BIBLIA NOVI TESTAMENTI ILLUSTRATA: IN WHICH The emphases of the words and the genuine meaning of the sayings are elicited from the sources, the context, and the analogy of Scripture:

II. The principal versions are compared with the Greek text, the sincerity of which is vindicated everywhere:

III. The expositions of both the ancients and the more recent interpreters are weighed, and the truer ones of the Fathers themselves, of B. Luther, and of other theologians are established in their own words:

Lutheri, & aliorum Theologorum propriis verbis stabiliuntur:

IV. Textual, historical, genealogical, and other doubts are resolved:

V. Apparent contradictions are discussed:

VI. Various questions, theoretical and practical, are solved:

VII. Most of the classical passages are treated professedly:

VIII. The corruptions of heretics and others are clearly refuted:

IX. The depravations and ψευδερμηνείαι (false interpretations) of Grotius are brought to a just examination and exploded; AND SO IT IS ESPECIALLY AND DILIGENTLY AIMED AT, THAT THE SINGLE LITERAL SENSE OF SCRIPTURE BE EVERYWHERE ASSERTED AND CONFIRMED, With the prefaces and partitions of the individual books prefixed, as well as the argument and distribution of any chapters, with also inserted, according to the wish of the learned, ALL THE ANNOTATIONS OF GROTIUS, inasmuch as they either contribute to the understanding of Scripture, or deserve observation, or are recalled for censure, SO ADORNED, THAT THEY MAY BE LIKE JUST COMMENTARIES: TOMUS II.

EXHIBITING THE UNIVERSAL APOSTOLIC EPISTLES, AND THE JOHANNINE APOCALYPSE.

By the Work and Study of D.

ABRAHAM CALOV, P.P. (Principal Professor)

IN THE ACADEMY OF WITTENBERG, AND SUPERINTENDENT GENERAL OF THE ELECTORATE OF SAXONY. DRESDEN AND LEIPZIG, At the expense of Johann Christoph Zimmermann.

IN RUDOLSTADT, PRINTED BY HEINRICH URBAN, IN THE YEAR

TO THE MAGNIFICENT, MOST NOBLE, MOST EXCELLENT MAN, LORD AUGUSTUS STRAUCH, JURISCONSULT, COUNT PALATINE OF THE EMPIRE, INTIMATE COUNCILLOR TO THE MOST SERENE ELECTOR OF SAXONY, ENVOY TO THE IMPERIAL DIET, ILLUSTRIOUS FOR HIS MOST EMINENT MERITS; TO HIS LORD AND PATRON, ONE OF THE FEW, HIS KINSMAN AND FELLOW GODFATHER, TO BE REVERED FOR ALL TIME.

AND LIKEWISE TO THE MOST REVEREND, MAGNIFICENT, MOST EXCELLENT MAN, LORD MARTIN GEIER, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY, SUPREME, AND MOST NOTABLY DESERVING OF THE ENTIRE CHURCH OF CHRIST, ECCLESIASTICAL COUNCILLOR TO THE MOST SERENE ELECTOR OF SAXONY, AND PRIMARY MINISTER FOR PRIVATE CONFESSIONS AND COURT SERMONS, HIS LORD, PATRON, KINSMAN, FELLOW GODFATHER, AND MOST CLOSELY UNITED BROTHER IN CHRIST, AND MOST HIGHLY TO BE HONORED,

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D., PRAYS WITH HIS WHOLE HEART FOR GRACE, PERPETUAL PEACE, THE ASSISTANCE OF THE SPIRIT OF COUNSEL, AND EVERY KIND OF HAPPINESS IN THE LORD JESUS.

Those who taste with the tips of their lips the Annotations of HUGO GROTIUS on the entire Scripture are greatly affected by his multivarious erudition, singular elegance, remarkable conformity, and the august structure of the work. Nor would I rashly detract that praise from the polished work of a GREAT MAN, from whose stupendous genius only stupendous things could proceed: provided he had not neglected the principal laws of interpretation.

Of which only four he suggests in the first chapter XLVI of Book II against heresies: These are the senses in which the words themselves are placed in the Scriptures.

The second we likewise exhibit in the words of the same most ancient Father from book IV, ch.

LXIII. The legitimate and safe exposition of Scripture is according to the Scriptures themselves.

The third is derived from the crisis of St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, in book I of De Trinitate: The best reader is he who expects the understanding of what is said from the things said, rather than imposing it, and who reports rather than brings, and does not force it to seem contained in the words which he had presumed to understand before the reading.

The fourth , finally, suffices the truly golden admonition of John of Constantinople, Archbishop, who earned the name Chrysostom from his golden river of Eloquence, in Psalm

II. As building is weak without a foundation, so is Scripture useless unless the scope is found.

These Rules , shining with their own light and beyond all exception, in the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, which uniquely exhibit to us the mind of GOD, that they must be religiously observed after preceding pious prayers, no one would rashly doubt: but that the same have been neglected, nay violated, in countless places by the Great Man, must be lamented.

For very frequently he leaves a sense that is quite clear and flowing from the letter itself, having devised a new and unheard-of interpretation which could have come into no one's mind.

Nor does he seek the sense so much from the mutual comparison of analogous Scriptures, or the authentic exposition of Prophetic books in the Apostolic writings, as from places that are entirely alien, or from exotic and profane writers.

But he is entirely intent on inserting preconceived opinions into the Holy Scriptures, and wherever he pleases, he introduces an ἰδίαν λύσιν, or private interpretation, serving his own hypothesis.

Finally, since the principal scope of Scripture is CHRIST JESUS, our GOEL and SAVIOR, he held Him in less account in the Old Testament, if he did not eliminate Him entirely; but in the New Testament, he did not exhibit Him as He manifested Himself as REDEEMER in obedience, both active and passive, in which our justice and redemption, and thus eternal salvation, are uniquely situated, but only as a HERALD of eternal life and a new LEGISLATOR.

In which manner, especially that golden Epistle of the Holy Apostle to the Romans was so badly depraved, and twisted from the Apostolic sense to Papal and Socinian corruptions. I outlined a syllabus of such depravations twenty-five years ago for the Patrons of Gdańsk in the preface to the ROMAN APOSTOLIC THEOLOGY, asserted through the vindication of XXII oracles. Now, since the order of interpretation and vindication of the books of the New Testament, after the completion, by divine gift, of the writings of the Old Testament, has led me to that divine COMPENDIUM of HOLY THEOLOGY, entrusted to the Coryphaeus of the Apostles by the primary Church, I judged that work not of a menial nature should be expended, so that I might not only wipe away the deceptions of Grotius and other sectarians; but that, while I might elicit the truest sense according to hermeneutical laws, and having asserted the genuine scope, I might expose it as if on the disk of the Sun. What has been achieved in this, I commit to your accurate judgment, O HIGHEST MEN, and especially to yours, Prince of the THEOLOGIANS of the modern Time, and leader of the interpreters of Scripture, to your most dexterous censure. But how much I owe to you, GREAT PATRONS, and how much I esteem your most eminent merits toward the Republic and the universal Church, I wished to testify by this public monument: praying to GOD, and about to pray, while His Spirit rules my limbs, that this twin Star may shine, with a most auspicious omen, for the REPUBLIC and the CHURCH, troubled on all sides, for as long as possible, that He may bless your Holier Counsels, and may He grant, through YOU, as chosen organs of GOD, countless benefits for the salvation of the Public Good, which is everywhere wavering or fleeing, to be stabilized and restored! Wittenberg, June 20, in the YEAR OF CHRIST 1673, in which I complete, by divine gift, the thirty-sixth year of my Doctorate. I

VIRO MAGNIFICO, NOBILISSIMO, EXCELLENTISSIMO, DN. AUGUSTINO Strauch/ JCto, COMITI PALATINO CÆSAREO, SERE- NISSIMI SAXONIÆ ELECTORIS CONSILIARIO INTIMO, AD COMITIA IMPERII LEGATO, EMINENTISSIMIS MERITIS ILLVSTRI; DN. ET PATRONO SUO NON E MULTIS, AFFINI ET COMPATRI ÆTATEM SUSPICIENDO.

NEC NON VIRO SUMME REVERENDO, MAGNIFICO, EXCELLENTISSIMO, DN. MARTINO GEIERO, DOCTORI THEOLOGO SUMMO, DEQVE UNIVERSA CHRISTI ECCLE- SIA PRÆCLARE MERITO, SERENISSIMO SAXONIÆ ELECTORI A CONSILIIS ECCLESIASTICIS, CONFESSIONIBUS PRIVATIS, ET CONCIONIBUS AULICIS PRIMARIIS, DN. PATRONO, AFFINI, COMPATRI ET FRATRI IN CHRISTO CONJUNCTISSIMO, MAXIMEQVE HONORANDO,

GRATIAM, PACEM PERENNEM SPIRITUS CONSILII ADSISTENTIAM, ET FELICITATEM OMNIGENAM IN DOMINO JESU TOTO PECTORE PRECATUR ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.

Qui primoribus labris Annotata HUGONIS GROTII in universam Scripturam degustant, maximoperè afficiuntur eruditione multivariâ, elegan-tiâ singulari, conformitate infigni, & structurâ operis augustâ. Neque laudem istam temerè derogârim operi exasciato VIRI MAGNI, à cujus ingenio stupendo non nisi stupenda proficisci potuêre: modò præcipuas interpretationis leges non neglexisset.

E quibus quatuor solum in primam II. adversus hæreses cap. XLVI. fuggerit: Is sensus sunt, quo ipfas dictionibus in Scripturis ponitur.

Alteram ejusdem Patris vetustissimi verbis itidem exhibemus è libro IV. c.

LXIII. Legitima & fine periculo est expositio Scripturæ secundum ipfas Scripturas.

Tertia eruitur è crisi S. Hilarii Pictavorum Episcopi libro I. de Trinitate: Optimus lector est, qui dictorum intelligentiam expectet ex dictis potius, quàm importer, & retulerit magis, quàm attulerit, nec cogat id videri dictis contineri, quod ante lectionem præsumserit intelligendum.

Quartam denique fufficit Johannis Constantinopolitani Archi-Episcopi ab aureo Eloquentiæ flumine Chrysostomi nomen promeriti monitum verè aureum in Pſalm.

II. Ut absque fundamento imbecillis est ædificatio, ita nisi invento scopo Scriptura est inutilis.

Hasce Regulas luce fuâ fulgentes, & exceptione omni majores, in S. Literarum, quæ mentem DEI unicè nobis exhibent, interpretatione præviis piis precibus, religiosè obſervandas esse, haud temerè quis ambigat: sed easdem innumeris in locis poſthabitas, imò violatas à viro Magno fuisse, queri oportet.

Frequentiffimè enim sensum perquam luculentum, & ex ipsa litera fluentem relinquit, novâ & inauditâ interpretatione, quæ nemini in mentem venire potuit, ex-cogitatâ.

Nec verò tam è Scripturarum analogarum mutuâ collatione, aut librorum Propheticorum in Scriptis Apostolicis authenticâ expositione sensum petit, quàm è locis prorsus alienis, aut scriptoribus exoticis & prophanis.

In eo autem totus est, ut præceptas opiniones S. literis inferat, & ubi, ubi lubet, ἰδίαν λύσιν, vel privatam interpretationem invehat, suæ inferviens ὑποθέσει.

Denique quum Scripturæ scopus præcipuus fit CHRISTUS JESUS, GOEL, & SALVATOR noster, Eundem in Veteri Testamento infuper habuit, fi non eliminavit penitus, in Novo verò Testamento non prout fefe ceu REDEMTOREM manifestavit in obedientia cùm activâ, tum paſſivâ justitia & redemtio nostra, adeòque falus æterna unicè fitâ est, sed tanquam PRÆCONEM solum vitæ æternæ, & LEGISLATOREM novum exhibuit.

Quo pacto inprimis aurea illa S. Apostoli ad Romanos Epistola tam pessimè depravata, & à sensu Apostolico ad Pontificias & Socinianas corruptelas detorta est. Syllabum ejusmodi depra-vationum ante hosce XXV. annos Patronis Gedanenfibus in præfatione THEOLOGIÆ APOSTOLICÆ ROMANÆ, per vindicias XXII. oraculorum adfertæ, adumbravi. Jam quum ordo interpretationis, & vindiciarum librorum Novi Testamenti, post expedita, divino munere, Veteris Testamenti scripta, me ad divinum illud SS. THEOLOGIÆ, ab Apostolorum Coryphæo primariæ Ecclesiæ creditum, COMPENDIUM deduxerit, operam non proleta-riam impendendam cenfui, ut non tantum offucias Grotianas, & aliorum sectariorum abſter-gerem; sed ut cùm maximè verum sensum, juxtà leges hermenevticas, eruerem, & genuino ſcopo adferto, in Solis veluti disco exponerem. Quid in eo præstitum fit, Vestro, VIRI SUMMI, accurato judicio, & Tuæ imprimis, THEOLOGORUM moderni Temporis Princeps, & interpretum Scripturæ antefignane, cenfuræ dexterrimæ committto. Vobis autem quantum debeam, PATRONI MAGNI, & quanti merita vestra in Rempublicam & Ecclesiam universam eminentissima, æstimem, testari hoc publico monumento volui: DEUM precans, & pre-caturus, dum Spiritus ejus regit artus, fervet hoc geminum Sydus, auspicatissimo omine, REIPUBLICÆ & ECCLESIÆ undiquaque turbatæ, quàm diutissimè, benedicat San&tioribus vestris Conſiliis, & innumerâ adhuc pro salute Boni publici paffim vacillante, aut fugiente, stabiliendâ ac reducenda per VOS, ceu Electa DEI organa, præstet emolumenta! ## 1:1 Introduction: J. N. J. [in the Name of Jesus] Introduction to the Annotations on the Golden Epistle of t
J. N. J. [In the name of Jesus] Introduction to the annotations on the golden Epistle of the Holy Apostle Paul to the Romans.

No one more worthy as an encomiast of the Holy Apostle, once you have departed from St. Peter, the Coryphaeus of the Apostles, is easily found than that golden mouth of Greek eloquence, JOHN, the Constantinopolitan Archbishop, who delivered eight entire homilies or sacred orations in his praise, but at the very threshold confessed that he was by no means equal to explaining his praises, nay, that no language suffices for this task, since that one soul possessed all the goods that are in men, and all those things fully, which are not only of men, but what is more, of angels. Regarding the Ministry of the Holy Apostle, and his efficacy and success, Homily IV of the same Holy [John] Chrysostom especially celebrated this. Chrysostom, that in the space of scarcely thirty years he progressed so much in virtue that he brought the Romans, and Persians, and Parthians, and Medes, and Indians, and Scythians, and Ethiopians, and Sauromatae, and Saracens, and absolutely the whole human race under the yoke of truth.

Although not only Schlichtingius, the noble Socinian, has dared to strip our Apostle of eloquence and power of speech, following the footsteps of ancient heretics according to Philastrius, but Origen himself, by no means the last of the ancient critics, and the great philologist of our century, Hugo Grotius, have scattered such things about the Teacher of the Gentiles as seem to detract from the praise of his eloquence: yet it was fitting that the Apostle should have been most eloquent and possessed of the highest power of speech, who persuaded not only Jews, but also Greeks, and the Athenians themselves, of the scandal and foolishness of the cross, and was held by the Lystrians to be Mercury, or the very God of Eloquence. Indeed, if one demands from a priest either Isocratic levity, or the bombast of Demosthenes, or the dignity of Thucydides, and the loftiness of Plato, the most eloquent of the Greek Fathers, whom I mentioned, acknowledges that the Apostle must be called unskilled in speech: but when I consider the whole character and nature of Pauline oratory more closely, I confess, he says, that I have found in Plato himself no similar grandiloquence, as often as it pleased him to thunder forth the mysteries of God, and no equal δεινότητα [power/vehemence] in Demosthenes, as often as he set out to terrify souls with the fear of divine judgment, or to admonish them, or to attract them to contemplate the goodness of GOD, or to exhort them to the duties of piety and mercy. But there is no reason why we should now defend the divine eloquence of the Apostle, which has been done by us in another place and day: and it shines with its own splendor from the divine Epistles more brightly than solar rays; not indeed with the allurements of words, or with adorned phrases, but with words which are spirit and life, not neat, curled, sprinkled with poppy and sesame, or woven from honeyed globules of words, as Seneca speaks, but commending itself by holiness and speech full of divine virtue: so that it is necessary to marvel, with Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book III, ch. 24, at the Apostle, who, being most powerful in both words and meanings, contains immense and countless Sacraments in a small body of Epistles: and to acknowledge that he was most truly called μεγαλoφωνότατον [most great-voiced] by Theodoret, and a river of eloquence by Jerome: whom, as often as that leader of critics reads, he seemed to himself not to hear words, but thunder.

We think we shall do a work more worth the effort if we strive rather to assert and vindicate the true meaning of the divine letters of the Apostle; how βαρειαι they are, and ισχυραι, those who had objected to his contemptible speech have even experienced, being convinced by the energy of his oratory and his equally grand and prepotent style of speaking. Worthy of mention is the judgment which Chrysostom passed in Homily III on the First Epistle to the Corinthians concerning a dispute between a certain Christian and a Gentile as to which of them, Paul or Plato, was more learned and eloquent. For when the Gentile tried to show that Paul was both rude and unlearned, he affirms that the Christian, on the contrary, rashly contended that Paul was more learned than Plato, and by that pact defeated the Gentile. For if Paul had been more eloquent than Plato, many could not have undeservedly asserted that Paul did not win by grace, but by eloquence. Wherefore Chrysostom judges that the Christian defended the Gentile cause, and the Gentile the Christian: for if Paul was unlearned, yet defeated Plato, his victory was surely most clear, as he enticed the unlearned disciples of the latter and converted them all to himself. From which it is sufficiently evident that the preaching was not done in human wisdom, but in divine grace. So much, clearly, does divine eloquence differ from human!

But Divine Eloquence is utterly enervated when the sense of the divine words, which is their form and soul, is overturned: for the power and efficacy of the word does not reside in the words without the sense, but in the sense and mind of the words. Wherefore let us feel that this is the business most given to us, that you may elicit The genuine sense of the Apostle’s letters must be diligently elicited and powerfully brought to bear against those who endeavor to pervert it. Among these, Hugo Grotius easily claims the first place for himself; for just as he did not fear to corrupt the Prophetic Oracles of the Old Testament as more than Jewish "vulgarities," and to despoil them of their own sense, so too did he distort the Apostolic letters with a truly Anti-Christian spirit, and deprive them of almost all the spirit and life which they possess from divine inspiration, having utterly evacuated the mysteries of the faith with which they are filled. This I showed ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (as in a sketch) some twenty-odd years ago, when I was writing the preface to the Roman Apostolic Theology, from the divine Epistle to the Romans: but because no work can be undertaken more worthy than that which is spent in solidly bringing forth the divine sense of this Epistle—which, as it is the first, is also, by the reckoning of all, the most excellent—come, let us undertake a work of immense study;

not relying on our own ingenuity, not leaning upon the help of Paul, nor invoking him by name, as Cornelius a Lapide does—for were we baptized in the name of Paul? (1 Cor. 1:13)—but placing all our trust in Him in whom Paul professed that he could do all things (Phil. 4:13), and who testified to Paul, "My grace is sufficient for thee: for power is made perfect in infirmity" (2 Cor. 12:9). To pious prayers, however, must be joined diligent and attentive reading, which the Apostle himself commends to us: "Attend unto reading" (1 Tim. 4:13); so that we may skillfully attain the true sense, and, as St. Peter warns (2 Pet. 3:16), carefully avoid and shun those things which "the unlearned and unstable wrest." Let us, therefore, turn and return the Pauline Epistles by day and by night—the Epistles without which, as the aforementioned Jesuit testifies, Melanchthon (no heretic he) was never accustomed to walk, to dine, to sup, or to lie down to sleep. And Cornelius could not deny that in this he had Chrysostom as his guide and predecessor—whose greatest praise in explaining the Pauline Epistles, he says, consists in this—reporting from George, Patriarch of Alexandria, the biographer of his life, that Chrysostom never let Paul slip from his hands, but read him assiduously and held his wisdom in the place of a miracle.

Nor do we ourselves, which we gladly profess with St. Chrysostom, know whatever we hold from the letters of the Holy Apostle through the industry and sharpness of the intellect, but rather from the fact that we adhere incessantly to that man, and are vehemently affected toward him. For those who love know and understand the things of their beloved, being solicitous for them, more than all others. And so, we promise with the same Prelate, if you are willing to attend to the reading with alacrity of mind, you will have need of nothing else besides. For the word of Christ is true when He says, "Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you." And although it is determined to follow Grotius κατὰ πόδα (step by step), the στρεβλῶτης (twister) of Grotius alone will not be defeated in such a way that the other modern heretics are not also largely satisfied, since in Grotius we have a certain instance, or rather a compendium, of the distortion of heretics of various kinds: who, as much as he excelled others in judgment and erudition, so much the more speciously and exquisitely did he distort the Scriptures to suit the various heresies from which he was, as it were, woven. But before we begin the Apostolic text of this golden key of Scripture and gem-like Theological Compendium, it is helpful to look briefly, at the very threshold, at those things which Grotius has in place of a preface. Δώη δὲ ἡμῖν ὁ κύριος σύνεσιν πᾶσι! (May the Lord give us understanding in all things!)

Latin:

J. N. J. AD ANNOTATA IN AUREAM S. APOSTOLI PAULI AD ROMANOS EPISTOLAM INGRESSUS.

NEmo dignior S. Apo- stoli encomiastes, cum a S. Petro discesseris, Apostolorum Cory- phaeo, facile reperitur aureo illo Eloquentiae Graecae ore, JOHAN- NE Constantinopolita- no Archi-Episcopo, qui octo integras homilias, vel orationes sacras in laudem ejusdem habuit, sed in limine ipso fassus est, nequaquam se explicandis ejus laudibus pa- rem esse, imo nullam linguam huic sufficere ne- gotio, siquidem omnia, quae in hominibus sunt bo- na, una illa possederit anima, & ea cuncta plene, quae non solum hominum sunt, sed quod amplius est, an- gelorum. De Ministerio autem S. Apostoli, & effi- cacia, ac successu ejus id imprimis homilia IV. cele- bravit S. Chrysostomus, quod annorum vix trigin- ta spacio in tantum virtute progressus sit, ut & Ro- manos, & Persas, & Parthos, & Medos, & Indos, & Scythas, & Aethiopes, & Sauromatas, & Sarace- nos, & omne prorsus humanum genus sub jugum miserit veritatis.

Quanquam vero Eloquentiam, ac dicendi vim non Schlichtingius tantum nobilis Socinianus, nostro Apostolo abrogare ausus sit, veterum hae- ticorum apud Philastrium vestigia legens, sed Ori- genes ipse Criticorum antiquorum minime po- stremus, & magnus seculi nostri Philologus Hugo Grotius, talia de gentium Doctore sparserint, quae laudi eloquentiae detrahere videantur: longe ta- men Eloquentissimum fuisse Apostolum, summa- que dicendi vi polluisse oportuit, qui non modo Judaeis, sed & Graecis, ipsisque Atheniensibus scan- dalum, & stultitiam crucis dicendo persuasit, & a Lystriis Mercurius, seu ipse Eloquentiae Deus habi- tus est. Equidem si a Sacerdote aut levitatem Iso- craticam, aut Demosthenis tumorem, aut Thucydi- dis dignitatem, & Platonis altitudinem quis exigat, agnoscit Graecorum Patrum, quem dixi, disertissi- mus imperitum sermone dicendum Apostolum: sed cum Orationis Paulinae totam indolem, & cha- racterem propius considero, nullam ego, inquit, in ipso Platone similem grandiloquentiam, quoties ipsi libuit Dei mysteria detonare, nullam in Demosthene parem dεινότητα comperisse me fateor, quoties ani- mos vel metu judicii divini perterrefacere, vel com- monefacere, vel ad contemplandam DEI bonitatem attrahere, vel ad pietatis ac misericordiae officia con- stituit exhortari. Verum non est, quod vindice- mus nunc divinam Apostoli eloquentiam, quod alio loco, & die a nobis factum: & effulget suo splendore ipsa e divinis Epistolis radiis solaribus clarius; non verborum quidem lenociniis, aut di- ctis phaleratis, sed verbis, quae spiritus & vita sunt, non comta, calamistrata, papavere & sesamo spar- sa, aut ex mellitis verborum globulis contexta, uti Seneca loquitur, sed sanctimonia, & divina virtutis plena oratione sese commendans: ut mirari ne- cessum sit, cum Eusebio lib. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 24. Apostolum, qui & in verbis & sensibus prepotens in parvo Epistolarum corpore immensa contineat, atque innumera Sacramenta: & agnoscere, verif- sime ipsum a Theodoreto μεγαλoφωνότατον, ab Hieronymo flumen eloquentiae dictum: quem quotiescunque legit, visus est sibi Criticorum ille antesignanus non verba audire, sed tonitrua.

Majus operae pretium nos facturos arbitra- mur, si veram potius literarum divinarum Apo- stoli sententiam adserere, ac vindicare annitemur; quae quam βαρειαι sint, atque ισχυραι, experti et- iam sunt, qui sermonem contemtibilem objecerant, de energia orationis ejus, grandique pariter & praepotenti dicendi genere convicti. Dignum commemoratu est judicium, quod de contentione Christiani cujusdam cum gentili, de Paulo & Pla- tone, uter eorum doctior, & disertior esset, tulit Chrysostomus homilia III. in Priorem ad Corin- thios. Quum enim gentilis ostendere conaretur, Paulum & rudem & indoctum, Christianum contra Platone Paulum doctiorem fuisse, temere contendis- se, eoque pacto gentilem vicisse, affirmat. Nam si Platone disertior Paulus fuisset, multi non in meri- to asserere potuissent, non gratia vicisse Paulum, sed facundia. Quamobrem gentilem causam defendis- se Christiani, Christianum vero gentilis, judicat Chrysostomus: nam si Paulus ineruditus fuit, vi- cit autem Platonem, profetto clarissima fuit ejus victoria, qui indoctos illius discipulos allexit, & ad se omnes convertit. Ex quo satis constat, non in sapientia humana predicationem factam esse, sed in divina gratia. Tantum scilicet interest eloquen- tiae humanae divina!

Quae vero Divina Eloquentia enervatur pe- nitus, cum sensus verborum divinorum, qui forma est, & anima eorum, evertitur: non enim in ver- bis absque sensu vis haeret, ac efficacia verbi, sed in sensu, & mente verborum. Quapropter id datum nobis maxime negotii esse sentiamus, ut eruas germanus sensus literarum Apostoli & eruatur diligenter, & adversus eos, qui pervertere eundem coriantur, adferatur potenter. Hos inter facile primas sibi vendicat Hugo Grotius, qui uti Prophetica Oracula Veteris Testamenti χυδαία plusquam Judaicâ corrumpere, suoque sensu spoliare minime veritus est, ita Spiritu vere Anti-Christiano literas Apostolicas detorsit, & omni propemodum Spiritu ac vita, quam ex divina habent inspiratione, privavit, fidei mysteriis, quibus referta sunt, prorsus evacuatis. Quod ὡς ἐν τύπῳ ante ipsos viginti, & quod excurrit annos, cum in Theologiam Apostolicam Romanam præfarer, è divina ad Romanos Epistola ostendi: sed quia dignior nulla suscipi potest opera, quam quæ divino hujus Epistolæ, cæteris ut priori, sic, omnium calculo, præstantiori sensui solidè adferendo impenditur, agite, aggrediamur opus ingentis studii; non proprio freti ingenio, non Pauli nixi ope, ejusve invocato, cum Cornelia a Lapide, nomine, nunquid enim in nomine Pauli baptizati sumus?

1. Cor. I. 13. sed omnem fiduciam in eum collocantes, in quo omnia se valere professus est Paulus Phil. IV. 13. quique testatus est Paulo, 2. Cor. XII, 9. Virtus mea in infirmitate perficitur. Precibus autem piis jungenda erit sedula, & attenta lectio, quam nobis commendat ipse Apostolus 1. Tim. IV. 13. Attende lectioni; ut sensum verum dextre assequamur, & ea, quæ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς κὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλῶσιν, S. Petro 2. Ep. III. 16. monente, folicite caveamus, ac declinemus. Diurna ergo, atque nocturna manu volvamus, ac revolvamus Epistolas Paulinas, fine quibus Melancthonem, nec hæreticum, nunquam incedere, nunquam prandere, nunquam cœnare, nunquam confidere aut cubare consuevisse, Jesuita prædictus testatur: inque eo Chrysostomum, cujus maximam in Paulinis Epistolis explicandis laudem constare ait, ipsum habuisse ducem, & antecessorem haud diffiteri potuit Cornelius, e vitæ ejus scriptore Georgio, Alexandrino Patriarcha, de Chrysostomo referens, quod nunquam siverit Paulum e manibus elabi, sed assidue eundem legerit, ac miraculi loco ejus sapientiam habuerit.

Neque vero nos ipsi, quod lubentes profitemur cum S. Chrysostomo, quicquid ex S. Apostoli literis tenemus, per industriam & acrimoniam intellectus cognoscimus, sed magis ex eo, quod viro illi indefinenter adhæremus, vehementerque erga illum affecti sumus. Ante alios siquidem omnes quæ dilectorum sunt, noverunt, & intelligunt, qui diligunt, utpote de illis solliciti. Et vos itaque, pollicemur cum eodem Antistite, si lectioni cum animi alacritate volueritis attendere, nullo alio præterea opus habebitis. Verus enim est sermo Christi, cum dicit, quærite, & invenietis, pulsate, & aperietur. Etsi vero constitutum fit, Grotium κατὰ πόδα sequi, non unius tamen ita Grotii στρεβλῶτης profligabitur, quin aliis etiam quibusvis hæreticis modernis magnam partem satisfiat, siquidem in Grotio instar quoddam habeamus, imo compendiu detorsionis hæreticorum varii generis: qui quantum præ aliis plurimis judicio & eruditione polluit, tanto speciosius, & exquisitius ad varias, ex quibus veluti consutus erat, hæreses Scripturas detorqueret. Antequam autem ipsum aureæ hujus clavis Scripturæ, gemmeique Compendii Theologici ordiamur Apostolicum textum, de iis, quæ præloqui loco habet Grotius, in limine ipso, paucis dispicere juvat. Δώη δὲ ἡμῖν ὁ κύριος σύνεσιν πᾶσι!

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of H. Grotius to the Annotations on the Epistle to the Romans
PREFACE OF H. GROTIUS TO THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS.

SECTION I. On the order of the Epistles.

The Pauline Epistles were not placed in the order of time by those who first compiled them into one volume, but according to the dignity of those to whom they were written.

Therefore, those to the Churches precede; the first is that to the Romans, on account of the majesty of that city.

ANTI-GROTIAN OBSERVATIONS.

The order of the Apostle’s Epistles is one of Collection, by which they were digested in the Biblical Codex; but another is that of Composition, by which they were written by Paul. The former is sufficiently known; for those that bear the author’s name in the inscription are placed before the Epistle to the Hebrews, which lacks an inscription: and of those, the ones sent to entire Churches are placed before those to individual persons; and in both orders, the larger ones generally precede the smaller. Nor does this Epistle to the Romans precede all others (in order of time), as many think, but only those which were written from Rome; it is later than the others, though not all of them, as Chrysostom warns. Furthermore, the Order of Composition appears to be this: seven of them were written before the captivity; the remaining seven were written in captivity.

Before the Captivity, the first was the former to the Thessalonians, given at Athens, from which city he first went to Corinth (Acts 18:1). For from Thessalonica he went to Beroea, and from there to Athens (Acts 17). To which Corinth he also returned, and sent this Epistle from there. The second is the latter to the Thessalonians, which he likewise wrote at Athens, as the subscription of both teaches.

Thus Theodoret and Athanasius in the Synopsis, as well as Oecumenius in the Scholia, hold that the former was written at Athens, gathering this from 1 Thess. 3:1-2. But Pererius, in his Prolegomena to the Romans, disp. II, no. 51, following Theodore Beza, concludes from verse 6 of the same chapter that this epistle was sent from Corinth, where Timothy, returning from Thessalonica, found Paul (Acts 18). This is also the argument of Baronius, T. 1, ad ann. LII. On this matter Justinianus speaks thus: "Although it is commonly thought to have been written at Athens, and Athanasius and Theodoret affirm this, yet it is more likely that it was given at Corinth: for the Apostle stayed at Athens only a very short time. Therefore, although he ordered Silas and Timothy to come to him, it is not certain whether they found him at Athens. For Luke indicates that they came to Paul when he was already at Corinth. Since, therefore, he names both in this epistle, it seems altogether credible that it was written at Corinth. I am not unaware that learned men do not approve this opinion, because it pleases certain heretics; but I praise their piety in attacking heretics; the reasons by which they refute this opinion, I do not likewise praise."

I follow this opinion, however, not because heretics followed it, but because it is most consistent with Luke’s history. Pererius also determines that the latter epistle, which Theodoret in his preface to the Romans and Chrysostom in his second to the Thessalonians say was written not long after, was written in the same place (Corinth), because Paul remained there for a year and a half. But since the ancients consistently agree, and Beza’s argument for Corinth is by no means solid, there is no reason for us to follow that novel opinion with Justinianus and Pererius. We shall say more on this matter in the Proem to the former Epistle to the Thessalonians.

The third is the former to Timothy, when he had left him at Ephesus (1 Tim. 1:3), before he came to Ephesus a second time (Acts 19), because he promises (1 Tim. 3:14) that he will come there. The fourth is the former to the Corinthians, written at Ephesus, when he might remain there for two years, Acts XIX. 9. The fifth, the latter to the Corinthians, written from Philippi, when having left Ephesus he set out for Macedonia and reached Philippi, which are on the first coast of Macedonia: Acts XX. 1. 2 Cor. IX, 4. Whence he promised that he would come to Corinth: which was done after he had traveled through Macedonia. Concerning the order, however, of these three, which we have called the third, fourth, and fifth, authors disagree. Pererius makes the third in order the first to the Corinthians, the fourth the latter, the fifth the first to Timothy. The sixth is to Titus, written according to some at Nicopolis, which is not far from Philippi. Which they gather from Tit. III. 12. But since Paul says he had decided to winter there, Pererius l. c. concludes that Paul, when he wrote that Epistle, had not yet been to Nicopolis, but had intended to go there. The subscription, which says it was written at Nicopolis, certainly seems doubtful. The order here also seems doubtful. Since this Epistle to Titus is perhaps not inappropriately held by B. Chemnitius in Exam. C. T. P. I. p. 25. to be the first in the preceding order of writing. The seventh is the Epistle to the Romans, written from Corinth. The rest were written at Rome, as the subscriptions testify: and thus the Romans are later. The eighth, namely, the Epistle to the Hebrews, sent from free custody, Heb. XIII. 23. The ninth to the Galatians, when he already bore the marks of the Lord in his body, Gal. VI, 17. which, however, Chrysostom says seems to him to be prior to the Epistle to the Romans. The tenth to the Ephesians, because he made mention of chains, Eph. VI, 20. The eleventh to the Philippians: whence the same order of these three is also observed in the Codex. The twelfth is that which he wrote to Philemon when he was already old. Chrysostom makes the Epistle to the Colossians the later, and therefore the thirteenth, because at the end of it it is said, Tychicus will make everything known to you, whom I sent with Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother. For he was that Onesimus, in whose name he composed the one which is to Philemon. The fourteenth and last is the second to Timothy c. IV. 6. Which order of writing is established generally by Theodoret in his preface, Flacius in his Gloss, Chemnitius l. c., Gerhard in his Epistle to the Romans, Cluver in his Orthotomia Apost., Pareus in his Commentary on Romans, and others. From whom, however, Ussher departs in his annals, observing this order: The first for him is the first to the Thessalonians; the second the latter to the same; the third to the Galatians; the fourth is, according to his opinion, the first to the Corinthians; the fifth the latter to the same; the sixth to the Romans. This is followed by the seventh to the Philippians; the eighth to Philemon; the ninth to the Colossians; the tenth to the Ephesians; the eleventh to the Hebrews. There follows these the twelfth, the first to Timothy; the thirteenth to Titus. He concludes finally, with the same Ussher counting, the fourteenth, the latter to Timothy.

Chrysostom warned about the use of this observed order, that knowing the time of the Epistles contributes not a little to treating questions; e.g., that he writes to the Romans and Colossians about the same things, but not in the same way, but to the former with great moderation, when he says (c. XIV.) receive the weak in faith, not to the judging of disputes. One indeed believes that he may eat anything. But another, who is weak, eats herbs. To the Colossians, however, although about the same things, yet not in this way, but with greater confidence. For if you have died with Christ, he says, (to Col. II.) why as if living in the world are you held by decrees? do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, etc. Chrysostom judges that no other cause for this difference is found than the time of the Epistles themselves. For in the beginning it was necessary to condescend, but with the passage of time, not so.

Furthermore, among those Epistles which were written to the Churches, the first is that which was destined for the Roman

Church, not because of the majesty of that city, as Grotius thinks with Theodoret, because the humility of Christ does not care for the pride of the world: not because of the preeminence of the Roman Church, as it seemed to Ambrosius Catharinus: for its regard before the Nicene Council, as Aeneas Sylvius testifies, was small: but because of the length of this Epistle, and especially because of its excellence and dignity, by which it surpasses all the rest, as Augustine Ep. CV. to Sixtus: this is the first, because it commends the grace of faith, which is the head and beginning of the Scriptures: which cause Theodoret also gives: namely, that it is the first because of the exact doctrine of every kind; and from those, Cornelius and Tirinus. And Flacius elegantly observes, since most of Paul's Epistles are very much accommodated to the reasons and circumstances of individual Churches or Persons; this of ours proposes general doctrine, necessary for all Churches, and is a common sermon, or a book methodically containing the principal heads of Christian doctrine: therefore it was sent most especially to this Church, because from there, as if from the seat of the whole Empire, citizens were sent out to all nations, and in turn the head of the world was frequented by men from all provinces.

SECTION II. Concerning the beginnings of the Roman Church.

There was, however, at Rome a certain beginning of the Church, made first, as at Antioch, by Christians of other provinces, whom business had led there: increased then by the preaching and miracles of Peter, whom the tricks of Simon Magus had drawn to Rome to be repressed by divine power around the beginnings of the Claudian principate, as the ancients have handed down.

It is not likely that the Church at Rome began merely from the occasion of trade: which Clement in the book of Recognitions, not rejected by Grotius, teaches that Barnabas first planted, in which Andronicus and Junias, as chief, or rather well-known, as the Syrian interprets the word ἐπίσημοι, are celebrated among the Apostles, and Priscilla and Aquila, and others, are adorned with their own eulogy, Rom. XVI. 37. Nor does Eusebius report that Peter came to Rome before about the end of his life, lib. III. c. 1. Therefore, he did not devote himself to increasing the Church at Rome from the beginnings of Claudius, as the Papists wish: indeed, the Magdeburg Centuries, l. I. II. c. X. p. 561, render it doubtful whether he was ever at Rome. Certainly, when Paul came to Rome in the year of Christ 59, there was no public Church there, much less an ordinary ecclesiastical ministry, or a Bishop, and Pontiff, or any trace of that same see; for the Jews were gathered to Paul, that they might know something about the sect of the Christians, Acts XXVIII. 22. Nor did Paul, who stayed there for two years and wrote several Epistles from there, ever make mention of Peter as being present in them: indeed, Cardinal Baronius himself testifies that Peter directed himself toward the West in the years 51 and 58, until he came into England. Pope Damasus, however, says that Peter finally came to Rome in the year of Christ 60, the 4th of Nero: finally, William, the teacher of Wycliffe, teaches that Peter did not even see Rome. Cf. Wolff. l. 1. Memorab. lect. p. 23.

SECTION III. Concerning the language in which the Epistle was written.

It is often asked why Paul, writing to the Romans, wrote in Greek rather than in Latin. I believe it was done because both he and his scribe, Tertius by name, although perhaps not entirely ignorant of the Latin language, could nevertheless dictate and write more correctly in Greek than in Latin: and because the Greek language was in daily use for all Romans, even women, as we learn from Juvenal: and it was better known to foreigners staying in Rome than the Roman language. Added to this was the fact that this Epistle, although properly sent to the Romans, contained all the defenses of the Christian religion in such a way that it was most worthy to have copies sent also to other Churches. But Greek, as Cicero says in defense of Archias, is read among almost all nations, while Latin is contained within its own truly narrow borders. Salmero, and not improbably in the judgment of Cornelius, thinks it was written not in Greek but in Latin, which the glossator also establishes in dist. IX, c. ut Veterum, and Lyranus on 1 Cor. 1. But Bellarmine, Cornelius, and others commonly reject this rightly. For all the Pauline Epistles were written in Greek, and Chrysostom and other Greek writers follow the Greek orthography. Add that this Epistle abounds in Grecisms, and that all interpreters easily agree that the original text is Greek. See what is said about the original language in the New Testament in the *Critici Sacri*. Grotius rightly gives this reason, that the Greek language was in daily use for all Romans, even women, and was better known to foreigners staying in Rome than the Roman language; and that Greek was then read among almost all nations. However, that reasoning of Grotius is not to be approved, that it was written in Greek rather than Latin because the Apostle himself and his scribe, Tertius by name, although perhaps not entirely ignorant of the Latin language, would nevertheless dictate and write more correctly in Greek than in Latin. For who will deny that the Apostle, by an infused gift, was most skilled in languages, and wrote or dictated through divine inspiration?

SECTION IV.

On the place and time the Epistle was written.

Origen proves that this Epistle was written from Corinth, not from those annotations which are read in certain codices written after the end of the Epistles (for those are neither ancient, nor are they found in all books, nor are they the same in those where they are found), but from arguments drawn from the Epistle itself: namely, because the Epistle is sent by Phoebe, a deaconess of the Church which was at Cenchreae, the port of the Corinthians; because among those who were then with Paul, and in whose name he greets the Romans, was Gaius, whom we say was a Corinthian (1 Cor. 1:14), and Erastus, whom we also say was a Corinthian (2 Tim. 4:20). It was written, however, not during Paul’s first arrival at Corinth, but during his second, mention of which is made in Acts 19:21. This is proven by comparing that passage with the one below in chapter 15:24. For in both places mention is made of the same journey which Paul had planned to Jerusalem; and because it is added in this Epistle that this journey, among other things, was intended for Paul to bring aid to the poor in Jerusalem, Chrysostom concluded from this that the two Epistles to the Corinthians had been written earlier, because in 1 Cor. 16:1 and 2 Cor. 9:1-2 those subsidies are being prepared. As for the place from which it was written, the interlinear author on the last chapter of Romans, as well as Haymo...

Athenis eam scriptam statuere: sed praeferenda Origenis sententia, quod Corinthi scripta sit, non tantum ob istas rationes, quod per Phoeben mittatur, ministram Ecclesiae in Cenchreis, portu Corinthiorum, Rom. XVI. 1. 27. quod salutet Apostolus nomine Caji hospitis, de quo perhibet ipse 1. Cor. I. 14. quod eundem e Corinthiis fere unicum baptizarit: & in nomine Erasti arcarii civitatis, Rom. XVI. 23. quem Corinthiis fuisse e 2. Tim. IV. 20. colligunt: Sed etiam ob subscriptionem: Non enim recedendum temere a subscriptionibus est, imprimis cum argumentis ex ipsa Epistola depromtis firmantur. [Translation:] establish that it was written at Athens: but Origen’s opinion is to be preferred, that it was written at Corinth, not only for those reasons—that it was sent by Phoebe, a minister of the church at Cenchreae, the port of the Corinthians, Rom. 16:1, 27; that the Apostle sends greetings in the name of Gaius, his host, of whom he himself testifies in 1 Cor. 1:14 that he was almost the only one of the Corinthians he baptized; and in the name of Erastus, the city treasurer, Rom. 16:23, whom they gather from 2 Tim. 4:20 to have been a Corinthian—but also because of the subscription: for one should not rashly depart from the subscriptions, especially when they are confirmed by arguments drawn from the Epistle itself.

It was written after Aquila and Priscilla had been prepared for Paul in the Gospel, Rom. 16:3-4, and the Apostle had filled all places from Jerusalem round about unto Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ, ch. 15:19. Therefore, it was not written when he first came to Corinth and was received into the hospitality of Aquila, Acts 18:1, but during his second arrival, when Priscilla and Aquila were staying in Rome, this Epistle was sent from Corinth, which Flacius observes was written around the 13th year of Claudius, the 55th of Christ, and the 22nd of the Apostle’s conversion: at which time he had determined to set out for Syria, intending to carry the alms of the Greeks there, Rom. 15:25.

SECTION V.

On the style and obscurity of the Epistle.

We are taught that there are many things of non-obvious sense in the writings of Paul, 2 Peter III. 16. The cause of this matter is partly common to Paul with the other Apostles, namely his Greek speech drawing many modes of speaking from Hebraism or even from the Syriasmus which was then in popular use; partly proper to Paul, namely his speech often abrupt, often interrupted, and not flowing with a premeditated order, but rushing with a certain impetus, as it had indeed come into his mind: Then the opinions of ancient and new teachers among the Hebrews are more incidentally drawn to those to whom they were known, than explained, concerning all of which see Jerome in his tenth question to Algasia.

But that this epistle to the Romans has more of this confusion than the others, Origen notes in that place which is related in the Philocalia, chapter nine. For he says that Paul seems not to insist on the purpose, namely that he often flies off from the started speech to another. To other difficulties in this Epistle this also is added, that he does not unfold the objections of the Jews, to which he responds, but strikes them through with a blow as being sufficiently known to those to whom he was writing: and because he states generally those things which are true ἐν τῷ πολὺ (in the main), which is most manifest in III. 10, but also ought to be extended with equal right to other things. Grotius, playing the Papias, and others think that many things of non-obvious sense are found in the writings of Paul. But although Peter indicates in 2 Epist. III. 16 that there are some things δυσνόητα (hard to understand) in the THINGS or MYSTERIES handed down by Paul, yet in WORDS, and the manner of treating them, let no one deservedly argue for obscurity, if anyone is willing to attend to the reading of the Apostle with alacrity of mind, Chrysostom in the preface to the Epistle to the Romans professed that nothing else besides this would be needed: but from this, he says, much destruction of heresies, from this innumerable evils have arisen, because the Scriptures are unknown. For just as those who are deprived of this light do not proceed rightly everywhere, so those who do not look to the rays of the divine Scriptures are compelled to sin continually, as walking in far worse darkness: that this may not happen to us, let us open our eyes to the SPLENDOR of the Apostolic words.

That his Greek speech draws something from Hebraism, or from the Syriasmus which was then in popular use, Grotius acknowledges to be common to him with the other Apostles; but he does not therefore demand obscurity, nor can he demand it, because the Apostle's idiom and its force is easily discerned by diligent reading, and by collation of the contexts, and of the other writings of the N.T., as well as of the Greek interpretation of the LXX interpreters, whence also obscurity, if any appears at first glance, is dispelled.

But that moreover the Pauline speech is accused, that it is often abrupt, often interrupted, and not so much with premeditated order, as with impetus, as it had indeed come into mind, rushing: this accusation is partly rash, because the speech is not so abrupt or interrupted that it cannot be supplied from the text, and the sense extracted: nor is it lawful to prescribe a mode of speech or style to the Spirit speaking through the Apostles: partly impious, since Scripture is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed), if it is esteemed as human speech, by which not what is dictated by the Holy Spirit, but whatever happens to come to mind, is poured out onto parchment or paper: whereas on the contrary, as Saint Peter says, prophecy (or canonical Scripture) was not brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit, 2 Ep. I. 21.

Saint Irenaeus indeed notes, l. III. c. 7, that the Apostle frequently uses hyperbata on account of the swiftness and impetus of the Spirit which is in him: but from this he by no means infers obscurity of Scripture, except for those who do not attend to the reading: since in such cases one ought to show the hyperbaton through reading, and preserve the consequent sense of the Apostle.

Nor is there any reason why the opinions of ancient and modern Hebrew teachers should be cited, which were touched upon by them more in passing, for those to whom they were already known, than explained. For what, I pray, are those opinions? Those which Jerome brings forward in the tenth question to Algasia, not so much from this Epistle of ours as from others, concern almost only a single passage, Col.

What is meant by *tapeinophrosyne* (humility) and *threskeia* (religion) of angels, what by *apheidia* (severity) of the body, what by *embateuon* (intruding into), etc.—these do not teach an inescapable obscurity. "Let us run," he says, "through each point, and, with Christ revealing it, let us unfold the obscurity of the senses and the words." That obscurity can therefore be unfolded; it is not inexplicable, provided that Christ, implored through prayers, reveals it. Furthermore, it cannot be proven that this Epistle is more rugged than the others: because Paul SEEMS not to stick to his purpose, and often flies off from the discourse he has begun to another; indeed, this SEEMS to be the case equally in the Prophets and other holy Scriptures, and sometimes even in other Pauline Epistles: yet no one easily concludes from that that anything is rugged. The *krisis* (judgment) of Origen deserves no weight here. Grotius refers this also to the difficulties, namely that he does not unfold the objections of the Jews to which the Apostle is responding: but it is clear from the Apostolic response itself what those were. And since Grotius acknowledges that the Ancients, especially Chrysostom, for the most part attained the sense of this Epistle well enough, from where did they have it, except from the text itself? Therefore, it is not so difficult or obscure that the sense cannot be extracted from it. Finally, because the Apostle enunciates generally what is true *epi to poly* (for the most part), even if it were observed at times; yet from the underlying subject matter and the *synecheia* (continuity) of the discourse, it could undoubtedly be discerned, so that there is no need to infer the true sense from elsewhere. The example, however, which is brought forward as most manifest from ch. III. 10, is not from Paul, but from David, and is deservedly held to be most false: for in those words *ouk estin dikaios oude heis* (there is no one righteous, not even one), there is no hyperbole, nor is the sentiment in the Psalms to be taken particularly, but universally, as was shown then from Ps. XIV. 1. It appears, however, from these things with what reverence Grotius is led toward the style of Holy Scripture and its author, the Holy Spirit Himself, by whose impulse the Apostle wrote. Against whom he belched forth similar *enkylemata* (accusations) in his special Commentary on the second part of ch. II of the Epistle of St. James, p. 18: that there are in that writer many *hyperbolas, parentheseis, anchyseis, hyperbata, anakoloutha*, superjections, interpositions, confusions, transitions, comparisons, unfinished and concise things, and other things said abruptly. Benedictus Justinianus is more modest in his argument on this Epistle; indeed, he does not fear to accuse such Aristarchuses of impudence. "Concerning the style," he says, "and the manner of speaking, it is not worth saying anything. Someone or other has said, indeed too impudently, that there is nowhere a more confused discourse, nowhere a speech more gaping with hyperbata, nowhere more frequently uncompleted in anantapodota." Although I do not deny that he labors at times with these vices of speech, whether by the fault of a third-party scribe, or the abundance of matter, or because the Holy Spirit neglects the pigments of speech, yet he almost always displays the solid and genuine nerves of eloquence.

...in many places teaches that Christ died for all, and that such faith as they preach has nothing in it that is true or useful. Others understand by faith all that obedience which is exhibited to the Gospel. But this does not agree with Paul’s manner of speaking, for he prefers love to faith, 1 Cor. XIII. 13, and says that faith performs its work through love, Gal. V. 6, openly distinguishing love, which is the chief part of that obedience, from faith. In reality, faith in the Pauline Epistles, and in that to the Hebrews, is an estimation thinking magnificently of God’s power, justice, goodness, and, if He has promised anything, of His constancy in performing it. That this is highly valued by God, and deservedly so, Philo shows in *On the Heir of Divine Things*. And this is what is said in this Epistle, that faith is imputed for righteousness, or righteousness is reckoned through faith. For it does not signify that Christ’s obedience, apprehended by faith, is held for our own, as some think: but that faith is judged by God to be an exceedingly good thing. For everything honorable is called "just" by the Hebrews. Thus, he who returns a pledge to a poor man, it is said to be righteousness to him, or he is said to have righteousness, Deut. XXIV. 13. Thus that vengeance which Phinehas took upon the idolaters is said to have been reckoned for righteousness, Ps. CVI. 30, where there is *chashav*, which is properly said of that which is referred into accounts, as Lev. XXV. 27, 50, 52; XXVII. 18; Num. XXIII. 9, or even into some census, as Deut. II. 11, 20; Josh. XIII. 3; 2 Sam. IV. 2. Thence, by a translation also customary among other nations, it is used of that which is of great or little value, or which is held as pleasing or unpleasing: as Gen. XXXI. 15; 1 Kings X. 12; 2 Chron. IX. 20; Hosea VIII. 12; Isaiah XXIX. 16. There is, however, a double construction with the same sense: it is imputed *into* righteousness, just as *elogisato eis misthosan* (it was reckoned for wages), 1 Sam. I. 13, or righteousness is imputed on account of this, in the way it is said *sophia logisthesetai* (wisdom shall be reckoned), Prov. XVII. 27. Both signify that some thing is held of such value, is valued as such. It is another thing when it is said that a man is justified by faith. For *dikaion* and *dikaiosyne* correspond sometimes to *tsadaq* in the *Qal*, which signifies to be just, as Gen. XXVIII. 26; Sirach XXXI. 5, or to appear just, just as that is said to be which appears: thus *hatsadaq* Ps. LI. 6, *dikaiothes* and *tsadaq* Ps. CXLIII. 2, *dikaiothesetai*: sometimes to the verb *tsadaq* in the *Piel* or *hitsdiq* in the *Hiphil*: which in their native sense signify to make just, that is, to purge from vices, to cleanse, to liberate, as we said Acts XIII. 38, 39, and thus it is taken in Psalm LXXIII. 13; Isa. LIII. 11; Dan. XII. 3 in the Hebrew; Ecclesiasticus XVIII. 20; 1 Cor. IV. 4; Rev. XXII. 11. And in this sense the Rabbis mostly use this word, as can be seen in the Zohar, in Rabbi Israel, and others. And because in this sense it is the same as to cleanse, therefore it is also said of the Temple in the *Niphal* for the *Hophal*, Dan. VIII. 14, *tsadaq qodesh*, which is translated *katharisthesetai to hagion* (the sanctuary shall be cleansed). It is also taken comparatively: thus Jerusalem justified Samaria, Ezek. XVI. 51; similar is this locution in Lucan: "And Mutina and Leucas made Philippi pure." See also Jer. III. 11. There is also another signification of this word departing somewhat from its property. Nor yet does it even so mean the same as to remit sins, as some think. It indeed has a use in the forum, yet not as simply to absolve. For it is said of the accuser no less than of the accused, Exod. XXIII. 7; Deut. XXVI. 1; 1 Sam. XV. 4; Prov. XXVII. 15, in which places it means to treat as just. Nor is it used only in matters of the forum, but also in other matters, and it signifies doing all that which it is fitting to be done to the just, for instance, to approve, Gen. XXXVIII. 29; Matt. XI. 19; XII. 39; Luke VII. 35; XVI. 15, 14; to praise, Eccles. I. 22; XXXI. 5; 1 Tim. III. 7; to do good, 1 Kings VII. 32; Ecclesiasticus IX. 15; Tob. XII. 3; Luke X. 20. The Ancients, and especially St. Chrysostom, deserve praise in every way, but the moderns are not to be spurned either. The writings of the great man Luther have truly brought great light to the Pauline Epistles, and even the German preface alone prefixed to this Epistle to the Romans: which the Papists try in vain to obscure, and Hugo Grotius, following in their footsteps, or at least pouring cold water upon them. Concerning the diverse interpretations of the Apostle’s writings, one may see our Preface prefixed to the *Orthotomia Apostolica* of the blessed Cluver, in which we praised Chrysostom, the Christian Demosthenes, for this reason especially: that, following Diodorus of Tarsus—as Nicephorus relates, with Socrates and Sozomen agreeing—whose student he was, he followed him in his mode of interpretation, just as the latter almost imitated Eusebius of Emesa, declining the subtleties of contemplation and being occupied only in the letter itself and the exposition of the historical sense. has been: whom he also handed down with such happiness, that he has not easily had an equal, let alone a superior, in the whole of Greece. But that he embraced the Epistles of Paul with more vehement love than other divine books, Georgius Alexandrinus, Patriarch, testifies in the life of Chrysostom.

Concerning B.

Concerning the blessed Luther, the judgment of the same [author], which Philippus teaches us in the preface to Tom. III. Concerning Luther, Erasmus was accustomed to say that no one was a more dexterous interpreter of all those whose letters exist after the Apostles: who, as the leader of the critics of the previous century (I point to Philippus), judged thus concerning the blessed Luther himself: The thing itself shows that Luther's expositions far excel the writings of other interpreters.

But above others B. Our Luther, in the explanation of faith, and the imputation of faith to righteousness, and justification by faith, and the remission of sins, was occupied in the golden preface of this Epistle, and in the commentaries on the twin Epistle to the Galatians to this one of ours: to which it must be attributed that, aided by the divine Spirit, the Christian world now possesses the light obscured under the Papacy, if not extinguished, laid bare, shining again through the darkness, and gleaming through the following century, which the Papists have in vain tried to obscure again, especially the Jesuit, and with equal, that is, equally vain success, the same notably Papizing Grotius has labored: First, as to the word of Faith, Faith, he says, some here have interpreted as a persuasion, by which someone believes that Jesus died for him by name, and to procure salvation for him in every way, or what amounts to the same thing among them, that he is predestined.

But these things are very different, in our opinion: that Christ died for someone, and that someone is predestined; and to believe in the redemption of Christ, and to believe that one is in the number of the elect. Nor do we call faith only persuasion, but confidence, and the fiducial apprehension and application of the redemption and merit of Christ, by which it is thus applied, and which makes both the passive and active obedience of the Redeemer Christ, as if he himself had performed it: by the example of the Apostle Gal.

II. 20. which has been shown against the Socinians alike and the Pontificians in the Socinismo profligato, and Mataologia Papistica, and also in the Exegemate Aug. Confess. Nor does it hinder this doctrine that Paul teaches that Christ died for all; because he died for all so that each one might be able to apply this to himself: just as the Apostle again leads the way 1.

Tim. I. v. 15. These things are subordinate, not opposed: indeed, unless Christ were believed to have died for all, no one could assume that he died for himself: so that nothing becomes truer, nothing more useful than this explanation of faith, and faith: because we must be found not having our own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is from the faith of Christ Jesus, Phil. III. 9. who was made righteousness for us by GOD, 1.

Cor. I. 30. But those are deservedly rejected who by faith understand all that obedience which is exhibited to the Gospel, in the sense in which they themselves receive these things.

This is Socinian, and Arminian, who confuse faith and obedience, which is the fruit of faith, and mix the law together with the Gospel, which are most distinct, Joh. I. 17. and in the article of justification are especially most diligently distinguished by the Apostle, when the law is a doctrine of works, the Gospel a doctrine of faith; the law works wrath and a curse, the Gospel becomes a proclamation of grace, and of the blessing which is exhibited to us in Christ, Galat. III. 8. seqq. Paul certainly openly distinguishes love from faith, which is the chief part of that obedience, Gal.

V. 6. as Grotius rightly [says]: But whoever falsely and perversely snatches at this, that Paul prefers love to faith, 1. Cor. XIII. 13. for it is not a question of justification there, nor is justifying faith properly compared with charity, which is the mother and origin of charity: finally, this is deferred to charity by reason of extensive quantity and duration. He also perverts the sense of that Gal.

V. 6. as if it were said that faith performs its work through love: for it is said working through love: which is not to perform its work, but to work through love, so that the works of love and charity, indeed love itself, may overflow from faith as from a cause and root: The work or proper act of faith is to behold Christ, Job. III. 14. 15. to apprehend, Job. I. 12. to put on, Gal. III. 27. also the application and appropriation of the righteousness of Christ, Phil. III. 9. in which its formal notion is situated: but it is not its proper work, but a consequence, which is working through love: which we have abundantly explained in the *Exeg.

A. C.* Cf. also the Harmonia Apostoli Pauli & Jacobi of B. Hülsemann. But, with Hugo Grotius as author, faith in the Pauline Epistles and in that to the Hebrews (which is also entirely Pauline, as we have proven in the vestibule of the Epistle to the Hebrews) is an estimation thinking magnificently of the power, justice, and goodness of GOD, and if he has promised anything, constancy in performing it. Which he wishes to teach from Philo Judaeus, who however has no supporting Prophets, Apostles, or Christian Doctors: although he teaches that it is magnified by GOD alone, but not that we obtain righteousness and salvation through that estimation, which does not follow from that in the least.

And where is this found in the Scriptures, whether Old or New Testament, from which alone what justifying faith is must be learned? Hypocrites and heretics, indeed Jews and Mohammedans themselves, think magnificently of the power, goodness, justice, and constancy of GOD; but shall we therefore ascribe saving faith to them?

But with the definition laid down, the thing defined cannot be denied. Therefore saving faith does not consist in the mere opinion and estimation of the mind, however magnificent, but besides knowledge and assent, not only concerning those divine attributes, but concerning whatever things are necessary to be believed for salvation, there is need of the trust of the heart and will, or the fiducial apprehension of Christ and his merits: which is the form and soul of justifying faith.

For since Christ, the only Mediator between God and men, died for us, or gave his soul as a ransom for all, 1. Tim. II. 6. and the same fulfilled the law for us, Rom. IX. 6. that we might be made the righteousness of GOD in him, 2. Cor. V. 21. and by his obedience we might be constituted righteous, Rom. V. 18. which his Satisfaction, undergone and paid in our place by his Passion and death, and obedience performed in our stead, cannot be another's or be reckoned to us, except through faith or fiducial application, therefore justifying faith is nothing else than the vicarious apprehension of the satisfaction and obedience of Christ our Mediator, by which each one claims and applies the same to himself individually, just as if he himself had rendered satisfaction to divine justice for his sins and full obedience to the divine law. Which Catholic faith Hugo Grotius defended in good part against the Socinian, in a special work published for the Satisfaction of Christ.

Who therefore dares to affirm that that faith, by which someone believes that Jesus died for him by name, and to procure salvation in every way, has NOTHING in it of TRUE or USEFUL?

Is it not most true that Christ died for all, and so also for each one of us? Did he not procure salvation for all, and so also individually for each one, by his death? And if this is true, is it not altogether, or truly, to be believed?

And does not each; specifically, faith in Christ Jesus is required for salvation Rom. X. 4. & 9. and so it is required that each one believe for himself specifically that Jesus died. I live, says the Apostle, in the faith of the Son of GOD (in the Son of GOD) who loved me, and gave himself for me Gal. II. 20. And this is entirely what is said in this Epistle about faith being imputed for righteousness: namely, that righteousness or obedience apprehended by faith is held to be ours, as almost the whole Christian world believes: for the band of Socinians is hardly worthy of the Christian name.

That the Roman Catholics do not entirely deny this imputation of Christ's obedience is evident from the declaration of the Walenburgs and others in Exeg. A. C. Artic. IV. proposed. But no one would easily say that our estimation, as if it were thinking magnificently about the power, justice, goodness, and truth of God, is imputed to us for righteousness, or that righteousness is reckoned through that estimation: he believes that nothing else is signified by that phrase, that faith is imputed for righteousness, than that faith or an estimation of such a kind is considered by God as exceedingly good; even if every honest thing were called just by the Hebrews, which does not appear from Deut.

XXIV. 13. Ps. CVI. 30., where that phrase imports something more than mere honesty and is gathered a posteriori, that works proceeding from faith are reckoned for righteousness, or that their righteousness is declared through those works and deeds, or that those works are held to be just, and are reckoned as just by the judgment of GOD, who sees and acknowledges them as proceeding from faith; but what is this to the present matter? We accept, however, that the word חַשַׁב which is used in Ps.

CVI. 30. is properly said of that which is referred to accounts, as in Lev. XXIV. 27. 50. 52. XXVII. 18. Num. XXIII. 7. or even to some census, as in Deut. II. 11. 20. Jos. XIII. 3. 2. Sam. IV. 2. But that a metaphorical meaning, by which it is said of that which is made of great or small value, or which is held as pleasing or unpleasing, should have a place, we entirely deny. For the rule of good interpretation is this, that we should not depart from the propriety of a word to a metaphorical or improper meaning without necessity: the proper meaning prevailing, it is manifest, from the observation of Grotius himself, that the obedience of Christ is so imputed to us that it is transferred to our accounts, and referred to our census; as if each of us had performed the same.

Although neither is this demonstrated by examples, that the word חַשַׁב to impute, PER SE is the same as to be made of great or small value: for in those examples also

Gen. XXXI. 15. 1. Reg. X. 12. 2. Par. IX. 20. Os. II. 12. Es. XXIX. 17. the word itself denotes nothing else than to be reckoned, just as the LXX. have simply rendered it in the same place by λογίζεσθαι to reckon, and it is not gathered except from added words or the context, how something is said to be reckoned, whether it is made of great value or not: Nor does that example 1. Sam. I. 13. καὶ ἐλογίσατο αὐτὴν ἡ ἐλίς μεθύουσαν and Eli reckoned her as drunk, or as a drunkard, fit well here: since here an abstract is held, not a concrete, and this phrase is far different from that, it is imputed to him for righteousness: if, however, you apply that thus, as there he reckoned her as drunk, Eli, thus God, faith objectively accepted, or faith which believes, will be said to be reckoned for righteousness. In the other example Prov. XVII. 28. ἀνόητῳ ἐπερωτήσαντι σοφίαν σοφία λογισθήσεται, to a fool asking for wisdom, wisdom shall be reckoned, that is, shall be estimated: for it is also estimated as wisdom, to seek wisdom. But from this the sense of the Apostolic phrase cannot be extracted: as if it were that righteousness is imputed on account of believing, as if righteousness were estimated on account of faith, when we are not justified on account of faith, but through faith, since that sense rather emerges thus, that our righteousness is estimated by faith objectively accepted, the faith by which it is believed, that is, the righteousness of Christ himself.

And just as in Lev. XVII. 4. it is said αἷμα λογισθήσεται τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ blood or the shedding of blood and the guilt and liability arising thence shall be imputed to the man, because namely he slaughtered the victims not before the door of the tabernacle, but in the camp, so that he is held guilty before GOD: so the obedience of Christ, which faith apprehends, is said to be reckoned to us for righteousness, so that thence we may be held just in the divine judgment. Just as the Lord is said not to impute ἀνομίαν 2. Sam. XIX. 19. & Ps. XXXII. 2. μακάριος, ᾧ μὴ λογίσηται κύριος ἁμαρτίαν, because in his judgment God does not impute sin to him, does not transfer it to his accounts, does not estimate it, or recall it to the census, so that he is held guilty of sins and punishment, so the obedience of Christ is imputed to us for righteousness, when in the judgment of GOD it is transferred to our accounts, is imputed to us, is reckoned and estimated as ours, so that we are held just, and blessed thence, and become saved. For from the opposition, and from the collation of such places, which the Holy Scripture confers, the force of the Apostolic phrase is estimated more correctly than from other places not parallel and alien. Nor indeed was it the Apostle's purpose to teach that faith is considered by GOD as an exceedingly good thing, but to explain how faith justifies, and to teach that man, through the apprehension of the redemption and righteousness or obedience of Christ, is justified, and obtains salvation, since namely his own sins are not imputed to him by GOD for guilt and condemnation, but on the contrary the obedience of Christ itself is imputed to him, when through faith man appropriates it to himself, for righteousness, so that he is held just therefore, and obtains blessedness.

Who doubts that the estimation of GOD's power, justice, goodness, and truth is an exceedingly good thing, pleasing to God? And what was the point of proving that there, where it had to be explained how a sinful man, condemned by the voice of the law on account of sins before the tribunal of GOD, is both absolved and declared just? which is done not on account of our works, because God justifies the ungodly, but solely on account of the redemption and righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith, as the Apostle teaches and demonstrates. And hence it is manifest that these are by no means different, when man is said to be justified through faith, and when faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, or righteousness is said to be imputed to the believer; as Grotius wishes, most wickedly perverting these things: but these are held by the Apostle as mutually explaining each other: for that faith, through which man is justified, is faith in Christ our Lord and Redeemer, and in the righteousness of God, or of Christ the θεανθρώπου, which is that righteousness χωρὶς νόμου without law, or without works of the law, revealed in the Gospel μαρτυρουμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου, καὶ τῶν προφητῶν Rom.

III. 21. because Christ is the end and completion of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes Rom. X. 4. and is made to us by GOD righteousness 1. Cor. I. 30. according to the creed of the faithful, which also obtained in the Old Testament, he himself is Jehovah our righteousness Jer. XXIII. 6. of whom all the Prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins Act. X. 43. whom God set forth, on account of the ἀπολύτρωσιν, which was made by him (when he gave his soul as ἀντίλυτρον for us Matth. XX. 18. Marc. X. 45. 1. Tim. II. 6.) ἱλαστήριον, a placament, or propitiatory through faith in his blood, for the ἔνδειξιν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτοῦ for the demonstration of his righteousness Rom. III. 24. 25. faith therefore apprehends ἀπολύτρωσιν the redemption of Christ, apprehends Christ, as the propitiatory (ἱλαστήριον) proposed by GOD, apprehends the propitiatory blood of Christ, and the redemption, both as by the same the propitiation and redemption (ἀπολύτρωσις) was made, and as he himself was poured out, in the place and stead of our blood, he apprehends the justice of Christ, which is offered and exhibited to us in the Gospel, that by the same apprehended we may be justified and by the obedience of our one mediator be constituted just Rom. V. 29.

This truly Apostolic doctrine, that he may pervert it, for the sake of the Papists if not also of the Socinians, Grotius feigns that the Apostle means something else entirely, when he teaches that justice is imputed through faith, or when he teaches that faith and justice are imputed, and when he asserts that we are justified through faith: which things, however, are to be accepted in the same sense, according to the mind of the Apostle: Because we are thus justified through faith apprehending the redemption and obedience of Christ, so that the obedience of Christ, both passive and active, is imputed to us for justice, by which the same is apprehended through faith, and is appropriated to us, so that thus we are not justified by our own proper obedience, but by the obedience of Christ, yet imputed to us, and by the obedience of him alone we are all constituted just, whoever we are justified; and therefore not faith, as it is believed, but that which is believed, that is, the proper object of faith, namely the obedience of Christ, is imputed to us for justice.

Is the word justification to be accepted here in a forensic sense?

And therefore the word Justification cannot here be accepted otherwise than in a forensic sense; by which he is said to be justified, who is absolved, and declared and pronounced just: because on account of Christ, our only Mediator and Redeemer and Advocate, who in our place and for the divine law performed obedience, which no one could perform perfectly, and for the sins, for which we had merited death, he himself, as our surety and sponsor, and ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) at once and piacular victim, underwent it, when we are absolved from sins, their guilt, and punishment by grace, then we are reputed just, as if we ourselves had performed the law of God, and that freely and out of mere grace: When constituted before the tribunal and judgment of God, accused by Moses and the Mosaic law, as unjust, and as guilty of various crimes and sins to be condemned by the force of divine justice, according to the strict justice (τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον) we were.

All things here are forensic, Judge, defendant, accuser, law, judgment of God, justice, condemnation, Mediator, satisfaction, placation of the judge, Advocate, absolution from guilt and punishment, justification: which those who deny to be judicial, deny that the sun shines at midday.

It is therefore mere perversity, when from a forensic signification a certain Physical justification is here feigned, as if sin were expelled, and justice infused, not otherwise than as cold being expelled heat is induced, when water is said to be heated.

Which is known to be done by the Papists.

What is it to justify according to the Papist-leaning Grotius?

That Grotius may pour cold water on these, he first observes that the verb δικαιοῦν, and δικαιοῦσθαι sometimes corresponds to צדק in Kal to be just, as Gen.

XXIX. 16. Syr. XXXI. 5. or to appear just, just as it is said to be, what appears, Psal. LI. 6. Psal. CXIII. 2. sometimes to the verb צדק in Piel, or הצדיק in Hiphil, which in their native sense signify to make just, that is, to purge from vices, to cleanse, to liberate, Psal. LXXII. 13. Is.
