LIII. 21. Dan. XII. 31. Ecclesiastic. XVIII. 22. 1. Cor. IV. 4. Ap. XXII. 11. but here it is not properly inquired about the verb צדק in Kal, but in Piel and Hiphil.

Alien Gen. 38, 16. therefore the place is Gen. XXIX. 16. she is just before me: for in Kal sometimes it is to be righteous.

Thus Job IV. 17. is rendered by the LXX. καθαρός ἐσαι. Ps. XIX. 10. The judgments of the Lord are just: likewise that Syr. XXXI. 5. ὁ ἀγαπῶν χρυσίον ὁ δικαιωθήσεται, he who loves gold shall not be justified, can also be accepted in a forensic sense: nor if that word be rendered there, will he not be just, it is therefore then with the Apostle, where there is discourse concerning the justification of man before the tribunal of God, it will be to be accepted in the same sense.

Nor Psal. CXLIII. 2. shall he be pure (καθαρός ἐσαι) and shall appear just: but rather is he just? because truly no one is just before God, if God wishes to enter into judgment with us, or to act with us according to the rigor of judgment.

And Psal. LI. 6. it can be rendered ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς, that thou mayest be declared just, or pronounced, and be acknowledged by all.

Now as far as the Hebrew verb in Piel, or Hiphil is concerned, no place could be produced, where it is to make just or to be made, or to be purged from vices, but always it is to absolve, or to be absolved from sins, or to pronounce or declare just, or to be declared.

Exod. XXIII. 7. Deut. XXV. 1. 2. Sam. XV. 4. 2. Par. VI. 23. Is. V. 23. c. XLV. 24.

The places which Grotius adduced to Acts XIII. 39. Job IV. 17. Dan. VIII. 14. are alien: for they do not pertain to these conjugations Piel, and Hiphil, but to the first: nor is there need that in Daniel Niphal be accepted for Hophal, as he himself wishes: for why can it not be rendered, it shall be cleansed in Psalm v. LXXIII. 13. the verb הצדיק is not had, he cleanses.

But the remaining places Is. LIII. 11. Dan. XII. 3. adduced by Bellarmine we have vindicated Exeg. Aug. Conf. art. IV. c. I. I. §. XI.

Christ indeed justifies us by the knowledge of himself, or through faith, not by infusing justice, but by absolving from sins, and by donating his own justice to us. Nor do the doctors of the word justify in such a way, that they infuse justice, and declare just ministerially (διακονικῶς) Matth. XII. 18. Joh. XX. 12. 2. Cor. V. 19.

Which sense also Syr. XIII. 22. can have, nor is that word accepted otherwise in 1. Cor.

It is certainly not there to be purged from vices: for what would this be, I am conscious of nothing, but in this I am not justified, that is, I am not purged or cleansed from vices? Nor Apoc. XXII. 11.

He who is just, let him be justified still, δικαιωθήτω ἔτι, the sense is, let him be justified more, or let him become more just, but let him be justified further, and no increment of justice is noted, but continuation and perseverance, that the just may not fall from justification, but study to persevere in that state. Finally, as to the comparative locution, when Jerusalem is said to have justified Samaria Ez. XVI.

51. certainly she did not make her just, but declared her by her own worst life to be more just than herself.

Thus therefore Grotius could not find from the Scriptures that meaning of justification which he makes most proper, as neither could Gardin. Bellarmine: which we showed in the cited place; He therefore betakes himself to the Hebrews, that in that sense, as it is to make just, the Rabbis use it, as in Zohar and elsewhere; but is the sense of the Apostolic phrase to be learned from them?

But it remains true, what we taught in the l. c., that the Hebrew word in the S. scriptures is nowhere accepted otherwise, than for absolution, or declaration of justice, whether it be judicial in the forum, or extrajudicial or outside the forum, whether it be used of God, or of creatures, whether truly, or falsely one is declared just, or is absolved.

Nor does Grotius profit a whit, whether he says that that signification departs somewhat from the property: For he did not prove it, nor could he prove it: or when he denies that it has the same value here, as to remit sins: because it suffices, that in justification the remission of sins is contained, even if with the remission of sins we are also declared just, or when he denies, that in the forum it is the same as to absolve, and wishes it to have the same value in certain places as to treat as just: in which our signification is contrary and manifest: as for instance Exod.

XXIII. 7. I will not justify, i.e. I will not absolve the impious.

Thus they are commanded Deut.

XXV. 1. To justify the innocent, that is, to absolve, 2 Sam. 15:4. & I will justify him, that is, I will absolve him, namely if he has a just cause: Prov. 17:15. He who justifies, that is, absolves the wicked, and condemns the just, is an abomination to the Lord. Nor in other places which it insinuates is the meaning different from that which we have stated. Matt. 11:19, Luke 7:35. Wisdom is said to be justified, that is, declared just. Matt. 12:37. By your words you will be justified, that is, you will be declared just, and by your words you will be condemned, Luke 16:15, ch. 18:9. they justify themselves, that is, they pronounce themselves just, and it is thus accepted also in 1 Kings 8:32, Luke 10:29, where it is rendered by Grotius as to do good. Finally, even if elsewhere to justify were to make just, what does this have to do with the Apostolic phrase, and must it therefore be accepted in this sense, what is said that GOD justifies the wicked, or justifies us through faith? Is this not a contradiction in terms, to be justified WITHOUT works of the law, that is, to be made just and pure, to be cleansed from vices, and to be adorned with inherent justice, he who, destitute of every good work, is nothing less than pure and just by inherent justice?

SECTION VII. Concerning the justice of man.

Since, therefore, in the primitive sense to justify is to make just or innocent, just as justice is twofold, the one which men perform by their own power, and which deserves praise among men, namely that exterior one, below 4:2, 9:32, the other interior, which God effects in us, and which is valid before God, or it is the same thing that we are justified by faith as that hearts are cleansed by faith, Heb. 10:22, that souls are cleansed through the obedience of the truth, 1 Pet. 1:22, and therefore Christ also did not heal the diseases of bodies except in believers, to show that souls are much more healed in this way. And indeed it was of all times that the interior purity of the soul should be born from faith, and grow from faith. Moreover, this pertains so much more excellently to the times of the Gospel, as the promises are both greater and more certain. Into a heart thus cleansed, as into a pure vessel, God pours His Spirit, the Spirit, I say, of Christ, full of the love of God and neighbor, and of all goodness. Chrysostom not badly on Gal. 3: ἡ δικαιοσύνη, τῶ πνεύματι τὴν χάριν ἐπεσπάσατο [righteousness drew grace to itself by the Spirit]. That Spirit then produces works with great abundance, no less divine and heavenly than were the use of tongues, prophecy, the expulsion of demons. Thus those who were צדיקים [righteous] become חסידים [pious], and ἁγιασμὸς [sanctification] follows δικαιοσύνην [righteousness], 1 Cor. 1:30. Not badly on this matter Lactantius: Then he ought to work justice more, when he has been made just, so that what he had done before for the healing of wounds, he may do afterwards for the praise and glory of virtue: likewise: And just as in rough fields, before you begin to sow, the fields must be purged by pulling up the thorns and cutting off the roots of all plants, so from our souls vices must first be removed, and then at last virtues must be inserted, from which the fruits of immortality sown through the word of God may arise. And the Church followed this order in the Sacraments, for after the κατήχησιν [catechesis] Baptism is given, that is, washing from sins, anointing follows, that is, the conferring of the Spirit, then the daily sacrifices τῆς ἀγάπης [of love]. Jerome: Baptism releases from prison, and once released, if he has labored, it promises rewards. But those who have that Spirit of God and keep it solicitously, God holds them as His own children, as born from Himself and similar to Himself, and gives them a certain right to eternal and heavenly goods. Since these things were so, that neither would the heart be cleansed except through faith in Christ, nor would that Spirit be poured into a heart thus cleansed, nor would God plainly acknowledge as His own those not endowed with that Spirit, it followed from this that the immense multitude of the Jews, as those who did not believe in Jesus, were excluded from those eternal and heavenly goods. That, indeed, Paul says is sad, but not absurd. For whatever appears to be done by God (and it appeared that Christians alone were gifted with the Spirit of GOD, both from their life, in which they far surpassed the others, and also from the signs of miracles, which ran into the sight of all) that altogether has a reason, even if it does not appear to us. Having prefaced this, Paul nevertheless shows that it is seen in some way, not why GOD ought to have done so, but why it was more fitting for Him. He adds that this very thing which was now happening had been foreshadowed by certain ancient figures. Concerning that predestination, about which many things are said in the Schools, there is no discussion here, nor indeed did it pertain to the matter, which Toletus excellently points out.

From these things which we have said, we think it is now manifest that our justice is spoken of in two ways, or is twofold: First, imputed, because faith is said to be imputed for justice, which justice is manifested χωρὶς νόμυ [without the law], Rom. 3:21, which God imputes χωρὶς ἔργων [without works], ch. 3:6. Then, inherent and begun: which has the law as a norm, and cannot be imagined without the works of the law: since those justified by faith ought not to live according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, and to serve not sin, but justice, Rom. 6:18, the former justice is alien and extrinsic, namely the obedience of Christ, Rom. 5:19, but it becomes ours through faith, by which we apprehend it, and through λογισμὸν [reckoning], or imputation, by which God imputes the same to believers: which is the cause of our justification. The latter is ours and intrinsic to us, which, namely, the Holy Spirit effects in believers: which is not the cause, but the consequence of our justification: therefore after the Apostle in chapters I, III, IV, and V had treated of the justice of God, of the justice which is from faith and through faith, of the justice which is imputed through faith, and had demonstrated that man is justified without the law: he proceeds in chapter VI to discourse concerning inherent justice, when those justified through faith apply their efforts and are devoted according to the law: so that, freed from sin, they may serve God in true justice and holiness. The former justice is perfect: because the obedience of Christ is absolute in all its parts and in all its degrees, which is reckoned to us in the judgment of God: the latter justice, however, is imperfect in many ways, and is destitute of the due perfection not only of degrees, but also of parts: which the Apostle teaches and proves primarily in Chapter VII by his own example.

Nor do the Papists deny, however sharp they may be, among whom is Gabriel Vasquez in 1. 2. T. II. disp. CCXXIII. c. I., that some extrinsic things, such as the merits and obedience of Christ, are imputed to us, and reckoned as if they were truly our own: Cardinal Bellarmine also acknowledges in l. II. de justif. c. X. §. 4. the imputation of the justice of Christ, which he teaches from Sess. VI. of the Council of Trent, c. VII., is conferred and applied to us in justification, although he contends that the justice inherent in us is also a true and absolute justice, to which, by the just judgment of God, glory is owed. The Walenburch brothers, c. XIV. de Unit. Eccl. c. XI. th. XXXIX. p. 831., have this to say on the matter: For the Council of Trent does not deny that men are justified by the imputation of the justice of Christ, but it denies that they are justified by imputation alone: And th. XLIX. Catholics, they say, do not doubt that the justice of Christ is extrinsic to us, and is the thing by and through which we are justified and absolved from sins, with justification taken in the forensic sense. The same brothers teach in c. VII. that Catholic Doctors hold that a person is pleasing to God before inherent justice is infused into him, and therefore they necessarily admit a double justice, one imputed, the other inherent: they also acknowledge, and indeed say that there is agreement between us and the Papists on this, that the justice inherent in us can be called begun with respect to the justice which the saints possess in heaven, and imperfect with respect to the justice of Christ given and imputed to us, as that which without doubt infinitely exceeds our justice. These things have been brought forward at length in the Exeg. Aug. Confess. art. IV. c. VIII. §. IX. et seqq. What, therefore, is that in which there is still disagreement in this chief article of faith? We have diligently shown that in the same place; and at the same time we have discussed the opinion of the Papists and the Syncretist Walenburch brothers.

Undoubtedly the Papists err when they contend that justification in the Scriptures is also taken for the bestowal of inherent justice, which they can show in no place of Scripture. They err when they [take] justification in its whole breadth with the imputation of the justice-

they wish to include the collation of inherent justice: for nowhere does it occur in that breadth, nor can it be that the word 'to justify' denotes at once in a forensic sense the absolution from sins, or the non-imputation of sins with the imputation of the merits and justice of Christ, and in a physical sense, as we might call it, the infusion or collation of inherent justice: nay, the Apostle so constitutes our justification before the tribunal of GOD by the remission, or non-imputation of our injustice, and the imputation of the justice of Christ, that he opposes it to inherent justice in this article, and thus in no way admits that the same concurs to our justification, but teaches openly that it is to be excluded entirely, and decrees that we are constituted just not by our own inherent justice, but solely by the obedience of the one Christ.

A new error, but more Socinian than Papist, reveals itself, when Grotius says that this pertains more excellently to the times of the Gospel, because, forsooth, the interior purity of the mind is born from faith, and grows from faith, in as much as the promises are both greater and more certain. For Scripture recognizes no such difference in that part of the times.

We believe, the Apostles decree, Acts XV. 10. that we are justified by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: just as our Fathers were.

Nor are the promises of the Gospel time greater: because in the promise made to the Patriarchs, and in the very first promise in Paradise, Gen.

III. 15. the remission of sins, spiritual blessing, and heavenly things, and salvation, and eternal life were contained: although these Evangelical promises were repeated and explained more clearly in the New Testament.

Nor indeed are they more certain to us than they were to the Patriarchs and other faithful of the Old Testament, whose faith is set before us as an example, Heb.

XI. or to Abraham himself, the father of believers, who believed in hope against hope, and in whose footsteps we all must follow: to whom the promise was made that he should be the heir of the world, Rom. IV. 13. that he should be the heir of the future world, or of eternal life, which was confirmed and sealed to the same by the Sacrament of Circumcision as by a seal of the justice of faith, v. 11. as in the New Testament the grace of God and eternal salvation is conferred and sealed to us through the Sacraments, so in the Old Testament it was done likewise through the Sacraments of that time.

Grotius says that after the catechism Baptism is given, that is, absolution from sins, followed by anointing, that is, the collation of the spirit, then the daily sacrifices of love.

But those who have that Spirit of God and keep it solicitously, he says that God holds them as born from himself and like to himself as his own children, and gives them the right to eternal and heavenly goods.

But in the designation of the Sacraments he sails for the Papists, while he introduces the sacrament of confirmation, nowhere instituted by Christ or the Apostles, and tacitly transforms the Sacrament of the Eucharist, to which the spiritual sacrifices of love were once joined in the exercise of charity, and were deservedly joined, into a Sacrifice: the accident and adjunct of the Sacrament are confused with the Sacrament itself.

Nor always after the

Which we have executed deliberately and solidly in the cited place: where we also called to account the Syncretism of Grotius, which he produced in his Annotations on the Cassandrian consultation. Here he makes a twofold justice: the one, which men perform by their own power, which deserves outward praise among men, namely that which he says is noted in Rom. IV. 2. IX. 32: the other interior, which God effects in us, and which is valid before God: and thus he says it is the same thing, that we are justified by faith, as that hearts are purified by faith, Heb. X, 22, that souls are purified by the obedience of truth, 1. Pet.

I. 22. But that twofold justice is not found in the cited places: nor does that distinction have any place in this article of justification, indeed any justice of the law, or which has the law as its norm, is excluded from the article of justification, because the justice by which we are justified before GOD, χωρὶς νόμου πεφανέρωται, Rom.

III. 21. Nor is it a matter in Rom.

IV. 2. c. IX. 32. only of external justice, but of any justice of works or of the law, of one's own (or inherent) justice, as is explained in c. X. 3. which is opposed to the justice of God, or of Christ, who is τέλος, the complement of the law for justice to every believer, Rom. X. 4. Therefore the Apostle does not wish to be found before the tribunal of GOD, having HIS OWN justice, which is from the law, whether external or internal: but he wishes to be found in CHRIST, having that which is through the faith of Christ, the justice of God in faith, Phil.

III. 9. Nor indeed are we justified by interior justice, which God effects in us, because this is a consequence of justification, which is by nature prior to this inherent justice.

Therefore, that which pertains to interior justice does nothing for our justification, by which we are justified through faith: Nor are hearts purified by faith otherwise than through faith in the blood of Jesus, Rom.

III. 25. who alone purifies us from all sin, 1. John I. 7. certainly not through our interior justice.

For faith is not interior justice: but it is distinguished from it as antecedent and consequent, cause and effect; and when souls are said to be purified in the obedience of truth, which is the paraphrase of faith, 1.

Pet. I. 22. it is hinted that this is done by the blood of that immaculate and uncontaminated lamb, v. 19. without which no justification occurs: which faith apprehends; as through ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος, 1. Pet. I. 2. and through that faith apprehending the purification of the blood of Christ, our hearts, the hearts of the faithful, are purified, Acts XV. 9. because the expiation made through the blood of Christ is appropriated to us through faith, and thus we are purified by the sprinkled blood of Christ: For the blood of Christ, who offered himself immaculate to GOD through the eternal spirit καθαριεῖ, purges our conscience from dead works, as the Apostle testifies, Heb.

IX. 14. Therefore, to be purified in the obedience of truth is to be purified through faith, by which one acquiesces and obeys the truth of the Gospel; which obedience of faith is designated in Rom. L.

5. c. VI. 17. c. XVI. 26. For faith embraces the most perfect expiation and cleanliness and purity of Christ offered in the word of the Gospel, and appropriates it to the believer; through this faith is then given the Spirit of justification, S. Gal. III. 2. which begins to purge the filth of sin through renewal, so that the faithful man becomes clean not only imputatively, 1. Cor. I. 30. but also inchoatively, and grows daily in this spiritual cleanliness, until it follows consummated in the other life. 1.

Cor. VI. 11. What of the fact that Grotius himself acknowledges that the interior purity of the mind (inherent) is born from faith, and grows from faith.

Therefore faith is not the interior purity of the mind itself, but its cause.

And afterwards, to the heart, he says, thus purified, that is, justified by faith, as to a pure vessel God infuses his Spirit: the Spirit, I say, of Christ, full of the love of God and of neighbor, and of all goodness: thus those who were חסרים צדיקים are חסרים and ἁγιασμός follows δικαιοσύνην.

1. Cor. I. 30. But what justice?

Certainly not inherent and inchoate; for that is not without ἁγιασμός, nor can it be feigned: Therefore imputed, because Christ is made justice to us by GOD, and we are rendered in him the justice of God through faith.

2. Cor. V. 21. But the removal or purging of vices from our minds, and the infusion of virtues, pertain equally to ἁγιασμός, and follow justice.

Neither, however, precedes justification, or pertains to the form of justification.

κατήχησιν Baptism is given, but only when adults are to be baptized.

De Furthermore, in Baptism there occurs not only a washing away of sins, but also an anointing and a conferring of the Spirit, who is poured out upon us richly, Tit. III. 6. In the Sacrament of the Eucharist, there occurs a confirmation of faith and a sealing of the righteousness of faith.

Nectalia These means, as we have already hinted, were not lacking to the faithful in the Old Testament. They had the Sacrament of initiation and regeneration, Circumcision: they had the Sacrament of confirmation and sealing, the Paschal lamb: nor were they destitute of the anointing or conferring of the Spirit, whom Moses, David, the Prophets, and other faithful ones had abundantly; how will this be denied?

And will they be excluded from the number of the children of God? Who then shall be heirs of eternal life? But if they are children of God, they are not destitute of the Spirit of God.

For those who are led by the Spirit of GOD, they are the children of God, Rom. IX. 14. And although it is certain that these things concur subjectively and exist together in time—to be born of God and to be a child of GOD, and to be justified through faith, and to have the Spirit full of the love of God and neighbor—yet in the order of nature these follow one another in such a way that there is first a need for regeneration, so that we may attain faith, then through faith justification occurs, and furthermore, the justified are renewed and sanctified through the H.

S. so that they may strive for the love of God and neighbor, because faith works through charity, Gal. V. 6. Whence in this Epistle the holy Apostle dealt first with the justification of faith, but afterwards finally with its fruits and effects, sanctification and the pursuit of good works.

Therefore, when the Apostle demonstrated that justification is only through faith in Christ, who was rejected by the Jews, to whom however He was once first promised, he therefore discourses on the rejection of the Jews, both to teach that they were not rejected by GOD out of some absolute decree, but because they themselves rejected the Messiah, in whom alone is the remission of sins and righteousness, and they attempted to set up their own righteousness, and wished to be justified and saved by their own obedience to the law, that righteousness which is rejected because it is from the faith of Christ.

Therefore, the Apostle also teaches that the promises made to the Jews, regarding spiritual and heavenly goods, do not pertain to them as Israelites, or as they are from Abraham according to the flesh, and that those who are children of the promise become participants in them solely out of the grace of God through faith, without their merits: nor does he show that anyone was absolutely rejected by them, even by the example of Pharaoh, namely how GOD rather, ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ (which shone forth especially in that example) endures σκεύη ὀργῆς κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν, Rom. IX. 22. But the riches of His grace shine forth from the fact that He called both Jews and Gentiles, and when He called the Gentiles, He did not reject the Jews in their entirety, even though they themselves rejected Christ, the remnant of whom ought to attain salvation v. 17. But that the Jews did not attain the righteousness of faith, the true righteousness, is because, as was predicted, they stumbled upon Christ, or the stone of stumbling, and did not confess that they were justified before GOD through the righteousness of Christ, but through their own righteousness: c.

IX. 30. ff. c. X. 3. f. wherefore the Lord wished to provoke the Jews to jealousy through the Gentiles, although in vain, v. 19. 20. 21. & and yet those whom He foresaw would believe in Christ c.

XI. 2. He by no means rejected, even if their number is not apparent to eyes or senses, just as the number of the faithful was hidden even in the time of Elijah v. 3. 4. 5. That the punishment of the unbelief of the faithless Jews had been predicted, v. 8. 9. 10. and that their παραπτώματι, by the singular direction of divine grace, and not by some fate, brought about salvation to the Gentiles εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτούς, not so that they (the Jews) remain rejected, if you look at the divine intention and the antecedent will, but rather so that the Gentiles, being emulated, might believe and be saved: and therefore also on the part of Israel a πώρωσις occurred, yet the Apostle did not wish the Romans to be ignorant of the mystery of divine Grace, that when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, also all Israel, whoever does not similarly refuse to be saved, at all times, with none excepted, with none precisely excluded or rejected by the force of the divine promises Is.

LIX. 20. Jer. XXXI. 33. is to be saved, v. 25. 26. because χαρίσματα, κλῆσις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀμεταμέλητα, as far as pertains to Him who concluded all under unbelief through the law, not so that He might pass over some by grace, or leave them concluded under sin and condemnation, but so that He might have mercy on all, according to the word of the Gospel v. 32. whence the Apostle concludes this treatment with admiration of the depth of the riches of grace, and wisdom, and the knowledge of God, and the unsearchable judgments of God.

E From which it is abundantly manifest that there is no treatment here of predestination c.

IX. X. XI. much less is any absolute predestination or preterition asserted, but the temporal rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles are dealt with in such a way that justification and blessedness, which is the principal scope of the whole Epistle, is taught not to depend on an absolute decree, nor on the merits and works of men, or one's own righteousness, but on the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and the righteousness of faith, so that the abyss of divine mercy, exhibited to the human race in Christ, may be celebrated on all sides: and that what the Apostle had said in the proposition of the Epistle may be acknowledged as true, that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to the Jew first and to the Greek, and it may be clearly understood how in it the righteousness of GOD is revealed, which is from faith to faith, and how the just shall live solely by faith, and there is no other reason for righteousness unto salvation, or for justifying faith, or for justification, or for life and salvation, than that they who receive the Gospel of God through faith, believe in Christ, and persevere in that faith, are justified and live eternally through the fiduciary apprehension of the righteousness of Christ by grace. Which is the sum of this whole golden Epistle.

Non But it is not taught in these chapters how that which was done in the New

Testament was prefigured by the figures of the ancients, nor that the examples of the ancients are brought forward only as figures, but that the very thing itself is placed there πρὸς ὄμμα and demonstrated, the reason for the continuity will teach: yet this one thing was truly observed by Grotius, who says: there is no discourse here about predestination: nor indeed did it pertain to the matter. SECTION VIII. Concerning the Remission of sins, what is it to the Apostle?

Etiam Many do not correctly understand what the remission of sins is in this Epistle.

God, by the prayers of Christ, on account of His supreme obedience, granted this, that He would not forsake the most corrupt human race, as He could, and harden it in sins, but would open ways, and indeed most magnificent ones, to all, through which they could attain that Holy Spirit and consequently eternal and heavenly goods. See, Chrysostom on Chapter IV of this Epistle, that it is much more to be justified than it is to be the remission of sins.

We have thought it necessary to explain these things at the very threshold, which might serve as a torch to the whole Epistle. Grotius warns that many do not correctly understand what the remission of sins is in this Epistle.

But he himself, more than almost all others, understood it less correctly: God, he says, by the prayers of Christ, on account of His supreme obedience, granted this, that He would not forsake the most corrupt human race, as He could, and harden it in sins, but would open ways, and indeed most magnificent ones, to all, through which they could attain that holy Spirit and consequently eternal and heavenly goods. could attain good things.

But who understands from this what the remission of sins is? He says that remission was not obtained for the human race by the satisfaction of Christ, which he had formerly opposed against Socinus, having always become worse, according to that of the Apostle 2 Tim. 3:13, not how the satisfaction of Christ is imputed to us through faith, so that we may actually obtain the remission of sins: he only commemorates the prayers and intercession of Christ; which indeed we do not exclude, but it has its weight from this, that Christ expiated our sins with his blood, propitiated God, and merited for us the remission of sins.

In what way those most magnificent things are, he does not openly explain here: but Scripture knows no other way than Christ, who says John 14:6, I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. And it is one thing indeed to have the remission of sins, which was sought here, and another the gift of the Holy Spirit, or as Grotius says, the Spirit full of the love of God and neighbor and all goodness: through which love and goodness certainly, he who thinks that we attain eternal and heavenly goods, does not seek the most magnificent way to eternal life, but one leading away from eternal life: which the Jews had chosen, of whom the Apostle says Rom. 9:31, Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness, etc. Ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God.

Finally, what Grotius says, that justification is much more than receiving the remission of sins, he proves from the Apostle, he cannot, who holds these as a kind of ὑπάλλον τι (hypallage); he even proves it from Chrysostom: for he often uses the remission of sins and justification interchangeably, and although he requires something more for justification in ch. 4 to the Romans, that however is not inherent or intrinsic righteousness, but imputed: and so he teaches with us that our justification is not completed by the imputation of our sins, with the imputation of the righteousness of Christ: which therefore is rightly described sometimes by the remission of sins or imputation negatively, sometimes by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, by which we are reputed just, affirmatively, in a sense not opposite, but the same: for the non-imputation alone constitutes us no otherwise than as it makes us free from the guilt and punishment of injustice, but the imputation of righteousness or obedience makes us just, Rom. V. 29. so that, absolved from the guilt and punishment of injustice, we are considered just, the righteousness or obedience of Christ being ascribed to us. Consider, says Chrysostom on ch. 4, p. 79, how great it is to believe certainly, to be persuaded, that God can not only free from punishment him who has spent his whole life in impiety, but also immediately make him just, and render him worthy of immortal honors at the same time. And he teaches how these cohere, the remission of sins, righteousness, and life: Where there is grace, there is also forgiveness: but where there is forgiveness, there will be no punishment: but with the punishment of justice removed through faith granted, there is nothing that prevents us from becoming heirs of his promise, which is by faith.

Finally, that Chrysostom held justification and liberation from sins, or the condonation of sins, in the same place, which he has at the end of ch. IV, they teach: For do not say, how shall we be able to be justified, when we are liable to so many and such great sins, he shows and demonstrates him who has atoned for all sins, as also from the faith of Abraham, through whom he was justified, and from the passion of the Savior, through whom we have been freed from sins, he might strengthen this discourse of his. And Grotius acknowledges in his annotations on Consult. Cass. art. IV that justification is taken for the remission of sins, and that Bellarmine, Pineda, Vega, and Salmeron admit that signification, which Nautantus in Eph. I confesses to be more familiar and more bad: indeed Grotius even gives counsel in the same place, that we should abandon the ambiguous word justification, and in its place use the word remission of sins and sanctification. If in its place the word remission of sins must be used, then certainly those Synonyms must be by a sure reason.

But that sanctification is joined to it does not contribute to the explanation of justification, but confuses justification with that which follows justification.

Grotius also observes on Luke 23:34 that the remission of sins is when God does not take away what is necessary for conversion: but that the remission is greater, by which God remits all punishments, and gives the right to eternal life. But in Luke 23:34, it is not only requested that what is necessary for conversion not be taken away, but as the words sound, that the guilt and punishment deserved by grace be remitted; and it is one thing not to take away those things which are necessary for conversion, and another to remit sins; even if the remission of sins has no place if what is necessary for conversion is taken away, nor does conversion happen. Furthermore, the donation of the right to eternal life is consequent to the remission of sins: it is not a greater remission: nor is there a greater or lesser in the remission of sins.

But who does not see in the Grotian explanation of the remission of sins a hidden ὑπάλλον τι (hypallage), both Papist and truly even Socinian? which therefore does not bring a torch to this Epistle, but obscures the light that shines in it.

What kind of thing that is, the annotations on Cassander teach.

Namely, Grotius has invented this process of God in the Gospel for the sake of the Papists and Socinians: that God recalls vicious men beyond his usual love to himself through the extraordinary miracles, precepts, and promises of Christ: that those who accommodate themselves to this vocation are purged by faith held in the word, where faith reaches such a degree that it produces a sincere purpose of obedience, to him who is such, that is, who has formed faith, sins are now fully forgiven: finally, that for retaining the right to eternal life, a constant pious operation is required, and especially abstinence from crimes, which devastate the conscience.

By which method nothing is attributed to the grace of God, nothing to the merit of Christ, nothing to the efficacy of truth, everything is ascribed to free will, to the divine vocation, where the man who assents has only recognized the precepts and promises confirmed by miracles, and that he is purged, and that sins are fully forgiven, and that the right to eternal life is acquired and retained, faith is furthermore feigned to be unformed, which is to be formed through the purpose of obedience, this finally is constituted prior to the remission of sins, and as its cause, and what other Pelagian paradoxes are fostered here, about which it is treated more fully in the cited place.

SECTION IX. On the Argument of the Epistle.

The sum and principal design of the Apostle Grotius did not set forth here, but he delivered it at sufficient length in his Comment. on James ch. II p. 17: namely that the Apostle Paul was then attacking the opinion of the Pharisees: that they could fruitfully obtain righteousness and salvation without faith, through observance of rituals, and abstinence from outward crimes, and that they owed that salvation to themselves from a συναλλάγματι or equitable covenant entered into with God: while Paul on the contrary showed that those rites instituted for a time were not of great worth in themselves; nor was abstinence from crimes worthy of so great a reward, especially since many who boasted of their observance of the law had not even kept that abstinence, after, namely, capital judgments, by fear of which they were restrained, had ceased among them, and the Roman laws or Governors connived at many misdeeds.

And that this reproach is cast in passing (in chapters 2 and 3 of Romans). But indeed, that the method of leading men to salvation, which God had roughly delineated in the affairs of Abraham and his descendants, but had most fully shown to be consummated in the Gospel, is most worthy of God, and most useful to men.

For by this method, there is excited in men modesty, when they hear that they are not led to the hope of eternal life by a contract, but through the mercy of GOD, and the remission of even grave sins, when the Law of Moses is also deaf and inexorable; that submission of mind is excited, when it understands that this way of arriving at salvation was revealed not by human wisdom, but by divine goodness. That hope is excited, because God is not going to deal with us by strict right, but according to kindness. That prayers are excited; to acknowledge such great benefits, to put away pride; and finally, that this firm persuasion concerning obtaining eternal life in this way, excites in us love toward GOD, and a zeal for patience, so that we desire to do and suffer everything, especially since Christ himself, the author of salvation, did not only teach this way, but also demonstrated it by his example.

But this extenuation of Mosaic rites and laws, and the communication of such great things to the Gentiles and aliens, done by GOD for the Jews, when it was difficult for the Jews to believe it, demonstrated that Paul (in chapters 9, 10, 11 to the Romans) [meant] that GOD does not owe anyone an account of his deeds, since both as creator he has masterly right over us, and eternal life and celestial happiness are not owed to man by nature.

Yet, without the fraud of these prescriptions, Paul shows that no plan could have been entered into that was more glorious to GOD, or more useful to men. And this is (he says) the chief purpose of the Pauline Epistle to the Romans, piously observed by all the ancients, although all do not interpret the individual members and words in the same way.

Among which, B. Hülfmann in Harmon. Pauli & Jacobi p. 118, not undeservedly desires first, that in such a laborious declaration of the Epistle's argument, Grotius makes no mention by any indication of the meritorious causes, which alone earned for us the favor of GOD, or the propitiator, whom GOD set forth for himself in his blood to justify man: Nor of the satisfactory causes for the guilt, for the impotence of men to keep the Law, which the same Apostle inculcates not once, and teaches that the Son of GOD was sent into the flesh, and made subject to death, etc. ch.

III. 23, 24, 25. IV. 25. V. 8, 9, 10. seq. VI. 5, 10. VII. 4, 24, 25. VIII. 3, 4, 32, 33, 34, 37, etc. which, I say, makes no mention of this principal cause of human salvation, but alleges only this as the impulsive cause of our mutual love toward Christ and his members, that Christ himself, the author of our salvation, not only taught this way of arriving at salvation, but also demonstrated it by his example, when yet it is confessed even among the Socinians: that the most vehement incentive to love Christ, and to endure calamities for love of him, is the death of Christ endured for men (so much more strongly, of course, for moving [us] to a like example of patience).

The fruit of which death, directly influencing our justification, the Apostle so often commends, and by demonstrating: how Adam's and our own transgressions directly and meritoriously cause our condemnation, so the actions and passions of Christ, that is, the observance of the Law, and the submission to an ignominious death, are directly and meritoriously caused to be our absolution from the guilt of condemnation, our reception into grace, our justification, Romans V. from v. 15 to the end, ch. VIII. 3, 4, 31, 32, 33, 34. Secondly, the chief argument of the Epistle is justification and salvation through faith in the merit of Christ, and satisfaction without our works.

The proper argument of the Epistle is justification and salvation through faith in the merit and satisfaction of Christ, without our works.

Which will be evident from the very analysis and Pauline treatment, and is confessed among the ancient Doctors of the Church, both Greek and Latin.

And Origen in Greek, lib. III. in Epist. ad Rom. v. 25. p. 501, has it thus: When he had said above that he had given himself as a redemption for all mankind, that he might redeem those who were held in the captivity of sins, while he tastes death for all without deceit: now he adds something more sublime, and says: Because God set him forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, by which, of course, through the sacrifice of his body he might make GOD propitious to men, and by this might show his justice, while he remitted to them preceding transgressions, which they had contracted by serving the worst tyrants at that time, when GOD was enduring and suffering these things to be done.

But he suffered for this, that after these things he might show his justice in this time. And afterwards p. 503. According to this, therefore, that he is a sacrifice (Christ), by the shedding of his blood he is made a propitiation in that he gives remission of preceding transgressions.

Which propitiation, however, comes to each of the believers by the way of faith.

Concerning justification, moreover, through faith without works, Origen thus [says] p. 504, when he had brought into the matter the examples of the thief and the sinful woman, Luke XXIII and VII. Concerning this, he says, from no work of the law, but for FAITH ALONE he says to her: Thy sins are remitted to thee: and again: thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace. But in many places of the Gospel we read that the Savior used this speech, that he says the cause of the believer's salvation is his faith. From all of which it is clear that the Apostle rightly judges that a man is justified through faith without the works of the law.

But perhaps someone hearing these things might be relaxed, and might take negligence in doing good, if faith alone suffices for justification. To whom we shall say: that after justification if anyone acts unjustly, without doubt he has spurned the grace of justification. Nor does anyone receive the remission of sins for this reason, that he might think the license to sin is given to him again. For indulgence is given not for future, but for past crimes.

One may have the opinion of Chrysostom from homil. IX. at the beginning of ch. V. But you consider for me, how EVERYWHERE the Apostle inculcates these two things, both what GOD has contributed on his part, and what ought to be brought on our part.

But those things on the part of GOD are various, and many, and more excellent. For he both died for us, and reconciled us, and brought us to faith, and conferred ineffable grace, ἡμεῖς δὲ τὴν πίστιν εἰσηνέγκαμεν μόνον. We bring faith ONLY.

And in ch. IV. almost from the beginning: Since the Jews were boasting of this first up and down, that Abraham, when he was a Patriarch, and then a friend of GOD, had received circumcision first of all: he wishes to show that he himself also was justified by faith: which indeed is an exuberance of great victory, for one to be saved from faith itself without works, would be nothing inconvenient. But that he who excels in merits and right deeds, is made just not from this, but from faith: that indeed was wonderful, and such as would most declare the power and strength of faith.

Which he also declares afterwards concerning that, and also at Gal. III. 6: Abraham, although he had studied good works, yet was justified by faith alone: much more will you be justified by faith alone.

And at Gal. III. 8. They (the Pseudo-Apostles) indeed were teaching: he who relies on faith alone is execrable: He on the contrary demonstrates that he who relies on faith alone is blessed.

And to this also tends the argument of Theodoret in this Epistle: which can be read at length in the work itself.

He repeats it, however, succinctly at the beginning of Tom. II. to ch. III. We have already said that the divine Apostle wishes to show that God and our Savior Jesus Christ was necessarily made man, and for that reason, concerning those who lived under it, the place he spoke, and proved that both those [Gentiles] had transgressed the natural law, and these [Jews] the Mosaic law, and that they were worthy of the ultimate punishment, and he imitated the best physician, who first teaches the gravity of the disease of the one who is suffering, and then applies the aid of medicines.

For thus he himself, when he had refuted the iniquity of both these and those, and had shown them to be both guilty and worthy of punishment, he then offers the medicine of faith, and teaches the kindness of the divine dispensation. And to verse. 24. 25.

BY FAITH ALONE brought forward, we have received the remission of sins: Since the Lord Christ offered his own body as a kind of price of redemption.

But the Lord Christ is GOD, and the propitiation, and the High Priest, and the Lamb, and in his own blood he procured our salvation, demanding from us faith alone.

(Jerome) From the Latins, Jerome in Epist. to the Gal.

He presents the summary of this and that Epistle thus: That in these two Epistles this argument is specially contained, that the ancient burdens of the law have been abrogated, with the grace of the Gospel creeping in, which not the blood of victims, but Faith would fulfill in the believing soul.

(Augustine) Augustine quest. II. to Simplicianus Vol. IV. of works, fol. 626. when he wishes to explain ch.

IX. to the Rom. First, he says, I hold the intention of the Apostle, which prevails through the whole Epistle, which I may consult.

This is, however, that no one may glory in the merits of works, of which the Israelite dared to glory, because they had served the law given to them, and from this had perceived the Evangelical grace as if it were owed to their merits, because they served the law: whence they did not want the same grace to be given to the Gentiles, as if they were unworthy, unless they undertook the Jewish Sacraments.

Which question that arose is turned over in the Acts of the Apostles: for they did not understand, because by the very fact that it is Evangelical grace, it is not owed to works: Otherwise grace is no longer grace.

And in many places he often testifies to this, proposing the grace of faith to works, not that he may extinguish works, but that he may show that works are not preceding grace, but consequent: so that, namely, no one may think himself to have perceived grace because he has worked well, but that he cannot work well unless he has perceived grace through faith.

But man begins to perceive grace from the time he begins to believe in GOD.

(Remigius) Remigius part.

3. vol. V. Biblioth. Patr. in the preface to this Epistle: He says that the Apostle interposes himself as a mediator between those converted from the Jews and the Gentiles, who were disputing about the superiority of one or the other, and shows: That none of them had been saved by merits, thus through the grace of Jesus Christ, because all, both Jews and Gentiles, were held under sin.

(Rupertus) Rupertus II.

Comment. on Hos. ch. IV. observes that this was the cause for the Apostle to treat the Epistle to the Romans, that he might restrain both Jews and Gentiles by enumerating the sins of both, and by showing the Sacrament of the Son of God, that those justified by faith might have peace with GOD through our Lord Jesus Christ: and that Hosea followed the same method, as often as he strikes or enumerates the sins of the nation, so often he ends the course of the Prophetic discourse in the coming of the Sacrament of the faith of the Son of GOD, that one can be justified and saved from sins NO OTHERWISE than through GRACE or FAITH: Nor are almost all the Papist Interpreters so ungrateful to Christ the Redeemer that they do not acknowledge in the argument and chief design of the Epistle that Christ is the meritorious cause of grace and salvation: concerning which, however, Grotius is silent here, who wished, as it seems, to gratify the Socinians.

Grotius wishes this third reason for salvation to be handed down by the Apostle, that through the mercy and grace of GOD and the forgiveness of sins we are led to the hope of eternal life, and that GOD is not going to deal with us by supreme right, but according to equity (κατ' ἐπιείκειαν), but that by this firm persuasion (concerning eternal life to be obtained in this way, namely, that if that persuasion arrives at the purpose of obeying, the benevolence of GOD is obtained, but is preserved by good merits, so that finally we may attain salvation), the love of GOD and the zeal for patience is excited in us, so that we desire to do and suffer nothing that is not, especially when Christ himself, the Author of salvation, [showed] that way.

That this is drawn from the pits of the Socinians, everyone sees.

Namely that faith is nothing other than the persuasion of obtaining eternal life through grace with the purpose of obedience: and that Christ showed this way of salvation by his own example.

If however Christ was an example to us in this, it is necessary that he himself also attained salvation through the gratuitous remission of sins, and through his own obedience obtained the same for himself.

Which impiety is worse than the Socinian.

Concerning sin, in what way does he open it?

Fourthly, that many who boasted of themselves concerning the law were only incidentally sprinkled, and that they had not even performed that innocence of abstaining from crimes, after, namely, the capital judgments, by the fear of which they were restrained, had ceased among the Jews, is detected as false from the very inspection of the treatment.

For ch. II. & III. Paul by design convicts all the Jews, from the Mosaic law, of sin, just as he had convicted the Gentiles from the law of nature, so that thus the foundation might be laid for justification by grace through faith, because the whole world becomes accountable (ὑπόδικος) to GOD, and all have sinned without distinction (διαβολῇ): concerning which Chrysostom: He had accused the Gentiles; He had accused the Jews.

He might express the discourse which faith produces.

For neither was nature nor the law of any help, nor could the written law provide more, but both burdened those who used these laws badly, and convicted them of being worthy of greater punishment, it remains that salvation must necessarily come through grace.

Theodoret above said that Paul in this imitated the best physician, who teaches first the gravity of the disease of the one who is suffering, and then applies the aid of medicines; but he is not to be considered the best physician who only incidentally inquires into the disease, and teaches about the same only perfunctorily.

Concerning the occasion of the sins increasing among the Jews. Fifthly, what Grotius introduces concerning the occasion of the sins increasing among the Jews, are neither true nor relevant.

Not true: because in the time of Pilate the Jews were not yet deprived of all criminal jurisdiction, nor do so few examples of the justice and severity of the Roman Governors occur, concerning the correction of even private crimes, if they were ever committed by the Jews: If those things are true, which Josephus commemorates concerning Valerius Gratus, Cumanus, Saturninus, Felix, and Porcius Festus, book.

XVIII. Antiquit. c. 4. 7. book XX. c. 6.

13. 14. and those which Baronius [wrote] to the year of Christ XXXIIX.

Montagu Analect. exercit.

VIII. sect. 1. 2. have handed down.

Not appropriate to this place, where it is not so much about particular vices, as about the natural corruption of men, and its tendency, as well as the daily fall into such flagrant crimes.

That is certainly certain, that the Apostle teaches and convicts that this corruption has extended as widely as the need for the grace of Christ has extended.

Namely, the Apostle demonstrates that all and each, as well Jews as Gentiles, as well infants as adults, are under sin from v. 10. to 19.

Which also is evident from v.

22. : Which root of evil the Apostle subsequently also pursues in Ch.

VI. & VII., whence Cornelius à Lapide: These verses of ch.

III.

10. seq. signify the corruption of man, and nature not healed through faith and grace.

For this whole [nature] is subject to sin, not to any one, but one to this, another to another sin, because all

mortals corrupted by the native vice of guilt, and so prone to evil, that they are compelled to endure a certain tyranny of sin.

VI. On the restriction of the words of the Apostle

Rom. III. 10. to certain persons Grotius on. to certain persons is accepted by the Socinians and Arminians, and is utterly adverse to the Pauline reasoning, and to the interpretation of the Papists themselves.

They, because the necessity of the grace of Christ is demonstrated here, by the removal of those things which could be objected as causes of salvation outside of Christ: such as were, on the part of the Jews, the observance of the Mosaic law, and on the part of the Gentiles, the observance of natural honesty.

The Apostle proves in chapters II and III that neither was observed nor could be observed by our own powers. Concluding all men, and the whole world, under sin with the most emphatic marks of universalism of every kind, and proving it by testimonies of Scripture that admit no restriction or exception.

To this, that the other Pontificians agree with Cornelius and Justinian, such as Card. Toletus, Benedictus Pererius, Salmero, Guilhelmus Estius and others, that it is not a question here of many, but of all men, not only of enormous crimes, but of the corruption of the whole nature.

Concerning which Estius is to be heard first: Here it is asked, how generally 'all' is to be taken, when he says that all are caused to be under sin. For it seems that it can only be inferred from the preceding that many are under sin; as from the Gentiles the philosophers, from the Jews those learned in the law. Since he has properly enumerated the crimes of these.

I answer: The mind of Paul is undoubtedly that all men without exception are to be concluded under sin; just as he also says in Gal. III. The Scripture concludes all under sin.

The first is evident from the scope of Paul. For he wishes to demonstrate that no one can be justified without the faith of Christ: which cannot be demonstrated unless he confesses that without it all are sinners. The testimonies of Scripture subjoined, which speak quite universally, prove the same thing, especially that: There is none that doeth good, no, not one.

From which he then again makes an inference universal, embracing all and singular men, saying: That every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become subject to GOD.

Nor is there need of more arguments in A MATTER SO MANIFEST. Add that Grotius himself in his commentary on the Decree of Holland and West Friesland for the peace of the Churches in the year 1614, concluded from this passage of the Apostle, all have sinned and come short of the glory of GOD, that no one, not even one, can or could merit the grace of GOD, by which we are justified. How much therefore he has changed from that!

VII. Whether and how Paul opposes the opinion of the Pharisees?

Seventh, that Paul opposes the opinion of the Pharisees, that they can obtain salvation and justice without faith, through the free observance of rituals, and abstinence from external crimes, and that such salvation is owed to them in a contract or equal covenant, can be admitted in a certain sense, yet the business is not solely with the Pharisees, but he is engaged in a didactic manner, and informs the Romans about true justification, and finally in chapters IX. X. XI. notes the false justice of the Pharisees: nor does he dispute in this Epistle about ceremonial laws: or by the works of the law, which he excludes from justification, does he note only ceremonial things, with the abstinence from evil actions, but all things which have the law as a norm, and he does not teach that works please GOD for the giving of salvation, nor finally under the Gospel, which is the power unto salvation to every one that believeth, does he include the doctrine of works, which arise from a heart purified by faith and from an abundance of temporal things, kindled by the care and love of GOD and neighbor, but the Gospel is solely to him a preaching of grace concerning the remission of sins, through faith in Christ, but he excludes from justification all works even those which have proceeded from faith, which alone are truly good, such as Abraham shone with above others, to whom nevertheless faith alone was imputed for justice, but all these things will be clearer in the Apostolic treatment, which Grotius has utterly perverted. Let these suffice for the present concerning the Grotian preface, and those who contribute to it.

SECTION X. THE ECONOMY OF THE EPISTLE

But I would like to add the οἰκονομίαν (economy) of the Epistle.

Which generally, in the manner of other Epistles that have an inscription, can be divided into the ἐπιγραφῇ (inscription), the ἐργασίᾳ (treatment), and the Epilogue or conclusion. The inscription contains the author, by whom it was written, v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. the object or those to whom the Epistle was written, and the prayer. The ἐργασία (treatment) then with the εἴσοδῳ (entrance) or exordium, partly eucharistic, v. 8. partly testifying of love, v. 9. etc. then with the proposition v. 16. 17. that justification, and life, or eternal salvation is announced and obtained for us solely through faith in the Gospel: then with the διεξόδῳ (digression) and the explanation of the proposition, especially as it pertains to the SUBJECT (which is like a narration), it is evident, up to chapter III. v. 20.

And thus far it is of the SUBJECT, with the implication of the END, namely of the sinful man, by which he is to be SAVED, the πεγνώσει (knowledge) which in the Practics deservedly precedes: which is followed further by the MEANS, by which man arrives at salvation, or the CAUSES OF JUSTIFICATION AND SALVATION, and what things are annexed or conjoined to them, the ἔκθεσις (exposition) from chapter

III. to chapter III. Concerning the means and causes of salvation, he is occupied partly in general, and that then by way of κατ' ἐξήγησιν ἀποδεικτικὴν (demonstrative explanation) by clarifying and confirming the true manner of justification up to the end of chapter IV, then by way of κατ' ἔνδειξιν (indication) vindicating that doctrine against the objections of those who calumniate the Apostolic justification in chapters VI and VII, and the Apostle treats of the scruples of temptations, and of the certainty of the hope of glory, partly specifically, as to the reprobation of the Jews, as also the calling of the Gentiles.

Which things having been thus set forth, exhortations to the study of holiness are subjoined, since sanctification is joined to justification by an indivisible bond.

The principal treatment therefore is twofold: partly Didactic, by which the proposition is confirmed, up to the end of chapter XI, concerning the righteousness of faith: partly paedeutic, by which moral corollaries concerning the duties of the justified are added up to chapter XVI exclusively. The didactic part first treats of justification and salvation in common up to Chapter IIX. inclusive. Then it treats particularly of the reprobation of the Jews from salvation, and the calling of the Gentiles, for the fuller illustration of the proposed theme, which is concerning the righteousness of faith, in three chapters IX. X. XI. so that it may be clear that no other manner and way of salvation is now open to the Gentiles, than that which was formerly proposed to the Jews, and which is still open to those who do not exclude themselves by obstinate unbelief in the promised Messiah. But since the Apostle here wished to present to the whole Church at once a compendium of all theology, having tasted beforehand its end, Salvation and eternal life, he places the Subject, which is to be justified and saved, namely sinful man subject to death, as in the place of πεγνώσεως (knowledge) in chapter I. from v. 18. to chapter III. v. 20. so that at the same time it may be evident from this, that all men concluded under sin, excluded from eternal salvation, nay, liable to eternal condemnation, and that no one can aspire to salvation and life by their own righteousness. Therefore, the subject is man the sinner, as one to be saved. From then on, therefore, the Apostle executes the causes and means of justification and salvation: first indeed ἐξηγητικῶς or by explaining the same in ch. III. Then indeed ἀποδεικτικῶς by demonstrating both a priori and a posteriori in ch. IV. The former from the example of Abraham and the testimony of David: the latter from the peace and tranquility of conscience, which complete the second and third arguments: as also ἀντιθετιτῶς, by instituting the opposition of Adam, through whom injustice and death, and of Christ, through whom justice and life were introduced, in ch. V. Which is the fourth argument of the Apostle. Finally, the consequence of justification, the pursuit of holiness, in ch. VI. and VII. as well as the certainty of salvation from v. 18 of ch. VIII. he examines: and this in such a way that he always keeps the primary scope and proper theme, justification by faith, before his eyes. And this in the general treatment.

In the special part, however, concerning the reprobation of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, first he vindicates both the justice and the mercy of God: that the Jews were not rejected or excluded from grace by an absolute good pleasure, ch. IX. then indeed he asserts the justice of Christ rejected by the Jews, ch. X. Finally, concerning the faith required by God, and the unbelief through which the Jews fell away (the Gentiles also could fall away), yet not with all hope of salvation taken away from them, which he confirms remains if they believe: with a universal conclusion of the treatment added at the end of ch. XI. But we will pursue these more accurately in the progress, §. 9.

The Paedeutic part is occupied partly with necessary things, partly with matters of indifference. In the former, he delivers rules both general in ch. XII. and special, as the order of the Magistrate in ch. XIII. towards the end of which he summarizes everything with the precept of Charity, with a reason added taken from the state of the converted. Concerning matters of indifference, however, he is occupied in ch. XIV. but in such a way that he does not neglect faith even here, which it behooves even the τὰ ἀδιάφορα, or indifferent things, to moderate: as it holds command, he urges mutual tolerance in ch. XV. In the conclusion begun in ch. XV. v. 14, he explains the primary cause of the letter: then he gives hope of his arrival, and commends himself to their prayers towards the end of ch. XV. which he seals with a vow; subjoining in ch. XVI. the commendation of Phoebe v. 1. & 2. Salutations to be delivered at Rome from v. 3-14, and with a general salutation from the Church of Christ added, v. 16, with an exhortation v. 17 seqq. and with a vow v. 20. he performs a special salutation in the name of others v. 21. and with repeated vows and a δοξολογίᾳ he finishes the Epistle.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM H. GROTII AD ANNOTATIONES IN EPISTOLAM AD ROMANOS.

SECTIO I. De ordine Epistolarum.

Epistolæ Paulinæ non temporis ordine locatæ sunt ab iis, qui eas primi in unum volumen compegerunt: sed pro dignitate eorum, ad quos scriptæ sunt.

Ideo præcedunt quæ ad Ecclesias, prima est, quæ ad Romanam, ob urbis ejus majestatem.

A N I M A D V E R S I O N E S A N T I - G R O T I A N Æ.

Ordo Epistolarum Apostoli alius est Collationis, quo digestæ sunt in Codice Bibliço; alius vero Scriptionis, quo fuerunt a Paulo exaratæ. Ille satis notus est; præmittuntur enim istæ, quæ autoris nomen in inscriptione præferunt Epistolæ ad Hebræos, inscriptione destitutæ: & ex istis, quæ ad integras Ecclesias expeditæ sunt his, quæ ad personas singulares: & in utroque ordine majores fere minoribus. Neque enim, quemadmodum multi putant, alias omnes antecedit (temporis ordine, hæc ad Romanos Epistola) sed eas tantum, quæ ex Roma sunt scriptæ, reliquis vero posterior est, licet non omnibus, monente Chrysostomo. Cæterum Ordo Scriptionis hic videtur: Septem earum ante captivitatem: reliquæ septem in captivitate scriptæ sunt.

Ante Captivitatem prima fuit prior ad Thessalonicenses Athenis data, ex qua urbe primum Corinthum adiit, Act. XIIX. 1. Thessalonica enim Berœam, & hinc Athenas profectus est, Act. XVII. Quo etiam Corintho rediit, & hanc Epistolam illic expedivit. Secunda est altera ad Thessalonicenses, quam Athenis itidem scripsit, ut subscriptio utriusque docet.

Ita Theodoretus, & Athanasius in synopsi, ut & Oecumenius in scholiis, priorem Athenis scriptam volunt, è 1. Thessal. III, 1. 2. id colligentes. At Pererius in Prolegomenis ad Romanos disp. II. num. 51. ex ejusdem cap. v. 6. præeunte Theodoro Beza, concludit, Corintho eam epistolam esse missam, ubi Thessalonica rediens Timotheus Paulum invenit, Act. XIIX. Quod etiam est Baronii T. 1. ad ann. LII. argumentum. Quo de Justinianus ita habet: Quamvis vulgo putetur Athenis scripta, idque Athanasius & Theodoretus affirment; vero tamen similius est, datam fuisse Corinthi: Nam Athenis brevi admodum tempore hæsit Apostolus: Quamvis igitur jusserit Silam & Timotheum ad se venire, non tamen constat, utrum illum Athenis deprehenderint. Lucas enim indicat, eos ad Paulum venisse, cum jam esset Corinthi. Cum igitur utrumque hac epistola nominet, credibile omnino videtur, eam Corinthi fuisse scriptam. Non me fugit, viris doctis hanc sententiam non probari, quia hæreticis quibusdam placet; sed pietatem laudo, quod hæreticos oppugnent; rationes, quibus hanc sententiam refellunt, non item.

Sententiam vero propterea sequor, non qua hæretici eam sequuti sunt, sed quia est Lucæ historia maxime consentanea. Posteriorem etiam, quam non multo post scriptam Theodoretus in præfat. ad Romanos, & Chrysostomus in II. ad Thessalonicenses. ajunt, ibidem (Corinthi) scriptam, quia illic per sesquiannum substitit Paulus, statuit Pererius. Sed quum veteres constanter consentiant, argumentum vero Bezæ solidū minime fit, quod pro Corintho adfert, non est, quod novellam illam sententiam cum Justiniano, & Pererio sequamur. Quæ de re dicturi sumus in Proœmio ad priorem ad Thessalonicenses.

Tertia est prior ad Timotheum, cum eum Ephesi reliquisset, 1. Tim. I. 3. priusquam altera vice Ephesum venisset. Act. XIX. quia promittit, 1. Tim. III. 14. illuc se venturum. Quarta est prior ad Corinthios Ephesi scripta, cum per biennium ibi subfifteret, A&t. XIX. 9. Quinta posterior ad Corinthum Philippis scripta, cum E- pheso relicta in Macedoniam profectus Philippos, qui sunt in prima Macedoniæ ora, attigit: A&. XX. 1. 2. Cor. IX, 4. Unde Corinthum se venturum pro- misit: quod factum post peragratam Macedoniam. De ordine támen harum trium, quam tertiam, quartam, & quintam diximus, discrepant autores. Pererius tertiam in ordine facit priorem ad Corin- thios, quartam posteriorem, quintam priorem ad Timotheum. Sexta ad Titum est, Nicopoli juxta quosdam scripta, quæ non procul Philippis distat. Quod colligunt è Tit. III. 12. Sed quum Paulus di- cat statuisse se illic hyemare, Pererius l. c. conclu- dit, Paulum cum eam scripsit Epistolam, nondum fuisse Nicopoli, habuisse tamen in animo, illuc ire. Dubia certe videtur subscriptio, quæ Nicopoli scriptam ait. Dubius etiã hic videtur ordo. Quum Epistola hæc ad Titum forte non incommode à B. Chemnitio in Exam. C. T. P. I. p. 25. præcedenti ordine Scriptionis prior habeatur. Septima est Epi- stola ad Romanos Corintho scripta. Reliquæ Romæ scriptæ sunt, ut subscriptiones testantur: adeoque Romani posteriores sunt. Octava videl. Epistola ad Ebræos, è libera missa custodia, Ebr. XIII. 23. Nona ad Galatas, quum ferret jam stigmata Do- mini in corpore suo, Gal. VI, 17. quam tamen prio- rem Epistolæ ad Romanos sibi videri ait Chrysosto- mus. Decima ad Ephesios, quia mentionem fecit vinculorum Eph. VI, 20. Vndecima ad Philippen- ses: unde idem ordo harum trium etiam in Codice observatur. Duodecima est, quam ad Philemonem jam senex scripsit. Quâ posteriorem, adeoque De- cimam tertiam Chrysostomus facit Epistolam ad Colossenses, quia in fine ejus dicitur, Tychicus omnia vobis nota faciet, quem misi cum Onesimo fi- do ac dilecto fratre. Erat enim is Onesimus, cujus nomine eam, quæ ad Philemonem est, composuit. De- cima quarta, & postrema est altera ad Timotheum c. IV. 6. Quem ordinem fere scriptionis consti- tuunt Theodoretius in præfatione, Flacius in Glossa, Chemnitius l. c. Gerhardus in Epistolam ad Rom. Cluverus in orthotomia Apost. Pareus in Com- ment. ad Rom. & alii. A quibus tamen discedit Usserius in annalibus hunc observans ordinẽ: Pri- ma ipsi est prior ad Thessalonicenses; secunda po- sterior ad eosdem; tertia ad Galatas; quarta est se- cundum ejus sententiã prior ad Corinthios; quinta posterior ad eosdem; sexta ad Romanos. Hanc excipit septima ad Philippenses; octava ad Phile- monem; nona ad Colossenses; decima ad Ephe- sios; undecima ad Ebræos. Sequitur has duode- cima, prior ad Timotheum; decima tertia ad Ti- tum. Concludit tandem, eodem numerante Usse- rio, decima quarta posterior ad Timotheum.

De usu observati hujus ordinis monuit Chryso- stomus, quod non modicũ faciat ad tractandas quæ- stiones cognitum Epistolarum tempus; Ex. gr. quod Romanis & Colossensibus de iisdem quidem rebus, sed non eodem modo scribat, sed illis cum magna at- temperatione, cum dicit (c. XIV.) infirmum fide suscipite, non ad dijudicationes disceptationum. Alius quidem credit vescendum esse quibuslibet. Alius autem, qui infirmus est, oleribus vescitur. Ad Colossenses vero licet de iisdem, non tamen hoc modo, sed majore fiduciâ. Si enim cum Christo, inquit, (ad Col. II.) mortui estis, ut quid velut in mundo vivẽ- tes decretis tenemini? ne tetigeris, ne gustaveris, neque contrectaveris &c. nullam aliam hujus dif- ferentiæ inveniri causam censet Chrysostomus, quàm ipsum Epistolarũ tempus. Nam principio quidẽ con- descendere oportuit, successu vero temporis non item.

Porrò inter eas, quæ ad Ecclesias scriptæ sunt Epistolæ, Prima est, quæ ad Romanam destinata

Ecclesiam, non ob urbis istius majestatem, uti cum Theodoreto censet Grotius, quia humilitas Christi non curat typhum seculi: non ob praeeminentiam Ro- manae Ecclesiae, uti visum fuit Ambrosio Catharino: nam illius ante Nicenum Concilium, Æneâ Sylvio teste, exiguus fuit respectus: sed ob Epistolae hujus prolixitatem, & imprimis ob ejusdem praestantiam, ac dignitatem, quâ reliquas omnes antecellit, ut Augustinus Ep. CV. ad Sixtum: prima haec est, eò quod gratiam fidei commendat, quae caput & initium est Scripturarum: quam causam etiã reddit Theodo- retus:quòd nempe ob exactam omnis generis dostri- nam prima sit; & ex illis Cornelius, ac Tirinus. Et eleganter observat Flacius, quum pleraeq; Episto- lae Paulinae, valde ad singularum Ecclesiarum, aut Personarum rationes, circumstantiasque accom- modatae sint; hanc Nostram generalem doctrinam, omnibus Ecclesiis necessariam, proponere, ac com- munem esse concionem, vel librum methodice praeci- pua doctrinae Christianae capita continentem: ideò potissimum etiam ad hancEcclesiam missum, quia inde tanquam è sede totius Imperii emittebantur ci- ves in omnes gentes, & vicissim ab omnium provin- ciarum hominibus caput orbis frequentabatur.

SECTIO II. De Ecclesiae Romanae primordiis.

ERat autem Romae initium quoddam Ecclesiae, factum primò, quomodo Antiochiz, à Christianis aliarum pro- vinciarum, quos illuc negotia perduxerant: Auctum deinde praedicatione & miraculis Petri, quem Simonis magi prae- stigiæ vi divinâ reprimendæ Romam traxerant circa initia Claudiani principatûs, ut veteres tradidêre.

Verisimile non est ex occasione tantum nego- tiationis cepisse Romæ Ecclesiam: quam Clemens in libro Recognit. non reprobatus à Grotio, Bar- nabam primùm plantasse docet, in qua Andronicus & Junias, ut præcipui, vel potius bene cogniti, ut Sy- rus interpretatur vocẽ ἐπίσημοι, inter Apostolos celebrantur, suoque elogio ornantur Priscilla, & Aquila, & alii,Rom.XVI.37. Neque Petrum prius, quam circa finem vitæ Romam venisse Eusebius tra- dit lib. III. c. 1. Non ergò inde ab auspiciis Clau- diani,uti Pontificii volunt,Romæ augendæ Eccle- siæ operam dedit: quem verò Romæ unquam fuis- se dubium reddunt Centur. Magdeburg, l. I.II. c.X. p.561. Sanè quum Paulus Romã venirét An.Chri- sti 59. nulla ibi publica erat Ecclesia,nedũ ordina- rium ministerium Ecclesiasticum, aut Episcopus, & Pontifex, vel ullum sedis ejusdem vestigium; congregati enim Judæi sunt ad Paulum, ut aliquid cognoscerent de sectâ Christianorum, Act.XXIIX.22. neque Paulus, qui illic per biennium substitit, & plures inde Epistolas scripsit, unquam Petri, ceu præsentis mentionẽ in illis fecit: imo testatur ipse Card. Baronius, Petrum An. 51. & 58. versus Occi- dentem se direxisse, usque dum in Angliam veni- ret. Damasus verò Papa Petrum demum An. Chr. LX. Neronis IV. Romam venisse ait: deniq; Guil- helmus Præceptor Wiclefi docet, Petrum ne vidisse quidẽ Romã. Conf.Wolff. l.1. Memorab. lect. p. 23.

SECTIO III. De Linguâ, quâ scripta Epistola.

QUæri solet, cur Romanis scribens Paulus, Græce potius scripserit quàm Latinè. Credo ideo factum, quod & ipse & scriba ejus, Tertius nomine, quanquam fortè Latini ser- monis non planè ignari, Græcè tamen rectius ille dictaret, hic scriberet, quàm Latinè: & quod Græca lingua Romanis omnibus, etiam fœminis, ut ex Juvenali discimus, in usu es- set quotidiano: peregrinis vero Romæ morantibus notior quam Romana. Accedebat, quod hæc Epistola quanquam Romanis propriè missa, ita omnia continebat religionis Christianæ munimenta, ut dignissima esset, cujus Exempla etiam ad alias Ecclesias mitterentur. Græca autem, ut Ci- cero ait pro Archiâ, leguntur in omnibus fermè gentibus, Latina suis finibus exiguis sanè continentur. Non Graece, sed Latine scriptam Salmero, nec improbabiliter, judice Cornelio, censet, quod & glossator statuit dis. IX. C. ut Veterum, & Lyranus in 1. Cor. I. Sed recte reprobant hoc Bellarm. Cornelius, aliique communiter. Siquidem omnes Epistolae Paulinae Graece scriptae sunt, ac Chrysostomus, aliique Graeci scriptores Graecum orthographum sequantur. Adde, quod Graecismis abundet haec Epistola, quodque in eo, quod Originalis textus Graecus fit, omnes interpretes facile consentiant. Vide, quae de lingua originali in N. T. in Critico sacro dicta sunt. Recte autem Grotius causam hanc reddit, quod Graeca lingua Romanis omnibus, etiam feminis in usu fuerat quotidiano, peregrinis vero Romae morantibus notior quam Romana; quodque Graeca tum in omnibus fere gentibus lecta sint. Non probanda tamen illa Grotiana ratio, ideo potius Graece, quam Latine scriptam, quod & ipse Apostolus & scriba ejus Tertius nomine, quamquam forte Latini sermonis non plane ignari, Grace tamen reætius ille dictaret, sic scriberet quam Latine. Nam Apostolum, ex dono infuso, linguarum fuisse callentissimum, & per θεοπνευστίαν scripsisse, aut diactasse ecquis inficiabitur?

SECTIO IV.

De loco & tempore scriptae Epistolae.

Corintho scriptam hanc Epistolam probat Origenes, ex illis annotationibus, quae in quibusdam codicibus post finem Epistolarum scriptae leguntur, (eae enim nec antiquae sunt, nec in omnibus libris reperiuntur, neque in quibus reperiuntur, eadem sunt) sed argumentis ex ipsa Epistola depromtis: quia scilicet mittitur Epistola per Phoeben, diaconissam Ecclesiae, quae erat Corinthi, portu Corinthiorum: quia inter eos, qui tum Paulo aderant, & quorum nomine Romanos salutat, erat Cajus, quem Corinthium fuisse dicimus 1. Cor. I. 14. & Erastus, quem & ipsum fuisse Corinthium dicimus 2. Tim. IV. 20. Scripta autem est non primo adventu Pauli Corinthum, sed altero, cujus mentio Actorum XIX. 21. Evincitur id collato isto loco cum eo, qui est infra XV. 24. Ultrobique enim ejusdem itineris, quod Hierosolyma Paulus instituerat, fit mentio: & quia in hac Epistola additur, id iter inter alia eo pertinere, ut Paulus subsidia pauperibus Hierosolymitanis adferret, inde collegit Chrysostomus, duas, quae sunt ad Corinthios, prius fuisse scriptas: quia 1. Cor. XVI. 1. & 2. Cor. IX. 1. 2. illa subsidia praeparantur. Locum unde scripta sit, quod attinet, autor interlinearis ad Rom. ult. ut & Haymon.

Athenis eam scriptam statuere: sed praeferenda Origenis sententia, quod Corinthi scripta sit, non tantum ob istas rationes, quod per Phoeben mittatur, ministram Ecclesiae in Cenchreis, portu Corinthiorum, Rom. XVI. 1. 27. quod salutet Apostolus nomine Caji hospitis, de quo perhibet ipse 1. Cor. I. 14. quod eundem e Corinthiis fere unicum baptizarit: & in nomine Erasti arcarii civitatis, Rom. XVI. 23. quem Corinthiis fuisse e 2. Tim. IV. 20. colligunt: Sed etiam ob subscriptionem: Non enim recedendum temere a subscriptionibus est, imprimis cum argumentis ex ipsa Epistola depromtis firmantur.

Scripta est, postquam Aquila & Priscilla Paulo in Evangelio paratae fuissent, Rom. XVI. 3. 4. & Apostolus ab Hierusalem per circuitum usque ad Illyricum omnia Evangelio Christi repleverat. c. XV. 19.
