Atque hactenus est SUBJECTI, cum implicatione FINIS, hominis nimirum peccatoris, qua SALVANDUS est, πεγνώσει quae in Praeticis merito antecedit: quam vero excipit porro MEDIORUM, quibus homo ad salutem pervenit, vel CAUSARUM JUSTIFICATIONIS ET SALUTIS, & quae iis annexa, vel conjuncta sunt, ἔκθεσις ex cap. III. c.

III. Circa media, & causas salutis occupatur partim in genere, idque tum κατ' ἐξήγησιν ἀποδεικτικὴν dilucidando & veram justificationis rationem confirmando usque ad finem capitis IV. tum κατ' ἔνδειξιν doctrinam illam vindicando adversus objectiones justificationem Apostolicam calumniantium cap. VI. & VII. & scrupulos tentationum, & de spei gloria certitudine agit Apostolus partim speciatim, quantum ad Judaeorum reprobationem, ut & gentilium vocationem.

Quibus ita expositis, adhortationes ad studium sanctitatis, cum justificationi indivulso nexu cohaereat sanctificatio, fubjunguntur.

Tractatio itaque principalis est bimembris: partim Didactica, quae confirmatur propositio, usque ad finem cap. XI. de justitia fidei: partim paedeutica, qua porismata moralia de officiis justificatorum adjiciuntur usque ad c. XVI. exclusive. Pars didactica primum de justificatione & salute tractat communiter usque ad Cap. IIX. inclusive. Deinde peculiariter de Judaeorum a salute reprobatione, & gentium vocatione agit, ad illustrationem uberiorem propositi thematis, quod est de justitia fidei capp. tribus IX. X. XI. ut nempe constet, non aliam salutis rationem ac viam jam patere gentibus, quam quae proposita olim Judaeis fuerit, atque etiamnum illis pateat, qui contumaci incredulitate in Mesiam promissum seipsos non excludunt. Quum vero hic Apostolus universae Ecclesiae simul totius Theologiae compendium exhibere voluerit, praelibato fine ejusdem, Salute & vita aeterna, Subjectum, quod justificandum est, & salvandum, hominem nempe peccatorem morti obnoxium, velut πεγνώσεως loco sistit c. I. à v. 18. ad c. III. v. 20. ut simul hinc pateat, omnes homines sub peccato conclusos, à Salute æternâ exclusos, imò condemnationi æternæ obnoxios esse, nec quenquam propriâ justitiâ ad Salutem ac vitam adspirare pos- se. Itaque Subjectum est homo peccator, quà sal- vandus. Dehinc ergò causas & media justifi- cationis & salutis exequitur Apostolus : Primò quidem ἐξηγητικῶς vel explicando eadem c. III. Deinde verò ἀποδεικτικῶς demonstrando cum à priori, tùm à posteriori c. IV. Illud ab exemplo A- brahæ, & testimonio Davidico: hoc à pace & tran- quillitate conscientiæ, quæ secundum & tertium ar- gumentum absolvunt: ut & ἀντιθετιτῶς, oppositio- nem Adami, per quem injustitia & mors, & Christi, per quem justitia & vita invecta est c. V. instituen- do. Quod est quartum argumentum Apostoli. Denique Consequentia justificationis, sanctitatis studium c. VI. & VII. nec non certitudinem Salu- tis à vers. 18. c. IIX. expendit : Idque ita, ut sem- per præcipuum scopum & thema proprium, justi- ficationem per fidem ante oculos habeat. Atque hæc in communi tractatione.

In speciali verò Judæorum reprobationem, & gentium vocationem concernente, Primùm divi- nam tùm justitiam, tùm misericordiam vindicat : quod non absoluto beneplacito rejecti, aut exclusi sint à gratiâ Judæi c. IX. tùm verò justitiam Christi adserit à Judæis reprobatam, c. X. Denique de fide à Deo requisitâ, & incredulitate, per quam excide- runt Judæi (excidere etiam possint Gentiles,) illis tamen non adempta omni spe salutis, quam super- esse, si crediderint, confirmat: Addita universali tractationis conclusione c. XI. extremo. Sed hæc ac- curatius in progressu persequemur, §. 9.

Pars Pædeutica occupatur partim in necessa- riis, partim in adiaphoris. Illic regulas tùm generales tradit c. XII. tùm speciales, quà ordinem Magistra- tus c. XIII. sub finem ejusdem summatim omnià complectens Charitatis præcepto, addita ratione à statu conversorum depromta. Circa adiaphora ve- rò occupatur c. XIV. sed ita ut fidem etiam hîc non negligat, quam ipsam quoque τὰ ἀδιάφορα, vel indifferentia moderari oportet: quà imperium obtinente, mutuam tolerantiam suadet c. XV. In Conclusione c. XV. v. 14. cœptâ, causam primariam literarum exponit: tùm adventûs sui spem facit, ac precibus ipsorum se commendat sub finem c. XV. quod voto obsignat; subjungens c. XVI. commen- dationem Phœbe v. 1. & 2. Salutationes Romæ ex- pediendas à v. 3. 14. additâque ab Ecclesiâ Christi salutatione generali, v. 16. cum adhortatione v. 17. seqq. & voto v. 20. aliorum nomine salutationem specialem peragit v. 21. & iterato vota, ac δοξολο- γίᾳ Epistolam finit.

## 1:1 Argument
ANNOTATIONS ON CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT.

The Apostle, after an inscription suitable to the scope and the beginning of the Epistle, proposes to deal with the righteousness of faith revealed in the Gospel, and leaves its necessity to be gathered from the fact that all men, by the force of divine justice, because of sin, by the very law of nature, are liable to death.

PARTITION.

The parts of the Chapter therefore are four: I. The inscription of the Epistle, from verse 1 to 8. II. The beginning from v. 8 to 16. III. The proposition, concerning the righteousness of faith v. 16, 17. IV. The narration, or explanation of the SUBJECT, also having the force of convincing of the necessity of the righteousness of faith v. 18 seqq.

PART I. INSCRIPTION OF THE EPISTLE. v. 1. Paul.

Concerning this name, see what is said in Acts XIII. 9.

The Apostle does not seem to have assumed that name only then, from the time he began to associate with the Romans: which Grotius, with Erasmus and some others, determined: or when he brought back the trophies of his victory from Sergius Paulus, the Proconsul of Cyprus, the first spoil of the Church, and raised a standard, so that he was called Paul from Saul, just as Roman generals and emperors brought back distinguished names for themselves and their families from the nations subjected by them, so that they were called Africanus, Creticus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus, Sarmaticus, which suspicion Jerome in his Epistle to Philemon, Claudius Espencaeus thinks is perhaps true, and the Socinian Crellius does not deny. But it seems rather that from the beginning, as Origen observed, the Apostle was double-named, called Saul among the men of his own nation, but Paul among the others, to whom this name was more familiar. For it is not easily read that the saints changed their names without the command of God: For it is not easily read that the saints changed their names without the command of God: Nor is any custom of naming from conquered enemies found in the Scriptures, as Espencaeus himself admits. And our man is called by both names even before the conversion of Sergius, Acts 13. There is no doubt, however, that the Hebrew name Saul was given to him at his circumcision; and it could have happened that he more willingly used the name Paul, when he was so called by others, both because it was better known and more common, and so that the Greeks and Romans, to whom it was pleasing and familiar, might more willingly recognize the word, of whom he professed himself a teacher, and because circumcision was now to be completely abrogated, primarily by the teaching of this Apostle, and Baptism was to be fully substituted in its place, with the Jewish Synagogue buried with honor.

A servant of Jesus Christ.

In the Old Testament those who were in great offices were called servants of the Lord, that is, of God, as Moses, Josh. 1:1, 14:7, 22:4, 1 Chron. 6:59; Joshua, Judg. 2:8; David, Ps. 132:10; Nehemiah, Neh. 1:6. In the New Testament also of Jesus Christ, who is also called their Lord.

Because in the O.T. men of God and Prophets were called servants, and in the N.T. the Apostles call themselves servants of Jesus Christ, it is manifest that Jesus Christ is the true God, for they did not serve creatures in their calling, but the one God, nor did they have their calling from mere men, but from God alone, called by God, not called by men, Gal. 1:1.

Called.

Called to perform the office no less magnificently than Moses, Exod. 3. Moses through an Angel of God, Acts 7:30. Paul through the Son of God himself.

An Apostle.

Concerning this word, see what is said at Matt. 10:2.

Grotius rightly says he was called no less magnificently than Moses, Exod. 3; but what he adds, that Moses was called through an Angel of God, Acts 7:30, and Paul through the Son of God, not only detracts from the magnificence of the Mosaic calling, which it is established was immediately from God, who appeared to him in the burning bush, Exod. 3, but also from that of Jesus himself, whom he makes equal to a created angel. But just as Paul was called through the Son of God in the flesh, so Moses was called through the same, while still not in the flesh, as we observed at Exod. 3.

Cæterùm Apostolum ab Episcopo ita distinguit Espensæus in 1. Tim. c. I. quod ille immediatè à Christo vocatus, certò habet S. S. ubique & in omnibus Ecclesiis docet, juxta illud Pauli 2. Cor. XII. Solicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum: unde Chrysostomus hom. XIX. in Matth. Apostolos vocat omnium Ecclesiarum Doctores. Episcopus verò per Furthermore, Espencæus in 1. Tim. c. I. distinguishes the Apostle from the Bishop in this way: that the former, called immediately by Christ, possesses the Holy Scriptures with certainty and teaches everywhere and in all Churches, according to that saying of Paul in 2. Cor. XII, "The care of all the churches": whence Chrysostom, hom. XIX. in Matth., calls the Apostles the teachers of all the churches. The Bishop, however, being called by men, presides over a certain place, does not have the Holy Spirit continuously, nor necessarily; he ought to receive the doctrine dictated by the Apostles, not also to introduce a new kind of doctrine. I would like the Roman Bishops to observe this. But the fact that the same Espencaeus notes from Theodoret on 1 Tim. 3, that those who are now called Bishops were once named Apostles, lacks the testimony of Scripture: Epaphroditus was indeed called an Apostle in Phil. 2:25, and others were called so in 2 Cor. 8:23, but they were Apostles of the Churches, not indeed of Jesus Christ: and in a far different sense, namely that they were sent by the Church, and were its legates, such as those who collected sacred funds. Compare Grotius on those passages. ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον Θεοῦ. מֻבְדָּל that is, set apart. Just as God is said to have set apart or separated the people of Israel from the peoples, Lev. 20:24, 26. The Church is also said to have set apart Paul, Acts 13:2, but by divine command. In Syriac here it is דאִתְפְּרֵשׁ as if Paul were saying that he could now more justly be called a Pharisee, separated from the others not by ritual institutions, but by extraordinary work. There is also ἀφορίσας in Gal. 1:15, but in a slightly different sense, as we shall say there. Concerning the word Gospel, see what has been said on the inscription of the Gospel according to Matthew.

It does not look so much to the sect of the Pharisees, who loved to be called separated, as to the divine segregation made from eternity, Gal. 1:15, Acts 9:15, regarding the ordination, and in the mission of the Apostle, regarding the execution carried out in time, Acts 13:2. ὁ προεπηγγείλατο διὰ τῶν προφητῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις. Which Gospel He had promised, namely God, whose name preceded, through the Prophets, not only by speech, but also by writings, which are accustomed to be better preserved. Do not be shaken by novelty, since that novelty was long ago predicted. See Luke 24:44, John 12:16, Acts 10:43, Heb. 8:8.

He is said to be separated unto the Gospel, which he distinguishes from the promise, although he gives assurance of it by this in v. 2. This was of the Prophets, namely the promise of the Messiah; that brings the announcement of the Messiah exhibited, or of the completion of the Prophecies, which was proper to the Evangelists and Apostles. But it is not a new Gospel, nor does it bring anything new, as far as the substance of the doctrine is concerned: for it hands down the same doctrine as the Prophets: it only testifies that what they had predicted was to be performed, has been completed or performed in Christ Jesus.

Latin:

ANNOTATA AD CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM.

APostolus post scopo convenientem inscriptio- nem, & exordium Epistolæ, proponit de justitia fidei in Evangelio revelatâ agere, ejusque necessita- tem inde colligendam relinquit, quòd omnes homi- nes, vi justitiæ divinæ, ob peccatum, ipsâ naturæ le- ge, morti obnoxii sint.

PARTITIO.

Partes ergò Capitis quatuor sunt: I. Epistolæ inscriptio, à versu 1. usque ad 8. II. Exordium à v. 8. ad 16. III. Propositio, de justitia fidei v. 16. 17. IV. Narratio, vel SUBJECTI explicatio, vim etiam habens convincendi justitiæ fidei necessitatem v. 18. seqq.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ INSCRIPTIO. vers. 1. Παῦλος.

De hoc nomine vide, quæ dicta Act. XIII. 9.

Nomen illud non videtur tùm demum, ex quo cum Romanis conversari cœpit, assumpsisse Apostolus: Quod cum Erasmo Grotius, aliique nonnulli statuêre: aut cùm à Sergio Paulo Cypri Pro-Consule, primo Ecclesiæ spolio, victoriæ suæ trophæa retulit, vexillumque erexit, ut Paulus è Saulo diceretur, uti Romani Duces, & Imperatores ex subjectis per eos gentibus insignia sibi, & familiis suis nomina reportarunt, ut Africani, Cretici, Adiabenici, Parthici, Sarmatici nuncuparentur, quam Hieronymi in Epist. ad Philem. suspicionem fortè veram esse Claudius Espensæus existimat, neque abnuit Socinista Crellius. Videtur autem potius ab initio, quemadmodum Origenes observavit, διώνυμος fuisse Apostolus, apud homines suæ gentis Saulus, apud cæteros verò Paulus nuncupatus, quibus hoc nomen familiariùs fuit. Nec enim leguntur facilè sancti sine Dei nutu mutasse nomina: Nec enim leguntur facilè sancti sine Dei nutu mutasse nomina: Neque ulla in Scripturis à devictis hostibus nominandi consuetudo, fatente ipso Espensæo, deprehenditur. Et vocatus utroque nomine noster est etiam ante conversionem Sergii Act. XIII. In circumcisione tamen nomen Sauli Ebræum ipsi datum esse, dubium non est; & fieri potuit, ut Pauli nomen, cùm ab aliis ita vocaretur, lubentius usurpârit, tùm quia notius & communius, tùm ut vocabulum lubentius, Græci ac Romani, quibus id gratiosum ac familiare erat, agnoscerent, quorum se Doctorem profitebatur, tùm quòd circumcisio jamjam abroganda penitus fuerit, doctrinâ imprimis hujus Apostoli, pleneque in ejus locum surrogandus Baptismus, Synagogâ Judaicâ cum honore sepultâ.

Δοῦλος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

In Veteri Testamento qui erant in magnis muneribus, dicebantur δοῦλοι κυρίου, id est, Dei, ut Moses Jos. I. 1. XIV. 7. XXII. 4. 1. Par. VI. 59. Josue Judic. II. 8. David Ps. CXXXI, 10. Nehemias Nehem. I. 6. In novo Testamento etiam Jesu Christi, qui & Dominus ipsorum dicitur.

Quia in V. T. servi dicebantur viri Dei & Prophetæ, ac Apostoli in N. T. se servos Jesu Christi vocant, manifestum est Jesum Christum verum DEum esse, non enim Creaturæ in vocatione suâ, sed uni DEO serviebant, nec ab hominibus ψιλοῖς, sed à DEO solo vocationem suam habebant, θεόκλητοι, non ἀνθρωπόκλητοι Gal. I. 1.

Κλητὸς.

Vocatus ad munus obeundum non minus magnificè, quàm Moses Exod. III. Moses per Angelum Dei, Act. VII. 30. Paulus per ipsum Dei Filium.

Ἀπόστολος.

De hac voce vide dicta ad Matth. X. 2.

Vocatum non minus magnificè, rectè dicit Grotius, quam Mosen Exod. III. sed quod addit, Mosen per Angelum DEI vocatum Act. VII. 30. Paulum per Filium DEI, eo magnificentiæ non tantùm vocationis Mosaicæ derogat, quem constat immediatè à Deo vocatum, qui in rubo ardente ipsi apparuit Ex. III. Sed etiam ipsius Jesu; quem angelo creato parem facit. At ut Paulus per Filium Dei ἔνσαρκον vocatus est, ita Moses per eundem vocatus est, adhuc ἄσαρκον, ut ad Exod. III. observavimus.

Cæterùm Apostolum ab Episcopo ita distinguit Espensæus in 1. Tim. c. I. quod ille immediatè à Christo vocatus, certò habet S. S. ubique & in omnibus Ecclesiis docet, juxta illud Pauli 2. Cor. XII. Solicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum: unde Chrysostomus hom. XIX. in Matth. Apostolos vocat omnium Ecclesiarum Doctores. Episcopus verò per homines vocatus certo loco praeest, S. S. non con- tinuo, nec necessario habet, dictatam ab Apostolis doctrinam accipere debet, non etiam novum do- ctrinae genus invehere. Quod observent, velim, Romani Episcopi. Quod vero idem Espensaeus e Theodor. ad 1. Tim. III. notat, qui nunc vocantur Episcopi, olim nominatos Apostolos, testimonio Scripturae caret: dictus quidem Epaphroditus A- postolus Philip. II. 25. dicti & alii 2. Cor. IIX. 29. sed Ecclesiarum Apostoli, non vero Jesu Christi: ac sensu longe alio, quod nempe ab Ecclesia missi fuerint, ejusque legati, quales erant, qui sacras pecunias colligebant. Confer. Grotius ad illa loca. ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον Θεοῦ. מֻבְדָּל id est, selectus. Sicut populum Israel dicitur Deus בָּדַל ἀφορίσαι aut διαχωρίσαι e populis Lev. XX, 24. 26. Dici- tur & Ecclesia ἀφορίσαι Paul. Act. XIV. 2. sed divino jussu. In Syriaco hic est דאִתְפְּרֵשׁ quasi diceret Paulus, se nunc ju- stius dici posse Pharisaeum, segregatum a caeteris non ritualibus institutis, sed opera eximia. Est & ἀφορίσας Gal. I. 15. sed sen- su paululum diverso, ut ibi dicemus. De voce Evangelii vide, quae dicta ad inscriptionem Evangelii secundum Matthaeum.

Non tam respicitur ad Pharisaeorum sectam, qui separati dici amabant, quam ad segregationem divi- nam ab aeternitate factam, Gal. I. 15. Act. IX. 15. quo- ad ordinationem, & in missione Apostoli, quoad exe- quutionem in tempore expeditam, Act. XIII. 2. ὁ προεπηγγείλατο διὰ τῶν προφητῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις. Quod Evangelium promiserat, Deus nempe, cujus no- men praecessit, per Prophetas, nec sermone tantum, sed & scriptis, quae melius servari solent. Nolite novitate percel- li, cum illa novitas pridem sit praedicta. Vide Luc. XXIV. 44. Joh. XII. 16. Act. X. 4. 43. Hebr. VIII. 8.

Ad Evangelium separatus dicitur, quod ab επαγ- γελια distinguit, quanquam ei ab hac fidem faciat v. 2. Haec Prophetarum fuit, promissio nempe Mes- siae; illud annunciationem de exhibito Messia in- fert, vel de complemento Prophetiarum, quae Ev- angelistarum & Apostolorum propria fuit. Non autem novum Evangelium est, aut aliquid novi adfert, quod ad doctrinae substantiam: nam ean- dem, quam Prophetae, tradit doctrinam: solum in Christo Jesu completum, vel praestitum esse testa- tur, quod illi praestandum esse, praedixerant.

## 1:3
V. 3. concerning His Son) This refers to that which preceded, Gospel. For it is explained of whom that discourse bringing good news treats. Who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh. That is, of Mary, Gal. 4:4, where the same word born, that is, began to exist. But Mary was of the descendants of David, Luke 2:5, Matt. 9:27, 12:23, 15:22, 20:30, 31, 21:9, 15, Mark 10:47, 48, Luke 1:32, 69, 17:38, 39.

That word denotes not only origin, but also begotten, as Erasmus translates it after Valla. If, however, you translate it as origin, it is not noted that the Son of God then finally began to exist simply, but that having been born from the seed of David according to the flesh, that is, the human nature, He began to exist, and thus became flesh, as is held in John 1:14: the Word became flesh. To say that the Son of God began to exist simply savors of Socinianism, as if He either did not exist at all before, or the Son of God is made by temporal birth: whereas on the contrary the Apostle says that Christ was indeed born according to the flesh from the seed of David: but defined as the Son of God not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit: and not born, as He is the Son of God, from the seed of David, but as He is flesh, or man; for this is according to the flesh.

Moreover, in that periphrasis of his calling and segregation, the Apostle immediately insinuates the sum of the Apostolic proclamation, both as a promise, just as it was announced through the Prophets in the Holy Scriptures, not only because writings are accustomed to be better preserved, but because God willed the Prophetic Scripture to be the perpetual Canon of the Church, and bound the Church to the same, as an infallible rule of believing: and also as the Gospel itself, which is announced through the Apostles: by which name here is not understood simply the promise of grace, as the Socinians wish, but the public proclamation concerning Christ exhibited: which namely is concerning the temporal birth of the eternal Son of God, from the seed of David according to the flesh, i.e., concerning His incarnation, and birth from the descendants of David: which concern the Person of Christ, and His partly divine nature, as He is the Son of God, begotten from eternity by the Father, partly also human, which is indicated by the word flesh, Isa. 40:8, John 1:14, 1 Tim. 3:16, according to which He was born from the seed and descendants of David, born of the Virgin Mary: which twofold nature He implies constitutes one hypostasis or person, because through that origin from the seed of David the Son of God assumed flesh, or human nature, into the unity of His divine hypostasis. He asserts that this divine nature of Christ was demonstrated when, in the days of His flesh, it was openly shown in virtue and divine power, and then especially in the resurrection from the dead according to the Spirit of sanctification, or by the infinite power of the divine nature: since it is the work of God alone to raise from the dead: or also from the resurrection onwards: which sense others embrace, because, exalted to the right hand of God, He showed His divine power and nature by the proclamation of the Apostles, the wonders of miracles, and the conversion of the Jews and Gentiles. And this is the first head, which is to be preached by the Apostles: namely, concerning the person of the Messiah: that the Son of God, according to the promises in the Old Testament, came into the flesh, begotten from the seed of David: the second is concerning the office of the Messiah, which is insinuated by the words ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν: because for this reason he came into the flesh, for this reason the Son of God died and rose again from the dead, that he might be our Jesus, or Savior, who would save us from our sins, Matt. I. 21. and Christ, that anointed Prophet, High Priest, and King, and our Lord, who, although he is our Lord by creation, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, would also claim us for himself in a peculiar way by the right of redemption, and acquire us for himself with his precious blood, εἰς λαὸν περιέσιον Tit. III. 14. through which grace we all receive grace (because outside of him there is no grace), through the obedience of faith, when indeed we render ὑπακοὴν to the Gospel through faith.

Latin:

V. 3. περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ) Hoc refertur ad illud, quod praecessit εὐ- αγγέλιον. Explicatur n. de quo agat ille sermo bona nuntians. τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ σάρκα. Id est, de Maria, Gal. IV. 4. ubi eadem vox γενόμενος, id est, cepit existere. Maria autem erat de posteris Davidis, Luc. II. 5. Matth. IX. 27. XII. 23. XV. 22. XX 30. 31. XXI. 9. 15. Marci X. 27. 48. Luc. I. 32. 69. XVII. 38. 39.

Vox illa non tantum ortum notat, sed etiam ge- nitum, ut post Vallam convertit Erasmus. Si ta- men ortum vertas, non notatur, quod tum demum ceperit existere ἁπλῶς Filius Dei, sed quod ex se- mine Davidis ortus secundum carnem, id est, natu- ram humanam, existere ceperit, adeoque factus sit caro, uti Johannis I. 14. habetur: ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο. Caepisse existere simpliciter Filium Dei, So- cinismum sapit, quasi aut plane non extiterit antea, aut Filius Dei per nativitatem temporalem fit: Cum contra Apostolus ortum quidem secundum carnem e semine Davidis Christum dicat: Filium autem Dei definitum non secundum carnem, sed se- cundum spiritum: nec ortum, ut Filius Dei est, e Davidis semine, sed qua caro, vel homo est; hoc enim est secundum carnem.

Caeterum in ista vocationis & segregationis suae περιφράσει Apostolus insinuat statim praeconii Apo- stolici summam, tum qua ἐπαγγελίαν, quemadmo- dum id praenunciatum fuit per Prophetas in Scriptu- ris Sacris, non solum, quod scripta melius servari soleant, sed quod Scripturam Propheticam Cano- nem perpetuum Ecclesiae esse voluerit Deus, & ad eundem Ecclesiam adstrinxerit, tanquam regulam credendi infallibilem: tum qua εὐαγγέλιον ipsum, quod per Apostolos annunciatur: quo nomine hic non simpliciter promissio gratiæ intelligitur, ut So- ciniani volunt, sed publicum de Christo exhibito præconium: quod nempe illud sit de æterni Filii Dei ortu temporali, è semine David secundùm carnem, h. e. de ejusdem incarnatione, & nativitate è poste- ris Davidis: quæ concernunt Christi Personam, ejusq; partim divinam naturam, quà est Filius Dei, ab æterno à Patre genitus, partim etiam humanam, quæ voce carnis indicatur Es. XL. 8. Joh. I. 14. 1. Tim. III. 16. secundùm quam ortus est è semine, ac posteris Davidis, natus è Mariâ virgine: quam geminam naturam unam hypostasin vel personam constituere innuit, quod per illam originem è se- mine David Filius DEI carnem, seu humanam na- turam in unitatem hypostaseos suæ divinæ assum- serit. Hanc autem divinam Christi naturam de- monstratam cùm in diebus carnis in virtute, ac potentia divina, palàm ostensa, tum imprimis in resurrectione à mortuis secundùm Spiritum San- ctificationis, seu infinita naturæ divinæ virtute fa- cta asserit: quum solius DEI opus sit resuscitare à mortuis: vel etiam inde à resurrectione: quem sen- sum alii amplectuntur, quia exaltatus ad dextram Dei divinam potentiam, ac naturam ostendit præ- conio Apostolorum, prodigiis miraculorum, con- versione Judæorũ, & gentium. Atque hoc primum est caput, quod prædicandum ab Apostolis: nimi- rum de persona Messiæ: quod Filius DEI secundum promissiones in V. T. in carnem venerit, è semine David procreatus: alterum est de Messiæ officio, quod vocibus ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν insinua- tur: quia ideo in carnem venit, ideò mortuus est, ac resurrexit à morte Filius DEI, ut esset Jesus no- ster, vel Salvator, qui salvaret nos à peccatis nostris, Matth. I. 21. & Christus unctus ille Propheta, Ponti- fex, & Rex, ac Dominus noster, qui quum per crea- tionem Dominus noster sit, cum Patre, & Spiritu S. jure redemtionis etiam nos sibi peculiariter vin- dicaret, ac sanguine suo pretioso sibi acquireret, εἰς λαὸν περιέσιον Tit. III. 14. per quam χάριν gratiam accipimus omnes (quia extrà eum nulla est gratia,) per obedientiam fidei, cum nempe Evangelio per fidem ὑπακοὴν præstamus.

## 1:4
v. 4. Τῦ ὁρισθέντος ὑἷ Θεῦ ἐν δυνάμει, κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης. The Syriac translates ὁρισθέντος as 'who was known': just as ותגזר Job XXII. 28 is translated by ὁρισθεὶς. But the Latin interpreters, even the most ancient, translate it as 'who was predestined,' as appears not only from the version which we use, but from the interpreter of Irenaeus III. 18. & 32. and from the Rufinian version of Origen on this passage, and from Hilary VII. de Trinitate, and from the Council of Toledo XI, 5. Epiphanius also, in heresy LIV, cites προορισθέντος, thinking that ὁρίζειν and προορίζειν mean the same thing. Thus, what is προώρισε γενέσθαι in Acts IV. 28 is the same as ὡρισμένη in chapter II. 23. In a similar sense we have ὡρισμένων, Luke XXII. 22. and ὥρισε, Acts XVII. 31. Thus also ὡρισμένος is used in Acts X. 42. But the abbreviated expression makes the meaning more difficult, which we shall endeavor to unfold. Jesus is called the Son of God in many ways: most popularly, because he was raised to the kingdom by God, in which sense the words of Ps. II, spoken concerning David when he attained the kingdom, are applied to Christ in Acts XIII, 33. and Heb. I. 5. V. 5. Moreover, this royal dignity of the Son of Jesus was predestined and prefigured even then, when, while leading a mortal life, he performed those great signs and wonders, which are denoted by the word δυνάμεων, often and singularly δυνάμεως as in Mark VI. 5. IX. 39. Luke IV. 36. V. 17. VI. 19. VIII. 46. IX. 1. Acts III. 12. IV. 33. VI. 8. X. 38. Jesus performed these signs through that spirit of holiness, i.e., the divine power, by which he had been sanctified from the beginning of his conception Luke I. 35. Mark II. 8. John IX. 36. Here, κατὰ σάρκα and κατὰ πνεῦμα are opposed concerning Christ, as also in 1 Pet. 3, 4. Jesus is therefore shown to be noble on the maternal side, inasmuch as he sprang from an earthly king, but more noble on the paternal side, inasmuch as he was made a heavenly king by God after the resurrection Heb. V. 9. Acts II. 30. & XXVI, 23. where there is similarly ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν, for ἀναστάσεως ἐκ νεκρῶν, as Peter speaks in 1. 3. and was destined for that kingdom even before, through so many miracles performed by the divine power proper to him and dwelling in him. Something similar is done in us. For we too are destined by the works of the Spirit to attain the kingdom after the resurrection. Irenaeus V. 8. But now we receive some part of his Spirit, for the perfection and preparation of incorruption. Novatian, concerning the Holy Spirit, who, acting in this way in us, that He may lead our bodies to eternity and to the resurrection of immortality, while He accustoms them to be mingled with heavenly power. But Chrysostom, in his discourse on the Holy Spirit, thinks it is a long transition, and that those words κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης, ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν χριστῦ refer to that phrase ἀφωρισμένου εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον: as if Paul were saying that he was rendered fit for the preaching of the Gospel through the Holy Spirit, who attained the resurrection of Christ, John VII. 39, Acts II. 33.

The Latin version cannot be defended, because ὁρισθεὶς is not predestined, nor does it signify the same thing according to the usage of the Greek language, for this is expressed by προορισθεὶς. And although it might be taken thus in some places (which in Acts II. 25, ch. X. 42, ch. XVII. 21 might indeed seem to be the case, but there it denotes designated, or defined by a certain reason, rather than PREDESTINED), here, however, it can by no means be taken in that way: whatever may be the case regarding Irenaeus and the Rufinian version of Origen; but it is known that Hilary not infrequently uses words in a catachrestic sense. The reason why it cannot be rendered thus is this: because the Son of GOD, who is understood here, is not so except through eternal generation from the Father: but by no means through anything temporary, for which He had been predestined beforehand, or from eternity. What Grotius says, that the Son is called [Son] in many ways, most popularly because He was raised to the kingdom by God, that is drawn from the pools of Socinianism: regarding which Socinianism may be considered defeated.

Nor indeed is that passage of Ps. II. 7, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you,' spoken of David, since such a thing was not said to any of the angels, Heb. I, nor adapted to Christ, by which He came to the kingdom, Acts XIII. 33, Heb. I. 5, ch. V. 5, but they uniquely belong to Christ, and define His eternal generation and sonship, which the Apostle explains in Heb. I. 3, according to which, indeed, He is the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης ϰ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως of God the Father: and that it was necessary for this that He should be the Messiah, Acts XIII. 33, and our eternal high priest, Heb. V. 5, demonstrates, because indeed no other Messiah and no other High Priest, who would deliver us, save us, and propitiate us by His offering and His Priesthood, was defined by GOD, except the eternal Son of GOD Himself, as David testifies in the second Psalm. Cf. what we said on Ps. II in the annotations. Nor anywhere in the Holy Scriptures are the name of the Son of God and King or Royal dignity used as equivalents; indeed, when the Son of GOD is described as King, that is the name of the person, but this is the name of the office and divinity; that is natural to Him, but this is accessory: because He Himself, when He was the natural Son of GOD, was made our Messiah, King, and Lord out of a most free economy. Therefore, it is taught only impiously that the sonship of the Son of GOD was then predestined and prefigured when He was performing signs while living a mortal life (because that was from eternity); indeed, it cannot even be said of the Royal dignity: which, although it was predestined from eternity, already had a place in act at His very birth; for He was not King only by designation in the days of His flesh, but was truly born King, as we showed against the Socinians in Socin. Proflig. Sect. VI. art. III. Tit. I. Quest. II. Therefore, the Son of GOD is called ὁρισθεὶς because He was declared, manifested, and demonstrated ἐν δυνάμει, through signs and wonders openly demonstrating divine and infinite power, John V. 19 ff., ch. X. 30, 38, Acts X. 38, because to perform miracles by one's own power belongs to none but divine and infinite power, Ps. LXXII. 18, Ps. CXXXVI. 4. Cf. Matt. X. 8, Luke IV. 36, John II. 11. Therefore, the Greek interpreters, to whom the force of the word is best known, and whom we therefore rightly prefer to the Latins here, explain ὁρισθέντος, that is, δειχθέντος, ἀποφανθέντος, κριθέντος, ὁμολογηθέντος; Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius. The Syriac translated it: and known: just as also in Acts II. 22, Christ is called ἀποδεδειγμένος δυνάμεσι, demonstrated by mighty works. Whence this opposition: made indeed the son of man through birth from the seed of David, but demonstrated that He is the Son of GOD through power, or signs and wonders, which Grotius acknowledges are denoted by the word δυνάμεως. Cf. Theol. Apost. Rom. Orat. IV. Here the Papists themselves desert the Vulgate version, and Isidore Clarius, Erasmus, Faber, Mariana, and Conzen correct it, striving to explain it either as an external definition or a declaration of predestination, although Tertullian and Jerome long ago read 'defined' or 'destined' here, and certainly understood it so. But by the spirit of holiness you may here more rightly understand the divine nature of Christ than either the third person of the Godhead or, as Grotius with the Socinians does, an unsubstantial divine force: which is falsely said to be noted in Luke I. 35, since there the Holy Spirit is indicated by His own characteristics, namely personal actions, and the Holy Spirit was the creator in the conception of Christ: whence Cocceius here wrongly understands the Son of GOD through the Holy Spirit in Luke I. 36: even though He was designated there by the power of the Most High. Nor is an unsubstantial force ever denoted in the Scriptures by the name of the Holy Spirit. But here, that the divine nature of Christ is to be understood by πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης, the cause and fountainhead of all sanctification, the antithesis itself teaches. For this Theological Rule must be held: When in Scripture Spirit and flesh are opposed to each other IN CHRIST, either expressly or interpretatively, as by flesh the human nature of Christ is indicated, so by spirit the divine nature of the same is indicated: See John I. 14, Rom. IX. 5, 1 Tim. III. 16, 1 Pet. III. 18, Heb. IX. 14, as also 1 Cor. XV. 45.

Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν) Chrysostom connects these with the following words, others with what preceded, ὑῦ αὐτῦ, so that this is an explanation of v. 5, δι' ὗ ἐλάβομεν χάριν κ̓ ἀποστολὴν. A hendiadys, that is, the great benefit of the grace of the apostleship. For he calls the conferred Apostolic office 'grace' elsewhere also, as below XV. 16, Gal. II. 9, Eph. III. 2, 7, 8, and he explains how great this benefit is in 1 Tim. I. 12. Δι ί, either through whom Jesus, or, if we follow Chrysostom, through whom the spirit, ἐλάβομεν χάριν, we have obtained.

The discourse concerning Christ is continued, therefore he is said to have received grace and Apostleship not through the Holy Spirit but through Christ. Nor is there need for a hendiadys, since the Apostle distinctly proclaims two benefits, both that he obtained grace, when he was the greatest of sinners 1 Tim. I. 15. 16. therefore using the plural number through the figure of communication he joins himself with others in this part: and that he received the Apostolic office, which was common to him with the rest of the Apostles 1 Cor. IV. 9. and was instructed with gifts necessary for that office, Rom. XII. 3. c. XV. 15.

The particle διὰ 'per' denotes here not the mediate cause, but the principal, as in John I. 3. Rom. XI. 36. Gal. I. 6. Heb. II. 10. Cocceius rightly here: 'It is not χάρις grace, certainly in this matter, unless of Him who has an architectural, autocratic, and despotic will, primary, lordly, plenary, who has εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος, the good pleasure of the will to forgive sins, to grant righteousness and life, to sanctify through His Spirit, John V. 21.' The same is also confirmed by the Apostleship of Paul, inasmuch as his conversion was brought about by divine authority and power, Acts IX. c. XXII. 6. his calling and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon him, perceived in the many languages which he spoke, in the miracles performed through him, in divine wisdom, and in the perfect knowledge of the highest mysteries; to say nothing of many other proofs. Since the Apostle received all these things from Christ, they confirm that He is truly the Son of God our Lord.

εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως. So also below XVI. 26. that is, that God may be obeyed through the faith held in the Gospel. The genitive often expresses the efficient cause. So also 1 Peter I. 22. Obedience is that toward which faith tends. below XV. 18. XVI. 19. 2 Cor. VII. 15. X. 5. 6. Philem. 21. 1 Peter I. 2. 18. 'that there may be obedience, not that there may be disputing about the nature of God,' says Chrysostom here.

The Vulgate less appropriately [translates it] 'to the obedience of faith'. More correctly 'for the obedience of faith to be rendered by the nations': yet it is not understood as the obedience which is the effect of faith: for he intends faith primarily, and consequently the obedience born from faith: nor is that alone intended, to which faith tends, but faith itself through the ἀποστολὴν of Paul was intended: therefore by the customary phrase of the Holy Scriptures, Faith itself is indicated, by which we obey the word of the Gospel, John VI. 29, 40, 1 John III. 23, so that the nations may obey by faith, by accepting the word of the Gospel with true trust of the heart. Thus faith is called obedience, Rom. VI. 17, 2 Cor. X. 5, 1 Pet. I. 2 (cf. 2 Thess. II. 13), and ὑπο- ταγὴ τῆς ὁμολογίας, 2 Cor. IX. 13, and ὑπακοὴ τῆς ἀληθείας, 1 Pet. I. 22. Not to believe, on the contrary, is τῇ ἀλη- θείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι, not to obey the truth, Gal. III. 1, and ἀπισία is ἀπείθεια, disobedience, John III. 36, 1 Pet. II. 8, not to be subject to the righteousness of Christ, Rom. X. 7. And why should faith not be ὑπακοὴ, or obedience, since in it there is προσοχὴ, ἀγάπη τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀποδοχὴ, τὸ διδόναι δόξαν Θεῷ, καταφυγὴ πεποίθησις, πλη- ροφορία, ἐλπὶς, τὸ μὴ φοβεῖσθαι, attentio, amor veritatis, ejus receptio, dare gloriam DEO, confuge- re, confidere, certum esse, sperare, non metuere, which are not in man without an obedient will, as Cocceius holds here. And thus the title fits the proposition and the Apostolic treatise. Others render it, 'that the nations may obey the faith', with this word taken objectively for the faith which is believed, or the doctrine of faith. But the matter comes to the same thing.

Latin:

v. 4. Τῦ ὁρισθέντος ὑἷ Θεῦ ἐν δυνάμει, κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης. Ὁρισθέντος Syrus vertit, qui cognitus est: quomodo per ὁρισθεὶς vertitur ותגזר Job. XXII. 28. At Latini interpretes etiam vetustissimi qui prædestinatus est, ut apparet non tan- tùm ex eâ, quâ utimur versione, sed ex Irenæi interprete III. 18. & 32. & ex Rufinianâ versione Origenis ad hunc lo- cum, & ex Hilario VII. de Trinitate, & ex Concilio Toleta- no XI, 5. Epiphanius quoque hæresi LIV. citat προορισθέν- τος, ratus idem valere ὁρίζειν & προορίζειν. Sic quod est προώ- ρισε γενέσθαι Act. IV. 28. idem est ὡρισμένη cap. II. 23. Pari sensu habemus ὡρισμένων, Luc. XXII. 22. & ὥρισε, Act. XVII. 31. Sic & ὡρισμένος sumitur Act. X. 42. Sed sensum difficilio- rem efficit curtata locutio, quam evolvere conabimur. Jesus Filius Dei multis modis dicitur: maximè populariter, ideò quòd in regnum à Deo evectus est, quo sensu verba Ps. II, de Davide dicta cùm ad regnum pervenit, Christo aptantur Act. XIII, 33. & ad Hebr. I. 5. V. 5. Hæc autem Filii sive regia dignitas Jesu prædestinabatur, & præfigurabatur jam tùm, cum mortale agens vitam magna illa signa & prodigia ede- ret, quæ δυνάμεων voce denotatur, sæpè & singulariter δυνά- μεως ut Marci VI. 5. IX. 39. Luc. IV. 36. V. 17. VI. 19. VIII. 46. IX. 1. Act. III. 12. IV. 33. VI. 8. X. 38. Hæc signa edebat Jesus per spiritum illum sanctitatis, i. e. vim divinam, per quâ ab ini- tio conceptionis sanctificatus fuerat Luc. I. 35. Mar. II. 8. Joh. IX. 36. Opponuntur hic de Christo ὁ σάρκα, & κατὰ πνεῦμα, ut & 1. Pet. 3, 4. Ostenditur ergò Jesus nobilis ex maternâ par- te, utpote ex rege terreno ortus, sed nobilior ex paternâ par- te, quippe à Deo factus rex cœlestis post resurrectionē Heb. V. 9. Act. II. 30. & XXVI, 23. ubi est similiter ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νε- κρῶν, pro ἀναστάσεως ἐκ νεκρῶν, ut loquitur Petrus l. 1. 3. & ei regno etiam ante destinatus per tot miracula facta vi divinâ ipsi propria, & in ipso habitante. Simile quid in nobis geri- tur. Nam & nos per opera Spiritus destinamur regno post resurrectionem adipiscendo. Irenæus V. 8. Nunc autem par- tem aliquam Spiritùs ejus sumimus, ad perfectionem & præparationem incorruptelæ. Novatianus, de Spiritu Sancto, qui id agens in nobis, ut ad æternitatem & ad resurre- ctionem immort. litatis corpora nostra perducat, dum illa in se assuefacit cum cœlesti virtute misceri. At Chrysosto- mus oratione de Spiritu Sancto putat esse longam trajectio- nem, & illa κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης, ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν χριστῦ referri ad illud ἀφωρισμένου εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον: quasi dicat Paulus se aptum redditum ad Evangelii prædicatio- nem per Spiritum Sanctum, qui resurrectionem Christi est consecutus, Joh VII. 39. Act. II. 33.

Latina versio defendi nequit, quia ὁρισθεὶς non est prædestinatus, nec idem ex usu Græcæ linguæ significat, hoc enim προορισθεὶς dicitur. Et tametsi alicubi sic acciperetur, (quod Act. II. 25. c. X. 42. c. XVII. 21. videri equidem posset, sed ibi potius designatum, aut certa ratione definitum, quàm PRÆDESTINATUM notat) hîc tamen ita sumi minimè potest: quicquid sit de Irenæo & Ruffinia- na Origenis versione; Hilarium autem vocibus καταχρηστικῶς non rarò uti, notum est. Ratio cur ita reddi non possit, hæc est: quia Filius DEI, qui hîc intelligitur, non est, nisi per æternam genera- tionem à Patre: nequaquam autem per aliquid temporarium, ad quod prædestinatus anteà, vel ab æterno fuerit. Quod Grotius ait, Filium mul- tis modis dici, maximè populariter ideò, quòd in re- gnum à Deo evectus sit, id è lacunis Socinismi hau- stum est: de quo Socinismus profligatus videatur.

Neque verò illa Ps. II. 7. Filius meus es tu, ego hodiè genui te, vel de Davide dicta, quum ne An- gelorum quidem ulli tale quid dictum sit Ebr. I. vel Christo aptata, quâ ad regnum venit, Act. XIII. 33. Ebr. I. 5. c. V. 5. sed unicè Christo conveniunt, ejusque æternam generationem, & υἱότητα defi- niunt, quam explicat Apostolus Ebr. I. 3. juxta quam nempè est ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης ϰ χαρακ- κτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως DEI Patris: & necessarium ad id fuisse, ut Messias esset, Act. XIII. 33. ac pontifex noster æternus Ebr. V. 5. demonstrat, quod nem- pe alius Messias, aliusque Pontifex, qui nos libe- raret, salvaret, ac oblatione, & Sacerdotio suo propitiaret, nullus definitus fuerit à DEO, nisi ipse æternus DEI Filius, teste Davide, Psalmo se- cundo, Conf. quæ Ps. II. in annot. diximus. Nec uspiam in S. literis nomen Filii Dei, & Regis vel di- gnitatis Regiæ κατ’ ἰσοδυναμίαν adhibentur, imò cum Filius DEI ut Rex describitur, illud est no- men personæ, hoc verò nomen officii, & divinita- tis, illud ei naturale est, hoc verò accessorium: quia ipse, quum naturalis DEI Filius esset, è liberrima οἰκονομίᾳ Messias, & Rex, ac Dominus noster fa- ctus est. Non ergò nisi impiè docetur, quod υἱό- της Filii DEI prædestinata tùm fuerit, ac præfigu- rata, cùm mortalem vitam agens signa ederet, (quia illa ab æterno fuit) imò nec de Regiâ dignitate id dici potest: Quæ ab æterno utique prædestinata, in ipsâ nativitate jam actu locum habuit; nam non designatione tantùm Rex fuit in diebus carnis, sed verè Rex natus est, ut contra Socinianos in Socin. Proflig. Sect. VI. art. III. Tit. I. Quæst. II. ostendi- mus. Itaque ὁρισθεὶς dicitur Filius DEI, quod declaratus, manifestatus, demonstratus sit, ἐν δυνά- μει, per signa & prodigia divinam & infinitam po- tentiam palàm demonstrantia Joh. V. 19. seqq. c. X. 30. 38. Act. X. 38. quia miracula, propriâ virtute, patrare non nisi divinæ, & infinitæ potentiæ est, Ps. LXXII. 18. Ps. CXXXVI. 4. Conf. Matth. X. 8. Luc. IV. 36. Joh. II. 11. Ideò Græci interpp. quibus optimè vis vocis nota, quos proinde Latinis me- ritò hîc præferimus, exponunt ὁρισθέντος, id est, δειχθέντος, ἀποφανθέντος, κριθέντος, ὁμολογη- θέντος, Origenes, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, Theodor. Theophyl. Oecumen. Syrus exposuit: & cognitus: quemadmodum etiam Act. II. 22. Christus dicitur ἀποδεδειγμένος δυνάμεσι demonstratus virtutibus. Unde hæc oppositio: factus quidem filius hominis per ortum è semine Davidis, demonstratus autem, quod sit Filius DEI, per virtutem, vel signa & pro- digia, quæ δυνάμεως voce notari agnoscit Gro- tius. Cons. Theol. Apost. Rom. Orat. IV. Deserunt hic Papistæ ipsi vulgatam versionem, & castigat eandem Isid. Clarius, Erasmus, Faber, Mariana, Conzen. vel de exteriori definitione, vel declaratio- ne prædestinationis exponere satagunt, quanquã jam olim Tertullian.& Hieron. hìc definitus, destina- tus legerint, certè intellexerint. Per spiritum autem sanctitatis hìc rectius divinam Christi naturam in- telligas, quàm vel tertiam personam Deitatis, vel ut Grotius cum Socinianis vim divinam ἀνυπόσατον: quæ Luc. I. 35. falsò notari dicitur, quum ibi Spi- ritus S. persona characteribus suis indicetur, actio- nes nempe personales, & S. S. δημιουργὸς fuerit in conceptione Christi : unde Coccejus hìc perperàm Luc. I. 36. per Spiritum S. Filium DEI intelligit: etsi per virtutem altissimi idem designatus ibi fue- rit. Nec uspiam sanè in scripturis Spiritus San- cti nomine vis ἀνυπόσατος denotatur. Hìc verò quod per πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης divina natura Christi intelligenda, Sanctificationis omnis causa, & Sca- turigo, antithesis ipsa docet. Tenenda enim Re- gula Theologica: Quando in Scriptura Spiritus & caro IN CHRISTO sibi opponuntur seu expressè, seu interpretativè, ut per carnem humana Christi natura ita per spiritum divina natura ejusdem in- digitatur: Vid. Joh. I. 14. Rom. IX. 5. 1. Tim. III. 16. 1. Pet. III. 18. Ebr. IX. 14. ut & 1. Cor. XV. 45.

Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν) Hæc Chrysostomus cum pro- ximis connectit, alii cũ eo, quod præcessit ὑῦ αὐτῦ, ut hoc sit v. 5. δι' ὗ ἐλάβομεν χάριν κ̓ ἀποστολὴν) illius ἐξήγησις. ἔν διὰ δυοῖν, id est, χάριν ἀποστολῆς beneficium ingens. Nam collatum munus Apostolicum & alibi χάριν vocat ut infra XV. 16. Gal. II. 9. Eph. III. 2. 7. 8. & quantum hoc sit beneficium explicat 1, Tim. I. 12. Δι ί, aut per quem Jesum, aut, si Chrysostomum sequimur, per quem spiri- tum, ἐλάβομεν χάριν זכינו.

Continuatur oratio de Christo, ideò non per Spiritum S. sed per Christum accepisse gratiam & Apostolatum dicitur. Nec opus est Hendyade, cum distinctè Apostolus prædicet duo beneficia, & quod gratiam consequutus sit, cum esset maxi- mus peccatorum 1. Tim. I. 15. 16. ideò plurali nu- mero usus per figuram communicationis se cum aliis hac parte conjungit : & quod Apostolicum munus acceperit, quod ipsi cum reliquis Aposto- lis commune fuit 1. Cor. IV. 9. donisque ad munus illud necessariis instructus, Rom. XII. 3. c. XV. 15.

Particula autem διὰ per non causam mediam, sed principalem hìc notat, uti Joh. I. 3. Rom. XI. 36. Gal. I. 6. Ebr. II. 10. Rectè hìc Coccejus : Non est χάρις gratia, certè in hoc negotio, nisi ejus, qui habet voluntatem ἀρχιτεκτονικὴν, αὐτοκρατορι- κὴν, καὶ δεσποτικήν, primariam, herilem, plenari- am, qui habet εὐδοκίαν τῦ θελήματος, beneplaci- tum voluntatis ad condonandum peccata, donan- dum justitiam, & vitam, sanctificandum per Spiri- tum suum, Joh. V. 21. Confirmat idem etiam Apo- stolatus Pauli, utpote conversio ejusdem divinâ autoritate & virtute facta, Act. IX. c. XXII. 6. voca- tio & effusio S.S. in ipsum, perspecta in linguis plu- rimis, quas loquutus est, in miraculis per ipsum patratis, in divina sapientia, & summorum myste- riorum perfectâ notitiâ; ut alia plurima documen- ta taceamus. Quæ cùm à Christo acceperit omnia Apostolus, eundem verè esse Filium Dei Domi- num nostrum, confirmant.

εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως. Sic & infra XVI. 26. id est, ut Deo obediatur per fidem Evangelio habitam. Genitivus sæpè causam efficientem exprimit. Sic & 1. Petri I, 22. Obedientia est id, quo tendit fides. infra XV. 18. XVI. 19. 2. Cor. VII, 15. X. 5. 6. Phi- len. 21. 1. Petr. I. 2. 18. ut obediatur, non ut disputetur de natura Dei, ait hic Chrysostomus.

Vulgata minùs commodè, ad obediendum fidei. Rectius ad obedientiam fidei à gentibus præstan- dam: non tamen obedientia, quæ fidei effectus est, intelligitur: nam fidem primariò intendit, conse- quenter obedientiam ex fide ortam: neque id so- lum, quò tendit fides, sed ipsa fides per ἀποστολὴν Pauli intendebatur: Phrasi ergò S. S. consuetâ in- dicatur Fides ipsa, quâ obedimus verbo Evangelii, Joh. VI. 29. 40. 1. Joh. III. 23. ut gentes fide obe- diant, verbum Evangelii acceptando verâ cordis fiduciâ. Sic fides obedientia vocatur Rom. VI. 17. 2. Cor. X. 5. 1. Petr. I. 2. (Cons. 2. Thess. II. 13.) & ὑπο- ταγὴ τῆς ὁμολογίας, 2. Cor. IX. 13. & ὑπακοὴ τῆς ἀληθείας, 1. Pet. I. 22. Non credere contrà est τῇ ἀλη- θείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι, veritati non obedire, Gal. III. 1. & ἀπισία est ἀπείθεια, inobedientia, Joh. III. 36. 1. Petr. II. 8. non subjici justitiæ Christi, Rom. X. 7. Et quidni fides ὑπακοὴ, vel obedientia esset, quum in ea sit προσοχὴ, ἀγάπη τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀποδοχὴ, τὸ διδόναι δόξαν Θεῷ, καταφυγὴ πεποίθησις, πλη- ροφορία, ἐλπὶς, τὸ μὴ φοβεῖσθαι, attentio, amor veritatis, ejus receptio, dare gloriam DEO, confuge- re, confidere, certum esse, sperare, non metuere, quæ sine voluntate obediente in homine non sunt, ut hic habet Coccejus. Atque ita titulus propositioni, & tractationi Apostolicæ congruit. Alii reddunt, ut gentes obediant fidei, voce hac objectivè accepta pro fide, quæ creditur, vel doctrina fidei. Sed res eodem recidit.

## 1:5
ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν.

Among all nations.

He understands not only the nations, but γενικῶς, all peoples, Jews equally and nations: because his Apostleship extended also to the Jews, and here it is described generally, even though it is meanwhile certain that he was peculiarly the Apostle of the nations by agreement, Rom. XI. 19, ch. XV. 16, Gal. II. 7, 1 Tim. II. 7, 2 Tim. I. 11.

ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ.

To the glory of Christ, 2 Cor. IV. 5, 1 Thess. I. 12.

The Greek Scholia not inappropriately refer it to the obedience of faith, or of the doctrine concerning faith, which is concerning the name of Christ, Acts X. 43, although it can also be taken τελικῶς for his name, or to the glory of the name of Christ: because the name of Christ is the object of saving faith, and the glory of Christ is the end of the same.

Latin:

ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν.

Apud omnes gentes.

Non tantùm gentes, sed γενικῶς, omnes populos, Judæos pariter & gentes intelligit: quia Apostola- tus ejus ad Judæos etiam se porrigebat, & hic ge- neratim describitur, etsi interim certum, quod pe- culiariter Apostolus gentium fuerit ex conventione Ro. XI. 19. c. XV. 16. Gal. II. 7. 1. Tim. II. 7. 2. Tim. I. 11.

ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ.

Ad gloriam Christi, 2. Cor. IV. 5. 1. Thess. I. 12.

Græcorum Scholia non incommodè referunt ad obedientiam fidei, vel doctrinæ de fide, quæ est de nomine Christi, Act. X. 43. quamvis etiam τελι- κῶς accipi possit pro nomine ejus, vel ad gloriam nominis Christi: quia Christi nomen est objectum fidei salvificæ, & gloria Christi est finis ejusdem.

## 1:6
V. 6. ἐν οἷς ἐστε καὶ ὑμεῖς.

You Romans, who came from Paganism to Christianity, such as Epaenetus, Amplias, Urbanus, Stachys, and others, who are named at the end of this Epistle.

Not only are the Romans who were converted from paganism pointed out, much less only those who are named at the end of the Epistle; but all who were at Rome, whether converted to the faith of Christ from the nations or from the Jews, as is evident from v. 7.

κλητοὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) The Apostle often adds this κλητοὶ when speaking to the faithful, so that they might understand that all their amendment and hope is from the most generous benefit of GOD, who had called them from on high while they were wrapped in grave crimes.

Latin:

V. 6. ἐν οἷς ἐστε καὶ ὑμεῖς.

Vos Romani, qui ex Paganismo ad Christianismum venistis, quales Epænetus, Amplias, Urbanus, Stachys, & alii, qui nominantur in fine hujus Epistolæ.

Non tantùm Romani indigitantur ex paganismo conversi, nedum illi soli, qui in fine Epistolæ nomi- nantur; sed omnes, qui Romæ erant, sive è genti- bus, sive è Judæis ad fidem Christi conversi, ut è v. 7. constat.

κλητοὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Sæpe hoc κλητοὶ addit Apostolus fidelibus loquens, ut intelligerent, omnem suam emenda- tionem & spem esse ex liberalissimo DEI beneficio, qui cri- minibus gravibus involutos ex alto vocasset.

## 1:7
v. 7. πᾶσι τοῖς ὖσιν ἐν Ῥώμῃ) Both to Jews and to those born elsewhere: and to those placed in dignity and to private citizens: and to the free-born and to freedmen and to slaves. For all are equal in Christ.

κλητοῖς ἁγίοις) He names both the benefit and the duty at the same time. It is the custom of epistles to place the dative with a verb understood.

χάρις ὑμῖν) That is, the favor, namely of GOD and of Christ as follows: that is to say, may it be present

And peace.

שלום all prosperous things. See Matt. X. 13. Mark V. 34. Luke VII. 50. VIII. 48. X. 5. XI. 21. XVI. 32. John XX. 2.

Just as by the name of grace is understood the gratuitous favor of GOD, the source of all benefits, by which He embraces us in Christ, forgiving our sins, and not indeed the benefits conferred out of grace metonymically, as Estius and Cornelius wish: so by the name of peace is indicated the peace of conscience, peace in God and with God, which arises from the reconciliation of GOD, as a consequence of Justification, Rom. V. 1. c. XIV 17. Luke XXIV. 36. John XX. 19. as is especially evident from the Apostolic wish in Phil. IV. 7., even though it is also customary among the Hebrews to wish for and include under the name of peace all prosperous things, and benefits both bodily and spiritual, Gen. XLIII. 27. Ps. CXIX. 165. Rightly Jerome in Epist. ad Cypr. Presbyt. All the Epistles of Paul at the beginning of the salutation do not have peace first, and thus grace, but before grace, and thus peace: so that with our sins forgiven we may obtain the peace of the Lord. Which he wishes from GOD as our author and Father, who adopted us as sons, and from Christ the Lord, as our Mediator and Redeemer, who by His death merited these things for us, and claimed us for Himself as His own possession.

PART II. THE EXORDIUM OF THE EPISTLE.

Latin:

v. 7. πᾶσι τοῖς ὖσιν ἐν Ῥώμῃ) Et Judæis & aliunde ortis: & in dignitate positis & privatis: & ingenuis & li- bertinis & servis. Omnes enim in Christo pares.

κλητοῖς ἁγίοις) Simul nominat & beneficium & officium. Dativum verbo subaudito ponete mos est epistolarum.

χάρις ὑμῖν) Id est favor nempe DEI & Christi ut sequitur: adsit scilicet

Καὶ εἰρήνη.

שלום prospera omnia. Vid. Matth. X. 13. Mar- ci V. 34. Luc. VII. 50. VIII. 48. X. 5. XI. 21. XVI. 32. Joh. XX. 2.

Uti gratiæ nomine gratuitus DEI favor, fons omnium beneficiorum, quo nos in Christo com- plectitur, peccata nobis remittens, intelligitur, non verò beneficia ex gratia collata μετωνυμικῶς, ut Estius, & Cornelius volunt: ita pacis nomine pax conscientiæ, pax in Deo & cum Deo, quæ ex reconci- liatione DEI oritur; indigitatur, ceu consequens Justificationis, Rom. V. 1. c. XIV 17. Luc. XXIV. 36. Joh. XX. 19. ut imprimis è voto Apostolico Phil. IV. 7. constat, etsi soleant etiam Ebræis pacis nomine voveri, & comprehendi prospera omnia, ac beneficia tàm corporalia, quàm spiritualia, Gen. XLIII. 27. Ps. CXIX. 165. Rectè Hieron. in Epist. ad Cypr. Presbyt. Omnes Epistolæ Pauli in salutationis principio non prius pacem habent, & sic gratiam, sed ante gratiam, & sic pacem: ut donatis nobis peccatis nostris pacem Domini consequamur. Quæ optat à DEO tanquam autore & Patre nostro, qui in filios nos adoptavit, & à Christo Domino, tanquam Mediatore & Redemtore nostro, qui morte sua nobis ea promeruit, sibique nos in peculium asseruit.

PARS II. EXORDIUM EPISTOLÆ.

## 1:8
V. 8. Πρῶτον.

It is the word of one beginning an Epistle. For until now there was the inscription. A similar Exordium of speech is in John VIII. 25.

It is not so much the word of one beginning, and of order, as of intention, and the same as 'first of all,' as also in John IX. 25. τὴν ἀρχήν. For before all things he gives thanks, as in other Epistles, 1 Cor. I. 4. Phil. I. 3. Col. I. 3. 1 Thess. I. 2. 2 Thess. I. 3. which he also warned ought to be done in 1 Thess. V. 18. Yet here begins the Exordium of the Epistle, in which he congratulates the Romans on their knowledge of the Gospel and their faith, and sets forth his desire to visit them, and explains why he has not yet come.

I give thanks to my God.

Chrysostom notes here and in the former to the Corinthians, that it is a sign of great affection, that he makes Him who is the God of all his own. That is frequent in David. Thus out of affection GOD calls Himself the GOD of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The fathers of the Old Testament gave thanks for earthly goods. The Apostles for those things which pertained to the glory of God even with their own greatest inconveniences and dangers.

The pronoun is of faith apprehending, and applying to itself the grace of GOD, as its own, John XX. 28. Gal. II. 20. as GOD has testified that He would be the GOD of the faithful, Gen. XVII. and He has everywhere professed Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of the Israelites. Wrongly, and in a Pelagian and Socinian spirit, Grotius here [says] that the Fathers of the O.T. gave thanks for earthly goods, [and] the Apostles for those things which pertained to the glory of GOD even with their own inconveniences. For what, did not the faithful of the O.T. also receive spiritual goods, and if they received them, were they ungrateful, and did they not give thanks to GOD for them equally as for earthly goods? Did they not also look to the glory of GOD in all things, and for His sake undergo even inconveniences and dangers? The whole History of the O.T. testifies to the contrary, as well as ch. XI of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and many other things here and there in the N.T.

through Jesus Christ) Just as Christians pray to the Father through Christ, so also through Christ they give thanks: that is, they acknowledge the benefits of the Father given to them through Christ. See John XIV. 14.

That your faith is spoken of in the whole world.

With great joy of the provincial Christians was that news received, that even at Rome, in the capital of the Empire, there were those who professed the same faith.

The announcement or report is not so much regarded as the truth of the same: consequently, the antecedent is given to be understood: namely, that their faith is such that it deservedly may be celebrated in the whole world.

Latin:

V. 8. Πρῶτον.

Est vox incipientis Epistolam. Nam hactenus inscriptio fuit. Simile sermonis Exordium Joh. VIII. 25.

Non tàm vox incipientis est, & ordinis, quàm intentionis, & idem quod imprimis, uti etiam Joh. IX. 25. τὴν ἀρχήν. Ante omnia enim gratias agit, ut in aliis Epistolis, 1. Cor. I. 4. Phil. I. 3. Col. I. 3. 1. Thess. I. 2. 2. Thess. I. 3. quod etiam fieri debere monuit 1. Thess. V. 18. Incipit tamèn hîc Epistolæ Exordium, quo gratulatur Romanis de cognitione Evangelii, ac fide, & desiderium eos invisendi exponit, atque excusat, cùr nondum venerit.

εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ μȣ.

Notat Chrysostomus hic & in priorem ad Corinthios, magni esse affectus, quod eum, qui est omnium Deus, sibi facit proprium. Frequens id in Davide. Sic ex affectu DEUS se DEUM dicit Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi. Gratias agebant patres Veteris Testamenti pro bonis terrenis. Apostoli pro iis, quæ ad Dei gloriam etiam cum ipsorum maximis incommodis & periculis pertinebant.

Pronomen est fidei apprehendentis, & applicantis sibi DEI gratiam, ceu propriam, Joh. XX. 28. Gal. II. 20. uti testatus est DEUS, se fidelium DEUM fore, Gen. XVII. & se Deum Abrahæ, Isaac, & Jacobi, Deum Israëlitarum passim professus est. Perperam, & Pelagiano, ac Sociniano Spiritu Grotius hîc Patres V. T. pro bonis terrenis gratias egisse, Apostolos pro iis, quæ ad DEI gloriam etsi cum ipsorum incommodis pertinebant. Quid enim, annon etiam fideles V. T. accepêre bona Spiritualia, & si accepêre, num ingrati fuerunt, neque DEO gratias æquè pro illis, ac terrenis bonis egerunt? annon & illi gloriam DEI spectarunt in omnibus, ejusque causâ etiam incommoda & pericula subierunt? Contrarium tota Historia V. T. testatur, nec non c. XI. Epist. ad Ebr. & multa alia passim in N. T.

διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Christiani sicut Patrem precantur per Christum, ita & per Christum gratias agunt: id est, agnoscunt beneficia Patris sibi per Christum data. Vide Joh. XIV. 14.

Ὅτι ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν καταγγέλλεται ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ.

Magno cum gaudio Provincialium Christianorum acceptus fuit ille nuncius, etiam Romæ, in capite Imperii, esse, qui eandem fidem profiterentur.

Non tàm respicitur annunciatio vel fama illa, quàm veritas ejusdem: ex consequenti intelligendum datur antecedens: quod nempe ipsorum fides talis sit, quæ meritò in toto orbe celebretur.

## 1:9
for God is my witness) This has the force of an oath: but in a most certain matter and one pertaining to GOD. See what we have said at Matt. V. 34.

v. 9. whom I serve in my spirit.

That is, with a willing mind, not resisting like Jonah. This is from the soul, Eph. VI. 6.

Not only voluntary service, that he did not wish to resist like Jonah, but religious worship is primarily designated, because in Spirit and truth, not by external work alone, he serves GOD with serious and sincere zeal, unfeignedly and unadulteratedly, John IV. 23.

in the gospel of his Son. I serve God, not by teaching legal rites, but a doctrine much more heavenly.

The Gospel is distinguished not only from legal rites, although these too were handed down from heaven, and in respect of author and origin there is no difference between legal rites and the Gospel; but also from the moral law, and indeed from the promise in the prophetic Old Testament. The Gospel of the Son of God is, however, called objective, because it is about the Son of God: although it is also from the Son of God, as its author, which it has in common with the law of God and prophecy.

that without ceasing I make mention of you) A sign of great affection, to remember friends in prayers not occasionally, but perpetually. You have similar passages in 1 Thess. 1:3, 2:13, 5:17, 2 Tim. 1:3.

Latin:

μάρτυς γάρ μου ἐστιν ὁ Θεός) Juramenti hoc vim habet: sed in re certissima & ad DEUM pertinente. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. V. 34.

v. 9. ᾧ λατρεύω ἐν τῷ πνεύματί μου.

Id est, volente animo, non renitens ut Jonas. Hoc est ἐκ ψυχῆς, Eph. VI. 6.

Non tantum voluntarium servitium, quod non reniti voluerit ut Jonas, sed cultus religiosus imprimis designatur, quod in Spiritu, & veritate, non externo tantum opere, DEO serio & sincero studio ἀνυποκρίτως, καὶ ἀκιβδήλως serviat, Joh. IV. 23.

ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τῦ ὑῦ αὐτῦ. Servio Deo, non docendo ritus legales, sed doctri- nam multò cœlestiorem.

Evangelium non tantùm à ritibus legalibus distinguitur, quamvis & hi cœlitùs traditi erant, ac ratione autoris & originis differentia nulla sit inter ritus legales, & Evangelium; sed à lege etiam mo- rali, nec non ab ἐπαγγελίᾳ vel promissione in V. T. Prophetica. Evangelium autem Filii DEI ob- jectivè dicitur, quod sit de Filio DEI: etsi etiam idem à Filio DEI, ceu autore sit, quod cum lege DEI ac Prophetiâ ipsi commune est.

ὡς ἀδιαλείπτως μνήμην ὑμῶν ποιῦμαι) Magni affe- ctus signum non interdum, sed perpetuo amicorum in pre- cibus meminisse. Similia habes 1. Thessal. I. 3. II. 13. V. 37. 2. Tim. I. 3.

## 1:10
v. 10. if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will of God, to come unto you) That 'if by any means' signifies that Paul was not certain whether he would obtain what he was praying for. Therefore he teaches us to pray under such a condition, if it be for the glory of God. 'To have a prosperous journey' is a frequent verb in the interpreters of the Old Testament, noted also by us often in the books of Tobit, Wisdom, Sirach, and Maccabees, corresponding to several Hebrew words, most frequently the word צלח. Therefore the sense is, I labor in my prayers, if by chance the will of God may grant me the happiness of coming to you. A similar construction is in 2 Macc. 10:23, 'to him who granted us the happiness of cleansing the Temple.' Thus also 'salvation' and 'rest' are said to 'have a prosperous journey' (prosper), Sirach 38:14 and Maccabees 3:16. 'Will of God' regarding the providence of God directing our affairs is used also by Ignatius to the Trallians, speaking of Polybius's arrival at Smyrna.

Latin:

v. 10. εἴπως ἤδη ποτὲ εὐοδωθήσομαι ἐν τῷ θελήματι τῦ θεῦ, ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Illud εἴπως significat non certum fuisse Paulum, an quod precabatur, consecuturus esset. Itaque docet nos orare tali sub conditione si id è gloria sit DEI. εὐοδῦν verbum est frequens in interpretibus Veteris Testamenti, notatum quoque à nobis sæpe in Tobia, Sapi- entiæ & Sirachidæ libris ac Maccabaicis, respondens He- bræis aliquot verbis, frequentissime verbo צלח. Itaque sensus est, laboro precibus meis, si forte DEI voluntas fe- licitatem mihi indulgeat ad vos veniendi. Similis con- structio 2. Macc. X. 23. τῷ εὐοδώσαντι καταρισθῆναι : qui felicitatem nobis dedit mundandi Templum. Sic & σω- τηρία & ἀνάπαυσις dicuntur εὐοδῦσθαι, Sirach. XXXVIII. 14. & Maccab. III. 16. θέλημα θεῦ de providentia DEI res nostras dirigente usurpat & Ignatius ad Trallenses de Poly- bii adventu Smyrnam agens.

## 1:11
v. 11. That I may impart unto you some spiritual gift) Not that I may receive something, for which reason most people come to Rome, but that I may give, and give not earthly things, but spiritual. He could have said doctrine, revelation, prophecy, but he prefers to use the word 'gift' (charisma), so that by his own example he may teach modesty.

to the end you may be established) He hints more than he expresses that the Romans were still tender in the faith. Thus also below 16:25, 1 Thess. 3:13, 1 Peter 5:12, Rev. 3:2, and elsewhere.

Latin:

v. 11. Ἱνα τι μεταδῶ χάρισμα ὑμῖν πνευματικὸν) Non ut accipiam aliquid, qua de causa plerique Romam ve- niunt, sed ut dem, & dem non terrena, sed spiritualia. Potuerat dicere doctrinam, revelationem, prophetiam, sed mavult usurpare vocabulum χαρίσματος, ut suo exemplo modestiam doceat.

εἰς τὸ στηριχθῆναι ὑμᾶς) Teneros adhuc fuisse Ro- manos in fide, innuit magis, quàm exprimit. Sic & infra XVI. 25. 1. Thess. III. 3. 1 Petri V. 20. Apoc. III. 2. & alibi.

## 1:12
v. 12. that is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me) Here 'to be comforted together' is governed by 'I long.' He softens what he had said by showing that not only would he bring some joy to them, but they also to him. He said 'in one another' improperly for 'in both,' in me and you. Demosthenes said this too, 'things toward one another.'

Latin:

v. 12. τῦτο δέ ἐστι συμπαρακληθῆναι ἐν ὑμῖν διὰ τῆς ἐν ἀλλήλοις πίστεως ὑμῶν τε καὶ ἐμῦ) Hic συμπαρακληθῆναι re- gitur ab ἐπιποθῶ. Emollit, quod dixerat, ostendendo non se tantùm illis, sed & illos sibi aliquid gaudii allaturos, ἐν ἀλλήλοις impropriè dixit pro in utrisque, in me & vobis. Dixit sic & Demosthenes, τὰ πρὸς ἀλλήλυς.

## 1:13
v. 13. and was let hitherto) Many have rightly warned that these things should be read parenthetically. For the preceding and following parts cohere with each other. He says this: The will to come to you was not lacking in me, although without success. But he had been hindered by other more urgent business of the Gospel, as he himself explains below 15:22. See a similar passage in Acts 16:6, 7. The necessity of the places in which Christ was unknown was more urgent.

That I might have some fruit among you) This fruit, of which he speaks, is both the increase of the Church through Apostolic miracles and the confirmation of the weak.

As even among the other Gentiles) He shows that he will not be useless to the Romans, since he had already been useful to many other nations: as he will say below 15:18, 19.

Latin:

v. 13. καὶ ἐκωλύθην ἄχρι τῦ δεῦρο) Rectè monuere complures hæc παρενθετικῶς legenda. Nam priora & po steriora inter se cohærent. Hoc dicit: Voluntas mihi non defuit ad vos veniendi, quanquam sine successu. Impe- ditus autem fuerat per alia negotia Evangelii magis urgen- tia, ut ipse explicat infra XV. 22. Simile vide Act. XVI. 6. 7. Magis urgebat necessitas locorum, in quibus Chri- stus erat ignotus.

Ἱνα καρπόν τινα σχῶ ἐν ὑμῖν) Fructus hic, de quo agit, est cùm incrementum Ecclesiæ per miracula Apostoli- ca, tum confirmatio infirmorum.

Καθὼς καὶ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσιν) Ostendit, non in- utilem se fore Romanis, cùm jam multis aliis gentibus fuisset utilis: ut dicet infra XV. 18. 19.

## 1:14
V. 14. both to the Greeks and to the Barbarians. Often the Apostles by synecdoche call all non-Judaizing people Greeks. But here Paul, adapting himself to the speech of the Greeks, distinguishes the human race into Greeks and Barbarians, as Thucydides does in the first book. Thus Ammonius: 'Barbarians, the non-Greek.' Plautus also calls the Romans barbarians. But Dionysius of Halicarnassus argues to the contrary in book 1, and proves that the Romans and other Italians are rather of Greek origin. But Paul here is not so much looking at origin as at customs; he calls those nations barbarian that were inferior, and those Greek that were more cultured. 'Greece, conquered, took the wild conqueror and brought arts to rustic Latium.' They are not called barbarians, as Grotius hints, so much because of their customs, as because of their foreign language, as is clear from 1 Cor. 14:11: for he does not look at more cultured and wilder customs; but he exhausts all peoples with this distinction, imitating the custom of the Greeks. For as the Hebrews call all other nations 'foreign' (la'az), Ps. 114:1, so the Greeks call other peoples barbarians. Strabo book 4.

Speaking with a thick mouth, he says, they called them barbarians at first, as if reproaching the harshness and roughness of their speech; then we abused it as a common gentile name in the division of nations, opposing barbarians to Greeks.

σοφοῖς τε κᾐ ἀνοήτοις) Just as nations differ in their customs, so too in their character: you would swear a Boeotian was born in thick air. The Apostle signifies, however, that the Gospel is so adapted to all men that it neither despises the stupid nor should it be despised by the ingenious.

ὀφειλέτης εἰμὶ) Namely, by the command of GOD, by which Paul was so obligated that he could not decline it without grave sin. 1 Cor. 9:16. A similar use of this noun is below in 15:27.

ὕτως) Just as I have preached the Gospel to other nations, so I wished to preach it to you also. For this ὕτως refers to that which preceded in verse 13.

Latin:

V. 14. ἕλλησί τε καὶ βαρβάροις. Sæpius Apostoli per συνεκδοχὴν omnes non Judai- zantes Græcos vocant. Sed hic Paulus Græcorum se locu- tioni aptans, humanum genus distinguit in Græcos & Bar- baros, ut Thucydides libro primo. Sic Ammonius: βάρ- βαροι, τὸ ἐχύ ἑλληνικόν. Etiam Romanos Plautus vocat bar- baros. Sed in contrarium disputat Dionysius Halicarnaf- sensis lib. 1. probatque Romanos, Italosque alios Græcæ magis esse originis. At Paulus non tàm hic originem re- spiciens, quàm mores, barbaras gentes vocat illas inferio- res, Græcas quæ cultiores essent. Græcia victa ferum victorem cepit & artes Intulit agresti Latio. Non tàm ob mores, ut Grotius innuit, bar- bari dicti non Græci, quàm ob peregrinam lin- guam, ut è 1. Cor. XIV. 11. liquet: nec enim cul- tiores & feriores mores respicit; sed omnès po- pulos hâc distinctione exhaurit, Græcorum mo- rem imitatus. Nam ut Ebræi reliquas gentes omnes לעז peregrinas vocant, Ps. CXIV. 1. sic Græ- ci reliquos populos dicunt barbaros. Strabo l. IV.

Crasso, inquit, loquentes ore initio vocarunt bar- baros, tanquam deductionem asperitatemque oris exprobrantes, deinde tanquam communi gentili nomine abusi sumus in nationum divisione, bar- baros Græcis opponentes.

σοφοῖς τε κᾐ ἀνοήτοις) Sicut moribus differunt gen- tes, ita & ingenio: Bœotam in crasso jurares aere natum. Significat autem Apostolus ita omnibus hominibus aptatum esse Evangelium, ut nec stupidos contemnat, nec ab ingeniosis contemni debeat.

ὀφειλέτης εἰμὶ) Nempe ex DEI imperio, quo obli- gatus ita erat Paulus, ut sine gravi crimine derrectare id non posset. 1. Cor. IX, 16. Similis usus nominis hujus in- fra XV. 27.

ὕτως) Sicut aliis gentibus Evangelium prædicavi, sic & vobis prædicare volui. Refertur enim hoc ὕτως ad id, quod præcessit commate 13.

## 1:15
v. 15. τὸ κατ᾽ ἐμὲ πρόθυμον) What is in my power, that is ready. Thus Plato said τὸ πρόθυμον παρεχόμενοι in the Laws, by metalepsis, of course.

Καὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐν Ῥώμῃ) I am no light-shunner; I showed that at Antioch, Athens, Ephesus, and Corinth: I am prepared to show it also in that most splendid city, Rome.

ἐ γὰρ ἐπαισχύνομαι τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τῦ χριςῦ) It is a metalepsis; I do not hide the Gospel of Christ, as those things of which we are ashamed are wont to be hidden. Let the initiates of Ceres and Liber and Libera among the Greeks, or the mystae and mystides of the Bona Dea at Rome, do this.

PART III. PROPOSITION.

Latin:

v. 15. τὸ κατ᾽ ἐμὲ πρόθυμον) Quod meæ est potesta- tis, id paratum est. Sic τὸ πρόθυμον παρεχόμενοι dixit Plato in legibus, per μετάληψιν scilicet.

Καὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐν Ῥώμῃ) Lucifuga non sum, ostendi id Antiochiæ, Athenis, Ephesi & Corinthi: paratus sum & in illa splendidissima urbe Roma ostendere.

ἐ γὰρ ἐπαισχύνομαι τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τῦ χριςῦ) Est με- τάληψις, Non occulto Evangelium Christi, sicut occultari solent quorum nos pudet. Hoc faciant Cereris & Liberi Liberæque apud Græcos aut Romæ Bonæ Deæ mystæ ac mystides.

PARS III. PROPOSITIO.

## 1:16
vers. 16. δύναμις γάρ Θεῦ ἐςὶν εἰς σωτηρίαν. God has never acted more powerfully to heal the souls of men, which is the way to eternal salvation, than now through the Gospel. So great a force of miracles has shone upon it and still shines. Therefore, it is called the arm of God in the mystical sense of Isaiah 53:1. See also 1 Cor. 1:18.

The proposition embraces the argument of the Epistle, which is the righteousness of faith revealed in the Gospel: to which, mention of the Gospel having been made, he adds: and the Apostle illustrates it with a Prophetic oracle: so that he may declare and establish what he had said in verse 2 concerning the Gospel foretold by the prophets. While, however, he calls the Gospel the power of GOD unto salvation, he does not imply that God acted powerfully at that time to lead men to salvation through the Gospel by employing signs and miracles: because it is not the power of miracles that is indicated here, but the Gospel itself is called the power of GOD, nor are miracles given for the sake of believers, but for the sake of unbelievers, 1 Cor. 14:22. Moreover, the Gospel is the power unto salvation to those who believe: it was not power only at that time, when it was attended by miracles, but from the very πρωτευαγγελίῳ, when indeed they did not have the ἐν- αγγέλιον or the very broad message concerning the Messiah exhibited, which was reserved for the New Testament, Ps. LXVIII. 12, Is. LII. 7, Luke V. 10, yet the ancients were not destitute of the ἐυαγγελίῳ, as it denotes a sermon of thanks concerning the remission of sins, Acts XV. 10, and they had Evangelical promises concerning grace and salvation, and also the ἐπαγγελίαν concerning the Messiah to come, in whom all promises are yea and amen, 2 Cor. I. 20, which were to them the power unto salvation: and thus even now the Gospel of God is power to us, where miracles have now ceased: nor finally does faith arise from prodigies, but through the word, and from the hearing of the word: Rom. X. 17. For although the word is confirmed by prodigies, so that assent may be given to it, yet that both assent, such as is required, and trust arise, there is need of the Holy Spirit, which He works not through miracles, but through the word. And therefore we are regenerated through the word of truth, James I. 18, and we are reborn from the word as from incorruptible seed, 1 Pet. I. 23. Miracles, however, are not the seed or the medium of our regeneration. And for that reason the word is called δύναμις Θεῦ, because it is excellently δυνατὸς or efficacious, the abstract being put for the concrete: as 1 Cor. I. 18. 2 Cor. 5:21. Eph. 5:8. It is called both Spirit and life, because it is spiritual, or rather animated and full of the Spirit, and truly living, and life-giving. John 6:36. It is not indeed a substantial or hypostatic power, just as Christ is called the power of God, Luke 1:37 and 1 Cor. 1:24, and the arm of God, Isa. 53:1, which latter passages Grotius rashly explains concerning the Gospel. It is, however, truly the power of God, not indeed materially by reason of the letters, the strokes, and the external sound, but formally, by reason of the divine sense understood, because it is θεόπνευστον [God-breathed], and through θεοπνευσία [divine inspiration] animated by divine power for illumination, conversion, vivification, and salvation, because through the word divine benefits are not only offered, but conferred; the mind is not only taught, but illuminated; the heart is not only moved, but converted; the Spirit is not only excited, but renewed; we are not only affected by the consolation of life, but truly vivified, nor are we only recalled into spiritual life through the power of the word, but we are also preserved for eternal life. Therefore, through the word, faith is kindled, John 17:20; through the word we are illuminated, 2 Pet. 1:29; through the word we are regenerated, Phil. 1:16; through the word we are purified, John 15:3; through the word we are sanctified, John 17:17; through the word we are saved, 1 Cor. 1:21. The word is the odor of life unto life, 2 Cor. 2:16. Rightly Ambrose at this place: The Apostolic preaching is the power of God, which invites to faith and gives salvation to every believer, while it forgives sins and justifies, so that he cannot be held by the second death. Therefore, this designates the first act and the intrinsic efficacy of the Gospel, which is not only objective and representative, like that of an image or a statue of Mercury, but effective, proportioned to conversion and salvation, because it is the power of God unto salvation.
