Nor is the power of informing attributed to the Gospel, as Socinus, the Arminians, and Schwenkfeld wish, but the power of converting; nor is it ascribed to it only for the sake of honoring it, as Calvin says, but it belongs to it truly and properly as an organic cause, to which the effect is altogether properly attributed. Cocceius confesses this in his Commentary. p. 43. when the Gospel is called the power of God, it is signified that it is a suitable instrument for converting souls and saving them, and that it attains that effect. But what he adds, that this happens because of the power or the efficacious will of God, of which this preaching is the instrument and ὄργανον [organ/tool], in that he does not exhaust the force of the Apostolic sentence: for this makes the Gospel itself the power of God, and does not distinguish power from the Gospel, nor does it make the power the will of God. For there lies hidden in it the τὸ ὕπουλον [the festering sore] of absolute grace: by the force of which the Calvinists do not leave this efficacy to the Gospel as if it were intrinsic, but wish the power of the Spirit to be added extrinsically in the absolutely elect, from an absolute good pleasure, whence Cocceius also denies, p. 44, that faith is from hearing alone, and requires the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as if the Holy Spirit did not work through the Gospel, but there were some immediate cooperation of his when the Gospel is preached; nor does faith arise from the proclamation of the Gospel unless that immediate operation is added, concerning which error see the Theol. Apost. Rom. art. 7 and System. Theol. Vol. 1.

To everyone who believes.

Just as medicine does not profit unless it is swallowed, so neither does the Gospel unless faith is had in it. For faith is the medium of salvation on our part, just as the word of the Gospel is on the part of God. And the proposition of the Epistle is contained in this Aphorism: namely, in this 16th and the following 17th theme. That the Gospel of Christ, or concerning Christ, is endowed with divine efficacy to confer salvation, both spiritual and eternal, to all who believe: without distinction of persons, whether they be Jews or Greeks, whether circumcised or uncircumcised: for the reason that in it the righteousness of God is revealed, proposed, offered, and conferred upon us, which is from faith to faith, according to the Prophetic promise, which Habakkuk has summarized: the just shall live by faith. In which aphorism the method of obtaining salvation through its causes is most briefly handed down: namely, that the principal efficient cause is God, whose word and power the Gospel is; the meritorious cause is Christ, because the Gospel is concerning Christ; the organic cause on the part of God is the word of the Gospel, as it reveals the righteousness of God; on our part it is faith, apprehending the righteousness of God revealed in the Gospel, and indeed the only one, because the GOSPEL is the power of GOD unto salvation to every BELIEVER: and the righteousness revealed in the Gospel is FROM FAITH TO FAITH, and the just shall live not by works, but by FAITH. The material cause is man, a sinner to be saved, or in need of salvation, without distinction of persons: the formal cause is the righteousness of God, apprehended by true faith: the final cause is life and eternal salvation. Therefore, the Gospel in this place is not the announcement of Christ exhibited, but the proclamation of grace and the remission of sins in Christ, who was to be exhibited in the Old Testament, and has been exhibited in the New, and in both he is proposed as the proper object of the Gospel and of faith. If the announcement of Christ exhibited is understood precisely, the Gospel was not in the Old Testament the power of God unto salvation. Therefore, one must either designate another medium in the Old Testament, or the Gospel concerning Christ was the medium of salvation for them. And the Apostle here treats universally of the article concerning justification by faith, and concerning the righteousness of faith proposed and revealed in the Gospel, abstracting from men of either the Old or the New Testament: since it is a general demonstration, and the same grace of our Lord Jesus Christ was necessary in both, Acts 15:10. Therefore he immediately alleges the Prophet as a witness, Hab. 2:4, just as St. Peter praised all the Prophets as witnesses to that matter, Acts 10:43; indeed, Paul also testifies in chapter 3:21 below, that the law, or the Mosaic and Prophetic writings alike, bear witness concerning this righteousness of God, which he says is revealed in the Gospel. It must therefore have been already handed down and made manifest in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, not finally by the Evangelists and Apostles in the New Testament. The Gospel must also have been proposed there concerning the righteousness of faith in Christ: or else the power of God unto salvation would have been lacking there, and the foundation of faith, from which saving faith is uniquely drawn, would have been lacking. Therefore, the voice of the Gospel is not to be taken here restrictively with Cocceius, for the announcement of Christ exhibited, but generally for the preaching of grace in Christ, so that the believers of the Old Testament may not be excluded from the Gospel, which is the power unto salvation, and from faith in the Gospel, through which is salvation, and the righteousness of faith, which is revealed in the Gospel. Nor is there any reason why we should distinguish revelation from indication with him, as if the righteousness of God were indeed indicated by Moses and the Prophets, but first revealed in the Gospel in the New Testament, so that the revelation of righteousness might denote the exhibition of that which was lacking for its perfect knowledge, preparation, and fullest fruit on earth. For although revelation in the New Testament is clearer, fuller, and more common, yet revelation of righteousness was not lacking in the Old Testament: just as the Apostle proves it here immediately from the Old Testament, as it is written. And was not that prophetic indication a revelation? was not righteousness revealed to the Prophets, and through the Prophets and prophetic writings to others, who heard and read them, and conceived faith from them? Or could faith have had a place without divine revelation? Certainly no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to ἀποκαλύψαι reveal, Matt. XI, 27. Or therefore The ancients did not know the Son, or have the ἀποκάλυψιν (revelation). Conf. Ps. V. 9. XL. 11. Isa. LIII. 1. 11. Jer. XXIII. 6. Dan. IX. 24. It was indeed revealed to the Prophets, and by them to the people, to the end that eternal righteousness was to be brought in by Christ, so that they might then apprehend it when revealed through faith, and live by it, not that it was reserved only for the faithful in the New Testament, which is the heresy of the Socinians. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. XIII. 8. And the Lamb of God was slain from the foundation of the world, Rev. XIII. 8, whence it is called the eternal Gospel, Rev. XIV. 6. And just as the whole Scripture, so also the Scripture of the Old Testament is distinguished into Law and Gospel, which are the two parts of the divine word, and thus the Gospel cannot be excluded from the Scripture of the Old Testament.

To the Jew first.

For the Gospel had to be announced to the Jews first by Jesus himself and to be announced by the Apostles, Acts III. 25, 26; XIII. 46. A similar expression below II. 9, 10, 11; Acts XVIII. 5.

Not that there is any distinction of persons with God, Acts X. 34; Rom. II. 2. But because the Messiah was promised peculiarly to the Patriarchs and Hebrews, Israelites, and Jews, and he came first to them, c. XV. 8, lest the Jews should now seem to be absolutely excluded from salvation. What that τό πρῶτον (the first) is, he explains at the beginning of c. IX; why he did not neglect it here in the proposition, the ἐξεργασία (elaboration) of c. IX, X, and XI teaches. Moreover, it is fitting for the Jews by reason of order, from the ὀικονομίᾳ (economy) of God, as those from whom the Gospel went forth, Isa. II. 3; Mic. IV. 2; Ps. CX. 2.

And to the Greek.

He speaks here in the Jewish manner. For the Jews knew the Greeks better, especially after the empires of the Macedonians.

Grotius thinks this opposition of Greeks and Jews is made because the Greeks were better known to the Jews than other nations: but that distribution, or manner of speaking, was not accepted only among the Jews, so that by that distribution of Jews and Greeks all peoples were accustomed to be comprehended. Therefore, by the name of Greeks, the Apostle embraces the Gentiles, and indeed all peoples who were distinguished from the Jews, Ps. CXLVII. 19, 20; Gal. III. 28, just as he deals later with Jews and Gentiles concluded under sin. For the Gospel is destined for salvation to those who are concluded under condemnation by the law, whether prescribed by Moses or only inscribed on the heart, that is, both to Jews and to Gentiles.

Latin:

vers. 16. δύναμις γάρ Θεῦ ἐςὶν εἰς σωτηρίαν. Nunquam potentius Deus id egit, ut hominum ani- mos sanaret, quæ via est ad salutem æternam, quàm nunc per Evangelium. Tanta ei affulsit & adhuc affulget vis mi- raculorum. Ideò brachium Dei dicitur sensu mystico E- saiæ LIII. 1. Vid. & 1. Cor. I. 18.

Propositio Epistolæ argumentum complecti- tur, quod est justitia fidei in Evangelio revelata: ad quam mentione Evangelii factâ accedit: eam- que illustrat Apostolus oraculo Prophetico: ut quod dixerat Versic. 2. de Evangelio prænuncia- to per prophetas, declaret ac stabiliat. Dum au- tem Evangelium potentiam DEI dicit ad salutem, non id innuit, quod potenter Deus id egerit isto tempore, ut homines ad salutem perduceret per Ev- angelium, adhibitis signis, & miraculis: quia non miraculorum δύναμις hic indigitatur, sed Evan- gelium ipsum δύναμις Θεῦ dicitur, nec miracula propter credentes, sed propter incredulos dantur, 1. Cor. XIV. 22. Evangelium autem credentibus potentia est ad salutem: neque isto tantum tempo- re potentia fuit, cùm miraculis stiparetur, sed in- de ab ipso πρωτευαγγελίῳ, cum non quidem ἐν- αγγέλιον vel ipsum latum nuncium de Messia exhi- bito habuerint, quod reservatum est Nov. Test. Psal. LXIIX. 12. Es. LII. 7. Luc. V. 10. ἐυαγγελίῳ tamen, ut concionem gratia de remissione peccato- rum notat, destituti non fuerint Veteres, Act. XV. 10. & promissiones Evangelicas habuerint de gratiâ, & salute, nec non ἐπαγγελίαν de Messia venturo, in quo omnes promissiones sunt na, & amen, 2. Cor. I. 20. quæ ipsis erant potentia ad salutem: atque ita etiamnum nobis Evangelium Dei potentia est, ubi jam cessarunt miracula: nec denique è prodi- giis fides oritur, sed per verbum, & ex auditu verbi: Rom. X. 17. Etsi enim per prodigia confirmetur verbum, ut eidem assensus præbeatur, tamen quod & assensus, qualis requiritur, & fiducia ori- tur, opus est Spiritûs S. quod non per miracula, sed per verbum ipse operatur. Ideoque per ver- bum veritatis regeneramur, Jac. I, 18. & ex verbo ceu semine incorruptibili renascimur, 1. Petr. I. 23. Miracula autem non sunt semen, aut medium no- stræ regenerationis. Atque eô nomine verbum di- citur δύναμις Θεῦ, quod sit excellenter δυνατὸς vel efficax, abstracto posito pro concreto: ut 1. Cor. I. 18. 2. Cor. V. 21. Eph. V. 8. dicitur & Spiritus & vita, quod Spirituale sit, vel potius Spiritu animatum & plenum, & verè vivum, ac vivificum. Joh. VI. 36. Non est quidem potentia substantialis, vel hypostatica, uti Christus virtus DEI dicitur Luc. I. 37. & 1. Cor. I. 24. ac brachium DEI Esa. LIII. 1. quæ posteriora loca temerè de Evangelio explicat Grotius. Est tamen vere potentia Dei, non qui- dem materialiter ratione literarum, apicum, & ex- terni soni, sed formaliter, ratione divini sensus in- tellectum, quia est θεόπνευστον, & per θεοπνευσίαν divinâ virtute animatum ad illuminationem, con- versionem, vivificationem & salutem, quia per ver- bum non offeruntur modò divina beneficia, sed conferuntur, non docetur tantum, sed illumina- tur animus; non movetur tantum, sed converti- tur cor, non excitatur tantum, sed renovatur Spi- ritus; non afficitur tantum solatio vitæ, sed revera vivificatur, nec tantum in vitam spiritualem revo- camur per verbi virtutem, sed conservamur etiam ad æternam vitam. Ideo per verbum fides accendi- tur Joh. XVII. 20. per verbum illuminamur 2. Petr. I. 29. per verbum regeneramur Phil. I. 16. per ver- bum purificamur Joh. XV. 3. per verbum sanctifi- camur, Joh. XVII. 17. per verbum salvamur 1. Cor. I. 21. Verbum est odor vitæ ad vitam 2. Cor. II. 16. Rectè Ambrof. ad h. l. Prædicatio Apostolica vir- tus DEI est, quæ invitat ad fidem & dat salutem omni credenti, dum peccata donat, & justificat, ut à secunda morte detineri non possit. Designatur er- go hic actus primus, & intrinseca efficacia Evan- gelii, quæ non est tantum objectiva & repræsenta- tiva, ut imaginis vel statuæ Mercurialis: sed effe- ctiva, proportionata ad conversionem, & salutem: quia potentia Dei ad salutem: Neque tantum vis informandi, ut Socin. Arminiani, Schwenkfeld. volunt, sed convertendi Evangelio tribuitur: nec id solum cohonestandi caussa adscribitur, ut Calvin. sed vere ac proprie ei convenit, ut caussæ organicæ: cui omnino effectus proprie tribuitur. Fatetur hic Coccejus in Comment. p. 43. quando Evange- lium dicitur potentia Dei, significari, id esse in- strumentum idoneum ad convertendum animas & eas salvandum, eumque effectum consequi. Quod v. addit id fieri propter potentiam sive vo- luntatem efficacem Dei, cujus hæc prædicatio in- strumentum atque ὄργανον est, in eo non exhaurit vim sententiæ Apostolicæ: hæc n. facit ipsum Ev- angelium potentiam Dei, non v. potentiam distin- guit ab Evangelio, nec potentiam facit voluntatem Dei. Latet enim in eo τὸ ὕπουλον absolutæ gratiæ: vi cujus non Evangelio hanc efficaciam, ceu intrin- secam relinquunt Calviniani, sed extrinsecus acce- dere volunt potentiam Spiritus in absolutè electis, ex absoluto beneplacito, unde etiam negat Cocce- jus p. 44. fidem esse ex auditu solo, & requirit coope- rationem S. S. quasi non per Evangelium operetur S. S. sed immediata ejus cooperatio quædam sit, cum prædicatur Evangelium; nec ex præconio Evangelii fides oriatur, nisi immediata illa opera- tio accedat, de quo errore Conf. Theol. Apost. Rom. ar. VII. & System. Theol. T. 1.

Πάντι τῷ πισέυοντι.

Sicut medicamentum non prodest nisi haustum, ita nec Evangelium nisi fides ei habeatur. Fides enim est medium salutis ex parte nostri, quemadmodum verbum Evangelii ex parte Dei. Et continetur in hoc Aphorismo propositio Episto- læ: hoc nim. 16. & seq. 17. themate. Quod Ev- angelium Christi, vel de Christo divinâ efficacia in- structum sit ad salutem conferendam cum spiritua- lem, tum æternam omnibus qui credunt: Sine di- scrimine personarum, sive Judæi sint, sive Græci, five circumcisi, sive incircumcisi: ideò quod in eo- dem reveletur, proponatur, offeratur, & conferatur nobis justitia Dei, quæ est ex fide in fidem, secundum promissionem Propheticam, quam summatim com- plexus est Abacuc, justus ex fide vivet. In quo apho- rismo ratio consequendi salutem per causas suas brevissime tradita est: quod nempe causa efficiens principalis sit Deus, cujus verbum & potentia est Evangelium; meritoria sit Christus, quia Evange- lium est de Christo, organica ex parte Dei sit ver- bum Evangelii, quà revelat justitiam Dei, ex parte nostri sit fides, justitiam Dei revelatam in Evange- lio apprehendens, & quidem unica, quia EVAN- gelium est potentia DEI ad salutem omni CRE- DENTI: & justitia revelata in Evangelio est EX FIDE IN FIDEM, & justus non operibus, sed FIDE vivet. Causa materialis est, homo pec- cator salvandus, seu salutis indigus, sine discrimine personarum: formalis est justitia Dei, verâ fide apprehensa: finalis vita & salus æterna. Evange- lium ergo hic loci non est annunciatio Christi ex- hibiti: sed concio gratiæ, & remissionis peccatorum in Christo, qui exhibendus in Vet. Test. erat, in Novo exhibitus est, utrobique ut objectum Evan- gelii, & fidei proprium propositus est. Si præcise annunciatio exhibiti Christi intelligatur, Evange- lium non fuit in Vet. Test. potentia Dei ad salu- tem. Proinde aut aliud medium in Vet. Test. de- signare oportet, aut Evangelium de Christo illis fuit medium ad salutem. Et tractat Apostolus hic universaliter articulum de justificatione per fidem, & de justitia fidei in Evangelio propositâ, & reve- latâ, abstrahendo ab hominibus seu Veteris, seu Novi Testamenti: quum demonstratio generalis sit, & eadem utrobique necessaria fuerit gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi Act. XV. 10. Ideo sta- tim allegat Prophetam in testimonium, Hab. II. 4. quemadmodum omnes Prophetas testes in eam rem laudavit S. Petrus, Act. X. 43. imo testatur etiam Paulus c. III. 21. infra, legem, seu scripta Mosaica pariter & Prophetica testimonium ferre de hac ju- stitiâ Dei, quam in Evangelio revelatam dicit. Oportet ergo eam in Scripturis Vet. Test. jam tra- ditam, ac patefactam esse, non demum ab Evange- listis & Apostolis in Nov. Test. Oportet Evange- lium illic etiam propositum esse de justitia fidei in Christum: aut defuerit illic potentia Dei ad salu- tem, defuerit fundamentum fidei, ex quo fides salvifica unicè hauritur. Non ergo cum Coccejo Evangelii vox restrictè hic accipienda, pro annun- ciatione Christi exhibiti, sed generatim pro concione gratiæ in Christo, ne ab Evangelio, quod est po- tentia ad salutem, & fide in Evangelium, per quam est salus, & justitia fidei, quæ in Evangelio revela- ta est, excludantur fideles Vet. Test. Neque est, quod cum ipso revelationem ab indicatione distin- guamus, quasi indicata quidem à Mose & Prophe- tis justitia Dei fuerit, sed revelata primùm in Ev- angelio in Nov. Test. ut revelatio justitiæ notet exhibitionem ejus, quod deerat ad illius perfe- ctam cognitionem, parationem, & plenissimum in terra fructum. Licet enim revelatio in Nov. Test. clarior, plenior, communior sit: non tamen in Vet. Test. defuit revelatio justitiæ: quemadmodum hic statim è Vet. Test. eam probat Apostolus, sicut scriptum est. Et annon indicatio illa Prophetica fuit revelatio? nonne revelata fuit Prophetis ju- stitia, & per Prophetas & scripta Prophetica aliis, qui audierunt & legerunt ea, ac fidem inde conce- perunt? aut num fides sine revelatione divinâ lo- cum habere potuit? Nemo utique novit Filium nisi Pater, & nemo Patrem nisi Filius, & cui Filius vult ἀποκαλύψαι revelare, Matth. XI, 27. aut ergo non novêre veteres Filium, aut ἀποκάλυψιν ha- buere. Conf. Pfal. V. 9. XL. 11. Efa. LIII. 1. 11. Jer. XXIII. 6. Dan. IX. 24. Revelata est utique Pro- phetis, & ab iisdem populo eo fine justitia æterna à Christo adducenda, ut revelatam per fidem tum apprehenderent, eâque viverent, non ut solum fidelibus in Nov. Test. eandem reservatam testa- rentur, quæ Socinianorum hæresis est. Jesus Christus enim heri, hodie, idem & in secula Ebr. XIII. 8. Et agnus Dei occisus est ab origine mundi Apoc. XIII. 8. unde Evangelium æternum dicitur, Apoc. XIV, 6. Et quemadmodum Scriptura universa, ita & Scri- ptura Vet. Test. in legem & Evangelium, quæ partes diræ sunt verbi divini, distinguitur, adeoque Ev- angelium è Scriptura Vet. Test. excludi non potest.

Ἰυδαίῳ τε πρῶτον.

Nam Judæis primùm ab ipso Jesu annunciatum & ab Apostolis annunciandum fuit Evangelium Act. III. 25. 26. XIII. 46. Similis locutio infra II 9. 10. 11. Actor. XVIII. 5.

Non quod ullum sit personarum discrimen apud Deum Act. X. 34. Rom. II, 2. Sed quod Pa- triarchis & Ebræis, Israëlitis, ac Judæis peculia- riter promissus fuerit Messias, ac primùm ad eos venit c. XV. 8. ne Judæi nunc à salute exclusi ab- solute videantur. Quid τό πρῶτον illud sit, c. IX. initio explicat, cur id hic in propositione non ne- glexerit, ἐξεργασία c. IX. X. & XI. docet. Conve- nit autem id Judæis ratione ordinis, ex ὀικονομίᾳ Dei, utpote à quibus exivit Evangelium Esa. II. 3. Mich. IV. 2. Ps. CX, 2.

Καὶ Ἕλληνι.

Hic more Judaico loquitur. Nam Græcos magis no- verant Judæi, maxime post Macedonum imperia.

Hanc oppositionem Græcorum, & Judæorum fieri putat Grotius ideò, quod Græci magis, quàm aliæ gentes noti Judæis fuerint: Verùm non pe- nes Judæos tantum recepta fuit illa distributio, vel loquendi ratio, ut ea distributione Judæorum & Græcorum omnes populi comprehendi consue- verint. Græcorum ergo nomine gentiles comple- ctitur Apostolus, & omnes adeo populos, qui à Judæis distinguebantur, Ps. CXLVII, 19. 20. Gal. III, 28. quemadmodum postea de Judæis & genti- libus sub peccato conclusis agit. Illis enim Evan- gelium ad salutem destinatum est, qui per legem, sive à Mose præscriptam, seu solùm cordi inscri- ptam conclusi sunt sub condemnatione, hoc est, tum Judæis, tum gentilibus.

## 1:17
v. 17. For the righteousness of God.

Righteousness which does not consist in outward deeds alone, but is effected by God, and as the work of God is pleasing to God. Thus below X. 3, the righteousness of God and one's own are opposed. You have the righteousness of God in this sense also below III. 22, 26; II Cor. V. 21; Jas. I. 20; II Pet. I. 1.

Inherent or our own righteousness is not meant: for the Apostle removes this as ἰδίαν (one's own) from justification, Rom. X. 3; Phil. III. 9, but imputed righteousness, which is Christ's, which he calls righteousness ἐκ πίστεως (from faith), here and Rom. IX. 30; c. X. 6, and διὰ πίστεως (through faith), Rom. II. 22. The righteousness of Christ v. 25, righteousness manifested without the law v. 21, righteousness imputed without the works of the law Rom. IV. 6, the righteousness of faith v. 11, 13, the righteousness which is through the faith of Christ Phil. III. 9, δικαίωμα (the requirement/righteousness) i.e., the righteousness of Christ Rom. V. 18, ὑπακοὴν (the obedience) of Christ v. 19, which St. Peter, 2 Epist. I. 1, called δικαιοσύνην τῦ θεῦ ἡμῶν κὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ (the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ). Wherefore, since here, and Rom. III. 22, as also c. X. 3, he calls the same δικαιοσύνην θεῦ (the righteousness of God), it is called the righteousness of God because it was ordained by God 1 Cor. I. 30, because it was performed by Christ, God blessed forever, and provided for us, Matt. III. 15; Rom. VIII. 3, 4; c. X. 4, because it is imputed to us by God for salvation, Rom. IV. 6, and because it is pleasing and acceptable to God, which he looks to uniquely when we stand before his tribunal, Rom. III. 24, 25, 28.

c. IV. 3. 4. 5. 2. Cor. V. 21. It is also called righteousness FROM GOD Phil. III. 6. both because it is the same from the divine ὀικονομίᾳ, and because it is from Christ, God and man, who has been made righteousness for us by God, 1. Cor. I, 30. and he himself יהוה צדקנו Jehovah our righteousness Jer. XXIII. 6. redounds to us, as one who in our place and stead was made under the law Gal. IV. 6. when he was not of himself subject to the law, but rather the Lord of the law Matth. XII. 8. he fulfilled all righteousness Matth. III. 15. and for that end he had come, not to destroy the law, but to fulfill the law, Matth. V. 17. and so the will of God, by his obedience, performed for us and in our place, by which he was made obedient even unto death, and that the death of the cross, he might do Phil. II. 8. Ps. XL. 8. Ebr. X. 9. in which divine will fulfilled by Christ, we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made once for all v. 10.

Wherefore that righteousness of God, of which James I, 20 speaks, is foreign here; for that can be done by us, but it is hindered by wrath; which therefore we are said to ποιεῖν, to do, 1. Joh. III. 10. but the righteousness which is treated here is not from us, but has been made righteousness for us by God 1. Cor. I. 30. and is only imputed to us by God through faith Rom. IV. 6. Grotius therefore, with the Papists, confuses inherent or begun righteousness, which is called God's because God effects it in the reborn and justified, not without them, because everyone who is born of God does righteousness, as John testifies in his 1st Epistle III. 10. And he delivers his members as weapons of righteousness Rom. VI. 13. and delivers himself not to sin, but to obedience unto righteousness v. 16. so that he may serve righteousness v. 18. after he has been freed from sin through justification. Which therefore does not precede justification, nor constitute it, but follows it, and is not its cause or form, but its effect.

Therefore the righteousness of God, of which we speak in this place, is not the essential righteousness of God itself, as Osiander wished, nor distributive righteousness, as Origen, nor our habitual or actual righteousness, as the Papists and the Papizing Grotius, but the righteousness and obedience of GOD himself, our Savior Jesus Christ, as both our Apostle and Saint Peter interpret. For it treats of that righteousness which is ἀποκαλύπτεται, revealed peculiarly by God, and is not evident outside that revelation: of that which is revealed in the Gospel, not in the law: which is proper to the Gospel, by which it is distinguished from the law; indeed which χωρὶς νόμε πεφανέρωται, is manifested without the law Rom. III. 21. But begun, inherent, habitual, infused righteousness is manifested in the law, and the law is its norm: but the law is utterly ignorant of imputed righteousness; only the Gospel reveals it, which is a mystery hidden for eternal times Rom. XV. 26. The law, that is, the Mosaic Scripture, with the Prophets, indeed bears witness to it, Rom. III. 21. But when the law is contrasted ἀντιδιηρημένως with the Gospel, it is revealed solely not in the law, but in the Gospel. Furthermore, the discourse here is of that righteousness which Moses and the Prophets pointed out: namely, that we are justified by it alone. But that is not righteousness inherent in us, but imputed, not ours, but God's or Christ's, Gen. XV. 6. (Rom. IV. 3.) Deut. XXX. 12. (Rom. X. 6.) Esa. LIX. 20. (Rom. XI. 26. 27.) Esa. LXI. 10. c. LXII. 1. c. XLIX. 25. c. XIV. 17. Jer. XXIII. 5. c. XXXIII. 16. Ps. XXII. 32. Ps. XL. 10. 11. Ps. XCVIII. 6. Conf. & Ps. IV. 2. Ps. V. 9. Ps. CXLIII. 1. 2. David calls it the righteousness OF GOD Ps. XCVIII. 2. the righteousness of Christ Ps. XCVII. 6. righteousness in Christ Es. c. XLV. 24. righteousness in which Christ establishes his kingdom Es. IX. 7. righteousness which the branch of righteousness is to prepare on earth, Jehovah our righteousness Jer. XXIII. 6. The righteousness treated here is that which is properly and solely God's, not ours, and is distinguished by the Apostle from our own righteousness Rom. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. But this is the righteousness of Christ, who has been made righteousness for us by God, but not habitual justice, or the actual justice of works; as that which is our own justice of the reborn, which we do and work, aided by the Holy Spirit, as those who are reborn: of an infused habit of justice, from which acts of justice arise in the reborn, Scripture knows nothing. It is a Papistic fiction. An infused habit of justice and holiness was in the Protoplasts at creation, or rather co-created, from which they were able to produce holy and just acts. But now, indeed, the Holy Spirit is given to us, and poured out upon us, Tit. III. 6. but it is nowhere said that a habit of justice is infused into us: nor is a habit of justice, if there is one (nor perhaps would 'disposition' be more correctly said than 'habit of justice' on account of its notable imperfection), prior in us to the acts of justice, but rather it is acquired through the acts of justice: because we are not renewed immediately, but gradually, and from day to day, we are transformed from glory to glory 2. Cor. III. 18. c. IX. 16. ἐπιτελῶντες ἁγιωσύνην perfecting sanctification 2. Cor. VII. 1. Furthermore, the justice treated here is that which is from faith, unto faith, which is through faith, which is of faith, and is established as the cause of our justification and salvation, by which we are justified and saved through faith. But this is not an inchoate or inherent justice, or what they call infused and habitual, or the actual justice of works. For this follows not only faith, but justification itself: but it is by no means the cause of justification according to the sense of the Apostle. Moreover, the Apostle treats here of that justice which is imputed to us by God, but is not found in us Rom. IV. 6. Phil. III. 9. But this is not to be understood of inherent or infused justice, which they call habitual; but solely of the justice of Christ: who, just as He was made sin for us in the judgment of God λογισικῶς, and imputatively, so also we are rendered the justice of God, pleasing and acceptable to GOD, which alone He deigns to accept for our justification, or we are just and are justified before God in His judgment ἐν αὐτῷ in Him, Christ Jesus, 2. Cor. V. 21. in His obedience and justice Rom. V. 18. 19. apprehended by us through faith, and imputed to us by GOD in His judgment. Finally, the matter here is of that justice which is χωρὶς ἔργων without works. But it is not permitted to invent an inherent or habitual or actual justice which is χωρὶς ἔργων: because under the name of works here comes adequately whatever is agreeable to the divine law, and conforms to its norm, whether it be a habit, or a disposition, or an act, whether it be something internal or external: and the adequate opposition is between the justice of works, which is from the law, and the justice of faith, which is from the Gospel: to the former is referred whatever of justice or holiness is in us intrinsically or subjectively, or is effectively from us, or exerts itself extrinsically: but the latter is the obedience of Christ alone, because we are constituted just not by each one's own obedience, but all by the obedience of the ONE man Christ θεανθρώπυ ὑπακοῇ, according to the Gospel. Rom. V. 18. Whence Augustine on the Spirit and the Letter, ch. IX. Divine justice, not Jewish, not Philosophical, by which, namely, God justifies us through Christ, and which makes us truly just in the eyes of God; And in Ps. XXX. hom. I. "Because you have not found my justice in me, deliver me in yours: that is, let that deliver me which justifies me, which makes a pious man out of an impious one, which makes a just man out of an unjust one: in Ps. LXX. in your justice deliver me: Not in mine, but in yours; for if in mine, I pray from those of whom he says: Ignorant of the justice of God, and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to the justice of God. And serm. VI. on the Words of the Apostle: God the Father made Christ himself, who had not known sin, sin for us, that we might be the justice of God in him. See two things: the justice of God, not ours: in him, not in us, as also serm. LXI. on the Words of the Lord. That we might be the justice of God

; in him: For if not in him: in no way justice. " But if in him, the whole of it goes to the Father for us: and also Tom. III. in Enchir. to Laur. §. XLI. for he himself " sin, that we might be justice, not ours, but God's; nor in us, but in him: just as he himself was sin, not his own, but ours, nor in himself, but in us. Likewise in Tract. III. on John. All who are from Adam with sin, are sinners: all who are justified through Christ, are just, not in themselves, but in him: for in themselves, if you ask, they are Adam: in him, if you ask, they are Christ's. To Augustine are ὁμόφωνοι others, both in the Latin and in the Greek Church: there S. Anselm on Rom. V. Through the justice of one coming unto all elect men, it has gone into justification, that by PARTICIPATION in the justice of Christ we might be justified. And S. Bernard Epist. CXC. which is to Innocent, Roman Pontiff. " For what could man, a slave of sin, bound by the Devil, do of himself to repair the justice once lost? Therefore, an ALIEN justice was assigned to him, since he lacked his own. Likewise: If one died for all, then all are dead, so that, namely, the satisfaction of one might be IMPUTED to all, just as that one bore the sins of all. And serm. to the knights of the temple c. XI. Death is put to flight in the death of Christ, and the JUSTICE of Christ IS IMPUTED to us. One sinned, and all are held guilty, and shall the INNOCENCE of ONE be reckoned to one alone? The sin of one worked death for all, and shall the JUSTICE of ONE restore life to one? Has the justice of God thus availed more to condemn than to restore? Or could Adam do more in evil than Christ in good? The sin of Adam IS IMPUTED TO ME, and the justice of Christ will not pertain to me? The same serm. LXI. on the Canticles. Lord, I will make mention of your justice alone. For it is indeed also mine. Indeed, you have been made righteousness for me by GOD. Also, the Roman Bishop Leo I, Epist. LXXII, which is to Juvenal, Bishop of Jerusalem, says: 'In order to restore the life of all, He took up the cause of all, and by paying for all the force of the old bond, which He alone among all did not owe, He made it void; and just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the INNOCENCE OF ONE all might be made innocent: from there righteousness flows into men, where human nature has been assumed.' It is pleasing to bring forward only one or two from the Greeks, although here they all easily agree. Chrysost. in Rom. V. hom. X: 'Since just as that one was made the cause of death brought in by the forbidden food for all who are from him, even though they did not eat from the forbidden tree: so also Christ, for His own, as many as are from Him, even though they have not performed righteousness, has been made the reconciler of righteousness, which He has given to us all through the cross.' Therefore, he also turns that 'through one' up and down, and brings it into the middle quite often, saying: 'Just as through one man sin entered the world, and in one transgression many died. And not as through one who had sinned had death come, so also the gift, and the judgment from one unto condemnation.' And again: 'Just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners': and so he repeats this word ONE again and again, so that you may be able, if at any time a Jew says to you, 'How could the world be saved through the merits of ONE Christ?', to say to him in turn, 'How was the world condemned because of the sin of one Adam?' Cyrillus Alex. l. de recta fide ad Reginas: 'It is absurd that we indeed have been made heirs of the punishment of our first parent, with corruption having been brought in through disobedience, but that we are not made participants of the righteousness of the second, who brings us back to life through His own greatest obedience.' When therefore the Scripture says: that many have been justified through the obedience of one, we do not say that a man simply like us was left in this, but rather one incarnate, and made obedient to the Father for us. For he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. Irenaeus, prior to all these, handed down the same in Book IV against heresies, ch. XIV. Whom we offended in the first Adam, not doing his commandment, but in the second Adam we have been reconciled, having been made obedient even unto death. And contemporary with Irenaeus, nay, older, Justin Martyr in his Epistle to Diognetus, p. 386. For what else could cover our sins than his righteousness? In whom else can we, wicked and ungodly, be considered righteous than in the Son of God alone? O sweet exchange! O unsearchable artifice! O benefits exceeding all expectation! that the iniquity of many might indeed be hidden in the one righteous one, and the righteousness of one might cause many unrighteous to be considered righteous! This was the Catholic faith concerning imputed righteousness; but under the Papacy it was wrapped in darkness more than Cimmerian or Egyptian. Which darkness having been dispersed, with the Sun of righteousness shining forth, Theander Luther brought into the open and illustrated. Those who strive to obscure and wrap the same in former darkness are about to render a grave account to GOD.

in it through this Gospel. ἀποκαλύπτεται. It is shown. The Gospel most perfectly teaches how one ought to live. See the passage Isaiah 62:1, 'until his righteousness goes forth as light.' See the same Isaiah and 56:1.

It is not only shown or revealed, but consequently the antecedent must be understood: it is revealed, that is, it is actually performed and exhibited: or so that that revelation is to be understood not only by way of manifestation, but also of efficacious operation: because the Gospel both manifests righteousness and effects and performs that we receive the same by faith, and thus attain righteousness, Rom. 10:17. Whence Lombard in this place: 'The Gospel reveals this righteousness by the effect itself, namely, while it gives faith to a man, through which he is justified.' Which Grotius interprets thus: 'The Gospel most perfectly teaches how one ought to live, is a falsehood.' It is not the function of the Gospel, promised through the Prophets, to teach perfectly how one ought to live: Moses and the Prophets handed that down perfectly, so that nothing is to be added to it, nor taken away, Deut. 4:2, ch. 12:32. The sum of the Law is: 'He who does these things shall live in them': of the Gospel, 'the righteous shall live by his faith,' Gal. 3:11, 12. The Law is the most perfect rule of living: the Gospel presents only the grace of GOD exhibited in Christ, and requires faith in Christ, John 1:17, ch. 3:16. Nor is righteousness to be understood otherwise than the Prophets taught would shine forth like light in the time of the N.T., which they testified was the righteousness of Christ, in whom alone we have righteousness, and we are justified, Is. 45:24, 25, ch. 53:11, ch. 55:1, ch. 56:1, ch. 62:1, Jer. 23:6, ch. 33:15, Dan. ch. 9:24. Cf. Ps. 72:1, 98:2, 3. But this righteousness is said to be revealed in the Gospel, because it is hidden from human reason, nor is anything of it known by the light of nature: nor is it contained in the Law, by which it is distinguished from the Gospel, but it is to be sought outside of it in Christ, who is the end of the Law, Rom. 10:4, John 1:18.

ἐκ πίσεως. That righteousness is born of faith. For heavenly promises and contrary threats, when believed as they ought to be, purge the soul from vices.

Righteousness is said to be of faith, not by reason of itself, but by reason of us, because the righteousness of GOD is prior to faith in itself: but that which is the same as ours or is imputed to us requires faith before it. For it is imputed through faith: therefore it is also called righteousness which is through faith. Grotius understands righteousness, of which faith is the mother: which, as Ambrose says, is the progenitor of every good action. But that righteousness is ours and inherent: which is not the subject here. Nor is it about that purging of the soul from vices, which heavenly promises and contrary threats provide; but about justification, or the remission of sins, which was obtained by the death of Christ and proposed in the Gospel, to be received by faith, Acts 10:43, ch. 13:38, 39.

εἰς πίστιν. For faith does not rest when it has produced righteousness, but perpetually flows into works. Which James teaches by the example of Abraham. For the faith of Abraham which Moses had placed at the beginnings of his piety, James placed at the height of his progress. Paul loves repeated words, as below 6:19, 2 Cor. 2 at the end. Similar is Ps. 134:8 and John 1:16. Clement of Alexandria well explains this passage in Strom. V, interpreting faith as the former which is relied upon, and the latter which is built upon it.

Although faith does not rest when it has produced righteousness, but perpetually flows into works, that is not indicated here. The influx or effect of faith is twofold: the first of justification and the remission of sins: the second of Sanctification: because faith is 'working through love.' By this latter it flows perpetually into works: but here the Apostle looks to the former, the 'operation': because he intends to explain the nature of justification. He says, however, 'from faith to faith,' not from the faith of the preachers, as Augustine, to the faith of the hearers, or as others, from the faith of the prophecies of the O.T. obscure to the clear faith of the N.T. or of the Apostles: or as Ambrose, from the faith of GOD promising to the faith of the one believing: because he deals solely with the faith of the subject to be justified, and righteousness is also called 'of faith' where GOD promising is not looked to, Rom. 9:30, ch. 10:6, but only the faith of the believer, and thus the Apostle indicates by that phrase both its perseverance and its increase. namely, that he may claim everything for faith alone, and teach that faith alone dominates in the matter of justification, because the righteousness of God is revealed, not that which is through works, or through a habit of holiness or charity, but that which is from faith to faith, that is, through faith alone, so that the continuity of the righteousness of faith may be expressed, and justification and salvation may be claimed entirely for faith: for faith does not begin justification dispositively, as the Papist Sophists wish, for charity to perfect it, but faith is the sole and unique cause of righteousness on our part: namely, that unique medium which apprehends righteousness, and retains it once apprehended, until we obtain the end of faith, the salvation of our souls 1 Pet. 1:9. There is no other righteousness of man in this life, except to live by faith, says Augustine in Ps. 93. Nor can the words of Clement of Alexandria in Strom. book 5 be accepted in this sense. It appears that the Apostle announces a twofold faith: or rather one, which receives increase and consummation. However, the transposition which Crellius establishes is not to be admitted: ordering it thus: The righteousness of GOD (that is, justification) from faith, (which is done through faith) is revealed in it (the Gospel) into faith, i.e., into this very thing, that faith may prevail among all, and reign everywhere. Comm. on this passage, p. 50. For without transposition the sense is clear and effective: the righteousness of GOD is revealed in the Gospel, from faith to faith: and the confirmation from the Prophet subjoined sufficiently teaches that all things are attributed to faith, even life itself for salvation, with which sense also the passage which Crellius compares agrees, 2 Cor. 3:18, we are transformed from glory to glory: indeed, even the Crellian interpretation: that justification both begins and is completely finished through faith, and procures salvation for man.

καθὼς γέγραπται) In Habakkuk, where see what has been said by us. It is no wonder if God does this now, which he also did of old, that he may do good to those who trust in him.

ὁ δὲ δίκαιος) A pious man.

ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται) God speaks in Habakkuk; but it is read now in the Hebrew as 'by his faith': But the ancient codices had 'by my faith' that is, in me: by waiting patiently for my promises, which I announced to them through Habakkuk and other Prophets, and by not failing into idolatry, as those of whom the Prophet had spoken a little before, shall live: that is, he shall obtain a return to his homeland. For to live often means to the Hebrews to be exempt from miseries and to live happily. Just as they were then delivered from the Babylonian captivity by having trust in GOD, so now from the captivity of sins and the punishments following it. And thus Habakkuk.

The Apostle confirms by the testimony of the Prophet, immediately in the Proposition itself, what he undertook to explain and assert from Hagg. II. 4, because it is not a new Gospel, but what GOD had long ago said he would deliver through the Prophets, v. 2. The Prophet is dealing, to be sure, even if from a special occasion, with justification and salvation to be obtained only through faith: the Prophet is not dealing with obtaining a return to the Homeland: as Grotius perverts it, whom we refuted in our Annotations on the Prophetic passage: and we have refuted what he suspects here, that the Hebrew Codices are corrupt, and that the ancients had 'by my faith', by expecting my promises. The Apostle is not dealing with the faith of GOD, but with the faith of believers, and with that same Prophet as interpreter: nor does he understand by faith the truth of divine promises; but that faith by which we are justified before God: and which he had indicated when he said, from faith to faith. Nor did the Apostle bring forward this passage otherwise than concerning our faith, the faith of believers, Gal. III. 11, Heb. X. 38, because there he dealt by design with justification through faith: here he exhorted to constancy in faith, and testified that he was indicating that faith which is ὑπόςασις ἐλπιζομένων, by which the ancient believers were distinguished. Nor do we read anywhere that GOD said 'my faith', in this sense, 'faith in me' or 'in my promises'. And what is chief, both the Prophet and the Apostle in parallel passages indicate that the just man lives not by another's faith, but by his own, so that everyone may believe and persevere in faith, because everyone lives by his own faith. Furthermore, just as the particle ב is sometimes turned by ἐκ, Deut. VI. 5, sometimes by διὰ 'through', Deut. XXXII. 21, sometimes it is taken simply as an ablative of instrument: so the Apostle said indiscriminately, ἐκ πίσεως, διὰ πίσεως, and πίσει, Rom. III. 28, 22, 25. Cornelius a Lapide tastes better here than Grotius. Habakkuk, he says, speaks not of the life of the body, but of the soul; not natural, but supernatural, namely of grace and justice, by which the just man, insofar as he is just, lives. For he opposes these two, namely to live, which he attributes to the just and faithful, and not to have a right soul, or to be displeasing to GOD, which he attributes to the unbeliever and the unjust. Moreover, the future verb ζήσεται, 'shall live', is used, by which the Hebrews are accustomed to denote perpetuity, as Buxtorf notes in Thesaur. l. 1. c. XII, because he intends to teach that spiritual life not only arises from faith, but is also continued by it: Whence Cornelius says that Habakkuk and the Apostle speak as much of the beginning of spiritual life as of the increase of justice and spiritual life: since this sentence, 'the just shall live by faith', is general and universal, pertaining as much to Jews as to Christians, as much to sinners who are first justified as to those who have already been justified. For the spiritual life of all of these begins, is preserved, and grows through faith. But Coster the Jesuit very badly perverts this golden aphorism in Enchir. p. 197, that the just man living by faith is nothing other than the just man directing and forming his whole life according to the norm of faith: For the Apostle is dealing here in the Proposition with justification, and intends to deal with it, not with the manner of living of the justified, and he declares the justice of faith from the Prophet, not however the holiness of life; nor do we obtain life through the holiness of life, according to the Apostle, but the Apostle takes it upon himself to explain how we are both justified and saved through faith in Christ. Finally, the Gospel is not a norm of living, but this is proper to the law. But see the Papal gloss in Orac. IX. Theol. Apostol.

Rom. I. 32. we have discussed. These things, therefore, concerning the Apostolic proposition. There follows

TREATMENT Or Apostolic Elaboration. FIRST PART DIDACTIC Informative CONCERNING THE JUSTICE OF FAITH. SECTION I. CONCERNING THE πρόγνωσιν (FOREKNOWLEDGE) OF THE SUBJECT.

PART IV OF THE FIRST CHAPTER NARRATION, OR EXPLANATION OF THE SUBJECT, CONVINCING OF THE NECESSITY OF THE JUSTICE OF FAITH.

Latin:

v. 17. Δικαιοσύνη γὰρ θεῦ.

Justitia quæ non in solis factis exterioribus consistit. sed à Deo efficitur, & ut Dei opus Deo placet. Sic infra X. 3. opponuntur θεῦ δικαιοσύνη & ἰδία. Dei justitiam habes hoc sensu & infra III. 22. 26. II. Cor. V. 21. Jac. I. 20. II. Petr. I. 1.

Non intelligitur justitia inhærens vel nostra: hanc enim ceu ἰδίαν removet Apostolus à justifica- tione Rom. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. sed justitia imputata, quæ est Christi, quam vocat justitiam ἐκ πίστεως ex fide, hic & Rom. IX. 30. c. X. 6. & διὰ πίστεως, Rom. II. 22. Justitiam Christi v. 25. justitiam sine lege ma- nifestatam v. 21. justitiam imputatam sine operibus legis Rom. IV. 6. justitiam fidei v. 11. 13. justitiam, quæ est per fidem Christi Phil. III. 9. δικαίωμα l. ju- stitiam Christi Rom. V. 18. ὑπακοὴν obedientiam Christi v. 19. quam S. Petrus 2. Epist. I. 1. δικαιοσύ- νην τῦ θεῦ ἡμῶν κὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, justitiam Dei nostri & Salvatoris Jesu Christi nuncupavit. Quapropter cum hic, & Rō. III. 22. ut & c. X. 3. ean- dem nuncupet δικαιοσύνην θεῦ, Dei justitia dicitur, quod à Deo eadem ordinata sit 1. Cor. I. 30. quod à Christo Deo benedicto in secula præstita, nobisq; cō- parata sit, Matt. III. 15. Rom. IIX. 3. 4. c. X, 4. quod à Deo imputetur nobis ad salutẽ Rom. IV. 6. quodq; Deo grata, & accepta sit, quam unicè respicit, cum coram tribunali ejus sistimur Rom. III. 24. 25. 28.

c. IV. 3. 4. 5. 2. Cor. V. 21. dicitur etiam justitia EX DEO Phil. III. 6. tum quod ex divina ὀικονομίᾳ ea- dem sit, tum quod ex Christo Deo & homine, qui nobis à Deo factus est justitia, 1. Cor. I, 30. & ipse יהוה צדקנו Jehova justitia nostra Jer. XXIII. 6. in nos redundet, utpote qui nostri loco & vice sub lege factus Gal. IV. 6. quum per se legi obnoxius non esset, sed potius Dominus legis Matth. XII. 8. justitiam omnem implevit Matth. III. 15. eoque fi- ne venerat, non ut legem solveret, sed ut impleret le- gem, Matth. V. 17. adeoque voluntatem Dei, obe- dientia sua, pro nobis & nostri loco, præstita, qua obediens factus est usque ad mortem eamque crucis, faceret Phil. II. 8. Ps. XL. 8. Ebr. X. 9. in qua vo- luntate divina à Christo impleta, sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factam v. 10.

Quapropter aliena hîc est illa δικαιοσύνη θεῦ, de qua Jac. I, 20. ea n. à nobis fieri potest, sed ira præ- peditur; quam proinde dicimur ποιεῖν facere, 1. Joh. III. 10. justitia vero, de qua hîc agitur, non à nobis sit, sed à Deo facta nobis est 1. Cor. I. 30. nobisq; solú imputatur à Deo per fidem Rom. IV. 6. Confundit ergo Grotius cum Papistis justitiam inhærentem vel inchoatam, quæ Dei dicitur, quod efficiat eam Deus in renatis & justificatis, non sine illis, quia omnis qui renatus ex Deo est, justitiam facit, teste Joh. I. Epist. III. 10. Deoque membra sua tradit ar- ma Justitiæ Rom. VI. 13. & seipsum non peccato, sed obedientiæ mancipat in justitiam v. 16. ut justitiæ serviat v. 18. postquam à peccato liberatus est per justificationem. Quæ proinde justificationem non antecedit, nec constituit, sed consequitur, & ejusdem non causa, aut forma, sed effectus est.

Justitia itaque Dei, de qua hoc in loco, non est ipsa essentialis Dei Justitia, ut Osiander volebat, nec justitia distributiva, ut Origenes, nec habitualis vel actualis justitia nostra, ut Papistæ & Grotius Papizans, sed justitia, & obedientia ipsius DEI servatoris nostri Jesu Christi, ut cùm Apostolus noster, tùm Sanct. Petrus interpretatur. De ea justitia enim agitur, quæ ἀποκαλύπτεται revelatur peculiariter à Deo, nec extra revelationem illam patet: de ea, quæ revelatur in Evangelio, non in le- ge: quæ Evangelii propria est, qua distinguitur à lege; imo quæ χωρὶς νόμε πεφανέρωται sine lege manife- statur Rom. III. 21. At justitia inchoata, inhærens, habitualis, infusa in lege manifestatur, ejusdemq; norma lex est: justitiam autem imputatam ignorat prorsus lex, revelat solum Evangelium, quæ my- sterium est æternis temporibus absconditum Rom. XV. 26. Testimonium quidem eidem perhibet lex, id est, Scriptura Mosaica, cum Prophetis, Rom. III. 21. At cum lex ἀντιδιηρημένως opponitur Evange- lio, non in lege, sed in Evangelio unice Eadem reve- lata est. Porro de ea justitia sermo hîc est, quam in- digitarunt Moses & Prophetæ: quod nempe eadem sola justificemur. At illa non justitia nobis inhæ- rens est, sed imputata, non nostra, sed Dei vel Chri- sti, Gen. XV. 6. (Rom. IV. 3.) Deut. XXX. 12. (Rom. X. 6.) Esa. LIX. 20. (Rom. XI. 26. 27.) Esa. LXI. 10. c. LXII. 1. c. XLIX. 25. c. XIV. 17. Jer. XXIII. 5. c. XXXIII. 16. Ps. XXII. 32. Ps. XL. 10. 11. Ps. XCVIII. 6. Conf. & Ps. IV. 2. Ps. V. 9. Ps. CXLIII. 1. 2. ju- stitiam DEI vocat David Ps. XCVIII. 2. justitiam Christi Ps. XCVII. 6. justitiam in Christo Es. c. XLV. 24. justitiam in qua firmat Christus regnum suum Es. IX. 7. justitiam quam paraturum est in terra ger- men justitiæ, Jehova justitia nostra Jer. XXIII. 6. De ea hîc agitur justitiâ, quæ propriè & unice Dei est, non nostra & à justitia nostra & propria distingui- tur ab Apostolo Rom. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. At hæc justi- tia Christi est, qui à Deo nobis factus est justitia, non vero justitia habitualis, vel actualis operum; utpote quæ nostra renatorum propria est justitia, quam à S. S. adjuti facimus, & operamur, qua re- nati: de habitu infuso justitiæ, è quo actus justi- tiæ oriuntur in renatis Scriptura nihil novit. Com- mentum est Papisticum. Infusus Protoplastis in creatione, vel potius concreatus fuit habitus justitiæ, & sanctitatis, ex quo actus sanctos & justos edere poterant. Jam verò Spiritus S. quidem nobis da- tur, & effunditur super nos, Tit. III. 6. justitiæ autem habitus nuspiam infundi nobis dicitur: nec prior est in nobis habitus justitiæ, si quis est, (nec disposi- tio forsan rectiùs, quam habitus justitiæ ob insi- gnem imperfectionem diceretur) actibus justitiæ, sed per actus justitiæ potius comparatur: quia non statim, sed paulatim, ac de die in diem renovamur, de claritate in claritatem transformamur 2. Cor. III. 18. c. IX. 16. ἐπιτελῶντες ἁγιωσύνην perficientes san- ctificationem 2. Cor. VII. 1. Adhæc de ea hic justitia agitur, quæ est ex fide, in fidem, quæ est per fidem, quæ fidei est, nostræque justificationis & salutis, qua per fidem justificamur, & salvamur, causa con- stituitur. At hæc non est justitia inchoata, vel inhæ- rens, aut quam infusam & habitualem vocant, aut actualis operum justitia. Hæc enim non fidem tan- tum, sed etiam justificationem ipsam consequitur: nequaquam vero causa justificationis est ex sensu Apostoli. Insuper de ea justitia hic agit Apostolus, quæ imputatur nobis à Deo, non invenitur vero in nobis Rom. IV.6. Phil. III. 9. At hoc non de justi- tia inhærente, vel infusa, quam vocant, habituali; sed de justitia Christi unice intelligendum: qui uti pro nobis factus est peccatum in judicio Dei λογι- σικῶς, & imputative, ita etiam nos reddimur justi- tia Dei DEO grata, & accepta, quam solam digna- tur suscipere ad nostri justificationem, vel justi su- mus & justifcamur coram Deo in judicio ejus ἐν αὐτῷ in ipso, Christo Jesu, 2. Cor. V. 21. in obedien- tia & justitia ejus Rom. V. 18. 19. a nobis per fidem apprehensa, nobisque a DEO in judicio ejusdem imputata. Denique de ea justitia hic res est, quæ χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus est. At justitiam inhæren- tem sive habitualem, sive actualem, quæ χωρὶς ἔρ- γων sit, fingere non licet: quia operum nomine hic adæquate venit, quicquid legi divinæ consenta- neum est, & ad ejus normam congruit, seu habitus, seu dispositio, seu actus sit, sive internum quid, sive externum: & oppositio adæquata est inter justitiam operum, quæ ex lege est, & justitiam fidei, quæ ex Evangelio: ad illam refertur, quicquid justitiæ aut sanctitatis in nobis intrinsece, vel subjective est, aut à nobis est effective, seu extrinsecus se exerit: hæc au- tem est solius Christi obedientia, quia non sua quisque obedientia, sed omnes UNIUS hominis Christi θεανθρώπυ ὑπακοῇ vel obedientia, juxta Evangelium justi constituimur. Rom. V.18. Unde Augustinus de Spir. & liter. c. IX. Justitia divina, non Judaica, non Philosophica, qua scilicet nos Deus justificat per Christum, quæque nos in ocu- lis Dei revera justos facit; Et in Psal. XXX. hom. I. "Quia non invenisti in me justitiam meam, erue me in tuam: hoc est, illud me eruat, quod me justificat, "quod ex impio pium facit, quod ex iniquo justum: in Pl. LXX. in justitia tua erue me: Non in mea, sed "in tua; si enim in mea, oro ex illis, de quibus ille ait: Ignorantes Dei justitiam, & suam volentes consti- "tuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti. Et serm. VI. de Verb. Apostoli: Ipsum Christum, qui non no- verat peccatum, DEUS Pater pro nobis peccatum "fecit, ut nos simus justitia Dei in ipso. Videte duo: justitia Dei, non nostra: in ipso, non in nobis, ut "& serm. LXI. de Verb. Dn. Ut nos simus justitia Dei

; in ipso: Si enim non in ipso: nullo modo justitia. " Si autem in ipso, totus nobis vadit ad Patrem: nec non Tom. III. in Enchir. ad Laur. §. XLI. ipse enim " peccatum, ut nos justitia, nec nostra, sed Dei; nec in nobis, sed in ipso: sicut ipse peccatum non suum, " sed nostrum, nec in se, sed in nobis. Item in Tract. III. in Joh. Omnes, qui ex Adam cum peccato, pec- " catores: omnes, qui per Christum justificati, justi, non in se, sed in illo: nam in se, si interroges, Adam sunt: in illo, si interroges, Christi sunt. Augustino " ὁμόφωνοι sunt alii cum in Latina, tum in Graeca Ec- clesia: illic S. Anshelmus in Rom. V. Per unius ju- " stitiam venientem in omnes homines electos itum est in justificationem, ut PARTICIPATIONE " justitiae Christi justificemur. Et S. Bernhardus Epist. CXC. quae est ad Innocent. Roman. Pontif. " Quid enim ex se agere poterat, ut semel amissam justitiam repararet, homo servus peccati, vinctus Diaboli? Assignata est ei proinde ALIENA, qui " caruit sua. Item: Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt, ut videlicet satisfactio " unius omnibus IMPUTETUR, sicut omnium peccata unus ille portavit. Et serm. ad milites tem- " pli c. XI. Mors in Christi morte fugatur, & Christi nobis JUSTITIA IMPUTATUR. Unus pecca- " vit, & omnes tenentur rei, & UNIUS INNO- CENTIA soli reputabitur uni? Unius peccatum omnibus operatum est mortem, & UNIUS JU- " STITIA uni vitam restituet? Itane Dei justitia magis ad condemnandum, quam ad restaurandum " valuit? Aut plus potuit Adam in malo quam Chri- stus in bono? Adae peccatum IMPVTATUR MI- " HI, & Christi justitia non pertinebit ad me? Idem serm. LXI. super Cantic. Domine memorabor ju- " stitiae tuae solius. Ipsa est n. & mea. Nempe factus es mihi tu justitia a DEO. Etiam Episcopus Roma- " nus Leo I. Epist. LXXII. quae est ad Juvenal. Hiero- " solym. Episc. ut a. repararet omnium vitam, rece- pit omnium causam, & vim veteris Chirographi, " quod solus inter omnes non debuit, pro omnibus solvendo vacuavit, & sicut per unius reatum omnes " facti fuerant peccatores: ita per UNIUS INNO- CENTIAM omnes fierent innocentes: inde in " homines manante justitia, ubi est humana suscepta natura. " E Graecis unum atque alterum solum adducere " libet, quamvis hic facile consonent omnes. Chry- sost. in Rom. V. hom. X. Quoniam quemadmodum " ille mortis ex vetito cibo inductae causa factus est omnibus, qui ex illo sunt, licet ex prohibito ligno " non comederint: sic & Christus suis quotquot ex ipso sunt, tametsi justitiam non fecerint, justitiae " factus est conciliator, quam per crucem omnibus nobis donavit. Propterea & illud per unum, sur- sum & deorsum versat, ac saepius in medium addu- " cit, dicens: Quemadmodum per unum hominem peccatum ingressum est mundum & in uno de- " licto mortui sunt multi. Et non sicut per unum, qui peccaverat, venerat mors, ita & donum, & ju- " dicium ex uno in condemnationem. Et iterum: Quemadmodum per inobedientiam unius homi- " nis peccatores constituti sunt multi: atque ita sub- inde repetit hanc vocem UNIUS, ut possis, si quando Judaeis tibi dicat, quomodo potuit orbis " per UNIUS Christi merita servari? vicissim illi di- cere, quomodo propter unius Adami peccatum " condemnatus est orbis? Cyrillus Alex. l. de recta fide ad Reginas: Absurdum est, nos quidem haere- " des factos supplicii primi parentis, corruptione per inobedientiam immissa: non a. fieri participes ju- " stitiae secundi, qui ad vita nos revehit per maxima suam obedientiam. Quando igitur dicit Scriptura: " ” per obedientiam unius justificatos esse multos, nō ” hominem simpliciter quempiam nobis similem in ” hoc derelictum esse dicimus, sed incarnatum po- ” tius, & obedientem pro nobis factum Patri. Non ” enim fecit peccatum, neque dolus inventus est in ” ore ejus. Irenæus hisce omnibus prior eadem tra- ” didit IV. adv. hæres. c. XIV. Quem in primo qui- ” dem Adam offendimus, non facientes ejus præ- ” ceptum, in secundo autem Adam reconciliati su- ” mus, obedientes usque ad mortem facti. Et Irenæo ” σύγχρονο̃ς, imo antiquior Justinus Martyr in Epist. ” ad Diognetum p. 386. Quid enim aliud peccata ” nostra potuit tegere, quam ejus justitia? in quo alio ” nos iniqui & impii pro justis haberi possumus ” quam in solo Dei Filio? O dulcem permutationem! ” O impervestigabile artificium! O beneficia exspe- ” ctationem omnem superantia! ut iniquitas quidem ” multorum in justo uno abscondatur, justitia a. u- ” nius faciat, ut multi injusti pro justis habeantur! ” Hæc fides Catholica fuit de justitia imputata; At ” sub Papatu tenebris plusquam Cimmeriis, vel ” Ægyptiacis involuta. Quam discussa caligine, ” affulgente Sole justitiæ, in apricum produxit, & ” illustravit, Theander Lutherus. Qui obfuscare, ” ac pristinis tenebris involvere eandem satagunt, ” DEO gravem reddituri sunt rationem.

ἐν αὐτῷ per hoc Evangelium. ἀποκαλύπτεται. Monstratur. Evangelium perfectissime docet, quo- modo vivendum sit. RespicMessages locus Es. LXII. 1. ἕως ἂν ἐξέλθῃ ὡς φῶς ἡ δικαιοσύνη. Vide eundem Esaiam & LVI 1.

Non tantum est monstratur, aut revelatur, sed ex consequente intelligendum est antecedens: revela- tur, id est, reipsa præstatur, & exhibetur: vel ut re- velatio illa non solum sit manifestationis, sed etiam efficacis operationis ratione intelligenda: quia Ev- angelium & manifestat justitiam, & efficit, ac præstat, ut eandem suscipiamus fide, adeoque justitiam consequamur Rom. X. 17. unde Lom- bardus in h. l. Hanc autem justitiam Evangelium revelat ipso affectus, scil. dum dat fidem homini, per quam justificatur. Quod Grotius ita interpreta- tur: Evangelium perfectissime docet, quomodo vi- vendum sit, πρεελότης est. Non hoc Evangelii est, promissi per Prophetas, perfecte docere, quomodo vivendum sit: tradidere id perfecte Moses, & Pro- phetæ, ita ut nihil ei addendum, neque demendum sit, Deut. IV. 2. c. XII: 32. Legis Summa est: Qui fe- cerit hæc, vivet in eis: Evangelii, justus fide sua vivet, Gal. III. 11. 12. Lex vivendi regula est perfectissima: Evangelium gratiam DEI solum sistit in Christo exhibitam, & fidem in Christum requirit Joh. I. 17. c. III. 16. Neque aliter justitia intelligenda, quam Prophetæ tempore N. T. instar lucis effulsuram docuere, quam de justitia Christi, in quo solo no- bis justitiam esse, nosque justificari testatus est, Es. XLV. 24. 25. c. LIII. 11. c. LV. 1. c. LVI. 1. c. LXII. 1. Jerem. XXIII. 6. c. XXXIII. 15. Daniel. c. IX. 24. Conf. Ps. LXXII. 1. XCIIX. 2. 3. Revelari autem di- citur hæc justitia in Evangelio, quia rationi huma- næ est abscondita, nec naturæ lumine quicquam de eadem constat: neque etiam in lege, qua ab Evan- gelio distinguitur, eadem habetur, sed extra eam in Christo quærenda est, qui finis legis est, Rom. X. 4. Joh. I. 18.

ἐκ πίσεως. Justitia illa ex fide nascitur. Nam promissa cœlestia & contrariæ minæ ita, ut oportet credita, animam a vitiis purgant.

Justitia dicitur ex fide esse, non ratione sui, sed ratione nostri, quia per se prior est fide justitia DEI: sed quæ eadem nostra est vel nobis imputatur, fidem ante se requirit. Nam imputatur per fidem: Ideo etiam dicitur justitia, quæ est per fidem. Grotius in- telligit justitiam, cujus fides mater est: quæ Ambro- sio dicente, omnis bonæ actionis est genitrix. Sed ea justitia est nostra & inhærens: de qua hic non agi- tur. Neque de illa animæ a vitiis repurgatione, quam promissa cælestia & contraria minæ præstant; sed de justificatione, seu peccatorum remissione, quæ morte Christi parta & in Evangelio proposita est, fide suscipienda Act. X. 43. c. XIII. 38. 39.

εἰς πίστιν. Non enim quiescit fides, ubi justitiam peperit, sed perpe- tuo influit in opera. Quod Abrahami exemplo docet Ja- cobus. Nam quam Abrahami fidem Moses circa initia pie- tatis ejus posuerat, Jacobus posuit in summo ejus progres- su. Amat Paulus voces repetitas, ut infra VI. 19. 2. Cor. II. in fine. Simile est Ps. CXXXIV. 8. & Joh. I. 16. Bene hunc lo- cum explicat Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. V. fidem inter- pretans priore quæ subsfruitur, posteriore quæ isti inædificatur.

Etsi fides non quiescat ubi justitiam peperit, sed perpetuo influat in opera, id tamen hic non indigi- tatur. Geminus est fidei influxus, vel effectus: pri- mus justificationis, & remissionis peccatorum: alter Sanctificationis: quia fides δι' ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη: Hoc posteriori influit perpetuo in opera: sed hic priorem, ἐνέργειαν respicit Apostolus: quia justifi- cationis rationem explicare instituit. Dicit autem ex fide in fidem, non ex fide prædicantium, ut Au- gust. in fidem audientium, aut ut alii, ex fide Pro- phetiarum V. T. obscura in claram N. T. vel Aposto- lorum: vel ut Ambrosius ex fide DEI promittentis in fidem credentis: quia de subjecti justificandi fide unice agit, & justitia ἐκ πίστεως etiam dicitur, ubi DEUS promittens non respicitur, Rom. IX. 30. c. X. 6. sed solum fides credentis, adeoque ejus tum perseverantiam, tum incrementum ea phrasi indi- cat Apostolus: ut nempe omnia fidei uni vindicet, ac in negotio justificationis solam fidem dominari doceat, quia justitia Dei revelatur, non quæ per ope- ra est, aut per sanctitatis vel charitatis habitum, sed quæ est ex fide in fidem, id est, per solam fidem, ut continuitas justitiæ fidei exprimatur, fideique in soli- dum justificatio ac Salus vindicetur: non enim in- cipit justificationem fides dispositive, ut Sophistæ Pontificii volunt, quam perficiat charitas, sed fides sola & unica justitiæ, ex parte nostri, causa est: uni- cum scilicet medium illud, quod justitiam appre- hendit, apprehensam retinet, donec fidem fidei, ani- marum salutem consequamur 1. Petr. I. 9. Non est alia justitia hominis in hac vita, nisi ex fide vivere, ait August. in Ps. XCIII. Neque hoc sensu etiam Clementis Alex. verba l. V. Strom. accipi possunt. Apparet Apostolum fidem duplicem annunciare: imo unam, quæ incrementum & consummationem susci- pit. Non admittenda autem trajectio, quam Crel- lius statuit: ita ordinans: Justitia DEI (id est, justi- ficatio) ex fide, (quæ fit per fidem) revelatur in ipso (Evangelio) in fidem, h. e. in hoc ipsum, ut fides apud omnes obtineat, & ubique regnet. Comm. in h. l. p. 50. Nam sine trajectione sensus luculen- tus est, & efficax: justitia DEI revelatur in Evan- gelio, ex fide in fidem: & confirmatio è Prophe- ta subjuncta satis docet, omnia fidei tribui, ipsam etiam vitam ad salutem, cui sensui quoque conso- nat locus, quem confert Crellius 2. Cor. III. v. ult. transformamur ex gloria in gloriam: imo ipsa Crel- liana interpretatio: quod & incipiat, & absolvatur penitus justificatio per fidem, hominique salutem pariat.

καθὼς γέγραπται) Apud Abacucum, ubi quæ à nobis dicta vide. Non mirum est si Deus hoc nunc faciat, quod & olim fecit, ut benefaciat in se confidentibus.

ὁ δὲ δίκαιος) Vir pius.

ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται) Loquitur apud Abacucum, Deus legitur autem nunc in Ebræo per fidem suam: Sed veteres co- dices habuere per fidem meam id est in me: expectando patienter mea promissa, quæ per Abacucum aliosque Pro- phetas ipsis annunciavi, & non deficiendo ad idololatriam, ut illi de quibus paulo ante Propheta egerat, vivet: id est consequetur reditum in patriam. Nam vivere Hebræis sæ- pe eximi miseriis & feliciter vivere. Sicut tunc fiduciam in DEUM habentes liberati sunt a captivitate Babylonica, ita nunc ex captivitate peccatorum, & pœnis eam conse- quentibus. Et sic hunc locum Habacuci usurpat Schem tob.

Confirmat Apostolus Prophetæ testimonio sta- tim in ipsa Propositione, quod explicandum, & as- ferendum sumpsit ex Hagg. II. 4. quia non novum Evangelium, sed quod olim DEUS προεπηγγείλα- το per Prophetas se traditurum dixerat, v. 2. Agit scilicet Propheta, etsi ex occasione speciali, de ju- stificatione & salute nonnisi per fidem consequenda: non vero de reditu in Patriam consequendo Pro- pheta tractat: ut pervertit Grotius, quem in Annot. nostris ad locum Propheticum confutavimus: & quod hic suspicatur, Codices Ebræos corruptos esse, & veteres habuisse per fidem meam, expectando mea promissa, profligavimus. Non de fide DEI, sed de fide credentium, agit Apostolus, & interprete eo- dem Propheta: nec promissionum divinarum veri- tatem per fidem intelligit; sed eam fidem, qua nos coram Deo justificamur: & quam indigitarat, cum dixit, ex fide in fidem. Neque aliter Apostolus ad- duxit hunc locum, quam de fide nostra credentiu, Gal. III. 11. Ebr. X. 38. quia illic de justificatione per fidem ex instituto egit: hic ad constantiam in fide hortatus est, eamque fidem se indicare testa- tus est, quæ est ὑπόςασις ἐλπιζομένων, qua veteres fideles claruerunt. Nec uspiam fidem meam legi- mus DEUM dixisse, hoc sensu, fidem in me, vel in pro- missa mea. Et quod præcipuum est, non aliena, sed sua fide vivere justum cum Propheta, tum Apo- stolus in locis Parallelis indicant, ut quisque cre- dat, & in fide perseveret, quia fide sua quisque vi- vet. Cæterum ut particula ב modo per ἐκ vertitur, Deut. VI. 5. modo per διὰ per, Deut. XXXII. 21, mo- do simpliciter ut ablativus instrumenti habetur: ita Apostolus promiscue dixit, ἐκ πίσεως, διὰ πίσεως & πίσει Rom. III. 28. 22. 25. Rectius hic sapit Gro- tio Cornel. a Lap. Habacuc, inquit, loquitur non de vita corporis, sed animæ; non naturali, sed super- naturali, gratia scilicet & justitiæ, qua justus, qua- tenus justus est, vivit. Opponit enim hæc duo, scilicet vivere, quod tribuit justo & fideli, & non habere rectam animam, sive displicere DEO, quod tribuit incredulo & injusto. Adhibetur autem ver- bum futurum ζήσεται, vivet, quo Ebræi perpetuita- tem notare solent, notante Buxtorf. in Thesaur. l. 1. c. XII. quia ex fide non solum oriri vitam spiri- tualem, sed eandem etiam continuari, docere in- stituit: Unde Cornel. Abacuc, & Apostolum loqui ait, tam de inchoatione vitæ spiritualis, quam de in- cremento justitiæ & vitæ spiritualis: cum hæc sen- tentia, justus ex fide vivit, sit generalis & uni- versalis, pertinens tam ad Judæos quam ad Chri- stianos, tam ad peccatores, qui primo justificantur, quam ad eos, qui jam justificati sunt. Omnis enim horum vita spiritualis incipit, conservatur, & cre- scit per fidem. Pervertit autem pessime hunc au- reum aphorismum Costerus Jesuita in Enchir. p. 197. quod justum ex fide vivere, nihil aliud sit, quam ju- stum ad fidei normam totam vitam dirigere, ac for- mare: De justificatione enim hic in Propositione agit Apostolus, & agere instituit, non de modo vi- vendi justificatorum, & justitiam fidei declarat e Propheta, non autem sanctitatem vitæ; neque per vitæ sanctitatem vitam consequimur, secundum Apostolum, sed quomodo per fidem in Christum & justificemur & salvemur, Apostolus explican- dum sibi sumit. Denique non Evangelium est vi- vendi norma, sed legis hoc est proprium. Sed Pontificiam glossam Orac. IX. Theol. Apostol.

Rom. I. 32. discussimus. Hæc ergo de propositione Apostolica. Sequitur

TRACTATIO Vel Ἐξεργασία Apostolica. PARS PRIOR DIDACTICA Informatoria DE JUSTITIA FIDEI. SECTIO I. πρόγνωσιν SUBJECTI CONCERNENS.

PARS IV. CAPITIS PRIMI NARRATIO, VEL SUBJECTI EXPLICA- TIO, CONVINCENS NECESSITA- TEM JUSTITIÆ FIDEI.

## 1:18
v. 18. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.

Namely, through the Gospel, which contains threats no less than promises. It begins, however, with threats, just as John the Baptist did. For men must first be terrified, just as Paul was cast to the ground. From heaven, that is, not by the inventions of men, but by divine revelation. See Matt. 21:25. Justin says the Gospel is brighter than the sun. For those who had not worshipped God by the sight of the sun were led by the hearing of the Gospel to worship Him, in his dialogue with Trypho.

The Apostolic elaboration now follows: and first indeed regarding the subject, which is to be led to salvation through the Gospel; then truly regarding the very causes of salvation. There it is demonstrated that ALL are concluded under the wrath of GOD by the force of the law, outside of the grace exhibited in Christ: and by this means the way is paved to the righteousness proposed in the Gospel: since no one can be justified by the law and the works of the law. For it was necessary for the righteousness of faith to be revealed in the Gospel if we are to obtain salvation: because in the law the wrath of GOD is revealed against all men on account of sin. The Apostle's treatment is also rightly resolved in this way, that he demonstrates by two kinds of arguments that righteousness and salvation are obtained by the faith of the Gospel: first by proving the damnation of all men, to which they have made themselves liable by their sins, both from Nature and from Scripture. For if all men are liable to sin and death outside of Christ, it is necessary that they obtain righteousness and life solely through faith in Christ. Then by confirming the form and manner of righteousness from Scripture, that it is necessary for us to be justified by faith without works, from chapter 3:21 up to chapter 6. The prior demonstration is expedited by the proposition in v. 17. GOD reveals His wrath from heaven upon all impiety and unrighteousness of all men. II. By confirmation (1.) general, from the wicked violation of universal or common divine revelation, in this manner: Those who wickedly violate the revealed truth of GOD, they are liable to the wrath of GOD and guilty of death. But all men violate it. The major premise is clear in itself, since the justice of GOD demands this, as is hinted in v. 32. Therefore, for the sake of proving the minor premise, it is taught both that God revealed Himself to men through creation, and that this manifestation was most wickedly violated by them, v. 21, ch. 1 to v. 12, ch. 2. (2) special, from the distinct transgression of the Jews and Gentiles, ch. 2:12, 25, v. 11. By refutation, ch. 2:25. IV. By conclusion, ch. 3:10-20. He says the wrath of GOD is revealed from heaven upon all impiety and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness. Such are all men outside the grace of Christ: whence all are liable to the wrath of God, by the force of divine law. What the Apostle asserts here generally about all, both by the force of his intention, because he wishes to conclude all under sin and death: and also by the force of the method of proof undertaken here: since he demonstrates that the revelation of wrath was made from heaven upon all through the law of nature and Scripture, and not upon some only: upon ALL, in whom τὸ γνωστὸν τῆ Θεẽ φανερόν ἐςι, which is manifest to every one of mortals, nay, is inscribed in the hearts of all. For although he afterwards explains specifically what things have followed them by the judgment of God, certainly horrible even by the dictation of nature and reason itself, who did not glorify God as God, and became vain in the thoughts of their heart, yet he teaches that the wrath of GOD is manifested upon all. Therefore Socinus, Praelect. c. 2, Enjedinus in Locis, and Arminius, resp. ad 31, wrongly understand certain men in particular. Crellius himself proves that all are to be understood, and observes at this place that the article τῶν is not διακριτικὸν, but αἰτιολογικὸν, from the Apostolic scope. Conf. B. Luth. Gloss. margin. ad h. l. But the wrath of God is not revealed through the Gospel, as Grotius wishes, who falsely says that it contains threats no less than promises, because ἐυαγγέλιον, which is known even from the force of the word, is a joyful message about the grace of God, the remission of sins, and salvation, and on account of the opposition of the Law and the Gospel, since threats and condemnation are attributed to the Law, they cannot belong to the Gospel, as it is contradistinguished from the Law: Although therefore in the proclamation of the Evangelists and of John the Proto-Baptist the beginning is made from threats, and men must first be terrified by the Law, which this Apostle also observed here, yet threats do not pertain to the Gospel itself, but to the Law, which in the Sacred ministry and practice ought to be joined, yet by their nature they are and remain most distinct. Grotius followed the Papists, Thomas, Dominicus a Soto, Toletus, Justinian, Bellarmine, Pererius, Cornelius, who thinks the words IN EO are to be repeated ἀπὸ κοινᾶ. Erasmus renders the word ἀποκαλύπλεται, it is uncovered, and opened: as if before the Gospel of Christ the wrath of God had been opened only to the Jews, if they had sinned, and now it is referred to all; but the statement is general, and the wrath of GOD was never not uncovered upon the impiety and injustice of any whatsoever, which the Gentiles also experienced.

It is said, however, to be revealed, because it lies hidden, intercepted as it were by a cloud of sins, until, that cloud being dispersed, the wrath of GOD against sins appears to human reason: which happens both through Scripture, and through the law of nature and conscience, and through the judgments of GOD, examples, and experience.

ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν) Against sins which are directed straight at God.

καὶ ἀδικίαν ἀνθρώπων) against sins against men. The Hebrews, writing in Greek, use ἀδικίας more broadly than the Philosophers, so that it signifies everything which is done toward men less than ought to be done by reason of some duty. Philo also joined these two, ἀδικίαν καὶ ἀσέβειαν, concerning the confusion of tongues: ἀδικίαν μὲν σπείροντες, ἀσέβειαν δὲ θερίζοντες. And he significantly said ἀνθρώπων, that is, not of the Jews only, but also of all nations. The Law of Moses pertained to the Jews alone.

By those words all sins are comprehended: by ἀσέβειαν indeed sins designated against the first Table of the Law; but by ἀδικίαν those against the second: the former is committed against God, the latter against one's neighbor. Nor did the Law pertain only to the Jews; even if it was first promulgated to them. For the moral Law looks to all: inscribed in all first at creation, but prescribed afterwards in the Decalogue and in a solemn repetition. For how else could the curse of the Law strike all who do not keep it, unless the Law pertained to all?

Τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων) He says of those men who so suppress the τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας concerning GOD, concerning his goodness and justice, concerning the honorable, through evil morals, that they do not appear any more than those who are held captive in a deep prison. That is similar in the old chorus. Ἄῤῥητες δὲ ὁπόσοι τὸ δίκαιον ἄγνσι ὑπὸ τᾶς ἀδίκω βωτᾶς ἄφανες. Paul takes ἀδικίαν here more generally than just now, so that it also embraces ἀσέβειαν, which the following will show. Origen against Celsus in the sixth book, when he had said: διὰ τῦτο δὲ καὶ τὸς τὰ ἀληθῆ περὶ θεῦ ὑπολαβόντας φαμὲν ὑποκεῖσθαι ταῖς τῶν ἁμαρ- τανόντων κολάσεσιν, he then subjoined these and the following words of Paul. The same author in the first book produces this confession of Celsus: ὅτι ἐςὶν ἀρχαῖος ἄνωθεν λόγΘ περὶ θεῦ! ἀεὶ, τὰ ἴδη σοφώταλα καὶ πόλεις, καὶ ἄνδρες σοφοὶ κατεγένοντο.
