The Greeks call those notions sometimes ἐννοίας, sometimes προλήψεις, as can be seen in Cicero, Academicorum II and de Finibus III. & Tusculanarum I. Justin calls them σπέρματα ἀληθείας in all. We have brought forward some things about them in lib. II. de Jure Pacis ac Belli XX. 45. & 46. Plutarch has more in his book on that subject against the Stoics. Tertullian de anima: Therefore no soul is without crime, because no soul is without the seed of good. The same against Marcion: The conscience of GOD is a gift to souls from the beginning. Cyprian de Idolorum vanitate: This is the sum of the offense, to be unwilling to acknowledge whom you cannot be ignorant of.

By truth are understood notions common to all: which therefore in themselves and by themselves are not mere errors and falsehoods, as some at Helmstedt have raved, especially Dan. Hoffmann, about whose error in natural and revealed Theology we have treated most abundantly: for even if errors adhere to the knowing subject, the natural notions themselves, to which they adhere, are not errors, but are adorned by the Apostle with the honorable name of ἀληθείας, and are openly distinguished from ἀδικία, with which they are joined by the fault of the subject. Here, however, this προσδιορισμὸς is not διακριτικὸς or restrictive, of those who hold the truth in injustice from others who do not hold the truth in injustice, but it is αἰτιολογικὸς or causal; therefore the wrath of GOD is revealed upon the impiety and injustice of any men whatsoever, because the truth is known to all, if not from the book of Scripture, certainly from the book of nature, which they indeed hold in injustice. For he discourses first generally about all men whatsoever, whether they be Jews or Gentiles, which is also observed here by Grotius: and about any impiety and injustice whatsoever, before he notes certain sins in particular. The object here therefore is not the Gentiles, but all men, who in themselves, or considered outside of Christ, are guilty both of ἀσεβείας or impiety toward GOD, and of ἀδικίας or injustice toward their neighbor, and are thus subject to wrath and condemnation, so that it is necessary to seek righteousness elsewhere. For there is none righteous, none seeking GOD. Rom. III. 10, 11. The matter therefore is not only about certain ones, as Grotius wishes, who so suppress the τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας about God, about his goodness, and justice, and about what is honorable through evil morals, that they no more appear than one who is detained captive in a deep prison. For there is no one who, being constituted outside the grace of Christ, does not sometimes so detain the same, that they do not appear otherwise, even if they are detained more by this than by another. As after the fall ἀδικία is common to all, so also is this, that all sometimes detain the truth ἐν ἀδικίᾳ: however much there may be degrees of impiety and injustice.

They are said, however, to be detained ἐν ἀδικίᾳ, because it is δίκαιον, and the law of God requires, that those common notions, therefore implanted by God, be rightly used, so that we do not neglect to seek God, nor remain in impiety and injustice. Acts XVII. 27. Nor indeed does Arminius have a just cause for wondering in art. 31. (which the blessed Hülsemann noted here) and Ostorodus in his Institutes, ch. 1, how those can be said to be injurious to God, or that they wrongfully withhold from God the worship due to him, who were not previously instructed by any grace or Spirit of God, who falsely suppose that the συνζητήσεις or practical collections about worshipping God elicited by man from the Creation and government of the world are not elicited by a natural faculty, but by a supernatural one, and thus are a certain most universal grace of God, which is commonly called natural instinct, when nevertheless it is from the beginning supernatural, just as Pelagius once denied that nature ought to be distinguished from divine grace, since the natural faculties themselves and their exercises, concerning divine objects, flow from the motion of divine grace, as can be seen from the Acts of Pelagius, ch. 15, 16, and ch., to which Augustine opposed his book on grace.

of Christ, in order to show by the Apostolic phrase that grace is understood not as of creation, or remaining from creation, but as obtained by the merit of Christ. See Vossius, Hist. Pel. book 3, on Christ.

Latin:

v. 18. ἀποκαλύπτεται γὰρ ὀργὴ Θεῦ ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῦ.

NEmpe per Evangelium continens minas non minus quam promissa. Incipit autem à minis, ut & Johan- nes Baptista. Perterrendi enim prius sunt homines, sicut Paulus in terram dejectus fuit. Ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῦ, id est, non ho- minum commentis, sed divina revelatione. Vid. Matth. XXI. 25. Evangelium, Justinus ait, sole esse lucidius. Nam qui solis conspectu Deum non coluerant, eos auditu Evangelii adductos, ut eum colerent, colloquio cum Tryphone.

Ἐξεργασία Apostolica jam sequitur: & primum quidem quoad subjectum, quod per Evangelium ad salutem perducendum; tum vero quoad ipsas sa- lutis causas. Illic demonstratur, OMNES sub ira DEI vi legis conclusos esse extra gratiam in Christo exhibitam: eoque vita sternitur ad justitiam in Evangelio propositam: siquidem nemo per legem, & opera legis justificari possit. Necessarium enim fuit in Evangelio revelari justitiam fidei, si salutem adipisci debeamus: quia in lege revelatur ira DEI in omnes homines propter peccatum. Recte etiam tractatio Apostoli ita resolvitur, quod duobus ar- gumentorum generibus demonstret, fide Evangelii obtineri justitiam & salutem: primum evincendo omnium hominum damnationem, cui se peccatis obnoxios fecerunt, cum e Natura, tum e Scriptu- ra. Si enim omnes homines peccato, & morti ob- noxii sunt extra Christum, necessum est, ut per fi- dem in Christum unice justitiam & vitam conse- quantur. Deinde formam & modum justitiæ e Scri- ptura confirmando, quod absque operibus fide nos justificari oporteat a c. III. 21. usque ad c. VI. Prior demonstratio expeditur propositione v. 17. DEUS iram suam de cælo revelat super impie- tatem, & iniquitatem omnem omnium hominum. II. confirmatione (1.) generali, ab universalis seu communis revelationis divinæ violatione nefaria, h. m. Qui revelatam DEI veritatem nefarie vio- lant, illi iræ DEI sunt obnoxii, & mortis rei. At omnes homines violant. Major per se luculenta est, quum hoc justitia DEI poscat, ut v. 32. innuitur. Minoris ergo probandæ gratia docetur, tum quod Deus revelarir se hominibus per creationem, tum quod ab iis iniquissime violata sit illa patefactio v. 21. c. I. ad v. 12. c. II. (2) speciali, à distincta præ- varicatione Judæorum & Gentilium c. II. 12. 25. v. II. Confutatione c. II. 25. IV. Conclusione c. III. 10. 20. Iram DEI dicit revelari de cælo super omnem im- pietatem & injustitiam hominum, qui veritatem in injustitia detinent. Quales omnes homines sunt extra gratiam Christi: unde omnes iræ Dei obno- xii sunt, vi legis divinæ. Quod hic generatim de omnibus asserit Apostolus, tum vi intentionis suæ, quia omnes sub peccato & morte concludere vult: tum etiam vi methodi probationis hic susceptæ: siquidem revelationem iræ super omnes factam cœlitus per legem naturæ & Scripturæ, demon- stret non super aliquos saltem: super OMNES, in quibus τὸ γνωστὸν τῆ Θεẽ φανερόν ἐςι, quod nemi- ni non mortalium manifestum, imo in cordibus omnium inscriptum est. Quamvis enim speciatim postea exequatur, quænam consequuta eos sint, ju- dicio Dei, horrenda certe vel ipsa natura & ratione dictante, qui Deum non glorificarunt, ut Deum, & vani facti sunt in cogitationibus cordis sui, super omnes tamen iram DEI manifestari docet. Perpe- ram ergo Socinus prælect. c. 2. Enjedinus in Locis & Arminius resp. ad 31. particulariter quosdam intelligunt homines. Omnes intelligendos pro- bat ipse Crellius ad h. l. articulum τῶν non esse dia- κριτικὸν, sed αἰτιολογικὸν observat, e scopo Aposto- lico.Conf.B.Luth.Gloss.margin.ad h.l. Non autem revelatur ira Dei per Evangelium, ut vult Grotius, quod minas non minus continere, quam promissa fal- so ait, quia ἐυαγγέλιον, quod vel ex vi vocis notum est, latum nuncium est de gratia Dei, remissione pec- catorum & salute, ac propter oppositionem legis & Evangelii, quum Legi minæ & condemnatio tri- buantur, Evangelio, qua contradistinguitur legi, convenire nequeunt: Etsi ergo in præconio Evan- gelistarum, ac Johannis Proto-Baptistæ initium à minis fiat, ac perterrendi prius lege sint homines, quod etiam hic Apostolus observavit, non tamen minæ ad Evangelium ipsum pertinent, sed ad legem, quæ in ministerio Sacro, & praxi conjuncta esse debent, natura tamen sua distinctissima sunt, & ma- nent. Sequutus est Grotius Papistas, Thomam, Dominicum a Soto, Toletum, Justinian. Bellarmin. Pererium, Cornelium, qui voces IN EO ἀπὸ κοινᾶ repetendas putat. Erasmus vocem ἀποκαλύπλεται reddit, retegitur, & aperitur: quasi ante Evange- lium Christi in solos Judæos aperta fuerit ira Dei,si peccassent, nunc referetur in omnes; Sed generalis est sententia, & nunquam non referata fuit DEI ira super quorumvis impietatem & injustitiam, quod experti etiam sunt gentiles.

Dicitur autem revelari, quia peccatorum nube velut intercepta latet, donec ea discussa humanæ rationi appareat ira DEI adversus peccata: quod fit tum per scripturam, tum per legem naturæ,& con- scientiam, tum per judicia DEI, exempla, & expe- rientiam.

ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν) Adversus peccata, quæ directe in Deum feruntur.

καὶ ἀδικίαν ἀνθρώπων) adversus peccata contra homines. ἀδικίας Hebræi Græce scribentes latius usurpant quam Phi- losophi, ut significet omne id, quod erga homines minus fit quam debet fieri ex officii alicujus ratione. Conjunxit hæc duo ἀδικίαν καὶ ἀσέβειαν etiamPhilo de linguarum confusio- ne: ἀδικίαν μὲν σπείροντες, ἀσέβειαν δὲ θερίζοντες. Et signifi- canter dixit ἀνθρώπων, id est, non Judæorum tantum, sed & omnium gentium.Lex Mosis ad solos Judæos pertinebat.

Vocibus illis peccata omnia comprehenduntur: per ἀσέβειαν quidem peccata contra primam legis Tabulam designata; per ἀδικίαν vero contra secun- dam: illa adversusDeum committitur,hæc adver- sus proximum. Neque vero lex tantum ad Judæos pertinebat; etsi iisdem promulgata primum fue- rit. Lex moralis enim ad omnes spectat: omni- bus inscripta primum in creatione, sed præscripta postmodum in Decalogo, ac folemni repetitione. Quomodo enim alias omnes ferire posset maledi- ctio legis, qui eam non servant, nisi ad omnes lex pertineret?

Τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων) Eorum inquit hominum, qui τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας de DEO, de ejus bonitate ac justitia, de honesto, per malos mores ita opprimunt, ut non magis appareant, quam qui in alto carcere captivi deti- nentur. Simile istud in choro vetere. Ἄῤῥητες δὲ ὁπόσοι τὸ δίκαιον ἄγνσι ὑπὸ τᾶς ἀδίκω βωτᾶς ἄφανες. ἀδικίαν hic Paulus generalius sumit quam modo, ut & ἀσέ- βειαν complectatur, quod ostendent sequentia. Origenes adversus Celsum sexto cum dixisset: διὰ τῦτο δὲ καὶ τὸς τὰ ἀληθῆ περὶ θεῦ ὑπολαβόντας φαμὲν ὑποκεῖσθαι ταῖς τῶν ἁμαρ- τανόντων κολάσεσιν, hæc deinde & sequentia Pauli verba sub- texit Idem libro primo, Celfi hanc producit confessionem: ὅτι ἐςὶν ἀρχαῖος ἄνωθεν λόγΘ περὶ θεῦ! ἀεὶ, τὰ ἴδη σοφώταλα καὶ πόλεις, καὶ ἄνδρες σοφοὶ κατεγένοντο. Notitias illas Græci modo ἐννοίας, modo προλήψεις vocant, ut apud Ciceronem videre est Academicorum II. & de Finibus III. & Tuscula- narum I. Justinus vocat σπέρματα ἀληθείας παρὰ πᾶσιν. De iis nos quædam attulimus lib. II. de Jure Pacis ac Belli XX. 45. & 46. Plura Plutarchus in ejus argumenti libro contra Stoicos. Tertullianus de anima: Propterea nulla anima fine crimine, quia nulla fine boni semine. Idem contra Marcio- nem: Animæ à primordio Conscientia DEI dos est. Cypria- nus de Idolorum vanitate: Hæc est summa delicti,nolle agno- scere quem ignorare non possis.

Per veritatem notitiæ intelliguntur omnibus communes: quæ proinde in se ac per se non sunt meri errores, & falsitates, uti nonnulli Helmstadii delirarunt, imprimis Dan. Hoffmannus, de quo errore in Theol, naturali & revelata uberrime egi- mus: etsi enim adhæreant subjecto cognoscenti errores, ipsæ tamen notitiæ naturales, quibus ad- hærent, errores non sunt, sed honorifico ἀληθείας nomine ornantur ab Apostolo, ac aperte discri- minantur ab ἀδικίᾳ, cum qua conjunctæ sunt, sub- jecti culpa. Hic vero προσδιορισμὸς non est δια- κριτικὸς vel restrictivus, τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων ab aliis, qui non detinent veritatem in injustitia, sed est αἰτιολογικὸς vel causalis; ideo su- per hominum quorumvis impietatem & injusti- tiam iram DEI revelari, quia omnibus nota est ve- ritas, si non è scripturæ, certe naturæ libro, quam vero in injustitia detinent. Prius enim generaliter de hominibus disserit quibusvis, sive Judæi, sive gen- tes sint, quod etiam hic observatum Grotio: & de impietate ac injustitia quavis, antequam in specie insignia quædam peccata notet. Objectum ergo hic sunt non gentiles, sed omnes homines, qua in sese, vel extra Christum considerati rei sunt tum ἀσεβείας seu impietatis in DEUM, tum ἀδικίας seu injustitiæ in proximum, adeoque iræ & damnatio- ni obnoxii, ut aliunde justitiam quærere oporteat. Nullus enim est justus, nullus requirens DEUM. Rom. III.10.11. Non ergo tantum de quibusdam res est, ut vult Grotius, qui τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας de Deo, de ejus bonitate, ac justitia, de honesto per malos mores ita opprimunt, ut non magis appareant, quam qui in alto carcere captivi detinetur. Nemo enim non extra gratiam Christi constitutus deti- net ita quandoq; easdem, ut non aliter appareant, etsi ab hoc plus detineantur,quam ab alio.Uti post lapsum ἀδικία communis omnibus est, ita & hoc, quod nonnunquam ἐν ἀδικίᾳ veritatem detineant omnes: utut impietatis, & injustitiæ gradus dentur.

Dicuntur autem ἐν ἀδικίᾳ detineri, quia δίκαιον est, & jusDei requirit,ut recte usurpentur commu- nes illæ notitiæ, ideo a Deo inditæ, ut Deum quæ- rere non negligamus, nec in impietate ac injustitia maneamus. Act. XVII. 27. Nec vero mirandi justa causam habet Armin.in art.31. (quod hic monuit B. Hülsemannus) & Ostorodus inst. c. l. quomodo ii possint dici injurii in Deum, seu quod cultum Deo debitum injuria ipsi subtrahant, qui nulla gratia aut Spiritu Dei antea fuerunt instructi, qui falso supponunt, συνζητήσεις seu collectiones Practicas de Deo colendo ex Creatione & gubernatione mundi ab homine elicitas, non elici facultate naturali,sed su- pernaturali, adeoque esse quandam universalissi- mam Dei gratiam, quæ vulgo vocetur naturalis in- stinctus, cum tamen a principio sit supernaturali, quomodo olim Pelagius negabat naturam gratia divinæ contradistingui debere, cum ipsæ naturales facultates earumq; exercitia, circa objecta divina fluunt ex motu divina gratia, uti videre est ex gestis Pelag.c.15.16.& c. cui opposuit August.lib.de gratia

Christi, ut oftenderet phrasi Apostolica gratiam non creationis, seu ex creatione residuam, sed me- rito Christi partam intelligi. Vid. Vossii Hist. Pel. l. 3. de Christo.

## 1:19
For God has manifested it to them) In various ways, concerning which Dio Chrysostom treats in his Olympic oration, which is well worth reading. Hence even those who had not known had an opportunity of knowing.

For the invisible things of him.) We see the actions of men, we do not see the actions of God, but we know them from his works.

Because that which is known of God is manifest in them) He calls that which can be known about God and is both easy and useful 'that which is known of God,' such as that He is most powerful and has authority over all things, as the Apostle will now explain. There are other things less necessary for directing life, and therefore more obscure. For this reason, Josephus against Apion, book 2, says that God is 'by power alone known to us, but what He is in essence is unknown in them,' this is to many among them, such as the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics, whose arguments on this matter, approaching the most ancient and most widely diffused tradition, are sufficient to convince Aristotle and Epicurus. See our first book on the Truth of the Christian Religion and the book of Wisdom 13 at the beginning, and what we have said there, and Acts 17:27.

The Apostle now begins to treat specifically of the acquired knowledge of God: namely, that the invisible things of God are known from visible creatures, or from the creation of the world, and he determines what those things are: and hence that even the Gentiles themselves are inexcusable, who could have known God, but did not worship Him as God: by the just judgment of God they were given over to uncleanness, a reprobate mind, and most grievous sins, and filled with all injustice, by their own fault. That this concerns natural knowledge, and not that which was revealed through the miracles of the Apostles, was most abundantly asserted in the book on the natural and revealed knowledge of God against Socinus: whom Crellius himself here deserts and refutes in his Commentary on this passage. The knowledge of God, says Ambrose on this passage, is implanted from this fabric of the world: For that God, who is by nature invisible, might also be known as visible, a work was made by Him, which would manifest the Maker by its visibility.

Lest it be objected that the knowledge of God has not been revealed to all, and therefore that not all have the truth known to them, so that they might hold it and become subject to the wrath of God; the Apostle teaches that to all 'that which is known of God' is manifest, that which it is helpful to know about God, through nature; whether this is accepted through 'acquired' knowledge, concerning which Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Theophylact speak, or through 'innate' and implanted knowledge alone. For those things which treat commonly of all are not to be restricted only to knowledge acquired through discourse and reasoning. For to 'that which is known of God,' which is manifest in all, belongs also whatever shines in the mind of man about God through those common notions without discourse, as in those who do not or cannot use reason and discourse, which is nevertheless inscribed on their minds, that there is a God. See what is in the Apostolic Oracles and the System of Theology. Volume II. We have spoken of these things. Whence the Apostle later treats both of acquired knowledge, which is had through the contemplation of the creature, v. 20, when he teaches that the book of the creature is openly exposed: and of innate knowledge, when he exhibits the work of the law inscribed on their hearts, and the dictate or book of conscience, c. 2:15.

From the creation of the world. From the beginning of the human race. Thus 'from' is taken in Matthew 13:35, 24:34, Luke 11:50. A similar expression is in John 15:27, and by consensus the Hebrews say from the creation of the world.

Although this can be rendered, from the beginning of the human race, or rather of the created world, without detriment to the sense, provided those words are not snatched with Socinus to the preceding words, which were invisible from the creation of the world, as if they could have been seen in the time of the Apostles, and with Socinus and Ostorod here the sense is extorted, that the promises and commands of God not known before by men could be seen through the miracles of Christ and the Apostles: but the sense remains, which the intention of the Apostle requires, that the invisible things of God could be seen from the creation of the world through facts or created works, namely His eternal power and deity; yet these words are more correctly taken concerning the means of knowing than concerning the time from which they could be known: because that preposition 'from' signifies 'out of' when it concerns the drawing of knowledge: Matthew 7:16, c. 24:32, Mark 13:28. Wisdom 13:3. But when the discourse is about time, it is not said 'from the creation,' but 'from the beginning of the creation,' Mark 10:6, c. 21:19, 2 Peter 3:4, 'from the foundation of the world,' Matthew 25:34, Hebrews 9:26, Revelation 13:8, c. 17:8. And it is better to understand 'creation' as the creatures themselves, since it is manifest that the Apostle intends that the Gentiles could know the Creator 'from the creation' and ought to have sought Him, so that they might honor Him as the one true God: but who 'worshipped the creature rather than the Creator,' v. 25.

A distortion, however, is when Grotius explains τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς as 'in many among them,' such as the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics; for the Apostle is not speaking restrictively about certain ones, but generally about all, and as Grotius previously said significantly, ἀνθρώπων, that is, not of the Jews only, but also of all nations: nor was τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ known only to those philosophers, or to those who felt more correctly about God than others and devoted effort to external honesty, but also to those who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and were given over to a debased mind: the Apostle teaches in v. 32 that the δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ was not unknown to all these, and thus asserts that what can be known about God is φανερὸν in all; that is, as far as it concerns inquiring into a further knowledge of God, so that no one may have an excuse. If it were φανερὸν only in some, the rest would certainly not be ἀναπολόγητοι, but would have something with which to excuse themselves. We have seen concerning Aristotle, whether he was devoid of the knowledge of God, in our book on the Nature and Revelation of the knowledge of God: It is the opinion of many that Epicurus did not deny God entirely, whom they wish to be considered ἄθεον; because while others worshipped gods, he did not acknowledge such ones. Nor do those who deny God with their mouth therefore not carry inscribed on their heart that there is a God. Indeed, they are convinced inwardly by the very dictate of nature and conscience that there is a God, however much they may dissemble it outwardly. For as Justin says in q. 1 to the Greeks, 'all confess that there is a God by a common notion.' And according to Damascene, l. 1 de Orth. fide c. III, 'the knowledge that there is a God is naturally sown in all by Him': That knowledge, that there is a God, is naturally implanted in all by Him.

Latin:

Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς αὐτοῖς ἐφανέρωσε) Variis modis, de quibus agit Dion Prusiensis in Olympica oratione lectu dignissima. Hinc & illi, qui non cognoverant, occasionem cognoscendi habuere.

Τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτῦ.) Hominum actiones videmus, Dei actiones non videmus, sed ex operibus eas cognoscimus.

Διότι τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φανερόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς) τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ vocat id quod de Deo sciri & facile potest & expe- dit, qualia sunt esse eum potentissimum, & jus habere in o- mnia, ut jam Apostolus explicabit. Sunt alia minus ad vitam dirigendam neceffaria, eoque obscuriora. Ideo Josephus con- tra Appionem ll. Deum dicit δυνάμει μὲν μόνον ἡμῖν γνώρι- μον, ὁποῖος δὲ κατ᾽ ὀσίαν ἄγνωστον ἐν αὐτοῖς, hic est mul- tis inter ipsos, ut Pythagoreis, Platonicis, Stoicis, quorum in hanc rem argumenta, accedentia ad vetustissimam latiffi- meque diffusam traditionem, convincendo Aristoteli & Epicuro sufficiunt. Vide librum nostrum primum de Ve- ritate Religionis Christianæ & librum Sapientiæ XIII. initio & quæ ibi, & Act. XVII. 27. à nobis dicta.

Incipit nunc Apostolus speciatim agere de noti- tia Dei acquisita : quod nempe invisibilia Dei è vi- sibilibus creaturis, vel è creatione mundi cogno- scantur, & quæ illa sint, determinat: atque hinc in- excusabiles esse etiam ipsos gentiles, qui Deum co- gnoscere potuerunt, eum autem non coluerint ut Deum: justo Dei judicio in immunditiem, sensum reprobum, ac peccata gravissima traditi, omnique injustitia, propria culpa, impleti. Quod autem de agnitione naturali, non vero ea, quæ per miracula Apostolorum patefacta, agatur, lib. de naturali & revelata DEI notitia adversus Socinum assertum fuit uberrime: quem hic deserit & refellit ipse Crellius in Comm. ad h. l. Notitia Dei, inquit Am- brosius in h. l. insita est ex hac mundi fabrica: Ille enim Deus, qui naturâ invisibilis est, etiam visibilis posset sciri, opus factum est ab eo, quod opificem visibi- litate sua manifestaret.

Ne obvertatur, non omnibus revelatam esse DEI notitiam, adeoque veritatem non habere o- mnes cognitam, ut eam detinere possint, ac iræ DEI obnoxii fiant; docet Apostolus, omnibus τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φανερὸν, id quod deDeo scire juvat, manifestum esse per naturam; sive per ἐπίκτητον, seu acquisitam notitiam, de qua Augustinus, Hiero- nymus, Ambrosius, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus hoc accipiunt, seu per ἔμφυτον solum, & insitam. Quæ enim communiter de omnibus agunt, non re- stringenda tantum ad notitiam per discursum & ratiocinationem acquisitam. Nam ad τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod in omnibus φανερὸν est, pertinet etiam, quicquid deDeo per communes illas notitias in ani- mo hominis sine discursu lucet, utpote in illis qui ratione ac discursu non utuntur, aut uti nequeunt, quod tamen mentibus inscriptum est, esse Deum. Videantur quæ in Oraculis Apostolicis, & System. Theol. Tom. II. de his diximus. Unde Apostolus postea & de acquisita notitia, quæ per intuitum creaturæ habetur, agit v. 20. quum creaturæ li- brum palam expositum esse docet : & de insita, quum opus legis cordibus inscriptum, & dictamen vel librum conscientiæ exhibet c. II. 15.

Ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου. Ab initio humani generis. Sic ἀπὸ fu- mitur Matth. XIII. 35. XXIV. 34. Luc. XI. 50. Similis locutio Joh.XV. 27. & eonsensu dicunt Hebræi מבּריאת העולם.

Quanquam reddi possit hoc, ab initio generis hu- mani, vel potius mundi conditi, citra detrimentum sensus, modo non rapiantur cum Socino illa ad præ- cedentia verba, quæ invisibilia fuerunt inde à con- dito mundo, quasi tempore Apostolorum conspici illa potuerint, & cum Socino & Ostorodo hic ex- torqueatur sensus, non cognita antea ab hominibus promissa Dei & mandata, per miracula Christi & Apostolorum conspici potuisse: sed sensus maneat, quem requirit intentio Apostoli, invisibilia DEI conspici inde à mundo condito per facta vel opera creata potuisse, æternam nempe potentiam & deita- ten; tamen rectius de medio cognoscendi, quam de tempore, ex quo cognosci potuerint, hæc verba ac- cipiuntur: quia præpositio illa ἀπὸ significat ex, quando de haurienda cognitione agitur: Matth. VII. 16. c. XXIV. 32. Marc. XIII.28. Sap.XIII.3.cum vero de tempore sermo est, non ἀπὸ κτίσεως dici- tur, sed ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως Marc. X. 16. c. XXI. 19. 2. Petr. III. 4. ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου Matth. XXV. 24. Ebr. IX. 26. Ap. XIII. 8. c. XVII. 8. & præstat κτίσιν de creaturis ipsis intelligere, quom manife- stum sit, id velle Apostolum, quod gentiles ἀπὸ κτίσεως ex creaturis cognoscere potuerint τὸν κτί- σαντα eumque inquirere debuerint, ut honora- rent ceu unum verum DEUM: qui vero ἐλάτρευ- σαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα; v. 25.

Detorsio autem est, cum Grotius τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς ex- plicat in multis inter ipsos, ut Pythagoreis, Platonicis, Stoicis; nam loquitur Apostolus non restricte de quibusdam, sed generaliter de omnibus, & ut antea Grotius significanter dixit, ἀνθρώπων, id est, non Ju dæorum tantum, sed & omnium gentium: neque illis solum Philosophis τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ notum fuit, aut qui de Deo rectius aliis senserunt, & honestati ex- ternæ operam dederut, sed etiam istis, qui gloriam Dei incorruptibilis in similitudinem imaginis cor- ruptibilis commutârunt, & in sensum reprobum dati sunt: quibus omnibus δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ non igno- tum fuisse docet Apostolus v. 32. adeoque φανερὸν manifestum in omnibus asserit, id quod de Deo sogno- sci potest; quantum scilicet interest ad inquiren- dum ulteriorem Dei notitiam, ut nemo excusatio- nem habeat. Si in quibusdam solum φανερὸν id es- set, reliqui certe non effent ἀναπολόγητοι, sed ha- berent, quo se excusarent. De Aristotele, an expers fuerit notitiæ Dei lib. de Nat. & Rev. Dei notitia vidimus: Nec Epicurum Deum prorsus negasse, multorum est sententia, quem ἄθεον habitum vo- lunt; quod quum alii deos colebant, tales non agnoverit.Neque qui ore negant Deum, cordi in- scriptum ideo haud gerunt, esse Deum. Imo con- vincuntur intrinsecus à proprio naturæ & consci- entiæ dictamine, quod sit Deus, utut id diffi- mulent extrinsecus. Nam ut Justinus q.1. adGræcos πάντες ὅτι ἐστὶν Θεὸς ὁμολογῶσι κοινῇ ἐννοίᾳ. Et se- cundum Damasc. l. 1. de Orth. fide c. III. πᾶσιν ἡ γνῶσις τῆ εἶναι Θεὸν ὑπ᾽ αὐτῷ φυσικῶς ἐγκατέ- σπαρται: Notitia illa, quod sit Deus, omnibus ab ipso naturaliter est insita.

## 1:20
τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα ) to the works, Wis. XIII. 1. Hellenistic Jews often translate מעשה as ποίημα, as in Ecclesiasticus VII. 14, 'behold the works of God.' So also Ps. CXLIII. 5. From the work, the operation is understood. A certain ancient writer not badly: 'for from the greatness and beauty of the creatures, their Creator is proportionately contemplated.' Plotinus: 'That to attribute the essence and constitution of this universe to chance and luck, as if it were irrational and possessed by a man who has neither mind nor sense, is clearly something that many and sufficient arguments have long since cried out against, demonstrating it.' The same elsewhere: 'Since the whole is consistent in its coming into being, he who contemplates this might perhaps admire it, as God having made me.' Tatian on God: 'We know this through His making, we grasp the invisible of His power by the works.' Athenagoras: 'Having so many things for piety, the order, the constant harmony, the magnitude, the color, the shape, the arrangement of the world.' This is what the Hebrews call ברית עולם from Isaiah XXIV. 5.

Καθοράται) That is, they are sufficiently apparent. And there is an oxymoron in 'the invisible are clearly seen.' The Hebrews love to express all internal and external senses with the word for seeing.

and His eternal power.

Power always enduring. Thus the word ἀΐδιος is taken, and in Jude 6, and in Symmachus Micah VII. 8, where others have 'to the mountain'.

(C) 4 others others εἰς αὐτό. That such is the power of God appears from the fact that living creatures are always being born, one after another, from the force which God has implanted in things. The power of men is fragile, and if not otherwise, it perishes with them themselves.

And divinity.

You have the word ὑπόστης and Wisdom 18:9. The Rabbis say אלהות and by that word they denote empire most especially. The same is גזות יהוה Isaiah 24:14. The craftsman has a right to his craft. Seneca, Epistle 95: The first worship of the gods is to believe in the gods: then to render to them their majesty, to render their goodness, without which there is no majesty. To know that they are those who preside over the world: who govern all things by their own power, who carry out the protection of the human race.

So that it might be clear what those invisible things of God are, which are clearly seen being understood through created things, and that they might not be drawn to mysteries revealed by the sole revelation of Scripture, the Apostle adds that they indicate His eternal power and divinity. But Socinus and Ostorodus, concerning divine promises, interpret eternal power perversely, and understand divinity as that which God perpetually wills us to do, against the force of the words, the usage of Scripture, and the intention and context of the Apostle. A promise is a relative thing, and is in God; and God can do many things which are not contained in His promises, and the power of God and divine promise are most different: finally, those things are not truly eternal, even if they are about eternal goods, but they come to be in time. But that which God perpetually wills us to do, to be called divinity, is both unheard of and absurdly invented. Grotius more correctly understands the power as always enduring; yet he does not thus attain the full sense of the word and the mind of the Apostle: for he indicates not only power from the part after, as they say, but also eternal from the part before: which it is certain is known by the light of nature. But by divinity, the same Grotius wrongly asserts that empire is most especially denoted, as by the Hebrew אלהות. We have taught elsewhere that the Hebrew word, from Arabism, denotes σέβασμα, a numen to be adored: and that the Greek θειότης is interchanged with θεότητι as synonyms: and so the Apostle teaches that both interminable power and divinity itself, by which GOD is what He is (which certainly is not by empire), are known by nature: so that not only the existence of God, eternity, and supreme power, but also that God is an independent and truly infinite Spirit, and so immaterial and incorruptible, can be concluded from created things. To this natural knowledge of God, the Gentiles are diametrically opposed, when they transformed divinity into the likeness of a corruptible image and of finite and dependent things.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὲς ἀναπολογήτες.

Construe with καθορᾶται. These properties of God appear sufficiently to convict those of an ungrateful mind who have not worshipped such a GOD. You have the word ἀναπολογήτε also below in 2:1 and in Cicero's letters to Atticus. The more knowledge, the less excuse. Luke 12:47, John 9:41, 15:24. He speaks, however, of the Gentiles for the most part; because there have always been few worshipping Greeks.

These things are not to be taken with Grotius concerning the Gentiles for the most part, but universally: for although there were sometimes some worshipping Greeks so called comparatively, with respect to others who were entirely alien to the worship of God, nevertheless no worship pleasing to God could be performed outside of Christ, since it is impossible to please God without faith (Heb. 11:6). Therefore, they worshipped God in their own way, not by the reason which GOD prescribed, which alone is pleasing to Him. For no one comes to the Father except through the Son (John 14:6). There is no worship of God pleasing to Him, unless Christ the Son is the altar. In this one man, in grace, we are pleasing to God, and we perform worship pleasing to God. Nor did the Gentiles acknowledge the true God, to whom they ought to have been led to be sought through that natural knowledge (Acts 17:27), who is none other than the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; therefore, as they were without Christ, so they were also atheists, by the judgment of the Apostle (Eph. 2:12). And here the Apostle convicts, not some, but ALL Gentiles, because they did not glorify God as God, even though that which is known of God was manifest in them; and for that reason, He makes them without excuse. Whence Lactantius, Inst. Book 6, ch. 9: Let us suppose it possible that someone might grasp true virtues by a natural and innate good, such as we have received Cimon to have been at Athens, who both gave alms to the needy and invited the poor and the naked: Nevertheless, when that one thing which is the greatest is missing, the acknowledgment of GOD, then all those goods are superfluous and empty. But that 'to be' here is to be taken not as final, but as consecutive, as Theophylact warns, which is to be observed against the Calvinists Piscator, Dan. Tossanus, and others, who understand it thus, that God indulged them the knowledge of Himself for this very purpose, that afterwards they might have nothing to allege. For the proper end of natural knowledge of God is that it may be a certain leading by the hand to a further acknowledgment of GOD proposed in the Word and revealed to the Church, which is called the pedagogical end: but this effect is accidental, that through it, those who neglect to seek further knowledge of God are rendered without excuse, not from the ordination or intention of God, but happening beyond the same: therefore 'to be' in this place is 'so as to be.' But the Leyden theologians are inept when, in the Censure of the Arminian Confession, ch. 11, class 7, they say they are inexcusable because God passed them by in the provision of sufficient grace. For thus, not they themselves would be without excuse, but God, who passed them by.

Meanwhile, those natural notices are not salvific, nor do they contribute anything to salvation, because salvation can by no means be ascribed to nature, but solely to grace: nor does the use of them contribute to conversion, even if abuse and neglect impede conversion; they lead us by the hand so that we may seek the Church, in which God has revealed Himself, they do not lead us into the Church, or to the saving knowledge of God; which is solely to be attributed to Christ received: Matt. 11:27, John 1:18. In this sense is to be taken that of Tertullian on the resurrection of the flesh: God sent before you nature as a teacher, intending to send prophecy also, so that you might more easily believe the prophecy as a disciple of nature. And that which Basil has in Homily 11 on the Hexaemeron: The world is a school for rational souls and a training ground for the knowledge of God.

Latin:

τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα ) τοῖς ἔργοις Sap. XIII. 1. Judæi Hellenistæ מעשה sæpe vertunt ποίημα ut Ecclesiastic VII. 14. ἴδε τὰ ποιήματα τοῦ Θεοῦ. Sic & Pf. CXLIII. 5. Ex opere intelligitur operatio. Vetus quidam non male: ἐκ γὰρ με- γέθους καὶ καλλονῆς κτισμάτων ἀναλόγως ὁ γενεσιεργὸς αὐτῶν θεωρεῖται. Plotinus: τὸ μὲν τῷ αὐτομάτῳ κὶ τύχῃ διδόναι τάδε τὰ παντὸς τὴν ὑσίαν καὶ ξύστασιν, ὡς ἄλογον κὶ ἀνδρὸς ἑτε νῦν, ἕτε αἴσθησιν κεκτημένε, δῆλον πᾶ καὶ πρὸ λόγε καὶ πολλοὶ καὶ ἱκανοὶ πρὸ τότε καταβεβόηκεν δεικνύντες λόγοι. Idem alibi: ἐπεὶ ἐν τὸ γενέσθαι ἀκόσυθον ἐστὶν ὁ ξύμπας, ὁ τῦτον θεωρῶν τάχα ἂν ἀγάσαι παρ᾿ αὐτᾶ, ὡς ἐμὲ πεποιηκως ὁ Θεὸς. Tatia- nus de Deo: τῦτο διὰ τῆς ποιήσεως αὐτῷ ἴσμεν, τὴν τῆς δυνά- μεως αὐτῷ τὸ ἀόρατον τοῖς ποιήμασι καταλαμβανόμεθα. Athenagoras: τοσαῦτα ἔχοντες πρὸς θεοσέβειαν ἐνίσχυα τὸ ἔντακτον, τὸ διαπαντὸς συμφωνον, τὸ μέγεθος, τὴν χρόαν, τὸ σχῆμα, τὴν διάθεσιν τῶ κόσμε. Hoc est quod Hebræi vo- cant ברית עולם ex Efaia XXIV. 5.

Καθοράται) Id est, satis apparent. Et est ὀξύμωρον in ἀόρατα καθορᾶται. Hebræi omnes sensus internos & exter- nos videndi vocabulo amant exprimere.

ἥτε ἀΐδι αὐτῷ δύναμις.

Potentia semper durans. Sic ἀΐδιος vox sumitur & Ju- dæ 6. apud Symmachum Michæ VII. 8. ubi alii εἰς τὸν ὄρος

(C) 4 alii alii εἰς αὐτό. Talem esse Dei potentiam inde apparet, quod animantia semper alia atque alia nascuntur ex vi quam De- us rebus indidit. Hominum potentia fragilis est, & si non aliter, cum ipsis intercidit.

Καὶ θειότης.

Habes vocem ὑπόστης & Sap.XVIII.9. Rabbini dicunt אלהות & ea voce imperium maximè denotant. Idem גזות יהוה Esa. XXIV. 14. Opisex jus habet in opi- ficium suum. Seneca Epistola XCVL. Primus est Deorum cultus Deos credere: Deinde reddere illis majestatem suam, reddere bonitatem, sine qua nulla majestas est. Scire illos esse qui præsident mundo: qui universa vi sua temperant, qui humani generis tutelam gerunt.

Ut quænam illa ἀόρατα Θεῦ sint, quæ per crea- turas νούμενα καθορᾶται, constaret, nec ad myste- ria sola revelatione Scripturæ patefacta ea trahe- rentur, addit Apostolus, æternam potentiam & divinitatem se indicare. Potentiam autem æter- nam perversè Socinus, & Ostorodus de promissis di- vinis interpretantur, ac divinitatem, id quod Deus perpetuo nos facere vult, intelligunt, adversus vim vocum,usum Scripturæ & intentionem ac contex- tum Apostoli. Promissio relativum quid est, & in Deo; & multa potest Deus, quæ promissis ejus non continentur, maximeq; diversa sunt potentia Dei, & promissio divina: denique illa verè æterna non sunt, etsi de æternis bonis sint, sed in tempo- re fiunt. Id autem, quod Deus nos perpetuo facere vult, θειότητα dici, & inauditum est, & absurde fin- gitur. Grotius potentiam semper durantem rectius intelligit; non tamen ita vocis sensum plenum, & mentem Apostoli assequitur: nam non tantum potentiam a parte post, ut loquuntur, sed a parte ante etiam æternam indigitat: quam lumine natu- ræ cognosci certum est. Per θειότητα vero idem Grotius,ut perEbræum אלהות imperium maxi- me denotari perperam asserit. Ebræum ex Arabi- smo notare σέβασμα numen adorandum: Græcum vero θειότης cum θεότητι commutari ceu Synonyma, alias docuimus: adeoq; tum interminabilem po- tentiam, tum divinitatem ipsam, qua DEUS, est quod est, (quod certe per imperium non est) na- tura cognosci docet Apostolus: ut non modo exi- stentiam Dei, æternitatem, summam potentiam, sed etiam quod Deus Spiritus independens, ac vere in- finitus sit, adeoq; immaterialis & incorruptibilis, e creaturis concludi possit.Cui naturaliDei cogni- tioni adversati è diametro gentiles sunt, cum θεό- τητα in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis, & re- rum finitarum,ac dependentium transformarunt.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὲς ἀναπολογήτες.

Construe cum καθορᾶται. Satis Dei proprietates istæ ap- parent ad convincendos ingrati animi qui talem DEUM non coluêre. Vocem ἀναπολογήτε habes & infra II. 1. & in Ciceronis ad Atticum Epistolis. Quo plus scientiæ, eo minus excusationis. Luc. XII. 47. Joh. IX. 41. XV. 24. Loquitur autem de gentibus ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ; quia pauci sem- per fuêre σεβόμενοι ἕλληνες.

Non de gentibus ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ hæc cum Grotio accipienda, sed universim: nam etsi fuerint quan- doq; aliqui σεβόμενοι ἕλληνες ita dicti συγκριτικῶς, respectu aliorum, qui alieni a cultu Dei prorfus fuêre, tamen cultus Deo gratus nullus extra Chri- stum præstari potuit, quum impossibile sit, Deo sine fide placere Ebr. XI. 6. suo ergo modô co- luerunt Deum, non ea, quam DEUS præcripsit, ratione, quæ sola ipsi grata est. Nemo enim venit ad Patrem nisi per filium Joh. XIV. 6. Nulla est gra- ta Dei, nisi Christus filius ara. In hoc uno homine in gratia nos grati Deo sumus, & cultum Deo gra- tum præstamus. Neque agnovere gentiles Deum verum, ad quem inquirendum per notitiam illam naturalem deduci debebant, Act. XVII.27. qui ali- us non est, quam Pater, Filius, & S. S. ideo ut χω- ρὶς χριστῶ, ita & ἄθεοι fuêre, judicio Apostoli Eph. II. 12. Et convincit hic Apostolus, non quosdam, sed OMNES gentiles, quod Deum non glorificârint, ut Deum, etsi τὸ γνωστὸν τᾶ Θεᾶ manifestum in ipsis fuerit; atque ideo illos ἀναπολογήτες facit. Unde Lactant. l. VI. Instit. c. 9. Putemus fieri posse, ut ali- quis naturali, & ingenito bono veras virtutes capiat, qualem fuisse Cimonem Athenis accepimus, qui & egentibus stipem dedit, & pauperes invitavit, & nu- dos: Tamen cum illud unum, quod est maximum, deest, agnitio DEI, jam illa bona omnia superva- cua sunt & inania.Illud autem εἰς τὸ εἶναι hic acci- piendum est non τελικῶς, sed ἐκβατικῶς, monente Theophylacto,quod contraCalvinianos Piscatorem, Dan.Tossanum,& alios observandum,qui ita intel- ligunt, quod Deus in hoc ipsum eis indulserit cogni- tionem sui, ut postea nihil haberent, quod prætexe- rent. Finis enim θεογνωσίας naturalis proprius est, ut sit manuductio quædam ad ulteriorem DEI agnitionem in verbo propositam, & Ecclesiæ pa- tefactam,quæ dicitur finis pedagogicus: hic autem effectus est accidentarius, quod per eam, qui negli- gunt ulteriorem Dei cognitionem inquirere, red- dantur ἀναπολόγητοι, non ex Dei ordinatione vel intentione,sed præter eandem eveniens: ideo εἰς τὸ εἶναι hoc loco est ὥςε εἶναι. Inepti autem sunt Leydenses,cum in Censura Confess. Armin. c. XI. cl. 7. inexcusabiliter ideo ajunt, quod suppedita- tione sufficientis gratiæ Deus eos præterierit. Sic enim non ipsi ἀναπολόγητοι forent, sed Deus, qui eos præteriit.

Interim notitiæ illæ naturales non sunt salvificæ, nec quicquam ad salutem faciunt,quia naturæ nul- lo pacto salus adscribi potest, sed unicè gratiæ: neq; usus earum confert ad conversionem, etsi ab- usus,& neglectus impediat conversionem;manudu- cunt nos, ut inquiramus Ecclesiam, in qua Deus se revelavit, non deducunt nos in Ecclesiam, aut ad salutarem Dei notitiam; quæ unice accepto fe- renda Christo est: Matth. XI. 27. Joh. I. 18. Hoc sensu accipiendũ est illud Tertulliani de resurrect. carnis: Præmisit tibi (Deus) naturam magistram, submissurus & Prophetiam, quo facilius credas Prophetiæ discipulus naturæ. Et quod habet Basili- us hom.XI. in hexaëm. ὁ κόσμος τῶν ψυχῶν λογι- κῶν διδασκαλεῖον καὶ τῆς θεογνωσίας παιδευτήριον.

## 1:21
V. 21. because knowing God.

By natural right, not familiar, as Tertullian speaks concerning spectacles, not a beautiful knowledge, but by periphrasis, as Clement Strom. VI. For certain philosophers ascended from visible things to intelligible things, as Origen says explaining this passage against Celsus III. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: The human mind has always deserved ill of God, first indeed by being undutiful toward Him, whom, although it understood Him in part, it did not seek. Hence understand what Tertullian says about the soul, that the soul of Socrates knew nothing clearly, who nevertheless the same Tertullian in the book On the Testimony of the Soul brings forward very many indications of natural knowledge of God. These two degrees of knowledge against Marcion the same Tertullian first distinguishes thus: We define God as first to be known by nature, then to be recognized by doctrine: by nature from works: by doctrine from preachings. And concerning the resurrection of the flesh: He set before you nature as a teacher, intending to submit also prophecy, so that you might more easily believe prophecy, being a disciple of nature. Lactantius: What pardon for their impiety can they hope for themselves, who do not acknowledge the worship of Him, whom it is not right for man to be entirely ignorant of? For (1) when they swear, and when they wish, (2) when they give thanks, they name not Jupiter or many gods, but God. To such an extent does truth itself, with nature compelling, break forth even from ignorant hearts.

The Apostle renders the cause why they have no excuse, who have detained the truth in injustice, because they knew GOD, if not through Scripture, yet through nature; and no one can plead ignorance. But they did not celebrate Him as GOD, nor did they give thanks, but indulging in their own speculations they became vain in their reasonings, and clearly in their heart they were darkened. There is therefore a twofold cause of ἀναπολογίας [inexcusability]: The one is a privative omission of the glory and thanksgiving due to God as Creator, as much as they could gather from nature, and such as natural equity dictates: the other is a positive one, namely the committed ignominy against God v. 23. Since the omission of the worship of God according to the guidance of nature was also followed by an omission of further inquiry concerning the true God and the Church: which, even though the Gentiles could not have instituted that inquiry through natural instinct without intervening report about GOD or the Church. To which contributes that saying of Tertullian in the Apology: The human mind has always deserved ill of God, first indeed, in that it was inofficious toward Him, whom, although it understood Him in part, it did not seek. For it is said γνόντες τὸν Θεὸν [knowing God], that they knew that God is, as Luther rendered it, restricting this knowledge to the question ὅτι [that], and that they could have drawn even from the book of nature itself that there is a certain eternal and omnipotent Deity to be worshipped by all with a holy mind Acts 17:25. As to who that one true God is, τὸν μόνον τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν [the only true God], Scripture alone reveals: where the terms of Nature and Scripture are deservedly to be distinguished: by nature we certainly know that God is, and in part what God is: but by no means who God is, or as Agur, what is the name of God? For this, he teaches, no one knows by nature Prov. 30:4. do you know this? Therefore rightly the Blessed Luther: The Gentiles knew divinity, but they did not rightly divide it: for they attributed it to false gods. This application, therefore, that we may rightly designate who that true God is, is learned from Scripture alone. What therefore Origen says against Celsus, book 2, concerning certain philosophers ἀνέβανον [ascending], ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρατῶν εἰς τὰ νοητὰ [from visible things to intelligible things], that is to be understood κατὰ τι [in a certain respect], by stopping within the hemisphere of natural knowledge. For to supernatural knowledge we cannot ascend except through revelation. And therefore the reason for ἀναπολογίας [inexcusability] is not to be established immediately in the subtracted legitimate worship, as is done by Toletus, Pererius, Salmeron, and others, who conclude from that that God is worshipped by the same principle from which He is known, and so can be worshipped according to the light of nature. But here the reason is determined under which the adoration of God [is to be understood], which is not to be extended to the worship which is to be rendered to God in Spirit and in truth John 4:13, but could only be done as much as was known of God and His worship by nature, by which they could glorify Him as God, as eternal, as powerful, and abstain from vices against nature and tending to the ignominy of God. v. 20, 22, seqq. Nor indeed should the example of Jethro, of the Midianites, of Hiram, and similar ones be brought forward as effects of natural instinct to inquire about the God of Israel, which could have been born from the mere contemplation of creatures without intervening report about God or the Church of the Israelites; but where such a report exists, there is a certain preaching of the word, and grace inherent in the word arriving and moving. Mark 4:26, Phil. 1:18, as the Blessed Hülsemann rightly warned here.

This is not to be restricted to certain ones, e.g., to the Academics and some others: no one of the Gentiles is excepted here: For even the wisest of all vanished in their reasonings. φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν [professing to be wise they became fools]: which Grotius understands of the seven sages themselves, so called before Pythagoras the philosopher assumed the name. Nor can the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics be absolved here from the vanity of their reasonings, even if others philosophized more correctly about God. Cicero himself denied that God exists, although under the persona of another, and by denying the foreknowledge of future events he denied God Himself, as Augustine observes, book 5 of The City of God, ch. 9. For either he denies that God exists, which indeed he attempted to do by introducing the persona of another in the books on the nature of the gods, or if he confesses that God exists, whom he denies to be prescient of future events, even so he says nothing other than what that fool said in his heart, there is no God. For he who is not prescient of all future events is certainly not God. What of the fact that it is a general sentiment, explaining what we are all like by nature? Namely, left to themselves, men, however wise in other things, are foolish in divine matters, and vanish, or are empty in their thoughts.

But they vanish in their reasonings, nor do they glorify God as God, both because they worship idols in place of the true God: and because they devise from their own ingenuity a mode of worshipping God besides and against the institution and word of God. Their foolish heart is also darkened, because they are destitute of true wisdom, and have an ἀνόητον [senseless] heart by nature Romans 3:11, and so they further darken it with their vain reasonings, and involve themselves more and more in darkness. Namely, the Apostle proves that the truth of the knowledge of God is held back in injustice by those who do not glorify the acknowledged God as God, who in His place even venerate images and idols. Which men have done over the whole world, inclined to that by nature.

And their senseless heart was darkened) Like the fault, such is the punishment. They had shaken off the light of reason: God took away from them even what remained. They were darkened in their understanding. Eph. IV. 18. Truly said Prov. XIX. 3. The foolishness of man perverts his way, that is, it corrupts his morals. How idolatry, which is now being discussed, brings about impiety. Impiety brings about the worst morals, we said regarding the book of Wisdom: Atticus the Platonist rightly says: The despair of providence is a thing ready for injustice.

Latin:

V. 21. διότι γνόντες τὸν Θεόν.

Naturali jure, non familiari, ut loquitur Tertullianus de spectaculis ἡ καλὴ ἐπίγνωσιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ περίφασιν,utClemens Strom. VI. Quidam enim Philosophi ἀνέβαφον ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρα- τῶν εἰς τὰ νοητὰ, ut ait hunc locum explicans Origenes con- tra Celsum III. Tertullianus in Apologetico: Semper huma- na mens male de Deo meruit, primo quidem ut inofficiosa ejus, quem cum intelligeret ex parte, non requisivit. Hinc intellige quod dicit de anima Tertullianus, nihil liquido sapuisse a- nimam Socratis, qui tamen ipse Tertullianus libro de Te- stimonio Animæ plurima adfert indicia notitiæ de Deo na- turalis.Duos hos notitiæ gradus adversus Marcionem pri- mo idem Tertullianus sic dispescit: Nos definimus Deum primum natura cognoscendum, dehine doctrina recognofcen- dum: natura ex operibus: doctrina ex prædicationibus. Et de resurrectione carnis: Præmisit tibi naturam magistram,sub- missurus & prophetiam, quo facilius credas prophetiæ, discipu- lus naturæ. Lactantius: Quam sibi veniam sperare possunt impietatis suæ, qui non agnoscunt cultum ejus, quem prorfus ignorari ab homine fas non est? Nam (1) cum jurant, & cum optant, (2) cum gratias agunt,non Jovem aut Deos multos, sed Deum nominant. Adeo ipsa veritas cogente natura etiam ab in- scitis pectoribus erumpit.

Causam reddit Apostolus, cur nullam habeant excusationem, qui veritatem in injustitia detinue- runt, quia cognoverunt DEUM, si non per Scripturam,tamen per naturam; & nemo ignoran- tiam possit prætexere. Non celebrarunt autem eum ut DEUM, aut gratias egêrunt, sed spe- culationibus propriis indulgentes vani facti ra- tiocinationibus suis, & planè in corde suo ἀσυνέ- obtenebrati sunt. Gemina ergo causa est ἀναπο- λογίας: Altera privativa omissio gloriæ & gratia- rum actionis Deo tanquam Creatori debitæ, quan- tam ex natura colligere potuêre, & qualem natu- ralis æquitas dictitat: altera positiva commissa scil. ignominia in Deum v. 23. Cum omissionem cultus Dei secundum ductum naturæ secuta etiam sit o- missio ulterioris inquisitionis de vero Deo & Ec- clesia: quam tametsi per naturalem instinctum si- ne interveniente fama de DEO aut Ecclesia eam inquisitionem gentiles instituere haud potuerint. Quo facit illud Tertull. in Apol. Semper humana mens male de Deo meruit, primo quidem, ut inoffi- ciosa ejus, quem cum intelligeret ex parte, non inquisi- vit. Dicitur enim γνόντες τὸν Θεὸν, quod sciverint, quod Deus sit, ut Lutherus reddidit, ad quæstionem ὅτι hanc notitiam restringens, quodque vel ex ipso naturæ libro haurire potuerint esse Numen quod- dam æternum atq; omnipotens ab omnibus sancta mente colendum Act XVII. 25. ut quisnam ille solus verus Deus sit, τὸν μόνον τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν sola Scri- ptura revelet: ubi distinguendi merito termini Na- turæ, & Scripturæ: per naturam utique Esse Deum novimus, & ex parte quid sit Deus: nullatenus au- tem quis Deus sit, vel ut Agur, quod sit nomen Dei? Hoc enim neminem naturâ novisse docet Prov. XXX. 4. nosti hoc? ideo recte B. Lutherus, Ethnici cognoverunt divinitatem, sed illam non recte divise- runt: attribuerunt enim diis falsis. Hæc itaque appli- catio, ut nempe quisnam sit ille verus Deus, recte designemus, è sola Scriptura discitur. Quod ergo Origenes contra Celsum l II. de quibusdam Philoso- phis ἀνέβανον, ait, ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρατῶν εἰς τὰ νοητὰ, id intelligendum κατὰ τι, sistendo intra hemisphæri- um naturalis cognitionis. Ad supernaturalem e- gnim non nisi per revelationem ascendere possu- mus. Ideoq; ratio ἀναπολογίας non constituenda immediate in subtracto cultu legitimo, uti a Toleto, Pererio, Salmerone & aliis fit, qui inde concludunt, Deum eodem principio, ex quo cognoscitur, adorari, adeoq; juxta naturæ lumen coli posse. Sed hic determinata est ratio sub qua adorationis Dei, quæ non extendenda ad cultum, qui Deo in Spiritu & veritate præstandus est Joh. IV. 13. sed tantum fie- ri potuit, quantum natura de Deo ejusq; cultu co- gnitum fuit, qua ut Deum, ut æternum, ut poten- tem glorificare, & à vitiis contra naturam, & ad ignominiam Dei vergentibus abstinere potuerint. v. 20. 22. seqq. Neq; vero exemplum Jethronis, Mi- dianitarum, Hiram & similia adferenda tanquam effectus naturalis instinctus ad inquirendum de Deo Israëlis, qui nasci potuerit ex sola contemplatione creaturarum sine interveniente fama de Deo aut Ecclesia Israëlitarum; ubi autem ejusmodi fama est, est quædam prædicatio verbi, verboque insita gratia perveniens & movens. Marc. IV. 26. Phil. I. 18. uti recte hic monuit B. Hülsemannus.

Non hoc restringendum ad quosdam e. g. ad Academicos, & alios nonnullos: nemo hic excipi- tur gentilium: Nam & sapientissimi quiq; evanue- runt in ratiocinationibus suis. φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν: quod de ipsis septem sapientibus ita nuncupatis antequam Pythagoras Philosophi sume- ret nomen, intelligit Grotius. Neq; hic Pythagorei, Platonici, Stoici à vanitate τῶν διαλογισμῶν absol- vi possunt: etiamsi rectius alii philosophati de Deo sint. Cicero ipse Deum esse, licet sub alterius perso- na, inficiatus est, & negando praescientiam futuro- rum Deum ipsum negavit, observante Aug. l. V. de Civ. Dei c. IX. Aut enim Deum esse negat, quod quidem inducta alterius persona in libris de Deorum natura facere molitus est, aut si esse confitetur De- um, quem negat præscium futurorum, etiam sic di- cit nihil aliud, quam quod ille dixit insipiens in cor- de suo, non est Deus. Qui enim non est præscius o- mnium futurorum non est utique Deus. Quid quod generalis sit sententia, quales simus omnes per natu- ram, explicans. Nimirum sibi relicti homines, ut- ut cætera sapientissimi, stulti sunt in rebus divinis, & evanescūt, vel inanes sunt in cogitationibus suis.

Evanescunt autem διαλογισμοῖς suis, nec De- um ut Deum glorificant, tum quia loco veri Dei colunt idola: tum quia ex proprio ingenio mo- dum colendi Deum præter & contra Dei institu- tum, & verbum excogitant. Obscuratum etiam in- sipiens cor eorum, quia vera sapientia destituun- tur, & ἀνόητον cor habent τῇ φύσει Rom. III. 11. adcoq; vanis suis διαλογισμοῖς ulterius id obscu- rant, seq; tenebris magis magisq; involvunt. Ni- mirum probat Apostolus ab iis veritatem cognitio- nis Dei detineri in injustitia, qui agnitum Deum non glorificant ut Deum, qui loco ejus etiam imagines, ac idola venerantur. Quod fecerunt toto ter- rarum orbe homines, ad id propensi natura.

Καὶ ἐσκοτίσθη ἡ ἀσύνετος αὐτῶν καρδία) Qualis culpa, tad lis pœna. Lumen rationis excusserant: Deus & quod resta- bat eis ademit. Fuerunt ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ. Eph. IV. 18. Vere dictum Prov. XIX. 3. Stultitia hominis pervertit viam ejus, id est mores corrumpit. Quomodo idololatria, de qua jam agitur, impietatem adferat. Impietas mores pessimos, diximus ad librum sapientiæ: Recte Atticus Platonicus: ἕτοι ἕτοιμοι τι χρῆμα πρὸς ἀδικίαν, ἡ τῆς προνοίας ἀπόγνωσις.

## 1:22
V. 22. Professing to be wise) When they called themselves or allowed themselves to be called wise. Thus were those seven most famous men in Greece called, before Pythagoras took the name of philosopher. Thus among the Romans Sempronius was called wise and Atilius wise, as we read in Pomponius on the origin of Law.

they became foolish) They were made fools. Full of empty conceit, as Timon used to say of them. They became foolish, namely, with God directing it. God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. 1 Cor. I. 21. Euripides well says: I hate a sophist who is not wise for himself, and Pacuvius: I hate men of idle work, of philosophical opinion, who, while they do not know the path for themselves, show the way to another: Add Jerem. X. 14.

Latin:

V. 22. Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ) Cum se dicerent aut se dici sinerent σοφοὺς. Sic appellati septem illi in Græcia notissimi, antequam Pythagoras philosophi sumeret nomen. Sic apud Romanos Sempronius dictus σοφὸς & Atilius sapiens, ut le- gimus apud Pomponium de origine Juris.

ἐμωράνθησαν) Stulti facti sunt. Κενῆς οἰήσεως ἔμπλεοι ἀσκεῖτο Ut dicebat de illis Timon. ἐμωράνθησαν nempe Deo diri- gente. ἐμώρανεν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν σοφίαν τῶ κόσμου τούτου. 1. Cor. I. 21. Bene Euripides: Μισῶ σοφιστὴν ὅστις ἐχ αὑτῷ σοφὸς, & Pacuvius: Odi homines ignava opera, philosophia sententia, Qui cum sibi semitam non sapiant, alteri monstrant viam: Adde Jerem. X. 14.

## 1:23
V. 23. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God) These are words taken from Ps. CVI. 20. just as the old reading had there his glory, just as also Jerem. II. 11. where God speaks, and the same word is he changed in the old books followed his glory the sense is, for the honor which they owed to God, they gave honor to a calf, to idols. The Scholiasts interpret the proper name of God as incorruptible, who neither perishes nor becomes worse.

In the likeness of an image of corruptible man) In the likeness is also in the aforementioned place of the Psalm, they translated the honor of God to the effigy of a calf. The same expression is in the matter of exchange Lev. XXVII. 10. likeness of an image is the figure which appears in an idol. Thus likenesses of idols 1 Macc. IV. 49. they called the very likeness of God. It is not real. For God does not have a form similar to a human, much less to worse animals. Empedocles on God: For neither is a human head adorned with limbs, nor do two branches spring from his back, nor feet, nor swift knees, nor hairy genitals. Xenophanes: He is not at all like mortals in body. Antiphanes: He is not seen with the eyes, he is like nothing; which agrees perfectly with those things which we have in Deut. IV. 15. Josephus against Apion II. For all matter is alien to the image of Him; and the most costly is worthless compared to His glory; and every art is a thoughtless imitation compared to the conception of Him; we do not conceive anything similar, nor is it holy to liken Him. For this reason, says Strabo, not only the Egyptians were blamed by Moses, who made God like wild beasts and cattle, but also the Greeks, adding: 'Who with any sense would dare to fashion an image similar to any of those among us?' Regarding the Persians, Herodotus says: 'But they also bring a charge of folly against those who make (statues), because they did not think the gods were human-shaped, as the Greeks do.' Thus also it seemed to Numa, says Plutarch, 'it is not holy to liken the better to the worse.' And Tacitus says of the Germans that it is not in accordance with the greatness of the celestials to liken them to any form of human face. No likeness of GOD is to be made, says Theodoret on Exodus XXXVIII. And Origen says in book 1 that this law is written in the hearts of men. And in book III. The common notion requires one to understand that God is the creator, that God is in no way corruptible matter, nor is He honored in inanimate materials fashioned by men; as if they were becoming images or certain symbols of Him, for which reason the things concerning statues are immediately said, that they are not gods; and the things concerning such creations, that they are not comparable to the creator, and a few things about the God over all, who created, and sustains, and governs the whole. And afterwards: 'But no less than these, one might proceed even if they think that things fashioned by base and most vile men are constructed for the honor of true gods.' Rightly, therefore, the writer in the Psalm and Paul in this place do not hold those images as images of GOD, but as those whose form they represent.

It is now declared by examples that men have vanished in their reasonings, and the consequences of a neglected inquiry into the true GOD are set forth: the first of which among the Gentiles was horrible idolatry; the second, v. 24, the uncleanness of foul lusts; the third, v. 27, a sink of most vile crimes. The first kind is directed against God; the second against themselves; the third primarily against their neighbor. A similar phrase is found in Ps. CVI, 20: where, however, Grotius rashly imagines a corrupted place, as if the old reading had כבודו, just as also in Jer. II. 11, when in both places the Hebrew text rightly has כבודם, their glory: for the glory of the Jewish people was, or certainly ought to have been, the Lord. Grotius here renders the particle ἐκ as 'to', as if to say they transferred the honor of GOD to the likeness of corruptible things. However, a more common sense can have a place, that they changed the glory of the incorruptible GOD by their reasonings and their will-worship into the likeness of an image, to an image similar to a corruptible man, so that ἐν is taken for εἰς: for ἤλλαξαν is not 'they transferred', but 'they changed': which they undoubtedly did, and worshipped such images instead of GOD. Learned are the things which Grotius brings forward from various authors to illustrate these points concerning the idolatry of the Gentiles: and Augustine has already shown this at length in book III of The City of God, ch. XII, and book IV, ch. X, that the Gentiles worshipped birds, serpents, cats, crocodiles, and even fever and pestilence as gods: on which places compare Ludov. Vivis' Commentary: Under this, he says, regarding the Romans, in the former place Augustine [speaks of] the protection of so many gods, whom can anyone count, native and foreign, celestial, terrestrial, infernal, marine, fountain-dwelling, river-dwelling: and as Varro says, certain and uncertain, and in all kinds of gods just as in animals, males and females? Under the protection of so many gods, therefore, Rome was established, and it ought not to have been agitated and afflicted by such great and horrible disasters, of which I shall recount a few from many. For it had gathered too many gods with their great smoke, as if by a given signal, for its protection: by instituting and providing temples, altars, sacrifices, and priests for them, it offended the supreme true God, to whom alone these things, when rightly performed, are due.

And of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things) This touches the Egyptians, who wanted to seem the wisest, most of all. Strabo in the cited place: 'How the Egyptians do not think rightly, likening the divine to wild beasts and cattle.' Philo on the same: 'Who make gods of dogs, wolves, and lions, and crocodiles, and many other wild beasts, both aquatic and land-dwelling, and winged.' Theophilus of Antioch, book I: 'What need is there for me to recount the multitude of animals worshipped by the Egyptians, creeping things and cattle and wild beasts, and birds, and aquatic creatures?' The Hebrew Sage mentions serpents specifically in the worship of the Egyptians in ch. XVI. And Virgil called them an 'all-monstrous god' regarding the same. Juvenal: 'Who does not know, Volusius, what kind of monsters mad Bithynian Egypt worships: one part adores the crocodile; another fears the Ibis gorged with serpents.' The golden image of the sacred ape shines, where the magic chords of half-statue Memnon resound, and ancient Thebes lies buried with its hundred gates. There they worship blue fish, here the river fish, there whole towns worship the dog. But not even the Romans are entirely free from this fault. Lucan, around the time of Paul: 'We have received your Isis into Roman temples, and half-human dogs.' And some Lares had a canine appearance. See also Philostratus VI. 9. Varro on them: 'They have the appearance of men and wild beasts and fish.' But some assume mixed sexes and diverse bodies.

Latin:

V. 23. Καὶ ἤλλαξαν τὴν δόξαν τῶ ἀφθάρτου Θεῶ) Sunt verba sumpta ex Ps. CVI. 20. sicut habuit ibi vetus lectio כבודו, sicut & Jerem. II. 11. ubi Deus loquitur, idemque verbum est המיר in libris veteribus sequebatur כבודו sensus est, pro honore quem Deo debebant, honorem habuere vitulo, simulacris. Dei proprium nomen ἄφθαρτος interpretantur Scholiastæ, qui nec interit, nec fit deterior.

Ἐν ὁμοιώματι εἰκόνος φθαρτῶ ἀνθρώπου) ἐν ὁμοιώματι est & in dicto Psalmi loco ב pro ad transtulerunt honorem Dei ad effigiem vituli. Eadem locutio in re commutatio- nis Lev. XXVII. 10. ὁμοίωμα εἰκόνος est figura quæ apparet in simulacro. Sic ὁμοιώματα εἰδώλων 1. Macc. IV. 49. ipsa Dei similitudinem dicebant. Attalis non est. Deus enim non habet formam humanæ similem, nedum pejorum ani- mantium. Empedocles de Deo. Οὔτε γὰρ ἀνδρομέη κεφαλὴ κατὰ γῦια κέκασται Οὐ μὲν ἀπαὶ νώτων γε δύο κλάδοι ἀίσσονται, Οὐ πόδες, ἐ θοὰ γῦν, ἐ μήδεα λαχνήεντα. Xenophanes: Οὔτι δέμας θνητοῖσιν ὁμοίοις Antiphanes: Ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐχ ὁρᾶται, ἐδενὶ ἔοικε' quod opti- me convenit cum iis quæ habemus Deut. IV. 15. Josephus contra Appionem II. πᾶσα μὲν γὰρ ὕλη πρὸς εἰκόνα τὴν τούτου ἀλλότριον· καὶ ἡ πολυτελὴς ἄτιμός ἐστι πρὸς τὴν ἐκείνου δόξαν· καὶ πᾶσα τέχνη πρὸς μίμησιν ἐπίνοιαν ἄτεκνον· οὐδὲν ὅμοιον εὖ τ’ ἐπινοοῦμεν, οὔτ’ εἰκάζειν ὅσιον. Ex hac caufa, ait Strabo, culpatos a Mose non Aegyptios tantum, qui feris ac pecudibus Deum similem facerent, sed & Græcos, qui homini: addens: τούτω τις ἂν εἰκόνα πλάττειν θαῤῥήσειεν νοῦν ἔχων ὁμοίαν τινὶ τῶν πάρ’ ἡμῖν; De Persis Herodotus: ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖσι ποιεῦσι (ἀγάλματα) μωρίην ἐπιφέρουσι, διότι οὐκ ἀνθρωποφυέας ἐνόμισαν τοὺς θεοὺς, καθάπερ οἱ ἕλληνες. Sic & Numæ visum ait Plutarchus, οὐχ ὅσιον ἀφομοιοῦν τὰ βελτίονα τοῖς χείροσιν. Et Germanis Tacitus non esse ex magnitudine cœleftium assimulari eos in ullam humani oris speciem. Nullum ὁμοίωμα DEO faciendum, ait Theodoreti ad Exodum XXXVIII. & scriptam hanc legem in hominum cordibus ait Origenes libro 1. Et libr. III. ἡ κοινὴ ἔννοια ἀπαιτεῖ ἐννοεῖν ὅτι θεὸς ἐποῖει, ὅτι θεὸς οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ὕλη φθαρτὴ, οὐδὲ τιμᾶται ἐν ἀψύχοις ὕλαις ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μορφώμενον; ὡς κατὰ εἰκόνα ἤ τινα σύμβολα ἐκείνου γιγνομέναις, διόπερ εὐθέως λέγεται τὰ περὶ ἀγαλμάτων, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶ θεοὶ· καὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν τοιούτων δημιουργημάτων, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶ σύγκριτα πρὸς τὸν δημιουργὸν, ὀλίγα τε περὶ τοῦ, ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ δημιουργήσαντος, καὶ συνέχοντος, καὶ κυβερνῶντος τὰ ὅλα. Et postea: οὐχ ἧττον δὲ τούτων βαίνοιτα κἂν νομίζοντες εἰς τίμην θεῶν ἀληθινῶν κατασκεύασθαι τὰ ὑπὸ βαναύσων καὶ φαυλοτάτων ἰδ’ ὅτε ἀνδρῶν κατασκευαζόμενα. Recte ergo scriptor in Psalmo & hoc loco Paulus imagines istas non pro DEI imaginibus habent, sed pro iis, quorum formam referunt.

Declaratur jam ab exemplis, quod evanuerint homines in suis διαλογισμοῖς & consequentia neglectæ inquisitionis veri DEI exponuntur: quorum primum apud gentiles fuit horrenda idololatria; alterum v. 24. fœdarum libidinum ἀκαθαρσία: tertium teterrimorum scelerum sentina v. 27. Primum genus adversus Deum; alterum adversus seipsos: tertium adversus proximum imprimis vergit. Phrasis similis Ps. CVI, 20. habetur: ubi tamen locum corruptum temere fingit Grotius, quasi vetus lectio habuerit כבודו, sicut & Jer. II. 11. quum utrobique textus Ebræus recte כבודם gloriam suam habeat: gloria enim populi Judaici erat, esse certe debebat Dominus. Particulam ἐκ hic reddit Grotius ad, q. d. transtulisse eos honorem DEI ad effigiem rerum corruptibilium. Potest autem sensus usitatior locum habere, quod gloriam DEI incorruptibilis διαλογισμοῖς suis, & ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ sua mutarint in similitudinem imaginis ad imaginem similem corruptibilis hominis, ut ἐν pro εἰς accipiatur: ἤλλαξαν enim non est transtulerunt, sed mutarunt: quod nimirum fecerint & pro DEO coluerint tales imagines. Erudita sunt, quæ ad hæc de idololatria gentilium illustranda ex autoribus variis adfert Grotius: & prolixe jam ostendit Augustinus. l. III. de Civ. Dei c. XII. l. IV. c. X. gentiles aves, serpentes, feles, Crocodilos, imo & febrem, pestem pro diis coluisse: in quæ loca Conf. Ludov. Vivis Commentarius: Sub hoc, inquit, de Romanis, priori loco August. tot deorum præsidio, quos numerare quis potest, indigenas, & alienigenas, cælestes, terrestres, infernos, marinos, fontanos, fluviales: & ut Varro dicit, certos atque incertos, in omnibusque generibus deorum sicut in animalibus, mares & fœminas? Sub hoc ergo tot deorum præsidio constituta Roma, non tam magnis & horrendis cladibus, quales ex multis paucas commemorabo, agitari, affligique debuit. Nimis enim multos deos grandi fumo suo tanquam signo dato ad tuitionem congregaverat: quibus templa, altaria, sacrificia, sacerdotes instituendo, atque præbendo, summum verum Deum, cui uni hac rite gesta debentur, offenderet.

Καὶ πετεινῶν, καὶ τετραπόδων, καὶ ἑρπετῶν) Hoc Aegyptios, qui sapientissimi videri volebant, maximè tangit. Strabo dicto loco: ὡς ἐκ ὀρθῶς φρονῶσιν οἱ Αἰγύπτιοι θηρίοις εἰκάζοντες καὶ βοσκήμασι τὸ θεῖον. Philo de iisdem: οἱ κύνας, λύκος, καὶ λέοντας, καὶ κροκοδείλους, καὶ ἄλλα πλείονα θηρία, καὶ ἔνυδρα, κj χερσαῖα, κj πτηνὰ θεοπλασοῦντες. Theophilus Antiochenus lib. I. τί μοι λοιπὸν καταλέγειν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν σεβομένων ζώων Αἰγύπτιοι, ἑρπετῶν δὲ κj κτηνῶν κj θηρίων, καὶ πετεινῶν, καὶ ἐνύδρων κηκτῶν: Serpentes speciatim in Ae- gyptiorum cultu memorat Sapiens Hebræus c. XVI. Omnigenumque Deum monstra dixit de iisdem Virgilius. Juvenalis: Quis nescit Volusi Bithynia qualia demens Ægyptus portenta colat: crocodilon adorat Pars hæc: illa pavet saturum serpentibus Ibin. Effigies sacri nitet aurea Cercopitheci, Dimidio magicæ resonant ubi Memnone chordæ Atque vetus Thebe centum jacet obruta portis. Illic cæruleos, hic piscem fluminis, illic Oppida tota canem venerantur. Sed nec Romani plane extra hanc culpam. Lucanus circa Pauli tempora: Nos in templa tuam Romana recepimus Isim, Semideosque canes. Et Laribus quibusdam canina erat species. Vide & Philostratum VI. 9. Varro de iis: Habitus illis hominum ferarumque & piscium. Quidam vero mixtos sexu, diversis corporibus induunt.

## 1:24
V. 24. Wherefore God also gave them up in the lusts of their hearts unto uncleanness) They deserted God, God in turn deserted them, not giving them divine laws, and allowing human ones to be depraved, not sending Prophets, and allowing Philosophers to slip into absurdities. He let them do what they pleased, even things most foul: so that those who had not honored God might dishonor themselves. What ἀκαθαρσία is here and below VI. 10, Gal. V. 19, Eph. IV. 19, V. 3, Coloss. III. 5, 1 Thess. II. 3, IV. 17, is the same as below 26, where this sense is repeated, 'to give up unto vile affections'. סגר is to be destitute of one's protection, to leave another to be ill-treated, Deut. XXIII. 15, XXXII. 30, 1 Sam. XXIII. 12. ἀκαθαρσία is נבלות in Hosea II. 10, Nahum III. 6, which elsewhere is ἄφροσύνη, 'impurities' to Cicero in the second Philippic. He shows there is no reason why the Romans should prefer themselves to those they called barbarians, such as the Scythians and Germans.

Idolatry was followed throughout the world by ἀκαθαρσία, a sink of foul lusts, which is introduced by the illative particle διὸ, as a punishment for idolatry, which is the source of all outrages and crimes. Therefore, they were delivered up by God, not effectively, as if God were the author of that impurity, as the Calvinists blaspheme; nor only permissively, and merely ἐκβατικῶς, but δικαστικῶς, and judicially. This just judgment of GOD is not a mere ἔκβασις, but it embraces both the dismissal into lusts, through divine abandonment (Acts 14:16; Ps. 81:13), and the delivery into the power of Satan, who drives them εἰς ἀκαθαρσίαν as an ἀκάθαρτος spirit (2 Tim. 2). Regarding the former, Ambrose says in this book: to deliver up is to permit, but not to incite or to send in, so that they might fulfill in action what they had conceived in their desires, aided by the Devil: regarding the latter, Augustine, book 20, On the City of God, chapter 19. God will send a working of error, by which He will permit the Devil to act, by His own just judgment, although he [the Devil] acts with an unrighteous and malicious intent. Rightly, therefore, Grotius here notes that παραδιδόναι is סגר, to leave one destitute of his protection to be ill-treated by another (Deut. 23:15; 32:30; 1 Sam. 23:12). And Bucer, Marloratus, and the Belgian interpreters acknowledge that the word παρέδωκεν is to be taken privatively regarding the non-prevention of more serious sins (Ps. 81:13; Acts 14:16), regarding the withdrawal of the grace required to resist sins (Matt. 25:28), and regarding the abandonment and delivery into the power of Satan, by whom, not with God as the instigator but as the judge decreeing it, men are solicited into worse crimes on account of their former ingratitude (1 Sam. 15:3; Matt. 6:11). Nor does that word occur anywhere regarding an immediate influence of God upon the will of the subject delivered up, but it always implies some intermediate cause influencing the subject delivered up, which even Gregory of Valencia, Schwaretz, and Johannes Malderus admit, appealing to the opinion of Thomas; add also Salmeron, Cornelius, and Estius, and Stapleton: who are therefore deservedly opposed to others, such as Bannez, Francis Sylvius, Didacus Alvarez, and the rest who assert the predetermination of the human will toward evil. Concerning which, see what was said in Volume II of the System of Theology, chapter 10, question 6, and Volume III, Article 6, question 5.

τῶ ἀτιμάζεσθαι τὰ σώματα αὐτῶν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. That is, per sefe: he says it thus, that they brought dishonor upon their own bodies, of their own accord, with no one compelling them. What more cruel thing could enemies do to a captured city? Theophylact understood it this way as well. A similar sense is in 1 Cor. VI. 18. The opposite is τὸ ἑαυτῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ 1 Thess. IV. 4.

Grotius's interpretation would not be to be disapproved of, when he explains ἐν ἑαυτοῖς by per sefe, that is, of their own accord with Theophylact, if he had confirmed this exception of the word with a parallel passage. For from a comparison of the passage 1 Cor. VI. 18, that cannot be gathered, but rather that such people sin against their own body: whence the Syrian did not render it quite conveniently as inter sefe. That, therefore, is indicated, that by the just judgment of GOD they are filled with ignominy and shame in themselves and in their own bodies, who robbed God of His glory. The Apostle himself explains this thus in v. 28, that they received the ἀντιμι- σίαν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.

Οἵ τινες μετήλλαξαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῦ Θεῦ ἐν τῷ ψεύδει) The same locution as above 23, and ἀλήθειαν Θεῦ for Θεὸν ἀληθῆ. For the true God they took imaginary ones. For ψεῦ- δος שׁקר is for the Hebrews a false GOD. As Is. XXVIII. 15, XLIV: 20, Jer. XIII. 25, XXIII. 14, Hos. VII. 1. Elsewhere, as Amos II. 4, those gods are called μάταια in an equal sense.

Καὶ ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα Ἐσεβάσθησαν κὰι ἐλάτρευσαν is וישׁתחו עבדו; the former word is accustomed to be said of sacrifices, and is translated σέβεσθαι Wis. XV. 6, 18; the latter of the bending of the body, which is accustomed to accompany sacred rites. Παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα; here the writer of the constitutions of Clement explains it as ἀντὶ τῦ κτίσαντος, and Hilary as passing over the creator: but παρὰ with the accusative, placed in a comparison, is accustomed to signify that which exceeds, as Exod. XXXVI. 4, Ps. XLV. 8, Luke XIII. 2, 4, Heb. III. 23. Thus also he said to Philo τῆς παρ᾽ ὑπη- κόυς ἄρχοντος διαφορὰν. Then indeed κτίσαντα is for the Hebrew הבורא, for the Hebrews, because they have few verbals, use participles in place of verbals; thus κτίσαντα is worth what κτιστῇ is 1 Pet. IV. 19. The sense therefore is: they treated the works with greater honor than the maker himself: whom if they acknowledged in any way, as the Platonists, they nevertheless instituted no sacrifices to him.
