They could say, as the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics said, that they did not think the same as the common people, that they did not follow civil theology or poetic theology, but natural, as Varro distinguished those things: that by Jupiter they understood the ether: by Juno, the air: by Neptune, the sea: by the Naiads, the springs: by Cybele, the outermost earth: by Dis and Proserpina, the bowels of the earth: by Ceres, the fruit-bearing power: by the Dryads, the lives of the trees: by Vulcan, fire: by Liber, the moisture implanted in bodies. Paul says, therefore, that not even in this way can they be excused, who bestowed the greatest worship they could upon the things themselves, but none upon the maker, or a meager one compared to that. But clearly as Josephus speaks of them in the second book against Apion: εἰς πλῆθος δόξαις προκατειλημένοι τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῦ δόγματος ἐξανέγκειν ἐκ ἐτόλμησαν. Doubtless because, as Plato said, τὸν μὲν ἗ν ποιη- τὴν κὰι πατέρα τῦ δὲ τῦ πάντων ἑυρεῖν τὸ ἔργον κὰι ἑυρόντα εἰς πάντων ἀδύνατον λέγειν, that is, it is not safe to say: concerning which matter we have brought forward more testimonies in the annotations to book IV of the truth of the Christian Religion. See also what Chrysostom has in this place against Plato. Seneca, dealing with received sacred rites: All of which, he says, the wise man will observe as commanded by laws, not as pleasing to the gods. The Gospel convicts these veils of evil custom, and injustice, and Paul in this place. Add to these the customs which had already prevailed in Rome in Paul's time. The dead Caesars were to be worshipped with divine honors, of whom Lucan: Fulminibus manes radiisque ornabit & astris, Inque Deum templis jurabit Roma per umbras. If any had perjured themselves by Caesar, they were punished most severely. If by GOD, they bore it with impunity.

Grotius did not prove that the former word is said of sacrifices: nor is the latter used only of the bending of the body: both denote religious worship. Nor indeed are the Gentiles argued against only because they exhibited to creatures the worship which they could [give] as the greatest, but to the maker none, or a meager one compared to that, but because they worshipped creatures besides the creator, just as the little word παρὰ is used in 1 Cor. III. 11, Gal. I. 8. For the Apostle also reproves those who, together with the supreme God, worshipped certain intermediate gods or even those of lesser nations. For he censures their entire idolatry, and vindicates εὐ- λογίαν & λατρείαν religious for God alone: but those also are accused of εἰδωλολατρείας who, alongside the true God, or together with the true God, religiously worship idols, Deut. XVII. 3, 2 Kings XVII. 3, who serve those who by nature are not Gods, Gal. IV. 8. Therefore it is taught that God alone is to be adored, Deut. VI. 13, ch. X. 20, Matt. IV. 10. And thus the ancients also used this passage against the Arians, because together with the supreme God they themselves worshipped one inferior to God, not ὁμούσιον to the Father. Athanasius, Cyril, Gregory of Nyssa, Nazianzen, others. Perhaps that Gloss pleased Grotius, so that the mark of idolatry might not be branded upon Papists and Socinians: who indeed cannot be absolved from the same, as long as they bestow divine worship upon creatures, not indeed passing over the creator, but together with the creator, which we have expressly demonstrated in Tom. II in Aug. Cons. Nor is there any reason for anyone to object that a μεταλ- λαγὴ of the truth of GOD into a lie is argued here, which is when the glory of the creator is bestowed upon a creature: for the exchange of truth into a lie is in any idolatry, which therefore the Apostle teaches is committed even then, when a creature is worshipped with the creator, not only when the divine honor is bestowed upon a creature with the creator left behind, or the creature is worshipped more than the creator.

Who is blessed for ever, amen. A frequent formula among the Hebrews, as Gen. IX. 26. XIV. 20. XXIV. 27. 31. But especially accustomed to be used, as the Jews warn, and Chrysostom noted here, when something has been narrated which has been done or said against majesty, so that by such an added poultice it may be shown that God's majesty is nevertheless safe. Paul adds εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας, to signify that God is most worthy of worship, praise, and honor not at some time, but at all times. And so that men may recognize this more and more, he adds the particle, amen, in a precative sense: as also below IX. 5. XI. 36. XV. 33. VI. 20. XVI. 24. 27. 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Gal. I. 5. VI. 18. Eph. III. 21. VI. 24. Phil. IV. 20. 23. Col. IV. 18. I. Thess. V. 28. 2. Thess. III. 18. 1. Tim. I. 27. VI. 21. 2. Tim. IV. 18. 22. Tit. III. 15. Philem. 25. Heb. XIII. 21. 25. 1. Petr. IV. 11. V. 11. 14. 2. Petr. V. 18. 2. Petr. III. 18. 1. Joh. V. 21. 2. Joh. 14. And in the Apocalypse several times.

It is taught not only that God is to be worshipped at all times by the words εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας: but that the worship and glory of God extend themselves into all eternity, into the everlasting ages of the heavenly blessedness that will never cease. For there is no reason why the word should be restricted to the present age, since the Holy Scriptures lift us up to celebrate the glory of God forever, which is the supreme end for which we were created, so that, namely, we may celebrate God not only here, but forever.

Latin:

V. 24. Διὸ καὶ παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τῶν καρδιῶν αὐτῶν εἰς ἀκαθαρσίαν) Deum deseruêre, Deus vicissim eos deseruit, non leges illis dans divinas, & humanas finens depravari, non Prophetas mittens, & Philosophos finens ad absurda prolabi. Sivit eos facere quod luberet, etiam summe fœda: ut qui Deum non honoraverant, semetipsos dehonestarent. Quid hic ἀκαθαρσία & infra VI. 10. Gal. V. 19. Eph. IV. 19. V. 3. Coloss. III. 5. 1.Thes. II. 3. IV. 17. id infra 26. ubi hic sensus repetitur εἰς πάθη ἀτιμίας παραδιδόναι סגר est a præsidio suo destitutum, alteri male tractandum relinquere Deut. XXIII. 15. XXXII. 30. 1. Sam. XXIII. 12. ἀκαθαρσία נבלות Oseæ II. 10. Nahum. III. 6. quod alibi ἄφροσύνη, impuritates Ciceroni secunda Philippica. Ostendit non esse cur Romani se iis quos barbaros vocabant, ut Scythis & Germanis præferant.

Idololatriam excepit per orbem ἀκαθαρσία fœdarum libidinum colluvies, quæ voce illativa διὸ adducitur, tanquam idololatriæ pœna, quæ omnium flagitiorum & scelerum fons est. Traditi ergo a Deo sunt non effective, quasi Deus autor sit illius impuritatis, ut Calviniani blasphemant; nec solùm permissive, ac tantum ἐκβατικῶς, sed δικαστικῶς, & judicialiter. Quod justum DEI judicium non mera ἔκβασις est, sed complectitur tum dimissionem in concupiscentiis, per desertionem divinam Act. XIV. 16. Ps. XXCI. 13. tum traditionem in potestatem Satanæ, qui eos εἰς ἀκαθαρσίαν ceu Spiritus ἀκάθαρτος agit, 2. Tim. II. de priori Ambrosius l. h. tradere, inquit, est permittere, non autem incitari aut immittere, ut ea, quæ in desideriis conceperant, adjuti a Diabolo explerent in opere: de posteriori Augustin. l. XX. de Civ. D. c. XIX. Deus mittet efficaciam erroris, qua Diabolum facere permittet, justo ipsius judicio, quamvis faciat ille iniquo, malignoque consilio. Recte ergo hic Grotius παραδιδόναι סגר est a præsidio suo destitutum alteri male tractandum relinquere. Deut. XXIII. 15. XXXII. 30. 1. Sam. XXIII. 12. Et agnoscunt Bucerus, Marloratus interpp. Belgici vocem παρέδωκεν privative accipiendam esse de non impediendis gravioribus peccatis Ps. LXXXI. 13. Act. XIV. 16. de subtractione gratiæ ad resistendum peccatis requisitæ Matth. XXV. 28. de derelictione & traditione in potestatem Satanæ, a quo non impulsore Deo sed decernente ita judice, ob pristinam ingratitudinem in pejora scelera homines solicitantur 1. Sam. XV. 3. Matth. VI. 11. Neque uspiam verbum iliud occurrit de immediata influentia Dei in voluntatem subjecti traditi, sed semper importat causam quandam intermediam influentem in subjectum traditum, quod fatentur etiam Gregorius de Valent. Schwaretz. & Job. Malderus ad Thomæ sententiam provocantes, adde & Salmeronem, Cornelium, Estium, Stapletonum: Qui proinde merito aliis, utpote Banni, Franc. Sylvio, Didaco Alvarez, & cæteris prædeterminationem voluntatis humanæ ad malum adstruentibus opponuntur. Quo de vid. quæ Tom. II. Syst. Theol. dicta, c. X. quæst. VI. & T. III. Art. VI. q. V.

τῶ ἀτιμάζεσθαι τὰ σώματα αὐτῶν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. Id est, per sefe: sic ait, ut ipsi corporibus suis dedecus inferrent, sua sponte,cogente nemine. Quid facerent hostes capta crudelius urbe. Sic accepit & Theophylactus. Similis sensus 1. Cor. VI. 18. Contrarium est τὸ ἑαυτῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ 1. Thef. IV. 4.

Non improbanda esset interpretatio Grotii, cùm ἐν ἑαυτοῖς exponit per sefe, id est, sua sponte cum Theophylacto, si loco parallelo hanc exceptio- nem vocis firmasset. Nam ex collatione loci 1. Cor. VI. 18. id colligi non potest, sed potius, quod in proprium corpus tales peccent: unde non satis commodè Syrus reddidit inter sefe. Id ergo indi- gitatur, quod justo DEI judicio in semetipsis & in propriis suis corporibus ignominia, & turpitu- dine repleantur, qui Deum sua spoliarunt gloria. Id ita explicat ipse Apostolus v. 28. quid ἀντιμι- σίαν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς receperint.

Οἵ τινες μετήλλαξαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῦ Θεῦ ἐν τῷ ψεύδει) Eadem locutio, quæ supra 23. & ἀλήθειαν Θεῦ pro Θεὸν ἀληθῆ. Pro Deo vero sumpserunt imaginarios. Nam ψεῦ- δος שׁקר Hebræis est DEUS falsus. Ut Es. XXVIII. 15. XLIV: 20. Jer. XIII. 25. XXIII. 14. Os. VII. 1. Alibi, ut Amos II. 4. vocantur Dii isti μάταια pari sensu.

Καὶ ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα Ἐσεβάσθησαν κὰι ἐλάτρευσαν est וישׁתחו עבדו prior vox de sacrificiis dici solet, & vertitur σέβεσθαι Sap. XV. 6. 18. posterior de flexione corporis, quæ sacris accedere solet. Παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα; hic ἀντὶ τῦ κτίσαντος explicat scriptor constitutionum Clementis: & præterito creatore Hilarius: sed παρὰ cum accusativo, in comparatione positum id quod excedit significare solet, ut Exodi XXXVI. 4. Ps. XLV. 8. Luc. XIII. 2. 4. Hebr. III. 23. Sic & Philoni τῆς παρ᾽ ὑπη- κόυς ἄρχοντος διαφορὰν dixit. Tum verò κτίσαντα est pro Hebræo הבורא nam Hebræi, quia pauca habent verba- lia, participiis utuntur vice verbalium, sic κτίσαντα valet quod κτιστῇ 1. Petr. IV. 19. Sensus ergò est: majori honore opificia affecêre quam ipsum opificem: quem si aliquo modo agnovère, ut Platonici, nulla tamen ei sacrificia in- stituerunt. Poterant dicere, sicut dixêre Pythagorei, Pla- tonici, Stoici, se non eadem cum plebe sentire, non civi- lem se sequi Theologiam aut poeticam, sed naturalem, ut ista distinguebae Varro: per Jovem se intelligere æthe- rem: per Junonem, aërem: per Neptunum, mare: per Naidas, fontes: per Cybelen, terram extimam: per Ditem & Proserpinam, terræ viscera: per Cererem, vim frugife- ram: per Dryadas, arborum vitas: per Vulcanum ignem: per Liberum, humorem corporibus insitum. Dicit ergo Paulus ne sic quidem eos excusari posse, qui rebus ipsis cultum detulerint quem potuère maximum, opifici vero nullum, aut præ illo tenuem. At planè ut Josephus de il- lis loquitur secundo contra Appionem: εἰς πλῆθος δόξαις προκατειλημένοι τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῦ δόγματος ἐξανέγκειν ἐκ ἐτόλμησαν. Nimirum quia, ut dicebat Plato, τὸν μὲν ἗ν ποιη- τὴν κὰι πατέρα τῦ δὲ τῦ πάντων ἑυρεῖν τὸ ἔργον κὰι ἑυρόντα εἰς πάντων ἀδύνατον λέγειν, id est, non tutum est dicere: quam ad rem plura testimonia attulimus annotatis ad lib. IV. de veritate Religionis Christianæ. Vide & quæ contra Plato- nem hoc loco habet Chrysostomus. Seneca de sacris agens receptis: Quæ omnia, inquit, sapiens servabit tanquam legi- bus jussa, non tanquam diis grata. Hæc mali moris vela- menta, injustitiæ convincit Evangelium, & hoc loco Pau- lus. Adde his mores, qui Romæ jam Pauli tempore inva- luere. Cæsares mortuos divinis colendi honoribus, de quibus Lucanus: Fulminibus manes radiisque ornabit & astris, Inque Deum templis jurabit Roma per umbras. Si qui per Cæsarem pejerassemt, gravissime puniebantur. Si per DEUM, ferebant id impune.

Vocem priorem de Sacrificiis dici non proba- vit Grotius: nec posterior solùm de flexione cor- poris adhibetur: utraque cultum religiosum notat. Nec verò gentiles tantum arguuntur ideò, quod creaturis cultum, quem potuêre maximum, opifici vero nullum, aut præ illo tenuem exhibuerint, sed quod creaturas præter creatorem coluerint, uti vo- cula παρὰ 1. Cor. III. 11. Gal. I. 8. adhibetur. Nam reprehendit Apostolus etiam eos, qui una cum summo Deo colebant deos quosdam medioxumos vel etiam minorum gentium. Taxat enim univer- sam eorum idololatriam, solique Deo vindicat εὐ- λογίαν & λατρείαν religiosam: εἰδωλολατρείας vero postulantur etiam isti, qui juxta verum De- um, vel una cum Deo vero idola religiose colunt, Deut. XVII. 3. 2. Reg. XVII. 3. qui serviunt iis, qui natura Dii non sunt. Gal. IV. 8. Ideo solum Deum adorandum esse docetur, Deut. VI. 13. c. X. 20. Matth. IV. 10. Atque ita veteres etiam usi sunt hoc loco contra Arianos, quod una cum summo Deo ipsi colerent inferiorem Deo, non ὁμούσιον Patri. Athanasius, Cyrillus, Gregor. Nyssenus, Nazian- zenus, alii. Placuit forsan illa Glossa Grotio, ne Papistis, & Socinianis inureretur idololatriæ nota: qui vero ab eadem absolvi non possunt, quousque non quidem præterito creatore, sed una cum crea- tore creaturæ cultum divinum deferunt, quod Tom. II. in Aug. Cons. ex professo demonstravi- mus. Nec est quod obvertat quis, quod μεταλ- λαγὴ hic arguatur τῆς ἀληθείας τῦ Θεῦ ἐν τῷ ψεύ- δει, quæ est, cum creatoris gloria creaturæ defertur: nam commutatio veritatis in mendacium est in qua- vis idololatria, quam proinde etiam tum com- mitti docet Apostolus, cum creatura colitur cum creatore, non solum cum relicto creatore honore divino afficitur, aut magis, quam creator colitur creatura.

Ὃς ἐςιν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας, ἀμήν. Frequens formula Hebræis, ut Gen. IX. 26. XIV. 20. XXIV. 27. 31. Sed præcipuè usurpari solita, quemadmo- dum Judæi monent, & hic notavit Chrysostomus, ubi ali- quid narratum est, quod factum dictumve sit contra maje- statem, ut tali addito malagmate ostendatur Deo suam majestatem nihilominus esse salvam. Addit Paulus εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας,, ut significet Deum non aliquo, sed omni tempore cultu, laude & honore esse dignissimum. Quod ut homines magis magisque agnoscant, addit precativo sensu particu- lam, amen: ut & infra IX. 5. XI. 36. XV. 33. VI. 20. XVI. 24. 27. 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Gal. I. 5. VI. 18. Eph. III. 21. VI. 24. Phil. IV. 20. 23. Col. IV. 18. I. Thess. V. 28. 2. Thess. III. 18. 1. Tim. I. 27. VI. 21. 2. Tim. IV. 18. 22. Tit. III. 15. Philem. 25. Heb. XIII. 21. 25. 1. Petr. IV. 11. V. 11. 14. 2. Petr. V. 18. 2. Petr. III. 18. 1. Joh. V. 21. 2. Joh. 14. Et in Apocalypsi aliquoties.

Non tantum omni tempore colendum esse Deum vocibus εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας docetur: sed cultum & gloriam Dei porrigere sese in omnem æternita- tem, in secula sempiterna cœlestis nunquam de- situræ beatitudinis. Non enim est, cur restringa- tur vox ad præsens seculum, quum ad gloriam Dei in æternum celebrandam nos evehat S. S. qui finis est supremus, ob quem conditi sumus, ut sc. non hic tantum, sed in æternum Deum celebremus.

## 1:26
V. 26. For this cause God gave them up) Paul does what we are accustomed to do after a long parenthesis, repeating the words placed earlier, 24.

unto vile affections) To infamous desires. For what is more infamous than, I will not say to serve pleasures, but not to be content with those things which nature has found, when nevertheless those which nature has given are sweeter. So true is it, what Tacitus said, that the magnitude of infamy is coveted by some and that for the prodigal it is the latest pleasure.

for their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature) He begins with women, whom modesty becomes most, even regarding natural pleasures, μετήλλαξαν with the particle εἰς, in the same sense in which we have had that word twice with the following ἐν, because the Hebrews place ב, which is translated both by εἰς and by ἐν. He touches upon the ulcer of those whom Phaedrus and Martial call tribades, Tertullian call frictrices, among whom was Sappho, most noble in genius and poetry, who speaks thus in Ovid: Lesbians who have made me infamous by being loved.

Rightly into infamous, on account of πάθος ἀτιμίας. Seneca Epist. 95, concerning the women of his own age: In lust they do not even yield to males, born to suffer. May the gods and goddesses destroy them: so perverse a kind of unchastity have they devised. Clement of Alexandria: for women act like men against nature. Akin to the word μετήλλαξαν, which is used here, and of equal meaning, is ἐναλλάσσειν: whence Aquila said ἐνηλλαγμένοις, Ose. IV. 14, pathics, who no less than those women were exchanging the duties of their sex, and of whom Paul will now treat.

Latin:

V. 26. Διὰ τῦτο παρέδωκεν ἀυτὸς) Facit Paulus quod post longam parenthesin facere solemus, repetens verba prius posita, 24.

εἰς πάθη ἀτιμίας) Cupiditatibus infamibus. Quid enim infamius quam non dicam servere voluptatibus, sed iis quæ natura reperit nòn esse contentum, cum tamen quas natura dedit sint suaviores. Adeo verum est, quod dixit Tacitus, magnitudinem infamiæ a nonnullis concupisci atque ejus apud prodigos novissimam esse voluptatem.

αἵτε γὰρ θήλειαι ἀυτῶν μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν) Incipit à fœminis quas maximè pudor decet, etiam circa naturales voluptates, μετήλλαξαν cum particu- la εἰς, eodem sensu quo id verbum sequente ἐν bis habui- mus, quia Hebræi ב ponunt, quod & per εἰς & per ἐν verti- tur. Tangit illarum ulcus quas tribadas vocant Phædrus & Martialis, Frictrices Tertullianus, quarum fuit, ingenio & poesi nobilissima Sappho, quæ apud Ovidium sic loquitur: Lespides infamem quæ me fecistis amatæ.

Recte in infamem, ob πάθος ἀτιμίας. Seneca Epist. 95. de sui seculi fœminis: Libidine vero ne maribus quidem ce- dunt, pati natæ. Dii illas Deæque male perdant: adeo per- versum commentæ genus impudicitiæ. Clemens Alexan- drinus: γὰρ γυναῖκες ἀνδρίζονται παρὰ φύσιν. Voci μετήλ- λαξαν, quæ hic usurpatur, affinis est & paris significatus ἐναλλάσσειν: unde ἐνηλλαγμένοις, dixit Aquila Ose. IV. 14. pathicos, qui non minus quam istæ fœminæ sexus officia commutabant, & de quibus jam aget Paulus.

## 1:27
V. 27. Likewise also the men leaving the natural use of the woman) In the Greek Epigram there is:

They love the female less, a small evil, because the mistress of Cyprus, nature, has given them a female instinct. Dirce, the offspring of irrational animals; for nature, of those, disdains the laws of union. For the female is joined to the male; but wretched men lead men into a strange marriage. To which corresponds that in the Epistle of Jude: But whatever they know naturally as irrational animals, in these they are corrupted. Plato in the first book of the Laws: It is to be believed that for the female and the nature of males coming together for the communion of generation, the pleasure concerning these things seems to be given according to nature; but of males with males, or females with females, is against nature. Plutarch in his Amatorius: the intercourse against nature with males, where he also calls this love 'bastard'. Maximus Tyrius in his tenth dissertation: But I have dared to touch male flesh, with unjust money male flesh; the mixing is unjust, the intercourse is barren; do you sow on rocks, do you plow sand? Transfer your joys to nature; turn your eyes to agriculture; already with fruitful pleasures

They burned in their lust for one another) He excellently uses the word for burning, as do the poets when dealing with loves. He calls that 'lust' which a little before he called 'desires'. For such a craving does not deserve the name of love. 'We say that such a one desires, but does not love,' says Maximus Tyrius.

Working out unseemliness) Maximus Tyrius, attaching some other 'seemly' or 'lawful' or 'truly erotic' habit. Thus 'nebalah' is translated as 'unseemliness' in Gen. XXXIV, 7.

And the recompense which was due for their error receiving in themselves) For it is no wonder if they themselves do what they narrate was done by the gods. Theophilus of Antioch: that they also introduced male-to-male cohabitations. And first of all they proclaim that the gods engage in unspeakable unions. Plutarch in his Amatorius says that Solon used this wicked pleasure: Diogenes Laërtius says that Zeno, the founder of the Stoic sect, did. But at Rome everything was full of such things. The same Theophilus, speaking about pederasty: it has been deemed worthy of privilege by the Romans, with them attempting to gather herds of boys, just as of brood mares. Which sense is in words nearly the same in Justin's second Apology. Horace in his Philosophical writings: If a little maid is at hand, or a slave boy, etc.

Seneca, writing at nearly the same time as Paul, Epist. 95: I pass over the herds of unhappy boys, whom, after the banquets are finished, the insults of the bedroom await. I pass over the troops of catamites described by nations and colors. Martial says that there was no one of such trembling or anxious modesty who feared to be caught in such an act. The Scantinian law had indeed forbidden the defilement of a boy, but only of a free-born one, establishing nothing about slaves. And that very law later fell into disuse. Force only began to be punished, and indeed in an equal manner whether against a boy or a woman, L. si postulaverit in fine D. de adulterio L. in eadem §. Præterea D. ad legem Juliam de vi publica. Tacitus on Tiberius: He sought the solitude of the sea out of shame for his crimes and lusts: with which he had burned so uncontrollably that, in royal fashion, he defiled free-born youth with outrages: nor did he have only beauty and graceful bodies, but in these modest boyhood, and in others the images of ancestors, as an incitement to his desire. And then for the first time were found words unknown before, 'sellarii' and 'spintriæ', from the filth of the place and the manifold endurance, and the slave who was proposed to seek, to drag in, to offer gifts to the willing, and threats against those who refused. See Suetonius on the same Tiberius 43. We have the word 'antimisthian' also in 1 Cor. VI. 13; that word signifies a reward equal to the work.

Latin:

V. 27. Ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ ἄῤῥενες ἀφέντες τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν τῆς θηλείας) In Græco Epigrammate est:

Θηλυτέρας φιλέουσι ὀλίγον κακὸν, ἕνεκα κείναις Κυπριδίας δάμυς πότνια δέδωκε φύσις. Δίρκαι, τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων γόνος· ἦ γὰρ ἐκείνων Φύσις, ἀτιμάζει θέσμια συζυγίης. Ἄρσενι γὰρ θήλεια συνάπτεται· οἱ δὲ ἄλεγεινοὶ Ἄνδρες ἐς ἀλλήλες ξέῖνον ἄγεσι γάμον. Cui convenit illud in Epistola Judæ: Ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα ἐπίστανται ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται. Plato de le- gibus primo: ἐπιστεόν ὅτι τῇ θηλείᾳ κὶ τῇ τῶν ἀῤῥένων φύ- σει εἰς κοινωνίαν ἰόσῃ τῆς γεννήσεως ἡ περὶ ταῦτα ἡδονὴ κατὰ φύσιν ἀποδεδόσθαι δοκεῖ· ἀῤῥένων δὲ πρὸς ἀῤῥένας, ἢ θηλειῶν πρὸς θηλείας παρὰ φύσιν. Plutarchus amatorio: ἡ παρὰ φύσιν ὁμιλία πρὸς ἀῤῥένας, ubi & amorem hunc νόθον vo- cat. Maximus Tyrius dissertatione decima: ἐγὼ δὲ ἕτλης θίγειν σαρκὸς ἄῤῥενος, ἀδίκω χρήματος σαρκὶ ἀῤῥεναι· ἄδικος ἡ μίξις, ἄγονος ἡ συνουσία· ἐπὶ πετρῶν σπείρεις, ψάμμος ἀροῖς; μετένεγκε τὰς ἐυφροσύνας ἐπὶ τὴν φύσιν· τρί- ψον ἐπὶ τὴν γεωργίαν τὰς ὀφθαλμὲς· ἐγκάρποις ἤδητι ἡδοναῖς

Ἐξεκαύθησαν ἐν τῇ ὀρέξει αὐτῶν εἰς ἀλλήλες) Egregiè vo- cem exardescendi usurpat, ut & Poëtæ ubi de amoribus agitur. Ὄρεξιν hic vocat quod paulò ante ἐπιθυμίας. Non enim amoris nomen meretur talis cupido. Ἐπιθυμεῖν λέ- γωμεν τῦτον, ἀλλ' ἐκ ἐρᾶν ait Maximus Tyrius.

Ἀσχημοσύνην κατεργαζόμενοι) Maximus Tyrius πρόσ- φυόμενος ἕτε τινὰ ἐυσχήμονα ἕτε νόμιμον, ἕτε ἐρατικὴν τῷ ὄντι ξυνήθη. Sic נבלה vertitur ἄσχημον Gen. XXXIV, 7.

Καὶ τὴν ἀντιμισθίαν ἣν ἔδει τῆς πλάνης αὐτῶν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἀπολαμβάνοντες) Nam quæ à Diis facta narrant, non mirum si & ipsi faciant. Theophilus Antiochenus: ὅτι μὲν κὶ τὰς συγγατὰς ἀῤῥενοκοιτίας εἰσηγήσαντο. Καὶ πρώτώς γε τὲς θεὸς κηρύσσεσιν ἐν ἀῤῥήτοις μίξεσι συγγίνεσθαι. Usum hac nefanda venere Solonem ait Plutarchus in amatorio: Ze- nonem Stoicæ Sectæ principem Diogenes Laërtius. Romæ verò omnia plena talium. Idem Theophilus περὶ παιδερα- στίας locutus: προνομίας ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων ἠξίωται, παίδων ἀ- γέλαις, ὥσπερ ἵππων φορβάδων, συναγείρειν ἀυτῶν πειραμέ- νων. Qui sensus verbis prope iisdem est apud Justinum Apologetico secundo. Horatius in scriptis Philosophicis Si ancillula præsto Sit, vel verna puer, &c.

Seneca eodem ferme quo hæc Paulus scribens tempore Epist. 95. Transeo puerorum infelicium greges, quos post trans- acta convivia, alii cubiculi contumeliæ expectant. Transeo agmina exoletorum per nationes coloresque descripta. Martia- lis ait, neminem fuisse tam trepidi aut solliciti pudoris, qui metueret in tali facto deprehendi. Scantinia quidem lex vetuerat stupra pueri, sed ingenui tantum, nihil de servis constituens. Et ea ipsa lex postea exolevit. Vis tantum puniri cœpit & quidem pari modo sive in puerum sive in fœminam L. si postulaverit in fine D. de adulterio L. in eadem §. Præterea D. ad legem Juliam de vi publica. Ta- citus de Tiberio: Solitudinem maris repetit pudore scelerum & libidinum: quibus adeo indomitis exarserat, ut more regio pubem ingenuam stupris pollueret: nec formam tantum & decora corpora, sed in his modestam pueritiam, in aliis imagi- nes majorum incitamentum cupidinis habebat. Tuncque pri- mum ignota ante vocabula reperta sunt sellariorum & spin- triarum ex fœditate loci ac multiplici patientia, propositique servi qui quærerent, pertraherent dona in promptos, minas ad- versus abnuentes. Vide Suetonium de eodem Tiberio 43. ἀντιμισθίας vocem habemus & 1. Cor. VI. 13. significat ea vox mercedem parem operæ.

## 1:28
V. 28. And even as they did not approve to have God in their knowledge;

Knowledge, in Hebrew 'da'ath', by metonymy signifies the worship of GOD, as can be seen in Prov. II. 7, Hos. IV. 1, 6, VI. 6. So also Col. I. 10. 'To approve' is often to judge: and taking the genus for the species, to estimate rightly, as below XV. 22. 'To have God' is to have Him propitious, as 2 John 9. The sense therefore is: they did not value God enough to acquire His favor by worshipping Him.

God Himself gave them over to a reprobate mind. There is an allusion in the words 'they did not approve' and 'reprobate'. They did not value GOD enough to worship Him. God gave them over to thoughts that are clearly to be rejected, for 'reprobate coin' is rejected money. Thus the word 'reprobate' is taken also in 1 Cor. IX. 7, Tit. I. 16, Heb. VI. 8, and elsewhere. Interpreters translate 'sig', which signifies dross, as 'reprobate'. Prov. XIV, 4, Isa. I. 22. The Latins call them 'rejected sheep', which are rejected on account of disease. We have 'mind' in this sense, so that it signifies the whole soul and its action, in Eph. IV. 17, 1 Tim. VI. 5, 2 Tim. III. 9, Tit. I. 15. Not far from this is that in the Greek tragedy: But when a divinity prepares evils for a man, he first harms his mind. Through 'knowledge' Grotius understands worship metonymically: others prefer to take it properly, and interpret 'to have' as 'to retain': because they did not approve of God in knowledge, so as to remain in the knowledge of God implanted, and that which they could acquire for themselves through the sight of creatures, or had acquired, nor did they use the same as was right: It can also be taken thus, as they did not approve or strive to have God in their knowledge, inquiring by way of natural cognition where the knowledge of God could be had, so God gave them over to a reprobate mind, into a mind so corrupt that they could feel or approve nothing right, and were carried by a blind impulse to do 'things not fitting', those things which in no way are decent and are repugnant to the law of nature itself. However, it cannot be approved that Grotius interprets 'to have God' as 'to have God propitious'. For the Apostle did not say simply 'to have God', but 'to have God in knowledge'. Nor could the favor of God or grace be acquired by them: because, destitute of faith, they could not please GOD, Heb. XI. 6. Furthermore, regarding what the Apostle said here and in the following verses, when he spoke of 'filled with all unrighteousness' concerning the wicked Venus of the Romans, Grotius notes that, although there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit wished to note it here at the same time, and thus far it is considered an excellent characterization of those times, especially at Rome, let us admit it in this place, yet it is not only those times, or only the Romans, that are looked at, but the Apostle teaches, by the force of the argument he is treating, what punishments and vices are accustomed to follow the neglect of the knowledge of God and the holding down of the truth in unrighteousness, to which we are all naturally inclined.

Ποιεῖν τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα) that is, εἰς τὸ ποιεῖν τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα. The Hebrews would say אשׁר לא יעשׂו, which the Greeks call ἃ μὴ χρεὼ. Lactantius, forgetful of what they were born for, compete with women in passivity.

Latin:

V. 28. Καὶ καθὼς ἐκ ἐδοκίμασαν τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει·

Ἐπίγνωσις Hebraice רעת per μετωνυμίαν cultum DEI significat, ut videre est Prov. II. 7. Os. IV. 1. 6. VI. 6. Sic & Col I. 10. δοκιμάζειν sæpe est judicare: & genere sum- to pro specie, rectum æstimare, ut infra XV. 22. θεὸν ἔχειν est habere propitium, ut II. Joh. 9. Sensus ergo est: non tanti fecerunt Deum, ut ejus favorem eum colendo sibi acquirerent.

Παρέδωκεν ἀυτὸς ὁ Θεὸς εἰς ἀδόκιμον νῦν. Est allusio in vocibus ἐδοκίμασαν & ἀδόκιμον DEUM non tanti fecêre quem colerent. Deus eos tradidit cogi- tationibus planè aspernandis, nam ἀδόκιμον νόμισμα est nummus rejectaneus. Sic vox ἀδόκιμος sumitur & 1. Cor. IX. 7. Tit. I. 16. Hebr. VI. 8. & alibi. סיג quod Scoriam significat per ἀδόκιμον vertunt interpretes. Prov. XIV, 4. Esa. I. 22. Latini rejiculas oves vocant, quæ ob morbum rejiciuntur. Νῦν hoc sensu ut totum animum ejusque actum significet, habemus & Ephes. IV. 17. 1. Tim. VI. 5. 2. Tim. III. 9. Tit. I. 15. Non longe abit hinc illud in Tragœdia Græca Ὅταν δὲ δαίμων ἀνδρὶ πορσύνῃ κακὰ Τὸν νῦν ἔβλαψε πρῶτον. Per ἐπίγνωσιν Grotius cultum metonymicè in- telligit: alii malunt propriè accipere, & ἔχειν in- terpretari retinere: quia non probarunt Deum in notitia, ut permanerent in notitia de Deo insitâ, & illa quam per creaturarum aspectum acquirere sibi poterant, vel acquisiverant, nec eadem, ut par erat, usi sunt: Accipi etiam ita potest, sicut non probarunt aut studuerunt, ut Deum in notitia haberent, vi naturalis cognitionis inquirentes ubi ἐπίγνωσις haberi posset Dei, ita in reprobum sensum dedit eosdem Deus, in mentem ita corruptam, ut nihil recti sentire vel probare possent, cæcoque impetu ferrentur ad faciendum τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα, ea, quæ nullatenus decent, ipsique naturæ legi repu- gnant. Non autem probari potest, quod Grotius θεὸν ἔχειν interpretatur Deum habere propitium. Non enim simpliciter θεὸν ἔχειν dixit Apostolus, sed θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει. Neque favor Dei, aut gratia ab ipsis acquiri poterat: quia fide destituti placere DEO non poterant, Ebr. XI. 6. Porrò quod hic & in sequentibus, cum πεπληρωμένυς πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ dixit Apostolus de Romanorum ne- fanda Venere & injustitia, annotat Grotius, etsi eam hic simul notare voluisse Spiritum S. dubium non sit, & hactenus egregium etiam χαρακτηρισμὸν illorum temporum, præsertim Romæ haberi, hoc loco admittamus, non tamen vel illa tempora so- lum, vel Romani tantum respiciuntur, sed quæ- nam pœnæ, & vitia sequi soleant neglectum τῇ γνωσῆ τῦ θεῦ, & detentionem veritatis in injusti- tia, ad quæ naturâ propensi omnes sumus, docet, vi argumenti, quod tractat Apostolus.

Ποιεῖν τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα) id est εἰς τὸ ποιεῖν τὰ μὴ κα- θήκοντα. Hebræi dicerent אשׁר לא יעשׂו ἃ μὴ χρεὼ dicunt Græci. Lactantius immemores quid nati sint, cum fœminis patientia certant.

## 1:29
V. 29. Πεπληρωμένυς πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ) There is a wonderful emphasis in this expression, and an excellent characterization of those times, especially at Rome, of which we have several descriptions also in Seneca's Epistles from about the same period. Since he had touched upon those things whose baseness was most prominent, he now touches upon other vices that were most widely spread, but reigning especially at Rome, all of which are indeed evil in themselves: but their depravity, having been covered over as it were by long-standing customs, needed to be pointed out by the Gospel. And first he mentions injustice, through which the Romans had become masters of the world, by often waging unjust wars and turning alliance into domination. See what we have said about the law of War and Peace, both in the Prolegomena and in book 1, chapter III, 21. that the Romans have nothing but what is stolen, that the cause of their warring is a deep desire for empire and riches, not entirely falsely in Sallust, Mithridates: Galgacus truly calls them in Tacitus the robbers of the world, whom neither the east nor the west has satisfied.

Πορνείᾳ) Here, under the name of fornication, do not understand only the congress of prostitutes, which old Cato praises in Horace; but also adulteries, as in Matthew 5:22. Gellius, from Varro, noted that that Sallust, whose history is full of censorious judgments, was caught in adultery. See what Horace has in book I, Satire II, and book II, Satire VII. Seneca says of the women of his time that the adultery of one was considered sordid, as if it were marriage. From Arrian we learn that women were accustomed to defend themselves with Plato's dogma concerning the community of women. See Seneca, Ep. XCVII. You have the adulteries of Tiberius and Gaius in Suetonius. Governors in the provinces imitated the deeds of the Emperors. 'A provincial wife who is somewhat pretty has I know not what power of attraction,' said Varro.

Πονηρίᾳ) πονηρία, malignity, depravity, malice, in the Glossary. Malice is a crafty and deceitful method of doing harm. You have an excellent example of it in Appian in the narration of those things which preceded the third Carthaginian war. You have the malice of the Roman Emperors in Tacitus, Annals XIII. The same Tacitus calls Tiberius cunning and obscure in covering up his crimes. That appeared then in other matters, and most especially in the overthrowing of Germanicus and the whole house of Drusus. Thus also Livia had overthrown the entire house of Augustus, in order to advance her own.

πλεονεξίᾳ) The arms of the Romans are most fierce against those from whom, when conquered, the greatest spoils are taken, says Mithridates: Petronius: 'If any hidden boundary existed beyond, if there were any land that might send forth yellow gold, it was an enemy, and with fates prepared for sad wars, riches were sought.' 'If the enemy is wealthy,' says Galgacus, 'he is greedy.' Seneca, that most eloquent accuser of avarice, within four years had prepared three thousand million sesterces, that is, as the learned think, fifteen million florins.

κακίᾳ) κακία is used by the Greeks, as Cicero noted, generally for all viciousness, just as Aristotle opposes κακίαν to ἀρετῇ. Where it is used specifically, it seems to denote the habit of harming others, such as Virgil describes: If you had not harmed someone, you would have died.

μυςὸς φθόνυ) A vice which Tacitus said was common to small and great cities. Of such people it was said long ago: Either some misfortune has happened to him, or some good to someone else. See Horace, Epist. II, concerning this.

φόνυ) This appears first in the wars of the Roman people, Seneca: We restrain homicides and individual murders. What of wars and the glorious crime of slaughtered nations? Neither avarice nor cruelty knows a limit. By decrees of the Senate and plebiscites, wars are waged, and things forbidden privately are ordered publicly. Then against slaves. Vedius Pollio threw a slave to lampreys for breaking a crystal cup. But especially in the amphitheater, where men were thrown to be slaughtered partly by beasts, partly by men, merely for the amusement of the people, which Christians like Tatian, Tertullian, Minucius, Arnobius, and Lactantius rightly reproach the Romans for. Now, indeed, for the Roman Emperors to condemn anyone to death on the slightest suspicions without a trial was so daily an occurrence that in Tacitus, Suetonius, and Dio nothing occurs more frequently, and when historians narrate such things, they beg the reader's indulgence for the weariness.

ἔριδος) Three forums full of lawsuits. Indeed, the philosophers themselves were also wranglers, of whom Timon says: And man-slaying strife wanders about, screaming, sister of man-slaying battle and discord, she who, blind, rolls around everywhere. Of which I have produced other things on this matter in the annotations to Book II of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

δόλο) Lucilius: To lay snares, as if they were enemies, all against all. Not every deceit was restrained by the courts. For Pomponius says it is permitted to mutually circumvent one another in the price of buying and selling, L. in causæ cognitione, D. de minoribus. Paulus the Jurist, L. item si §. quemadmodum D. Locati. This also is convicted of iniquity by the Gospel. See what we have said in Book II of the Law of War and Peace, ch. XII, 16, II, and 26.

κακοηθείας) It is translated as malignity in the Glossary, and Tacitus uses the word in this sense. It has a place when we take what we can interpret in a good light and twist it into a worse one, contrary to what the duty of love demands. 1 Cor. XIII. 6. Thus, the writer on the causes of corrupted eloquence says that mutual malignity was revealed between Calvus, Asinius, Brutus, Caelius, Caesar, and Cicero. This is the vice for which Plutarch criticizes Herodotus.

καταλάλος) In the Glossary, καταλαλῶ means to grumble, to speak against. The Hebrew נרף and כלם and certain others are translated this way. These signify those who more openly harmed the reputation of another, as many did at Rome, even under the guise of friendship. Such was that man in Horace: Who used me as a companion and friend at the Capitol. Who, from boyhood, asked for many things for my sake and did them, and I rejoice that he lives unharmed in the city. But yet I wonder how he escaped that judgment. Horace then adds: For these, the black juice of the cuttlefish: this is pure rust.

This Suetonius calls reproaching by excusing. Polybius: For this is a certain kind of calumny, to harm not by blaming, but by praising.

Θεοςυγείς) Those who wish θεοςύγος to be read here advise well, for it is a matter of vices, not punishments. They are rightly called haters of God or those abhorring God, as Cyprian cites in Epist. 68, who, as soon as anything adverse happened to them, accused the gods or denied Providence. Lucan: He will wait from high heaven for Thessalian slaughter, when he holds the thunderbolts. He will surely aim at Pholoe, he will aim at Aetna with fires, and the undeserving grove of Rhodope, and the threatening pines. He will strike this head with his snares instead.

Thus, the envy of the gods is the crime of the gods, that Pompey is exposed to the gods, you may read in the same author. Tacitus, Annal. XIV. Which things happened so without the care of the gods that many years later Nero continued his empire and crimes. How great the impiety of Caesar was, we have taught from Philo and others in that [commentary] on the Thessalonians. And the memory of that event was fresh when Paul wrote this Epistle.

ὑβριςὰς) ὑβριςὴς means contumelious in the Glossary. רעון in Prov. XV. 25 and elsewhere is translated as ὑβριςής. Aristotle says in his Rhetoric that it happens to both the young and the rich that they easily treat others indignantly. See in Gellius the story about the young man who slapped those he met. Tacitus, where he deals with the punishments of the Christians: Mockery was added to those perishing. To the same person is narrated Nero's insult to Thrasea as a forewarning of imminent slaughter. How Tiberius and Claudius mocked matrons more through contumely than through lust, see Suet. Tiber. 44, 45; Claudio 36.

ὑπερηφάνυς) ὑπερηφανία is pride, an evil innate to nobility, as Sallust says. Moreover, ὑπερηφανία, as Theophrastus defines it, is a contempt for everyone else except oneself. He has given us an excellent characterization of this vice. And there are many examples in Martial of those who would not admit others to kisses, who dined apart from banquets, and did other things of that kind. Galgacus in Tacitus says of the Romans: Whose pride you will have escaped in vain through compliance and modesty. But the same Tacitus notes the old and ingrained pride of the Claudian family, which had ruled Rome after Augustus, and into whose name Nero was adopted.

Latin:

V. 29. Πεπληρωμένυς πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ) Est mira ἔμφασις in hoc sermone, & egregius χαρακτηρισμὸς illorum tempo- rum, præsertim Romæ, quales descriptiones aliquot ha- bemus & in Senecæ Epistolis circa tempus idem. Cum hactenus ea attigisset, quorum turpitudo maximè emi- nebat, nunc alia tangit vitia latissime sparsa, sed Ro- mæ maxime regnantia, quæ omnia per se quidem sunt mala: sed eorum pravitas longis moribus velut obdu- cta opus habebat indicari ab Evangelio. Ac primum dicit injustitiam, per quam Romani facti erant orbis Do- mini, bella ferendo sæpe injusta, & societatem verten- do in dominatum. Vide, quæ diximus de jure Belli & Pacis, tum in Prolegomenis, tum lib. 1. c. III. 21. Roma- nos nihil nisi raptum habere, causam eis bellandi cupidinem profundam imperii, ac divitiarum, non planè falso apud Sal- lustium Mithridates: Galgacus vere apud Tacitum rapto- res orbis vocat, quos non oriens, non occidens satiaverit.

Πορνείᾳ) Hic sub πορνείας nomine non meretricios tantum congressus intellige, quos laudat apud Horatium priscus Cato; Sed & adulteria, ut Matth. V. 22. Sallusti- um illum, cujus plena censorii sententiis est historia in adulterio deprehensum notavit ex Varrone Gellius. Vi- de, quæ habet Horatius lib. I. Satyra II. & lib. II. Saty- ra VII. Seneca sui temporis fœminis dicit unius adul- terium sorduisse, quasi matrimonium esset. Ex Arriano discimus solitas se fœminas defendere Platonis dogmate de communitate mulierum. Vide Senecam Ep. XCVII. Tiberii & Caji adulteria habes apud Suetonium. Imperatorum fa- cta imitabantur in provinciis præsides. Habet nescio quid ἑλκυστικὸν, dicebat Varro, formosula provincialis uxor.

Πονηρίᾳ) πονηρία malignitas, pravitas, malitia, in Glos- sario. Malitia est versuta & fallax nocendi ratio. Ejus exemplum habes egregium in Appiano in narratione eorum quæ præcessere bellum Carthaginense tertium. Malitiam Imperatorum Romanorum habes apud Ta- citum Annalium XIII. Tiberium Tacitus idem vocat callidum & tegendis sceleribus obscurum. Apparuit id tum in aliis rebus, tum maximè in evertendo Germa- nico, & tota Drusi domo. Sic & Livia omnem Augusti domum everterat, ut suos proveheret.

πλεονεξίᾳ) Romanorum arma in eos acerrima, quibus victis spolia maxima sunt, dicit Mithridates: Petronius: Si quis finus abditus ultra, Si qua foret tellus quæ fulvum mitteret aurum Hostis erat, fatisque in tristia bella paratis Quærebantur opes. Si locuples hostis avari ait Galgacus. Seneca illo tam eloquens avaritiæ accusator intra quadriennium ter millies millies sestertium paraverat, id est, ut putant eruditi, quin- decim milliones florenorum.

κακίᾳ) κακία Græcis, ut Cicero notavit, generaliter su- mitur pro omni vitiositate, quomodo Aristoteles ἀρετῇ op- ponit κακίαν. Speciatim ubi sumitur, videtur notare con- suetudinem aliis nocendi, qualem describit Virgilius: Etsi non aliqua nocuisses, mortuus esses.

μυςὸς φθόνυ) Quod vitium parvis magnisque civitatibus commune dixit Tacitus. De talibus dictum olim: Aut illi nescio quid incommodi accidit, aut nescio cui aliquid boni. Vi- de de eo Horatium Epist. II.

φόνυ) Apparet id primum in bellis populi Romani Sene- ca: Homicidia compescimus & singulas cædes. Quid bella & occisarum gentium gloriosum scelus? Non avaritia, non cru- delitas modum nobit. Ex Senatusconsultis plebisque scitis bella exerceriur, & publicè jubentur vetita privatim. Deinde in servos. Vedius Pollio servum ob fractum crystallinum mu- renis objecit. Maximè verò in amphitheatro, ubi homines partim feris, partim hominibus trucidandi objiciebantur, tantum in oblectamentum populi, quod meritò Romanis exprobrant Christiani Tatianus, Tertullianus, Minutius, Arnobius, Lactantius. Jam verò Imperatoribus Romanis quosvis levissimis ex suspicionibus sine causæ cognitione morti addicere ita quotidianum, ut in Tacito & Suetonio, ac Dione non aliud frequentiùs occurrat, & cum talia nar- tant Historici, tædium Lectorem deprecentur.

ἔριδος) Tria fora plena litibus. Fuere verò Philosophi ipsi quoque vitiligatores, de quibus Timon: Φοιτᾷ δὲ βροτολοιγὸς ἔρις κατιὸν λελακυῖα, Νείκης ἀνδροφόνοιο κασιγνήτη καὶ ἐρίδη, Η' τ' ἀλαὴ περὶ πάντα κυλίνδεται. Cujus & alia in hanc rem produximus annotatis ad li- brum II. de veritate Religionis Christianæ.

δόλο) Lucilius: Insidias facere, ut si hostes sint, omnibus omnes. Non omnis dolus judiciis coërcebatur. Licere enim in pretio venditionis & emptionis se mutuo circumvenire, di- ドit Pomponius L. in causæ cognitione etiam D. de minori- bus. Paulus ICtus L. item si §. quemadmodum D. Locati. Hoc quoque per Evangelium iniquitatis convincitur. Vide quæ diximus lib. II. de Jure Belli & Pac. c. XII. 16. II. & 26.

κακοηθείας) Malignitas vertitur in Glossario, & hoc sensu eam vocem usurpat Tacitus. Locum habet, cum quæ pos- sumus in bonam partem interpretari, in pejorem rapimus contra quam exigit officium dilectionis. 1. Cor. XIII. 6. Sic inter Calvum, Asinium, Brutum, Cælium, Cæsarem, Ciceronem, mutuam malignitatem detegi ait Scriptor de causis corruptæ eloquentiæ. Hoc est vitium, cujus Hero- dotum arguit Plutarchus.

καταλάλος) In Glossario καταλαλῶ obgannio, obloquor. Vertitur sic Hebræum נרף & כלם & alia quædam. Signi- ficantur hic qui apertius famam alterius lædebant, ut multi Romæ, etiam amicitiæ specie. Talis ille apud Horatium: Me Capitolinis convictore usus amico. Quæ à puero est, causaque mea permulta rogatus Fecit & incolumis lætor quod vivit in urbe. Sed tamen admiror quo pacto judicium illud Fugerit. Addit deinde Horatius: His nigra succus loliginis: hæc est Ærugo mera.

Hoc Suetonius vocat excusando opprobrare. Polybius, καπιός γάρ ἐτι τις ὗτος ἔυχηται τρόπος διαβολῆς, τὸ μὲ ψέγον- τας, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπαινέτας λυμαίνεθαι.

Θεοςυγείς) Bene monent qui legi hic volunt θεοςύγος agitur enim de vitiis, non de pœnis. Recte autem dicuntur osores Dei aut abhorrentes à Deo, ut citat Cypr. Epist. 68. qui simul atque aliquid ipsis evenisset adversi, Deos incusa- bant, aut negabant Providentiam. Lucanus: Expectabit ab alto Æthere Thessalicas, teneat cum fulmina, cædes. Scilicet ipso petet Pholoen, petet ignibus æten, Immeritaque nemus Rhodopes, pinusque minantes. Cassibus hoc potius feriet caput.

Sic invidia Deorum crimen Deorum, Pompejum Deis objici, apud eundem legas. Tacit. annal. XIV. Quæ adeò si- ne cura Deûm eveniebant, ut multos post annos Nero imperium & scelera continuavevit Cæsi quanta impietas fuerit ex Philo- ne aliisque docuimus in illam Thessalonicenses. Et ejus rei recens erat memoria cum hanc Epistolam scriberet Paulus.

ὑβριςὰς) ὑβριςὴς contumeliosus in Gloss. רעון Prov XV. 25. & alibi vertitur ὑβριςής. Ait Aristoteles in Rhetoricis, & juvenibus & ditibus evenire,ut facile alios indigne habeant. Vide in Gellio historiam de juvene, qui alapas impingebat obviis. Tacitus ubi de pœnis Christianorum agit: Pereun- tibus addita ludibria. Eidem narratur Neronis in Thraseam contumelia prænuntia cædis imminentis. Quomodo Ti- berius & Claudius matronis per contumeliam magis quam per libidinem illuserint, vide Suet. Tiber. 44.45. Claudio 36.

ὑπερηφάνυς) ὑπερηφανία est superbia, agnatum, ut Sallu- stius ait, nobilitati malum. Est autem ὑπερηφανία, desiniente Theophrasto, καταφρόνησις πλὴν ἀυτῶ τῶν ἄλλων. Cujus vitii egregium nobis dedit χαρακτηρισμόν. Et complura sunt apud Martialem eorum, qui alios ad oscula non admittebant, qui à conviviis seorsim cœnabant,aliaque faciebant ejus generis. Galgacus apud Tacitum de Romanis: Quorum superbiam frustra per obsequium & modestiam effugeris. Claudio vero fa- miliæ quæ post Augustū Romæ imperaverat,cujus in nomen adscitus Nero,veterem & insitam superbiam notat idem Tac.

## 1:30
ἀλαζόνας) ἀλάζων is a boaster, a braggart, an arrogant person in the Glossary. In Theophrastus, too, there is one notation for ἀλαζονεία and another for ὑπερηφανία. And ἀλαζονεία for Plato is a disposition to pretend to good things, whether they are one's own or not. Theophrastus called it the expectation of certain good things that do not exist, where expectation is the excitement of an opinion: a description of such a man is excellent in the fourth book to Herennius, and in the fragments of Alexis, which we have edited, and not bad ones in the Epigrams of Martial. Such was Mucianus, a showman of everything he said and did by a certain art, according to Tacitus: and most of the Romans: Foul within, beautiful in a fair skin.

ἐφευρετὰς κακῶν) Gluttony is ingenious, says Petronius: where you should also see the following. Add what is said about the inventions of luxury in houses, in clothes, in banquets, vessels, gems, pearls, tables, and beds, which are many in Seneca, Pliny, and others.

γονεῦσιν ἀπειθεῖς) When Proculeius had complained about his son, that he was waiting for his death, and he had said that he was not waiting for it, he said, "Nay, I ask that you do wait." Let us consider what Tiberius did to Livia: after this letter was written, Nero to Claudius and Agrippina.

Latin:

ἀλαζόνας) ἀλάζων est jactator, gloriator, arrogans in Glos- sario. Apud Theophrastum quoque alia est ἀλαζονείας no- tatio, alia ὑπερηφανίας Et est ἀλαζονεία Platoni ἕξις προ- σποιητικὴ ἀγαθὸ ἢ ἀγαθῶν ἢ μὴ ὑπαρχόντων. Theophr. προσ- δοκίας dixit τινῶν ἀγαθῶν ἐκ ὄντων,ubi προσδοκία est excitatio opinionis: cujusmodi hominis descriptio est egregia quar- to ad Herennium & in Alexidis fragmentis, quæ nos edidi- mus, & in Martialis Epigrammatis non malæ. Talis Mu- cianus, arte quadam omnium, quæ diceret atque ageret o- stentator, Tacito: & Romanorum plerique: Introsum turpes, speciosi pelle decora.

ἐφευρετὰς κακῶν) Ingeniosa gula est, ait Petronius: ubi & sequentia vide. Adde quæ de commentis luxuriæ in ædi- bus, in vestibus, in epulis, vasis, gemmis, unionibus, men- sis, lectis multa apud Senecam, Plinium & alios.

γονεῦσιν ἀπειθεῖς) Proculejus cum questus esset de filio, quod mortem suam expectaret, & ille dixisset, se non expe- ctare, imo inquit, rogo expectes. Cogitemus quid fecerint Tiberius in Liviam: post hanc Epistolam scriptam Nero in Claudium & Agrippinam.

## 1:31
Vers. 31. ἀσυνέτως, ἀσυνθέτες.

It may seem to be a paronomasia, but it is not. Rather, two words were made from one word written in various ways. The Syrian reads only one, ἀσυνέτους, which is the true one. It is not about the vices of the intellect here, but of the will: and indeed the greatest ones, among which is perfidy, both in public treaties and in private contracts. Almost all historians note this vice in the Romans from the times of the third Punic War. See the examples of Servilius Galba and Cn. Domitius in Valerius Maximus VI. 6. Of Firmius Latus in Tacitus' Annals II. Of P. Egnatius in the same, XVI. He places the same in the sum of the evils of the Tiberian time, treacherous friendships, Annals IV.

Grotius rashly imagines here a corruption of the text: that two words were made from one word written in various ways. For no codex can be produced in which the word ἀσυνέτες is omitted. And the Greek text is wrongly corrected from the Syrian: since the Syrian, and any other version, ought to be measured by the standard of the Greek. Although it is primarily about the vices of the will here, the Apostle nevertheless noted not only these, but also the vices of the intellect, such as that they became vain in their reasonings, which pertains to the mind, and that their mind was darkened v. 21, that they were made foolish v. 22, which is of the spirit and mind, that they changed the glory of the incorruptible God not only in worship but also in the opinion of the mind v. 23, that they changed the truth of God into a lie v. 25, that they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, and that they have a reprobate mind v. 28. & those sins of injustice, fornication, avarice, malice, enmity, deceit, and so on, are committed also by the mind and the thoughts of the intellect, not only by the affection of the will and external work. Finally, that paronomasia pleased the Holy Spirit here, ἀσυνέτως, ἀσυνθέτως, because treaty-breakers please themselves greatly with the carnal prudence of the "reason of state," as they call it today: therefore, he pronounces those who commit perfidy in public treaties or in private contracts to be not at all prudent, but ἀσυνέτως. The Vulgate wrongly rendered it "incompositos." The word ἀσυνθετεῖν denotes to act treacherously, or to violate agreed-upon pacts. Ezra X. 10.

ἀσόργες) Devoid also of natural affection. The proof of this is that they forbade children to be raised, or ordered them to be exposed, if the number seemed burdensome, and that with impunity; for that reason, the father killing his son is not included in the Pompeian law on parricides. Tertullian in his Apology: How many of you, standing around and thirsting for the blood of Christians, can I strike in their consciences, even from among those of you who are most just and most severe judges against us, who kill their own children: for even if it differs in the kind of death, you certainly extinguish the spirit more cruelly in water, or expose them to cold and hunger and dogs. Justin has similar things in his Apology; hence it is that Tacitus, in the customs of the Jews which differ from those of the Romans, places: It is a sin to kill any of the agnates, where the word agnates is to be taken in the way that in law the testament is said to be broken by the agnation of one's own heir.

ἀσπόνδες) The Old Interpreter translates, implacable, not badly: for thus a war is called ἄσπονδος, which does not accept peace. Nor did the Syrian take it otherwise here. This fits well with the Romans of those times, of whom Tacitus denies it should have been hoped that those who had disturbed peace with the love of war would lay aside war with the love of peace, Histories II. Lucan:

Each is swept away by their own causes into wicked battles: for some, a polluted house and laws to be feared in peace, for others, hunger to be fled by the sword and the ruin of the world, faith to be confounded.

ἀνελεήμονας) The Romans were indeed merciless, even toward provincials, but especially toward slaves, of whom Seneca writes in Epistle XLVII: 'It is not permitted for unhappy slaves to move their lips, not even to speak. Every murmur is checked by the rod, and not even accidental sounds are exempt from lashes—a cough, a sneeze, a hiccup; silence interrupted by any voice is paid for with great pain. They stand hungry and mute all night long.' He adds: 'We do not have them as enemies, but we make them so.' Then he admonishes the master thus: 'Do you wish to consider that this person whom you call your slave was born from the same seeds, enjoys the same sky, breathes equally, lives equally, and dies equally?'

Juvenal on the morals of women: 'Put the cross on the slave: by what crime has the slave earned punishment? Who is the witness? Who brought the charge? Listen. No delay, I say, is too long when it concerns the death of a man. O madman! Is a slave a human being? He has done nothing, let it be. Thus I will, thus I command, let my will stand in place of reason.'

And later: 'On these he breaks rods: that one blushes from the lash; this one from the whip; there are those who pay torturers by the year.'

The same regarding men: 'He preaches a gentle mind and morals fair to minor errors, and thinks that the souls and bodies of slaves consist of the same material and equal elements: but does Rutilus teach this, who delights in the harsh noise of lashes, and compares no Siren to his whips, an Antiphates or Polyphemus of a trembling household, then happy as often as someone, the torturer having been called, is burned with a glowing iron because of two napkins?'

Regarding the governors of provinces, however, the same author says: 'If you break rods in the blood of allies, if you are delighted by the dull axes with a weary lictor.'

There is a not dissimilar description of those who depart from divine laws in Philo's work on humanity: 'One can see those who have departed from the holy laws as licentious, shameless, unjust, indecent, small-minded, quarrelsome, liars to their companions and perjurers, having sold their freedom for delicacies, unmixed wine, pastries, and beauty, for the enjoyment of the belly and what comes after the belly, the ends of which are the heaviest punishments of body and soul.' See Seneca, who makes a banquet in his own age—that is, the age in which Paul lived—and reproaches the same things you have here, in De Beneficiis, books 15 and 17.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἀσυνέτως, ἀσυνθέτες.

Videri potest esse παρονομασία, at non est. Sed ex una voce variè scripta duæ factæ sunt. Syrus nonnisi unam legit, ἀσυνέτους quæ vera est. Non de intellectus, sed de voluntatis vitiis hic agitur: Et quidem maximis, inter quæ est perfidia, tum in fœderibus publicis, tum in contractibus privatis. Notant id in Romanis vitium a Punici belli tertii temporibus historici propè omnes. Vide exempla Servilii Galbæ & Cn. Domitii apud Valerium Maximum VI. 6. Firmii Læti apud Tacitum Annalium II. P. Egnatii apud eundem XVI. Idem in summa malorum Tiberiani temporis ponit fallaces amicitias Anal. IV.

Temere fingit hic Grotius corruptelam textus: ex una voce variè scripta duæ factæ esse. Nullus enim produci co- dex potest, in quo vox ἀσυνέτες omittatur. Et perperam è Syro corrigitur Græcus textus: quum ad normam Græci exigenda sit Syri, & quævis alia versio. Quamvis verò de voluntatis hic imprimis agatur vitiis, non tamen ea sola, sed etiam intellectus vitia notavit Apostolus, utpote quod vani facti sint ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς, quod ad animum pertinet, & quod mens eorum obtenebrata sit v. 21. quod ἐμωράνθησαν, stulti facti sint, quod animi & mentis est v. 22. quod immu- tarint non tantum cultu, sed & mentis opinione gloriam Dei incorruptibilis v. 23. quod immutarint veritatem Dei ἐν τῷ ψέυδει v. 25. quod ἐκ ἐδοκίμασαν τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει, & quod mentem reprobam habeant v. 28. & committuntur illa peccata injustitiæ, fornicationis, avaritiæ, malitiæ, inimi- citiæ, doli, c'attonis &c. animo quoque ac cogitationibus men- tis, non solum voluntatis affectu & opere externo. Denique Paronomasia illa placuit hic Spiritui S. ἀσυνέτως, ἀσυνθέτως, quia fædifragi maximè sibi placent prudentia carnali rationis statûs, ut hodiè vocant: hos ergò minimè prudentes esse, sed ἀσυνέτως pronunciat, qui perfidiam in fœderibus publi- cis, sive in contractibus privatis committunt. Vulgatus incompositos malè reddidit. Verbum ἀσυνθετεῖν notat præ- varicari, seu pacta conventa violare. Esdr. X. 10.

ἀσόργες) Expertes etiam naturalis affectus. Ejus argu- mentum quod liberos, si numerus gravis videretur, aut tolli vetabant, aut jubebant exponi, idque impune; nam & id- eò in lege Pompeja de parricidis pater filium enecans non comprehenditur. Tertullianus Apologetico: Quot vultis in his circumstantibus, & in Christianorum sanguinem bianth bus ex ipsis etiam nobis justissimis, & severissimis in nos præsidi- bus apud conscientias pulsem, qui natos sibi liberos enecent: fi- quidem & de genere necis differt, utique crudelius in aqua Spi- ritum extorquetis,aut frigori & fami & canibus exponitis. Pa- ria habet Justinus in Apologetico; hinc est, quod Tacitus in Judæorum institutis à Romanorum discrepantibus ponit: Necare quemquam ex agnatis, nefas, ubi vox agnatis ita su- menda, quomodo in jure agnatione sui hæredis testamen- tum rumpi dicitur.

ἀσπόνδες) Vetus Interpres vertit,implacabiles, non male: nam sic ἄσπονδος πόλεμος dicitur, qui pacem non recipit, Nec aliter hic accepit Syrus. Bene convenit hoc in illorum temporum Romanos, de quibus Tacitus negat sperandum fuisse, ut qui pacem belli amore turbaverant, bellum pacis charitate deponerent, Historiarum II. Lucanus:

Quemque sua rapiunt scelerata in prælia causæ: Hos polluta domus legesque in pace timendæ, Hos ferro fugienda fames mundique ruina Permiscenda fides.

ἀνελεήμονας) immisericordes sane Romani, etiam in provinciales, at maxime in servos, de quibus Seneca Epi- stol. XLVII. Infelicibus servis movere labra, ne in hoc qui- dem, ut loquantur, licet. Virgâ murmur omne compefcitur, & ne fortuita quidem verberibus excepta sunt, tussis, sternuta- mentum, singultus, magno malo ulla voce interpellatum silen- tium luitur. Nocte tota jejuni mutique perstant. Addit: Non habemus illos hostes sed facimus. Deinde Dominum sic admonet: Vis tu cogitare istum quem servum tuum vocas ex iisdem seminibus ortum, eodem frui cœlo, æquè spirare, æquè vivere, æquè mori?

Juvenalis de fœminarum moribus: Pone crucem servo: meruit quo crimine servus Supplicium? quis testis? quis detulit? audi. Nulla, inquam, de morte hominis cunctatio longa est: O demens! ita servus homo est? nil fecerit, esto. Sic volo, sic jubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas.

Et postea: His frangit ferulas: rubet ista flagello; Hic scuticâ, sunt quæ tortoribus annua præstant.

De viris idem: Mitem animum & mores modicis erroribus æquos Præcipit, atque animas servorum & corpora nostra Materia constare putat paribusque elementis: An sabire docet Rutilus, qui gaudet acerbo Plagarum strepitu, & nullam Sirena flagellis Comparat, Antiphates trepidi laris aut Polyphemus, Tum felix quoties aliquis tortore vocato Uritur ardenti duo propter lintea ferro.

De provinciarum autem præsidibus hoc ejusdem: Si frangis virgas sociorum in sanguine, si te Delectant hebetes lasso lictore secures.

Est descriptio non dissimilis eorum, qui a divinis legibus desciscunt apud Philonem de humanitate: Τοὺς τῶν ἱερῶν νό- μων ἀποστάντας ἰδεῖν ἐστι ἀκολάστους, ἀναισχύντους, ἀδίκους, ἀσύ- μνους, ὀλιγοφρονας, φιλαπεχθήμονας, ψευδολόγους ἑταίροις καὶ ψευδορκίας, τὴν ἐλευθερίαν πεπρακότας ὀψῶν καὶ ἀκράτου, καὶ πεμμάτων, καὶ εὐμορφίας, εἰς τὰ τῆς γαστρὸς ἀπολαυσιν καὶ τῶν μετὰ γαστέρα, ὧν τὰ τέλη βαρύτατα ζημία σώματός τε καὶ ψυχῆς εἰσιν. Senecam suo, id est, ei quo Paulus vixit seculo convivium facientem & eadem quæ hic habes exprobran- tem vide XV, de beneficiis 15. & 17.

## 1:32
Verse 32. οἵτινες τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπιγνόντες. Having now completed that proof that the revelation of truth is violated by the human race, the Apostle now confirms the consequence of his inference, namely, that such people are subject to the wrath of God and to death, because this law of God is known to all by nature, that those who commit such things do not glorify GOD as GOD, they transmute the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of a corruptible creature, they pollute themselves with filthy lusts and injustice and other sins; in short, ALL those who in any way unjustly hold back the truth are worthy of death. Some, however, not only commit these things but also take pleasure in them: but those who do not take pleasure in the crimes of others, but point them out and condemn them, yet do the very things they condemn in others: and therefore they condemn themselves by their own judgment.

Verse same. τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. משפט אל as often in Ezekiel and others. This genitive signifies the efficient cause. For it is understood here as the law inscribed in human minds partly by reason and partly by tradition, that those who commit grave offenses are rightly punished; which we treated in Book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter XX. The Greeks also call the law of nature νόμον θεῖον.

Δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ here denotes the vindictive justice of God, by the power of which GOD punishes sins, which law is inscribed in human minds not by tradition (for things learned by tradition are never said to be inscribed on hearts) but τῇ Φύσει: because this law of God pertains to the natural knowledge of God: and finally, conscience dictates that punishment follows guilt, and that those who commit such crimes are worthy of death, from which we learn both that death is the punishment of sinners properly so called, and that Scripture attributes the vengeance of sins to the justice of God, not only to divine wrath: both of which we asserted against Socinus in Orac. XIV. Grotius understands this as bodily death and refers it to certain specific crimes, which the consensus of men testifies to be worthy of death; such as homicides, adulteries, and other foul lusts. But these words do not look only to certain crimes, which he has listed, but he pronounces concerning all those which the Apostle has brought forward in this catalog, that those who do τὰ τοιαῦτα, such things, are worthy of death. By which sentence he made all those transgressors whom he enumerated in a long series, as well as those who are subject to similar crimes, guilty. Therefore, he pronounces not only murderers and those defiled by foul lusts that deserve death, but also other transgressors of the law who unjustly hold back the truth, idolaters, those who do τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα, who are filled with all injustice, fornication, malice, avarice, wickedness, envy, contention, deceit, malignity, thieves, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, proud, boasters, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, without natural affection, implacable, merciless; these, I say, and all those similar to them, he pronounces worthy of death: which must therefore necessarily be understood of eternal death: as in Romans 6, the end, the wages of sin is called eternal death. For those who separate themselves from God through sin, and remain separated (not being converted to God), are worthy to be separated eternally from God, with the very law of nature dictating it, and conscience as judge. Conf. chap. II. 13.

that those who do such things are worthy of death) there are certain crimes which the consensus of men testifies to deserve death Acts XIII 28. XXIII. 29. XXV. 11. 25. XXVI. 31. XXVIII. 18. Such are homicides, adulteries, and other foul lusts, to which these words refer:

not only do them. They do this themselves, now this, now that, where the opportunity is given, but also consent to those who do them. This is worse than that, for someone led away by emotion sins who would not have sinned without it. But those who defend such things and teach that they are free from vice, truly sin more gravely. These are the סערים among the Chaldean Paraphrast Lev. XX. 5. concerning whom the Rabbis say that it is also treated in Levit. XXVI. 21. The word συνευδοκεῖν is also in the Maccabees and in Luke 11. 48. Acts VIII. 11. and XXII. 20. and in Clement in his Epistle. You praise those who act with you, Chrysostom says in this place, and after him others: Theophylact said to advocate. The Apostle touches here especially upon the philosophers, who were teachers of the peoples, and to whom therefore it ought to be imputed if the people sinned while they approved. For example, they taught that pederasty and any kind of incest were indifferent, not only the Epicureans, but also those severe Stoics, which not only Theophilus of Antioch teaches us, but also Sextus Empiricus, using the words of Zeno and Chrysippus, which one is ashamed to transcribe. Thus Aristotle and Cicero approve of the desire for revenge in the places we cited in the annotations II. for the Christian Religion. The same Aristotle wishes war against barbarians to be a certain kind of hunting, and therefore a thing just by nature: Politics I. 8. The same wishes it to be permitted to abort a fetus, as long as what is conceived does not yet have life, Polit. VII. 16. But all those philosophers who said that nothing is by nature dishonest, but that these things differ by human institutions, defend all crimes in summary. And as Justin explains their opinion, that there is no virtue, no vice, but that men by opinion alone consider these things either good or evil, which is the greatest impiety and injustice. Hence that is taken: for by law we consider the gods, and we live having defined what is unjust and what is just.

Likewise: What is shameful, if it does not seem so to those who practice it? See what we have brought forward concerning the Epicureans in book II. of the Law of War and Peace XX. 44. Appositely to that which is said here, Philo in his book on special laws: for not only those who do them are impious, but also as many as grant authority to those who do them with willing mind in the things being done (so it must be read, not with those who do them) Epist. XXI. For he is not immune from wickedness who ordered that it be done: Nor is he a stranger to the crime, whose consent, although the crime was not committed by himself, is yet publicly read. Sylvius book IV. For while spectators approve of these things and see them willingly, all perform them by sight and assent. Tacitus. It is called corrupting and being corrupted by the age.

The Vulgate rendered a far different sense in this verse: Who when they had known the justice of God, did not understand, that they who do such things are worthy of death, not only they who do them, but also they who consent to those who do them. That phrase DID NOT UNDERSTAND is added contradictorily. For if they knew this, how did they not understand? Or is there knowledge without understanding? Nor in the source, which Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact follow, is it said that those who consent are also worthy of death, but that the Gentiles not only do such things, but also consent to those who do them; where Bellarmine, in Book II of the Word of God, chapter XIII, urges in vain for the Vulgate, that it is worse to act evilly than to consent to those who act evilly. Because it is not a matter of simple consent here, but of those who συνευδοκῆσι τῷ κακῷ [consent to the evil]. Which is an incurable disease, as Theophylact says, and Erasmus acknowledges that this is graver than if you yourself fall, because the latter is often either a matter of chance or infirmity: The former is a matter of most pestilential flattery or most depraved malice. It was the duty of wise men to restrain the unlearned common people from these vices. But they not only did not do that, but also confirmed the madness of the people by their own authority: And Erasmus thinks that this opinion is proven by the very tenor of the discourse, because in chapter II, verse 1, it is added, therefore you are inexcusable, etc. Grotius also deserts the Vulgate here and defends the Greek text: that τὸ συνευδοκεῖν [consenting] is worse than the former: because one carried away by affection sins, who would often not sin without it. But those who defend such things and teach that they are free from vice, certainly sin more gravely. Cornelius à Lapide also agrees: This consenting is greater and worse than doing. For it arises from malice, whereas doing often proceeds from mere infirmity.

Latin:

Vers. 32. οἵτινες τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπιγνόντες. Absolutâ nunc illâ probatione, quod patefactio veritatis ab humano genere violetur, jam confir- mat Apostolus consequentiam suæ illationis, quod nempe tales iræ Dei & morti obnoxii sint, quia sc. hoc Dei jus notum omnibus naturâ est, quod qui ta- lia patrant, DEUM non ut DEUM glorificant, gloriam Dei incorruptibilis in imaginem corruptibi- lis creaturæ transmutant, libidinibus spurcis & in- justitiæ, aliisque peccatis se polluunt; breviter, OMNES illi, qui quacunque ratione veritatem in- justè detinent, morte digni sint. Aliqui tamen ea non modo patrent, sed etiam iisdem condelectentur: qui verò aliorum sceleribus non delectentur, sed ea indi- cent & damnent, ipsi tamen ea faciant, quæ in aliis damnant: ideoque suopte judicio se condemnent.

Vers. Eodem τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. משפט אל ut sæpe apud Ezechielem & alios. Genitivus hic causam efficientem significat. Intelli- gitur enim hic jus partim per rationem partim per traditionem inscriptum humanis mentibus, rectè pu- niri qui gravia delinquunt; quod tractavimus li- bro II. de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. XX. Etiam Græ- ci jus naturæ vocant νόμον θεῖον.

Δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ hic justitiam Dei notat vindi- catricem, vi cujus DEUS peccata punit, quod jus humanis mentibus inscriptum non per traditionem, (quæ enim per traditionem addiscuntur, inscripta cordibus nuspiam dicuntur) sed τῇ Φύσει: quia ad notitiam Dei naturalem hoc jus Dei pertinet: & conscientia denique dictitat culpam sequi pœnam, & dignos esse morte, qui ejusmodi crimina pa- trant, unde discimus & quod mors peccatorum pœ- na sit propriè dicta, & quod justitiæ Dei tribuat scri- ptura peccatorum vindictam non tantum ire divi- næ: quod utrumque adversus Socinum asseruimus Orac. XIV. Grotius de morte corporali intelligit, & ad certa quædam crimina refert: quæ mortem me- reri, consensus hominum testetur; ut sunt homici- dia, adulteria, & aliæ fœdæ libidines. At verba hæc respiciunt non quædam tantum, quæ recen- fuit, crimina, sed de omnibus, quæ adduxit Aposto- lus in hoc Catalogo pronunciat, quod qui τὰ τοι- αῦτα talia faciunt, morte digni sunt. Quâ sententiâ tum omnes illos prævaricatores fecit, quos longâ serie enumeravit, tum qui similibus criminibus obnoxii sunt. Non ergo tantum homicidas, & fœ- dis libidinibus, quæ mortem merentur, inquina- tos, sed etiam alios legis transgressores, qui veri- tatem injustè detinent, idolatras, qui faciunt τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα, impleti sunt omni injustitia, fornicatio- ne, malitia, avaritia, nequitia, invidia, contentione, dolo, malignitate, latrones, detractores, Dei osores, contumeliosos, superbos, jactabundos, inventores ma- lorum, parentibus non obedientes, insipientes, perfi- dos, naturalis affectus expertes, implacabiles, immi- sericordes; hos, inquam, omnes, iisq; similes morte dignos pronunciat: quod proinde de morte æterna intelligendum necessariò: uti Rom. VI. ult. sti- pendium peccati mors æterna dicitur. Qui enim à Deo sese per peccatú separant, & separati manent, (non convertuntur ad Deum) digni sunt, qui æter- num à Deo separentur, ipsâ etiam naturæ lege di- ctante, ac conscientiâ judice. Conf. cap. II. 13.

ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες ἄξιοι θανάτου εἰσὶ) sunt quæ- dam crimina, quæ mortem mereri consensus hominum te- statur Actor. XIII 28. XXIII. 29. XXV. 11. 25. XXVI. 31. XXVIII. 18. Talia sunt homicidia, adulteria & aliæ fœdæ libidines, ad quas hæc verba respiciunt:

οὐ μόνον ἀυτὰ ποιοῦσι. Faciunt ipsi modo hoc, modo illud, ubi datur occasio, ἀλλὰ καὶ συνευδοκοῦσι τοῖς πράσουσι. Hoc pejus illo, nam affectu abreptus peccat aliquis sine eo non peccaturus. At qui defendunt talia & docent vitio carere, sanè gravius delinquunt. Hi sunt סערים apud Pa- raphrasten Chaldæum Lev. XX. 5. de quibus agi etiam Le- vit. XXVI. 21. ajunt Rabbini. Verbum συνευδοκεῖν est etiam in Maccabæis & apud Luc. 11. 48. Act. VIII. 11. & XXII. 20. & apud Clementem in Epistola. ξυμπράττοις ἐπαινεῖς, hoc loco Chrysostomus, & post eum alii: Theophylactus dixit συνηγορεῖν. Philosophos hic maxime tangit Apostolus, qui erant Doctores populorum, & quibus proinde imputari de- bebat, si qua populus ipsis probantibus peccaret. Exempli causâ παιδεραστίαν & quosvis incestus esse ἀδιάφορα doce- bant non Epicurei tantum, sed & severi illi Stoici, quod non Theophilus tantùm Antiochenus nos docet, sed & Sextus Empiricus Zenonis & Chrysippi utens verbis, quæ pudet transcribere. Sic ultionis cupiditatem probant Aristoteles & Cicero locis, quos citavimus in annotatis II. pro Reli- gione Christianâ. Idem Aristoteles bellum in barbaros vult esse venatus quoddam genus, ac proinde rem naturâ justam: Politicorum I. 8. Idem abigere partum vult licere, quamdiu quod conceptum est, vitam nondum habet, Polit. VII. 16. Omnia autem facinora summatim defendunt illi Philoso- phorum, qui dixere nihil natura esse inhonestum, sed dif- ferre ista hominum institutis. Et ut Justinus eorum sen- tentiam explicat, μηδὲν εἶναι ἀρετὴν, μηδὲ κακίαν, δόξῃ δὲ μόνον τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἢ ἀγαθὰ ἢ κακὰ ταῦτα ἡγεῖσθαι, ὅπερ με- γίστη ἀσέβεια καὶ ἀδικία ἐσὶ. Hinc illud desumptum: νόμῳ γὰρ τοὺς θεοὺς ἡγούμεθα, Καὶ ζῶμεν ἄδικα καὶ δίκαι' ὡρισμένοι.

Item: Τί αἰσχρὸν, ἐν μὴ τοῖσι χρωμένοις δοκῇ; Vide quæ de Epicureis attulimus lib. II. de Jure Belli & Pacis XX. 44. Apposite ad id quod hic dicitur, Philo libro de legibus specialibus : ἀσεβέσι γὰρ οὐχ οἱ δρῶντες μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅσοι τοῖς δρῶσιν ἑκουσίῳ γνώμῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ δρωμένοις (ita legen- dum, non σὺν τῷ δρῶσιν) ἐξουσία ἐπιγράφουσιν Epist. XXI. Non est enim immunis à scelere, qui ut fieret imperavit : Nec est alienus à crimine, cujus consensu licet non à se admissum cri- men tamen publicè legitur. Sylvius lib. IV. Nam dum spectan- tes hæc comprobant ac libenter vident, omnes ea visu atque as- sensu agunt. Tacit. Corrumpere & corrumpi seculum vocatur.

Vulgata longe alium sensum reddidit hoc com- mate: Qui cùm justitiam Dei cognovissent, non in- tellexerunt, quoniam qui talia agunt digni sunt morte, non solum qui ea faciunt, sed etiam, qui con- sentient facientibus. Illud NON INTELLEXE- RUNT contradictorie additur. Si enim hoc cognoverunt, quomodo non intellexerunt? An- ne est cognitio sine intelligentia? Nec in fonte, quem sequuntur Chrysost. Oecum. Theophyl. dici- tur consentientes etiam morte dignos esse, sed non fa- cere modò talia Gentiles, verum etiam consentire facientibus; ubi nequicquam Bellarminus lib. II. de Verb. Dei cap. XIII. pro vulgata urget, quod pejus sit malè agere, quam consentire malè agentibus. Quia non de simplici consensu hic agitur, sed qui συνευδοκῆσι τῷ κακῷ. Qui morbus est immedica- bilis, dicente Theophyl. idque gravius esse, quam si ipse labaris, agnoscit Erasmus, propterea quod hoc sæpenumerò vel casus est vel infirmitatis: Illud vel pestilentissimæ adulationis, vel depravatissimæ ma- litiæ. Sapientum erat indoctam plebem ab his vitiis prohibere. At isti non solum id non fecerunt, sed etiam autoritate sua confirmarunt populi insaniam: Eamque sententiam ab ipso sermonis tenore, quod cap. II. 1. addatur, propterea inexcusabilis es, &c. probari censet Erasmus. Deserit etiam hic Gro- tius vulgatam, & textum Græcum tuetur: τὸ συν- ευδοκεῖν pejus esse priori: quia affectu abreptus pec- cat sæpe sine eo non peccaturus. At qui defendunt ta- lia, & docent vitio carere, sanè gravius delinquunt. Annuit quoque Cornel. à Lapide: Hoc consentire majus, & pejus est, quàm facere. Fit enim ex mali- tia, cùm facere sæpè ex mera infirmitate promanet.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT.

He teaches that all men, inasmuch as they judge others regarding their own guilt, are convicted by their own conscience that they are guilty in the judgment of God, and he confirms this specifically by the example of the Jews, whom he equates with the Gentiles before the tribunal of God.

DIVISION.

There are three parts: I. The common conviction of men, when they judge others regarding their own guilt, primarily from the law of nature, from verse 1 to 16. II. The special confusion of the Jews from the written law, from verse 17 to 26. III. The equal status of both Jews and Gentiles before God, from verse 26 to the last verse, 29.

PART I. THE COMMON CONVICTION OF MEN as self-condemned.

Verse 1. Therefore.

That is, since the matter stands as we have already said, so that that law, which is common to all men, dictates that there are certain crimes worthy of death. These ought to have been connected with the preceding chapter: But a new one should be begun there, tribulation and anguish.
