you are inexcusable.

See above 1. 20.

O man, everyone who judges.

From philosophers, one comes to the magistrates, who are called in Hebrew השופטים, οἱ κρίνοντες, οἱ κριταὶ. Under the name of magistrates, however, masters must also be included, who held domestic jurisdiction over their servants. He added this aptly, however, while writing to the Romans, from whom all the governors of the provinces also came.

You, O Roman, remember to rule the peoples with power. This is rightly connected with the preceding: since the matter stands thus, that the common law dictates to all men that those who commit such things are worthy of death; but it is not to be restricted to certain crimes only: for the Apostle embraces universally all who unjustly hold back the revealed truth: such as all men are by nature: their own conscience convincing them all: Nor are these things conveniently connected with the preceding chapter, unless the whole of the second chapter is glued to the first. For thus all things cohere in the same way, so that they can nowhere be torn away from the preceding: the ninth and tenth verses certainly explain the preceding ones, the seventh and eighth, in such a way that they cannot be conveniently separated. And since the last verse of chapter I coheres likewise with the penultimate, no beginning of a new chapter could be feigned more conveniently than from this inference, διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ. The Apostle had indeed convinced all that they were ἀναπολογήτους, in Chapter I; now, so that the mouth of all may be stopped more fully, as he hints in Chapter III. 19, he proceeds in convincing the human race, διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ ὦ ἄνθρωπε, calling man, whoever he may be, commonly and indefinitely, since no one is found who does not judge another at some time, as we are by nature blind in our own affairs, but lynx-eyed in the affairs of others. And therefore he now makes all ἀύτοκατακρίτους. For the argument is firm: he who judges another in those things which he himself commits, he condemns himself by his own judgment, and is truly ἀναπολόγητος. And so that the Apostle may teach more clearly that he is gathering this from the δικαιώματι, the right and justice of God known to all, he repeats and confirms what he had said about the right of God: We know indeed that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. Unless you would rather say that he composes his judgment with the right and justice of God, which is evident to all by nature, which will certainly follow, which everyone knows will be κατ' ἀλήθειαν, according to truth, upon those who do such things. The Apostle therefore shows that the judgment of God is prepared for those who judge others who act wickedly, and are themselves subject to the same sins which they condemn, refuting to that end the objection or exception concerning divine long-suffering and tolerance, which men interpret as if God despises human sins and wishes to leave them unpunished. Do you gather this, O man, who judge those who do such things, and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Is it not an absurd opinion to think that others are deservedly subject to human judgments, but that you, who are bound by the same vices, will escape the judgment of the most just Judge, God himself? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, and tolerance, and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God wishes to lead you to repentance? Know that you are invited by it to a change of mind. But if you harden yourself and, having spurned your conscience, become accustomed to committing crimes, you are heaping up for yourself treasures of punishments to be brought forth on the day of judgment. Therefore, these things cannot be restricted to the Jews, as Salmeron, Estius, à Lapide, and Hemmingius, to whom Calixtus is added, suggest; but they strike all men whatsoever, which is proven both by the συνέχεια with the preceding chapter, and the general appellation, O man, as well as the distribution of the human race into Jews and Gentiles, and the force of the whole demonstration and the genuine method of the Apostolic analysis.

Also vain is the gloss of Grotius, that the Apostle descends from philosophers to the magistrate, who are called according to the Hebrew style οἱ κρίνοντες, or οἱ κριταὶ, as is that of Cajetan, who explained it as concerning only those established in judgment, along with Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. For he had not dealt with philosophers alone before, nor does he address magistrates here, but indiscriminately any men whatsoever, who do themselves what they condemn in others. Nor are these things to be restricted only to hypocrites with Calvin and Bucer: but they are to be taken generally with Cyprian, book III to Quirinus, Origen, Augustine, Chrysostom, and Basil, as Toletus, Stapleton, Pererius, Maldonatus, and Justin acknowledge, and Martyr, Musculus, and Pareus affirm.

I fear Julia, when she ordered poison to be cooked. Sueton. XXXIV. Unchaste Vestal Virgins were buried alive: Nero committed violence against one of them, Sueton. 28. He who had abducted a free-born boy was punished with death, L. & eam D. ad L. Juliam de vi publica. For the Emperors this was a daily occurrence. See Suetonius, Nero 28. This license of the Emperors was imitated by governors in the provinces. If a slave had debauched a free-born boy, he did not escape the cross: this was permitted to masters over their slaves, and such boys were called 'delicate'. Cyprian: 'He who sits to judge crimes, commits them': But you may rightly extend this of Paul to private judgments about others. Thus David condemned himself before Nathan. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'For it is possible to see even those who do not wish to suffer the same things which they themselves inflict upon others, and in their consciences, as enemies, reproaching one another for the very things they do.' Salvian, book 1, on the Government of God: For in others they shudder at what they admit in themselves, in a wonderful way both accusers of the same crimes and sinners. They publicly execrate what they do in secret, and by this, while they think they are condemning others, they condemn themselves all the more by their own judgment. And afterwards: 'We are most severe to others, most indulgent to ourselves; austere to others, lax to ourselves. In the same crime we punish others, we absolve ourselves. It is truly an intolerable stubbornness and presumption, that we are unwilling to acknowledge guilt in ourselves, and yet dare to usurp judgment over others.' Chrysostom on sin and confession: 'But most men become advocates for their own sins, and accusers of the sins of others.' Nor did the wiser of the Romans fail to see this. Cicero, Verrine V: 'Everything for which you judge another, you must avoid yourself.' For not only the accuser, but not even the reprover is to be endured, who, while he criticizes a vice in another, is criticized for the same in himself. Horace, book 1, Sat. 3: 'I myself forgive myself, Maenius,' he says. 'This man is foolish and wicked and deserves to be marked.' Seneca on anger, book 1, 14: 'Let him consider how many things he does against good custom, how many of the things he has done require pardon, and he will soon be angry even with himself. For a just judge should not hold one opinion for his own case and another for someone else's.' Book II, 28: 'He who covets everyone's wife, and thinks there is a sufficiently just cause for loving because she belongs to another, does not want his own wife to be looked at, and is a most bitter exactor of fidelity while being perfidious himself, and pursues liars while being a perjurer himself, and as a calumniator bears it very badly if a lawsuit is brought against him; he does not want the chastity of his own little slaves to be tempted, he who did not spare his own. We have the vices of others before our eyes, our own are behind our backs.' Hence it is that a father, worse than his son, punishes his son's untimely banquets. He forgives nothing of another's injury who has denied nothing of his own: and the tyrant is angry at the murderer, and the sacrilegious man punishes thefts. A great part of mankind is that which is not angry at sins, but at sinners. Epist. XCIV: 'You know he is wicked who demands chastity from his wife, while he himself is a corrupter of the wives of others. You know that just as he has nothing to do with an adulterer, so you should have nothing to do with a mistress: And you do not do it.' IIX. Epist. 22: 'Do you know those who, slaves to all lusts, are so angry at the vices of others as if they envied them, and punish most severely what they most imitate?' Add what we have brought forward on this subject, not irrelevant, both in the prolegomena to Stobaeus, and to Matt. VII. 3, and book II of the Law of War and Peace XX. 3.

ἐν ᾧ is not here 'THEREFORE', or 'causal': but rather 'demonstrative', 'in that in which you judge another, you condemn yourself.' Grotius interprets this rashly regarding the Roman Emperors; the continuity and force of the Apostolic treatment convince that it must be taken of all. They can be alleged as an example; but it was not said peculiarly to them, nor about them. And Grotius is forced to admit that these things pertain also to private judgments about others. But that it should be extended only so far, and that it should not be conceded that it is Paul's proper and direct intention to argue against anyone generally, is not to be granted. That such is the character of men, the testimonies both of the Fathers and of the Gentiles, which Grotius himself collects, confirm: such as the saying of Chrysostom on sin and confession: 'But most men become advocates for their own sins, and accusers of the sins of others': And also that of Salvian, book 1, on the Government of God: It is truly an intolerable stubbornness and presumption, that we are unwilling to acknowledge guilt in ourselves, and yet dare to usurp judgment over others. Finally, that of Seneca on Anger, book 1, chapter 14: 'We have the vices of others before our eyes, our own are behind our backs.' For the Grotian point here regarding the just judgment of God, the ὁμοψηφία (unanimous vote), is to be well noted, that it is known to us by nature, as verse 2, reason itself teaches us this. And further: this knowledge of the incorrupt judgment of God sleeps in many, but is accustomed to be awakened around the time of death, as Plato observes in Republic 1. Cicero, book on Divination: 'Those who have lived otherwise than they ought, are then most especially penitent for their sins.' To which, indeed, Grotius himself confessed that the judgment of God, which is according to truth, was known to the Gentiles themselves by the guidance of reason against sins, and indeed that the final judgment was not unknown to them: And certainly, he says, the deduction was not so difficult, since God is just, but the wicked are often most happy in this life, that another judgment is to be expected. Beza and Piscator take the participle ἀγνοῶν outside of a question, as if the ignorance of a better cause were constituted as hardening. Which is repugnant to the whole treatment of the Apostle, who teaches that they both 'know' (ἐπιγνόντας) that they sin and judge others in what they sin, and despise the long-suffering of God, and by their own 'hardness of heart' (σκληροκαρδίᾳ) treasure up for themselves the wrath of God, and thus, knowing and prudent, become the cause of their own hardening and impenitence: when they could and ought to have known and understood that they were being led to repentance by the long-suffering of God. For every cause here is cast upon the voluntary hardness of man, not natural ignorance. Which is also to be noted against Cajetan, Faber Stapulensis, Estius, and Tirinus. And we have here in agreement Justinian and à Lapide, who [explain] that 'do you not know?' they interpret it reproachfully, certainly you could not, nor ought you to have been ignorant that such great kindness of God leads you to repentance. Τὸ γὰρ ἀυτὰ πράσσεις ὁ κρίνων) he says this also not to all, but to most. Vers. 2. οἴδαμεν δὲ) Reason itself teaches us this. Ὅτι τὸ κρῖμα τῦ Θεῦ ἐστι κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν ἐπὶ τὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντας) this follows from the very name of God. For we cannot conceive of God without justice. Εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν, ὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί. ἀλήθεια in this place is just judgment, giving nothing to favor or hatred, as below III. 7. 1. Cor. XIII. 6. The Hebrew אמונה is sometimes translated ἀλήθεια, sometimes δικαιοσύνη, often with the same meaning. This is opposed, as Chrysostom notes, to the judgments of the Romans, which were most corrupt. See concerning the Clodian judges Seneca, Epistle XCVI, where many things are excellently said, but this one in particular: When adultery was being committed for the sake of judging the accused. This knowledge concerning the incorrupt judgment of God sleeps in many, but is accustomed to be awakened around the time of death, as Plato observes in Republic 1. Cicero in his book on divination: Those who have lived otherwise than they ought, then especially repent of their sins. Nor indeed was the inference so difficult, since God is just, but the wicked are often most happy in this life, that another judgment is to be expected. Vers. 3. λογίζη δὲ τῦτο ὦ ἄνθρωπε) Do you think? Can you bring this into your mind? The Apostle does not address, as already warned, the Magistrates who judged according to the laws among the Romans, but any men indiscriminately. Ὁ κρίνων τὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντας) who judge those doing such things according to the laws, approved not only by the Romans, but by the consensus of all nations. Καὶ ποιῶν αὐτά) while you do the same things. Ὅτι σὺ ἐκφύξῃ τὸ κρῖμα τῦ Θεῦ) Diphilus speaks thus: Do you think, Nikeratos, that those who have died, having partaken of every luxury in life, have escaped the divine? Nor does that saying of Sophocles go far from this: A mortal must not overleap the blow. You have more in that sense in Stobaeus under the title of natural things, 7. Men escape crimes in three ways: because they are either unknown, or because no one is so powerful as to punish them, or because the law is broken through favor or price. None of these fall upon God; He knows all things, He can do what He wills, He judges from what is right. See Job XXXIV. 22. Vers. 4. ἢ τῦ πλέτε τῆς χρηστότητος αὐτῦ) רוב חסדך as Psalm V. 8. CVI. 7. רוב רחמיך LXIX. 17. Thus πλῦτος χάριτος is said in Ephes. I. 7. πλῦτος δόξης below IX. 23. Eph. I. 18. III. 16. Col. I. 27. πλῦτος in a similar sense as Simplicius uses it in his commentary on Epictetus. Philo said in the Allegories: ὑπερβολὴν τῶ πλύτου τῆς ἀγαθότητος Θεῦ. In a not dissimilar way, we have the word πλύτε below at IX. 23 and XI. 33.

With excellent words the Apostle celebrates the divine kindness: which exerts itself primarily in the bearing of any evils whatsoever: depicting not only χρησότητα, which is the sweetness of goodness and kindness, but the πλῦτον, the immense riches of such kindness, and not only the treasures of kindness, but also of grace and tolerance, and indeed of the highest μακροθυμίας and long-suffering. Here πλῦτος denotes a huge supply and abundance: and the πλῦτος τῆς χάριτος is proclaimed in Eph. I. 7, [and] the ὑπερβάλλων πλῦτος τῆς χάριτος in Eph. II. 7. χρησότης in general denotes a kindness that is convenient or useful to others, and pleasant and auspicious: The Syriac rendered it בסימות, sweetness, pleasant indulgence. The Hebrew טוב corresponds to it in Psalm XXVI. 5, Ps. XXXIV. 9, Ps. C. 5, Ps. CXLV. 7. Ἀνοχὴ, from ἀνέχειν, to sustain, expresses the patience by which He sustains us: Grotius explains it as a relaxation, a truce, from the Glossary. But Suidas distinguishes ἀνοχὴν, which he explains as ὑπομονὴν, patience, tolerance, and ἀνακωχὴν, by which he denotes a suspension of arms, a cessation of war, and a truce. Μακρόθυμος is said as if it were μακρύνων τὸν θυμὸν, delaying anger so that He does not punish immediately.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM.

HOmines universos utpote alios judicantes de propria culpa, quod rei sint in judicio Dei, suapte conscientia docet convinci, & spe- ciatim id Judæorum exemplo confirmat, quos gentibus coram Dei tribunali æquat.

PARTITIO.

Partes tres sunt: I. Communis hominum, cum alios judicant de reatu proprio, è lege imprimis na- turæ convictio à v. 1. ad 16. II. Specialis Judæorum è lege scripta confusio. à v. 17. ad 26. III. Utrorum- que Judæorum & gentilium coram Deo æqualis ratio, à v. 26. ad ultimum v. 29.

PARS I. COMMUNIS HOMINUM ceu ἀυτοκατακρίτων convictio.

Vers. 1. Διὸ.

Id est, cum ita se res habeat sicut jam diximus, ut jus il- lud, quod omnibus hominibus commune est, dictet esse quædam crimina morte digna. Debuerunt hæc connecti cum præcedente capite: Novum autem inchoari ibi, θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία.

ἀναπολόγητος εἶ.

Vide supra 1. 20.

ὦ ἄνθρωπε πᾶς ὁ κρίνων.

A Philosophis venitur ad Magistratus qui Hebræis השופטים οἱ κρίνοντες οἱ κριταὶ Sub Magistratuum au- tem nomine etiam Domini comprehendi debent, qui in ser- vos domesticam habebant jurisdictionem. Appositè au- tem hoc addidit ad Romanos scribens, ex quibus erant o- mnes etiam provinciarum rectores.

Tu regere imperio populos Romane memento. Rectè hoc cum superioribus connectitur: cum ita se res habeat, ut jus commune omnibus homini- bus dictet, morte dignos esse, qui talia patrant; sed non restringendum ad quædam tantum crimina: Nam Apostolus universim complectitur omnes, qui veritatem revelatam injustè detinent: Quales omnes homines sunt per naturam: Convincente omnes propria ipsorummet conscientia: Neque commodè hæc connectuntur cum præcedente ca- pite, nisi totum caput secundum primo congluti- netur. Ita enim in eodem cohærent omnia, ut divelli à præcedentibus nuspiam possint: comma certè nonum & decimum sic explicat præcedentia, septimum & octavum, ut commodè sequestrari nequeant. Et quum cap. I. v. ultimus cum penul- timo itidem cohæreat, nullum convenientius singi potuit initium capitis novi, quam ab hac illatione διό ἀναπολόγητος εἶ. Nimirum Apostolus omnes esse ἀναπολογήτυς convicerat, Cap. I. jam ut omnium os obstruatur plenius, uti Cap. III. 19. in- nuit, pergit in convincendo humano genere, διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ ὦ ἄνθρωπε, communiter & indesi- nitè hominem, quisquis fuerit, appellans, siquidem nemo reperiatur, qui non alium quandoque judi- cat, ut sumus naturâ in propriis cæci, in alie- nis lyncei. Ideoque omnes jam facit ἀύτοκατα- κρίτυς. Argumentum enim firmum est, qui alium in his judicat, quæ ipse patrat, ille seipsum proprio judicio condemnat, & vere est ἀναπολόγητος. Atque ut hoc ἐ δικαιώματι, jure & justitia Dei omnibus notâ se colligere doceat luculentius Apo- stolus, repetit & confirmat, quod de jure Dei dixe- rat: Scimus vero quod judicium Dei est secundum veritatem in eos, qui talia agunt. Nisi malis dice- re, quod cum jure & justitia Dei, quæ omnibus na- tura constat judicium ejus componat, quod certo sequuturum est, quod nemo non scit κατ' ἀλήθειαν secundum veritatem futurum super eos, qui talia fa- ciunt. Ostendit ergo Apostolus, paratum esse ju- dicium Dei illis, qui alios malè agentes judicant, & ipsimet iisdem, quæ damnant, peccatis obnoxii sunt, refellens eâ fini objectionem, vel exceptionem à longanimitate & tolerantia divinâ, quam eò in- terpretantur homines, ac si spernat Deus humana peccata, eademque inulta relinquere velit. Colligis- ne hoc, ó homo, qui judicas eos, qui talia agunt, & fa- cis ea, quod tu effugies judicium Dei? Annon absur- da opinio est, putare humanis judiciis alios meritò esse obnoxios, te vero, qui iisdem vitiis obligatus es, ipsiusmet Dei justissimi judicis elapsurum esse judicium? Aut an divitias bonitatis ejus, & tole- rentiæ, & longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans quod benignitas Dei ad pænitentiam te agere velit? Scias eâ te ad resipiscentiam invitari. Sin indurescis & spretâ conscientiâ patrandis sceleribus insuescis, thesauros tibi pœnarum colligis in die judicii expro- mendos. Non ergo cum Salmerone, Estio, à Lapi- de, Hemmingio, quibus accedit Calixtus, hæc ad Judæos restringi possunt; sed omnes omninò homi- nes feriunt, quod tum συνέχεια cum præcedente Capite, tum generalis appellatio, ώ homo, ut & di- stributio generis humani in Judæos & gentes, tum totius demonstrationis vis, & analyseos Apostoli- cæ genuina ratio comprobat.

Vana etiam est Grotii glossa, quod à Philosophis ad Magistratum, qui dicantur juxta Ebræum sty- lum οἱ κρίνοντες, sive οἱ κριταὶ descendat Apostolus, uti & Cajetani, qui de solis in judicio constitutis cum Theodor. Theophyl. & Oecumenio exposuit. Nam neque de Philosophis solis antea egerat, neque Ma- gistratus hìc compellat, sed promiscuè homines quosvis, qui, quod in aliis damnant, ipsi faciunt. Neque ad hypocritas solum cum Calvino & Bucero hæc restringenda: Sed generaliter cum Cypriano l. III. ad Quirin. Origene, August. Chrysost. Basilio accipienda, ut Tolet. Staplet. Perer. Maldon. & Justin. agnoscunt, & affirmant Martyr, Musculus, & Pareus.

Juliam timeo, cum venenum coqui juberet. Sueton. XXXIV. Incestae Virgines Vestales vivae defodiebantur: Nero uni earum vim intulit Sueton. 28. Puniebatur ca- pite, qui puerum ingenuum rapuisset L. & eam D. ad L. Juliam de vi publica. Imperatoribus id erat quotidianum. Vide Suetonium Nerone 28. Hanc Imperatorum licen- tiam imitabantur in provinciis praesides. Servus si inge- nuum puerum stuprasset, non effugiebat crucem: Dominis in servos id licebat & tales pueri dicebantur delicati. Cy- prianus: Qui sedet crimina vindicaturus, admittit: Sed & ad privata de aliis judicio recte hoc Pauli extendas. Sic David apud Nathanem semet damnabat. Justinus in col- loquio cum Triphone: ἰδεῖν γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοὺς μὴ τὰ αὐτὰ πα- θεῖν βουλομένους ἅπερ αὐτοὶ τοὺς ἄλλους διατιθέασι, καὶ ἐν συνειδή- σεσιν ἐχθροὺς ταῦτα ὀνειδίζοντας ἀλλήλοις ἅπερ ἐργάζονται. Salvianus 1. lib. de gubernatione Dei: In aliis nempe hor- rent, quod in se ipsis admittunt, mirum in modum & accusato- res eorundem criminum & peccatores. Exsecrantur publice quod occulte agunt, ac per hoc, dum damnare se caeteros pu- tant, ipsos se magis propria animadversione condemnant. Et postea: Aliis severissimi sumus, nobis indulgentissimi; aliis austeri, nobis remissi. In eodem crimine punimus alios, nos absolvimus. Intolerabilis sane & contumacia & praesumptio- nis, nec agnoscere volumus in nobis reatum, & audemus de aliis usurpare judicium. Chrysostomus de peccato & Confessio- ne: ἀλλ᾿ οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῶν μὲν ἰδίων ἁμαρτημάτων συνήγοροι γίνονται, τῶν δὲ ἀλλοτρίων κατήγοροι. Neque hoc videre Romanorum sapientiores. Cicero Verrina V. Omnia quae vindicaris in altero, tibi ipsi fugienda sunt. Etenim non modo accusator, sed ne objurgator quidem ferendus est, qui quod in alio vitium reprehendit, id in ipso reprehenditur. Ho- ratius libro 1. Sat. 3. Egomet mi ignosco Maenius, inquit. Stultus & improbus hic non est dignusque notari. Seneca de ira lib. 1. 14. Cogitet quam multa contra bonum morem faciat, quam multa ex his, quae egit, veniam desiderent, jam irascetur etiam sibi. Neque enim aequus judex aliam de sua, aliam de aliena causa sententiam ferat. lib. II. 28. Is qui nullius non uxorem concupiscit, & satis justam putat aman- di causam, quod aliena est, idem uxorem suam aspici non vult, & fidei acerrimus exactor est perfidus, & mendaces persequitur ipse perjurus, & litem sibi inferri agerrime calumniator pati- tur, pudicitiam servulorum suorum attentari non vult, qui non pepercit suae. Aliena vitia in oculis habemus, a tergo nostra sunt. Inde est, quod tempestiva filii convivia pater deterior filio casti- gat. Nihil alienae injuriae ignoscit, qui nihil sua negavit: Et homicide tyrannus irascitur, & punit furta sacrilegus. Ma- gna pars hominum est, quae non peccatis irascitur, sed peccanti- bus. Epist. XCIV. Scis improbum esse, qui ab uxore pudicitiam exigit, ipse alienarum corruptor uxorum. Scis ut illi nil cum adultero, sic nihil tibi esse habere cum pellice: Et non facis. IIX. Epist. 22. Nostine hos, qui omnium libidinum servi, sic aliorum vitiis irascuntur, quasi invideant & gravissime puniant, quae ma- xime imitantur? Adde, quae de hoc argumento non aliena attulimus, tum in prolegomenis ad Stobaeum, tum ad Matth. VII. 3. & lib. II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XX. 3.

ἐν ᾧ non est hic IDCIRCO, vel αἰτιολογικὸν: sed δεικτικὸν potius, in illo, in quo alium damnas, temetipsum condemnas. Temere id Grotius de Romanis Imperatoribus interpretatur, de omnibus accipiendum esse συνέχεια & vis tracta- tionis Apostolicae convincit. Exempli causa al- legari illi possunt; non autem iisdem peculiariter dicta sunt, aut de iisdem. Et fateri coactus Grotius est, haec pertinere etiam ad privata de aliis judicia. Sed eo tantum recte extendi, ac si non ea propria & directa sit Pauli intentio commu- niter quosvis arguere, non concedendum. Eam autem hominum indolem esse ea, quae ipse colli- git Grotius, cum Patrum tum Gentilium testimo- nia comprobant: utpote dictum Chrysostomi: de peccat. & confess. ἀλλ᾿ οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῶν μὲν ἰδίων ἁμαρτημάτων συνήγοροι γίνονται, τῶν δὲ ἀλλοτρίων κατήγοροι: Nec non istud Salviani l. 1. de Gubernat. Dei: Intolerabilis sane & contuma- cia & praesumtionis, nec agnoscere volumus in no- bis reatum, & audemus de aliis usurpare judi- cium. Denique illud Senecae de Ira lib. 1. cap. 14. Aliena vitia in oculis habemus, a tergo nostra sunt. Etenim probe notanda hic Grotiana de justo Dei judicio ὁμοψηφία, quod id natura nobis notum sit ad vers. 2. ipsa ratio hoc nos docet. Et porro: hac cognitio de incorrupto Dei judicio in multis dormit, sed excitari solet circa mortem, ut Plato observat de Republ. 1. Cicero l. de divinatione: hos, qui secus, quàm decuit, vixerunt, peccatorum suorum tum maximè pœnitet. Quibus utique ipse Grotius gentilibus ipsis rationis ductu judicium Dei, quod est secundum veritatem, adversus peccata cogni- tum fuisse, imò neque ignotum ipsis extremum judicium, confessus est: Nec sanè difficilis, in- quit, adeo erat collectio, cum Deus sit justus, mali autem sæpè in hac vita sint felicissimi, aliud expectari judicium. Beza & Piscator Participium ἀγνοῶν extra in- terrogationem accipiunt, quasi ignorantia melio- ris causæ indurationis constituatur. Quod uni- versæ Apostoli tractationi repugnat, qui & ἐπιγνόντας peccare & judicare alios, in quo pec- cant, & contemnere longanimitatem Dei eosdem, & σκληροκαρδίᾳ sua iram Dei sibi thesaurizare, adeoque scientes, prudentes sibi indurationis & impœnitentiæ causam existere docet: quum scire & intelligere poterant, ac debuerant, à Dei longa- nimitate se ad pœnitentiam agi. Omnis enim cau- sa hic in voluntariam hominis duritiem, non natu- ralem ignorantiam conjicitur. Quod etiam ad- versus Cajetanum, Fabrum Stapulensem, Estium, Tirinum, notandum. Et habemus hic consen- tientes Justinian. & à Lapide, qui illud ignoras? exprobratoriè interpretantur, certe ignorare nec poteras, nec debebas tantam benignitatem Dei te ad pœnitentiam ducere. Τὸ γὰρ ἀυτὰ πράσσεις ὁ κρίνων) hoc quoque dicit non omnibus, sed plerisque. Vers. 2. οἴδαμεν δὲ) Ipsa ratio hoc nos docet. Ὅτι τὸ κρῖμα τῦ Θεῦ ἐστι κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν ἐπὶ τὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντας) sequitur hoc ex ipso Dei nomine. Deum enim concipere non possumus sine justitia. Εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρὸν, ὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί. ἀλήθεια hoc loco est judicium justum, nihil dans gratiæ aut odio, ut infra III. 7. 1. Cor. XIII. 6. Hebræum אמונה interdum vertitur ἀλήθεια, interdum δικαιοσύνη sensu sæpe eodem. Oppo- nitur hoc, ut notat Chrysostomus, judiciis Romanorum, quæ erant corruptissima. Vide de Clodianis judicibus Se- necam Epistola XCVI. ubi multa egregie dicta, hoc verò imprimis: Cum stuprum committeretur rei judicandæ cau- sa. Hæc cognitio de incorrupto Dei judicio in multis dor- mit, sed excitari solet circa mortem, ut Plato observat de Republ. 1. Cicero l. de divinatione: Eos, qui secus quàm decuit, vixerunt, peccatorum tum maxime pœnitet. Nec sa- ne difficilis adeo erat collectio, cum Deus sit justus, mali autem sæpe in hac vita sint felicissimi aliud expectari judi- cium. Non alloquitur Apostolus, uti jam moni- tum, Magistratus, qui secundum leges judica- bant apud Romanos, sed quosvis homines pro- miscue. Ὁ κρίνων τὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντας) qui de illis judicas secundum leges, non Romanorum tantum, sed omnium gentium consensu probatas. Καὶ ποιῶν αὐτά) cum eadem facias. Ὅτι σὺ ἐκφύξῃ τὸ κρῖμα τῦ Θεῦ) loquitur sic & Diphi- lus: Οἶει συ τὺς θανόντας, ὦ Νικήρατε, Τρυφῆς ἁπάσης μεταλαβόντας ἐν βίῳ, Πεφευγέναι τὸ θεῖον; Nec longe abit Sophoclis illud: Δεῖ δὲ πληγὴν ἐκ ὑπερπηδᾷ βροτός. Plura habes in eum sensum apud Stobæum naturalium titulo 7. Homines tribus modis crimina ferunt impune, quia aut ignorantur, aut quia nemo tam potens, qui ipsos puniat, aut quia jus perrumpitur gratia aut pretio. Ho- rum nihil in Deum cadit, scit omnia, potest quæ vult, ex recto judicat. Vide Jobum XXXIV. 22. Vers. 4. ἢ τῦ πλέτε τῆς χρηστότητος αὐτῦ) רוב חסדך ut Psalm. V. 8. CVI. 7. רוב רחמיך LXIX. 17. Sic πλῦτος χάριτος dicitur Ephes. I. 7. πλῦτος δόξης in- fra IX. 23. Eph. I. 18. III. 16. Col. I. 27. πλῦτος pari sensu usurpat Simplicius ad Epictetum. ὑπερβολὴν τῶ πλύτου τῆς ἀγαθότητος Θεῦ dixit Philo in Allegoriis. Non dissimili modo πλύτε vocem infra habemus IX. 23. & XI. 33.

Præclaris verbis divinam Apostolus celebrat benignitatem: Quæ imprimis in malis quibusvis ferendis se exerit: Non χρησότητα tantum, quæ suavitatem bonitatis, & benignitatis, sed πλῦτον di- vitias talis benignitatis immensas, nec benignitatis solum thesauros, sed etiam gratiæ & tolerantiæ, imò & summæ μακροθυμίας & longanimitatis de- pingens. II. 7. χρησότης in genere notat benignitatem aliis commodam vel utilem, & gratam & auspica- tam: Syrus reddidit בסימות dulcedinem, suavem indulgentiam. Respondit ei Ebræum טוב Psalm. XXVI. 5. Ps. XXXIV. 9. Ps. C. 5. Ps. CXLV. 7. Ἀνο- χὴ ab ἀνέχειν sustinere, patientiam, qua sustinet nos, exprimit: Laxamentum, inducias exponit Gro- tius è Glossario. Μακρόθυμος dicitur qua- si μακρύνων τὸν θυμὸν tardans iram ne statim puniat

## 2:4
Καὶ τῆς ἀνοχῆς) thus also below at III. 26. In the Glossary: ἀνοχὴ, a relaxation, a truce.

Καὶ τῆς μακροθυμίας) אור אפים ἀγνοῶν) that is, not considering, for the Hebrew ידע is often to attend.

Ὅτι τὸ χρηστὸν τῦ Θεῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει) this is, in deferring punishments, the προηγύμενον Θεῦ θέλημα [the antecedent will of God]. Concerning which also 2 Pet. III. 9; then, after long patience, another [will] succeeds, of punishing more severely. Thus Wisdom XI. 24: ἐλεεῖς δὲ πάντας ὅτι πάντα δύνασαι καὶ παρορᾷς ἁμαρτήματα ἀνθρώπων εἰς μετάνοιαν. Philo in the Allegories: ὐδὲ τοῖς ἁμαρτάνυσιν εὐθὺς ἐπέξεισιν ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ δίδωσι χρόνον εἰς μετάνοιαν καὶ τῆς τῦ σφάλματος ἴασιν. Hence it is that the poets also give τῇ δίκῃ a slow foot. See the cited title of Stobaeus; μετάνοια signifies not only sorrow for sins, but also the amendment of life.

It is rightly explained concerning the antecedent will of God, by the power of which GOD seriously desires the salvation of all men, and strives to lead even the reprobate themselves to repentance through His kindness and long-suffering, 1 Tim. II. 1, 2 Pet. III. 9, Ezek. XXX. 22, ch. XXXIII. 11. The accumulation and emphasis of these words in describing the riches of divine kindness, which are opened up even to the reprobate, sufficiently teaches that this [will] is entirely sincere, not playful, and that the internal good pleasure of the mind corresponds to the external sign of the word, and it powerfully overthrows the absolute decree of the Calvinists.

Latin:

Καὶ τῆς ἀνοχῆς) sic & infra III. 26. in Glossario: ἀνοχὴ laxamentum, induciæ.

Καὶ τῆς μακροθυμίας) אור אפים ἀγνοῶν) id est non considerans, nam ידע Hebræum sæpe est attendere.

Ὅτι τὸ χρηστὸν τῦ Θεῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει) hoc est in differendis pœnis τὸ προηγύμενον Θεῦ θέλημα. De quo & 2. Petr. III. 9. succedit deinde post longam patientiam al- terum, puniendi gravius. Sic Sapientiæ XI. 24. ἐλεεῖς δὲ πάντας ὅτι πάντα δύνασαι καὶ παρορᾷς ἁμαρτήματα ἀνθρώ- πων εἰς μετάνοιαν. Philo Allegoriis: ὐδὲ τοῖς ἁμαρτάνυσιν εὐθὺς ἐπέξεισιν ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ δίδωσι χρόνον εἰς μετάνοιαν καὶ τῆς τῦ σφάλματος ἴασιν. Hinc est quod τῇ δίκῃ etiam Poëtæ dant βραδέα πόδα. Vide dictum titulum Stobæi, μετάνοια significat non dolorem solum ob peccata, sed & vitæ emendationem.

Rectè de antecedente Dei voluntate exponitur, vi cujus DEUS omnium hominum salutem seriò expetit, ipsosque etiam reprobos ejus testantlæ er- gò per benignitatem suam, & longanimitatem ad pœnitentiam perducere satagit 1. Tim. II. 1. 2. Pe- tri III. 9. Ezech. XXX. 22. c. XXXIII. 11. Quam sinceram omninò esse, non ludicram, ac benepla- citum internum animi externo verbi signo respon- dere cumulus & emphasis horum verborum in describendis divitiis benignitatis divinæ, quæ ipsis reprobis adaperiuntur, satis docet, & absolutum Calvinianorum decretum potenter profligat.

## 2:5
Καὶ τὴν σκληρότητά σου) but what is your hardness. Paul calls that hardness which Latin writers call a callus formed on the mind, namely by a long habit of vices. See Matt. XIX. 8, Mark XVI. 14. A similar use of the verb σκληρύνεσθαι is in Acts XIX. 9, Heb. III. 8, 13; the same is called ἀπαλγεῖν in Eph. IV. 19. Examples of such a constitution are in Pharaoh and King Saul.

Καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν) he explains more clearly what he had said by metaphor; however, ἀμετανόητον in this place is not one who cannot repent, but one who does not repent. In a similar way, ἀμετακίνητος is one who is not moved, 1 Cor. XV. 58.

Θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ ὀργὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς) The passage Deut. XXXII. 34, 35 is looked back upon, where it is thus in the Greek: ὐκ ἰδῦ ταῦτα συνῆκται παρ' ἐμοὶ καὶ ἐσφράγισται ἐν τοῖς θησαυροῖς μυ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐκδικήσεως ἀνταποδόσω. Philo, in the cited place of the Allegories, looking back to these words: Εἰσὶ γὰρ ὥσπερ ἀγαθῶν ὕτω κακῶν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ θησαυροὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ γάρ φησιν ἐκδικήσεως ἐσφραγίσθαι τὰς τῶν κακῶν θησαυρὸς. Plutarch also said: θησαυρὸς ὀργῆς. Furthermore, this is a Hebraizing locution, an active for a double active. Θησαυρίζεις, you store up, for you cause to be stored up, האוצר or הוספר, as in Nehemiah XIII. 8, or as in Job XXXVI. 13, השמו, in which way also ἀποθησαυρίζονται [is used], but it is placed in a good sense, 1 Tim. VI. 19. Thus βασιλεύειν is often to cause someone to reign. ὀργὴ, anger, for punishment. And the treasure of wrath is well opposed to the riches of goodness. And after ὀργὴν, [the word] to be rendered is understood from the passage of Deuteronomy.

To the treasure of divine kindness, which the impious spurn, a treasure—but an unhappy one—of wrath is opposed, or brought up as a reserve, which they collect for themselves according to the hardness of a heart that knows not how to repent. The verb θησαυρίζειν indicates that divine wrath is gradually accumulated, so that at length a treasure or huge supply, to be drawn out at the time of judgment, may arise; then it is said to be stored up with God, sealed in treasures, whatever vengeance is brought forth, Deut. XXXII. 34, 35, and God then opens His treasures, Jerem. L. 25. That σεαυτῷ is to be understood according to the opposition to divine goodness and the gracious intention, because an impenitent heart is the cause of such great evil to itself, when the goodness of God invites it to something else and desires it to be brought in. ἡμέρα ὀργῆς is called the final day with respect to the impenitent: because God has not placed the faithful εἰς ὀργὴν, 1 Thess. V. 9, for whom that is the day of ἀπολυτρώσεως.

Καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως καὶ δικαιοκρισίας Θεῦ) one through two, for ἀποκαλύψεως δικαιοκρισίας, so that he may speak more generally, which he is then about to explain more specifically. δικαιοκρισίας is well added, lest by the name of wrath an inordinate affection be understood.

Latin:

Καὶ τὴν σκληρότητά σου) quæ verò tua est durities. Duri- tiem id vocat Paulus, quod Latini Scriptores callum ob- ductum animo, longa scilicet vitiorum consuetudine. Vi- de Matth. XIX. 8. Marc. XVI. 14. Similis usus verbi σκλη- ρύνεσθαι est Actor. XIX. 9. Hebr. III. 8. 13. idem dicitur ἀπαλγεῖν Ephes. IV. 19. Exempla talis constitutionis in Pharaone & Saule Regibus.

Καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν) exponit clarius, quod per me- taphoram dixerat, ἀμετανόητον autem hoc loco est non qui pœnitentiam agere non potest, sed qui non agit. Pari modo ἀμετακίνητος qui non movetur. 1. Cor. XV. 58.

Θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ ὀργὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς) Respicicur lo- cus Deut. XXXII. 34. 35. ubi sic in Græco: ὐκ ἰδῦ ταῦτα συνῆκται παρ' ἐμοὶ καὶ ἐσφράγισται ἐν τοῖς θησαυροῖς μυ ἐν ἡμέ- ρᾳ ἐκδικήσεως ἀνταποδόσω. Philo dicto loco de Allegoriis ad hæc verba respiciens: Εἰσὶ γὰρ ὥσπερ ἀγαθῶν ὕτω κα- κῶν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ θησαυροὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ γάρ φησιν ἐκδική- σεως ἐσφραγίσθαι τὰς τῶν κακῶν θησαυρὸς. Dixit & Plu- tarchus: θησαυρὸς ὀργῆς. Præterea est hic locutio He- braizans, activum pro duplici activo. Θησαυρίζεις, asservas pro asservari facis האוצר ant הוספר cum Ne- hemia XIII. 8. aut cum Jobo XXXVI. 13. השמו quo- modo & ἀποθησαυρίζονται, sed in bonam partem ponitur. 1. Tim. VI. 19. Sic βασιλεύειν sæpe est facere ut quis regnet. ὀργὴ ira, pro pœna. Et benè Thesaurus iræ opponitur divitiis bonitatis. Et post ὀργὴν, subauditur reddendam, ex loco Deuteronomii.

Thesauro divinæ benignitatis, quem impii spernunt, thesaurus, at infelix, iræ opponitur, vel succenturiatur, quem sibi ipsis colligunt secun- dum duritiem cordis pœnitere nescii. Verbum θησαυρίζειν indicat paulatim coacervari iram di- vinam, ut tandem thesaurus vel copia ingens judi- cii tempore depromenda exfurgat; deinde recon- ditum apud Deum dicitur sigillatim in thesauris, quicquid ultionis expromitur, Deut. XXXII. 34. 35. & aperit tum Deus thesauros suos Jerem. L. 25. Illud σεαυτῷ secundum oppositionem ad divinam bonitatem & intentionem gratiosam accipien- dum, quod cor impœnitens sibi ipsi tanti mali cau- sa sit, cum bonitas Dei alio id invitet, ac inductum cupiat. ἡμέρα ὀργῆς dies extrema dicitur respectu impœnitentium: Quia fideles non posuit Deus εἰς ὀρ- γὴν 1. Thess. V. 9. quibus illa est dies ἀπολυτρώσεως.

Καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως καὶ δικαιοκρισίας Θεῦ) ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, pro ἀποκαλύψεως δικαιοκρισίας, ut generalius dicat, quod deinde explicaturus est specialius. Bene additum δικαιοκρι- σίας, ne nomine iræ affectus inordinatus intelligeretur.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. who will render to every man according to his works) Nothing is clearer; God will render good things for good deeds, and evil things for evil deeds. God, judging both these and those, looks back [to them]. Matt. XVI. 27, XXV. 35, and following. 2 Cor. V. 10. Apoc. II. 23, XX. 12, XXI. 12. This is the difference, that punishment cannot by justice exceed the measure of the crime: but a reward, if the liberality of the giver be added, can be greater than what the deeds are worth in themselves. Although, however, to promise such a reward was of immense liberality, yet where it has been promised, a right arises from it. But those to whom the promise was not made, such as the Patriarchs and the pious from among the Gentiles, they indeed hoped for a reward after this life, but by no means such a one. Therefore, when they speak of it, they name Hades, not the heavenly kingdom, but even these will receive more than they hoped for.

According to works the rendering will take place, but not according to the merits of works, nor on account of works. For even if retribution is owed to evil works by the force of divine justice, by which we deserve death (Rom. I. 32, ch. VI. last), yet good works do not deserve life, nor is eternal salvation owed to them by the force of justice as a form of retribution: because eternal life comes to us from grace, and is a χάρισμα τῦ Θεῦ, a purely gratuitous gift of God (Eph. II. 8, Rom. VI. 23), nor is there any proportion between works and eternal life (Rom. VIII. 18). To this truth accede, from among the Papists, all those who acknowledge that no merit properly so-called has a place here, and who do not even attribute to the works of the just the power of meriting, but only of obtaining, and that solely from the divine promise, not in themselves. Which is the opinion of Thomas Bradwardine, Scotus, Gregory, Ariminensis, Biel, Cassander, and many others. In support of which Cassander also cites Augustine, Jerome, Bernard, Thomas, Durandus, Adrian of Utrecht (afterwards Pope Adrian VI), and Ludovicus Clichtoveus. Which was likewise the declaration of Charles V and the remaining Roman Catholic Princes in the Consultation on Article 4 of the Augsburg Confession: as well as that of Thomas Waldensis, Conrad Clingius, Albert Pighius, and the authors of the anti-didagma of Cologne, and others. See what we have written concerning these matters on Article XX of the Augsburg Confession against the Walenburgers, who finally profess that there is no reason to think that the Lutherans are alien to the opinion of the Catholic Church; why then are we condemned by the Council of Trent? On which account we warned them there in a friendly manner, that they should obtain this from the modern Roman Church, namely, that it should decree with them (1) that it does not pertain to the Catholic faith that eternal life itself is the reward of good works. That it is enough, (2) if it be taught that the degrees of eternal life are the reward, and (3) that the reward here is to be established solely from the divine promise founded in the gratuitous goodness of God. (4) That an unworthy question is raised concerning the word 'condign'; if these and other things which we have observed there are obtained, we will acknowledge that the consensus which they claim will not be difficult.

Hugo Grotius, in his Consultations with Cassander, set forth his opinion thus: that the word merit and reward is used in the Holy Scriptures where it is a question of preserving the right to eternal life, and even a greater right to obtain greater rewards: and this for a twofold reason, both because those works, by the nobility of their origin, as having proceeded from the Word and Spirit of Christ and having been conformed to his example, have a certain aptitude for a reward that is not common, and then because GOD, as Augustine speaks, has made himself a debtor not by receiving anything, but by promising liberally. But in the Scriptures the word is nowhere read concerning the merit of eternal life, nor is eternal life itself called a reward. The Fathers indeed sometimes used the word merit, but only in a general sense, where it implies the bare consequence of a reward, by no means admitting merits properly so called, for which a proportion to the reward is required, in the cause of salvation. And they do not teach that a reward properly so called, which we call due, which we clearly earn by our works, but one improperly so called and undue, which is rendered out of grace, is in Holy Scripture. Furthermore, even if works arise from the Word and Spirit, they are nevertheless of such imperfection and impurity that they can by no means have the nature of merit properly so called: nor are they entirely conformed to the example of Christ, but they fail in many ways, and therefore they do not have an aptitude for the reward of heavenly life, much less are they meritorious of the same by condignity, and not even a merit by covenant, because no one keeps that covenant perfectly, as Gregory the Great rightly acknowledged in his 9th book of expositions on John 11, that all human justice is injustice. Nor is it true that GOD has made himself a debtor to render eternal life to our works, as it is not rendered to works, but is a gift of grace in Christ Jesus, Rom. 6:23.

But that Grotius says here that the promise of eternal life was by no means made to the Patriarchs, is from the pits of the Socinians, who make Christ the first herald of it in the New Testament. And that some hoped for a reward after this life, but by no means as much (as eternal life is), and when it is a question of it, it is named ᾅδην, not the heavenly kingdom, are dreams akin to the Rabbinical ones. Scripture does not recognize any other reward after this life except the heavenly kingdom, nor does it anywhere call ᾅδην a reward after this life, and that something other than the heavenly kingdom; but rather it designates by that name hell and the place of punishment for the impious. Finally, that he says the pious hoped for some reward after this life out of grace even without a promise, but would receive more than they hoped for, if he understands this of proselytes and those converted to the faith of the Patriarchs, the reasoning for them is the same as for the Patriarchs: if of others not converted, neither any hope, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit and arises from the Word of God, but a mere opinion or persuasion arising from the discourse of reason or tradition, is fitting for them, nor will any remuneration after this life fall to them: because they are reckoned in the Scriptures among the infidels, upon whom the wrath of God remains, which teach that a reward will be rendered after this life only to the faithful.

But to return to the Apostle, when he says that God will render according to works, our people rightly observe against the Papists that it is one thing to render according to works, that is, according to the testimony of works, which testify of internal faith or incredulity, but quite another to render something on account of works, that is, on account of the merit of works, which Gregory the Great already observed in his 7th Penitential Psalm. It is one thing to render according to works, and another to render on account of the works themselves. For in that which is said according to works, the quality of the works themselves is understood, so that whose works appear good, his also is the glorious retribution: they also rightly note: it is nowhere said διὰ τὰ ἔργα (on account of works), but κατὰ τὰ ἔργα (according to works): because works will indeed be a manifest rule of righteous judgment, but not a proportionate norm of merits. And it is no less well observed by our people that the Holy Scriptures do not use the word ἀντιδόσεως, which could be drawn by some appearance to a reward properly so called, but ἀποδόσεως, which is general, and also has a place when GOD, out of grace, crowns not our merits, but his own gifts. See what is brought against Cornelius and Bellarmine in Oracle 16. But above all it must be said in this place that this sentence is legal, as Flacius rightly observed in his Gloss, which is corrected by the Gospel applying to us the most ample justice of the works and fulfillment of the law of Christ, and freely forgiving sins. Just as believers are also freed from the curse of the whole law. For the Apostle is still engaged in that legal conviction or demonstration which he took from the law, so that he may conclude all men under condemnation; he has not yet begun to explain the Gospel or grace, or what GOD promised in the Gospel, life and glory. He is only occupied thus far in denying the perfect fulfillment of the law to all men, and thus in convincing that no flesh can be justified by works.

To those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality. For the διαμονὴ ψυχῆς (persistence of the soul) was not indeed believed with absolute certainty by the pious from among the Gentiles, but yet so that the opinion asserting it was believed to be more probable; κατ᾽ ὑπόμονην here is the same as δι᾽ ὑπομονῆς. For these particles are accustomed to be mixed, as in 1 Cor. 12:8, Eph. 3:3, and elsewhere. But then ὑπομονὴ, which properly signifies expectation, is placed here for constancy: because such expectation, as is described in Psalm 37:5 and elsewhere, is accustomed to produce constancy. Thus ὑπομένειν is to persevere, Matt. 10:22, and the singular here is for the plural: ἔργα ἀγαθὰ, for ἔργων ἀγαθῶν, as also below 15, 1 Cor. 13:14, 15, 15:50, 1 Thess. 1:3, 2 Thess. 1:11, 17, which is quite frequent where a totality of some things is signified. δόξα here signifies an illustrious state, as in Matt. 13:42. honor joined with praise, concerning which see John 12:18, 1 Pet. 1:7, immortality perpetual.

They are not understood as seeking the glory of works, as Beza translated against the distinction of the Greek text, the Syriac interpretation, and the Apostolic intention, but they are designated as seeking glory and honor and incorruptibility according to the perseverance of a good work, to whom eternal life is to be given, not because they obtain life through works or on account of the perseverance of works, for that is repugnant to the very proposition of the Epistle, the just shall live by faith, and to the whole treatment, which tends to this, that we are justified and saved by faith and not from works, but in the perseverance of works or those persevering in good works in faith or through faith in Christ they seek glory; which accords with the scope and doctrine of the Apostle. In which manner to those who seek God through faith, God is called a gracious μισθαποδότης, Heb. XI. 6. Nor therefore is the power of works indicated, much less merit in relation to eternal life, or the intention of such persons working, and persevering in a good work, that they strive to obtain and win eternal glory through good works, but the heirs of eternal life are described by perseverance in good, which is altogether required in them, although not as the cause and merit of eternal life, but as an argument of true faith, and a necessary consequent: Add that here the Apostle is still occupied in the proving of his cause from the law, according to which life is promised to works, but under the condition of perfect fulfillment, Lev. XVIII. 5. which, however, is demonstrated here to be performed by no one. For under the guise of an assertion, as

Flacius in Glossa p. 665 teaches that he spoke conditionally, as when he said that God in the final judgment will give to each according to his works, that to those indeed who through patience in well-doing seek glory and immortality, he will give eternal life. Likewise, that it will come to pass that honor, glory, and peace will befall everyone who does good, to the Jew as well as to the Greek. For where in the world is or was any mortal such that these great goods, namely eternal life itself, could befall him through his own works and innocence? but the law is often accustomed to speak thus conditionally under the shadow of an assertion, as if there were some who truly fulfilled the law, and to whom the rewards of the law would befall, when they only posit the condition that if ever any such observer of the law existed, such great rewards would befall him, as are those sayings: He who does these things shall live in them: if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: God will give to each according to his works. Which nature of legal expressions or the veil of Moses must be diligently observed.

Grotius has here ἐπιζητῦσι, but in the text is read the simple ζητῦσι: and he repeats from the preceding verse the verb ἀποδώσει, but others prefer to understand the verb δώσει, with the Syrian, since eternal life is a gift, not a repayment, so that the sense may be: He is about to render to each according to his works, to those indeed who perseveringly seek glory, honor, and incorruptibility in well-doing, he will give eternal life; but if this sentence is taken legally in the sense we have mentioned, the repetition of the verb ἀποδώσει will easily be able to have a place. Which legal sense I see is also approved by our blessed Gerhard. For although he himself thinks it can be explained evangelically by accommodation, that we who are justified by faith in Christ, who fulfilled the law in our place, ought henceforth to work well from faith, and through patience in well-doing seek glory and honor, that is, to walk constantly in good works as in a way, so that we may finally attain the ultimate goal, the possession of eternal life, through faith by grace; because eternal life is the end of faith 1 Pet. 1:9, good works are the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning, as Bernard says in his tract on grace and free will; he nevertheless prefers the legal sense, as most convenient: If the seeking of glory through patience in good works is taken legally, which most conforms to the Apostolic scope; the sense will be that the divine law promises eternal life to those who perfectly obey. But since because of the infirmity of the flesh no one perfectly fulfills the law in this life, Rom. 8:3, therefore these and similar promises of the law are rendered useless to us: hence we must flee by faith to Christ, who is the end of the law, Rom. 10:4, in whom the promises of God are yes and amen 2 Cor. 1:20. Grotius takes these words concerning the pious from among the Gentiles, but he does not explain whether he understands those persisting in Gentilism or proselytes: he says that the persistence of the soul was not indeed believed there with absolute certainty, but yet in such a way that the opinion asserting it was believed to be more probable, which is evident concerning Gentile philosophers and others not converted in Heathenism: who posited the immortality of the soul, and after the release from the body, a separated state, or persistence. That their goal in this was to attain some blessedness through patience or perseverance in well-doing is not difficult to teach. For that the Heathens, destitute of the revelation of the Word of God, not only believed in the immortality of the soul, but also certainly expected the highest eternal good from the Supreme Deity, even so much that they despised death itself in the hope of that, there exist not a few documents of that matter. Which we have brought forward

Decade of dissertations on the origin of Socinian Pseudo-Theology, p. 80 seqq. We present here Iamblichus, the preceptor of Chrysostom, who, having encompassed many things in few words, says: The soul will dwell with God, and will walk in heaven, which will serve it in place of a home: but that which has contaminated itself with crimes and wickedness will be thrust down to subterranean places, so that it may pay and endure the judgments which are exercised upon wicked souls. Add that the opinion of the recent heathens in the new world seems not to have been dissimilar, if faith is to be given to Jean de Léry, who in his history of the American voyage testifies concerning the Tupinambá, that they believe the souls of those who have cultivated virtue, flying beyond the highest mountains, lead a joyful life in most pleasant gardens with perpetual delights and dances: on the contrary, the shades of the slothful are snatched away to the Styx (so they call the Evil Spirit) and live with him amidst eternal torments.

Nor can there be any doubt that the Heathens devoted effort to good actions according to common notions about the distinction between just and unjust, so that they might attain that end, as far as they themselves recognized it: but since no one could perfectly fulfill the divine precepts concerning the love of God and neighbor, and they did not believe in Christ, who alone is the end of the law, they did not attain it at all. Zoroaster professed that one must hasten with all one's heart to the splendor of the Father: The end of man is to live by the mind, the life of the mind is God: and the only way to God is piety joined to knowledge: Mercurius Trismegistus posited. And no less clearly Zaleucus, the lawgiver of the Locrians, in the preamble of his laws: It is right, he says, for everyone to devote effort with all his might to be a good man, not so much in external life as in the purpose and destination of the mind, if only he wishes to be dear to God, and to prefer to lose all his wealth rather than to deviate a hair's breadth from praise, from honesty, from justice. And he teaches besides in the same place: That the gods are to be worshipped and honored as the parents and authors of all good things which are done with reason. And, so that anyone may be able to induce his mind to these things, he orders that men celebrated for the praise of honesty and probity be approached, by whose discussions he may be recalled from unjust deeds, both concerning the blessedness of life and the punishments of the wicked. What the opinion of Pythagoras was concerning religion, piety, justice, and honesty, his golden verses testify, by which he promises even heaven and deification to those who have established the mind as the best charioteer. Moreover, Pythagoras said that the end of this life is contemplation, the end of all contemplation is God, and the true blessedness of man is to become God. Thus Socrates, in Plato, teaches that for the sake of blessedness after death, we must strive with all our zeal so that in this life we may attain true Wisdom and virtue, and be sufficiently purged as far as the soul is concerned: because the reward is beautiful, and the hope great. Plato, however, says that piety is the highest virtue among men, which is toward God, and by it we are just and holy, and attain that blessedness, so that we may be rendered like unto God. But that it is impossible for us to be blessed in this life, but in the other, without doubt, those who have pursued virtue will receive blessedness in place of a reward. Epictetus in Enchiridion, chapter XXXVIII, says that the chief part of religion toward the immortal Gods is to have right opinions about them, so that we may believe both that they exist and that they govern all things well and justly: that we must obey them, and acquiesce in all things that happen, and follow them willingly, as things that are governed by a most excellent mind. Of the same author is this: If we have any mental capacity, what should we do but celebrate God assiduously and sing thanksgivings? If I were a nightingale, I would do what a nightingale does: but since I was born a rational man, what shall I do? I will praise God and I will never cease. But I seriously exhort you to do the same. Iamblichus, De Mysteriis, chapter XLV, discourses thus concerning happiness: You suspect, lest perhaps some other way to blessedness, besides divine worship, lies hidden, and you ask what that might especially be. But truly, since the essence of all good things is in the gods, and perfection is contained, and the first power, and the first principle of good things is there, we Priests alone, and those who have similarly dedicated themselves to the powers above, and have legitimately attained union with them, deservedly pursue with zeal the principle and end of all good things; in this state, indeed, both the contemplation of truth is present, and the consummation of intellectual knowledge. Simplicius, Commentary on Epictetus, on Chapter XXXVIII. That we may dedicate and consecrate the soul, he says, to God, whose author it is, by purging it, both by true thought concerning Him, and by a life in accordance with nature: So after it, the body also, given by Him, ought to be consecrated to Him, purged of stains as conspicuous as they are latent; And again: While the soul adheres to its cause as to a root, it is preserved, and has its perfection with which God created it: But if it has torn itself away from there, and has (as far as in it lies) deserted its own root, it withers and wastes away, having become base and weak, until, having returned from the beginning and been joined to its cause, it has recovered its perfection. What of the fact that Aristotle, who is commonly considered little religious, says somewhere: Nature serves man, so that he may sacrifice: His interpreter Alexander gives this reason for it, namely because all our happiness is placed in piety towards God, for we expect no reward except God alone, and we acquire Him, who is the highest good Himself, by worshipping Him. Moreover, Averroes himself confesses that nature has obligated us to magnify God with prayers and sacrifices. Which last point, however, concerning sacrifices, the Gentiles could not have had from nature or reason, as we have proven elsewhere against the Papists, but it must be believed that they had it from tradition, or conversation with the Jews, or propagation from them to other nations, and the imitation of these, or from κακοζηλίᾳ (bad emulation).

But as for the fact that Grotius says the Gospel has made us clearly certain of eternal life, not in the Socinian sense, which he himself invents, namely that there were no promises of eternal life in the O.T., but it is to be admitted solely in this way, that the Gospel hands down that method by which we uniquely attain eternal life. Which was indeed also proposed in the Pandects of the Old Testament, nay, in the very πρωτευαγγελίῳ (proto-evangelium) of Paradise, as we taught in our Commentary on Genesis at chapter III. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὃς ἀποδώσει ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἀυτῦ) Nihil planius, bonis factis bona, malis factis mala Deus reddet. Respicit Deus judicans & hæc & ista. Matth. XVI. 27. XXV. 35. & seq. 2. Cor. V. 10. Apoc. II. 23. XX. 12. XXI. 12. Hoc interest, quod pœna non potest per justitiam excedere mensuram criminis: Præmium autem, si accedat dantis li- beralitas, potest esse majus, quam quantum facta per se va- leant. Quanquam autem præmium tantum promittere immensæ fuit liberalitatis, tamen ubi promissum est, jus ex eo nascitur. Quibus vero promissio facta non est, ut Pa- triarchæ & pii ex gentibus, ii præmium post hanc vitam spe- rarunt quidem, sed neutiquam tantum. Ideò cum de eo loquuntur ᾅδην nominant, non regnum cœleste, sed & hi plus accipient, quam speraverunt.

Secundum opera fiet ἀπόδοσις, non vero secun- dum merita operum, nec propter opera. Nam etiamsi malis operibus debeatur retributio, vi ju- stitiæ divinæ, quibus meremur mortem Rom. I. 32. cap. VI. ult. bona tamen opera non merentur vi- tam, nec iisdem vi justitiæ debetur retributionis instar, æterna salus: quia vita æterna ex gratia no- bis obtingit, & est χάρισμα τῦ Θεῦ merè gratui- tum donum Dei Eph. II. 8. Rom. VI. 27. nec ulla est inter opera & vitam æternam proportio Rom. VIII. 18. Huic veritati accedunt è Papistis o- mnes illi, qui nullum propriè meritum hic locum habere agnoscunt, ac ne quidem justorum operibus merendi vim tribuunt, sed impetrandi solum, idque ex promissione tantum divina, non per se. Quæ Tho- mæ Brandvuardini, Scoti, Gregorii, Ariminensis, Bielis, Cassandri, & aliorum multorum est senten- tia: In quam etiam allegat Cassander Augustinum, Hieronymum, Bernhardum, Thomam, Durandum, Adrianum de Trajecto post Adrianum VI. Pontif. Rom. Ludovicum Clichtoveum. Quæ item Caro- li V. & reliquorum Principum Romano-Catholico- rum in Consultatione A. C. art. 4. declaratio fuit: nec non Thomæ Waldensis, Conradi Clingii, Alberti Piggii, & autorum anti-didagm. Colon. & aliorum. Vid. quæ de his ad art. XX. A. C. adversus Walen- burgicos, qui profitentur denique non esse, cur existi- mandum sit, Lutheranos à sententia Ecclesiæ Catholi- cæ alienos esse; cur ergo damnamur à Concilio Tri- dentino? Quo nomine monuimus illic eosdem amicè, id obtineant à moderna Romana Ecclesia, ut nempe decernat cum ipsis (1) non pertinere ad fidem Catholicam, quod ipsa vita æterna merces sit bonorum operum. Satis esse, (2) si doceatur, Gra- dus vitæ æternæ mercedem esse, & (3) mercedem hic unicè constituendam ex divina promissione in gra- tuita Dei bonitate fundata. (4) de voce condigni indignam moveri quæstionem, si hæc & alia, quæ ibi observavimus, obtinuerint, consensum, quem prætendant difficilem non fore, agnoscemus.

Hugo Grotius ad Consult. Cassandr. ita suam ex- posuit mentem : vocem meriti & mercedis in S. li- teris adhiberi, ubi agitur de conservando jure ad vi- tam æternam, & majore etiam jure ad majora præ mia adipiscendi : idque duplici de causa, tum quia opera illa nobilitate suæ originis, utpote profecta ex verbo & Spiritu Christi, & ad ejus exemplar con- formata aptitudinem quandam habeant ad præmium non vulgare, deinde quia DEUS, ut Augustinus lo- quitur, non aliquid accipiendo, sed liberaliter promittendo debitorem se fecit. At in Scripturis uspiam de vitæ æternæ merito verbum legitur, nec ipsa æterna vita merces dicitur. Patres quidem adhibuere nonnunquam vocem meriti, sed gene- rali tantum significatu, ubi nudam infert conse- quutionem præmii, neutiquam admittentes merita propriè dicta, ad quæ requiritur proportio ad præ- mium, in salutis causa. Neque mercedem propriè dictam, quam vocamus debitam, quam scilicet me- reamur operibus nostris, sed impropriè dictam & indebitam, quæ ex gratia retribuatur cum S. Scri- ptura tradunt. Porrò etsi opera ex verbo & Spi- ritu oriantur, ejus tamen imperfectionis, & impu- ritatis sunt, ut meriti proprie dicti rationem mi- nime habere possint: neque ex asse ad exemplar Christi conformantur, sed multis modis deficiunt, ideoque nec aptitudinem habent ad præmium vi- tæ cælestis, multò minus ex condigno meritoriæ e- jusdem sunt, ac ne meritum quidem ex pacto, quia nemo pactum illud perfecte servat, ut merito agnoverit Gregor. M. l. IX. expos. in Johan. XI. Omnem humanam justitiam injustitiam esse. Ne- que verum est, DEUM se debitorem reddendæ operibus nostris vitæ æternæ fecisse, utpote quæ non operibus redditur, sed gratiæ donum est in Christo Jesu Rom. VI. 23.

Quod autem hic Patriarchis promissionem vitæ æternæ nullatenus factam esse ait Grotius, è lacunis est Socinianorum, qui primum ejus præconem Christum in Nov. Testam. faciunt. Et quosdam præmium post hanc vitam, sed nequaquam tantum (quantum est vita æterna) sperasse, & cum de eo agitur ᾅδην id nominari, non regnum cœleste, somnia sunt Rabbinicis gemina. Scriptura aliud post hanc vitam præmium non agnoscit, præter regnum cœleste, nec ᾅδην uspiam præmium vocat post hanc vitam, idque aliud à cœlesti regno; sed isto nomine potius infernum, & supplicii impio- rum locum designat. Denique quod pios ex gra- tia sperasse etiam citra promissionem aliquod post hanc vitam præmium, sed plus accepturos, quàm sperarint, dicit, id si de proselytis & conversis ad fi- dem Patriarcharum intelligit, eadem de istis, quæ de Patriarchis est ratio: si de aliis non conversis, illis neque spes ulla, quæ donum Spiritus S. est, & è Verbo Dei oritur, sed mera opinio vel persuasio è rationis discursu, aut traditione oriunda, conve- nit, neque ulla post hanc vitam remuneratio ob- tinget: quia infidelibus, super quos manet ira Dei, accensentur in Scripturis, quæ solis fideli- bus retributum iri post hanc vitam præmium, docent.

Sed ut ad Apostolum redeamus, cum retribu- turum Deum secundum opera dicit, recte utique contra Pontificios observant nostrates, aliud esse secundum opera, id est, secundum testimonium ope- rum, quæ de interiore fide vel incredulitate te- stantur, aliud vero propter opera, id est, propter meritum operum aliquid reddere, quod etiam Gre- gorius M. jam observavit in Psal. VII. Pœnit. A- liud esse secundum opera reddere, & aliud, propter ipsa opera reddere. In eo enim, quod secundum opera dicitur, ipsa operum qualitas intelligitur, ut cujus apparuerint opera bona, ejus sit & retributio glorio- sa: rectè etiam notant: nuspiam dici διὰ τὰ ἔργα propter opera, sed κατὰ τὰ ἔργα secundum opera: quia opera erunt quidem manifesta δικαιοκρισίας regula, non autem proportionata meritorum norma. Nec minus observatur probè à nostris, quod S. S. non utatur verbo ἀντιδόσεως, quod ad mercedem propriè dictam quadam specie trahi posset, sed ἀποδόσεως, quod generale est, ac tum etiam locum habet, cum DEUS ex gratia non merita nostra, sed sua dona coronat. Quæ adversus Cornelium, & Bellarminum adferta vid. Oraculo XVI. Sed impri- mis hoc loco dicendum, quod hæc sententia lega- lis sit, ut recte observavit Flacius in Glossa, quæ ab Evangelio nobis Christi amplissimum operum ju- stitiam & impletionem legis applicante, ac pecca- ta gratis condonante corrigitur. Sicut & à totius legis maledictione credentes liberantur. Nam ver- satur Apostolus adhuc in legali convictione, vel de- monstratione illa, quam è lege desumpsit, ut omnes homines sub condemnatione concludat, nondum Evangelium aut gratiam, aut quod promiserit in Evangelio DEUS vitam & gloriam, explicare cœ- pit. In eo tantum adhuc occupatur, ut perfectam legis impletionem omnibus hominibus deroget, adeoque nullam carnem ex operibus justificari posse, convincat.

Τοῖς μὲν κατ᾽ ὑπομονὴν ἔργοῦ ἀγαθοῦ δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν, καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν ἐπιζητῦσι. Nam διαμονὴ ψυχῆς piis ex gentibus non quidem plane certo credita, sed ita tamen ut sententia eam adstruens probabilior crederetur, κατ᾽ ὑπόμονην hic idem est quod δι᾽ ὑπομονῆς. Solent enim istæ particulæ permisceri, ut 1. Cor. XII. 8. Eph. III. 3. & alibi. Tum vero ὑπομονὴ, quod propriè expectationem significat, po- nitur hic pro constantia: Quia expectatio talis, qualis de- scribitur Psal. XXXVII. 5. & alibi, constantiam solet produ- cere. Sic ὑπομένειν est perseverare. Matth. X. 22. & sin- gulare hic est pro plurali: ἔργα ἀγαθὰ, pro ἔργων ἀγαθῶν, ut & infra 15. 1. Cor. XIII. 14. 15. XV. 50. 1. Thessal. I. 3. 2. Thess. X. 11. 17. quod admodum frequens est, ubi rerum aliquarum universitas significatur. δόξα hic significat sta- tum illustrem, ut Matth. XIII. 42. τιμὴ conjunctum cum laude, de qua vide Joh. XII. 18. 1. Petr. I. 7. ἀφθαρσία per- petuum.

Non operum gloriam quærentes intelliguntur, quemadmodum Beza contra Græci textus distin- ctionem, Syriacam interpretationem, & Apostoli- cam intentionem transtulit, sed secundum perseve- rantiam operis boni, gloriam & honorem & incor- ruptibilitatem quærentes, designantur, quibus vita æterna danda, non quod per opera, vel propter ope- rum perseverantiam vitam consequantur, id enim repugnat ipsimet propositioni Epistolæ, justus ex fide vivet, totique tractationi, quæ huc tendit, fide & non ex operibus nos justificari, ac salvari, sed in operum perseverantia vel perseverantes in bonis operibus in fide vel per fidem in Christum glo- riam quærunt; quod Apostoli scopo & doctrinæ congruit. Quo pacto ἐκζητῦσιν iis, qui requirunt Deum per fidem, Deus gratiosus μισθαποδότης di- citur Ebr. XI. 6. Nec ergò indicatur operum vis, nedum meritum in ordine ad vitam æternam, aut intentio ejusmodi operantium, & in opere bono per- severantium, quod per opera bona consequi sata- gant, & impetrare gloriam æternam, sed descri- buntur hæredes vitæ æternæ à perseverantia in bo- no, quæ omninò in iisdem requiritur, etsi non æternæ vitæ causa & meritum, sed ut veræ fidei ar- gumentum, & consequens necessarium: Adde quod hic adhuc in causæ suæ evictione è lege oc- cupetur Apostolus, secundum quam operibus promissa est vita, sed sub conditione perfectæ imple- tionis, Lev. XVIII. 5. quam verò à nemine præsta- ri hic demonstratur. Sub specie enim assertionis, ut

Flacius in Glossa p. 665. docet, conditionaliter est loquutus, ut cum dixit Deum in extremo judicio unicuique secundum opera sua daturum esse, illis quidem qui per patientiam boni operis quærunt glo- riam ac immortalitatem, daturum esse vitam æter- nam. Item fore ut honor, gloria & pax contingat omni operanti bonum, Judæo simul & Græco. Ubi enim usquam aliquis mortalium talis est aut fuit, cui hæc tanta bona, nempe ipsa vita æterna, per sua opera innocentiamque contingere possit? sed solet crebro sic lex sub umbra assertionis condi- tionaliter loqui, tanquam si essent aliqui, qui verè legem præstarent, quibusque præmia legis con- tingerent, cum tantum ponant conditionem, quod si usquam aliquis talis observator legis exi- steret, illi contingerent tanta præmia, ut sunt illa dicta: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis: si vis in vitam in- gredi, serva mandata: Deus dabit unicuique secun- dum opera sua. Quæ natura legalium locutio- num aut velamen Mosis diligenter observandum est.

Grotius habet hic ἐπιζητῦσι, sed in textu legitur simplex ζητῦσι: & repetit è versu præcedente ver- bum ἀποδώσει, sed alii subintelligere malunt verbum δώσει, cum Syro, quum vita æterna χά- ρισμα sit, non ἀπόδοσις, ut sensus sit: Redditu- rus est unicuique secundum opera, his quidem, qui perseveranter in bene agendo gloriam, honorem, & incorruptibilitatem quærunt, dabit æternam vitam; sed si sententia hæc legaliter accipiatur eo, quo diximus sensu, repetitio verbi ἀποδώσει locum ha- bere facile poterit. Quem legalem sensum video etiam B. Gerhardo nostro probari. Etsi enim ipse Evangelicè per accommodationem explicari posse existimat, quod fide in Christum, qui nostri loco legem implevit, justificati debeamus impo- sterum ex fide benè operari, & per patientiam bo- ni operis gloriam & honorem quærere, id est, in bonis operibus tanquam in via constanter ambu- lare, ut ultimam metam, vitæ æternæ possessionem per fidem ex gratia tandem consequamur; quia vita æterna τέλος est fidei 1. Petr. I, 9. bona ope- ra sunt via regni, non causa regnandi, dicente Bernhardo tract. de grat. & lib. arbitr. præfert ta- men sensum legalem, ceu maximè convenientem: Si τὸ ζητεῖν δόξαν καθ’ ὑπομονὴν ἔργα ἀγαθῦ lega- liter accipiatur, quod maximè congruat scopo A- postolico; sensus erit, quod lex divina promittat æ- ternam vitam perfectè obedientibus. At cum propter infirmitatem carnis legem nemo in hac vita perfectè impleat, Rom. VIII. 3. ideo hæc & similes promis- siones legis redduntur nobis inutiles: proinde fi- de confugiendum est ad Christum, qui est τέλος legis, Rom. X. 4. in quo promissiones DEI sunt ναὶ καὶ ἀμήν 2. Cor. I, 20. De piis ex gentibus acci- pit hæc verba Grotius, sed non explicat, num in gentilismo persistentes, an proselytos intelligat: dicit διαμονὴν ψυχῆς illic non quidem plane certo creditam, sed ita tamen, ut sententia eam adstruens probabilior crederetur, quod de Philosophis gen- tilibus aliisque non conversis in Ethnicismo con- stat: qui animæ immortalitatem, & post solutio- nem à corpore, statum separatum, vel διαμονὴν sta- tuerunt. Quibus hunc scopum fuisse beatitudi- nem aliquam consequendi; per patientiam aut perseverantiam in benè agendo, haud difficulter docetur. Quod enim Ethnici verbi Dei revela- tione destituti non tantum immortalitatem animæ crediderint, sed & certò summum bonum sempiter- num à summo Numine expectarint, adeò etiam ut spe istius mortem ipsam contempserint, ejus rei non pauca exstant documenta. Quæ adduximus

Decade dissertation. de ortu Pseudo-Theol. Socin. pag. 80. seqq. Unum hic sistimus Jamblichum Chrysostomi Præceptorem, qui multa paucis complexus bona, inquit, anima habitabit cum Deo, & in cælo spaciabitur, quod ei domicilii loco erit: ve- rum quæ sese sceleribus & flagitiis contaminarit, ad subterranea loca detrudetur, ut judicia, quæ in sce- lestas animas exercentur, luat & perferat. Adde quod non absimilis videatur fuisse nuperorum gentilium sententia in novo orbe, si fides adhiben- da Johanni Lerio, qui in historia Americanæ navi- gationis de Toboupinambaultiis testatur, quod credant animas eorum, qui virtutem coluerint, post altissimos montes evolantes in amænissimis hortis perpetuis deliciis ac tripudiis lætum ævum agere: ignavorum contra manes abripi ad stygnam, (sic vo- cant Cacodæmonem) & cum eo sempiternos inter cruciatus vivere.

Neque dubium esse potest, ideò juxta κοινὰς ἐν- νοίας de discrimine justi & injusti bonis actionibus operam navasse Ethnicos, ut finem illum, quan- tum ipsi eundem agnovere, assequerentur: quum vero quia nemo perfectè implere præcepta divina de dilectione DEI & proximi, potuit, neque in Christum, qui solus est τέλ@ τꝫ νόμꝫ ipsi credi- dere, assequuti neutiquam sunt. Properandum toto corde ad splendorem Patris professus est Zoroaster: Finis hominis mente vivere, mentis vita Deus: & via ad Deum unica pietas cognitioni adjuncta: Sta- tuebat Mercurius Trismegistus. Nec minus præ- clare Zaleveus Locrensium Legislator in legum suarum proœmio: Par est, inquit, unumquemque pro virili dare operam, ut vir bonus sit, neque tant vita externa, quam animi proposito ac destinatione, si modo Deo charus esse velit, atque ut opum omnium jacturam facere malit, quam latum unguem defice- re à laude, ab honestate, à justitia. Docetque ibisdem præterea: Deos colendos esse, & honoran- dos, ut bonorum omnium, qua cum ratione fiunt, pa- rentes & autores. Et, ut ad hæc quisquis animum inducere possit, jubet accedere viros honestatis, & probitatis laude celebres, quorum disputatio- nibus tum de vitæ beatitate tum de improborum suppliciis ab injustis facinoribus revocetur. Quæ fuerit Pythagoræ de Religione, pietate, justitia, & honestate sententia, testantur aurea ejus verba, quibus cœlum etiam & ἀποθέωσιν promittit, qui aurigam mentem optimam constituerint. Quin & finem hujus vitæ esse dixit Pythagoras contempla- tionem, finem omnis contemplationis Deum, beati- tudinem vero hominis Deum fieri. Ita Socrates apud Platonem beatitudinis post mortem gratia omni studio adnitendum esse docet, ut in hac vita veram Sapientiam, ac virtutem consequamur, & satis, qua animam, purgemur: quia præmium pul- chrum sit, & species ingens. Plato verò pietatem summam apud homines virtutem esse, quæ erga Deum est, eaque nos justos & sanctos esse, ac beati- tudinem illam consequi, ut Deo similes reddamur. Fieri autem non posse, ut in hac vita beati simus, sed in altera haud dubiè, qui virtutem sectati fuerint, beatitudinem mercedis loco accepturos. Epictetus in Enchir. cap. XXXVIII. religionis erga Deos im- mortales illud præcipuum esse ait, rectas de eis habe- re opiniones, ut sentiamus & esse eos, & bene justeque administrare universa: parendum esse eis, & omni- bus eis, quæ fiunt, acquiescendum, & sequenda ultrò, ut quæ à mente præstantissima regantur. Ejusdem est illud: Si quid mente valemus, quid nobis agen- dum, nisi ut Deum assiduè celebremus, & gratiarum actiones canamus? Si luscinia essem, facerem, quod luscinia: Cum autem homo rationalis natus sim, quid faciam? laudabo Deum nec cessabo unquam. Vos vero ut idem faciatis, serio adhortor. Jambli- chus de myster. cap. XLV. ita differit de felicitate: Suspicaris, ne forte alia quædam ad beatitudinem, præter divinum cultum, via lateat, & quanam ista potissimum sit, interrogas. Sed profecto sit in diis bo- norum omnium essentia, perfectioque continetur, ac prima potestas, primumque bonorum illic est princi- piam, merito soli nos Sacerdotes, & qui similiter su- peris se dediderint, atque legitime unionem ad illos fuerint consequuti bonorum omnium principium atque finem studiosè prosequimur, in hoc utique statu & veritatis contemplatio adest, & intellectualis scientia consummatio. Simplicius Comment. in Epictet. super C. XXXVIII. Ut animum, inquit, Deo, cujus is autor est, dedicamus, & consecramus repurgando illum, tum vera de illo cogitatione, tum vita natura consentanea: Sic post eum corpus etiam ab ipso datum decet ei consecrari à maculis tam con- spicuis, quam latentibus repurgatum; Et rursus: Anima dum sua causæ tanquam radici inhæret, con- servatur, & suam habet perfectionem, cum qua Deus eam condidit: Si vero sese inde avellerit, & suam quasi radicem (quantum in ipsa est) deserue- rit, marcescit, & contabescit, turpis & infirma fa- cta, donec ab integro reversa, & suæ causæ conjuncta perfectionem suam recuperarit. Quid quod & Aristoteles, qui vulgo parum religiosus habetur, alicubi dicat: Homini natura inservit, ut sacrifi- cet: Cujus causam hanc reddit interpres ejus Alexander, quia scilicet in pietate erga Deum omnis felicitas nostra posita est, nullam quippe mercedem nisi Deum solum expectamus, hunc autem, qui sum- mum ipse est bonum, colendo acquirimus. Quin & Averrhoes ipse, naturam nos obligasse fatetur ad magnificandum Deum orationibus, & sacrificiis.
