Quod postremum tamen de Sacrificiis non ex na- tura, aut ratione habere potuere gentiles, quem- admodum adversus Pontificios alibi evicimus, sed è traditione, vel conversatione cum Judæis, aut pro- pagatione ab his ad alias gentes, harumque imita- tione, aut κακοζηλίᾳ habuisse credendum est.

Quod vero Grotius nos vita æterna plane certos fecisse Evangelium ait, non sensu Sociniano, quem ipse fingit, quod nempe in V. T. non fuerint pro- missiones æternæ vitæ, sed ita unicè admittendum, quod Evangelium eam rationem, qua vitam æter- nam unicè consequimur, tradat. Quod vero in Vet. Test. Pandectis etiam propositum fuit, imò in ipso πρωτευαγγελίῳ Paradisiaco, ut ad cap. III. 15. in Commentario nostro ad Genesin docuimus.

## 2:7
ζωὴν αἰώνιον) supply ἀποδώσει (He will give back). He will give them what men desire most. Posidippus: ὧν τοῖς θεοῖς ἄνθρωπος εὔχεται τυχεῖν. Τῆς ἀθανασίας κρεῖττον, οὐδὲν εὔχεται. (Of those things which a man prays to the gods to obtain. He prays for nothing better than immortality.)

The Gospel has made us clearly certain of this thing, and for this reason alone it should be valued most highly.

Latin:

ζωὴν αἰώνιον) supple ἀποδώσει. Dabit illis, quod homi- nes optant maxime. Posidippus ὧν τοῖς θεοῖς ἄνθρωπος εὔχεται τυχεῖν. Τῆς ἀθανασίας κρεῖττον, οὐδὲν εὔχεται.

Hujus rei certos nos plane fecit Evangelium, vel eo solo nomine faciendum maximi.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. Τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας.

That is, to those who are contentious. Thus the particle ἐξ among the Hebrews often denotes quality, as below III. 26, IV. 12, Galat. III. 7, Tit. III. 19. But understand ἐρίζουσι (those who contend) as against God, which is usually said of Idolatry. Thus Israel is בית המרי (the house of rebellion) Ezech. XII. 2, from the verb סרר (to rebel), which is translated as ἐρίζειν (to contend), Genes. XXVI. 35, 1 Sam. XII. 14, 15. Thus also the son סורר (rebellious) Deuter. XXI. 18, who is contumacious against his father. That complaint of God concerning the Hebrews has a similar sense: בעסוני כהבליהם (they provoked me with their vanities), παρεζήλωσάν με ἐν τοῖς εἰδώλοις αὐτῶν (they provoked me to jealousy with their idols). Deut. XXXII, 21.

καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι μὲν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.

Who do not follow the dictates of right reason, which is also called ἀλήθεια (truth) above at I. 18.

πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ.

But they follow injustice; ἀδικία (injustice) is taken here generally, so as to comprehend also ἀσέβειαν (impiety), as in the aforementioned place I. 18. πείθεσθαι (to be persuaded/to follow) means to follow, just as the Hebrews would say אחר השקר הלכים (walking after a lie).

Θυμὸς καὶ ὀργή.

It is understood, it is imminent. Where there is in the Hebrew אף which signifies grave wrath, the LXX are accustomed to place two words θυμὸς καὶ ὀργὴ, as is to be seen in Gen. XXVI. 43. Sometimes there are two words in the Hebrew also, as אף והחמה Deut. IX. 19. By that blazing wrath of God, however, a grave punishment is understood, which the following words explain more clearly.

We admit the Hebrew manner of speaking: since thus by a Hebrew phrase contentious sons are called sons of strifes, οἱ ἐξ ἐριθείας, who are of contention. In Suidas ἐριθεία is ἡ διὰ λόγων φιλονεικία, contention, which happens by words, as also ἡ μισθαρνία, mercenary work, or that which is performed for someone for the sake of receiving wages: if this latter meaning were to prevail, then punishment would be denounced both to such laborers and to those who pursue injustice: just as, on the contrary, glory is promised to believers and those who persevere in good work. But ἐριθεία in the Scriptures occurs only in the former sense for contention, 2 Cor. XII. 20, Gal. V. 20, Jas. III. 16, and thus the Syriac rendered it contentious or quarrelsome. Lyranus explains: whose soul always contends, and in whom συντήρησις, or the dictate of right reason, always murmurs back. By ἀπειθεῖς τῇ ἀληθείᾳ some understand those who do not believe the salutary doctrine proposed in the Gospel: which explanation is not inconvenient; and thus again in the preceding member, by the force of opposition, faith is tacitly included, as the beginning of a good work, and to which good works bear witness: but because the Apostle has not yet arrived at the Evangelical explanation of justification, we prefer the explanation of those who understand by the name of ἀληθείας here the true notions naturally implanted in the minds of men, as in chapter I. 18, 25. And they judge that those are said to be πειθομένως τῇ ἀδικίᾳ who pursue injustice, with the name of ἀδικίας taken generally, as it is opposed both to divine worship and to love of neighbor, which right reason dictates, in which sense he said in chapter I. 18 that they hold the truth of God in injustice, and thus Grotius not badly, καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι μὲν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ who do not follow the dictates of right reason: likewise ἀδικία is taken here generally, so that it also comprehends ἀσέβειαν.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας.

Id est τοῖς ἐρίζουσι. Sic ἐξ particula apud Hebræos sæpe qualitatem denotat, ut infra III. 26. IV. 12. Galat. III. 7. Tit. III. 19. ἐρίζουσι autem intellige, contra Deum, quod de Idololatria dici solet. Sic Israel בית המרי Ezech. XII. 2. à verbo סרר quod ἐρίζειν vertitur, Genes. XXVI. 35. 1. Sam. XII. 14. 15. Sic & filius סורר Deuter. XXI. 18. qui in patrem est contumax. Similem sensum habet illa Dei querela de Hebræis בעסוני כהבליהם παρεξή- λωσάν με ἐν τοῖς εἰδώλοις αὐτῶν. Deut. XXXII, 21.

καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι μὲν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.

Qui non sequuntur rectæ rationis dictata quæ & supra ἀλήθεια dicta est I. 18.

πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ.

Verum injustitiam sectantur, ἀδικία hic generatim sumi- tur, ut & ἀσέβειαν comprehendat, ut supra dicto loco I. 18. πείθεσθαι sectari, quomodo Gal. III. 1. V. 5. Hebræi di- cerent אחר השקר הלכים

Θυμὸς καὶ ὀργή.

Subauditur, imminet. Ubi est in Hebræo אף quod iram gravem significat, LXX. solent ponere voces duas θυμὸς καὶ ὀργὴ, ut videre est Gen. XXVI. 43. interdum & in Hebræo duæ sunt voces, ut אף והחמה Deut. IX. 19. Per iram autem illam exardescentem Dei μετατομικῶς gravis pœna intelligitur, quod clarius explicant sequentia.

Admittimus Ebræam loquendi rationem: quum ita phrasi Ebræa contentiosi filii rixarum dicuntur, οἱ ἐξ ἐριθείας, qui sunt ex contentione. Suidæ ἐριθεία est ἡ διὰ λόγων φιλονεικία, contentio, quæ fit verbis, ut & ἡ μισθαρνία opera mercenaria, vel quæ mercedis accipiendæ causa alicui navatur: quæ posterior significatio si obtineret, tum opera- riis ejusmodi, tum illis, qui injustitiam sectantur, pœna denunciaretur: ut ex adverso credentibus, & in bono opere perseverantibus gloria promissa. Sed ἐριθεία in Sacris priori tantum modo pro con- tentione occurrit 2. Cor. XII. 20. Gal. V. 20. Jac. III. 16. atque ita reddidit Syrus hic contentiosos, vel rixo- sos. Lyranus exponit: quorum anima semper con- tendit, & apud quos συντήρησις, seu dictamen rectæ rationis semper remurmurat. Per ἀπειθεῖς τῇ ἀληθείᾳ intelligunt nonnulli eos, qui salutari do- ctrina in Evangelio proposita non credunt: Quæ ex- plicatio non incommoda: atque ita iterum in membro præcedente vi oppositionis, fides tacitè in- cluditur, ceu boni operis principium, & cui testi- monium præbent bona opera: sed quia nondum Apostolus ad Evangelicam justificationis explica- tionem accessit, illorum præferimus explicatio- nem, qui veras notitias, naturaliter hominum men- tibus insitas nomine ἀληθείας hic intelligunt, ut cap. I. 18. 25. & πειθομένως τῇ ἀδικίᾳ dici censent, qui sectantur injustitiam, nomine ἀδικίας genera- liter accepto tum ut cultui divino, tum ut amori proximi, quem dictat recta ratio, opposita est, quo sensu cap. I. 18. dixit, eos veritatem Dei in in- justitia detinere, atque ita non male Grotius, καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι μὲν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ qui non sequuntur rectæ ra- tionis dictata: item ἀδικία hic generatim sumitur, ut & ἀσέβειαν comprehendat.

## 2:9
Vers. 9. θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία. Since he had hitherto shown how necessary the Gospel had been for the Gentiles, now he adds the Jews also, not a few of whom at Rome were opposing themselves to the Gospel. See the Acts at the end. These two words also of equal meaning signify the vehemence of evil, and correspond to the Hebrew צרה וצוקה as appears from the Greek of Isaiah XXX. 6. The word θλίψεως is everywhere obvious: the word στενοχωρία both in Isa. VIII. 21 and below VIII. 35, 2 Cor. VI. 4, XII. 10, στενοχωρεῖσθαι in Isa. XXVIII. 20 and elsewhere. Elsewhere στενοχωρεῖσθαι is more than θλίβεσθαι. The Latins also say 'angustiae' for misery.

ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀνθρώπου τοῦ κατεργαζομένου τὸ κακὸν. Soul is taken here for person, as often among the Hebrews. And understand the one working evil as such: for when a man's life is changed, God's decree is also changed. Ezech. XVIII.

Ἰουδαίου τε πρῶτον καὶ ἕλληνος. Just as he had preferred the Jew in privileges in I. 16, so he also prefers the same in punishments: for reason demands that he who receives more should be tormented more, if he has not responded to the benefit. The judgment of the will of God is more openly in the law divinely written and prohibiting homicides, adulteries, thefts, and other things of this kind, than in the mere collection of reason. Augustine well says in 'De vera Religione' chapter 6: The law prohibiting all sins doubles them: For it is not a simple sin to commit not only what is evil, but also what is forbidden. To this pertain those things which we shall have below IV. 15, V. 13, from which that of Tacitus, Annal. III, does not depart far: If you wish for what is not yet forbidden, you may fear that it will be forbidden: But if you have crossed forbidden things with impunity, there is neither fear nor shame any longer. Although, however, the things which are said here pertain properly to the punishments of the other life, yet God wished even beforehand to show by conspicuous signs His severity against the contumacious, the Romans indeed by sending in a most wicked tyrant, then very bloody civil wars: the Jews, however, by uprooting them utterly from their ancestral soil, with their republic and worship overturned.

That the Apostle had taught hitherto that the Gospel was necessary for the Gentiles, and now approaches the Jews themselves, which seemed to Grotius, does not appear. For he has rather dealt generally hitherto concerning natural knowledge, that by the same all may be convicted, whether they have revealed knowledge of Scripture or less. Nor does he now approach specifically the Jews, who were opposing the Gospel at Rome. For as he had dealt generally about all men before, he testified to the wrath of God revealed from heaven, which he demonstrated that all could have gathered even from nature itself: But he did not treat specifically only of the Gentiles, much less of the Romans: Which fiction Grotius devised, in order to elide the Apostolic scope, and to transform the Gospel into a legal sermon concerning a more perfect holiness, which legal admonitions, even if they were necessary for both the Gentile Romans and the Jews acting there, nevertheless did not contribute to the righteousness of faith and the salvation which the Apostle intended to teach. Although, therefore, he does not make specific mention of the Jew, because they not only had natural knowledge but also revealed, whence a heavier punishment was to be expected for them than for the Gentiles; yet he does not yet absolve the prior general demonstration concerning all men constituted under condemnation by the very dictate of nature: He only incidentally sprinkles in those heavier punishments of the Jews, being about to pass now to another special demonstration, in which the reason also shines forth, since a heavier punishment lies upon them. v. 12. Grotius rightly acknowledges that these things do not properly pertain to the punishments of the other life: What things, therefore, Grotius handed down here concerning the Romans punished by a most wicked tyrant and by very cruel civil wars, and concerning the πανωλεθρία of the Jews, do not properly apply here: Because generally all, both Jews and Gentiles, are concluded under wrath and condemnation who work evil. There is, however, no one who is excepted from this class, if they are viewed according to the law. And therefore for all, through that law which is impressed upon nature, the mouth is stopped. Nothing, therefore, does the Evangelical sentence, Ez. XVIII, contribute here, in which, however, no change of God is to be imagined: For these things are to be understood θεοπρεπῶς: God does not change in Himself, but a change may happen in divine effects, while He Himself remains immutable, Mal. III. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 9. θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία. Cum hactenus ostendisset, quam necessarium fuisset Gentibus Evangelium, nunc & Judæos addit, quorum non pauci Romæ Evangelio se opponebant. Vide acta in fine. Hæ quoque voces duæ paris significatus mali vehemen- tiam significant, respondentque Hebræis צרה וצוקה ut apparet ex Græco Esaix XXX. 6. Vox θλίψεως ubique obvia: vox στενοχωρία & Esa. VIII. 21. & infra VIII. 35. 2. Cor. VI. 4. XII. 10. στενοχωρεῖσθαι Esa. XXVIII. 20. & alibi. Alibi στενοχωρεῖσθαι plus est, quam θλίβεσθαι. La- tini quoque angustias pro miseria dicunt.

ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀνθρώπου τοῦ κατεργαζομένου τὸ κακὸν. Anima hic pro persona sumitur, ut apud Hebræos sæpe. Et operantem malum intellige qua talem: nam mutata ho- minis vita mutatur & Dei decretum. Ezech. XVIII.

Ἰουδαίου τε πρῶτον καὶ ἕλληνος. Sicut in privilegiis Judæum præposuerat I, 16. sic & eun- dem præponit in pœnis: id enim exigit ratio, ut qui plus accipit, eo plus crucietur, si beneficio non responderit. Apertius est judicium voluntatis Dei in lege divinitus scri- pta & prohibente homicidia, adulteria, furta, aliaque hu- jusmodi, quam in sola collectione rationis. Bene Augu- stinus de vera Religione cap. 6. Lex prohibens omnia deli- cta congeminat: Non enim simplex peccatum est, non solum malum, sed etiam vetitum committere. Quo pertinent ea, quæ habebimus infra IV. 15. V. 13. unde non longe abit il- lud Taciti Annal. III: Si velis quod nondum vetitum est, ti- meas ne vetetur: At si prohibita impune transcenderis, neque metus ultra, neque pudor est. Quanquam autem quæ hic dicuntur, ad pœnas vitæ alterius propriè pertinent, tamen voluit Deus etiam in antecessum conspicuis signis ostendere severitatem suam adversus contumaces, Romanos quidem, immittendo tyrannum pessimum, deinde bella civilia valde cruenta: Judæos autem, evellendo eos funditus à patrio so- lo eversa republica & cultu.

Hactenus gentilibus Evangelium necessarium fuisse, Apostolum docuisse, nunc Judæos ipsum adire, quod Grotio visum fuit, non apparet. Nam generatim potius hactenus de naturali notitia egit, quod per eandem convincantur omnes, sive reve- latam notitiam Scripturae habentes, seu minus. Neque jam specialiter ad Judaeos accedit, qui Romae Evangelio se opponebant. Nam uti communiter de omnibus hominibus egerat antea, usque reve- latam de coelo iram Dei testatus est, quam omnes vel ex ipsa natura colligere potuisse demonstravit: Non autem peculiariter tantum de gentibus, ne- dum de Romanis tractavit: Quod commentum Grotius excogitavit, ut scopum Apostolicum elide- ret, & Evangelium in concionem legalem, de per- fectiori sanctitate transformaret, quae legales ad- monitiones etsi & gentilibus Romanis & Judaeis, illic agentibus necessariae fuerint, tamen ad justi- tiam fidei, & salutem, quam docere intendebat Apostolus, non faciebant. Quamvis ergo Ju- daerum speciatim mentionem non faciat, quia illi non solum notitiam naturalem habebant, sed etiam revelatam, unde gravior ipsis poena exspe- ctanda, quam gentilibus; nondum tamen absol- vit priorem demonstrationem generalem de omni- bus hominibus natura ipsius dictatu, sub con- demnatione constitutis: Solum obiter inspergit graviora illa Judaeorum supplicia, ad alteram specia- lem jamjam transiturus demonstrationem, in qua etiam ratio effulget, cum ipsis gravior incumbat poena. v. 12. Recte autem agnoscit Grotius, hec proprie pertinere ad poenas vitae alterius: Quae ergo de Romanis per tyrannum pessimum punitis, & per civilia valde crudelia bella, deque Judaeorum πανωλεθρία hic tradidit Grotius, proprie huc non faciunt: Quia generatim omnes cum Judaei, tum gentiles, sub ira & condemnatione concluduntur, qui malum operantur. Non est autem ullus, qui ab hac classe excipiatur, si secundum legem spe- ctentur. Ideoque omnibus per legem eam, quae naturae impressa est, os obstruitur. Nihil ergo huc facit Evangelica sententia, Ez. XVIII. in qua tamen non fingenda aliqua Dei mutatio: Nam θεοπρεπῶς haec intelligenda: Deus in se non mu- tatur, sed in effectibus divinis mutatio contingat, ipso manente immutabili, Mal. III. 6.

## 2:10
Vers. 10. Δόξα δὲ καὶ τιμὴ) take as above 7. Καὶ εἰρήνη) all good things. For the Hebrews embrace all those things under the name of peace. By δόξαν is understood the glory of soul and body, by τιμὴν honor before God and the Angels, John XII. 26, by εἰρήνην peace in the conscience consummated, nor is ἡ δόξα ill opposed to τῇ θλίψει, τιμὴ to τῇ ὀργῇ, and εἰρήνη to τῇ στενοχωρίᾳ v. 9.

Vers. Eod. πάντι τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ ἀγαθὸν) namely from a mind divinely purified.

When glory and honor is said to every one working good, again it is not merit or a meritorious cause that is insinuated, but the condition of the subject is described, or rather it is likewise a legal sentence: Because in the law eternal life is promised under the condition of perfect obedience, and a curse is vibrated against those who in anything whatsoever transgress against the law, or do not keep ALL things which are written in the law, Deut. XXVI, 26.

Ἰουδαίῳ δὲ πρῶτον) because they will bear the first place in retribution.

Καὶ ἕλληνι) by ἕλληνα he here understands τὸν σεβόμενον, of which kind we said above there were few: Yet there were always some imitators of Melchizedek, and Job, and Jethro, and Naaman. See Acts X and XVII. 4. See also what we said about this matter in book 1, De Jure Belli & Pacis, and in the Annotations to that place.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Δόξα δὲ καὶ τιμὴ) accipe ut supra 7. Καὶ εἰρήνη) bona omnia. Hebraei enim ea omnia pacis nomine complectuntur. Per δόξαν gloria animae & corporis, per τιμὴν honor apud Deum & Angelos Johan. XII. 26. per εἰρήνην pax in conscientia consummata intelligitur, nec male ἡ δόξα opponitur τῇ θλίψει, τιμὴ ν. τῇ ὀργῇ & εἰρήνη τῇ στενο- χωρίᾳ v. 9.

Vers. Eod. πάντι τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ ἀγαθὸν) nempe ex ani- mo divinitus purgato.

Cum gloria & honor dicitur omni operanti bo- num, iterum non meritum, aut causa meritoria in- sinuatur, sed subjecti describitur conditio, vel po- tius sententia itidem legalis est: Quia in lege & vita aeterna promissa est sub conditione perfectae obedientiae, & maledictio in eos vibrata, qui in ullo tantum adversus legem praevaricantur, vel non servant OMNIA, quae in lege scripta sunt Deut. XXVI, 26.

Ἰουδαίῳ δὲ πρῶτον) quia primas in retributione fe- rent.

Καὶ ἕλληνι) ἕλληνα hic intelligit τὸν σεβόμενον quales pau- cos fuisse, supra diximus: Fuere tamen semper aliqui imi- tatores Melchisedeci, & Jobi, & Jethronis & Naamanni, Vide Actor. X. & XVII. 4. Vide & quae diximus hac de re lib. 1. de Jure Belli & Pacis, & in Annotatis ad eum locum.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. οὐ γάρ ἐστι προσωποληψία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ) προσωποληψία is to the Rabbis מַשׂוֹא פָּנִים, 18. 1. X. 34. The same sentiment as Deut. X. 17. He is said to respect a person who in judgment looks to something other than what comes into judgment. When God judges men, He does not look to origin, but to actions, Ephes. VI. 9. Coloss. III. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17. In distributing benefits, origin sometimes counts for something; in divine judgments, nothing.

Acceptio faciei to the Hebrews Gen. XIX. 21. c. XXV. 15.

προσωποληψία is forbidden to the Greeks, when they respect external things which strike the eyes and render a person commendable, but do not pertain to the cause itself, such as riches, honor, dignity, kinship, power, and the like. Lev. XIX. 16. Deuter. I. 17. cap. XVI. 19. Prov. XVIII. cap. XXIV. 24. Whence the acceptance of persons is described by Augustine in Ad 2. Ep. Pelag. lib. II. cap. 7, where he says that he who judges, leaving the merit of the cause about which he judges, favors one against another. But if anyone has two debtors, and wishes to forgive the debt to one and exact it from the other, he gives to whom he wishes, but defrauds no one. Nor is it to be called acceptance of persons when there is no iniquity. Grotius rightly: He is said to respect a person who in judgment looks to something other than what comes into judgment. When God judges men, He does not look to origin, but to actions, Eph. VI. 9. Col. III. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17. in distributing benefits, origin sometimes counts for something; in divine judgments, nothing.

The Papists abuse the Apostolic rule when they conclude from this that God does not predestine to life without foreseen merits, lest He be a προσωπολήπτης (respecter of persons). For it is not to be admitted so universally: He who distributes a reward without merits is a respecter of persons. It could be admitted concerning a reward given according to justice, but not according to grace, Cajetan in this place. Respect of persons, he says, is a vice contrary to justice, and has no place in liberal gifts. But eternal life is a χάρισμα, or a liberal gift of God, Rom. 6:23. And a distinction must be made between judicial and extrajudicial respect of persons; for that is especially a vice, by which in judgment a person is regarded—that is, some transitory condition not relevant to the matter itself, existing around the person—and in respect of it, one person is preferred to another in conferring upon him something which, by the debt of justice, is to be conferred upon the other, as in the Summa Angelica. in the entry 'Persona' it is described. But that does not happen in the judgment of God, since He adjudges life to believers without merits, and death to unbelievers because of merits. For to the latter no injury is done, because they have merited death, nor in the former is a person or condition regarded that is not relevant to the matter itself, but the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith. Finally, Cornelius à Lapide admits that when Scripture denies the respect of persons, it does not take it properly as a vice against distributive justice, but insofar as this respect of persons is opposed to the liberal indifference of God toward all men, as if to say: God does not care whether one is a Jew or a Greek, rich or poor; but He distributes His graces and His gifts indifferently to Gentiles as well as Jews, to the poor as well as the rich.

But as poorly as the Papists drag the Apostolic axiom to predestination from foreseen merits, so rightly do our people urge it against the absolute decree of the Calvinists. For that God should absolutely pass over some with His grace, only because it so pleases Him, is repugnant to this Apostolic sentence and to divine universal grace, which indifferently regards all men, without discrimination of persons: For He has concluded all under unbelief, that He might have mercy upon all, Rom. 11:32. Nor can that be reconciled with divine justice, that eternal punishments should be inflicted without any merit, from an absolute good pleasure. For it is unjust to sentence or afflict anyone with punishments without fault. For as Augustine rightly says, Book III against Julian the Pelagian, chapter 18: God is good, God is just: He can deliver without good merits, because He is good: He cannot damn anyone without merits, because He is just. Concerning God not being a respecter of persons, there are many places: Deut. X. 17. 2. Par. XIX. 7. Job. XXXIV. 19. Act. X. 34. Gal. II. 6. Eph. VI. 9. Coloss. III. 11. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 11. οὐ γάρ ἐστι προσωποληψία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ) προσω- ποληψία Rabbinis מַשׂוֹא פָּנִים, 18. 1. X. 34. Eadem sen- tentia, quo Deut. X. 17. Personam respicere dicitur, qui in judicio aliud respicit, quam quod in judicium venit, Deus cum homines judicat, non originem respicit, sed actio- nes Ephes. VI. 9. Coloss. III. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17. In benefi- ciis distribuendis aliquid interdum origo valet, in judiciis divinis nihil.

Acceptio faciei Ebraeis Gen. XIX. 21. c. XXV. 15.

προσωποληψία Græcis prohibita est, cum externa, quæ in oculos incurrunt, & personam commen- dabilem reddunt, ad ipsam vero causam non per- tinent, ut sunt divitiæ, honor, dignitas, cognatio, potentia, & similia respiciunt. Lev. XIX. 16. Deu- ter. I. 17. cap. XVI. 19. Prov. XVIII. cap. XXIV. 24. Unde acceptio personarum ab Augustino ad 2. Ep. Pelag. lib. II. cap. 7. describitur, ubi ille, qui judi- cat relinquens causæ meritum, de qua judicat, alteri contra alterum suffragatur. Si autem quispiam habeat debitores duos, & alteri vellet dimittere debi- tum, alterum exigere, cui vult, donat, sed neminem fraudat. Nec acceptio personarum dicenda est, quando iniquitas nulla est. Recte Grotius: Per- sonam respicere dicitur, qui in judicio aliud respicit, quam quod in judicium venit. Deus cum homines judicat, non originem respicit, sed actiones, Eph. VI. 9. Col. III. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17. in beneficiis distribuendis aliquid interdum origo valet, in judiciis divinis nihil.

Abutuntur autem Regulà Apostolicà Papistæ, quando hinc concludunt, Deum non prædestinare ad vitam absque prævisis meritis, ne sit προσωπο- λήπτης. Non enim ita universaliter admittenda est: Qui præmium distribuit sine meritis, acceptor est personarum. Admitti posset de præmio dando secundum justitiam, non autem secundum gratiam, Cajet. in h. l. Acceptio, inquit, personarum vitium est contrarium justitiæ, & non habet locum in libe- ralibus donis. Est autem vita æterna χάρισμα, seu liberale Dei donum Rom. VI. ult. Et distin- guenda est προσωποληψία judicialis, & extrajudi- cialis; illa enim potissimum in vitio est, qua in ju- dicio persona respicitur, id est, conditio aliqua transitoria, non congruens ad ipsam vim, existens circa personam, ejusque respectum, persona personæ præfertur in conferendo ei aliquid, quod ex debito justitiæ alteri est conferendum, ut in summ. Angelic. in voce Persona describitur. Id autem in judicio Dei non contingit, cum credentibus vitam adju- dicat citra merita, incredulis mortem propter me- rita. His enim non sit injuria, quia meriti sunt mortem, nec in illis respicitur persona seu condi- tio aliqua non congruens ad rem ipsam, sed meri- tum Christi vera fide apprehensum. Tandem fa- tetur. Corn. à Lap. cùm Scriptura negat acceptio- nem personarum, non accipere eam propriè pro vitio contra justitiam distributivam, sed quatenus acceptio hæc personarum opponitur indifferentiæ liberali Dei erga omnes homines q. d. Deus non cu- rat, an Judæus sit, an Græcus, an dives, an pauper; sed indifferenter suas gratias, suaque dona distri- buit tam gentilibus, quam Judæis, tam pauperi- bus, quam divitibus.

Quam malè autem ad prædestinationem è me- ritis prævisis trahunt Apostolicum axioma Papi- stæ, tam probè urgent id nostri adversus Calvinia- norum absolutum decretum. Quod enim Deus absolutè quosdam prætereat sua gratia, tantum quia ita placet, repugnat huic Apostolicæ senten- tiæ, divinæque universali gratiæ, quæ indifferen- ter respicit omnes homines, sine personarum discrimine: Omnes enim conclusit sub incredu- litate, ut misereatur omnium Rom. XI. 34. Neque conciliari potest illud cum divina justitia, quod pœnæ æternæ infligantur sine ullo merito, ex absoluto beneplacito. Nam injustum est, quenquam absque culpa suis pœnis addicere, vel afficere. Nam ut recte Augustinus lib. III. contr. Jul. Pelagian. ca- pit. 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est: non potest quenquam sine meritis damnare, quia justus est. Deo quod non sit προσωπολήπτης, loca plura sunt Deut. X. 17. 2. Par. XIX. 7. Job. XXXIV. 19. Act. X. 34. Gal. II. 6. Eph. VI. 9. Coloss. III. 11. 25. 1. Petr. I. 17.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. For as many as have sinned without law.

He calls that law here, which has been published by God by voice or in writing. ἀνόμως here is equivalent to בְּאֵין תּוֹרָה, that is, when they did not have such a law: This does not indeed take away the guilt, but it diminishes it, Luke XII. 43, 48, below IV. 15, V. 13, and in this state were the Gentiles, whom he calls Greeks, from the part better known to the Jews. The division of men into those under the law and those without law is found in 1. Cor. IX. 21.

shall also perish without law.

Those are said to perish who in any way fall away from that blessed life after this one, to which σώζεσθαι is opposed. See John X. 28, below XIV. 15, 1. Cor. I. 18, VIII. 11, 2. Cor. II. 15, IV. 3, 2. Thess. II. 10. This is what is mystically signified by the נִכְרַתְּ of the law. They shall perish without law, that is, they will be punished less, says Chrysostom, II. on Fasting.

and as many as have sinned in the law.

That is, when they had such a law. Thus בְּ is often placed by the Hebrews, and ἐν by our writers, as Matth. VI. 22, XVI. 27, XXV. 31, 2. Cor. XIII. 4, 2. Tim. I. 13; therefore what is said here and in III. 19 as in the law is explained below in 14 as those who do the things of the law. Understand sin here not in that most lax sense, but in a more restrictive and eminent one, in which sense those regenerated by God are said not to sin.

shall be judged by the law.

They will be brought to heavy punishments, the law convicting them, which they did not observe even in the most important and easiest matters to observe. Moses will accuse them: John V. 45. It was not just that if the crimes of some had not come to notice, or had escaped the severity of judges in some other way, they should escape punishment. Wherefore God himself had promised in the law that he would be the avenger of such, Lev. XVII. 10, XXXII. 2, 3, 5, 6, 17. But this vengeance is not always fulfilled in this life, but is often reserved for the day of judgment, as follows below in 16.

The general demonstration now being finished, a special one follows, likewise proving that all men are sinners and liable to punishment; which is this: Whoever violates the written or unwritten law sins and is liable to divine punishment. But the Greeks or Gentiles violate the unwritten law, namely, that which is impressed upon their hearts: the Jews, however, the written law or that prescribed by Moses. Therefore both Gentiles and Jews sin and are liable to divine punishment. He has the major premise in v. 12: For as many as have sinned without the written law shall perish without law: and as many as have sinned in the (written) law shall be judged by the written law, with which verse, the parenthesis being concluded, verse 16 seems to some to cohere: In the day when God shall judge the secrets of hearts according to my Gospel through JESUS Christ. The major premise is confirmed in v. 13, 14, 15. from law and justice: For not the hearers of the law are just before God, that is, justified, as the antithesis teaches, but the doers of the law shall be justified, or pronounced just. But those who have not only the unwritten but also the prescribed law, and violate it, are going to suffer so much the heavier punishments. Now as to the minor premise, he deals first with the Gentiles, v. 14. For he had not yet dealt with them specifically, even though the vices which he had recounted in chapter 1 had flourished in great part especially among the Gentiles. But he has no need to teach concerning them that they violated the law of nature, which was sufficiently evident already from the general argument: He only explains and confirms concerning them particularly that they are not ignorant of the law, but have it innate in their minds: Which he confirms both from their honest deeds according to the law and from the tribunal of their consciences within them. Blessed Gerhard also acknowledges this here, that that universal accusation of the human race, of which the Apostle had treated earlier, is now applied individually to the Gentiles and Jews: because the whole human race is contained within their scope. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law (namely, prescribed as the Jews do), by nature do the things of the law (he implies that they do not do all things, but many things commanded by the law by the instinct of nature or right reason alone), such people, not having the law, are a law unto themselves; they are described in such a way that they do not have a law prescribed from without, whether by promulgation, or by institution, or by any other external cause, but that by nature, and such as they are by themselves, they know what is to be done and what is to be avoided: For this is to be a law unto themselves, with no one dictating, to know by nature itself or the law of nature alone what is to be done, to know the distinction between honorable and base things. Grotius therefore perverts the sense of the Apostle, when he teaches that to sin here is not to be understood in the loosest sense of transgression against the law or ἀνομίᾳ, but in a more restricted and eminent sense, in which sense the regenerate are said not to sin, for the Apostle is intent on concluding the whole world outside of Christ under sin.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὅσοι γὰρ ἀνόμως ἥμαρτον.

Legem hic vocat eam, quæ à Deo voce, aut scripto pu- blicata est. ἀνόμως hic valet בְּאֵין תּוֹרָה, id est, cùm legem talem non haberent: Id culpam non tollit quidem, sed minuit Luc. XII. 43. 48. infra IV. 15. V. 13. & in hoc statu erant Gentes, quos Græcos a parte Judæis notiore ap- pellat. Per divisio hominum in τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον & ἀνόμους re- peritur 1. Cor. IX. 21.

ἀνόμως καὶ ἀπολοῦνται.

ἀπολοῦνται dicuntur quicunque ullo modo à vita illa post hanc beata excidunt, cui opponitur σώζεσθαι. Vide Joh. X. 28. infra XIV. 15. 1. Cor. I. 18. VIII. 11. 2. Cor. II. 15. IV. 3. 2. Thess. II. 10. Hoc est, quod mysticè signi- ficatur per legis נִכְרַתְּ. ἀνόμως καὶ ἀπολοῦνται, id est, mi- nus punientur, ait Chrysostomus II. de Jejunio.

καὶ ὅσοι ἐν νόμῳ ἥμαρτον.

Id est, cum legem talem haberent. Ita בְּ sæpè ponitur Hebræis, & ἐν nostris, ut Matth. VI. 22. XVI. 27. XXV. 31. 2. Cor. XIII. 4. 2. Tim. I. 13. ideo quod hic & III. 19. di- citur ἐν νόμῳ infra 14. explicatur τὰ τοῦ νόμου ἔχοντα. Peccare hic intellige non in significatu illo laxissimo, sed restrictio- re, & eminentiore, quo sensu per Deum regeniti negantur peccare.

διὰ νόμου κριθήσονται.

Gravibus suppliciis adducentur, lege eos convincente, quam non observarunt etiam in potissimis & facillimis ob- servatu. Moses eos accusabit: Joh. V. 45. Aequum non erat, ut si quorum crimina ad notitiam non pervenissent, aut alio aliquo modo effugissent judicum severitatem, pœ- nas effugerent. Quare talium se ultorem Deus ipse in le- ge promiserat, Lev. XVII. 10. XXXII. 2. 3. 5. 6. 17. Hæc autem ultio non semper in hac vita expletur, sed sæpe refer- vatur in diem judicii, ut sequitur infra 16.

Absoluta jam generali demonstratione specialis succedit, itidem probans, omnes homines peccato- res esse, & supplicio obnoxios; quæ hæc est: Qui le- gem scriptam, vel non scriptam violant, peccant & supplicio divino sunt obnoxii. At Græci seu Ethni- ci violant legem non scriptam, cordibus sc. ipsorum impressam: Judæi vero scriptam vel à Mose præ- scriptam. Ergo & Ethnici & Judæi peccant, & sup- plicio divino sunt obnoxii. Majorem v. 12. habet: Quicunque enim sine lege scripta peccarunt, sine lege peribunt: & quicunque in lege (scriptâ) peccarunt, per legem scriptam judicabuntur, cum quo versu, parenthesi interjectâ conclusâ, versus 16. cohære- re quibusdam videtur: In die, cum judicabit Deus occulta cordium secundum Evangelium meum per JESUM Christum. Confirmatur autem major v. 13. 14. 15. à jure & justitia: Non enim auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, hoc est, justificatur, ut ἀντίθεσις docet, sed factores legis justificabuntur, seu justi pronunciabuntur. Illi autem, qui legem non inscriptam modò, sed & præscriptam habent, & violant eam, tantò graviores pœnas daturi sunt. Jam quod ad minorem primùm de gentibus agit Apostolus, vers. 14. Hactenus enim speciatim de illis nondum egerat, etsi vitia quæ cap. 1. recen- fuerat magnam partem imprimis inter gentes vi- guerint. De illis vero non opus habet docere, quod legem naturæ violarint, quod satis constabat, jám è generali argumento: Explicat solum & con- firmat de iisdem particulariter, quod non ignaræ sint legis, sed mentibus eam habeant ingenitam: Quod tum à factis eorum honestis secundum le- gem, tum à conscientiarum tribunali in ipsis con- firmat. Agnofcit id etiam hic B. Gerhardus, uni- versalem illam humani generis accusationem, de qua prius egerat Apostolus, nunc sigillatim ad gentiles & Judæos applicari: quia illorum am- bitu totum genus humanum continetur. Quum enim gentes, quæ legem non habent, (præscri- ptam scilicet ut Judæi) τῇ φύσει naturaliter ea quæ legis sunt, faciunt, (non omnia, sed multa à lege præcepta eos facere solo naturæ seu rectæ rationis instinctu, innuit,) tales legem non habentes ipsi sibi sunt lex; describuntur ita quod legem extrinsecus præscriptam non habeant, sive per promulgatio- nem, sive per institutionem, sive per aliam quam- cunque externam causam, sed quod naturâ, & qua- les ipsi per se sunt, sciant quæ facienda & fugienda: Hoc enim est sibi ipsis legem esse, nemine dictante, solum naturâ ipsâ seu lege naturæ scire, quæ agen- da sunt, honestorum & turpium discrimen nosse. Pervertit itaque Grotius sensum Apostoli, cùm peccare hic non in significatu laxissimo de prævari- catione contra legem vel ἀνομίᾳ intelligendum esse docet, sed restrictiore & eminentiore, quo sensu re- geniti negantur peccare, nam in eo est Aposto-. lus, ut totum mundum extra Christum, sub pecca- to concludat.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. For not the hearers of the law) It matters little to learn precepts by heart, unless they are fulfilled in deed. A similar sentiment, but applied to the Gospel, is in James 1:28. Thus Epictetus on the books of Chrysippus: I would admire the interpreter, and up to this point there is nothing solemn; but when I find the interpreter, it remains to use the things commanded. This alone is solemn; but if I admire this very act of interpreting, what else have I become but a grammarian instead of a philosopher, except that instead of Homer I interpret Chrysippus? Therefore, rather, when someone says to me, 'Read Chrysippus to me,' I blush when I cannot show deeds similar and in agreement with the words. Explaining which, Simplicius cites that saying of Demosthenes: 'As every speech, if deeds are absent, appears something vain and empty.' Seneca: 'What do laws avail without morals?' Josephus: 'For knowledge is not enough, but one must also do the things commanded.' No sick person will be healed by the mere fact that he reads Hippocrates. Many have warned that these words and those that follow up to ἡμέρᾳ are parenthetical.

This proposition is not indeed formally and explicitly, yet materially and implicitly, hypothetical, as is clear from a comparison of Matthew 19:17, 'If you wish to enter into life (through obedience to the law) keep the commandments,' and Galatians 3:11, 'He who shall do these things shall live in them.' And therefore the blessed Luther rightly warned that a conditional statement asserts nothing indicatively, and that those sayings show not what men can do, but what they ought to do. Which, however, are not only an indication of our debt, but also like a tutor leading to Him who paid it for us, so that through the same we might be freed from the rigor of the demand. For since, as we warned in Theol. Apost. Roman. Orac. XVIII. p. 75, it is certain that there is no conflict among the Apostolic utterances, by which he now asserts that the doers of the law are justified, and now denies that anyone will be justified by the works of the law, and teaches that we are justified by faith alone without the works of the law, those same things must be reconciled from the Apostle himself. But they cannot be reconciled by a distinction between first and second justification, as if the former is done by faith, the latter by works: Or even by a distinction between works done without grace, and those done through grace, as if the former were excluded from justification, but the latter were the cause of justification. For these are the rotten inventions of the Sophists: concerning which it is so far from the case that they can bring even a tittle from the Apostolic writings, that they are rather soundly refuted by them, as will be taught in its proper place. But they are reconciled by the Apostle in this way, that a man could indeed be justified by the observance of the law, if he performed it perfectly: But not if there is anyone besides Christ who performs it, and therefore no one can be justified by the law. Whence the Apostle invincibly concludes that we shall be justified by faith in Christ without the works of the law, because indeed Christ performed the law in our place, and freed us from the curse of the law, under which we had been concluded because of sin. This saying, therefore, is legal, promising justification and life, but with the condition of perfect obedience. But to do the law, those are said to do, who continue in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. XXVII. 28. Gal. III. 20. Such doers of the law are altogether just, not only before men, but also before God, and through obedience to the law they obtain life, Lev. XVIII. 6. Luke X. 24. But because such a doer of the law is not given, thence also the law was not given, which could vivify, that is, justify, Gal. III. 21. Therefore the Apostle speaks of right, not of fact, because the law demands most perfect obedience, not only external, but also internal, nay, the highest integrity of the whole nature. But that such doers of the law are not given, he teaches here by design: so that he may conclude that no one is justified by the law. Let those things be seen which were said more fully concerning these in the oracles of the cited place. Grotius advises with others that these words and those which follow up to 'in the day' are parenthetical, but an accurate analysis teaches that there is no need for a parenthesis, since all things flow in order and make for the scope of the Apostle. But that he refutes only that sufficiently pestilent opinion of the Rabbis, that everyone who professes Judaism, however he may have lived, will have a part in the future age: Although it may be conceded to Grotius, yet the Apostle does not only do this, but rather teaches that all Jews, who sought to be justified before God through the law, are transgressors of the law, and are convicted of it through the law.

righteous before God) They have that righteousness which God rewards with eternal prizes. See above I. 17. The pestilent opinion of the Rabbis is refuted here, teaching that everyone who professes Judaism, however he may have lived, will have a part in the future age. Justin expresses this opinion thus: 'supposing that in any case to those who are from the seed according to the flesh of Abraham, even if they are sinners and disobedient toward God, the eternal kingdom will be given.'

But the doers of the law shall be justified) Here 'shall be justified' is the same as 'are righteous' in the preceding member, that is, 'tsadqu' in Kal: namely, just before God, as both the preceding and following things evince. But the condition which was just now understood concerning the Gentiles must also be understood here, namely, from a pure heart, as we said above 10. 'ha-qedoshim be-mitsvot', who sanctify themselves in the precepts, as the Hebrews speak. God gives His Spirit to the just: since He did not give it to the Hebrews while the law still remained, except to the 'blameless' according to the law. For without such zeal they were not just, Luke I. 6. But to whom He does not now give His Spirit, them He does not make certain of eternal life. Below he will say that the righteousness which avails before God does not come from the law of Moses, namely, distinct from those duties which were required even before the law.

Latin:

Vers. 13. οὐ γὰρ οἱ ἀκροαταὶ τοῦ νόμου) Parum refert me- moriter discere præcepta, nisi re impleantur. Par sententia, sed ad Evangelium applicata Jac. I. 28. Sic de Chrysippi libris Epictetus: Ζῆλῶ ἂν τὸν ἐξηγούμενον, καὶ μέχρι τούτων ἄπω σεμνὸν οὐδέν· ὅταν δὲ ἕυρω τὸν ἐξηγούμενον, ἀπολείπεται χρῆσθαι τοῖς παρηγγελμένοις. Τοῦτο ἀυτὸ μόνον σεμνόν ἐστιν· ἂν δὲ ἀυτὸ τοῦτο τὸ ἐξηγεῖσθαι θαυμάσω, τί ἄλλο ἢ γραμματικὸς ἀποτε- λέσθην ἀντὶ φιλοσόφου, πλὴν γε δὴ ὅτι ἀντὶ Ὁμήρου χρύσιππον ἐξηγοῦμαι; μᾶλλον οὖν ὅταν τις εἴπῃ μοι, ἐπαναγνῶθί μοι χρύσιππον, ἐρυθριῶ ὅταν μὴ δύνωμαι ὅμοια τὰ ἔργα καὶ σύμ- φωνα ἐπιδεικνύειν τοῖς λόγοις. Cui explicando Simplicius illud citat Demosthenis: ὡς ἄπας λόγος, ἂν ἀπῇ τὰ ἔργα, μάταιόν τι φαίνεται καὶ κενὸν. Seneca: Quid leges sine moribus Vanæ proficiunt? Josephus : ἡ γνῶσις γὰρ δεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ προταττόμενα πράττειν. Nemo ægrotus eo solo sanabitur, quod Hippo- cratem legat. Hæc verba & quæ sequuntur usque in ἡμέρᾳ esse παρενθετικὰ complures monuere.

Propositio hæc non quidem formaliter & ex- plicite, materialiter tamen & implicitè hypothetica est, ut è collatione Matth. XIX. 17. Si vis ingredi vitam (per legis obedientiam) serva mandata, & Galat. III. 11. Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis, liquet. Ideoque meritò monuit B. Lutherus conditiona- lem indicativè nihil afferere, eaque dicta non quid possint, sed quid debeant homines ostendere. Quæ tamen non tantum debiti nostri indicium sunt, sed etiam pædagogi instar ad eum, qui pro nobis id exsolvit, ut per eundem ab exactionis rigore libe- remur. Quum enim, ut in Theol. Apost. Roman. Orac. XVIII. p. 75. monuimus, certum sit, nullam inter effata Apostolica esse pugnam, quibus jam afferit, factores legis justificari, jam negat, quen- quam per opera legis justificatum iri, nosque sola fide absque legis operibus justificari docet, concilianda erunt eadem ex ipso Apostolo. Non autem con- ciliari possunt distinctione inter justificationem primam & secundam, quasi illa fiat per fidem, hec per opera: Vel etiam distinctione inter opera fine gratia facta, & per gratiam facta, quasi illa exclu- dantur à justificatione, hæc autem causa sint justi- ficationis. Nam hæc Sophistarum putida sunt commenta: De quibus tantum abest, ut vel api- cem ex Apostolicis scriptis afferre possint, ut foli- dè potius ex illis profligentur,quemadmodum suo loco docebitur. Ita vero conciliantur eadem ab Apostolo, quod justificari quidem homo posset per legis observantiam, si eam ex asse præstaret: Non autem si præter Christum ullus, qui præstet, ideo- que nemo possit justificari per legem. Unde invi- ctè concludit Apost. per fidem in Christum fine ope- ribus legis nos justificatum iri, quia nempe Chri- stus nostri loco legem præstitit,nosque ab execra- tione legis, sub qua propter peccatum conclusi eramus, liberavit. Dictum ergò hoc est legale promittens justificationem & vitam, sed cum con- ditione perfectæ obedientiæ. Facere autem legem- illi dicuntur, qui permanent in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, Deuter. XXVII. 28. Gal. III. 20. Tales factores legis omnino sunt justi, non solum coram hominibus, sed etiam apud Deum, & per le- gis obedientiam vitam consequuntur, Lev. XVIII. 6. Luc. X. 24. Quia vero talis ποιητὴς legis non datur, inde etiam non est data lex, quæ posset vivifi- care, id est justificare Gal. III. 21. De jure itaque lo- quitur Apostolus, non de facto, quod lex perfe- ctissimam obedientiam, non solum externam, sed etiam internam, imò summam totius naturæ inte- gritatem exigat. Tales autem legis factores non dari hic ex instituto docet: ut concludat neminem per legem justificari. Videantur quæ de his ube- rius in oraculis l. c. dicta. Grotius hæc verba & quæ sequuntur usque ἐν ἡμέρᾳ parenthetica esse cum aliis monet, sed accurata analysis docet nullâ opus esse parenthesi, cum omnia ordine fluant & ad scopum Apostoli faciant. Quod autem refellat tantùm illam Rabbinorum satis pestilentem sen- tentiam, omnem qui Judaismum profitetur, quomo- docunque vixerit, partem habiturum in futuro sæcu- lo: Etsi Grotio concedi possit, non tamen Apo- stolus id tantùm agit, sed potius Judæos omnes, qui per legem quærebant justificari coram Deo, legis transgressores esse, ac per legem de eo convinci docet.

δίκαιοι παρὰ τῷ θεῷ) Justitiam eam habent, quam Deus æternis præmiis repensat. Vide supra I. 17. Refellitur hic pestilens Rabbinorum sententia, docens omnem, qui Ju- daismum profitetur, 'quomodocunque vixerit, partem ha- biturum in futuro seculo. Hanc sententiam sic exprimit Justinus: ὑπολαμβάνοντες ὅτι πάντως τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς τῆς κατὰ σάρκα τῦ Ἀβραὰμ ὖσι, κἄν ἁμαρτωλοὶ ὦσι, καὶ ἀπειθεῖς πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, ἡ βασιλεία ἡ αἰώνιος δοθήσεται.

Ἀλλ' οἱ ποιηταὶ τῦ νόμυ δικαιωθήσονται) Hic δικαιωθήσονται idem est quod in præcedenti membro δίκαιοί εἰσι, id est, צדקו in Kal: justi nempe coram Deo, ut & præcedentia & sequentia evincunt. Intelligenda autem & hic conditio quæ modo de gentibus subintellecta est, nempe ex mundo corde, ut diximus supra 10. הקרשים במצות qui se sanctificant in præceptis, ut loquuntur Hebræi. Deus Spi- ritum suum dat justis: cum non dabat Hebræis manente adhuc lege nisi ἀμέμπτοις secundum legem. Nam sine tali studio justi non erant Luc. I. 6. Quibus autem nunc non dat Spiritum suum, eos certos non facit vitæ æternæ. In- fra dicet justitiam quæ coram Deo valet non contingere ex lege Mosis, nempe distincta ab iis officiis, quæ etiam ante legem requirebantur.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. For when the Gentiles who do not have the law) 'Gentiles', that is, 'ummot' or 'goyim', as the Jews call other nations. 'Not having the law', interpret as above 11.

By nature do the things of the law) 'Nature' here is opposed to 'law', it does not signify a disposition corrupted by evil education, but the right use of reason, the faculty of which is innate to man: nor does it exclude all the aids of God. Thus Aristotle distinguishes 'the just by nature' and 'the just by institution', and jurists distinguish natural and civil law. So also 1 Cor. XI. 14. Add here what we have brought from Josephus, Justin, and Clement to Matt. V. 17. By 'the things of the law' understand those which are commanded both by nature and by law, such as, 'Thou shalt not kill', 'Thou shalt not commit adultery', 'Thou shalt not steal'. Thus to know these would suffice for the Jews, it would suffice also for the Gentiles, although these had perceived it by the guidance of reason, the Jews also by the prescription of the law. But to the Gentiles that does not suffice. Therefore neither to the Jews: 'for God is no respecter of persons', as it excels.

Flacius wishes a Gentile to be introduced by a certain rhetorical concession: If there were such a one who did the law, he would be just without the written law and the ceremonies of the law, so that it may be shown that the external, shadowy, and ceremonial righteousness of the Jews is worth nothing. The cause of this explanation is that the argument of the knowledge inscribed on hearts may be eluded. For therefore Flacius contends that the opinion of the Apostle here is not assertive, but conditional, that it is not said that the law is inscribed on hearts, but if they did the things which are of the law, it would be inscribed; But the Apostle asserts both: To these he considers the Gentiles, such as they are after the fall, not such as they could be, or that such ought to be according to nature instituted at the beginning of creation, And to do 'the things of the law' is for them a certain thing, to perform what things are of the law, not all things which the law requires, and therefore he excludes here not the ceremonial law, but primarily the moral law from justification, when he teaches that we are justified by faith alone, not by works of the law. It could certainly seem that the present passage should be expounded hypothetically because of the particle 'when', which almost all interpreters accept hypothetically, but the text teaches that it must be assumed here affirmatively, not negatively: But the scope of the Apostle is to convince the Gentiles that the means of knowing were not lacking to them, and that they are inexcusable, even if instructed only by the light of nature, and the conclusion of the Apostle also proves that, namely, that the Gentiles sinning without the written law are to be condemned without the law, from the law of nature alone. And therefore to do well, and the excuse of conscience, and that they do certain 'things of the law', is from nature, as a principle of doing well in the Gentiles, but not indeed from faith, as Augustine book IV against Julian, or from a certain spiritual grace superadded to nature, as the Arminians, especially Arnoldus Corvinus against Molin. ch. XLI. 42. wish. Because otherwise a certain law written in the hearts of the Gentiles, who are without the law, would not be rightly inferred here: Hence Toletus, Bellarmine, Justinianeus, and Tirinus refute the opinion of Augustine here. But that the salvation of the Gentiles is wrongly built from this oracle by the Papists and some Calvinists, with the Pelagians leading the way, or even supernatural grace by the Arminians, we showed in oracle XIX, which can be compared here.

who do not have the law) Repeated for the sake of greater evidence, from that which had preceded. And note, the masculine is rendered to the neuter noun by that construction which is called 'according to the meaning', as Matt. XXVIII. 19. Acts XV. 17.

they are a law unto themselves.) That is, they provide for themselves that which the law does for the Jews. There is here a πλοκὴ, and at the same time an ὀξύμωρον. A similar ὀξύμωρον is below at 25: your circumcision has become uncircumcision. There is also a μετάληψις because the cause is named for the effect, although proceeding from another cause.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὅταν γὰρ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα) ἔθνη id est, אימות vel גוים quomodo Judæi vocant gentes alias. Non habentes legem, interpretare ut supra 11.

Φύσει τὰ τῦ νόμυ ποιῇ) Φύσις hic cum νόμῳ opponitur, non significat ingenium prava educatione corruptum, sed usum rectum rationis cujus facultas homini agnata est: neque omnia Dei auxilia excludit. Sic τὸ δίκαιον φύσει & τὸ δίκαιον θέσει distinguit Aristoteles, ac jurisperiti jus naturale ac ci- vile. Sic & 1. Cor. XI. 14. Adde hic, quæ ex Josepho, Ju- stino, & Clemente attulimus ad Matth. V. 17. τὰ νόμυ in- tellige illa, quæ & natura & lege præcipiuntur, ut, Non oc- cides, Non mœchaberis, non furaberis. Sic hæc nosse Ju- dæis suffeceret, suffeceret & gentibus, quanquam hæ ductu rationis, Judæi etiam legis præscripto id perceperant. At gentibus id non fufficit. Ergo nec Judæis: ὐ γὰρ προσω- πολήπτης ὁ θεὸς, ut præcellit.

Flacius Ethnicum per concessionem quandam Rhetoricam introduci vult: Si talis esset, qui le- gem faceret, eum sine lege scripta & ceremoniis legis justum fore, ut ostendatur, nihil valere Ju- dæorum externam, umbratilem ac ceremonialem justitiam. Causa hujus explicationis hæc est, ut eludatur argumentum notitiæ cordibus inscriptæ. Ideo enim contendit Flacius, Apostoli sententiam hîc non assertivam, sed conditionalem esse, non dici quod cordibus lex inscripta sit, sed si facerent quæ sunt legis, inscriptam fore; Sed Apostolus utrumque adserit: Ad hæc gentes considerat, qua- les sunt post lapsum, non quales esse possint, aut quod tales juxta naturam sub initium creationis institutam esse debeant, Et τὰ τοῦ νόμου facere ipsi est quædam, quæ legis sunt præstare, non omnia, quæ lex requirit, ideoque non ceremonialem legem, sed imprimis moralem hic excludit à justificatio- ne, cùm sola fide, non operibus legis nos justifica- ri docet. Videri sanè posset hypotheticè exponen- dum esse locum præsentem ob particulam ὅταν, quam omnes ferè Interpretes hypotheticè acci- piunt, sed subfumendum hîc esse affirmativè, non negativè, textus docet: Scopus autem Apostoli est convincere gentiles, quod non defuerint ipsis media cognoscendi, quodque inexcusabiles sint, etiamsi solo naturæ lumine instructi, atque id con- clusio etiam Apostoli probat, nimirum gentiles citra legem scriptam peccantes, citra legem con- demnandos esse, ex sola naturæ lege. Ideoque τὸ benè operari, & conscientiæ excusatio, & quod τὰ τοῦ νόμου quædam, quæ legis sunt, faciant, à na- tura est, ceu principio benè operandi in gentibus, non verò vel à fide, ut August. l. IV. contra Julian. vel à gratia quadam spirituali naturæ superaddita, ut Arminizni, imprimis Arnoldus Corvinus con- tra Molin. c. XLI. 42. volunt. Quia alias non re- ctè inferretur hîc lex quædam scripta in cordibus gentilium, qui sunt sine lege: Inde Augustini sen- tentiam refellunt hîc Toletus, Bellarminus, Justi- nianeus, Tirinus. Quod autem ex hoc oraculo perperam salus gentilium à Pontificiis & Calvinia- nis nonnullis, præeuntibus Pelagianis exstrua- tur, aut etiam supernaturalis gratia ab Arminianis, oraculo XIX. ostendimus, quod hîc conferri po- terit.

ἔτοιν νόμον μὴ ἔχοντες) Repetitum majoris evidentiæ cau- sa, ex eo, quod præcesserat. Et nota, neutro nomini reddi masculinum constructione ea, quæ dicitur κατὰ τὸ σημαινό- μενον, ut Matth. XXVIII. 19. Act. XV. 17.

ἑαυτοῖς εἰσι νόμος.) Id est, sibi id præstant, quod lex Ju- dæis. Est hic πλοκὴ, simul & ὀξύμωρον. Simile ὀξύμωρον infra 25. ἡ περιτομή σε ἀκροβυστία γέγονεν. Est & μετάληψις quia causa nominatur pro effectu, quamvis ex alia causa procedente.

## 2:15
Ver. 15. who show) by the innocence of their life, that is.

the work of the law) that is, that which the law effects in the Jews, namely the knowledge of the lawful and the unlawful. The virtue of the law is to command, forbid, permit, and punish, says Modestinus; Chrysippus says that a law is that which commands what must be done, and forbids what must not be done, which words Philo also uses, and, as we shall see now, Origen.

written in their hearts. This is indeed not a written, but a born law, as Cicero says in his speech for Milo: but the Apostle speaks elegantly, because the law of God was written on tablets, he says this one is written in the heart, mitigating the metaphor with this addition. And clearly Dion Chrysostom uses the same manner of speaking in his work on custom, under which name he also includes the law of nature. That the precepts were written in the heart of Adam. חקוקו בלב says the Hebrew Gedalia in the Shalshelet. Origen in the words which are related in the Philocalia: besides these, a law is spoken of, which according to common notions is sown in the soul, and as the scripture is named, the word written in the heart, commanding what must be done, and forbidding what must not be done. Tertullian against the Jews: Finally, before the law of Moses was written on stone tablets, I contend that there was a law not written, which was understood naturally, and was kept by the Fathers. For whence was Noah found righteous, if that justice of the natural law did not precede him? Whence is Abraham reckoned a friend, if not from the equity and justice of the natural law? The same in his work On the Soldier's Crown: Do you seek therefore the law of God? You have that common one in the public world, in natural tablets, to which the Apostle is also accustomed to appeal, as when in the matter of the veil, he says, does not nature itself teach us? As when he says to the Romans that the nations do by nature the things that are of the law, he suggests both the natural law and the legal nature: But also in the former Epistle: affirming that males and females changed the natural use of their condition into that which is against nature, in the retribution of their error in place of a penalty, he certainly advocates for the natural use. Hierocles on the Golden Verses: But wickedness is brought upon souls, because it is a turning away from the laws, the offshoots of right reason existing in nature and written upon it, which the human soul overlooks, and casts off its inclinations; and a proof that right reason exists in men is the blame

unjust in those things in which it makes no difference to him to judge justly, and the licentious temperately, and in general to use the bad with right impulses in those things in which he will turn away. And elsewhere: We accept these as the most sovereign principles of judgment, the goodness of God, and the law that has departed from us, the right law being cut off, and as it were a certain indwelling God having sinned. Again elsewhere: For the human soul would be in danger of not being supported through its turning aside into things contrary to nature. (For thus it ought to be read) but by the recall into things according to nature it is led back to its own essence and recovers pure the being which was defiled by the mixture of the passions.

It is certain that the law of God was written in the heart of Adam: of which there are remaining remnants, which are said here to be the work of the law written in the hearts of the Gentiles, and indeed of all men: But that Grotius, by the natural law, as he insinuates in the words of Tertullian, contends that Noah, or Abraham, or anyone else, was reputed just and a friend of God, he openly contradicts the Apostle, who here teaches that Abraham was justified by faith, and deduces the same concerning him, and Noah, and others in the Old Testament, Heb. XI. and confirms that without faith it is impossible to please God. We asserted this opinion against the Socinians, who deny that not only the knowledge of God, but also the distinction of just and unjust is in man by nature, and against Vorstius who agrees with them, and even against Flacius, when he says that it cannot be conceded that any true principles, or the knowledge of the one God, are in man by nature, Orac. XX. in Ep. ad Roman.

their conscience bearing witness together) that is, bearing witness. For Plato also uses the word to bear witness together, because he who bears witness helps the cause of someone. Thus also to testify is said to be testified together. Jerem. XI. 7. and between one another their thoughts accusing, or also defending) Philo in the book 'The worse attacks the better': For whether a man is found dwelling in each soul, then he is found to be ruler and king. Then he is judge and umpire of the contests of life. And there is a time when, having taken the rank of witness and accuser, he secretly convicts us from within, not allowing us to open our mouth, and taking up and bridling with the reins of conscience the headstrong and rebellious course of the tongue, he restrains it. And afterwards to the question why God questioned Cain, he answers: 'In order that the soul, having learned to make a defense by itself, may convict itself concerning the things about which it may be wrongly declaring, using neither an accuser nor a fellow-contestant.' And concerning the confusion of tongues: 'For all the most base are unaware of the thoughts concerning not being hidden, doing injustice to the divine, and having been unable to ward off the paying of the penalty entirely.' Hierocles: 'Having arrived here at the discourse of the whole of the commandments, gather for me the judgment, so that in the inner court of the soul, looking toward these as toward divine laws, you may make the judgment of things done well or badly. For whence will the calculation have the ability to examine us as having done things, and to praise us as about to do good things, if the fore-calculation does not receive certain laws according to which it is fitting to order life, and toward these direct the treasury of conscience, as toward a certain goal, our whole life.' Horace: Let this be a wall of bronze: To be conscious of nothing against oneself, to turn pale at no guilt. Juvenal: Yet why do you think those have escaped, whom the mind, conscious of a dire deed, holds astonished and beats with a silent lash, while the torturer within shakes the hidden whip? But the punishment is vehement, and much more cruel than those which the severe Caeditius and Rhadamanthus devised, to carry one's own witness in the breast night and day. And soon: ---- that they begin at last to feel what is right and wrong when the crimes are finished. To which is similar that of Tacitus: Only when the crime was completed was its magnitude understood. The poets depict this power of conscience excellently in Orestes, who, to Menelaus asking him in Euripides: 'Wretched Orestes, what disease destroys you?' answers: 'Consciousness, because I am conscious of having done terrible things.' And this of Menander is not to be despised: 'Whoever is conscious of something in himself, even if he be most bold, consciousness makes him most cowardly.' The Apostle appeals to the dictate of conscience, which he points out through thoughts accusing themselves in evil and excusing in good: He asserts that it is in the Gentiles by nature, which experience itself convinces. Origen, lib. II. in Epist. ad Roman. says it is a pedagogue joined to the soul, insofar as it is habitually considered, and by which Synesis is founded in it, or the act of conscience emerging from habit, which is otherwise called synderesis. Moreover, the act of conscience embraces both the testimony concerning a fact or non-fact, and the obligation to do and not to do, and the judgment excusing in good and accusing in evil. But the habit or synderesis dictates both what things are to be done and what are to be avoided, and obliges us to do the former and omit the latter. Whence it is also to be gathered that it is distinct from the faculty, because no faculty obliges, nor accuses, if it is not obeyed. But that this obligation arises from natural impression, not from one's own collection and judgment, is clear even from the fact that it is present even in those not using reason, and that it furthermore applies even to infants, who do not collect and judge. For infants and others not using reason, from where could they collect that obligation, have the law of nature inscribed, otherwise they would be guilty of neither sin nor punishment: For where there is no law, there is no sin, where there is no sin, there is no punishment.

• between one another) that is, in turn, or with alternating opinion. Thus we read concerning Nebuchadnezzar. Dan. V. 6. his thoughts were troubling him, but Musonius in Gellius V. 1. wishes him to bear such varied countenances and disparate senses, just as they have affected him and his conscience, the philosopher's treatment of both parts of the soul, either sincere or sick.

Latin:

Vers. 15. οἵτινες ἐνδείκνυνται) vitæ innocentia scilicet.

τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου) id est, id quod lex in Judæis efficit, nempe cognitionem liciti & illiciti. Legis virtus est impe- rare, vetare, permittere, punire, ait Modestinus; Chrysip- pus ait νόμον esse προσακτικὸν μὲν ὧν ποιητέον, ἀπαγορευτικὸν δὲ ὧν μὴ πρακτέον, quæ verba & Philo usurpat, &, ut jam vi- debimus Origenes.

γραπτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἀυτῶν. Est quidem hæc non scripta, sed nata lex, ut Cicero ait, pro Milone: sed eleganter Apostolus, quia lex Dei scripta erat in tabulis, hanc scriptam dicit in corde,hoc additamen- to translationem mitigans. Planeque idem loquendi ge- nus usurpat Dion. Chrysostomus περὶ ἕθες, sub quo nomine etiam jus naturæ comprehendit. In corde Adami scripta fuisse præcepta. חקוקו בלב ait Hebræus Gedalia Schab- scheleth. Origenes verbis, quæ in philocalia m relata sunt: παρὰ δὲ ταῦτα λέγεται νόμος, ὁ κατὰ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας ὑπο- σπαρμένος τῇ ψυχῇ κὴ ὡς ὀνομάζεται ἡ γραφὴ, ἐγγεγραμμένος τῇ καρδίᾳ λόγος, προστακτικὸς μὲν ὧν ποιητέον, ἀπαγορευτικὸς δὲ ὧν ὐ ποιητέον. Tertullianus adversus Judæos: Denique ante le- gem Moysi scriptam in tabulis lapideis, legem fuisse contendo non scriptam, quæ naturaliter intelligebatur, & à Patribus cu- stodiebatur. Nam unde Noe justus inventus, si non eum illa natu- ralis legis justitia præcedebat? unde Abraham amicus deputa- tur, si non de æquitate & justitia legis naturalis? Idem de Co- rona Militis: Quæris igitur Dei legem? habes communem istam in publico mundo, in naturalibus tabulis, ad quas & Apostolus solet provocare, ut cum in velamine ponendo, nec natura nos, inquit, docet? ut cum ad Romanos natura facere dicens natio- nes ea quæ sunt legis & legem naturalem suggerit, & naturam legalem: Sed & in priore Epistola: naturalem usum conditionis in non naturalem masculos ac fæminas inter se demutasse affir- mans retributione erroris in vicem pænæ, utique naturali usui patrocinatur. Hierocles ad aureum carmen: Ταῖς δὲ ψυχαῖς πονηρίαις ἐν ἐπιφέρεται, διότι ἀποστροφὴ ἔστι τῶν νόμων ἀπογιν- γματα τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ ἐν φύσει ἐνόντα καὶ ἐγγεγραμμένοι ἀυτῇ παρορᾷ ἡ ἀνθρωπα ψυχὴ τὰς προσπαθείας ἀποδυφλυμένει τε- μήριον δὲ τὸ εἶναι τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ἐν ἀνθρώποις, τὸ ἐγκτοὺ

ἄδικοι ἐν οἷς μηδὲν ἀυτῶ διαφέρι κρίνειν δικαίως, κὴ τὸν ἀκόλαστον σωφρονικῶς, καὶ ὅλως τὸν κακὸν ὀρθαῖς ἐπιβολαῖς χρῆσθαι ἐν οἷς ἀποστραφήσεται. Et alibi: τάυτας τῆς κρίσεως ἀρχὰς κυριω- τάτας ἀποδεχόμεθα, τὴν ἀγαθότητα τῦ Θεῦ, τὸν τε ἀποστάντας νόμον τὸν ἐν ἡμῖν παρατομόμενον ὀρθὸν νόμον, καὶ ὥσπερ τινὰ ἔνοικον Θεὸν πλημμελήκοτον. Rursus alibi: Κινδυνέυοι γὰρ ὡς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ὑποφέρεσθαι ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη ψυχὴ διὰ τῆς εἰς τὰ μὴ με- τὰ φύσιν ἐκτροπῆς. (Ita enim legi debet) τῇ δὲ εἰς τὰ κατὰ φύσιν ἀνακλήσει πρὸς τὴν ὀυσίαν τὴν ἀυτῆς ἐπάγεται κὴ ἀπολαμ- βάνει καθαρὸν τὸ εἶναι ὅ τῇ συμμίξει τῶν παθῶν ἐχραίνετο.

In corde Adami scriptam fuisse legem Dei cer- tum est: cujus residuæ sunt reliquiæ, quæ hic opus legis in cordibus gentium, omniumque adeò homi- num scriptæ dicuntur: Sed per naturalem legem, quod verbis Tertulliani insinuat Grotius, Noam, aut Abrahamum, aut quenquam alium, justum & amicum Dei reputatum, palam refragatur Apo- stolo, qui hîc Abrahamum fide justificatum docet, idemque de ipso, & Noah, aliisque in Veteri Te- stamento diducit Ebr. XI. ac sine fide impossibile esse, Deo placere, confirmat. Sententiam hanc ad- versus Socinianos non tantum Dei notitiam, sed & discrimen justi & injusti naturâ homini inesse negantes, & Vorstium iis accedentem, imò & Fla- cium, quum concedi non posse, ait, vera aliqua prin- cipia, aut notitiam unius Dei in homine inesse per naturam, contendit, asseruimus Orac. XX. in Ep. ad Roman.

συμμαρτυρούσης ἀυτῶν τῆς συνειδήσεως) id est, μαρτυρούσης. Nam συμμαρτυρεῖν pro testari etiam Plato usurpat, quia qui testimonium perhibet, causam alicujus adjuvat. Sic & te- stificari dicitur συμμαρτυρεσθαι. Jerem. XI. 7. καὶ μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων, ἢ καὶ ἀπο- λογουμένων) Philo libro pejorem insidiari meliori: εἴτε γὰρ ἄνθρωπον ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῇ ψυχῇ κατοικῶν, τότε μὲν ἄρχων καὶ βα- σιλεὺς ἐνρίσκεται. Τότε δὲ δικαστὴς καὶ βραβευτὴς τῶν κατὰ τὸν βίον ἀγώνων. ἔστι δὲ ὅτε μαρτύρων καὶ κατηγόρου λαβὼν τάξιν ἀφανῶς ἡμᾶς ἔνδοθεν ἐλέγχει, μηδὲ διᾶραι τὸ στόμα ἐῶν, ἀναλαμβανόμενός δὲ καὶ ἐπιστομίζων ταῖς τῆς συνειδότος ἡνίαις τὸν ἀυθάδη καὶ μετὰ ἀφηνιασμοῦ δρόμον γλωττης ἐπίσχη. Et postea ad quæstionem cur Cainum Deus interrogaverit, re- spondet: ἵν' ἡ μάθευσα καὶ ἀποκρίσεως ποιεῖσθαι ψυχὴ δι' ἑαυτῆς ἐλέγχῃ τὰ περὶ ὧν ἂν ᾖ κακῶς ἀποφαίνηται, μήτε κατηγόρω, μήτε συναγωνιστῇ χρωμένη ἑτέρῳ. Et de linguarum confu- sione: πάντες γὰρ οἱ φαυλότατοι λανθάνουσιν ἑνοίας περὶ τῦ μὴ λήσειν, τὸ θεῖον ἀδικῦντες, μήτε τὸ δίκην ὑφέξειν εἰσάπαν ἰσχύσας διακρούσασθαι. Hierocles: ἐνταῦθα γενόμενος τῦ λό- γυ τῶν ὅλων παραγγελμάτων ἄθροισόν μοι τὴν γνώμην, ἵνα τῷ ἔσω τῆς ψυχῆς δικαστηρίῳ πρὸς τᾶντα ὡς πρὸς θείους νόμους ἀπο- βλέπων, ποιῇ μὲν ἕυ ἢ κακῶς πεπραγμένων τὴν ἐπίκρισιν. πόθεν γὰρ ὁ ἐπιλογισμὸς ἕξει δοκιὰ μὲν ἐργασμένως ἡμᾶς ἐπισκέπτεω, χρηστὰ δὲ πράξοντας ἐπαινεῖν, εἰ μὴ ὁ προλογισμὸς νόμους τίνας λάβοι καθ' ὃς προσήκει τὴν ζωὴν τάττειν, καὶ πρὸς τύτους τὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ταμεῖον, ὡς πρός τινα σκοπὸν, ἐπευθύνειν τὸν ὅλον ἡμῶν βίον. Horatius: Hic murus aheneus esto: Nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa. Juvenalis: Cur tamen hos si tu Evasisse putas, quos diri conscia facti, Mens habet attonitos & surdo verbere cædit, Occultum quatiente animo tortore flagellum? Pœna autem vehemens, & multo sævior illis Quas & Cæditius gravis invenit & Rhadamanthus, Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem. Et mox: ---- quod fas Atque nefas tandem incipiunt sentire peractis Criminibus. Cui simile Taciti illud: Perfeclo demum scelere magnitudo ejus intellecta est. Egregiè hanc conscientiæ vim depingunt Poëtæ in Oreste, qui Menelao apud Euripidem quærenti: Ὀστέρα τλῆμον τίς σ' ἀπόλλυται νόσος; respondet: Ἡ σύνεσις, ὅτι σύνοιδα δείν' ἐιργασμένος. Est & hoc Menandri non spernendum: Ὁ συνισορῶν ἀυτῶ τι, κἂν ᾖ δρασύτατος, Ἡ σύνεσις ἀυτὸν δειλότατον εἶναι ποιεῖ. Ad dictamen conscientiæ provocat Apostolus, quòd per cogitationes & accusantes sese in malo & excusantes in bono indigitat: Eam autem naturâ inesse gentilibus, asserit, quod convincit ipsa expe- rientia. Origenes lib. II. in Epist. ad Roman. di- cit esse pædagogum animæ sociatum, prout nempe eadem habitualiter consideratur, & quâ in ea fun- datur Synesis, seu actus conscientiæ ex habitu emer- gens, qui dicitur aliàs συντήρησις. Cæterum actus conscientiæ complectitur tum testificationem de fa- cto vel non facto, tum obligationem ad faciendum, & non faciendum, tum judicium excusans in bono, & accusans in malo. Habitus autem vel Synteresis dictitat & quæ facienda, & quæ fugienda, & obligat nos, ut illa faciamus, hæc omittamus. Unde etiam eam à facultate distinctam esse colligere est, quia nulla facultas obligat, neque accusat, si ipsi non obediatur. Quòd autem ista obligatio oriatur ex naturali impressione, non ex propriâ collectione, & dijudicatione, id vel inde liquet, quòd etiam in- sit ratione non utentibus, quodque insuper infan- tibus etiam conveniat, qui non colligunt & dijudi- cant. Nam & infantes cæterique ratione non utentes, unde colligere possint eam obligatio- nem, habent legem naturæ inscriptam, alioquin enim neque peccati, neque supplicii rei essent: Ubi enim non lex, ibi nullum peccatum, ubi nul- lum peccatum, ibi nullum supplicium.

• μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων) hoc est vicissim, sive alternante senten- tia. Sic de Nabuchodonosore legimus. Dan. V. 6. οἱ δια- λογισμοὶ ἀυτῦ διετάρασσον ἀυτὸν, Musonius autem apud Gel- lium V. 1. Varios adeò vultus disparilesque sensus gerat, per- inde ut eum conscientiæque ejus affecerint, utrarumque animi partium, aut sincerarum, aut ægrarum Philosophi pertractio.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. in the day when God will judge) With the parenthesis finished, the Apostle returns to that which he had said, 'they will be judged' and assigns to it its time. But 'when' is put for 'in which', just as the Latins say 'he had at home from where he might learn', that is, from which. And in the manuscript for 'when' here is 'in which' with the same sense.

τὰ κρυπτὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων) that is, also τὰ κρυπτὰ, מסתרים. Thus also 1 Cor. IV. 5. Thales, being asked whether anyone doing evil could be hidden from God, said: not even one thinking it: For whoever thinks of any crime silent within himself, has the guilt of the deed, says Juvenal. Proving this very thing by a story taken from Herodotus.

according to my gospel through Jesus Christ. That is, through Jesus God will judge concerning the deeds and thoughts of men, plainly as I announce this to all peoples. See Acts X. 42, XVII. 31, 2 Tim. IV. 8. That expression according to my gospel is in a similar sense in 2 Tim. II. 8. But he well interposed the Gospel here, because it could not be established by reason alone through whom God would judge. But Paul added credibility to this truth by miracles.

Judgment is said to be future according to the Gospel, not simply, as if threats and even punishments pertained to the Gospel, as the Antinomians and Papists wish, but in a certain respect, both because eternal life will be adjudged to the Elect according to the Gospel, and because unbelief, as it is directed toward Christ, is declared in the Gospel, insofar as in the same the object is shown, the righteousness and merit of Christ, which the unfaithful reject, even if it is argued by the force of the law, and condemnation redounds from the law: for he who does not apply the merit of Christ to himself, he is under the law, and by the force of the legal covenant under a curse: and then especially, because we are taught that the judgment is to be instituted through Jesus Christ not in the law, but in the Gospel. Compare what we have handed down concerning these things in Oracle XXI.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὅτε κρινεῖ ὁ θεὸς) Absoluta παρενθέσει, redit Apostolus ad illud, quod dixerat, κριθήσονται & ei suum tempus assignat. Est autem positum ὅτε pro ᾧ, sicut eum Latini dicunt, habebat domi unde disceret, id est ex quo. Et in manuscripto pro ὅτε hic est ᾧ sensu eodem.

τὰ κρυπτὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων) id est, etiam τὰ κρυπτὰ, מסתרים Sic & 1. Cor. IV. 5. Thales interrogatus ecquis Deo latere posset male agens, dixit ne cogitans quidem: Nam scelus intra se tacitum qui cogitat ullum, Facti crimen habet, ait Juvenalis. Probans hoc ipsum historia de Herodoto deprompta.

κατὰ τὸ ἐυαγγέλιόν με διὰ ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ. Id est, per Jesum Deus judicabit de hominum factis ac cogitatis, planè sicut ego hoc omnibus populis annuntio. Vide Act. X. 42. XVII. 31. 2. Tim. IV. 8. Locutio illa κατὰ τὸ ἐυαγγέλιόν με pari sensu est 2. Tim. II. 8. Bene autem hic Evangelium interposuit, quia sola ratione constare non po- terat, per quem Deus esset judicaturus. Huic autem veri- tati Paulus fidem adstruebat miraculis.

Judicium secundum Evangelium dicitur futu- rum non simpliciter, ac si ad Evangelium perti- neant comminationes etiam atque supplicia, ut Antinomi, ac Pontificii volunt, sed secundum quid, tùm quia Electis adjudicabitur vita æterna secun- dum Evangelium, tùm quia incredulitas, quà in Christum fertur, in Evangelio declaratur, quate- nus in eodem monstratur objectum, Christi justi- tia, & meritum, quod respuunt infideles, etsi ar- guatur vi legis, ac condemnatio è lege redundet: qui enim meritum Christi sibi non applicat, ille sub lege est, ac vi pacti legalis sub maledictione: tùm imprimis, quia judicium instituendum esse per Jesum Christum non in lege, sed Evangelio do- cemur. Confer, quæ Orac. XXI. de his tradidi- mus.

## 2:17
Vers. 17. Behold, you are called a Jew. Which name was of religion at that time and signified μονόθεον, a worshiper of one God, which was no small honor. See below 28. At the same time there is an allusion to the origin of the word. Philo on the Allegories: to him who confesses one, Judah is a symbol: which he also repeats shortly after in the same book. And in the book on the Planting: he is called Judah who is interpreted as confession to the Lord. Therefore John in the Apocalypse denies that those who called themselves so were Jews in reality. II. 9.

and rest in the law. You lean upon נשען for שען is translated ἐπαναπάυεσθαι as in Ez. XXIX. 7. The same sense has נסמך in Is. XLVIII. 2.

which the LXX translate by ἀντιπεριῖζεσθαι. You place much security in the fact that you have the law given by God. See below 23.

and you boast in God. In this you take much pleasure in yourself, that you know the one, true God. The words of Isaiah XLV. 25 seem to be looked to.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἴδε σὺ Ἰυδαῖος ἐπονομάζῃ. Quod nomen erat religionis eo tempore & significabat μονόθεον, unius Dei cultorem, qui non modicus honos. Vi de infra 28. simul alluditur ad vocis originem. Philo de Allegoriis : τῷ μὲν ἓν ἐξομολογουμένῳ ὁ ἰύδας σύμβολον : quod & mox eodem libro repetit. Et libro de Plantatione: κα- λεῖται δὲ ἰύδας ὃς ἑρμηνέυεται κυρίῳ ἐξομολογήσεως. Ideò Johannes in Apocalypsi negat eos reverâ esse Judæos, qui se sic appellabant. II. 9.

καὶ ἐπαναπάυῃ τῷ νόμῳ. Inniteris נשען nam שען vertitur ἐπαναπάυεσθαι ut Ez. XXIX. 7. Eundem sensum habet נסמך Es. XLIIX. 2.
