quod per ἀντιπεριῖζεσθαι vertunt LXX. Multum præsidii in eo ponis, quod legem habeas à Deo datam. vide infra 23.

καὶ καυχᾶση ἐν Θεῷ. In eo multum tibi places, quòd unum, verumque Deum noris. Respici videntur verba Esaiæ XLV. 25.

## 2:18
Verse 18. and you know the will. You have learned what God wishes to be done not from a deduction of bare reason, but from the books of Moses and the Prophets.

After the Apostle thus convicts the Gentiles, he now turns himself to the Jews, to whom he indeed concedes the title, that they are called Jews, as if confessors, regarding revealed knowledge, that they have the law of God, or his word, or the acknowledgment of the true God, in whom or rather concerning whom (so that ἐν may be taken for περὶ: for to boast in God according to Is. XLV. 25 is of faith: but this is of vain boasting) they boast, and of his will revealed in the Word: and also the δοκιμασίας, the testing of those things which are more useful or more excellent according to the Word of God or the instruction of the divine law, v. 17, 18, with which from their tender years the Jews have been imbued through κατήχησιν or instruction made by living voice. 2 Tim. III. 15. Finally, the Mastership of others, that they are guides of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness, that is, of the Gentiles ignorant of the true God, Ps. LXXVI. 2, Ps. CXLVII. 19, 20. Is. IX. 1, ch. LXI. 1, they trusted that they were instructors of the unwise, masters of infants, and in a certain way they were, having an infallible form of knowledge and truth in the law. He brought forward these prerogatives in order to convict them of hypocrisy, that even if they boast of holiness, and put forward some appearance of external justice, they are destitute of the true and internal obedience of the heart, and thus he shows that they have deserved so much the more serious punishments. Afterwards he refutes and convicts the vices of the Jews; both Theoretical, because they teach others, or presume to teach, but do not teach themselves correctly: since they labored under gross ignorance concerning the Messiah and other divine matters, blind guides, unwise masters, destitute of the type of saving knowledge and truth: for all those things which they boasted of were the opposite: and then Practical, because they transgress against divine precepts, specifically those of the second table, by committing adultery, and thefts, daily usuries, and plunderings of their neighbor, lusts, and also by polluting themselves with polygamy, Matth. XIX. 3 and ch. V, and indeed those of the first table, by sacrilegiously changing the temple of God into a den of thieves, by selling sacrifices, by exchanging sacred shekels for common money in usurious money-changing, Luke XIX, Matth. XXI, John II. Furthermore, also by attributing to creatures the honor due to God, which cannot be done without sacrilege, since God is thus deprived of his glory, Is. XLII. 6, and also by denying that Christ alone is our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 6, by which means they were taking away the righteousness of God and setting up their own, Rom. IX and X, and then generally by transgressing the law, and by bringing ignominy upon God through the transgression of the law, since thus through them the name of God is blasphemed even among the Gentiles themselves. Is. LII. 5, Ez. XXXVI. 23.

And you test the things that differ) So also Philip. I. 10, in order that you may test the things that differ. Both passages look to the place of the law concerning cloven hoofs, the mystical sense of which is, namely, that lawful and illicit things must be distinguished by us, which deceive many by a narrow limit. Thus Philo explains that law in his book on agriculture, and adds that it is not enough, unless we also ruminate, that is, show that we remember where there is need. Barnabas does not go far away when he interprets the cloven-footed, with the approval of Clement of Alexandria, Strom. V. Those who meditate on the commandment of the word which they received. The same Barnabas refers this precept to the knowledge of both ages, as does Origen on Levit. XI.

being instructed out of the law) Indeed, taught from an early age out of the law, namely those distinctions of the lawful and the illicit, as the Syrian rightly takes it here, השמיע הוא, the κατήχησις, the שמעתא of the Rabbis. You have this word in Luke I. 4, Acts XVIII. 25, 1 Cor. XIV. 15, Gal. VI. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 18. καὶ γινώσκεις τὸ θέλημα. Quid Deus fieri velit non ex rationis nudæ collectione, sed ex libris Mosis & Prophetarum didicisti.

Postquam gentiles ita convincit Apostolus, nunc ad Judæos se convertit, quibus concedit fanè titu- lum, quod Judæi cognominentur, quasi confesso- res, quoad notitiam revelatam, quod legem Dei, vel verbum ejus habeant, vel agnitionem veri Dei, in quo vel potius de quo (ut ἐν accipiatur pro περὶ: nam in Deo gloriari juxta Es. XLV. 25. fidei est: hoc verò vanæ jactantiæ) gloriantur, & volun- tatis ejus in Verbo patefactæ: nec non δοκιμασίας probationis eorum, quæ utiliora, vel præstantiora sunt secundum Dei Verbum vel instructionem le- gis divinæ, v. 17. 18. quâ à teneris Judæi per κατή- χησιν vel institutionem vivâ voce factam imbuti sunt. 2. Timoth. III. 15. Denique Magisterium aliorum, quòd duces cæcorum, lumen eorum, qui in tenebris sunt, hoc est, gentilium verum Deum ignorantium, Ps. LXXVI. 2. Ps. CXLVII. 19. 20. Es. IX. 1. cap. LXI. 1. eruditores insipientium, Ma- gistros infantium se esse confiderent, & quodam- modo essent, habentes formam scientiæ & veritatis in lege infallibilem. Has prærogativas adduxit, ut hypocriseos eosdem convincat, quòd etsi ja- ctitent sanctitatem, & aliquam speciem externæ justitiæ præ se ferant, verâ & internâ obedientia cordis destituantur, adeoque tantò graviores pœ- nas eos promeritos esse, ostendat. Post redar- guit & convincit Judæorum vitia; cùm Theorica, quòd alios doceant, vel docere præsumant, seipsos verò rectè non doceant: siquidem crassâ ignoran- tiâ de Messia, aliisque rebus divinis laborarint cæ- ci ductores, insipientes Magistri, salutaris scientiæ & veritatis typo destituti: Omnia enim illa, quæ jactabant, contrario modo se habebant: tum Pra- ctica, quod contra præcepta divina tum speciatim, tabulæ quidem secundæ, mœchando, & furtis, quotidianis usuris, & expilationibus proximi, li- bidinibus, nec non polygamia sese polluendo, Matth. XIX. 3. & cap. V. primæ verò tabulæ, sacri- legè templum Dei in speluncam latronum com- mutando, sacrificia vendendo, siclos sacros com- muni pecunia quæstuosâ collybisticâ permutando prævaricentur, Luc. XIX. Matth. XXI. Joh. II. Adhæc etiam honorem Deo debitum creaturis tribuendo, quod sine sacrilegio fieri non potest, quum Deus ita gloria sua privetur, Es. XLII. 6. nec non solum Christum nostram esse justitiam negando, Jer. XXIII. 6. quo pacto justitiam Dei tollebant, propriamque erigebant Rom. IX. & X. tùm generatim legem transgrediendo, Deumque per transgressionem legis ignominia afficien- do, quum ita per ipsos nomen Dei inter ipsas etiam gentes blasphemetur. Es. LII. 5. Ez. XXXVI. 23.

Καὶ δοκιμάζεις τὰ διαφέροντα) Sic & Philip. I. 10. εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τὰ διαφέροντα. Uterque locus respicit ad locum legis de fissis ungulis, cujus mysticus sensus est scili- cet, distingui à nobis debere licita & illicita, quæ multos fallunt arcto limite. Sic eam legem explicat Philo libro περὶ γεωργίας, additque id non sufficere, nisi & ruminemus, id est, ostendamus nos meminisse ubi opus est. Barnabas non longe abit cum τὰ δίχηλα interpretatur, approbante & Alexandrino Clemente Strom. V. Τὺς μελετῶντας ὁ ἕλα- βον διάταλμα ῥήματος. Idem Barnabas hoc præceptum refert ad cognitionem utriusque seculi, ut & Origenes ad Levit. XI.

κατηχούμενος ἐκ τῦ νόμε) Quippe à prima ætate edoctus ex lege, illa scilicet discrimina liciti & illiciti, ut hic recte su- mit Syrus השמיע הוא κατήχησις שמעתא Rab- binis. Habes hoc verbum Luc. I. 4. Actor. XVIII. 25. 1. Cor. XIV. 15. Gal. VI. 6.

## 2:19
Verse 19. and you are confident) you persuade yourself. He addresses the Rabbis especially, who are also פקחים to the Hebrews, that is, seeing ones.

yourself to be a guide of the blind) That you are the one by whom all the Gentiles could be taught. So that this persuasion may be well expressed, the most magnificent titles are ascribed here to the Jews, according to their own judgment, and the vilest names to the Gentiles. In reality, God could say to those Jews: Who is blind but my servant? as from Is. XLII. 18, and blind guides of the blind, Matth. XV. 14. For even if they made proselytes from the Gentiles, they made them no better by their instruction or example, indeed even worse because of their empty trust in rituals. Matth. XXIII. 15.

A light of those in darkness) The Apostle expresses the same thing with many words. But he looks to the passage of Isaiah XLV. 6, which the Jews even now interpret as concerning themselves making many proselytes: And they are called by the Rabbis themselves, the light of the world.

Latin:

Vers. 19. πέποιθάς τε) tibi ipse persuades. Rabbinos præcipuè compellat, qui & פקחים Hebræis id est vi- dentes.

σεαυτὸν ὁδηγὸν εἶναι τυφλῶν) Te esse, à quo omnes gentes doceri possent. Ut bene exprimatur hæc persuasio, Ju- dæis hic adscribuntur, ex ipsorum judicio, tituli magnifi- centissimi, gentibus vilissima nomina. Reipsa Deus illis Judæis dicere poterat: Quis cæcus nisi servus meus? ut ex Esai. XLII. 18. & ὁδηγοὶ τυφλοὶ τυφλῶν. Matth. XV. 14. Nam etsi quos ex gentibus faciebant proselytos, eos ni- hilo faciebant aut institutione sua aut exemplo meliores, imo pejores etiam ob inanem in ritibus fiduciam. Matth. XXIII. 15.

Φῶς τῶν ἐν σκότῳ) Multis verbis rem eandem expri- mit Apostolus. Respicit autem locum Esaiæ XLV. 6. quem Judæi etiam nunc interpretantur de semetipsis mul- tos facientibus proselytos: Et Rabbini ipsis vocantur, lux mundi.

## 2:20
Vers. 20. παιδευτὴν ἀφρόνων מורה נככים, with which title Maimonides inscribed his book.

διδάσκαλον νηπίων) מרקק עוללים. Infants; understand here νεοφύτους (neophytes) in Judaism. Thus 1 Cor. III. 1. νήπιος, who is a νεόφυτος. 1 Tim. II. 6.

ἔχοντα τὴν μόρφωσιν τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐν τῷ νό- μῳ) μόρφωσις, or as Aquila speaks, μόρφωμα is the form of a thing which is seen, תאר or תכנית, and it is so taken in 2 Tim. III. 5. The meaning is transferred to the mind, because the figures of the things which we learn are as it were imprinted upon it, and those things are said to be μορφοῦσθαι (formed) in us, Gal. IV. 19. Thus the word תאר is translated μορφοῦσθαι in Isa. XLIV. 13 and 1 Sam. XXVIII. 14. Cicero said to know the form of honesty, the form of a good man; Horace, to form minds with studies; Cicero, to form the age with arts. Τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας for τῆς γνώσεως τῆς ἀληθείας: The form of the knowledge of that truth which is in the law. Paul does not wish anything to be taken away from the law; he acknowledges it to be true, that is, truly given by GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 20. παιδευτὴν ἀφρόνων מורה נככים quo titulo librum inscripsit Maimonides.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. ὁ ὖν διδάσκων ἕτερον, σεαυτὸν ὀυ διδάσκεις) It is a πλοκὴ (interweaving). For to teach in the second place signifies to stir oneself up to doing; they used to say, and did not do, Matt. XXIII. 3. The proverb was appropriate to them: Ἄλλων ἰατρὸς ἀυτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων (A physician of others, himself teeming with sores). Similar to which is Luke IV. 23. Philemon explains that sense thus: -- -- Τοὺς ἰατροὺς οἶδ᾽ ἐγὼ Ὑπὲρ ἐγκρατείας τοῖς νοσοῦσι εὖ σφόδρα Πάντας λαλοῦντας, εἶ τ' ἐπὰν πταίωσί τι Αὐτοὺς ποιοῦντας πανθ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἑῷεν πότε. Josephus in his address to the Jews, which is in the Jewish War, verse 26: ὑμῖν δὲ τί τῶν ἐνλογηθέντων ὑπὸ τοῦ νομοθέτου πέπρακται (But what of the things commanded by the lawgiver has been done by you?).

ὁ κηρύσσων μὴ κλέπτειν κλέπτεις) κηρύσσειν is to teach something openly, as Matt. III. 1, IV. 17, X. 27, in Syriac ברז. That infinitive κηρύσσειν here serves for a gerund. Stealing was both old and frequent among the Hebrews, Psalm L. 18, Prov. XXIX. 24. When Paul was writing these things, the memory of Anilaeus and Asinaeus in Babylonia was fresh among the Jews, to whom a huge multitude had flocked, who all lived only by plunder. Josephus, Antiquities XVIII, 12. Not long after, the leaders of the priestly families, having defrauded the lesser priests, took all the tithes for themselves. Josephus XX. 6. And the sicarii arose, ravaging everywhere with robberies. Josephus XX. 7. Josephus also in the aforementioned place of the War, verse 26, reproaches the Jews with κλοπὰς καὶ ἁρπαγὰς (thefts and robberies).

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὁ ὖν διδάσκων ἕτερον, σεαυτὸν ὀυ διδάσκεις) Est πλοκὴ. Nam docere secundo loco significat semet ad fa- ciendum excitare, dicebant, & non faciebant, Matth. XXIII. 3. Conveniebat illis proverbium: Ἄλλων ἰατρὸς ἀυτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων. Cui simile est Luc. IV. 23. Philemon eum sensum sic ex- plicat: -- -- Τοὺς ἰατροὺς οἶδ᾽ ἐγὼ Ὑπὲρ ἐγκρατείας τοῖς νοσοῦσι εὖ σφόδρα Πάντας λαλοῦντας, εἶ τ' ἐπὰν πταίωσί τι Αὐτοὺς ποιοῦντας πανθ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἑῷεν πότε. Josephus in sua allocutione ad Judæos, quæ est Belli Ju- daici vers. 26. ὑμῖν δὲ τί τῶν ἐνλογηθέντων ὑπὸ τοῦ νομοθέτου πέπρακται.

ὁ κηρύσσων μὴ κλέπτειν κλέπτεις) κηρύσσειν est palam ali- quid docere, ut Matth. III. 1. IV. 17. X. 27. in Syriaco ברז. Infinitivum illud κηρύσσειν hic valet pro Gerundio. Furari & vetus & frequens inter Hebræos Psalm. L. 18. Prov. XXIX. 24. Cum hæc scriberet Paulus, recens erat memoria Alinæi & Asylæi in Babylonia Judæorum, ad quos ingens multitudo confluxerat, qui omnes non nisi ex rapto vivebant. Joseph. Antiquit. XVIII, 12. Non multò post sacerdotalium familiarum principes frau- datis minoribus sacerdotibus decimas sibi totas abstule- re. Josephus XX. 6. & exorti sicarii rapinis ubique grassantes. Josephus XX. 7. Josephus quoque dicto lo- co de Bello vers. 26. κλοπὰς καὶ ἁρπαγὰς Judæis expro- brat.

## 2:22
Vers. 22. ὁ λέγων μὴ μοιχεύειν μοιχεύεις) And this vice was no less frequent from of old, as appears from the aforementioned place of the Psalm. Jerem. V. 8, Malach. III. 5. Talmudic books show that very many Rabbis were entangled in this and related vices, Akiba, Meir, Chanina, Eleazar. These were the fruits of a confidence placed in ceremonies alone. Josephus, among the crimes which he reproaches his countrymen with in the aforementioned place, also puts μοιχείας (adulteries). And Justin, disputing with Trypho, touches upon the lusts of the Masters among the Jews.

ὁ βδελυσσόμενος τὰ ἔιδωλα) ἔιδωλα (idols) are properly images: But the Hellenist Jews use that word when they deal with the gods of the nations, because only their images exist. They called the same gods βδελύγματα (abominations), by which word the Hebrew words are accustomed to be translated: שקצים גלולים אלילים תועבות. See what was said at Matt. XXIV. 15.

ἱεροσυλεῖς) It does not differ much to worship false gods and to rob the true one, which the priests did by not offering from the produce those things which the law of God commanded them, or certainly not such as was fitting. Malach. I. 8, 12, 13, 14, III. 10 where see the things said. Josephus in the stated place says that the Temple was profaned by the Jews in many ways.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὁ λέγων μὴ μοιχεύειν μοιχεύεις) Et hoc vi- tium non minus frequens ab antiquo, ut apparet dicto jam Psalmi loco. Jerem. V. 8. Malach. III. 5. Talmudici li- bri ostendunt plurimos Rabbinos huic & affinibus vitiis illigatos fuisse, Akibam, Meirum, Chanimam, Eleaza- rum. Hi fructus fuere fiduciæ in solis ceremoniis collo- catæ, Josephus inter crimina, quæ popularibus suis dicto loco exprobrat ponit & μοιχείας. Et libidines Magistro- rum inter Judæos attingit & Justinus cum Tryphone disputans.

ὁ βδελυσσόμενος τὰ ἔιδωλα) ἔιδωλα propriè sunt imagi- nes: Sed eam vocem usurpant Judæi Hellenistæ cum de diis gentium agunt, quia imagines tantum eorum exstant. Eosdem Deos vocabant βδελύγματα, qua voce verti so- lent Hebræi voces: שקצים גלולים אלילים תועבות. Vide, quæ dicta ad Matth XXIV. 15.

ἱεροσυλεῖς) Non multum distat falsos Deos colere & ve- rum spoliare, quod faciebant sacerdotes non offerendo ex proventibus ea, quæ lex Dei ipsis præcipiebat aut certè non qualia oportebat. Malach. I. 8. 12. 13. 14. III. 10 ubi dicta vide. Josephus dicto loco ait, Templum ab Judæis multis modis profanatum.

## 2:23
Verse 23. (you who boast in the law) as above 17. (through the transgression of the law you dishonor God) Transgression is a notable violation of the law. Moreover, it is a very emphatic antithesis: you bring ignominy upon God, of whose law you boast, as much as lies in you.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὃς ἐν νόμῳ καυχᾶσαι) ut supra 17. διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τῦ νόμε τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζεις) Παράβα- σις est מעל notabilis violatio legis. Est autem ἀντίθετον valde ἐμφατικὸν: Deum, de cujus lege gloriamini, quan- tum in vobis est, ignominia afficitis.

## 2:24
Verse 24. (for the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you) He does not cite the places, namely those known to the Jews to whom these things are written, Isaiah 52:5, Ezekiel 36:20, where there is (they profaned my holy name). The Gentiles were saying, behold what kind of religion is this, which produces such a life? An error, treating that which is not the cause as the cause.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τὸ γὰρ ὄνομα Θεῦ δι' ὑμᾶς βλασφημεῖται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι) Non allegat loca, nempe nota Judæis, quibus hæc scribuntur Esaïæ LII. 5. Ezech. XXXVI. 20. ubi est יחללו את שם קדשי ἐβεβήλωσαν τὸ ὄνομά με τὸ ἅγιον. Dicebant gentes, ecce qualis religio, quæ talem vitam pa- rit? Error, παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον.

## 2:25
Verse 25. (for circumcision indeed profits) as a part of legal obedience, from which the Jews did not yet understand themselves to be released: nor does Paul urge that.

The conviction of the Jews having been completed, the Apostle sets forth the refutation of two objections: the former is from the privilege and power of circumcision, the other from the absurdity that Paul seems to leave no eminence to the Jews over the Gentiles. The former is occupied in the preceding verse, that circumcision, as the Jews used it, does not allow them to be condemned: to which the Apostle responds that that power does not reside in circumcision unless one fulfills the whole law, speaking after the manner of men, in which way the Jews kept circumcision not as a Sacrament of grace, but as a certain precept of the law: which he confirms by comparing a Jewish transgressor with a frugal and just Gentile, so that it may be evident that circumcision of itself, or by the work performed, does not profit, but only brings utility to the just man, circumcised both in spirit and in body. For circumcision indeed, he says, profits if you observe the law: For he who is circumcised has become a debtor to the whole law, Galatians 5:3. But if you are a transgressor of the law, (which I have hitherto proven) your circumcision has become uncircumcision; God does not hold you any longer as circumcised, but as uncircumcised or foreskinned, Leviticus 26:41, Deuteronomy 10:16, chapter 30:6, Jeremiah 4:4, chapter 6:10, chapter 9:25, 26, Acts 7:51, Philippians 3:2, 3. If therefore the uncircumcision (the uncircumcised man) keeps the justice of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned for circumcision? Will not God hold the uncircumcised man for circumcised? And that which is by nature uncircumcision, fulfilling the law, will judge (thus is the uncircumcised man who observes the law, if such a one be given: this is a rhetorical fiction: for there is no one who fulfills the law), You, through the letter and circumcision (the preposition 'through' is taken for 'in', 'out of', or 'with', as has been observed also by Grotius: who is either that which you are out of the letter of the law and circumcision, or you found with the letter and circumcision; it can also have the place of a hendiadys, so that the sense may be, in the literal or external circumcision) will judge the transgressor of the law, that is, by comparison with himself he will convict your guilt, as Grotius rightly says from the collation of Matthew 12:42, to which, however, Hebrews 11:7 is wrongly drawn; for he judged, that is, he convicted Noah not by the comparison of his own justice, but by the preaching of the Word and the construction of the ark. Nor does 'nature' here denote the right use of reason, as Grotius wishes, but it is called uncircumcision by nature, because we are not circumcised by nature, but are foreskinned. Although indeed some have been found (which is urged by Grotius) who in uncircumcision, with hearts cleansed by faith, have served God, such as formerly Jethro, Naaman, Cyrus, Darius, and later the two centurions in the Gospel and Acts, and others, who are to be preferred to the circumcised Jews who are transgressors of the law, and will convict them in the day of judgment, yet none of them kept the law perfectly, none obtained salvation through the observance of the law: and therefore, as we have said, this is a fiction not unusual to rhetoricians about a Gentile who (the righteous requirements of the law)

(keeps, fulfills the law): and this is done from that hypothesis: if such a one were given, without doubt he would be preferred to a Jew, even if circumcised according to the letter of the law. Mention of the letter is made because in this comparison the circumcision of the Jew and the uncircumcision of the Gentile is not regarded, except according to the letter, insofar as the Jews, clinging only to the letter, were usurping it, and thought that the law was kept and the ordinance of God retained by the external circumcision of the foreskin. For if you look to the intention of GOD, circumcision ought to have been received as a medium of regeneration and salvation, and a seal of justice and faith: concerning which use there is no discussion here in that comparison of the Jew and the Gentile, whence, so that the Apostle may explain the matter more fully, he himself distinguishes between true and apparent, and truly false Judaism; and between literal, external, in the flesh, and spiritual or internal circumcision. For he is not a Jew who is one in the manifest, nor is that circumcision which is in the manifest, in the flesh, (pleasing to God) but he who is a Jew in the hidden (of the heart), and circumcision of the heart in the spirit (done), not in the letter (only according to the letter, and the external cutting off of the foreskin), whose praise is not from men (who look at external things), but from God. It is taught, therefore, that external and ceremonial observance of the law, or justice, is worth nothing in the judgment of God, but that internal purity of heart, perfect obedience to the law, and integrity of the whole nature are required: which, since they are found in no one, there is no justification from the law.

Nor is there any reason for the Papists to object, when the Apostle says that circumcision profits if the law is kept, that the law can be perfectly fulfilled by anyone: because hypothetical propositions posit nothing as being present: indeed, the inference must be inverted from the mind and scope of the Apostle: Because no one keeps the law perfectly, therefore circumcision looked at legally, as it was kept as a part of the law, profits no one for salvation, and thus the same judgment applies to other parts of the law, that they do not profit for salvation unless the whole law is kept in its entirety, which, however, no one can keep. Yet by this the use of circumcision is not evacuated, by which it is looked at evangelically, and had been ordained so that it might be a medium of regeneration and salvation. The Apostle is not, therefore, concerned to teach either that any of the Jews could perfectly fulfill the law, or that circumcision was of no benefit to any of the Jews, but that circumcision, when it is not used as a Sacrament of initiation or a seal of the righteousness of faith, is an obligation to keep the whole law, Gal. V. 3. The covenant entered into in circumcision did indeed require the fulfillment of the law, Gen. XVII. 1, but what was lacking to the circumcised person, the circumcised person could take by faith from the perfect obedience of Christ and apply to himself: because circumcision by divine institution was a means of salvation and a reminder and a seal of the coming blessed seed, Roman. IV. 11. the kind which is above 14. and it is clearly the same as if he had said, your circumcision shall be reckoned for circumcision, just as Paul will now speak in the opposite member. See what we have said in the Prolegomena to this Epistle. What the Greeks call ἀκροποσθίαν and the Latins præputium, as if it were προπόσθιον, the Hellenists call ἀκροβυσίαν. Gen. XVII. 11. 14. 23. 24. 25. XXXIV. 14. Exod. IV. 25. Levit. XII. 3. John V. 3. 1. Samuel XVIII. 25. 27. 2. Sam. III. 14. Jerem. IX. 24. 1. Maccab. 1. 17. from the name ἄκρουστον, which signifies obstructed at the highest part, whence also the verb is made ἀκροβυστᾶν Levit. XIX. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 25. περιτομὴ γὰρ ὠφελεῖ) ut pars obedientiæ lega- lis, qua se solutos nondum intelligebant Judæi: nec id ur- get Paulus.

Convictione Judæorum peracta confutationem duarum objectionum expedit Apostolus: Prior est à circumcisionis privilegio & virtute, altera ab absurdo, quod Paulus videatur nullam Judæis præ gentibus eminentiam relinquere. Prior versu præcedente occupatur, quòd circumcisio, quà Judæi utebantur, eos damnari non sinat: ad quam respondet Apostolus, circumcisioni virtutem illam non inesse, nisi quis totam legem impleat, loquendo κατ' ἄνθρωπον, quâ Judæi circumcisionem non ut Sacramentum gratiæ, sed ut legis quoddam præceptum servabant: quod confirmat, Judæum prævaricatorem cum Ethnico frugi & justo componendo, ut constet, circumcisionem ex se, vel opere operato non prodesse, sed tantum justo, tam spiritu, quàm corpore circumciso utilitatem adferre. Nam circumcisio quidem, inquit, prodest, si legem observes: Qui enim circumcisus est, debitor totius legis factus est, Gal. V. 3. Si autem prævaricator legis sis, (quod hactenùs evici) circumcisio tua præputium facta est, non amplius pro circumciso, sed pro incircumciso vel præputiato te habet Deus, Levit. XXVI. 41. Deuteron. X. 16. cap. XXX. 6. Jerem. IV. 4. cap. VI. 10. c. IX. 25. 26. Act. VII. 51. Philip. III. 2. 3. Si igitur præputium (præputiatus) legis justitiam custodiat, nonnè præputium illius in circumcisionem reputabitur? nonnè Deus incircumcisum habiturus est pro circumciso? Et judicabit id, quod ex naturâ est præputium legem consummans (ita est incircumcisus, qui legem observat, si talis detur: est hæc fictio Rhetorica: nemo enim est, qui legem consummet,) Te, per literam & circumcisionem (διὰ γράμματος καὶ περιτομῆς præpositio διὰ pro ἐν, ἐξ aut σὺν accipitur, ut Grotio etiam observatum: qui id vel ex legis literâ & circumcisione es, vel te cum litera & circumcisione repertum, potest etiam Hendyade locum habere, ut sensus sit, in literali, seu externâ circumcisione) prævaricatorem legis judicabit, id est, comparatione sui tuam culpam convincet, ut rectè Grotius è collatione Matth. XII. 42. quo tamen perperam trahitur Ebr. XI. 7. nam judicavit, id est, convicit Noah non suæ justitiæ comparatione, sed Verbi prædicatione, & arcæ exstructione. Neque hic Φύσις notat rectum rationis usum, uti Grotius vult, sed ἀκροβυσία ἐκ Φύσεως dicitur, quia naturâ non circumcisi, sed præputiati sumus. Quanquam verò aliqui reperti sint, (quod à Grotio urgetur) qui in præputio corde per fidem mundato Deo servierunt, quales olim Jethro, Naaman, Cyrus, Darius, postea centuriones duo in Evangelio, & Actis, & alii, qui Judæis circumcisis legis transgressoribus præferendi, eosque convincent in die judicii, nullus tamen eorum legem perfectè servavit, nullus per observantiam legis adeptus est salutem: ideoque, ut diximus, fictio hæc est Rhetoribus non insueta de gentili, qui τὰ δικαιώματα τῦ νόμε

φυλάσσει τὸν νόμον τελεῖ: & ex Hypothesi ista fa- cta: si daretur talis, sine dubio præferretur Judæo, etsi secundum literam legis circumciso. Literæ mentio fit, quia non respicitur in hac collatione circumcisio Judæi, & præputiati Ethnici non cir- cumcisio, nisi secundum literam, prout nempe Judæi literæ soli inhærentes eam usurpabant, & externa præputii circumcisione legem servari, or- dinationemque Dei retineri censebant. Nam si intentionem DEI respicias, debebat circumcisio ut medium regenerationis ac salutis, & sigillum ju- stitiæ ac fidei suscipi: de quo usu hic non agitur in illa comparatione Judæi & Ethnici, unde, ut rem uberius explicet Apostolus, distinguit ipse in- ter Judaismum verum & apparentem, & revera falsum; & inter literalem, externam, in carne, & spiritualem seu internam circumcisionem. Non enim qui in manifesto, Judæus est: neque quæ in manifesto, in carne, circumcisio est, (Deo placens) sed qui in abscondito (cordis) Judæus est, & cir- cumcisio cordis in spiritu (facta) non in litera (so- lum secundum literam, & externam præputii am- putationem) cujus laus non ex hominibus, (qui externa respiciunt) sed ex Deo est. Docetur er- go ita, externam, ac ceremonialem legis observan- tiam, aut justitiam nihil valere in Dei judicio, sed requiri interiorem cordis puritatem, perfectam le- gis obedientiam, & totius naturæ integritatem: quæ cum in nemine reperiantur, ex lege nulla est ju- stificatio.

Nec est quod objiciant Pontificii, quum Apo- stolus dicat, prodesse circumcisionem si lex servetur, posse a quopiam legem perfecte impleri: quia hypotheticæ propositiones nihil ponunt inesse: imo invertenda ex mente & scopo Apostoli est illa- tio: Quia nemo legem perfecte servat, ergo ne- mini ad salutem prodest circumcisio legaliter spe- ctata, qua servabatur ut pars legis, adeoque idem judicium est de aliis legis partibus, quod ad salutem non prosint, nisi ex asse tota lex servetur, quam vero servare potest nemo. Eo tamen non evacuatur usus circumcisionis, qua Evangelice eadem spectatur, & ordinata erat, ut medi- um esset regenerationis & salutis. Non ergo Apostolus in eo est, ut doceat, vel quod Judæo- rum aliquis perfecte legem implere potuerit, vel quod nulli Judæorum circumcisio profuerit, sed quod circumcisio, quando non usurpatur ut Sa- cramentum initiationis, aut signaculum justitiæ fidei, obligatio sit totius legis servandæ, Gal. V. 3. Requirebat quidem fœdus in circumcisione initum legis impletionem, Gen. XVII. 1. sed quod circumciso deerat, hoc ex perfecta Christi obe- dientia circumcisus fide desumere, sibique appli- care poterat: quia circumcisio ex divina in- stitutione erat medium salutis & commonefa- ctio, & sigillum venturi benedicti seminis, Ro- man. IV. 11. genus quod supra 14. planeque idem est, ac si dixisset, ἡ πε- ριτομή σου εἰς περιτομὴν λογισθήσεται, sicut jam loquetur Paulus in opposito membro. Vide, quæ diximus in Prole- gomenis ad hanc Epistolam. Quod Græci dicunt ἀκρο- ποσθίαν & Latini præputium, quasi προπόσθιον, id Helle- nistæ dicunt ἀκροβυσίαν. Genes. XVII. 11. 14. 23. 24. 25. XXXIV. 14. Exod. IV. 25. Levit. XII. 3. Johann. V. 3. 1. Samuel. XVIII. 25. 27. 2. Sam. III. 14. Jerem. IX. 24. 1. Maccab. 1. 17. à nomine ἄκρουστον, quod significat sum- ma parte obstructum, unde & verbum fit ἀκροβυστᾶν Le- vit. XIX. 23.

## 2:26
Vers. 26. if therefore the uncircumcision) And hence a Synecdoche of the part for the whole. For by the foreskin is understood a man who has a foreskin upon him. Thus below III. 30. IV. 9. XV. 8. circumcision is a circumcised man.

and the righteous requirements of the law) The Apostle here explains what he meant by law, namely מצות which is accustomed to be translated righteous requirements, and not by interpreters only, but also by Josephus, and where accurate speech is preserved, it signifies those things which are by their own nature honest, as we said on Luke I. 6. and book I. 9. of the Law of War and Peace.

Keep) He observes diligently, as in Matt. XIX. 20. Acts XXI. 24. Galat. VI. 13. and understand again, with a cleansed heart, such as were formerly Jethro, Naaman, perhaps also Cyrus, and Darius: Later two Centurions in the Gospel and Acts, and many others.

shall not his uncircumcision be reckoned for circumcision) the uncircumcised state will be worth just as much to him as the circumcised state is to the other, who is bound to circumcision, or thinks himself bound. The same Law and Action as for Titius.

Trojan and Tyrian shall be treated by me without distinction.

and shall judge the uncircumcision which is by nature) shall judge, that is, by comparison of itself it will convict your guilt. Thus the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba shall condemn the Jews Matt. XII. 42. where see what is said. Thus Noah shall condemn the world. Hebr. XI. 7. by nature is said here as above by contentiousness 8. And by nature is understood the right use of reason as above 4. The sense is: The uncircumcised man is he who follows right reason as his guide. Nor did the Syrian take it otherwise here.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐὰν ὖν ἡ ἀκροβυσία) Et hinc Synecdoche partis pro toto. Nam per præputium homo intelligitur, qui præ- putium in se habeat. Sic infra III. 30. IV. 9. XV. 8. περιτομὴ est homo circumcisus.

καὶ δικαιώματα τῦ νόμο) Apostolus hic explicat, quid mo- do intellexerit per νόμον, nempe מצות quod verti δικαιώ- ματα solet, nec ab interpretibus tantum, sed & à Josepho, & ubi accurata locutio servatur, significat ea, quæ suapte natura honesta sunt, ut diximus Luc. I. 6. & lib. I. 9. de Ju- re Belli & Pacis.

Φυλάσσῃ) Sedulo observat, ut Matth. XIX. 20. Act. XXI. 24. Galat. VI. 13. & subintellige rursus, corde mun- dato, quales olim Jethro, Naaman, forte & Cyrus, & Da- rius: Postea Centuriones duo in Evangelio & Actis, alii- que multi.

ὐχὶ ἡ ἀκροβυσία αὐτῦ εἰς περιτομὴν λογισθήσεται) tantun- dem illi valebit status præputiatus, quantum alteri, qui circumcisioni obligatus est, aut obligatum se putat, status circumcisus. Idem Jus Actio quod Titio.

Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine agetur.

καὶ κρινεῖ ἡ ἐκ φύσεως ἀκροβυσία) κρινεῖ, id est, compara- tione sui tuam culpam evincet. Sic Ninivitæ & regina Sa- bæ κατακρινῦσι damnabunt Judæos Matth. XII. 42. ubi di- cta vide. Sic Noe κατακρινεῖ τὸν κόσμον. Hebr. XI. 7. ἐκ φύσεως hic dictum ut supra ἐξ ἐριθείας 8. Et per φύσιν intel- ligitur rectus usus rationis ut supra 4. Sensus est: Præpu- tiatus is, qui rectam rationem ducem sequitur. Nec aliter hic accepit Syrus.

## 2:27
Vers. 27. fulfilling the law) that is, the righteous requirements of the law. And to fulfill here is the same as to keep just now, that is, to give effect. For the Hebrew עשה is accustomed to be translated by to fulfill, to accomplish, to complete.

the one who through the letter and circumcision is a transgressor of the law) Here through is the same as by or from just now, and above 7. according to: that is, it signifies an adjunct, and can be expressed by the preposition with, as also below IV. 11. XIV. 20. 2. Cor. III. 3. You, who violate the law, while you have both the letter of the law and circumcision. He said the letter of the law effectively, as if he were saying, the law is nothing else to you than Scripture. You show that you have it by reading, not by doing. You are a legalist, not a law-abiding man. Thus Celsus the Jurisconsult opposes the force and power of the law to words. Cassiodorus: To do the law is not to follow the words of the law outwardly, but to fulfill the mind and intention of the law obediently.

Latin:

Vers. 27. τὸν νόμον τελῦσα) id est, τὰ δικαιώματα τῦ νό- με. Et τελεῖν hic idem, quod modo φυλάσσειν, id est, effe- ctum dare. Nam עשה Hebræum per τελεῖν, ἐπιτελεῖν, συντελεῖν verti solet.

τὸ τὸν διὰ γράμματος καὶ περιτομῆς παραβάτην νόμε) Hic διὰ idem est, quod modo ἐκ vel ἐξ, & supra 7. κατὰ: id est, significat adjunctum, & potest per præpositionem cum exprimi, ut & infra IV. 11. XIV. 20. 2. Cor. III. 3. Te, qui legem violas, cum habeas & scriptum legis & circum- cisionem. Scriptum legis efficaciter dixit, quasi diceret, lex tibi nihil aliud est quam Scriptura. Ostendis eam te habere legendo, non agendo. Es νομικὸς, non νόμιμος. Sic sermæ vim ac potestatem legis verbis opponit Celsus Juris- Consultus. Cassiodorus: Legem facere non est verba legis exterius sequi, sed mentem & intentionem legis obedienter im- plere.

## 2:28
Vers. 28. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly) This must be construed with that which follows: whose praise is not from men, but from God. Not he who is a Jew outwardly, is by any means he whom God (I do not speak here of the judgment of men) approves and praises. He begins here a midrash in the Hebrew manner, that is, to oppose the mystical sense to the vulgar sense. Not much otherwise Arrianus of the Epictetans II. 1. a Jew in word, something else in deed. A Jew openly is he who draws his origin from Judah, and glories in that Is. XLVIII. who shows himself as such by his fringed garment, of which we treated in Matt. IX. 20.

And that which is outwardly, in the flesh circumcision) he explains that outwardly by in the flesh, that is, which, if an inquiry be made (as formerly after the times of Antiochus) can be seen in the flesh itself. It is not that which God principally or necessarily approves. Thus also Ephes. II. 11. of the so-called circumcision in the flesh.

But he is a Jew who is one inwardly) Rabbi Israel also speaks thus. God, as the eternal and best mind, looks most especially at the mind, a Jew inwardly, that is, who acknowledges God within in his heart, and confesses Him. For there is an allusion to the origin of the name, as we said above 17. and it appears in Apoc. II. 9.

If God is a spirit, as the poems tell us, He is to be worshipped by you especially with a pure mind.

See what we have said at John IV. 24 and in the prolegomena to the poetic sayings from Stobaeus and to book IV of the truth of the Christian Religion. ἐν κρυπτῷ, that is, in the heart. Thus more explicitly τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας. 1 Cor. XIV. 25. 2 Cor. IV. 2. Thus also τὰ κρυπτὰ, that is, thoughts, above 16 and above 42.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ὀὐ γὰρ ὁ ἐν φανερῷ Ἰυδαῖός ἐσι) Construen- dum hoc cum eo, quod sequitur: ᾗ ὁ ἔπαινος ὐκ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, ἀλλ’ ἐκ Θεῦ. Non is, qui exterius Judæus est, utique is est, quem Deus (de hominum judicio hic non ago) probat ac laudat. Incipit hic דרש more Hebræo, id est, sensum mysticum sensui vulgari opponere. Non multò aliter Ar- rianus Epictetorum II. 1. λόγῳ Ἰυδαῖον, ἔργῳ ἄλλοτι. Ju- dæus palam is, qui à Juda originem ducit, eaque gloriatur Es. XLVIII. qui se talem ostendit fimbriato habitu, de quo egimus Matth. IX. 20.

Ὀδὲ ἡ ἐν φανερῷ, ἐν σαρκὶ περιτομή) illud ἐν φανερῷ expo- nit per ἐν σαρκὶ, id est, quæ, si inquisitio fiat (ut olim post Antiochi tempora) in ipsa carne aspici potest. Non ea est, quam Deus præcipuè aut necessario probat. Sic & Ephes. II. 11. τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ ἐν κρυπτῷ Ἰυδαῖος) Loquitur sic & Rabbi Israel. Deus, ut mens æterna & optima, mentem potissimum spe- ctet ἐν κρυπτῷ Ἰυδαῖος, id est, qui intus in corde Deum agnoscit, καὶ ἐξομολογῦται. Alluditur enim ad originem nominis, ut supra diximus 17. & apparet Apoc. II. 9.

Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic tibi præcipuè purâ sit mente colendus.

Vide, quæ diximus ad Johan. IV. 24. & in prolegomenis ad dicta poetica è Stobæo & ad lib. IV. de veritate Religionis Christianæ. ἐν κρυπτῷ, id est, in corde. Sic explicatius τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας. 1. Cor. XIV. 25. 2. Cor. IV. 2. Sic & τὰ κρυπτὰ, id est, cogitata, supra 16. & sup. 42.

## 2:29
and circumcision of the heart in the spirit) That is, through the spirit, supply 'effected', whence this is called circumcision not made by hands Col. II. 11, which causes one to serve God through the Spirit. Phil. III. 3. This is that circumcision which the Prophets themselves demand and teach must be sought from God, Deuteronomy IX. 16, XXX. 6, Jeremiah IV. 4. Philo in his booklet on Circumcision notes the similarity of the circumcised part to the heart. And he adds that that exterior circumcision is a symbol of the cutting away of pleasures. In his book on sacrifices he even adds this: circumcise your hardness of heart, that is, the superfluous natures of the ruling faculty, which the immoderate impulses of the passions have sown and increased, and which the evil farmer of the soul, folly, has planted, cut away with haste, not the letter) not that which the letter you read especially prescribes. Plutarch in Numa, as if the secrets were not well entrusted to lifeless letters, by which reasoning they say the Pythagoreans did not commit their teachings to writing. the praise is not from men, but from God) We have said these things are to be connected with those which preceded in this and the previous verse, just as the Syriac seems to have accepted it, Men do not judge with certainty from the heart. God knows it and, just as He brings it about, so He follows it with praise and rewards. See below IV. 2, IX. 30, 31.

και περιτομὴ καρδίας ἐν πνεύματι) Id est, per spiritum, supple effecta, unde vocatur hæc περιτομὴ ἀχειροποίητος Col. II. 11. quæ facit, ut per Spiritum Deo serviatur. Phil. III. 3. Hæc est illa circumcisio, quam & ipsi Prophetæ exigunt, & à Deo expetendam docent, Deuteron. IX. 16. XXX. 6. Je- rem. IV. 4. Philo libello de Circumcisione notat τὴν πρὸς καρδίαν ὁμοιότητα τοῦ περιτμηθέντος μέρους. Additque, cir- cumcisionem illam exteriorem σύμβολον esse ἡδονῶν ἐκτο- μῆς. In libro vero de sacrificiis & hoc addit: περιτέμνεσθε τὰς σκληροκαρδίας, τόδε ἐστὶ τὰς περιττὰς φύσεις τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ, ἃς αἱ ἄμετροι τῶν παθῶν ἐπέσπειραν τε καὶ συν-ηύξησαν ὁρμαὶ, καὶ ὁ κακὸς ψυχῆς γεωργὸς ἐφύτευσεν, ἀφροσύνη, μετὰ σπουδῆς ἀποκείρεσθε, ἐ γραμμάτι) non ea præcipuè quam legis scriptum præ- cipit. Plutarchus Numa, ὡς οὐ καλῶς ἐν ἀψύχοις γράμμασι Φορευμένων τῶν ἀποῤῥήτων, ᾧ λογισμῷ φασι μηδὲ τοὺς Πυθα- γορικοὺς εἰς γραφὴν κατατίθεσθαι τὰ συντάγματα. ὁ ἔπαινος οὐκ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Hæc diximus cum iis, quæ hoc & superiori commate præcesserunt conne- ctenda, quomodo & Syrus videtur accepisse, Homines de corde certo non judicant. Deus id novit & id præcipue, sicut efficit, ita & laude & præmiis prosequitur. Vide in- fra IV. 2. IX. 30. 31.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

AS the Apostle taught that, with circumcision viewed legally, just as the Jews boasted of it, no prerogative or utility accrued to them in the judgment of God: so, even though they had an eminence over the nations in that the oracles of God were entrusted to them, from which they could have had true righteousness, nevertheless nothing accrues to them from that in the judgment of God, just as nothing is lost to the righteousness of God through their unbelief; for if He were to wish to test us with judgment, He could justly condemn all, yet He turns our injustice into the praise of His righteousness. Before whom, therefore, there is no prerogative for anyone, and thus he convicts all without distinction of condemnation through the law: and so he passes to the righteousness proposed in the Gospel, and to explaining justification through faith, through which likewise all boasting is excluded, and the grace of God is commended not only to the Jews, but also to the nations, and yet the law is not abolished, but is raised up and established. There are 4 parts: I. The dissolution of the objection concerning the eminence of the Jews, v. 1 and 2. II. The vindication of the constancy and righteousness of God, up to v. 9. III. The proof of the universal prerogative of all men concerning sin and condemnation excluded, to v. 21. IV. The demonstration of the righteousness of faith, up to the end of the chapter. The first three still pertain to the explanation of the subject to be justified. The fourth, however, begins the elucidation of the causes of justification and the demonstration of true justification.

PART I. The dissolution of the objection concerning the prerogative of the Jews.

Vers. 1. What then is the advantage of the Jew. Ecclesiastes VI. 11. The objection is proposed interrogatively: if the matter stands thus, that God approves only the purity of the heart without distinction of birth, and judges it worthy of His Spirit and consequently of the heavenly reward, what then does that people have as a prerogative, whom God so often calls His own peculiar people? or what is the profit of circumcision. Genesis XXXVII. 26. Psalm XXX. 10. If even the uncircumcised can be clean before God, why then was that exterior circumcision instituted? The Apostle's objection is not, as Grotius wishes, that the Jewish people, the peculiar possession of God, seem to have nothing of a prerogative if God approves only the purity of the heart without distinction of birth: because that purity of heart alone was certainly in this peculiar possession of God, and among the proselytes who joined themselves to it, not among the foreign nations, for these were without God in this world, Eph. II. 12, and were destitute of faith, by which hearts are purified, Acts XV. 9, nor could they have hope of a heavenly reward; indeed, they were strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope, as the Apostle says in the cited place, Eph. II. 12. But this is the force and reason of the objection: If the Jews are no less under condemnation than the Gentiles, by virtue of sin, which the Apostle had demonstrated, what then do the Jews have as a preeminence over the Gentiles? And what is the utility of circumcision? So that a reduction to absurdity is held here, since it ought to be placed beyond doubt that the Jews possess a notable prerogative over the Gentiles and that their circumcision has utility; does not that promiscuous condemnation of Jews and Gentiles on account of sin take away this prerogative of the Jews and the utility of circumcision? For if there is nothing more for the Jew than for the Gentile in terms of righteousness before God, there will certainly be no prerogative of Judaism, no utility of circumcision. Which is absurd, and altogether intolerable to the Jews. To which objection the Apostle replies first, regarding the prerogative, that it is indeed to be granted to the Jews, yet it is not such as if they obtain righteousness from the law; but it consists in this, that the oracles of God were entrusted to them: whence they could have the righteousness of faith, which the Gentiles could not attain except among the Jews; which prerogative is proclaimed in Ps. CXLVII. 19, 20. He has not dealt so with any nation. Cf. Ps. CIII. 7.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

UT circumcisione legaliter spectata, quem- admodum eam jactabant Judæi, nullam ipsis in judicio Dei prærogativam nec utilitatem accessisse docuit Apostolus: ita etsi habuerint eam præ gentibus eminentiam, quod eloquia Dei ipsis credita, unde justitiam veram habere potuerint, non tamen inde in Dei judicio ali- quid ipsis accedit, uti nec per eorum ἀπιστίαν ju- stitiæ Dei quicquam decedit; qui si judicio no- biscum experiri velit, omnes damnare justè posset, injustitiam tamen nostram vertit in lau- dem justitiæ suæ. Coram quo proinde nullam esse ullius prærogativam, adeoque omnes citra διαστολὴν condemnationis per legem convincit: atque ita ad justitiam in Evangelio proposi- tam, & justificationem per fidem explicandam transit, per quam itidem omnis gloriatio ex- cluditur, ac gratia Dei non Judæis tantum, sed gentibus etiam commendatur, neque tamen lex tollitur, sed erigitur, ac stabilitur. Partes IV. sunt: I. Objectionis de eminentia Ju- dæorum διάλυσις, v. 1. & 2. II. Constantiæ, & justi- tiæ Dei ἐκδίκησις, usque ad v. 9. III. Exclusa præ- rogativæ universalis omnium hominum de peccato & condemnatione ἔλεγξις, ad v. 21. IV. Justitiæ fi- dei ἔνδειξις, usque ad finem capitis. Priores tres pertinent adhuc ad subjecti justificandi explica- tionem. Quarta vero inchoat caussarum justifica- tionis dilucidationem & veræ justificationis de- monstrationem.

PARS I. Objectionis de prærogativa Judæorum διάλυσις.

Vers. 1. Τί οὖν τὸ περίσσον τοῦ ἰουδαίου. מה יותר Ecclesiastæ VI. 11. Objectio interrogative proponitur: si ita se res habet, ut Deus sine ortus discrimi- ne munditiem cordis solam approbet, Spirituque suo, & consequenter præmio cœlesti dignam judicet, quid ergo præcipuum habet populus ille, quem Deus toties suum pe- culiariter populum vocat? ἢ τίς ἡ ὠφέλεια τῆς περιτομῆς. מה בצע Gen. XXXVII. 26. Psalm. XXX. 10. Si etiam præputiatus Deo mundus esse potest, cur ergo instituta fuit illa exterior circumcisio? Objectio Apostoli non inde est, ut vult Gro- tius, quod nihil præcipui videatur habere populus Judaicus, peculium Dei, si Deus sine ortus discri- mine munditiem cordis solam approbet: quia sola illa cordis mundities utique erat in hoc Dei pecu- lio, & proselytis, qui se ad illum aggregabant, non in gentibus extraneis, hæ enim erant sine Deo in hoc mundo, Eph. II. 12. & fide destituebantur, quâ purificantur corda, Act. XV. 9. nec spem habere præmii cælestis poterant, imò peregrinæ erant à testamentis promissionis ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντες, ut lo- co laudato Eph. II. 12. Apostolus. Hæc autem est objectionis vis & ratio: Si non minus Judæi, quàm gentiles sub condemnatione sunt, vi peccati, quod demonstrarat Apostolus, quid ergò præcipui ha- bent Judæi præ gentibus? & quæ est circumcisio- nis utilitas? ut habeatur hic deductio ad absur- dum, quum extra dubium positum esse debeat, Ju- dæos prærogativa pollere insigni præ gentilibus ac circumcisionem suam habere utilitatem, annon illa promiscua Judæorum & gentilium ob pecca- tum condemnatio tollat hanc Judæorum præro- gativam, & utilitatem circumcisionis? Si enim nihil amplius Judæo, quàm Ethnico est Justitiæ coram Deo, nulla utique erit Judaismi prærogati- va, nulla circumcisionis utilitas. Quod absur- dum, & Judæis omninò intolerandum. Ad quam objectionem respondet Apostolus primùm, quod ad prærogativam, concedendam quidem eam Ju- dæis esse, non tamen illam esse, quasi justitiam ex lege obtineant; sed in eo sitam esse, quod ipsis cre- dita sint eloquia Dei: unde justitiam fidei habere poterant, quam gentiles non nisi apud Judæos consequi potuere; quæ prærogativa deprædica- tur Ps. CXLVII. 19. 20. Non fecit taliter omni na- tioni. Conf. Ps. CIII. 7.

## 3:2
Vers. 2. Much in every way.

Much properly corresponds to this 'abundant,' but according to the calculation, it also corresponds to the second member of the interrogation. He says this: The same piety before God is valid in both, but the Israelite or any circumcised person has easier access to reach it.

He does not indicate this: That the same piety before God is valid in both Jew and Gentile (because in the Gentile no piety has a place, Rom. XIV. 23, and the Apostle has gone on to deny proper righteousness to all, as much to Jews as to Gentiles) but that any Israelite has easier access to reach it: for the Apostle recognizes no distinction, v. 22. He concludes all Jews and Gentiles under sin, v. 9. He demonstrates that the grace of God in Christ is necessary for all; which he hints is proposed to all, although by reason of order first to the Jews, chap. I. v. 16. Formerly the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews, in which the way of salvation was revealed: and that was then their prerogative: We grant them these easier accesses to faith and to the means of faith.

For first indeed.

The beginning of the discourse, as above I. 8, where similarly 'indeed' is without an apodosis. But the Apostle does not finish this discourse here, but defers it to chap. IX. 4.

This discourse begun here is not continued in Rom. IX. 4, even though that prerogative is more fully illustrated there on occasion: nor is there need for an apodosis on account of the particle 'indeed,' which is used neatly at the beginning of a discourse, even if no adversative particle corresponds to it. But 'first' is not a bare beginning of a discourse, but rather indicates that which is chief in the prerogative of the Jews, which is brought forward here. Cf. Deut. IV. 32, 34.

That they were entrusted with the oracles of God.

They were entrusted in Puhal, that is, this the Jews have as a chief thing, that the oracles of God were given to them for safekeeping. It is the custom of the Greeks to construct passives with the case that the actives would govern: which our writers also often follow, and specifically in the passive 'to be entrusted,' 1 Cor. IX. 17, Gal. II. 7, 1 Thess. II. 4, 1 Tim. I. 11, Tit. I. 3. The oracles of God are rightly called all sayings proceeding from God, as Wisd. XVI. 11, Sirach XXXVI. 12, and living oracles, Acts VII. 38. But here they seem to be signified properly as oracles

foreshowing the Messiah, by whose indication the Jews could recognize him more easily than the Gentiles: which the Apostle says more explicitly below in 21, 22. See Ps. CXLVII. 19, CXIX. 38, 58, 162, in which places in the Greek it is 'oracles,' they are the very things which Paul often calls 'promises,' both in this Epistle and in that to the Galatians. How great a benefit this is, however, can be understood from those things which are said in Eph. III. 2.

Not only are the oracles pointing to the Messiah, or ἐπαγγελίαι (promises), noted, but all the λόγια (oracles) and utterances of God, the entire Scripture of the O.T.; nor did the benefit of divine grace exhibited to the Jews consist only in this, that by the benefit of those oracles the Messiah coming could be more easily recognized by them than by the Gentiles, since the Jews could have obtained salvation by believing in the promised Messiah before his exhibition and advent, Acts XV. 10. From this statement, however, the canonical books of the Old Testament are recognized, because only those books before Christ was exhibited belong to the Canon of the O.T. which were entrusted to the Jews, or pertain to the utterances and writings of God entrusted to the Jews: whence the Apocryphal books, as we call them, were rashly received into the Canon by the Council of Trent. For they were never entrusted to the Jewish Church as λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ (oracles of God). Toletus, Estius, Pererius, and Cornel. à Lap. certainly acknowledge this. that the Scriptures of the O.T. are signified here, to which, therefore, those Apocryphal books cannot belong. And Pererius observes, from Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Ambrose on this passage, that 'entrusted' signifies more than 'granted,' and that to entrust something to someone is to commit it to his proven and examined faith, and not only Eusebius, book VIII of the Preparation for the Gospel, ch. II, testifies to the faith and religion of the Jews in preserving the Canon of the O.T., but also Bellarmine, book II on the Word of God, ch. 2. Conf. Orac. XXII. But it must still be noted regarding this word that it seems also to tacitly involve the faith required of men: namely, the Apostle uses a word taken from faith, because those divine oracles entrusted to their faith ought also to have been received by them with faith, which was their primary aim, not, as was done, rejected through faithlessness.

PART II. The vindication of the constancy and justice of God.

Latin:

Vers. 2. πολὺ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον.

πολὺ propriè respondet isti περισσὸν, at κατὰ σύμψηφιν etiam membro secundo interrogationis. Hoc dicit: Ea- dem in utroque pietas apud Deum valet, sed ut ad eam perveniat Israelita sive circumcisus aliquis faciliores habet aditus.

Non id indigitat: Eandem in utroque Judæo & gentili pietatem apud Deum valere: (quia in gen- tili nulla pietas locum habet, Rom. XIV. 23. & omnibus tàm Judæis, quàm gentilibus hic justi- tiam propriam derogatum ivit Apostolus) sed ut ad eam perveniat Israelita aliquis, faciliores ipsos habere aditus: nullam enim διαςολὴν agnoscit Apostolus, v. 22. Omnes Judæos, & gentiles sub peccato concludit, v. 9. Omnibus gratia Dei in Christo opus esse demonstrat; quam omnibus pro- positam esse, etsi ratione ordinis prius Judæis, ca- pit. I. v. 16. innuit. Olim Judæis credita fuere τὰ λόγια τῶ Θεῶ, in quibus via salutis revelata est: at- que ea tunc fuit ipsorum prærogativa: Hos facilio- res aditus ipsis largimur ad fidem & ad media fidei.

πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ.

ראשית Inchoatio Sermonis, ut supra I. 8. ubi simili- ter μὲν est sine ἀποδόσει. Sermonem autem hunc hic non consummat Apostolus, sed differt in cap. IX. 4.

Sermo hic inchoatus non continuatur Rom. IX. 4. etsi uberius illa prærogativa ibidem ex occasio- ne illustretur: neque ἀναποδότῳ opus ob particu- lam μὲν, quæ concinnè in sermonis initio adhi- betur, etsi particula adversativa ei nulla respon- deat. τὸ πρῶτον autem non inchoatio sermonis nuda est, sed potius id, quod præcipuum est, in præ- rogativa Judæorum indicat, quod hic adfertur. Conf. Deut. IV. 32. 34.

ὅτι ἐπιςεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τῶ θεῶ.

פֿקדו in Puhal, id est, hoc Judæi habent præcipuum, quod illis in custodiam data sunt Dei oracula. Mos est Græcorum passiva construere cum eo casu, quem regerent activa: quod & nostri Scriptores sæpè sequuntur ac nomi- natim in passivo πισέυεσθαι 1. Corinth. IX. 17. Gal. II. 7. 1. Thessal. II. 4. 1. Timoth. I. 11. Tit. I. 3. λόγια τῶ Θεῶ אמרות אל dicuntur rectè omnia dicta à Deo profecta, ut Sapient. XVI. 11. Syrach. XXXVI. 12. & λόγια ζῶντα, Act. VII. 38. Sed hic propriè significari videntur oracula

Messiam præmonstrantia, quorum indicio Judæi facilius quàm gentes eum agnoscere potuerunt: quod & infra 21, 22. explicatius dicit Apostolus. Vide Ps. CXLVII. 19. CXIX. 38. 58. 162. in quibus locis in Græco est λόγια, ea ipsa sunt, quæ sæpè Paulus vocat ἐπαγγελίας tum in hac Epistola, tum in illa ad Galatas. Quantum verò hoc sit beneficium, in- telligi potest ex iis, quæ dicuntur Eph. III. 2.

Non modò oracula Messiam præmonstrantia, vel ἐπαγγελίαι notantur, sed universa λόγια & eloquia Dei, tota V. T. Scriptura; nec in eo tan- tum situm erat divinæ gratiæ Judæis exhibitæ be- neficium, quod beneficio istorum oraculorum Messias adveniens agnosci facilius potuerit ab ipsis, quam gentibus, siquidem in promissum Mes- siam credendo salutem consequi potuerint Judæi ante ejus exhibitionem, & adventum, Act. XV. 10. Ex hoc autem dicto libri canonici Veteris Testa- menti agnoscuntur, quòd illi solum libri ante Christum exhibitum ad Canonem Vet. Test. per- tineant, qui crediti sunt Judæis, vel ad eloquia, & scripta Dei Judæis credita spectant: unde libri Apocryphi, quos vocamus, temerè à Concilio Tri- dentino in Canonem recepti sunt. Nunquam enim illi Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, ut λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ, concredi- ti sunt. Agnoscunt utique Toletus, Estius, Pere- rius, Cornel. à Lap. Scripturas V. T. hîc significa- ri, ad quas proinde pertinere nequeunt libri illi Apocryphi. Et observat Pererius, è Chrysost. Theophyl. & Ambros. in h. l. quòd credita plus significet, quàm concessa, quodque credere alicui rem quampiam sit ejus fidei probatæ & perspectæ committere, ac testatur non Eusebius tantum l. VIII. de præpar. Evangel. c. II. de fide ac religio- ne Judæorum in asservando Canone Vet. Test. Sed etiam Bellarm. l. II. de Verbo Dei c. 2. Conf. Orac. XXII. Id autem circà hanc vocem adhuc monendum, quod videatur eadem etiam tacitè involvere fidem ab hominibus requisitam: nimi- rum utitur Apostolus voce à fide desumpta, quod oracula illa divina fidei ipsorum credita, fide etiam ab ipsis debuerint suscipi, quod ad præcipuum eorum Scopum, non, uti factum, reprobari per- fidiâ.

PARS II. Constantiæ & justitiæ Dei ἐκδίκησις.

## 3:3
For what if some did not believe?

As if he were saying, what then, if they did not use the benefit? The benefit did not cease to be such on that account. Ἀπιστεῖν (to disbelieve) here, as in Mark XVI. 16 and Acts XXVIII. 14, signifies a fault not common to the human race, but special, and avoidable by the help of God, if it is not neglected: about which matter we have said something in the Annotations at the end of book II on the truth of the Christian Religion. This manuscript has ἀπειθήκασι (they disobeyed), not badly; but the Apostle said 'some,' when he could have said 'most.' He is accustomed to use wit in this way. You have a similar instance below in XI. 17 and Heb. III. 16.

It does not regard only the Jews who lived around the advent of Christ, as it seems to Grotius, but also those who were unbelieving before Christ; because he speaks generally, nor does he restrict the discourse to certain times. No one's infidelity makes void the faithfulness of God. Whence it is gathered that those promises of God which do not include the hypothesis of faith are by no means rendered void by the infidelity of men: nor could the promise of the Messiah made to the Jews, who was to be raised up from their own seed, be made void by their infidelity. Nor indeed does anything depart from the faithfulness or constancy of God, as far as those promises are concerned which were made under the hypothesis of faith, because many of them are deprived of the fruit, because they lack faith. For thus the divine constancy and truthfulness are rather commended, in that those things which were promised under the hypothesis of faith, to those who are destitute of faith, He is unwilling to grant, nor does He grant. Rightly, therefore, this is opposed to the Calvinists, who deny that the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper are present to the impious on account of their infidelity, because the words of Christ's institution do not suspend the Sacramental presence from the faith of those receiving. But the Calvinists wrongly conclude from this axiom of the Apostle, the infidelity of men does not make void the faith of God, that those who have once been received into the covenant of grace with God are never excluded by God, nor do they fall from it through infidelity: because those promises include the hypothesis of faith. For although it is certain that God, as far as it lies in Him, wishes the covenant of grace to be kept, and testifies to His own faith and constancy in that He does not preclude a return to the covenant of grace for those who are failing, nor deny His grace to those who, after a fall, return to Him through conversion, which is rightly asserted against the Novatians and Socinians, because the gifts and calling of God are ἀμεταμέλητα Rom. XI. 29. and the Papists could also be pressed by this aphorism, when they assert that the covenant of God initiated with us in baptism is rendered so void by sins that no true consolation can any longer be sought from baptism by the penitent: yet it is not to be denied that the faithful can fall from the grace of God through infidelity, or lose faith through sins against conscience, for the reason that God is faithful and constant: because God never promised inamissible grace, or absolute perseverance in faith.

μὴ ἡ ἀπιστία αὐτῶν τὴν πίστιν τοῦ Θεοῦ καταργήσει) what Paul uses here concerning God, the same he uses concerning Christ 2. Tim. II. 13. εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν ἐκεῖνος πιστὸς μένει. God had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their posterity would be under His peculiar care; He did this both by other things and by promising and prefiguring the Messiah to them. He exhibited such a one, they did not follow Him, namely the majority, as this whole chapter is to be understood. See John I. 11. Understand: what wonder, therefore, if He transferred Himself to the Gentiles.

Latin:

Τί γὰρ εἰ ἠπίστησάν τινες.

Quasi dicat, quid tum, si illi beneficio usi non sunt? non ideo id beneficium esse desiit. Ἀπιστεῖν hic, ut Marci XVI. 16. Act. XXVIII. 14. significat culpam non communem humano generi, sed specialem, & Dei ope, si ea non negli- gatur, evitabilem: de qua re diximus aliquid in Annotatis ad finem l. II. de veritate Religionis Christianæ. Manu- scriptus hic habet ἀπειθήκασι non male, Τινὲς autem dixit Apostolus, cùm dicere potuisset, plerique. Ita solet χα- ριεντίζειν. Simile habes infra XI. 17. Hebr. III. 16.

Non Judæos tantùm respicit, qui sub adven- tum Christi vixere, ut Grotio videtur, sed etiam, qui ante Christum increduli fuere; quia ge- neraliter loquitur, nec ad tempora certa restrin- git orationem. Nullius infidelitas Dei fidem eva- cuat. Unde colligitur, illas Dei promissiones, quæ hypothesin fidei non includunt, per infide- litatem hominum minimè irritas reddi: neque promissio Messiæ Judæis facta, qui è semine ipso- rum excitandus erat, evacuari potuit per infideli- tatem eorum. Neque verò quicquam fidelitati vel constantiæ Dei decedit, quantùm ad illa pro- missa, quæ sub hypothesi fidei facta sunt, quod mul- ti eorum fructu destituantur, quia fide carent. Ita enim constantia potius divina ac veracitas commendatur, quòd quæ sub hypothesi fidei pro- missa sunt, iis, qui fide destituti sunt, concedere- nolit, nec concedat. Rectè ergo opponitur hoc Calvinianis, Christi corpus & sanguinem in S. Cœna, impiis ob infidelitatem eorum præstò esse, negantibus, quia verba institutionis Christi non suspendunt præsentiam Sacramentalem à fide per- cipientium. Malè autem Calviniani ex hoc axio- mate Apostoli, infidelitas hominum non evacuat fi- dem Dei, concludunt, quod illi, qui semel in fœ- dus gratiæ cum Deo recepti sunt, nunquam à Deo excludantur, nec per infidelitatem eodem exci- dant: quia promissiones illæ fidei hypothesin in- cludunt. Quanquam enim certum sit, quod Deus, quantum in ipso est, velit fœdus gratiæ ser- vatum, ac fidem & constantiam suam in eo teste- tur, quod reditum deficientibus ad fœdus gratiæ non præcludat, aut gratiam suam deneget illis, qui post lapsum per conversionem ad ipsum redeunt, quod contra Novatianos & Socinianos meritò asse- ritur, quia dona & vocatio Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα Rom. XI. 29. atque urgeri etiam possint hoc apho- rismo Pontificii, cum fœdus Dei in baptismo no- biscum initum per peccata ita irritum reddi asse- runt, ut ex baptismo à pœnitentibus nulla amplius vera peti possit consolatio: non tamen negandum, excidere posse fideles gratiâ Dei per infidelitatem, aut amittere fidem, per peccata contra conscientiam, ideo quod Deus fidelis & constans sit: quia nun- quam promisit Deus inamissibilem gratiam, aut absolutam perseverantiam in fide.

μὴ ἡ ἀπιστία αὐτῶν τὴν πίστιν τοῦ Θεοῦ καταργήσει) quod hic de Deo usurpat Paulus, idem de Christo 2. Tim. II. 13. εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν ἐκεῖνος πιστὸς μένει. Deus promiserat Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, posteritatem ipsorum, sibi peculiari curæ fore, fecit hoc tum aliis rebus, tum Messiam illis promitten- do & præfigurando. Exhibuit talem, ipsi eum secuti non sunt, nempe plerique quomodo totum hoc caput intelli- gendum est. Vid. Joh. I. 11. Subintellige: quid mirum er- gò, si ad gentes se transtulit.

## 3:4
μὴ γένοιτο) It is of one strongly dissenting. חס וחלילה See what was said at Matt. X. 22.

Verse 4. γινέσθω δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἀληθὴς, πᾶς δὲ ἄνθρωπος ψευστής.

The sense is: Let God appear constant in His promises, even if all men should fail in faith. We have dealt with this comparative manner of speaking at Matt. V. 18. To be for to appear is frequent in the books of the Hebrews, as below in verse 26; then truthful, for one who is of good faith: a liar for one who is of bad faith. And that the words are to be taken thus here is shown by the preceding context, and the comparison of that passage which we cited at Timothy, where πιστὸς is the same as ἀληθής here. And in very many places of the Old Testament נאמן and אמן which properly sounds ἀληθῆ, is translated πιστὸς. Greeks and Latins say ψεύδεσθαι and to lie of him who fails in faith. Deut. XXXII. 4. אל אמונה, in Greek Θεὸς πιστὸς, in Latin God is faithful.

The sense here is not only that God is to be acknowledged as constant in His promises, even if all men should fail in faith: nor is to be here, or in verse 26 below, to appear: but, let God be true, let it be acknowledged and believed that He is true, and that on the contrary all men are liars: which Ps. CXVI. 11, from which these words were brought, indicates: and here it is inculcated not only on account of the Jews, that the faith of God is not made void by their infidelity, but also with a view to the principal scope and demonstration, that indeed God, even if He had condemned all men, could not be argued to have violated faith, but would rather have the praise of demonstrated justice, so far is it from the case that the faith of God was rendered void on account of the punished perfidy of some: just as the allegation of Ps. LI. 6 confirms this: the sense of which here also seems to be: if God wishes to test by judgment, a just reason will stand for Him to condemn all men, no one will win in his own cause against God. For God is acknowledged as just when He convicts us of sin, He wins when He condemns us by the sentence of the law, as was done to David through Nathan. For thus the Apostle aims at the prefixed scope, that man cannot be justified before God by his own or inherent justice, or according to the law, but rather by His sentence is convicted as guilty of judgment and curse, and that being thus condemned by the law on account of sins, he is absolved solely through faith in Christ, and declared just to the praise of divine justice. In passing, however, he dilutes the objection, that our injustice commends the justice of God, teaching that this happens, not of itself, which he argues to be absurd, because thus it would follow that God is unjust, who inflicts punishment, but by the singular wisdom and goodness of God, who knows how to elicit good even from evil, not that evils are to be done so that goods may result; but that where sin had invaded the world, and condemnation on account of sin, God the Best and Greatest wished to provide for the salvation of men in such a way that the glory of His justice and of His immense goodness alike might shine forth. This is the genuine analysis, from which it is entirely left that all men without exception, or hyperbole, as infected with a habitual propensity to lying, are thus concluded under the guilt of sin by the sentence of the law. For by naming lying or a special sin, given the occasion, the other sins are connoted, which are afterwards more fully deduced by the Apostle. For in lying there is not only the highest baseness, but also the root of all iniquity.

Καθὼς γέγραπται) This is altogether to be referred to what follows, a similar expression in Acts VII. 42. XV. 15. & here above I.17. below 10. VIII. 36. IX. 13. 33. XI. 8. XV. 3. 9. 21. 1. Cor. II. 9. X. 7. 2. Cor. VIII. 15. IX. 9.

ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις συ) These are the very words of the LXX interpreters Ps. LI. 6. which both Paul and Luke follow much. Δικαιωθῇς, here is for the Hebrew תִצְדַק in Kal, that is, that you may appear just. For we said that this word is taken thus in the Prolegomena to this Epistle, and it is consistent with that which we just said about the word γενέσθω. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις for in your actions, a Hebrew expression.

Καὶ νικήσῃς ἐν τῷ κρίνεσθαί σε.

The LXX & Paul have expressed the sense well. The word in Hebrew is תִזְכֶּה, that is, that you may appear pure, but he who appears pure in a lawsuit, he wins, if you are judged, that is, if men wish to judge you, as the Syrian clearly here, ܒܥܝܢܐ, which is in the Hebrew, can be explained, either while you judge, or while someone judges you, for the noun is often understood among the Hebrews in verbs, especially in infinitives placed as gerunds. And as the Greeks preferred the latter sense, so also did the Apostle. The sense is: God called the Gentiles to the Gospel, but after the long contumacy of the Jews. What injury did He do to them? Their privilege remained safe for them.

The Apostle is not here treating of the rejection of the Jews after long-suffering, because no injury was done to them, on account of their long contumacy: but he is treating of this, that even if men wish to judge God, who condemns them, God wins, and is acknowledged as just in His word, because all are subject to the judgment of God, and by their own injustice they bear witness to the divine justice and truth. For just as David teaches that God does injury to no one, and that His judgments are just, however much men may judge them perversely; so the Apostle teaches that God remains truthful and faithful, but that all men are by nature liars and deceitful, and that when men judge God, who condemns them, God wins and prevails in His words and judgments, even if He condemns all, nor does the divine truth or faithfulness suffer any risk by that condemnation. Therefore it is not to be restricted to the Jews, much less to those who lived at the coming of Christ, so as to weaken the force of the Apostolic application, and the intention of the Apostle, which are stated and adduced generally and universally.

Latin:

μὴ γένοιτο) Est valde aversantis. חס ולה Vide, quæ dicta Matth. X. 22.

Vers. 4. γινέσθω δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἀληθὴς, πᾶς δὲ ἄνθρωπος ψευστής.

Sensus est: Appareat Deus constans in promissis, etiamsi vel omnes homines fidem fallant. De hoc comparativo genere loquendi egimus ad Matth. V. 18. Esse pro appare- re frequens in Hebræorum libris, ut infra 26. deinde verax, pro eo, qui sit bonæ fidei: mendax pro eo, qui malæ. Et ita hic sumendas voces ostendunt præcedentia, & collatio illius quem adduximus ad Timotheum loci, ubi πιστὸς idē est, quod hic ἀληθής. Et plurimis locis Vet. Testam. נאמן & אמן quod propriè ἀληθῆ sonat, vertitur πιστὸς. Græci & Latini di- cunt ψεύδεσθαι & mentiri eum, qui fidē fallit. Deut. XXXII. 4. אל אמונה, in Græco Θεὸς πιστὸς, in Latino Deus fidelis.

Non hic tantum sensus est, Deum constantem agnoscendum in promissis, utut vel omnes homi- nes fidem fallant: neque esse vel hic, vel v. 26. in- fra est apparere: sed, sit Deus verax est, agnosca- tur, & credatur, quod verax sit, quodque contrà omnes homines mendaces sint: quod Ps. CXVI.11. ex quo adducta hæc verba sunt, indicat: atque hic non modo ob Judæos, quod eorum infidelitate fi- des Dei non evacuetur, sed etiam intuitu principa- lis scopi, & demonstrationis inculcatur, quod nem- pe Deus, etiamsi omnes homines condemnafet, fidei violatæ argui minimè possit, sed justitiæ demon- stratæ laudem potius habiturus sit, tantum abest, ut ob vindicatam quorundam perfidiam fides Dei irrita reddita sit: quemadmodum id etiam allega- tio Psal. LI. 6. confirmat: cujus hic itidem vide- tur sensus: si judicio velit experiri Deus, justa illi constabit ratio ad damnandos omnes homines, nemo in sua causa vincet contra Deum. Justus enim agnoscitur Deus, cum peccati nos arguit, vincit, cum nos condemnat per legis sententiam, ut Da- vidi per Nathanem factum. Ita enim collineat Apostolus ad scopum præfixum, quod homo co- ram Deo justificari non possit per propriam vel in- hærentem justitiam, aut secundum legem, sed ejus sententiâ potius reus judicii & maledictionis con- vincatur, quodque ita condemnatus per legem propter peccata, unicè per fidem in Christum ab- solvatur, justusque declaretur ad laudem justitiæ divinæ. In transitu autem diluit objectum, inju- stitiam nostram Dei justitiam commendare, docens id fieri, non per se, quod absurdum esse arguit, quia ita sequeretur, Deum injustum esse, qui pœnam inferat, sed singulari sapientia & bonitate Dei, qui ex malo etiam novit elicere bonum, non quod mala sint facienda, ut eveniant bona; sed quod ubi peccatum invaserat mundum, & ob peccatum condemnatio, Deus O. M. ita consultum volue- rit saluti hominum, ut justitiæ pariter & bonitatis ejus immensæ gloria elucesceret. Hæc est genui- na analysis, è qua omninò relinquitur, omnes sine exceptione, vel hyperbole homines, ut habituali mentiendi pronitate infectos, ita sub peccati reatu conclusos esse, per legis sententiam. Nominato enim mendacio seu peccato speciali datâ occasio- ne, connotantur cætera peccata, quæ postmodum plenius deducuntur ab Apostolo. In mendacio enim non tantum turpitudo summa, sed radix et- iam omnis iniquitatis inest.

Καθὼς γέγραπται) Omnino hoc ad sequentia referen- dum, similis locutio Act. VII. 42. XV. 15. & hî̂c supra I.17. infra 10. VIII. 36. IX. 13. 33. XI. 8. XV. 3. 9. 21. 1. Cor. II. 9. X. 7. 2. Cor. VIII. 15. IX. 9.

ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις συ) Sunt ipsa verba LXX interpretum Ps. LI. 6. quos & Paulus & Lucas multum se- quuntur. Δικαιωθῇς, hî̂c est pro Hebræo תִצְדַק in Kal, id est, ut justus appareas. Sic enim id verbum sumi diximus in Prolegomenis ad hanc Epistolam, estque id congruens ei, quod modo diximus de voce γενέσθω. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις pro in actionibus tuis, Hebræa locutio.

Καὶ νικήσῃς ἐν τῷ κρίνεσθαί σε.

LXX. & Paulus sensum bene expressere. Verbum in Hebræo est תִזְכֶּה, id est, purus appareas, qui autem pu- rus apparet in lite, is vincit, si judiceris, id est, si homines de te judicare velint, ut clarè hî̂c Syrus, ܒܥܝܢܐ, quod est in Hebræo, potest exponi, aut dum tu judicas, aut dum aliquis de te judicat, nam nomen sæpè apud Hebræos in verbis subauditur, maximè in infinitivis gerundivè positis. Et posteriorem sensum sicut Græci prætulere, ita & Apostolus. Sensus est: Vocavit Deus gentes ad Evangelium, sed post longam Judæorum contumaciam. Quid injuriæ eis fecit? Salvum illis fuit suum privilegium.

Non hî̂c de Judæorum post diuturnam toleran- tiam rejectione, quòd illis nulla facta injuria, ob longam eorum contumaciam: sed de eo agit Apo- stolus, quod etiamsi homines judicare velint Deum, ipfos condemnantem, vincat, & justus agnoscatur in verbo suo Deus, quia omnes judicio Dei obnoxii sunt, & injustitiâ suâ justitiæ divinæ veritati testi- monium præbent. Ut enim David Deum nemini facere injuriam, ac justa ejus esse judicia, utut ho- mines præposterè judicent de iisdem, docet; ita Apo- stolus, veracem, & fidelem manere Deum, omnes verò homines mendaces naturâ esse, ac fallaces, & cum judicant Deum homines, qui ipsos condemnat, vincere, & obtinere Deum in verbis & judiciis suis, etiamsi condemnet omnes, nec quicquam periclita- ri eâ condemnatione divinam veritatem aut fidem. Non ergò ad Judæos, nedum ad eos, qui sub ad- ventum Christi vixere, restringenda, ad enervan- dam vim applicationis Apostolicæ, & intentio- nem Apostoli, quæ generaliter & universaliter di- cta & adducta sunt.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. εἰ δὲ ἀδικία ἡμῶν.

And here is a μίμησις, for Paul repeats the very words of the Jews who were at Rome. Now this objection of the Jews flowed mainly from the fact that the Gentiles, who had been immersed in idolatry and other vices, were said to have been adopted by God; those who believe this, they said, can sin safely. It is the same objection of Celsus in the words found in Origen: and here indeed the Apostle merely shows that what is inferred is impious, but the answer is deferred to chapter VI. And it is the same as that of Origen: the nations are not to be looked at as they were, but as they now are. Meanwhile, this also shows that the Jews at that time were no better than the nations. Furthermore, the Apostles taught that nothing was more glorious to God than that He had called all nations to Himself. And the occasion for that matter was given by the contumacy of the Jews. From these two very true things were born those false objections and calumnies which the Apostle refutes here.

Nor is there any trace here of either the rejection of the Jews or the calling of the nations. For the objections of the Jews are not being resolved here, because the nations, immersed in idolatry and other vices, were adopted by God, as if those who believe this concluded from it that one could safely sin: but the charges and objections, which were being woven from the Apostle's doctrine concerning the justice of God resisting from the very conviction of all men concerning injustice, are being solved.

Θεῦ δικαιοσύνην συνίστησι) that is, he makes it more conspicuous, as below V. 8. Thus συνιστάναι is used for to make attested, and Hesychius explains συνιστάναι as φανερῦν. Great is the goodness of God, in that He shows that the nations are also dear to Him.
