τί ἐρῦμεν) That is, do we say this for that reason, which is falsely objected against us? see below VI. 1.

μὴ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἐπιφέρων τὴν ὀργὴν) μὴ, that is, is not הֲ God, when He punishes us, (for ὀργὴ is frequent for punishment by metonymy in our authors) going to do us an injury? Thus it is said ἐπιφέρειν αἰτίαν in Acts XXV. 18, θλίψιν in Philippians I. 16. But this pertains to the fact that the Apostles were saying that God, having been deserted by the Jews, would in turn abdicate them from His protection, from which the greatest evils were about to come.

κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγω) אמרתי כדרך בני אדם as the Masters speak, or על־דברת בני אדם as it is in Ecclesiastes III. 18, that is, when I proposed that question, I used the words of some among you. Thus Solomon uses the words of the impious in Ecclesiastes. A similar manner of speaking is in 1 Corinthians IX. 8, Galatians III. 15. Thus ἀνθρωπίνως λέγω in VI. 19, I use commonly worn-out modes of speech. Thus, almost, κατ' ἄνδρα said Aeschylus in the Agamemnon. κατ' ἄνθρωπον Chrysippus in the third book on Justice, cited by Plutarch on the Stoics contradicting themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 5. εἰ δὲ ἀδικία ἡμῶν.

Et hî̂c μίμησις, nam ipsa verba Judæorum, qui Romæ erant, repetit Paulus. Objectio autem hæc Judæorum in. de maximè fluebat, quòd gentes, quæ idololatriæ aliisque vitiis immersæ fuerant, dicerentur à Deo adoptatæ, qui id credunt, ajebant illi, tutò peccare possunt. Est eadem ob- jectio Celsi verbis apud Origenem: & hî̂c quidem Apostolus duntaxat ostendit, quod infertur esse impium, responsum autem differt in caput VI. Estque idem cum illo Origenis: spectandas gentes non quales fuere, sed quales nunc sunt. Interim & hoc ostendit, Judæos illo tempore nihilo genti- bus fuisse meliores. Præterea docebant Apostoli, nihil Deo gloriosius, quàm quod omnes gentes ad se vocasset. Ei autem rei occasionem datam ex Judæorum contumacia. Ex his duabus rebus verissimis natæ sunt falsæ illæ obje- ctiones & calumniæ, quas hic refutat Apostolus.

Neque hic vel de Judæorum rejectione, vel de gentium vocatione ullum vestigium. Non enim objectiones Judæorum hic expediuntur, quod gentes idololatriæ aliisque vitiis immersæ, à Deo adoptatæ, quasi hinc collegerint, qui id credunt, tutò peccari posse: sed ἐγκλήματα & objectiones, quæ è doctrina Apostoli de justitia Dei reluctante ex ipsa hominum omnium convictione de injustitia, nectebantur, solvuntur.

Θεῦ δικαιοσύνην συνίστησι) id est, spectabiliorem facit, ut infra V. 8. sic est συνιστάναι pro testatum facere usurpant Demosthenes, & Hesychius συνιστάναι exponit φανερῦν. Magna Dei bonitas, quod gentes etiam cordi sibi esse ostendit.

τί ἐρῦμεν) Id est, an ideò hoc dicimus, quod nobis falso objicitur? vide infra VI. 1.

μὴ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἐπιφέρων τὴν ὀργὴν) μὴ, id est, nonne הֲ nonne Deus, cum nos puniet, (est enim ὀργὴ pro pœna μετωνυμίᾳ frequens nostris) injuriam nobis faciet? Sic di- citur ἐπιφέρειν αἰτίαν Actor. XXV. 18. θλίψιν Philip. I. 16. Hoc autem eò pertinet, quod dicebant Apostoli Deum ab Judæis desertum vicissim ipsos abdicaturum à tutela sua, unde maxima mala essent ventura.

κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγω) אמרתי כדרך בני אדם ut lo- quuntur Magistri aut על־דברת בני אדם ut est Eccl. III.18. id est, cum quæstionem istam proposui, usus sum ver- bis quorundam apud vos. Sic impiorum verbis utitur Sa- lomo in Ecclesiaste. Simile loquendi genus 1. Cor. IX. 8. Gal. III. 15. Sic ἀνθρωπίνως λέγω VI. 19. utor vulgo tritis loquendi modis. Sic fermè κατ' ἄνδρα dixit Æschylus Agamemnone. κατ' ἄνθρωπον Chrysippus tertio libro de Justitia, citatus à Plutarcho de Stoicis sibimet contradicen- tibus.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. μὴ γένοιτο) See above 3, but furthermore, this refers to the passage in Genesis XVIII. 25, where in the Hebrew it is חלילה לך For the following words are also taken from there.

ἐπεὶ πῶς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον) That is, in no way can we imagine God to be unjust, whom we acknowledge with Abraham as the judge of the world. These words, and those which preceded, κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγω and μὴ γένοιτο, are to be read equally as a parenthesis, for he pursues the objection begun from there.

Latin:

Vers. 6. μὴ γένοιτο) Vide supra 3. sed præterea hic respi- citur locus Gen. XVIII. 25. ubi in Hebræo est חלילה לך Nam & sequentia inde sumpta sunt.

ἐπεὶ πῶς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον) Id est, nullo modo pos- sumus Deum injustum imaginari, quem cum Abrahamo ju- dicem mundi agnoscimus. Hæc verba, & quæ præcessere κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγω & μὴ γένοιτο, pariter per παρένθεσιν le- genda sunt, nam objectionem cœptam inde persequitur.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια τῦ Θεῦ) Here the mimesis begun is continued. And ἀλήθεια here is good faith, just as ἀληθὴς above is tenacious of faith.

ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ψεύσματι) And ψεῦσμα here is infidelity, just as ψευδὴς above is unfaithful; and ἐν is for by.

ἐπερίσσευσε) was more abundant, that is, appeared more abundant, according to those things which we said above 4.

εἰς τὴν δόξαν αὐτῦ) whence the greater glory of God, namely from the calling of the nations.

Why am I still judged as a sinner? As if he were saying, God ought not to complain about that which pertains to His glory.

Latin:

Vers. 7. εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια τῦ Θεῦ) Hic continuatur cœ- pta μίμησις. Et ἀλήθεια hic est bona fides, sicut ἀληθὴς su- pra fidei tenax.

ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ψεύσματι) Et ψεῦσμα hic est infidelitas, quo- modo ψευδὴς supra infidus; & ἐν pro per.

ἐπερίσσευσε) abundatior fuit, id est, abundatior appa- ruit, secundum ea, quæ diximus supra 4.

εἰς τὴν δόξαν αὐτῦ) unde major Dei gloria, nempe ex gen- tium vocatione.

τί ἔτι καγὼ ὡς ἁμαρτωλὸς κρίνομαι) Quasi diceret, non debet Deus queri de eo, quod ad gloriam ejus pertinet.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. And not as we are slandered and as some say that we say, that we should do evil that good may come. Again, these things are to be read as a parenthesis. And not (as we are slandered and as some say that we say). For the Apostle cannot recite so foul and calumnious an objection in its entirety without interrupting himself twice to detest it: and it is a transposition, such as are many among the Hebrews. Why not μὴ ὅτι for ὅτι μὴ? For we have had ὅτι for why also in Mark 9:11 and 28. Why shall we not do evils, so that from them such a great good, namely the glory of God, may proceed? Paul in the parenthesis testifies by the way that this is indeed referred to himself and the Apostles, but by calumny, because the words of the Apostles were not reported in good faith, but in their place an illegitimate inference; and Clement of Alexandria, book III, gives an example of an anthypophora from this passage.

From the Evangelical Doctrine of justification, that blasphemy has arisen, by which even today our doctrine is traduced by Papists, that it hinders the pursuit of good works and induces a license to sin: since we deny that we are justified by works. Which, however, the Apostle judges unworthy of a response. For it is not therefore permitted to sin, so that righteousness may be obtained, because God justifies sinners by grace, without works of the law: for this is from the immense goodness and wisdom of God, that the glory of God is illustrated through sins, and that evil is directed to a good end, therefore it does not follow from evil in itself, but by accident: nor does God wish to absolve and justify us from sins so that we may indulge in sins, but so that, justified and freed from sins, we may serve God: just as the Apostle will teach later. Therefore, that impious inference or that scandal does not follow from the Apostolic doctrine in itself, but by accident.

We are taught here, however, that evils which are evil by nature and essence, namely the evils of fault, as they are called, are by no means and for no reason to be done so that good things may happen: for evils which are evil according to our sense, as Damascene distinguishes them in book IV of the Orthodox Faith, ch. XX, such as ignominies, persecutions, death itself, these can be admitted and tolerated for a good end, indeed they ought to be sustained for the glory of the divine name. It is one thing, therefore, when it is a matter of the active commission of evils, and another when it is a matter of the passive tolerance of evils: The former is never lawful, with whatever intention of end or pretext evils may be done; and so it is not permitted to consent even to lesser sins so that greater ones may be avoided, under that pretext of a case of necessity. That it can be permitted is not in doubt, but it is one thing to permit a lesser evil, another to consent to it. Rightly Cajetan on this passage: no sin, not even the smallest, is a medium that is eligible or to be done, so that even the most grave sins may be avoided: because even sound reason dictates that it is by no means good, or free from fault, which is in itself intrinsically evil and contrary to the will of God, however much the scope and end prefixed may be far the best: because a good end and intention cannot render an action good when it is evil by its nature, as Danaeus confesses in Christian Ethics. And therefore it is blasphemy against God when the Calvinists babble that God instigates to sins, or is the author and cause of sins, whether moral or physical, so that the glory of His justice may be illustrated through them. This tolerance of evils, however, is lawful, not only regarding those things which are evil and adverse to our sense, but also regarding those things which are evil by nature, when, namely, it is not in our power to remove those things which we tolerate, or when we are not bound to remove them by force, provided that we do not cooperate with them: Just as God Himself tolerates evils so that good things may happen. Thus also Matthew 19:8 is to be understood as having tolerated rash divorces, so that greater evils might be avoided in a stiff-necked people: to which, however, He did not consent, much less approve of them: but by the public voice of His law He perpetually accused and condemned them. See Profligatio Socinianismi.

whose judgment is just.

The Apostle does not value this saying of the Jews so highly that he laboriously solves it, holding it sufficient to detest it and call it a calumny, and indeed one worthy of punishment: quite rightly. For Aristotle also, in Nicomachean Ethics VI. 10, denies that euboulia is to be called that by which one attains what one ought, but not through that by which one ought. Thus Orestes avenged his father, but badly, having killed his mother by force, and therefore he is driven by the furies. Justin against Trypho: for if even his father and he himself were to act for the sake of human things, you did not do this as if serving by the will of God. Here Paul secretly predicts the destruction of the city and the Temple and the dissipation of the people.

That Paul secretly predicts here the destruction of the city and the temple, and the dissipation of the people, is rashly asserted by Grotius. For no trace of a prediction can be shown. It is not about the Judgment against the Jews, but against such mockers who were blaspheming the Apostolic Doctrine, whether they were or are Jews, or others, that is dealt with; much less about that final utter destruction of the Jews.

PART III. The universal conviction of all men concerning sin and condemnation.

Latin:

Vers. 8. καὶ μὴ καθὼς βλασφημούμεθα καὶ καθὼς φασί τινες ἡμᾶς λέγειν, ὅτι ποιήσωμεν τὰ κακὰ ἵνα ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀγαθά. Rursus hæc per parenthesin legenda sunt. καὶ μὴ (καθὼς βλα- σφημούμεθα κὴ καθὼς φασί τινες ἡμᾶς λέγειν) Nam Aposto- lus tam fœdam & calumniosam objectionem totam recitare non potest, ut non bis detestando interloquatur: & est transpositio, quales multæ apud Hebræos. μὴ ὅτι pro ὅτι μὴ, cur non? Nam ὅτι pro cur habuimus & Marc. IX. 11. & 28. Cur non agemus mala, ut indè tantum bonum, Dei scilicet gloria, proveniat? Paulus in parenthesi obiter te- statur, referri quidem hoc de se & Apostolis, sed per calu- mniam, quia Apostolorum verba non bona fide refereban- tur, sed vice eorum illegitima illatio, & ex hoc loco exem- plum ἀνθυποφορᾶς dat Clemens Alexandr. lib. III.

E Doctrina Evangelica de justificatione bla- sphemia illa enata, quà hodiè etiam nostra do- ctrina à Papistis traducitur, quòd studium bono- rum operum impediat, licentiam peccandi inducat: siquidem per opera nos justificari negemus. Quam verò Apostolus responso indignam judicat. Non enim ideò peccare licet, ut obtineatur justitia, quod Deus peccatores ex gratia, sine operibus legis justificet: nam hoc ex bonitate & sapientiâ Dei immensâ est, quòd per peccata illustretur Dei glo- ria, quodque malum dirigatur ad bonum finem, non ergo ex malo per se consequitur: sed per acci- dens: neque ideo à peccatis nos Deus absolvere ac justificare vult, ut peccatis indulgeamus, sed ut ju- stificati & liberati à peccatis, Deo serviamus: quemadmodum postea docebit Apostolus. Non ergo per se illa impia illatio, aut scandalum istud sequitur ex doctrina Apostolica, sed ex acci- denti.

Docemur autem hîc, nequaquam & nulla ra- tione facienda esse mala, quæ τῇ Φύσει & natura mala sunt, nimirum mala culpæ, quæ vocant, ut eveniant bona: nam mala, quæ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν αἴσθησιν secundum sensum nostrum mala sunt, ut di- stinguit ea Damascenus lib. IV. de orth. Fid. c. XX. uti sunt, ignominiæ, persecutiones, mors ipsa, ea ob finem bonum admitti ac tolerari possunt, imò ob gloriam nominis divini sustineri debent. Aliud ergo est, cùm de commissione malorum acti- vâ, aliud, cùm de tolerantiâ malorum passivâ agi- tur: Illa nunquam licita est, quacunque finis in- tentione aut προφάσει mala fiant; adeoque ne in minora quidem peccata consentire licet, ut eviten- tur majora, sub illo prætextu casûs necessitatis. Permitti posse non dubium est, sed aliud est per- mittere minus malum, aliud in illud consentire. Rectè Cajetanus in h. l. nullum peccatum, nec mi- nimum quidem medium est eligibile aut faciendum, ut peccata etiam gravissima vitentur: quia vel sana ratio dictitat id minimè bonum esse, aut culpâ va- care, quod per se est intrinsecè malum, Deique voluntati adversum, utut scopus finisque præfixus longè optimus sit: quia finis & intentio bona non posset actionem bonam reddere, quando naturâ suâ mala est, ut fatetur Danæus in Eth. Christ. Ideo- que blasphemia est in Deum, cum Calviniani Deum instigare ad peccata, vel peccatorum autorem ac causam esse sive moralem, sive physicam, ut per ea- dem illustretur justitiæ suæ gloria ganniunt. Hæc autem malorum tolerantia licita est, non modò quoad ea, quæ sensui nostro mala & adversa sunt, sed etiam quoad ea, quæ naturâ sunt mala, cum scilicet in potestate nostra non est, ut ea tolla- mus, quæ toleramus, aut cum ad ea vi tollenda non tenemur, dummodò iisdem non coopere- mur: Quomodo Deus ipse tolerat mala, ut eve- niant bona. Ita etiam Matth. XIX. 8. intelli- gendus est tolerasse divortia temeraria, ob majo- ra vitanda mala in populo duræ cervicis: in quæ tamen non consensit, nedum approbavit ea- dem: sed publicâ legis suæ voce eadem perpe- tuò accusavit & damnavit. Vid. Socinianism. pro- flig.

ὧν τὸ κρῖμα ἔνδικόν ἐστι.

Non tanti facit hoc dictum Judæorum Apostolus, ut operosè solvat, satis habens id detestari, & calumniam di- cere, & quidem pœna dignissimam: rectè admodum. Nam & Aristoteles Nicomacheorum VI. 10. negat ἐυβυλίαν di- cendam καθ' ἧν ὧ δεῖ μὲν τυγχάνει, ὅ μὲν τοι δι' ὃ ἔδει. Sic O- restes patrem ultus, sed malè, occisa per vim matre, ideo fu- riis agitatur. Justinus contra Tryphonem: εἰ γὰρ κὲ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῦ κὰι αὐτὸς παθεῖν ταῦτα αὐτοὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων γένοις ἐνήργησεν, ὑμεῖς ὠκ ὡς γνώμῃ Θεῦ ὑπηρετῦντες τῦτο ἐπράξατε. Latenter prædicit hic Paulus urbis & Templi excidium & populi dissipationem.

Prædicere hîc latenter Paulum urbis & templi excidium, & populi dissipationem, temerè à Gro- tio asseritur. Nullum enim prædictionis mon- strari potest vestigium. Non de Judicio adversus Judæos, sed contra tales empæctas, qui Doctri- nam Apostolicam blasphemabant, seu Judæi fue- rint aut sint, seu alii, agitur: multò minus de illa Judæorum novissimà πανωλεθρία̣.

PARS III. Universalis omnium hominum de peccato, & condemnatione ᄑλεγξις.

## 3:9
Ver. 9. τί ὖν; What then? Here the Apostle returns to that which he had begun to treat at the beginning of the chapter.

προεχόμεθα) An Attic expression for προέχομεν, προέχειν to excel, among Demosthenes and others. In the Glossary: προέχειν to excel. He proposes the question, do we Jews therefore excel the Gentiles?

οὐ πάντως. By no means.

He answers the question aptly. We excel, but not in all things. Not to the extent that the grace of the Gospel was not as necessary for us as it was for the Gentiles. Sometimes a negative particle placed before a universal among the Hebrews is accustomed to deny universally: but that does not fit this place, for it restricts what he had said above, that the surplus was great, namely in certain things. Therefore οὐ πάντως is worth here not in all things.

Some interpret this particle negatively and universally, in no way for πάντως οὐ, by transposition, as 1 Cor. V. 10; others restrictively, to whom Grotius here accedes: And indeed this sense could be admitted here: We excel, but not in all things, not to the extent that the grace of the Gospel was not as necessary for us as for the Gentiles, provided that grace is understood according to the mind of the Apostle, and the necessity is explained skillfully, and not perverted in the Grotian manner: namely, that only the time of the coming of Christ is regarded, because at that time the Jews were no less than the Gentiles of a most wicked life. Which distortion of the Apostolic sentence is to be detested. For he does not regard certain times, but men of all times; he does not deal with certain particular wickednesses, but the Apostle convicts the whole human race of being guilty of sin, so that he may prove that no one can be justified by the law. And therefore he concludes that the Jews and Greeks and thus the whole human race, which was then designated by that distribution, are under sin: and not only some of the Jews and Greeks, but ALL v. 9, and afterwards v. 19, the WHOLE WORLD is subject to God; not just the majority in the world. If therefore this question is taken concerning the prerogative of the Jews over the Gentiles, whether regarding the state of corrupted nature or regarding the respect of righteousness valid before God, the answer is rightly understood as universally negative; for in that there is no excellence of the Jews over the Gentiles at all: and the added argument confirms this sense, by which this prior Apostolic demonstration is summarized: for we have proven, says the Apostle, that both Jews and Gentiles are ALL under sin. If, however, all are under sin, they can in no way have any excellence or prerogative over others in justification before God.

προητιασάμεθα γάρ. For we have previously accused.

He proves that which he has already hinted at, more than he said, that the benefit of the Gospel was no less necessary for the Jews than for the Gentiles, προητιασάμεθα, we have previously accused, namely I. 17 concerning the Gentiles: II. 9 and following concerning the Jews.

It is not 'we have previously accused,' nor as the Vulgate, 'we have previously brought a charge,' but as the Greek Scholiast rendered it, ἠλέγξαμεν, we have argued and convicted with certain causes or reasons. In which manner the blessed Luther also rendered it. Therefore it does not regard c. I. 17, c. II. 9 and following, but the whole demonstration instituted thus far, and he embraces its sum here in place of a conclusion: because the prior demonstration, by which he proved us by consequence, or finished the matter with arguments, is now ended thus: and the same is now undertaken to be demonstrated by express testimonies of Scripture: which is the other kind of proof.

Ἰουδαίους τε καὶ Ἕλληνας πάντας ὑφ᾽ ἁμαρτίαν εἶναι. That is, that the Jews were no less than the Gentiles, when Christ arrived, of a most wicked life, although the former had received the law as a teacher, the latter philosophy. ὑφ᾽ ἁμαρτίαν εἶναι in this place, as appears from what follows, signifies to be addicted to grave vices, which is such as below VII. 14, he is said to be sold under sin, from which it further follows that that 'all' here is to be understood not plainly of individuals, but of the majority. Aristotle in the Poetics c. 20: for 'all' is said instead of 'many' even by metaphor. And Jerome says the same in epistle CXLVI, which is to Damasus, citing the places John X. 8, 1 Cor. IX. 22, Phil. II. 21, to which can be added the place John III. 31, 32, v. 26. Those times were indeed most corrupt, which Josephus sufficiently shows concerning the Jews, and Justin against Trypho, citing from the Psalms, which will now follow: and histories and poems concerning the Romans. Nevertheless, there were among the Jews some, such as Zacharias, Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna: and among the Gentiles, such as the two Centurions, the one mentioned in the Gospel, the other in the Acts: But these were nothing but a drop in the ocean. See the response to the Orthodox, ch. X. Faith speaks no less generally in Silius Italicus, book II. Force is worshipped and the sword claims the place of right for itself. And virtue has yielded to vice, behold, nations, look. No one is innocent, commerce preserves the peace of guilt.

The sense of the Apostle is perverted, as we have said, by Grotius, as if to be under sin were to be addicted to grave vices. Nor does that sense hold in ch. VII. 14, although there is also another phrase there, and the discourse is about a different subject, and Grotius very badly makes a particular out of a universal, so that πάντες here are not all, but only most. That was once the depravation of Pelagius in the Synod of Palestine, and recently of the Socinians in Volckel, book V. on true religion, ch. 5, Enjedinus, etc., and also the depravation of the Papists, Erasmus, Faber, Catharinus, Toletus, Salmeron, Jansenius, but one which the Holy Spirit now meets, since He not only said πάντες absolutely and universally, v. 4 and 9 and 12 and v. 23, and distributively embraced all by the mention of Jews and Greeks v. 9, Jews and Gentiles v. 29, but also collectively designated the whole world v. 19, and furthermore used a negative universal, οὐκ ἔστι δίκαιος, v. 10. οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σάρξ v. 20, and added an exclusive, οὐκ ἔστι ὀὐδὲ εἷς. v. 10 and 12, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς, so that not even one could perhaps be excluded or excepted from these: and he excluded every difference in that part, οὐ γάρ ἐστι διαστολὴ, v. 22, ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν, v. 12, so that those who still strive to recall these things to a particular sense openly and to his face contradict the Holy Spirit. Grotius therefore accomplishes nothing when he teaches that those times in which the Apostle wrote these things were most corrupt: for the Apostle is not dealing with the corruption of those times, but with the corruption of human nature, and he convinces the whole human race that it is under sin and subject to God outside the grace of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 9. τί ὖν; Quid ergo? Hic Apostolus redit ad id, quod tractare cœperat initio capitis.

προεχόμεθα) Attica locutio pro προέχομεν, προέχειν ex- cellere apud Demosthenem & alios. In Glossario: προέχειν excellere. Quæstionem proponit, an igitur nos Judæi præ- cellimus gentes?

οὐ πάντως.

Quæstioni apposite respondet. Præcellimus, sed non per omnia. Non eo usque, ut non tam nobis, quàm gentibus necessaria fuerit Evangelii gratia. Solet interdum negativa universali particulæ præposita apud Hebræos negare uni- versaliter: sed id huic loco non convenit, nam restringit, quod supra dixerat, πολὺ esse τὸ περίσσον, nempe in qui- busdam rebus. Itaque οὐ πάντως valet hic לא בכל.

HAnc particulam alii negativè universaliter interpretantur, nullo modo pro πάντως οὐ, per trajectionem, ut 1. Cor. V. 10. alii restrictè, quibus hic accedit Grotius: Et admitti sane posset hic sensus: Præcellimus, sed non per omnia, non eo usq; ut non tam nobis quam gentibus necessaria fuerit Evangelii gratia, modo gratia illa ex mente Apo- stoli intelligatur, & necessitas dextrè explicetur, non autem more Grotiano pervertatur: quòd nempe respiciatur tantum tempus adventus Chri- sti, quòd eodem non minus Judæi quàm gentes flagi- tiosissimæ vitæ fuerint. Quæ detestanda est senten- tiæ Apostolicæ detorsio. Non enim tempora cer- ta, sed omnium temporum homines respicit, non de flagitiis quibusdam particularibus agit, sed totum genus humanum peccati reum peragit Apostolus, ut neminem per legem justificari posse evincat. Ideoque concludit Judæos & Græcos adeoque to- tum humanum genus, quod tum ista distribu- tione designabatur, sub peccato esse: nec tantum quosdam è Judæis & Græcis, sed πάντας OMNES v. 9. ac postea v. 19. obnoxium esse TOTUM MUNDUM Deo; non plerosque tantum in mundo. Si ergò de prærogativa Judæorum præ gentilibus hic, sive quoad naturæ corruptæ statum, sive quoad justitiæ coram Deo valentis respectum attinet, hæc quæstio accipiatur, rectè universaliter negativè in- telligitur responsio; nam in ea nulla prorsus est Judæorum præ gentilibus præcellentia: atque hunc sensum argumentum additum confirmat, quò hæc demonstratio prior Apostolica summatim comprehenditur: evicimus enim, inquit Aposto- lus, quod & Judæi & gentes OMNES sub peccato sint. Si autem sub peccato omnes sunt, nullam in justificatione coram Deo ullatenus alii præ aliis habere possunt excellentiam, aut prærogati- vam.

προητιασάμεθα γάρ.

Probat id, quod jam innuit, magis, quàm dixit, Evangelii beneficium Judæis non minus quam gentibus fuisse neces- sarium, προητιασάμεθα, accusationem præstruximus, nempe I. 17. de gentibus: II. 9. & deinceps de Judæis.

Non est accusationem præstruximus, nec ut vul- gata, præcausati sumus, sed ut Græcus Scholiastes reddidit, ἠλέγξαμεν causis seu rationibus certis ar- guimus, & convicimus. Quo pacto etiam reddi- dit B. Lutherus. Non ergo c. I. 17. c. II. 9. & seqq. sed totam demonstrationem hactenus institutam respicit, ejusque summam hic conclusionis loco complectitur: quia prior demonstratio, quà per consequentiam nos evicit, vel argumentis rem con- fecit, nunc ita finitur: atque idem expressis Scri- pturæ testimoniis demonstratum jam suscipitur: quod est alterum probationis genus.

Ἰουδαίους τε καὶ Ἕλληνας πάντας ὑφ᾽ ἁμαρτίαν εἶναι. Id est, non minus Judæos quàm gentes, cùm Christus advenit, flagitiosissimæ fuisse vitæ, quamvis illi legem, hi philosophiam magistram accepissent. ὑφ᾽ ἁμαρτίαν εἶναι hoc loco, ut ex sequentibus apparet, significat gravibus vitiis addictos esse, qui talis est infra VII. 14. dicitur πεπραμένος ὑφ᾽ ἁμαρτίαν, unde porro sequitur, illud πάντας hic intelli- gendum non plane de singulis, sed de plerisque. Aristote- les Poeticorum c. 20. τὸ γὰρ πάντες ἀντὶ τοῦ πολλοὶ κᾀ μεταφο- ρὰν εἴρηται. Idemque dicit Hieronymus epistola CXLVI. quæ est ad Damasum, afferens loca Joh. X. 8. 1. Cor. IX. 22. Phil. II. 21. quibus addi potest locus Joh. III. 31. 32. v. 26. Erant sane corruptissima illa tempora, quod de Judæis satis ostendit Josephus, Justinus contra Tryphonem adducens ex Psalmis, quæ jam sequentur: de Romanis historiæ & poe- mata. Attamen erant inter Judæos quidam, quales Zacha- rias, Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna: & inter gentes, quales duo Centuriones, alter in Evangelio, alter in Actis memoratus: Sed hi nihil nisi gutta in mari. Vide responsum ad Ortho- doxos c. X. Non minus generaliter Fides loquitur apud Si- lium Italicum lib. II. Vis colitur jurisque locum sibi vindicat ensis. Et probros cessit virtus, en aspite gentes. Nemo insons, pacem servant commercia culpæ.

Pervertitur, ut diximus, à Grotio sensus Apo- stoli, quasi sub peccato esse, sit gravibus vitiis ad- dictos esse. Nec ille sensus c. VII. 14. obtinet, quam- vis etiam alia ibi phrasis, & de alio subjecto sermo sit, & pessimè ex universali particularem facit Gro- tius, ut πάντες hic sint non omnes, sed tantum ple- rique. Fuit ea Pelagii quondam in Synodo Palæ- stria depravatio, & Socinianorum nuper apud Vol- ckel. lib. V. de vera relig. c. 5. Enjedinum &c. nec non Pontificiorum, Erasmi, Fabri, Catharini, To- leti, Salmeronis, Jansenii depravatio, sed cui jam occurrit S. S. cum non solum absolutè universali- ter πάντες dixit, v. 4. & 9. & 12. & v. 23. & distributi- vè omnes complexus est Judæorum & Græcorum mentione v. 9. Judæorum & Ethnicorum v. 29. sed & collectivè totum mundum designavit vers. 19. ac prætereà negativa universali usus est, οὐκ ἔστι δίκαιος, v. 10. οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σάρξ v. 20. & exclusivâ addidit, οὐκ ἔστι ὀὐδὲ εἷς. v. 10. & 12. οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνός, ut ne unus quidem excludi, aut excipi ab his fortè possit: & omnem exclusit eâ in parte differentiam, οὐ γάρ ἐστι διαστολὴ, v. 22. ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν, v. 12. ut palam & in os contradicant Spiritui S. oporteat, qui adhuc ista ad particularem sensum revocare satagunt. Nihil ergò agit Grotius, cum corruptissi- ma fuisse tempora illa, quibus hæc scripsit Apostolus, docet: non enim de temporum istorum, sed de naturæ humanæ corruptione agit Apostolus, to- tumque genus humanum sub peccato, ac Deo obnoxium extra gratiam Christi esse, convincit.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. As it is written.

The times are such as were once described by David and others. Thus also Christ uses the words of the Prophets, first spoken about other times, but no less fitting for his own. See Matt. XIII. 14, Mark IV. 12, Luke VIII. 10, John XII. 40, Acts XXVIII. 26. Paul uses here various sentences, both from the Psalms and from Isaiah, not indeed always counting the words, but well expressing the sense, such as his memory suggested to him.

καὶ ὅτι δίκαιος οὐδὲ εἷς) Psalm XIV. 1 and LIII. 1, which two Psalms are in part conceived in the same words in the Hebrew. In the Greek Ps. XIV. it is οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν χρηστότητα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς; but in Ps. LIII. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν ἀγαθόν. טוב to the Hebrews signifies everything that is honest, and thus the Greeks often use the word for justice, according to that: ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ᾽ ἀρετή ἐστι. He is dealing with those who were with Saul.

Latin:

Vers. 10. καθὼς γέγραπται.

Tempora sunt talia, qualia olim à Davide & aliis descri- pta sunt. Sic & Christus Prophetarum verba usurpat, de aliis temporibus primum dicta, sed suis non minus conve- nientia. Vid. Matth. XIII. 14. Marc. IV. 12. Luc. VIII. 10. Joh. XII. 40. Act. XXVIII. 26. Utitur autem hic Paulus diversis sententiis tum ex Psalmis, tum ex Esaia, nec utique verba semper annumerans, sed sensum, qualem memoria ei suggerebat, bene exprimens.

καὶ ὅτι δίκαιος οὐδὲ εἷς) Psalm. XIV. 1. & LIII. 1. qui duo Psalmi ex parte iisdem verbis concepti sunt in Hebræo. In Græco Ps. XIV. est οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν χρηστότητα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς; at in Ps. LIII. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν ἀγαθόν. טוב Hebrais omne, quod honestum est, significat, & sic Græci sæpe justitiæ vo- cem usurpant, juxta illud: ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ᾽ ἀρετή ἐστι. Agit de iis, qui apud Saulem erant.

## 3:11
Vers. 11. οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ συνιῶν, οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ ἐκζητῶν τὸν Θεόν) He said more briefly what is more diffuse in Ps. XIV. Κύριος ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ διέκυψεν ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, τοῦ ἰδεῖν εἰ ἔστι συνιῶν ἢ ἐκζητῶν τὸν Θεόν. A good man had to be sought as if with a lamp. He is called intelligent here who uses his intellect rightly, just as the impious in the same Psalm is called a fool. But he is said to seek God to whom God is dear.

Latin:

Vers. 11. οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ συνιῶν, οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ ἐκζητῶν τὸν Θεόν) Bre- vius dixit, quod diffusius in Ps. XIV. Κύριος ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ διέ- κυψεν ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, τοῦ ἰδεῖν εἰ ἔστι συνιῶν ἢ ἐκζητῶν τὸν Θεόν. Quærendus erat quasi cum lucerna vir bonus. In- telligens hic dicitur, qui intellectu recte utitur, sicut impius in eodem Psalmo vocatur insipiens. Quærere autem Deum dicitur, cui Deus cordi est.

## 3:12
πάντες ἐξέκλιναν) Thus also in the Greek in the Psalms, to deviate from the paths outside the orbit of the right.

Vers. 12. ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν) And this from the Greek in the Hebrew יחדו נאלחו they have together become putrid. Now things that are such are not fit for eating; thus they are of no good use. Thus σαπροῖς are opposed to ἀγαθὰ εἰς χρείαν Eph. IV. 19.

Latin:

πάντες ἐξέκλιναν) Sic & in Græco in Psalmis, vias devias linire extra recti orbitam.

Vers. 12. ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν) Et hoc ex Græco in Hebræo יחדו נאלחו pariter putrefcant. Quæ autem talia sunt, esui non sunt idonea; sic illi nulli bono usui. Sic σαπροῖς opponuntur ἀγαθὰ εἰς χρείαν Eph. IV. 19.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν χρηστότητα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς) Here the Greeks in Ps. XIV. repeat the same words which we had at the beginning, and in Ps. LIII. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν ἀγαθὸν, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς. In the Hebrew οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς is in this member, in the former it is not. What David had said before, he repeats more effectively as a matter fully known to himself; χρηστότητα, or ἀγαθὸν ποιῶν, is the same here as δικαιοσύνη above, עשׂה טוב namely ὁ ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθὸν, as Paul spoke above II. 10.

Now the Apostle confirms with the sayings of Scripture the opinion which he had supported with arguments, concerning the universal guilt of the human race. Therefore the Grotian gloss is to be utterly rejected again, because he compares his own times with the Davidic ones; for David spoke of the whole human race, and so did Paul, who uses the Davidic testimony. For although he does not enumerate the very words of the passages brought from the Psalms, but expresses the sense, he did not do so as memory suggested it to him, but as the Holy Spirit inspired the same, by whom Φερόμενος he wrote these things, he delivered the same. Nor is it from Ps. XIV. alone, as some of the Papists, and especially the English apostate William Reynolds, wish, although in certain Greek codices and the Latin Vulgate these verses 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18 are found entire there, but they are taken from Paul, since they are neither held by Origen in the Hexapla, nor were they read in the time of Jerome, (see the preface sup. X. Libr. in Es.) nor are they found now in the more approved Greek Codices, nor do they pertain to the integrity of the Psalm, as Bellarmine admits, l. II. de Verb. Dei c. 2. and Franc. Luc. Brugens. in ann. Bibl. ad h. l. but they have been pieced together from different places of Scripture, as Jerome observed, and Grotius acknowledges here. Furthermore, that David in Ps. XIV. deals with those who were with Saul, which Grotius wishes here, whence will it be taught? In the annotations to Ps. XIV. he said that David meant that the age was as depraved as it had been before the flood. Now, however, he has limited it only to those who were with Saul. But by the annotations opposed to him, we have shown that it is not only about the corruption of actual sin, but also about that which was caused by original sin, not about the particular corruption of certain times and men, but about the universal corruption of the whole human race, extending to all times and to all subjects, that is being dealt with in the Davidic Psalm no less than in the Apostolic passage.

It is certainly taught here most clearly both that all men are subject to sin, and what kind of sin that is which is common to the whole human race. That the whole human race, ever since the fall of our first parents, is infected with sin, and that no one at all is to be entirely exempted from this lot, Holy Scripture has emphatically set forth (that we may show this again against the Socinians and the Socinianizing Grotius)

(1.) by an indefinite assertion. They have corrupted their way, they have perpetrated abominable deeds Ps. XIV. 1. Ps. LIII. 1. Contrition and misery are in their ways, Rom. III. 16. from Es. LIX. 7.

(2.) by an indefinite negation: they have not known the way of peace, there is no fear of God before their eyes Rom. III. 18. from Es. LIX. 8. and Ps. XXXVI. 2.

(3.) by a universal affirmation. ALL have turned aside, Psalm. XIV. 3. πάντες ἐξέκλιναν. Roman. III. 12.

(4.) by the common condition of all: everyone has turned aside alike, Ps. XIV. 3. or if you draw this adverb to what follows, they have become putrid or rancid alike. ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν, Rom. III. 12.

(5.) by a universal negation: There is none doing good, Ps. XIV. 1.

(6.) by the repetition of the same universal negation, v. 3. There is none that doeth good.

(7.) With the exclusion subjoined, not even one, v. 3.

(8.) Of the exclusion

by gemination: for the Apostle repeats the same in this manner: there is none righteous, no, not one: And there is none that doeth good, there is none so much as one, v. 10. & 12. (9.) by an emphatic amplification of universality: for in order to set before our eyes the universal depravity, the Psalmist introduces God looking around accurately, whether even one can be found, in the whole human race, who either understands God, as is fitting, and has a just knowledge of God and divine things, or seeks after God: who is either not corrupted in mind in perceiving spiritual things, or in will in embracing those things which are good, The Lord looked down from heaven? or upon those who were around Saul? by no means, but upon the whole human race? upon the children of men from the first parents: For the eyes of the Lord behold the hearts, counsels, and works of all men, that he may see, if there is any that understands, if there is any that seeks after God: whence the theme and argument of the Psalm is understood from the beginning of the proposition: who is the fool, saying in his heart, there is no God: that such by nature is every man. For no one is found in that accurate survey of God, who is understanding, no one, who is seeking after God. (10.) By the Apostolic explanation of the same. For where the Psalmist says that God saw whether there was any that understood, or sought after the Lord, the Apostle answers negatively v. 11. There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. (11.) By the universal distribution, which the Apostle institutes in verse 9, concluding that all Jews and Greeks are under sin. Which conclusion is to be understood according to the proof premised; in which he certainly does not treat of the specific crimes of some, but of the impiety and injustice of all men, Rom. I. 17. and convinces all, in whom is τὸ γνωστὸν τῶ θεῷ, and who acknowledge τὸ δικαίωμα θεῦ, of the same v. 19. 32. he shows that no man can be excused chap. II. 1., of whom some sinned without the (written) law, when they had the law inscribed on their heart; others sinned ἐν νόμῳ, i.e., both Gentiles and Jews chap. II. 12. 14. (12.) By the means of universal conviction, Rom. III. 10. which binds all whoever are ἐν νόμῳ or ὑπὸ νόμον: from which by chance no one is excepted; for the law convinces those who are under the law. But all men are under the law, not even excepting those who did not have the Mosaic law. (13.) By the definition of universal conviction, v. 19. ἵνα πᾶν σόμα φρα- γῇ, that EVERY MOUTH may be stopped. The Apostle intended that not the mouths of any one nation only, not of the Jews, but of ALL should be stopped. (14.) By the ἐξήγησις of the same, which he immediately subjoins: καὶ ὑπόδικος γένηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος τῷ Θεῷ, that ALL, or THE WHOLE WORLD, may be guilty before God. How can these things be restricted to the Jews? (15.) By the scope and intention of this definition. For this is the purpose of the Apostle, to teach that by the works of the law ALL FLESH shall not be justified, that is, no flesh, no man: since there is no one who is not condemned by the voice of the law. (16.) By the exclusion of difference, & γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ: There is no difference in this respect, whether of nations or of times, in the whole human race, v. 22. (17.) By the confirmation of the same, πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον, for ALL have sinned. But lest a hyperbole be feigned here again, it is not only most powerfully excluded c. V. 12. sq., but also here in this place: For those who ὑστερῦνται τῆς δόξης τῦ θεῦ: and if they wish to be justified, they have need of the grace of God, and have been redeemed by Christ, those the Apostle affirms to have sinned. But all men in general, such as they are by nature, after the fall, are destitute of the glory of God, and all have need of the grace of God, if they wish to be justified, and all are also redeemed, no one excepted, by Christ, which the whole Scripture teaches, and it is expressly set forth in Rom. V. (18.) By a new distribution of the human race. Which the Apostle divides into Jews and Gentiles, verse 29, and teaches that God has regard for all, and wills to be the God of both. Therefore, all those have sinned, as the Apostle testifies, and are destitute of the glory of God by nature, whose God have mercy. But God wills to be the God of all men, whether they be Gentiles or Jews, and He wills to have mercy on all. And here the conclusion of the Apostolic treatment fully agrees: Rom. XI. 32, He has shut up all under unbelief, that He might have mercy on ALL.

A noble example in Cleopatra. See also Aelian, book IX.

Latin:

Vers. 13. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν χρηστότητα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς) Hic Græci in Psal. XIV. repetunt eadem verba, quæ initio habuimus, & in Ps. LIII. οὐκ ἔστι ποιῶν ἀγαθὸν, οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς. In Hebræo οὐκ ἔστιν ἕως ἑνὸς in hoc membro est, in priori non est. Quod ante dixerat David, id efficacius repetit tanquam rem sibi plane compertam, χρηστότητα, aut ἀγαθὸν ποιῶν, hic idem est, quod δικαιοσύνη supra, עשׂה טוב nempe ὁ ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ut supra locutus est Paul. II. 10.

Jam confirmat Apostolus Scripturæ dictis sententiam, quam argumentis adstruxerat, de universali reatu generis humani. Reprobanda itaque omninò iterum glossa Grotiana, quod tempora sua cum Davidicis comparet; nam & David de toto humano genere loquutus est, & Paulus, qui Davidico utitur testimonio. Quamvis enim non annumeret ipsa locorum verba è Psalmis adducta, sed sensum exprimat, non tamen uti memoria hunc ei suggessit, sed ut Spiritus S. eidem inspiravit, à quo Φερόμενος hæc scripsit, eundem tradidit. Neque è solo Ps. XIV. ut nonnulli è Pontificiis, & imprimis Wilhelmus Reinholdus Apostata Anglus volunt, tametsi in Græcis codicibus quibusdam & vulgatâ versione Latinâ hi versus 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. & 18. integri illic reperiantur, ast è Paulo adsciti, quum nec ab Origene in Hexaplis habeantur, nec Hieronymi tempore lecti sint, (vid. præfat. sup. X. Libr. in Es.) neque reperiantur nunc in probatioribus Codicibus Græcis, nec ad Psalmi integritatem pertineant, fatente Bellarm. l. II. de Verb. Dei c. 2. & Franc. Luc. Brugens. in ann. Bibl. ad h. l. sed coagmentati sint è diversis Scripturæ locis, ut Hieronymus observavit, & agnoscit hic Grotius. Cæterum Davidem Ps. XIV. de iis agere, qui apud Saulem erant, quod hic vult Grotius, unde docebitur? In annotat. ad Ps. XIV. dixit, id velle Davidem, seculum esse tam depravatum, quam fuerat ante diluvium. Jam verò ad eos solum determinavit, qui apud Saulem fuere. Sed Annotatis ipsi oppositis ostendimus, non de corruptione peccati tantum actualis, sed de ea etiam, quæ per peccatum originale facta est, non de corruptione particulari certorum temporum & hominum, sed de corruptione universali totius generis humani, ad omnia tempora, & ad subjecta omnia se extendente non minus in Psalmo Davidico, quam loco Apostolico agi.

Docetur certè hic luculentissime tùm quod omnes homines peccato sint obnoxii, tum quale illud peccatum sit, quod toti generi humano commune est. Quod totum humanum genus inde à lapsu primorum parentum peccato infectum, quodque nemo prorsus ab hac forte penitus eximendus sit, emphaticè exposuit S. Scriptura (Ut hoc iterum contra Socinianos & Grotium Socinizantem ostendamus)

(1.) indefinitâ assertione. Corruperunt viam suam, abominanda perpetrarunt facinora Ps. XIV. 1. Ps. LIII. 1. Contritio & miseria in viis eorum, Rom. III. 16. ex Es. LIX. 7.

(2.) indefinitâ negatione: viam pacis non cognoverunt, non est timor Dei coram oculis eorum Rom. III. 18. ex Es. LIX. 8. & Ps. XXXVI. 2.

(3.) universali affirmatione. OMNES recesserunt, Psalm. XIV. 3. πάντες ἐξέκλιναν. Roman. III. 12.

(4.) communi omnium conditione: omnis recessit pariter, Ps. XIV. 3. vel si adverbium hoc ad sequentia trahas, pariter putidi aut rancidi facti sunt. ἅμα ἠχρειώθησαν, Rom. III. 12.

(5.) universali negatione: Non est faciens bonum, Ps. XIV. 1.

(6.) ejusdem universalis negationis repetitione, v. 3. Non est faciens bonum.

(7.) Subjunctâ exclusione, ne unus quidem, v. 3.

(8.) Exclusionis

geminatione: repetit enim eandem Apostolus hoc modo: non est justus, ne unus quidem: Et non est, qui faciat bonum, non est usque ad unum, v. 10. & 12. (9.) emphatica universalitatis amplificatio- ne: ut enim ob oculos ponat universalem depra- vationem, Deum introducit Psaltes accuratè circumspicientem, an vel unus inveniri possit, in toto humano genere, qui aut intelligat Deum, ut par est, ac de Deo & rebus divinis justam habeat notitiam, aut requirat Deum: qui aut mente cor- ruptus non sit in spiritualibus percipiendis, aut voluntate in iis, quæ bona sunt, amplectendis, Do- minus de cælo prospexit? an super eos, qui circa Saulem erant? minime, sed super universum ge- nus humanum? super filios hominum inde à primis parentibus: Oculi enim Domini intuentur homi- num omnium corda, consilia & opera, ut videat, si est intelligens, si est requirens Deum: unde thema & argumentum Psalmi ab initio proposi- tionis intelligitur: quis sit insipiens, in corde suo dicens, non est Deus: quod talis natura sit omnis homo. Nemo enim invenitur in illa accurata Dei perluistratione, qui sit intelligens, nemo, qui sit re- quirens Deum. (10.) Apostolica ejusdem expli- catione. Nam ubi Psaltes ait, Deum vidisse, an esset intelligens, vel requirens Dominum, respon- det Apostolus negativè v. 11. Non est, qui intelligat, non est, qui requirat Deum. (11.) universali distri- butione, quam versu 9. instituit Apostolus, con- cludens, omnes Judæos & Græcos sub peccato esse. Quæ conclusio secundum probationem præmis- sam intelligenda; in quà utique non de certis fla- gitiis nonnullorum, sed de impietate & injustitiâ omnium hominum agit, Rom. I. 17. omnesque, in quibus τὸ γνωστὸν τῶ θεῷ est, & qui agnoscunt τὸ δικαίωμα θεῦ, ejusdem convincit v. 19. 32. nemi- nem hominum excusari posse cap. II. 1. ostendit, quorum alii sine lege (scriptâ) peccarunt, quum legem cordi inscriptam habuerint; alii peccarunt ἐν νόμῳ, h.e. tum gentiles, tum Judæi cap. II. 12. 14. (12.) universalis convictionis medio, Rom. III. 10. quod stringit omnes quicunque ἐν νόμῳ vel ὑπὸ νόμον sunt: à quà forte nemo excipitur; illos enim convincit lex, qui sub lege sunt. At omnes homi- nes sunt sub lege, ne iis quidem exceptis, qui le- gem Mosaicam non habuerunt. (13.) universalis convictionis definitione, v. 19. ἵνα πᾶν σόμα φρα- γῇ, ut OMNE OS obstruatur. Non alicujus tantum gentis, non Judæorum, sed OMNIUM ora ob- structum iri voluit Apostolus. (14.) ejusdem ἐξη- γήσει, quam immediatè subjungit: καὶ ὑπόδικος γένηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος τῷ Θεῷ, ut obnoxius sit OMNIS, vel TOTUS MUNDUS Deo. Quomo- do hæc restringi possint ad Judæos? (15.) definitio- nis hujus scopo, & intentione. Hoc enim propo- situm est Apostoli, docere, quòd per opera legis OMNIS CARO non justificetur, id est, nulla caro, nullus homo: siquidem nullus non homo voce le- gis condemnetur. (16.) discriminis exclusione, & γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ: Nulla hac in parte est differentia, sive nationum, sive temporum, in toto genere hu- mano, v. 22. (17.) ejusdem confirmatione, πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον, OMNES enim peccârunt. Ne verò hic hyperbole iterũ fingatur, non modò excluditur ea validissimè c. V. 12. sq. sed etiã hîc loci: Qui enim ὑστερῦνται τῆς δόξης τῦ θεῦ: & si justificari velint, o- pus habent gratiâ Dei, & redempti à Christo sunt, illos peccasse affirmat Apostolus. At omnes in uni- versum homines, quales per naturā sunt, post lapsũ, destituuntur gloria Dei, gratiaq; Dei opus habent omnes, si justificari velint, & redempti etiam omnes sunt, nemine excepto, à Christo, quod tota Scriptura docet, & Rom. V. disertè expositum est. (18.) Nova generis humani distributione. Quod universum in Judæos & gentes dirimit Apostolus, vers. 29. omniumque Deum rationem habere, & illorum Deum esse velle, docet. Illi ergò omnes peccarunt, teste Apostolo, & gloria Dei destituuntur per naturam,quorum Deus vult esse Deus per gratiam, vel quorum misereri vult. At omnium hominum seu gentiles sint, seu Judæi, vult Deus esse, omnium vult misereri. Atque hic ex asse consonat tractationis Apostolicæ conclusio: Rom. XI.32. conclusit omnes sub incredulitate, ut OMNIUM misereretur.

Exemplum nobile in Cleopatra. Vide & Ælianum lib. IX.

## 3:13
Verse 13. Their throat is an open sepulchre. From Ps. 5:10, where the words in the Greek are the same as here. This Psalm describes men who are calumniators even to the point of bloodshed, such as many in royal courts. An open sepulchre is one that awaits a dead body. Thus Jeremiah 5:15 compares the quivers of the Chaldeans to an open sepulchre. In a similar way, the throat of those being discussed, that is, the voice proceeding from the throat, was waiting to see some dead person. Thus Eprius Marcellus: 'What have you to do with my dead man?' speaking of those whom he had driven to death by accusing them. Such, moreover, were many Jews even among the Christians. See the Acts of the Apostles.

with their tongues they have used deceit) these words also are verbatim from the Greek; the Seventy use the verb δολιῦν elsewhere, as in Num. 25:17, Ps. 105:25. In the Hebrew in this place is יַחֲלִיקוּן; that word in Prov. 28:23 is translated as 'flattering with the tongue.' For the most part, flatterers are also calumniators. ἐδολιῦσαν is a Boeotian termination. Thus we read εἴδοσαν, ἐμάθοσαν, ἤλθοσαν, and similar ones. Thus ἐλάβοσαν, 1 Macc. 11:48.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Τάφος ἀνεῳγμένος ὁ λάρυγξ ἀυτῶν. Ex Ps. V. 10. ubi in Græco eadem quæ hic verba. Describit hic Psalmus homines etiam in sanguinem calumnian- tes, quales in aulis multi. Sepulchrum apertum est, quod exspectat mortuum. Sic Chaldæorum pharetras sepulchro aperto comparat Jeremias V. 15. Pari modo eorum, de quibus agitur guttur, id est, vox à gutture procedens, exspectabat mortuum aliquem videre. Sic Eprius Marcellus, Quid tibi cum meo mortuo: de iis, quos accusando in mortem egerat loquens. Tales autem & Christianis erant Judæi multi. Vide Acta Apostolica.

ταῖς γλώσσαις ἀυτῶν ἐδολιῦσαν) etiam hæc verbotenus ex Græco, verbum δολιῦν alibi usurpant LXX. ut Num. XXV. 17. Es. CV. 25. In Hebræo hoc loco est יַחֲלִיקוּן id verbum Prov. XXVIII. 23. γλωσσοχαριτῶν. Plerumque adulatores etiam calumniatores sunt. ἐδολιῦσαν est Bœotica terminatio. Sic legimus εἴδοσαν, ἐμάθοσαν, ἤλθοσαν, & similia. Sic ἐλάβοσαν, 1. Macc. XI. 48.

## 3:13
the poison of asps is under their lips) From Ps. 140:4, where these same words are in the Greek. Those who harm others with their speech are said to have poison under their lips, as in James 3:8. But the worst poison is that of asps, which Aristotle in his History of Animals 8:29 reports to be incurable. Lucan, book 9, on the Asp: 'And a drop of thick poison fell: in no serpent is more concentrated.' Nicander on the same: 'The man is dragged along in evil, and the lashes bring him to the end of life.'

that whatsoever the law saith. The word Law is taken here more generally, so as to comprehend both the Psalms and the Prophets, just as in John 10:34, where we dealt with this matter: and we showed that the Hebrew word תּוֹרָה signifies everything that directs a man.

Latin:

ἰὸς ἀσπίδων ὑπὸ τὰ χείλη ἀυτῶν) Ex Ps.CXL. 4. ubi eadem hæc in Græco. Qui sermone suo aliis nocent, dicuntur habere venenum sub labiis, ut apud Jacobum III. 8. Pessimum autem venenum est aspidum, quod ἀνίατον esse tradit Aristoteles de Historia Animalium VIII. 29. Lucanus lib. IX. de Aspide: Et crassi gutta veneni Decidit: in nullo plus est serpente coactum. Nicander de eadem: κακάτη δ᾽ ἅτερ ὄλκεται ἀνὴρ, ῥηπιδοὶ δ᾽ ἐπὶ τῶκας ἄγει βιότοιο τελευτήν.

ὅτι ὅσα ὁ νόμος λέγει Νόμος vox hic generalius sumitur, ut & Psalmos comprehendat & Prophetas, quomodo & Joh. X. 34. ubi hac de re egimus: ostendimusque vocem Hebræam תּוֹרָה omne id significare, quod hominem dirigit.

## 3:14
whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness) From Ps. X. 7, where in the Greek: whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness: For the Greeks seem to have read מְרֹרוֹת for מִרְמוֹת, as it is in Deut. XXXII. 32; impious men are accustomed to both curse the pious and attack them with most bitter, and those deceitful, that is, false, curses. See Matt. V. 11, 44.

Latin:

ὧν τὸ ςόμα ἀρᾶς καὶ πικρίας γέμει) Ex Psal. X. 7. ubi in Græco: ὗ ἀρᾶς τὸ ςόμα ἀυτῦ γέμει καὶ πικρίας: Videntur enim Græci pro מִרְמוֹת legisse מְרֹרוֹת quomodo est Deut. XXXII. 32. solent homines impii pios & exsecrari & amarissimis, iisque dolosis, id est, falsis, maledictis impetere. Vide Matth. V. 11. 44.

## 3:15
Ver. 15. their feet are swift to shed blood) From Is. LIX. 7, where he describes the men contemporary with Manasseh, where the LXX [say]: and their feet run to wickedness, swift to shed blood. Paul said ὀξεῖς (swift) for ταχινοὶ (swift), with the same sense: for מִהֵר, which is here in the Hebrew, is translated ὀξὺς in Proverbs XXIII. 28, and ὀξέως in Isaiah VIII. 1. Nor is ὀξεῖς ἐπιβαλέσθαι otherwise [used] in Plutarch. In the Glossary: ὀξὺς, ὁ ταχὺς, nimble, swift.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες ἀυτῶν ἐκχέαι αἷμα) Ex Es. LIX. 7. ubi describit homines coævos Manassi, ubi LXX. οἱ δὲ πόδες ἀυτῶν ἐπὶ πονηρίαν τρέχουσι ταχινοὶ ἐκχέαι αἷμα. Paulus ὀξεῖς dixit pro ταχινοὶ, pari sensu: nam & מִהֵר, quod hîc in Hebræo est, ὀξὺς vertitur Proverb. XXIII. 28. & ὀξέως Esaiæ VIII, 1. Nec aliter ὀξεῖς ἐπιβαλέσθαι apud Plutarchum. In Glossario: ὀξὺς, ὁ ταχὺς pernix, velox.

## 3:16
Ver. 16. destruction and misery are in their ways) The same words in the Greek of the cited passage of Isaiah. The sense is, they do everything by force. This is most true of the Jews of those times. Hence the cause of their calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 16. σύντριμμα καὶ ταλαιπωρία ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἀυτῶν) Eadem verba in Græco dicti loci Esaiæ. Sensus est, omnia per vim agunt. Verissimum hoc de Judæis illorum temporum. Inde calamitatum causa.

## 3:17
Ver. 17. and the way of peace they have not known) In the Greek of Isaiah: and the way of peace they do not know. They do nothing that is of benefit to anyone. In Hebrew, someone is said to 'not know' that which he does not care about. Jerem. IV. 22, and above IV.

Latin:

Vers. 17. καὶ ὁδὸν εἰρήνης ὀυκ ἔγνωσαν) In Græco Esaiæ: καὶ ὁδὸν εἰρήνης ὀυκ οἴδασι. Nihil faciunt, quod cuiquam prosit. Hebræis nescire aliquis dicitur, quod non curat. Jerem. IV. 22. & supra IV.

## 3:18
Ver. 18. there is no fear of God before their eyes) These Greek words are in Ps. XXXVI. 1; the sense is: they have absolutely no regard for piety.

Now as to the quality of the sin of the human race, although the Apostle employs those circumlocutions which might seem to designate certain crimes or actual sins, if, however, everything is weighed more accurately, he describes the common misery of the human race by them, and that evil which by nature is in all since the fall, which Grotius, along with some Papists, denies in vain to please the Pelagians, Socinians, and Arminians; since it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking of the intrinsic and innate depravity of man from the universal corruption already asserted. But however not all may have been actually given over to such crimes, some of which are specifically mentioned, all and each are nevertheless not only capable and disposed toward them by natural depravity, as far as passive disposition is concerned, but also prompt and depraved regarding active and passive desire, Gen. VI. 5, chap. VIII. 21. Whence even some of the Papists, and among them Corn. à Lapide, when they see that the discourse is about such filthiness as is common to all men, acknowledge that these things must be understood of the state of the corrupt nature of the human race, and that they tend to show that all men lack the perfection due to them, and are in need of unmerited grace. Therefore, because actual malice is not universal, nor common to all men, much less can it be said of all in general that their throats are open sepulchres, exhaling the stench of sin, that all use their tongues for deceit, that the mouths of all are full of curses and bitterness, that the feet of all hasten to shed innocent blood, Augustine, lib. XII. de Civ. Dei c. XXII, rightly understands this here primarily of the habitual corruption of human nature, in which he has most of the better interpreters agreeing.

Although these things are taken from Ps. V. 10, where men who even slander unto blood are described, they are nevertheless applied here to man's natural proneness to evil. Which is designated, both in general and negatively, that there is no one righteous, v. 10, none understanding, none seeking God, v. 11, none doing good, v. 12, as human misery is expressed partly regarding the mind, partly regarding the will: and positively: partly regarding the recession from good, v. 12, partly regarding the conversion to evil, that we are all alike useless, nay, foul, rotten, and abominable, as is evident from a comparison of the Hebrew word in Ps. XIV. 3; and then in particular: regarding the principal members of man: such as (1.) the filthiness of the throat, which is like a most foul open sepulchre: For it is not said so because it awaits the dead, but because it emits a stench, as appears from the Psalm to which reference is made in v. 10. and which are then said here about the hastening of the feet to shed blood, confirm. (2.) the deceitfulness of the tongue, that it is by nature composed for nothing but deceits and frauds, from Ps. XXXVI. 4. (3.) the fraudulence of the lips, under which the poison of asps is hidden, from Ps. CXL. 4. (4.) the bitterness of the mouth, that it is full of nothing but curses, from Ps. X. 7. (5.) the swiftness of the feet, both to violence and to the flight from an innocent and peaceful life, from Is. LIX. 7 and Prov. I. 16. (6.) the impious turning away of the eyes from God, from Ps. LIX. 7. All of which exhibit the spiritual misery of the whole man, such as he is by nature, and outside of the grace of God; and although in the parallel passages they might perhaps be taken of actual malice, here however they are recalled to their source, and are to be understood primarily of habitual propensity and concupiscence, and the active verbs are to be explained according to the customary Hebraism, by which not only acts, but also habits and qualities are wont to be expressed by active verbs.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ὀυκ ἔςι Φόβος Θεῦ ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἀυτῶν) Sunt ista verba Græca in Ps. XXXVI. 1. sensus est: pietatem plane non respiciunt.

Jam quod ad qualitatem peccati generis humani, etsi Apostolus adhibeat eas περιφράσεις, quæ videantur facinora quædam, aut peccata actualia designare, si tamē accuratius expendantur omnia, communem miseriam generis humani iisdem describit, & malum illud, quod natura indè ab ortu omnibus post lapsum inest, quod nequicquam in gratiam Pelagianorum, Socinianorum, & Arminianorum negat Grotius cum Papistis nonnullis; siquidem de intrinseca & connata hominis pravitate Apostolum loqui ex universali corruptione jam asserta manifestum sit. Utut verò non omnes actu secundo talibus flagitiis dediti fuerint, quorum nonnulla speciatim commemorata sunt, omnes tamen & singuli non modo naturali pravitate ad ea habiles & dispositi sunt, quantum ad dispositionem passivam, sed etiam prompti & pravi quoad desiderium activum & passivum, Gen. VI. 5. cap. VIII.21. Unde è Pontificiis etiam nonnulli, & inter hos Corn. à Lap. cum videant de ejusmodi fœditate, quæ omnibus hominibus communis est, sermonem esse, agnoscunt de statu naturæ corruptæ generis humani hæc accipienda, eoque tendere, ut doceatur, omnes homines carere perfectione sibi debitâ, ac indigere gratiâ indebitâ. Quòd ergò actualis malitia universalis, omnibusque hominibus communis non sit, nedum de omnibus in universum dici possit, quòd guttura eorum sint sepulchra aperta, fœtorem peccati exhalantia, quòd omnes linguis utantur ad dolos, omnibus ora diris & amarulentiâ plena sint, omnium pedes ad effundendum innoxium sanguinem properent, meritò Augustin. lib. XII. de Civ. Dei c. XXII. de corruptione potissimum habituali naturæ humanæ hîc accipit, in quo plerofque Interpp. meliores consentientes habet.

Quamvis hæc è Ps. V. 10. petita, ubi homines in sanguinem etiam calumniantes describuntur, hîc tamen applicantur ad naturalem hominis ad malum pronitatem. Quæ designatur, tùm in genere & negativè, quòd non sit justus, v. 10. non intelligens nom requirens Deum, v. 11. non sit faciens bonum, v. 12. ut exprimitur miseria humana partim quoad mentem, partim quoad voluntatem: & positivè: partim quoad recessionem à bono, v. 12. partim quoad conversionem ad malum, quòd inutiles pariter omnes simus, imò fœtidi, putidi & abominabiles, ut è collatione verbi Ebraici Psal. XIV. 3. constat; tum in specie: quoad membra hominis præcipua: utpote (1.) gutturis fœditatem, quod est instar sepulchri aperti fœtidissimi: Non enim ita id dici, quòd expeĉtet mortuos, sed quod fœtorem emittat, ut è Psalmo apparet, ad quem respicitur v. 10. & quæ hic deinde de pedum festinatione ad profundendum sanguinem dicuntur, confirmant. (2.) linguæ dolositatem, quòd nonnisi ad dolos & fraudes naturâ composita sit è Ps. XXXVI. 4. (3.) Laborum fraudulentiam, sub quibus aspidum occultatur venenum, è Ps. CXL. 4. (4.) oris amarulentiam, quod nonnisi diris plenum è Psal. X. 7. (5.) pedum tum celeritatem ad violentiam,tum vitæ innocentis & pacificæ fugam ex Es. LIX. 7. & Prov. I. 16. (6.) oculorum declinationem à Deo impiam, ex Ps. LIX. 7. Quæ omnia exhibent spiritualem totius hominis miseriam, qualis is per naturam est, & extra Dei gratiam; & quamvis in parallelis forte locis de actuali malitia sumerentur, hîc tamen ad fontem suum ea revocantur, & de habituali maximè propensione ac concupiscentiâ accipienda sunt, & verba activa ex Ebraismo consueto explicanda, quo verbis activis non actus modò, sed etiam habitus & qualitates exprimi solent.

## 3:19
Verse 19. But we know) as if he were saying: This matter is known to those who have devoted effort to the sacred scriptures: from which Kimchi teaches this in his commentary on Ps. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 19. οἴδαμεν δὲ) quasi dicat: Res hæc nota est iis, qui sacris literis operam dedere: ex quibus id docet Kimchi ad Ps. XIV.

## 3:19
to them who are in the law) That is, to the descendants of Jacob, or to proselytes who have taken up the law. For these are said to be 'in the law,' above in 2:12, or 'under the law' below in 6:15, or 'under the law' in 1 Cor. 9:20. This rule also, although it is stated generally, certainly has exceptions, namely, unless an explicit mention of some foreign nation has preceded, as in the passage of Isaiah concerning the Chaldeans. And elsewhere: the burden of Egypt, the burden of Damascus, the burden of Edom, the burden of Nineveh.

that every mouth may be stopped) He brought this forward for this reason, that they might have nothing with which to defend themselves, since all these things apply to them, which God reproached the ancient Hebrews with, nor can they deny it. There is, however, a proverb among the Hebrews קפצה פיה עולה Job V. 15. & Ps. CVII. 42. iniquity has shut its mouth. In a similar sense, Plautus in the Miles [Gloriosus] uses the phrase to shut the tongue. This is ἀναπολόγητοι, as above I. 20. II. 1. καὶ ὑπόδικος γένηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος τῷ Θεῷ) ὑπόδικος חוב, that is, a debtor of punishments. Plato often uses this word in this sense. The whole world, that is, the greatest part of mankind, as 1 John V. 19, has deserved the most severe punishments, certainly not because of something innate, but because of treacherous and cruel deeds, such as have just been indicated. The reference is especially, as we have said, to the cruelty against Christians. The word νόμος here is not taken generally, to denote the Scripture of the O.T. as in John X. 34, but specifically concerning the law, by which this is opposed to the Gospel. Because men were to be convicted of sin from the law, so that it might be inferred that no one can be justified by the law, οἱ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ therefore are not only the descendants of Jacob with the proselytes, but all men: because all are ὑπὸ νόμον under the law, which some codices have here, which Grotius acknowledges to be the same as that ἐν τῷ νόμῳ. For in one sense the Jews are said to have sinned ἐν νόμῳ in the law, in opposition to the Gentiles, who sinned ἀνόμως without the law, c. II. 12; in another sense here, they are said to be ἐν τῷ νόμῳ in the law, that is, to be under the law, both Jews and Gentiles, who are all ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν v. 9, because they are subject to the law, from which condition no man is exempt: therefore the Apostle added this, so that every mouth may be stopped, and that the whole world may be ὑπόδικος, a debtor, namely, of punishments, as Grotius explains. But the whole world is not the greatest part of men, but the entire human race, which is wholly subject to the law, and bound to punishment because of the transgression of the law, of which he has convicted all men: not because of treacherous and cruel deeds, but because of original and innate sin, as has been shown thus far. That the cruelty of the Jews against Christians is especially referred to is asserted without proof. The matter is not about the Jews alone, who certainly were neither the whole world nor the greatest part of men, but the Apostle demonstrates that Greeks and Jews alike are ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν. And Grotius is forced to acknowledge at v. 20 that these things are said generally about men; how then does he restrict them to the Jews? Vers. 20. διότι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ. What he had said generally about men, he now adapts specifically to the Jews, pressing them more and more. The Apostle does indeed allude to that which we have in Ps. CXLIII. 2, but by an argument from the less credible to the more credible. If David, as not a bad man among kings, and well-versed in the law, confessed concerning himself and those like him, that if his life, from the time he had arrived at the knowledge of the law, were inspected by God, it could not be approved by God, what is to be thought of those whom David himself so execrates, and to whom the Jews of our time are similar? And δικαιωθήσεται in the Hebrew is לא יצרק in the Kal, it will not be, i.e., he will not appear righteous. See what is in the Prolegomena to this epistle. πᾶσα σὰρξ in the Hebrew is כל חי every living thing. Both words signify man. See Matt. XXIV. 22. And how that universality is to be taken in the words of David, appears from what was said above. But from this the Apostle infers that the law of Moses, in which the Jews placed more confidence than was right, as we saw above II. 17, when viewed by itself, that is, apart from those things which had been before the law, did not have the power to lead men to true and God-pleasing righteousness, since Abraham, without the law, far surpassed David, who was established under the law. The reason why the law did not have such power is because it contains promises limited only to the span of each man's life, whereas the promises made to Abraham extended themselves immensely beyond his death, under which Abraham suspected that something greater lay hidden, but, according to the proportion of the times, only faintly, whence his righteousness, although situated in the heart and pleasing to God, was nevertheless much weaker than that righteousness which most Christians of the first times exhibited throughout their whole life, namely, from baptism. Faith believes according to the measure of revelation: the purity of soul and life according to the measure of faith. Where God has bestowed more, He also demands more. Philosophers say that a certain firm facility is acquired by many acts. For thus Quintilian translates what the Greeks call ἕξιν. So also through many acts accustomed to the law, a certain righteousness is acquired that is valid among men, but not that interior one, which God especially desires and which alone God deems worthy of rewards not earthly, but heavenly or rather super-heavenly. Wherefore also Aben-Ezra in his Rhythmic work on the law calls the law by the name of a beginning.

The Apostle concludes the treatment of the former, which concerned the subject, namely, the whole human race, which he asserted to be concluded under sin and condemnation by the divine law, by virtue of divine justice: and because he concludes from the previous demonstration that no one can obtain righteousness and salvation from the law, not simply concerning the human race, over which the wrath of God is revealed because of impiety and injustice, but as it is to be justified and saved (for that is the object of Theology, of which this Epistle exhibits a certain compendium): For those who are under sin and condemnation through the law, they can in no way be justified by the works of the law. Therefore the Apostle does not here pass to the Jews of his own time, as Grotius perverts it; but he asserts generally that no man is justified by the law, and he does not only allude to Ps. CXLIII. 2, arguing from the less credible to the more credible, but he brings forward the words of the Psalms in place of proof, as being said not about David alone, but about all the living: Before you no living person will be justified: if, namely, you wish to enter into judgment or to act according to the law with men. For it is confessed that no living person, and no flesh, is no man, as Matt. XXIV. 12. Nor is it only inferred, as Grotius wishes, that the Law of Moses, viewed by itself, that is, apart from those things which were before the law, did not have such powers as to lead men to true and God-pleasing righteousness, but all power of justifying is also taken away from the law, nor is it taught that the law or the work of the law contributes anything to that righteousness which stands before God, because that righteousness is manifested not in the law, but in the Gospel, nay even without the law, as the Apostle affirms in Rom. I. 17. and here v. 21., and from the law there is only the knowledge of sin, and of the wrath pressing upon men because of sin, but not of righteousness or salvation: nor does the holy Apostle set out to demonstrate that the just man lives by the works of the law, but by faith. And what is that which was before the law of Moses, which makes for true God-pleasing righteousness? If you listen to the Apostle, it was the ἐπαγγελία (promise) concerning Christ: from which, therefore, and not from the law, the Apostle derives τὴν κληρονο- μίαν (the inheritance) in Gal. III. 18., but he teaches that the law was only brought in additionally, τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν (for the sake of transgressions), from which, however, there cannot be righteousness or justification, v. 19. 21. The reason, therefore, why the law did not have such powers is not because it contains only promises limited to the span of each man's life, for this is false, since the law promises eternal life to those who observe it, Lev. XVIII. 5., Luc. X. 28., Gal. III. 12. But because that condition of perfect observance can be fulfilled by no one after the fall: whence in Rom. VIII. 3. it is said to be weakened, with respect to us, so that it can no longer vivify us, διὰ σαρκὸς (through the flesh), because we are all carnal, and flesh, who are born of flesh, Joh. III. 5. Concerning which it is helpful to hear from the Papists themselves, Claudius Espencaeus in 1 ad Timoth. I. p. 8. Moreover, the law is given in that respect so that sin may be known, Rom. III. VII. There is therefore no hope of justification in its moral precepts, but in FAITH ALONE, Rom. III. (there is no doubt, that it is true and living) thus according to his method Aquinas, so much the more truly, the closer he is to the ancient Orthodox: for thus Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, not attacking the Law, but the evil teachers of the law: For since the institution and destination of the law is to justify man, and yet it cannot do so through the infirmity of the flesh, Rom. VIII. Act. XIII. its scope, legitimate use, and genuine intention is that it might lead us to Christ (who justifies) may send us back and lead us like a tutor. For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly have been by the law: but if righteousness is by the law, then Christ died for nothing, that is, in vain, Gal. 2. 3. Nor does Anselm, etc., think otherwise, following Augustine. But that Grotius trifles, saying that in the promise made to Abraham something greater lay hidden, and that he only suspected it, and that the Father of believers was at least tenuously [believing], and that therefore his righteousness was much thinner than that which most Christians of the first times exhibited, he has in large part from the Pelagians and Socinians. On the contrary, the Apostle teaches both in the following chapter 4 and in Heb. 9 that the most ample promises of the eternal inheritance itself were made to Abraham, and that he did not merely suspect it, but firmly believed it, and is therefore deservedly proposed to us as an example, nay, is established as the Father of believers, so that we may follow in his footsteps. Since, therefore, the faith of Abraham is so highly extolled by the Apostle, why does Grotius think so tenuously of it, and add that it was within the faith of Christians for the most part in the first times, which he sets before Christians as an idea for an example, and for which the Apostle even makes him the Father? An idea certainly cannot be held, which is much thinner than those to whom it is proposed as an idea. Nor is he to be considered the father of believers who is much inferior to his children in faith.

Nor does Grotius correctly define that righteousness which God regards in the justification of man, when he calls it the interior purity of the mind. On the contrary, the Apostle is entirely occupied with proving that we cannot stand before the tribunal of God by either our interior or our exterior righteousness, because that flesh cannot be justified before God by the law or the works of the law: but it would be justified by the law if justification were obtained on account of one's own righteousness, of which we spoke in the prolegomena.

That the Sophisms of the Papists may be resolved: it must be observed (1) that by the law here is not understood the ceremonial law, as if only ceremonial works were excluded from justification, as being abolished by the death of Christ, as Ederus, Alphonsus de Castro, Renatus Benedictus, Johannes de Daventria, and Alphonsus Varvesius, and Johannes Paulus Windick wish with Lombard: because the discourse there is about the law from which is the knowledge of sin, which is certainly from the moral law, Rom. 3:20 [7:7], whence Dominicus à Soto, Salmero, Toletus, Pererius, Estius, as also Bellarmine, lib. 1 de justif. cap. 19, acknowledge that not ceremonial works, but moral ones, or certain works of any law whatsoever, whether moral or ceremonial, are excluded here. (2) that by works of the law is not understood works done by the powers of nature alone, because here all works are excluded, and the Apostle deals not only with the Gentiles, but also with the Jews; nay, he acknowledges no good works done by the powers of nature alone, Rom. 14:23, which Vasquez also confesses in lib. 2, Tom. 2, Disp. 210, cap. 8, num. 73, namely that the Apostle never conceded such works as proceed from the powers of nature alone. Nor (3) are works of the law understood as only works done before faith without the grace of God from the mere knowledge of the law, or works of Jews not having faith in the redemption of Christ, as Salmero, Toletus, Stapleton, Bellarmine, Pererius, Estius, Becanus, Cornelius, Justinianus, Menuchius, Tirenus, Maldonatus, Vasquez, Valentianus, and others commonly contend; as if works done from faith were not excluded from justification, but only those which are done without the grace of God before faith: But the Apostle indefinitely excludes any works whatsoever, he even so opposes faith to works that he requires the former for justification, and removes the latter entirely, he teaches that righteousness is manifested not in the law, but uniquely in the Gospel, but works following faith are indeed consonant with the law: He asserts that we are justified solely by the grace of God and freely, and therefore not by works (by whatever name they come), Conf. Tit. 3:5, 2. Tim. 1:9, he decrees that that by which we are justified is not in us, but uniquely in Christ, and that we are justified solely by the redemption of Christ the Mediator, and concludes that a man is justified by faith without works: nor was the matter properly with Jews destitute of faith in Christ, but with Christians having faith in Christ, whom he nevertheless instructs are justified not by works done from faith, but solely by faith: furthermore, he excludes all boasting: which is not excluded if justification were obtained from our works following faith in Christ; nay, he affirms that the ungodly, not one instructed by works proceeding from faith, is justified, Rom. 4:5, and defines justification by the remission of sins and the imputation of faith for righteousness without works, Rom. 4:6, and especially confirms by the example of Abraham that we are justified without works by faith alone: excluding by this very example even those works which followed faith, because he proposes Abraham to be looked at in the middle of his course of good works, and concerning Abraham already gifted with the Spirit of grace, Vasquez himself admitting it, he denies that he was justified by works. Add that the occasion of the Apostolic disputation was that some wished to set up their own righteousness, but did not entirely reject Christ, or deny that the grace of God was necessary for performing works of piety or for obtaining the remission of sins. Nor indeed should it be doubted that Flacius rightly warned in the preface to this Epistle, that Paul, by proposing Abraham as an example of gratuitous or precarious justification and salvation through Christ, wished to refute that very empty boasting of the Jews concerning Father Abraham, who by his most illustrious virtues and merits had obtained righteousness and blessing for himself and all his descendants.

for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.

Lest anyone should think the law was entirely useless, he shows its excellent use, namely that those notices of base actions, which evil customs had especially obliterated during the sojourn in Egypt, were made conspicuous again by a manifest revelation of the divine will. Nature in some way indicates the divine will, but revelation, supported by so many miracles, does so much more. See below VII. 9. Νόμος, where it is used simply by Paul, signifies the law of Moses, as in II. 12. 14. 23. 25. ἐπίγνωσις is the same as γνῶσις, knowledge, or a little more, above I. 28. below X. 2. Eph. I. 17. IV. 13. Philip. I. 9. Coloss. I. 9. 10. II. 2. III. 10. 1. Tim. II. 4. 2. Tim. II. 25. III. 7. Tit. I. 5. & in Peter several times, thus also ἐπιγινώσκειν is γινώσκειν Matth. VII. 16. 70. above I. 32. & elsewhere.

The argument succinctly brought forward from the preceding points stands thus: If through the law there is only the recognition of sin, then certainly no one can be justified by the works of the law.
