But the former is true, therefore the latter is also. For since it has been shown thus far that the law only concluded all under sin, and argued the power of sin, namely that sin brings condemnation. But by the very law by which we are all condemned, because we all transgress it, by its observance certainly none of us can be justified. Whence Pererius, Justinianus, and Estius interpret it exclusively: through the law there is only the recognition of sin. And these things concerning the ἐξεργασία of the Apostolic and likewise DIDACTIC section, namely regarding the SUBJECTI πρόγνωσιν concerning man being justified and saved: who according to the law is convinced to be under a state of sin and condemnation, so that a παρασκευὴ may be made for the Evangelical doctrine concerning the true method of obtaining justification and salvation. There follows therefore

SECTION II. EXHIBITING AN EXPOSITION OF THE MEANS AND CAUSES OF JUSTIFICATION. MEMBER I. GENERAL.

The Apostle institutes an enumeration of the causes of justification in this Chapter III, in the remainder of its part, according to the proposed norm of this doctrine. Then he brings forward a demonstration from the example of Abraham and the Davidic testimony in chapter IV. Furthermore, from the posterior or consequent, namely the peace of conscience, he establishes justification through faith. Finally, he proposes the antithesis of Adam and Christ for the sake of greater elucidation and confirmation in chapter V. All of which we have observed to contribute to the Apostolic demonstrative exposition concerning the economy of the Epistle: these things having been thus dispatched, the Apostle appends a defense of this Evangelical doctrine, serving likewise for its further confirmation through Chapters VI, VII, and VIII.

SUBJECTION I. Presenting the confirmation of true doctrine. ARTICLE I. The argument from the rationale of the causes of salvation, why it is absolved, according to the partition handed down at the beginning of Chapter III.

PART IV OF CHAPTER THREE. THE IMPLANTATION OF THE JUSTICE OF FAITH.

τοῖς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ λαλεῖ) Id est, Jacobi posteris, aut proselytis, qui legem susceperunt. Hi enim dicuntur esse ἐν νόμῳ, supra II. 12. aut ὑπὸ νόμον infra VI. 15. vel ὑπὸ νόμον 1.Corinth. IX. 20. Hæc quoque regula, quanquam generaliter enunciatur, exceptiones sane habet, nempe nisi diserta mentio gentis alicujus extraneæ præcesserit, ut in Esaiæ loco Chaldæorum. Et alibi onus Ægypti, onus Damasci, onus Edom, onus Ninives.

ἵνα πᾶν τόμα φραγῇ) Hoc ideo attulit, ut nihil habeant, quo se tueantur, cum hæc omnia illis conve- niant, quæ veteribus Hebræis Deus exprobrarit, neque id negare possint. Est autem proverbium apud Hebræos קפצה פיה עולה Job. V. 15. & Ps. CVII. 42. iniquitati os occlusum est. Pari sensu occludere linguam Plauto in Milite. Hoc est ἀναπολόγητοι, ut supra I. 20. II. 1. καὶ ὑπόδικος γένηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος τῷ Θεῷ) ὑπόδικος חוב debitor pœnarum scilicet. Plato sæpe hanc vocem hoc sensu usurpat. Omnis mundus, id est, maxima pars hominum, ut 1. Joh. V. 19. pœnas gravissimas meruit non sane ob aliquid agnatum, sed ob facta perfida & crudelia, qualia modo indicata sunt. Respicicur maxime, ut diximus, sævitia in Christianos. Vox νόμος hic non accipitur generaliter, ut Scripturam V. T. notet Joh. X. 34. sed specialiter de lege, qua opponitur hæc Evangelio. Quia convincendi de peccato homines è lege erant, ut inferretur, neminem justificari posse per legem οἱ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ergo non sunt Jacobi posteri tantum cum proselytis, sed omnes homines: quia omnes sunt ὑπὸ νόμον sub lege, quod hic nonnulli codices habent, quod autem idem esse, cum illo ἐν τῷ νόμῳ agnoscit Grotius. Alio enim sensu dicuntur Judæi ἐν νόμῳ in lege peccasse in oppositione ad gentiles, qui ἀνόμως sine lege peccarunt, c. II. 12. alio hic ἐν τῷ νόμῳ εἶναι in lege, hoc est, sub lege esse dicuntur tum Judæi, tum gentes, qui omnes sunt ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν v. 9. quod nempe legi subjecti sint, à qua conditione nemo hominum exemptus est: ideo addidit Apostolus, ut omne os obstruatur, & ut totus mundus ὑπόδικος, debitor sit, pœnarum sc. ut explicat Grotius. Omnis autem mundus non est pars hominum maxima, sed universum genus humanum, quod totum legi obnoxium est, & ob transgressionem legis, cujus omnes homines convicit, pœnæ obstrictum: non ob facta perfida & crudelia, sed ob originale & agnatum peccatum, ut hactenus ostensum. Sævitiam Judæorum in Christianos maximè respici, precariò asseritur. Non de solis Judæis, qui utique nec totus mundus, nec pars maxima hominum erant, res est, sed Græcos pariter & Judæos ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν esse, demonstrat Apostolus. Et agnoscere cogitur Grotius ad v. 20. hæc generaliter dicta esse de hominibus; quomodo ergò ea ad Judæos restringit? Vers. 20. διότι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ. Quod generaliter de hominibus dixerat, jam Judæos magis magisque premens aptat ipsis specialiter. Alludit quidem Apostolus ad id, quod habemus Ps. CXLIII. 2. sed argumento à minus credibili ad magis credibile. Si David, ut inter reges non malus, & legis apprime gnarus, fassus est de se suisque similibus, si vita sua, ex quo ad legis notitiam pervenerat, inspiceretur à Deo, non posse eam Deo probari, quid de illis censendum est, quos ipse David adeò exsecratur, & quibus similes sunt nostri temporis Judæi? & δικαιωθήσεται in Hebræo לא יצרק in Kal, non erit, i. e. non apparebit justus. Vide, quæ in Prolegomenis ad hanc epistolam. πᾶσα σὰρξ in Hebræo כל חי omnis vivens. Utraque vox hominem significat. Vide Matth. XXIV. 22. Et in Davidis quidem verbis ista universalitas quomodo accipienda sit, ex supradictis apparet. At Apostolus hinc infert legem Mosis, in qua Judæi plus æquo fiduciæ collocabant, ut vidimus supra II. 17. per se spectatam, id est, seorsim ab iis, quæ ante legem fuerant, non eas habuisse vires, ut homines ad veram ac Deo placentem justitiam perduceret, quippe cum Abrahamus sine lege, Davidem sub lege constitutum multum superaverit. Causa cur lex tales vires non habuerit, est quia promissa tantum continet unius vitæ hominis cujusque spatio limitata, cùm facta Abrahamo promissa ultra mortem ejus in immensum se porrexerint, sub quibus & majus quiddam latere Abrahamus suspicatus est, sed pro ratione temporum tenuiter, unde & justitia ejus, quamvis in corde sita ac Deo placens, tenuior tamen multò fuit justitia ea, quam primorum temporum Christiani plerique per omne vitæ tempus, nempe à baptismo, exhibuere. Pro modo revelationis credit fides: pro modo fidei puritas animi ac vitæ. Ubi plus contulit Deus, plus etiam exigit. Ajunt Philosophi, multis actibus acquiri firmam quandam facilitatem. Ita enim Quintilianus vertit, quod Græci ἕξιν vocant. Sic & per actus multos legi con- suetos, gruentes acquiritur justitia quædam inter homines valens, non autem illa interior, quam præcipue desiderat Deus & quam solam dignatur Deus præmiis non terrenis, sed cœ- lestibus aut potius supercœlestibus. Quare & Aben-Esdra in opere Rhythmico de lege, legem vocat principii nomine.

Concludit Apostolus prioris tractationem, quæ subjectum concernebat, totum nempe genus huma- num, quod sub peccato, & condemnatione, lege di- vinâ, vi justitiæ divinæ conclusum esse, adseruit: & quia de genere humano, super quod ira Dei re- velatur ob impietatem & injustitiam, non simplici- ter, sed qua illud justificandum & salvandum est, (id enim objectum est Theologiæ, cujus compen- dium quoddam hæc Epistola exhibet,) justitiam & salutem ex lege neminem consequi posse, è su- periori demonstratione colligit: Qui enim per le- gem sub peccato & condemnatione sunt, illi per ope- ra legis justificari nullatenus possunt. Non ergo hic ad Judæos sui temporis transit Apostolus, uti Grotius pervertit; sed generatim nullum homi- nem per legem justificari asserit, nec tantum allu- dit ad Ps. CXLIII. 2. argumentando à minus credi- bili ad magis credibile, sed probationis loco verba Psalmis adducit, utpote non de solo Davide dicta, sed de omnibus viventibus: Coram te nullus vivens justificabitur: si scil. in judicium intrare, vel secun- dum legem agere velis cum hominibus. In con- fesso enim est, quod nullus vivens, & nulla caro sit nullus homo, ut Matth. XXIV. 12. Neque id tan- tum infertur, uti Grotius vult, quod Lex Mosis per se spectata, id est, seorsim ab iis, quæ ante legem fuerint, eas vires non habuerit, ut homines ad ve- ram ac Deo placentem justitiam perduceret, sed & adimitur omnis vis justificandi legi, nec quicquam legem ad justitiam illam, quæ coram Deo consi- stit, aut legis operam conferre docetur, quia non in lege, sed in Evangelio manifestata est illa justi- tia, imò sine lege, ut Rom. I. 17. & hic v. 21. affir- mat Apostolus, & ex lege solùm est cognitio pecca- ti, & iræ, ob peccatum homines prementis, non vero justitiæ aut salutis: nec per opera legis, sed ex fide justum vivere demonstrare instituit S. Apo- stolus. Et quid illud est, quod ante legem Mosis fuit, quod ad veram Deo placentem justitiam fa- ciat? Si Apostolum audias, ἐπαγγελία fuit de Christo: ex qua itaque, non ex lege, τὴν κληρονο- μίαν deducit Apostolus Gal. III. 18. legem autem subintroductam tantum, docet τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν transgressionum causa, ex qua vero nequeat esse justitia, vel justificatio, v. 19. 21. Causa ergò, cur lex tales vires non habuerit, non est, quia pro- missa tantum continet unius vitæ hominis cujusque spatio limitata, hoc enim falsum, quum promittat lex vitam æternam illis, qui observant eandem Lev. XVIII. 5. Luc. X. 28. Gal. III. 12. Sed quod con- ditio illa perfectæ observantiæ à nemine impleri possit post lapsum: unde Rom. VIII. 3. infirmata dicitur, nostri respectu, quo minus sc. nos vivificare amplius possit, διὰ σαρκὸς, propter carnem, quia omnes carnales sumus, & caro, qui de carne nati, Joh. III. 5. De quo audire juvat ex ipsis Pontificiis Claudium Espensæum in 1. ad Timoth. I. p. 8. Data autem ea parte lex est, ut peccatum cognoscatur, Rom. III. VII. Non est ergò in ejus moralibus spes justifica- tionis, sed in SOLA fide, Rom. III. (non dubium, quin vera & viva) sic pro sua methodo Aquinas, tantò ve- rius, quantò veteres Orthodoxos propius: sic enim Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Oecu- menius Legem non insectos, sed malos legis doctores: Cum enim legis institutum & destinatio sit hominem justificare, neq; verò id possit per infirmitatem carnis, Rom. VIII. Act. XIII. ejus scopus, usus legitimus, & germana intentio est, ut ad Christum (qui nos justificet) pædagogi instar nos remittat & adducat. Si enim data esset lex, quæ posset vivificare, verè ex lege esset justitia: Si autem per legem justitia, ergò Chri- stus gratis, id est, frustra mortuus est, Gal. II. III. Nec aliter ex Augustino Anshelmus &c. Quod verò Grotius in promissione Abrahamo facta, latuisse tantum majus quid, idque suspicatum esse, ac te- nuiter saltem Patrem credentium, adeoque justitiam ejus tenuiorem multò fuisse eâ quam plerique Chri- stiani primorum temporum exhibuere, nugatur, magnam partem à Pelagianis & Socinistis habet. Abrahamo contrà Apostolus factas fuisse pro- missiones amplissimas ipsius hæreditatis æternæ, neque suspicatum de ea tantum fuisse, sed firmiter eam credidisse, atque ideo in exemplum nobis merito proponi, imo Patrem credentium consti- tutum esse, ut ejus vestigiis insistamus, tum c. IV. sequenti, tum Ebr. IX. docet Apostolus. Quum ergo tantopere fides Abrahami extollatur ab Apostolo, cur tam tenuiter de ea sentit, eamque intra fidem Christianorum plerumque in primis temporibus adjicit Grotius, quam Christianis ideæ instar in exemplum sistit, & ob quam etiam ipsum Patrem facit Apostolus? Idea certè non potest haberi, quod multo tenuius est illis, qui- bus ideæ instar proponitur. Nec pater creden- tium habendus, qui filiis in fide multo est infe- rior.

. Nec justitiam illam, quam respicit Deus in ho- minis justificatione, rectè definit Grotius, cum eam interiorem puritatem animi dicit. Ex ad- verso in eo totus est Apostolus, ut nec per inte- riorem, nec per exteriorem nostram justitiam co- ram Dei tribunali nos consistere posse evincat, quia illa caro per legem vel opera legis justificari coram Deo non potest: justificaretur autem per legem, si ob justitiam propriam obtingeret justi- ficatio, de quo in prolegomenis diximus.

Papistarum Sophismata ut expediantur: obser- vandum (1) per legem hîc non intelligi ceremonia- lem legem, quasi opera tantum ceremonialia ex- cludantur à justificatione, utpote per mortem Christi deleta, ut cum Lombardo Ederus, Alphons. de Castro, Renatus Benedictus, Joh. de Daventriâ, Alphonsus Varvesius, Joh. Paulus Windick volunt: quia de lege illi sermo est, ex qua est agnitio pec- cati, quæ utique ex lege morali est, Rom. VII. 7. unde agnoscunt Dominicus à Soto, Salmero, Tole- tus, Pererius, Estius, ut & Bellarm. l. 1. de justif. cap. 19. non opera ceremonialia, sed moralia, vel certa opera cujuscunque legis, sive moralis, sive ceremonialis hîc excludi. (2) per opera legis non intelligi opera solis naturæ viribus facta, quia hîc omnia excluduntur opera, nec tantum de genti- libus, sed etiam Judæis agit Apostolus, imò nulla opera bona agnoscit solis naturæ viribus facta, Rom. XIV. 23. quod etiam Vasquez. fatetur in l. II. Tom. II. Disp. 210. cap. 8. num. 73. quod nempe Apostolus nunquam talia opera concesserit, quæ ex solis naturæ viribus proficiscuntur. Neque (3) per opera legis tantùm opera ante fidem sine Dei gratia facta ex sola legis notitia, aut opera Judæorum fidem in Christi redemptionem non habentium intelliguntur, ut Salmero, Toletus, Stapleton. Bellarm. Pererius, Estius, Becanus, Cor- nelius, Justinianus, Menuchius, Tirenus, Mal- donatus, Vasquez, Valentianus, aliique communi- ter contendunt; quasi opera ex fide facta non ex- cludantur à justificatione, sed quæ fiant sine Dei gratia ante fidem: Sed Apostolus indefinitè opera quævis excludit, fidem etiam ita operibus opponit, ut illam ad justificationem requirat, hæc omninò removeat, justitiam non in lege, sed in Evangelio unicè manifestatam docet, opera autem fidem consequentia utique consona legi sunt: Sola Dei gratia & gratis nos justificari asserit, adeoque non operibus (quocunque illa veniant nomine) Conf. Tit. III. 5. 2. Tim. I. 9. non in nobis, sed in Christo unicè esse id, unde justificemur, solaque Christi Me- diatoris redemptione nos justificari decernit, ac per fidem absque operibus justificari hominem con- cludit: neque ipsi res erat propriè cum Judæis fide in Christum destitutis, sed cum Christianis fidem in Christum habentibus, quos tamen non operi- bus ex fide factis, sed solum per fidem justificari instituit: omnem præterea gloriationem excludit: quæ non excluditur, si ex operibus nostris fidem in Christum consequentibus justificatio obtingat; imò impium, non vero operibus ex fide profectis instru- ctum justificari affirmat, Rom. IV. 5. & justifica- tionem per remissionem peccatorum, & imputatio- nem fidei in justitiam absque operibus definit Rom. IV. 6. ac cumprimis exemplo Abrahæ confirmat nos sine operibus sola fide justificari: excludens hoc ipso exemplo etiam opera ea, quæ fidem con- secuta sunt, quia Abrahamum in medio bono- rum operum cursu spectandum proponit, & de Abrahamo Spiritu gratiæ jam donato, fatente Vasquezio, negat, quod justificatus fuerit ex operi- bus. Adde, quod occasio disputationis Apostolicæ ea fuerit, quod nonnulli justitiam propriam erigere vellent, non autem Christum prorsus reproba- rent, vel gratiam Dei ad opera pietatis præstanda, aut ad remissionem peccatorum consequendam ne- cessariam esse inficiarentur. Neque sanè dubium esse debet, quod recte Flacius in præfat. in hanc Epist. monuit, quin Paulus proponendo Abraha- mum in exemplum gratuitæ aut precariæ per Christum justificationis salutisque illam ipsam inanem Judæorum gloriationem de Patre Abraha- mo, qui suis præclarissimis virtutibus & meritis sibi & omnibus posteris justitiam & benedictio- nem consequutus sit, redarguere voluerit.

διὰ γὰρ νόμο ἐπίγνωσις ἁμαρτίας.

Ne quis putaret legem planè fuisse inutilem, ostendit ejus usum egregium, nempe quod notitiæ illæ actionum turpium, quas mali mores in Ægyptiaco maximè incolatu obliteraverant, manifesta voluntatis divinæ revelatione factæ sunt rursus conspicuæ. Natura aliquo modo indicat divinam voluntatem, at multò magis revelatio tot fulta miraculis. Vide infra VII. 9. Νόμο, ubi simpliciter à Pau- lo ponitur, legem Mosis significat, ut II. 12. 14. 23. 25. ἐπί- γνωσις idem quod γνῶσις, cognitio, aut paulò amplius, su- pra I. 28. infra X. 2. Eph. I. 17. IV. 13. Philip. I. 9. Coloss. I. 9. 10. II. 2. III. 10. 1. Tim. II. 4. 2. Tim. II. 25. III. 7. Tit. I. 5. & apud Petrum aliquoties, sic & ἐπιγινώσκειν est γινώσκειν Matth. VII. 16. 70. supra I. 32. & alibi.

Argumentum è superioribus succinctè alla- tum, ita habet: Si per legem agnitio solùm peccati est, atique per opera legis nemo justificari potest. At verum prius est, E. & posterius. Cum enim hacte- nus ostensum, quod tantum lex sub peccato con- cluserit, & vim peccati arguerit, quod nempe pec- catum condemnationem afferat. Per quam vero legem condemnamur omnes, quia omnes eam transgredimur, per ejus sanè observantiam justi- ficari nemo nostrum potest. Unde Pererius, Justi- nianus & Estius exclusivè interpretantur: per le- gem tantum est agnitio peccati. Atque hæc de ἐξεργασία Apostolicæ ejusdemque DIDACTI- CÆ sectione priori, nimirum quoad SUBJECTI πρόγνωσιν de homine justificando & salvando: qui secundum legem convincitur esse sub statu pecca- ti & condemnationis, ut παρασκευὴ fiat ad doctri- nam Evangelicam de vera consequenda justitica- tionis & salutis ratione. Succedit itaque

SECTIO II. MEDIORUM ET CAUSARUM JUSTIFICA- TIONIS ἔΚΘΕΣΙΝ EXHIBENS. MEMBRUM I. GENERALE.

PRopositæ normæ hujus doctrinæ, causarum ju-stificationis ἐξαρίθμηsin instituit Apostolus hoc Capite III. parte ejus reliqua. Tum ἀπόδειξιν adducit ex exemplo Abrahæ, & testimonio Da- vidico c. IV. Porro à posteriori vel consequenti pa- ce scilicet conscientiæ justificationem per fidem stabilit. Denique ἀντίθεsιν Adami & Christi ma- joris dilucidationis & confirmationis gratia pro- ponit cap. V. Quæ omnia facere ad ἐξήγηsιν ἀπο- δεικτικὴν Apostolicam, circa οἰκονομίαν Epistolæ observavimus: Quibus ita expeditis subjungit Apostolus ἐκδίκισιν hujusce doctrinæ Evangelicæ, inservientem itidem ulteriori ejusdem confirma- tioni per Cap. VI. VII. & VIII.

SUBJECTIO I. Doctrinæ veræ βεβαίωσιν sistens. ARTICULUS I. Argumentum è causarum salutis ratione cur ab- solvitur, juxta partitionem sub initium Cap. III. traditam.

CAPITIS TERTII PARS IV. JUSTITIÆ FIDEI ἔΝΘΕΙΣΙΣ.

## 3:21
Ver. 21. But now (νυνὶ δὲ χωρὶς νόμε δικαιοσύνη Θεῦ πεφανέρωται) that is, in our times, most happy in this respect, the justice of God, that is, that which is most pleasing to God, as having been brought to the highest degree, appears by great things, namely from the most innocent life of Christians, without the law, that is, even without the law, even in those who are from the Gentiles, with no condition of that law intervening, who have been called and have obeyed the calling. It is clearly manifested (Πεφανέρωται נגלה), as in John III. 21, I Cor. IV. 11, and elsewhere. God alone indeed has the exact knowledge of the heart: But the perpetual tenor of the life of Christians of the Apostolic age, and their patience in evils, was such that it was not credible that these proceeded from anywhere else than from a cleansed heart; the gifts of the spirit were also added.

being witnessed by the law and the Prophets) in those oracles of which he spoke above in 2. You have the same sense above in I. 2, the word to witness (μαρτυρεῖν) with the same meaning in Acts X. 43, Hebrews VII. 8; concerning the matter, see John V. 39, 46.

There has been hitherto, as we have said, the first part of the didactic treatment concerning justification: dispatched primarily from the condition of the subject, and by way of negation (κατ’ ἄρσιν), through the removal of justification by the works of the law: now the Apostle proceeds to the other, about to execute the means and causes of justification and blessedness positively (κατὰ θέσιν): and while he undertakes this, he first insinuates the norm from which that doctrine is to be sought, and thus at the same time tacitly confirms again the thesis already exhibited in the proposition: For that norm is both proper, the Gospel, namely, in which he had said justice was manifested, Rom. I. 16, 17, which because it is opposed to the law, he now says manifests justice WITHOUT THE LAW, so that we may understand that the same is had from the Gospel alone, not partly from the law, partly from the Gospel: and also common, which is Holy Scripture, from which he says it is confirmed by the testimony of the law of Moses, or Mosaic Scripture in the Pentateuch, and of the Prophets, because by the name of Moses, or the law, and the Prophets, the entire writings of the O.T. are comprehended, Luke XVI. 29, c. XXIV. 27. But the Grotian perversity is to be detested: But now, that is, in our times, most happy in this respect, the justice of GOD, that is, that which is most pleasing to God, as having been brought to the highest degree, appears by great things, namely from the most innocent life of Christians, without the law, that is, even in those who are from the Gentiles, with no condition of that law intervening, who have been called and have obeyed the calling. Who ever, from the age of the Apostles, has heard such a gloss spoken of, or to whom did a sense of this kind come into mind, even through a fever? For here, with respect to the justice consisting before God, the time of the Apostolic age is being compared with the time of the Patriarchs and Prophets, so that the Apostle has attributed a more eminent degree and perfection of the justice which is imputed to us before the judgment of God to the men of his own time, over Abraham and other Patriarchs, and has made a judgment concerning a greater degree and perfection of Evangelical justice from the most innocent life of Christians, who have been called without any condition of the law. The Apostle certainly acknowledges no distinction (διαστολὴν) of times or nations regarding justification, nor does he attribute that justice, by which we solely consist before God, any less to the Patriarchs and Prophets and other believers in the Old Testament than to Christians, and he declares that it receives testimony from the law or the writings of Moses, and from the Prophets; furthermore, no difference of degrees has a place in that justice of faith: for since we are all justified by the OBEDIENCE OF THE ONE Christ, how can a difference of degrees, or a greater and lesser, be found or assigned in that obedience of one? Which certainly is always consistent with itself, and is never not most perfect, and most absolute in all degrees. Such as is also entirely required, if it is to consist and avail before God. And where does the Apostle have even a word about the innocence of the Christians of the first times of the New Testament? Where did he say that the justice of God appears from their life, or did he hint at it by the slightest indication? And what of that 'without the law' (χωρὶς νόμε) regarding their calling, that they were called with no condition of the law intervening? The entire context (συνέχεια) teaches that the Apostle is not here treating of the calling, but of justification; not of the Christians of the first times, but of any who are to be justified, without difference of times. But as he perverts the nature of justification, so Grotius completely perverts the proper Apostolic seat of this doctrine, clearer than the sun: defining justification, which the Apostle teaches is apprehended through faith, the obedience and justice of Christ, by the purification of the heart, and while he erects a proper justice with the Jews, he overturns the justice of Christ. Justification, according to the Apostle, is certainly one thing, situated in the non-imputation or remission of iniquities, and the imputation of justice or the obedience of Christ: the purification of the heart is another: which is a consequence of justification, and is rashly and sophistically confused with justification itself. The law is certainly the norm of the purity of the heart and of holiness: But this justice and justification, which the Apostle defines, does not have the law as its norm, but the Gospel, insofar as it is opposed to the law, and is manifested WITHOUT THE LAW, as the Apostle testifies. Purity of heart is ours subjectively: the righteousness, of which the Apostle speaks here, is not ours, but GOD’S, namely that of Christ, who is GOD blessed above all things forever, according to the Spirit, and the same according to the Fathers according to the flesh, that is, He is true God and true man, Rom. IX. 5. who for this reason is called Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 5. Which righteousness, or obedience, of the God-man Christ is indeed ascribed to us, so that we may be constituted righteous and justified before the tribunal of GOD, Rom. V. 19. But it is ours only imputatively, not subjectively: through the reception of faith, not through formal inherence. For the righteousness of GOD is now manifested, says the Apostle v. 21. the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, or into Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe. That νυνὶ now is not necessarily taken χρονικῶς or regarding time, but can be understood ἀντιθετικῶς, or even adversatively, as if to say. through the law is the manifestation, or recognition of sin. Contrariwise, or rather, but without the law that righteousness of God has been manifested, by which we are constituted righteous. It does not have the law as a norm, nor as a principle of knowing: but without the law πεφανέρωῒαι, If however the signification of time is admitted, the discourse will be about the degree of manifestation, not of righteousness: namely, not a greater degree of righteousness, but a greater light of the manifestation of the righteousness, which is THE SAME: and invariable, consisting in an indivisible, admitting of more and less in no way, since it is most absolute and most perfect in all numbers, parts, and degrees, thus the Apostle will indicate, in the time of the N. T. than was the light of the manifestation of the Same in the time of the O. T.

Latin:

Vers. 21. νυνὶ δὲ χωρὶς νόμε δικαιοσύνη Θεῦ πεφανέρωται) Nunc vero, id est, nostris temporibus hac in parte felicissi- mis, justitia Dei, id est, ea, quæ Deo summe placet, utpote ad summum perducta gradum, apparet rebus magnis, ex vita scil. innocentissima Christianorum, sine lege, id est, etiam sine lege, etiam in ill s, qui ex gentibus, nulla inter- cedente legis illius conditione, vocati sunt, & vocationi obtemperarunt. Πεφανέρωται נגלה clarè patesit, ut Jo- hann. III. 21. I. Cor. IV. 11. & alibi. Cordis quidem ex- actam notitiam solus habet Deus: Sed Christianorum Apostolicæ ætatis perpetuus vitæ tenor, ac malorum pa- tientia talis erat, ut non credibile esset hæc aliunde quàm ex mundato corde proficisci, accedebant & spiritus dona.

μαρτυρομένη ὑπὸ τῦ νόμε καὶ τῶν Προφητῶν) in illis ora- culis, de quibus locutus est supra 2. Idem sensus supra I. 2. verbum μαρτυρεῖν eodem significatu habes Act. X. 43. Hebr. VII. 8. de re vide Joh. V. 39. 46.

Fuit hactenùs, uti diximus, prima tractationis didacticæ de justificatione pars: à subjecti potissi- mum conditione, & κατ’ ἄρσιν, per remotionem ju- stificationis per opera legis, expedita: jam ad alte- ram procedit Apostolus, media & causas justifica- tionis & beatitudinis κατὰ θέσιν positivè exsequu- turus: quod dum aggreditur, normam prius insi- nuat, unde ea doctrina petenda sit, atque ita simul iterum tacitè thesin in propositione jam exhibitam confirmat: Ea enim norma est tum propria, Evan- gelium, nempe in quo manifestatam justitiam dixe- rat, Rom. I. 16. 17. quod quia legi opponitur, jam χωρὶς νόμε SINE LEGE manifestare justitiam di- cit, ut è solo Evangelio eandem haberi intelliga- mus, non partim ex lege, partim ex Evangelio: tùm communis, quæ est Scriptura S. unde testimonio eam confirmatam dicit legis Mofis, seu Scripturæ Mo- saicæ in Pentateucho, & Prophetarum, quia no- mine Mofis, vel legis, & Prophetarum universa scripta V. T. comprehenduntur, Luc. XVI. 29. c. XXIV. 27. Detestanda autem sφεκότης est Gro- tiana: Nunc verò, id est, nostris temporibus, hac in parte felicissimis, justitia DEI, id est, ea, quæ Deo summè placet, utpote ad summum perducta gra- dum, apparet rebus magnis, ex vita sc. innocentissi- ma Christianorum, sine lege, td est, etiam in illis, qui ex gentibus, nulla intercedente legis illius condi- tione, vocati sunt, & vocationi obtemperarunt. Quis unquam inde ab Apostolorum ætate fando talem audivit glossam, aut cui sensus ejusmodi vel per febrim in mentem venit? Comparari nempe hic respectu justitiæ coram Deo consistentis tem- pus ætatis Apostolicæ, cum Patriarcharum & Pro- phetarum tempore, ita ut justitiæ, quæ nobis coram Dei judicio imputatur, gradum eminentiorem & perfectionem tribuerit Apostolus hominibus sui temporis, præ Abrahamo, & aliis Patriarchis, & de majori gradu & perfectione justitiæ Evangelicæ ex vita innocentissima Christianorum judicium fe- cerit, qui sine ulla legis conditione vocati sint. Nullam utique Apostolus sive temporum, sive na- tionum, qua justificationem, agnoscit διαστολὴν, nec minus Patriarchis, & Prophetis, aliisque fide- libus in Vet. Test. tribuit eam justitiam, quà unicè coram Deo consistimus,quàm Christianis,eamque testimonium accipere à lege vel scriptis Mosis,& à Prophetis, perhibet, nulla adhæc graduum differen- tia in ista justitia fidei locum habet: quum enim justificemur omnes OBEDIENTIA UNIUS Christi, quomodo in illa unius obedientia gra- duum differentia, aut majus & minus inveniri vel assignari potest? quæ utique sibi semper constat, & nunquam non est perfectissima, omnibusque gra- dibus absolutissima. Qualis etiam omninò requi- ritur, si coram Deo consistere,ac valere debeat. Et ubi vel verbulum habet Apostolus de innocentia Christianorum primorum temporum Novi Testa- menti? ubi apparere justitiam Dei ex vita ipsorum dixit,aut minimo indicio saltem innuit? Et quid il- la χωρὶς νόμε ad vocationem eorum,quòd nulla in- tercedente legis conditione vocati sint? non utiq; hic de vocatione, sed de justificatione, non de Christia- nis primorum temporum,sed de quibusvis justifican- dis,sine differentia temporum,tractare Apostolum tota συνέχεια docet. Ut autem justificationis natu- ram, ita sedem hujus doctrinæ propriam Apostoli- cam locum præsentem sole clariorem prorsus per- vertit Grotius: justificationem, quam per fidem, obedientiam & justitiam Christi apprehendentẽ, fieri docet Apostolus, per cordis purificationem de- finiens, ac cum Judæis propriam erigens justitiam, Christi verò justitiam evertens.Aliud certè est ju- stificatio, secundum Apostolum, in non-imputatio- ne, vel remissione iniquitatum, & imputatione justi- tiæ, vel obedientia Christi sita: aliud cordis purifica- tio: quæ justificationis consequens est, temereq; ac sophistice cum justificatione ipsa confunditur. Munditiei cordis, & sanctitatis norma utique lex est: At hæc justitia, & justificatio, quam Apostolus definit, non legem pro norma habet, sed Evange- lium, quatenus id legi opponitur, & SINE LEGE manifestatur, teste Apostolo. Cordis mundities nostra est subjectivè: justitia,de qua hic Apostolus est, non nostra, sed DEI, Christi nempe, qui DEUS est super omnia benedictus in secula, quoad Spiritum, idemque ex Patribus secundum carnem, hoc est, Verus Deus, & verus homo est, Rom.IX.5. qui ob id dicitur Jehovah justitia nostra, Jer.XXIII. 5. Quæ Christi θεανθρώπε justitia, vel obedientia nobis quidem etiam adscribitur, ut eadem justi constituamur, ac justificemur, coram tribunali DEI. Rom. V. 19. Sed nostra est imputativè tan- tùm, non subjectivè: per fidei acceptionem, non per formalem inhæsionem. Justitia enim DEI nunc manifestatur, inquit Apostolus v. 21. justitia Dei per fidem Jesu Christi, vel in Jesum Christum, in omnes, & super omnes credentes. Illud νυνὶ nunc non necessariò χρονικῶς vel de tempore accipitur, sed intelligi potest ἀντιθετικῶς,vel etiã adversativè,q.d. per legem manifestatio est, vel agnitio peccati. Con- trà verd, vel, ast sine lege manifestata est justitia illa Dei, quâ nos justi constituimur. Ea non pro normâ, neque pro cognoscendi principio legem habet: sed sine lege πεφανέρωῒαι, Si tamen temporis signifi- catio admittatur, de manifestationis, non de justitia gradu sermo erit: nimirum non majorem justitia gradum, sed lucem majorem manifestationis justitia, quæ EADEM est: & invariabilis, in indivisibili consistens, magis, ac minús nullatenus admittens, quippe omnibus numeris, partibus, & gradibus absolutissima, ac perfectissima, ita indicabit Apo- stolus, tempore N. T. quàm fuerit lux manifesta- tionis Ejusdem V. T. tempore.

## 3:22
v. 22. Righteousness of God) a repetition. Through faith of Jesus Christ.

He shows from where that piety was born, namely from faith in Jesus Christ, i.e., in his truly heavenly promises, before which all things that are of this life and life itself are counted as nothing, which is a shortcut for extirpating all vices. Faith of Jesus Christ for in Jesus Christ. Thus faith of God Mark XI. 22. Faith of the name of Jesus, Acts III. 16. Faith of the son of God Gal. II. 20. Namely, the possessive case also designates the efficient cause and the Object or matter, about which it is. In the manuscript it is clearer: Through faith in Christ Jesus. There was also faith in the ancient Patriarchs, but not that which is now required, in Jesus as Christ.

εἰς πάντας καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας τὺς πιτεύονῒας.

εἰς signifies that that righteousness is in believers, ἐπὶ also that it appears. Faith in Christ when it has reached its maturity, that is, has filled the heart, produces that admirable and to God most acceptable purity and preserves the same. All, that is, as well those born from the Gentiles as from the Jews. In some manuscripts, and that one which I often praise, it is only: εἰς πάντας τὺς πιτεύονῒας.

In the demonstration of his theme the Apostle proceeds in such a way that he simultaneously delivers an explanation of the true sentiment concerning the Righteousness manifested in the law and the Prophets, which embraces the nerves of the proofs in itself, because from the nature and character of all the causes of Justification it is made clear what he set out to prove, namely that man is not justified by works, or his own obedience or righteousness, but by the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ through faith. Which was also observed by Flacius in his gloss. From here indeed (annotat. to v. 21.) up to the end of this chapter is first the proposition, and its exposition or explanation of righteousness through all causes, which it was necessary to do in this didactic genre, where the arduous things themselves had to be explained. The causes however are thus: I. The organic cause was premised on the part of God exhibiting this righteousness in the word with the O. T. Scriptures, for instance of Moses and the Prophets, then of the N. T. through the Apostles, who manifested it. Concerning which Chrysostom has it thus: He did not say, righteousness was given, but was manifested, removing the crime of novelty itself, for what has been manifested, is manifested as old and hidden. And not this alone, but what follows, show that this is not new: since where he said, it was manifested, he appended witnessed by the law and the prophets. Beware of troubling yourself, as if the thing itself temporal were new and foreign, for the law and the Prophets indeed already from the beginning foretold it. II. There follows the organic cause on our part receiving this righteousness of God offered in the word, which is faith. For the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ. III. The subject, which is indicated, when Righteousness is said to be into all and upon all who believe, into all and upon all believers. Which it proves both at once, or inculcates anew what was proved in the preceding: because, namely, there is no distinction: since all are both liable to sin, and destitute of the glory of God, and so are not otherwise than through faith in Christ, and by apprehending the righteousness of the God-man, righteous and are held before the tribunal of God. The subject therefore of Justification is man a sinner destitute of the glory of God, but who is from the faith of Christ; and so acknowledging his sins, and the lack of the glory of God, and seriously grieving, and by faith applying to himself the promise concerning the remission of sins through Christ. IV.

The efficient cause is marked as the principal one, as being the grace of God: because freely by his grace we are justified, by which pact again our merit and works are universally excluded; For if by grace, not by works, Rom. XI. 6. then the meritorious, which is insinuated partly by the word redemption made through Christ, with the most precious ransom intervening, which does not admit, but excludes our merits: For if justification could have been obtained by the merit of our obedience, what need would there have been for such a great ransom? If righteousness is through the law to be performed by us, Christ died in vain Gal. II. 22. partly by the type of the propitiatory or mercy-seat: because here Christ Jesus is the true mercy-seat, which God set forth for us through faith in his blood: which were shadowed forth in the O. T. when the Lord showed and manifested himself propitious with the blood of victims offered: so that to Christ, and to faith in Christ, both the most precious redemption from the evil of guilt and punishment, and the propitiation, and the obtaining of divine grace, reconciled to us by the blood of Christ, is to be ascribed solely. V. The Form of Justification, which is both the passing over or condonation of sins previously committed merely gratuitously, which does not happen except in and according to the mere tolerance and mercy of God: and the exhibition or showing of his righteousness, namely of Christ the God-man, while it is exhibited to us in the word, and is accepted by us through faith. VI. The final cause is the demonstration of the justice of God, namely that it may be clearly evident that He is just, who justifies anyone not without ἀπολυτρώσει (redemption) and propitiation, but has demonstrated His justice in this, that in His own Son, our sponsor, He punished the sins of the human race, and also His mercy, by which He justifies us not on account of our works or merits, but through faith in Jesus. By which reasoning the principal conclusion of the Apostle is again insinuated, and it is taught that the exhibition of the justice of Christ, with the remission of sins in this ἐνδείξει (demonstration) of divine justice and mercy in our justification, makes both sides, as they say, here, or to speak more correctly, formally completes the justification itself. Because the justice of God shines forth most of all from this, that sins, which as far as we are concerned are passed over or remitted ἐν ἀνοχῇ τῦ Θεῦ (in the forbearance of God), have been punished in Him as our Mediator: but it is of the divine mercy that, through faith in Jesus, that is, in His obedience both active and passive, when we make that same obedience our own and apply it to ourselves, He deigns to receive us into favor and pronounce us just. With these causes thus deduced and explained, it is concluded, as the Apostle had previously taught, by an invincible inference, both that no καύχησις (boasting) remains for us, not through the law of works, but through the law of faith itself v. 27, and that man is justified without the works of the law, by faith alone. The Apostle confirms this conclusion with an argument proposed by way of interrogation, v. 29, that God is not the God of the Jews only, to whom the law was solemnly given, but also of the Gentiles, who therefore proves Himself the same to all, justifying both the circumcision, or the Jews, and the uncircumcision, or the Gentiles, by the same reason, namely through faith, without any discrimination: and he adds a solution to the objection κατ’ ἀνθυποφορὰν (by way of counter-objection), by which the law might seem to have been given uselessly, and thus he teaches that not only is the law not abolished by this method of justification, but it is entirely established, because the law demands perfect obedience, which is only in Christ when apprehended by faith: so that the true method of justification is established on all sides, whether we look to the law or to the Gospel. And here is held at the same time an argument establishing the principal conclusion, from the absurd. For if man were justified by the works of the law, God would be the God of the Jews only, who alone receive the law, and not of the Gentiles. Which is absurd: since grace and blessing are promised to all peoples in Christ.

Now, that Grotius (v. 22) thinks the Apostle is showing whence that piety was born which shone forth in the life of Christians—namely, from faith in truly heavenly promises—is a Socinian and Arminian misinterpretation. Δικαιοσύνη Θεοῦ is not the piety of Christians, but the righteousness of Christ, God and man. It is not piety that is in believers and upon believers, which is rather of believers and follows faith; but the righteousness of God, which is said to be through faith in Jesus or into Jesus in believers and upon believers; because it is apprehended by them through faith, is imputed to them, and is their own. Faith held in truly heavenly promises, or ratification and συγκατάθεσις or assent, is not the proper and immediate cause of piety and a holy life. For do not many myriads of people apply faith to those things which Christ promised, who are neither devoted to true piety, nor shine with it in this world? And what more does faith in Jesus bring than that ratification of the promises of eternal life? Namely, the fiducial apprehension of the righteousness of God; because the righteousness of the God-man (Θεανθρώπου) was offered in the Gospel for this reason, that we might apprehend it by faith and make it our own. But then, if the promise of heavenly goods is sufficient for us to have true righteousness, what need was there for τῇ ἀπολυτρώσει or redemption, made by the expenditure of the precious blood of the Son of God? What necessity was there that God should set forth his Son as a propitiation (ἱλαστήριον) through faith in his blood, when without a ransom (λύτρῳ) and propitiation (ἱλασμῷ), that end could have been obtained by the promise of eternal life alone? Indeed, the Socinians act in such a way as to exclude the satisfaction of Christ here entirely, and to remove the propitiation of God made through Christ: in which, however, Grotius ought not to have yielded to them; since by that reasoning the very redemption (ἀπολύτρωσις) of Christ is overturned, as well as the proper force of the word propitiation (ἱλαστήριον), which Grotius himself once demonstrated against them in his Fidei Catholicae de Satisfact. Christi. Concerning which, let our Profligated Socinianism be compared, and what is said about these things in the Roman Apostolic Theology at this place. The Apostle does not teach what fruits faith in Christ produces in us, which follow justification, but how faith in Christ is the cause of justification; because, namely, righteousness comes not our own, but God's, into us and upon us, as we believe, through faith in Jesus—that is, when we apprehend Jesus and his righteousness by faith, by whose obedience and righteousness alone we are constituted righteous, Rom. V. 19. That εἰς πάντας [unto all] is not so much to be in believers subjectively, as it is to be given to believers through faith, and applied to them, so that it happens to believers, or redounds to all who believe, which is not done by way of communication (μεταδοτικῶς) or by way of transition (μεταβατικῶς), transfusively or transitively, but by way of reckoning (λογιστικῶς), imputatively, because it is transcribed and accounted to them in the judgment of God. There is added κ͵ ἐπὶ πάντας, and upon all: which is not added in vain; for it is noted that believers are covered by it as if by a shield against the lightning of the law, and are fortified against the heat of divine wrath, so that they are safe everywhere in the judgment of God. For Christ wishes to cover believers with his righteousness, as with a certain garment and tunic of salvation (Isa. LXI, Zech. III), and wishes to protect and fortify them with it as a shield (Gen. XV).

ἐ γάρ ἐστι διαστολὴ [for there is no distinction]) in this matter there is no difference; he thus explains what he had briefly said before: Τί ὖν προεχόμεθα; ϰ᾿απάντως [What then? are we better than they?] above in chapter 9, where see the remarks. Διαστέλλειν corresponds to the Hebrew בּדל [to distinguish].

Latin:

v. 22. Δικαιοσύνη δὲ Θεᾶ) ἐπαναφορά. Διὰ πίσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

Ostendit, unde illa pietas nata sit, nempè ex fide in Je- sum Christum, i. e. in promissa ejus vere cœlestia, præ quibus omnia, quę hujus vitæ sunt & vita ipsa nihili ducuntur, quod compendiũ est ad vitia omnia exscindenda. Fides Jesu Christi pro in Jesum Christum. Sic fides Dei Marci XI. 22. Fides no- minis Jesu, Act. III. 16. Fides filii Dei Gal. II. 20. Nempè ca- sus possessivus etiam efficientem causam & Objectum sive materiam, circa quam designat. In manuscripto planiùs est: Διὰ πίσεως ἐν Χρισῲ Ἰησοῦ. Fuit & in veteribus Patriarchis fides, sed non ea, quæ nunc requiritur, in Jesum ut Christum.

εἰς πάντας καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας τὺς πιτεύονῒας.

εἰς significat justitiam illam esse in credentibus, ἐπὶ etiam apparere. Fides in Christum ubi ad maturitatem suam per- venit, id est, cor implevit, parit illam admirabilem, Deoque acceptissimam puritatem eamdemque conservat. Omnes, id est, tàm ex gentibus natos, quàm ex Judæis. In manuscri- ptis nonnullis, & illo, quem sæpè laudo, est tantum: εἰς πάντας τὺς πιτεύονῒας.

In demonstratione thematis sui Apostolus ita pro- cedit, ut explicationem simul sententiæ veræ de Ju- stitiâ in lege & Prophetis manifestatâ, tradat, quæ nervos probationũ in se complectitur, quòd e cau- sarum omniũ Justificationis naturâ & indole id dis- palescat, quod probare instituit, hominem scilicet non justificari per opera, vel propriam obedientiã seu justitiam, sed per apprehensionem justitiæ Christi per fidem. Quod Flacio etiam observatum in glossâ. Hinc verò (annotat. ad v. 21.) usque ad finem capitis hujus est primum propositio, & ejus expositio aut ex- plicatio justitiæ per omnes causas, quod necesse fuit facere in hoc didascalico genere, ubi res ipsæ arduæ explicandæ fuerunt. Causæ autem ita habent: I. Præ- missa fuit causa organica ex parte Dei exhibẽtis hãc justitiam in verbo cùm V. T. Scriptis, puta Mosis & Prophetarũ, tum N. T. per Apostolos, qui eam ma- nifestàrunt. De quo Chrysost. ita habet: Non dixit, justitia data est, sed manifestata est, ipsum novitatis crimen amovens, nam quod manifestatum est, ut ve- tus & occultum manifestatur. Nec hoc solum, sed quæ sequuntur, ostendunt, hoc non esse novum: quippe ubi dixit, manifestata est, attexuit μαρτυρουμένη ὑπὸ τᾶ νόμου κὶ τῶ̃ν προφητῶν. Cave turbare, quasi res ipsa tẽ- poraria sit nova ac peregrina, eam n. tùm lex ac Pro- phetæ jam inde ab initio πρόελεγον prædixerunt. II. Sequitur causa organica ex parte nostri accipiens hanc justitiam Dei in verbo oblatam, quæ est fides. Justitia enim Dei per fidem in Jesum Christum. III. Subjectum, quod indicatur, cum Justitia dicitur esse εἰς πάνῒας κὶ ὑπὲρ πάνῒας τὺς πιτεύονῒας, in omnes & super omnes credentes. Quod utrumq; simul pro- bat, vel in antegressis probatũ denuo inculcat: quia sc. nulla est διαςολὴ: quum omnes & peccato sint ob- noxii, & gloria Dei destituti, adeoq; nonnisi per fidẽ in Christũ, & apprehendendo justitiam τᾶ θεανθρώπυ Dei hominis justi sint & habeantur coram tribunali Dei. Subjectum ergò Justificationis est homo pecca- tor gloriâ Dei destitutus, sed qui est ex fide Christi; adeoq; peccata sua, & carentiam gloriæ Dei agno- scens, serioq; dolens, & fide promissionẽ de remis- sione peccatorum perChristum sibi applicans. IV.

Causa efficiens signatur cũ principalis, utpote gratia Dei: quia δωρεὰν τῇ χάριτι αὐτῦ gratis gratia justifi- camur, quo pacto iterum meritũ nostrum & opera universim excluduntur; Si enim ex gratia, non ex operibus, Rom. XI. 6. tùm meritoria, quæ insinuatur partim voce ἀπολυτρώσεως redemptionis per Chri- stũ factæ, interveniente λύτρῳ pretiosissimo, quod non coadmittit, sed excludit nostra merita: Si enim nostræ obedientiæ merito justificatio obtineri po- tuisset, quid tanto λύτρῳ opus fuisset? Si per legem à nobis præstandam justitia, gratis mortuus est Chri- stus Gal. II. 22. partim typo ἱλαστηρία seu propitiato- rii: quia hic verũ est propitiatorium Christus Jesus, quod proposuit nobis Deus per fidẽ in sanguine ipsius: quæ adumbrata fuere in V. T. cum propitiũ se præ- buit & ostendit Dominus oblato victimarum san- guine: ut ita Christo, & fidei in Christum, & redemptio à malo culpæ ac pœnæ pretiosissima, & propitiatio, ac impetratio divinæ gratiæ, sanguine Christi nobis conciliata, adscribenda unice sit. V. Forma Justifi- cationis, quæ est tùm πάρεσις transmissio vel condo- natio peccatorum anteà commissorum merè gratui- tæ, quæ non fit nisi ἐν τῇ ἀνοχῇ τῦ Θεῦ, in & juxtà meram Dei tolerantiam, & misericordiam: tum ἔν- δειξις vel exhibitio justitiæ ejus, Christi nempè θεαν- θρώπε, dum ea nobis in verbo exhibetur, & à no- bis per fidẽ acceptatur. VI. Causa finalis est demon- stratio justitiæ Dei, ut nempè palam constet, ipsum justum esse, qui non sine ἀπολυτρώσει & propitia- tione justificat quenquam, sed justitiam suam in eo demonstravit, quod in ipso Filio suo; sponsore no- stro, peccata humani generis punivit, nec non mi- sericordia ejus, quà justificat nos non propter opera vel merita nostra, sed per fidem in Jesum. Quâ ratio- ne denuo conclusio principalis Apostoli insinuatur, & exhibitionem Justitiæ Christi, cum remissione pec- catorum in hac ἐνδείξει divinæ Justitiæ ac Misericor- diæ in nostri Justificatione, utramque, quod ajant, paginam hic facere, vel ut rectiùs dicam, ipsam Ju- stificationem formaliter absolvere, docetur. Quia justitia Dei pellucet inde maximè, quod peccata, quæ quoad nos ἐν ἀνοχῇ τῦ Θεῦ transmittuntur vel remittuntur, in ipso ceu Mediatore nostro punita sint: misericordia verò divinæ est, quod per fidem in Jesum, h. e. in obedientiam ejus tùm activam tùm passivam, cum eandem nostram facimus, nobísque applicamus, nos in gratiam recipere, & justos pro- nunciare dignatur. Quibus causis ita deductis, & expositis, concluditur, quod Apostolus anteà do- cuerat, per illationẽ invictam, tùm quod nulla no- bis supersit καύχησις, non per legem operũ, sed per ipsam fidei legem v. 27. tùm quod homo justificetur sine legis operibus, per solam fidem. Quam conclusio- nem firmat Apostolus argumento per Interroga- tionem proposito, v. 29. quod Deus non sit Judæorum tantùm Deus, quibus lex solenniter lata, sed etiam gentium, qui proinde omnibus eundem se probat, justificans & circumcisionem, seu Judæos, & præpu- tium, seu gentes eàdem ratione, per fidẽ nempe, sine ullo discrimine: additque solutionem objectionis κατ’ ἀνθυποφορὰν, quâ ita videatur lex inutiliter da- ta, adeoque docet, non modò legẽ non tolli hâc justi- ficandi ratione, sed stabiliri omninò, quia perfectam obedientiam exigit lex, quæ nonnisi in Christo est fide apprehenso: ut ita undiquaque vera justifica- tionis ratio astruatur, seu legem respiciamus, seu Evangelium. Et habetur hic simul argumentum conclusionem principalem stabiliens, ab absurdo. Si enim ex legis operibus justificaretur homo, Deus Ju- dæorum tantùm Deus esset, qui soli legem accipiunt, non gentium. Quod absurdum: siquidem omnibus populis gratia & benedictio promissa in Christo sit.

Jam quod Grotius v. 22. Apostolum ostendere putat, unde illa pietas nata sit, quæ in vita Christiano- rum effulsit, nimirum ex fide promissorum verè cœ- lestium, ψευδερμηνεία est Sociniana & Arminiana. Δικαιοσύνη Θεꭢ non est pietas Christianorũ, sed Ju- stitia Christi Dei & hominis. Non pietas est in cre- dentes & super credentes, quæ credentiũ potius est, & fidem sequitur: Justitia autem Dei, quæ est per fi- dem Jesu vel in Jesum in credentes, & super credentes esse dicitur; quia per fidem ab ipsis apprehenditur, illis imputatur, eorumq; propria sit. Fides promif- sionibus verè cœlestibus habita, seu ratihabitio & συγϰατάθεσις vel assensus non est causa propria & immediata pietatis, & vitæ sanctæ. Annon enim multæ myriades hominum fidem adhibent iis, quæ promisit Christus, qui neo veræ pietati dediti sunt, nec eâ in hoc mundo coruscant? Et amplius quid fides Jesu infert, quàm illam promissionum vitæ æ- ternæ ratihabitionem: nimirum fiducialem appre- hensionem justitiæ Dei; quia ideò in Evangelio Ju- stitia Θεανθρώπꭢ oblata est, ut fide eam apprehen- damus & nostram faciamus. Tum verò si promissio bonorum cœlestium sufficit ad id, ut justitiam veram habeamus, quid opus fuit τῇ ἀπολυτρώσει vel rede- ptione, impendio pretiosi sanguinis Filii Dei factâ? quid necessum fuit, ut Deus filium suum ἱλαστήριον proponeret per fidem in sanguine ipsius, quum sine λύτρῳ, & ἱλασμῷ, sola promissione vitæ æternæ fi- nis ille obtineri potuerit? Nimirum id agunt Soci- niani, ut Satisfactionem Christi hîc penitus exclu- dant, & propitiationem Dei per Christum factam re- moveant: in quo verò non debebat ipsis pollicem premere Grotius: quùm ea ratione evertatur ipsa ἀπολύτρωσις Christi, & vis propria vocis ἱλαστηρίꭢ, quod adversus eosdem demonstravit olim Gro- tius ipse in Fidei Catholic. de Satisfact. Christi ad- fert. quo de conferatur Socinismus noster profli- gatus, & quæ de his in Theologia Apostolica Romana ad h. l. Non quos in nobis pariat fides in Christum fructus, qui consequuntur Justificationem, sed quo- modo fides in Christum Justificationis causa sit, do- cet Apostolus; quia nimirum justitia non nostra, sed Dei in nos & super nos, qua credimus, venit, per fidem in Jesum, h. e. cum Jesum, ejusque Justitiam fide apprehendimus, cujus solius obedientia & ju- stitia justi constituimur, Rom. V. 19. Illud εἰς πάντας, non tàm in credentibus esse subjectivè, quàm crede- tibus per fidem donari, iisq; applicari, ut contingat credentibus, vel redundet in omnes, qui credunt, quod nõ fit μεταδοτικῶς, ἢ μεταβατικῶς, transfusivè vel transitivè, sed λογιστικῶς, imputativè, quia iis transcribitur & accensetur in judicio Dei; Additur κ͵ ἐπὶ πάντας, & super omnes: quod non frustrà ad- jectum; notatur enim, quod tegantur ea credentes veluti clypeo, adversus fulmen legis, & muniantur adversus æstum iræ divinæ, ut undiquaque in judi- cio Dei eadem tuti sint. Vult enim Christus justitia sua operire credentes, ceu vestimento quodam & tunicâ salutis Es. LXI. Zach. III. Gal. III. vult eos illa ceu scuto protegere ac munire Gen. XV.

ἐ γάρ ἐστι διαστολὴ) in hac re nullum est discrimen, sic ex- plicat, quod ante breviter dixerat: Τί ὖν προεχόμεθα; ϰ᾿απάντως supra 9. ubi dicta vide. Διαστέλλειν respondet Hebræo בּדל discernere.

## 3:23
v. 23. Πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον [For all have sinned].

It is not a wonder that God does not distinguish the Gentiles from the Jews in this matter, since all, that is, both those kinds of men, were held by the most grievous sins; thus we have had ἁμαρτάνειν [to sin] often.

The Apostle is not dealing with the special and more grievous sins of the Jews and Gentiles of a certain time, but with all men commonly, without distinction of ages and times in general, teaching that all men, without any exception, are guilty of sin, nor is ἁμαρτάνειν [to sin] taken otherwise, or only concerning more grievous sins, in Rom. II. 12; concerning the passages of John, see in their place. That word is general, just as ἁμαρτία [sin] also denotes sin generally: when one wanders or deflects from the scope or line of the divine law, 1 John III. 4; just as in Isocrates it is ἁμαρτάνειν τῆς ὁδοῦ, to wander from the way, and among Greek writers it is taken for to err, to be mistaken, to hallucinate, to do wrong, to sin in general, nor is it to be explained otherwise in the Scriptures, unless where a special determination in the text teaches it. And when the Apostle universally concludes all men under sin, to show that all are in need of the grace of God, the redemption of Christ, and the gratuitous remission of sins, how can this word be restricted only to more grievous sins in the present? Compare John III. 6, Rom. V. 12.

Καὶ ὑστερῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ [And fall short of the glory of God]. Therefore much is lacking to them, whereby they might be approved by GOD; ὑστερεῖσθαι [to fall short] is to have less than something (1 Cor. I. 7, XII. 24, 2 Cor. XI. 5, XII. 11, Heb. IV. 1). δόξα Θεοῦ [glory of God] is the approval of a man which is from God, as in John XII. 44. See below IV. 2.

This explanation could indeed be admitted if it is understood that all men generally have less, and that they lack what they ought to have: because they cannot be approved and pleasing to God for the reason that they are destitute of that perfection which God had conferred upon them in creation in his own image. But since ὑστερεῖσθαι [to fall short] is to be destitute, and δόξα Θεοῦ [glory of God] denotes the glory of God rather than the approval of a man by God, and δόξα Θεοῦ does not occur in chapter IV. 2, but rather καύχημα πρὸς τὸν Θεόν [boasting before God], the common explanation of the interpreters is not to be abandoned: especially because that privation and lack of the glory of God pertains most of all to the description of the state of man before justification, and here no respect is had to divine approval, but the defect of that glory which man had received from God is designated: whence it is gathered that the privation of the divine image is noted, which we all lack after the fall. For this was the glory granted to man by God in creation: and we are all destitute of it, after we lost the same in Adam, the consequence of which is that we cannot stand before God. ὑστερέω means I lack, Matt. XIX. 20, Mark X. 21, Luke XXII. 36; I am destitute, John II. 3, Heb. IV. 1, ch. XI. 37; I am needy, I am in want, Luke XV. 24, 1 Cor. VIII. 8, ch. XII. 24, Phil. IV. 12; just as ὑσέρημα is penury, Luke XXI. 4. That glory, of which we have been destitute through the fall, is restored to us through Christ. But concerning this, 1 Cor. III. 18, 1 Cor. XV. 43, Heb. II. 19, 1 Pet. I. 7, ch. V. 1. If, however, from a comparison of the passage Rom. IV. 2, anyone prefers to understand glory before God in this place, with Chrysostom and the blessed Luther and the blessed Gerhard, he will be able to explain it in this way: that no man can boast before the judgment of God, which is a consequence of the former, because, to wit, all have sinned.

Latin:

v. 23. Πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον.

Non mirũ est, Deũ hac in re gentes ab Judæis non distin- guere, cum omnes, id est, utraq; illa hominum genera gravif- simis peccatis tenerentur; Sic ἁμαρτάνειν habuimus & sæpè.

Non de peccatis specialibus iisque gravioribus Judæorum & gentium certi temporis, sed de omnium communiter hominum sine discrimine ætatum, & temporum in genere agit Apostolus, docens, omnes homines citra ullius exceptionem peccati reos es- se, nec aliter, aut de peccatis tantùm gravioribus τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν Rom. II. 12. accipitur; De locis Johannis suo loco. Verbum istud generale est, quemadmo- dum etiam ἁμαρτία generaliter peccatum notat: Cùm à scopo vel lineâ legis divinæ aberratur, vel deflectitur, 1. Joh. III. 4. uti apud Isocratẽ est ἁμαρ- τάνειν τῆς ὁδῶ, aberrare à viâ, & apud Græcos scri- ptores pro errare, falli, hallucinari, delinquere, pec- care in genere accipitur, nec aliter in Scripturis ex- plicandũ est, nisi ubi specialis determinatio in textu id docet. Et quum Apostolus universaliter omnes homines sub peccato concludat, ut ostendat, omnes indigere Dei gratiâ, redemptione Christi, ac gratuitâ remissione peccatorum, quomodo hoc verbum tantùm ad peccata graviora in præsenti restringi potest? Cons. Joh. III. 6. Rom. V. 12.

Καὶ ὑστερῦνται τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ. Ideò multum illis deest, quo minùs à DEO approben- tur, ὑστερεῖσθαι est minus aliquo habere 1. Cor. I. 7. XII. 24. 2. Cor. XI. 5. XII. 11. Heb. IV. 1. δόξα Θεῦ est approbatio hominis, quæ sit à Deo, ut Joh. XII. 44. Vide infra IV. 2.

Admitti quidem posset hæc explicatio, si gene- raliter omnes homines minus habere, iisqυe id deef- se, quod habere debebant, intelligatur: quia ideò Deo probari & placere non possunt, quia eâ desti- tuti sunt perfectione, quam Deus ipsis in creatione ad imaginem suam contulerat; Sed cum ὑστερεῖσ- θαι sit destitui, & δόξα Θεῦ gloriam Dei potiùs no- tet, quàm approbationem hominis à Deo, neq; c. IV. 2. δόξα Θεῦ occurrat, sed καύχημα πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, comūnis Interpp. explicatio deserẽda non est: im- primis quia privatio illa & carentia gloriæ Dei ad descriptionem statûs hominis ante justificationem maximè facit, nequè hîc respectus habetur ad ap- probationem divinam, sed defectus designatur ejus gloriæ, quam à Deo acceperat homo: unde priva- tione imaginis divinæ notari colligitur, quâ omnes caremus post lapsum. Hæc n. erat gloria homini à Deo cōcessa in creatione: & eâ destituimur omnes, postquam eandem in Adamo amisimus, cujus con- sequens est, quod consistere coram Deo nequea- mus. ὑστερέω est deficio Matth. XIX. 20. Marc. X. 21. Luc. XXII. 36. careo, destituor Joh. II. 3. Ebr. IV. 1. c. XI. 37. inops sum, egeo, Luc. XV. 24. 1. Cor. IIX. 8. c. XII. 24. Phil. IV. 12. uti ὑσέρημα est penuria. Luc. XXI. 4. Illa gloria, quâ per lapsum destituti sumus, per Christum nobis restituitur. De hâc verò 1. Cor. III. 18. 1. Cor. XV. 43. Ebr. II. 19. 1. Pet. I. 7. c. V. 1. Si tamen è collatione loci Rom. IV. 2. gloria apud Deũ intelligere quis hoc loco malit, cum Chrysost. & B. Luth. ac B. Gerhardo explicare poterit h. m. nemi- nem hominũ coram Dei judicio gloriari posse, quod consequens prioris est, quia scil. omnes peccârunt.

## 3:24
V. 24. being justified freely. But they are led to righteousness, even without the labor which is usually required for lesser virtues, that is, philosophical ones. For faith makes a shortcut of that labor, as appeared in Paul, and in many converted from Paganism and suddenly snatched to martyrdom. חִנָּם is properly opposed to expense, but labor is also said to be expended and something to be bought with labor; Epicharmus: The gods sell us all good things for our labors. But also, among the Jews and the nations, cleansing sacrifices cost a great deal of money. The Apostle looks to the words of Isaiah LV. at the beginning. The words of Lactantius III, 26, serve for the right understanding of this passage: Give me a man who is irascible, unbridled, and I will render him as placid as a sheep with a very few words of God. Give me a greedy, avaricious, tenacious man: I will now make him liberal and giving away his money with full hands. Give me one who is fearful of pain and death: he will now despise the cross, and fires, and the bull of Phalaris. Give me a lustful, adulterous, gluttonous man; you will now see him sober, chaste, continent. Give me a cruel and bloodthirsty man; that fury will now be changed into true clemency. Give me an unjust, foolish, sinful man: he will immediately be both equitable and prudent and innocent; for by one washing all malice will be abolished. Such is the power of divine wisdom, that when infused into the breast of man, it expels folly, the mother of sins, in one single assault, to effect which there is no need of payment, no need of books, no need of night-studies. These things are done freely, easily, safely, provided the ears are open and the breast thirsts for wisdom.

No comparison is instituted between the righteousness of faith and philosophical virtues (of which no trace appears), nor can virtue of man be understood here by righteousness, to which one might be led either through much labor or through a shortcut: because Paul is dealing with the justification of a sinful man before the tribunal and judgment of God, not with how Christians are led to piety and virtue as befits them. Therefore, the passage from Lactantius, Book III, ch. 26, has no bearing here: 'Such is the power of divine wisdom that, once infused into the human heart, it expels the mother of sins, folly, in a single stroke.' Grotius rightly observes that חנם and δωρεὰν are properly opposed to expense, and that labor is also said to be expended, and that the words of Isaiah ch. 55 at the beginning are being looked to: and that it is opposed to sacrifices among the Jews (the sacrifices of the Gentiles have no bearing here, as they draw their origin from zeal without knowledge and diabolical illusion) because cathartic sacrifices cost a great deal of money; whereas, on the contrary, we do not expend anything, nor do we attain righteousness by our labors, but freely and out of mere grace on account of the merit of Christ, since we can bring no merits to justification, nor can we acquire it by any labor. Therefore, by this word, the heterodoxy of the Papists is excluded, by which they contend that a man prepares and disposes himself for justification: for δωρεὰν means freely and gratuitously, just as δῶρον is a gratuitous gift, which is given freely. It is evident from the usage of Scripture that this particle is opposed both to price (Gen. 29:15, Ex. 21:2, Num. 11:5, 2 Kings 24:24, Matt. 10:8, 2 Cor. 11:7, Rev. 22:17) and to merit or demerit (1 Sam. 19:5, 25:31, 1 Kings 2:31, Ez. 16:10, Sir. 29:8, 10, 2 Thess. 3:8). Regarding which, Ambrose in loc.: 'We are justified freely, that is, by the gift of God, doing nothing, nor rendering anything in return; that is, we neither deserve it by preceding works, nor compensate for it by subsequent ones.'

v. 24. 'by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.' Christ, through his obedience, especially in his death, and the prayers accompanying it, obtained this from the Father, that He would not abandon and harden the human race immersed in grievous sins, but would give them a way to arrive at righteousness through Christ. Is. 53:4. This very thing, just as it is called 'forgiving sins' (Luke 23:34), so also is 'redeeming' or 'making redemption' (Luke 1:68), גאל or פדה, that is, to liberate, namely from the necessity of dying in sins, by opening a way through which it might be permitted to exit them. He rightly ascribes this liberation to divine goodness, because it was of the goodness of God to give Christ to us. John 3:16, below 8:32. Add Eph. 1:7.

He rightly explains grace as divine goodness, which is to be noted against the Papists, who understand by it an infused habit of righteousness, which is repugnant both to the proper meaning of the word, because χάρις denotes grace, just as χαρίζεσθαι is to forgive out of grace (Luke 7:42, 2 Cor. 2:9, 12:13), and to the usage of Scripture, because nowhere is such an infused habit expressed by the word χάριτος, and to the Apostolic scope, which is to teach that we are justified freely and by grace through the sole redemption of Christ, apart from our virtues, our righteousness, and our works and merits, solely by faith apprehending the righteousness and merit of Christ: and to the synonym by which χάρις is explained, through the mercy of God (Eph. 2:4, Tit. 3:5, 1 Pet. 1:3), and to the opposite, because grace in similar passages is opposed to works (Rom. 11:6, Eph. 2:8) and to debt (Rom. 4:4, 5), whence Cardinal Pighius, Book V on free will, acknowledges that that signification of grace, which denotes some quality of our soul uncreated by God, is fictitious; and Biel (II Sent. dist. 26) confesses that grace is taken actively for the gracious will of God giving liberally to all freely, not out of debt; and after the anathema of the Council of Trent, the Jesuit Pererius (Disp. 13 in loc.) teaches that the gratuitous goodness and kindness of God toward man is denoted here by that word, since Paul opposes the grace of God to the works of men: Cf. in Theol. Apost. Rom. orac. 31. Moreover, it is not liberation that is ascribed here to the goodness of God (although it must entirely be attributed to divine grace), but justification; because it is not explained whence redemption arose, but what is the cause of justification; namely, that it must be credited to the grace of God, yet not to an absolute grace, but one founded in the merit of Christ, or which comes to us on account of the redemption of Christ; by which He redeemed us, through the intervention of the ransom of His obedience, both active and passive, and the shedding of His most precious blood, from the wrath of God, sin, the power of Satan, death, and hell (1 Tim. 2:6, 1 Pet. 1:18, which was demonstrated against the Socinians in the aforementioned oracle 32), and thus He merited for us grace and the remission of sins, having expiated the wrath of God and rendered satisfaction to divine justice for the sins of the whole human race. Therefore, He did not only obtain by His redemption that God should give us a way to arrive at righteousness, but by the price of His blood having been paid, He satisfied for us and thus liberated us from the wrath of God, and procured for us the grace of God; indeed, this very obedience of His even to the death of the cross is that obedience through which we are constituted righteous (Rom. 5:18). For He was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him (2 Cor. 5:21), and He was made by God righteousness for us (1 Cor. 1:30); He Himself is our righteousness (Jer. 23:6), and in Him is righteousness for us (Is. 45:23). Nor is it the same thing to give a way to righteousness and to forgive sins; nor did Christ redeem us only by opening a way through which it might be permitted to exit the necessity of dying; nor, finally, do the words פדה and גאל import only that, but that by His death He satisfied for us and redeemed us from sin and death: just as was shown in the refutation of Socinianism, and proven by Grotius himself in his assertion of the faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ against Socinus.

Latin:

V. 24. δικαιώμενοι δωρεάν. Ad justitiam verò perducuntur, etiam sine labore, qui ad minores virtutes, id est, philosophicas requiri solet. Fides n. ejus laboris compendium facit, ut in Paulo apparuit, & in multis ex Paganismo conversis subitóq; raptis ad martyriũ. חִנָּם propriè opponitur impensæ, sed & labor impendi di- citur & emi aliquid labore; Epicharmus: τῶν πόνων πωλῦσιν ἡμῖν πάντα τ'ἀγαθ' οἱ Θεόι. Sed & magna pecunia constabant apud Judæos & gentes Sa- crificia καθαρτικά. Respicit Apostolus ad verba Esaiæ LV. in principio. Serviunt huic loco recte intelligendo verba Lactantii III, 26. Da mihi virum, qui sit iracundus, effrænatus, paucif- simis Dei verbis tam placidum quam ovem reddam. Da cupidum, ava- rum, tenacem: jam tibi eum liberalem dabo, & pecuniam suam plenis ma- nibus largientem. Da timidum doloris ac mortis: jam crucem, & ignes, & Phalaridis taurum contemnet. Da libidinofum, adulterum, ganeonem, jam sobrium, castum, continentem videbis. Da crudelem & sanguinis appe- tentem; jam in veram clementiam furor ille mutabitur. Da injustum, insipientem, peccatorem : continuò & æquus & prudens & innocens erit; uno enim lavacro malitia omnis abolebitur. Tanta divina sapientiæ vis est, ut in hominis pectus infusa matrem delictorum stultitiam uno semel impetu expellat, ad quod efficiendum non mercede, non libris, non luci- brationibus opus est. Gratis ista fiunt, facile, tutò, modo pateant aures, & pectus sapientiam sitiat.

Non instituitur comparatio justitiæ fidei cum virtutibus philosophicis, (quâ de nullum vestigium apparet) nequè per justitiam virtus hominis intel- ligi hic potest, ad quam sivē per labòrem multum, sive per compendium perducatur: quia de Justi- ficatione hominis peccatoris coram tribunali & judicio Dei agit Paulus, non quomodo ad pietatem & virtutem perducatur Christianos decentem. Nihil ergò huc facit locus Lactantii l. III. c. 26. Tanta sapientia divina vis est, ut in hominis pectus infusa matrem delictorum stultitiam uno semel im- petu expellat. Rectè autem observat Grotius חנם & δωρεὰν propriè opponi impensae, & laborem impen- di quoque dici, ac respici verba Es. c.LV. in prin- cipio: & opponi illud sacrificiis apud Judæos (gen- tium sacrificia nihil hùc faciunt, utpote quæ è κα- κοζηλίᾳ & illusione diabolica ortum trahunt) quia καθαρτικὰ sacrificia magnâ constabant pecunia; ubi contra nos haud impendimus quicquam, neq; laboribus nostris consequimur Justitiam, sed gra- tis & ex mera gratia propter meritū Christi, quum nulla merita ad justificationem adferre possimus, nulloc eam comparare labore. Ideò excluditur hac voce Papistarum ἑτεροδοξία, qua præparare & di- sponere sese hominem ad justificationem contendunt: δωρεὰν enim est gratis, & gratuitò, uti δῶρον donum est gratuitum, quod gratis donatum. Ex usu Scri- pturæ constat, opponi hanc particulam tùm pretio Gen. XXIX.15. Ex. XXI.2. Num. XI. 1. 2. Reg. XXIV. 24. Matth. X.8. 2. Cor. XI. 7. Ap. II. 5. tùm merito, seu demerito 1. Sam. XIX. 5, XXV. 31. 1. Reg. II. 31. Ez. XVI, 10. Syr. XXIX. 8.10. 2. Thess. III. 8. Quo de Ambrof. in h.l. Justificamur gratis, id est, dono DEI, nihil operantes, neque vicem reddentes, h.e. nec præ- cedentibus operibus meremur, nec sequentibus compensamus.

v. 24. τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ. Christus per obedientiam suam, maximè in morte, & preces ei accedentes hoc à Patre obti- nuit, ne is humanum genus gravibus peccatis im- mersum desereret atque obduraret, sed viam illis daret ad justitiam perveniendi per Christum. Es. LIII. 4. Hoc ipsum, sicut vocatur remittere pec- cata Luc. XXIII. 34. ita & ἀπολυτρῦν aut ποιεῖν λύ- τρωσιν Luc. I. 68. גאל aut פדה, id est, liberare, nempè à necessitate moriendi in peccatis, viam pa- tefaciendo, per quam exire ista liceret. Benè au- tem hanc liberationem adscribit bonitati divinæ, quia bonitatis DEI fuit Christum nobis dare. Joh. III. 16. infra VIII. 32. Adde Eph. I. 7.

Gratiam rectè explicat de bonitate divina, quod contra Papistas notandum, per eandem habitum justitiæ infusum intelligentes, repugnante tùm pro- prio vocis significatu, quia χάρις notat gratiam, uti χαρίζεσθαι est ex gratia cōdonare Luc. VII. 42. 2. Cor. II. 9. XII. 13. tùm usu Scripturæ, quia nuspiam voce χάριτος talis habitus infusus exprimitur, tùm Apo- stolico Scopo, qui est, docere, quod gratis, & ex gra- tia per solam redemptionem Christi, citra nostras vir- tutes, nostram justitiam, & opera ac merita nostra, solùm fide apprehendentes Christi justitiam & me- ritum justificemur: tùm Synonymo, quo χάρις ex- plicatur, per misericordiam Dei Eph. II. 4. Tit. III. 5. 1. Pet. I. 3. tùm opposito, quia gratia in locis similibus opponitur operibus Rom. XI. 6. Eph. II. 8. & debito Rom. IV. 4. 5. unde Cardinalis Pighius l. V. de lib. arbitr. commentitiam esse illam significationem gratiæ, quæ notet qualitatem aliquam animæ nostræ increatam à Deo agnoscit; fateturque Biel II. Sent. dist. 26. gratiam activè accipi pro gratiosa Dei vo- luntate dante omnibus liberaliter gratis, non ex debi- to; & post Concil. Tridentini anathema Jesuita Pererius Disp. XIII. in h. l. gratuitam Dei bonitatem & benignitatem erga hominem hîc illâ voce notari docet, siquidem Paulus operibus hominum gratiam Dei opponat: Conf. in Theol. Apost. Rom. orac. XXXI. Cæterum non hîc bonitati DEI adscribitur liberatio, (etsi ea omninò tribuenda sit divinæ gra- tiæ) sed justificatio; quia non unde orta sit ἀπολύ- τρωσις exponitur, sed quæ justificationis sit causa; quod nempe gratiæ DEI accepta ferenda illa sit, nec tamen gratiæ absolutæ, sed in merito Christi fundatæ, vel quæ propter ἀπολύτρωσιν Christi nobis obtingit; quâ redemit nos, interventu λύτρε obedientiæ suæ tùm activæ, tùm passivæ & effusione sanguinis sui pretiosissimi, ab irâ DEI, peccato, satanæ potestate, morte & inferno 1. Tim. II. 6. 1. Pet. I. 18. quod contra Socinianos l. c. orac. XXXII. demonstratum, adeoque meruit nobis gratiam, & remissionem peccatorum, expiatâ irâ DEI, & præstita satisfactione justitiæ divinæ, pro peccatis totius generis humani. Non ergò tantùm id obtinuit ἀπολυτρώσει sua, ut viam nobis daret Deus ad justitiam perveniendi, sed pretio sanguinis sui persoluto satisfecit pro nobis atque ita ab ira DEI nos liberavit, gratiamque DEI nobis comparavit; imò hæc ipsa ejus obedientia usque ad mortem crucis est obedientia illa, per quam nos justi constituimur Rom. V. 18. Factus enim est pro nobis peccatum, ut redderemur nos justitia in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. & factus est à Deo nobis justitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. ipse est justitia nostra, Jer. XXIII. 6. & in ipso nobis est justitia Es. XLV. 23. Neque idem est dare viam ad justitiam, & peccata remittere; nec tantum viam patefaciendo, quâ moriendi necessitate exire liceat, Christus nos redemit; nec deniquè id solùm voces פדה & גאל important, sed quod morte suâ pro nobis satisfecerit, & à peccato & morte nos redemerit: quemadmodum in Socinismo profligato ostensum, & ab ipso Grotio in assert. fidei de Satisfact. Christi contra Socinum evictum.

## 3:25
v. 25. whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood.

Ἱλαστήριον, כפרת, was called in the Old Testament the cover of the ark, upon which a certain cloud sent by God, sitting, made the people certain of his favor toward them. Lev. XVI. 2. Num. VII. 89. Thus also God, by holding those prayers of Christ as ratified and on account of them sending the Spirit upon the Apostles, John XIV. 16, showed that he wishes well to the human race. But when he adds through faith, he shows how each one might attain the effect of that goodness, that is, true righteousness, namely by having faith in the blood of Christ, that is, in the doctrine sanctioned by the blood of Christ, just as covenants were accustomed to be sanctioned by blood. See Matt. XXVI. 28. Justin against Trypho: no longer being cleansed by the blood of goats and sheep or the ashes of a heifer, but by faith through the blood of Christ and his death. And afterwards he says the passover was a figure of Christ, with whose blood, after the word of faith in him, they anoint their houses, that is, themselves, those who believe in him. But in the Manuscript, 'of faith' is missing.

Four things are to be observed here: (1) the divine πρόθεσις, which serves to explain the principal cause of Justification, the grace of GOD; because it was the grace of GOD that he set forth Christ as a propitiation; just as it is also of mere grace that he imputes to righteousness the faith looking toward this propitiation. For that πρόθεσις was made, both in the eternal counsel of God, 1 Pet. I. 20, and in the oracles of the Prophets, and in the types of the O. T., Apoc. XIII. 8, and in the mission and exhibition itself of Christ to the mediatorial office, 1 Tim. IV. 10, and in the preaching of the Gospel, by which he himself is clearly set forth to all as the true ἱλαστήριον, so that in him they may obtain the remission of sins and grace, whoever embrace it by faith. (2.) τὸ ἱλαστήριον: by which word it can be admitted that the cover of the ark is referred to, from which God formerly testified that he was propitious to the people, but not with respect only to the intercession of Christ and the mission of the Holy Spirit (which does not properly belong here), but with respect to the reconciliation made through the blood of Christ: for that ἱλαστήριον of the O.
