A similar way of speaking, in which there is a double meaning of the word GOD, substantive and appellative, appears in Luke 20:38, if you compare it with Matthew 22:32, where see what has been said by us; that God wills to be worshipped by the Gentiles and in turn to confer the highest goods upon them was most openly predicted by the Prophets, as in Malachi 1:11 and others.

Latin:

V. 29. ἢ Ἰδαίων Θεὸς μόνον, ὐχὶ καὶ ἐθνῶν; Ναὶ καὶ ἐθνῶν.

Est hic ratio, cur via per legem non fuerit optima: quia non conveniebat tot populis: neque enim omnium po- pulorum homines poterant venire sacrificaturi Hieroso- lyma. Θεὸς hic semel positum, sed in explicatione bis su- mendum. An DEUS ille verus, hujus mundi & humani generis opifex, vult tantùm DEUS, id est, sospitator atque ἐυεργέτης esse Judæorum, ut Judæorum multi existimant? Simile loquendi genus, cui inest duplex vocis DEI signi- ficatio, substantiva & appellativa, apparet Luc. XX. 38. si conferas Matth. XXII. 32. ubi quæ à nobis dicta vide, De- um autem velle & coli à gentibus & iis vicissim summa bona conferre, apertissimè prædictum erat Prophetis, ut Malach. I. 11. & aliis.

## 3:30
since God is one.

This is said in the same way as in the Poet: King Jupiter is the same for all. So also Ephesians 4:6 and Galatians 3:20.

who will justify.

That is, He justifies, the future used for the past in the Hebrew manner. That is very frequent where continuous acts are noted. What wonder, he says, if the supremely good One does this, that He makes others good?

circumcision by faith.

Jews, both born and proselytes, circumcision here [refers to] those themselves who are circumcised, as in Galatians 2:7, 8, 9, just as uncircumcision above in 2:26 and here immediately, those who retain the foreskin, that is, most of the Gentiles.

and uncircumcision through faith.

It appears that ἐκ, which preceded, and that which is here διὰ, have the same value. Hearts are purified through faith. See what was said in the prolegomena to this epistle.

The argument of the Apostle is not taken from a comparison of the legal way of salvation, that the way through the law was not the best, and that the Mosaic law was not suitable for all peoples, which is certainly equally false concerning the moral law (even if the ceremonial law was proper to the Jewish people), and it is certain and indubitable that no way of salvation is good and possible to be trodden after the fall in the law, since the yoke of the law is unbearable, Acts 15:10. and the Apostle Paul may judge it impossible after the fall to obtain salvation through the law Rom. 8:6, and thus no one can now be saved through the observance of the law, but this is the force of the argument: If GOD were to justify the Jews by one method and the Gentiles by another, He would not be one, that is, always like Himself, in the condemnation of all men and the conclusion under sin, so that He might have mercy on all: always like Himself both in justice and in mercy, in which the very nature and essence of GOD most unitively consists: nor would He be the God and savior of the Gentiles as much as of the Jews: because He gave and promulgated the law only to the Jews; for although some remnants of the law inscribed on the heart in the primeval creation still remain in the Gentiles, they do not have the law proposed, promulgated, and expounded to them as the Jews do, to whom were entrusted τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ Rom. 3:2, for He did not do so for every nation Ps. 147:19, 20. That GOD is the God of the Jews and the Gentiles, the Socinian Schlichtingius also explains by saying that He is of a propense will toward all and desires the salvation and conversion of all.

Do we then nullify the law through faith?

A new question containing an objection. If the matter stood thus, the Apostles could be seen to teach that the law was given uselessly. Καταργεῖν properly means to render useless, Luke 13:7, to say by metaleipsis that some thing is useless, such as that in Virgil: Now he surrounds the Phaethontiades with bitter bark. That is, he says they are surrounded. Likewise: — — who would sprinkle the ground with flowering herbs or introduce the shade of green springs?

That is, he would sing of the ground sprinkled and springs introduced. See also Jeremiah 1:10. διὰ τῆς πίςεως is a metonymy: that is, through those things which we preach concerning faith.

Latin:

ἐπείπερ εἷς ὁ Θεὸς.

Hoc ita dictum est quomodo apud Poëtam: Rex Juppiter omnibus idem. Sic & Eph. IV. 6. & Gal. III. 20.

ὃς δικαιώσει.

Id est, δικαιοῖ, futurum pro præterito more Hebræo. Frequentissimum id ubi notantur actus continui. Quid mirum, inquit, si summè bonus id agit, ut alios bonos fa- ciat?

περιτομὴν ἐκ πίσεως.

Judæos, & natos & adscititios περιτομὴ hic ipsi, qui cir- cumcisi sunt, ut Gal. II. 7. 8. 9. quomodo ἀκροβυσία suprà II. 26. & hic illico, ii, qui præputium retinent, id est, gen- tes pleræque.

καὶ ἀκροβυσίαν διὰ τῆς πίσεως.

Apparet ἐκ, quod præcessit, & quod hic est διὰ idem valere. Per fidem purgantur corda. Vide, quæ in prole- gomenis ad hanc epistolam dicta.

Argumentum Apostoli non à comparatione le- galis viæ salutis desumptum est, quod via per le- gem non fuerit optima, & Mosaica lex non conve- nerit omnibus populis, quod utique de lege mora- li æquè falsum est, (etsi lex ceremonialis populi Judaici propria fuerit) atque certum & indubi- tatum est, nullam salutis viam bonam & calcatu possibilem post lapsum superare in lege, siquidem jugum legis ἀβάσακτον sit, Act. XV. 10. & ἀδύνατον censeat Apostolus Paulus post lapsum, per legem consequi salutem Rom. IIX. 6. adeoque non possit ullus per legis observationem jam servari, sed hæc argumenti vis est: Si DEUS aliâ ratione Judæos, aliâ gentes justificaret, non esset unus, id est, sui sem- per similis, in condemnatione hominum omnium, & conclusione sub peccato, ut miseratur omni- um: similis sui semper tum justitia, tum miseri- cordia, in qua ipsa DEI natura & essentia unissi- mè una consistit: neque gentium æque, ac Judæo- rum Deus esset ac servator: quia Judæis tantùm legem dedit & promulgavit; etsi enim gentili- bus aliquid reliquiarum legis cordi inscriptæ in primæva creatione adhuc superfit, non tamen le- gem ita habent propositam, promulgatam & ex- positam, uti Judæi, quibus credita τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ Rom. III. 2. non enim taliter fecit omni natio- ni Ps. CXLVII. 19. 20. DEUM esse Judæorum & gentium Deum etiam Schlichtingius Socinianus ita explicat, quod in omnes propensâ sit voluntate omnium salutem ac conversionem desideret.

νόμον ὖν καταργῦμεν διὰ τῆς πίσεως.

Nova interrogatio continens objectionem. Si ita se res habebat, videri poterant Apostoli docere legem fuisse inu- tiliter datam. Καταργεῖν propriè est inutilem reddere, Luc. XIII. 7. per μετάληψιν dicere, rem aliquam esse inutilem, quale illud in Virgilio: Nunc Phaëtontiadas muscos circumdat amaræ Corticis. Id est, circumdatas dicit. Item: — — quis humum florentibus herbis Spargeret aut viridis fontes induceret umbra?

Id est, sparsam humum & fontes inductos caneret. Vide & Jerem. I. 10. διὰ τῆς πίςεως est μετωνυμία : id est, per ea, quæ de fide prædicamus.

## 3:31
May it not be.

Far be it. חלילה as above 3:4, 6, below 6:2, 15, 7:7, 13, 9:14.

but we establish the law.

The manuscript in the same sense ἱςάνομεν מעמיד we make to stand; that is, we defend its honor and its own: just as we say in Latin: the story stands on a straight foot. Doubtless the Apostles taught that through the law the baseness of sins is more rightly recognized, above 20. That civil society was preserved by it and to some extent, through fear of punishments, vices were repressed so they would not break out: Gal. 3:23. That Christ and the righteousness which Christ brought are promised in the law: above 21. But thus in many ways the law leads us to Christ, Gal. 3:24. And that Christ is the end proposed for the law, below 10:4. Tertullian, citing this passage concerning modesty, adds: We establish the law, namely in those things which are now introduced by the New Testament and prohibited even by a more cumulative precept. For 'You shall not commit adultery,' 'Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her, has already committed adultery with her in his heart': and for 'You shall not kill,' 'Whoever says to his brother Racha, shall be liable to Gehenna.' Query, whether the law of 'Not committing adultery,' to which 'Not coveting' has been added, is safe?

The Apostle's anthypophora is as follows: Although we say that justification is not from the works of the law, we do not therefore repudiate the law. Furthermore, the Vulgate must be corrected here, which less appropriately explained the word ἱςῶμεν as 'we establish.' To establish, says the blessed Gerhard on this passage, is of those things which are not yet, as in Virgil, 'the city which I establish': but it signifies the confirmation of those things which are. Nor does Grotius attain the mind of the Apostle when he renders it 'we defer its honor to it'; because the opposition of the words καταργῶμεν and ἱςῶμεν does not imply the deprivation of the honor owed to the law, or the deferring of it, but the evacuation or destruction of the law, and the confirmation or stabilization of the law. But in the Grotian explanation, as to how the law is stabilized through faith, the first reason, that through the law the baseness of sins is more rightly recognized, does nothing for the matter, for although this is done through the law; and the Apostles also taught this; yet here it had to be taught how the law is established through the doctrine of the Gospel and through faith, from which doctrine certainly not the acknowledgment of sin, but the revelation of the remedy for sin and of the punishment for sin is had; Nor does the other suit: because the doctrine of the Gospel delivers nothing concerning civil society, and furthermore that reasoning is foreign to the truth; for the law did not only make for the preservation of civil society and the repression of vices to some extent through the fear of punishments: but it prescribed true holiness, and prohibited and restrained any sins whatsoever, and that not only by threatening punishments and death, but also by promising rewards and life, if it should be observed and fulfilled, even if on account of the infirmity of the flesh it cannot be performed and fulfilled: whence at least it works wrath Rom. IV. 15. and condemnation 2. Cor. III. 9. not by its own fault and imperfection, or of itself, but by our fault, and by the vice and depravity of original sin, and thus accidentally. The third reason, that Christ and the righteousness which Christ brought are promised in the law, if the law is understood concerning the entire Mosaic Scripture, as in verse 21, is indeed true: but here it is a matter of the moral law, from which is the acknowledgment of sin, and which is the norm of true holiness. Which is opposed to the Gospel by the Apostle: and thus far only as a schoolmaster it leads us to Christ, Gal. III. 24, in that it convinces us of guilt and punishment, so that we may pant for him who has freed us from that guilt and punishment, whom indeed the moral law does not show, but the Ceremonial law shadowed forth, in the Evangelical promises, which together with the law have always flourished in the Church, more clearly shown and promised, in whom is the τὸ τέλος νόμου, not that Christ ends or abolishes the law, which would be against the Apostle, num do we make the law void through faith? God forbid, yea we establish the law: and against the express protestation of Christ Matt. V. 17. I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil it: But that he fulfils the law in our stead by his obedience, and makes that obedience ours or imputes it to us, and gives it through faith Rom. V. 15. 19. Tertullian's saying is to be reckoned among the chaff, of which not a few occur in that writer: For that new precepts were delivered by Christ neither agrees with the perfection of the law in the O. T., nor with the sermons of Christ, for the law itself also prohibited corrupt concupiscence and revilings, which Christ vindicated against the Pharisees who denied it, and went on to establish.

How therefore is the law established through the faith which is believed, that is, the doctrine of the Gospel? Schlichting also understands the faith which is believed in this place: you may take faith for the doctrine of faith Gal. I. 22. III. 2. s. 23. 26. (1.) because it shows Christ to be the τέλος and complement of the law Rom. X. 4. (2.) because believers use the law νομίμως, acknowledging from it the extreme corruption of their nature; whereas on the contrary hypocrites and Sophists wander from the true sense and use of the law, as if it were prescribed by external obedience only. (3.) because the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in believers, Rom. VIII. 4. while the righteousness of Christ, which is the perfect fulfilling of the law, is imputed to them through faith: (4.) because believers justified through faith are renewed by the Holy Spirit, so that they begin to offer spontaneous and inward obedience to the law, and thus through faith they arrive at works, that is, at obedience to the law, Gal. VI. 1. but they do not arrive at faith and justification through works, as hypocrites and heretics vainly attempt and contend. And these things concerning the third chapter to the Romans.

ARTICLE II. Proof from the testimony of the Scripture of the Old Testament.

Latin:

μὴ γένοιτο.

Longè absit. חלילה ut suprà III. 4. 6. infrà VI. 2. 15. VII. 7. 13. IX. 14.

ἀλλὰ νόμον ἱςῶμεν.

Manuscriptus eodem sensu ἱςάνομεν מעמיד stare fa- cimus; id est, honorem & suum defendimus : sicut Lati- nè dicimus : recto stat fabula talo. Nimirum docebant Apostoli per legem rectius agnosci peccatorum turpitudi- nem supra. 20. Societatem civilem per eam fuisse serva- tam & aliquatenus, pœnarum metu, repressa ne erumpe- rent vitia : Gal. III. 23. in lege promitti Christum & ju- stitiam, quam Christus attulit : suprà 21. At sic pluribus modis legem ducere nos ad Christum, Gal. III. 24. Chri- stum verò finem esse legi propositum infrà X. 4. Tertul- lianus de pudicitia hunc locum citans addit : Legem sisti- mus, scilicet in his, quæ & nunc Novo Testamento introdu- cta etiam cumulatiore præcepto prohibentur. Pro non mœcha- beris, Qui viderit mulierem ad concupiscendum, jam mœ- chatus est in corde suo : & pro Non occides; Qui dixerit fra- tri suo Racha, reus erit Gehennæ. Quære, an salva sit lex Non mœchandi, cui accessit, Non concupiscendi?

Ἀνθυποφορὰ Apostoli ita habet : Tametsi justi- ficationem non esse ex operibus legis dicamus, non tamen propterea legem repudiamus. Cæterum cor- rigenda hic vulgata, quæ minùs commodè expo- suit vocem ἱςῶμεν statuimus. Statuere, inquit B. Gerhard. in h. l. est eorum, quæ nondum sunt, ut apud Virgilium, urbem, quam statuo : sed stabi- lire confirmationem significat eorum, quæ sunt. Ne- que assequitur mentem Apostoli Grotius, dum reddit honorem ei suum deferimus ; quia opposi- tio verborum καταργῶμεν & ἱςῶμεν non infert honoris legi debiti privationem, ejusvè delatio- nem, sed legis evacuationem seu destructionem, & legis confirmationem seu stabilitationem. In explica- tione verò Grotiana, quo pacto lex stabiliatur per fidem prima ratio, quod per legem rectiùs agnosca- tur turpitudo peccatorum, nihil ad rem facit, nam quamvis hoc per legem fiat; idque Apostoli et- iam docuerint ; jam tamen hic docendum erat, quomodo per doctrinam Evangelii & per fidem lex stabiliatur, è qua doctrina certè non peccati agnitio, sed remedii peccati & supplicii pro pec- cato revelatio habetur; Neque altera convenit : quia doctrina Evangelii nihil tradit de civili socie- tate, & prætereà aliena est ratio illa à veritate; non enim tantùm ad societatis civilis conservatio- nem & aliqualem vitiorum per pœnarum metum repressionem faciebat lex : sed præscribebat veram sanctitatem, & prohibebat ac cohibebat quæli- bet peccata, idque non tantùm pœnas & mortem minando, sed etiam præmia & vitam promittendo, si observata & impleta fuerit, etsi propter infirmi- tatem carnis præstari & impleri non possit: unde saltem iram operatur Rom. IV. 11. & condemna- tionem 2. Cor. III. 9. non sui culpâ, & imperfectio- ne, vel per se, sed nostri culpâ, & peccati origina- lis vitio, ac depravatione, adeoque per accidens. Tertia ratio, quod in lege promittatur Christus & justitia, quam Christus attulit, si lex de universa Scripturâ Mosaica intelligatur, uti vers. 21. vera quidem est : sed hìc de lege morali, è quà agnitio peccati, quæque norma veræ sanctitatis est, res est. Quæ Evangelio opponitur ab Apostolo : & hacte- nus solùm ut pædagogus ad Christum nos ducit, Gal. III. 24. quà nempè convincit de culpa & pœ- nâ, ut anhelemus eum, qui nos ab ea culpa & pœna liberavit, quem verò lex moralis non osten- dit, sed lex Ceremonialis adumbravit, in promissio- nibus Evangelicis, quæ juxta cum lege semper in Ecclesia viguêre clariùs ostensum, & promissum, in quo τὸ τέλος νόμου, non quod legem finiat aut tollat Christus, quod esset contra Apostolum, num evacuamus legem per fidẽ? absit, imò legem stabilimus: & contra Christi disertam protestationem Matth. V. 17. Non veni legem tollere, sed implere: Sed quod legem nostri loco obedientiâ suâ impleat, eamque obedientiam nostram faciat vel nobis imputet, ac donet per fidem Rom. V. 15. 19. Tertulliani dictum, paleis, quarum non paucæ apud illum scriptorem occurrunt, accensendum: Nova enim præcepta à Christo tradita esse nec legis in V. T. perfectioni convenit, nec concionibus Christi, nam & lex ipsa concupiscentiam pravam ac convitia prohibuit, quam adversus Pharisæos id negantes Christus vindicavit, & stabilitum ivit.

Quomodo ergò per fidem, quæ creditur, id est, doctrinam Evangelii lex stabilitur? Fidem, quæ creditur, intelligit etiam Schlichting. in h. l.: possis fidem sumere pro doctrinâ de fide Gal. I. 22. III. 2. s. 23. 26. (1.) quia Christum τέλος & complementum legis monstrat Rom. X. 4. (2.) quia credentes νομίμως utuntur lege, agnoscentes ex ea extremam naturæ suæ corruptionem; cum contrà hypocritæ & Sophistæ à vero sensu & usu legis aberrent, q. externâ solùm obedientiâ eâ præscribatur. (3.) quia τό δικαίωμα legis impletur in credentibus, Rom. VIII. 4. dum Christi justitia, quæ est perfecta legis impletio per fidem ipsis imputatur: (4.) quia credentes per fidem justificati per Spiritum Sanctum renovantur, ut spontaneam & interiorem legi præstare incipiant obedientiam, adeoque fide perveniunt ad opera, id est, ad legis obedientiam, Gal. VI. 1. non autem operibus perveniunt ad fidem & justificationem, ut hypocritæ & hæretici frustrà conantur, & contendunt. Atque hæc de tertio capite ad Romanos.

ARTICULUS II. Probatio è Scripturæ Vet. Testamenti testificatione.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT.

The Apostle shows that a man is justified by faith, not by works, by the example of Abraham, to whom in the midst of his course of good works not works, but faith was imputed for righteousness without works, and by the testimony of David, concerning blessedness situated in the non-imputation of sins, and he teaches how faith was imputed to Abraham while he was yet in uncircumcision, and that he himself received circumcision only as a seal of the righteousness of faith, and that he is the example of justification for all, even the uncircumcised, who are of the faith of Abraham, as the Father of all believers, inasmuch as he believed in hope against hope, to whose example it behooves all also to believe, that faith may be imputed for righteousness, in GOD, who raised up Jesus delivered for our sins for our righteousness.

PARTITION.

There are three parts of the chapter, I. The confirmation of justification through faith from the example of Abraham and the testimony of David, to v. 8. II. The extension of the mode of Abrahamic justification to the Gentiles, to v. 13. III. The declaration of Abrahamic justifying faith, v. 14. to the end of the chapter.

PART I. CHAP. IV. Confirmation of justification through faith from the example of Abraham and the testimony of David.

V. 1. What shall we say then? That Abraham our father hath found according to the flesh?

The Jews, relying on the mighty works of their ancestors and especially of Abraham, thought that, however they lived, they would always remain the people of GOD, and that GOD would not deal as rigidly with them as with others, which they still persuade themselves of today. We have clear traces of this opinion in Matt. VI. 9, Luke III. 8, John VIII. 33, 37, 39, 40. Just as John the Baptist and Christ had opposed this harmful persuasion, so Paul also judged that it must be opposed here: and indeed in such a way that he turns back upon the Jews the argument taken from Abraham. An interrogation must be placed after ἐροῦμεν, as below VI. 1, what then is it that we say? Namely, do we say: that Abraham our father obtained (namely, the righteousness, which word had already preceded) by the flesh, that is, by his own powers? As if he were to say: by no means, the reasons for which negation he then gives. Flesh is opposed to divine revelation, Matt. XVI. 17, Gal. I. 16. To find corresponds to the Hebrew מצא, which very often signifies any kind of attainment, as in Gen. VI. 8, XVIII. 3, XIX. 19, XXXII. 5, XXXIII. 8, and often elsewhere: just as we noted that εὑρίσκειν is used among the Hellenistic Jews in Luke I. 30.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM.

Hominem fide, non operibus justificari Abrahami exemplo, cui in medio bonorum operum cursu non opera, sed fides imputata ad justitiam sine operibus, & Davidis testimonio, de beatitudine in non-imputatione peccatorum sitâ ostendit Apostolus, & quomodo Abrahamo adhuc in præputio fides imputata sit, & circumcisionem ipse solùm in sigillum justitiæ fidei acceperit, omnibus, etiam incircumcisis, qui fidei Abrahami sunt, ipsum justificationis exemplum esse docet, ceu Patrem omnium credentium, utpote qui in spem contrà spem credidit, ad cujus exemplum etiam omnes, ut fides imputetur ad justitiam, in DEUM, qui Jesum traditum propter peccata nostra resuscitavit propter justitiam nostram, credere oportet.

PARTITIO.

Partes capitis tres sunt, I. Justificationis per fidem ab exemplo Abrahami, & testimonio Davidis confirmatio ad v. 8. II. Modi justificationis Abramicæ ad gentiles extensio, ad v. 13. III. Fidei justificantis Abramicæ declaratio, v. 14. usque ad finem capitis.

PARS I. CAP. IV. Justificationis per fidem ab exemplo Abrami & testimonio Davidis Confirmatio.

V. 1. Τὶ οὖν ἐρῶμεν; Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν εὑρηκέναι κατὰ σάρκα;

Judæi majorum suorum ac præcipuè Abrahami virtu- tibus fisi putabant, quomodocunque viverent, se semper unos mansuros DEI populum, neque DEUM tàm rigi- dè cum ipsis, quàm cum aliis acturum, quod & nunc sibi persuadent. Hujus opinionis vestigia non obscura habe- mus Matth. VI. 9. Luc. III. 8. Joh. VIII. 33. 37. 39. 40. Huic noxiæ persuasioni, sicut Johannes Baptista & Chri- stus occurrerant, ita & hîc Paulus occurrendum censuit: & ita quidem, ut in Judæos retorqueat sumptum ab Ab- rahamo argumentum. Ponenda interrogatio post ἐρῶ- μεν, ut infrà VI. 1. quid est ergo, quod dicimus? Nempè an dicimus: Abrahamum patrem nostrum consecutum (justitiam scilicet, quæ vox jam præcesserat) per carnem, id est, propriis viribus? Quasi dicat: minimè verò, cujus negationis rationes deinde reddit. Caro opponitur divi- næ revelationi, Matth. XVI. 17. Gal. I. 16. Invenire re- spondet Hebræo מצא, quod sæpissimè qualemcunque adeptionem significat, ut Genes. VI. 8. XVIII. 3. XIX. 19. XXXII. 5. XXXIII. 8. & alibi sæpè: quomodo & apud Judæos Hellenistas εὑρίσκειν sumi notavimus Luc. I. 30.

## 4:2
V. 2. For if Abraham was justified by works.

If he appeared righteous, צדק in the Kal, by external deeds only, such as he could perform by himself.

he has a ground for boasting.

He has that in which he may confide, or from which he may hope for praise. Concerning the word καυχᾶσθαι, see above II. 17, 23.

but not before God.

Πρὸς here means before: we said in John I. 1, there is some just ground for boasting before God, below v. 2, 3, II. 7, 1 Cor. I. 31, 2 Cor. X. 17, Phil. III. 3. He who, in a civil manner, that is, by some external appearance, is innocent, can hope for temporary praise from men, not that eternal one from God: he has his reward, Matt. V. 5. For not doing wrong is not praise, says Philostratus in the Life of Apollonius VI, 2.

The mind of the Apostle is signally perverted. The Apostle did not aim only to teach that we are not justified by external obedience, much less to refute the vain persuasion of the Jews, who, relying only on the mighty works of their ancestors, thought that, however they lived, they would remain the people of GOD—which appears neither here nor in the other passages alleged; but to show that by the observance of the law, however much is performed by us, even if we did things equal to Abraham, no one is justified, and that we attain true righteousness not indeed by faith and works, but by faith alone. What the scope of the Apostle teaches, the total exclusion of the works of the law and its observance from the article of justification teaches, the entire continuity of the Apostolic disputation teaches, the arguments from the law of Moses, or the Pentateuch, from the example of Abraham, and from the Prophets, from the testimony of David adduced here, teach, as being those by which he proves what he had said in chapter III. 21, that righteousness indeed is obtained without the works of the law, yet is confirmed by the testimony of the law or the writings of Moses and the Prophets.

The Apostle brings forward the example of Abraham in the first place, not only as being very ancient, but also as most luminous in the Mosaic Genesis, and this indeed both because the Holy Spirit Himself wished to show in it the method of justification, Gen. XV. 4, and because the Jews, seeking righteousness in works, were accustomed to glory greatly in Abraham; and also because Abraham shone with mighty works, and yet in the midst of his course of good works it was pronounced concerning him that he was justified not by works, but by faith alone, so that the heresy of the false apostles might be overthrown, that faith and works are required together in order for us to be justified, or that a man is not justified by faith alone, but by faith and works. Concerning which Chrysostom, Homily VIII on the Epistle to the Romans, wishes to show also,

That Abraham was justified by faith, which was indeed a great excess of victory. For that he, to whom works are lacking, is justified by faith, was nothing absurd, but that he, who abounded in good works, was not just from them, but from faith, this indeed was to be wondered at, and it made the power of faith most manifest.

Wherefore Grotius perverts the Apostle's meaning here: first by changing the punctuation of the text: For thus all the codices read in a continuous discourse: Τί ὆ν ἐρῦμεν Αβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν ἐυρηκέναι κατὰ σάρκα; What then shall we say that Abraham our father has found according to the flesh? In no codex is there punctuation around the word ἐρῦμεν. Then he rashly repeats the word justice, when the question is complete: what shall we say, that Abraham has found according to the flesh? Thirdly, he explains that κατὰ σάρκα less correctly as concerning one's own powers. For although flesh is otherwise opposed to divine revelation, and in this Epistle to the Spirit, Chap. IX, 12. 13. yet that meaning is foreign here; because Abraham was already reborn, and is viewed not only according to his own powers, but as being most adorned with all virtues by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Nor can any man perform obedience pleasing to GOD or do good works by his own powers: since by nature we are bad trees, which cannot bear good fruits Matth. VII, 17. and we are dead in sin Eph. II. What good, however, would such a one work? Without me you can do nothing, says Christ John XV, 6. More correctly, therefore, others wish for works to be understood by the phrase κατὰ σάρκα, in which the Pseudo-Apostles sought the praise of justice, and which they required for justification, in which way they also wished for circumcision itself to be viewed as a work commanded by the law. The Apostle therefore denies that Abraham found anything κατὰ σάρκα according to the flesh, that is, by external circumcision and other works; because he explains soon v. 2. τὸ κατὰ σάρκα according to the flesh by the phrase ἐξ ἔργων from works; and he uses τὸ to find according to the flesh, for to be justified from works κατ᾽ ἰσοδυναμίαν as an equivalent. If he is justified from works, (thus the Apostle concludes) he has boasting; but he does not have boasting before GOD. Therefore he is not justified from works. Therefore that Popish gloss about works, done by the powers of nature, or without grace, since such things in reality are nothing and cannot be, is not to be admitted; which Grotius has here encrusted; Rightly Beza κατὰ σάρκα, that is, (as the Apostle himself explains) from works, suppose if we consider Abraham in himself, as circumcised. And Flacius in his gloss: The word according to the flesh here signifies from works, not without extreme contempt for the justice of works, just as Isaiah also says: All flesh is grass, and all his justice is like the flower of the field, and as is also held in Philipp. III. 4. & Gal. III. 3. having begun with the Spirit, are you now made perfect by the flesh: the cause of this locution is, because the flesh, that is, man himself in himself has and performs that justice, it is not freely imputed to him by GOD, even if he performs it now reborn, for this word also includes those works. Compare also B. Gerhard on this passage. B. Hülsemann in his vindication of the testimonies of Scripture, unpublished §. LXV. thus holds against Hemming and Hornæus in his repeated assertion, th. 14. and 120. from a collation of the Apostolic phrase it is manifestly evident that the Apostle uses that phrase according to the flesh in a far different sense when he speaks of circumcised Israelites, than when he speaks of Gentiles not yet converted. I say therefore, that Abraham to find according to the flesh, is the same as: Abraham to find through the circumcision of the flesh, which I prove, because the Apostle at the beginning of this dispute had explained this phrase thus

Chap. II. 28. ἡ ἐν σαρκὶ περιτομὴ, Circumcision, which is done in the flesh. Thus Gal. III. 3. where the question was, whether it was necessary for Gentiles converted to Christ to be circumcised, the Apostle calls circumcision a perfection in the flesh, if you began in the spirit, why will you now be made perfect in the flesh? where it is manifest that by flesh are understood not carnal sins, but the ceremony designated in the flesh. Thus Philipp. III. 3. 4. To trust in the flesh, does not signify to trust in works done by natural powers, but to trust in circumcision, as the consequences demonstrate, I am a Jew circumcised on the eighth day. This boasting about the state of circumcision the Apostle calls confidence in the flesh, and thus Rom. IV. 1. it is denied that Abraham found justice through the circumcision of the flesh, but on the contrary it is affirmed v. 11. that circumcision was a seal of the justice already received in the state of uncircumcision. Wherefore Pererius disp. 2. on this chapter, Justinianus and Estius confess that that phrase according to the flesh does not denote the powers of nature, but denotes the benefit of circumcision, and that this meaning is: Abraham our Father did not find justification through circumcision, but already before received justice before circumcision through faith alone, as is said in verse 11. Fourthly, that distortion is also to be rejected: If Abraham was justified from works, that is, if he appeared just by external deeds only, such as he could perform by himself; because Abraham could not perform truly good works by himself before regeneration, nor could any other unregenerate person: and works here are excluded in general; not only external deeds, works of the law, which are in every way in accordance with the law, not only as regards external obedience: but who can perform works of that kind after the fall? No mortal: so far is it from being the case that anyone can fulfill the law by the powers of nature alone, and by himself. Finally, it cannot be denied that Abraham appeared just through works, as those by which justice is demonstrated before men, as James testifies in chapter II. therefore the Apostle does not deny that here; but this is what he denies, as is evident from the whole discussion, namely that a man is justified before the divine tribunal by works, so that works contribute to justice consisting before GOD, whether it is asserted that the same consists only of works, or of faith and works together: because the Apostle opposes faith and works in the article of justification, and thus teaches that we are justified by faith alone, and that works contribute nothing to it. Fifthly, Grotius errs most gravely in this, as if the Apostle leaves Abraham boasting from works, and concedes it before GOD, not indeed from external works done by the powers of nature alone, when he was innocent in a civil manner, as he says, by which he would have obtained boasting only before men, but from works done through grace, whereas on the contrary the Apostle here denies boasting before God to works of any kind whatsoever, and that distinction of works done without grace and with grace is null, with the other member of the distinction, namely of good works done without grace, being wiped away. For those are nothing. This interrogation, says Illyricus, is a denial. Abraham our father obtained nothing by works: Therefore we shall obtain much less, since we are by no means his equals in piety. The Apostle is entirely concerned with teaching that men are justified entirely freely, having nothing at all in themselves by which they can be justified, and of which they can boast. Nor can that transposition of the ancients be approved, which Erasmus and Schlichtingius followed: What then shall we say that Abraham our father has found according to the flesh. For he is not called Father according to the flesh, but to have found according to the flesh: nor did the Apostle propose to himself to take away the praise of righteousness from Abraham simply, unless he had preferred to deter his adversaries with certain paradoxes, rather than to win them over to Christ little by little, but κατά τι, that is, of righteousness from works.

For what does the Scripture say.

Gen. XV. 6. After the promise of GOD made to Abraham concerning offspring, a thing unhoped for by him, was narrated. Paul cites the passage from the Greek.

Latin:

V. 2. εἰ γὰρ Ἀβραὰμ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη.

Si justus apparuit, צדק in Kal, factis tantùm exter- nis, qualia per se præstare poterat.

ἔχει καύχημα.

Habet in quo confidat, aut unde laudem speret. De voce καυχᾶσθαι vide suprà II. 17. 23.

ἀλλ' ὀ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν.

Πρὸς hîc valet apud: diximus Joh. I. 1. est aliquod κάυ- χημα justum apud Deum, infrà v. 2. 3. II. 7. 1. Cor. I. 31. 2. Cor. X. 17. Philip. III. 3. Qui ad civilem modum, id est, externa aliqua specie innocens, laudem potest ab ho- minibus sperare temporariam, non illam æternam à Deo: ἀπέχει τὸν μισθὸν αὑτῶ Matth. V. 5. τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀδικεῖν ἐκ ἔπαινος ait Philostratus de Vita Apollonii VI, 2.

Insigniter pervertitur mens Apostoli. Non id egit tantùm Apostolus, ut per externam obedien- tiam nos haud justificari doceret, nedum ut Ju- dæorum vanam persuasionem, qui nixi tantùm ma- jorum suorum virtutibus, quomodocunque vi- verent, se populum DEI mansuros putarint, quæ neque hic, neque aliis locis allegatis apparet, re- felleret; sed ut per legis observantiam, quanta quanta à nobis præstatur, etiamsi Abrahamo pa- ria faceremus, neminem justificari, ac ne qui- dem tùm per fidem, tùm per opera, sed per solam fidem nos justitiam veram consequi ostenderet. Quod docet Scopus Apostoli, docet legis ope- rum & observantiæ ejusdem omnimoda ex arti- culo justificationis exclusio, docet tota συνέχεια disputationis Apostolicæ, docent argumenta è lege Mosis, vel Pentatevcho, ab exemplo Abra- hami, & ex Prophetis è testimonio Davidis hic adducta, utpote quibus probat, quod cap. III. 21. dixerat, justitiam obtingere quidem sine operibus legis, testimonio tamen legis seu scriptorum Mosis & Prophetarum comprobari.

Adducit autem Apostolus imprimis exemplum Abrahami non tantùm, ceu admodum antiquum, sed etiam maximè luculentum in Genesi Mosai- câ, & quidem tùm quod ipse Spiritus Sanctus in eodem justificationis rationem ostendere voluit, Genes. XV. 4. tùm quod Judæi in operibus justi- tiam quærentes plurimum in Abrahamo gloriari consueverint; tùm quod Abraham insignibus virtutibus luxerit, quodque in medio bonorum operum cursu de eo tamen pronunciatum sit, quod non per opera, sed solùm per fidem justifi- catus fuerit, ut ita profligetur Pseudo-Aposto- lorum hæresis, fidem & opera simul requiri, ut justificemur, vel non solâ fide hominem justifi- cari, sed per fidem & opera. Quo de Chrysost. hom. IIX. in Epist. ad Rom. vult ostendere etiam,

Abrahamum ex fide justificatum esse, qui quidam erat victoriæ magnus excessus. Etenim eum, cui opera desunt, ex fide justificari, nihil erat absur- di, ast eum, qui bonis operibus abundaret, non in- de, sed ex fide fuisse justum, hoc verò admirandum fuit, fideique vim vel maximè manifestam fecit.

Quapropter pervertit hìc Apostoli senten- tiam Grotius: primùm textûs distinctionem im- mutando: Sic enim legunt codices omnes con- tinua oratione: Τί ὆ν ἐρῦμεν Αβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν ἐυρηκέναι κατὰ σάρκα; Quid igitur dicemus Abrahamum Patrem nostrum invenisse secundum carnem? In nullo vero codice interpunctio ha- betur circa vocem ἐρῦμεν. Deinde vocem ju- stitiæ temere repetit, cum quæstio completa sit: quid dicemus, invenisse Abrahamum secundum carnem? Tertiò illud κατὰ σάρκα minus recte ex- plicat de propriis viribus. Etsi enim caro, divinæ revelationi alias, & in hac Epistola Spiritui op- ponatur, Cap. IX, 12. 13. ea tamen significatio aliena hic est; quia Abraham jam renatus erat, nec solum secundum proprias vires spectatur, sed uti omnibus virtutibus gratia Spiritus S. erat or- natissimus. Neque propriis viribus quisquam hominum obedientiam DEO gratam præstare, vel bona opera facere potest: quum natura simus arbores malæ, quæ bonos fructus ferre nequeunt Matth. VII, 17. & mortui simus in peccato Eph. II. Quid autem boni talis operaretur? Sine me nihil potestis facere, inquit Christus Joh. XV, 6. Re- ctius itaq; voce κατὰ σάρκα alii respici volunt ope- ra, in quibus Pseudo-Apostoli laudem justitiæ quærebant, & quæ ad justificationem require- bant, quo pacto etiam ipsam circumcisionem, ut opus lege mandatum spectari volebant. Negat igitur Apostolus, Abrahamum κατὰ σάρκα secun- dum carnem, id est, externâ circumcisione aliisq; operibus quicquam invenisse; quia explicat mox v. 2. τὸ κατὰ σάρκα secundùm carnem voce ἐξ ἔρ- γων ex operibus; & τὸ invenire secundùm carnem, per justificari ex operibus κατ᾽ ἰσοδυναμίαν adhi- bet. Si justificatus est ex operibus, (ita conclu- dit Apostolus) habet gloriationem; sed non ha- bet gloriationem apud DEUM. Ergò non est justificatus ex operibus. Non ergò Papistica ista glossa de operibus, viribus naturæ, vel sine gratia factis, quum talia reverà nulla sint nec esse pos- sint, admittenda; quam hic incrustavit Grotius; Rectè Beza κατὰ σάρκα, id est, (ut ipse Aposto- lus explicat) ex operibus, puta si Abrahamum con- sideremus in sese, ut circumcisum. Et Flacius in glossa: Vox secundum carnem hic significat ex ope- ribus, non sine extremo contemptu Justitiæ operum, sicut & Isaias inquit: Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis justitia ejus sicut flos agri, & sicut etiam habetur Philipp. III. 4. & Gal. III. 3. cum Spiritu cœperi- tis, nunc carne consummamini: causa hujus locu- tionis est, quia caro, id est, homo ipse in se habeat ac præstet illam justitiam, non gratis ei à DEO imputetur, etiamsi eam præstet jam renatus, nam illa quoque opera vox hæc complectitur. Conf. & B. Gerhardum in h. l. B. Hülsemann. in vindi- cat. testimon. Script. ἀνεκδότῳ §. LXV. ita ha- bet contrà Hemming. & Hornæum in iterat. ad- sert. th. 14. & 120. ex collatione Phraseos Apo- stolicæ manifestè patet, Apostolum Phrasi illa secundùm carnem longo alio sensu uti, quando de Israëlitis circumcisis loquitur, quàm cum de gentibus nondum conversis loquitur. Dico ergo, Abrahamum invenire secundum carnem, perinde esse quod: Abrahamum invenire per circumcisio- nem carnis, quod probo, quia Apostolus initio hujus disputationis hanc Phrasin ita exposuerat

Cap. II. 28. ἡ ἐν σαρκὶ περιτομὴ, Circumcisio, quæ in carne fit. Sic Gal. III. 3. ubi quæstio erat, an gentiles ad Christum conversos necesse esset cir- cumcidi, Apostolus circumcisionem vocat con- summationem in carne, si spiritu incepistis, cur nunc in carne consummabitis? ubi manifestum est, per carnem non peccata carnalia, sed cere- moniam in carne designatam intelligi. Sic Phi- lipp. III. 3. 4. Confidere in carne, non significat confidere in operibus per vires naturales factis, sed confidere in circumcisione, ut consequentia demonstrant, Judæus sum circumcisus tertia die. Hanc gloriationem de statu circumcisionis vo- cat Apostolus confidentiam in carne, atque ita Rom. IV. 1. negatur Abrahamum invenisse justi- tiam per circumcisionem carnis, è contra autem affirmatur v. 11. quod circumcisio fuerit sigillum justitiæ jam acceptæ in statu præputii. Quam- obrem Pererius disp. 2. in hoc caput, Justinianus & Estius fatentur, Phrasin illam secundum carnem non notare vires naturæ, sed notare beneficium circumcisionis, & hunc sensum esse: Abraham Pater noster non invenit justificationem per cir- cumcisionem, sed jam antea accepit justitiam ante circumcisionem per solam fidem, ut dicitur vers. 11. Quartò reprobanda etiam illa detorsio: Si Abra- ham ex operibus justificatus est, id est, si justus apparuit factis tantùm externis, qualia per se præ- stare poterat; quia nec per se opera verè bona præstare poterat Abrahamus ante regeneratio- nem, nec quisquam alius non renatus: & ἔργα hic in universum excluduntur; non solùm facta exter- na, ἔργα τοῦ νόμου, quæ legi ex asse sunt consenta- nea, non tantùm quoad externam obedientiam: istius autem generis ἔργα ecquis post lapsum præ- stare potest? Nemo mortalium: tantùm abest, ut solis naturæ viribus, & per se legem quis implere valeat. Denique per opera apparuisse Abraha- mum justum, negari non potest, utpote quibus justitia demonstratur coram hominibus, teste Ja- cobo cap. II. non ergò id negat hîc Apostolus; sed hoc est, quod inficiatur, ut è tota tractatio- ne constat, hominem nempe justificari coram tri- bunali divino operibus, ita ut ad justitiam coram DEO consistentem opera conducant, sive solùm operibus eadem constare asseratur, seu fide & ope- ribus simul: quia fidem & opera in articulo ju- stificationis opponit Apostolus, adeoque sola fide nos justificari, nec quicquam ad id conferre ope- ra docet. Quintò gravissimè in eo errat Grotius, ac si Apostolus Abrahamo gloriationem ex operi- bus relinquat, & concedat apud DEUM, non quidem ex operibus externis solis naturæ viribus factis, cùm ad civilem, ut ait, modum innocens fuerit, quibus tantùm gloriationem apud homines obtinuerit, sed ex operibus per gratiam factis, quum ex adverso Apostolus hic gloriationem apud De- um operibus quibuscunque prorsus deroget, & distinctio illa operum sine gratia, & cum gratia factorum nulla sit, altero distinctionis membro bonorum nempè operum sine gratia factorum, in spongiam incumbente. Illa enim nulla sunt. Interrogatio hæc, inquit Illyricus, inficiatio est. Ab- rahamus Pater noster nihil consequutus operibus: Igitur multò minùs nos consequemur, cum ei pie- tate nequaquam pares simus. Totus in eo est Apostolus, ut doceat homines, quod gratis pror- sus justificentur, nihil omninò in se habere, quo possint justificari, & de quo possint gloriari. Nec illa trajectio veterum probari potest, quam Erasmus & Schlichtingius sequutus est: Quid igi- tur dicemus invenisse Abrahamum Patrem nostrum secundum carnem. Non enim Pater dicitur, se- cundùm carnem, sed invenisse secundùm carnem: nec proposuit sibi Apostolus justitiae laudem sim- pliciter Abrahamo adimere, nisi maluisset adver- sarios paradoxis quibusdam deterrere, quam Christum paulatim lucrifacere, sed κατά τι, id est, justitiae ex operibus.

τί γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ λέγει.

Gen. XV. 6. Postquam narrata fuit DEI promissio facta Abrahamo de sobole, re ipsi insperata. Citat locum Pau- lus ex Graeco.

## 4:3
V. 3. And Abraham believed God) He had faith in the promises of GOD, which itself presupposes (as the Schools say) an excellent estimation both of the power of GOD and of his most excellent faithfulness, from which also confidence in God arises. Philo, in his exposition of that passage from Genesis in the book on the heir of divine things, says: to God alone without any other intercession, to whom it is easy to believe because of the union with the mortal to which it is joined. Moreover, Abraham is called here אברהם by prolepsis, since in the Scriptures up to that time he is called אברם, Abram.

The promise of offspring is not being looked at here, but of the blessed seed, or rather the seed in the promised seed, because the Lord received that He Himself is the shield of Abraham, and his very great reward: concerning which promise we have spoken in the Commentary on Mosaic Genesis and in the Biblical illustrations on Gen. XV. Flacius rightly says: He believed not only in the multitude of the seed, but in that promise he looked especially to the preceding words, where GOD commanded him not to fear, but to confide in Him, and promised that He would be his shield and his most abundant reward, and in the blessed seed, in which alone both he himself and all mortals were to be blessed or liberated from the curse of God in Gen. III and of the law in Gal. IV. He also believed that GOD is his shield and a very abundant reward, as is promised to him there, in which all spiritual goods are contained. Grotius explains that 'he believed God' means he had faith in the promises of GOD, and says that it presupposes an excellent estimation both of the power of GOD and of his most excellent faithfulness, from which also confidence in God arises; thus far we admit this, provided that such estimation is not merely of opinion or persuasion, but of true faith divinely excited in us: because human persuasion alone does not suffice for true confidence in GOD; but this presupposes faith born from the word of GOD concerning the power and truth in divine promises, especially concerning the grace of GOD coming to us in Christ, and thus concerning the satisfaction and merit of Christ: which knowledge and συγκατάθεσις or certain and indubitable assent can be had only from the word of GOD, which must altogether precede confidence, if this is to be indubitable, and such as is described by πληροφορίαν (full assurance) in Rom. IV. 21, Heb. VI. 11, c. X. 22, and παρρησίαν (boldness) in Col. III. 12, Heb. III. 6, c. IV. 16. boasting Rom. X. 2. Courage Matth. IX. 22, Joh. XVI. 33.

and it was reckoned to him for righteousness.

So also 1 Macc. II. 52: Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness? That is, God held it as an excellent and very praiseworthy thing: as we explained in the Prolegomena from the passage Ps. CVI. 30. And deservedly indeed, not because all virtues which God requires are in faith, but because it is the greatest virtue and the mother and nurse of the others. Faith is the most perfect of virtues, said Philo in the aforementioned book: and at the end of the book on Abraham: the head of the praises of the wise man. In the book on languages: the most secure and most certain disposition. Thus in the book on Colonies he shows that: for a testimony of faith, he says, which the soul believed in God, not showing ingratitude from the results, but hanging and suspended from the expectation of future things and from good hope, and having considered without doubt that things not present were already present, because of the most certain faith of the one who promised. And in the book on Abraham himself: faith toward God is the consolation of life, the fullness of good hopes, the barrenness of evils, but the abundance of goods, the despair of misery, the knowledge of piety, the lot of happiness, improvement in all things, leaning upon the cause of all things, who is able to do all things, and wills the best. In the book on Cain, that faith is the best sacrifice which is offered to GOD. Justin clearly, as Paul here, applying the history of Abraham to us: being children of Abraham because of similar faith; for in the same way that he believed the voice of God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, in the same way we also, having believed the voice of God spoken again through the apostles of Christ, and preached to us through the prophets, let us renounce all things in the world until death. Clement, however, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, makes what is said here about Abraham general, speaking thus: And we therefore, having been called through His will in Christ Jesus, are not justified through ourselves, nor through our own wisdom or understanding or piety or works which we have wrought in holiness of heart, but through faith, through which the Almighty God has justified all who have existed from the beginning of time.

It was wrongly stated in the Prolegomena that the Apostle's phrase ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην is explained as: GOD held it as an excellent and highly praiseworthy thing; here the subject is justification: not, however, what God holds as an excellent thing. Nor is faith viewed as a quality or virtue, but insofar as it apprehends the merit or obedience of Christ. Nor is faith here considered in the category of action, or as a work, lest any work be mixed into justification, but in the category of relation, and with respect to Christ the blessed seed, who had promised that He would be a shield to Abraham, by averting any evils, and a very great reward by bestowing any good things: (as we showed in the Commentary on Gen. ch. XV. 6. and in the Biblical Illustrations of the O.T. at the same place) whom faith receives and embraces along with His merit. Therefore faith is opposed here, when it is imputed for righteousness, to works, and a man is said to be justified not as full of good works, but as endowed with faith v. 5. τῷ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ πιςεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ, λογίζεται ἡ πίσις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. Faith therefore apprehending Christ, who is Jehovah our righteousness Jerem. XXIII. 6. and has been made righteousness for us by GOD 1. Cor. I. 9. is imputed to us for righteousness, not by reason of itself, namely its own virtue, or action, and because of our τὸ πιςεύειν or believing: but by reason of the Object, or Christ apprehended: because the righteousness or obedience of Christ, both active and passive, apprehended by faith, is imputed to us in the divine judgment for righteousness, that is, it is reckoned for our righteousness and obedience, as if we ourselves had performed it. For if one died for all, then all died 2. Cor. V. 15. and God made Him, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, that we might be the righteousness of God in Him v. 21. whence by the obedience and righteousness of this one, many are constituted righteous Rom. V. 19. and in Him we have righteousness Is. XLV. 24. in Him shall all the seed of Israel be justified v. 25. And indeed the matter comes to the same thing, if it is explained orthodoxly, whether we say that faith is imputed for righteousness, or Christ apprehended by faith: because faith is nothing other than the apprehension of Christ and His righteousness; what difference is there, therefore, between the apprehension of Christ being imputed to us, and Christ apprehended being imputed to us. Mr. Dr. Sebastian Schmid, Coll. pr. Bibl. p. 304, explains the Mosaic words thus: Abraham believed GOD, and (the Lord) thought that (which He had promised) to him for righteousness. He had promised, however, so shall thy seed be: in which promise the Messiah was included. And so the Lord imputed the Messiah or the satisfaction of the Messiah, which was especially intended in the promise, to Abraham for righteousness, or thought of it for him as righteousness, or as that which is his righteousness.

Nor is there any reason for the Papists to object that imputation does not signify a mere estimation: but an estimation to which the truth itself corresponds: For as truly as our sins were imputed to Christ in the divine judgment, who for that reason bore them, so truly is the righteousness of Christ imputed to us by GOD, for which reason we are absolved from sins in the divine judgment, and are constituted, or pronounced, righteous. Which not even Cardinal Bellarmine himself, the chief Jesuit, de- could do, Book II on Justification, ch. X, v. 4. Christ is called our righteousness, since He satisfied the Father for us, and He so gives and communicates that satisfaction to us, when He justifies us, that it can be called our satisfaction and righteousness. And in this way it would not be absurd if someone were to say that the righteousness and merits of Christ are imputed to us, when they are given and applied to us, as if we ourselves had satisfied GOD. For thus speaks St. Bernard in Epistle 190 to Innocent: For if one, he says, died for all, then all have died, so that, you see, the satisfaction of one is imputed to all, just as that one bore the sins of all. This is Bellarmine, loc. cit. And in response to the 3rd argument: Our sins are imputed to Christ regarding the debt of satisfying, which He voluntarily undertook; thus, therefore, His righteousness is also imputed to us regarding the satisfaction which He performed for us; the same, ch. XI, response to the 2nd argument. This similitude (of a garment) can be adapted in a sound way, as also the example of the Patriarch Jacob (who put on the garment of the firstborn Esau, and being reputed as the firstborn obtained the blessing and inheritance from his Father, Gen. 27), to imputed righteousness, if one says that it is necessary that we put on the merits of Christ, and being covered by them in a certain way, we ask of GOD the indulgence of sins. For Christ alone could satisfy for our sins, and in fact satisfied out of justice, and that satisfaction is given and applied to us, and is reputed as ours, when we are reconciled to GOD and justified. This again is Bellarmine. Similarly, it was necessary for the most acute Gabriel Vasquez of the Jesuits to concede in 1. 2. Vol. II, disp. 23, ch. 1, that even things extrinsic to us are imputed to us for some effect, such as the merits and obedience of Christ, because not only those things which are within us, but also those of another, by the consideration of which something is given to us, are said to be counted as ours for some effect, as if they were truly ours. What? That Vasquez teaches that Catholics ought to confess this very kind of imputation and application of the merits of Christ (insofar as sins are said to be covered by imputation, and we are reputed just on account of Christ) for this purpose, that we may be rendered just. If you listen to the Walenburg brothers, on the unity of the Church, Book XIV, ch. XI, thesis 48. Catholics (Roman) do not doubt that the righteousness of Christ is a thing extrinsic to us, by and through which we are justified and absolved from sins, with justification taken in the forensic sense: indeed, in thesis 39, they assert that the Council of Trent itself does not deny that men are justified by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, but only denies that they are justified by imputation alone. Furthermore, the same brothers teach in ch. 8 that to impute anything to someone is the same as to count and reckon that thing among those which are his and pertain to him; and that the righteousness of Christ (by which they understand all that which Christ merited by acting and suffering, the active and passive righteousness of Christ) being imputed, the effect is the pardon of the offense, and the pardon of the guilt, and that through it a man is pleasing to GOD. It must be said, they say, Thesis 12, that through the righteousness of Christ given or imputed to us, a man becomes pleasing to GOD (for it is the merit of Christ given to us) because he is a participant in the righteousness of Christ, and therefore, speaking abstractly, he is considered just before GOD, as if he had in himself that from which he would be considered just; it cannot be that the righteousness of Christ is given to a man unless he also becomes pleasing to GOD through the righteousness given to him, unless he is considered just by his righteousness as if given to him. And Thesis 32. Festus Hommius asks: What is that righteousness which we must have, so that appearing before the tribunal of GOD we may be absolved in His judgment, and not condemned? If he speaks of judgment in this life, Catholics will answer that it is the righteousness imputed and given to us, as that which alone is the cause why we are not condemned on account of our sins, but are absolved from them. But we have dealt with these things more copiously in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession. art. 4, ch. 7, § 12.

Nor indeed is there any doubt among the Walenburgs that the form of justification is rightly constituted by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, when justification is taken in the forensic sense: which they do not deny is agreeable to the Scriptures, even if they invent another, but ἀτεργραφῆς, meaning of justification besides, which denotes absolute justification. Those brothers do indeed say, Thesis 27, that the imputation of the righteousness of Christ is the PROXIMATE CONDITION by which the complete account of justification, taken in the principal and forensic sense, is applied to us, and so they deny in the same place that the imputation of the righteousness of Christ is to that extent the form of justification: The imputation, they say, of the righteousness of Christ is the form of our justification, is said wrongly; because it is only a condition by which the imputed righteousness becomes ours in forensic justification. But this is only a logomachy: For imputation is taken either actively on the part of GOD who imputes, or passively, with respect to us, to whom the righteousness of Christ is imputed. In the former sense, the Walenburgs without doubt understand it to be the proximate condition: yet they do not deny that the righteousness imputed to us, or the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, by which the same is ours, apprehended through faith, is the form of justification. For Absolution, they say in Thesis 6, from sins in the judgment of GOD, the remission of sins, and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ is rightly called justification: and Thesis 11, 12. When justification is taken strictly for absolution, we have already said what its form is. Nor is there any doubt that the formal cause of justification taken in the forensic sense is the righteousness of Christ, and the imputation itself acts by way of a condition, so that it may be applied to the Subject. Likewise Thesis 31. When it is said that a man is just and is justified, it can be understood that the justice and merit and satisfaction of Christ are given or imputed to man, and then the formal cause, or rather the condition of the formal cause, so that it may be communicated by GOD to the subject itself, is the application on the PART OF GOD towards us. Thus far there is no dispute. Furthermore, Th. LVIII. No doubt, they say, can exist that we are formally and extrinsically named and called just by imputed justice, just as one is said to be free from a debt of payment for whom another pays. Add also th. XV. If it be asked whether we are constituted perfectly just in the judgment of GOD by the justice of Christ given and imputed to us? We shall answer: We are constituted, or rather considered and held to be perfectly just by that justice extrinsic to us, prior in reason than we are gifted by GOD with inherent justice, without prejudice in this to the judgment of the Church and of those who think more correctly.

But as for what other Papists, as well as Grotius, object regarding the example of Phinehas, to whom in Ps. 106:31 the deed is said to be imputed for justice: that is irrelevant; both because it is not a matter there of the justification of Phinehas before GOD, or of the justice of his person, since a man cannot be justified by one deed, but the fulfillment of the whole law is required if one is to be justified by deeds; but rather it is a matter of the divine approval of the zeal of Phinehas, and of the justice of this singular and heroic deed, which, since it might appear cruel on account of the violent and sudden process against the fornicators, was absolved and pronounced just by divine approval, as having proceeded from pious zeal for the glory of GOD; and also because the phrase there is different, when it is said to be imputed to Phinehas for justice unto generation and generation; by which it is openly hinted that that imputation is to be understood as one which could redound to his descendants, and therefore that it is not a matter of justification, by which someone is absolved from sins before the tribunal of GOD; because this does not pass over, or spread by its fruit and utility to descendants: nay, the Apostle testifies concerning it in this place v. 12, that it does not pertain to those who descend from Abraham through carnal generation, but who follow the footsteps of his faith: then because the deed of Phinehas was singular, and was not proposed for imitation, nor is that imputation unto righteousness to be drawn into an example of justification, as the Apostle testifies here concerning the imputation of faith made to Abraham, that it was written for our sake, to whom it will likewise be imputed, v. 23.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἐπίστευσε δὲ ὁ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ) Fidem DEI pro- missis habuit, quod ipsum praesupponit (ut loquuntur Scholae) egregiam existimationem & de potentia DEI & de optima ejus fide, unde & fiducia in Deum oritur. Phi- lo in loci illius ex Genesi expositione in libro de haerede rerum divinarum μόνῳ Θεῷ χωρὶς ἑτέρου προσπαρακλήσεως, ὦ ῥάδιον πιστεῦσαι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ θνητὸν ᾧ συνεζεύγματα συζυγίαν. Dicitur autem hic Abraham אברהם per πρό- ληψιν, cum in Scripturis ad id tempus vocetur אברם, Ἄβραμ.

Non respici hîc promissionem sobolis, sed bene- dicti seminis, imò semen in promisso semine, quia recepit Dominus, se esse scutum Abrahami, & mercedem ejus valdè magnam: de quà promissio- ne diximus in Comment. ad Genes. Mosaïc. & in Bibl. illustrat. ad Gen. XV. Rectè Flacius: Cre- didit ille non tantùm multitudinem seminis, sed in eâ promissione potissimùm respexit in verba praece- dentia, ubi DEUS jussit eum non timere, sed con- fidere in se, & promisit se fore ei scutum, & merce- dem ejus copiosissimam, & in benedictum semen, in quo solo tùm ipse, tùm & omnes mortales benedici seu à maledictione Dei Gen. III. & legis Gal. IV. li- berari oportebat. Credidit quoque, DEUM esse su- um scutum & mercedem copiosam valdè, ut ibi ei promittitur, in quo omnia spiritualia bona continen- tur. Quod τὸ ἐπίστευσε τῷ Θεῷ fidem DEI promissis habuit, exponit Grotius, eumque praesupponere ait egregiam existimationem, & de potentiâ DEI, & de optimâ ejus fide, unde & fiducia in Deo oriatur, hactenus admittimus, quà existimatio illa non tan- tùm opinationis vel persuasionis est, sed vera fidei divinitùs excitatae in nobis: quia sola persuasio humana ad veram in DEUM fiduciam non suffi- cit; sed praesupponit haec fidem è verbo DEI or- tam de potentiâ & veritate in promissionibus divi- nâ, imprimis de gratiâ DEI in Christo nobis ob- tingente, adeoque de satisfactione & merito Chri- sti: quae notitia & συγκατάθεσις vel assensio certa & indubia nonnisi è verbo DEI haberi potest, quam omninò antecedere fiduciam oportet, si haec debeat esse indubitata, & qualis describitur per πληροφορίαν Rom. IV. 21. Ebr. VI. 11. c. X. 22. παρ- ῥησίαν Col. III. 12. Ebr. III. 6. c. IV. 16. καύχησιν Rom. X. 2. Θάρσον Matth. IX. 22. Joh. XVI. 33.

καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

Sic & 1. Macc. II. 52. Ἀβραὰμ οὐκ ἐν πειρασμῷ εὑρέθη πι- στὸς, καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην; id est, Deus pro re egregia, valdequi laudabili id habuit: ut in Prolegome- nis exposuimus ex loco Ps. CVI. 30. Et meritò sanè, non quod in fide omnes sint virtutes, quas Deus requirit, sed quod virtus maxima caeterarumque est mater & altrix. τελειωτάτη ἀρετῶν πίστις, dixit Philo dicto libro: & fine libri de Abrahamo: τῶν ἐπαίνων τοῦ σοφοῦ κεφαλήν. Libro de linguis: τὴν ὀχυρωτάτην καὶ βεβαιοτάτην διάθεσιν. Sic libro de Coloniis illud ostendam εἰς μαρτυρίαν πίστεως, ait, ἣν ἐπίστευσεν ἡ ψυχὴ τῷ Θεῷ οὐκ ἐκ τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων ἐπιδεικνυμένη τὸ ἀχάριστον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ προσδοκίας τῶν μελλόντων ἀρτηθεῖσα καὶ ἐκκρεμασθεῖσα ἐλπίδος χρηστῆς, καὶ ἀνενδοί- αστα νομίσασα ἤδη παρεῖναι τὰ μὴ παρόντα, διὰ τὴν τοῦ ὑπο- σχομένου βεβαιοτάτην πίστιν. Et libro de ipso Abrahamo: ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν πίστις παρηγόρημα βίου, πλήρωμα χρηστῶν ἐλ- πίδων, ἀφορία μὲν κακῶν, ἀγαθῶν δὲ φορά, κακοδαιμονίας ἀπόγνωσις, εὐσεβείας γνῶσις, εὐδαιμονίας κλῆρος, ἐν ἅπασι βελτίωσις, ἐπερεισαμένη τῷ πάντων αἰτίῳ καὶ δυναμένῳ μὲν πάντα, βουλομένῳ δὲ τὰ ἄριστα. Libro de Caino ut optimum sacrificium, quod DEO offertur, fidem esse. Justinus plane, ut hic Paulus, historiam Abrahami nobis ap- plicans: τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ, διὰ τὴν ὁμοίαν πίσιν ὄντες· ὃν γὰρ τρόπον ἐκεῖνος τῇ φωνῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπίςευσε, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον, καὶ ἡμεῖς τῇ φωνῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῇ διὰ τῶν ἀποσόλων τοῦ χρισοῦ λαληθείσῃ πάλιν, καὶ τῇ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν κηρυχθείσῃ ἡμῖν, πιςεύσαντες, μέχρι τοῦ ἀποθνήσκειν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀποταξώμεθα. Clemens autem in Epistola ad Corinthios, quod hic de Abrahamo dicitur, generale facit sic loquens: Καὶ ἡμεῖς οὖν διὰ θε- λήματος αὐτοῦ ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησοῦ κληθέντες οὐ δι' ἑαυτῶν δικαι- ώμεθα, οὐδὲ διὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας σοφίας ἢ συνέσεως ἢ εὐσεβείας ἢ ἔργων ὧν κατειργασάμεθα ἐν ὁσιότητι καρδίας, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς πίσεως, δι' ἧς πάντας τοὺς ἀπ' αἰῶνος ὁ παντοκράτωρ Θεὸς ἐδικαίωσε.

Perperam ita Phrasin Apostoli ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην explicari, DEUS pro re egregiâ val- deq́; laudabili id habuit, in Prolegom. dictum est; De justificatione hic agitur: non verò, quid Deus pro re egregiâ habeat. Nec fides ut qualitas vel virtus spectatur, sed quatenus apprehendit meri- tum vel obedientiam Christi. Neque fides hîc at- tenditur in prædicamento actionis, vel ut opus, ne opus aliquod justificationi immisceatur, sed in prædicamento relationis, ac respectu Christi semi- nis benedicti, qui receperat se fore Abrahamo scu- tum, mala quævis avertendo, & mercedem valdè magnam bona quævis tribuendo: (ut in Com- ment. in Gen. c. XV. 6. & in Bibl. illustrat. V. T. ad eundem locum oftendimus) quem cum Me- rito suo recipit & complectitur fides. Ideò fides opponitur hîc, cum imputatur ad justitiam, ope- ribus, & justificari dicitur homo non operibus bonis plenus, sed ut fide præditus v. 5. τῷ μὴ ἐργα- ζομένῳ πιςεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ, λο- γίζεται ἡ πίσις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. Fides ergò ap- prehendens Christum, qui est Jehova justitia nostra Jerem. XXIII. 6. factus nobis à DEO est justitia 1. Cor. I. 9. imputatur nobis ad justitiam, non ra- tione sui, propriæ nempè virtutis, vel actionis, & ob nostrum τὸ πιςεύειν vel credere: sed ratione Objecti, vel Christi apprehensi: quia justitia vel obedientia Christi tùm activa, tùm passiva fide ap- prehensa nobis in judicio divino imputatur in justitiam, id est, pro nostrâ reputatur justitiâ & obedientiâ, ac si ipsi eam præstitissemus. Si enim unus pro omnibus mortuus est, utique omnes mortui sunt 2. Cor. V. 15. & Deus eum, qui non novit pecca- tum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut essemus justitia Dei in ipso v. 21. unde per unius istius obedientiam & ju- stitiam justi constituuntur multi Rom. X. 19. & in ipso nos habemus justitiam Es. XLV. 24. in ipso justi- ficatur omne semẽ Israël v. 25. Et sanè res eodem re- cidit, si orthodoxè explicetur, sive dicamus, fidem imputari in justitiam, seu Christum fide apprehen- sum: quia fides nihil aliud est, quàm apprehensio Christi & justitiæ ejus; quid ergò diversi est, Chri- sti apprehensionem nobis imputari, & Christum apprehensum imputari nobis. Dn. D. Sebastian Schmid. Coll. pr. Bibl. p. 304. ita explicat verba Mosaica: Credidit Abraham DEO, & cogitavit (Dominus) illud (quod promiserat) ipsi justi- tiam. Promiserat autem, sic erit semen tuum: in quâ promissione includebatur Messias. Itaque Do- minus Messiam seu Messiæ satisfactionem in pro- missione maximè intentam imputavit Abrahamo in justitiam, vel cogitavit illi tanquam justitiam, seu quod sit ejus justitia.

Nec est, quod obvertant Papistæ, imputationem non significare nudam existimationem: sed existi- mationem, cui veritas ipsa respondeat: Nam quàm verè imputata Christo sunt peccata nostra in ju- dicio divino, qui eadem ideo portavit, tàm verè imputatur nobis à DEO Christi justitia, qui ideò in judicio divino à peccatis absolvimur, & justi constituimur, vel pronunciamur. Quod nec ipse Bellarminus Cardinalis, ac præcipuus Jesuita ne- gare potuit, l. II. de Justif. c. X. v. 4. Dicitur Chri- stus justitia nostra, quoniam satisfecit Patri pro no- bis, & eam satisfactionem ita nobis donat, & com- municat, cum nos justificat, ut nostra satisfactio & justitia dici possit. Et hoc modo non esset absurdum, si quis diceret, nobis imputari Christi justitiam, & merita, cum nobis donantur, & applicantur, ac si nos ipsi DEO satisfecissemus. Sic enim loquitur S. Bernardus in Epistola CXC. ad Innocentium: Nam si unus, inquit, pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt, ut vid. satisfactio unius omnibus imputetur, sicut omnium peccata unus ille portavit. Haec Bellarm. l. c. Et resp. ad 3. argum. Imputantur Christo peccata nostra, quoad debitum satisfaciendi, quod ille sponte suscepit, sic igitur & nobis imputatur justitia ejus quoad satis- factionem, quam pro nobis praestitit; Idem c. XI. resp. ad 2. argum. Potest sano modo accommodari haec similitudo (indumenti) ut etiam exemplum Patriarchae Jacobi (qui vestem primogeniti Esavi induit, ac pro primogenito reputatus benedictionem & haereditatem a Patre obtinuit Gen. XXVII.) justitiae imputatae, si quis dicat, oportere, ut indua- mus Christi merita, & illis quodammodo tegi, pe- tamus a DEO indulgentiam peccatorum. Nam solus Christus pro peccatis nostris satisfacere potuit, & reipsa ex justitia satisfecit, & illa satisfactio nobis donatur & applicatur, & nostra reputatur, cum DEO reconciliamur & justificamur. Haec iterum Bellarminus. Similiter Jesuitarum acutis- simum Gabrielem Vasquezium concedere opor- tuit in 1. 2. Tom. II. disp. XXIII. c. 1. imputari nobis ad aliquem effectum etiam aliqua nobis ex- trinseca, ut merita & obedientiam Christi, quia non modo ea, quae nobis insunt, sed etiam aliena, intui- tu quorum nobis aliquid donatur, computari di- cuntur nostra ad aliquem effectum, ac si revera nostra essent. Quid? quod doceat Vasquezius, hoc ipsum genus imputationis & applicationis merito- rum Christi (quatenus peccata dicuntur tegi per imputationem, & justi nos reputamur propter Chri stum) fateri debere Catholicos ad hoc, ut nos justi reddamur. Fratres Walenburgicos si audias, de unit. Eccles. l. XIV. c. XI. th. XLIIX. Catholici (Romani) non dubitant, quin justitia Christi no- bis extrinseca sit res ea, per & propter quam justifi- camur & absolvimus a peccatis, justificatione in sensu forensi accepta: imo th. XXXIX. asserunt, ipsummet Concilium Tridentinum non negare ho- mines justificari, imputatione justitiae Christi, sed negare tantum sola imputatione justificari. Do- cent praeterea iidem Fratres c. IIX. imputare quic- quam alicui idem esse, atque inter ea, quae sunt ipsius, & ad eum pertinent, illud connumerare & recensere; ac justitia Christi, (per quam omne il- lud, quod Christus agendo, patiendoque promeruit, activam & passivam justitiam Christi intelligunt) imputata effectum esse condonationem offensae, & condonationem reatus, & quod per eam homo sit DEO gratus. Dicendum, inquiunt, Th. XII. quod per justitiam Christi nobis donatam seu imputatam homo fit DEO gratus (est enim meritum Christi nobis donatum) quia est particeps justitiae Christi, & proinde abstractive loquendo, justus censetur co- ram DEO, ac si in seipso haberet, unde justus cen- seretur, fieri non potest, ut justitia Christi homini donetur, nisi etiam gratus fiat DEO per justitiam sibi donatam, nisi censeatur justus a sua justitia tanquam sibi donata. Et Th. XXXII. Quaerit Fe- stus Hommius: Quaenam sit illa justitia, quam nos habere debemus, ut coram DEI tribunali com- parentes in ejus judicio absolvamur, & non con- demnemur? Si loquatur de judicio in hac vita, respondebunt Catholici, esse justitiam nobis impu- tatam & donatam, ut quæ sola sit causa, cur non con- demnemur ob peccata nostra, sed ab iis absolvamur. Sed de his copiosius egimus in Exegem. August. Confess. art. IV. c. VII. §. XII.

Neque vero dubium est penes Walenburgicos, formam justificationis recte constitui imputationem justitiæ Christi, cum justificatio sensu forensi acci- pitur: quem Scripturæ consentaneum esse, non inficiantur, etsi aliam, sed ἀτεργραφῆς, præterea fingant justificationis significationem, quæ abso- lutam justificationem notet. Dicunt quidem Fra- tres illi, Th. XXVII. imputationem justitiæ Christi esse CONDITIONEM PROXIMAM, qua princi- palis & in sensu forensi acceptæ justificationis com- pleta ratio nobis applicetur, adeoque negant ibi- dem eatenus imputationem justitiæ Christi esse for- mam justificationis: Imputationem, inquiunt, justi- tiæ Christi esse formam justificationis nostræ, male dicitur; quia est tantum conditio, qua justitia im- putata in justificatione forensi fit nostra. Sed hæc λογομαχία tantum est: Nam imputatio accipitur vel active ex parte DEI imputantis, vel passive, respectu nostri, quibus imputatur justitia Christi. Priori sensu conditionem proximam esse sine du- bio intelligunt Walenburgici: non tamen negant justitiam nobis imputatam, vel imputationem ju- stitiæ Christi, qua eadem nostra est, per fidem ap- prehensa, formam esse justificationis. Nam Ab- solutio, inquiunt Th. VI. à peccatis in judicio DEI remissio peccatorum, & imputatio justitiæ Christi recte dicitur justificatio: & Th. XI. XII. Quando justificatio restricte sumitur pro absolutione, que- nam sit ejus forma jam diximus. Neque enim du- bium est, quin justificationis in sensu forensi acceptæ causa formalis sit justitia Christi, ipsaque imputatio habeat se per modum conditionis, ut ea Subjecto ap- plicetur. Item Th. XXXI. Quando dicitur homo justus & justificari, id potest intelligi, quod homini detur seu imputetur justitia & meritum & satis- factio Christi, & tunc causa formalis vel potius conditio causa formalis, ut ipsa Subjecto a DEO communicetur, est applicatio ex PARTE DEI erga nos. Hactenus nulla lis est. Porro Th. LVIII. Nullum, inquiunt, potest esse dubium, quin forma- liter extrinsece justi nominemur, & dicamur, à ju- stitia imputata, sicut dicitur liber a debito solven- di, pro quo alius solvit. Adde & th. XV. Si peta- tur, an in judicio DEI perfecte justi constituamur justitia Christi nobis donata, & imputata? Respon- debimus: Nos justitia illa nobis extrinseca & per- fectissima constitui vel potius censeri haberique per- fecte justos prius ratione quam donemur a DEO justitia inhærente, salvo in hoc Ecclesiæ & rectius sen- tientium judicio.

Quod autem alii Pontificii, ut & Grotius ob- vertunt exemplum Phineæ, cui Ps. CVI. 31. factum imputatum dicitur ad justitiam: id ἀλλότριον est; tum quia ibi non de justificatione Phineæ coram DEO, vel de justitia personæ agitur, quum ex uno facto homo justificari non possit, sed requi- ratur totius legis impletio, si per facta justificari debeat; sed de approbatione zeli Phineæ divina, & de justitia facti hujus singularis & heroici, quod cum videri possit truculentum ob violentum & subitum processum adversus fornicantes, divina approbatione absolutum & justum pronuncia- tum est, utpote è pio zelo pro gloria DEI profe- ctum, tum quia phrasis ibi diversa est, cum im- putatum dicitur Phineæ in justitiam in generatio- nem & generationem; quo innuitur aperte, eam imputationem intelligendam esse, quæ redunda- re in posteros potuerit, adeoque non agi de justifi- catione, qua quis coram tribunali DEI à pecca- tis abfolvitur; quia hæc non tranfit, aut fructû & utilitate fua diffunditur ad pofteros: imo de ea hoc in loco Apoftolus v. 12. teftatur, quod non perti- neat ad eos, qui per carnalem generationem ex Abrahamo defcendunt, fed qui veftigia fidei ejus fectantur: tum quia factum Phineæ fingulare fuit, nec propofitum eft ad imitationem, neque illa im- putatio ad juftitiam in exemplum juftificationis tra- henda, uti hic de imputatione fidei Abrahæ factæ Apoftolus teftatur, quod fcripta sit propter nos, qui- bus pariter imputabitur, v. 23.

## 4:4
V. 4. To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt.

A similitude taken from men. Just as he who performs works for someone is not for that reason his friend; but receives a reward corresponding to the work; so also, he who by native strength, as he is able, obeys the commandments of GOD outwardly in some way, has a reward, is freed from punishments, and possesses the promised land in his own time: but he does not for that reason become a friend: which is said concerning Abraham in Isaiah LI. 8, 2 Chronicles XX. 7, James II. 27. Nothing makes friends except a similarity of wills. χάρις here signifies favor and friendship, as above II. 23, see what is below v. 1 and at Luke XVII. 10.

Latin:

V. 4. τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ μισθὸς ᾀ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα.

Similitudo ab hominibus defumpta. Sicut qui ope- ras alicui præftat, non ideo amicus eft illius; fed merce- dem accipit operæ refpondentem; fic etiam, qui nativa vi, ut poteft, DEI præceptis exterius aliquo modo pa- ret, habet mercedem, liberatur à fuppliciis, ac terram pro- miffam fuo tempore poffidet: fed non ideo fit amicus: quod de Abrahamo dicitur Efaiæ LI. 8. 2. Paral. XX. 7. Jacobi II. 27. Amicos non facit, nifi voluntatum fimili- tudo. χάρις hic favorem amicitiamque fignificat, ut fupra II. 23. vide quæ infra v. 1. & ad Lucam XVII. 10.

## 4:5
V. 5. But to the one not working.

That is, even if he does nothing, perhaps destitute of opportunity.

But to the one believing in Him who justifies the ungodly.

That is, to him who trusts in this GOD, so that by the work of GOD he may become good, even if he had previously been impious, that is, an idolater, such as Abraham had been, according to Philo in his book on Abraham, the book on migration, the book on piety, and the book on rewards: Josephus in his ancient history l. 8, and Maimonides in more than one place: which opinion is confirmed by the passage in Joshua XXIV. 2, although most Rabbis deny it.

His faith is reckoned unto righteousness.

That faith profits him greatly, being highly esteemed by GOD.

These strange glosses, newly devised, are plainly alien to the mind and treatment of the Apostle.
