There is no similitude here taken from men, but it is a matter of a twofold imputation that can be established in the judgment of GOD: namely, that one is from debt; when someone works with a view to a reward, to whom, if he works as is right, or as the divine law requires, the reward is not imputed from grace, but from debt; but another is from grace, when someone does not trust in works, but trusts solely in GOD, who freely justifies the ungodly through faith, to whom that faith is imputed unto righteousness. Nor does χάρις here denote friendship, but divine grace and mercy, as is clear from chapter III. 23, 24, where it is joined with the word δωρεὰν (freely), and from the opposite, because χάρις (grace) is opposed to τῷ ὀφειλήματι (to the debt), and also from the declaration of this grace in Romans V. 15 ff., c. XI. 6. Eph. II. 4 ff., where God is called rich in mercy, on account of this grace, and the riches of divine grace are proclaimed in the justification of man. It is not a matter of friendship, which is conciliated by a similarity of wills, but of justification before GOD: which the Apostle teaches is obtained not through works, but through faith alone, because Abraham's faith was imputed unto righteousness from grace, not from debt, and was imputed to μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ (the one not working), but only to the one believing; not that Abraham was destitute of works, or of the opportunity to do good, since these things were said of him in the midst of his course of good works: Abraham believed, and it was imputed to him unto righteousness, but so that it might be taught that in that imputation and justification GOD did not look at the works of Abraham, but solely at his faith: and that he did not work with a view to a reward, but trusted solely in the grace of GOD. Therefore, the Grotian interpretation openly contradicts the Apostolic sentiment: for the Apostle here proves his main theme by the example of Abraham, that man is justified by faith, not by works, because Abraham was justified from grace, and faith was imputed to him unto righteousness without works, as is evident from v. 6 and the parallel passage Gal. II. 5, 6 ff. And therefore he excludes the imputation which belongs to the worker, which is of reward, which is from debt. Grotius, on the contrary, wishes to maintain here an imputation through the performance of works, and indeed of a reward corresponding to the work, and proportionate, and therefore from debt. The Apostle, by the name τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ (the one working), does not mean him who obeys the commandments outwardly in some way, but him who relies on works performed in any way whatsoever and however great they may be, as the blessed Luther rightly understands, 'dem, der mit Wercken umgehet' (he who busies himself with works), as if the reward were to be given to him from debt, not from mere grace. Grotius, on the other hand, twists [the passage] toward him who, by the power of his nature, as he is able, obeys the commandments of GOD in some outward manner, and assigns to him both a reward, as he speaks, corresponding to his effort, and a liberation from punishments; which liberation, however, from the wrath of GOD and the penalty of sin is obtained only by the grace of GOD, just as GOD does not bestow a reward except out of grace, and only upon those whom He receives into grace, without whom we cannot please Him, Heb. XI. 6, nor does GOD remit the penalty without the remission of guilt: and those to whom He remits guilt and penalty, He does not disdain to honor with the status of friends, nay, of His own sons and heirs: because through faith He gave us the power τέκνα θεῦ γενέσθαι [to become children of God] Joh. I. 12, and we are all sons of GOD through faith in Christ Jesus Gal. III. 26.

But that χάρις signifies favor and friendship, not which we obtain by faith, but [which is] of our will in conformity with the divine, that indeed does not appear from Rom. II. 23, ch. V. 1, or even Luc. XVII. 10, although it is certain that the pursuit of such conformity follows faith and reception into grace, and is the fruit thereof. 1 Joh. III. 3. Everyone who has this hope in Him (which is trust itself in Christ, or certainly without it, it does not exist) sanctifies (ἁγνίζει purifies) himself, just as He is holy. Thus Chrysostom, with the Apostle, attributes the friendship of God not to our works, but to the merit of Christ: He reconciled, that is, He made them friends to Himself through Christ: For this is the admirable thing, not that GOD was made a friend only, but that He was a friend in such a way. How in such a way? Ἀφεὶς αὐτοῖς τὰ ἁμαρτήματα; ἄλλως γὰρ ὐκ ἦν: having dismissed their sins. For otherwise it could not be.

It is also mere distortion that 'to him who does not work' here means 'even if he does nothing,' perhaps being destitute of opportunity. For (1.) 'he who works' and 'he who believes' are simply opposed, so that righteousness is obtained not by the one working, but by the one believing, not through works but through faith. By that very fact, therefore, any works and the one working in any way are removed here: Works do nothing toward this righteousness. The one working, in that he works, does not attain justification at all. (2) That 'even if' Grotius rashly and of his own accord inserts, of which there is neither letter nor sense in the text. (3.) Abraham, whose example was brought forward to confirm the Apostolic theme, was neither destitute of the opportunity of working, nor did he lack good works; yet he did not attain righteousness by working, or by the act of working, but by believing, or as one believing, and by believing. (4.) The opportunity of working is never lacking to us, if not of working outwardly, at least as regards internal works: if not in effect, at least in affection: if not as regards ourselves, or as regards our neighbor, at least as regards GOD. (5.) He who is here the 'one who does not work' according to the Apostle, who DOES NOT WORK, but only BELIEVES, [is not] because works can be absent from faith as regards existence: because neither are any works good without faith, just as an effect cannot exist without a cause, nor can faith exist without works, just as a soul (in the body) can be cannot exist without motion, the sun's light without rays, but that faith alone, without works, apprehends and obtains righteousness, to the apprehension and attainment of which works contribute nothing, and have no influence, no regard. Charity certainly, in which is the sum of the law, does not extend itself to apprehending the Evangelical promise, or the remission of sins and righteousness promised by GOD freely, which faith alone apprehends, receives, embraces, and applies to itself, and thus also attains, procures, and obtains.

Furthermore, since the object of faith is established as ὁ δικαιῶν τὸν ἀσεβῆ, that is, GOD insofar as He has promised in the word of grace, or the Gospel, that He wills freely, and out of grace on account of the redemption of Christ, to justify the ungodly, that is, to remit to him all sins, and to pronounce him righteous, provided he believes, and does not reject this grace offered in the word of promise, but embraces and receives it by faith: is it not a perversion, when the believing in GOD who justifies is explained, entirely against the mind and scope of the Apostle, as referring to him who trusts in this GOD, not because He judicially justifies the ungodly, or absolves the ungodly person standing before His tribunal, without regard to works (which the ungodly person does not bring, nor can bring into judgment), solely seeking and embracing the grace of GOD by faith, from all impiety, but because he is going to be good by the help of GOD, even if he had previously been ungodly. For the ungodly is said to be justified, not he who was previously ungodly, but he who, on account of impiety, would still be condemned by the force of divine law when he appears before the throne of GOD, unless God, out of grace on account of Christ, who received, bore, and expiated our impiety and the sin of the whole world, and thus on account of the satisfaction of Christ, should remit and pardon to us, as He promises in the Gospel, the impiety and all sins of such an ungodly person, who flees to that grace and looks to it by faith. Who, when he has obtained the remission of sins, by the help of God, or aided by the Holy Spirit, thereafter strives for good works, and devotes effort to true holiness. Which works, indeed, according to the Rule of Augustine, follow the justified, but do not precede the one to be justified. And this faith, which we have spoken of, is said, according to the mind of the Apostle, not only to be highly esteemed by GOD, and not only to profit the believer greatly, but TO BE IMPUTED TO HIM FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS, so that he is held righteous before GOD, there being reckoned to him not his own righteousness, which is here excluded by the Apostle, but the mediatorial righteousness of Christ, which alone avails before GOD, apprehended by faith. For He has been made righteousness for us by GOD: and by the obedience of this one alone are we constituted righteous, as many as are justified.

Latin:

V. 5. τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ.

Id eft, etiamfi nihil operetur, occafione forte defti- tutus.

πισέυοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ.

Id eft, ei qui in hoc DEO fidit, ut DEI ope fiat bonus, etiamfi ante fuiffet impius, id eft, idololatra, qualis fuerat Abrahamus, fecundum Philonem libro de Abrahamo, libro περὶ ἀποικίας, libro de pietate & libro de præmiis: Jofe- phum antiquæ hiftoriæ l. 8. & Maimoniden plus uno loco: quam fententiam firmat locus Jofuæ XXIV. 2. quanquam Rabbinis plerisque id negantibus.

λογίζεται ἡ πίσις ἀυτῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

Illa fides ei plurimum prodeft, quippe à DEO magni æftimata.

Gloffæ hæ ftrahæ noviter excogitatæ plane alienæ funt à mente & tractatione Apoftolica. Non fimilitudo hic ab hominibus defumta habe- tur, fed de gemina, quæ in judicio DEI ftatui poffit, imputatione agitur: quod nempe alia fit ex debito; cum quis intuitu mercedis operatur, cui, fi operetur uti par eft, vel lex divina requirit, non ex gratia imputatur merces, fed ex debito; alia vero ex gratia, cum quis non confidit operibus, fed unice confidit DEO, gratis impium per fi- dem juftificanti, cui fides illa imputatur ad jufti- tiam. Nec χάρις hic amicitiam notat, fed gra- tiam & mifericordiam divinam, ut è cap. III. 23. 24. liquet, ubi cum voce δωρεὰν gratis conjungitur, & ex oppofito, quia τῷ ὀφειλήματι debito op- ponitur χάρις gratia, nec non è gratiæ hujus de- claratione Rom. V. 15. feqq. c. XI. 6. Eph. II. 4 feqq. ubi dives mifericordia Deus dicitur, ob hanc gra- tiam, & divitiæ gratiæ divinæ prædicantur in ju- ftificatione hominis. Non agitur de amicitia, quæ voluntatum fimilitudine conciliatur, fed de juftificatione coram DEO: quam non per opera, fed folum per fidem obtingere docet Apoftolus, quia ex gratia imputata fides Abrahæ ad juftiti- am, non ex debito, & μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ non operanti, fed tantum πισέυοντι imputata; non quod Abra- ham operibus deftitutus fuerit, aut occafione be- ne operandi, fiquidem in medio bonorum operum curfu hæc de ipfo dicta fint: Credidit Abraham, & imputatum eft ei ad juftitiam, fed ut doceatur, in imputatione illa & juftificatione non refpexiffe DEUM opera Abrahæ, fed unice fidem ejusdem: neque operatum eum effe intuitu mercedis, fed unice confifum fuiffe gratiæ DEI. Repugnat er- go palam interpretatio Grotiana Apoftolicæ fen- tentiæ: Apoftolus enim hic thema fuum princi- pale exemplo Abrahami probat, hominem justifi- cari fide, non operibus, quia ex gratia justificatus est Abraham, fidesque ei imputata est ad justitiam sine operibus, ut e v. 6. & loco parallelo Gal. II. 5. 6. seqq. constat. Ideoque imputationem exclu- dit, quæ operanti sit, quæ mercedis est, quæ ex de- bito. Grotius ex adverso hic tradi vult imputa- tionem per præstationem operum, & mercedis qui- dem operæ respondentis, & proportionatæ, adeo- que ex debito. Apostolus τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ nomine non eum, qui præceptis exterius aliquo modo pa- ret, sed qui operibus quomodocunque præstitis & quanta quanta illa sint, nititur, ut recte B. Lu- therus dem, der mit Wercken umgehet, intelligit, quasi ex debito tribuenda ipsi merces sit non ex mera gratia. Grotius contra ad eum, qui nativæ vi, ut potest, DEI præceptis exterius aliquo modo paret, detorquet, & ei tum mercedem, uti loqui- tur, operæ respondentem, tum liberationem a sup- pliciis assignat, quæ vero liberatio ab ira DEI, & pœna peccati, non nisi gratia DEI obtinetur, uti neque mercedem DEUS tribuit, nisi ex gratia, & iis solum, quos in gratiam recipit, cui sine fide placere non possumus Ebr. XI. 6. neque pœnam remittit DEUS sine remissione culpæ: & quibus culpam & pœnam remittit, illos amicorum, imo filiorum suorum, & hæredum axiomate non de- dignatur: quia per fidem potestatem dedit nobis τέκνα θεῦ γενέσθαι Joh. I. 12. sumusque omnes filii DEI per fidem in Christum Jesum Gal. III. 26.

Quod vero χάρις favorem amicitiamque signi- ficat, non quam fide consequimur, sed voluntatis nostræ cum divina conformatione, id vero è Rom. II. 23. c. V. 1. aut etiam Luc. XVII. 10. non appa- ret, etsi certum sit conformationis ejusmodi stu- dium fidem & receptionem in gratiam consequi, ejusque fructum esse. 1. Joh. III. 3. Omnis qui ha- bet hanc spem in eo (quæ est fiducia ipsa in Chri- stum, vel certe sine ea non est) sanctificat (ἁγνί-ζει purificat) se, sicut & ille sanctus est. Ita amici- tiam Dei non operibus nostris, sed merito Chri- sti tribuit cum Apostolo Chrysostomus: Recon- ciliavit, h. e. amicos sibi fecit per Christum: Hoc enim est admirabile, non quod amicus est factus so- lum DEUS, sed quod sic amicus. Quomodo sic? Ἀφεὶς αὐτοῖς τὰ ἁμαρτήματα; ἄλλως γὰρ ὐκ ἦν: dimissis peccatis. Aliter enim non poterat.

Mera etiam σρεβλότης est, τῷ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ hic esse, etiam si nihil operetur, occasione forte destitu- tus. Nam (1.) simpliciter opponitur ὁ ἐργαζόμε- νος, & ὁ πισεύων, ita ut non operanti, sed creden- ti, non per opera sed per fidem justitia obtingat. Eo ipso igitur quævis opera, & quomodocunque operans hic removentur: Opera nihil facere ad hanc justitiam. Operantem qua operatur justifica- tionem minime consequi. (2) Illud ʇʂɪ temere & de suo ingerit Grotius, cujus in textu nec li- tera nec sensus habetur. (3.) Abraham, cujus exemplum confirmando themati Apostolico ad- ductum est, neque occasione operandi destitutus fuit, neque operibus bonis caruit; nec tamen ju- stitiam consequutus est, ἐργαζόμενος operans, vel operando, sed πισεύων, vel credens, & credendo, (4.) Nunquam deest nobis operandi occasio, si non operandi extrinsece, saltem qua opera in- terna: si non effectu, saltem affectu: si non quoad nos ipsos, vel quoad proximum, saltem quoad De- um. (5.) Is, qui Apostolus hic ὁ μὴ ἐργαζόμενος est, qui NON OPERATUR, sed solum CREDIT, non quod opera à fide abesse possint, quoad exi- stentiam: quia nec opera ulla bona sunt sine fide, uti effectus esse nequit sine causa, nec fides esse potest sine operibus, uti anima (in corpore) esse nequit sine motu, solis lumen sine radiis, sed quod fides sola, sine operibus, apprehendat, & obtineat justitiam, ad cujus apprehensionem & consequu- tionem nihil cooperantur opera, nullumque in- fluxum, nullum respectum habent. Charitas certe, in qua summa legis est, non extendit sese ad ap- prehendendam promissionem Evangelicam, vel promissam DEI gratis remissionem peccatorum & justitiam, quam sola fides apprehendit, recipit, amplectitur, sibique applicat, adeoque etiam con- sequitur, impetrat & obtinet.

Porro fidei Objectum quum constituatur ὁ δι- καιῶν τὸν ἀσεβῆ, id est, DEUS quatenus promisit in verbo gratiæ, vel Evangelio, se gratis, & ex gratia propter redemtionem Christi velle justifica- re impium, id est, remittere ipsi omnia peccata, eumque justum pronunciare, modo credat, & hanc oblatam in verbo promissionis gratiam non re- spuat, sed fide amplectatur, & suscipiat: annon perversio est, cum τὸ credere in DEUM justifican- tem prorsus contra mentem & scopum Apostoli, de eo explicatur, qui in hoc DEO fidit, non quod judicialiter impium justificet, vel coram tribunali suo constitutum impium, citra intuitum operum (quæ non adfert, nec adferre potest in judicium impíus) solum fide gratiam DEI expetentem & amplectentem ab impietate omni absolvat, sed quod DEI ope bonus sit futurus, etiamsi ante fuisset impius. Justificari enim dicitur impius, non qui ante fuit impius, sed qui ob impietatem vi legis divinæ condemnandus adhuc esset, cum coram throno DEI comparet, nisi Deus ex gratia pro- pter Christum, qui impietatem nostram & pec- catum totius mundi in se recepit, tulit, & expia- vit, adeoque propter satisfactionem Christi no- bis, ut in Evangelio promittit, impietatem, & peccata universa, impio tali, ad gratiam illam con- fugienti eandemque fide suspicienti remitteret & condonaret. Qui, ubi remissionem peccatorum consecutus est, Dei ope, vel Spiritus S. adjutu, operibus bonis deinceps studet, veræque sancti- tati operam navat. Quæ vero opera, juxta Regu- lam Augustini, sequuntur justificatum, non vero præcedunt justificandum. Atque ista fides, quam diximus, ex mente Apostoli non modo à DEO multum æstimari, nec solum credenti plurimum prodesse dicitur, sed IMPUTARI EIDEM IN JUSTITIAM, ita, ut coram DEO justus habea- tur, accensita ei non justitia propria, quæ hic ex- cluditur ab Apostolo, sed justitia mediatoria Chri- sti, quæ sola coram DEO valet, fide apprehensa. Hic enim à DEO nobis factus est justitia: & hu- jus unius obedientia justi constituimur unice, quotquot justificamur.

## 4:6
V. 6. καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Δαβὶδ λέγει τὸν μακαρισμὸν τῶ ἀνθρώπω. Ps. XXXII. which the inscription teaches to be David's; μακαρισμὸς also for Aristotle and Ammonius is a congratulation and a proclamation of another's happiness.

ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων. Even if works are not yet present, because in that place of the Psalm no mention is made of works, but of a spirit devoid of guile, that is, sincere in the pursuit of piety.

Latin:

V. 6. καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Δαβὶδ λέγει τὸν μα- καρισμὸν τῶ ἀνθρώπω. Pl. XXXII. quam Davidis esse docet inscriptio, μακαρισ- μὸς etiam Aristoteli & Ammonio est gratulatio & prædica- tio felicitatis alienæ.

ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων. Etiamsi opera nondum adsint, quia in illo Psalmi loco nulla fit mentio operum, sed animi dolo carentis, id est, sin- ceri in pietatis studio.

## 4:7
V. 7. μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι. In the Hebrew נשוי פשע, those whose iniquity has been taken away, that is, those who have ceased to be wicked, just as David had changed his life after that crime against Uriah. The Greek has the same sense, but by metonymy. For GOD does not plainly pardon grave crimes, except to those who have already begun to change their life, Ezek. XVIII. Origen is undeservedly beaten here by some.

καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Just as in a healed body the wound does not appear, so neither in a healed soul do those crimes that once were. A subsequent benefit does not allow the injury to appear, says Seneca: so also innocence supervening through faith obliterates every stain from former offenses.

Latin:

V. 7. μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι. In Hebræo נשוי פשע, quibus ablata est improbitas, id est, qui improbi esse desierunt, sicut David post illud in Uriam facinus vitam mutaverat. Græcum eundem habet sensum, sed per μετωνυμίαν. Neque enim plane condonat DEUS gravia crimina, nisi iis, qui vitam jam mutare ince- perunt, Ezech. XVIII. Immerito hic à quibusdam vapulat Origenes.

καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Sicut in persanato corpore non apparet vulnus, ita nec in animo sanato ea quæ olim fuere crimina. Beneficium superveniens injuriam apparere non patitur, ait Seneca : sic & innocentia per fidem superveniens omnem ex priori- bus delictis labem obliterat.

## 4:8
V. 8. μακάριό ἀνὴρ ᾧ ὐ μὴ λογίσηται κύριό ἁμαρτίαν.

That is, in whom GOD finds nothing for which He may be angry with him. For חשׁב which is here translated λογίζεσθαι, Zech. VII. 10, is μνησικακεῖν. These things thus describe the friendship of man with GOD, χάριν θεῦ. The simile is drawn from the accounts of contracting parties, where he to whom something is imputed or charged as an expense, must pay it. See what we have said in Book II of the Law of War and Peace, XIX. 2, with the annotations.

This is the Apostle's proof: that David testifies that his blessedness and salvation belong to him to whom GOD imputes righteousness without works, that is, not his own righteousness: for that cannot be imputed without works, since it consists in works; but another's, which is none other than the righteousness of Christ. But how does David testify to this? When he says that they are blessed whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered: that the man is blessed to whom GOD does not impute sin. Whence it is clear that Paul considers it the same thing for GOD to forgive iniquities, to cover sins, and not to impute sins, as for GOD to impute righteousness without works: otherwise the Apostle's proof would be null. And therefore justification according to David is when sins are not imputed, when sins are forgiven and covered; according to Paul it is when righteousness is imputed without works: and consequently the non-imputation of sin and the imputation of righteousness without works, that is, of the righteousness of Christ, must in reality be one and the same thing. For when a person's own iniquity is not imputed to the ungodly, the ungodly is absolved and pronounced righteous; similarly, when the righteousness of another is imputed to the ungodly, it is necessary that the ungodly be absolved and pronounced righteous. The foundation, therefore, that the ungodly is absolved μὴ ἐργαζόμενω, not working, not bringing his own righteousness to the divine judgment, but only πιστεύων, believing and by faith apprehending the righteousness of Christ, is the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, or as Paul has it, His righteousness, which alone avails before GOD χωρὶς ἔργων without works, which alone—and not indeed works, and thus without works—GOD regards in the absolutory judgment, and credits to the ungodly man who is not working but believing. Even the Papists themselves acknowledge this emphasis of the word imputation in this place; Soto says: Paul explains in this most beautiful and most convenient speech both that which he had said, that faith is reckoned for righteousness, and most clearly the reason for our justification. For since we are not able to pay GOD, He Himself credits our debt to us, that is, He considers it as paid, provided only that we apply faith to Him who makes the promise. Salmero: To credit (for thus the Latin rendered the word imputed, to credit) is to remit a debt and to hold as paid that which is not paid. Hence the term of the jurists, accepti latio: which is done by question and answer, so that the debtor, who is not able to pay, says to the creditor: Do you have as accepted all that which I owed you? Upon his responding, I have, and I credit it, then the debtor is absolved from the debt and is held as a payer, even if no payment intervenes, and thus accepti latio is opposed to just payment. So he. But because GOD, without prejudice to His justice, cannot absolve a debtor unless a just payment intervenes, which the debtor cannot provide, He imputes the payment provided by the Mediator Christ to the ungodly man who is not working but believing in Christ, and thus credits the payment of Christ apprehended by faith as if the debtor himself had provided it. How Bellarmine above expressly stated, that Christ has satisfied, and so gives and communicates that satisfaction to us when He justifies us, that it can be called our satisfaction and righteousness, and so it is not absurd if someone says that the righteousness and merits of Christ are imputed to us, when they are given and applied to us, just as if we ourselves had made satisfaction. The Cardinal indeed adds, provided it is not denied that there is in us, besides this, a true and absolute righteousness to which, by the just judgment of GOD, not punishment but glory is due. But that is openly against the Apostle, who teaches that the righteousness of Christ is imputed in the judgment of GOD without works; and so he excludes inherent righteousness here, nay, he says that he justifies the ungodly, and μὴ ἐργαζόμενον. And how, by the just judgment of GOD, would glory be due to our works or to our inherent righteousness, when all must pray against the judgment of GOD according to righteousness, and flee to mercy alone? Furthermore, what need would there be before the judgment of GOD for the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, i.e., of another, if our inherent righteousness were a true and absolute righteousness to which glory is due? and shall we not thus be able to boast before GOD in our own works, if they are the same absolute righteousness to which glory is due by merit? Finally, whence does it come that we are not to suffer eternal punishments, and that we obtain remission of sin, if not from the righteousness of Christ? For the remission of guilt and eternal punishment is the effect of the satisfaction of Christ, which is conferred and applied to us by justification, as Bellarmine says διαρρήδην. But whence does it come that we have the remission of guilt and eternal punishment, from that same source it also entirely comes that we have eternal glory. For there is not one reason for the remission of guilt and eternal punishment, and another for eternal life and glory; which is equally χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ, a gift of GOD in Christ Jesus, and not indeed due to us by the just judgment of GOD for our inherent righteousness, Rom. VI. 23. Indeed, when the righteousness and merits of Christ are communicated and given to us, i.e., righteousness is imputed to us, guilt is remitted, and so it comes about that we are neither to suffer eternal punishments, and that we are to have eternal life, no differently than if we had never sinned, nay, had fulfilled the law, since Christ the Mediator both suffered the punishments for us and fulfilled the law, who, as Augustine says in his second explanation of Ps. XXII, made our faults his own faults, so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness. As Christ not only made satisfaction for our sins, but also performed perfect obedience to the law in our place, so not only is his satisfaction imputed to us, with our sins for which Christ made satisfaction not being imputed to us; for when one died for all, and made satisfaction, it is the same as if all had died, or had made satisfaction Cor. V. 14. but the righteousness or obedience of Christ, which he performed for us, is also imputed to us: because Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, Rom. X. 4. Thus 2 Cor. V. 21, both our sin is said to be imputed to Christ, and the righteousness of Christ to us: As therefore our sin, which is in us and not in Christ, is transferred to Christ by the decree and estimation of GOD, that is, it is estimated as if it were in Christ: so the righteousness of Christ, which is in Christ and not in us, is transferred to us by the estimation and decree of GOD, that is, it is estimated and accepted as if it were in us. Which imputation, however, is not a bare opinion and some imaginary figment; but it has a foundation: which foundation, however, is not in us, as we who are ungodly, so that in us there is rather a contrary foundation, not for righteousness but for wrath, if GOD wished to enter into judgment with us; but it is in the judgment and decree of GOD, who wills to impute the satisfaction and righteousness of Christ to us for justification, just as he imputed our sin to Christ for satisfaction, or the payment of punishment, and our debt of fulfilling the law, to which he himself was not a debtor by himself, for the fulfillment of the same for us. Rom. VIII. 3. Whence two modes (others say two parts) occur in the justification of the ungodly man who believes in GOD: one ςερητικὸς or privative, when that which is in man is not imputed to him, as if it did not exist in him, namely his sin and impiety; the other θετικὸς or positive, when that which is not in man, namely righteousness, is imputed to him, as if it existed in him, which is the very righteousness or obedience of Christ, as that by which we are constituted righteous. Rom. V. 19. For our own and inherent righteousness cannot be understood in this place, when righteousness is said to be imputed to us without works, as the Papists indeed wish; for (1.) it is a contradiction for our righteousness to be estimated without works; since our inherent righteousness consists in our works; nor can it formally exist without works, nay, our works are the inherent righteousness itself. (2.) Inherent righteousness is not imputed to us, but is infused, as the Papists wish; nay, what need is there to impute inherent righteousness, when it is in us, and is absolute righteousness, so that the acceptilation, which the Papists make an imputation, is by no means necessary here. (3.) Inherent righteousness is excluded from justification, when righteousness is said to be imputed to the μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ; because when the subject of justification and the imputation of righteousness is here constituted as μὴ ἐργαζόμενος ἀλλ' ὁ πισέυων, by that very fact he is regarded in the judgment of GOD not as endowed with inherent righteousness, but only as believing or apprehending the righteousness of Christ by faith. (4.) GOD is said to justify the ungodly man who believes: he does not therefore look upon one endowed with inherent righteousness when he justifies a man, or one in whom impiety has been expelled and righteousness has been infused into him; as the Papists contend. (5.) Justification and blessedness, or salvation, is his, to whom sins are remitted, veiled, and covered, and not imputed: not therefore his, in whom true and absolute justice is inherent, but his, to whom justice is imputed. (6.) The remission of sins, considered in itself, is nothing but imputative, so that it signifies no real change in man, but only the grace of GOD, not imputing to the believer the sin, which he nevertheless truly committed in act, and indeed even has in act. Since original sin remains throughout the whole life in the faithful, to be abolished indeed more and more, but never entirely, until we are fully delivered from the body of this death. (7.) All these things, which Paul brings forward from the Davidic Psalm, teach such a remission of sins. That is, not by which sins are abolished, so that they are not, but by which at least they are pardoned and not imputed, even though they still exist in man. Moreover, that ἄφεσις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν imports this: because GOD remits sins and offenses to us in the same way that we ought to remit them to our neighbor, Matt. VII. 12, 14. But we remit not by taking away, but by not imputing, and by pardoning; and as creditors remit a debt, which is done, not by working anything in the debtor, but only by not imputing our money to him, so that he may not pay what he owed. Such an imputation of justice is therefore designated here, which is the remission and non-imputation of injustice; but this does not agree with inherent justice; for if this be true and absolute, it can no more consist with sin and injustice or iniquity than absolute heat with cold. (8.) Such is the remission of iniquity here, by which it comes about that iniquities or sins are covered. But that which is present is covered and veiled, not indeed that which is not present, but has been taken away. Therefore, since sins are covered in justification, justification cannot consist in inherent justice: for inherent justice has no need to be covered, nor does it consist with sins which are covered. (9.) Justice, which is valid before GOD, must be perfect and conformable to the whole law; because God is a just judge, judging according to truth. But our inherent justice is not perfect in this way. (10.) The imputation of justice, of which the Apostle speaks here, is done according to grace v. 4. But inherent justice is imputed to the Subject, to whom it inheres, not according to grace, but according to debt, v. 5. (11.) That justice, which is imputed to us, has been manifested without the law; Rom. III. 21. But inherent justice pertains entirely to the law; because charity according to the Pontificians is that inherent justice which is the fulfillment of the law Rom. XIII. 10. (12.) The justice, which is imputed to us, is not ours Rom. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. But inherent justice is certainly ours. (13.) The justice which is imputed to us and is valid before GOD, is Christ's: nor does it become ours except through imputation 2. Cor. V. 21. And therefore it is not justice inherent in us (14.) The justice, which is imputed to us, is none other than that by which we are constituted just before the tribunal of God, but that is not our inherent justice, but the obedience of Christ Rom. V. 19.

What does Grotius say to these things? He repeats almost only Papistic cabbage: and he puts forward again those things which have been worn out more often. But in order that we may respond distinctly to these: (1.) χωρὶς ἔργων to him is, even if works are not yet present: Which misinterpretation has already been routed. (2.) But that he distinguishes works from a mind sincere in the study of piety, is a sophism: because by the name of works Paul includes not only external works, but also the internal affection of the mind, and whatever at all pertains to the law as a norm, since this justice has been manifested without the law. Rom. III. 21. (3.) That which David added, nor is there guile in his Spirit; that either does not apply here; because Paul did not bring it forward to declare justification, or if it is to be referred here also, it must be understood imputatively: that guile is not imputed to him. And that immunity from guile is either taken from the purification of the heart, which is done through the blood of Christ, Heb. IX. 15. 1. John I. 7. & through faith in Christ Acts XV. 9. or from the consequent holiness, and inherent justice: In the former way it does not differ from imputed justice: in the latter, however, it coheres with it in an inseparable bond, yet it ought not to be confused with the same. (4.) He interprets ἄφεσιν from the Hebrew as removal, clearly against the Apostolic and Davidic mind. For ἄφεσις ἀνομιῶν, is explained by David and the Apostle through the covering, and not the imputation of sin, nor is it accepted anywhere else than as the forgiveness of sin; where it signifies the removal of sin, not even Grotius could teach; much less a cessation from sin, where someone has ceased to be wicked; nor is GOD said to justify him who has ceased to be wicked, but the impious person who believes. The Hebrew phrase נשא פשע is used for the forgiveness, not the removal of iniquities Ex. XXXII. 32. c. XXXIV. 7. Num. XIV. 18. 1. Sam. XV. 26. Isa. XXXIII. 24. Ps. XXV. 18. Ps. XXXV. 3. nay even for human indulgence toward offenses, 1. Sam. XXV. 28. Gen. L. 17. But man does not in reality take away sin, or remove it from him who has sinned, but forgives the same. (5.) There is no need for a metonymy here, when it is a matter of the remission of iniquities; but the proper sense can have a place, nay it necessarily has one. Because the Apostle teaches that justification consists in the remission or forgiveness and non-imputation of sins, and the imputation of justice without works. Therefore he properly understands the remission of sins, and does not accept it for a consequent change of life for the better, or amendment, (6.) That GOD does not fully forgive grave crimes, except to those who have already begun to change their life Ezech. XVIII. is not taught in the Grotian sense, for GOD does not forgive only by half when He forgives, but entirely; nor does the forgiveness of grave crimes have any other way than that of light ones; but the remission of both is done out of grace: nor when amendment of life is required, is it constituted as either the cause or the antecedent condition of the remission of sins, but it pertains to the description of the subject, which follows the remission, and to the marks of true repentance. (7.) Origen's gloss is sufficiently violent, nor can it be excused: He said in this place that it is a great benefit when sins are dismissed; greater, when they are covered; greatest, when they are not imputed; for then they are so erased; that not even a trace appears. That sins are remitted to those who leave evil, covered to those who begin to do good; not imputed to those who have come to perfection, so that the root of all malice is amputated, so that no trace of wickedness can be found. Of which gloss neither a trace nor a footprint is found either here or elsewhere in Scripture, which ought not to be of private interpretation. Nor yet does it help either Grotius or the Papists. For according to the same, sins are remitted to those in whom the root of malice has not been amputated, in whom a trace of wickedness is still found, and thus to those to whom sins still adhere. Nor are those distinct, but remission of sins, covering, and non-imputation are held by David and the Apostle as the same things. Therefore they are rashly distinguished by subject by Origen. And who are those in whom the root of malice has been fully amputated, in whom not even a trace of wickedness is found? Is it perhaps the case that depraved concupiscence is not to be considered even the root, not even a trace of wickedness? Such perfection is certainly not of this life, in which we are renewed only in part and from day to day: nor do those things pertain to the description of justification: which the Apostle teaches to consist in the non-imputation of our injustice, and the imputation of the justice of Christ, not in the total eradication of malice. (8.) That comparison concerning a wound is irrelevant. The Apostle does not teach that the soul is healed in justification in such a way that no sin, the wound of the soul, remains: but that sin is covered, even if it remains: that the guilt is removed, even if the root is left behind. Wounds are said not to be covered, but healed. Sins are not healed, because the sinner is healed, not the sin, but covered. (9.) Furthermore, a benefit supervening does not allow an injury to appear, not because the injury ceases to be an injury, but because it is no longer reckoned, and because we forget the same. Moreover, our innocence cannot cause sin not to be imputed to us; the Papists themselves admit that this is the effect of the satisfaction of Christ, not of our justice or innocence, namely the remission of guilt, as also the pardon of eternal punishment. Nor does our innocence have the power to obliterate the stain from prior offenses, but divine indulgence is needed so that offenses may be remitted; the obliteration of which is nothing before the eyes of GOD that penetrate all things, unless GOD himself covers them with the justice of Christ, and cleanses us from sins by his blood, 1 John I. 7, unless he wills to forget them, Ezek. XVIII. 22, to cast them behind his back, Isa. XXXVIII. 17, to remove them far from us, Ps. CIII. 12, and to cast the same into the depth of the sea, so that they do not appear, Mic. VII. 19, and to hide his face from the same, Ps. LI. 11. (10.) Those things are as far apart as heaven and earth, that God does not impute sins, and that God does not find that for which he may be angry. For it is said that he does not impute sins to the ungodly: but it is not said that he does not find in the ungodly that for which he may be angry with him. He does not impute when He remits iniquities, or does He not deserve, because He remits, that GOD should be angry with him? And does not GOD deservedly become angry at iniquities? He does not impute, certainly, when He covers sins; but would He not be angry at them, by virtue of justice, He who hates and abominates sins, unless He covered them by virtue of grace and mercy? (11.) The word חָשַׁב is explained more than seventy times by λογίζω; and so it is also explained here by the Apostle; and Grotius, having dismissed that meaning and the Apostolic interpretation, snatches at the only passage in which it is explained by μνησικακεῖν: to be mindful of evil, Zech. VII. 10. κακίαν τõ ἀδελφõ μὴ μνησικακεῖτε. But what does this help Grotius? Who interpreted that in its own place: Let him not even allow the intention of harming anyone to come into his mind. For the explanation of Tertullian against Marcion. IV. He who, with the LXX, takes it more strictly concerning the restraining of the desire for private vengeance, that each one should not recall the malice of his neighbor, does not approve. Although neither interpretation is relevant to the present matter of the non-imputation of sin, since it is the same as GOD not finding that for which He should be angry. (12.) These three, the remission of iniquities, the covering of sins, and the non-imputation, describe not the friendship of man with GOD, but justification, or the imputation of righteousness without works. Meanwhile, there is no doubt that the justified are friends of GOD.

PART II. The extension of the modes of Abrahamic justification to the Gentiles.

Now the Apostle is acting to teach that justification by faith, which Abraham obtained, whom he brought forward as an example, pertains not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles: since faith was imputed to Abraham while he was still in uncircumcision, many years before the institution of circumcision: which he received, not that he might be justified through this work of circumcision, which the Pseudo-Apostles wanted, but that the righteousness of faith might be sealed in this very Sacrament as if by a seal: which happens to all, whether they be Jews or Gentiles, provided they are of the faith of Abraham, inasmuch as he is the Father of all believers.

Latin:

V. 8. μακάριό ἀνὴρ ᾧ ὐ μὴ λογίσηται κύριό ἁμαρτίαν.

Id est, in quo nihil invenit DEUS, ob quod ei succenseat. Nam חשׁב quod hic vertitur λογίζεσθαι Zach. VII. 10. μνησικακεῖν. Hæc ita describunt amicitiam hominis cum DEO, χάριν θεῦ. Similitudo tracta à contrahentium ratio- nibus, ubi is, cui aliquid imputatur aut expensum fertur, solvere id debet. Vide quæ diximus libro II. de Jure Belli & Pacis XIX. 2. cum annotatis.

Probatio Apostoli hæc est : Davidem testari, beatitudinem & salutem ejus esse, cui DEUS im- putat justitiam sine operibus, h. e. non propriam justitiam : ea enim non imputari potest sine ope- ribus, quum in operibus consistat; sed alienam, quæ nulla alia est, quam Christi justitia. Quo- modo vero id testatur David? Cum ait, beatos esse, quibus remissæ sunt iniquitates; & quorum tecta sunt peccata : beatum esse virum, cui non imputat DEUS peccatum. Unde liquet, Paulum pro iis- dem habere, DEUM remittere iniquitates, tege- re peccata, non imputare peccata: & DEUM im- putare justitiam sine operibus : Alioqui probatio Apostoli nulla esset. Ideoque justificatio secun- dum Davidem est, cum non imputantur peccata, cum remittuntur, teguntur peccata; secundum Paulum est, cum imputatur justitia sine operibus: ac proinde non imputatio peccati & imputatio ju- stitiæ sine operibus h. e. justitiæ Christi reipsa unum idemque sint necessum est. Cum enim impio non imputatur iniquitas propria, absolvitur impius, & justus pronunciatur; similiter cum impio impu- tatur justitia alterius, absolvi impium & justum pronunciari necessum est. Fundamentum ergo, quod impius absolvatur μὴ ἐργαζόμενω, justitiam propriam ad judicium divinum non adferens, so- lum πιστεύων, credens fideq; apprehendens Chri- sti justitiam, est imputatio justitiæ Christi, vel ut Paulus habet, ejus justitia, quæ sola coram DEO valet χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus, quam unice, non vero opera, adeoque sine operibus, DEUS respi- cit in judicio absolutorio, hominique impio, non operanti, sed credenti acceptam refert. Agnoscunt hanc vocis imputationis emphasin in hoc loco etiam ipsimet Papistæ; Soto: pulcherrima hæc, inquit, commodissimaque oratione explicat Paulus tum id, quod dixerat, reputatur fides ad justitiam, tum clarissime rationem nostræ justificationis. Cum enim nos solvendo non simus DEO, acceptum fert ipse nobis nostrum debitum, id est, pro accepto du- cit, si modo illi fidem pollicenti adhibeamus. Sal- mero: Acceptum ferre, (sic enim reddidit Latinus vocem imputavit, accepto ferre) est debitum re- mittere, & habere pro soluto, quod solutum non est. Hinc vox Jurisperitorum, accepti latio: quæ interrogatione & responsione fit, ut debitor, qui non est solvendo, dicat creditori: Id omne, quod tibi debebam, habesne acceptum? Quo respondente, ha- beo, acceptumque fero, tunc debitor à debito ab- solvitur, & habetur pro solutore, etiamsi nulla in- terveniat solutio, & ita accepti latio opponitur ju- stæ solutioni. Hæc ille. Sed quia DEUS salva justitia sua non potest absolvere debitorem, nisi interveniat justa solutio, quam vero debitor præ- stare nequit, solutionem à Mediatore Christo præstitam impio non operanti, sed in Christum cre- denti, imputat, atque ita acceptam fert solutio- nem Christi fide apprehensam, ac si debitor ipse eam præstitisset. Quomodo Bellarm. supra pro- fessus est, Christum satisfecisse, & eam satisfactio- nem ita nobis donare, & communicare, cum nos justificat, ut nostra satisfactio & justitia dici possit; adeoque non esse absurdum, si quis dicat, nobis im- putari Christi justitiam & merita, cum nobis do- nentur & applicentur, ac si nos ipsi satisfecissemus. Addit quidem Cardinalis, modo non negetur, in nobis praeterea, eamque veram & absolutam esse ju- stitiam, cui justo DEI judicio non debeatur poena, sed gloria. Sed illud aperte est contra Apostolum: qui imputari in Judicio DEI docet Justitiam Chri- sti sine operibus: adeoque hic excludit inhaerentem justitiam, imo impium justificare dicit, & μὴ ἐργα- ζόμενον. Et quomodo, justo DEI judicio, nostris operibus vel inhaerenti nostrae justitiae deberetur gloria, quum omnes oporteat deprecari judicium DEI secundum justitiam, & ad solam confugere misericordiam? Porro quid opus foret coram judicio DEI imputatione justitiae Christi, h. e. alie- nae, si nostra inhaerens justitia vera & absoluta justitia esset, cui gloria debeatur? & annon ita gloriari coram DEO poterimus, operibus nostris, si eadem sint absoluta justitia, cui ex merito de- beatur gloria? Denique unde fit, ut poenas da- turi non simus aeternas, & remissionem peccati consequamur, nisi a justitia Christi? nam remissio culpae & sempiternae poenae effectus est satisfactionis Christi, quae nobis justificatione confertur & appli- catur, ut διαρρήδην habet Bellarminus. Unde au- tem fit, ut remissionem culpae & poenae sempiter- nae habeamus, inde etiam omnino fit, ut habea- mus gloriam aeternam. Nam non alia est ratio remissionis culpae, & poenae sempiternae, alia vitae & gloriae sempiternae; quae aeque est χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ donum DEI in Christo Jesu, non vero nobis justo DEI judicio ob inhaerentem nostram justitiam debita Rom. VI. 23. Nimirum cum nobis commu- nicantur ac donantur justitia & merita Christi, h. e. imputatur nobis justitia, remittitur culpa, adeoque fit inde, ut nec poenas daturi aeternas, & ut vitam habituri simus aeternam haud secus, ac si nunquam peccassemus imo legem implevissemus, quandoqui- dem pro nobis Mediator Christus & poenas dede- rit, & legem impleverit, qui dicente Augustino ex- plicatione altera in Ps. XXII. delicta nostra sua delicta fecit, ut justitiam suam nostram justitiam faceret. Ut Christus non modo pro peccatis no- stris satisfecit, sed etiam nostri loco legi perfe- ctam praestitit obedientiam, ita non modo satis- factio ejus imputatur nobis, non imputatis nobis peccatis nostris, pro quibus Christus satisfecit; Nam cum unus pro omnibus mortuus est, & satis- fecit, idem est, ac si omnes mortui essent, vel satis- fecissent 2. Cor. V. 14. sed imputatur etiam nobis Christi justitia vel obedientia, quam pro nobis praestitit: quia Christus est finis legis, ad justitiam omni credenti Rom. X. 4. Ita 2. Cor. V. 21. & pecca- tum nostrum Christo, & justitia Christi nobis im- putari dicitur: Uti ergo peccatum nostrum, quod est in nobis & non in Christo, DEI decreto & aesti- matione transfertur ad Christum, id est, aestima- tur, ac si esset in Christo: ita Christi justitia, quae est in Christo & non in nobis, DEI aestimatione & decreto transfertur ad nos, id est, aestimatur & acceptatur, ac si esset in nobis. Quae tamen im- putatio non est nuda opinio, ac putatitium aliquod figmentum; sed fundamentum habet: quod vero fundamentum non in nobis quidem est, ut qui impii sumus, ita ut in nobis contrarium potius fundamentum sit non ad justitiam, sed ad iram, si DEUS nobiscum in judicium intrare vellet; sed in judicio & decreto DEI, qui Christi satisfactio- nem & justitiam nobis imputare vult, ad justifica- tionem, uti Christo nostrum peccatum imputavit ad satisfactionem, vel poenae lutionem, nostrum- que debitum implendæ legis, cui ipse debitor per se non erat, ad ejusdem pro nobis impletio- nem. Rom. IIX. 3. Unde duo in justificatione impii, credentis in DEUM modi (alii partes duas dicunt) occurrunt: unus ςερητικὸς privati- vus, cum id, quod homini inest, ei non imputa- tur, ac si non existeret in eodem, peccatum nem- pe & impietas ejusdem; alter θετικὸς seu positi- vus, cum id, quod non inest homini, justitia nem- pe, eidem imputatur, ac si in eodem existeret, quæ est ipsa Christi justitia, vel obedientia, ut- pote qua justi constituimur. Rom. V. 19. Nostra enim propria, & inhærens justitia intelligi non potest hoc loco, cum imputari nobis dicitur ju- stitia absque operibus, uti quidem Papistæ vo- lunt; nam (1.) nostram justitiam æstimari abs- que operibus, contradictio est; cum justitia no- stra inhærens in operibus nostris consistat; nec formaliter esse possit sine operibus, imo opera nostra sunt ipsa inhærens justitia. (2.) Inhærens justitia non imputatur nobis, sed infunditur, uti Papistæ volunt; imo imputare justitiam inhæren- tem quid opus est, cum ea in nobis sit, & abso- luta sit justitiæ, ut acceptilatio, quam imputatio- nem Papistæ faciunt, minime hic necessaria sit. (3.) Inhærens justitia à justificatione excluditur, cum μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ imputari justitia dicitur; quia cum hic justificationis & imputationis justitiæ Subjectum μὴ ἐργαζόμενος ἀλλ' ὁ πισέυων consti- tuitur, eo ipso non ut præditus justitia inhærente, sed solum ut credens seu fide apprehendens justi- tiam Christi in judicio DEI respicitur. (4.) DEUS justificare dicitur impium credentem: non ergo justitia inhærente præditum spectat, cum justificat hominem, vel qua expulsa est im- pietas, & infusa ipsi est justitia; uti Papistæ con- tendunt. (5.) Justificatio & beatitudo, vel salus est ejus, cui remittuntur, velantur, & teguntur, non imputantur peccata: non ergo ejus, in quo inhæsive est justitia vera & absoluta, sed ejus, cui imputatur justitia. (6.) Remissio peccatorum ipsa per se considerata non est nisi imputativa, ita ut nullam realem mutationem in homine signi- ficet, sed DEI tantum gratiam, non imputan- tem credenti peccatum, quod ille tamen vere actu commisit, imo etiam actu habet. Siquidem peccatum originale maneat per totam vitam in fi- delibus abolendum quidem magis magisque, sed nunquam penitus, donec plene liberemur à cor- pore hujus mortis. (7.) Talem remissionem peccatorum omnia hæc docent, quæ è Davidico Psalmo adducit Paulus. Hoc est, non qua abo- leantur peccata, ut non sint, sed qua saltim con- donentur & non imputentur, etsi adhuc existant in homine. Id autem ἄφεσις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν im- portat: quia ita remittit nobis DEUS peccata & offensas, uti nos proximo remittere debemus Matth. VII. 12. 14. at nos remittimus non aufe- rendo, sed non imputando, & condonando; & uti creditores remittunt debito, quod fit, non aliquid operando in debitore, sed tantum non imputan- do eidem æs nostrum, ut ne luat, quod debuit. Talis ergo justitiæ imputatio hic designatur, quæ fit injustitiæ remissio, & non-imputatio; non autem hoc convenit inhærenti justitiæ; hæc enim si vera & absoluta sit, cum peccato, & injustitia vel ini- quitate consistere non magis potest, quam calor absolutus cum frigore. (8.) Talis hic est iniqui- tatis remissio, qua fit, ut tegantur iniquitates, vel peccata. At tegitur & obtegitur id, quod inest, non vero id, quod non inest, sed ablatum est. Itaque cum obtegantur in justificatione pecca- ta, non potest in justitia inhærente consistere ju- stificatio: inhærens enim justitia opus non habet, ut tegatur, nec cum peccatis, quæ teguntur, con- sistit. (9.) Justitia, quæ coram DEO valet, per- fecta sit oportet, totique legi conformis; quia Deus justus judex est, judicans secundum verita- tem. At nostra inhærens justitia ita perfecta non est. (10.) Imputatio justitiæ, de qua hic Aposto- lus, fit secundum gratiam v. 4. At inhærens justi- tia imputatur Subjecto, cui inhæret, non secun- dum gratiam, sed secundum debitum, v. 5. (11.) Ju- stitia illa, quæ nobis imputatur, manifestata est sine lege; Rom. III. 21. At justitia inhærens per- tinet omnino ad legem; quia charitas juxta Pon- tificios est inhærens illa justitia, quæ impletio le- gis est Rom. XIII. 10. (12.) Justitia, quæ nobis imputatur, non est nostra Rom. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. At inhærens justitia utique nostra est. (13.) Ju- stitia quæ nobis imputatur & coram DEO valet, Christi est: nec nisi per imputationem nostra fit 2. Cor. V. 21. Ideoque non est justitia nobis inhæ- rens (14.) Justitia, quæ imputatur nobis, alia non est, quam illa, qua justi constituimur coram tri- bunali Dei, at illa est non nostra inhærens justi- tia, sed obedientia Christi Rom. V. 19.

Quid ad hæc Grotius? Repetit fere tantum crambem Papisticam: & ea, quæ sæpius protrita sunt, iterum apponit. Ad quæ vero ut distincte respondeamus, (1.) χωρὶς ἔργων ipsi est, etiam si opera nondum adsint: Quæ ψευδερμηνεία jam pro- fligata est. (2.) Quod vero opera à sincero in pietatis studio animo distinguit, σόφισμα est: quia nomine operum Paulus non tantum externa ope- ra, sed internum etiam affectum animi compre- hendit, & quicquid omnino ad legem ceu nor- mam pertinet, quum justitia hæc sine lege sit ma- nifestata. Rom. III. 21. (3.) Quod addidit David, nec est in Spiritu ejus dolus; id vel huc non facit; quia Paulus id non adduxit ad declarandam justi- ficationem, vel si huc etiam referendum, imputa- tive intelligendum: quod dolus ei non impute- tur. Et immunitas illa à dolo vel de purificatio- ne cordis accipitur, quæ fit per sanguinem Christi, Ebr. IX. 15. 1. Joh. I. 7. & per fidem in Christum Act. XV. 9. vel de consequente sanctitate, & ju- stitia inhærente: Priori modo à justitia imputata non differt: posteriori vero cum ea indivulso ne- xu cohæret quidem, nec tamen cum eadem con- fundi debet. (4.) Ἄφεσιν ex Ebræo per ablatio- nem interpretatur, plane contra mentem Apo- stolicam & Davidicam. Nam ἄφεσις ἀνομιῶν, à Davide & Apostolo per obtestionem, & non im putationem peccati exponitur, nec uspiam aliter, quam de peccati condonatione accipitur; ablatio- nem peccati ubi significet, nec ipse Grotius doce- re potuit; nedum cessationem a peccato, ubi quis desiit esse improbus; nec vero eum, qui improbus esse desiit, sed impium credentem DEUS justificare dicitur. Phrasis Ebræa נשא פשע de conda- natione, non ablatione iniquitatum adhibetur Ex. XXXII. 32. c. XXXIV. 7. Num. XIV. 18. 1. Sam. XV. 26. Esa. XXXIII. 24. Ps. XXV. 18. Ps. XXXV. 3. imo etiam de humana indulgentia adversus offen- sas, 1. Sam. XXV. 28. Gen. L. 17. At homo non au- fert revera peccatum, aut removet ab eo, qui pec- cavit, sed condonat eidem. (5.) Metonymia hic opus non est, cum de remissione iniquitatum agi- tur; sed proprius sensus locum habere potest, imo necessario habet. Quia justificationem in remis- sione vel condonatione & non imputatione pecca torum, & imputatione justitiæ sine operibus consti- stitere docet Apostolus. Proprie ergo remissionem peccatorum intelligit, non vero pro consequenti vita mutatione in melius, seu emendatione eam ac- cipit, (6.) DEUM non plane condonare gra- via crimina, nisi iis, qui vitam jam mutare ince- perunt Ezech. XIIX. sensu Grotiano non docetur, neque enim DEUS ex semisse tantum condo- nat cum condonat, sed ex asse; neque aliter gra- viorum criminum condonatio habet, quam levi- um; sed utrorumque remissio ex gratia fit: neque cum vita emendatio requiritur, ea vel causa vel conditio antecedens remissionis peccatorum con- stituitur, sed ad descriptionem subjecti facit, quod remissionem consequitur, & ad notas veræ pœni- tentiæ. (7.) Origenis glossa satis violenta est, nec excusari potest: Magnum beneficium esse, dixit in h. l. cum peccata dimittuntur; majus, cum tegun- tur; maximum, cum non imputantur; tunc enim ita deleri; ut ne vestigium quidem appareat. Re- mitti peccata iis, qui relinquunt malum, tegi iis, qui incipiunt bona facere; non imputari iis, qui ad perfectum venerunt, ita ut omnis malitiæ ra- dix amputetur, ut nullum inveniri possit nequitiæ vestigium. Cujus glossæ nec vola nec vestigium sive hic sive alibi in Scriptura, quæ non esse de- bet ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, reperitur. Neque tamen ju- vat ea vel Grotium vel Papistas. Nam juxta ean- dem remittuntur peccata iis, in quibus malitiæ radix amputata non est, in quibus adhuc nequitiæ invenitur vestigium, adeoque illis, quibus adhuc hærent peccata. Neque distincta illa sunt, sed pro iisdem habentur à Davide & Apostolo remif- sio peccatorum, obtectio & non imputatio. Te- mere ergo illa subjectis distinguuntur ab Orige- ne. Et quinam illi sunt, in quibus profus am- putata est radix malitiæ, in quibus ne vestigium quidem invenitur nequitiæ? Num forte concupi- scentia prava ne radix, ne vestigium quidem ne- quitiæ habenda? Talis utique perfectio non est hujus vitæ, in qua ex parte renovamur tantum & de die in diem: neque pertinent illa ad justifi- cationis descriptionem: quam in non imputatio- ne injustitiæ nostræ, & imputatione justitiæ Chri- sti consistere docet Apostolus, non in eradica- tione totali malitiæ. (8.) Simile illud de vulnere alienum est. Non ita sanari animam in justifica- tione docet Apostolus, ut vulnus animæ pecca- tum nullum supersit: sed ut peccatum tegatur, etiamsi remaneat: ut reatus tollatur, etsi radix relinquatur. Vulnera non tegi dicuntur, sed sa- nari. Peccata non sanari, quia peccator sanatur, non peccatum, sed tegi. (9.) Porro beneficium superveniens injuriam apparere non patitur, non quod injuria esse desinat injuria, sed quod non reputetur amplius, quodque obliviscamur ejus- dem. Innocentia autem nostra facere non potest, ut peccatum nobis non imputetur; id effectum esse satisfactionis Christi, non nostræ justitiæ, aut innocentiæ, fatentur ipsimet Papistæ, remissionem nempe culpæ, ut & condonationem pœnæ sempiter- næ. Nec obliterare labem ex prioribus delictis va- let nostra innocentia, sed opus est divina indul- gentia, ut remittantur delicta; quorum oblite- ratio nulla est coram oculis DEI omnia pene- trantibus, nisi DEUS ipse ea tegat justitia Christi, & sanguine ejus emundet nos à peccatis, 1. Joh. I. 7. nisi oblivisci velit eorum, Ezech. XIIX. 22. illa post tergum rejicere Esa. XXXIIX 17. a nobis elongare Ps. CIII. 12. eademque in profundum maris projicere, ne compareant Mich. VII. 19. & faciem suam ab iisdem abscondere. Ps. LI. 11. (10.) Toto cœlo illa distant, Deum non imputa- re peccata, & Deum non invenire ob quod succenseat. Nam impio non imputare peccata dicitur: non vero non invenit in impio, ob quod ei succenseat. Non imputat cum remittit iniquitates, an vero quod remittit, non meretur, ut ei succenseat DEUS? Et annon succenset merito DEUS ini- quitatibus? Non imputat sane cum tegit pecca- ta; num vero non succenseat illis, vi justitiæ, qui odit & abominatur peccata, nisi tegeret eadem vi gratiæ & misericordiæ? (11.) Verbum חָשַׁב plus- quam septuagies exponitur per λογίζω; atque ita etiam hic ab Apostolo explicatur; & Grotius missa illa significatione, & Apostolica interpreta- tione, unicum arripit locum, in quo per μνησικα- κεῖν exponitur: mali memorem esse Zach. VII. 10. κακίαν τõ ἀδελφõ μὴ μνησικακεῖτε. Quid vero hoc juvat Grotium? Qui illud in suo loco inter- pretatus est: Ne in animum quidem sibi venire patiatur consilium cuiquam nocendi. Tertulliani enim explicationem advers. Marcion. IV. qui cum LXX. strictius de vindictæ privatæ cupiditate in- hibenda accipit, malitiam proximi sui unusquisque ne recogitet, haud approbat. Quanquam neutra interpretatio ad rem præsentem de non imputa- tione peccati faciat, quum idem sit ac quod DEUS non inveniat, ob quod succenseat. (12.) Hæc tria, remissionem iniquitatum, obtectionem peccatorum, & non imputationem non amicitiam hominis cum DEO, sed justificationem, vel justitiæ sine operi- bus imputationem describunt. Interim justifica- tos amicos DEI esse nullum est dubium.

PARS II. Modi justificationis Abrahamicæ ad gen- tiles extensio.

Jam id agit Apostolus, ut doceat, justificatio- nem per fidem, quæ Abrahamo obtigit, quem in exemplum adduxit, non solum Judæos attinere, sed etiam gentes: siquidem Abrahamo adhuc in præputio existenti fides imputata sit, annis com- pluribus ante circumcisionis institutionem: quam acceperit, non ut per hoc circumcisionis opus justifi- caretur, quod Pseudo-Apostoli volebant, sed ut justitia fidei in ipso hoc Sacramento veluti sigillo obsignaretur: quæ omnibus obtingit, seu Judæi seu gentiles sint, modo fidei sint Abrahami, utpote qui Pater est omnium credentium.

## 4:9
V. 9. This blessedness.

To whom does that description of the blessed man apply?

ἐπὶ τὴν περιτομὴν.

To the circumcised, supply only: which the Latin rightly added here for the sense, a figure such as above III. 30.

ἢ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν.

Or indeed also to the uncircumcised? The same figure, which is above II. 10. The Hebrew עַל, which is translated ἐπὶ, often signifies the subject to which something applies, as appears in Gen. XXVII. 12. and elsewhere. The verb γίνεται is understood.

λέγομεν γὰρ.

Present for the already past. We said above 3.

Latin:

V. 9. ὁ μακαρισμὸς ἓν ὗτος.

Descriptio ista beati hominis cui convenit?

ἐπὶ τὴν περιτομὴν.

An circumcisis, supple tantum: quod hic recte ad sen- sum addidit Latinus, figura qualis supra III. 30.

ἢ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν.

An vero etiam non circumcisis? figura eadem, quæ supra II. 10. עַל Hebræum, quod ἐπὶ vertitur, sæpe sub- jectum significat, cui aliquid convenit, ut apparet Gen. XXVII. 12. & alibi. Subauditur verbum γίνεται.

λέγομεν γὰρ.

Præsens pro jamjam præterito. Diximus supra 3.

## 4:10
V. 10. How was it reckoned?

In what state of Abraham?

being in circumcision or in uncircumcision? He strikes the Jews here excellently, as the saying goes, in their own camp; they could say: we are caught by our own feathers. Similarly Justin, disputing with Trypho: 'For not even Abraham was testified by God to be righteous because of circumcision, but because of faith; for before he was circumcised, it was said concerning him: And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. And we, believing in God through Christ while in the uncircumcision of our flesh, and having the circumcision which profits those who possess it, that is, of the heart, hope to appear righteous and pleasing to God.' Abraham is said to have believed God for righteousness fourteen years at the least before, as some think twenty-five, before he was circumcised.

Latin:

V. 10. πῶς ἓν ἐλογίσθη.

In quo Abrahami statu?

ἐν περιτομῇ ὄντι ἢ ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ) Egregie hic cædit Judæos, ut dici solet, in suis ipsorum caltris dicere poterant: τοῖς ἀυτῶν πτεροῖς ἁλισκόμεθα. Similiter Justinus cum Tryphone disputans: ὐδὲ γὰρ Ἀβρα- ὰμ διὰ τὴν περιτομὴν δίκαιος εἶναι ὑπὸ θεõ ἐμαρτυρήθη ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν πίσιν, πρὸ τõ γὰρ περιτομηθῆναι ἀυτὸν, εἴρηται περὶ ἀυτõ, ὕτως˙ ἐπίςευσε δὲ τῷ Θεῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἓν ἐν ἀκροβυσίᾳ της σαρ- κὸς ἡμῶν πιστεύοντες τῷ Θεῷ διὰ τõ χριστõ, καὶ περιτομὴν ἔχοντες τὴν ὠφελῆσαν ἡμᾶς τὸς κεκτημένυς, τῆτ' ἐστὶ τῆς καρ- διας, δίκαιοι καὶ ἐυάρεστοι τῷ Θεῷ ἐλπίζομεν φανῆναι. Abra- ham quatuordecim ut minimam ante annis, ut quidam pu- tant XXV. dicitur credidisse DEO ad justitiam, priusquam fuit circumcisus.

## 4:11
V. 11. And he received the sign of circumcision:

The use of the genitive in place of apposition is not without example: but very many manuscripts, and that one in England, have 'of circumcision,' and the Syriac reads thus. That visible circumcision was a sign of the internal circumcision made through faith, which will also be called the righteousness of faith. These are the sensible signs, or symbols of the intelligible. Thus, external circumcision is also for Philo a symbol of the cutting off of pleasures. What Paul calls a sign here, he calls a type elsewhere, below V. 14, 1 Cor. X. 6, 11. Justin in his colloquy with Trypho: 'Why has this circumcision itself been given as a sign? But not as a work of righteousness.'

A seal of the righteousness of faith.

He calls the circumcision of the body a seal on Abraham's part: because just as witnesses, when they press a ring into an instrument, show that it is genuine, so also Abraham, by impressing upon himself the mark of circumcision, full of pain and mocked by outsiders, shows the righteousness, that is, the sincerity of his faith. For God had promised Abraham that a lineage would go forth into many nations; He had added that He would give the land of Canaan to his posterity, and furthermore, that He would be God, that is, a benefactor, both to him and to his posterity: and in testimony of the faith held in these promises, He had willed that that mark be imposed upon their bodies, as we read in Gen. XVII. 11. 'Seal' corresponds to the Hebrew 'oth' and signifies a signet ring, as can be seen in Cant. VIII. 6, Jer. XXII. 24, Ezech. XXVIII. 12. Haggai II. 24, whence it is also translated as 'ring' in Gen. XXXVIII. 18, 25, or even the carving itself which is in a ring or in precious stones: Exod. XXVIII. 11, 21, 36, XXXIX. 5, 12, 30. Hence the verb 'chatham,' which is 'to seal' in 1 Kings XXI. 8, Neh. XII, Ps. VIII. 8, IX. 10, Isa. VIII. 16, XXIX. 11, Jerem. XXXII. 10, 11, 44, Dan. VI. 17, IX. 24, XII. 4. Concerning the metaphorical use of this verb, we spoke at John III. 33. The author of the responses to the orthodox says that this seal was deservedly, that is, circumcision, impressed upon that part which by nature had been useless, but by faith had been made active: response CII. Chrysostom, however, compares circumcision to a mark impressed upon the skin of soldiers, which shows that they belong to the emperor.

Grotius, from the same words of the Apostle, makes external circumcision now a sign of internal circumcision, now a token and mark of the Lord's people: and he explains the righteousness of faith now by internal circumcision made through faith, now by the sincerity of the faith held in the divine promises concerning the lineage to go forth into many nations, concerning the land of Canaan to be given to his posterity, and that God would be God, that is, a benefactor, both to him and to his posterity: which Abram rendered attested by impressing upon himself the mark of circumcision. But circumcision is called a seal, not a purely indicative sign, nor merely a mark or token; and indeed a seal not of internal circumcision, but of the righteousness of faith, which is without the works of the law, which Grotius rashly confuses with internal circumcision; for the latter pertains to renewal and sanctification, nor can it be viewed without the works of the law: but the righteousness of faith imputed to Abraham in the article of justification or in the divine judgment is here presented 'without works'; and the sincerity of faith is one thing, the righteousness of faith imputed to Abraham, by which he was justified before God, is another. Sincerity is an attribute and affection of faith, but imputed righteousness is the Object of Abrahamic faith, just as the imputation of righteousness is the very form of justification. Although indeed we do not deny that circumcision was a mark and token of the Jewish people and easily admit that external circumcision can be called a sign of the internal, yet the Apostle is not dealing with that here; rather, he intends this: that Abraham, justified in uncircumcision through faith alone, received circumcision not in order to be justified, but so that the righteousness of faith without the works of the law might be sealed and confirmed in him by this Sacrament as if by a certain seal, so that he might thus be the Father of all who believe in uncircumcision, that righteousness might be imputed to them also, and all might in that manner, by the example of Abraham, believe in Christ, and through faith in Christ be justified by imputed righteousness without the works of the law, apart from the works or cooperation or merit of any, by the righteousness of Christ alone apprehended by faith and imputed to those who believe. But the Apostle calls the 'sign of circumcision' a seal of the righteousness of faith: for Circumcision was a sign of grace, or of the divine covenant, as the Syriac has interpreted it, a sign of the covenant, which is found in Gen. 17:11. But because it is not a merely σημαντικὸν (significative) sign, he adds the word σφραγῖδος (seal), because, to wit, it was a sealing and confirming sign. Whence it appears that circumcision was a means for adults, through which grace and righteousness were sealed to believers; but because infants also received it, so that grace might be equally sealed to them in that way, it is necessary that grace and righteousness were also exhibited and applied to infants through circumcision, since infants were destitute of any other means of application, and circumcision was divinely ordained so that they might be received into the covenant of grace through this Sacrament, and the same might be sealed and confirmed to them, to which therefore was annexed the promise of grace, of the remission of sins, and of eternal life, Gen. 17. Not that God wishes to be only a benefactor to those receiving circumcision, nor only that they ought to inherit the land of Canaan, which was an accidental promise, since even after the inheritance of the land of Canaan was received, the Sacrament of Circumcision still had to be dispensed and received; but that God wishes to be their God, by the gracious adoption of them as sons and heirs of eternal life, and to embrace and cherish them with His fatherly grace in this and the future age. Cf. Matt. 22:32, Luke 20:38, Rev. 21:3.

τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ (of that in uncircumcision).

Of that faith which he had even while not yet circumcised. And here as above [at verse] 10.

Why should the pronoun τῆς not be referred to righteousness as the principal object, which is treated here? The matter, however, comes to the same thing; because righteousness and faith cohere in an inseparable bond: whence also the Blessed Luther referred it to faith.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πατέρα πάντων τῶν πιστευόντων (that he might be the father of all them that believe).

Above [at verse] 10. Father is taken mystically: In which sense Philo also said father of words. Thus he is a Father who leads others by instruction or example. See what we have said at Matt. 13:19, John 3. Justin against Trypho: being children of Abraham because of similar faith.

These things are rightly accepted concerning the Father mystically and spiritually, who, to wit, is called Father not in respect of generation, as 2 Kings 2:12, but they are not rightly drawn to father of words, if the discourse is made concerning the hypostatic Word. For God is His Father not improperly, but properly, not by regeneration, but by eternal generation, Ps. 2:7.

δι᾽ ἀκροβυστίας (through uncircumcision).

διὰ here has the same value as ἐν just now. Thus, to have in hand, to be in the mouth of the people, even the more elegant Greeks say. See above 2:27.

See such a sense, if you please, in 1 Tim. 2:15, she shall be saved through childbearing, that is, in childbearing.

that righteousness might be reckoned to them also.

It is the same thing for righteousness to be imputed through faith, as for faith to be imputed for righteousness. For it signifies that praise is ascribed to someone by reason of faith. For praise is also called righteousness by metonymy. He has been deputed to righteousness, says Tertullian.

It can be admitted that it is the same thing for righteousness to be imputed through faith as for faith to be imputed for righteousness, in the Evangelical sense: For the righteousness of Christ is imputed by GOD to those who believe in Christ: that is, through faith: and faith, or the apprehension of the obedience of Christ, is imputed to believers for righteousness, no differently than if it were their own righteousness. But that praise is indicated by righteousness metonymically is a gloss, and an interpretation proper to Grotius. The Apostle is dealing with justification before the tribunal of God, not with the praise which we have before God by reason of faith; indeed, he excludes all boasting.

and the father of circumcision.

One must repeat from the preceding passage 'that he might be': and circumcision here is to be understood as that interior one of the heart.

Latin:

V. 11. καὶ σημεῖον ἔλαβε περιτομῆς:

Non caret exemplo usurpatio genitivi vice oppositio- nis: sed Manuscripti plurimi & ille in Anglia habet περι- τομῆς & sic legit Syrus, Circumcisio illa aspectabilis signum erat circumcisionis internæ factæ per fidem, quæ & justitia fidei jam dicetur. Sunt τὰ αἰσθητὰ σημεῖα, sive σύμβολα τῶν νοητῶν. Sic circumcisio exterior etiam Philoni σύμβολον ἡδονῶν ἐκτομῆς. Quod hic σημεῖον Paulus, id alibi τύπον infra V. 14. 1. Cor. X. 6. 11. Justinus in colloquio cum Tryphone: διάκυσπότι εἰς σημεῖον ἡ περιτομὴ αὐτὴ δέδοται; ἀλλ᾽ ὄχ ὡς ἔργον δικαιοσύνης.

Σφραγῖδα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίσεως.

Circumcisionem corporis vocat σφραγῖδα ex parte A- brahami: quia sicut testes, cum annulum imprimunt in- strumento, ostendunt id esse sincerum, sic & Abraham im- primens sibi notam circumcisionis, plenam doloris, & ir- risam apud exteros, ostendit justitiam, id est, sinceritatem fidei suæ. DEUS enim promiserat Abrahamo stirpem in multas gentes exituram; addiderat se daturum posteri- tati ipsius terram Canaanæam, ac præterea, se DEUM fu- turum, id est, εὐεργέτην, tum ipsi tum posteris ejus: & in testimonium fidei habitæ his promissis, voluerat notam illam corporibus imponi, ut legimus Gen. XVII. 11. σφρα- γὶς respondet Hebræo אותם significatque annulum si- gnatorium, ut videre est Cant. VIII. 6. Jer. XXII. 24. Ezech. XXVIII. 12. Aggæi II. 24. unde & δακτύλιον ver- titur Gen. XXXVIII. 18. 25. aut etiam ipsam sculpturam, quæ est in annullo aut in realia: Exod. XXVIII. 11. 21. 36. XXXIX. 5. 12. 30. Hinc verbum חתם quod est σφρα- γίζεσθαι 1. Reg. XXI. 8. Neh. XII. Pf. VIII. 8. IX. 10. Esa. VIII. 16 XXIX. 11. Jerem. XXXII. 10. 11. 44. Dan. VI. 17. IX. 24. XII. 4. De cujus verbi usu κατὰ μεταφορὰν dixi- mus Joh. III. 33. Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos ait merito σφραγῖδα hanc, id est, circumcisionem ei parti impressam, quæ per naturam inutilis, per fidem actuosa facta fuerat: responsio CII Chrysostomus vero circumcisionem comparat notæ impressæ in militum cutem, quæ ostendit eos ad imperatorem pertinere.

Grotius circumcisionem externam ex eisdem Apostoli verbis modo signum circumcisionis in- ternæ facit, modo tesseram & notam populi Domi- ni: & justitiam fidei jam explicat per circumcisio- nem internam factam per fidem, jam per sincerita- tem fidei habitæ promissis divinis de stirpe in mul- tas gentes exitura, de terra Canaan, posteritati dan- da, & quod Deus Deus, id est, εὐεργέτης futurus sit tum ipsi tum posteris ejus: quam testatam reddi- derit Abram notam circumcisionis sibi imprimen- do. At circumcisio σφραγὶς sigillum dicitur, non signum pure σημαντικὸν, nec nota vel tessera solum; & quidem sigillum non circumcisionis internæ, sed justitiæ fidei, quæ est sine operibus legis, quam te- mere cum circumcisione interna confundit Gro- tius; Nam hæc ad renovationem & sanctificatio- nem pertinet, nec sine operibus legis spectari po- test: fidei autem justitia Abrahamo imputata in articulo justificationis vel in judicio divino χωρὶς ἔργων hic sistitur; & aliud est sinceritas fidei, aliud justitia fidei imputata Abrahæ, qua justificatus est coram DEO. Sinceritas est attributum & affectio fidei, justitia vero imputata est Objectum Fidei Abrahamicæ, uti imputatio justitiæ est ipsa forma justificationis. Quanquam vero non negemus, circumcisionem notam & tesseram fuisse populi Judaici & externam circumcisionem internæ signum dici posse facile admittamus, non tamen id heic loci agit Apostolus, sed id potius vult, Abraha- mum in præputio justificatum per solam fidem, circumcisionem accepisse non ut justificaretur, sed ut justitia fidei sine operibus legis per hoc Sacra- mentum in ipso veluti sigillo quodam obsignaretur & confirmaretur, ut ita fuerit Pater omnium cre- dentium in præputio, ut ipsis imputetur etiam justitia, omnesque eâ ratione exemplo Abrahæ in Christum credant, & per fidem in Christum credant, & per fidem in Christum justificentur justitiâ imputatâ sine operibus legis, citra ope- rum sive συνέργειαν, sive meritum, Christi unius justitia fide apprehensa, & credentibus impu- tata. Σημεῖον autem περιτομῆς signum circumci- sionis sigillum justitiæ fidei dicit Apostolus: nam circumcisio signum erat gratiæ, vel fœderis divini uti Syrus interpretatus est, signum fœderis, quod habetur Gen. XVII. 11. quia autem non est signum mere σημαντικὸν, addit vocem σφραγῖδος, quod scil. signum fuerit obsignans & confirmans. Unde apparet, circumcisionem adultis medium fuisse, per quod obsignata fuit credentibus gratia & ju- stitia; quam vero quia infantes etiam suscepêre, ut illis eo modo pariter obsignaretur gratia, neces- sum est, infantibus gratiam & justitiam per circum- cisionem etiam exhibitam & applicatam fuisse, quum alio medio applicationis destituti fuerint infantes, & circumcisio ordinata divinitus, ut in fœdus gratiæ per hoc Sacramentum susciperen- tur, eademque obsignarentur & confirmarentur, cui proinde annexa fuit promissio gratiæ, remissio- nis peccatorum & vitæ æternæ Gen. XVII. non quod tantum εὐεργέτης esse velit Deus, circumcisionem suscipientibus, nec solum quod hæreditare terram Canaan debeant, quæ accidentalis fuit promissio, siquidem post hæreditatem terræ Canaan acce- ptam adhuc tamen Sacramentum Circumcisionis di- spensari & suscipi debuerit; sed quod Deus ipso- rum Deus esse velit, gratiosa eorum in filios & hære- des vitæ æternæ adoptione, gratiaque sua paterna eos in hoc & futuro seculo complecti, & fovere. Conf. Matth. XXII. 32. Luc. XX. 38. Ap. XXI. 3.

τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ.

Ejus fidei quam habuerat etiam nondum circumci- sus. & hic ut supra 10.

Cur non referatur pronomen τῆς ad δικαιοσύ- νην ceu præcipuum objectum, de quo hic agitur? Res tamen eodem recidit; quia justitia & fides in- divulso nexu cohærent: unde etiam B. Lutherus ad fidem retulit.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πατέρα πάντων τῶν πιστευόντων.

Supra 10. πατέρα sumitur mysticè: Quo sensu πατέρα λόγων dixit & Philo. Sic Pater est, qui aliis præit institu- tione aut exemplo. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XIII, 19. Joh. 3. Justinus contra Tryphonem: τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ διὰ τὴν ὁμοίαν πίστιν ὄντες.

Recte hæc de Patre mystice accipiuntur & spiri- tuali, qui scil. non generationis respectu Pater di- citur, ut II. Reg.
