II, 12. non autem recte ad πατέρα λόγων, si de λόγῳ ὑποστατικῷ sermo fit, trahuntur. Ejus enim Pater est Deus non improprie, sed pro- prie, non regeneratione, sed æterna generatione, Ps. II, 7.

δι᾽ ἀκροβυστίας.

διὰ hic idem valet, quod modo ἐν. Sic διὰ χειρὸς ἔχειν in manu habere, διὰ στόματος εἶναι in ore esse populo, dicunt etiam Græci elegantiores. Vide supra II, 27.

Talem sensum vide fis 1. Tim. II. 15. salvabitur διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, id est, ἐν τεκνογονίᾳ.

εἰς τὸ λογισθῆναι καὶ αὐτοῖς τὴν δικαιοσύνην.

Idem est justitiam imputari per fidem, quod fidem im- putari in justitiam. Significat enim ascribi alicui laudem fidei nomine. Nam & laus dicitur justitia per μετωνυμίαν. Justitiæ deputatus est, ait Tertullianus.

Admitti potest, idem esse justitiam imputari per fidem: quod fidem imputari in justitiam, sensu Ev- angelico: Nam Christi justitia imputatur a DEO credentibus in Christum: id est, per fidem: & fides seu apprehensio obedientiæ Christi imputatur cre- dentibus, in justitiam, non secus ac si ipsorummet esset justitia. Per justitiam autem laudem indigi- tari metonymice glossa est, & ἐπίλυσις Grotio pro- pria. De justificatione coram tribunali Dei agit Apo- stolus, non de laude, quam coram Deo habemus fidei nomine, imo gloriationem omnem excludit.

καὶ πατέρα περιτομῆς.

Repetendum ex superiori loco εἰς τὸ εἶναι: & περιτομὴ hic intelligenda interior illa cordis.

## 4:12
to those not of circumcision only.

Not to the Jews alone, to Israel, to the Idumeans and the descendants of Keturah, take 'from' here as above II. 8. 27. III, 26. 'To those' here is general: which is then divided into two members, unless you prefer with the Syrian to think that the words are transposed here, so that it might be 'to those from' instead of 'to those'. 'But also to those who walk in the steps of the faith of our father Abraham which he had in uncircumcision.' In the Hebrew manner he placed the noun for a demonstrative pronoun. Abraham is 'father' partially to all who imitate his faith, which faith he had even while uncircumcised. 'To walk in the steps', 'to go', 'to go into the tracks', 'to follow in the tracks' are expressions by metaphor, for 'to imitate', even among the elegant Greeks. The Hebrews say for the same thing הלך בדרך. For דֶרֶךְ is translated as 'track' in Prov. XXX. 19. The Apostle is not speaking of internal circumcision, but of external, as the whole context testifies: nor does he now join believing Jews or Abrahamites and other nations, so that there is need for a transposition of the little words, but he speaks with such care, 'of those not of circumcision only', that he may indicate that he is the Father of those who not only receive circumcision outwardly, but who also insist upon the footsteps of Abraham, i.e., imitate his faith; he applies the same here to believing circumcised persons; therefore he says 'our father' cautiously, that is, of the Jews, as if to say: just as Abraham is the Father of believers from the nations, because righteousness was imputed to him in uncircumcision, so also he is our Father, of believers from the Jews, because he received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith.

PART III. A declaration of the justifying faith of Abraham.

Latin:

τοῖς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον.

Non solis Judæis, Israëlis, Idumæis & Cethuræ po- steris, ex hic sume ut supra II. 8. 27. III, 26. τοῖς hic generale est: quod deinde dividitur in duo membra, nisi cum Syro mavis arbitrari trajectas hic voces, ut sit τοῖς ἐκ pro τοῖς. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σοιχῦσι τοῖς ἴχνεσι τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀκρο- βυτίᾳ πίσεως τῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ. More Hebræo nomen posuit pro demonstrativo pro- nomine. Pater μερικῶς est Abraham omnibus fidem suam imitantibus, quam fidem habuit etiam incircumcisus. σοι- χεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι βαίνειν, εἰς ἴχνη ἰέναι, κατ’ ἴχνη ἀκολυθεῖν sunt locutiones κατὰ μεταφορὰν, pro imitari, etiam apud elegantes Græcos. Hebræi pro eodem dicunt הלך בדרך. Nam דֶרֶךְ ἴχνος vertitur Prov. XXX. 19. Non de circumcisione interna loquitur Aposto- lus, sed de externa, teste toto contextu: nec jam conjungit Judæos credentes vel Abramitidas, & gen- tes alias, ut trajectione opus sit vocularum, sed cum cura ita loquitur, τῆς ὀυκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον, ut in- dicet Patrem esse eorum, qui nòn solum circumci- sionem extrinsecus suscipiunt, sed qui etiam insi- stunt vestigiis Abrahami, h. e. fidem ejus imitantur; applicat hic idem ad credentes circumcisos; ideo netanter dicit τῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Pater Noster, id est, Judæorum, q. d. sicut Abraham est Pater creden- tium ex gentibus, quia in præputio ipsi imputata est justitia, ita etiam Pater noster est credentium è Ju- dæis, quia circumcisionem sigillum justitiæ fidei accepit.

PARS III. Fidei justificantis Abrahamicæ declaratio.

## 4:13
V. 13 'For the promise to Abraham'. Supply 'was'. For that promise was not made to Abraham under the condition of observing the law of Moses, since that did not yet exist at that time. The same sense is in Gal. III. 18. This argument, that the law of Moses did not yet exist in the time of Abraham, understood of the moral law, is not true: For that is perpetual, as far as its substance is concerned, even if as far as circumstances and solemn promulgation are concerned, it, like the Ceremonial law, may be referred to Moses and his times. Meanwhile, it can be admitted that the promise was not made to Abraham under the condition of observing the moral law: but under the condition of faith; although it is more correctly explained that the promise was not made 'through the law', that is, through the righteousness of the law, as is evident from the antithesis immediately subjoined, 'but through the righteousness of faith'. The reason is explained in this way, why the seed of Abraham is not to be estimated from carnal propagation, but from faith, because, namely, Abraham himself by believing became a participant in the divine promise; and an approach is made to the declaration of the faith by which Abraham was justified, and by which it is necessary for us to be justified, who insist upon the same footsteps; which is now subjoined.

or to his seed. If not to him, then neither to his posterity; for the promise is the same: in the cited place Gen. XVII.

That he should be the heir of the world. He refers to that promise, 'In thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed,' which pertains more broadly than to the possession of Canaan alone, and embraces a great part of the world, which is the world by synecdoche. For from that promise, the posterity of Abraham, besides Judea, held Idumea and the rest of Arabia, and even no small part of Ethiopia. Which happiness bore a mysterious image of eternal happiness: which Philo also acknowledges and rightly explains in his book, 'Who is the heir of divine things,' and the writer to the Hebrews teaches us openly in XI. 9, 10, 13. Christ is the heir of all things, Heb. I. 1, II. 5, and following, and with Christ, Christians, below XI. 17, Apoc. II. 26. Because among the Hebrews, lands received by inheritance were inalienable, therefore every firm and perpetual possession is called by them נַחֲלָה, an inheritance, as in Ps. II. 8 and elsewhere.

It is false that by these words 'that he should be the heir of the world' in Jesus Grotianus, that promise is referred to: 'In thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed,' because although this promise in its own proper sense, that in the Messiah an all-embracing blessing, if you consider the antecedent will of God, may happen to all the families of the earth, that is, of the whole world, embracing above all the inheritance of the world, or of the other age, yet Grotius does not intend this; but he wishes that Judea, Idumea, and certain other places were promised in this way only to the posterity of Abraham; which come under the name of the world by synecdoche according to the Apostle. For this discourse is not about the promise made to Abraham his seed, nor is it about the promise of some earthly portion, but about the promise of a blessing of every kind, and above all a heavenly one, which pertains not only to the carnal seed of Abraham, but to all who are of the Abrahamic faith, whether they descend from him by carnal propagation or not: nor is that promise, in THEE shall be blessed, that is, in thy seed or in the Messiah arising from thee (Conf. Gen. XXII. 18. Gal. III. 8.) all the families of the earth. By the families of the earth is not indicated the object of the blessing, or the matter concerning which, or the form, if one likes to call it so, the possession of some parts of the earth, but the subject to whom that blessing pertains, namely, who can be participants of the promised blessing, and ought to be so by divine intention. Nor is a double sense to be admitted in that promise, a literal one concerning the possession of parts of the earth and a mystical one concerning the possession of a heavenly inheritance. Finally, what subject will then remain to whom that promise ought to accrue in that mystical sense? For the families of the earth are to be referred in this way to the promised thing, namely to the promised inheritance of the new earth of the other age, which is indicated by the world in a mystical sense according to Grotius. Therefore, no subject remains to whom that promise was made. But that passage concerning Christ as heir of all things, Heb. I. 2, is foreign to this place, by which is designated not the inheritance of Judea, Idumea, and a part of Arabia and Ethiopia, nor only the heavenly inheritance, but, as the words have it, the inheritance of ALL THINGS, which are in the whole nature of things. For he who says ALL THINGS, as the Apostle himself warns, excludes nothing, ch. II. 8, under which it is not doubted that the future world is also included: concerning which the Apostle speaks openly in ch. II. 5, when he teaches that the world to come is subjected not to Angels, but to Christ according to his human nature: as rightly Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Lyranus [say] on that passage: whom also most interpreters understand by the age to come, Heb. VI. 5. Conf. Is. LXV. 17, ch. LXVI. 21, Rom. VIII. 21, 2 Pet. III. 13, Rev. XXI. 1, as also Is. IX. 6, Heb. XI. 10, ch. XIII. 14, and also Matt. XII. 31, 39, ch. XXIV. 3, Mark X. 30, Luke XVIII. 30, ch. XX. 35. 1 Cor. I. 20, ch. II. 6, 8, ch. III. 18, 2 Tim. IV. 10, Tit. I. 1, 2.

The future world is to be understood here entirely by the word 'world', and indeed in a literal sense, not only a mystical one, which they invent: because the matter here concerns the method of obtaining blessedness and eternal salvation, and how the promise that he should be heir of the world accrued to Abraham and his seed, namely, that it is declared that the inheritance was promised to him and his seed, not through the righteousness of the law or of works, but through the righteousness of faith; which promise certainly concerns the heavenly inheritance; as is manifest from the following verse, even by the admission of Grotius himself; for he readily concedes that by the word 'heir' the inheritance of the goods of the future age is understood. However much, therefore, some Calvinists may wish believers to be understood by the word 'world', that sense agrees neither with the custom of Scripture, which nowhere understands only believers by 'world', nor does it accord with the scope or mind of the Apostle: because, contrary to what Beza wishes, 'heir of the world' is not the same as 'Father of believers', for this was not the promise made to Abraham and his seed concerning an inheritance to be obtained not through the law but through the righteousness of faith, nor is 'heir' ever the same as 'Father'; indeed, relatively, it is opposed to 'Father', nor is Abraham the heir of his children, much less can the seed of Abraham, to whom that same promise was also made, be called the Father of believers; but the inheritance of the world is the inheritance of the new heaven and the new earth of the other age, or of heavenly blessedness. Conf. Exam. doctr. Reform. de perf. Christ. p. 495 seqq. Moreover, that promise was made to Abraham and his seed, not only when the blessing in Christ was promised to all the families of the earth (conf. Eph. I. 3), but also when the Son of God testified to Abraham that He would be his exceeding great reward. Gen. XV. 3, Matt. V. 5, 12, Rev. II. 28, ch. XXII. 12, and established the eternal covenant of grace with him and his seed, which is that He wills to be the God of him and of his seed, Gen. XVII. 7, Matt. XXII. 32, Rev. XXI. 7.

but through the righteousness of faith.

Through the integrity of mind, which partly consists in faith, and partly is born and nourished from faith.

This is now a supreme distortion; since it perverts the entire treatment of the Apostle, and attributes to him the mind of the Pseudo-Apostles, who it is established ascribed justification and salvation to both faith and works, whom the Apostle openly contradicts here, and teaches that justification and salvation occur only through faith, not through works, and that we are justified and saved by faith alone. Furthermore, Grotius very badly confuses faith and works, which are opposed to each other in the article and moment of justification and salvation, when he says that integrity of mind partly consists in faith and partly is born and nourished from faith, and he is opposed to himself and speaks contradictory things. For if integrity of mind is born from faith and is its fruit, offspring, and effect, which we admit, because the Apostle says faith is working through love, Gal. V. 6. & Charity and works, and thus the integrity of the mind are fruits of faith, so that faith cannot formally consist in the integrity of the mind, just as a fruit cannot be the soul or the form of a tree. Furthermore, that the righteousness of faith is the integrity of the mind is diametrically opposed to the Apostle: who opposes the righteousness of the law, to which there is no doubt that integrity of the mind pertains, to the righteousness of faith, and restricts the promise to this, and refers the heavenly inheritance to it, but not to that. For that promise was not made to Abraham under the condition of observing the law, as Grotius himself admitted a little earlier. And against this depravation, that the righteousness of faith is the integrity of the mind, all the arguments militate which were previously opposed to the Papists, who here understand our righteousness as inherent, so that there is no need to do what has already been done.

But we must touch upon the ψευδερμηνεία of the Socinians, who, with Socinus leading the way in his book *de Justif.* p. 109, wish to imply at least this much from the Apostle: that there are no works which are of such value that we can be justified on account of their merit, but that works whatsoever and however considered are by no means excluded; in which manner Schlichtingius in his *Comment. ad Rom.* IV. 2 explains the Apostle: that to be justified by works is to be justified by the merits of works, by the power and dignity of the works themselves, but that no works can merit justification by their own power, unless they are perfect in every part. And at v. 4, f. 118: It must be maintained that the discourse is not about any work whatsoever, even an imperfect one, which in no way corresponds to a reward, but that the word for working κατ' ἐξοχὴν must be taken as referring to a perfect work that equals the reward or corresponds to it by a just analogy. And afterwards: For it is understood by 'reward' in this place a reward which corresponds in dignity to the labor, and which comes to the labor by its own nature, or is owed by equity and justice. For such a reward to the worker, that is, to him who fully satisfies his duty, or works perfectly, It is not usually given out of some grace, but out of debt, such as the reward is justice or justification, which by its own nature is owed to him who is void of all sin and crime. But from the word to impute, the Apostle proves that this reward was not given out of debt, but out of mere kindness without debt.

But this gloss does not at all agree with the Apostle's sentiment. For it is easily evident that works perfect in every part, and which by their own power deserve justification, are not meant here (1.) because the Apostle simply excludes works, not just the merits of works, and teaches that we are justified χωρὶς ἔργων without works. (2.) Works are and are called in the Scriptures not only works perfect in every part, but also those which in any way conform to the law. (3.) The Apostle teaches that our works, by whatever name they come, have no part here in the article of justification, and thus he always excludes works. (4.) Before justification there are no works in man, as they follow the justified, but do not precede the one to be justified, since the ungodly is justified: and justification consists in the remission of sins, not in the imputation of imperfect works, as if they were perfect. (5.) Whatever pertains at all to the law is excluded here from justification. But good works, whether they be perfect in every part or not, pertain to the law. (6.) What was the point of arguing against the merits of works, to teach that a man is not justified by works perfect in every part, when it is placed in the clearest light that there are no works perfect in every part, and that there is no one who so perfectly fulfills the law that he renders obedience to it most absolute in all numbers, parts, and degrees. (7.) The Apostle's argument is to be understood in such a way that the opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles is struck down, not admitted. Now if by works in this place only works perfect in every part are understood, the opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles will not be excluded; for they contended that a man is justified by both faith and works, but not by works perfect in every way. For thus faith would not be a work. (8.) The opposition of the justice of faith and the justice of the law or of works is adequate and immediate, so that it is certain that a man is justified by faith alone, with no works intervening or being added, and those things are inconsistent and incompatible, as we say in the Schools, that a man is justified by faith, or by the apprehension of the most perfect obedience of Christ, and that a man is justified by works, whether entirely or in part, that is, by his own obedience, so that these either by their own nature obtain justification, or at least contribute something to obtaining justification: for thus we shall not be justified by the justice or obedience of that ONE (namely, Christ). (9.) Although the Socinians indeed strive entirely to exclude here the merits of the obedience of Christ and his satisfaction, which are opposed by them in every way, yet those things are most firmly grounded in the Scriptures, and provide the foundation of justification asserted by the Apostle, and it is evident from the above, and especially solidly asserted in the Socinismo profligato. (10.) That by reward is understood a reward which corresponds in dignity to the labor, can be easily admitted; otherwise, some reward will also correspond to works that are not sufficiently perfect, namely, proportional to the labor. But justification is not regarded here in any way as a reward for our labors, as it consists in the non-imputation of sins; but where sins are only brought to the tribunal of the judgment of GOD, and only their remission is made, there the reward of labors or any work comes into no account: but is entirely excluded. (11.) Where no matter of boasting is left to us at all, there rewards or works do not come into account in any way. But in our justification no matter of boasting is to be left to us at all. (12.) A reward is said to be imputed to the worker not according to grace, but according to debt, in proportion to the ratio of labor and work; if he works perfectly, such a reward is also owed to him, i.e., a perfect one. But if he does work, or strives for good works, yet does not perfectly fulfill the law, if works come into any account before the divine judgment, as far as a man's justification is concerned, it will be necessary that at least some reward, proportional to the labor, should accrue to him by virtue of justice. But on the contrary, the Apostle teaches that in this business of justification no reward at all is owed to us, no place at all is left for our works: but all things are done freely and out of grace: that a reward is imputed to us only κατὰ χάριν, but not in any part κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα: But to the worker, however he may work, provided those works are good and not evil, a reward is imputed so far as he is regarded as a worker, not according to grace, but according to debt. Which the blessed Meisner also observed in his disputation on the primary end of faith, thesis LIX. The worker, although he may fail in some things, nevertheless demands his reward out of debt. And if the obedience is most imperfect, yet the reward, if any is given, is given because of the works, and therefore not according to grace, but according to debt. He adds: that the Apostle speaks not so much of the works themselves as of the worker and his intention in verse 8. To him who does not work, i.e., who does not seek salvation in works: because those who are to be saved must not entirely not work, but they must not work with this intention and opinion, that works are the meritorious cause of their salvation. (13.) Here therefore in justification, the Apostle presents man, as far as he is regarded by GOD, as μὴ ἐργαζόμενον, not working at all, but who rather, since he is ἀσεβὴς, ungodly, void of and destitute of every good work which he might bring into judgment before justification, only believes, and by faith apprehends the divine grace and mercy, and is justified by it. (14.) That reward is not justification, as it is the remission of sins and the non-imputation of iniquities: but whatever is to be rendered to τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ, if he were to work perfectly, eternal life would be rendered to him as a reward: if we were hirelings, not mere servants and slaves, to whom no reward belongs. Luke 17:11. But he who fulfills the law less perfectly, if the working in the judgment of God concerning justification were considered, would certainly not bring back eternal life, yet would bring back something as a reward. (15.) The scope of the Apostle is to exclude here all works, and likewise every worker, not only the worker κατ’ ἐξοχὴν, and to leave them no part in justification; and on the contrary to assert a purely gracious imputation: not that our imperfect works are imputed to us as if they were perfect, for this is repugnant to divine justice and does not at all accord with the judgment which is according to truth, but since the ungodly who are justified bring no good works to the judgment of God, only evils and sins, which God out of grace wills not to impute, but to forgive them their sins, and to impute righteousness without our works, that is, an alien righteousness, which is Christ's, with no parts left to our works, and thus in no way regarded in the divine judgment when God justifies the ungodly. (16.) A twofold imputation is alleged here: the one which is κατὰ χάριν, which alone has a place in the business of our justification, since God justifies the ungodly, not working, only believing: the other which is κατ’ ὀφέιλημα [according to debt], when works come into the account, and it is judged that some reward is owed to them in proportion to their labors. Blessed Gerhard says in Comm. on Rom. IV. 1. 2. The Apostle in this place establishes a twofold imputation, one according to debt: the other according to grace: Imputation according to debt regards the worker; imputation according to grace regards the believer. The former has its foundation in the man himself, to whom the imputation is made; the latter has its foundation not in him, to whom the imputation is made, but in the grace, mercy, and favor of the one imputing. (17.) This does not please Schlichting, therefore he prefers to understand the word δίδοται [is given] in the other part, or to claim that the Apostle is using an ἀκυρολογίας [improper speech], contending that the words of the Apostle are to be accepted in this way: But to the worker the reward is not imputed, i.e., it is given according to grace; but, to wit, it is given according to debt, adding: or finally it must be established that the Apostle, studying brevity, spoke somewhat less accurately, as is wont to happen in such concise speeches, and abused the word to impute especially in the latter part of the statement in some way, and extended it too broadly. Whether this is not to derogate from Holy Scripture? Let the wise judge. (18.) Finally, this σφεδλότης [subtlety] of the Socinian Apostolic phrase of being justified by faith without works comes down to this, that we are justified by possible works or whatever they may be, without impossible works and those perfect in every part, against which we have argued in the Exegesis of the Augustan Confession, art. VI. c. I. Compare. Blessed Meisner, in his dissertation on the primary end and effect of faith, thesis LI, who among other things urges the opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles in this manner: The Apostle excludes those works to which the Pseudo-Apostles and Pharisees ascribed salvation, and opposes them to faith. But the Pseudo-Apostles ascribed salvation to works begun, not most perfect, to obedience of the law not impossible, but possible and falling within the reach of men, with the mercy of God included, not excluded. Wherefore the Apostle also excludes those, and opposes them to faith, unless you wish to say absurdly and impiously that he fought with phantoms and either ignored or changed the state of the question. Likewise the argument from the uncertainty of salvation. For if this is given only from works, and indeed those which we can do: it will always be to be doubted whether we have also done everything, or whether we could have performed more? In which way eternal life is rendered for us clearly ambiguous. For the Racovian Catechism requires that if we wish to be saved, we do the will of God according to our highest strength, p. 383. Ostorodus, according to all our ability, c. 36. Inst. p. 308. Smalcius, with most perfect obedient zeal in the refutation of the thesis of Mr. Dr. Francius, page 202. But from where will anyone be rendered certain that he has always striven with all his strength and most perfect effort to obey the precepts of Christ? Finally, from the nature of works. If they are even the most perfect, and satisfy divine precepts on all sides, they can nevertheless merit nothing absolutely, by their own power, before God. Thus the Savior taught, Luke 17:10. That which is not given, nor asserted by anyone, the Pauline antitheses are poorly explained concerning it. But the absolute merit of works is not given, nor asserted by anyone; therefore the Pauline antitheses are poorly explained concerning it. This is Blessed Meisner.

Latin:

V. 13 ὁ γὰρ διὰ νόμυ ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῷ Ἀβραάμ. Supple ἐγένετο. Non enim promissio illa facta est Abra- hamo sub conditione observandi legem Mosis, quippe quæ nondum tunc erat. Idem sensus Gal. III 18. Hæc ratio, quod lex Mosis Abrahami tempore nondum fuerit, de morali lege intellecta, vera non est: Ea enim perpetua est, quantum ad substan- tiam, etiamsi quantum ad circumstantias & sole- mnem promulgationem ea, ut & lex Ceremonialis ad Mosen ejusque tempora referatur. Interea ad- mitti potest, promissionem Abrahamo factam non esse sub conditione observandi legem moralem: sed sub conditione fidei; quamvis rectius exponi non factam esse promissionem διὰ νόμυ id est, per justitiam legis ex antithesi pateat mox subjuncta, ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίσεως, sed per justitiam fidei. Exponi- tur autem ita ratio, cur Abrahæ semen nõ ex carnali propagatione sit æstimandum, sed ex fide, quia scil. Abraham ipse credendo particeps promissionis di- vinæ factus est; & accessus fit ad declarationem fi- dei, qua justificatus est Abraham, quaque nos oportet justificari, qui insistimus ejusdem vesti- giis; quæ jam subjungitur.

ἢ τῷ σπέρματι ἀυτῦ. Si non ipsi, ergo nec posteritati ejus; nam eadem est promissio: dicto loco Gen. XVII.

Τὸ κληρονόμον αὐτὸν εἶναι τῦ κόσμε. Respicit promissum illud, Benedictæ erunt in te omnes familiæ terræ, quod latius pertinet, quam ad solius Cana- nææ possessionem, & magnam mundi partem, quæ mundus κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν, complectitur. Nam ex eo promisso Abra- hami posteritas præter Judæam tenuit Idumæam & cætera Arabiæ, Æthiopiæ etiam non pauca. Quæ felicitas arca- nam gerebat imaginem æternæ felicitatis: quod & Philo agnoscit & recte explicat libro, τίς ὁ τῶν θείων πραγμάτων κληρονόμος & aperte nos docet scriptor ad Hebræos XI. 9. 10. 13. Christus πάντων κληρονόμος Hebr. I. 1. II. 5. & se- quentibus, & cum Christo Christiani infra XI. 17. Apoc. II. 26. Quia apud Hebræos res soli hæreditate acceptæ erant inalienabiles, ideo omnis firma atque perpetua possessio ipsîs dicitur נַחֲלָה hæreditas ut Ps. I. 8. & alibi.

Falsum est per hæc verba τὸ κληρονόμον ἀυτὸν εἶναι τῦ κόσμε Jesu Grotiano respici illam promis- sionem: Benedictæ in te erunt omnes familiæ terræ, quia etsi hæc promissio sensu suo proprio, quod in Messia omnibus familiis terræ, id est, totius mundi contingat, si voluntatem DEI antecedentem respicias, omnigena benedictio, complectens imprimis τὴν κληρονομίαν τοῦ κόσμου hæreditatem mundi, vel seculi alterius, non tamen id intendit Grotius; sed promissam ita tantum vult Abra- hami posteritati Judæam, Idumæam & alia quædam loca; quæ mundi nomine Synecdochice veniant pe- nes Apostolum. Non enim de ἐπαγγελίᾳ vel pro- missione Abrahæ posteritati tantum facta, sed & Abrahæ & semini ejus, non de promissione portio- nis alicujus terrenæ, sed de promissione benedi- ctionis omnigenæ, imprimis vero cælestis hic sermo est, quæ non tantum Abrahami semini carnali, sed omnibus, qui fidei sunt Abrahamicæ, seu ab ipso descendent carnali propagatione, seu non, compe- tit: nec promissionis illius, benedicto erunt in TE, hoc est, in semine tuo vel ex te oriundo Messia (Conf. Gen. XXII. 18. Gal. III. 8.) omnes familiæ terræ. Per familias terræ non benedictionis Objectum, vel materia circa quam, aut forma, si ita vocare libeat, possessio partium aliquot terræ, sed subje- ctum, ad quod pertineat benedictio illa, qui- nam nempe benedictionis promissæ participes esse possint, atq; ex intentione divina esse debeant, indigitatur. Neque admittendus est in illa pro- missione sensus geminus, literalis de possessione par- tium terræ & mysticus de possessione cælestis hære- ditatis. Denique quodnam tum remanebit Sub- jectum, cui obtingere debeat illa promissio, in isto sensu mystico. Nam familiæ terræ ad rem promis- sam sic referendæ, nimirum ad promissam hære- ditatem terræ novæ alterius seculi, quæ per τὸ κόσ- μον sensu mystico indigitatur juxta Grotium. Nul- lum ergo Subjectum remanet, cui facta sit illa pro- missio. Illud vero de Christo κληρονόμῳ πάντων Ebr. I. 2. alienum hic loci est, quo non hæreditas Judææ, Idumææ & partis Arabiæ & Æthiopiæ, nec hæredi- tas cælestis tantum, sed ut verba habent, hæreditas OMNIUM designatur, quæ sunt in universa re- rum natura. Qui enim OMNIA dicit, ut Apo- stolus ipse monet, nihil excipit c. II. 8. sub quibus πᾶσι etiam orbem futurum comprehendi, dubium non est: de quo vero aperte c. II. 5. agit Aposto- lus, cum τὴν μέλλουσαν οἰκουμένην non Angelis, sed Christo secundum humanam naturam subjectam esse docet: ut recte Theodorestus, Oecumenius & Lyran. ad illum locum: quem etiam per μέλλοντα αἰῶνα Ebr. VI. 5. plerique interpp. intelligunt. Conf. Es. LXV. 17. c. LXVI. 21. Rom. IIX. 21. 2. Pet. III. 13. Apoc. XXI. 1. ut & Es. IX, 6. Ebr. XI. 10. c. XIII. 14. nec non Matth. XII. 31. 39. c. XXIV. 3. Marc. X. 30. Luc. XIIX. 30. c. XX. 35. 1. Cor. I. 20. c. II. 6. 8. c. III. 18. 2. Tim. IV. 10. Tit. I. 1. 2.

Qui orbis futurus per τὸν κόσμον hic omnino in- telligendus est, & quidem sensu literali, non tan- tum mystico, quem fingunt: quia agitur hic de ratione consequendi μακαρισμὸν, beatitudinem & salutem æternam, & quo pacto Abrahamo & semini ejus ἐπαγγελία τὸ κληρονόμον αὐτὸν εἶναι τοῦ κόσμου obtigerit, nempe quod hæreditas ipsi promissa sit & semini ejus, non per justitiam legis vel operum, sed per justitiam fidei, declaratur; quæ ἐπαγγελία concernit utique cælestem hæreditatem; uti ex ver- su sequenti, fatente ipso Grotio, manifestum est; Ille n. voce κληρονόμος intelligi hæreditatem bono- rum futuri seculi ultro concedit. Utut ergo Calvinia- ni nonnulli voce κόσμου intellectos velint credentes, sensus tamen ille nec Scripturæ consuetudini, quæ nuspiam per κόσμον solos credentes intelligit, con- venit, nec Scopo aut menti Apostoli congruit: quia non, quod Beza vult, hæres mundi idem est, quod Pater credentium, hæc enim non erat promissio Abrahæ & semini ejus facta de hæreditate non διὰ νόμου ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίσεως consequenda, nec hæres uspiam idem est, quod Pater, imo relati- ve Patri opponitur, nec Abraham filiorum suo- rum hæres, nedum semen Abrahæ, cui utique ea- dem promissio etiam facta, Pater credentium dici potest; sed mundi hæreditas est hæreditas cæli novi & terræ novæ alterius seculi, vel beatitudinis cæle- stis. Conf. Exam. doctr. Reform. de perf. Christ. p. 495. seqq. Promissio autem illa Abrahæ & semi- ni ejus facta est, non solum cum omnibus familiis terræ benedictio in Christo promissa conf. Eph. I. 3. sed etiam cum filius DEI testatus est Abrahamo, se ei fore mercedem valde magnam. Gen. XV. 3. Matth. V. 5. 12. Ap. II. 28. c. XXII. 12. & fœdus gratiæ æter- num cum ipso, & semine ejus sancivit, quod velit esse Deus ipsius & seminis ejus Gen. XVII. 7. Matth. XXII. 32. Apoc. XXI. 7.

ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίστεως.

Per animi probitatem, quæ partim in fide consistit, partim ex fide nascitur aliturque.

Hæc jam est στρεβλότης palmaria; quum per- vertat universam tractationem Apostoli, eique mentem Pseudo-Apostolorum, quos & fidei, & operibus justificationem & salutem adscripsisse constat, affricet, quibus vero Apostolus hic palam contradicit, & justificationem & salutem solum per fidem, non per opera contingere, nec nisi sola fi- de nos justificari & salvari docet. Adhæc fidem, & opera, quæ in articulo & momento justificationis, ac salutis sibi opponuntur, pessime confundit Gro- tius, cum animi probitatem partim in fide consistere, partim ex fide nasci, alique ait, sibique ipsi adversus est, & contraria loquitur. Si enim ex fide nascitur animi probitas ejusque fœtus, proles, & effectus est, quod admittimus, quia Apostolus fidem δι' ἀ- γάπης ἐνεργουμένην dicit Gal. V. 6. & Charitas atq; opera, adeoque animi probitas fructus sunt fidei, utique in animi probitate fides formaliter consi- stere non potest, perinde uti fructus esse nequit a- nima, vel forma arboris. Porro πίσιν δικαιοσύνης justitiam fidei esse animi probitatem καδδιάμετρον contrariatur Apostolo: qui opponit Justitiam le- gis, ad quam animi probitatem pertinere nullum est dubium, justitiæ fidei, & ad hanc promissionem restringit, & hæreditatem cælestem refert, non vero ad illam. Non enim promissio illa facta est Abrahamo sub conditione observandi legem, ut paulo antea fassus est ipse Grotius. Atque adversus hanc depravationem, quod justitia fidei animi probitas sit, militant argumenta omnia, quæ Ponti- ficiis antea opposita fuêre, qui hic justitiam nostram, vel inhærentem intelligunt, ut opus non sit actum agere.

Socinianorum autem tangenda est ψευδερμη- νεία, qui præeunte antefignano Socino l. de Justif. p. 109. id saltem ab Apostolo innui volunt, nulla esse opera, quæ tanti sint, ut propter ipsorum meritum ju- stificari possimus, minime vero excludi opera quæcun- que & quomodocunque considerata: quo pacto Schlichtingius in Comment. ad Rom. IV. 2. expli- cat Apostolum: quod ex operibus justificari sit ex operum meritis, ipsorum operum vi, & dignitate justificari, mereri autem sua vi justificationem nulla opera posse, nisi ex omni parte perfecta. Et ad v. 4. f. 118. Statuendum est non de quovis opere etiam imperfecto, mercedi nequaquam re- spondente esse sermonem, sed verbum operandi κατ' ἐξοχὴν sumendum esse de opere perfecto & mer- cedem æquante eive justa analogia respondente. Et postea: Intelligitur enim per mercedem h. l. mer- ces, quæ labori dignitate respondeat, & quæ labori suâ naturâ obveniat, sive ex æquo & justo de- beatur. Ejusmodi enim merces operanti, h. e. ei qui officio suo plene satisfacit, sive perfecte operatur, non solet ex gratia aliqua, sed ex debito dari, qualis merces est justitia sive justificatio, quæ sua natura debetur illi, qui omni peccato & crimine est vacuus. Ex verbo autem imputandi probat Apostolus hanc mercedem non ex debito fuisse datam, sed ex mera be- nignitate citra debitum.

Quæ vero glossa Apostoli sententiæ haud qua- quam congruit. Non enim intelligi hic tantum opera ex omni parte perfecta, & quæ sua vi justifica- tionem mereantur; facile patet (1.) quia Aposto- lus simpliciter opera excludit, non tantum merita operum, & χωρὶς ἔργων absque operibus nos ju- stificari docet. (2.) Opera sunt & vocantur in Scripturis non tantum opera ex omni parte per- fecta, sed etiam ea, quæ quomodocunque legi conveniant. (3.) Nullas hic partes esse operibus nostris quocunque nomine veniant, in articulo justificationis, docet Apostolus, adeoque opera semper excludit. (4.) Ante Justificationem in homine nulla sunt opera, utpote quæ justifica- tum sequuntur, non vero justificandum præce- dunt, quum justificetur impius: & justificatio in remissione peccatorum consistat, non vero in im- putatione operum imperfectorum, ac si perfecta essent. (5.) Quicquid omnino ad legem pertinet, hic à justificatione excluditur. At opera bona seu perfecta illa sint omni ex parte, seu non, ad legem pertinent. (6.) Quid attinebat disputari contra operum merita, ut doceretur, hominem non justificari per opera omni ex parte perfecta, quum nulla esse opera omni ex parte perfecta, neminem esse, qui perfecte legem ita impleat, ut obedientiam eidem omnibus numeris, parti- bus & gradibus absolutissimam præstet, in luce manifestissima positum sit. (7.) Ita hæc intelligen- da est Apostoli disputatio, ut Pseudo-Apostolo- rum sententia feriatur, non admittatur. Jam si opera tantum omni ex parte perfecta per opera intelligantur hoc loco, non excludetur Pseudo- Apostolorum sententia; qui hominem & fide & operibus justificari contendebant, non autem operibus omnis modo perfectis. Sic enim fides opus non foret. (8.) Oppositio justitiæ fidei, & justitiæ legis, vel operum adæquata est, & imme- diata, ut fide solum, nullis operibus intervenien- tibus vel accedentibus hominem justificari con- stet, & ἀσύστατα illa sunt, & incompatibilia, uti loquimur in Scholis, hominem justificari fide, vel apprehensione obedientiæ Christi perfectissimæ, & ho- minem justificari operibus, sive ex asse, sive ex parte, id est, obedientia propria, ut hæc vel natura sua obtineat justificationem, vel saltim ad obtinen- dam justificationem etiam aliquid conferant: sic enim non justificabimur UNIUS illius (Christi nempe) justitia, vel obedientia. (9.) Quanquam vero Sociniani omnino id agant, ut merita obe- dientiæ Christi, & satisfactionem ejus hic ex- cludant, quæ omnibus modis ab ipsis oppugnan- tur, ea tamen in Scripturis fundatissima sunt, & fundamentum justificationis ab Apostolo assertæ præbent, & è superioribus patet, & imprimis solide assertum in Socinismo profligato. (10.) Per mer- cedem eam intelligi mercedem, quæ dignitate labori respondeat, admitti facile potest, cæterum etiam operibus non satis perfectis ita aliqua merces re- spondebit, proportionata nempe labori. Sed justificatio hic non ut merces laborum nostrorum ullatenus respicitur, utpote quæ in non-imputa- tione peccatorum consistit; ubi vero peccata tan- tum adferuntur ad tribunal judicii DEI, eorum- que solum fit remissio, ibi in censum nullum ve- nit merces laborum, aut opus ullum: sed peni- tus excluditur. (11.) Ubi nulla prorsus relinquen- tur da nobis est gloriationis materia, ibi nullo pacto merces vel opera in censum veniunt. At in ju- stificatione nostra nulla prorsus relinquenda no- bis est gloriationis materia. (12.) Operanti mer- ces imputari dicitur non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum, pro ratione proportionis labo- ris & operis; si perfecte operetur, merces etiam talis debetur ipsi, h. e. perfecta. Si autem ope- retur quidem, vel operibus bonis studeat, non tamen perfecte legem impleat, si opera in cen- sum aliquem veniant coram judicio divino, quan- tum ad hominis justificationem, necessum erit, ut merces ei obtingat saltim aliqua & proportio- nata labori, vi justitiæ. At ex adverso docet Apo- stolus, in hoc justificationis negotio nullam, nullam omnino mercedem nobis deberi, nullum, nullum omnino locum relinqui operibus nostris: sed omnia gratis, & ex gratia fieri: imputari nobis mercedem solum κατὰ χάριν, non autem ulla parte κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα: Operanti vero, quomodo- cunque operetur, modo bona illa, non mala sint opera, merces hactenus, qua ut operans respi- citur, non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum imputatur. Quod observavit etiam B. Meisnerus in disput. de primario fine fidei th. LIX. Operator, licet in quibusdam deficiat, ta- men mercedem suam ex debito postulat. Et si obe- dientia maxime sit imperfecta, tamen merces, si quæ datur, propter opera datur, adeoque non se- cundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Addit: quod non tam de ipsis operibus, quam de operan- te ejusque intentione loquatur Apostolus vers. 8. Ei qui non operatur, h. e. qui salutem in operi- bus non quærit: quia salvandi non debent plane non operari, sed tantum hac intentione ac opinione non debent operari, quod opera sint meritoria illorum salutis causa. (13.) Hic ergo in justificatione, hominem, quatenus respicitur a DEO, sistit Apostolus μὴ ἐργαζόμενον, nullatenus operantem, sed qui potius, quum ἀσεβὴς impius sit, omni bo- no opere, quod in judicium adferat, ante justi- ficationem vacuus, & destitutus, solummodo credat, & fide apprehendat gratiam & misericordiam di- vinam, eaque justificetur. (14.) Merces illa non est justificatio, utpote quæ est remissio peccato- rum, & non imputatio iniquitatum: sed quicquid retribuendum est τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ, si perfecte ope- raretur, vita æterna reddenda ipsi pro mercede fo- ret: si mercenarii, non servi meri & manci- pia, quibus nulla merces competit, essemus. Luc. XVII. 11. qui vero minus perfecte legem im- pleat, si τὸ operari in judicio DEI circa justifi- cationem respiceretur, non sane vitam æternam, aliquid tamen pro mercede reportarent. (15.) Sco- pus Apostoli est, ut opera omnia, ita operantem omnem, non tantum operantem κατ’ ἐξοχὴν hic ex- cludere, nullasque eis in justificatione partes re- linquere; & contra asserere mere gratiosam impu- tationem: non quod opera nostra imperfecta nobis imputentur, ac si perfecta essent, hoc enim re- pugnat justitiæ divinæ, & judicio, quod est secun- dum veritatem, haud convenit, sed cum nulla ad judicium DEI opera bona, solum mala & peccata adferant impii, qui justificantur, quod non imputare, sed remittere DEUS ex gra- tia velit ipsis peccata, & imputare justitiam sine operibus nostris, hoc est, alienam justitiam, quæ Christi est, nullis relictis partibus operi- bus nostris, adeoque nullatenus spectatis in judi- cio divino, cum justificat DEUS impium. (16.) Gemina hic allegatur imputatio: altera quæ sit κατὰ χάριν, quæ in negotio justificationis no- stræ unice locum habet, cum DEUS justificet impium, non operantem, solummodo credentem: altera quæ sit κατ’ ὀφέιλημα, cum in censum veniunt opera, iisque pro laborum proportione mercedem aliquam deberi judicatur. Duplicem, inquit B. Gerhardus in Comm. ad Rom. IV. 1. 2. Apostolus b. l. statuit imputationem, unam secundum debitum: alteram secundum gratiam: Imputatio secundum debitum respicit operantem; imputatio secundum gratiam respicit credentem. Illa fundamentum habet in ipso homine, cui fit imputatio, hæc fundamentum habet non in eo, cui fit imputatio, sed in gratia, misericordia & favore imputantis. (17.) Non hoc placet Schlichtingio, ideo subintelligere mavult in altera parte verbum δίδοται, aut ἀκυρολογίας postulare Apostolum, hoc pacto verba Apostoli accipienda esse contendens: Operanti autem non imputatur merces, h. e. secundum gratiam datur; sed scil. datur secundum debitum, addens: vel denique statuendum, Apostolum brevitati studendo minus quodammodo accurate, ut in ejusmodi concisis sermonibus fieri solet, fuisse locutum, & verbo imputandi in posteriori præsertim enunciati parte abusum aliquo modo, idque latius extendisse. Quod annon sit derogare Scripturæ Sacræ? cordati judicent. (18.) Denique σφεδλότης hæc Socinianorum phraseos Apostolicæ justificari fide sine operibus huc redit, nos justificari per opera possibilia vel qualiacunque, sine operibus impossibilibus & ab omni parte perfectis, adversus quam egimus in Exegem. Augustan. Confession. art. VI. c. I. Confer. B. Meisnerus disp. de primar. fin. & effect. fidei thes. LI. Qui inter alia urget Pseudo-Apostolorum sententiam h. m. Quibus operibus Pseudo-Apostoli & Pharisæi salutem adscribebant, illa excludit, fideique opponit Apostolus. Sed operibus inchoatis, non perfectissimis, obedientiæ legis non impossibili, sed possibili & in homines cadenti, inclusâ, non seclusâ DEI misericordia, salutem adscribebant Pseudo-Apostoli. Quapropter illa etiam excludit, fideique opponit Apostolus, nisi absurde impieque velis dicere, ipsum cum larvis pugnasse & statum quæstionis vel ignorasse, vel immutasse. Item argumentum ab incertitudine salutis. Si enim hæc datur non nisi ex operibus, & quidem iis, quæ facere possumus: semper dubitandum erit, an etiam omnia fecerimus, annon plus præstare potuerimus? quo pacto vita æterna nobis redditur plane ambigua. Nam Catechismus Racoviensis requirit, ut si salvari volumus, voluntatem DEI faciamus pro summis viribus nach dem höchsten Vermögen, p. 383. Ostorodus, secundum omnem facultatem nostram, nach allem besten Vermögen, c. 36. Inst. p. 308. Smalcius perfectissimo obedienti studio in refut. thes. Dn. D. Francii pag. 202. Unde autem quis certus reddetur, quod omnibus viribus & perfectissimo conatu semper studuerit præceptis Christi obtemperare? Denique ab operum natura. Si maxime perfectissima sint, & divinis præceptis undique satisfaciant, nihil tamen absolute, per vim suam, coram DEO mereri possunt. Ita docuit Salvator Luc. 17. 10. Quod non datur, nec à quoquám asseritur, de illo male exponuntur Paulinæ antitheses. Sed absolutum operum meritum non datur, nec a quoquam asseritur; Ergo de illo male exponuntur Paulinæ antitheses. Hæc B. Meisnerus.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. For if they which are of the law be heirs.

Here, having left the historical sense, he comes to the mystical. If those, he says, who outwardly fulfill the law of Moses, namely as they are such, obtain those goods of the future age ἐκ [from] again here as just now in 12.

κενόωται [is made void] corresponds to the Hebrew אָמַל in Jeremiah 14:4, 15:9; it signifies to lack strength. Thus you have κενῶσαι [to make void] also in 1 Cor. 1:17, 9:15, 2 Cor. 9:3. If the law of Moses was to be expected in this, his faith profited Abraham nothing.

and the promise is made of none effect.

Therefore that promise made to Abraham long before the law of Moses, lacked effect. κατήργηται [is made of none effect] as just now κεκένωται [has been made void], here signifies not the reception of an action, but existence itself: just as δεδικαίωται [has been justified] is sometimes 'was righteous': Thus Gal. 5:4, 11. בטל [to cease] is translated as ἀργεῖν [to be idle] in Ecclesiastes 12:3.

There is no trace of a mystical sense here. But from these things it is clear that κληρονομίαν τῦ κόσμου [the inheritance of the world] in the preceding is to be taken in the proper and literal sense concerning the inheritance of eternal life, which the Apostle teaches is not had from the law. He therefore is called ὁ ἐκ νόμου [he who is of the law] not who outwardly fulfills the law of Moses, but whom the Apostle previously called ἐργαζόμενον [working]: If those, says the Apostle, observe the law, as such is an heir of eternal life, faith is vain, and the promise is made void. For faith, which is the apprehension of the obedience of Christ, as it is imputed to the believer by the power of the divine promise, the righteousness of Christ, would be vain, if even in any part our righteousness alone and the fulfillment of the law contributed anything to obtaining the heavenly inheritance: because it would thus derogate from the obedience of Christ, that the obedience of one Christ would not suffice for our justification, and the divine promise would be made void, as it is had only in the Gospel, not in the law, nor does it require works of the law for salvation, but faith only in Christ: in sum, the whole Evangelical doctrine would be overturned, as we see happening among workers mixing the law and the Gospel, seeking justification not from faith alone but also from works, or neglecting the righteousness of faith, striving to set up their own righteousness, the Pharisees, Pontificians, Socinians, Majorists, Calixtines, and others of this bran who are heterodox. Blessed Luther is to be heard here concerning the parallel passage Gal. III. 17. in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, Vol. I, Jena Latin edition, fol. 351. He intends to infer this conclusion: If righteousness can be had from us through the law and its works, then the promise of the blessing of Abraham made is in vain, because without it we can be righteous through the law, or at least it itself is not enough to justify, if the righteousness of the law must be added. And thus the testament and promise of GOD is either superfluous or deficient, so that it is necessary for something else to be superadded. But both are most detestable; therefore the opposite is true: the righteousness of the law is neither necessary nor sufficient. Behold, a certainly most powerful argument. Let us see, therefore: In every testament there is a testator, there is one to whom the testament is made, there is the testament itself, there is the thing which is bequeathed or left. So here, GOD is the testator, for He Himself promises and bequeaths. Abraham and his seed are those to whom the testament is made, as heirs of GOD the testator. The testament is the promise itself, Gen. 21 and 17. The thing bequeathed is the inheritance itself, that is, grace and the righteousness of faith, namely the blessing of the nations in the seed of Abraham. If, therefore, the grace of the promise and the righteousness of GOD, exhibited through Christ (and thus by the testament of GOD confirmed through His death, nay, already executed and distributed), does not suffice unless you also have the righteousness of the law, does not the Testament of GOD, not only declared but also confirmed and fulfilled, become void, and is something superadded to it? which indeed ought to be done to the testament of a man. But if grace suffices, and the Testament of GOD is firm, it is evident that the righteousness of the law is not to be sought. The same in Rom. 4: If those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void, the promise is abolished. And a little later: The testament (says the Apostle) of God confirmed in Christ, ought not to be made void through the law and its justice. It would be made void, and would evacuate the promise entirely, if its works were necessary for justification, as if the grace of the promise were not enough or were impotent for our justification. Why indeed the Apostle here enters into a computation of time, when he teaches that the law was given many years after the promise, the blessed Luther explains excellently in that place, whose exegesis we rightly oppose to the Grotian ineptitudes concerning the argument from the priority of the divine promise made to Abraham with respect to the Mosaic law. But what he adds (the Apostle) 'which was made after 430 years, the law,' he seems to do by tapinosis against the law, as if he were saying: If the promise had been given after the law, it could have seemed to be obtained by the merit of the justice of the law. But now it is given by God without the works of the law, by grace, out of justice, so that even so many years before the law, much more before its justice, it was promised, with no one deserving it, no one asking for it, but by the sole mercy of God gratuitously promising. Why therefore will the law evacuate this promise of grace, now an exhibition, when the law had operated nothing toward either? And Rom. 3 he says, 'without the law the justice of God is manifested.' Indeed Rom. 4, the law has operated the contrary, while it rather operates wrath and increases offenses. Far be it, therefore, that justice should lean upon the law and our works; rather, let it lean upon the most faithful promise of God, who does not lie; even if we are made worse and more unworthy through the law.

For if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from the promise. That is, if the justice which was promised to Abraham in the blessing is from the works of the law and from us, the promise is evacuated and superfluous. It cannot be from us and from God at the same time, since He is truthful and we are liars. He proves this with the word that he has already said, that the promise is not evacuated by the law. Because (he says) if it is from the law, then the promise is evacuated by the law. Just as also Rom. 4: 'If heirs are from the law, the promise is abolished.' These are the words of the blessed Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἐἰ γὰρ ὁἰ ἐκ νόμυ κληρονόμοι.

Hic relicto sensu historico ad mysticum venit. Si illi, inquit, qui legem Mosis exterius implent, nempe qua tales sunt, adipiscuntur bona illa futuri seculi ἐκ rursum hic ut modo 12.

κενόωται respondet Hebræo אָמַל Jerem. XIV. 4. XV. 9. id significat vi carere. Sic κενῶσαι habes & 1. Cor. I. 17. IX. 15. II. Cor. IX. 3. Si lex Mosis expectanda in hoc fuit, nihil Abrahamo fides sua profuit.

καὶ κατήργηται ἡ ἐπαγγελία.

Ergo promissio illa multo ante legem Mosis facta Abrahamo, effectu caruere. κατήργηται ut modo κεκένωται, hic non susceptionem actionis, sed ipsam existentiam significat: sicut δεδικαίωται interdum est justus fuit: Sic Gal. V. 4. 11. בטל ἀργεῖν vertitur Ecclesiastæ XII. 3.

Nullum hic Sensus mystici vestigium est. Ex hisce autem patet, κληρονομίαν τῦ κόσμου in præcedentibus sensu proprio & literali accipiendam esse de hæreditate æternæ vitæ, quam non ex lege haberi docet Apostolus. Ille ergo dicitur ὁ ἐκ νόμου non qui legem Mosis exterius implet, sed quem ἐργαζόμενον antea dixit Apostolus: Si qui legem, inquit Apostolus, observant, qua talis hæres est vitæ æternæ, fides vana est, & evacua- tur promissio. Fides enim, quæ apprehensio est obedientiæ Christi, ut credenti imputatur vi promissionis divinæ, justitia Christi, vana foret, si vel ulla parte solum nostra justitia & legis impletio ad obtinendam hæreditatem cœlestem aliquid conferret: quia derogaretur ita obedientiæ Christi q. unius Christi obedientia non sufficiat ad nostri justificationem & evacuaretur promissio divina, utpote quæ in Evangelio solum, non in lege habetur, nec ad salutem opera legis requirit, sed fidem solum in Christum: summa, tota doctrina Evangelica everteretur, uti fieri videmus apud operarios legem & Evangelium commiscentes, justificationem non ex fide solum sed operibus etiam quærentes, vel neglecta fidei justitia justitiam propriam erigere satagentes Pharisæos, Pontificios, Socinianos, Majoristas, Calixtinos & hujus furfuris alios heterodoxos. Audiendus hic B. Lutherus de loco parallelo Gal. III. 17. in Comment. in Epist. ad Gal. Tom. I. Jen. Lat. f. 351. Intendit autem hanc inferre conclusionem: Si justitia potest haberi ex nobis per legem & opera ejus, jam frustranea est promissio benedictionis Abrahæ facta, Quia sine ea justi esse possumus per legem, aut certe ipsa non satis est, ut justificet, si legis justitia superaddenda est. Et sic testamentum & promissio DEI aut superfluit, aut deficit, ut necesse sit aliud superordinari. Utrumque autem detestabilissimum, ergo oppositum verum justitiam legis, neque necessariam, neque sufficientem. Ecce fortissimum certe argumentum. Videamus itaque, In omni testamento est testator, est cui fit testamentum, est ipsum testamentum, est res quæ testatur seu legatur. Ita hic, DEUS est testator, ipse enim promittit & legat. Abraham & semen ejus sunt, quibus fit testatio, ut hæredibus DEI testatoris. Testamentum est ipsa promissio Gen. 21. & 17. Res testata, est ipsa hæreditas, id est, gratia & justitia fidei scilicet benedictio gentium in semine Abrahæ. Si ergo, gratia promissionis, & justitia DEI, per Christum exhibita (& sic testamento DEI per mortem suam confirmato, imo jam executo & distributo) non sufficit, nisi & legis justitiam habeas, nonne jam Testamentum DEI, non nuncupatum modo, sed confirmatum & expletum quoque irritum fit, & aliquid ei superordinatur? quodne hominis Testamento quidem fieri debet. Si autem sufficit gratia, & Testamentum DEI firmum est, patet justitiam legis non esse quærendam. Idem Rom. 4. Si qui ex lege sunt, hæredes sunt, exinanita est fides, abolita promissio. Et paulo post: Testamentum (inquit Apostolus) Dei confirmatum in Christum, non debet irritum fieri per legẽ & justitiam ejus. Fie- ret autem irritum, & evacuaret promissionem omnino, si ejus opera ad justificationem necessaria forent, tanquam promissionis gratia non esset satis aut impotens, ad justificationem nostri. Cur vero hic temporis computum ineat Apostolus, cum docet, legem multis annis post promissionem da- tam, præclare ibidem explicat B. Lutherus, quam ejus ἐξήγησιν Grotianis ineptiis de argumento à promissionis divinæ Abrahamo factæ prioritate respectu legis Mosaicæ merito opponimus. Quod autem addit (Apostolus) quæ post 430. annos fa- cta est lex, per tapinosin facere videtur in legem, ac si dicat: Si promissio fuisset post legem data, poterat videri per justitiam legis merito impetrata. Nunc vero à Deo sine legis operibus, gratia, ex justitia da- tur, ut etiam tot annis ante legem, multo magis ante justitiam ejus fuerit promissa, nullis merentibus, nul- lis petentibus, sed sola Dei misericordia gratuito pro- mittente. Cur ergo lex evacuabit hanc gratiæ pro- missionem, nunc exhibitionem, cum ad utrumque lex nihil fuerit operata. Et Rom. 3. dicit, sine lege ma- nifestata est justitia Dei. Imo Rom. 4. contra ope- rata est lex, dum iram potius operatur, & offensiones auget. Absit ergo, ut justitia innitatur legi, & operi- bus nostris, imo innitatur fidelissimæ promissioni Dei, qui non mentitur; etiamsi nos per legem pejores & indigniores efficiamur.

Nam si ex lege hæreditas, jam non ex promis- sione. Id est, si justitia, quæ Abrahæ promissa est in benedictione, ex operibus legis, & ex nobis est, eva- cuata & superflua est promissio. Non potest idem ex nobis, & Deo esse, cum ipse verax, nos mendaces si- mus. Probat hoc verbo, quod jam dixit, promissio- nem non evacuari per legem. Quia (inquit) si ex lege, jam promissio evacuatur per legem. Sicut & Rom. 4. Si ex lege hæredes, abolita est promissio. Hæc B. Lutherus.

## 4:15
V. 15. 'For the law works wrath.' He shows what this law of Moses does, insofar as it is the law of Moses only, that is, insofar as it is distinguished from those precepts and interdicts which had been from the beginning. Namely, it brings a penalty upon grave sins, and indeed a certain one, and in many cases a lethal one, whereas before, crimes were in many cases overlooked, or had a penalty that was either light or arbitrary. We have taken ὀργὴν for penalty, as also above II. 5. 8. III. 5. See also Matthew III. 7. κατεργάζεσθαι is placed by interpreters also for 'asah and for pa'al, both of which signify an effect of any kind. Among the virtues of the law, Modestinus places 'to punish,' as we have said above.

Where there is no law, there is no transgression. That manuscript is better with ὗ δὲ; it does not say there is no sin, but that there is no 'stuy, that is, contempt of a law given by God not through collections, but expressly: and therefore there is less merit of punishment. See what we have said above II. 9. 12. III. 20.

With those trifles dismissed, concerning the law of Moses, insofar as it is the law of Moses only, and insofar as it is distinguished from those precepts which were from the beginning, since it is undoubted that the moral law, which is looked at here, was inscribed upon the heart in the primal creation of man, the remnants of which we still have in the law of nature after the fall; likewise concerning the penalty for grave sins, which is certain and in many cases lethal; since every transgression of the law brings in a curse and eternal death, and it was not a matter of penalty in the forum of the soil, but in the forum of heaven here: finally, with that lust for correcting the received codices from a single manuscript dismissed, where no necessity compels it; it is in the open that Grotius has wandered very far from the mind of the Apostle: who teaches that the law operates the wrath of God, or even if one likes, the penalty, but not a temporal one only, but also an eternal one, by the force of the curse promulgated in Deut. XXVII. 26, and that meritoriously, on account of the violated infinite justice of God: which, to wit, is not performed by us: and where there is no law, there does not have place a parabasin, that is, a transgression of the law: for not only contempt of the law, but any transgression of the same operates wrath: whence the Apostle concludes that the law cannot contribute anything to justification: and so neither does the justice of the law lead to that. For whatever only operates wrath, if it comes into the contention of judgment, or if God wishes to enter into judgment with us, it is most certain that it contributes nothing to our justification. But concerning the divine law, the former and the latter are true. But that the divine law only operates wrath is not the fault of the law but of us, because it cannot be fulfilled by us after we fell away from GOD through the fall of our first parents: 'But he who does not remain in all things which are written in the law is pronounced cursed,' Deut. XXVII. 26. and he who has kept the whole law, but has fallen in one thing at least, is guilty of ALL. James II. 10. Therefore, this is attributed to the law by accident, which by itself is the word of life and of salvation. The Papists do not wish to bear the exclusive, and they argue against the blessed Luther because he rendered it: 'Das Gesetz richtet nur Zorn an' (The law only works wrath). But the blessed Luther added the exclusive so that he might emphatically explain the mind of the Apostle, who concludes from there that the law does nothing at all or contributes nothing to justification and salvation, because the law operates wrath. In this immediate opposition, therefore, by which 'to justify,' i.e., to absolve from sin, and 'to operate wrath,' i.e., to accuse and condemn sin, are opposed to each other, the exclusive could rightly be added, that the law does not justify, but operates wrath, that is, that it only operates wrath. Cf. Luth. T. I. Jenens. Lat. on Galatians I. v. 12. p. 333. f. 1. as also part III. art. Smalcald. art. II.

Latin:

V. 15. ὁ γὰρ νόμος ὀργὴν κατεργάζεται. Ostendit quid faciat lex ista Mosis, quatenus est lex Mosis, tantum, id est, quatenus distinguitur ab iis præceptis & inter- dictis, quæ ab initio fuerant. Nempe infert pœnam gravibus peccatis & quidem certam, & in multis lethalem, cum ante cri- mina multis dissimularentur, alia pœnam haberent aut levem aut arbitrariam. ὀργὴν pro pœna habuimus & supra II. 5. 8. III. 5. Vide & Matth. III. 7. κατεργάζεσθαι ponitur apud in- terpretes & pro עשׂה pro פּעל, quorum utrumque effe ctionem qualemcunque significat. Inter virtutes legis Modesti- nus ponit punire, ut supra diximus.

ὧ γὰρ ὀὐκ ἔστι νόμος, οὐδὲ παράβασις. Melius Manuscriptus ille ὗ δὲ• non dicit non esse peccatum, sed non esse שׁטוי, id est contemptum legis à Deo non per collectiones, sed expressim datæ: ac proinde minus esse pœnæ meritum. Vide quæ diximus supra II. 9. 12. III. 20.

Missis næniis illis, de Mosis lege, quatenus est lex Mosis tantum, & quatenus distinguitur ab iis præceptis, quæ ab initio fuerunt, siquidem indu- bium sit, legem moralem, quæ hic respicitur, in pri- mæva creatione hominis cordi inscriptam fuisse, cujus reliquias adhuc quasdam in lege naturæ ha- bemus post lapsum; item depœna gravibus peccatis certa & in multis lethali; quum omnis transgres- sio legis maledictionem & mortem æternam infe- rat, nec de pœna in foro soli, sed in foro poli hic a- gendum fuerit: missa denique etiam illa libidine corrigendi codd. receptos ex unico M. S. ubi nul- la cogit necessitas; in aprico est, Grotium pluri- mum aberraffe à mente Apostoli: qui iram Dei vel etiam si libet, pœnam, sed non tamen temporalem tantum, verum etiam æternam legem operari do- cet, vi maledictionis Deut. XXVII. 26. promulga- tæ, idque meritorie, ob violatam infinitam Dei ju- stitiam: quà scil. a nobis non præstatur: & ubi non est lex, ibi non habere locum παράβασιν, id est, trans- gressionem legis: non enim tantum contemptus legis, sed quælibet transgressio ejusdem iram operatur: unde concludit Apostolus, non posse legem ad ju- stificationem quicquam conferre: adeoque nec ju- stitiam legis eo conducere. Quicquid enim tan- tum iram operatur, si in contentionem judicii ve- niat, vel si nobiscum Deus in judicium intrare ve- lit, id ad justificationem nostram nihil conferre certissimum est. At de lege divina verum prius & posterius. Quod autem lex divina tantum iram operetur, non sit legis sed nostri culpa, quia à nobis impleri non potest, postquam per lapsum primorum parentum à DEO defecimus: Qui au- tem non permanet in omnibus, quæ in lege scripta sunt, maledictus pronunciatur, Deut. XXVII. 26. & qui totam legem servarit, in uno vero saltem la- psus fuerit, OMNIUM reus est. Jac. II. 10. Per ac- cidens ergo hoc legi tribuitur, quæ per se verbum vitæ est, & salutis. Pontificii exclusivam ferre no- lunt, & B. Lutherum arguunt, quod reddiderit: Das Gesetz richtet nur Zorn an. Sed exclusivam addidit B. Lutherus, ut emphatice mentem Apo- stoli explicaret, qui inde concludit legem nihil omnino facere aut conferre ad justificationem & salutem, quia lex iram operatur. In hac ergo imme- diata oppositione, qua sibi τὸ justificare, h. e. à pecca- to absolvere, & τὸ iram operari, h. e. peccatum ac- cusare & damnare opponuntur, recte addi potuit exclusiva, quod lex non justificet, sed iram opere- tur, quod nempe ea tantum operetur iram. Conf. Luth. T. I. Jenens. Lat. ad Galat. I. v. 12. p. 333. f. 1. ut & part. III. art. Smalcald. art. II.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. Therefore it is of faith.

With respect to faith, namely, the promise, those excellent promises were made to Abraham. For this depends on those things which are above at 13.

That it might be according to grace.

Whence it came to pass that the promise was immense, inasmuch as it proceeded from the supreme benevolence of GOD as if to a friend, as we said above. He rewards a friend liberally, and the more liberally, the greater He Himself is. A hirer of labor repays labor with an equal recompense.

εἰς τὸ βεβαίαν εἶναι ἐπαγγελίαν παντὶ τῷ σπέρματι.

A second reason why God regarded faith, so that the pious, to whom no law had been given by God, might hope for equal things: οἱ σεβόμενοι ἕλληνες. Understand seed here mystically, as just now II. the name of the father.

ὦ τῷ ἐκτᾶ νόμο μόνον.

Not only to the Jews, whom he thus calls ἐκ νόμο, as just now ἐν περιτομῆς.

ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἐκ πίσεως Ἀβραάμ.

Αβραὰμ here is of the genitive case. He indicates those who have the faith of Abraham, that is, such as Abraham had had.

ὅς ἐσι πατὴρ πάντων ἡμῶν.

Of all who have ever truly believed in God, even before the times of Christ.

The promises were not made to Abraham because of faith or on account of faith, but to excite faith in Abraham. The promises are because of faith: which is from hearing and the announcement of the Word, but faith is not truly the cause of divine promises. Nor does the Apostle treat of that here. But he further explains and confirms his theme that therefore the remission of sins or justification and salvation have been obtained from faith and from that alone: For when he has shown that righteousness and salvation cannot be obtained from the law, he infers that it is ἐκ πίσεως, ἵνα κατὰ χάριν, so that it might be established that the same was made according to grace alone. Abraham was not yet a friend of GOD when he received the promise; but he was ungodly and an idolater when the promise was first made to him: which is pure grace done to him; but not for the sake of the remuneration of faith, and that not only for his sake; but εἰς τὸ βεβαίαν εἶναι τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν παντὶ τῷ σπέρματι, so that the promise might be made firm all the seed. For if the promise of the remission of sins and the inheritance of eternal life were obtained not from mere grace, not by faith alone, but from merit or debt in any part by works, it would by no means be firm for anyone, since one would always have to be in doubt whether those are our good works which are needed for justice and salvation to be obtained by us, just as Papists must always doubt, who even command others to doubt about this, whether they are justified and heirs of eternal life. Rightly does the blessed Gerhard observe here, p. 146, that certainty and firmness are attributed to the promise here not only by reason of itself, because it is certain on account of the truth and omnipotence of the one promising, but also by reason of us, because it is also most firm and most certain to us, insofar as we embrace it by faith and apply it to ourselves. Therefore, faith, apprehending the promise and confidently resting in it, is certainly a confidence utterly opposed to doubt.

By πᾶν τὸ σπέρμα are understood all, whether Jews, whom Grotius acknowledges are called here τὸ ἐκ τῆ νόμυ (σπέρμα); who are so called on account of the law of circumcision to which they were subject, yet at the same time having faith, by whose name they are called the seed of Abraham, but also the Gentiles, who, namely, are of the faith of Abraham, as the Father of ALL who believe. Therefore, that name is rashly restricted to the pious, to whom no law was given by God, τῆς σεβομένης ἕλληνας, as Grotius speaks; meanwhile, we do not deny that by τὸ σπέρμα believers are mystically understood, to whom alone the promise is firm.

Latin:

Vers. 16. διὰ τῦτο ἐκ πίσεως.

Respectu fidei nempe ἡ ἐπαγγελία, facta sunt Abra- hamo egregia illa promissa. Pendet enim hoc ex illis, quæ supra 13.

ἵνα κατὰ χάριν.

Unde factum est, ut promissum esset ingens, quippe procedens ex summa DEI benevolentia tanquam ad ami- cum, ut diximus supra. Amicum liberaliter remunerat, & tanto liberalius, quanto ipse major est. Conductor operæ operam pari hostimento repensat.

εἰς τὸ βεβαίαν εἶναι ἐπαγγελίαν παντὶ τῷ σπέρματι.

Altera ratio, cur fidem Deus respexerit ut paria sperare possent pii, quibus à Deo lex nulla erat data: οἱ σεβόμενοι ἕλ- ληνες. Semen hic intellige μυσικῶς, ut modo II. nomen patris.

ὦ τῷ ἐκτᾶ νόμο μόνον.

Non solum Judæis, quos ita vocat ἐκ νόμο, ut modo ἐν περιτομῆς.

ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἐκ πίσεως Ἀβραάμ.

Αβραὰμ hic est Genitivi casus. Illos indicat, qui fidem habent Abrahami, id est, qualem Abrahamus habuerat.

ὅς ἐσι πατὴρ πάντων ἡμῶν.

Omnium qui unquam vere in Deum credidêre, etiam ante Christi tempora.

Non causa fidei vel propter fidem facta sunt pro- missa Abrahamo, sed ut fidem excitarent in Abra- hamo. Promissa sunt causa fidei: quæ est ex auditu, & annunciatione Verbi, non vero fides est causa promissionum divinarum. Neque id hic agit Apo- stolus. Sed explicat & confirmat porro thema suum ideo ex fide eaque sola obtigisse remissionem pec- catorum vel justificationem & salutem: Quum enim ostenderit justitiam & salutem ex lege non posse obtineri, infert eam esse ἐκ πίσεως, ἵνα κατὰ χάριν ut secundum gratiam solum eandem factam esse constaret. Nondum erat tum amicus DEI Abraham, cum promissionem acciperet; sed im- pius erat & idololatra, cum primum ipsi promissio fieret: quæ est mera gratia ipsi facta; non autem remunerationis fidei causa, idque non tantum ipsius gratia; sed εἰς τὸ βεβαίαν εἶναι τὴν ἐπαγγελί- αν παντὶ τῷ σπέρματι, ut firma fieret promissio omni femini. Si enim non ex gratia mera, non fi- de solum, sed ex merito vel debito ulla parte ope- ribus promissio remissionis peccatorum & hære- ditas vitæ æternæ promissa obtingeret, nequaquam ulli firma eadem esset, siquidem semper ambigere oporteret, an ea sint bona nostra opera, quibus opus sit, ut obtingat nobis justitia, & salus, quem- admodum Papistas semper dubitare oportet, qui alios etiam de eo dubitare jubent, anne justi- ficati sint, & hæredes vitæ æternæ. Recte hic ob- servat B. Gerhard. p. 146. promissioni hic tribui certitudinem & firmitatem non solum ratione sui, quod ob veritatem & omnipotentiam promittentis sit certa, sed etiam ratione nostri, quod nobis quoque firmissima, & certissima sit, quatenus eam fide am- plectimur, nobisque applicamus. Utique ergo fides promissionem apprehendens & in ea fiducialiter re- cumbens, est fiducia dubitationi penitus opposita.

Per πᾶν τὸ σπέρμα intelliguntur omnes, sive Judæi, quos ita hic vocari τὸ ἐκ τῆ νόμυ (σπέρμα) agno- scit Grotius; qui sic vocantur, ob legem circumcisio- nis, cui subjecti erant, fidem tamen simul habentes cujus nomine semen Abrahæ dicuntur, sed etiam gentes, quat. scil. fidei sunt Abrahæ, ceu Patris OMNIUM credentium. Temere ergo nomen il- lud restringitur ad pios, quibus a Deo nulla lex da- ta, τῆς σεβομένης ἕλληνας, ut loquitur Grotius; In- terim per τὸ σπέρμα mystice intelligi credentes, np. quibus solis firma est promissio, non abnuimus.

## 4:17
v. 17. καθὼς γέγραπται.

Gen. XVII. 5. ὅτι πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν τέθεικά σε.

In these words is the reason for the changed name from Abram to Abraham, the letter ה added after י for the sake of euphony. Paul uses the mystical sense of these words here, allegorizing him as father who leads by example, as we have just said.

There is no reason why we should think the Apostle is pressing the mystical sense here, since neither should a mystical sense beyond the literal be admitted in one and the same saying, nor could the confirmation of faith be sought from the mystical sense alone (if it were admitted). Therefore, in the literal sense, we asserted in our Commentary on Genesis at ch. XVII. 4, p. 879, that Abraham was called the Father of many nations, since he is the Father of all who believe: For imagine, according to the literal sense, that the discourse here is about bodily propagation; how then will the Apostle demonstrate from that that Abraham is the Father of all who believe; and that those who obtain the promise do not obtain it by any other reason than through the faith by which Abraham obtained it, whether they be Jews or Gentiles, whether they have sprung from Abraham according to the flesh or not, provided they imitate Abraham by faith. Add that in v. 6 an amplification of the race is promised to the Patriarch. Which promise is not a tautological repetition of the former, but is distinguished from it, since it openly deals with the propagation of the seed; but this present one is explained by the Holy Spirit Himself concerning spiritual fatherhood, namely in this place, Rom. IV. 17. See more prolixly on this in the same place. That promise occurs in the very institution of circumcision, Gen. XVII, which the Apostle therefore brings forward here, so that it may be established that Abraham is called Father not only with respect to those who receive circumcision, but also with respect to those who believe from among the Gentiles.

κατέναντι ὗ ἐπίςευσε.

An interrogation must be added here. Having spoken of Abraham's faith, he asks before whom, that is, before what witness, Abraham believed. The Apostle is very fond of questions and inquiries, as has been noted by others and by Isidore of Pelusium. He himself, however, answers for himself.

Θεῦ.

That is, not indeed before men, from whom that faith was hidden, but before God.

τῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τῆς νεκρὸς

Since it is not a matter of the offering of Isaac, as in Heb. XI. 17, 18 and Jas. II. 21, but of the promised birth of that same Isaac, it appears that he

νεκρὸς here by metaphor is said of men decrepit and by nature useless for the function of begetting, as the Apostle himself will explain in clearer words presently; and the writer to the Hebrews XI. 12. Thus faith is dead, which does not of itself produce righteousness and consequently salvation. Conversely, ζωοποιεῖν חיה is to make useful for such a function. Thus to cure of leprosy is ζωοποιεῖν II Kings V. 7. He who nourishes is called ζωοποιεῖν Gen. V. 20. And he who delivers from evils Ps. LXXI. 20.

καὶ καλῶντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα.

Just as for the Hebrews to be called is often to be, so to call is to cause something to exist. For just as the Lord calling a servant causes him to come, so also God [calls] those things which neither are, nor are thought to be future. Thus that word is taken in Jer. XXXII. 23. Understand τὰ μὴ ὄντα as those things which are necessary for begetting, nourishing, and bringing forth offspring, δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν Heb. XI. 11. Philo on the constitution of the principate: τὰ γὰρ μὴ ὄντα ἐκάλεσεν, εἰς τὸ εἶναι τάξιν ἐξ ἀταξίας καὶ ἐξ ἀνομοίων ὁμοιότητας καὶ ἐξ ἑτεροτήτων ταυτότητας καὶ ἐξ ἀκοινωνήτων καὶ ἀναρμόστων κοινωνίας καὶ ἁρμονίας, ἐκ δὲ σκότους φῶς ἐργασάμενος. Thus Plutarch on Romulus, the founder of the new city: ποιῶν ἐξ οὐχ ὑπαρχόντων ἐκτάτω δόξαν.

Latin:

v. 17. καθὼς γέγραπται.

Gen. XVII. 5. ὅτι πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν τέθεικά σε.

In his verbis causa est mutati nominis Abram in Abra- ham, alifa litera ה post י εὐφωνίας causa. Horum verborum sensum mysticum hic usurpat Paulus, patrem ἀλληγορῶν eum qui exemplo præit, ut modo diximus.

Non est, quod hic sensum mysticum premere Apostolum censeamus, quum ne mysticus sensus præter literalem in uno eodemque dicto admitti debeat, nec e solo mystico sensu (si admittatur) fidei confirmatio peti possit. Literali itaque sensu Abrahamum Patrem multarum gentium dictum, quum Pater sit omnium credentium in Comment. in Genes. ad c. XVII. 4. p. 879. asseruimus: Finge enim secundum literalem sensum, sermonem hic esse de propagatione corporali, quomodo ergo Apostolus inde demonstrabit, Abrahamum Patrem esse omnium credentium; nec alia ratione promissionem consequi, qui consequuntur, quam per fidem qua Abraham eam adeptus est, sive Judæi sint, sive gentiles, seu ex Abrahamo secundum carnem prodierint, seu non, modo fide imitentur Abrahamum. Adde quod v. 6. amplificatio generis promittatur Patriarchæ. Quæ promissio non est ταυτολογικὴ prioris repetitio, sed ab eadem distinguitur, cum aperte de propagatione se- minis agat; hæc autem præsens de spirituali paterni- tate ab ipso Spiritu S. exposita sit, in hoc nempe lo- co Rom. IV. 17. vid. ibidem de hoc prolixius. Pro- missio illa in ipsa circumcisionis institutione oc- currit Gen. XVII. quam ideo hic adducit Aposto- lus, ut constet Abrahamum non tantum illorum respectu, qui circumcisionem suscipiunt, sed re- spectu eorum quoque, qui ex gentibus credunt, Patrem dici.

κατέναντι ὗ ἐπίςευσε.

Hic addenda interrogatio. De Abrahami fide locutus quærit coram quo, id est, quo teste, Abrahamus crediderit. Amat multum ἐρωτήσεις & πύσματα Apostolus, ut notatum tum aliis tum Isidoro Pelusiota. Ipse autem sibi respondet.

Θεῦ.
