Id est, non sane coram hominibus, quos fides ista latuit, sed coram Deo.

τῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τῆς νεκρὸς

Cum non de oblatione Isaaci agatur, ut Hebr. XI. 17. 18. & Jac. II. 21. Sed de ejusdem Isaaci ortu promisso, apparet eum

νεκρὸς hic per translationem dici homines decrepitos & per na- turam inutiles ad gignendi functionem, ut ipse Apostolus verbis apertioribus jamjam explicabit; & scriptor adHebraeos XI. 12. Sic fides mortua, quæ justitiam & consequenter salutem de se non edit. A contrario ζωοποιεῖν חיה eft ad talem functio- nem utiles facere. Sic curare a lepra est ζωοποιεῖν II. Reg. V. 7. dicitur ζωοποιεῖν & qui nutrit. Gen. V. 20. & qui a malis exi- mit Pf. LXXI. 20.

καὶ καλῶντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα.

Sicut Hebræis sæpe vocari est esse: ita vocare, facere ut quid exislat. Sicut enim Dominus servum vocans, facit ut veniat, sic & Deus res eas, quæ nec sunt, nec futuræ putantur. Ita sumitur id verbum Jerem. XXXII. 23. τὰ μὴ ὄντα intellige ea quæ fœ- tui gignendo, fovendo, pariendo sunt neceflaria, δύναμιν εἰς κατα- βολὴν Hebr. XI. 11. Philo de principatus constitutione: τὰ γὰρ μὴ ὄντα ἐκάλεσεν, εἰς τὸ εἶναι τάξιν ἐξ ἀταξίας καὶ ἐξ ἀνομοίων ὁμοιότητας καὶ ἐξ ἑτεροτήτων ταυτότητας καὶ ἐξ ἀκοινωνήτων καὶ ἀναρμόστων κοινωνίας καὶ ἁρμονίας, ἐκ δὲ σκότους φῶς ἐργασάμε- νος.. Sic Plutarchus Romulo novæ urbis conditore: ποιῶν ἐξ οὐχ ὑπαρχόντων ἐκτάτω δόξαν.

## 4:18
V. 18. ὃς Who, Abraham, concerning whom the question had been proposed. παρ᾽ ἐλπίδα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι ἐπίςευσεν.

This is an oxymoron, a figure which Paul loves; hope against hope, just as unwedded marriage, to be ignorant of what you know, nor could the captives be captured, and other similar things. He believed in hope, that is, in such a way that he hoped from God's promise, against hope, namely according to the laws of nature.

εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸν πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν

So that he might thus go before all Gentiles as an example. See above II. All those will be קוי יהוה according to Isaiah XL. 31.

κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον Gen. XV. 5.

Namely as the stars of heaven, which is understood here from the passage in Genesis. The Apostle takes those words, as also others above, in a mystical sense. Philo, both in his Allegories and in his work on the heir of divine things, understands by seed καθαρὰς φύσεις in the soul of Abraham having both brightness and their own motions like the stars, indeed above the stars. Paul, however, more correctly [understands] those who, after the example of Abraham, would have such lights in their soul, as if in a terrestrial heaven, celebrated among the Pythagoreans.

I rejoice in the pious among mortals as much as in Olympus.

It can be admitted, as far as the sense is concerned, that the interrogation in that κατέναντι ᾧ ἐπίστευσε, before whom Abraham believed, which he says signifies by the testimony and approval of God on account of spiritual knowledge, which has a place before GOD and renders us acceptable to him, that Abraham is not called the father of believers in a carnal sense. But this is to be observed primarily, that here the Apostle at the same time explains the nature of the object of faith, namely that he believed in God, who makes the dead alive, and calls those things which are not, as though they were, so that it is established that faith is directed toward both the power and the grace of God, and apprehends it, and by the same relies on hope against hope. Which he teaches by the example of Abraham indeed, who accepted by faith the promise concerning the birth of Isaac, but that promise was not strictly made on account of Isaac. But on account of that seed about to descend from Abraham through Isaac, in whom all the families of the earth are to be blessed, and therefore faith did not look primarily and in the first instance to the promise concerning Isaac, but rather to the promise concerning the blessed seed about to crush the head of the serpent and bring blessing to the whole world, and apprehended the same, by the power of which truly even those who are dead in sins are made alive, and those who are not children of God and heirs of life, but are excluded from that inheritance on account of sin, are called as such; which work of regeneration and justification is surely no less a work of divine power and grace than was the fecundation of Abraham and Sarah, and the work of creation itself: in which God properly called τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα, from which propriety of the words one should not easily depart. For therefore Abraham believed in God who makes the dead alive, that he could also make alive himself and his wife Sarah although they were barren, so that from his loins might yet arise the promised Messiah of the world, that blessed seed, because he had known that God also, by his infinite power and goodness, had called those things which are not in the primordial creation. Conf. 2 Cor. IV. 6. If, however, anyone looks directly at this place as our spiritual resuscitation from the death of sin and reception into grace, by which those who are not in grace, are not the people of God, are called so that they may be in grace, so that they may be the people of God, nay rather the children of God, Hos. 1:10, provided that an allusion at the same time to the work of the fecundation of Abraham and to the work of the primordial creation is left. In which manner the Apostle is to be considered to illustrate that in the following with a similar example of Abrahamic faith, as one who also believed in hope against hope, so that he might be in truth the Father of many nations, that is to say, of all believers, according to that which was said, so shall your seed be, namely, as are the stars of the heaven, Gen. 15:5. For this promise concerning so copious a seed could not be brought forward to prove that Abraham is the Father of believers, because it does not speak of a spiritual seed, but a carnal one: nor to demonstrate that Abraham believed that he was going to be the Father of believers, for this was only revealed to him divinely long after, when indeed his name was changed and the Sacrament of circumcision was instituted, Gen. 17. How therefore could it be brought forward here otherwise than to be commended by a similar example of the faith of Abraham, and indeed from the very seat in which Moses dealt with the justifying faith of Abraham and concerning his justification: as being that in which also that promise is read concerning the bodily multiplication of the seed of Abraham. Therefore the words εἰς τὸ εἶναι [are] not the Object of faith by reason of the promise, as the Syrian rendered it: He believed that he was going to be the Father of a multitude of nations, because that had not yet been promised to him, but the end of faith, by reason of divine direction, because God worked an outstanding faith also in the heart of Abraham, so that he might believe in hope even against hope, by which he himself might escape and be constituted divinely the Father of all believers, so that he might here go before all nations as an example, as Grotius does not badly [say] here. But that he believed παρ' ἐλπίδα εἰς ἐλπίδα, which indeed the Apostle looks to here, κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον ὕτως ἔσαι τὸ σπέρμα σε. Which words are rendered in the Vulgate: According to what was said, so that the passage Gen. 15:5 is brought forward here in place of a proof. Moreover, they can be explained either from that, or on account of that, which had been said to him, just as the particle κατὰ is sometimes the same as EX, Tit. 3:5. κατὰ ἔλεον by mercy, or PER, Heb. 6:3, by himself, Mark 1:27, by power, or PROPTER, Phil. 4:11. Because from that promise, and through it, and on account of it, Abraham believed in hope against hope, so that there is no need here to have recourse to a mystical sense with Grotius. And the Apostle explains here what he had said, that Abraham had believed IN hope, so that he might hope from the promise of God, just as he will pursue afterwards, what it is to be ABOVE or AGAINST hope, that he believed against the laws of nature. Or if you render it with the Vulgate: According to that which was said to him, the reason is rendered not of the immediately preceding [statement], that he is the Father of many nations, because those are distinct promises, but of that which was said in v. 17, that he believed in God who makes the dead alive, by accepting this concerning the fecundation of the dead bodies of Abraham and Sarah. In whatever way you take it, it is certain that the Apostle is delivering here a description of that true and living faith, through which he has taught us thus far that we are justified, which by the example of Abraham rests in firm trust in the power and goodness of God.

Latin:

V. 18. ὃς Qui Abrahamus, de quo proposita fuerat quæstio. παρ᾽ ἐλπίδα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι ἐπίςευσεν.

Est hic ὀξύμωρον, quam figuram amat Paulus; Spes in- sperata, quomodo innupta nuptiæ, nescire quod scias, nec capti potuere capi, aliaque similia. Credidit in spem, id est, ita ut speraret ex Dei promisso, contra spem, nempe secundum naturæ leges.

εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸν πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν

Ut sic omnibus Gentibus exemplo præiret.Vide fupra II. omnes illi erunt קוי יהוה juxta Esaiam XL. 31.

κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον Gen. XV. 5.

Nempe ut stellæ cæli, quod ex loco Geneseos hic subaudi- tur. Sumit autem Apostolus illa verba, ut & alia supra, in sensu mystico. Philo cum de Allegoriis, tum de hærede rerum divinarum, per semen intelligit καθαρὰς φύσεις in Abrahami animo habentes & fulgorem & motus suos ad fiderum instar, imo supra sidera. Paulus vero rectius eos, qui ad exemplum Abrahami tales in animo, velut in terrestri cælo, luces essent habituri, celebratum apud Pythagoricos.

Εὐσεβέσιν δὲ βροτῶν γανύμαι τόσον ὅσσον ὀλύμπῳ.

Admitti potest, quantum ad sensum in illo κα- τέναντι ᾧ ἐπίςευσε interrogatio, coram quo credi- derit Abraham, quod teste & approbante Deo significare ait ob cognitionem spiritualem, quæ co- ram DEO locum habet eique nos gratos reddit, non carnalem Abrahamum vocari credentium patrem. Id autem imprimis observandum, quod hic Apo- stolus simul objecti fidei rationem explicat, quod nempe crediderit in Deũ, qui mortuos vivificat,& vocat ea,quæ nõ sunt,ut sint ut constet fidem inDei tum potentiam, tum gratiam ferri,eamque appre- hendere, atque eâdem in spem contra spem inniti. Quod exemplo quidem Abrahæ promissionem de Isaaci ortu fide acceptantis docet, sed nec illa pro- missio κυρίως ob Isaacum facta. Sed ob semen illud per Isaacum exAbrahamo descensurum, in quo be- nedicenda omnes familiæ terræ, neque adeo fides in promissionem πρώτως & primario, sed potius in promissionem de semine benedicto contrituro ca- put serpentis & benedictionem toti mundo alla- turo respexit, eandemque apprehendit, vi cujus vere etiam illi, qui in peccatis mortui sunt, vivifi- cantur, & qui non sunt filii Dei, & hæredes vitæ, sed ab ea hæreditate ob peccatum excluduntur, ut tales sint, vocantur; quod regenerationis & ju- stificationis opus non minus sane est potentiæ & gratiæ divinæ opus, quam erat fœcundatio Abra- hæ & Saræ, ipsumque creationis opus: in qua pro- prie vocavit Deus τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα, a qua pro- prietate vocum facile non discedendum. Nam ideo credidit Abraham Deo mortuos vivificanti, se quoque cum Sara conjuge etsi effœtos vivifica- re posse, ut ex lumbis suis adhuc oriatur promissus mundi Messias semẽ illud benedictum,quia nove- rat Deum etiam pro infinita sua potentia & boni- tate vocasse ea, quæ non sunt in primæva creatio- ne. Conf.2.Cor.IV.6. Si tamen directe quis respicit hoc loco spiritualem nostram è morte peccati resuscitationem & in gratiam receptionem, qua ii, qui non sunt in gratia, non sunt Dei populus, vocantur, ut sint in gratia, ut sint Dei populus, imò filii Dei Os. I. 10. non refragabimur, modò allusio simul ad opus fœcundationis Abrahæ, & ad opus creationis primævæ relinquatur. Quo pacto censendus est Apostolus id in sequentibus simili fidei Abrahamicæ exemplo illustrare, utpote qui etiam in spem contra spem crediderit, ut esset revera Pater multarum gentium, credentium sc. omnium, secundum illud quod dictum est, sic erit semen tuum, scil. sicut sunt stellæ cæli Gen. XV. 5. Nam hæc promissio de tam copioso semine non adferri poterat ad probandum, quod Abraham Pater credentium sit, quia non loquitur de semine spirituali, sed carnali: neque ad demonstrandum, quod Abraham crediderit, quod Pater futurus esset credentium, hoc enim longè post demum ipsi divinitus revelatum fuit, cum nempe nomen ipsius mutaretur, & circumcisionis Sacramentum institueretur, Genes. XVII. Quomodo ergò aliter hic adferretur, quam ut simili exemplo fidei Abrahæ commendetur, & quidem ex ipsa sede, in qua Moses de fide Abrahæ justificante, deque justificatione ipsius egit: utpote in qua etiam illa promissio legitur, de multiplicatione corporali seminis Abrahæ. Idcirco verba εἰς τὸ εἶναι non Objectum fidei ratione promissionis, uti Syrus reddidit: Credidit, quod futurus esset Pater multitudinis gentium, quia id nondum promissum ei erat, sed finem fidei, ratione directionis divinæ, quia Deus fidem operatus insignem & in corde Abrahami, ut in spem etiam contra spem crederet, quo evaderet ipse ac constitueretur divinitus Pater omnium credentium, ut hic omnibus gentibus exemplo præiret, ut non malè hic Grotius. Quod vero credidit παρ' ἐλπίδα εἰς ἐλπίδα, quod quidem hic respicit Apostolus, κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον ὕτως ἔσαι τὸ σπέρμα σε. Quæ verba in vulgata redduntur: Secundum quod dictum est, ut probationis loco hic adducatur locus Gen. XV. 5. Explicari autem possunt vel ex isto, aut propter istud, quod dictum erat ei, uti particula κατὰ idem quandoque est, quod EX Tit. III. 5. κατὰ ἔλεον ex misericordia, vel PER Ebr. VI. 3. per semetipsum, Marc. I. 27. per potestatem, vel PROPTER Phil. IV. 11. Quia ex ista promissione, & per eam, ac propter eam Abraham credidit in spem contra spem, ut non opus sit hic ad sensum mysticum cum Grotio confugere. Et explicat hic Apostolus, quod dixerat in SPEM credidisse Abrahamum, ita ut speraret ex Dei promisso, quemadmodum postea persequetur, quid sit SUPRA vel CONTRA spem, quod contra naturæ leges crediderit. Aut si cum vulgata reddas: Secundum id, quod dictum est ei, ratio redditur non immediatè præcedentis, quod Pater multarum gentium sit, quia distinctæ illæ sunt promissiones, sed ejus, quod v. 17. dicebatur, quod crediderit Deo vivificanti mortuos, accipiendo hoc de fœcundatione mortuorum corporum Abrahæ & Saræ. Quocunque modo accipias, certum est, tradere hic Apostolum descriptionem illius veræ & vivæ fidei, per quam justificari nos hactenus docuit, quod exemplo Abrahæ in potentia & bonitate Dei firma fiducia acquiescat.

## 4:19
Verse 19. καὶ μὴ ἀσθενήσας τῇ πίσει) Those are said to be ἀσθενεῖν τῇ πίσει who doubt about some matter, as the passage below 14:1 shows, compared with 1 Cor. 8:7, 12, ἀσθενεῖν τῆς διανοίαις, 1 Macc. 11:49. The opposite is τὸ πληροφορεῖσθαι, which will follow presently.

ἐκατενόησε) That is, he did not remain looking at it, for he did consider this indeed as we see in Gen. 17:17. But he expelled this thought from his mind, trusting in God who was promising; therefore that καλεῖντος here signifies a permanent act, as sometimes the Hebrew נבט and this Greek word [do], Heb. 3:1.

τὸ ἑαυτῦ σῶμα νενεκρωμένον) Namely, to that function of which we spoke above [in verse] 17.

But how [was it] already dead then, when long afterwards Abraham had children from Keturah? Gen. 25:1. Augustine replies, book 16, On the City of God, ch. 28, that in the generation of Isaac, Abraham had received a singular gift of generating from God, which he retained afterwards even after the death of Sarah.

ἑκατονταέτης πυ ὑπάρχων. From Gen. 17:17, there are those who say that one year was lacking, therefore that πυ was added. Thus the Greeks say: δέκα πυ, about ten.

and the deadness of the womb of Sarah. A womb no longer fit for conception, being that of a ninety-year-old woman. Philo, in his book On the Heir of Divine Things, says this womb is an image of the kind of soul which, having renounced things that fall under the senses, begins to conceive from God.

Latin:

Vers. 19. καὶ μὴ ἀσθενήσας τῇ πίσει) Ἀσθενεῖν τῇ πίσει dicuntur, qui aliqua de re dubitant, ut ostendit locus infra XIV. 1. collatus cum 1. Cor. VIII. 7. 12. ἀσθενεῖν τῆς διανοίαις 1. Macc. XI. 49. Oppositum est τὸ πληροφορεῖσθαι quod modo sequetur.

ἐκατενόησε) Id est, non mansit id respiciens, nam consideravit hoc quidem ut videmus Gen. XVII. 17. Sed hanc cogitationem expulit animo fretus Deo pollicente, ergò il- lud καλεῖντος hic fignificat actum permanentem, ut aliquo- ties Hebræum נבט & Græcum hoc Hebr. III. 1.

τὸ ἑαυτῦ σῶμα νενεκρωμένον) Nempe ad illam functionem, de qua diximus fupra 17.

At quomodo jam tum emortuum; quum diu postea Abraham ex Kethura liberos fufceperit? Gen. 25. 1. Refpondet Augustin. l. XVI. de Civit. Dei c. 28. quod in generatione Ifaaci Abraham singulare do- num generandi divinitus acceperit, quod postea etiam post Sara obitum retinuerit.

ἑκατονταέτης πυ ὑπάρχων. Ex Gen. XVII. 17. sunt, qui ajunt unum defuisse annum, ideo adjectum illud πυ. Sic Græci dicunt: δέκα πυ, circi- ter decem.

καὶ τὴν νέκρωσιν τῆς μήτρας σάρρας. Uterum non ultra conceptui aptum, utpote anus no- nagenaria. Hunc uterum Philo libro de hærede re- rum divinarum, imaginem ait genere animæ, quæ à re- bus in fenfum cadentibus abdicata ex Deo concipere in- cipit.

## 4:20
Ver. 20. But regarding the promise of God. The Syriac translator did not render this εἰς badly as 'against'. The more proper meaning 'concerning' can also be conveniently retained: he did not doubt concerning the promise, as it is used in Acts 2:25, Eph. 5:32. Although that preposition εἰς, meaning 'against', is not unusual; see Luke 7:30, 1 Cor. 8:12.

He did not waver through unbelief. Through unbelief, that is, through lack of faith. To waver here, as also in Matt. 21:21, Mark 11:23, 14:23, James 1:6, is the same as to doubt in Matt. 14:31, 28:17, and to be of two minds and to waver in Philo, as we said at the aforementioned place in Matt. 15.

We add what the blessed Gerhard has on these matters on page 150. The noun 'through unbelief' is added either restrictively, if 'to waver' is taken generally for investigation; or exegetically, if it is taken specifically for doubt. He did not waver through unbelief, he did not dispute through unbelief. For he is said to waver who leans toward both sides, doubtful toward which judgment he ought to incline. The Syriac has the verb 'atphalag', which, when transferred by metaphor to the soul, signifies being divided into different opinions, just as the poet sings of such a division: 'The uncertain crowd is split into opposing factions. And he divides his swift mind, now hither, now thither.' Matt. 14:31, Mark 11:23. This corresponds to the Greek verb 'to doubt', to be as it were at a crossroads, to be in suspense, to be driven from here to there, just as ships are driven by waves, and as meteors in the air, to incline now hither, now thither with a suspended and doubtful mind. Whence it is rightly gathered that faith is confidence, because the wavering of unbelief is opposed to it, James 1:6.

But he was strengthened in faith. This passive here has the force of the Hebrew Hithpahel, for which the Hebrews themselves often put either Kal or Niphal. Thus Ps. 52:9, in the Hebrew it is in Kal 'oz', in Greek in the passive 'he was strengthened', both meaning 'he strengthened himself'. Although Abraham is said to have strengthened himself, this must be understood as being by the incitement and most present help of God. For we are said to be able to do even those things which we can do through God.

Give glory to God. He is said to give glory to God who either does or says, or, as Abraham here, thinks that which is honorable to God, or that which is consistent with the attributes of God. See Luke 17:18 and what was said at Matt. 26:63.

He gave glory to God, namely the glory of divine truth and omnipotence. For faith gives glory to God; unbelief affects Him with ignominy. 1 John 5:10.

Latin:

Verf. 20. εἰς δὲ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τῦ Θεῦ. Hoc εἰς per contra non male transtulit Syrus. Retineri etiam commode potest magis propria fignificatio pro DE: de promiffione verò non dubitavit, ufurpatur Actor. II. 25. Eph. V. 32. Quanquam nec illa, quæ propofitio εἰς est adver- sus inusitata sit, vid. Luc. VII. 30. 1. Cor. VIII. 12.

ὐ διεκρίθη τῇ ἀπισίᾳ. τῇ ἀπισίᾳ, id est δι᾽ ἀπιστίας, διακρίνεσθαι hic, ut & Matth. XXI. 21. Marci XI. 23. XIV. 23. Jac. I. 6. idem est, quod δισάζειν Matth. XIV. 31. XXVIII. 17. διδοιάζειν & ἐπαμφοτε- ρίζειν Philoni, ut diximus ad dictum locum Matth. XV.

Addimus quæ B. Gerhardus de his habet p. 150. Nomen τῇ ἀπισίᾳ additum vel limitativè, si τὸ δια- κρίνεσθαι generaliter accipiatur pro disquisitione; vel exegeticè, si specialiter accipiatur pro dubitatione. ὐ διεκρίθη τῇ ἀπισίᾳ non hæsitavit, non disceptavit incredulitate. Dicitur enim διακρίνεσθαι, qui in utramque partem propendet, dubius quonam judicio suo inclinare debeat? Syrus habet verbum אתפלג quod per metaphoram, ad animam translatum si- gnificat in diversas sententias divisus fuit, sicut Poe- ta de ejusmodi divisione canit: Scinditur incertum studia in contraria vulgus. Atque animum celerem, nunc huc nunc dividit illuc. Matth. XIV. 31. Marc. XI. 23. Respondet hoc verbo Græco δισάζειν, in bivio quasi versari, in suspenso esse, hinc illuc agitari, sicut naves fluctibus agitata, & sicut meteora in aëre, suspenso ac dubio animo modò huc modò illuc inclinare. Unde rectè colligitur, quod fides sit fiducia, quia opponitur ei διάκρισις τῆς ἀπιστίας Jac. I. 6.

ἀλλ᾽ ἐνεδυναμώθη τῇ πίσει. Passivum hoc hic valet quod Hebræum Hithpahel, pro quo & ipsi Hebræi sæpe ponunt aut Kal aut Niphal Sic Ps. LII. 9. in Hebræo est in Kal עז Græce in Passivo ἐνδυ- ναμώθη utrumque pro firmavit fese. Quanquam autem se firmaffe dicitur Abrahamus, intelligendum hoc est Dei ex- citatu & ope præsentissima. Posse enim dicimur etiam, quæ per Deum possumus.

δὸς δόξαν θεῷ. Dare gloriam Deo dicitur, qui aut facit aut dicit, aut, ut hic Abrahamus, cogitat id, quod Deo honorificum est, sive id, quod Dei proprietatibus convenit. Vide Luc. XVII 8. & quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 63.

Dedit Deo gloriam, puta gloriam veritatis & omnipotentiæ divinæ. Fides enim dat Deo glo- riam, incredulitas eum afficit ignominia. 1. Jo- han. V. 10.

## 4:21
Ver. 21. And being fully persuaded. To be fully persuaded is to be filled with something, as appears in Ecclesiastes 8:11, where in the Hebrew 'mala' means to be full. Thus also 2 Tim. 2:4, 4:17. Hence the translation was drawn to persuasion, because where someone does not doubt, but holds a matter as certain, his heart is said to be full of such a thing. See below 14:6. Hence the full assurance of hope and faith, Heb. 6:11, 10:22. 'Fully persuaded' is also used in Isocrates in the Trapeziticus.

The word 'to be fully persuaded' implies not only persuasion, but firm confidence, when someone is carried with full sails of confidence toward that thing in which he trusts, a metaphor taken from ships; nor is it to be referred, as the Vulgate renders it most fully, to the intellect, but rather to the will; and the heart, as 2 Tim. IV. 5. την διακονιαν συ πληροφορησον, perform your ministry with great confidence of spirit. Conf. Col. II. 2. 1 Thess. II. 2. Heb. X. 12. Eccles. VIII. 11. επληροφορηθη καρδια: it concerns the preposterous and damnable confidence which men conceive in their sins from the delay of punishment. As απιστια is rendered here as diffidence in the Vulgate, so one must admit, by the force of opposites, that πιστιν is confidence. And this πληροφορια, which the Apostle attributes to Abraham, denotes not only the certainty of the assent of knowledge, but also the strength of confidence. Therefore he says that he believed in hope against hope. Basil. in Ethic. Defin. 8. One must not hesitate, he says, and doubt in those things which are spoken by the Lord, but hold for certain that whatever is the word of God is true and powerful, even if nature protests, for this is the struggle of faith. Theophyl. in c. IV. ad Rom. Abraham, beyond all human hope, trusted in the divine will, he did not hesitate, i.e., he had absolutely nothing about which he might waver, but was immediately made stronger through faith. Add from the Papists Cajetan, Comment. in Gen. XV. 4. Moses does not say that Abraham believed God, but in God, for this is more. For to believe God is to have faith in his words as truthful, but to believe in God adds, moreover, confidence in God; and Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, in Harm. Evang. cap. 32. The name of faith is most rightly said in the Gospels, when salvation or the attainment of all that we desire is attributed to it, to embrace both, namely, both that firm assent in believing things about God and Christ, and the confidence conceived from his omnipotent goodness. Conf. our blessed Meisner, disp. de natura fidei justific. c. II. Th. XLV., where against the Papists he proves with XIII arguments from the Scriptures that faith is confidence. We add only what our same blessed Meisner has in explaining the metaphor of the word πληροφοριας, disp. de primar. fine & effect. fidei th. CVIII: Great is the likeness of ships sailing with full sails, and of minds conceiving something with full persuasion and hope. Faith justifying is truly an impelled ship: Confirmed by the word of God and the Spirit bearing witness, it is carried most swiftly, breaks through everything, and seizes and claims for itself the grace of God, the forgiveness of sins, and other gifts. And just as ships running most swiftly nowhere stick, do not delay for reefs, quicksands, and hidden rocks, but tend forward in a most direct course: so faith does not hesitate in the least, does not limp, does not tremble, but, inflated by the truth of the word, the constancy of the promises, and the breeze of the Holy Spirit, it is accustomed to be carried in a direct and most consistent course, as if secure from every shipwreck, toward God, sin, and the promised goods. Such a πληροφορια was very notable in the blessed Luther, of whom Flacius writes thus in his booklet on the word Fides, part 2, q. 66: Often when I have watched Dr. Martin Luther of pious memory going into the temple with full confidence in God and a joyful and erect countenance, and have weighed his actions, which were clearly worthy of Elijah himself, I have seemed to myself to see that great Venetian ship (which they call a Galleon) proceeding against the enemy with all sails inflated by the wind. Although it is notable for its size, beauty, and speed, it nevertheless has that special glory, that having been attacked with the greatest force so many times by the Turks and other impious men, it remained victorious against all in the end. Thus, indeed, the Evangelical doctrine of faith alone justifying makes heroes out of the most timid, and victors out of the defeated; of which comfort and strength other religions, which suggest that all or the greatest hope of salvation should be placed in works, completely deprive us. This was our late predecessor, the blessed one.

That what he has promised he is also able to do) Namely God, which name preceded; επαγγελλεσθαι is always used deponentially in these books for to promise. Promises are held as certain things if there is no doubt about either the will or the power of the one promising. That God wills what he promises is easily believed. Those who think that God is nothing other than nature itself doubt his power.

Latin:

Vers. 21. καὶ πληροφορηθείς. Plane persuasum habens, πληροφορεῖσθαι est impleri ali- qua re, ut apparet Ecclesiastæ VIII. 11. ubi in Hebræo מלא plenum esse. Sic & 2. Tim. II. 4. IV. 17. Hinc ducta translatio ad persuasionem, quia ubi quis non dubitat, sed rem pro certa habet, ejus cor dicitur tali re esse plenum. Vide infra XIV. 6. Hinc πληροφορία ἐλπίδος & πίσεως Hebr. VI. 11. X. 22. πληροφορηθείς plene persuasus est etiam apud Isocratem Trapezitico.

Non persuasionem tantum, sed firmam fidu- ciam τὸ πληροφορεῖσθαι infert, cum quis q. plenis πληροφο- velis fiducia sua fertur ad eam rem, qua confidit, εὔδαι- metaphora a navibus desumpta; nec cum vulgata reddente plenissime sciens & Papistis referendum ad intellectum, sed ad voluntatem potius; & cor, ut 2. Tim. IV. 5. την διακονιαν συ πληροφορησον mini- sterium tuum magna animi fiducia peragito. Conf. Col. II. 2. 1. Thess. II. 2. Ebr. X. 12. Eccles. VIII. 11. επληροφορηθη καρδια: agitur de praepostera & da- mnabili fiducia, quam homines ex dilatione poenae in peccatis suis concipiunt. Ut απιστια per diffi- dentiam hic redditur in vulgata, ita fateri, vi contra- riorum, oportet, πιστιν esse fiduciam. Et πληροφορια haec, quam Abrahae tribuit Apostolus, non tantum notat certitudinem assensus notitiae, sed etiam robur fiduciae. Ideo in spem contra spem eum credidisse dicit. Basil. in Ethic. Defin. 8. Non est haesitandum, inquit, & dubitandum in iis, quae a Domino dicuntur, sed pro certo habendum, quodcunque Dei verbum verum esse & potens, etiamsi natura reclamet, nam hoc certamen est fidei. Theophyl. in c. IV. ad Rom. Abraham prae- ter omnem spem humanam divinae voluntati fuit con- fisus, non haesitavit h. e. nihil prorsus habuit, quod ille ambigeret, quin statim per fidem fortior est effe- ctus. Adde e Pontificiis Cajetanum Comment. in Gen. XV. 4. Moses non dicit Abrahamum credi- disse Deo, sed in Deo, hoc enim plus est. Nam cre- dere Deo est fidem habere illius verbis, ut veracibus, credere autem in Deo insuper addit fiduciam in Deo; & Jansenium Episc. Gandaviens. in Harm. Evang. cap. 32. Rectissime dicitur nomen fidei in Evangeliis, cum ei tribuitur salus, aut consecutio omnium quae volumus, complecti utrumque nem- pe & assensum illum firmum in credendis de Deo & Christo, & fiduciam ex illius omnipotente bo- nitate conceptam. Conf. B. Meisneri nostri disp. de natura fidei justific. c. II. Th. XLV. ubi contra Pontificios XIII. argumentis e Scripturis probat fidem esse fiduciam. Addimus solum, quae in ex- plicanda vocis πληροφοριας metaphora pulchre idem B. Meisnerus noster disp. de primar. fine & effect. fidei th. CVIII. habet: Magna est convenien- tia navium plenis velis navigantium, & animorum plena persuasione ac spe aliquid concipientium. Vere incitata navis est fides justificans: Confirmata ver- bo Dei & spiritu testimonium perhibente, fertur celer- rime, perrumpit omnia, gratiam Dei, peccatorum ve- niam & alia dona sibi rapit ac vendicat. Et veluti naves celerrime currentes nusquam haerent, non mo- rantur scopulos, syrtes & saxa latentia, sed rectissimo cursu antrorsum tendunt: sic fides minime haesitat, non claudicat, non trepidat, sed veritate verbi, constantia promissionum, & aura Spiritus S. inflata, recto con- sentissimoque cursu, tanquam secura de omni naufra- gio, in Deum peccatum & bona promissa ferri consue- vit. Talis πληροφορια valde insignis fuit in B. Lu- thero, de quo Flacius in libello de vocabulo Fidei part. 2. q. 66. ita scribit: Saepe quum piae memoriae D. Martinum Lutherum plena in Deum fiducia, lae- taque & erecta fronte in templum vadentem intui- tus sum, ejusque actiones plane ipso Elia dignas perpendi, visus mihi sum Venetam illam longe ma- ximam navim (quam illi Galeonem vocant) o- mnibus velis vento inflatis contra hostes pergen- tem cernere. Quae cum magnitudine, pulchritu- dine & celeritate sit insignis, illud tamen habet prae- cipuum decus, quod toties a Turcis aliisque im- piis summa vi oppugnata ad extremum contra o- mnes victrix permansit. Ita nimirum doctrina Ev- angelica de sola fide justificante ex timidissimis he- roas, ex debellatis victores facit; quo solatio & ro- bore nos prorsus privant religiones aliae, quae vel omne vel maximam in operibus spem salutis ponendam esse suggerunt. Haec o μακαριτης noster antecessor.

Ὅτι ὃ ἐπήγγελται δυνατός ἐσι καὶ ποιῆσαι) Nempe Deus, quod nomen præcessit, ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι semper deponaliter ponitur in his libris pro promittere. Promissa pro rebus certis habentur, si nec de voluntate nec de potentia promis- tentis dubitatur. Deum velle quod promittit facilè credi- tu est. De potentia illi dubitant, qui nihil aliud Deum es- se putant, quam ipsam naturam.

## 4:22
V. 22. Therefore it was also reckoned to him for righteousness) That faith was held for an extraordinary and very praiseworthy thing. This statement, that Abraham's faith was accepted by God as a great thing, was placed by Moses in Gen. XV. 6 before Ishmael was born: but since the reason for equals is equal, it is rightly referred by Paul to the faith concerning the birth of Isaac, and by James to that faith which shone forth in the offering of Isaac. For if the beginnings of faith please God, much more do its increments: nor are there any works of the pious into which faith does not flow.

Latin:

V. 22. διὸ καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) Illa fides ha- bita est pro egregia re ac valdè laudabili. Hæc sententia, fidem Abrahami à Deo pro re magna acceptam, posita fuit à Mose Gen. XV. 6. ante natum Ismaelem: sed cum pa- rium par sit ratio, rectè & à Paulo ad fidem de ortu Isaaci, & à Jacobo ad eam fidem, quæ in oblatione Isaaci emicuit, refertur. Fidei enim si initia Deo placent, multò magis incrementa: nec ulla sunt piorum opera, in quæ fides non influat.

## 4:23
Vers. 23. But it was not written for his sake alone. Rightly, for Moses placed those histories about Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph before his laws, so that by that example he might excite everyone to piety. Philo notes this. Thus also the deeds and punishments of the impious were written to deter others, 1 Corinth. X. 11. But when Paul says 'us' here, he understands Christians specifically, as the following things show.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐκ ἐγράφη δὲ δι' ἀυτὸν μόνον. Rectè, nam historias illas de Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, ac Josepho legibus suis præposuit Moses, ut eo exemplo omnes ad pietatem excitaret. Notat id Philo. Sic & im- piorum facta & pœnæ scripta sunt ad deterrendos alios 1. Corinth. X. 11. Cum autem ἡμᾶς hic dicit Paulus, specialiter Christianos intelligit, ut ostendunt sequen- tia.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. To those who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. You have almost the same words in 1 Petr. I. 21. This is a faith greater than the faith of Abraham. For Abraham and Sarah were dead figuratively, Jesus truly and perfectly.

The Apostle does not teach here that the faith of Christians is greater than the faith of Abraham, but he sets forth the faith of Abraham as an example to all Christians, and he established him as defined by divine ordination for all believers, and he wants us all to walk in his footsteps: Nor was the Object of the faith by which Abraham was justified any other than that of the faith by which we are justified: For the Apostle teaches by this very fact that he himself also believed in Christ, insofar as he had to be delivered for our sins and justified for our justification, because it was written not for Abraham alone, but also for us who believe this, that this faith is likewise reckoned to us for righteousness, just as it was reckoned to Abraham. Conf. Act. XV. 11. Abraham was not justified in that he believed, whether that his seed was to be multiplied like the stars of heaven, or that his dead body was to be animated and endowed with new life and γεννητικῇ through fecundation; but in that he believed in the blessed seed, which by his death was to take away the curse, and by his resurrection was to bring the blessing, which was to be a shield to him against the diabolical power, and a great reward unto an eternal inheritance. For by the same covenant by which we are justified and saved, by the same covenant was Abraham also justified and saved, inasmuch as he is set forth as an example of believers, and of those who through faith obtain righteousness and salvation. Just as there is but one way of obtaining life and salvation: No one comes to the Father except through me, says Christ, John XIV. 6. There is salvation in no other, nor is there any other name given, in which it is necessary to be saved, says Peter, Acts IV. 12. Hence all the Prophets bear witness, that all who believe in his name must obtain remission of sins, Acts X. 43. There is no διαστολὴ here, Rom. III. 22, 23, 24. Through that one δικαίωμα or satisfaction, the benefit of liberation comes unto all men εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς, unto justification of life, ch. V. 18. Through the righteousness of that one, many are constituted righteous, as many, that is, as are justified, ver. 19. Since that διὸ καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην was not written for Abraham's sake alone, but for us all, whoever are justified, it is necessary that we be justified by the same reason as Abraham, and that the same thing be imputed to us for righteousness which was imputed to Abraham, and vice versa: otherwise neither the example of Abraham, nor the proof of the Apostle would fit, nor would those things be consistent with themselves, that that concerning imputation for righteousness was not written for Abraham's sake only, but also for us who believe in him, who raised Jesus from the dead for the sake of our righteousness, having been delivered up to death for our sins. The matter is too clear, that the object of justifying faith, and that which is imputed for righteousness, is the same with respect to us and with respect to Christ, and that both our faith and Abraham's look to God, who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, as having been delivered by God to death for our sins, and after the expiation of our sins was made by his death, raised again for our justification. Which light of the Apostolic dissertation cannot be obscured by that Grotian gloss, that faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, at least in the sense that Abraham's faith was held to be an excellent and highly praiseworthy thing. For faith is not celebrated as an excellent thing, but as that which was imputed to Abraham for righteousness, and is similarly imputed to us for righteousness, as we taught before.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τοῖς πισέυεσιν ἐπὶ τὸν ἐγείραντα Ἰησοῦν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ἐκ νεκρῶν. Eadem fermè verba habes 1. Petr. I. 21. Hæc est fides major fide Abrahami. Nam Abrahamus & Sara mortui erant figuratè, Jesus verè atque perfectè.

Non hic Apostolus majore Christianorum fidem, esse fide Abrahami docet, sed Christianis omnibus Abrahami fidem in exemplum sistit, eumq; omnium credentium divinâ ordinatione definitum consti- tuit, atq; in vestigiis ejus nos omnes incedere vult: Neque aliud Objectum fidei, quâ justificatus est Ab- raham, fuit, quàm est fidei, qua nos justificamur: Nam & ipsum in Christum credidisse, quatenus propter peccata nostra tradi, propter justificatio- nem nostram justificari debuit, Apostolus hoc ipso docet, quod non propter Abrahamum solum, sed et- iam propter nos, qui hoc credimus, scriptum sit, impu- tari hanc fidem itidem nobis ad justitiam, uti Abra- hæ imputata fuit. Conf. Act. XV. 11. Non justifica- tus Abraham est, quà credit, sive quod semen suum instar stellarum cæli multiplicandum sit, sive quod corpus suum emortuum vita q. nova & γεννητικῇ per fœcundationem animandum & dotandum sit; sed quà credidit in semen benedictum, quod morte sua maledictionem ablaturum, resuscitatione be- nedictionem allaturum, quod ipsi scutum adversus diabolicam potestatem, & merces magna ad æter- nam hæreditatem futurum erat. Quo enim pacto nos justificamur & salvamur, eodem pacto & Abra- ham justificatus & salvatus est, utpote qui in exem- plum credentium, & per fidem justitiam & salutem consequentium sistitur. Quemadmodum non nisi unica est ratio consequendi vitam & salutem: Ne- mo venit ad Patrem nisi per me, inquit Christus Joh. XIV. 6. Non est in ullo alio salus, nec est aliud nomen datum, in quo oporteat salvari, ait Petrus Act. IV. 12. Hinc testimonium perhibent omnes Prophetæ, quod re- missionem peccatorum oporteat consequi omnes, qui credunt in nomine ejus Act. X. 43. Nulla hic est dia- στολὴ Rom. III. 22. 23. 24. Per unius illius δικαίωμα vel satisfactionem in omnes homines venit beneficium liberationis εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς, in justificationem vi- tæ c. V. 18. Per unius illius justitiam multi consti- tuuntur justi, quotquot sc. justificantur, vers. 19. Quum illud διὸ καὶ ἐλογίσθη ἀυτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην non propter Abrahamum solum scriptum sit, sed propter nos omnes, quicunque justificamur, opor- tet eadem ratione nos justificari, ut Abraha- mum, idemque nobis imputari in justitiam, quod Abrahamo imputatum est, & vice versâ: alioqui nec exemplum Abrahæ, nec probatio Apostoli quadraret, neque illa sibi constarent, quod illud de imputatione in justitiam non propter Abrahamum tantum scriptum id esse, sed etiam propter nos cre- dentes in eum, qui Jesum propter peccata nostra in mortem traditum justitiæ nostræ causâ ex mortuis suscitavit. Res nimis clara est, objectum fidei ju- stificantis, & id, quod in justitiam imputatur idem esse respectu nostri, & respectu Christi, & nostram & Abrahami fidem respicere in Deum, qui Jesum Dominum nostrum ex mortuis suscitavit, utpote à Deo traditum in mortem propter peccata nostra, & post expiationem peccatorum nostrorum mor- te ipsius factam resuscitatum propter nostri justifi- cationem. Quæ dissertationis Apostolicæ lux ob- scurari nequit illâ glossâ Grotiana, quod imputata fides in justitiam dicatur, eo saltim sensu, quod pro egregia re & valde laudabili habita sit Abrahæ fides. Non enim celebratur fides ut res egregia, sed ut quæ imputata fuerit Abrahæ in justitiâ, ac similiter nobis in justitiam imputatur, ut antea docuimus.

## 4:25
Vers. 25. ὃς παρεδόθη. By God the Father: namely to death, which is also implied below VIII. 32. See what we have said at Matt. XVIII. 22. Reference is made to the Greek version of Isaiah LIII. 6. Κύριος παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν. διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν, καὶ ἠγέρθη διά τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν.

He could have said, who both died and rose again, that he might justify us from sins, that is, deliver us. But loving parallelism, he joined sins, which are the death of the soul, to death, and the attainment of righteousness, which is the resuscitation of the soul, to the resurrection. He wonderfully both draws us away from sins and leads us to righteousness, because we see that Christ did not fear death as a testimony to his doctrine, which is contrary to sins and calls us to righteousness, and that he was raised by God, so that the highest authority might be reconciled to the same doctrine, see 1 Pet. I. 3.

The death of Christ is not viewed here only as a martyrdom or testimony of the doctrine which he sealed with his death, but as a satisfaction for sins, which Grotius himself asserted against Socinus in his Defensio Fidei Catholicae de Satisfactione Christi, and it has been prolixly asserted by us in Socinismus Profligatus: nor does Christ's fortitude draw us away from sins and lead us to righteousness only because he did not fear death as a testimony to his doctrine, which is contrary to sins and calls us to righteousness, for the sake of which thing there would have been no need for the only-begotten Son of God himself to undergo death, since such things have been seen in very many martyrs, who certainly did not fear to undergo death as a testimony to their doctrine, but the very death of Christ was a ransom and a counter-ransom for our sins, because of which, having been taken upon himself—since sins are the meritorious cause of death—Christ was delivered to death for us, that one might die for all 2 Cor. V. 15. Nor is there talk here of this drawing away from sins; but of the expiation of sins made through the death of Christ, or the satisfaction rendered for sins, which is the meritorious cause of our justification, not only a cause morally moving us to desist from sins.

Furthermore, the Apostle does not say that Christ was raised by God so that the authority of his doctrine might be reconciled, which could have been reconciled to him by miracles and by testimony from heaven, had the Jews not been so hardened, but διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν for our justification. And if the only-begotten Son of God was delivered to death and raised from death for the sake of doctrine alone to be confirmed by the martyrdom of death and the miracle of resurrection, so that others might be delivered from sins and destruction through his doctrine, could not the same have been done through the death and resurrection of other martyrs, just as some of the ancient faithful were raised, and appeared to many, as St. Matthew testifies c. XXVII. 53. What need, therefore, would there have been for the Son of God himself, that God blessed forever above all, to be delivered to death and raised for that reason? The Apostle teaches something far different here, namely that the death of Christ was brought about not only on the occasion of our sins, not only for the confirmation of the doctrine of Christ drawing us away from sins, but for the merit of our sins, because the words διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν introduce the meritorious cause of the death of Christ, that Christ, having been delivered, sustained the punishment of our sins by divine counsel and decree, so that he might deliver us from the same; which is taught at length in Is. c. LIII. and that we are reconciled to God by the death of Christ, and are justified, and therefore, just as the death of Christ was the cause or motivating reason for decreeing to us the remission of sins, justification, and salvation, so we are not justified before God and do not obtain salvation otherwise than by having apprehended the satisfaction of the death of Christ; which is the scope of the Apostolic demonstration and treatment in this chapter. Therefore, he describes the faith which is imputed to us for righteousness in such a way that it is directed toward God, who raised Jesus from the dead, as having been delivered for our sins; because that resurrection from the dead is an infallible document of the fullest satisfaction and expiation of our sins, and of reconciliation with God, made through the death of Christ, which if it had not been made, God would by no means have raised this Mediator and our sponsor, who gave himself as a ransom 1 Tim. II. 4, from death to communicate and distribute his righteousness or our justification to us. Christ is not, therefore, said to have been raised for our justification in exactly the same way as He was delivered by God unto death for our sins, since here the death of Christ is established as the meritorious cause of the expiation of our sins, just as our sins were the meritorious cause of the death of Christ, because by the merit of our sins He Himself was delivered unto death in our place, so that we, by the merit of His death, might be freed from sin and its punishment, death: but concerning the resurrection of Christ, this cannot be asserted to the same extent, namely, that Christ by His resurrection merited righteousness for us: the merit of which was also CONFIRMED TO HAVE BEEN CONSUMMATED by His exclamation on the cross, τετέλεσται, it is consummated, John XIX 30. Therefore, Scripture speaks in different ways of the death of Christ and of His resurrection. For it says that Christ suffered and died both for our sake and in our stead: but that He rose again not in our stead, but only for our sake.

Although, therefore, theologians sometimes call the resurrection of Christ the meritorious cause of our justification, they nevertheless understand the term merit only in a general sense, as the blessed Gerhard advised in his commentary on this passage, responding to the question: Whether the resurrection of Christ pertains to the merit performed for us, in this manner: the name of merit is accepted either generally for everything that pertains to our justification, or specifically for that which Christ performed for us, and which we ought to have performed. In the former sense, the resurrection of Christ pertains to merit, because the resurrection of Christ was required for our justification in certain respects; but in the latter respect, it does not pertain to merit, because Christ rose again for our sake, but not in our stead, whereas He suffered and died not only for our sake, but also in our stead. In what respects, however, the resurrection of Christ was required for our justification, the blessed Gerhard explains thus: Namely, 1. by reason of manifestation and confirmation, because the resurrection of Christ is evident testimony that satisfaction has been fully made for our sins, and perfect righteousness has been brought in. To this pertains that of Chrysostom, Homily IX on Romans: In the resurrection it was shown that Christ had died not for His own sins but for ours. For how would He have risen if He had been a sinner? But if He was not a sinner, He was crucified for others. 2. in respect of application; If Christ had remained in death, He would not have been the victor over death, nor would He have been able to bestow upon us the righteousness obtained at such a dear price, Rom. V. 10. c. VIII. 34. with respect to actual absolution from sin, as God punished our sins in Christ, which were imposed and imputed to him as our sponsor; so also by raising him from the dead he ipso facto absolved him from our sins, which were imputed to him, and consequently also absolved us in him: to which he refers the cited passages 1. Cor. XV. 17. 2. Cor. V. 21. Eph. II. 5. Gal. II. 12. 13. Phil. III. 8. 9. 10. 1. Pet. I. 3. Where, however, it is to be observed that the manifestation and confirmation of the expiation of sins and the demonstration of the victory over death do indeed convince our faith, but do not contribute to the merit of Christ; but he distinguishes the application of the righteousness of Christ entirely from the merit of Christ, and that the resurrected Christ is the efficient cause of the application, but that the resurrection of Christ is not meritorious either of the righteousness of Christ or of its application; finally, that we are absolved from sin in the resurrected Christ is admitted thus far, that since he himself is absolved from our sins imputed to him, the expiation of our sins is certain for us, just as our vivification is also certain for us, and our resurrection from the dead to a blessed life, on account of which certainty, resting upon the merit of the death of Christ confirmed by the resurrection of Christ, we are said to be vivified in Christ and to have risen with Christ Ef. VI. 2. Eph. II. 5. But these things do not properly contribute to the meritorious cause of justification: since it is clear that they only contribute to strengthening faith on our part, or to the application through the Gospel of the righteousness obtained for us by Christ, for which the resurrection of Christ is a prerequisite, though not meritoriously. Nor should it be overlooked that the Apostle, as he says that Christ died for our sins, does not say that the same was resurrected for our δικαιωσύνην righteousness, which is otherwise opposed to sins, but διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν for our justification, because neither the faith which is needed for justification could be ἄμεταπτώτως immutably certain, nor could the righteousness be applied to us by Christ, if Christ had not been resurrected from the dead.

The Papists, however, pervert the opinion of the Apostle when they contend that he means here that the death of Christ was an example of the death of sins, and the resurrection an example of internal renewal and regeneration, through which we might walk in newness of life, see Bellarm. l. II. de justif. c. 6. because the subject here is not the death of sins, or renewal and newness of life, of which the Apostle only begins to treat in chapter VI, but the non-imputation or remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness, or justification: nor does the particle διὰ import an exemplary cause, but a meritorious one for our sins, and a final cause for our justification. Moreover, that there is need for the application of the passion of Christ for the justification of which the Apostle treats, Suarez himself acknowledges T. II. in part. III. Thomæ disp. XLIV. p. 478. Christ through his passion sufficiently destroyed sin, yet in order that we might be justified, and sin might be effectively remitted to us, it was necessary that the passion of Christ be applied to us through living faith. Which application is made through imputation, as the Apostle teaches. Finally, it is to be observed here that the Apostle notably says that he who is to be justified, or he to whom faith ought to be imputed for righteousness, must believe in God, who resurrected Jesus, who was delivered for our sins, for our justification; so that he teaches us to direct our faith to that which God made us most certain of in the resurrection of Jesus, namely, the satisfaction rendered to him, no less than in the death, into which he delivered Jesus for our sins, and thus into the very meritorious satisfaction of the Lord Jesus; and that this faith is imputed to us for righteousness, especially since, as the Apostle testifies, God the Father resurrected the Son as the cause of this our justification, so that this might also be established for us by this infallible document concerning the expiation of sins, and so that we might believe without doubt that Christ himself, our Mediator, applies to us also, by the decree and will of God the Father, the righteousness which he obtained for us.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὃς παρεδόθη. A Deo Patre: nempe in mortem, quod & infra subaudi- tur VIII. 32. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XVIII. 22. Re- spicitur Græca versio Esaïæ LIII. 6. Κύριος παρέδωκεν αὐ- τὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν. διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν, καὶ ἠγέρθη διά τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν.

Potuerat dicere, qui & mortuus est & resurrexit, ut nos à peccatis justificaret, id est, liberaret. Sed amans παρίσωσιν morti conjunxit peccata, quæ sunt mors animi, resurrectio- ni autem adeptionem justitiæ, quæ est animi resuscitatio. Mire nos & à peccatis retrahit & ad justitiam ducit, quod vi- demus Christum mortem non formidâsse pro doctrinæ suæ peccatis contrariæ & ad justitiam nos vocantis testimonio, & à Deo resuscitatum, ut eidem doctrinæ summa concilia- retur auctoritas, vide 1. Petr. I. 3.

Mors Christi non spectatur hic solum ut marty- rium vel testimonium doctrinæ, quam morte ob- signavit, sed ut satisfactio pro peccatis, quod contra Socinum asseruit ipse Grotius in defens. fid. Cathol. de Satisfactione Christi, & prolixe assertum à no- bis est in Socinismo profligato: nec tantum à peccatis retrahit, & ad justitiam ducit Christi fortitudo, quod mortem non formidarit pro doctrinæ suæ peccatis contrariæ, & ad justitiam nos vocantis te- stimonio, cujus rei gratia non opus fuisset ipsum- met Dei unigenitum Filium mortem subire, quum in martyribus plurimis talia conspecta sint, qui mortem utique non formidarunt, in testimonium doctrinæ suæ subire, sed ipsa mors Christi λύτρον fuit & ἀντίλυτρον pro peccatis nostris, propter quæ in se suscepta, quum peccata causa meritoria sint mor- tis, Christus traditus in mortem est pro nobis, ut unus pro omnibus moreretur 2. Cor. V. 15. Nec de hac re- tractione à peccatis hic sermo est; sed de expiatione peccatorum per mortem Christi factâ, vel satisfactio- ne pro peccatis præstitâ, quæ est meritoria causa nostræ justificationis, non tantum causa moraliter nos movens, ut à peccatis desistamus.

Porrò non resuscitatum dicit Apostolus Chri- stum à Deo, ut doctrinæ ejus autoritas conciliare- tur, quæ per miracula & per testificationem de cœ- lis fatis conciliari ipsi poterat, modo Judæi adeo in- durati non fuissent, sed διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν pro- pter justificationem nostram. Et si doctrinæ solum per mortis martyrium & resuscitationis miraculum confirmandæ causa Filius Dei unigenitus in mor- tem traditus & à morte resuscitatus est, ut alii per doctrinam ejusdem à peccatis & exitio liberaren- tur, annon idem per aliorum martyrium mortem & resuscitationem fieri potuisset, quemadmodum quidam è fidelibus priscis resuscitati sunt, multisq; apparuerunt teste S. Matthæo c. XXVII. 53. Quid ergò opus fuisset ipsummet Filium Dei Deum illum benedictum in secula super omnia in mortem ideò tradi & resuscitari? longè aliud hic docet Aposto- lus mortem nempe Christi factam fuisse non occasione tantum peccatorum nostrorum, non solum ob confirma- tionem doctrinæ Christi nos à peccatis retrahentis, sed ob meritum peccatorum nostrorum, quia verba διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν inferunt meritoriam cau- sam mortis Christi, traditum, adeo peccatorum nostrorum pœnam Christum divino consilio & decreto sustinuisse, ut nos ab eadem liberaret; quod prolixè docetur Es. c. LIII. nosque Christi morte Deo reconciliatos esse, ac justificari, ac proinde ut mors Christi causa vel ratio motiva fuit ad decernendam nobis remissionem peccatorum, justificationem & salutem, ita non aliter nos coram Deo justificari & salutem consequi nisi apprehensa satisfactione mortis Christi; qui scopus est de- monstrationis & tractationis Apostolicæ in hoc capite. Idcircò fidem, quæ nobis imputatur in justi- tiam, ita describit, quod in Deum feratur, qui Jesum resuscitavit è mortuis, ceu traditum propter peccata no- stra; quia illa resuscitatio è mortuis documentum est infallibile plenissimæ satisfactionis & expiationis peccatorum nostrorum, ac reconciliationis cū Deo, per morte Christi factæ, quæ si facta nō esset, Deus hunc Mediatorem & sponsorem nostru, qui semet- ipsu dedit ἀντίλυτρον 1. Tim. II. 4. neutiquam è mor- te ad communicandam & distribuendam nobis ju- stitiam suam vel justificationem nostram resusci- tasset. Non ergo eâdem omnino ratione Christus dicitur propter justificationem nostram resuscitatus, quemadmodum propter peccata nostra in mortem à Deo traditus est, quùm hic mors Christi causa meri- toria expiationis peccatorū nostrorum, uti peccata nostra causa meritoria fuere mortis Christi, con- stituitur, quod merito peccatorum nostrorum ipse in mortem traditus sit nostri loco, ut nos merito mor- tis ejus à peccato ejusque pœna morte liberemur: De resuscitatione Christi verò id non adeò asseri possit, quod nempe Christus sua resurrectione no- bis justitiam meruerit: cujus etiam meritum morte CONSUMMATUM FUISSE exclamatio ejus in cruce τετέλεσται consummatum est Joh. XIX 30. con- firmavit. Ideò diversimodè de morte Christi, & de resurrectione ejus loquitur Scriptura. Christum enim passum & mortuum dicit & propter nos & pro nobis: resurrexisse autem non pro nobis, sed tantum propter nos.

Quanquam ergò quandoque Theo- logi resurrectionem Christi causam meritoriam nostræ justificationis dicunt, vocem meriti tamen intelligunt tantum generaliter, uti monuit B. Gerh. in comment. ad h. l. ad quæstionem: An resurrectio Christi pertineat ad meritum pro nobis præstitum h.m. respondens: nomen meriti accipitur vel γενικῶς pro omni eo, quod pertinet ad nostram justificationem, vel εἰδικῶς pro eo, quod Christus pro nobis præstitit, ac nos præstare debebamus. Priori sensu resurrectio Christi pertinet ad meritum, quia ad justificationem nostram requirebatur Christi resurrectio certis respectibus; po- steriori autem respectu non pertinet ad meritu, quia Christus resurrexit propter nos, non autem pro nobis, passus autem est & mortuus non solum propter nos, sed etiam pro nobis. Quibus autem respectibus ad ju- stificationem nostram requisita fuerit Christi re- suscitatio, ita explicat B. Gerh. Nimirum 1. ratione manifestationis, ac confirmationis, quia resurrectio Christi est evidens testimonium, quod pro nostris peccatis plenè sit satisfactum, & justitia perfecta ad- ducta. Quo facit illud Chrysost. hom. IX. adRom. In resurrectione ostensum est, Christum non propter sua sed nostra peccata fuisse mortuum. Quomodo enim sur- rexisset, si peccator fuisset? si vero peccator non fuit, propter alios crucifixus est. 2. respectu applicationis; Si Christus in morte mansisset, non fuisset mortis victor, nec potuisset nobis justitiam tam caro pretio partam applicare Rom. V. 10. c. VIII. 34. respe- ctu actualis à peccato absolutionis, ut punivit Deus peccata nostra in Christo, quæ ipsi ut sponsori no- stro erant imposita atque imputata; ita quoque ex- citando eum à mortuis ipso facto absolvit eum à nostris peccatis, ipsi imputatis, ac proinde etiam nos in ipso absolvit: quo refert dicta 1. Cor. XV. 17. 2. Cor. V. 21. Eph. II. 5. Gal. II. 12. 13. Phil. III. 8. 9. 10. 1. Pet. I. 3. Ubi tamen observandum, manifestatione & confirmationem expiationis peccatorum & victo- riæ mortis demonstrationem ad fidem quidem no- stram facere, non autem ad meritum Christi; appli- cationem verò justitiæ Christi à merito Christi omni- nò distinguit, & Christum resuscitatum causam ef- ficientem esse applicationis, non autem resurrectio- nem Christi meritoriam esse vel justitiæ Christi vel applicationis ejusdem, deniq; in Christo resuscitato nos absolvi à peccato, hactenus admitti, quod eo- dem absoluto à peccatis nostris ipsi imputatis, cer- ta nobis sit peccatorū nostrorum expiatio, quem- admodū etiam certa nobis est vivificatio, & à mor- tuis ad beatam vitam resuscitatio, ob quam certitu- dinem merito mortis Christi per resuscitationem Christi confirmato innixam nos vivificari dicimur in Christo & cum Christo resurrexisse Ef. VI. 2. Eph. II. 5. Sed hæc ad meritoriam causam justifica- tionis propriè non faciunt: Quum solum ad fidem ex parte nostri firmandam, aut justitiæ à Christo no- bis partæ per Evangelium applicationem, ad quam prærequiritur Christi resuscitatio, non tamen me- ritòriè, illa facere in aprico sit. Nec prætermit- tendum quod Apostolus, uti dicit, Christum mor- tuum esse propter peccata nostra, non eundem dicat resuscitatum propter δικαιωσύνην justitiam nostram, quæ peccatis alias opponitur, sed διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἤμω̃ν propter justificationem nostram, quia nec fides, qua opus est ad Justificationem ἄμεταπτώτως certa esse, nec à Christo applicari nobis justitia potuis- set, si Christus à mortuis resuscitatus non fuisset.

Pervertunt autem sententiam Apostoli Papistæ, cum id eum hic velle contendunt, mortem Christi exemplar fuisse mortis peccatorum, resurrectionem autem exemplar renovationis & regenerationis in- ternæ, per quam innovitate vitæ ambulemus, vid. Bellarm. l. II. de justif. c. 6. quia hic non agitur vel de morte peccatorum, vel de renovatione & novitate vitæ, de quibus cap. VI. demum agere incipit Apo- stolus, sed de non imputatione vel remissione pecca- torum, & imputatione justitiæ, vel justificatione: nec causam exemplarẽ, sed meritoriam importat parti- cula διὰ propter peccata nostra, & causam finalem propter justificationem nostram. Ad justificatio- nem autem, quâ de agit Apostolus, applicatione opus esse passionis Christi agnoscit ipse Svarez T. II. in part. III. Thomæ disp. XLIV. p. 478. Christus per passionem suam sufficienter destruxit peccatum, ta- men ut nos justificaremur, & efficaciter remitteretur nobis peccatum, oportebat passionem Christi nobis ap- plicari per fidem vivam. Quæ applicatio per impu- tationem fit, docente Apostolo. Denique observan- dum hic, quod notanter Apostolus dicat justifican- dum, vel eum, cui fides imputari debet ad justitiam, credere debere in Deum, qui Jesum propter peccata nostra traditum propter justificationem nostram resu- scitavit; ut sc. fidem nostram respicere doceat in id, quod Deus nos quàm certissimos fecit de satisfa- ctione sibi præstita in resuscitatione nempe Jesu, non minus quam in mortem, in quam propter peccata nostra Jesum tradidit, adeoque in ipsam Domini Je- su satisfactionem meritoriam; eamque fidem nobis imputari ad justitiam, imprimis cum, Apostolo teste, hujusce justificationis nostræ causa Deus Pa- ter Filium resuscitavit, ut & constaret nobis hocce documento infallibili, de expiatione peccatorum, & ut Christum ipsum Mediatorem nostrum, eam, quam nobis peperit justitiam nobis quoque decre- to & voluntate Dei Patris applicare indubitato cre- damus.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Justification through faith is declared a posteriori from the peace of conscience, and the confidence of access to God, and the hope of future glory; which is strengthened by the love of God and the satisfaction of Christ for us. Since through the sin of one man guilt came upon all, but the gift of grace through Christ frees not only from one sin, but from all: and since sin was rendered more effective through the law for condemnation, grace must be held to be much more effective, not only by freeing us from the dominion of sin and death, but also by reigning through righteousness unto life in Christ.

There are three parts: The first is exegetical, in which he declares, and by declaring establishes, justification through faith from the consequent, peace with God, up to verse 11. The second is demonstrative, in which from the antithesis of the first and second Adam he confirms gratuitous justification through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ up to v. 19 inclusive. The third is preparatory, in which he prepares the way for himself for objections, instructing us concerning the law, as to what it profited, namely not for justification, but for the exaggeration of sin, and the amplification of the grace of God in Christ. Furthermore, if we attend to the entire economy of the Pauline disputation, the third and fourth argument of the principal theme of confirmation occurs here: namely, the proof of the justification of faith a posteriori or from the consequent, i.e., from the peace of conscience: as from the similarity and comparison of the origin of injustice and justice, and the collation of Adam and Christ. Whence the Apostle, having finished the duty of proof, about to proceed to the vindication, or the defending of the doctrine concerning justification through faith, prepares the way for himself, reminding us of the cause of the law having entered in.

ARTICLE III. Argument a posteriori, from the peace of conscience.

PART I. OF THE CHAPTER, exegetical. Declaring justification by faith a posteriori.

Vers. 1. Δικαιωθέντες ὐν ἐκ πίστεως. Therefore cleansed from sins through faith. εἰρήνην ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν. We enjoy the friendship of God. See what is above IV. 4. Here εἰρήνη, which is there, and now soon χάρις. Just as Abraham was the friend of God, Jas. II. 23. so also are we. διὰ τῦ κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ. To him after God we owe thanks. He now expresses the cause. Vers. 2. δι᾽ ὗ καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν τῇ πίστει εἰς τὴν χάριν ταύτην. From whom we have both other benefits, and this one most of all, that he gave us the causes for believing, so that thus through faith we might arrive at that friendship and benevolence of God. Προσάγειν corresponds to the Hebrew כנס and קרב, whence πρόσαγωγη both here and Eph. II. 18. III. 12. is access to a thing or person. For τῇ πίστει in the Manuscript ἐν τῇ πίστει, which is more customary for Paul, and repeated letters are accustomed to fall out easily.

Of justification, which is done through faith, and not from works, this is the consequence, that we have peace of conscience, acquiescing in the grace of God, of which we are certain; peace with God, who from being angry with us has become appeased, our sins having been forgiven, and we having been received into grace, and adopted to the inheritance of salvation. Whence is the Apostolic theme, that we are justified not by works but by faith alone, confirmed a posteriori from this peace and tranquility of conscience? For that is true justification which produces tranquility of conscience; but it is not justification by works, but that which is done by faith, that produces tranquility of conscience. For suppose it is required for justification that our works be obtained, whether by them alone or joined with faith, the conscience could never be tranquil, because we could never be certain whether we have performed such and so many works as are required for justification. Which is also the reason why Papists and other Workers must doubt the grace of God, who also teach that we cannot be certain of the same, whence the dogma of the certainty of grace was condemned in the Council of Trent. But what is this other than to condemn the Apostolic dogma? inasmuch as the Apostle here so prolixly establishes that those justified by faith have peace with God, have access to God with confidence, stand in grace, and glory on account of the hope of the glory of God: glorying also in calamities themselves, nay, glorying in the calamities themselves, because we are certain that they cannot intercept our heavenly blessedness, but that through tribulations we enter into the kingdom of God. Acts 14:22. Justification, however, is wrongly explained by Grotius as cleansing from sins, which he understands as sanctification; since it consists not in sanctification, but in the remission of sins, as the Apostle testifies, of which sanctification is the consequence. Wrongly also are εἰρήνη and χάρις confused: for the latter is the principle and cause of justification; the former, however, is the effect and consequence, namely, peace with God, which we have not only on the part of the thing, because God has been made propitious to us through faith in Christ, but also regarding the certainty of our mind, because the grace and love of God has been poured out into the hearts of those who have been justified. And thus through faith we have not only the love of benevolence, or propitiation, because God is appeased toward us through Christ, and we apprehend his grace and propitiation by faith, but also the love of friendship, because God holds us as friends, nay, as sons; of which divine love we are made certain through the Holy Spirit.

By εἰρήνη therefore is understood both reconciliation with God, because πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν is added, and the quiet and tranquility of conscience: which consists in the sense and certainty of that reconciliation. Which εἰρήνη we have through our Lord Jesus Christ, in respect of merit, inasmuch as he acquired the same for us, and through faith in Christ by reason of apprehension and application. The Apostle adds that through Christ we also have προσαγωγὴν to that grace in which we stand, justified by faith: which is not to be understood as an introduction to grace, insofar as it was acquired by Christ, i.e., we have been introduced to grace by the death of Christ; but insofar as it has been applied to us on account of Christ in justification, because τῇ πίστει, in faith and through faith, we have that introduction: where nothing is added or taken away from the sense, whether the preposition ἐν is added to τῇ πίστει or not added; since the sense is the same, even if the preposition is not expressly added. Moreover, the word ἐσχήκαμεν can also not badly be taken in the present tense, as Luther rendered it, wir haben einen Zugang; because as we have been introduced to grace in justification by faith, so, being justified, we always have access to grace, and can approach the same with confidence, not otherwise than as the faithful in the Old Testament approached the mercy seat. Eph. 2:18. Heb. 4:16. Before we were reconciled to God through Christ, we were compelled to flee from God and hide ourselves before his face, Gen. 3:8; but after we have been reconciled to God by faith in Christ, a perpetual and free access to divine grace lies open to us.

ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν. In which, namely, faith we stand, that is, we guard ourselves against sins. For just as he who sins is said to fall, Heb. 4:2, Jas. 5:12, so he who abstains from sinning is said to stand, below 14:4, 1 Cor. 10:12. This is the past tense for the present, in the Hebrew manner. Although for us to stand by faith, it is necessary that we guard ourselves against sins, by which we fall from faith, Rom. 14:4, 1 Cor. 10:12, yet these are not the same: to stand by faith, and to abstain from sin. For they stand by faith who persevere in confidence, who retain faith, and thus remain unmoved in the grace of God; but faith having been lost or shaken off, we are no longer in the grace of God, nor can we stand before God, much less persist intrepidly, or have access to the grace of God. ςῆναι does not simply signify to stand, but also to persist in a station, to remain in firm confidence, a metaphor drawn from the battle line, in which brave soldiers do not yield even a foot's breadth to the enemy, says B. Gerhard.

καὶ καυχώμεθα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ. We are supported by the hope of that glory which we are to receive from God, according to the promises of Christ. Καυχᾶσθαι is to lean upon something, as we said above 2:17, 23. Thus עלץ, which is to rejoice, is translated both by καυχᾶσθαι and by κατακαυχᾶσθαι, as also עלז and רנן, which are of equal meaning. Καυχᾶσθαι implies more than to lean upon or be supported by something, which Grotius could not deny, since he also explained it by TO REJOICE. But to glory still differs, even if it is joined with joy; for we do not glory except in those things in which we rejoice; we are accustomed TO GLORY concerning a thing glorious to us, or in which we judge our glory to be situated; and therefore those justified by faith are said to glory in hope, or on account of the hope of the glory of God, because, namely, they certainly hope that they will be partakers of heavenly glory: they glory, however, not in their works, but uniquely in Christ: for he who wishes to glory, let him glory in the Lord, Jer. 9:25. Cor. I. 31. 2. Cor. XI. 7. Gal. VI. 14. The glory of God is called heavenly glory, both efficiently, because it is given by God, and objectively and formally, because this glory consists in God and the enjoyment of God.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Declaratur a posteriori justificatio per fidem a pace conscientiae, & fiducia accessionis ad Deum, ac spe futurae gloriae; quae e Dei dile- ctione & Christi pro nobis satisfactione fir- matur. Quandoquidem per unius quidem peccatum in omnes reatus venerit, donum vero gratiae per Christum non ab uno peccato tantum, sed ab omnibus liberat: & quum peccatum per legem efficacius redditum sit ad condemnationem, multo magis efficax ha- benda gratia, non tantum liberando nos a do- minio peccati & mortis, sed etiam dominan- do per justitiam ad vitam in Christo.

PArtes tres sunt: Prima ἐξηγητικὴ, qua declarat, & declarando statuminat justificationem per fi- dem e consequenti, pace cum Deo, usque ad vers. 11. Secunda est ἀποδεικτικὴ, qua ex antithefi Adami primi & secundi confirmat justificationem gratui- tam per imputationem justitiae Christi usque ad v. 19. incl. Tertia est παρασκευαστικὴ, qua viam sibi parat ad objectiones, de lege nos instruens, ad quid il- la profuerit, nimirum non ad justificationem, sed ad peccati exaggerationem, & gratiae Dei in Christo am- plificationem. De caetero si universam οἰκονομίαν disputationis Paulinae attendamus, occurrit hic ar- gumentum tertium & quartum βεβαιώσεως thema- tis principalis: utpote probatio justificationis fidei a posteriori vel consequenti pace sc. conscientiae: ut e similitudine & comparatione ortus injustitiae & justitiae, & collatione Adami & Christi. Unde munere probationis defunctus Apostolus ad ἐνδί- κησιν progressurus, seu vindicandum doctrinam de justificatione per fidem, viam sibi parat, commone- faciens de Causa subingressa legis.

ARTICULUS III. Argumentum a posteriori, e pace con- scientiae.

PARS I. CAPITIS ἐξηγητικὴ. Declarans justificationem per fidem a posteriori.

Vers. 1. Δικαιωθέντες ὐν ἐκ πίστεως. Mundati igitur a peccatis per fidem. εἰρήνην ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν. Amicitia Dei fruimur. Vide quae supra IV. 4. Hic εἰ- ρήνη, quod ibi, & jam mox χάρις. Sicut Abraham amicus Dei fuit, Jac. II. 23. sic & nos. διὰ τῦ κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ. Ei post Deum gratiam debemus. Causam jam expri- met. Vers. 2. δι᾽ ὗ καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν τῇ πίστει εἰς τὴν χάριν ταύτην. A quo tum alia habemus beneficia, tum hoc vel maxi- mum, quod ille nobis dedit credendi causas, ut sic per fidem perveniremus ad illam Dei amicitiam & benevolentiam. Προσάγειν respondet Hebraeo כנס & קרב, unde πρόσαγω- γη tum hic, tum Eph. II. 18. III. 12. est aditus ad rem vel per- sonam. Pro τῇ πίστει in Manuscripto ἐν τῇ πίστει, quod Paulo usitatius, & solent facile excidere literae repetitae.

Justificationis, quae per fidem fit, & non ex ope- ribus, hoc consequens est, quod pacem conscientiae, acquiescentis in gratia Dei, de qua certi sumus, ha- beamus; pacem cum Deo, qui ex irato nobis factus est placatus, peccatis nobis remissis, nobisq; in gra- tiam receptis, & ad haereditatem salutis adoptatis. Unde à posteriori firmatur ex hac pace & tranquillitate conscientiæ thema Apostolicum, quod non operibus, sed fide solum justificemur. Ea enim est vera justificatio, quæ parit tranquillitatem conscientiæ; at non justificatio per opera, sed quæ per fidem fit, conscientiæ parit tranquillitatem. Pone enim requiri ad justificationem nostra opera, sive iisdem solis, sive cum fide junctis obtinenda sit justificatio, nunquam tranquilla esse poterit conscientia, quia nunquam certi esse poterimus, utrum talia ac tanta opera, qualia & quanta ad justificationem requiruntur, præstiterimus. Quæ causa etiam est, quod Papistis & Operariis cæteris dubitandum sit de gratia Dei, qui etiam docent, nos certos de eadem esse non posse, unde dogma de certitudine gratiæ damnatum est in Concilio Tridentino. Quid verò hoc aliud est, quàm dogma Apostolicum damnare? siquidem Apostolus hic tam prolixè adstruit, justificatos per fidem pacem habere cum Deo, accessum habere ad Deum cum fiducia, stare in gratia, & gloriari ob spem gloriæ Dei: gloriari etiam in ipsis calamitatibus, imò de calamitatibus ipsis gloriari, quod certi simus easdem non posse nobis intervertere cœlestem beatitudinem, sed per tribulationes nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Act. XIV. 22. Justificatio autem perperam à Grotio per mundationem à peccatis, quam ille de sanctificatione intelligit, explicatur; quum non in sanctificatione, sed peccatorum remissione consistat, teste Apostolo, cujus consequens est sanctificatio. Perperam etiam confunditur εἰρήνη & χάρις: nam hæc principium & causa est justificationis; illa verò effectum, & consequens est, pax nempe cum Deo, quam habemus non tantum ex parte rei, quia Deus nobis propitius factus est, per fidem in Christum, sed etiam quoad certitudinem mentis nostræ, quia gratia & dilectio Dei effusa est in cordibus eorum, qui justificati sunt. Atque ita per fidem habemus non tantum amorem benevolentiæ, vel propitiationis, quia placatus nobis Deus est per Christum, ejusque gratiam, & propitiationem fide apprehendimus, sed etiam amorem amicitiæ, quia Deus nos ut amicos habet, imò ut filios; de quo amore divino certi reddimur per Spiritum S.

Per εἰρήνην ergò tum reconciliatio cum Deo intelligitur, quia additur πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, tum conscientiæ quies & tranquillitas: quæ in sensu & certitudine illius reconciliationis consistit. Quam εἰρήνην habemus per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, respectu meriti, siquidem eandem nobis acquisiverit, & per fidem in Christum ratione apprehensionis, & applicationis. Addit Apostolus, per Christum etiam nos habere προσαγωγὴν ad illam gratiam, in qua stamus, justificati per fidem: quod non de adductione ad gratiam, quatenus ea à Christo acquisita est, intelligendum, q. d. adducti sumus ad gratiam, morte Christi; sed quatenus ea nobis applicata est propter Christum in justificatione, quia τῇ πίστει in fide & per fidem eam habemus adductionem: ubi nihil sensui accedit, aut decedit, sive præpositio ἐν addatur τῇ πίστει, sive non addatur; quum sensus idem sit, etiamsi expresse addita non sit præpositio.
