Potest autem verbum ἐσχήκαμεν etiam non malè in præsenti accipi, ut Lutherus reddidit, wir haben einen Zugang; quia ut in justificatione per fidem adducti sumus ad gratiam, ita justificati accessum semper ad gratiam habemus, & cum fiducia ad eandem accedere possumus, non secus atque accedebant ad propitiatorium fideles in Vet. Test. Eph. II. 18. Ebr. IV. 16. Antequam Deo per Christum reconciliaremur, cogebamur Deum fugere, nosque coram facie ipfius abfcondere, Gen. III. 8. sed postquam fide in Chriftum Deo reconciliati fumus, patet nobis perpetuus & liber ad gratiam divinam aditus.

ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν. In qua nempe fide stamus, id est, cavemus nobis à pecca- tis. Nam sicut qui peccat cadere dicitur, Hebr. IV. 2. Jac. V. 12 sic stare, qui à peccando abstinet, infra XIV. 4. 1 Cor. X. 12. Est hic præteritum pro præsente, more Hebræo. Etfi ad id, ut fide stemus, opus fit, ut caveamus no- bis à peccatis, quibus fide excidimus, Rom. XIV. 4. 1. Cor. X. 12. non tamen hæc idem sunt, stare fide, & à peccato abstinere. Nam fide stant, qui perseverant in fiducia, qui fidem retinent, & ita immoti persi- stunt in gratia Dei; fide autem amissa, vel excussa, non amplius sumus in Dei gratia, nec stare coram Deo, nedum consistere possumus intrepidè, aut accesfum habere ad gratiam Dei, ςῆναι non simpli- citer fignificat stare, verum etiam in statione per- sistere, in firma fiducia permanere, metaphora ducta ab acie, in qua strenui milites ne latum quidem pe- dem hosti cedunt, ait B. Gerhardus.

καὶ καυχώμεθα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ. Fulcimur spe gloriæ illius, quam à Deo accepturi sumus, secundum promissa Christi. Καυχᾶσθαι est aliqua re inniti, ut diximus supra II. 17. 23. Itaque עלץ quod est gaudere vertitur & per καυχᾶσθαι, & per κατακαυχᾶσθαι, ut & עלז & רנן quæ paris sunt fignificatus. καυχᾶσθαι plus infert quàm inniti aliquâ re, vel sulciri, quod Grotius diffiteri non potuit, cum per GAUDERE id etiam exposuit. Sed gloriari ad- huc differt, etsi cum gaudio conjunctum sit; non enim gloriamur nisi de his, in quibus gaudemus; De re nobis gloriosa, vel in qua sitam esse gloriam nostram censemus GLORIARI solemus; ideoque gloriari dicuntur justificati per fidem in spe, vel ob spem gloriæ Dei, quod nempe certò sperent, se gloriæ cœlestis participes fore: gloriantur autem non in operibus suis, sed unicè in Christo: nam qui gloriari vult, glorietur in Domino Jer. IX. 25. 1. Cor. I. 31. 2. Cor. XI. 7. Gal. VI. 14. Δόξα τοῦ Θεοῦ vocatur cœlestis gloria, tum efficienter, quia à Deo datur, tum objectivè, & formaliter, quod in Deo & fruitione Dei consistat hæc gloria.

## 5:3
Verse 3. And not only. We do not only rejoice in that hope.

but we also glory in tribulations. This is the proper effect of that great, that is, Christian faith: to rejoice in adversities which happen for the sake of the name of God and Christ. See the example in Acts 5:41, which you would seek in vain in the Old Testament. Add 2 Cor. 7:4, 8:2.

But what difference between the Old and New Testament is sought here? Had not the Apostle brought forward the example of Abraham and David for justification by faith? Had he not ordered us to follow in the footsteps of Abrahamic faith? Now, that glorying is a consequence of the justification of faith. Nor are there lacking in the Old Testament both precepts and examples of the Patriarchs regarding glorying in adversities, if you diligently weigh the history of Moses, Job, David, Daniel and his companions, and the Maccabees, and search the exhortations in the Psalms and among the Prophets. See Job 1:21, Ps. 23:4, Ps. 55:11 ff., Ps. 68:4, Ps. 71:8, 23, Ps. 73:28, Ps. 97:11, 12, Ps. 116:13, etc.

knowing that tribulation worketh patience. Namely, in believers. Tertullian translates ὑπομονή as sufferentia, others more Latinly as tolerantia or patientia: understand it as that by which we willingly endure any evils for the sake of God. Rabbi Israel has beautiful things, quite in agreement with Paul, concerning the utility of adversities in his book On the Soul, chapters 28 and 33.

It does not work patience by itself, but accidentally, in that it is joined with faith, or in believers. The Papists wrongly gather from this the merits of works or sufferings: because our sufferings are not worthy of the glory to come, Rom. 8:18, nor is affliction the cause of patience, whether physical or moral, much less peculiarly meritorious, but it works patience only, because patience follows in believers: which patience is exercised and tested through affliction: but the Holy Spirit works patience in believers in afflictions and through afflictions; because He uses afflictions so that they may learn to tolerate evils patiently; so that, having placed their faith in divine promises, they may sustain themselves and overcome evils, aided by divine grace. The sufferings of Christ alone are a λύτρον, ours are either punishments, or trials, or testimonies; they cannot be a lytron and expiation before God.

And patience, trial. Exploration, namely of oneself: for by suffering a man learns his own strengths. Elsewhere that name is taken with respect to others, but in James 1:3 τὸ δοκιμὸν is placed metonymically for the adverse things themselves.

Rightly Blessed Gerhard, outside the cross we are mere theorists, in the cross the true and living practice of the article concerning gratuitous justification is proposed. Sirach 34:10. Thomas also metonymically accepts in James 1:3 τὸν δόκιμον in this way: tribulation works patience.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὦ μόνον δὲ. Non tantum gaudemus ea spe.

ἀλλὰ καὶ καυχώμεθα ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσιν. Hic proprius effectus magnæ illius, id est, Christianæ fi- dei, gaudere adversis, quæ propter Dei & Christi nomen eveniunt. Exemplum vide Act. V. 41 quale in Veteri Te- stamento frustra quæras. Adde 2. Cor. VII. 4. VIII. 2.

Quæ verò hic differentia Vet. & Novi Test. quæ- ritur? Annon Abrahami & Davidis exemplum ad justificationem per fidem adduxerat Apostolus? annon nos insistere vestigiis fidei Abrahamicæ jusserat? Justificationis autem fidei consequens est illa gloriatio. Neque desunt gloriationis in adver- sis cum præcepta, tum Patriarcharum exempla in Vet. Test. Si Mosis, Jobi, Davidis, Danielis & Sociorum, ac Maccabaicam historiam diligenter expendas, & paræneses in Psalmis, & apud Prophe- tas scruteris. vid. Job. I. 21. Pf. XXIII. 4. Ps. LV. 11. seqq. Pf. LXVIII. 4. Ps. LXXI. 8. 23. Ps. LXXIII. 28. Pf. XCVII. 11. 12. Ps. CXVI. 13. &c.

εἰδότες ὅτι ἡ θλίψις ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται. Nempe in credentibus. ὑπομονὴν sufferentiam vertit Tertullianus, alii Latinius tolerantiam aut patientiam: eam intellige, per quam Dei causa mala quævis libenter tolera- mus. De utilitate adversorum pulchra & Paulo fatis con- sentientia, habet Rabbi Israël de anima c. 28. & 33.

Non per se operatur patientiam, sed per acci- dens, quâ cum fide conjuncta est, vel in credenti- bus. Pontificii perperam merita operum vel passio- num inde colligunt: quia non condigna sunt passio- nes nostra gloria Rom. VIII. 18. neq; afflictio causa est Patientiæ, seu Physica seu moralis, nedum peculia- riter meritoria, sed κατεργάζεται patientiam so- lùm, quia in credentibus consequitur patientia: quæ patientia exercetur & probatur per θλίψιν: Spiritus S. autem in afflictionibus & per afflictiones operatur in credentibus patientiam; quia utitur afflictionibus, ut discant patienter tolerare mala; ut fide promissis divinis habitâ se sustentent, & ma- la superent, adjuti divinâ gratiâ. Solius Christi passiones λύτρον sunt, nostræ vel τιμωρίαι sunt, vel δοκιμασίαι, vel μαρτύρια, lytron & expiatio apud Deum esse nequeunt.

ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ δοκιμὴν. Explorationem, nempe sui ipsius: nam patiendo discit homo suas vires. Alibi sumitur id nomen respectu alio- rum, at Jac. I. 3. τὸ δοκιμὸν ponitur μετωνυμικῶς pro ipsis rebus adversis.

Rectè B. Gerhardus, extra crucem sumus meri Theorici, in cruce vera & viva praxis articuli de gra- tuita justificatione proponitur. Sirach. XXXIV. 10. Metonymicè etiam Thomas Jac. I. 3. accipit τὸν δό- κιμον h. m. tribulatio operatur patientiam.

## 5:4
Verse 4. And trial, hope. For he who knows that he suffers the hardest things for God's sake, his hope is kindled more and more, both from God's goodness, to whom it is not fitting not to reward such patience, and from the promise of Christ, Mark 5:12, John 16:20.

Those who are conformed in the cross to the image of the Son of God are confirmed by this, that they are also to be conformed to the same at some time in glory. Romans 8:29.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἡ δὲ δοκιμὴ ἐλπίδα. Nam qui scit se durissima pati Dei causa, ejus spes magis magisque accenditur, tum ex Dei bonitate, cui non conve- nit talem patientiam non munerare, tum ex promisso Chri- sti Marc. V. 12. Joh. XVI. 20.

Qui in cruce conformantur imagini Filii Dei, ex eo confirmantur, quod etiam eidem aliquando conformandi sint in gloria. Rom. VIII. 29.

## 5:5
Verse 5. And hope does not put to shame) That is, hope founded on God's promises does not fail. The expression is taken from Psalm 22:6, and is a metonymy, because usually those who have placed their faith in vain promises are accustomed to be ashamed. See also Sirach 2:10. Augustine noted a gradation in this period, a figure which the Apostle loves, as can be seen below in 8:39, 10:14.

because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

He says this: we have the less reason to doubt the outcome of the thing hoped for, because we have also received the Holy Spirit as a pledge from God. The love of God is to be understood here, by which God loves men, as can be seen below in [chapter] 8. The Spirit poured out upon Christians, that is, abundantly given, is spoken of in Acts 2:17, 18, 33, 10:45, Titus 3:6. But here the love of God itself is said to be poured out, that is, abundantly testified to the minds of men. For everyone conscious of the gifts he had received rightly concluded from that, that the love of God was great toward him. Those who wish to break faith are not accustomed to give such great things in return. Add 2 Corinthians 1:21, 22, Ephesians 1:14.

These things are more correct than the glosses of the Papists, who explain it not of the active love of God, by which He loves us, but of the passive, by which He is loved by us: and from this they wish to carve out the charity poured into us or infused as the form of our justification. But the Apostle is dealing here with the consequences of justification, not with its causes or its form. Nor is the outpouring to be understood physically, but, as Grotius acknowledges—who otherwise gladly gratifies the Papists—the love of God is said to be poured out, that is, abundantly testified to the minds of men. It is explained thus in the commentary which is ascribed to Ambrose, concerning the Charity by which GOD loves us. We have the pledge of charity in us through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Which interpretation was also approved by the Glossa Ordinaria, Dominicus à Soto, Cajetan, Toledo, Justinianus. Which explanation is also evident from the context. For the Apostle proves that hope does not put to shame, because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts. This proof is firm, being from the love of God toward us, by which our hope is solidly sustained and supported; but it is too weak if from the love of us toward God, which wavers greatly, and is in many ways imperfect, and contaminated, because of the stain of depraved concupiscence which remains in us. Only the love of God toward us, which we have in us from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, can seal the hope of the heavenly inheritance in us. Compare 1 John 3:13, 16, and it is hinted that it deals with the Charity of God toward us in verse 8, which God Himself commends; compare chapter 8, last verse.

Not to mention that the word 'outpouring,' which implies abundance, does not so well befit our Charity toward GOD; since our love toward God is lacking rather than abounding in us. Therefore Chrysostom explains it concerning the charity which God showed toward us: with whom Theophylact and Oecumenius agree, as does Primasius. Which charity poured out in us is not as a subjective inherence, but as a manifestation, and as an effect, or the sense of the same poured out in our hearts, Psalm 34:9, as the Jesuit Pererius himself admits; whether we read 'diffused' or 'poured out,' nothing else is signified by that word, except that the charity of God has been openly and evidently declared.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἡ δὲ ἐλπὶς ὐ καταισχύνει) Id est, spes in Dei pro- missis fundata non fallit. Locutio sumpta ex Psal. XXII. 6. & μετωνυμία, quia plerumque pudere eos solet, qui vanis pollicitationibus fidem habuêre. Vide & Sirach. II. 10. Notavit in hac periodo gradationem Augustinus, quam fi- guram amat Apostolus, ut videre est infra VIII. 39. X. 14.

ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ Θεῦ ἐκκέχυται ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν διὰ πνέυματος ἁγίε τῦ δοθέντος ἡμῖν.

Hoc dicit: eo minus dubitandum habemus de rei spera- tæ eventu, quia etiam arrham à Deo accepimus Spiritum Sanctum, Dei dilectio hic intelligenda, quâ Deus homines diligit, ut videre est infra 8. Spiritus effusus in Christianos, id est, ubertim datus dicitur Act. II. 17. 18. 33. X. 45. Tit. III. 6. Hic vero ipsa Dei dilectio effusa dicitur, id est, ab- undanter testata hominum animis. Nam quisque sibi con- scius donorum, quæ acceperat, recte inde colligebat, ma- gnum in se esse Dei amorem. Non solent tam magna pro mutuo ii dare, qui fidem volunt fallere. Adde 2. Corinth. I. 21. 22. Eph. I. 14.

Hæc rectius se habent, quàm Papistarum glos- sæ, qui non de dilectione Dei activâ, quâ nos di- ligit, sed passiva, quâ diligitur à nobis, explicant: & effusam in nos vel infusam charitatem formam justificationis nostræ hinc exsculpere volunt. At de consequentibus justificationis hic agit Apostolus, non de causis ejusdem vel formâ. Neque effusio physicè intelligenda, sed, ut agnoscit Grotius, alias libenter Papistis gratificans, dilectio Dei effusa di- citur, id est, abundanter testata hominum animis. Ita explicatur in commentario, qui adscriptus est Ambrosio, de Charitate, quâ nos DEUS diligit. Pignus charitatis habemus in nobis per Sp. S. qui da- tus est nobis. Quam interpretationem etiam pro- bavit Glossa ordinaria, Dominicus à Soto, Cajeta- nus, Toletus, Justinianus. Quæ explicatio etiam patet è contextu. Probat enim Apostolus spem non confundere, quia charitas Dei effusa est in cordi- bus nostris. Firma est hæc probatio è dilectione Dei erga nos, quâ solidè sustentatur & fulcitur spes nostra; at nimis infirma à dilectione nostri er- ga Deum, quæ maximè vacillat, multisque modis imperfecta est, & contaminata, ob eam, quæ in nobis reliqua est, pravæ concupiscentiæ labem. Solius Dei amor erga nos, quem ex testimonio S. S. in nobis habemus, potest obsignare spem hæ- reditatis cœlestis in nobis. Conf. 1. Joh. III. 13. 16. & de Charitate Dei erga nos agi vers. 8. innuitur, quam Deus ipse commendat, conf. c. VIII. v. ult.

Ut taceam, quod Charitati nostræ erga DEUM non adeò conveniat verbum effusionis, quod abun- dantiam importat; quum deficiat potius, quàm abundet in nobis amor erga Deum. Ideò de cha- ritate ἣν περὶ ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεδείξατο explicat Chry- sostomus: cui consonat Theophyl. Oecumen. ut & Primasius. Quæ charitas effusa in nobis non qua inhaesionem subjectivam, sed quâ manifestationem, & quâ effectum, vel sensum ejusdem in cordibus nostris effusum, Psal. XXXIV. 9. fatente ipsomet Pererio Jesuitâ; sive legamus diffusa sive effusa, non aliud eâ voce significatur, nisi quod charitas Dei apertè ac evidenter declarata sit.

## 5:6
Ver. 6. For while Christ

This γὰρ is not connected with the preceding, but is a new argument to prove God's love toward us, rising from the less credible to the more credible. Others have read here εἰ, others εἰς τὸ: but ἔτι is correct, and is construed with ὄντων ἀσθενῶν, just as it will follow shortly, ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν.

Why should it not be connected with the preceding? Is there not also a most effective consolation here against afflictions, that Christ died for us when we were still weak sinners and ungodly, and therefore, having justified us and received us into grace, he cannot abandon us in adversities? And is it not a most brilliant testimony of the love of God, that he delivered his Son to death for us, and consequently, after we have now been reconciled ourselves, we should certainly have hope of salvation from him?

when we were weak.

When we had not yet received the strength to serve God.

at the time.

At a time opportune for that matter, John 13:1, 17:1, Gal. 4:4. When the weeks of Daniel had been completed: when kingdoms had been destroyed.

That appointed time does not apply here: because a comparison is being instituted between the antecedent state, when we were still ungodly, and the present state, after we have been justified; and he teaches that Christ died for us even then, when we were still ungodly, nay, his enemies; how much more, therefore, will he save us now, when we have been justified and made his friends? Whence that κατὰ καιρὸν is explained later by ἔτι in verse 8.

for the ungodly.

That is, even for the ungodly, such as many were not only among the Gentiles, but also among the Jews. Those whom he calls ἀσεβεῖς here, he calls ἁμαρτωλοὺς shortly after, in a more eminent sense, just as it has been noted by the learned that among the Hebrews רשעים and חטאים are accustomed to be taken for the same thing. The Greek interpreters also, for both those Hebrew words, sometimes say ἀσεβεῖς, sometimes ἁμαρτωλοὶ. See what we have said in Book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, ch. XX. 44.

died.

He died for this reason, that those sinners might be led to faith, which faith relies principally upon the death and resurrection of Christ. See above 4:25.

The ungodly are not only many, but all. For there is no διαςολὴ. We have all sinned Rom. III. 21. Which the Apostle teaches in this place at v. 12 and following, how sin has invaded all, and all have been made subject to sin and death. Nor did Christ die only for some, but for all 2. Cor. V. 15. having been made a propitiation for the sins of the whole world 1. Joh. II. 2. which Grotius also acknowledged at v. 8. Nor did he die only so that sinners could be led to faith, relying chiefly on the death and resurrection of Christ; but so that he might make satisfaction for them; it is not the resurrection that is treated here, upon which Grotius thinks faith primarily relies, but the death of Christ: who himself died for the ungodly, i.e., in their place and stead, as the word ὑπὲρ is understood in Gen. IV. 35. c. XXX. 2. Ex. VII. 1. Lev. XVII. 11. Job. II. 4. Es. XLIII. 4. Prov. XI. 8. Luc. XXII. 19. 20. Joh. X. 15. c. XI. 51. 52. c. XIII. 38. cap. XIV. 17. Act. XXI. 25. 1. Cor. I. 13. cap. V. 7. cap. XV. 29. 1. Thess. V. 9. 10. Phil. V. 13. 1. Pet. II. 27. c. IV. 1. 1. Joh. III. 16. Ebr. II. 9., and is here rendered by the Syriac by the word חלף, implying exchange: which sense the parallel passage 2 Cor. V. 14. 15. confirms, and the allusion to sacrifices, which were substituted in place of transgressors: Cf. Levit. XVII. 11. and what has been adduced in Socinismo Profligato p. 387. seqq. and what Grotius himself has handed down in fid. Cathol. de Satisf. Christi.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἔτι γὰρ χριστὸς.

Hoc γὰρ non connectitur cum prioribus, sed novum est argumentum ad probandum Dei in nos amorem, à minus credibili ad magis credibile assurgens. Legerunt hic alii εἰ, alii εἰς τὸ: sed ἔτι rectum est, & construitur cum ὄντων ἀσθε- νῶν, quomodo mox sequetur, ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν.

Cur non connectatur cum prioribus? annon & consolatio hic efficacissima habetur adversus affli- ctiones, quod Christus pro nobis, cum adhuc in- firmi peccatores & impii essemus, mortuus sit, adeoque nos justificatos & in gratiam receptos non possit relinquere in adversis? & luculentissi- mum charitatis Dei testimonium, quod pro nobis Filium suum in mortem tradiderit, ac proinde postquam reconciliati jam ipsi simus, certò spera- re ab ipso habeamus salutem?

ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν.

Cum nondum vires accepissemus ad serviendum Deo.

κατὰ καιρὸν.

Tempore ad eam rem opportuno, Joh. XIII, 1. XVII. 1. Gal. IV. 4. Exactis hebdomadibus Danielis: destructis regnis.

Non facit huc tempus illud constitutum: quia in- stituitur comparatio status antecedentis, cum adhuc impii essemus, & præsentis, postquam justificati sumus; & Christum etiam tum, cum adhuc impii essemus, imò inimici ejus, pro nobis mortuum do- cet; quanto ergo magis nunc, cum justificati & amici ejus facti sumus, nos servabit? unde illud κατὰ καιρὸν exponitur postea per ἔτι vers. 8.

ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν.

Id est, etiam pro impiis, quales multi non inter gentes tantum, sed & inter Judæos. Quos hic dicit ἀσεβεῖς, mox dicit ἁμαρτωλοὺς, sensu scilicet eminentiore, quomodo He- bræis רשעים & חטאים pro eodem sumi solere notatum est eruditis. Græci quoque interpretes pro utraque illa voce Hebræa modo dicunt ἀσεβεῖς, modò ἁμαρτωλοὶ. Vi- de quæ diximus libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. XX. 44.

ἀπέθανε.

Ideò mortuus est, ut illi peccatores ad fidem perduci possent, quæ fides præcipue nititur morte Christi & resurre- ctione. vide supra IV. 25.

Impii non multi tantum sunt, sed omnes. Nulla enim est διαςολὴ. Omnes peccavimus Rom. III. 21. Quod v. 12. & deinceps hoc loco docet Apostolus, quomodo peccatum omnes invaserit, omnesque peccato & morti obnoxii facti sint. Neque tan- tum pro nonnullis, sed pro omnibus mortuus est Christus 2. Cor. V. 15. factus propitiatio pro pecca- tis totius mundi 1. Joh. II. 2. quod ad v. 8. etiam agnovit Grotius. Nec mortuus solum est, ut pec- catores ad fidem perduci possent, nitentem præci- puè morte & resurrectione Christi; sed ut pro iis satisfaceret; non de resurrectione hic agitur, quâ niti fidem imprimis Grotius censet, sed de morte Christi: qui pro impiis ipse mortuus est, h.e. loco, & vice eorum, uti vox ὑπὲρ Gen. IV. 35. c. XXX. 2. Ex. VII. 1. Lev. XVII. 11. Job. II. 4. Es. XLIII. 4. Prov. XI. 8. Luc. XXII. 19. 20. Joh. X. 15. c. XI. 51. 52. c. XIII. 38. cap. XIV. 17. Act. XXI. 25. 1. Cor. I. 13. cap. V. 7. cap. XV. 29. 1. Thess. V. 9. 10. Phil. V. 13. 1. Pet. II. 27. c. IV. 1. 1. Joh. III. 16. Ebr. II. 9. ac- cipitur, & hic à Syro per vocem חלף commuta- tionem inferentem redditur: Quem sensum locus parallelus 2. Cor. V. 14. 15. confirmat, & allusio ad sacrificia, quæ surrogabantur vice prævaricatorum: Conf. Levit. XVII. 11. & quæ Socinismo Profligato adducta sunt p. 387. seqq. quæque tradidit Grotius ipse fid. Cathol. de Satisf. Christi.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die.

The Syriac reads for the unrighteous. In a very good sense. It is a great thing, what I have said. This is very rare, that anyone should be willing to meet death for a bad man. He speaks according to the opinion of the Philosophers and Jews. Seneca: I will help one who is about to perish, but so that I do not perish myself, unless I am to be the reward of a great man or a great thing. The same sense is in the letter of Epicurus to Pythocles, Philo: scarcely standing firm, knowing that they are about to become a loss on the road of profit.

The translation of the Syriac is not to be preferred nor admitted here, since the Greek reading is correct: for the Apostle exaggerates what he had said, that Christ died for us ungodly ones: for scarcely FOR A RIGHTEOUS MAN does one die, as the Vulgate has it. Which Jerome in Epist. ad Algasium quæst. VII. accepts as a matter of fact, as does also B. Luther, but because the Apostle is dealing with sinners and the ungodly, the person is more correctly understood. Grotius indeed wishes τάχα here to be easily, so that it may be opposed to μόλις. But Suidas has observed that τάχα also sometimes is perhaps, by chance, by accident, or by fortune. As the Vulgate also rendered it. For for a good man perhaps one might dare to die, whence by way of correction the Apostle subjoined this, for for a good man perhaps one even dares to die, that it happens indeed perhaps, but rarely, that one should die for a righteous man. Grotius admits that it is a concession. Furthermore, although τολμᾷν is to endure, as Grotius teaches from the examples τολμᾷ ἱκετεύειν, τολμᾷ ἀπέχεσθαι: it nevertheless connotes boldness, which the Syriac expressed as אמרח he was bold, and the Latin: Because it is a remarkable species of boldness to undergo death itself in the place of another.

Latin:

Vers. 7. μόλις γὰρ ὑπὲρ δικαίου τὶς ἀποθανεῖται.

Syrus legit ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων. Sensu optimo. Magnum est, quod dixi. Est hoc perrarum, ut quis pro homine malo mortem velit oppetere. Loquitur ex sententia Philosophorum ac Judæorum. Seneca: Succurram perituro, sed ut ipse non peream, nisi si futurus ero magni hominis aut magnæ rei merces. Idem sensus in epistola Epicuri ad Pythoclem, Philo: μόλις ἀνυπόσταμοι εἰδότες ἐπ’ ὀδοῦ λυσιτελοῦ παρανάλωμα γενησόμενοι.

Non præferenda nec admittenda hic Syri translatio, quum rectè se habeat Græca lectio: exaggerat enim Apostolus, quod dixerat Christum mortuum esse pro nobis impiis: vix enim PRO JUSTO quis moritur, ut vulg. habet. Quod Hieronym. in Epist. ad Algasium quæst. VII. de re accipit, ut & B. Luther. sed quia de peccatoribus & impiis agit Apostolus, persona rectiùs intelligitur. Vult quidem Grotius τάχα hic esse facilè, ut opponatur τῷ μόλις. Sed observavit Suidas, τάχα etiam quandoque esse fortasse, fortè, casu, vel fortuna. Uti reddidit quoque vulgatus. Nam pro bono forsitan quis audeat mori, unde per correctionem hæc subjunxit Apost. ὑπὲρ γὰρ ἀγαθῦ τάχα τὶς καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν, contingere quidem fortè, sed raro, ut quis pro justo moriatur. Συγχώρησιν esse admittit Grotius. Porrò τολμᾷν etsi sustinere sit, ut Grotius ab exemplis τολμᾷ ἱκετεύειν, τολμᾷ ἀπέχεσθαι docet: connotat tamen audacia, quam Syrus expressit אמרח ausus fuit, & Latinus: Quia audaciæ insignis species est, ipsam mortem alterius loco adire.

## 5:8
Ver. 8. But God commends His own love toward us.

This is the love of God preceding toward the whole human race indiscriminately. 'Commends', makes conspicuous, as above III. 5. He ascribes this to God, because He delivered up His own Son, He did not spare His own Son.

That while we were yet sinners Christ died for us.

He repeats with words slightly changed in the same sense what he had said, as something excellent and to be impressed upon the memory. we shall be saved by his life. By his life. Every life contains within itself the power of acting: and what should Christ rather do, to whom all power has been given, than deliver from evils those for whom he has done and suffered so much in order to restore them to the favor of the Father?

and not only. It is little that I have said, that he will deliver us from evils.

but also boasting in God through Jesus Christ. Supply: we are. As the Syrian received it, that is, we lean upon the promises of God made through Christ, and we trust that we shall furthermore obtain good, and eternal, and greatest things. See what is above 4. and Heb. III. 6.

Others more correctly explain it concerning the comparison of future glory and present grace, that the justified boast not only of that, but also of the state in which they now are. For previously a comparison had already been instituted by the Apostle between the liberation from wrath and destruction made through the death of Christ, and the heavenly glory of blessedness, which consists in God and the enjoyment of him. Now, therefore, for the reborn he claims not only boasting of the hope of glory, of which v. 2 and 3, or of a future state: but also boasting of present blessedness, as regards spiritual communion with God, and the enjoyment of God and a foretaste of eternal life. The Apostle had reasoned thus: if we have been reconciled to God, when we were enemies, through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled and freed from wrath, shall we be saved through his life, for the enjoyment of the glory of God, as many, that is, as make that reconciliation our own through faith: since we have been reborn into a living hope through his resurrection from the dead 1 Pet. I. 3. Compare Eph. II. 5. Theophylact explains these things thus: He seems to be speaking of the same matters, even though the meanings which are expressed by the comparisons are different, for he previously proposed that we were bound by sins, and then, by introducing justification through comparison, he inferred: when we were sinners, he justified us through death, and he will save those who are justified by much more. But now, repeating both the life and death of Christ, he explains the meaning again by comparing them in this way, saying: If we were reconciled then through the blood and death of Christ, shall we not be saved now in his life? He who did not even spare his own Son, who offered him up for the sake of reconciling us by his death, will he not even now, especially in his life, render us saved? Now, therefore, the Apostle attributes something more to the faithful, namely, that they not only have cause to boast in Christ of future blessedness, but that they also boast in this very thing, of present salvation, because they feel God to be propitious, and experience the love of God, and in it taste the mighty works of the world to come Heb. VI. 5. For concerning the present state, which the particle νῦν indicates, the faithful not only boast in the hope of the sons of God, but they can also boast in God himself and his actual communion, into which they have come through the reconciliation of his Son: which is the highest happiness, the highest glory, 1 John I. 3. 4.

through whom we have now received the reconciliation. Now, that is, even now we have received the reconciliation. Said metonymically, that is, we have received the effect of that reconciliation, the Holy Spirit, whom God would not have given to us unless we had been clearly restored to his favor. Here that second act is expressed more openly, of which we spoke above 10. The peace of subjects with a king is then perfect, when the subjects have obeyed those conditions which the king had prescribed.

There is no need for metonymy here. The discourse is not about the Holy Spirit, but about the reconciliation, by the act of which we are indeed made participants in justification, which, because we receive it through Christ when we apprehend his merit through faith, we can be certain that we shall be saved in him from destruction, and shall receive heavenly salvation, if we stand in faith and persevere.

ARTICLE IV. Illustration and Confirmation of the righteousness of faith from a comparison of the origin of injustice and justice. SECOND PART demonstrative. Proving justification through faith from the comparison of the first and second Adam.

Latin:

Vers. 8. συνίσησι δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην εἰς ἡμᾶς Θεός.

Hæc est dilectio Dei προηγουμένη erga omne humanum genus indistinctè. συνίσησι, conspicuam facit, ut supra III. 5. Deo hoc adscribit, quia is Filium suum tradidit, filio suo non pepercit.

ὅτι ἔτι ἀμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανε.

Repetit paulùm mutatis verbis sensu eodem quod dixerat, ut egregium & memoriâ infœgendum. σωθησόμεθα διὰ τῆς ζωῆς ἀυτῶν. Per vitam ipsius. Vita omnis vim agendi in se continet: & quid potius agat Christus, cui omnis potestas data est, quam ut malis eximat eos, pro quibus in gratiam patris re- ponendis tam multa fecit ac passus est?

ἡ μόνον δὲ. Parum est quod dixi, fore ut malis nos eximat.

ἀλλὰ καὶ καυχώμενοι ἐν τῷ θεῷ διὰ ἱησῦ χρισῦ. Supple sumus. Quomodo accepit Syrus, id est, Dei pollicitis per Christum factis innitimur, atque confidimus nos insuper bona & æterna, & maxima consecuturos. Vide quæ supra 4. & Hebr. III. 6.

Alii rectius explicant de comparatione gloriæ futuræ, & gratiæ præsentis, quod non solum de illa glorientur justificati, sed etiam de statu, in quo nunc sunt. Nam antea jam instituta ab Apostolo erat comparatio liberationis ab ira, & exitio per mortem Christi factæ, & gloriæ cælestis beatitudinis, quæ in Deo ejusque fruitione consistit. Jam ergò renatis vindicat non glorionem tantum de spe glo- riæ, de qua v. 2. & 3. vel de statu futuro: sed etiam gloriationem de præsenti beatitudine, quoad spiri- tualem cum Deo communionem, Deique fruitionem & πρόγευσιν æternæ vitæ. Nimirum ita college- rat Apostolus: si reconciliati sumus Deo, cum ini- mici essemus, per mortem Filii ejus, quantò magis reconciliati & ab ira liberati, servabimur per vi- tam ejus, ad fruitionem gloriæ Dei, quotquot sc. reconciliationem illam per fidem nostram faci- mus: Siquidem regeniti sumus in spem vivam per resurrectionem ejus ex mortuis 1. Petr. I. 3. Confer. Eph. II. 5. Theophylactus hæc ita explicat: Vide- tur de rebus iisdem habere sermonem, tametsi diver- sa sint sensa, quæ comparationibus exprimuntur, su- perius namque illud, esse nos scilicet peccatis obstri- ctos, proposuit, deinceps justificari subjiciens per com- parationem intulit, cum peccatores essemus, justifi- cavit per mortem, & longè magis justificatos salva- bit. Nunc vero & Christi vitam & mortem repe- tens, rursum comparando explicat sensum hoc pacto, inquiens: Tunc quidem conciliati per Christi san- guinem & mortem fuimus, nunc vero ejus in vita haud salvi efficiemur? Qui etiam nec proprio Filio pepercit, qui illum morte conciliandi nos gratia ob- tulit, nonne vel impræsentiarum maximè illius in vita salvos nos reddet? Jam ergò aliquid amplius fidelibus tribuit Apostolus, quod scilicet non mo- dò gloriari habeant in Christo de futurâ beatitu- dine, sed quod etiam eo ipso glorientur, de præ- senti salute, quod Deum sentiant propitium, & amorem Dei experiantur, atque in eo virtutes venturi seculi degustent Ebr. VI. 5. De præsenti enim statu, quem particula νῦν indicat, non solùm in spe filiorum Dei gloriantur fideles, sed etiam in Deo ipso & actuali ejus κοινωνίᾳ gloriari possunt, in quam per καταλλαγὴν Filii ejus devenerunt: quæ summa est felicitas, summa gloria, 1. Jo- han. I. 3. 4.

δι ἗ νῦν τὴν καταλλαγὴν ἐλάβομεν. Νῦν, id est, jam nunc accepimus reconciliationem. Di- ctum μετωνυμικῶς, id est, accepimus effectum istius reconci- liationis Spiritum Sanctum, quem Deus non dedisset nobis, nisi planè in gratiam suam repositis. Hic apertius expri- mitur actus ille secundus, de quo diximus supra 10. Pax sub- ditorum cum rege tunc perfecta est, cum subditi eis condi- tionibus paruere, quas rex præscripserat.

Nulla opus hic metonymia. Non de Spiritu S. sed de reconciliatione, quâ nempe ejus actu parti- cipes reddimur in justificatione sermo est, quam quia per Christum accipimus, cum per fidem ap- prehendimus meritum ejus, servatum nos iri in ipso ab exitio, & cœlestem accepturos salutem, si in fide stemus, ac perseveremus, certi esse possu- mus.

ARTICULUS IV. Illustratio & Confirmatio justitiæ fidei è collatione ortus injustitiæ & justitiæ. PARS SECUNDA ἀποδεικτικὴ. Probans justificationem per fidem à primi & secundi Adami comparatione.

## 5:9
we shall be saved by him from the wrath.

That is, we shall be snatched from the common destruction which awaits the ungodly. A similar expression 1 Thess. I. 10.

Again we warn that Justification does not consist in internal purity and righteousness, but in the remission of sins and the imputation of the Righteousness of Christ, without our works, which the Apostle taught in chapters III. and IV. For we are justified ἐν τῷ αἵματι in his blood, that is, by and on account of his blood, because through it justification has been acquired for us; therefore there is no need for a participation, and the blood of Christ is understood as apprehended by faith, or his bloody death endured in our place, or the satisfaction of Christ, insofar as we apply it to ourselves by faith; Thus the bloody death of Christ is proposed as the Object of faith, but faith is the organic cause of justification, as they call it.

Latin:

σωθησόμεθα δι αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς.

Id est, eripiemur à communi exitio, quod impios manet. Par locutio 1. Thess. I. 10.

Iterum monemus, Justificationem non in interna puritate, & justitia, sed in remissione peccatorum & imputatione Justitiæ Christi, sine operibus nostris consistere, quod cap. III. & IV. docuit Apostolus. Justificamur enim ἐν τῷ αἵματι in sanguine, id est, per & propter sanguinem ejus, quia per eundem nobis est acquisita justificatio; ideò opus non est μεταλήψει, & intelligitur sanguis Christi per fidem apprehensus, vel mors ejus cruenta nostri loco exantlata, vel satisfactio Christi, quatenus fide eam nobis applicamus; Ita mors cruenta Christi ut Objectum fidei proponitur, fides autem causa est justificationis organica, ut vocant.

## 5:10
Vers. 10. For if when we were enemies.

For all the ungodly are enemies to God Jac. IV. 4. They do not love God, 1 Joh. IV. 20.

we were reconciled to God through the death of his son.

That is, God, having been most grievously injured by us, when he gave his son to death for our sake, showed that he was not so far angry that he would not be willing to return into favor with us under good conditions. This is what καταλλάττεσθαι is here, not fully of course, but in part: to that effect as 2 Cor. V. 19.

That is, after God has come to terms with us, understand the conditions which we have accepted and to which we have complied. For often under the words of the first act, the second acts are understood. See similar things in John VI. 44, XVII. 6.

The Apostle has sufficiently taught that God was entirely angry with the human race on account of sin, and that all men were concluded under death and condemnation by the force of the law; but that we have been reconciled to God through the death of His Son is to be attributed to the immense love of God, revealed in the Gospel: Nor was that reconciliation made only in a certain respect, but fully, nay, most fully, as being through the death of the very Son of God, the only-begotten, consubstantial with the Father, the true and supreme God with the Father. It is impious to say that the reconciliation of the Son of God is not full or is only semi-full, or that we have been reconciled only in a certain respect through the death of the Son of God; nor was God reconciled to us only on the condition that He would be willing to return to favor with us under good conditions: but iniquity has been fully expiated, Dan. IX. 24, God has been made propitious to us entirely, if I may so speak. 1. John II. 2. We have been redeemed most perfectly by Christ, as being by a ransom far most precious, the blood of God Himself. Matt. XX. 28, Mark X. 45, 1 Tim. II. 6, 1 Pet. I. 18, Luke I. 68, Rom. III. 24, concerning which matter it was expressly treated in the Socinianism overthrown. And what are these good conditions here? Is it that by our own righteousness or good works we may finally obtain full reconciliation, and God may return to favor with us, and justify us? But the Apostle refutes this by design, and has taught that we are justified by grace, through the redemption of Christ, by faith alone. If by grace, not by works, otherwise grace would not be grace, Romans XI. 6; if through the redemption of Christ, then not by our righteousness, otherwise it could not be attributed solely to the ransom and redemption of Christ. If by faith apprehending the payment made for us by Christ, then not by the intervention of our own satisfaction or righteousness. We have not been redeemed, reconciled, or our sins expiated under a condition, but simply, most perfectly, most fully: as far as merit and acquisition are concerned, even if as far as actual fruit and application are concerned, faith is needed: which indeed is nothing other than the appropriation of that expiation and satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ. Because if one died for all, this is the same (in the judgment of God) as if all had died. 2 Cor. V. 15.

For one will hardly die for a righteous man) It is a concession. You may find some among the Gentiles and Jews who expose themselves to dangers for a good man: as Jonathan for David: as Damon and Pythias in Valerius Maximus IV. 7. Lactantius V. 10. For why are those Pythagorean friends praised by you, of whom one gave himself to the tyrant for the other in the same death, and the other, at the appointed time, when his sponsor was already being led away, made his presence known and freed him by his intervention, whose virtue would not be held in such glory, because one was willing to die for a friend, the other even for his pledge, if they were thought to be fools. 'Perhaps' here is 'easily', the opposite of that which preceded 'scarcely': such is that:

Perhaps even the blameless are blamed.

And 'to dare' is not to be bold, but to endure, just as 'he dares to supplicate', 'he dares to abstain', frequently among the Greeks.

Latin:

Vers. 10. εἰ γὰρ ἐχθροὶ ὄντες.

Nam impii omnes Deo sunt inimici Jac. IV. 4. Deum non amant, 1. Joh. IV. 20.

κατηλλάγημεν τῷ Θεῷ διὰ τοῦ θανάτο τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ.

Id est, Deus à nobis gravissimè læsus, cum filium suum nostri causa morti dedit, ostendit se non eo usque iratum, ut non sub bonis conditionibus in gratiam redire nobiscum vellet. Id hic est καταλλάττεσθαι, non plenè scilicet, sed κατάτι: ad illum effectum ut 2. Cor. V. 19.

Id est, postquam Deus nobiscum venit ad conditiones subintellige quas nos accepimus iisque paruimus. Nam sæpe sub verbis actus primi intelliguntur actus secundi. Similia vide Joh. VI. 44. XVII. 6.

Omninò iratum Deum generi humano fuisse propter peccatum, omnesque homines conclusos fuisse sub morte, & condemnatione vi legis, Apostolus satis docuit; Quod verò reconciliati simus Deo, per mortem Filii ejus, immensæ Dei dilectioni acceptum ferendum est, in Evangelio patefactæ: Neque tantùm καταλλαγὴ illa secundum quid facta est, sed plenè, imò plenissimè, utpote per mortem ipsiusmet FiliiDei unigeniti ὁμουσίη cum Patre, veri & summi cum Patre Dei. Impium est ἄπτσμα non plenam vel semiplenam esse reconciliationem Filii Dei, vel secundum quid tantum reconciliatos nos esse per mortem Filii Dei; Neque ad quid illum esse tantum reconciliatus est Deus, ut sub bonis conditionibus in gratiam nobiscum redire vellet: sed expiata est plenè iniquitas Dan. IX. 24. propitius nobis factus est ex asse, ut ita loquar, Deus. 1. Joh. II. 2. redempti sumus perfectissimè à Christo, utpote λύτρῳ longè pretiosissimo sanguine ipsius Dei. Matth. XX. 28. Marc. X. 45. 1. Tim. II. 6. 1. Pet. I. 18. Luc. I. 68. Rom. III. 24. quà de re ex professo actum in Socinismo profligato. Et quænam hic bonæ illæ conditiones? an ut justitiâ nostrâ, vel operibus bonis consequamur demum plenam reconciliationem, & in gratiam nobiscum redeat Deus, nosque justificet? At hoc ex instituto refellit Apostolus, & ex gratia, per redemptionem Christi, sola fide nos justificari docuit. Si ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia Roman. XI. 6. si per ἀπολύτρωσιν & redemptionem Christi, non ergò nostrâ justitiâ, alioqui λύτρω & ἀπολυτρώσει Christi unicè id tribui non posset. Si ex fide apprehendente solutionem Christi pro nobis præstitam, ergo non interventu propriæ nostræ satisfactionis, aut justitiæ. Non sub conditione nos redempti, reconciliati, aut peccata nostra expiata sunt, sed simpliciter, perfectissimè, plenissimè: quantum ad meritum & acquisitionem, etsi quantùm ad actualem fructum & applicationem fide opus sit: quæ vero nihil aliud est, quam appropriatio illius expiationis & satisfactionis ac reconciliationis Christi. Quia si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, idem hoc est (in judicio Dei) ac si omnes mortui essent. 2. Cor. V. 15.

ὑπὲρ γὰρ ἀγαθῦ τις καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν) Est συγχώρησις. Aliquos in gentibus & Judæis invenias, qui pro viro bono se periculis objiciant: ut Jonathan pro Davide: ut Damon & Pythias apud Valerium Maximum IV. 7. Lactantius v. 10. Quid enim illi familiares Pythagoræi laudantur à vobis, quorum alter se tyranno eadem mortis pro altero dedit, alter ad præstitutum tempus, cum jam sponsor ejus duce- retur, præsentiam sui fecit, eumque interventu suo liberavit, quorum virtus in tanta gloria non haberetur, quod alter pro amico, alter etiam pro fide mori voluit, si stulti putarentur. τάχα hic est facile, oppositum ei, quod præcessit μόλις: tale illud:

τάχα μὲν καὶ ἀναίτιοι αἰτιῶντα.

Et τολμᾷν non est audere, sed sustinere, sicut τολμᾷ ἱκετεύειν, τολμᾷ ἀπέχεσθαι, frequenter apud Græcos.

## 5:12
Verse 12. Therefore.

Since these things are so, as we have said. For therefore is not rendering the cause of the things said before, but is interpreting an ancient mystery from the things said before as if they were certain: but this is it here: that the things which were done through Adam, their opposites ought to have been done through Christ. He explains the same in 1 Cor. XV. 22.

Although you may render it thus: since these things are as we have said: namely that such is the fruit of justification by faith; nevertheless the comparison of the first and second Adam, to which it proceeds, can contribute to the further confirmation of justification by faith: because just as from the first Adam arose the perpetual restlessness of conscience, so through the second has been restored peace and tranquility, which it is not permitted to enjoy, except insofar as through faith we are rendered partakers of his righteousness by divine imputation out of grace, just as we have been made partakers of the disobedience and sin of the first man, by the imputation of the same guilt, by the power of divine justice.

ὥσπερ δι ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπυ ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε.

By Κόσμον here understand the human race, to whom Adam first gave an example of sinning. Why did he not say Eve? Because the Hebrews are not accustomed to trace genealogies through women.

Not only by imitation, which was the heresy of Pelagius, did the sin of Adam reach his descendants, but also by carnal propagation, whence it is called Original sin: as also by the imputation of Adam's transgression. Namely, the sin of one man came into the world, and upon the whole human race, both because in one man we all sinned, as the Apostle will teach a little later, and because, the habitual condition having been contracted through the apostasy of Adam, when he fell from his primordial rectitude, that primordial rectitude and integrity could not be propagated to his descendants, but corruption and obliquity were propagated, into which the concreated rectitude degenerated: and he begat children not in the image and likeness of God, which he lost, but in his own image and likeness, which he contracted through sin, Gen. V. 3.

Καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος.

That is, the diminution of powers, the cause of weariness, pains, diseases, and of the death that would follow from these, as we said regarding Genesis. But someone might say that immortality was not promised to Adam, even if he had obeyed God, and by nature he was χοϊκὸς, made into a living soul, not into a life-giving spirit, 1 Cor. XV. 45. I grant it, but if he had obeyed the divine precept, whether he would have remained in Paradise forever, or whether something greater would have been ordained for him thereafter, is both uncertain to us and was uncertain to him. Certain Hebrews think it would have come to pass that after a very long and happy life, God would have freed his soul from his body without any trouble or pain, which they call not מות, that is, to die, but נשיקה or the kiss of peace. Others think that what happened to Enoch and Elijah would have happened to him: But let others judge of this matter: while we hold that which the wise Hebrew says, that by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, II. 24. And what the son of Sirach says, that through a woman the beginning of sin was made, and from that it is that we die, XXV. 33.

By θάνατον is understood not the diminution of powers, the cause of death, but death itself or mortality: For why should we depart from the proper meaning of the word? Grotius, however, mixes in many falsehoods besides.

(1.) That immortality was not promised to Adam, even if he had obeyed God. For just as God had threatened death to Adam, and that eternal, if he did not obey, Gen. II. 17, so by the force of contraries, if he had persisted in integrity and obedience, he would have attained eternal life and celestial and blessed immortality.

(2.) That he was mortal by nature, because he was χοϊκὸς,

made εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν [into a living soul] 1 Cor. 15:45. But it is one thing to have been χοϊκὸν [earthly] & earthly, and another to have been mortal: because he was earthly by reason of his origin, from the earth, and breath in the earth, but not by reason of mortality, because he was created ἐπ' ἀφθαρσία [for incorruption] Wis. 2:13. It is likewise one thing to have been made εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν [into a living soul] and an animal life subject to earthly necessities, and another to a life corruptible and obnoxious to earthly calamities, miseries, and death: which things finally followed the fall and had no place before the fall; concerning which see what we said in Vol. IV, Syst. Theol., last question, toward the end. However, that opposition of the second Adam, who was made εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν [into a life-giving spirit], is correct, because it respects the hypostatic union and communication, by virtue of which the second man, Christ, according to the flesh or human nature, is a participant of the life-giving Spirit and has the power of vivifying: which is able to vivify us to eternal life: so that we who have only animal life from Adam, may obtain eternal life from Christ; we who are procreated earthly from the earthly, may be made heavenly from the Lord from heaven, so much so that we may also obtain from the latter spiritual bodies, which we receive as animal bodies from the former. And since the diminution of powers had no place outside of sin, it must be confessed that man was not mortal by his own nature. (3.) Is it uncertain to us whether, if Adam had obeyed the divine precept, he would have remained in Paradise forever, or whether something greater would have been ordained for him thereafter? But how is this uncertain, if indeed man was created not for this earthly, but for another heavenly life? And since death entered into the world by the envy of the Devil, but before that there was not in nature φάρμακον ὀλέθρου [a poison of destruction] or ruin in the world Wis. 1:24, nor would death, which is the dissolution of soul and body, have had a place, nor could men have remained in Paradise, as it could by no means be capable of the whole multitude of the human race, if none of them had been translated into heaven: whence it is altogether consistent that what happened to Enoch and Elijah would have happened to others also after their life was spent. (4.) That this was uncertain to Adam: But what was by no means uncertain to him, since Adam was created in the image and likeness of God ἐν ἐπιγνώσει [in knowledge], in the knowledge and wisdom of divine things, he could by no means be ignorant of it; and created in true justice and holiness, ἐπ' ἀφθαρσία [for incorruption], he easily perceived that immortality was given to him, not that he should live eternally in Paradise, but that, having performed obedience to God, he would at length be raised to a heavenly and blessed immortality: indeed, from the threat of death for disobedience, it was easy to conclude that eternal life would be granted to the obedient. Concerning which there is not easily any doubt in anyone, except this Sceptic of ours. Compare what is said in the Commentary on Genesis, on chapters II and III, and in Vol. IV, Syst. Theol.

Καὶ ὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπως ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν [And so death passed unto all men]. It reached all the descendants of Adam, by the very law of origin, through which their bodies, drawing their substance and qualities from such a body, could not but be obnoxious to all the evils we have mentioned. For with that benefit removed through the tree of life, the human body remained like that of other living creatures, perishable and fragile like a pot made from clay. In this sense the Hebrews say that death came to his descendants from the sin of Adam, as the Chaldean Paraphrast on Ruth 4 and Ecclesiastes 7, the writer of the Life of Moses more than once, Jarchi, Hana Barhaina in Beresith Rabba. Cyril against the Anthropomorphites, chapter VIII: οἱ γεγονότες ἐξ ἀυτᾶ ὡς ἀπὸ φθαρτῶ φθαρτοὶ γεγόνασιν [those who are born of him, as from a corruptible one, have become corruptible]: see also what follows there.

Grotius assumes that the human body, outside the use of the tree of life, was by its own nature perishable and fragile like a pot made from clay. But we have expressly refuted that in the places cited against the Pelagians, Socinians,

Baptists, and Calixtines. We do not wish to do what is already done. However, they were not procreated mortal from mortals after the fall by the mere law of origin, but by the power of divine justice; and not without the guilt of sin, but on account of sin; for it is more than the punishment of sin, and it is alien to the justice of God to afflict with death those who are entirely devoid of sin. Therefore the Apostle adds expressly that all men have sinned: and he teaches that this is the cause why death διη̃λθεν [passed through] unto all men.

ἐφ᾽ ᾦ πάντες ἥμαρτον [in whom all have sinned].

It is frequent for the Hebrews to use a metonymy, saying sin for punishment, and to sin for to undergo punishment: whence also, as the figure proceeds further by metalepsis, those are said to חטא [sin] who bear some evil even without guilt, as Gen. 31:37 and Job 6:24, where חטא is translated by δυσπραγεῖν [to fare ill]. Ἐφ᾽ ᾦ [in whom] here is by whom, just as ἐν [in] is taken with the dative, Luke 5:5, Acts 3:16, 1 Cor. 8:11, Heb. 9:17. Chrysostom on this passage: ἐκείνου πεσόντος καὶ οἱ μὴ φαγόντες ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου γεγόνασιν παρ᾽ ἐκείνου πάντες θνητοί [he having fallen, even those who did not eat from the tree have become, through him, all mortal]. After these words follows a long parenthesis here up to verse 8, where the discourse returns to what was begun. The Greeks call this kind of speaking hyperbaton, and it is usually much softened if the words or the sense placed before are repeated with the addition of 'I say' or 'therefore', as below in verse 12, that is, as I had begun to say.

That metonymy is wrongly introduced here: since one must not depart from the literal property, and the Apostle speaks accurately and distinctly of guilt and punishment, of sin and death; and does not interchange these: but a metalepsis is added much worse, and it is imagined that some evil is inflicted by God without guilt: because neither is any example of that metalepsis given (for an inspection of the passages Gen. XXXI. 37, Job VI. 24 shows that such a μετάληψιν does not occur in them) and it is most alien to divine justice to inflict evil without guilt and merit: but the Apostolic passage is most basely depraved, since it is the Apostle's purpose in it to explain how death drew its origin from the sin of Adam, not that he himself was made subject to death only on account of sin; but that all men are subjected to death on account of sin: ἐφ᾽ ᾦ πάντες ἥμαρτον, which some render causally, 'in that all have sinned,' by which agreement the sin of all is constituted the cause of death, as regards all, and not merely the sin of Adam: Grotius explains it, 'THROUGH WHOM,' namely that through Adam all ἥμαρτον: which sounds and must be rendered, 'HAVE SINNED,' (for the Apostle had already said in the preceding words that all are subject to evils and death, and indeed through Adam) and thus death passed unto all men, where Grotius, having in vain abandoned the propriety of the word, understands by death pains and diseases and various evils, although we readily concede that these are not excluded. Some render ἐφ᾽ ᾦ as 'IN WHOM,' namely Adam, that in him all have sinned; because as we were all created in him in the image of God, so he sinning, we sinned in him, as in a common stock, since we were all in his loins, as most of the ancients have explained: concerning which see Theol. Apost. Rom. at this passage. B. Hulsemann proves this explanation in his annotations on the δυσκέπτοις: That the relative, ᾦ, in ἐφ᾽ ᾦ in this place is of the masculine gender and denotes the person of Adam, in whom all his posterity have sinned, and is not neuter, nor does it denote the merit of death or condemnation, is persuaded by 1. the opposition between the individual Adam and Christ, in this verse, and verses 14, 15, 16, etc., where always one is opposed to one. 2. because such a species of sin is understood, which, apart from the revealed law of Moses, was not reckoned as sin, which species must necessarily be understood not of actual sins, but of original sin alone, as the passages c. I. 32, c. II. 14, 15, c. VII. 7 & 9 show. 3. because this species of sin is expressly distinguished from actual transgression in v. 14, in so far as it is committed by the deliberation and destined will of individual persons. Wherefore not only have the Netherlanders here departed from the version of Luther, and they translate that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ as 'in which they all have sinned,' but they also render the reason: because the Apostle in a similar matter, when he disputes about the original causes of death and human life in 1 Cor. 15:22, takes the particle ἐν for the causal διὰ as in this chapter 5:16, 17, 18, 19. Concerning ἐπὶ used causally, see Mark 2:4, Phil. 1:3, Heb. 9:17, 2 Cor. 1:4, ch. 7:4, 1 Cor. 1:2, Matt. 15:33, Mark 8:4, and ἐν ᾧ in Rom. 8:3. And Socinus himself admits in book 4 de Servat. c. 6, p. 480 in Sibrandus, that that ἐπὶ in v. 14, ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας, ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι, must be explained first subjectively, but the other causally. Our Luther indeed translates it causally, not subjectively, 'dieweil sie alle gesuͤndiget haben' [because they all have sinned], but he supposed not only the stain contracted from Adam, but also the participation in the actual transgression of Adam, as is evident from his gloss to v. 18. and 10. B. Er. Schmidius: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. In whom all (men) have sinned. Namely, in that one man Adam. For ἐπὶ is often used for ἐν. Hesiod, Works: Μέτρον δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστον. Moderation is best in all things. Pindar, Olymp. 1: Ἐπ᾽ ἄλλοισιν ἄλλοι μεγάλοι. Some excel in some things, others in others. Thus Matt. 18:5, Rom. 4:18, 5:2, Phil. 1:3, etc. And from this guilt no man can exempt himself, so that whoever dares to do this becomes a blasphemer. 1 John 1:10. Grotius did not prove that a hyperbaton must be admitted here. Others more correctly posit an anantapodoton: because it is clear that the apodosis is missing for the protasis in verse 12, even though it can be gathered from v. 18.

Latin:

Vers 12. διὰ τῦτο.

Hæc cum ita se habeant, ut diximus. Est enim לכן διὰ τῦτο, non reddentis causam ante dictorum, sed ex ante di- ctis tanquam certis mysterium vetus interpretantis : Id au- tem hic est : quæ per Adamum gesta sunt, eorum contraria debuisse geri per Christum. Idem explicat 1. Cor. XV. 22.

Quanquam sic reddas : hæc cum ita se habeant ut diximus : nimirum quod talis sit justificationis per fidem fructus; nihilominus ea ad quam acce- dit collatio primi & secundi Adami ad ulteriorem confirmationem justificationis per fidem facere potest : quia ut à primo Adamo orta est perpetua inquietudo conscientiæ, ita per secundum reddita est pax & tranquillitas, quâ frui non licitum, nisi quatenus per fidem imputatione divinâ ex gratiâ justitiæ ejus participes reddimur, quemadmodum participes facti sumus inobedientiæ & peccati pri- mi hominis, imputatione culpæ ejusdem, vi divi- næ justitiæ.

ὥσπερ δι ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπυ ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε.

Κόσμον hic intellige genus humanum, cui peccandi exem- plum primus dedit Adamus. Cur non Evam dixit ? quia Hebræi non solent γενεαλογεῖν per fœminas.

Non tantum per imitationem, quæ Pelagii erat hæresis, peccatum Adami attigit posteros, sed etiam per carnalem propagationem, unde Originale peccatum dictum: ut & per transgressionis Adami- cæ imputationem. Nimirum venit in mundum, & super totum genus humanum peccatum unius hominis, tum quia in uno homine peccavimus omnes, ut paulò post Apostolus docebit, tum quia contracta per apostasiam Adami conditione ha- bituali, quum à primæva rectitudine defecit, non potuit primæva illa rectitudo & integritas in po- steros propagari, sed propagata fuit corruptio, & obliquitas, in quam degeneravit concreata recti- tudo: genuitque liberos non ad Dei imaginem & similitudinem, quam deperdidit, sed ad imaginem & similitudinem suam, quam per peccatum con- traxit Gen. V. 3.

Καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος.

Id est, virium imminutio, causa lassitudinis, dolorum, morborum & ex his secuturæ mortis, ut ad Genesin dixi- mus. Atqui immortalitas Adamo, etiamsi Deo paruisset, dicat aliquis, promissa non erat, & natura erat χοϊκὸς, factus εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν non εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν, 1. Cor. XV. 45. Fa- teor, at, si præcepto divino paruisset, mansissetne in Para- diso semper, an majus aliquid deinde de eo constitutum fuisset, & nobis incertum est, & ipsi incertum fuit. Hebræi quidam existimant futurum fuisse, ut post vitam felicem longissimam Deus ei sine ulla molestia ac dolore animum è corpore liberaret, quod ipsi non מות, id est, mori, sed נשיקה aut osculum pacis vocant. Alii putant eventurum ei fuisse id, quod Enocho & Eliæ evenit: Sed de hac re alii judicent: dum illud teneamus, quod ait sapiens Hebræus, diaboli in- vidia mortem in mundum intrasse, II. 24. Et quod Sirachi- des, per mulierem initium factum peccandi, & inde esse quod moriamur XXV. 33.

Per θάνατον non virium imminutio, causa mor- tis, sed mors ipsa vel mortalitas intelligitur: Cur enim à proprietate vocis discedamus? Admiscet autem præterea falsa plurima Grotius.

(1.) Immortalitatem Adamo etiamsi Deo paruisset, promissam non fuisse. Nam uti mortem Deus minatus erat Adamo, eamque ætérnam, si non paruerit. Gen. II. 17. ita vi contrariorum, si perstitisset in in- tegritate & obedientia, vitam æternam & immor- talitatem cœlestem ac beatam consequutus fuisset.

(2.) Naturâ mortalem fuisse, quia χοϊκὸς erat,

factus εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν 1. Cor. XV. 45. sed aliud est χοϊκὸν & terrenum fuisse, aliud mortalem: quia ter- renus fuit ratione originis, de terra, & flatus in ter- ra, non autem ratione mortalitatis, quia ἐπ' ἀφθαρ- σία conditus fuit Sap. II. 13. Aliud item est factum fuisse εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν in animam viventem, & vi- tam animalem terrenis necessitatibus subditam, aliud ad vitam corruptibilem, & terrenis calamita- tibus, miseriis ac morti obnoxiam: quæ demum lapsum sequuta sunt nec ante lapsum locum ha- buere; quo de vid. quæ Tom. IV. Syst. Theol. quæst. ultim. sub finem diximus. Oppositio tamen illa Adami secundi, qui factus est εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν in Spiritum vivificantem recte se habet, quia respicit unionem & communicationem hypostaticam, vi cujus secundus homo Christus secundum carnem vel natu- ram humanam Spiritus vivificantis particeps est, & vim vivificandi habet: quæ nos ad vitam æternam vivificare valet: ut qui ab Adamo vitam animalem tantum habemus, a Christo vitam æternam conse- quamur; qui a terreno terreni procreamur, a Domi- no de cælo cælestes efficiamur, adeo ut etiam corpora nostra, quæ ab illo ψυχικὰ animalia accipi- mus, ab hoc πνευματικὰ spiritualia consequamur. Et quum virium imminutio nulla extra peccatum lo- cum habuerit, non fuisse hominem natura sua mortalem fatendum erit. (3.) Incertum nobis esse, an si præcepto divino paruisset Adam, mansissetne in Paradiso semper, an majus aliquid deinde de eo con- stitutum fuisset? Qui vero hoc incertum, siquidem primo conditus fuerit homo non ad hanc terre- nam, sed ad alteram cælestem vitam? Et quum Dia- boli invidia mors in mundum intraret, antea vero non fuerit in natura φάρμακον ὀλέθρου venenum per- ditionis vel exitii in mundo Sap. I. 24. neque mors, quæ animæ & corporis solutio est, locum habuisset, neque in Paradiso manere homines potuissent, ut- pote qui capax minime esse poterat universæ mul- titudinis generis humani, si nemo eorum transla- tus in cælum fuisset: unde omnino consentaneum est, id quod Enocho & Eliæ evenit, aliis etiam post transactam vitam eventurum fuisse. (4.) Incertum id Adamo fuisse: Quod vero minime incertum ei fuit, siquidem Adam conditus ad imaginem & si- militudinem Dei ἐν ἐπιγνώσει, in cognitione & sa- pientia rerum divinarum, ignorare id minime po- terat; & in justitia & sanctitate vera, ἐπ' ἀφθαρσία creatus, immortalitatem sibi datam, non ut æter- num in Paradiso viveret, sed ut præstita Deo obe- dientia tandem ad cælestem & beatam immortali- tatem eveheretur, facile sentiebat: imo ex commi- natione mortis ob inobedientiam, concludere in promptu erat, obedienti vitam æternam concessum iri. De quo non facile penes ullum dubium est, præter hunc Scepticum nostrum. Conf. quæ & Comment. in Genesin, ad c. II. & III, & Tom. IV. Syst. Theol. dicta.

Καὶ ὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπως ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν. Pervenit ad omnes Adami posteros, ipsa lege originis, per quam non poterant non omnibus, quæ diximus, malis ob- noxia esse corpora, ex tali corpore substantiam suam & qua- litates ducentia. Sublato enim beneficio illo per arborem vitæ, manebat corpus humanum quale cæterorum animan- tium, caducum ac fragile velut testa ex humo facta. Hoc sensu ajunt Hebræi mortem ex peccato Adami venisse ad po- steros ejus, ut Paraphrastes Chaldæus Ruth. IV. & Ecclesia- stæ VII. Scriptor vitæ Mosis plus semel, Jarchi, Hana Barhai- na in Beresith Rabba. Cyrillus adversus Anthropomorphi- tas cap. VIII. οἱ γεγονότες ἐξ ἀυτᾶ ὡς ἀπὸ φθαρτῶ φθαρτοὶ γεγόνασιν: vide & quæ ibi sequuntur.

Assumit Grotius, corpus humanum extra usum arboris vitæ natura sua caducum ac fragile fuisse veluti testam ex humo factam. Sed id locis citatis ex professo profligavimus in Pelagianis, Socinianis,

Raptistis, & Calixtinis. Nolumus actum agere. Non autem post lapsum ipsa originis lege mortales ex mortalibus procreati sunt, sed vi justitiae divinae; neque citra culpam peccati, sed propter peccatum; plus enim est poena peccati, & alienum est a justitia Dei, cum morte afficere eos, qui peccati prorsus expertes sunt. Ideo addit Apostolus diserte, quod omnes homines peccarint: atq; hanc causa esse, quod διη̃λθεν pertransiit in omnes homines mors, docet.

ἐφ᾽ ᾦ πάντες ἥμαρτον.

Frequens est μετωνυμία Hebraeis dicere peccatum pro poena, & peccare pro poenam subire: unde & procedente longius figura per μετάληψιν חטא sive peccare dicuntur qui malum aliquod etiam sine culpa ferunt, ut Gen. XXXI. 37. & Job. VI. 24. ubi חטא vertitur per δυσπραγεῖν. Ἐφ᾽ ᾦ hic est per quem, quomodo ἐν cum Dativo sumitur, Luc. V. 5. Act. III. 16. 1. Cor. VIII. 11. Hebr. IX. 17. Chrysostomus hoc loco: ἐκείνου πεσόντος καὶ οἱ μὴ φαγόντες ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου γεγόνασιν παρ᾽ ἐκείνου πάντες θνητοί. Post haec verba sequitur longa hic παρένθεσις ad comma usque 8. ubi reditur ad coeptum sermonem. Id genus dicendi Graeci ὑπέρβατον vocant, soletque id multum emolliri, si voces eadem aut sensus ante positus repetatur addito inquam vel ergo, ut infra v. 12., id est, ut dicere coeperam.

Metonymia illa hic male invehitur: quum a proprietate literae discedendum non sit, & Apostolus accurate ac distincte loquatur de culpa & poena, de peccato & morte; non vero haec commutet: longe pejus autem metalepsis additur, & malum aliquod sine culpa divinitus infligi fingitur: quia nec ullum metalepseos istius exemplum datur (in illis autem Gen. XXXI. 37. Job. VI. 24. talem μετάληψιν non occurrere inspectio locorum datur) & a justitia divina alienissimum est malum infligere sine culpa, & merito: pessime autem Apostolicus locus depravatur, cum in eo Apostolo propositum sit exponere, quomodo mors a peccato Adami originem traxerit, non quod tantum morti obnoxius ipse factus sit propter peccatum; sed quod omnes homines morti propter peccatum subjiciantur: ἐφ᾽ ᾦ πάντες ἥμαρτον, quod aliqui reddunt causaliter, eo quod omnes peccarint, quo pacto peccatum omnium causa mortis constituitur, quoad omnes, non vero tantum peccatum Adami: Grotius id exponit, PER QUEM, quod nempe per Adamum omnes ἥμαρτον: quod sonat & reddendum est, PECCARUNT, (nam quod omnes malis & morti obnoxii sint & quidem per Adamum, verbis antecedentibus jam dixerat Apostolus) & sic in omnes homines mors pertransiit, ubi nequicquam relicta vocis proprietate Grotius per mortem dolores & morbos & mala varia intelligit, etsi ea non excludi facile annuamus. Nonnulli ἐφ᾽ ᾦ reddunt IN QUO, Adamo, sc. quod in ipso peccarint omnes; quia ut in ipso omnes ad imaginem Dei conditi eramus, ita ipso peccante, in ipso peccavimus, tanquam in communi stipite omnes, quum omnes in lumbis ejus fuerimus, ut plerique veterum exposuere: quo de vid. Theol. Apost. Rom. ad h. l. Probant hanc explicationem B. Hulsemann. in annot. δυσκέπτοις: Relativum, ᾦ, ἐφ᾽ ᾦ hoc loco esse masculini generis & notare Adami personam, in qua omnes posteri peccaverunt, non neutrius neque notare meritum mortis seu condemnationis suadent 1. oppositio inter individuum Adami & Christi, hoc versu, & 14. 15. 16. seqq. ubi semper unus uni opponitur. 2. quia talis species peccati intelligitur, quae citra revelatam legem Mosis, non aestimata fuit pro peccato, qua species utique non de actualibus peccatis, sed de solo originali necessario intelligenda est, ut dictorum c. I. 32. c. II. 14. 15. c. VII. 7. & 9. 3. quia haec species peccati expresse distinguitur a transgressione actuali v. 14. in quantum videl. deliberatione & destinata voluntate singulorum individuorum committitur. Quamobrem non solum Belgae hic discesse- runt à versione Lutheri, & illud ἐφ᾽ ᾧ vertunt, in wel- chem sie alle gesuͤndiget haben, sed rationem etiam reddunt: quia Apostolus in simili materia, quando de causis originalibus mortis & vitæ humanæ disputat 1. Cor. XV. 22. particulam ἐν sumat pro causali διὰ ut hoc cap. V. 16. 17. 18. 19. De ἐπὶ causaliter usurpato vide Marc. II. 4. Phil. I. 3. Ebr. IX. 17. 2. Cor. I. 4. c. VII. 4. 1. Cor. I. 2. Matth. XV. 33. Marc. VIII. 4. & ἐν ᾧ Rom. VIII. 3. Et fatetur Socinus ipse l. 4. de Ser- vat. c. 6. p. apud Sibrandum 480. illud ἐπὶ v. 14. ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας, ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι primum quidem subjectivè, alterum verò causaliter esse expo- nendum. Lutherus quidem noster causaliter non sub- jectivè vertit, dieweil sie alle gesuͤndiget haben, sed supposuit non solum labem contractam ex Adamo, ve- rum etiam participationem de actuali transgressione Adami, ut patet ex glossa ejus ad v. 18. & 10. B. Er. Schmidius: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. In quo omnes (homines) peccarunt. Nempe in uno illo homine Adamo. Nam ἐπὶ, pro ἐν, sæpe usurpatur. Hesiod. ἔργ: Μέτρον δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστον. Modus in omni- bus rebus optimus est. Pindar. Olymp. á. Ἐπ᾽ ἄλ- λοισιν ἄλλοι μεγάλοι. Alii in aliis excellunt. Sic Matth. 18. 5. Rom. 4. 18. 5. 2. Phil. 1. 3. &c. Atque ab hoc reatu nemo hominum sese eximere potest, ut qui hoc ausit, blasphemus fiat. 1. Joh. 1. 10. Hyperbaton hic admittendum esse non probavit Grotius. Alii ἀνανταπόδοτον rectius statuunt: quia ἀπόδοσιν omissam esse ad πρότασιν vers. 12. in aprico est, etsi ea è v. 18. colligi possit.

## 5:13
Verse 13. ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ. 'For until the law sin was in the world.' A 'men' is understood here. He gives the reason why he said all men were dead because they drew their origin from Adam, because no law was given to them which threatened the penalty of death to those who transgressed. He does not deny that there was sin, such as that of Cain, of the men who were in the time of the flood, of the citizens of Sodom, of the brothers of Joseph, of Pharaoh, who was contemporary with Moses, and of others. Ἄχρι νόμου, that is, before the law of Moses, which assigns death to grave crimes.

ἁμαρτία δὲ ἐκ ἐλλογεῖται μὴ ὄντος νόμου. 'But sin is not imputed when there is no law.' In the manuscript it is ἐκ ἐλλογεῖτο: and both the Syriac and Theophylact read it no differently. Paul also uses the verb ἐλλογεῖν in that letter to Philemon. The correct phrasing would have been ἐνελογεῖτο: but we have other examples of a missing augment. The sense is: It was not imputed in such a way that it could be called the cause of death, namely in individual men. For God did not then punish individual men, but whole generations of men, and in them even children guilty of no committed act. But the law says concerning individuals, 'let him die the death.' Namely, with God himself about to inflict death, if judges were to cease or were ignorant of it.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ. Subauditur hic μὲν. Causam reddit, cur dixerit omnes homines ideò mortuos, quod ex Adamo ortum traherent, quia lex nulla illis data erat, quæ transgredientibus mortis pœnam minaretur. Non negat fuisse peccatum, ut Caini, hominum, qui fuere diluvii tempore, Sodomæ civium, fra- trum Josephi, Pharaonis, qui Mosi coævus fuit & aliorum. Ἄχρι νόμου, id est, ante legem Mosis, quæ gravibus facinori- bus pœnam ascribit, mortem.

ἁμαρτία δὲ ἐκ ἐλλογεῖται μὴ ὄντος νόμου. In Manuscripto ἐκ ἐλλογεῖτο: nec aliter legit & Syrus & Theophylactus. Verbum ἐλλογεῖν etiam in illa ad Philemo- nem Paulus usurpat. Recta locutio fuerat ἐνελογεῖτο: Sed omissi augmenti habemus & alia exèmpla. Sensus est: Non in id imputabatur ut causa possit dici mortis, nempe in sin- gulis hominibus. Non enim singulos tunc homines Deus puniit, sed genera tota hominum & in illis etiam pueros nullius commissi reos. At lex de singulis dicit morte mo- riatur. Nempe Deo ipso mortem inflictu͵ro, si cessarent aut rem ignorarent judices.

## 5:14
V. 14. ἀλλ᾽ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μώσεως. 'Nevertheless,' he says, 'death exercised its power over individual men from the age of Adam to the age of Moses,' that is, for nearly two thousand five hundred years, not a short space of time. βασιλέυειν is מָלַךְ, to exercise its power, as below 21, 6:21. Thus the wise Hebrew said ἅδε βασίλειον in 1:14. ἀπὸ and μέχρι are accustomed to be placed for the notation of time, as in Acts 10:30.

The mind of the Apostle is clearly inverted, who teaches that sin exercised its power in the world unto death up to the law of Moses. Since therefore sin could not be imputed unto punishment or death while the law did not exist; it is necessary that the law existed, even before Moses, if indeed death reigned from Adam unto Moses. Although therefore they did not have a law prescribed from without, yet they were not without law, inasmuch as it was inscribed upon their hearts in the first creation: and so by its power it was not permitted for them to sin with impunity, but sin was imputed to them unto condemnation. For if death had a place before the law, then certainly sin, which is the cause of death, also had a place, and vice versa; because sin was in the world, which is not, nor is it imputed, when no law at all exists, it is necessary that some law also existed then, even if the law had not yet been promulgated by Moses. The Apostle had said that sin, and through sin death, passed unto all men: Lest that be doubtful concerning men before the law, he adds that before the law was solemnly promulgated, sin also was in the world, which, because it was imputed while death reigned through sin from Adam unto Moses, even upon those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, what is more certain than that the law existed before Moses, because sin is the transgression of the law, 1 John 3:4, and where there is no law, there is no transgression; where there is no transgression of the law, there it cannot be imputed unto punishment. Ἀλλὰ ἐβασίλευσεν, 'but death reigned,' is as it were an assumption, so that the whole conclusion may have it thus: Where sin is not imputed, there death cannot reign on account of sin: But death did reign on account of sin from Adam unto Moses. Therefore, before Moses, and hence also from Adam, sin was imputed. Furthermore, where sin is imputed, there it is necessary that the law exist. For when the law does not exist, imputation does not occur. Although therefore Paul seems to affirm that there was no law before Moses: yet Paul does not affirm that, but rather speaks hypothetically; sin would not be imputed if there had been no law. But Grotius goes into all other things; he denies that death is on account of sin, contrary to the most clear opinion of Paul, his whole treatment, and the very evidence of the matter, and he pretends that Paul teaches: that all men died for this reason, not because the guilt of sin or sin pertains to all, but because they draw their origin from Adam, as Schmalzius in refut. disp. 2. Franz. de pecc. orig. p. 45. He asserts that men, on account of the propagation itself which they have from Adam, are liable even to eternal death, although they have not sinned: which is utterly false and contrary to divine justice; since they are liable to punishment not on account of the propagation of nature alone, which is such, but on account of the propagation of a corrupted nature and on account of the communion of Adam's sin. God can and is accustomed to help those who do not deserve it with the praise of his clemency: but he cannot punish those who have not sinned WITHOUT THE OVERTHROW OF JUSTICE, says Augustine, book II of the imperfect work. Furthermore, it is openly false that no law was given to men which threatened the penalty of death to those who transgressed it. For both to Adam, and in his person to all men, a law was prescribed under the threat of death, Gen. II. 17, and it is inscribed in all men by nature, by the force of which the δικαίωμα of God is known to them by nature, that sinners are worthy of death, Rom. I. 32. Furthermore, it is false, and contrary to the Apostle, that sin was not imputed before Moses so that it could be called the cause of death with regard to individual men; because the Apostle teaches with a clear voice that death passed through to all men on account of sin, and reigned over all. Finally, it is false that God punished only kinds of men before the Mosaic law, since it is evident that individual men were also punished, by the example of Cain, Phamon, Ger, Onan, and others: and it would have been an injustice if individual men liable to guilt and the gravest sins had not been punished, because guilt, by the force of divine justice, demands punishment.

καὶ ἐπὶ τὲς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παρα- βάσεως Ἀδὰμ.

It prevailed even over those who had committed nothing similar to Adam, such as Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph. Because ἁμαρτάνειν is ambiguous and in some sense can be attributed to all men who have lived for some time: therefore he explains distinctly of what kind of sin he is treating here, namely of such a kind that it can be considered equal to that which Adam had committed. Grave transgressions are accustomed to be compared to the transgression of Adam, Hosea VI. 7.

Indeed, death reigned not only over them, but even over infants themselves, who although they were guilty of no actual, deliberate sin, nevertheless became liable to death on account of sin, and death reigned over them through sin, because the sting of death is sin, 1 Cor. XV. 47. Therefore, by a transgression similar to Adam's, not only grave sin is designated, but any deliberate sin whatsoever, inasmuch as death holds sway even over those who have not committed actual sin, such as embryos that are extinguished in the womb, and newborn infants; whence St. Augustine, along with other ancient Fathers, asserted original sin from this passage against the Pelagians, which Grotius here seems to have perverted for the sake of the new Pelagians and Socinians.

Who is the type of the one to come.
