That death, indeed, as we have already said, followed from the law of nature, but one which God could easily have prevented, had He not willed Adam to be a figure of Christ, though with a different manner of generation and contrary effects. ὁ μέλλων is said here with respect to the time of Adam and thenceforth up to the law, he who is the last Adam, 1 Cor. 15:46. So also Col. 2:17, the word μελλόντων looks back to earlier times. τύπος is a figure, according to which something else is more fully accomplished, Exod. 25:40. Thus 1 Cor. 10:6, 11, it is called ἀντίτυπος, Heb. 11:24.

It is Pelagian to say that death followed from the law of nature, which St. Augustine refuted in Book XX of The City of God, ch. 15, teaching that it is agreed among CHRISTIANS who truly hold the CATHOLIC FAITH that even the death of the body itself was not inflicted upon us by the LAW OF NATURE, by which God made no death for man, but by the merit of sin: because God, avenging sin, said to man, in whom we all were then, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall go.' In the Council of Milevis, anathema was pronounced against this opinion of Grotius, which is repeated in the Canon Law, dist. IV, de consecr. c. 142: 'Whoever teaches that Adam, the first man, was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body, that is, would depart from the body not by the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.'

Although God could indeed have easily prevented even the sin by whose merit death was inflicted, and consequently death itself, He did not therefore fail to prevent it because He willed Adam to be a figure of Christ, but because He willed man to be of free will, to whom He imparted sufficient strength so that he could have guarded himself against seduction, having created him in His own image and likeness in true wisdom and holiness, whence He did not will to draw him back from sin by force. Not that He permitted sin or introduced death so that he might be a figure of Christ, but because Adam was about to sin and to merit death, He promised Christ as the second Adam, so that just as from that first one sin and death passed to all men, so from this second Adam righteousness and life might come to us.

In what way the Apostle calls Adam a type of Christ, not as figures are otherwise called types in the Old Testament, but because here a certain likeness and comparison is found; and that of things more dissimilar than similar. For as there would have been no need for Christ as mediator in the state of integrity, so there was no place there for a type of Christ; but in the fall and its consequences, he can be constituted a type of Christ, properly so called, all the less, the more disparate those things are: the fault of Adam and the penalty of death, and the righteousness of Christ and the gift of life, Rom. 6:last verse. Therefore, this is not such a figure here, according to which something else is more fully accomplished, but in which something else clearly contrary is found, as Grotius himself acknowledges a different manner of generation and contrary effects.

Latin:

V. 14. ἀλλ᾽ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μώσεως. Attamen, inquit, vim suam exercuit mors in homines sin- gulos ab Adami ætate ad Mosis ætatem, id est, per annos fer- mè bis mille quingentos, non breve spatium. βασιλέυειν מָלַךְ est vim suam exercere ut infra 21. VI, 21. Sic ἅδε βα- σίλειον dixit sapiens Hebræus I. 14. ἀπὸ & μέχρι poni solent ad temporis notationem ut Act. X. 30.

Planè invertitur mens Apostoli, qui peccatum usque ad legem Mosis in mundo vim suam exercuisse ad mortem docet. Quum ergo peccatum non exi- stente lege imputari non posset ad pœnam vel mortem; necessum est legem extitisse, etiam ante Mosen, siquidem dominata sit mors ab Adamo us- que ad Mosen. Etsi ergo non habuerint legem ex- trinsecus præscriptam, tamen non sine lege fuere, ut- pote quæ cordibus eorum in prima creatione in- scripta fuit: adeoque vi ejus non licebat impunè ipsis peccare, sed peccatum imputatum ipsis fuit ad condemnationem. Si enim mors locum habuit an- te legem, utique etiam peccatum, quod est causa mortis, habuit locum, & vice versa, quia peccatum in mundo fuit, quod non est, neque imputatur, nul- lâ planè lege existente, oportet etiam legem ali- quam tum extitisse, etiamsi à Mose lex nondum promulgata fuerit. Dixerat Apostolus, in omnes peccatum, & per peccatum mortem transiisse: Id ne dubium sit de hominibus ante legem, addit, ante le- gem solenniter promulgatam etiam peccatum in mundo fuisse, quod quia imputatum est dominan- te morte per peccatum, ab Adamo usque ad Mo- sen, etiam in eos, qui non peccarunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adamica, quid certius est, quàm legem ante Mosen fuisse, quia peccatum est transgressio legis 1. Joh. III. 4. & ubi non est lex, ibi non est prævaricatio, ubi prævaricatio legis non est, ibi nec imputari po- test ad pœnam. Ἀλλὰ ἐβασίλευσεν sed dominata est mors, est veluti assumptio, ut ita tota conclusio ha- beat: Ubi peccatum non imputatur, ibi dominari non potest mors propter peccatum: Atqui mors dominata est propter peccatum ab Adamo usq; ad Mosen. E. ante Mosen inde etiam ab Adamo pec- catum imputatũ est. Porrò, ubi peccatum imputa- tur, ibi legem esse oportet. Nam lege non existente non fit imputatio. Etsi ergò videatur Paulus affir- mare, non fuisse legem ante Mosen: non tamen id af- firmat Paulus, sed hypotheticè potius loquitur; non imputatum esset peccatum, si nulla lex fuisset. At Gro- tius in alia omnia it; mortem contra luculentissimã Pauli sententiam, totamq; ejus tractationẽ & ipsam rei evidentiam, negat esse ob peccatum, fingitque Paulum docere: ideò mortuos esse omnes homines, non quod peccati reatus vel peccatum omnes attineat, sed quod ex Adamo ortum trahant, uti Schmalzius in refut. disp. II. Franz. de pecc. orig. p. 45. homines propter ipsam propagationẽ, quam ex Adamo habent, morti etiam æternæ obnoxios esse, etsi non peccarint as- serit: quod oppidò falsum, & divinæ justitiæ con- trarium; cùm non ob propagationem solum naturæ, quæ talis, sed ob propagationem naturæ corruptæ, & ob communionem peccati Adami posteri pœnæ obnoxii sint. Quo de subvenire non merentibus potest, & solet Deus cum laude clementiæ: punire autem non peccan- tes non potest SINE EVERSIONE JUSTITIÆ ait August. l. II. op. imperfecti. Falsum adhæc est aper- tè, nullam datam legem esse hominibus, quæ transgre- dientibus mortis pœnam minaretur. Nam & Adamo, atque in ejus persona omnibus hominibus lex præ- scripta est sub comminatione mortis Gen. II. 17. & inscripta omnibus hominibus est naturâ, vi cujus δι- καίωμα Dei ipsis naturâ notum est, quod peccatores digni sint morte Rom. I. 32. Falsum insuper est, & Apostolo contrarium, non in id imputatum pecca- tum fuisse ante Mosen, ut causa possit dici mortis, quoad singulos homines; quia in omnes homines propter peccatum mortem pertransiisse, & domi- natam esse super omnes λευκᾶδι φωνῇ docet Apo- stolus. Falsum denique genera tantùm hominum Deum ante legem Mosaicam puniisse, siquidem etiam singulos homines punitos esse, exemplo Caini, Pha- monis, Ger, Onan, & aliorum constat: & injustitia fuisset, si singuli homines culpæ ac peccatis gra- vissimis obnoxii puniti non fuissent, quia culpa, vi justitiæ divinæ, postulat pœnam.

καὶ ἐπὶ τὲς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παρα- βάσεως Ἀδὰμ.

Etiam in eos valuit, qui nihil simile Adamo commiserant, quales Abel, Noë, Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus Josephus. Quia ἁμαρτάνειν ambiguum est & aliquo sensu omnibus ho- minibus, qui aliquandiu ætatem egêre, tribui potest: ideò distinctè explicat, de quo peccandi genere hic agat, nempe de tali, quod par censeri possit ei, quod Adamus commise- rat. Solent graves transgressiones comparari transgres- sioni Adami, Oseæ VI. 7.

Imò non tantum in eos dominata est mors, sed etiam in infantes ipsos, qui etsi nullius peccati actualis proæretici rei fuere, tamen morti obnoxii facti sunt propter peccatum, & mors in eos domina- ta est per peccatum, quia aculeus mortis est peccatum 1. Cor. XV. 47. Designatur ergò per transgressio- nem similem Adamicæ, non tantum peccatum grave, sed quodcunque peccatum proæreticum, siquidem in illos etiam dominatur mors, qui peccatum proæreticum non admisere, utpote in embryones, qui in utero extinguuntur, & in infantes recens natos, unde peccatum originis ex hoc loco contra Pelagianos asseruit S. August. cum aliis antiquis Patribus, quẽ in gratiam novorũ Pelagianorum,Socinianorũ, hic pervertisse videtur Grotius.

ὅς ἐστι τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος. Mors quidem illa, ut jam diximus, secuta est ex naturæ lege, sed quam Deus facile impedire potuisset, nisi voluisset Adamum figuram esse Christi, diversa tamen gignendi ratione & effectibus contrariis. ὁ μέλλων hic dicitur respectu habito ad tempus Adami & deinceps ad legem usque, is qui Ἀδὰμ ἔσχατος. 1. Cor. XV. 46. sic & Col. II. 17. vox μελλόντων respicit priora tempora. τύπος est figura,ad quam aliud quid plenius efficitur Exod. XXV. 40. Sic 1. Cor. X. 6. 11. dicitur ἀντίτυπος, Hebr. XI. 24.

Pelagianum est mortem sequutam esse ex naturæ lege, quod prosligavit S. August. l. XX. de Civit. Dei c. 15. docens, id constare inter CHRISTIANOS veraciter CATHOLICAM tenentes FIDEM, etiam ipsam nobis corporis mortem non LEGE NATURÆ, qua nullam mortem homini Deus fecit, sed merito inflictan esse peccati: quoniam peccatum vindicans Deus dixit homini,in quo tunc omnes eramus,terres es, & in terram ibis. In concilio Milevitano anathema dictum est huic Grotii sententiæ: quod in Jure Canonico repetitur dist. IV. de consecr. c. 142. Quicunque docet Adam primum hominem mortalem factum, ita ut sive peccaret, sive non peccaret, moreretur in corpore, h. e. de corpore exiret non peccati merito, sed necessitate naturæ, anathema sit.

Quamvis verò Deus etiam peccatum, cujus merito inflicta est mors, adeoque ipsam mortem facilè impedire potuisset, non tamen ideò non impediit, quod voluerit Adamum Christi figuram esse, sed quia hominem liberi arbitrii esse voluit, cui vires sufficientes indidit, ut à seductione sibi cavere potuisset, condito eodem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam in sapientiâ & sanctitate verâ, unde vi retrahere à peccato noluit: Non ut figura Christi esset, vel peccatum permisit, vel mortem immisit, sed quia Adam peccaturus,& mortem meriturus erat, Christum promisit alterum Adamum, ut quemadmodum ab illo primo peccatum & mors in homines universos transiit, ita ab hoc secundo Adamo justitia & vita in nos perveniret.

Quo pacto Apostolus Adamum τύπον dicit Christi,non uti aliàs figuræ in V. T. dicuntur typi, sed quod hic similitudo quædam & comparatio; eademque dissimilium magis, quam similium deprehendatur. Nam uti Christo mediatore opus non fuisset in statu integritatis, ita nec typo Christi ibi locus erat; in lapsu verò & consequentibus ejusdem tanto minus typus Christi constitui potest, propriè ita dictus, quanto magis disparata illa sunt, Adami culpa & mortis pœna, & Christi justitia ac vitæ donum Rom. VI. v. ult. Non ergò hic talis figura est,ad quam aliud quid plenius efficitur, sed in qua aliud quid planè contrarium deprehenditur, uti Grotius diversam gignendi rationem & effectus contrarios ipse agnoscit.

## 5:15
Verse 15. 'But not as the trespass, so also is the free gift.' He wishes to say this: in neither, indeed, is there anything unjust; but yet it is more fitting for God to make one author of life than one of death. χάρισμα is called what is soon after δώρημα, any benefit, as below 11:28, 2 Cor. 1:11. But παράπτωμα corresponds to the Hebrew words פֶּשַׁע, מַעַל, עָוֹן and similar ones, which signify a grave violation of divine law. But here that word is understood together with its effect, which will now be explained. God loves more to do good than to do harm. And life is more pleasing to God than death.

The Apostle does not mean what is more fitting for God; nor indeed did God make the author of death, or cause Adam to be the author of death, because God in no way made death, and He created Adam immortal, and for a blessed life, not so that he might be the author of death. But this is what the Apostle means in that comparison of dissimilars or 'dissimilarity,' as the Scholastics say: that the gift or benefit in Christ is greater than the evil or sin and transgression in Adam, by reason of greater power and effect: because in the ONE sin of Adam all indeed died, or were made subject to death; but the grace and benefit exhibited in Christ frees us not only from that one sin, but from ALL sins. Therefore, a certain likeness and unlikeness is given here. The likeness is in this, that each propagates what is his own to his own; the unlikeness is in this, that Adam propagates sin and destruction to his own by carnal generation; Christ communicates righteousness and life to His own by regeneration: which the χάρισμα embraces, by which it is noted that it descends from the grace of God exhibited in Christ, that God shows favor to man on account of Christ: which is also called δώρημα in verse 16, and that the power of that righteousness and salvation which is from Christ is more effective than the power of sin and death arising from Adam, partly by reason of sin, because from Adam there is the guilt of one sin, from Christ liberation from many or all sins, verse 16, partly by reason of death, because indeed Adam brought in death and condemnation, but Christ not only renders us immune from death and condemnation, but also confers upon us that salvation and life which Adam did not have. Concerning which see Chrysostom in his commentary. on this passage, that one sin could indeed introduce death, but grace did not take away only that one sin, but also those which entered after it. Furthermore, that not only were sins taken away, but righteousness was provided, and that Christ profited us not only as much as Adam harmed us, but much more and far more.

For if by the one man's trespass the many died. The many, that is, almost all except Enoch, and if there were any others by chance, of whom it is not written. The same is meant here by the one man's trespass, which was just now by sin.

The many are spoken of here in respect to the one, because not only one, but by far the most died by the sin of one, that is, they became liable to death, or guilty of death; but that those many are all men the Apostle had already taught in verse 12, namely that death passed through to all. Whence it is plain that the many are spoken of only comparatively and in respect to the one, when in reality they are all, from whom neither Enoch, nor Elijah, much less others whom Grotius rashly suspects, are to be excepted: because even if they did not properly die, they were nevertheless mortal and guilty of death; and they experienced something analogous to death in their translation, namely by putting off the mortal body, that they might put on the immortal, or while immortality absorbed mortality. To which the rule concerning words that often signify not the act but the obligation pertains, Ps. 27:9, Heb. 5:4, cf. Gen. 2:17. Therefore from the word the many, the Pelagians and Socinians cannot infer that sin harms posterity not by propagation but by imitation of Adam's example, or that it does not harm all, but only many; because these many are all: many were constituted sinners, that is, all, who in reality are many. See Augustine, Book VI against Julian, chapter 12. And Pareus himself admits in this place that the name many is not taken in opposition to all, but indefinitely for a great and infinite multitude, as if one were to say there are many fish in the sea, thus verse 18, 19, Dan. 12:5.

much more) Much more easily. For that is more difficult to believe than this, and yet it has appeared to be true.

But how is that more difficult to believe, that by the offense of one many died, which is of justice? Since in Adam, the common stock, God entrusted to all men both His image, to which immortality pertained, and that having been lost by Adam, the image of God was destroyed, and immortality was lost, which he had received for himself and his posterity. This certainly, which in

To the Son of God, that God manifested in the flesh, may justice and salvation be obtained for us, through his obedience even unto death, confessedly a great mystery, 1 Tim. III. 15. And it is so much the more difficult to believe, by how much it is greater, that through the death of one, life is restored, and through the justice of one, justice is restored to many who were dead in sins, and condemned to eternal death by the force of divine justice and truth. What then is that πολλῷ μᾶλλον, much MORE? The Apostle is looking at the magnitude and greater efficacy of the matter, as we have said, not at what is easier or more difficult to believe. And if one wishes to hint at the cause, the grace of God, ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ, is much MORE powerful, because mercy rejoices against judgment, κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως, Jas. II. 13. Much MORE powerful, or prevailing, is the gift in grace, δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι, because in that grace is given that which is in that one man Jesus Christ in a singular way, μονοτρόπως, who is not a mere man, ψιλάνθρωπος, but God-man, θεάνθρωπος, true, great, and God blessed above all forever: and therefore that which is exhibited to us in him, the gift of justification and salvation, is founded in the very justice and expiation performed by God for us, by which we obtain the remission of sins and a perfect justice valid before the tribunal of God. Add also that the grace of God appeared much more illustriously than the power of sin, namely in the life, death, and resurrection of Christ, and in the benefits which are obtained in Christ. Tit. II. 14. c. III. 6.

The grace of God and the gift, ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ) Here he said grace, χάρις, where before he said gift, χάρισμα, the cause for the effect. The divine justice, which has come to Christians, is both a great benefit and provoked by no merits of ours: therefore it is called a gift.

In the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, ἐν χάριτι τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Grace, χάρις, in this place signifies the benevolence of Christ toward the human race.

There is no need for that metonymy. The Apostle speaks properly and accurately, not confusing grace, χάριν, and gift, χάρισμα, which are distinguished as cause and effect: for grace, χάρις, is of God, τοῦ θεοῦ, which abounded, ἐπερίσσευσε, unto us all, and from that grace flows the gift, ἡ δωρεὰ, and the free gift, τὸ χάρισμα, whence it is said the gift in grace, ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι, the gift of justice and life, not indeed from a certain absolute grace of God, but that of the one man Jesus Christ, τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, that which is in that one man, or is exhibited to us on account of that one man. It is in that one, because from his fullness we all receive grace for grace, χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος, John I. 14. It is through that one man, because through his obedience, both active and passive, it was procured and acquired for us. Therefore, grace, χάρις, here is not the benevolence of Christ, but the grace of God, which comes to us in Christ.

It abounded unto the many, Εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐπερίσσευσε) Unto many, that is, unto all who have believed in Christ, which is the beginning of a new nature. It abounded, ἐπερίσσευσε, that is, appeared more abundantly, see above III. 7. and Matt. V. 20. יתר.

By the force of the Apostolic comparison and the amplification of grace, which is instituted here, grace is said to have redounded, that is, to have been copiously poured out, not only upon believers but upon ALL men: just as the Syriac word יתר is said of both quantity and quality, it abounded, it excelled. Otherwise, the evil which redounded from Adam unto all would be more abundant than the good which redounded in Christ unto very few, as if only unto believers. Which is to be noted against the Calvinian particularity.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀλλ' ὀυχ ὡς παράπτωμα,ὕτω καὶ τὸ χάρισμα. Hoc vult dicere: in neutro quidem quicquam iniqui: sed tamen Deo convenientius esse, unum facere vitæ auctorem, quam unum mortis. χάρισμα, dicitur quod mox δώρημα beneficium quodvis, ut infra XI. 28. 2. Cor. I. 11. παράπτωμα verò respondet vocibus Hebræis עוֹל מַעַל פֶּשַׁע & similibus, quæ violationem legis divinæ gravem significant. Hic vero ea vox intelligitur simul cum suo effectu, qui jam explicabitur. Deus magis amat prodesse quam nocere. Et vita Deo gratior quam mors.

Non id vult Apostolus, quid Deo convenientius sit; neq; verò Deus autorem mortis fecit, vel fecit, ut Adam autor esset mortis, quia nullatenus Deus fecit mortem, & Adamum immortalem condidit, atque ad beatam vitam, non ut mortis autor esset. Sed p hoc est, quod in illa comparatione dissimilium vel dissiparantia, uti loquuntur Scholastici, vult Apostolus: quod ampliùs sit donum vel beneficiu in Christo, quàm malum vel peccatum & delictum in Adamo ratione majoris virtutis & effectus: quia in UNO Adami peccato quidem mortui sunt omnes, seu morti facti sunt obnoxii; at gratia & benefi- cium in Christo exhibitum non liberat nos solum ab uno illo peccato, sed ab OMNIBUS peccatis. Si- militudo ergo hic quædam datur & dissimilitudo. Similitudo in eo, quod uterque quod suum est in suos propaget, dissimilitudo in eo, tum quod Adam in suos peccatum & exitium carnali generatione propaget; Christus suis justitiam & vitam per re- generationem communicet: quam τὸ χάρισμα complectitur, quo notatur, quod ex Dei gratia in Christo exhibita descendat, quod Deus homini propter Christum gratificatur: quod & δώρημα v. 16. dicitur, tum quodvis illa justitiæ, & salutis, efficacior sit, quæ à Christo est, quam vis peccati & mortis ab Adamo oriunda, partim ratione peccati, quod ab Adamo unius peccati reatus sit, à Christo liberatio à plurimis vel omnibus peccatis v.16.par- tim ratione mortis, quod nempe Adam mortem & condemnationem invexerit, Christus verò non so- lum à morte & condemnatione nos immunes præ- stet, sed etiam salutem & vitam eam nobis confe- rat,quam Adam non habuit. Quo de Chrysostom. in comment. ad h. l. quod mortem unum quidem peccatum introducere potuerit, gratia verò non uni- cum illud solum abstulerit peccatum, sed & ea, quæ post illud ingressa sunt. Deinde, quod non solum peccata sint sublata, sed & justitia præstita, & quod non solum tantum nobis Christus profuerit, quantum nocuerit Adam, sed & multò plus & longè magis.

εἰ γὰρ τῷ τῶ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι οἱ πολλοὶ ἀπέθανον. Οἱ πολλοὶ, id est, ferè omnes excepto Enocho, & si qui fortè fuere alii, de quibus id scriptum non est. Idem est hic τῷ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι, quod modo δι ἁμαρτίας.

Πολλοὶ hic dicuntur respectu unius, quia non unus tantum, sed longè plurimi mortui unius pec- cato sunt, id est, morti obnoxii, vel mortis rei facti sunt, plures autem illos esse omnes homines jam do- cuerat Apostolus v. 12. quod nempe mors in omnes pertransierit. Unde planum est solùm συγκριτικῶς, & respectu τῶ ἑνὸς dici τὲς πολλὲς, quum revera sint omnes, è quibus nec Enoch, nec Elias, nedum alii, quos temerè suspicatur Grotius excipiendi: quia etiamsi illi propriè mortui non sint, mortales ta- men & mortis rei fuere; & aliquid morti ἀνάλογον in sua μετάθεσει sensere, exuendo nempe corpus mortale,ut immortale induerent, vel dum immor- talitas absorpsit mortalitatem. Quò facit Regula de verbis quæ sapè non actum sed debitum significant Ps. XXVII. 9. Ebr. V. 4. conf. Gen. II. 17. Ideo è voce οἱ πολλοὶ Pelagiani, ac Sociniani colligere ne- queunt, non propagatione sed imitatione exemplo Adami peccatum posteris nocere aut quod non omnibus noceat, sed multis tantum; quia multi hi sunt omnes: Multi constituti sunt peccatores, id est omnes, qui revem sunt multi. vid. Aug. l. VI. contr. Jul. c. 12. Et fatetur Pareus ipse h. l. nomen multi non sumi in oppositione ad omnes, sed indefinitè pro magna & infinita multitudine, ut si quis dicat, in mari esse multos pisces, sic v. 18. 19. Dan. XII, 5.

πολλῷ μᾶλλον) Multò facilius. Nam illud quàm hoc difficilius creditu, & tamen verum esse apparuit.

Quî verò illud difficilius creditu unius delicto multos mortuos, quod justitiæ est? Siquidem in Adamo communi stirpe omnibus hominibus & imaginem suam,ad quam immortalitas pertinebat, concredidit Deus, eaque ab Adamo amissa,imago Dei deperdita, & immortalitas amissa fuerit,quam pro se & posteris suis acceperat. Hoc certè, quod in

Filio Dei, Deo illo in carne manifestato, nobis ju- stitia & salus obtingat, per obedientiam ejus usque ad mortem, ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον esti. 1. Tim. III. 15. credituque tantò difficilius, quantò majus est, per unius mortem vitam, per unius justitiam multis justitiam restitui in peccatis mortuis, & ad æter- nam mortem, vi justitiæ, & veritatis divinæ con- demnatis. Quid ergo illud πολλῷ μᾶλλον, multò MAGIS? rei magnitudinem & efficaciam majorem, ut diximus, respicit Apostolus, non quid creditu fa- cilius aut difficilius sit. Et si causam quis subinnui velit, multò MAGIS ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ gratia Dei va- let, quia κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως Jac. II. 13. Multo MAGIS valet, vel prævalet δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι donum in gratia, quia in illa gratia id datur, quæ est in uno illo homine Jesu Christo μονοτρόπως singu- lari, qui non ψιλάνθρωπος, sed θεάνθρωπος est, verus, magnus, & super omnia in secula benedictus Deus: ideoque fundatum est illud, quod nobis in eo exhibetur justificationis & salutis donum in ipsa Dei pro nobis præstita justitia & expiatione, qua remissionem peccatorum & justitiam perfectam coram Dei tribunali valentem consequimur. Adde & quod multò illustrius apparuerit Dei gra- tia, quàm peccati vis, in vita nempe, morte & re- surrectione Christi, & beneficiis, quæ in Christo obtingunt. Tit. II. 14. c. III. 6.

ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ) Hic χάρις dixit quod ante χά- ρισμα, causam pro effectu. Justitia divina, quæ Christianis obtigit, & magnum est beneficium, & nullis à nobis meritis provocatum : ideo donum dicitur.

ἐν χάριτι τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) χάρις hoc loco significat benevolentiam Christi in genus humanum.

Non opus est illa metonymia. Propriè & accu- ratè loquitur Apostolus, χάριν & χάρισμα non confundens, quæ ut causa & effectum distinguun- tur: Nam χάρις est τοῦ θεοῦ quæ ἐπερίσσευσε in nos omnes, & ex illa χάριτι fluit ἡ δωρεὰ & τὸ χάρι- σμα, unde dicitur ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι donum justitia & vitæ, non quidem è gratia quadam Dei absoluta, sed τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ea, quæ est in uno illo homine, vel ob unum illum hominem nobis ex- hibetur. In uno illo est, quia è plenitudine ipsius ac- cipimus omnes χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος, gratiam pro gra- tia Joh. I. 14. Per unum illum hominem est, quia per ejus obedientiam tum activam tum passivam nobis parta est, & acquisita. Non ergo χάρις hic est benevolentia Christi, sed gratia Dei, quæ in Christo nobis obtingit.

Εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐπερίσσευσε) In multos, id est, in omnes, qui in Christum credidere, quod initium est novæ naturæ. ἐπερίσσευσε, id est, abundantius apparuit, supra III. 7. & Matth. V. 20. יתר.

Vi comparationis Apostolicæ & amplificatio- nis gratiæ, quæ hic instituitur, non in credentes tantùm, sed OMNES homines redundasse, id est, copiose effusa esse dicitur gratia : uti verbum Syri יתר & de quantitate & qualitate dicitur abundavit, excelluit. Alias abundantius esset malum, quod ab Adamo in omnes, quàm bonum, quod in Christo in paucissimos utpote credentes solùm redunda- vit. Quod contra particularitatem Calvinianam notandum.

## 5:16
Verse 16. And not as by one that sinned, the gift, Καὶ ὀυχ ὡς δὲ ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος ἡ δωρεὰ) There is a double ellipsis. For both after by one, δι' ἑνὸς, the noun death, θάνατος, is understood from the verb they died, ἀπέθανον, which had preceded, and after the gift, ἡ δωρεὰ, is understood has, ἔχει. The gift is not in the same state as that death which followed from one sin. The benefit was much more efficacious than the harm. But in what that difference consists, he now explains.

Namely in this, that while the guilt of sin indeed came upon descendants from the transgression of Adam: the obedience of Christ, however, frees us not only from that one sin alone, but from all the guilt of all sins.

For the judgment indeed from one, Τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρῖμα ἐξ ἑνὸς) Judgment, κρῖμα, משפט, here signifies the constitution of God, to which the sin of Adam gave occasion.

Not by occasion only, as the Pelagians and Socinians wish, but by merit, sin became the judgment, τὸ κρῖμα, or the sentence of God, the guilt of which reached unto all. If anyone testifies that only the death of the body, and not also sin, passed through one man into the whole human race, he will attribute injustice to God, as is held in the Synod of Orange c. II. because, namely, it is an injustice for a man to be subjected to death on the occasion of sin without sin.

Unto condemnation, εἰς κατάκριμα) It is frequent for the Hebrews to name the cause for the effect, even if it proceeds from another cause. Thus, because the condemned are accustomed to die, condemnation is said here for death.

There is no necessity why we should posit a metalepsis here. The proper meaning of the word should rather be retained: and κα- τάκριμα is to be understood as eternal condemnation, which, by divine judgment, by merit of sin, and on account of sin, has been established and decreed: just as, conversely, by the merit of Christ, on account of Christ's obedience, there comes to us, according to the Apostolic ἀντίθεσιν, τὸ δικαίωμα, justification and eternal salvation. Just as he previously dealt with temporal death, brought in through Adam: so now he deals with eternal death or condemnation, inflicted by merit of sin. For by the merit of Christ we are not only freed from the penalty of temporal death, which for us who believe in Christ no longer results in a penalty, but in a benefit, but we are also freed from eternal death, and we attain and obtain eternal life.

τὸ δὲ χάρισμα) He understands here faith, which is also called the gift of God in Eph. II. 8: because, with God revealing it, nothing of the sort happened by merits.

Faith is indeed a gift of God, John VI. 29, Phil. I. 29, which, however, is not said in Eph. II. 8, for there it is taught that salvation is the gift of God: but in this place χά- ρισμα denotes that gift of God which He gives to us for justification, namely by communicating and imputing to us the obedience and righteousness of Christ, so that through the same we may not only be freed from τῷ κατακρίματι, but also attain τὸ δικαίωμα, and thus be justified before the tribunal of God.

ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων) With the occasion taken from many sins.

εἰς δικαίωμα) To a righteous life or perpetual obedience: in which way δικαίωμα is also used below in verse 18. Thus in Job XXXIV. 27, דרכיו, which is his ways, the seventy translate as δικαιώματα αὐτῶ. Therefore the Apostle used the singular noun here, so that he might signify one and a constant tenor of life. The Apocalypse spoke in the plural for the same thing: τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων XIX. 8.

What is that 'occasion from many sins'? Sins did not only give the occasion for κρίματος εἰς κατάκριμα, but they entirely deserved it. But by that most eminent gift of God, which He gave to the whole world out of immense love, and which is appropriated to believers through faith, John III. 16, we are freed not only from the guilt of the one Adamic fall, but from many offenses, or all falls, namely sins, whatever and however great they may be, and thus we are justified in the judgment of God, Acts XIII. 38. Grace, says Augustine, l. 1. contr. Jul., does not kill only that one sin, but also the sins entering after it. From many offenses, therefore, that is, from all: for if we were not freed from all offenses, it would not be true justification, true blessedness. Cf. Acts XIII. 38, Rom. IV. 6. He who offends in one is guilty of all. James II. 10. τὸ δικαίωμα, because here it is opposed to τῷ κα- τακρίματι, denotes justification; just as the latter denotes condemnation, and not a righteous life, or perpetual obedience. For what kind of opposition would that be, between death, which Grotius understands by condemnation, and perpetual obedience, which he understands by δικαίωμα?

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ ὀυχ ὡς δὲ ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος ἡ δωρεὰ) Est ἔλ- λειψις duplex. Nam & post δι' ἑνὸς subauditur nomen θάνα- τος ex verbo ἀπέθανον, quod præcesserat, & post ἡ δωρεὰ subauditur ἔχει. Non sic se habet donum, ut illa mors ex uno peccato consecuta. Multò efficacius fuit beneficium quam noxa. In quo autem ea differentia sita sit jam explicat.

Nimirum in eo, quod ex Adæ quidem delicto reatus peccati in posteros venerit : Christi verò obe- dientia non ab uno solùm illo peccato, sed ab omni omnium peccatorum reatu nos liberet.

Τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρῖμα ἐξ ἑνὸς) Κρῖμα משפט constitutionem Dei hic significat, cui occasionem dedit peccatum Adami.

Non occasione tantum, ut Pelagiani & Sociniani volunt, sed merito peccatum factum est τὸ κρῖμα vel judicium Dei, cujus reatus ad omnes pervenit. Si quis mortem tantum corporis, non autem & pec- catum per unum hominem in omne genus humanum transiisse testatur, injustitiam Deo dabit, habetur in Synodo Arausicanâ c. II. quia scilicet injustitiæ est morti hominem subjici occasione peccati citra peccatum.

εἰς κατάκριμα) Frequens est Hebræis causam nominare pro effectu, quamvis ex alia causa procedente. Ita, quia damnati mori solent, damnatio hic dicitur pro morte.

Nulla est necessitas, cur metalepsin hic ponamus. Propria potius vocis significatio retinenda: & κα- τάκριμα de condemnatione æternâ, quæ, judicio di- vino, merito peccati, & propter peccatum consti- tuta, & decreta sit, intelligenda: quemadmodum vicissim merito Christi propter Christi obedien- tiam nobis obtingit juxta Apostolicam ἀντίθεσιν τὸ δικαίωμα justificatio & salus æterna. Ut antea de morte temporali egit, per Adamum invectâ: ita jam de morte æterna seu condemnatione, merito peccati inflicta agit. Christi enim merito non tantum à pœna mortis temporalis liberamur, quæ nobis in Christum credentibus jam non in pœ- nam cedit, sed in beneficium, verum liberamur etiam à morte æterna, & consequimur atque obti- nemus vitam æternam.

τὸ δὲ χάρισμα) Intelligit hic fidem, quæ & Ephes. II. 8. donum Dei dicitur: quia Deo revelante nihil tale meritis contigit.

Fides est quidem donum Dei Joh. VI. 29. Phil. I. 29. quod tamen Eph. II. 8. non dicitur, ibi enim salutem donum Dei esse docetur: at hoc loco χά- ρισμα notat illud donum Dei, quod nobis ad justi- ficationem donat, obedientiam nempe, & justitiam Christi nobis communicando, & imputando, ut per eandem non modò à τῷ κατακρίματι liberemur, sed etiam τὸ δικαίωμα consequamur, adeoque co- ram tribunali Dei justificemur.

ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων) Occasione sumpta ex multis peccatis.

εἰς δικαίωμα) Ad vitam rectam sive perpetuam obedien- tiam: quomodo δικαίωμα & infra 18. Sic Jobi XXXIV. 27. דרכיו quod est vias ejus, septuaginta vertunt δικαιώματα αὐτῶ. Ideò nomen singulare hic usurpavit Apostolus, ut unum ac constantem vitæ tenorem significaret. Apocalypsis pluraliter pro eodem dixit: τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων XIX. 8.

Quid illud occasione ex multis peccatis? Non oc- casionem tantum κρίματος εἰς κατάκριμα dede- runt peccata, sed id omnino meruerunt. Dono au- tem illo Dei eminentissimo, quod toti mundo ex immensa dilectione dedit, quodque per fidem ap- propriatur credentibus Joh. III. 16. non ex reatu tantum unius peccati lapsus Adamici, sed è multis delictis, vel lapsibus omnibus, nempe peccatis, qualia & quanta illa etiam sint, liberamur, adeoque in judicio Dei justificamur Act. XIII. 38. Gratia, inquit Augustin. l. 1. contr. Jul. non unum tantum illud interficit peccatum, sed & post illud introeuntia peccata. Ex multis ergo offensis, hoc est, ex omnibus: nam si non ab omnibus offensis liberaremur, non esset vera justificatio, vera beatitudo. Conf. Act. XIII. 38. Rom. IV. 6. Qui in uno offendit, omnium est reus. Jac. II. 10. τὸ δικαίωμα, quia hic opponitur τῷ κα- τακρίματι, justificationem notat; uti hoc conde- mnationem, non vero rectam vitam, seu perpetuam obedientiam. Quænam enim illa foret opposi- tio, inter mortem, quam per condemnationem Grotius intelligit, & obedientiam perpetuam, quam per δικαίωμα?

## 5:17
Vers. 17. εἰ γὰρ) He shows how great that righteous life is, which we obtain by the gift of God, from the fact that it draws with it eternal life and happiness.

τῷ τοῦ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι) He repeats what he had said above in 15, but so that he may introduce something greater than before. In the Manuscript it is, ἐν ἑνὶ παραπτώματι.

He shows not how great a good a righteous life is, but how great justification is, which we obtain by the gift of God: for our obedience does not draw eternal life and happiness along with it, inasmuch as it is otherwise owed to GOD, and moreover is altogether imperfect and impure, Luke 17:10, Rom. 8:3, Phil. 3:7, 8, but justification does; because those whom He justified, them God also glorifies, Rom. 8:30. And this is that greater thing which the Apostle now introduces: that we are not only freed from all sins through Christ, but also that by his merit we attain eternal life. Which he now also illustrates by the contrast of the first Adam, but so as to attribute far more to the second Adam: because, namely, by the demerit of Adam we were not only constituted sinners, but also guilty of eternal death; but by the merit of Christ we are not only justified and freed from sin and from eternal death, but we also attain eternal life and blessedness, both of which good and gift befall us by the sole obedience of Christ apprehended through faith, without any works or merits of our own, so that it might be given solely by grace. And thus that great herald of the righteousness of Christ both illustrates his principal theme clearly and demonstrates it equally with an Apostolic Spirit.

Death reigned.

As above, 12.

He meant to say 14. He is not, however, dealing here with the dominion of death unto temporal destruction, but unto eternal condemnation: over which, by the force of the divine threat in Gen. 2:17, death reigned through sin, or the Devil who has the power of death, Heb. 2:14.

Through the one.

That is, by nature passing from one into all.

Pelagianism and Socinianism are again being encrusted; the Apostle had said in verse 16 'through one who sinned,' and he always inculcates sin as the cause of death, and therefore here also as the cause of condemnation: for death did not obtain dominion over all through nature as such, but through nature corrupted, passing from one into all. For under a just GOD, no one can be miserable (let alone condemned), as Augustine teaches in Book 1 of the Imperfect Work, unless he deserves it. Evil, says the same Bishop of Hippo in Book 3 against Julian, ch. 6, if they (the descendants of Adam) drew none from their origin, they would never be born with even bodily vices. For God, who is the creator of souls, is also the creator of bodies, who certainly would not inflict vices upon human nature in its very creation without cause.

Much more.

Much more easily, as above, 15.

Those who [receive] the abundance of grace.

He calls it the abundance of grace in the Hebrew manner, that is, most abundant grace, the benevolent manifestation of the divine will made through Christ.

And of the gift of righteousness.

The gift of righteousness, again a Hebraism, for righteousness which is given as a gift. See above 15. It is said to be given as a gift, because it is obtained through faith, which is the gift of GOD, as we said above 16.

Receiving.

That is, those who were willing to receive, and thus received in reality: thus also John 1:12.

That abundantly good grace does not consist in the manifestation of the divine will's benevolence, but is the very grace of justification, that GOD justifies the ungodly, provided he believes, out of mere grace and mercy. Which is indeed announced in the Gospel, Acts 13:38, but it is not the announcement of the Gospel itself, which we embrace through faith: just as that gift overflowing from grace signifies a most abundant gift, a gift of righteousness, or most abundant righteousness, which GOD offers to us through the Word. Faith is therefore described here through the taking or reception and apprehension of the grace and righteousness of Christ, which is given as a gift and imputed to us. Which the Papists utterly pervert, turning grace into inherent righteousness, and the abundance of the donation or of the righteousness given, into most abundant righteousness given to us as a gift—concerning which more abundant righteousness see Matthew 5:20—into an abundance of infused gifts, entirely against the mind of the Apostle, both in the parallel, Ephesians 2:7, where he explains the abundance of grace by the exceeding riches of his grace: and in other sayings of Scripture, which teach that we receive not only an abundance of gifts, but only the firstfruits of the Spirit, Romans 8:23, and testify that we labor under great infirmity because of the remnants of the flesh, Romans 7:14 ff., Galatians 5:17. Add that in verse 20 it is sufficiently clear what this abundance of grace is here, where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. That this cannot be explained of inherent righteousness is clear.

They shall reign in life.

He speaks of two great things, and most pleasing to men, life and kingdom, or immortality and highest honors. See 1 Cor. 4:8, 2 Tim. 2:12, Rev. 5:20, 20:4, 22:5.

through the one Jesus Christ.

Through the Prince of life. Acts III. 15. For He was the first to make manifest that eternal life which lay hidden in darkness, the first to attain it: the same will also confer it upon those who draw a new nature from Him.

The faithful, accepting the most abundant grace of GOD, and the most abundant righteousness of Christ, which is given as a gift out of grace, reign in life, both in the kingdom of grace in the spiritual life, and in the kingdom of glory in the eternal and heavenly life, through Christ, who has made us kings unto GOD Rev. I. 6. chap. V. 10. Which is a far greater good that redounds from Christ than was the evil that proceeded from Adam. For he only propagated death with sin to his descendants; but Christ not only delivers us from sin and death by His passion and death, but has also acquired for us by His obedience and righteousness a heavenly, blessed life, and the kingdom of glory, which are goods Adam did not possess. That Grotius, with Pelagius and Socinus, does not fear to obliterate the merit of Christ, as far as in him lies, attributing nothing more to Christ here than the first announcement of eternal life, and the first access to it, or that He was the first to attain the same, and thus went before us by His example. Both of which are false; for eternal life was announced long ago, and preached by the Prophets: nor did Christ first attain eternal life in terms of the order of time, since Enoch and Elijah were translated into eternal life in soul and body, and if you listen to Grotius, perhaps even more; not to mention that no reasoning of example has a place here. For Christ was devoid of sin and perfectly Holy, such as no others are, whence no one would be entering heaven after His likeness and example if we had to enter it by our own innocence and holiness. But that Christ confers eternal life upon us, that is common to Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor does it pertain to the merit of Christ: just as our regeneration is also a work common to the Holy Trinity, not proper to Christ. For we are born of GOD John I. 13. and of the Spirit John III. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εἰ γὰρ) Ostendit quantum sit ista vita recta, quam Dei dono adipiscimur, ex eo, quod secum trahit æternam vitam ac felicitatem.

τῷ τοῦ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι) Repetit quod dixerat supra 15. sed ut majus aliquid quam ante inferat. In Manuscripto est, ἐν ἑνὶ παραπτώματι.

Non quantum bonum vita recta, sed quantum justificatio sit, quam Dei dono adipiscimur, osten- dit: neque enim obedientia nostra secum trahit æternam vitam ac felicitatem, utpote alias DEO debita, adhæc imperfecta admodum & impura Luc. XVII. 10. Rom. IIX. 3. Phil. III. 7. 8. sed justificatio; quia quos justificavit, eos etiam glorificat Deus Rom. IIX. 20. Et hoc est majus illud, quod infert jam Apostolus: non tantum ab omnibus peccatis nos liberari per Christum, sed etiam merito ejus vitam æternam nos consequi. Quod jam etiam ἀντιθέ- σει primi Adami illustrat, sed ut secundo Adamo longe amplius tribuat: quia nempe Adami de- merito non peccatores solum constituti sumus, sed etiam rei æternæ mortis; Christi autem merito non justificamur tantum, & liberamur à peccato, & à morte æterna, sed consequimur etiam vitam & beatitudinem æternam, quod utrumque bonum & donum obtingit nobis sola Christi obedientia per fidem apprehensâ, sine ullis nostris operibus, aut meritis, ut donaretur unice gratia. Atque ita the- ma suum principale & illustrat præclare, & de- monstrat pariter Spiritu Apostolico Magnus ille justitiæ Christi præco.

ὁ Θάνατος ἐβασίλευσε.

Ut supra 12.

Volebat dicere 14. Non autem de dominio mor- tis jam agit ad internecionem temporalem, sed ad condemnationem æternam: ad quam omnino vi comminationis divinæ Gen. II. 17. dominabatur per peccatum mors, vel qui potestatem mortis ha- bet Diabolus Ebr. II. 14.

διὰ τῶ ἑνὸς.

Id est, per naturam ex uno in omnes transeuntem.

Iterum incrustatur Pelagianismus, & Socinia- nismus δι ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος dixerat Apostolus v. 16. & semper inculcat peccatum ut causam mortis, adeoque etiam hic ut κατακρίματος condemnatio- nis causam: Non enim per naturam qua talem, sed per naturam corruptam ex uno in omnes transeun- tem mors in omnes obtinuit imperium. Neque enim sub DEO justo miser esse (nedum condemnari) quisquam, docente August. l. 1. oper. imperf. nisi mereatur, potest. Malum, inquit idem Hipponen- sis Episcopus l. III. c. Julian. c. 6. si nullum ex ori- gine traherent, (posteri Adami) nunquam cum vi- tiis vel corporalibus nascerentur. Deus enim qui est animarum, ipse est etiam corporum conditor, qui utique humanæ in ipsa conditione naturæ vitia non infliget immerito.

Πόλλῳ μᾶλλον.

Multo facilius, ut supra 15.

ὁι τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος.

Abundantiam gratiæ more Hebraico, id est, gratiam abundantissimam vocat, benevolam patefactionem divinæ voluntatis factam per Christum.

Καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης.

Δωρεὰ δικαιοσύνης, rursum Hebraïsmus, pro justitia, quæ dono datur. Vide supra 15. Dono autem dari dicitur, quia per fidem obtingit, quæ est donum DEI, ut diximus supra 16.

Λαμβάνοντες.

Id est, qui voluerunt accipere, & sic acceperunt re- ipsa: sic & Joh. I. 12.

Gratia illa abundanter bona non consistit in be- nevola voluntatis divinæ patefactione, sed est ipsa gratia justificationis, quod ex mera gratia & mi- sericordia impium DEUS, dummodo credit, ju- stificet. Quæ annunciatur quidem in Evangelio, Act. XIII. 38. sed non est ipsa Evangelii annuncia- tio, quam amplectimur per fidem: uti donum il- lud ex gratia redundans abundantissima, donum justitiæ, vel justitiam abundantissimam signifi- cat, quam nobis offert per Verbum DEUS. Fi- des ergo hic per λῆψιν seu receptionem & appre- hensionem gratiæ & justitiæ Christi, quæ dono datur & imputatur nobis, describitur. Quæ Pa- pistæ penitus pervertunt, gratiam in justitiam in- hærentem, & abundantiam donationis seu justitiæ donatæ, justitiam abundantissimam dono nobis da- tam, de qua abundantiore justitia Matth. V. 20. convertentes in abundantiam donorum infusorum, prorsus contra mentem Apostoli, tum in paralle- lo, Eph. II. 7. ubi περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος explicat per ὑπερβάλλοντα πλοῦτον τῆς χάριτος: Tum in aliis Scripturæ dictis, quibus nō tantum περισσείαν do- norum, sed tantum primitias Spiritus nos accipere docet Rom. IIX. 23. & magna infirmitate ob carnis reliquias laborare testatur Rom. VII. 14. sqq. Gal. V. 17. Adde quod v. 20. satis luculentum sit, quæ- nam hic sit περισσεία χάριτος, ubi abundavit de- lictum, ibi ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις. Quod utique de inhærente justitia explicari non posse, liquet.

Ἐν ζωῇ βασιλεύσουσι.

Duo magna dicit & hominibus gratissima, vitam & regnum, sive immortalitatem & summos honores. Vide 1. Cor. IV. 8. 2. Tim. II. 12. Apoc. V. 20. XX. 4. XXII. 5.

διὰ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ.

Per vitæ principem. Act. III. 15. Etenim vitam il- lam æternam in tenebris latentem primus apertam fecit, primus eam est consecutus: idem etiam novam de se natu- ram trahentibus eam conferet.

Fideles acceptantes gratiam abundantissi- mam DEI, & abundantissimam justitiam Chri- sti, quæ dono datur ex gratia, regnant in vita, tum in regno gratiæ in vita spirituali, tum in regno gloriæ in vita æterna ac cœlesti, per Chri- stum, qui nos fecit reges DEO Ap. I. 6. cap. V. 10. Quod longe majus est bonam, quod à Christo redū- dat, quam erat malum, quod ab Adamo est profe- ctum. Ille enim tantum mortem in posteros cum peccato propagavit; Christus autem non tantum à peccato & morte nos liberat, passione & morte sua, sed vitam etiam cœlestem, beatam, & re- gnum gloriæ, quæ bona Adam non habuit, no- bis acquisivit obedientia & justitia sua. Quod meritum Christi obliterare, quantum in ipso est, cum Pelagio & Socino non veretur Grotius, Chri- sto nihil amplius hic tribuens, quam vitæ æternæ primam annunciationem, & aditum primum, vel quod eandem primum consequutus sit, adeoque exemplo suo nobis præiverit. Quod utrumque falsum est; Nam annunciata vita æterna est jam olim; & per Prophetas prædicata: neque pri- mus vitam æternam quoad ordinem temporis adiit Christus, quum Enoch & Elias in vitam æternam anima & corpore translati sint, & si Grotium au- dias, forte etiam plures; ut taceam, quod nulla hic exempli ratio locum habeat. Christus enim fuit expers peccati & perfecte Sanctus, quales nulli alii sunt, unde ad ejus instar & exemplum nulli in- gressuri essent cœlum, si propria innocentia & sanctitate id ingredi deberemus. Quod vero Chri- stus nobis vitam æternam confert, id commune ipsi est cum Patre & Spiritu S. nec ad meritum Christi pertinet: quemadmodum etiam regeneratio nostra opus est S. S. Trinitatis commune, non Christo proprium. Nascimur enim ex DEO Job. I. 13. & ex Spiritu Joh. III. 5.

## 5:18
Verse 18. Therefore then.

Here, after a long parenthesis, in which he incidentally showed a certain disparity in the comparison he had instituted, he returns to that which he had begun to say above in verse 12. 'Therefore' is that of one repeating an interrupted discourse. You have a similar hyperbaton and repetition of a discourse begun through 'therefore' in Philippians II. 1. 5.

As by one trespass unto all men unto condemnation.

Supply 'it came to pass', the matter proceeded. The Hebrews, when they designate some state, which 'unto' signifies, place it in place of the nominative, as Gen. II. 20. 'they shall be unto one flesh'. And 1 Cor. XV. 45. 'it became unto a living soul': whence also the Syriac translated this 'unto condemnation' and what will follow 'unto justification' by nominatives.

so also through one righteous act.

That is, of obedience, as he now explains: he calls that obedience of Christ through the whole time of his life even unto death by the singular number δικαίωμα, on account of its uniform tenor, as we said above 16.

Unto all men.

Understand all who themselves believe as is fitting, which is the beginning, as we have said, of the new nature.

Unto justification of life.

There comes to them a liberation from sins, which liberation is the cause of eternal life. The genitive among our writers, from Hebraism, has various meanings. Here it is a designator of the thing effected.

There is no parenthesis here: everything stands correctly without it, nor is that comparison alien to the Apostle's treatment, but it makes for it in the highest degree; indeed, it pertains to both the explanation and the confirmation of the principal theme. Nor, therefore, was this comparison made incidentally, but of set purpose and diligently. The Ἄρα here is rather that of one inferring than of one repeating and returning to previous matters; for he concludes from those things which the Apostle has already treated, and here he completes the demonstration of his theme from that most elegant antithesis of Adam and Christ; i.e., therefore, as through the transgression of one (Evil or guilt or τὸ κρῖμα guilt, which is gathered from the preceding) upon all men (it came) unto condemnation, so through the righteousness of one (a benefit, or a gift, or τὸ χάρισμα) upon all men it came, unto justification of life. In what way Adam and Christ are opposed to one another, the παράπτωμα or transgression of the former, the δικαίωμα or satisfaction of the latter; from the former arises the κρῖμα or judgment, the guilt and communion of the Adamic transgression; but from the latter redounds the χάρισμα or gratuitous benefit; the gift and imputation of satisfaction. Finally, there are compared the κατάκριμα or eternal condemnation arising from the judgment, and the justification of life redounding to us from the gift of righteousness, by which we are liberated from sins and rendered heirs of eternal life. The interpretation of the Syriac, and the observation of Grotius, can easily be admitted here; yet that which I have stated is fuller, and simpler and more convenient. For the Syrian has it thus: As through the transgression of one comes condemnation to all sons of men; So through the righteousness of one is justification of life unto all sons of men: by which reasoning that which is held in the following verse is expressly brought forward as a cause, why both condemnation through the transgression of one, and justification of life through the δικαίωμα of one, arose, because, to wit, by the disobedience of one many are constituted sinners, and on the contrary by the obedience of one many are constituted righteous. However, the δικαίωμα did not redound unto all for justification by reason of actual justification, but by reason of merit and the acquisition of salvation; because for actual justification and the fruition of salvation, faith is necessary. Furthermore, δικαίωμα is defined by the Philosopher in V. Eth. Nicom. c. 7. the correction of an injury, which is either active, which is done through a legitimate action and the execution of a judicial sentence, or passive, which is done through satisfaction, when the guilty party who committed the injury pays the due penalties. To which pertains that of Michael of Ephesus in chapter 19 of the Ethics: δικαιώεσθαι is said to receive justice, and it is said of one receiving that which was taken from him by an unjust person, and it is said also of him who is punished by law. Satisfaction in general is that performance which frees the debtor of a penalty from the penalty; or by which as much is done as is sufficient to correct the injury, just as penal satisfaction is the payment of a penalty, which is done by suffering for the transgression, or to extinguish the obligation which was from the transgression. Therefore, since it is a question here of the δικαίωμα of our Christ performed in our place, there is no doubt that his satisfaction is expressed by this name; so that consequently here in verse 18, the meritorious cause of absolution from sins, which occurs in our justification, is designated as a δικαίωμα or satisfaction, and in verse 19 the meritorious cause of the imputation of righteousness is subjoined.

of Christ, which likewise is in justification, is named the obedience of Christ. Certainly, just as by the merit of the Adamic transgression, by force of the law, judgment came upon all unto condemnation, so by the merit of the satisfaction of Christ, not for one sin only, but for all sins, according to the Gospel, the imputation of the satisfaction of Christ is procured for all unto justification or absolution from sins, so that they may obtain eternal life: and just as by the merit of the disobedience of Adam all were constituted sinners and unjust, by force of divine justice, the disobedience of Adam being imputed to all, so also by the merit of the obedience of Christ, by force of the divine gracious will, all can and ought to be constituted just, the obedience of Christ being imputed to them. Therefore, τὸ δικαίωμα and ἡ ὑπακοή are not simply the same, because by the former penal satisfaction is designated, but by the latter the fulfillment of the law (for Christ performed both for us for the sake of our justification): Conf. Our Königsberg disputations concerning the truth of the satisfaction of Christ. Elegantly Augustine, book II, on original sin, ch. 2: In the case of these two men the Christian faith properly consists, since through one we were sold under sin, through the other we are redeemed from sins (which is the satisfaction performed by passion and death), since the former destroyed us in himself by doing his own will, not His by whom he was made; the latter saved us in himself by not doing his own will, but His by whom he was sent; which is the active obedience of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἄρα ὖν.

Hic post longam παρενθηκην, in qua obiter institutæ comparationis disparitatem ostendit quandam, redit ad id, quod dicere cœperat supra 12. ἄρα est repetentis interru- ptum sermonem. Simile hyperbatum & repetitionem ser- monis inchoati per ἄρα habes Philipp. II. 1. 5.

Ὡς δι᾽ ἑνὸς παραπτώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπες εἰς κατάκριμα.

Supple ἐγένετο res processit. Hebræi, ubi statum aliquem designant, quod valet εἰς, ponunt vice nominativi ut Gen. II. 20. ἔσονται εἰς σάρκα μίαν. Et 1. Cor. XV. 45. ἐγένετο εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν: unde & hoc εἰς κατάκριμα & quod sequetur εἰς δικαίωσιν Syrus per Nominativos transtulit.

ὕτω καὶ δι᾽ ἑνὸς δικαιώματος.

Id est, ὑπακοῆς, ut jam explicat: eam obedientiam Chri- sti per omne vitæ tempus ad mortem usque vocat singulari numero δικαίωμα, ob uniformem ejus tenorem, ut diximus supra 16.

Εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους.

Intellige omnes, qui ipsi sicut oportet credunt, quod ini- tium est, ut diximus, novæ naturæ.

Εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς.

Evenit eis liberatio à peccatis, quæ liberatio causa est vitæ æternæ. Genitivus apud nostros scriptores ex He- braismo varias significationes habet. Hic rei effectæ de- signativus est.

Nulla hic παρενθήκη: omnia recte se habent absque ea, nec aliena est à tractatione Apostoli illa comparatio, sed maxime ad eam facit, imo ad the- matis principalis tum explicationem tum confirma- tionem pertinet. Neque obiter ergo, sed ex insti- tuto & sedulo facta est hæc comparatio. Ἄρα hic po- tius est inferentis, quam repetentis, & ad priora re- deuntis; Nam concludit ex iis, quæ jam pertra- ctavit Apostolus, atque demonstrationem hic conficit sui thematis ex illa ἀντιθέσει elegantissima Adami & Christi; h. m. ergo sicut per unius delictum (Malum vel reatus aut τὸ κρῖμα reatus, quod è su- perioribus colligitur) super omnes homines (venit) in condemnationem, ita per unius justitiam (bene- ficium, vel donum vel τὸ χάρισμα) super omnes homines venit, ad justificationem vitæ. Quo pacto opponuntur sibi Adam & Christus, illius παράπτω- μα delictum, hujus δικαίωμα satisfactio; ex illo or- tum κρῖμα vel judicium, delicti Adamici reatus & communio; ex hoc autem redundat χάρισμα vel beneficium gratuitum; satisfactionis donum & imputatio. Deniq; comparantur è judicio oriens κατάκριμα vel condemnatio & mors æterna, & è do- no justitiæ in nos redundans justificatio vitæ, qua à peccatis liberamur, & vitæ æternæ hæredes reddi- mur. Syri autem interpretatio, & Grotii obser- vatio admitti hic facile potest; plenior tamen illa est, quam dixi, & simplicior ac convenientior. Sy- rus enim ita habet: Sicut per unius delictum fit condemnatio omnibus filiis hominum; Sic per unius justitiam est justificatio vitæ in omnes filios homi- num: qua ratione id, quod versu sequenti habe- tur, causæ instar expresse adducitur, cur & con- demnatio per unius delictum, & justificatio vitæ per unius δικαίωμα orta, quia scil. peccatores con- stituuntur per unius inobedientiam multi, & contra per obedientiam unius multi constituuntur justi. Non autem in omnes redundavit δικαίωμα ad ju- stificationem ratione actualis justificationis, sed ratione meriti & acquisitionis salutis; quia ad actualem justificationem, & salutis fruitionem opus est fide. Cæterum δικαίωμα definitur à Philosopho V. Eth. Nicom. c. 7. ἐπανόρθωμα τῆς ἀδικίας injuriæ correctio, quæ vel activa est, quæ per actionem legitimam & sententiæ judiciariæ exequutionem fit, vel passiva, quæ fit per satis- factionem, cum reus, qui injuriam fecit, pœnas de- bitas luit. Quo facit illud Mich. Ephesii in cap. 19. Ethic. δικαίζεσθαι jus accipere dicitur, & de acci- piente id, quod sibi ablatum fuit ab injusto, & dici- tur de eo quoque qui jure plectitur. Satisfactio in genere est ea præstatio, quæ debitorem pœnæ à pœna liberat; vel qua tantum fit, quantum satis est ad injuriam corrigendam, uti pœnalis satisfactio est persolutio pœnæ, quæ luendo delicto fit, vel ad perimendam obligationem, quæ fuit è delicto. Ideo cum de δικαιώματι Christi nostri loco præstito hic agatur, satisfactionem ejus hoc nomine exprimi dubiu non est; Ut proinde hic v. 18. causa meritoria absolutionis à peccatis, quæ fit in justificatione nostra, utpote δικαίωμα vel satisfactio designetur, & v. 19. subjungatur causa meritoria imputationis justitiæ

Christi, quæ itidem in justificatione sit, nominata Christi obedientia. Nimirum uti merito transgressionis Adamicæ, vi legis, judicium in omnes venit ad condemnationem, ita merito satisfactionis Christi non pro uno tantum peccato, sed pro omnibus peccatis, secundum Evangelium, imputatio satisfactionis Christi omnibus parta est ad justificationem vel absolutionẽ à peccatis, ut vitam consequi possint æternam: & uti merito inobedientiæ Adami peccatores & injusti constituti sunt omnes, vi justitiæ divinæ, omnibus imputata Adami inobedientia, ita & merito obedientiæ Christi, vi divinæ gratiosæ voluntatis, omnes constitui possunt & debent justi imputata ipsis Christi obedientia. Non ergo simpliciter idem est τὸ δικαίωμα & ἡ ὑπακοὴ, quia per illud pœnalis satisfactio, per hanc vero legis impletio (utramque enim pro nobis præstitit Christus justificationis nostræ causa) designatur: Conf. Disputationes nostræ Regiomontanæ de veritate satisfactionis Christi. Eleganter August. l. II. de peccat. orig. c. 2. In horum duorum hominum causa proprie fides Christiana consistit, quum per unum venundati sumus sub peccato, per alterum redimamur à peccatis (quæ est satisfactio passione & morte præstita) quum ille nos in se perdidit faciendo voluntatem suam, non ejus, à quo factus est; iste nos in se salvos fecit non faciendo voluntatem suam, sed ejus, à quo missus est; quæ est obedientia Christi activa.

## 5:19
V. 19. For as by the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners.

It is again a metonymy. They were treated as if they had sinned in act, namely because they were addicted to death. Thus the word sinner is taken in 1 Kings 1:21 and elsewhere. He said the many here again, when he had just said all, except perhaps one or another.

so also by the obedience of the one.

Through the perpetual obedience of Christ, consistent with his own doctrine, and rewarded by God with the highest prize. See Philippians 2:8, 9.

The many shall be constituted just.

The future for a durable present. And many, that is, believers, in such a way as it is fitting to believe. You see here that 'shall be constituted just' is the same as 'shall be justified' or 'are being justified', and with the abstract placed in place of the concrete, in the Hebrew manner, 'they become righteousness' 2 Cor. 5:21. Moreover, the passage of Isaiah 53:11 is obscurely referred to: 'By his knowledge shall my righteous servant make many righteous.' They shall be made righteous, namely before God, and consequently shall also obtain divine rewards in their own time.

A metonymy is rashly invented, and in the Socinian manner the sentence of the Apostle is perverted. The Apostle does not teach how we are treated on account of the disobedience of Adam, as Grotius does, but what kind of persons we have been constituted: namely, sinners and unjust through the imputation of the disobedience of Adam; nor is it a matter here of death, but of sin, which in this accurate treatment the Apostle has distinguished from death as a cause from an effect. The passage 1 Kings 1:21 is irrelevant. For there the particle כ can conveniently be understood, according to a custom accepted among the Hebrews: we shall be as sinners. But here there is no place for it. Moreover, πολλοὶ are here said to be absolutely those who were just now called πάντες: therefore all are to be understood, nor can any one be excepted. For there is no διαςολὴ here as in Romans 3:21; all were in the loins of Adam, all sinned in him (verse 12), therefore all were constituted sinners, and upon all condemnation came. Moreover, the obedience of Christ is not proposed to us here as being rewarded in Christ with the highest prize, but as performed for us, and imputable to us all; through which we all can be constituted just, and by the intention of the most gracious divine will, ought to be. And that is rightly said to be the future used for the durable present, and that the passage of Isaiah, which Grotius notably corrupted in his Annotations on Isaiah 53:11, is here not obscurely looked back upon. We have therefore here the justice and obedience of Christ, which is imputed to us in our justification, in the divine judgment through faith, or is apprehended with faith, just as the disobedience of Adam was imputed to his posterity. For just as here we are constituted sinners by the imputation of the disobedience of Adam, so we are constituted just by the imputation of the obedience or justice of Christ.

The Papists Bellarmine, Becanus, and others gather from this comparison that the obedience of Christ is not the formal cause of our justification, but the efficient; since the obedience of Christ is opposed to the disobedience of Adam, and as we are said to be constituted unjust through the latter, so we are said to be constituted just through the former. But we are constituted unjust through the disobedience of Adam not formally, but efficiently and meritoriously. But these are not opposites; indeed, neither could the disobedience of Adam make us unjust, nor the obedience of Christ make us just, unless we were constituted unjust by the former and just by the latter imputatively. For if the disobedience of Adam and the obedience of Christ were not imputed to us, neither that nor this would be ours. For they are singular and individual acts, and therefore proper to those by whom they are done, and personal. But for proper and personal acts to be formally common is a contradiction. And therefore it must be imputed, and consequently it is necessary that the very disobedience of Adam was imputed to his posterity, and it is no less necessary that the obedience of Christ be imputed to us. But the disobedience of Adam would not be imputed to us unless Adam had merited by his disobedience this penalty, that the disobedience should be imputed to himself for condemnation, and to all his posterity: because Adam was the one in whom the whole human race was considered to exist, and in whom it had received original justice by nature; whence the apostasy and disobedience of Adam was considered the apostasy and disobedience of the whole human race, which was in his loins, and in Adam all sinned, and thus even then, when Adam sinned, the whole human race was condemned, and made guilty of apostasy and disobedience against GOD; whence also to Augustine original sin, which we draw from Adam through carnal generation, is called the penalty of the first sin, or the disobedience of Adam. But how could the penalty of the first sin be in the posterity, unless that first sin were imputed to the posterity? And Bellarmine admits (l. IV. de amiss. grat. c. 10) that the sin of Adam is so imputed to all his posterity, as if all had committed the same sin, citing the saying of St. Bernard: The fault of Adam is ours, because although in another, we nevertheless sinned, and it was imputed to us by the just judgment of God, though secretly. Similarly, the obedience of Christ could not be imputed to us, unless Christ had merited by performing obedience to the law, that that obedience should be imputed to us, as being performed for us: because Christ was the one who was substituted in the divine judgment in our place, not only that he might pay the penalty of sin for us, and satisfy divine justice, 1 Cor. V. 14, 21, but also that he might fulfill the law for us, and perform the obedience which we could not perform, Rom. VIII. 3, ch. X. 4, Gal. IV. 6; therefore his obedience is considered the obedience of the whole human race, and when it is apprehended by us by faith, it becomes our obedience through λογισμὸν and imputation in the judgment of God, as truly as if we ourselves had performed it. Thus, therefore, Christ is the cause of our justification both efficiently and meritoriously, because he performed obedience to GOD in the place of the human race, and formally, because the obedience of Christ is imputed to our faith, and being apprehended through faith, it is reckoned as ours in the judgment of God. If you say that no one is constituted just except through inherent justice, I say to the contrary, that he is truly just before God to whom another's justice, namely Christ's, is imputed. For since this is done by GOD, it must also be truly done. We are therefore just, and truly just before GOD through this imputed justice, and indeed much more so, and much more augustly, than those who are reckoned by their own inherent justice. If with Stapleton you say that καθισθήσονται implies inherent justice, just as a servant is said to be set over all goods (Luke XII. 44) and someone is said to be constituted an enemy of GOD (Jas. IV. 4): I reply that τὸ καθισῆναι does not precisely signify something inherent, but the truth and certainty of that which is done; but that it is done in one way or another does not matter. Thus a wall is constituted white through inherent whiteness; someone is constituted Lord over goods not through inherence, but through σχέσιν; someone is constituted a friend of GOD through the affection of God loving, which inheres in GOD, not in him who is loved. Therefore, through the imputed justice of Christ we can be constituted truly just before God, and no one is constituted lord over goods or an enemy or friend of GOD more truly by his Lord. Chamier in Panstr. de justif. l. XXI. c. 2. The excellent sentiments of the Fathers pertain here, notably illustrating the Apostolic passage: Justin Martyr in expos. fid. says: Since by this sin Adam subjected the human race to death, and rendered all nature liable to debt, the Son, being GOD and man, revoked and abolished the transgression and fall of Adam, and insofar as he was man, he lived a life without crime innocently, and underwent voluntary death, by his highest and exact conduct indeed obliterating the fall, covering it so that it might not be seen, but by his unmerited death extinguishing the debt. The same in Epist. ad Diognet. What else could cover our sins than his justice? In whom else could we wicked and impious ones BE ACCOUNTED JUST, than in the Son of GOD alone: O sweet exchange! O unsearchable artifice! O benefits exceeding all expectation! so that the iniquity of many is indeed hidden in one just man, but the justice of one causes many unjust men to be held as JUST. Irenaeus, book V, against heresies, chapter XIV. For by dissolving the disobedience of man which had been made from the beginning in the tree, he was made obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross, healing that disobedience which had been in the tree. Whom we offended in the first Adam by not doing his commandment, in the second Adam we have been reconciled, being made obedient even unto death: which is explained in C. XV concerning the donation of the justice of Christ: He gives to us, he says, that which is for our easier conversation and subjection. Ambrose on 2 Cor. IV. 1. As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. For Adam is the form of death, the cause of sin, but Christ is the form of life on account of justice. Cyril of Alexandria, Vol. III, book on the right faith to the Queen: It is absurd that we, indeed, having been made heirs of the punishment of our first parent, with corruption having been introduced through disobedience, should not also become participants in the justice of the second, who brings us back to life through that greatest obedience. Therefore, when Scripture says that by the obedience of one many have been justified, let us not say that a man simply like us was left to this, but rather the Son, incarnate and made obedient to the Father for us. And book XI on John, c. 25. Just as in the transgression of the first man, as in the first-fruits of our race we were addicted to death, hearing in that first one, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall return,' in the same way I also think that through the obedience and justice of Christ, in as much as he subjects himself to the law, although he was the author of the law, the blessing and vivification, which is through the spirit unto life, penetrated our nature. Item l. XII. c. 16. Just as condemnation penetrated into all through the first Adam; so the blessing of the justified Christ has been extended through one to all. Paul testifies to this, saying: For just as through the transgression of one into all men unto condemnation, so also through the righteousness of one into all men unto justification of life: We were therefore sick through the first Adam with the disease of disobedience and curse, but we have been enriched through the second Adam through obedience and blessing.

For the author of the law as God, kept the mandates of the law as man. Athanasius on the incarnation of the Word. It is impossible for purity and innocence to be exhibited in human nature, unless God is believed to be in the flesh, who introduced into the world righteousness free from all sin, of which because we have been rendered PARTICIPANTS, we shall live and be saved: For that saying, there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin, pertains in common to all men. Whence he descended from heaven, who was about to give IMMACULATE righteousness from himself. The same against those who afflict our race with damage because he denies that the Savior took the firstfruits from our nature. It is necessary, and most necessary, to believe the Scripture. S. to confess the firstfruits from our race, to celebrate the singular Love of the one assuming into the human race, to be astonished at the miracle of the great economy and dispensation, not to fear the execration of the law, (for Christ freed us from the curse of the law) TO ASCRIBE THE FULFILLMENT OF THE LAW made from the firstfruits (Christ) TO THE WHOLE MASS, λογίζεσθαι TO IMPUTE. Gregory of Nyssa orat. II. on the Canticles. Christ, with the filth of my sins TRANSFERRED INTO HIMSELF, COMMUNICATED HIS PURITY to me, and made me a PARTICIPANT of the beauty which is in him. St. Augustine T. IX. tract. III. on John. All who are from Adam with sin, are sinners; all who are justified through Christ, are just not in themselves, but in HIM, for if you ask in themselves, they are Adam, if you ask in him, they are Christ's. The same Serm. VI. on the words of the Apostle. T. X. Christ himself, who had not known sin, God the Father made sin for us, that we might be the righteousness OF GOD in him: see two things, THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD, not OURS, in HIM, not in US. Item Tom. XIII. on the words to Laurent. C. XL. He himself therefore is sin, that we might be righteousness, and not ours, but GOD'S; and not in us, but in him. Just as he himself is sin, not his own, but ours, and not in himself, but in us. And T. IIX. in Enarr. Ps. XXX. Conc. I. in your righteousness rescue me, and strip me. Because you did not find my righteousness in me, rescue me in yours, that is, let that rescue me, which justifies me, which makes the impious pious, which makes the unjust just. Add what he has in Ep. XXIII. to Boniface. From Adam we contracted guilt, because we were in Adam, when he sinned. Chrysostom hom. X. on chapter V. to the Romans. For this reason, insisting upward and downward on this word ONE, he brings it constantly into the middle, when he says: Just as through one man sin entered into the world; and, if by the sin of one many died; and, not as through one who had sinned, had death come, so also the gift; and, judgment from the transgression of one unto condemnation, and again, for just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, nor does he desist: so that when the Jew says to you, In what way by one king acting, Christ, the whole world was made safe? you may be able to answer him: In what way by one Adam disobeying

the whole world was condemned? Leo I. Epist. LXX. to Juvenal. But in order to repair the life of all, he received the cause of all, and the force of the old handwriting, which he alone among all did not owe, by paying for all he emptied, so that just as through the transgression of one all had been made sinners, so through the righteousness of one all might be made INNOCENT, righteousness flowing thence into men, where human nature was assumed. Anselm on chapter V. to the Romans. Through the righteousness of one coming into all elect men, it went into justification, so that by PARTICIPATION IN THE RIGHTEOUSNESS of Christ they might be justified. Bernard Ep. CXC. to Innocent. Man who owed, man who pays. For if one, he says, died for all, then all are dead, so that clearly the satisfaction of one might be IMPUTED to all, just as that one bore the sins of all. Item: What could man, a servant of sin, bound by the devil, do of himself to repair the RIGHTEOUSNESS once lost? Therefore, an ALIEN righteousness was assigned to him, who lacked his own. And serm. to the knights of the temple cap. XI. Death is put to flight in the death of Christ, and Christ's righteousness is IMPUTED to us. And further: one sinned, and all are held GUILTY. And shall the INNOCENCE of one be REPUTED to one alone? Did the sin of one work death for all, and shall the RIGHTEOUSNESS of one restore life to one? Therefore did the righteousness of GOD avail more to condemn than to restore? Or could Adam do more in evil, than Christ in good? Shall Adam's sin be imputed to me, and shall Christ's RIGHTEOUSNESS not pertain to me?

PART III.

Preparatory, reminding concerning the cause of the law that entered in.

Latin:

V. 19. Ὥσπερ γὰρ διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς τῶ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπω ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεσάθησαν οἱ πολλοὶ.

Est rursus μετωνυμία. Ita tractati sunt, quasi peccassent actu, nempe quia addicti sunt morti. Sic vox peccatoris sumitur 1. Regum I. 21. & alibi. Πολλοὶ hic rursum dixit, cum modo dixerit πάντας omnes, excepto forte uno aut altero.

ὅτω καὶ διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τῶ ἑνὸς.

Per obedientiam Christi perpetuam, doctrinæ ipsius congruentem, & à DEO repensatam summo præmio. Vide Philipp. II. 8. 9.

Δίκαιοι κατασήσονται οἱ πολλοὶ.

Futurum pro præsente durabili. Et multi, id est, credentes, sic ut credi oportet. Vides hic δίκαιοι κατασήσονται idem esse quod δικαιωθήσονται aut δικαιῦνται, & posito abstracto vice concreti, more Hebræo, δικαιοσύνη γίγνονται II. Cor. V. 21. Respicitur autem non obscure locus Esaiæ LIII. 11. Per sui notitiam justos faciet justus servus meus multos. Justi fient nempe apud Deum, ac proinde & divina præmia suo tempore consequentur.

Temere fingitur μετωνυμία, & more Sociniano pervertitur sententia Apostoli.
