V. 5. εἰ γὰρ σύμφυτοι γεγόναμεν τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ.

Græcis συμφύεσθαι dicuntur, quæ in unum coalescunt, ut plantæ quædam Luc. VIII. 7. unde sumta translatione de amicitia usurpatur apud Platonem ac Plutarchum. Er- go αὐτοῦ hic subauditur ex sequente Genitivo αὐτοῦ, ut sæpe. Coaluimus Christo, ad instar ejus mortui, nempe cupiditatibus, ut ille vitæ functionibus.

ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐσόμεθα.

Nempe σύμφυτοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς ἀναστά- σεως. Ita instar ejus resurgemus. Prior similitudo est ge- neris, hæc speciei, sive generis proximi. Ubi rebus molestis opponuntur solatia, usurpari solent particulæ εἰ & ἀλλά. Sic apud Virgilium:

Si non ingentem foribus domus alta superbis, Mane salutantum totis vomit ædibus undam. Post versus deinde aliquot sequitur: At secura quies & nescia fallere vita Discs opum variarum &c.

Confirmatur ab Apostolo ea, quæ de Ba- ptismi fine dixerat, quia in Baptismo nos mortis Christi ὁμοιώματι reddimur σύμφυτοι, ideo & re- surrectionis ejus. Alludit Apostolus ad institionem vel implantationem nostri, qua Christo inserimur, per Baptismum, ceu arbori vitæ Ap. XXII. v. 11. & viti veræ Joh. XV. 1. 5. atque olivæ Rom. XI. 17. 18. 19. & ex ipso spiritualem succum haurimus, ut conformes ipsi reddamur, in morte & resurrectio- ne: & colligit Apostolus: Si Christo implantati sumus, ut simus ipsi similes in morte, etiam implan- tati erimus ei, ut similes ipsi simus in resurrectione. Chrysost. hic habet: Plantationis nomine fructum, quem ex ea accepimus significat. Quemadmodum enim corpus Christi in terra sepultum fructum at- tulit, orbis salutem: ita & nostrum in Baptisimate sepultum fructum attulit justitiam, sanctificationem, adoptionem & alia innumera bona, feret autem & postremo resurrectionis donum.

## 6:6
V. 6. τοῦτο γινώσκοντες.

Let us only think on this and fix it in our mind. We have noted that γινώσκειν and similar words are sometimes used in this way at John 15:18.

ὅτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη.

He proceeds to take many likenesses from the cross, death, and resurrection of Christ and to adapt to them allegorical types of speech: which itself is called עש ר by the Hebrews. The old man here and in Eph. 4:22, Col. 3:9 is the subject for the adjunct, for the old humanity, that old way of living in man, which is also called nature. To this metonymy Paul also added personification, in which he delights greatly. For he attributes to an inanimate thing, that is, to an accident, that which belongs to living beings. He says that that old nature was co-crucified, that is, crucified after the likeness of Christ: because just as one arrives at the end through the cross not without grievous pain, so that nature is not extinguished without pain. For self-love and thence the appetite for pleasures is innate to man: then long habit is something hard to wash away. But faith overcomes these difficulties.

There is certainly an analogy and a certain likeness between the crucifixion of Christ and the crucifixion of the old man. But the particle σὺν does not denote likeness, but simultaneity, so to speak, and communion: that we ought to know that when Christ was crucified, our old man, or sin, was also crucified at the same time: because He had taken our sin upon Himself, so that sin might be nailed to the cross with Him also, for He bore sin to the wood of the cross (1 Pet. 2), and by that very act He destroyed sin, by taking away from sin both its condemnatory power, or power to mortify us, and by acquiring for us the power to mortify sin; both of which By his crucifixion Christ merited that he not only obtained for us the remission of sins, but also the gift of the Holy Spirit, by whose power our true man might be mortified. Therefore our old man is said to have been crucified with him. Cocceius, however, observes here in his Commentary, p. 313, that it is not for nothing that the Apostle mentions crucifixion in this place, not content to have denoted death as the cause of the death by which we die to sin. Indeed, crucifixion provides a manifest argument that Christ bore the curse, Gal. III. 13. Through crucifixion, therefore, all that which is from the curse and which confirms the curse has been abolished. Man, as he is born, is born under a curse, and therefore is born depraved and evil and a slave of sin. But crucifixion took away the curse. For reconciliation was made through it for those who were given to Christ and joined with him. Therefore, through crucifixion it has been brought about that our old man must be abolished. Now sin is called παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος partly by reason of its origin, which is so ancient, because it draws its rise from Adam after he fell into sin. Because man's first condition is to be born in sin, therefore it is called old: partly by reason of the deformation of the faculties and parts of man, which is so great that he is considered as another man if he is compared with man in the state of integrity or renewal, even though by reason of substance there is no diversity: such as the Manichaeans and Flacians dreamed of; τὸ μετὰ ὑποκείμενον, Chrysost. in ch. IV to the Ephes. αὐτὸ δὲ μεταβολὴ κατὰ τὸ συμβεβηκός. We defend, says Tertullian, l. de resurrect. carn., that the oldness and newness of man pertain to a moral, not a substantial difference.

ἵνα καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας.

Καταργεῖν, here is to kill, as the following words show. A body is said to be killed when it is despoiled of life, Matt. X. 28. But Paul elegantly attributes a body to sin, that is, to the habit of sinning, because it is like a certain structure consisting of many members, that is, vices, Col. III. 5. Thus he also attributes a body to death below: A flock, a people, a legion are bodies among the Jurisconsults, and the body of the state in Livy, the Body of colleges in Gaius the Jurisconsult. Cicero also transferred it to inanimate things when he said the body of books in Latin and Greek σῶμα. But the translation is bolder where a body is given to accidents, just as Virgil said the body of the kingdom.

τῷ μηκέτι δυλεύειν ἡμᾶς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ.

Τῷ for ἕνεκα τῦ, as often elsewhere. Therefore, that we may not henceforth serve sin or a vicious habit, as we served before, δυλεύειν to serve, is a word of middle signification. For we are said to serve GOD, Matt. VI. 24, Acts XX. 19, Eph. VI. 7, 1 Thess. I. 9, and Christ below XIV. 18, XVI. 18, Coloss. III. 24, and the law of GOD below VII. 25, and righteousness, below VI. 19, and on the contrary Mammon, Matt. VI. 24, Idols, Gal. IV. 19, pleasures and desires, Tit. III. 3, impurity, VI. 19, corruption, 2 Pet. II. § 19. Thus also in Latin we say to serve life, health, posterity, the interests of the people, dignity: and on the contrary love, desires, anger. Seneca: The mind, once moved and shaken, serves that by which it is impelled.

He says body of sin, because he had said the old man; the body of sin, therefore, not substantially as the Flacians wanted, nor only collectively, as Grotius, since body is the same as a multitude; but metaphorically, he points it out with an analogy to the old man: just as by the same similitude he also attributes members to sin, namely vices of various kinds, both because they exert themselves through the various faculties and members of man, and because a heterogeneous body is constituted from them, and because it exerts various operations, and those so great and such, as if it were a certain living body, and subsisting by itself, Col. III. 4. But the old man was crucified with Christ for this reason, that not this or that sin only might be abolished, but the whole body of sin with all its members, so that henceforth we may not serve any sin, for thus sin is abolished, as far as dominion is concerned, when one does not serve it. It is destroyed, says Anselm and the interlinear Gloss, not so that it does not exist, but so that we are not compelled to serve.

Latin:

V. 6. τοῦτο γινώσκοντες.

Modo hoc cogitemus & infigamus animo. Sic γινώσκειν ἡμῖν, & voces similes interdum sumi notavimus ad Joh. XV. 18.

ὅτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη.

Pergit ex cruce, morte & resurrectione Christi multas sumere similitudines & eis aptare ἀλληγορικὰ loquendi ge- nera: quod ipsum עש ר dicitur Hebræis ὁ παλαιὸς ἄνθρω- πος hic & Eph. IV. 22. III. 9. est subjectum pro adjuncto, pro ἡ παλαιὰ ἀνθρωπότης, vetus illa in homine vivendi ratio, quæ & natura dicitur. Ad hanc μετωνυμίαν adjun- xit Paulus & προσωποποιΐαν, qua delectatur plurimum. Tri- buit enim rei inanimatæ, id est, accidenti id, quod est ani- matorum. Veterem illam naturam concrucifixam dicit, id est, ad similitudinem Christi crucifixam: quia sicut per crucem non sine gravi dolore ad exitum pervenitur, ita illa natura sine dolore non extinguitur. Est enim sui amor & inde voluptatum appetitus agnatus homini: deinde longa consuetudo δυσέκνιπτόν τι. Sed has difficultates fi- des superat.

Datur omnino analogia & similitudo quædam crucifixionis Christi, & crucifixionis veteris homi- nis. Sed particula σὺν non similitudinem notat, verum simultatem, ut ita dicam & communionem: quod cum Christus crucifixus est, simul etiam ve- terem nostrum hominem, vel peccatum crucifi- xum esse, scire debeamus: quia peccatum no- strum in se susceperat, ut cruci affigeretur cum ipso etiam peccatum, attulit enim peccatum in lignum crucis 1. Petr. II. eoque ipso peccatum destruxit, peccato & vim condemnatoriam seu nos mortificandi adimendo, & vim mortifican- di peccatum nobis acquirendo; quod utrumque crucifixione sua promeruit Christus, quod non modo remissionem peccatorum nobis impetra- vit, sed etiam Spiritus S. donationem, cujus vir- tute verus noster homo mortificetur. Ideo ve- tus noster homo cum ipso crucifixus dicitur. Ob- servat autem hic Coccejus in Comment. p. 313. non de nihilo esse, quod Apostolus crucifixionem hoc in loco memorat, non contentus mortem denotasse causam mortis, qua morimur peccato. Nempe cru- cifixio manifestum argumentum præbet, quod Chri- stus exsecrationem tulerit Gal. III. 13. Per crucifi- xionem igitur id omne abolitum est, quod est ab execratione & quod execrationem confirmat. Ho- mo, ut nascitur, sub execratione nascitur, & ideo pravus malusque nascitur ac servus peccati. Atqui crucifixio abstulit exsecrationem. Reconciliatio enim per eam facta est eorum, qui Christo dati sunt & cum ipso conjuncti. Ergo per crucifixionem est effectum, ut veterem hominem nostrum aboleri opor- teat. Vocatur autem peccatum παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος partim ratione originis, tam annosæ, quia ab Ada- mo postquam lapsus in peccatum est, ortum tra- hit. Quia prima hominis conditio est nasci in peccato; ideo vetus dicitur: partim ratione insi- gnis facultatum & partium hominis deformationis, quæ tanta est, ut velut alius homo censeatur, si cum homine in statu integritatis vel renovationis con- feratur, tametsi substantiæ ratione nulla sit diversi- tas: qualem Manichæi & Flaciani somniârunt; τὸ μετὰ ὑποκείμενον, Chrysost. in cap. IV. ad Ephes. αὐτὸ δὲ μεταβολὴ κατὰ τὸ συμβεβηκός. Vetusta- tem & novitatem hominis, inquit Tertull. l. de re- surrect. carn. ad moralem non ad substantialem differentiam pertinere defendimus.

ἵνα καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας.

Καταργεῖν, hic est occidere, ut ostendunt sequentia. Oc- cidi dicitur corpus, cum vita spoliatur Matth. X. 28. Cor- pus autem peccato, id est, consuetudini peccandi elegan- ter tribuit Paulus, quia est veluti compages quædam mul- tis constans membris, id est, vitiis, Col. III. 5. Sic & morti corpus infra tribuit: Grex, populus, legio apud Juriscon- sultos corpora sunt, & corpus civitatis apud Livium, col- legiorum Corpus apud Cajum Jurisconsultum. Transti- lit & ad inanimata Cicero, cum dixit librorum corpus La- tine & Græce σῶμα. Sed audacior est translatio, ubi acci- dentibus datur corpus, quomodo Virgilius dixit corpus regni.

τῷ μηκέτι δυλεύειν ἡμᾶς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ.

Τῷ pro ἕνεκα τῦ, ut sæpe alibi. Ideo ne posthac pecca- to sive consuetudini vitiosæ serviamus, sicut ante serviimus, δυλεύειν servire, vox est mediæ significationis. Nam & DEO dicimur servire Matth. VI. 24. Act. XX. 19. Eph. VI. 7. 1. Thess. I. 9. & Christo infra XIV. 18. XVI. 18. Co- loss. III. 24. & legi DEI infra VII. 25. & justitiæ, infra VI. 19. & contra Mammonæ Matth. VI. 24. Idolis Gal. IV. 19. voluptatibus & cupiditatibus Tit. III. 3. impuritati VI. 19. corruptioni 2. Petr. II. § 19. Sic & Latine dicimus servire vitæ, valetudini, posteritati, populi commodis, di- gnitati: & contra amori, cupiditatibus, iracundiæ. Seneca: Commota semel & concussa mens ei servit à quo impellitur.

Corpus peccati dicit, quod veterem hominem dixerat; Corpus ergo peccati non substantialiter uti Flaciani volebant, neque collective tantum, ut Grotius, cum corpus idem est, quod multitudo; sed metaphorice, cum analogia ad veterem hominem indigitat: quemadmodum eadem similitudine membra etiam peccato tribuit, varii nempe generis vitia, tum quod per diversas facultates & membra hominis sese exerunt, tum quod corpus heterogeneum ex iisdem constituatur, tum quod variis operationibus easque tantas ac tales exserat, ac si esset corpus quoddam vivum, & per se subsistens Col. III. 4. Ideo autem cum Christo crucifixus est homo vetus, ut aboleatur non hoc vel illud tantum peccatum, sed totum peccati corpus cum omnibus membris suis, ut posthac non ser- viamus ulli peccato, nam ita aboletur peccatum, quantum ad dominium, quando non servitur ei- dem. Destruitur, inquit Anshelmus & Glossa in- terlin. non ut non sit, sed ne nos cogamur servire.

## 6:7
V. 7. ὁ γὰρ ἀποθανὼν δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.

That is, he is free from sin, or he no longer serves sin. For it is not for the dead to sin. The Syriac rightly translates here with Basil, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylact, he has been freed from sin. For in that sense, as we said in the Prolegomena, δικαιοῦσθαι is very often used in this Epistle, as also Acts XIII. 38, 39. Peter said in the same sense πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας 1 Pet. IV. 1. But it is a metaphor here from like to like: for he who is dead is not properly justified, that is, cleansed or made righteous, and not even freed, if we follow the propriety of the words: but because it is true that he no longer serves sin, therefore he is said to be freed first, then also justified by metonymy: thus the best writers say that he who is dead is free from hatred, envy, disease, troubles. Thus death is called medicinal by Aeschylus, because, as he himself explains: Οὐδὲν ἄλγος ἅπτεται νεκρῶν. Thus also Euripides: Θανὼν ἄν εἴη μᾶλλον εὐτυχέστερος. Moreover, this sentiment of Paul, like many others, is taken from the sayings of the Rabbis. For in the Talmud we have: כיון שארם מת נעשה חפשי מן המצות that is, As soon as a man is dead, he is made free from the commandments. If free from the commandments, also free from sin. Paul, however, adapts this by way of an underlying meaning to him who has died to sin, as he spoke above in verse 2. The dead do not return to their former life. Thus, neither should he who has truly died to sin return to his former life.

Some indeed explain this sentiment of the Apostle as referring to natural death, and there is no doubt for us that there is an allusion to natural death, because in it we are freed from sin, whence we not inappropriately use this aphorism, that after death sin is no longer required of the reborn, nor any punishment, because he who has died in faith is justified and freed from sin, as can be urged from the similarities of the protasis or the foundation of the metaphor, or the similarity, which is gathered from the apodosis or the use of the metaphor, namely in what third respect it is applied. However, it seems here, as far as the present subject is concerned, that that aphorism, 'he who has died is justified from sin,' directly concerns that spiritual death by which one has died to sin, of which the Apostle had treated in verse 2. Therefore, just as those who depart in faith are justified from both the guilt and the punishment of sin, and are raised to eternal salvation, so those who die to sin are justified from sin and are constituted heirs of eternal life: not that the death of sin is the cause of justification, but that they are connected by an inseparable bond, nor does anyone die to sin unless he is justified from sin, and that dying to sin is proper to the justified in the fourth mode, as they call it. But that does not exhaust the force of the Apostolic aphorism, nor does it suit the simplicity of the Apostolic diction, that he who is naturally dead no longer serves sin (for he no longer serves righteousness in this age either, indeed he produces no operations in this age, being deprived of light and life, Ps. 6:6), and is to that extent freed from sin, and by a transfer of terms said to be justified: nor do those things have any relevance in this place, that he who is dead is free from hatred, nor is it in any way true or likely that Paul drew these things from the sayings of the Rabbis or the Talmud, much less many other things; since it is established by no document that those Talmudic writings already existed or were held in esteem in the age of the Apostle, nor is it to be believed that the Holy Spirit, by whose impulse Paul wrote, would have wished to honor the impious and blasphemous writings of the Talmud in such a way. But if these things necessarily cohere with the fact that to be justified or freed from guilt and punishment is to be and to die to sin, according to the Apostolic doctrine, by what right can the Apostolic doctrine be argued, as if it permitted those who are justified to live in sins, so that Grace may abound in them? In what sense can that suspicion of v. 2 be admitted: The dead do not return to their former life; thus neither should he who is truly dead to sin, such as those who are justified by faith, return to a former life. But that dying to sin is here understood from the crucifixion of the old Adam with Christ, which argument the Apostle still pursues and presses, is apparent: therefore he subjoins, if we have died with Christ (not certainly by natural death to sin) we shall also live with Christ.

Latin:

V. 7. ὁ γὰρ ἀποθανὼν δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.

Id est, liber est à peccato, sive non ultra servit peccato. Mortuorum enim non est peccare. Recte hic Syrus cum Basilio, Chrysostomo, Oecumenio, Theophylacto vertit liberatus est à peccato. Eo enim sensu, ut in Prolegomenis diximus, sæpissime δικαιοῦσθαι usurpatur in hac Epistola, ut & Act. XIII. 38. 39. Petrus eodem sensu dixit πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας 1. IV. 1. Est autem Metaphora hic à simili ad simile: non enim proprie justificatur, id est, mundatur aut justus fit qui est mortuus, ac ne liberatur quidem, si proprietatem verborum sectemur: sed quia verum est, eum non servire amplius peccato, ideo liberari primum, deinde per μετάληψιν etiam justificari dicitur: sic eum qui mortuus sit, liberum esse ab odio, invidia, morbo, mo- lestiis dicunt optimi scriptores. Sic mors medica dicitur Æschylo, quia, ut ipse explicat: Οὐδὲν ἄλγος ἅπτεται νεκρῶν. Sic & Euripides: Θανὼν ἄν εἴη μᾶλλον εὐτυχέστερος. Est autem hæc Pauli sententia, ut multa alia, sumpta ex dictis Rabbinorum. Nam in Thalmude habemus: כיון שארם מת נעשה חפשי מן המצות id est, Simul quis est mortuus, factus est liber à præceptis. Si à præceptis liber, etiam à peccato liber. Paulus autem hoc aptat per ὑπόνοιαν ei qui mortuus est peccato, ut locu- tus est supra 2. Mortui non redeunt ad vitam priorem. Sic nec qui peccato vere est mortuus, ad priorem vitam redire debet.

Sententiam hanc Apostoli, de morte naturali explicant sane nonnulli, neque dubium nobis est, alludi ad naturalem mortem, quod in ea libere- mur à peccato, unde non incommode hoc apho- rismo utimur, post mortem non amplius peccatum à renatis exigi, aut pœnam ullam, quia mortuus in fide, justificatus & liberatus est à peccato, uti è similitudinibus πρότασις vel fundamentum meta- phoræ, aut similitudinis, quod ex ἀποδόσει vel usu metaphoræ colligitur, in quonam nempe tertio adhibeatur, urgeri potest. Cæterum videtur hic, quantum ad præsentem materiam ille aphori- smus, qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato, di- recte concernere mortem illam spiritualem, qua peccato quis mortuus est, de qua v. 2. egerat Apo- stolus. Ut ergo qui in fide decedunt, justifican- tur à peccati & culpa & pœna, & ad æternam sa- lutem evehuntur, ita qui peccato moriuntur, à pec- cato justificantur, & hæredes æternæ vitæ consti- tuuntur: non quod causa justificationis sit mors peccati, sed quod connexa illa sint indivulso nexu, nec moriatur quis peccato, nisi qui justificatur à peccato, quodque τὸ mori peccato justificatorum proprium sit in quarto modo, quod vocant. Id vero non exhaurit vim Aphorismi Apostolici, nec simplicitati dictionis Apostolicæ convenit, quod naturaliter mortuus non serviat amplius pec- cato, (nam nec justitiæ amplius servit in hoc se- culo, imo nullas operationes in hoc seculo edit, utpote luce, ut vita orbatus Ps. VI, 6.) atque ea- tenus liberetur à peccato, ac per μετάληψιν ju- stificari dicatur: nec ad rem quicquam hoc in lo- co faciunt illa, quod qui mortuus est, liber sit ab odio, nec ullatenus vero est simile, Paulum ex di- ctis Rabbinorum, vel Thalmude hæc, nedum multa alia deprompsisse; quum Thalmudica illa scripta Apostoli ætate jam extitisse aut in pretio fuisse, nullo documento constet, nec Spiritum Sanct. cujus impulsu Paulus scripsit, ita honorare vo- luisse Thalmudis impia, & blasphema scripta, cre- dendum sit. Si autem hæc necessario cohærent justificari vel liberari à culpa & pœna esse & mori peccato, juxta doctrinam Apostolicam, quo jure argui potest Apostolica doctrina, quasi justifica- tis permittat vivere in peccatis, ut exuberet in ipsis Gratia? Quo sensu ὑπόνοια illa v. 2. admitti potest: Mortui non redeunt ad vitam priorem; sic nec qui peccato vere est mortuus, quales sunt, qui justificati sunt per fidem, ad vitam priorem re- dire debet. Tò mori autem peccato hic intelligi, è crucifixione veteris Adami cum Christo, quod ar- gumentum adhuc exequitur & premit Apostolus, apparet: ideo subjungit, nos si cum Christo mortui simus (peccato non certe morte naturali) etiam cum Christo victuros esse.

## 6:8
V. 8. But if we have died with Christ.

Ei here is, since, as appears from what was posited above 2. Θεοῖν χρισῷ is according to the likeness of Christ, just as we recently had to be buried together.

we believe,

We hold for certain, if we rely on the promises made through Christ.

that we shall also live with him.

Namely in eternity, in a heavenly and most happy life. The same sense 2 Tim. II. 11. which he said elsewhere we shall reign together 1 Cor. IV. 8. and following in the stated place to Timothy.

The proper and native sense of the particle can be kept very well: If indeed we have died with Christ; which is evident from the above, where the old Adam was said to be crucified with Christ, and we were said to be justified and dead to sin. Hence therefore he infers what is consequent from this doctrine: We believe, he says, and we profess, that one must not live in sin, but must live with Christ, who rose burdened by no sin, living a divine life, so that with him we may live this divine spiritual life here, and eventually be raised to a heavenly and blessed life. Σὺν χρισῷ is not according to the LIKENESS of Christ, but implies COMMUNION with Christ. For we do not imitate Christ in this, whether we die by natural death, or we die to sin, because Christ died, not out of necessity, but by will, nor did he know any sin: but he was made sin for us, which no one can imitate, but we have died with Christ partly on the cross of Christ, because Christ bore our sins on the wood of the cross, 1 Pet. II. 34. and our old man was crucified with Christ, partly in Baptism, where having been made partakers of the cross and death of Christ we have not only obtained the remission of sin and been justified, but have also been enriched and renewed by the power of the spirit, and thus are dead to sin: which are evident from the above. B. Mylius comment. in this place p. 240. following, he says the old man was crucified with Christ, that we are dead with Christ, because the crucifixion and death of Christ is communicated to us as a gift, as a power, as an example: as a gift by which we are justified; as a power, by which the old man is killed in us, and the new is aroused, as an example, so that looking to the cross of Christ, and the death of Christ, we may conform ourselves to that type. For unless the power of innate sin has first been extinguished in us, and a new force has been added, which breathes new vigor into us, the example of the imitation of Christ is proposed in vain. Therefore, that we must also live with him pertains not to another life here, or a heavenly one, but to this spiritual life, which the Apostle teaches is incumbent upon us by the force of the Evangelical doctrine of justification: just as he also weaves this thread in the following, that we ought to live not to sin, but to GOD, which certainly looks to this age. For the death of sin, as long as we are in the flesh, is only begun, not perfected, then finally being consummated, when we shall end this life:

and therefore we are said to be dead to sin only inchoatively, if you look primarily at the sense of sin, which does not cease, except with the sense of life: even if in respect to dominion the faithful are thus far truly dead to sin, because they do not serve the tyranny of sin, and they so extinguish its vigor, that sin cannot rule over them. Moreover, he uses the word of believing πιστεύομεν, so that he may teach that his faith and profession not only do not favor the desire of sinning, or the life of sin, but also embrace with the renunciation and death of sin, the spiritual and divine life by which we live in the spirit to GOD. Some of our own also refer the word συζήσομεν to eternal and blessed life in the heavens, whom the note of the future tense moves. But, although it is certain that he cannot live there with Christ who has lived here with the devil: it is nevertheless simpler if, with B. Mylius, a perpetual pursuit of a new life, as long as we are pilgrims in this world, is said to be noted as needing to be continued: or with Flacius, that both lives are comprehended here together, both that of new obedience and that future one of eternal happiness.

Latin:

V. 8. εἰ δὲ ἀπεθάνομεν σὺν χριστῷ.

Ei hic est, quandoquidem, ut apparet ex positis supra 2. Θεοῖν χρισῷ est ad similitudinem Christi, quomodo modo habuimus συνταφῆναι.

πιστεύομεν,

Pro certo habemus, sisi promissis per Christum factis.

ὅτι καὶ συζήσομεν ἀυτῷ.

Nempe in æternum, vita cœlesti & felicissima. Idem sensus 2. Tim. II. 11. quod alibi dixit συμβασιλεύσομεν 1. Cor. IV. 8. & seqq. dicto ad Timotheum loco.

Particulæ & proprius & nativus sensus retineri optime potest: Si vero mortui sumus cum Christo; quod è superioribus constat, ubi vetus Adam cum Christo crucifixus, ac justificati peccato mor- tui dicebamur. Hinc ergo infert, quid ex hac do- ctrina consequens sit: Credimus, inquit, & profi- temur, non in peccato vivendum esse, sed conviven- dum esse Christo, qui surrexit nullo peccato onustus, vitam divinam vivens, ut cum ipso divinam hic vivamus vitam spiritualem, & ad vitam cælestem ac beatam aliquando evehamur. Σὺν χρισῷ non est ad SIMILITUDINEM Christi, sed infert COMMUNIONEM cum Christo. Non enim imitamur in eo Christum, sive cum morte natu- rali morimur, seu cum peccato morimur, quia Christus mortuus est, non ex necessitate, sed vo- luntate, neque peccatum ullum novit: factus ve- ro est pro nobis peccatum, quod nemo imitari po- test, sed cum Christo mortui sumus partim in cru- ce Christi, quia Christus nostra peccata in lignum crucis tulit, 1. Petr. II. 34. & vetus noster homo cum Christo crucifixus est, partim in Baptismo, ubi cru- cis & mortis Christi participes facti non remissio- nem peccati tantum consequuti & justificati sumus, sed etiam virtute spiritus ditati & renovati sumus, adeoque mortui peccato: quæ è superioribus pa- tent. B. Mylius comment. in h. l. p. 240. seqq. crucifixum dicit veterem hominem cum Christo, mortuos nos cum Christo, quod communicetur no- bis crucifixio & mors Christi ut donum, ut virtus, ut exemplum: ut donum quo justificamur; ut vir- tus, qua in nobis interimïtur vetus homo, & ex- citatur novus, ut exemplum, ut in Christi crucem, & mortem Christi respicientes nos ad illum ty- pum conformemus. Nisi enim prius in nobis ex- tincta sit virtus innati peccati, & vis nova acces- serit, quæ nobis vigorem novum aspiret, frustra imitationis Christi exemplum proponitur. Quod ergo cum ipso vivendum etiam nobis sit non ad alteram hic, vel cœlestem vitam, sed ad hanc spi- ritualem vitam pertinet, quam nobis incumbere vi doctrinæ Evangelicæ de justificatione, docet Apostolus: quemadmodum etiam in sequentibus hoc filum pertexit, quod non peccato, sed DEO vivere debeamus, quod utique ad hoc seculum spectat. Mors enim peccati, quoad in carne su- mus, inchoatur tantum, non perficitur, tum de- mũ consummando, quando vitam hanc finiemus:

ideoque mortui peccato dicimur inchoative tan- tum, si sensum imprimis peccati respicias, qui non cessat, nisi cum sensu vitæ: etsi qua dominium ha- ctenus vere mortui fideles peccato sint, quia pec- cati tyrannidi non serviunt, & vigorem ejus sic extinguunt, ut dominari ipsis peccatum non va- leat. Verbum autem credendi πιστεύομεν adhibet, ut fidem & professionem suam doceat non modo non favere studio peccandi, vel vitæ peccati, sed complecti etiam cum abdicatione & morte pec- cati, vitam spiritualem & divinam qua spiritu vi- vimus D E O. Referunt & è nostris nonnulli verbum συζήσομεν ad vitam æternam ac bea- tam in cœlis, quos movet nota futuri temporis. Sed, quanquam certum sit, non posse illic cum Christo vivere, qui hic vixit cum diabolo: sim- plicius tamen est, si cum B. Mylio, perpetuum vitæ novæ studium, quamdiu in hoc mundo peregri- namur continuandum notari dicatur: vel cum Flacio uttaque vita hic simul comprehendatur, tum ista novæ obedientiæ, tum illa futura æternæ felicitatis.

## 6:9
V. 9. Εἰδότες.

Take as above γινώσκοντες.

Ὅτι χριστὸς ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐκ ἔτι ἀποθνήσκει.

He dies no more. Death is to him the cause of immortality.

Θάνατος ἀυτᾶ ἐκ ἔτι κυριεύει.

This is the cause of the preceding statement: He dies no more, because he is also in a place where death has no power. See John XVI. 10. and what is said there: He is placed outside the territory of death.

Neither concerning the cause nor the place of Christ's immortality is anything held here; if the cause is sought, why Christ dies no more, it is rendered in v. 10, because in that he died, he died unto sin once for the expiation of sin, therefore that being expiated he dies no more; nor does death have dominion over him, not because he is in the heavens, where death has no power, but because, satisfaction having been rendered for the sin for which he underwent death, he took the sting from death, so that death can fix its poisonous barb neither into him as our sponsor, nor into any of those who believe in him. Moreover, it is said ἐκ ἔτι κυριεύει, not because it had dominion over Christ before, because death could not have dominion over Christ, being the victor of death, who by his death became the poison of death, Hos. XIII. 14, whom it was impossible to be held by death, Acts II. 14. John XIV. 30. who is so far from having been overcome by death, that in death itself he was the author of life, Acts III. 15, willingly meeting death for us, so that he might destroy and evacuate through his death him who has the power of death, and might deliver us from the fear of death. Heb. II. 15, 16. The particle therefore ἐκ ἔτι introduces a simple negation, as in Acts XIII. 34, when it is said μηκέτι no more to return to corruption, because he never saw corruption, nor could he see it. Ps. XVI. 20. Urb. Pierius therefore wrongly concluded from this passage against B. Mentzer (collat. A. C.) that death had previously held dominion over Christ: Since death does not hold dominion even over the pious, but they themselves have been made kings, and triumph over death.

The Apostle, however, pursues his argument, which he had proposed from the connection of death and life, namely that if we have died with Christ, we can and ought to believe certainly that we shall also live with him, knowing this, that just as Christ died unto sin, but being raised from the dead dies no more, but lives unto God: so also we, having died unto sin, live unto God in Christ Jesus our Lord, and just as sin or death does not have dominion over Christ who is revived, so also sin ought not to rule over us, that we should obey it unto death, since Christ died to sin, that he might free us from the guilt and dominion of sin. Which some explain by a mere similitude: As Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more, so also after we have been spiritually raised with Christ from the death of sin, we ought no longer to indulge in sin, since sin is the spiritual death of the soul; but the cause is simultaneously included, why sin cannot rule over the justified and those believing in Christ, which is communion with Christ, because Christ not only acquired this for us by his death, having died to sin for us, but we also are one with Christ through faith. For how else could we gather from λογίζεσθαι that we are dead to sin, but alive to GOD, unless that inference had a foundation? which is partly remote, the merit of Christ, who died for our sin, and partly near, our communion with Christ through faith, through which we draw from him, as branches from their vine, the life-giving sap of renewal, and thus daily die more and more to sin, and learn to live to GOD.

Latin:

V. 9. Εἰδότες.

Sume ut supra γινώσκοντες.

Ὅτι χριστὸς ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐκ ἔτι ἀποθνήσκει.

Non ultra moritur. Mors ei causa immortalitatis.

Θάνατος ἀυτᾶ ἐκ ἔτι κυριεύει.

Hæc est causa præcedentis dicti: Non ultra moritur, quia est & in loco ubi mors vim non habet. Vide Joh. XVI. 10. & ibi dicta: Positus est extra territorium mortis.

Nec de causa, nec de loco immortalitatis Chri- sti hic quicquam habetur; Causa si quæratur, cur amplius non moriatur Christus, v. 10. reddita est, quia quod mortuus est, peccato mortuus est semel ob expiationem peccati, eo ergo expiato non amplius moritur; nec mors in ipsum dominatum habet, non ideo, quia in cœlis est, ubi mors vim non habet, sed quia præstita pro peccato satisfacti- one, ob quod mortem subiit, morti stimulum ade- mit, ut nec in ipsum ceu sponsorem nostrum, nec in quenquam credentium in ipsum mors aculeum venenatum figere possit. Dicitur autem ἐκ ἔτι κυ- ριεύει non quod antea dominium in Christum ha- buerit, quia Christo dominari mors non potuit, utpote mortis victori, qui morte sua venenum factus est mortis, Hos. XIII. 14. quem impossibile erat a morte κρατεῖσθαι vinci, Act. II. 14. Joh. XIV. 30. qui tantum abest, ut superatus à morte fuerit, ut in ipsa etiam morte fuerit ἀρχηγὸς ζωῆς, dux vitæ Act. III. 15. mortem ultro oppetens pro no- bis, ut eum, qui potestatem habet mortis, per mor- tem suam καταργήση destrueret & evacuaret, nos- que à metu mortis ἀπαλλάξη liberaret. Ebr. II. 15. 16. Particula ergo ἐκ ἔτι simplicem negationem infert, uti Act. XIII. 34. cum dicitur μηκέτι non amplius reversurum in corruptionem, quia nun- quam corruptionem vidit, nec videre potuit. Ps. XVI. 20. Male ergo Urb. Pierius ex hoc loco con- cludebat contra B. Mentzer. collat. A. C. mortem antea Christo dominatam esse: Quum ne piis qui- dem mors dominetur, sed ipsi facti Reges sint, & de morte triumphent.

Persequitur autem argumentum suum Apo- stolus, quod à connexione mortis & vitæ pro- posuerat, quod nempe si cum Christo mortui simus etiam cum ipso nos victuros certo credere possimus, ac debeamus id scientes, quod uti Chri- stus peccato mortuus, at excitatus è mortuis non amplius moritur, sed Deo vivit: ita etiam nos pecca- to mortuos Deo vivere in Christo Jesu Domino no- stro, & uti non dominari peccatum vel mors Christo redivivo potest, ita etiam nobis non dominari debeat peccatum, ut & obediamus ad mortem, siquidem Christus peccato mortuus sit, ut nos a reatu & domi- nio peccati liberaret. Quod per nudam similitudi- nem exponunt nonnulli; Sicut Christus ex mortuis resuscitatus non amplius moritur, ita quoque post- quam cum Christo spiritualiter ex morte peccati su- scitati sumus, non amplius debemus peccato indul- gere, cum peccatum sit spiritualis mors animæ; sed causa simul comprehenditur, cur non domi- nari possit peccatum justificatis, & credentibus in Christum, quæ est communio cum Christo, quod non tantum hoc nobis acquisiverit morte sua Christus, mortuus peccato pro nobis, sed nos et- iam unum simus cum Christo per fidem. Nam quomodo alias λογίζεσθαι colligere possemus, nos mortuos esse peccato, vivere autem DEO, nisi collectio illa fundamentum haberet? quod est partim remotum, Christi meritum, qui pro peccato nostro mortuus est, partim propinquum nostra per fidem cum Christo communio, per quam ex ipso tanquam palmites ex sua vite succum vi- vificum renovationis haurimus, & ita quotidie magis magisque peccato morimur, & DEO vi- vere discimus.

## 6:10
V. 10. For in that he died.

Here ὃ, like the Hebrew אשׁר, refers not to any noun, but to the complex; as if he were to say: for as far as it pertains to the fact that Christ died. A similar mode of speaking is in Gal. II. 20.

he died unto sin once for all.

Ἁμαρτία, corresponding, as we have said, to the Hebrew לחטאת, is very often taken for the punishments of sins; Christ once finished with those evils which he was enduring on account of our sins. And thus you may not wrongly interpret the word ἁμαρτιῶν in Heb. V. 3, VII. 27, so that it is understood that Christ offered prayers to GOD that he might be freed from those evils which he was experiencing on account of our sins.

but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God.

He lives to the honor of GOD, he cares for nothing but the things of GOD. Aristides: For he who lives under GOD and has neglected human affairs.

Latin:

V. 10. ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανε.

Hic ὃ ut אשׁר Hebræum non ad nomen aliquod, sed ad complexum refertur; quasi dicat: quantum enim at- tinet, quod mortuus est Christus. Simile loquendi genus Gal. II. 20.

τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ.

Ἁμαρτία respondens, ut diximus לחטאת Hebræo, sæ- pissime sumitur pro pœnis peccatorum; Christus semel defunctus est malis illis quæ ob peccata nostra sustinebat. Et sic non male interpreteris vocem ἁμαρτιῶν Hebr. V. 3. VII. 27. ut intelligatur Christus obtulisse preces DEO ut ab illis malis, quæ ob peccata nostra sentiebat, liberaretur.

ὃ δὲ ζῇ, ζῇ τῷ Θεῷ.

Vivit in honorem DEI, nihil nisi res DEI curat. Ari- stides: Τὸν γὰρ ζῶντα ὑπὸ Θεῷ καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμά- των ἠμεληκότα.

## 6:11
V. 11. Likewise also you reckon.

Think thus. Reckon, translates Tertullian in 'De Pudicitia'. For we noted above at III. 28 that λογίζεσθαι is taken in this way.

To be dead indeed to sin.

Here do not take ἁμαρτίαν figuratively, but properly. Thus it is necessary that the meanings of words sometimes vary, to which allusions of this kind are pleasing. He repeats here what he had said above in verse 2.

But living to God.

That is, you are preserved in life for this purpose, that whatever of life remains to you, you should spend it on God. For duty rather than its execution is noted here.

In Christ Jesus our Lord.

That is, through Jesus Christ: because since He is our Lord by right of redemption and by paternal constitution, He demands from us this which I have said under that right.

The observation concerning the article is not inconvenient: which was also Beza's. Erasmus, Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide, Adamus Conzen, and most of our own say that ὃ is put for ὅτι. Valla translates it in the neuter gender: For that which is dead. In which manner Hilary also reads in book IX de Trinit., who refers that first ὃ ἀπέθανεν to the human nature, but the latter, ὃ δὲ ζῇ, to the divine nature. But Beza rightly judges that this interpretation neither fits the passage and is less safe, and favors the Arians. B. Weller indeed retains the neuter, but prefers to understand it of any other than Christ, and explains the phrase 'to die to sin' as 'to die away from sin,' as it is taken in verses 2 and 11. But that I may say this with all respect to the late lamented, that ἐφάπαξ does not fit, nor even the subject. For what is it: That which is dead to sin, is dead once for all? Wherefore we judge that this sentiment should be taken rather of Christ, with Ambrose, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, B. Rungius, B. Balduinus, and most others. For the immediately preceding things treat of Him; with which these things cohere through a causal particle. And that ἐφάπαξ concerning Christ occurs elsewhere, when there is discourse of His death, Heb. VII. 27, c. X. 10. Christ is also rightly said to be dead to sin, in that He died by expiating sin, and by abdicating it, or for the abolishing of sin as far as regards guilt and dominion, indeed even as regards the sense and the incentive, so that τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ may be FOR SIN: just as He lives to GOD by glorifying Him, or for the magnifying of the glory of GOD in the Church, or FOR GOD: whence it is to be gathered that those who, once liberated from sins, have said farewell to carnal desires, ought no longer to succumb to dead works, but to institute a life to the honor of GOD, in Christ the Lord, who liberated them from sin. Whence it is again evident that the gratuitous righteousness of faith and the merit of Christ do not establish a license for sinning, but exclude it, and are defended by the Apostle for the sake of excluding it. But that ἁμαρτία is taken here for the punishments of sins in this sense, 'Christ died once to the punishments of sins,' or 'He has finished with those evils which He sustained on account of our sins,' that departs from the propriety of the word and the usage of speaking received by the Apostle: Christ is said to have died because of sins, and for sins, but not for the evils which He sustained on account of our sins, not for the punishments of sin.

Nor does the passage Heb. V. 3 or c. VII. 27 teach that ἁμαρτία is taken for those evils which Christ felt on account of our sins: for He is compared with a Priest offering for sins, which offering was indeed made because of sins, and to expiate sins: and at the same time the difference is shown, that the priests of the O.T. indeed had the necessity to offer for their own sins; but Christ, void of all sin, offered only for our sins. And how did CHRIST feel evils on account of our sins? Is it because our sins were the meritorious cause, but the evils were the punishments of our sins, which Christ took upon Himself and bore? Thus to die to sin will be to pay the penalty of our sins, and to satisfy for our sins, which sense agrees with our explanation; but is it on the occasion of our sins, or so that He might draw us away from sins, which the Socinians want? in which manner ἁμαρτία is not even taken for punishment. But it cannot be taught that the word חַטָאת is taken in this way, which either denotes sin, or certainly by metonymy a punishment, or a sacrifice for sin, nowhere an evil which does not have the nature of a punishment. Furthermore, what is this, that Christ died to afflictions and death? And who does not see how different those things are, to die to sin, and to have finished with afflictions, or to be liberated from afflictions? Nor indeed does the beauty of the comparison and the force of the inference perish if sin is taken properly; as Christ died once because of sin, so that He ought not, nor can He, die anymore, but now lives always to God: So we also must die to sin spiritually, so that we may not live again to sins, but henceforth to God. For if He died once because of the guilt and merit of our sins, and cannot or ought not to undergo death again through and because of our guilt; it is just that we who have died to sins through baptism should not indulge in sins, and contract new guilt, but strive to live to GOD, lest we crucify Christ as it were again by our sins. But that gloss of Grotius is inept, 'Christ has finished once with afflictions, and is now immune from them, and therefore it is fitting that we also be immune from sins,' as we warned against a similar gloss of the Socinian Crellius in Socinismo profligato, page 402. What? That in the preceding verse 10 concerning Christ, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ cannot be taken otherwise than in the following verse 11 concerning the faithful. But here λογίζεσθαι, reckon (which is both more usual and more convenient here than reputate, and holds its place entirely in Rom. III. 28), that you are dead indeed τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, it is clear that the word for sin must be taken not figuratively, but properly, and Grotius acknowledges this. However, it does not appear that there is only an allusion here; rather, the method of his treatment shows that the Apostle is establishing a proof, and is refuting the calumny of those who contradict him, both from the merit and the example of Christ. Whence neither should that ζῶντας δὲ τῷ θεῷ be taken otherwise here in the consequent than in the antecedent: and thus to live to GOD is not to be preserved in life so that one may live to GOD, but being dead to sin, or to the service of sin, to live spiritually to GOD, and to consecrate one's whole life to GOD. Which St. Peter said, ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν, 1 Epist. II. 24, where he expressed ἀπογίνεσθαι, as Beza translated it, to be made outside, disjointed and separated (as Ambrose translates it, to be separated), but he translated it with the Vulgate, that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness. Paul said ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας in verse 13, because we rise again from spiritual death, that we may live to GOD. Which death is not of the reborn, who die to sin until they are raised up through the grace of the Spirit in conversion to spiritual life, and live to righteousness. Which is called the first resurrection, Apoc. XX. 6.

But that Grotius, in his letter to the Hebrews, understands ἁμαρτιῶν as the mortal condition of the body, and here understands ἁμαρτίαν as a mortal body, such as a body subject to sin, is destitute of the example of the Holy Scriptures, nor does it agree with the words or the mind of the Apostle. For in Heb. V. 3, the sin for which the Priest offered is properly understood as that of the people and of the Priest himself, not indeed the condition of a mortal body: but here, if τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ were a mortal body, how is Christ said to have died in a mortal body, so that by his example or in his likeness we might die to sin? Since that likeness demands that we also reckon ourselves dead in a mortal body, if Grotius wishes to speak consistently? How also will the body of Christ be called sin metonymically, because it is subject to sin, when Christ knew no sin?

Latin:

V. 11. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς λογίζεσθαι.

Sic cogitate. Reputate, vertit Tertullianus de pudici- tia. Ita enim λογίζεσθαι sumi notavimus supra III. 28.

Ἑαυτὸς νεκρὸς μὲν εἶναι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ.

Hic ἁμαρτίαν non figurate sume, sed proprie. Sic ne- cesse est interdum vocum significatus varient, quibus allu- siones istiusmodi allubescunt. Repetit hic quod dixerat supra 2.

Ζῶντας δὲ τῷ Θεῷ.

Id est, in id vos in vita servatos, ut quicquid vitæ vobis restat, id Deo impendatis. Officium enim magis quam ejus executio hic notatur.

Ἐν χρίσῳ Ἰησῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.

Id est, per Jesum Christum: quia cum Dominus noster sit redemtionis jure & constitutione paterna, hoc quod dixi sub jure à nobis exigit.

Observatio de articulo non incommoda est: quæ etiam Bezæ fuit. Erasmus, Pererius, Corne- lius à Lapide, Adamus Conzen & plerique nostri ὃ pro ὅτι positum dicunt. Valla neutro genere vertit: Quod enim mortuum est. Quo pacto et- iam legit Hilarius lib. IX. de Trinit. qui prius illud ὃ ἀπέθανεν refert ad corpus humanum, poste- rius autem, ὃ δὲ ζῇ ad divinam naturam. Sed eam interpretationem neque loco convenire & minus tutam esse, atque Arrianis favere recte censet Beza. B. Wellerus neutrum quidem retinet, sed de quovis alio, quam Christo mavult intelligere, & phrasin peccato mori explicat demori peccato, uti v. 2. & 11. accipitur. Sed ut pace τῷ μακαρίτῃ id dicam, non congruit illud ἐφάπαξ ac ne Subje- ctum quidem. Quid enim est: Quod mortuum est peccato, demortuum est semel? Quapropter de Christo potius accipiendam esse hanc sententiam censemus cum Ambrosio, Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Oecumenio, B. Rungio, B. Balduino, & aliis ple- risque. De hoc enim immediate antecedentia agunt; cum quibus haec per particulam causalem cohaerent. Et de Christo illud ἐφάπαξ alias, cum de morte ejus sermo est, occurrit Ebr. VII. 27. c. X. 10. Christus etiam recte τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ peccato mortuus dicitur, qua mortuus est expiando peccato, & abdicando, vel ad peccatum abolendum quan- tum ad reatum & dominium, imo quoad sensum etiam atque fomitem ut τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ sit PROPTER PECCATVM: quemadmodum vivit DEO glo- rificando, vel ad gloriam DEI in Ecclesia ampli- ficandam, seu PROPTER DEUM: unde collige- re est, qui semel a peccatis liberati valedixere carnalibus desideriis, eos non amplius succumbe- re debere mortuis operibus, sed vitam in DEI honorem instituere, in Christo Domino, qui eos a peccato liberavit. Unde iterum constat, gratui- tam fidei justitiam & meritum Christi licentiam peccandi non stabilire, sed excludere, eique ex- cludendae ab Apostolo propugnari. Quod autem ἁμαρτία hic pro poenis peccatorum accipiatur hoc sensu, Christus semel mortuus est poenis peccatorum, vel defunctus est malis illis quae ob peccata nostra sustinebat, id a proprietate vocis & loquendi usu Apostolus recepto recedit: Christus propter pec- cata, & pro peccatis mortuus dicitur, non autem pro malis, quae ob peccata nostra sustinuit, non pro poenis peccati.

Neq; locus Ebr. V. 3. aut c. VII. 27. docet ἁμαρ- τίαν pro malis illis accipi, quae sensit Christus ob peccata nostra: nam comparatur cum Sacerdote pro peccatis offerente, quae oblatio utique fiebat propter peccata, & ad expianda peccata: & mon- stratur simul differentia, quod Sacerdotes quidem V. T. necessum habuerint pro suis peccatis offer- re; Christus autem peccati omnis expers, non- nisi pro nostris peccatis obtulerit. Et quomodo ob peccata nostra CHRISTUS mala sensit? Num quod peccata nostra causa fuerint meritoria, mala vero poenae peccatorum nostrorum fuerint, quae in se suscepit, & portavit Christus? ita peccato mori erit poenam peccatorum nostrorum luere, & pro peccatis nostris satisfacere, qui sensus cum no- stra explicatione congruit; num vero occasione peccatorum nostrorum, vel ut nos a peccatis abs- traheret, quod Sociniani volunt? quo pacto ne quidem pro poena accipitur ἁμαρτία. At hoc mo- do vocem חַטָאת accipi doceri nequit, quae vel peccatum notat, vel certe per metonymiam poe- nam, aut sacrificium pro peccato, nuspiam malum, quod rationem poenae non habet. Porro quid hoc est, Christum mortuum esse afflictionibus & morti? Et quis non videt, quam diversa illa sint, mori pec- cato, & defungi afflictionibus, vel liberari ab af- flictionibus? Nec vero perit comparationis de- cus & illationis vis, si proprie accipiatur pecca- tum; ut Christus ob peccatum mortuus est semel, ut amplius mori neque debeat, neque possit, sed Deo nunc semper vivat: Sic nobis quoque moriendum est peccato spiritualiter, ne denuo peccatis, sed Deo deinceps vivamus. Si enim propter culpam & me- ritum peccatorum nostrorum semel mortuus est, nec iterum per & propter culpam nostram mor- tem subire potest, aut debet; aequum est, ut qui peccatis mortui sumus per baptismum, non in- dulgeamus peccatis, novamque culpam contra- hamus, sed DEO vivere studeamus, ne Christum peccatis nostris veluti denuo crucifigamus. Glossa vero illa Grotii inepta est, Christus defunctus est semel afflictionibus, & immunis jam ab iisdem est, ideoque convenit, ut & nos immunes simus a peccatis, ut contra similem Crellii Sociniani glossam mo- nuimus in Socinismo profligato pag. 402. Quid? quod in antecedenti de Christo vers. 10. τῇ ἁμαρ- τίᾳ aliter accipi non possit, quam in consequenti v. 11. de fidelibus. Hic verò λογίζεσθαι Colligite, (quod & usitatius & convenientius hic est, quam reputate, & Rom. III. 28. omninò locum habet) vos mortuos quidem τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, non figuratè, sed propriè accipiendum esse peccati vocem, luculen- tum est, & agnoscit id Grotius. Allusionem au- tem solùm hic esse non apparet, imò probatio- nem instituere Apostolum, & à merito & exemplo Christi refellere calumniam contradicentium tra- ctationis ejus ratio docet. Unde nec illud ζῶν- τας δὲ τῷ θεῷ aliter hic in consequenti accipi debet, quàm in antecedenti : adeoque vivere DEO est, non in vita servatum esse, ut DEO vivatur, sed mortuum peccato, vel servitio peccati, DEO spi- ritualiter vivere, omnemque vitam DEO conse- crare. Quod S. Petrus dixit ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν. 1. Epist. II. 24. ubi ἀπογίνεσθαι expressit Beza extra fieri sejun- ctum ac separatum esse (ut Ambrosius vertit sepa- rari) transtulit autem cum Vulgata, ut peccatis mor- tui justitiæ vivamus. ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας dixit Pau- lus vers. 13. quod è morte spirituali resurgamus, ut vivamus DEO. Quæ mors est non renatorum, qui peccato immoriuntur, donec per gratiam Spiri- tûs in conversione resuscitentur ad vitam spiri- tualem, ac justitiæ vivant. Quæ resurrectio prima dicitur Apoc. XX. 6.

Quod verò Grotius ad Luc. II. 27. ἁμαρτιῶν nomine conditionem mortalem corporis, in Episto- la ad Hebræos, & hic ἁμαρτίαν corpus mortale, qua- le est corpus peccato obnoxium, intelligit, exemplo S. literarum destituitur, neque verbis aut menti Apostoli convenit. Nam Ebr. V. 3. peccatum, pro quo Sacerdos offerebat, propriè intelligitur tum populi, tum Sacerdotis ipsius, non verò conditio corporis mortalis : Hic verò τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ si sit corpo- re mortali, quomodo Christus mortuus corpore mor- tali dicitur, ut exemplo vel ad similitudinem ejus nos peccato demoriamur? Quum similitudo illa postulet, ut nos etiam mortuos nos corpore morta- li reputemus, si consequenter loqui velit Grotius? Quomodo etiam corpus Christi peccatum dicetur metonymicè, quia peccato subjectum, quum Chri- stus peccatum non novit?

## 6:12
V. 12. Let it not reign. Let it exercise its power. See above V. 4.

In your mortal body. He rightly added this epithet; for when he reminds us of our mortality, he easily signifies that we must think of another life, and that labors, which are certainly not long-lasting, are not to be feared.

To obey it. Namely, to sin. He speaks as if of an infamous mistress, whom it is unworthy to serve.

In its desires. The desires of the body, if a bridle is not present, lead to sin, James I. 15; wherefore not only are illicit desires to be suffocated in their beginnings, but also the body is not to be indulged further than nature requires, so that it may learn to obey the better part.

Latin:

V. 12. Μὴ ὔν βασιλευέτω. Vim suam exerceat. Vide supra V. 4.

Ἐν τῷ θνητῷ ὑμῶν σώματι. Benè adjecit hoc ἐπίθετον; cum enim mortalitatis no- stræ nos admonet, facilè significat de vita altera cogitan- dum, nec formidandos labores haud sanè diuturnos.

Εἰς τὸ ὑπακύειν ἀυτῇ. Nempe τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ. Loquitur tanquam de infami he- ra, cui servire indignum sit.

Ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις ἀυτῶ. Corporis cupiditates, si frænum non adsit, ad peccatum ducunt Jac. I. 15. quare non tantùm illicitæ cupiditates suffocandæ sunt in suis initiis, verum etiam corpori non ultra indulgendum, quàm natura exigit, ut parére discat parti meliori.

## 6:13
V. 13. Neither present your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin. Understand members here as all parts of the body, even the interior ones, as also in Col. III. 5. You will rightly translate ὅπλα as instruments. For Eustathius teaches that the Greek word is taken thus in his commentary on the Iliad Δ; thus also Servius says that they are called arms in Latin, regarding that passage of Virgil: 'And the arms of Ceres.' Likewise: 'It must be said what the arms are for the hardy farmers.' And the Hebrew כּלי is every instrument, which is sometimes translated as ὅπλον. Παρισάνειν is indeed usually said of members, Luke I. 19, John XV. 22, 1 Sam. XVI. 22, Ps. CXXXV. 2. But because it is a question here of members as if they were instruments, you will rightly translate παριστάνετε as 'hand over,' as in Matt. XXVI. 53, IX. 41, or 'have,' as in Acts I. 3, 2 Tim. II. 15. Ἀδικίας is placed generally, as above I. 18, and refers to actions in this place, just as ἁμαρτία refers to the custom or quality itself.

But present yourselves to GOD. As above 11.

As alive from the dead. See above 4.

And your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. Here the word δικαιοσύνης is extended to all honest actions, and extends just as broadly as the contrary one which we just had, ἀδικίας. Our body is of a middle quality, which it is permitted to use both badly and well.

The Apostle concludes this treatment with this argument: Those who are justified, freed from the guilt of sin, dead to sin, rise again to spiritual life; therefore, they ought not to grant dominion to sin, to which they are dead, in their body, nor accommodate their members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but use the same rightly, so that they may serve God alone. For since by justification the guilt of sin is indeed taken away, but the remnants of sin still remain in us, it is necessary to suppress them and mortify the flesh, but not to loosen the reins of concupiscence, or permit dominion to the flesh. Let not sin therefore reign, says the Apostle, and he repeats that again in v. 14. Attributing to sin not tyranny, but a kingdom, as Theodoret observes: because a tyrant commands unwilling subjects; but a King commands those who are willing, over whom he is set; and that sin still remains in us is hinted at by the word Dominion: concerning which see August. tract. XL. in Joh. He does not say, let it not be, but let it not reign. For as long as you live, it is necessary for sin to be in your members, at least let it be taken away from it, so that what it commands may not be done; then also when he calls the body ϑνητὸν mortal: for because of the remnants of sin, we are subject to diseases and death: by which reminder of our mortality he wishes us to be recalled also from the servitude of sin: so that since our body is mortal, we should not indulge in sin, seeing that at any moment death could overwhelm us, and precipitate us into eternal death. But the fact that he makes mention of the body and members is not to be taken as if it reigns only in the body, while the soul is immune from depraved desires, nor can it be subjected to the dominion of sin, but because sin reveals itself more openly in the body and bodily members, and because by not permitting the dominion of sin in the body and bodily members, sin cannot break out into action, or fully exert its force, or even acquire those strengths by which it might captivate us and reduce us to miserable servitude, and conversely the force of concupiscence and desires is diminished and broken, while such dominion is not permitted: where, however, the mortification of the old man and of depraved interior concupiscence must not be neglected, nor the subjection, restraint, and repression of the desires bursting forth from it, lest we indulge in them or take pleasure in them, since in that also we sin most gravely, and offend God who searches the hearts and reins, so that from there easily follows the ὑπακοὴ, which the Apostle forbids and wishes to guard against.

The word παραστήσατε is military, alluding to a soldier who, stationed in the battle line, directs his weapons against the enemy, just as παραστάτης, as Henri Estienne notes, signifies one who girds the side of another, Conf. Matth. XXVI. 53. For our life is a continuous battle against the sin dwelling in us Rom. VII. 23. Gal. V. 17. Thus also the Apostle used the word for weapons, as Chrysostom teaches, to show that a serious war also threatens, for which reason we have need of strong armor, and likewise of a generous spirit, and one who is well-versed in the nature of that same war, but then above all a Leader; and a leader is indeed at hand, always prepared to bring reinforcements, with strong weapons prepared for us by him, but it remains that we be endowed with that will which handles weapons decently and according to use, just as one who obeys the leader's command takes up arms for the fatherland.

Latin:

V. 13. Μηδὲ παρισάνετε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν ὅπλα ἀδικίας τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ. Membra hic intellige omnes corporis partes, etiam in- teriores, ut & Coloff. III. 5. Ὅπλα rectè verteris instru- menta. Ita enim sumi Græcam vocem docet Eustachius ad Iliados Δ. sic & arma dici Latinis Servius ad illud Vir- gilii : Cerealiaque arma. Item: Dicendum & quæ sint duris agrestibus arma. Et Hebræum כּלי est omne instrumentum, quod nonnun- quam ὅπλον vertitur. Παρισάνειν solet quidem de mem- bris dici Lucæ I. 19. Joh. XV. 22. 1. Sam. XVI. 22. Psal. CXXXV. 2. Sed quia hic de membris velut instrumentis agitur, παριστάνετε rectè verteris, tradite, ut Matth. XXVI. 53. IX. 41. aut habete ut Act. I. 3. 2. Tim. II. 15. Ἀδικίας generaliter ponitur, ut suprà I. 18. & refertur ad actiones hoc loco, sicut ἁμαρτία ad ipsam consuetudinem sive qualitatem.

Ἀλλὰ παραστήσατε ἑαυτοὺς τῷ Θεῷ. Ut supra 11.

Ὡς ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας. Vide supra 4.

Καὶ τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν ὅπλα δικαιοσύνης τῷ Θεῷ. Hic δικαιοσύνης vox ad omnes actiones honestas extendi- tur, & æque latè patet atque contraria quam modo habui- mus ἀδικίας. Corpus nostrum mediæ est qualitatis, quo & malè & benè uti licet.

Concludit Apostolus hanc tractationem hoc argumento: Justificati à peccati reatu liberati pec- cato demortui resurgunt ad spiritualem vitam; er- gò peccato, cui demortui sunt, dominium concedere non debent in corpore suo, nec membra peccato ac- commodare ceu arma injustitiæ, sed iisdem rectè uti, ut DEO uni serviant. Quum enim per justi- ficationem peccati reatus quidem tollatur, rema- neant autem in nobis adhuc peccati reliquiæ, eas deprimere ac carnem mortificare oportet, non verò concupiscentiæ fræna laxare, aut dominium carni permittere. Non dominetur ergò peccatum, ait Apostolus, idque denuo repetit v. 14. Pecca- to tribuens non tyrannidem, sed regnum obser- vante Theodoreto: quia tyrannus invitis subditis imperat; Rex verò iis volentibus, quibus impe- ratur; Et superesse adhuc peccatum in nobis tum voce Dominii innuit: quo de August. tract. XL. in Joh. Non ait, non sit, sed non regnet. Quamdiu enim vivis, peccatum necesse est esse in membris tuis, saltem illi auferatur, ne fiat, quod jubet; tùm etiam cum ϑνητὸν mortale corpus dicit: ob reliquias enim peccati, morbis & morti obnoxii sumus: quâ commonefactione mortalitatis nostræ à pec- cati etiam servitute nos revocatos vult: ut cum mortale sit corpus nostrum, peccato non indulgeamus, siquidem quolibet momento mors opprimere nos possit, nosque in æternam mor- tem præcipitare. Quod autem corporis & mem- brorum mentionem facit, non eò accipiendum, pus & ac si in corpore tantùm dominetur, anima verò à pravis desideriis immunis sit, nec peccati dominio subjici possit, sed quod in corpore & membris cor- poreis apertius sese exserat peccatum, quodque non permisso dominio peccati in corpore ac mem- bris corporeis, nec in nervum ita erumpere pec- catum, aut vim suam plene exerere, aut vires et- iam eas acquirere possit, quo nos captivet, & in miseram servitutem redigat, & ex adverso immi- nuatur ita ac frangatur vis concupiscentiæ & de- sideriorum, dum non permittitur tale dominium: ubi tamen intermittenda etiam non est veteris ho- minis, & pravæ concupiscentiæ interioris mortifi- catio, ac desideriorum inde prorumpentium sub- actio, cohibitio, & repressio, ne qua iisdem in- dulgeamus, aut delectemur, quum in eo etiam gravissimè delinquamus, & Deum corda & renes scrutantem offendamus, ut facile inde sequatur ὑπακοὴ, quam prohibet & præcavere vult Apo- stolus.

Verbum παραστήσατε militare est, alludens ad militem, qui in acie constitutus arma contra hostes dirigit, ut & παραστάτης notante Heinrico Stephani significat eum, qui latus alicujus cingit, Conf. Matth. XXVI. 53. Vita enim nostra conti- nua pugna est adversus peccatum in nobis habi- tans Rom. VII. 23. Gal. V. 17. Sic & armorum ver- bo usus Apostolus, Chrysostomo docente, often- dit bellum quoque grave imminere, quâ de causâ armatura nobis forti opus est, generoso item animo, quique belli ejusdem naturam probè calleat, tùm vero ante omnia Duce; ac dux quidem præsto est, ad ferendas suppetias semper paratus, fortibus ab eo armis nobis apparatis, superest autem, ut eâ vo- luntate præditi simus, quæ decenter atque ex usu arma pertractet, sicut ducis dicto parens arma pro patria sumit.

## 6:14
V. 14. For sin shall not have dominion over you.

This is not a warning, but a consolation, as if he were saying: I promise you an easy victory, provided you are not ψιψάσπιδες (shield-less). The powers of sin to defeat you are not now what they once were. In a similar sense the Psalmist uses the word ימשׁלו in Psalm 19:14.

For you are not under law, but under grace.

A metonymy. For χάρις (grace) is said for the Gospel, which is the word of grace in Acts 14:3. A similar expression is in Acts 13:43. Because the Law promised nothing above earthly things, it did not give sufficient strength for cleansing the soul. But the Gospel, having heavenly promises, gives great strength to those who are willing to use it. This is treated more fully at the end of the seventh chapter. You have ὑπὸ νόμον (under law) also in Galatians 4:21.

The Apostle entirely repeats the former warning, so as to impress it the more upon the mind, and urges a new reason from the state and condition of the justified, in which, however, we do not deny that a consolation lies in the easy victory, provided we are not slothful, or easily cast away the shield of faith, and use the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, as is fitting. But it savors of the Pelagian error that the powers of sin are not now what they once were under the Old Testament. Regarding the passage in Psalm 19:14, those things which are held here in the commentary of the blessed Dr. Weller may be compared. Therefore, the Apostle promises the reborn victory against sin from the fact that they have been gifted with grace, which causes both that the lusts of the flesh be mortified, and that the infirmities of the indwelling sin be forgiven them: and he warns from this that we should not suffer ourselves to be enslaved to sin, lest we fall from that grace. Therefore, to be under the law is to be under the curse of the law and its rigorous exaction, which requires perfect obedience. Whence to be under grace is not to fulfill the law under the protection of grace, which Pererius wants, for this can be done by no one; but to be reconciled through faith in Christ, liberated from the curse and coercion of the law, and thus renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, by the power of which we can resist, and readily, without the coercion of the law, we do resist evil desires and the dominion of sin; so that thus both the grace of the remission of sins and of renewal may be understood; for then all the commandments of God are reckoned as done, when whatever is not done is forgiven. And in the Gospel we are made certain that an initiated obedience is pleasing to God through faith, if the person is reconciled to Him. Therefore there is no need for the trope of metonymy, so that χάρις (grace) is taken for the Gospel: nor are the Law and the Gospel opposed to each other in this, whether as to the object, that the Law promised nothing above earthly things, but the Gospel has heavenly promises, or as to the effect, that the Law did not give sufficient strength to cleanse the soul, but the Gospel gives great strength to those who are willing to use it, which hypotheses are merely Pelagian and have been refuted elsewhere; but the difference between the Law and the Gospel, with the Apostle as author, lies in this, that the Law requires perfect obedience if anyone wishes to obtain eternal salvation, but the Gospel demands faith, only believe, and you shall be saved: the Law demonstrates, argues, terrifies, condemns, and kills sin; the Gospel consoles, saves, and gives life: the Law shows good works, but does not provide the strength to perform them, but the Gospel bestows the Holy Spirit (Galatians 3, 4, 5; 2 Corinthians 3; Jeremiah 31:33) by the power of which we may obey the Law. The argument therefore from the dignity of the justified occurs here in two ways: First, that they are free from the dominion of sin and the law, and therefore ought not to subject themselves to sin: Second, that they are servants of righteousness; and therefore ought to serve it. Sin therefore shall not have dominion over you; I say it shall not have dominion, neither by right, nor in fact: not by right, both because you have been liberated through Christ, and because you are dead to sin; nor in fact, because sin without the law can do nothing. But you are not under the law, but under grace.

PART II OF CHAPTER VI. Refuting the other objection from the state of the justified, that they are not under the law, but under grace, and therefore have license to sin.

Latin:

V. 14. ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν ὀυ κυριέυσει.

Non est hoc monitum, sed solatium, quasi dicat: faci- lem vobis spondeo victoriam, modò ne sitis ψιψάσπιδες. Non eæ nunc vires sunt vires peccati ad vos debellandos, quæ olim fuêre. Simili sensu vocem ימשׁלו usurpat Psalmographus XIX. 14.

ὀ γάρ ἐσε ὑπὸ νόμον, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ χάριν.

Metonymia. Dicitur enim χάρις pro Evangelio, qui est λόγος χάριτος Act. XIV. 3., Similis locutio Act. XIII. 43. Lex quia nihil promittebat supra terrestria, non satis vi- rium dabat ad animum mundandum. Evangelium verò promissa habens cœlestia, vires dat magnas uti volentibus. Tractatur hoc uberius fine capitis septimi. ὑπὸ νόμον ha- bes & Gal. IV. 21.

Repetit omninò Apostolus prius monitum, ut eò magis id menti imprimat, novamque rationem à statu & conditione justificatorum urgeat, in quâ verò etiam solatium latere à facili victoria non abnuimus, dummodò non ignavi simus, aut faci- lè clypeum fidei abjiciamus, & gladio Spiritûs, verbo DEI, ut decet, utamur. Id verò errorem Pelagianum sapit, quod nunc eæ non sint peccati vires, quæ olim sub V. T. fuerint. De loco Psalm. XIX. 14. conferri poterunt, quæ hic habentur in Comment. B. Dn. D. Welleri. Promittit ergò Apostolus renatis victoriam adversus peccatum ex eo, quod donati sint gratia, quæ efficit tùm ut carnis concupiscentiæ mortificentur, tùm ut adhærentis peccati infirmitates ipsis remittantur: monetque inde, ut non patiamur nos servitio man- cipari peccato, ne excidamus illâ gratiâ. Sub lege igitur esse est sub legis maledictione, & rigorosa exactione esse, quæ perfectam requirit obedien- tiam. Unde sub gratia esse, non est, sub præsidio gratiæ legem implere, quod vult Pererius, hoc enim à nemine fieri potest; sed per fidem in Christum reconciliatum, à maledictione & coactione legis li- beratum, adeoque Spiritûs S. gratiâ renovatum esse, vi cujus resistere possumus, & prompti, sine coactione legis, resistimus pravis desideriis, & dominio peccati; ut ita tùm gratia remissionis pec- catorum, tùm renovationis intelligatur; Tunc enim omnia Dei mandata facta reputantur, quan- do quicquid non fit ignoscitur. Et in Evangelio certi reddimur, quod inchoata obedientia per fi- dem DEO grata sit, si persona ipsi sit reconci- liata. Non ergò opus est metonymiæ tropo, ut χάρις pro Evangelio accipiatur: nec in eo lex & Evangelium sibi opponuntur, sive quod ad obje- ctum, q. lex nihil promiserit supra terrestria, Ev- angelium verò promissa habeat cœlestia, sive quod ad effectum, quod lex non satis virium de- derit ad mundandum animum, Evangelium verò vires det magnas uti volentibus, quæ hypotheses merè Pelagianæ alias profligatæ sunt, sed in eo, Apostolo autore, sita est legis & Evangeli diffe- rentia, quod lex requirat obedientiam perfectam, si quis salutem æternam adipisci velit, Evange- lium verò fidem postulet, tantùm crede, ac salvabe- ris: lex peccatum demonstret, arguat, terreat, da- mnet, occidat; Evangelium consoletur, salvet, & vivificet: lex monstret bona opera, sed vires non sufficiat præstandi, Evangelium vero Spiritum S. largiatur Gal. III. IV. V. 2. Cor. III. Jer. XXXI. 33. vi cujus legi obediamus. Argumentum itaque à dignitate justificatorum geminum hic occurrit: Primum quod liberi sint à peccati & legis dominio, ideoque peccato se subjicere non debeant: Al- terum quod mancipes sint justitiæ; ideoque servire ei debeant. Peccatum igitur non dominabitur vo- bis; non inquam dominabitur, nec de jure, nec de facto: non de jure, tum quia liberati estis per Christum, tum quia mortui peccato; nec de fa- cto, quia peccatum sine lege nihil potest. At vos non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia.

PARS II. CAPITIS VI. Objectionem alteram à statu justificatorum, quod non sint sub lege, sed sub gratia, adeoque peccandi licentiam habeant, refellens.

## 6:15
V. 15. What then? What follows from these things which we have said? Is it that which the enemies of the Gospel say we teach?

ἁμαρτήσομεν. Even here the Manuscript has ἁμαρτήσωμεν, let us sin, correctly. For it is an imitation of the words which the enemies used, as above 1. ἐπιμένωμεν. Let us sin, that is, let us continue to indulge in vices.

μὴ γένοιτο. Far be it, as above 1. and often elsewhere.

The force of the objection is this: What then, shall we sin? (not indeed, shall we be sinning, much less continue to indulge in vices? For those who are justified do not indulge in vices; and therefore it is not for them to continue in that) Since we are under grace, not under law: the law does not concern us, and therefore we are not bound to obedience to the law. Thus it is perversely gathered from that which the Apostle had said, that we are not under the law, who said this only by reason of the curse, the compulsion, and the rigorous exaction, but not by reason of obedience and observance. Therefore the Apostle explains the state and condition of the justified: so that this objection may be satisfied, and he utterly denies the consequence μὴ γένοιτο, far be it: for from the fact that the justified are not condemned by the voice of the law, are not compelled to the compliance of the law, are not under the strict rigor of the law, but under the grace of the Gospel, it by no means follows that they are in no way under the law, that they ought not to learn the will of God from the law, what is to be done and what is to be omitted, nor to compose themselves to the observance of the law. Although we are not ὑπόνομοι, we are nevertheless not ἄνομοι but ἔννομοι. Conf. 1 Cor. IX. 21. Indeed, he proves the contrary partly from the very state of the justified, that they have surrendered themselves into service not to sin, but to Christ, according to the form and norm of the doctrine of the Word, which is completed by the law and the Gospel; partly from the end, scope, and goal of justification. Since the end of justification is both sanctification and the gift of eternal life: which the justified could by no means attain if they wished to serve sin, from which there is nothing but shameful fruit and an unhappy outcome, eternal death. The Apostle proposed the former argument in v. 16, 17, 18, 19, the latter in v. 20, 21, 22, 23.

ἐκ οἴδατε. Again he clearly shows what he teaches, so that the Christians at Rome may have something to oppose with Paul's words to the Jewish detractors.

Latin:

V. 15. τί ὖν. Quid ex his sequitur, quæ diximus? An illud quod inimici Evangelii nos docere dicunt?

ἁμαρτήσομεν. Etiam hic Manuscriptus habet ἁμαρτήσωμεν peccemus, Rectè. Est enim μίμησις verborum, quæ usurpabant ini- mici, sic supra 1. ἐπιμένωμεν. Peccemus, id est, pergamus indulgere vitiis.

μὴ γένοιτο. Longè absit ut supra 1. & alibi sæpè.

Vis objectionis hæc est: Quid igitur, num pec- cabimus? (non verò num peccemus, nedum per- gamus indulgere vitiis? Justificati enim non in- dulgent vitiis; ideoque eorum non est pergere in eo) Quum simus sub gratia, non sub lege: lex ad nos non spectat, neque proinde legi obedientia adstrin- gimur. Ita perversè colligitur ex eo, quod Apo- stolus dixerat, nos non esse sub lege, qui hoc tantum dixit ratione maledictionis, coactionis, & rigorosæ exactionis, non autem ratione obedientiæ & ob- servationis. Idcircò explicat Apostolus statum & conditionem justificatorum: ut huic objectioni satisfiat, ac consequentiam penitus negat μὴ γέ- νοιτο, longe absit: nam ex eo, quod non conde- mnentur justificati voce legis, non cogantur ad obsequium legis, non sub stricto rigore legis sint, sed sub gratia Evangelii, neutiquam sequitur, quod nullatenus sub lege sint, quod nec ex lege debeant voluntatem Dei discere, quid agendum quid omittendum, nec sese componere ad obser- vationem legis. Etsi non simus ὑπόνομοι, non tamen sumus ἄνομοι sed ἔννομοι. Conf. 1. Cor. IX. 21. Quin contrarium probat partim ex ipso justificatorum statu, quod se in servitium addixerint non pec- cato, sed Christo, secundum formam & normam doctrinæ Verbi, quod lege & Evangelio absolvi- tur; partim è justificationis fine, scopo & termino. Siquidem finis justificationis sit tùm sanctificatio, tùm vitæ æternæ donatio: quem assequi justificati minimè possint, si peccato servire velint, unde non nisi pudendus fructus & infelix exitus, mors æter- na. Prius argumentum proposuit Apostolus v. 16. 17. 18. 19. posterius v. 20. 21. 22. 23.

ἐκ οἴδατε. Rursum clarè ostendit quid doceat, ut habeant Christia- ni Romæ, quod Pauli verbis opponant Judæis obtrectato- ribus.

## 6:16
V. 16. That to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves to whom you obey, whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness.

There are two Masters, sin and life according to the Gospel, which is here called the Gospel by metonymy. To which you enslave yourselves is your choice, as if at a Pythagorean crossroads. But so that you may choose well, see what the outcome of each empire is. On this side death, and indeed eternal death, because Christ does not die again to resolve it: on that side righteousness, that is, praise for righteousness. Because δῦλοι is here constructed with the genitives ἁμαρτίας and ὑπακοῆς, therefore ᾧ is repeated twice, not with

δῦλοι is construed, but it is a dative having the force of a Latin ablative, as if he were saying: By this very fact that you surrender yourselves, by this very fact that you induce your mind to obey either sin or the Gospel, by this, I say, very fact you enter upon the way either to death or to the praise of righteousness.

Latin:

V. 16. ὅτι ᾧ παρισάνετε ἑαυτὸς δύλες εἰς ὑπακοὴν δῦλοί ἐςε ᾧ ὑπακύετε, ἤτοι ἁμαρτίας εἰς θά- νατον, ἢ ὑπακοῆς εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

Duo sunt Domini, peccatum & vita secundum Evange- lium, quæ hîc per μετωνυμίαν Evangelium dicitur. Utri vos mancipetis vestra electio est, tanquam in bivio Pytha- gorico. Sed ut benè eligatis, videte quis sit utriusque im- perii exitus. Hinc mors & quidem æterna, quia Christus non iterum moritur, ut eam solvat: inde justitia, id est, laus pro justitia. Quia δῦλοι hic construitur cum geniti- vis ἁμαρτίας & ὑπακοῆς, ideo ᾧ bis repetitum non cum

δῦλοι conftruitur, sed est dativus vim habens ablativi lati- ni, quasi dicat: Hoc ipso quod vos mancipatis, hoc ipso quod in animum inducitis, parere aut peccato aut Evan- gelio, hoc, inquam, ipso viam initis aut ad mortem, aut ad justitiae laudem.

## 6:17
V. 17. But thanks be to God.

Just as for the Gospel, so also for the success of the Gospel, thanks are always to be given. Above I. 8.
