that you were slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were delivered.

There is here first a Hebraism of the past tense with a copulative conjunction, in place of a participle. For he does not give thanks to God because they served sin, but because those who served sin afterwards obeyed the Gospel: ἐκ καρδίας, that is, not outwardly only, but within the recesses of the mind, with sincere faith. The same kind of speaking is in Deut. IV. 29. VI. 5. XI. 13. XIII. 3. Mark XII. 30. Luke X. 27. 1 Tim. I. 5. 2 Tim. II. 22. See also what we said at Matt. XXII. 37. εἰς τύπον διδαχῆς, that is, you obeyed according to that manner which the doctrine of the Gospel prescribes. Thus κατὰ τύπον is taken in Heb. VIII. 5. from the passage in Exodus XXV. 40. where in the Hebrew is תבנית which elsewhere is translated as pattern, elsewhere as arrangement, form, likeness. That παρεδόκατε has the same value as παρελάβετε קבלתם. See what we said at Matt. XV. 2. For the Greeks are accustomed from active verbs, even those which govern a dative of the person, to form passives and to add to them an accusative of the thing, as ἐπιστεύθησαν λόγια above III. 2. ἐπιστεύθην τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον 1 Tim. I. Thus also elegant Greeks say ἐπιτρέπομαι δίαιταν and similar things. The Gospel is called teaching in John VII. 16, 17. Acts V. 28. XIII. 12. below XVI. 17. 2 John 9. It is תלמוד but the opposite to the Jewish one.

The Apostle's first argument holds thus: To whom anyone has addicted himself into service, to him he ought to show himself obedient. But the justified have addicted themselves to Christ into service. Therefore they ought to show themselves obedient to Christ. The major premise is confirmed: because those who addict themselves to service, bind themselves εἰς ὑπακοὴν to obedience, and so they are truly the slaves of him whom they obey. The minor premise is clear of its own accord: because the justified addict themselves to service to Christ for the reason that He liberated them from sin and death. Therefore the pronoun of the person in the dative ὧ is not to be left indeterminate and without application, but Christ the Lord or GOD from v. 11 and 13 is here looked to: to whom we serve τῇ ὑπακοῇ εἰς δικαιοσύνην through obedience unto righteousness: just as τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ to sin or disobedience one serves the devil εἰς θάνατον unto death. The Apostle changes the cases, because those who are slaves, whether of sin or of obedience, serve or present themselves as slaves either to the Devil or to Christ and GOD. He opposes sin and obedience, because sin is truly disobedience. He also opposes death and righteousness: because to live in injustice is spiritual death, and the beginning and cause of eternal death. However, righteousness is understood here not of the person, but of a good conscience, not imputed, but begun, not of absolution, but of renovation. Therefore the masters are not sin and life according to the Gospel—which, how would it be called the Gospel metonymically here, when the word Gospel does not appear here at all?—but the masters are the Devil and GOD, to whom one serves when we are slaves either of sin or of obedience. Nor is righteousness here praise for righteousness, but it properly denotes holiness of life. For we obey, not that we may bring back praise or glory, but εἰς δικαιοσύνην unto righteousness, that we may be just and holy, and have the righteousness of a good conscience. Which, even if it obtains praise by divine grace, yet we are not justified before GOD through it, nor do we aspire to eternal salvation, concerning which the holy Apostle says in 1 Cor. IV. 4: I am not conscious of anything against myself, yet I am not justified by this. Nevertheless, praise will be to each one from GOD; the major proposition is a rule taken from the law of nations: To whom anyone has given himself to serve, his slave he is thereafter, just as among the Jews some sold themselves voluntarily into slavery v. 16. The minor proposition v. 17 should have been put simply thus: But you gave yourselves into slavery to GOD and His righteousness; for we are reminded that we were before miserable slaves of the Devil and sin, but having been liberated from there through Christ, we have been made slaves of GOD and righteousness. Therefore we must see carefully that we do not relapse into our former slavery. Added here, moreover, is an amplification from thanksgiving, so that we may consider that this benefit is both huge, and whose it is, and that thanks are owed to GOD, and finally that it is to be retained with the greatest zeal. τύπῳ διδαχῆς; it is not the manner which the doctrine of the Gospel prescribes; for in the Gospel the laws of living are not contained; but faith alone is required for justification and salvation: therefore by the pattern of teaching, the form of heavenly doctrine, which is completed by the whole law and Gospel, is understood, in which pattern we have the form and manner both of believing, as far as the Gospel is concerned, and of living, as far as the law is concerned. Rightly the blessed Gerhard: The sense of the Apostle is that for the faithful Romans, since they have been translated from that state in which they previously served sin, a certain reason and form of doctrine has been proposed, which they might use thereafter as a rule of faith and life; that they might conform themselves to it, and express their faith and life exactly according to it.

Latin:

V. 17. χάρις δὲ τῷ θεῷ.

Sicut pro Evangelio, ita & pro successu Evangelii gra- tiae semper habendae sunt. Supra I. 8.

ὅτι ἦτε δῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ὑπακούσατε δὲ ἐκ καρ- δίας εἰς ὃν παρεδώκατε τύπον διδαχῆς.

Est hic primum Hebraismus praeteriti cum copulativa conjunctione, vice participii. Non enim Deo gratias agit quod servierint peccato, sed quod qui servierunt peccato, postea obedierunt Evangelio: ἐκ καρδίας, id est, non ex- terius tantum, sed intra animi recessus, sincera fide. Idem loquendi genus Deut. IV. 29. VI. 5. XI. 13. XIII. 3. Marc. XII. 30. Luc. X. 27. 1. Tim. I. 5. 2. Tim. II. 22. Vide & quae diximus Matth. XXII. 37. εἰς τύπον διδαχῆς, id est, obedistis ad eum modum, quem doctrina Evangelii prae- scribit. Sic κατὰ τύπον sumitur Hebr. VIII. 5. ex loco Exodi XXV. 40. ubi in Hebraeo תבנית quod alibi vertitur πα- ράδειγμα, alibi διάταξις, μορφὴ, ὁμοίωμα. Illud παρεδό- κατε idem valet quod παρελάβετε קבלתם. Vide quae di- ximus ad Matth. XV. 2. Solent enim Graeci ab activis, et- iam quae dativum personae regunt, formare passiva & eis addere accusativum rei, ut ἐπιστεύθησαν λόγια supra III. 2. ἐπιστεύθην τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον 1. Tim. I. Sic & elegantes Graeci dicunt ἐπιτρέπομαι δίαιταν & similia. Evangelium vocatur διδαχὴ Joh. VII. 16. 17. Act. V. 28. XIII. 12. infra XVI. 17. 2. Joh. 9. est תלמוד sed oppositum Judaico.

Argumentum Apostoli prius ita habet: Cui quis in servitium se addixit, illi sese obsequentem praebere debet. At justificati se Christo in servitium addixere. Ergo debent sese obsequentes Christo prae- bere. Major confirmatur: quod qui servitio ad- dicunt sese, εἰς ὑπακοὴν ad obedientiam sese ob- stringunt, adeoque servi etiam ejus demum vere sunt, cui obediunt. Minor ultro patet: quia Chri- sto ideo sese in servitium addicunt justificati, quod eosdem a peccato, & morte liberavit. Non ergo indeterminate & sine applicatione relinquendum est pronomen personae Dativum ὧ, sed Christus Dominus vel DEUS e v. 11. & 13. hic respicitur: cui servimus τῇ ὑπακοῇ εἰς δικαιοσύνην per obedien- tiam ad justitiam: quemadmodum τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ peccato vel inobedientia servitur diabolo εἰς θάνα- τον ad mortem. Permutat Apostolus casus, quia qui servi sunt sive ἁμαρτίας, sive ὑπακοῆς, servi- unt vel servos se sistunt aut Diabolo, aut Christo & DEO. Opponit ἁμαρτίαν & ὑπακοὴν, quia peccatum vere est inobedientia. Opponit & θάνα- τον καὶ δικαιοσύνην: quia in injustitia vivere mors est spiritualis, & initium & causa mortis aeternae. Intelligitur autem hic justitia non personae, sed bo- nae conscientiae, non imputata, sed inchoata, non absolutionis, sed renovationis. Domini ergo non sunt peccatum, & vita secundum Evangelium, quae quomodo hic metonymice Evangelium dicere- tur, quum vox Evangelii hic plane non occurrat? sed Domini sunt Diabolus & DEUS, quibus ser- vitur, cum servi sumus vel peccati, vel obedien- tiae. Neque justitia hic est laus pro justitia, sed proprie notat sanctitatem vitae. Obedimus enim, non ut laudem reportemus, vel gloriam, sed εἰς δικαιοσύνην ad justitiam, ut justi & sancti simus, & justitiam bonae conscientiae habeamus. Quae etsi laudem consequatur divina gratia, non tamen per eandem vel justificamur coram DEO, vel ad sa- lutem aeternam adspiramus, de quo S. Apostol. 1. Cor. IV. 4. Nihil quidem mihi conscius sum, non tamen in eo justificatus sum. Laus tamen erit uni- cuique a DEO; Major propositio est regula e jure gentium desumpta: Cui se quis dedit ad ser- viendum, ejus servus posthac est, sicut apud Ju- daeos aliqui se ultro vendebant in servitutem v. 16. Minor propositio v. 17. simpliciter ita poni de- bebat: At vos dedistis vos in servitutem DEO & justitiæ ejus; Monemur enim nos fuisse antea mi- sera mancipia Diaboli & peccati, sed inde per Christum liberatos servos factos esse DEI & justi- tiæ. Videndum igitur nobis solerter esse, ne in pristinam servitutem relabamur. Addita autem hic est amplificatio à gratiarum actione, ut cogi- temus, tum ingens esse hoc beneficium, tum cu- jus sit, tum DEO gratias deberi, tum denique summo studio esse retinendum. τύπῳ διδαχῆς· non est modus, quem doctrina Evangelii præscri- bit; in Evangelio enim leges vivendi non haben- tur; sed unicè fides requiritur ad justificationem & salutem: proinde per τύπον διδαχῆς forma do- ctrinæ cælestis, quæ universa lege & Evangelio absolvitur, intelligitur, in quo typo habemus for- mam & modum tum credendi, quantum ad Ev- angelium, tum vivendi, quantum ad legem. Re- ctè B. Gerhardus: Sensus Apostoli est, fidelibus Romanis, cum translati sint ab eo statu, in quo prius serviebant peccato, certam doctrinæ rationem ac for- mam esse propositam, quâ illi imposterum pro fidei ac vitæ regulâ uterentur; ad eam sese conformarent, & fidę ac vitæ ad amussim exprimerent.

## 6:18
· But having been set free from sin·

It is the same as δικαιωθέντες, as we also said in the Prolegomena to this Epistle, and it is proven from that which we just had in verse 7. But the word ἐλευθερωθέντες was more appropriate here, because δῦλοι preceded it several times. A cruel enemy had captured you: GOD took you out from there. The word ἐλευθερῦν and similar ones love to have the preposition ἀπὸ or ἐξ after them for the Hebrew מן, as below VI. 22. VIII. 2. 21. Deut. VII. 8. XIII. 5. XXI. 8. 1. Paralip. XVII. 21. and often elsewhere. Thus also Plato: ἀπὸ τῶν βαρβάρων ἐλευθερώσα τὴν πόλιν. ·

V. 18. ἐδωλώθητε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ.

We said above in 6 that δουλέυειν is also taken in a good sense, as here δουλωθῆναι, that is, to be made a slave, to be assigned, to be enslaved; and the word δικαιοσύνης here is general, as above in 13.

The reborn are said to be liberated from sin, because they have been liberated both from the guilt of sin in justification, and from the dominion of sin in renewal; because sin and righteousness are mutually opposed to each other, therefore liberation from sin brings with it an obligation to serve righteousness. Therefore the Apostle attributes to the justified both liberty and servitude: for they are free, because, having been liberated from both the guilt and dominion of sin, they no longer serve sin, but are led by the spirit of liberty, and offer spontaneous worship and obedience to GOD: but they are servants, because they do not have the license to do whatever they wish at their own discretion, but have a norm of living prescribed in the law; which servitude, however, is without coercion, and is a voluntary or free servitude.

Latin:

· ἐλευθερωθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας·

Idem est quod δικαιωθέντες, ut & in Prolegomenis ad hanc Epistolam diximus, & evincitur ex eo, quod habui- mus modo commate 7. sed congruentior hic fuit vox ἐλευθερωθέντες, quia δῦλοι præcessit aliquoties. Crudelis hostis vos ceperat: DEUS vos inde exemit. Amant vox ἐλευθερῦν & similes post se præpositionem ἀπὸ vel ἐξ pro Hebræo מן ut infra VI. 22. VIII. 2. 21. Deut. VII. 8. XIII. 5. XXI. 8. 1. Paralip. XVII. 21. & alibi sæpè. Sic & Plato: ἀπὸ τῶν βαρβάρων ἐλευθερώσα τὴν πόλιν. ·

V. 18. ἐδωλώθητε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ.

Diximus supra 6. δουλέυειν etiam in honestam partem sumi, ut hic δουλωθῆναι, id est, servum fieri, addici, manci- pari & δικαιοσύνης vox hic generalis est, ut supra 13.

Liberati à peccato dicuntur renati, quod & à reatu peccati liberati sint in justificatione, & à do- minio peccati in renovatione; Quia peccatum & justitia sunt sibi invicem opposita, ideò liberatio à peccato affert secum obligationem ad servien- dum justitiæ. Tribuit ergò Apostolus justificatis & libertatem, & servitutem: Liberi enim sunt, quia à peccati & reatu & dominio liberati non amplius peccato serviunt, sed spiritu libertatis du- cuntur, & DEO spontaneum cultum & obsequium præstant: Servi autem sunt, quia non habent li- centiam quidvis agendi pro arbitrio, sed normam vivendi in lege præscriptam habent; quæ tamen servitus est sine coactione, & voluntaria, vel libe- ra servitus.

## 6:19
V. 19. ἀνθρώπινον λέγω.

That is, I express spiritual meanings through similarities of common things known to you. Is it not fair that he who has been liberated by a king from savage enemies should serve his king well? See what we said above in III. 5. regarding John III. 12.

διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν.

He is not dealing here with vices, but with the slowness of the intellect. Thus ἀσθενὴς is used in 1 Cor. VIII. 7. and ἀσθενῶν below in XIV. 1. 1 Cor. VIII. 11. And σὰρξ in this place is indeed a mind broken to handle earthly things, such as were especially the minds of the Romans.

You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with power. Therefore he takes the similarity from empires.

A certain human thing: because of the proposed similarity concerning servitude and liberty, with which he had compared the flight from sin and obedience to righteousness: namely, a heavenly and spiritual matter with a terrestrial and civil one, in a human manner, although that similarity is far inferior in reality, and does not exactly correspond.

By ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς [weakness of the flesh] is understood not only the infirmity of the intellect, but of the whole subject, insofar as all faculties labor under infirmity due to the remnants of sin: by which name, in human fashion, one must speak not only with the Romans, but with all the reborn, so that they may both grasp and embrace these things better: for those things which are proposed under the form of illustrious similitudes are more easily understood and explained. Therefore, the blessed Gerhard does not wrongly understand by ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς a carnal and rude intellect, provided that it is not said exclusively, but that the carnal propensity of the will is also included. For on account of this also, there is need of συγκαταβάσει [condescension] in instruction; since when the mind has been corrected regarding the equity of a matter through clear similitudes, the will becomes more willing to obey: to whose infirmity, therefore, one must also bring aid. To this effect is what Desid. Heraldus notes on Martial, that ἀνθρωπίνως λαλεῖν [to speak humanly] is to use popular words. See other explanations in B. Balduinus.

ὥσπερ γὰρ παρεστήσατε.

You, Romans, who now profess Christ, see what I say, and what you ought to answer those Jews, not only with words, but also with deeds.

Δοῦλα τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ [Slaves to uncleanness]. See above I. 24. καὶ τῇ ἀνομίᾳ [and to lawlessness].

By the name of Ἀνομίας [lawlessness] understand all those things which are done against the law of human society, such as those things about which [I spoke] above I. 27. 30. 31.

εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν [unto lawlessness].

So that you became worse daily. For that is the way of habit. By that formula of speaking, τῇ ἀνομίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν [to lawlessness unto lawlessness], an increase with continuation is altogether denoted. Psalm 84:7, 144:13.

ὕτω νῦν παραστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ [so now present your members as slaves to righteousness].

Do I demand anything unjust, when I wish you to apply as much diligence in cultivating virtues as you applied in cultivating vices? Procopius, II Vandalicorum, not wrongly: Those who are successful in the things in which they sinned might bring forward a more becoming defense.

Εἰς ἁγιασμὸν [unto sanctification].

That is, so that you may make progress daily in holiness. For the power of habit is equal in either direction: indeed, it is stronger toward the good. See what we said on Matt. 11:30. An argument from comparison is involved here: With as much zeal as you once served sin before regeneration and justification, with so much zeal must you now serve righteousness after regeneration and justification. For the reason of contrary masters requires this. But before regeneration you served sin with great promptness and alacrity, because you also offered your services to sin itself. Which is to exhibit or present your members to sin. However, a parity of habit does not hold here, and it is false that habit is stronger toward the good, which even the ἀσθένεια τῆς σαρκὸς [weakness of the flesh] refutes. Whence it is gathered from the lesser to the greater regarding what is owed, not what is done: If you once served sin with singular zeal, with how much greater zeal must you now serve righteousness?

Latin:

V. 19. ἀνθρώπινον λέγω.

Id est, sensus spirituales exprimo per similitudines rerum vulgarium & vobis notarum. Nonne æquum est, ut regi suo bene serviat, qui per regem à sævis hostibus liberatus est? Vide quæ diximus supra III. 5. ad Joh. III. 12.

διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν.

Non de vitiis, sed de intellectus tarditate hic agit. Sic ἀσθενὴς usurpatur 1. Cor. VIII. 7. & ἀσθενῶν infra XIV. 1. 1. Cor. VIII. 11. Et σὰρξ hoc quidem loco est ingenium- fractum tractare res terrestres, qualia erant præcipuè in- genia Romanorum.

Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento. Ideò ab imperiis sumit similitudinem.

Humanum quoddam: ob propositam simili- tudinem de servitute & libertate, cum quâ fugam peccati & obedientiam justitiæ comparaverat: rem scilicet cælestem & spiritualem cum terrenâ & civili, more humano, quamvis similitudo illa longè reipsâ inferior sit, nec exactè congruat.

Per ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς non intellectûs infirmitas modò, sed totius subjecti, quatenus ob reliquias peccati omnes facultates infirmitate laborant, in- telligitur: quo nomine, humano more, non cum Romanis tantum, sed cum omnibus renatis loquen- dum est, ut & capere & amplecti ea melius pos- sint: faciliùs enim tùm intelliguntur, tùm expe- diuntur, quæ sub forma illustrium similitudinum proponuntur. Ideò non malè B. Gerhardus per ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς intelligit carnalem & rudem intellectum, dummodò non exclusivè id dicatur, sed voluntatis etiam carnalis propensio compre- hendatur. Nam & hujus gratia συγκαταβάσει o- pus est in informatione; quum mente de rei æqui- tate, per similia luculenta correctâ, voluntas luben- tior eat in obsequia: cujus proinde infirmitati etiam succurrendum. Quo facit quod Desid. Heraldus ad Martal. notat ἀνθρωπίνως λαλεῖν esse popularibus verbis uti. Alias explicationes vid. apud B. Balduinum.

ὥσπερ γὰρ παρεστήσατε.

Vos, Romani, qui nunc Christum profitemini, videte quid dicam, & quid Judæis illis respondere debeatis non verbis tantum, sed & rebus.

Δοῦλα τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ. Vide supra I. 24. καὶ τῇ ἀνομίᾳ.

Ἀνομίας nomine ea omnia intellige, quæ contra legem societatis humanæ fiunt, qualia sunt illa, de quibus supra I. 27. 30. 31.

εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν.

Ita ut quotidiè pejores fieretis. Is enim mos est con- suetudinis. Per istam loquendi formulam τῇ ἀνομίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν omninò cum continuatione incrementum notatur Psalm. XXCIV. 7. CXLIV. 13.

ὕτω νῦν παραστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ.

An iniquum aliquid exigo, cum volo vos tantum dili- gentiæ adhibere in colendis virtutibus, quantum adhibui- stis in colendis vitiis? Procopius II. Vandalicorum non malè: Οἱ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐυδοκιμῦντες οἷς ἥμαρτον, ἐυκρεπεστέραν τὴν ἀπολογίαν εἰσκοὶ φέροιεν.

Εἰς ἁγιασμὸν.

Id est, ita ut quotidiè progressum faciatis in sanctitate. Par enim vis consuetudinis in utramque partem: imò ad bonum fortior. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XI, 30. Involvitur hic Argumentum à comparatis: Quanto studio olim ante regenerationem & justifi- cationem serviistis peccato, tanto studio nunc ser- viendum est justitiæ post regenerationem & justifica- tionem. Id enim ratio contrariorum Domino- rum requirit. Atqui ante regenerationem magnâ promtitudine & alacritate serviistis peccato, quia & officia vestra peccato ipsi obtulistis. Quod est exhibere seu sistere membra peccato. Non ve- ro hic paritas consuetudinis obtinet, & falsum est fortiorem esse consuetudinem ad bonum, quod vel ἀσθένεια τῆς σαρκὸς refellit. Unde de debito, non de facto à minori ad majus colligitur: Si studio sin- gulari olim serviistis peccato, quanto majori studio serviendum nunc est justitiæ?

## 6:20
V. 20. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.

That is, you did not even think about that which was honorable and pleasing to God. So also now, think of nothing that is shameful and displeasing to God. Apply equal effort. It is apparent here that the word ἐλεύθερος is used in a good sense and in a bad sense, no less than δοῦλος.

Latin:

V. 20. Ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ.

Id est, ne cogitabatis quidem de eo, quod honestum ac Deo gratum esset. Sic & nunc nihil cogitate, quod turpe sit Deoque displiceat. Parem adhibete operam. Apparet hic vocem ἐλεύθερος, in re bona & in re mala dici, non minus quam δῦλος.

## 6:21
V. 21. What fruit then did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?

The only fruit was infamy among the good. This is clear, because even you, having now become good, cannot remember them without shame. If the recollection effects this, what does the thing itself do?

It is an ellipsis. For he wishes to say this: Such was the thing itself. But if you look to the end or outcome, it was none other than death, namely without hope of a better life: For neither did GOD promise anything good to those living in such a way, nor does the human mind itself, conscious of such things, dare to hope for any good, as Plato testifies in the first book of the Republic. Τέλος here is עקב, which is sometimes translated as τὰ ἔσχατα, sometimes as ἀνταπόδοσις.

By death is understood not temporal death, but death or the separation of the soul from the body, but eternal and infernal death: which is the penalty of the slavery of sin, when repentance is not practiced. Furthermore, in one way the τέλος of sins is called eternal death, in another way the τέλος of faith is called the salvation of souls and eternal life, 1 Pet. 1:9. Here it is a bare consequence, because eternal life follows perseverance in faith: there, however, sins merit death, and the wages of sin is death. Τέλος, however, as the blessed Mylius notes on p. 253, is not taken here ethically, for that for the sake of which something is done; for no one sins with the intention that he might die: but it is used for a limit and outcome.

Latin:

V. 21. Τίνα ὖν καρπὸν εἴχετε τότε ἐφ’ ὅις νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε;

Fructus unicus erat infamia apud bonos. Liquet hoc, quia & ipsi boni jam facti sine pudore eorum meminisse non potestis. Si hoc efficit recordatio, quid res ipsa?

Est ἔλλειψις. Vult enim hoc dicere : Talis erat res ipsa. Quod si finem sive exitum respicitis, is nullus alius erat quam mors, nempe sine spe vitæ melioris: Neque enim DEUS ita viventibus quicquam promisit boni, neque ipsa per se mens humana talium sibi conscia quicquam boni spe- rare audet, ut Plato testatur de Republica prim. Τέλος hic est עקב quod modò vertitur τὰ ἔσχατα, modò ἀνταπόδοσις.

Per mortem intelligitur non mors temporalis, sed mors aut separatio animæ à corpore, sed mors æterna, & infernalis: quæ pœna est servitutis peccati, cum non agitur pœnitentia. Cæterùm aliâ ratione τέλος peccatorum dicitur mors æterna, alia ratio- ne τέλος fidei, salus animarum & vita æterna vo- catur 1. Petr. I. 9. Hic nuda est consequentia, quia vita æterna sequitur perseverantiam in fide: ibi verò peccata merentur mortem, & peccatorum stipendium est mors. Τέλος autem, notante B. My- lio p. 253. non Ethicè hìc accipitur, pro eo, cujus gratia fit aliquid; Nemo enim eo consilio peccat, ut moria- tur: sed pro termino atque eventu ponitur.

## 6:22
V. 22. But now.

This is opposed to that ὅτε γὰρ: as if he were to say, things have changed much. See above 19.

Having been set free from sin.

As above 18.

But having been enslaved to God.

Enslaved to GOD. Above he said τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ 18. namely, he who serves goodness and honest things, serves GOD also: because GOD has always loved this and has most clearly commanded it in the Gospel.

You have your fruit unto holiness.

Here is the fruit for the present, that daily you become holier and on that account also more honorable among good men. This is opposed to the infamy which he signified when he also spoke of a memory devoid of shame.

But the end, eternal life.

He opposes end to end, life to death, and not a brief or finite one, but truly eternal.

Those converted to Christ are said to be indeed freedmen of sin, but servants of GOD, than which servitude no liberty can be given more precious. The fruit of this servitude is said to be not Sanctification itself, because Christ alone has been made sanctification for us by GOD: but UNTO SANCTIFICATION. For although it is certain that the pious are renewed by the Spirit of the mind, yet unless another Sanctification is added, which flows from Christ into us, we cannot please GOD.

Latin:

V. 22. Νυνὶ δὲ.

Hoc opponitur illi ὅτε γὰρ: quasi dicat, multùm mu- tatæ sunt res. Vide supra 19.

Ἐλευθερωθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.

Ut supra 18.

Δουλωθέντες δὲ τῷ Θεῷ.

Mancipati DEO. Supra dixit τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ 18. nimi- rum qui bonitati rebusque honestis servit, & DEO servit: quia DEUS hoc semper amavit & in Evangelio apertissimè præcepit.

Ἔχετε τὸν καρπὸν ἡμῶν εἰς ἁγιασμὸν.

Hic in præsens est fructus, quod quotidiè evaditis san- ctiores ac propter id etiam honoratiores apud bonos. Op- ponitur hoc infamiæ, quam significavit, cum & memoriam dixit pudoris haud consortem.

Τὸ δὲ τέλος, ζωὴν αἰώνιον.

Finem fini opponit, morti vitam, nec brevem aut defi- turam, sed verè æternam.

Dicuntur conversi ad Christum liberti quidem peccati, DEI verò servi esse, quâ servitute libertas nulla dari potest pretiosior. Fructus hujus servi- tutis dicitur non ipsa Sanctificatio, quia Christus solus factus est nobis à DEO sanctificatio: sed AD SANCTIFICATIONEM. Quamvis enim pios renovari Spiritû mentis certum sit, nisi tamen alia accedat Sanctificatio, quæ ex Christo in nos dima- nat, DEO placere non possumus.

## 6:23
V. 23. For the wages of sin is death.

It is a comparison taken from military service, which is itself a kind of servitude, most known to the Romans. Ὀψώνια are properly those things which are given to be eaten for bread, a usage which has remained in the Latin language; formerly the provisions themselves were given to the soldier, afterwards money was given for them, but the old name remained. In the glossaries: ὀψώνιον is a daily allowance: Polybius among others uses it thus. Thence the word passed also to the Jews as אפסניא as we said at Luke III. 14. and therefore our writers use it as if it were known to all, as appears not only here and in the cited place of Luke, but also 1 Cor. IX. 7. He wonderfully calls the evil which is rendered for wicked deeds a reward, since a reward is usually rendered for labor. There is a similar μετάληψις in Cicero when he said: A great reward has been given to my error. But Seneca also spoke of the reward of vices.

But the gift of GOD is eternal life.

Kings are accustomed to give to excellent soldiers, besides their pay, crowns, laurels, and honors. He compares eternal life to these donatives, not because it is not given to those who have served well, but because it is much greater than the merit, being an eternal and heavenly thing. Eternal life could indeed be called a reward, as it is often called, but the name of a donative is more noble. Nor is the article added in vain, and at the same time that order of speaking is inverted which had been in the former member in contrast. For this is what he means: But the donative which GOD gives to those serving Him is not something harmful, like death, nor something trivial, as in the Roman military, but it is the greatest thing, immortality and heavenly joys. Where one renders much more for a work than the work is worth, It can be called both a reward and a gift: for it partakes of both. But here the nature of a gift promised under a condition and given after the condition has been fulfilled prevails.

Although eternal life is given to those who serve God, it is not, however, rendered for work or service; both because this service is very imperfect, and joined with innumerable defects, which by their nature deserve death, and because eternal life is a χάρισμα and a purely gratuitous gift of God, which we in no way deserve, but obtain by mere grace. χαρίζομαι is not simply to bestow, but to bestow freely, as Phavorinus notes: χαρίζομαι; οὐ μόνον τὸ δωρεῖσθαι ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ χάριν τινὶ ποιεῖν. Whence Chrysostom, Homily X: Eternal life is neither a debt, nor a retribution for labors, but a gratuitous gift of divine bounty. Jerome, Vol. 1, Epistle 108: Where there is grace, it is not a retribution for works, but a bounty of the giver. Compare Romans 11:6, Ephesians 2:8, 1 Timothy 6:21. 1 Peter 3:8. Both because life is given to us not on account of our merits or works, but in Christ Jesus our Lord, who acquired life for us by his merits and death, and gave himself for the life of the world, John 6:51; he gave his soul as a price of redemption for us, Matthew 20:28, Mark 10:45, 1 Timothy 2:5. And therefore life procured by Christ is given to us only in Christ Jesus apprehended by faith, John 3:16, 36, ch. 6:47, Acts 4:12, ch. 10:43, ch. 13:39; and because the Apostle did not say that eternal life is ὀψώνια, the wages of our service, in the same way as he said death is the wages of sin: but having changed the kind of speech, he called life a χάρισμα. Since in the preceding verses he delighted in an antithesis of similarity, and remained in the same kind of speech, as for instance concerning the service of sin, that it is freedom from righteousness; concerning its fruit, that it is shameful; concerning its end, that it is death; and on the contrary concerning the service of God, that it is freedom from sin; concerning its fruit, that it makes for our sanctification; concerning its end, that it is eternal life; here he varies the kind of speech, and indeed calls death the wages of sin, as ὀψώνια in Luke 3:14, 1 Corinthians 9:7, denote wages, which are paid out of merit for military service and labor; but he does not call life wages, but a purely gratuitous gift, which is conferred upon us solely on account of Christ's merit, and in Christ and his merit apprehended by faith, without regard to or merit of any work of ours, so that we may understand that, although it is conferred upon us because we serve God having been freed from sin, nevertheless eternal life is not conferred upon us on account of the service rendered to God, but is a gift just as gratuitous as justification itself.

Holy antiquity studiously observed this precision of the Apostle's words, which is to be diligently noted against the Papists and Socinians: especially St. Chrysostom, Homily 12: Having named the wages of sin, when speaking of good things he did not keep the same order: for he did not say, the reward of your good deeds, but the grace of God: showing that they were not freed by their own strength, nor did they receive what was a debt, nor is that which is given to them either a retribution or a remuneration for labors, but all things came to pass by grace, and that he gave them through the Son. And Theodoret in this place: when he spoke of eternal life which is rendered to righteousness, he did not say it was a reward, but grace: for eternal life is a gift of God. For even if someone has performed supreme or absolute righteousness, nevertheless eternal things do not correspond in equilibrium to temporal labors; and Fulgentius, Book 1 to Monimus: From grace is given not only to the justified a good life, but also to the glorified eternal life. But why is death called wages, but eternal life grace, unless because the former is rendered, the latter is given. And Theophylact: Death is the wages of a transgression. Wages is called the money which is spent by a prince for the provisions of soldiers; sin therefore, to us whom it had held as slaves, paid back death as the reward of service: but he called what is to come from God grace, not a reward: just as if he were to say: For you will not receive rewards for labors, but all these things come to pass through grace in Christ Jesus, who works and effects these things. Nor did St. Augustine (to whom the Papists are accustomed to appeal here) think otherwise in Enchiridion, chapter 107: wages are rendered as a debt for the work of military service, they are not given; if grace is not gratuitous, it is not grace. Likewise, Vol. 2, Works, Epistle 105 to Sixtus: Fighting most vigilantly against the plague of pride, he says, the wages of sin is death. Rightly wages, because it is owed, because it is worthily paid back, because it is rendered by merit: then, lest righteousness should exalt itself from human merit, just as human merit is not doubted to be sin, he did not report it from the contrary by saying: the wages of righteousness is eternal life, but, he says, the grace of God is eternal life. And he added this, in Christ Jesus our Lord, so that it might not be sought by any other way than through the mediator. Thus St. Augustine. But also some of the Papists have had the eyes of their minds pierced by the rays of truth here: namely, Cardinal Cusanus, and Cardinal Cajetan: The former says, it is to be noted here that the Apostle hints that death is owed to sin out of justice, for the name of wages seems to signify this; but that eternal life is from the gratuitous gift of God. The latter indeed: He does not say that the wages of righteousness is eternal life; but the gift of God is eternal life, so that we may understand that we do not attain eternal life as an end from the merits of works, but from the gratuitous gift of God, for which reason he adds, in Christ our Lord. Behold merit, behold righteousness, whose wages is eternal life, but to us a gift, by reason of Jesus Christ himself. Therefore eternal life is not both wages and a gift, nor does it partake of both; nor is it a gift promised under the condition of our obedience: but it is given by mere grace. For grace is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way, as Augustine says again, with the Apostle leading the way in Romans 11:6. Compare the Theology of the Apostle Paul to this place.

Latin:

V. 23. Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος.

Est similitudo sumpta de militia, quæ & ipsa servitus quædam est, maximè nota Romanis. Ὀψώνια propriè sunt, quæ ad panem vescenda dantur, qui usus in latina lingua remansit; Olim species ipsæ dabantur militi, postea pro eis pecunia data est, sed mansit vetus nomen. In glossa- riis: ὀψώνιον diarium: utitur sic inter alios Polybius. In- de & ad Judæos transiit vox אפסניא ut diximus ad Luc. III. 14. & ideo velut omnibus notam usurpant nostri scri- ptores, ut apparet non tantum hic & dicto Lucæ loco, sed & 1. Cor. IX. 7. Mire autem mercedem dixit malum, quod pro pravis factis redditur, cum merces labori reddi soleat. Similis μετάληψις apud Ciceronem cum dixit: Data est merces errori meo magna. Sed & Seneca vitiorum dixit mercedem.

Τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τῦ Θεῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος.

Solent reges egregiis militibus præter stipendium dare coronas, laureas, honores. His donativis comparat vitam æternam, non quod non detur benè meritis, sed quod multo sit major merito, quippe res æterna & cœlestis. Poterat quidem vita æterna & merces dici, ut sæpe dici- tur, sed nobilius est nomen donativi. Neque articulus frustra additur, simulque invertitur is ordo loquendi, qui in priori membro ἀντιθέτως fuerat. Hoc enim vult. At quod donativum DEUS dat sibi militantibus, id non est noxium aliquid, ut mors, ut leve aliquid, ut in militia Romana, sed est res maxima, immortalitas & gaudia cœlestia. Ubi quis pro opere multò plus reddit, quam quanti est opera, potest id & merces dici & donum: trahit enim de utroque. Sed hic prævalet doni sub conditione promissi & post con- ditionem impletam dandi natura.

Etsi donatur vita æterna DEO servientibus, non tamen redditur pro opere vel servitio; tùm quia servitium hoc valdè est imperfectum, & cum innumeris defectibus, qui mortem naturâ sua merentur, conjunctum, tùm quia χάρισμα & me- rè gratuitum donum DEI est vita æterna, quam nullatenus meremur, sed ex mera gratia conse- quimur. χαρίζομαι non est simpliciter largiri, sed gratis largiri, ut Phavorinus notat χαρίζομαι; ὀ μό- νον τὸ δωρὲμαι ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ χάριν τινὶ ποιῶ. Unde Chrysost. hom. X. Vita æterna neque debitum est, neque laborum retributio, sed divini muneris donum gratuitum. Hieronymus T. 1. Ep. IIX. Ubi gra- tia, non operum retributio, sed donantis est largi- tio. Conf. Rom. XI. 6. Ephes. II. 8. 1. Tim. VI. 2. 1. Pet. III. 8. tùm quia datur nobis vita non propter nostra merita, vel opera, sed in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, qui nobis meritis & morte suâ vitam acqui- sivit, & se dedit pro mundi vita, Job. VI. 51. animam suam pretium redemptionis dedit pro nobis. Mat- thæi XX. 28. Marc. X. 45. 1. Tim. II. 5. Ideoque vita à Christo parta donatur nobis non nisi in Chri- sto Jesu fide apprehenso Joh. III. 16. 36. c. VI. 47. Act. IV. 12. c. X. 43. c. XIII. 39. tùm quia Apostolus non dixit vitam æternam esse ὀψώνια stipendium servitutis nostræ, quemadmodum mortem stipen- dium peccati dixit: sed mutato sermonis genere, vitam dixit χάρισμα. Quum in præcedentibus in ἀντιθέσει similitudine gavisus sit, & in eodem ser- monis genere permanserit, utpote de servitio pec- cati, quod sit libertas à justitia, de ejus fructu, quod ignominiosus sit, de ejus fine, quod mors sit, & ex adverso de servitio DEI, quod sit libertas à peccato, de ejus fructu, quod faciat ad nostri sanctificatio- nem, de ejusdem fine, quod sit vita æterna, hic va- riat dicendi genus, & mortem quidem stipendium peccati dicit, uti ὀψώνια Luc. III. 14. 1. Cor. IX. 7. stipendium notant, quod pro militia & labore ex merito persolvitur, vitam autem non stipendium di- cit, sed donum merè gratuitum, quod ob Christi me- ritum, & in Christo ac merito ejus fide apprehenso nobis unicè confertur, nullius operis nostri intui- tu, aut merito, ut intelligamus, etsi conferatur no- bis, quia à peccato liberati DEO servimus, non ta- men propter servitium DEO præstitum vitam æ- ternam nobis conferri, sed æquè gratuitum donum esse, atque ipsam justificationem.

Quam verbo- rum Apostoli ἀκρίβειαν adversus Pontificios & Soci- nianos sedulò notandam studiosè observavit San- cta antiquitas: imprimis D. Chrysost. homil. XII. peccati stipendium cum nominâsset, de bonis verba fa- ciens non eundem servavit ordinem: neque enim di- xit, merces rectè factorum vestrorum, sed gratiam Dei: ostendens illos suo Marte liberatos non esse, neque quod debitum esset, accepisse, nec id quod datum est illis, esse aut retributionem aut remunerationem laborum, sed omnia gratiâ obvenisse, & quod ea per Filium dederit. Et Theodoret. in h. l. cum dixit de vita æterna quæ redditur justitiæ, non dixit eam esse mercedem, sed gra- tiam: est enim donum DEI vita æterna. Etsi enim quis summam vel absolutam justitiam præstiterit, ta- men temporalibus laboribus æterna in æquilibrio non respondent; Et Fulgentius l. 1. ad Monimum: Ex gratia datur non solum justificatis vita bona, sed etiam glorificatis vita æterna. Cur autem mors sti- pendium, vita vero æterna gratia dicitur, nisi quia illa redditur, hæc donatur. Et Theophylactus: De- licti stipendium mors est. Stipendium vero pecu- nia dicitur, quæ militibus à principe ad commeatum expenditur; peccatum igitur nobis, quos servos ha- buerat, servitutis in præmium mortem retribuebat: gratiam autem non mercedem dixit à DEO futuram: perinde ac si inquiat: Non enim laborum accipietis præmia, sed per gratiam fiunt hæc omnia in Christo Jesu, qui hæc operatur & efficitat. Nec aliter S. Augustinus (ad quem hic provocare solent Papi- stæ) in Enchir. cap. CVII. stipendium pro opere mi- lititæ debitum redditur, non donatur, gratia nisi gra- tuita sit, gratia non est. Item T. II. Oper. Epist. CV. ad Sixtum: Adversus elationis pestem vigilan- tissime militans, stipendium, inquit, peccati mors. Rectè stipendium, quia debetur, quia digne retri- buitur, quia merito redditur: deinde ne justitia de humano se extolleret bono merito, sicut humanum me- ritum malum non dubitatur esse peccatum, non à con- trario retulit dicens: stipendium justitiæ vita æter- na, sed gratia, inquit, DEI vita æterna. Et hæc ne præter mediatorem alia aliqua via quæreretur, adje- cit, in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Hæc S. Au- gustinus. Sed & nonnullis è Pontificiis hic verita- tis radji oculos perstrinxêre: Cardinali nempe Cusano, & Cardin. Cajetano: Ille notandum hic, in- quit, quod innuit Apostolus ex justitia peccato deberi mortem, nomen enim stipendii videtur hoc significare; Vitam autem æternam esse ex dono DEI gratuito. Hic verò: Non dicit, quod stipendia justitiæ vita æterna; sed donum DEI vita æterna, ut intelliga- mus non ex operum meritis, sed ex gratuito DEI do- no assequi nos pro fine vitam æternam, propter quod subdit, in Christo Domino nostro. Ecce meritum, ec- ce justitia, cujus stipendium est vita æterna, nobis au- tem donum, ratione ipsius Jesu Christi. Non ergò & stipendium & donum est vita æterna, nec de u- troque trahit; neque donum est sub conditione obedientiæ nostræ promissum: sed ex mera gra- tia donatur. Gratia enim non est gratia ullo mo- do, si non sit gratuita omni modo, uti iterum Augu- stinus, præeunte Apostolo Rom. XI. 6. Confer. Theol. Apost. Rom. ad h. l.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

ARGUMENT, AND DIVISION.

The Apostle, intending to further illustrate the state of the justified, how they are under grace, not under law, teaches that the law is as it were dead to the reborn, and thus they are no longer subject to its condemnation and exaction, by the similitude of a wife free from the law of her husband, he being dead, but joined to Christ, another husband, to bring forth fruit to GOD, whereas before regeneration they brought forth unhappy fruits: Not that the law itself is of itself either sin or the cause of sin: but that it makes sin manifest, whence also accidentally sin is irritated by the law and kills man: by the vice of that depravity, which not only exists in us before regeneration and justification, and begets death through the law, but also adheres to the reborn, so that they do not do what they would, and also captivates them under the law of sin, so that they anxiously desire final liberation; meanwhile giving thanks to GOD through Christ our Lord, that they can serve His law with their mind, immune from condemnation by the merit of His redemption; Which benefit he subjoins and explains in the following chapter.

There are three parts: The first is allegorical, by which, through a similitude from the law, and specifically from the matrimonial law, he illustrates the condition of the reborn, who are not under the law, as being different from the state of the non-reborn, who are under the law that condemns and compels, and he illustrates it as being most different, and teaches that they, being joined to Christ, bear fruit to God, up to verse 6 inclusive. The second is apologetic, by which he defends the law, that it is neither sin nor the cause of sin, but by arguing against sin, it excites the guilt of our depraved concupiscence and vicious desires, and brings death, since it is in itself holy, just, and good, from v. 7 up to v. 14 exclusive. The third is complaining, by which the Apostle complains about the evil of concupiscence, which still adheres to him, even though he is reborn, hindering the good that he wills, and resisting the law of the mind; on account of which he sighs, seeking to be delivered from the body of this death, and giving thanks to God for the liberation accomplished through Christ, from v. 14 up to the end of the chapter.

PART I. Allegorical-didactic. Illustrating the difference between the state of the non-reborn and the reborn from matrimonial law.

Vers. 1. Do you not know, brothers. For I speak to those who know the law.

Here Paul directs his discourse to the Jews alone, whom he calls brothers even by birth of the flesh, as below X. 1. But here he opens a great mystery, revealed first of all the Apostles to Paul, among many things divinely disclosed to him 2 Cor. XII. 1. 7, that even the Jews, who following the discipline of Christ had progressed much in it, were no longer bound by the bond of the law given through Moses. The Apostolic decree, which is in Acts XV, deals only with those who had been called from the Gentiles, and Paul kept himself within those limits for a long time, as is evident in Acts XVI. 4. It was not yet the time to open this, which God signified not obscurely, when He allowed not only the temple to be destroyed, but also the law itself to be carried in the triumph of the Romans. He says that he is addressing those not ignorant of the law, because it was the custom of the Jews, who did not live in extreme poverty, to imbue their children from an early age with the reading and knowledge of the law.

The mind of the Apostle is completely perverted by Grotius. For this epistle was directed not to the Jews alone, but to all the converted, and to the whole Roman Church consisting equally of Gentiles and Jews, who were all brothers spiritually; nor is such a mystery revealed here concerning liberation from the obligation of the Mosaic law, which Grotius rashly asserts was taught to Paul in the third heaven, where the things he heard were mere ῥήματα ἄῥῥητα, and it had already been handed down in the Prophetic writings that the ceremonial law was to be abrogated and the forensic law was to cease with the Jewish Polity; nor was the definition in the Jerusalem council made concerning the Gentiles only, but also concerning the Jews: which was this, that neither circumcision, nor the observation of the ceremonial law, nor the fulfillment of the moral law is necessary for obtaining salvation, but that we obtain salvation by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ alone in the New Testament, just as the faithful in the Old Testament obtained salvation by that alone. Nor does the Apostle deal here with the ceremonial law, but rather with the moral, whose function is to condemn and kill. But Grotius contends that these things were directed to the Jews alone, so that he might insert his own fabrication, as if Paul were describing the Hebrew race in this chapter, what it was first before the law, then after the law, as we have observed elsewhere.

that the law has dominion over a man.

It has right and power over him, as a master over servants. Thus we have κυριεύειν in Luke XXII. 25. It is common for the Hebrews to personify the law; see chapter VII of Rabbi Ishmael on the Soul. Similar things are in Is. I. 2. v. 14. Jerem. XXXI. 15. Job VIII. 8.

for as long as he lives.

As long as the law lives, so long it is not extinct. For an abrogated law is dead, that is, it does not have the force of binding, it lives in the heir. See what was said in book II of The Law of War and Peace, chapter IX.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO.

Justificatorum statum, quomodo sub gratia sint, non sub lege, porro illustraturus Apostolus, legem quasi demortuam esse renatis, atque ita ejus condemnationi, & exactioni non amplius eos esse obnoxios, similitudine uxoris à lege mariti, hoc defuncto liberæ, sed Christo, alteri marito copulatos fructus DEO parere, quum ante regenerationem infelices fructus ediderint docet: Non quod lex ipsa per se vel peccatum vel cau- sa peccati sit: sed quod peccatum patefa- ciat, unde & per accidens peccatum per legem irritetur hominemque occidat: vitio ejus pravitatis, quæ non modo ante rege- nerationem & justificationem nobis inest, & mortem gignit per legem, sed etiam re- natis adhæret, ut ea non agant, quæ velint, & captivet quoque eosdem sub peccati le- gem, ut anxie finalem liberationem desi- derent; DEO interim per Christum Do- minum gratias agens, quod mente servi- re legi ejus possint, redemptionis ejus me- rito immunes à condemnatione; Quod beneficium sequenti capite subjungit & explicat.

Partes tres sunt: Prima ἀλληγορικὴ, quâ per si- militudinem à lege, & in specie à lege matrimoniali conditionem renatorum, qui non sub lege sunt, diversam à non renatorum statu, qui sub lege con- demnante & cogente sunt, maximè diversam illu- strat, eosque Christo copulatos fructus Deo parere docet usque ad vers. 6. inclus. Altera ἀπολογητικὴ, quâ legem defendit, quod ea nec peccatum sit, nec peccati causa, sed peccatum arguendo culpâ pravæ nostræ concupiscentiæ & desideria vitiosa excitet, & mortem afferat, quum per se sancta, justa & bo- na sit à v. 7. usque ad v. 14. excl. Tertia σχετλιαστικὴ, quâ conqueritur Apostolus de malo concupiscen- tiæ, quod sibi, etsi renato, adhuc adhæret, bonum quod vult impediente, & repugnante legi mentis; ob quod suspirat, liberari expetens à corpore hu- jus mortis, Deoque gratias pro liberatione per Christum factâ, agens à v. 14. usque ad finem capitis.

PARS I. Ἀλληγορικο-διδακτικὴ. E lege matrimoniali statûs non-renatorum & renatorum differentiam illustrans.

Vers. 1. ἡ ἀγνοεῖτε ἀδελφοὶ. γινώσκουσι γὰρ τὸν νόμον λέγω.

Hic Paulus Sermonem ad solos Judæos dirigit, quos fra- tres vocat etiam carnis ortu, ut infra X. 1. Magnum autem hic aperit mysterium primo omnium Apostolorum Paulo, inter multa divinitus ei patefacta 2. Cor. XII. 1. 7. revela- tum, etiám Judæos, qui Christi disciplinam sectantes mul- tum in ea profecissent, non obligari ultra vinculo legis per Mosen datæ. Decretum Apostolicum, quod est Act. XV. de solis agit, qui ex gentibus vocati erant, & intra eos limi- tes diu se tenuit Paulus, ut patet Act. XVI. 4. Nondum tempus erat & hoc aperiendi, quod Deus non obscurè si- gnificavit, cum non templum tantum sivit dirui, sed & ipsam legem in triumpho Romanorum portari. Ait se legis non ignaros alloqui, quia is mos erat Judæorum, qui non in summa viverent egestate, liberos suos à prima ætate im- buere lectione & notitia legis.

Pervertitur prorsus mens Apostoli à Grotio. Nam nec ad solos Judæos, sed ad omnes conversos, totamque Ecclesiam Romanam ex gentibus pari- ter & Judæis constantem directa est hæc epistola, qui omnes fratres erant spiritualiter, nec de libe- ratione ab obligatione legis Mosaicæ tale hîc myste- rium panditur, quod Paulum in tertio cælo edo- ctum temerè asserit Grotius, ubi quæ audivit, me- ra ῥήματα ἄῥῥητα fuere, & abrogandam esse legem ceremonialem ac cessaturam cum Politia Judaica legem forensem, in scriptis Propheticis jam tradi- tum erat, neque in concilio Hierosolymitano de gen- tibus solum, sed etiam de Judæis definitio facta: quæ hæc erat, quod nec circumcisio, legisque cere- monialis observatio; nec legis moralis impletio ad sa- lutem consequendam necessaria sit, sed quod solá gratiâ Domini nostri Jesu Christi salutem adipsca- mur in Novo Test. æque uti eà solà adepti salutem sunt fideles in Vet. Testam. Nec de lege ceremoniali hic agit Apostolus, sed de morali potius, cujus est condemnare & occidere. Ad solos autem Judæos hæc directa esse contendit Grotius, ut ingerat commentum suum, quasi Paulus, imprimis Ebræum genus in hoc capite describat, quale illud fuerit pri- mum ante legem, deinde post legem, uti aliàs obser- vavimus.

ὅτι ὁ νόμος κυριεύει τῦ ἀνθρώπε.

Jus potestatemque in eum habet, ut dominus in servos. Sic κυριεύειν habemus Luc. XXII. 25. Legem προσωποποιεῖν frequens Hebræis; Vide caput VII. Rabbini Ismaëlis de Anima. Similia Es. I. 2. v. 14. Jerem. XXXI. 15. Job. VIII. 8.

εἰς ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ.

Quamdiu lex vivit, tamdiu extincta non est. Lex enim abrogata mortua est, id est, vim obligandi non ha- bet, in hærede vivit. Vide, quæ dicta libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. IX.

## 7:2
For the married woman is bound by law to the living husband.

He takes an example from the law of marriage. To her the wife remains bound, while the marriage remains, and through it the law of marriage, and that for the use of the husband, whom the law regards as one in such a way that, he being dead, the law also is extinguished as far as the woman is concerned. ὕπανδρος γυνὴ that is, married. It is translated thus, תחת האיש Num. V. 29. & אשת עץ Prov. VI. 24. & 29. Sirachides also speaks thus IX. 10. XLI. 27. ζῶντι ἀνδρὶ, for the use of the living husband.

This is what the Apostle means, that both the law is dead to the faithful, and they are dead to the law, inasmuch as they have been freed from its formidable sentence of perpetual damnation and from dire servitude. Which he illustrates by a comparison of the past state before regeneration and justification and the present state of the justified, having employed a similitude drawn from the marriage of husband and wife, and from the matrimonial law. For as according to the law of matrimony a woman is tied to a husband while he lives, but upon his death the obligation ceases; so the unregenerate were bound to the law, and ὑπὸ νόμον by reason of both the curse of the law and the dire servitude to which it drives with rigorous exaction and horrible threatening: For since the unregenerate live in the flesh and follow the desires of the flesh, they are exposed to the damnation of the law, and however much they may do certain things according to the law, that is nevertheless servile obedience, not proceeding from the freedom of the Spirit, but extorted by the oldness of the letter and the threats of the law and in many ways imperfect. But because the regenerate and justified are as it were dead to the law, or the law is dead to them, the law no longer has such power of binding: for the justified have been released from the guilt of sin and condemnation, and are no longer subject to the rigorous exaction of the law. Therefore they are now dead to that importunate husband, or the law itself is dead to them, and they themselves are freed from its bond through Christ, who both took away the curse of the law and bestowed the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they might serve Him spontaneously.

V. 2. But if the husband should die.

To whom that law alone devoted effort. What he says here about death can also be said about repudiation, which itself is also the death of a marriage.

A bill of divorce and a divorce in fact dissolved a marriage, not by divine law, certainly not by the force of matrimonial law: because in the beginning it was not so, Matthew XIX, as we said regarding that passage. Nor yet, with Bellarmine, book on matrimony, ch. 16, is it to be gathered from this passage that the bond of marriage is never dissolved except by death alone, because it is also dissolved by fornication, Matthew XIX, as Erasmus and Cajetan admit.

She is discharged from the law of the husband.

She is freed from the law of marriage, which was the law of the husband, because, as I said, it provided for the husband: although that τῶ ἀνδρὸς can be absent, just as it is absent in very many manuscripts. Καταργεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῦ νό- με is to be freed from the law, as the following things show, because he who is freed from some master is in a way dead to him. See above VI. 2. Not much otherwise is καταργεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῦ χριστῦ said in Gal. V. 4. It corresponds to ἀργεῖν & καταργεῖσθαι to the Hebrew בטל which is to cease. Just as the same thing is ἁμαρτίαν ἀποθανεῖν for us, that we are ἁμαρτίᾳ, so the same thing is νόμον καταργεῖσθαι for us, or we ἀπὸ τῦ νόμε; in that locution the right is regarded, in this the necessity of acting according to the right. Thus also Cicero changes the words, where he deals with money owed and with thanks owed. See Gellius 1. 4. but the Apostle preferred to use that locution which would offend the Jews less.

Latin:

ἡ γὰρ ὕπανδρος γυνὴ τῷ ζῶντι ἀνδρὶ δέδεται νόμῳ.

Exemplum sumit in lege conjugii. Ei uxor manet de- vincta, manente conjugio, & per id lege conjugii, idque in usum mariti, quem lex unum ita respicit, ut eo extincto etiam lex quoad fœminam extinguatur. ὕπανδρος γυνὴ id est, nupta. Sic vertitur, תחת האיש Num. V. 29. & אשת עץ Prov. VI. 24. & 29. Loquitur sic & Sirachides IX. 10. XLI. 27. ζῶντι ἀνδρὶ, in usum viri viventis.

Hoc est, quod vult Apostolus, & legem fideli- bus, & hos legi esse mortuos, utpote qui ab illius formidabili sententia damnationis perpetuæ, & servitute dirâ liberati sunt. Quod illustrat com- paratione statûs præteriti ante regenerationem & justificationem ac statûs præsentis justificato- rum, adhibitâ similitudine à conjugio mariti & uxoris, & à lege connubiali depromtâ. Ut enim secundum legem matrimonii mulier viro alligata est, dum ille vivit, eo autem demortuo cessat obligatio; ita non renati obligati legi fuêre, & ὑπὸ νόμον ratione tùm maledictionis legis, tum diræ servitutis, ad quam adigit cum rigorosa exa- ctione, & horrenda comminatione: Quum enim non renati vivant in carne, ac sequantur carnis de- sideria, damnationi legis expositi sunt, & utut ma- ximè quædam agant secundum legem, id tamen ser- vile est obsequium, non profectum à libertate Spi- ritûs, sed per vetustatem literæ, & minas legis ex- tortum multisque modis imperfectum. Quia vero demortui quasi legi sunt renati & justificati vel lex mortua illis est, vim talem obligandi lex non ha- bet amplius: nam justificati soluti sunt à reatu pec- cati & condemnatione, nec amplius subjecti legis rigorosæ exactioni. Marito ergo isti importuno jam demortui, vel lex ipsa iis demortua, ipsique à vinculo ejus liberati sunt, per Christum, qui & maledictionem legis sustulit, & Spiritum S. largi- tus est ipsis, ut spontè sibi serviant.

V. 2. ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ἀνὴρ.

Cui sola lex illa operam dabat. Quod de morte hic di- cit, idem de repudio dici potest, quod & ipsum mors est conjugii.

Libellus repudii, & divortium de facto solvebat conjugium, non de jure divino, non certè vi legis matrimonialis: quia in primordio non erat sic Mat- thæi XIX. ut ad illum locum diximus. Nec ta- men cum Bellarm. l. de matrim. c. 16. ex hoc loco colligendum, nunquam conjugii vinculum solvi, nisi per mortem tantùm, quia etiam per fornicationem solvitur Matth. XIX. fatente Erasmo & Cajetano.

κατήργηται ἀπὸ τῶ νόμε τῶ ἀνδρὸς.

Liberata est à lege conjugii, quæ erat lex viri, quia viro, ut dixi, consulebat: quanquam abesse potest illud τῶ ἀνδρὸς sicut abest in plurimis manuscriptis. Καταργεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῦ νό- με est à lege liberari, ut sequentia ostendunt, quia qui à do- mino aliquo liberatur, ei mortuus est quodammodo. Vide supra VI. 2. Non multò aliter καταργεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῦ χριστῦ dicitur Gal. V. 4. Respondet ἀργεῖν & καταργεῖσθαι Hebræo בטל quod est desinere. Sicut idem est ἁμαρτίαν ἀποθανεῖν nobis, quod nos ἁμαρτίᾳ, sic idem νόμον καταργεῖσθαι nobis, aut nos ἀπὸ τῦ νόμε; in illa locutione jus respicitur, in hac secundum jus agendi necessitas. Sic & Cicero voces com- mutat, ubi de pecunia debita, & de gratia debita agit. Vide Gellium 1. 4. sed maluit Apostolus ea locutione uti, quæ Ju- dæos minus offenderet.

## 7:3
Vers. 3. ἄρα ὖν ζῶντος τῶ ἀνθρὸς. And therefore while that marital law is still living.

she shall be called an adulteress.

Χρηματίζειν means to be called, as Greek writers also often use it, and Luke Acts XI. 26. μοιχαλὶς נאפת Prov. XXX. 20 Ezech. XVI. 37. XXIII. 45. Hosea III. 1. Mal. III. 5.

Moreover, this verbal word is taken for a real one, shall be called for SHALL BE, as Is. VII. 14. Matt. V. 9. Luke I. 32. Beza notes that it is to be so called that she is held to be an adulteress by the consent of all. If she becomes another man's. היתה לאיש זר Levit. XXII. 13. Just as one is said to have a Chrysis who sleeps with her, so a woman is said to be had by a man or to be to a man. For that is said to be to someone, which is had by him.

But if the husband dies, she is free from the law. Here he explains what it is for the law to be dead to her.

So that she is not an adulteress. So that she is not an adulteress, she is not held by the penalties of adultery.

Having become another man's. Whether through marriage or otherwise. For even if she admits something of the sort without marriage, she sins: but not against the law concerning adulteresses.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἄρα ὖν ζῶντος τῶ ἀνθρὸς. Ac proinde vivente etiam lege illa maritali.

μοιχαλὶς χρηματίσει.

Χρηματίζειν est appellari, quomodo & Græci scriptores sæpe usurpant, & Lucas Act. XI. 26. μοιχαλὶς נאפת Prov. XXX. 20 Ezech. XVI. 37. XXIII. 45. Oseæ III. 1. Mal. III. 5.

Hæc autem vox verbalis sumitur pro reali, ap- pellabitur pro ERIT, ut Es. VII. 14. Matth. V. 9. Luc. I. 32. Beza notat, quod sit ita vocari ut omnium consensu adultera habeatur. ἐὰν γένηται ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ. היתה לאיש זר Levit. XXII. 13. Sicut habere Chryfi- dem dicitur, qui cum ea cubat, ita haberi mulier a viro sive esse viro. Nam esse alicui dicitur, quod ab eo habetur.

ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἀνὴρ, ἐλευθέρα ἐσὶν ἀπὸ τῦ νόμε. Hic explicat, quid sit legem ei esse mortuam.

Τῦ μὴ εἶναι ἀυτὴν μοιχαλίδα. Ita ut non sit adultera. non teneatur adulterii poenis.

γενομένην ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ Sive per nuptias, sive aliter. Nam etiamsi aliquid tale sine nuptiis admittat, peccat: sed non in legem contra adulteras.

## 7:4
V. 4. So that, my brethren, you also. You Jews also.

You were put to death to the law. The same thing as the law was put to death to you. For in these figurative expressions those things are reciprocal, as we said above 2. You have no need of the law.

Through the body of Christ. Through the body of Christ, crucified, that is. For Christ's cross and death, among other things, also obtained this from the Father, that the authority of that law should be removed. Eph. II. 15. 16. Coloss. II. 14. These passages were the reason why Ebion did not accept Paul's epistles.

We have already noted before that these things are rashly restricted to the Jews and ceremonial laws, since they pertain also to the Gentiles, and to the moral law, whatever may be the case regarding Ebion's opinion. The Apostle teaches that believers are joined through a second marriage to another man, namely to Him who rose from the dead: which is not only for Jews, but also for converted Gentiles, and indeed so that hereafter they may bear to Him, to whom they are joined through faith, not pernicious fruits, but fruits of faith and righteousness, just as a wife is accustomed to bear and bring forth fruit for her husband alone. Which is likewise true of all the justified. But Tertullian rashly from those words, if she joins herself to another man, in De Monogamia c. 13, concluded that she prejudices herself of adultery who passes to second vows: whereas the Apostle speaks expressly of that conjunction or marital intimacy with another man, which happens while the husband is living: but upon his death he permits freedom to the woman, as being free by the law of the former husband. The Apostle says we are mortified to the law, not dead; to indicate that this liberation from the curse of the law depends on something other than our own powers. But this is what the Apostle means: just as a wife marries another when her husband is dead, as she is able to marry; so also we, being mortified to the law, have married another, namely Christ. Furthermore, just as he says we are dead to the law, so he had previously said we were dead to sin: because the law and sin, even if they fight against each other, nevertheless conspire in our destruction, both regarding guilt, while sin takes its power from the law 1. Cor. XV. 56. and conversely the law accuses and condemns because of sin, and regarding the exciting of vicious impulses. For the law, accusing and condemning because of sin, excites us to anger and rage against itself and God, and feeling the internal malice, the law urging and condemning, it seethes all the more, like fire poured upon quicklime with water, when it sees no power of obedience.

Moreover, the Apostle does not say that the law is dead to us, in such a way that it is abrogated so that it no longer pertains to us in any part. That was the madness of the Antinomians, but he says that we are dead to the law, that is, that we are so far finished with the law that the judgment of GOD, which is revealed in it, no longer has any right or power over us: namely, as regards the curse, as regards the rigor of its exaction, and as regards servile compulsion: Meanwhile, another kind of death is given, by which we are so through the mortification of the old Adam, through the renewal of the Spirit, dead to the law, so that it can no longer excite depraved desires in us, which used to happen in the unregenerate. The end, however, of this liberation from the bond of the law is not that we may henceforth wander freely, released from all marriage, just as it is optional for a widow whose husband has died to return to second nuptials, but this death was brought about for this end, that we might be bound by the bond of a new marriage, namely, that which exists with Christ, whose primary law it is that we should bear fruit for GOD. This is to be understood both of the debt and of the ability, because we are now bound by a stricter right than before, and we are also instructed with a greater aid of the Spirit and grace. Hos. II. 19. 2. Cor. XI. 2. Eph. V. 30. This passage therefore contains a clear apology for the present disputation, as the blessed Mylius aptly advised: It seems to conflict somewhat with the preceding chapter, and not to excite a zeal for piety, but rather to provide a license for sinning, because the law is said to be abrogated; yet the thing itself teaches the contrary. For he does not argue about this abrogation with any other purpose than that, with the bond of a new marriage established with Christ, he may lead us to higher reasons for piety and to the very true fountain of spiritual obedience, so that the closer the union we enjoy with Christ, the more we may understand ourselves to be bound not only by a heavier debt of living well, but also to be instructed with a greater aid for performing those debts.

Grotius rightly explains the words διὰ τῶ σώματος as the crucified body of Christ: because that mortification, by which we die to the law and the law dies to us, is to be attributed to the merit of the crucifixion and death of Christ, so that we may be freed from the curse and compulsion of the law. Conf. Col. I, 22. 2. Pet. II. 24. Crellius does not deny that the body of Christ is to be explained by the death of Christ, by which the new covenant was sanctioned, and consequently the old was abolished at the same time: but what he adds, that if the resurrection of Christ had not followed, his death would have brought little momentum to establishing the New covenant and abrogating the old, and hardly anyone would have adhered to the discipline of Christ after deserting the law: this is from the hypotheses of the Socinian heresy. Scripture, on the contrary, everywhere attributes the sanction of the new covenant to the death of Christ, which covenant is one of grace and the remission of sins, since it proclaims it to have been obtained by the blood and death of Christ; nor does it command us to desert the law as imperfect, so that we may adhere to the discipline of Christ as a more perfect law, because Christ did not increase the law or make it more perfect by his teaching, but fulfilled it by the obedience performed for us: Therefore, the Apostle teaches not that the law is simply to be deserted, but that we are free from the condemnation and rigor of the law, and enjoy the grace of Christ. Mention is made of the resurrection of Christ, not because this contributed greater momentum to sanctioning the covenant of grace, which is nowhere taught, but because Christ had to rise again for the sake of establishing the covenant of grace sanctioned by his death and rendering us actual participants in it, and because one must be married to the living, not the dead, which reason Crellius admits: But what Crellius says, that with the resurrection of Christ having followed, whoever believes that it followed CANNOT BUT desert all other disciplines and apply themselves to CHRIST, proceeds from a most false principle, both because the resurrection of Christ was only a confirmation of the doctrine of Christ, and because the knowledge of eternal life (which is had from the resurrection of Christ) causes us to obey Christ: when, on the contrary, infinite myriads of men, doubting nothing about the resurrection of Christ, nothing about the existence of eternal life, do not obey Christ, but their own depraved desires: and because by the example of Christ we can aspire to eternal life through obedience: Concerning which, in Socinismo profligato, and in the Examination of Crellius's treatise on the causes of the death of Christ. But the Papists are by no means to be heard here, who wish sins to be expiated by their own afflictions, and substitute their own body for the body of CHRIST with a huge crime, concerning which there is no need for us to say how they are caught in the act.

that you should belong to another.

The Church is compared to a bride 2 Cor. XI. 2. Eph. V. 39.

to him who was raised from the dead.

He who has himself been made a new man also demands a new life.

that we might bear fruit for God.

So that from the sowing of Christ we might fruitfully bring forth works much better than those of the great part of men had been under the state of the law. He pursues the similitude. For offspring in marriage are also called fruit. Ps. CXXVII. 4. Luke VI. 42.

Latin:

V. 4. ὥστε ἀδελφοί με καὶ ὑμεῖς. Etiam vos Judaei.

ἐθανατώθητε τῷ νόμῳ. Idem quod ὁ νόμος ὑμῖν ἐθανατώθη. Nam in his figura- tis locutionibus ista reciprocantur, ut diximus supra 2. Le- ge opus non habetis.

διὰ τῦ σώματος τῦ χρισῦ. Per corpus Christi, crucifixum scilicet. Nam Christi crux & mors inter caetera, & hoc a Patre impetravit, ut legis illius imperium tolleretur. Eph. II. 15. 16. Coloss. II. 14. Hi loci in causa fuere, cur Pauli epistolas non reciperet Ebion.

Ad Judaeos & leges ceremoniales haec temere restringi jam ante notavimus, quum ad gentes etia pertineant, & ad legem moralem, quicquid sit de Ebionis sententia. Junctos fideles esse per secundum q. conjugium viro alteri docet Apostolus, nimirum ei, qui ex mortuis resurrexit: quod non est tantum Judaeorum, sed etiam gentilium conversorum, & quidem ut posthac illi, cui per fidem copulati sunt, pariant non fructus perniciosos, sed fructus fidei & justitiae, sicut uxor suo marito soli parere & fru- ctificare solet. Quod itidem est omnium justifica- torum. Temere autem ex illis verbis si se junxerit alteri viro Tertull. de Mongo c. 13. collegit, adulte- rii se praejudicare, quae ad secunda vota transit: quum Apostolus diserte de ea cum altero viro conjun- ctione, vel consuetudine maritali loquatur, quae fit vivente marito: eo autem defuncto mulieri li- bertatem permittat, utpote lege viri prioris libere. Mortificatos a. nos legi dicit Apostolus, non mor- tuos; ut indicet aliunde hanc a legis maledictione liberationem, quam a nostris dependere viribus. Hoc autem vult Apostolus: quemadmodum uxor mortuo marito alteri nubit, ut nubere potest; ita & nos mortificatos legi, alteri nempe Christo nupsif- se. Porro ut legi mortuos nos dicit, ita antea peccato mortuos dixerat: quia lex & peccatum, etiamsi in- ter se pugnent, in perdendis tamen nobis conspi- rant, tum quoad reatum, dum peccatum vim suam ex lege sumit 1. Cor. XV. 56. & contra lex ob pecca- tum accusat & damnat, tum quoad vitiosos motus excitandos. Lex enim ob peccatum accusans & damnans, nos ad iram fremitumque contra se & Deum excitat, & interna malitia sentiens legem urgentem, & damnantem, tanquam ignis in calce viva perfusus aqua, tanto magis exaestuat, quum virtutem obsequendi haud videat.

Caeterum non dicit Apostolus legem nobis esse mortuam, quod ita abrogata sit, ut nulla sui parte ad nos amplius pertineat. Qui Antinomorum furor erat, sed dicit, nos legi mortuos esse, id est, nos eate- nus legi defunctos esse, ut judicio DEI, quod in ea patefactum est, non sit in nos jus amplius aut pote- stas: scilicet quoad maledictionem, quoad rigorem exactionis, & quoad servilem coactionem: Interim datur alia mortis species, qua per mortificationem veteris Adami sic sumus, per renovationem Spiri- tus, legi mortui, ne possit ea in nobis amplius pra- vas cupiditates excitare, quod in non renatis fieri consuevit. Finis autem liberationis istius a legis vinculo est, non ut deinceps libere vagemur, so- luti omni conjugio, sicut viduae defuncto marito arbitrarium est ad secundas nuptias reverti, sed eo fine facta est ista mors, ut novi conjugii vinculo constringamur, nimirum quod cum Christo inter- cedat, cujus ea lex primaria, ut DEO fructum fera- mus. Quod & de debito & de facultate intelligen- dum est, quia & arctiori nunc quàm antea jure ob- stringimur, & majori etiam Spiritus & gratiæ ad- miniculo instruimur. Hos. II. 19. 2. Cor. XI. 2. Eph. V. 30. Luculentam ergò locus iste præsentis dis- putationis apologiam, ut commode monuit B. Mylius, continet: Videtur ea cum præcedenti capite pugnare nonnihil, & non excitare studium pietatis, sed parere potius peccandi licentiam, quod lex esse ab- rogata dicitur; Atqui contrarium res ipsa docet. Non enim alio consilio de abrogatione ista disputat, quàm ut novi matrimonii vinculo cum Christo constituto, ad sublimiores pietatis rationes, & verum ipsum spiritualis obedientiæ fontem adducat, ut quo arctiori cum Christo conjunctione fruimur, eo nos non gra- viori tantùm bene vivendi debito obstrictos, sed & majori ad præstanda debita adminiculo instructos esse intelligamus.

Rectè autem verba διὰ τῶ σώματος exponit Grotius per corpus Christi crucifixum: quia cruci- fixionis & mortis Christi merito tribuenda est illa mortificatio, quâ morimur legi, & lex moritur nobis, ita ut liberemur à maledictione, & coactione legis. Conf. Col. I, 22. 2. Pet. II. 24. Crellius non diffite- tur per corpus Christi explicandum esse per mortem Christi, quà novum fœdus fuit sancitum, ac proin- de vetus simul abolitum: quod verò addit, nisi re- surrectio Christi subsecuta fuisset, mors ejus exiguum ad Novum fœdus stabiliendum & vetus abrogan- dum attulisset momentum, & vix quisquam desertâ lege Christi disciplinæ adhæsisset: hoc ab hypothefi- bus hærefeos Socinianæ est. Scriptura contra mor- ti Christi passim tribuit fœderis novi sanctionem, quod fœdus est gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum, quum sanguine & morte Christi partum deprædi- cat; nec legem ceu imperfectam deserere jubet, ut Christi disciplinæ, ceu perfectiori legi adhæreamus, quia Christus legem non auxit aut perfectiorem reddidit doctrinâ, sed implevit obedientia pro nobis præstita: Proinde non legem simpliciter deserendam, sed nos à legis condemnatione & rigore liberos esse, gratiàque Christi frui, docet A- postolus. Resurrectionis autem Christi mentio sit, non quod hæc majus momentum ad fœdus gratiæ sanciendum contulerit, quod nuspiam docetur, sed quod fœdus gratiæ morte Christi sancitum stabi- liendi, nosque actu ejusdem participes reddendi gratiâ resurgere debuerit Christus, & quod vivis, non mortuis nubendum sit, quam rationem Crellius admittit: Quod verò ait Crellius, subsecutâ resur- rectione Christi, quicunque eam subsecutam fuisse credunt, NON POSSUNT NON deserere omnes alias disciplinas & CHRISTO sese applicare, ex fal- sissimo principio procedit, tùm quod resurrectio Christi tantùm confirmatio fuerit doctrinæ Christi, tùm quod notitia vitæ æternæ (quæ habetur à resur- rectione Christi) faciat, ut obsequamur Christo: quum ex adverso infinitæ myriades hominum ni- hil de resurrectione Christi, nihil de existentiâ vitæ æternæ dubitantes, Christo haud obsequan- tur, sed pravis suis desideriis: tùm quod exemplo Christi per obedientiam adspirare possimus ad vi- tam æternam: De quibus in Socinismo profligato, & Examine tract. Crelliani de causis mortis Christi. Nullatenus verò audiendi hic Pontificii, qui pro- priis afflictionibus expiari peccata volunt, pro cor- pore CHRISTI suum corpus ingenti scelere sub- stituunt, de quo non opus est, ut dicamus, quam ἐπαυτοφόρῳ deprehendantur.

εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ.

Ecclesia sponsæ comparatur 2. Cor. XI. 2. Eph. V. 39.

τῷ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγερθέντι.

Qui factus ipse homo novus vitam etiam novam postulat.

ἵνα καρποφορήσωμεν τῷ Θεῷ.

Ut ex Christi satu fœcundi edamus opera multò meliora, quam fuerant magnæ partis hominum sub statu legis. Per- sequitur similitudinem. Nam & partus in matrimonio fru- ctus dicuntur. Psal. CXXVII. 4. Luc. VI. 42.

## 7:5
Ver. 5. For when we were in the flesh.

Few under the state of the law were spiritual, and those who were such, were not such by the sole power of the law. But most were carnal, having no or only a slight hope of another life, and therefore addicted to this life, and to the conveniences and pleasures of this life, whence in such great matter sin is easily born.

the passions of sins.

Desires leading to sin. Thus this word is taken also in Gal. V. 24.

which were by the law.

The participle is missing. Chrysostom supplies 'manifested' or 'made known', rightly from what follows.

was active in your members.

ἐνεργεῖσθαι is a deponent verb, and it is usually placed even without an explicit accusative: as when it is said πίστις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη Gal. V. 6. See also 2 Cor. I. 16. Eph. III. 20. Col. I. 29. 2 Thess. II. 7. Jas. V. 16. Then ἐν for per, in the Hebrew manner. He says, therefore, that those desires produced their work through the internal and external parts of the human body. Concerning which, see above VI. 13.

so as to bear fruit unto death.

Paul also personifies death; the desires are the fruit, that is, they provide the very man as fodder for death.

The state of the law is not compared here with the state of the Gospel; or the Old Testament with the state of the New Testament, but the state of the unregenerate with the state of the regenerate, where those who were spiritual (πνευματικοὶ) in the time of the Old Testament were indeed not so few, unless speaking comparatively, yet none of them was made spiritual by the sole power of the law: since the ancients had knowledge not only of the law, but also of the Gospel, or of the Evangelical promises, and having apprehended them by faith, they were justified, and furthermore sanctified by the grace of the Holy Spirit, renewed, and made spiritual (πνευματικοὶ). Indeed, the ancients could certainly have a hope of eternal life, not a faint one, but a certain one, from the word of God, from the promises made in the writings of the Prophets, which are above all exception: because eternal life was contained in them, as Christ testifies in John V. 39, and eternal salvation could be had from them, as the Apostle testifies in 2 Tim. III. 15.
