However, that the knowledge and promise of eternal life were reserved for the times of the New Testament is a Pelagian-Socinian hypothesis, which alone did not make men spiritual (πνευματικοὺς): since countless people under the New Testament, while doubting nothing about eternal life, nevertheless remain carnal and addicted to the comforts and pleasures of this life: nor is sin born any less easily now under the New Testament than it was born formerly under the Old Testament. Moreover, under the state of sin before regeneration, we are not only all inclined by nature (τῇ Φύσει) to sin, but we also cannot not sin; because every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is ONLY EVIL all the days of life, from earliest infancy, Gen. VI. 5, ch. VIII. 21. To be in the flesh is not to be under the state of the law, in the Grotian sense: by which this is the same as saying, in the time of the Old Testament; otherwise ALL who existed in the time of the Old Testament would have been in the flesh (ἐν σαρκὶ), which is clearly false. But ALL the unregenerate are in the flesh (ἐν σαρκὶ) and are carnal (σαρκικοὶ): because whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, John III. 5, who also, without distinction of the times of the Old and New Testaments, are all said to be under the law (ὑπὸ νόμον), that is, under the curse and servitude of the law, and not under grace: and because in the flesh are the affections of sins, and wicked desires, indeed on the occasion of the proposed law (which is able only to terrify and drive one to perform duty, but is not sufficient for grace and the strength to do it), but by the vice of corrupted nature they flourish more and more in the members of the unregenerate: for the reason that man, by a certain natural depravity, strives repeatedly toward what is forbidden, and desires to pursue what is denied. In which manner the unregenerate produce fruits that are at least truly pestiferous and lethal, where there is no grace of liberation; the prohibition of sins increases the desire to sin, as Augustine says somewhere. Crellius in this passage acknowledges that to be in the flesh here signifies being held by the flesh or appetite as if by certain chains: and that the affections are not only not restrained by the law, but are even more irritated and exasperated. The Apostle notably says that the affections of sin are not from the law, but through the law, not as if they were not in us before, but partly because they are revealed by the ministry of the law: and partly because when the law is set against them like a barrier, they are rendered far more sharp and vehement. Concerning which, see Augustine, Questions to Simplicianus I. Sin is increased by the law, first because it is known through it, then because it is more irritated by it.

We always strive for what is forbidden and desire what is denied.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ.

Pauci sub statu legis erant πνευματικοὶ, & qui tales erant, non erant tales ex sola vi legis. Plerique verò erant σαρκικοὶ, nullam aut tenuem spem habentes vitæ alterius, ac proinde addicti huic vitæ, & hujus vitæ commodis ac voluptatibus, unde in tam magna materia facile nascitur peccatum.

τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν.

Cupiditates ad peccatum ducentes. Sic hæc vox sumi- tur etiam Gal. V. 24.

τὰ διὰ τῦ νόμυ.

Deest participium. Chrysostomus supplet φανόμενα, aut γνωριζόμενα, rectè ex sequentibus.

ἐνεργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν.

ἐνεργεῖσθαι est deponens, ac poni solet etiam non ex- presso accusativo: ut cum dicitur πίστις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργυ- μένη Gal. V. 6. Vide & 2. Cor. I. 16. Eph. III. 20. Col. I. 29. 2. Thess. II. 7. Jac. V. 16. Deinde ἐν pro per, more Hebraico. Di- cit ergò cupiditates istas opus suum edidisse per humani cor- poris partes internas & externas. De quibus supra VI. 13.

εἰς τὸ καρποφορῆσαι τῷ θανάτῳ.

Etiam mortem προσωποποιεῖ Paulus, cupiditates fructum, id est, pabulum morti præbent ipsum hominem.

Non hic comparatur status legis, cum statu Ev- angelii; vel Veteris Testam. cum statu Novi Test. sed status non renatorum cum renatorum statu, ubi qui πνευματικοὶ erant tempore V. T. non quidem adeò pauci tantum fuere, nisi comparatè loquendo, non tamen ex sola vi legis ullus eorum spiritualis factus est: siquidem non legis solùm, sed etiam Ev- angelii, vel promissionum Evangelicarum notitiam habuêre veteres, iisque fide apprehensis justificati sunt, & porro sanctificati per Spir. S. gratiam, re- novati ac πνευματικοὶ facti sunt. Spem verò vitæ æternæ non tenuem, sed certam habere ex verbo Dei omnino poterant veteres, ex promissis, in scriptis Prophetarum factis omni exceptione superiori- bus: quia in iis habebatur vita æterna teste Christo Joh. V. 39, & ex iis salus æterna haberi poterat, teste Apostolo 2. Tim. III. 15. Notitiam autem ac pro- missionem vitæ æternæ reservatam esse temporibus N. T. hypothesis Pelagio-Sociniana est, quæ sola non faciebat πνευματικοὺς: quum innumeri sub N. T. nihil ambigentes de vita æterna carnales tamen maneant, & addicti hujus vitæ commodis, ac vo- luptatibus: neque minus facile nunc peccatum nascatur sub N. T. quam olim natum fuit sub V. T. Sub statu autem peccati ante regenerationem non mo. do proclives sumus omnes τῇ Φύσει ad peccatum, sed & non possumus non peccare; quia omne figmen- tum cogitationum cordis humani TANTUM MALUM est omnibus diebus vitæ, inde à prima in- fantia Gen. VI. 5. c. IIX. 21. In carne esse, non est sub statu legis esse, sensu Grotiano: quo hoc idem est, quod tempore Vet. Test. alioquin OMNES, qui tempore V. T. extitêre fuissent ἐν σαρκὶ in carne, quod liquidò falsum est. Sed ἐν σαρκὶ sunt, & σαρ- κικοὶ OMNES non renati: quia, quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est, Joh. III. 5. qui etiam omnes, citra discrimen temporum Veteris & Novi Test. dicun- tur esse ὑπὸ νόμον, sub lege, id est, sub maledictione, & servitute legis, & non sub gratia: & quia in carne sunt affectus peccatorum, & desideria prava ex oc- casione quidem propositæ legis (quæ nonnisi terre- re & adigere valet ad officium præstandum, gratiã autem & vires ad id non sufficit) vitio autem cor- ruptæ naturæ magis magisque vigent in membris non renatorum: eo quod homo naturali quadam pravitate in vetitum subinde nititur, cupitque ne- gata persequi. Quo pacto non renati fructus sal- tim pariunt verè pestiferos & lethales, ubi non est gratia liberationis, auget desiderium peccandi pro- hibitio peccatorum, uti alicubi Augustinus. Crellius in h. l. agnoscit esse in carne h. l. significare carne seu appetitu constrictum veluti vinculis quibusdam te- neri: & affectus per legem non tantùm non cohiberi, sed magis adhuc irritari & exasperari. Notanter Apostolus non ex lege, sed per legem affectus pec- cati esse, ait, non q. antea in nobis non sint, sed par- tim quia legis ministerio patefiant: partim vero cum lex illis tanquam obex opponatur, reddantur longè acriores, ac vehementiores. Quo de Aug. Quæst. ad Simplic. I. Peccatum augetur per legem, primum quia per illam cognoscitur, deinde, quia ma- gis per eam irritatur.

Nitimur in vetitum semper cupimusque negata.

## 7:6
Verse 6. But now we have been discharged from the law. He repeats the word which he had placed in the first part of the comparison above in 2.

Others explain 'freed from the law' as being rendered useless to the law. But we are freed from the law not simply, but 1. regarding the curse, since the justified are immune from the curse, 2. regarding servile compulsion: because we have been gifted with the Spirit of liberty. 3. regarding the rigor of exaction: because even begun holiness pleases God, when the person is reconciled through faith. 4. regarding the power of irritation: which the law has in the unregenerate, not by its own fault, but by the guilt of corrupt nature: which, just as it is restrained in the regenerate, so they are not irritated by the law to sin, but are rather excited to the pursuit of holiness.

ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα.

Other codices have ἀποθανόντος, of which reading Origen also makes mention. Just as it appears Chrysostom also read it from his interpretation: ὁ δεσμὸς δι᾽ ὅ κατειχόμεθα ἐνε- κρώθη. Christ dying killed the law of Moses, which held the Jews bound to itself: just as the law of marriage [holds] a woman. Κατέχω corresponds to the Hebrew חזק, which is to possess.

Since the Greek codices consistently have ἀπο- θανόντες, with which the Syrian interpreter also agrees, one must not depart from that reading, and it can be rendered by subauditing the word ἐκείνῳ 'dead to that' in which, or by which they were detained, or 'dead' i.e. to the law, of which mention was made before, in which, or also insofar as we were held constrained by it; for κατειχόμεθα implies force and violent detention, Matt. XXI. 38, Luke IV. 42, Rom. I. 18. Thus, therefore, we are dead to the law, insofar as we were detained by it, because that bond is broken, by which the law held us liable, which was primarily guilt, and condemnation. We are warned here about the use of the law in the unregenerate: which is this, that it constrains, and as it were holds captive with the bond of guilt and condemnation those who have not yet been freed. It would therefore be most absurd to feign that its use is to justify. Nor is this perversion unlike [the case] if someone accused of a capital crime were seen to be bound by the executioner, in order to obtain the ornaments of equestrian dignity. Concerning the emphasis of the word κατέχειν, let B. Wellerus be consulted on this passage.

ὥστε δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος.

That we may serve God, namely, with a new spirit, that is, of Christ. A frequent Hebraism, καινότητι πνεύματος, for πνέυματι καινῷ. He rightly said 'new spirit,' which had not been given before the resurrection of Christ. John VII. 39. See also 1 Cor. III. 6.

καὶ ὀ παλαιότητι γράμματος.

He calls the law of Moses the old letter. Old letters are wont to vanish. Heb. VIII. 13. Rhetoricians also often say 'the writing' for the law, thus also above II. 27, 29, 2 Cor. III. 6, 7.

Not a new Spirit, but the newness of the Spirit is designated here, but much less is the new Spirit called by that name, because it was finally given after the resurrection of Christ; what is held in John VII. 39 must be understood in a certain respect: namely, with respect to the visible effusion made at the feast of Pentecost, not simply: for the faithful of the Old Testament also had the Holy Spirit; but by 'the letter' is understood the letter of the law, which is so called, both by reason of its origin, because the Decalogue was described in letters on tablets, and of condition, because just as a letter is otherwise mute and dead, so the letter of the law itself after the fall is unable to change the heart, and contributes absolutely nothing toward performing what it requires. By the Spirit, however, the Holy Spirit is understood, effectively instructing us and renewing us in such a way that we can perform actions pleasing to GOD. Furthermore, oldness is attributed to the letter of the law, because in the old man nothing but oldness, and not indeed the grace of the Spirit, has a place; but newness is attributed to the spirit, not only in time, because this grace of the Spirit is later and is appropriate only to the reborn, but also in effect, because it produces new works in believers, and clothes the mind with new light and the will with new motions. We serve, therefore, in the newness of the Spirit, not in the oldness of the letter, not when the faculty of nature is exerted to the utmost according to the prescription of the law, but when those regenerated by the Spirit of GOD attune themselves to the good pleasure of GOD with new motions, and when we obey GOD not according to the external discipline of the law, but with true piety of mind, not according to that servile obedience which consisted of the letter, not in spirit, but with a spontaneous Spirit and with obsequies flowing from an ardent affection of the soul. B. Asselmann, Heptad. quaestion. illustrium p. IV. th. 9, explains the letter from Augustine l. XV. c. Faust. Manich. c. 8, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Ambrose, through the law of Moses exercising and punishing itself in the oldness of nature: the Spirit through the grace of the Gospel liberating and showing itself through the newness of life, comparing Rom. II. 27. seqq., where the letter is preached concerning the Spirit of the flesh, concerning the circumcision of the heart, and 2. Cor. III. 6. 7., where the letter is enunciated concerning the Old Testament or the law, and its proper effect is assigned to it, to kill; the Spirit concerning the New Testament or the Gospel, whose proper effect is established to be to give life. This is B. Asselmann. But if we wish to be precise, as is fitting, the Spirit is properly distinguished from the Gospel: just as the letter is also distinguished from the law, because the Spirit works through the Gospel, and is the principal cause of our newness, as the Gospel is the organic cause. Therefore the Gospel is called τοῦ πνεύματος or of the Spirit in the oblique case, but not indeed τὸ πνεῦμα in the nominative case: the law also is not the letter itself, but the letter is something accidental to the law: since the law is an image of divine justice, to which it happens that it is found in its own way in the oldness of the letter, and that it is written in our heart by the Spirit of GOD, and thus shines forth in the newness of the Spirit.

PART II OF CHAPTER VII. Apologetic. Vindicating the holiness of the law.

Latin:

Vers. 6. νυνὶ δὲ κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τῶ νόμȣ. Repetit verbum, quod in comparationis parte priore po- fuerat supra 2.

Liberati à lege alii exponunt, inutiles legi reddi- ti. Liberati autem sumus à lege non simpliciter, sed 1. quoad maledictionem, cum justificati immu- nes sint à maledictione, 2. quoad servilem coactio- nem: quia Spiritu libertatis donati sumus. 3. quoad rigorem exactionis: quia inchoata etiam sanctitas Deo placet, cum persona est reconciliata per fidem. 4. quoad virtutem irritationis: quam in non rena- tis habet lex non sui vitio, sed naturæ corruptæ culpâ: quæ uti compescitur in renatis, ita non irri- tantur illi per legem ad peccandum, sed excitantur potius ad sanctitatis studium.

ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα.

Alii codices habent ἀποθανόντος, cujus lectionis & Ori- genes meminit. Quomodo & Chrysostomum legisse ap- paret ex ejus interpretatione: ὁ δεσμὸς δι᾽ ὅ κατειχόμεθα ἐνε- κρώθη. Christus moriens interfecit legem Mosis, quæ Ju- dæos sibi alligatos habebat: sicut lex conjugii fœminam. Κατέχω respondet Hebræo חזק, quod est possidere.

Quum codices Græci constanter habeant ἀπο- θανόντες, quibus etiam Syrus interpres consonat, ab ea lectione non est discedendum, & reddi potest subintelligendo vocem ἐκείνῳ mortui illi, in quo, seu à quo detinebantur, vel mortui sc. legi, cujus antea mentio facta, in qua, vel etiam quatenus eâ constricti detinebamur; κατειχόμεθα enim vim & violentam detentionem infert Matth. XXI. 38. Luc. IV. 42. Rom. I. 18. Sic ergò legi sumus mortui, qua- tenus illâ detinebamur, quia vinculum illud ru- ptum est, per quod lex nos habuit obnoxios, quod imprimis reatus fuit, & damnatio. Monemur hic de usu legis in non renatis: qui is est, ut constringat, & q. captivos detineat vinculo reatus & damnatio- nis eos, qui nondum liberati sunt. Absurdissimum ergò fuerit eum illius usum fingere, ut justificet. Nec dissimilis est hæc perversio, quàm si quis capi- tis reus à carnifice constrictus videatur, ut eque- stris dignitatis ornamenta consequatur. De em- phasi vocis κατέχειν conferatur B. Wellerus ad h. l.

ὥστε δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος.

Ut serviamus Deo scilicet, novo spiritu, id est, Christi. Hebraismus frequens, καινότητι πνεύματος, pro πνέυματι καινῷ. Rectè spiritum novum dixit, qui ante resurrectionem Christi datus non fuerat. Joh. VII. 39. Vide & 1. Cor. III. 6.

καὶ ὀ παλαιότητι γράμματος.

Legem Mosis vocat literam vetustam. Literæ vetustæ solent evanescere. Hebr. VIII. 13. Scriptum etiam Rhetores sæpe dicunt pro lege, sic & supra II. 27. 29. 2. Cor. III. 6. 7.

Non novus Spiritus, sed novitas τῶ πνέυματος. Spiritûs hic designatur, multò verò minus eo no- mine Spir. novus dicitur, quod demum post resurre- ctionem Christi datus sit; quod Joh. VII. 39. habetur, secundum quid intelligendum: nimirum respectu visibilis effusionis, in festo Pentecostes factæ, non simpliciter: nam & fideles Veteris Testamenti Spiritum S. habuêre; Per literam autem intelligi- tur legis litera, quæ ita dicitur, tùm ratione originis, quia literis Decalogus in tabulis descriptus fuit, tum condicionis, quia ut alias litera muta est, & mor- tua, ita & ipsa legis litera post lapsum cor immuta- re non valet, & ad præstandum id, quod requirit vi- rium plane nihil confert. Per Spiritum autem Spi- ritus Sanctus intelligitur nos efficaciter instruens, & ita renovans, ut actionibus DEO placitis de- fungi possimus. Cæterum literæ legis tribuitur vetustas, quia in veteri homine nil nisi vetustas, non vero gratia Spiritus locum habet; spiritui autem novitas tribuitur, non tempore tantum, quod hæc Spiritus gratia posterior sit, & renatis tantum con- veniat, sed effectu etiam, quia nova in credentibus opera edit, mentem nova luce, voluntatem novis motibus induit. Servimus ergo in novitate Spiri- tus, non in vetustate literæ, non cum ad præscriptum legis facultas naturæ pro virili excutitur, sed cum Spiritu DEI regenerati novis motibus ad bene- placitum DEI sese attemperant, & cum non juxta externam legis disciplinam, sed vera animi pietate non juxta servilem illam obedientiam, quæ literæ constabat, non spiritu, sed Spiritu spontaneo & obsequiis ab ardenti animorum affectu promanan- tibus, DEO paremus, B. Asselmann. Heptad. quæ- stion. illustrium p. IV. th. 9. ex Augustino l. XV. c. Faust. Manich. c. 8. Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Theo- phylacto, Oecumenio, & Ambrosio explicat literam per legem Mosis in vetustate naturæ se exerenten & punientem: Spiritum per gratiam Evangelii li- berantem, & per vitæ novitatem se ostendentem, conferens Rom. II. 27. seqq. ubi litera prædicatur de carnis Spiritu, de cordis circumcisione, & 2. Cor. III. 6. 7. ubi litera enuncietur de Testamento Vete- ri vel lege, eique proprius effectus assignatur, occi- dere; Spiritus de Test. Novo vel Evangelio, cujus proprius effectus constituatur vivificare. Hæc B. Asselmannus. Verum si prout par est, ἀκριβολογεῖν velimus, proprie Spiritus ab Evangelio distinguitur: uti etiam litera a lege, quia Spiritus per Evangelium operatur, & causa est novitatis nostræ principalis, u- ti Evangelium, organica. Ideo Evangelium τοῦ πνεύ- ματος vel Spiritus in casu obliquo, non vero τὸ πνεῦ- μα in casu recto dicitur: Lex etiam non est ipsa li- tera, sed litera aliquid accidens est legis: quum lex sit ἀπεικόνισμα justitiæ divinæ, cui accidit, quod in literæ vetustate suo modo reperiatur, & quod in corde nostro Spiritu DEI scribatur, adeoque in novitate Spiritus refulgeat.

PARS II. CAPITIS VII. ἀπολογητική. Legis sanctitatem vindicans.

## 7:7
Vers. 7. What then shall we say.

What then is it that we say? as in IV. 1, VI. 1. For he returns to the other calumny objected against him, that the law is the cause of sin, and for that reason evil.

that the law is sin.

It is a metonymy; do we say, as they slander, that the law is the cause of sin?

God forbid.

He rejects this far from himself, as above III. 6. 31. VI. 2. 15. Jerome expresses the force of the objection thus in Vol. III, Quæst. VIII to Algasia: But if under the entering law (which teaches what we ought to do, and forbids what we ought not to do) we are carried by our own vice and incontinence against the legal decrees: the law seems to be the cause of sin, which, while it forbids concupiscence, is known in a certain way to inflame it: There is a secular maxim among the Greeks: Whatever is permitted is less desired; Therefore, on the contrary: Whatever is not permitted receives the tinder of desire. But Jerome meets that objection there in this way: Just as medicine is not the cause of death if it shows deadly poisons, although evil men abuse these for death and either kill themselves or plot against their enemies: So also the law was given to show the poisons of sins, and to restrain with the bridle of the law a man badly abusing his liberty, who was previously carried along improvidently and was falling down precipices, and to teach him to walk with composed steps. From the words of the Apostle it could be gathered thus. That which 1. had to be mortified through the body of Christ 2. through which are the παθήματα of sins; 3. from which we have been freed, 4. to which we had to die, that we might serve God, is either sin, or the cause of sin. But such is the law. Therefore. But from the response of the Apostle denying the consequence: Μὴ γένοιτο Far be it, and declaring himself thus, but I did not know sin except through the law, but having received an occasion, sin through the commandment produced in me all concupiscence, it is clear: That a distinction must be made partly between the origin of sin and its manifestation, that through the law are the παθήματα of sins not effectively, but declaratively, because things are said to happen even then when they are revealed; partly between that which is by itself, and that which is by accident or ἀφορμητικῶς: That the law of God was to be mortified by accident, and we to be freed from it, and to have died to it, insofar as it brings condemnation and forces us to servile obedience: which is to be attributed to the vice of our corruption, not to the nature of the law by itself; which is just, holy, and good; That through the law of God also the παθήματα of sins are in us ἀφορμητικῶς only and occasionally, and that likewise, because we are carried by our own vice and incontinence against legal decrees. Phil. Melanchthon has it thus here in Vol. IV on this passage, p. 134. But the question is instituted in the text for the sake of declaration: Whether the law is an evil thing, since it increases sin, because in accusation hearts flee from God, and horribly rage against him. Paul answers by Translation: that the law is a ministry of death, is not by the fault of the law, but because of our sin. For since this depraved nature is not conformable to the law, but full of darkness and doubts, and is without fear, without love, without trust in God, and is of ineffable contumacy, finally since it is without God, when the wrath of God is shown through the law, it cannot sustain it, but flees, and would wish itself or God to be reduced to nothing, as it is written Luke 23. You will say to the mountains, fall upon us. Paul says, therefore, that the effect of the law is to show and accuse sin: Afterwards, guilty nature rages against God.

ἀλλὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου. That is, I would not have known it so exactly. For these things are said comparatively. See above III, 20.

Not only comparatively, but these things are true simply; For there is no recognition of sin except from the law; which, however, is both inscribed on our heart and truly prescribed by Moses. And in this latter way of considering, or if the discourse is about the Mosaic law, it is certain that we know sin more exactly than through the law of nature and the remnants of the divine image, which still remain after the fall.

τὴν δὲ γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν. It is to be noted in this place, and subsequently, that Paul speaks in the first person, not because he is dealing with himself: but because for the sake of modesty he prefers to express odious things in this way, which he himself calls μετασχηματίζειν 1 Cor. IV. 6. You have similar kinds of speaking 1 Cor. VI. 10. 12. X. 23. 29. 30. XIII. 2. Gal. II. 18. Chrysostom on 1 Cor. XII. σὺ τὰ φορτικὰ ἐπὶ τὸ οἰκείου προσώπου γυμνάζει. Jerome on Daniel: He enumerates the sins of the people because he is one of the people, in his own person, which we also read the Apostle doing in the epistle to the Romans. Nor indeed do such things not occur elsewhere. The Scholiast of Horace on epistle VIII, book 1. He reproves Celsus for moroseness and inconstancy, yet so that what he criticizes in him, he transfers to himself, so that he may reprove more freely. Thus in the Art of Poetry: -- I labor to be brief: I become obscure. Likewise, To preserve the described turns and colors of works. Why, if I cannot, am I greeted as a Poet though I am ignorant? And -- I avoided the fault of the two-toothed one: I did not deserve praise. -- Scholiast: He puts himself for any other. Thus also Lucian Κροῖσος ἐμοί. You have a similar position of the first person for an uncertain one in Ambrose on Duties 1. 48. But the Apostle here describes the Hebrew race under the first person, as it was, for the most part, first before the law: then after the law. ἐκ ἤδη, namely that there is sin, which is understood from what precedes. Before the law, most men thought themselves innocent if they had taken another's wife or property without violence and theft. For this is what the law calls to covet, for example, if someone sees a little coldness arising between husband and wife, he fosters it and fans it so that the husband, impatient of the troubles, may separate her from himself: or he instructs a lustful youth with money, having accepted his goods as a pledge, so that when he does not pay, he may retain those goods for himself as forfeited. Many think these are not crimes, but the inventions of a clever mind. Thus also in the matter of lusts, the Hebrews acknowledge that many things were wicked which were restrained by no punishments. Lactantius: The fear of laws did not suppress crimes, but removed license. For laws could punish offenses, they could not fortify the conscience. And so, whereas before they were done openly, they began to be done secretly: rights were even circumvented.

if the law had not said you shall not covet:

לא תחמר Exodus 20:14. לא תאוה Deuteronomy 5:18. understand another's wife, house, servant, ox, ass. The law therefore, so solemnly promulgated by GOD, brought it about that no Israelite could doubt that such deceits were to be reckoned as sins. ἐπιθυμεῖν is to deprive. See Matthew 19:18 and Mark 10:11 and what we have said there.

There is no trace here of such a transformation. That the Apostle is speaking rather of himself, all his words openly testify, which we showed in the Apostolic Theology on Romans, having adduced the opinions of the ancients and arguments which broke the ankles of this Pelagian, Socinian, and Arminian gloss. But that the Apostle is describing the Hebrew race, as it was for the most part first before the law, then after the law, is likewise openly false. For he relates it concerning him in his own person and by his own example, what kind of people those are who are not reborn by the fault of their own vicious and corrupt nature, and to what extent the law of nature itself is obliterated in them, and almost deleted, because they do not understand that concupiscence is sin: and how he himself under Pharisaism, even though he had the law, did not recognize it, as one who likewise obliterated and depraved the law of Moses with their own corruptions, and said that it was the very sentence of the law itself, which Grotius says men for the most part fostered before the law, as we observed on Matthew 5. Nor indeed did the law in any way favor rash divorces, which was noted both there and on Matthew 19, but this was the fault of Pharisaic misinterpretation. Therefore it is no wonder that the Apostle himself, informed by the Pharisees, did not hold concupiscence for sin before his conversion, even though the law makes it sin clearly and brightly enough, while it is prohibited in the Decalogue itself as a most grave sin: You shall not covet. For the Pharisees did not hold the interior motions of wicked concupiscence for sin, as is read even in the Talmud, Kiddushin: God does not reckon an evil thought as a work. But the Papists act as midwives to the Pharisees, and to some extent also the papizing Grotius; who think that the concupiscence prohibited in the law is not the unorganized and involuntary motions of wicked concupiscence, but only formed or voluntary concupiscence, when, namely, we consent to an internal vicious motion, as from the Papistic interpreters, Salmeron, Toledo, Cornel. à Lapide, Pererius, Conzenius, Justinianus, and Bellarmine, book 5, On the loss of grace.

chapter 10. it is evident; But against whom the Apostle here opposes himself, teaching that even the first and involuntary motions of concupiscence, which we do not approve, to which we do not consent, which we do not will, are prohibited; and that not only voluntary concupiscence is sin, is evident also from the fact that we can know that concupiscence from elsewhere than from the Mosaic law, and the Gentiles, destitute of divine law, had knowledge of it, which Justinianus and Salmeron prove from the very laws of Lycurgus should be held as sin. But the Apostle here deals with that concupiscence, the knowledge of which he had only through the law: and thus not only of voluntary

and formed, but also of involuntary. Of that concupiscence which takes occasion to produce vicious voluntary motions and in them as it were lives and exerts its life, which he teaches is sin even when it seems dead, v. 8, 9. Of that concupiscence which seduces us, v. 11, which the Apostle complains clings to him, so that it does the things which he does not will, but hates, v. 15, to which he does not consent, but from which he abhors by the law of the mind, by which he is reborn, v. 23. Therefore he does not deal only with voluntary concupiscence, to which we consent. Therefore Chrysostom, homily 6 on Matthew, says we will render an account, not only of those things which we have committed voluntarily, but also those which we have committed involuntarily, and we shall give an account of those things which we did willingly and those which we did unwillingly: and Augustine, Epistle 197 to Agelius, teaches that this precept, you shall not covet, is not fulfilled in this life, but that in this life we only strive toward that place where it will be fulfilled. And the Papists finally admit that involuntary concupiscence is also called sin, but only originally, because it arose from sin, and efficiently, because it leads to sin: but with the Apostle again resisting: who teaches that it is formally sin, as being prohibited by the law. For whatever is lawlessness, or prohibited by divine law, it cannot be doubted that it is formally sin, 1 John 3:4. And the Apostle calls it sin more than once, and indeed for that reason by which he denies that the law is sin, by which he teaches that sin is recognized from the law: Sin, which seduces us, because of which we are carnal, sold under sin; sin dwelling in us, which not only does evil, and works wicked desires, but is also itself evil, v. 21. ἐϰ ἀγαθὸν v. 18. contrary to the good and holy law, v. 16. repugnant to the law of the mind of the regenerate, and taking them captive under the law of sin, v. 23. making us serve the law of sin, contrary to the divine law v. 25. from which the Apostle seeks to be delivered and desires with groaning, v. 24. All of which things proclaim with a loud voice that this concupiscence is sin in the true sense of the word. Not to mention that it is a rule of good interpretation that one must not depart from the literal meaning of the text, without a cause shown in the Scriptures themselves, in matters to be believed. But no such cause appears. Augustine indeed calls concupiscence the cause of sin in such a way that he makes it sin itself, book V against Julian, ch. 2. Concupiscence, he says, of the flesh against which the good Spirit lusts, is also sin, because there is in it disobedience against the dominion of the mind, and it is the punishment of sin, because it was rendered to the merits of the disobedient: and it is the cause of sin by the defection of the one consenting, and by the contagion of the one harming. Nor does Cardinal Cajetan deny that concupiscence, of which the Apostle treats here, is also formally sin, affirming it in so far as it is a part of original sin. Not only did Augustine precede him, as we have said, and Ambrose, whom Bellarmine admits calls concupiscence a vice, iniquity, and delight contrary to the command of God, book V on the loss of grace, ch. 22, but also Lombard, II Sentences, dist. 21, from the corruption of the flesh arises an illicit motion, and a depraved titillation, and therefore temptation, which is from the flesh, is not without sin. And book III, dist. 19. We still await the redemption of the body, but according to the soul we have already been redeemed in part, not in whole, from guilt, not from punishment; nor entirely from guilt; for we have not been so redeemed from it that it does not exist, but that it does not dominate. And Thomas, part III, qu. 41, art. 1, ad 3. Temptation which is from the flesh cannot be without sin, because it happens through delight and concupiscence, and as Augustine says, book IX of the City of God, ch. 4. It is some sin, when the flesh lusts against the Spirit. Even in the Council of Trent itself, when that opinion of the Fathers Augustine, Ambrose, Lombard the Master, and Thomas (which is ours) was being condemned, Antonius Marinarius the Carmelite warned: That concupiscence, which is the same before and after Baptism, is of itself indeed sin, as Saint Paul testifies, and that it fights even in the regenerate against the law of GOD, to which whatever is repugnant must necessarily be sin, the baptized person is nevertheless excused, who has put on Christ, and is clothed with him: and after the Council, Stapleton, book III on concupiscence in the regenerate, ch. 2, confessed that concupiscence is a certain iniquity, and sometimes an obliquity, not only against the dominion of the mind, but even against the law of God. And Cassander in Consult. art. II acknowledged that if you define the nature of sin in that vice and iniquity, languor, infirmity, and disease, which must be resisted by the Spirit lest it beget illicit acts, concupiscence is not ineptly so called. But whither those disputes of the Papists finally tend or depart, that the first and indeliberate motions of concupiscence are truly not sin, those opinions can teach which the Practitioners and Moralists among them have defended. e.g. Molanus, Theol. Pract. ch. 27, Concl. 1, propos. 4. that many impure thoughts and imaginations are not sins: Toletus, book IV, Instruct. Sacerd. ch. 13. When a man, moved by some anger or other passion, not noticing the words he was uttering, uttered a blasphemy, it is not a mortal sin. Book V, instr. ch. 9, when a man utters a contumelious word not from full deliberation, it is not a mortal sin; and ch. 6, when someone is seized by a sudden motion so that he is not in possession of his reason, and kills another, he is free from mortal sin. To this also pertains that of Gregory of Valentia, book on Celibacy, ch. VI. When the Apostle says, it is better to marry than to burn, to burn does not signify the same as to be burned by the flame of lust, for this is not evil in itself, etc.

But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence.

ἡ ἁμαρτία, here is the habit of sinning, which had been before the law, it also brought forth those evil deceits after the law, but how? ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, that is, having obtained impunity from the precept: because no punishment was opposed to that precept, such as was opposed to adulteries and thefts: therefore it was despised: which is a sign that those who indulged in these evils abstained from those others not for the love of honesty, but for fear of punishment. Demosthenes also uses ἀφορμὴν for impunity: and it is said, as the Scholiast of Thucydides explains, that from which one starting is saved. Thus also in Gal. V. 13 this word is taken. Many interpreters explain ἀφορμὴν as occasion, and think that the same thing is said here as in the common proverb: We strive for what is forbidden: to which agrees that of Seneca: Homicides began with the law, and the punishment showed them the crime. And that of Tacitus: To engage in usury and extend it into interest was unknown: and therefore it was more observed than if it had been forbidden. You have something of the sort and concerning sodomy in Lampridius in Severus. I do not deny that these things, as they are in some, so they do not happen so commonly as those to which Paul refers. To the above-mentioned interpretation well agrees what Maimonides says in the Guide for the Perplexed III. 41, that a man cannot be torn away from an unusual habit of sinning except by heavy punishments.

There is various corruption and falsehood here: First, that ἡ ἁμαρτία is the habit of sin. It is clear from the text that not the habit of sinning, but depraved concupiscence, the cause of all depraved desires, or original sin, is indicated here by the word ἁμαρτίας: which the Pharisees did not consider to be sin, nor would the Apostle, taught by them, have known it to be sin, unless, being more rightly informed in the School of the Holy Spirit, he had understood that the law against coveting prohibits the same thing.

Then, that he interprets ἀφορμὴν as impunity: Because there is nothing about the impunity of depraved concupiscence here or elsewhere in Scripture: nor does it fit this place: where he does not extenuate depraved concupiscence, but exaggerates it, and teaches that it is not only sin, and not only the cause of depraved desires, but also brings death. Thirdly, that it obtained this impunity for ἁμαρτίαν from the precept. For how could a divine precept grant impunity, when he is pronounced cursed who has not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. XXVII. 26, and he who has offended in one, or has transgressed, is held guilty of the whole law, James II. 10. But what Grotius says fourthly, that no punishment was opposed, such as was opposed to adulteries and thefts: One must distinguish between the forum of the soil and the forum of the pole; for although there is no punishment for concupiscence in the forum of the soil or human forum, yet in the forum of the pole and divine, the punishment of the curse awaits it. Nor indeed (5.) can the use of the word ἀφορμῆς for impunity be taught from the Scriptures in Gal. V. 13. The usual and common meaning can certainly be retained: for which there is no reason why we should depart here: since the received interpretation is entirely correct, that the occasion of transgression is taken from the interdict, by the vice of corrupt nature. Since we always strive for what is forbidden, because of the power of original concupiscence. Sixthly, it does not deserve approval that Grotius says this does not happen so commonly, that man strives for what is forbidden, if it is a question of his natural proclivity and the power of concupiscence: which is entirely the matter here. For every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil ALL THE DAYS. On the contrary, however, it does not happen so commonly that where a political punishment has not been sanctioned, the habit of sinning always rushes into such sins because of such impunity: since by the fear of the Deity and the dictate of conscience, or by the benefit of the Holy Spirit of regeneration and grace, even those who have been ensnared by the habit of sinning are not rarely drawn back, even if they know they are not thereby rendered liable to punishments in the forum of the soil. This, therefore, is what the Apostle says: that concupiscence takes occasion from the divine interdict or precept to omit those things which are commanded, to commit those things which are forbidden, and thus, setting aside the divine will, to indulge its own depraved desires: and those not of one, but of every kind, which has an influence on all sins, and instigates and solicits us to all sins: To this (concupiscence), therefore, it is not to be imputed as a fault of the law that that original evil generates πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν every actual concupiscence, taking occasion from the prohibiting law: by which prohibition it is irritated, when it ought to be restrained. Desperate diseases are exacerbated by remedies. Thus, to the law of the members, most things become sweet for the very reason that they are forbidden by the law of GOD. For such is the depravity of our nature that the more exquisitely a sin is forbidden in the law, the more it strives toward the contrary. For it tends toward its own liberty, which seems as if bound by the chain of the law, and thus it strives to break that bond. You see, says St. Chrysostom on this passage, how he frees the law from all blame: for sin (not the law), having taken the occasion, increased concupiscence: and thus the contrary of what the law intended was done, which was not of malice, but of infirmity. For when that which we desire is forbidden, the flame of concupiscence is rendered stronger by it; but that is not from the law: for it indeed forbade concupiscence, that it might lead us away from it: but this sin is your own sloth and evil mind, which abuses that which is good for the contrary. But the blame is not to be ascribed to the physician, but to the patient, who has used the medicine badly. Nor, however, does the Apostle rush into all desires, or designate flagrant acts of every kind: for the discourse is not about external actions, but only about the affections of the mind and internal motions: nor is it expressed what has been done, but what could be done through an innate propensity toward evil. Nor is there any reason for the Jesuit Adam Contzen to object that concupiscence is from GOD, and therefore is not sin: because concupiscence is viewed here, not insofar as it is a natural affection, implanted by GOD, but insofar as it degenerated from concreated justice through the fall, and thus either is not directed toward the due object, or is not directed in the due manner. Concupiscence considered physically and absolutely is neither good nor evil, but morally and relatively to the law it is either good or evil. Here, however, it is manifest that the discussion is about concupiscence as the depraved source and fountain of every depraved desire and actual evil.

For without the law sin is dead. Dead, that is, it does not have the force which it ought to have; See above VI. 2. Thus faith is dead, which does not lead a man to righteousness. And this is said comparatively. For sin less disturbs the conscience when the divine law is not present.

What is that force of the habit of sinning, if this is understood through sin, which it ought to have? And had not Grotius said before and apart from the law that men judged themselves innocent, even if they had fraudulently transferred another's property or wife to themselves? Why then would the habit of sinning not have obtained its force then? Nor indeed is that comparison of dead faith to be approved: as if faith is called dead from its effect or inefficacy, because it does not have the force of leading to righteousness; when it is rather called dead from a defect of form, because it is destitute of true and living assurance, which is the life of faith, whence it follows that it does not lead to righteousness. Furthermore, where there is no law, there is no sin; and therefore it cannot trouble or disturb the conscience, nor be considered dead: for of a non-entity there are no attributes. The Apostle speaks therefore of the Mosaic law, that without it sin is dead: because although we are never without the law of nature, it is nevertheless obliterated in us by depraved concupiscence, so that it cannot so well explain its force. But the law of Moses was solemnly promulgated and recorded in the Scriptures, so that the conscience might be the more effectively disturbed. For there are no terrors of conscience where the law does not yet stir the sleeper. Now, that the law of nature does not demonstrate the atrocity of guilt and offense, and does not so terrify the conscience, is caused by the depravity from the fall of our first parents: since it does not even show that fountain and source of all evil. Therefore, there is absolutely a need for a divinely revealed law, so that there may be a full acknowledgment of sin and the conscience may be disturbed, as is fitting.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν.

Quid ergo est, quod dicimus? ut IV. 1. VI. 1. Recurrit enim ad calumniam alteram sibi objectam, legem causam esse peccati, & ob id malam.

ὅτι νόμος ἁμαρτία.

Est μετωνυμία, dicimusne nos, ut illi calumniantur, le- gem esse causam peccati?

μὴ γένοιτο.

Longe id a se rejicit, ut supra III. 6. 31. VI. 2. 15. Objectionis vim ita exprimit Hieronymus T. III. Quæst. IIX. ad Algasiam: Quod si sub intrante lege (quæ docet, quid facere, & prohibet, quid non fa- cere debeamus) vitio nostro & incontinentia fera- mur contra scita legalia: videtur lex esse causa pecca- ti, quæ dum prohibet concupiscentiam, quodammodo eam inflammare cognoscitur: Secularis apud Græcos sententia est: Quicquid licet, minus desideratur; Ergo e contrario: Quicquid non licet, fomitem accipit desi- derii. Occurrit autem illic Hieronymus Objectio- ni isti hoc pacto: Quomodo medicina non est causa mortis, si ostendat venena mortifera, licet his mali ho- mines abutantur ad mortem & vel se interficiant, vel t, insidientur inimicis: Sic & lex data est, ut peccatorum venena monstret, & hominem malè libertate sua abu- tentem, qui prius ferebatur improvidus, & per præci- pitia labebatur, freno legis retineant, & compositis doceat incedere gressibus. E verbis Apostoli sic colli- gi poterat. Id quod 1. mortificandum fuit per cor- pus Christi 2. per quod peccatorum sunt παθήματα; 3. à quo liberati sumus, 4. cui mori debuimus, ut Deo serviamus, aut peccatum est, aut peccati causa. At talis est lex. Ergò. E responsione verò Apostoli con- sequentiam negantis: Μὴ γένοιτο Absit, & sese ita de- clarantis, sed peccatum non cognovi nisi per legem, sed occasione acceptâ peccatum per præceptum genuit in me omnem concupiscentiam, patet: Distinguendum esse partim inter peccati originem, & ejusdem mani- festationem, quod per legem sint παθήματα pecca- torum non effectivè, sed declarativè, quia tùm etiam res fieri dicuntur, cum patesiunt; partim inter id, quod per se est, & quod ex accidenti vel ἀφορμητι- κῶς: Legem Dei ex accidenti mortificandam fuis- se, nosque ab eâ liberari, eidemque demori debuis- se, quatenus ea affert damnationem & nos cogit ad obedientiam servilem: quod nostræ corruptionis vitio, non legis naturæ per se tribuendum; quæ ju- sta, sancta est, & bona; Per legem Dei etiam παθή- ματα esse peccatorum in nobis ἀφορμητικῶς tan- tùm & occasionaliter, idque itidem, quod vitio no- stro & incontinentia feramur contra scita legalia. Phil. Melancht. hic ita habet T. IV. in h. l. p. 134. Est autem in textu declarandi causa instituta quæstio: Num lex sit res mala, cum augeat peccatum, quia in accusatione corda fugiunt Deum, & horribiliter fre- munt adversus eum. Respondet Paulus per Transla- tionem: quod lex est ministerium mortis, non sit legis vitio, sed propter nostrum peccatum. Cum enim hæc depravata natura non sit conformis legi, sed plena te- nebrarum & dubitationum, & sit sine timore, sine dile- ctione, sine fiducia Dei, & sit inenarrabilis contumacia, denique cum sit sine Deo, quando per legem ostenditur ira Dei, non potest eam sustinere, sed fugit, & vellet se aut Deum in nihilum redigi, sicut scriptum est Luc. 23. Dicetis montibus, cadite super nos. Ait ergò Paulus, effectum legis esse ostendere & accusare peccatum: Postea natura rea fremit adversus Deum.

ἀλλὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου. Id est, non ita exactè nossem. Dicuntur enim hæc com- paratè. Vide supra III, 20.

Non comparatè tantùm, sed simpliciter hæc vera sunt; Nam nonnisi è lege est agnitio peccati; quæ tamen est tùm cordi nostro inscripta, tùm verò à Mose præscripta. Atque hoc posteriori conside- randi modo, vel si de lege Mosaica sermo fit, cer- tum est nos exactius peccatum cognoscere quàm per legem naturæ, & reliquias imaginis divinæ, quæ post lapsum adhuc superant.

τὴν δὲ γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν. Notandum est hoc loco, ac deinceps Paulum in prima persona loqui, non quod de se agat: sed quod modestiæ causa res odiosas sic exprimere malit, quod ipse dicit μετασχημα- τίζειν 1. Cor. IV. 6. Similia loquendi genera habes 1. Cor. VI. 10. 12. X. 23. 29. 30. XIII. 2. Gal. II. 18. Chrysostomus ad 1. Cor. XII. σὺ τὰ φορτικὰ ἐπὶ τὸ οἰκείου προσώπου γυμνάζει. Hieronymus ad Danielem: Peccata populi quia unus è popu- lo est, enumerat persona sua, quod & Apostolum in epistola ad Romanos facere legimus. Neque vero non & alibi talia oc- currunt. Scholiastes Horatii ad epistolam VIII, lib 1. Repre- hendit Celsum morositatis & inconstantiæ, ita tamen ut quod in eo carpit, in se transferat, quo reprehendat liberius. Sic in arte poetica: -- brevis esse laboro: Obscurus fio. Item Descriptas servare vices operumque colores. Cur ego si nequeo ignoroque Poëta salutor? Et -- Vitavi bidentique culpam: Non laudem merui. -- Scholiastes: Se autem ponit pro quovis alio. Sic & Lucia- nus Κροῖσος ἐμοί. Similem positionem primæ personæ pro incerta habes apud Ambrosium de officiis 1. 48. Apostolus autem hic sub prima persona describit Hebræum genus, quale fuit, ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ, primum ante legem: deinde post legem. ἐκ ἤδη, nempe εἶναι ἁμαρτίαν, quod ex superiori subauditur. Ante legem homines plerique se infontes putabant, si absque vi & furto alienam uxorem aut rem ad se traduxissent. Hoc enim est quod lex vocat concupiscere, puta videns aliquis frigufculum nasci inter virum & uxorem, fovet illud accenditque ut molestiarum impatiens maritus illam à se segreget: aut juvenem luxuriosum pecunia instruit, rebus ejus pignori acceptis, ut illo non solvente res eas sibi ut commissas retineat. Hæc multi non scelera esse putant, sed solertis ingenii commenta. Sic & in libidinum genere agnoscunt Hebræi multa fuisse improba, quæ nullis pœnis coërcebantur. Lactantius: Metus legum, non scelera comprimebat, sed licentiam submovebat. Poterant enim leges delicta punire, conscientiam munire non poterant. Itaque ante palam fiebant, clam fieri cœperunt: circumscribi etiam jura.

εἰ μὴ ὁ νόμος ἔλεγεν ἐκ ἐπιθυμήσης:

לא תחמר Exodi XX. 14. לא תאוה Deut. V. 18. subaudi uxorem alterius, domum, servum, bovem, asinum. Lex igitur à DEO tam solenniter promulgata effecit, nequis Israelita dubitare posset, quin tales doli peccatis accensendi essent. ἐπιθυμεῖν est ἀποστερεῖν. Vide Matth. XIX. 18. & Marc. X. 11. & ibi à nobis dicta.

Nullum hic vestigium talis μετασχηματισμõ. De se potius loqui Apostolum, omnia ejus verba palàm testantur, quod ostendimus in Theol. Apost. Rom. adductis veterum sententiis, & argumentis, quæ huic Pelagianæ, Socinianæ, & Arminianæ glossæ talos fregerunt. Describere verò Apostolum Ebræum genus, quale fuit ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ primum ante legem, deinde post legem, apertè itidem falsum. Nam de eo in sua persona proprioque exemplo tradit, quales sint non renati culpâ naturæ suæ vitiosæ, & corruptæ, & quatenus lex ipsa naturæ in iis obliterata est, & propemodum deleta, quod non intelligant concupiscentiam esse peccatum: & quomodo ipse sub Pharifaismo, etsi legem habuerit, id non cognoverit, utpote qui legem Mosis corruptelis suis itidem obliterarunt & depravarunt, & eam etiam ipsius legis sententiam esse ajebat, quam ante legem homines plerosque fovisse, dicit Grotius, ut ad Matth. V. observavimus, Nec verò lex ullatenus velificabatur temerariis divortiis, quod tùm illic, tùm ad Matth. XIX. annotatum, sed ψευθερμηνείας Pharisaicæ hæc erat culpa. Ideò non mirum Apostolum ipsum à Pharisæis informatum concupiscentiam non habuisse pro peccato ante conversionem, etsi satis clarè & luculenter eam peccatum lex faciat, dum eadem in ipso Decalogo ceu gravissimum peccatum prohibetur: Non concupisces. Pharisæi enim interiores concupiscentiæ pravæ motûs non habebant pro peccato, uti in Talmude etiam Kiddufch legitur: Cogitationem malam non reputat Deus pro opere. Obstetricantur autem Pharisæis Papistæ, & quadantenus etiam Grotius papizans; qui concupiscentiam in lege prohibitam non pravæ concupiscentiæ motus inordinatos, eosque involuntarios sed solum concupiscentiam formatam seu voluntariam esse existimant, cum sc. nos consentimus interno vitioso motui, ut ex Interpp. Papisticis, Salmerone, Toleto, Cornel. à Lapide, Pererio, Conzenio, Justinian. & Bellarmino l. V. de amiss. grat.

c. 10. constat; Quibus verò hic sese opponit Apostolus etiam, concupiscentiæ motûs primos & involuntarios, quos non probamus, quibus non consentimus, quos non volumus, prohibitam esse docens; nec solam voluntariam concupiscentiam peccatum esse, vel inde constat, quod illam concupiscentiam etiam aliunde, quàm ex lege Mosaica cognoscere possimus, ejusque notitiam gentiles lege divinâ destituti habuerunt, quam pro peccato habendam esse Justinianus, & Salmero ex ipsis Lycurgi legibus probant. De eâ autem concupiscentiâ agit hic Apostolus, cujus cognitionem tantùm per legem habuit: adeoque non de voluntaria tantũ

& formata, sed etiam de involuntaria. De illa con- cupiscentia, quæ occasionem sumit ad vitiosos mo- tus voluntarios & in iis veluti vivit ac vitam exerit, quam etiam tùm cum mortua videtur ἁμαρτίαν esse v. 8. 9. docet. De illa concupiscentia, quæ nos sedu- cit v. 11. quam Apostolus sibi adhærescere queritur, ut ea faciat, quæ non vult, sed odio habet v. 15. in quæ non consentit, sed à quibus abhorret lege mentis, vel quâ renatus est v. 23. Non ergo de concupiscentia voluntaria tantum agit, in quam consentimus. Ideò Chrys. hom. VI. in Matth. nos rationem reddituros dicit, non eorū tantum, quæ voluntariè commisimus, sed etiam quæ involuntariè, ϰᾀ ὧν ἑκόντες, ϰᾀ ὧν ἀεϰόντες ἡμάρ]ομεν, δώσομεν λόγον: & Aug. Ep.cxcvii.ad A- gel.docet, hoc præceptū, non concupisces, in hac vita non impleri, sed in ea nos tantum tēdere ad eū locum, ubi implebitur. Et admittunt tandem Papistæ invo- luntariam etiam concupiscentiam peccatum dici, sed tantùm originaliter, quia à peccato orta, & efficien- ter, quia ad peccatum inducit: sed repugnante ite- rum Apostolo: qui formaliter eam peccatum esse docet, utpote lege prohibitam. Quicquid n. ἀνομία, vel lege divina prohibitum est, id formaliter pec- catum esse dubitari nequit 1. Joh. III. 4. Et vocat id Apostolus plus vice simplici peccatum, & quidem eâ ratione, quâ legem peccatum esse negat, quâ è lege peccatum agnosci docet: Peccatum, quod nos seducit, ob quod nos carnales sumus, venundati sub pecca- tum; peccatum in nobis habitans, quod non tantum facit malum, & prava desideria operatur, sed etiam ipsum est ϰαϰὸν v. 21. ἐϰ ἀγαθὸν v. 18. legi bonæ & san- ctæ contrarium, v. 16. repugnans legi mentis renato- rum, & captivans eos sub legem peccati, v. 23. faciens nos servire legi peccati, legi divinæ contrariæ v. 25. à quo liberari expetit ac cum gemitu desiderat A- postolus, v. 24. Quæ omnia veri nominis peccatum esse hanc concupiscentia λευκάδι φωνῇ clamitant. Ut taceam, quod à proprietate literæ discedendum non esse, citra causam in ipsis Scripturis monstra- tam, in rebus credendis regula sit bonæ interpreta- tionis. Qualis vero causa nulla comparet. Augusti- nus sanè ita peccati causam dicit concupiscentiam, ut ipsam etiam peccatum faciat, l. V. contr. Julian. c. 2. Concupiscentia, inquit, carnis adversus quam bonus concupiscit Spiritus, & peccatum est, quia inest illi inobedientia contra dominatum mentis, & pœna pec- cati est, quia reddita est meritis inobedientis: & causa peccati est defectione consentientis, & contagione no- centis. Neque abnuit Cardinalis Cajetanus, concupi- scentiam, de quâ hic agit Apostolus, peccatum etiam esse formaliter, pro quanto est pars peccati originalis, affirmans. Præivit non tantum Aug. ut diximus, & Ambrosius, quem concupiscentiam vocare vitium, iniquitatem, & delectationem mandato Dei adversa Bellarminus fatetur l. V. de amiss. grat. c. 22. sed et- iam Lombardus II. sentent. dist. 21. ex carnis corru- ptione suboritur motus illicitus, & titillatio prava, ideoque tentatio, quæ ex carne est, non sit sine peccato. Et l. III. dist. 19. Adhuc expectamus redemtionē cor- poris, secundum animam verò jam redempti sumus ex parte, non ex toto, à culpâ, non à pœna; nec omnino à culpa; non n. sic ab ea redemti sumus, ut non sit, sed ut non dominetur. Et Thomas part. III. qu. 41. art. 1. ad3. Tentatio quæ est à carne, non potest esse sine pecca- to, quia fit per delectationem & concupiscentiam, & sicut dicit Aug. l. IX. de Civ. Dei c. 4. Nonnullum pec- catum est, cum caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum. Etiam in ipso Concilio Trid. cum condemnaretur sententia illa Patrum Augustini, Ambrof. Lombardi Magistri, Thomæ, (quæ nostra) Antonius Marinarius Carmelita monuit: Concupiscentiam, quæ eadem est ante & post Baptismum, ex se quidem esse peccatum attestante Divo Paulo, eam etiam in renatis pugnare tum lege DEI, cui quicquid repugnat, peccatum esse, necesse est, baptizatum nihilominus excusari, qui Christum induerit, eoque vestiatur: & post Con- cilium Stapletonus l. III. de concup. in renat. c. 2. fassus est concupiscentiam esse quandam iniquita- tem, & aliquando obliquitatem, non modo contra dominatum mentis, verum etiam contra legem Dei. Et Cassander in Consult. art. II. agnovit, si peccati rationem in vitio illo & iniquitate, languore, infir- mitate, ac morbo constituas, cui Spiritu resisten- dum sit, ne actus illicitos gignat, concupiscentiam non ineptè dici. Quò autem expediant, abeantve tan- dem illæ Pontificiorum disputationes, quod con- cupiscentiæ primi & indeliberati motûs verè non sint peccatum, sententiæ illæ docere possunt, quas Practici & Moralistæ inter eos propugnarunt. v. g. Molanus Theol. Pract. c. 27. Concl. 1. propos. 4. multas cogitationes & imaginationes impuras non esse peccata: Toletus l. IV. Instruct. Sacerd. c. 13. Cum homo irâ aliquâ vel alia motus passione, non adver- tens verba, quæ proferebat, protulit blasphemiam, non est mortale peccatum. l. V. instr. c. 9. cum homo pro- fert verbum contumeliosum non ex plena deliberatio- ne, non est mortale peccatum; & c. 6. cum aliquis mo- tu repentino correptus adeò, ut non sit rationis com- pos, alterum occidit, à peccato mortali liber est. Quo etiam facit illud Gregorii de Valent. l. de Cœlib. c. VI. Cum dicit Apostolus, melius est nubere quam uri, uri non idem significat, quod flamma libidinis uri, hoc enim per se malum non est &c.

ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς κατειρ- γάσατο ἐν ἐμοὶ πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν.

ἡ ἁμαρτία, hic est peccandi consuetudo, quæ ante legem fuerat, ea etiam post legem dolos illos malos peperit, at quomodo? ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, id est, impu- nitatem nacta à præcepto: quia præcepto isti nulla pœna erat opposita, qualis erat opposita adulteriis, & furtis: ideò contemnebatur: quod signum est eos, qui istis malitiis in- dulgebant, ab illis aliis abstinuisse non honesti amore, sed pœnæ metu. Ἀφορμὴν pro impunitate etiam Demosthenes usurpat: & dicitur, ut explicat Thucydidis Scholiastes, ἐξ ἧς ὁρμώμενός τις σώζεται. Sic & Gal. V. 13. Sumitur hæc vox. Multi interpretes ἀφορμὴν exponunt occasionem, putantque idem hic dici, quod vulgari proverbio: Nitimur in vetitum: cui convenit Senecæ illud: Homicidæ cum lege cœperunt, & illis facinus pœna monstravit. Et Taciti: Fenus agitare & in usuras extendere ignotum: ideoque magis servabatur, quam si vetitum esset. Quale quid & περὶ ἀρσενοκοιτίας habes apud Lampridium Severo. Hæc sicut in quibusdam ita se habe- re non nego, ita non ita communiter eveniunt, qualia sunt ad quæ respicit Paulus. Supra dictæ interpretationi benè congruit quod dicit Maimonides ductore dubitantium III. 41. ab insolita peccandi consuetudine non posse hominem avelli, nisi gravibus pœnis.

Varia hic est corruptela & falsitas: Primò quod ἡ ἁμαρτία peccati consuetudo sit. Non peccandi cõ- suetudinem, sed pravam concupiscentiam, causam desideriorum omnium pravorum, vel peccatum ori- ginale, voce ἁμαρτίας hic indigitari è textu claret: quam pro peccato non habebant Pharisæi, nec Apostolus ab iis edoctus novisset peccatum esse, nisi rectiùs in Schola Spiritûs S. informatus legem de non concupiscendo eandem etiam prohibere in- tellexisset.

Deinde, quod ἀφορμὴν de impunitate interpretetur: Quia nihil de impunitate pravæ con- cupiscentiæ sive hic, sive alibi Scriptura: nec ea huic loco convenit: ubi non extenuat pravam concupiscentiam, sed exaggerat, eamque non mo- do peccatum esse, nec modò causam esse pravo- rum desideriorum, sed etiam mortem inferre do- cet. Tertio impunitatem eam nactam esse ἁμαρ- τίαν à præcepto. Quomodo enim præceptum di- vinum impunitatem concederet, quum maledictus pronuncietur, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis Deut. XXVII. 26. & qui in uno offenderit, vel prævaricatus fuerit, totius le- gis reus habeatur Jac. II. 10. Quod verò quarto ait Grotius, nullam oppositam pœnam, qualis adulteriis opposita & furtis: Distinguendum inter forum soli, & poli; licet enim concupiscentiæ nulla sit pœna in foro soli seu humano, tamen in foro poli & divino pœna maledictionis eam manet. Ne- que verò (5.) è Scripturis usus vocis ἀφορ- μῆς pro impunitate doceri potest Gal. V. 13. Reti- neri certè potest usitata & communis significatio: à quâ cur hic discedamus causa nulla est: quum o- mnino rectè se habeat recepta interpretatio, quod ab interdicto occasio sumatur transgressionis, vitio na- turæ corruptæ. Siquidem in vetitum semper nita- mur, ob concupiscentiæ originalis vim. Sextò cal- culum non meretur, quod non ita communiter hoc evenire, ait Grotius, quod in vetitum nitatur ho- mo, si de naturali ejus proclivitate, & concupiscen- tiæ vi agatur: de quâ hic omnino res est. Omne enim figmentum cogitationum cordis humani tantùm ma- lum est OMNIBUS DIEBUS. Ex adverso verò non ita communiter hoc evenit, quod ubi pœna po- litica sancita non est, ob ejusmodi impunitatem semper peccandi consuetudo in ea peccata ruat: quũ metu Numinis & conscientiæ dictamine, vel rege- nerationis & gratiæ Spiritus S. beneficio non rarò retrahantur etiam, qui peccandi consuetudine ir- retiti fuêre, etsi pœnis in foro soli se obnoxios in- de haud reddi norint. Hoc ergò est, quod ait A- postolus: Concupiscentiam occasionem capere ex interdicto vel præcepto divino, ea, quæ præcepta sunt, omittendi, ea, quæ vetita sunt, committendi, adeoque, divina voluntate posthabitâ, propriis suis desideriis pravis indulgendi: iisque non unius, sed omnis generis, quæ influentiam habet in omnia peccata, & nos instigat ac solicitat ad omnia peccata: Huic ergò (concupiscentiæ) non legis culpæ imputandum est, quod malum illud origi- narium gignat πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν omnem concupisce- tiam actualem, occasionem accipiens à lege prohi- bente: quâ prohibitione irritatur, cum compesci debeat. Desperati morbi remediis exasperantur. Sic legi membrorũ eo ipso dulcia fiunt pleraque, quia lege DEI sunt prohibita. Tanta enim est na- turæ nostræ depravatio, ut quo exquisitius in lege prohibetur peccatum, eo magis in contrarium ni- tatur. Tendit enim ad libertatem suam, quæ vin- culo legis quasi adstricta videtur, adeoque illud vinculum rumpere nititur. Cernis, inquit, S. Chrys. in h. l. quemadmodum legem omni culpa liberet: Oc- casione quippe sumptâ peccatum (non lex) concupi- scentiam auxit: atque ita contrarium ab eo, quod lex volebat, factum est, id quod non erat malitiæ, sed in- firmitatis. Cum enim quod concupiscimus prohibetur, eo redditur validior concupiscentiæ flamma; verum non à lege est istud: ipsa quippe concupiscentiam pro- hibuit, ut ab ea nos abducat: peccatum verò hoc est so- cordia tua animusque malus eo, quod bonum est, in contrarium abutitur. Culpa autem non adscribenda est medico, sed ægroto, qui pharmaco malè usus est. Neque tamen ideo Apostolus in omnia desideria ruit, aut omnis generis flagitia designavit: non n. de actionibus externis, sed affectionibus animi & mo- tibus internis solùm sermo est: nec quid factum sit, sed quid per insitam propensionem ad malum fieri potuerit, exprimitur. Nec est, quod Adam à Conzen Jesuita obvertat, concupiscentiam à DEO esse, & propterea non esse peccatum: quia concupiscentia hic spectatur, non quatenus affectus est naturalis, à DEO inditus, sed quatenus à concreata justitia degeneravit per lapsum, adeoque aut non fertur in debitum objectum, aut non fertur debito modo. Con- cupiscentia physicè & absolutè considerata nec bona est nec mala, sed moraliter & relatè ad legem vel bona est vel mala. Hic autem de concupiscentia prava scaturigine & fonte omnis pravi desiderii malique actualis agi in propatulo est.

χωρὶς γὰρ νόμε ἁμαρτία νεκρὰ. Νεκρὰ, id est, vim non habet, quam debet; Vide supra VI. 2. Sic fides νεκρὰ, quæ hominem ad justitiam non per- ducit. Et hoc comparatè dictum. Minus enim peccatum conscientiam convellit, ubi lex divina non adest.

Quænam est illa vis consuetudinis peccandi, si hæc per ἁμαρτίαν intelligitur, quam illa habere debet? Et annon ante & citra legem Grotius di- xerat infontes se judicasse homines, etiamsi dolis ma- lis alienam rem aut uxorem ad se traduxissent? Quidni ergò enim vim suam tùm obtinuisset con- suetudo peccandi? Nec verò collatio illa fidei mortuæ probanda est: quasi fides νεκρὰ dicatur ab effectu vel inefficacia, quod vim non habeat ad justitiam perducendi; quum potius à formæ de- fectu mortua dicatur, quod verà & vivà πληροφορίᾳ destituatur, quæ est vita fidei, unde consequens est, quod ad justitiam non perducat. Porrò ubi nulla lex est,ibi nullum peccatum; ideoque nec conscië- tiam angere vel convellere potest, neq; νεκρὸν cen- seri: Non entis enim nulla sunt attributa. De lege ergò Mosaìcà loquitur Apostolus, sine ea pecca- tum mortuum esse: quia etsi nunquam simus sine naturæ lege, ea tamen in nobis obliteratur per pra- vam concupiscentiam,ut non adeò possit vim suam explicare. At lex Mosis solemniter promulgata, inque Scripturas relata est, ut conscientia eò effi- cacius convellatur. Terrores enim conscientiæ non sunt, ubi lex nondum excitat dormientem. Quo minus autem lex naturæ reatûs & offensæ atro- citatem commonstret, & conscientiam adeò ter- reat, depravatio ex lapsu primorum parentum fa- cit: quum ne quidem fontem atque scaturiginem illam omnis mali ostendat. Ideò omnino opus est lege divinitus revelatà, ut plena possit esse peccati agnitio & conscientia, prout par est, convellatur.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. But I was alive without the law once.

That is, I myself, as he says below 25. that very one, whom I signify under this pronoun I: that is, the Israelite race lived even before the law, namely in Egypt. See Ezek. XVI. 4. XXIII. 2.

But when the commandment came. The law having been given to the Israelites.

Sin lived. It had a conscience convicted more openly than before, its foulness was more manifest. I think it is read more correctly as lived than revived.

The pronoun I sufficiently teaches that the Apostle is speaking of himself: but that invention is colder than ice, that I myself denotes another, and indeed the Israelite race, such as it lived before the law in Egypt. No mention is made by any word of the Israelite race. Nor is it about the time of the promulgated law: but it is about the arrival of the law into our hearts: namely, how before that law penetrates, sin is dead, but then lives when the law arrives, or penetrates our hearts. Where death and life are understood not as to the thing, but as to the sense. For there is no sense of sin without the law: and therefore it seems dead: but when the commandment comes, it lives. Blessed Mylius rightly calls it dead, not because sin does not exist or does not work, for it is always very fruitful: but because it is felt little or nothing by us; for the law is the force of sin, says the Apostle (1 Cor. XV.), but without the law sin is not acknowledged nor does it press upon man. For the judgment of God is not acknowledged; Sin therefore being as it were lulled to sleep and sleeping at the doors, one lives securely Gen. IV. Furthermore, as the death of sin is only apparent, not true; when sin is not felt; so the Apostle was flourishing, i.e., he seemed to himself to live and to be most rightly with GOD, when he was without the law, that is, when the law did not exercise its force in him, and he did not yet know his sin from the law. For there was no disturbance in his mind, nor was his conscience terrified. For things are said to be then when they are seen, and words to be and to do are sometimes taken phenomenally and reputatively Matt. XIII. 12. Phil. III. 7. just as Augustine also explained this passage l. 1. i. c. 9. to Boniface: I seemed to myself to live. For the Apostle was ignorant that the interior affections of the heart were sin under Pharisaism, nor do we acknowledge them, unless taught from the word of GOD, much less their source, depraved concupiscence and original sin. Therefore he was secure, and trusted in external righteousness. Phil. III. 7. But when the law was preached, sin revived, i.e., not only did sin receive increments (accidentally) but its atrocity also became more and more known, and the wrath of GOD against sin was rendered more manifest by degrees. The Apostle therefore wished to set himself as an example, partly for the sake of energy, since discourse becomes more illustrious by examples; partly for the sake of persuasion. For he shows that he speaks of nothing except what he has found out by his own sense and experience. For then one is taught most usefully, when each person, descending into himself, can take a living experiment of the doctrine from himself. The law is therefore said to approach when it is felt to exercise its force. Then therefore sin is discovered to live, which before seemed dead; whence this use of the law, consisting in mortification, proceeds in this order: since the Apostle, after the manifestation of sin, now brings in mortification, namely that the law brings death. 1. Desires are increased by the occasion of the law. 2. Sin sleeps for a time. 3. Security encroaches. 4. Sin revives. Then from the terrors follows death, that is, that tremendous consternation, by which a man sees his destruction before his eyes, and is so crushed that he feels himself nowhere equal to sustaining the burden of sin. Thus Philippus: When the law came, that is, now accusing the heart, so that it might feel the wrath of God against my uncleanness, hypocrisy, and security, there sin revived, that is, it became more restless, and was of itself the cause of terrors, flight, and indignation against GOD, and this very consternation is death: therefore it is added: But I died, just as he says to the Corinthians, The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the Law. And in this chapter: That sin might become exceedingly sinful, that is, very guilty, this is, in true terrors and the sense of the wrath of GOD the magnitude of sin is discerned in some way, which secure and idle men lightly regard, etc. I died, says Blessed Weller, that is, I felt myself guilty of death and damnation. Conf. Gen. XX. 3. Num. XXXV. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἐγὼ δὲ ἔζων χωρὶς νόμε ποτὲ.

Id est, αὐτὸς ἐγὼ, ut dicit infra 25. ille nempe, quem sub hoc pronomine ego significo: id est, genus Israe- liticum vixit & ante legem,in Aegypto scilicet. Vide Ezech. XVI. 4. XXIII. 2.

ἐλθύσης δὲ ἐντολῆς. Datâ Israëlitis lege.

ἡ ἁμαρτία ἔζησεν. Apertius quàm ante convictam habuit conscientiam, magis patuit ejus fœditas. Puto rectius legi ἔζησεν quàm ἀνέζησεν.

De se loqui Apostolum pronomen ἐγὼ satis do- cet: glacie vero frigidius est commentum illud, αὐτὸς ἐγὼ alium, & quidem genus Israëliticum, qua- le vixit ante legem in Aegypto notare. Nullo verbo generis Israëlitici mentio facta. Nec de tempore pro- mulgatæ legis: sed de legis adventu in corda nostra agitur: quomodo nempe antequam ea penetret lex, peccatum mortuum, vivat autem deinde cum lex advenit, vel corda nostra penetrat. Ubi mors & vita non quoad rem, sed quoad sensum intelligi- tur. Nullus enim sensus est peccati, sine lege: ideo- que mortuum videtur: sed veniente præcepto vi- vit. Rectè B. Mylius mortuum appellat, non quod non sit, aut non operetur peccatum, valdè enim sem- per fructuosum est: sed quia nihil aut parum à nobis sentiatur; vis enim peccati lex est, inquit A- postolus (1. Cor. XV.) sine lege autem peccatum non agnoscitur nec premit hominem. Judicium enim Dei non agnoscitur; Peccato ergò sopito quasi & ad fores dormiente, securè vivitur Gen.IV. Porrò ut mors peccati apparens tantum est, non ve- ra; cum peccatum non sentitur; ita vigebat, h. e. vivere sibi videbatur Apostolus & rectissimè cum DEO habere,cum sine lege esset,id est,cum lex vim suam in ipso non exerceret, & ex lege peccatum suum nondum cognosceret. Turbationis enim nihil erat in animo, nec terrebatur conscientia. Res enim tùm esse dicuntur, cum videntur, & verba esse ac facere nonnunquam φαινομένως & reputati- vè accipiuntur Matth. XIII. 12. Phil. III. 7. uti et- iam Augustinus hunc locum exposuit l. 1. i. c. 9. ad Bonif. vivere mihi videbatur. Interiores enim cordis affectus peccatum esse ignorabat Aposto- lus sub Pharisaïsmo, neque nos eos agnoscimus, nisi edocti è verbo DEI, nedum fontem eorum pravam concupiscentiam & peccatum originale. Ideò securus erat, & in externa justitia confidebat. Phil. III. 7. Cum autem lex prædicaretur, revixit peccatum, h. e. non incrementa tantum capiebat peccatum (per accidens) sed atrocitas etiam ejus magis magisque innotescebat, & ira DEI adver- sus peccatum manifestior subinde reddebatur. Se ergò in exemplum sistere voluit Apostolus, par- tim ἐνεργείας ergò, siquidem illustrior fiat exem- plis oratio; partim πιθανολογίας gratia. Nihil enim loqui se ostendit, nisi quod sensu atque experien- tiâ suapte compertum habeat. Tunc enim utilis- simè docetur, cum in se quisque descendens do- ctrinæ vivum experimentum ex seipso capere po- test. Accedere ergò lex dicitur, cum sentitur, vim suam exerere. Tum ergo peccatum vivere depre- henditur, quod antea mortuum videbatur; unde hoc ordine procedit iste usus legis in mortificatio- ne consistens: siquidem Apostolus post manifesta- tionem peccati, jam mortificationem adferat, quod nempe lex mortem inferat. 1. Cupiditates oc- cafione legis augentur. 2. dormit ad tempus pecca- tum. 3. ingruit securitas. 4. reviviscit peccatum. In- de ex pavoribus mors, id est, consternatio illa tre- menda sequitur, quâ interitum suum homo ante oculos videt, & sic atteritur, ut oneri peccati sus- tinendo nusquam se parem esse sentiat. Ita Phi- lippus: Veniente lege, id est, jam accusante cor, ut sentiretur iram Dei adversus immunditiem meam, Hypocrisin & securitatem, ibi peccatum revixit, id est, factum est inquietius, & fuit per se causa pavorum, fugæ & indignationis adversus DEUM, & hæc ipsa consternatio est mors: ideò additum est: Ego autem mortuus sum, sicut ad Corinth. inquit, Aculeus mortis peccatum est, Potentia vero pec- cati Lex est. Et in hoc capite: Peccatum sit excel- lenter peccatum, id est, valde reum, hoc est, in ve- ris pavoribus & sensu iræ DEI cernitur aliquo mo- do peccati magnitudo, quam securi & ociofi homines leviter curant &c. Mortuus sum, inquit B. Wel- lerus, id est, sensi me mortis & damnationis reum. Conf. Gen. XX. 3. Num. XXXV. 3.

## 7:10
But I died.

Most men were dying in their vices, without any hope of a better life Heb. II. 15.

The Apostle is not speaking of Israelites stubbornly persisting in sins and dying in impenitence, but of himself and his own example, for others when sin revives in them, and the conscience is convinced. By death is understood not natural destruction, which is called the first death, but the terrors of eternal death, which arise from sin, and are a certain foretaste and prelude of the second death, which is eternal. Blessed Baldu. correctly expressed the sense p. 132. I was alive once (he says) without the law ver. 9. as if he were saying, when I was still a Pharisee, and had not correctly examined the law, because it also forbade the vicious interior affections of the heart, I seemed to myself to live beautifully, and to please God: but now I have died, that is, I am guilty of death and condemnation; and the commandment, which was for life, was found to be for me, that is, for death, that is, I finally understood the precepts of the law, in which, not yet having been correctly understood, I seemed to myself to have life and salvation, to produce death and damnation.

V. 10. And the commandment which was unto life was found by me.

The moral precepts of the law were a part of that obedience which is owed to God: and in that sense they did not indeed give that eternal life, but they led to it. See what we said at Matt. XIX. 17. εὑρέθη was discovered by the event itself.

this.

That very thing.

unto death.

Supply ἄγειν: by the event, of course: because, to be sure, the habit of sinning had grown so strong that it required greater remedies.

Latin:

ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον.

Homines plerique in vitiis suis moriebantur, sine ulla spe vitæ melioris Hebr. II. 15.

Non de Israëlitıs præfracte in peccatis perseve- rantibus & in impœnitentia decedentibus, sed de se & exemplo suo, aliis cum peccatum in iis revi- viscit, & conscientia convincitur, agit Apostolus. Per mortem intelligitur non naturalis interitus, quæ mors prima dicitur, sed terrores mortis æternæ, qui ex peccato oriuntur, & mortis secundæ, quæ æterna est, prægustus quidam sunt, & præludium. Sensum rectè expressit B. Baldu. p. 132. Ego vive- bam aliquando (inquit) fine lege vers. 9. quasi di- ceret, cum adhuc Pharisæus essem, nec rectè inspexis- sem legem, quod illa etiam interiores cordis affectûs vitiosos prohiberet, videbar mihi pulcrè vivere, Deoque placere: nunc autem mortuus sum, hoc est, mortis & condemnationis reus; & inventum est mihi mandatum, quod erat ad vitam, hoc esse, ad mortem, boc est, intellexi demum præcepta le- gis, in quibus nondum recte intellectis vitam & sa- lutem me habere mihi videbar, mortem & damna- tionem parere.

V. 10. καὶ εὑρέθη μοι ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωήν.

Erant præcepta legis moralia pars ejus obedientiæ, quæ Deo debetur : & eo sensu vitam illam æternam non dabant quidem, sed ad eam ducebant. Vide, quæ diximus Matth. XIX. 17. εὑρέθη deprehensa est ipso eventu.

αὕτη.

Illa ipsa.

εἰς θάνατον.

Supple ἄγειν : eventu scilicet : quia nimirum ita in- valuerat peccandi consuetudo, ut majoribus egeret re- mediis.

## 7:11
for sin.

That habit of drawing to itself the things of others under a certain appearance of right.

Vers. 11. having taken occasion through the commandment.

Having obtained impunity through that precept, to which no penalty is attached either in the Decalogue or elsewhere. See what we said at Matt. V. 20.

deceived me.

The precept is said to have done that to which it gave occasion. Men were deceived by the hope of obtaining impunity from God even after this life, in which they were miserably mistaken, just as many Jews are deceived now.

and through it killed.

It gave an occasion why men might not arrive at true justice, and consequently at heavenly life.

The previous depravations, enriched by others, recur. The law entirely promised life to those keeping it, Lev. XVIII. 6. Luke X. Gal. II. Therefore it is said here ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωήν. But because no one after the fall can keep it, it does not give life, and does not even lead to it: but it is a schoolmaster to Christ, the author of life. Therefore the law is found to be εἰς θάνατον unto death for us, not by its own fault, but by the vice of our depraved nature.
