Not only regarding those who have contracted a habit of sinning and of drawing to themselves the things of others under the appearance of right; but regarding all: because no one lives devoid of this depraved concupiscence, and of that evil adhering to us by nature, of which the Apostle complains. But how did sin deceive the Apostle, how does it deceive us? Not by the hope of impunity, received through the law: for from the habit of drawing to oneself the things of others under a certain appearance of right, no hope of impunity can even be presumed from the law, which could not even be hoped for in the forum of the earth, since such deceits are not rarely detected and laid open; much less in the forum of heaven: if indeed they can in no way escape or be hidden from God, the καρδιογνώστην. Sin therefore deceives, having taken occasion διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, not because the law of itself makes for deception, but because things forbidden by law are desired more, and thus men are deceived by those desires through their own fault, seduced by depraved concupiscence, and through the same (law) not only is an occasion given of killing and exclusion from heavenly life, but men are truly mortified, although not by the fault of the law, which of itself is unto life, and does not kill and mortify except by accident. But sin kills by working death and condemnation, which the law threatens, partly because, agitated by the terrors of conscience, we taste the punishment of death here, while it attempts to precipitate us into the abyss of despair, partly because it is also the cause of death itself, unless the grace of God comes to our aid. The Apostolic aphorism must be carefully noted here: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐξαπατᾷ, sin deceives. For it both entices us to obedience by its appearance, presenting itself under the guise of good and desirable, and when obedience is rendered to it, it will always find, either in itself or in the objects or in the subjects, a source from which it may attempt fraud. Therefore, this whole imposture ought deservedly to beget in us a hatred of sin. But the Apostle does not teach simply that the law is unto death, but it was found, he says, to be unto me unto death. Therefore he shows that the matter and proper cause of that effect resides in himself, not in the law. But concerning the law itself he says expressly: that the law was given unto life.

And furthermore: The law itself indeed is holy, and (in particular) the commandment (concerning not coveting) is holy, and just and good: so that the law itself may not be believed to be the cause of either deception or death. And therefore there is no need, as with Flacius, part I. Clavis under the word deceive, that we should take those things concerning deception only declaratively, that is, it declared me deceived. For as it is a question of the killing itself, not of its declaration, so also it is a question of the deception itself, and there is added here ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα, because it deceives only occasionally διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς; but the declaration of deception through the commandment or law does not happen only occasionally; but directly. It is everywhere properly attributed to sin, which was ascribed to the law only by accident. For it is sin, which, irritated by the precepts of the law, deceives man, so that he may consent to an evil thing, and yet imagine for himself some holiness, until at last, stripped of all defenses, and contaminated on all sides by sins, he feels nothing but the terrors of eternal death.

Latin:

ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία.

Illa consuetudo per speciem quandam juris ad se trahen- di res alienas.

Vers. 11. ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς.

Impunitatem nacta per illud præceptum, cui neque in Decalogo, neque alibi ulla pœna apposita est. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. V. 20.

ἐξηπάτησέ με.

Dicitur præceptum id fecisse, cui occasionem dedit. De- cepti homines fuere spe impunitatis etiam post hanc vitam à Deo consequendæ, in quo miserè fallebantur, ut & nunc falluntur multi Judæi.

καὶ δι᾽ αὐτῆς ἀπέκτεινεν.

Occasionem dedit, cur homines non pervenirent ad ve- ram justitiam, & consequenter ad vitam cœlestem.

Recurrunt priores depravationes aliis locuple- tatæ. Lex omninò vitam promittebat servanti- bus eam, Lev. XVIII. 6. Luc. X. Gal. II. Ideo di- citur hic ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωήν. Sed quia nemo post lapsum eam servare potest, vitam non dat, ac ne ducit quidem ad eam: sed pædagogus est ad Chri- stum vitæ auctorem. Deprehenditur ergo lex εἰς θάνατον ad mortem nobis esse, non suopte, sed na- turæ nostræ depravatæ vitio. Non quoad eos tantum, qui consuetudinem peccandi, & per spe- ciem juris ad se res alienas trahendi contraxere; sed quoad omnes: quia nemo expers vivit hujus pra- væ concupiscentiæ, & mali istius nobis naturâ ad- hærescentis, de quo conqueritur Apostolus. Quo- modo autem decepit Apostolum peccatum, quomo- do nos decipit? Non spe impunitatis, per legem ac- ceptâ: non enim de consuetudine per speciem quandam juris ad se trahendi res alienas aliqua impunitatis spes vel præsumi potest è lege, quæ ne quidem in foro soli sperari potuit, quum doli ta- les non rarò detegerentur & patefiant; nedum in foro poli: siquidem Deum καρδιογνώστην minimè fugiant, aut latere possint. Decipit ergo peccatum occasione acceptâ διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, non quod lex per se ad deceptionem faciat, sed quia lege vetita ma- gis desiderantur, adeoque illis desideriis decipiun- tur homines propriâ culpâ, seducti à prava concu- piscentia & per eandem (legem) non occasio tan- tum datur occisionis & exclusionis è vita cœlesti, sed vere mortificantur homines, licet non culpâ le- gis, quæ per se ad vitam est, nec nisi ex accidenti oc- cidit, & mortificat. Occidit autem peccatum mortem & condemnationem, quam lex minatur, operando, partim quà terroribus conscientiæ ex- agitati pœnam mortis hic prægustamus, dum in barathrum desperationis nos præcipitare cona- tur, partim quà causa etiam est ipsius mortis, nisi gratia Dei nobis subveniat. Notandus hic sedulò aphorismus Apostolicus: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐξαπατᾷ, pec- catum decipit. Nam & ad obsequium specie sua nos allicit, sub ratione boni & appetibilis sese si- stens, & cum obsequium ei præstatur, semper vel in se ipsa vel in objectis vel in subjectis inveniet, un- de fraudem intentet. Hæc ergo tota impostura odium peccati in nobis meritò parere debet. Non autem simpliciter Apostolus docet, legem esse ad mortem, sed reperta est, inquit, mihi ad mortem. Ergo in se, non in lege effectus istius materiam & causam propriam residere ostendit. De lege au- tem ipsâ expressè dicit: legem datam esse ad vitam.

Et porrò: Lex ipsa quidem sancta, & (in specie) præceptum (de non concupiscendo) sanctum, ac justum & bonum: ne vel deceptionis, vel mortis causa credatur ipsa lex. Ideoque non opus est, ut cum Flacio, part. I. Clavis voce decipere, illa de de- ceptione tantum declarativè accipiamus, id est, de- ceptum me declaravit. Ut enim de ipsâ occisione, non de ejusdem declaratione, ita & de ipsâ de- ceptione agitur, & additur hîc ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα, quod occasionaliter tantum decipiat διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς; at deceptionis declaratio per præceptum vel le- gem non fit occasionaliter tantùm; sed directè. Peccato ubique propriè tribuitur, quod legi per accidens tantum adscribebatur. Peccatum enim est, quod præceptionibus legis irritatum decipit hominem, ut consentiat in rem malam, & tamen sibi sanctitatem aliquam imaginetur, donec tan- dem omnibus præsidiis destitutus, peccatis autem undique contaminatus, nihil nisi mortis æternæ terrores persentiscat.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος. It commands nothing that is not right, even if it permits certain less perfect things. It has stopped the mouth of calumny, concerning which he had begun to treat above in 7.

καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ. Also that commandment, Thou shalt not covet.

ἁγία. It is holy, that is, agreeing with the will of God. Ps. XIX. 9. and Ps. CXIX.

καὶ δικαία. It demands nothing unjust.

and good. It is useful to all in itself.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος. Nihil præcipit, quod non rectum sit, etsi quædam mi- nùs perfecta permittat. Obstruxit os calumniæ, de qua age- re cœperat supra 7.

καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ. Etiam illud præceptum, Non concupisces.

ἁγία. Sanctum est, id est, Dei voluntati congruens. Ps. XIX. 9. & Ps. CXIX.

καὶ δικαία. Nihil iniqui exigit.

καὶ ἀγαθή. Utilis est omnibus per se.

## 7:13
Vers. 13. Did then that which is good become death to me? That is, the cause of sin, the same expression as above.

God forbid. Far be it that it should be called the cause of eternal death: Understand it as the cause in itself, for things that are causes by accident are improperly called causes, since they are rather certain occasions, and not given for that purpose, but seized upon.

but sin. Supply, was truly and in itself the cause of that death.

that sin might appear. φανῇ is the same as εὑρέθη, as in 2 Cor. XIII. 7. above VII. 10. and ἵνα is 'so that'. For the outcome is signified.

through that which is good. Construe with φανῇ, for by the law it is understood where sin goes.

working death. Bringing about death. An expression similar to that which is above IV. 15. φαίνεται and similar words love to be joined to participles, which the Latins translate by infinitives. Thus φαίνεται in Thucydides: φαίνομαι προθυμούμενος in Demosthenes: φαίνεται συνεωρακώς, φαίνεται ποιήσας in Plutarch's Numa. How can he hope for eternal life who knows that he remains in those things which God so severely forbids?

that sin might become exceedingly sinful. So that from this that habit of sinning becomes guilty in the highest degree. Ἁμαρτωλὸς signifies guilty: חטא 1 Kings I. 21. καθ' ὑπερβολὴν is used by Paul for 'exceedingly' 1 Cor. XII. 31. 2 Cor. I. 8. IV. 17. Gal. I. 13. It is the same as ὑπερεκπερισσῶς לאט Job XV. 11. That habit cannot be proven guilty more excellently than when it is shown not only to harm others for a time, but also to harm him in whose power it is to harm eternally.

through the commandment. Through which it is convinced that it is exceedingly displeasing to God.

The law is called holy by reason of its efficient and material cause: because it is from God, who is most holy, and is occupied with holy commanded objects; it is formally just, because it is an ἀπεικόνισμα of divine justice and a rule for our own; it is good by reason of its end: because it promises temporal and eternal goods. If it is holy and just, then it is not itself the cause of deception; if it is good, then it is not the cause of death and condemnation. And this is the Apostolic apology for the law. But because the Apostle had said that sin kills through the commandment, another doubt still arises: how can that which is good become, or be made, death or the cause of death? Which the Apostle denies, saying, God forbid! explaining how sin through the good, that is, the law, has worked death: not indeed that we should remain under death and condemnation, but that it might appear how great an evil sin is, inasmuch as it is sinning beyond measure through the law, that is, enormously evil and destructive, so that in this way the destruction is to be attributed not to the law, but to sin. It is not, therefore, only a matter of the habit of sinning, much less only of the habit of snatching away through fraud those things which belong to our neighbor: but it is a matter of sin commonly, and of that very depraved concupiscence itself: and how Grotius said that impunity was left to that habit not only in the Decalogue, but also elsewhere in the Scriptures, if the same thing brings with it the guilt of eternal death, by the force of the law and of Holy Scripture, which is certainly the most grievous of all punishments, and cannot consist with impunity. We see thus also that there is no need for those words φανῇ διὰ τῶ ἀγαθῶ to be drawn back, since they cohere excellently with the following participle, so that it may appear that sin through the good, that is, the law, works or begets death in me, and thus sin would become sinning in a greater measure through the commandment. It is an antanaclasis. But sin does not appear through the law only by reason of guilt and punishment, i.e., as most destructive, but also by reason of fault: because it offends God most greatly, and is contrary to divine justice, as B. Luther, Tom. IV, Jen. p. 532, has it, sin becomes sinning beyond measure, that is, it is shown that sin is truly as great as He is great who is offended by sin: whom, however, heaven and earth cannot contain.

PART III. σχετλιασική (Expostulatory). Exhibiting the Apostle's complaint concerning the power of depraved concupiscence.

Latin:

Vers. 13. τὸ οὖν ἀγαθὸν ἐμοὶ γέγονε θάνατος. Id est, causa peccati, eadem locutio, quæ supra.

μὴ γένοιτο. Absit, ut causa mortis æternæ dicatur: Intellige causam per se, nam per accidens causæ, impropriè causæ dicun- tur, cum occasiones quædam sint potius, nec in id datæ, sed arreptæ.

ἀλλὰ ἡ ἁμαρτία. Supple, fuit verè ac per se causa mortis illius.

ἵνα φανῇ ἡ ἁμαρτία. Idem φανῇ quod εὑρέθη, ut 2. Cor. XIII. 7. supra VII. 10. & ἵνα est ita ut. Significatur enim eventus.

διὰ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ. Construe cum φανῇ, per legem enim intelligitur, quo eat peccatum.

κατεργαζομένη θάνατον. Adducens mortem. Locutio similis ei, quæ supra IV. 15. φαίνεται & voces similes amant jungi participiis, quæ Latini per infinitiva vertunt. Sic φαίνεται apud Thucydidem: φαίνομαι προθυμούμενος apud Demosthenem: φαίνεται συ- τεωρακώς, φαίνεται ποιήσας apud Plutarchum Numa. Quo- modo vitam æternam sperare potest, qui norit se in eis ma- nere, quæ Deus tam severe vetat?

ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία. Ita ut hinc summoperè rea fiat illa peccandi consuetudo. Ἁμαρτωλὸς reum significat: חטא 1. Reg. I. 21. καθ' ὑπερ- βολὴν usitatum Paulo pro eximiè 1. Cor. XII. 31. 2. Cor. I. 8. IV. 17. Gal. I. 13. Idem est ὑπερεκπερισσῶς לאט Job. XV. 11. Non potest excellentius rea peragi ista consuetudo, quàm cùm ostenditur non aliis tantum ad tempus nocere, sed etiam ei penes quem est nocere æternum.

διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς. Per quam convincitur Deo summoperè displicere.

Sancta dicitur lex ratione causæ efficientis & ma- terialis: quia à Deo sanctissimo est, & circa ob- jecta præcepta sancta occupatur: justa est formali- ter, quia justitiæ divinæ ἀπεικόνισμα, nostræ re- gula est; bona est ratione finis: quia bona tempo- ralia & æterna promittit. Si sancta & justa, non ergo ipsa deceptionis causa: si bona, non ergò causa mortis, & condemnationis. Atque hæc apologia est legis Apostolicæ. Quia verò Apostolus dixe- rat, peccatum per præceptum occidere, dubium aliud adhuc suboritur: quomodo id, quod bonum factum sit, aut fiat mors, vel causa mortis? Quod in- ficiatur Apostolus, absit! explicans: quomodo pec- catum per bonum, id est, legem operatum sit mor- tem : non quidem, ut nos sub morte, & condemna- tione maneamus, sed ut appareat, quantum malum sit peccatum, utpote quod per legem sit supra modum peccans, id est, enormiter malum & exitiosum, ut ita non legi exitium, sed peccato tribuendum sit. Non ergo tantum de consuetudine peccandi, ne- dum tantum de consuetudine per fraudes ea, quæ proximi sunt, ad nos rapiendi : sed de peccato com- muniter, deque ipsa prava concupiscentia agitur : & quomodo impunitatem non solum in Decalogo, sed & alibi in Scripturis illi consuetudini relinqui dixit Grotius, si eadem reatum mortis æternæ in- fert, vi legis & Scripturæ S. quæ utique pœna omnium gravissima, cum impunitate consistere nequit. Videmus ita etiam opus non esse, ut ad verbum φανῇ illa διὰ τῶ ἀγαθῶ retrahantur, cum optimè cohæreant cum consequenti participio, ut appareat peccatum per bonum, id est, legem mihi operari vel gignere mortem, adeoq; fieret majorem in modum peccatum peccans per præceptum. Est antanaclasis. Non verò tantum peccatum ratio- ne reatus & pœnæ apparet per legem, h. e. exitiosum maximè, sed etiam ratione culpæ : quod maximè Deum offendat, & justitiæ divinæ contrarium sit, ut B. Luther. Tom. IV. Jen. p. 532. habet, fit pecca- tum supra modum peccans, id est, ostenditur pecca- tum verè tam magnum esse, quam magnus est, qui peccato offenditur : eum verò cœlum & terra capere non potest.

PARS III. σχετλιασική. Querelam Apostoli de vi pravæ concupiscentiæ exhibens.

## 7:14
Verse 14. οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός. He now shows the reason why something else follows in man from the law than that which the law has proposed by itself. The nature of the law, he says, is one thing: that of a great part of men is another. The law has proceeded from God, who is pure spirit and subject to no evil affections. John IV. 24. Also, dealing with human law, Aristotle, Politics III. 16, says that he who sets the law over things sets God himself over them, because the law is ἄνευ ὀρέξεως νῦς (reason without desire). Schemtob says that the law dwells in the mind.

ἐγὼ γὰρ σαρκικός εἰμι. That is, the greater part of the Jews is carried away by affections which arise from the flesh. Thus σαρκικαὶ ἐπιθυμίαι (fleshly lusts) 1 Pet. II. 11.

πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν. They are like Ahab, of whom Elijah predicts that in 1 Kings XXI. 20. Whence we also learn that this passive πεπραμένος has the force of a reciprocal. For in Hebrew it is the Hithpahel התמכרך לעשות הרע, you sold yourself to do evil: where in the Greek it is πέπρασαι ποιῆσαι τὸ πονηρὸν. That is, you delivered yourself: which very words you have taken from there also in 1 Macc. I. 17. It was permitted by Hebrew law to sell oneself into slavery. But because delivery with dominion follows from a sale, therefore the name of sale is used for those consequences, even where a sale has not intervened. Thus God is said to have sold the Israelites for their sins, Deut. XXXII. 30, and Judges ch. II. 14, III. 8, IV. 2. Thus also Isa. L. 1. So by a like metaphor the Latins say a man is enslaved to vices. What is 'to sell' here is called 'to take captive' below. For men become servants in two ways, by sale and by right of war: the effect is the same.

After he has vindicated the divine law, or taught that all the fault is to be ascribed to depraved concupiscence, the Apostle groans that he still experiences its power, even though he is already regenerate and justified; and this is because he is not yet entirely spiritual, but is still in part carnal, since although he has received the firstfruits of the Spirit, the remnants of the flesh still survive, by which he is wonderfully fatigued. This he executes laboriously, to confound and crush the perfection of one's own righteousness, which the Pharisees peddled, so that the praise may remain solely to the grace of God and the redemption of Christ, and justification be asserted for faith alone. Therefore, both a long lamentation concerning the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate, up to verse 23 inclusive, and a vigorous thanksgiving for the liberation wrought by Christ, are held here, v. 24. In that [passage] he first institutes a comparison between the spiritual law and his carnal self, v. 14, as if he were saying, the highest perfection of the law is the highest corruption of my nature. Therefore, there can be no perfect fulfillment of the law in me: then he establishes in himself diverse principles of acting; the flesh, which does that which the Spirit disapproves; and the Spirit, which disapproves and does not will, but hates, what he does according to the flesh, v. 15; he says that this [the Spirit] consents to the law, v. 16; he distinguishes the former [the flesh] from himself, as sin dwelling within, and the subject in which it dwells, and as not working that which he does not will, nor approve, namely. ἑκουσίως voluntarily from that which works it in him by dwelling in him, v. 17, for which he further complains of his own ἀδυναμίᾳ (weakness), that the willing indeed is present with him, but not the doing, v. 18, 19, which, however, he says is not done by him, but by the indwelling sin, v. 19; furthermore, he also complains particularly of this, that when he wills to do good, evil is joined to him, παρακείμενον (lying near), which hinders it, v. 21; that when he delights in the law of God according to the inward man, he sees another law in his members, rebelling against the law of his mind and rendering him captive to the law of sin which is in his members; because of these, therefore, such diverse, nay, altogether mutually adverse principles, spirit and flesh, inward and outward man, law of the mind and law of the members, he not only acknowledges and groans that his own righteousness is very imperfect and subject to many impurities, but also sighs under that misery, wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from this body of this death? But collecting himself in spirit, he at the same time gives thanks to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, because we have been liberated through the same not only regarding the guilt of condemnation, because there is no κατάκριμα in us, who receive and embrace him as Jesus, and Christ and our Lord with true faith, but also regarding the dominion of sin, because they serve the law of God with their mind even if they still serve the law of sin with their flesh: because they have not been renewed ὁλικῶς and perfectly, but μερικῶς and in part, until we are fully liberated from the body of this death. From which it is most clear that the discourse is about the reborn, as one in whom flesh and spirit have their place, and who enjoys the liberation made through Christ by faith, and gives thanks to God with a devoted mind. Therefore he does not teach that the nature of the law is one thing and that of a great part of men is another, but he compares himself, as still in part carnal, with the law which is entirely spiritual. For the law is spiritual not only by reason of the efficient cause, because it is from God, but also by reason of the material cause, because it demands spiritual obedience, not only exterior but interior, not only of the members but also of the heart and spirit; and formal: because it is a doctrine not of political or carnal wisdom, but spiritual: and also by reason of the final cause, because it ought to make us spiritual, as far as its proper end is concerned, even if by our fault it does not attain it, and it promises spiritual and heavenly goods to those who perform obedience. Grotius therefore does violence to the text by taking it as referring to the greater part of the Jews carried away by their affections: those things which Paul affirms of himself and by his example of other reborn persons. Nor indeed is he so σαρκικὸς as the unregenerate in John 3:5, in which way also οἱ νήπιοι ἐν χριστῶ are called σαρκικοί 1. Cor. 3:1, and therefore he calls himself carnal, not only by reason of conception and birth, Ps. 51:7, Col. 3:6, but by reason of the remnants of the flesh and the adhering viciousness, since in the Saints flesh and spirit have their place entirely, as Christ testifies in Matt. 26:41, and the Apostle in Gal. 5:17. For regeneration does not abolish flesh and blood, but adds grace and spirit to them, which may correct what is vicious and gradually according to the measure of grace may perfect each one, says B. Mylius here. Let us also hear Philip on this passage: But I am carnal, etc. He (the Apostle) himself interprets what he calls the carnal nature, namely, the whole man, sold under sin, that is, a slave of sin and death, just as this antithesis is illustrated below: The mind of the flesh is death. Likewise, it is enmity against God, etc. But by the name of Spirit is understood the Holy Spirit Himself and the corresponding motions in the saints kindled by the Holy Spirit, life, light, and joy resting in God, the flame of love toward God; thus, conversely, the flesh and the mind of the flesh are to be understood as the whole unregenerate man. Not only in the appetite of the senses and in the heart is there contumacy against God, namely, unjust fires of loves, hatreds, and vengeance, but also in the higher part, namely, in the intellect of the unregenerate man, there is darkness and a great chaos of doubts about God, and the will is without fear, without love of God, without joy resting in God, either despising God or fleeing Him with horrible trembling, and is without God who gives life, gives joy, and governs. Such a man without God is called flesh according to all the powers of the soul. These are the words of Philip, who still understands these things as concerning the state of sin, but he accepts those things which follow further in the complaint of Paul as concerning the state of regeneration. For thus he proceeds to this passage: But first Paul narrates what the carnal nature is according to itself, because he says: I am sold under sin, that is, snatched into slavery, for the phrase is taken from captives who were sold and were slaves. Thus, he says, the carnal nature according to itself is a slave of sin and death, and can neither put off depravity and death, nor draw back justice and life by itself, but the Son of God regenerates man by the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit. Although the beginnings of new light and spiritual motions are kindled in the regenerate, yet in this mortal life the remnants of the former disease still cling to the carnal nature: therefore a struggle follows, in which the Word and the Holy Spirit mortify those remnants; Paul describes this struggle shortly. But when he uses the word, Sold, he looks to the saying of Isaiah 52: You were sold for nothing, you have been redeemed without silver. Where God objects to the devil the injustice, as if he were to say: I will act in a just order. The devil snatched you from me by fraud, and neither paid me a price, nor gave you promises. It is just, therefore, in turn, that I recover my property, without a price given to the robber. For just as a thing is not to be bought back from a thief or robber, but is restored to the Lord without a price by a just judge: So God recovers the human race, paying nothing to the unjust and wicked robber, the Devil. He said, therefore, You were sold for nothing, that is, you were unjustly dragged into slavery by the fraud of the devil, and neither was a price paid to God nor were promises given to men. Therefore, you are redeemed again for nothing; I will not give a price to the devil, and I will receive you by my mercy, since you cannot give me a price. Thus far again Philip. But it seems more appropriate that these things also: I am carnal, sold under sin, because they cohere in the Apostolic complaint, refer to the Apostle expressing the state of those regenerate in himself. For which reason the Apostle indeed calls himself πεπραμένον ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν with a similar phrase to that by which Ahab is said to be sold to sin, 1 Kings 21:20. The words of the Apostle, however, are to be accepted with a qualification: namely, regarding the flesh and congenital concupiscence, if you look at its power and effort, because he uses a prosopopoeia, which, as much as is in itself, wishes to enslave him entirely to itself, just as those who are sold to someone are his slaves entirely: and it wishes to captivate him thoroughly under its obedience, v. 23. And there is, moreover, not in vain the Hithpael form used concerning Ahab, you sold yourself to serve evils, which is not found here, but the simple passive πεπραμένος, I am sold: furthermore, there he is said to be sold to sin before the Lord, which is wont to be said of voluntary sins, and those committed with a high hand before the Lord, or crying out to heaven. Cf. Gen. 18, 2 Kings 17:17, which cannot be said of this subject, who groans under sin, and deplores that misery, and seeks to be liberated. And therefore we see that Grotius has played very badly with the Socinians who snatch such passages to this place, against whom it was dealt with in the Theological Apostolic Romans. It only hints at this in this passage with that phrase: just as a buyer has a right to a sold thing, so he is not yet entirely exempted from the power of sin. And the Apostle himself explains in the following what he had said about his own sale: For just as slaves and purchased servants are dragged where they do not want, and are slaves who are forced to live for another's will, so the Apostle testifies that he is snatched by innate depravity, from which he himself nevertheless abhors. He indicates, therefore, that he is not entirely exempted from the right of sin, but confesses that he sometimes feels the goads of sin, which attempt to enslave him to sin, having snatched him from the good, although they cannot bring that into effect.

Latin:

Vers. 14. οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός. Ostendit jam causam, cur ex lege aliud in hominem con- sequatur, quam id, quod per se lex propositum habet. Alia, inquit, natura est legis : alia magnæ partis hominum. Lex à Deo profecta est, qui est spiritus purus nullisque malis af- fectibus obnoxius. Johan. IV. 24. Etiam de humana lege agens Aristoteles Politicorum III. 16. ait eum, qui legem præficit rebus, Deum ipsum præficere, quia lex sit ἄνευ ὀρέξεως νῦς. Legem in mente habitare ait Schemtob.

ἐγὼ γὰρ σαρκικός εἰμι. Id est, major pars Judæorum affectibus abripitur, qui ex carne oriuntur. Sic σαρκικαὶ ἐπιθυμίαι 1. Pet. II. 11.

πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν. Similes sunt Achabo, de quo Elias id prædicat 1. Reg. XXI. 20. Unde etiam discimus, passivum hoc πεπραμένος habere vim reciproci. Nam sibi in Hebræo est Hithpahel התמכרך לעשות הרע vendidisti te ad malè agendum: ubi in Græco πέπρασαι ποιῆσαι τὸ πονηρὸν. Id est, tradidisti te : quæ ipsa verba inde desumpta habes & 1. Macc. I. 17. Li- cebat jure Hebræo semet in servitutem vendere. Quia verò ex venditione sequitur traditio cum dominio, ideò vendi- tionis nomen pro illis consequentibus usurpatur, etiam ubi venditio non intercessit. Sic Deus dicitur Israëlitas ob pec- cata vendidisse inimicis Deuteron. XXXII. 30. & Judicum cap. II. 14. III. 8. IV. 2. Sic & Esa. L. 1. Sic pari tralatione hominem mancipatum vitiis dicunt Latini. Quod hic est vendere, infra dicitur αἰχμαλωτίζειν. Servi enim fiunt duo- bus modis, venditione, & belli jure : effectus idem.

Postquam legem divinam vindicavit, vel pravæ concupiscentiæ omnem culpam transcribendam docuit, ejus vim sese etiamnum experiri, inge- miscit Apostolus, etiamsi renatus jam sit, & justifi- catus; idque ideo, quia nondum ex asse spiritualis, sed ex parte adhuc carnalis est, quum Spiritus qui- dem primitias acceperit, sed carnis adhuc reliquiæ superent, à quibus mirum quantum fatigetur. Id quod operosè exequitur, ad confundendam & contundendam perfectionem propriæ justitiæ, quam venditabant Pharisæi, ut unicè laus ma- neat gratiæ Dei, & redemptioni Christi, soliusque fidei adseratur justificatio. Ideò tum de concu- piscentia in renatis reliqua prolixa lamentatio, ad vers. 23. inclus. tum pro liberatione a Christo facta nervosa gratiarum actio hic habetur v. 24. In illa primum inter legem spiritualem, & se carnalem comparationem instituit v. 14. q. dicat, summa le- gis perfectio est, summa naturae meae corruptio. Ergo nulla esse in me potest perfecta legis impletio: tum in se diversa agendi principia constituit; carnem, quae hoc agit, quod improbat Spiritus; & Spiritum, qui reprobat nec vult, sed odit, quod agit secundum carnem v. 15. hunc legi consentire ait v. 16. illam a se distinguit, ceu peccatum inhabitans, & subjectum, in quo id habitat, & tanquam non operans illud, quod non vult, nec probat scil. ἑκουσίως voluntarie ab eo, quod in se habitando id operatur v. 17. ob quod por- ro de sua ἀδυναμίᾳ queritur, quod velle quidem sibi adsit, non autem facere v. 18. 19. quod tamen non se, sed inhabitans peccatum facere ait v. 19. insuper de eo peculiariter etiam queritur, quod sibi, bonum facere volenti malum adjunctum sit, παρακείμενον quod id impediat v. 21. quod cum delectatur lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem, aliam lege in mem- bris suis videat, legi mentis suae rebellante & se capti- vum reddentem legi peccati, quae in membris suis est, ob haec ergo tam diversa, imo sibi invicem prorsus adversa principia spiritum & carnem, interiorem & exteriorem hominem, legem mentis & legem mem- brorum non modo valde imperfectam esse justitiam propriam, multisque impuritatibus obnoxiam agnoscit & gemit, sed etiam sub illa miseria suspi- rat, miser ego homo! quis me liberat ex hoc corpore mortis hujus? Sed recolligens se spiritu, gratias si- mul agit Deo, per Jesum Christum Dominum no- strum, quod liberati per eundem simus non modo quoad reatum condemnationis, quod nullum in nobis sit κατάκριμα, qui eum ceu Jesum, & Christu ac Dominum nostrum vera fide suscipimus, & am- plectimur, sed etiam quoad peccati dominiu, quod mente servant legi Dei etsi adhuc carne legi peccati serviant: quia renovati non sunt ὁλικῶς & perfecte, sed μερικῶς & ex parte, donec plene a corpore mor- tis hujus liberemur. E quibus luculentissimum est, quod de renato sermo sit, utpote in quo caro & spiritus suum locum habent, quique liberatione per Christum facta per fidem fruitur, ac Deo de- vota mente gratias agit. Non ergo aliam naturam esse legis, aliam magnae partis hominu esse docet, sed se ceu ex parte adhuc carnalem cum lege prorsus spirituali componit. Spiritualis enim est lex non tantum ratione causae efficientis, quia a Deo est, sed etiam ratione causae materialis, quia spirituale obse- quium, non exteriorem solum, sed interiorem, non membrorum tantum, sed etiam cordis & spiritus obedientiam postulat; & formalis: quia doctrina non politica aut carnalis sapientiae, sed spiritualis esse: nec non ratione finalis causae, quia nos spiri- tuales efficere, quantum ad finem proprium debe- bat etsi vitio nostro eum non assequatur, & spiritua- lia ac caelestia bona promittit, obedientiam prae- stantibus. Vim itaque textui facit Grotius, de ma- jori parte Judaeorum affectibus abrepta accipi: eas, quae Paulus de se & exemplo suo aliis renatis affir- mat. Neque vero ita σαρκικὸς est, uti non renati Joh. III. 5. quomodo etia οἱ νήπιοι ἐν χριστῶ σαρκι- κοὶ dicuntur 1. Cor. III. 1. ideoq; vocat se carnalem, non tantum ratione conceptionis & nativitatis, Ps. LI. 7. Col. III. 6. quam ratione reliquiarum car- nis & adhaerentis vitiositatis, quum in Sanctis caro & spiritus omnino locum habeant teste Christo Matth. XXVI. 41. & Apostolo Gal. V. 17. Non enim carnem & sanguinem regeneratio abolet, sed gratiam & spiritum eis adjungit, qui quod vitiosum est emen- det, & paulatim pro modulo gratiæ unumquemque perficiat, ait hîc B. Mylius. Audiamus etiam de hoc loco Philippum: Ego autem carnalis sum &c. In- terpretatur ipse (Apostolus) quid nominet carnalem naturam, scilicet, totum hominem, venundatum sub peccatum, id est, servum peccati & mortis, sicut & infra hæc antithesis illustratur: Sensus carnis mors est. Item, inimicitia est adversus Deum &c. Ille au- tem appellatione Spiritus intelligitur ipse Spiritus S. & à Spiritu S. accensi congruentes motus in sanctis, vita, lux, & lætitia acquiescens in Deo flamma dile- ctionis erga Deum, sic è regione caro & sensus carnis intelligantur, de toto homine non renato. Non solùm in appetitu sensuum & in corde est contumacia con- tra Deum, videlicet, injusta incendia amorum, odio- rum, vindictæ sed etiam in superiore parte, videlicet, in intellectu hominis non renati, sunt tenebræ & m magnum chaos dubitationum de Deo, & voluntas est sine timore, sine dilectione Dei, sine lætitia acquiescen- te in Deo, aut contemnens Deum, aut horribili fre- mitu fugiens eum, & est sine Deo vivificante, lætifi- cante, & gubernante. Talis homo sine Deo dicitur caro secundum omnes animæ potentias. Hæc Philip- pus, qui hæc adhuc intelligit de statu peccati, ea ve- rò, quæ in querela Pauli porrò sequuntur de statu regenerationis accipit. Ita enim pergit ad h. l. Primum autem narrat Paulus, qualis sit natura car- nalis secundum sese, quia inquit: Venundatus sum sub peccatũ, id est, raptus in servitutem, phrasis enim sumpta est à captivis, qui vendebantur & erant ser- vi. Ita, inquit, naturam carnalem secundum sese ser- vam peccati & mortis esse, nec posse deponere pravita- tem & mortem, nec retrahere per sese justitiam & vitam, sed Filius Dei voce Evangelii & Spiritu S. regenerat hominem. Quanquam autem initia novæ lucis & motuum spiritualium in renatis accendun- tur, tamen in hac mortali vita hærent adhuc in na- tura carnali reliquiæ prioris morbi: Sequitur ergò lucta, in qua verbum & Spiritus S. mortificant reli- quias illas, hanc luctam mox describit Paulus. Cum autem utitur vocabulo, Venundatus, intuetur dictum Esaiæ LII. Gratis venundati estis, sine argento redi- memini. Ubi Deus objicit diabolo injustitiam, quasi dicat: Agam justo ordine. Diabolus vos fraude mihi eripuit, & neœ, mihi solvit pretium, neœ, vobis dedit promissa. Justum est igitur vicissim, me rem meam recuperare, non dato pretio prædoni. Sicut enim à fure aut prædone res non rursus emenda est, sed sine pretio per judicem justum restituitur Domi- no: Ita Deus recuperat genus humanum, nihil sol- vens injusto & scelerato prædoni Diabolo. Dixit igitur, Gratis venundati estis, id est, injustè in servi- tutem pertracti estis fraude diaboli, nec Deo solutum est pretium neque hominibus data promissa. Rur- sus igitur gratis redimemini, non dabo pretium dia- bolo, & vos recipiam mea misericordia, cum mihi pretium non possitis dare. Hactenus iterum Phi- lippus. Sed convenientius videtur etiam hæc: Car- nalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum, quia cohærent in querela Apostolica, ad Apostolum in se renato- rum statum exprimentem referre. Quapropter se quidem πεπραμένον dicit Apostolus ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρ- τίαν phrasi simili, quà Achabus venundatus dicitur ad peccatum 1. Reg. XXI. 20. Apostoli tamen ver- ba secundum quid accipienda: nempè quoad carnẽ & concupiscentiam congenitam, si ejus vim & cona- tum, quia Prosopopœia utitur, respicias, quæ quan- tum in ipsa est, eum sibi mancipare totum vult, uti qui alicui venundati sunt, mancipia ejus prorsus sunt: & captivare ipsum penitus vult sub obse- quium suum v. 23. Estque præterea non frustra de Achabo forma Hithpaelica adhibita temetipsum vendidisti ad serviendum malis, quæ hic non repe- ritur, sed passivi simplicis πεπραμένος venditus sum: adhæc ibi venundatus ad peccandum coram Domi- no dicitur, quod de peccatis voluntariis, & elato q. brachio patratis coram Domino comparentibus, vel in cœlum clamantibus dici solet. Conf. Ge- nef. XVIII. 2. Reg. XVII. 17. quale quid de hoc sub- jecto, quod sub peccato gemit, eamq; miseriam de- plorat, & liberari expetit, dici non potest. Ideoq; pessimè cum Socinianis talia loca huc abripienti- bus hic collusisse Grotium videmus, adversus quos in Theol. Apost. Rom. actum fuit. Id tantum innuit h. l. ista phrasi: quemadmodum jus est emptori in rem venditam, ita se potestati peccati nondum planè exem- ptum esse. Et explicat in seqq. Apostolus ipse, quod de sua venditione dixerat: Nam quemadmodum mancipia, & servi emptitii trahuntur, quo nolunt, & servi sunt, qui alienæ voluntati vivere coguntur, ita Apostolus rapi se testatur ab innata pravitate, unde ipse etiam nihilominus abhorreat. A jure er- gò peccati se non omninò exemptum esse indicat, sed stimulos peccati se interdum etiam sentire fa- tetur, qui ipsum à bono abreptum peccato manci- pare conantur, licet id in effectum dare nequeant.

## 7:15
Verse 15. For what I work, I do not know.) That is, I do not approve. For thus the Hebrews take ידע, Isa. 1:6, Hos. 8:4, and the Hellenists γινώσκειν, Sir. 18:26, Matt. 7:23, where we have brought forward other passages. Such is Medea in Euripides: And I understand indeed what evils I am about to do. But passion is stronger than my counsels. And in Ovid: - - I see better things and approve them, I follow the worse. And Laius in the Tragedy: Nothing of those things which you advise me has escaped me. But nature forces me, though I have the judgment. Which Greek passages Clement brings forward for this matter in Stromata II. Plutarch, correcting that from the tragedy Atreus: Alas, alas, this is already a divine evil for men, when someone knows the good, but does not use it. He says: It is beastly and irrational, and pitiful to know the better, and to be led by the worse through incontinence and weakness. He rightly says: through incontinence. For there are many more incontinent than intemperate. And men are described here from the greater part of themselves. See what we have said at Matt. 13:9. In this passage γινώσκειν, which in those things which we have brought forward is μανθάνειν, μὴ λεληθέναι, εἰδέναι, γνώμην ἔχειν. Paul in Trinummus, I was not able to do, wretch, as it would have been fitting for me to be a scribe.

Medea has nothing to do with this, nor whatever Grotius has collected here from the Gentiles; for it is not a struggle of the sensitive appetite against the intellectual, or a contention of reason and will, which the unregenerate experience when they choose and follow things they do not approve of in their mind, carried away by the affections of the will: but the struggle of the spirit and the flesh, which has no place except in the regenerate, is discussed here: which is sufficiently evident from the example of the Apostle, provided he is speaking of himself. Moreover, B. Balduinus not badly notes that that οὐ γινώσκω I do not understand can be taken either of sense, so that the intellect is accused because it does not know its sins so exactly, many of which are hidden, just as he teaches that many things happen to him against his will; or of affection, so that the depravity of the flesh is accused because it performs those things which he himself does not approve.

For what I will, this I do.) You may rightly translate θέλω potentially, as what I would will, according to those things which we said at Matt. XXVI. 39, although it can also be taken in the indicative, provided you know that it is not a matter here of a certain constitution and decree of the will, but of a light desire. Both the mind and carnal affections act upon the volitional, but the latter, as being closer to the executive, act more strongly, while the mind acts more languidly, unless aided by great supports. Arrian in the second book of the Epictetean discourses has a passage similar to this: for since he who sins does not will to sin, but to do right, it is clear that what he wills he does not do, and what he does not will he does.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι ὐ γινώσκω.) Id est, non ap- probo. Nam sic ידע sumunt Hebræi, Ef. I. 6. Os. VIII. 4. & Hellenistæ γινώσκειν Sir. XVIII. 26. Matth. VII. 23. ubi alia loca attulimus. Talis est Medea apud Euripidem: Καὶ μανθάνω μὲν οἷ̓ δρᾶν μέλλω κακά. Θυμὸς δὲ χρείσσων τῶν ἐμῶν βελευμάτων. Et apud Ovidium: - - Vldeo meliora proboque Deteriora sequor. Et Lajus in Tragœdia: Λέληθεν ὐδὲν τῶν δὲ μ᾽ ὧν σὺ νεθετεῖς. Γνώμην δ᾽ ἔχοντα μ᾽ ἡ φύσις βιάζεται. Quæ Græca loca ad hanc rem adducit Clemens Stroma- tum II. Plutarchus corrigens illud ex Tragœdia Atreo: Αἶ αἶ τοδ᾽ ἤδη θεῖον ἀνθρώποις κακὸν, Ὄταν τις εἰδῇ τ᾽ ἀγαθὸν, χρῆται δὲ μή. Ait: θηριῶδες μενῦν καὶ ἄλογον, καὶ οἰκτρὸν εἰδότα τὸ βέλτιον, ὑπὸ τῦ χείρονος ὑπ᾽ ἀκρασίας, κὶ μαλακίας ἄγεσθαι. Rectè ait: ἐξ ἀκρασίας. Multò enim plures sunt ἀκρατεῖς quam ἀκόλαστοι. Et describuntur hic homines ex majore sui parte. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. XIII. 9. In hoc loco γινώσκειν, quod in illis, quæ attulimus μανθάνειν, μὴ λεληθέναι, εἰδέναι, γνώμην ἔχειν. Paulus Trinummo, scribam ut esse me deceret, facere non quibam miser.

Nihil huc Medea facit, aut quicquid hic gemi- num è gentilibus collegit Grotius; Non enim de appetitus sensitivi adversus intellectualem pugna, vel de rationis, & voluntatis contentione, quam non re- nati experiuntur, cum ea, quæ non probant men- te, eligunt tamen, & sequuntur voluntatis affecti- bus abrepti: sed pugna spiritus & carnis, quæ non locum habet, nisi in renatis, hic disseritur: quod exemplo Apostoli satis constat, siquidem de semet- ipso loquatur. Illud autem ὐ γινώσκω non intelligo non malè notat B. Balduinus accipi posse vel de sensu, ut accusetur intellectus, quod tam exactè non cognoscat peccata, quorum multa occulta, quemadmodũ multa sibi contra voluntatẽ contin- gere docet; vel de affectu, ut accusetur carnis pra- vitas, quod ea operetur, quæ ipse non approbat.

ὃ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τῦτο πράσσω.) Θέλω rectè vertas potentia- liter, quod vellem, secundum ea, quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 39. quanquam & in indicativo sumi potest, dum no- ris non agi hic de certa constitutione decretoque voluntatis, sed de levi desiderio. Agunt εἰς τὸ θελητικὸν & mens & car- nales affectus, sed hi ut propiores τῷ τελεστικῷ, agunt vali- dius, at mens languidius, nisi magnis adjuta præsidiis. Ar- rianus Epicteteorum secundo locum habet huic similem: ἐπεὶ γὰρ ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ὐ θέλει ἁμαρτάνειν, ἀλλὰ κατορθῶσαι, δῆ- λον ὅτι ὃ μὲν θέλει ὐ ποιεῖ, καὶ ὃ μὴ θέλει ποιεῖ.

## 7:16
Vers. 16. But what I hate, this I do.) Understand μισῶ just like θέλω just now, concerning a certain sudden and easily vanishing motion.

But if what I do not will, this I do) Since indeed I do those things which I would not will to do.

I agree with the law that it is good. As those of whom the Satirist says: Let them see virtue and pine away that they have abandoned it. σύμφημι means I assent, even to Sophocles and Euripides. But then to the Hebrews to say is to think.

The Apostle is not dealing with a light desire of the will, but teaches that he wills seriously and vehemently according to the spirit, which he does not do because of the fault of the flesh: because this willing is joined with that consent of the law and the approval of those things which the law requires, and with hatred of the contrary, which hatred Grotius would wrongly have understood as a certain sudden and easily vanishing motion, because the Apostle indicates a grave and serious hatred of sin, which is accompanied by abomination and detestation. This is a conclusion, as the blessed Mylius observes; for thus the Apostle gathers: If we ourselves, in the part in which we are reborn, do not approve of sin, much less can the perpetration of sin be imputed to the law, or the law be accused of some vice. To whom then is it to be imputed here? Since it ought to be ascribed neither to the person himself who is reborn, nor to the law, it remains that it be attributed to innate depravity. Which the Apostle now further explains.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἀλλ᾽ ὃ μισῶ, τῦτο ποιῶ.) Intellige μισῶ sicut modo θέλω, de motu quodam subitaneo & facile evane- scente.

εἰ δὲ ὃ ὐ θέλω τῦτο ποιῶ) Quando quidem ea facio, quæ facere nollem.

σύμφημι τῷ νόμῳ ὅτι καλὸς.) Ut illi, de quibus Saty- ricus: Virtutem videant intabescantque relicta. σύμφημι est assentior, etiam Sophocli & Euripidi. Tum verò Hebræis dicere est, cogitare.

Non de levi desiderio voluntatis agit Apostolus, sed serio & vehementer se velle secundum spiri- tum, quod non agit ob carnis vitium, docet: quia hoc velle junctum est cum consensu illo legis & approbatione eorum, quæ lex requirit, & cum odio contrarii, quod proindè odium malè Grotius de motu quodam subitaneo & facilè evanescente intellectum velit, quia Apostolus odium peccati grave ac serium, quod est cum abominatione & detestatione, indicat. Συμπέρασμα hoc est, obser- vante B. Mylio; Sic enim colligit Apostolus: Si ne nos ipsi qua parte renati sumus, peccatum ap- probamus, multò minùs legi perpetratio peccati imputari, aut illa vitii cujusdam insimulari potest. Cui ergo hic imputandum? quum nec ipsi, qui re- natus est, nec legi adscribi debeat, superest, ut id innatæ pravitati tribuatur. Quod nunc porrò ex- plicat Apostolus.

## 7:17
Verse 17. But now it is no longer I that do this. Now therefore, that is, after the law has been given, the man, that is to say the whole man, no longer does evil. For there is something in man that resists: what this is, he will now explain.

The particle now is not here a distinction of time, as if he were now speaking of those who lived after the law was given, and previously of those who acted before the law, as Grotius foolishly and perversely claims: but it is illative: because he is dealing with one subject, not with different ones: and there is no trace of a distinction of times or subjects: and as he hints here, with Grotius agreeing, that the whole man does not do evil, so he had also indicated this in the preceding passages: namely, that he does not will what he does, but holds it in hatred, that he consents rather to the law of God in his mind, even if he is carried away by the affections and evil concupiscence, so that he acts against the law. Therefore, a distinction of times, before and after the law, has no place here. Nor is it to be ascribed to the law that man does not do evil in his entirety, or that there is something in man that resists, namely the inner man, and the law of the mind consenting to the law of God. For it is necessary to attribute renewal not to the law, but to the grace of God in Christ. The Apostle here distinguishes himself into two parts, and that by reason of the same time: because at the same time he attributes to himself both the not willing and the working, and denies of himself that he works evil, and testifies of that which is in him, that it works it: he teaches therefore that he both works and does not work it in one respect and another. Namely, he denies that he works evil, because he does not work it as a whole; for in the part in which he was reborn, he wholly abhorred that which the remaining part of him nevertheless designated: by which means he shows that the operation of evil is not his own any longer, but is to be held as clearly belonging to another. Thus far, therefore, having championed the law, he had transferred all the blame of evil onto himself, whose corruption was such that what he did not will, he did, and what he willed, he omitted. Lest anyone should take this as said in such a way as if the Apostle left no place for the spirit and the regeneration of the faithful, he again uses a translation which champions his own cause and that of all the regenerate, both by way of negation, denying that he is the operator of that evil of which he complains, and by way of affirmation, attributing the designation of that evil to sin.

But the sin that dwells in me. That long-ingrained habit of sinning, which we have shown is also called nature from Evenus and others in Book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis XII. 26. But the verb to dwell is well added to this habit, as also below in 18 and 20; wickedness does not lodge with them, but dwells, to imitate Seneca. But on the contrary, the Holy Spirit dwells in those who are cleansed, Rom. VIII. 9, 1 Cor. III. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 17. νυνὶ dὲ ὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι τῦτο.) Nunc er- go, id est, post legem datam, non amplius homo, totus scili- cet, malè agit. Est enim aliquid in homine, quod repugnat: quod quid sit, jam explicabit.

Particula νυνὶ non est hic distinctiva temporis, quasi jam loquatur de iis, qui post legem datam vixere, antea de iis, qui ante legem egerint, ut ineptit & pervertit Grotius: sed est illativa: quia de uno subjecto, non de diversis agit: & nullum est distinctionis temporum vel subjectorum vesti- gium: & ut hic innuit, Grotio annuente, non to- tum hominem malè agere, ita etiam in antecedenti- bus id indicarat: dum sc. se non velle, sed odio habere quod facit, se consentire potius legi Dei in mente sua, etsi abripiatur ab affectibus & pravâ concupiscen- tiâ, ut contra legem agat. Non ergò hic distinctio temporum locum habet, ante, & post legem. Neque etiam legi hoc adscribendum, quod homo non totus malè agat, vel quod in homine sit, quod repugnet, homo sc. interior, & lex mentis legi Dei consentiens. Nam renovationem non legi, sed gratiæ Dei in Chri- sto acceptam ferre oportet. Distinguit autem hic Apostolus semetipsum in duas q. partes, idq; ratio- ne ejusdem temporis: quia eodem tempore, sibi ipsi & τὸ non velle, & τὸ operari tribuit, & de se negat, quod malum operetur, & de eo, quod in se est, testa- tur, quod illud id operetur: Se ergo κατ' ἄλλο, καὶ ἄλλο id & operari & non operari docet. Nimirum negat se operari malum, quia non operatur totus; Nam quâ parte renatus erat, totus abhorrebat ab eo, quod reliqua tamen sui parte designabant: quo pacto nequidem operationem mali suam esse amplius, sed pro aliena planè habendam ostendit. Hactenus ergo legi patrocinatus culpam mali omnem in se transtulerat, cujus ea esset corruptio, ut quod nollet, faceret, quod vellet, omitteret. Quod ne quis ita dictum acciperet, quasi nihil spi- ritui & regenerationi fidelium loci relinqueret Apostolus, rursus translatione utitur, quæ suæ re- generatorumq; omnium causæ patrocinatur, cùm κατ' ἄρσιν negando se mali illius, de quo conqueri- tur, operatorem esse, tum κατὰ θέσιν, peccato acce- ptam referendo mali istius designationem.

ἀλλ' ἡ οἰκῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία.) Inolita illa pridem pec- candi consuetudo, quam & naturam dici ex Eveno & aliis ostendimus lib. II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XII. 26. Benè au- tem huic consuetudini additur verbum οἰκεῖν, ut & infra 18. 20. non divertit apud illos nequitia, sed habitat, ut Senecam imitemur. Sed contra in emundatis habitat Spiritus San- ctus, Rom. VIII. 9. 1. Cor. III. 16.

## 7:18
Verse 18. For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good. When man is named, sometimes the whole is understood, sometimes the name is attributed to the parts by synecdoche. Thus, what he said here, in me, he interprets concerning the flesh and the affections arising from the flesh. In these there was hardly anything of good, although in the mind there was some knowledge of good, as he will now say more fully. But in Christians, such as most were in those first times, even the affections themselves were corrected through faith and the Spirit, and the body itself was a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. VI. 19, no less than the Temple was once the dwelling place of the divine Majesty. We rightly say that flesh also includes the affections: indeed, it is often taken for those alone, as 1 Cor. V. 5. Tertullian in his book On Modesty explains this passage thus: For even if he denied that good dwells in his flesh, it was according to the law of the letter, in which he was: but according to the law of the Spirit, to which he attaches us, he frees us from the infirmity of the flesh: for the law, he says, of the Spirit of life has manumitted you from the law of delinquency and death.

It is not a question of an ingrained habit or a state of sinning contracted through frequent acts, which has passed into nature; such a custom and habit of sinning has no place among the regenerate, but it is a question of innate depravity, and original sin, of evil concupiscence, which is in all, even in the regenerate themselves. The Apostle says that this sin dwells in him: because it is intimately in him, and has fixed a firm seat in us after the fall: and as an inhabitant enjoys the house by right, and does not emigrate from there until another place of dwelling has been provided, so sin sits in man, and enjoys its right, and does not depart until the tabernacle of the body has been destroyed. And how does Grotius ascribe to men after the law an ingrained habit of sinning, which passes into nature, when he says that man by the force of the law no longer does evil in his entirety, from which he would much less contract a habit of sinning by frequent evil actions? But the Apostle speaks of himself, I know, he says, emphatically claiming for himself this knowledge, which escapes many others, indeed the greatest part of men, as a kind of store of hidden wisdom: that in me, that is, in my flesh: he therefore restricts this to the flesh: excepting the spirit, which is immune from this stain; By flesh, however, he does not mean human nature itself, which the Manichaeans make essentially evil, because our body is the temple of the Holy Spirit itself 2 Cor. VI. 19. nor only the sensitive appetite, which pleases the Papists, who attribute repugnance and depravity to it alone, as if we had a mind and will of integral nature, having suffered only a violation of the lower faculties; but he understands the corruption of the whole man, and of all his powers, everything that is not reborn. By Spirit likewise designating the whole man, insofar as he is reborn. In me, that is, in my flesh does not dwell good, says the Apostle: He denies simply that good dwells in the flesh. In the unregenerate therefore, who are nothing but flesh, John III. 6. not only is it to be judged that there is hardly anything of good, but NOTHING of good is in them; For whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. XIV. 23. but in Christians, although the affections are corrected through faith and the Spirit, and the body itself is their dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, insofar as they are reborn, yet because the flesh is still in them, and corruption adheres to the affections, and to the members of the body; good does not dwell in them, that is, in their flesh, but evil lies close to them, v. 21.

For to will is present with me, but to perform that which is good I find not.) In the manuscript instead of I find not is not, namely it is present. Far from me is the power of doing good.

Latin:

V. 18. Οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι ὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοὶ, τῦτέσιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί με, ἀγαθόν.) Homo cum nominatur, modo totus intelligitur, modo κατ᾿ συνεκδοχὴν tribuitur id nomen partibus. Sic quod hic dixit, in me, interpretatur de carne & affectibus ex carne orientibus. In his vix quicquam erat boni, quanquam in mente erat aliqua boni cognitio, ut jam amplius dicet. At in Christianis, quales pleriq; erant primis illis temporibus, ipsi etiam affectus erant correcti per fidem ac Spiritum, & corpus ipsum habitaculum erat Spiritus Sancti 1. Cor. VI. 19. non minus quam olim Templum erat Majestatis divinæ habitaculum. Rectè dicimus σάρκα etiam affectus includere: imò sæpè pro illis solis sumitur, ut 1. Cor. V. 5. Tertullianus libro de pudicitia hunc locum sic explicat: Nam etsi habitare bonum in carne sua negavit, sed secundum legem literæ, in qua fuit: secundum autem legem Spiritus, cui nos annexit, liberat ab infirmitate carnis: lex enim, inquit, Spiritus vitæ manumisit te à lege delinqventiæ & mortis.

Non de inolita consuetudine, vel habitu peccandi contracto per frequentes actus, qui in naturam abierit; qualis consuetudo & habitus peccandi penes renatos locum non habet, sed de connata pravitate, & peccato originali, de concupiscentia mala, quæ omnibus inest, etiam ipsismet renatis, agitur. Quod peccatum in se habitare dicit Apostolus: quia intimè ipsi inest, & firmam sedem in nobis fixit post lapsum: & ut incola jure domus fruitur, nec inde prius emigrat, quàm de alio habitandi loco prospectum sit, ita peccatum insidet homini, & suo jure fruitur, nec excedit prius, quàm tabernaculum corporis destructum sit. Et quomodo peccati consuetudinem inolitam, quæ in naturam abit, hominibus post legem adscribit Grotius, quum hominem vi legis non amplius totum malè agere dicat, unde multo minus frequentibus actionibus malis habitum peccandi contrahet? de se verò loquitur Apostolus, Scio, inquit, hanc scientiam emphaticè sibi vendicans, quæ alios plurimos, imò maximam partem hominum fugiat, ceu penus quædam reconditæ sapientiæ: quod in me, h. e. in carne mea: restringit ergo hoc ad carnem: spiritum excipiens, qui à labe hâc immunis sit; Per carnem autem non naturam humanam ipsam, quam Manichæi essentialiter malam faciunt, quia corpus nostrum ipsius Spiritus S. templum est 2. Cor. VI. 19. non appetitum tantum sensitivum, quod Pontificiis placet, ei soli repugnantiam & pravitatem tribuentibus, quasi inferiorum duntaxat facultatum violationem passi mentem ac voluntatem integræ naturæ habeamus; sed corruptionem totius hominis, omniumque ejus virium, intelligens omne id, quod non renatum est. Per Spiritum itidem totum hominem designans, quatenus renatus est. In me, id est, in carne mea non habitat bonum, inquit Apostolus: Negat simpliciter bonum in carne habitare. In non renatis ergo, qui nonnisi caro sunt, Joh. III. 6. non tantum vix quicquam boni esse censendum est, sed NIHIL boni in iis; Quicquid enim non est ex fide, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. in Christianis vero, etsi affectus correcti per fidem ac Spiritum, & corpus ipsum eorum habitaculum sit Spiritus S. qua renati sunt, tamen quia adhuc caro in illis est, & affectibus adhæret corruptio, & membris corporis; bonum in ipsis, h. e. in carne ipsorum non habitat, sed malum adjacet ipsis, v. 21.

τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν ὐχ ἐυρίσκω.) In manuscripto pro ὐχ ἐυρίσκω est ὐ, nempè παράκειται. Longe à me abest bene agendi vis.

## 7:19
Vers. 19. For the good that I would I do not, but the evil which I would not that I do.) He clearly attributes to the Jew the speech which Lactantius IV. 24 attributes to the pagan: I wish indeed not to sin, but I am overcome. For I am clothed in fragile and weak flesh, this is what lusts, what is angry, what grieves, what fears to die. And so I am led uncertain, and I sin not because I wish, but because I am compelled. I myself also feel that I sin, but the necessity of fragility impels me, which I cannot resist. And what wonder is it that they have held up such veils for their vices, when many who go by the name of Christian use this very speech, as if Paul were speaking of himself already corrected, already an Apostle, and this is not only of this age, but also of others, from the time when that first purity began to decline. That is apparent from the life

Of Andronicus in Nicetas Choniates. But we ought not to marvel at this, since even in the age of the Apostles there were those who would twist these words of Paul and similar ones to their own destruction. 2 Pet. III. 16. Thanks be to God that the best, that is, the Christians of the first three centuries, understood this passage as it ought to be understood, dictated by that Spirit by whom their life was governed.

That these things are to be understood of a Jew will never be taught from the consensus of the first three centuries. The Pelagians indeed contended that some profane, incontinent, lustful, unregenerate man was being described, which opinion was also interpolated by Erasmus, Ursinus, Castellio, and F. Socinus under the name of Prosper Dysidaeus, as well as under his own name, then in Part I of De Servatore, ch. 4, p. 30, and by the Arminians and other heretics. But that it was handed down by the ancient Fathers through the first three centuries and accepted by Christians at that time cannot be proven. Certainly no one besides Origen can be brought forward; but his commentaries are most impure, and it is no wonder that he, being too addicted to Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy, defended the τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον (free will). And by what argument, I ask, will such a thing be taught from the text? If a Jew not converted and destitute of the grace of the Gospel is understood, how are the inner man and the law of the mind attributed to him, which do not befit any but the regenerate, and those who are through regeneration and renewal Eph. III. 19. I do not see, says Augustine, ch. X to Boniface, how a man under the law could say: I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, since that very delight in the good, by which he does not even consent to evil, not from fear of punishment but from love of justice (for this is what it means to delight with) must be attributed to nothing but grace. Augustine indeed felt the same as the Pelagians, but afterwards he retracted his opinion, concerning which in Book VI, ch. II against Julian: Afterwards I yielded to better and more intelligent men, or rather, which must be confessed, to the truth: so that I might see that in those words of the Apostle there is the groaning of the saints struggling against carnal concupiscences. And he appeals in the same place to Augustine. to the opinion of the Fathers: I am not the only one or the first to have understood this passage in this way, by which your heresy is overturned, in the way it is truly to be understood: nay rather, I myself had previously understood it otherwise, or rather had not understood it. Hence it happened that I understood these things in the way that Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the OTHER holy and well-known Doctors of the Church understood them, who also felt that the Apostle himself struggled strenuously against carnal concupiscences, which he did not wish to have, and that he testified to this same conflict of his in those words of his. Nor did St. Jerome go in a different direction, whom the adversaries are accustomed to praise for themselves, but only from his commentaries; which, however, are judged by not a few to have been written under his name by some Pelagian infected with error. But he himself has it thus in Dial. II against the Pelagians. And daily according to the Apostle, who had said, for good does not dwell in my flesh, the saints groan, saying: My loins are filled with illusions, and there is no soundness in my flesh, (Ps. XXXVIII. 8.) Nor is it absurd that a regenerate man should be at the same time the old and the new man, should do evil, and hate it according to one thing and another, and feel the battle of the flesh against the Spirit; nay, without this there would be no exercises of repentance in the regenerate, and they would be warned in vain to put off, lay aside, mortify the old man, and resist concupiscence, not to walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit, and by the Spirit to mortify the deeds of the flesh. Those who write or feel the contrary have either never felt their own heart, or if they have felt it, and have not found anything of the old man in themselves, they are mere non-men, that is, notable hypocrites.

There is no reason why we should think that these things which are said here cannot be said except of those whom the concupiscence of the flesh held so subjugated that they did whatever it impelled them to do: which it is madness to believe of the Apostle; since even an innumerable multitude of saints, so as not to fulfill the concupiscence of the flesh, lust against the flesh in the spirit: Which Augustine also says he once thought, Book VI against Julian, ch. II. Rather let us conclude, as the holy Father testifies he believed afterwards when he yielded to better and more intelligent men to the truth, that although the saints are spiritual in their mind, they are still carnal because of this corruptible body which weighs down the soul, nay, they are entirely captive in that part under the law of sin, which is subject to the motions of desires to which they do not consent: which he therefore warns in Book 1 of Retractations, ch. 23. What the Apostle says, we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, I certainly did not wish to be taken from the person of him who was already spiritual, but of a man placed under the LAW, not yet under GRACE. For thus I previously understood these words, which I later considered MORE DILIGENTLY after reading certain translators of the divine utterances, whose authority moved me, and I saw that it could also be understood of the Apostle himself, what he says: We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, which I showed as diligently as I could in those books which I recently wrote against the Pelagians. And a little later: But in those books we showed that these words are better understood even of a spiritual man, and one already established under grace, because of the BODY OF FLESH, which is not yet spiritual, but will be in the resurrection of the dead: AND BECAUSE OF THE CONCUPISCENCE OF THE FLESH ITSELF: with which the saints struggle in such a way, not consenting to it for evil, that they are nevertheless not without those motions, which they resist while they struggle against them: but they will not have them in that life, where death will be swallowed up in victory.

Moreover, it must be observed that there is one state, of which Paul speaks in verses 5 and 6, 'When we were in the flesh, the affections of sins which were by the law did work in our members, etc.', which is the state of the unregenerate: and another, of which the Apostle discourses here: For to be in the flesh, as also to live or walk according to the flesh, signifies to consent to the desires of the flesh and to indulge them totally, which the UNREGENERATE do without a struggle. But to feel the affections and desires of the flesh within oneself, to deplore them, to struggle against them, and sometimes even to be overcome in the struggle, can entirely happen to the REGENERATE. The reason is: because the unregenerate are wholly flesh and carnal; the regenerate are not wholly spiritual, but are still in part flesh: inasmuch as they are not yet fully renewed, whence they are to be renewed from day to day. They are spiritual, in so far as they have a mind illuminated by the Spirit of God, a will turned toward God, sensuality in part mortified, and the locomotive faculty dedicated to justice: thus they delight in the law of God, they hate evil, they will the good, and they do it; finally, they serve God. But they are also carnal, in so far as many ignorances and doubts still cling to the mind, and depraved inclinations, appetites, and desires in the heart and sensuality: hindering the will and the locomotive faculty in the good, and drawing them toward evil. This contrariety, struggle, and contention of principles, desires, motions, and finally actions, remains in the Saints until they put off the flesh entirely and lay aside this mortal body of sin.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὁ γὰρ ὁ θέλω ποιῶ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλ᾽ ὃ ὐ θέλω κακὸν τῦτο πράσσω.) Plane Judæo eum sermonem tribuit, quem pagano Lactantius IV. 24. Volo equidem non peccare, sed vincor. Indutus enim sum carne fragili & imbecilla, hæc est, qua concupiscit, quæ irascitur, quæ dolet, quæ mori timet. Itaque ducor incertus, & pecco non quia volo, sed quia cogor. Sentio me & ipse peccare, sed necessitas fragilitatis impellit, cui repugnare non possum. Et quid mirum, illos talia vela obtendisse vitiis suis, cum hoc ipso sermone, tanquam Paulus de se jam correcto, jam Apostolo loqueretur, multi utantur nomine Christiani, nec id hujus tantum est seculi, sed & aliorum, ex quo labescere cœpit prima illa puritas. Apparet id ex vita

Andronici apud Nicetam Choniatem. Verum id mirari non debemus, cum & Apostolorum ætate fuerint, qui in suam perniciem verba Pauli hæc & similia detorquerent. 2. Pet. III. 16. Deo laus sit, quod optimi, id est, trium pri- morum seculorum Christiani hunc locum sic ut oportet intellexerint, dictante illo spiritu, per quem vita ipsorum regebatur.

De Judæo hæc intelligenda esse, è trium primo- rum seculorum consensu nunquam docebitur. Pe- lagiani quidem, hominem aliquem profanum, in- continentem, libidinosum, non renatum describi contendebant, quam etiam sententiam interpola- runt Erasmus, Ursinus, Castellio, F. Socinus sub nomine Prosperi Dysidæi, ut & sub proprio nomi- ne, deinde part. I. de Servat. cap. 4. pag. 30. & Ar- miniani, aliique hæretici. Sed ab antiquis Patri- bus per tria secula priora eam traditam, & à Chri- stianis tum susceptam esse probari nequit. Nul- lus utique præter Origenem adferri potest: cujus verò commentaria impurissima sunt, quem Phi- losophia Platonica & Aristotelica nimis addictum τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον defendisse, mirum non est. Et quo, obsecro, argumento tale quid docebitur è textu? Si Judæus non conversus & gratia Evangelii desti- tutus intelligitur, quomodo ei homo interior, & lex mentis tribuitur, quæ non conveniunt, nisi renatis, & per regenerationem ac renovationem Eph. III. 19. Non video, inquit Augustinus c. X. ad Bonif. quomodo diceret homo sub lege: Conde- lector lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem, cum ipsa delectatio boni, qua etiam non consentit ad malum, non timore pœnæ, sed amore justitiæ (hoc est enim condelectari) nonnisi gratiæ deputanda sit. Sen- sit quidem etiam Augustinus cum Pelagianis, sed postmodum sententiam suam retractavit, quo de lib. VI. cap. II. contr. Julian. Postea melioribus & intelligentioribus cessi, vel potius, quod fatendum est, veritati: ut viderem, in illis Apostoli vocibus gemi- tum esse sanctorum contra carnales concupiscentias dimicantium. Et provocat ibidem Augustin. ad Patrum sententiam: Non ego solus aut primus sic istum locum intellexi, quo evertetur hæresis vestra, quemadmodum verè intelligendus est: imò verò eg prius cum aliter intellexeram, vel potius non intel- lexeram. Hinc factum est, ut sic ista intelligerem, quemadmodum intellexit Hilarius, Gregorius, Ambrosius & CÆTERI Ecclesiæ Sancti, notique Doctores, qui & ipsum Apostolum adversus carna- les concupiscentias, quas habere nolebat, strenuè conflixisse, eundemque conflictum suum illis suis ver- bis contestatum fuisse, senserunt. Neque in diver- sum abiit S. Hieronymus, quem pro se laudare so- lent adversarii, sed è commentariis solum ejus; quæ vero sub ipsius nomine ab aliquo Pelagiano errore infecto scripta à non paucis censentur. Ipse verò sic habet Dial. II. contr. Pelagian. Et quotidiè juxta Apostolum, qui dixerat, non enim ha- bitat in carne meâ bonum, ingemiscunt Sancti, di- centes: Renes mei impleti sunt illusionibus, & non est sanitas in carne meâ, (Ps. XXXVIII. 8.) Ne- que verò absurdum est, ut homo renatus sit simul vetus, & novus homo operetur malum, & odio ha- beat illud secundum aliud & aliud, & pugnam sen- tiat carnis adversus Spiritum; imò sine hoc nulla forent exercitia pœnitentiæ in renatis, & frustra commonefierent illi, ut exuant, deponant, mor- tificent veterem hominem, & concupiscentiæ re- sistant, non secundum carnem ambulent, sed se- cundum Spiritum, & Spiritu opera carnis mortifi- cent. Qui contrarium scribunt vel sentiunt, vel in sinum suum nunquam palparunt, aut si palpa- runt, nec de veteri homine aliquid in se repere- runt, sunt meri non homines, h.e. insignes hypocritæ.

Non est, quod ita censeamus, dici ista, quæ hic di- cuntur, non posse nisi de iis, quos ita haberet con- cupiscentia carnis subjugatos, ut facerent, quic- quid illa impelleret: quod de Apostolo demen- tis est credere; cum etiam innumerabilis multitudo Sanctorum, ne concupiscentiam carnis perficiat, con- tra carnem spiritu concupiscat: Quod & sese quon- dam putasse ait August. lib. VI. contr. Julian. c. II. quin potius ita statuamus, quemadmodum postea, cum melioribus & intelligentioribus cessit, se cre- didisse veritati, perhibet S. Pater, quod Sancti cum mente sint spirituales, adhuc tamen isto corruptibili corpore, quod aggravat animam, carnales sint, imò eà omninò parte captivi sint sub lege peccati, quæ desi- deriorum, quibus non consentiunt, motibus subja- cent: qui proinde monet l. 1. Retract. c. 23. Quod ait Apostolus, scimus, quia lex spiritualis est, ego autem carnalis sum, utique non ex persona ejus ac- cipi volui, qui jam spiritualis erat, sed hominis sub LEGE positi, nondum sub GRATIA. Sic enim prius hæc verba sapiebam, quæ postea lectis quibus- dam divinorum translatoribus eloquiorum, quorum me moveret autoritas, consideravi DILIGENTIUS & vidi, etiam de ipso Apostolo posse intelligi, quod ait: Scimus, quoniam lex spiritualis est, ego autem carnalis, quod in eis libris, quos contra Pelagianos nuper scripsi, quantum potui, diligenter ostendi. Et paulò post: Sed in illis libris etiam spiritualis homi- nis, jamque sub gratia constituti melius intelligi ver- ba ista monstravimus, propter CARNIS CORPUS, quod spirituale nondum est, erit autem in resurre- ctione mortuorum: ET PROPTER IPSAM CAR- NIS CONCUPISCENTIAM: cum quâ ita con- fligunt Sancti, non ei consentientes ad malum, ut ta- men eis motibus, quibus repugnantibus resistunt, non careant in hac vitâ: non eos autem habebunt in illa, ubi mors absorbebitur in victoriam.

Cæterum observandum, alium esse statum, de quo Paulus v. 5. 6. Cum in carne essemus, affectûs peccatorum per legem vigebant, in membris nostris &c. qui est non renatorum: alium, de quo hic dis- serit Apostolus: Nam esse in carne, ut & vivere, vel incedere secundum carnem, significat carnis cupidi- tatibus consentire, & indulgere totaliter, quod sine lucta faciunt NON RENATI. At carnis affectus & desideria in se sentire, deplorare, eis reluctari, & aliquando etiam in lucta superari in RENATOS omninò cadere potest. Ratio est: quia non re- nati toti caro, & carnales sunt; renati non sunt to ti spirituales, sed ex parte adhuc caro sunt: utpote nondum plenè renovati, unde de die in diem reno- vandi sunt. Spirituales sunt, in quantum habent mentem Spiritu Dei illustratam, voluntatem ad Deum conversam, sensualitatem ex parte mortifi- catam, locomotivam justitiæ dicatam: sic lege Dei delectantur, malum oderunt, bonum volunt, & agunt, denique Deo serviunt. Sed & carnales sunt, in quantum multæ adhuc ignorantiæ & dubitatio- nes hærent in mente, inclinationes, appetitiones, desideria prava in corde & sensualitate: impedien- tia voluntatem & locomotivam in bono trahentis ad malum. Ista principiorum, desideriorum, mo- tuum, actionum denique contrarietas, lucta & contentio manet in Sanctis, donec carnem penitus exuant, & mortale hoc corpus peccati deponant.

## 7:20
Vers. 20. εἰ δὲ ὃ ὐ θέλω, ἐγὼ τῦτο ποιῶ, ὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ κατερ- γάζομαι αὐτὸ, ἀλλ’ ἡ οἰκῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία. He repeats what he had said in verse 17, but adds a complication, with 'I' taken twice, in a different sense. It is the man who consents to sin, but not all parts of him, since the mind of the man dictates otherwise, which increases the guilt.

There is no reason why a different sense of the word ἐγὼ should be admitted: since in the former 'what I do not will, I', and in the latter

ὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ ἐργάζομαι [I no longer do it myself], let him speak the same of himself under the same quality, namely, in that part in which he is reborn, that he neither wills nor works the very thing which he works, because it is not he himself, but sin dwelling in him that does and works it: The Apostle therefore distinguishes himself, as he is reborn, from the sin dwelling within him. He says that he neither wills nor does evil, nay rather that he does this, which he does not will, and that he does not even perform it entirely, but that the sin dwelling in him works it, that is, that depraved concupiscence which, after the fall, has found a fixed domicile in us. Meanwhile, it is not only the will that consents to sin, much less only the sensitive appetite, with the mind of man dictating otherwise, but just as the corruption of original sin has infected the whole man and all his faculties, so also there is an aberration in the mind, which the will follows, desiring nothing except what is proposed by the mind under the guise of good. Although, however, the whole man thus does evil, he does not work it as he is reborn and spiritual, but as he is carnal, and because, not yet being fully renewed here, he still carries about with him depraved concupiscence and the corruption of all his faculties: for as he is reborn, he does not will, but rather hates evil and wishes to be so desired by concupiscence, tempting him to evil, and the flesh lusting against the spirit. Hence, therefore, the guilt is not increased, nor does the Apostle wish this; nay, rather, because he so greatly abhors evil in the Spirit, he deplores that propensity of his toward evil, and his misery, that he must perpetually struggle with sin. Who would say that this serves to increase evil? The indwelling sin is that impure fountain from which every kind of filth, by which even the reborn are sometimes defiled, flows forth; if they were without it, they would never sin: but as long as they have it lurking within them, they cannot be immune from sin. Into this fountain, therefore, the Apostle deservedly derives all guilt; this, however, he does again, not to excuse the sinning reborn, but to animate them more, being established in the struggle against an internal enemy.

Latin:
