Vers. 20. εἰ δὲ ὃ ὐ θέλω, ἐγὼ τῦτο ποιῶ, ὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ κατερ- γάζομαι αὐτὸ, ἀλλ’ ἡ οἰκῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία. Repetit, quod dixerat 17. sed addit πλοκὴν, ἐγὼ bis sumpto, sensu diverso. Homo est, qui consentit peccato, sed non omnes partes, hominis mente diversum dictante, quod culpam auget.

Non est, quod admittatur diversus vocis ἐγὼ sensus: cum in priori ὅ ὐ θέλω ἐγὼ, & in posteriori

ὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ ἐργάζομαι idem de seipso sub eadem qualitate loquatur, se sc. qua parte renatus est, nec velle, nec operari idipsum, quod operatur, quia non ipse, sed inhabitans in ipso peccatum id facit & operatur: Se ergo qua renatum discriminat Apo- stolus a peccato in sese habitante. Se nec velle, nec facere malum, imo hoc facere, quod non vult, ne- que etiam se omnino id perpetrare, ait, sed pecca- tum in se habitans id operari, id est, pravam illam concupiscentiam, quae post lapsum fixum in no- bis domicilium nacta est. Interim consentit pec- cato non tantum voluntas, nedum solum appeti- tus sensitivus, hominis mente diversum dictante, sed uti corruptio peccati originalis totum homi- nem omnesque facultates ejus infecit, ita & in mente est aberratio, quam sequitur voluntas nihil appetens, nisi quod sub ratione boni a mente pro- ponitur. Quanquam vero ita totus homo malum faciat, non tamen qua renatus & spiritualis est, id operatur, sed qua carnalis est, & quia nondum hic plene renovatus, concupiscentiam pravam, & cor- ruptionem omnium facultatum adhuc circum- fert: nam qua renatus est, non vult, sed odit po- tius malum & optat ita desiderari a concupiscen- tia, se ad malum tentante, & carne concupiscente adversus spiritum. Inde ergo culpa non augetur, nec id vult Apostolus, imo potius quia tantopere Spiritu abhorret malum, suam istam ad malum propensionem, & miseriam, quod perpetuo cum peccato sibi colluctandum sit, deplorat. Quis hoc ad malum augendum facere dixerit? Peccatum in- habitans est impurus ille fons, ex quo omne genus sordium, quibus etiam renati quandoque inqui- nantur, promanat, absque quo si essent, nunquam peccarent: quamdiu vero in se latentem habent, peccati immunes esse non possunt. In hunc igitur fontem omnem culpam merito derivat Aposto- lus; Id vero rursus facit, non ut peccantes renatos excuset, sed ut in lucta constitutos adversus intesti- num hostem magis animet.

## 7:21
Vers. 21. ἐυρίσκω ἄρα τὸν νόμον τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοὶ ποιεῖν τὸ καλὸν, ὅτι ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται. [I find then the law, that to me who wills to do good, evil is present.] Here ἐυρίσκω is 'I experience,' which he soon calls βλέπω [I see], in the manner of the Hebrews, who call all senses, even interior ones, by the word for seeing. I experience, he says, even a law different from the law of God; what is that law? That although I wish to do well, evil is nevertheless closer to me: whence this? From the flesh: not that the flesh forces anyone to sin, but that it greatly patronizes the habit of sinning, as he now says. The flesh loves all things that delight it. But many things of that kind cannot be had without sin: therefore the flesh, which is within us, favors the habit of sinning, while the law of God sounds only outwardly.

This evil παρακείμενον [present] is not from the flesh, but is the flesh itself. For by the flesh is not understood the muscular substance of man, or the human body itself, but the depravity and original corruption which is opposed to the Spirit, the old and exterior man opposed to the new and interior man, the law of the members and of sin, opposed to the law of the mind and of God. Although, however, the indwelling sin in v. 18 is distinguished from the flesh in which it dwells in v. 18 and 20, that distinction is made only when the flesh is taken not abstractly, for the depravity and original sin itself, but concretely, so that it implies a subject: I know that in ME, that is, in my flesh, good does not dwell, or sin dwells: in me, namely, insofar as I am still carnal. For the material subject is man, the formal is as he is still carnal. Grotius wrongly says that the habit of sinning is that indwelling sin, since sin dwells in us from our first birth, whereas the habit of sinning is only contracted later from frequent acts of sin, and it would not be so conveniently said to dwell in man. Furthermore, if evil is from the flesh, that is, from the body itself viewed by reason of its substance, is not God constituted the author and cause of sin, as He is the cause and author of the body, especially if the rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, i.e., of the body and the affections of the body against the mind, which Grotius with the Papists maintains, is natural? For the cause of a cause is the cause of the thing caused. Which, however, is impious and blasphemous. The flesh, of which Paul treats, entirely solicits us, tempts us, and unless it is subdued by the Spirit, necessitates and forces us to sin. But that the body tempts and forces us to sin is false. The body is no less good, and a creature of God, than the soul. Therefore, the body does not of itself, and by reason of its substance, tempt, move, or force us to sin; nor does it patronize the habit of sinning; nay, because the soul is the πρῶτον δεκτικὸν [first recipient] of sin, the soul rather, insofar as it is not regenerated, tempts and forces us to sin, and favors the habit of sinning. It is not for the flesh, when it denotes our body, to love those things which delight it, but this belongs to the soul, among which there are not a few things contrary to the law of God. And it is fitting for the soul to work evil, even if it is sometimes done through the flesh; the body never does evil without the soul: but the soul performs very many evils without the body, namely, interior motions and depraved desires, which do not depend on the body, as is evident from the example of the evil Angels, and as everyone experiences in himself. There is, therefore, no reason why sin should be restricted to the body, and thus the mind and will, or the soul, be held immune from sin.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐυρίσκω ἄρα τὸν νόμον τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοὶ ποιεῖν τὸ καλὸν, ὅτι ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται. Ἐυρίσκω hic est experior, quod mox βλέπω dicit, more Hebraeorum, qui sensus omnes etiam interiores, videndi vocabulo appellant. Experior, inquit, etiam legem diver- sam a lege Dei, quae illa lex? quod quanquam bene agere malum tamen mihi est propius : unde hoc? ex carne: non quod caro quemvis cogat peccare, sed quod consuetudini peccandi, ut jam dicit, multum patrocinetur. Caro omnia amat, quae se delectant. Multa autem ejus generis haberi sine peccato non possunt: ideo peccandi consuetudini favet caro, quae intra nos est, cum lex Dei exterius tantum sonet.

Malum hoc παρακείμενον non est ex carne, sed ipsa est caro. Non enim per carnem substantia ho- minis musculosa, vel ipsum corpus humanum, sed pravitas & corruptio originalis intelligitur, quae Spiritui opponitur, vetus & exterior homo oppo- situs homini novo & interiori, lex membrorum & peccati, opposita legi mentis & Dei. Quanquam vero peccatum inhabitans v. 18. distinguatur a car- ne, in qua habitat v. 18. & 20. ea tamen distinctio fit solum, cum caro non abstractive, pro ipsa pra- vitate & peccato originali, sed concretive accipi- tur, ut subjectum implicet : Scio, quod in ME, id est, in carne mea non habitet bonum, vel habitet pecca- tum: in me nempe quatenus adhuc carnalis sum. Subjectum enim materiale homo est, formale qua adhuc carnalis. Perperam vero Grotius consue- tudinem peccandi dicit esse peccatum illud inhabi- tans, quum inhabitet nos peccatum inde a primo ortu, consuetudo autem peccandi postmodum de- mum contrahatur a frequentibus peccati actibus, neque inhabitare hominem ita convenienter dica- tur. Porro si malum est ex carne, hoc est, ex cor- pore ipso ratione substantiæ suæ spectato, annon Deus constituirur autor & causa peccati, utpotè qui causa est & autor corporis, imprimis si rebellio carnis adversus spiritum, h. e. corporis & affectuum corporis adversus mentem, quod Grotius cum Pa- pistis vult, naturalis sit. Causa enim causæ est cau- sa causati. Quod verò impium est & blasphe- mum. Caro, de qua Paulus agit, omninò nos soli- citat, tentat, & nisi subigatur Spiritu, necessitat, & cogit nos ad peccatum. At corpus nos tentare & cogere ad peccandum, falsum. Corpus non mi- nus bonum, & creatura Dei est, quam anima. Non ergo corpus per se, & ratione substantiæ suæ ad peccatum nos tentat, movet aut cogit; nec consue- tudini peccandi patrocinatur; imò quia anima est πρῶτον δεκτικὸν peccati, anima potius quatenus non regenita est, ad peccatum nos tentat, & cogit, favetque peccandi consuetudini. Carnis, cum corpus nostrum notat, non est amare ea, quæ se de- lectant, sed hoc animæ est, inter quæ legi Dei ad- versa etiam non pauca sunt. Et animæ convenit operari malum, etsi id per carnem quandoque fiat; Corpus nunquam sine anima malum facit: animæ autem sine corpore mala plurima patrat, interiores sc. motus, & prava desideria, quæ non dependent à corpore, ut exemplo malorum Angelorum con- stat, & quisq; in sese experitur. Non ergo est, quod peccatum ad corpus restringatur, & ita mens & vo- luntas, vel anima à peccato immunis habeatur.

## 7:22
Vers. 22. Συνήδομαι τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ. [I delight in the law of God.] אבתי לתורת for אבה is translated by συνήδομαι in Deut. XIII. 8. This is what he just said: σύμφημι τῷ νόμῳ ὅτι καλός [I consent to the law that it is good]. It is a metonymy. For it is properly the function of the mind to approve, not to rejoice: but it is customary for the names of proximate effects to be attributed to their causes.

according to the inner man. The inner man and the new man are not the same, nor are the outer man and the old man the same. The old and new man signify their qualities by the name of the subject. But when it is said the inner and outer man, the name of the whole is given to the parts by synecdoche. There are always in man an inner and outer man, that is, the mind and the body with its affections. But where the new man is, there the old has ceased to be. He who is here the inner man, is the hidden man of the heart 1 Pet. III. 4. the man dwelling in each one in the soul. In his book, Philo says that the worse lies in wait for the better, where he also says that he is the one who invisibly reproves us from within. But in his book on agriculture he calls the same the ruling man, and adds, what else would the man in each of us be but the mind? But in his book on the meeting for the sake of preliminary studies, he says that God ought to be praised by us also for the mind, which is strictly the man in man, the better in the worse. Hierocles, interpreting that golden poem, says that 'thee' is placed for the man who truly is and for the rational essence, and elsewhere it is said if man is a rational soul with a connatural mortal body. For so it must be read there, since for the Pythagoreans the mind alone is man, the rest are not parts, but instruments of man. But Paul speaks with the common people. For Plautus also greeted the inner man. Tertullian on the resurrection: Thus the term, man, is in a way the buckle of two associated substances: under which term they cannot be, unless they are coherent. Furthermore, the Apostle prefers the inner man to be understood not so much as the soul, but as the mind and the spirit, that is, not the substance itself, but the flavor of the substance.

As the old and new man, so also the outer and inner man signify their qualities by the name of the subject, and are taken in the same sense in the Scriptures. Whence by the inner man spiritual renewal in the reborn man is designated. By which name the renewal of the Spirit and the putting on of the new man is joined Eph. IV. 23. 24. Therefore such contrary attributes are assigned to the internal and external man. The internal man hates and turns away from the deeds of the external, consents to the law of God that it is good, does not work evil, to will is present with him, he delights in the law of God, he serves the law of God. The external man is carnal, sold under sin, does what the internal man does not want, has sin as an inhabitant, does not have good dwelling in him, does not find how to perform good, does evil, fights against the law of the mind, a captive under the law of sin, it serves the flesh. Therefore, by the outer man, the body with its affections is not understood, nor by the inner, the mind. For Scripture nowhere speaks in such a way; indeed, the Apostle names the mind of the flesh in Col. II. 18 and Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς in Rom. VIII. 7. And affections are not only of the body, but primarily of the soul; which are either vicious or devoid of vice. If you understand those, sin will be attributed to the body, by reason of its substance and in itself, and God will be constituted the cause of sin. If they are devoid of vice, how then are they contrary to the law of God? Nor do mind and body complete the man, as essential parts, but body and soul, to which besides the mind also the will pertains, which Grotius here distinguishes from the mind, when he says it is properly of the mind to approve, not to rejoice, which is of the will. Although, therefore, body and soul with their affections are always in man, they are not, however, always with vicious affections, nor do these pertain to the parts of man. They were indeed without them in the state of integrity: They will be without them in the state of perfection of the other life: But in the state of the fall and sin, after renewal, just as the outer and inner man, in the Apostolic sense, is always in man in this life, so also the old and new man is always in him: for where the new man is, the old has not entirely ceased to be: because we are renewed μερικῶς in part, not ὁλικῶς in whole; and thus both the old and new man concur in one subject, which is both carnal and spiritual, but in part. For the oldness of the flesh always struggles with the newness of the Spirit, and the remnants of the old man well consist with the firstfruits of the Spirit and the beginnings of the new man. For we receive here only the firstfruits of the Spirit: and our newness is only begun, as it is to be consummated finally in the other life, when τὸ τελείον, the perfect, shall come, and τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται, and that which is in part shall be destroyed 1 Cor. XIII. 10. Thus ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπός, is ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος, 1 Peter III. 4. certainly the mind of man will not be denoted by that. For the mind is not the hidden man of the heart: since the mind is in every man, but that hidden man of the heart is not found in every one, as he who is πολυτελὴς before God, and whose praise is from God Rom. II. 29. Meanwhile, the ornament, which is here opposed to outward adornment, is of spiritual gifts and virtues, and pertains to the new, internal, and spiritual man. And Ambrose understands this in book 1 de offic. c. 18. πνεῦμα most rightly concerning the spirit of man renewed by the Holy Spirit, which is the best ornament of women, namely a spirit meek and gentle, and distinguished by other virtues. Thus also 2 Cor. IV. 16 it is said that through the cross ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος is corrupted, as he who is to be crucified and mortified: and ὁ ἔσωθεν RENOVARI from day to day: which cannot be understood of body and soul; because through the cross the body is not crucified nor is the soul renewed. For this διαφθορὰ and ἀνακαίνωσις is of body and soul: since the old man must be entirely destroyed and corrupted, and the new man made both in body and soul. Add that in Eph. III. 16 ἔσω ἄνθρωπος is not called the mind, or the will, or the soul of man: because we are commanded to be strengthened κραταιωθῆναι by the Holy Spirit εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον into the inner man, but we are not strengthened into our soul, but into the increase of the Spirit, and of our renewal. The opinions of Philo and the Philosophers do not come into account here, where we are not in the School of Pythagoras, but of the Holy Spirit. Although not even the Philosophers admit that the mind alone is man, and the rest not parts but instruments of man: which error we have elsewhere refuted in the Arminians and Anabaptists. For the soul and body of man are essential parts according to sounder Philosophy, and therefore man is not soul alone, much less mind alone. But Paul here does not speak of the parts of man considered Physically and Philosophically, much less with the common people: but of the state of man viewed Theologically, and the diverse principles of acting in the same after regeneration. Nor does Tertullian favor the inventions of Grotius, understanding not the substance of man itself, but the flavor of the substance through the inner man. And Grotius himself contradicts himself: For while he himself favors the Pythagorean opinion here, at c. VIII. 11 he reproves Origen, because he speaks too Pythagorically about body and soul.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Συνήδομαι τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ. אבתי לתורת nam אבה per συνήδομαι vertitur Deut. XIII. 8. Hoc est, quod modo dixit: σύμφημι τῷ νό- μῳ ὅτι καλός. Est μετωνυμία. Nam propriè mentis est ap- probare, non gaudere: sed solent causis tribui proximo- rum effectuum nomina.

κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον. Non idem est ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος & ὁ καινὸς, nec idem ὁ ἔξω & ὁ παλαιὸς. Vetus, & novus homo nomine subjecti signi- ficant ejus qualitates. At cum dicitur ὁ ἔσω & ὁ ἔξω ἄνθρω- πος, nomen totius per συνεκδοχὴν datur partibus. Semper in homine sunt homo interior & exterior, id est, mens & corpus cum suis affectibus. At ubi est novus homo, ibi ve- tus esse desiit. Qui hîc ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος, is est, ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος 1. Pet. III. 4. ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῇ ψυ- χῇ κατοικῶν. Philoni libro pejorem meliori insidiari, ubi & eum esse ait, qui ἀφανῶς ἡμᾶς ἔνδοθεν ἐλέγχει. At libro de agricultura eundem vocat τὸν ἡγεμόνα ἄνθρωπον, additque ἄνθρωπος δὲ ὁ ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν τίς ἄν εἴη πλὴν ὁ νοῦς; At libro περὶ τῆς εἰς προπαιδεύματα συνόδου, dicit Deum à nobis lauda- ri debere etiam ἐπὶ τῷ νῷ, ὃς κυρίως ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ, κρείττων ἐν χείρονι. Hierocles ὁ μέσ᾽ ἀνίσου in aureo illo car- mine interpretans, ait illud σε poni ἐπὶ τῷ ὄντως ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ τῆς λογικῆς ουσίας, & alibi dicitur εἰ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ψυχὴ λογι- κὴ, μετὰ συμφυῦς θνητῦ σώματος. Ita enim ibi legendum nimirum Pythagoricis mens sola homo est, cætera non par- tes, sed instrumenta hominis. At Paulus cum vulgo lo- quitur. Nam & Plautus salutem dixit interioris hominis. Tertullianus de resurrectione: Ita vocabulum, homo, con- sociatarum substantiarum duarum quodammodo fibula est: sub quo vocabulo non possunt esse, nisi cohærentes. Porrò Apo- stolus interiorem hominem, non tam animam quam mentem atque animum intelligi mavult, id est, non substantiam ipsam, sed substantiæ saporem.

Ut vetus & novus homo, ita etiam homo exterior & interior nomine Subjecti ejus qualitates signifi- cant, eodemque sensu in Scripturis accipiuntur. Unde per interiorem hominem renovatio spiritua- lis in homine renato designatur. Quo nomine renovatio Spiritus, & induitio novi hominis con- jungitur Eph. IV. 23. 24. Ideò interno & externo homini tam contraria attributa assignantur. In- ternus homo odit & aversatur facta externi, con- sentit legi Dei, quod bona sit, non operatur malum, velle ipsi adjacet, condelectatur lege Dei, servit legi Dei. Externus homo carnalis est, venundatus sub peccatum, facit, quæ non vult internus homo, pecca- tum habet incolam, non habet in se bonum inhabi- tans, non invenit, ut efficiat bonum, facit malum, re- pugnat legi mentis, captivus sub lege peccati, fervit carni. Non ergo per exteriorem hominem corpus cum suis affectibus, per interiorem mens intelligitur. Nuspiam enim ita Scriptura loquitur; imò Apost. mentem carnis Col. II. 18. & Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς Rom. VIII. 7. nominat. Et affectus non tantum corporis, sed imprimis animæ sunt; qui vel vitiosi sunt, vel expertes vitii. Si illos intelligas, corpori, ratione substantiæ suæ & per se peccatum tribuetur, & Deus causa peccati constituetur. Si vitii expertes sunt, quî ergò adversi legi Dei? Neq; mens & corpus absolvunt hominem, ceu partes essentiales, sed corpus & anima, ad quam præter mentem etiam voluntas pertinet, quam hic à mente distinguit Grotius, cum propriè mentis esse dicit approbare, non gaudere, quod est voluntatis. Licet ergò semper in homine corpus & anima sint cum suis affectibus, non tamen semper cum affectibus vitiosis sunt, neque hi ad partes hominis pertinent. Erant utique sine illis in statu integritatis: Erunt sine illis in statu perfectionis alterius seculi: In statu autem lapsus & peccati, post renovationem ut homo exterior & interior, sensu Apostolico, semper in homine est in hac vita, ita etiam semper in eo est vetus & novus homo: neque enim ubi novus homo est, ibi vetus esse desiit penitus: quia renovamur μερικῶς ex parte, non ὁλικῶς ex asse; adeoque & vetus & novus homo concurrunt in uno subjecto, quod & carnale est, & spirituale, sed ex parte. Superat enim semper cum novitate Spiritus vetustas carnis, & reliquiæ veteris hominis cum primitiis Spiritus & initiis hominis novi probè consistunt. Accipimus enim hic tantum primitias Spiritus: & inchoatur solum nostra novitas, utpote consummanda demum in altera vita, cum veniet τὸ τελείον, perfectum, & τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται, & id quod ex parte est destruetur 1. Cor. XIII. 10. Sic ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπός, est ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος, 1. Petri III. 4. non certè mens hominis eo notabitur. Mens enim non est occultus cordis homo: quum mens in quovis homine sit, non autem in quovis occultus ille cordis homo reperiatur, utpote qui πολυτελὴς est coram Deo, & cujus laus ex Deo est Rom. II. 29. Ornatus interim, qui exteriori ornatui hic opponitur, donorum est spiritualium & virtutum, & ad novum, internum & spiritualem hominem pertinet. Et intelligit Ambrosius l. 1. de offic. c. 18. πνεῦμα rectissimè de spiritu hominis renovato per Spiritum S. qui optimus est mulierum ornatus, spiritus nempe mansuetus, & lenis, aliisq; virtutibus insignis. Sic etiam 2. Cor. IV. 16. dicitur per crucem ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος corrumpi, utpote qui crucifigendus & mortificandus est: & ὁ ἔσωθεν RENOVARI de die in diem: quod intelligi non potest de corpore & anima; quia per crucem non crucifigitur corpus nec renovatur anima. Nam & hæc διαφθορὰ & ἀνακαίνωσις est corporis & animæ: quum vetus homo totus destrui & corrumpi debeat, & novus homo fieri & corpore & anima. Adde, quod Ephes. III. 16. ἔσω ἄνθρωπος non dicatur mens, aut voluntas, aut anima hominis: quia jubemur virtute κραταιωθῆναι per Spiritum S. εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον in interiorem hominem, in animam autem nostram non corroboramur, sed in incrementum Spiritus, & renovationis nostræ. Philonis & Philosophorum sententiæ hic non veniunt in censum, ubi non in Schola Pythagoræ, sed Spiritus S. versamur. Quanquam nec Philosophi mentem solam hominem esse, cætera non partes sed instrumenta hominis, admittant: quem errorem in Arminianis, & Anabaptistis alias profligavimus. Anima enim & corpus hominis partes sunt essentiales juxta sa- niorem Philosophiam, ideoque homo non est sola anima, nedum sola mens. Paulus verò hic non de partibus hominis Physicè considerati Philosophicè, multò minus cum vulgo loquitur: sed de hominis Theologicè spectati statu, & diversis in eodem post regenerationem agendi principiis. Nec Tertullia- nus commentis Grotii favet, non substantiam ipsam hominis, sed substantiæ saporem per interio- rem hominem intelligens. Et contradicit sibi Gro- tius ipse: Nam quum hic ipse Pythagoricæ sententiæ faveat ad c. VIII. 11. Origenem reprehendit, quod nimis Pythagoricè de corpore & anima loquatur.

## 7:23
Verse 23. βλέπω δὲ ἕτερον νόμον ἐν τοῖς μέλεσί μου.) Thus he calls the strong appetites of the flesh: יצר הרע to the Hebrews.

ἀντιςρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ νοός με.) Paul loves much to place the same words in various senses. To him it is the law of God or of Moses: it is of the mind, that is, the judgment concerning the honest and the base: it is the law of the members, that is, the appetites containing the flesh: it is the law of sin, that is, the very habit of sinning. Thus we have had ἁμαρτίαν, θάνατον, δικαιοῦν with one meaning and another. The honest mind approves, the flesh approves sweet things, whether those be honest or not: whence it happens that often the flesh, not tamed by reason, opposes the mind, which he here calls ἀντιςρατεύεσθαι, a metaphor drawn from warfare, from whence he had also just derived ὀψώνιον. Moreover, the Hebrews knew that all wars waged with the Canaanites and their neighbors bore the image of this internal war. Porphyry also said Νόμον τοῦ νοὸς in his book περὶ ἀποχῆς lib. 1.

and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.

Ἐν τῷ νόμῳ is written incorrectly here, since more correct books have τῷ νόμῳ. He says this: the vehemence of the affections arising from the flesh, favoring the habit of sinning, was subjecting most Jews to that same habit. He continues the metaphor taken from war. For he who is captured by the law of war becomes the slave of the captor, as we said in Book III of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, chapter VII. There is a law of Moses on this matter in Deut. XX. 4. He also places the habit of sinning in the members, because it is exercised through all parts of the body. See above VI. 13. 19. Simplicius uses the same simile in his commentary on Epictetus: ἄλογον ὄρεξιν τὸν λόγον κινήσασα (that is, having moved us to desires according to it) κὴ αἰχμάλωτον λαβοῦσα. Paul, however, composes two pairs: To the law of God the mind is present: to the law of sin the flesh is present.

Not the appetites of the flesh, which are acts, but the habit of depraved concupiscence, that is, original sin, is so called: which the ancient Hebrews also point to by יצר הרע from Gen. VI. 5 and VIII. 21, as Grotius himself admits in his commentary on Luke II. 22, that the Hebrews call that viciousness which is born in men יצר הרע. It is called a law in our members: because just as a law commands and promises, so depraved concupiscence both commands or impels us to sin, and ensnares us with the pleasures that will supposedly follow. However, it is unusual for an act of vicious appetite to be called a law. It is said to be this law in the members, not because it properly concerns and affects the corporeal substance of the members, but because it brings about the depravity which exerts itself in the corrupted members of the old man: nor are only external members understood, but also the interior faculties, which are like members, because the old man works through them and consists in them. For even Socinus (Prosper Disydaeus) admits that he is called the exterior man for this reason, because he occupies the whole man in soul and body, and uses all the man's members as weapons. For he seems to call them members here because he had spoken of the flesh: because as he places sin in the flesh, so he places the law of sin in the members: and because he had named the external man; just as he commands to mortify the members τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς which are upon the earth, Col. III. 5, which he elsewhere called crucifying the flesh, Gal. V. 24, and mortifying τὰς πράξεις τῶ σώματος through the Spirit, Rom. VIII. 13. If, however, one prefers to understand corporeal members, it must be said that the law of sin is referred to them because sin finally reveals itself there, and does not contain itself within the confines of the mind and heart. He uses the name of law for everything that rules and moderates our actions: and the law of the mind is called the propensity of the faithful soul toward obedience to the divine law, so called because it reigns most powerfully within; but by calling it the law of sin and of the members, he alludes to the dominion which sin has in a man not fully regenerated, but in a regenerate man only in part, namely in the flesh: just as the statutes of tyrants, however iniquitous, are also called laws. judgment concerning honorable and base things, by the law of the members the appetites contained in the flesh, and by the law of sin the very habit of sinning. For the law of the members and the law of sin are the same, as is clear from the words of the Apostle ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τῷ ὄντι ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι μου, and as we have said, it designates not only the appetites and affections of the body, or of sensuality, resisting the judgment of reason, but the propensity of all faculties and powers, and of all members toward evil, and that same habitual and intimately inherent propensity, which affects dominion over us and strives to render us slaves to its lust, which we find primarily in the superior faculties, the mind and the will. The law of the mind, however, is the propensity of the regenerate man, which likewise must be established not in the mind alone, although primarily in it, but in all the faculties and powers of the soul and body of the regenerate and faithful man, by which we are incited and governed so that we embrace the good, flee and abhor the evil, by which we consent in the Spirit to the law of God, and delight in it. For he does not speak here as some Jew under the law without grace, much less as a pagan, in whom there is a struggle of reason and appetite, but as an Apostle, as one regenerate and under grace, in whom there is a struggle of the flesh and the spirit: as one indeed regenerate, but not yet so renewed that he is not still agitated by various waves of carnal desires, and has need to struggle perpetually with the desires of depraved concupiscence: and thus under his own person he describes the condition and state of the faithful justified by faith in Christ, as far as concerns a renovation that is still very imperfect, and joined with a perpetual struggle of the flesh and the Spirit. The words ἀντιστρατευόμενον and αἰχμαλωτίζοντά με are entirely military, and those two contrary principles are presented as athletes struggling and fighting among themselves, Gal. V. 17, with the concupiscence of the flesh fighting against the propensity and concupiscence of the Spirit: the outcome of which contest is not rarely sorrowful, if indeed the concupiscence which is in us, as we are still carnal, or which dwells in our flesh, vehemently fighting against the Spirit and the law of our mind, strives not only always and in all ways and with all powers to subjugate us, but also sometimes renders us captive, and subjugates us under the law of the members. For although active verbs are often to be explained not of the effect, but of the endeavor, Gen. XXXVII. 21, Deut. XXVI. 5, Acts VII. 26, 1 Cor. X. 33, 2. Cor. X. 5, it cannot nevertheless be denied that the flesh sometimes prevails, and subjugates even the regenerate, even against their will, so that it even precipitates them into voluntary and graver sins, so that they shake off faith and fall from the grace of God, sometimes partially and totally, sometimes also finally, even if they have been truly regenerate and justified. Whence they are warned to watch diligently, that those who stand may see that they do not fall, that they may resist the desires of the flesh and embrace the same, that they may crucify the old man with his depraved desires, that they may mortify the works of the flesh by the Spirit, and other most frequent exhortations of this kind. Which would be entirely in vain if either the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit had no place in the regenerate, or if, once it were posited, the Spirit always prevailed, and the flesh could not subjugate us; the former of which Grotius asserts with the Pelagians and Socinians, but the latter the Calvinists contend with the Anabaptists.

Latin:

Vers. 23. βλέπω δὲ ἕτερον νόμον ἐν τοῖς μέλεσί μου.) Sic vo- cat carnis appetitus validos: יצר הרע Hebræis.

ἀντιςρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ νοός με.) Multum amat vo- ces easdem Paulus variis sensibus ponere. Est illi lex Dei sive Mosis: est mentis, id est, judicium de honestis & turpi- bus: est lex membrorum, id est, appetitus carni continen- tes: est lex peccati, id est, ipsa peccandi consuetudo. Sic ἁμαρτίαν, θάνατον, δικαιοῦν alio atque alio significatu ha- buimus. Mens honesta approbat, caro dulcia, sive illa ho- nesta sint, sive non: unde fit, ut sæpè caro ratione non edo- mita, menti adversetur, quod hic dicit ἀντιςρατεύεσθαι tra- latione ducta à militia, unde & ὀψώνιον modo deduxerat. Norant autem Hebræi omnia bella cum Chananæis eorum- que vicinis gesta hujus belli interni gerere imaginem. Νό- μον τοῦ νοὸς dixit & Porphyrius περὶ ἀποχῆς lib. 1.

καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντά με ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τῷ ὄντι ἐν τοῖς μέλεσί μου.

Ἐν τῷ νόμῳ male hic scribitur, cum libri correctiores ha- beant τῷ νόμῳ. Hoc ait: vehementia affectuum ex carne orientium favens consuetudini peccandi, eidem consuetu- dini subjiciebat Judæos plerosque. Continuat translatio- nem à bello desumptam. Nam qui belli lege capitur, is ca- pientis servus fit, ut diximus libro III. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. VII. Est ea de re Mosis lex Deut. XX. 4. Ponit autem etiam consuetudinem peccandi in membris, quia per omnes partes corporis exercetur. Vide supra VI. 13. 19. Eadem si- militudine utitur Simplicius ad Epictetum: ἄλογον ὄρεξιν τὸν λόγον κινήσασα (τυτέστιν ἡμᾶς τὲς κατ᾿ αὐτὴν ἐπιθυμίας) κὴ αἰχμάλωτον λαβοῦσα. Paulus autem duo componit paria : Legi Dei adest mens: Legi peccati adest caro.

Non appetitus carnis, qui actus sunt, sed habi- tus pravæ concupiscentiæ, h. e. peccatum originale ita vocatur: quod etiam per יצר הרע Ebræi an- tiqui è Gen. VI. 5. c. VIII. 21. indigitant, fatente ipsomet Grotio ad Luc. II. 22. Hebræos vitiosi- tatem illam, quæ hominibus agnascitur, vocare יצר הרע. Lex vocatur in membris nostris: quia ut lex præcipit, ac pollicetur, ita concupiscentia pra- va & præcipit vel impellit, ut peccemus, & volu- ptatibus ceu inde sequuturis nos inescat. Actum autem appetitûs vitiosi legem dici, insolens est. In membris vero dicitur esse hæc lex, non quod ipsam substantiam corpoream membrorum propriè concernat, & afficiat, sed quod pravitatem, quæ in corruptis veteris hominis membris se exerit, effi- ciat: nec membra tantum intelliguntur externa, sed interiores quoque facultates, quæ veluti membra sunt, quod per easdem operetur homo vetus, & in iisdem consistat. Nam & Socinus (Prosper Disy- dæus) fatetur, quod ideo homo exterior dicatur, quod totum hominem animo & corpore occupet, omnibusque hominis membris pro armis utatur. Membra enim vocare hic videtur, quod carnem dixerat: quia ut in carne peccatum, ita in membris legem peccati po- nit: & quod externum hominem nuncuparat; uti membra τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς quæ super terra sunt, morti- ficare jubet Gal. II. 3. quod alias dixit crucifigere car- nem Gal. V. 24. mortificare τὰς πράξεις τῶ σώματος per Spiritum Rom. VIII. 13. Si tamen membra corpo- rea intelligere quis malit, dicendum ad ea referri legem peccati, quod ibi tandem peccatũ se prodat, nec intra mentis & cordis claustra se contineat. Le- gis autem nomine utitur pro omni eo, quod re- git & moderatur actiones nostras: & lex mentis vocatur propensio fidelis animæ ad obedientiam divinæ legis, sic appellata, quod intus potissimum regnet; legem autem peccati & membrorum vocans alludit ad imperium, quod peccatum habet in ho- mine non regenerato plenariè, in renato verò ex par- te, nimirum in carne: quemadmodum tyranno- rum etiam statuta, quantumvis iniquissima, leges vocantur. Fallitur autem Grotius, cum per legem mentis judicium de honestis & turpibus, per legem membrorum appetitus carni continentes, per legem peccati ipsam peccandi consuetudinem intelligit. Nam lex membrorum, & lex peccati, idem sunt, ut è verbis Apostoli ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τῷ ὄντι ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι με liquet, & ut diximus, non tantùm appetitus & affectus corporis, vel sensualitatis, re- pugnantes judicio rationis designat, sed propensio- nem omnium facultatum & virium, omniumque membrorum ad malum, eandemque habitualem & intimè inhærentem, quæ imperium in nos affectat, nosque libidinis suæ mancipia reddere satagit, quam imprimis in facultatibus superioribus, mente & voluntate invenimus. Lex autem mentis est propensio hominis regeniti, quæ itidem, non in mente solùm, etsi præcipuè in ea, sed in omnibus facultatibus & viribus animæ & corporis hominis renati & fidelis constituenda est, qua incitamur & gubernamur, ut bonum amplectamur, malum fu- giamus & abominemur, qua consentimus Spiritu legi Dei, eaque delectamur. Loquitur enim hic non Judæus quidam, sub lege extra gratiam, nedum paganus, in quo pugna rationis & appetitûs, sed Apostolus, quà renatus & sub gratia, in quo pugna carnis & spiritus: ut renatus quidem, sed nondum ita renovatus, quin variis adhuc agitetur cupidita- tum carnalium fluctibus, & perpetuò cum pravæ concupiscentiæ desideriis dimicare opus habeat: adeoque sub persona sua describit conditionem & statum fidelium justificatorum per fidem in Chri- stum, quantum ad renovationem valdè adhuc im- perfectam, & cum perpetua lucta carnis & Spiri- tus conjunctam. Verba ἀντιστρατευόμενον & αἰχμα- τωτίζοντά με omnino sunt militaria, & sistuntur ita illa duo contraria principia tanquam athletæ inter se luctantes, & pugnantes Gal. V. 17. concupiscen- tiâ carnis pugnante adversus propensionem & concupiscentiam Spiritûs: cujus certaminis even- tus non rarò luctuosus est, siquidem concupiscen- tia, quæ in nobis, qua carnales adhuc sumus, vel in carne nostra habitat, vehementer dimicans adver- sus Spiritum & legem mentis nostræ nos subjugare non tantum semper, & omnibus modis atque vi- ribus conetur, sed etiam quandoque nos captivos reddat, & subjuget sub legem membrorum. Quan- quam enim verba activa sæpè non de effectu, sed de conatu exponenda sint Gen. XXXVII. 21. Deut. XXVI. 5. Actor. VII. 26. 1. Cor. X. 33. 2. Cor. X. 5. non negari tamen potest, quin quandoque præva- leat caro, & subjuget etiam renatos, etsi contra vo- luntatem eorum, ita ut præcipitet etiam eosdem in peccata voluntaria, & graviora, ut fidem excu- tiant, gratiaque Dei excidant, nonnunquam ὀλι- κῶς & totaliter, nonnunquam etiam τελικῶς & fina- liter, etiamsi verè renati, & justificati fuerint. Un- de monentur, ut sedulò vigilent, ut qui stant, vi- deant, ne cadant, ut carnis desideriis resistant ean- demque complescant, ut veterem hominem cruci- figant cum pravis suis desideriis, ut opera carnis Spi- ritu mortificent, & quæ hujus generis aliæ sunt fre- quentissimæ paræneses. Quæ omninò frustra- neæ forent, si vel lucta carnis & Spiritus in renatis locum non haberet, vel eâ positâ Spiritus semper prævaleret, nec caro nos subjugare valeret; quo- rum illud Grotius cum Pelagianis & Socinianis ad- serit, hoc vero Calviniani cum Anabaptistis con- tendunt.

## 7:24
Vers. 24. ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος. He adds an exclamation or lamentation suitable to such a man as he had described. For he is truly miserable whom the thoughts of his own mind daily beat and tear apart. ταλαίπωρος שָׁדוּד.

τίς με ῥύσεται. For the law cannot do that. Therefore liberty must be sought elsewhere.

ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου. He calls it σῶμα θανάτου not a mortal body, but metaphorically a vicious body, which he called ἁμαρτίαν above VI. 6, which is thus called σῶμα θανάτου because of the effect, because it takes away from those enslaved to it the hope of eternal life. Genitives among the Hebrews and the Hellenists imitating them are often used for adjectives, as here the body of death, that is, the death-dealing body; the odor of death, that is, a lethal odor; the tree of life, that is, the life-giving tree.

Grotius inverts everything: by flesh he understands the body, when he ought rather to understand the depravity by the phrase and style of the Apostle: but now by the body of death he understands not the mortal body itself, as the words imply, but metaphorically a depraved body, nay, even sin itself. But although it may be admitted that by death sin may be understood metonymically, because it is the cause of death, or even metaphorically, so that spiritual death is noted, and a body obnoxious to death, because that depraved concupiscence is truly the death of the soul, and renders man most deadly, so that he desires to be freed from so great an evil: yet by the voice of the body of death, depravity and sin itself are not denoted in the Grotian sense: but if anyone should wish to make the body of death a synonym for the flesh and the law of the members, as if depraved concupiscence were like some body, which consists of various members, embracing the entire structure of vices, since it includes all vices as members of the old man, at least virtually, if not formally, that would not be foreign to the sigh of the Apostle: who desires this above all, that he may be thoroughly freed from the flesh, and from the body referring to spiritual death, and bringing eternal death, and he gives thanks to God, because he procured that liberation through Jesus Christ. Thus the blessed Mylius calls the body of sin a corrupt and depraved nature, with which he struggles. Therefore he does not desire death, which would be the mark of either an imprudent or an impatient man; but he speaks of sin and corruption, and sighs that he may be rid not of the punishment, but of the sin. The blessed Balduinus, however, takes the body of death through a Hebraism for the mortal body, in which that struggle of flesh and spirit is found, as long as the vital spirit survives in it: so that he thus seeks a blessed departure, and desires to be freed from this mortal body on account of the flesh or depraved concupiscence perpetually adhering to it, and wearying itself. But in what way he does not seek to be freed from this body because it is obnoxious to diseases and mortality, but because sin dwells in this mortal body, and cannot be laid aside except with the body. Ταλαίπωρος, ὁ τλάων τὸν πῶρον: πῶρος is a callus, a stony hardness of the joints: ταλαίπωρος is miserable, afflicted, wretched. Plato: τὸν ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ τε ταλαίπωρον μοι, that is, τῷ τηλικῷ, as the Scholiast explains: whence ταλαίπωρος is one who is constantly pressed by the burdens of mournful calamities, and vexed by perpetual disturbances and internal assaults, walks about squalid and as if half-dead: See. The blessed Weller. Suidas says that πῶρον is an affliction, an evil, and misery, on the authority of Antimachus. His interpreter Æmilius Portus adds that the Eleans say πωρεῖν for πενθεῖν, that is, to mourn, to lament on account of a disaster received.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος. Addit exclamationem sive ταλανισμὸν homini tali, qua- lem descripserat, convenientem. Verè enim miser est, quem animi sui cogitationes verberant quotidiè atque dila- niant. ταλαίπωρος שָׁדוּד.

τίς με ῥύσεται. Lex enim id non potest. Aliunde ergò quærenda li- bertas.

ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου. σῶμα θανάτου vocat non corpus mortale, sed μεταφορι- κῶς corpus vitiosum, quod ἁμαρτίαν dixit supra VI. 6. quod sic ob effectum dicitur σῶμα θανάτου, quia ea mancipatis adimit spem vitæ æternæ. Genitivi Hebræis & eos imitan- tibus Hellenistis sæpè sunt pro adjectivis, ut hic corpus mortis, id est, mortiferum: odor mortis, id est, odor letha- lis; arbor vitæ, id est, vivifica.

Omnia invertit Grotius: per carnem intelligit corpus, cum vitiositatem potius phrasi & stylo Apo- stoli intelligere deberet: jam verò per corpus mor- tis non corpus ipsum mortale, ut verba inferunt, sed μεταφορικῶς corpus vitiosum, imò ἁμαρτίαν pec- catum ipsum intelligit. At quamvis admitti pos- sit per θάνατον intelligi peccatum metonymicè, quia causa est mortis, vel etiam metaphoricè, ut mors spi- ritualis notetur, & corpus morti obnoxium, quia prava illa concupiscentia verè mors animæ est, & hominem maximè mortiferum reddit, ut deside- ret à tanto malo liberari: non tamen voce corporis mortis ipsa vitiositas & peccatum denotatur sensu Grotiano: si vero quis corpus mortis Synonymum facere velit carni & legi membrorum, ut prava con- cupiscentia instar alicujus corporis, quod variis membris constat, universam vitiorum compagem, quum omnia vitia ceu membra veteris hominis saltim virtualiter, si non formaliter complectatur, non alienum id à suspirio Apostoli fuerit: qui hoc maximè desiderat, ut à carne, & corpore mortem spiritualem referente, & mortem æternam inferen- te penitus liberetur, & Deo gratias agit, quod per Christum Jesum illam liberationem procuravit. Ita B. Mylius corpus peccati appellat corruptam & vitiatam naturam, cum qua conflictetur. Non ergo mortem optat, quod vel imprudentis, vel im- patientis foret; sed de peccato & corruptione loqui- tur, & non pœna, sed peccato se defungi posse suspi- rat. B. Balduinus tamen corpus mortis per Ebraïsmum accipit pro corpore mortali, in quo pugna ista carnis & spiritus invenitur, quamdiu spiritus vitalis in eo superat: ut beatam ἀνάλυσιν ita expetat, & liberari ex hoc corpore mortali de- sideret propter carnem vel pravam concupiscen- tiam perpetuò adhærentem, & sese fatigantem. Quo vero pacto non ex corpore hoc liberari ex- petit, quia morbis & mortalitati est obnoxium, sed quia in corpore hoc mortali habitat peccatum, nec nisi cum corpore deponi potest. Ταλαίπωρος, ὁ τλάων τὸν πῶρον: πῶρος callus lapidosa durities ar- ticulorum: ταλαίπωρος miser, afflictus, ærumno- sus. Plato: τὸν ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ τε ταλαίπωρον μοι, id est, τῷ τηλικῷ, ut exponit Scholiastes: unde ταλαί- πωρος est, qui calamitatum luctuosarum oneribus premitur assiduè, & perpetuis turbationibus & incur- sationibus vexatus internis squalidus & quasi semi- mortuus incedit: Vid. B. Wellerus. Suidas πῶρον di- cit ærumnam esse, malum & miseriam authoritate Antimach. Interpres ejus Æmilius Portus addit πωρεῖν Elei dicunt pro πενθεῖν, id est, lugere, pro- pter cladem acceptam lamentari.

## 7:25
Verse 25. I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.) These things are clearly to be read as a parenthesis, which being omitted, the rest coheres with what follows. But the Apostle interposed that parenthesis, just as he did another above at III. 6., to cut off the handle from those who wrongly interpret his words, as if he were to say, I indeed [say] these things in the first person out of a certain modesty: But in truth, if I must speak of myself without metaphor, I am not the man who feels such lacerations, since God has liberated me through Jesus Christ, that is, through the Gospel and His Spirit, from that body of sin, for which I give thanks both to the Father as the supreme cause, and to Christ as the subordinate cause. Origen, whom Ambrose and other ancients follow, rightly explained this passage. We have had the thanksgiving expressed in equal words above at I. 8.

ἄρα οὖν ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ.

Not I myself, but that I, that is, that man whom he described under the pronoun of the first person. Thus in a table of relationships, the hypothetical person is called 'I' by others.

τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ Θεῦ.

He says that he serves the law of God, because he is compelled to confess that it is good.

τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας.

Because the flesh or body provides service to custom, and carries out its dictates. Flesh is properly a part of the body, but it is very often taken for the body, as you will see if you compare Leviticus 16:27 with Hebrews 13:11. And thus certain ancients, commemorating the institution of the Eucharist, say that Christ said, This is my flesh.

This is now mere distortion and depravation of the Apostolic sentiment; for not only is the text torn apart by a violent method, but the mind and intention of the Apostle are twisted into a sense that is clearly alien. According to the text, the person who complains about the evil adjacent to him and desires to be liberated from it is not different from the one who gives thanks for the liberation, but it is one and the same person, the same Apostle, which the pronoun of the first person, used perpetually without variation or designation of another person, teaches; and so that we may not doubt it, after the same thanksgiving, the holy Apostle, repeating the sum, names himself again, and that more emphatically: 'I myself' (ipse ego): where Grotius tries in vain to escape by distinguishing those, 'I myself' and 'that I': because it is most manifest that the Apostle is speaking of himself, nor does any trace of another person appear. Nor does it stand in the way that the same person who laments so miserably gives thanks. For this contrary affection of sadness and joy, of lamentation and thanksgiving, is born from consideration: for before he had looked at sin, hence there was matter for groaning; here he looks at grace, from which matter for triumph is born. Thus, gathering himself from the midst of his groaning, he sings a joyful song of victory for his liberation: which, even if he has not yet obtained it in its fullness, which we shall finally possess in the blessed dissolution, whence he sighs and desires that liberation: he nevertheless had it, not only by reason of merit, but also in the undoubted hope and foretaste and preliminary draught of heavenly happiness; indeed, he even had a gracious liberation in act by the virtue of the merit of Christ, both in the liberation from the guilt and condemnation of sin through justification, and in the gracious assistance of the Holy Spirit through sanctification, so that he might be able to extricate himself more and more from the snares and attempts of the flesh, to resist them, and by destroying the outer man, be more fully renewed day by day according to the inner man. Although, however, one must always struggle with the concupiscence of the flesh, and the remnants of the old self still adhere to us, those are nevertheless so covered by the cloak of the justice of Christ that they do not come into the sight of God, and there is nothing of condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus through faith. Thanks are therefore also given, because he has been liberated from the servitude of sin; whence it is that he can serve the law of God according to the mind or the inner man, whereas otherwise in the state of sin before regeneration we serve nothing but the law of sin. The Apostle therefore testifies that it is to be credited to that liberation made through Christ that he can serve the law of God with his mind: and although he still serves the law of sin with his flesh, he has to expect a plenary liberation even from the incentive of sin and

sense. That explanation is also cold, that he serves the law of God who is compelled to confess it to be good: for this is not to serve, unless we also wish to say that the Devil thus serves the law of God, and any most flagitious person whatsoever. For both the Devil, and every most wicked person, is compelled to confess that the law of God is good. Nor is the exposition of the other member any better: To serve the law of sin with the flesh; because the flesh, or body, offers service to the custom of sin, and executes its dictates; for not only the body obeys the custom of sinning, but primarily the soul: and it has already been warned before that by flesh here the body, or by the law of sin the custom of sinning, is not denoted. But let these things suffice concerning Chapter VII.

Latin:

Vers. 25. εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν.) Hæc planè per παρενθήκην legenda, qua omissa cætera cum sequentibus cohærent. Illam autem παρενθήκην interposuit Apostolus, sicut & aliam su- pra III. 6. ad ansam præcidendam malè verba sua capien- tibus quasi dicat, ego quidem hæc in prima persona per modestiam quandam elocutus sum : At revera si sine figura mihi de memetipso loquendum sit, non is ego sum, qui tales laniatus sentiam, cum Deus me per Jesum Christum, id est, per Evangelium & Spiritum ejus, ab isto corpore peccati liberarit, unde & Patri ut summæ causæ, & Christo ut causæ subordinatæ gratias ago. Ita rectè hunc locum explicavit Origenes, quem Ambrosius & veteres alii sequuntur. Gratiarum actionem paribus expressam verbis habuimus supra I. 8.

ἄρα οὖν ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ.

Non ipse ego, sed ille ego, id est, is homo, quem sub primæ personæ pronomine descripsit. Sic in tabula cognationum ὁ ὑποθέτικὸς ab aliis vocatur ego.

τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ Θεῦ.

Servire illum dicit legi Dei, quia eam bonam fateri cogitur.

τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας.

Quia caro sive corpus consuetudini ministerium præbet, ejusque dictata exsequitur. Caro proprie est pars corporis, sed sæpissime pro corpore sumitur, ut videbis, si conferas Levit. XVI. 27. cum Hebr. XIII. 11. Et sic quidam veteres commemorantes institutionem Eucharistiæ, ajunt Christum dixisse, Hæc est caro mea.

Hæc jam mera στρεβλότης est, & depravatio sententiæ Apostolicæ; non enim tantum discerpitur textus violentâ ratione, sed & mens, & intentio Apostoli in plane alienum sensum detorquetur. Secundùm textum non diversa est persona, quæ queritur de malo sibi adjacente, & desiderat ab eo liberari, & quæ gratias agit pro liberatione, sed est una eademq; persona, idem Apostolus, quod pronomen primæ personæ perpetuò adhibitum sine variatione aut alterius personæ designatione docet, ac ne dubitemus de eo, post eandem gratiarum actionem, summam repetens S. Apostolus, se denuò nominat, idq; ἐμφατικωτέρως: ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ ipse ego: ubi effugere frustrà conatur Grotius, distinguens illa, ipse ego, & ille ego : quia manifestissimum est, de sese Apostolum loqui, nec ullum apparet alterius personæ vestigium. Neque verò obstat, quod gratias agat idem, qui tam miserabiliter lamentatur. Nam contrarius hic tristitiæ & lætitiæ, lamentationis, & gratiarum actionis affectus ex consideratione nascitur: Ante enim peccatum respexerat, hinc gemitûs fuit materia; Hìc in gratiam respicit, ex quo triumphi materia nascitur. Ita ex medio gemitu se recolligens ἐπινίκιον lætum canit pro liberatione: quam & si plenariam nondum obtinuerit, quâ in beata ἀναλύσει demùm potimur, unde suspirat & desiderat eam liberationem: habebat tamen non tantùm ratione meriti, sed etiam in spe indubitata & προγεύσει ac προποτισμῷ cœlestis felicitatis, imò habebat etiam actu gratiosam liberationem virtute meriti Christi, tum in liberatione à reatu & condemnatione peccati, per justificationem, tum in assistentia Spiritus S. gratiosa per sanctificationem, ut magis magisque à carnis insidiis, & conatibus sese expedire, eisdem resistere, & hominem exteriorem destruendo secundùm interiorem hominem plenius de die in diem renovari possit. Quamvis verò cum concupiscentia carnis semper colluctandum sit, & reliquiæ vetustatis nobis adhuc adhæreant, illæ tamen justitiæ Christi pallio ita teguntur, ut in conspectum Dei non veniant, nihilque in iis condemnationis sit, qui per fidem sunt in Christo Jesu. Gratiæ ergò etiam aguntur, quod liberatus à peccati servitute sit; unde est, quod possit servire legi Dei secundum mentem vel hominem interiorem, quum alias in statu peccati ante regenerationem nonnisi peccati legi serviamus. Testatur ergo Apostolus, liberationi isti per Christum factæ acceptum ferendum esse, quod mente servire possit legi Dei: & quamvis adhuc carne legi peccati serviat, expectare habeat plenariam liberationem etiam à peccati fomite &

sensu. Frigida etiam est illa explicatio, servire legi Dei illum, qui eam bonam fateri cogitur: nam hoc non est servire, nisi etiam Diabolum ita legi Dei servire & quemvis omnino flagitiosissimum dicere velimus. Nam & Diabolus, & nemo non sceleratissimus fateri cogitur, legem Dei bonam esse. Neque melior est alterius membri ἔκθεσις: Carne servire legi peccati; quod caro, sive corpus, consuetudini peccati ministerium praebeat, ejusque dictata exequatur; non enim corpus tantum consuetudini peccandi paret, sed imprimis anima: neque per carnem hic corpus, vel per legem peccati consuetudinem peccandi notari jam ante monitum. Sed haec de Capite VII. sufficiant.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

On the occasion of thanksgiving for liberation by Christ, the Apostle returns to the exhibition of grace in Christ, by which those who are through faith in Christ Jesus, and walk according to the Spirit, are immune from condemnation, having been liberated from the law of sin and death: the causes of which liberation he explains: and he treats particularly of the Subject, the faithful walking not according to the flesh but the Spirit, and of the ultimate end, eternal life: and in that way he confirms the certainty of the hope of glory from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, from the evidence of sufferings, from the sighing and desire of all creatures, and primarily of the reborn themselves, aided by the Spirit, and also from the eternal purpose of God, and the Mediatorial office of Christ, and finally concludes that the faithful can be torn away by nothing from the grace or love of God in Christ Jesus.

There are two parts: The former concerning the exhibition of grace in Christ up to verse 14 inclusive. The latter concerning the certainty of the hope of glory from verse 15 to the end. B. Mylius makes three parts according to the ratio of the three obstacles to hope: so that in the first the Apostle may explode the terrors of the law; in the second he may demolish the reefs of adversities; in the third he may remove the scruples of infirmities, and show that all these things are invalid for weakening the hope of the pious.

PART I. Concerning the exhibition of grace in Christ.

The Apostle had celebrated, around the end of the preceding chapter, God, who delivers us through Jesus Christ from the body of this death, concerning which grace he had vehemently complained: And therefore, since in the primary treatment, after the doctrine concerning gratuitous justification through faith in Christ had been set forth, he had handed down something concerning the preservation of justified believers in grace, how they consist in it, and glory in the hope of future glory in chapter V, he had around that former point concerning the preservation of justifying grace cleared up the doubts intervening in the doctrine concerning gratuitous justification, as for instance then in chapter VI, whether one must persevere in sin so that grace may be more efficacious? and whether it is permitted for those who are not under the law, but under grace, to sin? then in chapter VII, how we are not under the law: and what the law pertains to the reborn, and primarily, how impossible it is for the law, which is spiritual, to be fulfilled even by those who are reborn, since they must perpetually struggle against the flesh: to whom, however, the grace of God in Christ uniquely provides aid. And the Apostle has dealt with these things thus far diligently, and in such a way that he would never lose sight of the principal theme concerning Justification through faith, and would firmly assert it, which is not undermined by the discussion of those doubts, but is more and more established. To this treatment, therefore, instituted for the confirmation of the justified in grace, he now returns, those doubts having been resolved: since he teaches further, both a priori, that there is no condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus through faith, even if they sometimes unwillingly serve the law of sin, and a posteriori, that they walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, he proves the same v. 1. A priori from the Evangelical doctrine, through which we are freed from the law of sin and death, he deduces this v. 2. Clarifying the causes of this redemption v. 3. 4. both κατ' ἄφσιν, that this was impossible for the law; namely, by way of the proper fulfillment of the law: and κατὰ θέσιν; the principal cause of the grace of God, the meritorious one, the Son of God sent into the flesh, in whom He satisfied for sin, and fulfilled the law for us: the formal one, of the fulfillment of the law imputed to us; which he had already taught sufficiently abundantly that it is done through faith; the material one, or of the Subject, that they are those who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit: whence a posteriori he undertakes to prove the confirmation in grace from the study of the holy life of the justified; from the contrary fruit of the carnal and spiritual φρόνημα v. 5. 6. 7. 8. and the indwelling of the Spirit of God and of Christ in the faithful, and its own adjunct, spiritual life, v. 9. 10. and its effect, resurrection to eternal life v. 11. with an added admonition concerning the duty of the reborn, that they should not live according to the flesh, lest they die, but by the spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh, and lead a spiritual life v. 12. 13. since this is the property of the sons of God, to be led by the Spirit of God, v. 14.

Vers. 1. Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα.) He repeats the discourse which he had left at the end, as these things are now read, of the sixth chapter; for there he had said that eternal life is certainly laid up for those who order their life according to the Gospel. Here an objection immediately occurred: But many Christians do not observe the law of Moses; they are not גרי צדק. Paul now answers, that it is so far from the case that they are subject to divine condemnation on that account, that not even the Jews are held by the law of Moses any longer, if only they understand their own goods, and live according to the prescription of Christ. Κατάκριμα here, as also above V. 16., is the same as death VI, 23., namely eternal.

Τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ πνεῦμα.) To those who, through Jesus Christ, or through the Gospel, have been brought so far that they do not go where the affections of the flesh drag them, without discrimination, but having obtained the Holy Spirit, constantly obey His customs.

It is not a question here of the attainment of eternal life through the observance of the commandments of God, because that we can attain life in such a way is repugnant to the whole Apostolic treatment; indeed, the Apostle teaches here entirely that the fulfillment of the law is impossible even for the reborn; nor is it treated here in any word whether Christians are held to observe the Ceremonial law of Moses, as גרי צדק, strangers or proselytes of righteousness, much less is it taught that the Jews are no longer held by the law of Moses: but this is what the Apostle delivers, that we are all immune from the curse and condemnation of the law, as many as are in Christ Jesus, in whom, however, we are not, except through faith in Him, indicating those who are in Christ, namely τοὺς ἐν χρισῷ ὄντας. To whom we are grafted through Baptism Gal. III. 27. and are made His children through faith John I. 12. not that the sin which dwells in us is not worthy of condemnation, which the Papists wish, but that it does not result in condemnation for us, who receive the grace exhibited to us in Christ by true faith, and so take care, lest by walking according to the flesh we fall from the same. The Apostle does not say that there is no sin, nothing condemnable in the reborn, but no condemnation. For although there are certain sins in them, which by their nature are indeed damnable: yet condemnation has no place, and it is certain that not the sin but only the guilt is removed. Namely, he teaches that no condemnation is to be feared by the faithful, however much sin may still adhere to them. Concerning which see Bened. Justinian. in h. l. although in truth there are also in the just impure motions, which have their origin from a depraved nature, they are not however imputed to them, but are pardoned through faith in Christ. Furthermore, it is one thing to serve the law of sin in the flesh, when one serves the law of God with the mind, which is affirmed of the reborn, because they are not entirely spiritual, chap. VI. v. ult., another thing to walk not according to the spirit, but according to the flesh, which has no place in the reborn, nor can it consist with the grace of God or justifying faith. Because there is an unwilling servitude, here a voluntary occupation in executing those things which the flesh dictates: for to walk implies the study and voluntary and malicious frequenting of sin Ps. I. 1. There the flesh indeed struggles against the spirit but does not predominate over it, here however the flesh predominates. The reborn therefore, even if they still feel the weaknesses of the flesh, do not however walk according to the flesh, or indulge in carnal desires.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Occasione εὐχαριστίας pro liberatione Christi, redit Apostolus ad gratiae in Christo exhibitionem, qua immunes sunt à condemnatione, qui per fidem in Christo Jesu sunt, & secundum Spiritum ambulant, liberati à lege peccati, & mortis: cujus liberationis causas explicat: & de Subjecto, fidelibus non secundum carnem sed Spiritum ambulantibus, & fine ultimo, vitâ aeternâ peculiariter tractat: eoque pacto spei gloriae certitudinem à Spiritûs S. testimonio, passionum τεκμηρίῳ, creaturarum omnium, ipsorumque imprimis renatorum suspirio & desiderio, à Spiritu adjuto, nec non ab aeterno Dei proposito, officioque Christi Mediatorio confirmat, & denique fideles nullâ re divelli à gratia vel dilectione Dei in Christo Jesu posse concludit.

PArtes duae sunt: Prior de gratiae in Christo exhibitione usque ad v. 14. inclus. Posterior de spei gloriae certitudine v. 15. usque ad finem. B. Mylius tres partes facit pro ratione trium obstaculorum spei: ut in prima terriculamenta legis displodat Apostolus; in secunda adversitatum scopulos demoliatur; in tertia infirmitatum scrupulos eximat, & haec omnia ad infirmandam spem piorum invalida esse ostendat.

PARS I. De gratiae in Christo exhibitione.

Celebrarat Apost. circa finem cap. praecedentis Deum, qui nos à corpore mortis istius, cujus gratia vehementer questus erat, per Jesum Christum liberat: Ideoque quum in primaria tractatione, post expositam doctrinam de gratuita per fidem in Christum justificatione, de fidelium justificatorum in gratia conservatione, quomodo in ea consistant, & de spe gloriae futurae glorientur cap. V. aliquid tradiderit, circa prius illud de gratiae justificantis conservatione expedivit dubia doctrinae de gratuita justificatione intercedentia, utpote tum cap. VI. anne in peccato perseverandum sit, ut gratia sit efficacior? & anne illis, qui non sub lege, sed sub gratia sunt, peccare liceat? tum cap. VII. quomodo non simus sub lege: & quid lex renatos attineat, atque imprimis, quam impossibile sit, legem, quae spiritualis est, ab iis etiam, qui renati sunt, impleri, quippe quibus perpetud dimicandum est adversus carnem: quibus verò unicè subvenit gratia Dei in Christo. Et haec hactenus sedulo, atque ita egit Apostol. ut principale thema de Justificatione, per fidem, nunquam non respiceret, solideq; adse- reret, quod per dubiorum illorum discussionem non subruitur, sed magis magisque stabilitur. Ad hanc ergo tractationem ob justificatorum confir- mationem in gratia institutam nunc, dubiis illis so- lutis, redit: cum porrò tum à priori, quod nihil condemnationis in illis sit, qui per fidem in Christo Jesu sunt, etsi inviti quandoq; legi peccati serviant, docet, tum à posteriori, quòd non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum ambulent, idem comprobat v. 1. A priori è doctrinâ Evangelicâ, per quam libe- ramur à lege peccati & mortis, id deducit v. 2. Causas hujus redemptionis dilucidans v. 3. 4. tum κατ' ἄφ- σιν, quod impossibile hoc legi fuerit; nimirum per modum propriæ impletionis legis: tum κατὰ θέσιν; causa principalis gratiæ Dei, meritoria, Filii Dei in carnem missi, in quâ satisfecit pro peccato, & im- plevit legem pro nobis: formalis, imputatæ nobis impletionis legis; quod per fidem fieri jam satis abundè docuerat; materialis, vel Subjecti, quod illi sunt, qui non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiri- tum ambulant: unde à posteriori è studio vitæ sanctæ justificatorum in gratia confirmationem probare aggreditur; à carnalis & spiritualis φρονήματος contrario fructu v. 5. 6. 7. 8. & Spiritus Dei ac Christi in fidelibus inhabitatione, ejusque tum proprio ad- juncto, spirituali vitâ, v. 9. 10. tum effectu, resuscita- tione ad æternam vitam v. 11. addita comonitione, de renatorum debito, ut scil. non vivant secundum carnem, ne moriantur, sed spiritu carnis opera mor- tificent, & vitam spiritualem peragant v. 12. 13. si- quidem hoc sit filiorum Dei proprium, Spiritu Dei agi, v. 14.

Vers. 1. Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα.) Repetit sermonem, quem reliquerat fine, ut nunc ista leguntur, capitis sexti; namque ibi dixerat, vitam æternam illis certo esse reposi- tam, qui secundum Evangelium vitam suam instituunt. Hic statim occurrebat objectio: Atqui multi Christiano- rum legem Mosis non observant; non sunt גרי צדק. Respondet jam Paulus, tantum abesse, ut ob id damnationi divinæ subjaceant, ut ne Judæi quidem lege Mosis ampliùs teneantur, si modò bona sua intelligant, & ex præscripto Christi vivant. Κατάκριμα hic ut & supra V. 16. est idem, quod mors VI, 23. nempè æterna.

Τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ πνεῦμα.) Iis, qui per Jesum Christum, sive per Evangelium eousque perducti sunt, ut non eant, quo carnis affectus ra- piunt, sine discrimine, sed Spiritum S. adepti, ejus moribus constanter obsequantur.

Non hîc de vitæ æternæ per observantiam præ- ceptorum Dei consequutione agitur, quia ita nos vitam consequi posse, toti tractationi Apostolicæ repugnat, imò impossibilem legis impletionem etiam renatis esse, hic omninò docet Apostolus; nec de eo, an Christiani teneantur legem Mosis Ce- remonialem, ut גרי צדק advenæ vel proselyti justi- tiæ, observare ullo verbo hîc tractatur, multò mi- nùs docetur nec Judæos ampliùs lege Mosis teneri: sed hoc est, quod tradit Apostolus, nos omnes à legis maledictione & condemnatione immunes esse, quot- quot in Christo Jesu sumus, in quo verò non su- mus, nisi per fidem in ipsum, τοὺς ἐν χρισῷ scil. ὄντας, Christo insitos indigitans. Cui inserimur per Ba- ptismum Gal. III. 27. ejusque filii reddimur per fi- dem Joh. I. 12. non quod peccatum, quod in nobis habitat, non sit condemnatione dignum, quod Pa- pistæ volunt, sed quod in condemnationem nobis id non cedat, qui gratiam in Christo nobis exhibi- tam verâ fide suscipimus, adeoq; cavemus, ne am- bulando secundum carnem eâdem excidamus. Non dicit Apost. nullum peccatum, nihil condemnabile esse in renatis, sed nihil damnationis. Nam quam- vis peccata quædam in ipsis sint, quæ naturâ suâ damnabilia utique sunt: tamen condemnatio lo- cum non habet, & non peccatum sed reatum tantum tolli certum est. Nimirum fidelibus nullam metuendam esse condemnationem docet, utut iis adhuc adhæreat peccatum. Quo de Bened. Justinian. in h. l. quanquam revera etiam in justis motus impuri, qui à naturâ depravatâ ortum habent, insunt, non tamen iis feruntur impensi, sed per Christi fidem condonantur. Cæterum aliud est servire carne legi peccati, cum legi Dei mente servitur, quod de renatis, quia non prorsus spirituales sunt, affirmatur cap. VI. v. ult. aliud ambulare non secundum spiritum, sed secundum carnem, quod in renatis locum non habet, nec cum gratia Dei aut fide justificante consistere potest. Quia ibi invita servitus est, hìc voluntaria in iis, quæ caro dictitat, exequendis occupatio: nam τὸ ambulare studium, & frequentationem peccati voluntariam & malitiosam infert Pf. I. 1. Ibi caro luctatur quidem adversus spiritum non autem ei prædominatur, hìc verò prædominatur caro. Renati ergò etsi imbecillitates carnis adhuc sentiant, non tamen secundum carnem ambulant, aut carnalibus desideriis indulgent.

## 8:2
Vers. 2. ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος.) So much more perfect than the law of the mind, as the new creation surpasses the old: so much also more perfect than the law of Moses, as the solid law excels the shadows.

τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.) τῆς ζωῆς, that is, ζωοποιοῦ, of that Spirit, I say, who leads to eternal life, which Christ is about to give.

ἠλευθέρωσέ με ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου) He has freed me (that is, any truly Christian person. For now he uses the first person in another sense) first from the habit of sinning, then also from eternal death, which necessarily follows that habit. For by the word of sin here, nothing comes except τὰ προαιρετὰ, as Clement explains Strom. II. Thus ἁμαρτάνειν is also taken in the epistle of John.

By the law of the mind is not designated the natural judgment concerning the honest and the base, as Grotius was persuaded, but the propensity to render obedience to the divine law, opposed to the law of sin, or of the propensity to sin, and of the depraved concupiscence, which is in our members: but by the law of the spirit of life we admit that the doctrine of the Gospel itself is noted, which is also in the commentary of Ambrose. is explained, as the name of law is wont to be used generally for doctrine; which doctrine is of the Spirit, both concerning life in Christ Jesus, objectively, and formally νόμος ζωοποιῶν a vivifying law, but solely in Christ Jesus, and his obedience and merit, whether this epithet is to be referred to the πνεῦμα, or to the νόμον τοῦ πνεύματος, because it is of this νόμος that we are treating here as the τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ and proper subject, and to the same that liberation is attributed ὀργανικῶς, by which we have been liberated from the law of sin, from depraved concupiscence, and thus also from every sin redundant therefrom, but not indeed only from the custom of sinning and proaretic sins, as also from the law of death. For we are not liberated from other sins by one reason, and from proaretic sins and the custom of sinning by another, but there is one and the same liberation from all sins according to Evangelical doctrine: namely, through the death of Christ as regards acquisition, and through faith in Christ, as regards application, or the actual remission of sins and justification: Since there is need for the gratuitous remission of all sins; and it is necessary to obtain the remission of all sins through faith in Christ, Acts 10:43.

Furthermore, in the primeval creation, when man was created in the image and likeness of God, it is certain that the law of the mind was not imperfect but perfect, from the nature of the image of God and the concreated Original Justice, to which we are renewed by the new creation, as the Apostle testifies in Eph. 4:24. But the Gospel is different in its whole genus from the law impressed in the primeval creation, and from the Mosaic law, which as it is here It is not the Ceremonial one that is being viewed, having a shadow of things to come, but the Moral one, content with the Decalogue: for the Gospel is a proclamation freely of the remission of sins and the righteousness of Christ: for which there was no need in the state of primeval integrity, nor could it be imbued in any way through the moral law, as it is something of which the moral law knows nothing, notifying nothing but sin, and working wrath and condemnation, whence the law and the Gospel are most poorly confounded by Grotius in the Pelagian, Socinian, and Papistic manner, whence also not inappropriately the blessed Mylius, the blessed Balduinus, and others understand the Mosaic law by the law of sin and death, from which is the recognition of sin and death and condemnation.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος.) Tantò perfectior lege mentis, quantum nova creatio superat veterem: tantò etiam perfectior lege Mosis, quantum lex solida præstat umbris.

τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.) τῆς ζωῆς, id est, ζωοποιοῦ, illius inquam Spiritus, qui ad vitam æternam ducit, quam Christus daturus est.

ἠλευθέρωσέ με ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου) Liberavit me (id est, quemvis verè Christianum. Jam enim primam personam alio sensu usurpat) primum à peccandi consuetudine, deinde etiam à morte æterna, quæ consuetudinem illam necessario sequitur. Nam peccati voce hic non veniunt nisi τὰ προαιρετὰ, ut explicat Clemens Strom. II. Sic ἁμαρτάνειν etiam in Johannis epistola sumitur.

Per legem mentis non naturale judicium de honestis & turpibus, uti persuasus fuit Grotius, sed propensio ad obsequium legi divinæ præstandum, opposita legi peccati, vel propensionis ad peccandum, & concupiscentiæ pravæ, quæ est in membris nostris, designatur: per legem autem spiritus vitæ ipsam Evangelii doctrinam notari admittimus, quæ & in Ambros. comment. exponitur, uti legis nomen generaliter usurpari pro doctrina solet; quæ doctrina Spiritûs est, tum de vita in Christo Jesu, objectivè, tum formaliter νόμος ζωοποιῶν lex vivificans, sed unicè in Christo Jesu, ejusq; obedientia & merito, sive ad πνεῦμα, sive ad νόμον τοῦ πνεύματος hoc epitheton referendum, quia de hoc νόμῳ hic ceu τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ & subjecto proprio agitur, eidemque liberatio illa tribuitur ὀργανικῶς, quâ à lege peccati, à prava concupiscentia, adeoque etiam omni peccato inde redundante, non verò tantum à peccandi consuetudine & proareticis peccatis, ut & à lege mortis liberati sumus. Non enim alia ratione à cæteris peccatis liberamur, aliâ à peccatis proareticis & peccandi consuetudine, sed una eademque est secundum doctrinam Evangelicam à peccatis omnibus liberatio: per mortem sc. Christi quantum ad acquisitionem, & per fidem in Christum, quantum ad applicationem, vel actualem peccatorum remissionem & justificationem: Quum omnium peccatorum gratuita remissione opus sit; & omnium peccatorum remissionem per fidem in Christum consequi oporteat, Act. X. 38.

Porrò in creatione primævâ cum homo conditus est ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei, non imperfectam sed perfectam fuisse legem mentis è naturâ imaginis Dei, & Justitiæ Originalis concreatæ certum est, ad quam creatione nova renovamur, teste Apostolo Eph. IV. 24. Evangelium verò toto genere diversum est à lege in primævâ creatione impressa, & à lege Mosaica, quæ prout hîc spectatur non illa Ceremonialis est, umbram ha- bens rerum futurarum, sed Moralis Decalogo con- tenta: nam Evangelium est concio gratis de re- missione peccatorum & justitia Christi: qua nec in flatu primævæ integritatis opus fuit, nec per legem moralem quicquam ullatenus imbui potuit, utpo- te de qua lex moralis nihil novit, non nisi pecca- tum notificans, & iram atque condemnationem operans, unde pessime lex & Evangelium a Gro- tio more Pelagiano & Sociniano ac Papistico, con- funditur, unde etiam non incommode B. Mylius, B. Balduinus & alii per legem peccati & mortis le- gem Mosaïcam intelligunt, ex qua est agnitio pec- cati & mors ac condemnatio.

## 8:3
Vers. 3. τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆ νόμο ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρ- κός. This refers not to any noun, but to the whole complex that follows, such a construction as we also had recently at VII. 21. For this is what it says: that which Christ performed, the law of Moses could not perform, because the flesh, that is, the carnal affections of the Jews, had carried away its strength. See Acts XIII. 38 & Heb. IX. 15. The Latin translated τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆ νόμῳ well: For what was impossible to the law. For the possessive case added to such adjectives is worth the same as the dative: just as the evil of man and the evil to man are the same. ἀσθένει, it could not, it failed, בָּשָׁל. In a similar sense τὸ ἀσθε- νὲς τῆς ἐντολῆς is said in Heb. VII. 18. ἐν ᾧ here means 'because,' in the Hebrew manner.

This annotation is correct: provided that 'flesh' is not restricted to the carnal affections of the Jews, as it belongs to everyone, without distinction of Jews and Gentiles, and is still found even in the regenerate, as is evident from the preceding chapter and Gal. V. 17. Nor can Grotius deny that the first person is used here of any Christian or regenerate person. But there is no reason why he should take it in a different sense than in the preceding chapter; indeed, it is most clear that one and the same Apostle is speaking both here and there, and setting himself as an example of the regenerate, who, just as he had previously proposed himself as an example of infirmity and imperfection, so now he constitutes himself an example of consolation.
