Moreover, the προκαταρκτικὴ (preliminary) cause is noted here, by which the necessity of the intervention of such a great advocate is shown. For only two modes of bringing salvation in general are signified to have a place, of which the one is τῶ ἀκριβοδικαίῳ, which consists in the perfect observation of the divine law: the other τῆς ἐπιεικείας, which implies the gratuitous mercy of God. The Apostle pronounces the former mode to have been ἀδύνατον, not indeed simply and in itself (for the law, just as it contains the perfect norm of divine justice, so it promises life and salvation to its observers) but κατὰ τι κὶ ἐκ τῶ συμβεβηκότος: insofar as this ἀδυναμία (impossibility) comes to it from human infirmity. For the law could save, if it could be kept by men. But because it cannot, neither can it save. Whence the former mode of salvation is left to be impossible. Impelled therefore by necessity itself, God is shown to have embraced the other mode of bringing human salvation, as the blessed Mylius has it here on p. 278. Philippus has it thus: The grammatical syntax must be correctly explained. This is its series: Since it was impossible for the law, namely to take away sin, because the law could not be done through the flesh, God sent his son, etc.

ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτῦ ὑιὸν πέμψας. Namely, into the world. But God is said to send when he gives commands, as we said at John IV. 34. See also Jer. I. 7.

That mission is not only to be restricted, with the Socinians, to commands or the imposition and instruction of an office, but since the Son of God was sent from heaven into the world, it involves both his pre-existence before the ἐνσάρκωσιν (incarnation) and the incarnation itself, although with relation to the office which was entrusted to him, as we showed in the Exercitation on the προϋπάρξει (pre-existence) of the Son of GOD.

ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας. That is, that he might be treated in such a way as guilty ones are accustomed to be treated, Isa. LIII. 12, Mark XV. 28, Phil. II. 8.

Τὸ ὁμοίωμα σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας does not look only to the passion of Christ, that he was treated in such a way as guilty ones are accustomed to be treated, which could not even have happened unless he had taken our sin and guilt upon himself, without which also τὸ ὁμοίωμα σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας could not be attributed to him: nor does it designate only the likeness of our nature, that Christ is only ὁμοιώσιος (of like substance) to us, not ὁμούσιος (of the same substance), which is repugnant to the truth of Christ's human nature, and indeed even to our redemption: for τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον (that which is not assumed is not healed), as the rule of antiquity has it: but the Son of God is said to be sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, because while assuming true flesh or human nature consubstantial with us, he nevertheless had to be made similar to our sinful flesh, but without sin: because, being destitute of his own sin, since he knew no sin, and was that holy of holies, from the very first moment of conception, he willed to take our sin upon himself, so that he might be made sin for us, or a sacrifice for sin. That is therefore called ὁμοίωμα or likeness, not of flesh simply, but of sinful flesh. But Grotius rashly excludes this taking upon himself of our sins here, just as he also noted at Luke II. 22, that it signifies neither vice nor fault, but the condition of a mortal body in this place. Which, however, does not at all suit the use of the word ἁμαρτίας. And although that likeness of sinful flesh, in which Christ came, altogether embraces the mortal condition and other θνητὰς δυσχερείας (mortal difficulties), which Christ voluntarily took upon himself, yet the taking upon himself of our sin is not to be excluded, but included: so that the likeness of sinful flesh is attributed to him both by reason of guilt and by reason of misery and the punishment also taken upon himself for us.

καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας) For sins: for it is the same as διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα above IV. 25. Thus περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν 1 Cor. XV. 3 & Gal. I. 4, and thus the Syrian rightly accepted these words.

κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ) By his own flesh, that is to say, delivered to death, he killed sin. For κατακρίνειν is used for to kill, just as κατάκριμα for death, because the condemned are accustomed to be killed: he killed it indeed, that is, he provided us with the strength to kill it. To kill is to take away its efficiency. Thus there is here a μετάληψις, or a multiplication of figures. See what is above at IV. 25. It is, however, cleverly said. He himself, who seemed to be condemned by sin, condemned sin.

Others take these words περὶ ἁμαρτίας as referring to the sacrifice for sin: because Christ willed to be made a victim for us and for our sins. Thus Philippus: Let the phrase be observed: God condemned our sin in the flesh for sin, that is, in Christ the victim, offered for sin. For the phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας signifies a sacrifice for sin. Thus in Leviticus the Greek reading always speaks, and in the same way in the Greek reading of Isaiah it is said: ἐὰν δῶται περὶ ἁμαρτίας ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ ὄψεται σπέρμα μακρόβιον. In the Hebrew text the preposition is not added, but it is read thus: Because he shall place his soul as a sin-offering, he shall see long-lived seed. But from the Greek reading of Leviticus the phrase περὶ ἁμαρτίας is most well-known. But why we should admit a double figure in the verb κατακρίνειν here, no reason appears: so that, for instance, first κατακρίνειν should be understood as killing, and furthermore killing as the provision of strength to kill, when the proper meaning of condemnation, which occurs in v. 1, has a place: Namely, God condemned the merits of sins or sins as the meritorious cause, which had earned the condemnation of us all, in our flesh or nature assumed by the only-begotten Son, inasmuch as he had taken upon himself the sins of us all, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν the sin of the world, which he himself as that Lamb of God was bearing, John I. 29. But it is not said that the Son of God himself, who seemed to be condemned by sin, condemned sin, but

God condemned sin in His Son, in the flesh assumed by Him, inasmuch as He willed to bear our sin, was bound to, and therefore also to pay for the same. Philip notes this emphasis in the word condemned: As a judge condemning a murderer first pronounces him guilty, afterwards executes him: So God, condemning sin, when the innocent Son was made a victim, first snatched from sin the authority to accuse us, afterwards destroys it entirely, when He renders to us eternal life and complete righteousness.

Latin:

Vers. 3. τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆ νόμο ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρ- κός. Hoc refertur non ad nomen aliquod, sed ad totum com- plexum quod sequitur, qualem constructionem & modo habuimus VII. 21. Hoc enim dicit: id quod Christus præ- stitit, nequisse legem Mosis præstare, quia caro, id est, car- nales Judæorum affectus vires ejus retulerant. Vide Act. XIII 3.8. & Hebr. IX. 15. τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆ νόμῳ bene tran- stulit Latinus: Nam quod impossibile erat legi. Casus enim possessivus talibus adjectivis additus, idem valet, quod dati- vus: sicut idem est malum hominis & malum homini. ἀσθένει minus potuit, excidit, בָּשָׁל. Pari sensu τὸ ἀσθε- νὲς τῆς ἐντολῆς dicitur Hebr. VII. 18. ἐν ᾧ hic valet, quia, more Hebraico.

Recte se habet hæc annotatio: modo caro non ad carnales Judæorum affectus restringatur, utpote quæ omnium est, sine discrimine Judæorum & gen- tium, & in renatis etiam adhuc reperitur, ut e cap. præced. & Gal. V. 17. constat. Neque enim diffiteri potest Grotius primam personam hic de quovis Christiano vel renato adhiberi. Cur vero alio sensu accipiat ut cap. præced. ratio nulla est; imo unum eundemq; Apostolum & hic & illic lo- qui, seq; in exemplum renatorum sistere, luculen- tissimum est, qui uti se exemplum antea proposue- rat infirmitatis & imperfectionis: ita nunc exem- plum se constituit consolationis. Notatur autem hic causa προκαταρκτικὴ quâ necessarius fuisse tanti assertoris interventus ostenditur. Duo enim dun- taxat in universum salutis afferendæ modi locum ha- bere significantur, quorum alter est τῶ ἀκριβοδικαίῳ, quod observatione perfectâ legis divinæ consistat: al- ter τῆς ἐπιεικείας, quæ gratuitam Dei misericordiam implicat. Priorem modum ἀδύνατον fuisse Apostolus pronunciat, non ἁπλῶς quidem & per se (Lex enim quemadmodum perfectam divinæ justitiæ normam continet: ita suis observatoribus vitam & salutem promittit) sed κατὰ τι κὶ ἐκ τῶ συμβεβηκότος: quate- nus nimirum ex infirmitate humana hæc illi ἀδυνα- μία accedit. Posset enim salvare lex, si ab homini- bus servari posset. At quia non potest, nec illa sal- vare potest. Unde prior salutis modus impossibilis esse relinquitur. Necessitate igitur ipsâ impulsus Deus, afferendæ salutis humanæ modum alterum amplexatus fuisse ostenditur, uti hic habet B. Mylius p. 278. Philippus ita habet: Grammatica Syntaxis recte explicanda est. Hujus hæc est series: Cum esset impossibile legi, scilicet tollere peccatum, eo quod per carnem lex non poterat fieri, Deus misit filium suum &c.

ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτῦ ὑιὸν πέμψας. Nempe in mundum. Mittere autem Deus dicitur, ubi mandata dat, ut diximus ad Joh. IV. 34. vide & Jer. I. 7.

Missio illa non solum cum Socinianis ad man- data vel muneris impositionem & instructionem re- stringenda, sed quum e cœlo Filius Dei in mun- dum missus sit, & præexistentiam ante ἐνσάρκωσιν & ipsam incarnationem ejusdem, licet cum rela- tione ad officium, quod eidem demandatum est, involvit, uti Exercit. de προϋπάρξει Filii DEI ostendimus.

ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας. Id est, ut tractaretur sic, quomodo nocentes tractari so- lent, Esa. LIII, 12. Marc. XV. 28. Philipp. II. 8.

Τὸ ὁμοίωμα σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας non respicit so- lum passionẽChristi, quod ita tractatus fit,quomodo nocentes tractari solent, quod ne quide fieri potuis- set, nisi peccatum nostrum & culpam in sese susce- pisset, sine quo etiam τὸ ὁμοίωμα σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας ipsi tribui non posset: nec similitudinem tantum na- turæ nostræ designat, quod solum ὁμοιώσιος nobis sit Christus, non ὁμούσιος, quod veritati humanæ Christi naturæ repugnat, imo etiam redemptioni nostræ: nam τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, uti ha- bet vetustatis regula: sed in similitudine carnis pec- cati missus dicitur Filius Dei,quod assumens quide veram carnem seu humanam naturam nobis con- substantialem, similis tamen fieri nostræ carni pec- catrici debuerit, sed absque peccato: quia proprio destitutus peccato, quum non norit peccatum, & sanctus ille sanctorum fuerit, inde a primo conce- ptionis momento, nostrum peccatum in se suscipe- re voluerit, ut fieret pro nobis peccatum, vel hostia pro peccato. Id ergo dicitur ὁμοίωμα vel similitudo non carnis simpliciter, sed carnis peccatricis. Hanc autem susceptionem peccatorum nostrorum hic temere excludit Grotius, uti etiam ad Luc. II. 22. notavit, neque vitiositatem neq; vitium, sed conditio- nem mortalis corporis hoc loco significare. Quod ve- ro vocis ἁμαρτίας usui haud convenit. Et tametsi illa similitudo carnis peccati, in qua venit Christus, omnino mortalem conditionem, & alias θνητὰς δυσχερείας complectatur, quas sponte in se susce- pitChristus, peccati tamen nostri susceptio non ex- cludenda, sed includenda: ut tum ratione culpæ, tum ratione miseriæ & pœnæ quoque pro nobis susceptæ ὁμοίωμα carnis peccatricis ipsi tribuatur.

καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας) Propter peccata: idem enim est, quod διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα supra IV. 25. Sic περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν 1. Cor. XV. 3. & Gal. I. 4. & ita recte hæc verba acceptit Syrus.

κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ) Per carnem suam sci- licet morti traditam interfecit peccatum. Nam κατακρίνειν dicitur pro interficere, sicut κατάκριμα pro morte, quia damnati interfici solent: interfecit vero, id est, inte ficisendi vires nobis præstitit. Interficere est efficientiam adimere. Ita est hic μετάληψις, sive figurarum multiplicatio. Vide, quæ supra IV. 25. Est autem argute dictum. Ipse, qui damnatus peccato videbatur, damnavit peccatum.

Alii hæc περὶ ἁμαρτίας accipiunt de hostia pro peccato: quia Christus victima pro nobis, & pro pec- catis nostris fieri voluit. Ita Philippus: Observetur phrasis: Deus damnavit peccatum nostrum in carne pro peccato, id est, hostia Christo, oblata pro peccato. Nam phrasis περὶ ἁμαρτίας significat hostiam pro peccato. Sic in Levitico Græca lectio semper loquitur, & eodem modo in Græca lectione Esaiæ dicitur: ἐὰν δῶται περὶ ἁμαρτίας ἡ ψυχὴ ἀυτᾶ ὄψεται σπέρμα μακρόβιον. In textu Hebræo non additur Præpositio, sed sic legitur: Quia ponet peccatù animam suam, vi- debit semen longævum. Sed ex Levitici Græca lectio- ne phrasis περὶ ἁμαρτίας notissima est. Cur vero hic duplicem figuram in verbo κατακρίνειν admittere debeamus nulla apparet ratio: ut nempe primum κατακρίνειν pro interfectione, & porro interfectio, pro virium ad interficiendum subministratione intel- ligatur, cum propria condemnationis significatio, quæ v. 1. occurrit, locum habeat: Nimirum merita peccatorum vel peccata ceu causam meritoriam, quæ condemnationem nostrum omnium merue- runt, Deus condemnavit in carne vel natura nostra a Filio unigenito assumpta, utpote qui in se susce- perat nostra omniu peccata, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν peccatum mundi, quod ipse ceu agnus ille Dei ferebat Joh. I. 29. Non autem dicitur ipse Filius Dei, qui damna- tus peccato videbatur, damnasse peccatum, sed

Deus damnavit peccatum in Filio suo, in carne ab ipso assumpta, siquidem nostrum peccatum ferre voluerit, debuerit adeoque etiam pro eodem lue- re. Notat hanc Emphasin in voce damnavit Phi- lippus: Ut judex damnans homicidam, primùm pro- nunciat eum reum esse, postea interficit eum: Sic Deus damnans peccatum, cum filius innocens sit fa- ctus victima, primum eripuit peccato autoritatem nos accusandi, postea omnino delet, cum reddit nobis eternam vitam & justitiam integram.

## 8:4
Ver. 4. that the requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us.

That we might perform all things which in the law of Moses are honest in themselves, which are called משׁפָּטים, just as those which are added are called חֻקּים ἐντολαὶ, where the Hebrews speak distinctly. However, those who are truly Christians perform those things which are honest in the law of Moses, and in them greater things, as we said above III. 31, not because Moses commanded, but because Christ did, who also gave the strength.

The requirement of the law is fulfilled not by us, for we are too powerless for that v. 3, but in us: when indeed the obedience of Christ is imputed to us; who for that end willed to undergo in His own flesh the condemnation which was owed to our sin by virtue of the law, having performed obedience to the law, so that we might not only be free from condemnation, but also His obedience might be imputed to us, and thus the requirement of the law, the whole right of the law, both as the penalty which it requires from us on account of the transgression of the law, to which He had taught that we are all liable, and as the obedience which it demands most exactly from us, might be fulfilled in us, by the satisfaction and righteousness of Christ, or His obedience both passive and active, applied to us through faith, which God wills to impute to us for righteousness. That not all the commandments of the law are regarded here, but only some, which, namely, concern those things which are honest in themselves, is a Grotian invention: since the requirement of the law embraces all precepts which, namely, concern us all, or the whole human race, indeed even the right which the law has over us, by requiring both satisfaction for sins and the most perfect obedience, both of which the Apostle teaches were performed in our place by Christ and are imputed to us, so that the right of God might be fulfilled in us. But while Grotius establishes Christ as a lawgiver with Moses, he contradicts John, who asserts that the law indeed was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Christ Joh. I. 18.

to those who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

He repeats what he had said above, 1, to show that he is dealing with Christians in reality and name, such as most were who professed Christianity at the time of the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἵνα τὸ δικαίωμα τῦ νόμε πληρωθῇ ἐν ἡμῖν.

Ut nos præstaremus omnia, quæ in lege Mosis per se ho- nesta sunt, quæ dicuntur משׁפָּטים, sicut ea, quæ sunt ad- dita, vocantur חֻקּים ἐντολαὶ, ubi distinctè loquuntur He- bræi. Præstant autem, qui vere sunt Christiani, illa, quæ in lege Mosis honesta sunt, & in illis majora, ut diximus su- pra III. 31. non quia Moses jussit, sed quia Christus, qui & vires dedit.

Impletur τὸ δικαίωμα τῦ νόμε non à nobis, ad id enim nimium impotentes sumus v. 3. sed ἐν ἡμῖν in nobis: cùm nimirum obedientia Christi imputa- tur nobis; qui eo fine in sua carne subire voluit condemnationem, quæ peccato nostro debèba- tur vi legis, præstita legi obedientia, ut nos à con- demnatione non modo liberi essemus, sed etiam obedientia ejus nobis imputaretur, & ita τὸ δι- καίωμα τῦ νόμε jus legis universum, tum quà pœ- nam, quam requirit à nobis ob legis transgressio- nem, cui omnes nos obnoxios esse docuerat, tum quà obedientiam, quam exactissimam à nobis po- stulat, impleretur in nobis, satisfactione & justitia Christi, vel obedientia ejus tum passiva, tum acti- va, nobis applicata per fidem, quam imputare no- bis vult Deus ad justitiam. Respici hìc non omnia mandata legis, sed nonnulla tantum, quæ scil. con- cernunt ea, quæ per se honesta sunt, commentum Grotianum est: quum τὸ δικαίωμα τῦ νόμε omnia præcepta complectatur, quæ sc. nos omnes, seu to- tum genus humanum concernunt, imò etiam jus, quod lex habet in nos, tum satisfactionem exigen- di pro peccatis, tum obedientiam perfectissimam requirendo, quam utramque nostri loco à Christo præstitam nobis imputari, ut impleatur jus Dei in nobis, Apostolus docet. Christum autem dum Grotius cum Mose νομοθέτην constituit, Johanni contradicit, qui legem quidem per Mosen datam, gratiam autem & veritatem per Christum factam asserit Joh. I. 18.

τοῖς μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατῦσι ἀλλὰ κατὰ πνεῦμα.

Repetit, quod dixerat supra, 1. ut ostendat, se agere de Christianis re & nomine, quales plerique erant, qui Chri- stianismum profitebantur crucis tempore.

## 8:5
Ver. 5. for those who are according to the flesh.

These, who are possessed by the affections of the flesh, which he called passions above. Thus we had a city full of idols in the Acts.

See Acts XVII. 16. Yet not those who are possessed by the affections of the body, which Grotius understands by flesh, but those who are possessed by the affections of depraved concupiscence, and are truly carnal, not yet regenerate, they alone mind the things which are of the flesh: And it is sufficiently evident that body here is not flesh, because the mind is attributed to the flesh in verse 6. Blessed Balduinus p. 148 presents the connection thus: Lest under this consolation (concerning immunity from condemnation) hypocrites might also hide, who boast of faith in words but deny it in deeds; now the Apostle proceeds to describe the truly faithful by their effects, and to propose their chief works, and to institute a long and truly Apostolic exhortation to the pursuit of good works, lest by sins against conscience we shake off faith and the grace of God: for those who do this, they certainly cannot be immune from the condemnation of the law. An opposition is therefore instituted between the spiritual and the carnal 1. by reason of carnal prudence, because these mind only carnal things, but those spiritual things. 2. by reason of effects and properties: because carnal wisdom is deadly, adversarial to God, rebellious to the law of God, and invalid for performing those things which the law requires. But concerning the mind of the Spirit, that it is life and peace; and that the spiritual have the indwelling Holy Spirit, moderating their senses, thoughts, and actions, and directing them to a salutary end.

to mind the things of the flesh. Φρονεῖν & φρόνημα in Paul are usually referred not to the intellect, but to the pursuit: see what we have said at Matt. XII. 23. Actions frequently follow the constitution of the mind. See what [we said] at Matt. VII. 18.

Why do we refer [it] only to pursuit and will, and not also to the mind and intellect? For we first understand with the mind, and the thoughts and figments of our mind are occupied only with those things which are of the flesh, since the natural man does not understand the things which are of the Spirit of God, 1 Cor. II, 14. And the will follows the error of the mind, choosing as good what is in reality evil, even if it is presented by the mind under the guise of good.

but they who are according to the Spirit. Those who are possessed by the Spirit of God, which now comes to pass only through Christ.

the things of the Spirit. That is, they pursue holy things, such as that Spirit is.

Latin:

Vers. 5. οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ὄντες.

Hi, qui possidentur à carnis affectibus, quæ παθή- ματα dixit supra. Sic κατείδωλον urbem in Actis habui- mus.

Vid. Act. XVII. 16. Non tamen, qui à corporis, quod per carnem intelligit Grotius, sed qui à pra- væ concupiscentiæ affectibus possidentur, & verè σαρκικοὶ carnales sunt, nondum regeniti, illi tan- tum ea, quæ carnis sunt, sapiunt: Et corpus hic non esse carnem, satis constat, quia τῇ σαρκὶ tribui- tur Φρόνημα prudentia vers. 6. Nexum ita exhibet B. Balduinus p. 148. Ne sub hac consolatione (de immunitate à condemnatione) etiam hypocritæ latere possint, qui fidem crepant verbis, factis autem abnegant; jam pergit Apostolus describere verè fide- les ab effectibus, eorumque opera præcipua propone- re, & prolixam vereque Apostolicam instituere ex- hortationem ad studium bonorum operum, ne pecca- tis contra conscientiam fidem & gratiam Dei excu- tiamus: quod qui faciunt, ii sanè à condemnatione legis immunes esse non possunt. Instituitur ergo op- positio inter spirituales, & carnales 1. ratione pru- dentiæ carnalis, quod hi tantum carnalia sapiant, illi verò spiritualia. 2. ratione effectuum & pro- priorum: quod sapientia carnalis mortifera sit, Deo adversaria, legi Dei rebellis, & ad ea, quæ lex re- quirit, præstanda, invalida. De φρονήματι πνεύ- ματος vero quod sit vita & pax; quodque spiritua- les habeant inhabitantem Spiritum S. sensus, cogita- ta, & actiones ipsorum moderantem, & ad saluta- rem finem dirigentem.

τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς φρονεῖν. Φρονεῖν & φρόνημα Paulo non ad intellectum, sed ad stu- dium solet referri: vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. XII. 23. So- lent animi constitutionem actiones frequenter sequi. Vide, quæ ad Matth. VII. 18.

Cur tantùm ad studium & voluntatem, non ad mentem etiam atque intellectum referamus? Nam prius mente sapimus, & cogitata, atque figmenta mentis nostræ circa ea, quæ carnis sunt, tantum oc- cupantur, quum animalis homo non intelligat ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, 1. Cor. II, 14. & errorem men- tis sequitur deinde voluntas eligens pro bono, quod malum revera est, etsi à mente sub specie boni ag- geratur.

οἱ δὲ κατὰ πνεῦμα. Qui possidentur à Dei Spiritu, qui nunc nonnisi per Christum contingit.

τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. Id est, student rebus sanctis, qualis est ille Spiritus.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. for the mind of the flesh is death. Here he gives the reason why he said above that he was also delivered from death, because that pursuit of complying in all things with the affections of the flesh leads to death, and that eternal. See above VI. 21. VII. 10. 11. 24. Φρόνημα here is the same as יֵצֶר Gen. VI. 5. He called it death here for the cause of death, as above VII, 12.

Not only the pursuit of complying in all things with bodily affections, but also the errors, doubts, and ignorances of the mind when it is left to itself, indeed the very τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, prudence, and whatever the unregenerate mind is most capable of, whatever is most excellent in it, is death, or the cause of death: because every figment of the human heart is only evil, Gen. VI. 5. compare our Commentary on Mosaic Genesis p. 648 seqq. regarding that passage, and regarding this Apostolic passage, what we have argued at length against the Papists and Socinians in Exegem. August. Confess. art. V. c. III. §. 5. Philip rightly names it the sense of the flesh in this place, Paul, not only appetites or affections in the heart, such as loves, hatreds, joy, sadness, the fires of lusts, anger, but also in the higher part, darkness and doubts about God, about providence, and about the word of God. Likewise, in the will, aversion from God, distrust, blind security, contempt of the judgment of God, indignation and rage against God. Paul calls all these φρόνημα σαρκὸς, and the name φρόνημα embraces thoughts and affections. He also meets the Papist objection, which it is pleasing to observe here, in what way this happens: But they object, why does he say the sense of the flesh is enmity against God, when nevertheless there are many good items of knowledge in man, such as numbers and the laws of nature? Likewise, good affections, such as στοργαὶ? I answer: Paul speaks principally of thoughts about God, such as they are in the unregenerate mind, in which there is at the same time great confusion of doubts. Then also of affections toward God, such as they are in the unregenerate will and heart. In the secure there is contempt of the judgment of God: in the terrified, as in Saul, Judas, there is indignation and rage against God, and there is manifold contumacy in the heart against the Law of God, nor are the στοργαὶ governed by order. Paul preaches about these interior evils when he says that the flesh cannot be subject to the law of God. And in this place, the necessary doctrine concerning the distinction between external discipline and interior obedience must be held. For even after the fall of our first parents, this freedom of the will in man remains, to be able to govern the Locomotive, that is, the external gestures of the limbs. Such is still the nature of the nerves, founded by God with wonderful art, that they can obey thought and will, because God wills that external limbs be restrained and coerced by human diligence, and He wills that the distinction be understood in some way we may know that God is the most free agent. Nor does Paul speak of these external gestures when he says: That the flesh cannot be subject to the law of GOD, but he speaks of interior obedience, because faith ought to have shone in man, believing with firm assent the threats and promises of GOD, and rightly acknowledging the Son of God, and in the heart there ought to have been conformity with God, ardent love of God, true fear. Finally, the heart ought to have been the Temple of God, without any depraved inclination, and without depraved motions, but a man not reborn cannot even begin this interior obedience. Concerning these interior darknesses and doubts and evil inclinations it is said: The flesh cannot be subject to the law of God.

τὸ δὲ φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος ζωὴ καὶ εἰρήνη. That is, it is the cause of life and happiness, which the Hebrews call by the name of peace. See above II. 10.

That the study of holy things is the cause of life and happiness, or of eternal salvation, is the heresy of the Papists and Socinians, not the sentiment of Scripture, not the doctrine of the Apostle. He who attributes justification, and likewise life and eternal salvation, not to the study of piety or holiness, but to faith, to the merit of Christ, and to the grace of God, Rom. IV. 6. Eph. II. 8. 9. Moreover, that doctrine which the Spirit delivers is called the prudence of the Spirit, namely the Gospel, which he had called the law of the Spirit in v. 2, to bring life and peace, which is not only exhibited in the same, but is conferred through it, as the instrument of the Holy Spirit, and is the word of life Phil. II. 16. and the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes Rom. I. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 6. τὸ γὰρ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς θάνατος. Hic rationem reddit, cur supra dixerit etiam à morte se liberatum, quia studium illud carnis affectibus per omnia obsequendi ad mortem eamque æternam ducat. Vide su- pra VI. 21. VII. 10. 11. 24. Φρόνημα hic idem, quod יֵצֶר Gen. VI. 5. Mortem hic dixit pro causa mortis, ut supra VII, 12.

Non tantum studium corporalibus affectibus per omnia obsequendi, sed etiam mentis cum sibi relin- quitur, errores, dubitationes, ignorantiæ, imò ipsum τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς prudentia, & quicquid ma- ximè valet mens non renata, quicquid in ea præ- stantissimum est, mors est, vel mortis causa: quia omne figmentum cordis humani tantum malum est Gen. VI. 5. conf. de illo loco Commentarium no- strum ad Genesin Mosaicam p. 648. seqq. & de hoc Apostolico loco, quæ adversus Pontificios & Soci- nianos disputavimus prolixè in Exegem. August. Confess. art. V. c. III. §. 5. Rectè Philippus in h. l. Sensum carnis nominat Paulus, non tantùm appeti- tiones seu affectus in corde, ut amores, odia, lætitiam, tristitiam, incendia libidinum, iram, sed etiam in superiore parte caliginem & dubitationes de Deo, de providentia & de verbo Dei. Item, in voluntate aversionem à Deo, diffidentiam, cæcam securitatem, contemptum judicii Dei, indignationem & fremi- tus adversus Deum. Hæc omnia nominat φρόνημα σαρκὸς, ac nomen φρόνημα complectitur cogitationes & affectus. Occurrit etiam Pontific. objectioni, quod hic etiam observare libet, quo pacto id fiat: Sed objiciunt, cur ait sensum carnis inimicitiam esse adversus Deum, cum tamen in homine sint multæ bone notitiæ, ut numeri & leges naturæ. Item, boni affectus, ut στοργαὶ? Respondeo: Loquitur Paulus principaliter de cogitationibus de Deo, quales sunt in mente non renata, in qua simul magna confusio est dubitationum. Deinde & de affectibus erga Deum, quales sunt in voluntate & corde non renato. In se- curis est contemptus judicii Dei: in perterrefactis, ut in Saule, Juda, est indignatio & fremitus adver- sus Deum & est multiplex contumacia in corde con- tra Legem Dei, nec στοργαὶ reguntur ordine. De his interioribus malis concionatur Paulus, cum ait, car- nem non posse subjici legi Dei. Ac tenenda est hoc loco doctrina necessaria de distinctione externæ disci- plinæ & interioris obedientiæ. Nam etiam post lapsum primorum parentum hæc libertas voluntatis in homine reliqua est, posse regere Locomotivam, id est, externos membrorum gestus. Adhuc talis est na- tura nervorum, mirabili arte a Deo condita, ut obe- dire cogitationi & voluntati possint, quia Deus vult externa membra franari, & coerceri humana dili- gentia, & vult aliquo modo intelligi discrimen inter agens liberum & non liberum, ut sciamus, Deum esse agens liberrimum. Nec de his externis gestibus lo- quitur Paulus cum ait: Carnem non posse legi DEI subjici, sed loquitur de interiore obedientia, quia in homine debebat lucere fides, firma assensione credens comminationibus, & promissionibus DEI, & recte agnoscens Filium Dei, & in corde debebat esse confor- mitas cum Deo, ardens dilectio Dei, verus timor. De- nique cor debebat esse Templum Dei, sine ulla prava inclinatione, & sine pravis motibus, sed homo non re- natus hanc interiorem obedientiam ne quidem in- choare potest. De his interioribus tenebris & dubi- tationibus & malis inclinationibus dicitur: Caro non potest subjici legi Dei.

τὸ δὲ φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος ζωὴ καὶ εἰρήνη. Id est, causa est vitæ ac felicitatis quam Hebræi pacis no- mine appellant. Vide supra II. 10.

Studium rerum sanctarum causam esse vitæ, ac felicitatis, vel salutis æternæ, Papistarum & Soci- nianorum hæresis est, non Scripturæ sententia, non Apostoli doctrina. Qui non studio Pietatis vel sanctitatis, sed fidei, merito Christi, & gratiæ Dei tribuit, ut justificationem ita & vitam ac salutem æternam Rom. IV. 6. Eph. II. 8. 9. Dicitur autem prudentia Spiritus doctrina illa, quam Spiritus tra- dit, Evangelium nempe, quod νόμον τοῦ πνεύμα- τος v. 2. dixerat, vitam & pacem adferre, quæ non in eodem tantum exhibetur, sed per illud, ceu ὄρ- γανον Spiritus S. confertur, estque verbum vitæ Phil. II. 16. ac potentia Dei ad salutem omni cre- denti Rom. I. 16.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. διότι τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς τὸν Θεὸν. It is enmity with GOD, that is, it conducts itself just as enemies are wont to do. The name of the cause for the effect. See Jas. IV. 4.

τῷ γὰρ νόμῳ Θεοῦ οὐχ ὑποτάσσεται. It is carried wherever it pleases, not where the Law of GOD points. You may aptly apply here, not wrongly, but in a more eminent sense, what Agatho said: — πρὸς τὸ τιτράχοεδον δ᾽ ὅλοι, Τὴν ἡδονὴν, ἐπιθυμίαν, λύπην, φόβον. Ασπήσεώς γε καὶ μάχης πολλῆς δέοι. Οὗτοι γὰρ, ἤτοι καὶ διὰ σπλάγχνων ἀεὶ Χωρῶσι καὶ κυκῶσιν ἀνθρώπων κέαρ.

οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται. For the Law is something defined. Desires are infinite. You have similar kinds of speaking in 1 Cor. II. 14. 1 John III. 9.

Ἐμφατικώτερον is the Pauline locution; for he did not place the abstract without cause, saying not only inimical, but enmity itself and hostility against God: because of the supreme repugnance of the mind of the flesh; whence he adds, not only that it is not carried where the law points, but that it cannot even be carried; and not even be subject to the law of God, because of the force of depraved concupiscence innate in us: which neither Agatho, nor any other of the pagans deprived of the light of the word of GOD, understood, much less could express. Concerning which see the loc. cit. in Exegem. A. C.

Latin:

Vers. 7. διότι τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς τὸν Θεὸν. Est inimicitia cum DEO, id est, ita se gerit, sicut so- lent inimici. Causæ nomen pro effectu. Vide Jac. IV. 4.

τῷ γὰρ νόμῳ Θεοῦ οὐχ ὑποτάσσεται. Fertur qua lubet, non qua monstrat DEI Lex. Non ma- le huc, sed sensu eminentiore aptes quod dixit Agatho: — πρὸς τὸ τιτράχοεδον δ᾽ ὅλοι, Τὴν ἡδονὴν, ἐπιθυμίαν, λύπην, φόβον. Ασπήσεώς γε καὶ μάχης πολλῆς δέοι. Οὗτοι γὰρ, ἤτοι καὶ διὰ σπλάγχνων ἀεὶ Χωρῶσι καὶ κυκῶσιν ἀνθρώπων κέαρ.

οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται. Lex enim definitum est aliquid. Cupiditates infinitæ. Similia loquendi genera habes 1. Cor. II. 14. 1. Joh. III. 9.

Ἐμφατικώτερον est locutio Paulina; non enim præter causam abstractum posuit, non inimicam tantum dicens, sed ipsam inimicitiam & hostilita- tem adversus Deum: ob summam repugnantiam τοῦ φρονήματος τῆς σαρκὸς; unde addit, non tan- tum, quod non feratur, qua monstrat lex, sed quod ne quidem ferri possit; ac ne subjici quidem legi Dei, ob vim pravæ concupiscentiæ nobis in- genitæ: quam nec Agatho, nec alius quisquam pa- ganorum luce verbi DEI destitutus intellexit, nedum exprimere potuit. Quo de l. c. in Exe- gem. A. C.

## 8:8
V. 8. οἱ δὲ ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντες Θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται. Those who are such as I have described can no more please God than rebels subject to a king. How then would God give them the supreme gift, that is, eternal happiness?

Latin:

V. 8. οἱ δὲ ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντες Θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται. Qui tales sunt, quales descripsi, Deo placere non magis possunt, quam regi subditi rebelles. Quomodo ergo Deus illis daret summum munus, id est, felicitatem æternam?

## 8:9
V. 9 ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σαρκὶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν πνεύματι. He addresses Christians, both Jews and foreigners. What he just said according to the flesh and according to the spirit, he now says in the flesh and in the spirit, just as the Greeks call him who is possessed by God 'in-godded'. The simile is taken from those who are surrounded on all sides by guards and are in their power.

εἴπερ πνεῦμα Θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν. Here too is the effect for the cause; for he wishes to say: If, however, you have so imbibed faith, and have been cleansed in soul, that that celestial aura deigns to dwell in you. There is no need for that metonymy of the cause: nor does it fit well enough. For the indwelling Spirit is the cause of the cleansing of the soul, which Grotius understands, not indeed the effect. Through faith the Holy Spirit dwells in us, which indwelling is followed by sanctification. But the argument here is sought a posteriori from the indwelling of the Spirit, which reveals itself through effects, to establish justification: For it is certain that those in whom the Holy Spirit dwells are justified through faith, since the Holy Spirit dwells in us through salvific and vivifying faith.

Latin:

V. 9 ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σαρκὶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν πνεύματι. Christianos tam Judæos quam alienigenas alloquitur. Quod modo dixit κατὰ σάρκα & κατὰ πνεῦμα, nunc dixit ἐν σαρκὶ κἀ ἐν πνεύματι, sicut ἔνθεον dicunt Græci eum qui a Deo possidetur. Similitudo sumpta ab iis, qui custodibus undi- que sepiuntur, & in eorum sunt potestate.

εἴπερ πνεῦμα Θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν. Est & hic effectus pro causa; vult enim dicere: Si tamen ita fidem imbibistis, & animo mundati estis, ut dignetur in vobis habitare aura illa cælestis. Non opus est illa metonymia causæ: nec ea satis convenit. Nam Spiritus inhabitans causa est mun- dationis animi, quam Grotius intelligit, non vero effectus. Per fidem habitat in nobis Spiritus S. quam inhabitationem sequitur sanctificatio. Ar- gumentum autem hic a posteriori ex inhabitatione Spiritus, quæ se per effecta prodit, petitur, ad sta- biliendam justificationem: Nam in quibus Spiri- tus S. habitat, illos per fidem justificatos esse cer- tum est, quum per fidem salvificam & vivificam nos inhabitet Spiritus S.

## 8:10
v. 10. εἰ δέ τις πνεῦμα χριστῦ ἐκ ἔχει. He rightly said Spirit of Christ what he just called Spirit of God, because after the revelation of the Gospel that Spirit is not given except through Christ John XIV. 15. 16. 17. 26. and he is said to have it in such a way as a house is said to have a master.

Nay, the πνεῦμα Θεῦ is called the πνεῦμα χριστῦ, because it proceeds from both from eternity, from God the Father, and from the Son of God: and is sent by both in time.

ἐκ ἔσιν ἀυτῦ.

He is not yet fully Christ's. For to believe and to be baptized is not enough.

He directly contradicts Christ in this: who says in Mark 16:16, he who shall have believed and shall have been baptized, shall be saved. Grotius on the contrary: To believe and to be baptized is not enough. Although indeed these things are sufficient for us to be Christ's, nevertheless we discern a posteriori whether someone is Christ's, if he has the Holy Spirit; because we are indeed Christ's through justification, but neither the indwelling of the Holy Spirit nor sanctification can be separated from justification: since they are its necessary consequences.

εἰ δὲ χρισός ἐν ὑμῖν,

Here ἐν is taken differently than above. In you, as in his temple, namely through the Spirit, who is called by Tertullian the vicar of Christ.

τὸ μὲν σῶμα νεκρὸν δι ἁμαρτίαν.

We said above that body and flesh are used indiscriminately by the Hebrews. We have often taken flesh for the affections congruent to the flesh. Thus also here is placed the body, which in Christians is said to be dead, that is, stripped of that former liberty of acting according to its own desires, on account of sin, that is, for the sake of avoiding sin, just as someone is said to flee on account of enemies.

τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ζωή.

And here is a metonymy, for the cause of life. Just as death, that is, the cause of death in verse 13.

διὰ δικαιοσύνην.

Because it works in us a righteousness not human, but divine, which righteousness is not obscurely called here the cause of eternal life.

Latin:

v. 10. εἰ δέ τις πνεῦμα χριστῦ ἐκ ἔχει. Recte πνεῦμα χριστῦ dixit quod modo πνεῦμα Θεῦ, quia post Evangelii patefactionem Spiritus ille non datur nisi per Christum Joh. XIV. 15. 16. 17. 26. & habere sic dicit, sicut domus dicitur habere dominum.

Imo πνεῦμα Θεῦ dicitur πνεῦμα χριστῦ, quia ab utroque ab æterno procedit, à Deo Patre, & à Fi- lio Dei: & ab utroque in tempore mittitur.

ἐκ ἔσιν ἀυτῦ.

Nondum plene Christi est. Nam credere & baptizatum esse non sufficit.

Directe hoc contradicit Christo: Qui Marc. XVI. 16. qui crediderit, inquit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Grotius contra: Credere & bapti- zatum esse non sufficit. Quanquam vero hæc ad id sufficiant, ut Christi simus, à posteriori tamen di- gnoscimus an Christi quis sit, si habeat Spiritum S. quia Christi sumus quidem per justificationem, sed nec inhabitatio Spiritus S. nec sanctificatio à ju- stificatione separari potest: cum necessaria ejus- dem sint consequentia.

εἰ δὲ χρισός ἐν ὑμῖν,

Hic ἐν aliter quam supra sumitur. In vobis, tanquam in templo suo, nempe per Spiritum, qui Christi vicarius Ter- tulliano dicitur.

τὸ μὲν σῶμα νεκρὸν δι ἁμαρτίαν.

Diximus supra corpus & carnem Hebræis promiscue sumi. Carnem pro affectibus carni congruentibus sæpe ha- buimus. Ita & hic ponitur corpus quod in Christianis di- citur esse mortuum, id est, exutam pristina illa qui suis agen- di libertate, propter peccatum, id est ad vitandum peccatum, sicut dicitur aliquis fugere propter hostes.

τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ζωή.

Et hic μετανομία est, pro causa vitæ. Sicut mors, id est, mortis causa 13.

διὰ δικαιοσύνην.

Quia operatur in nobis justitiam non humanam, sed divinam, quæ justitia non obscure hic dicitur causa vitæ æternæ.

## 8:11
ver. 11. But if the Spirit of him that raised Christ from the dead dwell in you.

The Spirit of God the Father & of Christ, as we have already said. But here he is called the Spirit of the Father, because his primary origin is from thence, nor did he say simply of the Father, but with an epithet most pertinent to the matter, of him who raised Christ from the dead.

He that raised Christ from the dead.

That same Father, to whom as the principal cause the resurrection of Christ is wont to be attributed, Acts III. 15. IV. 18. V. 30. XIII. 38. Above IV. 24. 1 Cor. VI. 14. & elsewhere.

shall also quicken your mortal bodies.

ζωοποιήσει is the same as ἐγερει יחיה. You have this word in this sense in John V. 21. and it is also above IV. 17. 1 Cor. XV. 28. Gal. III. 21.

by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.

The other reading is not a little better, διὰ τὸ ἐνοικῶν ἀυτῦ πνεῦμα ἐν ὑμῖν, as the Syrian, the Latin, Origen, Chrysostom, Oecumenius & others read. Just as Christ, because he had in himself that divine nature, which is called the Word by John, and by others the Spirit, as we said at Mark II. 8, for that very reason it was not right for him to remain in death, but it was necessary that he be raised up, as Paul clearly says above I. 4, Peter 1. III. 18, & the writer to the Hebrews IX. 14, so GOD also does not suffer those to whom he has given his Spirit to remain in death. For he does not give it, that he may take it away: but he gives it as an earnest, that is, a part of the price, to give assurance that the price itself, that is, eternal life, will also follow 2 Cor. I. 22. V. 5. Ephes. I. 14.

B. Balduinus, p. 149, notes that the objection of the faithful is answered here in our chapter. For they could say, what kind of spirituality is this in us? And can we be better than others who wallow in pleasures? Since we too must struggle with death and other calamities, just as others do? Who then knows whether we are going to prevail in that struggle? The Apostle answers this objection by concession, that the reborn are indeed still subject to death and calamities on account of the sin still clinging to them; yet they have the Holy Spirit dwelling within them, who, if they themselves do not place an obstacle through stubborn persistence, but walk according to the leading of the Holy Spirit, will continually preserve spiritual life in them, will resist the desires of sin, and will finally guard them for the everlasting life of eternal happiness, which He promises they will attain as certainly as the eternal Father raised His Son from the dead. Doubtless from the fact that Christ dwells in us through faith, Eph. 3:17, the body is indeed dead on account of sin, that is, subject to death, yet the Spirit bestows life on account of the righteousness of Christ, which alone—and not our human righteousness—is the cause of eternal life, and alone can be opposed to the sin that wounds the infinite righteousness of God, which cannot be satisfied by human righteousness, but solely by the righteousness of God, that is, of Christ the θεανθρώπꙋ (God-man). Cardinal Cajetan acknowledged this sense: 'Striving for brevity,' he says, 'Paul describes us as similar to Christ, from Christ dwelling in us, so that just as Christ had a mortal body and a living spirit: so our body is dead, that is, mortal, but the Spirit is living.' But the dissimilarity lies in the cause: that our body is dead on account of our own sin; original sin is therefore common to all men except Christ: but the Spirit lives for life, on account of justification. And here too there is a dissimilarity in the cause; because the life of the Spirit of Christ does not depend on righteousness, but was blessed from the beginning; but the life of the Spirit of those in whom Christ dwells is on account of the righteousness of Christ, by which He satisfied God, by paying the price of human redemption: on account of that righteousness, however, extrinsically (meritoriously) and through participation in it intrinsically, is the life of those in whom Christ dwells. Thus Cajetan, with Oecumenius, understands the spirit of man because of the antithesis of the body, and the Spirit as intelligent: in which way Estius observes that the spirit of man is said to be life on account of righteousness, because not only does he himself live through righteousness, but he also makes the man whose spirit it is live through the same righteousness, as a kind of spiritual life of the man himself. The same Estius notes, however, that in the Greek and Syriac codices 'life' is read instead of 'lives': and those who read it in this way generally understand the Spirit not as man's, but as God's, in this sense: If Christ is in us, therefore His Spirit is your life, that is, He bestows life upon you, and makes you live through righteousness, etc. But that σῶμα (body) is understood as flesh, and flesh is further taken for the affections congruent with the flesh, and thus the body is said to be dead, that is, stripped of its original freedom of action, on account of sin, that is, to avoid sin, are merely precarious Grotian glosses. For why should we not take 'body' properly? Why should we not understand death properly, the meritorious cause of which is certainly sin, which the preposition διὰ (through/on account of) sufficiently designates? But because the body is inhabited by the Holy Spirit, even though it is subject to death on account of sin—for the root of this, since it still remains in us, must be afflicted by that cross and this body of ours must finally be abolished by death, so that sin may finally be utterly exterminated from it—nevertheless it lives through the indwelling Spirit, that is, it enjoys spiritual life, on account of the righteousness of Christ, which

is imputed through faith. (Others understand by the Spirit the part in us that is regenerated, which he says lives on account of justification, because spiritual life in this age is an effect of justification: which spiritual life certifies us of the eternal life which we begin here in the Spirit: there we will continue it eternally among the blessed in spirit and body, cf. B. Balduin. in h. l. p. 149.) Whence it also follows further from the same indwelling of the Spirit that τὰ θνητὰ σώματα (the mortal bodies) are to be resurrected, certainly not the flesh, or our carnal affections: but our very mortal bodies. In the phrase where resurrection is attributed to the Father as the principal cause, if it is opposed to the Son, Arianism must be avoided; for whatever the Father does, ταῦτα eadem ἡ ὁμοίως (these same things likewise) the Son does.

Latin:

vers. 11. εἰ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα τῦ ἐγείραντος χρισὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ὀικεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν.

Spiritus Dei Patris & Christi, ut jam diximus. Hic vero Spiritus Patris dicitur, quia inde prima ejus origo est, neque simpliciter dixit Patris, sed cum elogio maxime ad rem per- tinente, ejus qui suscitavit Christum è mortuis.

ὁ ἐγείρας τὸν χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν.

Idem ille Pater, cui ut principali causæ tribui solet Christi resurrectio Act. III. 15. IV. 18. V. 30. XIII. 38. Supra IV. 24. 1. Cor. VI. 14. & alibi.

ζωοποιήσει καὶ τὰ θνητὰ σώματα ὑμῶν.

Idem est ζωοποιήσει quod ἐγερει יחיה. Hoc sensu verbum hoc habes Joh. V. 21. est & supra IV. 17. 1. Cor. XV. 28. Gal. III. 21.

διὰ τῦ ἐνοικῶντος ἀυτῦ πνεύματος ἐν ὑμῖν.

Non paulo melior est lectio altera, διὰ τὸ ἐνοικῶν ἀυτῦ πνεῦμα ἐν ὑμῖν quomodo legere Syrus, Latinus, Origenes, Chrysostomus, Oecumenius & alii. Sicut Christum, quia in se habuit naturam illam divinam, quæ Johanni λόγος vocatur, aliis etiam Spiritus, ut diximus ad Marc. II. 8. ob id ipsum æquum non fuit manere in morte, sed eum resu- scitari oportuit, ut clare dicunt Paulus supra I. 4. Petrus I. III. 18. & scriptor ad Hebr. IX. 14. ita non patitur etiam DEUS in morte manere eos, quibus dedit Spiritum suum. Neque enim dat eum, ut auferat: sed dat, ut arrhabo- nem, id est, partem pretii, ut fidem faciat, ipsum etiam pretium, id est, vitam æternam secuturam 2. Cor. I. 22. V, 5. Ephes. I. 14.

Responderi hic objectioni fidelium monet in cap. nostro B. Balduinus p. 149. Dicere enim po- terant, qualisnam est hæc in nobis spiritualitas? & numquid meliores esse possumus cæteris, qui volupta- tibus diffluunt? siquidem & nobis cum morte & aliis calamitatibus conflictandum sit, æque ac cæteris? quis ergo scit, utrum in ista lucta simus superaturi? Huic objectioni respondet Apostolus per concessionem, esse quidem renatos etiam morti & calamitatibus ob- noxios propter peccatum in ipsis adhuc hærens; ha- bere tamen ipsos Spiritum Sanctum in se habitantem, qui, si modo ipsi non obstinata pertinacia obicem posuerint, sed ad ductum Spiritus S. ambulaverint, vitam in ipsis spiritualem subinde conservabit, desideriis peccati resistet, & tandem ad sempiter- nam vitam æternæ felicitatis custodiet, quam tam certo adepturos pollicetur, quam certe Pater æternus filium suum à mortuis resuscitavit. Ni- mirum ex eo, quod Christus in nobis habitat per fidem Eph. III. 17. corpus quidem mortuum propter peccatum, id est, morti subjectum, vitam tamen Spiritus largitur propter justitiam Christi scil. quæ sola, non vero humana nostra justitia, est causa vitæ æternæ, & opponi sola potest peccato infinitam DEI justitiam lædenti, cui satis fieri non potest humana justitia, sed unice justitia DEI hoc est Christi θεανθρώπꙋ. Quem sensum agno- vit Cardin. Cajetanus: Brevitati, inquit, studens Paulus similes nos Christo describit, ex Christo in- habitante in nobis, ut quemadmodum Christus ha- buit corpus mortale & spiritum vivum: ita cor- pus nostrum est mortuum hoc est mortale, Spiri- tus vero vivus. Sed dissimilitudo est penes causam: quod corpus nostrum est mortuum propter pecca- tum proprium; peccatum ergo originale est com- mune omnium hominum excepto Christo: Spiritus vero vivit pro vita, propter justificationem. Et hic quoque est dissimilitudo penes causam; quia vita Spi- ritus Christi non pendet à justitia, sed ab initio beata fuit; vita vero Spiritus eorum, in quibus habitat Christus, est propter justitiam Christi, quâ satisfecit Deo, solvendo pretium redemtionis humanæ: propter illam autem justitiam extrinsece (meritorie) & per participationem ejus intrinsece est vita eorum, in quibus habitat Christus. Ita Cajetanus cum Oecu- menio Spiritum hominis propter antithesin corpo- ris, & Spiritus intelligens: quo pacto Estius Spiri- tum hominis vitam dici propter justitiam observat, quia non tantum ipse per justitiam vivit, sed etiam ho- minem, cujus est Spiritus per eandem justitiam vivere facit, tanquam ipsius hominis vita quædam spiritua- lis. Notat autem idem Estius in Græcis ac Syriacis Codd. pro vivit legi vita: & qui hoc modo legunt, fere Spiritum intelligere non hominis, sed DEI, hoc sensu: Si Christus in nobis est, igitur Spiritus ejus vita ve- stra est, id est, vitam vobis tribuit, ac vivere vos fa- cit per justitiam &c. Per σῶμα autem carnem in- telligi, & carnem porro pro affectibus carni con- gruentibus accipi, & ita corpus dici mortuum, id est, exutum pristina agendi libertate, propter peccatum, id est, ad vitandum peccatum, glossæ sunt Grotianæ mere precariæ. Cur enim non corpus proprie acci- piamus? cur non intelligamus mortem proprie, cujus causa meritoria utique est peccatum, quam præpositio διὰ satis designat? Corpus vero quia inhabitatur a Spiritu S. etsi propter peccatum mor- ti subjectum sit, hujus enim radix, cum adhuc in nobis reliqua sit, ea cruce affligendum & morte tandem abolendum est hoc corpus nostrum, ut tandem prorsus ex eo peccatum exterminetur; tamen per inhabitantem Spiritum vivit, id est, vita spirituali fruitur, propter justitiam Christi, quæ

| per fidem imputatur. (Alii per Spiritum intel- ligunt partem in nobis regeneratam, quam vivere dicit propter justifrcationem, quia vita spiritualis in hoc seculo effectus justificationis est : quæ vita spi- ritualis nos certificat de vita æterna, quam hic in Spiritu inchoamus : ibi Spiritu & corpore æternũ inter beatos continuabimus, Conf. B. Balduin. in h. l. p. 149.) Unde etiam porro ab eadem inhabita- tione Spiritus est, quod resuscitanda sint τὰ θνητὰ σώματα, non certe caro, aut affectus nostri carna- les : sed ipsa corpora nostra mortalia. In phrasi, quod Patri ut principali causæ tribuatur resurrectio, si opponatur Filio, cavendus est Arianismus ; Quæ enim operatur Pater, ταῦτα eadem ἡ ὁμοίως operatur Filius.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. ἄρα οὖν, ἀδελφοὶ, ὀφειλέται ἐσμὲν, ὐ τῇ σαρκὶ. τῦ κατὰ σάρκα ζῆν. (Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.) It is understood from the reason of the opposite, and from those things which follow: ἀλλὰ πνέυματι τῦ κατὰ πνεῦμα. (but to the Spirit, to live according to the Spirit.) Whoever has given great things, has wished for great things to be repaid to him. God gave His Spirit so that we might use it. Clemens Strom. II. τοῖς εἰληφότα τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἐκ ἔτι ἁμαρτάνειν χρή. (Those who have received the forgiveness of sins ought no longer to sin.) Otherwise, those who do so are said to grieve the Holy Spirit, Eph. 4:30, nay even to quench Him, 1 Thess. 5:16, since such a great guest wishes to be cared for: otherwise He bids farewell to the lodging.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἄρα οὖν, ἀδελφοὶ, ὀφειλέται ἐσμὲν, ὐ τῇ σαρκὶ. τῦ κατὰ σάρκα ζῆν. Subauditur ex ratione oppositi, & ex iis,quæ sequun- tur : ἀλλὰ πνέυματι τῦ κατὰ πνεῦμα. Quisquis magna dedit, voluit sibi magna rependi. Deus Spiritum suum dedit, ut eo utamur. Clemens Strom. II. τοῖς εἰληφότα τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἐκ ἔτι ἁμαρτάνειν χρή. Aliter, qui faciunt, ii dicuntur Spiritum Sanctum do- lore afficere Eph. IV. 30. imo & extinguere 1. Thess. V. 16. cum cura haberi vult tam magnus hospes : alioqui valedi- cit hospitio.

## 8:13
V. 13. εἰ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ζῆτε, μέλλετε ἀποθνήσκειν. (For if you live according to the flesh, you are about to die.) Namely, without the hope of a better life, which those who have it seem to sleep rather than die. God does not give the highest good to those who despise His commandments.

εἰ δὲ πνεύματι τὰς πράξεις τῦ σώματος θανατῦτε. (But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body.) There is a metonymy here. For he said 'deeds' (πράξεις) when he wished 'sufferings and desires' (παθήματα καὶ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας) to be understood, as in Gal. 5:24, or 'the mind of the flesh' (φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς), as above, from which the 'deeds' arise. But just as ζωοποιεῖν (to make alive) for the Hellenists is often 'to preserve in life': Neh. 9:6, Ps. 71, Ecclesiastes 7:13, so also is θανατῦν (to put to death) 'to retain in death.' Moreover, evil desires are already killed before the Spirit enters into the heart. See above 6:6.

ζήσεσθε. In a clearly happy life, which is called eternal life. The word θανατῦν is rashly removed from its proper meaning; so that it may not denote to mortify, but to retain in death, which is a clearly unusual meaning: nor does the reason added accord with the truth. Because pains must be taken throughout the whole life for mortifying the desires and for crucifying the flesh. Moreover, the abuse of this opinion by the new Helmstedt Majorists in the Calixtine Harmony has been refuted as heretical: who wrongly infer from it the necessity of good works for salvation: for although the actions of the flesh, which are here called πράξεις τῦ σώματος Gal. V. 19. are called ἔργα τῆς σαρκὸς, so that we may not fall from life, yet good works are neither the cause of salvation, nor necessary for salvation: because those who are reborn are already in the spiritual life, and have obtained salvation, through faith; it is important, therefore, that they do not fall from that salvation, but be further preserved in it through faith: but they do not remain in faith, but lose the same, who, not mortifying the works of the flesh by the Spirit, permit the same to reign and dominate in the mortal body, and live according to the flesh. Rightly the blessed Mylius on this passage, f. 286. The Apostle teaches that life is a companion to the pursuit of piety, yet in such a way that it is signified not as a cause, but only as a consequence, lest anyone, taking a holiday from this, should construct a merit of eternal life. For from the effect of faith it is inferred that he who lives well will live eternally: because from the effect the judgment is made concerning the cause itself, that is, from works concerning faith. For no one mortifies the works of the flesh, unless he is endowed with a true and living faith. Rightly, therefore, are they said to be about to live, who mortify the works of the flesh: because from this it is evident that they have faith, by which life and righteousness are properly apprehended: just as from the movement of the body a judgment is made concerning the life of a man, although the movement does not constitute life itself.

Latin:

V. 13. εἰ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ζῆτε,μέλλετε ἀποθνήσκειν. Nempe sine spe vitæ melioris, quam qui habent, dormire potius, quam mori videntur. Deus summum bonum non dat sua præcepta spernentibus.

εἰ δὲ πνεύματι τὰς πράξεις τῦ σώματος θανατῦτε. Est hic μετωνυμία. Nam πράξεις dixit, cum vellet intel- ligi παθήματα καὶ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας, ut Gal. V. 24. aut φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, ut supra, ex quibus oriuntur αἱ πράξεις. Sicut autē ζωοποιεῖν Hellenistis sæpe est in vita conservare : Neh. IX. 6. Ps. LXXI. Ecclesiastæ VII. 13. ita & θανατῦν in morte reti- nere. Sunt autem jam interfectæ cupiditates malæ prius- quam in cor intret Spiritus. Vide supra VI. 6.

ζήσεσθε. Vita plane felice, quæ æterna vita dicitur. Verbum θανατῦν temere à proprietate remo- vetur ; ut non mortificare notet, sed in morte reti- nere, quæ significatio plane inusitata est : neque ratio adjuncta vero litat. Quia cupiditatibus mortificandis, & carni crucifigendæ per totam vi- tam opera danda est. Cæterum abusus hujus sen- tentiæ novorum Majoristarum Helmstadienfium in Harmon. Calixtino Hæretica profligatus est : qui perperam inde bonorum operum necessita- tem ad salutem colligunt : nam etsi Spiritu morti- ficanda sint actiones carnis, quæ hic πράξεις τῦ σώματος Gal. V. 19. ἔργα τῆς σαρκὸς dicuntur, ut vita non excidamus, non tamen bona opera vel causa salutis sunt, vel necessaria ad salutem : quia jā in vita sunt spirituali, & salute potiti sunt renati, per fidem ; Interest ergo, ut illa salute non excidant, sed porro in ea per fidem conserventur : non au- tem in fide manent, sed eandem amittunt, qui Spiritu opera carnis non mortificantes eadem in corpore mortali regnare & dominari permittunt, & secundum carnem vivunt. Recte B. Mylius in h. l. f. 286. Docet Apostolus pietatis studio comitem esse vitam, sic tamen ut non causa, sed consequentia tantum significetur, ne quis hinc male feriatus, vitæ æternæ meritum extruat. Ab effectu enim fidei col- ligitur, victurum esse æternum, qui bene vivit : quia ex effectu de causa ipsa, id est, ex operibus de fide sit judicium. Nemo enim mortificat opera carnis, nisi qui vera ac viva fide præditus est. Recte ergo vi- cturi dicuntur, qui opera carnis mortificant : quia hinc fidem eos habere constat, qua proprie vita & justitia apprehenditur : sicuti ex motu corporis de vita hominis sit judicium, quamvis motus vitam ipsam non constituat.

## 8:14
v. 14. ὅσοι γὰρ πνέυματι Θεῦ ἄγονται. They are led, that is, they are animated, as in Virgil:

The mind moves the mass. Thus also Gal. V. 18. He treats of those who have the law of GOD in their heart, of whom Isaiah LI. 7 prophesies.

These are the sons of God.

In an excellent way. For if Adam was called the son of GOD, as we said at Luke III. 38, because God had breathed into him the spirit of earthly life, how much more those into whom God has breathed the Spirit of holiness? See 1 John III. 1.

The cause of adoption is not the insufflation of the Holy Spirit, but regeneration and faith. For we are all sons of GOD through faith in Christ Gal. III. 25, and as many as received him, which happens through faith, to them he gave power to be sons of GOD, who believe in his name John I. 12. But the consequence of regeneration and faith is the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is given to the regenerate and the faithful, whom we do not receive from the works of the law, but from the hearing of faith. Gal. III. 2. Because you are sons of GOD, GOD sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts c. IV. 6.

PART II. CONCERNING THE CERTAINTY OF THE HOPE OF GLORY.

After he has asserted that we are immune from condemnation, the Apostle now desires to render us certain of eternal salvation: that we have both in Christ through faith, both liberation from the law of sin and death, and eternal salvation, where in place of sin, righteousness will be obtained, and in place of death, eternal life: against which, lest we fall away through voluntary sins, he had warned. He therefore proves the certainty of the hope of glory, where both the arguments of the proof and the conclusion or inference are to be observed. As to the former, since he had finally said that the sons of GOD are led by the Holy Spirit, he now seeks from that the first argument for the certainty of the hope of glory, namely from the gift of the Holy Spirit, that we have received not the spirit of bondage, but of adoption v. 15, through which we are rendered certain of the heavenly inheritance v. 16, provided we patiently sustain afflictions with Christ v. 17, 18. The second is from the manifestation of the sons of GOD, desired by the sighing of other creatures v. 19, 20, 21, 22, and of the believers themselves v. 23, 24, 25. The third is from the aid of the Holy Spirit v. 26, 27. The fourth from the eternal purpose of GOD v. 28, 29, 30. The fifth from the mediatorial office of the Son of GOD, both by reason of redemption v. 31, 32, 33, and by reason of intercession v. 34. As to the conclusion, the Apostle infers that nothing can separate us from the grace and love of GOD through an induction of various calamities, which we overcome through faith v. 35, 36, 37, and he proves this by his own example, that he is most certain that nothing can tear him away from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord v. 38, 39.

Latin:

v. 14. ὅσοι γὰρ πνέυματι Θεῦ ἄγονται. Aguntur, id est, animantur, sicut apud Virgilium :

Mens agit molem. Sic & Gal. V. 18. De iis agit, qui in cor- de habent legem DEᴵ, de quibus vaticinatur Esaias LI. 7.

ὕτοί εἰσιν ὑιὸι θεῦ.

Excellenti modo. Nam si Adam dictus DEI filius, ut diximus ad Lucam III. 38. quia Deus ei inflasset vitæ terre- stris spiritum, quanto magis ii, quibus inflavit Deus sancti- tatis Spiritum? Vide 1. Joh. III. 1.

Causa τῆς ὑιοθεσίας non est insufflatio Spiritus Sancti, sed regeneratio & fides. Omnes enim filii DEI sumus per fidem in Christum Gal. III. 25. & quotquot eum receperunt, quod fit per fidem, iis dedit potestatem, ut sint filii DEI, qui credunt in nomen ejus Joh. I. 12. Consequens autem re- generationis & fidei est Spiritus S. donatio, qui re- natis & fidelibus donatur, quem non accipimus ex operibus legis, sed ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως. Gal. III. 2. Quia estis Filii DEI, misit DEUS Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra c. IV. 6.

PARS II. DE SPEI GLORIÆ CERTITUDINE.

Postquam à condemnatione immunes nos as- seruit, jam salutis æternæ certos nos reddere cu- pit Apostolus: quod utrumque in Christo per fi- dem habeamus, tum liberationem à lege peccati, & mortis, tum salutem æternam, ubi loco peccati ju- stitia, loco mortis vita æterna obtinebitur: quâ, ne per peccata voluntaria excidamus, monuerat. Probat ergo certitudinem spei gloriæ, ubi & argu- menta probationis, & συμπέρασμα vel illatio con- clusionis observanda. Quod ad illa, quum filios DEI à Spiritu S. agi postremo dixerit, inde nunc primum certitudinis Spei gloriæ argumentum pe- tit, nimirum à Spiritu S. dono, quod non Spiritum servitutis, sed adoptionis acceperimus v. 15. per quē de hæreditate cœlesti certi reddimur v. 16. modo cum Christo patienter afflictiones sustineamus v. 17. 18. Alterum à manifestatione filiorum DEI, suspirio tum creaturarum aliarum v. 19. 20. 21. 22. tum ipsorummet fidelium v. 23. 24. 25. desiderata. Tertium à Spiritus S. subsidio v. 26. 27. Quartum ab æterno DEI proposito v. 28. 29. 30. Quintum à Filii DEI mediatorio officio, tum ratione redemtio- nis v. 31. 32. 33. tum ratione intercessionis v. 34. Quod ad συμπέρασμα, infert Apostolus nihil nos seque- strare à gratia & dilectione DEI posse per inductio- nem variarum calamitatum, quæ per fidem supe- ramus v. 35. 36. 37. idque suo exemplo comprobat, quod quam certissimus sit, nihil se divellere posse à dilectione DEI, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro v. 38. 39.

## 8:15
v. 15. For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear.

He calls the servile affection here the spirit of bondage, of those abstaining from evil solely for fear of present punishment, such as was the state of the greatest part of the Jews under the law of Moses. He rightly calls this servile. For servants generally abstain from harms, not for love of the master, but for fear of the cross or the hanging lash. Thus Horace: If a servant says to me, I have not stolen, I have not run away, I have my reward, you are not lashed with thongs, I say, I have not killed a man: you will not feed the crows on the cross. Aristotle: They are worse who do this not for shame, but for fear, not avoiding the shameful but the painful. The word spirit is frequent among the Hebrews for an affection, whence it is also accustomed to be taken for both anger and love. Thus also 1 Cor. II. 12, IV. 21, Gal. VI. 1, what is here spirit of bondage to fear, is the same as spirit of timidity. II Tim. I. 7.

but you have received the spirit of adoption.

He did not think it enough to say the spirit of liberty, but said of adoption. For those who are adopted, if they are servants, both become free from servants, and sons. Sons made by law are called thetous in Greek law. The verb is to adopt, whence the name adoption, which comprises both arrogation and adoption as specifically called by the Romans. The Apostle could have taken a likeness from natural generation itself, but it was more convenient for this passage to take it from adoption, because he mentions at the same time the prior state, as if it were servile.

in which we cry, Abba Father.

He imitates the voices of children coaxing their fathers, as we said at Mark XIV. 36. This article ὁ has the force of a vocative, as in Aristophanes, ὁ παῖς φέρε & ὁ Ξανθίας for Ξανθία. From the Syriac אבא is the Greek Ἀφφίς. Moreover, it is the custom of those coaxing to repeat either the same words, as Matt. VII. 22, or those of equal meaning, as Psalm VIII. 1. The Apostle recites the words which Christians were uttering immediately after baptism.

Latin:

v. 15. ὀὐ γὰρ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα δυλείας πάλιν εἰς φόβον.

Spiritum servitutis hic vocat affectum servilem metu so- lo pœnæ præsentis à malo abstinentium, qualis erat status maximæ partis Judæorum sub lege Mosis. Merito autem servile hoc vocat. Nam servi plerumque noxis abstinent, non domini amore, sed metu crucis aut pendentis habenæ. Sic Horatius: Nec furtum feci, nec fugi si mihi dicat Servus, habes pretium, loris non ureris, aio Non hominem occidi: non pasces in cruce corvos. Aristoteles: χείρους δὲ ὕσοι ὀὐ δι᾿ αἰδῶ, ἀλλὰ διὰ φόβον αὐτὸ δρῶσι ὀὐ φεύγοντες τὸ αἰσχρὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ λυπηρόν. רוּחַ πνεῦμα pro affectu frequens Hebræis, unde & pro ira & pro amo- re sumi solet. Sic & 1. Cor. II. 12. IV. 21. Gal. VI. 1. quod hic πνεῦμα δυλείας εἰς φόβον, idem πνεῦμα δειλίας. II. Tim. I. 7.

ἀλλ᾽ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα ὑιοθεσίας.

Non satis habuit dicere Spiritum libertatis, sed dixit adoptionis. Nam qui adoptantur, si servi sint, & liberi ex servis fiunt, & filii. Filii lege facti θετοὶ dicuntur in jure Græco. Verbum est ὑιοθετεῖν, unde nomen ὑιοθεσία, quod & arrogationem & adoptionem specialiter Romanis dictam comprehendit. Poterat & ab ipsa naturali genera- tione similitudinem sumere Apostolus, sed ut ab adoptione fumeret, huic loco convenientius fuit, quia simul meminit status prioris, quasi servilis.

ἐν ᾧ κράζομεν, Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ.

Imitatur puerorum patribus blandientium voces, ut di- ximus ad Marc. XIV. 36. Articulus ὁ hic habet vim vocativi, ut Apud Aristophanem, ὁ παῖς φέρε & ὁ Ξανθίας pro Ξανθία. Ex Syriaco אבא est Græcum Ἀφφίς. Tum vero mos est blandientium repetere aut voces easdem, ut Matth. VII. 22. aut paris significatus, ut Psal. VIII. 1. Recitat autem Apo- stolus voces quas statim à baptismo enunciabant Chri- stiani.

## 8:16
v. 16. the Spirit himself.

That Spirit given by GOD.

bears witness with our spirit.

That is, he bears witness. Thus we had the same compound word for the simple one above at II. 17. Our spirit here is our mind, as 1 Cor. II. 11, 2 Cor. VIII. 1; for the word רוח among the Hebrews is very polysemous, and Paul, as we have said, hunts for similarities of words, even in different meanings; which kind the Greeks call antanaclasis: such as in Plautus: 'May he blunt the edge of the eyes in the edge of the enemies.'

that we are children of God.

Just as the Sparti recognized their lineage from the spear sign impressed upon their body, and the Pelopidae from their shoulder whitening like ivory. GOD does not give such a gift except to those whom He wishes to have as sons.

For it is a servile or filial affection; but the Spirit is indicated by the Apostle, whom he denies to be a Spirit of bondage, and makes a Spirit of adoption, who is indeed the Holy Spirit himself, as being He in whom and through whom we cry: Abba Father, and who is distinguished from our spirit when in verse 16 the Apostle adds, 'the Spirit himself,' signifying that he is speaking of that same Spirit 'bearing witness with our spirit,' where an antanaclasis is feigned in vain: which the pronouns 'himself' strongly exclude. Nor does the Apostle speak of an effect of the Holy Spirit, but of the Holy Spirit who is called 'the deep things of God,' 1 Cor. II. 10, 11, 12, as also 2 Tim. I. 7. Compare Gal. IV. 6. He does not distinguish the Spirit of bondage and of adoption as if they were different Spirits, but designates the same Spirit by different effects, because the Holy Spirit works bondage and fear through the law, when man, struck by the knowledge and sense of sins, dreads and trembles, and is compelled to obedience by the threat of punishments, in the manner of servants who are forced to do their duty by fear of the lash: and through the Gospel He exhibits grace, and regenerates us, and makes us certain of adoption; the same Spirit is spoken of in the Gloss, but is called differently on account of different works. Therefore the Apostle builds up the certainty both of present grace and also of the hope of glory, first from the nature of the Spirit of the reborn, because He is a Spirit of adoption, not of bondage: Those who have received a Spirit not of bondage, but of adoption, they have no need to fear whether they are in the grace of GOD, but are certain that they are children of GOD, heirs of GOD. But the reborn, and those who have been justified through faith in Christ, have received a Spirit not of bondage but of adoption; therefore. Next, from the matter of the testimony; because the Spirit testifies to our spirit that we are children of God: That which the Holy Spirit testifies and confirms to our spirit, of that we are undoubtedly certain; because the testimony of the Holy Spirit is most certain, and absolutely indubitable, and he who does not believe it makes God a liar, 1 John V. 10. Beautifully Chrysostom in this place: When the Spirit testifies, what ambiguity is left? For if any man or angel, or some other power of this kind, were to promise something, one might rightly doubt. But that supreme essence, which both grants this very thing which it promises, and has even commanded us to pray, bearing witness to us, who could henceforth doubt this dignity? compare John XV. 26. The Papists [hold] the certainty of grace Those who attack the infallible [testimony], in order to defend the decree of the Council of Trent, say that this testimony is not through some expressed word, that is, through revelation, but through the experience of a certain inward sweetness and peace, which does not beget certainty, except a conjectural one, as Bellarmine holds, Book III on Justification, ch. 9. I reply that this testimony is not ἄμεσον and immediate, without the Word, to which fanatical spirits and enthusiasts are accustomed to appeal, but ἔμμεσον and mediate, which comes about through the Word: For although in the Word of God there are not singular propositions about this or that individual, nevertheless under universal propositions everyone can undoubtedly subsume, and conclude infallibly, with the application made to oneself: and the experience which we perceive thence in the heart, as the fruit of the Word, which is Spirit and life, and the power of GOD unto salvation to every one that believeth, John VI. 63. Rom. I. 16. is not merely conjectural, but infallible. Thus, when the Holy Spirit testifies in His Word: Whosoever believes in the Son of GOD, they certainly have remission of sins, Acts X. 43, and are children of GOD, John I. 12, Gal. III. 26, the believer subsumes: I believe in the Son of GOD: for he who believes, through a reflexive act, knows that he believes: and thence he undoubtedly concludes that he has remission of sins, that he is a child of GOD; and the Holy Spirit effects in the heart of such a believer certainty and sealing, and thus an inward taste and experience of this grace, indeed a foretaste of eternal life, because such are those who have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, Heb. VI. 5. Furthermore, an experimental affection cannot exist in the will if there is not a prior knowledge in the mind. Therefore, from the knowledge of our sonship arises the experience of sweetness and peace. Cf. Blessed Weller on this passage. Bellarmine also objects that in the Greek Codex it is held, not as in the Latin, that the Holy Spirit bears witness to our Spirit, but that the Holy Spirit bears witness together with our Spirit, and that this testimony is nothing else but the prayer itself, by which we say, Abba Father. I reply that Grotius acknowledges that the Latin version here expresses the sense of the Greek text, and rightly so; and that the testimony of the Holy Spirit is one thing, and our prayer is another: From the testimony of the Holy Spirit arises that confident prayer of ours, of which, however, the Holy Spirit Himself is also the author, through whom we cry, Abba Father. Whence the whole argument is here presented from the confident prayer of the reborn. Whosoever through the Holy Spirit cry Abba Father, they are certain that they are children of God. But the reborn through the Holy Spirit cry Abba Father. Therefore, the reborn are certain that they are children of God. But what Bellarmine objects that even sinners, as also heretics, say to GOD, Our Father, who art in heaven, and yet they are not true children of GOD. I reply that they do not say it through the Holy Spirit, nor is this about hypocritical prayers, but about true and serious ones, such as fall only to the reborn, not about presumption and vain boasting, but about the testimony and gracious operation of the Holy Spirit, which is in the faithful alone. Concerning which the Apostle says: No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. XII. 3; just as those who believe know that they believe, so those who are led by the Holy Spirit know that they are ruled by Him, and not by another: and they can prove and test themselves, whether they are in the faith, 2 Cor. XIII. 5, unless perhaps they are reprobates, which the Apostle adds, implying that doubt is not of the faithful, but is a sign of reprobation. And the word κράζομεν is emphatic: In which WE CRY: by which the invocation of the pious is described, Ps. XXIX. 1, 2, 5. Jer. XI. 11, noting the highest desire of the soul joined with filial confidence, just as the Son of GOD Himself cried to GOD the Father, Heb. V. 7. The word אבא also denotes a gentle and kind Father, and implies a benevolent affection, from אבה, he acquiesced, willed well, desired. Whence Bernard: The prayer, which grows sweet with the paternal name, provides me with confidence that all my petitions will be obtained. Cf. Mark XIV. 36, John XI. 42.

Latin:

v. 16. αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα.

Spiritus ille a DEO datus.

συμμαρτυρεῖ τῷ πνεύματι ἡμῶν.

Id est, μαρτυρεῖ. Sic eandem vocem compositam pro simplici habuimus supra II. 17. πνεῦμα ἡμῶν hic est animus noster, ut 1. Cor. II. 11. 2. Cor. VIII. 1. vox enim רוח apud Hebræos est valde πολύσημος, & Paulus, ut diximus, vo- cum similitudines venatur, etiam in significatu diverso; quod genus Græci ἀντανάκλασιν vocant: qualis apud Plautum: Oculorum præstinguat aciem in acie hostibus.

ὅτι ἐσμὲν τέκνα Θεῷ.

Sicut Sparti ex lanceæ signo impresso corpori, Pelopidæ ex humero eboris in modum candicante genus suum nosce- bant. DEUS tale donum non dat nisi iis quos pro filiis habere vult.

Nam affectus servilis, aut filialis; sed Spiritus in- digitatur ab Apostolo, quem negat servitutis esse Spiritu, & Spiritu facit υἱοθεσίας vel adoptionis, qui utique ipse Spiritus S. est, utpote in quo, & per quem clamamus: Abba Pater, quique à nostro Spiri- tu distinguitur cum vers. 16. addit Apostolus, αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα, significans se de eodem illo Spi- ritu loqui συμμαρτυρεῖ τῷ πνεύματι ἡμῶν, ubi frustra antanaclasis fingitur: quam fortiter exclu- dunt pronomina αὐτὸ τὸ. Nec vero de effectu Spi- ritus S. sed de Spiritu S. qui vocatur τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ, loquitur Apostolus 1. Cor. II. 10. 11. 12. ut & 2. Tim. I. 7. Conf. Gal. IV. 6. Spiritum servitutis, & adoptionis non distinguit ceu diversos Spiritus, sed eundem Spiritum à diversis effectis ita designat, quod Spiritus S. per legem servitutem ac timorem operetur, cum homo notitia & sensu peccatorum perculsus paveat, & contremiscat, & ad obe- dientiam tenore pœnarum cogatur, servorum more, qui metu flagrorum officium facere co- guntur: & per Evangelium gratiam exhibeat, nosque regeneret, & de υἱοθεσίᾳ certos reddat; Idem Spiritus dicitur in Glossa, sed propter diversa opera dissimiliter vocatur. Adstruit ergo Aposto- lus certitudinem tum præsentis gratiæ, tum etiam spei gloriæ à Spiritus S. testimonio primum è natu- ra Spiritus renatorum, quia est Spiritus adoptionis, non servitutis: Qui acceperunt Spiritum non ser- vitutis, sed adoptionis, illi non opus habent pave- re, an sint in gratia DEI, sed certi sunt, se esse filios DEI, hæredes DEI. At renati, & qui per fidem in Christum justificati sunt, acceperunt Spiritum non servitutis sed adoptionis; E.
