Deinde è testifi- cationis materia; quia Spiritus testatur nostro spiritui, quod simus filii Dei: Quod nostro spiritui testificatur & confirmat Spiritus S. de eo nos in- dubitato certi sumus; quia testimonium Spiritus Sancti certissimum est, & prorsus indubitatum, cui qui non credit, Deum mendacem facit 1. Joh. V. 10. Pulcre Chrysost. in h. l. Quando Spiritus testatur, quænam relinquitur ambiguitas? Si enim homo quispiam vel angelus, aut alia certe hujusmo- di quædam potestas aliquid promitteret, merito quis- piam dubitaverit. Suprema vero illa essentia, quæ & hoc ipsum largitur, quod promittit, atque adeo orare etiam jussit, testimonium nobis perhibente, quisnam de dignitate hac deinceps dubitare poterit? conf. Joh. XV. 26. Pontificii certitudinem gratiæ infallibilem impugnantes, ut Concilii Tridenti- ni decretum tueantur, hoc testimonium non esse per verbum aliquod expressum, id est, per reve- lationem, sed per experimentum cujusdam suavita- tis & pacis internæ, ajunt, quæ non gignat cer- titudinem, nisi conjecturalem, ut habet Bellarm. I. III. de justific. c. 9. Resp. esse hoc testimonium non ἄμεσον & immediatum, sine Verbo, ad quale solent fanatici Spiritus, & Enthusiastæ provoca- re, sed ἔμμεσον & immediatum, quod mediante ver- bo fit: Quamvis enim in verbo Dei non habean- tur propositiones singulares de hoc vel illo indi- viduo, tamen sub universalibus propositionibus indubitato quisque subsumere potest, & conclu- dere infallibiliter, applicatione ad sese facta: & quod inde percipimus experimentum in corde, tan- quam fructum Verbi, quod Spiritus & vita est, & potentia DEI ad salutem omni credenti Joh. VI. 63. Rom. I. 16. non est conjecturale tantum, sed infal- libile. Ita cum Spiritus S. in verbo suo testatur: Quicunque credunt in Filium DEI, illi certo ha- bent remissionem peccatorum Act. X. 43. & sunt filii DEI Joh. I. 12. Gal. III. 26. subsumit fidelis: Ego credo in Filium DEI: qui enim credit, per actum reflexum, scit, se credere: atque inde indubitato concludit, se habere remissionem peccatorum, esse filium DEI; efficitque Spiritus S. in corde hu- jusmodi fideli certitudinem & obsignationem, adeo- que interiorem gustum & experimentum hujus gra- tiæ, imo πρόγευσιν vitæ æternæ, quia talis est γευ- σάμενοι καλὸν θεῦ ῥῆμα, δυνάμεις τε μέλλοντος αἰῶνος Ebr. VI. 5. Porro experimentalis affectus esse non potest in voluntate, si non in mente prævia sit notitia. Ideo ex cognitione filiationis nostræ ori- tur experimentum suavitatis & pacis. Conf. B. Wellerus in h. l. Excipit & Bellarm. in Codice Græco haberi, non ut in Latino, quod Spiritus S. testimo- nium reddat Spiritui nostro, sed Spiritum S. simul testari cum Spiritu nostro, & hoc testimonium nihil esse alind nisi ipsam orationem, quâ dicimus, Abba Pater. Resp. Versionem Latinam hic sensum exprimere textus Græci agnoscit, & recte, Grotius; & aliud esse Spiritus S. testificationem, aliud nostram oratio- nem: E testificatione Spiritus S. oritur illa fidu- cialis nostra oratio, cujus tamen autor etiam est ipse Spiritus S. per quem clamamus, Abba Pater. Unde totum argumentum hic exhibetur è fiduciali renatorum oratione. Quicunque per Spiritum S. clamant Abba Pater, illi se esse filios Dei certi sunt. At renati per Spiritum S. clamant Abba Pater E. renati certi sunt se esse filios Dei. Quod vero ob- vertit Bellarm. quod etiam peccatores, ut & hæreti- ci dicant DEO, Pater noster, qui es in cælis, & tamen non sunt veri filii DEI. Resp. non dicere eos per Spir. S. neque hic de precibus hypocriticis, sed de veris seriisque, quales tantum in renatos cadunt, non de præsumtione & gloriatione vana, sed de te- stificatione & operatione gratiosa Spiritus S. agi, quæ est in solis fidelibus. De quo Apostolus ne- mo potest Jesum dicere Dominum, nisi per Spirit. S. 1. Cor. XII. 3. uti qui credunt, se credere sciunt, ita qui aguntur à Spiritu S. se ab illo, non alio regi sciunt: & probare ac tentare semetipsos possunt, an in fide sint 2. Cor. XIII. 5. nisi forte reprobi sunt, quod addit Apostolus innuens, dubitationem non esse fidelium, sed signum esse reprobationis. Et emphatica est vox κράζομεν: In quo CLAMA- MUS: quâ piorum invocatio describitur Ps. XXIX. 1. 2. 5. Jer. XI. 11. notans summum animi defide- rium cum fiducia filiali conjunctum, quemadmo- dum & ipse Filius DEI clamavit ad DEUM Pa- trem, Ebr. V. 7. Vox etiam אבא blandum & beni- gnum Patrem notat, & affectum benevolum in- nuit, ab אבה acquievit, bene voluit, concupivit. Unde Bernhardus: Oratio, quæ paterno dulcefcit nomine, omnium petitionum mearum impetranda- rum fiduciam mihi præstat. Conf. Marc. XIV. 36. Joh. XI. 42.

## 8:17
Verf. 17. εἰ δὲ τέκνα καὶ κληρονόμοι.

The sentiment is suitable not only to the Israelite law, Num. XXVII, but also to the law of the nations. For a certain tacit law assigns the inheritance of parents to children, L. cum initio D. de bonis damnatorum. But it is more likely that Paul looked to the Hebrew law, and therefore τέκνα here are sons, not because what he says cannot be adapted to either sex of Christians, but because by the law of Moses sons are necessarily heirs, daughters only if sons are lacking. And the word τέκνον is accustomed to be said especially of a son, Matthew XXI. 28.

κληρονόμοι μὲν Θεῦ.

In the word heir here, the right of succeeding to the goods of the deceased is not looked to, but a firm and inalienable possession, such as was the landed property among the Hebrews which they call נחלה, and the Hellenists κλῆρος, κληρονομία, κληροδοσία: sometimes κατάσχεσις, which word Stephen also uses twice in his speech. Thus the patrimony of Abraham and the gifts are distinguished, Gen. XXV. 4, 5. With God, heavenly felicity takes the place of a patrimony.

συγκληρονόμοι δὲ χρισῦ.

As the firstborn, in which way He is called below 19, Matth. I. 2, Luke II. 7, here, 29, Coloss. I. 15, Hebr. I. 6. We shall reign, but under Christ, and through Him. For He is clearly the heir of all things, Hebr. I. 2, we by the title of a trust.

And from the certainty of sonship the Apostle further gathers the certainty of the inheritance; from the certainty of present grace, the certainty of future glory: which, even if it be hypothetical, if, that is, we do not fall away from divine grace through sins, nevertheless by reason of the paternal affection of our GOD, whose gifts are without repentance, no doubt can exist for us, provided we persevere in the faith and avoid sins against conscience, by which faith is shaken. Since, however, eternal life is here called an inheritance, by which name it also comes in Matth. XIX. 24, ch. XXV. 34, 1 Cor. XV. 58, Gal. III. 24, Eph. I. 18, ch. V. 5, Col. III. 24, Tit. III. 7, Heb. I. 14, ch. XI. 8, 1 Petr. V. 4, Jac. II. 5, it is manifest that the merits of works, which the Papists bring forward, are excluded. For whatever we obtain by the title of inheritance, that we do not obtain or acquire by the merits of works. Nor is there any reason for Papists to say that an inheritance can also come about under a condition, for God has promised us eternal life not under the condition of works or merits, but by the title of inheritance alone: by which we are sons; but we are not sons through works, but through faith. Natural reason, as is held in l. 7. cum ratio ff. de bonis damnatorum, as a certain tacit law assigns the goods of parents to their children. Eternal life is not a servile or mercenary inheritance, but a filial one. And jurists distinguish between a condition and a mode: that a condition is the cause both of obtaining and losing an inheritance, but a mode not observed is indeed a cause of losing the inheritance which you possess, but not a cause of acquiring it: so that a mode may be admitted, lest by sins against conscience and will we fall from the inheritance Gal. V. 20. 21. nor are good works for that reason a condition, much less causes, of obtaining the heavenly inheritance. For the sole cause is ὑοθεσία or adoption. When the Apostle calls us heirs of GOD, this can be understood both originally, because that inheritance is from GOD, who adopted us as sons, and objectively and materially, because God is our inheritance, since He gives Himself to us, and in the other life God will be all in all to us 1. Cor. XV. 24. We are co-heirs of Christ, not as He is πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως the firstborn before all creatures, which belongs to Him according to His divine nature, and by eternal generation from the Father, and therefore those testimonies of Col. I. 15, Heb. I. 6 do not apply here, nor does that by which he is the firstborn of Mary, Matt. I. 25, Luke II. 7; for thus he does not have uterine brothers who could be called co-heirs with him by right of brotherhood: but as he willed to be the firstborn among many brothers, Rom. VIII. 29, which name is attributed to him metonymically, since he is not called so by reason of some generation, but by reason of the inheritance which he himself receives first, not by propriety of time; for thus Enoch and Elijah were already partakers of the same before, but by nature, because by entering the Holy of Holies he himself found eternal redemption for all, even for Enoch and Elijah, Heb. IX. 12, and having been made perfect, he himself became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, ch. V. 9, among whom were also Enoch and Elijah.

If indeed we suffer together. Namely with Christ, that is, if we endure all adversities with constant patience, as Christ did. He rightly added the condition, because a salutary birth does not give life unless it is accepted and guarded, as Cyprian says. See Matt. X. 33, Gal. VI. 9.

That we may also be glorified together. He adds the cause why we ought to endure those evils constantly, namely with a certain hope of future glory. The same sense is in 2 Tim. II. 11, 12.

Passions are not a meritorious condition, but a mode or order which GOD has established and observes in admitting men to the eternal inheritance. For the sole cause established was adoption. Now he explains how the children of GOD are to be admitted to the heavenly inheritance: which is taught from the example of the co-heir Christ, who also entered into his glory through passions, Luke XXIV. 25, 26, but did not merit glory for himself by passions, inasmuch as he had to merit it for us, not for himself; and therefore we too are said to enter the kingdom of heaven through afflictions, Acts XIV. 22, but not because of afflictions; then from the denied proportion between our passions and future glory: for a cause cannot be in the whole genus worse and more ignoble than its effect, whence our afflictions cannot be considered the cause of eternal life: and since there ought to be a proportion between merits and that which is rendered for merits, how can our passions merit eternal glory, between which there is no proportion at all, as the Apostle warns in the following verse.

Latin:

Verf. 17. εἰ δὲ τέκνα καὶ κληρονόμοι.

Sententia est conveniens non tantum Israëlitico, Num. XXVII. fed etiam gentium juri. Nam lex quædam tacita liberis parentum hæreditatem addicit L. cum initio D. de bonis damnatorum. Sed magis est, ut jus Hebræum respe- xerit Paulus, ideoque τέκνα hic sunt ὑοὶ, non quod non utrique sexui Christianorum aptari possint, quæ dicit, sed quod jure Mosis filii necessario hæredes, filiæ non nisi filiis deficientibus. Et folet vox τέκνον eximie de filio dici Matthæi XXI. 28.

κληρονόμοι μὲν Θεῦ.

In voce hæredis hic non respicitur jus succedendi in bona defuncti, sed possessio firma atque inalienabilis, qua- lis erat rerum soli apud Hebræos quæ vocantur נחלה, & Hellenistis κλῆρος, κληρονομία, κληροδοσία: interdum κα- τάσχεσις, qua voce & Stephanus in oratione sua bis utitur. Sic distinguuntut patrimonium Abrahami & munera Gen. XXV. 4. 5. Apud Deum patrimonii locum habet, cœlestis felicitas.

συγκληρονόμοι δὲ χρισῦ.

Tanquam πρωτοτόκυ, quomodo vocatur infra 19. Matth. I. 2. Luc. II. 7. hic, 29. Coloss. I. 15. Hebr. I. 6. Regnabimus, sed sub Christo, & per eum. Nam ille diferte est κληρονόμ πάντων Hebr. I. 2. nos fidei commissi titulo.

Et certitudine τῆς ὑότητος colligit porro Apo- stolus certitudinem τῆς κληρονομίας; è gratiæ præsen- tis certitudine, gloriæ futuræ certitudinem: quæ etsi hypothetica sit, si sc. non per peccata excidamus divinâ gratiâ, tamen ratione affectus paterni DEI nostri, cujus dona sunt ἀμεταμέλητα, nullum no- bis dubium esse potest, dummodo in fide perseve- remus & peccata contra conscientiam, quibus excutitur fides, caveamus. Quum autem hic vita æterna hæreditas dicatur, quo etiam nomine venit Matth. XIX. 24. c. XXV 34. 1. Cor. XV. 58. Gal. III. 24. Eph. I. 18. c. V. 5. Col. III. 24. Tit. III. 7. Ebr. I. 14. c. XI. 8. 1. Petr. V. 4. Jac. II. 5. manifestum est excludi operum merita, quæ Papistæ afferunt. Quicquid enim hæreditatis titulo consequimur, id operum meritis non impetramus, aut acquiri- mus. Nec est, quod dicant Papistæ hæreditatem etiam sub conditione posse contingere, nam vitam æternam nobis promisit Deus non sub conditio- ne operum vel meritorum, sed hæreditatis solius titulo: quâ sumus filii; non autem filii sumus per opera, sed per fidem. Ratio naturalis, ut habetur l. 7. cum ratio ff. de bonis damnatorum, quasi lex quæ- dam tacita addicit liberis bona parentum. Vita æterna non est servilis vel mercenaria hæreditas, sed filialis. Et distinguunt JCti inter conditionem, & modum: quod conditio causa sit & impetrandæ & amittendæ hæreditatis, modus autem non ob- servatus causa quidem amittendæ hæreditatis sit, quam possides, non vero acquirendæ causa: ut adeo modus admitti possit, ne peccatis contra conscien- tiam & voluntatem hæreditate excidamus Gal. V. 20. 21. nec tamen bona opera idcirco conditio, ne- dum causæ sint consequendæ hæreditatis cœlestis. Causa enim unica est ὑοθεσία vel adoptio. Cum hæredes DEI nos dicit Apostolus, intelligi hoc po- test tum originaliter, quod à DEO sit illa hæ- reditas, qui nos adoptavit in filios, tum objective & materialiter, quod Deus sit nostra hæreditas, quia seipsum nobis donat, & in altera vita nobis Deus erit omnia in omnibus 1. Cor. XV. 24. Cohæ- redes Christi sumus, nõ quâ is est πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως primogenitus ante omnes creaturas, quod ei convenit secũdum divinam naturam, & per æternã à Patre generationem, adeoque huc etiam illa non spectant testimonia Col. I. 15. Ebr. I. 6. nec qua is Mariæ primogenitus est Matth. I. 25. Luc. II. 7. sic enim non habet fratres uterinos, qui sibi fraterni- tatis jure cohæredes dici possint: sed qua is primo- genitus esse voluit inter fratres multos Rom. IIX. 29. quod nomen ipsi tribuitur metonymice, quum non dicatur ita, ratione generationis cujusdam, sed ra- tione hæreditatis, quam primus ipse accipit, non proprietate temporis; sic enim Enoch, & Elias jam ejusdem consortes antea fuère, sed naturæ, quia Sanctum sanctorum ingrediendo ipse æternam re- demtionem pro omnibus etiam Enocho & Elia invenit Ebr. IX. 12. & τελειωθεὶς perfectus ipse fa- ctus est αἶτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίυ causa salutis æternæ omnibus obsequentibus ipsi c. V. 9. inter quos etiam Enoch fuit & Elias.

ἔιπερ συμπάσχομεν. Nempe Christo, id est, si constanti patientia adversa omnia toleremus, sicut Christus fecit. Bene adjecit condi- tionem, quia nativitas salutaris non accepta, sed custodita vivificat, ut ait Cyprianus. Vide Matth. X. 33. Gal. XI. 9.

ἵνα καὶ συνδοξασθῶμεν. Causam addit, cur tolerare mala illa constanter debea- mus, spe certa scilicet futuræ gloriæ. Idem sensus 2. Tim. II. 11. 12.

Passiones non conditio sunt meritoria, sed modus vel ordo, quem DEUS in hominibus ad æternam hæreditatem admittendis constituit, & observat. Causa enim unica constituta erat ὑιοθεσία, vel ado- ptio. Jam explicat, quomodo filii DEI admitten- di sint ad cœlestem hæreditatem: quod cum ab exemplo cohæredis Christi docetur, qui per passiones etiam ingressus est in suam gloriam Luc. XXIV. 25. 26. non vero passionibus sibi meritus est gloriam, utpote quam nobis, non sibi mereri debuit; ideo- que & nos per afflictiones ingredi regnum cœlo- rum dicimur Act. XIV. 22. non vero propter affli- ctiones; tum à negata passionum nostrarum & glo- riæ futuræ proportione: non enim causa toto ge- nere deterior & ignobilior esse potest effectu suo, unde afflictiones nostræ causa censeri nequeunt vitæ æternæ: & quum inter merita, & id, quod red- ditur meritis, proportio intercedere debeat, quo- modo passiones nostræ gloriam æternam mereri possunt, inter quæ nulla omnino est proportio, ut v. seq. monet Apostolus.

## 8:18
V. 18. For I reckon. That is: for I always think this, as you also ought to think. Thus we had the word to reckon above III. 28 and VI. 11. Some of the ancients translate it, I weigh; not badly.

For the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. For what proportion is there? We endure brief things, we expect eternal things. Chrysostom notes that Paul opposes to patience not a relief from evils, which is directly opposed to it, but something much greater, glory from patience, and says that this glory will be revealed in us, that is, around us, because we already have a right to it now, but it does not appear to all, Col. III. 3, 4. The word worthy is derived from things that are weighed. For that which hangs by weight for the sake of an example is said to draw, that is, to pull, to lead. Plutarch uses it thus in the life of Demosthenes. Hence the scale in Festus by which the beam of the balance is inserted. Homer uses the word worthy thus: — of which we are worth one — If you throw into one scale the adversities which must be borne, and into the other the goods which are expected, the one in which the goods are will weigh down immensely. The same sense is in 2 Cor. IV. 17.

I reckon here is not just I think, or, as the Vulgate has it, I repute, but it is I conclude by reason, i.e., with things properly weighed, both with the magnitude of future glory and the afflictions of the present time

of the present momentary time, whether they are compared intensively or extensively, I cannot conclude and determine otherwise than that these sufferings are not worthy of future heavenly glory; Augustine, for not condign, as the Vulgate has it, said unworthy in book V of the City of GOD, ch. 18, and XXIII, quest. num. 67, as also Ambrose in book I of interpretation, ch. I. Beza rendered it as not at all equal: just as Tremellius also interpreted the Syriac text. For it implies equality. Therefore equality is denied, worthiness is denied, the proportion of passions is denied: and therefore merit is excluded, unworthily indeed, with Ambrose saying in the place cited, for the comparison of consolation, not for the fruit of redemption. What is so excellent, or whose life on earth is such, that it can equal heavenly glory? What is more sublime than Paul, who underwent so many dangers, absorbed so many pains and infirmities? In these, which he underwent in the name of Christ, he died daily, as he himself says, and he judged that he suffered nothing unworthy (more correctly, condign) in this time for such hope and expectation of glory. But if our passions do not merit glory, much less do works merit it. For it is more grievous to sustain passions for Christ than to devote effort to piety: and the highest degree of obedience is that perseverance in passions, whence Papists assign a higher degree to martyrs among the saints. But if anyone from the time Adam was created until the consummation of the world were to struggle against Satan and sustain afflictions, he would accomplish nothing great, in respect of the glory which he is about to attain. For he will reign for infinite ages together with Christ, says Macarius, hom. XV. Similarly Anselm in this place. If anyone were to suffer all the bitterness of punishments which can be suffered in the time of the present life, all those passions would not be a worthy merit for the attainment of future glory, which will be revealed in us with every veil removed, when we will perceive that which the eye has not seen: And of measure. If a man were to serve God for a thousand years, even most fervently, he would not merit by condignity to be in the kingdom of heaven for half a day.

Nor is there any exception for the Papists, who, although our works have no proportion in themselves to eternal glory, because they nevertheless lean upon the immense merit of Christ, and proceed from the infinite power of the Spirit dwelling in man and impelling the same to act, are in their own way also infinite; for those things contribute nothing to the condignity of our works, being merely extrinsic to them, such as would be the meritorious cause, the immense merit of Christ, and the efficient cause, the infinite power of the Holy Spirit: and it is entirely foreign to the Scriptures that Christ suffered so that by His merit He might obtain for our works the power of meriting, whom on the contrary they teach to have suffered for our sins, and to have made satisfaction for them, and thus to have acquired for us the gratuitous remission of sins.

Latin:

V. 18. λογίζομαι γάρ. Id est: hoc enim semper cogito, ut & vos cogitare de- betis. Sic verbum λογίζεθαι habuimus supra III. 28. & VI. 11. Veterum quidam vertunt, expendo; non male.

ὅτι ὐκ ἄξια τὰ παθήματα τῦ νῦν καιρῦ πρὸς τὴν μέλλεσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι εἰς ἡμᾶς. Quæ enim proportio? toleramus brevia, expectamus æterna. Notat Chrysostomus patientiæ opponere Paulum non levamentum à malis, quod directe ei opponitur, sed aliquid multo majus, gloriam ex patientia, & dicere eum, futurum ut in nos, id est, circa nos reveletur hæc gloria, quia jam nunc jus ad eam habemus, sed quod non omnibus appareat Coloff. III. 3. 4. ἄξιυ vox deducta est ex rebus, quæ ponderantur. Nam quod pondo exempli causa pen- det, dicitur τουτον ἄγειν, id est, trahere, deducere. Uti- tur sic Plutarchus in vita Demosthenis. Hinc agina apud Fe- stum qua inferitur scapus trutinæ. Homerus ἄξιυ vocem sic usurpat: — τῶν δ’ ἑνὸς ἄξια ἑσμὲν — Si in alteram lancem injicias adversa, quæ ferenda sunt, in alteram bona, quæ expectantur, immensum propendebit, in qua sunt bona. Idem sensus 2. Cor. IV. 17.

Λογίζομαι hic non est tantum cogito, aut, ut vul- gata habet, reputo, sed est ratione colligo, & con- cludo, q. d. rebus probe ponderatis cum futuræ gloriæ magnitudine, tum afflictionum τῦ νῦν καιρῦ

præsentis momentanei temporis sive intensive, seu extensive comparentur, non aliter concludere possum, ac statuere, quam non esse digna hæc παθήματα futura cœlesti gloria, August. pro non condignis, ut vulgata habet, indigna dixit l. V. de Civ. DEI cap. 18. & XXIII. quæst. num. 67. ut & Ambrosius lib. I. de interp. cap. I. Beza reddidit minime paria esse: prout etiam Tremellius Syrum textum interpretatus est. Nam שוה æqualitatem infert. Negatur ergo æqualitas, negatur dignitas, negatur proportio passionum: ideoque excluditur meritum indigne utique, Ambrosio l. c. dicente, ad consolationis comparationem non ad fructum re- demptionis. Quæ est tam præclara, cujusve vita in terra, ut adæquare cœlestem gloriam possit? Quid sublimius Paulo, qui tantum periculorum subiit, tantum dolorum, atque infirmitatum absorpuit? In his, qui Christi nomine subiit passionibus, quoti- die, ut ipse dicit, moriebatur, & nihil indignum (rectius condignum) perpeti se in hoc tempore pro tanta gloriæ spe, atque expectatione censebat. Si au- tem passiones nostræ non merentur gloriam, multo minus opera merentur. Nam gravius est passiones sustinere propter Christum, quam pie- tati operam navare: & supremus gradus obe- dientiæ est illa in passionibus perseverantia, unde martyribus gradum superiorem inter sanctos as- signant Papistæ. Si autem quisque ex quo crea- tus est Adam usque ad consummationem mundi dimi- caret contra Satanam & sustineret afflictiones, nihil magni perageret, respectu gloriæ, quam consecu- turus est. Regnabit enim in infinita secula una cum Christo, ait Macarius hom. XV. Similiter Anshel- mus in h. l. Si quis pateretur omnes pœnarum a- cerbitates, quæ in tempore præsentis vitæ sufferri possunt, non essent omnes illæ passiones dignum me- ritum ad consecutionem futuræ gloriæ, quæ ablato omni velamine revelabitur in nobis, quando perci- piemus illud, quod oculus non vidit: Et de men- sur. Si homo mille annis serviret Deo etiam ferven- tissime, non mereretur ex condigno dimidium diem esse in regno cœlorum.

Neque ullius bili est exceptio Papistarum, quod etsi opera nostra nullam per se habeant proportionem ad æternam gloriam, quia tamen innituntur im- menso Christi merito, & ab infinita Spiritus virtute in homine habitantis eundemque ad agendum im- pellentis proficiscuntur, suo modo etiam infinita sunt; Nam illa nihil faciunt ad operum nostro- rum condignitatem, utpote iis mere extrinseca, qualis foret tum causa meritoria Christi meritum immensum, tum efficiens, infinita Spiritus Sancti virtus: & à Scripturis alienum prorsus est Chri- stum passum esse, ut merito suo nostris operibus merendi virtutem obtineret, quem contrà pas- sum docent pro peccatis nostris, & pro illis satis- faceret, adeoque nobis gratuitam remissionem peccatorum acquireret.

## 8:19
V. 19. For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. Here there are those who understand by creature the Christians, who are a new creation: but they are not called creature simply and without addition. Nor does the discourse cohere sufficiently if the creature and the sons of God are the same. Origen takes creature to mean the body of individual Christians, as if souls alone were the sons of God: too Pythagorically and not in the manner of Paul. It is more true that creature is used here, as the Hebrews use בריה, for this universe which we behold, in which sense creature is used in Judith 9:13, 16:17, Wisdom 2:6, 5:18, 16:24, 19:6. And that there is a reference here to the passage of Ecclesiastes saying that all this is vanity, that is, subject to vanity, v. 20, to vanity it was subjected, as Paul will now speak: because, namely, in a perpetual cycle some things are born and others perish, namely animals and plants and metals, and parts of the earth, of the sea, of the air, and even of the heavens and the stars, according to the opinion of the ancients.

Philo on Cain: for the sun and the moon and the whole heaven and world, inasmuch as they are not self-governing, and are moved and carried continuously, it is right to say that they suffer hardship, and the clearest proof of this is that the annual seasons are idle. For the very things that hold together the movements in heaven change, at one time with northern, at another with southern, at another with other parts the revolutions, and being itself changed and cooled and twisted through all turnings, it is tested as suffering in its own experiences, since the thing that holds together is the cause of change, weariness, and it is not customary to speak at length about the things on land or under water, which govern their general and partial turnings to the greatest extent. For these things, being much more numerous than the celestial ones, according to what is likely, admit of weakness, inasmuch as they partake most of the moist and earthy substance. But after the conflagration a much better and purer machine is expected II. 2 Pet. 3:13, where by the Hebrew custom the new sum of things is understood by the name of heaven and earth, even if perhaps not divided into heaven and earth. But just as personifications are frequent among all writers, so also among the sacred ones, as when heaven and earth are ordered to listen, when mountains are said to have exulted, and seas and rivers to have trembled, as in Deut. 23:1, Ps. 114. You have similar things in Jer. 57:6, Hos. 13:14. And when not only sense, but also speech is attributed to them, as in Isa. 55:12, Baruch 3:34, Hab. 2:12. But above others Paul loves to personify, now the law, now sin, now death, and here the visible nature of things. Christians began to be treated badly from the times of Claudius. Paul consoles them in two ways; first, that the whole universe of things is subject to the changes and destruction of things. But it would be foolish to wish for oneself what the world does not have: concerning which matter see the chorus of Seneca in Thyestes at the end of act 4. & the letter of Sulpicius to Cicero, and Seneca to Helvidia. Then that the Apostles daily suffer many vexations and insults, but Christians ought not to refuse that lot which the Apostles bear willingly; the eager expectation of the creation, is the creation itself eagerly expecting, in the Hebrew manner. Eager expectation signifies here and in Phil. 1:20, an attentive expectation, such as is that of those who stand with head raised, when they await someone about to come from afar, which Herodotus, Euripides, Aristophanes, and others call to look out for. In the Glossary: I look out for, I await. Josephus also uses it. Cicero to Atticus 9.10 you will await the future there. What then does it mean that the nature of things awaits so attentively? The manifestation of the sons of God, that is, that time when it will appear to all that they are sons of God, who are indeed now, but are not thought to be. But it will appear when God makes them like himself, 1. 1 John 3:2, but the Apostle uses the word revelation, because the glory that is to be revealed had preceded. That this whole nature was founded for the sake of men, not only Moses established, but also the best of the Philosophers. You ought not therefore to be reformed into a better state except when men will be reformed. And Origen follows this sense, which we have now explained, elsewhere, namely in the book against Celsus 4, when having spoken about the Sun and Moon he says: concerning which we agree that they await the revelation of the sons of God.

Grotius removed only two opinions: but we have observed many more in Theol. Apost. Rom. orac. 62. The first, that Christians and the just are understood, Gregory the Great in comment. Job 3, book 4, Mor. ch. 41, and Lyranus, as well as Cajetan, Catharinus, and Salmeron in this place foster, which Socinus especially defends in his reply to the defense of the Tr. Luke 1, book 4, p. 170. But it is rightly opposed by Grotius, that creation nowhere absolutely denotes a new creature or the reborn, which however he will be seen to contradict himself on Col. 1:15. And here the sons of God, for whose glory to be revealed the creature groans, and the creature itself groaning are distinguished. Grotius did not propose the other opinion, which is Origen's, correctly enough: For he did not understand these sighs concerning human bodies, but concerning animals, which he attributes to the Sun, Moon, and other creatures, book 1, On First Principles, ch. 7. This vanity is the bodies into which souls existing before the body were thrust down because of their sins, and such bodies are also the Sun, Moon, and indeed even the earth and the heavens. But all these have souls, which existed before them, and consequently they themselves can sin, and will undergo the judgment of Christ just as men. These bodies therefore properly await the resurrection, and properly hope and groan to be freed from corruption. Which opinion both collapses by its own futility, and as heretical was deservedly rejected by Epiphanius, heresy 64, and Jerome in his letter to Avitus. For the rest, if Origen thinks somewhere that creation is the body of individual Christians, but the children of God the soul alone, Grotius rightly rejects this statement as too Pythagorean, and not according to the custom of Paul. But why did he himself at the previous chapter v. 21, in the explanation of the Pauline sentiment concerning the inner man, praise the Pythagorean opinion, that the mind alone is man, and the rest are not parts, but instruments of man?

But as for the present opinion of Grotius, even if he correctly explains the subject as concerning creatures destitute of reason, of which those are especially understood here which were first destined by God for the uses of men, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius among the Greeks, Hilary and Ambrose and indeed even Origen himself, as is observed here also by Grotius, among the Latins, and almost all among our own, establish. But as for the predicate, that expectation of the revelation of the sons of GOD is indeed correctly explained by Prosopopoeia, but the cause of the expectation is less correctly handed down, that the whole of man was subjected to vanity, that is, because of perpetual vicissitude it is subject to vanity, Ecclesiastes. I. 2. 8. because here that vicissitude is not regarded, but the creature is said to be subject to vanity on account of the abuse of men, and the servitude, which it is forced against its will to provide for sins: nor are all creatures liable to destruction while this age lasts, even if they are to perish at the consummation of the age, which is certain regarding the heaven and the stars, whatever may be the opinion of certain ancients: nor does the Apostle use that argument of consolation, that the whole universe of things is liable to changes and destruction, for what παράκλησις can redound to the faithful from that? Nor is the object which the creature awaits the reformation of itself into a better state, but ἡ ἀποκάλυψις the manifestation, or revelation of the sons of GOD. Concerning the reformation of creatures, neither here nor elsewhere is anything held in the Scriptures, and indeed they were created for the sake of man, to whom they provide use, but in this, not in the future age; nay, we believe on the authority of Peter, 2 Ep. III. 13, that at the consummation of the world all creatures will be destroyed by ἐμπύρωσιν, not indeed reformed after the ἐμπύρωσιν, who makes mention of the creation of a new heaven and a new earth, not of the reformation of creatures into a better state, as men will be reformed; nor does he understand by the creation of the machine of a new heaven and earth a production from nothing after the destruction of the former; but he so adumbrates for us the things of the future age by the things of this age, as if we were to have a new heaven and a new earth, illustrating future blessedness parabolically, when nevertheless he testifies that there will no longer be a sun to shine, nor the splendor of the moon, but that the Lord will be for an everlasting light, and Grotius himself acknowledges that by the Hebrew custom the name of heaven and earth is understood as the new sum of things, even if perhaps distinguished into heaven and earth, concerning which in its own place, with God; since it is otherwise certain from the Scriptures that the heaven and the earth, and all creatures devoid of reason, will substantially perish, and that mansions are already prepared for us with the Father, John XIV. 2, in the heavenly Jerusalem, that the spirits of just men made perfect are already acting with many myriads of angels and Christ Jesus, Heb. XII. 23, and that the heavenly kingdom is prepared for the elect from the foundation of the world ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, Matt. XXV. 34.

Latin:

V. 19. ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀπο- κάλυψιν τῶν ὑῶν τῦ Θεῦ ἀπεκδέχεται. Hic κτίσιν sunt, qui intelligant Christianos, qui nova sunt creatura: sed ii simpliciter & sine additamento κτίσις non vocantur. Neque satis cohæret sermo, si iidem sunt κτίσις & υἱοὶ τῦ Θεῦ. Origenes κτίσιν de corpore accipit singulorum Christianorum, quasi τίκεται Θεῦ sint animæ solæ: nimis Pythagorice & non ex more Pauli. Verius est κτίσις hic dici, ut Hebræis בריה hoc universum, quod conspicimus, quo sensu κτίσις dicitur Judith IX. 13. XVI. 17. Sap. II. 6. V. 18. XVI. 24. XIX. 6. Et respici hic locum Ecclesiastæ dicentis totum hoc esse vanitatem, id est, vani- tati subjectum l. 2. S. ματαιότητι ὑπετάγη, ut Paulus jam loquetur: quia scilicet perpetuo orbe alia gignuntur alia in- tereunt, animalia scilicet & plantæ & metalla, & partes terræ, maris, aëris etiam cœli ac syderũ, secundũ veterũ sententiā.

Philo de Caino : ἥλιος γὰρ καὶ σελήνη καὶ τὸν συμπάντα οὐρανὸν τε καὶ κόσμον, ἅτε οὐκ ὄντα αὐτεξούσια, καὶ κινόμενα καὶ φερόμενα συνεχῶς, θέμις εἰπεῖν κακοπαθεῖν καὶ τὸ κουότα μαρτύριον ἧς ἀργός εἰσιν οἱ ἐτήσιοι ὧραι. Τά τε γὰρ συνεκτικώτατα τα τῶν ἐν οὐρανῷ τας κινήσεις ἐναλλάττει , πότε μὲν βορείοις, τότε δὲ νοτίοις, τότε δὲ ἀλλοίας μοίραις τὰς περιφορὰς, ἅ τε αὐτῆς ἀναινόμιος καὶ ψυχόμενος κἠ πάσας τροπὰς ἐλικαπόμενος ἐν ταῖς ἰδίων πα- θημάτων ἐλέγχεται καμνων, ἐπεὶ τὸ συνεκτικώτατον μεταβολῆς αἴτιον, κάματος, ἀνήθες δὲ ἐστι περὶ τῶν χερσαίων ἢ καθ' ὕδατος μακρηγορεῖν τὰς καθόλου καὶ μετὰ μέρη τροπὰς αὐτῶν ἐπὶ μή- κισον διέποντα. Ταῦτα γὰρ πολὺ πλέω τῶν μεταρσίων, κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς ἀσθένειαν ἐνδέκεται, ἅτε πλεῖσον μετέχοντα τῆς ὑγᾶ- τας κἠ γεώδες ὕσιας. Expectatur autem post ἐμπύρωσιν multo melior puriorque machina II. Petr. III. 13. ubi Hebraico more cœli & terræ nomine nova rerum summa intelligitur, etsi forte non in cœlum terramque distincta. Sicut autem frequentes sunt προσωποποιΐαι apud omnes scriptores, ita & apud sacros, ut cum audire jubentur cœlum & terra, cum montes exultasse, maria & amnes trepidasse dicuntur, ut Deut. XXIII. 1. Pf. CXIV. Similia habes Jer. LVII. 6. Oseæ XIII. 14. Et cum non sensus tantum, sed & locutio eis af- fingitur, ut Esa. LV, 12. Baruch. III. 34. Habac. II. 12. Supra cæteros autem Paulus amat προσωποποιεῖν, nunc legem, nunc peccatum, nunc mortem, & hic naturam rerum aspe- ctabilem. Cœperunt Christiani à Claudii temporibus male tractari. Eos Paulus dupliciter consolatur; primum quod tota rerum universitas rerum vicibus & interitioni sit obno- xia. Stultum autem sit sibi optare, quod mundus non ha- bet: De qua re vide chorum Senecæ in Thyeste fine actus IV. & epistolam Sulpitii ad Ciceronem, & Senecam ad Hel- vidiam. Deinde quod Apostoli quotidie multas patiantur vexationes & contumelias, non debeant autem Christiani eam fortem recusare, quam Apostoli libenter ferant; ἡ ἀπο- καραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως, est ipsa κτίσις ἀποκαραδοκῶσα, more Hebræo. Significat ἀποκαραδοκία hic & Philipp I. 20. atten- tam expectationem, qualis est eorum, qui stant capite arre- cto, cum aliquem opperiuntur è longinquo venturum, quod καραδοκεῖν dicunt Herodotus, Euripides, Aristopha- nes, alii. In Glossario: καραδοκῶ exspecto. Usurpat & Jo- sephus. Cicero ad Atticum IX.10 τὸ μέλλον ibi καραδοκή- σεις. Quid ergo dicit opperiri tam attente rerum naturam? Patefactionem filiorum Dei, id est, tempus illud cum omni- bus apparebit esse filios Dei, qui nunc sunt quidem, sed non putantur esse. Apparebit autem cum Deus eos faciet sibi si- miles, 1. Joh. III. 2 utitur autem Apostolus voce ἀποκαλύ- ψεως, quia præcesserat τὴν μέλλυσαν δόξαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι. Totam hanc naturam hominum causa conditam, non Mo- ses tantum statuit, sed & Philosophorum optimi. Non de- bes ergo reformari in statum meliorem nisi cum homines reformabuntur. Et hunc, quein jam explicavimus, sensum alibi sequitur Origenes, libro nempe contra Celsum IV. cum de Sole & Luna locutus dicit: περὶ ὧν ὁμολογῦμεν ὅτι τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν ὑῶν τῶ Θεῶ ἀποδέχονται.

Duas tantum sententias removit Grotius: lon- ge autem plures observavimus in Theol. Apost. Rom. orac. LXII. Primam quod Christiani & ju- sti intelligantur Gregorius M. in comment. Job. III. l. IV. Mor. c. 41. & Lyranus, nec non Cajet. Cathar. & Salmer. in h. l. fovent, quam imprimis Socinus propugnat in resp. ad def. Tr. Luc. I. IV. p. 170. Cui vero merito opponitur à Grotio, quod κτίσις absolute nuspiam notet novam creaturam vel re- natos, qui tamen in eo ἑαυτομαχεῖ ad Col. I. 15. pa- tebit. Et distinguuntur hic filii Dei, ob quorum gloriam revelandam creatura ingemiscit, & crea- tura ipsa ingemescens. Sententiam alteram quæ Origenis est, non proposuit satis recte Grotius: Non enim de corporibus humanis, sed de animali- bus, quas Soli, Lunæ, & aliis creaturis tribuit, hæc suspiria intellexit l. 1. περὶ ἀρχῶν c. 7. Vanitas hæc sunt corpora in quæ animæ ante corpus existentes ob peccata sua sunt detrusæ, & talia corpora sunt etiam Sol, Luna, imo & terra & cæli. Hæc autem omnia habent animas, quæ ante ea extiterunt, ac consequêter possunt ipsa peccare, judiciumque Christi æque ac ho- mines subibunt. Hæc ergo corpora proprie expectant resurrectionem, & ut à corruptione liberentur, pro- prie sperant & ingemiscunt. Quæ vero opinio & futilitate sua concidit, & tanquam hæretica merito ab Epiphanio hæref. LXIV. & Hieronym. in Epist. ad Avitum reprobata est. De cætero si alicubi ita sent Origenes, quod κτίσις sit corpus singulorum Christianorum, τέκνα Θεoῦ vero anima sola, recte ceu nimis Pythagorice hoc dictum, & non ex more Pauli, rejicit Grotius. Cur vero ipse ad cap. præced. v. 21. in Paulinæ sentētiæ de interiori homine explicatione, Pythagoricam opinionem, quod mens sola homo sit, cætera non partes, sed instrumenta hominis, laudavit?

Quod vero ad præsentem Grotii sententiam attinet, etsi recte is subjectum explicet de creatu- ris ratione destitutis, quarum præcipue illæ hic in- telliguntur, quæ usibus hominum à Deo primum destinatæ sunt, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Oe- cumenius è Græcis, Hilarius & Ambrosius imo etiam Origenes ipse, uti hic observatum quoque Grotio, è Latinis, & plerique omnes è nostris, sta- tuunt. Quod vero ad prædicatum, expectatio illa revelationis filiorum DEI probe quidem per Pro- sopopæiam exponitur, sed expectationis causa mi- nus recte traditur, quod totum hominis ματαιότη- τι ὑπετάγη, id est, ob perpetuam vicissitudinem va- nitati obnoxium sit, Ecclesiast. I. 2. 8. quia non respi- citur hic illa vicissitudo, sed vanitati subjecta crea- tura dicitur propter abusum hominum, & servi- tium, quod ad peccata invita ipsi præstari cogitur: nec omnes creaturæ interitui obnoxiæ sunt, dum durat hoc seculum, etsi in consummatione seculi interituræ sint, quod de cælo ac syderibus constat, quicquid sit de veterum quorundam sententia: nec eo consolationis argumento utitur Apostolus, quod tota rerum universitas vicibus & interitioni sit obnoxia, quænam enim inde παράκλησις ad fi- deles redundare potest? Neque objectum quod expectat creatura, est reformatio ipsius in meliorem statum, sed ἡ ἀποκάλυψις manifestatio, vel revela- tio filiorum DEI. De reformatione creaturarum, neque hic, neque alibi quicquam habetur in Scri- pturis, & conditæ quidem illæ sunt propter homi- nem, cui usum præstant, sed in hoc, non in futuro se- culo; imo in consummatione mundi creaturas omnes per ἐμπύρωσιν destructum, non vero post ἐμπύρω- σιν reformatum iri, Petro autore credimus, 2. Ep. III. 13. qui creationis novi cæli & novæ terræ men- tionem facit, non creaturarum in statum meliorem reformationis, veluti homines reformabuntur; nec per creationem machinæ novæ cæli & terræ è ni- hilo post prioris destructionem, productionem in- telligit; sed ita rebus hujus sæculi res futuri seculi no- bis adumbrat, ac si novum cœlum ac novam terrā habituri simus, parabolice futuram beatitudinem illustrans, quum tamen neque solem amplius fore ad lucendum, nec splendorem lunæ, sed Dominum fore in lucem sempiternam testetur, agnoscatque ipse Grotius, Ebraico more cæli & terræ nomine no- vam rerum summam intelligi, etsi forte in cælum & terram distinctam, quo de suo loco, cum Deo; quum de cætero è Scripturis constet substantialiter interi- turæ cœlum & terram, & creaturas omnes rationis expertes, & paratas jam esse nobis mansiones apud Patrem Joh. XIV. 2. in Hierosolyma cælesti, jam agere Spiritus justorum perfectorum cum multis my- riadibus angelorum & Christo Jesu Ebr. XII. 23. re- gnumque cæleste electis à constitutione mundi ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου paratum esse, Matth. XXV. 34.

## 8:20
V. 20. For the creature was made subject to vanity.

He calls the inconstancy and mutability of things vanity, as appears from the passage of Ecclesiastes, and from Ps. XXXIX. 6. ὑπετάγη signifies, is subject, a passive for a neuter.

Not willingly.

All things having sense love their own preservation, and if we believe some, there are none which do not have some sense, although it is not called by that name by all. Thus above Philo: ἐκ ὄντα ἀντιξέσια, Tertullian says that an unwilling condition succeeded to vanity.

but because of him who subjected it.

GOD had indeed created beautiful things, but perishable ones. Tertullian in 'De Corona', and others, refer this to the time after the sin, which can be accepted if one looks only at the harm which comes to men from other things. And in the 'Apologeticus', Tertullian refers this to the creation itself: 'The reason which composed the universe out of diversity, so that all things might consist of rival substances under unity, of the void and the solid, of the animate and the inanimate, of the comprehensible and the incomprehensible, of light and darkness, of life itself and death, preserves the age also in such a defined and distinct condition, that this first part, from the beginning of the things which we inhabit, flows down in temporal age to the end; but the following one, which we await, is propagated into infinite eternity.' When, therefore, the end and the middle boundary, which intervenes, shall have arrived, so that the species of the world itself, which is opposed to that disposition of eternity in the manner of a hall, is also transformed, being equally temporal, then the whole human race will be restored to expunge what it has earned of good or evil in this age.

in hope.

He continues the personification, and this coheres with 'was subjected'.

Latin:

V. 20. τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη.

Ματαιότητα vocat rerum inconstantiam ac mutabilita- tem, ut apparet ex Ecclesiastæ loco, & ex Ps. XXXIX. 6. ὑπετάγη singnificat, subest, passivum pro neutro.

ἐχ ἑκῦσα.

Res sensum habentes omnes amant sui conservationem, & si quibusdam credimus, nullæ sunt, quæ non aliquem sensum habeant, quanquam is non eo ab omnibus nomi- ne appelletur. Sic supra Pihlo: ἐκ ὄντα ἀντιξέσια, Con- ditionem invitam vanitati succedisse ait Tertullianus.

ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα.

Pulcra quidem creaverat DEUS, sed caduca. Tertul- lianus de corona, & alii hoc referunt ad tempus post pec- catum, quod recipi potest, si sola spectetur noxa, quæ à re- bus aliis ad homines pervenit. Ac in Apologetico Ter- tullianus ad ipsam creationem hoc refert: Quæ ratio uni- versitatem ex diversitate composuit, ut omnia æmulis substan- tiis sub unitate constarent ex vacuo & solido, ex animali & inanimali, ex comprehensibili & incomprehensibili, ex luce & tenebris, ex ipsa vita & morte, eadem ævum quoque ita de- finita ac distincta conditione conservat, ut prima hæc pars ab exordio rerum, quas incolimus, temporali ætate ad finem defluat; sequens vero quam expectamus, in infinitam æterni- tatem propegetur. Cum ergo finis & limes medius, qui in- terhiat, adfuerit, ut etiam mundi ipsius species transforme- tur æque temporalis, quæ illi dispositioni æternitatis aulæ vi- ce opposita est, tunc restituetur omne humanum genus ad ex- pungendum quod in isto ævo boni seu mali meruit.

ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι.

Prosequitur προσωποπεΐαν & cohæret hoc cum ὑπετάγη.

## 8:21
that the creation itself also will be liberated from the bondage of corruption.

Here he interprets what he had called 'vanity', and that which he had said was subjected, he now calls bondage, and opposes to it 'to be liberated'. Similar is that of Euripides:

To bear the yoke of necessity.

Into the freedom of the glory of the children of GOD.) 'Of the glory of the children of GOD' has here a signification of time. He says, it will receive freedom from vanity or destruction then, when the children of GOD shall arrive at that eternal glory. Tertullian against Hermogenes: 'Then there will be an end to death, when its ruler, the devil, shall have gone into the fire which GOD prepared for him and his angels, having first been relegated to the pit of the abyss, when the revelation of the children of GOD shall have redeemed the creation (thus he is accustomed to translate κτίσιν) from the evil everywhere subject to vanity, when with restored innocence and integrity of condition the cattle shall have agreed with the beasts, and little children shall have played with serpents, when the father shall have placed the enemies under the feet of the son, namely, the workers of evil.' The last of which are not far from the opinion of the Rabbis, who think that even mute animals will attain a better state when men rise again. See Manasseh on the resurrection. Philo in the book 'On Rewards': 'It is not beyond hope that the animals will be tamed in their minds.' And afterwards: 'Then also the kinds of scorpions and snakes and other reptiles will have their poison rendered inactive.' Good fathers are accustomed to honor even the servants of their children for the sake of the children.

We have previously warned that the subjection of bondage is wrongly understood as the mutability of creatures: to which the word 'subjection' does not even correspond, which the Apostle did not use rashly, but to indicate forced service: for 'it was subjected' is not 'it is merely under', but 'it has been subjected', and therefore it does not look to the property of nature, but to subjection and bondage coming from elsewhere, nor does the notion of 'involuntary' fit: by which word, even if used metaphorically, it is noted that this happens to things contrary to nature, and as if they were unwilling, but not that they were created such by GOD: nor is he who subjected things to vanity God, whether in that he created them perishable, or in that after the sin he willed them to be harmful to men: But man, who through the abuse of creatures subjects them to vanity: which here is not an inherent, blameless mutability or vicissitude, but rather a usurped, detestable bondage, to which man drags it away as if it were unwilling. But it is called 'bondage of corruption', not because vicissitude and corruptibility is a certain bondage of the creature, by which it aspires to incorruptibility exempt from vicissitude, as if to true freedom: because (1.) Every creature was created by GOD such as He willed it to be, and through that creation, by the most wise judgment of God Himself, each was very good, just as the whole universe was distinguished into its species, of which the good and great God willed some to be corruptible, some incorruptible. And therefore (2.) The creature, on account of this condition of its own and its specific perfection due to the will and good pleasure of GOD for each, cannot be introduced by the Holy Spirit as groaning and grieving most vehemently, just as 'birth pangs' imply infernal pains and the most exquisite pains of those giving birth. How can this servitude be established as involuntary and lamentable, when every creature serves it in its own kind at the nod of the Creator, and executes His will, so that it may celebrate God its Creator in its own way? Is this the δουλεία φθορᾶς? Is it a servitude of such a kind from which it might deservedly seek to be liberated? See Ps. 148:1 seqq. v. 8, 9, 10. What kind of liberation is that from this servitude? For it is understood to be liberated from φθορᾷ & δουλείᾳ τῆς φθορᾶς, if corruptibility is designated by that, or it is considered to be brought about by total destruction and annihilation: or by reformation into a better state and condition: If the former, then the creature will groan, so that it may be liberated from that perfection in which it was created very good by God, so that it may be reduced from being to non-being, which is absurd. If the latter, it contradicts Scripture, which is ignorant of and excludes such a reformation; since it leaves no creature to the other world besides man and the angels, and testifies that heaven and earth will utterly cease to be, Ps. 102:27, Matt. 5:18, ch. 24:35, Mark 13:13, Luke 16:17, ch. 21:13, 2 Pet. 3:7, 10, so that they will no longer exist in the other world, Job 14:2, Psalm 72:7, Rev. 10:6, ch. 20:1, ch. 21:1. And it affirms that God alone will be all in all to the elect, 1 Cor. 15:28. And will all plants and shrubs in turn grow green again, will brute animals, birds, fish, serpents, and any reptiles, the beasts of the earth, after they have long since expired, be recalled to life in turn, and enjoy a new and far better state? Grotius himself would scarcely have said this, who did not even dare to say that the earth, distinct from heaven, would have a place in the new world: Nor could even Socinus himself, the worst of the most recent heretics, bear the Paccian opinion that brute animals are one day to be resurrected to incorruptibility, nor did any of the Calvinists dare to approve of a similar monstrous opinion of their Lucas Trelcatius. Who among the sounder sort would deem the trifles of even some Papists, such as those of Cornelius à Lapide on Rev. 22:8 and similar ones, that rivers, trees, and fruits will exist in the other life, and that the blessed will enjoy them in the heavenly Paradise, more worthy of his approval than the fables of the Jews and Muhammadans about the pleasures of the other world? One must certainly wonder at Grotius not rejecting Jewish commentaries, which are truly unworthy of refutation. What therefore remains, but that the δουλείαν φθορᾶς from which the creature is introduced as groaning so much to be liberated, is that servitude to which it is subjected against its will, and involuntarily, when it would rather serve at the nod and will of GOD, and perpetually praise Him, than objectively detract from the glory of the divine name, or serve blasphemy, idolatry, murders, fornications, and other scandals of that kind, by which the name and law of GOD are disparaged, just as, for example, the day and the sun are forced to serve with light, the night with darkness, the earth with the sustenance of such, etc., to those who commit such things. Which is a servitude of φθορᾶς, of corruption, because creatures are corrupted in respect to their end and use, which were created for the glory of GOD and the use of man, not for the ignominy of the Creator and abuse of such a kind: and that servitude contributes to the corruption and destruction of man as the cause of his death and condemnation, and also to the corruption of the creatures themselves, since GOD can no longer bear the abuse of the best creatures, and will therefore destroy them, which the antediluvian world experienced in great part in the universal cataclysm, and creatures devoid of reason are from time to time accustomed to experience in general punishments, whence they are described as if not only brute animals and the earth; but even heaven itself and the stars are affected by the same, Isa. XIII. 9. ch. XXIV. 4. Jer. IV. 23. ch. XV. 9. Ez. XXXII. 7. Am. VIII. 9. Mich. III. 6. B. Gerhard T. IX. on the consummation of the age §. 55. seems to understand by the word φθορᾶς [corruption] corruptible man, to whom when one is a servant, one is a servant to what is corruptible: all men, he says, are mortal and corruptible; because therefore creatures serve impious men who wickedly abuse them, therefore through this service they undergo δουλείαν φθορᾶς [the bondage of corruption]. But because not only the impious are mortal and corruptible, but also the pious, service to the impious, and indeed rendered to impiety itself, is best understood by ματαιότητα [vanity], and δουλείαν φθορᾶς [the bondage of corruption], to which creatures are read to be subject in this age. Which also pleased B. Gerhard, illustrating it with the example of wine: Thus wine is a good and excellent creature of GOD, but it is forced in this life to serve the desires of drunkards. This is that bondage of corruption, to which that creature is subject not willingly, hence it groans and according to the Apostolic prosopopoeia seeks to be freed from this bondage, for it chooses rather not to be, and to go into nothingness; than to serve the abuse of drunkards, and by this reason to war as it were against its creator. Let the same judgment be held regarding the remaining creatures of GOD. The creature is said to be freed not from corruption, but from the bondage of corruption: because they are freed from the bondage of corruption, which they are forced to render to impious men, although they themselves do not become free from corruption, but are subject to corruption and destruction. But why the Apostle uses this phrase, Gerhard explains thus §. 59. But for this reason he preferred to say that the creature is to be freed from the bondage of corruption, rather than that it will totally perish, both because he wished to use such a phrase as could also be predicated of man, and yet in respect to man would not be opposed to destruction. Now indeed total destruction and corruption on the last day does not apply to men, but liberation from the bondage of corruption is also common to men; and because he wished to persist in that allegorical prosopopoeia and metaphorical hyperbole, by which he gave certain acts of reason to irrational creatures, as if to say: If creatures subject to the abuse of the impious in this life were participants of sense and reason, they would prefer total annihilation rather than such bondage. But we perceive this sense of the creature anxiously aspiring to liberation when creatures deny their operations to human uses, when the earth is shaken by violent motions, when immense floods occur, when the very laws and barriers of nature are seen to be loosened and broken. For then the machinery of the world is to be thought to pant for its liberation with certain sighs, as it were, and a heavy sob, as B. Mylius has it here. Furthermore, that the signification of time is noted by the words εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν [into the liberty] is not poorly noted by Grotius; but so that the sense may be fuller, we have advised that it be added in Theol. Apost. Rom. because by the destruction of the creatures that served vanity, the glorious liberty and immunity from all manner of vanity will be the more illustrious and certain: because then for the children of GOD one GOD will be all in all, nothing will appear subject to vanity, nothing to the bondage of corruption, nor will we any longer need their use, nor will we have need to fear their abuse, because they will cease to be entirely, and will no longer remain.

Latin:

ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ὑπὸ τῆς δυλείας τῆς φθορᾶς.

Hic interpretatur, quod ματαιότητα dixerat, & id, quod subjici dixerat, nunc vocat servitutem, & ei opponit, libe- rari. Simile illud Euripidis:

Τὸ τῆς ἀνάγκης ἐ λέγειν ὕσον ζυγόν.

Ἐς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τῶ Θεῶ.) Τῆς δό- ξης τῶν τέκνων τῶ Θεῶ habet hic temporis significationem. Libertatem, inquit, à vanitate sive interitu accipiet tunc, cum filii DEI ad gloriam illam æternam pervenient. Ter- tullianus adversus Hermogenem: Tunc erit morti finis, cum præses ejus diabolus abierit in ignem, quem præparavit illi DEUS & Angelis ejus, prius in puteum abyssi relegatus, cum revelatio filiorum DEI redemerit conditionem (sic κτίσιν ver- tere solet) à malo ubique vanitati subjectam cum restituta innocentia & integritate conditionis pecora condixerint bestiis, & parvuli de serpentibus luserint, cum pater filio posuerit ini- micos sub pedes, utique operarios mali. Quorum ultima non absunt a Rabbinorum sententia, qui existimant etiam mu- ta animantia meliorem statum adeptura cum homines re- surgent. Vide Manassem de resurrectione. Philo libro de Præmiis: ἐκ ἀπελπίστου ὅτι ἐξημερωθήσεται τῶν κατὰ διά- νοιαν κὰι τὰ ζῶα ἡμερωθήσεται. Et postea: τότε κὰι σκορπίων γένη κὰι ὄφεων κὰι τῶν ἄλλων ἑρπετῶν ἄπρακτον ἕξει τὸν ἰόν. Solent boni patres in honorem filiorum etiam servos eorum ornare.

Servitutis subjectionem perperam de mutabili- tate creaturarum intelligi antea monuimus: cui neque consonat subjectionis verbum, quo non te- mere usus est Apostolus, sed ut coactum servitium indicaret: ὑπετάγη enim non est, nude subest, sed subjecta est, ideoque non respicit proprietatem na- turæ, sed subjectionem & servitutem aliunde ac- cedentem, nec involuntarii notio convenit: quà voce etsi metaphorice adhibita notantur præter na- turam hoc rebus accidere, ipsisque veluti invitis, non vero tales à DEO conditas esse: nec ille qui res vanitati subjecit est Deus, sive qua creavit eas caducas, seu qua post peccatum noxias homini- bus esse voluit: Sed homo, qui per abusum crea- turarum easdem vanitati subjicit: quæ hic non est insita inculpabilis mutabilitatis aut vicissitudinis, sed potius usurpata detestandæ servitutis, ad quam quasi invitam eam abripit homo. Dicitur autem δυλέια τῆς Φθορᾶς, non quod vicissitudo & cor- ruptibilitas servitus quædam sit creaturæ, qua ad incorruptibilitatem vicissitudinis expertem adspi- ret, ceu ad veram libertatem: quia (1.) Creatura quæque condita est à DEO, qualem eam esse voluit, & per illam creationem judicio ipsius Dei sapientissimo quælibet fuit valde bona, uti uni- versitas tota in species suas distincta, quarum alias Deus optimus Maximus voluit corruptibiles, ali- quas incorruptibiles. Ideoque (2.) Creatura ob hanc sui conditionem & specificam perfectionem ad arbitrium & beneplacitum DEI cuivis debitam, non potest à Spiritu S. introduci ceu gemens & vehementissime dolens, uti ώδίνες infernales dolo- res & dolores parturientium exquisitissimos im- portant. (3.) Quomodo hæc servitus statui po- test invita & lamentabilis, cum quævis creatura ad nutum creatoris in suo genere eam serviat, & voluntatem ejus exequatur, ut Deum creatorem suum more suo celebret. Anne hæc est δουλεία φθορᾶς? An est servitium ejusmodi à quo libe- rari merito expetat? Vid. Ps. CXLIIX. 1. seqq. v. 8. 9. 10. Qualis est illa liberatio ab hac ser- vitute? Nam à φθορᾷ & δουλείᾳ τῆς φθορᾶς velli- berari intelligitur, si corruptibilitas designetur ea, vel fieri censetur per destructionem omnimodam, & annihilationem: vel per reformationem in me- liorem statum & conditionem: Si illud, tum crea- tura ingemiscet, ut ab ea perfectione, in qua valde bona condita est à Deo, liberetur, ut ab esse ad non esse redigatur, quod absurdum. Si posterius, repu- gnat Scriptura, quæ talem reformationem ignorat, & excludit; cum præter hominem & angelos nul- lam creaturam alteri seculo relinquat, ac cælum & terram penitus desitura testatur Ps. CII. 27. Matth. V. 18. c. XXIV. 35. Marc. XIII. 13. Luc. XVI. 17. c. XXI. 13. 2. Petr. III. 7. 10. ita ut amplius fu- tura non sint in altero seculo Job. XIV. 2. Psalm. LXXII. 7. Ap. X. 6. c. XX. 1. c. XXI. 1. Deumque solum electis futurum esse omnia in omnibus af- firmat, 1. Cor. XV. 28. & num plantæ & frutices omnes vicissim revirescent, num animalia bruta, volucres, pisces, serpentes, & quælibet reptilia, be- stias terræ, postquam pridem expirarunt, vicissim in vitam revocabuntur, novoque statu longe me- liori gaudebunt? Vix id dicturus fuisset ipse Gro- tius, qui ne quidem terram à cœlo distinctam in novo seculo locum habituram dicere ausus fuit: Nec vel Socinus ipse hæreticorum novissimorum pessimus Paccianam sententiam, quod bruta ani- mantia ad incorruptibilitatem olim resuscitanda sint, ferre potuit, vel Calvinianorum quisquam simile opinionis portentum Lucæ sui Trelcatii ap- probare ausus est. Papistarum etiam nonnullo- rum nugas, utpote Cornelii Lapidei ad Ap. XXII. 8. & similium, quod fluvii, arbores, & poma in altera vita futura sint, quodque iisdem fruituri be- ati sint in Paradiso cœlesti, ecquis saniorum cal- culo suo magis dignabitur, quam Judæorum & Muhametanorum fabellas de alterius seculi volu- ptatibus. Mirari sane oportet Grotium non ab- nuentem Judaicis commentis, quæ vero indigna sunt refutatione. Quid ergo superest, quam ut δουλείαν φθορᾶς à qua ut liberetur creatura, tanto- pere ingemiscens introducitur, sit illa servitus, cui subjicitur præter voluntatem suam, & invita, quum mallet potius ad nutum & voluntatem DEI servire, eumque perpetuo laudare, quam nominis divini gloriæ detrahere objective, vel blasphemiæ, idololatriæ, cædibus, scortationibus, & id genus aliis scandalis, quibus nomini & legi DEI derogatur, inservire, uti v. g. dies, & sol lumine, nox tenebris, terra talium sustentatione &c. iis qui talia desi- gnant inservire cogitur. Quæ φθορᾶς corruptio- nis est servitus, quia corrumpuntur creaturæ ratio- ne finis & usus sui, quæ ad gloriam DEI & usum hominis, non ad ignominiam Creatoris, & ab- usum ejusmodi conditæ sunt: & servitus illa facit ad corruptionem, & interitum hominis ceu causa mortis & condemnationis ejusdem, nec non ad ipsa- rummet creaturarum corruptionem, cum DEUS abusum optimarum creaturarum non amplius ferre potest, easque ideo destruet, quod in cata- clysmo universali mundus antediluvianus ma- gnam partem expertus est, & rationis expertes creaturæ in generalibus suppliciis experiri subin- de solent, unde illa ita describuntur, ac si non modo animantia bruta & terra; sed etiam cœlum ipsum & sydera iisdem afficiatur, Esa. XIII. 9. c. XXIV. 4. Jer. IV. 23. c. XV. 9. Ez XXXII. 7. Am. IIX. 9. Mich. III. 6. B. Gerhardus T. IX. de con- summ. Seculi §. 55. videtur sub voce φθορᾶς homi- nem corruptibilem intelligere, cui cum servitur, corruptibili servitur: omnes homines, inquit, sunt mortales & corruptibiles; quia ergo creaturæ inserviunt hominibus impiis nequiter eas abuten- tibus, ideo per hoc servitium subeunt δουλείαν φθο- ρᾶς. Quia vero mortales & corruptibiles non im- pii tantum sunt, sed etiam pii, servitium impiis, & quidem ad impietatem ipsam præstitum opti- me per ματαιότητα, & δουλείαν φθορᾶς intelligi- tur, cui creaturæ in hoc seculo subjectæ esse legun- tur. Quod etiam B. Gerhardoplacuit, exemplo vini illustranti: Sic vinum est bona & præclara DEI creatura, sed cogitur in hac vita servire cu- piditatibus ebriosorum. Hæc est illa servitus cor- ruptionis, cui creatura illa subjecta est non volens, inde ingemiscit & juxta prosopopœiam Apostoli- cam expetit ab hac servitute liberari, eligit enim potius non esse, & in nihilum abire; quam abusui ebriosorum inservire, & hac ratione contra crea- torem suum quasi militare. Idem judicium esto de reliquis DEI creaturis. Creatura liberanda dici- tur non à corruptione, sed à servitute corruptionis: quia liberantur à servitute corruptionis, quam ho- minibus impiis impendere coguntur, cum liberæ ipsæ non fiant à corruptione, sed corruptioni & interitui obnoxiæ sint. Cur autem hac phrasi uta- tur Apostolus, ita explicat Gerhardus §. 59. Ideo vero maluit dicere, creaturam liberandam à servi- tute corruptionis, quam totaliter interituram, tum quia voluit usurpare talem phrasin, quæ etiam de homine prædicari posset, nec tamen hominis respe- ctu interitui esset opposita. Jam vero totalis interi- tus ac corruptio in die novissimo hominibus non competit, liberatio autem à servitute corruptionis hominibus est etiam communis; tum quia voluit in prosopopœia allegorica & hyperbole illa metapho- rica, quâ creaturis irrationalibus actus quosdam rationis dedit, persistere, q. d. Si creaturæ abusui impiorum in hac vita subjectæ sensus ac rationis essent participes, præoptarent potius omnimodam an- nihilationem, quam talem servitutem. Sensum au- tem istum creaturæ anxie ad liberationem aspi- rantis tum nos percipimus, cum operationes suas creaturæ usibus humanis negant, cum motibus vio- lentis terra concutitur, cum immensæ exundationes fiunt, cum leges ipsæ ac repagula naturæ solvi rum- pique videntur. Tum enim suspiriis q. quibusdam & gravi singultu, ad liberationem suam anhelare, machina mundi putanda est, ut habet hic B. My- lius. Cæterum verbis εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν temporis significationem notari non male notat Grotius; sed ut plenior sit sensus, addendum monuimus in Theol. Apost. Rom. quod destructione creaturarum quæ vanitati servierunt, libertas gloriosa, & immu- nitas à vanitate omnimoda eo illustrior certiorque futura sit: quia tum filiis DEI unus DEUS erit omnia in omnibus, nihil vanitati, nihil servituti corruptionis obnoxium comparebit, nec eorum usu amplius indigebimus, nec abusum eorum me- tuere opus habebimus, quia prorsus esse desinent, nec amplius supererunt.

## 8:22
V. 22. For we know that the whole creation groans together and travails in pain together until now.

All parts of the world together sigh and are in labor until now, namely that they may be freed. It is a metaphor taken from a woman, who gives birth with great pain and groaning, expecting to be freed from her burden. Στενάζειν [to groan] is also of those giving birth. Which

Not only is the whole world a participant in these evils.

Latin:

V. 22. οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις συστενάζει καὶ συνωδίνει ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν.

Omnes simul mundi partes suspirant & parturiunt ha- ctenus, nempe ut liberentur. Est translatio sumpta à fœmina, quæ cum magno dolore ac gemitu parturit, expe- ctans, ut onere liberetur. Στενάζειν est etiam parturien- tium. Quod

Non tantum totus mundus istorum malorum est par- ticeps.

## 8:23
But also we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves.

But also we, he says, that is, the Apostles, feel and lament the same evils. But he denotes the Apostles by an excellent circumlocution, when he names those who have received the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, which happened to the other Apostles on the day of Pentecost, but to Paul shortly after that admirable calling from heaven. Ἀπαρχὴ [firstfruits] is תרומה [terumah], that which was consecrated to God before the tithes, whence it began to be said of all those who precede others in time, as can be seen in XI. 16. XVI. 5. 1. Cor. XV. 20. 23. XVI. 15. Jas. I. 18.

waiting for the adoption.

For there is a twofold adoption, one in the spirit, which happens here, as we saw above 14. 15. the other in the whole man and before all. See John I. 12. Luke XX. 36. Therefore because the word was ambiguous, he explains it by apposition.

the redemption of our bodies.

Redemption of souls happens here when they are purged from vices; of bodies it will happen then, when they revive free from all evils. Thus ἀπολύτρωσις is used in Luke 21:28, Eph. 1:14, 4:30, 31, Heb. 11:35.

Latin:

Ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοὶ τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῦ πνεύματος ἔχοντες καὶ ἡμεῖς αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ςενάζομεν.

Sed & nos, inquit, Apostoli scilicet, eadem mala senti- mus ac plangimus. Apostolos autem egregia circumscri- ptione denotat, cum illos nominat, qui primitias accepere Spiritus S. quod Apostolis aliis contigit Pentecostes die, Paulo vero paulo post admirabilem illam de cœlo voca- tionem. Ἀπαρχὴ est תרומה id quod ante decimas Deo sacrabatur, unde dici cœpit de omnibus iis, qui alios tem- pore antecedunt, ut videre est XI. 16. XVI. 5. 1. Cor. XV. 20. 23. XVI. 15. Jac. I. 18.

ὑοθεσίαν ἀπεκδεχόμενοι.

Est enim duplex ὑιοθεσία altera in spiritu, quæ hic sit, ut vidimus supra 14. 15. altera in toto homine ac coram omni- bus. Vide Joh. I. 12. Luc. XX. 36. Ideo quia vox erat am- bigua, per appositionem eam explicat.

τὴν ὑπολύτρωσιν τῶν σωμάτων ἡμῶν.

Ἀπολύτρωσις animorum hic fit cum à vitiis purgantur; corporum tunc fiet, cum ea ab omnibus malis libera re- viviscant. Sic ἀπολύτρωσις sumitur Luc. XXI. 28. Eph. I. 14. IV. 30. 31. Hebr. XI. 35.

## 8:24
V. 24. For by hope we were saved.

That is, we do not yet have eternal salvation, but we hope for it. Thus Cicero said that a matter is in hope, which does not exist, but is hoped for.

but hope that is seen.

Here he spoke of hope for the thing which is hoped for. When that is seen and possessed, it ceases to be hoped for. Thus also faith is the evidence of things not seen, Heb. 11:1.

Latin:

V. 24. τῇ γὰρ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν.

Id est, salutem æternam non habemus adhuc, sed spera- mus. Sic Cicero dixit in spe esse negotium, quod non ex- sistit, sed speratur.

ἐλπὶς δὲ βλεπομένη.

Hic spem dixit pro re, quæ speratur. Ea ubi videtur & habetur, desinit sperari. Sic & πίσις πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀ βλεπομένων Hebr. XI. 1.

## 8:25
V. 25. For what one sees, why does he also hope for?

Why should he hope for it further? For it is an indicative for a subjunctive. In the manuscript which I often praise, it is 'why does he also wait for'.

Latin:

V. 25. ὃ γὰρ βλέπει τις, τί καὶ ἐλπίζει;

Cur ultra id speret? Est enim indicativus pro Subjun- ctivo. In Manuscripto, quem sæpe laudo, est τί καὶ ὑπο- μένει

## 8:26
V. 26. But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.

That is, that hope is not unfruitful in us, but produces an excellent virtue, a strong tolerance of evils. See above V. 4.

Although Oecumenius, Aretius, and even Salmero explain these things as concerning only the Apostles: yet they are more correctly understood as all the faithful. If the Apostle had said, but not only they, but we also have the first fruits of Christ or the Spirit, these things might perhaps be restricted to the Apostles: but when he says, we who have the first fruits of the Spirit, he includes himself and all the reborn: For he speaks of those who groan together with creatures devoid of reason, who await the ὑοθεσίαν, who desire τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν the redemption of the body, who have been saved in hope, whose infirmities the Holy Spirit relieves, all of which remaining predicates are not proper to the Apostles, but common to all the reborn and the faithful. Moreover, the reborn are said here to have the first fruits of the Spirit by reason of the tithes or the entire harvest, which is to be expected in the blessed life. Whence it is clear that believers in this life do not attain the whole fullness, but only the first fruits of the Spirit; whereby it happens that perfect holiness is by no means to be expected from them here. And that argument of the Apostle demands this, which he draws for the certainty of the hope of eternal glory from the groaning of creatures and especially of the reborn themselves, because while the former groan that they may be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the children of GOD, the reborn indeed seek the liberation of their bodies and the full fruition of τῆς ὑοθεσίας in the heavenly inheritance: Therefore, just as the groaning of the former is not in vain, so much less can the sighs of the reborn be fruitless, even if they have salvation only in hope as yet, nor can the thing which they hope for be seen. Doubtless it is taught that the support of hope, even when placed among afflictions, is so certain and firm concerning future glory, that even the most afflicted creatures depend upon the appearance of that glory; but the saints, however afflicted most gravely afflicted, because they already have the firstfruits of the Spirit, are as certain as can be of the full enjoyment of adoption, and anxiously await the same, as something that would undoubtedly happen to them, just as the harvest itself certainly followed the firstfruits. Chrysostom notes that the Apostle spoke of the liberation of the body, not of the soul, because he looked partly to the origin of evils, and partly to their seat. For as sin is propagated with the seed from which we are born, so it can never be extirpated from the body except through death. Regarding the difference between faith and hope, Philip holds this: Faith and hope differ, because faith receives in the present the remission of sins, and reconciliation, or the imputation of righteousness on account of the Mediator, and brings peace, that is, joy to the heart that has felt true terrors: as it is said, Being justified by faith we have peace with God. And by this faith, struggling out of the sorrows of the underworld, we approach GOD, we rightly acknowledge and invoke Him, as it is said to the Ephesians: Through him we have boldness to approach in confidence through faith in him. Thus faith receives in the present reconciliation, and the earnest of future goods, namely the Holy Spirit, and is an apprehensive and quieting virtue. But hope is the expectation of future liberation, which explanation is preceded by the knowledge of the promise and assent, and the confidence receiving reconciliation, as David, having heard the promise, being uplifted, afterwards begins to hope for liberation.

ὡσαύτως δὲ. Furthermore: יחד which is explained now by ὡσαύτως, now by μετὰ ταῦτα.

καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα. The Spirit of GOD, promised and given by Christ above 11. & 14., whence He is also called the Spirit of Christ 9. The third consolation of Christians follows here from the help of the Spirit.

συναντιλαμβάνεται ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν. Συναντιλαμβάνεται is to be of help, as in Luke X. 40. and by metonymy to console. Ἀσθένειαι [weaknesses] for the Apostle are sorrows from adverse things as 1 Cor. II. 3. 2 Cor. XI. 30. XII. 5. 10. Gal. II. 13. Hebr. IV. 15. V. 2. XI. 34. Also ἀσθενεῖν is used 2 Cor. XI. 29. XIII. 9. The Hebrew עצר is translated as πόνος, ὀδύνη, ἀσθένεια. That Spirit consoles our distress.

τὸ γὰρ τὶ προευξώμεθα καθὸ δεῖ ἐκ οἴδαμεν. The Latins refer καθὸ δεῖ to ἐκ οἴδαμεν. We do not know sufficiently. Naturally, man prays excellently in adverse things: and such are almost the prayers even of the good, under the old and carnal testament. See the Psalms.

ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα ὑπερεντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σεναγμοῖς ἀλαλήτοις. Στεναγμοί are אנחות [sighs] of those laboring under a heavy burden 1 Cor. V. 2. whence it is also transferred to the internal motions of the mind. Ἀλαλήτοι, that is, even without a voice. The Jews thought no prayers were valid unless voices were at least expressed within the lips. Christians do not lose prayers conceived by the mind alone. Ὑπερεντυγχάνει is of advocates, who dictate desires to their clients. But that is attributed to the Holy Spirit because He dictates prayers to God for us. Moreover, the Spirit teaches us to pray to God for those things which are glorious to GOD, our own reasons being set aside, nay, even with our own disadvantage, if the matter should so turn out. See an example in Paul, Philip. I. 20. 21. 22. 23. 24. 25. and in the friends of Paul, Acts XXI. 14. In like manner, Gal. IV. 6. that Spirit is said to cry out, that is: to excite us to cry out. In the Church, the deacon in a certain way bears the image of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

V. 26. εἰ δὲ ὃ ὀὐ βλέπομεν, ἐλπίζομεν, δι᾽ ὑπομονῆς ἀπεκδεχόμεθα.

Id est, spes ista non infructuosa est in nobis, sed egre- giam virtutem operatur, malorum fortem tolerantiam. Vide supra V. 4.

Etsi de solis Apostolis Oecumenius, Aretius, Sal- mero etiam hæc explicent: rectius tamen intelli- guntur omnes fideles. Si dixisset Apostolus, non solum autem illi, sed & nos Christi vel Spiritus pri- mitiæ, restringi forte ad Apostolos hæc possent: sed cum dicit, nos qui primitias Spiritus habemus, se & renatos universos complectitur: Nam de il- lis loquitur, qui juxta cum creaturis rationis ex- pertibus ingemiscunt, qui ὑοθεσίαν expectant, qui τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν redemtionem corporis deside- rant, qui in spe salvi facti sunt, quorum infirmi- tates sublevat Spiritus S. quæ & reliqua prædicata omnia non Apostolis sunt propria, sed omnibus renatis & fidelibus communia. Primitias autem Spiritus hic habere dicuntur renati ratione deci- marum vel integræ messis, quæ expectanda in bea- ta vita. Unde patet, quod credentes in hac vita non plenitudinem totam, sed primitias tantum Spiritus assequantur; Quo fit, ut perfecta sancti- tas ab ipsis hic minime expectanda sit. Et postu- lat id argumentum Apostoli, quod pro certitudi- ne spei gloriæ æternæ depromit à gemitu crea- turarum ipsorumque imprimis renatorum, quod cæteræ quidem ingemiscant, ut liberentur à ser- vitute corruptionis in libertatem filiorum DEI, renati vero expetant liberationem corporum, & fruitionem plenam τῆς ὑοθεσίας in cœlesti hæredi- tate: Ut ergo illarum gemitus frustraneus non est, ita multo minus renatorum suspiria irrita esse pos- sunt, etsi spe adhuc tantum habeant salutem, ne- que videri possit res, quam sperant.
