Nimirum ita certum ac firmum esse spei etiam inter afflictio- nes positæ de futura gloria præsidium docetur, ut ab illius gloriæ apparitione creaturæ etiam afflictissimæ pendeant; Sanctos autem utut affli- gantur gravissime, quia Spiritus primitias jam ha- bent, esse quam certissimos de plena υἱοθεσίας frui- tione eandemque expectare anxie, utpote quæ ipsi indubitato contingeret, æque uti primitias certo messis ipsa sequebatur. Corporis liberatio- nem dixisse Apostolum, non animæ, Chrysostomus annotat, quod ad originem malorum respexerit partim, partim ad sedem. Nam ut cum semine, ex quo nascimur, propagatur peccatum, ita nisi per mortem extirpari ex corpore nunquam po- test. De fidei & spei differentia Philippus ita ha- bet: Differunt fides & spes, quia fides in præsentia accipit remissionem peccatorum, & reconciliatio- nem, seu imputationem justitiæ propter Mediato- rem, & adfert pacem, id est, lætitiam cordi, quod sensit veros pavores: ut dicitur, Justificati fide pa- cem habemus apud Deum. Et hac fide ex doloribus inferorum eluctantes accedimus ad DEUM, recte eum agnoscimus invocamus, ut ad Ephes. dici- tur: Per hunc audemus accedere in fiducia per fi- dem ejus. Ita fides accipit in præsentia reconcilia- tionem, & arrabonem futurorum bonorum, vide- licet Spiritum Sanctum, & est virtus apprehensiva & quietativa. Sed spes est expectatio futuræ libe- rationis, quam explicationem antecedunt notitia promissionis & assensus, & fiducia accipiens reconci- liationem, ut David audita promissione erectus postea incipit sperare liberationem.

ὡσαύτως δὲ. Præterea: יחד quod modo per ὡσαύτως, modo per μετὰ ταῦτα explicatur.

καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα. Spiritus DEI supra 11. & 14. à Christo promissus & da- tus, unde & Christi Spiritus dicitur 9. Tertia hic sequitur Christianorum consolatio ab auxilio Spiritus.

συναντιλαμβάνεται ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν. Συναντιλαμβάνεται est auxilio esse, ut Luc. X. 40. & per μετωνυμίαν solari. Ἀσθένειαι Apostolo sunt dolores ex re- bus adversis ut 1. Cor. II. 3. 2. Cor. XI. 30. XII. 5. 10. Gal. II. 13. Hebr. IV. 15. V. 2. XI. 34. Sit & ἀσθενεῖν su- mitur 2. Cor. XI. 29. XIII. 9. עצר Hebræum vertitur πό- νος, ὀδύνη, ἀσθένεια Spiritus ille molestiam nostram so- latur.

τὸ γὰρ τὶ προευξώμεθα καθὸ δεῖ ἐκ οἴδαμεν. Latini καθὸ δεῖ referunt ad ἐκ οἴδαμεν. Non satis sci- mus. Naturaliter homo orat eximie rebus adversis: & ta- les ferme sunt preces etiam bonorum, sub veteri & carnali testamento. Vide Psalmos.

ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα ὑπερεντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σεναγμοῖς ἀλαλήτοις. Στεναγμοί sunt אנחות suspiria sub onere gravi labo- rantium 1. Cor. V. 2. unde & ad internos animi motus transfertur. Ἀλαλήτοι, id est, etiam sine voce. Judæi nul- las preces valere censebant, nisi voces saltem intra labia exprimerentur. Christiani etiam solo animo conceptas preces non perdunt. Ὑπερεντυγχάνει est advocatorum, qui clientibus desideria dictant. Id autem Spiritui Sancto ideo tribuitur, quia preces ad Deum nobis dictat. Docet autem nos Spiritus precari Deum ea, quæ DEO sunt gloriosa, ra- tionibus nostris sepositis, imo & cum nostro, si ita res ferat, incommodo. Exemplum vide in Paulo, Philip. I. 20. 21. 22. 23. 24. 25. & in amicis Pauli Act. XXI. 14. Pari modo Gal. IV. 6. clamare dicitur Spiritus ille, id est: ad claman- dum nos excitare. In Ecclesia diaconus imaginem quodam- modo gerit Spiritus Sancti.

## 8:27
V. 27. ὁ δὲ ἐρευνῶν τὰς καρδίας. Which is an epithet of GOD. Ps VII. 10. Jerem. XI. 29. XVII. 10. XX. 12. Act. I. 24. v. 8.

Οἶδε τί τὸ φρόνημα τῷ πνεύματος, ὅτι κατὰ Θεὸν ἐντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἁγίων. Ἐντυγχάνει is said here more briefly, for ὑπερεντυγχάνει. He knows what the Spirit intends, namely to direct the prayers of the saints according to GOD, by suggesting to them to pray for those things which serve GOD. Κατὰ θεόν here is the same as κατὰ τὸ θέλημα ἀυτᾶ 1 Joh. V. 14. It is understood, however, that GOD cannot but hold such prayers as pleasing, even if they are not expressed in words.

This third argument of the certainty of hope of glory—although we do not deny that this is also proposed for consolation along with others on account of the afflictions of the faithful—is from the intercession of the Holy Spirit. For since the Spirit Himself dictates to us the prayers by which we pant for the redemption of the body, those cannot be in vain. Therefore, the Holy Spirit not only succors our infirmity in our afflictions and lifts it up (ἀντίληψις is such a support as that of porters carrying burdens, when they grow weary under them, or totter, and obtain some help and relief from a helping hand, Conf. here B. Weller in comm. p. 500.) but also, when we do not know what we ought to do, He suggests it to us, as advocates are accustomed to do for clients. Grotius explains τὸ ὑπερεντυγχάνειν quite conveniently here: with which B. Luther agrees in his explanation of Ps. VI. Tom. V. Altenburg. and in conc. 1. Isleb. Tom. IIX. Altenb. p. 517. as also in the same Tom. p. 64. Philip: Here it is asked: by what distinction is Christ elsewhere called an intercessor for us, but here the Holy Spirit is called an intercessor? I answer: Christ is an intercessor because He is the Redeemer, and by His merit appeases the wrath of the eternal Father. But the Holy Spirit is an intercessor, in that He moves us to invocation according to the saying: You have received the Spirit, by whom we cry Abba Father. Likewise Zach. XII. I will pour upon the House of David the Spirit of grace and of prayers. The Son is an intercessor because He is the Redeemer, who paid the price, so that He might satisfy the justice of GOD, and the wrath of GOD might be appeased. But the Holy Spirit intercedes after the wrath has been appeased by the Son, in such a way that He kindles in us invocation, according to the saying: I will pour upon the house of David the Spirit of grace and of prayers, that is, the Spirit testifying in consolation through the Gospel, that God receives us, and is propitious to us, and kindling us to invocation, and gladdening our hearts with acquiescence in GOD &c. and the ἐξήγησις of our B. Mylius: that the Holy Spirit is our guide and author for praying rightly, who suggests both words to the mouth, and motions to the heart, and helps and inflames us, so that prayers may become acceptable to GOD; as also B. Ægid. Hunnius: He is said to pray, while he makes us pray, while he excites, forms, and directs these very prayers, these groanings within us, kindles our heart and the affection of praying, and provides the final confidence in praying: Likewise Blessed Balduinus: The Holy Spirit is said to pray then, when he makes us pray, he groans for us then, when he sends into us pious groanings and sighs to GOD, renders prayers in us fervent and ardent, and kindles confidence in our souls concerning infallible hearing. Blessed Wellerus: he intercedes, that is, he instigates us to prayers, makes us cry out, and excites the more sluggish. Whom Blessed Augustine preceded in tract VI on John. Therefore the Holy Spirit does not groan in himself, by himself in that Trinity, in that blessedness, in that eternity of subsistence, but he groans in us, because he makes us groan. Add also Origen, Chrysostom, and among the Papists, Toletus, Saa, Justinianus, concerning whom more at Job. However, the comparison of Grotius concerning the Deacons neither befits the dignity of the Holy Spirit, nor is it suitable for expressing the matter: since the Holy Spirit inspires and suggests the very prayers to the hearts of the pious, as Grotius admits. Concerning those ἀλαλήτοις στεναγμοῖς, our Blessed Mylius not inaptly says: In the notation of the trope, which is annexed, Augustine in Epistle 121 to Proba says that we labor with a certain learned ignorance. Interpreters say that the groanings are called ineffable, because we ourselves do not utter what we seek: But with the Spirit instigating, we conceive those vows in our breast. For it happens not rarely to the pious, that they only sigh, and do not discern to where they should turn themselves in praying. Meanwhile, while they are thinking nothing of it, indeed ignorant of what is being done, the Holy Spirit moderates those sighs excited by himself from within, and as if into sight

of GOD may come, he brings about. But above all, B. Luther has explained this very clearly, according to his custom, in his commentary on Galatians IV, later volume, T. III, Jena edition, Latin, which passage is worthy of being compared here: 'But those prayers, stirred up in the faithful by the Holy Spirit, cannot be ineffectual, since God, the searcher of hearts (who knows the mind of the Spirit, that is, who understands and looks upon those groans stirred up by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect), holds those prayers as valid, approves and hears them: because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to God; that is, he stirs up such motions and prayers in the pious, which are pleasing and acceptable to God through Christ, as having proceeded from children, upon whom he has sealed his fatherly grace with the Spirit of adoption.' As B. Hunnius has it here.

Latin:

V. 27. ὁ δὲ ἐρευνῶν τὰς καρδίας. Quod DEI ἐπίθετον. Ps VII. 10. Jerem. XI. 29. XVII. 10. XX. 12. Act. I. 24. v. 8.

Οἶδε τί τὸ φρόνημα τῷ πνεύματος, ὅτι κατὰ Θεὸν ἐντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἁγίων. Ἐντυγχάνει hic brevius dictum, pro ὑπερεντυγχάνει. Novit, quid studeat Spiritus, nempe sanctorum preces di- rigere secundum DEUM, suggerendo eis illa precari, quæ DEO serviant. Κατὰ θεόν hic idem, quod κατὰ τὸ θέλημα ἀυτᾶ 1. Joh. V. 14. Subintelligitur autem tales preces DEUM non posse non gratas habere, etiamsi verbis non exprimantur.

Tertium hoc est argumentum certitudinis spei gloriæ etsi in consolationem hoc etiam cum aliis propositum esse ob afflictiones fidelium non ne- gemus, à Spiritus S. intercessione. Quum enim ipse Spiritus nobis dictet preces, quibus anhelemus redemtionem corporis, illæ irritæ esse non pos- sunt. Spiritum S. ergo non tantum in afflictio- nibus nostris infirmitati nostræ succurrere, eam- que sublevare (ἀντίληψις sustentatio est talis, qua- lis bajulorum onera ferentium, cum sub iis fati- scunt, aut labascunt, à socia manu adminiculi & levationis aliquid consequuntur, Conf. hic B. Weller. in comm. p. 500.) sed etiam cum nesci- mus, quid agere debeamus, nobis id suggerit, uti advocati clientibus solent. Τὸ ὑπερεντυγχάνειν satis convenienter hic explicat Grotius: cui con- sonat B. Lutherus in explicat. Ps. VI. Tom. V. Altenburg. & in conc. 1. Isleb. Tom. IIX. Altenb. p. 517. ut & Tom. eodem p. 64. Philippus: Hic quæritur: quo discrimine alibi Christus dicatur in- terpellator pro nobis, hic vero Spiritus Sanctus di- catur interpellator? Respondeo: Christus est inter- pellator, quia est Redemptor, & suo merito placans iram æterni Patris. Sed Spiritus S. est interpella- tor, in quantum nos movet ad invocationem juxta dictum: Accepistis Spiritum, quo clamamus Abba Pater. Item Zach. XII. Effundam super Domum Da- vid Spiritum gratiæ & precum. Filius est inter- pellator, quia est Redemtor, qui persolvit pretium, ut satisfaceret justitiæ DEI, & placaretur ira DEI. Sed Spiritus S. interpellat post placatam iram per Filium, sic, ut accendat in nobis invocationem, juxta dictum: Effundam super domum David Spiritum gratiæ & precum, id est Spiritum testificantem in consolatione per Evangelium, quod Deus nos reci- piat, & sit nobis propitius, & accendentem nos ad invocationem, & lætificantem corda acquiescentia in DEO &c. & B. Mylii nostri ἐξήγησις: quod Spiritus S. nobis dux atque autor sit ad recte pre- candum, qui & verba ori, & motus cordi sugge- rat, nosque adjuvet, & inflammet, ut preces DEO fiant acceptabiles; nec non B. Ægid. Hunnii: Ora- re dicitur, dum nos orare facit, dum has ipsas pre- ces, hos gemitus in nobis excitat, format, dirigit, cor nostrum & precandi affectum accendit, & finalem fiduciam in precando subministrat: Item B. Bal- duini: Tunc Spiritus S. orare dicitur, quando nos orare facit, tunc ingemiscit pro nobis, quando pios gemitus & suspiria ad DEUM nobis immittit, pre- ces in nobis ferias ac ardentes reddit, fiduciamque in animis nostris de exauditione infallibili accendit. B. Welleri: intercedit, id est, ad preces nos insti- gat, clamantes nos facit, & segniores excitat. Qui- bus præivit B. August. tract. VI. in Joh. Non er- go Spiritus S. in semetipso, apud semetipsum in illa Trinitate, in illa beatitudine, in illa æternita- te subsistentiæ gemit, sed in nobis gemit, quia ge- mere nos facit. Adde & Origenem, Chrysostomum, Pontificiis Toletum, Saa, Justinian. de quo plu- ra ad Job. Simile tamen Grotii de Diaconis nec dignitati Spiritus S. convenit, nec rei exprimendæ idoneum est: quum cordibus piorum inspiret & suggerat Sp. S. ipsas preces, fatente Grotio. De illis ἀλαλήτοις στεναγμοῖς non inconcinne B. My- lius noster: In notatione τᾶ τρόπυ, quæ annexa est, Augustinus Ep. CXXI. ad Probam ait, nos laborare docta quadam ignorantia. Interpretes dicunt, in- effabiles dici gemitus, quia non ipsi effamur, quod petimus: Sed Spiritu instigante vota ista in pectore concipimus. Contingit enim non raro piis, ut tan- tummodo suspirent, & quo se se precando vertant, non dispiciant. Interim illis minime cogitantibus, imo quid agatur ignorantibus, Spir. S. suspiria ista à se ipso excitata, intus moderatur, atque ut in conspectum

DEI veniant, efficit. Sed imprimis præclare hæc expofuit B. Lutherus, pro more suo, in commen- tario Gal. IV. poster. T. III. Jenens. Lat. qui locus dignus est, ut hic conferatur: Preces autem istæ per Spiritum S. excitatæ in fidelibus non possunt esse irritæ, quandoquidem Deus scrutator cordium (qui novit sensum Spiritus, id est, qui intelligit & afpi- cit, gemitus illos a Spiritu sancto in cordibus electo- rum excitatos) is ratus habet eas preces, approbat & exaudit : quoniam Spiritus secundum DEUM intercedit pro sanctis; hoc est, suscitat hujusmodi motus & preces in piis, quæ DEO per Christum gratæ & acceptæ sint, tanquam profectæ à filiis, quibus gra- tiam suam paternam Spiritu adoptionis obsignavit. Ut hic habet B. Hunnius.

## 8:28
V. 28. And we know.

The fourth consolation follows, derived from the fact that all those adversities happen to Christians, not from some general permission of God, but from a special decree, which tends to their own good: and this is understood both from elsewhere, and because God cannot but love those who love him in the highest degree.

that to those who love God all things work together for good.

Even adversities are an aid to them for the increase of virtues and reward. The manuscript not badly: 'God works all things together for good.' Plato's statement in the first book of the Republic does not depart far from this: 'And shall we not agree that for the one beloved of God, all things that come from the gods come to pass as well as possible?'

to those who are called according to his purpose.

That is, who accommodate themselves to the whole will of God. For 'purpose' (prothesis), just as in human affairs (Acts 13:23, 27:13, 2 Tim. 3:11), so in God it is will, below 9:11. There is a certain 'purpose of the ages,' as concerning the sending of the Messiah (Eph. 3:11). But it is not a matter of that here, as the following shows. 'Called' (kletoi), however, are called by Paul those who obey the one calling, as above 1:6, 1:24. So also Rev. 17:14.

Latin:

V. 28. Οἴδαμεν δὲ.

Sequitur quarta consolatio, inde ducta quod omnia illa adversa Christianis eveniant, non ex generali quodam DEI permissu, sed ex decreto speciali, quod ad ipsorum bonum tendat: idque tum aliunde intelligi, tum quia Deus se dili- gentes non possit non summe diligere.

ὅτι τοῖς ἀγαπῶσι τὸν θεὸν πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθὸν.

Etiam adversa illis adminiculo sunt ad incrementa vir- tutum & præmii. Manuscriptus non male: πάντα συνεργεῖ ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν. Non longe hic abit Platonis illud pri- mo de Republica: τῷ δὲ θεοφιλεῖ οὐχ ὁμολογησομέν γε ἀπὸ θεῶν γίγνεσθαι πάντα γίγνεσθαι ὡς οἷον τε ἄριστα.

τοῖς κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοῖς ὖσι.

Id est, qui se ad omnem DEI voluntatem accommodant. Nam πρόθεσις sicut in hominibus Act. XIII, 23. XXVII. 13. 2. Tim. III. 11. sic in DEO est voluntas, infra IX. 11. Est quædam πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων ut de Messia mittendo Eph. III. 11. Sed de ea hic non agitur, ut ostendunt sequentia. Κλητοὶ autem apud Paulum dicuntur ii, qui vocanti obe- diunt, ut supra I. 6. I. 24. Sic & Apoc. XVII. 14.

## 8:29
V. 29. For whom he foreknew.

For those whom he already approved beforehand as believing in his Son. Just as 'to know' (yada, ginoskein) is to approve, above 7:15, so 'to foreknow' (proginoskein) is to approve beforehand, as below 11:2.

and he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

A double ellipsis. For both 'type' is missing at the beginning and 'to become' at the end. 'Conformed to the image' is the same as 'conformed to the image' (dative), just as we have 'conformed to the body' in Philippians 3:21, just as 'impossible to the law' above is equivalent to 'impossible to the law' (dative). He calls 'image' the exemplar, to which something else is fashioned, which elsewhere is 'type', 'likeness', 'pattern' (tabnit). Christ was obedient in the most atrocious sufferings, and thus arrived at that heavenly kingdom. By the same way God has pre-constituted to lead those who believe in Christ. Thus Paul in Phil. 3:9 says that he was made a participant of the sufferings of Christ, and thus 'conformed to his death,' and that in the hope of resurrection. Thus above 8:17, if we suffer together, we shall also attain glory together. Thus Christ is said to be crowned with glory and honor because of his suffering, having been made the prince of eternal salvation (Heb. 2:9, 10) to those, namely, who are called his brothers and participants of his flesh and blood there because of this likeness. And in the same Epistle 12:2, we are commanded to run the race of endurance, looking to Jesus, the prince and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, and despised the shame. So also 2 Tim. 2:12: If we endure, we shall also reign together, namely with Christ. God is said to 'predestine' whatever he constitutes before it happens (Acts 4:28). 'Before the ages' is not added here as in 1 Cor. 2:7. But 'predestine' is never used except of good things. 'Rasham', which the Syrian placed here for that 'predestined', signifies 'constituted': for it is translated by 'to appoint' (tattein) in Dan. 6:12, by 'to command' (epitattein) in Dan. 6:9, by 'to enjoin' (entattein) in Dan. 5:26, 27, 6:10, 10:21.

The fourth argument for the certainty of the hope of glory, by which, namely, they themselves can boast even in afflictions, is from the eternal purpose of GOD: by the power of which all things, even evils themselves, work together for the good of the faithful, of which they themselves are most certain: as those who know this from the word of GOD, and are rendered certain by their calling, which they have received through faith. That word, however, συνεργεί, does nothing for the συνεργείᾳ of free will, since it concerns the divine direction of things happening to the faithful, so that those things may cooperate and contribute their σύμβολον to their good. Nor does it, with Calvin. πάντα are to be extended, so that they apply to sins, as if even those were ordained by God to serve for the greater glory of the elect: for it is a question here of calamities and afflictions, and not of the evils of fault, as is manifest from verses 15, 16, 17; meanwhile, we do not deny that, having foreseen the fault of men, GOD even so directs it that it tends to our good, which, however, happens ἐκβατικῶς and συμβεβηκότως, by reason of the sin, nor should it be snatched at to mean that GOD intended the sin or is the author of it, August. book on corruption and grace, ch. IX. God, he says, works together for good with those who love him, to such an extent that even if any of them deviate and go astray, he makes this very thing turn out for their good, by which they return more humble and more learned. πρόθεσις here is not the bare will of GOD, but the purpose, which the word itself implies; κλητοὶ, however, are called not by reason of obedience and accepted calling, but simply from the calling itself: for although we admit that those who are looked upon here and are called called are truly faithful, it is not, however, by the force of the word κλητοὶ that this is inferred, much less do the called denote those who accommodate themselves to every will of GOD, for this is not in us, nor does the calling alone provide it, but there is need of further divine grace: although even with that approaching, there is not found anyone who is accommodated to EVERY will of GOD: Even if the reborn strive for it, and as much as is in them, labor and devote effort, if yet you look at the whole phrase, by which they are called κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοὶ, from it you will more correctly gather that those are understood who accept the calling through faith, and persevere in it; For that πρόθεσις comprehends the purpose of GOD: as that which has proposed and decreed them to be made conformable to the image of his son; not indeed by some absolute decree, but by a certain defined τάξει of means: which while they do not neglect, they are called κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοὶ, called according to that purpose of GOD, and thus far they conduct themselves conformably to the order included in the purpose of GOD: not indeed by rendering themselves worthy of divine grace, as the Papists and Arminians wish, but by not spurning or neglecting it, nor rejecting or putting behind the ordained means. Concerning which in the Disputations on Predestination. In which the calling does not follow the event παρὰ πρόθεσιν, it happens κατὰ πρόθεσιν. Nor does the word προέγνω denote approval here, but foreknowledge; those whom he foresaw would believe or would receive the calling, those he also predestined, that they might be made conformable to the image of the Son of GOD, not only by reason of suffering, but also by reason of glorification; not that either Christ by his obedience merited his glory for himself, or the faithful by their obedience can merit or obtain it, for they are justified and saved not by their own, but by Christ's obedience, as the Apostle had taught above in verses 18, 19; but that by that order GOD leads us to glory, namely by preceding afflictions, Acts XIV. 21, Rom. VIII. 17, Phil. III. 9. And although πρὸ αἰώνων is not added here as in 1 Cor. II. 7, there can be no doubt, however, that that προορισμὸς was made from eternity. Compare Eph. I. 4. See concerning this oracle the Theological Apostolical Rom. oration LXIII.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.

The antecedent is for the consequent. For this is what it wishes to say: that Christians might be led through the footsteps of Christ, as the firstborn brother. The same sense, which is in the aforementioned second chapter to the Hebrews. See also what was brought forward above at 17.

But he is called the firstborn among many brothers, not by reason of the resurrection, which the Socinians want, as if he were then newly begotten and made the Son of God, because he obtains τὴν ὑιότητα through eternal generation from the Father, not through resuscitation, even if δι ἀναστάσεως ἐν δυνάμει he was declared the Son of God Rom. 1:4; nor by reason of glorification, which the Socinians likewise contend, that in his exaltation he put on another nature and received a new life, which fiction is repugnant to Scripture, saying that Christ was glorified in the same body in which he suffered and was crucified here; but by reason of the right of firstborns and dignity, since the principal inheritance and kingdom were owed to the firstborn, as was also the Priesthood. Therefore Christ, having discharged the Priesthood in his death as far as the offering of his body is concerned, is glorified and exalted in the heavens and performs priestly intercession there for us, and fully exercises royal power in heaven and on earth, having been constituted heir of all things Heb. 1:3. But he is called the firstborn among many brothers because he has made us, as brothers, also priests and kings before God Apoc. 1:6, 5:10, here in the kingdom of grace and hereafter in the kingdom of glory, where we are to be co-heirs of Christ.

Latin:

V. 29. ὅτι ὃς προέγνω.

Quos enim ut filio suo credentes approbavit jam ante. Sicut ידע γινώσκειν est approbare, supra VII. 15. sic προ- γινώσκειν prius approbare, ut infra XI. 2.

καὶ προώρισε συμμόρφες τῆς εἰκόνος τᾶ ὑᾶ ἀυτᾶ.

Duplex ἔλλειψις. Nam & initio deest τύπως & in fine γενέσθαι. Συμμόρφες τῆς εἰκόνος idem quod συμμόρφες εἰκόνι, quomodo σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι habemus Philipp. III. 21. sicut ἀδύνατον τῷ νόμῳ supra valet ἀδύνατον τῷ νό- μῳ. Vocat autem εἰκόνα exemplar, ad quod aliquid aliud effingitur, quod alibi τύπος, ὁμοίωμα תבנית. Christus in passionibus atrocissimis obediens fuit, & sic ad regnum illud cœleste pervenit. Eadem via Deus præconstituit, du- cere Christo credentes. Sic Paulus Phil. III. 9. ait se par- ticipem factum passionum Christi, ac sic συμμορφόμενον τῷ θανάτῳ ἀυτᾶ idque in spem resurrectionis. Sic supra VIII. 17. si una patimur, & una gloriam adipiscemur. Sic Christus dicitur propter passionem coronatus gloria & ho- nore, factus esse princeps salutis æternæ Hebr. II. 9. 10. iis scilicet qui ibidem propter hanc similitudinem fratres ejus & participes carnis & sanguinis ejus vocantur. Et in ea- dem Epistola XII. 2. jubemur stadium tolerantiæ decur- rere, spectantes in principem & consummatorem fidei Je- sum, qui ob propositum sibi gaudium crucem pertulit, ignominiamque contempsit. Sic & 2. Tim. II. 12. Si tole- ramus, etiam una, nempe cum Christo, regnabimus. Προορί- ζειν dicitur Deus quidquid ante constituit, quam fiat Act. IV. 28. Non additur hic πρὸ αἰώνων ut 1. Cor. II 7. Nun- quam autem usurpatur προορίζειν nisi de bonis rebus. רשם quod hic pro illo προώρισε posuit Syrus, signifi- cat constituit: vertitur enim per τάττειν Dan. VI. 12. per ἐπιτάττειν Dan. VI. 9. per ἐντάττειν Dan. V. 26. 27. VI. 10. X. 21.

Quartum certitudinis spei gloriæ argumen- tum, qua sc. gloriari ipsi possint etiam in afflictio- nibus est ab æterno DEI proposito: vi cujus omnia etiam mala ipsa fidelibus operantur in bonum, quo de ipsi quam certissimi sunt: utpote qui hoc è verbo DEI sciunt, & è vocatione sua, quam per fidem suscepêre, certi redduntur. Illud autem συνεργεί, nihil pro liberi arbitrii συνεργείᾳ facit, cum de rerum fidelibus evenientium directione divina, ut cooperentur illa, & σύμβολον suum conferant in eorum bonum, agatur. Neque etiam cum Calvin. πάντα extendenda sint, ut ad peccata, q. etiam illa divinitus ordinata sint, ut ad majorem electorum gloriam inserviant: nam de calamitatibus & afflictionibus, non vero de malis culpæ hic agitur, ut è v. 15. 16. 17. manifestum est; interim non diffitemur, prævisa culpa hominum DEUM etiam ita eam dirigere, ut vergat in nostrum bonum, quod tamen ἐκβατικῶς & συμβεβηκότως fit, ratione peccati, nec eo rapiendum q. DEUS intenderit peccatum ejusve autor sit, August. l. de corrupt. & grat. c. IX. Deus diligentibus se, inquit, cooperatur in bounm usque adeo prorsus omnia, ut etiam, si qui eorum deviant, & exorbitant, hoc ipsum eis faciat proficere in bonum, quibus humiliores redeunt atque doctiores. πρόθεσις hic non est nuda voluntas DEI, sed propositum, quod vox ipsa infert; κλητοὶ autem dicuntur non ratione obsequii, & acceptatæ vocationis, sed simpliciter ab ipsa vocatione: nam quamvis admittamus eos, qui hic respiciuntur & vocati dicuntur vere esse fideles, non tamen vi vocis κλητοὶ hoc infertur, multo minus vocati notant eos, qui se ad omnem DEI voluntatem accommodant, hoc enim non est in nobis, nec vocatio sola id præstat, sed opus est ulteriori divina gratia: quamvis ea etiam accedente non inveniatur quisquam, qui ad OMNEM voluntatem DEI accommodetur: Etsi renati id annitantur, & quantum in ipsis est, allaborent, operamque navent, si tamẽ phrasin totam respicias, qua κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοὶ dicuntur, ex ea rectius colliges intelligi eos, qui vocationem per fidem acceptant, & in ea perseverant; Nam id πρόθεσις propositum DEI comprehendit: utpote quod eos sibi proposuerit ac decreverit conformes fieri imagini filii sui; non quidem absoluto quodam decreto, sed certo mediorum τάξει definito: quam dum non negligunt κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοὶ secundum illud propositum DEI vocati dicuntur, & hactenus conformiter se ordini in proposito DEI incluso gerunt: non quidem dignos se reddendo divina gratia, ut Pontificii & Arminiani volunt, sed eam non spernendo aut negligendo, nec media ordinata respuendo aut posthabendo. De quo in Disputationibus de Prædestinatione. In quibus vocatio non assequitur evẽtum παρὰ πρόθεσιν, κατὰ πρόθεσιν id fit. Neque vox προέγνω approbationem hic notat, sed prævisionem, quos credituros prævidit vel suscepturos vocationem, illos etiam prædestinavit, ut conformes fiant imagini Filii DEI, non modo ratione passionis, sed etiam ratione glorificationis; non quod vel Christus per obedientiam sibi gloriam suam promeruerit, vel fideles per suam obedientiam eam mereri aut impetrare possint, non enim hi propria, sed Christi obedientia & justificantur, & salvantur, uti supra V. 18. 19. docuerat Apostolus; sed quod eo ordine DEUS ad gloriam nos perducat, præviis nimirum afflictionibus Act. XIV. 21. Rom. IIX. 17. Phil. III. 9. Etsi vero non addatur hic πρὸ αἰώνων ut 1. Cor. II. 7. dubium tamen esse nequit, quin προορισμὸς ille ab æterno factus sit. Conf. Eph. I. 4. Vide de hoc oraculo Theol. Apost. Rom. orat. LXIII.

εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.

Est antecedens pro sequente. Hoc enim vult dicere: ut Christiani per Christi, tanquam fratris primogeniti, vestigia ducerentur. Idem sensus, qui dicto capite secundo ad Hebræos. Vide & quæ allata supra 17.

Primogenitus autem inter multos fratres dici- tur, non ratione resurrectionis, quod Sociniani vo- lunt, q. tum noviter genitus sit, & factus DEI Filius, quia τὴν ὑιότητα obtinet per æternam à Pa- tre generationem, non per resuscitationem, etsi δι ἀναστάσεως ἐν δυνάμει declaratus sit Dei Filius Rom. I. 4. nec ratione glorificationis, quod itidem So- ciniani contendunt, quod in exaltatione aliam na- turam induerit, novamque vitam acceperit, quod commentum Scripturæ repugnat, eodem corpo- re Christum glorificatum esse dicens, in quo hic passus & crucifixus est; sed ratione juris primoge- nitorum & dignitatis, siquidem primogenito præ- cipua hæreditas & regnum debebatur, ut & Sacer- dotium. Proinde Christus in morte Sacerdotio, quantum ad oblationem corporis sui defunctus, glorificatus & exaltatus in cœlis & Sacerdotali ibidem pro nobis intercessione fungitur, & Regia potestate plenarie utitur in cœlo & in terra, con- stitutus hæres omnium Ebr. I. 3. Primogenitus autem inter multos fratres dicitur, quia nos ceu fratres etiam Sacerdotes & Reges fecit coram DEO Apoc. I. 6. c. V. 10. hic in regno gratiæ & olim in regno gloriæ, ubi cohæredes Christi futuri sumus.

## 8:30
V. 30. ὃς δὲ προώρισε.

One must repeat here ἀπὸ κοινῦ, to be conformed to the image of his Son.

τούτες καὶ ἐκάλεσε.

Namely to sufferings; for it appears that the word for calling is taken in this way in 1 Pet. 2:20, 21, 'But if when you do good and suffer, you endure, this is grace before God. For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that you should follow in his steps.' The sense is similar in that 1 Thess. 3:3, 'that no one should be moved by these afflictions, for you yourselves know that we are appointed for this.' God is said to call the pious to sufferings, where he not only does not hinder the causes of them, but also disposes them.

καὶ ὃς ἐκάλεσε τέτες καὶ ἐδικαίωσεν.

These he also made righteous, that is, he provided them with the strength to persevere in the obedience of his righteousness. For δικαιῶν is said not only of the beginning, but also of the progress.

ὃς δὲ ἐδικαίωσε.

Namely with effect, provided they themselves do not neglect the gift.

Τότες καὶ ἐδόξασε.

That is, he decreed to adorn with glory. Thus also Eph. 1:4 'he chose', it is valid, 'he decreed to choose'. Thus Christ is said to have had glory before the world was, John 17:5, as we have explained there with the ancients. Thus grace is said to have been given to us in Jesus before times eternal, 2 Tim. 1:9, that is, it was decreed to be given. See to what a gradation the Apostle has brought this; Chrysostom explains ἰσόζασε, he adorned with wondrous gifts.

By calling, a calling to sufferings is not understood, but to the kingdom of grace and glory, even though suffering is also divinely appointed for the called, by which name they are said by Peter to be called to it, and by Paul to be placed for it, 1 Pet. 2:20, 1 Thess. 3:3. Nor is 'to justify' here to make just, or to provide the strength to persevere in obedience: but just as the Apostle has used the word 'justification' hitherto, it ought to be understood in a forensic sense: nor should a new meaning, unused by the Apostle, be invented for the word. For where is 'to justify' the same for the Apostle as 'to make just'? Where is it to provide the strength to persevere in the obedience of justice? Finally, 'he glorified' is not 'he decreed to glorify', but the past tense is used for the future on account of the certainty of the matter. Nor Eph. 1:4 ἐξελέξατο is not 'he decreed to choose', but 'he chose', nor is Christ said in John 17:5 to have had glory before the world was by reason of decree and predestination, but by reason of the actual possession of glory, which he had from eternity as God, even though he asked for and received it in time as man. Concerning the entire Apostolic gradation, however, we have dealt expressly in Oration 64. We add what the blessed Hülsemann has in his Vindiciae Scripturae, § 88. From that antistrophe of the particles ὃς καὶ τέτες, Rom. 8:30, 'whom he foreknew, these he also predestined', etc., 'whom he justified, these he also glorified', etc., it by no means follows that it cannot be committed by man that this connection of one benefit with another be broken, or that it cannot be committed by a justified man that he not be glorified, which Bareus, Beza, Marloretus, Groffius, and most others contend at this passage. For the Apostle says what God intends on his part, and to what end he calls and justifies men, namely, that he may also glorify the same. But this is by no means a discourse about the inability of man to hinder his own glorification after he has been justified; it is not the inability of man, but of tyrants, the Devil, miseries, and persecutions that is opposed in this place to the power and benevolence of God, as is clear to the eye from the words immediately following, v. 31: 'What then shall we say? If God is for us, who is against us?' v. 35: 'Who shall separate us?' etc. That the voluntary sins of the justified can separate them from the love of God, the Apostle not only did not deny in this place, but openly asserted in the words just preceding, v. 13 and 14, where he speaks to the regenerate: 'If you live according to the flesh, you will die,' etc. Therefore, a fallacy of opposites is committed by the Calvinists in the exposition of this saying, when they oppose man's inability to lose justification to divine grace, when they should have opposed the power of the Devil and the power of divine grace; nor does anything follow more for the impossible severance of glorification and justification from the antistrophe of those particles ὃ and τέτο than they can conclude from the words of the Apostle in the preceding chapter, 7:15 and 19: ὃ 'what I do not want, τῦτο πράσσω this I do'. Therefore the Apostle always sinned and could never act against the instinct of concupiscence; how absurd it is if they were to collect such things. That master takes whomever he receives into his discipline and makes them excellently learned. Therefore no student can tear himself away from his discipline without emerging excellently learned. For the discourse is about the intention of the Master, not about the inability of the students to hinder the effect of that good intention. See the Hague Colloquy on Art. 1, p. 159 seqq. Thus the declaration of Christ, John 6:39: 'This is the will of my Father, that whatever he has given me I should lose nothing of it,' does not prevent the exception that Judas could have perished by his own fault, even though he was of the number of those whom the Father gave to the Son, etc. John 17:12: 'I kept those whom you gave me, and none of them perished except that one son of perdition,' etc. But from that very fact the entirely gratuitous nature of human salvation is clear. The foreknowledge of God is, predestination proceeds from the same: God calls: God justifies: the same glorifies. Here, therefore, man did nothing. Augustine shows this same thing also by another reasoning: He says, God foreknew and predestined before we were: he called when we were turned away; he justified when we were sinners. Let no one therefore say, God called me because I worshipped God. How would you have worshipped if you had not been called? If you already were, you would not be predestined: unless you were turned away, you would not be called: unless you were impious, you would not be justified: unless you were earthly and abject, you would not be glorified. To him be glory: Because we were not when we were predestined; because we were turned away when we were called; because we were sinners when we were justified. See the blessed Mylius, p. 303.

Latin:

V. 30. ὃς δὲ προώρισε.

Repetendum hic ἀπὸ κοινῦ, conformari ad exemplar Filii sui.

τούτες καὶ ἐκάλεσε.

Nempe ad passiones; nam sic sumi verbum vocandi ap- paret 1. Petr. II. 20. 21. ἀλλ᾽ εἰ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καὶ πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε, τῦτο γὰρ χάρις παρὰ Θεῷ. Εἰς τῦτο γὰρ ἐκλήθητε, ὅτι καὶ χριστὸς ἔπαθεν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, ἡμῖν ὑπολιμπάνων ὑπο- γραμμὸν, ἵνα ἐπακολυθήσητε τοῖς ἴχνεσιν ἀυτῦ. Par sensus in illa 1. Thess. III. 3. τῷμηδένα σαίνεσθαι ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι ταύ- ταις, ἀυτοὶ γὰρ ὄιδατε ὅτι εἰς τῦτο κείμεθα. Dicitur DEUS pios vocare ad perpessiones, ubi causas earum, non modo non impedit, sed & disponit.

καὶ ὃς ἐκάλεσε τέτες καὶ ἐδικαίωσεν.

Hos & justos fecit, id est, vires eis præstitit perseverandi in justitiæ suæ obedientia. Nam δικαιῶν non de initio tan- tum, sed & de progressu dicitur.

ὃς δὲ ἐδικαίωσε.

Nempe cum effectu, ipsis donum tantum non negli- gentibus.

Τότες καὶ ἐδόξασε.

Id est, decrevit gloria decorare. Sic & Eph. I. 4. elegit, valet, decrevit eligere. Sic Christus gloriam habuisse di- citur priusquam mundus esset Joh. XVII. 5. uti ibi cum veteribus exposuimus. Sic gratia in Jesu data nobis dici- tur ante tempora sæcularia 2. Tim. I. 9. id est, decreta dari. Vide, quo gradationem istam Apostolus deduxerit, Chry- sostomus ἰσόζασε exponit, ornavit donis mirificis.

Per vocationem non vocatio ad passiones intel- ligitur, sed ad regnum gratiæ & gloriæ, etsi vocatis etiam definita sit divinitus passio, quo nomine ad id vocati à Petro, & ad id positi dicuntur à Pau- lo 1. Petr. II. 20. 1. Thess. III. 3. Neque justificare hic est justos facere, vel vires perseverandi in obe- dientia præstare: sed quemadmodum hactenus justificationis vocem adhibuit Apostolus, sensu forensi intelligi debet: nec nova, Apostolo inusi- tata, in verbo significatio fingenda. Ubi enim justificare Apostolo idem est, quod justos facere? ubi vires præstare perservandi in justitiæ obedien- tia: Denique glorificavit, non est decrevit glorifi- care, sed præteritum ponitur pro futuro ob rei certitudinem. Nec Eph. I. 4. ἐξελέξατο est decre- vit eligere, sed elegit, nec Joh. XVII. 5. gloriam ha- buisse dicitur Christus priusquam mundus esset ratione decreti & prædestinationis, sed ratione actu- alis gloriæ possessionis, quam habuit ab æterno, ut Deus, etsi petierit & acceperit in tempore ut ho- mo. De gradatione autem Apostolica universa ex professo egimus orat. LXIV. Addimus quæ habet B. Hülsem. in vindic. script. §. 88. Ex Anti- strophe illa particularum ὃς καὶ τέτες Rom. VIII. 30. quos prævidit, hos prædestinavit &c. quos justifi- cavit hos glorificavit &c. nequaquam sequitur non posse committi ab homine, ut hæc connexio unius beneficii cum alio rumpatur, seu non pos- se committi ab homine justificato ne glorifice- tur, quod Bareus, Beza, Marloretus, Groffius & plerique ad hunc locum contendunt. Dicit enim Apostolus, quid Deus à parte sua intendat, & quo fine homines vocet & justificet, nempe ut eosdem etiam glorificet. Nequaquam vero hic sermo est de impotentia hominis ad impediendam glorifica- tionem suam postquam justificatus est; non ho- minis sed Tyrannorum, Diaboli, ærumnarum & persecutionum impotentia opponitur h. l. poten- tiæ & benevolentiæ DEI, ut ex verbis immedia- te sequentibus ad oculum patet v. 31. quid igitur dicemus, si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? v. 35. Quis nos separabit &c. quod autem justificato- rum voluntaria peccata ipsos possint separare ab amore DEI, non solum non negavit h. l. Aposto- lus, sed verbis paulo præcedentibus aperte asse- ruit v. 13. & 14. ubi ad regenitos loquitur, si se- cundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini &c. Itaque committitur à Calvinianis in expositione hujus dicti Elenchus oppositorum, quando hominis impotentiam ad amittendam justificationem op- ponunt gratiæ divinæ, cum Diaboli potentiam & gratiæ divinæ potentiam opponere debuissent, nec quicquam sequitur magis pro impossibili di- vulsione glorificationis & justificationis ex Anti- strophe illarum particularum ὃ & τέτο quam ex dictis Apostoli capite præcedenti VII. 15. & 19. ὃ quod non volo, τῦτο πράσσω hoc facio possunt concludere. Ergo Apostolus semper peccavit nec potuit unquam contra instinctum concupiscen- tiæ agere; quam absurdum est, si colligerent h.m. Magister ille quoscunque in disciplinam suscipit, egregie doctos reddit. Ergo nullus discipulus potest proripere se ex ejus disciplina, quin egre- gius doctus evadat. Sermo enim est de intentio- ne Magistri non de impotentia discipulorum ad impediendum effectum illius bonæ intentionis. Vid. Colloquium Hagiense ad art. I. p. 159. seqq. Sic declaratio Christi Joh. VI. 39. Hæc est volun- tas Patris mei, ut quicquid dederit mihi nihil per- dam ex eo, non impendit exceptionem quod Ju- das sua culpa potuerit perire, etsi fuerit ex nume- ro eorum, quos Pater dedit Filio &c. Joh. XVII. 12. Custodivi eos quos dedisti mihi, & nemo periit ex illis nisi unus ille filius perditionis &c. Patet au- tem ex eo ipso gratuita plane salutis humanæ ratio. Prævisio DEI est, prædestinatio ab eodem proficisi- tur: vocat DEUS: justificat DEUS: glorificat idem. Hic ergo homo nihil fecit. Augustinus alia ratione hoc ipsum etiam commonstrat: Prævidit, inquiens, & prædestinavit Deus, antequam essemus: vocavit, cum aversi essemus; justificavit, cum pec- catores essemus. Nemo ergo dicat, ideo me vocavit Deus, quia colui DEUM. Quomodo coluisses, si vo- catus non fuisses? Si jam esses, non prædestinareris: nisi aversus esses, non vocareris: nisi impius esses, non justificareris: nisi terrenus & abjectus esses, non glorificareris. Ipsi gloria: Quia non eramus, quando sumus prædestinati; quia aversi eramus, quando su- mus vocati, quia Peccatores eramus, quando sumus justificati. Vid. B. Mylius p. 303.

## 8:31
V. 31. τί ἂν ἐρῦμεν πρὸς ταῦτα.

That is, what do we infer from these? For we noted above that ἐρῦμεν is used by the Apostle in the present tense as well; furthermore, πρὸς ταῦτα also signifies "on account of these things" in Aristophanes.

If God is for us,

Here 'if' has the force of 'since': for he assumes what he had established, that God is for us Christians, since he directs all things toward adorning us with the highest goods.

Latin:

V. 31. τί ἂν ἐρῦμεν πρὸς ταῦτα.

Id est, quid ex his inferimus? Nam ἐρῦμεν apud Apo- stolum in præsenti etiam tempore poni supra notavimus, Tum πρὸς ταῦτα etiam Aristophani significat propter hæc.

ἐἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν,

ἐἰ hic valet, quandoquidem : assumit enim, quod ad-struxerat, Deus pro nobis Christianis est, quandoquidem omnia ad nos summis bonis ornandos dirigit.

## 8:32
V. 32. Who indeed did not spare his own Son. What in Abraham had been a sign of love toward GOD, Gen. XXII. 12, that is in GOD a sign of benevolence toward men. In the Greek of Genesis: you did not spare your son.

but for us all he delivered him up. That is, for all men. The same sense as above, V. 8. If he valued any men so highly, how much more will he value men who have faithfully obeyed him? Concerning the verb παραδιδόναι, see above IV. 25.

how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? It is easier to give to those who have already been made friends than to those who are still enemies; and it is easier to give anything else than the Son.

This is the conclusion of the present chapter, in the judgment of the blessed Mylius, p. 303. For because he has demonstrated thus far that neither the thunderbolts of the law, nor the peals of afflictions, nor even the flashes of one's own sins are powerful enough to weaken the anchor of hope, he concludes that the pious are placed in the safest asylum of hope. But for this consequence, an antecedent is posited, and that varied four times, and always figured by the scheme of interrogation. And first, for that which he could have said, that the hope of the pious is most certain, he posits this: that no one can be against us. This statement, according to the quality of the subject matter, is not to be taken absolutely. For that enemies will not be lacking to the pious, Christ himself is a most certain witness and prophet. But that they so oppose us that they can tear away the hope of heavenly life, that indeed is what the Apostle denies. Which he does not merely assert, however, but fortifies with a reason, namely, because God is for us. These are the words of the blessed Mylius. But in our opinion, the Apostle proceeds to a new argument for the certainty of the hope of the reborn, which he draws from the mediatorial office of Christ: both as to Redemption and as to intercession. For since temptations could arise for the faithful concerning perseverance, and indeed even concerning the present state of grace, and our faith cannot either arise or be sustained concerning the gratuitous remission of sins and salvation unless we are in every way certain of the grace of God exhibited to all in Christ, the Apostle inculcates the same thing here, especially for the certainty of the hope of glory, how GOD the Father, by delivering his own Son for us all, and by justifying the faithful for the sake of the Son, and Christ the Son of GOD, both by dying for us and rising again and sitting at the right hand of GOD for our sake, and by interceding for us, exhibits love and grace to us, so that from this we may be most certain that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ, nothing from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Grotius rightly explains those words 'for us all' here as referring to ALL men, which sense the text demands. For if he had meant believers only, there would have been no need for the particle of universality to be added. For there was no reason why anyone should suspect that Christ was given for some believers and not for all. Moreover, in the human race as a whole, because there is a great deal of difference, lest this should seem to have stood in the way of divine charity, Christ is said to have been delivered not only for us, but also for all; as the blessed Mylius warns, and as the confirmation of our faith, to which these things are dedicated, requires. For under universal propositions, that Christ was delivered unto death for all men, everyone can subsume and apply to himself individually the merit of Christ, so that faith, which is the apprehension of the merit of Christ, and the justification of faith, which is the divine imputation of the same made to believers, may stand firm for him, and thus, being certain of the merit of Christ pertaining to himself, they may have hope that they will attain the end of faith, eternal salvation, which Christ likewise merited for all by his death. But those words, 'how will he not also with him graciously give us all things,' although they seem to speak particularly of the faithful, for whom the Son of God was not only delivered, which is common to all men, but to whom the Son was also given out of grace in justification, with a peculiar approbation being added. It can, however, be taken generally: because the Son was given to us not only in justification, which is proper to the faithful, but also in the incarnation, which is a gift made to the whole world, John III. 16, 1 John IV. 14, Isa. IX. 6. And thus the Apostle's collection holds its place according to the Grotian interpretation: If he valued any men so highly, how much more will he value men who have faithfully obeyed him or believe: And it is easier to give to those who have already been made friends than to those who are still enemies; (cf. Rom. V. 9.) and it is easier to give anything else than the Son. To those, therefore, to whom God has made this great gift his own, which happened in the justification of the faithful, how would he not graciously give them all other things, how would he not give them salvation itself and eternal life, for whose sake he gave his Son to the whole world, for whose sake he particularly appropriated this gift to the faithful, by imputing to them the satisfaction and righteousness of the Son through faith, so that they might indeed have eternal life in the Son, 1 John V. 11, 12. This sweetest inference must be strongly impressed upon the mind: because in it the most solid hope of eternal life is held. How would GOD not GRACIOUSLY GIVE US ALL THINGS with the SON? For what greater gift did he have to graciously give us than his own Son, the only-begotten Son, the Son who is of one substance with the Father, the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his nature.

Latin:

V. 32. ὅς γε τῦ ἰδίε ὑῦ ἐκ ἐφείσατο. Quod in Abrahamo signum fuerat amoris in DEUM Gen. XXII. 12. id in DEO signum benevolentiæ adversus homines. In Græco Geneseos : ἐκ ἐφείσω τῦ ὑἱῦ σε.

ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν. Id est, pro omnibus hominibus. Idem sensus, qui supra V. 8. Si tanti fecit homines quosvis, quanti facturus est homines sibi fideliter obsecutos ? De verbo παραδιδόναι vide supra IV. 25.

πῶς ὀχὶ σὺν ἀυτῶ τὰ πάντα ἡμῖν χαρίσεται. Facilius est dare amicis factis, quam adhuc hostibus; & facilius omne aliud quàm filium.

Conclusio hæc est præsentis capitis, judicio B. My- lii p. 303. Nam quia neque legis fulmina neque affli- ctionum tonitrua neque propriorum etiam peccato- rum fulgura, ad infirmandum spei anchoram satis esse valida posse, demonstravit hactenus: pios in tu- tissimo spei asylo collocatos esse colligit. Positum est autem pro consequente isto antecedens, idque quater variatum, & interrogationis schemate semper figu- ratum. Ac primum pro eo, quod dicere poterat, spem piorum esse certissimam, illud ponit, Neminem con- tra nos esse posse. Hoc enunciatum pro subjecta ma- teriæ qualitate, non absolute accipiendum est. Nam inimicos piis non defore, Christus ipse testis & vates est certissimus. Sed qui ita nobis adversantur, ut spem vitæ cælestis convellere queant, id vero est, quod Apostolus pernegat. Quod non modo tamen illa effert: sed ratione munitam nimirum, quia Deus sit pro nobis. Hæc B. Mylius. Nostra autem sententia progreditur Apostolus ad novum argu- mentum certitudinis spei renatorum, quod depro- mit à munere Christi mediatorio: tum qua Redem- tionem, tum qua intercessionem. Quum enim ten- tationes suboriri possent fidelibus de perseveran- tia, imo & de statu præsenti gratiæ, neque fides no- stra possit vel oriri, vel sustentari, de gratuita re- missione peccatorum & salute nisi omnimodo certi simus de gratia Dei omnibus in Christo ex- hibita, eandem subinde & hic imprimis in certi- tudinem spei gloriæ inculcat Apostolus, quomodo & DEUS Pater Filium suum pro nobis omni- bus tradendo, & fideles ob Filium justificando, & Christus Filius DEI tum moriendo pro nobis, & resurgendo ac considendo ad dextram DEI nostri causa, tum intercedendo pro nobis, amorem & gra- tiam nobis exhibeat, ut inde quam certissimi simus nihil nos separare posse ab amore Christi, nihil à dilectione DEI, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Recte hic Grotius illa ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων de OMNIBUS hominibus explicat, quem sensum postulat textus. Si enim credentes solos intellexis- set, particula notæ καθόλε addita nihil opus fuisset. Nihil enim causæ erat, cur pro aliquibus credenti- bus, non pro omnibus datum esse Christum quisquam suspicari queat. Cæterum in genere humano univer- so, quia plurimum discriminis inest, ne hoc obstitisse divinæ caritati videretur, non pro nobis tantum: sed pro omnibus etiam traditus esse Christus dici- tur; Monente B. Mylio, & requirit fidei nostræ con- firmatio, cui hæc sunt dicata. Nam sub universa- libus propositionibus, quod Christus pro omni- bus hominibus traditus in mortem sit, subsumere quisque & in individuo sibi applicare potest meri- tum Christi, ut fides, quæ est apprehensio meriti Christi, & justificatio fidei, quæ est imputatio di- vina ejusdem credentibus facta sibi constet, atque ita certi de merito Christi se attinente finem fidei salutem æternam, quam morte sua itidem omni- bus promeruit Christus, se consecuturos sperare habeant. Illi autem πῶς οὐχὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα ἡμῖν χαρίσεται etsi videantur peculiariter de fide- libus loqui, pro quibus non tantum traditus est Dei Filius, quod omnibus hominibus commune est, sed quibus etiam Filius ex gratia donatus est in justi- ficatione accedente peculiari approbatione. Po- test tamen generaliter accipi: quia donatus no- bis Filius est non tantum in justificatione, quæ fi- delium propria, sed etiam in incarnatione, quæ donatio toti mundo facta est Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. IV, 14. Esa. IX. 6. Atque ita locum habet collectio Apostoli juxta interpretationem Grotianam: Si tanti fecit homines quosvis, quanti facturus est ho- mines fideliter sibi obsecutos vel credentes: Et faci- lius est dare amicis factis, quam adhuc hostibus: (conf. Rom. V. 9.) & facilius omne aliud, quam Filium. Quibus ergo Deus hoc tantum donum proprium fecit, quod contigit in justificatione fi- delibus, quomodo illis non gratificaretur alia o- mnia, quomodo non ipsam salutem & vitam æter- nam, cujus gratia mundo toti donavit Filium, cu- jus gratia peculiariter appropriavit hoc donum fidelibus, imputata illis Filii satisfactione, & ju- stitia per fidem, ut nempe in Filio habeant vitam æternam, 1. Joh. V. 11. 12. Dulcissima hæc illatio fortiter menti imprimenda: quia in ea spes vitæ æternæ habetur solidissima. Quomodo non cum FILIO nobis DEUS GRATIFICARETUR OMNIA? quod enim majus donum habuit quod nobis gratificaretur, quam Filium proprium, Filium unigenitum, Filium ὁμοούσιον, splendorem gloriæ & characterem hypostaseos suæ.

## 8:33
V. 33. Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect.

He fortifies Christians more closely against the judgments of crimes which were being aimed at them even though they were innocent. Who shall accuse the elect of GOD? that is: Who at last are they who dare to accuse them? namely, little men. In a similar sense, what is it, we have Ps. VIII. 5. & who therefore, what is my life or the thought of my father: for how little and how little, 1 Sam. XVIII. 18. The elect of GOD, that is, those whom God values most highly. See Matt. III. 17. & XX, 16

God is the one who justifies.

It is God who considers them as just, as they truly are, and wishes to treat them as such. Let others call them whatever most odious names they wish: their innocence is perceived and pleasing to God. Reference is made to the passage Job XXXIV. 29. If He grants peace, who is there who can condemn?

Latin:

V. 33. τίς ἐγκαλέσει κατὰ ἐκλεκτῶν Θεῦ.

Propius munit Christianos adversus criminum judicia. quæ ipsis innocentibus intentabantur. Quis accusabit ele- ctos DEI? id est: Qui tandem sunt, qui eos accusare au- dent? nempe homunciones. Simili sensu, quid est, habe- mus Ps. VIII. 5. & quis ergo, quæ mea vita aut cogitatio patris mei: pro quantillus & quantilla, 1. Reg. XVIII. 18. Electos DEI, id est, eos, quos Deus maximi facit. Vid. Matth. III. 17. & XX, 16

Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν.

Deus est, qui eos pro justis, ut revera sunt, habet & ut tales vult tractare. Vocent eos alii, quam volent, odio- sissimis nominibus: Deo eorum innocentia perspecta ac grata est. Respicitur locus Jobi XXXIV. 29. Ipso conce- dente pacem quis est, qui condemnet?

## 8:34
V. 34. Who is he that condemneth.

Who at last are they who condemn them? Mortal and evil judges.

Christ who died.

Who died for us.

Yea rather, and is risen again.

Nay, even for our sake He was raised from the dead, namely so that we might know that He will be our judge. See above IV. 35. & Acts XVII. 31.

Who also is at the right hand of God.

King of kings, Lord of lords. For that is what is signified by the right hand of GOD. See what is at Matt. XX. 21. & at 15, supply sitting.

That this pertains to the remnants of sin: Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s Elect, notes B. Mylius, as he does other things regarding the law and afflictions: who may be seen here. Yet these things are not said only of the Christians of those times, although they pertain to them entirely, nor are they spoken only of the causes of judicial accusations, but against all accusations, even in the divine judgment: not only on account of the accusations of petty men, but primarily also on account of diabolical accusations, because Satan accuses us before GOD night and day, Apoc. XII, 10. The Apostle thus lifts up all the Elect of GOD of all times, by which name he does not specifically understand those who are predestined to eternal salvation, but all the faithful: who are called elect, both because of grace, or because GOD holds them in the highest regard, and because of excellence, for that is called elect which is choice and excellent, as being worthy to be chosen before others, just as Christ is called the elect stone, that is, the precious one, Is. XXVIII. 16. 1 Pet. II. 6. which dignity the faithful do not have from themselves, but in Christ, in whom they are also uniquely beloved, Eph. I. 6. Thus Rufus is called elect, Rom. XVI. 13. That elect lady, to whom St. John was writing, 2 Epist. v. 1. and her sister v. 13. All the elect are holy and beloved, Col. III. 12. But the passage Matt. III. 17 is cited less correctly. For in that the name elect does not occur, and the discourse is about the consubstantial Son of GOD. But the grace of justification is opposed to this accusation of the elect: It is God who justifies, i.e., absolves: for when justification and a judge, before whom the accusation was made, are opposed to the accusation which takes place in judgment, he justifies those who were accused, what else is that justification but an absolution? But GOD does not justify by holding them as just, as they truly are, and by treating them as such: For thus no one would be held innocent and just before GOD: Job IX. 2. Ps. CXLIII. 2. but out of mere grace by absolving from sins for the sake of the only-begotten Son, and by freely remitting sins, and by imputing and attributing to us the innocence and justice of the Son, as the Apostle had taught in chapters III and IV, from which he proceeds further here by asking v. 34. Who is it that condemns? not speaking of mortal judges: but removing everyone universally: that no one, not even Satan himself, indeed not even the divine law or our own conscience can condemn us. But just as he opposed absolution to our accusation, so he opposes the death and satisfaction of Christ to condemnation, because by dying for us he underwent condemnation in our place, and made satisfaction for our sins. How therefore should he condemn us, when Christ himself was willing to be condemned for us, and to make satisfaction, which satisfaction of his is imputed to us through faith. 2 Cor. V. 14, 21. Nor indeed did Christ only die for us, but he also rose again, namely not only so that we might know that he who is our redeemer will be our judge, but also for our justification, Rom. IV. 25, so that he might make us more certain of his justice and satisfaction, or active and passive obedience, and impart the same to us through faith. Is. LIII. 11. He also sat down at the right hand of GOD reigning over all, as King of Kings and Lord of lords, not that this is signified by the phrase right hand of GOD, but by the whole phrase: because the right hand of God is the immense and infinite virtue and power of God, Acts IV. 24, c. V. 31, Matt. XXV. 34, Luke XXII. 69, Heb. I. 3, c. VIII. 1, c. XII. 2, whence he sat at the right hand of God, insofar as he, having been made a participant of the same divine virtue, rules over all things with divine power and authority, Matt. XXVIII. 19, Ps. CX. 1, 3, Eph. I. 20, et seqq. Heb. I. 3, 13, c. II. 6, which rule of Christ exalted at the right hand of GOD concerns especially the Church, as his elect people, since he gathers the Church to himself through the word and Sacraments, and governs, protects, and preserves the same, against enemies both spiritual and bodily, in the kingdom of grace, until he leads and raises the same to the kingdom of glory: whence under this Lord, who is the same Redeemer, and our brother, we can be safe and tranquil, and dwell confidently, certain of future glory, Jer. XXIII. 6, c. XXXII. 15.

we also had in the Maccabees. In a similar sense Christ is said to intercede for them, Heb. VII. 25, that is, to commend to GOD those who trust in him: to obtain the Spirit for them. Earthly kings condemn Christians. The heavenly King is so far from condemning that he deems them worthy of his patronage.

So that he may render us certain and confidently secure of salvation on every side, he adds the intercession of Christ for us to the satisfaction of the death of Christ, and the resurrection that followed, and the exaltation to the right hand of GOD: to the offering made for us, he adds the appearance before the face of God in heaven, which is done eternally for us: to the kingly office of Christ, that eternal office of his Priesthood, by which he perpetually intercedes for us. Conf. 1 John II. 1, Heb. IX. 25. Therefore the Apostle does not look only at those whom Christian kings were condemning in his time, but whom God himself, the supreme King, could by right condemn; but he teaches that they will not be condemned, provided they believe in Christ, but will obtain eternal salvation, from the fact that Christ has freed us from condemnation, having died for us, and acquired eternal salvation for us, but also that he intercedes continually before the Father for the sake of our salvation, whom we are certain is always heard by the Father, John XI. 42. This is opposed to the law, says the blessed Mylius p. 356, the Apostle attributes condemnation to it, for this is proper to the law in a corrupt nature, that it should strike with the thunderbolt of a curse. But the Apostle opposes four things to this, and those each in Christ, so that just as authority accrues to the law from GOD, whose will it proposes and executes: in turn, he compares the authority of our redemption from the person of Christ. The first, however, is the death of Christ, in whose sentence, passed through the mouth of Pilate, Christ sustained condemnation, so that condemnation might be expiated by condemnation. Resurrection is subjoined to death, as the complement of the justification to be brought. For Christ was delivered up for our sins: but he rose again for our justification. To understand what force all these things have, two others are subjoined: the sitting at the right hand of the Father, and the intercession for us, by the former of which the power, and by the latter the will of Christ is signified; and that it may not be understood that either is lacking in Christ, it is said that Christ entered into that heavenly Sanctuary with this very purpose, that He might provide for our salvation. The same Peter testifies in Acts 5:31: Him hath God exalted with His right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins. And Hebrews 8:1: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. Therefore, the present passage contains, as it were, a cornucopia of all comforts, by which the terrors of the law are to be dispelled. We add the explanation of Philippus, who on p. 154. He amplifies, he says, (the Apostle) at the end the certainty of grace and deliverance, by the mention of the pledge given, namely, the redeemer and intercessor, and at the same time refutes objections. For two terrible arguments meet the eyes, which impel men to doubt. The sight of our uncleanness, which clings to all, even those not having sins against conscience; for conscience always argues: God does not hear sinners: I am a sinner: Therefore I am not in grace. Then the sight of external miseries, concerning which it reasons thus: The righteous ought to be well. The Church is most afflicted and not only small, but also deformed by domestic wounds. These two arguments do not lightly shake the minds of all men. And by the former argument the Monks were so moved that they taught that in this life one must always doubt whether we are in grace, and they approve of this doubt, and say it is humility. Against this foul error, the voice of the Gospel most constantly teaches that doubt must be overcome by faith,

who also makes intercession for us.

Understand ἐσίν. He Himself, who died for our sake. He who was raised for our sake, and sat down at the right hand of the Father, is He who commends our affairs to God: for this mean- thus, that those converted to God may establish that their sins are truly remitted for the sake of the Son, and that for his sake they are pleasing to God, although there still cling to us not sins against conscience, but defects and depraved inclinations and the flame of depraved affections, which we nevertheless resist. Here Paul answers that faith relies on the merit and intercession of the Son of God, not on our dignity, and there is mention of both things, merit and intercession. Let this consolation, therefore, be first in sight, which is proposed in the merit of Christ, or sacrifice, namely, that in conversion believers are truly received and are pleasing to God on account of this victim, even if the remnants of sin still cling to the converted. Doubt must therefore be overcome, because the doubter disputes whether the merit of Christ is sufficient, or prefers his own sins to the merit of Christ against the saying: Grace abounds over the offense. Therefore he says here: Who shall accuse the elect, since it is God who justifies, as if he were saying, even if the remnants of sin cling to the converted, yet God justifies them on account of the Son. But concerning intercession, let us know that the application of the merit of Christ is made to us at all times, before the eternal Father through the Mediator himself praying for us. Thus merit and intercession are joined. Merit is the obedience of Christ satisfying the justice of God to appease his wrath. Intercession is the constant appeal for us, as it is said in Heb. VII, Always living to intercede for them. And in this place at Rom. VIII, Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us, that is, who reigns with the Father, and sees the heart of the Father, and in that secret counsel intercedes for us, and carries our groans to the Father, who receives us for the sake of the Son, according to the saying: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Let this consolation always be in sight, even if we are very weak and unworthy, yet we are pleasing, because here the Son by his merit appeases the Father, and always intercedes for us, and covers us with the application of his merit, lest the immense divine wrath be poured out upon us. To this let the saying also be accommodated: You are a Priest forever. Likewise, the whole prayer said before the agony, which is the perpetual voice of the Mediator at all times. The words of application are: I sanctify myself for them, that is, I offer myself. Likewise, I pray not for them only, but for those who will believe through their word, that they may be one in us. Likewise, that your love may be in them, with which you love me. But God the Father certainly hears this intercessor, according to the saying: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as an inheritance.

Latin:

V. 34. Τίς ὁ κατακρίνων.

Qui tandem sunt, qui eos damnant? Judices mortales & mali.

χριστὸς ὁ ἀποθανὼν.

Qui pro nobis est mortuus.

μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐγερθείς.

Imo etiam nostri causa ex mortuis est excitatus, nempe ut sciremus illum fore nobis judicem. Vide supra IV. 35. & Act. XVII. 31.

Ὅς καὶ ἔστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ Θεῦ.

Rex regum, Dominus dominantium. Id enim per dex- tram DEI significatur. Vide quæ ad Matth. XX. 21. & ad 15, subaudi καθεζόμενος.

Ad reliquias peccati hoc pertinere: Quis accu- sabit Electos, notat B. Mylius uti alia ad legem & afflictiones: qui hic videatur. Non autem hæc de Christianis tantum istorum temporum dicuntur, etsi ad illos omnino pertineant, nec tantum causæ accusationum judicialium dicuntur, sed adversus omnes accusationes, in judicio etiam divino: non tantum ob homuncionum accusationes, sed imprimis etiam ob accusationes diabolicas, quia accusat nos Satanas coram DEO nocte ac die, Apoc. XII, 10. Electos DEI universos omnium temporum ita erigit Apostolus, quo nomine non specialiter eos, qui ad salutem æternam prædesti- nati sunt intelligit, sed fideles quosque: qui electi dicuntur, tum ob gratiam, vel quod DEUS eos maximi faciat, tùm ob præstantiam, nam electum dicitur, quod eximium & præstans est, ut dignum quod præ aliis eligatur, quomodo Christus lapis electus, id est, pretiosus dicitur Es. XXVIII. 16. 1. Pet. II. 6. quam verò dignitatem fideles non ex se habent, sed in Christo, in quo etiam unicè dilecti sunt Ephes. I. 6. Ita electus dicitur Rufus, Rom. XVI. 13. Electa famina illa, ad quam S. Jo- hannes scribebat 2. Epist. v. 1. & soror ejus v. 13. Electi omnes ἅγιοι καὶ ἠγαπημένοι Coloff. III. 12. Minus autem rectè adducitur locus Matth. III. 17. Nam in illo nomen ἐκλεκτὸς non occurrit, & ser- mo est de Filio DEI consubstantiali. Opponitur autem huic electorum accusationi justificationis gratia: Deus est, qui justificat, h. e. absolvit: nam accusationi, quæ fit in judicio, cum opponitur δικαίωσις & judex, coram quo facta est accusatio, justificat eos, qui accusabantur, quid aliud justifi- catio illa, nisi absolutio est? Non autem justificat DEUS pro justis, ut reverà sunt, habendo, & ut tales tractando: Sic enim nemo coram DEO in- nocens, & justus haberetur: Job. IX. 2. Ps. CXLIII. 2. sed ex mera gratia propter Filium unigenitum à peccatis absolvendo, & gratis peccata remitten- do, & innocentiam ac justitiam Filii nobis accen- sendo, & tribuendo, ut c. III. & IV. docuerat A- postolus, undè progreditur hic porrò quærendo v. 34. Quis est, qui condemnet? non de judicibus mortalibus loquens: sed in universum omnes re- movens: neminem, ac ne Satanam ipsum, imò nec legem divinam aut conscientiam nostram nos condemnare posse. Ut autem accusationi nostræ opposuit absolutionem, ita condemnationi Christi mortem & satisfactionem, quia moriendo pro no- bis condemnationem nostri loco subiit, & pro peccatis nostris satisfecit. Quomodo ergò nos condemnet, quum pro nobis Christus ipse con- demnari voluerit, ac satisfacere, quæ ejus satis- factio nobis per fidem imputatur. 2. Cor. V. 14. 21. Nec verò mortuus tantùm pro nobis est Chri- stus, sed resurrexit etiam, nempè non modò, ut sciremus, eum nostrum fore judicem, qui redemtor noster est, sed etiam ob justificationem nostram, Rom. IV. 25. ut justitiæ & satisfactionis suæ, vel obedientiæ activæ & passivæ nos certiores red- deret, eandemque nobis per fidem impertiret. Es. LIII. 11. Consedit etiam ad dextram DEI re- gnans super omnia, ceu Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium, non quod per vocem dextræ DEI hoc significetur, sed per integram phrasin: quia dextra Dei est virtus & potentia Dei immensa & infinita Act. IV. 24. c. V. 31. Matth. XXV. 34. Luc. XXII. 69. Ebr. I. 3. c. VIII. 1. c. XII. 2. unde sedit ad dextram Dei, quatenus ejusdem divinæ parti- ceps factus virtutis dominatur super omnia divinâ δυνάμει & ἐξουσίᾳ Matth. XXVIII. 19. Ps. CX. 1. 3. Eph. I. 20. seqq. Ebr. I. 3. 13. c. II. 6. quod regimen Christi ad dextram DEI exaltati concernit im- primis Ecclesiam, ceu populum ejus electum, quum per verbum & Sacramenta sibi colligat Ec- clesiam, eandemque gubernet, protegat & con- servet, adversus hostes tùm spirituales, tùm corpo- rales, in regno gratiæ, donec perducat & evehat eandem ad regnum gloriæ: unde sub hoc Domi- no, qui idem Redemtor est, & frater noster tuti & tranquilli esse possumus, & confidenter habitare certi de futura gloria, Jer. XXIII. 6. c. XXXII. 15.

su ἐντυγχάνειν & ἔντευξιν habuimus etiam in Maccabaicis. Pari sensu Christus dicitur ἐντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν Hebr. VII. 25. id est, eorum, qui ipsi confidunt re, DEO com- mendare: Spiritum ipsis impetrare. Reges terreni Chri- stianos damnant. Rex cælestis adeò non damnat, ut di- gnos censeat suo patrocinio.

Ut undiquaque nos certos & confidenter se- curos de salute reddat satisfactioni mortis Chri- sti, & consequutæ resurrectioni, & evectioni ad dextram DEI addit intercessionem Christi pro no- bis: oblationi pro nobis factæ apparitionem coram vultu Dei in cælis, quæ pro nobis æternum fit: Regio Christi muneri æternum illud Sacerdotii ejus munus, quò perpetuò interpellat pro nobis. Conf. 1. Joh. II. 1. Ebr. IX. 25. Non ergò respicit solùm eos Apostolus, quos suo tempore Reges Christiani damnabant, sed quos jure Deus ipse Rex supre- mus damnare posset; quos verò non condemna- tum iri, modò in Christum credant, sed æternam sa- lutem consequuturos esse inde docet, quod à con- damnatione nos Christus liberârit, mortuus pro nobis, & salutem æternam nobis acquifiverit, sed quod etiam apud Patrem nostræ salutis causâ ju- giter intercedat, quem verò semper exaudiri à Pa- tre certi sumus Joh. XI. 42. Legi hoc oppositum est tropæum, inquit B. Mylius p. 356. ei Apostolus tribuit condemnationem, proprium enim hoc est le- gis in corrupta quidem naturâ, ut maledictionis ful- men firingat. Huic autem opponit Apostolus qua- tuor, eaque singula in Christo, ut quia legi autoritas accedit ex DEO, cujus ea voluntatem proponit, & exequitur: vicissim ex persona Christi, redemtionis nostræ autoritatem comparat. Primum autem est mors Christi, in cujus sententia per os Pilati lata con- damnationem Christus sustinuit, ut condemnatio condemnatione expiata sit. Morti resurrectio sub- jungitur, ceu complementum justificationis afferendæ. Traditus est enim Christus propter peccata nostra: resurrexit autem propter justificationem nostram. Quæ quam vim omnia habeant, ut intelligatur, duo alia subnectuntur, sessio ad dextram Patris, & in- tercessio pro nobis, quorum illo potestas, hoc voluntas Christi significatur, quarum neutra, ut deeffe Christo intelligatur, hoc ipso consilio in cælesle illud Sacra- rium ingressus esse Christus dicitur, ut saluti nostræ consulat. Testatur idem Petrus Act. V. 31. Hunc ipsum Deus dextra sua erectum, ducem & Serva- torem constituit, ut daret Israeli pænitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Et Hebr. VIII. 1. Talem habemus Pontificem, qui sedet ad dextram throni Majestatis in cælis. Continet ergò præsens locus quasi cornu quoddam copiæ consolationum omnium, qui- bus terriculamenta legis displodenda sunt. Addi- mus Philippi explicationem, qui p. 154. Ampli- ficat, inquit, (Apost.) in fine certitudinem gratiæ & liberationis, mentione dati pignoris, scilicet, re- demtoris & intercessoris, & simul refutat objectio- nes. Duo enim terribilia argumenta incurrunt in oculos, quæ impellunt homines ad dubitandum. Con- spectus nostræ immunditiæ, quæ hæret in omnibus, etiam non habentibus delicta contra conscientiam; semper enim disputat conscientia: Deus peccatores non exaudit: Ego sum peccator: Non igitur sum in gratia. Deinde conspectus externarum ærumna- rum, de quibus sic ratiocinatur: Justus debebat be- nè esse. Ecclesia est afflictissima & non solùm exi- gua, sed etiam deformis domesticis vulneribus. Hæc duo argumenta non leviter concutiunt omnium ho- minum animos. Ac priori argumento fic moti sunt Monachi, ut docuerint, in hac vita semper dubi- tandum esse, an simus in gratia, & hanc dubitatio- nem approbent, & dicant esse humilitatem. Ad- versus hunc tetrum errorem constantissime docet vox Evangelii, vincendam esse fide dubitationem,

ὃς καὶ ἐντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν.

Subintellige ἐσίν. Is ipse, qui nostri causa mortuus. Qui nostri causa resuscitatus est, & ad dextram Patris conse- dit, is est, qui nostras res Deo commendat: nam hoc sen- sic, ut conversi ad Deum statuant, verè sibi remitti peccata propter Filium, & propter eum se placere Deo, quanquam adhuc haerent in nobis non peccata contra conscientiam, sed defectus & pravae inclina- tiones & flamma pravorum affectuum, quibus ta- men repugnamus. Hic respondet Paulus fidem niti merito & intercessione Filii Dei, non nostra dignita- te, & sit utriusque rei mentio, meriti & intercessio- nis. Primum igitur sit in conspectu haec consolatio, quae proponitur in merito Christi, seu sacrificio, vi- delicet, quod in conversione verè recipiantur & placeant Deo credentes propter hanc victimam, et- iamsi adhuc haerent in conversis reliquiae peccati. Vincenda est igitur dubitatio, quia dubitans dis- putat, an meritum Christi sufficiat, aut antefert sua peccata merito Christi contra dictum: Gratia exuberat supra delictum. Ideò hic inquit: Quis accusabit electos, cum Deus sit, qui justificat, quasi dicat, etiamsi haerent in conversis reliquiae peccati, tamen eos justificat Deus propter filium. De inter- cessione verò sciamus applicationem meriti Christi ad nos fieri omni tempore, coram aeterno Patre per ipsum Mediatorem deprecantem pro nobis. Sic con- juncta sunt meritum & intercessio. Meritum est obedientia Christi satisfaciens justitiae Dei ad pla- candam iram. Intercessio est assidua appellatio pro nobis, sicut Ebr. VII. dicitur, Semper vivens, ut in- tercedat pro eis. Et hoc loco ad Rom. VIII. Qui est ad dextram Dei, qui & interpellat pro nobis, id est, qui regnat cum Patre, & videt pectus Patris, & in illo arcano consilio pro nobis intercedit, & nostros gemitus ad Patrem perfert, qui propter filium nos recipit, juxta dictum: Quicquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Haec consolatio semper in conspectu sit, etiamsi valdè infirmi & indigni su- mus, tamen placemus, quia hic Filius merito suo pla- cat Patrem, & semper pro nobis intercedit, & tegit nos applicatione meriti sui, ne in nos effundatur in- gens ira divina. Huc accommodetur & dictum: Tu es Sacerdos in aeternum. Item, tota precatio an- te agonêm dicta, quae est perpetua vox Mediatoris omni tempore. Verba applicationis sunt: Ego me pro eis sanctifico, id est, offero. Item, Oro non pro ipsis tantùm, sed pro credituris per verbum eo- rum, ut unum sint in nobis. Item, ut dilectio tua in eis sit, qua me diligis. Hunc deprecatorem au- tem certò exaudit Deus Pater, juxta dictum: Po- stula à me, & dabo tibi gentes haereditatem.

## 8:35
V. 35. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ.

The love of Christ, as shortly the love of God is that love with which God loves those who love him. See above 28, 32, and below 37, 39. Moreover, the word χωρίζω is significantly placed.
