For it is accustomed to be used of Jewish divorces, Matt. XIX. 6, Mark X. 9. But he says τίς, and answers concerning things, because he also personifies things. In these words Augustine rightly noted the vehemence.

Tribulation or distress.

Tribulation, or distress, the Latin translator renders: as Salvianus also cites in II against avarice. We spoke of these words above II. 9. Tertullian translates θλίψιν as pressure.

or persecution.

To persecute is to expel, as we said at Matt. V. 10. Thus Christians in Claudian times were driven from Rome together with the Jews, as Suetonius testifies.

or famine, or nakedness, or danger.

Which we see often happened to Christians, 2 Cor. XI. 26, 27.

or sword.

He understands the sword of civil power, as in XIII. 4. Indeed, the Christians at Rome had not yet been treated with such cruelty as to lead to death, but what had happened to James in Judea, Acts XII. 2, could likewise happen to Christians elsewhere,

V. 36. As it is written: For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.

Those who wish these things to be read in parentheses advise correctly. Paul shows in passing that, even if the cruelty of enemies should reach the point of bloodshed, such patience would not lack an ancient example taken from Psalm XLIV. Paul follows the version of the LXX. We are killed daily, that is, now this one, now that one, from the people. Πρόβατα σφαγῆς, sheep kept for this purpose, that they may be slaughtered.

Latin:

V. 35. Τίς ἡμᾶς χωρίσει ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τῦ Χρισῦ.

Ἀγάπη τῦ Χρισῦ, ut mox ἀγάπη τῦ Θεῦ est ea dilectio, qua Deus se diligentes diligit. Vide supra 28. 32. & infrà 37. 39. Est autem verbum χωρίζω significanter positum. Solet enim de Judaicis divortiis usurpari Matth. XIX. 6. Marc. X. 9. τίς autem dicit, & respondet de rebus, quia etiam res προσωποποιεῖ. In his verbis δείνωσιν rectè nota- vit Augustinus.

Θλίψις ἢ στενοχωρία.

Tribulatio, an angustia, vertit Latinus: quomodo etiam citat Salvianus II. contra avaritiam. De his vocibus dixi- mus supra II. 9. Tertullianus θλίψιν vertit pressuram.

ἢ διωγμὸς.

Διώκειν est expellere, ut diximus ad Matth. V. 10. Sic Christiani Claudianis temporibus una cum Judaeis pulsi Roma, teste Suetonio.

ἢ λιμὸς, ἢ γυμνότης, ἢ κίνδυνος.

Quae saepè evenisse Christianis videmus 2. Cor. XI. 26. 27.

ἢ μαχαίρα.

Gladium civilis potestatis intelligit, ut XIII. 4. Nondum quidem ad mortem usque Romae in Christianos saevitum fuerat, sed quod Jacobo evenerat in Judaea Actor. XII. 2. idem & alibi Christianis evenire poterat,

| V. 36. Καθὼς γέγραπται· Ὅτι ἕνεκά σου θανατούμε- θα ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν· ἐλογίσθημεν ὡς πρό- βατα σφαγῆς.

Rectè monent, qui hæc legi volunt ἐν παρενθέσει. Obi- ter oftendit Paulus, etiamsi ad sanguinem hostium sævitia perveniret, talem patientiam non carituram veteri exemplo petito ex Psalm. XLIV. Sequitur Paulus versionem LXX. Occidimur quotidiè, nempè nunc hic, nunc ille, de popu- lo. Πρόβατα σφαγῆς, pecudes in hoc asservatæ, ut ma- ctentur.

## 8:37
V. 37. But in all these things we more than conquer.

He answers the questions. So far are those things from separating us from the love of GOD, that we more than conquer in all of them, that is, we triumph over them. Paul loves to compound words with ὑπὲρ, as we noted above in V. 20. There is a passage in Marcus Antoninus, book IX, concerning the ready spirit of Christians toward death.

through him that loved us.

Not by our own powers, but by those given by GOD. See what we had above in V. 1, 2, 3.

These are again rashly restricted to the Claudian times and the persecutions of the Romans, when they look in general to all times and serve for the consolation of all. Nor is Psalm XLIV. 15 brought forward merely for the sake of example or comparison; but the fulfillment of that prophecy is taught, which sounds primarily concerning the Apostolic Church. Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, and other Holy Doctors, following the authority of the Apostle, have explained it thus: A conclusion is brought in here from the arguments already made, and the Apostle's certainty concerning eternal salvation is taught, because this hope could not be snatched from him by any calamities, nor could this good be intercepted: which, however, was not peculiar to the Apostle alone, nor did it arise from immediate revelation, as Papists, who command us to doubt of salvation, are accustomed to object, but was deduced from the arguments treated thus far: in which matter the Apostle sets himself as an example to all other reborn people.

Latin:

V. 37. ἀλλ’ ἐν τούτοις πᾶσιν ὑπερνικῶμεν.

Respondet interrogatis. Tantum abest, ut ista nos à DEI dilectione separent, ut illa omnia plus quam vinca- mus, id est, de iis triumphemus. Amat Paulus verba com- ponere cum ὑπὲρ, ut notavimus suprà V. 20. De Chri- stianorum prompto in mortem animo locus est apud Mar- cum Antoninum libro IX.

διὰ τοῦ ἀγαπήσαντος ἡμᾶς.

Non nostris, sed à DEO datis viribus. Vide, quæ habui- mus supra V. 1. 2. 3.

Temerè iterum hæc restringuntur ad tempora Claudiana, & persecutiones Romanorum: quùm in genere ad omnia spectent tempora, omnium- que solatio cedant. Nec exempli vel similitudi- nis tantùm causâ Psal. XLIV. 15. adducitur; sed complementum illius vaticinii docetur, quod de Apostolocâ Ecclesiâ imprimis sonat. Ambrosius, Hieronymus & Augustinus aliiqne S. Doctores, autoritatem sequuti Apostoli ita exposuêre: In- fertur autem hic συμπέρασμα ex argumentis jam factis, & docetur certitudo Apostoli de salute æternâ, quod nullis calamitatibus hæc spes ipsi eripi possit, aut hoc bonum intercipi: Quæ ve- rò non Apostoli solius propria erat, neque è reve- latione immediatâ oriebatur, ut Papistæ dubitare jubentes de salute, excipere solent, sed ex argu- mentis hactenus pertractatis deducebatur: quâ in re aliis renatis omnibus se in exemplum sistit Apostolus.

## 8:38
V. 38. For I am persuaded.

The Latin interpreter translates well: I am certain. Thus in Plato's Apology: πέπεισμαι ἐγὼ ἑκὼν μηδένα ἀδικῆσαι ἀνθρώπων. I am certain that I have willingly done injury to no man. Thus below in XIV. 14. οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι. Elsewhere it signifies opinion or hope.

that neither death.

That is, the fear of death.

nor life.

The hope of life.

nor angels.

Evil ones, of course, who are called angels of Satan 2 Cor. XII. 7.

nor principalities nor powers.

They are greater angels in the kingdom of Satan, who are called both principalities and authorities Eph. VI. 12. principality, authority, power 1 Cor. XV. 24. Just as also among the angels of light the more eminent are called by equal terms Ephes. I. 21. Coloss. II. 1. 16. But we have truly said that these names were taken from the Persian empire, under which the Hebrews had once lived. For principalities are רבני Dan. IV. 12. V. 2. powers שרין Esth. II. 18. just as authorities שלטני from שלט which is to have authority to the Chaldeans, from whence the Persians had taken many things, as we showed in Esther and Ezra. Thus principalities or rulers are ראשין Job XII. 24. XXXIX. 25. and in Ezekiel and Ezra: lordships or dominions משלות Dan. XI. 3. 4. 5. It is, however, the custom of all Oriental peoples to use abstract nouns for concrete ones.

things present nor things to come.

Neither the evils which we now feel, nor if any more grievous ones threaten, as certainly the most exquisite torments were threatening, crosses, flayings of the skin, burnings alive.

Latin:

V. 38. πέπεισμαι γὰρ.

Benè vertit Latinus interpres: Certus sum. Sic in Pla- tonis Apologia: πέπεισμαι ἐγὼ ἑκὼν μηδένα ἀδικῆσαι ἀν- θρώπων. Certus sum, me spontè nemini fecisse injuriam. Sic infra XIV. 14. οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι. Alibi opinionem aut spem significat.

ὅτι ὔτε θάνατος.

Id est, metus mortis.

ὔτε ζωὴ.

Spes vitæ.

ὔτε ἄγγελοι.

Mali scilicet, qui Angeli Satanæ dicuntur 2. Cor. XII. 7.

ὔτε ἀρχαὶ ὔτε δυνάμεις.

Sunt Angeli majores in regno Satanæ, qui appellantur & ἀρχαὶ & ἐξουσίαι Eph. VI. 12. ἀρχὴ, ἐξουσία, δύναμις 1. Cor. XV. 24. Sicut etiam inter Angelos lucis eminentiores pa- ribus vocabulis appellantur Ephes. I. 21. Coloss. II. 1. 16. Verè autem diximus nomina hæc sumpta ex imperio Per- sico, sub quo olim Hebræi vixerant. Nam ἀρχαὶ sunt רבי בני Dan. IV. 12. V. 2. δυνάμεις שרין Efth. II. 18. sicut ἐξουσίαι שלטני à שלט quod ἐξουσιάζω Chaldæis, unde multa sumserant Persæ, ut ad Estherem & ad Esdram osten- dimus. Sic ἀρχαὶ sive ἄρχοντες sunt ראשין Job. XII. 24. XXXIX. 25. & apud Ezechielem & Esdram: κυριότητες sive κυρείαι משלות Dan. XI. 3. 4. 5. Est autem omnium po- pulorum Orientalium abstracta usurpare pro concretis.

ἐνεστῶτα ὔτε μέλλοντα.

Nec quæ nunc sentimus mala, nec si qua graviora im- minent, ut certè imminebant tormenta exquisitissima, cru- ces, cutis detractiones, vivicomburia.

## 8:39
V. 39. nor height.

The hope of honors; you have height for honors in the Greek of Job XXII. 14.

nor depth.

Fear of ignominy. He rightly placed these in the last position, to which often succumb even those who despise death.

nor any other creature.

Or any other thing. For even those things which are not substances are said to be created, as can be seen in the son of Sirach 11:16, 39:34, 41:11. will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Having spoken before of Christ's love for us, he adds the love of God for us, which Christ has reconciled for us.

The very weight of the words and the matters themselves testify that these things bring not merely an opinion or moral certainty alone, but a divine certainty and hope, superior to every exception. Nor is it merely the fear of death that is indicated, but death itself: namely, that we cannot be separated even by death from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus: nor by ζωὴν is only the hope of life indicated, but life itself, which, however happy it may be, can in no way separate us from GOD: nor by ἐνεστῶτα καὶ μέλλοντα are only calamities indicated, but all things in general, whatever they may be, whether present, or imminent and future: nor finally by ὕψωμα, καὶ βάθος are the hope of honors and the fear of ignominy indicated; but the highest honors themselves, and extreme ignominy, indeed whatever is highest, whatever is lowest, are understood. The interlinear gloss understands by height the elevation of Satan, by depth the hell which Satan threatens. That by principalities and powers different choirs of evil angels are understood is less clear: since angels have already been named; from whom ἀρχαὶ καὶ δυνάμεις are placed disjunctively, whence principalities and powers are understood indefinitely by others. Philippus understands by ἀρχὰς tyrants, by δυνάμεις the whole hosts of persecutors; by height the wisdom of heretics and other impious men; by depth the common errors of the mob. Therefore, the Apostle confirms us concerning the certainty of divine grace. For he declares that there is nothing in the whole world by which the love of GOD can be subverted for the pious, or rendered doubtful and uncertain. Therefore, the world will cease to be what it is before anything of all things can exclude the pious and believers from the love of GOD. From which it follows how certainly the pious know that this world still endures, of which they themselves are even now a part: that they themselves can be so certain of the grace and love of GOD, that to doubt it would be nothing other than to wonder whether the world still endures: as our blessed Mylius has it here on page 309. But Grotius is mistaken in his interpretation, with a preconceived opinion, as if the discourse were about the times of the Apostle, and these things were written for consolation only for those times, when rather the Apostle wished to make all the reborn certain by his own example, concerning future glory, so that they might not doubt it in the least, or think that that hope and promised inheritance could be subverted for them by anything. It is pleasing to append the paraphrase of Antonius Marinarus, a Carmelite, in the second Oration at the Council of Trent itself, where the dogma was sanctioned concerning the uncertainty of grace, held against this sanction handed down in the History. of the Council of Trent by Petrus Suavis: What is it that anyone should speak to me of diffidence? Who shall separate me from the charity and trust of my GOD, who contains all things by His power, rules all things by His command, moderates all things by His wisdom, embraces all things with His mind, bends all things to His will wherever He pleases, and binds them wherever He pleases, whose charity toward me was so great that He handed over the only Son, whom He loved uniquely, to the horrible cross, so that I might be sprinkled and redeemed by His blood, namely that He Himself might be a Father to me, and Christ a brother. But what greater love or solicitude is there than that of a Father toward a son, especially of that Father who is as much more clement than others as He is more sublime? Wherefore neither the flatteries of that age, nor the allurements of this flesh, nor those thunderbolts of Satan, nor the frauds of heretics, nor the delights of friends, nor the prayers of those near to me, nor the piety of parents, nor the fury of peoples, nor the cruelty of tyrants, whether they wish to terrify with threats, or deprive of fortunes, or banish into exile, or destroy by any kind of death, shall ever at any time tear me away from God the Best and Greatest, from the omnipotent Lord, from the most indulgent Father, if the sky should fall, if the earth should vanish, if the world should tumble headlong, I shall be erect in Him: if an angel from heaven should contend to persuade me otherwise, I shall say to him anathema. O happy trust of the Christian heart! O blessed piety of the Evangelical heart! O secure trust of the Christian mind! which commits vows, counsels, studies, efforts, duties, diligence, industry, fortunes, in every place, at every time, in all things, to the one God, who makes no one who trusts in Him vain. Whence Alphonsus de Castro confessed in book VII, on heresies, under the word Grace: that many most learned men have asserted the certainty of faith concerning present grace, and that the doctrine concerning the uncertainty of grace did not please all the Fathers of the Synod of Trent, since many of them wished to defend the certainty of salvation. And these things also to Chapter VIII.

Latin:

V. 39. ὔτε ὕψωμα.

Spes honorum ὕψωμα pro honoribus habes in Græco Job. XXII. 14.

ὔτε βάθος.

Metus ignominiæ. Meritò postremo loco hæc posuit, quibus succumbunt sæpè etiam, qui mortem contemnunt.

ὔτε τις κτίσις ἑτέρα.

Aut res ulla alia. Nam etiam, quæ substantiæ non sunt, dicuntur ἐκτίσθαι, ut videre est apud Sirachiden XI. 16. XXXIX. 34. XLI. 11. δυνήσεται ἡμᾶς χωρίσαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.

Locutus ante de Christi in nos amore 35. addit & Dei in nos amorem, quem nobis conciliavit Christus.

Non opinionem tantùm aut certitudinem solum moralem, sed divinam, omnique exceptione su- periorem certitudinem & spem hæc inferre ipsa momenta verborum, & rerum testantur. Nec verò metus tantùm mortis, sed ipsa mors indicatur: quod scil. ne morte quidem separari à dilectione DEI possimus, quæ est in Christo Jesu: nec per ζωὴν tantùm spes vitæ, sed vita ipsa, quæ quantum- vis felicissima, minimè nos à DEO separare potest: nec per ἐνεστῶτα καὶ μέλλοντα solùm calamitates, sed omnia in genere, quæcunque tandem illa fue- rint, seu præsentia, seu imminentia & futura: nec denique per ὕψωμα, καὶ βάθος spes honorum, & metus ignominiæ; sed honores ipsi summi, & igno- minia extrema, imò quicquid est summi, quic- quid imi intelliguntur. Glossa interlinearis per altitudinem elevationem Satanæ, per profundita- tem infernum, quem minatur Satanas, intelligit. Per principatus & virtutes diversos Angelorum malorum choros intelligi minùs luculentum est: siquidem Angeli jam nominati fuerint: à quibus disjunctivè ponuntur ἀρχαὶ καὶ δυνάμεις, unde prin- cipatus & virtutes indefinitè ab aliis intelligun- tur. Philippus per ἀρχὰς tyrannos, per δυνάμεις agmina tota persequentium; per altitudinem sapi- entiam hæreticorum & aliorum impiorum: per profunditatem communes vulgi errores intelligit. De divinæ ergò gratiæ certitudine confirmat nos Apostolus. Nihil enim in universo mundo esse pro- nunciat, quo interverti piis, aut dubia atque incerta effici dilectio DEI queat. Prius ergo mundus desi- net esse quod est, quàm à dilectione DEI rerum o- mnium quicquam pios & credentes excludere queat. Ex quo id consequens est, quàm certò mundum istum adhuc durare norunt pii, cujus ipsi etiamnum ali- quactiam pars sunt: tàm certos ipsos esse de gratia & dilectione DEI posse, ut de ea dubitare, nihil aliud sit, quam utrum mundus etiamnum duret, ambigere: ut hic habet B. Mylius noster pag. 309. Fallitur autem Grotius in interpretamento suo, præconceptâ opinione, qs. de temporibus Apostoli sermo sit, & calamitatibus solum illorum tempo- rum hæc in solatium scripta sint, quùm potiùs re- natos omnes certos reddere suo ipsius exemplo voluerit Apostolus, de futura gloria, ne ullate- nus de ea dubitent, aut spem illam, & promissam hæreditatem ullâ re sibi interverti posse censeant. Subjungere placet paraphrasin Antonii Marina- rii, Carmelitæ, in secunda Oratione in ipso Con- cilio Tridentino, quo sancitum dogma fuit de in- certitudine gratiæ habitâ contra hanc sanctionem traditam in Histor. Concil. Trident. Petri Suavis: Quid est, quod de diffidentia mihi loquatur aliquis? Quis me separabit à charitate & fiducia DEI mei, qui sua potentia omnia continet, suo imperio omnia regit, sua sapientia omnia moderatur, sua mente omnia complectitur, suo arbitrio omnia flectit quo libet, & quo libet, constringit, cujus tanta fuit erga me charitas, ut unicum, quem unicè diligebat fili- um, ad horribilem tradiderit crucem, quo essem il- lius sanguine aspersus atque redemptus, nempe ut ipse mihi sit Pater, & Christus frater. Quæ autem ma- jor aut dilectio aut sollicitudo, quàm Patris erga filium, præsertim ejus Patris, qui tantò est aliis cle- mentior, quantò sublimior? quamobrem neq; ejus seculi blanditiæ, neq; hujus carnis illecebræ, neque illa Satanæ fulmina, neque hæreticorum fraudes, neque amicorum deliciæ, neque necessariorum preces, neque parentum pietas, neque populorum furor, neœ́ tyrannorum crudelitas, seu minis perterrere, seu fortunis privare, seu in exilium ablegare, seu quolibet mortis genere perdere voluerint, à Deo Opt. Max. à Domino omnipotente, à Patre indulgentissimo, ullo unquam tempore me divellent, si cœlum ruat, si terra evanescat, si orbis illabatur præceps, ego in eum erectus ero: si angelus de cœlo aliud mihi persuadere contendat, dicam ei anathema. ô felicem Christiani pectoris fiduciam! ô beatam Evangelici pectoris pietatem! ô securam Christianæ mentis fiduciam! quæ vota, quæ consilia, quæ studia, conatus, officia, diligentiam, industriam, fortunas, omni loco, omni tempore, omnibus in rebus, uni Deo committit, qui neminem in se confidentem, vanum facit. Unde fassus est Alphonsus de Castro l. VII. ad hæres. voce Gratia: multos viros doctissimos certitudinem fidei de præsente gratia adstruxisse, & doctrinam de incertitudine gratiæ non placuisse omnibus Synodi Tridentinæ Patribus, siquidem multi eorum certitudinem salutis defendere voluerint. Atque hæc etiam ad VIII. Caput.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

MEMBER II. SPECIAL.

Wherein it is taught that the Apostolic doctrine concerning justification by faith in Christ shines forth from the very rejection of the Jews and the salvation of the Gentiles.

After the general treatment of justification by faith in Christ, and its consequences, such as the pursuit of holiness and the assurance of salvation, concerning which the Apostle asserted the righteousness of faith against the calumnies of adversaries and the scruples of temptations: now the Apostle discourses specifically on the rejection of the majority of the Jews, in such a way as to vindicate his doctrine: For since the Jews argued that it followed from the Pauline doctrine that the Jewish people were for the most part rejected by God and excluded from the hope of salvation, inasmuch as they pursued the righteousness of the law, but did not at all accept the righteousness handed down by the Apostle: If, however, the Jewish people were for the most part and almost entirely rejected, the divine promise would be in jeopardy: the Apostle is engaged in this: to show that no other way of salvation is now open to the Gentiles than that which was once proposed to the Jews, but which is now neglected by them, and to teach that the Word of God is by no means made void, but rather that the truth of the promises of grace is confirmed, when those from among the Jews are rejected who seek righteousness not by faith, but by the law, while the Gentiles, embracing the righteousness of faith, obtain salvation. He vindicates, moreover, primarily both the Mercy and the Justice of God concerning the rejection of the Jews and the salvation of the Gentiles in chapter IX, which pertains to the principal efficient cause of justification. Then, indeed, he also asserts concerning this same righteousness of Christ as the meritorious and formal cause in chapter X. Finally, the organic cause, faith, apprehending the grace of God and the righteousness of Christ, in chapter XI.

SUBJECTION I. Vindicating the truth of the promises of grace, and in them the equity of both divine justice and mercy.

CHAPTER IX.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle first testifies to his extreme sorrow on account of the rejection of most of the Jews, as being his brethren according to the flesh, and enriched by GOD with many axioms; then he asserts the truth of the promises of grace, even though they have been rejected, since the enjoyment of them pertains not to those who pursue the righteousness of the law, but to those who accept the promises by faith—such as were not so much the Israelites anymore, as the Gentiles: which he illustrates with types from the house of Abraham and Isaac, so that it may be clear who are the children of the promise: thence he demonstrates from divine oracles against the Jews the equity of the purpose concerning justifying and saving men not by works, but through faith in Christ, not so much from the most free right of GOD, as from the most wholesome tempering of divine justice and mercy: which shines forth even in the very extreme hardening, where the great patience of GOD in the vessels of wrath, and the riches of grace in the vessels of glory, shine forth, and both the adoption of the Gentiles and the preservation of the remnant of Israel are purely of grace, and the Gentiles attain the righteousness of faith only out of grace, whereas the Jews, pursuing the righteousness of the law, stumble against Christ as a stone of offense, and thus by no means attain true righteousness.

There are four parts: I. Παθητικὴ, testifying to the Apostle’s sadness and grief over the anathema of his Israelite brethren, up to v. 6. II. Διδακτικὴ, illustrating by types the truth of the promises of grace, which only the children of the promise enjoy through faith, up to v. 13. III. Ἀπολογητικὴ, vindicating the equity of GOD’S purpose in showing mercy to the faithful and reprobating and hardening the unfaithful, showing in the former the riches of grace, and in the latter the great patience of GOD, up to v. 25. IV. Βεβαιωτικὴ, further confirming from the Scriptures the grace of GOD in the adoption of the Gentiles and justification through faith in Christ: by which He also preserves a holy seed from the Israelites, while the rest seek the righteousness of the law in vain.

PART I. OF CHAPTER IX. Pathetic, declaring the sadness and sorrow of the Apostle concerning the reprobate Jews.

Vers. 1. I speak the truth in Christ.

When the Apostle had said and proven with great arguments that no one is so pleasing to GOD that He would wish to give him the highest good, unless he be endowed with the Spirit of GOD, and that God does not give this Spirit except to the justified, that is, to those cleansed in heart—which at this time can happen to no one except through faith in Jesus Christ, which was manifest from the very conspicuous gifts of the Spirit, which did not occur except to those believing in Jesus—he saw that the Jews would easily conclude what followed from this, namely, that the Jewish people considered for the most part were no longer the people of GOD, but that the people of GOD was the Christian Church, consisting for the greatest part not of Jews, but of foreigners who had been idolaters. Both of which things vehemently conflicted with those opinions which the Jews had drawn from their Masters, that the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob would always hold the chief place before God, and that although they committed many sins, God would pardon them, both because of the virtues of their ancestors and because of their profession of the true Religion. Intending to answer these, he prepares to show that God never so bound Himself to the descendants of the Patriarchs that He did not retain for Himself the liberty of punishing the contumacious, and of pardoning and bestowing benefits upon others, even if they were guilty, and that this was signified by certain ancient figures and furthermore by examples and sayings. Whatever it may appear that God is doing, such as this matter of the gifts of the Spirit bestowed upon the Church, but taken away from the multitude of the Jews, that is to be held as right, and it is of great rashness to dispute against it. God owes the reasons for His benefits and mercy to no one. When he had crushed their audacity with these prefaces; he then shows that no way could have been entered upon by GOD, which would be either more glorious to Himself, or more useful to the human race. Moreover, the whole treatment, which is divided into the three chapters that will now follow, is rather obscure, not only for reasons common to this whole epistle, about which we have spoken in the Prolegomena to this epistle, but also because, by showing himself fair in wondrous ways to Jews and Gentiles, he mixes sweet things with bitter, and bitter with sweet, and makes unobserved transitions from these to those, and from those to these, and often loves to hint more than to say. And first, because, having been often treated badly by the Jews, while on the contrary held in the highest honor among the Christians called from the Gentiles, it could be believed that he was either hostile to the former or more inclined toward the latter, he removes this suspicion far from himself, and indeed by employing an oath by Christ, which ought to be held of no less account in the new covenant than the oaths made by God in the old covenant, because God has now handed over all power of ruling and protecting the Church to Christ. I speak the truth in Christ, that is, by Christ. A similar expression is in Dan. XII. 7. ὤμοσεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα; Jerem. V. 7. ὤμνυον ἐν τοῖς οὐκ οὖσι θεοῖς. And μαρτύρομαι ἐν κυρίῳ Eph. V. 17. Paul calls upon GOD and Christ together as witnesses 1. Tim. V. 21.

I do not lie.

I do not speak for the sake of favor, as flatterers are accustomed to do.

My conscience bearing witness with me.

Συμμαρτυρύσης is the same as μαρτυρύσης, as we said II. 15. VIII. 16. It is commonly said: Conscience is a thousand witnesses.

in the Holy Spirit.

Not that conscience of the Gentiles, which now accuses them, now excuses them, but the conscience which is in the Holy Spirit, that is, is ruled by the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

MEMBRUM II. SPECIALE.

Quo doctrinam Apostolicam de justificatione per fidem in Christum elucere ex ipsâ Judæorum plerorumœ́ rejectione gentiumœ́ salvatione, docetur.

Postquam in genere de justificatione per fidem in Christum, ejusque consequentibus, ut putà studio sanctitatis, & certitudine salutis, circa quæ Apostolus justitiam fidei adversus calumnias adversariorum & scrupulos tentationum asseruit, actum est: jam in specie de Judæorum plerorumque rejectione ita disserit Apostolus, ut suam doctrinam vindicet: Quum enim argu- erent Judæi, ex Paulina doctrina sequi, populum Judaicũ secundùm maxi- mam partem à Deo rejectũ, & à salu- tis spe exclusum, utpote qui legis justi- tiam sectabatur, justitiam verò ab Aposto- lo traditam minimè suscipiebat: Si autem populus Judaicus maximam partem & propemodum totus rejectus sit, periclita- ri divinam promissionem: Apostolus in eo est: ut non aliam salutis viam jam pa- tere gentibus, quam quæ olim proposita fuit Judæis, quæ verò nunc ab his postha- beatur, ostendat, Verbumque Dei minimè irritum fieri doceat, sed veritatem pro- missionum gratiæ potius confirmari, cum illi ex Judæis rejiciuntur, qui non ex fide, sed ex lege justitiam quærunt, gentes au- tem justitiam fidei amplectentes salutem consequuntur. Vindicat autem imprimis Dei tùm Misericordiam, tùm Justitiam circa Judæorum rejectionem, genti- umque salvationem c. IX. quæ ad cau- sam efficientem principalem justifica- tionis pertinet. Deinde verò adserit etiam circa eandē justitiam Christi ceu causam meritoriam & formalem c X. Deniq; causam organicam fidem gratiam Dei & justitiã Christi apprehendentem c. XI,

SUBJECTIO I. Promissionum gratiæ veritatem, & in iisdem divinæ tùm justitiæ, tùm misericordiæ æquitatem vindicans.

CAPUT IX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

„ Testatur Apostolus primum dolorem sum- „ mum ob Judæorum plerorumque rejectionem, „ utpote fratrum secundum carnem, & multis „ axiomatibus à DEO ditatorum, tùm verò asse- „ rit promissionum gratiæ veritatem, etsi illi rejecti „ sunt, quandoquidem illarum fruitio non eos, qui „ justitiam legis sectantur, sed qui fide promissio- „ nes acceptant, quales non tàm Israëlitæ amplius „ erant, quam gentes, attineat: quod typis è domo „ Abrahæ & Isaaci illustrat, ut qui filii promissio- „ nis sint, constet: inde æquitatem propositi de ju- „ stificandis & salvandis hominibus non ex operi- „ bus, sed per fidem in Christum, non tàm è jure „ DEI liberrimo, quàm è temperamento justitiæ & „ misericordiæ divinæ saluberrimo ex oraculis di- „ vinis adversùs Judæos demonstrat: quæ in ipsa „ etiam extrema induratione effulgeat, ubi magna „ DEI patientia in vasis ignominiæ, divitiæ verò „ gratiæ in vasis gloriæ elucescunt, & tùm adoptio „ gentium, tùm sospitatio reliquiarum Israëlis merè „ gratuita est, gentesque nonnisi ex gratiâ justitiam „ fidei assequuntur, quum Judæi justitiam legis se- „ ctantes in Christum ceu lapidem offensionis im- „ pingant, adeoque veram justitiam haudquaquam „ consequantur.

PArtes quatuor sunt: I. Παθητικὴ, tristitiam & dolorem Apostoli de Israëlitarum fratrum anathemate testans usque ad v. 6. II. Διδακτικὴ, ve- ritatem promissionum gratiæ, quibus solum fruun- tur filii promissionis, per fidem, typis illustrans, usque ad v. 13. III. Ἀπολογητικὴ, æquitatem propo- siti DEI fidelibus misericordiam exhibentis, infi- deles reprobantis, & indurantis vindicans, osten- dens in his divitias gratiæ, in illis verò magnam DEI patientiam usque ad v. 25. IV. Βεβαιωτικὴ, è Scripturis ulteriùs confirmans DEI gratiam in adoptione gentium & justificatione per fidem in Christum: quâ etiam sanctum semen ex Israëlitis servat, cæteris frustrà justitiam legis sectantibus.

PARS I. CAPITIS IX. Παθητικὴ, Tristitiam & dolorem Apostoli de reprobatis Judæis declarans.

Vers. 1. Ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν χρισῷ.

Cum dixisset & magnis argumentis evicisset Apostolus, neminem DEO ita placere, ut ei summum bonum dare velit, nisi qui Spiritu DEI donatus sit, hunc autem Spiri- tum non dare Deum nisi justificatis, id est, corde munda- tis, quod hoc quidem tempore nemini contingere potest, nisi per fidem in Jesum Christum, quod manifestum erat ex ipsis conspicuis Spiritus donis, quæ non contingebant nisi in Jesum credentibus; videbat facilè collecturos Ju- dæos quod hinc sequebatur, nempe populum Judaicum consideratum ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ non ultra esse populum DEI, sed populum DEI esse Ecclesiam Christianam constantem maxima sui parte non ex Judæis, sed ex alienigenis, qui ido- lolatræ fuissent. Quorum utrumque vehementer pugna- bat cum iis opinionibus, quas Judæi ex Magistris suis hau- serant, Posteros Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi semper præci- puo apud Deum loco fore, & quamvis multa delinque- rent, Deum ista condonaturum, tùm ob majorum virtutes, tùm ob professionem veræ Religionis. His responsurus, parat ostendere Deum nunquam ita se adstrinxisse posteris Patriarcharum, ut non libertatem sibi retineret puniendi contumaces, & aliis quamvis sontibus ignoscendi ac bene- faciendi, idque figuris etiam quibusdam antiquis ac præ- terea exemplis dictisque significatum. Quidquid Deum facere appareat, quale hoc est de donis Spiritus collatis in Ecclesiam, ablatis verò à multitudine Judæorum, id pro re- cto habendum, magnæque esse temeritatis contra id dispu- tare. Beneficiorum suorum & miserationis rationes Deum debere nemini. His præfationibus cùm audaciam contu- disset; ostendit deinde, non potuisse à DEO ullam iniri viam, quæ aut ipsi esset gloriosior, aut humano generi uti- lior. Est autem tota tractatio, quæ in tria, quæ nunc se- quentur, capita divisa est, obscurior, non modò ob causas toti huic epistolæ communes, de quibus in Prolegomenis ad hanc epistolam egimus, verùm etiam quia miris modis æ- quum se præbens Judæis & gentibus, amaris dulcia, dulci- bus amara miscet, & ab his ad illa, ab illis ad hæc inobser- vatos facit transitus, ac sæpè amat plus innuere, quàm dice- re. Ac primùm, quia sæpè malè tractatus à Judæis, contra in summo honore habitus apud Christianos è gentibus vo- catos, credi poterat, aut infensus illis, aut in hos propensior, suspicionem hanc longè à se amolitur, & quidem jurejuran- do adhibito per Christum, quod non minoris haberi debet in novo fœdere, quam juramenta in veteri fœdere per Deum facta, quia Deus omnem jam potestatem Ecclesiæ regendæ ac tuendæ Christo tradidit. Veritatem dico in Christo, id est, per Christum. Similis locutio Dan. XII. 7. ὤμοσεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα; Jerem. V. 7. ὤμνυον ἐν τοῖς οὐκ οὖσι θεοῖς. Et μαρτύρομαι ἐν κυρίῳ Eph. V. 17. DEUM simul & Christum testes advocat Paulus 1. Tim. V. 21.

ὀὐ ψεύδομαι.

Non loquor in gratiam, ut aretalogi solent.

Συμμαρτυρύσης μοι τῆς συνειδήσεώς με.

Συμμαρτυρύσης idem est, quod μαρτυρύσης, ut diximus II. 15. VIII. 16. Dici vulgò solet: Conscientia mille testes.

ἐν πνέυματι ἁγίῳ.

Non illa gentium conscientia, quæ ipsas modò accusat, modò excusat, sed conscientia, quæ est in Spiritu Sancto, id est, per Spiritum Sanctum regitur.

## 9:2
V. 2. that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.

These latter words are from Ps. XIII. 3. יגון בלבבי יומם He says that it grieves him exceedingly that the greatest and most numerous of the Jews were outside the state of true righteousness and the divine Spirit and eternal salvation.

He attributes to the Apostle a mind here that is utterly foreign and contrary to the Holy Scriptures. 1. The Apostle did not argue that eternal life is not granted unless to those gifted with the Spirit of GOD, and that these are not such unless they have been cleansed in heart, that is, sanctified: but he dealt first with justification situated in the remission of sins, which is obtained through faith in Christ, then with the consequent sanctification of the same, and the pursuit of holiness, and finally with the certainty of the salvation of the justified: but the Apostle neither established justification in the purging and sanctification of the heart, nor taught that the Holy Spirit is given after such a cleansing of the heart, whether our Apostle or any other θεόπνευστος Doctor. Furthermore, that justification happens only at this time through faith in Christ is repugnant to the Scriptures: which know of only one way and method of justification and salvation, which is through faith in Christ, c. III. 16. XIV. 6. Acts IV. 12. c. X. 43. Rom. III. IV. V. which even now in the rejection of the Jews and the adoption of the Gentiles appears in these very chapters, as the Apostle teaches of set purpose, namely in this place, ch. X. and XI. Thirdly, the Apostle made no mention in the preceding treatment of the conspicuous gifts of the Holy Spirit: much less did he leave it to be gathered from the bestowal of the same that the Jewish people for the most part are no longer the people of GOD: but rather, while intimating the reprobation of the Jews not without sorrow, he taught that the same neither conflicts with the truth of the promises, and further confirmed this doctrine concerning gratuitous justification through faith in Christ, both because he set forth the supreme cause, the divine justice tempered with Mercy, especially in ch. IX., and the meritorious and formal cause, the righteousness of Christ proposed in the Gospel, in ch. X.

ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE.

as well as the organic cause of faith, to which the righteousness of Christ is imputed: on account of the lack of which the unbelieving Jews are reprobated in ch. XI, just as the riches of mercy and the unsearchable abysses of the judgments of GOD are celebrated, and to God alone be glory: toward the end of ch. XI. Fourthly, therefore, he does not assert the freedom of GOD in punishing the contumacious and in pardoning and benefiting others, however guilty, but the Apostle so defends the truth of the divine promises, concerning the reprobation of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, that he demonstrates the righteousness of GOD shining forth together with mercy from the same, and by no means endangered.

5. Fifthly, concerning the gifts of the Spirit bestowed upon the Church, but taken away from the multitude of the Jews, nothing appears here; but the divine mercy and justice concerning the calling and justification of both Jews and Gentiles is vindicated, so that gratuitous justification through faith in Christ may be established. Which is the proper and principal theme of the Apostolic Didactic treatment. 6. Sixthly, although it is of great rashness, with the Apostle as author, to dispute against the economy of grace and divine justice, he does not teach that God uses his absolute right, but that he acts in such a way that his mercy shines forth everywhere no less than his justice. 7. Seventhly, it is no wonder to accuse this whole treatment of chapters IX, X, and XI of obscurity. Hugo, since he errs at the very threshold and scope of the Apostolic disputation, which is to establish everywhere gratuitous justification through faith in Christ, even in the fact that the Jews are excluded from salvation and that the Gentiles are led by GOD to salvation. Nor indeed, seventhly, does the Apostle remove the suspicion of either hatred toward those or excessive love toward these, whether because he was often treated badly by the Jews or because he was held in the highest honor among the Christians called from the Gentiles, but he testifies to his sadness out of pious συμπαθείᾳ [sympathy] that they have become ἀνάθεμα [anathema], so that he might the more gain some; but concerning the Gentiles, who were asserted into the place of the Jews by the just judgment of GOD, he discourses, deducing all things from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in order to make them jealous of a non-people and lead them to faith in Christ, so that once that unique way of salvation is known, they might not neglect to enter it: since those who have fallen through unbelief can in turn be grafted in, warning also the Gentiles not to be proud because of the grace shown, lest they too be cut off. By an oath, moreover, he testifies to the affection of pain and sadness (as being in a matter far most grave and deeply incredible) that he himself even wishes to become ἀνάθεμα ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ [anathema from Christ] for his brethren according to the flesh, so that he might move their bowels, whereby he might both find faith, and, having recognized such an affection of love in the Apostle of Christ, they might be induced to faith in Christ, convinced by the clear testimonies of the sacred writings. In the name of Christ, however, whose Apostle he professes himself to be, he lays down an oath, as one to whom, as GOD blessed above all things forever, this truly divine honor is owed, that one must swear in his name: by no means, however, is that distinction to be admitted here, that in the Old Testament oaths were made by God, not by the Son of God; but in the New, by the Son of GOD: for this one is the same GOD with the Father, John X. 30, and is to be honored as the Father is honored, John V. 23, and in his name every tongue of theirs ought to swear, and to him the knees of all ought to bow, as to the one true GOD, outside of whom there is no other, as many as ever have been, are, or shall be, namely, whoever shall one day appear before his tribunal on the pantocritic day, Is. XLV. 22, 23, Rom.

XII. 11. Phil. II. 10. Nor is the concession of all power for the sake of ruling and protecting the Church the cause and reason for religious worship, of an oath to be performed in the name of Christ, but the true and supreme Deity or divine nature, since this worship and honor is owed to none but the true and supreme GOD. Exod. XXII. 11. Deut. VI. 13. X. 20. Josh. XXIII. 7. Is. XIX. 18. LXV. 16. Jer. IV. 2. V. 2. 7. XII. 16. Cf. Gen. XI. 23. XXIV. 12. Josh. II. 12. 1 Sam. XXIV. 22. Ps. LXIII. 12. Dan. XII. 7. Zeph. I. 5. Zech. V. 4. Heb. VI. 16. Rev. X. 5. Nor indeed for any other reason was force and power over the Church and over all things that are in heaven and on earth in time granted to Christ according to his human nature, or should religious worship be deferred to him, than because the human nature was assumed into the very hypostasis of the Son of GOD, by the power of which προσλήψεως [assumption] and hypostasis of the Son of GOD and of his infinite majesty and glory, the very human nature of Christ was truly made a participant: which those who deny pass over into the camp of Nestorius. And therefore from this Apostolic testimony, since he appeals both to Christ and to the Holy Spirit as a witness καρδιογνώστην [knower of hearts] and avenger of perjury, the ancient Doctors of the Church were accustomed to demonstrate the same Deity of both the Son and the Holy Spirit with the Father against the Arians and the Pneumatomachians. The Apostle, intending to testify to his supreme pain, manifests not only λύπην [grief] or sadness, but λύπην μεγάλην [great grief], and not only that, but ὀδύνην [anguish], by which word the pains of those in labor and the most exquisite infernal pains are wont to be expressed, and the same ἀδιάλειπτον [unceasing], having no intermission, no end, or constant and perpetual, and that in his HEART, opening up the innermost recesses of his soul and the bowels of his heart to them. He adds this, moreover, because it would be most incredible, unless the Apostle were testifying to it in Christ, with his conscience attesting to him in the Holy Spirit, that is, confirming it by an oath laid down in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Latin:

V. 2. ὅτι λύπη μοι ἐστὶ μεγάλη καὶ ἀδιάλειπτος ὀδύνη τῇ καρδίᾳ με.

Hæc posteriora sunt ex Ps. XIII. 3. יגון בלבבי יומם Dicit summè sibi dolere, quod Judæorum maximi & pluri- mi erant extra statum veræ justitiæ & divini Spiritus ac sa- lutis æternæ.

Prorsus alienam hîc, & S. literis adversam af- fingit mentem Apostolo. 1. Non id egit Aposto- lus, quod vita æterna non concedatur nisi Spiritu DEI donatis, hi autem non sint, nisi corde mun- dati, id est, sanctificati sint: sed primùm de justi- ficatione sità in peccatorum remissione, quæ per fidem in Christum obtinetur, tùm de consequenti ejusdem sanctificatione, & sanctitatis studio, ac denique de certitudine salutis justificatorum egit: neutiquam verò vel justificationem in cordis pur- gatione & sanctificatione constituit, vel Spiritum S. post ejusmodi mundationem cordis dari docuit sive Apostolus noster, sive quisquam alius Doctor θεόπνευστος. Deinde hoc solum tempore per fidem in Christum justificationem contingere, Scri- pturæ repugnat: quæ nonnisi unicam justificatio- nis & salutis viam & rationem novit, quæ est per fidem in Christum, c. III. 16. XIV. 6. Actor. IV. 12. c. X. 43. Rom. III. IV. V. quam etiamnum in Ju- dæorum rejectione & gentium adoptione appa- rere his ipsis capp. ex instituto docet Apostolus nimirum h. l. c. X. & XI. Tertiò de conspicuis Spi- ritûs S. donis nullam in superiori tractatione men- tionem fecit Apostolus: nedum ex eorundem do- natione colligendum reliquit, Judaicum populum ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ non ultra esse DEI populum: sed po- tiùs Judæorum reprobationem non sine dolore innuens, eandem neque pugnare cum veritate promissionum, & confirmare ulterius hanc de gratuità per fidem in Christum justificatione do- cuit, tùm quia causam supremam, justitiam di- vinam Misericordià temperatam, imprimis c. IX. tùm quà causam meritoriam & formalem Chri- sti justitiam in Evangelio propositam, cap. X.

ANNOTATA AD EPIST.

tùm quà causam organicam fidem, cui imputatur Christi justitia : ob cujus defectum Judæi increduli reprobantur c. XI. ut & divitiæ misericordiæ, & abyssi judiciorum DEI imperscrutabiles celebran- tur, Deoq; uni sit gloria : sub finem cap. XI. Quar- 4. tò non ergò libertatem DEI in puniendis contu- macibus, & aliis quamvis sontibus ignoscendi ac benefaciendi asserit, sed veritatem promissionum divinarum ita tuetur, circa reprobationem Judæ- orum & vocationem gentium Apostolus, ut justi- tiam DEI unà cum misericordia effulgere ex eadem, nullatenùs verò periclitari demonstret.

5. Quintò, de donis Spiritûs collatis in Ecclesiam, abla- tis verò à multitudine Judæorum hic nihil compa- ret, Misericordia verò & justitia divina circa vo- cationem & justificationem cùm Judæorum, tùm gentium vindicatur, ut justificatio gratuita per fi- dem in Christum statuminetur. Quod est pro- prium & principale tractationis Apostolicæ Dida- 6. cticæ thema. Sextò quanquam temeritatis magnæ, Apostolo Autore, sit disputare contra œconomiam gratiæ, & justitiæ divinæ, non tamen absoluto jure suo uti Deum docet, sed ita agere, ut undiquaque non minùs misericordia ejus effulgeat, quàm ju- 7. stitia. Septimò non mirum est obscuritatis arguere totam hanc tractationem IX. X. XI. Hugonem, quùm in ipso limine & scopo Apostolicæ disputa- tionis aberret, qui est stabilire undiquaque gra- tuitam per fidem in Christum justificationem et- iam in eo, quod Judæi à salute excludantur, quod- que gentes ad salutem à DEO perducantur. Nec verò septimò Apostolus, sive quod malè à Judæis sæpius tractatus, sive quod apud Christianos è gen- tibus vocatos summo in honore habitus suspicio- nem seu odii in illis seu amoris nimii in hos amo- litur, sed Judæis è pia συμπαθείᾳ tristitiam, quod ἀνάθεμα facti sint, testatur, ut eò magis nonnul- los lucrifaciat; de gentibus verò in locum Judæo- rum justo DEI judicio adsertis, in horum impri- mis gratiam è Scripturis Vet. Test. omnia dedu- cens differit, ut eos zelare faciat in non populo & ad fidem in Christum perducat, quo unicà illa sa- lutis viâ cognitâ eam inire non negligant: quùm exsisi per incredulitatem vicissim inseri possint, præmonens etiam gentes, ne ob gratiam exhibi- tam superbiant, ne & ipsæ exscindantur. Jurejuran- do autem testatur doloris & tristitiæ affectum, (ut- pote in re longè gravissimâ, & penitùs incredibili ) quod vel ipse velit ἀνάθεμα fieri ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ pro fratribus secundùm carnem, ut viscera eorum commoveat, quo & fidem inveniat, & cognito tanto amoris affectu in Apostolo Christi, ad fi- dem in Christum, convicti sacrarum literarum lu- culentis testimoniis inducantur. In Christi autem nomine, cujus Apostolum se profitetur, juramen- tum deponit, utpote cui ceu DEO super omnia benedicto in secula hunc honorem verè divinum deberi, ut in nomine ejus jurandum sit, testatur : neutiquam verò hic discrimē illud admittendum, quod in Vet. Test. juramenta per Deum facta sint, non per Filium Dei; in Novo autem per Filium DEI: Hic enim idem est cum Patre DEUS, Joh. X. 30. & honorandus est, sicut honoratur Pater, Joh. V. 23. & in ipsius nomine omnis eorum lingua jura- re, eique omnium genua flecti debent, tanquàm uni vero DEO, extra quem non est alius, quot- quot unquam fuêre, sunt, aut erunt, quicunque nempè aliquando in die pantocritico coram ejus tribunali comparituri sunt Es. XLV. 22. 23. Rom.

XII. 11. Phil. II. 10. Neque concessio omnis po- testatis Ecclesiæ regendæ ac tuendæ causa & ratio est cultûs religiosi, juramenti in nomine Christi bræstandi, sed vera & suprema Deitas vel natura divina, quum nonnisi vero & supremo DEO hic cultus & honor debeatur. Exod. XXII. 11. Deut. VI. 13. X. 20. Jos. XXIII. 7. Es. XIX. 18. LXV. 16. Jer. IV. 2. V. 2. 7. XII. 16. Conf. Genes. XI. 23. XXIV. 12. Jos. II. 12. 1. Sam. XXIV. 22. Ps. LXIII. 12. Dan. XII. 7. Zeph. I. 5. Zach. V. 4. Ebr. VI. 16. Apoc. X. 5. Nec verò alia ratione vis & potestas in Ecclesiam & in omnia, quæ sunt in cælo & in terra, in tempore concessa est Christo secundùm humanam naturam, vel cultus religiosus ei defer- ri debet, quàm quia humana natura assumpta est in ipsam hypostasin Filii DEI, vi cujus προσλήψεως & hypostaseos Filii DEI & majestatis, ac gloriæ ejus infinitæ verè ipsa humana natura Christi par- ticeps facta est: quod qui negant, in castra Ne- storii transeunt. Ideoque ex hoc testimonio A- postolico, cum & ad Christum provocat & ad Spi- ritum S. ceu testem καρδιογνώστην & vindicem per- jurii, utrorumq; & Filii & Spiritus S. eandem cum Patre Deitatem antiqui Doctores Ecclesiæ ad- versus Arianos, & Pneumatomachos demonstrare soliti sunt. Dolorem autem summum testaturus Apostolus, non tantùm λύπην vel tristitiam, sed λύπην μεγάλην, nec eam solùm, sed ὀδύνην, quâ voce dolores parturientium, & infernales exqui- sitissimi exprimi solent, eandemque ἀδιάλειπτον, nullam intermissionem, nullum finem habentem vel jugem & perpetuam, idque in CORDE suo, intima animi penetralia & cordis viscera, ipsis ad- aperiens, manifestat. Addit autem hoc, quia ma- xime incredibile id foret, nisi in Christo, attestan- te sibi conscientia in Spiritu S. id testaretur Apo- stolus, h. e. jurejurando, in nomine SS. Trinitatis deposito, confirmaret.

## 9:3
V. 3. For I myself was wishing.

The imperfect is used for the optative, which is frequent among the Greeks, whether with or without the addition of ἂν, as in Acts 25:22. The phrase ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ has emphasis. I myself, who am compelled to say these ill-omened things about them.

ἀνάθεμα εἶναι.

Ανάθεμα for ἀναθεματισθεὶς, as in 1 Cor. 12:3, 15:1, 21, Gal. 1:8, 9, from the Hebrew חרם or חרמא, which the Syriac has here. Thus גלות, deportation, is put for the deported.

ἀπὸ τῦ Χριστῦ.

That is, from the Church of Christ, which is called Christ in 1 Cor. 12:12, Gal. 3:27. Just as it was the custom among the Hebrews for wives to be called by the husband's name, Isa. 4:1. He says this: I would wish not only to lack the honor of the Apostleship, but even to be most contemptible among Christians, such as those who are excommunicated. In the epistle of Ignatius to the Romans we read: κόλασις τῦ διαβόλυ ἐπ' ἐμὲ ἐρχέσθω, μόνον ἵνα Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ ἐπιτύχω.

ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τῶν συγγενῶν μ8 κατὰ σάρκα.

That is, if by that means I could lead them to true righteousness and to eternal salvation. I do not wish them ill to such a degree, being joined to me by the bond of blood.

This explanation of the Apostolic vow is too diluted; and it deviates rashly from the propriety of the word χριστῦ, because by it not Christ, but the Church of Christ is designated, in which manner the passage Gal. 3:27 is also perverted, which Grotius nevertheless interpreted more correctly in his annotations on the same, concerning Christ himself; nor is being ἀνάθεμα from Christ, or even from the Church of Christ, to be most contemptible among Christians: those very parallel passages 1 Cor. 12:3, 16:31, Gal. 1:8, 9 prove otherwise: because exclusion from GOD and eternal blessedness, which is in the enjoyment of GOD, is designated by the calculation of the best interpreters, both ancient and recent; whence they laboriously dispute how he could vow this GREAT evil, and wish it for himself instead of the Jews.

The Apostle, most certain of his own salvation, and seeking and panting for the same with the highest desires, as is right. But the ἐπίλυσις (solution) of that difficulty will be easier if it is observed that these words are to be taken in the Optative, OPTAREM (I would wish), not in the Indicative, OPTO (I wish): and that consequently they are uttered hypothetically and hyperbolically, under a hypothesis, to wit, that is impossible: since the Apostle, being by far most certain of eternal salvation, testifies that he would so wish, if it were possible, because he was certain through the Holy Spirit that this was impossible, in order to exaggerate the abundance of his love. He loves his brethren so greatly, and desires their salvation, that he would desire to redeem it even at the cost of his own salvation, if he could, so that he himself alone might become an ἀνάθεμα (anathema) for such an innumerable crowd: which, however, he does not say as one prodigal or negligent of his own salvation, but out of an abundance of πληροφορίας (full assurance), because he was infallibly certain that the same was laid up for him in heaven, and that he could in no way be excluded from it; the words therefore are not those of one doubting about salvation, nor of one putting it after the salvation of others, but of the greatest πληροφορίας (full assurance) of faith, and of an affection of human love, such and as great as can fall into a mere man: as if to say, I would wish to redeem your salvation even at the loss of my own, if I could; but I am most certain that this is among the impossibilities, that I can in no way be separated from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus, and also that you can in no way be redeemed from Christ by my anathema: for Christ alone was made anathema by God for all, 2 Cor. 5:21. Meanwhile, however, by this very attestation of an impossible thing, I wished to manifest the sincerity of my love: just as Moses also, with the same πληροφορίᾳ (full assurance) of mind concerning his own name being indelible from the book of life before God himself, testified to the sincerity of his love and his most serious intercession, 'either forgive the people, or blot me out of the book which you have written,' Exod. 32:32, being entirely certain and secure that he could by no means be blotted out from thence; the prayer of Christ, Matt. 26:39, can be compared in a certain way. Father, if it is POSSIBLE, let this cup pass from me: which was not the word of one doubting whether this is possible, which, given the divine decree, he notes as absolutely impossible, nor of one so much averting the cup, which he had promptly and of his own authority received to drink in our place, but of one testifying to the immense bitterness of the cup of the fury and divine wrath, which blazes against the sins of the whole world, speaking thus hypothetically, and assuming an impossible hypothesis, so that he might manifest how full of bitterness and horrible fury that cup is. Thus, therefore, most people understand these things concerning the lack of eternal blessedness, not that Paul and Moses effectively wished for it, which they knew to be impossible, but only hypothetically, if in any way without any guilt that could be a means for obtaining pardon for the people; and that those things are not to be understood properly, as they sound, but figuratively, to testify to love. But such desires, although they are ineffective for acting, are nevertheless of the greatest moment and effective, both for declaring love and also for obtaining thanks. For friends are accustomed to use similar prayers to do violence in a certain way to their friends, and to extort what they want, as if a Son most dear to his Father were to plead for the fault of an unruly brother from the Parent in this way: either forgive my brother, or kill me, or deprive me of your inheritance; for he knows that the Parent will do anything rather than that latter thing. I know that Jerome, in his questions to Algasia, quest. 9, not denied by Photius, and among the more recent writers, Pererius and Andr. Rivetus on Exod. 32:32, take these things concerning temporal destruction: The Apostle, says Jerome, wishes to perish in the flesh, so that others may be saved in the Spirit, to pour out his own blood, so that the souls of many may be preserved. Thus therefore Moses also wished to become anathema, so that the people might not be blotted out by the Lord because of sin: but they were not ignorant that this was alien to the justice of God, that the soul which has sinned, it itself ought to die, Ez. 18:20, Deut. 24:16, nor does an ἀνάθεμα ἀπὸ χριςῦ (anathema from Christ), and being blotted out from the book which God wrote, bring only bodily destruction: therefore we judge that these things are to be understood rather in the way we have said. And thus Chrysostom, book 1 on compunction of heart: The love of Christ so bound his whole mind, that even this, which was more lovable to him than all others, to be with Christ, he would again despise that very thing, if it so pleased Christ, and would suffer to be deprived of the kingdom of heaven, which seemed to be the reward of labors, for Christ nonetheless, and would consider it desirable to be made anathema from Christ himself for Christ. Whence rightly Lippomanus on the passage in Ez. 33:32. That Moses said this not out of perturbation of mind, but out of the fire of most ardent charity, and out of secret familiarity and confidence toward God, or by way of hyperbolic speech, by which something is frequently said by way of excess without a lie to insinuate the magnitude of his affection: according to which mode also the Apostle, Rom. 9, 'I myself wished to be anathema,' etc. For thus both were so affected for the salvation of the Jews, that if it were permitted to say (which yet itself was impossible to happen), they would in a certain way desire to be blotted out of the book of life and separated from the Lord, rather than that they should perish, although they themselves were certain that God would not blot them out of the book of life. B. Mylius: He affirms that he would redeem the salvation of his people with his own eternal destruction, if it were lawful and could be done: so far is he from not sympathizing from his heart with the destruction of the same. When the affection of those who love blazes up, it proceeds even to impossibilities. Thus also B. Aegid. Hunnius: Nor indeed does the Apostle here wish or do anything against the love of Christ, but rather all this proceeds from the magnitude of the love with which his heart burned toward Christ and his glory, while he loves him so greatly that he uniquely desires him to be acknowledged, received, and loved by very many; and therefore, as has been said, he desires to redeem it with his own perpetual destruction, if it could be done. Which was indeed a very remarkable and plainly heroic movement, and an ineffable desire for the salvation of his people, proceeding from the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

V. 3. ἠυχόμην γὰρ ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ.

Est imperfectum pro optativo, quod frequens Græcis, sive addito, sive non addito ἂν, ut Act. XXV. 22. Ἔμφα- σιν habet ἀυτὸς ἐγὼ. Ego ipse, qui hæc malè ominata de il- lis cogor dicere.

ἀνάθεμα εἶναι.

Ανάθεμα pro ἀναθεματισθεὶς quomodo 1. Cor. XII. 3. XV. 1. 21. Gal. I. 8. 9. ex Hebræo חרם aut חרמא quod hic habet Syrus. Sic גלות deportatio pro deportatis ponitur.

ἀπὸ τῦ Χριστῦ.

Id est, ab Ecclesia Christi, quæ Christus vocatur 1. Cor. XII. 12. Gal. III. 27. Sicut mos erat apud Hebræos uxo- res vocari de mariti nomine, Es. IV. 1. Hoc dicit, velim non modò carere honore Apostolatus, verum etiam con- temptissimus esse inter Christianos, quales sunt, qui ex- communicati sunt. In Ignatii epistola ad Romanos legi- mus: κόλασις τῦ διαβόλυ ἐπ' ἐμὲ ἐρχέσθω, μόνον ἵνα Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ ἐπιτύχω.

ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τῶν συγγενῶν μ8 κατὰ σάρκα.

Id est, si ea ratione illos ad justitiam veram & ad æter- nam salutem possem perducere. Adeò illis malè non vo- lo, quippe sanguinis vinculo mihi conjunctis.

Nimis diluta hæc est voti Apostolici explicatio: & temerè à vocis χριστῦ proprietate deflectitur, quod per eam non Christus, sed Ecclesia Christi designetur, quo pacto etiam locus Galat. III. 27. pervertitur, quem tamen rectiùs in annotatis ad eundem interpretatus Grotius est, de ipsomet Chri- sto; neque ἀνάθεμα à Christo, vel etiam ab Ec- clesia Christi fieri est contemptissimum esse inter Christianos: aliud ipsa illa loca parallela 1. Cor. XII. 3. XVI. 31. Gal. I. 8. 9. evincunt: quia ex- clusio à DEO & beatitudine æternâ, quæ est in fruitione DEI, designatur interpp. optimorum & veterum, & recentiorum calculo; unde ope- rosè disputant, quo pacto hoc TANTUM ma- lum vovere, & præ Judæis sibi optare potuerit

Apostolus, de salute sua certissimus, eandemque summis, ut par est, votis expetens, & anhelans. Sed facilior erit istius difficultatis ἐπίλυσις, si ob- servatum fuerit, quod in Optativo hæc accipienda, OPTAREM, non in Indicativo, OPTO: quod- que proinde hypotheticè prolata sunt, & hyperbo- licè, sub hypothesi scil. impossibili : quandoqui- dem Apostolus longè certissimus de salute æterna, ita se optaturum, si possibile foret, ideò testetur, quia per Sp. S. certus erat, impossibile hoc esse, ad exaggerandam ubertatem amoris sui. Tan- toperè nempè amat suos fratres, eorumque desi- derat salutem, ut vel salutis suæ dispendio redime- re eam, si posset, cuperet, ut unus ipse pro tàm in- numerabili catervâ ἀνάθεμα fieret: quod verò non ceu prodigus, aut negligens salutis suæ dicit, sed ex πληροφορίας abundantiâ, quod infallibiliter certus esset, sibi eandem repositam esse in cœlis, seque ab eadem excludi nullatenùs posse; Verbâ ergò sunt non dubitantis de salute, non eandem posthabentis aliorum saluti, sed πληροφορίας fidei maximæ, & affectûs Amoris humani, qualis & quantuscunque in ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον cadere potest: q. d. vellem vel salutis meæ jacturâ vestram salu- tem redimere, si possem; certissimus autem id ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων esse, tùm separari me nullatenus pos- se à dilectione DEI, quæ est in Christo Jesu, tùm etiam anathemate meo à Christo vos redimi mi- nimè posse: Christus enim solus anathema à DEO factus pro omnibus, 2. Cor. V. 21. Interim vel hâc tamen rei impossibilis attestatione sinceritatem Amoris mei manifestare volui: quemadmodum & Moses eadem animi πληροφορίᾳ de nomine suo è libro vitæ indelebili apud DEUM ipsummet amoris & intercessionis suæ maximè seriæ since- ritatem testatus est, aut remitte populo, aut dele me de libro, quem scripsisti, Exod. XXXII. 32. cer- tus omninò atque securus, maximè se deleri inde non posse; Conferri potest certa ratione oratio Christi, Matth. XXVI. 39. Pater, si POSSIBILE, transeat à me calix iste: quæ non erat dubitantis, an possibile hoc sit, quod decreto divino posito no- tat prorsus ἀδύνατον, nec aversantis adeò calicem, quem promptè & αὐτεξουσίως nostri loco epota- re receperat, sed testantis immensam acerbitatem poculi furoris & iræ divinæ, quæ exardescit ad- versus peccata totius mundi, hypotheticè ita lo- quens, & hypothesin impossibilem assumens, ut quàm plenus amarore & horribili furore sit calix ille, manifestaret. Sic ergò de carentia beatitudinis æternæ hæc intelligunt plerique, non quod effica- citer id voluerint Paulus & Moses, quod sciebant impossibile esse, sed solùm hypotheticè, si quomodo citrà ullam culpam illud posset medium esse ad veniam populo obtinendam; quodque illa non propriè, ut sonant, sed figuratè intelligenda sunt, ad amorem testandum. Qualia verò desideria, licet inefficacia sint ad agendum, maximi tamen momenti & effiacia sunt, tùm ad amorem decla- randum, tùm etiam gratiam impetrandam. So- lent enim amici similibus precibus vim quodam- modò amicis facere, & quod volunt, extorquere, ut si Filius Patri charissimus culpam fratris im- morigeri à Parente hoc modo deprecaretur: vel fratri ignosce, vel occide me, aut hæreditate tuâ me priva; scit enim Parentem quidvis potiùs, quàm illud posterius facturum. Novi, quod Hieronymus ad Algas. quæst. IX. non abnuente Photio, & è re- centioribus Pererio, Andr. Riveto ad Ex. XXXII. 32. de interitu temporali hæc accipiat: Vult Apo- stolus, inquit Hieronymus, perire in carne, ut alii salventur in Spiritu, suum sanguinem fundere, ut multorum animæ conserventur. Sic ergo & Moses anathema fieri voluit, ne populus à Domino de- leatur propter peccatum: sed & hoc non ignora- bant à justitia DEI alienum esse, vt cujus anima, quæ peccavit, ipsa mori debet, Ez. XVIII.20. Deut. XXIV.16. nec ἀνάθεμα ἀπὸ χριςῦ, ac deleri è libro quem scripsit Deus, solum interitum corporalem infert: ideò eà potius, ut diximus, ratione hæc in- telligenda esse censemus. Atque ita Chrysost. l. 1. de compunct. cord. Ita totam ejus mentem devin- xit amor Christi, ut etiam hoc, quod ei præ cæteris omnibus amabilius erat, esse cum Christo, rursum id ipsum, si ita placeret Christo, contemneret, sed & cælorum regno, quod videbatur laborum esse remu- nerationem, pro Christo nihilominus carere patere- tur, & ab ipso etiam Christo anathema effici pro Christo optabile haberet. Unde rectè Lippomanus ad locum Ez. XXXIII. 32. Id non ex perturbatione animi, sed ex ardentissimæ charitatis incendio, & ex occulta familiaritate, & confidentia ad Deum dixif- se Mosen, sive per hyperbolicæ loquutionis modum, quâ frequenter aliquid per excessum dicitur sine mendacio ad insinuandum affectionis suæ magnitu- dinem: juxta quem modum etiam Apostolus Rom. IX. Optabam ego ipse anathema &c. Sic enim ambo erant Judæorum saluti affecti, ut si di- cere liceret, (quod tamen ipsum fieri erat impos- sibile) quodammodo deleri de libro vitæ & sepa- rari à Domino, quam eos perire desiderarent, licet ipsi certi essent, quod eos Deus de libro vitæ non deleret. B. Mylius: Exitio suo sempiterno, si ita fas sit, & fieri queat, salutem populi sui se redem- pturum affirmat: tantum abest, ut non ex animo exitio ejusdem condoleat. Affectus amantium cum exardescit, procedit etiam ad impossibilia. Sic etiam B. Ægid. Hunnius: Neque verò hic Apostolus quicquam contra dilectionem Christi optat, aut fa- cit, quin potiùs ex magnitudine dilectionis, quâ pe- ctus ipsius erga Christum ejusœ, gloriam ardebat, hoc totum proficiscitur, dum tantoperè eum diligit, ut ipsum à quàmplurimis agnosci, recipi & diligi uni- cè desideret; idœ, ut dictum est, suo perpetuo exitio, si fieri posset, redimere cupiat. Qui sanè insignis ad- modum planéq; heroicus fuit motus, & ineffabile de- siderium salutis sui populi, profectum à Spiritu S.

## 9:4
V. 4. ὅιτινές εἰσιν ἰσραηλῖται (who are Israelites).

Who are the posterity of Jacob, to whom the name of Israel was given by God.

whose is the adoption.

For the Israelites are called children of GOD, Deut. XIX. 1. Exod. IV. 22. namely on account of the benefits of this life, which GOD had granted them, not on account of the promises of eternal life, as Christians.

Nowhere is adoption restricted to the benefits of this life, nor did God grant only those to the Israelites, but to the believers He also promised and granted the remission of sins, righteousness, and salvation, which adoption altogether brings, which was as it were peculiar to the Israelites, because the Lord had entrusted His word to them in particular, and the true Church was in their assembly, although not all Israelites were therefore children of GOD, but only the believers. So also today adoption is a prerogative peculiar to the Church, not that all who are in the Church are truly children of God; but that in the Church He gathers to Himself children through the Word and Sacraments. But those who are children of God have not only temporal goods, by virtue of divine promises, but also heavenly ones, 1 Tim. IV. 8. if indeed they are children, they are also heirs, Rom. VIII. 16. What kind of sonship or adoption is that without an inheritance? Brentius, however, explains this prerogative of the Jews very well, p. 660. in h.l. This was the great glory of the Israelites, that God had adopted their nation as children. For He says concerning the family of Abraham, I will be their God, they shall be my people. And again: Israel is my firstborn son.

Israel. What then shall we say to these things? Have all Israelites been saved because of this benefit of God? And have all uncircumcised nations perished? By no means. For adoption here is to be understood in such a way that God chose the Israelites primarily, from whose Church he might gather, by a general ordination, his own children: just as at this time there is an adoption of the nations, not that all nations are saved, but that God gathers generally from the nations the heirs of his heavenly goods. Meanwhile, however, in those times when Christ had not yet arrived, they believed in the true God, namely him who promised the blessing of the nations through the seed of Abraham, and they obtained eternal salvation, even if they were not of the external people of Israel. Thus the Ninevites, thus Naaman the Syrian, thus those who, from the sermons and decrees of the monarchs Nebuchadnezzar and Darius (in Daniel ch. 3. and 6.) believed in the God of Israel, were saved: and that was not done by a general ordination, for in that way the election pertained only to the Israelites, but it was done by special grace and prerogative. Since, therefore, those were Jews to whom the adoption pertained generally, it is a stupendous thing that they have been rejected by God, and it is no wonder that many doubted concerning Christ, since he was not received by the Jews.

and the glory.

That is, the ark, which עֹז 1 Paralip. XVI. 7. 2 Paral. VI. 41. Ps. LXIII. 3. LXXVIII. 61. It is usually translated עֹז as strength, power, glory, although properly glory is כָּבוֹד the majesty of God shining forth at the Ark 1 Sam. II. 12. in the said Ps. LXIII.

Glory is not to be restricted to the ark, which, even if it was once so called because the glory of the Lord was manifested at it, yet it is not evident that it was preserved for the Israelites up to the times of the Apostle. But if this excellence or prerogative is understood concerning ancient times, it will perhaps sufficiently suit this name, but there is no doubt that this is something more than to be restricted to the ark. For the glory and dignity of this people consisted in more things than that material ark alone, and what prevents it from being extended to all things that contribute to the glory of the same, besides those expressly recounted here? Whence the blessed Hunnius also refers here to the magnificence of the miracles by which God exalted and illustrated this people in the world before all nations.

and the covenants.

That is, the words of the covenant written on the two tablets Exod. xxxiv. 28. The Hebrews call them לֻחוֹת בְּרית. By this name can also be comprehended circumcision and the sprinkling of blood, which are also called by the very word of covenant. Gen. XVII. 10. Exod. XXIV. 8.

Neither the tablets of the covenant nor the sprinkling of blood itself were properly the covenant, and circumcision was a medium and Sacrament of the covenant of grace: therefore the Testaments are rather the covenants themselves, concerning which Jerem. XXXI. Namely, the old testament, and the new legal and evangelical: which, as they are the proper goods of the Church, so they also formerly belonged to the Israelitic people, when it constituted the Church.

and the giving of the law.

Which to the Hebrews is מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, all those constitutions given through Moses for binding the society of the people.

That axiom consists in this, that in this people God deigned to promulgate his law solemnly: which dignity happened to no people, by which the people of the Lord are not rarely celebrated. And not only the promulgation of the Decalogue is comprehended, but the entire pandects of the Israelitic laws, by which the form of the Jewish Republic was constituted and governed.

עבודת, by which name come all sacrifices, but especially the Paschal lamb, as can be seen in Exodus 12:25, where in the Greek it is Φυλάξατε τὴν λατρείαν ταύτην. He understands the priesthood, indeed the entire divine worship, which flourished among the people of the Lord, and not merely the offering of sacrifices and the celebration of the Paschal lamb.

and the promises.

That is, εὐλογίαι ברכות, those famous, but earthly promises of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, which Philo calls ἆθλα.

Again the Pelagian-Socinian error recurs, concerning mere earthly promises. And yet those earthly promises in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 not only concern the Israelite people, but even now most of them are fulfilled in Christians, who devote effort to the law of God and piety, nor do they encompass merely earthly things: for God promises in Leviticus 26:12, I will dwell among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. But those whose God is God, to them He is God not only in this age, but forever, Matthew 22:32, Revelation 21:7. Thus God promised in Deuteronomy 29:9, God will raise you up as a holy people, just as He swore to you, which certainly cannot be restricted to merely earthly things: and are there not many other promises extant in Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets than those two places? Are not many spiritual and heavenly goods also promised here and there to the people of the Lord in the Old Testament? But the promises referred to here are whatever were made to the people of the Lord and the faithful (such as the Israelites were in the Old Testament), in particular also those by which the Messiah was promised to this people; because He had to descend from the Israelites, appear among them, reveal Himself by word and miracles, preach the Gospel to them above others, and execute the work of redemption among them, and by suffering, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, fulfill the prophetic predictions, and send forth the scepter of His kingdom from Zion: such remarkable and excellent promises we know were made to this people above all others.

Latin:

V. 4. ὅιτινές εἰσιν ἰσραηλῖται.

Qui sunt posteritas Jacobi, cui à DEO Israëlis nomen datum est.

ὧν ἡ ὑιοθεσία.

Vocantur enim Israëlitæ filii DEI, Deut. XIX. 1. Exod. IV. 22. nempè ob beneficia hujus vitæ, quæ DEUS eis in- dulserat, non ob promissa vitæ æternæ, ut Christiani.

Nuspiam restringitur ὑιοθεσία ad beneficia hujus vitæ, nec ea tantùm indulsit Deus Israëlitis, sed cre- dentibus etiam remissionem peccatorum, justiti- am & salutem promisit & concessit, quam omninò ὑιοθεσία infert, quæ Israëlitarum erat veluti pro- pria, quod ipsis peculiariter verbum suum credi- derit Dominus, & in cœtu ipsorum vera fuerit Ecclesia, etsi non ideò omnes Israëlitæ Filii DEI fuerint, sed soli credentes. Ita & hodiè ὑιοθεσία Ecclesiæ proprium est ἀξίωμα, non quod omnes, qui in Ecclesia sunt, filii Dei reverà sint; sed quod in Ecclesia per verbum & Sacramenta sibi colligat Filios. Qui autem Filii sunt Dei, non tantum bo- na temporalia, vi promissionum divinarum, ha- bent, sed etiam cœlestia, 1. Tim. IV. 8. si filii utique κληρονόμοι & hæredes sunt Rom. IIX.16. Qualis illa filiatio vel ὑιοθεσία sine hæreditate? Optimè autem hanc prærogativam Judæorum explicat Brentius, p. 660. in h.l. Hæc fuit magna Israëlitarũ gloria, quod Deus adoptaverit gentem ipsorũ in filios. Dicit enim de familia Abrahami, ego ero Deus illorum, erunt populus meus. Et iterum: Filius meus primogenitus, Israël.

Israël. Quid ergò ad hæc dicemus? Num propter hoc Dei beneficium omnes Israëlitæ salvi facti sunt? & o- mnes gentes incircumcisæ perierūt? Nihil minus. Ad- optio enim hîc sic intelligenda est, quod Deus elegerit præcipuè Israëlitas, ex quorum Ecclesia colligeret, ge- nerali ordinatione, suos filios: quemadmodum & hoc tempore adoptio est gentium, non quod omnes gentes salvæ fiant, sed quod Deus colligat generaliter ex gen- tibus hæredes cælestium suorum bonorum. Intereà autem illis temporibus, quibus Christus nondum advenerat, crediderunt in verum Deum, nimirum eum, qui promisit benedictionem gentium, per semen Abrahæ, consecuti sunt æternam salutem, etiamsi non fuerunt de externo populo Israël. Sic Ninivitæ, sic Naëman Syrus, sic illi, qui ex concionibus & De- cretis Monarcharum Nebucadnezaris & Darii, (apud Danielem cap. 3. & 6.) crediderunt in Deum Israëlis, salvi facti sunt: idque non est factum gene- rali ordinatione, sic enim electio pertinebat tantùm ad Israëlitas, sed factum est speciali gratia & præro- gativa. Cum igitur Judæi illi fuerint, ad quos ad- optio generaliter pertinuerit, stupenda res est, quod sint rejecti à Deo, & mirum non est, quod multi du- bitarverint de Christo, cum non reciperetur à Judæis.

καὶ ἡ δόξα.

Id est, arca, quæ עֹז 1. Paralip. XVI. 7. 2. Paral. VI. 41. Ps. LXIII. 3. LXXVIII. 61. Solet autem verti עֹז ἰσχὺς, δύναμις, δόξα, quanquam propriè δόξα est כָּבוֹד majestas Dei apud Arcam relucens 1. Sam. II. 12. dicto Ps. LXIII.

Gloria non restringenda ad arcam, quæ etsi olim ita vocata, quod ad eam gloria Domini ma- nifestaretur, tamen ad tempora usque Apostoli conservatam esse Israëlitis, non constat. Si verò hæc ἐξοχὴ, vel prærogativa de temporibus anti- quis intelligatur, nomini huic fortè satis conve- niet, sed hoc tamen amplius esse, quam ut ad ar- cam restringatur, dubium non est. Nam pluribus constabat δόξα & dignitas hujus populi, quàm so- lâ illâ materiali arcâ, & quid vetat, quò minus ad omnia, quæ ad δόξαν ejusdem faciunt, præter illa hic expressè recensita, id extendatur. Unde B. Hunnius magnificentiam miraculorum huc etiam refert, quibus Deus populum istum in orbe coram omnibus gentibus extulit & illustravit.

καὶ αἱ διαθῆκαι.

Id est, verba fœderis scripta in duabus tabulis Exod. xxxiv. 28. Eas Hebræi vocant לֻחוֹת בְּרית. Potest hoc nomine comprehendi & circumcisio, & aspersio sanguinis, quæ & ipso fœderis vocabulo appellantur. Gen. XVII. 10. Exod. XXIV. 8.

Nec tabulæ fœderis, nec ipsa sanguinis aspersio propriè fœdus erant, & circumcisio medium fuit & Sacramentum fœderis gratiæ : Testamenta ergô ipsa fœdera potius sunt, de quibus Jerem. XXXI. Testamentum nempè vetus, & novum legale, & Ev- angelicum: quæ, ut propria sunt Ecclesiæ bona, ita & Israëlitico populo, cùm constituebat Eccle- siam, olim conveniebant.

καὶ ἡ νομοθεσία.

Quæ Hebræis מַתַּן תּוֹרָה omnes illæ constitu- tiones per Mosen datæ ad vinciendam populi so- cietatem.

Axioma illud in eo consistit, quod in hoc popu- lo Deus dignatus est legem suam solemniter pro- mulgare: quæ dignitas nulli populo accidit, à quâ non rarò celebratur populus Domini. Nec De- calogi tantùm promulgatio, sed universæ legum Israëliticarum pandectæ comprehenduntur, qui- bus Reip. Judaicæ forma constituta & guberna- ta fuit.

עבודת quo nomine veniunt sacrificia omnia, sed præcipuè agnus Paschalis, ut videre est Exodi XII. 25. ubi in Græco Φυλάξατε τὴν λατρείαν ταύτην. Sacerdotium, imò universum cultum divinum intelligit, qui vigebat in populo Domini, non ve- rò tantùm sacrificiorum oblationem, & agni Pa- schalis celebrationem.

καὶ αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι.

Id est, εὐλογίαι ברכות, præclara illa, sed terre- stria promissa Levit. XXVI. & Deut. XXVIII. quæ ἆθλα vocat Philo.

Iterum recurrit error Pelagio-Socinianus, de meris terrestribus promissis. Atqui promissiones illæ terrestres Lev. XXVI. Deut. XXVIII. nec so- lum populum Israëliticum attinent, sed etiamnum pleræque implentur in Christianis, legi DEI & pietati operam navantibus, neque merè terrestria complectuntur: nam promittit Deus Lev.
