XXVI. 12. Ego in vobis habitabo, & Deus vester ero, & vos populus meus eritis. Quorum verò Deus est Deus, illis non hoc seculo tantùm Deus est, sed in æter- num Matth. XXII. 32. Apoc. XXI. 7. Ita promisit Deus Deut. XXIX. 9. Deus te eriget in Sanctum populum, sicut juravit tibi, quod sanè restringi ne- quit ad merè terrestria: & annon plura alia in Mo- se, Psalmis & Prophetis extant promissa, quàm illis binis locis? Annon multa passim spiritualia & cælestia bona etiam promissa sunt populo Do- mini in Vet. Testamento? Promissiones autem hic respiciuntur, quæcunque factæ sunt populo Domini ac fidelibus, (quales in Vet. Test. fuêre Israëlitæ) in specie etiam illæ, quibus promissus est Messias huic populo; quod ex Israëlitis descende- re, inter eos comparere, seque verbo & miraculis patefacere, illis præ aliis Evangelium prædicare, & in illis opus redemptionis exequi, ac patiendo, moriendo, resurgendo, & adscendendo in cælum vaticinia Prophetica implere, sceptrumque regni è Zione emittere debuerit: Qualia insignia pror- sus, & excellentia promissa huic populo præ omni- bus aliis facta novimus.

## 9:5
whose are the fathers.

Those whom those great men Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob touch by right of blood, whom God remembers so willingly, Exodus 6:3, Leviticus 26:42, and who are called the Fathers by excellence in Exodus 3:13, 16, 4:5, 13:5, and elsewhere.

and from whom is Christ according to the flesh.

Not according to the divine nature which is in Him, but according to the human nature. See above 1:3. The phrase 'according to the flesh' is opposed to 'according to the spirit.' By the former the human nature is denoted, by the latter the divine: and the particle 'the' indicates a distinction, and introduces something else, according to which Christ is God blessed forever, namely the divine nature of Christ, who is the same according to the human nature from the Fathers. Compare John 1:14, Romans 1:3, 1 Timothy 3:16, Hebrews 2:14, 1 Peter 3:18. Therefore, the truth of the personal union of the divine and human nature is established from this.

who is over all, God blessed forever.

This can rightly be understood thus concerning Christ, because when it is said 'over all,' the Father is tacitly excepted, 1 Corinthians 15:27. But it appears from the Syriac that the ancient codices had: 'who is over all, blessed forever,' which better suits the customary speech of Paul, who, when he speaks of the Father and the Son, is accustomed to attribute the name of God to the Father, and the name of Lord to the Son. And Erasmus noted that it was so in the ancient codices of Cyprian, that Hilary also read it so, and that Chrysostom did not seem to read it otherwise. And it was enough for this passage indeed to say that this privilege of the Jews, that Christ was born from them, was greater than all others, because praise and honor are owed to Christ above all, that is, even above Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Amen.

Thus we have had Amen inserted, and above in the praise of God I. 25. so also below XI. 36. and XVI. 27. Gal. I. 5. Eph. III. 21. Philip. IV. 20. 1. Tim. I. 17.

This annotation sails in favor of the Socinians, by which it is feigned that the name Θεῦ is an interpolation or an insertion: But rashly. There is no reason for us to dwell here on Erasmus, who not infrequently prepares κρησφύγεῖα (hiding places) for the Arians in the Scriptures. Nor can the Syriac (although it is falsely cited here by Grotius) or even any Latin codex prejudice the universal Greek codices and the consistent reading of the purer Latin and other Fathers. Moreover, that the omission of the name of God better suits Paul's manner of speaking is futile: because it is known from Acts XX. 28, 1 Tim. III. 16, and Tit. II. 14 that Paul calls Christ God. But this contributed most of all to the ἐξοχὴν (preeminence) of the people, whom the Apostle wished to extol with his highest honors, that Christ is from them, not only more eminent than all the Patriarchs (as Hugo weakens the force of the eulogy), but that God blessed forever over all things: Nor indeed is such eminence designated by those words, if the word Θεῦ is even neglected, but the dignity and majesty of the divine nature is expressed. For he who is blessed forever over all things is the true and essential God. Rom. I. 25, Luke I. 68, 2 Cor. I. 3, ch. XI. 31, Eph. I. 3, 1 Pet. I. 3. Since Erasmus saw this clearly, he snatched this eulogy away from Christ and toward the Father, by inserting a period, through a certain feigned exclamation, so that it might not serve to establish the Deity of Christ. Yet this depravation could not be approved even by Socinus himself, as noted in Vol. III of the System. Theol. page 46: where this passage is treated at length, and it is observed that the word Θεὸς is found not only among other Fathers, but also among Cyprian and Hilary in the better editions (while the others lie in error), as well as in the Syriac Interpreter. Which the German Racovian version of Socinus did not omit. Therefore, Cassianus, lib. III de Incarnat., says best: When Paul says that Christ is God, this suffices for Christians; but when he adds that he is GOD blessed over all things, he excludes every blasphemy of perfidious assertion. Let Theol. Apost. Roman. orac. LXVII be compared. The Syriac has it thus: From whom Christ appeared in the flesh, who is over all things, whose are the praises and blessings forever and ever. Amen.

We add, for the sake of vindicating the illustrious passage and argument of the Deity of Christ, what we prepared about thirty years ago against the Socinians concerning the same, as it has not yet been communicated to the Church of Christ. For this testimony of the eternal Deity of Christ is most worthy of being solidly vindicated.

Various arguments can be drawn from this. (1) That Christ is called absolutely Θεὸς, God: which name is not attributed absolutely except to the one and only true GOD. (2) That he is said to be ἐπὶ πάντων. For he who is simply and universally ἐπὶ πάντων, over all things, is true GOD by nature: since only one and the only GOD is simply ἐπὶ πάντων, over all things. (3) That he is called ἐυλογητός. Because this epithet is not claimed for anyone except the one and only true GOD in the Holy Scriptures, which is demonstrated by an induction of Sacred passages, Mark XIV. 61, Luke I. 68, Rom. I. 25, 2 Cor. I. 3, II. 31, Eph. I. 3, 1 Pet. I. 3, and is conceded by Enjedinus himself, p. 265, to such an extent, he says, that ἐυλογητός is a peculiar epithet for GOD, that it is read to be attributed to NO ONE except Him in the New Testament. Hence it happens that when only that word ἐυλογητῦ is placed, God the Father is understood, as in Mark XIV. 61. (4) That he is named God ἐυλογητὸς εἰς αἰῶνας, with the particle of confirmation ἀμήν added. For this description and glorification is proper to the eternal GOD, according to the tenor of the Holy Scriptures and the style of the Apostle himself: Rom. I. 25, They served the creature besides the Creator: ὅς ἐστιν ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας Ἀμήν. 2 Cor. XI. 31, ὁ Θεὸς, God and Father

of our Lord Jesus Christ knows, ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, both of which passages are similar to ours. There is a twin doxology familiar to the Apostle, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ἀμὴν, which is proper to the same one true and eternal GOD, as is evident from the induction of passages. Rom. XVI. 27, Phil. II. 20, Heb. XIII. 21, 1 Pet. V. 11, etc. But it is attributed to Christ in 2 Pet. III. 18, as also in 2 Tim. IV. 18. (5) That he is preached not only as εὐλογητὸς, but as ἐπὶ πάντων εὐλογητὸς, blessed over all things. For besides the fact that the name εὐλογητὸς placed by itself and absolutely sufficiently implies that Christ is the true God, whom the Hebrews call that supreme and blessed one, הקדוש ברוח הוא that is, הקדש and that name blessed היתב that is, השם יתברך, what is clearer than that by this whole eulogy ἐπὶ πάντων εὐλογητὸς, blessed over all things, the supreme God himself is designated, who alone is, and is called, blessed over all things. (6) That in Christ the flesh, or human nature, and the Deity, or his divine nature, are clearly distinguished, when it is said that Christ is from the Fathers τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, which pertains to the flesh or human nature, and yet that he is also θεὸν εὐλογητὸν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, God blessed forever, which, since it is denied to be by reason of the flesh or human nature by the force of the Apostle's words, it remains that there is another more sublime nature in Christ, according to which he himself is God blessed forever. Adam Goslavius was indeed forced to acknowledge to Bebel, part 1 against Kekerm. ch. I, page 5, that the particle τὸ added (in the words τὸ κατὰ σάρκα) signifies nothing else than that Christ, as much as he is, is not from the Jews, but only according to the flesh. Therefore, besides the flesh or human nature, there must be something else in Christ that is not from the Jews, according to which he is God blessed forever, which pertains no less to constituting Christ than the flesh does. Which what else can it be than the Deity itself, through which he is God blessed forever, just as through the flesh or human nature he is man. (7) But we now urge most of all that description, and that complete one, which confirms our faith absolutely apodictically: Whoever is God blessed forever over all things, he is the true and essential God. But Christ is God blessed forever over all things. E. The major premise is proved, first, because this is a description proper to the true and eternal God, and from a description or definition to the thing defined, the consequence is invincible; second, because this eulogy is claimed in the scriptures for the one and only GOD: therefore, he to whom this very thing is attributed must be believed to be that one true God; third, because the eminence of the supreme God is inferred by this phrase, when it is said ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς; fourth, because a truly divine glorification befits none but the one God, which is expressed in these words: εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας; finally, because not only has the universal Church, ever since the time of the Apostles, accepted this description as a periphrasis of the true, supreme, and eternal God himself, but even the adversaries themselves are compelled to admit and acknowledge it, that it befits none but the one true and eternal God. Cassian. l. 3. de incarnat. When Paul says that Christ is God, this suffices for Christians; but when he adds that he is God over all, by that he excludes every blasphemy of a perfidious assertion. Enjedinus, in the cited place, says that this argument is very valid in the scriptures, because, forsooth, wherever this encomium is read, it is always attributed to the Father as the true and eternal God, and therefore, so that the analogy of scripture may be preserved, he concludes that here too it must be understood of the same: he proves the antecedent by an induction of passages. Thus, therefore, the analogy of scripture cannot be preserved, as Enjedinus admits, unless it be admitted that here too by it that the true and eternal GOD is designated by this title, as to whom alone this title and epithet is always attributed and claimed in the scriptures, as Enjedinus confesses and confirms. Socinus, however, Smalcius, and others, while they act to ensure that by a new interpretation this title is claimed for GOD the Father in this place, sufficiently testify that they are convinced in their own conscience that it is proper to the one true GOD. Indeed, when they wish this to be understood of the Father, they grant, even if unwillingly, that this is a description of the true and eternal GOD no less than the description of the true and eternal GOD is when it occurs in Rom. 1:25 and 2 Cor. 11:31, not to mention that the name of GOD occurs here subjectively, in which manner Socinus, Smalcius, and other adversaries sharply contend that it can only suit the one and only eternal GOD. The Apostle's own words exhibit the minor premise: for he confesses concerning Christ that he is not only from the Fathers according to the flesh, but that the same is also God over all, blessed for ever; which therefore the whole Church has always understood of Christ, because it could not do otherwise by the force of the Apostle's words, nor did Socinus, Goslavius, Nicolaides, or the Racovian Catechism deny that those words are to be referred to Christ, whose own words we shall produce later.

The adversaries strive in every way, but in vain, to obscure the sun of this truth with various mists, Enjedinus in expl. loc. Socin. against Wujek p. 263 and 355, Smalcius ref. disp. Grav. de pers. Christ. p. 3 seqq., Goslavius part 1 against Kekerman c. 5, Volckel de ver. relig. p. 426 and 468, Schlichting l. Trin. p. 234 and 254. First questioning the reading of the text, then the interpretation, and finally our inference. Whence (1) from the annotations of Erasmus on the N.T. at this place they object that the word God is suspect here: since Cyprian, Hilary, and Chrysostom did not read it, but it seems to have been added by Enjedinus, by someone too zealous for the Divinity of Christ and an enemy of the Arians. (2) Those words, who is over all, etc. are not to be referred to Christ who was named immediately before, but a period ought to be placed before him, which separates those from the preceding, so that they may be referred absolutely to GOD, just as if it had been written expressly: He who is over all, let him be God blessed for ever; Socinus says there is no reason why this opinion of Erasmus should be rejected; Enjedinus, however, strives to confirm the same also with the argument that, forsooth, this title is everywhere attributed not to Christ, but to the Father. (3) The word GOD is not placed here absolutely, since 'over all' is added, by which Socinus wishes to indicate that the name God is to be taken for Lord or divine Master. (4) The word ἐπὶ πάντων, 'over all', is not to be taken so absolutely universally that nothing at all is excluded outside of him of whom there is speech, since the Father is excepted in 1 Cor. 15:27. Thus the word 'all' can be rendered 'everyone', but the word 'everyone' is accustomed to be referred only to men, says Socinus p. 265. (4) That there is nothing over all except that one God of Israel is not simply true, but only so if that 'being over all' is understood from his own nature, or from himself, and the word 'all' is taken absolutely universally. But that Christ is over all by the gift of God, and that he does not have it by his own nature, nor is he over all absolutely and universally. (7) Smalcius objects that Paul indeed says of the eternal God that he is blessed for ever, but he does not say that whoever is God blessed for ever is the eternal God. Those words in Rom. 1:25 signify the eternal God because they are expressly predicated of the Creator. But in Rom. 9:5 they do not signify the eternal God because they are said of Christ, who is from the Fathers according to the flesh. (8) Goslavius replies to the argument from the distinction of the particle κατὰ σάρκα in the cited place p. 67, that κατὰ σάρκα is also said elsewhere of others who are merely men, as in Rom. 4:1 and 9:3. And these are the principal exceptions of the adversaries, which must now be discussed in order.

As to (1). Response: All Greek copies read the word θεὸς, nor has it ever been found to be missing in any. Those who have compared the most approved and ancient copies testify to this: Stephanus, Aldus, Theodor Beza, Isaac Casaubon, and Erasmus himself: nor is there anyone who has observed the contrary in that Greek Codex. Moreover, Latin editions agree with the Greek codices, as does the very ancient Syriac translation. Ancient commentators and Doctors also read that word: Irenaeus, Origen, Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Hilary, Epiphanius, Cyril of Alexandria, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Idacius Clarius, Augustine, Fulgentius, etc. Finally, there is no reason why it should be held as suspect. In the editions of Cyprian l. 2 advers. Jud. c. 5, which omit it, it is manifest that it is a scribe's error, since both the inscription of this chapter and the consideration of the places produced in the same prove that those are testimonies produced by which the name of GOD is expressly claimed for the Son of God. But if the name of God had not been read in this place, how could Cyprian have counted this testimony among those by which the name of GOD is expressly ascribed to Christ? Add that Jacobus Pamelius found the name God in all the manuscripts, both his own and those which Manutius and Morelius used, whence he did not omit it in his edition of Cyprian, just as it is not omitted in the Goulartian edition. Let the same judgment be held concerning the place of Hilary in Ps. 122, since he cites the saying of Paul for the purpose of proving that Christ is God; whence Erasmus himself in his annotations to Rom. 9:5 p. 415 confesses that the name God seems to have been omitted through the carelessness of scribes. The Parisian edition of Hilary expressly added this: The same is also read in Hilary, book IV and VIII de Trinitate. Regarding Chrysostom, Erasmus notes at least that he does not use the weapon of this testimony against the Arians, and that his commentary on this passage is somewhat obscure. But that Chrysostom did not find the word θεὸς in his codices cannot be inferred from Chrysostom, nor did Erasmus assert that, because he adds that Chrysostom read that word, but that the text had been punctuated differently. In vain, therefore, does Enjedinus suspect, and most rashly, that it seems to have been added by some enemy of the Arians, since it has never been discovered in any instance that it was missing. And how can it seem to have been added by an enemy of the Arians, when it was read before the Arians were born by Tertullian, c. 13, adv. Praxean, who, he says, can call Christ alone God, just as the same Apostle, who is God blessed for all eternity, indeed even by Cyprian himself, as has already been noted, and also by Irenaeus, who in book III against heresies, c. 18, cites it thus: whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all blessed for ever.

As to (2.) I reply: That punctuation, devised by Enjedinus, is 1) Entirely new, and hitherto unheard of in the Church. 2) Contrary to all Greek codices, since no trustworthy and approved exemplar can be produced in which a hypostigma or point is placed after the word κατὰ σάρκα, but only a comma or small stroke is found. 3) That exclamatory epiphonema does not agree with the preceding thanksgiving and doxology. Because the Apostle is engaged in testifying to his sympathy and most animated affection: Great sorrow is mine, he says v. 2, and continual grief in my heart. I myself wished, he continues v. 3, to be anathema for my brethren, whose glory he now describes, and among other things, that from them is Christ according to the flesh. Who therefore now abruptly into a doxology depart. What is the cause or reason for the same? He grieves, he wishes, he does not congratulate. He commemorates their dignity, not to celebrate God, but to exaggerate the cause of his grief and his vow of anathema. (4.) Nor does that doxology fit the following parts any better. For the Apostle continues his discourse, and indeed in such a way that no place is granted for an explanation of that kind being inserted. For how would those things cohere, I could wish to be anathema for my brethren etc. of whom is Christ according to the flesh: Who is over all God blessed for ever, Amen. But not that the word of GOD has failed. Therefore no continuity, no connection is left. (5.) The scope of the Apostle is to extol the dignity of the Jewish nation, which among other things he confirms primarily from this, that Christ is of them according to the flesh, and from the height of this dignity, that he is God over all blessed for ever. For what is more evident than this analysis? he rightly said he was mourning, says Theodoret in this place, because from them is a certain Lord according to the flesh, who is God over all; but they themselves have fallen from nobility, and have become alienated from that surname. (6.) Socinus gives the reason why the interpretation of Erasmus should be rejected: It is this, that since the simple name, Blessed, signifies the same thing as that he is Blessed, it is almost always accustomed to be placed before the one to whom it refers, but very rarely placed after. Here, however, the word God is placed before, l. c. p. 263. (7.) The Syriac interpretation referred it expressly to Christ: From the Jewish nations appeared the Messiah in the flesh, who is GOD over all, to whom are praises and blessings for ever and ever Amen. So also the Latin Vulgate. (8.) The universal Church, from the times of the Apostles, as far as is evident from public documents, has followed the simple tenor of the words, which is liable to no error. Thus Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian, Ambrose book 1 de Sp. S. chapter 3, Hilary, Epiphanius heresy LVII of the Noetians chapter 2, Cyril of Alexandria Ep. to Anastas. Tom. I. p. 2, Fulgentius l. 1 to Trasimund, Theodoret, Jerome, Augustine, Idacius Clarius book against Varimund, Novatian l. de Trin. chapter 13 & 30, Theophylact in this place etc. (9.) What of the fact that Socinus himself, and his disciples, acknowledge that those words are referred to Christ skillfully. Socinus l. c. I easily concede, he says, that all the words of the cited Pauline testimony are to be referred to Christ. Catech. Racov. chapter 1. S. Paul calls him, who according to the flesh was from the fathers, a God over all blessed. Goslavius l. c. We most willingly concede that in this place Christ is referred to by the word GOD. Val. Smalcius l. de divin. Christ. c. 12. Justly does this belong to the Lord Jesus Christ, that Paul called him GOD blessed for ever. Theoph. Nicolaides, contra Albert. Borkowsky de Eccles. c. 8. We call Christ GOD with St. John ch. I, with Thomas John XX, with Paul Rom. IX. 5, on account of his divinity, and that true and proper. Conf. Johan. Volckel. de V. R. p. 426. Joh. Crell. Tr. de uno DEO Lat. fat. 2. c. 3. & Schlichting. l. c. finally the Racovian version of the N. T., having rejected the Erasmian, follows the Vulgate punctuation, by the force of which the name GOD is necessarily referred to Christ.

To (3.) Resp. If the word GOD used absolutely and simply denotes the true and essential GOD, that addition, that he is over all blessed for ever, will not diminish the force of this signification, but rather will confirm it. The word over all can be referred either to the word blessed, and thus God blessed over all can be understood not just as some divine ruler, but as the true and essential GOD, who alone is that blessed God over all; or to the word God and then he who is over all God, who is over all God again cannot fit some divine man at least endowed with dominion, but implies God himself of Gods, as one who alone is God over all. What? does God over all, Ephes. IV. 6. denote only a divine ruler, is it not an express periphrasis of that one GOD?

To (4.) Resp. There is nothing that teaches that the word over all placed absolutely and universally should be restricted, since the Apostle is engaged in celebrating the Deity of Christ, and proclaims it in such a way that he does not derogate or diminish anything, but exalts it over all. Add that it is the exact same manner of speaking that occurs concerning God the Father Eph. IV. 6, who is called God over all. But what is the cause that one and the same manner of speaking, without any indication of diversity, when it occurs concerning the Father, must denote the supreme God, because he is absolutely over all, but when it occurs concerning the Son of GOD it does not denote the supreme God, who is absolutely over all. Therefore we conclude: God who is over all, according to the received phrase of scripture, is the true and supreme God, as is most manifest from Eph. IV. 6. But Christ is God who is over all. E. Likewise: He who is called by the Apostle God who is over all, is that supreme GOD: But Christ is called by the Apostle God who is over all. E. Christ is that supreme God. If you say that the reason for the place Eph. IV. 6 and this present one is unequal, because there it is about the Father, here about Christ, what is this other than begging the question? The predicate is exactly the same, and it can be taught that its sense is not different here and there, of the Apostle. But it is frivolous that the word all is not taken absolutely universally, because the Father is excepted. 1 Cor. XV. 27. For besides that the Apostle there teaches at least that the Father is excepted, where he explains how all things are subject to Christ according to human nature, since here the according to the flesh is not looked at, as far as the flesh or human nature is concerned, but as he is God blessed for ever: Socinus himself confesses that the word all is then taken absolutely universally, when nothing OUTSIDE OF GOD, about whom the discourse is, is excepted. But outside of Christ God, nothing at all is excepted, when it is said that he is over all. For the Father is not outside of Christ, and neither is the Holy Spirit, but one with Christ, 1 John V. 7. Nothing therefore is excepted from the nature of Christ, by which he is God blessed for ever, over which Christ is not. But as the Father is not different from the nature of Christ, because he is that God blessed for ever, so he is no less proclaimed to be over all than Christ, and thus by that very fact, both that Christ is equally as the Father that God blessed for ever, and that he is equally as the Father called GOD over all, the very identity of nature with the Father is concluded. Who therefore would not laugh at the trifles about the exception of the Father? But Schlichtingius infers, when the Father is said to be over all, not even Christ is excepted. But however Christ may not be excepted according to the flesh, Christ is nevertheless excepted, as he is God blessed for ever. For thus he himself is no less than the Father proclaimed God over all. Who therefore would not be excepted? Is the same thing above itself in the same respect?

To (5.) Resp. Even if the word all is rendered 'all men', the Deity of Christ will not be diminished. For who would doubt that he who is God blessed over all is the God of gods? And how is Christ only proclaimed God over all men? Is he not also over other creatures? Why should that same phrase, when it occurs concerning GOD the Father, θεὸς ἐπὶ πάντων, be rendered GOD over all, but concerning Christ it should not be so rendered? Is not Christ before ALL THINGS, and do ALL THINGS consist in him? Col. I. 17. Latin interpreters and commentators certainly rendered it over ALL THINGS, Tertullian, Cyprian, Novatian, Ambrose, Hilary, Idacius Clarus, Fulgentius, and others. Nor does the Vulgate interpreter render it otherwise. Since Socinus himself, Smalcius, and others do not once allege this saying thus, blessed over ALL THINGS. Enjedinus page 266. What else, he says, will the adversaries conclude from this, than that Christ is over all, is God, is blessed for ever. All of which we confess one by one concerning Christ, as being also testified elsewhere.

To (6.) Resp. He who is over all by his own nature, or even he who is over all things taken absolutely, he is the one GOD of Israel. Both these propositions belong to the adversaries. We subsume: Christ, who is GOD blessed for ever, is over all by nature: The same is over all things taken absolutely. This latter we have now obtained: and it is especially evident from Col. I. verse 17. Whoever is before ALL THINGS taken absolutely, before all Creatures, he is also over ALL THINGS, taken absolutely, that is to say, over all Creatures. But the former is evident from this: Because it implies a contradiction in the adjunct, for GOD blessed for ever to have anything over all, as he is such, not by his own nature, but by gift and by grace. For thus he would not be God properly, let alone that blessed GOD, least of all the blessed GOD over all. He who is over all, as such, cannot depend on anything else; otherwise he would not be over all, but would have someone superior to himself in power, on whom he himself depends, and that would be held to be what is over the rest. What is moved concerning Christ being raised over all by the Father by grace, is foreign and irrelevant. For this did not happen to Christ as he is GOD blessed for ever, for if he was before all things, he was not finally constituted over all in time: But it is τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, as regards the Flesh, or human nature.

To (7.) Resp. Paul teaches concerning no one else than the eternal GOD, that he is GOD blessed for ever, nor does any other God-inspired writer. The whole Holy Scripture claims this title, and the praises that are twin to it, for the one and only eternal God: nor can any passage be brought forward from the Scriptures to the contrary. Therefore the proposition remains unmoved: Whoever is GOD blessed for ever, is this true and essential eternal God, which the adversaries will be able to infringe with no argument. Furthermore, since this is a periphrasis and a proper description of GOD, the inference cannot but be invincible. To whomever the proper description of the eternal GOD applies, he is the eternal GOD. Finally, if those passages Rom. I. 25. and 2. Corinth. XI. 31. are compared, what is more evident than this demonstration, that he who in Apostolic phrase is GOD blessed for ever, is the true and essential GOD, as those passages of the Apostle testify: But Christ, in Apostolic phrase, is GOD blessed for ever. For one must not look at how those words can be taken according to Socinian corruptions, but what they import and signify in Apostolic phrase. Therefore Christ is the true and essential GOD. Where it is replied most ineptly that in those passages indeed the eternal GOD is designated, because it is expressly about the Creator: but here not at all, because it is about Christ, who is from the Fathers. For what is this here except a most vain begging of the question? And would not the eternal GOD have been designated in Rom. I. 25., if by chance the name of Creator had not been added? Does not that very phrase εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας import a periphrasis of the true and essential GOD? Then we also see that the name of Creator is not added in 2. Cor. XI. 31. and yet the true and natural GOD is understood, when it is said ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας: nay even, when the word εὐλογητῷ occurs only absolutely, as in Mark XIV. 61. the eternal GOD is designated, how much more here, where GOD over all is celebrated as εὐλογητὸς for ever. Although indeed it is about Christ, who is from the Fathers according to the flesh, that we are dealing here, in what way we ourselves acknowledge Christ not to be eternal, yet it is not because he is from the Fathers or according to the flesh that he is called GOD blessed for ever: But as we warned before, those things are distinguished in Christ, that according to which he is from the Fathers, or flesh, or human nature, and that according to which he is GOD blessed for ever over all: According to which that Christ is also the Creator, besides the fact that it is sufficiently evident from this, that no one other than the God blessed for ever is the Creator, is expressly asserted in Col. I. 16. Heb. I. 2. and elsewhere. What then is that opposition between God the blessed Creator, and Christ God blessed? Because Adam by reason of his body is from the earth, is he also to be said to be from the earth by reason of his soul, which GOD peculiarly breathed into him? Certainly Christ, who by reason of the Flesh is from the Fathers, is no more to be said to be from the Fathers by reason of his divinity.

To (8.) Resp. That the reason is different when the word κατὰ σάρκα is used of other men, and when it is used of Christ: nor can one conclude from that usage to the present usage of the word. In Romans IV. verse 1. Abraham is denied to have found anything according to the flesh. In Chapter IX. verse 3. the Jews are called Paul's kinsmen κατὰ σάρκα. But here Christ is said to be from the Jews τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, as far as the flesh is concerned, who also exists as GOD blessed over all. Who does not see the difference? Since in those places the flesh is not distinguished from the Deity, which is done clearly here, by the force of which distinction, just as human nature is understood by the flesh, so by Θεὸν εὐλογητὸν etc. the divine nature must necessarily be understood. Schlichtingius, on page 254, admits that human essence is understood by 'flesh,' where he says that Christ, with respect to his essence, which was flesh or human (essence), is said to have sprung from the Israelites. Volckelius, in the place cited on page 469, does not deny that divinity is attributed to Christ, but he denies that the divinity which Paul seems to attribute to Christ signifies the divine nature of substance. But Scripture knows no other Deity (properly and truly so called) than that of the divine essence. Just as humanity is nothing other than human nature itself, so too is Deity nothing other than divine nature itself. Just as a man is a man through human essence, so GOD is not [GOD] except through Deity, or divine essence. The opposition admits of no other interpretation than that, just as human nature is understood by 'flesh,' so in the other member the divine nature is insinuated, when He is called GOD blessed forever over all things. Enjedinus concludes in the same manner on page 368. He expressly states this (1. Timoth. III. 15.) is opposed to flesh. Therefore, if flesh signifies human nature, God cannot signify anything but divine nature. This is Enjedinus. Which (divine nature) is also always and everywhere inferred, when in the Scriptures the word God is properly employed, or is used absolutely, or God blessed, or God over all is expressed, how much more when all those things are joined, which cannot be taken otherwise according to the tenor of the Holy Scriptures, than that the divine nature is inserted. Hence Theodoret in this place says that it was sufficient for declaring the Deity of the Lord that he added according to the flesh, but just as in the preface when he had said, Made of the seed of David according to the flesh, he subjoined, declared the Son of GOD in power: so here when he had said According to the flesh, he added, God, who is blessed for ever; that he might show the difference of nature, and deservedly mourning might teach, &c. Compare what we have said in our Anti-Crellius Exam. I. Sect. 2. c. 3. And so much for the present concerning this passage.

PART II. Didactic concerning the truth of the promises of grace made to the Israelites.

Latin:

ὧν οἱ πατέρες.

Quos jure sanguinis contingunt magni illi viri Abra- ham, Isaac & Jacob, quorum tam libenter Deus meminit, Exod. VI. 3. Lev. XXVI. 42. & qui per excellentiam Patres dicuntur Exod. III. 13, 16. IV. 5. XIII. 5. & alibi.

καὶ ἐξ ὧν ὁ χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα.

Non secundùm τὸ Θεῖον quod in ipso, sed secundùm τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. Vide supra I. 3. Τὸ κατὰ σάρκα opponitur τῷ κατὰ πνεῦμα. Illo humana, hoc divina natura notatur: & particu- la τὸ distinctionem refert, ac aliud quid, secundùm quod Christus est Deus benedictus in secula, infert, nimirum divinam Christi naturam, qui idem se- cundùm humanam naturam est ex Patribus. Conf. Joh. I. 14. Rom. I. 3. 1. Timoth. III. 16. Ebr. II. 14. 1. Pet. III. 18. Constat ergo hinc unionis persona- lis divinæ & humanæ naturæ veritas.

ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων Θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας.

Potest hoc de Christo rectè sic intelligi, quia cum dicitur super omnia, tacitè excipitur Pater 1. Cor. XV. 27. Sed ex Syro apparet, veteres codices habuisse: ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων ἐν- λογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, quod consuetæ locutioni Pauli me- lius convenit, qui cùm de Patre & Filio loquitur, Patri no- men Dei, Filio nomen Domini tribuere solet. Et sic fuisse in vetustis codicibus Cypriani, sic etiam legisse Hilarium, nec aliter videri legisse Chrysostomum, notavit Erasmus. Et satis erat huic quidem loco, dicere hoc privilegium Ju- dæorum, quod ex illis natus esset Christus omnibus aliis majus esse, quia Christo laus & honor debetur supra omnes, id est, etiam supra Abrahamum, Isaacum & Jacobum.

ἀμήν.

Sic Amen insertum habuimus, & supra in Dei laudatione I. 25. sic & infra XI. 36. & XVI. 27. Gal. I. 5. Eph. III. 21. Philip. IV. 20. 1. Tim. I. 17.

Socinianis velificatur hæc annotatio, quâ fingitur nomen Θεῦ esse βεμβολιμαῖον vel irreptitium: At temerè. Erasmus non est quod hic moremur, qui non rarò Arianis κρησφύγεῖα in Scripturis parat. Neque vel Syrus, (quanquam hic falsò adducatur à Grotio) vel etiam codex aliquis Latinus præjudicare Græcis codicibus universis, & purioribus Latinis aliorumq; Patrum lectioni constanti potest. Pauli autẽ locutioni magis convenire omissionem nominis Dei, futile est: quia Paulum Christum Deum dicere ex Act. XX. 28. 1. Tim. III. 16. Tit. II. 14. notum est. Id autem vel maxime faciebat ad ἐξοχὴν populi, quem summis suis dignitatibus extollere volebat Apostolus, quod ex ipsis Christus sit, non tantum Patriarchis omnibus eminentior (uti vim elogii enervat Hugo) sed Deus ille benedictus in secula super omnia: Neque verò illis verbis, si negligatur etiam vox Θεῦ, talis solùm eminentia designatur, sed divinæ naturæ dignitas, & majestas exprimitur. Is enim, qui est super omnia benedictus in secula, est verus & essentialis Deus. Rom. I. 25. Luc. I. 68. 2. Cor. I. 3. c. XI. 31. Eph. I. 3. 1. Pet. I. 3. Quod cum probè videret Erasmus, non ad Christum, sed ad Patrem hoc elogium, interjecto puncto, per fictitiam quandam exclamationem abripuit, ne Deitati Christi adstruendæ inserviret. Cujus vero depravatio ne ipsi quidem Socino probari potuit, ut annotatum T. III. Syst. Theol. pag. 46: ubi pluribus de hoc loco actum, & observatum, non tantùm apud alios Patres, sed etiam apud Cyprianum & Hilarium in editionibus melioribus (cæteris in mendo cubantibus) ut & penes Syriacum Interpretem vocem Θεὸς reperiri. Quam nec versio Racov. Socin. Germanica prætermisit. Optimè ergò Cassianus lib. III. de Incarnat. Quando Paulus dicit, Christum esse Deum, hic sufficit Christianis; quando verò addit, esse DEUM benedictum supra omnia, omnem blasphemiam perfidæ assertionis excludit. Conferatur Theol. Apost. Roman. orac. LXVII. Syrus ita habet: Ex quibus apparuit Christus in carne, qui est super omnia, cujus sunt laudes & benedictiones in seculum seculorum Amen.

Addimus pro vindicando illustri loco & argumento Deitatis Christi, quæ ante XXX. circiter annos de eodem contra Socinianos expedivimus, utpote nondum cum Ecclesiâ Christi communicata. Dignissimum enim est hoc æternæ Deitatis Christi testimonium, quod solide vindicetur.

Varia autem hinc argumenta peti possunt. (1) quod Christus absolutè vocetur Θεὸς, Deus: quod nomen absolutè non tribuitur, nisi soli & uni vero DEO. (2.) quod dicatur esse ἐπὶ πάντων. Qui enim simpliciter & universaliter est ἐπὶ πάντων super omnia, is est verus naturâ DEUS: quum non nisi unus & solus DEUS simpliciter sit ἐπὶ πάντων, super omnia. (3.) quod vocetur ἐυλογητός. Quia hoc epitheton non nisi uni & soli DEO vero vindicatur in S. literis, quod ex inductione locorum Sacrorum demonstratur, Marc. XIV. 61. Luc. I. 68. Rom. I. 25. 2. Cor. I. 3. II. 31. Eph. I. 3. 1. Pet. I. 3. & ab ipso Enjedino conceditur p. 265. usque adeò, inquit, peculiare epitheton est DEO ἐυλογητός, ut NULLI præterquam ipsi in Novo Testamento attributum legatur. Hinc fit, ut posita solùm illa ἐυλογητῦ voce Deus Pater intelligatur, ut Marc. XIV. 61. (4.) quod nominetur Deus ἐυλογητὸς εἰς αἰῶνας, additâ particula confirmationis ἀμήν. Hæc enim descriptio & glorificatio æterni DEI propria est, secundum tenorem sacrarum literarum, & ipsius Apostoli stylum: Rom. I. 25. Servierunt creaturæ præter Creatore: ὅς ἐστιν ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας Ἀμήν. 2. Cor. XI. 31. ὁ Θεὸς, Deus & Pater

Domini nostri Jesu Christi novit, ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, qui uterque locus nostro similis est. Gemina est δοξολογία Apostolo familiaris, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ἀμὴν, quæ eidem uni vero & æterno DEO propria est, ut è locorum inductio- ne constat. Rom. XVI. 27. Phil. II. 20. Ebr. XIII. 21. 1. Petr. V. 11. &c. Christo autem tribuitur 2. Pet. III. 18. ut & 2. Tim. IV. 18. (5.) Quod non tantùm εὐλογητὸς, sed ἐπὶ πάντων εὐλογητὸς super omnia benedictus prædicatur. Nam præterquam quod nomen εὐλογητὸς per se & absolute positum satis innuat, Christum esse verum Deum, quem Hebræi summum & benedictum illum vocant, הקדוש ברוח הוא id est, הקדש & nomen illud benedictum היתב id est, השם יתברך quid cla- rius est, quam elogio isto toto ἐπὶ πάντων εὐλογητὸς super omnia benedictus ipsum summum Deum de- signari, qui solus super omnia benedictus est, & di- citur. (6.) Quod luculenter distinguatur in Chri- sto caro, seu humana natura, & Deitas, vel divina ejus natura, cum dicitur Christus esse ex Patribus τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, quod ad carnem seu humanam na- turam attinet, & esse tamen quoque eum θεὸν εὐλο- γητὸν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, Deum benedictum in secula, quod quum ratione carnis vel humanæ naturæ esse negetur vi verborum Apostoli, relinquitur in Chri- sto aliam esse sublimiorem naturam, secundum quam ipse sit Deus benedictus in secula. Agno- scere sanè coactus fuit Adam Goslavius à Bebelno part. 1. contr. Kekerm. c. I. pag. 5. particulam τὸ appositam (in verbis τὸ κατὰ σάρκα) nihil aliud si- gnificare, quàm Christum, quantus, quantus est, non esse ex Judæis, sed solum secundùm carnem. E. præ- ter carnem vel naturam humanam aliud esse opor- tet in Christo, quod non sit è Judæis, secundùm quod sit Deus super omnia benedictus in secula, quod ad Christum constituendum non minus per- tineat, quàm caro. Quod quid aliud esse potest, quàm ipsa Deitas, per quam est Deus super omnia benedictus in secula, uti per carnem vel humanam naturam est homo. (7.) Urgemus autem nunc potissimum descriptionem illam, eamque inte- gram, quæ prorsus apodicticè confirmat nostram fidem: Quicunque est super omnia Deus benedi- ctus in secula, is verus & essentialis Deus est. At Christus est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula. E. Major probatur tùm quia hic descriptio est veri & æterni Dei propria, à descriptione autem vel definitione ad definitum, invicta est consequentia: tùm quia elogium hoc soli & uni DEO vindicatur in scripturis: Cui ergò id ipsum tribuitur, is cre- dendus est unus ille verus Deus: tùm quia emi- nentia summi Dei hac phrasi infertur, dum dicitur ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς: tùm quia glorificatio verè divina non nisi uni Deo convenit. Quæ exprimitur hisce verbis: εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας; tùm deniq; quia non tantùm universa Ecclesia inde ab Apo- stolorum tempore hanc descriptionem suscepit, ceu περίφρασιν ipsius veri, summi, & æterni Dei, sed & adversarii ipsi id admittere & agnoscere co- guntur, eandem non nisi uni vero & æterno Deo convenire. Cassian. l. 3. de incarnat. Quando Paulus dicit, Christum esse Deum, hoc sufficit Christianis; quando verò addit, esse Deum super omnia, eo omnem blasphemiam perfidæ assertionis excludit. Enjed. l. c. argumentum hoc admodum validum in scripturis esse ait, quod nimirum, ubicunque hoc encomium le- gitur, illud semper attribuatur Patri ceu vero & æterno Deo, adeoque, ut scripturæ analogia salva sit, hic quoque de eodem intelligendum esse conclu- dit: Antecedens ex inductione locorum probat. Ita ergò analogia scripturæ salva esse non potest, fatente Enjedino, nisi admittatur, hic quoque eo elogio designari verum & æternum DEUM, ut cui soli hoc elogium & epitheton semper attribuitur, & vindicatur in scripturis, profitente & confirmante Enjedino. Socinus verò, Smalcius, & alii, dum id agunt, ut nova interpretatione hoc elogium DEO Patri hoc in loco vindicetur, satis testantur, sese in conscientia sua convictos esse, id uni vero DEO proprium esse. Sanè cum illi de Patre hoc acce- prum volunt, largiuntur vel inviti, veri & æterni DEI descriptionem hanc esse non minus, atque veri ac æterni DEI descriptio est, cum Rom. I. 25. & 2. Cor. XI. 31. occurrit, ut taceam, quod nomen DEI hic subjectivè occurrat, quo pacto id non nisi uni & soli æterno DEO convenire, Socinus, Smal- cius, & alii adversarii acriter contendunt. Mino- rem ipsa Apostoli verba exhibent: de Christo enim profitetur, quod non tantum sit ex Patribus secundum carnem, sed quod idem etiam sit ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας; quod proinde tota Ecclesia semper de Christo intelle- xit, quia aliter, vi verborum Apostoli, non potuit, nec inficiatus Socinus, Goslavius, Nicolaides, Ca- tech. Racov. verba illa ad Christum referenda, quorum verba propria postmodum producturi sumus.

Hujus veritatis solem variis nebulis obscurare, omnibus modis, sed frustra, satagunt adversarii, Enjedinus in expl. loc. Socin. contra Wujek pag. 263. & 355. Smalcius ref. disp. Grav. de pers. Christ. pag. 3. seqq. Goslavius part. 1. contra Kekerman. c. 5. Volckel. de ver. relig. p. 426. & 468. Schlich- ting. l. Trin. p. 234. & 254. Primò lectionem textus, deinde interpretationem, denique nostram illatio- nem sollicitantes. Unde (1.) ex annotationibus E- rasmi in N. T. ad h. l. obvertunt, vocem Deus hic suspectam esse: quum Cyprianus, Hilarius, Chryso- stomus eam non legerint, sed addita videatur En- jedino, ab aliquo Divinitatis Christi nimis studioso, & Arianorum hoste. (2.) Verba illa, qui est super omnia, &c. non referenda esse ad Christum proximè nominatum, sed ante ipsum punctum statui debere, quod illa à superioribus sejungat, ita ut ad DEUM absolute referantur, perinde ac si disertè scriptum fuisset: Ille qui est super omnia, DEUS sit benedi- ctus in secula; quæ Erasmi sententia cur rejicia- tur, nullam esse causam Socinus ait; Enjedinus ve- rò eandem etiam argumento confirmare nititur, quod nimirum ubique hoc elogium non Christo, sed Patri tribuatur. (3.) Vocem DEUS absolute hic positam non esse, quum addatur super omnia, quo indicari vult Socinus, nomen Deus pro Do- mino seu Dominatore divino accipiendum esse. (4.) Vocem ἐπὶ πάντων, super omnia non esse ita prorsus universè accipiendam, ut nihil omninò extra illum, de quo est sermo, excludatur, quum Pater excipiatur 1. Cor. XV. 27. Sic vocem πάντων reddi posse omnes, vocem autem omnes ad homines tantum referri solere, ait Socin. pag. 265. (4.) Nihil esse super omnia, nisi illum unum Deum Israël̈is, non esse simpliciter verum, sed ita tantum, si istud esse super omnia intelligatur ex natura sua, sive ex seipso, & vox omnia universaliter prorsus acci- piatur. Christum autem ex dono Dei esse super omnia, neq; id natura sua habere, nec super omnia absolute & universaliter esse (7.) Smalcius excipit, Paulum quidem de æterno Deo dicere, eum esse be- nedictum in secula, at non dicere, quicunque est Deus benedictus in secula, eum esse æternum Deum. Verba illa Rom. I. 25. æternum Deum significare, quia de Creatore disertè prædicantur. At Rom. IX. 5. æternum Deum non significare, quia de Christo, qui est secundum carnem ex Patri- bus, dicta sunt. (8.) Goslavius ad argumentum è distinctione particulà τὸ κατὰ σάρκα indigitatà re- gerit l. c. p. 67. quod etiam alibi de aliis dicatur τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, qui duntaxat homines, ut Rom. IV. 1. c. IX. 3. Atque hæ sunt adversariorum præcipuæ exceptiones, quæ ordine discutiendæ jam erunt.

Quod ad (1.) Resp. Vocem θεὸς omnia legunt exemplaria Græca, nec in ullo unquam deprehen- sa est eadem defuisse. Testantur id, qui probatissi- ma & antiquissima contulere exemplaria, Stepha- nus, Aldus, Theodor. Beza, Isaacus Casaubonus, & Erasmus ipse: nec quisquam est, qui contrarium observavit in illo Codice Græco. Consonant in- super Græcis codd. latinæ editiones, ut & transla- tio perantiqua Syriaca. Legerunt vocem eam et- iam tractatores & Dd. veteres, Irenæus, Origenes, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Ambrosius, Hilarius, Epi- phanius, Cyrillus Alexandr. Chrysostomus, Theodo- retus, Idacus Clarius, Augustinus, Fulgentius, &c. Denique causa nulla est, cur suspecta habenda sit. In editionibus Cypriani l. 2. advers. Jud. c. 5. eam omittentibus manifestum est mendum librariorũ, quandoquidem & ἐπιγραφὴ vel inscriptio hujus- ce capitis, & locorum eodem productorũ confide- ratio evincat, ea producta esse testimonia, quibus nomen DEI Filio Dei expresse vindicatur. Si verò hoc in loco nomen Dei haud lectum fuisset, quo- modo Cyprianus testimonium istud inter ea re- censere potuisset, quibus expresse nomen DEI Christo adscribitur? Adde, quod Jacobus Pamelius nomẽ Deus in omnibus MM.SS. invenerit, tũ suis, tum quibus usi sunt Manutius & Morelius, unde in editione sua Cypriani non omisit, uti nec in editio- ne Goulartiana omittitur. De Hilarii loco in Ps. CXXII. idem esto judicium, quũ is ideò citet Pauli dictum, ut probet, Christum esse Deum; unde Era- smus ipse in annot. ad Rom. IX. 5. p. 415. fatetur, in- curià librariorum nomen Deus omissum videri posse. Addidit id expresse Parisiensis Hilarii editio: Legitur quoq; eadem apud Hilarium l. IV. & IIX. de Trinit. De Chrysost. notat saltim Erasmus, quod non utatur hujus testimonii telo adversus Arianos, & quod subobscurus sit ejus in hunc locũ Comen- tarius. Quod verò non deprehenderit Chrysost. in suis codd. vocem θεὸς non licet è Chrysost. depre- hendere, nec id asseruit Erasmus, quia addit, Chrysost. vocem eam lectam, textum autem aliter di- stinctum fuisse. Frustrà itaque suspicatur Enjedinus, & perquàm temerè, additam videri ab aliquo Aria- norum hoste, quum in nullo unquam deprehensa fuerit eadem defuisse. Et qui ab Arianorum hoste addita videri potest, quum lecta sit ante Arianos natos à Tertulliano c. 13. adv. Prax. qui solam Chri- stum, inquit, potest Deum dicere, sicut idem Aposto- lus, qui est Deus benedictus in omne ævum, imò & ab ipso Cypriano, uti jam monitum, nec non ab Irenæo, qui l. III. adv. hæres. c. 18. ita id adducit, quorum Pa- tres, & ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est Deus super omnia benedictus in secula.

Quod ad (2.) Resp. Interpunctio illa, ab Enje- dino excogitata, 1) Nova prorsus, & antehac inau- dita in Ecclesia. 2) Omnibus Codd. Græcis con- traria, quũ nullum fide dignum & probatum exem- plar proferri possit, in quo hypostigma vel punctũ positum sit post vocem κατὰ σάρκα, sed coma vel virgula tantum reperiatur. 3) Non congruit epi- phonema illud exclamatoriũ εὐχαρισικω̂ν & δοξο-λογικω̂ν antecedentibus. Quia versatur Apostolus in testando συμπαθείας & amoris animatissimi af- fectu: Tristitia mihi magna est, inquit v. 2. & conti- nuus dolor cordi meo. Optabam ego ipse, pergit v. 3. anathema esse pro fratribus, quorum jam describit gloriam, & inter alia, quod ex iis sit Christus secun- dum carne. Qui ergò jam ex abrupto in δοξολογίαν abiret. Quæ causa vel ratio ejusdem? dolet, optat, non gratulatur. Commemorat dignitatem ipso- rum, non ut Deum celebret, sed ut causam doloris & voti anathematis exaggeret. (4.) Nec magis congruit ea δοξολογία consequentibus. Conti- nuat quippe Apostolus sermonem, & quidem ita, ut nullus interjectæ ejusmodi explicationi locus concedatur. Quomodo enim illa cohærerent, optabam esse anathema pro fratribus &c. ex quibus est Christus secundùm carnem: Qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula, Amen. Non autem quod exciderit verbum DEI. Nulla igitur συνέχεια, nulla συνάφεια relinquitur. (5.) Scopus Apostoli est, extollere dignitatem gentis Judaicæ, quam in- ter alia imprimis inde confirmat, quod ex iisdem sit Christus secundùm carnem, & ex summa digna- tionis hujus eminentiâ, quod is sit super omnia DEUS benedictus in secula. Quid enim eviden- tius hac ἀναλύσει? meritò lugere se dixit, ait Theo- dor. in hoc loco, quod ex ipsis sit quidam Dominus secundùm carnem, qui est Deus super omnia; ipsi autem à nobilitate exciderunt, & ab illo cognomine alieni facti sunt. (6.) Socinus reddit rationem, cur Erasmi interpretatio rejicienda sit: Ea hæc est, quod cum simplex nomen, Benedictus, idem signi- ficat, quod Benedictus sit, semper ferè soleat ante- poni ei, ad quem refertur, perrarò autem postponi. Hic autem præmittitur vox Θεὸς, l. c. p. 263. (7.) Syriaca interpretatio illam retulit expresse ad Christum: Ex gentibus Judaicis apparuit Messias in carne, qui est DEUS supra omnia, cui sunt lau- des & benedictiones in seculum seculorum Amen. Sic & Vulgata Latina. (8.) Universa Ecclesia inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, quantum ex publi- cis constat documentis, sequuta simplicem verbo- rum tenorem nulli errori obnoxium. Ita Irenæus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Cyprianus, Ambrosius lib. 1. de Sp. S. cap. 3. Hilarius, Epiphanius hær. LVII. Noëtianorum cap. 2. Cyrill. Alexandr. Ep. ad A- nastas. Tom. I. p. 2. Fulgent. l. 1. ad Trasim. Theo- doret. Hieronymus, Augustinus, Idacus Clarius lib. contr. Varimund. Novatianus l. de Trin. cap. 13. & 30. Theophylact. in h. l. &c. (9.) Quid quod Socinus ipse, ejusque discipuli cum agnoscant ver- ba illa ad Christum referri dexterè. Socinus l. c. Facilè concedo, inquit, verba prolati Paulini testi- monii omnia ad Christum referenda esse. Catech. Racov. cap. 1. S. Paulus nennet den, welcher nach dem Fleisch aus den Vätern gewesen, einen GOtt über alle gebenedeyet. Goslavius l. c. Liben- tissime concedimus h. l. vocabulo DEI Christum re- ferri. Val. Smalcius l. de divin. Christ. c. 12. Ju- stè hoc Domino Jesu Christo competit, quod eum Pau- lus appellavit DEUM benedictum in secula. Theoph. Nicolaides, contra Albert. Borkowsky de Eccles. c. 8. Christum appellamus DEUM cum S. Johanne cap. I. cum Thoma Joh. XX. cum Paulo Rom. IX. 5. ob divinitatem, eamque veram & propriam. Conf. Johan. Volckel. de V. R. p. 426. Joh. Crell. Tr. de uno DEO Lat. fat. 2. c. 3. & Schlichting. l. c. deni- que versio Racov. N. T. Germanicâ reprobatâ E- rasmianâ vulgatam interpunctionem sequitur, vi cujus ad Christum necessariò nomen DEUS re- fertur.

Ad (3.) Resp. Si vox DEUS absolutè & sim- pliciter adhibita verum & essentialem DEUM notat, vim hujus significationis non imminuet, sed confirmabit potius additamentum illud, quod sit super omnia benedictus in secula. Tò super omnia referri potest vel ad vocem εὐλογητὸς, at- que ita DEUS benedictus super omnia non dominator tantum aliquis divinus intelligi potest, sed verus & essentialis DEUS, qui solus est be- nedictus ille super omnia Deus; vel ad vocem θεὸν & tùm ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς, qui est super omnia Deus rursus non convenire potest homini alicui divino saltem dominio prædito, sed ipsum Deum Deorum, utpote qui solus Deus est super omnia importat. Quid? num θεὸς ἐπὶ πάντων, Ephes. IV. 6. divinum tantum dominatorem denotat, annon DEI illius unius expressa est περίφρασις?

Ad (4.) Resp. Nihil est, quod vocem ἐπὶ πάντων absolutè & universaliter positam restrin- gendam esse doceat, quum in celebranda Deita- te Christi versetur Apostolus, eamque ita depræ- dicet, ut non deroget, aut imminuat quicquam, sed super omnia evehat. Adde, quod eadem prorsus loquendi ratio sit, quæ de Deo Patre Eph. IV. 6. occurrit, qui θεὸς ἐπὶ πάντων dicitur. Quæ verò causa, quod una eademque loquendi ratio, absque diversitatis indicio, cum de Patre occur- rit, denotare debeat Deum summum, quod ab- solutè sit super omnia, cum autem de Filio DEI Deum summum non denotet, qui sit absolutè su- per omnia. Proinde concludimus: Deus ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, qui est super omnia, secundùm phrasin scripturæ receptam, est verus & summus Deus, ut ex Eph. IV. 6. manifestissimum est. At Christus est Deus ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, qui super omnia est. E. Item: Qui ab Apostolo vocatur θεὸς ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, est summus ille DEUS: At Christus ab Apostolo vo- catur θεὸς ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων. E. Christus est summus ille Deus. Si dicas, disparem esse rationem loci Ephes. IV. 6. & hujusce præsentis, quod ibi de Patre, hic de Christo agatur, quid hoc aliud, quam principium petere? Idem prorsus est prædica- tum, nec diversum ejus sensum esse hic & illic, Apostoli, doceri potest. Id verò frivolum est, non accipi prorsus universè vocem πάντων, eò quod Pater excipiatur. 1. Cor. XV. 27. Nam præ- terquam, quod Apostolus ibi saltem doceat, Pa- trem excipi, ubi quomodo Christo sint omnia subjecta secundum humanam naturam explicat, quum hic non spectetur τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, quantum ad carnem, vel humanam naturam, sed quà est Deus benedictus in secula: Fatetur ipse Soci- nus, tùm prorsus universè accipi vocem πάντα, cum nihil EXTRA DEUM, de quo est sermo, excipitur. At extra Christum Deum nihil omni- nò excipitur, cum dicitur esse super omnia. Pater enim non est extra Christum, ut & nec Spiritus S. sed unum cum Christo, 1. Joh. V. 7. Nihil itaque à Christi natura, qua est Deus benedictus in secu- la, diversum excipitur, super quod Christus non sit. Pater autem uti diversus non est à Christi natura, quia is est Deus benedictus ille, ita non minus, quàm Christus super omnia esse depræ- dicatur, adeoque eo ipso tum quod Christus æquè ut Pater sit Deus ille benedictus in secula, tùm quod æquè ut Pater DEUS dicatur super omnia, ipsa identitas naturæ cum Patre concluditur. Quis ergò non rideret nugas de exceptione Patris? At infert Schlichtingius, cum Pater dicitur super omnia, ne Christus quidem excipitur. Verum utut Christus non excipiatur τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, quod ad carnem attinet, excipitur tamen Christus, quà est Deus benedictus in secula. Ita enim ipse non minus quàm Pater prædicatur θεὸς ἐπὶ πάντων, Deus su- per omnia. Qui ergo non exciperetur? Num idem est supra seipsum secundum idem?

Ad (5.) Resp. Si maximè reddatur vox πάν- των omnes, non imminuetur Deitas Christi. Qui enim Deus est benedictus super omnes, eum Deum Deorum esse quis dubitet? Et quî Christus tan- tum Deus super omnes homines prædicetur? An- non etiam est super alias Creaturas? Cur eadem illa phrasis, cum de DEO Patre occurrit θεὸς ἐπὶ πάντων, reddenda DEUS supra omnia, de Christo autem ita non reddenda? Annon Christus ante OMNIA, & OMNIA in ipso consistunt? Col. I. 17. Latini certè Interpp. & tractatores reddidere super OMNIA, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Novatianus, Ambrosius, Hilarius, Idacus Clarus, Fulgentius, aliique. Nec aliter reddit Vulgatus interpres. Quum quod ipse Socinus, Smalcius, & alii non semel hoc dictum ita allegent, super OMNIA benedictus. Enjedinus pag. 266. Quid hinc aliud, ait, consequentur adversarii, quàm quod Christus sit super omnia, sit Deus, sit benedictus in secula. Quæ omnia nos de Christo, utpote alibi quoque testata, sigillatim confitemur.

Ad (6.) Resp. Qui est super omnia naturâ suâ, vel etiam qui est super omnia universè prorsus accepta, ille est unus DEUS Israëlis. Hæc utraque propositio est adversariorum. Subsumimus: Christus, qui est DEUS benedictus in secula, est super omnia naturâ: Idem est super omnia universè prorsus accepta. Hoc posterius jam obtinuimus: & è Col. I. vers. 17. cumprimis constat. Quicunque est ante OMNIA prorsus universè accepta, ante omnes Creaturas, ille etiam est super OMNIA, prorsus universè accepta, super omnes scil. Creaturas. Prius autem inde patet: Quia implicat contradictionem in adjecto, DEUM benedictum in secula super omnia, quà talis est, habere aliquid non naturâ suâ, sed dono & ex gratia. Ita enim nec DEUS foret proprie, nedum benedictus ille DEUS, minimè omnium benedictus DEUS super omnia. Qui super omnia est, is, quà talis, non potest aliunde dependere; alioquin non super omnia foret, sed haberet aliquem sese superiorem potestate, à quo ipse dependeat, idque habeatur, quod super reliqua sit. Quod movetur de Christo à Patre è gratia evecto super omnia, ἀλλότριον est κὶ ἐξαγώνιον. Non enim hoc contigit Christo, quà est DEUS benedictus in secula, si enim ante omnia fuit, non demum in tempore constitutus est super omnia: Sed τὸ κατὰ σάρκα quantum ad Carnem, seu humanam naturam.

Ad (7.) Resp. Paulus de nullo alio, quam de æterno DEO docet, quod sit DEUS benedictus in secula, nec quisquam alius scriptor θεόπνευστος. Tota Scriptura S. uni & soli æterno Deo hoc elogium, & quæ ei gemina sunt præconia vendicat: nec ullus in contrarium è Scripturis proferri potest locus. Immota ergò manet propositio: Quicunque est DEUS benedictus in secula, est verus & essentialis hic æternus Deus, quam nullâ infringere poterunt adversarii instantiâ. Præterea cum hæc sit περίφρασις, & descriptio DEI propria, non potest non invicta fieri illatio. Cuicunque descriptio convenit æterni DEI propria, is æternus est DEUS. Denique si loca illa Rom. I. 25. & 2. Corinth. XI. 31. conferantur, quid evidentius hac ἀποδείξει, is, qui Apostolicâ Phrasi est DEUS benedictus in secula, est verus & essentialis DEUS, testibus illis locis Apostoli: At Christus, Apostolicâ phrasi, est DEUS benedictus in secula. Non enim videndum, quo pacto possint voces illæ accipi secundum corruptelas Socinianas, sed quid phrasi Apostolicâ importent & significent. E. Christus est verus & essentialis DEUS. Ubi non nisi ineptissimè regeritur, iis locis quidem æternum DEUM designari, quia de Creatore disertè agitur: hic vero minimè, quia de Christo, qui est è Patribus. Quid enim hic præterquam vanissima principii petitio? Et num Rom. I. 25. non designatus fuisset æternus DEUS, si fortę Creatoris nomen additum non fuisset? Annè ipsâ illâ phrasi εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας importatur περίφρασις veri & essentialis DEI? Tum etiam videmus non addi nomen Creatoris 2. Cor. XI. 31. & intelligitur tamen verus & naturalis DEUS, cum dicitur ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας: imò etiam, cum absolutè tantum vox εὐλογητῷ occurrit, ut Marc. XIV. 61. DEUS æternus designatur, quantò magis hic, ubi DEUS super omnia εὐλογητὸς in secula celebratur. Quanquam verò de Christo, qui est è Patribus secundum carnem, hic agatur, quo pacto Christum non esse æternum ipsimet agnoscimus, non tamen quàd est è Patribus vel secundum carnem, dicitur DEUS benedictus in secula: Sed ut anteà monuimus, distinguuntur illa in Christo, secundum quod est è Patribus, vel caro, aut natura humana, & id secundum quod est DEUS benedictus in secula super omnia: Juxta quod Christum etiam Creatorem esse, præterquam quod ex eo satis constet, quod non alius quam Deus benedictus in secula Creator sit, expressè asseritur Col. I. 16. Ebr. I. 2. & alibi. Quæ ergò illa oppositio, inter Deum benedictum Creatorem, & Christum Deum benedictum? Num quia Adam ratione corporis è terra est, etiam ratione animæ è terra esse dicendus est, quam peculiariter ei DEUS inspiravit: Non magis certè Christus, qui ratione Carnis est è Patribus, dicendus est è Patribus esse ratione divinitatis?

Ad (8.) Resp. Dispartimam esse rationem, cum vox κατὰ σάρκα de aliis hominibus usurpatur, & cum de Christo: nec ex illo usu concludi posse ad præsentem vocis usum Roman. IV. vers. 1. Abraham negatur, quid ἐυρηκέναι secundum carnem Cap. IX. vers. 3. Judæi dicuntur Pauli cognati κατὰ σάρκα. Hic autem Christus dicitur è Judæis esse τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, quod ad carnem attinet, qui & DEUS existit super omnia benedictus. Quis non videt diversitatem? Quandoquidem illis in locis non distinguitur caro à Deitate, quod hic luculenter fit, vi cujus distinctionis, ut per carnem humana natura, ita per Θεὸν εὐλογητὸν &c. divina natura intelligenda venit necessariò. Humanam autem essentiam per carnem intelligi fatetur Schlichtingius pag. 254. ubi Christum essentiæ suæ respectu, quæ caro, seu humana (essentia) fuit, ex Israëlitis ortum dici ait: Divinitatem etiam Christo tribui non negat Volckelius loc. cit. pag. 469. sed constare negat divinitatem, quam Paulus Christo tribuere videtur, divinam significare naturam substantiæ. At nullam aliam Deitatem (propriè & verè ita dictam) novit scriptura, quàm divinæ essentiæ. Ut humanitas alia non est ab ipsâ humanâ naturâ, ita nec Deitas ab ipsâ divinâ naturâ. Ut homo per humanam essentiam est homo, ita DEUS non est, nisi per Deitatem, seu essentiam divinam. Oppositio non admittit aliter, quam ut per carnem intelligitur humana natura, ita in membro altero insinuatur divina natura, cum DEUS benedictus in secula dicitur super omnia. Ad eundem modum concludit Enjedinus pag. 368. Disertè hoc (1. Timoth. III. 15.) opponitur carni. E. si caro humanam significat naturam, non Deus poterit nisi divinam significare naturam. Hoc Enjed. Quæ (divina natura) etiam semper & ubique infertur, cum in Scripturis Dei vox propriè adhi- betur, vel absolutè usurpatur, vel Deus benedictus, aut Deus super omnia exprimitur, quantò magis cum omnia illa conjunguntur, quæ non possunt aliter accipi secundum tenorem S. literarum, quàm ut divina inseratur natura. Inde Theodo- retus in h. l. ad declarandam Domini Deitatem id satis fuisse, ait, quod addidit τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, sed quemadmodum in proœmio cum dixisset, Factus ex semine David secundum carnem, subjunxit, de- finitus est Filius DEI in virtute: ita hic cum dixisset Secundùm carnem, adjecisse, Deum, qui est bene- dictus in secula; ut naturæ differentiam ostenderet, & meritò lugens doceret, &c. Conf. quæ diximus in Anti-Crellio nostro Exam. I. Sect. 2. c. 3. Et tan- tum impræsentiarum de hoc loco.

PARS II. Διδακτικὴ de veritate promissionum gratiæ Israëlitis factarum.

## 9:6
v. 6. But it is not as though the word of God hath taken none effect.

Although these things are true, he says, yet it cannot be that the word of God should be void, namely those threats which God in the law Levit. XXVI. 14. Deut. XXVII. 15. XXVIII. 15. Josh. XXIV. 20. and elsewhere, often pronounces against the contumacious Israelites. Thus Deut. IV. 30. all these words shall find thee, that is, those threats. οὐχ οἷον to the Rabbis is it is impossible. ἐκπίπτειν is to be made void 1 Sam. III. 19. there let none of his words fall to the ground, so also Joshua XXI. 45.

For they are not all Israel, who are of Israel.

The cause of the name, for which Jacob was called Israel by God, does not belong to all who are sprung from Jacob, Gen. XXXII. 28. see Josephus on this history. That name, as Tertullian rightly understood, belongs especially to the Martyrs, for they surpass the Angels in this part, that, which is the greatest honor, it happens to them to die for God. Justin disputing against Trypho: But you, understanding nothing of these things nor preparing to understand, since you are children of Jacob according to the fleshly seed, expect to be saved in every way; but that you are deceived in these things also has been demonstrated to me in many places. Philo on Nobility: But these are common boundaries for all men, not to be proud of great families if they lack virtue. But there are also other judgments of common things; for the virtues of ancestors do not profit at all those who are caught in reprehensible and blameworthy actions, even if they are not convicted by others, but by their own conscience, which alone is not led astray by the chances of words from any judges. The Apostle does not treat of the truth of threats, but of divine promises, weighing the doubt, how this has been fulfilled, when the Israelites have become anathema from Christ, for whom he himself had wished to become anathema. For to these were given those promises of grace. Whence, to remove that scruple, he teaches that not all are Israel who descend from Israel or Jacob, that not all are genuine Israel, and that they do not deserve this name with Jacob, who obtained it through faith: and so that those are finally true Israelites who conquer with Israel through faith Gen. XXXII.

Latin:

v. 6. ὐχ οἶον δὲ ὅτι ἐκπέπτωκεν ὁ λόγος τῶ Θεῦ.

Quanquam hæc vera sunt, inquit, tamen fieri nequit, ut irritus sit sermo Dei, nempè minæ illæ, quas Deus in lege Levit. XXVI. 14. Deut. XXVII. 15. XXVIII. 15. Joh. XXIV. 20. & alibi, sæpe adversus contumaces Israëlitas pronun- ciat. Sic Deut. IV. 30. εὑρήσεσί σε πάντες οἱ λόγοι ὗτοι, id est, minæ istæ οὐχ οἷον Rabbinis est אי אפשר ἐκπίπτειν נפל est irritum fieri 1. Sam. III. 19. ἐκ ἔπεσεν ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν λόγων ἀυτὲ ἐπὶ γῆν, sic & Josuæ XXI. 45.

ἐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ ἰσραὴλ ὗτοι ἰσραὴλ.

Non omnibus ex Jacobo ortis competit causa nominis, propter quam Jacobus à Deo vocatus est Israël, Genes. XXXII. 28. ad quam historiam Josephum vide. Convenit id nomen, ut Tertullianus rectè intellexit, eximiè Marty- ribus, Angelos enim hac parte superant, quod, qui maxi- mus est honos, pro Deo mori eis contingit. Justinus con- tra Tryphonem disputans: ὑμεῖς δὲ μηδὲν τύτων νενοηκότες μηδὲ νοεῖν παρασκευαζόμενοι, ἐπειδὴ κατὰ τὸ σαρκικὸν σπέρμα τῦ ἰακὼβ τέκνα ἐστὲ, πάντως σωθήσεσθαι προσδοκᾶτε ἀλλ' ὅτι κ ἐκ τύτοις ἑαυτὲς πλανᾶτε ἀποδέδεικταί μοι ἐν πολλοῖς. Philo de Nobilitate: Ἀλλ' ὗτοι μὲν ἔσωσαν κοινοὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ὅροι τὲ μὴ ἐπὶ μεγάλοις γένεσι σεμνύνεσθαι τῆς καλοκαγαθίας ἀμοιρῦντας. ἐκδίκη δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι δίκᾳ τῶν κοινῶν ἐξαιρέτοι τῶν γὰρ τῷ γένες ἀρχηγετῶν εἰσιν ὥς οἱ τῶν προγόνων ἀρεταὶ συνόλως ὐδὲν ὤνησαν ἐπ' ἐπιλήπτοις κὶ ὑπαιτίοις πράξεσιν ἑλόγ- τας, εἰ καὶ πρὸς ἑτέρε μηδενὸς ἐλεγχθεῖος, ἀλλ' ἐν ὑπὸ τῦ συν- ειδότος, ὃ μόνον ἐξ ἀπάτων δικατήρων τύχαις λόγων ἐ παρά- γεται. Non de veritate comminationum, sed promis- sionum divinarum agit Apostolus, dubium expen- dens, quomodo hæc impleta sit, quum ἀνάθεμα à Christo facti sint Israëlitæ, pro quibus ipse optasset anathema fieri. His enim datæ illæ promissiones gratiæ. Unde ut scrupulum illum eximat, non omnes Israël esse, qui ex Israële vel Jacobo descen- dunt, non omnes genuinos esse Israël, & hoc no- men, cum Jacobo, qui id per fidem obtinuit, me- reri, docet: adeoque eos demum Israëlitas veros esse, qui cum Israële per fidem vincunt Gen.XXXII.

## 9:7
v. 7. Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children.

Understand it in full right, so that they are heirs supra VIII. 17. Neither Ishmael, nor the sons from Keturah are heirs to Abraham, but Isaac alone, Gen. XXV. 5. 6. Philo on Nobility: The first was a father of many children from three wives, not for the enjoyment of pleasure, but for the hope of multiplying the race. But from many only one was shown to be the heir of the paternal goods, and all the others, having failed in sound judgment and having copied nothing of the begetter, were sent away, alienated from the celebrated nobility. And speaking of rewards concerning Abraham: He had many children, but all except one were suspicious, who, having taken hold of the cables of the race, anchored safely.

But in Isaac shall thy seed be called.

Genes. XXI. 12. where also the LXX. in Isaac shall thy seed be called. That is, through Isaac will a most noble lineage come to you; For קרא to call, signifies to be famous.

Latin:

v. 7. ἐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶ σπέρμα Ἀβραὰμ πάντες τέκνα.

Intellige pleno jure, ita ut hæredes sint supra VIII. 17. Neque Ismaël, neque ex Cethura filii hæredes Abrahamo, sed Isaac solus, Gen. XXV. 5. 6. Philo de Nobilitate πολύ- παις ἦν ὁ πρῶτος ἐκ τριῶν παιδοποιησάμενος γυναικῶν, ἐ δι' ἡ- δονῆς ἀπόλαυσιν, ἀλλὰ δ' ἐλπίδα τῶ πληθῦναι τὸ γένος. ἀλλ' ἐκ πολλῶν εἷς μόνον ἀπεδείχθη κληρονόμος τῶν πατρῴων ἀγαθῶν, οἱ δ' ἄλλοι πάντες γιώμης ὑγιῶς σφαλέντες καὶ μηδὲν τῶν τῦ γεν- νήσαντος ἀπομαξάμενοι διωκίσθησαν ἀπαλλοτριωθέντες τῆς ἀοιδί- μυ ἐυγενείας. Et de præmiis de Abrahamo locutus: ὗτος πολλὲς μὲν ἔσχε παῖδας, ἅπαντας δὲ πλὴν ἑνὸς ὑποτίες, ὃς τὰ πείσματα τῦ γένες ἐκηδησάμεν@ ἀσφαλῶς ὠνερμίσατο.

ἀλλ' ἐν ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα.

Genes. XXI. 12. ubi & LXX. ἐν ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα. Id est, per Isaacum continget tibi stirps nobilissi- ma; Nam קרא claudat, significat celebrem esse.

## 9:8
v. 8. That is,

This word is that of one explaining a latent ὑπόνοιαν, which is called דרש by the Hebrews. It signifies in this history not only that an example of divine liberty exists, but also a figure of those things which are now being transacted. Therefore, elsewhere Paul, referring to this very history concerning Isaac and Ishmael, says that these things are ἀλληγορούμενα Gal. IV. 24.

the children of the flesh.

They, I say, are certainly not those whom God cherishes with a fatherly and singular affection. Thus the seed of GOD Malach. II. 15.

but the children of the promise are counted for the seed.

Λογίζεται εἰς σπέρμα, that is, they are treated by God as his sons. Thus ἐλογίσθη δίκαιος in Clement in the Constitutions, that is, he was treated by GOD in such a way as righteous men are accustomed to be treated.

The Apostle absolutely intends this, if we weigh the matter correctly: just as not all who were the seed of Abraham were his children by full right, so that they might be heirs, and that that notable promise which was made to Isaac might pertain to them, as it was proper to this one alone, according to the oracle Gen. XXI. 12. In Isaac shall thy seed be called: so not all who are children κατὰ σάρκα are reckoned into the spiritual seed, or are children of GOD; but τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, the children of the promise, are those who receive it through faith, or who become partakers of the promise, just as children of light, who have been illuminated by God, Luc. XVI. 8. Joh. XII. 36. Eph. V. 8. 1. Thess. V. 5. children of the resurrection, who become partakers of the blessed resurrection Luc. XVI. 36. here the Apostle called the faithful the seed of Abraham, and heirs according to the promise Gal. III. 29. and Abraham the Father of believers Rom. IV. 11. because Abraham embraced the word of promise by faith Gen. XIIX. 10. For it was not a matter of doubt among the Jews that not all who descend carnally from Abraham are without distinction children of GOD, and therefore there was no need to prove it. Wherefore by τὰ τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς, children of the flesh, the Apostle does not understand those descending carnally from Abraham, but since the children of the promise are the faithful embracing the promise by faith, by way of opposition the children of the flesh are those who seek righteousness not from faith, but from works; in which way Rom. IV. 1. 2. τὸ κατὰ σάρκα is taken, that is, from works: and Gal. IV. 22. Ishmael and Isaac are a type of the covenant of bondage or of works, and of grace or of faith: and a little later the Apostle will interpret the scope of the types brought in here v. 11. 12. so that the purpose of GOD, according to election, might remain firm, not from works, but from the grace of him who calls. For these words, from him who calls, from grace, from gift, through faith, according to the promise, explain one another, and therefore that opposition of the children of the flesh and of the promise, and of our works and of the grace of him who calls, declare one another: so that the children of the flesh are those who pursue righteousness and salvation through the works of the law, but the children of the promise are those who seek righteousness and salvation through faith in Christ. That therefore the word of promise embraces only the children of the promise, with the children of the flesh excluded, the Apostle illustrates in this place with a double type: one taken from the house of Abraham, the other from that of Isaac, so that Isaac and Jacob are types of all the children of the promise, but Ishmael and Esau of the children of the flesh. As therefore Isaac had to be reckoned into the seed, and Ishmael not, so, because Isaac is a type of the children of the promise, and Ishmael of the children of the flesh, those, the children of the promise alone, ought to be reckoned into the spiritual seed, these, the children of the flesh, ought not to be reckoned. Nor is it indeed incongruous that he who was born of the bondwoman and by the power of the flesh is constituted a type of the children of the flesh, but he who was born of the free woman, and by the power of the promise, when the flesh was now worn out, becomes a type of the children of the promise. The explanation of the blessed Jacob Weller, p. 540, also comes to this. Τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς, children of the flesh, are not absolutely reprobated: for in this sense this phrase comes nowhere: nor even those who live according to the flesh Rom. VIII. 1. c. IV. 13. Gal. V. 13. 19. that is, they indulge in carnal desires: nor is the derivation or generation simply carnal from the Fathers noted here, although this prerogative is by no means excluded here in an absolute sense, in which respect Paul above called his Jews kinsmen according to the flesh, ch. IX. 3. But those are called children of the flesh here, who seek righteousness from works and the law, Rom. IV. 1. 2. and Gal. IV. 22. mystically Ishmael born according to the flesh, designates the covenant of servitude or of works, Isaac the covenant of grace and faith. Thus Gal. III. 23. 28. and 29. children of the flesh and Jews persecuting others are equivalent: Children of promise, and those who adhere to Christ, inasmuch as they suffer persecution. But the Apostle introduces the examples of Isaac and Ishmael in this place not as examples, but as types, in this sense: Just as Isaac was not born from the natural powers of Abraham and Sarah, but from the efficacy of the divine promise Gen. XVIII. 18. Thus, those are not to be held as genuine children of God who are born only according to the flesh from the holy Patriarchs, or even seek righteousness through the works of the law: but those who are children of promise, that is, who embrace the promise by faith. Thus v. 9. ἐπαγγελίας ὁ λόγος is the word of promise, which is received by faith Hebr. XI. 11.

Latin:

v. 8. τετέστι,

Hæc vox est explicantis ὑπόνοιαν latentem, quod דרש dicitur Hebræis. Significat in hac historia non tantùm exemplum exstare divinæ libertatis, sed & figuram eorum, quæ nunc geruntur. Itaque alibi Paulus hanc ipsam de Isaaco & Ismaële historiam referens, dicit hæc esse ἀλληγορούμενα Gal. IV. 24.

ἐ τὰ τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς.

Non illi, inquam, utique sunt, quos Deus paterno ac singulari affectu fovet. Sic semen DEI Malach. II. 15.

ἀλλὰ τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας λογίζεται εἰς σπέρμα.

Λογίζεται εἰς σπέρμα, id est, à Deo tractantur ut filii sui. Sic ἐλογίσθη δίκαιος apud Clementem in Constitutio- nibus, id est, ita à DEO tractatus est, ut homines justi tra- ctari solent.

Apostolus omninò id vult, si rem rectè expen- damus: uti non omnes, qui semen Abrahæ fuêre, filii ejus erant pleno jure, ut hæredes essent, & ad ipsos promissio illa insignis spectaret, quæ Isaa- co facta est, utpote quæ huic uni erat propria, jux- ta oraculum Gen. XXI. 12. In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: ita non omnes, qui κατὰ σάρκα filii sunt, reputantur in semen spirituale, vel Filii DEI sunt; sed τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, liberi promissionis sunt, qui eam per fidem suscipiunt, vel qui promis- sionis fiunt participes, uti filii lucis, qui à Deo illu- minati sunt, Luc. XVI. 8. Joh. XII. 36. Eph. V. 8. 1. Thess. V. 5. filii resurrectionis, qui beatæ resurre- ctionis participes fiunt Luc. XVI. 36. hic fideles di- xit Apostolus σπέρμα τῦ Ἀβραὰμ, κὰ κατ’ ἐπαγγε- λίας κληρονόμυς Gal. III. 29. & Abrahamum Patrem credentium Rom. IV. 11. quia Abraham verbum promissionis fide amplexus est Gen. XIIX. 10. Non enim id dubium apud Judæos fuit, non omnes, qui carnaliter ab Abraham descendunt, sine discri- mine DEI filios esse, ideoque id probare opus non erat. Quapropter per τὰ τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς filios carnis non intelligit Apostolus carnaliter descen- dentes ab Abrahamo, sed quum filii promissionis sint fideles promissionem fide amplectentes, vi op- positionis filii carnis sunt, qui non ex fide, sed operibus justitiam quærunt; quomodo Rom. IV. 1. 2. τὸ κατὰ σάρκα accipitur, id est, ex operibus: & Gal. IV. 22. Ismaël & Isaac typus sunt fœderis servitutis vel operum, & gratiæ vel fidei: & paulò post Apostolus scopum typorum hic adductorum interpretabitur v. 11. 12. ut propositum DEI, secun- dùm electionem, firmum maneat, non ex operibus, sed ex gratiâ vocantis.
