Hæ enim voces, ex vocan- te, ex gratia, ex dono, per fidem, secundùm promis- sionem, explicant se mutuò, ideoque & oppositio illa filiorum carnis & promissionis, & operum no- strorum ac gratiæ vocantis sese mutuò declarant: ut filii carnis sint, qui per opera legis justitiam & salutem confectantur, filii autem promissionis, qui fide in Christum justitiam & salutem quærunt. Quod ergò verbum promissionis solos filios pro- missionis exclusis filiis carnis complectatur, dupli- ci typo illustrat h. l. Apostolus: uno ex domo Abra- hami, altero ex Isaaci desumto, ita ut Isaac & Ja- cob sint typi omnium filiorum promissionis, Ismaël verò & Esav filiorum carnis. Ut itaque Isaac cen- seri debuit in semen, Ismaël non item, sic, quia Isaac typus est filiorum promissionis, Ismael filio- rum carnis, illi, promissionis filii soli debent re- putari in semen spirituale, hi filii carnis, non de- bent reputari. Nec inconcinnè sanè ille, qui ex ancillâ & vi carnali natus erat, typus filiorum car- nis constituitur, ille verò, qui ex liberâ, & vi pro- missionis, ubi caro jam esset effæta, typus fit filio- rum promissionis. Huc redit etiam explicatio B. Jacobi Welleri p. 540. Τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς, Filii car- nis non sunt absolutè reprobati: hoc enim sensu nul- libi hæc phrasis venit: neque etiam qui secundùm carnem vivunt Rom. VIII. 1. c. IV. 13. Gal. V. 13. 19. id est, cupiditatibus carnalibus indulgent: nec nota- tur etiam simpliciter carnalis derivatio sive genera- tio ex Patribus, quamvis hæc prærogativa hic ἀπολό- μως haud excludatur, quo respectu supra Paulus Ju- dæos suos συγγενεῖς secundum carnem dixit cap. IX. 3. sed Filii carnis dicuntur hîc illi, qui ex operibus & lege justitiam sectantur Rom. IV. 1. 2. & Gal. IV. 22. mysticè Ismael secundum carnem natus, fœdus ser- vitutis vel operum, Isaac fœdus gratiæ & fidei de- signant. Sic Gal. III. 23. 28. & 29. æquipollent filii carnis & Judæi persequentes alios: Filii promissio- nis, & qui Christo adhærent, quippe persecutionem patiuntur. Exempla vero Isaaci & Ismaelis Apo- stolus h. l. non παραδειγματικῶς, sed τυπικῶς in- troducit, hoc sensu: Quemadmodum Isaac non est natus ex viribus naturalibus Abrahæ & Saræ, sed ex efficacia divinæ promissionis Gen. XVIII. 18. Sic non sunt habendi pro genuinis Dei filiis, qui tantum secun- dum carnem ex sanctis Patriarchis geniti sunt, aut etiam per opera legis justitiam quærunt: sed qui sunt filii promissionis, h. e. qui promissionem fide ample- ctuntur. Sic v. 9. ἐπαγγελίας ὁ λόγος promissio- nis sermo est, qui fide receptus est Hebr. XI. 11.

## 9:9
Vers. 9. For this is the word of promise.] Which is written Gen. XVII. 10.

At this time I will come.] In the LXX the Angel speaks thus in the name of God: I will return and come to you at this time in the future, and Sarah your wife shall have a son. I will come, that is, God. First, that which is born is not by the powers of nature, but by divine power, like Isaac: then, that it is by the intervention of a promise. For it is begotten through the Evangelical promises. This also may be added, that Ishmael was of a wild disposition, Isaac of a mild one, which distinction Philo observes: But a mild disposition is proper to Christians. Matth. XXVII. 27. 1. Cor. IV. 21. Gal. V. 22. Eph. IV. 2. Coloss. III. 12.

That the Angel speaks in the name of God Gen. XVIII. 10. is not to be conceded, that it was the Son of God who spoke those things, who appeared to Abraham accompanied by two Angels as companions, has been shown at that place both in the Commentary on Genesis and in the Illustrated Bibles.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐπαγγελίας γὰρ ὁ λόγος οὗτος.] Qui scribitur Gen. XVII. 10.

κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον ἐλεύσομαι.] In LXX. Angelus Dei nomine sic loquitur: ἐπαναστρέφων ἥξω πρὸς σὲ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον εἰς ὥρας, καὶ ἕξει υἱὸν Σάρρα ἡ γυνή σου. Veniam ego, Deus scilicet. Primum quod nasci- tur non naturæ viribus, sed vi divina, ut Isaacus: deinde quod intercedente promisso. Gignitur enim per promissa Evangelica. Potest & hoc addi, quod Ismael feræ, Isaac miti fuit ingenio, quod discrimen Philo observat: Ingenium autem mite proprium Christianorum. Matth. XXVII. 27. 1. Cor. IV. 21. Gal. V. 22. Eph. IV. 2. Coloss. III. 12.

Angelum Dei nomine loqui Gen. XVIII. 10. haud concedendum, Filium Dei loquutum ista esse, qui duobus Angelis comitibus stipatus Abrahæ appa- ruit, ad locum illum & in Commentario in Genesin, & in Bibliis illustratis ostensum.

## 9:10
Vers. 10. And not only.] There is here an aposiopesis, a figure which the Apostle often uses: The sense is: not only that which we have already said is a proof of that which we wish to infer.

but also Rebecca.] Rebecca teaches us the same. Rebecca for the history of Rebecca.

having conception from one Isaac our father. Who had offspring from one Isaac our Father, namely a double one at the same time, which is tacitly understood from the opposite word one. For Philo also observes that some great mystery lay hidden in that so early predicted distinction of the twins. The places are in the book on Allegories at the end of the book on Cain and Abel, and on Nobility. Koite, corresponding to shekhavah and mishkav, in the first sense is a bed: then by metonymy of the adjunct, the bedchamber, it is thus expressed as intercourse, as can be seen below XIII. 13. Hebr. XIII. 4. which is called the bed of seed Lev. V. 16. 17. 18. XVIII. 20. XXII. 4. Num. V. 12. Then by a further going figure or metalepsis, the seed itself, that is, the offspring, as here. But these words have emphasis, lest perhaps someone might refer what he had said about Ishmael to a difference of mother or time.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἓ μόνον δὲ] Est hic ἄποσιώπησις, qua figura sæpe utitur Apostolus: Sen- sus est: non solum id, quod jam diximus, documentum est ejus, quod inferre volumus.

ἀλλὰ καὶ Ῥεβέκκα.] Rebecca idem nos docet. Rebecca pro Rebeccæ historia.

ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν. Quæ genituram habuit ex uno Isaaco Patre nostro, nempe duplicem eodem tempore, quod tacitè ex opposita voce ἑνὸς subintelligitur. Nam & Philo observat, mysterium aliquod magnum latuisse in illo geminorum tam maturè prædicto discrimine. Loci sunt libro de Allegoriis fine li- bri de Caino & Abele, ac de Nobilitate. Κοίτη respondens שכבת & משכב primo sensu est cubile: deinde per με- τωνυμίαν adjuncti κοιτῶνος sic exprimitur ἡ συνουσία, ut videre est infra XIII. 13. Hebr. XIII. 4. quæ dicitur κοίτη σπέρματος Lev. V. 16. 17. 18. XVIII. 20. XXII. 4. Num. V. 12. Deinde per longiùs euntem figuram sive μετάληψιν ipsum σπέρμα, id est, genitura, ut hic. Habent autem hæc verba ἔμφασιν, ne fortè, quod de Ismaele dixerat, ad matris aut temporis diversitatem aliquis referret.

## 9:11
Vers. 11. For when they were not yet born, nor had done any good or evil. Thus also Philo says of the same in the Allegories: Jacob and Esau, the one a ruler and leader and master, but Esau a subject and slave, he says were such while still in the womb. He begins to unfold the hidden mystery. God preferred him who would be born later to him who was born earlier. The infants not yet born could have done nothing good or evil. What does this portend? That God would likewise prefer a believing people to a non-believing people, so that He might regenerate the believers through His Spirit, with no regard had for either the legal works which the Jews had done, or the idolatrous worship and other crimes in which those from the Gentiles had been involved, no more than if they had never existed. For often in the sacred writings they are placed as equals, not to be, and not to be considered, as Hebr. VII. 3.

that the purpose of God according to election might remain. Therefore this was said, that it might remain, that is, that it might be proven by this argument (for the Hebrews say this by amad to stand, which the Greeks in many places translate to remain) the will of God (namely, free) in those things which pertain to preference, that is, that He might prefer one to another. For all that is called by the name of election, for the Hebrew bahar, which is for the most part translated to elect, is translated by proairein Deut. VII. 6. X. 15. Prov. I. 29.

from her who says.

Thus, that we are saved through faith, is a gift of God, for it is not from works Eph. I. 9. God saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works: but according to His own will 2. Tim. I. 9. See above III. 24. IV. 6. and the things said there and below XI. 6. A new creation does not look back at what has been done before.

but from the one who calls.

God calls through promises. Therefore, the word of promise and the calling amount to the same thing.

Latin:

Vers. 11. μήπω γὰρ γεννηθέντων, μηδὲ πραξάντων τὶ ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακόν. Sic & Philo de iisdem in Allegoriis: τὸν ἰακὼβ κᾐ τὸν Ἡσαῦ, τὸν μὲν ἄρχοντα καὶ ἡγεμόνα, καὶ δεσπότην, τὸν δὲ Ἡσαῦ ὑπήκοον καὶ δοῦλον, ἔτι κατὰ γαστρὸς ὄντας, φησὶν εἶναι. Incipit evol- vere mysterium latens. Prætulit Deus eum, qui posterius nasceretur, eo, qui prius. Infantes nondum nati, nihil bo- ni aut mali agere potuerant. Quid hoc portendit? Deum itidem prælaturum populum credentem, populo non cre- denti, ut credentes regeneret per Spiritum suum, nulla ha- bita ratione aut operum legalium, quæ Judæi fecerant, aut cultus idololatrici & aliorum criminum, quibus involuti fuerant illi ex gentibus, non magis, quam si ea nunquam ex- stitissent. Sæpe enim in sacris literis ponuntur quasi paria, non esse, & non considerari, ut Hebr. VII. 3.

ἵνα ἡ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόθεσις μένῃ. Ideò hoc dictum est, ut maneret, id est, ut probaretur hoc argumento (nam id Hebræi dicunt per עמד stare, quod Græci multis in locis vertunt μένειν) voluntas Dei (libera scilicet) in iis, quæ pertinent ad prælationem, id est, ut al- terum alteri præferat. Id enim omne ἐκλογῆς dicitur no- mine, nam בחר Hebræum, quod plerumque vertitur ἐκλέ- γειν, per προαιρεῖν vertitur Deut. VII. 6. X. 15. Prov. I. 29.

ἐκ τῆς λέγων.

Sic, quod per fidem servamur, Dei est donum, non enim ex operibus Eph. I. 9. Servavit nos Deus & vocavit voca- tione sancta, non secundum opera nostra : sed secundum suam voluntatem 2. Tim. I. 9. Vide supra III. 24. IV. 6. & ibi dicta & infra XI. 6. Nova creatio, quæ ante acta sunt, non respicit.

ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς καλῶντος.

Vocat Deus per promissa. Itaque eodem recidunt ἐπ- αγγελίας λόγος καὶ κλῆσις.

## 9:12
Vers. 12. It was said to her, that the greater shall serve the lesser.) Josephus rightly perceived that the peoples are to be understood here under the designation of the parents. Thus Jacob & Israel are used throughout for the descendants of Jacob, Esau & Edom for the Idumeans. And it preceded in Genesis: Two peoples are in your womb. Moreover, it was fulfilled in the times of David, as is evident in 1 Sam. VIII. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἐῤῥέθη ἀυτῇ, ὅτι ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι.) Sub parentum designatione intelligi hic populos recte per- cepit Josephus. Sic Jacob & Israel pro Jacobi posteris, E- sau & Edom pro Idumæis passim. Et præcessit in Genesi: Duo populi in utero tuo. Est autem impletum Davidis tem- poribus, ut patet 1. Sam. VIII. 14.

## 9:13
as it is written.] There is an ellipsis here. The full sentence is: Which prophecy was truly fulfilled, as we find it written by Malachi.

I have loved Jacob, but I have hated Esau.) That is, I preferred the Israelites, although they were guilty of grave crimes, to the Idumeans. For this meaning of the word to hate & to reproach, as in the Prophets, so in Paul, suffices for what they are treating in their argument. And this expression is customary in comparisons among the Hebrews, as appears in Gen. XXIX. 31 in the Hebrew & Deut. XXI. 15 & 2 Sam. XVI. 7, Prov. XIII. 24 & in Matt. VI. 24 & Luke XIV. 26, John XII. 25. Malachi clearly says that this was established by God in his benefits, to prefer the Israelites to the Idumeans, and that this was apparent even then and would be more apparent, namely in the times of Hyrcanus, concerning whom see Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews XIII. 19. If these very things are referred to an underlying meaning, they correspond to the Idumean people, the Israelite people, as the former born of God: to the once Israelite people, the now Christian people, as the latter born of God: but the servitude of the Idumeans signifies the viler condition of the old Jewish people, who never had promises except earthly ones, and gifts of the Spirit very infrequently. Barnabas: Let us see if this people is the heir, or the first, and the covenant is for us, or for them. Hear now concerning the people what the scripture says: And Isaac prayed concerning Rebecca his wife because she was barren and she conceived. Then Rebecca went out to inquire of the Lord, and the Lord said to her: Two nations are in your womb and two peoples in your belly, and one people shall excel another, and the greater shall serve the lesser. You ought to perceive who is Isaac and who is Rebecca, and in whom it has been shown that this people is greater than that. Tertullian against the Jews: Therefore, since the people or nation of the Jews is prior in time, and greater through the grace of the first dignity in the law, but ours is lesser in age, as having attained the knowledge of divine mercy in the last space of the age, without doubt according to the edict of the divine utterance the prior and greater people, that is, the Jewish, must serve the lesser, and the lesser people, that is, the Christian, must overcome the greater. And afterwards: But our people, the lesser, that is, the posterior, having abandoned the idols which it previously served, has turned to the same God from whom Israel, as we mentioned above, had departed. For thus the lesser people overcame the greater people, while it obtains the grace of divine dignity, from which Israel has been repudiated. The same author, book III against Marcion: Jacob, who is indeed a figure of the posterior people of preference, that is, of ours. Cyprian, Testimonies against the Jews, book I. That two peoples were predicted, the greater and the lesser, that is, the old one of the Jews, and the new, which was to be from us, in Genesis: And the Lord said to Rebecca: two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly. And one people shall overcome another, and the greater shall serve the lesser: Philo, just as he did not perceive the whole matter because he did not believe, so he did not entirely depart from it when he says in his book on Abel and Cain that the evil and good natures are signified by Esau and Jacob, the former being the prior, the latter the more excellent, and not much later, explaining the same thing, he says: Thus indeed that which is oldest in time will be wickedness, but that which is in dignity and honor and glory is virtue. And on the waking Noah: And they bring in a sequence to the birth of Jacob, who is younger than Esau, because folly is our companion from youth, but he who is the end of the good is late-born in power and older. Who in the same book also allegorizes eloquently both about the heel being seized and about the right of the firstborn being sold. Likewise about the snares of Esau against Jacob in his book that the worse plots against the better: and how the one obeyed his belly, the other his parents and God, in his book on Nobility: and how the former was harsh and wild, the latter mild and gentle, in his book on rewards and punishments. But just as it is pleasant to pursue gently things of this kind insofar as they have some shadow of true and certain doctrine, so it is boorish and witless to make all comparisons equal in every respect and to invent doctrines from them. Tertullian rightly warns that matters are not to be commended from symbols, but parables from matters, for in comparisons not all things can correspond to the mirror. And Chrysostom, that which is to be used, for the sake of which the comparison was instituted, the rest is to be sent away. The Apostle wishes for God the freedom of dispensing His own benefits. Especially those through which one arrives at true justice: not indeed that for certain persons not yet created, with an eternal constitution having no causes, every way of arriving there is blocked. What in persons is Ishmael and Esau, that in the rendering are the Jews relying on the privilege of human origin. What in persons is Isaac and Jacob, that in the rendering are Christians born from divine promises, later in time, earlier in God's gifts.

We agree in most of these things without difficulty with Grotius. Who followed Jacobus Arminius in the Appendix to the examination of Perkins' Predestination, and the Remonstrants in the clear explanation of chapter IX to the Romans in the Synodical Writings, p. 96 et seqq. Whose opinion we praised in the Apostolic Theology. The Remonstrants, in oration LXVIII, [say that] the Apostolic proof in this later type of Jacob and Esau, of whom the former was loved, the latter held in hatred, before they had done anything either good or evil, was brought in for this end, that it might be concluded that the purpose of God according to election is firm, not from works, but from Him who calls, i.e., that it does not concern the children of the flesh, who are from works, but the children of promise, who are from faith, by which one obeys God who calls, [and they] hold it thus: if the purpose according to election remains, from Him who calls, but not from works, it follows that those who are from the works of the law, and seek justice and salvation through the law, are not contained in that purpose, but only those who obey God who calls and promises through faith, or who accept the divine calling and promise. But that the former is true is taught from the type of Esau and Jacob, by which both were signified, that God's purpose is according to election, then that it remains from Him who calls and not from works; the former, because one is preferred to the other, which is a sign of a purpose according to election: the latter, because the elder Esau is hated and subjected, but the younger Jacob is loved and preferred, which is a sign that this purpose is not firm from works; but from Him who calls, i.e., that God loves those who seek justice and salvation through faith in Christ, but hates those who pursue the same from the works of the law. These are the words of Arminius, who, as far as this type is concerned, also observes that he who was born first bears the figure of the children of the flesh and of the old or former covenant, or of the Jews, who by the zeal of the law sought justice and life through it, and he who was later, [bears the figure] of the children of promise and of the later or new covenant, or of those who pursued justice and faith through faith in Christ. Similarly, the Remonstrants explained their mind, that the Apostle is not dealing with the giving of faith, how and to whom God wishes to give faith, but with the giving of justice, how and whom He wishes to justify and adopt, and that he is defending this thesis against the exceptions of the Jews. That it had been God's purpose from ancient times to justify, adopt, and bless not those who seek justice from the law, but those who believe in the promises of God revealed in the Gospel, and that God in this is not unjust, [but] has the right and power to do this most freely; whence it is not difficult to gather that the controversy between the Apostle and the unbelievers was not properly about their own rejection, but about the doctrine of the Apostle, from which that rejection had to follow, the sum of which was that justice and adoption are not from the works of the law, but from the faith of Christ. They urge, among other things: That the purpose of God according to election is more correctly understood as the divine decree concerning the salvation of men according to the Apostolic phrase, than as election into a peculiar possession and people of God; and that it can in no way be explained as a purpose of giving faith, or the grace necessary for faith: because thus those words 'not from works' would be in vain. For who said that faith is given from works, so that this had to be denied? And the rationale of the types answers neatly if it is said that the justice of works and of faith, of the old and new covenant, is being represented. But if it is asserted that regard is had to the giving or denial of faith, it cannot be explained conveniently. For how will the younger be called, to whom faith is given, [and] the elder, to whom faith is denied, [and] how will it signify, moreover, not having faith? But rightly the elder is the people of workers, because they are prior to the people of believers, [and] the younger is the people of believers, as being posterior. Likewise, it conveniently denotes not having the freedom of the children of God to serve. The analysis of the whole chapter also holds together best with that theme and state of the question admitted concerning justification by faith, which does not seem so plain if it is said to be dealing primarily and in itself with the rejection of the Jews, or even with the collation of faith or the denial of the same, as the comparison of both analyses can teach. This state of the question, the Remonstrants say, agrees as much as possible with the scope of the Apostolic treatment set forth in this epistle, [and] excellently illustrates the continuity with the previous chapters. For the Apostle had previously taught expressly that man is uniquely freed through faith in Christ, both from the curse of sin, by which he is subjected to condemnation, and from the dominion of the same, by which he is enslaved to the service of sin, since the curse is not taken away except through gracious justification, which is done only through Christ; but liberation from the dominion of sin must be done through renewal, which is likewise a gift of God in Christ flowing from being planted together with Him. Whence it follows that only Christians, who have true communion with Christ, are true children of God and heirs of eternal life, who do not call upon God as their Father in lethal and servile fear, as under the law, but in undaunted and filial παῤῥησίᾳ, and are able to serve Him: Thus he now defends in the first place that saving doctrine against the Jews, as far as concerns the decree of God regarding the justifying and saving of men, not from the works of the flesh or the law, but through faith in Christ, demonstrating its truth from divine oracles from verse 6 to 13, and demonstrating its equity from the free right of God from verse 14 to 23, to the end of the chapter. They add, moreover, that verse 15 deals with the mercy of God, by which sins are remitted, but those things necessarily presuppose faith, and thus the translation is instituted not concerning the giving of faith, but concerning justification through faith. Thus, in the first place, the Apostle explicitly explains his scope in verse 16, that righteousness, sonship, and inheritance are not of him who runs, or who pursues it through the works of the law, but of God, who has mercy on the faithful and those who believe in Christ. And therefore it is a matter of the mercy of God in justifying the faithful. Similarly, when God is said to harden whom He wills in verse 17, it is only the unbelieving, and those who stubbornly reject the offered grace, that He hardens (Isa. 6:9, 8:12, Rom. 9:33, ch. 11:7, 1 Pet. 2:8), as is evident even from the example of Pharaoh himself, who, having been called so many times through the word and miracles, was hardened while rejecting the grace of God, as the Mosaic history testifies. Whence it is manifest that those words are to be understood not of an absolute denial of faith, but of the hardening and reprobation of those who do not believe and who reject the grace of God. It is added that verse 21, a vessel for honor or dishonor, is not a vessel for faith or unbelief, or one to whom God wills to give or not give the grace to believe, but a vessel for honor is a vessel for inheritance, blessing, and glory, as is explained in verse 23 concerning the faithful, just as vessels for dishonor are the unbelievers themselves. What Grotius has toward the end will have to be amended from these things, indeed even from those things which Grotius himself had premised: What is in the protasis as Ishmael and Esau, that in the apodosis are the Jews pursuing the righteousness of works.

What is in the purpose of Isaac & Jacob, that is in the fulfillment [for] believers embracing the righteousness of faith: who are also not undeservedly called children of the promise, because they are born from divine promises.

B. Hülsem. in Vind. Script. §. 90. against the Calvinists observes this especially: The words of promise & election, of will and the purpose of good pleasure of love, v. 7. 8. 9. 11. 12. 18. Of compassion v. 16. 18. Of mercy v. 23. All of which are said to be causes of gratuitous election, are by no means absolute and do not exclude the foreknowledge of faith to be received by man through that preventing and accompanying grace, [and] all preaching of the divine word, but all these words are correlative with faith, and presuppose it, but are opposed only to works, [and] exclude only works, both internal and external, which are done with the purpose of obtaining salvation through them. Which is proved both from chapter IX itself to the Romans, and from the scope & connection of this whole Epistle. The former, that the will of showing mercy, the purpose, election, &c. do not exclude but presuppose faith, as their correlate, is proved, both in general from the fact that no divine promise can be applied, nor can its firmness consist, nor can it be held as a promise, if it is taken absolutely, & without the supposition of faith Rom. IV. 16. therefore not by faith [is] the inheritance, so that it may be by grace, so that the promise may be firm, to Gal. III, 18. If the inheritance is by the law, it cannot be by promise, but GOD willed to confer it upon Abraham by promise; therefore so that the promise might be given by the faith of Jesus Christ to believers, the inheritance could not be acquired by works v. 22. From these things said, I say, it is clear that there is not given any promise of grace or decree concerning human salvation, which in its intuition, or as regards the exclusion of faith, is absolute. Wherefore nothing is more frequent in the writings of the Calvinists [than] this Elenchus of opposites, if we are elected from the mere will & good pleasure of GOD, it follows that GOD did not foresee faith in man as a supposition and Hypothesis necessary on the part of the one to be saved; the contrary is clear from these things said, that no promise & decree of salvation can be feigned without the supposition of the correlation between promise and faith. The latter, namely that those words of purpose, decree, election &c. exclude only works, [and] are opposed only to works, not to faith, is clear through the induction of the Apostolic Phrase itself chapter IX to the Romans, where v. 11. 16. 30. 31. 32. the will of God showing mercy is expressly opposed to works, [and] excludes the will, striving, and course of man to obtain salvation through his own works v. 11. When they had done nothing good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might remain firm, not from works, but from the grace of the caller it was said to them &c. The greater shall serve the lesser &c. v. 16. Salvation & election are not of the one willing and running, but of God showing mercy v. 30. The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have attained righteousness. But Israel, who was pursuing righteousness most of all, has not attained righteousness. Why? because they were striving for righteousness not by faith, but as if by works of the law. This determination of the opposition between gratuitous election & works, and this subordination of faith & gratuitous election in this very matter or treatment of the question concerning predestination, most clearly shows that the Calvinists err in the Elenchus of opposites, when they oppose gratuitous election & the foreknowledge of faith, when they ought to have opposed gratuitous election & the foreknowledge of works. Let them produce for us any example from the entire sacred code, of opposed faith & gratuitous election. Then we argue thus: In the same sense that the Apostle was [wont] throughout the whole Epistle to the Romans to oppose promise & works, [and] to subordinate faith & promise, in the same sense it is presumed that he used these phrases also in the continuation of the doctrine concerning gratuitous salvation through faith, which Calvin, Musculus, Beza, Aretius, Gwalther, Piscator in the summaries of this Epistle confess is continued throughout the whole Epistle to the Romans, not only in Chapters II. III. IV. V. VI. but also VIII. IX. X. XI. XII. XV. But the Apostle everywhere throughout this whole Epistle treats the promise & the economy of grace in such a way that he everywhere excludes only works, [and] never faith, which is clear by the induction of Chapter III. 16. 17. seqq. Chapter IV. 13. 14. 16. 20. 21. & IX. 8. 9. c. XV. 8. Gal. III. 19. that this is likewise clear from the induction of the words προγνώσεως & προθέσεως of foreknowledge & purpose, as often as they are preached concerning the Economy of eternal salvation, they are everywhere opposed only to works, nowhere to faith. Rom. VIII. 29. XI. 23. 1. Pet. I. 2. Rom. VIII. 28. IX. 11. Ephes. I. 11. & most clearly 2. Tim. I. 9. οὐ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν. The third argument is such: In the same sense that works & gratuitous justification are opposed, [and] faith & gratuitous justification are subordinated, in the same sense gratuitous election & works are opposed, [and] faith & gratuitous election are subordinated. The Apostle shows the connection of the major [premise] Rom. VIII. 30. & IX. 30. 31. 32. We have shown that such as is the relation between faith & justification, such it is between faith & predestination, but gratuitous justification & works are so opposed, that they do not exclude, but include faith, [and] justification & faith are subordinated, so that faith in the order of nature is prior to justification. Therefore also gratuitous predestination & works are so opposed, that they do not exclude faith, [and] they are so subordinated, that in the order of nature and in the sign of the reason of God predestining, the reception of faith is prior to the decree of predestination or the decree of saving.

PART III. CHAPTER IX. Apologetic, vindicating the equity of the purpose of God concerning saving believers [and] condemning unbelievers.

Latin:

καθὼς γέγραπται.] Est hic Ellipsis. Plena sententia. Quod vaticinium revera impletum est, ut scriptum reperimus à Malachia.

Τὸν Ἰακὼβ ἠγάπησα, τὸν δὲ Ἡσαῦ ἐμίσησα.) Id est prætuli Israelitas, quanquam gravium criminum reos Idumæis. Nam hæc significatio vocis μισεῖν & ὀνειδίζειν, ut in Prophetis ita in Paulo sufficit ei, quod tractant argumento. Et est lo- cutio ista in comparationibus usitata apud Hebræos, ut ap- paret Gen. XXIX. 31. in Hebræo & Deuteron. XXI. 15. & 2. Sam. XVI. 7. Proverb. XIII. 24. & in Matth. VI. 24. & Luc. XIV. 26. Joh. XII. 25. Dicit Malachias plane hoc constitutum Deo in beneficiis suis præferre Israelitas Idu- mæis, idque & nunc apparere & magis appariturum, Hyr- cani nempe temporibus, de quibus vide Josephum Anti- quæ Historiæ XIII. 19. Hæc ipsa si ad ὑπόνοιαν referantur, respondent populo Idumæo, populus Israeliticus, ut prius à Deo genitus : populo olim Israelitico, populus nunc Chri- stianus, ut posterius à Deo genitus: Servitus autem Idu- mæorum significat conditionem viliorem populi veteris Judaici, qui promissa nunquam habuit nisi terrestria, & do- na Spiritus valde infrequentia. Barnabas: ἄπ' ἴδωμεν εἰ ὗτος ὁ λαὸς κληρονόμος, ἢ ὁ πρῶτος, καὶ ἡ διαθήκη εἰς ἡμᾶς, ἢ εἰς ἐκείνους. ἀκούσατε νῦν περὶ τῶ λαῶ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή: ἐδεῖτο δὲ Ἰσαὰκ περὶ Ῥεβέκκας τῆς γυναικὸς ἀυτῶ ὅτι στεῖρα ἦν καὶ συνέλαβ βε. Εἶτα νοῦς ἐξῆλθε Ῥεβέκκα πυθέσθαι παρὰ κυρίου, καὶ εἶπε κύ ριος πρὸς ἀυτήν· Δύο ἔθνη ἐν τῇ γαστρί σε καὶ δύο λαοὶ ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ σε, καὶ λαὸς λαῦ ὑπερέξει, καὶ ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσ- σονι. αἰσθάνεσθαι ὀφείλετε τίς ὁ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ τίς ἡ Ῥεβέκκα, καὶ ἐπὶ τινῶν δέδεικεν ὅτι μείζων ὁ λαὸς ἔτος ἢ ἐκεῖνος. Tertullia- nus adversus Judæos: Itaque cum populus seu gens Judæorum anterior sit tempore, & major per gratiam primæ dignationis in lege, noster vero minor ætate, utpote in ultimo seculi spatio ad- eptus notitiam divinæ miserationis, procul dubio secundum edi- ctum divinæ locutionis prior & major populus, id est, Judaicus, serviat necesse est minori, & minor populus, id est, Christia- nus superet majorem. Ac post: Noster vero populus minor, id est, posterior, relictis idolis, quibus ante deserviebat, ad eundem Deum conversus est, à quo Israel, ut supra memoravimus, absces- serat. Sic namque populus minor populum majorem supera- vit, dum gratiam divinæ dignationis consequitur, à qua Israel est repudiatus. Idem lib. III. adversus Marcionem: Jacob, qui quidem posterioris ex prælationis populi figura est, id est, no stri. Cyprianus Testimoniorum contra Judæos lib. I. Quod duo populi sint prædicti, major & minor, id est, vetus Judæo- rum, & novus, qui esset ex nobis futurus, in Genesi: Et dixit Do- minus Rebeccæ: duæ gentes in utero tuo sunt, & duo populi de ventre tuo dividentur. Et populus populum superabit, & major serviet minori: Philo sicut non totam rem pervidit, quia non credidit, ita non plane abscessit, cum dicit libro de Abe- le & Caino per Esavum & Jacobum significari naturas ma- lam & bonam, illam priorem, hanc excellentiorem, ac non multo post id ipsum explicans ait: ὕτω μὲν δὲ τὰ χρόνῳ πρεσβύτα ἔσεσται κακία, τὰ δὲ ἀξιώματι κὶ τιμῆς κὶ ἐυκλείας ἡ ἀρετή. Et de evigilanti Noe: καὶ ἀκολουθίαν ἐπάγουσι Ἰακὼβ γενέσει μὲν τῶ Ἡσαῦ νεώτερος, ὅτι, ἀφροσύνη ἡλικίας ἡμῖν ἐστὶ σύντροφο, ὀψίγονος δ' ὁ τὸ καλῶ τέλος δυνάμει καὶ πρεσβύτερος. Qui eodem libro & de calce arrepta, & de ju- re natatium vendito facunde ἀλληγορεῖ. Item de insidiis Esavi in Jacobum libro pejorem insidiari meliori: & quo- modo alter ventri, alter parentibus ac Deo paruerit, libro de Nobilitate: & quomodo durus & Sylvester ille, hic mi- tis ac placidus, libro de præmiis & pœnis. Cæterum sicut res ejusmodi quatenus umbram aliquam habent veri cer- tique dogmatis, leniter prosequi suave est, ita omnes com- parationes per omnia æquare, & inde dogmata commi- nisci, agreste atque infacetum est. Recte monet Tertul- lianus, non ex symbolis materias commendandas, sed ex materiis parabolas, neque enim in comparationibus omnia ad speculum respondere posse. Et Chrysostomus, uten- dum id, cujus causa instituta est comparatio, mittenda cæ- tera. Salvam vult Deo Apostolus libertatem dispensan- dorum beneficiorum suorum. Præsertim eorum, per quæ ad veram justitiam pervenitur: non verò personis quibus- dam nondum creatis, æterna constitutione nullas habente causas, præclusam omnem eò perveniendi viam. Quod ἐν προσώποις est Ismael & Esau, id ἐν ἀποδόσει sunt Judæi privilegio humanæ originis freti. Quod ἐν προσώποις Isaac & Jacob, id ἐν ἀποδόσει Christiani ex promissis divinis geni- ti, posteriores tempore, priores Dei donis.

Annuimus in plerisque hisce haud difficulter Grotio. Qui Jacobum Arminium in Appendice ad examen Prædestinationis Perkinsianæ, & Re- monstrantes in explicat. dilucid. cap. IX. ad Rom. in Script. Synodal. p. 96. seqq. sequutus est. Quo- rum sententiam laudavimus in Theol. Apost. Rem. orat. LXVIII. probationem Apostolicam in hoc posteriori typo Jacobi & Esavi, quorum ille dile- ctus, hic odio habitus, antequàm quicquam vel boni vel mali fecissent, in hunc finem adducto, ut concludatur propositum Dei secundum electionem firmum esse, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante h. e. non concernere filios carnis, qui sunt ex operibus, sed filios promissionis, qui sunt ex fide, qua Deo vocanti pa- retur, sic habere: si propositum secundum electio- nem manet, ex vocante, non autem ex operibus, sequitur, illos, qui ex operibus legis sunt, & per le- gem justitiam & salutem sectantur, illo proposito non contineri, sed illos tantum, qui Deo vocanti, & promittenti per fidem parent, seu vocationem & promissionem divinam acceptant. At prius ve- rum esse docetur ex typo Esavi & Jacobi, quo utrumque significatum est, Dei propositum esse secundum electionem, deinde id manere ex vo- cante & non operibus; illud quidem, quia unus sit alteri prælatus, quod est signum propositi secun- dum electionem: hoc quia major Esau sit exosus & subjectus, minor vero Jacob amatus & præla- tus, quod est signum, id propositum non esse ex operibus firmum; sed ex vocante h. e. Deum ama- re illos, qui fide in Christum justitiam & salutem quærunt, odisse vero illos, qui eandem ex operi- bus legis consectantur. Hæc Arminius, qui, quod ad hunc typum attinet, etiam observat, il- lum, qui prior esset natus, gerere figuram filiorum carnis & fœderis veteris seu prioris, vel Judæorum, qui zelo legis per illam quærebant justitiam & vi- tam, & qui posterior, filiorum promissionis & fœde- ris posterioris vel novi, seu illorum, qui per fidem in Christum justitiam & fidem sectabantur. Simili- ter mentem suam exposuere Remonstrantes, Apo- stolum non de datione fidei agere, quomodo & qui- bus Deus velit dare fidem, sed de datione justitiæ, quomodo & quos velit justificare & adoptare, at- que hanc thesin defendere contra Judæorum exce- ptiones. Deo propositum fuisse inde ab antiquis tem- poribus non eos, qui ex lege justitiam quærunt, sed qui Dei in Evangelio revelatis promissionibus credunt, justificare, adoptare, beare, Deumque in eo non esse injustum, jus habere ac potestatem id faciendi liber- rimum; unde non difficile est colligere, contro- versiam inter Apostolum & incredulos propriè non fuisse de ipsorum rejectione, sed de doctrina Apostoli, unde illam consequi necesse erat reje- ctionem, cujus summa erat, justitiam & adoptio- nem non esse ex operibus legis, sed ex fide Christi. Urgent inter alia: Propositum Dei secundum ele- ctionem rectius de decreto divino de salute hominum intelligi juxta phrasin Apostolicam, quam de electio- ne in peculium & populum Dei; de proposito autem dandi fidem, vel gratiam necessariam ad fidem nul- latenus explicari posse: quia sic frustranea forent verba illa non ex operibus. Quis enim dixit, fidem ex operibus dari, ut hoc negandum fuerit? & con- cinnè respondet typorum ratio, si justitia operum & fidei, veteris & novi fœderis, repræsentari dica- tur. Si autem ad fidei dationem vel negationem re- spectus haberi asseratur, commodè explicari non poterit. Quomodo enim minor vocabitur, cui fi- des datur, major, cui fides negatur, servire insuper quomodo significabit fidem non habere? At rectè major est, populus operariorum, quia prior populo fidelium, minor populus fidelium, utpote posterior. Commodè item servire notat libertatem filiorum Dei non habere. Totius etiam capitis analysis optimè sibi constat admisso illo themate & quæ- stionis statu de justificatione fidei, quæ non ita pla- na videtur, si πρώτως & per se de rejectione Judæo- rum, vel etiam de collatione fidei aut negatione ejusdem agi dicatur, ut utriusque ἀναλύσεως colla- tio docere potest. Status etiam iste, inquiunt Re- monstrantes, scopo Apostolicæ tractationis in hac epistola præstituto quam maximè congruit, συνέχειαν cum superioribus capitibus egregie illustrat. Ille enim antea docuerat Apostolus ex professo, quod ho- mo unicè per fidem in Christum liberetur, tum à pec- cati maledicto, per quod damnationi subjicitur, tum ab ejusdem dominio, per quod peccati servitio man- cipatur, quum maledictio non auferatur, nisi per gratiosam justificationem, quæ tantum fit per Chri- stum; liberatio verò à dominio peccati fieri debeat per renovationem, quæ pariter est donum Dei in Christo fluens ex complantatione cum ipso. Unde consequitur, solos Christianos, qui veram habent cum Christo communionem, esse veros Dei fi- lios, & vitæ æternæ hæredes, qui non in lethali & servili metu, quemadmodum sub lege, sed in im- perterrita & filiali παῤῥησίᾳ Deum Patrem suum invocant, eique servire possunt: Ita tuetur jam imprimis salutiferam illam doctrinam adversus Ju- dæos, quantum ad decretum Dei de justificandis & salvandis hominibus, non ex operibus carnis vel le- gis, sed per fidem in Christum, oraculis divinis ejus veritatem à vers. 6. ad 13. è jure autem Dei liberris mo ejus æquitatem demonstrans à vers. 14. ad 23. ad finem capitis. Addunt insuper, quod v. 15. de mi- sericordia Dei agatur, quâ peccata remittuntur, ea verò necessariò præsupponunt fidem, adeoque non de fidei datione, sed de justificatione per fidem trans- latio instituatur. Ita imprimis explicat disertè scopum suum Apostolus v. 16. quod justitia, filia- tio & hæreditas sit non currentis, seu per opera legis eam sectantis, sed Dei, fidelium & credentium in Christum miserentis. Ideoque agitur de misericor- dia Dei in justificandis fidelibus. Similiter cum indurare Deus dicitur, quem vult v. 17. siquidem nonnisi infideles, & qui oblatam gratiam pertina- citer respuunt, induret Es. VI. 9. c. VIII. 12. Rom. IX. 33. cap. XI. 7. 1. Pet. II. 8. ut vel ex ipso Pharaonis exemplo constat, qui toties vocatus per verbum & miracula gratiam Dei rejiciens induratus est, te- ste Historia Mosaica. Unde manifestum, non de absoluta denegatione fidei, sed de induratione & re- probatione eorum, qui non credunt, gratiamque Dei reprobant, verba illa exaudienda esse. Acce- dit, quod v. 21. vas ad decus vel dedecus non sit vas ad fidem vel incredulitatem, aut cui Deus gratiam ad credendum dare, vel non dare velit, sed vas ad de- cus fit vas ad hæreditatem, benedictionem, & glo- riam, uti v. 23. de fidelibus explicatur, quemad- modum vasa ad dedecus sunt ipsimet infideles. Quæ Grotius sub finem habet, ita emendanda ex hisce erunt, imò ex illis etiam, quæ præmiserat Grotius ipse: Quod ἐν προθέσει est Ismael & Esau, id ἐν ἀποδόσει sunt Judæi operũ justitiam sectantes.

Quod ἐν προθέσει Isaac & Jacob, id ἐν ἀποδόσει credentes justitiam fidei amplectentes: qui promis- sionis filii etiam inde non immerito dicuntur, quod ex promissis divinis geniti.

B. Hülsem. in Vind. Script. §. 90. contra Cal- vinianos id imprimis observat: Vocabula promif- sionis & electionis, voluntatis & propositio beneplaci- ti dilectionis, vers. 7. 8. 9. 11. 12. 18. Miserationis v. 16. 18. Misericordiæ v. 23. Quæ omnia dicun- tur esse causæ gratuitæ electionis, nequaquam esse ab- soluta & excludere prævisionem fidei ab homine reci- piendæ per prævenientem illam gratiam concomitan- tem, omnem verbi divini prædicationem, sed hæc vo- cabula omnia esse correlativa cum fide, & supponere eam, opponi autem solis operibus, excludere sola ope- ra, tum interna, tum externa, quæ fiunt cum propo- sito consequendi salutem per ea. Quod probatur tum ex ipso capite IX. ad Rom. tum ex scopo & connexio- ne totius hujus Epistolæ. Prius, quod voluntas mi- serendi, propositum, electio, &c. non excludant sed sup- ponant fidem, tanquam correlatum suum probatur, tum in genere ex eo, quod nulla divina promissio ap- plicari possit, neque constare possit ei sua firmitas, nec haberi possit pro promissione, si absolute, & citra sup- positionem fidei sumatur Rom. IV. 16. propterea ex fide non hæreditas, ut sit per gratiam, ut firma sit pro- missio, ad Gal. III, 18. Si ex lege est hæreditas, non potest esse ex promissione, DEUS autem voluit eam conferre Abrahamo per promissionem; ideò ut pro- missio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus, non potuit hæreditas acquiri per opera v. 22. Ex his in- quam dictis patet, non dari ullam promissionem gra- tiæ aut decretum de salute humana, quod intuitu, seu quoad exclusionem fidei sit absolutum. Quapropter nihil frequentius est in scriptis Calvinianorum Elen- cho hoc oppositorum, si ex mera voluntate & bene- placito DEI electi sumus, sequitur DEUM non præ- vidisse fidem in homine tanquam suppositionem & Hypothesin ex parte salvandi necessariam; contra- rium patet ex his dictis, non posse fingi ullam pro- missionem & decretum salutis citra suppositionem correlationis inter promissionem & fidem. Poste- rius, nempe vocabula ista propositi, decreti, electio- nis &c. excludere sola opera, opponi solis operibus, non fidei patet per inductionem ipsius Phraseos Apostoli- cæ cap. IX. ad Rom. ubi v. 11. 16. 30. 31. 32. expresse voluntas Dei miserentis opponitur operibus, exclu- dit voluntatem, contentionem, & cursum hominis ad salutem per opera sua consequendam v. 11. Cum nihil boni vel mali fecissent, ut propositum Dei secun- dum electionem firmum maneret, non ex operibus, sed ex gratia vocantis dictum est eis &c. Major ser- viet minori &c. v. 16. Salus & electio non sunt vo- lentis & currentis, sed Dei miserentis v. 30. Gentes, quæ non sectabantur justitiam, consecutæ sunt justi- tiam. Israel autem, qui vel maximè sectabatur ju- stitiam, non est assecutus justitiam. Quare? quia non ex fide, sed velut ex operibus legis contendebant ad justitiam. Hæc determinatio oppositionis inter gratuitam electionem & opera, atque hæc subordina- tio fidei & electionis gratuitæ in hac ipsa materia seu tractatione quæstionis de prædestinatione, clarissimè ostendit, fallere Calvinianos Elencho oppositorum, quando gratuitam electionem & fidei prævisionem opponunt, cum gratuitam electionem & operum præ- visionem debuissent opponere. Edant nobis ullum exemplum ex universo codice sacro, oppositæ fidei & gratuitæ electionis. Deinde sic argumentamur: Quo sensu fuevit Apostolus per totam Epistolam ad Romanos opponere promissionem & opera, subordi- nare fidem & promissionem, eodem sensu præsumi- tur his phrasibus etiam usus in continuatione doctri- na de gratuita salvatione per fidem, quam tota Episto- la ad Roman. non solum Cap. II. III. IV. V. VI. sed etiam VIII. IX. X. XI. XII. XV. continuari, Calvi- nus, Musculus, Beza, Aretius, Govalthêrus, Pisca- tor in summariis hujus Epistolæ confitentur. Sed Apostolus ubique per totam hanc Epistolam promis- sionem & œconomiam gratiæ sic tractat, ut ubique sola opera, nunquam fidem excludat, quod patet in- ductione Capitis III. 16. 17. seqq. Cap. IV. 13. 14. 16. 20. 21. & IX. 8. 9. c. XV. 8. Gal. III. 19. quod id item patet ex inductione vocabulorum προγνώσεως & προ- θέσεως prævisionis & propositi, quoties de Oeconomia æternæ salutis prædicantur, ubique opponi solis operi- bus nuspiam fidei. Rom. VIII. 29. XI. 23. 1. Pet. I. 2. Rom. VIII. 28. IX. 11. Ephes. I. 11. & clarissimè 2. Tim. I. 9. 8 κατά τα έργα ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν. Tertium argumentum tale est: Quo sensu opera & gratuita justificatio opponuntur, fides & gratuita justificatio subordinantur, eodem sensu gra- tuita electio & opera opponuntur, fides & gratuita electio subordinantur. Connexionem majoris osten- dit Apostolus Rom. VIII. 30. & IX. 30. 31. 32. Osten- dimus qualis est σχέσις inter fidem & justificationem, talem esse inter fidem & prædestinationem, sed justi- ficatio gratuita & opera sic opponuntur, ut non ex- cludant, sed includant fidem, justificatio & fides sub- ordinantur, ut fides ordine naturæ sit prior justifica- tione. Ergo & prædestinatio gratuita & opera sic op- ponuntur, ut non excludant fidem, ita subordinantur, ut ordine naturæ & in signo rationis Dei prædesti- nantis receptio fidei prior sit decreto prædestinationis seu decreto salvandi.

PARS III. CAPIT. IX. Apologetica æquitatem propositi Dei de salvan- dis fidelibus, damnandis infidelibus vindicans.

## 9:14
Vers. 14. τί ἂν ἐρῶμεν. What then do we say? We have said that Paul uses this little preface when he wishes to remove a calumnious interpretation of his doctrine. μὴ ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ. Do we teach this, which they whisper that we teach, that certain things are done unjustly by God? That which adheres to Him, or can rightly be attributed to Him, is said to be with God. They express this very thing in Deuteronomy XXXII. 4 in Greek thus: ὧν ἔσιν ἀδικία ἐν αὐτῷ. μὴ γένοιτο. And we have had this often. It is, however, the expression of one who is strongly averse. Far be it that we should say this, which is plainly repugnant not only to the aforementioned passage of Deuteronomy, but also to the whole book of Job, and to infinite other places, and finally to the very nature of God:

τῷ γὰρ Μωσῇ λέγει. Namely, after all had sinned concerning the calf. Exod. XXXIII. 19. Vers. 15. ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω. In the Greek, οἰκτείρω is better, as if he were to say, I will do in him that which shall seem good to me. Lords and Kings are accustomed to speak thus, as often as they do not wish to render reasons for their constitution, even if they have some. God can do the same by supreme right in bestowing or denying His benefits, in pardoning and punishing sins, not because the reasons for the distinctions are not clear to Him, but because it is not necessary that they be known to men. See what we have brought to the aforementioned passage of Exodus. The writer of the book on the life and death of Moses explains those words of God thus: I owe nothing to anyone, I give my own freely. Non autem hoc dicit Paulus, that he cannot render some reasons for this dispute, of which he has treated thus far (for he will indeed render some), but that before he comes to that, he wishes to tame the audacity of the contradictor. Politicians also say of Princes: It is not for us to estimate whom they exalt above others and for what reasons: that the supreme judgment of things is given to them, the glory of obedience left to the subjects; that it is illicit and dangerous to inquire into their hidden thoughts and if they are preparing something more refined, and that we cannot therefore attain them: that a soldier ought to be as ignorant of some things as he is knowledgeable: that military affairs are maintained by obeying, not by questioning the commands of leaders: that he is a bad soldier who prefers to interpret the commands of leaders rather than to execute them. It could suffice for us that God wishes to give eternal goods to no one, unless he be just within; ad consequendam eam justitiam, to attain that justice, the way must be entered upon which He Himself shows, and demonstrates to be certain by the gifts of His spirit.

Those words, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, were not brought forward to tame the boldness of those who contradict, nor do they have any commerce with our internal and inherent righteousness, but they set forth the divine mercy shining primarily in the purpose of God according to election, or the most gracious decree concerning the justifying of those who believe in Christ, than which no more illustrious document of immense and incomprehensible divine mercy can be given, which, however, is neither absolute, as the Calvinists wish, nor does it look to our internal righteousness or our works, but it has mercy on us in view of the sole merit of Christ apprehended through faith. The sum of the Evangelical sermon is contained in that which the Son of God held before Moses after he had averted the wrath of God from the people by his prayer and intercession, magnificently and most excellently describing the divine mercy, how gracious, clement, and merciful He is in pardoning and remitting sins

Exod. XXXIV. 6. 7., a summary of which is prefixed here: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious. That out of mere and undeserved grace and mercy He both remits sins and receives sinners into favor without any merit of their own, not because of their internal righteousness or because of the merits of works, but freely and out of His immense kindness and clemency, just as the Apostle infers from there: It is not therefore of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. So that the matter may be more fully established: it must be observed (1.) that the word of showing mercy can be explained as the power of showing mercy, since words signifying action, according to the Hebrew idiom, are accustomed to denote the power of acting, namely that God is bound to no one to show mercy, but has the free power of showing mercy to whom He wills, just as in v. 21 it seems to be explained concerning power. However, the liberty of mercy has no commerce with the Calvinistic absolute mercy of God. For it is one thing for the mercy of God to be free, another for it to be absolute. The former excludes at least the necessity of obligation and the respect of merits, but the latter excludes every respect whatsoever, and thus also removes the intuition of faith. That, therefore, is what the Apostle teaches, that no one ought to rely on the merit of his own will or course, but that all things must be referred to the most free will and grace of God, in which alone our salvation is situated. He forbade, says Augustine in qu. in Exod. qu. 154, a man to glory as if in the merits of his own virtues, so that he who glories, may glory in the Lord; thus also Chrysostom explains that antithesis; To will and to run is a work, but to trust relies not on one's own labors, but on the kindness of God. But if you ask to whom the kindness of God extends, or whom God wills to show mercy; the Apostle answers generally in Rom. XI. 13. God has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all; therefore the mercy of God embraces the whole human race, as far as the antecedent will is concerned, yet God specifically cherishes the faithful with the same, as far as the consequent will is concerned. Wherefore also the mercy of God is merely gratuitous in itself, nor are our merits or works required for the enjoyment of the same, but only a fiducial apprehension of grace. However, the Apostle is properly occupied here in vindicating the equity and justice of the decree by which He determined to justify, adopt, and save the faithful or those who believe in Christ, which pertains to the consequent will. For since this seemed unjust to the Jews, that God should exclude those who pursued the righteousness of works, but adopt those who apprehend grace only by faith; the Apostle meets them, and teaches that God is by no means unjust in this dispensation of salvation, having rendered a twofold reason: the former is drawn from the liberty of divine mercy, and frees God from the crime of injustice with respect to the justification and adoption of the faithful; the latter is taken from the just illustration of divine power and glory, and frees God from injustice with respect to the reprobation of the unfaithful and the workers. The present reason, therefore, relies on the most free mercy of God in choosing the faithful to life, and reprobating the workers and the unfaithful. In the state of integrity, God had placed righteousness and life in the obedience of the law, and condemnation and death in its transgression. Since, therefore, now through the Evangelical covenant He excludes in a manner entirely contrary those who strive for righteousness and life through the law from righteousness and life, but renders others, who do not do that but only believe in Christ, participants of righteousness and life; and the Jews, against whom the Apostle disputes, argued God or this purpose of God and the Evangelical covenant of injustice; but the Apostle absolves it from injustice by this most certain document, that God, moved by mercy alone, made such a decree, to whom it is free to determine, yet with justice moderating, whom He wills to show mercy, and whom He wills to become participants of righteousness and life, since because of the violated condition and the impotence of performing the law, it was either of divine mercy to strike a covenant of grace with man, or of just rigor, however, to punish man without hope of pardon.

Latin:

Vers. 14. τί ἂν ἐρῶμεν. Quid ergo dicimus? Hac præfatiuncula diximus uti Pau- lum, ubi calumniosam suæ doctrinæ interpretationem vult amoliri. μὴ ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ. An hoc docemus, quod illi nos docere susurrant, à Deo quædam injuste fieri? Apud Deum esse dicitur id, quod ei adhæret, aut jure ei attribui potest. Hoc ipsum Deuter. XXXII. 4. sic eloquantur Græce: ὧν ἔσιν ἀδικία ἐν αὐτῷ. μὴ γένοιτο. Et hoc sæpe habuimus. Est autem longissimè aversan- tis. Absit, ut hoc dicamus, quod non tantum dicto Deu- teronomii loco, sed & toto libro Jobi, infinitisqué aliis lo- cis, ipsi denique Dei naturæ planè repugnat:

τῷ γὰρ Μωσῇ λέγει. Nempe postquam circa vitulum omnes peccaverant. Exod. XXXIII. 19. Vers. 15. ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω. In Græco διχτείρω melius, quasi dicat, faciam in eo, quod mihi visum erit. Solent sic loqui Domini ac Reges, quoties constitutionis suæ causas nolunt reddere, etiamsi aliquas habeant. Idem Deus summo jure facere potest in benefi- ciis suis elargiendis, aut negandis, in peccatis condonandis & vindicandis, non quod non ipsi rationes discrimimum constent, sed quod nihil necesse sit eas cognitas esse homi- nibus. Vide, quæ attulimus ad dictum Exodi locum. Scriptor libri de vita & morte Mosis verba illa Dei sic expli- cat: Nemini quicquam debeo, gratis do mea. Non autem hoc dicit Paulus, quod non hujus disputationis, de qua egit hactenus, rationes aliquas possit reddere (nam & reddet aliquas) sed quod priusquam eo veniat, edomare velit con- tradictoris audaciam. Etiam de Principibus dicunt Politi- ci: Non esse nostrum, æstimare, quem supra cæteros & qui- bus de causis extollant: summum illis datum esse rerum ar- bitrium, subditis obsequii gloriam relictam; abditos eorum sensus, & si quid excultius parant exquireré, illicitum, an- ceps, nec ideò nos posse assequi: militem tam nescire quæ- dam, quam scire oportere: Parendo, non imperia ducum sciscitando, res militares contineri: malum esse militem, qui imperia ducum interpretari malit quam exequi. Suffi- cere nobis poterat, nemini Deum velle dare bona æter- na, nisi qui intus justus sit; ad consequendam eam justitiam, viam ineundam, quam ipse monstret, & certum esse osten- dat donis spiritus sui.

Verba illa, Miserebor cujus miserebor, non ad- ducta sunt ad edomandam contradictorum auda- ciam, nec quicquam commercii habent cum inter- na & inharente nostra justitiâ, sed divinam sistunt misericordiam elucentem imprimis in proposito Dei secundum electionem, vel decreto gratiosissimo de justificandis, qui credunt in Christum, quo nullum illustrius dari potest documentum immensæ, & in- comprehensibilis divina misericordia, quæ verò nec absoluta est, uti Calviniani volunt, nec inter- nam nostram justitiam vel opera nostra respicit, sed intuitu solius meriti Christi per fidem appre- hensi nostri miseretur. Summa nempe concionis Evangelica in eo continetur, quam coram Mose postquam iram Dei deprecatione & intercessione suâ à populo avertisset, Filius Dei habuit, magnifi- cè & perquam excellenter describentis misericor- diam divinam, quàm gratiosus, clemens, & miseri- cors sit in condonandis & remittendis peccatis

Exod. XXXIV. 6. 7. cujus breviarium hic præmit- titur, Miserebor, cujus miserebor & gratiosus ero, cui gratiosus ero. Quod ex mera & immerita gra- tia & misericordia & remittat peccata, & in gra- tiam recipiat peccatores sine ullo ipsorum merito, non ob internam eorum justitiam, vel ob operum merita, sed gratis, & ex immensa sua benignitate & clementià, quemadmodum inde infert Aposto- lus: Non est ergò volentis, nec currentis, sed miseren- tis Dei. Ut res plenius constet: observandum (1.) verbum miserendi de potestate miserendi explicari posse, cum verba actionem significantia ex idiotismo Hebræo soleant agendi potestatem notare, quod nempe Deus ad miserendum nulli sit obstrictus, sed liberam habeat potestatem miserendi, cujus vult, uti v. 21. de potestate explicari videtur. Li- bertas autem misericordiæ nihil commercii habet cum absoluta misericordia Dei Calvinistica. Aliud quippe est misericordiam Dei esse liberam, aliud eam esse absolutam. Illud excludit saltem necessi- tatem obligationis, & meritorum respectum, hoc au- tem omnem prorsus respectum excludit, adeoque fidei quoque intuitum removet. Id ergo est, quod docet Apostolus, neminem debere in voluntatis suæ aut cursus merito recumbere, sed omnia ad li- berrimam Dei voluntatem & gratiam referenda esse, in qua solum nostra salus sita est. Prohibuit, inquit August. in qu. in Exod. qu. 154. hominem velut de propriarum virtutum meritis gloriari, ut qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, sic etiam eam antithesin exponit Chrysostomus; Velle & currere opus est, confidere autem non propriis laboribus, sed Dei benignitate nititur. Si autem quæras, ad quos se extendat Dei benignitas, vel quorum velit Deus misereri; Respondet Apostolus generatim Rom. XI. 13. Conclusit Deus omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereretur; ideò misericordia Dei complectitur totum genus humanum, quantum ad voluntatem antecedentem, eâdem tamen speciatim Deus fovet fideles, quantum ad voluntatem consequentem. Quo- circa & in sese gratuita merè est misericordia Dei, nec ad fruitionem ejusdem requiruntur merita vel opera nostra, sed solum fiducialis gratiæ apprehen- sio. Versatur autem propriè hic Apostolus in vin- dicanda æquitate & justitia decreti, quo constituit fideles vel credentes in Christum justificare, adopta- re & salvare, quod ad voluntatem consequentem pertinet. Cum enim hoc Judæis injustum videre- tur, quod Deus eos, qui operum justitiam secta- bantur, excluderet, eos autem, qui fide tantum ap- prehendunt gratiam, adoptaret; occurrit illis Apo- stolus, Deumque minime injustum esse hac salutis dispensatione, docet, redditâ geminâ ratione: prior à libertate misericordiae divinae ducta est, & liberat Deum à crimine injustitiae, respectu justificationis & adoptionis fidelium; posterior desumpta est à justa divinae potentiae ac gloriae illustratione, liberatque Deum ab injustitia, respectu reprobationis infidelium & operariorum. Praesens ergò ratio nititur liber- rima Dei misericordia in eligendis ad vitam fideli- bus, reprobandis operariis & infidelibus. In inte- gritatis statu posuerat Deus justitiam & vitam in obedientia legis, condemnationem & mortem in ejus transgressione. Cum itaque nunc per foedus Evangelicum contrario prorsus modo illos, qui per legem ad justitiam & vitam contendunt, à ju- stitia & vita excludat, alios verò, qui id non fa- ciunt, sed tantum credunt in Christum, justitiae & vitae participes reddat; et injustitiae arguebant Deum, vel propositum hocce Dei, foedusque Ev- angelicum Judaei, contra quos disputat Apostolus; sed absolvit Apostolus id ab injustitia, hoc certissi- mo documento, quod Deus solâ misericordiâ mo- tus, tale decretum fecerit, cui liberum est statuere, justitiâ tamen moderante, quorum velit misereri, & quasnam velit justitiae & vitae participes fieri, quandoquidem ob conditionem violatam, & prae- standi legem impotentiam, aut misericordiae fuerit divinae, foedus gratiae cum homine pacifci, aut rigo- ris justi tamen, hominem absque spe veniae punire.

## 9:16
Vers. 16. So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Since the Hebrews have few adverbs and conjunctions, they almost use the copula in their place. And so here, of him who wills and of him who runs, is worth the same as, of him who runs, as he pleases. This business, which is being treated, is not in the judgment of any man, but of God. For He could without injury leave all who have sinned gravely to their own disease, and apply no medicine: much more to prescribe to them what kind of medicine He wills. He proceeds from the lesser to the greater, that is, the more incredible.

Here the effort and zeal of the workers, the will and faculty of free will, are excluded, and it is taught that the entire business of salvation is to be attributed to the mercy of God alone. Therefore, nothing is left to our own powers, for which the Pelagians and Papists contend, nor yet is election to salvation claimed for the absolute grace of God, which is what the Calvinists want: because although salvation does not depend on our works, the Calvinists themselves cannot deny that faith is necessary for obtaining salvation, nor is the issue here the gift of faith, but justice and salvation, which the Jews sought from the works of the law; on the contrary, the Apostle teaches that justice and salvation do not rely either on the will of man, or free will, or his laborious course and zeal, but on the mercy of God alone, which is apprehended by faith. Conf. oracul. LXIX. Just as to run is to advance with great diligence and haste: so here it denotes the ardent zeal of the workers (the work-holy), just as the Jews truly sweated over the acquisition of eternal life Acts XXVI. 7. And thus the word for running is used in a bad sense Jer. II. 25. Prov. I. 16. c. VI. 18. etc. says our blessed Weller here.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἄρα οὖν οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος, οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐλεοῦντος Θεοῦ. Hebraei cum pauca habeant adverbia & conjunctiones, fermè eorum vice utuntur copula. Itaque hic volentis & currentis, idem valet, quod currentis, quà libet. Non est hoc negotium, de quo agitur, in hominis cujusque arbitrio, sed Dei. Posset enim sine injuria omnes, qui gravia pecca- runt, morbo suo relinquere, nec ullam adhibere medicinam: multo magis eis qualem velit medicinam praescribere. Procedit à minori ad majus, id est, magis incredibile.

Excluditur hic conatus & studium operario- rum, voluntas & facultas liberi arbitrii, & uni Dei misericordiae tribuendum esse docetur, universum salutis negotium. Non ergò viribus nostris, pro quibus Pelagiani & Pontificii dimicant, quicquam relinquitur, nec tamen absoluta Dei gratia electio ad salutem vindicatur, quod volunt Calviniani: quia etsi non ab operibus nostris dependeat salus, fi- dem tamen ad salutem consequendam necessariam esse, nec ipsimet Calviniani diffiteri possunt, neque hic de fidei donatione, sed de justitia & salute agitur, quam ex operibus legis quaerebant Judaei; ex ad- verso vero docet Apostolus justitiam & salutem non niti vel voluntate hominis, aut libero arbitrio, vel cursu studioque ejusdem laborioso, sed sola Dei misericordia, quae fide apprehenditur. Conf. oracul. LXIX. Currere ut est magna cum diligen- tia & festinatione progredi: sic hic ardens studium operariorum (der Werckheiligen) notat, quem- admodum Judaei sudabant verè circa acquisitionem vitae aeternae Act. XXVI. 7. Et ita vox currendi in malo usurpatur Jer. II. 25. Prov. I. 16. c. VI. 18. &c. ait hic B. Wellerus noster.

## 9:17
Vers. 17. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ τῷ Φαραὼ. That is, in Holy Scripture it is said to Pharaoh; a similar locution is in Mark XV. 28. John VII. 38. 42. XIX. 24. 37. Galatians III. 22. IV. 30. Holy Scripture is said to speak, because the Holy Spirit speaks in Scripture, who is united to His word, so that the word of God is spirit and life John VI. 64. living and effective Hebrews IV. 12. and the power of God unto salvation Romans I. 16. by the force of which union of the Spirit and the word, such things are attributed to Scripture itself, that it speaks, that it judges John XII. 48. that it concludes under sin Galatians III. 22. that it is more penetrating than a two-edged sword, and reaches even to the marrow and bones Hebrews IV. 12. that through Scripture we are enlightened, regenerated, converted, and saved.

For for this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. In the Greek it is Exod. IX. 16. For this cause you have been preserved, that I may show my strength in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. What Paul translates, I have raised you up, and the LXX, you have been preserved, is in the Hebrew העמרתיך, that is, I have made you stand. But just as to make alive is said by the Hebrews of one who preserves in life, so to make stand, ἐγείρειν, is said of one who does not impel to ruin. This Pharaoh was oppressing with the harshest servitude the people who worshipped God, not conquered in war, but received into protection on account of the merits of Joseph. Admonished by God concerning this injustice, and indeed with great signs and wonders added, he had contumaciously resisted. For that is what ἐβαρύνθη ἡ καρδία Φαραὼ signifies, Exod. VII. 14. VIII. 15. For it is Kal for Hithpael, and the sense is, he himself made his heart heavy, as is openly explained in VIII. 15. where in the Hebrew it is Pharaoh made his heart heavy: and IX. 35. where in the Greek it is, ἐβά- ρυνεν αὐτὲ τὴν καρδίαν. God could have immediately struck down a man so contumacious, he did not do this, but kept him alive, so that he might bring forth more signs of his power concerning him, which were to procure great glory for God, as is said in Nehem. IX. 10. Sirach. XVI. 15. A heavy heart is called that which does not allow itself to be moved from its purpose. Whom God could by right have destroyed, him he could also by right have left to his own disease, and not apply medicine, which God can by right do against all the contumacious. But what measure of contumacy to expect for this, I do not say is necessary, but convenient to the divine goodness as well as severity, no one knows exactly except himself.

Tertullian against Marcion II. He hardens the heart of Pharaoh: but he had deserved to be supplied for destruction, who had already denied God, who had already so often proudly shaken off his messengers, who had already added the labor of work to the people. Finally, in what way the Egyptian had long been guilty before God of gentile idolatry, worshipping the Ibis and the crocodile sooner than the one God. But the reason is also to be noted, by which God is said to have aggravated and hardened the heart of Pharaoh, namely, lest he should dismiss the people: for it is about that which is treated here. If God had made the evils which he had sent to last, the waters turned into blood, frogs, lice, flies, pestilence, it ought not to be doubted that Pharaoh would have dismissed the people. But because God immediately took away those evils, that matter increased his contumacy. Origen in the fragment which we have of the Philocalia, chapter XX, explaining that place of Exodus and this of Paul: It is not absurd also to soothe such things from custom, often with kind masters saying to servants who are worn out on account of their kindness and long-suffering, I have made you wicked, and, I have become the cause to you of such great sins. For it is necessary to hear the sense and the power of what is said and not to cavil, not hearing the intention of the word. For Paul, having clearly examined these things, says to the impenitent: Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God. For what the Apostle says to the sinner, let it be said to Pharaoh, and these things might be understood very fittingly as being announced to him according to the hardness and impenitent heart, storing up for himself wrath, the hardness not being able to be proven so clearly to have become manifest, if the signs had not happened or had happened, but not so many and such great ones. In the preceding, Origen had argued many excellent things against those who posited Pharaoh as earthy and plainly unamendable by the necessity of nature. And after these words which we have now produced, he has many others worthy of reading. Pharaoh therefore hardened himself and for a long time, but God hardened Pharaoh by not taking him out of life, nor by using that dispensation of his powers by which he could have immediately crushed his hardness, but rather by another, which would make his contumacy more and more known to the human race, and at length also the justice of God in punishing him. But there is in Pharaoh an image of the Jewish people from the times of Christ and thereafter. God had sent to them not Moses, but his Son with innumerable signs. He could have immediately avenged their contumacy, but he did not wish to, he allowed them to act in peace for almost forty years. In the meantime, having become worse daily, they brought infamy upon themselves among all nations, so that when at length their destruction happened, although most sad, it was nevertheless believed to be below their evil merits, with Joseph himself as witness.

Grotius does not badly weigh the Hebrew and Greek phrase and the whole passage, which the Calvinists abuse most badly: To whom these things can be entirely opposed; that (1.) not an incitement to hardening, but a preservation in life, in the Hebrew manner of speaking, is intimated. (2.) that Pharaoh, having been admonished by God concerning the injustice against the Israelites, and concerning their dismissal, contumaciously resisted, and so hardened his own heart, but was not hardened by God. (3.) that God preserved in life a contumacious man, whom he could have immediately struck down, not so that he might struggle more, but, since he foresaw that he would struggle, so that he might bring forth more signs of power concerning him, which were to procure great glory for God throughout the world. (4.) that the name of God was to be glorified in this way, not only by reason of power, but also by reason of long-suffering, patience, and divine thanks. Which shone forth in a most illustrious manner in this example of supreme obstinacy, and is presented here by the Apostle himself to be weighed. (5.) God did not intend by these same miracles the further hardening of Pharaoh, but rather wished to drive Pharaoh to the dismissal of His people, and to lead him to the glorious acknowledgment of His name. Whence also the servants of Pharaoh acknowledged the power of God Exod. IX. 20. X. 7. XII. 38. And Pharaoh himself chap. VIII. 20. IX. 27. X. 16. Nor did God absolutely wish to declare His power in Pharaoh, but in so far as he persisted in his disobedience; He indulged the one hardening himself, so that when he was incurable, He might show His power among foreigners by these same miraculous punishments, as we have warned in Theolog. Apost. Rom. (6.) that because of his contumacy and the hardening of his heart, God could rightly destroy Pharaoh, and rightly also leave him to his own disease, and thus, according to His consequent and judicial will, He left him. What measure of contumacy it was fitting for the goodness or the severity of God to await or to abandon in order that Pharaoh might be destroyed, must be left to God. (7.) Pharaoh altogether deserved both divine abandonment and destruction and ruin, not only because of his detestable tyranny and cruelty toward the people, but also because of that supreme contumacy and resistance against God, after he had been warned especially by great signs and wonders. (8.) When God is said to have hardened Pharaoh, namely so that he would not dismiss the people, it is explained that this was done in such a way that He immediately removed those evils which He had sent, and by that agreement accidentally increased his contumacy; as is beautifully illustrated by Origen in the Philocalia by the example of a master who, through kindness and long-suffering, is said to have made his servants wicked, or to have been the cause of the sins committed by them. (9.) Therefore, after Pharaoh hardened himself and that for a long time, God is said to have hardened Pharaoh, not by infusing further hardness, but by not taking him away from life, and not crushing his hardness, as He could have, not because He decreed his destruction by any absolute decree or good pleasure, but because He wished to manifest his contumacy more and more to the world, and at length also to reveal His justice in punishing him. (10.) Moreover, by the preservation of Pharaoh and the patient tolerance of the same, God equally invited him to repentance: as in Rom. II. 4. it is said generally that He invites us to repentance through His μακροθυμίαν; therefore He does not intend his ruin and destruction, but rather his conversion and salvation, and an example for others. Which the same Origen excellently illustrates in his commentary on this passage, book VII, p. m. 580. Let us suppose either a head of a household or a King has seen the time when those who have committed many things against morals and discipline ought to have been amended, and has chosen someone very harsh, and much harsher than these very ones who are to be corrected, who for his own crimes is now no longer worthy of amendment but of death. Wishing, therefore, for his destruction to profit the amendment of the others, sending him to those whom he desires to be corrected by his death, he says to him: Because for this very thing I have raised you up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be announced in all the earth. Do you see, because he did not say: Because for I have made you for this very thing; otherwise the blame would seem to be referred to the Creator; but he says: For this very thing I have raised you up, that is, so that through the malice of your mind, which you sought for yourself by living unbridledly and without the fear of God, both a useful and fruitful correction may be inflicted upon others, and a most famous destruction may be conferred upon you yourself as an example for posterity. (11.) It is therefore now clear how the hardening of Pharaoh is attributed to God, certainly not as it was a sin, but as it was the punishment of that same sin, and that God hardened him not ἐνεργητικῶς or effectively by injecting or increasing hardness, but ἀποφαντικῶς by not taking away nor blunting the hardness contracted by his own fault, and συμβεβηκότως by both preserving and tolerating him in life, and by not immediately taking away evils and punishments, and also ἐγκαταλειπτικῶς by abandoning him and withdrawing grace: concerning which see St. Augustine, Epistle CV. God does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting grace: as also παραδοτικῶς, by delivering him into a reprobate sense, Rom. I. 28. Rightly therefore St. Augustine, Sermon XXCVIII. on the season: It must be most certainly believed that not the violence of God, but his own iniquity and indomitable pride caused Pharaoh to be hardened so many times against the commandments of God. (12.) The Apostle uses this example, however, to show that God enjoys the free power of rejecting the working Jews, because He can also harden the unfaithful and refractory altogether. Since there is a great parity between the Jews and Pharaoh. For just as the latter refused to believe the words of the Lord, which were announced to him through Moses and Aaron, and were confirmed by miracles: So the former refused to believe the word of the Gospel, which was preached to them by Christ, and was confirmed by many miracles: As the former persisted contumaciously in infidelity and disobedience, so also did the latter. And since it is a graver sin not to believe the Son than the servant, the sin of the Jews was certainly graver, who denied faith to the Son himself, as the Apostle concludes Heb. II. 1. & c. III. 1. seq., just as we also observed in the cited place. Compare what we have said about this example in the Old Testament illustrated in the Bible regarding Exodus.

ἄρα ὇ν θέλει ἐλεᾷ.) He softens whom He wills for reasons known to Himself. There are various kinds of divine mercy, the dispensation of which is free to God. The greatest of these is that by which He corrects the vices of men, which He often does not by treating them gently, but by chastising them sharply.
