Origen brings forward this very argument, treating this same point in the Philocalia, chapter XXVI, a notable passage from 2 Maccabees VI. 12. and following, where it is shown that this is most of all a matter of divine mercy, not to allow those who sin to act according to their own will for long, but to apply discipline to them immediately.

Latin:

Vers. 17. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ τῷ Φαραὼ. Id est, in S. Scriptura dicitur Pharaoni; Similis locutio Marci XV. 28. Job. VII. 38. 42. XIX. 24. 37. Galat. III. 22. IV. 30. Scriptura S. loqui dicitur, quia Spiritus S. in Scri- ptura loquitur, qui verbo suo unitus est, ita ut ver- bum Dei sit spiritus & vita Joh. VI. 64. vivum & ef- ficax Ebr. IV. 12. & potentia Dei ad salutem Rom. I. 16. vi cujus unionis Spiritus & verbi scripturae ipsi ta- lia tribuuntur, quod loquatur, quod judicet Joh. XII. 48. quod sub peccato concludat Gal. III. 22. quod penetrantior sit gladio ancipiti, & pertingat usque ad medullam & ossa Ebr. IV. 12. quod per Scriptura il- luminemur, regeneremur, convertamur, salvemur.

Ὅτι εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε, ὅπως ἐνδείξωμαι ἐν σοὶ τὴν δύ- ναμίν μου, καὶ ὅπως διαγγελῇ τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ. In Græco est Exod. IX. 16. ἕνεκα τούτου διετηρήθης, ἵνα ἐν- δείξωμαι ἐν σοὶ τὴν ἰσχύν μου, καὶ ὅπως διαγγελῇ τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ. Quod Paulus vertit, ἐξήγειρά σε & LXX. διετηρήθης, in Hebræo est העמרתיך, id est, stare te feci. Sicut autem vivificare Hebræis dicitur, qui in vita conservat, ita stare fa- cere, ἐγείρειν, qui non impellit in ruinam. Pharao iste po- pulum Dei cultorem, non bello victum, sed ob Josephi me- rita in tutelam receptum durissimo servitio premebat. A Deo de hac injustitia admonitus, & quidem magnis signis prodigiisque additis, contumaciter obstiterat. Id enim va- let ἐβαρύνθη ἡ καρδία Φαραὼ Exod. VII. 14. VIII. 15. Est enim Kal pro Hithpael, & sensus est, ipse cor suum grave reddidit, sicut apertè explicatur VIII. 15. ubi in Hebræo est Pharao grave fecit cor suum: & IX. 35. ubi in Græco est, ἐβά- ρυνεν αὐτὲ τὴν καρδίαν. Hominem tam contumacem potue- rat Deus illicò prosternere, non fecit hoc, sed eum vivum servavit, ut plura etiam potentiæ suæ signa circa eum ede- ret, quæ Deo magnam gloriam erant paritura, ut dicitur Nehem. IX. 10. Sirach. XVI. 15. Grave cor dicitur, quod à proposito dimoveri se non patitur. Quem perdere jure potuerat Deus, eum jure poterat etiam suo morbo relin- quere, nec adhibere medicinam, quod Deus jure potest ad- versus omnes contumaces. Quam verò mensuram contu- maciæ ad hoc expectare, non dico, necessarium sit, sed con- veniens divinæ quà bonitati quà severitati, nemo exactè novit nisi ipse.

Tertullianus adversus Marcionem II. Indurat cor Pha- raonis: sed meruerat in exitium subministrari, qui jam negave- rat Deum, qui jam legatos ejus toties superbus excusserat, qui jam populo laborem operis adjecerat. Postremo qua Ægyptius olim Deo reus fuerat gentilis idololatria, Ibin & crocodilum ci- tius colens quam Deum unum. Notanda vero etiam ratio, qua usus Deus dicitur aggravasse & indurasse cor Pharao- nis, nempe ne populum dimitteret: nam de eo hic agitur. Si Deus fecisset durare mala quæ immiserat, aquas verfas in sanguinem, ranas, ciny phes, muscas, pestilentiam, dubitari non debet, quin Pharao dimissurus fuerit populum. Quia vero Deus mala illa statim sustulit, ea res illi auxit contu- maciam. Origenes in fragmento quod habemus philoca- liæ cap. XX. locum illum Exodi & hunc Pauli éxplicans: ἐκ ἄτοπον δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ συνηθείας τὰ τοιαῦτα παραμυθήσασθαι, πολ- λάκις τῶν χρηστῶν δεσποτῶν φασκόντων τοῖς διὰ τὴν χρηστότητα καὶ τὴν μακροθυμίαν ἐκτριβομένοις οἰκέταις τὸ ἐγώ σε πονηρὸν ἐποίησα, καὶ, ἐγώ σοι αἴτιος γέγονα τῶν τηλικούτων ἁμαρτημάτων. δεῖ γὰρ τὸ τῆς ἀκροᾶσαι καὶ τῆς δυνάμεως τῇ λεγομένη καὶ μὴ συκο- φαντεῖν, μὴ κατακούοντας τοῦ βελήματος τοῦ λόγε. ὁ γὰρ Παῦλος ταῦτα σαφῶς ἐξετάσας φησὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀμετανοητα· ἢ τοῦ πλούτο τῆς χρηστότητος αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀνοχῆς καὶ τῆς μακροθυμίας κατα- φρονεῖς, ἀγνοῶν ὅτι τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ Θεῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει. και τὰ δὲ τὴν σκληρότητά σου καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν, θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ ὀργὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως δικαιοκρισίας Θεῦ. ἃ γὰρ λέγει πρὸς τὸν ἁμαρτάνοντα ὁ Ἀπόστολος, λεγέσθω πρὸς τὸν Φαραὼ, καὶ πάνυ ἁρμοδίως νοηθείη ταῦτα ἀπαγγελλό- μενα αὐτῷ κατὰ τὴν σκληρότητα καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν, θησαν ρίζοντα ἑαυτῷ ὀργὴν τῆς σκληροτήτος ἐκ ἂν ἐλεγχθείσης ὕτως εἰδὶ Φανερᾶς γεγενημένης, εἰ μὴ τὰ σημεῖα ἐγέγονε ἢ ἐγεγόνει μὲν, μὴ τοσαῦτα δὲ καὶ τηλικαῦτα. In præcedentibus Ori- genes multa egregia disputaverat contra eos, qui Pharaonem χοϊκὸν & plane ex naturæ necessitate inemendabilem statue- bant. Et post hæc, quæ jam produximus verba, multa alia habet digna lectu. Induravit ergo se Pharao & diu, indu- ravit autem Deus Pharaonem non auferendo eum ex vita, neque utendo ea virium suarum dispensatione, qua statim duritiem ejus potuerat contundere, sed aliâ potius, quæ ma- gis magisque cognitam faceret humano generi ipsius contu- maciam, ac tandem quoque Dei in eo puniendo justitiam. Est autem in Pharaone imago populi Judaici à Christi tem- poribus ac deinceps. Miserat Deus ad eum populum non Mosen, sed Filium suum cum signis innumeris. Potuerat eorum contumaciam statim ulcisci, sed noluit, sivit eos in pace agere per annos fermè quadraginta. Interea temporis pejores effecti quotidie, infamiam sibi accersivere apud omnes gentes, ita, ut cum tandem excidium eis evenit quanquam tristissimum, esse tamen infra eorum mala me- rita crederetur, ipso teste Josepho.

Non malè expendit Grotius phrasin Ebræam & Græcam totumque locum, quô pessimè abutun- tur Calviniani: Quibus hæc omninò opponi pos- sunt; quòd (1.) non excitatio ad indurationem, sed conservatio in vita, more loquendi Hebraico, in- nuatur. (2.) quod Pharao de injustitia adversus Israelitas, deque eorum dimissione à Deo admoni- tus contumaciter obstiterit, adeoque cor suum ob- duravit, non autem à Deo induratus sit. (3.) quod hominem contumacem, quem illicò prosternere potuit, in vita conservavit Deus, non ut obluctaretur amplius, sed, quum prævideret eum obluctaturum, ut plura potentiæ signa circa eum ederet, quæ Deo magnam per orbem terrarum paritura erant gloriam. (4.) quod nomen Dei sic glorificandum fuerit, non solum ratione potentiæ, sed etiam ratione longanimitatis, patientiæ, & gratiæ divinæ. Quæ illustrissima ratione in hoc exemplo summæ obstinationis effulgebat, & ab ipso Apostolo hic expendenda sistitur. (5.) non intendebat Deus iisdem miraculis Pharaonis ulteriorem indurationem, sed adigere potius volebat Pharaonem ad populi sui dimissionem, & adducere ad gloriosam sui nominis agnitionem. Unde & servi Pharaonis agnoscebant Dei potentiam Exod. IX. 20. X. 7. XII. 38. Et Pharao ipse cap. VIII. 20. IX. 27. X. 16. Nec absolutè voluit Deus in Pharaone suam declarare potentiam, sed in quantum ille in inobedientia sua perseverabat; indulgebat indurescenti, ut cum insanabilis esset, potentiam suam apud exteros iisdem miraculosis pœnis ostenderet, ut in Theolog. Apost. Rom. monuimus. (6.) quod ob contumaciam & indurationem cordis Pharaonem jure Deus perdere, jure etiam suo morbo relinquere potuerit, adeoq; juxta voluntatem consequentem & judiciariam reliquerit. Quam mensuram contumaciæ ad hoc ut perderetur Pharao expectare vel deserere divinæ aut bonitati aut severitati convenerit Deo relinquendum est. (7.) Meruit omninò Pharao cum derelictionem divinam, tum perditionem & exitium, non tantum ob detestandam tyrannidem, & sævitiam in populum, sed etiam ob summam illam contumaciam & obluctationem adversus Deum, postquam imprimis magnis signis, & prodigiis commonefactus esset. (8.) Cum indurasse Deus Pharaonem dicitur ne scilicet populum dimitteret, id explicatur eâ factum ratione, quod mala illa, quæ immiserat, statim ab illo sustulerit, eoq; pacto per accidens contumaciam illius auxerit; uti ab Origene in Philocalia pulchrè illustratur exemplo heri, qui per benignitatem & longanimitatem servos dicitur pravos fecisse, aut causa exstitisse peccatorum ab iis designatorum. (9.) Postquam ergò Pharao semetipsum induravit idque diu, Deus indurasse Pharaonem dicitur, non duritiem ulteriorem immittendo, sed cum ex vita non auferendo, neque duritiem, uti poterat, contundendo, non quod ejus perditionem absoluto aliquo decreto vel beneplacito decreverit, sed quia contumaciam ejus ita magis magisque orbi manifestare, ac tandem etiam justitiam suam in eo puniendo patefacere voluit. (10.) Conservatione autem Pharaonis & patienti ejusdem tolerantia Deus eundem æquè invitavit ad pœnitentiam: uti Rom. II. 4. generatim dicitur nos per μακροθυμίαν suam ad pœnitentiam invitare, non ergò intendit ejus exitium & perditionem, sed potius ejus conversionem & salutem, aliorumque exemplum. Quod eximiè illustrat idem Origenes in comm. ad h. l. lib. VII. p. m. 580. Ponamus vel Patremfamilias vel Regem vidisse tempus, quo emendari debuissent hi, qui contra mores & disciplinam multa commiserunt, & elegisse durissimum aliquem, & his ipsis, qui corripiendi sunt, multò duriorem, qui pro sceleribus suis jam non sit dignus emendatione sed morte. Volens ergò interitum ejus ad emendationem proficere cæterorum, mittens eum ad illos, quos morte ejus corrigi cupit, dicit ei: Quia ad hoc ipsum te suscitavi, ut ostendam in te virtutem meam, & ut annunciem nomen tuum in universa terra. Videnim, quia non dixit: Quia ad hoc ipsum te feci; alioquin ad conditorem referri videretur culpa; sed ait: Ad hoc ipsum te suscitavi, hoc est, ut per animi tui malitiam, quam tibi infrenite & sine Dei timore vivendo quæsisti, & in alios irrogetur utilis & fructuosa correctio, & in te ipsum ad posteritatis exemplum famosissimus conferatur interitus. (11.) Patet ergò jam, quomodo induratio Pharaonis Deo tribuatur, nimirum non ut peccatum fuit, sed uti fuit peccati ejusdem supplicium, quodque induravit Deus non ἐνεργητικῶς vel effectivè duritiem immittendo, vel augendo, sed ἀποφαντικῶς non auferendo nec retundendo duritiem propriâ culpâ contractam, & συμβεβηκότως tùm conservando & tolerando eum in vita, tùm mala, & pœnas statim tollendo, nec non ἐγκαταλειπτικῶς deserendo & gratiam subtrahendo: de quo S. August. Epist. CV. Non obdurat Deus impertiendo malitiam, sed non impertiendo gratiam: ut & παραδοτικῶς, tradendo eum in sensum reprobum, Rom. I. 28. Rectè itaque S. August. Serm. XXCVIII. de tempore: Certissime credendum est, quod Pharaonem non Dei violentia, sed propria iniquitas & indomabilis superbia contra Dei præcepta toties indurari fecerit. (12.) Utitur autem hoc exemplo Apostolus, ut ostendat Deum liberâ gaudere potestate reprobandi operarios Judæos, quia indurare etiam omninò potest infideles & refractarios. Quum magna sit paritas inter Judæos & Pharaonem. Ut enim hic verbis Domini credere renuebat, quæ ipsi per Mosen & Aaronem annunciabantur, & miraculis confirmabantur: Ita illi verbo Evangelii credere recusabant, quod ipsis à Christo prædicabatur, multísque miraculis confirmabatur: Ut ille in infidelitate & inobedientia contumaciter perseverabat, ita & hi. Et quum gravius sit peccatum, Filio non credere quàm servo, Judæorum profectò gravius fuit peccatum, qui Filio ipsi fidem denegarunt, ut concludit Apostolus Ebr. II. 1. & c. III. 1. seq. quemadmodum etiam l. c. observavimus. Conf. quæ ad Exodum in Bibliis V. T. illustratis de hoc Exemplo diximus.

ἄρα ὇ν θέλει ἐλεᾷ.) Emollit, quos vult ob causas sibi cognitas. Varia sunt divinæ misericordiæ genera, quorum libera Deo est dispensatio. Eorum maximum id, quo hominum vitia corrigit, quod sæpe facit non tam leniter tractando, quam acriter castigando. Adducit ad hanc rem Origenes hoc ipsum argumentum tractans Philocaliæ cap. XXVI. locum insignem ex 2. Maccab. VI. 12. & sequentibus, ubi ostenditur, maximè hoc esse misericordiæ divinæ, non diu sinere ex sententia agere eos, qui peccant, sed statim illis adhibere disciplinam.

## 9:18
ὃν δὲ θέλει σκληρύνει.) σκληρύνειν corresponds to the verb חזק which is likewise used in Scripture no less than כבד βαρύνειν, and in the same sense. First, God predicts, having seen Pharaoh's hardness, that He would harden his heart, Exod. IV. 21. then it is said that He hardened it, VII. 22. VIII. 19. 36. where in the Hebrew it is, and he hardened, namely himself, the heart of Pharaoh. It is also said that God hardened the heart of Pharaoh, IX. 13. X. 20. 27. XI. 10. XIV. 4. 17. Pharaoh hardened himself by voluntary obstinacy: God hardened Pharaoh, that is, He allowed him to become harder, and showed what he was like (for both are accustomed to be signified by active verbs among the Hebrews) by preserving him, as we have said, alive and treating him more gently than he deserved, so that He might later compensate for the slowness of the punishment with its severity. See the cited passage from Maccabees, and those of Origen which we have indicated. Kimchi adds in the word שקר that God hardens the minds of men by hiding His counsels from them, giving an example in Pharaoh and Sihon.

That explanation of the words, He has mercy therefore on whom He wills, does not seem foreign to those which precede: He softens whom He wills, for reasons known to Himself; among other things, by sharply chastising the vices of men: He hardens whom He wills by permitting that one should become harder, and by keeping him alive, and treating him more gently than he deserves. But if this sentence is taken more generally, the Calvinists can nevertheless carve nothing out of it for their horrible dogma, that the absolute will of God is established as the cause of hardening. For it can be said (1.) that the words of the Apostle are to be understood not of the action, but of the power of acting. Namely, that God has the power of hardening whom He wills. (2.) That that will is not absolute, regarding no merits of man, but that only the freedom of the divine will is hinted at by the Apostle, which, however, is not to be opposed to divine justice or truth. (3.) that the hardening, as it is ascribed to God, is not a sin, but the punishment of sin, otherwise God would be established as the direct cause of sin, which the sounder Calvinists acknowledge to be blasphemous. But if it is a punishment for sin, it certainly presupposes sin. Therefore, it neither can nor ought to be ascribed solely to the absolute will of God. It is to be noted, therefore, that hardening is viewed in two ways: 1. as it is a sin. 2. as it is the punishment of preceding sins. In the former way, it is ascribed to men and the Devil, to the latter as suggesting and blinding, 2 Cor. IV. 3. Eph. II. 2. to the former as consenting, and hardening themselves by spontaneous malice, and therefore they are said to turn their backs to God, Zech. VII. 11. to close their eyes, Is. VI. 10. John XII. 40. to stop their ears, Matt. XIII. 15. to harden their necks, Acts VII. 15. to have a forehead of brass, Is. XLVIII. 4. to make their face harder than a rock, Jer. V. 3. to harden their heart, 1. Sam. VI. 9. to foster a reprobate mind, Rom. I. 28. to have a seared conscience, 1 Tim. IV. 2. as also a spirit of compunction, Rom. XI. 8. and a mind that knows not how to repent, Rom. II. 5. finally to contract a callus in hardness, Eph. IV. 18. In the other way, it is ascribed to God, or even to His ministry, Is. VI. 10. and to this indeed μετωνυμικῶς or for the declaration of divine judgment: But to the former κυρίως, and it is nothing else than the most just judgment itself, by which the contumacy of men is avenged through the withdrawal of grace, and delivery into the power of Satan.

God, therefore, is not the cause of hardening in so far as it is sin, whether directly or indirectly, whether by effecting, or by commanding, or by approving, which can be evident (1.) from the nature of God, because his immutability, goodness, and supreme perfection prevent any sin from being able to come from God. (2.) from the divine prohibition, that we should not harden our hearts Ps. XCV. 8. (3.) From God's complaint, that men have hardened themselves, Exod. X. 3. (4.) From the punishment with which he affects those who harden themselves. For he is not the author of the hardening of whom he himself is the avenger. But in so far as hardening is a punishment for sin, it is ascribed to God, not because he himself is the author of the hardness of heart, but because God, as a punishment for preceding sins, permits the reprobate to be hardened, deserts them with his grace, and finally delivers them to Satan. Which judicial acts being posited, the sin of hardening follows. When, therefore, God is said to harden, it is by no means to be understood ἐνεργητικῶς or effectively, as if God infuses hardness, or efficiently cooperates toward hardening, but 1. συγχωρητικῶς on account of permission, as in Is. LXIII. 17 it is said, You have made us to err, i.e., you have permitted it, as is explained in Ps. LXXXI. 12. 2. ἀφορμητικῶς on account of the occasion which the reprobate take from those things which God does. Whence it is ascribed to God at least συμβεβηκότως, and by accident. Thus God is said to concur in hardening, partly σωστικῶς by preserving the reprobate and tolerating those who are hardened, partly ὑλικῶς by offering the means which men abuse to their own perdition, so that they are hardened more and more, when God wishes them to act toward repentance. 3. ἐγκαταλειπτικῶς on account of desertion, because he deserts the reprobate with his grace, or also ἀφαιρετικῶς, because he takes away whatever softness of heart there might be, by withdrawing grace. Matth. XIII. 12. 4. παραδοτικῶς on account of delivery into a reprobate mind, and into the further power of Satan Rom. I. 28. But that God does not wish to harden except those who reject the grace offered, the whole Scripture proves. See Prov. I. 24. seq. Eph. V. 1. seq. Jerem. XXXII. 33. Matth. XXIII. 37. Luc. XIV. 21. Job. III. 18. 36. XVI. 8. seq. 2. Thess. I. 8. II. 10. Therefore, the will here is not absolute, but presupposes the rejection of the grace offered. What of the fact that the very sin of hardening confirms this sufficiently, because hardening formally includes the rejection of grace and the hardening of the heart against the word of God? Therefore, hardening cannot be imputed to the absolute will of God without manifest contradiction. Origen's interpretation is again correct here: But what he says, he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills, he hardens: he seems to take this from those things which are written in Exodus. For there he says: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, that he may not let the people go. The heart of Pharaoh was hardened in this way: God did not wish to give sudden and full vengeance upon him. For although it was a consummation of malice, yet through his patience he had not excluded even for him the opportunity of conversion: and therefore he used against him first lighter, then also gradually increasing blows. But what God was doing through patience, from this he was hardened to contempt, storing up for himself a greater path, so that it is fitting to say to him that which the Apostle writes, do you despise the riches of his goodness and longsuffering, not knowing that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath. Therefore, God does not harden whom he wills, but he who has not wished to obey patiently is hardened.

wills, yet in such a way that he is not the author or approver or positive cause of the hardness, he does not undeservedly accuse those who harden themselves. The Apostle hints at this concerning God in four ways and arguments primarily: 1. because those who harden themselves are vessels of wrath; but wrath presupposes sin; 2. because God at least tolerates, but does not approve of their hardness; 3. because they are tolerated in great longsuffering, and therefore God does not wish that they be hardened, but that they be converted; Rom. II. 4. 4. because they are called vessels prepared for destruction, namely by their own fault. Therefore not by the absolute will of God. Although we admit that some will of God is irresistible, yet that which exerts itself in election to eternal life, or in the ordinary donation of faith, is not irresistible, just as the Apostle teaches here. Which that objection would certainly constrain, if this will of God were irresistible. For why does God complain about us, when we do not believe, if he has decided by an absolute decree to give faith to these, and to deny it to others, and to his will, according to which he wills to give or not to give it, no one can resist?

Vers. 18. ἐρεῖς ἄν μοι. You say, stubborn Jew.

Latin:

ὃν δὲ θέλει σκληρύνει.) σκληρύνειν respondet verbo חזק quod itidem in Scriptura usurpatur non minus quam כבד βαρύνειν, & sensu eodem. Primum prædicit Deus conspecta Pharaonis duritie, se cor ejus induraturum Exod. IV. 21. deinde dicitur induruisse VII. 22. VIII. 19. 36. ubi in Hebræo est, & induravit, nempe se, cor Pharaonis. Dicitur & Deus indurasse cor Pharaonis IX. 13. X. 20. 27. XI. 10. XIV. 4. 17. Pharao semet obduravit voluntariâ obstinatione: Deus Pharaonem, id est, sivit duriorem fieri, ac qualis esset, ostendit (utrumque enim per verba activa apud Hebræos significari solet) servando, ut diximus, vivum molliusquè eum tractando quàm merebatur, ut postea tarditatem supplicii gravitate compensaret. Vide dictum locum ex Maccabaico, & Origenis, quæ indicavimus. Addit Kimchi in verbo שקר indurare Deum animos hominum, consilia sua ipsos celando, exemplum dans in Pharaone & Seone.

Non aliena ab istis, quæ antecedunt, videtur illa verborum, Miseretur igitur quorum vult, explicatio: Emollit, quos vult, ob causas sibi cognitas; inter alia, vitia hominum acriter castigando: indurat quem vult permittendo, ut durior quis fiat, ac servando vivum, molliusque eum, quàm meretur tractando. Si verò generalius accipiatur hæc sententia, nihil tamen Calviniani pro horribili suo dogmate, quod causa indurationis constituatur absoluta Dei voluntas inde exsculpere possunt. Dici enim po- test (1.) non de actione, sed de agendi potestate ver- ba Apostoli esse intelligenda. Deum nempe pote- statem habere indurandi, quem vult. (2.) Volunta- tem illam non esse absolutam, nulla merita hominis respicientem, sed innui tantum ab Apostolo vo- luntatis divinæ libertatem, quæ tamen non est op- ponenda divinæ vel justitiæ, vel veritati. (3.) indu- rationem, quà Deo ascribitur, non esse peccatum, sed pœnam peccati, alioquin Deus directè causa peccati statueretur, quod blasphemum esse, sanio- res agnoscunt Calviniani. Si autem pœna est pec- cati, præsupponit utique peccatum. Proinde nec potest, nec debet absolutæ Dei voluntati unicè ascribi. Notandum itaque indurationem bifariam spectari: 1. uti peccatum est. 2. ut est præcedentium peccatorum supplicium. Priori modo hominibus & Diabolo ascribitur, huic ut suggerenti & excæcanti 2. Cor. IV. 3. Eph. II. 2. illis ut consentientibus, & spontaneâ malitiâ sese indurantibus, ideoque dicun- tur illi Deo tergum obvertere, Zach. VII. 11. oculos occludere Es. VI. 10. Joh. XII. 40. aures obserare Matth. XIII, 15. cervicem indurare Act. VII. 15. fron- tem habere æneam Es. XLVIII. 4. faciem petra ob- firmatiorem reddere Jerem. V. 3. cor aggravare 1. Sam. VI. 9. mentem reprobam fovere Rom. I. 28. conscientiam cauteriatam habere 1. Tim. IV. 2. ut & Spiritum compunctionis Roman. XI. 8. animumque pœnitere nescium Rom. II. 5. denique callum in du- ritie contrahere Eph. IV. 18. Altero modo ascribi- tur Deo, vel etiam ejusdem ministerio, Es. VI. 10. & huic quidem μετωνυμικῶς vel ob declarationem judicii divini: Illi autem κυρίως, estque nihil aliud, quàm ipsum judicium justissimum, quo vindicatur hominum contumacia per gratiæ subtractionem, & traditionem in potestatem Satanæ.

Non ergo Deus indurationis in quantum illa peccatum est, causa est sive directè, sive indirectè, sive efficiendo, sive præcipiendo, sive approbando, quod patere po- test (1.) è Dei naturâ, quia immutabilitas, boni- tas, & perfectio ejusdem summa obstat, quò minus à Deo ullum peccatum esse possit. (2.) ex prohibi- tione divina, ne obduremus corda Ps. XCV. 8. (3.) E Dei querela, quod homines seipsos indurarint, Exod. X. 3. (4.) E pœna, quà afficit eos, qui se in- durant. Non enim indurationis autor est, cujus ipse est ultor. Quà verò induratio pœna est pecca- ti, Deo ascribitur, non quod ipse autor sit duritiei cordis, sed quod Deus in pœnam peccatorum præ- cedentium reprobos permittat indurari, eosdem gratiâ sua deserat, tandemque Satanæ tradat. Qui- bus actibus judicialibus positis, sequitur peccatum indurationis. Cùm ergò Deus indurare dicitur, neutiquam id intelligendum est ἐνεργητικῶς vel ef- fectivè, quasi Deus immittat duritiem, vel efficien- ter ad indurationem cooperetur, sed 1. συγχωρη- τικῶς propter permissionem uti Es. LXIII. 3. dicitur, Fecisti nos errare, i. e. permisisti, ut exponitur Psal. XXCI. 13. 2. ἀφορμητικῶς propter occasionem, quam ex iis, quæ Deus agit, sumunt reprobi. Unde Deo id ascribitur saltem συμβεβηκότως, & ex accidenti. Ita concurrere dicitur Deus ad indurationem, par- tim σωστικῶς conservando reprobos, & tolerando eos, qui indurantur, partim ὑλικῶς media offeren- do, quibus abutuntur homines ad sui perditionem, ut magis magisq; indurentur, cum Deus illis agere eos velit ad pœnitentiam. 3. ἐγκαταλειπτικῶς ob desertionem, quod gratiâ sua deserat reprobos, vel etiã ἀφαιρετικῶς, quod mollitiem cordis qualem- cunque auferat, subtractâ gratiâ. Matth. XIII. 12. 4. παραδοτικῶς ob traditionem in sensum reprobum, & in ulteriorem Satanæ potestatem Rom. I. 28. Quod autem non velit Deus indurare nisi eos, qui gratiam oblatam aspernantur, universa Scriptura comprobat. Vid. Prov. I. 24. seq. Ef.V. 1. seq. Je- rem. XXXII. 33. Matth. XXIII. 37. Luc. XIV. 21. Job. III. 18. 36. XVI. 8. seq. 2. Theff. I. 8. II. 10. Non ergo absoluta hic est voluntas, sed supponit oblatæ gratiæ reprobationem. Quid quod etiam ipsum indurationis peccatum id satis confirmet, quia in- duratio formaliter includit reprobationem gratiæ, & obfirmationem cordis adversus verbum Dei. Non ergò citra manifestam contradictionem in- duratio imputari potest absolutæ Dei voluntati. Rectè iterum hic se habet Origenis interpretatio: Quod autem dicit, cui vult, miseretur, & quem vult, indurat: ex his, quæ in Exodo scripta sunt, videtur affumere. Ibi enim dicit: Indurabo cor Pharaonis, ut ne dimittat populum. Indurabatur cor Pharao- nis, hoc modo: noluit Deus subitam & plenam dare in eum vindictam. Quamvis enim effet consumma- ta malitiæ, tamen per patientiam suam nec ipsi facul- tatem conversionis excluserat: & ideò primò leviori- bus, tum etiam paulatim ingravescentibus in eum verberibus utebatur. Sed quod Deus gerebat per pa- tientiam, ex hoc ille indurabatur ad contemptum, majorem sibi viam recondens, ita ut ad ipsum dici conveniat illud, quod scribit Apostolus, an divitias bonitatis & longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans quo- niam patientia Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit? Se- cundum duritiem autem tuam & cor impœnitens thesaurizas tibi ipsi iram in die iræ. Non ergò, quem vult, Deus indurat, sed qui patienter obtemperare noluerit, induratur.

vult, ita tamen ut duritiei non sit autor vel approba- tor seu causa positiva, is non immeritò accusat eos, qui indurescunt. Id verò de Deo quatuor po- tissimum modis & argumentis innuit Apostolus: 1. quia, qui indurescunt, sunt vasa iræ; Ira autem præsupponit peccatum; 2. quia Deus tolerat sal- tem, non autem approbat eorum duritiem; 3. quia in longanimitate multâ tolerantur, ideoque non vult Deus, ut indurentur, sed ut convertantur; Rom. II. 4. 4. quia dicuntur vasa præparata ad in- teritum, propriâ scil. suâ culpâ. Non ergo volun- tate Dei absoluta. Quanquam verò admittamus, voluntatem aliquam Dei esse irresistibilem, ea ta- men, quæ exerit sese in electione ad vitam æternam, vel in fidei donatione ordinaria irresistibilis non est, quemadmodum hic docet Apostolus. Quem cer- tè objectio illa stringeret, si irresistibilis hæc Dei voluntas foret. Quid enim conqueritur Deus de nobis, quum non credimus, si fidem his dare, aliis negare absoluto decreto constituit, ejusque voluntati, secundum quam illam dare aut non da- re vult, nemo resistere possit?

Vers. 18. ἐρεῖς ἄν μοι. Dicis tu Judæe pertinax.

## 9:19
τί ἔτι μέμφεται.) Why then does God blame us? Thus μέμφεσθαι is used in Hebr. VIII. 8. and likewise 2. Maccab. II. 7.

τῷ γὰρ βουλήματι ἀυτᾶ τίς ἀνθέςηκε;) It is a Hebraism. For both the indicative is put for the subjunctive: and the past for any time: as if he were to say; τίς ἀνθιςῇ; Who can resist his will? It is a proverb worn by use among the Hebrews, as appears in Gen. I. 19. as indeed the Latin interpreter accepted it. Thus 2. Paralip. XX. 6. to God: ὃς ἐςι πρός σε ἀντιςῆναι. The Jews opposed this to Paul. If God does not wish to heal except through faith, and does not give us faith, why are we accused? For a man would oppose himself in vain to God willing something. The answer was ready for the Apostle: that this is true in those things which God wills to be brought about without condition. Here the matter is different: for although God does not wish to heal except those believing in Jesus, that they do not believe is a cause in themselves, which answer the Apostle will insinuate shortly in verse 29 and will execute more broadly in the following chapters. But before he does that, he prudently crushes the Jewish ferocity: deservedly indeed, for that Paul saw that the Christians had become the people of God was apparent from the things themselves, that is, from the most excellent purity of life and the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit.

Latin:

τί ἔτι μέμφεται.) Cur ergo Deus nos incusat? sic μέμ- φεσθαι sumitur Hebr. VIII. 8. sic & 2. Maccab. II. 7.

τῷ γὰρ βουλήματι ἀυτᾶ τίς ἀνθέςηκε;) Est Hebraïsmus. Nam & indicativus ponitur pro subjunctivo: & præteritum pro quovis tempore: quasi dicat; τίς ἀνθιςῇ; Quis possit voluntati ejus obstare? est proverbium tritum usu inter He- bræos, ut apparet Gen. I. 19. ut quidem accepit Latinus in- terpres. Sic 2. Paralip. XX. 6. ad Deum: ὃς ἐςι πρός σε ἀντιςῆναι. Hoc opponebant Judæi Paulo. Si Deus non vult sanare nisi per fidem, & fidem nobis non dat, cur nos accusamur? Nam Deo aliquid volenti homo frustra se op- ponat. Responsio erat parata Apostolo: verum hoc esse in iis, quæ Deus sine conditione vult effecta dare. Hic aliam esse rem: nam quanquam Deus sanare non vult nisi in Jesum credentes, ut non credant in ipsis esse causas, quam respon- sionem insinuabit Apostolus mox 29. & latius exequetur capitibus sequentibus. Sed antequam id faciat, prudenter contundit Judaicam ferociam: meritò sanè, nam quod di- debat Paulus Christianos factos Dei populum, apparebat rebus ipsis, id est, ex excellentissima vitæ puritate & donis Spiritus eximiis.

## 9:20
σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενῷ τῷ Θεῷ.) Who are you, that is, how small are you, who dare to answer God, that is, to dispute against those things which you see God doing? This also is taken from a saying frequent among the Hebrews, the sense of which you have in Job. IX. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. XXXIV. 31. 32. 33. 34. 35. Dan. IV. 32. Even men are accustomed to say to a servant yesterday, go away, answerer. Emperor M. Antoninus in book X.X. ὀργὰς γὰρ κρὴ ἀυτὸς, ὅτι σῦτο παραζητῶν δικαιολογῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν.

μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα τῷ πλάσαντι, τί με ἐποίησας ὕτως.) This also taken from usage appears in Isa. XXIX. 16. and XLV. 9. It indicates nothing else, however, than that men ought not to criticize the deeds of God their maker. τί με ἐποίησας ὕτως, that is, why did you treat me thus? For even in that sense among the Greeks and our own, ποιεῖν has an accusative for the dative, as appears in Matth. V. 44. and according to some copies XXVII. 22. Luc. XV. 14.

Η ἐκ ἔχει ἐξεσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τᾶ πηλᾶ ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ φυράμα- τος ποιῆσαι ὃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν σκέυθ, ὃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν.) The potter has the right not only to make from the same clay what vessels he wishes, but also to break those made, and from vessels for food, if he wishes, to make chamber pots. See Wisd. XV. 7. where ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ πηλᾶ, which is here, ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ φυράματῷ. For φύραμα, which is accustomed to be used especially of flour, is general, and signifies anything mixed, as in the geoponics, φύραμα κονίας κὶ βολίτε. What is here εἰς τιμὴν σκέυθ is there καθαρῶν ἔργων δῦλα σκένη: what is here εἰς ἀτιμίαν, is there ἐναντία. But Jeremiah XVIII. 6. shows that this simile does not correspond in all things, where he uses the same simile of the potter and the clay, and immediately adds that God adjusts his counsels to the counsels of men. Let the passage be seen and another similar to it of Sirach XXXIII. 14, 15. where after the simile of the potter and the clay it is added: ἐπιδῶσαι ἀυτοῖς κατὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἀυτᾶ. This ὁμοίωσις [likeness] is therefore not to be pressed further here, lest we wish to become censors and judges of those things which God does. That simile in the Gospel of Matthew XX. 14, 15: Take what is yours, and go. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? But because the word φύραμα [lump] appears here, I cannot omit a passage of Philo concerning the sacrifices of Abel and Cain: It is such: τὸ τοῖυν φύ- ραμα, τὸ χρῆ τ' ἀληθὲς λέγειν, ἡμεῖς ἐσμὲν ἀυτοὶ, συμπεφορημέ- νοι καὶ συγκεκραμένοι πλείσων ὀσιῶν ἵνα ἀποτελεσθῶμεν. φυ- χεὸν γὰρ δεητε, καὶ ξηρᾶ ὑγρᾶ, δυνάμεων ἐναντίας, μίξας τὸ ἀνα- κερασάμενΘ ὁ χοσοπλάσης ἐν ἐκ πασῶν ἑκασον ἡμῶν ἀπειργά- σατο συνέφιξαμα ὤφ᾽ ὦ καὶ φύραμα ἄρηται. But in the second book of Plato's Republic, where the varied state of men is discussed, God is called ὁ πλάσσων [the molder].

These things are correct. But the Calvinists, on the other hand, vainly attempt to establish from this simile the horrible dogma, which its own author calls that of absolute Reprobation. To whom we respond in general: 1. That parabolic theology is not argumentative. 2. That every simile is also dissimilar. 3. That similes are not to be extended beyond the scope of the author. 4. And therefore that every member of a comparison is not always to be examined too subtly, if only the intention and application made by the author are clear. In particular, however, we note: I. That the comparison here is instituted between God and the potter, as also between man and the potter's work: 1. by reason of power. 2. by reason of the making in itself. 3. by reason of the unworthiness of the making in relation to the potter. 4. That the thing made ought not to ἀνταποκρίνεσθαι [answer back]. But no comparison is instituted here, either by reason of the parity of the mass in relation to the diverse vessels, or by reason of the origin and cause of the ignominy, as if God so makes every man for disgrace, or gathers together vessels of wrath for destruction, as the potter is the maker of the pot, in that it is the same as a vessel of dishonor, or as if there were no disparity in the mass of the human race, from which some are chosen, others are reprobated, as the clay behaves in the same way, from which both vessels of honor and of ignominy are prepared; for such an application can neither be reconciled with the analogy of faith, nor will it ever be demonstrated from the words or the scope of the Apostle. II. The absolute right of God is shadowed forth in the power of the potter, but not any absolute decree of God. For the power of God is one thing, the exercise of that power is another. Thus God had the power, once the human race had fallen into sin, to reprobate all without exception as vessels of wrath, but he did not therefore use this right of his, but having pity on the human race, he willed that only those who were finally unbelieving should be reprobated, but he chose believers for glory. III. The Calvinists do not yet agree in unfolding this simile, as to what mass is understood, from which they think other vessels were gathered together for dishonor. Some understand the mass to be man not yet created but still to be created. Others, man as he has been created. Others, as he has been both created and fallen into sin. Those who support the latter view refute the former opinions, and that most rightly, among whom Pareus in his Commentary on this passage teaches that the damned mass is properly the object of election and reprobation, of mercy and wrath, and he proves this with an indissoluble argument. For God predestined such men from eternity as he calls and justifies in time, namely, those lying in the mass of perdition. IV. If, therefore, the human race fallen into sins is that mass, it is asked whether those who are prepared for glory and those who are gathered together for destruction in the eternal decree of God behave in exactly the same way? Where we cannot decide this more rightly than according to the aforementioned argument of Pareus. God predestined such men as he justifies in time. He reprobated from eternity such as he condemns. But he does not justify or condemn them as they sinned in Adam, but as they either believe in Christ or do not believe. Therefore, even in the decree of Predestination, the mass of the human race ought to be viewed not simply as it was made subject to sin in Adam, but as it is in Christ through faith, or outside of Christ through unbelief.

Latin:

σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενῷ τῷ Θεῷ.) Tu quis, id est, quan- tulus es, qui Deo respondere audeas, id est, contra ea, quæ Deum facere vides, disputare? Est & hoc sumptum ex dicto frequenti apud Hebræos, cujus sensum habes Job. IX. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. XXXIV. 31. 32. 33. 34. 35. Dan. IV. 32. Etiam homines heri servo dicere solent, abi responfator. M. Anto- nius Imperator libro Χ.Χ. ὀργὰς γὰρ κρὴ ἀυτὸς, ὅτι σῦτο παρα- ζητῶν δικαιολογῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν.

μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα τῷ πλάσαντι, τί με ἐποίησας ὕτως.) Hoc quoque ex usu sumptum apparet Efa. XXIX. 16. & XLV. 9. Nihil autem aliud indicat, quam non debere homines re- prehendere facta Dei opificis sui. τί με ἐποίησας ὕτως, id est, cur me sic tractasti? Nam etiam in illo sensu apud Græcos & nostros ποιεῖν pro dativo habet accusativum, ut apparet Matth. V. 44. & secundum quædam exemplaria XXVII. 22. Luc. XV. 14.

Η ἐκ ἔχει ἐξεσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τᾶ πηλᾶ ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ φυράμα- τος ποιῆσαι ὃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν σκέυθ, ὃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν.) Jus habet figulus non modo ex eodem luto facere, quæ velit vasa, sed & facta refringere, & ex esculentis, si velit, facere matulas. Vide Sap.XV. 7. ubi ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ πηλᾶ, quod hic est, ἐκ τᾶ ἀυτᾶ φυράματῷ. Nam φύραμα, quod de farina maximè usurpat solet, generale est, & quidvis mixtum significat, ut in geo- ponicis, φύραμα κονίας κὶ βολίτε. Quod hic εἰς τιμὴν σκέυθ ibi καθαρῶν ἔργων δῦλα σκένη: quod hic εἰς ἀτιμίαν, ibi ἐναν- τία. Verum hanc similitudinem non in omnibus responde- re ostendit Jeremias XVIII.6. ubi eadem utitur figuli ac lute similitudine, statimque subjicit Deum hominum consiliis sua attemperare consilia. Videatur locus & alter ei similis Sirachidæ XXXIII. 14, 15. ubi post similitudinem figuli & luti additur: ἐπιδῶσαι ἀυτοῖς κατὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἀυτᾶ. Non ulte- rius igitur premenda hic ὁμοίωσις, quam ne eorum, quæ Deus agit, hòs' velimus effe censores ac judices. Simile illud in Evangelio Matth. XX. 14. 15. Tolle quod tuum est, & abi. Annon licet mihi de meo facere, ut volo? Quia vero φυρά- ματῷ vox hic apparet, non possum omittere Philonis lo- cum de sacrificiis Abelis & Caini: Est is talis: τὸ τοῖυν φύ- ραμα, τὸ χρῆ τ' ἀληθὲς λέγειν, ἡμεῖς ἐσμὲν ἀυτοὶ, συμπεφορημέ- νοι καὶ συγκεκραμένοι πλείσων ὀσιῶν ἵνα ἀποτελεσθῶμεν. φυ- χεὸν γὰρ δεητε, καὶ ξηρᾶ ὑγρᾶ, δυνάμεων ἐναντίας, μίξας τὸ ἀνα- κερασάμενΘ ὁ χοσοπλάσης ἐν ἐκ πασῶν ἕκασον ἡμῶν ἀπειργά- σατο συνέφιξαμα ὤφ᾽ ὦ καὶ φύραμα ἄρηται. Platoni vero de Republica secundo, ubi de vario agitur hominum statu, Deus vocatur ὁ πλάσσων.

Rectè hæc se habent. Frustra autem ex adver- so Calviniani ex hoc simili stabilitum eunt dogma horribile, quod vocat ipse ejus Autor de absoluta Reprobatione. Quibus in genere respondemus 1. Theologiam Parabolicam non esse argumentati- vam. 2. Omne simile esse quoque dissimile. 3. Si- milia non esse extendenda ultra scopum autoris. 4. Ideoque non semper quævis comparationis membra subtilius rimanda esse, si constet modo intentio & applicatio ab autore facta. In spe- cie verò notamus: I. Collationem hic institui Dei & figuli, ut & hominis cum figmento figuli: 1. ra- (O) 4 tione potestatis. 2. ratione facturae in se. 3. ratione indignitatis facturae in ordine ad figulum. 4. Quod factura non debeat ἀνταποκρίνεσθαι. Non autem instituitur hic comparatio, vel ratione paritatis massae in ordine ad vasa diversa, vel ratione originis & causae ignominiae, quasi Deus ita ad dedecus faciat quoque hominem, vel ad interitum coagmentet vasa irae, uti figulus est fictor ollae, quà eadem est vas dedecoris vel quasi nulla sit disparitas in massa generis humani, ex qua alii eliguntur, alii repro- bantur, uti lutum sese eodem modo habet, ex quo & vasa decoris & ignominiae parantur, talis enim applicatio nec cum analogia fidei conciliari po- test, nec è verbis vel scopo Apostoli unquam de- monstrabitur. II. Absolutum Dei jus adumbratur in potestate figuli, non autem decretum aliquod Dei absolutum. Aliud enim est potestas Dei, aliud potestatis illius exercitium. Ita Deus potestatem habuit prolapso genere humano in peccatum omnes prorsus reprobare ceu vasa irae, non autem ideò hoc jure suo usus est, sed misertus humani ge- neris reprobatos tantum voluit finaliter incredu- los, credentes autem elegit ad gloriam. III. Cal- viniani nondum conveniunt in simili hoc evol- vendo, quaenam massa intelligatur, ex qua illi cen- sent vasa alia ad dedecus coagmentata. Nonnulli massam intelligunt hominem nondum creatum sed adhuc creandum. Alii hominem, quà crea- tus est. Alii quà & creatus & in peccatum lapsus. Priores sententias refellunt illi, qui po- steriori adstipulantur idque rectissimè, è quibus Pareus in Comment. ad h. l. docet, massam damna- tam propriè esse objectum electionis & reprobationis, misericordiae & irae, idque argumento probat adia- λύτῳ. Tales enim homines praedestinavit Deus ab aeterno, quales vocat, justificat in tempore, nempe in massa perditionis jacentes. IV. Si ergò genus hu- manum in peccata prolapsum massa illa est, quaeritur utrum eodem prorsus modo sese habeant tum illi, qui praeparantur ad gloriam, tum illi, qui coagmen- tantur ad interitum in aeterno Dei decreto? Ubi pariter rectius id decidere non possumus, quàm juxta praedictum argumentum Parei. Tales ho- mines praedestinavit Deus, quales justificat in tem- pore. Tales ab aeterno reprobavit, quales con- demnat. Non autem justificat aut condemnat eos, quà in Adamo peccarunt, sed quà vel credunt in Christum, vel non credunt. Itaque etiam in Prae- destinationis decreto massa generis humani spe- ctari debet non simpliciter, quà in Adamo ob- noxia facta peccato, sed quà per fidem est in Christo, vel extra Christum, per incredulitatem.

## 9:22
Verse 22. εἰ δὲ ὁ Θεὸς [But if God]. After the pride of those who contradict the manifest deeds of God has been repressed, he gradually opens up the causes of that divine dispensation, as far as it is lawful for men to know them. Εἰ δὲ [But if] has nothing here that is rendered to it by an ἀπόδοσις [apodosis]. It therefore means: What then if? That is, what is unjust in that?

It is so; no ἀπόδοσις [apodosis] is repeated here: and therefore in the preceding verse 21, when the potter is discussed, a πρότασις [protasis] of a simile is not to be established, which the Calvinists are accustomed to establish: as if it follows how God is compared with the potter: since the argument is taken not from a parity, but rather from the lesser to the greater; if it is permitted to the potter to adorn a vessel of honor and of ignominy from the same material that does not differ, and in this his free power shines forth, how much more is it permitted to God, who is most free, to show his longsuffering in tolerating the vessels of ignominy, which adapted themselves to ἀτιμίαν [dishonor], and to reveal the riches of his goodness in the vessels of glory? The disparity itself teaches that there is no πρότασιν [protasis] and ἀπόδοσιν [apodosis]: For on one side the ignominy is final, since a vessel of ignominy formed by the potter is and remains such by the intention of the potter; but that vessels of ignominy, when the discourse is about men, cannot rise up to be vessels for honor was rightly condemned in the Synod of Arles, Ep. to Lucidus: There the potter makes vessels of ignominy and of honor equally with joy; here, however, God does not make vessels of ignominy, but he tolerates those who, by their own fault, have turned out to be such, not without sorrow. The potter proceeds by free will, but the process of God rests on justice, not indeed on simple good pleasure. Chrysostom here prefers to call it an ὑπόδειγμα [example] rather than to establish a simile constant in its own πρότασις [protasis] and ἀπόδοσις [apodosis], and concerning this example he has this (page 195.) Here, therefore, the Apostle wishes to do nothing else than to persuade the hearer to obey God as much as possible and more than can be said, and to demand an account from him about nothing. For just as the potter, he says, makes what vessels he wishes from the same mass, and no one contradicts him: so also here, when he affects some of the same human race with punishment and others with honor, do not be a curious and anxious investigator of the cause, but adore him alone, and imitate the clay, and just as it follows the hands of the potter, so do you follow his judgment: who dispenses these things. For he does nothing rashly or by chance, even if you are ignorant of the mystery of his wisdom. You, moreover, permit the potter to fashion dissimilar and different vessels from the same mass, and you do not count it a fault. But do you demand an account from God of both punishments and honors? And do you not grant that he himself knows who is worthy and who, in turn, is unworthy? Nevertheless, what I said before, the example itself is to be accepted in this one thing only, namely, that one ought not to contradict God: but rather to yield to his incomprehensible wisdom. For examples ought to be greater than the things proposed, and those for which they are brought forward, and indeed, so that they may affect the hearer more. For unless they were greater, and had a greater hyperbole, they could not sting and shame the contradictor as they ought. The speech, however, in this and the following verse is incomplete, concerning which B. Mylius: The final causes are explained on both sides, in the damning of the impious, the demonstration of divine justice and power: in the saving of believers, of divine mercy. The whole speech has an ἀποσιώπησιν [aposiopesis]: For after he said if it so pleases, on both sides to God, etc. With the speech suspended, he suggests to the reader the sense of the next speech, namely, who is man, who dares to answer back, or to call God to judgment.

Vers. eod. Θέλων ὁ Θεὸς ἐνδείξασθαι τὴν ὀργὴν καὶ γνώρισαι τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτῶ) Wishing to show his severity against the impious Jews and his power to execute his judgments even through the Romans. For the Apostle hints at that desolation predicted by Daniel and Christ: τὸ δυνατὸν, as above II. 4. τὸ χρηστὸν, neuters of adjectives for denominatives, in the Greek manner.

ἤνεγκεν ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ σκέυη ὀργῆς κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν.) Σκέυη ὀργῆς can be said in a double sense, either those by whom, or those in whom God executes his judgments. For through both, as through instruments, the severity of God, which is here called ὀργὴ, shines forth. Here it must be taken in the latter sense. Conversely, σκέυo- ἐκλογῆς Acts IX. 15, a chosen instrument: And likewise σκέυη- εἰς τιμὴν, εἰς ἀτιμίαν, σκέυη- εἰς τιμὴν 111. 2. Tim. II. 21. σκέυη- τῆς λατρεργίας Heb. IX. 21. Dicuntur autem σκέυη ὀργῆς men certainly not by nature, but by long and hardened malice, most worthy indeed, in whom God may set forth the gravest examples: such as were most of the Jews in those times: the same are called σκέυη κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν, where in the manner of the Hebrews, who have few verbals, a participle is put for a verbal: clearly as the Hebrew נכון which signifies apt, and is accustomed to be translated by ἕτοιμος from the verb כון, which is sometimes translated ἑτοιμάζω, sometimes καταρλίζω as Ps. LXVIII. 10. LXXIV. 16. LXXXIX. 38. In this sense we had καληρλισμένοι also in Luke VI. 40. They are apt for destruction who have deserved a dire end. Such God does not destroy immediately, but gives them time for repentance, which is shown here by those words ἤνεγκεν ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ and above II. 4. where there is the same word μακροθυμίας; and it follows τὸ χρηστὸν τᾶ Θεᾶ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει. Quæ omnia apertissimum faciunt all of which make it most clear that there is no reference here to men nakedly as creatures of God, or descendants of Adam, but as similar to Pharaoh. There is in Eusebius, Preparation VIII, a passage of Philo by him not foreign to what is treated here: (GOD) provides for the living who are under accusation, at once giving them time for amendment, and at the same time not overstepping the merciful nature in Himself, of which the suffering is a virtue and has become philanthropy. Thus also 2 Macc. VI. 14: the Master waits, being long-suffering, until they have reached the fulfillment of their sins to punish them.

Latin:

Vers. 22. εἰ δὲ ὁ Θεὸς. Post repressam superbiam manifestis Dei factis obtre- ctantium paulatim dispensationis illius divinae causas ape- rit, quantum quidem eas hominibus scire fas est. Εἰ δὲ hic nihil habet, quod ei reddatur per ἀπόδοσιν. Valet itaque: Quid tum si? Id est, quid in eo iniqui?

Sic est; nulla hic repetitur ἀπόδοσις: ideoque nec versu praecedenti 21. cum de figulo agitur, simi- litudinis πρότασις constituenda, quam Calviniani constituere solent: quasi jam sequatur, quo pacto Deus componatur cum figulo: quum non à pari, sed à minori ad majus potius argumentum desuma- tur; si figulo licet vas honoris & ignominiae ex eàdem nil discrepante materia adornare, inque eo ejusdem libera potestas effulget, quantò magis licet Deo sum- mè libero, suam ostendere in tolerandis vasis ignomi- niae, quae seipsa adaptarunt ad ἀτιμίαν, longanimi- tatem, & in vasis gloriae patefacere divitias suae boni- tatis? Non esse πρότασιν & ἀπόδοσιν disparitas ipsa docet: Nam ex una parte ignominia est finalis, cum vas ignominiae à figulo formatum tale sit ac maneat intentione figuli; vasa autem ignominia, cum de hominibus sermo est, non assurgere posse, ut vasa sint in honorem in Synodo Arelatensi Ep. ad Lucid. merito damnatum fuit: Illic parat figulus æquè vasa ignominiæ atque honoris cum gaudio; hic verò non facit Deus vasa ignominiæ, sed qui suâ culpâ talia evasêre, eos tolerat non absque cordo- lio. Figulus procedit liberâ voluntate, Dei autem processus nititur justitiâ, non verò simplici bene- placito. Chrysostomus hic mavult ὑπόδειγμα vel exemplum dicere, quàm similitudinem suâ προτάσει & ἀποδόσει constantem statuere, & de exemplo hoc ita habet (pag. 195.) Hic igitur (Apostolus) aliud nihil agere vult, quàm ut persuadeat auditori, ut maximoperè & supra quam dici possit, Deo pa- reat, nullaque de re ab eo rationem exigat. Quem- admodum enim figulus, ait, ex eadem massa, quæ vult, vasa facit, ac nullus contradicit: ita & hic eo- dem ex hominum genere alios quidem supplicio, alios autem honore dum afficit, ne curiosus solicitusque sis causæ pervestigator, sed hunc adorato tantum, & lu- tum imitare ac quemadmodum illud figuli manus sequitur: sic & tu sententiam ejus: qui hæc dispensat. Nihil enim temerè nec fortuito facit, ut etiam ignores sapientiæ arcanum. Tu porrò figulo permittis, ut mas- sa ex eadem, dissimilia ac differentia vasa fingat, nec vitio vertis. A Deo autem rationem exigis tum sup- pliciorum, tum honorum? nec concedis, ut sciat ipse, quis dignus, quis rursus indignus sit? Veruntamen quod prius dixi, in unum hoc solùm accipiendum est ipsum exemplum, quod videlicet non oportet Deo con- tradicere: quin potius incomprehensibili illius sapien- tiæ concedere. Nam exempla oportet majora esse propositis, iisque pro quibus ea in medium adducun- tur, & quidem, ut auditorem magis afficiant. Nam nisi majora essent, majoremque haberent hyperbolen, ea non quemadmodum oportet, contradicentem per- stringere ac pudefacere possent. Oratio autem in hoc & sequenti versu incompleta est, de quo B. Mylius: Exponuntur autem utrinque fimales causæ, in da- mnandis impiis, justitiæ & potentiæ: in salvandis cre- dentibus, misericordiæ divinæ demonstratio. Oratio tota ἀποσιώπησιν habet: Nam postquam dixit si ita libeat, utrinque Deo &c. Suspensâ oratione, lectori sensum proximæ orationis suggerit, nimirum, quis est homo, qui responsare ausit, aut in jus vocare Deum.

Vers. eod. Θέλων ὁ Θεὸς ἐνδείξασθαι τὴν ὀργὴν καὶ γνώρισαι τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτῶ) Volens ostendere in impios Judæos seve- ritatem suam & potentiam ad judicia sua exsequenda etiam per Romanos. Innuit enim Apostolus desolationem illam a Daniele & Christo prædictam: τὸ δυνατὸν, ut supra II. 4. τὸ χρηστὸν, neutra adjectivorum pro denominativis, more Græco.

ἤνεγκεν ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ σκέυη ὀργῆς κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν.) Σκέυη ὀργῆς duplici sensu. dici possunt aut per quos, aut in quos Deus judicia sua exsequitur. Nam per utrosque tanquam per instrumenta Dei severitas, quæ hic ὀργὴ dicitur, elucet. Hic sumendum id in sensu posteriore. Contra σκέυo- ἐκλογῆς Act. IX. 15. instrumentum electum: Et modò σκέυη- εἰς τιμὴν, εἰς ἀτιμίαν, σκέυη- εἰς τιμὴν 111. 2. Tim. II. 21. σκέυη- τῆς λατρεργίας Heb. IX. 21. Dicuntur autem σκέυη ὀργῆς homines certè non ex natura, sed ex lon- ga indurataque malitia, dignissimi scilicet, in quos Deus gra- vissima edat exempla: quales erant Judæi plerique illis tem- poribus: dicuntur eidem σκέυη κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν, ubi more Hebræorum, qui pauca habent verbalia, partici- pium ponitur pro verbali: planè ut Hebræum נכון quod aptum significat, & per ἕτοιμος verti solet à verbo כון, quod modò ἑτοιμάζω vertitur, modò καταρλίζω ut Pf. LXVIII. 10. LXXIV. 16. LXXXIX. 38. Hoc sensu καληρλισμένοι habui- mus & Luc. VI. 40. Apti ad interitum sunt, qui dirum exitium meruêre. Tales Deus non illicò perdit, sed tempus illis dat ad resipiscentiam, quod hic ostendunt illa ἤνεγκεν ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ & supra II. 4. ubi est eadem vox μακροθυμίας; & sequitur τὸ χρηστὸν τᾶ Θεᾶ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει. Quæ omnia apertissimum faciunt non respici hic homines nudè ut crea- turas Dei, aut Adami posteros, sed ut similes Pharaoni. Est apud Eusebium Præparationis VIII. Philonis locus ab eo, quod hic tractatur, non alienus : προμηθεῖται δὲ (DEUS) τῇ τῶν ὑπαιτίων ζῶντων, ἅμα μὲν καιρὸν εἰς ἐπανόρθωσιν αὐτοῖς διδὺς, ἅμα δὲ τῇ τὴν ἰλεως φύσιν αὐτῷ μὴ ὑπερβαίνων ἧς ὁ παθὸς ἀρετὴ κῂ Φιλανθρωπία γέγονεν. Sic & 2. Macc. VI. 14. ἀνα- μένοι μακροθυμῶν ὁ δεσπότης μέχρι τῷ καταντήσαντω αὐτὲς πρὸς ἐκπλήρωσιν ἁμαρτιῶν κολάσαι.

## 9:23
Verse 23. And that He might make known the riches of His glory. Paul is accustomed to call every abundance riches, as above II. 4, XI, below 33, 2 Cor. VIII. 2, Eph. I. 7, II. 7. The riches of glory here and Eph. I. 18 and Coloss. I. 27 is immense glory. But the subject here is the outpouring of the gifts of the Spirit, which was supremely glorious to God. And that He might make known, that is, He did this both for other reasons and to show, etc. For opposites shine forth from opposites.

On vessels of mercy. Men in whom God wonderfully shows His goodness. The Hebrew chesed is accustomed to be translated by mercy, and to be used even where no misery has preceded.

Which He prepared beforehand for glory. For honor to be begun here, to be perfected in the other life. But how He prepared them for this, the following things explain; to predestine and to prepare beforehand is not found except concerning good things.

Latin:

Vers. 23. καὶ ἵνα γνωρίζῃ τὸν πλῦτον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῦ. Paulus omnem abundantiam solet πλῦτον vocare, ut su- pra II. 4. XI. infra 33. 2. Cor. VIII. 2. Eph. I. 7. II. 7. πλῦ- τῷ δόξης hic & Eph. I. 18. & Coloss. I. 27. est ingens gloria. Agitur autem hic de effusione donorum Spiritus, quæ Deo fuit summè gloriosa. Καὶ ἵνα γνωρίζῃ, id est, fecit hoc tum ob alias causas, tum ut ostenderet &c. Nam contraria ex contrariis elucescunt.

ἐπὶ σκέυη ἐλέυς. Homines in quibus Deus bonitatem suam mirificè osten- dit. חסד Hebræum per ἔλεος verti solet, & usurpari etiam ubi nulla præcessit miseria.

ἃ προητοίμασεν εἰς δόξαν. Ad honorem hic inchoandum, perficiendum in vita alte- ra. Quomodo autem eos ad id præparaverit, explicant se- quentia προορίζειν & προετοιμάζειν non invenitur nisi de re- bus bonis.

## 9:24
Verse 24. Even us whom He called, not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles. Us, that is, the Christians, whom God has called, with effect of course, that is, led to obedience, born partly from the Jews, partly from other nations. Words of counsel and labor are often taken in such a way that they include the outcome as well, as to give 2 Tim. II. 6, I. 9. See above VIII. 30. And here is explanatory of that which preceded.

These things likewise are rightly said thus against the Calvinists, that vessels fitted for destruction are not adopted by God, but rather their merit is indicated, and that those are said to be fit for destruction who have deserved it, and that men are not regarded merely as creatures of God, or as descendants of Adam, but as similar to Pharaoh. How, however, these are determined toward the desolation predicted by Daniel and Christ, does not appear. Concerning which Chrysostom, homily XVI, should rather be heard. Consider further his integrity and infinite wisdom, for when he could, while dealing with those who are subjected to punishment, bring forward not Pharaoh, but those who had sinned from among the Jews, and by this reasoning make the discourse clearer, and then show that where the parents are the same, where the sins are the same, some indeed have perished, but others have been gifted with mercy, and thus persuade that it is no longer to be doubted if some from the Gentiles also had been saved, the Jews having perished: but Paul, when he could do this, nevertheless, so as not to make the discourse invidious, brings forward the argument and proof of punishment from a barbarian, so that he might not be forced to call them vessels of wrath: but those who have obtained mercy he takes from the people of the Jews, although he uses what is sufficient for the defense of God. Because he, when he had understood that he was preparing himself as a vessel of perdition, nevertheless contributed his own offices: tolerance, gentleness, and not simply gentleness, but much gentleness, and he did not wish to exercise that argument even in the Jews. We have spoken more fully about these things against the Predestinations in the Apostolic Theology of the Roman Oracles LXXII. The Apostle speaks otherwise, indeed, about the vessels of mercy; otherwise about the vessels of wrath; the former he says were prepared by God for glory: the latter he simply calls fitted. Nor indeed does he make God, but man himself, the cause of both the sin by which he is a vessel of wrath, and of the destruction and ruin. 1. Because the Apostle is occupied here in commending the long-suffering of God, which he says is great, even with respect to the vessels of wrath, but not in declaring severity, of which he has no primary account here, even though he indicates the vessels of wrath. If the Adversaries reply that the Apostle is explaining how God wished to show wrath; we will answer that the Apostle only hints at this, that when God could have declared His wrath against the vessels of wrath, He still made His long-suffering or patience attested. 2. The Apostle calls them vessels of wrath, not which God either destined or prepared for wrath, but which deserve the wrath of God, and with which God is angry. But of those with whom He is angry, He is certainly not the author, in that He is angry with them, Wisd. XI. 25. But if He were the maker of the vessels of wrath as such, he would certainly necessarily be established as the cause of sin, which Pareus acknowledges to be blasphemous. 3. God is said to endure the vessels of wrath in much long-suffering, i.e., to invite them to repentance by His kindness, Rom. II. 4, cf. 2 Pet. III. 9. For this is the primary end of the long-suffering and tolerance of God, intended by God in itself, as can be seen from the loc. cit. Therefore it is not hinted that God Himself joins men together for destruction, since He intends the exact opposite by that long-suffering, namely their repentance and salvation. 4. That God only tolerates, He is not the author or approver of it. For what we love and approve, we embrace, but what displeases us, we tolerate with averted minds. But God is said only to tolerate the vessels of wrath. 5. Vessels of wrath are understood either commonly as sinful men worthy of wrath or subject to the wrath of God, or specifically as infidels. It is clear that the former sense has no place here, since in that way all men are by nature children of wrath Eph. II. 3 and subject to God Rom. III. 19; but if infidels are understood, it is manifest that their joining together is not from God. For that joining together is either taken as they are composed for infidelity; which cannot be ascribed to God, unless we wish to call God the cause of infidelity, or as infidels are destined or prepared for destruction. But if it were said of God at all, it would have to be ascribed not to his absolute will, but to his just judgment, by which he condemned them to destruction on account of their unbelief. But this is 1. not ascribed to God here. 2. removed from God elsewhere; Thy destruction is from thyself, O Israel, Hos. XIII. 9. 3. Nor does the word κατηρτισμένα allow it to be ascribed to God, which is to be understood not of an extrinsic destination, but rather of an internal disposition, by which the ungodly adapt, dispose, and fit themselves for destruction through unbelief and the sins flowing from it, when God wishes them to be fitted for faith and salvation through his word. See Matt. IV. 21, ch. XXI. 16, Mark I. 19, 2 Cor. III. 11, Gal. VI. 1, Heb. X. 5, ch. XIII. 21, 1 Pet. V. 10. Which word, however, we can also understand simply with Grotius, so that those called κατηρτισμένοι are ἕτοιμοι, apt for destruction, who have deserved the same. We also praise Grotius's observation concerning the words προορίζειν and προετοιμάζειν, as being consistent with the Scriptures, because it is not found except in reference to good things: And Zanchius himself, among the Calvinists, admits this, as do Martyr, Whitaker, and Keckermann, that Scripture uses the word Predestination only concerning Election, and does not indeed extend it to reprobation. See Appendix Exam. doctr. Reform. de Person. Christi page 493. But the fact that God is said to demonstrate both his wrath and his power, when he tolerates the vessels of wrath, which by their own fault have deserved wrath, implies that with the manifestation of the wrath and power of God against the refractory, as appears most clearly in the example of Pharaoh, there is joined and shines forth the great long-suffering of God, because he tolerates for no small time even the vessels of wrath themselves: which have deserved nothing but severity and destruction, for which they adapted themselves by their own fault: but concerning the vessels of mercy he says that God makes known in them the riches of his glory, namely of his glorious mercy, inasmuch as he himself prepares them for glory out of his immense grace, without any merit of their own. In this way he asserts again both the justice and the mercy of God, neither of them absolute, but both tempered in the business of eternal salvation. The things which Chrysostom has here are worthy; let them be brought forward: Pharaoh was a vessel of wrath, that is, a man, kindling the wrath of God through his own hardness. For having obtained the immense gentleness of God, he was by no means becoming better, but remained uncorrected: and so he called him not only a vessel of wrath, but also prepared for destruction, that is, made ready, by himself indeed, and by his own nature. For God did not omit anything of those things which would make for his correction and amendment: nor did he omit anything of those things which would destroy him and deprive him of all pardon. But yet God, although he knew this well, bore it with much gentleness, wishing to lead him to repentance. For if he had not wished this, he would not have exhibited even such great gentleness: but when he did not wish to use gentleness for repentance, but prepared himself for wrath, God used him for the correction of others, through the kind of punishment with which he afflicted him, both rendering others more addicted and intent upon the pursuits of virtue, and making his own power seen in this way. For that God does not wish his strength to be made known in this way, but in another, namely through his beneficence and liberality towards us: this indeed he declared in every way right from the beginning. And a little later: But truly after he used prolonged gentleness, in order to lead him to repentance, and he did not repent: he bore him for a long time, at once indeed declaring his goodness, and at the same time also his power, unless he wished to make some profit from this great gentleness and tolerance. Therefore, just as by taking punishment from him who had remained uncorrected, he showed his power: so by pitying most sinners who had returned to repentance, he rendered his kindness seen and proven to us, and he did not say, kindness: but glory, showing evidently that this very thing is most of all the glory of God, and that it is primarily his care and study. And after some many things: God, since he is very good, shows the same goodness in both. For he did not only pity those whom he was saving, but also Pharaoh himself, as much indeed as was in him. For both he and the latter obtained the same gentleness. If he was not saved at all, the blame for the whole matter came from his own mind: for he received the parts and offices of God no less than those who were saved. These are the words of Chrysostom: It is also pleasing to add the interpretation of our B. Mylius: Each part of this speech, he says, deserves accurate consideration: 1. As regards the damned, the figure of a likeness is retained, and the impious are called vessels, and indeed vessels of wrath. This appellation applies to them in two ways. For first, they are the impious, whom God uses as rods, not only to afflict one another: but also to chastise the sins of the Elect. But that expression suits them better, because they are the impious, into whom God will finally pour the dregs of his wrath. 2. He shows how such vessels are made. For he calls them not destined, as some interpret: but prepared for destruction: but not prepared by God, as the Sacramentarians blasphemously bring to this passage: but prepared both by themselves, and by the devil. 3. He teaches how God uses them. He tolerates, he says, them and sustains them in much patience. It is tolerance that he does not immediately cut them off, thus indeed inviting them to repentance: it is tolerance that he does not strike them except when iniquity and the measure of sins are complete: it is likewise of tolerance that he for the most part accumulates them with various benefits in the meantime. 4. But the end of their damnation is that God may produce proofs of both his wrath and his power. That these are likewise vessels of believers and the elect: but they are called vessels of divine mercy, both because they are those through and for whom God bestows mercy upon the human race: and indeed primarily, because he pours out the bowels of his mercy upon them. For these are truly those whom God properly pities and clearly not only privatively: but also collatively, as they speak in Hosea 2:19. 2. Furthermore, such vessels are said to be made specifically by divine preparation. Which was not said at all about the former: That the sentence of the Prophet may stand, Thy destruction is from thyself, O Israel: only from me is thy salvation. And the preposition (in the word προητοίμασεν) has a singular emphasis. For as we do not have it from ourselves that we exist (for it would follow that we were prior to our very birth) so it is signified that it is not from ourselves that we are such: because the beginning of this very birth is far more ancient than we ourselves. For what the Apostle says elsewhere, if anyone has cleansed himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, the Apostle is not arguing there about that preparation or the cause of election, nor is he patronizing free will, as if it were in the power and strength of men to aggregate themselves to the number of the children of God: and to be the authors of their own adoption; but only an admonition is proposed, by which he orders believers to be unlike the impious, who wallow in any filth whatsoever, and commands the faithful, who have already been elected and called, to accommodate themselves to pure uses. Therefore, he simply calls them only to holiness, and advises that which was said elsewhere by the same, Be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord, touch no unclean thing. 3. The end is added, the manifestation of the riches of his glory, that is, of his immense goodness. This is the more remote end; the nearer one is that which the Apostle mentions elsewhere, God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. Thus far B. Mylius.

PART IV. Confirmative.

Further confirming the grace of God in the adoption of the Gentiles and justification through faith in Christ, while most Jews seek the righteousness of the law in vain.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὃς καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ἡμᾶς ὀ μόνον ἐξ ἰυδαίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν. Nos, id est, Christianos, quos Deus vocavit, cum effectu scilicet, id est, ad obedientiam perduxit, genitos partim ex Judæis, partim ex aliis gentibus. Verba consilii & laboris sæpe ita sumuntur, ut simul & eventum includant, ut dare 2. Tim. II. 6. I. 9. Vide supra VIII. 30. καὶ hic est ἐξη- γητικὸν ejus quod præcessit.

Hæc itidem rectè ita contra Calvinianos dicta, quod non à Deo σκέυη κατηρτισμένα vasa adopta- ta sint, sed potius indicetur meritum eorum, & quod apti ad interitum dicantur, qui eum merue- re, quodque non respiciantur homines nudi ut creaturæ Dei, aut ut Adami posteri, sed ut similes Pharaoni. Quomodo tamen hæc ad desolationem à Daniele & Christo prædictam determinentur, non apparet. Quo de potius audiendus Chrysosto- mus homil. XVI. Considera porro illius probitatem ac sapientiam infinitam, nam quum posset, de iis, qui supplicio adficiuntur agens, non Pharaonem, sed eos, qui ex Judæis peccavissent, proferre, atque hac ratio- ne orationem apertiorem reddere tum ostendere, quod ubi iidem parentes, ubi eadem peccata, alii quidem perierint, alii autem misericordia donati fuerint, sicque persuadere non amplius dubitandum esse, si ex gentibus quoque nonnulli salvi effecti essent, Judæis perditis: sed id Paulus quum posset, tamen ut ne ora- tionem invidiosam redderet, supplicii quidem argu- mentum ac probationem à barbaro profert, ut ne illos videlicet iræ vasa appellare cogatur: eos autem, qui misericordiam assequuti sunt, à Judæorum populo as- sumit, quanquam, quod satis est, pro Deo defensione utitur. Quod is videlicet quum intellexisset illum admodum seipsum præparantem vas perditionis, ta- men sua officia contulerit: tolerantiam, lenitatem, nec simpliciter lenitatem, sed multam lenitatem, nec in Judæis quidem id argumenti voluit exercere. Ple- nius de his diximus contra Prædestinationes in Theol. Apost. Rom. Orac. LXXII. Aliter utique loquitur Apost. de vasis misericordiæ; aliter de va- sis iræ; Illa à Deo præparata dicit ad gloriam: hæc simpliciter dicit κατηρτισμένα. Nec vero Deum sed hominem ipsum facit causam tum peccati quo est vas iræ, tum interitus & exitii. 1. Quia versatur hic Apostolus in commendanda Dei longanimitate, quã multam esse dicit, etiam respectu vasorum iræ non autem in declaranda severitate, cujus hic primariò rationem non habet, tametsi vasa iræ indicat. Si reponent Adversarii, Apostolum explicare, quo- modo Deus voluerit ostendere iram; respondebi- mus, Apostolum id tantum innuere, quod cum Deus potuerit iram suam adversus vasa iræ declara- re, testatum adhuc fecerit μακροθυμίαν vel longa- nimitatem suam. 2. Vasa iræ dicit Apostolus, non quæ Deus vel destinavit vel præparavit ad iram, sed quæ iram Dei merentur, & quibus Deus irascitur. Quibus autem irascitur, eorum certè non est autor, quà illis irascitur Sap. XI. 25. Quod si vasorum iræ, quà talium opifex esset, utique necessariò causa peccati statueretur, quod blasphemum esse agnoscit Pareus. 3. Perferre dicitur vasa iræ Deus ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ h. e. benignitate sua invitare ad pœnitentiam Rom. II. 4. conf. 2. Pet. III. 9. Hic enim est finis primarius μακροθυμίας & tolerantiæ Dei, per se à Deo intentus, ut è loc. cit. videre est. Non ergo ipse Deus coagmentare innuitur homines ad interitum, cum intendat prorsus contrariū illâ μακροθυμίᾳ pœnitentiam nempe & salutem eorum. 4. Quod Deus tolerat tantum, ejus non est autor vel approbator. Quod enim amamus & approbamus, id amplexamur, quod verò displicet, animis aversis toleramus. At vasa iræ tolerare tantum dicitur. 5. Vasa iræ vel intelliguntur communiter homines peccatores irâ digni aut iræ Dei obnoxii, vel specialiter infideles. Illum sensum hic locum non habere patet, cum eo modo omnes homines naturâ sint filii iræ Eph. II. 3. & obnoxii Deo Rom. III. 19. si autem infideles intelligantur, manifestum est, coagmentationē eorum non esse à Deo. Nam illa coagmentatio vel accipitur, quà illi sunt ad infidelitatem compositi; quod Deo adscribi nequit, nisi Deum causam infidelitatis dicere velimus, vel quà infideles ad interitum destinati aut præparati sunt. Quod si omnino de Deo diceretur, non absolutæ ejus voluntati, sed judicio justo adscribendum foret, quo propter infidelitatem eos ad interitum addixit. Verum id 1. hic non adscribitur Deo. 2. alibi removetur à Deo; Perditio tua ex te Israel Os. XIII. 9. 3. Nec vox κατηρτισμένα id admittit, ut Deo adscribatur, quæ non de extrinseca destinatione, sed de interna potius dispositione accipienda, quà impii semetipsos infidelitate & ex eâ manantibus peccatis ad interitū adaptant, disponunt, & coagmentant, cum eos Deus per verbum suum velit aptatos ad fidem & salutem. Vid. Matt. IV. 21. c. XXI. 16. Marc. I. 19. 2. Cor. III. 11. Gal. VI. 1. Ebr. X. 5. c. XIII. 21. 1. Pet. V. 10. Quam tamen vocem etiam cum Grotio simpliciter intelligere possumus, ut κατηρτισμένοι dicti sint ἕτοιμοι apti ad interitum, qui eundem meruêre. Laudamus quoque observationem Grotii de verbis προορίζειν & προετοιμάζειν, ceu Scripturis consentaneam, quod non inveniatur nisi de rebus bonis: Et fatetur è Calvinianis Zanchius ipse, ut & Martyr, Witakerus, Keckermannus, Scripturam voce Prædestinationis solum uti de Electione, non verò eam ad reprobationem extendere. Vid. Appendix Exam. doctr. Reform. de Person. Christi pag. 493. Quod verò Deus dicitur demonstrare & τὴν ὀργὴν & τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτõ, cum tolerat vasa iræ, quæ suâ culpâ iram meruêre, eo innuitur, quod cum iræ Dei & potentiæ ejusdem manifestatione adversus refractarios, ut in exemplo Pharaonis luculentissimè apparet, conjuncta sit, & effulgeat magna Dei longanimitas, quod non exiguo tempore toleret etiam ipsa vasa iræ: quæ nil nisi severitatem meruêre, & interitum, ad quem sese propriâ culpâ adaptarunt: de vasis autem misericordiæ ait, quod patefaciat Deus in iisdem divitias gloriæ suæ, gloriosæ nempe misericordiæ, utpote quæ ipse ex immensa gratia præparat, ad gloriam, sine ullo suo merito. Quo pacto iterum cum justitiam tum misericordiam Dei, neutram verò absolutam, utramque temperatam in negotio æternæ salutis adserit. Digna sunt, quæ hic habet Chrysostomus; quæ adducantur: Vas iræ erat Pharao, hoc est homo, Dei iram accendens per suam duritiem. Dei enim le- nitatem ingentem nactus, melior nequaquam evade- bat, sed incorrectus manebat: itaque illum non so- lum ira vas vocavit, sed & ad perditionem prepara- tum, hoc est, apparatum, à se quidem, & suopte inge- nio. Neque enim Deus quicquam prætermisit eorum, quæ ad illius correctionem emendationemq; facerent: neque ille quicquam omisit eorum, quæ ipsum perde- rent omnique venia privarent. Sed tamen hæc Deus, quum probè nosset, tulit multa cum lenitate, volens ipsum ad pœnitentiam adducere. Si enim hoc no- luisset, ne lenitatem quidem tantam exhibuisset: ubi autem noluit ille lenitate ad pœnitentiam uti, sed seipse ad iram præparavit, usus est illo Deus ad alio- rum correctionem, per supplicii genus, quo illum af- fecit, cum alios ad virtutis studia addictiores, inten- tioresque reddens, tum suam ipsius potentiam hac ra- tione spectatam faciens. Quod enim non vult Deus sic suum robur innotescere, sed aliter, nempe per be- neficentiam, liberalitatemque erga nos suam: id verò modis omnibus jam inde ab initio declaravit. Et paulò post: At vero posteaquam prolixa uteretur lenitate, ut illum ad pœnitentiam adduceret, illum autem non pœniteret: tulit illum ad multum tem- pus, simul quidem declarans suam bonitatem, simul autem & potentiam, nisi vellet ille lucrum aliquod facere à multa hac lenitate, ac tolerantia. Ergo quemadmodum sumpto de eo, qui incorrectus per- manserat supplicio, potentiam ostendit suam: ita ple- rosque peccatores ad pœnitentiam reversos misera- tus, benignitatem nobis suam spectatam probatamque reddidit, nec dixit, benignitatem: sed gloriam, osten- dens videlicet, quod hoc ipsum maximè gloria Dei est, quodque ea cura ac studio illi imprimis est. Et post aliquam multa: Deus admodum bonus quum sit, in utrisque eandem ostendit bonitatem. Etenim non eos modo, quos servabat, miseratus est, sed & Pharao- nem ipsum, quantum quidem in ipso fuit. Eandem enim lenitatem & illi & hic sunt assequuti. Qui si servatus minimè fuit, rei totius culpa ab illius animo accidit: nam Dei partes atque officia nihilo minus ac- cepit, quam qui servati sunt. Hæc Chrysostomus: Addere etiam placet B. Mylii nostri interpretatio- nem: Partes orationis bujus singulæ, inquit, accu- ratam considerationem merentur: 1. Quoad damna- tos, retinetur similitudinis figura, & vasa appellan- tur impii, ac vasa quidem iræ. Bifariam illis hæc appellatio competit. Primum enim impii sunt, qui- bus Deus ceu virgis utitur, non tantum ad affligen- dum sese mutuo: sed ad castiganda etiam Electorum peccata. Sed magis ipsis dictio ista convenit, quia impii sunt, in quos tandem Deus fæces iræ suæ effun- det. 2. Quomodo talia vasa fiant, ostendit. Vocat enim non destinata, ut quidam interpretantur: sed apparata ad interitum: non autem apparata à Deo, quemadmodum blaspheme huic loco afferunt Sacra- mentarii: sed apparata tum à seipsis, tum à diabolo. 3. Quomodo Deus istis utatur, docet. Tolerai, in- quit, ea ac sustinet in multa patientia. Tolerantia est, quod non statim exscindit eos, sic nimirum illos ad pœnitentiam invitans: tolerantia est, quod nonnisi completa iniquitate & mensura peccatorum plectit ipsos: tolerantiæ itidem est, quod plerumque variis etiam interim beneficiis cumulat. 4. Finis autem damnationis eorum est, ut & iræ & potentiæ suæ do- cumenta Deus edat. Quod credentes & electos hi iti- dem vasa: sed misericordiæ divinæ vasa appellantur, tum quia illi sunt, per & propter quos generi buma- no misericordiam præstat Deus: tum verò imprimis, quia in bos viscera misericordiæ suæ idem effundit.
