For as many as strive to establish their own righteousness, that is, think themselves abundantly furnished with their own, are not capable of the righteousness of God, to which they most rightly subject themselves who, depressed by the acknowledgment of their own corruption and injustice, with the Publican groan: Be merciful to me a sinner, O GOD. That faith is the way through which the Righteousness of God (he understands INTERNAL) can be obtained ἄτερ γραφῆς is said: faith is the cause of the love of God Gal. V. 6. but not the way to love or internal righteousness. Nor was internal righteousness rejected by the Jews; who rather strove to set up THEIR OWN righteousness, and were persuaded that they performed to the law from themselves no less internal than external obedience, and thus all the righteousness of the law, and therefore they rejected the righteousness of Christ. Nothing here is held concerning the way through which the Righteousness of GOD is obtained, in no word is faith constituted as the way to righteousness. Nor is the persuasion of Wisdom here reproved in the Jews, but that they set up their own Righteousness, by which they wished to obtain Salvation through their own righteousness and the fulfillment of the law, but rejected the Righteousness of Christ and the fulfillment of the law for us, performed by Christ. But this false interpretation relies on the false hypothesis that the law of Moses was only a way to the Gospel: that the law of Moses was imperfect, and the Gospel exhibits more perfect laws: which we have elsewhere refuted in the Socinians.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἀγνοῦντες γὰρ τὴν τῶ Θεῦ δικαιοσύνην.

Id est ἐκ Θεῦ, ut dicitur Philipp. III. 9. Justitia illa vera & interna ac DEO grata à Deo ipso se revelante, & homi- nes ad se vocante proficiscitur. Cujus exemplum in Abra- hamo Paulus supra dedit IV. 2. 3. De hac Judæi plerique non cogitabant.

Cardinem disputationis Apostolicæ non attin- git Grotius, Papistico-Remonstranticis, & Socinia- nis occupatus opinionibus. Ideoque omnia in il- la disputatione pervertit. Non de justitia INTER- NA vel INHÆRENTE, quam illi causam forma- lem justificationis faciunt, sed de IMPUTATA CHRISTI justitia, quam formalem justificationis nostræ causam esse supra asseruerat Apostolus, hic sermo est. Nam agitur hic de justitia, quæ (1.) χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus nobis obtingit (2.) Quæ nobis imputatur per fidem. (3.) De justitia vel OBEDIENTIA CHRISTI, qua nos justificari docuerat. (4.) de justitia, quæ est ἐκ πίστεως ex fide, ut v. 30. cap. præced. dictum, non ἐξ ἔργων νόμε, ex operibus legis, quæ postulat opera perfectissima, sine ullo defectu, Deut. XXVII. 26. (5.) de justitia non nostra vel propria, quia τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην propriam justitiam erigere volebant Judæi, quod reprobat Apostolus, sed ALIENA, adeoque Chri- sti justitia. Nam propria justitia opponitur aliena, justitiæ nostræ justitia Christi, justitiæ inhærenti, justitia imputata, justitiæ operum, justitia fidei, ju- stitiæ legali, justitia Evangelica. (6.) De justitia, quam habemus non per propriam legis impletio- nem, hæc enim impossibilis est nobis, Rom. IIX. 3. sed per impletionem à Christo factam nostri loco, qui est τέλος νόμε εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῶ πισέυοντι. Justitia ergo illa dicitur ἡ τῶ Θεῦ δικαιοσύνη, non modo quod à DEO revelata, nam & ea justitia, quæ in lege exhibetur à DEO, à quo lex est, reve- lata dici potest, nec solum quod à DEO, homines ad se vocante, proficiscatur : siquidem etiam obe- dientia, quæ legi præstatur, DEO adscribenda sit, ceu autori & causæ nostræ renovationis & sancti- ficationis, à quo & velle est, & perficere: sed quod sit ipsiusmet DEI justitia, Christi nempe DEI il- lius benedicti in secula super omnia, qui est Jeho- vah, justitia nostra, Jerem. XXIII. 5. quæ ἐκ Θεῦ di- citur Phil. III. 9. quia Christus factus est nobis à Deo justitia 1. Cor. I. 30. & ex gratia Dei unice est, quod justitia Christi nostra est justitia, nobis- que imputatur. Paulo aliter qua verba, justitiam Dei, sed sensu tamen eodem reddidit B. Mylius P. 343. Justitiam DEI appellat, non quâ ille in judi- cando utitur, dum piis præmia tribuit, de impiis pœ- nas exigit : sed quam nobis in filio suo communicat, & quá nos solá in judicio ipsius consistere possumus. Giselber. l. IIX. Altercat. (apud B. Wellerum p. 582.) ita habet: Justitiam DEI dico, non qua Deus justus est, sed qua induit hominem, cum gratis justi- ficat impium. Huic justitiæ testimonium perhibent Lex & Prophetæ. Lex quidem hoc ipso, quod ju- bendo & minando, & neminem justificando satis in- dicat, dono DEI justificari hominem per Spiritum vivificantem : Prophetæ autem, quia id, quod prædi- xerunt, Christi implevit adventus. Quam vero justitiam non esse nostrammet propriam, vel in- hærentem INTERNAM justitiam Apostolus Phil. III. 9. clare testatus est, ut inveniar IN IPSO (Christo) non habens MEAM justitiam, τὴν ἐκ νόμε, eam, quæ est EX LEGE, (inhærens illa & in- terna nostra justitia annon ex lege est, annon à le- pe præscribitur & juxta legem ceu regulam æsti- manda est, eique confidere debet?) ἀλλὰ τὴν διὰ πίσεως, sed eam, quæ est per fidem Christi, vel in Christum τὴν ἐκ θεῦ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῇ πίσει, illam quæ est ex Deo JUSTITIAM in fide: Ex DEO est, quia ex mera Dei gratia est: quod justitiam non nostram, qualẽ lex requirit, quam nemo nostrûm in se invenit, nec invenire potest post lapsum : quia lex spiritualis est, nos autem carnales sumus, sed alienam, ipsius nempe CHRISTI destinavit, & or- dinavit, eandemque nostræ loco suscipit, nobisque imputat per fidem, quæ nonnisi in fide & per fi- dem nobis obtingit, cum nempe fide eandem ap- prehendimus: atque ita nobis eadem accensetur, ac si propria nostra esset justitia. Atque hujus exemplum in Abrahamo Paulus dedit supra c. IV. 2. 3. cui imputata est fides in justitiam, quam SINE OPERIBUS, adeoque etiam sine interna illa in- hærente justitia docuit v. 5. 6. De hac Christi ju- stitia, plerique Judæi non cogitabant, propriam erigere conantes justitiam, teste Apostolo.

καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην ζητῦντες ςῆσαι. ἱσάναι העמיד est inter alia approbare potestatem, ac jus alicui tribuere. Judæi plerique pro causa salutis æternæ constituere volebant, justitiam illam externam, quæ per frequentes actiones paratur & in societate humana aliquid valet. Est καθῆκον, non κατόρθωμα, ut distinguit Cicero libro tertio & quarto de finibus, & de officiis primo.

Vocem propriæ justitiæ pervertit Grotius, ac si EXTERNAM tantum justitiam notet: annon enim INTERNA etiam justitia habenda pro ju- stitia illa propria; aut num Judæi tantum EX- TERNAM justitiam pro causa salutis æternæ habebant, non vero justitiam INTERNAM. Herebant utique utplurimum in exterioribus, sed internam tamen justitiam, utpote dilectionem Dei ex tota mente, ex tota anima, ex toto corde etiam urgebant, ut tum Legisperiti, Luc. X. 37. tum Pharisæorum Matth. XXII. 37. exemplo con- stat. Paulus autem, qui temere ex Cicerone, nihil de justitia Evangelii edocto, æstimatur, reprobat Judæorum sententiam, non solum quatenus ex- ternam tantum urgebant justitiam, quo de nullus apex habetur, sed quatenus PROPRIAM justi- tiam erigebant, & causam salutis constituébant cum internam, tum externam illam justitiam de qua Moses scribit, de legis præceptis inquiens, Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis, ut v. 5. habetur: qui vero non externam tantum præscripsit aut postulavit obe- dientiam vel justitiam, sed imprimis internam mentis, animæ, cordis & quidem totius mentis, animæ, totius cordis, sub ea perfectione, quæ in nemine mortalium invenitur: unde confugien- dum nobis ad Christum, qui est τέλος νόμου com- plementum legis, & factus nobis à DEO est justi- stitia. Recte ad hunc vers. B. Mylius: Propriam justitiam vocat, quæ propriorum operum merito con- stat, quamque ex semetipsis homines habent. Sta- biliendi vocabulo infirmitas ejus notatur. Stabili- tur enim quod in se labascit & vacillat, ideoque ful- cris opus habet, quibus stabiliatur. Sed irritus co- natus altero verbo notatur. Quæritur enim stabili- tio hec duntaxat: non obtinetur.

τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐχ ὑπετάγησαν.

Bene monent viri eruditi, esse hic formam passivam pro reciproca: Niphal, ut Hebræi loquuntur pro Hithpael: quâ de locutione egimus ad Act. XIII. 48. Non subjecerunt se justitiæ DEI, id est, viam non iniêre, per quam ea compara- ri possit, fidem scilicet. Multi ad sapientiam pervenirent, nisi pervenisse se putarent. Idem Judæis illis evenit. Non dissimile est illud Philonis: εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ οἱ δόξαντες ἐπιμελεῖσ- θαι, (nempe σπερμάτων ἐλπίδος) φιλαυτίαν, πρὸ εὐσεβείας ἀσπασάμενοι, τὰς αἰτίας τῶν κατορθωμάτων ἀνέθηκαν ἑαυτοῖς, ὑπαιτίου δὲ πάντες ἦτον, μόνον δὲ ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιον, ὁ ἀναθεὶς τὴν ἐλπίδα Θεῷ.

Non admittenda illa glossa, non subjecerunt se justitiæ DEI, id est, viam non iniêre, per quam ea comparari possit, fidem scilicet. Plus dicit Aposto- lus: non subjecerunt se justitiæ Dei, id est, non admi- serunt justitiam DEI, repudiarunt eandem, quia Christum ipsum, qui Jehovah est justitia nostra, reprobârunt. Quomodo admitterent, vel susci- perent per fidem Justitiam Christi, qui Christum ipsum rejecerunt, & damnârunt: Μείωσις ergo est: subordinari vel subjicere sese Christi justitiæ nolue- runt, pro: reprobarunt penitus Justitiam Christi, uti sprevisse consilium DEI de salute dicuntur Luc. VII. 30. & repulisse verbum DEI Act. XIII. 46. Emphasin etiam in voce subjicere probe observa- vit B. Mylius: Quod Judæos justitiæ DEI non sub- jectos fuisse dicit, id est, non humiliatos coram DEO, ut se miseros esse & gratiâ ac misericordiâ DEI opus habere faterentur, ac justitiam, quam ipsis DEUS in Christo offerret, fide apprehenderent. Causa hujus mali ex præcedéte membro pendet. Quotquot n. suam Justitiam stabilire satagunt, id est, propria se abun- de instructos putant, justitia DEI non sunt capaces, cui rectissime se subjiciunt, qui suæ corruptionis & injustitiæ agnitione depressi, cum Publicano ingemiscunt: Propitius esto mihi peccatori ô DEUS. Fidem esse viam, per quam comparari possit Justi- tia Dei (INTERNAM intelligit) ἄτερ γραφῆς di- citur: fides causa est dilectionis Dei Gal. V. 6. non autem via ad dilectionem vel justitiam internam. Nec interna justitia reprobata à Judæis est; qui po- tius erigere nitebantur PROPRIAM justitiam, & à sese legi præstari non minus internam, quam ex- ternam obedientiam, omnemque adeo legis justi- tiam, persuasi erant, ideoque justitiam Christi re- probabant. Nihil hic de via, per quam comparatur Justitia DEI, habetur, nullo verbo fides via ad ju- stitiam constituitur. Nec persuasio Sapientiæ hic in Judæis reprehenditur, sed quod erigerent propriam Justitiam, quo propria justitia legisque impletione Salutem consequi vellent, Christi vero Justitiam & impletionem legis pro nobis, à Chri- sto præstitam, reprobarent. Nititur autem hæc ψευδερμηνεία falsa hypothesi, quod lex Mosis via tantum fuerit ad Evangelium: Mosis lex imper- fecta fuerit, Evangelium leges perfectiores exhibeat: quam in Socinianis alias profligavimus.

## 10:4
V. 4. For Christ is the end of the law.

That is, the law of Moses was only a way to the Gospel: τέλος is the goal of life, as above VI. 21. 22. 1. Tim. I. 5. The same sense Gal. III. 24. and above III. 31. and VIII. 4. Hebr. VII. 19: Christ is often put for the Gospel, as we also said above IX. 32. love is the fulfillment of the law, below XIII. 10.

unto righteousness to everyone that believeth.

Those who believe in Christ, namely truly and perseveringly, these are led through that Faith to the righteousness of GOD. This is the hinge of this whole dispute, to distinguish internal righteousness from external and to show that there is no way to the internal today except through Christ.

A new distortion: that by Christ the Gospel is to be understood. But why descend from the proper signification of the word Christ to a metonymical one and understand the doctrine of Christ? And Grotius indeed asserts that Christ is often put for the Gospel, but he produces no passage. Nor is the Gospel to be understood by the stone of stumbling in the preceding chapter V. 32, but Christ himself, who is also called the rock of offense Is. IIX. 14. For this is spoken of the Lord, who is our sanctification, not of the Gospel. Neither is the law of Moses ever said to be a way to the Gospel, nor the Gospel the goal of the law of Christ, much less is it taught in the Holy Scriptures that the law of Moses is imperfect, but the Gospel of Christ delivers far more perfect laws; indeed that is most false, since the law is most perfect, admitting neither addition nor diminution: nor does that have anything to do with the matter in this place: since the Apostle delivers a far different distinction between the law and the Gospel, that the law demands perfect obedience, and promises life under the condition of the perfect fulfillment of the Lord's precepts: but the Gospel of Christ presents righteousness and obedience, both active and passive, and promises life and salvation through faith in Christ. If the end of the commandment is love out of a pure heart 1 Tim. I. 5, and therefore it behooves the commandment or law to deliver or prescribe such love: in which sense love is also called the fulfillment of the law Rom. XIII. 10, because, to wit, love is prescribed in the law, and when love is performed, such as is prescribed there, the law is fulfilled. Therefore that love is not finally prescribed by Christ, since love is not called the fulfillment of the Gospel, but of the law. Furthermore, that τέλος is the goal of the way does not fit the passage 1 Tim. I. 5: for the goal of the Mosaic law is not love, but rather the fulfillment, and consequently these things are said in the same sense, that love is the fulfillment of the law, and is the end of the commandment. But above VI. 21. 22. sanctification is not constituted as a way to eternal life, but eternal life is called the end or consequence of sanctification: just as the consequence and end of the fruits of the service of sin is death. Wherefore if the passage 1 Tim. 1. 5 is to be compared, where we said that fulfillment is signified by the word τέλος, Christ is called the fulfillment and complement of the law, because in him we have the fulfillment or performance of the law: he himself, however, fulfilled the law not for his own sake, because he was the Lord of the law, but for us unto righteousness to everyone that believeth, so that believers might be justified by his obedience. Rom. V. 18. Besides, he notes that τέλος properly signifies consummation and complement, which, since it cannot be understood here by reason of abrogation or cessation, because it is not a matter of the abrogation of Ceremonies, as August. b. II against the adversaries of the law and the Prophets c. 7, Gregor. M. hom. XVI. in Ezech., but of the moral law, which has not been abrogated; it must certainly be understood as its fulfillment. For Christ did not come to destroy the law; but to fulfill the law Matth. V. 17. And thus also Augustine elsewhere, namely in Ps. IV. The end of the law, he says, is Christ. For here end signifies perfection, not consumption. Whom Haymo follows: Christ is said to be the end of the law, not the consumption, but the fulfillment and consummation of the law and the Prophets unto righteousness to everyone that believeth: Conf. Victor. Strigel. in this place, who notes from Eustathius on Homer that τέλος signifies the perfection and consummation of a work. And thus the commentary ascribed to Ambrose also explains it. Furthermore, Christ is called the end of the law unto righteousness. Therefore the end of cessation is not noted, but that of fulfillment which righteousness requires. Wherefore it remains that Christ is the complement of the moral law, that is, he who performed most perfectly whatever the moral law demanded. For it demanded both punishment for sins committed, and exact observance to be performed, for our righteousness & salvation; and therefore Christ both paid the former and fulfilled the latter, that the law might be fulfilled, which it was impossible to pay. But as to the remaining words εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πισεύοντι, by them the end of that fulfillment of the law is designated, righteousness, which is through faith. But that righteousness which is apprehended through faith is not our righteousness, but Christ's obedience & righteousness, which the Apostle taught at length above in c. III. v. 22. & seq., c. IV. 5., c. V. 18, 19. Whence also in Phil. III. 9. he removes our righteousness, that he may establish Christ's righteousness: Who was made unto us righteousness by God 1. Cor. I. 30. so that he who glories, may glory only in the Lord. But above all, the scope must also be weighed, which here is that the Jews are justly rejected, who attempt to set up their own righteousness, and reject the righteousness of GOD v. 3. who pursued righteousness from the works of the law, and neglected the righteousness which is from faith cap. IX. 32. but the righteousness of GOD is the righteousness of Christ, whom in c. IX. 5. he had called God blessed forever, since he had also inculcated the righteousness and obedience of Christ as δικαίωμα in the preceding chapters, and here urges faith in Christ, when he declares the righteousness of faith. But the righteousness of Christ is not essential, which certainly cannot become ours, but the righteousness of the mediatorial office, which consists in the satisfaction and fulfillment of the law, performed by Christ for us, and is to be apprehended through faith, so that it may become ours by application, which is not ours by performance; Moreover, from the opposition of one's own righteousness and another's, of the righteousness of our works, and of faith in Christ, it is clearly evident that it is not the fulfillment of the law by us that is urged, but that the fulfillment of the law, which we have in Christ, is hinted at, having been done for us. Which finally the subjoined proofs also teach, of which later. Therefore, as we have said, Grotius did not touch the hinge of the Apostolic disputation, who only wishes to distinguish internal righteousness from external, and to show that for man there is no way to internal righteousness except through doctrine of Christ. Nothing also occurs here concerning the means or the way of knowing internal righteousness, nor concerning the distinction between external and internal righteousness: But concerning the distinction between proper and imputed righteousness, legal and Evangelical, as is also manifest from the Apostolic confirmation.

Latin:

V. 4. Τέλος γὰρ νόμου χρισὸς.

Id est lex Mosis via tantum fuit ad Evangelium: τέλος est vitæ meta, ut supra VI. 21. 22. 1. Tim. I. 5. Idem sensus Gal. III. 24. & supra III. 31. & VIII. 4. Hebr. VII. 19: Chri- stus sæpe ponitur pro Evangelio, ut & supra diximus IX. 32. πλήρωμα νόμου ἀγάπη, infra XIII. 10.

εἰς δικαιοσύνην πάντι τῷ πιστεύοντι.

Ii qui Christo credunt, nempe vere ac perseveranter, hi per istam Fidem perducuntur ad justitiam DEI. Hic est cardo totius disputationis hujus, distinguere justitiam inter- nam ab externa & ostendere ad internam hodie nullam esse viam nisi per Christum.

Nova στρεβλότης: per Christum intelligendum esse Evangelium. Cur vero à propria vocis Christi significatione ad metonymicam descendendum & doctrina Christi intelligenda? Et Christum pro Ev- angelio sæpe poni asserit quidem Grotius, nullum ve- ro locum producit. Nec præced. cap. V. 32. per λί- θον προσκόμματος Evangelium intelligendum est, sed Christus ipse, qui & petra scandali dicitur Es. IIX. 14. Hoc enim de Domino, qui est sanctificatio nostra, non de Evangelio effertur. Neque vel lex Mosis via ad Evangelium, vel Evangelium Christi legis meta uspiam dicitur, multo minus id docetur an S. literis, quod imperfecta fit lex Mosis, Evan- gelium vero Christi legis longe perfectiores tra- dat, imo falsissimum id est, siquidem lex longe perfectissima sit, nec additionem ac diminutio- nem admittens: nec id hoc loco quicquam ad rem facit: quum longe aliam legis & Evangelii distin- ctionem tradat Apostolus, quod lex perfectam obedientiam postulat, ac vitam promittat sub con- ditione perfectæ præceptorum Domini adimple- tionis: Evangelium vero Christi justitiam & obe- dientiam tum activam, tum passivam sistat, & per fidem in Christum vitam & salutem promittat. Si τέλος præcepti est dilectio ex corde puro I, Tim. I. 5. ideoque præceptum vel legem oportet talem dilectionem tradere vel præscribere: quo sensu etiam ἀγάπη πλήρωμα νόμου Rom. XIII. 10. dicitur quod scil. in lege præscribatur dilectio, & cum di- lectio præstatur, qualis ibi præscribitur, lex im- pleatur. Non ergo à Christo demum illa præscripta est dilectio, siquidem non Evangelii πλήρωμα di- catur ἀγάπη, sed legis. Porro τέλος via metam esse loco 1. Tim. I. 5. non convenit: non enim meta legis Mosaicæ est dilectio, sed potius πλήρω- ma, ac proinde eodem sensu hæc dicuntur, dile- ctionem esse τὸ πλήρωμα νόμου, & esse τὸ τέλος τῆς παραγγελίας. Supra vero VI. 21. 22. sanctificatio nõ constituitur via ad vitam æternam, sed finis sancti- ficationis vel consequens dicitur vita æterna: sicut & fructuum servitii peccati consequens & finis est mors. Quapropter si conferendus locus 1. Tim. 1. 5. qua vocem τέλος, ubi πλήρωμα significari dixi- mus, Christus πλήρωμα & complementum legis dicitur, quia in ipso habemus legis impletionem vel praestationem : ipse vero legem implevit non sui causa, quia Dominus erat legis, sed pro nobis εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πισεύοντι ad justitiam omni credenti, ut obedientia ejus justificientur creden- tes. Rom. V. 18. Adhaec notat τέλος proprie consum- mationem & complementum, quod cum hic intelli- gi nequeat ratione abrogationis seu defitionis, quia non de abrogatione Ceremoniarum agitur, ut Au- gust. l. II. contr. advers. leg. & Proph. c. 7. Gregor. M. hom. XVI. in Ezech. sed de lege morali, quae abrogata non est; intelligendum utique est de ejus- dem adimpletione. Non enim venit Christus κα- ταλῦσαι solvere legem; sed πληρῶσαι adimplere le- gem Matth. V. 17. Atque ita etiam Augustinus alibi, nimirum in Ps. IV. Finis legis, inquit, Christus. Hic enim finis perfectionem non consumtionem signi- ficat. Quem Haymo sequitur : Christus dicitur esse finis legis non consumtio, sed impletio & consumma- tio legis & Prophetarum ad justitiam omni credenti : Conf. Victor. Strigel. in h. l. qui ex Eusthatio in Homerum notat, τέλος significare operis perfe- ctionem & consummationem. Atque ita explicat etiam commentarius Ambrosio adscriptus. Prae- terea dicitur Christus finis legis ad justitiam. Non ergo desitionis finis notatur, sed impletionis quem requirit justitia. Quocirca relinquitur Christum esse complementum legis moralis, h. e. eum, qui quicquid exigebat lex moralis, praestitit perfectis- sime. Exigebat autem illa tum poenam pro pec- catis commissis, tum exactam observantiam prae- standam, ad justitiam & salutem nostram; Ideo- que & illam persolvit & hanc adimplevit Christus, ut lex impleretur, quam impossibile erat solvi. Quod autem ad verba reliqua εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πισεύοντι iis finis illius impletionis legis desi- gnatur, justitia, quae est per fidem. Ea autem justitia quae per fidem apprehenditur, non est nostra ju- stitia, sed Christi obedientia & justitia, quod supra c. III. vers. 22. & seq. c. IV. 5. c. V. 18. 16. prolixe do- cuit Apostolus. Unde & Phil. III. 9. nostram justi- tiam removet, ut Christi justitiam stabiliat: Qui factus est nobis a Deo justitia 1. Cor. I. 30. ut, qui gloriatur, in Domino unice glorietur. Sed imprimis etiam scopus perpendendus est, qui hic est, Judaeos juste reprobari, qui propriam erigere conantur justi- tiam, & justitiam DEI reprobant vers. 3. qui per- sequebantur justitiam ex operibus legis, negligebant justitiam, quae est ex fide cap. IX. 10. justitia autem DEI est justitia Christi, quem c. IX. 6. Deum be- nedictum in secula dixerat, quandoquidem & in superioribus δικαίωμα obedientiam & justitiam Christi inculcarit, & hic fidem in Christum urgeat, cum justitiam fidei declarat. Non autem est ju- stitia Christi essentialis, quae utique nostra fieri non potest, sed justitia mediatorii muneris, quae in sa- tisfactione & impletione legis consistit, a Christo pro nobis praestita, & per fidem apprehendenda est, ut nostra fiat applicatione, quae nostra non est praestatione; Ex oppositione insuper justitiae pro- priae & alienae, justitiae operum nostrorum, & fidei in Christum luculenter constat, non propriam urgeri legis impletionem a nobis, sed impletio- nem legis, quam habemus in Christo innui, factam pro nobis. Quod denique etiam probationes sub- junctae docent, de quibus postea. Non itaque, ut diximus, attigit Grotius cardinem disputationis Apostolicae, qui tantum velit distinguere internam justitiam ab externa, & ostendere, ad internam justitiam homini nullam esse viam nisi per doctrinam Christi. Nihil etiam de medio vel viâ cognoscendi justitiam internam, nec de distinctione externæ & internæ justitiæ hic occurrit: Sed de distinctione justitiæ propriæ & imputatæ, legalis & Evangelicæ, uti etiam è confirmatione Apostolica manifestum.

## 10:5
V. 5. For Moses writes the righteousness which is of the law, that the man who does these things shall live in them. The Manuscript is not a little better: For Moses writes that the man who does the righteousness which is of the law shall be sought in it, just as the Latin also reads, from the Greek Lev. XVIII, 5. but there 'in them' refers to the commandments: here 'in it' refers to righteousness, with equal sense. 'In' is worth 'by', shall live, that is, shall be long-lived, as the Chaldean interprets. The righteousness of the law is not such obedience, which falls to the lot of no one, but the law is considered together with its expiations. In this way, to those who direct their deeds according to the law, the law promises a long and prosperous life. This is the reward of deeds. Deut. XXXII, 47.

The received Greek codices, which agree here entirely, are wrongly hurried into a suspicion of error, nor does the M.S. to which Grotius appeals differ in sense: whence the Latin indeed reads no otherwise, or has expressed the sense. Nor did the Latin follow the LXX Interpreters: whom indeed the Apostle followed. Therefore one must adhere rather to the authentic words of the Apostle than to the Latin text: which furthermore does not agree with Moses: for in Moses there is no mention of righteousness; how then can the pronoun be referred to it, so that it is forced to be 'in it' (righteousness) and not 'in them' (the commandments of which express mention is found) and thus all Greek codices are amended not according to Moses, but according to a certain M.S. perhaps adorned from the Latin. As to the sense of the words of Moses, it is not a question of long temporal life, but of eternal and heavenly; and the Chaldean also understands it, as we noted at Lev. XVIII. 5., nor did the Apostle accept it otherwise: for he is not occupied here with how we might be able to obtain a long life, but he treats of salvation and eternal life. And the obedience of the law is removed, because although the law promises eternal life, it nevertheless requires perfect and in all respects absolute obedience, which no one can perform. Legal expiations, however, do not pertain to this saying, which is merely legal, since expiations are a certain representative or visible Gospel, if I may so say, because the sentence of the Gospel concerning the expiation made through Christ and the remission of sins was represented and expressed in those Levitical shadows. Furthermore, the first confirmation of the Apostle from Moses occurs here, from the comparison of legal righteousness and Evangelical righteousness, which is through faith. For to legal righteousness Moses most openly requires perfect and absolute observance of the commandments of GOD, if anyone wishes to live through the law or to obtain eternal salvation. But since such observance can be performed by no one, it is manifest that we cannot obtain salvation through the law. But concerning the righteousness of faith, the Apostle again uses the words of Moses Deut. XXX. 12.

Latin:

V. 5. Μωσῆς γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὅτι ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς. Non paulo melius Manuscriptus: Μωσῆς γὰρ γράφει ὅτι τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου ὁ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπος ζητεῖται ἐν αὐτῇ, quomodo & Latinus legit, ex Græco Levit. XVIII, 5. sed ibi ἐν αὐτοῖς refertur ad προστάγματα: hic ἐν αὐτῇ ad δικαιοσύνην, pari sensu. Εν valet per, vivet, id est, longævus erit, ut interpretatur Chaldæus. Justitia legis non est talis obedientia, quæ nulli contigit, sed lex consideratur una cum suis expiationibus. Hoc modo secundum legem facta sua dirigentibus lex vitam promittit longam ac prosperam. Hæc est factorum merces. Deut. XXXII, 47.

Perperam in suspicionem erroris abripiuntur codices Græci recepti, qui hic ex asse consentiunt, nec in sensu discrepat M. S. ad quem provocat Grotius: unde Latinus non aliter quidem legit, seu sensum expressit. Nec LXX. Interpp. sequutus est Latinus: quos vero sequutus Apostolus. Est ergo adhærendum potius verbis authenticis Apostoli, quam Latino textui: qui præterea Mosi non convenit: nam in Mose nulla est δικαιοσύνης mentio; qui ergo pronomen ad eam referri potest, ut cogatur ἐν αὐτῇ (δικαιοσύνῃ) non vero ἐν αὐτοῖς (προσάγμασι quorum diserta mentio invenitur) & ita emendantur non juxta Mosen, sed secundum M. S. quoddam forte è Latino adornatum Græci codices universi. Quod ad sensum verborum Mosis non de vita longæva temporali, sed æternâ & cælesti agitur; eamque intelligit quoque Chaldæus, ut ad Lev. XIIX. 5. monuimus, nec aliter accepit Apostolus: non enim hic in eo occupatur, quomodo vitam longævam obtinere possimus, sed de salute & vita æterna agit. Et removetur legis obedientia, quia etsi promittat lex vitam æternam, requirit tamen perfectam omnibusque numeris absolutam obedientiam, quam nemo præstare potest. Expiationes autem legales ad hoc dictum non pertinent, quod mere legale est, quum expiationes sint Evangelium quoddam repræsentativum vel visibile, ut ita dicam, quia sententia Evangelii de expiatione per Christum factâ & remissione peccatorum in umbris illis Leviticis repræsentata & expressa fuit. Cæterum occurrit hic prima Apostoli confirmatio è Mose, à comparatione justitiæ legalis, & justitiæ Evangelicæ, quæ est per fidem. Ad legalem enim justitiam requirit Moses apertissime perfectam & absolutam præceptorum DEI observantiam, si quis per legem velit vivere vel salutem æternam adipisci. Quum vero observantia ejusmodi à nemine præstari possit, manifestum est, salutem nos consequi non posse per legem. De justitia vero fidei iterum utitur Apostolus verbis Mosis Deut. XXX. 12.

## 10:6
V. 6. But the righteousness which is of faith speaks thus. That is, he who has obtained the righteousness of GOD through faith in Christ, gives thanks to God for so manifest a benefit. Righteousness for one who has obtained righteousness, a Hebraism of the abstract for the concrete, such as election for the elect, circumcision for the circumcised.

Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven. The words are from Deut. XXX. 12. spoken there by Moses, to show that the knowledge of the law is not difficult to acquire, as we said there. Do not say in your heart, that is, do not think, a locution frequent among the Hebrews: Philo, that every good man is free: 'And yet what need is there of a long journey or of seafaring for the investigation and search of virtue, the roots of which the maker did not cast far, but thus near to you, just as the wise lawgiver of the Jews says there: in your mouth and in your heart, and in your hands.' And in the book on rewards and punishments: 'For the commandments are not excessive and heavier than the strength of those who use them, nor does the good stand far off or beyond the sea, or in the ends of the earth, so as to require a long-lasting and distant journey, nor was it suddenly snatched from here to heaven'

the colonies, so that someone, lifted up high and winged, might with difficulty reach it, and be able to [attain] these. But it is near and very close, established in three parts of those things which are in each of us, in the body, and in the heart and in the hands, in word and in thought and in deeds.' From which two [passages] of Philo note in passing that he himself follows the LXX version, who read more in the Hebrew than we have, namely 'and in your hands'. But Paul applies the words of Moses to the Gospel by an argument from the greater. Those who wish to signify a thing that is extremely difficult are accustomed to use the similitude of an ascent into heaven, and a descent to the underworld: Eteocles in the Phoenissae: 'I would go to the risings of the sun of the stars and beneath the earth.' Where the Scholiast: 'I could have the prize to go to heaven or to descend to Hades.' Tertullian against the nations II. Diogenes being consulted what is done in heaven, 'I never ascended,' he said.

But why should we say here that the abstract is put for the concrete, righteousness for the justified? And whence will it be taught that Moses is treating of the ease of the knowledge of the law, when Grotius acknowledges that the Apostle explains the place in a far different way? Shall we believe that the Apostle either did not perceive the mind of Moses, or knowingly and prudently brought forward his words in an alien sense beyond it?

that is, to bring Christ down.

That is, is an explanation of the underlying thought as above IX. 8. That, he says: Who shall ascend into heaven, is just as if you should say: Who will go into heaven, that he may make Christ descend from there? Understand that there is no need for us to labor over it. God has done this. See John III. 13. and the things said there. The Syrian follows this sense here, and often the infinitive is in place of 'that' with the potential.

Latin:

V. 6. ἡ δὲ ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοσύνη ὕτω λέγει. Id est, is qui per fidem in Christum justitiam DEI adeptus est, Deo gratias agit pro tam exposito beneficio. Justitia pro justitiam consecuto Hebraismus abstracti pro concreto, qualis ἐκλογὴ, pro electo, περιτομή pro circumcisis.

μὴ εἴπῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σού, τίς ἀναβήσεται εἰς τὸν ὀρανὸν. Verba sunt ex Deuter. XXX. 12. dicta ibi à Mose, ut ostenderet non esse difficilem acquisitu legis cognitionem, ut ibi diximus. Ne dicas in corde tuo, hoc est, ne cogites, locutio frequens Hebræis: Philo, omnem virum bonum esse liberum: καίτοι τίς ἡ μακρᾶς ὁδοιπορίας ἢ τῶ θαλαττεύειν ἐστὶ χρεία πρὸς ἔρευναν καὶ ζήτησιν ἀρετῆς, ἧς τὰς ῥίζας ὁ ποιῶν ἐ μακρὰν ἀλλ᾽ ἕτω σοὶ πλησίον ἐβάλλετο, καθάπερ κἀκεῖ ὁ σοφὸς τῶν ἰκδαίων νομοθέτης φησὶν: ἐν τῷ στόματί σου καὶ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου, καὶ ἐν ταῖς χερσί σου. Et libro de præmiis & pœnis: Οὐ γὰρ ὑπέρογκοι καὶ βαρύτεραι τῆς τῶν χρησομένων δυνάμεως αἱ προστάξεις εἰσὶν, ἐδὲ μακρὰν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐφέστηκεν ἢ πέραν θαλάσσης, ἢ ἐν ἐσχατίαις γῆς, ὡς δεῖσθαι πολυχρονίε καὶ παρατόπε ἀποδημίας, ἐδ᾽ ἐξαίφνης ἐσύλατο τὴν ἐντεῦθεν εἰς ἐραν

τὰς ἀποικίας, ἵνα τις μετέωρος κὴ πτηνὸς ἀρθεὶς μόλις ἐφίκηται, κὴ τέτων δυνηθῇ. πλησίον δ' ἐσὶ καὶ ἐγγύτατον τρισὶ μέρεσι τῶν καθ' ἕκαςον ἡμῶν ἐνιδρυμένον σώματι, κᾀ καρδίᾳ κᾀ χερσὶ, λόγῳ κᾀ διανοίᾳ κᾀ πράξεσι. Ex quibus duobus Philonis obiter no- ta ipsum sequi LXX. versionem, qui in Hebræo plus legerunt quam nos habemus, nempe κᾀ ἐν χερσί σου Paulus autem verba Mosis Evangelio applicat argumento a majori. So- lent qui rem perquam difficilem volunt significare, uti simi- litudine ascensus in cœlum, & descensus ad inferos: Eteo- cles Phœnif. Ἄςρων ἂν ἐλθοιμ' ἡλίου πρὸς ἀνατολὰς καὶ γῆς ἔνερθεν. Ubi Scholiastes: ἆθλον ἠδυνάμην εἰς ὐρανὸν ἐλθεῖν ἢ εἰς ᾅδου κα- τελθεῖν. Tertullianus adversus nationes II. Diogenes con- sultus quid in cœlo agatur, Nunquam inquit ascendi.

Cur vero hic abstractum dicamus positum pro concreto, justitiam pro justificato? Et unde docebi- tur de facilitate cognitionis legis Mosen agere, quum aliter longe explicare locum Apostolum agnoscat Grotius. Num Apostolum aut non per- cepisse mentem Mofis, aut præter eam alieno sen- su scientem prudentem verba ejus adduxisse cre- demus?

τουτέςι χριστὸν καταγαγεῖν.

Τουτέςι est explicatio ὑπονοίας ut supra IX. 8. Illud, in- quit: Quis ascendet in cœlum, perinde est, quasi dicas : Quis in cœlum ibit, ut Christum inde faciat descendere ? Intellitge nihil opus de eo nos laboremus. Deus hoc fecit. Vide Joh. III. 13. & ibi dicta. Hunc sensum hic sequitur Syrus, & sæpe infinitivus est vice ἵνα cum potentiali.

## 10:7
V. 7. Or who shall descend into the abyss.

In the Greek of the seventy elders it is 'beyond the sea,' but it is credible that in other versions it was 'into the abyss' or 'beyond the abyss.' For to the Hellenists, the abyss is often the great sea, as also in the son of Sirach 16:18. But because that word signifies everything that is deep, Paul preferred to use this word, so that he might transfer it to the seat of the dead. See what we have said on Luke 8:19. However, in these proverbial expressions, even if no ambiguous word occurred, such a change has nothing wrong with it, as long as the same meaning always remains, as here for the purpose of signifying difficulty. Thus some say you would more easily send a camel through the eye of a needle, others an elephant. Clement in his Epistle to the Corinthians called the abyss 'the unsearchable things.'

that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.

That is just as if you were to say: Who will go to the lowest places, so that he may restore to life Christ, buried in body, kept in soul in a place which God knows, and composed again? Nor indeed is there any need for us to labor over this. God has also accomplished this for us.

Grotius therefore seems to take the Apostle's words concerning the truth of the descent and resurrection of Christ: or rather concerning the fact that we have no need to labor to either bring Christ down from heaven or raise him from the earth, because God accomplishes these things for us. We have said a few things about the different interpretation of the words, both of Moses and of the Apostle, in the Theologia Apostolica Romana. We note, however, primarily that the words of Moses are to be accepted as they are explained here by the Holy Spirit, who is the best and only infallible interpreter of himself. Nor do we judge that Moses indicated one thing, and Paul, bringing forward the Mosaic passage as a place of proof, intended another. Furthermore, that the scope of the treatment and the arguments of the proof explain each other, and that the latter are directed entirely to the former. With these things supposed, and everything properly weighed, we still acquiesce in that which we taught thirty-two years ago in the Theologia Apostolica Romana at the Academy of Königsberg, and afterwards asserted at Danzig in a public disputation concerning the apostolic sense of the Mosaic words, and the genuine scope of this demonstration, namely that the Apostle explains the ease of justification through faith, both because he had previously shown the impossibility of justification through the law, and because he now asserts that the word of faith is not remote, but near, that is, obvious to all who grasp the grace of God, and he deduces this at length with other clearer sayings concerning the righteousness of faith, and also concerning the proclamation of the Gospel, by which that righteousness is exposed and proposed to all. This, therefore, is what the Apostle wants: that there is no reason why we should strive to fly into heaven or cast ourselves into the abyss, that we may seek salvation, but that the word of faith is near us, inasmuch as it is both in our mouth and in our heart through the preaching of the Apostles, and so the righteousness of faith is accessible to all, because the word has been preached to all. For from the preaching and hearing of the word, faith is conferred, but through faith righteousness is apprehended, and eternal salvation is obtained. Therefore, our merits and works and efforts are at least removed here, and thus the grace of God is established in our justification. What the Apostle had said above, that it is not of him who runs, nor of him who wills, but of GOD who shows mercy, he says here, that it is not of those who either fly into heaven or submerge themselves into the abyss, that they may obtain righteousness, and that the word of faith is near to all, and that there is need of faith alone. Moreover, the Apostle employs those undoubted articles of faith concerning Christ's ascension into heaven and resurrection, because those who attempt to ascend to heaven by their own works and merits do nothing other than deny that Christ descended from heaven or ascended into heaven for the sake of our salvation; nay, they deny that Christ was raised from the dead, both of which, however, were most certain and most attested. He therefore leads them to an absurdity, that they deny the first elements of Christianity, such as Christ's descent from heaven as well as his ascension and resurrection; that is, they render the whole faith void, 1 Cor. 15:14, whoever attempts to establish the righteousness of works. For what need would there have been for Christ to descend for the sake of our redemption, and furthermore to ascend into heaven to intercede for us, nay, even to rise from the dead to seal our justification, if we could ascend to heaven by our own righteousness, or so fulfill the law that we might attain eternal life through it? The ἔκθεσις of our blessed Mylius does not dissent from this explanation, who also refutes a similar gloss of the Grotian exposition on page 346. Others, he says, refer those words to knowledge, seduced by the sense of the Mosaic words, as if the Apostle were saying, it is not so hidden that there is need to ascend to heaven, etc., but the reasons immediately subjoined by Paul do not correspond. Others refer verse 6 and 7 to human curiosity. I refer them to the supplements of works in the cause of righteousness. He explains these things, however, from the apostolic antithesis of legal righteousness and the righteousness of faith, in which he observes four members: 1. 1. The Law. 2. Deeds or works. 3. The property of works. 4. The perfection of works, but that impossible one. To these four, he says, four other things are opposed in this other part of the antithesis: 1. To the Law of Moses is opposed the word which the Apostles preached, but by way of excellence the Gospel is understood. For they did not indeed abstain from the preaching of the law; but they had been appointed by Christ principally for the preaching of the Gospel. 2. To works, faith is opposed: not as if these are in themselves conflicting, but because they are considered according to the condition of the subject matter, namely, if the righteousness of works is opposed to the righteousness of faith. 3. To the property of works in the cause of righteousness, Christ with his obedience and redemption is opposed: 4. To the impossible perfection, which renders the cause of salvation from the law uncertain, is opposed partly the absolute perfection of salvation and righteousness obtained, which is evident even from this, that neither in heaven nor among the dead is anything left that should weary us with the care of completing it in the least; partly the most evident certainty. For as it cannot be taken away from heaven, that is, that Christ does not reign at the right hand of the Father; as it is a sin to seek the same among the dead, so the reason for salvation asserted by Christ is not uncertain. In almost the same manner, orthodox theologians in the Colloquy of Altenburg explained this passage: that there is no reason for us to strive to fly into heaven or to cast ourselves into the abyss, that we may seek salvation, but that the word of faith is near us, which is both in our mouth and in our heart through the preaching of the Apostles, so that thus our merits, works, and efforts are at least removed, and the grace of God is established. Nor is the explanation of blessed Weller on page 590 foreign to the scope. It is not that you should flee to the moral law and seek righteousness in it, which cannot be found here, but it is necessary that you confess Christ, the coming Messiah, and revere him with your whole heart, having received the spiritual circumcision, which is done without hands, by the power of the merit of Christ, to that Lord your God, verse 10. Do not say in your heart, who will ascend into heaven, and will prepare a place for me there; who will descend into the abyss, and will deliver me from death? Look to the promised Messiah, who will fulfill the law for you, will snatch you from hell, and will lead you with him into heaven. This doctrine concerning the coming Messiah is near you in your mouth and in your heart, that is, sufficiently clearly and perspicuously revealed and inculcated to you, so that you may now recite it with your mouth and publicly confess it, and likewise embrace it with your heart and true faith, provided you have allowed God to work in you through the word, and have not resisted out of malice. Chrysostom on this passage. There is no need, he says, that you be saved either by having traveled a long journey, or by having sailed across the sea, or by having overcome mountains, but if you wish to cross even your own threshold, it will be permitted to you to attain salvation even while sitting at home. For it is in your mouth and in your heart, from whence you may seek salvation. Cocceius explains it thus: The righteousness of faith says this: The righteousness of Christ, placed in public, commands one to say this, that is, to believe, or forbids one to doubt concerning the descent from heaven and the resurrection from the dead of him who could bring the law of faith: but it commands one to believe in him who descended from heaven and rose from the dead. Furthermore, he who weighs the whole connection and sequence of the passage will not easily call into doubt our explanation provided earlier. Therefore the word of Faith is explained, in that it consists in our believing that God raised Jesus, who was delivered for our sins, from the dead, and it is concluded that nothing else is required on our part for righteousness and salvation than that we believe in Christ; which the other proofs further illustrate, the one from Is. XXIX. v. 16. He who believes in him shall not be put to shame. Where nothing else is required for us to be freed from eternal ignominy than faith in Christ. The other is taken from Joel II. 32. Whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved: Where likewise nothing else is required for salvation except faith in Christ, because the invocation of the name of the Lord is an effect of faith in Christ: Whence it is added in verse 14. How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? The Apostle has therefore sufficiently established that only faith in Christ is required for righteousness and salvation, and indeed insofar as Christ is the fulfillment of the law, which faith he teaches is denied to no one, while he demonstrates that the word, through which GOD wills to excite faith, is divinely set forth to all; so that it thus holds true, if any perish, they do not perish by the fault of God, but because they reject the grace of God that is proposed.

However, it seems that this must still be observed on account of the Mosaic sentiment in Deut. XXX., that Moses refers to the entire doctrine of the divine word, which also embraces the Gospel: since he immediately preaches about conversion to GOD, which is done with the whole heart and the whole soul, verse 11, for the sake of which the circumcision ἀχειροποίητος (made without hands) had been delivered, which there is no doubt pertains to the Evangelical promises: not to mention that the sum of the new covenant, which is described in Jerem. XXXI. 33, is contained in it. And we have here the Hebrews in agreement, as noted by Vatablus; who, at Deut. XXX. 14, says it is diligently to be observed, from the consensus of the Hebrews, that this chapter pertains to the kingdom of Christ, whence also one of them says that there is a promise in this place that under King Messiah circumcision of the heart would happen to all who are of the covenant, citing Joel ch. II. 28.

Latin:

V. 7. ἤ τίς καταβήσεται εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον.

In Græco LXX. senum est πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης, sed cre- dibile est in aliis versionibus fuisse εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον vel πέραν τῆς ἀβύσσου. Nam Hellenistis ἄβυσσος sæpe est mare ma- gnum, ut & Sirachidæ XVI. 18. Sed quia ea vox omne, quod profundum est, significat, inde hâc voce uti maluit Paulus, ut eam ad sedem mortuorum transferret. Vide, quæ diximus ad Lucam VIII. 19. In proverbialibus autem istis locutionibus etiamsi vox nulla occurreret ambigua, mutatio talis nihil habet mali, dum semper maneat sensus idem, ut hic significandæ difficultatis. Sic alii dicunt fa- cilius camelum transmittas per foramen acus, alii elephan- tem. Ἄβυσσον, τὰ ἀνεξιχνίασα dixit Clemens in Epistola ad Corinthios.

τουτέςι χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναγαγεῖν.

Illud perinde est, quasi dicas : Quis ad loca infima ibit, ut inde Christum corpore sepultum, anima in loco quem Deus novit custoditum, re compositum in vitam restituat ? Nec de hoc quidem opus nos laborare. Deus & hoc pro nobis effecit.

Videtur ergo Grotius de veritate descensus & resurrectionis Christi verba Apostoli accipere : vel potius de eo, quod nos opus non habeamus la- borare, ut Christum vel de cœlo deducamus vel è terra resuscitemus, quia Deus hos pro nobis efficit. De diversa verborum tum Mosaicorum, tum A- postoli interpretatione diximus nonnulla in Theol. Apost. Rom. Notamus autem imprimis ita Mofis verba esse accipienda, uti hic à Spiritu S. qui opti- mus & solus infallibilis sui est interpres, explican- tur. Nec aliud Mosen indigitasse, aliud Paulum Mofaicum locum probationis loco adducentem voluisse censemus. Deinde scopum tractationis & argumenta probationis sese mutuo explicare, at- que hæc ad illum omnino directa esse. Quibus sup- positis, omnibusque probe expensis, adhuc in eo acquiescimus, quod in Theologia Apostolica Ro- mana ante hos XXXII. annos in Academia Regio- montanâ docuimus, & postmodum Dantisci Di- sputatione publicâ adseruimus de sensu verbo- rum Mosaicorum Apostolico, ac scopo genuino hujus demonstrationis, quod nempe explicet Apostolus facilitatem justificationis per fidem tum quia antea impossibilitatem justificationis per legem ostenderat, tum quia non remotum, sed prope esse verbum fidei h. e. omnibus obvium, qui gratiam Dei prensant, nunc asserit, idque prolixe deducit aliis clarioribus dictis, de justitia fidei, nec non de præconio Evang. quo omnibus exposita & proposita est ea Justitia. Hoc E. vult Apostolus: non esse quod vel in cœlum volitare contendamus vel in abyssum nos præcipitemus, ut quæramus salutem, sed prope nobis esse verbum fidei, quippe quod & in ore & in corde nostro est per Apostolorum præconiũ, adeo- que fidei justitiam omnibus esse obviam, quia omni- bus verbum prædicatum. E verbi autem præconio & auditu fides confertur, per fidem vero apprehen- ditur Justitia, & obtinetur salus æterna. Remo- ventur ergo saltem hic merita & opera ac conatus nostri, & stabilitur ita Dei gratia in nostri justifi- catione. Quod supra dixerat Apostolus, non esse currentis, neque volentis, sed miserentis DEI, id hic ait, non esse eorum, qui vel in cælum volitent, vel in abyssum se submergant, ut justitiam obtineant DEI verbumque fidei prope omnibus esse, solaque fide opus esse. Adhibet autem Apostolus articulos illos fidei indubios de Christi ascensu in cælum & resurrectio- ne, quod illi, qui conantur operibus & meritis suis cœlum conscendere, nihil aliud agant, quam quod negent Christum salutis nostræ causa de cælo descien- disse vel in cælum ascendisse, imo inficiêntur, Chri- stum à mortuis resuscitatum esse quod utrumque ta- men erat longe certissimum testatissimumq;. De- ducit ergo eos ad absurdum, quod negent prima Christianismi elementa, utpote Christi tum descien- sum è cælo tum ascensionem & resurrectionem quoq;. h. e. totam fidem irritam reddant, 1. Cor. XV. 14. quicumque operum Justitiam stabilire conantur. Quid enim opus fuisset, ut Christus descēderet no- stræ redemptionis gratiâ, & porro ascenderet in cœlum ad interpellandum pro nobis, imo ut re- surgeret etiam à mortuis ad obsignandam justifi- cationem nostram, si propriâ justitiâ nos cœlum conscendere possimus, vel legem ita adimplere, ut per eandem vitam æternam consequamur? Non abnuit huic explicationi B. Mylii nostri ἔκθεσις, qui etiam Grotianæ expositioni similem glossam con- futat fol. 346. Alii, inquit, ad notitiam verba ista re- ferunt, seducti sensu verborum Mosaicorum, quasi di- cat Apostolus, non ita est abscondita, ut sit opus ad cœlum ascendere &c. sed rationes à Paulo statim subjunctæ non respondent. Alii ad curiositatem hu- manam referunt v. 6. & 7. Ego ad supplementa ope- rum refero in causa justitiæ. Explicat vero hæc ex ἀντιθέσει justitiæ legalis & justitiæ fidei Apostoli- câ, in quà quatuor observat membra: 1. Legem. 2. Facta sive opera. 3. Proprietatem operum. 4. Per- fectionem operum, sed illam impossibilem. Qua- ternis his, inquit, quaterna alia in altera hac ἀντιθέ- σεως parte sunt opposita: 1. Legi Mosis opponitur ver- bum, quod predicabant Apostoli, κατ' ἐξοχὴν autem intelligitur Evangelium. Nam & legis predicatione side non abstinebant quidem; verū ad Evangelii præ- dicationẽ præcipue constituti à Christo fuerant. 2. Ope- ribus fides opponitur: non quasi hæc sint per se pugnan- tia, sed quia pro subjecta materia conditione conside- rantur, nimirum si justitia operum, Justitiæ fidei oppo- natur. 3. Proprietati operum in causa justitiæ, Chri- stus cum sua obedientia & redemptione opponitur: 4. Perfectioni impossibili, quæ incertam salutis cau- sam ex lege reddit, opponitur partim absoluta salutis & justitiæ parta perfectio, quæ vel inde patcat, quia ne- que in cælis, neque apud inferos relictum sit, quod nos cura illius consummandæ vel minima fatigare debeat: partim certitudo evidentissima. Quam enim non possit cælo detrabi, id est, non regnare ad dexteram Patris Christus: quam sit nefas eundem inter mor- tuos quærere, tam non esse incertam salutis à Christo assertæ rationem. Ad eundem fere modum expli- carunt hunc locum Theologi orthodoxi in Collo- quio Altenburg. non esse quod vel in cælum voli- tare contendamus, vel in abyssum nos præcipitemus, ut quæramus salutem, sed prope nobis esse verbum fidei, quod & in ore & in corde nostro est per Apostolorum præconium, ut ita removeantur saltem merita, ope- ra, & conatus nostri, & stabiliatur Dei gratia. Ne- que aliena à scopo est B. Welleri explicatio p. 590. Non est, ut ad legem moralem confugias, & in ea quæras justitiam, quæ hic inveniri nequit, sed opor- tet, ut Christum, venturum Messiam, confitearis, & reverearis toto corde, suscepta circumcisone spiri- tuali, quæ fit sine manibus, vi meriti Christi, ad istum Dominum Deum tuum vers. 10. Ne dixeris in corde tuo, quis ascendet in cælum, & locum ibi mihi parebit; quis descendet in abyssum, & è morte me liberabit? Respice promissum Messiam, qui pro te implebit legem, te ex inferno eripiet, & in cælum secum adducet. Hæc doctrina de venturo Messia, prope te est in ore tuo & in corde tuo h. e. satis clare & perspicue revelata & tibi inculcata, ut illam ore jam recitare & publice confiteri, corde itidem & vera fide amplecti queas, modo Deum in te operari per verbum passus fueris, & non repugnaveris ex malitia. Chrysost. in h. l. Non opus est, inquit, ut aut longo itinere emenso, aut pernavigato mari, aut su- peratis montibus salveris, sed si ipsum etiam limen transgredi volueris, licebit tibi domi quoque sedenti salutem consequi. In ore namque tuo & in corde tuo est, unde salutem petas. Coccejus ita explicat: Justitia fidei ita dicit: Justitia Christi in publico posita jubet hoc dicere h. e. credere, vel vetare dubitare de descen- su ex cælo & resurrectione ex mortuis ejus, qui legem fidei afferre potuerit: jubere autem credere in eum, qui descendit è cælo & resurrexit ex mortuis. Cæ- terum nostram explicationem antea traditam non facile in dubium vocabit, qui totam συνέχειαν & ἀκολουθίαν loci expendet. Ideo explicatur ver- bum Fidei, quod in eo consistat, ut credamus, quod Deus Jesum traditum propter peccata nostra resus citaverit è mortuis, nihilque aliud requiri ad Justitiam & salutem concludatur ex parte nostri, quam ut credamus in Christum; id quod ulterius illustrant cæteræ probationes, altera ex Es. XXIX. v. 16. Qui credit in eum, non pudefiet. Ubi nihil aliud requiritur, ut ab ignominia æterna libere- mur, quam fides in Christum. Altera desumitur è Joel. II. 32. Qui invocaverit nomen Domini ser- vabitur: Ubi pariter nihil aliud requiritur ad sa- lutem nisi fides in Christum, quia invocatio nomi- nis Domini est fidei in Christum effectus: Unde additur vers. 14. Quomodo invocabunt, in quem non crediderint? Satis ergo stabilivit Apostolus, re- quiri solùm fidem in Christum ad Justitiam & sa- lutem, & quidem in quantum Christus est comple- mentum legis, quam fidem nemini denegatam esse docet, dum verbum, per quod DEUS fidem ex- citare vult, omnibus expositum divinitus demon- strat; ut ita obtineat, si qui pereunt, non Dei culpa perire, sed quod gratiam Dei proposita reprobent.

Id autem adhuc ob Mosaicam sententiam Deut. XXX. observandum videtur, quod Moses doctrinam universam verbi divini, quæ etiam Ev- angelium complectitur, respiciat: siquidem im- mediate prædicat de conversione ad DEUM, quæ fit toto corde, totaque anima vers. 11. cujus cau- sa tradita erat circumcisio ἀχειροποίητος, quam ad Evangelicas promissiones spectare nullum est dubium: ne dicam quod eâdem summa novi fœ- deris, quod Jerem. XXXI. 33. describitur, com- prehendatur. Et habemus hic consentientes Ebræos, notante Vatablo; qui ad Deut. XXX. 14. diligenter, inquit, observandum, ex consensu Ebræo- rum caput hoc ad regnum Christi pertinere, unde etiam quidam illorum dicit, hoc loco promissionẽ esse, quod sub Rege Messia omnibus, qui de fœdere sunt, circumcisio cordis contingeret, citans Joëlem c. II. 28.

## 10:8
V. 8. The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.

These are the very words of the Seventy, except that * σφόδρα is added there. The sense in Moses is: there is no other work than that the law be read daily and kept in mind.

That is, the word of faith.

That is, again, is an explanation of the underlying meaning. This which can truly be said to be so easy is the Gospel, which is the word of God below 17, Eph. II. 17, Heb. VI. 9, XI. 3; but the word of faith, just as the hearing of faith Gal. III. 2, III. 5, the word of faith 1 Tim. III. 6, that is, that word which is received through faith.

Which we preach.

Which I and the other Apostles teach, both to the Jews and to the Gentiles.

The sense in Moses is not one thing, and another in the Apostolic citation: as if Moses were speaking of the ease of understanding the law, provided the law is read daily and kept in mind. But the Apostle is speaking of the ease of the Gospel; because the Apostle explained that which Moses said was near, that it is the word not of the law, but of the Gospel, and it is necessary that the text and the explanation of the text agree, and they must deal not with disparate things, such as Law and Gospel, but with the same things, if the explanation is to be sound. But the Apostle expressly says, that is, the word of faith, teaching that by that very word of which Moses spoke, it is not the law but the word of faith, which, just as Moses preached in his time, since the Gospel has always been handed down in the Church along with the law, so the Apostles in the New Testament especially explained it, and preached it to all throughout the world. It is not a bare explanation of the underlying meaning, but an interpretation of the genuine and literal sense of the Mosaic text that is designated by the word that is in the preceding; and here, by the same word, an interpretation of the subject, which is the word, of which it is asserted that it is near, is introduced, that it is the word of faith. Regarding that, Cocceius holds this: Paul explains the words of Moses, first denying, then affirming. Moses says: Do not say, who will ascend into heaven? Paul says that this is the same as, do not bring Christ down from heaven, i.e., believe that Christ has descended from heaven, and that there is no need for him to descend now. For thus he would descend again. For to bring down is to wish or demand that Christ descend. Moses says: Do not say, who will cross over the sea? For that, the Apostle says: Who will descend into the abyss? and interprets: do not bring Christ back from the dead, i.e., believe that Christ has risen from the dead, and that there is no need for him to die and rise again. The context concerning the universal and clear preaching of the Gospel refutes the opinion of certain Papists, Bellarmine, Salmeron, and Cornelius à Lapide, as if this were not a discourse about the ease and evidence of the proposition of the word, but about the ease of apprehension or observation from our own powers, and Estius is deservedly opposed to them, explaining those phrases, to ascend into heaven, to descend into the abyss, as referring to the inability to know anything from overly remote principles (cf. Prov. XXX. 4, Isa. XIV. 13, Am. IX. 2, John VII. 9): but they are refuted above all by the scope of the Apostle, which is clearly contrary, namely, to exclude whatever is ours, our powers, our merit, our righteousness, and to claim everything for the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and the righteousness of faith.

PART II. OF CHAPTER TEN. A further demonstration of the righteousness of faith from the Prophets.

Latin:

V. 8. Ἐγγύς σέ τὸ ῥῆμά ἐστιν ἐν τῷ στόματί σου καὶ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου.

Sunt ipsa verba LXX. senum, nisi quod ibi additur * σφόδρα. Sensus in Mose est: nihil aliud opus quam legem quotidie legi ac animo retineri.

Τουτέστι τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως.

Τουτέστι rurfum est explicatio ὑπονοίας. Hoc quod esse tam facile vere dici potest, est Evangelium, quod ῥῆμα Θεοῦ infra 17. Eph. II. 17. Hebr. VI. 9. XI. 3. ῥῆμα vero πίστεως, quomodo ἀκοὴ πίστεως Gal. III. 2. III. 5. λόγος πίστεως 1. Tim. III. 6. id est, id verbum, quod per fidem recipitur.

Ὃ κηρύσσομεν.

Quod ego & Apostoli alii docemus, & Judæos, & gentes.

Non alius est sensus in Mose, alius in allegatio- ne Apostolica: q. Moses loquatur de facilitate legem intelligendi, modo lex quotidie legatur, animo- que retineatur. Apostolus vere loquatur de fa- cilitate Evangelii; Quia illud, quod obvium esse dixit Moses, exposuit Apostolus, quod sit verbum non legis, sed Evangelii, & convenire oportet tex- tum, & explicationem textus, nec de disparatis, qualia sunt Lex & Evangelium, sed de iisdem agant necessum est, si proba sit explicatio. Diserte au- tem Apostolus τότεστι τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως, docens, eo ipso verbum illud, quo de loquutus est Moses, non legem sed verbum fidei esse, quod ut Moses suo tempore prædicavit, quum semper in Eccle- sia cum lege Evangelium traditum sit, ita impri- mis Apostoli in N. T. exposuere, omnibusque per orbem prædicarunt. Non nuda ὑπονοίας explica- tio, sed sensus genuini & literalis textus Mosaici interpretatio voce τουτέστι in superioribus desi- gnata est: & hic eadem voce Subjecti, quod est τὸ ῥῆμα, de quo essertur, quod prope sit, interpre- tatio infertur, quod id sit verbum fidei. De illa Coccejus ita habet: Verba Mosis primo negantia, deinde & affirmantia explicat Paulus. Moses dicit: Ne dicas, quis ascendet in cœlum? Paulus dicit, id tantundem esse atque, ne deducas Christum de cœlo, b. e. Crede Christum descendisse de cœlo, & non esse opus, ut jam descendat. Nam sic iterum descenderet. Nam deducere esse optare vel flagi- tare ut Christus descendat. Moses dicit: Ne dicas, quis transibit ultra mare? Pro eo dicit Apostolus: Quis ascendet in abyssum? & interpretatur: ne reducas Christum ex mortuis h. e. Crede Christum resurrexisse ex mortuis, & non esse opus, ut iterum moriatur & resurgat. Pontificiorum quorundam, Bellarmini, Salmeronis, Cornel. à Lapide senten- tiam, quasi hic non sermo sit de facilitate & evi- dentia propositionis verbi, sed de facilitate appre- hensionis, vel observationis ex viribus nostris, refel- lit contextus de universali, & luculentâ prædi- catione Evangelii, iisque merito opponitur Estius, phrases illas, ascendere in cœlum, descendere in abyssum, de impotentia cognoscendi aliquid ex nimium remotis principiis, (Conf. Prov. XXX. 4. Esa. XIV. 13. Am. IX. 2. Joh. VII. 9.) explicans: sed imprimis refelluntur è Scopo Apostoli, qui pla- ne contrarius est, nimirum excludendi, quicquid nostrum est, nostras vires, nostrum meritum, nostram justitiam, & gratiæ DEI, merito Christi ac justitia fi- dei omnia vendicandi.

PARS II. CAP. DECIMI. Ulterior justitiæ fidei è Prophetis demonstratio.

## 10:9
V. 9. That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus.

If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is your Lord. He made mention of the mouth because the mouth is named by Moses. Otherwise, he understands all parts of the body synecdochically; for just as some deny God by their deeds, Tit. I. 16, so others acknowledge Jesus as Lord by their deeds.

and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead.

For God does not value deeds, so that they might be rewarded eternally, unless they proceed from a purified heart. But the heart is purified through faith, and especially that by which it is believed that Jesus was raised by GOD, namely for this purpose, that we might know both his precepts to be divine and his promises to be certain, both because of the authority given to him and because of the conspicuous example of life restored. The two things which we have here, to confess and to believe, you have also in 1 John 4:15 and 5:1. That piety which God loves is not a difficult thing, Philo also acknowledges in his book on those who sacrifice: for he says, the mind asks of you, O God, nothing heavy and complex or difficult to perform, but something very simple and easy. These things are to love him as a benefactor. Chrysostom: It requires only intention and faith, O the labors and sweats

you will be saved.

You will arrive at eternal life.

This is a very bad depravation of the Apostle's words. (1) He deals with confession of the mouth, but not with deeds, which are performed through whatever parts of the body. (2) So that we may understand that not just any works are noted, but the confession of faith, he brings in the sentiment of Joel concerning invocation: if anyone shall call upon the name of the Lord, he shall be saved, v. 13, just as he brings forward the testimony of Isaiah concerning faith: Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame. (3) For salvation he does not require deeds or works, but faith alone. Which has been established thus far from the whole treatment. What perversity it is, therefore, that works are here thrust into the business of salvation, against the whole connection and Apostolic intention. (4) It is not a question here of the ease of piety, but of the ease of justification and of justifying faith, since we obtain salvation through faith, and faith is obtained from the word, which is obvious to all and not at all difficult. (5) Faith, by which our hearts are purified, is the apprehension of the expiation of Christ, whose blood alone cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7, and purges from dead works, Heb. 9:15, but it is not a bare knowledge and assent concerning the resurrection of Christ, by which the precepts and promises of Christ might be confirmed: for the precepts, because Christ gave no others, nor other promises than those which were given and proposed in the Old Testament, did not need new confirmation, nor was Christ dead and raised primarily and especially for the confirmation of his doctrine, to which he had abundantly reconciled faith by his very illustrious and most frequent miracles: His death was a ransom, not a testimony, the resurrection was a proof of the satisfaction rendered by the payment of the ransom. Nor indeed have all those who believe that Jesus was raised from the dead obtained salvation by that knowledge alone approved by assent, because even the demons themselves believe: and that obedience and piety redound from that knowledge and assent, and that this obedience and piety is the form of saving faith, are Socinian hypotheses and therefore truly heretical. See Socinus on the causes why one should believe the Gospel, etc. Moreover, those words 'to confess the Lord Jesus' and 'to believe that God raised him' are joined in the same sense as was said before concerning Christ's descent from heaven and his reduction from the abyss or resurrection: For he who descended is the Lord from heaven, who therefore came from heaven to this earth that he might be our Jesus, who is said to be the same one recalled from the abyss when he was raised, so that it might be implied that he was even in the abyss of hell itself, when for the sake of our salvation he willed to descend into the infernal pit, in which there is no water. Because of some Papists, with Thomas 2.2, q. 2, art. 5, and the Syncretists, with M. Anton. de Dominis, book VII, on the Resurrection, ch. 11, gathering from this passage that by explicit faith nothing further is necessary to be believed, or even, which the Synergists especially desire, that it is required for communion with the Church, Regarding what is contained in this Apostolic summary of things to be believed, it is to be noted that it was not the Apostle's intention to enumerate here all and singular things to be believed, but only to bring forward the main heads, and especially those which were necessary here for the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and for explaining the faith of justification; and furthermore, that the remaining mysteries of faith are comprehended under the articles of the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of Christ, and not excluded.

Latin:

V. 9. Ὅτι ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃς ἐν τῷ στόματί σου κύριον ἰησοῦν.

Si ore fatearis Jesum esse Dominum tuum. Oris fecit mentionem, quia os nominatur à Mose. Alioqui συνεκδο- χικῶς omnes corporis partes intelligit; nam sicut negant quidam DEUM factis Tit. I. 16. ita alii factis Jesum Domi- num agnoscunt.

καὶ πιστεύσῃς ἐκ τῇ καρδίᾳ σου ὅτι Θεὸς αὐτὸν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν.

Facta enim non æstimat Deus, ut ea in æternum remu- nerentur, nisi quæ ex corde mundato proficiscuntur. Mun- datur autem cor per fidem, & eam maximè, qua creditur, Jesus à DEO resuscitatus, in hoc scilicet, ut & præcepta ejus noscamus esse divina, & promissa certa, tum propter au- ctoritatem ei datam, tum propter vitæ redditæ conspicuum exemplum. Duo, quæ hic habemus, confiteri & credere, habes & 1. Joh. IV. 15. & V. 1. Pietatem illam, quam Deus amat, non esse rem difficilem, agnoscit & Philo libro de sa- crificantibus : αἰτεῖται γὰρ φησιν ἡ διάνοια παρὰ σοῦ ὁ θεὸς οὐδὲν βαρὺ καὶ ποικίλον ἢ δύσεργον, ἀλλ᾽ ἁπλοῦν μάλα καὶ ῥά- διον. Ταῦτα δέ ἐσιν ἀγαπᾷν αὐτὸν ὡς ἐνεργέτην. Chrysosto- mus: Γνώμης μόνης δεῖται καὶ πίσεως, ὦ πόνων καὶ ἱδρώτων

σωθήσῃ.

Ad vitam æternam pervenies.

Pessima hæc est depravatio verborum Aposto- li. Qui (1.) de oris confessione agit, non autem de factis, quæ per corporis partes quas cunque expe- diuntur. (2.) ut non quævis opera, sed confessio- nem fidei notari intelligamus, adducit sententiam Joëlis, de invocatione: si quis invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit, v. 13. quemadmodum de fide adfert Esaiæ testimonium: Omnis qui credit in eum, non confundetur. (3.) ad salutem non requirit fa- cta vel opera, sed unicè fidem. Quod hactenus ex tota tractatione constitit. Quæ ergò perversitas est, quod hic ingerantur opera in negotio salu- tis, contra totam συνέχειαν & intentionem Apo- stolicam. (4.) Non hic de pietatis facilitate agi- tur, sed de facilitate justificationis & fidei justifi- cantis, siquidem salutem consequamur per fidem, fides autem è verbo, quod omnibus obvium, mi- nimeque difficile est, obtineatur. (5.) Fides, quæ purificantur corda nostra, est apprehensio expiatio- nis Christi, cujus sanguis solum nos mundat ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. & purgat ab operibus mortuis, Ebr. IX. 15. non verò est nuda notitia, & assensus de resurrectione Christi, qua confirmata sint & præcepta, & promissa Christi: præcepta enim, quia non alia Christus dedit, nec alia promissa, quam in V. T. data sunt, & proposita, non indi- gebant novâ confirmatione, nec mortuus ac re- suscitatus primò ac præcipuè Christus fuit ob do- ctrinæ suæ confirmationem, cui fidem miraculis suis perquam illustribus & frequentissimis abundè conciliârat: Mors ejus λύτρον non μαρτύριον fuit, resuscitatio satisfactionis τῶ λύτρῳ persolutione præstitæ documentum. Nec verò omnes illi, qui- bus creditum Jesum resurrexisse à mortuis, sola illa notitia assensu probata salutem adepti, quod credunt etiam ipsimet dæmones: & ex ista no- titia atque assensu redundare obedientiam & pieta- tem, atque hanc obedientiam ac pietatem formam esse fidei salvificæ, hypotheses sunt Socinianæ adeo- que verè hæreticæ. Vid. Socinus de caus. cur cre- dat Evangel. &c. Cæterum conjunguntur illa κύριον ἰησοῦν Dominum Jesum confiteri, & credere, quod Deus ipsum resuscitârit, sensu eodem, quo anteà dictum, de Christi descensu de cœlo; & de ejus reductione ex abysso, vel resuscitatione: Nam qui descendit, Dominus est de cœlo, qui ideò de cœlo in hanc terram venit, ut esset noster Jesus, qui idem revocatus ex abysso dicitur, cum resusci- tatus est, ut innuatur, eum etiam in abysso fuisse ipsius inferni, quum nostræ salutis gratia in lacum infernalem, in quo non est aqua, descendere vo- luerit. Ob Pontificios nonnullos, cum Thoma 2. 2. q. 2. art. 5. & Syncretistas, cum M. Anton. de Dominis l. VII. de Refurr. c. 11. ex hoc loco colli- gentes fide explicitâ nihil porrò creditu necessa- rium esse, aut etiam, quod Synergistæ maximè volunt, ad communionem Ecclesiæ requiri, quam quæ hac Apostolica credendorum summa contineantur, notandum, Apostolo propositum non fuisse omnia & singula credenda hic recen- sere, sed summa tantum capita adferre, & impri- mis ea, quæ hic ad differentiam legis & Evangelii, & ad justificationis fidem explicandam necessaria erant; ac præterea sub articulis incarnationis, passionis, & resurrectionis Christi reliqua fidei mysteria comprehendi, non vero excludi.

## 10:10
V. 10. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness.

Through faith the righteousness of the heart is acquired, as we have often said.

and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

There is here a similar synecdoche, such as we have already noted. For he who perseveres in the solid profession of Christianity, he is saved.

The Apostle does not say that righteousness is acquired through faith, much less does he speak of INTERNAL righteousness, which Grotius understands, but he says that it is believed with the heart unto righteousness; because the faith of the heart apprehends the righteousness offered in the word of the Gospel, and the heart makes it its own through faith, so that he who believes in Christ may be justified before GOD; but when he says that confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, he by no means understands by the mouth, synecdochically, all parts of the body, nor by confession any good works whatsoever; because as the word of GOD is said to be in the heart and mouth, with the mouth taken properly, not synecdochically, so also here the mouth, by which confession is made, is to be taken properly, not synecdochically: but he joins faith and confession, because faith indeed never happens without confession, whether virtual and of the first act, or actual or of the act, as they call it, of the second, whether express, or tacit and interpretative: whence confession and the celebration of the name of the Lord is attributed even to infants, Ps. 8, even if they do not yet know how to use their tongue, as they celebrate in their own way, by the virtue of the Holy Spirit poured out upon them in Baptism, with mind and spirit, which must also be held regarding mute believers: who certainly would have to be excluded from salvation if actual oral confession were simply necessary for salvation: otherwise, in those who can use their tongue, faith breaks forth into the celebration and oral confession of the name of the Lord. But the Apostle has no further intention here than to teach that we obtain righteousness by faith alone; namely, the imputed righteousness of Christ, of which the Apostle is speaking, and that we are justified, and likewise that we obtain salvation by faith alone, and that because of such great grace of God we should glory in the Lord, and celebrate and confess Him. For the words of the Apostle are not to be taken in a divided sense; as if something else were required for salvation than what is required for justification, of which he had taught in chapter IV that the causes are the same, but that the grace of God and the righteousness of Christ the Savior, by which we are both justified and obtain eternal salvation, are to be proclaimed with the mouth no less than they are to be apprehended with the heart. For just as it would be absurd if the objects of faith and confession were divided, as if the object of faith were indeed the resurrection of Christ, but not that Jesus is Lord; and the object of confession were indeed the Lord Jesus, but not the resurrection; so also it is not fitting that righteousness should be subjected only to faith, but not to salvation, and that only salvation, but not righteousness, should be subjected to confession or celebration and glorying in GOD; since Isaiah, describing our justification, says in chapter XLV. 25, speaking of Christ (Cf. Rom. XIV. 11. Phil. II. 10.) In the Lord, he says, all the seed of Israel shall be justified, and shall glory in Him: and Paul, teaching that Christ has been made for us righteousness by God, warns that we ought to glory solely in Christ, both as to justification and as to salvation and eternal glorification, 1 Cor. I. 30, 31. Regarding which glorying, the present Apostolic passage is elegantly explained in the Colloquy of Altenburg, as noted by Schlüsselburg in the Catalogue of Heretics, ch. on the Majorists, p. 8, 13. These are the words: With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, is a description of true and saving faith, by which we apprehend imputed righteousness. And it is opposed to legal righteousness, which wants to descend now into heaven, now into the abyss, as the context of the discourse shows: For the Justitiaries, who think they can merit righteousness by their own works, are vehemently tormented, and in various struggles, various works and ways, they attempt to appease GOD, and to merit righteousness and salvation: but the righteousness of faith is faith kindled in the heart, apprehending the imputed righteousness of the obedience and merit of Christ, which then confesses salvation with the mouth, that is, it glories in this benefit of Christ exhibited to us, and not only embraces it with faith kindled and burning in the heart, but also proclaims and celebrates it with the mouth and a grateful voice.
