Therefore, neither the Majorist nor the Papist will be able to obtain anything from these words for the necessity of good works for salvation, unless they wish to add the preaching of the grace of GOD, or glorying in the one Lord Jesus, to good works; that is, if they wish to contradictorily establish that the exclusion of works and the thesis of the one righteousness of Christ is the position of our works, and the exclusion of the grace of GOD and the righteousness of Christ (because if by grace, not by works, Rom. XI. 6; if through the obedience of one Christ, not through our own obedience), destroying their own hypothesis. Some of our own explain the word ὁμολογεῖσθαι as the proclamation of the Gospel, such as the blessed Chemnitz and the blessed Weller, because ὁμολογία is used in this way in Heb. III. 1, ch. IV. 4, ch. X. 23, Rom. XV. 9, 1 John IV. 2. Heb. XIII. 15, but we stand by the explanation given, because both the faith of the heart and the confession of the mouth are uttered concerning one and the same subject; for neither the celebration of the grace of GOD exhibited in Christ, nor the fiducial invocation of the name of the Lord with that publican in Luke XVIII. 13, O God, be merciful to me the sinner, pertain to the works of the Law, which the Papists establish as necessary for salvation, and which the Apostle excludes from the circle of justification and salvation: that confession here is not a work, but an act of faith by which one believes in Christ, and that it stands in a correlative relation to the primary object of faith, the blessed Henricus Höpfner, Disp. XI. on justification. th. 57. et seqq. he excellently proved, from the scope of the Apostle, from the special example of this confession v. 13, from the necessary connection or harmony of the mouth and heart, and from the mutual permutation of attributes, which are distinctly predicated of the heart's desire of faith and the confession of the mouth: for he meant that the Apostle wished to join the heart and the mouth, through which faith in Christ exercises itself, just as he showed in the object and principle of faith, the word of the Gospel, that the mouth and heart are joined in understanding and apprehending; for faith is from hearing, the hearing of the proclamation, which is done by the mouth, that is, the perception of the preached word, is through the word, which perception is done by the heart.

Latin:

V. 10. καρδία γὰρ πιστεύεται εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

Per fidem acquiritur cordis justitia, ut sæpe diximus.

στόματι δὲ ὁμολογεῖται εἰς σωτηρίαν.

Est hic similis Synecdoche, qualem jam notavimus. Nam qui in professione solida Christianismi perseverat, is servatur.

Apostolus non per fidem acquiri Justitiam di- cit, nedum de INTERNA Justitia loquitur, quam Grotius intelligit, sed corde credi ait ad Justitiam; quia fides cordis apprehendit in verbo Evangelii oblatam justitiam, eamque suam facit cor per fi- dem, ut ita coram DEO justificetur, qui in Chri- stum credit; ore autem cum fieri confessionem ad salutem ait, neutiquam per os Synedochice omnes partes corporis, nec per confessionem bona opera quæcunque intelligit; quia ut in corde & ore dici- tur esse verbum DEI, ore proprie accepto, non Synecdothice, ita etiam hic os, quo fit confessio, proprie, non Synecdothice, accipiendum: sed fi- dem & confessionem conjungit, quod fides qui- dem nunquam fit sine confessione, seu virtuali & actus primi, seu actuali vel actus, quem vocant, secundi, seu expressâ, seu tacita & interpretativâ: unde & infantibus confessio & celebratio nomi- nis Domini tribuitur Pf. IIX. etsi linguâ uti adhuc nesciant, utpote qui suo more celebrant, virtute Spiritus S. in Baptismo super ipsos effusa Domi- num, mente atque animo, quod etiam de mutis fi- delibus habendum: qui certe à salute excludendi essent, si simpliciter necessaria esset actualis oralis confessio ad salutem: cæterum penes eos, qui lin- qua uti possunt, prorumpit fides in celebrationem & confessionem nominis Domini oralem. Apo- stolo autem nihil amplius hic propositum est do- cere, quam quod solâ fide consequamur Justitiam; imputatam nempe justitiam Christi, de quâ sermo est Apostolo, & justificemur, solâ item fide conse- quamur salutem, quodque ob tantam Dei gratiam gloriemur in Domino, eumque celebremus & con- fiteamur. Nec enim in sensu diviso accipienda verba Apostoli; quasi aliud requiratur ad salu- tem, quam quod ad justificationem requiritur, cu- jus utriusque easdem causas esse cap. IV. docue- rat, sed quod non minus ore prædicanda, quam corde apprehendenda sit divina gratia, & Christi Servatoris justitia, qua unice & justificamur & sa- lutem æternam consequimur. Quemadmodum enim absurdum foret, si dividerentur objecta fidei & confessionis, quasi fidei quidem objectum sit re- surrectio Christi, non autem quod Jesus sit Domi- nus; confessionis vero objectum sit Dominus Jesus, non autem resuscitatio; ita etiam non convenit, ut fidei tantum Justitia, non vero salus, confessioni vel celebrationi & gloriationi in DEO vero tan- tum salus, non vero justitia subjiciatur; siquidem Justificationem nostram describens Esaias c. XLV. 25. In Domino, inquit, de Christo loquens (Conf. Rom. XIV. 11. Phil. II. 10.) justificatur omne semen Israël, deque eo gloriabitur: & Paulus docens, quod Christus nobis à Deo factus sit Justitia, monet, nos unice in Christo gloriari debere, tum qua Ju- stificationem, tum qua salvationem & glorifica- tionem æternam 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. De qua gloriatione eleganter exponitur in Colloq. Altenb. locus præ- fens Apostolicus, notante Schlüffelburg. in Catal hæret. c. Majoristas p. 8. 13. Sunt autem hæc verba: Corde creditur ad Justitiam, ore autem fit con- fessio ad salutem, descriptio veræ & salvificæ fidei, quà justitiam imputativam apprehendimus. Ac op- ponitur justitiæ legali, quæ nunc in cœlum, nunc in abyssum vult descendere, ut contextus orationis osten- dit: Nam Justitiarii, qui se propriis operibus justi- tiam mereri posse arbitrantur, vehementer angun- tur, & in variis luctis, variis operibus & modis conantur DEUM placare, & justitiam & salutem promereri: sed justitia fidei est, fides in corde ac- censa, apprehendens Justitiam imputativam obedi- entia & meriti Christi, quæ deinde ore confitetur sa- lutem, hoc est gloriatur de hoc Christi beneficio no- bis exhibito, & id ipsum non solum fide in corde accensa & ardente amplectitur, sed etiam ore & gra- ta voce prædicat & celebrat.

Non ergo quicquam ex his verbis vel Majo- rista vel Pontificii pro bonorum operum neces- sitate ad salutem obtinere poterunt, nisi prædica- tionem gratiæ DEI, vel gloriationem in uno Domino Jesu operibus bonis accensere velint; hoc est, exclusionem operum & θέσιν unius justitiæ Christi esse positionem operum nostrorum, & exclusio- nem gratiæ DEI, & justitiæ Christi, (quia si ex gratia, non ex operibus Rom. XI. 6. si per unius Christi obedientiam, non per propriam nostram obedientiam) suæ ὑποθέσει διαλέοντες contradicto- rie statuere velint. Nonnulli è nostris vocem ὁμο- λογεῖσθαι de præconio Evangelii explicant, utpote B. Chemnit. & B. Wellerus, quod ὁμολογία sic usur- petur Ebr. III. 1. c. IV. 4. c. X. 23. Rom. XV. 9. 1. Job. IV. 2. Ebr. XIII. 15. sed subsistimus in tradita ex- plicatione, quia de uno eodemque Subjecto effer- tur & fides cordis & confessio oris; Nam nec cele- bratio gratiæ DEI in Christo exhibitæ, nec invo- cati fiducialis nominis Domini cum publicano illo Luc. XIIX, 13. ὧ Θεὸς ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτω-λῷ, ad opera legis, quæ Papicolæ necessaria statu- unt ad salutem, quæque Apostolus è circulo justi- ficationis & salvationis excludit, faciunt: Con- fessionem hic non esse opus, sed actum fidei quà creditur in Christum, & correlative se habere ad objectum fidei primarium B. Henricus Höpfnerus Disp. XI. de justificat. th. 57. seqq. eximie pro- bavit, ex scopo Apostoli, ex speciali confessionis hu- jus exemplo v. 13. ex necessaria connexione sive har- monia oris, & cordis & ex mutua permutatione attributorum, quæ de fidei desiderio cordis & con- fessione oris distincte prædicantur: voluisse enim Apostolum cor & os, per quod fides in Christum sese exercet, conjungere, sicut in fidei objecto & principio verbo Evangelii intelligendo & appre- hendendo ostendit conjuncta sunt os & cor; fides enim ex auditu est, præconii, quod ore fit, auditus, id est perceptio prædicationis auditæ, est per ver- bum, quæ perceptio corde fit.

## 10:11
V. 11. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ· πᾶς ὁ πισέυων ἐπ’ αὐτόν ὐ καταιχυνθήσεται.

In the place cited at the end of the chapter which preceded. And both there and here he takes the words of Isaiah in a mystical and more excellent sense. There it is, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, here ἐπ’ αὐτόν. In an equal sense: In the Hebrew it is implied.

Latin:

V. 11. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ· πᾶς ὁ πισέυων ἐπ’ αὐτόν ὐ καταιχυνθήσεται.

Loco citato fine capitis, quod præcessit. Et ibi & hic sumit verba Esaiæ in sensu mystico & excellentiore. Ibi est, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, hic ἐπ’ αὐτόν. Sensu pari: In Hebræo id sub- auditur.

## 10:12
V. 12. Ὀ γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ ἰεδαίε τε καὶ Ἕλληνⓒ.

All who are upright within are pleasing to GOD. But such are now many from the nations, as appears from the holiness of life, the patience under evils, and the gifts of the Spirit. See above II. 14.

ὁ γὰρ αὐτὸς κύριⓒ πάντων.

Κύριⓒ in this place signifies יהוה, for which he said Θεὸς above III. 29.

Abounding unto all who call upon him. Abounding, namely, in grace. Thus, the riches of grace is spoken of in Eph. I. 7. Abounding in goodness unto all. See above II. 4. IX. 23.

Latin:

V. 12. Ὀ γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ ἰεδαίε τε καὶ Ἕλληνⓒ.

Omnes qui intus recti sunt, DEO placent. Tales autem nunc sunt multi ex gentibus, ut apparet ex vitæ sanctitate, malorum patientia, donis Spiritus. Vide supra II. 14.

ὁ γὰρ αὐτὸς κύριⓒ πάντων.

Κύριⓒ hoc loco valet יהוה, pro quo dixit Θεὸς su- pra III. 29.

πλυτῶν εἰς πάντας τὺς ἐπικαλῦντας ἀυτὸν. Πλυτῶν nempe χάριτι. Sic πλῦτος χάριτος dicitur Eph. I. 7. Abundans bonitate in omnes. Vide supra II. 4. IX. 23.

## 10:13
V. 13. For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. He who shall call, namely with his whole heart, shall be saved; understand this here in a mystical sense, the pledge of which was to be the deliverance from the destruction of Jerusalem. See Acts II. 21. and what is said there.

As is the assertion, so also must be the proof. Since, therefore, this proof concerns faith alone; it is manifest that the assertion, or the theme of the Apostle, must be taken as regarding faith alone, not piety and the observance of the precepts of GOD or good works; he who shall have believed in him. That this is free from doubt is clear from the first oracle from Isa. XXVIII. 16. Which Grotius indeed takes in a mystical sense only concerning Christ, but that the Prophet prophesied of Christ in a literal sense, we have both taught in those annotations, and it is evident from this Apostolic demonstration. For proofs are not wont to be made from a mystical sense in such arduous disputes, but from a literal sense. It is rightly observed, however, that 'upon him' is the same as 'on him': because the discourse is about placing trust in Christ. To this one alone, therefore, is deliverance from all confusion, and consequently eternal glory, vindicated. And this, as the Apostle interprets, without distinction, whether one be a Jew or a Gentile. Grotius inserts or substitutes in place of the trust, which the Apostle designated from the Prophet, internal rectitude, which, even if it be joined with trust, does not however avail here, where it had to be proven that we are not justified, nor do we obtain salvation, by our own righteousness, but by the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith, who alone is that precious fundamental stone upon which we are built up, Eph. II. 20. 1 Pet. III. 6. Therefore the riches of the mercy of the Lord are celebrated over all who call upon the Lord with true trust of heart, but our good works or internal rectitude are not asserted.

The invocation of the name of the Lord in the other oracle, Joel II. 32, also brings in nothing other than faith in the merit of Christ; which is the basis of invocation pleasing to GOD, nay, its soul and form, nor is it taken in any other sense than to express refuge in the merit of Christ alone, in whom alone is our hope and trust. For he who betakes himself to this name with true trust is saved, Prov. XVIII. 10, besides which name no other is given under heaven in which it behooves us to be saved, Acts IV. 12. The gloss concerning deliverance from the destruction of Jerusalem, and the invention concerning a double literal and mystical sense, we have exploded in the annotations to that Prophetic passage, which may be consulted.

PART III. The necessity and propagation throughout the world of the Word of the Gospel, by which the righteousness of faith is announced.

Latin:

V. 13. πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσεται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίε σωθήσεται. Qui invocaverit, toto nempe animo, servabitur; intel- lige hic in sensu mystico, cujus arra futura erat liberatio ab excidio Hierosolymorum. Vide Act. II. 21. & ibi dicta.

Qualis est assertio, talis & probatio esse debet. Quum ergo hæc probatio solum concernat fidem; qui crediderit in eum, proinde de sola fide, non de pietate & observantia præceptorum DEI vel bonis operibus assertionem, vel thema Apostoli accipi debere, manifestum est. Quod è primo oraculo ex Es. XXVIII. 16. dubietate vacat. Quod in sen- su quidem mystico solum de Christo accipit Gro- tius, sed sensu literali de Christo vaticinari Pro- phetam tum illis in annotatis docuimus, tum ex hac ἀποδείξει Apostolica patet. Non enim pro- bationes fieri solent è sensu mystico, in ejusmodi arduis disputationibus, sed è sensu literali. Recte autem observatur ἐπ’ αὐτῷ idem esse, quod ἐπ’ αὐτὸν: quia de fiducia in Christum collocanda ser- mo est. Huic ergo soli liberatio ab omni con- fusione, adeoque gloria sempiterna vindicatur. Idque interprete Apostolo, fine discrimine, seu Judæus quis sit, seu Ethnicus. Grotius ingerit vel substituit loco fiduciæ, quam designavit è Prophe- ta Apostolus, internam rectitudinem, quæ etsi cum fiducia conjuncta sit, huc tamen non facit, ubi probandum erat, non nostra justitia, sed justitia Christi per fidem apprehensa, qui unus est lapis ille pretiosus fundamentalis, cui nos superstrui- mur Eph. II. 20. 1. Petr. III. 6. justificari, & salutem adipisci. Ideo celebrantur divitiæ misericordiæ Do- mini, super omnes, qui Dominum vera cordis fi- ducia invocant, non vero adseruntur nostra opera bona, vel rectitudo interna.

Invocatio etiam in al- tero oraculo Joel. II. 32. nominis Domini nihil aliud infert, quam fidem in meritum Christi; quæ invocationis, DEO gratæ, basis est, imo anima & forma, nec alio sensu accipitur, quam ut exprimat refugium ad Christi unius meritum, in quo solo nostra est spes & fiducia. Qui enim ad hoc no- men sese vera fiducia recipit, servatur Prov. XIIX. 10. extra quod nomen aliud non est datum sub cœlo, in quo servari oporteat Act. IV. 12. Glos- sam, de liberatione ab excidio Hierosolymorum, & commentum de duplici sensu literali & mystico ex- plosimus in annot. ad locum illum Propheticum, quæ videantur.

PARS III. Verbi Evangelii, quo justitia fidei annunciatur, necessitas & per orbem propagatio.

## 10:14
V. 14. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? V. 15. And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach except they be sent? As it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace.

All these words contain an objection to the statements of the Apostle. The objection, however, is as follows: The Apostles did not arrive in all places in which there are Jews, for instance in remote parts of Syria and Egypt; where they were not, they did not preach the word of the Gospel; where it was not preached, it was not heard: where it was not heard, it could not be believed. But why they came here and did not come there depends on GOD directing, who is said here to send, as also in Jer. I. 7, of which mission, performed for us by divine warning, you have examples in Acts XIII. 2, XVI. 6, 7, 8, 9, XX. 23, XII. 21. It seems therefore, says he who objects, that the cause still lies in GOD why many Jews perish eternally, if it is as you say, that without internal righteousness no one can obtain eternal salvation, and that at this time one cannot obtain such righteousness without faith in Jesus, which faith requires hearing, hearing requires preaching, and preaching requires being sent, that is, divine direction. If what is said were true, we learn from John XV. 22 that this excuse would not be lacking in its own reason. To that 'how shall they preach' must be understood in the Hebrew manner 'the preachers,' who are the same as 'those who preach the gospel.' For 'to preach the gospel' is also used deponentially, as in Luke II. 10, III. 18, IV. 18, VIII. 1, IX. 6, Acts V. 42, VIII. 4, 12, 40, X. 36, XIII. 32, XII. 1, 15, 21, XV. 35, XVII. 18. That passage which is employed to weaken the objection is from Isa. LII. 7, where in the Hebrew: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that is, who makes to hear peace, who brings good tidings of good. In the Greek LXX it is read: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good tidings of the hearing of peace, as one bringing good tidings of good. But from the Hebrew and this passage of Paul at the same time, it appears it should be read: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those bringing good tidings of the hearing of peace, of those bringing good tidings of good. We have said, however, that in the former sense these things are spoken of Jeremiah, but yet in such a way that even the ancient Jews understood these things to pertain more eminently to the times of the Messiah. Therefore, he who makes this objection proves that it would have been just that, from this prophecy, the Apostles should have been directed by GOD into all places in which Jews lived, which had not been done, when in the meantime the Apostles had reached many Gentiles and had preached to them.

For a fuller explanation concerning the righteousness of Christ, which is a mystery hidden from the wise of the world, the Apostle establishes the necessity of the proclamation of the Gospel, not approaching it on the occasion of an objection to the same, as seemed to Grotius, but directly. The connection of these is adamantine: There is no invocation without trust, and we invoke no one unless we believe in him and place our trust in him: Furthermore, there is no faith except concerning him of whom we have heard: Moreover, there is no hearing without a proclamation and a proclaimer, and finally there is no proclaimer without a mission. The Apostle teaches that neither Jews nor Gentiles were destitute of these, first from Isaiah 52:7, which passage Grotius falsely explains concerning Jeremiah in the literal sense, which he calls the primary one for himself, whereas there is only one sense of any given saying, but the Rabbis acknowledge that it pertains to the times of the Messiah, and that according to the proper and literal sense, concerning which we have spoken in the Illustrated Bibles in the annotations on Isaiah. Isaiah understands each one of those evangelizing, because they announce everything with one mouth, ὁμοφώνως; therefore the Apostle substituted 'those evangelizing' in the plural, so that the Prophet might look to the unanimous harmony of many, and the Apostle to the plurality of the persons evangelizing; who indeed were all sent out into the whole world, even if the word first sounded in Judea. For God is said to have manifested his holy arm before the eyes of all nations, so that the ends of the whole world might see the salvation of the Lord, verse 10. Moreover, the description of the proclaimers of the word of righteousness squares excellently, who are messengers not of the Law or of such a Gospel as might contain precepts more difficult than the Mosaic laws, since those were already in themselves ἀβάστακτα (unbearable): but εὐαγγελιζόμενοι (evangelizing), joyful and auspicious proclaimers, announcing PEACE and GOOD THINGS. These, antithetically, as the blessed Mylius teaches on page 353, look to the ministry of the law, and at the same time set forth the sum of the Gospel. The Law works wrath and threatens punishments, both of which are in the category of evils. By the Gospel, peace is announced, peace indeed, not with the world, which Christ did not come to bring, but peace with God, because it proposes the word of reconciliation. By which name even the feet of those evangelizers are to be considered beautiful. Which words, because the Roman Pontiff applies them to the kissing of his own feet, we consider to be held not so much in the category of abuse as of sacrilege.

Latin:

V. 14. πῶς ὖν ἐπικαλέσονται εἰς ὃν ἐκ ἐπίσευσαν; πῶς δὲ πισεύσυσιν ὕ ὐκ ἤκυσαν. V. 15. πῶς δὲ ἀκύσυσι χωρὶς κηρύσσοντος. Πῶς δὲ κηρύξυσιν ἐὰν μὴ ἀποσῶσι· καθὼς γέγραπται ὡς ὡραῖοι οἱ πόδες τῶν ἐναγγελιζομέ- νων εἰρήνην.

Hæc omnia verba continent objectionem ad dicta Apo- stoli. Est autem objectio talis, Apostoli non pervenere in loca omnia, in quibus sunt Judæi, puta in remota Syriæ & Ægypti; ubi non fuere, non prædicarunt verbum Evange- lii; ubi prædicatum non est, auditum non est: ubi audi- tum non est, credi non potuit. At cur huc venerint: illuc non venerint, pendet à DEO dirigente, quod hic dicitur mittere, ut & Jer. I. 7. cujus missionis nobis divino monitu factæ exempla habes Act. XIII. 2. XVI. 6. 7. 8. 9. XX. 23. XII. 21. Videtur ergo, dicit is, qui objicit, adhuc causa in DEO esse, cur multi Judæi æternum pereant, si ita est, ut ais, ut sine justitia interna nemo salutem æternam adipi- sci possit, neque hoc tempore justitiam talem adipisci sine fide in Jesum, quæ fides auditum requirit, auditus prædicationem, prædicatio immissionem, id est, directio- nem divinam. Si vera essent, quæ dicuntur, non cari- turam suâ ratione hanc excusationem discimus Joh. XV. 22. Ad illud πῶς δὲ κηρύξουσι subintelligendum more He- bræo οἱ κήρυκες, qui iidem εὐαγγελιζόμενοι. Nam εὐαγ- γελίζεσθαι etiam deponentialiter ponitur ut Luc. II. 10. III. 18. IV. 18. VIII. 1. IX. 6. Act. V. 42. VIII. 4. 12. 40. X. 36. XIII. 32. XII. 1. 15. 21. XV, 35. XVII. 18. Locus ille, quâ objectioni infirmandæ adhibetur est ex Esa. LVII. 2. ubi in Hebræo: Quam pulchri super montes sunt pedes ejus, qui evangelizat, id est, Audire facit pacem, qui evangelizat bo- num. In Græco LXX. legitur: ὡς ὥρα ἐπὶ τῶν ὄρεων ὡς πόδες εὐαγγελιζομένη ἀκοὴν εἰρήνης ὡς εὐαγγελιζομένη ἀγαθά. Sed ex Hebræo simul & hoc Pauli loco apparet legendum: Ὡς ὡραῖοι ἐπὶ τῶν ὄρεων οἱ πόδες εὐαγγελιζομένε ἀκοὴν εἰρή- νης, οἱ εὐαγγελιζομένε ἀγαθά. Diximus autem, sensu prio- re dici hæc de Jeremia, sed ita tamen, ut etiam veteres Ju- dæi intellexerint hæc eminentius convenire in tempora Messiæ. Probat ergo is, qui objectionem hanc facit, æquum fuisse, ut ex hoc vaticinio Apostoli à DEO dirige- rentur in omnia loca, in quibus viverent Judæi, quod fa- ctum non erat, cum interim ad multos alienigenas perve- nissent, iisque prædicassent Apostoli.

Ad pleniorem explicationem de justitia Chri- sti, quæ mysterium est sapientibus mundi abscon- ditum, Apostolus necessitatem præconii Evange- lici adstruit, non occasione objectionis ad eandem accedens, quod Grotio visum, sed directè. Nexus horum est adamantinus: Nulla est invocatio sine fiducia, neminem v. invocamus, nisi in quem credi- mus: & fiduciam collocamus: Nulla porro est fi- des nisi de eo, quo de audivimus: Nullus autem est auditus sine præconio, & præcone, nullus denique est præco sine missione. His autem non destitutos esse, sive Judæos, sive gentiles, docet Apostolus primum ex Es. LII. 7. quem locum falso de Jeremia, sensu literali, qui prior ipsi dicitur, cum nonnisi unus dicti cujusvis sensus sit, explicat Grotius, in tem- pora autem Messiæ convenire agnoscunt Rabbini, idque juxta proprium & literalem sensum, quo de in Bibliis illustratis ad annot. Esaiana diximus. Evangelizantium unumquemque intelligit Esaias, quia uno ore ὁμοφώνως omnem annunciant; ideo Evangelizantes in plurali substituit Apostolus, ut ita Propheta ad consonantiam plurimum una- nimem, Apostolus ad personarum Evangelizan- tium pluralitatem respiciat; qui vero omnes in totum orbem emissi sunt, etsi in Judæa verbum primum sonuerit. Nam manifestasse dicitur Deus brachium suum sanctum coram oculis omnium gentium, ut totius mundi fines videant salutare Domini vers. 10. Præclare autem quadrat descri- ptio præconum verbi justitiæ, qui nuncii sunt non Legis aut talis Evangelii, quod legibus Mosaicis dif- ficiliora præcepta contineat, quum illa jam fuerint per se ἀβάστακτα: sed εὐαγγελιζόμενοι læti & fau- sti præcones, PACEM & BONA annunciantes. Hæc ἀντιθετικῶς, docente B. Mylio f. 353. legis ministe- rium respiciunt, & simul summam Evangelii pro- ponunt. Lex iram operatur, & interminatur sup- plicia, quod utrumque est in parte malorum. Evan- gelio pax nunciatur, pax nimirum, non cum mundo, quam Christus non venit mittere: sed pax cum Deo, quia verbum reconciliationis proponit. Quo no- mine vel pedes etiam Evangelizantium istorum spe- ciosi existimandi sunt. Quæ verba, quod ad pedum suorum oscula Pontifex Romanus accommodat, non in abusus magis, quam sacrilegii parte habendum esse ducimus.

## 10:16
V. 16. ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντες ὑπήκουσαν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ (But not all obeyed the gospel). Paul responds in a twofold way: first, that those cannot use this excuse to whom the Apostles had been present, and who had not obeyed the Gospel when it was preached with such great miracles and heard so well, who were very many, as appears from the Acts. Those are said to obey the Gospel or the word of God who prepare themselves for that life which the Gospel prescribes, as in 2 Thess. 1:8 and 3:14. Hence the obedience of faith, that is, from faith, above in 1:5, as we said there: the obedience of the truth, 1 Pet. 1:22.

For Isaiah says.

That same Isaiah, whose words he who made the objection has used, also predicted this, in a more abstruse sense, of course, in which sense he cites these words also in John XII. 38.

Lord, who has believed our report?

As if he were to say, few. What had happened in Isaiah's time was about to happen again for similar reasons. Ἀκοὴ here, in the Hellenistic manner, like שמועה among the Hebrews, is the word which is heard, as in Matt. IV. 24, XIV. 1, XXIV. 6, Mark I. 28.

This is not a response to the objection, but rather the cause is explained why, although that salvation has been announced to all, not all are saved, because, to wit, not all have believed the Gospel: which is indicated by the word ὑπήκουσαν. For thus we observed above at I. 5 that the obedience of faith was spoken of there; add also c. XVI. 26. So also in 1 Pet. I. 22 it is called the obedience of the truth. Nor is it taken otherwise in 2 Thess. I. 8. And the passage of Isaiah demands this sense; because there the Gospel is described by the announcement of peace and of good things (τῶν ἀγαθῶν), and not indeed by the injunction of commandments to be performed: the other subjoined passage also demands that sense: Who believes our report? For it is not a matter there of the hearing of legal precepts, which are for the most part known by nature, but of the hearing and revelation of the Evangelical doctrine: which the men of God evangelizing peace received both in the O.T. and in the New, otherwise unknown to all human reason, concerning Christ the just servant of God and his emptying as well as his exaltation, concerning the arm of the Lord and the salvation of our God (Conf. Is. LIII, etc. & c. LII. 10). In this chapter of Isaiah LIII, certainly, our justification is established not in our works, but solely in the fiducial recognition of the just servant of God, who laid down his life for us and made satisfaction, or by his obedience both active and passive, v. 11; and therefore that classic passage, than which none exists clearer concerning the satisfactory passion of Christ in the whole O.T., has been most appositely adduced in the present case. But as for the more than Jewish distortion of it proposed by Grotius at Is. c. LIII and repeated here in the Bibl. Illustrat. we have abundantly refuted. Ἀκοὴ here does not denote fame, as in Matt. V. 24, c. XIV. 1, c. XXIV. 6, Mark I. 28, but the hearing of the Prophets, which they received from the Lord and which they announced. For what sense would it be: Who believes our report? that is, our fame? Those passages are therefore foreign, not parallel. The sense, however, is, who believes those things which we have received by hearing, revealed to us by the Lord? For the Prophetic discourses were made from the revelation of the Lord, nor did they preach other things than those which they had received from the Lord speaking to them, whether by internal or even external ἀκοῇ or hearing.

Latin:

V. 16. ἀλλ᾽ 8 πάντες ὑπήκουσαν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ. Respondet Paulus duplici modo: primum illos non posse excusatione hâc uti, quibus adfuissent Apostoli & qui Evangelio prædicato tantis cum miraculis & bene au- dito non paruerant, qui erant valde multi, ut ex Actis ap- paret. Ὑπακούειν εὐαγγελίῳ aut τῷ λόγῳ Θεῦ dicuntur, qui se parant ad eam vitam, quam præscribit Evangelium ut 2. Thess I. 8. & III. 14. Hinc ὑπακοὴ πίστεως, id est, ex fide, supra I. 5. ut ibi diximus: ὑπακοὴ τῆς ἀληθείας 1. Petr. I. 27.

Ἡσαΐας γὰρ λέγει.

Idem ille Esaias, cujus verbis usus est, qui objectionem fecit, hoc quoque prædixit, in sensu scilicet abstrusiore, quo sensu hæc verba adducit & Joh. XII. 38.

Κύριε τίς ἐπίστευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν.

Quasi diceret pauci. Quod Esaiæ tempore evenerat, iterum erat eventurum paribus de caussis. Ἀκοὴ hic Hellenistico more, ut שמועה apud Hebræos, est sermo, qui auditur, ut Matth. IV. 24. XIV. 1. XXIV. 6. Marci I. 28.

Non Responfio hæc ad objectionem est, sed potius caussa explicatur, cur, cum omnibus annunciata sit illa salus, non omnes salventur, quia scil. non omnes credidêre Evangelio : quod per verbum ὑπήκουσαν indicatur. Nam ita ὑπακοὴν πίστεως supra I. 5. dictam ibi observavimus, adde & c. XVI. 26. Ita etiam 1. Petr. I. 22. ὑπακοὴ τῆς ἀληθείας dicitur. Nec aliter 2. Thess. I. 8. accipitur. Et hunc sensum postulat locus Esaiæ ; quia ibi per annuntiationem pacis, & τῶν ἀγαθῶν bonorum, non vero per præceptionem mandatorum præstandorum describitur Evangelium : postulat etiam illum sensum alter subjunctus locus : Quis credit auditui nostro? Non enim ibi de auditu præceptorum legalium, quæ magnam partem natura nota sunt, sed de auditu & revelatione doctrinæ Evangelicæ agitur: quam accepêre viri DEI evangelizantes pacem cum in V. T. tum in Novo, omni humanæ rationi cæteroqui incognitam, de Christo servo DEI justo ejusque tum exinanitione, tum exaltatione, de brachio Domini & salutari DEI nostri (Conf. Ef. LIII, &c. & c. LII. 10.) In hoc certe capite Esaia LIII. non in nostris operibus, sed unice in agnitione fidutiali servi DEI justi, qui pro nobis animam suam posuit, & satisfecit, vel obedientia ejus cum active tum passive constituitur nostra justificatio, v. 11. ideoque quam appositissime locus ille classicus, quo clarior non extat de passione Christi satisfactoria in toto V. T. adductus est, in præsenti. Cujus vero detorsionem plus quam Judaicam à Grotio ad Ef. c. LIII. propositam & hic repetitam in Bibl. Illustrat. V. T. profligavimus abunde. Ἀκοὴ hic non famam notat, ut Matth. V. 24. c. XIV. 1. c. XXIV. 6. Marc. I. 28. sed auditum Prophetarum, quam à Domino accepere, quemque annunciarunt. Nam quis sensus foret : Quis credit auditui nostro? id est, fama nostra? Aliena ergo illa sunt loca, non parallela. Sensus autem est, quis credit illis, quæ auditione accepimus à Domino nobis revelata? Conciones enim Propheticæ fiebant ex revelatione Domini, nec alia illi prædicabant, quam quæ à Domino sibi loquente seu interna, seu etiam externa ἀκοῇ vel auditione acceperant.

## 10:17
So then faith comes by hearing.

Coming to the other part of the response, he concedes what had been assumed, that faith is not except from hearing. Ἄρα here means indeed. The Scholiasts note that it is taken for ὡς ἔοικε, both in Hesiod and in Apollonius.

and hearing by the word of God.

That hearing is of the divine word, that is, of the word sent by God; he concedes this also.

Here there is not another response: but a further explanation and deduction of the proof is held. Ἄρα is ordinarily THEREFORE. And this is inferred from the preceding. Therefore faith is from the hearing of the word of God. For faith cannot be had except from the Word of God. Which, therefore, must be heard or read. Word and faith are related. The word is preached for the sake of faith: nor does faith ordinarily have a place outside the word of God. For we do not receive faith enthusiastically and immediately, but acoustically and mediately through the hearing of the word, where, however, by the naming of the word, the Sacrament of Baptism is not excluded, which is also a medium of regeneration and faith. Because Sacraments are a certain word of God, not indeed audible but visible, yet they are not without the word; nay, they consist of the word both of command and of promise, nor are they Sacraments without it. But that hearing is διὰ ῥήματος Θεοῦ through the word of GOD, namely, the preached word: for it concerns the proclamation of those sent by the Lord: But through the preached word, the hearing of mystical things and those to be believed for salvation is obtained, not without the preaching of the word. Therefore, that men are accused in the name of infidelity is an indication that not only the guilt of the fault, but the proper and proximate cause of the evil itself, nay, the whole of it, adheres in men, who, if they wished, what they could and ought to wish, were certainly going to believe. Commonly, these sentences seem to have some contradiction if it is said: That faith is a gift of GOD, and that the proper cause of why one does not believe adheres in man. And the fanatics respond: That many do not believe the Gospel because God does not wish it, who, if He wished, could bestow faith upon all: but that God does not wish it by a hidden, yet not unjust, counsel. These are monsters of doctrines. Indeed, no one can take faith to himself unless it is given divinely; but truly the Lord is prepared to give faith to those who studiously hear His word. This is indeed placed in the power of men, as B. Mylius most correctly says here.

Latin:

Ἄρα ἡ πίστις ἐξ ἀκοῆς.

Veniens ad alteram responsionis partem concedit, quod sumptum erat, fidem non esse nisi ex auditu. Ἄρα hic valet sane. Notant Scholiastæ sumi pro ὡς ἔοικε & apud Hesiodum & apud Apollonium.

ἡ δὲ ἀκοὴ διὰ ῥήματος Θεῦ.

Auditus ille est verbi divini, id est, verbi à DEO missi etiam hoc concedit.

Non hic altera responsionis: sed probationis ulterior explicatio & deductio habetur. Ἄρα ordinarie est IGITUR. Et infertur hoc è superioribus. Igitur ex auditu verbi DEI fides. Non enim nisi ex Verbo Dei haberi potest fides. Quod proinde audiendum est vel legendum. Relata sunt verbum & fides. Verbum prædicatur ob fidem: nec extra verbum Dei locum habet fides ordinarie. Non enim ἐνθουσιαστικῶς & ἀμέσως fidem accipimus, sed ἀκουστικῶς & ἐμμέσως per auditum verbi, ubi tamen nominato verbo non excluditur Sacramentum Baptismi, quod etiam medium est regenerationis & fidei. Quia Sacramenta sunt verbum quoddam Dei non quidem ἀκουστὸν sed ὁρατὸν, non tamen sunt sine verbo, imo verbo tum mandati tum promissi constant, nec sine illo Sacramenta sunt. Auditus autem illa est διὰ ῥή- ματος Θεῒ per verbum DEI scil. prædicatum: nam de præconio agitur missorum à Domino: Per verbum autem prædicatum auditus rerum mysticarum & credendarum ad salutem obtine- tur, non sine verbi prædicatione. Quod ergo in- fidelitatis nomine accusantur homines, indicio est, non culpæ tantum reatum; sed mali ipsius causam quoque propriam ac proximam, imo omnem hærere in hominibus, qui si vellent, quod velle poterant ac debebant, utique credituri erant. Vulgo contrarie- tatis quippiam videntur habere hæ sententiæ, si di- catur: Fidem donum DEI esse, & in homine pro- priam hærere causam, quo minus credat. Et fa- natici respondent: Non credere multos Evangelio, quia Deus nolit, qui, si vellet, omnibus posset largiri fidem: nolle autem Deum occulto quidem, non ta- men injusto consilio. Hæc monstra sunt dogmatum. Fidem quidem nemo sibi sumere potest, nisi detur divinitus; At vero paratus est dare Dominus fidem, verbum suum studiose audientibus. Id quod est sane in facultate hominum positum, ut hic rectissime B. Mylius.

## 10:18
V. 18. ἀλλὰ λέγω μὴ ἤκουσαν.

But this being granted, he says, I ask whether those whom you excuse have heard nothing at all about the Gospel. Paul wishes to deny that, and illustrates the matter with a comparison.

Μενοῦνγε) But indeed. εἰς πᾶσαν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν.

We have said at the place in the Psalm that the LXX Interpreters read קולם for קום in the Hebrew. The starry heaven is in one place: and yet its voice and words are heard everywhere, that is, its power is understood. In a similar way, since the Apostles were in the more illustrious cities, and there both preached and performed miracles, as in Jerusalem, Caesarea, Joppa, Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth, Thessalonica, from there the fame of such great things reached all the lands in which the Jews lived, and that is sufficient. Thus Paul denies that Agrippa could be ignorant of those things which had been done by Jesus, because, forsooth, those things had not happened in some corner, but in illustrious places. Acts XXVI. 26. We have said that this is the reason why the Apostles were not permitted to go into Asia, because a sufficiently clear fame could have reached there from the cities of Pisidia and Pamphylia. In Latin, φθόγγος αὐτῶν and ῥήματα αὐτῶν is referred to ὀυρανοὺς, which the Hellenists pronounce in the plural, as the Hebrews do שמים, even where there is mention of only the air or only the starry heaven. Similar is what Philo said about the law of Moses: τῶν νόμων τὸ κλέος ὡς ἀπολέλοιπε διὰ πάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης καὶ τῶν τῆς γῆς τερμάτων ἔφθακεν. See what Paul said above about the faith of the Romans I. 8. and Acts VII. 6. and Colossians I. 6. Clement about Paul: δικαιοσύνην διδάξας ὅλον τὸν κόσμον.

I repeat what I said, that this is not a response to an objection, but that the Apostle is continuing his ordinary treatment; that God does not fail men in His grace, provided they themselves admit the word of grace: and that that announcement of the Gospel concerning Christ and His righteousness did not happen to a few certain ones, with the rest excluded, but that it ought to have happened through the whole world, and did happen, in the tenor of Psalm XIX, so that as widely as the proclamation of the natural heavens announcing the glory of GOD extends, so widely has the proclamation of the Apostles evangelizing the grace of GOD spread itself, to whom, as mystical heavens, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, is carried through the world. But how an allusion is made in the Psalm to the heavens, the sun, and the proclamation of other creatures, and the metaphor has a place, or how the Davidic prophecy is brought in here, we have discussed at length concerning its explanation. Paul does not only illustrate the matter he is dealing with by a comparison, but he confirms that which he said about the word of the Gospel, about the righteousness of Christ, that it is not far off but obvious to all, with a new argument, and just as he had proved it by the testimony or prophecy of the Prophet Isaiah, so he now further confirms it with the Davidic prophecy: in which the course of Christ rising from on high in the work of redemption and calling, and of the word of GOD recreating souls, exhilarating the heart, illuminating the eyes, and affecting the palate with sweetness and pleasantness, from which we know the grace of GOD in the remission of sins, so that with confidence we may also seek pardon for hidden offenses, that is, the word of the Gospel, is treated. And thus it appears that this passage also has been most aptly brought to the present matter, in which the Apostle treats of the gratuitous remission of sins, and of the righteousness of Christ, and thus of justification, as well as of the word of the Gospel, by which that is announced: Φθόγγος for קוָם is called their (the Apostles') rule, because the Evangelical sound, as Luther says (T. II. Jen. Lat. f. 216), is that rule according to which the Church is built. Furthermore, we admit that of Ambrose: where the presence of a preaching man was lacking, the sound and fame nevertheless arrived, just as the report of the miracles performed had reached all nations, and that of Jerome on ch. XXIV of Matthew: I do not think any nation has remained that does not know the name of Christ. Such a generic and universal preaching not even the Calvinists themselves can deny, however sharply they may dispute against the grace of universal calling. What of the fact, says Chamier (Panstrat. Cath. T. II. l. XVI. c. 4), that Jerome and others take that preaching broadly, not only for the labors of pastors, but also for the hearing of the report? If this is so, who would likely deny that either those Indians, whom Rufinus observes as neighbors to Parthia, into which histories report Thomas to have traveled, heard nothing of Christ from their neighbors? Or the Poles, Vandals, and Moravians from the Germans? Add that the Holy Scriptures have been translated into various languages known throughout the world, whence knowledge of Christ could be drawn in the whole world. For the Apostles were commanded to preach through the whole world not less by writings than by living voice. Therefore, where the foot of the Apostles did not come, there came their fame or their Scripture. The rest that might be desired here should be sought from the annotations to the book of Psalms. However, both the Calvinists and, among the Papists, Cajetan, Gentianus, Hervæus, Salmero, and Pererius, oppose the Apostolic scope when they restrict the universal assertion, since the Apostle takes away every excuse from the unbelievers by asserting the calling of all, and makes the proclamation as universal as the light and heat of the sun extend universally to all, by force of the metaphorical expression, as we explained in the place cited.

Latin:

V. 18. ἀλλὰ λέγω μὴ ἤκουσαν.

Sed hoc concesso, inquit, quæro, an illi, quos excusatum is, omnino nihil de Evangelio audierunt. Id negare vult Paulus, & rem simili illustrat.

Μενοῦνγε) At enim. εἰς πᾶσαν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν.

LXX. Interpretes in Hebræo legisse קולם pro קום diximus ad Psalmi locum. Cœlum astriferum uno in lo- co est: & tamen ejus vox & verba ubique locorum au- diuntur, id est, vis ejus intelligitur. Pari modo cum Apo- stoli in illustrioribus urbibus fuerint, ibique & prædicave- rint, & miracula fecerint, ut Hierosolymis, Cæsareæ, Joppæ, Antiochiæ, Ephesi, Corinthi, Thessalonicæ, inde fama re- rum tantarum pervenit ad omnes terras, in quibus habi- tabant Judæi, idque sufficit. Sic Agrippam negat Paulus ignarum esse posse eorum, quæ ab Jesu gesta erant, quia scilicet illa non in angulo aliquo, sed in locis illustribus contigissent. Act. XXVI. 26. Hanc esse causam diximus, cur Apostoli non permissi sint in Asiam ire, quia ex Pisidiæ & Pamphyliæ urbibus fama satis clara illuc pervenire po- tuerat. In Latino φθόγγος αὐτῶν & ῥήματα αὐτῶν refer- tur ad ὀυρανοὺς, quod Hellenistæ pluraliter enunciant, ut He- bræi שמים, etiam ubi aut de solo aëre, aut de solo astrifero cœlo mentio est. Simile est, quod de lege Mosis dixit Philo: τῶν νόμων τὸ κλέος ὡς ἀπολέλοιπε διὰ πάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης καὶ τῶν τῆς γῆς τερμάτων ἔφθακεν. Vide, quæ de Romanorum fide supra dixit Paulus I. 8. & Act. VII. 6. & Coloss. I. 6. Clemens de Paulo: δικαιοσύνην διδάξας ὅλον τὸν κόσμον.

Repeto, quod dixi, non esse responsionem ad ob- jectionem, sed prosequi Apostolū ordinariam suam tractationem; quod non desit Deus hominibus suā gratia, modo ipsi admittant verbum gratiæ: quodq; illa Evangelii de Christo ejusq. justitia annuncia- tio non paucis quibusdam obtigerit, cæteris exclu- sis, sed quod per totum orbem fieri debuerit, & fa- cta sit, tenore Ps. XIX. adeo ut quam late patet præconium cælorum naturalium gloriam DEI an- nuntiantium, tam late se diffuderit præconium Apostolorum gratiam DEI Evangelizantium, qui- bus ceu cælis mysticis per orbem fertur Christus Sol justitiæ. Quomodo autem vel in Psalmo allu- sio fiat ad cælos, solem & creaturarum aliarum præ- conium, & metaphora locum habeat, vel hic ad- ducatur Davidicum vaticinium, circa ejus expli- cationem late disseruimus. Non illustrat tantum Paulus rem, de qua agit, simili, sed confirmat id, quod dixit de verbo Evangelii, de justitia Christi, quod non procul sed omnibus obvium sit, novo argumento, & uti probarat id testimonio vel vaticinio Prophetæ Esaiæ, ita idem ulterius jam confirmat vaticinio Davidico: quo de cursu Chri- stiorientis ex alto in opere redemptionis & vocatio- nis, & de verbo DEI animas recreante, cor exhila- ranti, oculos illuminante, & palatum dulcedine ac suavitate afficiente, ex quo cognoscimus gratiam DEI in remissione peccatorum, ut cum fiducia etiam occultorum delictorum, condonationem expetere possimus, h. e. de verbo Evangelii, agitur. Atq; ita apparet etiam hunc locum appositissime adductum esse ad præsentem materiam, quâ de remissione peccatorum gratuitâ, deque justitiâ Chri- sti, adeoque de justificatione, nec non de verbo Evangelii, quo illa annunciata tractat Apostolus: Φθόγγος pro קוָם Regula eorum (Apostolorum) dicitur, quia sonus Evangelicus, Luthero T. II. Jen. Lat. f. 216. dicente, regula illa est, juxta quam ædi- ficatur Ecclesia. De cætero admittimus illud Am- brosii: ubi prædicantis hominis præsentia defuit, so- nus tamen & fama pervenit, sicut pervenerat opi- nio factarum virtutum in omnes gentes, & Hiero- nymi in c. XXIV. Matth. Non puto aliquam re- mansisse gentem, quæ Christi nomen ignoret. Qua- lem genericam & universalem prædicationem nec ipsi Calviniani inficiari possunt, utut acriter ad- versus gratiam vocationis universalis disputent. Quid quod, inquit Chamier panstrat. Cath. T. II. l. XVI. c. 4. Hieronymus atque alii illam prædicatio- nem latè accipiant, non tantum pro pastorum labo- ribus, sed etiam pro auditione famæ? quod si est, quis verisimiliter neget, aut Indos illos, quos Par- thia proximos Ruffinus observat, in quam profectum esse Thomam tradunt historiæ, nihil inaudivisse de Christo à vicinis? aut Polonos, Vandalos, Moravos à Germanis? Adde quod S. literæ in varias linguas per orbem notus conversæ sint, unde in universo mundo notitia de Christo hauriri potuit. Non minus enim scriptis, quam vivâ voce prædicare per mundum universum jussi sunt Apostoli. Quo ergo non venit pes Apostolorum, eo venit fama vel Scriptura eorum. Reliqua quæ hic desiderari pos- sunt, petantur ex annotatis ad librum Psalmorum. Repugnant autem tum Calviniani, tum è Papistis quoque Cajetanus, Gentianus, Hervæus, Salmero, Pererius Apostolico scopo, cum universalem asser- tionem restringunt, siquidem Apostolus incredu- lis omnem excusationem adimat assertâ vocatione omnium, & tam universale faciat præconium, quam universaliter sese ad omnes extendit lumen, & calor solis, vi metaphoricæ loquutionis, ut l. c. ex- pedivimus.

## 10:19
V. 19. But I say, did Israel not know?

I now ask you in turn: Can it be said at all that the fame of the Apostles did not reach some Israelites? Paul wishes to say that this clearly cannot be said plausibly. Therefore, the fault lies in them, which was also predicted in a mystical sense by Moses and the Prophets.

It is not a counter-question, because no question preceded it. Nor is any doubt raised about the fame of the Apostles among the Jews. But about the calling and conversion of the Gentiles, could the future occurrence of that, so to speak, have escaped the Israelites? Or should it not have been clear to them from the Holy Scriptures themselves that the Gentiles would be called, and indeed that they would become participants and partners of the grace of GOD in Christ even with the Israelites themselves? This he teaches both from Moses and also from Isaiah. If, however, one prefers to refer this entirely to the knowledge of the Gospel which the Israelites could have had (although the analysis already given is more convenient), he will have Chrysostom not disagreeing: Did Israel not hear the Gospel, did it not know its power and efficacy? i.e., it heard it entirely, it knew it entirely, but by its own stubbornness and obstinacy it does not wish to believe and obey it.

πρῶτος Μωϋσῆς λέγει. Moses, who precedes the other Prophets in time, says this: I will provoke you to jealousy by a no-people, by a foolish nation I will anger you. This is taken from the version of the Seventy elders, Deut. XXXII. 21, except that there it is 'them' twice, where here it is 'you', with the same meaning: for it is clear that it concerns the Israelites; A 'no-people' by way of emphasis, there the Philistines, here all who had bad laws and had been insane about idols. For true wisdom is the knowledge of God, Deut. IV. 6. There God provoked the Israelites to emulation and anger by granting victories to the Philistines: here, however, by giving the gifts of His Spirit to those whom the Israelites believed unworthy of the name of people.

Again, a different meaning of Moses and a different one of the Apostle is imagined: when, on the contrary, the opinion of both ought to be the same, since otherwise four terms would arise in the Apostle's argument, or it could do nothing for the matter: for what is it, that Israelites were once provoked to emulation and anger by the Philistines through the victories of the latter, for the demonstration of the present matter, that the Gentiles have attained righteousness not before the Israelites by adoption, and have become a nation or people of the Lord, which once had not been the people of the Lord? That Moses treats of the provocation of the Israelites to zeal through the conversion of the Gentiles is evident even from this allegation and proof of the Apostle. Compare what was said on that passage.

Latin:

V. 19. Ἀλλὰ λέγω μὴ ἐκ ἔγνω Ἰσραὴλ.

Ego nunc te vicissim interrogo: An omnino dici possit ad aliquos Israëlitas non pervenisse fama de Apostolis. Di- cere vult Paulus id plane probabiliter non dici posse. Ita- que in ipsis hærere culpam, quæ etiam in mystico sensu præ- dicta à Mose & Prophetis.

Non est ἀντερώτημα, quia non præcessit ἐρώτη- μα. Nec de fama de Apostolis penes Judæos du- bium movetur. Sed de vocatione & conversione gen- tium, anne illius futuritio, ut ita dicam, Israëlitas latere potuerit? vel annon ex ipsis S. literis hoc ipsis exploratum esse debuerit, gentes vocatum iri, imo cum ipsis etiam Israëlitis gratiæ DEI in Chri- sto participes & consortes evasuros. Quod cum ex Mose docet, tum etiam ex Esaia. Si tamen omnino ad notitiam Evangelii, quam habere po- tuerant Israëlitæ, hæc referre malit (quamvis tra- dita jam ἀνάλυσις convenientior sit) habiturus est non abnuentem Chrysostomum; Nunquid Israël non audivit Evangelium, nunquid non ejus vim & efficaciam cognovit? q. d. omnino audivit, omnino cognovit, sed suâ pertinacia & obstinatione non vult credere illique obedire.

πρῶτος Μωϋσῆς λέγει. Moses qui cæteros Prophetas tempore præcedit, hoc dicit: ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ' οὐκ ἔθνει, ἐπὶ ἔθνει ἀσυνέτῳ παροργιῶ ὑμᾶς. Sumpta hæc ex versione LXX. senum Deut. XXXII. 21. nisi quod ibi bis αὐτοὺς, ubi hic ὑμᾶς, sensu eodem: appa- ret enim de Israëlitis agi; Gens non gens κατ' ἔξυγμασον, ibi Philistini, hic omnes qui malas habuerunt leges, & cir- ca idola insaniverant. Vera enim sapientia est Dei cogni- tio Deut. IV. 6. Ibi Deus ad æmulationem & iram excita- vit Israelitas, victorias largiendo Philistinis: hic vero dona spiritûs sui dando illis, quos populorum nomine indignos credebant Israëlitæ.

Iterum alia mens Mosis alia Apostoli fingitur: quum contra eandem oporteat esse utriusque sen- tentiam, siquidem alias in argumento Apostoli quatuor termini orituri sint, aut ad rem nihil id facere queat: nam quid hoc, quod à Philistinis olim Israëlita ad æmulationem & iram excitati sint per victorias istorum, ad demonstrationem rei præsentis, quod gentes præ Israëlitis adoptione ne consecutæ sint, & gens vel populus Domini evase- rint, quæ olim non fuerant populus Domini? De provocatione Israëlitarum ad zelum per gentium conversionem Mosen agere vel ex hac Apostoli al- legatione & probatione constat. Confer quæ ad illum locum dicta.

## 10:20
V. 20. But Isaiah is very bold and says) That is, he speaks boldly or freely. Plutarch also uses the verb ἀποτολμᾶν.

I was found by those who did not seek me, I became manifest to those who did not ask for me. In the Greek of Isaiah LXV. 1, in reverse order: I became manifest to those who did not ask for me, I was found by those who did not seek me.

We said at that passage that the LXX interpreters read ודרשתי and that it concerns in the first sense those who were delivered beyond hope in the times of Antiochus. 'To those who did not ask for me', that is, to those not consulting me. But this is very well adapted to so many peoples to whom the Gospel came, when they were thinking nothing of God or the worship of God, which the Apostles often and deservedly proclaim as a huge benefit. This does not differ from that of Philo in the book, That God is unchangeable: 'It often happens that those who seek laboriously fail, while those without care find easily even what they had not thought of.' See also above X. 30.

Latin:

V. 20. Ἡσαΐας δὲ ἀποτολμᾷ καὶ λέγει) Id est, ἀποτολμῶν sive παῤῥησιάζων λέγει. Verbo ἀποτολμᾶν utitur & Plu- tarchus.

εὑρέθην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ζητῦσιν, ἐμφανὴς ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσι. In Græco Esaiæ LXV. 11. ordine inverso: ἐμφανὴς ἐγενόθην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσιν, εὑρέθην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ζητῦσιν.

Diximus ad eũ locũ interpretes LXX. legisse ודרשתי & agi primo sensu de iis qui præter spem liberati sunt An- tiochi temporibus. Ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσι, id est, me non consu- lentibus. Optime autem id aptatur tot populis, quibus advenit Evangelium, cum nihil de Deo, Deive cultu cogi- tarent, quod ingens beneficium sæpe ac merito prædicant Apostoli. Non abludit hic illud Philonis libro, Deum esse immutabilem: συμβαίνει δὲ πολλάκις τοῖς μὲν ἐπικόπως ζη- τῦσιν ἀποτυγχάνειν, τοῖς δ' ἄνευ Φροντίδος ῥᾷτα καὶ ἃ μὴ δι- ενοήθησαν εὑρίσκειν. Vide & supra X. 30.

## 10:21
Πρὸς δὲ τὸν ἰσραὴλ λέγει.) God, of course, which is often understood even in the Prophets. Πρὸς here means 'against'. For GOD accuses Israel, not addressing him, but speaking about him.

“All the day long I have stretched out my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.” These are the very words of the LXX interpreters, although transposed without any loss of sense, following with a few words interposed those very words of Isaiah which we have already had. Moreover, these words refer to those Jews who had followed the party of Antiochus. If such could exist among the Jews then, what wonder if such are found even now? Ἐκπετανύειν is the Hebrew פָּרַשׂ, to call with open arms. Ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα, a people not only disobedient, but also contumaciously opposing commands. For with two words the seventy elders thought it should be translated, סורר, which is translated both by ἀπειθοῦντα and by παραῤῥεοντὰ. And we have said at Luke 11:34 that the word ἀντιλέγειν is used among our writers not only of words, but also of things.

Regarding the phrase ἀποτολμᾷ καὶ λέγει, let the emphasis be noted, that it is CONFIDENTLY he says: because the Hebrews are accustomed to place a verb in the place of adverbs, Psalm 102:3, Gen. 25:1, 5, 30:31, Job 10:16. Concerning this oracle, which Grotius perverts both as to the reading and as to the sense, we have already acted sufficiently in the Annotations on Isaiah. Those things are not only applied to the Gentiles and Israelites in the New Testament by the Apostle; but they were predicted concerning them by the Prophet. For it cannot be shown by any proof that they look to the times of Antiochus. And the proof of the Apostle ought to be consistent with itself, who [shows] that the conversion of the Gentiles brought about by the Apostles had been predicted long ago by Isaiah, and also the very disobedience and incredulity of the Israelites: that He was found by those not seeking or inquiring for Him, and without any merit of their own, or course and labor, He manifested Himself, but to this people He stretched out the hand of grace in vain for the whole day, as being incredulous and refractory. so that the Israelites, when they do not obtain salvation, have themselves to blame, because they did not apprehend the grace of God exhibited in Christ, but remained in unbelief and ἀντιλογίᾳ or contradiction; that, for example, the Gentiles enjoy salvation, they ought to attribute not to their own merits or works, but solely to the grace of GOD, who out of grace called them, converted them, and adopted them into his own people, since the Lord manifested himself to those not seeking him, and was thus found by them, and apprehended by true faith, outside of which grace of GOD they were an ἀσύνετον ἔθνος, a foolish nation destitute of the knowledge of the true GOD, in whom σύνεσις and true wisdom consist. In which manner it remains again that justification is purely gratuitous and happens solely through faith in Christ, which appears no less in the Gentiles than in the Israelites, according to the oracles of the Scriptures, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι. Moreover, God is said metaphorically or figuratively to have stretched out his hands, i.e., to have voluntarily and liberally offered his grace. For thus are those accustomed to act who wish to promptly testify to their benevolence, so that they might, as it were, invite and entice with their very hands. 2. A note of time is added, All the day, that is, for a very long time. There is a most sweet type in this metaphor, not unlike that which is held in Matt. XXIII. 37 and Luke XIII. 34. As there is nothing more effective than this for consoling fearful minds, so there is nothing more powerful for destroying that dogma of impiety concerning an absolute decree of damnation and reprobation. For either the Jews had not been created and destined by GOD for damnation; or that stretching out of hands was a mockery: But it is impious to think this. The truth of the former, therefore, will by no means be able to be obscure; so that we may explain this in the words of our blessed Mylius: whom, speaking ἀυτοφώνως, we bring forward again and again on purpose.

SUBSECTION III. Exhibiting faith as the organic cause of justification, with the opposed unbelief, with respect to the Jews as well as the Gentiles.

Concerning the organic cause on the part of GOD, and the hand of GOD offering and giving, or divine grace by the word of the Gospel, the Apostle has already spoken, when he expounded the evangelical righteousness, which is learned only by the revelation of GOD: Now he asserts primarily the organic cause on our part, namely, saving faith, as our hand apprehending the gift of GOD, which is offered to us through the word of the Gospel, and that with a view to both the Jews and the Gentiles.

Latin:

Πρὸς δὲ τὸν ἰσραὴλ λέγει.) Deus scilicet, quod sæpe et- iam in Prophetis subauditur. Πρὸς hic valet adversus. Israë- lem enim accusat DEUS, non eum alloquens, sed de eo loquens.

Ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν ἐξεπέτασα τὰς χεῖράς με πρὸς λαὸν ἀπει- θοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα.) Sunt ipsa verba, quanquam sine ul- lo sensus detrimento transposita, LXX. interpretum, se- quentia paucis vocibus interpositis illa ipsa Esaiæ quæ jam habuimus. Respiciunt autem hæc illos Judæos, qui Antio- chi partes erant secuti. Si tunc tales esse potuêre in Judæis, quid mirum si & nunc tales inveniãtur? Ἐκπετανύειν כרש est obviis ulnis advocare. Ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα, po- pulum non modo obedientem, sed & contumaciter se opponentem jussis. Duobus enim verbis LXX. senes ver- tendum putavêre סורר quod & per ἀπειθοῦντα & per πα- ραῤῥεοντὰ vertitur. Et vocem ἀντιλέγειν apud nostros non de verbis tantum, sed & de rebus usurpari diximus ad Lu- cam 11. 34.

Circa phrasin ἀποβολμᾷ καὶ λέγει notetur empha- sis, quod sit CONFIDENTER plane dicit: quia ver- bum adverbiorum loco ponere solent Ebræi Psal. CII. 3. Gen. XXV. 1. 5. XXX. 31. Job. X. 16. De hoc oraculo, quod & quantum ad lectionem, & quoad sensum pervertit Grotjus, actum jam affatim in Annot. ad Esaiam. Non aptantur tantum illa gen- tibus & Israëlitis in N. T. ab Apostolo; sed prædi- cta de illis sunt à Propheta. Nam ad tempora An- tiochi ea spectare nullo documento ostendi po- test. Et constare sibi debet probatio Apostoli, qui gentium conversionem per Apostolos factam ab Esaia jam olim prædictam esse, ipsamq; etiam Isra- ëlitarum ἀπειθείαν & incredulitatem: quod ab il- lis non quærentibus vel requirentibus invẽtus sit, ac sine ipsorum merito, vel cursu & labore, sese mani- festarit, ad hoc vero frustrà per totũ diem manum gratiæ extenderit, utpote incredulos & refractarios ut ita Israëlitæ, cum salute non potiuntur, sibi im- putare habeant, quod nempe gratiam Dei in Chri- sto exhibitam non apprehenderint, sed in incredu- litate & ἀντιλογίᾳ vel contradictione permanse- rint; quod v. gentes fruantur salute, non suis me- ritis aut operibus, sed unice gratiæ DEI acceptum ferre debeant, qui ex gratia eos vocavit, conver- tit, & in populum suum adoptavit, cum iis non quærentibus Dominum, Dominus sese manifesta- rit, adeoq; ab iisdem inventus, ac verâ fide appre- hensus fuerit, extra quam DEI gratiam fuêre ἀσύ- νετον ἔθνος gens stulta destituta cognitione veri DEI, in qua σύνεσις ac vera sapientia consistit. Quo pa- cto iterum manet, justificationem esse mere gratui- tam fierique unice per fidem in Christum, quod in gentibus non minus apparet, quam in Israëlitis, juxta Scripturarum oracula, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι. Di- citur autem Deus μεταφορικῶς ἡ ὑποτυπωτικῶς expandisse manus suas, i. e. ultro gratiam suam large obtulisse. Sic enim solent facere, qui prompte be- nevolentiam suam testari volunt, ut manibus ipsis invitent quasi atque alliciant. 2. Temporis nota ad- ditur, Tota die, id est, longissimo tempore. Suavis- simus in hac metaphora typus inest, haud dissimilis illi, qui Matth. XXIII. 37. & Luc. XIII. 34. habe- tur. Quo ut nihil est ad consolandas pavidas men- tes efficacius: ita validius nihil ad profligandum il- lud impietatis dogma, de absoluto damnationis & re- probationis decreto. Nam aut ad damnationem conditi & destinati Judæi à DEO non fuerant; aut lusus fuit ista manuum expansio : At hoc impium est cogitare. Prioris ergo veritas obscura esse nullo modo poterit; ut hæc verbis B. Mylii nostri expli- cemus: quem ἀυτοφώνως loquentem data operâ iterum iterumque adducimus.

SUBSECTIO III. Fidem ceu causam organicam justificationis, cum op- positâ incredulitate respectu Judæorum æque ac gentium, exhibens.

De causa organica ex parte DEI, & manû DEI offerentis & dantis, vel gratia divi- na verbo Evangelii jam dixit Apostolus, cum justitiam Evangelicam, quæ non nisi revelatione DEI discitur, exposuit: Jam causam organicam ex parte nostri im- primis adserit, fidem nempe salvificam, ceu manum nostram donum DEI appre- hendentem, quod per verbum Evange- lii nobis offertur, idque intuitû tum Ju- dæorum, tum gentium.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle teaches that the Israelites were not rejected from salvation, whose faith God foresaw, and that God even now preserves a remnant for himself, as in the time of Elijah, not indeed out of the merit of works, but out of grace, namely those who are not hardened: and that the fall of the Israelites is indeed the salvation of the Gentiles, but that the Israelites are provoked by it out of the intention of GOD to a good emulation: and that their ἀποβολή (rejection) is not in itself the reconciliation of the rest of the world. But for the rest, on account of the firstfruits and the holy root, the mass and the branches also have their own holiness, by virtue of the covenant initiated with the Fathers, and that the branches of the olive tree can in turn be grafted in, and therefore the Gentiles ought not to boast, since they were broken off because of unbelief, while they themselves stand through faith, and therefore they ought to humbly acknowledge not only the severity of GOD toward the Israelites, but also his goodness toward themselves; since very many of the Israelites are to be saved, to whom the Redeemer was peculiarly promised, and the covenant of grace concerning the remission of sins was given, whence there is still some ἐκλογὴ (election) of them, whose Fathers the Lord specially adopted, knowing not how to repent; In summary, that the cause of the destruction of the Jews resides in unbelief, as that of the calling of the Gentiles resides in the mercy of the Lord; for GOD has concluded all under unbelief by the voice of the law, so that he might have mercy on all according to the doctrine of the Gospel: therefore, the inexhaustible riches of the mercy and Wisdom of GOD are to be acknowledged here, the latter, because no one can penetrate the mind and counsels of the Lord in the economy of salvation; the former, because no one is able to merit grace, and to him alone all glory is due, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things, both in general and especially in the matter of salvation.

There are four parts (I.) The Didactic, which is about the Israelites not being rejected out of an absolute good pleasure, but in part saved on account of foreseen faith, out of grace, while the others are hardened on account of unbelief, up to verse 10. (II.) The Apologetic-exhortatory, which contains an apology for the grace of GOD, that it was not by force of an absolute purpose and decree of his own that the Israelites fell, but that rather their ruin happened by their own fault, while salvation indeed came to the Gentiles out of grace, so that they themselves might be provoked to emulation, since on account of the holy root not all hope is cut off for the branches, but that they can be grafted in again, having been cut off through unbelief, provided they do not persevere in the same: and that the Gentiles stand or remain grafted in out of grace through faith, otherwise they are to be cut off: Then an exhortation directed to the Gentiles, that they should not be proud, but having acknowledged both the wrath and the grace of GOD, they should adhere to grace through faith, lest they be cut off, up to verse 24. (III.) The Demonstrative, concerning the Israelites being saved in great part, by virtue of the promise of Isaiah concerning the Redeemer from Zion, and the covenant of grace concerning the remission of sins, as well as the calling of the Patriarchs; of whom, although many do not believe, not a few are yet to believe, and through faith in the grace of GOD are to obtain mercy together with the Gentiles, up to verse 31. (IV.) The Conclusive, by which all things hitherto treated in this article concerning justification are summarized, that all things were concluded under unbelief through the law, which the Apostle had taught concerning the Subject, so that God might have mercy on all in Christ, by virtue of the doctrine of the Gospel, which he had expounded concerning the mode and means of justification and salvation: and from there the Apostle admires the riches of both the mercy and the Wisdom of GOD, and attributes glory to him.

PART I. CHAPTER XI. DIDACTIC. Concerning the Israelites to be saved in part on account of foreseen faith, the others being hardened through unbelief.

V. 1. Λέγω ἆν.

I say therefore, namely to that objection which will now be rehearsed.

There is no objection here: but as is evident from the analysis already delivered, it is a fuller explanation and confirmation of the proposed theme, especially as regards faith exhibited in the grace of God in Christ, as the sole medium of salvation on our part, from a comparison of the salvation of the Jews to be saved in a remnant and of the Gentiles grafted in through the excision of the former.

μὴ ἀπώσατο ὁ Θεὸς τὸν λαὸν ἀυτᾶ.

In the manuscript here, no less than below, is added, ὃν προέγνω. Which I think is correct. And thus it appears that Origen, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and other Greeks read it: so that it is the best antithesis of the words προέγνω and ἀπώσατο. For προέγνω in Hebrew idiom is 'he previously approved': concerning which idiom we spoke above VIII. 29. But ἀπώσατο corresponds to its contrary in the Hebrew געל, רחק, נטש, מאס זנח, ורף, דחה, all of which are used in the sense of contempt, but most of them in their primitive force signify to remove from oneself, to drive away, to cast off, and they have been deflected to that other meaning because we are accustomed to remove from our sight those things which we loathe. Therefore, he whom Paul answers in the dispute asks whether Paul means this, that the same people previously loved by God are now despised by Him. Why so variously? Not much differently than Gideon in Judges VI. 13. μήτεχὶ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐξήγαγεν ἡμᾶς κύριος, καὶ νῦν ἐξέῤῥιψεν ἡμᾶς; Paul, about to answer, first in his usual manner rejects this statement.

May it not be. Far be that.

For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.

As if he were to say, if I were to say this, that all Israelites without exception were hateful to GOD, then I myself would be without any hope of salvation and would be suffering so much in vain. For I myself am not only sprung from Abraham, but also from Israel, namely through Benjamin. He explains his origin specifically, so that there may be less doubt about it. See Philipp. III. 5.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Docet Apostolus nec Israëlitas reprobatos esse à salute, quorum fidem prævidit Deus, & reliquias sibi, ut tempo- re Eliæ, etiamnum servare Deum, non quidem ex ope- rum merito, sed ex gratia, eos scil. qui non indurati sunt: & casum quidem Israëlitarum salutem esse gentium, sed eâ provocari ex intentione DEI Israëlitas ad bonam æmu- lationem: nec per se illorum ἀποβολὴν esse mundi reliqui reconciliationem. De cætero vero ob primitias & radicem sanctam, massam & ramos suam etiam habere sanctita- tem, vi fœderis cum Patribus initi, & inseri vicissim posse ramos oleæ, ideoque gloriandum non esse gentibus, quum illi defracti sint propter incredulitatem, ipsi vero stent per fidem, ac proinde non modo severitatem DEI erga Israë- litas, sed etiam bonitatem erga se humiliter agnoscere de- beant; siquidem plurimi ex Israëlitis omnino salvandi sint, quibus peculiariter Redemptor promissus est, & fœ- dus gratiæ de remissione peccatorum datum, unde adhuc aliqua ἐκλογὴ eorum est, quorum Patres specialiter ado- ptavit Dominus pœnitere nescius; Summatim causam exitii Judæorum residere in incredulitate, uti vocationis gentium in misericordia Domini; conclusisse enim DEUM omnes sub incredulitate voce legis, ut omnium secun- dum doctrinam Evangelii misereretur: ideo inexhaustas hic agnoscendas esse divitias misericordiæ, & Sapientiæ DEI, hujus, quia nemo mentem & consilia Domini in œco- nomia salutis penetrare potest; illius, quia nemo gratiam mereri valet, ipsique uni omnis gloria debetur, à quo, per quem, & in quo sunt omnia, tum in universum tum impri- mis in salutis negotio.

Partes quatuor sunt (I.) Διδακτικὴ est de Israë- litis non ex absoluto beneplacito reprobatis, sed ex parte ob prævisam fidem, ex gratia servatis, cæte- ris ob incredulitatem induratis, usque ad v. 10. (II.) Ἀπολογητικο-παραινετικὴ, quâ tum apologia continetur, pro gratia DEI, quod non vi abso- luti propositi & decreti sui effecerit, ut ruerent Israëlitæ, sed quod potius ruina ipsorum culpâ facta, salus vero ex gratia gentibus ideo etiam ob- tigerit, ut ipsi ad æmulationem provocentur, si- quidem ob radicem sanctam ramis non decollet omnis spes, quin inseri possint vicissim per incre- dulitatem excisi, modo non perseverent in eadem: quodque gentiles ex gratia insiti per fidem stent, vel maneant insiti, alioquin exscindendi: Tum parænesis ad gentiles directa, ne superbient, sed a- gnita DEI & irâ, & gratiâ per fidem adhæreant gratiæ, ne exscindantur, usque ad vers. 24. (III.) ἀποδεικτικὴ de Israëlitis magnam partem salvandis, vi promissionis Esaiæ de Redemptore è Zion, & fœ- deris gratiæ de remissione peccatorum, nec non vocationis Patriarcharum; quorum etsi multi non credant, non pauci tamen adhuc credituri, & per fidem in gratiam DEI una cum gentibus miseri- cordiam consecuturi sint, usque ad v. 31. (IV.) Συμπερασματικὴ, quâ summatim omnia in hoc articulo de justificatione hactenus pertractato com- prehenduntur, quod per legem omnia conclusa sint sub incredulitatem, quod circa Subjectum do- cuerat Apostolus, ut omnium Deus misereretur in Christo, vi doctrinæ Evangelii, quod circa mo- dum & media justificationis & salutis exposuit: atque inde admiratur Apostolus divitias tum mi- sericordiæ DEI, tum Sapientiæ, eique gloriam tribuit.

PARS I. CAPITIS XI. DIDACTICA. De Israëlitis ex parte ob prævisam fidem ser- vandis, cæteris per incredulitatem induratis.

V. 1. Λέγω ἆν.

Dico igitur, nempe ad eam, quæ jam retitabitur, obje- ctionem.

Nulla hic objectio: sed ut ex analysi jam tradi- tâ patet, thematis propositi, quantum imprimis ad fidem in gratiam DEI in Christo exhibitam, ceu salutis medium ex parte nostri unicum, ube- rior è συγκρίσει salutis Judæorum in reliquiis sal- vandorum & gentilium per istorum excisionem insitarum explicatio & confirmatio.

μὴ ἀπώσατο ὁ Θεὸς τὸν λαὸν ἀυτᾶ.

In manuscripto hic non minus quam infra additur, ὃν προέγνω. quod rectum puto. Et ita apparet legisse Ori- genem, Chrysostomum, Oecumenium & Græcos alios: ut optimum sit ἀντίθετον verborum προέγνω & ἀπώσατο. Nam προέγνω Hebræâ locutione est prius approbavit: de qua locutione diximus supra IIX. 29. ἀπώσατο vero ei contrarium respondet Hebræis געל, רחק, נטש, מאס זנח, ורף, דחה, quæ omnia in despectus significatu usurpantur, pleraque autem primitiva vi significant à se removere, depellere, abjicere, ad alterum autem illum significatum ideo deflexa sunt, quod, quæ aversamur, ea à conspectu nostro solemus amovere. Quærit ergo is, cui Paulus disputanti respondet, an hoc velit Paulus, eun- dem populum prius amatum à DEO nunc ab eo despici. Quo tam varie? Non multo aliter Gedeon Judicum VI. 13. μήτεχὶ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐξήγαγεν ἡμᾶς κύριος, καὶ νῦν ἐξέῤῥιψεν ἡμᾶς; Responsurus Paulus primum more suo aversatur hoc dictum.

μὴ γένοιτο. Longe id absit. Non dereliquit Deus populum suum,

καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ Ἰσραηλίτης εἰμὶ ἐκ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ φυλῆς Βενιαμίν.

Quasi dicat, si hoc dicerem, omnes omninò Israelitas DEO exosõs, jam & ego sine ulla spe salutis essem & fru- stra tanta perpeterer. Sum enim & ego non tantum ex Abrahamo ortus, sed & ex Israele, nempe per Benjami- num. Designate originem suam explicat, quo minus de ea dubitetur. Vide Philipp. III. 5.

## 11:2
V. 2. God has not cast away his people whom he foreknew.

He answers the objection with an open negation. GOD never loved the whole people sprung from Israel in such a way that he led them all to true justice and the salvation that accompanies it, but only some. Therefore, those whom he approved in this and those whom he now despises are not the same or entirely equal. That some were rejected by GOD was nothing new. See Deut. XXIX. 28, where in the Greek it is ἐξέβαλον ἀὐτός.

The received text is rashly called into suspicion of corruption, as the reading of the Greeks undoubtedly arose from the second verse. However, one codex cannot prejudice all the others. The sense is: that GOD did not cast away his people simply: both because he did not cast away the whole, and because he did not do so out of mere good pleasure; but whom he did not cast away and how, is explained in verse 2. The Apostle proves the former, that he did not cast away all, by his own example: he explains the latter, whom he did not reprobate, in v. 2. Nor is that προέγνω rightly taken by Grotius. For it is not, he approved beforehand, but he foreknew: nor is it used in that sense in Rom. VIII. 29. It is not an approval of piety, but a foreknowledge of faith that is designated by the Apostle. For election is made from foreknown faith, 1. Petr. I. 2, 2. Thess. II. 13. Therefore GOD did not reprobate those whose faith he himself foreknew in the Israelite people. But what does it have to do with this, that the Lord did not despise his people whom he previously approved? or that those whom he approved and those whom he now despises are not the same? For there could be no doubt about that, that the Jewish people were once approved by GOD, and that this people is different from that one: but the Apostle is discussing how, and for what cause, God now reprobates or casts away his people. For Paul belonged to that people, as far as the kinship of blood is concerned, and he deals with those brothers of his according to the flesh, whom he lamented above as cast away: teaching that they were not cast away out of mere hatred by GOD, nor were they all reprobated, for he did not cast away those whom he foreknew would believe, but only the incredulous and hardened. For God knows his own, 2. Timoth. II. 9. Therefore he says that the whole people was not cast away, because he foreknew the same, that is, because he both knows now who believe, and knows who will one day believe in Christ, who are never to be reckoned among the cast away, even if he seems to have cast away almost the whole people. Which he illustrates with a similar example, how in the time of Elijah, when the Prophet believed that he alone survived among the true worshippers of GOD, the Lord kept for himself seven thousand of the faithful in secret, applying that to the present matter. Therefore, the foreknown people, the people not rejected, saying the Author of the book on the calling of the Gentiles, book 1, ch. 10, these are they who are justified in Christ; and what seems to be said of all Israel is shown only in those whom grace and Election made the rest. Therefore Chrysostom and the Greek scholia on this passage: ἐκ ἀπώθητε ἀπὸ Θεῦ, ἀλλ’ ἑαυ- τὺς ἀπωθεῖτε. You are not rejected by GOD, but you reject yourselves. The LXX express the word געל with this verb ἀπωθεῖν, which is to remove with disgust and nausea. See Ezech. XVI. 5, 44, 45. They also express the word מאס in this way, to cast away something with a certain disgust as abominable. Jer. VII. 29, Amos II. 4, ch. V. 21, as נטש and פרע to abandon, to strip bare. The Jews are said to ἀπωθεῖσθαι λόγον, to turn away from, to reject the Gospel, Act. XIII. 46, ch. VII. 37. Therefore they themselves were not cast away out of simple hatred, but because they rejected and reprobated the Gospel of God.

Or do you not know what the Scripture says in Elijah? That is, in that part of the book of Kings, which, because it contained the affairs of Elijah, is therefore called by his name by metonymy.

as he makes intercession to God against Israel. λέγων is absent in the Manuscript. Well: for just as ἐντυγχάνειν ὑπέρ τινος is to commend the business of someone, so ἐντυγχάνειν κατά τινος is to accuse someone. See 1. Macc. VIII. 32, X. 61, 63, 64, XI. 21.
