Abjectionem Israelis, mollibus usus vocabulis, lapsum & diminu- tionem appellat : plenitudinem ejusdem, vocat con- versionem locupletem, qua non sigillatim, sed grega- tim quasi convertantur Judæi, sive pridem facta illa fuiffet; sive deinceps etiam quandocunque tandem futura sit. Si præteritum tempus sumatur, id in- nuit Apostolus, si credidissent maximè Judæi, id sa- lutem gentilium minimè impediturum fuisse. Præ- dicatio enim Evangelii nihilominus dimanaffet ad gentiles, idque majori etiam cum fructu, si gentiles id etiam à gente Judæa, unde id profectum erat, com- muniter fuisse receptum conspexissent. Si futurum sumatur, solennis & luculenta populi Israelitici fu- tura esse conversio ab Apostolo significatur. Hæc B. Mylius: qui futurum quidem sumi; sed nos præ- teritum potius respici deinde docebimus. Quo pacto etiam B. Hunnius: Verum hic potuisset objici: si igitur ex lapsu Judæorum ditati sunt gentiles, se- quitur, ut, si stetissent in fide Judæi, gentiles non fuerint ad consortium fidei admittendi. Respondet Apostolus per inversionem: Si lapsus fuit occasio vo- cationis gentium; multo magis plenitudinem Judæo- rum inservituram fuisse conversioni gentium. Expli- cant illa se mutuò, παράπτωμα αὐτῶν & ἥττημα αὐτῶν, uti πλῦτος κόσμα & πλῦτος ἐθνῶν : non paucitas credentium è populo Israelitico, salus fuit gentium : sed diminutio vel abjectio, quà ob παρά- πτωμα capitis diminutionem, & honoris sui, qui fuerant populus DEI gloriosus, ἥττημα passi sunt. Diminutionem enim ἥττημα propriè & ex commu- ni usu importat, non verò paucitatem. Et culpæ adjungenda erat pœna. Neque jam de credenti- bus, sed de incredulis, non de reliquiis salvando- rum, sed de multitudine pereuntium Israelitarum sermo est. Adeoque de præterito potius accipi- mus, quam de futuro, de eo, quod contingere po- tuisset, non de eo, quod continget. Addimus de voce ἥττημα, quæ hîc B. Wellerus noster habet p. 629. Ipsum verò ἥττημα ab ἡττᾶσθαι deductum, mi- litare est. Sunt enim νίκη καὶ ἥττη ἀντισρέφοντα, ac ut illud victoriam, sic hoc cladem significat, & ea, quæ ex clade prævenire solent, 2. Pet. II. 19. 20. hinc vocabulum מס quod LXX. per ἥττημα reddidère Esa. XXXI. 8. B. Luth. in vernacula: und deine junge Mannschafft wird zinßbar werden. Est igi- tur ἥττημα ἰυδαίων defectus seu accubitus Judæorum, qui in spirituali pugna victi à Diabolo, & propriâ malitiâ succumbentes, omnem DEI gloriam & gra- tiam perdiderunt, & hanc Ethnicis gaudentibus tot spoliis Esa. IX. 41. reliquerunt.

## 11:13
V. 13. For I say to you the Gentiles.

Since he had said many things thus far to refute the unbelieving Jews, and to confirm those who had believed, Paul now turns his discourse to the Christians gathered from the Gentiles especially by his own labor, and warns them, lest on account of the gifts received from GOD, they should live too securely, or despise the Jews as utterly lost, or hold them in hatred.

Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles. From Christ's designation Acts IX. 15. and the revelation of the Holy Spirit made to the Church Acts XIII. 2. which Peter himself acknowledged, Gal. II. 7. not that Paul did not also go to the synagogues, and indeed always in the first place, nor that Peter did not, as with Cornelius, convert other foreigners, but that Peter betook himself especially to those places in which there were very many Jews, conversely Paul where there were very many foreigners.

I glorify my ministry. I then declare the happiness of my work, when I say that many have been converted from the Gentiles. He soothes their minds, just as he had done above in chapters IX and X concerning the Jews, so that they would not take too harshly what he was about to subjoin.

So also Flacius in his gloss: The apostrophe is directed specifically to the Gentiles, by which he wins their confidence in what he says, affirming that he ought not to be suspected by them, as if he attributed too much to the Jews, since he rather desires to extol the Gentile church and the preaching done to them, as being their own proper Apostle: which, however, he does not do out of hatred for the Jews, but with a good intention of provoking the Jews to emulation and imitation, as they hear of the piety, zeal, and glorious ministry of the Gentiles.

Latin:

V. 13. ἡμῖν γὰρ λέγω τοῖς ἔθνεσιν.

Cum multa hactenus dixiffet ad refutandos Judæos in- credulos, & ad confirmandos, qui crediderant, nunc ad Chri- stianos ex gentibus sua potissimum opera collectos Paulus sermonem vertit, eosque monet, ne propter dona à DEO accepta, nimis aut securi viverent, aut Judæos ut planè deploratos contemnerent, odiove haberent.

ἐφ’ ὅσον μέν εἰμι ἐγὼ ἐθνῶν ἀπόσολος. Ex Christi destinatione Act. IX. 15. & revelatione Spiri- tus Sancti facta Ecclesiæ Act. IX. 2. quod Petrus ipse agno- vit, Gal. II. 7. non quod non & Paulus synagogas, & quidem primo semper loco adierit, nec quod, non Petrus, ut Cor- nelium, ita alios alienigenas converterit, sed quod Petrus præcipuè in ea se loca conferebat, in quibus plurimi erant Judæi, contrà Paulus ubi plurimi alienigenæ.

τὴν διακονίαν με δοξάζω. Meæ tunc operæ felicitatem prædico, cum dico multos esse ex gentibus conversos. Ita præmulcet animos, ut & supra fecerat capitibus IX. & X. circa Judæos, ne durius ac- ciperentur, quæ erat subjuncturus.

Sic etiam Flacius in glossa: Apostrophe est spe- cialiter ad gentiles directa, qua sibi fidem conciliat in iis, quæ dicit, affirmans, se non debere illis esse su- spectum, tanquam nimium quid Judæis tribuat, cum ille potius gentilem ecclesiam & prædicationem illis factam extollere cupiat, utpote eorum proprius A- postolus: quod tamen ipsum non odio Judæorum faciat, sed bono studio ad æmulationem imitatio- nemque provocandi Judæos, audientes gentilium pie- tatem, zelum & gloriosum ministerium.

## 11:14
V. 14. If I may provoke to jealousy my flesh and save some of them. That I speak of so great a multitude of Gentiles converted, I do this among other things, so that I may provoke the Jews to imitation, which is to bring salvation to the Jews themselves. See above II. He calls his flesh those joined to him by birth of blood: above IX. 3. in a Hebrew idiom, which you have in Gen. XXIX. 14, XXXVII. 26. ἵπως is that of one not despairing.

Latin:

V. 14. εἴπω παραζηλώσω με τὴν σάρκα καὶ σώσω τινὰς ἑξ αὐτῶν. Quod de tanta multitudine Gentium conversa loquor, id inter alia facio, ut Judæos ad imitationem provocem, quæ ipsis Judæis salutem sit paritura. Vide supra II. Car- nem suam vocat junctos sibi ortu sanguinis: supra IX. 3. locutione Hebræa, quam habes Gen. XXIX. 14. XXXVII. 26. ἵπως est non desperantis.

## 11:15
V. 15. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world. ἀποβολὴ from ἀποβάλλειν, which is the same as ἀπωθεῖν, which we had just now in verse 1, and with ἐκβάλλειν, which is in Deut. XXIX. 28. God had cast off the Jews, who had despised the Gospel; on that occasion the world, that is, very many from the Gentiles, have been reconciled to GOD, that is, have obtained a certain special friendship of GOD, have become the people of GOD, 2 Cor. V. 19, 20. For they saw the Gospel, which the Jews were opposing with such hatred, proven from the scriptures of the Jews. There are many degrees of divine καταλλαγῆς, as also of remission, to be distinguished according to the subject matter.

What is the receiving if not life from the dead? Πρόσληψις is the opposite of τῇ ἀποβολῇ. Προσλαμβάνειν from which comes πρόσληψις. הקריב in its primary meaning is to make near to oneself: thence by translation to take into one's protection, just as GOD receives those who believe the Gospel. He speaks, however, of the assumption of a great multitude of Jews.

If not life from the dead. That is, the highest joy; for the Hebrews, just as they call sadness by the name of death, so they call joy by the name of life. He means this: since this joy is to be so great, sustain the Jews patiently, just as GOD sustains them, and pray to GOD earnestly for them, and do not despise them.

These things are more correctly explained by our blessed Hunnius: If the rejection of the Jews is the reconciliation of the world, that is, a certain occasion for reconciliation and for calling the Gentiles (for the Ishmaelites were one people, but the nations alien to the Israelites constituted the rest of the world, whence Paul testifies that the Gospel was announced in the whole world, Col. I. 23), how much more should the assumption of the Jews be considered the reconciliation of the world. For certainly the Gentiles could rather have been offended by the example of the unbelief of the Jews, so that they themselves would not receive that Messiah whom the Jews, as the proper people of the Messiah, were so greatly repudiating. On the contrary, if the Jews had believed, by this very example the Gentiles could have been much more enticed and invited, so that the assumption of the Jews would have been salutary to the Gentiles, and life from the dead, in that not only the Jews, but by the example of the Jews, the Gentiles also would have been transferred from the kingdom of darkness and death into life. Πρόσληψις is assumption, adjunction, πρόσκλισις, coaptation: and it is opposed to τῇ ἀποβολῇ, rejection: but the reconciliation of the world is explained or illustrated and amplified by life from the dead, because that reconciliation is understood, by which those who were dead in sins obtain life and are made alive, as the Apostle teaches concerning the Gentiles in Eph. 2:1, 5, that they were dead in sins and made alive in Christ: of which reconciliation the Apostles were ministers, 2 Cor. 5:18. Since, therefore, the reconciliation of the world happened on the occasion of the rejection (τῆς ἀποβολῆς) of the Israelites, why should not the reconciliation (καταλλαγὴ) have come to the world through the reception (πρόσληψιν) or assumption of the unbelieving Jews? Indeed, what is the reception (τίς ἡ πρόσληψις) if not life from the dead (ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν)? What else would that assumption be, if not a joyful vivification of the world? Although, however, the reconciliation and life from the dead are to be understood not separately, but jointly with respect to both Jews and Gentiles, because to both, insofar as they believed, reconciliation with God and vivification occurred; and both remained under the wrath of God and in death outside of faith in Christ, who alone is our propitiation and our life; yet the reconciliation is peculiarly adapted to the Gentiles, as those who were outside the covenant, 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers from the covenants of promise, and without God in the world,' Eph. 2:12. To the Jews, however, life is adapted, both because the Jews seemed to themselves to live most of all, and to have eternal life in the Scriptures, John 5:39, to whom, however, Christ says in John 8:24, 'unless you believe that I am he (what I have told you), you will die in your sins'; and because by the assumption of the Jews the whole world could seem to revive, after reconciliation and life had already come to the Gentiles. Philipp. part 4. Oper. in his commentary on this passage has it thus: He attaches the consequence thus: Your ruin profited the Gentiles, but not simply the ruin, but much more your fullness, that is, the safe part that was to believe, which was to be provoked by the example of the Gentiles; therefore, the rest among the Jews are to be converted. This remaining part he calls the fullness, that is, the complement of the entire Church to be converted from the seed of Abraham; thus also afterwards an amplification is added: if the rejection of the Jews profited, how glorious will be the restoration, which is to be as a resurrection from the dead. He signifies, therefore, that the remaining greater part was rejected because it was bewitched by the persuasion that they were the people of God and the Church on account of their race, the Law, ceremonies, and merit; nor did they understand the Church to be anything other than this Jewish polity. But now these who are received will learn that the polity is one thing, the Church another; the promise of bodily goods one thing, the promise of grace and eternal life another. They will teach the whole Church, Gentiles and Jews, as if they were dead, that righteousness and eternal life are rendered on account of the Messiah, and through him, not on account of the law or the merits of men.

Latin:

V.15. εἰ γὰρ ἀποβολὴ αὐτῶν καταλλαγὴ κόσμε. ἀποβολὴ ab ἀποβάλλειν quod idem cum ἀπωθεῖν, quod ha- buimus modo commate 1. & cum ἐκβάλλειν quod est Deut. XXIX. 28. despexerat Deus Judæos, qui Evangelium con- tempserant, ea occasione mundus, id est, plurimi ex gen- tibus, DEO sunt reconciliati, id est, specialem quandam DEI amicitiam adepti, facti sunt DEI populus, 2. Cor. V. 19. 20. videbant enim ex scripturis Judæorum probatum Evangelium, quod Judæi tanto odio oppugnabant. Multi sunt gradus divinæ καταλλαγῆς, ut & remissionis, distin- guendæ pro materia.

τίς ἡ πρόσληψις εἰ μὴ ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν. Πρόσληψις contrarium est τῇ ἀποβολῇ. Προσλαμβάνειν unde πρόσληψις. הקריב primo significatu est propinquum sibi facere: inde per translationem in tutelam suam reci- pere, sicut DEUS suscipit credentes Evangelio. Loquitur autem de assumptione magnæ Judæorum multitudinis.

εἰ μὴ ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν. Id est, summum gaudium; Nam Hebræi sicut tristitiam mortis, ita gaudium vitæ nomine appellant. Hoc vult: cum tantum futurum sit hoc gaudium, sustinete Judæos pa- tienter, sicut DEUS eos sustinet, & serio DEUM pro eis orate, neque eos contemnite.

Rectius hæc à B. Hunnio nostro explicantur: Si rejectio Judæorum est reconciliatio mundi, id est, occasio quædam reconciliationis & vocanda- rum gentium, (nam Ismælitæ unus erant populus, gentes verò alienæ ab Israëlitis mundum reliquum e universum constituebant, unde in mundo toto Ev- angelium annunciatum esse Paulus testatur Coloff. Col. I. 23. I. 23.) quantò magis assumti Judæorum reconci- liatio mundi habenda. Nam certe gentiles potius offendi potuissent exemplo incredulitatis Judæorum, ut nec ipsi reciperent eum Messiam, quem Judæi tanquam proprius Messiæ populus tantopere repu- diarent. Econtra si Judæi credidissent; hoc ipso exemplo multo magis allici & invitari potuissent gentiles, ita ut assumptio Judæorum gentibus falu- taris fuerit futura, & vitæ ex mortuis, quæ nonnisi tantùm Judæi, sed Judæorum exemplo etiam gentes ex regno tenebrarum & mortis in vitam fuissent translatæ. Πρόσληψις est assumptio, adjunctio, πρόσκλισις, coaptatio: & opponitur τῇ ἀποβολῇ rejectioni: Κα- ταλλαγὴ verò κόσμυ explicatur vel illustratur & amplificatur per ζωὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν, quod ea re- conciliatio intelligatur, quâ qui in peccatis- mortui sunt: vitam consequuntur & vivificantur ut de gentibus Apostolus Eph. II. 1. 5. docet, eos in peccatis mortuos, in Christo vivificatos esse: cu- jus reconciliationis ministri fuere Apostoli 2. Cor. V. 18. Quum itaque reconciliatio mundi occasione τῆς ἀποβολῆς Israëlitarum acciderit, quidni per πρόσληψιν vel assumptionem incredulorum Judæo- rum obtigisset mundo καταλλαγὴ? Imò τίς ἡ πρόσ- ληψις εἰ μὴ ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν, quæ illa assumptio nisi vita ex mortuis, quid aliud futura fuisset, quàm læta orbis vivificatio? Etsi verò ita non sejunctim, sed conjunctim respectu utriusque & Judæorum & gentium accipienda καταλλαγὴ & ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν, quia utrisque, quà credebant, reconciliatio cum DEO & vivificatio obtingebat; utrique & sub ira DEI, & in morte hærebant extra fidem in Chri- stum, qui solus est propitiatio nostra & vita nostra; peculiariter tamen hòc aptatur gentibus reconci- liatio, ut quæ extra foedus fuêre ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ. Eph. II. 12. Ju- dæis v. vita tum quia Judæi sibi maximè vivere vi- debantur, & in Scripturis habere vitam æternam Ioh. V. 39. quibus verò Christus Ioh. IIX. 24. nisi credideritis, quod ego sim (quod vobis dixi) morie- mini in peccatis vestris; tum quia assumptione Ju- dæorum totus reviviscere mundus videri poterat, postquam gentibus jam reconciliatio & vita obti- git. Philipp. part. IV. Oper. in comment. ad h. l. ita habet: Consequens sic attexit: Ruina vestra pro- fuit gentibus, sed non simpliciter ruina, verum multo magis plenitudo vestra, id est, pars incolumis creditu- ra, quæ provocanda fuit gentium exemplo, sunt er- gò reliqui inter Judæos convertendi. Hanc reli- quam partem nominat plenitudinem, id est, comple- mentum integræ Ecclesiæ convertendæ ex semine Ab- rahæ; sic & postea amplificatio additur, si abjectio Judæorum profuit, quàm gloriosa erit restitutio, quæ est futura quasi resurrectio ex mortuis. Significat autem ideò reliquam majorem partem rejectam esse, quia fuit fascinata persuasione, se esse populum Dei & Ecclesiam, propter genus, Legem, Ceremonias, & meritum: nec aliud intellexerunt esse Ecclesiam, nisi hanc politiam Judaicam, nunc verò hi, qui recipiun- tur, discent, aliud esse politiam, aliud Ecclesiam, aliud promissionem bonorum corporalium, aliud pro- missionem gratiæ & vitæ æternæ. Discent toti Eccle- siæ, gentibus & Judæis, velut mortuis, reddi justitiam & vitam æternam propter Messiam, & per eum, non propter legem aut merita hominum.

## 11:16
v. 16. 'If the firstfruits are holy, so is the lump.' These things which follow also pertain to this, so that those called from the Gentiles might not for that reason separate the Jews from themselves because they were addicted to the rites of the law: for just as the spirit of Ebion began to show itself among the Jews, so the Spirit that later agitated Marcion began to show itself among Christians made from the Gentiles. Against both these kinds of men the Apostles had grave struggles. So difficult is it to maintain the middle way. 'Firstfruits' (ἀπαρχὴ) generally corresponds to the Hebrew terumah (תרומה). That was the liberality which was offered to God from the ripe fruits before the tithes. It is also called reshit (ראשית), as in Deut. 18:4, 26:2. That oblation having been made, it was permitted to cook the rest of the grain and eat it. That grain, because it was taken for cooking, is therefore called here 'lump' (φύραμα), which some in Latin call matter, others mass. It was holy, that is, permitted for human use, just as food is said to be sanctified through prayers, and a wife to her husband, 2 Cor. 7:14, 1. Tim. 4:5. In like manner, just as Abraham was holy, so also his descendants imitating his faith, and therefore they ought not to be separated from the Church as if they were profane. Philo says the whole Jewish nation is as it were 'firstfruits' (ἀπαρχὴν) to God in his book on the creation of a prince.

This reason is nothing. For the converted Gentiles did not turn away from the Jews who embraced the faith of Christ: since the Jews rather withdrew themselves from the Gentiles, as being uncircumcised. Nor is the Apostle speaking of the descendants of Abraham imitating his faith, whom no one desired to be separated from the Church as if they were profane: rather, the Gentiles rejoiced that they had approached the polity of Israel, and were no longer guests to the covenants of promise. Cf. Eph. 2:2, 3; Mic. 4:1 ff.; Luke 24:47; Acts 2:39, 41; ch. 4:4; ch. 10:36, 45. Nor is it about internal and spiritual holiness, which is nothing without faith, and belongs neither to the mass because of the firstfruits, nor to the branches because of the root, because just as the just man lives by his own faith, so it is necessary for each one to be justified through his own faith, Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17. Acts 15:11. But it is about external and ecclesiastical holiness, which is attributed to the Israelite people because God struck a covenant with their ancestors the Patriarchs, and adopted that people as his own possession: to whom belonged the promises and the covenants, Acts 2:39; Rom. 9:4. For the medium of internal holiness is not carnal generation, but spiritual regeneration. Therefore, it is not to be admitted with the Calvinists that holy children are procreated from faithful and holy parents. Because by nature we are all children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. Christians are not born, but made, says Tertullian, Apol. ch. 17. However, that external holiness, that those born in the Church enjoy the rights of the Church, is not to be denied, in which way also the children of Christians are called holy, 1 Cor. 7:14. They have a right to the thing, not in the thing. Whence also Camero, in the school of Calvin, accepted these things not concerning spiritual holiness, but ecclesiastical, that they have a right to the privileges of the Church. It is about that holiness that is treated here, by virtue of which access to the same grace was open to the posterity of the Patriarchs, according to the divine promises, of which, however, the Israelites could not become participants in act, except through faith. For God did not enter into the pact of the covenant with the Fathers only, but with the whole nation, whence it was not among the impossibilities for the posterity to aspire to salvation, provided they did not reject Christ through infidelity, but received his Gospel. The Apostle's simile concerning the firstfruits and the mass sufficiently teaches that it is not about internal holiness. For the offering of the firstfruits contributed nothing intrinsically to the lump, but only σχετικῶς (relatively) on account of the divine command rendered the same edible, or lawful to be eaten, but not indeed fit: for it did not attain this internal fitness and goodness through the offering of the firstfruits; so also the descendants do not have from their firstfruits, the Patriarchs consecrated to God, that they possess spiritual and internal holiness, but they are holy only σχετικῶς (relatively) and extrinsically, in that they are able to enjoy the rights of the Church and the promises of God.

And if the root is holy, so are the branches. Another similitude tending to the same point. The name ῥίζα (root) is here taken συνεκδοχικῶς (synecdochically) for the whole trunk, from which the branches extend: and it is put for the Hebrew עֵץ (tree), which is translated sometimes as ῥίζα (root), sometimes as στέλεχος (stem).

Latin:

v. 16. εἰ δὲ ἡ ἀπαρχὴ ἁγία καὶ τὸ φύραμα. Hæc, quæ sequuntur, eò etiam pertinent, ne ex Genti- bus vocati Judæos ideò, quod legis ritibus addicti essent, à se segregarent: nam sicut Ebionis spiritus inter Judæos, ita Spiritus, qui Marcionem postea agitavit, inter Christianos è gentibus factos incipiebat se ostendere. Contra utrumque hoc hominum genus gravia fuere Apostoli certamina. Adeò difficile est servare mediocritatem. Ἀπαρχὴ plerumque respondet Hebræo תרומה. Ea erat liberalitas, quæ de frugibus maturis Deo offerebatur ante decimas. Vocatur & ראשית ut Deut. XVIII. 4. XXVI, 2. Ea oblatione facta reliquum frumenti coquere & eo vesci licebat. Id frumen- tum, quia ad coquendum sumebatur, ideò hîc vocatur Φύραμα, quod Latine alii materiam, alii massam vocant. Ea sancta erat, id est, usui humano permissa, sicut cibus dicitur per preces sanctificari, & uxor viro 2. Cor. VII, 14. 1. Tim. IV, 5. Pari modo sicut Abrahamus sanctus fuit, ita & posteri ejus fidem ejus imitantes, ac propterea non debent veluti profani ab Ecclesia segregari. Philo totam gentem Judaicam Deo esse velut ἀπαρχὴν dicit libro de constituen- do principe.

Hæc causa nulla est. Nam gentes conversæ non aversabantur Judæos fidem Christi amplexos: quum Judæi potius à gentibus, utpote incircumci- sis sese subtraherent. Nec de posteris Abrahami fidem ejus imitantibus sermo est Apostolo, quos veluti profanos ab Ecclesia nemo segregatos cu- piebat: quin gauderent potius gentes, se accessisse ad politiam Israelis, nec amplius hospites esse à testamentis promissionis. Conf. Ef. II. 2. 3. Mich. 4. 1. seqq. Luc. XXIV. 47. Act. II. 39. 41. c. IV. 4. c. X. 36. 45. Nec de sanctitate interna & spirituali, quæ sine fide nulla est, neque soli massæ convenit, ob primi- tias, aut ramis ob radicem, quia ut justus fide suâ vi- vet, ita per fidem cujusque propriam justificari ceu e jusdem oportet Hab. II. 4. Rom. I. 17. Act. XV. 11. sed de sanctitate externa & Ecclesiasticâ; quæ Israe- litico populo tribuitur, quod cum majoribus eo- rum Patriarchis fœdus pepigerit Deus, & populum illum in peculium adoptarrit: cujus erant promissio- nes & testamenta Act. II. 39. Rom. IX. 4. Sanctitatis enim internæ medium non est carnalis generatio, sed spiritualis regeneratio. Non ergò cum Calvinia- nis admittendum, quod ex fidelibus & sanctis paren- tibus sancti procreentur liberi. Quia natura omnes sumus filii iræ Eph. II. 3. Christiani non nascuntur, sed fiunt, ait Tertull. Apol. c. XVII. Sanctitas autem illa externa, quod in Ecclesia nati juribus Ecclesiæ fruantur, neganda non est, quo pacto etiam liberi Christianorum sancti dicuntur 1. Cor. VII. 14. Ha- bent jus ad rem, non in re. Unde etiam Camero, in Calvini schola, non de sanctitate spirituali, sed Ec- clesiastica hæc accepit, quod jus habeant ad privile- gia Ecclesiæ. De illa agitur hîc sanctitate, vi cujus po- steritati Patriarcharum aditus ad gratiam eandem patebat, secundum divina promissa, quorum verò actû participes Israelitæ fieri non poterant, nisi per fidem. Non enim cum Patribus tantum, sed cum tota gente Deus pactum fœderis iniit, unde non erat ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων posteritatem ad salutem ad- spirare, modò non reprobet Christum per infide- litatem, sed Evangelium ejus suscipiat. Similitudo Apostoli de primitiis & massâ, satis docet, de inter- na sanctitate non agi. Nam oblatio primitiarum ni- hil intrinsecè conferebat massæ, sed σχετικῶς tan- tum ob mandatum divinum reddebat eandem ve- scibilem, vel ad vescendum licitam, non verò a- ptam: hanc enim internam aptitudinem & bonita- tem non consequebatur per primitiarum oblatio- nem; ita & posteri non à primitiis suis Patriarchis Deo consecratis habent, quod spirituali & interna sanctitate polleant, sed σχετικῶς tantum & extrin- secè sancti sunt, quod juribus Ecclesiæ & promissis Dei frui possint.

καὶ εἰ ἡ ῥίζα ἁγία καὶ οἱ κλάδοι. Altera similitudo eodem tendens. Nomen ῥίζης hîc su- mitur συνεκδοχικῶς pro toto trunco, unde se rami exten- dunt: poniturque pro Hebræo עֵץ quod modò ῥίζα modò στέλεχος vertitur.

## 11:17
V. 17. But if some of the branches were broken off. Εἰ δὲ (But if) here signifies although. Although, he says, some branches were broken off. He uses the language of farmers, who break off useless branches. See John 15:2. Virgil: -- or the highest shoots are broken off from the tree. Cicero for Caecina: who would break off a branch of a tree from those passing by, he understands by that the very thing which he had called ἀποβολὴν (casting away) before, שֶׁרֶשׁ (root) in Ps. 52:7, and it is an ἐυφημισμὸς (euphemism) when he says 'some' instead of 'by far the most'.

But you, being a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them) he addresses one person for all: among them, that is, placed among the branches of that tree. Ovid: Let grafting come: let branch adopt branch. There are, however, several kinds of grafting, one of which is called by the Greeks ἐνοφθαλμισμὸς (budding), by the Latins inoculation, which here seems to be signified by ἐγκεντρίζειν (to graft in), a word which Theophrastus also uses. Rightly, however, both Ambrose and Jerome note that in this matter the greater benefit of God is described, because it is against the custom of farmers to insert wild shoots into a mild tree, since the contrary is usually done, which is also frequent among writers on agriculture, and can be understood from this elegant Epigram: The wild pear, formerly a bastard of the forest soil, a trunk of beast-grazed wilderness, now through alien branches I bloom as a cultivated tree, bearing fruit not for myself, but for my own branches. Great thanks to you, O planter, for your labor, because of you, the wild pear is grafted among the fruit-bearing trees.

Philo on Curses: that God welcomes virtue springing from ignoble birth, letting the roots be, but accepting the shoot from the stem because it has changed and been tamed toward fruitfulness. Paul indicates this same thing here figuratively, which he had said more openly in IV. 11. He said olive tree rather than another tree, because it is both beautiful and fruitful, Ps. LII. 10, and kings and priests are anointed with it. See what is at Zech. IV. 3.

and a fellow-partaker of the root and of the fatness of the olive tree) It is a hendiadys. For he wishes to say: of the fatness of the root of the olive tree, for from the root the sap is diffused to the branches, and that properly belongs to the olive tree, Jud. IX. 9. You have been made a partaker of the promises which God made to Abraham, accepted mystically. See Matt. XXII. 23. Fellow-partaker חבר.

It pleases some, with Origen, to understand Christ by the root: who is from the Israelites according to the flesh, to which root we are grafted by faith v. 20, and which carries us v. 17, 18. But because it is a matter of holiness not spiritual, which is had in Christ, but only Ecclesiastical and external, it is better to accede to others, with great consensus, who accept this similitude also concerning the Fathers. Yet there is no need that we understand the name of root synecdochically concerning the whole trunk: rather, just as first-fruits does not denote the whole mass synecdochically, but the first-fruits, so also the root is to be understood properly, and not indeed concerning the whole trunk. For the branches have life and vigor from the root, and indeed the whole trunk too, which is more correctly comprehended under the word of the branches than under the word of the root. For the root carries the trunk with the branches. That in them, the Syriac interprets as in the place of them, but it is correctly explained as being placed among the branches of that tree. B. Luther renders it among them. For a partaker of the root and of the fatness of the olive tree is of the radical fatness, or that flowing from the root of the olive tree. The fabrication concerning the mystical sense of the promises made to Abraham has been exploded elsewhere: namely, in the Commentary on Genesis, and in the Illustrated Bibles of the O.T.

Latin:

V. 17. εἰ δέ τινες τῶν κλάδων ἐξεκλάσθησαν. Εἰ δὲ hîc valet quamvis. Quamvis, ait, quidam rami de- fracti sunt. Utitur voce agricolarum, qui inutiles ramos defringunt. Vide Joh. XV. 2. Virgilius: - - aut summas defringi ex arbore plantas. Cicero pro Cæcinna: qui prætereuntes ramum defringerent arboris, id ipsum intelligit quod ἀποβολὴν ante dixerat שֶׁרֶשׁ in Ps. LII. 7. & ἐυφημισμὸς est, cum dicit quidam pro longè plurimis.

σὺ δὲ ἀγριέλαιος ὢν ἐνεκεντρίσθης ἐν αὐτοῖς) unum aliquem alloquitur pro omnibus: ἐν αὐτοῖς, id est, positus es inter ramos illius arboris. Ovidius: Venerit insitio: fac ramum ramus adoptet. Sunt autem insitionis plura genera, quorum unum dici- tur Græcis ἐνοφθαλμισμὸς, Latinis inoculatio, quod hîc vi- detur significari per ἐγκεντρίζειν, qua voce & Theophrastus utitur. Rectè autem notant & Ambrosius & Hieronymus in hac re eo majus describi Dei beneficium, quod contra morē est agricolarum seros surculos miti arbori inserere, cum con- trarium fieri soleat, quod & apud rei rusticæ scriptores fre- quens est, & intelligi potest ex hoc eleganti Epigrammate ἡ πάρος ἐν δρυμοῖσι νόθης ζώδωρος ἀρούρης. (Callimachi: Ἄχρὰς, θηροβότω πρέμνον ἐρημοσύνης, Ὀθνείοις ὄζοισι μετέμφυλος ἥμερα θάλλω, ὐκ ἐμοὶ ἡμετέροις κλωσὶ φέρουσα φάρος. πολλή σοι φυτουργὲ πόνω χάρις ἕνεκα σεῖο Ἀχρὰς ἐν ἐυκάρποις δένδρεσιν ἐγκατέφομαι.

Philo de Diris: ὅτι τὴν ἐκ δυσγενείας ἀρετὴν φυομένην ὁ θεὸς ἀσπάζεται, τὰς μὲν ῥίζας ἐῶν χαίρειν, τὸ δὲ στελεχόθεν ἔρνος, ὅτι μετέβαλεν ἡμερωθὲν πρὸς εὐκαρπίαν, ἀποδεχόμενος. Idem autem hic figuratè indicat Paulus, quod apertius dixerat IV. 11. oleam autem potius dixit quam aliam arborem, quia & pulchra, & fructifera est Psal. LII. 10. & ex ea unguntur reges & sacerdotes. Vide quæ ad Zach. IV. 3.

καὶ συγκοινωνὸς τῆς ῥίζης καὶ τῆς πιότητος τῆς ἐλαίας ἐγένου) Est ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Vult enim dicere: τῆς πιότητος τῆς ῥίζης τῆς ἐλαίας, nam à radice succus ad ramos diffunditur, & propriè id convenit oleæ Jud. IX. 9. Particeps factus es promissorum, quæ Deus fecit Abrahamo, mysticè acceptorum. Vide Matth. XXII. 23. Συγκοινωνὸς חבר.

Nonnullis placet cum Origene per ῥίζαν Christum intelligere: qui ex Israelitis est secundum carnem, cui radici inserimur per fidem v. 20. quæque nos portat v. 17. 18. sed quia de sanctitate agitur non spirituali, quæ in Christo habetur, sed Ecclesiastica & externa solum, præstat aliis, magno consensu hanc similitudinem etiam de Patribus accipientibus accedere. Non tamen opus est, ut nomen ῥίζας Synechdochicè intelligamus de toto trunco: imo uti ἀπαρχὴν non Synechdochicè totam massam, sed primitias notat, ita etiam radix propriè intelligenda, non verò de toto trunco. Nam ex radice habent κλάδοι vitam & vigorem, imò & truncus totus, qui rectius sub voce τῶν κλάδων comprehenditur, quam sub voce ῥίζας. Nam radix portat truncum cum ramis. Illud ἐν αὐτοῖς, Syrus interpretatur loco illorum, sed rectè exponitur positus esse inter ramos illius arboris. B. Lutherus reddit unter sie. Consors enim radicis & pinguedinis oleæ est pinguedinis radicalis, seu ex radice oleæ profluentis. Commentum de mystico sensu promissorum Abrahæ factorum aliàs explosum est: in Comment. nempè in Genesin, & Bibliis illustratis V. T.

## 11:18
v. 18. Do not boast against the branches. Do not despise the broken-off branches, much less those still adhering. The word to boast against Jer. L. 30, Zech. X. 12, Jer. L. 10, Jas. II. 13, III. 14, in Ps. LII. 3, why do you boast, you boast.

But if you boast, you do not carry the root, but the root you. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and other pious fathers owe you nothing, you owe them much: and because of them, also to their descendants.

It is not a matter here of not despising branches still adhering, but of the broken-off branches v. 19. Concerning the word to boast against, B. Wellerus says thus: to boast against is to toss one's neck against someone; which gesture those use who trample others with their pride, and indeed break forth into open insult. Let the passage Jer. L. 11 be weighed, where the LXX expressed this with this word, and immediately the effect of this arrogance, which is trampling, is added. Furthermore, the Jews are compared to the cut-off and broken-off branches. For just as these are held as castaways: so now the condition of the Jews is said to be similar. The prior and modern condition of the Gentiles is set before the eyes: from the former, they are compared to wild olive trees: from the present, they are called grafted shoots, who participate in a foreign sap and stock. Hence therefore immediately the first, and indeed the second argument of exhortation is connected: That the Gentiles must not be proud against the Jews: 1. because they do not have it by nature, but have received this by grace, whatever happiness they now obtain in the kingdom of Christ. The second argument, because they do not carry the root; but are carried by the root, that is, the Christian doctrine and religion did not take its origin from them, but first went out from the Jews, according to that Is. II. 3, The Law went out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Thus B. Mylius.

Latin:

v. 18. μὴ κατακαυχῶ τῶν κλάδων. Noli despicere ramos defractos, multò magis adhuc adhærentes. Verbum κατακαυχᾶσθαι Jer. L. 30. Zach X. 12. Jer. L. 10. Jac. II. 13. III. 14. in Ps. LII. 3. מה־תתהלל τί ἐγκαυχᾷ.

εἰ δὲ κατακαυχᾶσαι, ὁ σὺ τὴν ῥίζαν βαστάζεις, ἀλλ' ἡ ῥίζα σε. Abrahamus, Isaacus Jacobus, & alii pii patres nihil tibi debent, tu illis multum: & propter illos etiam posteris.

De non despiciendis ramis adhuc adhærentibus hic non agitur, sed de ramis defractis v. 19. De voce κατακαυχᾶν ita B. Wellerus: κατακαυχᾶν est, cervicem contra aliquem jactare; quo gestu utuntur, qui alios suo fastu conculcant, imò in contumeliam apertam se prorumpunt. Expendatur locus Jer. L. 11. ubi LXX. דצת hoc verbo expresserunt, & statim effectus hujus arrogantiæ, quæ est conculcatio, adjicitur. Porrò Judæi decisis defractisque ramis conferuntur. Nam uti hi pro abjectamentis habentur: ita nunc Judæorum similis dicitur esse conditio. Gentilibus prior & moderna conditio ob oculos proponitur: ex priori, oleastris comparantur: ex præsenti, surculi insititii appellantur, qui alieno succo & stipite participant. Hinc ergò statim primum, imò alterum etiam exhortationis argumentum nectitur: Non esse gentilibus contra Judæos superbiendum: 1. quia non ex natura habeant, sed per gratiam hoc acceperint, quidquid jam felicitatis in regno Christi obtinent. Secundum argumentum, quia non ipsi radicem gestent; sed à radice gestentur, hoc est doctrina & religio Christiana non ab ipsis ortum duxerit, sed à Judæis primum exierit, secundum illud Es. II. 3. Ex Sion exivit Lex, & verbum Domini de Jerusalem. Ita B. Mylius.

## 11:19
v. 19. You will say then. He sets down the words of certain Christians from the Gentiles, just as he previously set down those of the Jews.

The branches were broken off that I might be grafted in. God, by rejecting the Jews, made a place for me.

Latin:

v. 19. ἐρεῖς ŧν. Dicis igitur. Verba ponit Christianorum quorundam ex gentibus, sicut ante Judæorum posuit.

ἐξεκλάσθησαν οἱ κλάδοι ἵνα ἐγὼ ἐγκεντρισθῶ. Deus Judæos abjiciendo, mihi locum fecit.

## 11:20
v. 20. Well. You have spoken well, that is. A formula of one approving a statement, as also

one, indeed well. The full expression of Mark XII. 23, Luke XX. 39, John IV. 17.

τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ ἐξεκλάσθησαν. They were broken off because of unbelief. σὺ δὲ τῇ πίσει ἕστηκας. But you have stood in faith, that is, you have remained in the tree until now. For עמד is often translated by μένειν.

μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει. Just as we said above (VIII. 5. 7. 27) that φρονεῖν is taken not of the intellect, but of the affection, so here and in 1 Tim. VI. 17, ὑψηλοφρονεῖν is to be proud, to which ταπεινοφρονεῖν is opposed. Thus Euripides said φρονεῖν μέγα. Menander, φρονεῖν μέγισον. And those who are such are called ὑπέρφρονες. Conversely, the modest are said to φρονεῖν θνητὰ, φρονεῖν ἀνθρώποις ἴσα. Pride is a huge vice, especially regarding those things which we have as given by God.

The Apostolic exhortation, as blessed Weller noted here, is offered in a triple form: do not boast (v. 18), do not be puffed up in mind (v. 20), do not be arrogant in yourself (v. 25). The difference between these is this: Φρόνιμον εἶναι ἐν ἑαυτῷ is of private judgment, which a man superstitiously assumes about himself. Whence follows ὑψηλοφρόνησις, where the mind swells toward others and affects nothing but great things. From this is born κατακαύχησις, the contempt of others. Paul begins from the latter, as from the worst fruit of the worst tree, so that he may finally propose that this too must be avoided.

ἀλλὰ φοβῦ. Faith excludes fear on account of temporal things: but not the fear of offending God (Phil. II. 12).

Therefore, it is not a doubt about salvation that is to be understood with the Papists, but rather a pious solicitude about retaining faith and the grace of God: since the scope of the Apostle is to dissuade the converted Gentiles from carnal confidence and security. Such pious solicitude and filial fear is so far from removing the certainty of faith that it is rather a fruit of true faith and follows it (Phil. II. 12). It is evident from this that true believers can fall from salvation, otherwise that exhortation would be in vain, nor would there be a danger that someone grafted into the olive tree and made a partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree might be broken off: which the Apostle nevertheless hints at here (cf. v. 17, 18, 22). But the Calvinists are in vain who deny this, and corrupt the text against the mind of the Apostle concerning hypocritical faith: for hypocrites were neither grafted into the olive tree through faith, nor were they made partakers of the radical fatness of the olive tree: nor can it be said of them that they stand by faith, when others were broken off because of unbelief; which antithesis sufficiently teaches that true faith, not hypocritical, is indicated.

Latin:

v. 20. καλῶς. Benè dixisti scilicet. Formula dictum approbantis, ut &

ἓν ἔνγε καλῶς γε. Plena locutio Marci XII. 23. Luc. XX. 39. Joh. IV. 17.

τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ ἐξεκλάσθησαν. Ob incredulitatem defracti sunt. σὺ δὲ τῇ πίσει ἕστηκας. Tu verò in fide stetisti, id est, hactenus mansisti in arbo- re. Nam עמד sæpe per μένειν vertitur.

μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει. Sicut φρονεῖν diximus supra VIII. 5. 7. 27. non de intelle- ctu, sed de affectu sumi, ita hic & 1. Tim. VI. 17. ὑψηλοφρο- νεῖν est superbire, cui opponitur ταπεινοφρονεῖν. Sic φρονεῖν μέγα dixit Euripides. Menander φρονεῖν μέγισον. Et qui tales sunt, ὑπέρφρονες dicuntur. Contra modesti, φρονεῖν θνητὰ, φρονεῖν ἀνθρώποις ἴσα. Superbia ingens vitium, ma- ximè circa ea, quæ à Deo data habeamus.

Parænesis Apostolica, quod hic notavit B. Wel- lerus, triplici forma offertur: ne glorieris vers. 18. ne efferaris animo v. 20. ne sis arrogans apud te- metipsum v. 25. Differentia vero hæc inter ista est: Φρόνιμον εἶναι ἐν ἑαυτῷ judicii privati est quod de se superstitiosè homo sumit. Unde sequitur ὑψηλο- φρόνησις, quæ erga alios mens tumet, & nonnisi ma- gna adfectat. Hinc nascitur κατακαύχησις con- temtus aliorum. A posteriori initium facit Paulus, tanquam à fructu pessimo pessima arboris, ut tandem & hanc fugiendam proponat.

ἀλλὰ φοβῦ. Timorem ob res temporales excludit fides: non etiam timorem Deum offendendi Phil. II. 12.

Non ergò dubitatio de salute cum Papistis intel- ligenda, sed pia potiùs sollicitudo de fide ac gratia Dei retinenda: quum scopus Apostoli sit dehor- tari gentiles conversos à carnali confidentia & se- curitate. Ejusmodi sollicitudo pia, & filialis timor tantum abest, ut certitudinem fidei tollat, ut po- tius veræ fidei fructus sit, eandemque sequatur Phil. II. 12. Patet autem inde, verè credentes ex- cidere posse saluti, aliàs frustranea foret illa paræ- nesis, neque periculum subesset, nequis oleæ in- sertus & consors radicis & pinguedinis oleæ fa- ctus defrangatur: quod tamen hic innuit Aposto- lus, conf. v. 17. 18. 22. Frustra autem sunt Calvin. qui hoc negant, atque de fide hypocritica textum contra Apostoli mentem corrumpunt: nam hypo- critæ nec inserti sunt oleæ per fidem, nec partici- pes pinguedinis radicalis oleæ facti sunt: nec de illis dici potest, quod fide stent, cum alii per ἀπι- σίαν defracti sunt; quæ ἀντίθεσις satis docet, fidem veram, non hypocriticam indigitari.

## 11:21
v. 21. εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ὀυκ κλάδων ἐφείσατο. He did not spare them, so as not to break them off.

μήπως ὀὐδέ σε φείσεται. In the manuscript, which I often praise, there is only εἰ δὲ οὐ φείσεται, just as the Syrian also reads. Namely, if you also fall away from the faith, as they did (1 Tim. I. 19; IV. 1), whence all are seriously warned to remain in the faith (1 Tim. II. 15; 2 Tim. IV. 7; 1 Cor. VI. 13).

There is no reason why the particle μήπως occurring in the received codices should be omitted: which here is not of one doubting, but of one certainly asserting, as is evident from v. 22. Beza fixes an ellipsis here from Matt. XXV. 9, as if to say: see that you do not fall away. Ambs rendered it thus: If God did not spare the branches growing in their nature and their root, when He was the root to them, how much more will He not spare you also? In these verses 19, 20, 21, blessed Mylius notes a third argument, to which the transition is made through an anticipation: for the objection (ὑποφορά) of the Gentiles is placed, seeking an argument for their own excellence from the very fact of the rejected Jewish people and the substituted Gentiles. The Apostle's response first has a concession, for he does not deny the alleged fact. But he recalls them to consider the cause and manner of the fact. For it is not what is done, but why and how it is done, that matters most. But they expressly assign the cause as unbelief: not understanding some common one, but an enormous and monstrous one, to overcome which neither sermons nor any miracles could have been sufficient. To this, on the contrary, he opposes faith from person of the Gentiles. For he declares that it is by faith that they stand, that is, that they are occupied in the kingdom of grace: thus indeed hinting that, if faith is cast off, they themselves will suffer the same thing as the Jews. Whence it is that, having repeated the proposition, he concludes thus: That the Gentiles must not be proud, but must walk cautiously and providently: since in an equal crime of unbelief, God will spare the Gentiles much less than the Jews. The reason for the assertion is explained by a customary metaphor, by which words it is not, however, signified what kind of people the Jews were by nature, as if they were better than the rest in this respect; but in a discourse instituted by way of comparison, this alone is hinted, that this was the prerogative of the Jews over the Gentiles, that by long-continued use, it could seem to have been as it were natural in them: which, that it is adventitious to the Gentiles of late, appears quite manifestly. The argument of the present passage is such: Unbelief can be less unpunished in the Gentiles than it was in the Jews. The pride of the Gentiles against the Jews is not without the manifest crime of unbelief. Therefore, it cannot be immune. Philippus p. 172 observes here a prediction concerning the excision of the Gentiles: Paul prophesies concerning the ruin of the Church of the Gentiles. The event shows this. Immediately after the disciples of the Apostles, horrible sects arose, and when gradually greater lacerations were made, Mahomet found the minds of many prepared for a plausible and political kind of doctrine, by which the Gospel is utterly destroyed. Thus in all Africa and in a great part of Asia, the Churches were utterly destroyed. And in Europe the Papacy established manifold idolatry, invocations of dead men, the profanation of the Lord's Supper in the Mass, and in the carrying about of the host. Likewise satisfactions, and Monasticism; likewise, it extinguished the doctrine concerning the offices of the persons of the Godhead, and concerning Justification. And then the Pontiffs openly exercise cruelty against those who embrace the purity of the Gospel. This desertion in the greatest part of the human race Paul predicts here, and yet among these ruins God preserves some remnants, lest the whole human race be born in vain and only for destruction.

Latin:

v. 21. εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ὀυκ κλάδων ἐφείσατο. Non pepercit eis, quo minus defringeret.

μήπως ὀὐδέ σε φείσεται. In Manuscripto, quem sæpe laudo, tantum est εἰ δὲ οὐ φεί- σεται, quomodo & Syrus legit. Nempe, si & tu à fide defi- cias, ut illi 1. Tim. I. 19. IV. 1. unde seriò monentur omnes manere in fide 1. Tim. II. 15. 2. Tim. IV. 7. 1. Cor. VI. 13.

Non est cur omittatur particula μήπως in Co- dicibus receptis occurrens: quæ verò hic non du- bitantis est, sed certò asseverantis, ut è v. 22. patet. Ellipsin autem hic figit Beza è Matth. XXV. 9. q. d. vide ne excidaris. Ambs ita reddidit: Si Deus non pepercit ramis crescentibus in natura sua, & radice sua, quum esset ipsis radix, quanto magis non parcet tibi etiam? In versibus hisce 19. 20. 21. tertium ar- gumentum notat B. Mylius, ad quod transitus fit per occupationem: Ponitur enim gentium ὑποφο- ρὰ, ex ipso facto abjecti populi Judaici, & gentilitatis surrogatæ, argumentum præstantiæ suæ petentium. Responsio Apostoli primum concessionem habet, non enim diffitetur factum allegatum. Sed ad causam & modum facti considerandum eosdem revocat. Non enim in eo quid fiat, sed cur & quomodo fiat, quid- que plurimum interest. Causam verò expresse assignant infidelitatem: non vulgarem aliquam in- telligens: sed enormem ac monstrosam, cui expu- gnandæ neque conciones neque miracula ulla sa- tis esse potuerint. Huic ex adverso fidem opponit ex persona gentilium. Hi enim quod stent, hoc est, in re- gno gratiæ versentur, fide factum esse pronunciat: ita nimirum subindicans, fide profligata, idem ipsos pas- suros, quod Judæos. Unde est, quod repetita proposi- tione sic colligit: Non superbiendum esse gentilibus, sed cautè & provide ambulandum: siquidem in pari infidelitatis crimine, gentilibus multo minus parsu- rus sit Deus, quam Judæis. Ratio assertionis consueta metaphora exponitur, quibus verbis non tamen signifi- catur, quales naturâ fuerint Judæi, quasi cæteris hâc parte meliores fuerint; sed comparatè instituto sermo- ne, hoc duntaxat innuitur, præ gentilibus hanc fuisse Judæorum prærogativam, ut usu diuturno, quasi na- turale in ipsis videri queat fuisse: quod adventitium nuper gentilibus esse, satis manifeste appareat. Argu- mentum loci præsentis tale est: Infidelitas minus im- punis esse in gentilibus potest, quàm fuit in Judæis. Su- perbia gentilium contra Judæos non caret manifesto infidelitatis crimine. Ergò immunis esse nequit. Phi- lippus p. 172. observat hic prædictionem de excisio- ne gentium: Vaticinatur Paulus de ruina Ecclesiæ gentium. Id eventus ostendit. Statim post discipulos Apostolorum exortæ sunt horribiles sectæ, & cum paulatim dilacerationes majores fierent, invenit Ma- hometus præparatos multorum animos ad genus do- ctrinæ plausibile & politicum, quo prorsus deletur Ev- angelium. Ita in tota Africa & in magna parte Asiæ, prorsus Ecclesiæ deletæ sunt. Et in Europa Papatus constituit multiplicem idololatriam, invocationes hominum mortuorum, profanationem cœnæ Domini in Missa, & in circumgestatione. Item satisfactiones, & Monachatus; item, extinxit doctrinam de officiis personarum divinitatis, & de Justificatione. Et tunc palàm exercent Pontifices sævitiam in eos, qui puri- tatem Evangelii amplectuntur. Hanc desertionem in maxima parte generis humani prædicit hic Paulus, & tamen inter has ruinas servat Deus reliquias ali- quas, ne totum genus humanum frustra & tantùm ad exitium nascatur.

## 11:22
v. 22. Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God.

In the Glossary: ἀπότομον rigid. Thus ἀπότομος ὀργὴ, ἀπότομος κρίσις. Wisd. 5:20, 6:5. Thus ἀποτόμως severely 2 Cor. 13:10, Tit. 1:13. The origin of the word is from physicians, who cut off infected limbs. Also to the Hebrews חרוץ is συντέμνων Dan. 9:2, whence חרון which is translated σκληρότης in Isaiah 28:27.

Chrysostom is apposite here; He does not say, see therefore your merits, or your labors, but the goodness of GOD, showing that the whole was done from heavenly grace, and instructing the believer to tremble.

if you continue in his goodness.

That is, if you retain the goodness of God toward you. Thus faith is called ἔλεος below in verse 31. If you do what David says of himself in Psalm 52:10, I have hoped in the mercy of God for ever.

Although we remain in the goodness of God through faith, and retain it: yet faith is not itself the χρηστότης or goodness of GOD: nor is it called ἔλεος in verse 31, although it is a work of divine mercy that we believe and persist in faith.

Latin:

v. 22. ἴδε ὖν χρηστότητα καὶ ἀποτομίαν Θεῦ.

In Glossario: ἀπότομον rigidum. Sic ἀπότομος ὀργὴ, ἀπό- τομος κρίσις. Sap. V. 20. VI. 5. Sic ἀποτόμως severe 2. Cor. XIII. 10. Tit. I. 13. Origo vocis à medicis, qui membra infe- cta abscindunt. Etiam Hebræis חרוץ est συντέμνων Dan. IX. 2. unde חרון quod σκληρότης vertitur Esaiæ XXVIII. 27.

Appositè hîc Chrysostomus; Non dicit, vide igi- tur merita tua, aut labores tuos, sed DEI bonitatem, ostendens, quod universum ex superna sit gratia fa- ctum, instituensque credentem, ut tremat.

ἐὰν ἐπιμείνῃς τῇ χρηστότητι.

Id est, si Dei adversus te bonitatem retines. Sic fides vocatur ἔλεος infra 31. Si facias quod de se dicit David LII. 10. ἤλπισα εἰς τὸ ἔλεος τῦ Θεῦ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.

Etsi per fidem maneamus in bonitate Dei, eam- que retineamus: non tamen fides est ipsa χρησότης vel bonitas DEI: neque ἔλεως vocatur v. 31. quam- vis misericordiæ divinæ opus sit, quod credamus & in fide persistamus.

## 11:23
v. 23. otherwise you also will be cut off.

Ἐπὶ here is otherwise, as above in chapter 3. Plato uses it thus both in the Gorgias and in the Hippias Minor. Before he spoke of the breaking off of branches; here of the axe being applied. Tender branches are broken; those who have stood long in the tree are cut out. See Matt. 3:10.

and they also, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in.

If the cause ceases, the effect will cease.

For God is able to graft them in again.

There is nothing except unbelief that prevents God from taking them back for his own and treating them as a father. A similar way of speaking is above IV. 21, below XIV. 4, 2 Corinthians IX. 8, 1 Timothy II. 12, Hebrews XI. 19.

The cause is therefore shown for which the Jews were rejected, namely unbelief, and it is taught in turn that they can be grafted into the olive tree if they cease to be unfaithful; just as to continue in kindness is to remain in a state of grace, which comes about through faith: and thus to retain constantly faith in Christ, in whom alone the goodness and grace of God is apprehended.

For if you were cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree. Paul coined this word good olive tree, so that he might better oppose it to the wild olive tree, at the same time looking back, as he often does in this whole discourse, to Psalm LII, where there is a green olive tree, in the Greek a fruit-bearing olive tree.

How much more. How much more easily. How we have had 'more' also above in verses 9, 10, 13. The effect of an art is easier where nature assists.

Latin:

v. 23. ἐπεὶ κὰι σὺ ἐκκοπήσῃ.

Ἐπὶ hîc est alioqui, ut supra III. Utitur sic & Plato tum in Gorgia, tum in Hippia minore. Ante locutus est de ra- morum defractione; hîc de adhibita securi. Teneri rami franguntur; exciduntur qui diu in arbore stetère. Vide Matth. III. 10.

κὰι ἐκεῖνοι δὲ ἐὰν μὴ ἐπιμείνωσι τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ ἐγκεντρισθήσονται.

Si cesset causa, cessabit effectum.

δυνατὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς πάλιν ἐγκεντρίσαι αὐτές.

Nihil est præter incredulitatem, quod Deum impediat eos rursum pro suis assumere & paternè tractare. Simile lo- quendi genus suprà IV. 21. infra XIV. 4. 2. Corinth. IX. 8. 1. Tim. II. 12. Hebr. XI. 19.

Ostenditur ergò causa ob quam reprobati sint Judæi ἀπισία, ac docetur vicissim eos inseri posse oleæ, si infideles esse desinant; uti ἐπιμένειν ἐν χρηστότη- τι est permanere in statu gratiæ, quod per fidem fit: adeoque constanter retinere fidem in Christum, in quo uno bonitas, & gratia Dei apprehenditur.

εἰ γὰρ σὺ ἐκ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἐξεκόπης ἀγριελαίου καὶ παρὰ φύσιν ἐνεκεντρίσθης εἰς καλλιέλαιον. Vocem hanc καλλιέλαιον finxit Paulus, ut melius eam opponeret ἀγριελαίῳ, simul respiciens, ut sæpè, in hoc omni sermone ad Ps. LII. ubi est יַרְעַן זַיִת, in Græco ἐλαία κατάκαρπος.

πόσῳ μᾶλλον. Quantò facilius. Quomodo μᾶλλον etiam supra habui- mus vers. 9. 10. 13. Facilior est artis effectus, ubi natura adjuvat.

## 11:24
Those by nature. Namely the branches born from Abraham. Will be grafted into their own olive tree) Thus Ovid called his own tree: That the tree may scarcely bear the burden which its own has produced.

In the simile, the assistance of nature has a place. But take care not to carry that into the application. For nature contributes nothing, the Abrahamic lineage contributes nothing, from which the grafting of the Israelites, who were broken off through unbelief, might be easier. That 'how much more' is therefore 'how much more,' with a view indeed to the promises made to the Patriarchs and the holy root, but for the reason we have stated, and not 'how much more easily': Blessed Weller notes from Augustine on Psalm LXX two miracles in the grafting of the wild olive into the olive; one is that he (the Apostle) says the wild olive was grafted into the olive, when on the contrary the olive is accustomed to be grafted into the wild olive. The other is that that wild olive grafted into the olive produced not the fruit of the wild olive, but of the olive, when in natural grafting the opposite happens: since that which is grafted is the very thing that grows and bears fruit, not of the tree into which it is grafted, but of the shoot which was grafted. Whence the Apostle rightly calls this grafting contrary to nature.

PART III. APODICTIC. Concerning the Israelites to be saved in great part.

v. 25. For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery. A mystery is a hidden thing, which men cannot know unless God gives it, as 1 Corinthians XV. 51, Revelation X. 7, XVII. 7, Daniel II. 18, 19, 27, 28, 29, 30, 47, IV. 6. It is also said of the secrets of men, Tobit XII. 6, Judith II. 2, Sirach XXII. 24, XXVII. 16, 17, 21, 2 Maccabees XIII. 21.

Lest you be wise in your own estimation. From Proverbs III. 7, where in the Greek: 'Do not be wise in your own estimation,' according to the LXX, 'do not be wise' according to other interpreters. In the Hebrew it is: 'Do not be wise in your own eyes.' This manuscript has 'in yourselves,' just as in Isaiah V. 21, 'and those who are prudent in themselves.' The sense is: Do not think yourselves to be so prudent that you think you can foresee by your own ingenuity what is to come.

The Apostle first proposes the theme which is to be proved: then the arguments proving it. He adorns the theme with the eulogy of a mystery, that it is truly a hidden and concealed thing, which GOD has decreed concerning the Jews, which no one can penetrate, or know in any way, without divine revelation. Chrys. hom. XIX. in Rom. Μυστήριον ἐνταῦθα ἀγνοόμενον καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον λέγων καὶ πολὺ μὲν τὸ θαῦμα πολὺ δὲ τὸ παράδοξον ἔχον. Then indeed he brings forward the reason why he proposes it: namely, lest the Gentiles should be παρ' ἑαυτοῖς φρόνιμοι, the force of which Grotius has not grasped, 'lest you think yourselves so prudent that you think you can foresee future things by your own ingenuity'; for this very thing was already sufficiently expressed by the word μυστηρίs: since, as Grotius admits, a mystery is a hidden thing, which men cannot know unless GOD grants it. Therefore others express it more correctly, 'lest you grow insolent within': because φρόνιμος here refers not to prudence but to disposition, by a formula of speaking customary in Holy Scripture, by which the proud are said to be wise in their own eyes, as in Prov. III. 7.

ὅτι πώρωσις ἀπὸ μέρους τῷ Ἰσραὴλ γέγονεν. He said ἀπὸ μέρους here, as above 'some of the branches', by a mild expression, when he wished to signify the majority: ἀπὸ μέρους and ἐκ μέρους are frequent in Paul, where he wishes to say 'not all', or 'not entirely'.

Some refer the word ἀπὸ μέρους to time, that Israel has been hardened ἀπὸ μέρους for a time, but without an example, or a parallel passage, in the N.T. Therefore it is more correctly understood of a certain part of the Jews: which

It is the explanation of Augustine, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others; and it is confirmed both from the mode of speaking, because τὰ ἐπὶ μέρυς and τὰ ἐν μέρει are particular things to the Philosopher: τὸ μὲν μέρος which is of my parts; and then from verse 7. The election has obtained it, but the rest were ἐπωρώθησαν, that is, hardened.

until the fullness of the Gentiles shall come in. Fullness here, as above in 12, is a huge multitude of Gentiles easily exceeding the number of the Jews who did not believe. This was fulfilled through the journeys of Paul, many of which he undertook after this epistle was written. And by 'shall come in,' the people of God are to be understood.

and so all Israel shall be saved. He alludes to the saying of the Hebrews: that every Israelite would have a part in the world to come. And as the Apostles often do, drawing this into a better sense, he signifies that it will be true of the true Israel, that is, of those who will imitate the patience of Jacob or Israel in evils, of the Israel of GOD, as he speaks to the Galatians VI. 16. At the same time, however, he hints that the time is at hand when not a few, as before, but a certain great multitude of Jews would embrace Christ; and that happened first when the Jews saw fulfilled what Christ had said, that the idols of the Romans, that is, the military standards, would appear in the sight of the temple, concerning which we have spoken at Matthew XXIV. 15. For then many who embraced Christianity, together with the previously existing Christians, were exempted from the evils that were to follow. These are those sealed in Revelation VII. For just as formerly in the time of Nebuchadnezzar all who had followed the law of Moses, and were therefore said to be sealed by ת, that is, תורה, Ezekiel IX. 4, were freed from the destruction of many: so then were those who bore the sign of the cross in their heart. After that, however, with the city razed and the Temple destroyed, when the truth of the prophecies of Christ appeared much more clearly, and the burden of personal servitude had broken the ferocity of many, which had also happened formerly in the Babylonian exile, many Jews clearly embraced Christ, with Vespasian and Titus not hindering it. Justin, addressing in the person of Trypho: 'In the same way that God then brought wrath because of those seven thousand, in the same way even now He has not yet brought or is bringing judgment, knowing that still day by day some are being discipled into the name of His Christ and are leaving the way of error, who also receive gifts, each as he is worthy, being enlightened through the name of this Christ.' For one receives the spirit of understanding, another of counsel, another of strength, another of healing, another of foreknowledge, another of teaching, another of the fear of God.

He therefore takes that 'until' exclusively and determinately, so that it may be 'up to the time when,' and thus a certain limit is defined for the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles, upon the completion of which the hardening of Israel is finally to cease; he limits that entry to the journeys of Paul; but this is partly precarious, resting on no evidence; it also partly assumes a foundation that is too slippery, that 'fullness' designates such a multitude of Gentiles as would easily exceed the number of the Jews who did not believe; and it is partly false: because the hardening does not only happen to Israel until that time, but lasts in the Israelite people to this very day. Furthermore, that the Apostle alludes to the saying of the Hebrews, that every Israelite would have a part in the world to come, whence, I ask, is it certain, or whence will it be taught that that saying was even in use at that time, or by what example will it be shown that the Apostles often draw such things into a better sense?

As for the meaning of the Apostolic mystery, various opinions are found concerning it: Most think that a notable conversion of the Jews is predicted toward the end of the world, among whom the Chiliasts believe that a certain bodily kingdom is to be erected by Christ in Judea itself over the Jewish people at Jerusalem for a thousand years, such as Socinus reports in Miscellanea, pp. 50, 51, that there were some among his own, which opinion, however, he himself rejects as false, absurd, and pernicious.

A similar fiction is read in the 'Onus Ecclesiae' by a Papal writer, adorned in the year 1519, and reprinted in the year 1620, concerning the Jews to be converted after the Anti-Christ is killed, and to reign with Christ on these earths for a thousand years, in the state which he thus calls the seventh state of the Church: concerning which see chapter LXVI, page 362. In that seventh state, he says, the carnal Church will be finished, if indeed the Jews and all the tribes of Israel, together with the rest of the Gentiles of the whole world, are converted to the faith of Christ, the Apostle being witness, 'blindness in part has happened to Israel,' etc. 3. Those who in the School of Calvin have championed Chiliasm have likewise attempted to prove from this passage a most notable conversion toward the end of the world: such as Curio, a Professor at Basel, who in his book on the amplitude of the kingdom of Christ strives to prove that the number of those to be saved will be much greater than those to be damned, and that all Jews must be converted to the true recognition of the Messiah before the last day of judgment. Piscator, with the final conversion of the Jews, fosters not only Chiliasm, but also the resurrection of the martyrs before the universal resurrection, whom he also says will ascend into heaven and reign there with Christ. Thomas Brightman the Englishman in his commentary on Revelation at chapter XX, page 663, says that the 'beloved city' is that multitude of believing Jews par excellence, who will finally be enrolled from here into the flock of the truly believing. But especially, in a peculiar diatribe, Joh. Henr. Alstedius, following his Piscator, labored to assert a most happy millennium after the destruction of the kingdom of the great Anti-Christ from the thousand years of the Apocalypse, and to establish the kingdom of the resurrected martyrs on these earths, and deduced the universal conversion of the Jews to be in the future toward the end of the world from our Apostolic passage, page 119. Christians, he says, Easterners burning with zeal for Christ and penetrating into Asia itself will provoke the Jews to zeal Rom. XI. and spiritual Babylon will be a prey to all nations: into which opinion he snatches many other testimonies of Scripture, and brings forward the consent of certain other Doctors from the Reformed. Nor have we observed that Grotius in his Annotations on Luke XXI. 24. is alien to this opinion of the Chiliasts regarding this passage.

Others, although they abhor the error of the millenarians, nevertheless enrich the final conversion of the Jews with other inventions, which was done both by other ancients, and by Augustine l. XX. C. D. c. 29. concerning Elijah converting the Jews at the last time, and by Chrysostom homil. LIIX. on Matthew and homil. XIX. on the Epistle to the Romans, and also by Theodoret on this passage. For after the nations have received the preaching, they also (the Jews) will believe, when the great Elijah has come, and has brought to them the doctrine of the faith: as also Bede on this passage. But the more audacious Papists pronounce the opinion concerning Elijah returning to be either of the faith, or next to the faith, as Schvarez has it, Tom. II. in I. Thom. disp. LV. and they contend that the contrary is, if not heretical, at the very least next to heresy, with Bellarmine l. III. de Rom. Pont. c. 3. But the most audacious of all are Malvenda and Cornelius à Lapide, who even define the number of those to be converted, which the former in l. II. de Anti-Christo c. 17. p. 202. not only says with Pererius from l. XV. on Daniel is so great that, compared to the fewness of those who are to remain in impiety, it can be rightly and truly said that all Israel will believe: but he also asserted in the following page that in the Apocalypse the number 144,000 is the number of the Jews, not of all universally who will then believe, since that will be much greater, but only of those who, after having received the faith of Christ, will be slaughtered for it by the Anti-Christ; finally, that after the Anti-Christ has been killed and plunged into hell by lightning, the conversion of the Jews will be most fully accomplished. This Cornelius à Lapide indeed says on Apoc. VII. that at the end of the world, 12,000 from each of the tribes of the Jews will be converted to Christ, etc.

But some of our own Theologians, who detest both the dream of the Chiliasts and the Judaico-Papistic invention concerning the return of Enoch and Elijah, nevertheless believe that the Apostle in this place predicts a certain notable conversion of the Jews to take place near the end of the world. Blessed Mylius makes the Apostle argue thus on this passage: There will finally be before the end of the world a splendid conversion of the Israelite people to Christ; therefore they are not to be insulted on account of their present rejection. This a mystery, adds Blessed Mylius, the Apostle calls it, because unless this had been predicted specifically by the Apostle, it would scarcely have entered anyone's mind. Although some think that Christ also looked to this in Luke 21:24. This illustrious prophecy, since it has not yet been fulfilled, we shall hold it as certainly to be fulfilled before the day of the Lord descends. B. Ægid. Hunnius institutes this paraphrase: I say to you this singular mystery, that that blinding of Israel or of the Jewish people is not total, but only in part: which is to have a place until that great fullness of the nations is completed, and thus then all Israel (by whom synecdochically a certain greatest part of the Jewish people is understood according to the customary manner of Scripture) will be saved, converted, namely, to the true Messiah, when the Jews, taught by their infinite exile and wearied by the excessive but vain expectation of the Messiah (whom they were just then auguring would come), will at length weigh the matter more deeply by the grace of God; namely, that the times appointed for the advent of the Messiah have long since been completed; and therefore no other can be acknowledged as the Messiah, except him who has already been acknowledged before the public testimony of the world as the true Messiah and declared in the Gospel. B. Hunnius adds, however, that he prescribes his opinion to no one: It has pleased [me] to speak thus concerning the meaning of the words of Paul, meanwhile prejudicing no one; but wishing from the heart that the Jews might at some time approach the Church in great number before that last advent of Christ, and be saved together with the fullness of the nations. And who would not wish for this? B. Balduinus on this passage, p. 719. It appears that D. Paul is prophesying about a certain illustrious conversion of the Jews, a great part of whom will acknowledge the Messiah before the last day, and will aggregate themselves to the faith of the Christians: which prophecy, although it is not yet fulfilled, it is not to be doubted that it will certainly have its event, the time is known to God alone, therefore it is a mystery to us. B. Andr. Keslerus, in an inaugural disputation held at Jena in the year 1627, concerning the citations of the Old and New Testament. c. 1. th. 7. explains concerning the future conversion of the Jewish people, by which, although not all Jews entirely, yet a great number are to be converted: To which opinion is also brought B. Gesnerus, B. Meisnerus in his Commentary on Hosea 3, B. Jacob. Martini, B. Helvicus, in his Elenchus Judaicus, B. Hafenrefferus in his Templum Ezechielis, p. 313. B. Brentius is also added: but although he, in earlier times while he was adorning his Commentary on Hosea, which was done in the year 1531, acceded to that opinion, his second thoughts, however, teach that his views were otherwise in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, written in the year 1564, that is, 33 years later. Lucas Lossius, however, so concedes to this opinion that he does not entirely reject that opinion of the ancients concerning Enoch and Elijah, but leaves it in the middle, as he affirms that nothing certain can be affirmed and established concerning it.

From the Reformed, not a few favor the general conversion of the Jews around the last times, and Gisbertus Voëtius especially takes the present Apostolic passage concerning it, who defended the same in Vol. 2 of his Select Disputations, p. 127, and for his opinion—by what right or wrong others may see (for in compiling authors he is for the most part more copious than accurate)—he did not hesitate to praise Martyr, Beza, Deodatus, Junius, Piscator, Pareus, Willet, Rollock, the English theologians, authors of the new and publicly received translation, as also those who edited the ecclesiastical notes in the entire Bible in the year 1645, the authors of the new Belgian translation; the French translation publicly received there in the hypothesis of the chapter: to which he further adds Danaeus in his Christian Ethics, book 2, chapter 13, Franciscus Lambertus in his commentary on Revelation 20, Cellarius in his treatise on the Works of God, Du Plessis in his admonition to the Jews, Tilenus in his Syntagma. Vol. 2, disp. 34. Polanus, Syntagma, book 6, chapter 59, and book 7, chapter 22. Cameron in his Myrothecium on Romans 11:30, p. 169, and Capellus there in his Spicilegium, p. 101. Cunaeus, On the Hebrew Republic, book 1, chapter 18. John Weemse of Lathocker, treatise on degenerate sons, part 4, section 8. Perkins, treatise on the end of the world, Brightman on Revelation 15, 16, and 20. Justus Heurnius on undertaking the legation to the Indians, chapter 4. Forbes in his Instructio Historico-Theologica, p. 221. Jacob Laurentius in his 'Paul the Hard to Understand', p. 295 and 464. Prideaux in his Theological Works, part 2, Oration 6, p. 50. Hull in his English commentary on 2 Peter 3, 519. William Gouge in his English treatise to the Jews; Maccovius in his Collegium disputations, part 2, disp. 17. But we have noted before that the opinion of Brightman and Piscator approaches Chiliasm: Martyr, however, expects a new Anti-Christ, I know not whom, but very doubtfully, being also entirely doubtful concerning the general conversion of the Jews in his commentary. on this passage, whom he says will perhaps return and acknowledge their Messiah, when the Anti-Christ has been killed by the spirit of Christ's mouth: Likewise: it may also happen that, when the Jews have believed, and the nations have helped after some time, as is the nature of the flesh, some security and license may arise, especially if the Anti-Christ follows, whence an infinite number, both from the Jews and from the nations, may be alienated from Christ. Forbes expects not only the conversion of the Jews, but also of the Mohammedans; Danaeus conjectures that the Christians are not to be aggregated to the Jews, but the Christian Church is to be transferred to the Jews. John Heurnius, however, has strange divinations concerning these, which I do not think it worth the effort to bring forward. Pareus, however, does not so much assert that a conversion of a great quantity of Jews will happen at the end of the world, as he denies that it can be defined: he says that it is held with probable faith concerning the end of the world, but he immediately adds: Since it is a mystery, it is not permitted to define it; thus Zwingli and Bullinger are also ambiguous. There is no time to examine the others brought forward by Voëtius.

Voetius says that Christopher Besold in his Pentadecades and Hugo Grotius in book II of De veritate religionis, section 8, state the same thing regarding men of doubtful or varied religion; but a man of most extensive reading ought not to have passed over Georg Calixt, who refers the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles and the Jewish people into the Church to the signs of the Last Judgment, in his book on the supreme judgment published at Helmstedt in the year 1635, p. 27, who, as in other matters, wished to be singular here also, and not in one way only:

(1.) Since it is certain, in his opinion, that some large and populous nations have heard nothing at all of the Gospel within 400 or 500 years (whatever may have been the case in earlier centuries), it seems entirely consistent that God should cause the Gospel to be preached to these very people before He puts an end to the affairs of the world. But from where will this certainty be taught? From where will anyone who wishes to applaud this opinion convince us that what is said is entirely consistent?

(2.) that the nations which have not yet been converted to Christ, and the very most obstinate nation of the Jews, will at length be converted, St. Paul teaches not obscurely in Romans 11:25. But which are those nations not yet converted to the faith? Calixt later names on page 29 the Persians, Tartars, and most of the Indians, as well as the Chinese: but just as he was undoubtedly mistaken about the Persians, Tartars, and Indians, that they were never converted to Christ and that the Gospel was never brought to them, since the Persians even have the New Testament in their own language, nor are they or the Tartars or Indians entirely destitute of the knowledge of Christ; so Calixt himself is mistaken about the Chinese, that some had at some time penetrated to them who announced the Gospel, and that he had attempted to prove this by some evidence, who described those nations,

Janus Gonzalez de Mendoza, the Augustinian, whom he says were never in that place, so that they could be ranked among the nations that are reckoned by the Christian name, but that all ought to be in that place at some time; but that truly had to be taught without begging the question, and it ought to be consistent with Scripture, if anyone wishes to believe it with Calixtus. Nor indeed does the Apostle hand down anything concerning the nations hitherto, i.e., not yet converted up to our own times, but he speaks of his own age, or of the time in which he wrote that, in which he indicates that the fullness of the nations had not yet entered: but nowhere does he teach that all nations are to be converted to Christ. But the fullness of the nations, says Calixtus, I cannot take otherwise than for the universality of the nations, to such an extent that no people to whom the appellation of nation or race is appropriate is missing. But why can it not be taken otherwise? Because the fullness is spoken of in this way in Ps. 24:1. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, that is, whatever is on the earth, with no part of it excepted at all; add Ps. 50:12, Ps. 89:12, Ps. 96:11, Ps. 98:7. So he. But according to this parallelism, not only will no nation be excepted, but not even any man among the nations. And what necessity is there that the fullness of the nations be understood of all nations precisely? Since the definition of the fullness can be taken from GOD, as in the parallel passages which Calixtus likewise compared here, Gal. 4:4, Eph. 1:10, the fullness of time is not taken in such a way that no portion of time is excepted, but of the time which had been divinely predetermined to be exactly completed, in which sense, according to Calixtus himself, these things are to be explained. (3.) He interprets the whole of Israel being saved thus: that it will come to pass that just as all Germany (for example) is said to be Christian, so also all Israel may be said to have received Christ. But such and so great a conversion of the Israelites to Christ or reception of the faith of Christ toward the end of the world, after all nations have been brought to the faith of Christ, neither has anyone of our own people, to whom Calixtus nevertheless appeals, believed, nor will it be easy to bring forward the suffrage of any Catholic Doctor from antiquity. Ambrose, in his book on Joseph, the last chapter, hints at something concerning the blindness being taken away from the Jewish people in the last times, but he did not teach that all Israel according to the flesh was to be converted to Christ. Hilary, in Ps. 58, says that the Jews, who are meanwhile dispersed among almost all nations, will be liberated at the consummation; but he handed down nothing concerning the whole race being converted to Christ after the nations and peoples of all nations. But Calixtus had no one else to praise besides these two Fathers.
