Our own people, however, who judge that the conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world is established from this passage, say that a significant and notable multitude of them will be converted, yet not that all Israel will receive Christ in such a way as all Germany, for example, is said to be Christian: nor can that be said of the ten tribes of Israel, as we taught in the Annotations to Hosea ch. 3, v. 5; nor is it believed by our Theologians that that conversion will happen after the nations of the whole earth have been converted. And what is to be said of the race of the Mahometans and Turks? Is that also going to embrace the Christian faith? Are all the peoples who are under the Sun going to turn out to be Christian, so that throughout the whole world all nations, races, and peoples are to profess faith in Christ; and will there be no nation left that cannot be called Christian in this most recent time, even if perhaps in this, that, or the other nation some few might remain alien to the Christian faith; just as Calixtus speaks of the Jews, that all Israel can be said to be going to receive Christ, even if then also some few among the Jews might perhaps refuse to give their name to Christ, provided they are few compared to the rest?

Our Theologians have never thought about such a universal conversion of the nations and Jews, which ought to be considered an undoubted sign that will precede the final judgment, because they could see nothing about it in Scripture. Edward Brerewood, the Englishman, in his investigation of languages and religions, ch. 14, observes that if the whole world, as far as it is known, is distributed into thirty equal parts, the Christians possess scarcely five portions, but he assigns six portions to the Muhammadans, and nineteen to the pagans; will therefore those six parts of the Muhammadans and those nineteen of the Pagans, and will also, besides those, the whole Magellanic land first embrace Christianity, and then also will so many myriads of Jews dispersed throughout the whole world, whether in dispersion or gathered together, profess the Christian name as one people? That has hardly come into anyone's mind besides Calixtus. And indeed it might seem that that opinion of Calixtus cultivates a token of familiarity with the new and subtle Chiliasm, of which the blessed Cramer, part 2, on the kingdom of Christ, ch. 4, p. 310, makes mention, and elsewhere I remember a certain new and subtle Chiliastic opinion of some commentator on the Apocalypse concerning the Evangelical kingdom; who posits that there will be an utter destruction of the Anti-Christ, both Turkish and Roman, before the end of the world: and that the Church will be ecumenical and Catholically Evangelical, with all heresies deleted, and all persecutions, pressures, wars, and tyranny ceasing; and that for a thousand years, i.e., a time almost long, but precisely known to GOD. In which state of the Evangelical kingdom, however, he rejects whatever savors of Judaism, and likewise whatever savors of political dominion. He does not admit an utter binding of the devil, as far as each private individual is concerned: he removes the bodily conversation of Christ, and likewise the bodily resurrection of the faithful and the judicial administration of the saints: so that this opinion is close to the sentiment of Johannes Erasmus (with the sole exception of Arianism), of which we spoke above. But because this opinion was suppressed in the first egg, before it was hatched, it is enough to have forewarned the reader with these few words. Calixtus indeed anticipated, lest he might seem to have determined such a thing concerning the abolition of all heresies; nevertheless, he says, although, what is still lacking to the fullness of the Gentiles, and the whole of Israel furthermore will enter into the house of God and the visible Church, before that great day comes; there will nevertheless be such dissensions and wars among men professing the Christian name, such wickedness and security, such corruption, moreover, of doctrine, even though it be most manifest from the Holy Scriptures, such, I say, craftiness or violence in twisting and adapting them to human senses and desires, that towards the coming of the Lord it will be entirely as he himself predicted: When he comes, will he find faith on the earth? These are his words: but if you define heresies according to the mind of Calixtus, who deemed neither Papism nor Calvinism subject to heresies, and the Socinians concerning the denied SS. Trinity, Deity and incarnation and the satisfactory passion of the Son of God, which chapters they protest they cannot perceive as revealed in the Holy Scriptures, he would perhaps have likewise deemed them to be absolved from heresy by the force of his own hypotheses, then that deletion of heresies would not have been difficult, I think, to have been granted by him to the happiness of the latest age, which he believed would be entirely Christian. Finally, is that σωθήσεται of the Apostle to embrace the Christian name, or does that entry of the fullness of the Gentiles at least imply the profession of Christianity? Does the Apostle not rather treat of conversion and salvation, than of external profession only, which is also that of hypocrites? Certainly those who in Israel were preserved from Baalitish idolatry belonged to the invisible Church and the assembly of the faithful known to God, they did not constitute the external assembly of the visible Church.

Furthermore, not a few interpreters and doctors, both ancient and modern, judge that there is no prediction here of a notable, let alone a universal, conversion of the Jews, which is to be expected toward the end of the world, or they consider such a conversion to be only doubtful and ambiguous. Our blessed Luther, in Vol. VII of the Jena German edition, in his Epistle on the Sabbatharians of the year 1538, pp. 38 and 41, despairs of the conversion of the Jews, and although in his tract 'vom Schemhamphoras' of the year 1543, Vol. VIII of the Jena German edition, fol. 121, he says that the Jews will survive until the end of the world, they will nevertheless be wanderers throughout the world like Cain, according to the prediction of Psalm 59. and only the dregs of the people, he says, and Jerusalem will be trodden down until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled, that is, until the end of the world, he teaches from Luke 21: but in the preface of that same tract, fol. 109, he has this to say about modern Jews: 'In short, they are young devils, damned to hell; but if there is still something human in them, such writing may be of use and benefit to them; let whoever wishes hope for the whole lot, I have no hope there, nor do I know of any Scripture for it; we cannot even convert our own Christians, the great crowd, we must be content with the small flock, how much less is it possible to convert all these devil's children: for that some derive such a delusion from the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, as if all Jews were to be converted at the end of the world, is nothing; St. Paul means something quite different.' B. Joh. Bugenhagius, the faithful assistant of B. Luther, agrees with him in the argument of Ps. LIX, Comment. p. 98. The Spirit of Christ predicts a dreadful judgment for the Jews, because they denied the Gospel, as an example to others. They are now exiles, wandering among the nations, struck with blindness, fury, and madness, teaching or speaking nothing but blasphemies against Christ. As hungry dogs go around the city, seeking food and yet not finding it, so they themselves at evening, or at the end of the world after the age of the Apostles, will be forsaken; they will wander everywhere as exiles and outcasts, under foreign and most harsh empires, from one land to another, seeking a corner where they might again find remnants of a kingdom or of leaders, but in vain, for they will not be satisfied, but will endure until the end of the world without a leader, without a kingdom, without a priesthood, and will be thrust down into hell. B. Joh. Brentius, whose commentaries our blessed Luther valued highly in this place, explained the mind of the Apostle thus: 'You will be cut off,' says the Apostle, 'but they will be grafted in, because blindness has happened to Israel, not so that the whole nation should perish entirely, but it happened to it for various reasons, but in large part for this reason, that while the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, that is, while many of the Gentiles obtain salvation through Christ, in the meantime some also of the Jews might be converted to Christ, and thus all Israel, gathered as much from the Gentiles as from the Jews, might be saved.' Paul indeed seems to signify in this place that after all those (for this is the fullness of the Gentiles) who have been ordained from the Gentiles to eternal life have been gathered to the Church, then also all the Jews who remain should be converted to Christ. Which benefit of God we are so far from envying the Jews that we even pray for it. But I think the present event of things explains the true opinion of Paul, namely, that he thinks the Jews are not so blinded that absolutely none of them are converted to Christ and obtain salvation, but rather that in the meantime, while the Gentiles are the Church of God and enjoy heavenly benefits, some also of the Jews approach the Church and become saved, so that thus All Israel, namely the spiritual one, gathered as much from the Gentiles as from the carnal Israel, becomes one fold and is adorned with one heavenly glory. Philippus Melancthon in his commentary on this place, which is found in Vol. III, p. 1027, adds, he says, a prophecy about the conversion of the Jews, which perhaps is to be understood thus: 'It will come to pass that from time to time until the end of the world some of the Jews will be converted.' For I do not know whether he means that there still remains some conversion of a great multitude toward the end of the world. That, since it is a mystery, let us commit to God; Isaiah's prophecy preaches about the liberation of the people, namely that of which the Gospel speaks properly, that is, about the remission of sins. And it is a sweet sentiment, because it clearly teaches that in the New Testament the remission of sins is to be preached. This liberation of the people is to be understood from then, from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, to the end. And in another commentary on Romans on this place, Vol. IV, p. 172, he adds also Paul's prophecy about the conversion of the Jews, which I understand thus: that it will come to pass that from time to time until the end of the world some of the Jews will be converted; Isaiah's statement preaches about the coming of the Messiah. When he was born of a virgin, then he taught openly, gave testimonies, was made a victim, rose again, sent the Holy Spirit, and began the preaching of the Gospel. But let the whole sermon of Isaiah in chapter 59 be noted, because it contains both the sweetest doctrine about the benefits of Christ and about the Church; it shows what the true Church is, and affirms that there will always be one: 'The Redeemer shall come out of Zion': where the emphasis of the word should be noted; a Redeemer is one who, having given a price, frees another. 'And he shall turn away iniquities from Jacob'; therefore Christ is sent, so that he may truly blot out the sins of all who believe in him. And let the entire benefit be considered; he restores life and eternal righteousness, just as Daniel also speaks. Then Isaiah adds there a sermon concerning the Church: This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, My spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, and out of the mouth of your seed, from now and forever; that is, this is the true Church, in which sounds the word given to Isaiah concerning the redeemer taking away sin, and in it believers are certainly sanctified by the Holy Spirit, such a Church he affirms will always remain, although at times it is more, at times less frequent. Thus far Philip. Osiander renders this paraphrase of the Apostle's words: For I do not want you, says Paul, to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, which has hitherto been incredible to the Jews; I will recall this to your memory, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation; more correctly: so that you may not be puffed up in spirit among yourselves: Because (it is an expletive particle) blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved, that is, blindness has happened to the Israelites, not so that all Jews should perish, but so that meanwhile, while the Gentiles are converted in great numbers, many of the Jews also may be saved: and thus all Israel (that is, the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles) may obtain salvation. (But let us not exterminate the Jews from the world for that reason, because there are still some elect among that people, to be brought back to the Christian faith before their death.) The Weimar Paraphrase retains the same sense: Blindness (and hardness of heart) has happened (to the people of) Israel in part (to some Jews), so long, until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, (so long as the calling and conversion of the Gentiles in great numbers lasts) And so all Israel shall be saved. (that meanwhile, while the Gentiles are converted to Christ in great numbers, also many many of the Jews will obtain salvation, and thus the whole Israel, namely the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, will obtain salvation.) The same opinion is held by the blessed Johann Pappus, an eminent theologian of Strasbourg, in his commentary on Hosea 3:4. As far as that question pertains to the universal conversion of the Jews who are to survive before the last day, I consider it a fabrication of the same sort as that concerning the Antichrist who is to arise from the lineage and tribe of Dan and is to reign for three years and a half. It is not indeed our place to deny repentance to any human being, whether Jew or Gentile: but neither is it our place to invent a universal conversion of any nation, which the Holy Scriptures have not predicted. For that passage to the Romans, if it is looked into more deeply, not only does not confirm this opinion for which it is brought forward, but even clearly overturns it. For in this also lies that great mystery, which Paul proclaims in other epistles, that all Israel is to be saved, consisting of the remnant of the Jews and the fullness of the Gentiles: nor does Paul affirm that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, others from carnal Israel are still to be enlightened, but he announces that immediately after the fullness of the Gentiles, all Israel will be saved: that is, according to the doctrine of chapter 9 and also this chapter 11, that the spiritual Israel is to be considered, and its gathering from Jews and Gentiles. In almost the same manner, the blessed Dr. Daniel Cramer, part II, on the Kingdom of Christ, chapter IV, question VI, p. 332, explained the testimony of the Apostle, except that he did not take 'Israel' collectively of the Gentiles and Israelites according to the flesh, but of these alone in the latter verse: We concede that under the name 'Israel' the Apostle does not understand believers, but Jews according to the flesh; meanwhile, however, the whole difficulty is in these words, where he says: 'All Israel will be saved.' For it is asked whether Paul promises some illustrious and universal conversion of all and singular Jews, so that the Jews in crowds and simultaneously before the last day are to acknowledge Jesus Christ and are still to come to the Christian faith? But that this is not the mind of the Apostle is clear from a comparison of the words which the same man predicts concerning the fullness of the Gentiles. For just as the conversion of the Gentiles did not happen simply in a catholic and simultaneous way, but successively, sporadically, and gradually; so we concede that the Jews are to be converted sporadically and successively, and that already now quite a few have been converted, and from time to time not a few are being converted, who in the eyes of God are gathered and most notably enrolled, and constitute no small multitude. As we recently received from the living report of a certain Greek, very many Jews are being converted annually to the Greek Church under the Turkish Emperor. So much so that there is no need to establish that this Apostolic prophecy has not yet been fulfilled, as some wish. For although the conversion of the Jews seems too rare to us in these places, yet it is not non-existent. Although even in these places, where the portion of Jews is minimal, their conversion is rare, yet elsewhere in the more remote parts of Asia and Africa, where we said above that the Church is dispersed throughout the whole world, there is no doubt that frequent accessions of Jews to the Christian faith are taking place. Therefore, as far as that universal sign (ALL) is concerned, it looks to different and distinct times: namely 1. to the time of the Old Testament, 2. to the primitive Church, 3. to the Church which is to be in times more remote from the age of the Apostles. For that after the gathering of the Gentiles in these last and immediately preceding centuries, there will be an accession of Jews to the Church, no less than it had already happened in the time of the Apostles, that indeed is what the Apostle asserts in the mystery. So that thus all Israel, that is, as much that which was in the ancient Old

Testament times, as that which lived in the primitive Church, and indeed also that which is to survive in our centuries, and thus all Israel of all times, by the continuous increase of the Church, is to be saved and led to the knowledge of Jesus Christ. This is what the Apostle means in these words. The same was taught by the blessed Dr. Brochmand in his System on the Last Judgment, Question XIII. When the Apostle says: 'And so all Israel would be saved,' he does not mean this: that all Israel is to be converted to God in its own time, but the mind of the Apostle is that God is so far from having cast off His people by some absolute decree, that the Jews will all be saved to the last man, if, having cast off their unbelief, they place their hope in the Savior Jesus. For that this is the genuine mind of the Apostle Paul is so plain from the context itself that one can hardly contradict it. Therefore, the Israel to be saved is not just anyone from Israel, whether he believes or is an unbeliever: but all Israel to be saved is the Israel whom God foreknew, that is, whom He foresaw would be faithful. For Paul himself brings forward this interpretation in verse 2: 'God has not cast off His people whom He foreknew.' For just as unbelievers are said not to be known by God (Matthew 7:23), so believers are said to be foreknown (2 Timothy 2:19; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). The blessed Dr. Hülsemann agrees with this explanation in his unpublished commentary, whose entire explanation, because it is not publicly available, I am pleased to transcribe: Just as the fullness of the Gentiles about to enter into the Church does not signify all and singular Gentiles, neither of one nor of all ages, but that whole fullness which God has determined to call and bring to the Gospel: as John 10:16, 11:52, Acts 10:35, 1. Pet. I. 1. 2. et seqq. thus, by way of opposition, the fullness of Israel, or the whole Israel to be converted, by no means signifies the whole Jewish nation, all and singular, and indeed to be converted to Christ in the extreme or very last times before the destruction of the world. But by the force of the opposition, and also by the force of the phrase by which the Apostle is accustomed to circumscribe Israel in this matter, it signifies the whole number of the elect Jews, and that not at one peculiar moment of time, but to be called throughout the whole course of the New Testament; which is most greatly proved from those testimonies which the Apostle alleges from Isaiah in the place of a middle term. For these testimonies do not speak of a certain conglomeration of the whole Jewish nation, nor of an effect precisely future at the end of the age, but of the singular grace of the New Testament in its own seat, and therefore they are also applied elsewhere to the common benefits of all Christians, namely Heb. VIII. 8, X. 16, 2 Cor. III. 16. Compare the things said above concerning the πληρώματι [fullness] both of the Jews and of the Gentiles, v. 12 et seqq., and of the Jews in the first place. If this fullness were to be understood concerning the number of Jews to be converted at the time of the millennium, it would necessarily follow that after that universal conversion of the Jews, another conversion of all and singular of the Gentiles must also be expected, because the Apostle expressly says: just as from the lapse and fall of the Jews a universal conversion of the Gentiles followed, so from the conversion of the Jews a much more similar conversion of the Gentiles would follow: but the latter is absurd, therefore the former is also. And consequently the fullness of Israel or the whole Israel necessarily denotes the whole crowd of the elect, that is, some, as the Apostle expressly calls them, τινὰς ἐξ ἀυτῶν [some of them] v. 14. Our blessed Weller also embraced this opinion in his commentary, page 644. The Apostle judges that some from among the Jews are perpetually to be converted, and that the whole Israel, i.e., the son of promise, is at some time to receive the inheritance together with the Gentiles. Thus Osiander testifies that at different times Jews were baptized in great numbers and enrolled into the college of the Church, cent. V. lib. I. c. 24, cent. VI. lib. IV. c. 4 and 5, p. 244, 245, cent. VII. lib. II. c. 7, p. 95. We do not deny (which, however, is demonstratively evinced from this place it cannot, but it is known to God alone) that it is still possible, out of the singular mercy of God, that some notable number of Jews may approach the kingdom of the Messiah before his glorious return: that this may certainly come to pass, we pray with all our heart. The blessed Joh. Cluverus in Orthod. Apostol. on this passage explains it thus: The sense is: blindness has not befallen all Israelites, but only to a certain part, and only insofar as it was supplied by the assumption of the Gentiles. For πλήρωμα denotes also a supplement, Matt. IX. 16, Mark II. 21, which sense the comparison of verse 19 and the context argues to obtain here, dealing with the substitution of the Gentiles in the place of the fallen Jews. And thus, with the Gentiles supplying the place of those blinded, all Israel, not of the flesh, which it never is, but the one foreknown by God, i.e., the Israel of God, Gal. VI. 16, shall be saved. The blessed Dölingius in Anti-Christo τυμβογέρω book IV, ch. 9, p. 198. The exposition has it thus: Until the fullness of the Gentiles shall have entered, or as long as the doors of divine grace shall be open to the Gentiles, so long also will it be permitted to the Jews to enter by them with equal right; nay, even by them they are to enter, if indeed blindness has not befallen all the Jews, but only in part, so that thus all Israel, the entire assembly of the elect, gathered as much from the Jews as from the Gentiles, whom the Apostle calls the Israel of God in Gal. VI. 16, might be saved, and through faith in Christ might attain eternal salvation. Therefore this saying of the Apostle pertains not only to the last age, but to the whole duration of the New Testament, and most of all to the first four centuries, in which it is evident from the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles that many thousands of Jews received the Gospel, whom it is not doubted that they furthermore also educated their families and children in the faith of Christ for several generations, whence, having gradually forgotten their gentile name and origin, they were designated by no other name than the rest of the Christians, their holy seed meanwhile, and that which originated from Abraham according to the flesh, being nonetheless propagated throughout the most extensive world. The paraphrase of the blessed D. Danhwerus, a friend most closely joined to me while he lived, on the mystery of the Apostolic Apocalypse, p. 114, is this: I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, which I shall now disclose to you, a mystery hitherto unknown, paradoxical to reason, a secret of the heavenly court, stupendous, lest you be of haughty brow among yourselves, because spiritual blindness has happened in part as to number and degree to the Israel according to the flesh, until that time when the fullness or some great forest of the Gentiles shall have entered together into the kingdom of grace, at which very time, while it is running and finished, the Jewish nation shall be cleared by some great and solemn and exotic illumination, and thus its faith will stand by the prophecies of the Old Testament. Thus the whole Israel of God, not only the Israel from the Gentiles, but also the one converted in throngs from the Jews wandering here and there in the world, chosen by God according to the foreknowledge of the divine order observed, shall be saved. The blessed Danhwerus approves this on p. 106. Dölingius's opinion, that it is possible that some Jews may be converted toward the end of the world, but whether this will certainly happen cannot be affirmed, since no peculiar indication of that matter exists in the whole Scripture. Nor are those entirely alien to this opinion who, when they see from this Apostolic passage that it is not clearly established that a great number of Israelites will be converted AT THE END of the world, leave the matter in the middle, which we observe to have been done by our blessed Gerhard: inasmuch as he, having brought forward the foundations of both the affirming and the denying opinion, wished to define nothing, but concluded this question thus: What kind and how great the conversion of the Jews will be precisely before the completion of this oracle cannot be known apodictically. At least, therefore, that this oracle is not yet fully completed, and whether such and so great a multitude of Israelites is still to approach by a simultaneous conversion, so that it might seem that the whole Israel overcoming at that time would be saved, that indeed he did not determine at all. The blessed Menzerus also, even though he believed that opinion to be more probable which posits that the conversion of a great multitude will happen toward the end of the world, did not, however, interpret the word ALL ISRAEL as the whole Israel then to exist, but as all the faithful from the Israelites from the Patriarchs down to the end of the world, Vol. I, Giessen disputations in the analysis of ch. XI to the Romans. To us that interpretation seems closer to the scope of the Apostle regarding a great multitude of Jews to be converted to the Christian faith before the end of the world, so that the sense may be: Many of the Jews are already rejected, so that on this occasion the Gentiles substituted in their place might attain salvation. But it will come to pass that, with the Gentiles called to Christ throughout the whole world, there will never be lacking some from the Jews, and indeed toward the end of the world by far the most, who by the profession of the same doctrine will join themselves to them, as partakers of the same grace with them, so that thus the whole Israel, i.e., that entire multitude of believing Jews, from the Patriarchs to the very end of the world, may be saved. The opinion of the blessed Meisnerus on Hos. III, p. 326, regarding the conversion of the Jews before the last day, comes to almost the same thing: This conversion of the Jews, he says, 1. happens successively and particularly, when from time to time some pass over to Christianity. 2. or simultaneously and notably, when according to the said predictions the Jews shall be converted to Christ in some more notable way. And these things concerning our theologians. The blessed Matth. Hoe, Vol. II, is also accustomed to be brought forward for this opinion. Apoc. p. 506, but he rather asserts that a most extensive conversion of the Jews before the end of the world is predicted here in this place, loc. cit.

From the Reformed, however, Voetius himself grants the ὁμοψηφίαν [unanimity of vote] in Vol. II, disp. sel., p. 127, of his Calvin, Hyperius, and Wollebius in Compend. Theol., to whom must be added also Rivetus, commentary on Hosea III, p. 216, that this mystery, which the Apostle unfolds from the Prophets, concerns only the conversion of the Israel of God, or the spiritual Israel, i.e., the fullness of the Gentiles and the remnant from the Jews, who, partly converted then by the Apostles, and partly to be converted subsequently until the end of the world, although few, are to be converted.

From the Fathers, Origen contributes to this in ch. XI, from whom it is helpful to cite a few things a little more fully, so that it may be clear how truly he is alleged by Voetius for the contrary opinion: 'But who this "all Israel" is, who will be saved, or what this "fullness of the Gentiles" will be, God alone knows, and His only-begotten Son: and if there are any who by chance are His friends, to whom He might say: "I will no longer call you servants, but friends: because I have made known to you all things which I have heard from the Father." This, however, can also occur to our understanding, that just as Israel, as long as it remains Israel according to the flesh and has not also become a true Israelite according to the spirit, seeing God with the mind, cannot attain to salvation: so neither can all the Gentiles altogether be saved, unless those which shall have been found within the fullness, whatever that is, which is named by the Apostle.' Thus, therefore, the mystery of God is handled by a certain ineffable dispensation of His wisdom, so that even when a soul has procured for itself a lot of evils, He, who knows how to dispose all things, makes its rejection and punishment the salvation of others. But that also seems to me to be considered more diligently in the passage, that he does not say that this blindness has happened to all Israel, but in part. For the remnant according to the election of grace have been saved. Concerning which remnant also Isaiah had prophesied, saying: "Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed." These remnants, therefore, are compared in blessedness with the fullness of the Gentiles: but the others, who are blinded from Israel, are compared to those Gentiles who could not attain to the fullness. If, therefore, those things which are found in the words of the Prophets concerning Scriptures containing blessedness by promises, if they concern Israel, pertain to those remnants which have been elected: if they concern the nations, they look to the fullness. But if any sad things are said, if indeed they are said of Israel, they are without doubt referred to those remaining and who have been blinded, but if of the nations, they surely constrain those who are outside the fullness. Jerome, who is also sometimes praised by the other side, comment. on Is. XI. In that day, in which the root of Jesse rose up for a sign of the peoples, or as the ruler of the nations, the Lord will apply his hand a second time, so that by no means according to our Judaizers at the end of the world, when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel may be saved; but let us understand all these things in the first advent. Ambrosiaster was also rashly brought forward by Voetius, who teaches nothing about a notable conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world; he only teaches that those who have returned to the faith will be received, and, he says, with the abundance of the nations admitted, the darkness will be wiped away from the eyes of the Jews: indeed, he accepts that the saying of Isaiah brought forward by the Apostle refers to the successive and daily conversion of the Israelites: There shall come out of Zion, he who may deliver: The reason for this example, he says, always remains, as long as there are those who believe: For this Lord Jesus, who is promised to come from the heavens for the liberation of the human race, he himself daily remits sins to those converted to him, and does not immediately condemn those not believing, but waits, knowing they can progress to the acknowledgment of God. Nor was Theophylact brought forward from the truth, whose interpretation holds thus: What will that mystery be? Namely, that the Jews will not be entirely faithless, but that there is blindness on their part. For most of them, whom God had foreknown, have attained faith, and hereafter many are to believe. And furthermore: Their fathers were already long ago from the beginning elected by God; therefore God will not allow them to perish entirely, but, if they shall have believed, he will receive them.

However, some other Fathers, Augustine lib. XX. de C. D. c. 29. John Chrysostom hom. LVIII. in Matth. Theodoret ad h. l. and Bede, fascinated by the opinion about Enoch and Elijah returning at the last time before the judgment, which then, as Augustine says, will become most famous in the sermons and prayers of the faithful, asserted entirely that that notable conversion of the Jews would happen a little before the last day. Which opinion, however, was false, and rests on nothing but the apocryphal book of Sirach, and that same one less skillfully translated into Latin c. XLIV. (and XLIX.) and the ψευδερμηνείᾳ (false interpretation) of the words of Christ Matth. XVI. 11.

Therefore, as to the mind of the Apostle, that he does not speak about a simultaneous or universal conversion of the Israelites, or one of a great multitude, to be in the last times of the world, and still to be expected. We readily give our assent to B. Luther and others of our own already praised, and we judge that this oracle should be accepted as referring rather to a successive conversion coming from time to time until the end of the world, so that from that time of the Apostle, not a small, but an altogether great number of Israelites is still to arrive at faith and eternal salvation. The reasons which are brought forward for this opinion, and can be brought forward, are certainly more pregnant. For first, the Apostle unfolds the mystery, not from some hidden decree of absolute predestination, from which most Reformed deduce the other opinion about a great multitude of Israelites to be converted at the last time, nor to be explained by a miraculous or extraordinary conversion through Enoch and Elijah returning from Paradise, which are figments of the human brain, not divine mysteries; but concerning justification through faith in Christ regarding the nations equally and the Israelites, which is the proper argument of the Apostolic dissertation: namely, that because of unbelief most Israelites were indeed blinded and hardened, yet the approach is not closed to the whole nation, but that not a few are to be saved from time to time through faith, just as salvation comes to the nations through faith, and while the fullness of the nations enters, also some from the Israelites are to enter at every time; if indeed a final blindness did not happen to all in general, but to Israel only ἀπὸ μέρους (in part). Truly this is a mystery, both by reason of the persons, that in the nation of the Israelites, by whom the Lord of glory was crucified, the author of life killed, by whom also Christ is daily torn apart by perpetual blasphemies, and the means of salvation are stubbornly and impiously rejected, there are still many who attain salvation: then by reason of the times, that even during the entry of the nations, and with the greatest part of the Israelite nation persisting, indeed with whole visible congregations dispersed here and there of Apellas in that stubborn obstinacy, so that no greater hope of Jews to be saved appears than seemed to be the case in the time of Elijah concerning the Israelites, yet in all ages here, there, and yonder some are to be converted to the faith of Christ, and together with the faithful from the nations, through faith in the one Savior of the world are to attain salvation, then by reason of the duration of grace, that until the πλήρωμα (fullness) of the nations enters and the times of the nations are fulfilled Luke XXI. 24. i.e., until the consummation of the age, the door is left open and unlocked for the Israelites, the most perverse enemies of Christ and truly ἀσπόνδοις (implacable), so that they themselves may also enter, and are to enter from time to time, until at length also their number, defined by God from the foreknowledge of faith, is completed, and thus πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ all Israel may be saved. If it was a notable mystery that the Gentiles should be συγκλη- ρόνομοι, σύσσωμοι, and συμμέτοχοι of the promise in Christ through the Gospel, Eph. III. 5. sqq., even though the promise had been made to all the nations of the earth long ago in the blessed seed of Abraham, why should it not be considered a singular mystery that, with the Israelite nation hardened through the greatest ἀπισίαν, a πώρωσις nevertheless happened to them only ἀπὸ μέρους, and hope is still granted concerning the remaining ones, not a small number, being saved, out of the infinite mercy of God. Although, therefore, it has been in the open that some of the Jews are converted daily, this is nevertheless proposed as a mystery: that from now on the conversion of the Jews is to be expected from time to time while the fullness of the Gentiles continues, and that not just a few of them will be converted, but a good many, since blindness has befallen Israel only ἀπὸ μέρους, so that when πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ is to be saved, a great future accession is still indicated within that time until the consummation of the age, which will contribute not a little to the fulfilling of all that Israel. Voetius is therefore in vain, in that he claims the Apostle inculcated nothing new, nothing besides what had already been said in chapters IX, X, and XI, and nothing of a mystery concerning the conversion of the Jews in v. 25 and following, provided that that conversion is understood as being from v. 2, 4, 7, and no other more illustrious one. For it has already been noted that a more frequent and notable conversion is indicated, both by reason of number or multitude, and by reason of times and duration. Nor is there any reason for Voetius to warn that the Apostle is accustomed to use the word 'mystery' to signify a future thing still latent in its causes. For it is also used in Eph. III. 4, 12 regarding a thing that was already happening and was not entirely latent in its causes, namely the conversion of the Gentiles, as also regarding a thing already done, the incarnation of God, 1 Tim. III. 16; and the greatest part of the future conversion of the Jews was certainly still latent in its causes.

Furthermore, the word ἀπὸ μέρους, 'in part,' abundantly teaches that the Apostle wished to signify something that happened to a part of the Israelite nation in respect to the whole of Israel, not only of that time, nor even only of the last times, but of all future ages; because he prophesies about future times in general, and not about the last times only, nay, he even embraces his own age, and looks simultaneously at the Israelites dispersed everywhere in all places and nations: from whom, to some part both of his own age and of the following times, at least a πώρωσις (hardening) has happened, with remnants always remaining, which are saved in every age. B. Dannh. notes in Apocal. myst. Apostol. p. 108 that ἀπὸ μέρος (in part) is said here not only by reason of number: it says in part (so August. Ep. LIX.), because not all were blinded. For there were some of them who knew Christ. And not only by reason of time, as Ambrosius explains at this place, but also by reason of degree, which πώρωσις admits: for there are given increments of blindness: just as also some are more easily converted to the true light than others, and perceive divine grace.

Thirdly, the word γέγονεν (has happened) refers no less to the past time, because that blinding of the Jews is observed primarily in the days of Christ's flesh, John 1:5, 11; 12:40 (cf. Isa. 6:9), as also afterwards in the time of the Apostle, Acts 28:26-27, than to the future, and that not only or primarily the last time—for no indication is found here that the extreme times before the final judgment are primarily regarded—but of all ages and centuries: just as history and fulfillment have taught, that which from the time of Christ and the Apostles has been continued until now, which the Apostle says here: πώρωσις ἀπὸ μέρος τῷ ἰσραὴλ γέγονεν (a hardening in part has happened to Israel). But the best interpreter of prophecies is the event.

Fourthly, that ἄχρις ὗ (until) must be well observed, by which the end and limit of the blinding of the Israelites is designated, namely, that it will not have an end except with the end of the world: for this is the ordinary meaning of the word, from which therefore one should not rashly depart: in which the Israelitic people indeed have this peculiar trait, that that πώρωσις (hardening) remains perpetually, which is not easily found in other nations. For as its sins were most great, and its ingratitude incomparable against the greatest benefits shown to this people above others, so by the just judgment of God such and so long-lasting a hardening happened to it above others; but since it is indicated that the πώρωσις (hardening) happened to it only in part, room is still left for the conversion of some, and because that ἀπὸ μέρος (in part) is continued until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, so that all Israel may be saved, it is manifest that conversion will also happen from time to time until that limit designated by the Apostle.

Fifthly, the whole phrase ἄχρις ὗ τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ (until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered) does not denote any limit of the centuries immediately following the Apostle, or any other before the last day, both because the event has proven that through these sixteen centuries and what has passed since this oracle was promulgated, the hardening has still happened to Israel in part, and because in the parallel passage, Luke 21:24, concerning the earthly Jerusalem being trodden down by the Gentiles ἄχρι πληρωθῶσι καιροὶ ἐθνῶν (until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled), the limit is established as the end of the world, since the signs that will precede the final coming of Christ are immediately added, v. 25: And there shall be signs, etc. Therefore Euthymius rightly understands by the times of the Gentiles those which will last until the consummation of the Gentiles and of the whole world. For it is not indicated that Jerusalem will ever be recovered by the Jews, but that it is to be possessed and trodden down as long as there are Gentiles upon the earth. Cf. Dan. 9:27. But the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles extends without doubt as long as the times last, or until they are fulfilled; τὸ πλήρωμα καιρῶν ἐθνῶν (the fullness of the times of the Gentiles) and τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν (the fullness of the Gentiles) explain each other. Therefore, it is taught that with the entering Gentiles, whose fullness will finally follow with the consummation of the age, not a few Israelites also, because the hardening happened to them only in part, will enter and be converted to faith in Christ. Which likewise has been proven by the event: for even in the Apostle's own time, although that πώρωσις (hardening) lasted in part of Israel (Acts 28:26), a great number of Israelites were converted, just as James with the other brothers reported to Paul at Jerusalem: see how many myriads there are of Jews τῶν πεπιστευκότων (who have believed), Acts 21:20. Which passage must be well observed.

Sixthly, B. Dannh. observes that the word εἰσέλθῃ (has entered/enters) denotes not only the past but also the future, 1 Cor. 11:25, Gal. 3:19, Matt. 5:20, 10:11, 18:3, Mark 6:10, 10:15, Luke 9:4, 18:17, Rev. 21:27, and thus explains it in this way on p. 112: εἰσέλθῃ, i.e., it will enter in the future, and it has entered in the past. The Latins explain both the past and future sense in the subjunctive with one word, introiverit (has entered). This εἰσέλευσις (entry), as he notes, alludes to an entry into some kingdom (Matt. 23:13), a city (Matt. 19:3), a house (Luke 10:5), a sheepfold (John 10:1), through the narrow gate (Matt. 7:13), as if by violence, just as is accustomed to happen in a dense mass of an entering army. Therefore, the entry into both the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of glory of a great multitude of Gentiles is designated, the number of which is known to God alone. Therefore, the Apostle of the Gentiles prophesies not only concerning that which is finally to happen in the last times, but that which, from the time of the πωρώσει (hardening) of the Jews after the manifestation of Christ, whom they rejected through ἀπιστίαν (unbelief), was bound to occur until the consummation of the age. Wherefore, there is no reason why we should concede to Voetius that the Apostle is speaking of a future conversion of the Jews, not yet begun at that time, so that the conversion of the Jews might follow the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles: for this, as we have observed, is finally terminated by the consummation of the age. Moreover, that sense—that when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in such a way that there is no longer any entry for them, then the Jewish nation alone is to occupy the kingdom of heaven—is discordant and most alien to the scope of the Apostle.

Seventhly, the words καὶ ὕτω can be taken either χρονικῶς (temporally), as 'and then,' as Estius understands it, because at the consummation of the age all Israel will be saved, or τροπικῶς (tropically), so that it is the same as 'thus,' 'in such a way,' 'so,' as if to say: 'So and thus it is true, what the Prophets predicted would be, that all Israel shall be saved.' Neither sense hinders the explanation given, but the temporal signification is especially appropriate, because the salvation and eternal blessedness of the elect follows the consummation of the Church or of the kingdom of Israel and of the world or age. In which manner this present passage again corresponds to the parallel cited in Luke 21:24.

Eighthly, πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ (all Israel) is explained by some as the Israel of God, Galatians 6:16, which they say consists of the fullness of the Gentiles and the faithful Israelites of all times: but in our judgment it is better that it be understood as Israel according to the flesh, which both the use of that word in the preceding verses and the apposition of the πληρώματος (fullness) of the Gentiles demand: yet not as it rejoices in carnal generation, but as it is truly Israel at the same time. For πᾶς (all) or the whole Israel is understood, just as the πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν (fullness of the Gentiles), and just as by the fullness of the Gentiles all the nations which have been divinely defined κατὰ πρόγνωσιν τῆς πίςεως (according to the foreknowledge of faith) are indicated, but not indeed all nations, much less the individuals of all nations in the universe: so all Israel indicates not the whole Israelite nation in general and all its individuals, but denotes all the Israel foreseen by God, the people of God whom he foreknew, Rom. XI. 2. whom he inscribed in the book of life, Dan. XII. 1. 2. Therefore, the points which Voetius opposes to our explanation are of no moment; for what he objects first, that the syncategorema πᾶς implies universality, but does not suit a small number: it does not hinder us. For in our opinion, more are comprehended by this syncategorema than according to the Voetian interpretation. For there are more elect of all times from Israel than the faithful Israelites whom he hopes will be converted all at once before the final judgment. These do not constitute a certain body; for they are understood either as contemporaries before the last day, such as even Voetius himself does not admit will all and singular, without exception, be converted, or successively very many in later times; to constitute a peculiar universality or a certain determined body of these, which is called πᾶς ἰσραὴλ, is inconvenient: because others are added to that multitude from time to time: but the assembly of the elect from the Israelites is best called πᾶς ἰσραὴλ: not that all Israelites according to the flesh are elect, but that all those who from them belong to the Israel of God, and are truly Israel, just as Jacob was adorned with that name, Gen. XXXII.

But as for what Voetius further urges, that the πᾶν of this nation is expressly opposed to the remnant or the few excepted and exempted from that nation, v. 5. 6. 7. 8. Resp. It is not opposed to the remnant, but embraces them; because it comprehends all Israelites who have ever been and will be until the end of the world, whom, namely, God foreknew.

Ninthly, the word σωθήσεται does not sound of a bare profession of Christianity, or conversion to the Christian religion, but of salvation: that all Israel is about to obtain salvation. Conf. Rom. X. 13. Act. II. 41. Therefore, it is not a question of the simultaneous bringing of Israelites to the Christian religion under the final times, but the successive conversion and justification of Israelites until the end of the world is tacitly vindicated, while blindness still befalls others of the same, but it is directly taught that, just as the fullness of the Gentiles, so also all Israel, who from the Israelites according to the flesh is truly Israel through faith, and such perseveres, and departs, is eternal, so that not a total rejection of the Israelitic people is to be presumed, but the conversion of a great multitude is to be believed.

Tenthly, therefore, we can here urge the reason of parity with the blessed Gerhard, who holds as follows: As the conversion of the Gentiles was not done once and for all, but successively, so the Jews seem to be converted here and there and successively, which, if all who are converted by Christians, especially in Greece, are counted, will constitute a not contemptible multitude. Since in the time of the Apostles many myriads were counted, Acts XXI. 29, and one myriad contains ten thousand, how great the number of converted Jews in Jerusalem alone was, is manifest. If, when the affairs of the Jews were flourishing, so many myriads came to the gain of Christ, who, after those same affairs were taken away, will calculate those who in other corners of the earth, dispersed throughout the whole world (witness Philo in the embassy to Gaius. Conf. Joseph. l. IV. c. 12.) endured to be called by the pipe of the best Shepherd: for the sermons and enticements sent forth to those who were in the dispersion were not without success, as R. Dannh. has it here, l. c. p. 27. And Osiander reports that Jews were received into the bosom of the Church in great numbers at different times, Cent. V. l. 1. c. 34. Cent. VI. l. 4. c. 4. & 5. Cent. VII. l. 2. c. 7. Conf. also the Ecclesiastical History of Hottinger. When in the year of Christ 1412, Jerome of the Holy Faith, formerly a Jew, but

converted to Christ, publicly recited in Spain before the Roman Pontiff Benedict XIII and the Cardinals in a most crowded assembly of Christians and Jews the book written by himself against the Jews, more than 5000 Jews were converted to Christ, as is mentioned on the frontispiece of the book.

Eleventhly, there is added the argument of the Apostle drawn from the testimonies of the Old Testament: which certainly ought to agree with both the oracle and the theme being demonstrated. But these can by no means be understood of the conversion of the Israelites under the latest times, but speak most openly of the first coming of Christ, Is. LIX. 20, and of the times of the New Testament, Jer. XXXI. 31. 34. Which reason, if it alone be attended to, invincibly builds up our opinion, and convinces us that we cannot accede to those who wish it to be predicted here that the conversion will happen only at the end of the world. For thus the testimonies brought by the Apostle would not square, as they can by no means be restricted to the latest times of the world. The blessed Dannh. embraces these testimonies with such a Syllogism: Every covenant of God is irrevocable, fixed in eternal tablets, never to be rescinded: for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable, as regards the order and the whole of the people. The covenant concerning the Jewish nation not being utterly rejected, though now an enemy, but beloved according to election, for the sake of the Fathers, and to be restored again, is the covenant of God that must be saved. Therefore, both Prophets deliver the minor premise, in the places alleged, and the context.

Twelfthly, the remaining arguments of the blessed Luther and others contribute to this, which intercede against such a general conversion of the Jews, which some believe will happen at the end of the world. Those are collected briefly by the blessed Gerhard; that, namely, such a conversion is not to be expected 1. because of the triple curse to which the Jews are subject, first the general one, Deut. XXVII. 15, then the proper one spontaneously attracted by those words: His blood be upon us and our children, Matt. XXVII. 25, and finally that pronounced by Christ himself through the mouth of David, Ps. LXIX. 34, CIX. 17. 2. because of the stubborn rejection of the means of conversion and salvation. For they blaspheme Christ in their synagogues, calling him Thalui, and upon the mention of his deeds they add, let his name be blotted out, and they spit three times upon the ground; they accustom their children from their earliest childhood to curse Christ and the Virgin Mother of God; if anyone refutes their errors from the word of God, they stop their ears, etc. 3. because of Paul's prediction that the revelation of the Anti-Christ will be the last most memorable work of God before the end of the world, 2 Thess. II. 8. but if a universal conversion of the Jews were to intervene between the revelation of the Anti-Christ and the end of the world, the Apostle would not have set forth the nearest sign of the coming of Christ. 4. because of the duration of the calling of the Gentiles, which in Luke XXI. 24, 25 seems to extend until the end of the world. Finally, because of the prediction of Christ and the Apostles concerning the scarcity of believers and the multitude of heresies and corruptions toward the end of the world: with which that explanation can in no way be reconciled. To say nothing of the fact that the blessed Dannhauer also refutes that opinion concerning the final conversion from those things which precede here: since this explanation does not cohere with them: For it does not follow, he says: You Romans ought to lower your crests, not to oppress the Jews, because after the passage of sixteen centuries they will still be converted in great numbers: It could be retorted thus: let these things be said to those Romans who are to live then, what is it to us, the latest of men? whom, as we do not know, so neither can we despise? If the Jews contemporary with us are not to be despised, because from these dark ones after many centuries the children of light will arise. Therefore we today are to be held in hatred, because at some time the Anti-Christ will proceed from us. The blessed Dannhauer adds that this explanation is incongruous for the Jews contemporary with the ancient Apostle: for what does a remedy for blindness help those Jews who lived then, if it is deferred so very long? will the covenant stand firm for him with the whole people, if it is salutary to the whole people so late? He also urges the connection of the context in this way: In chapter X, salvation depends on the chain of the divine order: Faith comes from hearing, etc. But ordinary conversion has no place where the whole nation is most densely dark, and hemmed in by such great darkness that, just like those Egyptian ones, no star can dissipate it, extremely blind, extremely obstinate, recalcitrant against all pedagogy, and stubbornly resisting all the means of the divine order. Here there is need for more than an ordinary divine action. But it is permitted to doubt at the very least that God will break through adamantine hearts with such power. The blessed one urges the consequences in the context. In chapter XI, the fatherly heart is revealed as universally and equally merciful to all: For God has shut up all, etc. But how is it catholic, how is it equal, if the shower of divine converting grace is only late and abundant in the evening of the world, while in the earlier circle of centuries it distills dews sparingly? Finally, the same man urges the absurdities: Imagine the outcome of this Apostolic Prophecy suspended until the very last age of the centuries, how great will be the inequality of the Jews and the Gentiles (in the reconciling, equalizing, and conciliating of whom the Apostle is entirely occupied), the former excluded from the kingdom of heaven for so many centuries, the latter accepted for so many centuries? And these things concerning those matters.

It remains that we speak of the opinion of Grotius. He restricts this statement about all Israel being saved to the time then imminent; he says that it was indeed fulfilled concerning the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles through the journeys undertaken by Paul after this Epistle was written. But the fullness of the Gentiles had not yet entered when the Apostle undertook various journeys, since countless numbers from the Gentiles have entered after the death of the Apostle, and even now are entering, and are about to enter until the end of the world, Luke XXI. 24. Nor can πᾶς ἰσραὴλ be restricted to those times which were then most imminent: whatever may be the case regarding what he says, that a certain great multitude of Jews had then embraced Christ, and that this first happened when military signs were seen in the sight of the temple. Add that it is falsely accepted that this σωθήσεται refers only to the profession of Christianity, when it should be understood concerning eternal salvation. Nor indeed is there any evidence of such a multitude converted to the Christian religion at that age, which could be called πᾶς ἰσραὴλ. What of the fact that Grotius himself in his work on the truth of the Christian Religion accepts the Apostolic passage concerning the notable conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world? But the passage in Apoc. VII is irrelevant here. For the faithful who are sealed are understood to be not only from the nation of Israel, but from all nations: because that benefit of sealing is common to all the faithful, 2 Cor. I. 21, as spiritual Israelites, Rom. IX. 6, 8. For just as the carnal Israel had twelve tribes, so this spiritual one is gathered from all nations, tribes, and peoples, and languages. Certainly, the distinctions of all the tribes of Israel have long since been utterly abolished. For the ten tribes, as can be seen in 2 Kings XVII. were so dissipated by Salmanassar the Assyrian, that from that time no one could say that this or that Jew was from this or that of the ten tribes. Then Emperor Titus also so dissipated the tribe of Judah, that now no one can say that he is from that tribe, as was rightly observed by the blessed Pappus in his commentary on the Apocalypse, MS, citing the blessed Dannhauer, l. c. p. 64. Then the faithful who are sealed are not to be converted at last, but are already converted and to be guarded from the dangers of falling and apostasy, and sealed as the most cherished pledges of God. Cf. the blessed Dannhauer in Antichristosophia, Sect. I, art. 9, page 320. But the Apocalypse is by no means dealing with a signature made to that end, so that the sealed might be exempted from the common evils of the Jews. But concerning that passage of the Apocalypse, in its own place, God willing.

Latin:

οἱ κατὰ φύσιν. Nempe κλάδοι ex Abrahamo nati. ἐγκεντρισθήσονται τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐλαίᾳ) Sic suam arborem dixit Ovidius: Ut sua quod peperit vix ferat arbor onus.

In similitudine locum habet naturæ adjutorium. Id verò cave ne in applicationem trahas. Nihil e- nim natura, nihil prosapia Abrahamica confert, un- de facilior sit insitio Israëlitarum, qui per incredu- litatem defracti sunt. Illud ergò πόσῳ μᾶλλον est quantò magis, intuitu nempe promissorum Patriar- chis factorum & radicis sanctæ, sed eâ, qua diximus ratione, non verò quantò facilius: Notat B. Wel- lerus ex Augustino super Psal. LXX. duo miracula in oleastri in olivam insertione, unum est, quod di- cat (Apostolus) oleastrum insertum esse in oliva, cum è contrario oliva inferi soleat in oleastro. Alte- rum quod oleaster ille insertus in oliva, non oleastri, sed olivæ fructus protulerit, cum in naturali insertione contrarium accidat: siquidem id, quod inseritur, ipsum est, quod crescit fructumque fert, non arboris in qua inseritur, sed surculi, qui fuit insertus. Unde Apo- stolus hanc insertionem παρὰ φύσιν merito vocat.

PARS III. APODICTICA. De Israëlitus magnam partem salvandis.

ν. 25. ὀ γὰρ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο. Μυστήριον est res arcana, quam homines nisi Deo dante scire nequeunt ut 1. Cor. XV. 51. Apoc. X. 7. XVII. 7. Dan. II. 18. 19. 27. 28. 29. 30. 47. IV. 6. Dicitur & de hominum arca- nis Tob. XII. 6. Judith II. 2. Sirach. XXII. 24. XXVII. 16. 17. 21. 2. Macc. XIII. 21.

ἵνα μὴ ἦτε παρ' ἑαυτοῖς φρόνιμοι. Ex Proverb. III. 7. ubi in Græco: μὴ ἴσθι φρόνιμος παρὰ σεαυτῷ, secundum LXX. μὴ ἴσθι σοφὸς secundum alios in- terpretes. In Hebræo est: Ne sis sapiens in oculis tuis. Ma- nuscriptus hic habet ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, quomodo Esaïæ V. 21. καὶ οἱ συνετοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. Sensus est: Ne existimetis vos ita esse prudentes, ut vestro ingenio putetis vos, quæ futura sunt, posse prænoscere.

Proponit Apostolus primò thema quod pro- bandum: deinde argumenta probantia. Thema or- nat elogio mysterii, quod verè res arcana & abscon- dita sit, quod DEUS de Judæis decreverit, quam nemo penetrare possit, aut cognoscere ullatenus, sine divina revelatione. Chrys. hom. XIX. in Rom. Μυστήριον ἐνταῦθα ἀγνοόμενον καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον λέγων καὶ πολὺ μὲν τὸ θαῦμα πολὺ δὲ τὸ παράδοξον ἔχον. Tum verò causam; cur id proponat, adfert: nimi- rum ne gentiles παρ' ἑαυτοῖς φρόνιμοι sint, cujus vim non assecutus est Grotius, ne existimetis vos ita prudentes esse, ut vestro ingenio putetis futura vos posse prænoscere; nam hoc ipsum jam voce μυστηρίs satis expressum erat: siquidem Grotio fatente myste- rium res arcana sit, quam homines nisi DEO dante scire nequeunt. Proinde alii rectius exprimunt, ne intus insolefcatis: quod φρόνιμος h. l. non ad pru- dentiam sed ad affectum referatur, usitatâ in S. lite- ris loquendi formulâ, quâ dicantur superbi sapere in oculis suis, ut Prov. III. 7.

ὅτι πώρωσις ἀπὸ μέρους τῷ Ἰσραὴλ γέγονεν. ἀπὸ μέρους hic dixit, ut supra τίνες τῶν κλάδων, molli locu- tione, cum significare vellet plurimos: ἀπὸ μέρους & ἐκ μέρους frequentia Paulo, ubi vult dicere non omnes, aut no omnino.

Vocem ἀπὸ μέρους ad tempus nonnulli referunt, ἀπὸ μέρους quod ad tempus obduratus sit Israël, sed citra ex- emplum, vel locum parallelum, in N.T. Ideò rectius de parte quadam Judæorum accipitur: quæ

Augustini, Chrysostomi, Theodoreti & aliorum est explicatio; & confirmatur cum ex modo loquendi quia τὰ ἐπὶ μέρυς & τὰ ἐν μέρει sunt Philosopho particularia: τὸ μὲν μέρος quod mearum est partium; tum e vers. 7. Electio consequuta est, reliqui vero ἐπωρώθησαν obdurati sunt.

ἄχρις ὗ τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ. Πλήρωμα hic, ut supra 12. est ingens multitudo gentium facile exuperans Judæorum numerum, qui non crediderunt. Impletum autem hoc per itinera Pauli, quorum multa suscepit post scriptam hanc epistolam. Introierint autem, intelligi Dei populum.

καὶ ὕτω πᾶς ἰσραὴλ σωθήσεται. Alludit ad dictum Hebræorum: omnem Israelitam partem habiturum in futuro sæculo. Et ut sæpe faciunt Apostoli, in sensum meliorem hoc trahens, significat id verum fore de vero Israele, id est de iis, qui Jacobi sive Israelis patientiam in malis imitabuntur, de Israele DEI, ut loquitur ad Gal. VI. 16. Simul autem innuit adesse tempus, quo non pauci, ut antea, sed magna quædam multitudo Judæorum Christum esset amplexura; id autem evenit primum cum videre Judæi impletum quod Christus dixerat, idola Romanorum, id est, signa militaria apparitura in conspectu templi, qua de re diximus ad Matth. XXIV. 15. Tunc enim multi Christianismum amplexi simul cum ante factis Christianis exempti sunt secuturis malis. Hi sunt illi signati Apoc. VII. Nam sicut olim Nabuchodonosoris tempore omnes, qui legem Mosis erant secuti, & propterea, per ת id est, תורה signati dicuntur, Ezech. IX. 41. liberati sunt a multorum exitio: ita tunc qui crucis signum gerebant in corde. Post id vero, excisa urbe, exciso Templo, cum jam multo clarius veritas vaticiniorum Christi appareret, servitutis etiam personalis onus multorum fregisset ferociam, quod & in Babylonico exilio olim evenerat, multi plane Judæi Christum amplexi sunt, Vespasiano & Tito id non impedientibus. Justinus in persona Tryphonis alloquens: ὃν ἐπὶ τρόπον διὰ τὰς ἑπτακισχιλίας ἐκείνας τὴν ὀργὴν ἐπέφερε τότε ὁ Θεὸς, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ νῦν ὐδέπω τὴν κρίσιν ἐπήνεγκεν ἢ ἐπάγει, γινώσκων ἔτι καθ’ ἡμέραν τινὰς μαθητευομένες εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τῦ χριστῦ αὐτῦ καὶ ἀπολείποντας τὴν ὁδὸν τῆς πλάνης, οἳ καὶ λαμβάνυσι δόγματα, ἕκαστος ὡς ἀξιοί ἐστι, φωτιζόμενοι διὰ τῦ ὀνόματος τῦ χριστῦ τύτυ. ὁ μὲν γὰρ λαμβάνει συνέσεως πνεῦμα, ὁ δὲ βυλῆς, ὁ δὲ ἰσχύος, ὁ δὲ ἰάσεως, ὁ δὲ προγνώσεως, ὁ δὲ διδασκαλίας ὁ δὲ φόβε Θεῦ.

Accipit ergò illud ἄχρι exclusivè & determina- te, ut sit, usque dum, adeoque definiatur certus terminus ad ingressum πληρώματος gentium, quo finem consequuto demum cessatura sit πώρωσις Israelis; Introitum autem illum finit cum itineribus Pauli; sed hoc partim precarium est, nullo nitens documento; partim etiam supponit fundamentum nimis lubricum, quod πλήρωμα talem multitudinem gentium designet, quæ facile exsuperet Judæorum, qui non crediderunt, numerum; partim falsum est: quia πώρωσις non tantum eousque Israeli contingit, sed in hunc usque diem durat in populo Israelitico. Porrò alludere Apostolum ad dictum Ebræorum, omnem Israelitam partem habiturum in futuro seculo, unde, obsecro, constat, aut unde docebitur saltem dictum illud tum in usu jam fuisse, aut quo exemplo ostendetur, quod talia sæpe Apostoli in sensum meliorem trahant?

Quod ad mysterii Apostolici sententiam, variæ reperiuntur de eadem opiniones: Plerique censent prædici conversionem insignem Judæorum, sub finem mundi, è quibus Chiliastæ credunt regnum quoddam corporale ad mille annos à Christo in ipsa Judæa super Judaicum populum Hierosolymis erigendum, quales inter suos nonnullos fuisse Socinus, in Miscell. p. 50. 51. perhibet, quam tamen sententiam ceu falsam, absurdam & perniciosam ipse reprobat.

Simile commentum legitur in Onere Ecclesiæ Scriptoris Pontificii Anno 1519. adornato: Anno 1620. recuso, de Judais post occisum Anti-Christum convertendis, & mille annis cum Christo in his terris regnaturis, in statu, quem ita vocat, septimo Ecclesiæ: de quo c. LXVI. p. m. 362. In illo septimo statu, inquit, finietur carnalis Ecclesia, siquidem Judai & omnes tribus Israel una cum cate- ris gentibus totius terrarum orbis ad fidem Christi convertentur teste Apostolo, cæcitas ex parte contin- git in Israel, &c. 3. Qui in Calvini Schola Chilia- smum propugnarunt, pariter ex hoc loco conver- sionem maximè insignem sub finem mundi proba- re conati sunt: utpote Curio Professor Basileensis, qui libr. de amplit. regni Christi probare satagit, numerum salvandorum multo majorem fore, quam damnandorum, & Judæos omnes ante extremum ju- dicii diem ad veram Messiæ agnitionem convertendos esse. Piscator cum conversione Judæorum novissi- ma non Chiliasmum tantùm fovet, sed etiam mar- tyrum resurrectionem ante universalem resurrectio- nem, quos etiam ascensuros in cælum dicit, ac ibi cum Christo regnaturos. Thomas Brightmannus An- glus in Apocal. ad c. XX. p. 663. Dilectam urbem esse illam κατ' ἐξοχὴν multitudinem credentium Judæorum ait, qui hinc tandem in gregem verè credentium adscribentur. Sed imprimis ex profes- so peculiari Diatribâ Joh. Henr. Alstedius Piscato- rem suum sequutus è mille annis Apocalypticis millenarium felicissimum, post destructum magni Anti-Christi regnum asserere, regnumque marty- rum resuscitatorum in hisce terris statuminare la- boravit, ac Judæorum universalem conversionem sub finem mundi futuram ex loco nostro Aposto- lico deduxit p. 119. Christiani, inquiens, Orientales zelo Christi ardentes & in ipsam Asiam penetrantes provocabunt ad zelum Judæos Rom. XI. & Babylon spiritualis præda erit omnibus gentibus: in quam sen- tentiam multa alia Scripturæ testimonia abripit, & consensum aliorum quorundam Doctorum è Re- formatis adducit. Nec alienum esse ab hac Chilia- starum opinione Grotium in Annot. ad Luc. XXI. 24. circa locum istum observavimus.

Alii etsi abhorreant à millenariorum errore, Judæorum tamen conversionem novissimam aliis commentis locupletant, quod tum ab aliis vete- ribus factum, tùm ab Augustino l. XX. C. D. c. 29. de Elia ultimo tempore Judæos converso, & à Chrysost. homil. LIIX. in Matth. & homil. XIX. in Epist. ad Rom. nec non à Theodoreto ad h. l. Postquam enim gentes prædicationem susceperunt, illi etiam (Judæi) credent, ubi magnus Helias venerit, & fidei doctri- nam iis attulerit: ut & Beda in h. l. Sed audaciores Papistæ sententiam de Elia redituro aut esse de fide, aut fidei proximam pronunciant, ut habet Schva- rez. Tom. II. in I. Thom. disp. LV. & contrarium si non hæreticum, ad minimum hæresi proximum esse contendunt, cum Bellar. l. III. de Rom. Pont. c. 3. Audacissimi verò omnium sunt Malvenda & Cor- nelius à Lapide, qui etiam numerum convertendo- rum definiunt, quem ille l. II. de Anti-Christo c. 17. p. 202. non solum cum Pererio è l. XV. in Daniel. tantum esse ait, ut præ eorum, qui in impietate mansu- ri sunt, paucitate rectè & verè dici possit, omnis Israel crediturus: sed etiam seq. p. in Apoc. 144000. nu- merum esse Judæorum asseruit, non omnium univer- sè, qui tunc credituri sint, quoniam is multò major e- rit, sed eorum duntaxat, qui post fidem Christi susce- ptam pro ea ab Anti-Christo trucidabuntur; denique interfecto & in infernum fulminibus demerso Anti- Christo plenissimè peragendam Judæorum conversio- nem. Hic verò Cornelius Lapideus ad Apoc. VII. in fine mundi, inquit, ex singulis Judæorum tribubus 12000. convertentur ad Christum &c.

E nostris verò Theologis nonnulli, qui & so- mnium Chiliastarum, & commentum Judaico - Papisti- cum de reditu Enochi & Eliæ maximè detestantur, Apostolum tamen hoc loco notabilem quandam Judæorum conversionem sub finem mundi futuram prædicere credunt. B. Mylius in h. l. ita argumen- tantem facit Apostolum: Futura est tandem ante- finem mundi luculenta populi Israelitici ad Christum conversio, Ergò istis non est insultandum propter ab- jectionem præsentem. Mysterium hoc, addit B. My- lius, appellat Apostolus, quia nisi in specie ab Aposto- lo hoc predictum fuisset, in mentem vix cuiquam ve- nisset. Tametsi huc aliqui respexisse etiam Christum arbitrentur Luc. XXI, 24. Hoc vaticinium illustre, cum nondum sit impletum, implendum esse certò per- suasum habebimus, priusquam dies Domini ingruat. B. Ægid. Hunnius hanc instituit paraphrasin: Dico vobis singulare hoc mysterium, excæcationem illam Israelis seu populi Judaici non esse totalem, sed ex parte tantùm: quæ locum habitura est, donec ma- gna illa plenitudo gentium complebitur, & sic deinde totus Israel (per quem Synechdochicè maxima quæ- dam populi Judaici pars juxta usitatum Scripturæ morem intelligitur) salvabitur, conversus scil. ad verum Messiam, quando Judæi infinito suo exi- lio edocti & nimia sed vana expectatione Messiæ (quem modò venturum esse augurabantur) fatigati, tandem rem altius per DEI gratiam expendent; nimirum tempora omnino adventui Messiæ dicta jampridem completa; & proinde non posse alium pro Messia agnosci, præter eum, qui jam ante publico orbis testimonio pro vero Messia sit agni- tus & in Evangelio declaratus. Addit autem B. Hunnius, se nemini hâc sententiâ suâ præscribere: Hæc de sententia verborum Pauli dicere placuit, ne- mini interim præjudicans; optans autem ex animo, ut Judæi aliquando magno numero ad Ecclesiam an- te ultimum illum Christi adventum accedant, & una cum plenitudine gentium salventur. Ecquis v. hoc non optaret? B. Balduinus ad h. l. p. 719. Appa- ret D. Paulum vaticinari de illustri quâdam con- versione Judæorum, quorum magna pars ante novis- simum diem Messiam agnoscet, & ad Christianorum fidem se aggregabit: quod vaticinium etsi impletum nondum est, non tamen dubitandum, quin suum cer- tò habiturum sit eventum, tempus soli Deo notum est, ideò mysterium nobis est. B. Andr. Keslerus, in inau- gurali disput. Jenæ habitâ Anno 1627. de Dictor. V. & N. T. allegat. c. 1. th. 7. de populi Judaici fu- turâ conversione explicat, quâ licet non omnes omni- nò Judæi, tamen magno numero sint convertendi: In quam sententiam adducitur, etiam B. Gesne- rus, B. Meisnerus in Comment. in Hos. III. B. Jacob. Martini B. Helvicus, in Elench. Judaic. B. Hafenrefferus in Templ. Ezech. p. 313. Addi- tur & B. Brentius: sed quanquam ille prioribus temporibus dum Commentarium in Hoseam ad- ornaret, quod Anno 1531. factum, illi accesserit sententiæ, φροντίδες tamen δευτέρας ejusdem alias fuisse è Commentario in Epist. ad Roman. anno 1564. hoc est 33. annis post conscripto docent. Lu- cas verò Lossius ita concedit huic sententiæ, ut etiam veterum illam de Enocho & Elia opinionem non planè reprobet, sed in medio relinquat, utpote de qua nihil certi affirmari & constitui posse affirmat.

E Reformatis generali Judæorum circa novissi- ma tempora conversioni favent non pauci, atque de eâ accipiunt imprimis locum præsentem Apo- stolicum Gisbertus Voëtius, qui eandem T. II. select. Disp. p. 127. propugnavit ac pro sua sententia, quo jure quàve injuriâ viderint alii (nam in compilan- dis autoribus plerumque magis copiosus est, quam accuratus) laudare non dubitavit Martyrem, Be- zam, Deodatum, Junium, Piscatorem, Pareum, Willetum, Rollocum, Anglos Theologos autores no- væ, & publicæ receptæ translationis, ut & illos, qui notas q. Ecclesiasticas in universa Biblia edidére An. 1645. autores novæ translationis Belgicæ; translatio- nem Gallicam publicè ibi receptam in hypothesi capi- tis: quibus porrò addit Danæum in Ethica Christia- nál. 2. c. 13. Francisc. Lambertum in comment. ad A- poc. 20. Cellarium tr. de Oper. Dei, Plessæum in ad- monit. ad Judæos, Tilenum Syntagm. T. 2. disp. 34. Polanum Syntagm. l. 6. c. 59. & l. 7. c. 22. Cameronem in myrothec. ad Rom. XI. 30. p. 169. & Capellum ib. in spicileg. p. 101. Cunæum de Republ. Hebræor. l. 1. c. 18. Job. Weemsum à Lathocker. tract. de filiis degeneran- tibus part. 4. sect. 8. Perkinsum tract. de fine seculi, Brigsbman. in Apoc. 15. & 16. & 20. Justum Heurnium de Legatione ad Indos capessendâ cap. 4. Forbesium in Instruct. Historico-Theol. p. 221. Jacob. Lauren- tium in Paulo δυσνόητῳ p. 295. & 464. Prideaux in Operib. Theol. part. 2. Orat. 6. p. 50. Hullum in com- mentar. Anglico ad 2. Petr. 3. 519. Wilhel. Gouge in tract. Anglico ad Judæos; Maccovium in Colleg. disp. part. 2. disp. 17. Sed Brightmanni & Piscatoris sen- tentiam Chiliasmo accedere antea notavimus: Martyr verò novum, nescio quem, Anti-Christum expectat, sed valdè dubiè, dubius etiam omninò de Judæorum generali conversione in comment. ad h. l. quos fortasse redituros ait & suum agnituros Messiam, cum Anti-Christus spiritu oris Christi fue- rit interfectus: Item: poterit etiam fieri, ut, cum Ju- dæi crediderint, & gentes juverint post aliquod tem- pus, ut ingenium est carnis, oriatur aliqua securitas & licentia, præsertim si Anti-Christus sequatur, un- de infinitus numerus cum Judæis, tum ex gentibus à Christo alienetur. Forbesius non tantùm Judæorum, sed & Mahummedanorum conversionem expectat; Daneus non Judæos ad Christianos aggregandos, sed Ecclesiam Christianam ad Judæos transferendam esse conjicit. Job. Heurnius verò miras habet de his- ce divinationes, quas adducere operæ pretium non puto. Pareus verò ad finem mundi futuram conversionem magnæ Judæorum copiæ non tàm asserit, quàm definiri posse negat: probabili fide, id de fine mundi teneri ait, sed statim subjungit: Cum sit de mysterio, id definiri non licere; sic ambigui et- iam sunt Zwinglius & Bullingerus. Cæteros à Voë- tio adductos excutere haud vacat.

Ex dubiæ aut variatæ religionis hominibus idem statuere ait Voëtius Christophorum Besoldum in Pentadec. & Hugonem Grotium l. II. de verit. Re- lig. l. 2. sect. 8. sed præterire non debuerat vir dif- fusisimæ lectionis Georgium Calixtum ad signa ex- tremi Judicii referentem introitum plenitudinis gen- tium & populi Judaici in Ecclesiam, libro de supre- mo judicio Helmstadii anno 1635. edito p. 27. qui ut in aliis, hic etiam singularis esse voluit, non uno in modo:

(1.) Quum certum sit, ejus sententiâ, nonnullas gentes amplas & populosas intrà annos 400. aut 500. (quicquid fuerit de prioribus seculis) de Evangelio nihil omnino audivisse, planè consenta- neum videri, ut his ipsis antequam rebus mundi finem imponat (Deus) Evangelium prædicari faciat. Un- de verò certitudo ista docebitur? unde fidem fa- cturus est, quisquis applaudere huic opinioni vo- luerit, id quod dicitur planè consentaneum esse?

(2.) quod gentes, quæ hactenus ad Christum con- versæ non sunt, & ipsam obstinatissimam Judæorum gentem tandem conversum iri haud obscure doceat S. Paulus Roman. XI 25. sed quænam illæ gentes sunt hactenus ad fidem nondum conversæ? No- minat postea Calixtus pag. 29. Persas, Tartaros, & plerosque Indos, nec non Sinenses: sed uti sine dubio, de Persis, Tartaris & Indis falsus fuit, nunquam illos ad Christum conversos, nunquam Evangelium ipsis delatum fuisse, quum Persæ etiam N. T. in lingua sua habeant, nec notitiâ Christi omninò destituan- tur, aut Tartari aut Indi; ita de Sinensibus falsus ipse Calixtus est, ad eos quoque aliquando penetrasse, qui Evangelium annunciaverint, idq; indiciis aliquot probare conatum esse, qui eas gentes descripsit,

Janum Gonzalem de Mendoza Augustinianum, quos eo loco quidem nunquam fuisse ait, ut inter gentes, quæ Christiano nomine censentur, collo- cari potuerint, sed omnes eo loco aliquando esse debe- re, id verò absque petitione principii docendum erat, & è Scriptura constare oportet, si quis cum Calixto id credere velit. Nec verò quicquam tra- dit Apostolus de gentibus hactenus, h. e. ad nostra usque tempora nondum conversis, sed de suâ ætate loquitur, vel de tempore, quo illa scripsit, quo non- dum intraffe plenitudinem gentium indicat: nuspiam autem docet, omnes gentes ad Christum conversum iri. At plenitudinem gentium aliter, inquit Calix- tus, accipere non possum, quàm pro universitate gen- tium eatenus, ut nullus populus, cui nationis vel gentis appellatio conveniat, desideretur. Cur verò non possit aliter accipi? Quia ita plenitudo dicitur Ps. XXIV. 1. Domini est terra & plenitudo ejus, id est, quicquid in terra est, nulla prorsus revel parte ejus exceptâ; Adde Psal. L. 12.
