Nor indeed is the subject here the consequent divine will, but the antecedent, as they call it: not the special mercy toward the faithful, but the universal mercy toward miserable sinners, convicted of disobedience, and constrained under the same: and therefore not how God now affects these, now those with good things, when they have believed; but how he has deigned to have mercy on all men, according to the doctrine of the Gospel, because all have been concluded under sin through the law. By which argument the Apostle confirms the common misery of men and the disobedience and the universal grace and mercy of God, which he had said, that the door of grace was not closed to the Jews in general, even if a hardening had happened to them, which he had taught had not happened to the whole Israelite nation, but only to a part of it, since God has mercy on both Jews and Gentiles by the power of his immense grace, with which he embraces the whole human race. We have dealt expressly with this golden aphorism against the Calvinists who restrict the mercy of God in oracle LXXV. This only is to be observed here, that the word disobedience in this aphorism is not to be taken precisely of the unbelief of actual contumacy, but of original, since indeed God has also had mercy on many who were not under the unbelief of actual contumacy, as is evident from the example of infants, and the word disobedience also occurs concerning those to whom the Gospel was not actually preached, Eph. II. 2, Col. III. 6. and that what the Apostle called disobedience here, he calls sin in Gal. III. 22; since sin by its nature is joined with nothing but unbelief and contumacy: since by the power of original sin we are disobedient, nor can we not be such, before God converts us by the illumination of the mind and the creation of a new heart, and unbelief is the primary sin, the fountain and source of all others. For the scope of the Apostle is not to teach that whoever are saved are saved by the mercy of God: but to explain the order by which men are led to salvation, namely so that first they are concluded under sin, but then they may be able to enjoy the mercy announced in the Gospel unto salvation, which he does not say is of a few, but of all. Therefore the Apostle does not speak definitely of these or those Jews or Gentiles, but indefinitely of the Gentiles who have obtained mercy, and the Jews by no means absolutely excluded from mercy. He says all are concluded by the voice of the law under sin, not that they may perish, but that God may have mercy on all. Pareus acknowledged this in this place regarding the former member concerning the universal misery of men: God concluded all men under the prison of contumacy; from which it is given to none to escape, except through the mercy of the heavenly judge. Therefore our universal misery and the mode of liberation is briefly indicated. Other Calvinists also acknowledge this, commonly referring this saying to the fall of Adam, which however they falsely impute to the efficacious decree of God. Because God concluded all under disobedience not actively by working or effecting unbelief, but convictively, by arguing, convincing and condemning: not causally, but judicially, by which voice of the law, or legal and judiciary sentence, all men are accused of guilt, convicted of sin, and condemned because of sin, and are as it were cast into prison, and held as captives, the slaves of eternal condemnation, Deut. XXVII. 26. Compare the Greek Interpreters Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, and the Greek Scholia in this place. But in the Syntagma of the Reformed Confessions in the Repetition of the Saxon Confession, title concerning the remission of sins and justification, p. 247, the doctrine of universal grace is also proved from this place: It is most certain that the preaching of repentance pertains to all men, and accuses all men, so also the promise is universal, and brings the remission of sins to all according to those universal sayings: Come to me all, etc. John III. Rom. XI. God concluded all, etc. Thus Philip also reckons this promise in Rom. XI. in his response to the Bavarian articles, 21, p. 819, adding these memorable things to the universal sayings: What faith can there be, if the mind is driven away from the promise by these thunderbolts? Perhaps the promise pertains nothing to you, expect violent seizures and coercion; I know that more horrible disputations are moved by some, of which there certainly ought to be some limit: Therefore to these, who are in the assembly of the called, and are in sorrows, I propose the universal promise, nor do I place contradictory wills in God, and I often think of the agony of a certain holy man, who repeatedly uttered this voice before death: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. We have seen Luther himself in a certain agony of his, I and others, often repeating this saying: He concluded all under sin, that he might have mercy on all. In his commentary on this place, Vol. IV. Oper. p. 173. it has it thus concerning this Apostolic epiphonema: To be concluded under sin is not to be understood idly, but it embraces guilt, terror, judgment, and the punishments of sin, as if he were saying, all are guilty, all will be subject to the judgment of God, to death and to afflictions, just as David was concluded under sin when he was driven into exile, when he was tormented with horrible pains, according to the saying, God is a consuming fire; but he argues sin, not so that men may be left in sin and destruction, but so that they may be liberated through the Son. Here, therefore, consolation is immediately added: that he may have mercy on all. Gratuitous reconciliation is promised, which must be opposed to the temptation concerning merit, or concerning dignity, and the promise is universal: let us oppose this universal particle to the temptation concerning particularity, nor let us be disturbed by Stoic and Manichaean disputations, let us know that the Son of God himself brings forth this universal promise (Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, I will refresh you) from the bosom of the eternal Father, let us not imagine contradictory wills in God, but let us believe the Son of God sent for this very purpose, that he might be the messenger, witness, pledge, and sealer of the divine promise, as he says: God so loved the world, that everyone who believes in him should not perish. See, if you please, more of these ἐμόψηφα concerning the Apostolic sentiment, inferring universal grace, collected from the Calvinists themselves, in the declaration of Hermann Hildepr. p. 174. seqq.

O the depth of the riches.) Depth signifies the same thing as abyss, as in 1 Cor. 2:20 [sic], Apoc. 2:24. It refers, however, to the three following things, which he denies can be penetrated. Riches here is to be understood as abundance, namely of goodness, which name is added above in 2:4; he says it is impenetrable, namely, how God formerly endured the contumacy of the Gentiles, and then of the Jews, for so long.

and of wisdom.) That wisdom also is impenetrable, because he did not call the Gentiles until after the contumacy of the Jews had been shown to the world.

and of the knowledge of God.) This too is impenetrable, how he moved both the dispositions of the Gentiles and of the Jews, so that he might draw the former to himself by miracles never heard of, and the Jews partly by envy toward the Gentiles, and partly by extreme calamities. In Ps. 139:6, פלאיה דעת ממני. Thy knowledge is wonderful, too high for me to attain.

In this exclamation, the absolute Calvinist patrons of the decree of Predestination triumph. But Grotius rightly observes that the inexhaustible riches of divine kindness and mercy are celebrated here, no less than the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God; because the Apostle himself distinguishes the depth of the riches by the particle 'and' from the depth of the wisdom and also of the knowledge of God: whence he admires the depth of divine mercy no less than divine Wisdom, as St. Chrysostom also notes. It is pleasing to append what is held here in the manuscript notes of B. Hülsemann: This exclamation, by the force of its connection, praises the wisdom and goodness of GOD, who from the fall of the Jews raises up the salvation of the Gentiles. But it can by no means be shown to be for the exercise of God's punitive justice, for which a meritorious cause on the part of the punished man cannot be given, as Calvin, Beza, Martyr, and Pareus himself extend this passage. And all Calvinistic impiety, when it cannot be excused, is accustomed to be covered as if by this shield, which the Remonstrants noted in the Hague Conference, Brand. ed., p. 191. But if the sense of this exclamation is to be explained according to the nature of those things which immediately preceded, v. 32, the Apostle admires only that incomprehensible knowledge and benevolence of God, declaring through the manifestation of sin and iniquity on one side, and of his remedy and goodness on the other, not severity nor absolute reprobation, but rather his benevolence, so that it is great impudence to restrict the judgments and ways of God, because they have the benefits of God as objects in this place, to an absolute decree of reprobation, which Bertius also once agitated at length in his 'Hymenæus Desertor'. See ed. 1, p. 708 seq. Cocceius recognizes here the conclusion of the Apostolic treatment of justification, namely that he has shown, (1.) that all are in need of the justice of God. (2.) that it is by faith, and not by the law, and was given before the law, and was not abolished by the law, and is now manifested without the law. (3.) that it is true justice. (4.) that it belongs both to the Gentiles, and indeed to the Jews who were cast off for a time; yet so that in their own time they are to be reassumed: and thus that it is dispensed according to an immutable Testament: he demonstrates in summary that this whole doctrine is consistent with the glory of God: and thus, what he had said around the beginnings of this treatment, ch. 3:23, 27, he now as it were concludes.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Συνέκλεισε γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τὺς πάντας εἰς ἀπείθειαν) Id est, vicibus res agitur. Olim vos convicti inobedientiæ, nunc illi. Συγκλείειν est convincere, ut Gal.III. 22. ubi est ὑπὸ, eodem sensu, quo hîc εἰς, nimirum quia qui criminis alicujus convincuntur, tenentur ita constricti, ut effugium, id est, excusationem non habeant.

ἵνα τὺς πάντας ἐλεήσῃ.) Modò hos, modò illos bonis affi- cit,ubi crediderint. Agitur enim hîc non de communi Dei bonitate in genus humanum, sed de ea, qua credentes pro- sequitur.

Non tantum convictio, sed simul etiam ipsa constrictio, quæ per legem fit, condemnantem homines ob ἀπείθειαν, ut cogantur misericordiam implorare,ac pædagogi instar lex iisdem sit ad Chri- stum, ut loco parallelo Gal. III. habet Apostolus, designatur. Nam non tantum agnitio peccati est ex lege, Rom. III. 19. 20. sed operatur etiam lex iram, c. IV. 15. & maledictionem, Gal. III. 10. seqq. Nec verò de consequenti voluntate divina hîc agitur, sed de antecedente, quam vocant: non de misericordia erga fideles speciali, sed de misericordia erga miseros peccatores, de ἀπειθείᾳ convictos, & sub eâdem constrictos universali: ideoq; non de eo, quomo- do Deus modò hos, modò illos bonis afficiat, ubi crediderint; sed de eo, quomodo omnium homi- num misereri dignatus est, secundum doctrinam Evangelii, quia omnes per legem sub peccato con- clusi sunt. Quo argumento communis hominum miseria & ἀπειθείας & universalis Dei gratiæ & mi- sericordiæ confirmat Apostolus, quod dixerat, Ju- dæis non in universum occlusam esse gratiæ ja- nuam,etsi iis acciderit πώρωσις,quam non evenisse toti Israëliticæ genti, sed parti tantum ejusdem do- cuerat, quum & Judæorum & gentium Deus mise- reatur vi immensæ suæ gratiæ, quà totum genus humanum complectitur. De aureo hoc apho- rismo contra Calvinianos misericordiam Dei re- stringentes egimus ex professo oraculo LXXV. Id tantum hîc observandum, ἀπειθείας vox in hoc aphorismo accipi non præcisè de actualis contuma- ciæ infidelitate, sed de originali, siquidẽ etiam Deus misertus multorum est, qui non fuêre sub incredu- litate actualis contumaciæ, ut exemplo infantum constat,& vox ἀπειθείας etiam de iis occurrat,qui- bus actu prædicatum non fuit Evangeliũ Eph.II.2. Col.III.6. & quod hîc ἀπείθειαν dixit Apostolus,id Gal.III.22. ἁμαρτίαν vocet; siquidem peccatum naturâ suâ nonnisi cum incredulitate, & contumaciâ conjunctum sit: quum vi originalis peccati ἀπει- θεῖς simus, nec possimus non tales esse, priusquam Deus nos convertat mentis illuminatione, & cor- dis novi creatione, ac infidelitas primarium sit pec- catum,fons & scaturigo cæterorum omnium. Sco- pus enim Apostoli non est docere, quod misericor- diâ Dei salventur,quicunq́; salvantur: sed explicare ordinem,quo ad salutem homines perducantur,ni- mirum ita,ut primùm concludantur sub peccatum, tùm verò misericordiâ in Evangelio annunciatâ frui possint ad salutem, quod non dicit paucorum esse, sed omnium. Ideò Apostolus non definitè loquitur, de his, vel illis Judæis aut gentibus, sed ἀορίστως de gentibus misericordiam consecutis, & Judæis à misericordia neutiquā absolutè exclusis. Omnes conclusos dicit voce legis sub peccatum,non ut pereant, sed ut omnium misereatur Deus. Quod agnovit quantum ad prius membrum de universa- li hominum miseria Pareus in h. l. Deus conclusit omnes homines sub contumaciae carcere; unde evade- re nulli datur, nisi per misericordiam caelestis judicis. Miseria igitur nostra universalis & liberationis mo- dus breviter indicatur. Agnoscunt & alii Calvinia- ni communiter hoc dictum ad lapsum Adami refe- rentes, quem verò falsò Dei efficaci decreto impu- tant. Quia conclusit Deus omnes sub ἀπειθείᾳ non ἐνεργητικῶς operando, seu efficiendo incredulita- tem, sed ἐλεγχτικῶς, arguendo, convincendo & con- demnando: non αἰτιατῶς seu causaliter, sed δικα- στικῶς & judicialiter, qua voce legis, seu legalis ac judiciariae sententiae rei arguuntur omnes ho- mines, convincuntur de peccato, & condemnan- tur ob peccatum, ac velut in carcerem compin- guntur, ac captivi detinentur aeternae condemna- tionis mancipia, Deut. XXVII. 26. Conf. Graeci In- terpp. Chrysost. Theodoret. Oecum. & Scholia Grae- ca in h. l. In Syntagmate verò Confessionum Refor- matarum in Repetitione Conf. Saxon. tit. de remiss. peccat. & justif. p. 247. etiam gratiae universalis do- ctrina ex hoc loco probatur: Certissimum predica- tionem poenitentiae ad omnes homines pertinere, & accusare omnes homines, ita & promissio universalis est, & omnibus affert remissionem peccatorum jux- ta illa dicta universalia: Venite ad me omnes &c. Joh. III. Rom. XI. Conclusit omnes Deus &c. Sic accenset etiam Philippus hanc promissionem Rom. XI. in resp. ad Bavaric. artic. 21. p. 819. dictis uni- versalibus haec addens ἀξιομνημόνευτα: Quae potest esse fides, si depellatur mens à promissione his fulmi- nibus? Fortassis nihil ad te pertinet promissio, expe- cta violentos raptus & coactionem; scio alias dispu- tationes horridiores à quibusdam moveri, quarum certè modum aliquem esse oportet: Ergò his, qui sunt in cœtu vocatorum, & sunt in doloribus, propono universalem promissionem, nec pono contradictorias in Deo voluntates, & saepè cogito agonem cujusdam sancti viri, qui subinde repetebat hanc vocem ante mortem: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Vi- dimus ipsum Lutherum in suo quodam agone ego & alii saepè repetentem hoc dictum: Conclusit omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereretur. In comment. ad h. l. T. IV. Oper. p. 173. ita habet de hoc epiphone- mate Apostolico: Concludi sub peccatum, non est otiosè intelligendum, sed complectitur reatum, pavo- rem, judicium & pœnas peccati, quasi dicat, omnes rei sunt, omnes erunt subjiciendi judicio Dei, morti & afflictionibus, ut David erat conclusus sub pecca- tum, cum pelleretur in exilium, cum horribilibus do- loribus excruciaretur, juxta Dictum, Deus ignis con- sumens est, arguit autem peccatū, non ut relinquan- tur homines in peccato & exitio, sed ut per Filium li- berentur. Hic igitur mox consolatio addita est: ut omnium misereatur. Promittitur gratuita reconci- liatio, quae opponenda est tentationi de merito, seu de dignitate, & promissio universalis est: hanc particu- lam universalem opponamus tentationi de particu- laritate, nec turbemur Stoicis & Manichaeis disputa- tionibus, sciamus ipsum Filium Dei hanc promissio- nem universalem (Venite ad me omnes, qui labora- tis & onerati estis, ego reficiam vos) proferre ex sinu aeterni Patris, non fingamus in Deo contradictorias volūtates, sed credamus Filio Dei misso ad hoc ipsum, ut sit nuncius, testis, pignus & obsignator divinae pro- missionis, sicut inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat. Plura hisce ἐμόψηφα de sententia Apostolica, gratiam universa- lem inferente, ex ipsis Calvinianis collecta, vide sis in declaratione Hermanni Hildepr. p. 174. seqq.

ὦ βάθος πλύτε.) βάθος significat idem, quod ἄβυσσος, ut 1. Cor. II. 20. Apoc. II. 24. Refertur autem ad tria sequentia, quæ negat posse penetrari. Πλῦτος hic intelligenda abundantia, nempè bonitatis, quod nomen additur supra II. 4. eam ait esse impenetrabilem, nempè quomodo Deus olim gentium, deinde Judæorum contumaciam tamdiu pertulerit.

κὶψ σοφίας) Impenetrabilis & illa sapientia, quod gentes non vocaverit, nisi post ostensam Mundo Judæorum contumaciam.

κὶψ γνώσεως Θεῦ.) Est & hoc impenetrabile, quomodo permoverit & Gentium ingenia & Judæorum, ut illos quidem miraculis nunquam auditis, Judæos verò partim invidia in gentes, partim summis calamitatibus ad se pertraheret. In Ps. CXXXIX. 6. פלאיה דעת ממני. Mirabilis scientia tua præ quam ut eam assequar.

In hâc exclamatione triumphant Calviniani absoluti Prædestinationis decreti patroni. Rectè autem Grotius observat celebrari hic potius divitias inexhaustas divinæ benignitatis & misericordiæ, non minùs quàm profunditatem sapientiæ & cognitionis Dei; quia τὸ βάθος τῦ πλύτε distinguit ipse Apostolus per particulam κὲ à profunditate sapientiæ ut & cognitionis Dei: unde non minus profunditatem divinæ misericordiæ admiratur, quam Sapientiæ divinæ, notante etiam S. Chrysostomo. Placet adscribere, quæ hic in notis MSS. B. Hülsemanni habentur: Exclamatio hæc vi connexionis laudat sapientiam & bonitatem DEI, ex Judæorum casu suscitantis gentium salutem. Nequaquam verò ostendi potest ad exercitium justitiæ Dei punitivæ, cujus causa meritoria ex parte hominis puniti dari non possit, quomodo Calvinus, Beza, Martyr, Pareus ipse, hunc locum extendunt. Et omnis impietas Calvinistica, quando excusari non potest, solet quasi hoc umbone tegi, quod in Collatione Hagi. notarunt Remonstr. edit. Brand. p. 191. At verò si hujus exclamationis sensus exponendus est juxta naturam eorum, qui proximè præcesserunt, v. 32. admiratur Apostolus solam eamq; incomprehensibilem scientiam & benevolentiam Dei, declarantis per ostensionem peccati & iniquitatis ab unâ, remedii autem & bonitatis suæ ab alterâ parte, non severitatem neque absolutam reprobationem, sed potius benevolentiam suam, ut magna impudentia sit κρίματα & ὁδὺς Θεῦ, quia pro objectis habent hoc loco beneficia Dei, restringere ad absolutum reprobationis decretum, quod olim etiam Bertius in Hymenæo desertore multis exagitavit. Vide edit. 1. p. 708. seq. Conclusionem tractationis Apostolicæ de justificatione agnoscit hic Coccejus, quod nempè ostenderit, (1.) omnes justitia Dei indigere. (2.) eam esse ex fide, & non ex lege, & datam fuisse ante legem, & non sublatam per legem, & nunc manifestatam esse sine lege. (3.) eam esse veram justitiam. (4.) eam esse & gentium, & quidem Judæis per tempus abjectis; ita tamen, ut suo tempore sint reassumendi: atque adeò dispensari ex Testamento immutabili: hanc omnem doctrinam compendio demonstrat esse consentaneam gloriæ Dei: atq; ita, quod circa initia hujus tractationis dixerat, cap. III. 23. 27. id jam quasi concludit.

## 11:33
Ver. 33. How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out.) He calls the decrees of God 'judgments', in the Hebrew manner. The passage in Ps. 36:7 is referred to, where in the Greek: Thy judgments are a great abyss. You have 'judgments' in a similar sense in Ps. 119:91 and elsewhere. By 'ways', however, he understands those reasons through which God brings his decrees to their end. But Paul wishes to say this: I, whom God has honored with many revelations, have touched upon some parts of the divine dispensation, but far more things lie hidden from me, and what I have touched upon, I admire, I do not fully perceive. In Job 5:9 we read: I will call upon the Lord and Master of all, who does great and unsearchable things, glorious and extraordinary. And 9:10, who does great and unsearchable things, glorious and extraordinary. Origen against Celsus: For there are certain connections and sequences, unspeakable and indescribable, concerning the economy of the different human souls. Arnobius, book II. For it is not easy for anyone to see the mind of God, or by what ways he has ordered his affairs; man, a blind animal and ignorant of himself, can of his own accord follow the reasons. What ought to be done, when, or by what kind, the father, moderator, and Lord of all things knows alone. Salvianus: It is not therefore not just, what the divinity does, because man is not able to grasp divine justice. Just as God is more than human reason, so it ought to be more to me than reason that I know all things are done by God. The Hebrews note on Num. 15: One must not curiously inquire after the works of God: for he has done all things wisely, even if they are hidden from the eyes of the wise.

Such is the decree concerning the restoration of the human race, that both the divine justice may be satisfied and the mercy of God may shine forth; such is the way of justification and salvation of man through faith in Christ, and of condemning the incredulous; in which one ought to admire the depth of divine grace and wisdom. But why he made such decrees for men, and chose such a reason and way of salvation, that indeed is to us unsearchable and past finding out. Which must also be held concerning the dispensation of divine grace, how and why GOD dispenses grace either to these or to those; where indeed the reason for salvation or justification is not hidden, but revealed in the Gospel, namely that we obtain justice and salvation solely through faith in Christ: but the cause why he chose that reason for salvation, and the mode of the divine economy and its reasons, cannot be perceived and penetrated by us, why e.g. he calls now these, now those to the Church, why he grants the light of the Gospel to this nation and not to that, why he delayed the solemn calling of the Gentiles for so long, why he leads the Jews to the recognition of Christ at these or those times here or there, and not others or elsewhere, etc. An exclamation is added, says Philip, which breaks off the disputation, because although God is equal, and immediately in the beginning published the promise concerning the Mediator, and willed it to be known to all posterity, and for all posterity to remain in the true acknowledgment and invocation of God, and very often repeated the voice of the promise, and again gathered the Church: yet after a huge multitude presently forgot the promise, and horrendous furies followed. Human reason asks many things, why such a great multitude perishes in all ages, why so few are saved; why the Church is a dissipated and oppressed assembly, without certain authority and without beautiful order; why the impious multitude excels in empires, glory, wealth, many excellent virtues, wisdom and fortitude, why the devils are permitted to rage with such madness against this weak human nature. These and many other things exercise human thoughts, but Paul in this exclamation signifies that not all the counsels of God can be comprehended by human reasonings, but that the revealed word of God must be embraced, and one must not fall away from it, and these huge benefits which He offers must be received and retained with thankful minds, and His goodness and the justice of God must be celebrated. Afterwards in that eternal School we shall learn the causes of the divine counsels, just as it is very often commanded: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. Likewise, to the law and to the testimony, if they speak not according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. Likewise, this is my beloved son, hear him.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ὡς ἀνεξερεύνητα τὰ κρίματα αὐτῦ κό ἀνεξιχνίασοι αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτῦ.) κρίματα vocat Dei decreta, more Hebræo. Respicitur locus Ps. XXXVI. 7. ubi in Græco: τὰ κρίματά συ ἄβυσσος πολή. Habes κρίματα pari sensu Ps. CXIX. 91. & alibi. Per vias autem intelligit rationes illas, per quas decreta sua Deus ad exitium perducit. Hoc autem vult dicere Paulus: Ego, quem multis revelationibus Deus honestavit, dispensationis divinæ partes aliquas attigi, sed multò plura me latent, & quæ attigi, admiror, non pervideo. Jobi V. 9. legimus: Κύριον δὲ τῶν πάντων δεσπότην ἐπικαλέσομαι, τὸν ποιῦντα μεγάλα κό ἀνεξιχνίασα, ἔνδοξά τε κό ἐξαίσια. Et IX. 10. ὁ ποιῶν μεγάλα κό ἀνεξιχνίασα ἔνδοξά τε καὶ ἐξαίσια. Origenes adversus Celsum: εἰσὶ γάρ τινες εἱρμοὶ κό ἀκολυθίαι ἄφατοι κό ἀνεκδιήγητοι περὶ τῆς τῶν τὰς ἀνθρωπίνας ψυχὰς διαφόρυ οἰκονομίας. Arnobius lib. II. Neque enim promptum est cuiquam Dei videre mentem, aut quibus modis ordinavit res suas, homo, animal cæcum & ipse se nesciens, ultro potest mtionibus conse- qui. Quid oporteat fieri, quando, vel quo genere ipse cuncta- rum rerum pater, moderator & Dominus scit solus. Salvianus: Non ideo non justum est, quod divinitas agit, quia capere sinæ divina justitia homo non valet. Sicut plus Deus est, quam hu- mana ratio, sic mihi plus debet esse quam ratio, quod à Deo agi cuncta cognosco. Hebræi notant ad Num. XV. Non est cu- riosè quærendum post opera Dei: omnia enim sapienter fecit, tametfi abscondita sint ab oculis sapientum.

Tale est decretum de generis humani reparatio- ne, ut & justitiæ divinæ satisfiat, & misericordia Dei elucescat, talis via de justificatione & salvatio- ne hominis per fidē in Christum, & de condemnan- dis incredulis; in quibus admirari oportet divinæ gratiæ & sapientiæ profunditatem. Cur autem ho- minibus talia decreta fecerit, & talem rationem ac viam salutis elegerit, id verò nobis est ἀνεξερεύνητον καὶ ἀνεξιχνίαστον. Quod etiam de dispensatione di- vinæ gratiæ habendum, quomodo & cur DEUS dispenset gratiam sive his, sive illis; ubi quidem abscondita non est salutis vel justificationis ratio, sed revelata in Evangelio, quod nempè per fidem in Christum unicè justitiam & salutem consequamur: Causa autem, cur eam salutis rationem elegerit, & modus οἰκονομίας divinæ ejusdemq; rationes à no- bis percipi ac penetrari non possunt, quare e. g. modò hos, modò illos vocet ad Ecclesiam, quare huic, non illi nationi lucem Evangelii concedat, quare solennem gentium vocationem eousque distu- lerit, quare Judæos his illisve temporibus hic illic ad agnitionem Christi perducat, non alios aut ali- bi &c. Exclamatio addita est, inquit Philippus, quæ abrumpit disputationem, quia quanquam Deus est æqualis, & statim initio edidit promissionem de Me- diatore, & voluit omnibus posteris notam esse, & omnes posteros manere in vera agnitione & invoca- tione Dei, & sæpissimè repetivit vocem promissionis, & rursus collegit Ecclesiam: tamen postquam ingens multitudo subinde oblita est promissionis, & secuti sunt horrendi furores. Multa quærit humana ratio, quare tanta multitudo omnibus seculis pereat, cur tam pauci fiant salvi; cur Ecclesia sit dissipatus & oppressus cœtus, sine certo imperio & sine pulchro ordine; cur impia multitudo antecellat imperiis, glo- ria, opibus, multis excellentibus virtutibus, sapien- tia & fortitudine, quare in hanc imbecillem natu- ram humanam tanta rabie grassari diabolis permit- tatur. Hæc & alia multa exercent humanas cogita- tiones, sed Paulus in hac exclamatione significat, non omnia consilia Dei humanis ratiocinationibus com- prehendi posse, sed amplectendum esse verbum Dei re- velatum, nec ab eo deficiendum esse, & gratis menti- bus hæc beneficia ingentia, quæ offert, accipienda & retinenda esse, & ipsius bonitatem & justitiam Dei celebrandam esse. Postea in illa æterna Schola causas consiliorum divinorum discemus, sicut sæpissimè præ- ceptum est: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Item, ad legem & ad testimonium, si non dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit eis matutina lux. Item, hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite.

## 11:34
Vers. 34. For who hath known the mind of the Lord, or who hath been his counsellor?) These words are taken from the LXX, Isaiah XL. 13, 14. Earthly kings have counsellors who know their innermost secrets. But God does not admit men to His counsels. We do indeed know certain counsels of God, but those revealed by God, Matt. XI. 27, John I. 18, XV. 14, 15, 1 John V. 20, 1 Cor. II. 16, and those very things are a small part of the counsels of God. Wis. IX. 18, And thy counsel who hath known, except thou gavest wisdom, and sentest thy holy spirit from above? Sir. XVIII. 3, To whom hath he given power to declare his works? and who shall find out his noble acts? [Who shall number the strength of his majesty? and who shall also tell out his mercies? As for the wondrous works of the Lord, there may nothing be taken from them, neither may anything be put unto them, neither can the ground of them be found out.

The depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God in the hidden and unsearchable judgments and ways of the Lord is confirmed by a passage of Isaiah: concerning the depth of the riches of the grace of God in the justification and salvation of men without regard to works or merits, the rest treat: Who has first given to God, that it might be repaid to him? etc.

Latin:

Vers. 34. τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νῦν κυρίου, ἢ τίς σύμβουλος ἀυτῦ ἐγένε- το.) Sunt hæc verba sumpta ex LXX. Esai. XL. 13. 14. Re- ges terreni habent consiliarios, qui intima ipsorum nove- rint. At Deus ad sua consilia homines non admittit. Sci- mus quidem Dei consilia quædam, sed à Deo patefacta, Matth. XI. 27. Johann. I. 18. XV. 14. 15. 1. Johan. V. 20. 1. Corinth. II. 16. & ea ipsa exigua pars sunt consiliorum Dei. Sap. IX. 18. βουλὴν δέ σου τίς ἔγνω εἰ μή συ ἔδωκας σοφίαν, κὴ ἔπεμψας τὸ ἅγιόν σου πνεῦμα ἀπὸ ὑψίστων. Sir. XI. 3. τίνι ἐξε- ποίησει ἐξαγγεῖλαι τὰ ἔργα ἀυτῦ, κὴ τίς ἐξιχνίασει τὰ μεγαλῶια ἀυτῦ; [κράτG μεγαλωσύνης ἀυτῦ τίς ἐξαριθμήσεται, καὶ τίς προσθήσει ἐκδιηγήσασθαι τὰ ἐλέη ἀυτῦ; ὐκ ἔστιν ἐλαττῶ- σαι, ὐδὲ προσθῆναι, καὶ ὐκ ἔστιν ἐξιχνιάσαι τὰ θαυμάσια τῦ κυρίου.

Τὸ βάθος sapientiæ, & cognitionis Dei in judiciis viisque Domini absconditis & impervestigabilibus confirmatur loco Esaiano: de profunditate ver divitiarum gratia Dei in justificatione & salvation hominum citra intuitum operum aut meritorum agunt reliqua: Quis prior dedit Deo, ut retribua tur ei. &c.

## 11:35
V. 35. Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him. There are those who take this in the sense which is in Job XLI. 2: Who has anticipated me, that I should repay? But 'καὶ' is placed for 'ut' [that]. For this sentence says this: Who has anticipated God with gifts, so that he should be obliged to return the favor? The sentence, however, tends in the same direction as that in the Gospel of Matthew XX. 14: Take what is yours, and go. As if the Apostle were saying: If the reasons for the divine dispensation brought forward by me thus far do not satisfy anyone, let him consider that this is not a matter of returning thanks, but of bestowing a benefit: and one must be the arbiter of one's own benefit. Liberality has its name from liberty.

Merits are therefore excluded from the justification and salvation of men, and consequently also from election to salvation, which Estius acknowledges here, departing in that part, as far as election is concerned, from Pighius, Becanus, and other Papists: The sense, he says, of the Apostle is that no one can anticipate the beneficence of God by any merit of his own, whence it follows that every opinion of merit is to be excluded from Election or divine Predestination. Indeed, it follows that it is also to be excluded from justification and salvation. For the Apostle is properly treating of this here. Nor are we elected to salvation from eternity by any other reason than that by which we are led to salvation in time.

Latin:

V. 35. ἢ τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ, κὶ άνταποθήσεται αὐτῷ. Sunt, qui in hunc sensum sumunt, quod est Jobi XLI. 2 מי הקדימני ואשלם. Est autem καὶ positum pro ut Hoc enim dicit hæc sententia: Quis prior Deum muneribus ut vicem reddere debeat? Sententia autem eodem tendit, quo illud in Evangelio Matth. XX. 14. Tolle, quod tuum est, & va- de. Quasi dicat Apostolus: Si cui rationes divinæ dispen- sationis à me hactenus allatæ non satisfaciunt, cogitet non de reddenda gratia, sed de beneficio dando hic agi: bene- ficii autem sui quemque oportet esse arbitrum. Liberalitas à libertate nomen habet.

Excluduntur itaque merita à justificatione, ac salute hominum adeoq; etiam ab electione ad sa- lutem, quod agnoscit hic Estius, discedens eà parte, quantum ad electionem, à Piggio, Becano, aliisque Pontificiis: Sensus, ait, Apostoli est, neminem ullo suo merito beneficentiam Dei prævenire posse, unde sequitur ab Electione seu Prædestinatione divina omnem meriti opinionem esse excludendam. Imò sequitur etiam à justificatione & salvatione exclu- dendam esse. Nam de hâc propriè hic agit Apo- stolus. Nec alia ratione ab æterno ad salutem electi sumus, quàm quâ in tempore ad salutem perducimur.

## 11:36
Vers. 36. For from him, and through him, and to him are all things. From him all men are called to salvation, through him they receive good things, and that is so that they may honor him. 'ἐξ' signifies the operating cause, as 1 Cor. I. 30 and elsewhere: 'διὰ', the cooperating cause: 'εἰς' indeed the end, that for the sake of which something is done. You have those two, 'εἰς' and 'ἐξ', also in 1 Cor. VIII. 6. 'Πάντα' refers to that whole dispensation of which he has treated. Similar is what Theocritus says of King Ptolemy: And let Ptolemy be mentioned among the first, and the last, and the middle. To him be glory for ever. Amen.) Whatever things God does are not to be judged by us, but are to be received with veneration and praise. We have had similar epiphonemata twice above, I. 25, IX. 5. Thus Deut. XXXII. 3: Give greatness to our God.

Although this final doxology can be taken particularly concerning those things which pertain to the calling to the kingdom of grace and to our salvation, it is nevertheless general and extends itself to all the works of God. For since all things are from God the Father, and through God the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as the pious ancients have explained this, August. lib. I. c. 6. de Trinit., Hilary lib. VIII. de Trinit., Basil de Spiritu S. To this triune God alone is glory due for all things, and even most especially for those things which he does in our salvation to be procured from mere grace regarding our works or merits, so that we may have to profess: Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory; yours is the mercy, but to us is due confusion of face, Ps. CXV. 1. Dan. IX. 7. Basil. M. orat. XVI. de Spir. S. calls the Father in Creation the 'prokatarktiken' [pre-initiating] cause, the Son the 'demiurgiken' [creative], the Holy Spirit the 'teleiotiken' [perfecting]. From God the Father, as far as the business of salvation is concerned, are all things, inasmuch as he gave us the Son, and with him gives all things. Roman. VIII. 31, 33. Through the Son of God are all things; because the Son of God acquired and merited for us all things that pertain to our salvation, and through and on account of him we obtain all things, the remission of sins, righteousness, and salvation. In the Holy Spirit are all things, because the Holy Spirit works in us regeneration, conversion, faith, and sanctification, and all good things and spiritual gifts, to his own honor and glory, so that we may be consecrated to him as to the Spirit of glory, 1 Pet. IV. 1, and he himself may dwell in us as in his temple, 1 Cor. III. 16. Which 'eulogian' [blessing] the Apostle seals with the word Amen; so that all the pious may also sing along here, Amen. To us, says St. Augustine, serm. CXLV. de Tempor., consideration, admiration, trembling, exclamation, because there is no penetration. But to him what? Glory for ever. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ὅτι ἐξ αὐτῶ, κὶ δι' αὐτῶ, κὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα. Ab ipso omnes homines ad salutem vocantur, per ipsum bona accipiunt, idque ut ipsum honorent. ἐξ, causam ope- rantem significat, ut 1. Cor. I. 30. & alibi: διὰ, cooperan- tem: εἰς verò τέλος, id cujus causa fit aliquid. Duo ista εἰς & ἐξ habes & 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Πάντα refertur ad totam illam, de qua egit, dispensationem. Simile est, quod de Pto- læmeo Rege dicit Theocritus: Αἰδζῶν δ' αὖ Πτολεμαῖον ἐνὶ πρώτοισι λεγέσθω, Καὶ πύματος, κὶ μέσσος. αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν.) Quæcunque Deus agit, non à nobis dijudicanda, sed cum veneratione & laude exci- pienda sunt. Similia epiphonemata habuimus bis supr. I. 25. IX. 5. Sic Deut. XXXII. 3. δότε μεγαλωσύνην τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν.

Δοξολογία hæc finalis etsi peculiariter accipi de iis possit, quæ ad vocationem ad regnum gratiæ, & ad salutem nostram faciunt, generalis tamen est, & ad omnia Dei opera se extendit. Quum enim omnia ex ipso Dei Patre, & per ipsum Filium Dei, & ad ipsum Spiritum Sanctum sint, uti hæc pii veteres exposuère, August. lib. I. c. 6. de Trinit. Hilarius lib. VIII. de Trinit. Basilius de Spiritu S. Soli huic triuni Deo pro omnibus, adeoque vel maximè pro iis, quæ in salute nostra circa opera vel merita no- stra ex mera gratia procuranda agit, debetur glo- ria, ut profiteri habeamus: Tuo nomini, Domine, non nobis gloria; tua est misericordia, nobis verò de- betur confusio faciei, Ps. CXV. 1. Dan. IX. 7. Basil. M. orat. XVI. de Spir. S. Patrem in Creatione vocat causam προκαταρκτικὴν, Filium δημιυργικὴν, Spi- ritum S. τελειωτικὴν. A Deo Patre, quantum ad negotium salutis, sunt omnia, utpote qui dona- vit nobis Filium, & cum eo donat omnia. Ro- man. VIII. 31. 33. Per Filium Dei omnia sunt; quia Filius Dei nobis acquisivit & promeruit omnia, quæ ad salutem nostram faciunt, & per ac propter ipsum consequimur omnia, remissionem peccato- rum, justitiam & salutem. In Spiritum Sanctum sunt omnia, quia Spiritus S. in nobis operatur re- generationem, conversionem, fidem, & sanctificatio- nem, & omnia bona, & dona spiritualia, in sui ipsius honorem & gloriam, ut ei consecremur ceu Spiritui gloriæ, 1. Pet. IV. 1. ac ipse in nobis habitet tanquam in templo suo, 1. Cor. III. 16. Quam ἐυλογίαν voce Amen obsignat Apostolus; ut pii omnes ipsi quoq; hic succinant, Amen. Nobis, inquit S. Augustin. serm. CXLV. de Tempor. consideratio, admiratio, tremor, exclamatio, quia nulla penetratio. Ipsi autem quid? Gloria in seculorum. Amen.

## 12:1 Argument
THE LATTER PÆDEUTIC PART OF THE EPISTLE. Presenting exhortations or admonitions to the study of the holiness of life. SECTION I. CONCERNING NECESSARY DUTIES. SUBJECTION I. Presenting general rules. CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Exhortations to the duties of piety toward God, of a sober mind regarding ourselves, of charity regarding others, both in the administration of gifts and offices, and in the exhibition of mercy and love. To which are subjoined warnings regarding those things which are to be observed in carrying out duties, and in love toward the needy, strangers, and persecutors, and which are necessary for 'homonoian' [concord] and for fostering and promoting peace even with enemies.

Two parts can be established: The former contains exhortations concerning the due duties of the justified, up to v. 10 inclusive. The latter presents warnings concerning certain 'proskemenois' [things lying before/incidental matters] to be observed regarding duties, up to v. 21.

PART I. CHAP. XII. Concerning the due duties of the justified.

The Grotian distribution rests upon a false hypothesis, namely that the law is perfected through the Gospel, as if the law in itself had not been perfect, but had needed to be enriched and perfected as to its precepts by further additions through the Gospel, and that the Gospel, insofar as it is distinguished from the law, delivers more perfect moral precepts: which Pelagian, Socinian, and Arminian heresy, which most wretchedly corrupts, nay, utterly overturns the whole doctrine concerning justification hitherto delivered by the Apostle, namely that we are justified by faith in Christ without works, and is therefore not unwelcome to the Papists, we have noted more than once in Grotius. It stands thus here:

When Paul had taught that no one now attains to that righteousness which leads to eternal life, except through faith had in the Gospel, and that God had most serious reasons for why He so ordained it, and had solved those things which are wont to be objected, coming to the admonitions he shows in reality what he had said above in passing, that the law is perfected through the Gospel, and that by going through the individual parts of the Mosaic law, first the ritual, then that which governs judgments, XII. 1. Lastly that which governs morals, XII. 8. And he begins first with the ritual or Levitical, the chief of which are sacrifices, and among sacrifices עולה, that is, ὁλοκαύτωμα.

That the rituals of chapter XII are perfected is foreign to the truth. There is an allusion in v. 1 to sacrifices, or the secondary end of sacrifices is explained; which, as they were primarily offered for the sake of prefiguring Christ, the propitiation, chapter III. 24, who died and was offered for us, c. V. 8, for our redemption c. III. 4, and that we might be reconciled to God through His death c. V. 10, and shadowed forth the true sacrifice of the New Testament that was to come: so secondarily they reminded [men] of spiritual sacrifices, not only in the New Testament, but also to be offered by the faithful in the Old Testament, who even then were bound to present themselves to God as a living, holy, and to God pleasing sacrifice, and were reminded of this through the Levitical sacrifices. Nor indeed in chapter XII is regard had only to those rituals, what is done in v. 1: For the remaining part deals with morals, or the duties of piety, sobriety, and charity, even though Grotius draws all these to the Levitical; just as chapter XII regards not only judgments, but the entire Polity, and in it prescribes duties owed both to the Magistrate and to all persons whatsoever. Moreover, from that order, that the Apostle delivered the precepts of good works after the doctrine of faith had been premised, Dr. Georgius Major himself, in Vol. II of his Works, fol. 1, confesses that Paul shows by the very series of the doctrine that believers are justified freely, without any merits of good works, by faith ALONE, and that the doctrine of good works is to be separated from the righteousness of faith as far as heaven is distant from earth, and the rising from the setting sun, and that works are in no way to be mixed with the doctrine of justification. For faith alone, apprehending the Mediator, is the efficient cause, on account of which a believer's faith is imputed to him for righteousness. But thus, having been justified by faith alone, that is, on account of the Mediator alone, gifted with the remission of sins, with righteousness and the Holy Spirit, and having been made good trees, they ought afterwards to be filled with the fruit of righteousness, which comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God, Philippians 1.

Vers. 1. παρακαλῶ ὖν ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ. That is, since what I have said is so, I will give you admonitions consequent to that doctrine. This is the custom of Paul, which other ancients followed, to be accustomed to append the ethical after the dogmatic.

διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τῶ Θεῶ. By those properties of God described in Exodus 34:6. The Hebrews are accustomed, when they indicate the magnitude of mercy, to use the plural רחמים οἰκτιρμὸς, as in Nehemiah 1:11 and often in the Psalms.

παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν. παραστῆσαι is הקריב, otherwise προσφέρειν, which word you have concerning the burnt offering in Leviticus 1:2 and following. And θυσία is called a general name by excellence for a burnt offering, and therefore עולה is translated θυσία in Exodus 10:25, 29:42, Numbers 23:3, 28:13, Joshua 22:27, Job 1:5, Ezekiel 44:11. He shows by one example that rituals are fulfilled by more solid things, which correspond to those shadows from the opposite side: the Jews offer a dead body, you a living body, that is, together with the body, its actions: for to act is to live. He says the same thing here with an allusion to sacrifices (similar allusions to which you have in Philippians 2:17, 4:18), which is simply 1 Corinthians 6:20.

He draws the exhortation entirely from the preceding by the illative word in this place. For those justified by faith must strive for holiness, lest they fall away from faith and righteousness; nor is faith either idle, but ἐνεργυμένη δι᾿ ἀγάπης, working through charity toward God and neighbor, Galatians 5:6, nor does it allow believers to be idle and unfruitful, but rather that they supply virtue in faith, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge abstinence, in abstinence patience, in patience piety, in piety brotherly love, in brotherly love charity, 2 Peter 1:5 seqq. He calls them brothers because of the common regeneration and heavenly inheritance, and at the same time he implies by the name of brother that those who do not observe this exhortation are unworthy. 1 Corinthians 5:11. Therefore he exhorts and asks διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τῶ Θεῶ, through the mercy of God, which is the principal cause of our Justification, so that, mindful of the mercies shown to us, which is the greatest reason for loving GOD, and the best incentive of Love toward God who has mercy on us, and how grateful to us is the divine grace, lest, namely, we fall away from it, we may present our bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. And through the mercy of God we are cleansed from sin, and are constituted priests of God, Revelation 1:5, 6; 5:9, 10, and are brought in Christ, in whom alone we can approach God, so that we may present ourselves to him, and be thankful to him, John 14:6, Hebrews 11:6.

The word παραστῆσαι is sacrificial, because animals separated from the flock were presented before the Lord in the holy place ordained by Him, Leviticus 3:7, 12.

Mention of our bodies is made, not that the soul is excluded; for we cannot offer the body without the soul: and therefore in the oblation of the body is included the oblation of the soul, but the Apostle wished to name the body particularly, both because by this way of speaking the part by which we are more priests is more evidently distinguished from that part by which we are more the sacrifice; and because the body is required for a sacrifice, insofar as through it God is honored among others. By the word ϑυσίας, not only the burnt offering is regarded, because other sacrifices also were offered in the Old Testament, which prefigured the reasonable service. Cocceius observes a threefold sacrifice: 1. By which God is honored as creator, which is man and those things which are of man; while he consecrates himself and all his things to God. 2. By which God is honored and sanctified and justified as a judge justifying the ungodly justly and holily. And this is the ransom for sin, Ascham, that is, satisfaction or the expiation of guilt or fault. This is typically from cattle and in the shedding of blood: truly it is the obedience and death of the Mediator, which we represent to God when we approach God in the faith of the Mediator. 3. By which God is honored as merciful, which is ἐυχαρισικὸν. Which last is here primarily regarded. By ϑυσίαν ζῶσαν not only is an opposition in relation to the sacrifices of the O.T., which were offered dead, not living, insinuated, but also spiritual life, which is through faith, as well as the mortification of affections and desires, because those justified by faith ought to consider themselves dead to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus our Lord: It is shown, says the blessed Glassius in Exeg. Epist. T. I. p. 1090, at the same time the principle of this sacrifice, which is the vivification of the Holy Spirit through the word of life, of which Eph. I. 4. 5, as well as the opposite, that sins and dead works are, Heb. IX. 14. As much as is taken away from sins in the mortification of the flesh, so much is added to spiritual life in Christ and to this living sacrifice: Then the end and the consequent reward, which is eternal life, the hope of which is also called living 1. Pet. I. 4. Let us hear also those words of Luther in his enarrations on this passage, f. 164. Those sacrifices of the Old Testament were oxen, sheep, and goats, which as soon as they began to be sacrifices, life was taken from them, for they were slaughtered, burned with fire, and consumed by the priests. But this sacrifice of the New Testament is wonderfully constituted, so that it is indeed slaughtered at the same time, and yet lives; nay, the more it has been killed and slaughtered, the better and more strongly it lives. According to that in Rom. VIII. If you have mortified the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live. And Col. III. You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

ἁγίαν.) In the Law, whatever is offered to God is called holy, as Lev. XII. 4. Matth. XXIII. 19. how much more the bodies of men justified from all vices, that is, cleansed.

The flesh of the sacrifices was also called holy in the Old Testament, but typically; because it was consecrated as a symbol of the holy oblation of Christ, and a figure of our body to be consecrated to God, and to be sacrificed through zeal and charity, which the heavenly fire signified. Because those things are from the Holy Spirit, therefore our victim is called holy, not because of perfection, which is not found here, but because of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit by which we are sanctified, Rom. XV. 16. Which sanctification is not to be confused with justification. For the latter consists in the remission of sins and cleansing from sins, which is done by the blood of the Son of God, 1. Joh. I. 7. and is perfect: but the former is done by the renewal of us through the power of the Holy Spirit, but in this life it is imperfect, because we are not rendered πνευματικοὶ spiritual in every part, since there still remain relics of the flesh, and the flesh always lusts against the Spirit, Roman. VII. 14. seqq. Gal. V. 6. Sacrificialia Vet. Test. B. Glassius, he says, l. c. [loco citato], were called holy and consecrated to GOD, because they were separated from the rest of the flock according to His word and institution, and indeed such as were without bodily defect, as appears from Levit. I. 3. 10. c. XIV. 4.: and the blood of these, when finally brought to God, was poured out in honor and as a type of the future Messiah. Behold a pleasant figure of the holiness of spiritual sacrifices! Christians and believers are holy, because they are sanctified and consecrated to God through the word of GOD, which sanctifies all things 1. Tim. IV. 5. John XV. 3. c. XVII. 17. They are holy, because they are selected from the flock of profane worldly men, and are removed in spirit from earthly things John XVII. 16. They are holy, because they seriously study holiness and purity, and live ἀνεγκλητοι [blameless] 1. Thess. IV. 3. Hebr. XII. 14. 1. Petr. I. 14. 15. 16. They are holy, because they consecrate all their own to the honor of their Savior, and do not blush or refuse to shed their blood for his glory and confession. Apoc. XII. 11. Origen l. IX. in Ep. ad Rom. Those who mortify their members, offer a living beast rationally, and fulfill the law of sacrifices, which is in Leviticus, according to a spiritual understanding. If they conquer pride, they sacrifice a calf; if they overcome anger, a ram; if lust, a goat; if they prune the wandering and slippery flights of thoughts, doves and turtledoves. Chrysostom in h. l. [hunc locum]. The sacrifice of Christians, he says, is a matter of the mind and spiritual: for the temple is the breast of man, for the beast is the body of man; this is the affection of the flesh, for fire is the charity of God, etc.

ἐυάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ [well-pleasing to God]. A burnt offering is called ὀσμὴ ἐυωδίας τῷ κυρίῳ [a sweet-smelling savor to the Lord] Levit. I. 9. 13. 17. And often elsewhere. That applies much more to the bodies and actions of Christians, as can be seen in 2. Cor. II. 15. Philipp. IV. 18.

In order for a sacrifice to please GOD, it is necessary that it be offered through faith: just as the Levitical sacrifices also had to be offered by faith, without which it is impossible to please God. Hebr. XI. 4. 6. This sacrifice must be offered in Christ as the altar; because no one is pleasing to GOD except Christ the Son, the altar Ebr. 13. 10. 15. 16. Apoc. IIX. 3, Of which altar Cocceius also understands the passages in Is. 54. 7. Their (the strangers') burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be for acceptance upon MY altar: and Ps. LI. 21. Then shall calves ascend upon Thine altar.

τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ὑμῶν [your reasonable service]. The Levitical λατρεία [service] עבודה was δι᾽ ἀλόγων [by irrational things], that is, by beasts. For all mute living creatures are called ἄλογα [irrational] Sap. XI. 15. in the Glosses, animals ζῶα ἄλογα [irrational creatures]. Hence ἀλογευθῆναι [to be treated as irrational] in the canons. But we offer a body, in which is a mind possessed of most excellent reason, and actions directed by reason. Thus Peter called it λογικὸν γάλα [reasonable milk] 1. II. 2. The victim of the burnt offering was entirely consumed in honor of God: so also it is necessary that vicious affections be consumed in us: what fire is there, faith ascending to heaven is here.

Others prefer that λογικὴν [reasonable/verbal] be said, with the Syrian Interpreter, from λόγῳ Θεῦ [the Word of God], because the λατρεία [service] is to be instituted not according to the lead and norm of our reason, but according to the prescription and form of the word of GOD, as 1. Petr. II. 2. according to them λογικὸν γάλα [reasonable/verbal milk] is verbal milk: Which they observe against the Socinians, as those who from this word constitute human reason as the rule of divine worship and religion. But because there is an allusion to the Levitical sacrifices, it is better that the host and λατρεία [service] be called λογικὴν [reasonable] with respect to the matter, because it is done not through the offering of cattle, but of our bodies, than by reason of the principle, whether efficient or directing.

Latin:

PARS EPISTOLÆ POSTERIOR PÆDEUTICA. Paracleses vel adhortationes ad studium Sanctitatis vitæ exhibens. SECTIO I. DE OFFICIIS NECESSARIIS. SUBJECTIO I. Regulas generales sistens. CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Paracleses ad officia pietatis ergà Deum, sobriæ mentis quoad nos, charitatis quoad alios, tum in donorum & officiorum administratione, tum in misericordiæ & dilectionis exhibitione. Quibus monita subjiciuntur, quoad ea, quæ in officiis expediundis, quæque in dilectione erga indigentes, peregrinos, persequentes observanda, & ad ὁμόνοιαν & concordiam, ac pacem etiam cum hostibus fovendam & promovendam necessaria sunt.

Partes duæ constitui possunt: Prior Adhortationes, de justificatorum officiis debitis continet, usque ad v. 10. inclus. Altera monita, de προσκημένοις quibusdam circa officia observandis, exhibet, usque ad v. 21.

PARS I. CAP. XII. De Justificatorum debitis officiis.

Grotiana distributio falsa nititur hypothesi, nimirum legem per Evangelium perfici, quasi lex in se non fuerit perfecta, sed quantum ad præcepta per Evangelium ulterioribus accessionibus locupletari ac perfici debuerit, & Evangelium prout à lege distinguitur, præcepta moralia perfectiora tradat: quam Pelagianam, Socinianam & Arminianam hæresin, quæ totam doctrinam de justificatione ab Apostolo hactenus traditam, quòd nempe per fidem in Christum sine operibus justificemur, pessimè corrumpit, imò penitùs evertit adeoque Pontificiis non ingrata est, plus simplici vice in Grotio notavimus. Ita autem hîc habet:

Cum docuisset Paulus, neminem nunc ad justitiam eam, quæ ad vitam æternam ducit, pertingere, nisi per fidem Evangelio habitam, Deumque cur ita constitueret gravissimas habuisse causas, & ea, quæ objici solent, solvisset, ad monita veniens reipsa ostendit, quod supra dixerat obiter, per Evangelium legem perfici, idque per singulas eundo legis Mosaicæ partes, ritualem primum, inde eam, quæ regit judicia, XII. 1. Postremò eam, quæ mores, XII. 8. Ac primum incipit à rituali sive Levitico, cujus præcipuum sacrificia, & inter sacrificia עולה, id est, ὁλοκαύτωμα.

Ritualia cap. XII. perfici à vero alienum est. Alluditur v. 1. ad sacrificia, vel explicatur finis sacrificiorum secundarius; quæ uti πρώτως ob ἱλαστήριον perfectione Christum, cap. III. 24. qui pro nobis mortuus & oblatus est, c. V. 8. ad nostram ἀπολύτρωσιν c. III. 4. & ut per mortē ipsius Deo reconciliaremur c. V. 10. ipsum præfigurandi causâ oblata sunt, & venturum verum sacrificium Nov. Test. adumbrarunt: ita δευτέρως commonebant de sacrificiis spiritualibus, non tantum in Novo Testamento, sed etiam à fidelibus in Vet. Testam. offerendis, qui tùm quoque Deo sese in hostiam viventem, sanctam & DEO placentem sistere debebant, atque de eo per sacrificia Levitica commonefiebant. Nec verò cap. XII. solùm ad ista ritualia respectus habetur, quod v. 1. fit: Pars enim reliqua de moralibus, vel officiis pietatis, sobrietatis & charitatis agit, etsi hæc omnia ad Levitica trahat Grotius; quemadmodum cap. XII. non solùm judicia, sed Politiam universam respicit, inque ea cùm Magistratui, tum quibusvis omninò debita officia præscribit. Ex ordine autem illo, quod præmissa doctrinâ fidei præcepta bonorum operum tradidit Apostolus, D. Georgius Major ipse Tom. II. Oper. f. 1. fatetur, Paulum ipsâ doctrinæ serie ostendere, credentes justificari gratis, sine ullis bonorum operum meritis, SOLA fide, & doctrinam bonorum operum à justitia fidei tam procul segregandam, quantum cælum à terra, ortus ab occidente distat, & nullo modo opera cum justificationis doctrina miscendæ esse. Sola enim fides Mediatorem apprehendens est causa efficiens, propter quam credenti fides sua imputatur ad justitiam. Sic autem fide sola, id est, propter solum Mediatorem justificati, donati remissione peccatorum, justitiâ & Spiritu Sancto, & facti bonæ arbores, debent postea esse impleti fructu justitiæ, qui contingit per Jesum Christum, ad gloriam & laudem Dei, Philipp. I.

Vers. 1. παρακαλῶ ὖν ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ. Id est, cum quæ dixi, ita se habeant, monita vobis dabo doctrinam istam consequentia. Mos is est Pauli, quem secuti alii veteres, post τὸ δογματικὸν, subjungere solent τὸ ἠθικὸν.

διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τῶ Θεῶ. Per illas proprietates Dei descriptas Exod. XXXIV. 6. Solent Hebræi, cum magnitudinem misericordiæ indicant, usurpare plurale רחמים οἰκτιρμὸς, ut Nehem. I. 11. & in Psalmis sæpè.

παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν. παραστῆσαι הקריב, aliter προσφέρειν, quam vocem habes de holocausto Levit. I. 2. & sequentibus. Et θυσία nomen generale per excellentiam dicitur de holocausto, ideoque עולה vertitur θυσία Exod. X. 25. XXIX. 42. Num. XXIII. 3. XXVIII. 13. Jos. XXII. 27. Job. I. 5. Ez. XLIV. 11. Ostendit uno exemplo ritualia perfici per res solidiores, quæ umbris istis ex adverso respondeant: Judæi offerunt corpus mortuum, vos corpus vivum, id est, una cum corpore actiones ejus: nam agere est vivere. Idem hic dicit cum allusione ad sacrificia, (cui similes allusiones habes Philip. II. 17. IV. 18.) quod simpliciter 1. Cor. VI. 20.

Deducit omninò adhortationem è superioribus voce illativâ h. l. Justificatos enim per fidem oportet sanctitati studere, ne fide ac justitia excidant; neque fides vel otiosa est, sed ἐνεργυμένη δι᾿ ἀγάπης operosa per charitatem erga Deum & proximum, Gal. V. 6. vel ἄργος κὴ ἀκάρπως otiosos esse sinit & infructuosos credentes, quin porrigant in fide virtutem, in virtute scientiam, in scientia abstinentiam, in abstinentia patientiam, in patientia pietatem, in pietate amorem fraternitatis, in amore fraternitatis charitatem, 2. Pet. I. 5. seqq. Fratres vocat ob comunem παλιγγενεσίαν & cælestem κληρονομίαν, ac simul innuit fraterno nomine indignos esse, qui hanc adhortationem non observant. 1. Corinth. V. 11. Ideò autem hortatur & rogat διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τῶ Θεῶ per misericordiam Dei, quæ causa est principalis Justificationis nostræ, ut miserationum nobis exhibitarum memores, quæ maxima ratio est amandi DEUM, & optimum incentivum Amoris erga Deum miserentem nostri, & quàm grata nobis est divina gratia, ne sc. excidamus eâdem, corpora nostra sistamus hostiam viventem, sanctam, placentem Deo. Et per miserationem Dei mundamur nos à peccato, & constituimur sacerdotes Dei, Apoc. I. 5. 6. V, 9. 10. & adducimur in Christo, in quo solo nos accedere possumus ad Deum, ut nos ei sistamus, eique grati simus, Joh. XIV. 6. Ebr. XI. 6.

Verbum παραστῆσαι sacrificiale est, quia pecora ex grege segregata sistebantur coram Domino in loco sancto ab ipso ordinato Lev. III. 7. 12.

Corporum nostrorum mentio fit, non quod anima excludatur; nam non possumus offerre corpus si- ne animà: ideoq; in oblatione corporis compre- henditur oblatio animæ, sed peculiariter corpus nominare voluit Apostolus, tum quia hoc loquen- di modo pars, quâ magis suntus Sacerdotes, evi- dentius ab ea distinguitur parte, quâ magis sumus sacrificium; tum quia corpus requiritur ad sacrifi- cium, quatenus per illud Deus honoratur apud alios. Voce ϑυσίας non ὁλοκάυτωμα tantùm respi- citur, quia alia etiam sacrificia in Vet. Test. offe- rebantur, quæ figurabant λατρείαν λογικὴν. Coc- cejus triplex observat sacrificium: 1. Quo honora- tur Deus ut creator, quod est homo & ea, quæ sunt hominis; dum se & omnia sua Deo consecrat. 2. Quo honoratur ac sanctificatur ac justificatur Deus ut ju- dex justificans impium justè & sanctè. Et hoc est ly- tron pro peccato, Ascham, h.e. satisfactio vel luitio reatus aut culpæ. Hoc typicè est ex pecudibus & in effusione sanguinis: verè est obedientia & mors me- diatoris, quam repræsentamus Deo, quando in fide Mediatoris accedimus ad Deum. 3. Quo honoratur Deus ut misericors, quod est ἐυχαρισικὸν. Quod postremum hîc imprimis respicitur. Per ϑυσίαν ζῶσαν non tantum oppositio in ordine ad sacrificia V. T. quæ mortua, non viva offerebantur, insinua- tur, sed vita etiam spiritualis, quæ per fidem est, nec non mortificatio affectuum & cupiditatum, quia justificati per fidē reputare sese debent mor- tuos peccato, viventes autem Deo in Christo Jesu Domino nostro: Ostenditur, inquit B. Glassius in Exeg. Epist. T. I. p. 1090. simul hujus sacrificatio- nis tum principium, quod est vivificatio Spiritus S. per verbum vitæ, de qua Eph. I. 4. 5. tum opposi- tum, quod peccata & opera mortua sunt, Heb. IX. 14. Quantum peccatis in mortificatione carnis continua decedit, tantum accedit spirituali vitæ in Christo & viventi huic sacrificio: Tum finis & consequens præmium, quod est vita æterna, cujus spes etiam di- citur viva 1. Pet. I. 4. Audiamus & Lutheri illa in enarrat. h. l. f. 164. Sacrificia illa Vet. Test. boves, oves & hædi erant, quæ simul atque sacrificia incipie- bant esse, vita illis adimebatur, mactabantur enim, igne cremabantur & à Sacerdotibus consumebantur. At hoc Novi Testam. sacrificium mirè comparatum est, ut simul mactetur quidem, & vivat tamen, imò quantò plùs occisum fuerit & mactatum, tantò vivit meliùs & fortius. Juxta illud Rom. VIII. Si facta carnis Spiritu mortificaveritis, vivetis. Et Col. III. Vos mortui estis, & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo.

ἁγίαν.) In Lege sanctum dicitur, quidquid Deo oblatum est, ut Lev. XII. 4. Matth. XXIII. 19. quantò magis hominum corpora ab omnibus vitiis justificata, id est, repurgata.

Dicebatur & in Vet. Test. sacrificiorum caro sancta, sed typicè; quia consecrata erat in Symbo- lum sanctæ oblationis Christi, & figuram corporis no- stri Deo consecrandi, & sacrificandi per zelum & charitatem, quam significabat ignis cælestis. Quia illa à Spiritu S. sunt, ideoque sancta dicitur victima nostra, non propter perfectionem, quæ hîc non in- venitur, sed ob inhabitationem Spiritus S. quâ san- ctificamur, Rom. XV. 16. Quæ sanctificatio non confundenda cum justificatione. Hæc enim con- sistit in peccatorum remissione & purgatione à peccatis, quæ fit sanguine Filii Dei, 1. Joh. I. 7. ac perfecta est: illa verò fit renovatione nostri per virtutem Spiritus S. sed in hac vita imperfecta est, quia non reddimur πνευματικοὶ spirituales ex omni parte, quum supersint adhuc reliquiæ carnis, & caro semper concupiscat adversus Spiritum, Ro- man. VII. 14. seqq. Gal. V. 6. Sacrificialia Vet. Test. pora inquit B. Glassius l. c. sancta & DEO conse- crata vocabantur, quia ad verbum & institutum ejus à grege reliquo segregabantur, & talia quidem, quæ sine corporis vitio erant, ut ex Levit. I. 3. 10. c. XIV. 4. apparet: & horum demum ad Deum adductorum sanguis in honorem & typum futuri Messiæ funde- batur. En sanctitatis spiritalium sacrificiorum ju- cundam figuram! Sancti sunt Christiani & creden- tes, quia per verbum DEI, quod omnia sanctificat 1. Tim. IV. 5. sanctificantur & Deo consecrantur Jo- han. XV. 3. c. XVII. 17. Sancti sunt, quia à grege ho- minum profanorum mundano selecti, & à terrenis ani- mo remoti sunt Joh. XVII. 16. Sancti sunt, quia san- ctitati ac puritati serio student, & ἀνεγκλητοι vivunt 1. Thess. IV. 3. Hebr. XII. 14. 1. Petr. I. 14. 15. 16. San- cti sunt, quia omnia sua honori Salvatoris sui conse- crant, & sanguinem pro ejus gloria & confessione fun- dere non erubescunt vel renuunt. Apoc. XII. 11. Origenes l. IX. in Ep. ad Rom. Qui membra sua mortificant, bestiam viventem rationabiliter offe- runt, & legem sacrificiorum, quæ in Levitico est, secundum spiritalem intelligentiam complent. Si superbiam vincunt, immolant vitulum, si iracun- diam superant, arietem; si libidinem, hircum; si va- gos & lubricos cogitationum resecant volatus, colum- bas & turtures. Chrysostomus in h. l. Christiano- rum, inquit, sacrificium res est animi & spiritualis: pro templo est pectus hominis, pro pecude corpus ho- minis; hoc est affectus carnis, pro igne est charitas Dei & c.

ἐυάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ. Holocaustum dicitur ὀσμὴ ἐυωδίας τῷ κυρίῳ Levit. I. 9. 13. 17. Et alibi sæpe. Id multo magis Christianorum corpori- bus & actionibus competit, ut videre est 2. Cor. II. 15. Philipp. IV. 18.

DEO ut hostia placeat, necessum est, ut per fidem offeratur: quemadmodum & sacrificia Le- vitica fide erant offerenda, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere.Ebr. XI. 4.6. In Christo ut altari offerenda est hæc hostia; quia nulla est grata DEO nisi Christus Filius ara Ebr. 13. 10. 15. 16. Apoc. IIX. 3, De quo altari etiam intelligit Coccejus locaEs.54.7. Holocausta eorum (peregrinorum) & sacrificia eo- rum in acceptationem erunt super altari MEO: & Ps. LI. 21. Tunc ascendent in altare Tuum vituli.

τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ὑμῶν. Λατρεία עבודה Levitica erat δι᾽ ἀλόγων, id est, per pe- cudes. Nam omnia muta animantia ἄλογα vocantur Sap.XI. 15.inGlossis animalia ζῶα ἄλογα.Hinc ἀλογευθῆναι in cano- nibus.Nos vero offerimus corpus,in quo est animus rationis excellentissimæ compos, & actiones ratione directas. Sic λογικὸν γάλα dixit Petrus 1. II. 2. Holocausti victima tota consumebatur in honorem Dei: sic & vitiosos affectus in nobis consumi oportet: quod ibi ignis, id hic fides in cœ- lum ascendens.

Alii λογικὴν dici malunt, cùm Syro Interp. à λό- γῳ Θεῦ Verbo Dei, quod non juxta rationis nostræ ductum & normam, sed juxta verbi DEI præscri- ptum & formam instituenda sit λατρεία, si DEO placere debeat, uti 1. Petr.II.2. juxta ipsos λογικὸν γάλα est lac verbale: Quod adversus Socinianos observant, utpote qui ex hac voce rationem hu- manam regulam cultûs divini & religionis consti- tuunt. Sed quia alluditur ad sacrificia Levitica, præstat λογικὴν dici hostiam & λατρείαν respectu materiæ, quod non per pecorum, sed corporum nostrorum oblationem fiat, quam ratione principii sive efficientis, sive dirigentis.

## 12:2
V. 2. Τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τῆ νοὸς ὑμῶν [by the renewing of your mind]. Now he explains what the washings of the Priests signify. What do the Levitical washings have to do with the innovation of the mind? If the Apostle had said purification, those washings could be brought here. But Grotius wished to drag everything in this chapter to the Levitical rites, although, as they say, by the neck. But lest the body alone

seem to be consecrated to God, the Apostle also requires the innovation of the mind: so that the body may be holy, and the mind may be renewed from the Adamic and carnal oldness to a spiritual newness. By which pact the restoration of the divine image, which especially shone in the mind or soul, lost through the fall, is indicated, which is by the innovation of our mind. Conf. Col. I. 9. Eph. IV. 22.

μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ [be not conformed to this world]. That is, do not lead a life similar to men who love this age, whom you renounced in baptism. Thus Peter said συσχη- ματίζεσθαι ἐπιθυμίαις [to be conformed to the lusts] 1. Ep. I. 14. Plutarch also uses that word, for which Columella said to be configured. Opposed to this is μεταμορφοῦσθαι [to be transfigured]. Seneca letter VI. Understand, Lucilius, that I am not only being amended, but transfigured. Thus Pliny XVII. 24 said that almonds are transfigured from sweet into bitter, who also VII. 55 calls the Pythagorean μετα- σωμάτωσιν [transmigration] a transfiguration. And Suetonius relates that Nero attempted to transfigure Sporus into a female nature. The transfiguration, of which Paul treats here, as he himself adds, is through the innovation of the mind: for he said זפק [spirit] for mind here συνεκδοχικῶς [synecdochically]. Indeed also עור [skin] and כבד [liver] is translated in Is. XL. 13. these signify in the burnt offering the head and the liver, which are the first things placed on the altar Levit. I. 7.

Sobriety of mind is required in the justified: lest they be configured to the age, that is, to men dedicated to the age or world, alienated from God and the life which is in God, who are drunk with the pleasures of the world Eph. IV. 17. sqq. 1. Petr. IV. 3. 1. Thess. IV. 7. just as on the contrary we are commanded to be conformed to God, 2. Cor. III. conf. 1. John II. 16. c. V. 19. Act. II. 40. Gal. I. 4. For the transformation is not substantial, such as the μεταμόρφωσιν [transfiguration] that fanatics invent in the renovation of man, but accidental, as regards the knowledge of the mind and the affections, and the desires of the will, or heart.

to test for yourselves what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God. You are mystical Levites. It is the duty of the legal Levites to examine victims according to the law of Leviticus XXII, Deuteronomy XV. 21, XVII. 1, to which there is also an allusion above II. 18. Clement in his epistle calls this μαμωσκοπεῖν: yours is to examine which actions please God. Τέλειον corresponds to the Hebrew תמים which in Leviticus I is translated as ἄμωμον and in Exodus XII. 5 as τέλειον. But what he called ἐυάρεστον here corresponds to the Hebrew לרצון in Leviticus XXII. 21, where the LXX translate it as εἰς δεκτὸν. Δεκτὸν is used in Leviticus I. 3 & 4, Jeremiah VI. 20, Malachi II. 13. פחור is also said of victims and signifies fat ones in Leviticus XXVII. 10, where the LXX translated it as καλὸν, which Paul here calls ἀγαθὸν. Thus he transferred all the praises of victims to better things. He said θέλημα metonymically for those things which God loves, as in 1 Thessalonians IV. 3; what he had said in general, he now brings down to the species of things.

This testing is not of the sacrifice which is to be offered to God, but of the will of God, and it is not only theoretical but practical, so that we may not only know what the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God is, or what is good according to the will of God, pleasing or acceptable to God, and perfect: but that we may also strive to do and execute it. For words of knowledge are often to be understood in Scripture with the affection of the heart and the effect of the work; compare 1 Corinthians XV. 19. That there is a reference to the duty of the Levites to examine victims does not appear, because it is not explained what kind of victims our bodies are to be presented to God as, but it is taught how we ought to be conformed to God and the divine will, not to the world or the age: for which thing's sake this sacred testing, and an accurate one at that, is necessary. It is necessary to look to God not only as the end, but as the exemplar, and not to the world or the age. Moreover, this is the will of God, our sanctification, 1 Thessalonians IV. 3. The will of God is good, who detests evil and requires good, and therefore prescribes both what is to be avoided and what is to be done in the law, the most perfect norm of our life. The will is called εὐάρεσον because it is well-pleasing to the Lord when we strive to conform ourselves to it: perfect, because He wills that we strive to be perfect, just as He Himself is perfect. Matt. 5, last verse. Although we do not attain this perfection here, we must nevertheless strive toward it.

Latin:

V. 2. Τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τῆ νοὸς ὑμῶν. Nunc explicat quid significent lotiones Sacerdotum. Quid lotiones Leviticæ ad innovationem mentis? Si purgationem dixisset Apostolus, huc lotiones il- læ adferri possent. Sed voluit Grotius omnia in hoc capite abripere ad Leviticos ritus, licet obtor- tò, quod dicitur, collô. Ne autem solum corpus

Deo consecrandum videatur, requirit Apostolus etiam mentis innovationem: ut corpus sanctum sit, & mens à vetustate Adamica & carnali reno- vetur ad novitatem spiritualem. Quo pacto ima- ginis divinæ, quæ præcipue effulgebat in mente vel animo, per lapsum amissæ reparatio indicatur, quæ sit innovatione mentis nostræ Conf. Col. I. 9. Eph. IV. 22.

μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ. Id est, ne vitam ducite similem hominibus amantibus seculum hoc, cui vos in baptismo renunciaftis. Sic συσχη- ματίζεσθαι ἐπιθυμίαις dixitPetrus 1. Ep.I.14.Utitur eo verbo & Plutarchus, pro quo Columella dixit configurari. Huic oppositum est μεταμορφοῦσθαι transfigurari. Seneca episto- la VI. Intellige, Lucili, non emendari me tantum, sed trans- figurari. Sic amygdalas ex dulcibus in amaras transfigurari dixit Plinius XVII. 24. qui & VII. 55. Pythagoricam μετα- σωμάτωσιν transfigurationem appellat. Et Suetonius Ne- ronem narrat conatum transfigurare Sporum in muliebrem naturam. Transfiguratio, de qua hic agit Paulus, ut ipse addit per innovationem animi: nam זפק pro animo hic di- xit συνεκδοχικῶς. Quippe & עור & כבד vertitur Esa. XL. 13. hoc significant in holocausto caput & jecur, quæ prima impo- nuntur altari Levit. I. 7.

Sobrietas mentis requiritur in justificatis: ne con- figurentur seculo, id est hominibus seculo vel mun- do deditis, à Deo & vita, quæ in Deo est, alienis, qui voluptatibus mundi ebrii sunt Eph.IV.17.sqq. 1.Petr.IV.3.1.Thess.IV.7. uti ex adverso conformari Deo jubemur, 2. Cor. III. conf. 1. Job. II.16. c. V. 19. Act. II. 40. Gal. I. 4. Non enim transformatio est substantialis, qualem μεταμόρφωσιν fanatici comminiscuntur in hominis renovatione, sed acci- dentalis, quoad notitiam mentis & affectus, & cupi- ditates voluntatis, vel cordis.

εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς, τὶ τὸ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐυάρεστον καὶ τέλειον. Estis Levitæ mystici. Levitarum legalium est, exami- nare victimas ex lege Levit, XXII. Deut. XV. 21. XVII. 1. quo & allufum fupra II. 18. Id μαμωσκοπεῖν vocat in episto- la Clemens: vestrum, quæ actiones Deo placeant. Τέλειον respondet Hebræo תמים quod Levit. 1.vertitur ἄμωμον & Exod. XII. 5. τέλειον. Quod autem hic dixit ἐυάρεστον, respondet Hebræo לרצון Levit. XXII.21. ubi εἰς δεκτὸν ver- tere LXX. δεκτὸν Levit. I. 3. & 4. Jerem. VI. 20. Malach. II. 13. פחור etiam de victimis dicitur, & pingues significat Levit. XXVII. 10. ubi καλὸν verterunt LXX. quod hic ἀγα- θὸν Paulus. Ita omnes victimarum laudes ad res meliores transtulit. Θέλημα dixit μετατωνυμικῶς pro iis, quæ DEUS amat, ut 1. Thess. IV. 3. quod in genere dixerat, nunc ad rerum species deducit.

Hæc δοκιμασία non est τῆς θυσίας, quæ DEO offerenda, sed τῶ θελήματῶν τῆ Θεᾶ, voluntatis DEI, neque solum Theoretica, sed Practica, ut nempe non cognoscamus modo, quæ sit voluntas DEI bona, placens & perfecta, vel quodnam juxta Dei voluntatem bonum sit, DEO placens vel ac- ceptum, & perfectum: sed id etiam agere atque exequi studeamus. Verba enim cognitionis sæpe in Scriptura intelligenda cum affectu cordis & effe- ctu operis, Conf. 1. Cor. XV. 19. Respici ad Levita- rum munus, examinandi victimas, non apparet, quia non, quales victimæ corpora nostra DEO sistenda sint, explicatur, sed quomodo DEO & voluntati divinæ, non mundo vel seculo, confor- mari debeamus, docetur: cujus rei gratia sacrâ hàc δοκιμασίᾳ, eaque accurata opus est. Intueri Deum oportet non ut terminum tantum, sed ut exemplar, non autem mundum vel seculum. Hæc autem voluntas DEI est, sanctificatio nostra, 1. Thess. IV. 3. Bona est DEI voluntas, qui detesta- tur malum, & requirit bonum, ideoque & fugien- da & facienda præscribit in lege, perfectissima vitæ nostræ norma. Εὐάρεσον τὸ θέλημα dicitur, quia beneplacitum est Domino, cum ei nos conforma- re studemus: τέλειον, quia vult, ut perfecti esse contendamus, quemadmodum ipse perfectus est Matth. V. v. ult. Quam perfectionem etsi hic non assequamur, ad eam tamen eniti oportet.

## 12:3
V. 3. For I say through the grace given to me. That is, by Apostolic authority, but just as he refers everything that others have, so also what he himself had, to the goodness of God, in order to teach modesty, which becomes Christians all the more, the greater the things are that they have received. There is therefore here a metonymy of the cause for the effect.

to everyone who is among you. That is, to all who are in the Church, whether Jews or Christians.

not to think more highly than one ought to think. It is almost the same as to be high-minded, 11.20. Moreover, it is an infinitive for an imperative, in the Greek manner, as below 15. Do not take more upon yourselves than is fitting. Levites ought not to arrogate to themselves what belongs to the Priests, nor Priests what belongs to the High Priests. Diotrephes sinned against this precept, 3 John 9, and almost all authors of schisms.

but to think so as to be sober-minded. Sobriety here signifies modesty. Thus also among the Greeks, to be arrogant and to be sober-minded are opposed, as in Sotades: If you are arrogant, this is a swelling of folly. But if you are sober-minded, this is a gift of the Gods. A similar paronomasia is found in Charondas: let each of the citizens profess to be sober-minded rather than to be wise.

This also pertains to the sobriety of mind and judgment, so that we may think modestly of ourselves, and not indeed be wise beyond what is right. For to think among the Greeks signifies to feel or to be wise, and to understand, just as wisdom is both wisdom and prudence: Origen, Erasmus, and others accept it in the former sense, so that no one may be puffed up in spirit, just as to be high-minded is to be arrogant, to think sublimely of oneself; in which way Chrysostom warns that humility or modesty is indicated here.
