By the other meaning it is hinted that we should not rashly presume to attain those things which are above us, just as when heretics attempt to discuss the mysteries of the faith by reason, which is to think more highly than one ought. However, both are easily joined, because both are a matter of arrogance, whether we puff ourselves up in spirit, or attempt those things which are above us. However, it is not certain that there is a reference here to the Levites, nor is it strictly about affecting the offices of others, or at least this arrogance alone, which consists in affecting higher duties, is not designated: in the way that some interpreters say that arrogance and immodesty of feeling and thinking are prohibited, so that they also wish meddlesomeness, as that which arises from it, to be interdicted by Musculus, B. Hieronymus, Weller, B. Glassius, etc. But this exhortation pertains to all: because that thinking more highly than one ought is such a vice that it is innate in all, and that thinking so as to be sober-minded is incumbent upon all. Furthermore, the Apostle does not say, to all of you, (as Musculus warns) but to everyone living among you, so that it may not be thought to be a certain general and common admonition, such as are usually despised, but so that each one, of whatever status and condition, may privately understand that this is said to him.

to each as God has distributed a measure of faith. There is a transposition here, for as to each, such as are many in Paul. Let each one conduct himself according to the gifts which he has received from God, namely according to the measure of the faith which he has; for what Cyprian says about internal gifts: As much of capacious faith as we bring there, so much of overflowing grace we draw: the same was true in those first times also concerning gifts that were visible externally. See Matt. 17.20. Therefore the measure of faith, which he soon calls the analogy of faith, is the very measure of grace given according to the measure of faith. See below 6. Eph. 4.7. 1 Cor. 12.7. Cicero first translated analogy as proportion, whom other Latins have followed. Jerome against Jovinian 2. As much of the grace of Christ is poured in, as we are able to draw. Here also there is an allusion to the ministries of the Levites: for some things were imposed upon the young, others upon those advanced in age, others upon the old, as we said on Luke 3.23. Add Num. 4.1. Chronicles. 15.15. those old things were types of ours, Heb. 9.24. In that first Church, instead of faith there were gifts, instead of gifts there were ministries. For the election took place without thanks, without canvassing, without frauds, with the Holy Spirit directing. Tertullian in the Apology: The approved elders preside, having obtained this honor not by price, but by testimony. For no thing of God is established by price. Clement in his Epistle: he said gift metonymically, for the function itself: as it was placed in his gift.

It contributes to sobriety or modesty if we look at the variety of gifts which God has distributed to different people, and each one humbly acquiesces in those gifts which have been granted to him, and does not think of himself beyond what is right, or presume to be wise. B. D. Hieron. Weller, with B. D. Jac. Weller praising him, says this passage is about concord, when each one recognizes the measure of his gift, and takes the greatest care against meddlesomeness, so that he does not break into another's vocation, but does this, that he may perform the duties of his own vocation rightly and prudently, and recognizes, reveres, and promotes the gifts and efforts of others, etc. Moreover, it is called the measure of faith, either because faith receives the measure which the Lord grants, for it is a hand receiving and grasping, when the hand of divine grace extends itself to us in its largesses, which is the munificent hand of GOD giving; or because faith here is knowledge and cognition, the measure of which God divides and distributes to each as He wills, as is taught in 1 Cor. 12. Others understand spiritual gifts metonymically by faith, as those which come to the pious along with faith, and are consequences of faith: such as are the knowledge of spiritual things, love and zeal for GOD, the pursuit of piety, etc., which are sanctifying gifts, which are not found in the same measure in all, and also ministering gifts, which are likewise distributed in various ways in the Church. But these seem to be understood especially from verses 4 and 5. Although these things may fall even upon the unfaithful and hypocrites, here, however, the faithful are regarded, as they are true and living members of the mystical body of Christ, who through faith and confident prayer obtain them, Jas. 1:5-6, and use them πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον, 1 Cor. 12:7. Let everyone know, therefore, that there is a certain μέτρον of the gift which he has received from GOD: why then should he boast as if he had received the whole fullness? Let him know that he has received from elsewhere whatever good he has: why then should he boast as if he had not received it, 1 Cor. 4:7. Let him know that he has received it from God: therefore, through humility, let him attribute all things as received from Him, and render them as with a grateful mind, and use them for His glory: Let him know that God distributes his gifts of the Spirit piece by piece (ἐμέρισεν), and has given to others also their portion: let no one, therefore, despise others, as if they were devoid of the gifts of GOD and χαρισμάτων, as the blessed Glassius holds here. However, the comparison of the analogy of faith does not fit here, which differs greatly from the measure of faith. The analogy of faith is one and the same; but the measure of faith varies greatly. Nor is there any trace here that regard is had for the duties of the Levites, as Grotius has invented.

Latin:

V. 3. λέγω γὰρ διὰ τῆς χάριτος δοθείσης μοι. Id est, pro auctoritate Apostolica, sed sicut omnia, quæ alii habent, ita & quæ ipse habebat, ad Dei bonitatem re- fert, ut modestiam doceat, quæ Christianos tanto magis decet, quanto majora sunt quæ accepêre. Est ergo hic με- τωνυμία causæ pro effectu.

πάντι τῷ ὄντι ἐν ὑμῖν. Id est, omnibus qui in Ecclesia estis, sive Judæi, sive Chri- stiani.

μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ᾽ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν. Idem est ferme quod ὑψηλοφρονεῖν XI. 20. Est autem in- finitivus pro imperativo, more Græco, ut infra 15. Nolite plus animorum sumere, quam oportet. Non debent Le- vitæ sibi arrogare, quæ sunt Sacerdotum, nec Sacerdotes, quæ sunt summorum Sacerdotum. Contra hoc præceptum peccavit Diotrephes III. Joh. 9. & ferme omnes Schisma- tum autores.

ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν. Σωφροσύνη hic modestiam significat. Sic & Græcis op- ponuntur ἀλαζονεῦν & σωφρονεῖν, ut apud Sotaden: Ἀν ἀλαζονῇς, τῦτ᾽ ἀνοίας ἐσὶ φρύαγμα. Ἀν δὲ σωφρονῇς τῦτο Θεῶν δῶρον ὑπάρχει. Similis παρονομασία apud Charondam: προσποιεῖσθω δ᾽ ἕκα- στος τῶν πολιτῶν σωφρονεῖν μᾶλλον ἢ φρονεῖν.

Pertinet & hoc ad sobrietatem mentis ac judicii, ut modeste de nobis sentiamus, non vero ultra quam par est sapiamus. φρονεῖν enim Græcis signi- ficat sentire vel sapere, & intelligere, uti Φρόνησις Sa- pientia est & prudentia: Priori sensu Origenes, Era- smus, & alii accipiunt, ne quis efferatur animo, uti ὑψηλοφρονεῖν est arrogantem esse, sublime de se sen- tire; quo pacto Chrysostomus monet, hic indicari ταπεινοφροσύνην seu modestiam. Altero significatu innuitur, ne temere ea, quæ supra nos sunt, assequi præsumamus, utpote cum hæretici ratione discu- tere tentant mysteria fidei, quod est ὑπερφρονεῖν. Facile autem utrumque conjungitur, quia arro- gantiæ utrumque est, sive animo nos efferamus, sive ea, quæ supra nos sunt, tentemus. Non autem constat hic ad Levitas respici, nec de affectandis alienis officiis proprie agitur, vel certe sola hæc ar- rogantia, quæ in affectandis muneribus sublimio- ribus sita est, non designatur: quomodo nonnulli Interpp. ita arrogantiam & immodestiam sentiendi & sapiendi prohibitam dicunt, ut πολυπραγμο- σύνην, utpote quæ ex illa oritur, interdictam etiam velint Musculus, B. Hieronym. Weller. B. Glassius &c. Ad omnes autem pertinet hæc παράκλησις: Quia illud ὑπερφρονεῖν tale est vitium, quod omnibus est annatum, & illud τὸ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν omni- bus incumbit. Cæterum non dicit Apostolus, omnibus vobis, (ut monet Musculus) sed cuilibet in- ter vos versanti, ut non putetur esse generalis & com- munis quædam admonitio, quales plerumque contemni solent, sed ut quisque, cujuscunque status & conditionis, privatim intelligat, hoc sibi dictum.

ἑκάστῳ ὡς ὁ Θεὸς ἐμέρισεν μέτρον πίστεως. Est hic transpositio, pro ὡς ἑκάστῳ, qualia multa apud Paulum. Quisque se gerat pro donis quæ à Deo accepit, nempe pro modo ejus, quam habet, fidei; Nam quod de internis donis ait Cyprianus: Quantum illuc fidei capacis afferimus, tantum gratiæ inundantis haurimus: idem primis illis temporibus etiam de donis extra conspicuis verum erat. Vide Matth. XVII. 20. Itaque μέτρον πίστεως, quod mox dicit ἀναλογίαν πίστεως, est ipsa mensura gratiæ data pro modo fidei. Vide infra 6. Eph. IV. 7. 1. Cor. XII. 7. Ἀναλο- γίαν proportionem primus vertit Cicero, quem secuti sunt Latini alii. Hieronymus adversus Jovinianum II. Tantum gratiæ Christi infunditur, quantum valemus haurire. Etiam hic illuditur ad Levitarum ministeria: alia enim impone- bantur juvenibus, alia provectis, alia senibus, ut diximus ad Luc. III. 23. Adde Num. IV. 1. Paralipp. XV. 15. erant illa vetera nostrorum ἀντίτυπα, Hebr. IX. 24. In prima illa Ecclesia pro fide erant dona, pro donis ministeria. Fiebat enim electio sine gratia, sine ambitu, sine fraudibus, Spi- ritu Sancto dirigente. Tertullianus Apologetico: Præsi- dent probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio, sed testimonio adepti. Neque enim pretio ulla res Dei constat. Clemens in Epistola: μετωνυμικῶς χάρισμα dixit, pro ipsa functione: καθὼς ἐτέθη ἐν τῷ χαρίσματι αὐτὲ.

Ad σωφροσύνην vel modestiam facit, si varieta- tem donorum quæ alia aliis Deus distribuit, re- spiciamus, & quisque iis donis, quæ sibi concessa sunt, humiliter acquiescat, nec ultra, quam par est, de se sentiat, aut sapere præsumat. B. D. Hieron. Wellerus laudante B. D. Jac. Wellero, locus hic, inquit, est de concordia, cum quisque agnoscit men- suram doni sui, & summopere cavet πολυπραγμο- σύνην, ne in alienam vocationem irrumpat, sed id agit, ut vocationis suæ officia recte ac prudenter fa- ciat, & aliorum dona & conatus agnoscit, revere- tur, & provehit. &c. Μέτρον autem πίσεως dicitur, sive quod fides accipiat mensuram, quam concedit Dominus, est enim manus accipiens & apprehen- dens, cum se manus divinæ gratiæ in largitionibus ad nos extendit, quæ est munifica manus DEI dan- tis; sive quod fides hic notitia & cognitio sit, cujus μέτρον mensuram partitur Deus ac distribuit cuique prout vult, ut 1. Cor. XII. docetur. Alii per fidem metonymice dona spiritualia intelligunt, utpote quæ una cum fide piis obtingant, & consequentia fidei sint: uti sunt, cognitio rerum spiritualium, amor & zelus DEI, studium pietatis &c. quæ do- na sunt sanctificantia, quæ non eadem mensura penes omnes reperiuntur, nec non dona mini- strantia, quæ itidem diversimode in Ecclesia dis- tribuuntur. Sed hæc præcipue intelligenda viden- tur è vers. 4. & 5. Quæ etsi in infideles & hypo- critas quoque cadant, hic tamen respiciuntur fideles, utpote qui vera & viva membra sunt corporis Christi mystici, qui per fidem & fidu- cialem orationem ea impetrant Jac. I. 5. 6. iisque utuntur πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον 1. Cor. XII. 7. Sciat ergo quilibet μέτρον certum esse ejus, quod accepit à DEO, doni: quid igitur quasi de tota plenitudine accepta gloriaretur? Sciat se accepisse aliunde, quidquid bo- ni habet: quid igitur gloriaretur, quasi de non acce- pto: 1. Cor. IV. 7. Sciat à Deo se accepisse: Ergo per humilitatem omnia ipsi accepta ferat, & quasi grato animo reddat, inque gloriam ejus usurpet: Sciat Deum distribuere particulatim (ἐμέρισεν) sua dona Spiritus, & aliis etiam suam dedisse portionem: ne igitur alios quisquam contemnat, ac si donorum DEI & χαρισμάτων essent expertes, ut hic habet B. Glas- sius. Non autem hic quadrat collatio ἀναλογίας τῆς πίσεως, quæ maxime differt à μέτρῳ πίσεως. Analogia fidei una eademque est; mensura autem fidei maxime variat. Neque etiam ullum hic vesti- gium, quod ad Levitarum munia respectus ha- beatur, uti Grotius commentus est.

## 12:4-5
V. 4. 5. For just as in one body we have members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, the many, are one body in Christ, and each one members of one another. The comparison of the human body with a social body, such as the body of a republic, is frequent among all writers, to which Menenius Agrippa drew a likeness from the human body in that speech which Livy has in book II. Such is the body of the Christian Church, to which the Apostle adapts likenesses taken from the human body, not only here, but also 1 Cor. 12:12 and following. Eph. 4:25, 5:30. Clement in his Epistle to the Corinthians: Let us take our body; the head without the feet is nothing, so neither are the feet without the head. And the smallest members of our body are necessary and useful to the whole body. But all breathe together and use one subjection for the saving of the whole. Paul said πρᾶξιν by metonymy for function, which Menenius called ministry in the speech already indicated. We are one body in Christ, that is, through Christ, who was the joiner of that body; Tertullian in his Apology: We are a body from the consciousness of religion and the unity of discipline, and the covenant of hope. Καθ' εἷς, that is, individually, concerning which word we spoke at Mark 14:19; it is constructed here with the plural by synthesis. He said, however, ἀλλήλων

members & here & Eph. IV. 25. As we say in Latin, my fellow citizen, my fellow townsman, concerning those who are of the same city or municipality with us.

By that simile the Apostle indicates both the cause of sobriety and modesty, and at the same time insinuates mutual love with due humility of mind. For God willed that there be diverse members in one body for diverse uses, so that one might not claim everything for itself, and despise or look down upon another in comparison to itself. Beautiful are the things which B. Luther has here, reducing to four heads what are hinted at by this simile:

1. That all members have their offices and acts in the body for the reason that they are its members, and they are by no means members because they work with their offices and acts, as if they had earned that, etc. Thus no one arrives by his own works at being a member of the body of Christ, but because he has already been made that by the grace of God, therefore he does good works, etc.

2. That individual members are content with their own offices and dignity, and envy nothing of others, even if they excel, etc. Thus true Christians do not envy one another, etc.

3. That no one serves itself, but all serve others and the whole body, etc. Than which a more convenient example of love cannot be given, etc.

4. That whatever member suffers with another when it is afflicted or in pain; and again rejoices with it if it enjoys any convenience or delight, etc. Thus it is for Christians to συμπάχειν καὶ συγχαίρειν (suffer and rejoice together) with one another, as far as is honest, in the Lord, etc. Concerning the wonderful harmony, brotherly love, and sympathy of all the members, let both B. Wellers also be consulted. But this simile is not to be snatched away by the Papists to mean that there is a visible head of the spiritual members in the Church: for he does not refer these members to a visible head (about which there is deep silence in Scripture), but to the invisible Christ, from whom alone all the members of the mystical body depend.

Latin:

V. 4. 5. Καθάπερ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι μέλη ἔχομεν, τὰ δὲ μέλη πάντα ὐ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχει πρᾶξιν, ὕτως οἱ πολλοὶ ἓν σῶμά ἐσμεν ἐν χρισῷ, ὁ δὲ καθ᾽ εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη. Frequens est apud omnes scriptores comparatio corpo- ris humani cum corpore sociali, quale est corpus reipublicæ, ad quod similitudinem à corpore humano deduxit Mene- nius Agrippa, ea oratione, quam habet Livius libro II. Tale est Ecclesiæ Christianæ corpus, cui similitudines ab huma- no corpore sumptas aptat Apostolus, non hic tantum, sed & 1. Cor. XII. 12. & sequentibus. Eph. IV. 25. V. 30. Cle- mens in Epistola ad Corinthios: λάβωμεν τὸ σῶμα ἡμῶν· ἡ κε- φαλὴ δίχα τῶν πόδων ἐδὲν ἐσιν, ὕτως ἐδὲ οἱ πόδες δίχα τῆς κεφα- λῆς. Τὰ δὲ ἐλάχισα μέλη τῆ σώματος ἡμῶν ἀναγκαῖα κὴ ἔυ- χρησά εἰσιν ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι. ἀλλὰ πάντα συμπνεῖ κὴ ὑποτα- γῇ μιᾷ χρῆται εἰς τὸ σώζεσθαι ὅλον. Πρᾶξιν dixit Paulus per μετωνυμίαν functionem, quod ministerium dixit Me- nenius indicata jam oratione. Sumus unum corpus in Christo, id est, per Christum, qui corporis istius compactor fuit; Tertullianus Apologetico: Corpus sumus de conscien- tia religionis & disciplinæ unitate, & spei fœdere. Καθ' εἷς, id est, singuli, qua de voce diximus ad Marcum XIV. 19. con- struitur hic cum plurali κατὰ σύνθεσιν. Dixit autem ἀλλήλων

μέλη & hic & Eph. IV. 25. Sicut Latine dicimus, civis meus municeps meus, de iis qui nobiscum ejusdem sunt civitatis aut municipii.

Similitudine ista Apostolus & causam sobrietatis & modestiae indicat, & cum debita animi demissione mutuam dilectionem simul insinuat. Nam ideo diversa membra Deus in uno corpore esse voluit, ad diversos usus, ne unum omnia sibi vendicet, & alterum prae se contemnat vel despiciat. Pulcra sunt, quae hic habet B. Lutherus, ad quatuor capita reducens, quae hac similitudine innuuntur:

1. Quod omnia membra ideo in corpore sua habent officia & actus, quod ejus membra sunt, & nequaquam ideo membra sunt, quod operantur suis officiis & actibus, quasi id meruissent &c. Sic nemo suis operibus eo pervenit, ut membram corporis Christi sit, sed quia jam id est per gratiam DEI factus, ideo bona operatur &c.

2. Quod singula membra suis officiis & dignitate contenta sunt, nihil aliis, etsi praestent, invident &c. Sic Christiani veri sibi invicem non invident &c.

3. Quod nullum sibi ipsi, sed omnia aliis & toti corpori inserviunt, &c. Quo non potest commodius dilectionis exemplum dari &c.

4. Quod membrum quodlibet alii, ubi adfligitur aut dolet, compatitur; rursus etiam congaudet, si qua fruitur commoditate vel oblectatione, &c. Sic Christianorum est, sibi invicem συμπάχειν καὶ συγχαίρειν, quoad honesta, in Domino, &c. De mirifica membrorum omnium ἁρμονίᾳ, Φιλοσοργίᾳ & συμπαθείᾳ videatur etiam B. Wellerus uterque. Nõ autem haec similitudo cum Papistis eo abripienda, quod caput visibile membrorum spiritualium in Ecclesia desur: non enim ad visibile caput haec membra refert, (de quo altum silentium in Scriptura) sed ad invisibile Christum, à quo unice membra omnia corporis mystici dependent.

## 12:6
V. 6. Having then gifts according to the grace that is given to us, differing. Various gifts, according to that liberality which God has exercised toward us. For that is what he said here, to give grace.

Whether prophecy. It is to be understood in the individual members, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think so as to think soberly. Let each contain themselves within their limits. The gift of Prophecy was once rare, frequent in the Christian Church Acts XIII. 1. XV. 32. 1 Cor. XII. 28. 29. XIV. 29. 37. 38. Eph. III. 5. IV. 11. concerning the Apostles, of whom the first rank, he said nothing, because they did not lack admonition.

According to the analogy of faith. That is, for prophecy, either greater, such as Moses had, or lesser, such as other Prophets had, which God willed to bestow upon him according to the measure of faith. Let him be content with this measure, and not go beyond what has been revealed to him.

The primary point is not that each person should contain themselves within the limits of their office, but the Apostle teaches how each ought to use the gifts divinely given, so that one may be a member of another and serve them with his gifts, and each may administer his own duty for the common good 1 Cor. XII. 7. For that cannot conveniently be repeated from the common source for individual members, e.g., if anyone has prophecy, the Apostle does not hint that he should contain himself within the limits of Prophecy, but how the prophecy ought to be constituted, namely that he should have it according to the analogy of faith: if anyone has a ministry, let him be wholly occupied in the ministry: if anyone teaches, that he should show himself diligent in teaching, if anyone exhorts, that he should be diligent in exhortation: not that he should contain himself within the limits of doctrine: he who gives, that he should do it in simplicity: he who rules, let him rule with care and diligence: he who shows mercy, let him do it with cheerfulness. The Apostle therefore said nothing, because he gives precepts here to the disciples of the Apostles, and because he is writing to the Romans, among whom there were no Apostles. In the first place, therefore, he warns about Prophecy, which is the foundation of the remaining offices; but Prophets are not understood as those who have immediate revelations, but those who interpret the Scriptures, as this word is taken 1 Cor. XIV. 13. 29. 32. 1 Thess. V. 20. 1 Tim. IV. 14. 2 Pet. I. 20. Since, indeed, it is not for these to bring forth new Prophecies or revelations, but to search out, elicit, and propose the Prophecies or revelations contained in the Holy Scriptures. For a rule could not be prescribed to those, how they ought to prophesy, since they acted by the immediate impulse of the Holy Spirit, whatever they did: but for these a norm is prescribed, namely that they should interpret the Scriptures in such a way that their interpretation is analogous to the faith. But Grotius, along with Martyr, Piscator, and Cornel. à Lapide, wrongly understands the measure of revelation by the analogy of faith: for the measure of revelation is one thing, the analogy of faith is another: which is constituted here as the norm for Prophecies, insofar as it is had from the Scriptures, as they are the sole principle and foundation of faith. The analogy of faith, therefore, is the conformity of the doctrine of faith clearly exposed in the Holy Scriptures, which is done in those places especially where each doctrine has its own proper seat. Therefore, the interpretation of Scripture ought to be done according to Scripture, so that more obscure passages may be explained by clearer ones, since Scripture is its own interpreter, and not of private interpretation 2 Pet. I. 20. Thus Anselm explains: According to the reason of faith, that is, that we should speak or think nothing outside the rule of faith. So also most other interpreters, and from the Papists, Salmero l. 18. disp. 2. in Epist. ad Rom. Bellarmine, Book III, On the Word of God, chapter 10. Guilielmus Estius on this passage: according to the reason or congruence of faith, that is, in such a way that it follows the dictate of right faith. From the Reformed, Toffanus on this passage, Cocceius, and others. From our own, all without exception, none that I know of excepted. The analogy of faith is called the consensus and harmony of the heads and articles of the Christian religion, says B. Mylius. The sense is, as B. Jacob Weller says, that those who are interpreters of Scripture should take pains that the interpretation be analogous to faith, that is, that it agrees with the articles of faith and the principal heads of Christian doctrine revealed in Scripture. Regarding the sense of Grotius, which Piscator also taught, the blessed man holds this: The exposition of Piscator and others is rejected, because 1) the universal condition placed in verse 3 would thus be ascribed specifically to only one member of prophecy, which is absurd. For that is attributed to all in verse 3. 2) If the analogy of faith in this passage were the same as the capacity of our understanding of faith, then that understanding would be offered to us either through an extraordinary cause or through ordinary means: If the former, enthusiasm would be introduced; if the latter, it would follow that, because we must perpetually ascend to further knowledge, this very norm would be clearly imperfect; and thus this norm could never be any norm, since our knowledge is never perfect. Nor indeed is the gift of prophecy distributed according to the measure of faith. For many have faith who are destitute of the gift of prophecy.

Latin:

V. 6. ἔχοντες δὲ χαρίσματα κατὰ τὴν χάριν τὴν δοθεῖσαν ἡμῖν διάφορα. Dona varia, pro ea liberalitate, quam in nos Deus exercuit. Id enim dixit hîc διδόναι χάριν.

εἴτε προφητείαν. Subaudiendum in singulis membris, μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν. Contineant se intra limites singuli. Donum Prophetiae olim rarum, frequens in Ecclesia Christiana Act. XIII. 1. XV. 32. 1. Cor. XII. 28. 29. XIV. 29. 37. 38. Eph. III. 5. IV. 11. de Apostolis, quorum primus gradus, nihil dixit, quod illi admonitionis non egerent.

κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς πίστεως. Id est, pro prophetia, aut majore, qualem Moses habuit, aut minore qualem Prophetae alii, quam Deus ipsi pro modo fidei elargiri voluit. Hac mensura contentus sit, nec egrediatur sibi revelata.

Non id imprimis agitur, ut intra limites officii se quisque contineat, sed quomodo donis divinitus datis quisque uti debeat, docet Apostolus, ut alter alterius membrum sit eique donis suis inserviat, & quisque suũ munus πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον administret 1. Cor. XII. 7. Non enim commode illud penes singula membra repeti potest ἀπὸ κοινῦ v. g. si quis prophetam habet, non innuit Apostolus, ut intra limites Prophetiae se contineat, sed quomodo comparata esse debeat prophetia, ut nẽpe habeat eam secundum fidei analogiam: si quis ministerium habeat, is in ministerio totus versetur: si quis doceat, ut in docendo se praebeat sedulum, si quis exhortetur, ut in exhortatione diligens sit: non ut intra limites doctrinae se contineat: qui impertit, ut in simplicitate id faciat: qui praeest, cum curâ & diligentiâ praesit: qui miseretur, in hilaritate id praestet. Apostolus ideo nihil dixit, quod hîc det praecepta Apostolorum discipulis, quodque Romanis scribat, inter quos non erant Apostoli. Primo loco ergo de Prophetia monet, quae fundamentum est reliquorum officiorum; Non autem Prophetae intelliguntur, qui revelationes immediatas habent, sed qui Scripturas interpretantur, uti vox hæc accipitur 1. Cor. XIV. 13. 29. 32. 1. Thess. V. 20. 1. Tim. IV. 14. 2. Petr. I. 20. Siquidem horum qui- dem non sit novas Prophetias vel relationes pro- ferre, attamen Prophetias vel relationes in S. li- teris contentas scrutari, eruere, ac proponere. Illis enim regula præscribi non poterat, quomodo va- ticinari debeant, quum immediato Spiritus S. im- pulsu egerint, quicquid egerunt: his autem norma præscribitur, ut nempe sic interpretentur Scriptu- ras, ut interpretatio ipsorum fidei sit analoga. Per analogiam autem fidei perperam cum Martyre, Pi- scatore, Cornel. à Lapid. intelligit Grotius mensu- ram revelationis: aliud enim est mensura revela- tionis, aliud analogia fidei: Quæ hîc norma Pro- phetias constituitur, quatenus è Scripturis ead. ha- betur, utpote quæ unicum principium & funda- mentum sunt fidei. Analogia ergo fidei est conformitas doctrinæ fidei in Scripturis Sacris lu- culenter expositæ, quod in iis imprimis locis, ubi quæque doctrina propriam suam sedem ha- bet factum. Scripturæ ergo interpretatio secun- dum Scripturam fieri debet, ut obscuriora loca per luculentiora explicentur, quum Scriptura sui ipsius interpres, non vero ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως sit 2. Petr. I. 20. Sic Anshelmus exponit: Secundum rationem fidei, id est, ut extra regulam fidei nihil loquamur, aut sapiamus. Sic etiam alii plerique Interpp. & ex Pontificiis Salmero l. 18. disp. 2. in Epist. ad Rom. Bellarm. l. III. de Verbo DEI c. 10. Guilb. Estius in h. l. secundum rationem seu congruentiam fidei, id est, sic, ut sequatur rectæ fidei dictamen. E Refor- matis Toffanus in h. loc. Coccejus & alii. E nostris omnes in universum, nemine quod sciam excepto. Analogia fidei capitum atque articulorum religionis Christianæ consensus atque harmonia appellatur, ait B. Mylius. Sensus est, B. Jacobo Wellero dicente, qui sunt interpretes Scripturæ, operam dent, ut inter- pretatio sit analoga fidei, h. e. congruat cum articu- lis fidei & principalibus doctrinæ Christianæ capi- tibus in Scriptura revelatis. De Grotii vero sen- su, quem Piscator etiam tradidit, ita habet ὁ μα- καρίτης: Piscatoris & aliorum expositio rejicitur, quia 1.) conditio universalis posita v. 3. sic adscribe- retur in specie uni tantum membro prophetiæ scilicet quod absurdum. Omnibus n. v. 3. istud tribuitur. 2.) Si analogia fidei h. l. idem esset ac capacitas intellige- tiæ fidei nostræ, tunc illa intelligentia esset vel per ex- traordinariam causam nobis oblata, vel per ordina- ria media: Si prius, Enthusiasmus introduceretur: si posterius, sequeretur: quia perpetuo debemus ad ulteriorem cognitionem adscendere, ipsam hanc nor- mam plane esse imperfectam; Et sic nunquam pote- rit hæc norma esse aliqua norma, cum nostra cognitio nunquam sit perfecta. Neque vero donum prophe- tiæ pro mensura fidei distribuitur. Multi enim fidem habent, qui dono Prophetiæ destituti sunt.

## 12:7
εἴτε διακονίαν, ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ.

Supply σωφρονεῖν. This is the office of פנים, about which Maimonides has much in Volume III; see Acts 6.

Cocceius takes the word Διακονία or Ministry with such breadth that it also includes teaching and exhortation; but those are more correctly said to be brought forward as parts of prophecy; just as the others that follow are established here as parts of the ministry; so that in this way sacred functions are generally distributed into prophecy and ministry, and subsequently their parts are explained specifically, first indeed those of prophecy, which are doctrine and exhortation, then truly those of the ministry, which are of those who distribute, those who preside, and those who show mercy, of whom the former are the overseers of alms; the latter are the overseers of order and discipline in the Church, and the last are those who [care for] the sick, the exiled, and the afflicted, etc.

they take care. Buxtorf in his Talmudic Lexicon indeed explains the word חזן as a Deacon or minister of the Synagogue, but notes that it was his primary duty to lead the Church in prayer or supplications and singing, to preside over the legal reading, teaching what and how it should be read, and similar things which pertained to sacred matters, whence it is also taken for a cantor or precentor: how this fits this passage does not appear, since it is placed in order before the teachers: whence that opinion which we have mentioned is to be preferred, that it is a general name. For as a species it could by no means be placed in the Ecclesiastical order before the others which follow.

whether he who teaches, in teaching. Whether he who teaches, supply 'let him be'. But the Manuscript has 'whether teaching', supply 'having'. The teachers are the rank next to the Prophets. Acts 13:1, 1 Cor. 12:28, 19, Eph. 4:11. They were those who were set over many Churches to instruct those who presided over individual Churches, such as Titus in Crete, the senior Bishops in Africa, and Metropolitans elsewhere. In Judaism, the 'mufleim be-chokhma' or 'rabbanim' made for the Sanhedrin corresponded to these. You have doctors named in the ninth canon of the first Council of Caesaraugusta.

Latin:

εἴτε διακονίαν, ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ.

Supple σωφρονεῖν. Hoc est munus פנים de quo multa Maimonides Tomo III. vide Act. VI.

Διακονίας vel Ministerii vocem ea amplitudine accipit Coccejus, ut complectatur etiam τὴν διδα- σκαλίαν & τὴν παράκλησιν; sed illa rectius ceu par- tes τῆς προφητείας adductæ dicuntur: quemadmo- dum cætera, quæ sequuntur, partes τῆς διακονίας hic constituuntur; ut ita generaliter functiones sa- cræ in Prophetiam & Diaconiam distribuantur, & deinceps specialiter earum partes exponantur, primo quidem prophetiæ, quæ sunt doctrina, & exhortatio, deinde vero διακονίας, quæ sunt τῶν μεταδιδόντων, τῶν προϊσαμένων, τῶν ἐλεόν- των, quorum illi sunt Eleemosynarum præfecti: isti præfecti ordinis, & disciplinæ in Ecclesia, hi vero, qui ægrotorum, exulum, & afflictorum &c.

curam gerunt. Vocem חזן exponit quidem Bux- torf. in Lex Talm. de Diacono vel ministro Syna- gogæ, sed hujus maxime fuisse oratione sive precibus & cantu Ecclesiæ præire, præesse lectioni legali, do- cendo quod & quomodo legendum sit, & simili- bus, quæ ad sacra pertinebant, unde & pro cantore vel præcentore accipi notat : quod quomodo huic loco conveniat, non apparet : quum præmittatur ordine τοῖς διδασκαλοῖς: unde præferenda illa, quam diximus, sententia, quod generale sit no- men. Nam ut species in ordine Ecclesiastico præ- mitti cæteris, quæ sequuntur, minime poterat.

εἴτε ὁ διδάσκων, ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ. εἴτε ὁ διδάσκων, supple sit. At Manuscriptus εἴτε διδασκα- λίαν, supple ἔχων, οἱ διδάσκαλοι proximus à Prophetis gra- dus. Act. XIII. 1. 1. Cor. XII. 28. 19. Eph IV. 11. Erant il- li, qui multis Ecclesiis erant impositi ad instruendos eos, qui Ecclesiis singulis præerant, quales Titus in Creta, seniores Episcopi in Africa, alibi Metropolitæ. His respondebant in Judaismo מופלאים בחכמה sive רבנים Synedrio facti. Habes doctores nominatos Canone nono Concilii Cæsar-Augustani primi.

## 12:8
V. 8. whether he who exhorts, in exhortation. Here is signified the presbyter, 'laboring in the word' 1 Tim. 5:17, that is, the Bishop, to whom corresponded in Judaism the 'chacham ha-gadol' or 'memuneh', or 'rosh ha-kahal', or 'resh kenishta'. See on Matt. 9:18, Heb. 13:7, and in the Epistle of Clement.

If teachers are the rank next to the Prophets, why is 'ministry' interposed? Therefore, it is not noted here as a rank distinct from the Prophets, but since 'prophecy' is a genus, denoting the interpretation of Scripture, and it comprehends under itself 'teaching' and 'exhortation', it is specifically about these special parts of the Prophets that we are dealing here. However, those who teach here are not the same as the teachers in 1 Cor. 12:28 and Eph. 4:11, where the ranks of those who teach in the Church are recounted in order, nor are Archbishops, or senior Bishops, or Metropolitans understood by them in this place; just as those who exhort are not Bishops or presbyters, for such an opposition of those who exhort and those who teach is nowhere founded in the Scriptures, nor can it be taught from Antiquity. Therefore, two offices of the Prophets or those interpreting Holy Scripture are indicated: both 'teaching' or instruction concerning the doctrine of faith; and 'exhortation' or admonition, which is both hortatory, toward piety and holiness, and consolatory against temptation and affliction, of which the former (I designate 'teaching') is theoretical, the latter (consider 'exhortation') is practical; both ought to be instituted from the interpretation of Scripture, made according to the analogy of faith. They are separated for this reason, that some are more instructed with the gifts of admonishing, just as God is accustomed to distribute His gifts in various ways.

he who distributes, in simplicity. He understands the rich man. Opulence is indeed a temporal good, but when it is conferred for the uses of the poor, it becomes spiritual. 'Metadidōnai' is to make others participants of one's own goods. Luke 3:11, above 1:11, Eph. 4:28, 1 Thess. 2:8. You have that word also in the Interpreters of Job 31:17, Prov. 11:26. 'Simplicity' is usually opposed to deceitfulness, because the deceitful are double-minded, others are outside: but sometimes it is put for liberality as in 2 Cor. 7:2, 9:3, they do not pretend to have less than they have: they are not detractors of their own wealth.

Now follow the distinct functions of the Deacons, whom the Apostle mentioned. Those 'distributors', however, are not precisely the rich, since they are understood rather as administrators of ecclesiastical goods and prefects of alms: who dispense the goods of the Church, and thus others' goods, not their own. Which office was especially necessary in the primitive Church, in which the communion of goods flourished, Acts 2:42, 44, not that all lived in the same houses as in a 'koinobion', and had nothing of their own, but that for the sustenance of the poor they were accustomed to contribute a good part of their goods, and for that reason they sometimes even sold houses and lands, and contributed their prices to the uses of the Church, Acts 4:34. The dispensers of those collections were at first the Apostles themselves, afterwards Deacons appointed for that purpose, Acts 6:2, who are here specifically called 'distributors': and upon them is enjoined 'simplicity', which is to be opposed to fraud: so that, namely, they do not alienate anything from the goods of the Church, nor defraud anyone to whom distribution ought to be made, but that they dispense everything with a sincere mind, and without deceit and the gain of their own advantage. 'Simplicity' is also attributed to others giving from their own, 2 Cor. 8:2, ch. 9:3, 1 Chron. 29:9, when in that also a simple and sincere mind, intent on divine honor, the use of the Church, and the advantage of one's neighbor, is required. But duplicity of heart and hypocrisy ought to be absent.

he who presides, in diligence.

Those who preside here and in 1 Thess. 5:12, who are also 'those who rule' in 1 Tim. 5:17, are the presbyters, the 'parnasim' or 'zeqenim', of whom Tertullian says: 'The approved elders preside.' It was the duty of these to attend diligently to the morals of each, to warn the wavering, to correct the fallen with censure, to prescribe the time and manner of penance, and sometimes even to relax it. This care was called 'diligence'.

Therefore, those in charge of discipline and good order in the church are noted, such as governors, besides the ministers of the church, upon whom that care likewise rests today, are Superintendents and whoever are in charge of Ecclesiastical Consistories. Coccejus says that by the name of those who preside and those who stand before, are signified those who stand before others; namely, those who place themselves before others and defend their cause and right, as patrons. In which the care of necessities and governance is contained, 1 Tim. 3:4, 5, 12.

he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

He calls those 'showing mercy' here who attended to the sick, whom a later age called parabolani, because among other things, the law of the Parabolani in the Theodosian Code concerning Bishops and the law of the Parabolani in the Justinian Code under the same title. Cheerfulness in this place signifies readiness of mind, just as he is also called a cheerful giver in 2 Cor. 9:7; and so the Hebrew word for favor in Prov. 18:22 and 19:12 is translated as cheerful and cheerfulness by the Septuagint interpreters, but by others as good pleasure in Isa. 60:10, showing mercy.

Coccejus refers to this the 'helps' and 'healings' of 1 Cor. 12:28, but there it is a matter of the miraculous gift of healings; here it is about the duty toward the sick and other needy persons; nor does it appear how 'helps' ought to be restricted only to Deacons of this kind. Therefore, they are those showing mercy, who take care of the sick, the afflicted, and the exiles, which, even if it can be understood in a general sense, whether they do it by private care and compassion, or are destined for it and obligated by a public office; yet here the discourse is properly about such Ecclesiastical offices, to which also elderly and pious widows were applied, 1 Tim. 5:9 and Acts 6:1, for whom provision was made in the same manner at the same time. And thus Estius also explains it: although he admits that the common opinion of the interpreters is that the Apostle here passes from the precept of using spiritual gifts well, to precepts common to all; and he proves our opinion from the fact that this precept has a similar form to the preceding ones. But the things that follow, as they are common, so they differ in form from the seven above. And therefore the Apostolic rule is transferred by parity to the compassion of private individuals, when it is applied to it, but not, as Coccejus wishes, that those showing mercy and those contributing are distinguished in such a way that the former give from their own, but the latter from another's, namely from those things which have been collected in the Church for the use of the poor.

Cheerfulness, however, is required primarily for compassion in distributing alms, as in general to anyone, 1 Cor. 9:7, so also in those things which are dispensed from the public treasury, so that the friendly face of the one cheering may refresh the one to whom mercy is shown no less than the benevolent hand of the one pitying, such as a cheerful giver whom God loves. Almsgiving is, according to Chrysostom, to give in such a way that you rejoice that you are giving and think that you are receiving rather than giving. It is necessary for one bestowing mercy upon another, so that he may have it again, Chrysost. hom. XXXVI. to the people of Antioch, to rejoice, not to be indignant. For how is it not absurd, if one relieving another's sadness is himself sad? For it is no longer almsgiving. For you show the extreme of cruelty and inhumanity, because you have freed another from sorrow. Conf. Syr. IV. 8. cap. XXXV. 21. Tob. IV. 9.

Latin:

V. 8. εἴτε ὁ παρακαλῶν, ἐν τῇ παρακλήσει. Hic significatur presbyter, κοπιῶν ἐν λόγῳ 1. Tim. V. 17 id est, Episcopus, cui respondebat in Judaismo חכם הגדול sive ממנה, aut ראש הקהל, aut ריש כנישתא Vide ad Matth. IX. 18. Hebr. XIII. 7. & in Epistola Clementis.

Si διδάσκαλοι proximus à Prophetis gradus, cur interponitur διακονία ? Non ergo hîc ut distinctus à Prophetis gradus notatur, sed quum προφητεία genus sit, Scripturæ interpretationem notans, & ea comprehendat sub se διδασκαλίαν, καὶ παράκλησιν, de his Prophetarum partibus specialibus εἰδικῶς hic agitur. Non autem οἱ διδάσκοντες hic iidem sunt, qui διδάσκαλοι 1. Cor. XII. 28. Eph. IV. 11. ubi gradus docentium in Ecclesia ordine recen- sentur, neque vel Archi-Episcopi, aut Episcopi Se- niores, aut Metropolitæ per eos hoc loco intelli- guntur; uti nec οἱ παρακαλῶντες Episcopi sunt, aut presbyteri, talis enim oppositio τῶν παρακαλῶν- των & τῶν διδασκάλων nuspiam in Scripturis fun- data est, nec ex Antiquitate doceri potest. Offi- cia ergo Prophetarum seu Scripturam S. interpre- tantium duo indicantur: tum διδασκαλία seu in- stitutio de doctrina fidei; tum παράκλησις seu com- monefactio, quæ & adhortatoria est, ad pietatem & sanctitatem, & consolatoria adversus tentationẽ & afflictionem, quorum illud (διδασκαλίαν indi- gito,) theoreticum, hoc παράκλησιν puta) practi- cum est ; utrumque ex interpretatione Scripturæ, secundum analogiam fidei factâ, institui debet. Quæ ea de causa disjunguntur, quod nonnulli ma- gis instructi sint donis commonefaciendi, prout Deus diversimode dona sua distribuere solet.

ὁ μεταδιδοὺς, ἐν ἁπλότητι. Divitem intelligit. Est quidem opulentia bonum tem- porale, sed cum in usus pauperum confertur, fit spirituale. Μεταδιδόναι, est alios participes suorum bonorum facere. Luc. III. 11. supra I. 11. Eph. IV. 28. 1. Thess. II. 8. Habes id verbum & in Interpretibus Job. XXXI. 17. Prov. XI. 26. Ἁπλότης fallacitati opponi solet, quia dolosi sunt duplices, alii extra : sed interdum pro liberalitate ponitur ut II.Cor. VII. 2. IX. 3. non præ se ferunt minus se habere, quam ha- beant : non sunt detractatores opis propriæ.

Sequuntur jam Diaconorum, quos dixit Apo- stolus, distinctæ functiones. Μεταδιδόντες autem illi non sunt præcise divites, quum administrato- res potius bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, & Eleemosy- narum præfecti intelligantur: qui Ecclesiæ, & ita aliena, non sua bona dispensant. Quod officiũ im- primis in Ecclesia primitiva necessarium fuit, in qua vigebat bonorum communio, Act. II. 42. 44. non quod in iisdẽ ædibus omnes velut in κοινοβίῳ vixerint, nihilque habuerint proprium, sed quod ob sustentationem pauperum bonam partem bono- rum suorum conferre soliti sunt, eaque de causa etiam domos ac fundos, quandoque vendiderint, ac pretia eorum in usus Ecclesiæ contulerint Act. IV. 34. Istarum collectarum dispensatores primo ipsi erant Apostoli, post Diaconi ad id constituti Act. VI. 2. qui hic speciatim μεταδιδόντες dicuntur: iisque injungitur ἁπλότης Simplicitas, quæ fraudi opposita esse: ne sc. quidpiam de bonis Ecclesiæ alienent, nec quemquam, cui distributio fieri de- bet, defraudent, sed ut animo sincero, & sine dolo proprique commodi lucro dispensent omnia. Alias etiam de suo largientibus ἁπλότης tribuitur 2. Cor. IIX. 2. c. IX. 3. 1. Chron. XXIX. 9. quum & in eo animus simplex & sincerus, honori divino, Ecclesiæ usui, & proximi commodo intentus, re- quiratur. Cordis vero duplicitas & hypocrisis abesse debeat.

ὁ προϊστάμενος, ἐν σπυδῇ.

Προϊσάμενοι hic & 1. Thess. V. 12. qui & προεστῶτες 1. Tim. V. 17. sunt οἱ πρεσβύτεροι הפרנסים sive הזקנים, de qui- bus Tertullianus: Præsident probati quique seniores. Horum erat diligenter attendere ad singulorum mores, monere ti- tubantes, lapsos censurâ corrigere, præscribere pœnitentiæ tempus & modum, interdum & relaxare. Hæc cura σπυδὴ dicebatur.

Præfecti ergo disciplinæ & ἐυταξίας in Ecclesiæ conservandæ notantur, quales gubernatores, præ- ter ministros Ecclesiæ, quibus illa cura itidem ho- die incumbit, Superintendentes sunt & quicunque Ecclesiasticis Consistoriis præfecti sunt. Coccejus προϊσαμένων, inquit, & προεστώτων nomine signifi- cantur q. ante alios stantes; nempe qui se sistunt pro aliis & eorum causam & jus defendunt, tanquam patroni. In quo cura necessariorum & gubernatio continetur, 1. Tim. III. 4. 5. 12.

ὁ ἐλεῶν, ἐν ἱλαρότητι.

Ἐλεῶντας hic vocat, qui ægrotis aderant, quos posterios ætas parabolanos vocavit, L. quia inter cætera L. Parabo- lani C. Theodosiano de Episcopis & L. Parabolani C. Ju- stin. titulo eodem. ἱλαρότης hoc loco promptitudinem ani- mi significat, quomodo & ἱλαρὸς δότης dicitur 2. Cor. IX. 7. itaque רצון Prov. XVIII. 22. & XIX. 12. ἱλαρὸν & ἱλαρό- της vertitur interpretibus LXX. at aliis εὐδοκία Esa. LX. 10. ἐλεῶν.

Coccejus huc refert ἀντιλήψεις & ἰάματα 1. Cor. XIV. 28. sed ibi de dono sanationum miraculoso agi- tur; hic de officio erga ægrotos, & alios indigentes; nec apparet, quomodo ἀντιλήψεις ad hujus ge- neris Diaconos tantum restringi debeant. Sunt ergo ἐλεῶντες, qui ægrotorum, afflictorum, exulum, curam gerunt, quod etsi in genere intelligi possit, sive privata cura & miseratione id agant, seu ad id destinati sint, & publico munere obligati; hic tamẽ proprie de muneribus ejusmodi Ecclesiasticis ser- mo est, ad quod etiam viduæ vetulæ ac piæ adhi- bitæ sunt 1. Tim. V. 9. & Act. VI. 1. quibus eadem ratione simul prospectum fuit. Atque ita explicat etiam Estius: etsi fateatur, communem Interpp. sententiam esse, Apostolum hic transire à præcepto bene utendi spiritualibus, ad præcepta omnibus com- munia; probatque nostram sententiam inde, quod hoc præceptum formam similem habeat cum præce- dentibus. Quæ vero sequuntur, uti communia sunt, ita formâ à septem superioribus differant. Ideoque regula Apostolica à pari transfertur ad privato- rum commiserationem, cum de ea adhibetur, non vero ut Coccejus vult, ἐλεῶντες & μεταδιδόντες ita distinguuntur, quod illi de suo largiantur, hi vero de alieno, de his nempe quæ in Ecclesia in usum pauperum collecta sunt.

Hilaritas autem requi- ritur imprimis ad commiserationem, in dstribuen- dis eleemosynis, ut in genere quibusvis 1. Cor. IX. 7. ita etiam in illis, quæ è publico dispensantur æra- rio, ut non minus exhilarantis amica facies, quam miserantis benevola manus illum reficiat, cui mi- sericordia exhibetur, qualem hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Eleemosyna est, Chrysostomo d Eleemosyna autore, sic dare, ut gaudeas te dar putesque te accipere magis, quam dare. Oportet al teri misericordiam impendentem, ut iterum habe Chrysost. hom. XXXVI. ad popul. Antiochen gaudere, non indignari. Nam quomodo non abfur dum, si solvens alterius tristitiam ipse tristetur? No enim finis amplius eam esse eleemosynam. Nam mores, quod alium a mœrore liberaveris, extrema præfers crudelitatis ac inhumanitatis significatio nem. Conf. Syr. IV. 8. cap. XXXV. 21. Tob. IV. 9.

## 12:9
Vers. 9. Love without hypocrisy.

Supply ἔστω (let it be). Just as in the following it is understood ἧτε (you may be). Just as the Levites were brothers among themselves Levit. XXI. 6. Deut. XVIII. 7. so also you. You have the word ἀνυπόκριτος also in Wisd. V. 13. XVIII. 6. and Jas. III. 17. It is attributed to love, not here only, but also 2 Cor. VI. 6. 1 Pet. 1. 22. To faith, 1 Tim. I. 5. 2 Tim. I. 5.

Abhorring that which is evil, cleaving to that which is good.

Namely, just as the Levites had formerly adhered to Moses and then to Phinehas, with burning hatred of idolatry. Exod. XXII. 26. XXV. 11. Deut. XXXIII. 9.

Again, the Levites are introduced rashly and without indication from the text; and we ought to show love not only to brothers, but even to enemies themselves, as the Apostle will warn later v. 20. It concerns brotherly love (Φιλαδελφίᾳ) in v. 10. Furthermore, love (ἀγάπη) according to Aretius is said to be from 'doing exceedingly' (ἄγαν ποιεῖν), because it is industrious. The word 'abhorring' (ἀποστυγῦντες) implies such hatred as we pursue hell itself with, or the Devil, since it is derived from Styx or hell. The word 'cleaving' (κολλώμενοι) is derived from glue, because we ought to adhere most closely to the good, and it is used concerning the combination of husband and wife, Matt. XIX. 5. Eph. V. 21. and also concerning the mystical union of the faithful with Christ, 1 Cor. VI. 17. Things to be avoided and things to be done are usually comprehended in this way: hating evil, cleaving to that which is good. See Ps. XXXIV. 18. Isa. I. 16. Acts XXVI. 18. Eph. IV. 22. seqq. Here this is specially warned concerning love, because in order for love to be sincere, and not against GOD, evil must be hated, but the good must be adhered to; and therefore communion is not to be had with the wicked, so that evil is approved, and the good are to be loved, so that we may seem to cleave to goodness itself (τῷ ἀγαθῷ). And therefore in the love of one's neighbor this rule is primarily to be observed: abhorring that which is evil, cleaving to that which is good.

In brotherly love, kindly affectioned one to another.

Aristotle, Xenophon, and even Cicero in his letters to Atticus use this word 'kindly affectioned' (φιλοστόργοι). Hence you have the adverb 'kindly' (φιλοστόργως) in 2 Macc. IX. 21. It signifies a vehement affection of loving.

In honor preferring one another.

The same sense is in Philipp. II. verse 3. The lesser Levites yielded to the greater; you yourselves yield to anyone. Let this be a contest among you. 'Preferring' (προηγεῖσθαι) here is to set before oneself, to consider more worthy, 'esteeming them better' (ἡγεῖσθαι ὑπερέχοντας) in the cited place to the Philippians.

In the Vulgate, the object of 'kindly affection' (Φιλοστοργίας) is less correctly established as brotherly love (Φιλαδελφία) itself. 'In brotherly love, loving one another,' concerning which Thomas is therefore rashly subtle here; therefore, from the Roman correction, it is read 'IN CHARITY'; brotherly love ought to be such among the faithful as the innate and natural affection (στοργὴ) is accustomed to be, such as is between father and son. But in order that honor may be fostered and preserved among us, it is necessary that one not only pursue another with honor, but also anticipate him. Phil. II. 3. 4. Blessed Balduinus gives the reason: This is the nurse of brotherly charity, which removes all suspicion of contempt or hatred: and the dignity of human nature requires it, in which is the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, and the image of GOD, now after the fall restored in some way, on account of which man owes his honor to man, according to that 1 Pet. II. 17. Honor all men.

PART II. CHAP. XII. Apostolic admonitions concerning the pursuit of holiness.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἀγάπη ἀνυπόκριτος.

Supple ἔστω. Sicut in sequentibus subauditur ἧτε. Sicut Levitæ inter se fratres erant Levit. XXI. 6. Deut. XVIII. 7. sic & vos. Vocem ἀνυπόκριτος habes & Sap. V. 13. XVIII. 6. & Jac. III. 17. Tribuitur dilectioni, non hic tantum, sed & 2. Cor. VI. 6. 1. Petr. 1. 22. Fidei, 1. Tim. I. 5. 2. Tim. I. 5.

ἀποστυγῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν, κολλώμενοι τῷ ἀγαθῷ.

Nempe sicut Levitæ olim Mosi ac deinde Phinez adhæ- serant, ardenti odio idololatriæ. Exod. XXII. 26. XXV. 11. Deut. XXXIII. 9.

Iterum temere, & citra textus indicium immi- scentur Levitæ; Nec tantum fratribus ἀγάπην exhibere debemus, sed ipsis etiam inimicis, ut postea monebit Apostolus v. 20. De Φιλαδελφίᾳ agitur v. 10. Cæterum ἀγάπη juxta Aretium dici- tur ab ἄγαν ποιεῖν, quia operosa est. Verbum ἀπο- στυγῦντες odium tale infert, quo infernum prose- quimur ipsum, vel Diabolum, quum à Styge seu inferno deducatur. Verbum κολλώμενοι à glutine deductum est, quod arctissime adhærescere bono debeamus, & de combinatione maris & uxoris adhibetur Matth. XIX. 5. Eph. V. 21. nec non de unione fidelium mystica cum Christo 1. Cor. VI. 17. Solent autem ita fugienda & facienda comprehen- di, odio habentes malum, adhærentes ei, quod bonum est. Vid. Ps. XXXIV. 18. Es. I. 16. Act. XXVI. 18. Eph. IV. 22. seqq. Hic specialiter id monetur circa dilectionem, quia ut amor sincerus sit, nec adver- sus DEO, odio habendum malum, bono autem ad- hærendum; ideoque nec cum malis communio habenda, ut approbetur malum, & boni diligendi, ut τῷ ἀγαθῷ bonitati ipsi adhærescere videamur. Ideoque in dilectione proximi hæc imprimis obser- vanda regula, ἀποστυγῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν, κολλώμενοι τῷ ἀγαθῷ.

τῇ Φιλαδελφίᾳ εἰς ἀλλήλες Φιλόστοργοι.

Utuntur hac voce φιλοστόργοι, Aristoteles, Xenophon, Cicero etiam ad Atticum. Hinc adverbium φιλοστόργως habes II. Macc. IX. 21. Significat vehementem amandi af- fectum.

Τῇ τιμῇ ἀλλήλες προηγύμενοι.

Idem sensus Philipp. II. vers. 3. Levitæ minores cede- bant majoribus, vos ultro cuivis concedite. Sit hoc in- ter vos certamen. Προηγεῖσθαι hic est sibi præponere, po- ttiorem ducere, ἡγεῖσθαι ὑπερέχοντας dicto ad Philippenses loco.

In vulgata minus recte Objectum Φιλοστοργίας constituitur ipsa Φιλαδελφία. Charitatem frater- nam invicem diligentes, de quo proinde temere subtilis est hic Thomas; Ideo ex castigatione Ro- mana legitur CHARITATE; Amor fraternus talis esse inter fideles debet, qualis congenita & naturalis στοργὴ esse solet, qualis est inter patrem & filium. Ut vero honor inter nos foveatur & con- servetur, opus est, ut alter alterum honore non prosequatur modo, sed etiam præveniat. Phil. II. 3. 4. Causam reddit B. Balduinus: Est hæc virtus nu- tricula fraternæ charitatis, quæ removet omnem su- spicionem contemtus, aut odii: & requirit eam di- gnitas humanæ naturæ, in qua domicilium est Spi- ritus Sancti, & imago DEI, jam post lapsum qua- litercunque restaurata, propter quam homo homini suum honorem debet, juxta illud 1. Petr. II. 17. Omnes honorate.

PARS II. CAP. XII. Monita Apostolica circa studium sanctitatis.

## 12:11
V. 11. Not slothful in zeal.

The Levites were girded, Ezek. XLIV. 18, as Propertius said, 'girded temple-attendants.' For the function of the temple-attendants at Rome was that which the Levites had at Jerusalem. That is a sign of the diligence which Christians ought to show in every good work.

Fervent in spirit.

As with the fire of the pots of the Levites, Mic. III. 3, 1 Sam. II. 13, and following, Ezek. XXIV. 4.

Serving the Lord.

Which is said excellently of the Levites, Num. I. 50, VIII. 15, Deut. X. 1, Sam. II. 13, Ezek. XLV. 4, 5.

Nothing here about the Levites. Nor in the whole chapter. An allusion to the Priests was made near the beginning; nowhere to the Levites. Those glosses, therefore, are merely arbitrary. But these and the following admonitions of the Apostle exhibit rules which are observed: 1. concerning the pursuit of piety toward God, where there is need for alacrity in discharging the parts of one's duty, and fervor of spirit, or zeal for piety, v. 10; the observation of time and the occasion for doing good, hope, joy, tolerance of adversities, and unwearied prayer, v. 12; (2) concerning the duty of charity toward one's neighbor, by which beneficence and hospitality, v. 13, forgiveness and sympathy, v. 15, and harmony, v. 16; (3) concerning the duty of sobriety toward ourselves, where is required: Humility, v. 16; Modesty, v. ibid.; Meekness, v. 17; the pursuit of peace, v. 18; and finally, the moderation of anger and vengeance, v. 19 and 20. In the pursuit of piety, therefore, and the acts of the duty divinely entrusted to us, there is need above all that we be not slothful in zeal, and fervent in spirit. One must act alacritously and fervently in what is incumbent upon each person, as Mylius says here; for to be sluggish is not for men, but for dormice. For time slips away, and opportunities flow by. 'Fervent in spirit.' This is greater than the former. For he is fervent who is entirely inflamed with zeal. Yet while the Apostle requires the fervor of the Spirit, he quite clearly disapproves of the zeal of the flesh, which is not according to knowledge. And he utterly rejects the 'fervor of the times,' which is in great praise of moderation for some. And therefore let us be neither fervent nor lukewarm, Rev. III. 16. Furthermore, he wishes the faithful not to be sluggish, but ready for labors and cheerful in acting. And since this fervor is stirred up by the Spirit of GOD, our spirit also, that is, our mind, should be fervent with the love of God and of our neighbor, and with other holy virtues, as Aretius holds here. Zesis signifies an effervescence of the spirits around the heart. Compare 2 Tim. I. 6, 1 Thess. V. 19. 'He is fervent in spirit,' says Basil in the Shorter Rules, no. 259, 'who does the will of God with ardent zeal, insatiable desire, and assiduous diligence, in the charity of Christ Jesus our Lord.' To the pursuit of piety belongs most especially that rule: 'Serving the Lord,' because we ought to serve God as our ONLY LORD with holy devotion, obedience, and humility, nor should we allow ourselves to be drawn away by anything from the service (douleia) owed to God. The Holy Scriptures do not recognize a distinction in religious worship between service (douleia) and worship (latreia). But it claims for GOD ALONE service (douleia) just as much as worship (latreia), when it is a matter of the worship of the first table and religious worship. And thus the Syriac, the Vulgate, and also Beza and Casaubon, along with Basil in Ethics definition 68, Chrysostom, and Theophylact, read 'the Lord' (to kyrio) in this place. And the Greek interpreters connect these with the preceding. as Erasmus notes, in this way: loving, honoring, and cherishing one another, you will show worship to the Lord, because whatever duty is expended upon a neighbor reaches the Lord himself. B. Luther, however, embraced another reading, which has 'the time' (to kairo), with Erasmus in his German version, but in such a way that he leaves it free which reading one might prefer to follow: in his commentary on this place. It is not yet clear which reading I should pronounce the truer. For it is not absurd to read 'serving the time,' so that we may understand the Apostle to admonish us to accommodate ourselves to the time. And it can also be read not inappropriately, serving the Lord; let each follow whichever he pleases. But he adds: But I embrace the other reading, being fervent in time, which is the same as, accommodate yourselves to the time, and manage it well, so that all things may be done by you in their time. This, according to Ps. 1, is to bear fruit in its time. Erasmus also prefers it in his annotations on this passage. Which καιροδουλεια consists not in the conformation of the mind and actions to the customs of the age, which the Apostle had forbidden in v. 2, but in the holy observation of the time granted by God, so that we do not neglect the time of grace and gracious visitation, Jer. VIII. 7, 2 Cor. VI. 2, 3, Luke XIX. 44, and that we observe the opportunity of doing good and benefiting others, Gal. VI. 10, Eph. V. 16, Col. IV. 5. and modestly and with honesty, in suitable places and with suitable persons, and at a suitable time, let us speak the faith of religion, but not indeed everywhere and inopportunely, casting words of religion at an unfavorable time, through which perhaps scandal is excited; as Ambrosiasler holds. Blessed Mylius: To serve the time is not to accommodate oneself to the customs of the age, which he expressly forbade above, Rom. XII. 2, or like a polypus, to change oneself into all forms, which the ἀλλοπρόσωποι do. Nor finally to be like a ship's side always leaning, everywhere studious of its own advantage: but in indifferent matters, referring all things to the use of public edification, by the Pauline example becoming all things to all men, 1 Cor. IX. 22. Nor does the word δουλεύοντες truly oppose this reading, as Beza thinks. Since, as Blessed Er. Schmid notes, we even read καιρῷ δουλεύειν in the Epigrams; and Eudæus cites καιρῷ δῦλον from Gregory. And all things cohere well, whether it is said that the pious are advised that if any inconvenience should happen, they should take this in good part, or whether καιροδουλία is explained by the ways already proposed. Blessed Beza himself also observes that this reading is found in Origen and the ordinary gloss; which the Basel edition also, as well as the Tigurine, Argentine, Stephanus, Schmid, and others retain. Which our own opinion also seems to be preferable. In this way also the so-called Ambrosian reads, refuting the other reading as inconvenient. But also the most ancient MSS., as Fr. Lucas reports, which prefix arguments of the chapters to the books, inscribe the 48th chapter of this Epistle concerning serving the time.

Latin:

V. 11. τῇ σπουδῇ μὴ ὀκνηροί.

Levitæ erant succincti Ezech. XLIV. 18. quomodo Propertius dixit, succinctas popas. Nam Poparum Romæ ea erat functio, quæ Levitarum Hierosolymis. Id signum sedulitatis, quam in omni bono opere præstare debent Christiani.

τῷ πνεύματι ζέοντες.

Sicut igne ollæ Levitarum Mich. III. 3. 1. Samuel. II. 13. & sequentibus Ezech. XXIV. 4.

τῷ κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες.

Quod eximie de Levitis dicitur Num. I. 50. VIII. 15. Deut. X. 1. Sam. II. 13. Ezech. XLV. 4. 5.

Nihil hic de Levitis. Nec in toto capite. Ad Sacerdotes allusio sub initium facta; nuspiam ad Levitas. Glossæ ergo illæ mere arbitrariæ sunt. Monita autem hæc & sequentia Apostoli regulas exhibent, quæ observantur 1. circa studium pietatis erga Deum, ubi opus est alacritate in expediundis officii partibus, & fervore spiritus, vel zelo pietatis v. 10. observatione temporis & occasionis bene agendi, spe, lætitia, adversorum tolerantia, oratione indefessa v. 12. (2.) circa officium charitatis erga proximum, qua beneficentiam & hospitalitatem v. 13. ignoscentiam & συμπαθείαν v. 15. & ὁμόνοιαν v. 16. (3.) circa debitum sobrietatis erga nos ipsos, ubi requiritur: Humilitas v. 16. Modestia v. eod. Mansuetudo v. 17. studium pacis, v. 18. denique iræ & vindictæ moderatio v. 19. & 20. In pietatis ergo studio & actibus officii divinitus concrediti opus imprimis est, ut simus studio non pigri, & spiritu fervidi. Alacriter & fervide agendum, quod cuique incumbit, ut hic Mylius, Torpere autem non hominum, sed glirium est. Labitur n. tempus, effluunt occasiones. Spiritu ferventes. Hoc priori proximo majus est. Fervet enim, qui totus inardescit studio. Dum tamen Spiritus fervorem requirit Apostolus, carnis zelum, qui non est secundum scientiam, haud obscure improbat. Temporum vero, qui aliquibus in magna moderationis laude est, prorsus repudiat. Ideoque nec ferventes simus, nec tepidi Apoc. III. 16. Porro impigros vult fides non esse, paratos ad labores, hilares ad agendum. Et cum DEI Spiritu excitetur fervor iste, noster quoque Spiritus h. e. animus ferveat amore Dei, & proximi, aliisque sanctis virtutibus, ut hic habet Aretius. Ζέσις significat effervescentiam Spirituum circa cor. Conf. 2. Tim. I. 6. 1. Thess. V. 19. Spiritu fervens est, ait Basil. in Regul. brevior. n. 259. qui ardenti studio & inexplebili cupiditate, & assidua diligentia voluntatem Dei facit, in charitate Christi Jesu Domini nostri. Ad Pietatis studium vel maxime pertinet illa Regula; τῷ κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες, quod Deo tanquam UNI DOMINO Nostro servire debeamus sancta devotione, obedientia, & humilitate, nec ulla re à δουλείᾳ Deo debita nos abstrahi patiamur. Non agnoscit S.S. discrimen in cultu religioso τῆς δουλείας & λατρείας. Sed DEO UNI æque δουλείαν uti λατρείαν vendicat, cum de cultu primæ tabulæ & religioso agitur. Atque ita legit hoc loco τῷ κυρίῳ Syrus, Vulgatus, nec non Beza & Casaubonus cum Basilio in Ethicis definit. 68. Chrysostomo & Theophylacto. Et connectunt hæc cum superioribus Græci Interpp. notante Erasmo, hoc modo: amantes, honorantes, & adamantes invicem Domino cultum exhibebitis, quod quicquid officii proxime impenditur, ad ipsum Dominum pervenit, B. Lutherus tamen aliam lectionem, quæ habet τῷ καιρῷ, cum Erasmo amplexus est in versione Germanica, sed ita, ut liberum hoc relinquat, quamnam lectionem quis sequi malit: in enarrat. h. l. Nondum liquet, utram veriorem lectionem pronunciem Neque enim absurdum est legere, servientes tempori, ut intelli- gamus monere Apostolum, ut tempori nos accommo- demus. Et potest etiam non incommodè legi, servien- tes Domino; Quisque sequatur, utram libuerit. Addit autem: Sed ego alteram lectionem amplector fervientes tempori, quod perinde est, accommodate vos tempori, & probè ipsum dispensate, ut omnia suo tempore à vobis fiant. Id juxta Ps. 1. est fructum ferre in suo tempore. Eam etiam præfert Erasmus in ann. ad h. l. Quæ καιροδουλεια consistit non in animi & actionum juxta mores seculi conformatio- ne, quam prohibuerat Apostolus v. 2. sed in san- cta temporis à Deo concessi observatione, ut tempus gratiæ & gratiosæ visitationis non negligamus, Jer. IIX. 7. 2. Cor. VI. 2. 3. Luc. XIX. 44. & occasionem bene operandi & aliis benefaciendi observemus Gal. VI. 10. Eph. V. 16. Col. IV. 5. & modestè & cum ho- nestate, aptis locis & personis, & apto tempore religio- nis fidem loquamur, non verò passim & importunè, tempore inimico verba religionis injiciamus, per quod fortè scandalum excitatur; ut Ambrosiasler habet. B. Mylius: Tempori servire, non est, moribus seculi se accommodare, quod supra disertè vetuit, Rom. XII. 2. aut Polypi instar, in omnes se mutare formas, quod faciunt ἀλλοπρόσωποι. Neque denique infœlicius la- tus navis incumbentem semper, commodi sui passim studiosum esse: sed in rebus mediis, ad usum ædifica- tionis publicæ referentem omnia, exemplo Paulino omnibus omnia fieri 1. Cor. IX. 22. Nec vero adver- satur huic lectioni vox δουλεύοντες, uti Beza putat. Siquidem notante B. Er. Schmidio etiam in Epi- grammatibus καιρῷ δουλεύειν legamus; & Eudæus καιρῷ δῦλον ex Gregorio alleget. Et cohærent omnia probè, sive dicatur moneri pios, ut si quid incommodi accideret, hoc boni consulant, sive modis jam propositis καιροδουλία exponatur. Observat etiam Beza ipse, quod habeatur hæc le- ctio in Origene & glossa ordinaria; quam Basileensis quoque editio, nec non Tigurina, Argentina, Ste- phanus, Schmidius aliique retinent. Quæ nostra quoque sententia præferenda videtur. Hoc mo- do etiam legit Ambrosianus dictus, alteram lectio- nem ceu incommodam refutans. Sed & antiquissi- ma MSS. referente Fr. Luca, quæ libris argumenta capitum præfigunt, hujus Epistolæ 48. caput de tempori inserviendo inscribunt.

## 12:12
V. 12. Rejoicing in hope.

Not with the hope of tithes and similar revenues, but with the hope of eternal life. Thus it is fulfilled spiritually in Christians, which had been said concerning the Levites: God is their portion, Num. XVIII. 20.

Patient in tribulation.

Just as the duty of the Levites had been to carry the tabernacle, so you, for the sake of the Church, sustain anything.

Continuing steadfastly in prayer.

This also was proper to the Levites. Ezra IX. 5, XI. 17.

What does the joy of the Levites on account of the hope of tithes have to do with this? Or were the joy and pleasure of the Levites only tithes or similar revenues? Was there no hope of eternal life for them, no joy in the Lord? What does the carrying of the tabernacles have to do with this, which pertained to their ordinary duty, and was not like a cross? But these admonitions of the Apostle cohere: Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, instant in prayer: because hope, patience, and prayer must be together, and when they are together, we rejoice even in adversities on account of the hope of a better life, the nature of patience, and the virtue of prayer, Rom. V. 2, James I. 2. Hope fosters the Christian soul, adds alacrity, and fills us with joy. Then indeed it also wonderfully consoles, and makes us strong in afflictions, and impels us to prayers and praises of GOD. Therefore we are patient in tribulations, being animated by hope, and imbued with joy on account of a solid hope; which overcomes all afflictions: especially when we are instant in faithful prayer: that is, frequently, confidently, and

perseveringly we solicit divine grace with prayers: which requirements of prayer are insinuated by the word προσκαρτερῶντες. For prayer overcomes afflictions, increases hope, and makes us cheerful, as being certain and secure of being heard, and committing all things to the divine will. Faith pours forth prayer, prayer poured forth obtains firmness for faith, as Augustine says in Sermon XXXVI on the Words of the Lord. Philosophy also teaches hope, as Blessed Mylius holds, but a false one, indeed one that is nothing. For it teaches one to hope, but in such a way that if it happens that one is deceived, one remembers that nothing alien to hope has happened to oneself. Hence it must always be doubtful, and joined with fear. Christian hope, always certain of a happy end, expels fear and the rancors of the flesh, complaints, and overcomes all evils with joy. Akin to this, indeed as it were its offspring, is tolerance in affliction. To both of which ardor and constancy of prayers is not undeservedly joined; for these are not the fruits of natural powers: but gifts to be obtained from heaven through prayers.

Latin:

V. 12. τῇ ἐλπίδι χαίροντες.

Non spe decimarum similiunique obventionum, sed spe vitæ æternæ. Ita spiritualiter impletur in Christianis, quod de Levitis dictū fuerat: Deus portio ipsorū Num. XVIII. 20.

τῇ θλίψει ὑπομένοντες.

Sicut Levitarum munus fuerat ferre tabernaculum, ita vos Ecclesiæ causa quidvis sustinete.

τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερῶντες.

Erat & hoc Levitarum proprium. Esdræ IX. 5. XI. 17.

Quid huc facit gaudium Levitarum ob spem de- cimarum? aut num Levitarum gaudiū & voluptas solum erant decimæ aut similes obventiones? Nū ipsis nulla spes vitæ æternæ, nullum gaudium erat in Domino? Quid huc portatio tabernaculorum, quæ ad ordinarium munus eorum pertinebat, non ve- ro crucis instar erat? Cohærent autem ista Apo- stoli monita: Spe gaudentes, in tribulatione patien tes, orationi instantes: quia, spes, patientia & oratio simul esse debent, & cum simul sunt, etiam in ad- versis gaudemus ob spem vitæ melioris, patientiæ indolem, & orationis virtutem, Rom. V. 2. Jac. I. 2. Spes animum Christianum fovet, alacritatem ad- dit, & gaudio nos perfundit. Tum vero mirifice etiam consolatur, ac fortes reddit in afflictionibus, & ad orationes & laudes DEI impellit. Ideo in tribulationibus patientes sumus, spe nimirum ani- mati, & gaudio ob spem solidam delibuti; quod omnes afflictiones superat: imprimis ubi oratione fideli instamus: hoc est frequenter, fiducialiter &

perseveranter precibus divinam gratiam solicita- mus: quæ orationis requisita voce προσκαρτερῶν- τες insinuantur. Oratio enim afflictiones superat, spem auget, nosque hilares reddit, utpote de ex- auditione certos, & securos, ac voluntati divinæ omnia committentes. Fides fundit orationem, ora- tio fusa fidei impetrat firmitatem dicente Augustino Serm.XXXVI. de Verb. Dom. Docet spem etiam Philosophia, ut habet B. Mylius, sed falsam, imo quæ nulla est. Sperare enim docet, verum sic, ut si falli contingat, nihil à spe alienum sibi accidisse memine- rit. Hinc dubia semper sit oportet, & cum metu con- juncta. Spes Christiana de fine læto semper certa, me- tum expellit & carnis rancores, querelas, mala omnia gaudio semper superat. Huic cognata, imo hujus quasi propago est tolerantia in afflictione. Cui utrique ar- dor & constantia precum haud immerito conjungitur; Neque enim naturalium virium hi sunt fructus: sed dona cœlitus per preces impetranda.

## 12:13
V. 13. ταῖς χρείαις τῶν ἁγίων κοινωνοῦντες, τὴν φιλοξενίαν διώκοντες. Some codices have had μνείαις: and indeed this was also the duty of the Levites, to celebrate the memory of great men, concerning which matter we have spoken to the son of Sirach. But I prefer this more accepted reading. The Levites used to feast with the poor and the strangers from the tithes: But Paul exhorts the mystical Levites, that they themselves should receive the poor and strangers from their own means. Διώκειν here is to pursue, as above IX. 30. In the following verse to persecute, as Matt. V. 10. 11. where see the remarks.

The reading of the Greek codices is rightly preferred, even though not only did Ambrosiaster read 'Memories', but Optatus also cites this passage in this way (l. II. contr. Donatist.), Chrysologus (Serm. CXX.), Gregory (l. II. in Epist. ad Optim. & pop. Germ.), the Milanese Missal, which they call Ambrosian, and indeed even Hilary in 'Constantius Augustus', and Rufinus in his 'Commentary on Origen' testifies that that reading is held more in Latin codices. But he who also preferred the reading of the Greek codices: which Guilh. Estius proves not only from the Syriac and Latin editions, but also from the constant consensus of the Greek codices, and teaches that it is very consistent with similar Apostolic precepts in Gal. VI., Phil. IV., 1 Tim. VI., Heb. XIII., 2 Cor. VIII. & IX., and the last chapter of 1 Cor. Moreover, it is even more appropriate to the text than the other reading: because when they recognized that patron of theirs, they wished to snatch it into the same meaning, i.e., that the memory of the holy poor should be held: whether by private communication of temporal goods, or in solemn collections, which are accustomed to be made for the poor. But this is not to COMMUNICATE in the memories of the saints. However, they are rightly said to communicate in the necessities of the saints, not so much those who have a certain communion of tribulations, which is accustomed to make the cross more tolerable, as those who succor their indigence, and make their own resources common to brothers laboring in want, just as χρεία is taken for indigence in 1 John III. Therefore this rule is joined with the precept of Hospitality towards exiles and the wretched, to whom we ought not to deny hospitality. Erasmus notes that the Apostle says 'communicating', not 'assisting', because it is a commerce between the giver and the receiver, and he who gives a benefit gains more than he who receives. And that it is not said ἀνάγκαις, but χρείαις, which sounds more of use, or having need. Which he warned of for this reason, because some think we ought not to assist our neighbor except in extreme necessity. But Turrianus (l. IV. defens. Ep. Pontif. c. 14) is inept, explaining 'necessity of the saints' as the punishments of the dead; which are to be relieved by prayers and alms: since we neither know for certain that they are saints, who, namely, have died in the faith, and we are certain that the faithful are not afflicted by any punishment after death, but enjoy beatitude; but we are commanded to pursue, i.e., to follow after hospitality: as to follow after charity * and peace † so that not only is it not to be denied, but even to be offered promptly, and that it is to be done with diligent zeal so that we may be able to exercise hospitality, and that holy pilgrims and exiles are even to be sought out, so that we may be able to receive them into hospitality, which the Apostle also advised Heb. XIII. 1. Do not forget hospitality, and benefit were shown to himself: I was a stranger, and you took me in Matt. XXV. 35.

Latin:

V. 13. ταῖς χρείαις τῶν ἁγίων κοινωνοῦντες, τὴν φιλοξενίαν διώκοντες. Quidam codices habuêre μνείαις: & sane Levitarum & hoc erat, celebrare memoriam virorum magnorum, de qua re ad Sirachiden diximus. Sed hoc receptius præfero. Levi- tæ cum pauperibus & peregrinis de tertiis decimis epula- bantur: At Paulus mysticos Levitas hortatur, ut ipsi de suo pauperes & peregrinos excipiant. Διώκειν hic est sectari, ut supra IX. 30. In commate sequente insectari, ut Matth. V. 10. 11. ubi dicta vide.

Recte præfertur Græcorum codicum lectio, etsi non Ambrosiafter tantum Memoriis legerit, sed & ita locum hunc citet Optatus l. II. contr. Donatist. Chysolog. Serm. CXX. Gregorius, l.II. in Epist. ad Optim. & pop. Germ. Missale Mediolanense, quod Ambrosianum vocant, imo etiam Hilarius in Con- stantium Augustum, & Ruffinus in Comment. Ori- gen. eam lectionem magis haberi in Latinis Codd. testetur. Qui vero etiam prætulit Græcorum codd. lectionem: quam Guilh. Estius non tantum è Syria- cis & Latinis editionibus, sed etiam è constanti Græcorum codd. consensu comprobat, ac valde con- sentaneam similibus Apost. præceptis Gal. VI. Phil. IV. 1. Tim. VI. Ebr. XIII. 2. Cor. IIX. & IX. 1. Cor. ult. docet. Est autem etiam magis conveniens textui, quam altera lectio: quod quū istius patroni agno- scerent, in eandem sententiam illam abripere vo- luêre, q. d. memoriam habendam esse sanctorum pau- perum: seu privata communicatione bonorum tem- poralium, sive in collectis solemnibus, quæ in paupe- res fieri solent. Sed hoc non est sanctorum memo- riis COMMUNICARE. Necessitatibus autem sanctorum communicare recte dicuntur, non tam qui tribulationum communionem quandam ha- bent, quæ crucem reddere solet tolerabiliorem, quam qui indigentiæ eorum succurrūt, & faculta- tes suas fratribus inopia laborantibus communes faciunt, uti χρεία pro indigentia habetur 1. Joh. III. Ideo conjungitur hæc regula cum præcepto Hospi- talitatis erga exules ac miseros, quibus hospitium non denegare debemus. Erasmus notat, quod Apostolus communicantes dicat, non subvenien- tes quod commercium sit inter dantem & accipien- tem, & plus lucrifaciat, qui dat beneficium, quam qui accipit. Et quod nō ἀνάγκαις dicatur, sed χρεί- aις, quod magis sonat usum, sive opus habere. Quod ideo submonuit, quod quidam non nisi in extrema necessitate putant debere nos subvenire proximo. Ineptus autem est Turrianus l. IV. defens. Ep. Pon- tif. c. 14. Sanctorum necessitate de defunctorum pœnis explicans; quæ orationibus & eleemosynis suble- vandæ sint: siquidem nos, nec quinâ sancti sint, qui sc. in fide decesserint, certo sciamus, & fideles nulla post mortem pœna affici, sed beatitudine frui, certi simus; Sectari autē, i. e. persequi hospitalitatē jubemur: ut charitatem prosequi * & pacem † ut non modo non denegandum esse hospitium, sed etiam prom- pte offerendum, studioque sedulo id agendum, ut hospitalitatem exercere possimus, & vel quæren- dos esse sanctos peregrinos & exules, doceat, ut hospitio eos excipere possimus, quod Apostolus etiam monuit Ebr. XIII. 1. Hospitalitatem nolite oblivisci, & celebraturus est Christus, ac si ipsi hoc beneficium exhibitum sit: Hospes eram, & collegistis me Matth. XXV. 35.

## 12:14
V. 14. Bless those who persecute you, bless and do not curse.
