Just as in the old law the Levites used to pronounce the blessings of GOD Deut. X. 8. XXVII. 12. but others the curses. See Matt. V. 44.

The Apostle commands forgiveness, which is not the least part of love and mercy Luke VI. 36. 37. so that we may so pardon those who persecute us, that we not only do not think of revenge, much less retaliate by the deed itself, but that we even bless them, both with wishes and prayers for them and their conversion, and with deeds and benefits, or verbal and real blessing. However, Erasmus's interpretation is not to be approved: Speak well of those who persecute you. Because from the antithesis, do not curse, it is clear that blessing is not taken for praise. Furthermore, it is to be noted on account of Grotius, that curses were not lawful in the Old Testament either, but whatever were pronounced against sins were pronounced in the name of GOD, so that transgressors might be struck by the curses of the law from GOD, unless they did penance.

Latin:

V. 14. ἐὐλογεῖτε τὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς, ἐυλογεῖτε κὶ μὴ καταρᾶσθαι.

Sicut in veteri lege DEI ἐυλογίας pronunciabant Levitæ Deut. X. 8. XXVII. 12. ἀρὰς vero alii. Vide Matth. V. 44.

Præcipit Apostolus ignoscentiam, quæ non po- strema pars dilectionis & misericordiæ est Luc. VI. 36. 37. ut ita persequentibus nos condonemus, ut non modo non cogitemus de ultione, nedum opere ipso retribuamus, sed ut etiam benedicamus ipsis, tum votis & precibus pro ipsis, eorumque conversione, tum factis & beneficiis, seu bene- dictione verbali & reali. Non tamen probanda Erasmi interpretatio: Bene loquamini de iis, qui vos insectantur. Quia ex antithesi, non maledica- tis, patet, benedictionem non accipi pro laude. Cæterum ob Grotium notandum, nec in V. Test. ἀρὰς licitas fuisse, sed quæcunque pronunciatæ sint adversus peccata, nomine DEI pronunciatas esse, ut legis maledictis à DEO ferirentur præva- ricatores, nisi pœnitentiam agerent.

## 12:15
V. 15. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep.

An allusion to the two gates of the temple, of which one was for the bridegrooms, the other for the mourners; the Levites used to say things appropriate to both.

The Apostle commands sympathy both in joyful and in sad circumstances, which is the companion of true love. There appears no evidence that there is an allusion to the temple gates and the duties of the Levites. However, the distinction of the blessed Luther in his Enarrations on this passage between rebuking and cursing is not to be neglected here. This, he says, wishes that evil may come to someone; that does this, and is engaged in this, that the evil which is present may be driven away. Whence also Christ indeed rebuked the Jews and quite harshly, while he called them a brood of vipers, children of the devil, hypocrites, blind, foolish, liars, etc. But we never read that he cursed, that is, wished that they might be oppressed by these or other evils; nay, he wished for nothing so much as to free them once and for all from all evils, etc.

Latin:

V. 15. χάιρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων, κὶ κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων.

Allusum ad duas templi portas, quarum una erat spon- sorum, altera lugentium; utrisque convenientia dicebant Levitæ.

Συμπάθειαν tum in lætis, tum in mæstis casibus præcipit Apostolus, quæ veræ dilectionis comes est. Alludi ad templi portas & Levitarum munia, nullo apparet indicio. Non negligenda autem hic B. Lutheri distinctio in Enarr. h. l. inter increpare & imprecari. Hoc inquit, optat, ut malum alicui adveniat; Illud hoc agit, & in hoc est, ut, quod ma- lum adest, pellatur. Unde & Christus increpavit quidem Judæos atque satis dure, dum vocaret proge- niem viperarum, filios diaboli, hypocritas, cæcos, stultos, mendaces, &c. At nunquam legimus, male precatum, id est, optasse, ut his, aut aliis malis pre- merentur, imo nihil æque optavit, quam semel eos malis omnibus liberare, &c.

## 12:16
V. 16. Being of the same mind toward one another.

That is, be of one mind among yourselves. For that to be of the same mind 2 Cor. XIII. 11. Phil. II. 2. and toward one another, among yourselves, as below, XIV. 19. 1 Thess. III. 12. just as among yourselves Mark IX. 50. John XIII. 35. below XV. 5.

He enjoins ὁμόνοιαν [concord], and τὸ ὁμοθυμαδὸν [being of one mind], that we may think the same thing and be unanimous; since without this ὁμονοίᾳ [concord] Φιλαδελφία [brotherly love] cannot subsist. But because for the same it is necessary that we rightly govern ourselves, as to our mind, will, and affections, therefore he also prescribes certain rules concerning these, which now follow. Whence that sense of Estius is to be preferred to the interpretation: Let others be affected with the same mind toward one another, nor because anyone excels in wealth, honors, birth, or power, should he therefore think himself better. For that which Estius thinks, that our explanation hardly admits the Greek, is vain: τὸ αὐτὸ εἰς ἀλλήλας φρο- νῦντες, which he renders: Thinking the same toward one another mutually, but why could that not be accepted concerning ὁμονίᾳ [concord]?

μὴ τὰ ὑψηλὰ φρονῦντες [not minding high things].

He repeats what he had said above XI. 21. & above 3.

ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι [but being carried away with the lowly].

Following the examples of the most modest. For he who leads is said to συναπάγειν [lead away together], Exodus XIV. 6; he who follows the one leading is συναπάγεσθαι [to be carried away together], Gal. II. 13, 2 Pet. III. 17. The Levites also ought to serve even the poorest of the common people in offerings and to provide refuge for the miserable.

It is repeated from the above-mentioned XI. 25, where see the notes. Do not be such as most of the learned among the Jews from the Levites, who called others out of contempt the people of the land.

First indeed he requires modesty and humility, that we may not mind things more sublime than is fitting, but follow the humble, or consent to the humble, or condescend, or in neither, so that it may correspond to the preceding τὰ ὑψηλὰ, not high, but humble, let us follow. To this study of humility also pertains the following rule: that we be not wise in our own eyes. For that persuasion of prudence causes us to mind high things, not to follow humble ones. Chrysostom and Theodoret explain it thus: Do not think your own counsels suffice for you, as if you did not need the counsel of others, do not attribute too much to your own prudence.

Latin:

V. 16. τὸ ἀυτὸ εἰς ἀλλήλας φρονῦντες.

Id est, concordes inter vos estote. Id enim τὸ ἀυτὸ φρο- νεῖν 2. Cor. XIII. 11. Philipp. II. 2. & εἰς ἀλλήλας, inter vos, ut infra, XIV. 19. 1. Thess. III. 12. sicut ἐν ἀλλήλοις Marci IX. 50. Joh. XIII. 35. infra XV. 5.

Præcipit ὁμόνοιαν, & τὸ ὁμοθυμαδὸν, ut idem sentiamus, & unanimes simus; siquidem sine hac ὁμονοίᾳ consistere nequeat Φιλαδελφία. Quia ve- ro ad eandem opus est, ut nosmetipsos rite guberne- mus, qua animum, voluntatem, & affectus, ideo de iis etiam præscribit certas regulas, quæ jam se- quuntur. Unde præferendus sensus ille Estii in- terpretationi: Sint eodem animo alii erga alios af- fecti, nec quia quisquam opibus, honoribus, genere, potentia præstat, ideo meliorem se putet. Quod enim existimat Estius nostram explicationem Græca vix admittere, vanum est: τὸ αὐτὸ εἰς ἀλλήλας φρο- νῦντες, quod reddit: Idem erga vos mutuo sentien- tes, cur vero id non de ὁμονίᾳ accipi posset?

μὴ τὰ ὑψηλὰ φρονῦντες.

Repetit quod supra dixerat XI. 21. & supra 3.

ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι.

Modestissimorum exempla sectantes. Nam qui ductat dicitur συναπάγειν, Exodi XIV. 6. qui ductantem sequitur συναπάγεσθαι Gal. II. 13. 2. Petr III. 17. Levitæ etiam pau- perrimo cuique de plebe in oblationibus servire debebant & refugium præbere miseris.

Repetitur ex supra dicto XI. 25. ubi notata vide. Nolite esse, quales eruditi apud Judæos plerique è Levitis, qui cæteros per contemptum vocabant populum terræ.

Primo quidem requirit modestiam & humilitatem, ne sublimiora, quam par est, sapiamus, sed humiles sequamur, vel humilibus consentiamus, vel condescendamus, aut in neutro, ut respondeat præcedenti τὰ ὑψηλὰ non alta, sed humilia, sectemur. Ad hoc humilitatis studium pertinet etiam sequens regula: ne simus prudentes apud nosmetipsos. Nam illa persuasio prudentiæ facit, ut alta sapiamus, non sectemur humilia. Chrysost. & Theodor. ita explicant: Ne putetis vestra consilia vobis sufficere, q. aliorum consilio non egeatis, ne nimium vestræ prudentiæ tribuatis.

## 12:17
V. 17. μηδενὶ κακὸν ἀντὶ κακõ ἀποδιδόντες [rendering to no one evil for evil].

It is not permitted to you what was permitted to those Levites, to kill idolaters without judgment: Christ did not permit that to you. It was permitted to them to demand an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth: it is not permitted to you.

προνοόμενοι καλὰ ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων [providing things honest in the sight of all men].

The manuscript has, ἐνώπιον τῶ Θεῶ, and before all men, just as you have the same admonition in 2 Cor. 8:21. This also follows the example of the Levites, who performed their duties in the temple of GOD, with all the people watching. The expression itself is taken from Prov. 3:4, προνοõ καλὰ, where in the Hebrew it is שכל, which signifies to provide diligently.

It was never permitted for the Levites or others to kill idolaters or other transgressors without a trial, unless they were caught in the act; but such deeds, noted in the Holy Scriptures, were heroic and are not to be rashly imitated; private vengeance was never permitted in the Old Testament. Regarding those things which are held in Matt. 5, to that passage it is said: As he has done, so let it be done to him, Levit. 24:19, Deut. 19:21; it is said to the judges, therefore it has nothing to do with private vengeance. For this is forbidden to private individuals in Prov. 24:29: Do not say: as he has done to me, so I will do to him. However, private vengeance is prohibited in this place in such a way that we are commanded even to provide for good things ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων before all men, and thus even for those who have shown us evil. For so it is read among the Greek Commentators, Origen, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others, so that the rest is from 2 Cor. 8. For let us provide good things, not only before GOD, but also before men, which Estius thinks was added by someone. But these things are not said in an absolute sense, as Grotius seems to accept with Estius, that we ought to provide what is good and honest, but relatively in order to those who have shown us evil; which sense the antithesis demands, and which the Greek Commentators proved, as Estius admits, that is to say, it is not enough for you not to return evil for evil, but also to provide good things, that is, to study to do well and to consult the well-being of all men, even if they are enemies and have deserved ill of you. Nor is it necessary that the same sense should obtain here as in 2 Cor. 8:21. For there is another subject matter and another context.

Latin:

V. 17. μηδενὶ κακὸν ἀντὶ κακõ ἀποδιδόντες.

Non licet vobis quod Levitis illis licebat, sine judicio occidere idololatras: vobis id Christus non permisit. Illis licebat oculum poscere pro oculo, dentem pro dente: vobis id non licet.

προνοόμενοι καλὰ ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων.

Manuscriptus habet, ἐνώπιον τῶ Θεῶ, καὶ ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων, quomodo idem monitum habes 2. Cor. VIII. 2. Hoc quoque ad exemplum Levitarum, qui in templo DEI, inspectante omni populo, mandata faciebant. Locutio ipsa desumpta est ex Prov. III. 4. προνοõ καλὰ ubi in Hebræo שכל, quod diligenter procurare significat.

Nunquam illud Levitis aut aliis licitum fuit, sine judicio occidere idololatras, vel alios prævaricatores, nisi ἐπ' αυτοφώρῳ deprehenderentur: qualia vero facta, in S. literis notata, Heroica fuere, nec temere imitanda sunt; Nunquam privata vindicta licita fuit in V. T. De iis vero, quæ habentur Matth. V. ad illum locum dictum: Sicut fecit, ita fiat ei Levit. XXIV. 19. Deut. IX. 19. judicibus dictum est, nihil ergo id ad vindictam privatam. Nam privatis hoc interdictum est Prov. XXIV. 2. Ne dicas: sicut fecit mihi, ita faciam ei. Prohibetur autem hoc loco ita vindicta privata, ut jubeamur etiam καλὰ prospicere ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων coram omnibus hominibus adeoque etiam pro iis, qui κακὰ nobis exhibuêre. Sic enim legitur apud Græcos Commentatores, Origenem, Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, & alios, adeo, ut cætera è 2. Cor. IIX. Procuremus enim bona, non solum coram DEO, sed etiam coram hominibus, addita à quopiam censeat Estius. Non autem sensu absoluto, ut cum Estio Grotius videtur accipere, hæc dicta, quod quæ bona & honesta sunt procurare debeamus, sed relative in ordine ad eos, qui nobis malum exhibuêre; quem sensum antithesis postulat, & probarunt fatente Estio Græci Commentatores, q. d. non sufficiat vobis pro malo malum non reddere, sed etiam bona providere, id est, studere bene facere, ac bene consulere omnibus hominibus, quamvis etiam inimicis ac male de vobis meritis. Nec necessum est, ut idem sensus hic obtineat, qui 2. Cor. IIX. 21. Est enim ibi alia materia & alius contextus.

## 12:18
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, living peaceably with all men.

Even with idolaters, according to the spirit of Christ, Luke 9:56. This means to say, be friends of all, if it is possible: If it is not possible on both sides, at least be friends on your part. Εἰρηνέυειν corresponds to the Hebrew words שלם, שלום, and שקט, which signify to live tranquilly and amicably with someone.

God is not so eager for anything as to bind us together with mutual bonds of charity, says Chrysostom, hom. 16 in Matt. cf. Jer. 26:7, Mark 9:50, Rom. 14:19. Those two cautions of the Apostle should properly be observed: 1. if possible, that is, without prejudice to the truth and to piety; 2. as much as in us lies, that we suffer nothing to be lacking in us which makes for fostering or establishing concord. But the Irenic Syncretists abuse this sentiment, since they [seek peace] not with the truth preserved, but with the dissent concerning heavenly truth preserved, against the rule of GOD, Zech. VIII. 16: Only love truth and peace, and the admonition of the Apostle, Eph. IV. v. 15, where by ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ we are commanded to grow in charity while embracing divine truth.

Latin:

εἰ δυνατὸν, ἐξ ὑμῶν, μετὰ πάντων ἀνθρώπων εἰρηνέυοντες.

Etiam cum idololatris, secundum Christi spiritum Luc. IX. 56. Hoc vult dicere, omnium amici este, si fieri potest: Si non poteit utrinque, certe ex vestra parte amici este. Εἰρηνέυειν respondet vocibus Hebraicis שלם, שלום, & שקט quæ significant tranquille & amice cum aliquo vivere.

Nihil ita studet Deus, quam nos mutuis charitatis nexibus colligare, ait Chrysostomus, hom. XVI. in Matth. cons. Jer. XXVI. 7. Marc. IX. 50. Rom. XIV. 29. Dux illæ cautiones Apostoli probe observentur 1. si fieri potest, salva sc. veritate, ac pietate. 2. Quantum in nobis est, ut nihil in no- BIS desiderari patiamur, quod ad concordiam fo- vendam vel sanciendam facit. Abutuntur autem hac sententia Irenici Syncretistæ, siquidem illi non salva veritate, sed salvo dissensu de cælesti veritate pacem suadeant, contra regulam DEI Zach. IIX. 16. Tantum veritatem & pacem diligite, & Apostoli monitum Eph. IV. v. 15. ubi ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ veritatem divinam amplectentes in charitate cre- scere jubemur.

## 12:19
V. 19. μὴ ἑαυτὸς ἐκδικῶντες, ἀγαπητοὶ. That is, avenging, as the following shows: just as the Syrian also understood it and the Greek interpreters, nor did the Latin mean anything else when it said, defending: For Christians used that word in the sense of avenging, as we said in the annotations to Book I, Chapter III, § 3, on the Law of War and Peace.

Therefore Thomas and Lyranus do not correctly understand defense, explaining it as the preparation of the mind, since the Apostle is occupied in prohibiting private vengeance: just as Jerome also reads 'avenging' here in Book III, Apol. adv. Ruffin., and Sedulius and Chrysologus read 'punishing', and in that sense Cyprian used the word 'defense' in his book On Patience, near the end: And let us not hasten to be defended (that is, avenged) before the Lord with an irreligious haste: and Tertullian, Book II, against Marcion, c. 18: 'To me defense, and I will defend,' which now in the Vulgate follows thus: to me vengeance, I will repay.

ἀλλὰ δότε τόπον ὀργῇ. That is, do not occupy the punishment which GOD will inflict upon him, by Himself or by His minister, of whom He is about to speak shortly. Leave time for GOD. Thus he is said to give place to the devil who opens an approach to himself for him, Eph. IV. 27.

That place is to be left to the wrath of GOD, which is wont to be noted by the word 'wrath' used absolutely, Rom. XI. 5, c. IV. 25, Eph. II. 3, 1 Thess. II. 16 (cf. Prov. XX. 22), is interpreted also by the Greeks, Ambrosiaster, Augustine in his exposition of Ps. LXXVIII, Musculus also, Drusius, and likewise Lombard and Aquinas: as also Basil in his shorter rules, response 244, who however adds also another interpretation, which is also that of Ambrose, Book 1, On Duties, c. 21, that one must yield to the wrath of an adversary, by the example of the Patriarch Jacob, who yielded to his brother's wrath. But the former sense is simpler, and agrees with the example of Christ, of whom Peter says, 1 Epist. 23: He committed Himself to Him who judges justly; and also with the following proof from Moses: vengeance is mine. Indeed, to give place is either to provide an opportunity to someone, or to yield. Heinsius also embraces the former sense, but understands it of one's own wrath, not of GOD's: and thus he notes that the admission of wrath, but our own and brief, is indicated: but this is against the mind of the Apostle, who teaches not that place should be left for our own wrath, but rather that it should be restrained, adding antithetically 'but do not avenge yourselves.' Therefore we adhere to the opinion of the Greeks, which the blessed Chemnitius also embraced: We do not do private vengeance for our enemies, but we intercept the course of the wrath of GOD, which is destined for them, and we avert it from them, and derive it upon ourselves. Whoever therefore desires vengeance upon his enemies, let him commend it to GOD. Thus also place is given to the wrath of GOD.

γέγραπται γὰρ· Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω. Ἐμοὶ here means, it pertains to me. In the Hebrew לי נקם ושלם לעת 'to me vengeance and retribution in time.' The LXX translated 'in the day of vengeance I will repay.' It is the Lord's to punish servants, not fellow-servants. But God granted this right in the old law in certain cases even to individuals, as in the avenger of blood. But in the Gospel, where nothing is to be given to the passions, punishment is either of GOD, or of the public law, which itself also lacks passions.

That it is false, indeed, that there was another reason for vengeance under the law than now in the N.T., is evident even from this argument, brought by the Apostle from Moses.

For since he proves from the law that vengeance must be left to GOD, how was private vengeance granted under the law? The reason for the vengeance of blood was special and symbolic and typical: which itself, however, was circumscribed by the rules of GOD the supreme judge. That Socinian opinion of Grotius has been refuted elsewhere. Paul, however, brings forward that Scripture according to the Hebrew TRUTH, as Estius speaks, in which it is held word for word: To me vengeance and retribution. For the LXX have it somewhat differently: In the day of vengeance I will repay. Those, therefore, who exercise their own vengeance fly into the office of GOD: and that which GOD reserved for Himself to be executed either immediately, or mediately through the magistrate, they snatch to themselves through sacrilege, nay, they become guilty of lese-majesty.

Latin:

V. 19. μὴ ἑαυτὸς ἐκδικῶντες, ἀγαπητοὶ. Id est, ulciscentes, ut sequentia ostendunt: quomodo & Syrus accepit & Græci interpretes, nec aliud voluit La- tinus, cum dixit, defendentes: Nam Christiani eam vocem in ulciscendi sensu sumebant, ut diximus in annotatis ad Lib. I. cap. III. §. 3. de jure Belli ac Pacis.

Non ergo recte defensionem intelligunt Thomas & Lyranus, exponentes de præparatione animi, quum occupetur Apostolus in prohibenda vin- dicta privata: uti etiam hic ulciscentes legit Hie- ronymus l. III. Apol. adv. Ruffin. & Sedulius, ac Chrysologus vindicantes, atque eo sensu voce de- fensionis usus est Cyprianus lib. de Patient. sub fin. Nec defendi (id est, vindicari) ante Dominum ser- vi irreligiosa festinatione properemus: & Tertull. l. II. contr. Marcion. c. 18. Mihi defensam, & ego defendam, quod jamjam in Vulg. ita sequitur: mi- hi vindicta, ego retribuam.

ἀλλὰ δότε τόπον ὀργῇ. Id est, ne occupate pœnam, quam ei infliget DEUS, per se aut per ministrum suum, de quo paulo post acturus est. Relinquite tempus DEO. Sic diabolo locum dare dicitur, qui ei aditum ad se aperit Ephes. IV. 27.

Iræ DEI, quæ voce iræ absolute posita notari solet Rom. XI. 5. c. IV. 25. Eph. II. 3. 1. Thess. II. 16. (conf. Prov. XX. 22.) locum relinquendum esse, etiam Græci, Ambrosiaster, August. in expos. Ps. LXXIIX. Musculus etiam, Drusius, nec non Lom- bardus, & Aquinas interpretantur: ut & Basilius in Regul. brev. resp. 244. qui tamen addit etiam aliam interpretationem, quæ etiam Ambrosii est l. 1. Offic. c. 21. iræ adversarii cedendum esse, exemplo Patriarchæ Jacobi, qui fratris iræ cessit. Sed prior sensus simplicior est, & exemplo Christi convenit, de quo Petrus 1. Epist. 23. Tradebat ju- dicanti juste; nec non sequenti probationi è Mose, mihi vindicta est. Nimirum locum dare, est vel copiam facere alicui, vel cedere. Priorem sensum amplectitur quoque Heinsius, sed de iræ propria, non DEI intelligit: adeoque admissionem iræ, sed nostræ & brevis indigitari notat: at contra men- tem Apostoli; qui non nostræ iræ locum relin- quendum, sed eam potius coërcendam esse do- cet, addens ἀντιθετικῶς μὴ ἐκδικεῖτε δὲ αὐτὸς. Pro- inde sententiæ Græcorum inhæremus, quam etiam B. Chemnitius amplexus est: Vindicta privata non ære facimus hostibus, sed cursum iræ DEI, quæ ipsis destinatur, intercipimus, & ab illis avertimus, & in nos derivamus. Qui igitur cupit ultionem de ini- micis suis, DEO illam commendet. Ita etiam locus datur iræ DEI.

γέγραπται γὰρ· Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀντα- ποδώσω. Ἐμοὶ hic valet, ad me pertinet. In Hebræo לי נקם ושלם לעת mihi ultio & retributio in tempore. LXX. verterunt ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐκδικήσεως ἀνταποδώσω. Domini est pu- nire servos, non conservorum. Sed Deus hoc jus in lege ve- teri in certis casibus etiam singulis tribuit, ut in vindice sanguinis. At in Evangelio, ubi nihil dandum affectibus, pœna est aut DEI, aut legis publicæ, quæ & ipsa affectibus caret.

Id vero falsum esse, quod sub lege alia ultionis ratio fuerit, quam nunc in N. T. vel ex hoc argu- mento, ab Apostolo è Mose adducto, patet.

Quum enim è lege probat, DEO relinquendam vindictam, quomodo sub lege privata vindicta concessa fuit? De vindicta sanguinis specialis & Symbolica ac typica fuit ratio: quæ ipsa tamen DEI supremi judicis regulis fuit circumscripta. Sociniana illa Grotii opinio alias profligata est. Adducit autem eam ScripturamPaulus secundum Hebraicam VERITATEM, ut Estius loquitur, in qua ad verbum habetur: Mihi vindicta & retri- butio. Nam LXX. paulo secus habent: In die vindictæ retribuam. Qui ergo vindictam exer- cent propriam in DEI officium involant: & id quod DEUS vel immediate, & mediate per magi- stratum exequendum sibi reservavit, per sacrile- gium ad se rapiunt, imo læsæ majestatis rei eva- dunt.

## 12:20
V. 20. ἐὰν ὖν πεινᾷ ὁ ἐχθρὸς, ψώμιζε αὐτὸν, ἐὰν διψᾷ, πότιζε αὐτόν.

By two most well-known examples all kinds of benefits are indicated, as in Matt. XXV. 35. ψωμίζειν is frequent among the LXX for טעם, חברד, האכיל. You have the same in 1 Cor. XIII. 3 and Wis. XVI. 20. Sir. XV. 3. Thus also ποτίζω is placed for נסכד, גמיא, שקה. Moreover, these words and the following are taken from Prov. XXV. 21, 22. And there indeed they are counsels: in the Gospel they are precepts. Tertullian against Scapula: For thus by discipline we are commanded to love even our enemies, and to pray for those who persecute us, so that this may be our perfect and proper goodness, not a common one. For to love friends is for everyone: but to love enemies is for Christians alone. That rancid distinction between counsels and precepts, worn thin by our people against the Papists, is snatched up by Grotius in another sense for this purpose, in favor of the Socinian heresy: who argue that new precepts were delivered in the Gospel, and when we demonstrate the same from the Old Testament, they say that there they were proposed only as counsels. But the precept concerning loving enemies in the Old Testament is clear in Exod. XXIII. 4, Lev. XIX. 18, from which an evident example of such love is read in 2 Chron. XXVIII. 15. Compare on this passage Paulinus, B. Balduin, q. 11. Tertullian's opinion is nothing against us: for it is truly the part of believers and the reborn alone to observe that law concerning loving enemies. Nor indeed does this precept, which was noted by Estius, oblige only in extreme necessity, as some (especially Pererius) explain, but as often and whenever right reason dictates that a neighbor suffering necessity must be helped. On the word ψωμίζειν, with Erasmus leading the way, Cornel. a Lap. noted an emphasis; it signifies, he says, to feed indulgently, just as if putting in bread bit by bit, or thrusting morsels into the mouth, just as mothers do for little ones, or birds for their chicks, inserting food into the mouth; or to offer food cut into small pieces to be eaten, which is done among some toward those who are singularly favored at banquets.

Latin:

V. 20. ἐὰν ὖν πεινᾷ ὁ ἐχθρὸς, ψώμιζε αὐτὸν, ἐὰν διψᾷ, πότιζε αὐτόν.

Duobus notissimis exemplis omnia beneficiorum ge- nera indicantur,ut Matth. XXV. 35. ψωμίζειν frequens apud LXX. pro טעם, חברד, האכיל. Habes idem 1. Cor. XIII. 3. ac Sap. XVI. 20. Sir. XV. 3. Sic & ποτίζω po- nitur pro נסכד, גמיא, שקה. Sunt autem hæc verba & sequentia desumta ex Prov.XXV. 21. 22. Et ibi qui- dem consilia sunt: in Evangelio præcepta. Tertullianus contra Scapulam: Ita enim disciplina jubemur diligere ini- micos quosque, & orare pro eis, qui nos prosequuntur, ut hæc sit perfecta & propria bonitas nostra, non communis. Amicos enim diligere omnium est: inimicos autem solorum Christianorum. Rancida illa distinctio inter consilia & præcepta, à nostris in Papistis protrita, à Grotio alio sensu huc abripitur, in gratiam Socinianæ hæreseos: qui pugnant in Evangelio nova præcepta traditá esse, & cum eadem è Vet. Test. demonstramus, ibi ea tantum instar consiliorum proposita fuisse, ajunt. Sed præceptum de inimicis diligendis in Vet. Test. luculentum est Exod. XXIII. 4. Lev. XIX. 18. unde exemplum talis dilectionis evidens legitur 2. Par. XXIIX. 15. Conf. ad h. l. Paulinum B. Balduin. q. 11. Tertulliani sententia nihil adversus nos: nam vere solorum fidelium & renatorum est, legem illam de inimicis diligendis observare. Neque vero præceptum hoc, quod ab Estio notatum, ob- ligat in sola necessitate extrema, quomodo non- nulli (imprimis vero Pererius) exponunt, sed quo- ties, & quandocunque recta ratio dictat proximo ne- cessitatem patienti subveniendum esse. In voce ψω- μίζειν, præeunte Erasmo, emphasin notavit Cor- nel. à Lap. significat, inquit, indulgenter pascere, veluti minutatim inslipato pane, sive bolos in os in- gerere, sicut matres parvulis, aves pullis cibum in os inserunt; aut frustulatim concisum cibum ad co- medendum offerre, id quod apud aliquos sit erga eos, quibus singulariter favetur in conviviis.

## 12:21
V. 21. For in doing this, you will heap coals of fire upon his head.

It appears from the passage in Proverbs that it concerns divine punishment, which is accustomed to be expressed everywhere through the likeness of fire. The sense is: if the other person cannot be recalled to a better mind by that great patience and beneficence of yours, a heavy punishment hangs over him. We are said to do that for which we provide the occasion, as in Luke XVI. 9. Tertullian in his book On Patience: You strike that wicked man more by enduring: for he will be beaten by Him for whose sake you endure.

Nay, it is not a question there of procuring divine punishment for an enemy but of reconciling his mind; that by the duties of beneficence we might inflame him, as it were, with living coals to mutual charity. In the former way, indeed, it is interpreted toward evil by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Photius in Oecumenius, Eucherius in the Questions on the New Testament, Flacius in the Gloss, William Estius, and others. But it is interpreted more correctly toward good by Jerome, Book 1, Dialogue against the Pelagians, ch. 9. Coals of fire, he says, you will heap upon his head, not for a curse and condemnation, as MOST think, but for correction and repentance; so that, overcome by benefits, refined by the fervor of charity, he may cease to be an enemy. Jerome in Epist. ad Hedeb. q. 1. and Augustine l. III. de doctr. Christian. c. 16. pursue this meaning at greater length. Since this can be understood in two ways, one way as to harm, the other as to provide: let charity rather recall you to repentance, so that in by which the pride of him who grieves that he was an enemy to the man by whom his misery is relieved is healed. The context certainly favors this latter interpretation, because the Apostle exhorts to the love of enemies, and to the pursuit of reconciliation and peace; Now this reconciliation and concord can be repaired primarily by benefits. For as Augustine has it in l. de catech. rudib. c. 4.: There is no greater invitation to love than to anticipate by loving. And too hard is the soul that, if it was unwilling to bestow love, is unwilling to repay it. St. Augustine also proves that explanation elsewhere, in Enarrat. Ps. LXXIIX. and at the end of Serm. de quat. quæstion. which is 26. de diversis, as well as Primasius, and other Latins, as also the author of the exposition of Ps. XCIII. which is among the works of Jerome. Cæsarius in homil. IV. which is held among the Sermons of Augustine de temp. n. 168. Beda, Jansenius in comm. in Prov. Salom. Saà, Mariana, Menochius, Cornel. à Lapide, Martin. à Rada part. II. singul. l. 1. c. II. p. 129. Nor does the exposition of Mercer in Prov. dissent, that you will so burn and move him, that with enmity laid aside he is rendered a friend to you, or at least does not harm you; or B. Franzius de interpret. Script. orac. XLIII. although he applies this simile a little differently; just as heads after washing are both dried and sweetly stroked, warmed, etc. (according to that of Isa. XLVII. 17. there are no coals to warm themselves, etc.) so the enemy also will feel a peculiar sweetness having been fed or refreshed by you. B. Hunnius delivers our exposition, and provides an augmentation for confirming it in his analysis, that just as the Apostle had already warned that vengeance should be committed to GOD, so now he is occupied in that which it is fitting for us to do when we have been harmed by others, with the authority of Solomon produced. B. Balduin also delivers the same in h. l. B. Glassius in Domin. III. post Epiph. tex. Epist. This is taken from Prov. XXV. 22. and the sense is: do good to your enemy, in whatever way you can. (for a species of ἀγαθεργίας is put for the genus itself) For thus you will win him over and soften him, so that by your services and benevolence, as if by certain coals, he may be inflamed into mutual love. In his heart charity is cold, but by these holy coals he will again be warmed, with the unjust flame of hatred and anger removed. In the place of Proverbs it is added: And the Lord will repay you, i.e., that gentle preservation with your neighbor, by which you both patiently bore the enemy, and moreover mitigated him with kindness, and brought him back to a sounder mind, He will abundantly repay you. From the Reformed, Aretius has it thus: Others interpret, your benefit will be a greater cause of damnation for him. Which sentiment seems to console the afflicted, i.e., do good in all ways to your enemy, thus you will conquer him, and he will be more severely damned. But since the affection of charity is repugnant to these thoughts, I prefer to follow another sense, viz. your benefit will be a burning coal to him, by which he will finally be inflamed to love you, and you will be an occasion for him to repent; thus that coal will be praiseworthy, and honorable to you: for what utility or even honor will there be for you, if you do good to an enemy with that end, that he may be damned? Nor are those alien to this sense, as far as the thing itself is concerned, who indeed explain the Proverbial locution otherwise, but admit the other ἔκθεσιν at the same time, or leave both free. Calvin says, I take it simply, that his mind will be broken in one direction or the other. For certainly by benefits the enemy will either be softened, or if he is of such atrocity that he is not at all tamed, he will nevertheless be burned and will seethe by the testimony of his conscience, by which he will feel himself overwhelmed by our kindness. Sanctius in Esaiae XXXV. The sense is: for injuries received confer benefits upon your enemies, for then those benefits will be like coals, which you will heap upon your enemies, either because in that way enemies are tormented when they see injuries compensated by benefits, or because we will reconcile his mind to us, and inflame it into love for us. B. Mylius: Because thus either the anger of GOD will be more accumulated against him, unless he repents: or the torments and anxiety of his mind will lead to his own accusation by his own testimony. Dn. D. Geiero, to heap coals upon another's head is the same, from a comparison of Prov. VI. 28. as to do something intolerable, by which the enemy is to be vehemently moved to lay aside hatred, or unless he has done this because of the unamendable malice of his mind, he will procure for himself great torments of punishment, not otherwise than if the bread by which he was fed had turned into mere coals for him.

They still bring forward another explanation, Sanctius the Jesuit in Esa. XIII. and others, You will heap coals of fire, that is, you will suffuse his face with redness, so that then, shamed by your kindness and conquered by charity, he may yield and convert his hatred into Love. But Cornel. à Lapide rightly judges concerning it in h. l.: This sense is weaker and colder.

μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τῶ κακῶ.

He is conquered by evil, that is, by an evil action, who imitates the evil. Solon, prince of the Syracusans, answered the Spartan legate cordially in Herodotus VII.: ξένε Σπαρτῆτα ὀνείδεα κατιόντα ἀνθρώπῳ φιλίῳ ἐπανάγει τὸν θυμὸν, σὺ μὲν τοὶ ἀποδεξάμενος ὑβρίσματα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, ὃ μὲ πείσεις ἀσχήμονα ἐν τῇ ἀμοιβῇ γενέσθαι.

ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακὸν.

Evil is conquered by bearing it: contrary to what happens in the public contests of the Greeks and Romans. Seneca de beneficiis VII. 30. just as the vices of bodies, so those of minds must be treated gently; often what delay has unfolded, the stubbornness of the one pulling it has snapped. And in the following chapter: Persistent goodness conquers the wicked, nor is anyone of a mind so hard and hostile against things to be loved, that he does not love even if he is drawn to good things. This whole chapter is Isocratic, it has such dense ἰσόκωλα and ἀντίθετα.

The Apostle had inculcated gentleness 1. κατ᾽ ἄφεσιν or negatively v. 19. Not avenging yourselves. 2. Κατὰ θέσιν or affirmatively v. 20. If therefore he hungers &c. Now therefore 3. κατ᾽ ἀντίθεσιν or oppositively he describes the same v. 21. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. He who flares up into mutual hatred and κακοχεγίαν, is overcome by evil or sin, and thus becomes its slave, and consequently has given himself into the power of Satan. But he who treats an enemy benevolently, he overcomes evil with good, and thus is truly a most valiant victor, because he overcomes not only another, but also himself and his own depraved affections, and therefore, since that cannot be done without faith 1 John V. 4, he is rendered more certain that he is endowed with living faith, and thus is a regenerated son of GOD. To avenge oneself, says Ambrose l. 1. offic. c. 36, is not an act of fortitude, but of abjection and timidity; he is overcome by an enemy, he does not overcome, who avenges himself. If we were to show gentleness, says Chrysostom on this passage, we would be insuperable to all, nor would any injury reach us. Ask an enemy, does he not grieve, does he not consider himself overcome, when you laugh, when you despise his injuries? The Apostle demands in this place, as Musculus teaches, such constancy in doing good to enemies, that we allow ourselves in no way, and by no injuries, to be driven from that purpose, but like soldiers we should constantly defend our place and rank, which is to do good to all, to do evil to no one, so that we may be found true sons of our heavenly Father.

SUBSECTION II. CONTAINING SPECIAL RULES.

Latin:

V. 21. Τῦτο γὰρ ποιῶν, ἄνθρακας πυρὸς σωρέυσεις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῦ.

Apparet ex Proverbiorum loco de pœna divina agi, quæ per ignis similitudinem passim exprimi solet. Sen- sus est: si alter illa tanta tua patientia ac beneficentia ad meliorem mentem revocari non potest, gravis ei impen- det pœna. Dicimur facere, cui rei occasionem præbemus, ut Luc. XVI. 9. Tertullianus libro de Patientia: Plus im- probum illum cadis, sustinendo: ab eo enim vapulabit, cujus gratia sustines.

Imo non de pœna divina inimico concilianda sed de animo ejus reconciliando ibi agitur; quod officiis beneficentia eum q. vivis carbonibus ad mu- tuam charitatem inflammare possimus. Priori qui- dem modo in malum exponitur à Chrysostomo, The- ophylacto & Photio apud Oecumenium. Eucher. in quæst. Nov. Test. Flacio in Glossa, Guilhelmo Estio & aliis. Sed rectius in bonum interpretatur Hiero- nymus l. 1. Dial. c. Pelag. c. 9. Carbones, inquit, ignis congregabis super caput ejus, non in maledictum & condemnationem, ut PLERIQUE existimant, sed in correctionem & pœnitudinem; ut superatus beneficiis, excoctus fervore charitatis, inimicus esse desistat. Quem sensum pluribus exequitur Hieron. in Epist. ad Hedeb. q. 1. & Augustin. l. III. de doctr. Chri- stian. c. 16. Hoc cum possit dupliciter intelligi, uno modo ad nocendum, altero ad praestandum: ad pœ- nitentiam te potius charitas revocet, ut intelligas, carbones ignis esse urentes pœnitentiæ gemitus, qui- bus superbia sanatur ejus, qui dolet se inimicum fuisse hominis, à quo ejus miseriæ subvenitur. Con- textus sane huic posteriori favet interpretationi, quia ad dilectionem inimicorum, & reconciliatio- nem ac pacem sectandam adhortatur Apostolus; Ista autem reconciliatio & concordia resarciri imprimis beneficiis potest. Nam ut August. l. de catech. rudib. c. 4. habet: Nulla est major ad amorem invitatio, quam prævenire amando. Et nimis durus est animus, qui dilectionem si nolebat impendere, nolit rependere. Probat etiam illam ex- plicationem S. Augustinus, alibi, in Enarrat. Ps. LXXIIX. & in fine Serm. de quat. quæstion. qui est 26. de diversis, nec non Primasius, aliique Latini, ut & autor exposit. Ps. XCIII. qui est inter opera Hieronymi. Cæsarius in homil. IV. quæ habetur inter Serm. Augustini de temp. n. 168. Beda, Jan- senius in comm. in Prov. Salom. Saà, Mariana, Menochius, Cornel. à Lapide, Martin. à Rada part. II. singul. l. 1. c. II. p. 129. Nec abnuit expositio Merceri in Prov. ita eum ures & movebis, ut simul- tate deposita tibi amicus reddatur, aut certe tibi non noceat; aut B. Franzii de interpret. Script. orac. XLIII. licet paulo aliter hoc simile applicet; sicut prunis capita post lotionem tum siccantur, tum suaviter demulcentur, foventur &c. (secundum illud Esa. XLVII. 17. non sunt prunæ, quibus cale- fiant &c.) ita inimicus quoque peculiarem sentiet suavitatem à te cibatus vel refectus. Tradit au- tem nostram expositionem B. Hunnius, ejusque confirmandæ augmentum in analysi submini- strat, quod uti vindictam DEO committendam jam ante monuerat Apostolus, ita nunc in eo occu- petur, quod nos facere conveniat, quando ab aliis læsi sumus, productâ autoritate Salomonis. Tradit eandem quoque B. Balduin. in h. l. B. Glassius in Domin. III. post Epiph. tex. Epist. Desumptum hoc ex Prov. XXV. 22. & sensus est: inimico be- nefac, quâcunque potes ratione. (ponitur enim spe- cies ἀγαθεργίας pro ipso genere) Sic enim ipsum lucraberis atque emollies, ut officiis tuis & benevo- lentia, veluti prunis quibusdam, in mutuam dile- ctionem exardescat. In corde ejus charitas friget, sed his sanctis prunis iterum calesiet, amotâ odii & iræ injustâ flammâ. In loco Proverbiorum additur: Et Dominus reddet tibi, h. e. mansuetam illam cum proximo conservationem, qua & inimicum patienter tulisti, & beneficentia insuper eum mi- tigasti, & ad saniorem mentem reduxisti, abunde tibi rependet. E Reformatis Aretius ita habet: Alii interpretantur, erit illi beneficium tuum ma- jor causa damnationis. Quæ sententia videtur con- solari afflictos, q. d. benefacito omnibus modis ini- mico tuo, sic vinces illum, & gravius damnabitur. Sed cum affectus charitatis his cogitationibus re- pugnet, malo alium sensum sequi, scil. beneficium tuum erit illi carbo ignitus, quo inflammabitur tan- dem ad te amandum, & eris illi occasio resipi- scendi; sic ille carbo laudabilis erit, tibique hone- stus: nam quæ erit tibi utilitas aut etiam honestas, si eo fine benefacias inimico, ut damnetur? Nec alieni sunt ab hoc sensu, quantum ad rem ipsam qui Proverbialem quidem loquutionem aliter ex- ponunt, at alteram ἔκθεσιν, simul admittunt, vel liberam utramque relinquunt. Calvinus, Ego, in- quit, simpliciter accipio, quod animus ejus frange- tur in alterutram partem. Nam certe beneficiis aut emolletur hostis, aut si tanta atrocitate erit, ut nihil mansuescat, uretur tamen & aestuabit testimonio conscientiae, qua se obrutam sentiet benignitate nostra. Sanctius in Esaiae XXXV. Sensus est: pro injuriis acceptis beneficia confer in inimicos, tunc enim illa beneficia erunt instar carbonum, quos congeres in inimicos, aut quia eo modo excruciantur inimici, cum vident injurias beneficiis compensari, aut quia illius animum nobis conciliabimus, & in nostri amorem inflammabimus. B. Mylius: Quia sic vel cumulatior futura ira DEI contra ipsum, nisi resipiscat: vel tormenta & anxietas animi proprio testimonio ad sui ipsius accusationem adductura sint. Dn. D. Geiero, carbones super alterius caput congerere idem est, è collatione Prov. VI. 28. ac facere aliquid intolerabile, quo vehementer movendus inimicus sit, ad deponendum odium, vel nisi hoc ob inemendabilem animi malitiam fecerit, magnos poenarum sibi conciliabit cruciatus, haud aliter ac si panis, quo cibatus est, ipsi in meros versus sit carbones.

Adferunt adhuc aliam explicationem Sanctius Jesuita in Esa. XIII. & alii, Carbones ignis congeres, id est, rubore suffundes faciem illius, ut tum beneficentia pudefactus, & charitate victus cedat, odiumque in Amorem convertat. Sed de ea recte Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l. judicat: Hic sensus repis & frigidior est.

μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τῶ κακῶ.

Vincitur à malo, id est, ab actione mala, qui malos imitatur. Solon Syracusarum princeps apud Herodotum VII. Spartae Legato respondit cordate: ξένε Σπαρτῆτα ὀνείδεα κατιόντα ἀνθρώπῳ φιλίῳ ἐπανάγει τὸν θυμὸν, σὺ μὲν τοὶ ἀποδεξάμενος ὑβρίσματα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, ὃ μὲ πείσεις ἀσχήμονα ἐν τῇ ἀμοιβῇ γενέσθαι.

ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακὸν.

Vincitur malum ferendo: contra quam in Graecorum Romanorumque publicis certaminibus. Seneca de beneficiis VII. 30. ut corporum, ita animorum molliter vitia tractanda sunt; saepe quod explicavit mora, pertinacia trahentis abruptum est. Et capite sequenti: Vincit malos pertinax bonitas, nec quisquam tam duri infestique adversus diligenda animi est, ut etiam si tractus bonos non amet. Est totum hoc caput Isocraticum, adeo densa habet ἰσόκωλα & ἀντίθετα.

Mansuetudinem inculcarat Apostolus 1. κατ᾽ ἄφεσιν seu negative v. 19. Non vosmetipsos ulcifcentes. 2. Κατὰ θέσιν seu affirmative v. 20. Si igitur esurit &c. Jam ergo 3. κατ᾽ ἀντίθεσιν seu oppositive eandem describit v. 21. Ne vincaris à malo, sed vincas malum bono. Qui mutuum in odium & κακοχεγίαν exardescit, à malo seu peccato vincitur, & ita ejus servus fit, & per consequens in potestatem Satanae se dedit. Qui vero inimicum benevolenter tractat, is malum vincit bono, & sic vere victor est fortissimus, quia tam alium, quam seipsum & pravos suos affectus vincit, adeoque cum id sine fide fieri nequeat 1. Joh. V. 4. certior redditur, quod viva fide sit praeditus, atque ita regenitus DEI filius. Vindicare se, inquit Ambrosius l. 1. offic. c. 36. non est actus fortitudinis, sed abjectionis & timiditatis; vincitur ab inimico, non vincit, qui se vindicat. Si mansuetudinem exhiberemus, inquit Chrysostomus in h. l. effemus omnibus insuperabiles, nec ulla ad nos injuria perveniret. Roga inimicum, annon doleat, annon censeat se victum, cum rides, cum contemnis ejus injurias? Exigit hoc loco, Musculo docente, Apostolus tantam constantiam benefaciendi inimicis, ut nullo pacto, nullisque injuriis nos ab eo proposito depelli sinamus, sed more militum constanter locum nostrum & ordinem tueamur, qui est benefacere omnibus, malefacere nemini, ut inveniamur germani Patris nostri caelestis filii.

SUBSECTIO II. REGULAS SPECIALES COMPLECTENS.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

This treats of the obedience to be rendered to the Magistrate as a divine ordinance, not only for the sake of punishment, but also for the sake of conscience, and of the tribute to be paid to him for protection: as well as of the debt, both civil and spiritual, which is love, in which the fulfillment of the law consists, to be rendered, and also of the works of darkness to be put off, and the armor of light to be put on, and the time of grace to be instituted with a decent walk.

The present chapter is therefore completed by three exhortations: I. It is concerning our debt regarding the Magistrate, as to subjection and the payment of tribute, up to verse 6 inclusive. II. Concerning the debt, both civil and spiritual, regarding one's neighbor, up to verse 10. III. Concerning the debt of each decent attire and action in the day of gracious light, regarding governing oneself rightly in piety, up to verse 14.

PART I.

Debt toward the Magistrate. Πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐξυσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις ὑποτασσέσθω.

With the use of the ritual law and that pertaining to morals completed, he comes to that part which pertains to public authority and civil society: and he shows in this part that the laws of Moses are not abolished by Christians, as those who, if they lived in Judea, would have to obey those laws, but are made equal with the laws of other nations not repugnant to GOD. Nor does it stand in the way that the law of Moses was given by GOD; since the empires that are outside Judea and their authority also have their origin from GOD. At the same time he cuts off the difficulty of many in Judea, who, because it was said in Deut. XVII. 15 that a king was to be chosen from their brothers, that is, fellow countrymen, inferred that no obedience was owed to foreigners, tacitly hinting that that law was valid when the Hebrew people were of their own right; but after they had come under the Roman Empire by the judgment of GOD, they were to be obeyed no less than a Jewish king or the Sanhedrin of the Jews, just as Jeremiah commanded that Nebuchadnezzar be obeyed, just as the Prophets obeyed the Chaldeans and Persians. This admonition was all the more necessary because he had said above that Christians were free from the law of Moses, from which some incautious person could have inferred that neither the political law of Moses for the Hebrews, nor other civil laws for Christians, imposed any necessity of obeying: which he shows to be contrary to itself from the origin and use of empires. Πᾶσα ψυχή. Even Prophets and Bishops. For both the Prophets and the high priests of the old covenant had been under the power of Kings and the Sanhedrin. Ἐξυσία corresponds to the Hebrew שלטן and the Chaldean שׁלטן, by which authority is signified. Moreover, ὑπερέχουσαι is added, so that princes and kings and those who by any other name are guardians of the public state may be understood, as Seneca speaks of Clemency in book IV, whose constituted power is at the same time the power of those who rule peoples under them, namely for the part mandated to them, as Peter explains this in 1 Ep. II. 13, 14, where there is similarly βασιλεῖ ὡς ὑπερέχοντι. Ὑποτασσέσθω, that is, let him obey in all things which are not against GOD. For it is a Niphal for a Hitpahel: which we have shown elsewhere to be most frequent in the verb τασσέσθαι and its compounds. If evil is inflicted on those who keep the precepts of GOD for this very reason, let them not resist, but patiently endure it.

As for what we said first regarding the distinction between ritual and forensic law, we spoke of it at the beginning of chapter XII. Nothing is contained in this chapter that pertains to the ritual law, whether to explain, perfect, or abrogate it. In the first verse at least, there is an allusion to sacrifices, and their end, which is a secondary one, is presented. Furthermore, as regards this second present chapter, nothing is found in it concerning the laws proper to the Jewish Republic. Obedience and subjection toward the Magistrate pertain to the moral law, not the forensic; it is of natural law, common to all, and not of the law proper to the Hebrews. It is expressed in the Decalogue, nay, inscribed in the minds of men at their primeval creation: and therefore the remnants of this law are to be found among all nations, even the most barbarous. Therefore, there was no need in the third place to show that the laws of Moses are not in that part abolished by Christians, since it is known in nature even to Gentiles who do not admit the Christian faith: nor do those things which are handed down here concerning subjection toward the Magistrate flow from Judaism, nor is it taught here that the laws of the Jews concerning the obedience owed to the Magistrate are to be equated with the laws of other nations. Fourthly, there is no indication of a precise difficulty concerning the election of Kings from among their brethren prescribed in Deut. XVII. 25, nor is anything hinted at concerning the abrogation of that law. That necessity indicated by Grotius from chapter VII. 4, with the genuine meaning of that passage having been handed down, now vanishes. But it is most correctly noted here that that universal πᾶσα ψυχὴ includes even Prophets and Bishops. Which overturns the Papacy, and especially the total exemption of clerics from the jurisdiction of the secular Magistrate, and from the subjection and obedience to be rendered to him. The command is universal; Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; Therefore, either the Pope is not a soul, or he ought to be subject by divine law. Bernard, Ep. XLII: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers: If every one, then yours too. Who excepts you from the universality? If anyone tries to except, he tries to deceive. To which the Imperial constitutions contribute: Let all live according to the law, even if they belong to the divine house, l. 10. C. de mandat. princip. & l. Presbyteri C. de Episcopis. But Bellarmine, l. II. de R. P. c. 29, contends in vain that Paul here establishes even Ecclesiastical jurisdiction itself; since it is clear from the attribution of the sword and the required tax that the discourse is about the Political Magistrate: such as the pagan one at Rome then was, and about obedience in civil matters; in which, as Estius admits, all commentators agree, both ancient and modern, both Greek and Latin. Salmero on this passage: The ancient Fathers, he says, and especially August. Epist. LIV. to Marcion, and Chrysostom in the present passage, interpret this place only concerning secular power, which the context itself also indicates when it says, he does not bear the sword in vain. Pererius and Toletus on this passage likewise grant this consensus of almost all the ancients: to whom add Lombard and Thomas on this passage. And Salmero proves this opinion from the occasion of the Apostolic precept, which the heresy of the Gaulonites had provided, who denied that obedience and tax were owed to Caesar or other profane princes, because of the liberty of the law received from GOD, to whom alone they asserted they were subject: The same Salmero adds: Regarding this passage of Paul, and the aforementioned sense of the expositors, it must be said that the power of a pagan Principality not yet incorporated into the Church has all as subjects, because they belong to that Republic over which they preside, as members, whether they be Gentiles, or Christians, or Clerics, or Bishops, or Apostles: and this by the LAW OF NATURE, just as now the Princes of the Turks are over the Christians, and the Princes who reside in their own place.

Although it is indeed permitted to Princes to dismiss certain persons from their jurisdiction and hand them over to be judged by others, they are not thereby entirely exempted from the subjection and jurisdiction of those princes, but the same jurisdiction remains as to its species, origin, and form, at least it is exercised through different persons by profession or some accident. For he who receives a privilege does not cease to be subject to him from whom he received it;

And that obligation of natural and divine law is one which cannot be derogated from; however, the exemption is only of human law, not divine, and the entire exercise of ecclesiastical jurisdiction concerning matters and actions of such a kind, which are by their nature civil, as Johan. Hofmeister and Georg. Cassander acknowledge on the last article of the abuses of the Aug. Conf., and Claudius Espensaeus in his digression XI on the 1st Epistle to Timothy. But it must be held, against Beza ch. 1 and Hadrian Saravia the Belgian in his book on the order of Bishops, that such jurisdiction could be conferred by the civil Magistrate upon ecclesiastical persons, namely Bishops and others, for the sake of order and reverence, without sin and without violation of this Apostolic command. Thus, therefore, this Apostolic warning is rightly applied to them also, in so far as such jurisdiction has been conferred by Princes upon Bishops and other ecclesiastical persons, which those who are subject to it are bound to value and revere by virtue of this communicated power.

For there is no authority except from God, and the authorities that exist are appointed by God.

GOD rules and changes all empires after the calling of the Gentiles, not only by that common providence through which He leaves many things to the natural order, but by a wisdom tempered to the needs of the subjects, or, if they have deserved it, to their punishments. God did this also in times past on several occasions, Prov. VIII. 2, Ps. LXXVI. 7, Dan. II. 21, 37. But Christ willed that this be believed and held for certain universally by Christians, John XIX. 11. Following Him in this place, Paul says that no empire now comes to pass unless GOD gives it His authority, just as a king gives it to governors: so that this may be better understood, he says that all empires which exist, that is, as long as they remain and endure, are constituted by GOD, that is, receive their authority, no less than if those kings had been anointed by Prophets, as indeed the kings of Syria were. In the Constitutions of Clement we have: You shall fear the king, knowing that his appointment is from the Lord. Irenaeus V. 24. For by whose command men are born, by His command also are kings constituted, suited to those who are ruled in those times. Tertullian in his Apology: We look up to the judgment of GOD in Emperors, who set them over the nations. The same to Scapula: A Christian is an enemy to no one, much less to the Emperor, whom, knowing him to be constituted by his GOD, it is necessary that he should both love, and revere, and honor, and wish him safe.

The reason is of the preceding precept, but not, as Bellarmine wishes against Barclay ch. 3, an application of general doctrine to the civil Magistrate, since the Apostle also dealt in general with power, whether secular or spiritual; thus Thomas in this place. First he (the Apostle) sets forth the instruction, secondly he assigns the reason. See also Cajetan in this place. But it is impious and inept that Stephanus Junius Brutus, author of the Vindiciae against Tyrants, or on the legitimate power of the people over the prince, q. I and III, under that universal EVERY SOUL, includes even the soul of the supreme Magistrate, that this question should in turn be subject to the people, with the added reason that that abstract term 'power' is not restricted to the concrete term of a prince or King, but is said indefinitely as POWER, abstracting from the person or persons with whom that power ought to be composed. Impious, because Paul Tit. III. 1 and Peter 1. Epistle II. 13 ff. not only restricts this faculty or authority to the Prince, contradistinguished from those hearers to whom he was writing, but also, as a remedy for iniquity, if those individuals should perhaps abuse that jurisdiction, teaches that the jurisdiction of the people over such Kings is not then to be usurped, but that vengeance is to be committed to GOD, S. Peter 1 Eph. II. 18 ff. Which remedy he also prescribes to servants concerning the abuse of the power of a master, from whom, however, one could appeal to the civil power or that of the Republic. Eph. VI. 9, Tit. II. 10 ff., Col. III. 25. It is inept, however, because by this reasoning a circle would always be given, and the Republic would be disturbed where and when either the jurisdiction of the Magistrate over the people, or the jurisdiction of the people over the Magistrate, was to be exercised. But in those Republics where jurisdiction is so constituted and, as it were, distributed, that in certain specific cases it can and ought to be exercised by the community, and has been suspended or derogated, as regards certain cases, from him or them who preside, there is one and the same jurisdiction, and it remains and is exercised at least in certain specific cases through different persons, as the blessed Hülsemann advised in his annotations to this place in his unpublished works, which also against Anton. Machiavelli book 1 ch. 9, and against Rossaeus or Guilb. Gifford, author of the Calvino-Turcismus in his book on the just judgment of the Republic against impious and heretical Kings ch. 209, Irenaeus Philalethes (whom Jacob Revius in his Examination of Episcopius-Vedelius p. 14 reports to be Ludovicus Molineus), likewise Buchanan and Hotman, whom Rivetus does not dare to excuse any more than Junius Brutus, as well as Dav. Pareus, whose pages on this place were burned at Oxford and London by Royal authority, concerning which Rivetus likewise: it is not our task to guarantee all his propositions and distinctions (see Apolog. on the truth of the peace of the Church p. 117), and it is to be noted concerning other Monarchomachs. Compare Luther Vol. III. Jena Germ. on Christian Authority, and Vol. VI and VII on Self-Defense. Suarez against the King of England book VI, Defense of the Catholic faith ch. 6. The King of England himself in his Apology for the oath of fidelity, and both Barclays in their writings published against Bellarmine, as also Arnisaeus in his book on the authority of Princes, where, as if in passing, it must be noted concerning the opinion of the blessed Luther, which the blessed Hülsemann observed in his Breviarium extensum ch. XX p. 394, that some things subscribed simultaneously in the name of Luther, Bugenhagen, Cruciger, and Melanchthon are supposititious, which the style argues, and which D. Matthaeus Ratzenberger, Archiatrist of the laudable memory of John Frederick, Elector of Saxony, shows in Hortleder Vol. II on the Smalcaldic War. book 1, last chapter, for the year 1552.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Agitur hic de obedientia Magistratui præstan- dâ ceu divinæ ordinationi non ob pœnam tantum, sed etiam ob conscientiam, & tri- buto ob protectionem eidem solvendo: nec non de debito tum civili, tum spirituali, quod est dilectio, in qua legis impletio consistit, reddendo, ut & de operibus te- nebrarum deponendis, & armis lucis in- duendis, ac tempus gratiæ decenti ambu- latione instituendâ.

Tribus ergo absolvitur caput præsens exhor- tationibus: I. est de debito nostro quoad Magistra- tum, quà subjectionem & tributi pensionem, usque ad vers. 6. incl. II. de debito tum civili tum spiri- tuali, quoad proximum, ad v. 10. III. de debito cu- jusque decentis vestitus & actionis in die gratiosæ lu- cis, quoad semetipsum rite in pietate gubernan- dum, usque ad v. 14.

PARS I.

Debitum erga Magistratum. Πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐξυσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις ὑποτασσέσθω.

Absoluto usu legis ritualis & ad mores pertinentis, ve- nit ad illam partem, quæ ad imperium publicum societa- temque civilem pertinet: ostenditque in hac parte Mosis leges non aboleri à Christianis, ut qui, in Judæa si vive- rent, illis legibus parendum haberent, sed æquari cum alia- rum gentium legibus DEO non repugnantibus. Nec ob- stare, quod Mosis lex à DEO esset lata; cum & quæ extra Judæam sunt imperia eorumque autoritas, à DEO habe- ret originem. Simul præcidit difficultatem multorum in Judæa, qui ideo quod dictum sit Deut. XVII. 15. regem legendum à fratribus, id est, popularibus, inferebant exter- nis nullam deberi obedientiam, tacite innuens illam le- gem valuisse, cum sui juris esset populus Hebraicus; post- quam vero DEI judicio sub Romanorum Imperium de- venerat, illis quoque non minus quam regi Judæo, aut Judæorum Synedrio parendum, sicut Nabuchodonosori pareri præcepit Jeremias, sicut Prophetæ Chaldæis & Per- sis paruerunt. Erat autem hæc admonitio eo magis ne- cessaria, quod supra à lege Mosis liberos dixerat Christia- nos, unde incautus aliquis inferre potuerat, neque legem Mosis politicam Hebræis, neque alias leges civiles Chri- stianis ullam injicere parendi necessitatem: quod contra se habere ostendit ex imperiorum origine & usu. Πᾶσα ψυ- χή. Etiam Prophetæ & Episcopi. Nam & Prophetæ & summi Sacerdotes veteris fœderis sub Regum ac Synedrii potestate fuerant. Ἐξυσία respondet Hebræo שלטן & Chaldæo שׁלטן, per quæ significatur imperium. Additur autem ὑπερέχουσαι, ut intelligantur principes regesque & quocunque alio nomine sunt tutores status publici, ut Se- neca loquitur de Clementia libro IV. quorum constituta potestate simul constituta potestas est eorum, qui sub il- lis regunt populos, nimirum pro mandata ipsis parte, ut hoc explicat Petrus 1. Ep. II. 13. 14. ubi similiter est βασιλεῖ ὡς ὑπερέχοντι. Ὑποτασσέσθω, id est, pareat in omnibus, quæ contra DEUM non sunt. Est enim Niphal pro Hitpahel: quod in verbo τασσέσθαι & inde compositis frequentissi- mum esse, alibi ostendimus. Si DEI præcepta servantibus ob hoc ipsum malum inferatur, non resistant, sed patienter id sustineant.

Quod primum ad distinctionem ritualis & fo- rensis legis, diximus de ea ad c. XII. initium. Ni- hil isto capite habetur, quod ad legem ritualem seu explicandam seu perficiendam seu abrogan- dam spectet. Primo saltim commate ad sacrificia alluditur, finisque eorum isque secundarius ex- hibetur. Quod porro secundo hoc præsens caput attinet, de legibus Judaica Reipublicæ propriis ni- hil in eodem reperitur. Obedientia & subjectio erga Magistratum ad legem moralem, non foren- sem pertinet: Juris est naturalis omnibus commu- nis, non vero juris Ebræorum proprii. In Deca- logo expressa, imo in mentibus hominum in pri- mæva creatione inscripta: ideoque legis hujus re- liquias apud omnes gentes etiam maxime barba- ras reperire est. Non ergo tertio opus erat osten- dere leges Mosis ea parte non aboleri à Christianis, siquidem etiam Ethnicis Christianam fidem non admittentibus in natura notum sit: nec à Judai- smo illa fluunt, quæ de subjectione erga Magi- stratum hic traduntur, aut æquari Judæorum le- ges de obedientia Magistratui debita cum alia- rum gentium legibus hic docetur. Quarto nul- lum est indicium præcisæ difficultatis circa electio- nem Regum è fratribus Deut. XVII. 25. præscri- ptam, nec de legis istius abrogatione quicquam in- nuitur. Necessitas illa è cap. VII. 4. à Grotio in- dicata, tradita genuina loci istius sententia jam evanescit. Id autem rectissime hic animadversum, universalem illam πᾶσα ψυχὴ etiam Prophetas & Episcopos comprehendere. Quod Papatum ever- tit, imprimis autem exemtionem omnimodam cle- ricorum à jurisdictione Magistratus secularis, & subjectione & obedientia ei præstanda. Manda- tum est universale; Omnis anima potestatibus su- pereminentibus subjecta esto; Ergo aut Papa non est anima, aut subjectus esse debet divino jure. Bernhard. Ep. XLII. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: Si omnis & vestra. Quis vos excipit ab universitate? Si quis tentat excipere, conatur decipere. Quo faciunt Imperatoriæ con- stitutiones: Omnes secundum legem vivant, etiamsi ad divinam domum pertineant l. 10. C. de mandat. princip. & l. Presbyteri C. de Episcopis. Frustra autem contendit Bellarminus l. II. de R. P. c. 29. Paulum hic constituere ipsammet etiam jurisdictio- nem Ecclesiasticam; siquidem ex attributione gla- dii, & requisito censu liqueat, de Magistratu Poli- tico sermonem esse: qualis tum gentilis Romæ erat, & de obedientia in rebus civilibus; in quo, fatente Estio, consentiunt omnes commentatores, tam veteres quam recentiores, tam Græci, quam Latini. Salmero in h. l. Patres, inquit, veteres, & prasertim August. Epist. LIV. ad Marcion. & Chry- sostomus præsenti loco hunc locum de potestate secu- lari tantum interpretantur, quod & ipse contextus subindicat, cum ait, non sine causa gladium portat. Pererius & Tolet. in h. l. itidem largiuntur hunc veterum fere omnium consensum: quibus adde Lombardum & Thomam in h. l. Et probat hanc sententiam Salmero ex occasione præcepti Apo- stolici, quam præbuerat Gaulonitarum hæresis, ne- gantium obedientiam & censum deberi Cæsari, aliis- ve principibus profanis, propter libertatem legis à DEO susceptæ, cui soli se subjectos esse asserebant: Addit idem Salmero: Ad hunc Pauli locum, & ex- positorum sensum prædictum, dicendum est, quod po- testas Ethnici Principatus nondum Ecclesiæ incorpo- rata subditos habet omnes, quia ad eam Rempublic. cui præsident, tanquam membra, pertinent, sive Ethnici, sive Christiani, sive Clerici, sive Episcopi, sive Apostoli: & hoc ex JURE NATURÆ, ut modo Turcarum Principes supra Christianos, & Principes, qui suo loco resident.

Quanquam vero Principibus liceat quasdã per- sonas dimittere ex sua jurisdictione, & judicandas aliis tradere, non tamen ita eximuntur omnino, à subjectione & jurisdictione illorum principum, sed manet jurisdictio eadem quoad speciem, originem & formã, saltem exercetur per diversas professio- ne seu accidente quodam personas. Neq; enim pri- vilegiũ accipiens cessat subesse ei, à quo acceperat;

& obligatio illa juris naturalis & divini est, cui derogari non potest; exemtio autem juris tan- tum humani est, non divini, totumque exerciti- um jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticae circa res & actio- nes ejusmodi, quae naturà suâ civiles sunt, uti agnoscunt Johan. Hofmeisterus, & Georg. Cassan- der ad ultimum articulum abusuum Aug. Conf. & Claudius Espensaeus digress. XI. in 1. Epist. ad Timoth. Potuisse autem ordinis & reverentiae causa conferri jurisdictionem talem à civili Ma- gistratu Ecclesiasticis personis, utpote Episcopis, aliisque citra peccatum, & citra violationem hu- jus mandati Apostolici, contra Bezam cap. 1. & Hadrianum Saraviam, Belgam l. de ordin. Episc. tenendum. Sic ergo ad eos etiam recte applica- tur in tantum hoc monitum Apostolicum, in quan- tum à Principibus collata est Episcopis aliisque Ecclesiasticis personis ejusmodi jurisdictio, quam vi hujus communicatae potestatis, æstimare & re- vereri tenentur, qui illi subjecti sunt.

ὁ γάρ ἐστιν ἐξυσία εἰ μὴ ὑπὸ θεῦ, αἱ δὲ ὖσαι ἐξυσίαι ὑπὸ θεῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσί.

Imperia omnia post vocationem gentium, DEUS re- git ac mutat non communi tantum illa providentia, per quam multa relinquit naturali ordini, sed sapientia attem- perata subditorum utilitatibus, aut, si ita meruerint, poe- nis. Fecit hoc & olim Deus aliquoties Prov. VIII. 2. Ps. LXXVI. 7. Dan. II. 21. 37. At Christus hoc universaliter à Christianis credi & pro certo haberi voluit Joh. XIX. 11. Quera sequens hoc loco Paulus, nullum ait imperium nunc contingere nisi DEO autoritatem ei suam dante, sic- ut rex dat præsidibus: quod ut rectius intelligatur, ait, omnia imperia, quæ sunt, id est, quamdiu manent ac du. rant, à DEO constitui, id est, autoritatem suam accipere, non minus quam si reges illi per Prophetas uncti essent, ut quidem Syriæ reges. In Clementis Constitutionibus habemus: τὸν βασιλέα φοβηθήσῃ εἰδὼς ὅτι τῦ κυρίε ἐσὶν ἡ χειροτονία. Irenæus V. 24. Cujus enim jussu homines na- scuntur, hujus jussu & reges constituuntur, apti illis, qui illis temporibus regnantur. Tertullianus in Apologetico: Nos judicium DEI suspicimus in Imperatoribus, qui gentibus illos præfecit. Idem ad Scapulam: Christianus nullius hostis est, nedum Imperatoris, quem sciens à DEO suo constitui, necesse est ut & ipsum diligat, & revereatur, & honoret, & salvum velit.

Ratio est antecedentis præcepti, non autem ut Bellarminus contra Barclajum c. 3. vult generalis doctrinæ applicatio ad civilem Magistratum, q. in genere de potestate sive seculari sive spirituali etiam egerit Apostolus; Ita Thomas in h. l. Pri- mo ponit (Apostolus) documentum, secundo ra- tionem assignat, Vid. & Cajetanus in h. l. Impium autem atque ineptum est, quod Stephanus Junius Brutus autor vindiciarum contra Tyrannos, seu de legitima potestate populi in principem, q. I. & III. sub universali ista OMNIS ANIMA, etiam supremi Magistratus animam comprehendit, q. istam populo vicissim oporteat esse subjectam, addita ratione, quia abstractum illud potestas, non restringatur ad concretum principis, seu Regis, sed indefinite dicatur POTESTAS abstrahendo cum quo vel quibus subjectis componi debeat illa pote- stas. Impium, quia Paulus Tit. III. 1. & Petrus 1. Epist. II. 13. seqq. facultatem istam seu ἐξυσίαν non solum restringit ad Principem contradistin- ctum illis auditoribus, quibus scribebat, sed et- iam pro remedio iniquitatis, si qua forte abute- rentur ista individua jurisdictione, non tum usur- pandam jurisdictionem populi in tales Reges, sed vindictam DEO esse committendam docet S. Petrus 1. Eph. II. 18. seqq. Quod remedium etiam servis præscribit circa abusum potestatis herilis, à qua tamen provocari poterat ad potestatem ci- vilem seu Reipublicæ. Eph. VI. 9. Tit. II. 10. sqq. Col. III. 25. Ineptum est autem, quia semper hac ratione daretur circulus, & turbaretur Respubl. ubi & quando vel Magistratus jurisdictio in populum, vel populi jurisdictio in Magistratum esset exercenda. In illis autem Rebuspublicis, ubi jurisdictio sic constituta est, & quasi distributa, ut in certis quibusdam casibus exerceri possit & debeat à communitate & suspensa vel derogata sit, quoad certos casus ei, vel eis, qui præsunt, una est & manet jurisdictio ac saltem in certis quibusdam casibus exercetur per diversas personas, ut monuit B. Hülsemannus in annot. ad h. l. ἀνεκδότοις, quæ etiam contra Anton. Machiavello l. 1. c. 9. & contra Rossæum sive Guilb. Giffordum, autorem Calvino-Turcismi libro de just. Reipubl. in Reges impios & hæretic. animadversione c. 209. Irenæum Philalethen (quem Ludovicum Molineum esse tradit Jacobus Revius Examini Episcopio-Vedeliani p. 14.) Buchananum item & Hottomannum, quos æque ut Junium Brutum excusare non audet Rivetus, nec non Dav. Pareum, cujus pagellæ in h. l. Oxonii & Lundini Regia autoritate exustæ sunt, de quo Rivetus itidem: nostrum non est præstare ejus omnes propositiones & distinstiones (vid. Apolog. de ver. pac. Ecclesiæ p. 117.) aliosque Monarchomachos observandum. Conf. Lutherus T. III. Jen. Germ. von der Christl. Obrigkeit, & Tom. VI. & VII. von der Gegenwehr. Schwarez. contr. Reg. Angl. libr. VI. defens. Cathol. c. 6. Rex ipse Angliæ in Apol. pro juram. fidelit. & Barclajus uterque in scriptis contra Bellarm. evulgatis ut & Arnifæus l. de autor. Princip. ubi ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ circa B. Lutheri sententiam monendum, quod observavit B. Hülsemannus in Breviar. extens. c. XX. p. 394. nonnulla simultaneo Lutheri, Bugenhagii, Crucigeri, Melanchthonis nomine subscripta supposititia esse, quod arguat stylus, & ostendant D. Matthæus Ratzenberger Joh. Friedr. Elector. Saxon. laud. memor. Archiater, apud. Hortlederum Tom. II. de Bello Smalcald. l. 1. cap. ult. ad ann. 1552.

## 13:2
V. 2. So that he who resists the authority resists the ordinance of God.

Ἀντιτάσσεσθαι, that is, to oppose oneself by force, just as GOD opposes Himself to the impious, Prov. III. 34, Jac. IV. 6, 1 Petr. V. 5. The Syrian here used [a word meaning] one who rises up against: not badly. For the Apostle refers to the deed of Judas the Gaulonite and his followers, whose examples many of the Jews were shortly to follow against the express prohibition of Christ, no less unhappily than Galba, Otho, and Vitellius in the Roman Empire. And note that the edict of GOD is called here, lest anyone oppose force to kings. For this is διαταγὴ, which in Ezra VII. 10, Heb. XI. 23 is διάταγμα and διάταξις in Ps. CXIX. 9, just as the Roman Emperors called their constitutions in Greek, ἀντιτασσόμενοι again passive in sound, reciprocal in sense.

But those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves.

No less than among the Jews, who opposed themselves to the Sanhedrin, Deut. XVIII. 12, or to the king, 1 Kings II. 43, or to a parent, Deut. XXI. 18; he who does this is called סורר ומורה, disobedient and rebellious, which has the same value as ἀντιτασσόμενος. Κρῖμα λήψονται, they will bear the penalty. Thus Matt. XXIII. 14. For words concerning good things are accustomed to be transferred to bad ones, as in 2 Cor. XI. 24.

We have noted such an occasion also just now from Salmeron: the same was also observed by Benedictus Justinianus on this passage. Josephus is the author that among the Jews there was a certain sect of Gaulonites, sprung from a certain Judas the Gaulonite, etc., which denied that census and obedience were owed to Caesar, etc. Deluded by the same or a very similar error, those who misinterpreted Christian liberty were once those who thought that those who had given their names to Christ were released from civil laws and entirely free from the power of Princes. And so Christians were once ill-spoken of among the infidels, as if they were less obedient to Princes and Magistrates, etc. Paul therefore removes this false and impious suspicion in the present passage. Estius also agrees in this place. Jerome had preceded them in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus. The dogma of Judas the Galilean was still flourishing at that time and had very many followers, therefore the Apostle teaches that believers ought to be subject to principalities and powers.

Latin:

V. 2. ὥστε ὁ ἀντιτασσόμενος τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ διαταγῇ ἀνθέστηκεν.

Ἀντιτάσσεσθαι hoc est, per vim se opponere, sicut DEUS impiis se opponit Prov. III. 34. Jac. IV. 6. 1. Petr. V. 5. Syrus hic posuit, qui contra insurgit: non male. Respicit enim Apostolus factum Judæ Gaulonitæ & sectatorum ejus, quorum exempla brevi contra expressum Christi interdictum secuturi erant Judæorum multi non minus infeliciter, quam in Romano imperio Galba, Otho Vitellius. Et nota DEI edictum hic dici, ne quis regibus vim opponat. Est enim hic διαταγὴ quod Esdræ VII. 10. Hebr. XI. 23. διάταγμα & διάταξις Ps. CXIX. 9. quomodo & Romani Imperatores constitutiones suas Græce appellabant, ἀντιτασσόμενοι rursum passivum sono, sensu reciprocum.

Οἱ δὲ ἀνθεστηκότες ἑαυτοῖς κρῖμα λήψονται.

Non minus quam apud Judæos, qui Senedrio se opponebant Deut. XVIII. 12. aut regi 1. Reg. II. 43. aut parenti, Deut. XX. 18. qui id facit, dicitur סורר ומורה ἀπειθὴς, καὶ ἐρεθιστὴς, quod idem valet, quantum ἀντιτασσόμενος. Κρῖμα λήψονται pœnam ferent. Sic Matth. XXIII. 14. Solent enim verba de rebus bonis ad malas transferri, ut 2. Cor. XI. 24.

Talem occasionem notavimus etiam modo ex Salmerone: Observata eadem quoque Benedicto Justiniano in h. l. Josephus autor est apud Judæos fuisse quandam sectam Gaulonitarum à quodam Juda Gaulonita ortam &c. quæ negabat censum & obedientiam Cæsari deberi &c. Eodem vel persimili errore delusi malè Christianam libertatem interpretantes fuerunt olim, qui existimarent, eos, qui Christo nomina dedissent, legibus civilibus solutos esse, ac penitus liberos à Principum potestate. Itaque male olim audiebant Christiani apud infideles, quasi Principibus ac Magistratibus minus essent obse- quentes, &c. Hanc igitur falsam atque impiam su- spicionem Paulus in præsenti amolitur. Consonat & Estius in h. l. Quibus præiverat Hieronymus in comment. Epist. ad Tit. Judæ Galilæi per illud tem- pus dogma adhuc vigebat & habebat plurimos secta- tores, idcirco docet Apostolus principatibus & pote- statibus credentes debere esse subjectos.

## 13:3
V. 3. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil.

After the argument from origin, he adds another from utility, for the sake of which governments were established, namely that with wickedness repressed, the good may live more safely. Good kings fulfill this most fully, and bad ones also to some extent, if only for their own sake. And although sometimes some vice intervenes, it is nevertheless always better that there be princes than that there not be. For as Tacitus rightly says: There will be vices as long as there are men, but these are not continuous and are compensated for by the intervention of better things. And just as sterility or rains and other evils of nature, so the luxury or avarice of those in power must be tolerated. See what we have discussed at length about this matter in the first book of the Law of War and Peace III. 4. and in the annotations to that place. From which also explain those things which follow in Paul. Agrippa in his speech to the Jews, which is in Josephus, Jewish War II. 28. says that no one was sent by the Roman Magistrates to harm the good. Cicero II. de legibus: Laws affect the wicked with punishment, and defend and protect the good. In the Manuscript it is read: ἐκ εἰσὶ φόβος τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἔργῳ, ἀλλὰ τῷ κακῷ. Rightly, provided you know that there is a metonymy of the effect for the cause: for the work is put for the worker.

A single manuscript codex is not rightly preferred to all others whatsoever. Estius explains it thus: Princes (as indeed they are such) are not to be feared by those who do good, but by those who do evil. It is more correctly added as a limitation, that they are not to be feared by the good, but by the bad, by right.
