He calls them Ἄρχοντες, princes, leaders, whom he previously called ἐξουσίας, powers: embracing all, the highest, the middle, the lowest, but properly civil ones, to whom the right of the sword belongs; he calls good and bad works not theologically, but civilly such, i.e., virtues and vices, commanded or prohibited by the laws of each territory or city; which laws are both divine, of which the Magistrate ought principally to be the guardian, lest they be violated, and human, common, or municipal, or positive, by which external discipline suitable and necessary to any Republic is sanctioned: therefore he calls works admitted according to or against these laws good or bad. Moreover, a twofold end of the Magistrate is designated, both the secondary, the fear of the wicked, and the primary, the praise of the good.

Do you wish then not to fear the authority? Do what is good.

He shows that he means the same thing when he says authority, and when he says rulers.

and you will have praise from it.

They will say, 'Caius Seius is a good man, only that he is a Christian,' as it is in Tertullian. When Paul was writing this, there was no persecution of Christians in Rome. The Jews had also returned to Rome. Philo expresses this sense thus: 'confirming punishments for the unjust, as honors for the just,' in his Book on the Judge.

Latin:

V. 3. Οἱ γὰρ ἄρχοντες ὀυκ εἰσὶ φόβος τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων, ἀλλὰ τῶν κακῶν.

Post Argumentum ab origine, alterum addit ab usu, cujus causa constituta sunt imperia, nempe ut improbita- te repressa, tutius vivant boni. Hoc autem plenissime præ- stant boni reges, mali quoque aliquatenus, vel sui causa. Et quanquam interdum aliquid vitii intervenit, nunquam tamen non satius est esse principes, quam non esse. Nam ut recte Tacitus: Vitia erunt, donec homines, sed neque hæc continua & meliorum interventu pensantur. Et quomodo sterilitatem aut imbres & cætera naturæ mala, ita luxus vel avaritia dominantium toleranda. Vide, quæ de hac re fuse disseruimus libro primo de Jure Belli ac Pacis III. 4. & in annotatis ad eum locum. Unde & ea quæ apud Pau- lum sequentur, explica. Agrippa in oratione ad Judæos, quæ est apud Josephum belli Judaici II. 28. ait nullos à Romanis Magistratibus missos ut bonis noceant. Cicero II. de legibus: Leges improbos supplicio afficiunt, & defendunt ac tuentur bonos. In Manuscripto legitur: ἐκ εἰσὶ φόβος τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἔργῳ, ἀλλὰ τῷ κακῷ. Recte, dum noris μετα- νυμίας esse effecti pro causa: nam opus ponitur pro ope- rante.

Non recte præfertur Manuscriptus codex uni- cus aliis quibusvis omnibus. Explicat autem ita Estius: Principes (ut quidem tales sunt) non sunt metuendi bene agentibus, sed male. Rectius addi- tur limitatio, quod timendi non sint bonis, sed malis, de jure. Ἄρχοντες autem principes, duces vo- cat, quos prius ἐξουσίας potestates: omnes com- plectens, summos, medios, imos, sed proprie ci- viles, quibus convenit jus gladii; Bona vero & mala opera vocat non Theologice, sed civiliter ta- lia, h.e. virtutes & vitia, legibus cujusque territo- rii vel civitatis præcepta vel prohibita; quæ leges sunt tum divinæ, quorum principaliter Magistra- tus debet esse custos, ne violentur, tum humanæ communes, aut municipales, seu positivæ, quibus disciplina externa cuivis Reipubl. conveniens & necessaria sancitur: opera igitur secundum vel contra leges has admissa, vocat bona vel mala. Designatur autem geminus finis Magistratus, tum secundarius, timor malorum, tum primarius laus bonorum.

Θέλεις δὲ μὴ φοβεῖσθαι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ποίει.

Ostendit idem se significare, cum dicit ἐξουσίαν, & cum dicit ἄρχοντας.

καὶ ἕξεις ἔπαινον ἐξ αὐτῆς.

Dicent Bonus vir Cajus Sejus, tantum quod Christianus, ut est apud Tertullianum. Cum hæc scriberet Paulus, non sæviebatur Romæ in Christianos. Etiam Judæi Romam redierant. Philo hunc sensum sic exprimit: τιμωρίας δὲ ἐπ' ἀδίκοῖς, ὡς ἐπὶ δικαίοις τιμὰς, βεβαιώσασαι, Libro de judice.

## 13:4
V. 4. For he is God's minister to you for good.

He means the same as Seneca in Epistle LXXIII. 'They seem to me to err who think that those who are faithfully devoted to philosophy are contumacious and refractory, and contemners of magistrates and kings, or of those by whom public affairs are administered. On the contrary, none are more grateful to them: and not undeservedly: for they provide more to none than to those to whom it is permitted to enjoy tranquil leisure.' Therefore, these to whom public security provides access to the purpose of living well, it is necessary that they honor the author of this good as a parent. And just as in this matter magistrates profit the wise much, so also the wise, especially Christians, profit magistrates the most; for by correcting many, and rendering them better, even than human laws command, they remove from them a great source of severity, and cause them to rule more placidly. Justin treats this beautifully in his Apology II, and Chrysostom several times.

But if you do evil.

Against the laws of civil society.

If nothing else, let the fear of punishment deter you. For he is speaking to every man.

For he does not bear the sword in vain.

For he does not bear the sword in vain is a litotes for he bears the sword for a grave cause. In the Talmudic writings, that saying about the Hebrew King is frequent: The King who bears the sword. He rightly adapts this to all kings: for the right of all is now equal. And the Roman Emperors wore a dagger, which Tacitus in the third book of his Histories interprets as the right of life and death over citizens. It is permitted to them to kill, which is not permitted to others. Irenaeus V. 24. And for this reason the magistrates themselves, having the laws as a garment of justice, whatever they shall have done justly and lawfully, they shall not be questioned concerning these, nor shall they pay penalties.

He teaches that the magistrate is deservedly feared by the wicked by two arguments; first, because he is armed with the sword, which he may draw against the wicked; then, because in the place of God, as his minister, he ought to restrain the crimes of the wicked with punishments; but it is said without foundation that Paul took these things concerning the sword from the Talmudic writings: because it is not established that those Talmudic writings are older than the Apostolic letters. Nor does the Apostle have what he proposed in the Scriptures from the Talmud, but from his own divine inspiration. Moreover, by the sword is understood metonymically the power of drawing the sword, under which are comprehended at the same time weapons of every kind and coercive power: and it seems that the old custom of wearing a sword is being looked at, or the way in which swords, fasces, and axes were carried before the Magistrate as a symbol of power. But the Socinians assume the improper and synecdochical meaning of the word 'in vain' in such a way that they render ambiguous the power of drawing the sword against criminals: for it is indicated that power is granted to the magistrate up to the sword, so that he himself can also properly wield the dagger or sword. Schlichting acknowledges this here from the lectures of Crellius, rendering this paraphrase: For the power was not given to him in vain to strike with the sword, and to avenge evildoers, and the right of life and death was granted: he who has this power can much more impose lesser punishments and fines. The same Schlichting stated in his own commentary on this passage: Not in vain. That is, he has the right and power even to strike with the sword, that is, to deprive evildoers of life, whose crimes, to wit, deserve this punishment. For if the Magistrate did not have this right and power, he would carry the sword in vain, which is an instrument for beheading and depriving a man of life. But from where does he have this right and power if not from GOD himself, whose minister he is, especially since he performs such a ministry that cannot be carried out without the right and power of the sword. For otherwise it would not be well for the good, that is, the good could in no way be safe and secure from the bad through the Magistrate.

For he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil.

Εἰς ὀργὴν is said metonymically, for in punishment. Philo in the said book on the Judge, concerning the guilty: having done not from (whence) but things worthy of wrath.

Latin:

V. 4. Θεῦ γὰρ διάκονός ἐστί σοι εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν.

Idem vult quod Seneca Epistola LXXIII. Errare mihi videntur, qui putant philosophiæ fideliter deditos contumaces esse ac refractarios, & contemptores magistratuum ac regum, eorumve per quos publica administrantur. E contrario enim nulli adversus illos gratiores sunt: nec immerito: nullis enim plus præstant, quam quibus frui tranquillo otio licet. Itaque hi quibus ad propositum bene vivendi aditum confert securi- tas publica, necesse est, ut auctorem hujus boni ut parentem colant. Ac sicut hac in re magistratus multum sapientibus prosunt, ita & sapientes, præcipue Christiani, plurimum magistratibus; Nam multos corrigendo, & meliores red- dendo, etiam quam leges humanæ præcipiunt, detrahunt illis magnam severitatis materiam, efficiuntque ut placidius imperent. Tractat hoc pulchre Apologetico II. Justinus & Chrysostomus aliquoties.

ἐὰν δὲ κακὸν ποιῇς.

Contra leges societatis civilis.

Si non aliud, formido pœnæ te absterreat. Loquitur enim homini cuivis.

ὀ γὰρ εἰκῆ τὴν μάχαιραν φορεῖ.

ὀ γὰρ εἰκῆ est λιτότης pro gravi de causa gladium gerit. In Thalmudicis frequens illud est de Rege Hebræo: Rex qui portat gladium. Id recte aptat ad reges omnes: par enim nunc omnium jus. Et Romani Imperatores pugio- nem gerebant, quod jus vitæ necisque civium interpreta- tur Tacitus historiarum III. Licet illis interficere, quod aliis non licet. Irenæus V. 24. Et propter hoc & ipsi magistratus indumentum justitiæ leges habentes, quæcunque juste & legitime fecerint, de his non interrogabuntur, neque pœnas dabunt.

Magistratum merito sceleratis timeri duobus argumentis docet; tum quod gladio armatus sit, quem stringat in sceleratos; tum quod Dei loco, ceu minister ejus coërcere pœnis scelera impro- borum debeat; Paulum autem è Thalmudicis hæc de gladio sumpsisse, citra fundamentum dicitur: quia Thalmudica illa Apostolicis literis antiquiora esse, non constat. Nec è Thalmude, sed è divina inspiratione sua habeat Apostolus, quæ in Scriptu- ris proposuit. Cæterum per gladium metonymi- ce intelligitur potestas gladium stringendi, sub quo comprehenduntur simul omnis generis arma & potestas coäctiva: & respici videtur mos vetus gla- dii gestandi, vel quo præferebantur Magistratui gladii, fasces, secures in symbolum potestatis. Te- mere autem vocis impropriam & synecdochicam significationem Sociniani ita assumunt, ut gladii contra facinorosos stringendi potestatem com- prehendi ambiguam reddant: nam usque ad gla- dium potestatem magistratui concessam esse, ita ut proprie dictum ensem vel gladium etiam ipse stringere possit, indicatur. Quod agnoscit hic ex prælectionibus Crellii Schlichtingius, hanc red- dens paraphrasin: Neque enim frustra potestas illi data est gladio feriendi, atque ulciscendi maleficos, ac jus vitæ necisque concessum: quam potestatem qui habet, is multo magis minora supplicia ac mulctas potest irrogare. Idem in proprio commentario tradidit Schlichtingius ad h. l. Non frustra. Id est, habet jus & potestatem etiam gladio feriendi, id est, vitæ privandi maleficos, quorum scil. maleficia pœ- nam hanc mereantur. Nam si jus & potestatem hanc Magistratus non haberet, frustra omnino gla- dium gereret, qui instrumentum est capitis detrun- candi, & hominem vitæ privandi. Unde autem hoc jus & potestatem habet nisi ab ipso DEO, cujus minister est, præsertim cum tale ministerium gerat, quod sine gladii jure ac potestate obiri non possit. Neque enim aliter bonis bene esset, id est, boni à ma- lis per Magistratum tuti ac securi esse ullo modo possent.

Θεῦ γὰρ διάκονός ἐσιν ἔκδικος εἰς ὀργὴν τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι.

Εἰς ὀργὴν dictum est μετωνυμικῶς, pro in pœnam. Philo dicto libro de Judice, de nocente: δεδρακὼς ἐκ όλίυ (πόθεν) ἀλλ' ὀργῆς ἄξια.

## 13:5
V. 5. Wherefore it is necessary to be subject.) Sophocles: are they rulers? honor them on account of wrath. Not only for fear of the punishment which the laws threaten.

but also for conscience' sake.

Because Christ commanded it, Matt. XXII. 21.

Latin:

V. 5. διὸ ἀνάγκη ὑποτάσσεσθαι.) Sophocles : ἄρχοντές εἰσιν' τίμή; ἐμότον διὰ τὴν ὀργὴν. Non solo pœnæ metu quam leges minantur.

ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν.

Quia Christus id præcepit Matth. XXII. 21.

## 13:6
V. 6. For for this cause pay ye tribute also. Not only for fear of what is committed, but also because Christ so willed it; in the already mentioned passage of Matthew. Justin Martyr in Apology II: And we strive everywhere to pay taxes and tributes to those appointed by us, as we were taught by him. Tatian: Does the king command to pay tribute? I am ready to provide it. Tertullian in the Apology: The rest of the taxes will give thanks to the Christians, who pay them faithfully, as we abstain from defrauding another.

For they are ministers of God.

What he had twice called ministers (diaconos), he now calls ministers (leiturgous). Thus the Hebrew משרת is sometimes translated as minister (leiturgos), sometimes as servant (diaconos).

persevering in this very thing. חזקים, that is, assiduous in this very thing, namely that by the right of GOD he may punish the wicked for the protection of the innocent. Those who serve man have need of a wage: those serve GOD in a great and useful matter, even for the Church. This precept of Christ is not new: but the obedience to be rendered to the Magistrate was already commanded in the Old Testament, Deut. XVII. 12, Prov. XXIV. 22, nay, it is enjoined by the law of nature, Gen. XLI. 40. The Apostle therefore warns that one must obey not only because of wrath, or the punishment of men, and especially of GOD himself, but also because of conscience, through which not the consciousness of benefits, which are provided to subjects by the Magistrate, as the Greek Interpreters wish, but the dictate of conscience and the fear of divine offense is insinuated; because the argument is taken not from utility, but from necessity: nor is the Apostle accustomed to name conscience in any other sense: Obedience therefore produces a good conscience, which is the approval of our mind rightly judging and testifying to us that we have done right things approved by GOD and men. This approval is followed by the joy of the heart resting in this approval of GOD and men. Προσκαρτεροῦντες Erasmus renders as 'incumbentes' (applying themselves). The Vulgate, 'servientes' (serving). Augustine, book 4 of De Doctrina Christiana, ch. 29, translates as 'perseverantes' (persevering). Properly, προσκαρτερεῖν denotes continuous and diligent care, which is joined with great patience, on account of the weight of the burden. And thus he describes the most burdensome office of the Magistrate, who must be perpetually intent upon this very work, namely the defense of the good and the restraining of the wicked, and therefore finds it necessary to expend even great costs. Thus it is used in Mark III. 9, Acts I. 24 concerning prayers, Acts II. 24, Rom. XII. 13, as the blessed Weller has it. The argument is taken from equity: For because the Magistrate is intent upon this with such diligence, that he presides in the place of GOD, it is equitable that subjects should bring back some retribution to them. For the laborer is worthy of his hire. Luke X. v. 7, 1 Cor. IX. 7.

PART II. Debt toward one's neighbor.

Latin:

V. 6. διὰ τῦτο γὰρ καὶ φόρυς τελεῖτε. Non tantum metu commissi, sed etiam quia Christus ita voluit; Matthæi dicto jam loco. Justinus Martyr Apolo- getico II. φόρυς δὲ καὶ εἰς φορὰς τοῖς ὑφ' ἡμῶν τεταγμένοις πανταχῦ πρὸ πάντων πειρώμεθα φέρειν, ὡς ἐδιδάχθημεν παρ' ἀυτῦ. Tatianus: προσατίω φόρυς τελεῖν ὁ βασιλευς; ἕτοιμος παρέχειν. Tertullianus Apologetico. Cætera svectigalia gratias Christianis agent ex fide pendentibus, qui alieno fran- dendo abstinemus.

λειτυργοὶ γὰρ Θεῦ εἰσι.

Quod bis dixerat διακόνυς, nunc dicit λειτυργὺς. Ita משרת Hebræum modo λειτυργὸς vertitur, modo διάκονος.

εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο προσκαρτεροῦντες. חזקים, id est, assidui in hoc ipsum, nempè ut DEI jure malos puniat ad innocentium tutelam. Qui homini serviunt, mercede opus habent: illi DEO serviunt in re magna utilique, etiam Ecclesiae. Non est novum hoc Christi praeceptum: sed obedientia Magistratui praestanda jam in Vet. Test. mandata Deut. XVII. 12. Prov. XXIV. 22. imò naturae lege injuncta est Gen. XLI. 40. Monet ergò Apostolus, non tantùm ob iram, vel poenam tùm hominum, tùm ipsius imprimis DEI parendum esse, sed etiam propter conscientiam, per quam non conscientia beneficiorum, quae subditis praestantur à Magistratu, ut Graeci Interpp. volunt, sed dictamen conscientiae & metus offensionis divinae insinuatur; quia non ab utili, sed à necessario desumptum est argumentum: nec alio sensu conscientiam solet nuncupare Apostolus: Obedientia igitur parit bonam conscientiam, quae est approbatio mentis nostrae rectè judicantis & testificantis nobis, quod recta fecerimus DEO & hominibus probata. Quam approbationem sequitur laetitia cordis acquiescentis in hac approbatione DEI & hominum. Προσκαρτεροῦντες Erasmus reddit incumbentes. Vulgatus, servientes. Augustinus l. 4. de Doctrin. Christ. c. 29. vertit perseverantes. Propriè προσκαρτερεῖν notat continuam & diligentem curam, quae cum magna patientia, ob oneris gravitatem, conjuncta est. Atque sic describit officium maximè molestum Magistratûs, qui εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο huic ipsi operi, defensioni scilicet bonorum & coërcendis malis perpetuò intentus esse debet, & ideò magnos etiam sumptus impendere necesse habet. Sic usurpatur Marc. III. 9. Act. I. 24. de precibus, Act. II. 24. Rom. XII. 13. ut habet B. Wellerus. Argumentum ab aequitate desumtum est: Quia enim Magistratus tanta sedulitate in id intentus est, ut loco DEI praesit, subditis aequum est, ut retributionem aliquam ab iis reportet. Dignus enim operarius est mercede sua. Luc. X. v. 7. 1. Cor. IX. 7.

PARS II. Debitum erga proximum.

## 13:7
Verse 7. Render therefore to all their dues. Not only to kings, but also to governors, procurators, tax collectors, ministers of kings. τὰς ὀφειλὰς, that is, τὰ ὀφειλόμενα (the things owed), as in Matt. XVIII. 32, in the Glossary: ὀφειλὴ (debt) a debt. Τῷ τὸν φόρον, τὸν φόρον, τῷ τὸ τέλος, τὸ τέλος. Τῷ, that is, ᾧ (to whom), supply 'is owed' from the former. Just as the Poets, so also the Apostles often change articles. And so, just as here the prepositive article is used in place of the subjunctive article, so the subjunctive is used in place of the prepositive below in XN. 2. 5. Φόρος and τέλος differ just as 'tributa' (tributes) and 'vectigalia' (taxes) do for the Latins; taxes are given for merchandise; tributes for land or head. Some call φόρους 'εἰσφορὰς' (contributions), as also Justin in the words just cited. But we have said enough about these words at 1 Macc. X. 32. Josephus also distinguishes φόρους and εἰσφορὰς in the Jewish War II. 1. Φόρος corresponds to the Hebrew מס. Τῷ τὸν φόβον, τὸν φόβον, τῷ τὴν τιμὴν, τὴν τιμὴν. By the name Φόβος (fear) he understands anxious caution, lest we admit anything that might offend them: by the name of τιμῆς (honor) all signs of reverence. We do not deny that these things still concern the Magistrate in particular. Because taxes and tributes are imposed by them and are owed to them: and fear and honor are to be shown especially to them: but since the Apostle speaks generally, 'Render therefore to all their dues,' I do not see why the debts to be rendered to ALL, to whom we are obligated in civil society, should be restricted to Magistrates, or to Kings, Governors, Procurators, tax collectors, ministers of kings: nor indeed are debts owed only to them, but also to others in civil society, just as it is manifest especially concerning fear and honor, which also pertain to 'the dues,' that they are owed to any superiors whatsoever, such as also Masters, Parents, Teachers, and others who are not established in the Magistracy. Ex. XX. 12. Deut. V. 16. 1 Tim. VI. 1. 1 Pet. II. 18. Sir. III. 9. But Augustine rightly says concerning the Magistrate, book of Questions on the Old and New Testament, q. 35: The King bears the image of GOD, therefore he is to be honored and loved, if not for his own sake, at least for the sake of his vocation and function. Concerning the words Φόρ and τέλ, others say thus: Φόρ is properly tribute, which is paid from things born of the earth, from 'φέρειν' (to bear). Τέλος is a tax, which is paid for things that are transported and exchanged in contracts, from 'τελεῖν' (to complete). Jurists say that tribute is paid to the Prince or the treasury for immovable goods, law 2, Code concerning provisions and tributes; tax for movable goods, law 'universi', Code concerning taxes. Budaeus, however, teaches from Strabo that Φόρον is properly the census of property and persons, as the Syrian rendered it here, head-money: but τέλ is a tax, which is paid for imported or exported merchandise: whence 'ἀτέλεια' (immunity) from taxes. But that these words are not so exquisitely distinguished is evident even from the preceding verse: 'for this cause you pay tributes'.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἀπόδοτε οὖν πᾶσι τὰς ὀφειλὰς. Non regibus tantùm, sed & praesidibus, procuratoribus, publicanis, ministris regum. τὰς ὀφειλὰς, id est, τὰ ὀφειλόμενα, ut Matth. XVIII, 32. in Glossario: ὀφειλὴ debitum. τῷ τὸν φόρον, τὸν φόρον, τῷ τὸ τέλος, τὸ τέλος. Τῷ, id est, ᾧ, supple ὀφείλεται ex priore. Sicut Poëtae, ita & Apostoli saepè articulos commutant. Itaque sicut hic articulus praepositivus, vice articuli subjunctivi, ita subjunctivus vice praepositivi infra XN. 2. 5. Φόρος & τέλος sic differunt, quomodo Latinis tributa & Vectigalia, Vectigalia pro mercibus dantur; Tributa pro solo aut capite. Quidam φόρους vocant εἰσφορὰς, ut & Justinus verbis modò adductis. Sed satis diximus de his vocibus ad 1. Macc. X. 32. Φόρους & εἰσφορὰς distinguit & Josephus belli Judaici II. 1. Φόρος respondet Hebraeo מס. τῷ τὸν φόβον, τὸν φόβον, τῷ τὴν τιμὴν, τὴν τιμὴν. Φόβος nomine intelligit sollicitam cautionem, ne quid admittamus, quod eos possit offendere: τιμῆς nomine omnia reverentiae signa. Peculiariter ista concernere adhuc Magistratûs inficias haud imus. Quia ab illis imponuntur, illisque debentur vectigalia, & tributa: & exhibendus imprimis ipsis timor, & honor: sed quum generaliter loquatur Apostolus, ἀπόδοτε οὖν πᾶσι τὰς ὀφειλὰς, non video, cur debita CUNCTIS reddenda, quibus obligati sumus in civili societate, restringenda sint ad Magistratus, vel ad Reges, Praesides, Procuratores, publicanos, ministros regum: nec verò ὀφειλαὶ tantùm illis, sed etiam aliis in societate civili debentur, quemadmodum imprimis de timore & honore, quae etiam ad τὰς ὀφει- λας pertinent, manifestum est: quod superioribus quibusvis, utpote etiam Dominis, Parentibus, Praeceptoribus, & aliis, qui in Magistratu constituti non sunt, debeantur. Ex. XX. 12. Deut. V. 16. 1. Tim. VI. 1. 1, Pet. II. 18. Syr. III. 9. Rectè autem de Magistratu August. l. qq. V. & N. T. q. 35. Imaginem DEI Rex gestat, idcircò colendus & amandus est, si non propter se, saltim vocationis & functionis suae causa. De vocibus Φόρ & τέλ alii ita: Φόρ propriè tributum est, quod penditur de rebus terrâ nascentibus ἀπὸ τῶ φέρειν. Τέλος est vectigal, quod solvitur pro rebus, quae transvehuntur, & permutantur in contractibus ἀπὸ τῶ τελεῖν. JCti dicunt, tributum Principi vel fisco solvi pro bonis immobilibus, l. 2. C. de annon. & trib. vectigal pro bonis mobilibus, l. universi C. de vectigal. Budaeus tamen ex Strabone docet, Φόρον propriè esse censum facultatum & personarum, uti Syrus hic reddidit, argentum capitis: τέλ autem vectigal, quod pro mercibus importatis vel exportatis penditur: unde ἀτέλεια immunitas vectigalium. Non autem has voces adeò exquisitè distingui vel è vers. anteced. patet: διὰ τῦτο γὰρ ὴ Φόρες τελεῖτε.

## 13:8
V. 8. Owe no man anything, but to love one another.

By the occasion of the word 'dues' he passes from the part of the Political Law to that which instructs morals, and shows that those precepts, just as they had been before Moses, so also remain now, but with the supplements which Christ added worthy of himself. Moreover, it is cleverly said: other debts are paid, and do not remain: the debt of love is always both being paid, and remains.

It is false that this commandment was added by Christ and was not delivered in the Old Testament: because Christ inculcated it from nowhere else than from the books of the Old Testament, Matt. 22:39, Luke 10:25. Nor did the Apostle warn of any supplements added to the law by Christ; rather, he taught these things concerning love of neighbor, and that we should not sin against him by violating the wife, body, or fortunes of our neighbor, from the law and the very commandments of the Decalogue. Concerning that debt, St. Augustine, Vol. II, Epist. 62 to Coelestinus the Deacon: 'I always owe charity, which alone, even when rendered, always keeps the debtor in debt. For it is rendered when it is expended; yet it is owed even if it has been rendered, because there is no time when it should not already be expended, nor is it lost when it is rendered, but rather it is multiplied by being rendered. For it is rendered by having it, not by lacking it.' And since it cannot be rendered unless it is had, nor can it be had unless it is rendered—nay, even when it is rendered by a man, it grows in the man, and is acquired as much the greater as it is rendered to more people. Blessed Selneccerus rightly warned concerning the cause of the debt, reconciling the present and the preceding verse: 'Two sayings of Paul expressed in this place must be reconciled, namely: Render to all their dues, and owe no one anything, except to love one another. The former saying speaks of civil obligation, owed from mutual duty and other contract; the latter saying speaks of natural and divine obligation, which remains perpetually from the commandment of God, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." And this obligation provides many things, even those not owed by civil obligation: as a rich man ought to help Lazarus when he can, although the magistrate does not punish the rich man for omitting this duty; thus we all owe many duties to our neighbor, even if we are not bound to these by civil obligation. Blessed Luther expresses the matter thus, not inelegantly: 'The sense is, you Christians ought to owe, not as the heathens, out of necessity, binding by law, but as sons, freely, prompted by charity.' In which let a double debt be noted, the one of law, the other of love. By the debt of law we are bound before men, from which others have some right toward us, and which they may demand from us by law; from this debt to the magistrate we pay tax, tribute, honor, etc. The other debt is that of charity, by which Christians voluntarily make themselves servants to others, concerning which Paul says in 1 Cor. 9, 'when I was free, I made myself a servant to all,' etc. No law of men requires or vindicates this debt, etc.

ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἕτερον. That is, any man whatsoever, adorned with the image of the same GOD, sprung from the same first parents.

νόμον πεπλήρωκε. He added what is lacking to the Law of Moses, מַלֵא. For he who only executes the precepts of Moses, to him something is still lacking, Matt. 19:20.

A most perverse depravity: which is first of all new and insolent; for where in the Scriptures is 'to fulfill the law' to perform more than what the law requires? Secondly, it is false: because no one can do that: and indeed not even perform that which the law demands, let alone more, Acts 15:10, Rom. 8:4. Finally, it is an injury to the Mosaic law, as if something were lacking to it: which is indeed celebrated with the praise of perfection, because nothing can be added to it, nothing taken away, Deut. 4:2, 12:32. Nor can that turgid response of the youth educated in the School of the Pharisees, Matt. 19:20, derogate from it, which was not approved by Christ, but convicted of manifold defect and imperfection.

Latin:

V. 8. μηδενὶ μηδὲν ὀφείλετε, εἰ μὴ τὸ ἀγαπᾷν ἀλλήλες.

Occasione vocis ὀφειλὰς transit à Legis Politicae parte ad eam, quae mores instruit, ostenditque ea praecepta, sicut ante Mosen fuerant, sic & nunc manere, sed cum supplementis, quae se digna Christus adjecit. Est autem argutè dictum caetera debita solvuntur, nec manent: dilectionis debitum semper & solvitur, & manet.

Falsum est hoc praeceptum à Christo adjectum, in V. Test. traditum non esse: quia non aliunde, quàm è V. T. libris Christus id inculcavit Matth. XXII. 39. Luc. X. 25. Nec de ullis supplementis à Christo legi additis quicquam monuit Apostolus, imò haec de Amore proximi, & ne adversus illum, violando uxorem, corpus, vel fortunas proximi peccemus, lege ipsísque praeceptis Decalogi docuit. De illo debito S. Augustin. T. II. Epist. LXII. ad Coelestin. Diacon. Semper debeo charitatem, quae sola etiam reddita semper detinet debitorem. Redditur enim cum impenditur: debetur autem, etiamsi reddita fuerit, quia nullum est tempus, quando impendenda jam non sit, nec cum redditur, amittitur, sed potiùs reddendo multiplicatur. Habendo enim redditur, non carendo. Et cum reddi non possit, nisi habeatur, nec haberi potest, nisi reddatur, imò etiam cum redditur, ab homine, crescit in homine, & tantò major acquiritur, quantò pluribus redditur. Rectè autem de causa debiti monuit B. Selneccerus, concilians praesentem & antecedentem versum: Concilianda sunt duo dicta Pauli hoc loco expressa, videlicet: Reddite omnibus debita, & nemini quicquam debeatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis. Prius dictum loquitur de obligatione civili, debitâ ex officio mutuo, & alio contractu: Posterius dictum loquitur de obligatione naturali, & divinâ, quae perpetuo manet ex praecepto DEI, diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum. Et haec obligatio praestat multa, etiam non debita obligatione civili: ut dives debet Lazaro opitulari cum possit, quamvis Magistratus non punit divitem omittentem hoc officium: sic nos omnes debemus proximo nostro multa officia, etiamsi ad haec obligatione civili non simus obstricti. B. Lutherus rem ita exprimit, non inconcinnè: Sensus est, debere debetis vos Christiani, non ut Ethnici, ex necessitate, obstringente lege, sed ut filii, liberè monente charitate. In quo notetur duplex debitum, alterum legis, alterum dilectionis. Legis debito coram hominibus obligamur, ex quo alii juris aliquid erga nos habeant, & quod jure à nobis postulent: ex hoc debito Ma- stratui persolvimus vectigal, tributum, honorem &c. Alterum debitum charitatis est, quo se Christiani ultrò servos alii addicunt, de quo Paulus 1. Cor. IX. cum essem liber, omnium feci me servum &c. Hoc debitum nulla lex hominum requirit, aut vin- dicat &c.

ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἕτερον. Id est, hominem quemvis, ejusdem DEI imagine orna- tum, iisdem ortum primis parentibus.

νόμον πεπλήρωκε. Is adjecit, quod Legi Mosis deest, מַלֵא. Nam qui Mosis tantùm præcepta exequitur, ei adhuc aliquid deest, Matth. XIX. 20.

Perversissima depravatio : quæ primùm nova & insolens; nam ubi in Scripturis legem implere est plus præstare, quàm quod lex requirit; Deinde falsa: quia nemo id potest: ac ne præstare qui- dem id, quod lex postulat, nedum ampliùs Actor. XV.10. Rom.VIII.4. Denique injuria est in legem Mosaicam, quasi ei aliquid desit: quæ verò perfe- ctionis laude celebratur, quia nihil ei addi, nihil detrahi potest, Deut. IV. 2. XII.32. neque ei de- rogare poterit turgida illa juvenis in Schola Pha- risæorum informati responsio, Matth. XIX. 20. à Christo non probata, sed defectus & imperfectio- nis multiplicis convicta.

## 13:9
V. 9. τὸ γὰρ, ὐ μοιχεύσεις, ὐ φονεύσεις. He recites the precepts in the order in which the LXX read them in their Hebrew text in Exodus, as we have shown in our more extensive exposition of the Decalogue.

ὐκ κλέψεις, ὐ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις, ὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις: ὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις here means, you shall not act so as to attract to yourself the property of others under some favorable pretext. You shall do nothing in fraud of the law. See above, ch. 7, and what is said there.

κᾀι εἴτις ἑτέρα ἐντολὴ. Namely, of the same nature, demanding that which we owe to one another, for instance, to honor parents: and others, which are in the law, but outside the Decalogue.

ἐν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται. It is comprehended in summary. בִּכְלִילָה. Thus Aquila at the beginning of Genesis translates בְּרֵאשִׁית as κεφαλαίῳ, that is, together, as Philoponus explains on Genesis. Thus the Hebrews say: נפש וגומר כל-התורה כלילה באהבת יהוח בכל לב ובכל. The whole law is ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται in this: Love God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your substance. And this precept of loving GOD, and the other of loving one's neighbor, are called by the Hebrews, as others have noted, כְּלָלִים גְּדוֹלִים, that is, great summaries. Greek authors call it ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, which the Latins call the confection of a cause. Augustine: in which the cause is repeated in summary, which they call ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ, that is, in this precept, for thus the Hebrews excellently use the word דָבָר.

ἐν τῷ ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σοῦ ὡς ἑαυτὸν. In this precept, not of the law, but of Christ, Matt. 19:19. The Law indeed commands that the neighbor be loved, Lev. 19:18, but by the name of neighbor the Law understood him who was subject to the same law, as we have shown on Matt. 5:43. Nor did that formula comprehend those by whom someone had been gravely injured, which the Evangelical one does, Matt. 5:44. Neighbor before the law is any man whatsoever, Gen. 11:3. So also in the Gospel, which was given not to every people but to all, Luke 10:33. Therefore those precepts of the law are comprehended in that precept of Christ, as a part in a whole, which also has many other parts.

But how is this precept not of the law, but of Christ, when the youth, educated in the School of Moses, not of Christ, professes that he has fulfilled it? Matt. 19:20. Therefore it could not have been unknown to him. And why could he not have had it from the law, in which it is most expressly handed down in Lev. 19:18? But the false interpretation is to be detested, which understands by the name of neighbor in the law not just anyone, but only the Jew who was subject to the same law, and does not comprehend him by whom one has been gravely injured. Which Pharisaic corruption Christ himself refuted, as was shown in Matt. 5: and the enumerated precepts of the Decalogue, which the Apostle teaches are recapitulated in this summary, evidently refute it. Whoever, says St. Augustine, l. 1. de Doctr. Christian. c. 30. thinks that the Apostle did not give the precept concerning every man, is forced to confess, which is most absurd and wicked, that it seemed to the Apostle that it is not a sin if someone commits adultery with the wife of a non-Christian or an enemy, or kills her, or covets her property. But if he is bound to say this, it is manifest that every man is to be considered a neighbor, because evil is to be done to no one. Cf. Exod. 26:4, Lev. 19:17, 18, Prov. 25:21, 22, Luke 10:3. And how is it that in these precepts it is ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται, recapitulated and comprehended in summary, whatever precepts there are of the second table, when it is handed down by the Apostle, but not when it is handed down in the law, which nevertheless was also repeated and approved by Christ as the summary of the law of the second table, Matt. 22:39, 40. It is also inept, what Grotius quibbles: that those precepts of the law are comprehended in that precept of Christ, which he had taught, as a part in a whole, which also has many other parts: for neither can other parts be given, especially because of the added clause, καὶ εἴτις ἑτέρα ἐντολή: for whatever other one is brought forward, it is already comprehended by that clause, and how could it be called a summary complex, which in many ways exceeds those things which it reduces into a summary? That locution is either taken from the conclusions of rhetoricians, which certainly do not contain more than the speech itself, but only exhibit the summary of the speech, or from arithmetic calculations, where we embrace the sum of numbers, which, if it be just, cannot exceed the smaller or partial numbers.

Latin:

V. 9. τὸ γὰρ, ὐ μοιχεύσεις, ὐ φονεύσεις. Recitat præcepta eo ordine, quo LXX. in suo Hebræo textu ea legerunt in Exodo, ut ostendimus in fusiore nostra ad Decalogum expositione.

ὐκ κλέψεις, ὐ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις, ὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις: ὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις hic valet, non ages ut aliena prætextu quodam favorabili ad te attrahas. Nihil facies in fraudem legis. Vide supra VII. & ibi dicta.

κᾀι εἴτις ἑτέρα ἐντολὴ. Nempè ejusdem naturæ, id exigens quod alter debe- mus alteri, puta honorare parentes: & alia, quæ sunt in le- ge, sed extra Decalogum.

ἐν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται. Summatim comprehenditur. בִּכְלִילָה. Sic Aquila in principio Geneseos בְּרֵאשִׁית vertit κεφαλαίῳ, id est, simul, ut exponit ad Genesin Philoponus Sic dicunt Hebræi: נפש וגומר כל-התורה כלילה באהבת יהוח בכל לב ובכל Lex tota in hoc ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται: Dilige Deum toto corde & tota anima atque substantia. Et hoc præ- ceptum DEI amandi, & alterum amandi proximi, dicuntur Hebræis, ut alii notarunt, כְּלָלִים גְּדוֹלִים, id est, sum- mæ magnæ. Græci auctores ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν vocant, quod Latini causæ confectionem. Augustinus: in quibus causa summatim repetitur, quam vocant ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ, id est, in hoc præcepto, nam sic Hebræi דָבָר exi- miè usurpant.

ἐν τῷ ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σοῦ ὡς ἑαυτὸν. In hoc præcepto non legis, sed Christi, Matth. XIX. 19. Jubet quidem & Lex diligi proximum, Levit. XIX. 18. sed proximi nomine Lex intelligebat eum, qui eidem legi sub- jectus esset, ut ostendimus ad Matth.V. 43. Neque verò ea formula comprehendebat eos, à quibus læsus graviter esset aliquis, quod facit Evangelica, Matth. V. 44. Proximus an- te legem homo quivis. Genes. XI. 3. Sic & in Evangelio, quod non omni populo sed omnibus datum est, Luc. X. 33. Comprehenduntur igitur illa legis præcepta in isto Chri- sti præcepto, ut pars in toto, multas etiam alias partes habente.

Quî verò hoc præceptum non legis est, sed Christi; quum juvenis in Schola Mosis, non Chri- sti informatus profiteatur id se implevisse? Matth. XIX. 20. ideò non potuit ei ignotum esse. Et quidni ex lege id habere potuerit, in qua expres- sissimè id traditum Lev. XIX. 18. Ψευδερμηνεία au- tem detestanda est, legem proximi nomine non quemlibet, sed Judæum solùm, qui eidem legi sub- jectus erat, intelligere, nec eum comprehendere, à quo graviter quis læsus. Quam corruptelam Pharisaicam Christus ipse retudit, ut Matth. V. ostensum: & evidenter refellunt enumerata De- calogi præcepta, quæ in hac summa recapitulari docet Apostolus. Quisquis, inquit S. August. l. 1. de Doctr. Christian. c. 30. arbitratur non de omni homine Apostolum præcepisse, cogitur fateri, quòd absurdissimum & sceleratissimum est, visum fuisse Apostolo, non esse peccatum, si quis aut non Christia- ni aut inimici adulteraverit uxorem, aut eam occi- derit, aut ejus rem cupierit. Quod si devinctus est dicere, manifestum est omnem hominem proximum esse deputandum, quia erga neminem operandum est malum. Conf. Exod. XXVI. 4. Levit. XIX. 17. 18. Prov. XXV. 21. 22. Luc. X. 3. Et quomodo in istis præceptis ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται recapitulatur, & sum- matim comprehenditur, quicquid præceptorum est tabulæ secundæ, cum ab Apostolo id traditur, non autem cum in lege id traditum est, quod tamen à Christo etiam repetitum, & approbatum, ceu summarium legis tabulæ secundæ, Matth. XXII. 39. 40. Ineptum etiam est, quod Grotius tricatur: illa legis præcepta in isto Christi, quod docuerat, præ- cepto comprehendi, ut partem in toto, multas et- iam alias partes habente: nam neque partes aliæ dari possunt, imprimis ob clausulam additam, καὶ εἴτις ἑτέρα ἐντολή: nam quæcunque adferatur alia, illâ clausulâ jam comprehensa est, & quomodo summaria diceretur complexio, quæ multis mo- dis illa, quæ in summam redigit, excedit? Loquu- tio illa vel è Rhetorum conclusionibus desumta, quæ utique non plus continent, quam ipsa oratio, sed summam tantùm Orationis exhibent, vel ab A- rithmeticis computationibus, ubi summam nume- rorum amplectimur, quæ excedere non potest, si justa sit, numeros minores vel partiales.

## 13:10
V. 10. Love works no evil to his neighbor. I think the reading of certain codices, which the ancient Greek interpreters follow, is more true, τῷ πλησίον, love, that is, he who loves another, does nothing evil to another. If nothing evil, therefore he will neither violate his marriage, nor his life, nor will he steal his property.

Love is the fulfillment of the law. For it contains more than the law. It is a dragnet for every injury.

The former false interpretation recurs; love is not said to contain more than the law requires, for how could it contain more? but to perform or fulfill the law. For this is what it is to be the fulfillment of the law: that he who loves his neighbor performs or fulfills the law, as far as the second table is concerned, as Schlichting also explains in his commentary, p. 304. To fulfill the law is to execute the law with deeds and works: and fulfillment, πλήρωμα, that is, execution: not that there is anyone who fulfills the law even as regards the second table only, since not even a single precept of the law can be performed or perfectly fulfilled by us, much less all of them, whence it is to be granted neither by reason of the perfection of the parts of the law, nor by reason of degrees; but because those things are said hypothetically, and are to be understood as regards the perfection of the law, which is to be sought by us and pursued by all means, but cannot be obtained in this imperfection; therefore rightly B. Mylius p. 389. The words of the Apostle indeed hold thus: Whoever loves his neighbor, has fulfilled the law; but he understands love, such as the law requires; but whether there is or has been anyone who has fulfilled it, or indeed whether it is even possible for such a one to exist in this world, he does not say. Therefore, it is not shown what is done, or can be done, in the actions of men, but the idea of the commandment is proposed by the Apostle, which will be fulfilled only in the other life; but now it is inculcated for this reason, that we may be admonished as to what we ought to seek by faith, and where we ought to send our hope ahead. To which Augustine adds, as it seems to me, in that justice which is to be perfected, he has progressed much in this life who, by progressing, has known how far he is from the perfection of justice. It is said of no one, except of Christ alone, that he fulfilled the law. Those who are said to have served the Lord with their whole heart, 1 Kings 15:5, 2 Kings 23:25, nevertheless did not fulfill the law; because because that service is not understood according to the rigor of the law, but according to the sincerity of the heart, which not hypocritically, or with a divided heart, but with a sincere one, and in such a way that they have consecrated their whole heart to GOD, as far as the readiness of the Spirit is concerned, even if as far as the infirmity of the flesh is concerned, they were not always able to carry out what they intended and strove for.

PART III. The duty of every Christian, as to how he ought to govern himself piously in the light of the Gospel.

Latin:

V. 10. ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν 8 κατεργάζεται. Puto veriorem esse lectionem quorundam codicum, quam sequuntur veteres Interpp. Græci, τῷ πλησίον, dile- ctio, id est, qui alterum diligit, alteri nihil facit mali. Si nihil mali, ergò nec matrimonium ejus, nec vitam violabit, nec res surripiet.

πλήρωμα ἓν νόμυ ἡ ἀγάπη. Plus enim continet, quàm lex. Est everriculum omnis injuriæ.

Recurrit prior ψευδερμηνεία; Non plus conti- nere dicitur dilectio, quàm lex requirit, quomo- do enim plus contineret? sed præstare vel imple- re legem. Hoc enim est esse πλήρωμα νόμου: ut, qui proximum diligit, legem, quantum ad tabu- lam secundam, præstet vel impleat, ut explicat et- iam Schlichting. in comment. p. 304. implere le- gem est legem factis & operibus exequi: & imple- tio, πλήρωμα, id est, exequutio: non quod detur, qui legem vel quoad secundam tantùm tabulam impleat, quùm ne unicum quidem legis præce- ptum præstari vel perfectè impleri à nobis possit, nedum omnia, unde id neque ratione perfectio- nis partium legis, neque ratione graduum conce- dendum est; sed quod hypotheticè illa dicta, & quoad perfectionem legis intelligenda, quæ à no- bis expetenda modisque omnibus ambienda est, sed obtineri in hac imperfectione non potest; Ideò rectè B. Mylius p. 389. Sic quidem habent verba Apostoli: Quisquis diligit proximum, legem implevit; sed dilectionem intelligit, qualem lex re- quirit; An autem sit vel fuerit, qui eam impleve- rit, imò an etiam esse in hoc mundo possit, non dicit. Non ergò quid in actionibus hominum fiat, aut fieri possit, ostenditur, sed idea mandati ab Apostolo pro- ponitur, quod in altera demum vita implebitur; nunc autem ideò inculcatur, ut quid fide exposcere, quo spem præmittere debeamus, admoneamur. Cut Augustinus id subjungit, quantum mihi videtur, in ea, quæ perficienda est justitia, multum in hac vita ille profecit, qui quàm longè sit à perfectione justitiæ, proficiendo cognovit. De nemine, nisi de uno Christo dicitur, quod impleverit legem. Qui Domino serviisse dicuntur toto corde, 1. Reg. XV. 5. 2. Reg. XXIII. 25. non tamen legem impleverunt; quia quia non illa servitus intelligitur, secundum rigo- rem legis, sed secundum sinceritatem cordis, quod non hypocriticè, aut corde dimidiato, sed sincero, & ita, ut totum cor DEO consecrarint, quoad prom- titudinem Spiritûs, etsi quantum ad carnis infir- mitatem, non id exequi semper valuêre, quod in- tenderunt, & fategerunt.

PARS III. Debitum cujusvis Christiani, quà semetipsum in luce Evangelii piè gubernandum.

## 13:11
V. 11. καὶ τῦτο.

This καὶ τῦτο has special force, and refers to that which had long preceded, that we are always debtors of love.

Others refer it to all the preceding admonitions, with whom Crellius and Schlichting also agree. Others prefer to render καὶ τῦτο as ALSO, This, or even now, and besides. We prefer to refer it to all the preceding exhortations, i.e., And this, which we have said, you will observe all the more, because you know, etc. For there are contained here such special precepts, as those which the reborn ought to observe regarding governing themselves piously in sobriety, chastity, moderation of anger, and care of the body, that at the same time, by that comparison and reason which the Apostle applied to this exhortation (from the day of the light of the Gospel), he has elegantly and summarily embraced all parts of Christianity, as if for the sake of an epilogue and recapitulation: so that finally, comprehending everything in a few words with this sweet picture of the present state, he might leave stings in the minds of the faithful, to perform their duties with alacrity. Therefore he warns not only in general about the WORKS of darkness, and about all the armor of light, and about honest walking, which extend much more broadly than those things which he had specifically designated as pertaining to honest conversation: But he also commands that we put on the Lord Christ Jesus; which is done through faith, and that we not be devoted to or intent upon the lusts of the flesh, by which name those things come.

εἰδότες τὸν καιρὸν.

Considering what the time is now.

ὅτι ὥρα ἡμᾶς ἤδη ἐξ ὕπνε ἐγερθῆναι.

He takes the comparison from military matters, as he often does, as in 2 Cor. X. 4, 1 Tim. I. 18, 2 Tim. II. 3, Eph. VI. 17, 1 Thess. V. 8. Cicero in his defense of L. Murena regarding a leader: the sound of the trumpets rouses him. Horace.

Nor is the soldier roused by the harsh trumpet.

The blessed Hieron. Weller explained the emphasis of the word in this place. There is emphasis in the word to awake. For the Apostle signifies that those who embrace the doctrine of the Gospel are called to huge and manifold struggles and dangers. Because all who burn with true love and zeal for learning, professing, and propagating the doctrine of the Gospel, these are attacked from without by the world, that is, by tyrants, who rage against the fortunes and bodies of the pious. But within, they are tormented by the fiery darts of the Devil, that is, by internal fears. Both enemies, namely the world and the Devil, strive equally, and do so with the greatest zeal, so that they may either deter us from the doctrine of the Gospel by the fear of punishments, or, having ensnared us with the allurements of pleasures, call us away from it and drag us into destruction. Therefore, ἐγερθῆναι, that is, to rise, signifies vigilance, diligence, assiduity, and the most keen zeal for doing good. Finally, to be keen, alert, attentive, and diligent in the word, faith, invocation, and all exercises of faith, and to keep watch against the snares of the Devil. He exhorts, therefore, as the blessed Jacob Weller notes on page 698, that after the light of the Gospel has arisen and been scattered throughout the whole world, they should recognize that opportunity of the present time: that they should not sleep through the perpetual lethargy of ignorance and carnal security, but should embrace the true doctrine with serious study, cast off their former conversation, and walk in newness of life: and that they should know that they will lose the true religion and neglect the time of grace by an easy occasion and in a moment, unless they watch diligently. Compare 2 Cor. VI. 2. Gal. VI. 10. Is. LV. 6.

now our salvation is nearer.

He speaks as if of those besieged, who must escape with great courage through the midst of the enemy.

than when we believed.

That is, than when we began to believe. For such words sometimes signify the beginning, sometimes the progress, sometimes the end. Thus Exod. IV. 20, in Hebrew and Latin: from the time that you have spoken to your servant: in Greek: ἀφ' ἧς ἤρξω λαλεῖν τῷ θεράποντί σου. Thus Nehem. VIII. 3, אוֹר is said for the beginning of light, as Kimchi explains on that word.

The blessed Glassius agrees: 'to believe' is most simply explained as 'to begin to believe,' or to approach the Christian faith for the first time, and to be established as it were in the dawn of faith. Heinsius, Sacred Exercises on this passage: πιστεύειν is here clearly used in an incomplete sense, so that it means 'when you first began to believe.' And compare the word מָלַךְ, βασιλεύειν, which is frequently said of him who first begins to reign: ἐβασίλευσεν Ωσηε, ἐβασίλευσεν Ἀχαζ, etc. For examples of that canon, that completive verbs are to be understood inchoatively, see the Sacred Grammar, p. 220. Now our salvation is nearer, (these are the words of the most learned Flacius in the Key to Scripture, part 1, col. 974) than when we believed; that is, by degrees the doctrine is more illustrated, religion is more widely scattered, the experience of the divine presence and of spiritual things is increased for us, and finally other gifts also grow and increase; and therefore, although salvation was certain for us even at the beginning when we believed, yet now everything is as it were clearer and more certain to us. Some, not inappropriately, apply here the metaphor from those who run in a stadium, who the further they progress, the closer they approach the goal. For thus the beginning of our conversion is like the entry into the starting blocks of the stadium, the continuation and increase of faith is like the running in the stadium, and finally, heavenly glory itself is like the goal.

Latin:

V. 11. καὶ τῦτο.

Hoc καὶ τῦτο valet præsertim, & refertur ad id, quod lon- gè præcesserat, dilectionis nos semper esse debitores.

Alii ad omnia monita antecedentia referunt, cum quibus etiam facit Crellius, & Schlichting. Alii καὶ τῦτο malunt reddere ETIAM, Hoc, vel adhuc, & præterea. Nos referre malumus ad omnes ante- cedentes paræneses, q. d. Et hoc, quod diximus, tantò magis observabitis, quod sciatis &c. Habentur enim hic ita specialia præcepta, quà ea, quæ renati quoad seipsos piè gubernandos in sobrietate, castitate, iræ moderamine, corporis προνοίᾳ observare de- bent, ut simul illâ similitudine & ratione, quam ad hanc parænesin adhibuit Apostolus, (à die lucis Evangelicæ) universas Christianismi partes ele- ganter & summariter complexus sit, veluti epilogi & ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως gratiâ: ut postremo paucis omnia comprehendens suavi istâ statûs præsentis picturâ, aculeos in animis fidelium relinquat, ad alacriter exequendum debita officia. Ideò non tantùm in genere de OPERIBUS tenebrarum mo- net, deque armis lucis universis, de honesta ambu- latione, quæ latiùs omninò patent, quàm illa, quæ peculiariter designârat, ceu pertinentia ad hone- stam conversationem: Sed jubet etiam induamus Dominum Christum Jesum; quod per fidem fit, & ne carnis concupiscentiis, quo nomine illæ veniant, dediti aut intenti simus.

εἰδότες τὸν καιρὸν.

Considerantes, quale jam sit tempus.

ὅτι ὥρα ἡμᾶς ἤδη ἐξ ὕπνε ἐγερθῆναι.

Similitudinem sumit à re bellica, ut sæpè ut 2. Cor. X. 4. 1. Tim. I. 18. 2. Tim. II. 3. Eph. VI. 17. 1. Thess. V. 8. Ci- cero pro L. Muræna de duce: illum buccinarum cantus ex- suscitat. Horatius.

Nec excitatur classico miles truci.

Emphasin vocis exposuit B. Hieron. Wellerus in h. l. Est emphasis in vocabulo expergisci. Significat enim Apostolus, eos, qui doctrinam Evangelii am- plectuntur, vocari ad ingentia & multiplicia certa- mina atque pericula. Quia omnes, qui ardent ve- ro amore & studio discendi, profitendi, & propagan- di doctrinam Evangelii, hi foris à mundo, id est, tyrannis oppugnantur, qui in fortunas & corpora piorum grassantur. Intus verò ignitis telis Diaboli, hoc est, internis pavoribus excruciantur. Ambo hostes, scil. mundus & Diabolus, pariter conantur, & summo studio id agunt, ut nos aut metu suppli- ciorum à doctrina Evangelii deterreant, aut illece- bris voluptatum inescatos nos inde avocent, atque in exitium inde pertrahant. Significat igitur ἐγερθῆ- ναι, id est, surgere, vigilantiam, diligentiam, assi- duitatem, & acerrimum studium benè operandi. Denique in verbo, fide, invocatione, & omnibus exer- citiis fidei acres, exporrectos, attentos & assiduos esse, & excubias agere, contra insidias Diaboli. Hor- tatur itaque, notante B. Jacobo Wellero pag. 698. ut postquam lux Evangelii exorta, & per totum terrarum orbem sparsa sit, opportunitatem istam præsentis temporis cognoscant: non dormitent per- petuum ignorantiæ & securitatis carnalis veter- num, sed serio studio amplectantur doctrinam ve- ram, abjiciant pristinam conversationem, & in vitæ novitate ambulent: & sciant, se facili occasione & momento veram religionem amissuros, & tempus gratiæ neglecturos esse, nisi assiduè advigilaverint. Confer 2. Cor. VI. 2. Gal. VI. 10. Es. LV. 6.

νῦν ἐγγύτερον ἡμῶν ἡ σωτηρία.

Loquitur tanquam de obsessis, qui magno animo per medios hostes debent evadere.

ἢ ὅτε ἐπιστεύσαμεν.

Id est, quam cùm credere cœpimus. Verba enim talia interdum initium, interdum progressum, interdum exitum significant. Sic Exod. IV. 20. in Hebræo & Latino: ex quo locutus es ad servum tuum: in Græco: ἀφ' ἧς ἤρξω λαλεῖν τῷ θεράποντί σου. Sic Nehem. VIII. 3. אוֹר dicitur pro initio lucis, ut explicat Kimchi in ea voce.

Consonant B. Glassius: Simplicissimè exponitur credere, pro incipere credere, seu ad fidem Chri- stianam primum accedere, & in fidei quasi diluculo constitutum esse. Heins. exercit. sacr. in h. l. πιστεύ- ειν hîc manifestè ἀτελῶς ponitur, ut sit, cum pri- mùm credere cœpistis. Conferque τὸ מָלַךְ βα- σιλεύειν, quod crebrò dicitur de eo, qui regnare pri- mum incipit: ἐβασίλευσενος Ωσηε, ἐβασίλευσεν Ἀ- χαζ &c. Canonis illius, quod verba completiva sint inchoativè intelligenda, exempla videantur in Gram- matica sacrâ p. 220. Nunc propior est nobis salus, (verba sunt doctissimi Flacii in clave Script. part. 1. col. 974.) quàm cùm credidimus; id est, sub- inde magis tùm doctrina illustratur, tùm religio latius spargitur, tùm experientia præsentiæ divi- næ ac rerum spiritualium nobis augetur, tùm de- nique etiam alia dona crescunt & augentur, eoq; quamvis & initio cùm credidimus, certa nobis fuit salus, tamen nunc omnia nobis veluti clariora ac certiora sunt. Quidam non inconcinnè huc ap- plicant metaphoram ab iis, qui in stadio currunt, qui quò longiùs progrediuntur, eò propiùs acce- dunt ad metam. Sic enim initium conversionis no- stræ simile est ingressui in carceres stadii, continua- tio & incrementum fidei est simile cursui in stadio, denique ipsa cœlestis gloria est similis metæ.

## 13:12
V. 12. the night is far spent.

A great ignorance of good things. Προέκοψεν, has finished its course: עָבַר as here the Syriac. It has passed. Cyprian.

and the day is at hand.

The day has reached us: the Evangelical light has shone forth. Thus Lam. IV, what had been said before as קָרַב ἤγγικε, is explained by בָּא ἦλθε. Similar sense in 1 Thess. V. 4, 5, 6.

Others prefer that a comparison be instituted between this life and the future life. Some between the time of the Old and New Testament. But it is said more correctly to compare the time before conversion with the time of conversion. Compare Eph. IV. 18, V. 8, 11, 13, 14, 1 Thess. V. 5 seqq., Tit. II. 11, 12, Is. LX. 1, 2.

Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness

What these are, he explains in the following clause.

and let us put on the armor of light.

That is, bright: shining armor becomes soldiers, as that one in Plautus: Take care that the splendor of my shield be brighter than the rays of the sun are wont to be, when the sky is clear. But what the weapons of the Christian militia are, he explains in Eph. VI. 13. and following.

The works of darkness are called any crimes whatsoever, fighting against the law of GOD, because they are done by the author of darkness, Col. I. 13: they proceed from the primeval and original darkness of the ignorance of the mind and the depravity of the will, Eph. IV. 18: they are performed in darkness, Joh. III. 20: and they cast one into outer darkness, Matth. XXII. 13. Which, before conversion, were securely designated in 1. Cor. VI. 9. 1. Pet. IV. 3. are now commanded to be laid aside no differently than clothes are taken off and laid aside, Eph. IV. 22. On the contrary, however, the armor of light must be put on: he does not say garments, but armor: because not so much that we may be clothed, as that we may be fitted for spiritual battle against the devil, the world and the flesh, it is necessary, 2 Cor. 10:4. There are, however, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which He Himself instructs us for this warfare, Eph. 6, which are therefore called weapons of light, because they descend from the Father of lights, Jas. 1:17, are performed by a man illuminated by the Holy Spirit, are tested by the light of the divine word, and shine and gleam before God and men, Eph. 5, Matt. 5, and serve to overthrow the spirit of darkness, and are fitting for the children of light and candidates for eternal glory, Phil. 2, finally because the prize of the warfare of the weapons of light is laid up in the heavenly and eternal light, 2 Tim. 4:6.

Latin:

V. 12. ἡ νὺξ προέκοψεν.

Magna rerum bonarum ignorantia. Προέκοψεν, cursum suum peregit: עָבַר ut hîc Syrus. Transivit. Cyprianus.

ἡ δὲ ἡμέρα ἤγγικεν.

Pervenit ad nos dies: affulsit lux Evangelica. Sic Lam. IV. quod prius dictum fuerat קָרַב ἤγγικε, exponitur per בָּא ἦλθε. Par sensus 1. Thess. V. 4. 5. 6.

Alii comparationem institui malunt inter hanc & futuram vitam. Nonnulli inter Vet. & Novi Test. tempus. Sed rectiùs conferri dicitur tempus ante conversionem cum conversionis tempore. Conf. Ephes. IV. 18. V. 8. 11. 13. 14. 1. Thess. V. 5. seqq. Tit. II. 11. 12. Es. LX. 1. 2.

Ἀποθώμεθα ὖν τὰ ἔργα τῶ σκότους

Quæ qualia sint, explicat cominate sequenti.

καὶ ἐνδυσώμεθα τὰ ὅπλα τῶ φωτός.

Id est, φωτεινά: arma fulgentia decent milites, ut ille apud Plautum: Curate, ut splendor meo sit clypeo clarior; quam solis radii esse olim, cum sudum est, solent. Quæ verò sint Christianæ militiæ arma, explicat Ephes. VI. 13. & se- quentibus.

Opera tenebrarum dicuntur scelera quævis, cum lege DEI pugnantia, quia autore Principe tene- brarum Col. I. 13. fiunt: à tenebris primævis & originalibus ignorantiæ mentis, & pravitatis vo- luntatis proficiscuntur, Eph. IV. 18. in tenebris per- aguntur, Joh. III. 20. & in tenebras exteriores præ- cipitant, Matth. XXII. 13. Quæ ante conversionem securè designata 1. Cor. VI. 9. 1. Pet. IV. 3. jam deponi jubentur non secus atque vestes exuuntur, & deponuntur, Eph. IV. 22. Ex adverso verò in- duenda sunt arma lucis: non dicit vestimenta, sed arma: quia non tam ut vestiamur, quàm ut ad pugnam spiritualem aptemur contra diabolum, mundum & carnem, opus est, 2. Cor. X. 4. Sunt autem χαρίσματα Spiritûs Sancti, quibus ipse nos instituit ad hanc militiam, Eph. VI. quæ ideò ar- ma lucis dicuntur, quia à Patre luminum descen- dunt, Jac. I. 17. ab homine illuminato à Sp. S. per- aguntur, ad lucem verbi divini exiguntur, & lu- cent, ac fulgent coram DEO & hominibus, Eph. V. Matth. V. & Spiritui tenebrarum profligando inserviunt, filiis lucis & candidatis æternæ gloriæ conveniunt, Phil. II. denique quia in luce cœlesti & æternâ militiæ armorum lucis brabæon repo- situm est, 2. Tim. IV. 6.

## 13:13
V. 13. as in the day, let us walk honestly. Those who proceed by day go with a composed step. Ovid: Night and love and wine suggest nothing moderate. Tacitus, Histories 4: night had removed all shame. Thus it befits us, who are possessors of such great light, to do all things as honestly as possible.

Luther: By day no one does what he is accustomed to do in the dark; everyone respects another and prepares himself so that he may live honestly. It is commonly said: Night is free from shame; that is true, which is why men do things at night for which they would be ashamed by day; but the day possesses shame and demands honest conversation. The Christian life ought to be in the same state, namely, that you admit nothing of which you could be ashamed, even if the whole world were to see all your affairs. For he who lives and works in such a way that he finds it difficult for all his affairs to be seen and heard by everyone, and for his whole life to be known openly to all, he lives a life entirely unworthy of Christ.

not in revelries) revelries are nocturnal amours, whence to revel. See the Idyll of Theocritus on the reveller, and Wis. 14:23, 2 Macc. 6:4.

and in drunkenness) For it is also customary to drink by night: 1 Thess. 5:7.

and in chambering) chambering is the congress of a man with a woman, as we said above 9:10. He said chamberings in the plural, however, to express promiscuous cohabitation, concerning which, what and how many evils follow, Chrysostom eloquently discourses here in his own manner.

and in wantonness) Wantonness is a Greek word extending quite broadly and comprehending all things that are done lasciviously and lustfully, but here I should think those things are understood which are done against the laws of the sexes. For Aeschines also uses it in this sense against Timocrates. In the Glossary, wantonness is unchastity. Seneca concerning such: for the hiding of which no night is dark enough, book 1 of Nature, ch. 16.

These are not all the works of darkness which the Apostle commands to be put off in this place, as it seemed to Dr. Majus: but because he still adheres to the simile of those waking from sleep, those things are particularly mentioned which leisure and security, or torpor and sleep, are accustomed to draw with them; such as banquetings and drunkenness, chamberings and lasciviousness, which fight against the sixth commandment: and those things which are connected to them, contention and fervor, which are opposed to the fifth commandment. Just as, on the contrary, by the weapons of light, not so much the contrary virtues, such as temperance, sobriety, chastity, modesty, the pursuit of concord, and long-suffering, are designated, as those which are set forth in the armory of the Holy Spirit for the sacred panoply, Eph. 6:11 ff., such as truth, justice, the Gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of hope, the sword of the divine word, the darts of prayers: to which spiritual weapons those things which the Apostle requires here concerning an honest walk are rather to be considered as aids, and things added, or requisites necessary for that purpose, so that those weapons may be rightly handled and we may fight bravely with them, rather than to be confused with the armor itself: just as temperance, chastity, and the flight from anger and undue emulation indeed pertain to the requisites of a good soldier, but are not his weapons themselves. In which manner to the Apostle 1. Thess. 5:6, 8, it pleased him to distinguish vigilance and sobriety from the weapons themselves which are to be put on, of faith, love, and hope. There is an ellipsis here of the preposition in, to be repeated from the preceding, in revelries. A revel, however, as Erasmus notes, is to the Greeks the god of drunkenness (whom indeed, because of the homophony, they wish to be Chemosh, that idol of the Moabites, of which mention is made in Num. 21:29, 1 Kings 11:33, Jer. 48:46, as Drusius notes in his Animadversions, book 1, ch. 56). And by the same name a more forward and youthful banquet is called. Indeed, lascivious songs and dances are also called revels by the Greeks: whence comedy is also named. Aretius on this passage: a revel is a scurrilous banquet, in which witticisms and freer taunts reign. The Syrian has for revelries in music, understanding by synecdoche those lavish banquets, concerning which Job 21:12, Isa. 5:11, 12. Amos 6:5, 6, which, besides exquisite foods, also have joined to them profane, filthy, and dishonest music, as the blessed Glassius observes, p. 107.

There is no reason, however, why we should so restrict those words chamberings and wantonness; since sins of every kind against the sixth commandment are comprehended by them, (chamberings, according to Hesychius, are called desires of women and those who lie in wait,) and wantonness is spoken of more generally in Scripture, Mark 7:22, Gal. 5:19, Eph. 4:19, 1 Pet. 4:3, 2 Pet. 2:18, Jude v. 4, Wis. 14:25. The interpreter of Demosthenes in the Oration against Meidias has it thus: We say that he is called wanton who partakes of neither justice nor virtue. Yet wantonness is spoken of particularly concerning lasciviousness. Philo, book 1 of the Life of Moses, through the obscene lust and forward petulance of women. Lucian, more wanton than donkeys, since this animal is most lustful. Budaeus says that wantonness is used for obscenity and the shameful habit of debauchery. They derive the word from Selge, a town founded by the Lacedaemonians, in which some place temperate and frugal men, with Strabo book XII and Suidas in the entry ἀσέλγεια, so that α becomes privative: others make its citizens wicked and petulant, so that α becomes intensive. See Scapula in his Lexicon. Pliny, Book XV, Natural History, ch. 7, and Book XXIII, ch. 4, mentions Selgitic oil, which is very useful for the nerves. They report that the Selgitae invented lasciviousness, so that they might restore strength lost through luxury and lust and strengthen weakened nerves. The Syrian and Arab translated it as 'not in lascivious beds'.

μὴ ἔριδι κὰι ζήλῳ) By metonymy, he understands here by strife, revilings; by zeal, that is, anger, fights. Thus Clement said in his Epistle to the Corinthians, 'the zeal that leads to death.' Both usually follow, both violence and whoredom: Epicharmus: 'From sacrifice came the feast, from the feast came drinking. B. How pleasant it is to me. A. From drinking came the revel, from the revel came insolence. From insolence came the lawsuit, from the lawsuit came the condemnation.' The same: 'From slander comes reviling; from this, the fight.' Eubulus concerning the mixing bowls of wine: 'The first is for health, the second for love, the third for sleep. The fourth is no longer ours, it is of insolence; the fifth is of shouting, the sixth of revelry, the seventh of black eyes.' Mnesitheus concerning wine: 'To those who drink it in moderation and mixed, it brings cheerfulness; but if you exceed, it brings insolence.'

Rightly B. Glassius: The Apostle joins in this verse three pairs of vices, which disturb the whole world and are the most common of all: namely, luxury in food and drink, lasciviousness with its softness, and pride of mind with its contention and emulation. Thomas Aquinas in this place says that the Apostle sets forth those things which pertain to the corruption of the appetite: 1. The concupiscible, whose corruption is intemperance (1) regarding foods: not in banquetings; (2) regarding drink: and drunkenness; (3) regarding bodily rest: not in chamberings; (4) regarding venereal matters: and wantonness. 2. The irascible, not in strife and envying.

Latin:

V. 13. ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατῶμεν. Qui de die procedunt, eunt composito gradu. Ovidius: Nox & amor vinumque nihil moderabile suadent. Tacitus historiarum IV. omnem pudorem nox ademerat. Ita nos de- cet lucis tantæ compotes omnia agere quàm honestissimè.

Luther. Die nemo operatur, quæ in tenebris solet operari, quilibet alterum veretur, & comparat se, ut vivat honestè. Vulgò dicitur: Nox pudore va- cat, id verùm est, quare & ea homines noctu faciunt, quorum ipsos die puderet; dies autem pudore pol- let, exigit conversationem honestam. Eodem se ha- bere modo debet vita Christiana, nempe ut nihil ad- mittas, cujus te pudere possit, etiamsi omnia tua uni- versus orbis videret. Nam qui ita vivit & operatur, ut ægrè ferat, sua omnia ab omnibus videri, & audi- ri, totamque vitam suam palàm cunctis innotescere, is omninò Christo indignam vitam vivit.

μὴ κώμοις) κῶμοι sunt nocturnæ amationes, unde κω- μάζειν. Vide Idyllium Theocriti κωμαστὴν, & Sap. XIV. 23. 2. Macc. VI. 4.

καὶ μέθαις) Nam & potari solet de nocte: 1. Thess. V. 7.

καὶ κοίταις) κοίτη est congressus viri cum muliere, ut di- ximus supra IX. 10. Dixit autem pluraliter κοίτας, ut ex- primeret concubitus vagos, ex quibus quæ & quot sequan- tur mala, facundè hic edisserit suo more Chrysostomus.

καὶ ἀσελγείαις) Est ἀσέλγεια vox Græca satis latè patens, & omnia comprehendens, quæ lascivè, libidinoseque fiunt, sed hîc ea intelligi putem, quæ fiunt contra sexuum leges. Nam & Æschines contra Timocratem hoc sensu utitur. In Glossario ἀσέλγεια impudicitia. Seneca de talibus: quibus abscondendis nulla satis atra nox est, libro 1. de Natura c.16.

Non hæc sunt opera tenebrarum universa, quæ deponere jubet hîc loci Apostolus, quod D. Ma- jori visum: sed quia inhæret adhuc similitudini evigilantium è somno, peculiariter illa comme- morantur, quæ otium & securitas, vel torpor & so- mnus secum trahere solet; uti sunt comessationes & ebrietates, cubilia & lascivia, quæ contra præ- ceptum sextum pugnant: & quæ connexa illis sunt, contentio, & fervor, quæ quinto præcepto adversan- tur. Quemadmodum ex adverso per arma lucis non tàm virtutes contrariæ, quales sunt temperan- tia, sobrietas, castitas, verecundia, studium concor- diæ, & longanimitatis, designantur, quàm illa, quæ in armamentario Spiritus S. ad πανοπλίαν sacram sistuntur, Eph. VI. 11. seqq. uti sunt veritas, justitia, Evangelium pacis, scutum fidei, galea spei, gladius verbi divini, tela orationum: ad quæ arma spiri- tualia ea, quæ hic circa honestam ambulationem requirit Apostolus, quædam potiùs adminicula censenda sunt, & προσκείμενα, vel requisita ad id necessaria, ut arma illa rectè tractentur, iisque fortiter præliemur, quàm cum armatura ipsa con- fundenda: quemadmodum temperantia, castitas, fuga iræ & æmulationis indebitæ ad requisita boni militis quidem pertinent, non verò ipsa ejus ar- ma sunt. Quo pacto Apostolo 1. Thess. V. 6. 8. vi- gilantiam & sobrietatem ab ipsis armis, quæ in- duenda sunt, fidei, dilectionis & spei distinguere placuit. Ellipsis autem hìc est præpositionis ἐν in, ex præcedentibus repetenda, ἐν κώμοις. Κῶμος autem, annotante Erasmo, Græcis Deus est temu- lentia (quem quidem ob ὁμοφωνίαν כמוש Camos effe volunt, idolum illud Moabitarum, cujus Num. XXI. 29. 1. Reg. XI. 33. Jer. XLVIII. 46. fit mentio, notante Drufio animadverf. l. 1. c. 56.) Eodemque nomine vocatur convivium procacius ac juvenile. Quin & cantiones ac faltationes lafciva Gracis κῶ- μοι dicuntur: unde & comœdia dicta est. Aretius in h. l. κῶμος comestatio est fcurrilis, in qua fales & dicteria liberiora regnant. Syrus pro κῶμοις habet בזמרא in Mufica, per Synecdoch. intelligens illa profufa convivia, de quibus Job. XXI. 12. Ef. V. 11. 12. Amos VI. 5. 6. quæ præter exquifitos cibos conjunctam etiam habent Muficam profanam, fpur- cam & inhoneftam, ut obfervat B. Glaffius p. 107.

Non autem est, cur voces illas κοίταις ἠ ἀσελ- γείαις ita restringamus; quum peccata omnis ge- neris contra fextum præceptum iis comprehen- dantur, (Κοίται juxta Hefychium γυναικῶν ἐπιθυ- μίαι & ἐμβασικοῖται dicuntur,) & ἀσελγέιαι ge- neralius dicantur in Scriptura, Marc. VII. 22. Gal. V. 19. Eph. IV. 19. 1. Pet. IV. 3. 2. Pet. II. 18. Jud. v. 4. Sap. XIV. 25. Interpres Demofthenis in Orat. κατὰ Μειδίε ita habet: Φαμὲν δὲ ἡμεῖς, ὅτι ἀσελγὴς λέγεται, ὅ μὴ μετέχων, μητὲ δικαιοσύνης, μητὲ ἀρετῆς. Dicitur tamen peculiariter ἀσέλ- γεια de lafcivia. Philo l. 1. de vita Mofis, διὰ τῆς τῶν γυναικῶν ἀσελγείας ἠ ἀγονασίας, per mulie- rum obfcænam libidinem, & protervam petulantia. Lucianus, ἀσελγέσεροι τῶν ὄνων, asinis lafciviores; fiquidem hoc animal libidinoffiffimum fit. Budæus ἀσέλγειαν dicit adhiberi pro obfcænitate, & stu- prorum flagitiofa confuetudine. Deducunt vo- cem à Selge, oppido à Lacedæmoniis condito, in quo aliqui homines temperantes & frugales, cum Strabone l. XII. & Suidá in dictione ἀσέλγεια, col- locant, ut α fit ςερητικὸν : alii cives ejus faciunt im- probos, & petulantes, ut α fit epitheticon. Vid. Scapula in Lex. Plinius Lib. XV. H. N. c. 7. & L. XXIII. c. 4. Selgitici olei meminit, quod nervis valdè utile. Id Selgitarum inveniffe lafciviam tra- dunt, ut vires luxu & libidine deperditas reftitue- rent nervosque debilitatos confirmarent. Syrus & Arabs expofuere pro μὴ κοίτας ἀσέλγεσι.

μὴ ἔριδι κὰι ζήλῳ) μετωνυμικῶς per ἔριν hîc intelligit convicia, per ζῶλον, id eft, iram, pugnas. Sic τὸν εἰς θάνα- τον ἄγοντα ζῆλον, dixit Clemens in Epistola ad Corinthios. Utrumque confequi folet, tum violentiam, tum scortatio- nem: Epicharmus: ἐκ μὲν θυσίας Θοίνα, ἐκ δὲ θοίνης πόσις ἐγένετο Β. χάριεν ώς γέ μοι Α. ἐκ πόσιος δὲ κῶμος κώμου δ' ἐγένετο υνανία. Ἐκ δὲ υνανίας δίκη γονετ’ ἐκ δίκης δὲ καταδίκη. Idem: Ἐκ διαβολᾶς ἡλοιδορία· ἐκ ταύτης ἡ μάχη. Eubulus de vini crateribus: ὁ δετότατος ἐκ ἔτι Ἡμίτερος ἐς' ἀπ' ὕβρεως ὁ δὲ πέμπτος βοῆς Ἕκτος δὲ κώμου· ἕβδομος δ' ὑπωπίων. Mnefitheus de vino: Τοῖς δὲ μέτριον πίνετι κὰι κεκραμένον, Εὐθυμίαν Φέρει· ἂν δ’ὑπερβάλης, ὕβριν.

Rectè B. Glaffius : Conjungit hoc verfu Apo- ftolus tria paria vitiorum, quæ totum orbem per- turbant, & omnium vulgariffima funt: videl. lu- xum in cibo & potu, lafciviam cum fua mollicie, & mentis fuperbiam cum fua contentione, & æmu- latione. ## 13:14
V. 14. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

Chrysostom says that even in his own time a frequent mode of speaking was: ὁ δεῖνα τὸν δεῖνα ἐνεδύσατο [so-and-so put on so-and-so], to signify a certain intimate conjunction. Thus χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε [you have put on Christ] Gal. III. 27. Thus also the new man is said to be put on Eph. IV. 24. Coloss. III. 10. and mercy Coloss. III. 12. To put on Christ is to imbibe his qualities. Just as it is said that a man is put on by a garment, and a garment by a man, so a man puts on the spirit, and the spirit a man, Jud. VI. 34.

: and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts.

Make no provision for the flesh: And because this generally stated [precept] could be taken wrongly, as if health were not to be cared for, he added, for the fulfilling of lusts, clearly, and indiscriminately, as Epicurus said: ὀ γὰρ ἔγωγε ἔχω τί νοήσω τ᾽ ἀγαθὸν, ἀφαιρῶν μὲν τὰς διὰ χυλῶν ἡδονὰς, ἀφαιρῶν δὲ τὰς δι᾽ ἀφροδισίων κὴ τὰς δὶ ἀκροαμάτων κὴ τὰς διαμορϕὰς [For I for my part have no notion of the good, if I take away the pleasures of taste, and take away the pleasures of sex, and the pleasures of listening, and the pleasures of beauty]. Πρόνοιαν ποιεῖν [to make provision], the same as προνοεῖν [to provide], above XII. 17. 1. Tim. V. 8. שכל [sekel].

We admit that a certain conjunction with Christ is noted: which, however, is through faith, inasmuch as by it we put on Christ, Gal. III. 26. 27. i.e., we apprehend the righteousness and obedience of Christ, and apply the same to ourselves, just as a garment is accustomed to be assumed and applied, concerning which garment of righteousness [see] Isaiah LXI. 10, which is also the wedding garment, which is required in worthy guests Matth. XXII. 11, that garment by which we can uniquely cover our spiritual nakedness, or τὴν αἰσχύνην τῆς γυμνότητος [the shame of the nakedness] of our own, Apoc. III. 18. XVI. 15, with which He himself surrounds, clothes, and adorns us, Es. LXI. 10. Joh. III. 29, and which it is necessary to receive from Him, Apoc. III. 18. But the putting on of the new man is one thing, the putting on of Christ is another: the latter happens in regeneration, and through faith: the former happens in renovation, and through sanctification. To the putting on of the new man pertains the putting on of mercy, and of other virtues, Col. III. 12. but not to the putting on of Christ, which is here accurately distinguished from the putting on of works and the armor of light: for no tautology, or vain repetition in such a concise explanation of an Apostolic similitude, is to be established here: but according to the blessed Mylius, it has the sense of the argument rather than of the explanation, i.e., it will thus come to pass that it will be openly evident that they themselves were once truly clothed with Christ in baptism. For baptism is that by which they put on Christ, as many as enjoy it, Gal. III. 27. By the study of good works, Christ is not so much put on as shown to have been put on. Moreover, many things are said to be done when they begin to be made more manifest; or, which seems more convenient: when he wishes the reborn man, as a Christian soldier, to be armed with spiritual weapons against enemies, when he wishes him ἐυσχημόνως περιπατεῖν [to walk becomingly], as is fitting in the day of the Evangelical light, by fleeing those things which are of the night, 1. Thessal. V. 7. and not involving himself in the works of darkness; now, how we can both fight against enemies and walk ἐυσχημόνως [becomingly], he summarizes in two admonitions: If, namely, first we have put on Christ through faith, by which we have need especially for battle and victory, Eph. VI. 16. 1. Joh. V. 1. and furthermore, if we have πρόνοιαν τῆς σαρκὸς [provision for the flesh], the provident care of the flesh, which easily conspires with external enemies, Satan and the world, lest we consent to its lusts, and be ensnared or seduced by them. We ought to make provision for the flesh, or take care of it, lest it rush εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν [into lust], into wicked concupiscence, as it is prone to do; and thus we ought to look around accurately and providently, and take care, which is insinuated by the word προνοίας [provision], lest the flesh deceive us with its lusts, and prevail over the spirit, inasmuch as it always lusts against the spirit, Gal.
