V. 17. whence it is necessary to abstain

| from fleshly lusts which war against the soul, 1. Pet. II. 11. and by the spirit to mortify the deeds of the body, Rom. VIII. 13. Grotius, however, confuses the care of the body and of health, which is not attended to here, nor is it connected to the putting on of Christ, or homogeneous, and pertains to the Medical School rather than the Theological: and τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν [provision for the flesh], which is to be understood concerning the provident management of the flesh, and circumspect government, lest we assent to the flesh that suggests evil, but restrain the same as we ought, and subject it, and crucify it with all its lusts, Galat. V. 24. Some say that in the same sense σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν [provision for the flesh] is that which the flesh provides and suggests; and thus prohibiting that we make provision for the flesh, or that which the flesh suggests, for the perpetrating of wicked lusts. The blessed Luther followed the sense of Theophylact: who holds as follows: Nothing certainly hinders that the flesh should be provided for, but he enjoins that it should not be indulged for pleasure and luxury; just as if he were to say, account is to be taken of the flesh only for health, not for continence. For it could not be called providence, which would excite a flame and fire for the flesh, and would kindle for it a furnace of fire and hell. Similarly Philip, Dr. Georgius Major, Beza, David Pareus, Cornel. à Lapide, Estius, B. Mylius, B. Hunnius. B. Balduinus says, Make no provision for the flesh in its desires. He does not prohibit all care of the flesh, but at least that which is in desires, that is, he wishes excess to be avoided, lest the wicked affections adhering to our nature become an irritant to us toward lasciviousness, by which all fervor of piety and all study of honesty is extinguished. B. Erasmus Schmidius says, otherwise it is permitted to make provision for the flesh, provided it is not done for the sake of lust. But the word σαρκὸς usually designates flesh rather than body, and that signification is more suitable by which the restraint of depraved desires is joined with the putting on of Christ through faith: in which we have Flacius in his Gloss agreeing; Glassius, l. c., and Tirinus on this passage. Grotius here agrees with the Socinian interpreters, among whom, for Crellius in this place, to put on Christ is to embrace the same manner of life which Christ both commanded and taught by the example of his life: moreover, he judges that the command by the Apostle not to take thought for the flesh regarding desires is so ordered, that such care of the body should not be undertaken, and that it should not be indulged to such an extent that it luxuriates and grows into various desires, and prepares itself to satisfy them. Schlichtingius from Bukoviz on the former member: to be put on, he says, is said of the person of someone, when he is expressed by a certain imitation and assimilation. Thus, therefore, we also ought to put on the person of the Lord JESUS Christ, so that we may imitate and express his most holy manners in all things. But where in the sacred writings the putting on of Christ is taken in such a way that his imitation is designated, it is not possible to find: nor does that phrase 'to put on the person of Christ' occur anywhere, nor are his virtues and manners understood here through Christ. Concerning the latter, Schlichtingius holds thus: The flesh is indeed to be cared for, since it is the dwelling place of the soul, and an instrument, and a part of us, nor do I forbid any care of the flesh, but this I wish, that you do not take thought for the flesh regarding desires. But the Apostle did not intend here to prescribe care for health or bodily necessity; nor is the Apostle's sentence twofold; that is, he does not both command to take thought for the flesh, or to care for those things which are necessary for the body for sustenance, which no one doubted was lawful and necessary for this life: and not to indulge in the flesh's desires: which is entirely different from that. But there is one simple meaning: that we should not take providential care of the flesh, that is, of depraved carnal concupiscence, to satisfy its lusts. The word σαρκὸς, placed once in the same clause, cannot have a double meaning, and thus denote synecdochically both the body at the same time, i.e., an essential part of man, and metaphorically carnal concupiscence, so that the former is to be cared for, but of the latter no πρόνοια is to be had: nor is carnal concupiscence only of the body, but primarily of the soul, which is its πρῶτον δεκτικόν. Finally, if the word σαρκὸς were taken for the human body, so that care for it were commanded, but lusts or concupiscences were at the same time prohibited, the Apostle would not have used a purely negative command, 'make no provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts': not to mention that he had already warned before about avoiding bodily lusts, namely, that they should not indulge in carousing, nor drunkenness, nor sacrifice only to Vacuna, and sleep, not in beds, nor surrender themselves to Venus, not in impurities. After such a long exhortation against bodily lusts, luxury, softness, and lasciviousness, instituted κατὰ μερισμὸν and part by part, what was the point of now adding a warning not to take care of the body for the sake of lust.

Latin:

V. 14. ἀλλ᾽ ἐνδύσασθε τὸν Κύριον ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.

Ait Chrysostomus, etiam suo tempore loquendi genus srequens fuisse : ὁ δεῖνα τὸν δεῖνα ἐνεδύσατο, ad significandam intimam quandam conjunctionem. Sic χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε Gal. III. 27. Sic & novus homo indui dicitur Eph. IV. 24. Coloss. III. 10. & misericordia Coloss. III. 12. Christum in- duere, est qualitates ejus imbibere. Sicut dicitur & homo indui veste, & vestis ab homine, sic homo induit spiritum, & spiritus hominem, Jud. VI. 34.

: καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε εἰς ἐπιθυμίας.

Carnis curam ne gerite : Et quia hoc generaliter dictum malè poterat accipi, quasi nec valetudo curanda esset, ad- didit, ad cupidines, explendas scilicet, & indistinctè, ut Epi- curus dixit : ὀ γὰρ ἔγωγε ἔχω τί νοήσω τ᾽ ἀγαθὸν, ἀφαιρῶν μὲν τὰς διὰ χυλῶν ἡδονὰς, ἀφαιρῶν δὲ τὰς δι᾽ ἀφροδισίων κὴ τὰς δὶ ἀκροαμάτων κὴ τὰς διαμορϕὰς. Πρόνοιαν ποιεῖν, idem quod προνοεῖν, supra XII. 17. 1. Tim. V. 8. שכל.

Conjunctionem quandam cum Christo nota- ri admittimus : quæ verò sit per fidem, utpote quâ induimus Christum, Gal. III. 26. 27. h. e. appre- hendimus Christi justitiam & obedientiam, ean- demque nobis applicamus, uti vestis assumi & applicari solet, de qua veste justitiæ Esaiæ LXI. 10. quæ etiam vestis nuptialis est, quæ in hospitibus dignis requiritur Matth. XXII. 11. vestis illa, quâ nuditatem nostram spiritualem, vel τὴν αἰσχύνην τῆς γυμνότητος nostræ, unicè tegere possumus, Apoc. III. 18. XVI. 15. quâ ipse nos circumdat, vestit & ornat, Es. LXI. 10. Joh. III. 29. quamque ab ipso accipere oportet, Apoc. III. 18. Alia verò est induitio novi hominis, alia induitio Christi: hæc fit in regeneratione, & per fidem : illa fit in reno- vatione, & per sanctificationem. Ad novi homi- nis induitionem pertinet induitio misericordiæ, & aliarum virtutum, Col. III. 12. non autem ad in- duitionem Christi, quæ hic ab operum & armo- rum lucis induitione accuratè distinguitur : non enim hic aliqua ταυτολογία, aut in tàm concinnâ similitudinis Apostolicæ explicatione inanis re- petitio statuenda : sed juxtà B. Mylium quidem argumenti potius, quàm explicationis sensum hoc habet, q. d. sic futurum ut Christo vere ipsos semel indutos fuisse in baptismo palam constet. Baptismus enim est, quo Christum induunt, quotquot eo fru- untur, Gal. III. 27. Bonorum operum studio non tàm induitur, quam indutus esse Christus ostenditur. Multa autem tùm dicuntur fieri cum incipiunt fieri manifestiora; vel, quod convenientius vide- tur: quum renatum ceu militem Christianum ve- lit armatum spiritualibus armis, adversus hostes, quum velit eum ἐυσχημόνως περιπατεῖν, ut in die lucis Evangelicæ par est, fugiendo ea, quæ noctis sunt, 1. Thessal. V. 7. & tenebrarum operibus sese non involvendo; jam quomodo & pugnare con- tra hostes, & ἐυσχημόνως ambulare possimus, sum- matim duobus monitis complectitur : Si nempè primùm Christum induerimus per fidem, quâ vel imprimis ad pugnam & victoriam opus est, Eph. VI. 16. 1. Joh. V. 1. & porrò πρόνοιαν τῆς σαρκὸς, providam curam carnis, quæ facilè conspirat cum hostibus externis, Satana & mundo, habeamus, ne in ejus concupiscentias consentiamus, illisque in- escemur aut seducamur. Carnis πρόνοιαν ποιεῖσθαι, vel curam ejus gerere debemus, ne εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν, in pravam concupiscentiam, uti prona est, ruat; adeoque accurate & provide circumspicere, & cu- rare debemus, quod voce προνοίας insinuatur, ne caro nos suis concupiscentiis decipiat, ac spiritui prævaleat, utpote quæ semper concupiscit adver- sus spiritum, Gal. V. 17. unde oportet ἀπέχεσθαι

| τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν αἵτινες στρατεύονται κατὰ | τῆς ψυχῆς, 1. Pet. II. 11. & πνεύματι τὰς πράξεις τοῦ σώματος θανατοῦσθαι, Rom. VIII. 13. Con- fundit autem Grotius corporis & valetudinis cu- ram, quæ hìc non attenditur, neque induitioni Christi connexa, vel homogenea est, & ad Scho- lam Medicam potiùs, quàm Theologicam pertinet: & τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν, quæ de carnis provi- do regimine, & circumspectâ gubernatione, ne malesuadæ carni assentiamur, sed eandem com- pescamus ut debemus, ac subjiciamus, & cru- cifigamus cum omnibus concupiscentiis, Galat. V. 24. intelligenda. Nonnulli eodem sensu σαρ- κὸς πρόνοιαν dicunt illud esse, quod caro providet & suadet; adeoque prohibens ne faciamus car- nis curam, vel id, quod suadet caro, ad concupi- scentias pravas perpetrandas. B. Lutherus se- ctatus est Theophylacti sensum : qui ita habet: Nihil sanè quò minùs carni providendum sit, impedat, sed illi ne ad voluptatem & luxum in- dulgeatur, injungit; perinde ac si dicat, carnis duntaxat ad sanitatem, non ad continentiam ha- benda est ratio. Nec enim dici providentia pos- set, quæ carni flammam & incendium excitaret, & ignis caminum & gehennam illi succenderet. Similiter Philippus, D. Georgius Major, Beza, David Pareus, Cornel. à Lapide, Estius, B. Mylius, B. Hunnius. B. Balduinus, Carnis, inquit, cu- ram ne feceritis in desideriis. Non prohibet omnem carnis curam, sed eam saltem, quæ sit in deside- riis, hoc est, excessum vitari vult, ne pravi af- fectus naturæ nostræ adhærentes, nobis irritamen- to siant ad lasciviam, quâ extinguitur omnis fer- vor pietatis, omne studium honestatis. B. Erasmus Schmidius, alias, inquit, licet τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν ποιεῖσθαι, modò ne id fiat εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. Sed vox σαρκὸς carnem potius, quùm corpus designare so- let, & convenientior est illa significatio, quâ cum induitione Christi per fidem conjungitur cu- piditatum pravarum coërcitio: in quo consen- tientem habemus Flacium in Glossa : Glassium, l. c. & Tirinum in hunc loc. Grotius hic Soci- nianis interpretibus consonat, è quibus Crellio in hoc loco Christum induere est eandem vitæ rationem amplecti, quam Christus tùm præcepit tùm vitæ exemplo docuit: Carnis autem curam non gerendam esse ad cupiditates ab Apostolo ita juberi censet, ne hujusmodi corporis cura sus- cipiatur, eique tantùm indulgeatur, ut luxuriet, & in varias cupiditates excrescat, atque ad eas explendas sese accingat. Schlichtingius à Buko- viz de priori membro : indui, inquit, dicitur persona alicujus, cum is imitatione quadam & assimilatione exprimitur. Sic igitur & nos perso- nam Domini JESU Christi induere debemus, ut ejus sanctissimos mores in omnibus imitemur, & exprimamus. Sed ubi in sacris Christi indui- tio ita accipiatur, ut ejus imitatio designetur, non invenire licet: neque uspiam occurrit phra- sis illa induere personam Christi, aut hîc per Chri- stum intelliguntur ejus virtutes, ac mores. De posteriori sic habet Schlichtingius: Curanda qui- dem est caro, cum sit animi habitaculum, & in- strumentum, ac pars nostri, neque ego cuiquam curationi carnis interdico, sed hoc volo, ne carnis curam geratis ad cupiditates. Sed non præscribe- re hic curam sanitatis, aut necessitatis corporalis voluit Apostolus; neque gemina est Apostoli sen- tentia; hoc est, non jubet & carnis curam gere- re, vel ea, quæ corpori necessaria ad sustentatio- nem sunt, curare, quod licitum, & ad hanc vitam necessarium esse, nemini dubium erat: & carnis cupiditatibus non indulgere: quod ab illo prorsus diversum est. Sed unica est sententia simplex: ne providam curam carnis, id est, pravæ carnalis con- cupiscentiæ geramus, ad explendas ejus libidines. Vox σαρκὸς in eodem colo semel posita non po- test geminam habere significationem, adeoque & synecdochicè corpus simul notare, partem sc. ho- minis essentialem, & metaphoricè carnalem con- cupiscentiam, ut illud quidem curandum sit, hu- jus verò πρόνοια non sit habenda: neque carna- lis concupiscentia tantùm corporis est, sed impri- mis animæ, quæ ejus est πρῶτον δεκτικόν. Denique si vox σαρκὸς pro corpore humano acciperetur, ut cura ejus præcepta, libidines verò vel concupi- scentiæ prohibitæ simul sint, non purè negativum adhibuisset mandatum Apostolus, carnis provi- dentiam ne geratis ad libidines: ut taceam, quod de vitandis corporeis libidinibus jam anteà monu- erit, ne sc. commessationibus, nec ebrietati indul- geant, nec Vacunæ tantùm litent, & somno, non in cubilibus, nec Veneri sese mancipent, non in impudicitiis. Post tàm prolixam à corporeis libi- dinibus, luxu, mollitie, ac lascivia dehortationem κατὰ μερισμὸν & per partes institutam, quid attine- bat nunc addere monitum, ne curam corporis ad libidinem gerant.

## 14:1 Argument
SECTION II. Admonitions concerning things indifferent. CHAPTER XIV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Concerning the weak in faith in matters of indifference, such as not judging the distinction of foods and days, provided they serve their own Lord, by whom we are all to be judged; and not giving offense, so that a neighbor is not lost because of such external things, in which the kingdom of GOD is not situated, and that peace and mutual edification may prevail; and finally, not offending one's own conscience, which happens when the things we do in these matters do not proceed from faith.

There are two parts: I. Concerning not judging the weak, up to verse 12 inclusive. II. Concerning the rules by which the use of things indifferent is to be governed: such as love, so that a neighbor is not lost; and peace and mutual edification; as well as the preservation of an uninjured conscience, up to verse 23.

PART I. CONCERNING NOT JUDGING THE WEAK REGARDING THINGS INDIFFERENT.

From that commandment of love, about which he had begun to treat, Paul deduces excellent consequences, extremely necessary for those times and places. Many Jews converted to Christ not only wanted to observe, and impose upon others to observe, the commandments of Moses, even the ritual ones, Acts XV. These men detested those called from the Gentiles who did not observe these commandments. On the other hand, those called from the Gentiles, conscious of the liberty given through Christ, wanted to exclude the Jews living in a Jewish manner from their communion, XI. 18, 21, from which a schism was going to follow, and would have hindered the progress of the Gospel wonderfully in its very beginnings. To meet this evil, Paul institutes a middle way, and warns the Jews who had believed in Christ to follow their own opinion in such a way that they abstain from condemning with the crime of impiety those who thought otherwise. And those called from the Gentiles, that they should not shun the communion of those, even though they lived in a Jewish manner, and that they should not despise them as unskilled. These two types of men exercised the Apostles much, and while he accommodates himself now to these, now to those, according to the circumstances of time and place, and reduces both to moderation, he makes known both his prudence and his goodness. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho expresses this Apostolic temperament thus: 'I answered, O Trypho, and there are some who do not dare to have communion or fellowship with such people. I agree with them, but if they themselves, because of the weakness of their judgment, wish to observe as many of the things of Moses as they can, which we understand were ordained because of the hardness of the heart of the people, along with hoping in this Christ and keeping the eternal and natural acts of justice and piety, and choose to live with Christians and the faithful, as I said before, not persuading them either that they must be circumcised like them, or keep the Sabbath, or keep other such things, they ought to be accepted as kinsmen and brothers.'

It is helpful to hear Chrysostom regarding that occasion, whom Theophylact has followed here step by step: 'There were very many of the believing Jews who, since they were held by the conscience of the law even after they had believed, still kept the observance of foods, not yet daring to shake off the yoke of the law entirely in every respect. Lest they be marked as blameworthy by the remaining Christians, as those who abstained from swine's flesh, avoiding all eating of meat entirely, they ate only herbs, so that what they were doing might seem not a legal observance, but rather a fast. Again, there were others who, since they were more perfect, keeping not even one small observance of the law, were troublesome and burdensome to these weak observers of the law by criticizing, accusing, and casting them into sadness.' The Apostle, therefore, fearing that those more perfect ones, wishing to correct what was a trifle, might subvert the whole, and while they tried to lead the weak into the indifference of foods, might cause them to fall away entirely from the faith, and while they studied to correct everything in general that concerns temporary things before the maturity of a convenient time, might inflict damage: namely, that by that continuous rebuke they might, being dulled, recoil from the confession of Christ, and thus persist uncorrected on both sides: See what prudence he used, and in what way he heals both parties with his customary wisdom. For he did not dare to say to those criticizing the legal observance that they were doing wrong, lest he harden the weak in the observance of the law: nor again that they were doing well, lest he make the more vehement ones more intense in accusing; therefore he instituted a measured rebuke. Chrysostom shows not inelegantly by what artifice the Apostle accomplished this.

Him that is weak in the faith.

He calls him weak in the faith here, who has indeed embraced Christianity, but does not fully know all things revealed by Christ or His Spirit, and especially that mystery which Paul began to open in the seventh chapter. Epiphanius notes that such were the Nazarenes in Palestine. Thus Horace: I am a little weaker, that is, more scrupulous. Cyril explains this word well against Julian VII: 'We eat with a pure conscience, giving glory to God, as having granted us the use of all edible things freely and without harm; but if anyone is weak in these matters, and does not have a healthy and sound mind, but thinks that some things are truly sacrificed to idols, not having reached the genuine faith, we sit with them, just as some trainers exercise young boys, leading them up little by little to the most perfect experience of the matter.' Emperor Constantine in Eusebius: 'One must yield to the weaker out of a spirit of forgiveness.'

Receive.

Into the fellowship of the Church, just as those who receive someone into hospitality are said to receive him, Acts 18:26, 28:2. For the Church is compared to a house above in 11:25. This admonition is taken from those things which were said about Christ in Matthew 12:20.

The Apostle is not dealing with the weak, who have indeed embraced Christianity but do not fully know all its mysteries, being joined to the Church, but with those who are still rooted or firm, even if they easily suffer offense: and concerning those who are still struggling with some ignorance of the benefits of Christ, who are to be taken up or assumed, so that we not only tolerate them, although living according to their custom, and still differing from us for the time being in the use of indifferent things, but also with a spirit of meekness let us instruct and inform them. The weak part constantly needs greater care, whence the Apostle, turning to the strong and powerful, says: receive the weak in faith. But those who err in the foundation of the faith, heretics, are not to be judged as weak in faith; whence the Calvinists, Massonius in Anat., Joh. Bergius in Regul. Apostol. wrongly abuse this passage for receiving the Reformed into the communion of the Church. For to such, not even a greeting is to be said, according to St. John, 2 Epist. v. 10. But those who were not sufficiently informed in the article concerning Christian liberty, cf. 1 Cor. VIII. 9, chap. IX. 22, such as were the weak Jews in comparison to the converted Gentiles: concerning whom Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact explain it in this place, Basil in Regul. brevior. n. 64, Clemens Alex. l. II. Pædag. c. 1. The Word of God, says Vedelius in acc. Armin. p. 14. c. 22, prescribes that not those who err in the faith, but the weak, should be tolerated.

Not to disputes of thoughts.

Not taking upon yourselves to judge their thoughts: namely, whether they use legal things as necessary, or as useful. Διακρίνειν to judge, Matt. XVI. 3, 1 Cor. VI. 5, Job IX. 14, XV. 5, Ecclesiastes III. 18, 2 Sam. XIX. 9, Lev. XXIV. 11, Exod. XVIII. 16, διαλογισμοὶ thoughts, Matt. XV. 19, Mark VII. 21, Luke II. 35, V. 22, VI. 8, IX. 46, 47, XXIV. 38, above I. 21, 1 Cor. III. 20.

According to this explanation, it is forbidden that we judge the consciences of the weak, which are open to God alone: that we do not inquire too anxiously into their thoughts, and either sadden them with such scrupulous examination, or untimely render them, being offended, alienated from the faith, by interpreting everything sinisterly and taking it in the worse sense. In which manner St. Augustine in c. VII. Rom. Neither let us judge, he says, his thoughts, that is, as if we dared to pass sentence on another's heart, which we do not see. Others, however, understand διάκρισιν as hesitation, so that we receive the weak, but not to the hesitation or fluctuation of thoughts, or disputation, so that we render him hesitant and doubtful, or scrupulous in thoughts or conscience, so that he is carried hither and thither by various winds of thoughts, as in Acts XI. 12, μηδὲν διακρινόμενος nothing hesitating, Matt. XXI. 21, μὴ διακριθῆτε, do not hesitate. Thus Blessed Luther, do not confuse the consciences. But the matter, as to the sense, comes to the same thing: Since one must not dispute with the weak about indifferent things, lest they be offended. For because in the most pious there is great force partly of religious custom, partly of conscience, they are by no means to be blunted or confused, but while they admit nothing in their deeds that publicly offers offense or incurs manifest violation of the faith, in other matters one must easily acquiesce, and they themselves are to be borne, cherished, and peacefully informed or corrected.

Latin:

SECTIO II. Monita de Indifferentibus. CAPUT XIV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

De infirmis in fide in adiaphoris, utpote de dif- crimine ciborum & dierum non judican- dis, modò Domino suo serviant, à quo ju- dicandi sumus omnes; nec scandalo dando, ut perdatur proximus ob talia externa, in quibus situm non est regnum DEI, & ut pax & ædificatio mutua obtineat; nec of- fendendâ denique propriâ conscientiâ, quod fit, cum non ex fide procedunt, quæ in his agimus.

Partes duæ sunt: I. De infirmis non judican- dis, usque ad v. 12. inclus. II. De regulis, qui- bus adiaphororum usus gubernandus: utpote di- lectionis, ne proximus perdatur; ac pacis & ædi- ficationis mutuæ; nec non conservationis illæsæ con- scientiæ, usque ad v. 23.

PARS I. DE INFIRMIS NON JUDICANDIS CIRCA ADIAPHORA.

Ex illo dilectionis, de quo agere cœperat, præcepto egregia Paulus consectaria deducit, illis temporibus ac lo- cis perquam necesfaria. Judæi multi ad Christum conversi non modo servare volebant, & aliis servanda imponere præcepta Mosis, etiam ritualia, Act. XV. Hi vocatos ex gen- tibus ista præcepta non servantes aversabantur. Contra vo- cati è gentibus, conscii datæ per Christum libertatis, Ju- dæos Judaicè viventes à sua communione volebant ex- cludere, XI. 18. 21. unde secuturum erat schisma, & mirè in ipsis initiis obstiturum Evangelii processibus. Huic ma- lo ut occurrat Paulus, mediam instituit viam, & Judæos, qui in Christum crediderant, monet, ita sequantur suam opinionem, ut à damnandis crimine impietatis, qui aliter sentiebant, abstineant. Ex gentibus verò vocatos, ne il- lorum, quamvis Judaicè viventium, communionem defu- giant, & ut imperitos spernant. Multum Apostolos exer- cuere duo ista hominum genera, quorum dum nunc his, nunc illis se accommodant pro tempore ac locorum ratio- ne, utrosque verò ad mediocritatem reducunt, cognitam faciunt suam & prudentiam, & bonitatem. Justinus in col- loquio cum Tryphone temperamentum hoc Apostolicum sic exprimit: Εἰσὶν, ἀπεκρινάμην, ὦ Τρύφων, καὶ μηδὲ κοινω- τῶν ὁμολίας ἢ ὁσίας τοιούτοις τολμῶντες. οἷς ἐγὼ & συναινός εἰμι, ἀλλ' ἐὰν αὐτοὶ διὰ τὸ ἀσθενὲς τῆς γνώμης τὰ τὰ ὅσα δύ- νανται νῦν ἐκ τῶν Μωσέως, ἃ διὰ τὸ σκληροκάρδιον τὸ λαᾶ νοῦμεν διατετάχθαι, μετὰ τὸ ἐπὶ τᾶτον τὸν Χρισὸν ἐλπίζειν κὴ τὰς αἰωνίας καὶ φύσει δικαιοπραξίας καὶ ἐυσεβείας φυλάττειν βέλωνται, καὶ αἱρῶνται συζῆν τοῖς χρισιανοῖς καὶ πιςοῖς, ὡς προεῖπον, μὴ πείθοντες αὐτὲς μήτε δεῖν περιτέμνεσθαι ὁμοίως αὐτοῖς, μήτε σαββατίζειν, μήτε ἄλλα ὅσα τοιαῦτά ἐσι τηρεῖν, ὡς ὁμοσπλάγχνους καὶ ἀδελφοὺς δεῖν ἀποφαίνεσθαι.

De occasione illa juvat audire Chrysostomum, quem hîc κατὰ πόδα sequutus est Theophylactus: Erant quamplurimi credentium Judæorum, qui cum legis conscientia, etiam posteaquam credide- rant, detinerentur, ciborum adhuc custodiebant ob- servantiam, nondum planè in universum legis au- dentes excutere jugum. Illi ne à reliquis Christia- nis veluti reprehensibiles notarentur, ut qui à suillâ carne abstinerent, omnem omninò carnis esum vitan- tes, holeribus tantummodò vescebantur, ut, quod fa- ciebant, non legalis observatio, sed jejunium magis videretur. Rursus alii quidem erant, qui cùm per- fectiores essent, ne unam quidem legis observatiun- culam custodientes, infirmis istis legis observantibus vituperando, accusando, inque mæstitiam conjicien- do, molesti erant & graves. Veritus itaque Aposto- lus, ne perfectiores illi, quod minutum erat emenda- re volentes, totum subverterent, & dum infirmos in ciborum indifferentiam subducere conarentur, effi- cerent, ut prorsus ex fide deciderent, dumque ante convenientis temporis maturitatem omnia in uni- versum quæ temporaria concernunt, corrigere stu- derent, damnum inferent: nimirum quòd continuâ illâ increpatione obtusi à Christi confessione resili- rent, atque ita utrobique inemendati persisterent: Vide, quâ usus sit prudentiâ, & quo pacto consueta suâ sapientiâ utrisque medeatur partibus. Neque enim legalem observantiam carpentibus audebat dicere, quòd malè facerent, ne in legis observatione obfirmaret infirmos: neque rursus quòd benè face- rent, ne vehementiores illos in accusando redderet; commensuratam itaque increpationem instituit. Quod quo artificio exequutus Apostolus sit, non ineleganter ostendit Chrysostomus.

Τὸν δὲ ἀσθενῦντα τῇ πίσει.

Ἀσθενῦντα vel ἀσθενῆ τῇ πίσει, hic vocat, qui Christia- nismum quidem amplexus est, sed non omnia à Christo, aut Spiritu ejus revelata pernoscat, præcipuè verò myste- rium illud, quod septimo capite aperire cœpit Paulus. Ta- les fuisse in Palæstina Nazaræos notat Epiphanius. Sic Ho- ratius: sum paulò infirmior, id est, scrupulosior. Cyrillus ve- cem hanc benè explicat contra Julianum VII. ἐσθίομεν δὲ συνειδότι καθαρῷ, Θεῷ τὴν δόξαν ἀνάπτοντες, ὡς ἁπάντων ἡμῶν τῶν ἐδωδίμων ἐλευθεραντε καὶ ἀζήμιον χαρισαμένῳ τὴν χρῆσιν· εἰ δὲ ἀσθενεῖ τις ἐν τύτοις ὑγιά τε ἕπω κὴ ἔυρωσον ἔχων τὸν νῦν, οἴεται δὲ εἶναί πη τι ἱερόθυλα ἀληθῶς, ἕπω βεβηκότε περὶ τὸ γνήσιον εἰς πίςιν, συγκαθισάμεθα, ὥσπερ τινὲς παι- δοτρίβαι διαγυμνάζοντες τὰ μειράκια ἀναβιβάζοντές τε κατὰ βραχὺ πρὸς τελιοτάτην τῷ πράγματος ἐμπειρίαν. Con- stantinus Imperator apud Eusebium: ἀσθενεστέροις δεῖ ὑπο- κατακλίνεσθαι λόγῳ συγγνώμης.

Προσλαμβάνεσθε.

Societate Ecclesiæ, sicut qui hospitio aliquem accipiunt, dicuntur eum προσλαμβάνειν, Act. XVIII. 26. XXVIII. 2. Ecclesiæ enim domui comparatur suprà XI. 25. Sumitur hæc admonitio ex iis, quæ de Christo dicta Matth. XII. 20.

Non de infirmis, qui Christianismum quidem amplexi sunt, sed non omnia ejus mysteria per- noscunt, sociandis Ecclesiæ, sed de iis, qui adhuc radicati aut firmi sunt, etiamsi facile offensam pa- tiantur, agit Apostolus: deque iis, qui cum ali- qua adhuc beneficiorum Christi ignorantiâ confli- ctantur, suscipiendis vel assumendis, ita ut non to- leremus tantùm eos, licet more suo viventes, & in rerum mediarum usu adhuc pro tempore à no- bis discrepantes, sed etiam Spiritu mansuetudinis eos erudiamus, & informemus. Infirma pars ma- jore perpetuo cura opus habet, unde & ad valen- tem & fortem conversus dicit Apostolus : infirmum in fide suscipite. Non autem infirmi in fide judi- candi sunt hæretici, qui in fidei fundamento errant; unde perperam Calviniani, Massonius in Anat. Joh. Bergius in Regul. Apostol. hoc loco abutun- tur ad suscipiendos Reformatos in communio- nem Ecclesiæ. Talibus enim ne Ave quidem di- cendum secundum S. Johannem 2. Epist. v. 10. Sed qui in articulo de libertate Christiana informati satis non erant, Conf. 1. Cor. VIII. 9. cap. IX. 22. quales infirmi fuere Judæi in συγκρίσει ad Ethni- cos conversos: de quibus explicat id August. Chry- sost. Theophyl. h. l. Basil. in Regul. brevior. n. 64. Clemens Alex. l. II. Pædag. c. 1. Verbum Dei, inquit Vedelius in acc. Armin. p. 14. c. 22. præscribit, ut non errantes in fide, sed infirmi tolerentur.

Μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν.

Non sumentes vobis dijudicandas ipsorum cogitatio- nes : nempe an legalia ut necessaria usurpent, an ut utilia. Διακρίνειν dijudicare Matth. XVI. 3. 1. Cor. VI. 5. Job. IX. 14. XV. 5. Ecclesiastæ III. 18. 2. Sam. XIX. 9. Lev. XXIV. 11. Exod. XVIII. 16. διαλογισμοὶ cogitationes Matth. XV. 19. Marc. VII. 21. Luc. II. 35. V. 22. VI. 8. IX. 46. 47. XXIV. 38. suprà I. 21. 1. Cor. III. 20.

Juxta hanc explicationem prohibetur, ne judi- cemus infirmorum conscientias, quæ soli Deo pa- tent: ne in ipsorum cogitationes nimis anxiè in- quiramus, eosque scrupulosiori ejusmodi exami- ne vel contristemus, vel intempestivè offensos à fide alienos reddamus, sinistrè interpretando omnia, & in partem deteriorem abripiendo. Quo pacto S. August. in c. VII. Rom. Neque dijudice- mus, inquit, cogitationes ejus, id est, quasi ferre au- deamus sententiam de alieno corde, quod non vide- mus. Alii tamen διάκρισιν de hæsitatione intel- ligunt, ut suscipiamus infirmum, sed non ad hæsi- tationem vel fluctuationem cogitationum, vel dis- ceptationem, ut ipsum hæsitantem & dubium, vel scrupulosum reddamus in cogitationibus vel con- scientia, ut variis cogitationum ventis huc illuc rapiatur, uti Act. XI. 12. μηδὲν διακρινόμενος ni- hil hæsitans, Matth. XXI. 21. μὴ διακριθῆτε, non hæ- sitaveritis. Sic B. Lutherus, verwirret die Gewis- sen nicht. Sed res, quoad sensum, eodem recidit: Cum infirmis non de indifferentibus disceptandum esse, ne offendantur. Quia enim in piissimis qui- busque magna est partim religiosæ consuetudinis, partim conscientiæ vis, minimè obtundendi sunt, aut confundendi, sed dum in factis nihil admit- tant, quod publicè offensionem præbeat, aut in manifestam fidei violationem incurrat, in cæteris facilè acquiescendum, ipsique ferendi, fovendi, & placidè informandi aut corrigendi sunt.

## 14:2
v. 2. One believes he may eat all things.

Supply it is permitted. He thinks it is lawful to eat all things. Πάντα, that is, all kinds of food.

but he who is weak eats herbs.

An argument from the greater. Those are to be tolerated who think one must abstain from all living things, which some did out of a certain religion, others because they thought it better. That this was done out of religion, Aelius Spartianus teaches us, speaking of the Emperor Julian: But often, when there was no religion, he dined on herbs and legumes without meat. Therefore Sextus Aurelius Victor rightly calls him a harsh teacher of living well. Of those who thought it better, let the example be Sextius the Philosopher, whom Seneca mentions in epistle CVIII, and says that he himself also once followed his example and abstained from animals. That Sextius therefore used to say, as Origen reports, the use of living things is indifferent; but abstinence is more rational. Concerning which matter there exists a learned booklet by Porphyry. And that Xenocrates and Polemon thought so for physical reasons, Clemens notes in Strom. VII. Philo adds in the place which Eusebius preserved at the end of the 8th of the Preparation: Wherefore even until

– to whom the principle of temperance is to abstain from all things (namely animals) – using herbal greens, and in the fruits of trees as a pretext for pleasant enjoyment. Where it is clearly explained what is said here, eating herbs. Josephus attributes abstinence from living things to Daniel and his companions in Antiquities XII. To the Essenes; Philo attributes the same in the book on the contemplative life. That this was ancient among many nations, especially among the Priests of the Egyptians and the Cretans and the Eleusinians, and among certain of the Persian magi, Jerome shows in II against Jovinian. Among the Indians also many observe this, and Abenesdra noted on Gen. XLVI. 32 that this is ancient for the Indians. Many among the Christians imitated this, some because they thought it better, others out of a scrupulous opinion. Clemens Pædag. II. Matthew the Apostle indeed partook of seeds and nuts and herbs – without meat. Augustine l. XX. c. 21. to Faustus, says that James the brother of the Lord used seeds and herbs, not meat nor wine. The Apostolic Canon distinguishes between those who abstained through exercise, and those who execrated things created by God. For thus Canon 21 holds: If any bishop or priest, or deacon, or at all of the clerical list, abstains from marriage and meat and wine, not for exercise, but for abomination, forgetting that all things are very good, and that God made man male and female, but blaspheming, slanders the creation, either let him be deposed or corrected and cast out of the church. Likewise also laymen. Therefore we learn that Tatian and others were rejected from the Church because they introduced as a necessary dogma, as of marriage, so of abstinence from living things. Irenaeus mentions this in l. 30 & 31. Origen also well distinguishes these two kinds of those who abstain in Against Celsus IV. Observe also in the difference the cause of the abstinence from living things by those of Pythagoras and the ascetics among us, for those abstain from living things because of the myth concerning the transmigrating soul;

And if anyone, having lifted up a dear son, should slaughter him, praying, great fool. But we, even if we do such a thing, we do it because we buffet the body and bring it into bondage, and we wish to put to death the members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and we do everything indeed so that we may put to death the deeds of the body. And Zonaras on the said Apostolic Canon says that it is lawful for some to abstain: for the sake of self-control, not because they loathe them. With which agrees the Ancyran Canon XIV. It seemed that those who are in the clergy, presbyters or deacons, and who abstain from meats, ought to be compelled to touch the meats, and if they should loathe them, so as not even to eat vegetables cooked with meats, and should not submit to the canon, they should be removed from their order. Tertullian, book II, on the apparel of women: Do not some interdict to themselves the very creature of God, abstaining from wine and edible animals, the fruits of which are subject to no danger or anxiety, but offer to God the humility of their soul in the chastisement of their diet also? Prudentius in the third hymn of the Cathemerinon:

Far be that hunger that craves to tear apart bloody feasts with the slaughter of cattle. Let the wild, untamed nations have lunches from the killing of four-footed beasts: let the blade of a vegetable, let the pod pregnant with manifold legumes feed us with harmless feasts.

Eusebius, History IV. 3. For to Alcibiades, one of them who was living very austerely and partaking of nothing at all before, but using only bread and water, and attempting to live in this way even in prison, it was revealed to Attalus, after the first struggle which he finished in the amphitheater, that Alcibiades was not doing well, not using the creatures of God, and leaving behind a pattern of stumbling for others. And Alcibiades, being persuaded, partook of all things freely and gave thanks to God. The same history is held in the martyrology of Ado on the 4th of the Nones of June, where these words are: wishing to take no food, but content with salt and bread, he used it with water. Chrysostom praises in II Cor. IX those who are able to be satisfied with legumes. There was in his time Olympias, a deaconess of the Church of Constantinople, who abstained from all living things, as Palladius testifies. And in Action II of the eighth Synod mention is made of those who ate no meats. They could therefore be tolerated among Christians, not only those who did so for the sake of exercise, but also those who abstained from living things out of opinion or ancient custom, provided they did not proceed to such a degree of confidence as to abominate others living differently.

At length here, but irrelevantly, Grotius brings forward examples both of heathens and of Christians who, either out of religion or because they thought it better, abstained from all living things: but those of the heathens here are irrelevant, as is manifest where it concerns those weak in faith. Christians from Christian liberty, and some bodily chastisement, abstained, but did not constitute religion or some part or necessary condition of worship in it, nor did they hold such abstinence for a fast. And Grotius himself observes that the Apostolic Canon, which they call the XXI, distinguishes between those who abstained through exercise, and those who cursed things created by God, and Tatian and others rejected by the Church, because they introduced as a necessary dogma, as of marriages, so of ἐμψύχων ἀποχὴν, as Irenaeus testifies in book I, chapters 30 and 31. But what he concludes: Therefore those could be tolerated among Christians not only who abstained for the sake of exercise, but also who abstained from opinion or ancient custom regarding living things, provided they did not proceed to such confidence that they abhorred others living differently; that can indeed be admitted, but the opinion of necessity, and of worship, or of religion, ought also to have been absent: which limitation Grotius here neglected for the sake of the Papists: for the saints, whose abstinence is perhaps celebrated in Ecclesiastical History, did not abstain from certain foods out of superstition or religion (the persuasion of which outside the word of God is true ἐθελοθρησκεία, or superstition) but out of Christian liberty, or out of a certain weakness of faith; otherwise than is done in the Papacy, where the opinion of religion, necessity, and merit is attached to such abstinence. But the Apostle here speaks of those weak in faith, who, converted from the Jews, abstained from meats, and ate only herbs, which weak persons he advises should be borne. There were, to be sure, those who with a secure and ready mind ate whatever foods without distinction: and there were found in turn others, who, hindered by the weakness of their conscience, abstained from some things, and judged that they ought to eat herbs rather than other foods. Here, while the Apostle does not weigh the deed of either party by itself with a judgment of guilt or reproach, he teaches that the observance of the thing in either direction is indeed free, yet he indicates not obscurely that the free use of indifferent things approaches closer to the praise of faith than abstinence and choice. For he compares, as Theophylact rightly does with Chrysostom, the imperfect one with him who has attained perfection, and indicates that he who is perfect in faith, trusting, eats all things indifferently: but the more imperfect one, as one who is wavering and unstable, has herbs for food. It is therefore fair that the weaker one should be cared for rather than offended. But the prohibition imposed upon consciences under the law of necessity, such as that of meats, milk, butter, and cheese in the Papacy, he calls elsewhere the doctrine of demons, 1 Tim. IV. 3. Concerning which Erasmus on this passage: Today we see among Christians there is almost more superstition in the choice of foods than there ever was among the Jews. Nor are these things tolerated now, but they constitute absolute piety in them, for the sake of the others we fight with every kind of weapon, by these we judge, we avert, we execrate our neighbor, as if he were little of a Christian, by these we most foolishly please ourselves.

ὁ ἐσθίων. Namely, meats from animals.

τὸν μὴ ἐσθίοντα. One who does not eat [meat]. Abstaining from living creatures and for that reason content with vegetables.

μὴ ἐξουθενείτω. As if rude and unskilled. Concerning the word ἐξουθενεῖν see what we said on Mark VIII. 31, IX. 12.

καὶ ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων. Some follower of Pythagoras.

τὸν ἐσθίοντα. Using a promiscuous diet.

Ne damnet, that is, hold as a lost cause.

Latin:

v. 2. Ὃς μὲν πισεύει φαγεῖν πάντα.

Supple ἕξιναι. Putat licere omnibus vesci. Πάντα, id est, omnis generis edulia.

ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐθίει.

Argumentum à majori. Tolerandi sunt ii, qui ab omni- bus animatis abstinendum putant, quod quidam faciebant religione quadam, alii, quod id melius existimarent. Reli- gione id factum multis docet nos Ælius Spartianus de im- peratore Juliano loquens: Sæpe autem nulla existente reli- gione, oleribus leguminibusque contentus sine carne cœnaverit. Ideo eum asperum rectè vivendi præceptorem vocat Sex- tus Aurelius Victor. Eorum, qui id melius existimarent, ex- emplum sit Sextius Philosophus, cujus meminit Seneca epi- stola CVIII. ejusque exemplum se quoque aliquando secu- tum ait animalibus abstinuisse. Dicebat ergo is Sextius, re- ferente Origene, ἐμψύχων χρῆσις μὲν ἀδιάφορος; ἀποχὴ δὲ λογικώτερον. Qua de re extat eruditus Porphyrii libellus. Atque ita sensisse physicis de causis Xenocratem & Polemo- nem notat Clemens Strom. VII. Addit Philo in loco, quem servavit Eusebius in fine 8. præparationis: Διὸ κὴ μέχρι τῶν

– οἷς λόγος ἐγκρατείας ἀπαξαπάντων ἀπέχεσθαι (ζώων nempe) – λαχανώδει χλοῇ, κᾀν καρποῖς δένδρων προσσχήμασιν ἡδίσῃ ἀπο- – λαύσει χρωμένοι. Ubi clarè explicatur, quod hic dicitur λά- χανα ἐσθίων. Abstinentiam ab animatis Danieli & sociis, bus ejus tribuit Josephus antiquæ historiæ XII. Essenis ; idem tribuit Philo libro de vita contemplativa. Vetus id . fuisse apud plurimas gentes, maximè apud Aegyptiorum Sacerdotes & Cretensium & Eleusine, apud quosdam etiam Persarum magos ostendit Hieronymus II. contra Jovinia- num. Apud Indos etiam multi id observant, & vetus id esse Indis notavit Abenesdra ad Gen. XLVI. 32. Imitati d sunt id in Christianis multi, alii, quòd id melius putarent, i alii scrupulosa opinione. Clemens pædag. II. Ματθαῖος . μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος σπερμάτων καὶ ἀκροδρύων καὶ λαχάνων – ἄνευ κρεῶν μετελάμβανεν. Augustinus l. XX. c. 21. ad Fau- stum, Jacobum ait fratrem Domini seminibus & oleribus usum, non carne nec vino. Canon Apostolicus distinguit . inter eos, qui per exercitationem abstinebant, & eos, qui t execrabantur res à Deo conditas. Sic enim habet Canon 21. Εἴ τις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὅλως τοῦ καταλόγου τοῦ ἱερατικοῦ γάμου καὶ κρεῶν καὶ οἴνου, οὐ δι' ἄσκησιν, ἀλ- λὰ διὰ βδελυγίαν ἀπέχηται, ἐπιλαθόμενος, ὅτι πάντα καλὰ λίαν, καὶ ὅτι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλὰ βλασ- φημῶν διαβάλλοι τὴν δημιουργίαν, ἢ καθαιρείσθω ἢ διορθούσθω καὶ . τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἀποβαλλέσθω. ὡσαύτως καὶ λαϊκοὶ. Ideo Ta- tianum & alios ab Ecclesia rejectos discimus quod tanquam dogma necessarium introducerent, ut nuptiarum ita ἐμψύ- χων ἀποχήν. Meminit Irenæus l. 30. & 31. Duo ista gene- . ra abstinentium bene & Origenes distinguit contra Celsum IV. ὅρα δὲ κᾀν τῇ διαφορᾷ τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς τῶν ἐμψύχων ἀποχῆς τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πυθαγόρου καὶ τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀσκητῶν, ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ διὰ τὸν περὶ ψυχῆς μετενσωματουμένης μῦθον ἐμψύχων ἀπέ- χονται·

κᾔτις φίλον υἱὸν ἀείρας Σφάξει ἐπευχόμενος μέγα νήπιος. ἡμεῖς δὲ κᾀν τὸ τοιοῦτο πράττομεν, ποιοῦμεν αὐτὸ, ἐπεὶ ὑπωπιά- ζομεν τὸ σῶμα καὶ δουλαγωγοῦμεν, καὶ βουλόμεθα νεκροῦν τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, πορνείαν, ἀκαθαρσίαν, ἀσέλγειαν, πάθος, ἐπι- θυμίαν κακὴν, καὶ πάντα γε πράττομεν, ἵνα τὰς πράξεις τοῦ σώ- ματος θανατώσομεν. Et Zonaras ad dictum Canonem A- postolicum licite abstinere aliquos ait: δι' ἐγκρατείαν, οὐ βδελυττομένους. Quocum convenit Ancyranus Canon. XIV. τοὺς ἐν κλήρῳ πρεσβυτέρους ἢ διακόνους ὄντας, καὶ ἀπεχομένους κρεῶν, ἔδοξεν ὀφείλεσθαι καὶ ἅπτεσθαι φύλασθε κρεατεῖν, εἰ δὲ βδελύττοιντο, ὡς μηδὲ τὰ μετὰ κρεῶν βαλλόμενα λάχανα ἐσθίειν, καὶ μὴ ὑπείκοιεν τῷ κανόνι, πεπαῦσθαι αὐτοὺς τῆς τάξεως. Tertullianus lib. II. de cultu fœminarum: Numquid non aliqui ipsam Dei creaturam sibi interdicunt, abstinentes vi- no & animalibus esculentis, quorum fructus nulli periculo aut sollicitudini adjacent, sed humilitatem anima suæ in victus quoque castigatione Deo immolant? Prudentius hymno κα- θημερινῶν tertio:

Absit enim procul illa fames Cædibus ut pecudum libeat Sanguineas lacerare dapes. Sint feræ gentibus indomitis Prandia de nece quadrupedum: Nos oleris coma, nos siliqua Fœta legumine multimodo Paverit innocuis epulis.

Eusebius hist. IV. 3. Ἀλκιβιάδη γάρ τινος ἐξ αὐτῶν lex Chri- stianis πάνυ αὐχμηρῶς βιοῦντος, καὶ μηδενὸς ὅλως τὸ πρότερον μεταλαμβάνοντος, ἀλλ' ἢ ἄρτου μόνου κᾀν ὕδατι χρωμένου, πειρω- μένου τε καὶ ἐν εἱρκτῇ οὕτω διάγειν, Ἀττάλῳ, μετὰ τὸν πρῶτον ἀγῶνα ὃν ἐν τῷ ἀμφιθεάτρῳ ἤνυσε, ἀπεκαλύφθη, ὅτι μὴ καλῶς ποιοίη ὁ Ἀλκιβιάδης, μὴ χρώμενος τοῖς κτίσμασι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἄλλοις τύπον σκανδάλου ὑπολειπόμενος. πεισθεὶς δὲ Ἀλκιβιά- δης πάντων ἀνέδην μετελάμβανε, καὶ ηὐχαρίστει τῷ Θεῷ. Ha- bet eandem historiam in martyrologio Aonis ad IV. Nonas Junii, ubi hæc verba: nihil cibi volens accipere, sed contentus sale & pane cum aqua utebatur. Laudat Chrysostomus in II. ad Cor. IX. τὸν ὀσπρίοις δυναμένων ἀρκεῖσθαι. Fuit ipsius temporibus Olympias diaconissa Ecclesiæ Constantinopoli- tanæ, quæ ab omnibus animatis abstinebat, teste Palladio. Et in Actione II. Synodi octavæ fit mentio eorum, qui car- nibus nullis vescebantur. Poterant ergò tolerari inter Chri- stianos non modo, qui exercitamenti causa, verum etiam, qui ex opinione aut veteri more animatis abstinebant, dum nec eò procederent confidentiæ, ut alios aliter viventes ab- ominarentur.

Prolixè hîc, sed alienè Grotius adducit exem- pla tùm Ethnicorum, tùm Christianorum; qui vel religione, vel quia id melius existimarunt, ab omnibus animatis abstinuêre: sed illa Ethnicorũ hîc ἀλλότρια esse, ubi de infirmis in fide agitur, manifestum. Christiani è libertat. Christiana, & corporis ali- qua castigatione abstinuere, non autem in eo re- ligionem vel partem quandam aut conditionem necessariam cultus constituere, vel abstinentiam talem pro jejunio habuere. Et observat ipse Gro- tius, Canonem Apostolicum, quem vocant, XXI. distinguere inter eos, qui per exercitationem abs- tinuere, & eos, qui exsecrati sunt res a Deo condi- tas, ac Tatianum & alios ab Ecclesia rejectos, quod tanquam dogma necessarium introducerent, ut nuptiarum, ita ἐμψύχων ἀποχὴν, teste Irenaeo l. I. cap. 30. 31. Quod verò concludit: Poterant er- gò tolerari inter Christianos non modò, qui exerci- tamenti causà, verùm etiam, qui ex opinione aut veteri more animatis abstinebant, dum ne eò pro- cederent confidentia, ut alios aliter viventes ab- ominarentur; id admitti quidem potest, sed ab- esse etiam debuit opinio necessitatis, & cultus, aut religionis: quam limitationem in gratiam Papi- colarum neglexit hic Grotius: non enim sancti, quorum abstinentia fortè celebratur in Historia Ecclesiastica, ex superstitione aut religione, (cu- jus persuasio extra Dei verbum vera est ἐθελοθρη- σκεία, vel superstitio) sed è Christiana libertate, vel ex quadam fidei infirmitate a certis cibis abs- tinebant; secus atque in Papatu fit, ubi religio- nis, necessitatis, & meriti opinio tali abstinen- tiae affingitur. Apostolus verò hic de infirmis loquitur in fide, qui e Judaeis conversi à carnibus abstinebant, & olera tantùm manducabant, quales infirmos ferendos esse monet. Erant nimirum, qui secura & parata mente esculentis quibusvis citra discrimen vescebantur: ac reperiebantur vicissim alii, qui conscientiae imbecillitate impe- diti aliquibus abstinebant, & oleribus potiùs, quàm aliis cibis vescendum sibi judicabant. Hic dum neutrius partis factum Apostolus per se cul- pae, aut reprehensionis judicio gravat, liberam equidem esse rei in utramvis partem observatio- nem docet, liberum tamen rerum mediarum usum propius ad laudem fidei accedere, quàm ab- stinentiam & delectum, haud obscurè innuit. Comparat enim, ut rectè cum Chrysostomo Theo- phylactus, cum imperfecto qui fit perfectionem ad- eptus, innuitque, perfectus quidem in fide confisus, indifferenter omnia comedit: imperfectior verò, ut- pote qui nutabundus sit & instabilis, holus habet in esum. AEquum est igitur, ut curetur potiùs quàm offendatur infirmior. Prohibitionem autem sub lege necessitatis conscientiis impositam, qualis in Papatu est carnium, lactis, butyri, casei, doctrinam daemoniorum aliàs appellat, 1. Tim. IV. 3. De qua Erasmus in hunc loc. Hodie videmus inter Christianos propè plus esse superstitionis in ciborum delectu, quàm unquam fuerit apud Judaeos. Nec ista jam tolerantur, sed his absolutam constituunt pietatem, pro illis omni telorum genere depugnamus, ex his judicamus, aversamur, execramur proxi- mum, ceu parum Christianum, ex his nobis stultis- simè placemus.

ὁ ἐσθίων. Nempe carnes ex animalibus.

τὸν μὴ ἐσθίοντα. Abstinentem ab animatis & ob id oleribus conten- tum.

μὴ ἐξουθενείτω. Tanquam rudem atque imperitum. De verbo ἐξουθε- νεῖν vide, quae diximus ad Marcum VIII. 31. IX. 12.

καὶ ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων. Pythagorae sectator aliquis.

τὸν ἐσθίοντα. Promiscuo victu utentem.

Ne damnet, id est, pro deplorato habeat.

## 14:3
ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς αὐτὸν προσελάβετο.

God called the Gentiles without any law of foods.

Latin:

ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς αὐτὸν προσελάβετο.

Deus gentes vocavit sine ulla ciborum lege.

## 14:4
Who are you that judges another man's servant?

Indeed, where you have no law of the Lord, who are you, whether Jew or Pythagorean, who dare to claim such a right for yourself?

To his own master he stands or falls.

That is, by the judgment of the Lord he will bring a sentence either for himself or against himself. He is said to stand who is the victor in a case, as in Psalm 1:4. Those who receive a judgment against themselves are said to fall in a case, even among the Latins.

But he shall be made to stand.

It is a good omen.

For God is able to make him stand.

Here 'powerful' is taken as above in chapter 11. That scrupulous opinion will not prevent God from saving him by His sentence, if he has lived in a Christian manner otherwise. In the manuscript it is: 'For He is powerful,' as in 2 Corinthians 13:3.

He addresses the more perfect, as Theophylact teaches, so that just as he turns them away from contempt of their neighbor, so he dissuades them from judging others. For both things were practiced by those who had progressed more in the faith. For they both despised and judged the less perfect. On the other hand, Theophylact also notes that the Apostle is comforting him, while he does not imply that he has collapsed entirely. Furthermore, I do not object that 'to stand' here means to be the victor in a case, and 'to fall' means to receive a judgment against oneself: because with what conscience anyone either eats or abstains must be left to be judged by the Lord alone, by whose judgment one either stands or falls; if, however, 'to fall' is to be taken as a good omen, because he is to be raised up in turn: for so far should rash condemnation of companions in religion be from pious minds, that they ought to flee even a sinister omen as far as possible.

Latin:

σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ κρίνων ἀλλότριον οἰκέτην.

Nempe ubi Domini legem habes nullam, quis tu es aut Judæe aut Pythagorista, qui id juris tibi vindicare audeas?

τῷ ἰδίῳ κυρίῳ στήκει ἢ πίπτει.

Id est, Domini judicio aut pro se aut contra se sententiam feret. Stare dicitur, qui in causa victor est, ut Psal. I. 4. Cadere causa dicuntur & Latinis, qui judicium contra se referunt.

σταθήσεται δὲ.

Est benè ominantis.

Δυνατὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς στῆσαι αὐτὸν.

Δυνατὸς hic sumitur, ut suprà XI. Scrupulosa ista opinio Deum non impediet, quominus eum sententia sua servet, si cætera Christianè vixerit. In Manuscripto est: Δυνατεῖ γάρ, ut 2. Cor. XIII. 3.

Perfectiores, docente Theophylacto, alloquitur istiusmodi, ut quemadmodum eos à proximi contemptu avertit, sic ne alios judicent, dehortatur. Utrunque enim id factitabant, qui magis in fide profecerant. Nam & minus perfectos aspernabantur & judicabant. Rursum autem solari etiam notat Theophylactus Apostolum, dum non prorsus eum collapsum infert. Cæterùm non repugno, hic stare esse in causâ victorem esse, cadere judicium contra se referre: quia quâ conscientiâ quis vel manducet vel abstineat, uni Domino judicandum relinquendum, cujus judicio quis vel stat, vel cadit; si tamen cadere benè ominandum, quòd erigendus sit vicissim: ita enim abesse procul à piis mentibus debet temeraria sociorum religionis damnatio, ut omen etiam sinistrum defugere quàm longissimè debeant.

## 14:5
v. 5. One person esteems one day above another.

When he had dealt with foods, he came to another kind of ritual, concerning feast days and non-feast days according to the law. 'Esteems' means judges, as in 1 Corinthians 2:2. Thus 'I judge enemies' means I consider them as enemies, in Demosthenes. 'Day above day': day before day, in the way 'para' is taken by the Greek interpreters in Psalm 45:8. Thus we also had above in 1:25. He prefers Sabbaths, Passover, Pentecost, the Feast of Tabernacles, and new moons to other days. Thus the Hebrews were accustomed to say concerning the Passover night: How much does this night excel other nights?

but another esteems every day.

That is, he considers every day equally holy, serving God from new moon to new moon, from Sabbath to Sabbath, according to the prophecy of Isaiah LXVI. 23.

Concerning the distinction of days, which those converted from the Jews observed, but not those who had come to the faith of Christ from the Gentiles, the Apostle warns equally that neither these nor those are to be judged, provided each person is certain in his own mind and does nothing against his conscience. However, while it is permitted that every day be considered equally holy, the Christian constitution and custom concerning the observance of feast days is not contradicted: for this can be observed without prejudice to Christian liberty in honor of God and for the edification of the Church, provided that superstition is absent and a yoke is not imposed upon consciences. But that the Apostles themselves initially observed feasts with the Jews was not done out of a law of necessity, because they knew the ceremonial law had already expired, but out of a certain συγκατάβασις, and for the sake of infirmity, until the Synagogue, as Augustine speaks, was buried with honor, and the doctrine of Christian liberty was rendered more confirmed among the people. Which then he so far did not permit to be rendered ambiguous by such, that he condemned the observation and distinction of days as unworthy, in the name of the weak and beggarly elements of the world, for Christians, Coloss. II. 16. Gal. IV. 9. 10. on account of the vice, namely superstition, and the annexed opinion of necessity, which was being spread by the wickedness of the Pseudo-Apostles. For indifferent things are not ἀδιάφορα, when they are urged to be observed under an opinion of necessity, or carry scandal and superstition with them.

ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείτω. Manuscript: ἕκαστος τῷ ἰδίῳ νοὶ πληροφορείτω. The Hebrews say איש ימלא את לבו, that is, let each one enjoy his own knowledge. Thus Ecclesiastes 8:12: ἐπληροφορήθη καρδία υἱῶν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸ πονηρόν: in committing evils he pleased himself. For πληροφορεῖσθαι is also put for πληροῦσθαι. Thus πληροφορηθέντες ἀγάπης in Clement's epistle. The sense here is the same as in that Sophoclean line: Ὅτωι δὲ μὴ ταῦ' ἐστιν ἐν γνώμῃ φίλα, Κεῖνόν τ' ἐκεῖνα στεργέτω, κἀγὼ τάδε. And Evenus: Καὶ πρὸς μὲν τούτους ἀρκεῖ λόγος, ὃς εἰς πάλαισιν: Σοὶ μὲν ταῦτα δοκεῖν τ' ἐστὶν, ἐμοὶ δὲ τάδε.

Thus Grotius for the Vulgate, which has it thus: let each one abound in his own sense. But that could not recommend itself even to the Papists themselves: and as Justinianus acknowledges, it provided an occasion for erring; as if the Apostle wished here to approve whatever anyone undertakes in his own religion with a good intention of mind: and that permission of any sense whatsoever might easily introduce a vicious and scandalous Libertinism: since to abound in one's own sense is a vice, and of a brazen face, according to Salmeron, and of a headstrong man, and of an obstinate mind, as Erasmus testifies, and πληροφορεῖσθαι in the Scriptures does not imply abundance and fullness, but a most firm persuasion and certainty, Rom. 4:21, Luke 1:1, so that the mind is clearly ἀμετάπτωτος in its opinion, and does not hesitate or fluctuate in conscience in any way. For whatever is not from faith is sin. But if we ought to be certain in the use of indifferent things, that it is not joined with the vice of superstition and scandal, much more ought everyone to be certain in matters of faith: by which is proscribed and condemned both the impious Pyrrhonism and Skepticism of the Remonstrants, of M. Henricus Nicolaus, and of those like them who dispute on both sides about most articles of faith and eliminate the necessity of believing: and also the gloomy dogma of the Papists concerning the uncertainty of grace: for if everyone ought to have a certain πληροφορία in his own mind, there will certainly be no need to doubt about the grace of God. This, therefore, is what the Apostle wants, as interpreted by the blessed Mylius, p. 399: that no one should undertake anything in this kind of matter feignedly or with a fluctuating mind: but that everyone should act according to his conscience: and should undertake those things for which he can render a certain and indubitable account to GOD from His word. For there are many recesses of human hearts, and most people wander wonderfully in their own thoughts; there are those who are delighted by new and monstrous opinions: others itch with a lust for dissenting from others: others consult their own religion for an uncertain outcome. Here the Apostle recalls everyone to the judgment of conscience and the analogy of faith. For nothing stabilizes the mind unless it has proceeded from that certainty. Theophylact rightly says with Chrysostom: When it is a matter of dogmas, there is no need at all that we be led by our own sense, but rather those things which we have received from others are to be held, even if an angel sent down from heaven should announce otherwise. But when a contention arises concerning abstinence from foods, or other things of that kind, if there are any among the neophytes who are failing, or who need indulgence, severity is to be relaxed for them, not tightened.

Latin:

v. 5. Ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν.

Cum de cibis egisset, venit ad alterum genus ritualium, circa dies festos & non festos ex lege. κρίνει æstimat ut 1. Cor. II. 2. Sic κρίνω πολεμίους pro hostibus habeo, apud Demosthenem. ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν : diem præ die, quomodo παρὰ sumitur à Græcis Interpretibus Psalm. XLV. 8. Sic & suprà habuimus I. 25. Præfert Sabbata, Pascha, Pentecosten, σκηνοπηγίαν, interlunia diebus aliis. Sic solebant Hebræi dicere de nocte Paschali: Quantum præstat hæc nox aliis noctibus?

ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν.

Id est, quemvis diem pariter sanctum habet, serviens Deo ab interlunio ad interlunium, à Sabbato ad Sabbatum, secundum vaticinium Esaiæ LXVI. 23.

De discrimine dierum, quod è Judæis conversi observabant, non autem qui ex gentilibus ad fidem Christi accesserant, monet æquè Apostolus non judicandos esse sive hos, sive illos, modò quisque in sua mente certus sit, nec quicquam contra conscientiam agat. Dum autem quemvis diem pariter sanctum haberi permittitur, constitutioni & consuetudini Christianæ de observandis festis diebus non contradicitur: hæc enim salva libertate Christiana observari potest in honorem Dei, & ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ: dum absit superstitio, & conscientiis jugum non imponatur. Quod autem Apostoli ipsi initio festa cum Judæis observarunt, non factum ex lege necessitatis, quia legem ceremonialem jam expirasse noverant, sed ex συγκαταβάσει quâdam, & in gratiam infirmitatis, donec Synagoga cum honore, uti Augustinus loquitur, sepeliretur, & doctrina libertatis Christianæ confirmatior in populo redderetur. Quam deinde talibus adeò non permisit, ambiguam reddi Spiritus Sanct. ut observationis & discriminis dierum infirmorum & egenorum mundi elementorum nomine tanquam indignam, Christianis damnârit, Coloss. II. 16. Gal. IV. 9. 10. ob vitium sc. superstitionis, & annexam necessitatis opinionem, quæ Pseudo-Apostolorum impro- bitate spargebatur. Adiaphora enim non sunt ἀδιάφορα, cum sub necessitatis opinione obser- vanda urgentur, aut scandalum & superstitionem secum trahunt.

ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείτω. Manuscriptus: ἕκαστος τῷ ἰδίῳ νοὶ πληροφορείτω. Hebræi dicunt איש ימלא את לבו, id est, fruatur quisque sua scientia. Sic Ecclesiastæ VIII. 12. ἐπληροφορήθη καρδία υἱῶν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸ πονηρόν: in malis per- petrandis sibi placuit. Ponitur enim πληροφορεῖσθαι etiam pro πληροῦσθαι. Sic πληροφορηθέντες ἀγάπης in Clementis epistola. Sensus hic idem est, qui in isto Sophocleo: Ὅτωι δὲ μὴ ταῦ' ἐστιν ἐν γνώμῃ φίλα, Κεῖνόν τ' ἐκεῖνα στεργέτω, κἀγὼ τάδε. Et Eveni: Καὶ πρὸς μὲν τούτους ἀρκεῖ λόγος, ὃς εἰς πάλαισιν: Σοὶ μὲν ταῦτα δοκεῖν τ' ἐστὶν, ἐμοὶ δὲ τάδε.

Hæc ita pro Vulgatâ Grotius, quæ sic habet: unusquisque in suo sensu abundet. Sed ea nec ipsis Papistis sese probare potuit: & Justinianeo agno- scente occasionem errandi præbuit; quasi quic- quid bonâ intentione animi sui suscipit quisque in religione suâ, approbatum hic velit Aposto- lus: ac illa sensus cujuslibet permissio facilè Liber- tinismum vitiosum & scandalosum invehat: quum abundare suo sensu vitii sit, & refractæ frontis, se- cundum Salmeronem, & hominis præfracti, & ob- stinatæ mentis, teste Erasmo, & πληροφορεῖσθαι in Scripturis non inferat abundantiam & plenitudi- nem, sed firmissimam persuasionem, & certitudi- nem, Rom. IV. 21. Luc. I. 1. ut animus plane sit in sententia sua ἀμετάπτωτος, nec ullatenus hæsitet, aut fluctuet in conscientia. Quicquid enim non est ex fide, peccatum est. Si autem certi esse de- bemus in usu rerum indifferentium, quòd non cum superstitionis vitio & scandalo conjunctus sit, multò magis quisque certus esse debet in rebus fidei: quo proscribitur & damnatur tùm impius Pyrrhonismus, & Scepticismus Remonstrantium, M. Henrici Nicolai, & similium de plerisque fi- dei articulis in utramque partem disputantium, & necessitatem credendi eliminantium: tùm do- gma Papistarum tetricum de incertitudine gratiæ: Si enim quisque in mente sua πληροφορίαν certam habere debet, dubitandum utique non erit de gratiâ Dei. Hoc ergò vult Apostolus, interprete B. Mylio p. 399. neminem fictè, neminem fluctuam- te animo in hoc genere rerum suscipere quicquam debere: sed quemvis agere tùm pro conscientia de- bere: tùm ea suscipere, quorum ex suo verbo ra- tionem DEO reddere certam atque indubitatam possit. Multi enim sunt cordium humanorum re- cessus, & mirificè cogitationibus suis plerique vagan- tur; sunt, qui delectantur novis & monstrosis opi- nionibus: alii libidine dissentiendi ab aliis pruriunt: alii in eventum incertum religioni suæ consulunt. Hic ad judicium conscientiæ, & fidei analogiam Apostolus revocat universos. Mentem enim nihil stabilit, nisi ex istâ certitudine profectum. Rectè cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: Cùm de do- gmatibus agitur, nequaquam est opus, ut nostro sen- su ducamur, quin erunt quæ ab aliis accepimus te- nenda, vel si angelus è cælo demissus diversa denun- tiet. Cùm verò de ciborum abstinentia contentio oritur, vel aliis istiusmodi, si qui sunt ex neophytis, qui delinquunt, vel indulgentiâ egeant, laxanda his erit, non intendenda severitas.

## 14:6
v. 6. ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν, κυρίῳ φρονεῖ. Φρονεῖν with the accusative signifies in these writings to devote effort to some thing, as we saw above 8:3, 12:16. Κυρίῳ, that is, in honor of God. He observes feast days with a pious mind, because he thinks that this pleases God in the Jews.

καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν τῷ κυρίῳ ὐ φρονεῖ.

And he who dedicates all days equally to God, looks to nothing else in this than the honor of God.

καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων. Any meats whatsoever, that is.

Κυρίῳ ἐσθίει. He consecrates this act of eating also to God.

εὐχαριστεῖ γὰρ τῷ Θεῷ. He gives thanks to God for what is given, as was the custom of the Jews and Christians. We spoke about this custom in Matt. 14:19, 15:36, 26:25.

κὰι ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐκ ἐσθίει. He abstains, because he thinks that is safer, and by that he shows that he is reverent toward God.

and gives thanks to God. For that very temperance which he uses.

The Apostle confirms, as B. Mylius holds here, his judgment concerning the approval of both actions, and that by a reason taken from the common end of both actions, and the similarity of the manner. Both he who distinguishes days, and he who does not distinguish, does it for the Lord, that is, in obedience to the word, and for the glory of the divine name: the former because he knows that the Jewish observation of days is not necessary after the coming of Christ: the latter, because he understands that it was divinely commanded to the Jewish people, and not yet abrogated. In which sense, although there is error: because he is nevertheless led by the conscience of a divine command, and has a probable cause for his ignorance, from his recent conversion to Christianity, faith is said not to be extinguished by that error; but to be weakened: and he will be judged not to labor under or sin against conscience: but to err and hallucinate in knowledge. The manner of the actions is also posited as the same in both cases, which is joined with thanksgiving. Conf. 1 Tim. IV. 4. Tit. I. 15.

Latin:

v. 6. ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν, κυρίῳ φρονεῖ. Φρονεῖν cum accusativo significat in his scriptis, operam alicui rei dare, ut vidimus suprà Vlll. 3. Xll. 16. Κυρίῳ, id est, in honorem Dei. Observat dies Festos pio animo, quòd hoc in Judæis Deo placere existimet.

καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν τῷ κυρίῳ ὐ φρονεῖ.

Et ille, qui dies omnes pariter Deo dedicat, nihil aliud in hoc, quàm Dei honorem, respicit.

καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων. Quasvis carnes scilicet.

Κυρίῳ ἐσθίει. Hunc quoque vescendi actum Deo consecrat.

εὐχαριστεῖ γὰρ τῷ Θεῷ. Deo pro datis gratias agit, ut mos erat Judæorum & Christianorum. De hoc more diximus Matth. XIV. 19. XV. 36. XXVI. 25.

κὰι ὁ μὴ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐκ ἐσθίει. Abstinet, quòd id tutius existimet, & eo ostendit, se Dei reverentem esse.

κὰι εὐχαριστεῖ τῷ Θεῷ. Pro ipsâ illâ, quâ utitur, temperantiâ.

Confirmat Apostolus, ut hic habet B. Mylius, judicium suum de facti utriusque approbatione, id- que ratione ex communi actionum utriusque fine, & modi similitudine desumta. Uterque & discernens dies, & non discernens, Domino id facit, id est, in obsequium verbi, & gloriam nominis divini: hic quia dierum Judaicam observationem post adven- tum Christi non necessariam esse novit: ille, quia eam populo Judaico divinitùs mandatam, nondum abrogatam esse intelligit. In quo sensu, quamvis error est: quia tamen mandati divini conscientiâ ducitur, & ignorantiæ suæ probabilem, ex novellâ ad Christianismum conversione, habet causam, fides errore isto non exstingui; sed infirmari dicitur: & non conscientia laborare, aut peccare: sed scientiâ errare atque hallucinari judicabitur. Modus actio- num utrobique idem etiam ponitur, qui sit conjun- ctus cum gratiarum actione. Conf. 1. Tim. IV. 4. Tit. I. 15.

## 14:7
v. 7. For none of us. Of us, who are Christians. lives to himself, and no one dies to himself; for whether we live, we live to the Lord, whether we die, we die to the Lord. That is, we ought to consecrate, and are prepared to consecrate, both our life, and all things of life, and death itself, to Christ, who has made us his own. Is this not so great a thing, that for the sake of these trifles they ought to be overlooked?

Latin:

v. 7. ὀὐδεὶς γὰρ ἡμῶν. Nostrum, qui Christiani sumus. ἑαυτῷ ζῇ, καὶ ὀὐδεὶς ἑαυτῷ ἀποθνήσκει; ἐάν τε γὰρ ζῶμεν, τῷ κυ- ρίῳ ζῶμεν, ἐάν ἀποθνήσκωμεν, τῷ κυρίῳ ἀποθνήσκομεν. Id est, Christo, qui nos suos fecit, & vitam, & vitæ omnia, & ipsam mortem consecrare debemus, & parati sumus. Nonne hoc tantum est, ut propter hæc levicula dissimulari debeant?

## 14:8
v. 8. Whether we live, whether we die, we are the Lord's. See Eph. I. 21. Nothing is the property of servants. All things are the Lord's. We are servants of Christ, bought with the highest price, his own blood. This is what follows.

Latin:

v. 8. ἐάν τε ἐν ζῶμεν, ἐάν τε ἀποθνήσκωμεν, τῷ κυρίῳ ἐσμὲν. Vide Eph. I. 21. Servorum nihil est proprium. Omnia sunt Domini. Nos servi Christi sumus, empti summo pre- tio, ipsius sanguine. Hoc est, quod sequitur.

## 14:9
v. 9. For to this end Christ both died and rose and lived again, that he might have dominion both over the dead and the living. This dominion is owed to him by the decree of the Father, who for this reason allowed him to die, that he might raise him, and raised him, that he might give him heavenly life, joined with royal power in the Church, and for the Church. In the Manuscript there is only died and lived. And thus the Latin and Theophylact seem to have read.

The Apostle digresses into a common place, having employed a comparison from servants, over whom masters formerly had the right of life and death; therefore he teaches that power over life and death belongs to Christ the Lord: so that it may be established that we are Christ's own not only in this life, but also in death: and since civil masters have dominion only over the living, but can no longer rule over dead servants: he warns that Christ rules even over the dead, indeed that he died and revived for this reason, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living, not that Christ merited glory for himself by his death, but that by acquiring us for himself with his blood he obtained that he might have as servants us, over whom Satan ruled because of sin, liberated from the power of darkness, translated into his kingdom, over whom he rules both in this and in the other life, in the kingdom of grace and glory. Therefore, these things are not to be taken, as with the Socinians and Pontificians, to whom Grotius seems to incline here, as if Christ had acquired for himself by his death any dominion or glory, but since he was Lord over all, even before his death, that he willed to die for us, and to rise again, that he might claim us for himself,

he could certainly have had a heavenly life, without the intervention of death, had he not been destined to die for us; nay, he was in the form of God, before he freely took upon himself the mortal hardships, and royal power, as one born a King, since he had all things whatsoever in his hands, even in the days of his flesh, Matt. XI. 27. John III. 35. ch. XIII. 3. but as far as concerns the possession or ownership: But as for the use or enjoyment, he had emptied himself of his power for the sake of our redemption; meeting death for us, so that he might merit for us grace and salvation, but not that he might acquire for himself Royal power and Dominion. Or he says this to persuade you, (as Theophylact's interpretation has it,) that the Lord of those who are weaker will take care of them, so that they may eventually return to the way, because he both shed his blood and underwent death, so that he might have right and authority over us. By what means, therefore, does he not also provide for those who have been reduced to his service, and for whose sake he has suffered so much.

Latin:

v. 9. εἰς τῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς καὶ ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέση καὶ ἀνέζησεν, ἵνα καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων κυριεύσῃ. Debetur ei hoc Dominium ex Patris decreto, qui ideò eum mori sivit, ut suscitaret, suscitavit, ut vitam ei cœlestem daret, conjunctam cum regia potestate in Ecclesiam, & pro Ecclesia. In Manuscripto tantùm est ἀπέθανε κὰι ἔζησε. Et sic videtur legisse Latinus & Theophylactus.

Digreditur Apostolus in locum communem, adhibitâ à servis similitudine, in quos Domini quondam jus vitæ, & necis habebant; ideò Chri- sto Domino potestatem in vitam & mortem con- venire docet: ut nos non tantùm in hac vita, sed etiam in morte Christo proprios esse constet: & quum Domini civiles tantùm in vivos dominium habeant, in mortuos autem servos dominari am- pliùs nequeant: Christum in mortuos etiam dominari, monet, imò ideò mortuum esse, & revixisse, ut & mortuorum & viventium Do- minus esset, non quòd meruerit sibi gloriam Christus morte sua, sed quòd nos sibi sanguine suo acquirens obtinuerit, ut nos, quibus domi- nabatur ob peccatum Satanas, servos haberet, liberatos à potestate tenebrarum, translatos in regnum suum, quibus dominetur & in hac, & in altera vita, in regno gratiæ & gloriæ. Non ergò cum Socinianis & Pontificiis, ad quos incli- nare hìc videtur Grotius, hæc eò accipienda, quasi morte suâ sibi Christus dominium, vel gloriam aliquam acquisiverit, sed quum Dominus fuerit super omnia, etiam ante mortem, quòd pro nobis mori voluerit, & resurgere, ut nos sibi vendicaret;

vitam utique cœlestem habere, citra mortis inter- ventum, poterat, nisi pro nobis moriendum fuis- set, imò in forma Dei erat, antequam τὰς θνητὰς δυσχερείας liberè affumeret, & regiam potestatem, utpote Rex natus, quin omnia omninò in mani- bus habebat, etiam in diebus carnis, Matth. XI. 27. Ioh. III. 35. c. XIII. 3. sed quantum ad κτῆσιν, vel possessionem: Cæterum quod ad χρῆσιν, vel usurpa- tione potestate sua sese evacuaverat nostræ redem- tionis gratiâ; pro nobis mortem oppetens, ut sci- licet nobis gratiam, & salutem promereretur, non autem ut sibi potestatem Regiam & Dominium acquireret. Vel hoc ait, tibi ut suadeat, (ut habet interpretatio Theophylacti,) Dominum eorum, qui imbecilliores sunt, suscepurum curam, ut in viam redeant tandem, quia & sanguinem fuderit, & sub- ierit mortem, ut in nobis jus & imperium habeat. Quo ergò pacto non & illis prospiciat, qui in ejus sint servitutem redacti, & quorum causâ sit tàm mul- ta perpessus.

## 14:10
v. 10. But you, why do you judge your brother? You, Christian, observing the rites of the law, why do you consider another as impious who is no less than you fulfilling the precepts of Christ?

Or why do you also despise your brother? You, Christian, believing yourself free from rites, why do you despise another living as a Christian as if he were unskilled because he does not yet sufficiently understand that right given by Christ? Concerning the word ἐξουθενεῖν see above,

For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Why do you usurp his office? It is his to judge concerning hidden things. He alone knows how much knowledge each person has received, how much ought to be required of him according to the measure of his talent. The tribunal is attributed to Christ as judge, both in 2 Cor. V. 10. and they are accustomed to stand whose case is being handled. Divine matters, however, are accustomed to be explained after the manner of human ones.

Latin:

v. 10. σὺ δὲ κρίνεις τὸν ἀδελφόν σου. Tu Christiane legis ritus observans, cur pro impio ha- beas alterum non minus quam tu præcepta Christi implen- tem?

ἢ καὶ σὺ τί ἐξουθενεῖς τὸν ἀδελφόν σου. Tu, Christiane, liberum te à ritibus credens, cur alte- rum Christianè viventem aspernaris tanquam imperitum quòd jus illud à Christo datum nondum satis intelligat? De verbo ἐξουθενεῖν vide supra,

Πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Quid occupas illius officium? Illius est de occultis judi- care. Solus novit, quantum cognitionis quisque accepe- rit, quantum ab eo pro talenti sui modo exigi debeat. Tribunal Christo ut judici attribuitur, & 2. Cor. V. 10. & stare solent, quorum causa tractatur. Solent autem res divinæ ad humanarum modum explicari.

## 14:11
v. 11. For it is written. Is. XLV. 23. As I live, says the Lord. In the Hebrew and Greek of Isaiah: I swear by myself. This oath of God, however, is accustomed to be expressed in other places by the words: As I live: as Is. XLIX. 18. XVII. 16. 19. XVIII. 3. XX. 3 Zeph. II. 9. God speaks to Isaiah: but also the honor which is held for Christ returns to the Father as the Author,

that to me every knee shall bow. Thus also the LXX in the cited place of Isaiah, and it is understood, he shall bow himself, in which way the Hebrew תִכרַע is taken

of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth. These do not belong here, nor are they contained in the better books, nor does the Syriac read it, nor the Arabic, nor Origen, nor Chrysostom, nor Oecumenius. It crept in here in certain books from the passage Phil. II. 10.

and every tongue shall confess to God. In the Hebrew and Greek: every tongue shall swear by God. But the sense is correctly expressed: for as we said regarding the passage of Isaiah, all worship of God is accustomed to be expressed by one species, that is, by an oath, as in Isaiah XIX. 18. Rightly, therefore, Paul, unfolding that figure, rendered the genus for the species.

That God the Father is not speaking in Isaiah, but the Son of God himself, was sufficiently shown both from this undoubted testimony of the Apostle, who teaches that knees are to be bowed to him according to the Prophet, before whose throne he says we must be placed; and from that Isaianic passage, when we treated that Prophetic oracle: which, although it deals with the faith and confession of Christ, which is required of all in this life, is nevertheless aptly applied to the final judgment, in which Christ, that universal Lord of all the living and the dead, will be openly acknowledged by all men. For it is the same Lord, in whom one must believe here, and whom all ought to confess, to whom all knees must be bowed on the day of the Almighty; and it is enough for the Apostle to be taught that by the Prophet, that Christ is the Lord, to whom all who are to be saved ought to bow their knees; and the Apostle here manifests that this will be acknowledged by all in the final judgment, both those who have obtained salvation through faith, and those who remain under the wrath of God because of unbelief; adding also the name to God, when in the Hebrew it is simply, and every tongue shall swear, and not to God
