the name, as Grotius believed without inspecting the text, has been added: because that confession, in the Lord (JESUS) is righteousness, is to God the Father, whom he distinguishes from the Son, to whom the Apostle indicates by the second-person pronoun that knees are to be bowed, looking to the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and it tends to the honor of God the Father, by whom Christ was made righteousness for us, 1 Cor. I. 30. whence Phil. II. 11. every tongue, says the Apostle, shall confess, that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father. Moreover, besides the fact that the citation of this passage exhibits a notable testimony for establishing the eternal Deity of Christ, it also contains signs by which the divine majesty of the man Christ is indicated: For both the judgment, which God the Father gave to his Son not as God, but because he is the son of man, and the universal genuflection, which has the indication of religious worship, openly prove that Christ, in respect of the flesh assumed, shares that glory which is naturally proper to the Divinity. Conf. Joh. V. 22. 2. Cor. V. 10.

Latin:

v. 11. γέγραπται γάρ. Es. XLV. 23. ζῶ ἐγὼ, λέγει Κύριος. In Hebræo & Græco Esaiæ: κατ' ἐμαυτοῦ ὀμνύω. Hoc autem Dei juramentum aliis locis exprimi solet per verba: Vivo ego: ut Es. XLIX. 18. XVII. 16. 19. XVIII. 3. XX. 3 Soph. II. 9. Deus loquitur ad Esaiam: sed & honor, qui Christo habetur, ad Patrem ut Auctorem redit,

ὅτι ἐμοὶ κάμψει πᾶν γόνυ. Sic & LXX. dicto Esaiæ loco, & intelligitur, κάμψει ἑαυ- τὸ se flectet, quomodo sumitur Hebræum תִכרַע

ἐπουρανίων, καὶ ἐπιγείων, καὶ καταχθονίων. Hæc huc non pertinent, neque habentur in libris melio- ribus, neque Syrus id legit, neque Arabs, neque Origenes neque Chrysostomus, neque Oecumenius. Irrepsit huc in quibusdam libris ex loco Philipp. II. 10.

καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ Θεῷ. In Hebræo & Græco: ὀμεῖται πᾶσα γλῶσσα τὸν Θεόν. Sed sensus rectè expressus est: nam ut ad Esaiæ locum diximus, cultus omnis Dei per speciem unam, id est, per juramen- tum exprimi solet, ut Esaiæ XIX. 18. Rectè igitur Paulus figuram illam evolvens, pro specie genus reddidit.

Non loqui Deum Patrem apud Esaiam, sed ipsummet Filium Dei, tùm ex indubitato hocce Apostoli testimonio, qui ei juxtà Prophetam, cur- vanda esse genua docet, coram cujus throno nos si- stendos esse, ait; tùm è loco isto Esaiano satis ostensum fuit, cùm oraculum illud Propheticum tractavimus: quod etsi de fide & confessione Chri- sti agat, quæ ab omnibus requiritur in hac vita, aptè tamen ad extremum judicium, in quo Chri- stus Dominus ille universalis omnium vivorum & mortuorum ab omnibus hominibus palam agno- scetur, applicatur. Idem enim est Dominus, in quem hìc credendum, quemque confiteri omnes debent, cui omnium genua flectenda in die pan- tocritico; & satis est Apostolo id doceri à Prophe- ta, Christum esse Dominum, cui omnes salvandi ge- nua flectere debeant; id autem in novissimo judicio ab omnibus, tùm qui per fidem salutem adepti, tùm qui ob incredulitatem sub ira Dei manent, agnitum iri per SpiritumS. hîc manifestat Aposto- lus; adjiciens etiam nomen τῷ Θεῷ, cum in Ebræo simpliciter, & jurabit omnis lingua, nec τῷ Θεῷ

nomen, uti Grotius non inspecto textu credidit, additum sit: quia confessio illa, in Domino (JESU) justitia, sit Deo Patri, quem distinguit à Filio, cui genua flectenda Apostolus pronomine secundæ personæ indicat, S. S. Trinitatis mysterium respiciens, & in honorem Dei Patris vergit, à quo factus est nobis Christus justitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. unde Phil. II. 11. πᾶσα γλῶσσα, inquit Apostolus, ἐξομολογήσεται, ὅτι Κύριος Ἰησῦς Χρισὸς εἰς δόξαν Θεῦ πατρός. Præterquam verò, quòd loci istius allegatio pro æterna Deitate Christi stabilienda insigne testimonium exhibeat, simul etiam notas continet, quibus divina hominis Christi majestas subindicatur: Nam & judicium, quod Deus Pater Filio suo non quà Deus, sed quia filius hominis est, dedit, & genuflexio universalis, quæ religiosi cultûs indicium habet, palàm evincunt, Christum ex parte assumtæ carnis communicare eam gloriam, quæ est Divinitatis naturaliter propria. Conf. Joh. V. 22. 2. Cor. V. 10.

## 14:12
v. 12. So then each of us shall give an account of himself to God.

Whether he has answered to the measure of knowledge which he received. Δώσει for ἀποδώσει, just as in Luke XVI. 2. ἀπόδος τὸν λόγον, and Heb. XIII. 17 ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες, and 1 Pet. IV. 5. ἀποδώσυσι λόγον. So also Dan. VI. 2.

It is taught that in general an account must be rendered, yet we do not deny that these things, which the Apostle treats here, are specifically included. Since therefore everyone is to bear his own burden, not another's, and indeed everyone will have enough to do in rendering an account of his own affairs, this ought rightly to recall us to modesty, lest we rashly usurp the roles of judging others.

PART II. CONCERNING THE RULES BY WHICH THE USE OF INDIFFERENT THINGS IS TO BE GOVERNED.

Latin:

v. 12. Ἄρα ὖν ἕκαστος ἡμῶν περὶ ἑαυτῦ λόγον δώσει τῷ Θεῷ.

An responderit mensuræ cognitionis, quam accepit. Δώσει pro ἀποδώσει, quomodo Lucæ XVI. 2. ἀπόδος τὸν λόγον, & Hebr. XIII. 17 ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες, & 1. Pet. IV. 5. ἀποδώσυσι λόγον. Sic & Dan. VI. 2.

In genere rationem reddendam esse docetur, non tamen abnuimus, specialiter hæc, quæ tractat hìc Apostolus, comprehendi. Cùm ergò quilibet suum, non alienum onus portaturus sit, & verò quisque suarum rerum rationem quod reddat, habiturus abundè sit, meritò hic ad modestiam nos revocare debet, ne vices judicandi alios temerè usurpemus.

PARS II. DE REGULIS, QUIBUS ADIAPHORORUM USUS GUBERNANDUS.

## 14:13
v. 13. Let us not judge one another anymore.

For that is dangerous in doubtful matters, because whatever judgment you have passed on another, such will be passed on you, Matt. VII. where see the sayings.

but judge this rather.

Supply 'to be done'. A similar expression 1 Cor. VII. 37. There is, however, an ἀντανάκλασις, with κρίνωμεν and κρίνατε in a different sense.

Not to put a stumbling block or a scandal before a brother.

That is, do not rashly give anyone an occasion either for not approaching Christianity or for receding from it; the former is signified by the word πρόσκομμα, the latter by σκάνδαλον, which is the graver term. See Matt. IV. 6. 1 Cor. VIII. 9. Matt. V. 49. XIII. 41. XVIII. 7. below XIV. 20. 21. Now both the Jews, who wished to impose the yoke of the law upon the unaccustomed Gentiles, and the Christians from among the Gentiles, who repelled from the Church the Jews who were hesitant in this matter, were doing this. We cannot avoid all occasions of others' falls, but those are to be avoided to which we are driven by no necessity or utility.

Indeed, some rules concerning indifferent things can be gathered from the above, such as (1.) that the weak are not to be disturbed regarding indifferent matters, v. 1. (2.) Nor are they to be rashly despised or judged, v. 3. (3.) That nothing is to be done with a hesitant mind, v. 4. 5. (4.) That all things are to be directed toward obedience to the word and the glory of the divine name and performed with thanksgiving, v. 6. But those things deal properly with the receiving of the weak, or were brought in as an example of arguments for their sake. Now, however, the Apostle directs and circumscribes the use of these indifferent things with certain rules: such as 1. That no stumbling block or scandal be placed before a brother: since nothing is unclean in itself, but only to him who judges something to be unclean, v. 13. 14. 2. That charity ought to be the guide in the use of indifferent things, so that a brother is not lost on account of food or other indifferent things, v. 15. 3. That an opening is to be avoided, lest our good be blasphemed, v. 16. 4. Those things which make for peace and mutual edification are to be followed, v. 19. 5. Nothing is to be done when the conscience is in doubt, v. 22.

Latin:

v. 13. Μηκέτι ἀλλήλυς κρίνωμεν.

Periculosum enim id in rebus dubiis, quia quale de alio judicium tuleris, tale de te feretur, Matth. VII. ubi dicta vide.

ἀλλὰ τῦτο κρίνατε μᾶλλον.

Supple faciendum. Similis locutio 1. Cor. VII. 37. Est autem ἀντανάκλασις, κρίνωμεν & κρίνατε sensu diverso.

Τὸ μὴ τιθέναι πρόσκομμα ἀδελφῷ ἢ σκάνδαλον.

Id est, ne occasionem temerè detis alicui, aut non accedendi ad Christianismum, aut ab eo recedendi, illud πρόσκομμα, hoc σκάνδαλον voce, quæ gravior est, significatur. Vide Matth. IV. 6. 1. Corinth. VIII. 9. Matth. V. 49. XIII. 41. XVIII. 7. infrà XIV. 20. 21. Hoc autem faciebant & Judæi, qui gentibus insuetis imponere volebant legis jugum, & è gentibus Christiani, qui Judæos hac in re hæsitantes ab Ecclesiâ repellebant. Occasiones omnes alienorum lapsuum vitare non possumus, sed vitandæ sunt eæ, ad quas necessirate nulla aut utilitate impellimur.

Regulæ quidem nonnullæ è superioribus colligi possunt, de adiaphoris, utpote (1.) infirmos non esse quoad indifferentia perturbandos, v. 1. (2.) Nec temerè contemnendos aut judicandos v. 3. (3.) Nihil animo hæsitabundo faciendum esse, v. 4. 5. (4.) Ad obsequium verbi & gloriam nominis divini dirigenda & cum gratiarum actione peragenda esse omnia, v. 6. Sed illa propriè de infirmis suscipiendis agunt, aut eorum causâ rationum instar adducta sunt. Nunc autem dirigit & circumscribit Apostolus certis regulis usum ipsorum adiaphororum: utpote 1. Ne fratri ponatur offendiculum, aut scandalum: quum per se nihil immundum sit, sed illi solùm, qui immundum aliquid judicat, v. 13. 14. 2. Charitatem debere esse directricem in usu indifferentium, ne propter cibum vel alia adiaphora frater perdatur, v. 15. 3. Vitandam esse ansam, ne bonum nostrum blasphemetur, v. 16. 4. Sectanda esse ea, quæ pacis sunt, & mutuæ ædificationis, v. 19. 5. Nihil faciendum disceptante conscientiâ, v. 22.

## 14:14
v. 14. I know and am persuaded in Christ Jesus. That is, through Christ, who revealed this to me more openly than to others. See above VII.

that nothing is common through it. By itself, that is, by nature. κοινὸν בּוּל. See what was said on Matt. XVII. & Act. VII. 14. Certain nations even eat serpents. He assumes, however, that no law was given to the nations concerning that matter: and he had already shown before that it was taken away from the Jews.

unless to him who considers anything to be common, to him it is common. Because nothing is lawful to him who believes something is unlawful, while he believes it. We spoke about this axiom in book II. of the Law of War and Peace XXIII. 2. λογιζομένῳ to one thinking, as above II. 3. III. 28. VI. 11. VIII. 18.

He does not say that he has knowledge from Christ, but that he is persuaded in Christ Jesus that nothing is common by itself: because that is from the liberty obtained through Christ, through whom, and under whom, that Levitical distinction of clean and unclean things was abrogated, which was not of nature, but only of position and ceremonial ordinance, so that, on the contrary, to those believing in Christ, that is, to the clean, all things are clean, Tit. I, 15. But if any impurity adheres to things, the Apostle teaches that it is not from the property or quality of nature, but is accidental, namely from the opinion and conscience of one judging wrongly. But if it happens that things created are misused by the impious, this does not prejudice the use of good things in those matters. For the abuse of the impious does not contaminate the things themselves. But in these matters, conscience is the best judge for everyone, for whoever considers something as illicit, although it may not be such, yet by that very fact he is bound to abstain through conscience, until he has been taught more correctly. But what if conscience can make a sin out of a non-sin, can it also make a non-sin out of a sin? By no means: because God himself has defined in his word what is a sin, which man cannot change. It is one thing in matters indifferent by themselves, in which there is no sin by itself; but which things God himself judges as such, depends on the affection of the user. Therefore the Papists, who by infinite laws establish as unclean things which are not such, will one day be condemned by these very laws, because they acted against them while their conscience resisted, v. 15. if indeed because of food your brother is grieved. That is, if you defend your liberty in such a way that you reproach him for his lack of skill. Τὸ βρῶμα מַאֲכוֹל in the Law and the Talmudic writings.

you no longer walk according to love. Love, from which this whole discourse flows, not only wants those to be tolerated who do not yet see everything, but also that our liberty be curtailed for their good. It is an argument from the greater to the less. The foundation, however, is in the passage of Hosea VI. 6.

do not destroy him with your food, for whom Christ died. Christ died for all men, among whom are also those who will perish, John III. 16. 1. Timoth. II. 4. 5. 6. 2. Pet. II. 1. III. 9. Hebr. X. 29. Clearly the same as what is said here 1. Cor. VIII. 11. He who does not understand that liberty, and for that reason sees himself treated more harshly, can easily be led to doubt the Gospel first, and then to think otherwise. Wherefore such minds are to be treated gently, and if possible, taught, not blunted. μὴ ἀπόλλυε לֹא תֹאבַר.

Not only is the neighbor thus saddened while his lack of skill is reproached, but especially while he is judged or condemned for the use of indifferent things, as if he were a prevaricator. Rightly, however, is universal redemption by Christ asserted from this, that Christ also died for and made satisfaction for those who perish, which is a brilliant argument against the absolute and fatal decree of Predestination, and the dogma of the Calvinists full of despair, concerning the redeemed being only the absolutely elect.

Latin:

v. 14. οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Id est, per Christum, qui mihi hoc apertiùs, quàm aliis revelavit. Vide supra VII.

ὅτι οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι' αὐτό. Per se, id est, naturâ. κοινὸν בּוּל. Vide, quæ dicta Matt. XVII. & Act. VII. 14. Etiam serpentibus gentes quædam vescuntur. Supponit autem, nullam esse de ea re gentibus legem datam: & ab Judæis ablatam jam antè ostenderat.

εἰ μὴ τῷ λογιζομένῳ τι κοινὸν εἶναι, ἐκείνῳ κοινόν. Quia nihil licitum ei, qui illicitum aliquid credit, dum id credit. Diximus de hoc axiomate libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XXIII. 2. λογιζομένῳ existimanti, ut supra II. 3. III. 28. VI. 11. VIII. 18.

Non notitiam à Christo se habere dicit, sed per- suasum esse in Christo Jesu, quòd nihil per se com- mune sit: quia id à libertate per Christum partâ est, per quem, & sub quo abrogatum discrimen illud mundorum adque immundorum Leviticum, quod non φύσεως fuit, sed tantum θέσεως & ordinatio- nis cæremonialis, quam ex adverso credentibus in Christum, id est, mundis, omnia sint munda, Tit. I, 15. Si quæ autem rebus adhærescat impuritas, eam non ex naturæ proprietate seu qualitate, sed acci- dentariam esse, nempe ex opinione & conscientia perperam judicantis, docet Apostolus. Quod si ab impiis res conditas malè usurpari contingat, hoc bonorum usui in rebus istis non præjudicat. Neque enim impiorum abusus res ipsas contami- nat. Sed in his conscientia unicuique judex opti- mus est, quisquis enim pro illicito aliquid habet, licet tale non sit, tamen eo ipso per conscientiam abstinere tenetur, donec rectiùs edoctus fuerit. Quid verò si conscientia ex non peccato potest pecca- tum facere, num etiam ex peccato potest facere non peccatum? Minimè verò: quia quod peccatum sit, Deus ipse in verbo suo definivit, quod homo mu- tare non potest. Aliud est, in rebus per se indiffe- rentibus, in quibus per se peccatum non est; quas verò tales Deus ipse judicat, qualis est affectus usurpantis. Ideò Papistæ, qui infinitis legibus im- munda statuunt, quæ talia non sunt, his ipsis legi- bus olim condemnabuntur, quòd repugnante conscientiâ contra easdem egerint, v. 15. εἰ δὲ διὰ βρῶμα ὁ ἀδελφός σου λυπεῖται. Id est, si libertatem tuam ita defendis, ut ipsi imperitiam exprobres. Τὸ βρῶμα מַאֲכוֹל in Lege & Talmudicis.

οὐκέτι κατὰ ἀγάπην περιπατεῖς. Dilectio, unde totus hic sermo fluit, non modò vult tole- rari eos, qui nondum omnia pervident, sed etiam illorum bono libertatem nostram circumcidi. Est argumentum à majori ad minus. Fundamentum autem in loco Oseæ VI. 6.

μὴ τῷ βρώματί σου ἐκεῖνον ἀπόλλυε, ὑπὲρ οὗ Χριστὸς ἀπέθανε. Christus pro omnibus hominibus mortuus est, in quibus sunt & illi, qui peribunt, Joh. III. 16. 1. Timoth. II. 4. 5. 6. 2. Pet. II. 1. III. 9. Hebr. X. 29. Planè idem, quod hic dicitur 1. Cor. VIII. 11. Qui istam libertatem non intelligit, & ob id duriùs tractari se videt, facile eò perduci potest, ut de Ev- angelio dubitet primùm, deinde & sequius existimet. Qua- re leniter tractanda, & si fieri potest, edocenda, non obtun- denda sunt ingenia & ejusmodi. μὴ ἀπόλλυε לֹא תֹאבַר.

Non tantùm ita contristatur proximus, dum exprobratur ipsi imperitia, sed imprimis dum ob usum indifferentium judicatur vel condemnatur, quasi prævaricator. Rectè autem asseritur hinc universalis Christi redemtio, quod etiam pro illis mortuus sit, & satisfecerit Christus, qui pereunt, quod argumentum luculentum est adversus abso- lutum & fatale Prædestinationis decretum, & de- sperationis plenum dogma Calvinianorum, de re- demtis solis absolutè electis.

## 14:16
v. 16. Let not then your good be blasphemed. The Syriac and Latin read our, well: and the good succinctly for the good work. The same manner of speaking is in the Epistle to the Philippians. The good is Christian liberty: but if schisms arise from it, it is ill-spoken of among outsiders.

Others more correctly understand the good as the doctrine of the Gospel, which ought to be in the place of the highest treasure for us, lest it become liable to such blasphemies, as if the hinge of the Christian religion consisted only in food and drink: whence, lest such a thing be established, the Apostle informs about it, in what the kingdom of God is situated. Therefore it is the title of the Christian religion that it is called good by way of excellence, nay indeed it is the highest good.

Latin:

v. 16. μὴ βλασφημείσθω ὖν ὑμῶν τὸ ἀγαθὸν. Syrus & Latinus legerunt ἡμῶν, benè: & τὸ ἀγαθὸν suc- cinctè pro τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἔργον. Idem loquendi genus in Epi- stola ad Philippenses. Bonum est libertas Christiana: sed si inde schismata oriantur, malè audit apud extraneos.

Alii rectiùs bonum intelligunt de doctrina Ev- angelii, quæ summi thesauri loco nobis esse de- beat, ne illa fiat blasphemiis ejusmodi obno- xia, quasi cardo religionis Christianae tantum con- sistat in cibo & potu : unde ne tale quid statuatur, de eo informat Apostolus, in quonam situm sit re- gnum Dei. Religionis ergo Christianae titulus est, quod ἐξοχικῶς bonum dicatur, imo vero sum- mum bonum sit.

## 14:17
v. 17. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink.

It is a metonymy. The right to the heavenly kingdom is not obtained by drinking or eating, 1. Cor. VIII. 8. There is need of other acts. We had a similar manner of speaking above VIII. 6.

but righteousness.

Innocence. The passages of Isaiah LIV and LXII are referred to.

and peace,

That is, the pursuit of peace.

and joy in the Holy Spirit.

The care of gladdening others through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, but not of irritating them, which he just called λυπεῖν. See above I. 12.

Latin:

v. 17. ὀὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ βρῶσις καὶ πόσις.

Est μετωνυμία. Non bibendo neque edendo paratur jus ad regnum coeleste, 1. Cor. VIII. 8. Aliis actibus opus. Si- mile loquendi genus habuimus supra VIII. 6.

ἀλλὰ δικαιοσύνη.

Innocentia. Respiciuntur loca Esaiae LIV, & LXII.

καὶ εἰρήνη,

Id est, pacis studium.

καὶ χαρὰ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ.

Cura exhilarandi alios per dona Spiritus Sancti, non au- tem eos irritandi, quod modo dixit λυπεῖν. Vide supra I. 12.

## 14:18
v. 18. For he who in these things serves God,

Through such acts.

is well-pleasing to God and approved by men.

He will be able to promise himself both the favor of God and praise from pious men. We had the word ἐυαρέστου above XII. 1. 2. ἐυάρεστος τῷ Θεῷ, that is, טוב לפני אלהים. δόκιμος is one who is approved, as below XVI. 10. 1 Cor. XI. 19. 2 Cor. X. 18. XIII. 7. 2 Tim. II. 15. Jas. I. 12. It is properly said of gold or money, as can be seen in Gen. XXIII. 16. 1 Kgs. X. 18. Zech. XI. 13. 2 Chr. IX. 17. XXVIII. 18. XXIX. 4.

This is a most unworthy corruption of the golden Apostolic Aphorism: by which it is taught not by what things the kingdom of God is acquired, but in what it consists, both negatively, that it is not situated in the use of food and drink or similar indifferent things: for the genus is designated by the species: and positively, that it consists in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. And it is false, and diametrically contrary to Apostolic doctrine, that the Kingdom of God is acquired or obtained by our own righteousness or innocence, pursuit of peace, and care of gladdening others through the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For it is not by our obedience or righteousness, but by the righteousness and obedience of Christ alone that we are constituted righteous, Rom. V. 19, ch. X. 4, which the Apostle clearly taught is done χωρὶς ἔργων, without our works; nor do we prepare for ourselves a right to the heavenly kingdom through our innocence, but it is prepared for us through the merit and obedience of Christ; and therefore those are condemned who strive to erect their own righteousness here, so that they might obtain salvation through it, and thus derogate from the righteousness of Christ, ch. IX and X. Nor did Isaiah teach otherwise, but he referred us solely to the righteousness of Christ, ch. XLV. 24, 25, and taught that we are justified through faith in this righteous servant of God, ch. LIII. 11, and therefore that we are to be clothed in the robe of the righteousness of Christ, ch. LXI. 10, as one who has been made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. I. 30, and in whom we are made the righteousness of God, 2 Cor. V. 21, whom we put on by faith, as the Apostle testifies, Gal. III. 26. Wherefore the RIGHTEOUSNESS of faith, which the Apostle asserted in this whole treatment, is understood, when the Kingdom of God is said to be righteousness, and not indeed the righteousness of works, whether moral or ceremonial. And this is the reason why the Apostle wished to append to his treatment concerning justification by faith an instruction concerning adiaphora, namely to teach that he wished works of the ceremonial law to be no less excluded and removed than those of the moral, as inept for justification, since it is accomplished by faith alone, without works, and that Christian righteousness is something other than works of this kind, as the Augsburg Confession observes in the article concerning the distinction of foods. Now peace here does not denote a desire for concord, or external peace with others, but the internal peace and tranquility of conscience, concerning which the Apostle had discoursed in Rom. V, inasmuch as it immediately redounds in the hearts of believers from justification through faith, and which alone can keep [them] in Christ Jesus unto life eternal, Phil. IV. 7. in which we have solid and true joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. V. 1. et seqq., because we are certain of the grace of God and the heavenly inheritance: than which full assurance nothing more joyful, nothing more desirable can befall us: which also provides us with a certain foretaste, or some anticipation of the mighty works of the future age, Heb. VI. 5. These three, therefore, the righteousness of Christ, which we apprehend through faith; peace with God the Father, which the justified enjoy on account of Christ, and joy in the Holy Spirit, which arises from our justification and peace of conscience, are truly the kingdom of GOD; and the enjoyment of the Holy Trinity; which we have in the kingdom of grace, is completed by these three things laid before us, or treasures, than which the faithful and the elect of the Lord possess nothing more precious. By joy in the Holy Spirit is understood that gladness which the faithful themselves perceive in their own heart, of which the holy Psalmist Ps. LXIX. 4. and the holy Apostle Phil. IV. 5. is understood, but not that with which they themselves imbue and exhilarate others. Blessed Hunnius explains and paraphrases it thus: Those adiaphorous and middle things are so constituted that with a good conscience you can, for the sake of the weak, abstain from their use when there is need. For the kingdom of God, begun in this age and to be consummated in the other, is not placed in these indifferent things, in food and drink; but is defined by other far greater and necessary things, namely, righteousness, which we obtain by faith in Christ: then peace of conscience and joy, not earthly, but spiritual, and, as Peter names it, ineffable and glorified, with which the reborn, by the consideration of the benefits of Christ, exult in their hearts through the Holy Spirit. And in the cited places n. VI. Note the description of the kingdom of God; which is not defined by earthly goods, but by those clearly divine and heavenly, righteousness availing before God, than which there is nothing more important to a Christian man; likewise peace of conscience, which, as the Apostle testifies, surpasses all understanding, Philip. IV. Likewise sincere and solid joy, with which the pious always rejoice in the Lord, and in the most pleasant sense of divine grace rest most sweetly, and are as it were inebriated by the torrent of His benefits, and are refreshed to a sense of immortality. Which, although they are only begun in the kingdom of grace; yet they are certainly a kind of taste of the perpetual blessedness of the children of God, which will be fully perfected in the kingdom of glory, where, adorned with the garment of eternal righteousness, we shall enjoy perpetual peace of God, exulting with ineffable and truly glorified joy, which will never be contaminated by any sickness anywhere for eternity. Just as the Prophet Isaiah preaches about this joy of the elect in the blessed life, ch. XV. XXXV. LXV. and Rev. VII. Similarly Blessed Balduinus: The kingdom of God is considered insofar as it is either the kingdom of grace, in this age, or the kingdom of glory, in the other life. In neither case is anything promoted by the use or eating of food formerly prohibited in the Law: for as Christ speaks elsewhere: the kingdom of God does not come with external observation Luke XVII. 20. But there are other far greater things in which the kingdom of God consists, three of which are recounted here: (1.) righteousness, that indeed by which we are reputed just before the judgment of God, and which we obtain only by faith in Christ. (2.) peace, which we have before God through Christ. (3.) joy, by which he understands the tranquility of conscience, which is the beginning of eternal life, and results from the former. For those who are justified by faith have peace with God, Rom. V. thence is perpetual exultation even in adversities: for such people glory in tribulations, because they have a continual feast in a good conscience. Thus also Pareus from the Reformed: He understands the righteousness of faith, about which he had argued at length above, internal peace, the tranquility of conscience or cheerfulness, which follows justification, ch. V. From the two is mixed a third, gladness, with which we always exult in the Lord, and glory under the hope of the glory of GOD ch. V. 2. Pareus adds to the righteousness of faith the righteousness of the cause, and to peace

and internal conscience an external love of peace, and a zeal for peace, which was also done by Flacius; But although these things cohere; the former as cause and effect, as root and fruit, the latter as necessary connections, because a zeal for concord accompanies faith, and is necessary for the faithful so as not to disturb the peace of conscience; yet such diverse things cannot be noted by one word in the same place, and if all consequences and connected things are to be referred to the meaning of the word, what will not be noted by the same word at the same time? The Apostle speaks of those things in which the kingdom of God and salvation properly consist: not indeed those things which are to be done by those established in the kingdom of God. For concerning these things it follows now under the word of service, which is proper to subjects in this kingdom, as those who serve God alone, and are comprehended by that one word: For he who in these things serves Christ, is acceptable to GOD, and approved by men: not he who serves Christ in food and drink, but he who in the righteousness of faith, peace of conscience, and joy in the Holy Spirit performs the due services to this his Lord, through whom he obtains and possesses those things, and thus enjoys the goods and treasures of the kingdom of God: for he does not teach through what we may serve Christ, but with what those who truly serve the Lord are instructed: that indeed, possessing the righteousness of faith and peace with God, and imbued with spiritual gladness, they may serve Christ with the greatest alacrity. For without these there is no service of Christ well-pleasing to God, and our zeal ought to be occupied in retaining these three: which will render us more pleasing to God and men than if, with no regard for the weak, we used all foods indifferently. But the service itself, by which we both truly serve Christ our Lord, and please our God, and are rendered approved to men, is situated both in faith, without which it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI. 6. and in charity, or the love of God and neighbor: whence it is manifest that neither food nor drink, nor other external things of that kind, contribute anything to the kingdom of God, nor to service in the kingdom of God, by which, however, those who seemed strong to themselves were disturbing the weak; by which also the Pope with his clergy, exalting themselves in the name of spiritual things, vehemently disturb their subjects today; so much so that some do not hesitate to constitute these three in the abstinence prescribed in the Papacy, which is from certain kinds of foods, as we see in Estius in this place.

(1.) Estius’s [view on] justice, because by such abstinence we make satisfaction to God for sins committed against Him: which is no less injurious to the justice of God, which certainly does not demand abstinence from certain foods in place of satisfaction for sins, nor is it content with that, but demands eternal punishment and requires most perfect obedience, than it is to the satisfaction and merit of our one Redeemer Christ Jesus, who alone paid the penalty for our sins and performed the obedience due to the law in our place. (2.) [His view on] peace, whereby through abstinence we subjugate the flesh to the Spirit; because neither does abstinence from certain foods do anything toward subjugating the flesh, nor does that subjugation produce a solid peace of conscience; because it is in many ways imperfect, and more often fails: whence no true tranquility, but mere doubt arises, if peace with God within ought to rely upon the subjugation of the flesh. Finally (3.) the joy of the Holy Spirit, because through abstinence from food and drink the mind is rendered more alert for contemplating divine things: but although this is true in its own way regarding abstinence and fasting in the true sense, it is not true regarding the choice of foods; yet joy in the Holy Spirit arises and overflows not from contemplation, but from the gratuitous remission of sins and justification, and interior peace, and tranquility of conscience.

Latin:

v. 18. ὁ γὰρ ἐν τούτοις δουλεύων τῷ Θεῷ,

Per tales actus.

ἐυάρεστος τῷ Θεῷ καὶ δόκιμος τοῖς ἀνθρώποις.

Is & Dei favorem sibi polliceri poterit, & laudem ab ho- minibus piis. Vocem ἐυαρέστου habuimus supra XII. 1. 2. ἐυάρεστος τῷ Θεῷ, id est, טוב לפני אלהים δόκιμος est, qui probatur, ut infra XVI. 10. 1. Cor. XI. 19. 2. Cor. X. 18. XIII. 7. 2. Tim. II. 15. Jac. I. 12. Proprie de auro aut pe- cunia dicitur, ut videre est Genes. XXIII. 16. 1. Reg. X. 18. Zach. XI. 13. 2. Paralip. IX. 17. XXVIII. 18. XXIX. 4.

Indignissima haec est corruptela aurei Aphori- smi Apostolici : quo non, quibus rebus compare- tur regnum Dei, sed, in quibus consistat, docetur, tum ἀποφατικῶς, quod non situm sit in usu cibi & potus aut similium rerum indifferentium : per spe- ciem enim genus designatur : tum θετικῶς, quod consistat in justitia, pace, & gaudio in S. S. Et fal- sum est, atque Apostolicae doctrinae e diametro contrarium, Regnum Dei propria nostra justitia vel innocentia, pacis studio, & cura exhilarandi alios per dona Spiritus S. acquiri vel comparari. Non enim nostra obedientia vel justitia, sed unius Christi justitia & obedientia nos justi constitui- mur, Rom. V. 19. cap. X. 4. quod χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus nostris fieri luculenter docuit Apostolus; nec jus nobis ad regnum coeleste paramus per no- stram innocentiam, sed id paratum nobis est per Christi meritum & obedientiam; ideoque damnan- tur, qui propriam hic erigere justitiam satagunt, ut per eam salutem consequantur, adeoque justi- tiae Christi derogant, cap. IX. & X. Nec aliud Esaias tradidit, sed unice ad justitiam Christi nos remisit cap. XLV. 24. 25. & per fidem in hunc Dei servum justum nos justificari docuit cap. LIII. 11. atque ideo intuendos esse tunica justitiae Christi, cap. LXI. 10. utpote qui nobis factus est a Deo ju- stitia, 1. Cor. I. 30. & in quo efficimur justitia Dei, 2. Cor. V. 21. quem fide induimus, teste Apostolo Gal. III. 26. Quapropter JUSTITIA fidei, quam asseruit Apostolus in tota hac tractatione, intelli- gitur, cum Regnum Dei justitia esse dicitur, non vero justitia operum, sive moralium, sive ceremonia- lium. Atque haec causa est, cur tractationi suae de justificatione per fidem Apostolus etiam sub- jungere voluerit informationem de adiaphoris, ut nempe doceret, non minus exclusa & remota sese velle opera legis ceremonialis, quam moralis, ceu inepta ad justificationem, quippe quae sola fit fide, sine operibus, & justitiam Christianam aliud quid- dam esse, quam hujusmodi opera, ut artic. de discrim. ciborum observat Aug. Confessio. Pax autem hic non notat concordiae studium, seu pa- cem externam cum aliis, sed internam conscientiae pacem, ac tranquillitatem, de qua Rom. V. disserue- rat Apostolus, utpote quae e justificatione per fide immediate redundat in cordibus credentiu, qua- que sola custodire potest in Christo Jesu ad vitam æternam Phil. IV. 7. in quâ habemus solidum & verum gaudium in Spiritu S. Rom. V. 1. seqq. quia certi sumus de gratia Dei & hæreditate cœlesti: quâ πληροφορίᾳ nihil lætius, nihil exoptatius nobis obtingere potest: quæ etiam nobis præbet quod- dam πρόγευσμα, vel προπολισμὸν aliquem virtutũ futuri seculi, Ebr. VI. 5. Hæc ergò tria, Justitia Christi, quam per fidem apprehendimus; pax cum Deo Patre, quâ fruuntur justificati propter Chri- stum, & gaudium in Spiritu S. quod è nostra ju- stificatione, ac pace conscientiæ oritur, verè sunt regnum DEI; & SS. Trinitatis fruitio; quam in regno gratiæ habemus, hisce tribus προσκειμένοις, vel κειμηλίοις absolvitur, quibus nihil pretiosius obtinent fideles, & electi Domini. Per gaudium in Spiritu S. lætitia illa, quam fideles ipsi in corde suo percipiunt, de quâ Hiero-Pfaltes Ps. LXI IX. 4. & S. Apostolus Phil. IV. 5. intelligitur, non verò quâ alios iidem perfundunt & exhilarant. B. Hun- nius ita explicat & παραφράζει: Res adiaphoræ illæ & mediæ ita sunt comparatæ, ut bonâ conscientiâ pos- sitis in gratiam infirmorum, ab usu earum, cùm opus est, abstinere. Nam regnum Dei in hoc seculo in- choatum, & in altero consummandum, non est po- situm in rebus his indifferentibus, in cibo & potu; sed aliis longè majoribus & necessariis rebus defini- tur, nempe justitia, quam fide in Christum obtine- mus: deinde pace conscientiæ & gaudio, non terreno, sed spirituali, &, ut Petrus nominat, ineffabili atque glorificato, quo renati, consideratione beneficiorum Christi, per Spiritum S. in cordibus suis exultant. Et in LL. CC. n. VI. Notanda descriptio regni Dei; quod non terrenis bonis definitur, sed divinis planè & cœlestibus, justitia coram Deo valente, quâ nihil prius est homini Christiano; pace item conscientiæ, quæ, teste Apostolo, superat omnem intellectũ, Philip. IV. Gaudio item sincero atque solido, quo pii in Do- mino gaudẽt semper, & in jucundissimo sensu divinæ gratiæ dulcissimè requiescunt, ac veluti torrente be- neficiorũ ipsius inebriantur, & ad sensum immorta- litatis reficiuntur. Quæ licet in regno gratiæ inchoa- ta tantum sint; tamen sunt certè quidam veluti gustus perpetuæ beatitudinis filiorũ Dei, quæ plenè perficie- tur in regno gloriæ, ubi sempiternæ justitiæ indumen- to exornati, pace Dei perpetuâ perfruemur, exultan- tes gaudio inenarrabili, & verè glorificato, quod nul- la uspiam ægritudine in æternum contaminabitur. Sicut de hoc electorum gaudio in vita beata Pro- pheta Esaias concionatur, cap. XV. XXXV. LXV. & Apoc. VII. Similiter B. Balduinus: Regnum Dei consideratur quatenus vel regnum gratiæ est, in hoc seculo, vel regnum gloriæ, in altera vitâ. Utrobique nihil promovetur usu vel esu cibi in Lege olim pro- hibiti: nam ut alibi Christus loquitur: regnum Dei non venit cum externa observatione Luc. XVII. 20. Sunt verò alia longè majora, in quibus regnum Dei consistit, quorum tria hîc recensentur: (1.) justitia, ea nimirum, quâ coram Dei judicio justi reputamur, quamque non nisi fide in Christum obtinemus. (2.) pax, quam habemus coram Deo per Christum. (3.) gaudium, per quod intelligit tranquillitatem con- scientiæ, quæ est initium vitæ æternæ, & ex prioribus resultat. Nam qui justificati sunt fide, pacem habent cum Deo, Rom. V. inde est perpetua exultatio etiam in adversis: tales enim gloriantur in tribulationibus, quia juge convivium habent in bona conscientia. Ita & è Reformatis Pareus: Justitiam intelligit fi- dei, de qua prolixè disputârat suprà, pacem inter- nam, conscientiæ tranquillitatem seu εὐθυμίαν, quæ justificationem sequitur, cap. V. Ex duobus miscetur tertium lætitia, quâ semper exultamus in Domino, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ DEI c. V. 2. Addit Pareus justitiæ fidei justitiam causæ, & paci

& internæ conscientiæ externam Φιλησυχίαν, & stu- dium pacis, quod etiam à Flacio factum; Sed quan- quam ista cohæreant; illa ut causa & effectus, ut radix & fructus, hæc ut connexa necessaria, quia concordiæ studium comitatur fidem, & ad pa- cem conscientiæ non turbandam fidelibus est ne- cessarium; una tamen voce tàm diversa in eodem loco notari non possunt, & si ad vocis significatum consequentia, & connexa referenda omnia, quid non eadem voce simul notabitur? De iis loquitur Apostolus, in quibus regnum Dei & salus propriè consistit: non verò quæ in regno Dei constitutis agenda sunt. De his enim jam sub voce servitutis sequitur, quæ propria est subditorum in hoc regno, utpote qui soli Deo serviunt, & unâ voce illa com- prehenduntur: Qui enim in his servit Christo, ac- ceptus est DEO, & probatus hominibus: non qui in cibo, & potu servit Christo, sed qui in justitiâ fidei, pace conscientiæ, & gaudio in Spiritu S. huic suo Domino, per quem illa consequitur & possidet, adeoque bonis & thesauris regni Dei fruitur, debita præstat servitia: non enim, per quæ Christo serviamus, docet, sed quibus instru- cti sint, qui Domino verè serviunt: quòd nempe justitiam fidei, & pacem cum Deo possidentes, ac lætitiâ spirituali delibuti summâ alacritate Christo serviant. Sine his enim nulla est servitus Christi ἐυάρεstος τῷ Θεῷ, & in istis tribus retinendis occu- patum debet esse studium nostrum: quod nos Deo & hominibus gratiores reddet, quàm si nullo eum respectu infirmorum cibis omnibus indiffe- renter utamur. Servitus autem ipsa, quâ & Chri- sto Domino nostro verè servimus, & Deo nostro placemus, hominibusque probati reddimur, sita est tùm in fide, sine quâ impossibile est Deo pla- cere, Ebr. XI. 6. tùm in charitate, vel dilectione Dei & proximi: unde nec ad regnum Dei, nec ad servitutem in regno Dei cibus vel potus, aut alia ejusmodi externa quicquam facere manifestum est, quibus tamen, qui firmi sibi videbantur, infir- mos perturbabant; quibus etiam Papa cum clero suo, sese spiritualium nomine efferentes, sibi sub- ditos vehementer hodie perturbant; adeò ut etiã nonnulli in abstinentia in Papatu præscriptâ, quæ est à certis ciborum generibus, non dubitent hæc tria constituere, uti in Estio videmus in h. l.

(1.) Estiana justitiam, quod per ejusmodi abstinentiam Deo pro peccatis in eum commissis satisfaciamus: quòd non minùs justitiæ Dei, quæ utique non poscit abs- tinentiam à certis cibis loco satisfactionis pro peccatis, nec eâ contenta est, sed pœnam exigit æternam, & obedientiam requirit perfectissimam, quàm satisfactioni, & merito unius Redemptoris nostri Christi Jesu, qui solus pœnam pro peccatis nostris luit, & obedientiam legi debitam nostri loco præstitit, injuriosum est. (2.) Pacem, quà per abstinentiam subjugamus carnem Spiritui; quia nec abstinentia à certis cibis quicquam facit ad subjugandam carnem, nec subjugatio illa pacem conscientiæ solidam parit; quia multis modis imperfecta est, & sæpiùs deficit: unde nulla vera tranquillitas, sed mera dubitatio oritur, si niti sub- jugatione carnis pax cum Deo interior debeat. Denique (3.) gaudium Spiritus Sancti, quod per abstinentiam cibi & potûs mens reddatur alacrior ad contemplandum divina: sed quamvis de absti- nentia & jejunio veri nominis id suo modo verum sit, non verò de ciborum delectu, gaudium tamen in Spiritu Sancto non ex contemplatione, sed è gratuitâ remissione peccatorum & justificatione, ac interiori pace, ac tranquillitate conscientiæ oritur ac redundat.

## 14:19
v. 19. Therefore let us pursue the things of peace. As above 17. and the things of edification one toward another. The faithful are the temple of God 1. Corinth. III. 16. 17. VI. 19. 2. Cor. VI. 16. That temple is built by good teachings and examples. And here must be referred mystically those things which are in Moses concerning the Tabernacle: and in the history of the Kings concerning the Temple.

The things which are of peace can either be understood as those things which make for internal peace: for we must seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness Matth. 6, 33. so that we may be solicitous for our own salvation before all things; then indeed also for those things which make for the edification of the Church: to which pertains mutual love, peace and concord, or those things are understood which make for peace with one's neighbor, and for mutual edification among us; because in v. 15 he had warned that we should walk in charity, and that charity should be the directress and moderatrix of the use of intermediate and indifferent things, so that when the Apostle has dealt with spiritual peace in the preceding verse, he now warns of ecclesiastical peace, which is born from that, and is necessarily joined with it. For those who have peace with God also cultivate peace with the household of God: those who do not cultivate peace with their brothers, in them there is no solid peace with God, or tranquility of conscience, which is disturbed by nothing more than by enmity and contention. It is indicated therefore that by that untimely use of indifferent things not only external peace, but also internal peace is hindered: not only the edification of one's neighbor, but also one's own salvation is disturbed. To edify one's neighbor is to do those things which make for the neighbor's instruction in the faith, for the correction of his life, and which make the infirm person stronger and better; just as to destroy is to do those things which alienate the neighbor from the faith, and corrupt him in life. Cf. 2. Cor. 13, 10. Eph. 4, 12. It is a metaphor from architects, who are occupied in building a house, and provide mutual help to one another when there are many of them: just as we also are commanded to build ourselves into the house of God, 1. Petr. II. 5. and no less also to study the edification of one's neighbor, 1. Cor. XIV. 26. Blessed Hunnius makes this inference in the present place: Since the kingdom of God is not constituted in those intermediate things; we should deservedly hold to the rule of charity regarding their use or abstinence, pursuing those things which are of peace; which make for the edification of the infirm.

Latin:

v. 19. ἄρα ὖν τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης διώκωμεν. Ut fupra 17. κὰι τὰ τῆς ὀικοδομῆς τῆς ἐις ἀλλήλυς. Fideles sunt templum Dei 1. Corinth. III. 16. 17. VI. 19. 2. Cor. VI. 16. Id templum ædificatur bonis documentis & exemplis. Et huc myfticè referenda, quæ apud Mofem sunt de Tabernaculo : & in hiftoria Regum de Templo.

Ea quæ sunt pacis, vel intelligi possunt, quæ ad pacem internam faciunt : quærendum enim primû regnum Dei & justitia ejus Matth. 6, 33. ut ita de no- stra salute ante omnia simus foliciti ; tum verò etiã de iis,quæ ad ædificationẽ Ecclefiæ faciunt: ad quam spectat mutua dilectio, pax & concordia, vel intel- liguntur ea, quæ ad pacem cum proximo faciunt, & ad mutuam inter nos ædificationem;quia v.15. mo- nuerat,ut in charitate ambulemus,& charitas dire- ctrix sit & moderatrix usus rerum mediarum & in- differentiû, ut quum verfu præced. de pace spirituali egerit Apostolus, jam de pace Ecclefiastic. moneat, quæ ex illa nascitur, & cũ illa conjuncta est neceffa- riò. Qui enim pacem habent cum Deo, pacem etiã colunt cum domesticis Dei : qui cum fratribus pa- cẽ non colunt, in illis non est solida pax cum Deo, aut tranquillitas conscientiæ, quæ nullâ re magis disturbatur, quàm inimicitiâ & contentione. Indi- catur itaque,intempestivo illo usu rerum adiapho- rarum non pacem externam tantùm, sed etiam in- ternam impediri : non ædificationem tantùm proxi- mi, sed salutem etiam propriam turbari. Edificare proximum est ea facere, quæ ad proximi in fide in- formationem, in vitæ correctionem faciunt, cumque infirmus sit,firmiorem & meliorem faciunt; uti de- struere est ea facere,quæ proximum à fide alienant, & in vita corrumpunt. Conf. 2. Cor. 13, 10. Eph. 4, 12. Metaphora est ab architectis, qui in domo ex- truenda occupantur, & mutuas sibi, cum plures sunt, præstant operas : uti & nos ipsos in domum Dei extruere jubemur, 1. Petr. II. 5. nec minus etiã ædificationi proximi studere, 1. Cor. XIV. 26. Illa- tionem hanc in præsenti loco facit B. Hunnius: Cùm regnum Dei non sit constitutum in rebus illis mediis; meritò circa usum vel abstinentiam earum charitatis regulam teneamus, sectantes, quæ pacis sunt ; quæ ad ædificationem infirmorum faciunt.

## 14:20
v. 20. Do not for the sake of food destroy the work of God. He persists in the figure of the Temple begun. See Matth. 26, 6.

what is here καταλύειν, that is φθείρειν * שחת in Hebrew. That happens by bitter altercations, through which truth is often lost, and charity certainly is.

All things indeed are clean. Namely foods, both by their own nature, and by the permission of Christ. The same is said in Tit. 1, 15.

but it is evil for the man who eats with offense. Διά here has the value of μετά, as above II. 27. IV. 11. 2. Cor. III. 11. for κακὸν understand the food: the thing for the action. His action is evil, who through it rashly provides an occasion for another to recede from the Gospel, while he sees himself treated contumeliously.

The work of God is destroyed both in ourselves, and in our neighbor, who is likewise reborn from God. Because with such contentions divine regeneration cannot consist, as far as we ourselves are concerned, and when the neighbor is affected with scandal and is lost through food, which the Apostle had said in v. 15, the work of God is destroyed in him also. And the following things teach that the destruction of the work of God in us is especially referred to, because we are a new creature in Christ 2. Cor. V. 17. and the work of God created in Christ Jesus, Eph. II. 10.: because it is said to be evil for a man eating with a stumbling block (of his neighbor), that food, or the use of food, which is joined with the stumbling block of the neighbor. Yet it is rightly said that the work of God in the neighbor is also noted. Chrysostom says that he calls the salvation of the infirm brother the work of God. Others understand faith by the work of God Joh. VI. 29. And the weak faith of a neighbor is also a work of God pleasing to God: which is destroyed when the weak one is alienated from the faith by a stumbling block. It is not, however, a light fault, but a horrible theomachia, to destroy the work of God, and to wantonly demolish that which God is building.

Latin:

v. 20. μὴ ἕνεκεν τῶ βρώματος κατάλυε τὸ ἔργον τῶ Θεῶ. Persistit in cœpta Templi figura. Vide Matth. 26, 6.

quod hîc καταλύειν, id φθείρειν * שחת Hebraicè. Id sit a- cerbis altercationibus, per quas veritas sæpe, caritas certò amittitur.

πάντα μὲν καθαρά. Nempe βρώματα,tum suapte naturâ, tùm Christi permissu. Idem dictum Tit. 1, 15.

ἀλλὰ κακὸν τῶ ἀνθρώπῳ διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίοντι. Διὰ ita hîc valet μετά, ut fupra II. 27. IV. 11. 2. Cor. III. 11. κακὸν subaudi τὸ βρῶμα : res pro actione. Mala est ejus actio,qui per eam temerè occasionem præbet alteri receden- di ab Evangelio, dum se contumeliose tractari videt.

Destruitur opus Dei tùm in nobis ipsis, tùm in proximo,renato itidem exDeo. Quia cum con- tentionibus talibus consistere nequit divina rege- neratio, quoad nosmet ipsos, & cùm scandalo af- ficitur & perditur proximus per cibum, quod v.15. dixerat Apostolus, opus Dei etiam in ipso destrui- tur. Et vel imprimis destructionem operis Dei, in nobis, quia nova sumus creatura in Christo 2. Cor. V. 17. & Dei opus conditi in Christo Jesu, Eph. II. 10. respici, sequentia docent : quia κακὸν malum dici- tur homini cum offendiculo (proximi) vescenti, in cibus ille, vel usus cibi, qui cum proximi offendi- culo conjunctus est. Opus tamen etiam Dei in proximo notari rectè dicitur. Opus Dei vocat fra- tris infirmi salutem, ait Chrysostomus. Alii fidem per opus Dei intelligunt Joh. VI. 29. Estque etiam in- firma fides proximi opus Dei placens Deo : quod destruitur, cum infirmus offendiculo à fide aliena- tur. Non autem est levis culpa, sed horribilis θεο- μαχία, opus Dei destruere, & id, quod Deus ædi- ficat, petulanter demoliri.

## 14:21
v. 21. It is good not to eat meat, nor to drink wine.

The positive is used for the comparative, as in Matt. 18:8, 9. The sense is the same in 1 Cor. 8:13. We ought to endure anything rather than drive a brother to ruin by our unnecessary action.

nor in that by which your brother stumbles. Supply 'to do'. And 'in which' is equivalent to 'by which', in the Hebrew manner.

Some wish to see here a reference also to things sacrificed to idols and wine that is poured out in libation to idols, but it is rather a matter of not offending the Jews who abstained from things that were forbidden in the Law. The Apostle exhorts the stronger ones that if they see the weak offended by the eating of meat forbidden by the Law, such as pork or hare, they should yield their right and abstain from all meats, or even wine, rather than place a stumbling block before weak brothers by their liberty, so that either they themselves do the same with a wavering conscience, or they oppose them as profaners of the divine law. It is an abuse, however, when Jerome prohibits virgins and widows from eating meat and drinking wine based on these verses. See his Epistle to Fulvia on keeping widowhood, to Salvia on the same, to Eustochium on guarding virginity. For the Apostle teaches that this is not evil in itself, but becomes evil by accident, on account of scandal. 'If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat' (1 Cor. 8:13). And therefore the Papists in vain prove from this passage their doctrine concerning the distinction of foods, which Paul called a doctrine of demons in 1 Tim. 4:3, as was done by the Jesuit Bailius in his Catech. controv. tr. II. q. 11. For the Apostle gave this warning without distinction regarding all foods by which we place a stumbling block before a neighbor: nor does he prohibit certain foods, but teaches that scandal is to be avoided in any of them, as Thomas and Estius acknowledged in this place.

v. same. or is offended or is weak.

These are absent in the Manuscript: nor does the Syriac read them.

These, however, could more easily have fallen out of a few copies than be added to most. And there is an emphasis, making for a greater intensity of exhortation: since the weak one easily stumbles, or if he does not stumble, at least some scandal is given to him, or he is disturbed in his weakness. All of which, as far as possible, must be avoided.

Latin:

v. 21. καλὸν τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν κρέα,μηδὲ πιεῖν οἶνον.

Melius est Positivum pro comparativo, ut Matt. 18, 8. 9. Idem sensus 1. Cor. 8, 13. Quidvis potiùs nobis sustinendum est, quàm ut facto nostro non necessario fratrem in ruinam impellamus.

μηδὲ ἐν ᾧ ἀδελφός σε προσκόπτει. Supple, facere. Et ἐν ᾧ, valet per quod, more Hebræo.

Nonnulli hîc idolothyta, & vinum, de quo libatur idolis, respici etiam volunt, sed de Judæis potiùs abstinentibus ab iis, quæ in lege vetita erant, non offendendis agitur. Hortatur firmiores Apostolus, ut si esu carnis lege vetitæ, utpote suillæ vel leporinæ offendi infirmos videant, de suo jure cédant, & vel omnibus carnibus, imò vino etiam abstineant, quàm libertate suâ fratribus infirmis offendiculum ponant, ut aut ipsi idem faciant fluctuante conscientia, aut eos ceu divinæ legis profanatores adversentur. Abusus autem est, cum Hieronymus ex his virginibus & viduis prohibet vesci carnibus, bibere vinum. Vid. Epist. ad Fulviam de servanda viduitate, ad Salviam de eadem, ad Eustochium de custodienda virginit. Docet enim Apostolus, per se malum id non esse, sed ex accidenti malum fieri, ob scandalum. Si esca facit, ut offendatur frater meus, non vescar carnibus in æternum 1. Cor. 8. 13. Ideoque frustrà Papistæ ex hoc loco doctrinam suam, quam dæmoniorum Paulus dixit 1. Tim. 4. 3. de discrimine ciborum probant, ut à Bailio Jesuita in Catech. controv. tr. II. q. 11. factum. Nam Apostolus sine discrimine de omnibus cibis hoc monuit, quibus proximo offendiculum ponimus: nec prohibet certos cibos, sed in quibusvis scandalum vitandũ docet, ut agnovit Thomas & Estius in h. l.

v. eod. ἢ σκανδαλίζεται ἢ ἀσθενεῖ.

Hæc absunt in Manuscripto: neque legit Syrus.

Hæc verò facilius excidere poterant paucis Exemplaribus, quàm adjici plerisque. Et emphasis est, ad paræneseos majorem δεινότητα faciens: quũ facilè impingat infirmus, aut si non impingat, scandalũ saltem quoddã ei detur, aut in infirmitate suâ turbetur. Quæ omnia, quoad fieri potest, cavenda.

## 14:22
v. 22. You have faith.

πίσις here is that persuasion by which one believes that what he does is lawful: the assent of the conscience: אמונה to the Hebrew teachers. Chrysostom and Oecumenius read these with an interrogative mark: rightly.

Faith here implies not only a bare persuasion, but also true knowledge.

κατὰ σεαυτὸν ἔχε ἐνώπιον Θεῦ.) That is, use it when you have no other witness whom you might offend.

μακάριος ὁ μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτὸν ἐν ᾧ δοκιμάζει.

Happy is he who does not condemn himself (for κρίνειν is used for κατακρίνειν frequently) in that thing which he prefers, that is, which he undertakes to do. He expresses the same thing thus in 1 John 3:21: ἐὰν ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν μὴ καταγινώσκῃ ἡμῶν, παῤῥησίαν ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν.

Latin:

v. 22. σὺ πίσιν ἔχεις.

πίσις hîc est persuasio ea, per quam quis credit licitum esse id, quod facit: assensus conscientiæ: אמונה magistris Hebræis. Cum interrogandi notâ hæc legerunt Chrysostomus & Oecumenius: rectè.

Non nudam tantùm persuasionem, sed veram etiam notitiam fides hîc infert.

κατὰ σεαυτὸν ἔχε ἐνώπιον Θεῦ.) Id est tunc utere, cum alium non habes testem, quem offendas.

μακάριος ὁ μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτὸν ἐν ᾧ δοκιμάζει.

Felix qui semet non damnat (κρίνειν enim pro κατακρίνειν per frequens) in eâ re quam præfert, id est, quam agendam suscipit. Idem sic eloquitur 1. Joh. III. 21. ἐὰν ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν μὴ καταγινώσκῃ ἡμῶν, παῤῥησίαν ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν.

## 14:23
v. 23. ὁ δὲ διακρινόμενος.

He who doubts, he who hesitates. See the cited passage in De Jure Belli ac Pacis. Διακρίνειν means to doubt, as in Matthew 21:21 and above in 4:20; see the notes on those passages.

ἐὰν φάγῃ, κατακέκριται. By himself, of course.

ὅτι ὐκ ἐκ πίσεως. Not with a firm persuasion that what he does is lawful. For that is an excellent maxim: 'What you doubt, do not do,' found in Cicero, and common in the proverb of the Hebrews.

πᾶν δὲ ὃ ὐκ ἐκ πίσεως, ἁμαρτία ἐσιν.

It is a sin, whatever is done without the conscience assenting. This warning concerns the Jews who had become Christians, that they should not do by the example of others that which they themselves either did not think lawful, or certainly were very doubtful about. After these words in that manuscript which we often use, no less than in other very ancient manuscripts, there follow three verses which we have at the end of the Epistle. And it appears that Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact read them in this place. It seems Paul intended to finish the Epistle here at first, but later, having obtained a little more time than he had hoped for, added certain other things. Marcion's copies ended the epistle here, according to Jerome.

It is indicated that he has not only progressed well in the School of the Holy Spirit who does not judge or condemn himself in that thing which he chooses and by which he uses his Christian liberty: but that this is required so that his happiness or salvation may not be endangered. For he who doubts whether something is lawful or not, and nevertheless he uses it with a hesitating conscience, by this very fact he tacitly reproves and condemns himself and his deed in his own conscience; because it is not from faith. For faith alone, following the guidance of the shining word, clearly confirms our conscience, so that we may know whether anything pleases or displeases God, and be undoubtedly certain. Therefore, he who eats, concerning which he doubts whether it is lawful to eat it, sins: whence a general axiom is subjoined: Whatever is not from faith, is sin. Although this seems to sound concerning the faith of conscience, because it is inculcated on the occasion of certainty and the full assurance of the mind regarding indifferent things: yet it must be taken generally, because the Apostle infers his conclusion from that universal maxim, and thus it is verified also entirely concerning the faith of dogmas, and concerning saving faith itself: indeed, if our mind ought to be unchangeable concerning adiaphora, much more so concerning things necessary to be believed. If in the use of indifferent things full assurance is needed, much more in the apprehensive and applicative practice of those things which are presented to our faith, to be applied to us. If those things, says the blessed Balduinus in this place, p. 250, which are done without that faith, by which we believe something is permitted in indifferent things, are sin; much more will those things be sins, which are done without a certain trust of the heart in Christ. And thus we can rightly adapt this saying of the Apostle from hypothesis to thesis, or even from a lower species of faith to a higher. For it is a general aphorism true of every faith: Whatever is done without faith, is sin; whether historical faith is understood, or the faith of conscience, or faith in Christ, etc. Nothing, therefore, prevents this saying from being able to be explained also concerning justifying faith, although here it is applied to another species. These are the words of B. Balduinus: by which he solves the sophism of Bellarmine, book V, on free will, chapter 10: as if this axiom does not pertain to faith in Christ: because it speaks directly not of justifying faith, but of a certain persuasion of the heart, that those things which are done are not unpleasing to God. Which consequence is commonly wont to be denied, with the antecedent granted. I do not see, however, why this should be granted, that that Apostolic aphorism does not speak here directly of justifying faith. For although the conclusion of the Apostle concerns adiaphora, he who eats of some food while doubting, that is, wavering and doubting, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius interpret, is condemned: yet the middle term, because it is not from faith (but whatever is not from faith, is sin), can be most excellently explained concerning justifying faith. Whatever is not from faith, not from faith in Christ, or is done without that faith, is sin, and makes one guilty of condemnation. But this, that one eats with a wavering conscience, is not from faith in Christ, or is done without that faith. Therefore, this is sin, etc. But lest what is said about eating without or from faith seem inconvenient, the admonition of the Apostle must be recalled, Colossians 3:17: EVERYTHING whatsoever you do in word or in work, ALL THINGS in the name of the Lord JESUS CHRIST, giving thanks to GOD and the Father through him. How in the name of Jesus Christ, if not through faith in Christ? How giving thanks to God through Christ, if without faith in Christ? Every action, therefore, which ought to be well-pleasing to God, must necessarily proceed from faith in Christ. It is of that faith that we are treating here, he who lacks which, is condemned. But this faith is in Christ, the faith by which we obtain salvation, as Christ testifies in John 3:17, following. The Apostle does not speak here of the dictate of conscience, or the persuasion, or the credulity of some impious person, inducing this or that into the mind; but of the certainty of a faithful man, who has been established in the kingdom of God through faith, verse 17. Of the faith by which righteousness is obtained: of the faith by which peace

and the tranquility of conscience relies; of the faith through which joy in the Holy Spirit is had; of the faith by which Christ must be served, so that we may be acceptable to God. He treats of brothers, whether weak or robust in faith, not of the impious; and he wishes actions to be done by faith in the Lord, even those that are intermediate and indifferent, verse 6. He who regards the day, regards it to the Lord, he who eats, eats to the Lord: of the faith by which we have something persuaded in the Lord Jesus, verse 14, which is the mother of charity, according to which one must walk, verse 15. Compare Galatians 5:5. Nor indeed is there need only of certain knowledge and firm assent for this faith: lacking which, whatever is done is sin: but primarily of a true and solid full assurance of application, and trust in Christ, by which hearts ought to be purified, Acts 15:10, which alone renders the conscience tranquil and secure, Romans 5:1, and without which it is impossible to please God, Hebrews 11:6. Therefore he requires here that everyone should be πληροφορούμεν in his own mind, v. 5. Rightly, therefore, B. Well. in h.l. The sense is: Whatever is not from the faith of Christ Jesus, in whom alone we know what things are common and unclean, and what are not, is sin. Furthermore: Whoever lacks this faith, his actions are not approved by God, and consequently whatever is done by him who lacks faith, or who is an unbeliever, that is sin. See Aug. l. 4. contr. Julianum c. 3. & de Nuptiis & concupiscentia c. 3. The Apostle speaks of those who ought to be of the same mind, to think the same thing mutually, according to Christ Jesus, in the following chapter, verse 5; who ought with one mind, with one mouth, to glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, verse 6; and who through patience and consolation have a living hope, verse 4; whom he commands to receive one another, by the example of Christ, who received us, verse 7; which is not of any but those who believe in Christ; for whom, therefore, he himself prays that GOD of hope may further fill them with all JOY in the Holy Spirit and PEACE in believing, or through faith, verse 13; of whom he is persuaded that they are filled with all knowledge, and can mutually exhort one another, verse 14. From all of which it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking of justifying faith when he says: Whatever is not from faith, is sin. Through this faith, the holy Patriarchs and their works pleased God, the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 11. And therefore pains must be taken that we may be in this faith, 2 Cor. XIII, and that the things which we do may be done from faith. But they cannot be done from faith unless it is certainly established to us that they are approved by the word of the Lord (from which faith is), nay, unless the person doing them is endowed with faith in the Lord.

Therefore, those words in v. 22, Σὺ πίσιν ἔχεις, are also rightly understood concerning faith: Do you have faith in Christ? Have it to yourself before God. See to it that you first approve your faith, but see also that you do not judge yourself in those things which you approve and do outwardly: that you do not do them with a wavering conscience. For thus you will not be blessed, but you will condemn yourself: and so you will testify that you are not truly endowed with faith, which does not consist with hesitation, but is situated in πληροφορίᾳ. Therefore, the Apostle delivers a new rule concerning adiaphora in v. 22, that they are to be used in such a way that nothing is done with a wavering conscience, but he is not still pursuing the prior rule concerning avoiding the stumbling block of one's neighbor. Which is to be well observed. For with that neglected, the text concerning saving faith, about which the Apostle has dealt throughout this whole Epistle, is rendered sufficiently obscure and intricate: as if the discourse were about the faith, as they call it, of conscience, or about the knowledge of the use of adiaphora, lest we abuse it with the scandal of the weak; concerning which it had already been dealt with before. And Salmero observes in Disp. 9, book 4, on the Epistle to the Romans, that there are not lacking (besides Augustine) other Fathers who teach that faith in this place is not to be taken for conscience, which is the rule of human actions, but for the assent of the catholic faith, or the assertion of dogmas; and that Augustine is of that opinion, so that the opposite acceptance of faith he did not approve of as new and unheard of. Most rightly, therefore, from this passage, whatever is done without faith is sin, Saint Augustine concluded that all the works of unbelievers, which are done without faith and the special help of grace, are sins, l. IV. contra Julian. c. 3. Whatever good is done by man, and is not done for that reason for which true wisdom commands it ought to be done, even if it may seem good in terms of duty, it is sin because of the not-right end. There can be no true virtue except in him who is just, but no one can be just without faith. And l. III. ad Bonifac. c. 5. Without faith, those things which seem to be good works are turned into sins, for whatever is not from faith is sin. See also l. 1. de Nupt. & Concupisc. cap. 3. &c. whence Salmero confesses l. c. that Augustine often uses the testimony of the Apostle, whatever is not done from faith, &c. to prove that every act of unbelievers is sin. With which Prosper agrees in sentent. 105. All the life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good: for where the recognition of the eternal and unchangeable will is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best of morals. And in the Epigrams: For every work of piety, unless it arises from the seed of true faith, is sin. Cassander brings forward more to that effect from Basil and Chrysostom in Consult. art. VI. Gregory the Great l. II. Moral. c. 25. If faith, he says, is not first born in our heart, the rest also cannot be good, even if they seem good. Bernard serm. XXII. in Cant. What have you philosophers to do with virtues, you who are ignorant of Christ, the power of God? Ordinary Gloss on this passage: All the life of unbelievers is sin. Thomas on c. 15. John at the words, without me you can do nothing: he has blocked the way of the proud, and especially of the Pelagians, who say that they can do the good works of virtues and of the law from themselves without help. Whence Cassander l. c. teaches that the followers of Thomas reject the opinion of Scotus, that a man from purely natural powers and general help can prepare himself for grace by congruity: appealing to the consent of John Driedo: but Ambrosius Catharinus in the Council of Trent itself argued that the works of unbelievers, who are not stirred by God to believe, are truly sins, and he cited not only Augustine for that matter, but also St. Ambrose, St. Prosper, Anselm and others among the Fathers, likewise Gregory of Rimini and Cardinal Fisher, as noted by Father Suavis in Hist. Conc. Trid. l. II. Pesantius alleges to that effect Altisiodorensis, Alensis, and Capreolus in l. 2. quæst. 109. art. 2. The Jesuit Tanner T. II. Theol. Scholast. Disp. VI. q. 3. & T. III. Disp. 1. q. 8. also adduced Michael Baius and Cassalius. For even if the virtues of the Gentiles are in agreement with right reason and the light of nature, Augustine nevertheless does not hesitate to call them sins, not because they are evil actions in their own kind and materially, but because they are done neither by a person pleasing to God, nor for a right end, since nothing makes a person pleasing to God except faith in Christ: whence those virtues are called sins not intrinsically and in their nature, but extrinsically when viewed in the judgment of God, because they were done without faith: nor can they be called good works, because faith is the soul of good works, (but good works are not the soul of faith,) and when it is lacking, nothing can be called a good work. Wherefore one must judge differently concerning the works of unbelievers in the judgment of GOD than in the judgment of men. For that which deserves the highest praise before men can be vicious before God: according to that saying of Jerome: Every virtue without Christ is in vice. Whence it appears how great a difference there is between the virtues of believers and unbelievers: the former please God even when barely begun, because they are done from faith; the latter displease even in an excellent degree, because they are done without faith. Lombard l. II. Sentent. distinct. XLI. lit. A. It is not unreasonably asserted by some that all the actions and wills of a man without faith are evil, which, once faith is had, exist as good, whence the Apostle says, everything which is not from faith is sin, which Augustine, explaining it, says, all the life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good. Add John Ferus l. 1. in Matth. VIII. p. 125. You see therefore, that not only is it not good, but it is evil, whatever is done outside of faith: and Thomas Bradwardine l. II. de causa Dei adversus Pelag. cap. 5. proves this at length from Augustine. Finally, Bellarmine himself had to confess l. 1. de justific. c. 21. that before faith nothing good can be done: and akin to these is what is held in the Canon Law c. cum Paulus, Caus. 1. quæst. 1. from Gregory: Since Paul says, no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus, it is consequently proved that where Christ is not the foundation, the edifice of no good work exists.

We add to these things what our blessed HÜLSEMANN hands down to us as clearly ὁμόψηφος (of the same mind) concerning the present passage, because they have not yet been published: Whatever is not from faith, &c. It is indeed true that the word faith, according to the nature of the objects about which it is predicated, signifies either knowledge or assent only, or also trust in the benevolence of GOD towards us, and the complacency of our actions before GOD. In both ways we assert that the word faith is taken here, not only for the knowledge of a lawful thing, but also for the benevolent will of GOD towards us approving our deed. For Paul expressly asserts in verse 17 that this trust in the benevolence of GOD towards us is required to tranquilize our conscience. & following, when he not only says indefinitely what are the attributes of a Christian man living in the kingdom of grace, namely righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, but that also, whether eating or not eating, he enjoys these benefits, and is εὐάρεστος τῷ Θεῷ (well-pleasing to God): in which sense the word πίστεως (faith) in verse 22 is also taken, not only for the knowledge of lawfulness or permission. Wherefore the Apology of the Augsburg Confession and our theologians rightly extend this saying not only to the elective works of the Papists, which are destitute of the word of GOD and consequently of faith, against Bellarmine II. de Monachis c. 16. but also to the works of the Gentiles, which are destitute of faith or true trust in the True God, against the same Bellarmine. V. On grace ch. 10. For although it may be conceded, what he himself, what Suarez in part I of Thomas T. II. book 2. chapter 10, what Stapleton in his antidote to this passage, what Cornelius and Estius object, that Paul here did not have regard to the object of faith, which is the imputation of the merit of Christ; it suffices, however, for the object of that faith, of which Paul treats here, to be the benevolence and complacency of GOD toward our actions: but what is the meritorious cause of such complacency, this must be proved from elsewhere: and with the benevolence of GOD toward us established as the object of the faith of which there is discourse here, the cause of such benevolence is also necessarily admitted, even if in one intuition, or in one secondary act of such faith, as Paul describes here, not all causes or all instruments of our salvation are comprehended. Hence the inference of the Papists, with whom Arminius also sides, is inept. to the 31st article, article 15. The faith of which Paul speaks does not have as its adequate object that special confidence that sins are remitted or are to be remitted to oneself through the imputation of the merit of Christ: Therefore the faith of which there is discourse here is not the justifying faith of the Lutherans. For it suffices, as we have said, for this faith to have as its object also the benevolence of God toward us: which being posited, the meritorious cause of this benevolence is also posited, and the mode of applying it is certainly by no reasoning excluded.

Thus Augustine, Book 4 against Julian, chapters 3 and 4. Prosper, Fulgentius, and others, following Origen, explain it concerning the lack of faith in Christ: whom Pererius shamelessly refutes in Disputation 5. Toletus, however, in annotation 5, calls it a probable opinion. Let the reader compare the exposition of Origen, Augustine, and other Fathers with that of certain Latins, even the Lateran Council under Innocent III, Canon 41, the torture by which they explain faith in this place juridically as a just title of acquired possessed property: That which is not of faith is sin, they say, we define by synodal judgment: that no prescription or possession of any thing beyond 30 or 40 years is valid without good faith, i.e., without a just title of initial acquisition. These are the words of the blessed Lord Socer. What Grotius adds concerning the three verses, even though he reports some diversity of the codices, is nevertheless wrongly and not sufficiently religiously snatched at, in that he wished Paul to end the Epistle here, but later, having unexpectedly obtained more time, added certain other things. For those things do not accord with divine inspiration and direction. And that the things which are held at the beginning of the following chapter up to the prayer of this treatment, the epilogikon, pertain to this place, its own continuation sufficiently teaches, and further confirmation from the Holy Scriptures along with other things, which it is not likely to have happened by chance. Compare Justinian and Estius on this place.

Latin:

v. 23. ὁ δὲ διακρινόμενος.

Qui dubitat, qui hæsitat. Vide dictum locum de Jure Belli ac Pacis. Διακρίνειν est dubitare, ut Matth. XXI. 21. & suprà IV. 20. quibus locis dicta vide.

ἐὰν φάγῃ, κατακέκριται. A semetipso scilicet.

ὅτι ὐκ ἐκ πίσεως. Non cum firma persuasione licitum esse quod facit. Optimum enim illud: Quod dubitas, ne feceris, apud Ciceronem, tritum & Hebræorum proverbio.

πᾶν δὲ ὃ ὐκ ἐκ πίσεως, ἁμαρτία ἐσιν.

Peccatum est, quicquid sit conscientia non adstipulante. Hoc monitum Judæos, qui Christiani facti erant, spectat, ne aliorum exemplo id facerent, quod ipsi aut licitum non putabant, aut certè valdè de eo dubitabant. Post hæc verba in Manuscripto illo quo sæpe utimur, non minus quam in aliis Manuscriptis vetustissimis, sequuntur commata tria, quæ fine Epistolæ habemus. Et hoc loco illa legisse apparet Chrysostomum, Oecumenium, Theophylactum. Videtur Paulus primum hîc finire voluisse Epistolam, sed postea aliquantò plus, quam speraverat, nactus temporis, alia quædam adjecisse. Marcionis exemplaria hic epistolam finiebant, teste Hieronymo.

Id indicatur, eum non tantùm benè in Schola Sp. S. profecisse, qui non judicat aut condemnat seipsum in ea re, quam eligit, & quà ex libertate Christiana utitur: Sed id ne beatitudo vel salus ejus periclitetur, requiri. Qui enim dubitat, num aliquid licitum sit, nec ne, & nihilominus eo utitur hæsitante conscientiâ, hoc ipso se suum- que factum tacitè in conscientia sua reprehendit, & condemnat; quod id non ex fide sit. Nam fi- des sola, ductum prælucentis verbi sequens, no- stram conscientiam planè confirmat, ut num quid Deo placeat, aut displiceat, sciamus, & indubi- tatò certi simus. Qui ergò edit, de quo dubi- tat, num eo vesci liceat, peccat: unde axioma generale subjungitur: Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Quamvis autem de fide conscien- tiæ hoc sonare videatur, quod occasione certi- tudinis & πληροφορίας animi circa res indifferen- tes id inculcetur: γενικῶς tamen accipiendum, quia ex illa maxima universali conclusionem suam infert Apostolus, adeoque de fide dogma- tum, deque ipsa salvifica fide omninò etiam ve- rificatur: imò si de adiaphoris animus noster de- bet esse ἀμετάπτωτος, multò magis de rebus credi- tu necessariis. Si in usu rerum indifferentium πλη- ροφορία opus est, multò magis in praxi apprehen- sivâ & applicativâ ea, quæ fidei nostræ sistuntur, nobis applicanda. Si ea, inquit B. Balduinus in h. l. p. 250. quæ absque ista fide fiunt, quâ credimus aliquid esse concessum in rebus adiaphoris, peccatum sunt; multò magis peccata erunt, quæcunque fiunt absque certâ fiduciâ cordis in Christum. Atque sic dictum hoc Apostoli ab hypothesi ad thesin, vel etiam ab inferiore specie fidei ad superiorem rectè accom- modare possumus. Est enim generalis Aphorismus de omni fide verus: Quicquid absque fide fit, pecca- tum est; sive intelligatur fides historica, sive fides conscientiæ, sive fides in Christum &c. Nihil igitur obstat, quo minus etiam de fide justificante hoc di- ctum explicari queat, licet hîc ad aliam speciem ap- plicetur. Hæc B. Balduinus: quibus σόφισμα Bel- larmini l. V. de lib. arbitr. cap. 10. solvit: quasi hoc axioma non pertineat ad fidem in Christum: quia directè loquatur non de fide justificante, sed de per- suasione certâ cordis, quod ea, quæ fiunt, Deo non ingrata. Quæ consequentia negari communiter solet, concesso antecedente. Non video autem, cur hoc concedendum sit, quòd Aphorismus ille Apostolicus hîc non loquatur directè de fide justificante.
