Quanquam enim conclusio Aposto- li concernat adiaphora, qui edit de cibo aliquo διακρινόμενος, id est fluctuans & dubitans, ut Chry- sost. Theoph. & Oecum. interpretantur, condemna- tur: medius terminus tamen, quia non ex fide (quod autem non ex fide, peccatum est,) de fide justificante optimè exponi potest. Quicquid non ἐκ πίστεως, non ex fide in Christũ, vel absq; illa fide fit, peccatum est, & condemnationis reum facit. At hoc, quod edit quis fluctuante conscientiâ, non ex fide in Christum, vel absque fide illa fit. E. hoc peccatum est, &c. Ne autem inconveniens videatur, quod dicitur de esu absque vel ex fide, recolendum est Apostoli monitum Coloss. III. 17. OMNE quodcunque facitis in verbo aut in opere, OMNIA in nomine Domini JESU CHRISTI, gratias agentes DEO & Patri per ipsum. Quo- modo in nomine Jesu Christi, nisi per fidem in Chri- stum? Quomodo gratias agentes Deo per Chri- stum, si absque fide in Christum? Omnis ergò actio, quæ Deo εὐάρεστος esse debet, ex fide in Chri- stum procedat necesse est. De illa fide hic agitur, quâ qui caret, κατακέκριται condemnatus est. At hæc fides est in Christum, fides, quâ salutem con- sequimur, teste Christo Joh. III. 17. seq. Non loqui- tur hîc Apostolus de conscientia dictamine, aut per- suasione, vel credulitate impii alicujus, hoc vel illud in animum inducentis; sed de certitudine hominis fidelis, qui in regno Dei constitutus est per fidem, v. 17. De fide, quâ justitia obtinetur: de fide, quâ pax

& tranquillitas conscientiæ nititur; de fide, per quam gaudium in Spiritu S. habetur; de fide, quâ Christo serviendum est, ut accepti simus Deo. Agit de fratribus seu infirmis, seu robustis in fide, non de impiis; & actiones fide in Dominum fieri vult, et- iam medias & indifferentes v. 6. Qui curat diem, Domino curat, qui vescitur, Domino vescitur: de fi- de, quâ persuasum quid habemus in Domino Jesu, v. 14. quæ mater charitatis est, secundum quam am- bulandum est, v. 15. Conf. Gal. V. 5. Neque verò tantùm notitiâ certâ, & assensione firmâ opus est ad hanc fidem: quâ deficiente peccatum est, quicquid fit: sed imprimis verâ, solidâque applicationis πλη- ροφορίᾳ, & fiduciâ in Christum, quâ oportet corda purificari Act. XV. 10. quæ sola reddit conscientiam tranquillam & securam, Rom. V. 1. & sine quâ im- possibile est placere Deo, Ebr. XI. 6. Ided requirit hic, ut unusquisque in mente sua sit πληροφορούμεν v. 5. Rectè ergò B. Well. in h.l. Sensus est: Quicquid non est ex fide Christi Jesu, in quo unicè cognoscimus, quæ communia & immunda sunt, quæ non, peccatum est. Porrò: Quisquis hac fide caret, ejus actiones Deo non probantur, ac proinde quod ab illo, qui fide caret, seu qui infidelis est, sit, id peccatum est. Vid. Aug. l. 4. contr. Julianum c. 3. & de Nuptiis & concupiscentia c. 3. Loquitur Apostolus de iis, qui τὸ ἀυτὸ φρονεῖν, idem sentire mutuò debent, secundum Christum Je- sum c. seq. v. 5. qui ὁμοθυμαδὸν unâ mente, uno ore Deum & Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi glo- rificare debent, v. 6. quique per patientiam & conso- lationem spem vivam habent, v. 4. quos se mutuò as- sumere jubet, exemplo Christi, qui nos assumsit, v. 7. quod non nisi eorum est, qui in Christum credunt; quibus proinde ipse precatur, ut eosdem DEUS spei porrò impleat omni GAUDIO in Spiritu S. & PA- CE ἐν τῷ πιστεύειν in CREDENDO, vel per fidem v. 13. de quibus persuasus est, quod sint πεπληρωμέ- νοι impleti omni notitiâ, seque mutuò exhortari pos- sint, v. 14. E quibus omnibus manifestum est, de fi- de justificante Apostolum loqui, cum ait: Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Per hanc fidem placuis- se Deo S. Patriarchas, & opera ipsorum, docet Apost. Ebr. XI. Ideoque opera danda, ut in hac fide simus, 2. Cor. XIII. & ut quæ facimus, ex fide fiant. Ex fide autem fieri non possunt, nisi ea è verbo Domini (è quo fides est) probari, certò nobis con- stet, imò nisi persona ea faciens, fide in Dominum prædita sit.

Proinde de fide etiam illa verba v. 22. Σὺ πίσιν ἔχεις rectè accipiuntur: Habesne fidem in Christum? Secundum teipsum habe coram Deo. Illi vide ut im- primis probes fidem tuam, sed vide etiam, ut ne ju- dices temetipsum in iis, quæ probas, & facis ad ex- tra: ne ea titubante conscientiâ facias. Ita enim non beatus eris, sed temetipsum condemnabis: adeo- que te verè præditum non esse fide, testaberis: quæ non consistit cum hæsitatione, sed in πληροφορίᾳ sita est. Novam ergò de adiaphoris regulam v. 22. tradit Apostolus, iis ita utendum esse, ut nihil fiat ti- tubante conscientiâ, non verò priorem regulam de vitando proximi offendiculo adhuc persequitur. Quod probè observandum. Nam eo neglecto tex- tus de fide salvifica, de qua totâ hàc Epistola egit Apostolus, satis luculentus, intricatus redditur: quasi de fide, quam vocant, conscientiæ, sermo sit, vel de notitia de usu adiaphororū, ne eâ abutamur cum scandalo infirmorum; quo de antea jam actum erat. Et observat Salmero Disp. 9. l. 4. in Epist. ad Rom. non deesse (præter August.) alios Patres, qui fidem hoc loco non pro conscientiâ, quæ regula est actionum hu- manarum, sed pro assensu fidei catholicæ, sive asser- tione dogmatum accipiendam esse, doceant; & in ea sententia ita esse Augustinum, ut oppositam fidei acceptionem tanquam novam & inauditam non probârit. Rectissimè ergò ex hoc loco, quicquid fit sine fide, peccatum est, omnia infidelium opera, quæ sine fide & speciali auxilio gratiæ fiunt, peccata esse, conclusit Sanct. Augustinus l. IV. contra Julian. c. 3. Quicquid boni fit ab homine, & non propter hoc fit, propter quod fieri debere vera sapientia præcipit, etsi ab officio videatur bonum, ipso non recto fine peccatum est. Nulla potest esse vera virtus, nisi in eo, qui justus est, justus autem nemo esse potest sine fide. Et l. III. ad Bonifac. c. 5. Sine fide qua videntur bona opera in peccata vertuntur, quicquid enim ex fide non est, peccatum est. Vide & l. 1. de Nupt. & Concupisc. cap. 3. &c. unde Salmero fatetur l. c. Augustinum sæpe uti testimonio Apost. quicquid non fit ex fide, &c. ad approbandum, omnem infidelium actum peccatum esse. Cui consonat Prosper. in sentent. 105. Omnis infidelium vita peccatum est, & nihil est bonum sine summo bono: ubi enim deest agnitio æterna & incommutabilis voluntatis, falsa virtus est etiam in optimis moribus. Et in Epigrammatis: Omne etenim pietatis opus, nisi semine recta exoritur fidei, peccatum est. Plura in eam sententiam è Basilio, & Chrysostomo adfert Cassander in Consult. art. VI. Gregor. M. l. II. Moral. c. 25. Si fides, inquit, non prima in corde nostro gignitur, reliqua quoque bona esse non possunt, etsi bona videantur. Bernhardus serm. XXII. in Cant. Quid vobis Philosophis cum virtutibus, qui Dei virtutem Christum ignoratis? Glossa ordinar. in h. l. Omnis infidelium vita est peccatum. Thom. in c. 15. Joh. ad verba, sine me nihil potestis facere: om obstruxit superborum, & præcipuè Pelagianorum, qui dicunt, bona opera virtutum & legis sine adjutorio ex seipsis facere posse. Unde Thomæ sectatores Cassander l. c. docet rejicere Scoti sententiam, hominem ex puris naturalibus, & auxilio generali se ad gratiam de congruo præparare: ad consensum Joh. Driedonis provocans: Ambrosius verò Catharinus in ipso Concilio Tridentino propugnabat opera infidelium, qui à Deo non excitantur ad credendum, verè esse peccata, neque solum Augustinum in eam rem citabat, sed & D. Ambrosium, D. Prosperum, Anshelmum aliosque è Patribus, item Gregorium Ariminens. & Cardin. Rossensem, notante P. Suavi Hist. Conc. Trid. l. II. Pesantius allegat in eam sententia Altisiodorensem, Alensem, & Capreolum in l. 2. quæst. 109. art. 2. Tannerus Jesuita T. II. Theol. Scholast. Disp. VI. q. 3. & T. III. Disp. 1. q. 8. adduxit etiam Michaelem Bajum & Cassalium. Nam etsi virtutes gentilium rectæ rationi & lumini naturæ consentaneæ sint, non dubitat tamen easdem peccata appellare Augustinus, non quòd in suo genere & materialiter actiones malæ sint, sed quia nec à persona Deo grata, nec recto fine fiunt, siquidem nihil personam Deo gratam reddat, nisi fides in Christum: unde virtutes illæ peccata vocantur non intrinsecè & in natura sua, sed extrinsecè in judicio Dei spectata, quia absque fide facta: nec bona opera dici possunt, quia fides anima est bonorum operum, (non verò bona opera anima fidei,) quâ deficiente nihil bonum opus appellari potest. Quapropter aliter judicandum de operibus infidelium in judicio DEI, quàm in judicio hominum. Potest enim id quod coram hominibus summam meretur laudem, vitiosum esse coram Deo: juxta illud Hieronymi: Omnis virtus absque Christo in vitio est. Unde apparet, quantum discrimen sit inter virtutes fidelium & infidelium: illæ vix inchoatæ Deo placent, quia ex fide factæ; hæ etiam in excellenti gradu displicent, quia absq; fide factæ. Lombardus l. II. Sentent. distinct. XLI. lit. A. Non irrationabiliter à quibusdam adstruitur, quòd omnes actio- nes & voluntates hominis sine fide mala sint, qua fide habita bona existunt, unde Apostolus ait, omne, quod non est ex fide, peccatum est, quod exponens Augustinus ait, omnis vita infidelium peccatum est, & nihil bonum est sine summo bono. Adde Job. Ferum l. 1. in Matth. VIII. p. 125. Vides igitur, nedum bonum, sed malum esse, quicquid extra fidem fit: & Thomam Bradvardin. l. II. de causa Dei ad- versus Pelag. cap. 5. ex Augustino id prolixè pro- bantem. Denique fateri Bellarm. ipse debuit l. 1. de justific. c. 21. ante fidem nihil boni fieri posse: & affine illis est, quod habetur in jure Canonico c. cum Paulus, Caus. 1. quæst. 1. ex Gregorio: Cùm Paulus dicat, fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest præter id, quod positum est, quod est Christus Jesus, consequenter probatur, quia ubi Christus non est fundamentum, nullius boni operis est ædi- ficium.

Addimus hisce quæ B. HÜLSEMANNUS noster de præsenti loco nobis planè ὁμόψηφος tradit, quia ea nondum edita sunt: Quicquid non est ex fi- de, &c. Verum quidem est, vocem fidei pro ratione objectorum, de quibus prædicatur, significare vel notitiam vel assensum tantùm, vel etiam fiduciam de benevolentia DEI erga nos, & complacentia a- ctionum nostrarum coram DEO. Utroque modo afferimus hic sumi vocem fidei, non tantùm pro no- titia rei licitæ, sed etiam pro benevola voluntate DEI erga nos approbante factum nostrum. Hanc enim fiduciam de DEI benevolentia erga nos corre- quiri ad tranquillandum conscientia nostræ, ex- pressè asserit Paulus vers. 17. & seq. quando non solùm indefinitè ait, quæ sint attributa hominis Christiani in regno gratiæ versantis, scilicet justi- tia, pax & gaudium in Spiritu S. sed quòd etiam comedens vel non comedens fruatur his beneficiis, & sit εὐάρεστος τῷ Θεῷ: quo sensu etiam vocabulum πίστεως vers. 22. sumitur, non solùm pro notitia li- citentiæ sive permissionis. Quamobrem Apologiæ Augustanæ Confessionis & Theologi nostri dictum hoc rectè extendunt non solum ad electitia opera Papistarum, quæ verbo DEI, & consequenter fide destituuntur, contra Bellarmin. II. de Mona- chis c. 16. sed etiam ad opera gentilium, quæ fide seu verâ fiduciâ in Verum Deum destituuntur, con- tra eundem Bellarm. V. de gratia c. 10. tametsi enim concedi possit, quod ipse, quod Suarezius in par- tem I. Thomæ T. II. l. 2. cap. 10. quod Stapleso- nus in antidoto ad h. l. quod Cornelius & Estius objectant, Paulum hic non respexisse ad objectum fidei, quod sit imputatio meriti Christi; sufficit tamen objectum ejus fidei, de qua hic agit Pau- lus, esse benevolentiam & complacentiam DEI erga actiones nostras: quæ autem sit causa meri- toria talis complacentiæ, hoc aliunde proban- dum est: & constituta benevolentiâ DEI erga nos, pro objecto fidei, de qua hic sermo est, neces- sario etiam admittitur causa talis benevolentiæ, et- si uno intuitu, sive uno actu secundo talis fidei, qua- lem hic describit Paulus, non omnes causæ aut omnia instrumenta salutis nostræ comprehendantur. Pro- inde inepta est collectio Papistarum, cum quibus etiam Arminius facit respons. ad 31. art. articu- lo 15. fides, de qua Paulus loquitur, non habet pro objecto adæquato specialem illam fiduciam peccata sibi remissa, vel remittenda esse per imputatio- nem meriti Christi: Ergò fides, de quâ hic ser- mo est, non est fides justificans Lutheranorum. Nam sufficit, ut diximus, fidem hanc habere pro objecto etiam benevolentiam Dei erga nos: quà positâ etiam ponitur causa meritoria hujus benevolentiæ, & modus applicandi eam, certè nullâ ratione excluditur.

Sic August. IV. contra Julian. cap. 3. & 4. Prosper, Fulgentius, aliique, Originem secuti, de defectu fidei in Christum exponunt: quos impudenter 5. Disp. refutat Pererius. Toletus autem annot. 5. vocat sen- tentiam probabilem. Conferat Lector Origenis, Au- gustini, aliorumque Patrum expositionem, cum quo- rundam Latinorum, etiam Concil. Later. sub Inno- centio III. Canone 41. torturam, qua exponunt fidem hic loci juridice pro justo titulo, acquisitæ rei possessæ: Quod non est ex fide, peccatum est, id Synodali judi- cio definimus, inquiunt: quod nulla præscriptio sive possessio alicujus rei ultra 30. vel 40. valeat absque bona fide, i. e. absque justo titulo prima acquisitionis. Hæc B. Dominus Socer. Quod Grotius attexit de tribus versibus, etiamsi Codicum aliquam diversi- tatem referat, eo tamen perperam, nec satis re- ligiose abripitur, quod voluerit Paulus hic finire Epistolam, sed postea temporis plus insperato nactus alia quædam adjecerit. Non enim ea congruunt divinæ inspirationi, & directioni. Et quæ habentur initio capitis sequentis usque ad votum tractatio- nis hujus ἐπιλογικὸν, huc pertinere, satis docet e- jusdem continuatio, & ulterior e S. literis confir- matio cum aliis, quæ fortuito accessisse, verisimile non est. Confer. Justinian. & Estius in h. l.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV.

ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

The Apostle pursues the subject concerning the weak, and teaches that we should tolerate them and not please ourselves, by the example of Christ, who did not please himself, but for the sake of the zeal of pleasing God bore reproaches, as David testifies: which he says was written for the sake of our instruction: adding a prayer that all with one mind may glorify God: and he further admonishes that we should accept one another, just as Christ accepted us, both the Jews, to whose fathers the promise was made, and also the Gentiles, which David and Isaiah predicted concerning them: concluding with prayers for fuller joy and peace in faith. Then indeed he excuses the boldness of his writing by the duty of his office, which he was performing among the Gentiles, Christ granting it: on account of which, being hindered by various travels from coming to Rome until now, he promises his arrival when he will set out for Spain with alms, exhorting them to help him with their prayers, and he adds an epilogikon prayer.

There are two parts: The former is hortatory concerning bearing the infirmities of one's neighbor, and mutual acceptance, with a pious prayer both interspersed and subjoined up to verse 13. The latter is excusatory, partly of the writing, partly of the delayed arrival, with a request for their prayers, and a prayer for divine grace, up to the end of verse 33. The former pertains to the completion of the Apostolic treatment: The latter to the epilogue of this Epistle, which constitutes its final part, begun here, to be completed in the following chapter.

PART I. OF CHAPTER XV. HORTATORY. Concerning bearing the infirmities of one's neighbor, and mutual acceptance.

verse 1. We who are strong. He calls those more advanced in the knowledge of things strong here, to whom the weak are opposed above. Thus, strong in speech. Luke 25:19; Acts 7:22.

to bear the infirmities of the weak. A similitude drawn from companions on a journey, of whom those who are stronger relieve the less strong of a portion of their burdens. Cicero says, to lighten a burden. To bear one another's burdens, the Apostle here, Galatians 6:2. But the argument seems to be drawn from the law of Exodus 23:5, in this way: If the beast of an enemy must be relieved, how much more a human friend? The sense is, we ought to bear the errors of others gently.

and not to please ourselves. To please in this place, as also in 1 Corinthians 10:33, is to do a pleasing thing, just as Xenophon also said to please a neighbor. It is a metonymy of the effect for the cause.

Latin:

CAPUT XV.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Persequitur Apostolus materiam de infirmis, & ut eos toleremus, nec nobismetipsis placea- mus, exemplo Christi, docet, qui non sibi ipsi placuit, sed ob Zelum Deo placendi oppro- bria, Davide teste, tulit: quod nostræ do- ctrinæ causa scriptum ait: addito voto, ut o- mnes una mente Deum glorificent: monet- que porro, ut assumamus nos mutuo, quem- admodum Christus nos assumpsit, tum Ju- dæos, quorum Patribus promissio facta, tum etiam gentiles, quod de his David & Esaias prædixerit: concludens vota ple- nioris gaudii & pacis in fide. Tum vero excusat scriptionis παῤῥησίαν officii sui debi- to, quo inter gentes, Christo dante, fungeba- tur: ob quod peregrinationibus variis Ro- mam venire eousque impeditus, promittit adventum suum cum in Hispaniam cum Eleemosynis proficiscetur, exhortans eos- dem, ut precibus suis sese juvent, votumque ἐπιλογικὸν subjicit.

PArtes duæ sunt: Prior est adhortatoria de fe- rendis proximi infirmitatibus, & assumtione mutua, pio voto tum intermixto, tum subjuncto usque ad v. 13. Altera est excusatoria partim scri- ptionis, partim dilati adventus, cum petitione pre- cum ipsorum, & voto gratiæ divinæ, usque ad finem v. 33. Illa pertinet ad tractationis Apostolicæ com- plementum: Hæc ad Epistolæ hujus Epilogum, qui partem ultimam ejusdem constituit, hic cœ- ptam, sequenti capite absolvendam.

PARS I. CAPITIS XV. ADHORTATORIA. De ferendis proximi infirmitatibus, & assum- tione mutua.

vers. 1. Ὀφείλομεν ἡμεῖς οἱ δυνατοὶ. δυνατοὺς hic vocat provectiores in rerum cognitione, qui- bus oppositi supra ἀσθενεῖς. Sic δυνατὸς ἐν λόγῳ. Luc. XXV. 19. Act. VII. 22.

τὰ ἀσθενήματα ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν. Similitudo ducta ab itinerum sociis, quorum validiores qui sunt, minus validos parte sarcinarum levant. Onus al- levant, dicit Cicero. ἀλλήλων βάρη βαστάζειν, hic Apostolus Gal. VI. 2. Videtur autem argumentum duci ex lege Exo- di XXIII. 5. hoc modo: Si sublevandum est jumentum ini- mici, quantò magis homo amicus? Sensus est, leniter fer- re nos debet aliorum hallucinationes.

κὰι μὴ ἑαυτοῖς ἀρέσκειν. ἀρέσκειν hoc loco, ut & 1. Cor. X. 33. est rem gratam fa- cere, quomodo & Xenophon dixit γείτονι ἀρέσκειν. Est me- tonymia effectus pro causa.

## 15:2
v. 2. For each of you. A manuscript, each of us, which coheres better with the preceding.

let him please his neighbor for good unto edification. We ought not to gratify another in all things, but in those things which result in his own good, that is, through which he can become better. For after for good is understood his, as above 8:28 and 13:4, and its interpretation is that unto edification, concerning which see above 14:19. Let him please, that is, he ought to know that this is to be cared for by him.

Latin:

v. 2. ἕκαστος γὰρ ὑμῶν. Manuscriptus, ἕκαστος ἡμῶν, quod cum præcedentibus melius cohæret.

τῷ πλησίον ἀρεσκέτω εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν. Non in omnibus gratificari alteri debemus, sed in iis, quæ ipsius bono cedunt, id est, per quæ fieri melior potest. Nam post εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν subauditur αὐτῦ, ut supra VIII. 28. & XIII. 4. & ejus interpretatio est illud πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν, de quo vide supra XIV. 19. ἀρεσκέτω, id est, scire debet hoc sibi curan- dum.

## 15:3
v. 3. For even Christ. That is, he who ought to be for an example to us, 1 Pet. II. 21.

did not please himself. He did not seek sweet things for himself.

but. Supply 'he did', as above XIV. 23.

as it is written, the reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me. These are the words of David, who is a figure of Christ, in the Psalm according to the Hebrews LXIX. 10. See Matth. XXVII. 39, 40, 41, 42. Christ endured all these things for the sake of God and men.

I continue to treat of the infirm; but blessed Luther not without reason warns that here those are also regarded who do not err only in indifferent matters, but who are overtaken by infirmity in some sin, concerning whom he also taught in Gal. VI. 2, that one ought to bear the burdens of another. See Vol. II. Jena Latin, fol. 328. What he says is this: if we are not firm, and seem spiritual to ourselves, we ought not to compare ourselves to those who are not such, or do not seem so, nor please ourselves in the defect of a brother, just as the Pharisee in the Gospel pleased himself in the defect of the publican and of all men, nor should the brother be displeasing for that reason, because he cannot, nor has what we can and have, but we ought to sustain this defect of his in a spirit of gentleness, taking care that we so treat him that we may please him in gentleness and tolerance of such a kind, until, provoked by our good, he imitates us, and is built up by us in that manner. Wherefore this must be done, not how we may please ourselves and he be displeased, but in what way we may so please him, that he may become better. Therefore the Apostle commands to bear the infirmities of the weak, and that this may be done, he warns that we should not attempt to please ourselves: which most people take concerning self-will or self-love as the cause of the contrary vice, namely, impatience. For those who please themselves, and admire their own things, are accustomed to be more rigid censors of others. But we easily admit that these things are explained concerning the pursuit of one's own advantage. For he who seeks only what is his own, and what is pleasant to himself, he pleases himself, he indulges himself, and therefore does and pursues only things that please himself, and does not serve his neighbor, much less bear his infirmities with his own burden and annoyance. Which sense the example of Christ and the Davidic passage concerning the same confirms: because Christ did not indulge himself, or seek what is his own, and what is sweet to himself, but wished to serve the glory of God the Father and our salvation, by enduring even reproaches and most grievous sufferings, both on account of zeal for the house of the Lord, and on account of the salvation of the human race: concerning which insults and sufferings, and the causes of the same, Psalm 69 treats expressly, as they say. Theophylact preceded with this explanation along with Chrysostom: When he said that it behooved us to sustain, he teaches how that may be done, if, namely, we require nothing of those things which are our own. And at v. 2 he brings Christ into the middle, that he may argue to us by his example how life is to be lived. For it was permitted to him to vindicate himself from any reproach and insult, and not to suffer those things which he suffered, if he had preferred to please himself, that is, if he had sought what was in his own interest. Similarly, the Greek Scholia explained it through τὰ ἑαυτῶ σκοπεῖν, to intend only those things which might tend to our own advantage. Beza renders it, to indulge ourselves. Estius: They are said by the Apostle to please themselves who acquiesce in their own good, not solicitous that it may be well for others also: just as those were doing whom he reproves in the previous chapter, who were so acquiescing in their own knowledge and faith, which they had concerning the indifference of foods and the cessation of legal requirements, and were using it in such a way that they did not avoid the scandals of others, nor did they at all sustain their infirmities. In this way Christ did not please himself. For he did not indulge himself; he was not so content with his own good, although he himself was most excellent and most blessed, that he did not also care for the salvation of others. For for us men, and for our salvation he descended from the heavens, suffered, was crucified and died. Flacius in his gloss: First, he commands that we should with all zeal tolerate and lift up the infirmities and inconveniences of our neighbor: then, that we should not serve and indulge only ourselves and our own conveniences. Thus also at the beginning of the preceding chapter he ordered us to take up the infirm brothers. He says, however, that we ought to do this, namely, because the divine command obliges us, and because we were not born only for ourselves, and were not adorned with gifts by God, but also for our neighbor. To please ourselves does not here signify properly Φιλαυτίαν, by which someone too much magnifies and loves himself: but the zeal of pleasing oneself, or seeking only one's own advantage and pleasures, and (as he spoke above in verse 7) living for oneself. The effect of pleasing is put for the endeavor. To indulge or to comply you could not badly translate. And afterwards: He illustrates and confirms this latter member of the proposition by the example of Christ, whose every action is our instruction, and whom we ought deservedly to imitate. He indeed did not come to be served, but to serve others, as he himself says. Thus also in Philippians chapter two the Apostle argues copiously from the example of Christ. He says therefore that he did not please himself, or attempt to please, or indulge himself, or have leisure or live for himself, but for the Father, and that by sustaining for his sake all the greatest reproaches and crosses, which he also proves by the cited sixty-ninth Psalm. The concise speech can easily be supplied in this way: but by the greatest zeal and having no regard for himself, by promoting the glory and will of the Father, he drew upon himself the persecution and reproaches of men, as it is written, etc. For thus the Lord there testifies that his zeal is the cause of persecution for him. These things Flacius. To which contribute those things of Christ in John 5:30. I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me. To which sense the antithesis also serves: that we should not please ourselves, but each one of us should please his neighbor, that is, should strive to please, not for evil, whether of loss or of vice, but for good; not for destruction, but for edification; by which not any utility, but an excellent utility is noted, just as buildings, from which the metaphor is taken, are of notable use to us. Which debt the law of Christian charity demands, that namely one should not destroy another, but build him up. We do not deny the reading in the first person. For fewer read ὑμῶν, your. For some Latin manuscript copies also exhibit our, with which both the Syriac text and Augustine, reciting this place in his book On the Morals of the Manichaeans, chapter 14, agree: and that reading corresponds to the preceding part, in which the first person had been expressed, as Estius here observed, having put the Vulgate version after. In this, however, Grotius maintains the old view, that he explains the Psalm, which according to the connection of the context and the evidence of the Apostolic explanation and of other divinely inspired writers in the New Testament, prophesies entirely concerning Christ, according to the letter concerning David: whom we have refuted in the Annotations to the book of Psalms. What was predicted concerning the reproaches of the Father falling back upon Christ, B. Brentius rightly

, explains in his Commentary on the Psalms, both concerning the blasphemies with which the Pharisees and the rest of the crowd of the Jewish nation impiously affected God by their doctrine and their hypocritical religion or rather superstition, and especially concerning the reproaches which they cast upon Christ hanging on the cross, being openly contumelious against God himself, saying: he trusts in God, let him deliver him now, if he wants him: which blasphemies fell upon Christ, and although they burned and consumed him most grievously in his soul, nevertheless he received them with the greatest obedience and patience, and although he could have vindicated them by present lightning or a chasm of the earth, he preferred to gratify the calling of God his Father than to please himself and importunately show his majesty. William brings forward and proves another sense. Estius: Thus for those reproaches I grieved, so that for them as if they were my own sins, to appease your wrath against those who were admitting these things, I humbled myself even to the death of the cross: paying back what I did not steal: (as is said in the same Psalm) in which matter I declared how much care I had for their salvation. But the former interpretation is simpler: and the Psalmist speaks not of the grief of Christ because of the malice of those reproaching, and the expiation of this, but of the patient toleration of reproaches to fulfill the will of the Father and acquire salvation for the human race. B. Luther interprets it thus in the place cited: See the example of Christ, who treated us in this way, so that he did not insult our sins, did not glory in the form of God, nor in all things which he had and could do, but emptied himself, and did that by which he might please us for the provocation of good, while he bore our sins upon himself, and did not reject or desert us, so evil and unworthy. For if he himself had acted as we act toward our neighbors, he would have redeemed no one; but if we act toward our neighbors as he does toward us, we will despise no man, however much a sinner or difficult he may be. Thus also Erasmus in this place: He is pleased with himself who serves his own advantage, and draws what he does to his own profit: which kind of man is called by the Greeks Φίλαυτοὶ, not only on account of arrogance, but also on account of the pursuit of private advantage. From which vice Christ was very far removed, who spent his whole self upon us. Origen also noted here that the vice of Φιλαυτίας is condemned. But as it is written, Reproaches, and the rest) And this statement is little finished, but the contrary part is to be understood: Christ did not please himself, but displeased himself: that is, he did not serve his own advantages, but at his own inconvenience he consulted our advantages, just as it is written, the reproaches of them that reproached, etc.

Latin:

v. 3. κὰι γὰρ ὁ χριστὸς. Is scilicet, qui nobis pro exemplari debet esse, 1. Pet. II. 21.

ὐχ ἑαυτῷ ἤρεσεν. Non quæsivit sibi dulcia.

ἀλλά. Supple fecit, ut supra XIV. 23.

καθὼς γέγραπται οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ τῶν ὀνειδιζόντων σε, ἐπέπεσον ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ. Verba sunt Davidis, qui figura Christi, psalmo juxta He- bræos LXIX. 10. Vide Matth. XXVII. 39. 40. 41. 42. O- mnia hæc sustinuit Christus Dei ac hominum causa.

De infirmis agere pergi; sed non præter rem monet B. Lutherus, hîc respici etiam illos, qui non in rebus mediis tantum errant, sed qui infirmitate in aliquo delicto præoccupantur, de quibus etiam Gal. VI. 2. docuit, quod alter alterius onera portare de- beat. Vid. T. II. Jen. Lat. f. 328. Quod dicit hoc est: si non sumus firmi, & spirituales nobis videmur, non debemus nos eis comparare, qui tales non sunt, aut non videntur, nec nobis placere in defectu fratris, sic- ut Pharisæus in Evangelio, de publicani defectu & omnium hominum sibi placebat, nec debet ideo fra- ter displicere, quia non potest, nec habet, quod nos pos- sumus & habemus, sed sustinere debemus hunc ejus defectum in spiritu lenitatis, id curantes, ut nos sic tractemus eum, quo ei placeamus in lenitate & tole- rantia ejusmodi, donec provocatus nostro bono, nos imitetur, & ex nobis isto modo ædificetur. Quare id agendum est, non quomodo nobis placeamus & ille displiceat, sed quo modo nos ei sic placeamus, quo me- lior fiat. Portare ergò jubet Apostolus infirmorum ἀσθενήματα, idque ut fiat, monet, ne nobis ipsis pla- cere conemur: quod plerique de ἀυθαδείᾳ vel Φι- λαυτίᾳ ceu causa vitii contrarii, impatientiæ nimi- rum, accipiunt. Qui enim sibi ipsis placent, & sua mirantur, in alios rigidiores censores esse solent. Sed facilè admittimus, hæc de studio proprii com- modi explicari. Qui enim quærit tantùm, quæ sua sunt, sibique grata, is sibi placet, sibi indulget, ideo- que tantùm sibi placentia agit, ac sectatur, non verò proximo servit, nedum ejus infirmitates cum onere, & molestia sua portat. Quem sensum ex- emplum Christi, & locus Davidicus de eodem con- firmat: quia Christus non indulsit sibi, aut quæsi- vit, quæ sua sunt, sibique suavia, sed Dei Patris glo- riæ, nostræque saluti inservire voluit, opprobria etiam ac passiones gravissimas sustinendo, tùm ob zelum pro domo Domini, tùm ob salutem gene- ris humani: de quibus contumeliis ac passionibus, & causis earundem Psal. 69. ex professo, quod di- cunt, agitur. Præivit hac explicatione cum Chrys. Theophylactus: Cùm diceret oportere nos sustinere, docet quemadmodum fieri id queat, si ea videlicet quæ nostra sunt, nil requiramus. Et ad v. 2. Christum producit in medium, ut arguat nobis ejus exemplo vivendam. Illi namque licebat sese à quovis opprobrio, & contumelia vindicare, neque ea, quæ passus est, perpeti, si sibi ipsi placere maluisset, hoc est, si quod sua intererat, conquisisset. Similiter Græca Scholia exposuère per τὰ ἑαυτῶ σκοπεῖν, tantùm intendere ea, quæ in nostrum commodum vergere possint. Beza reddit, indulgere nobis met ipsis. Estius: Apostolo dicuntur sibi placere, qui acquiescunt in bono suo, non solliciti ut & aliis benè sit: quemadmodum faciebant, quos reprehendit capite superiori, qui in sua, quam de ciborum indifferentia & legalium cessatione habebant, scientiá ac fide ita conquiescebant, sicque eâ utebantur, ut aliorum scandala non vitarent, nec omnino infirmitates eorum sustinerent. Hoc modo Christus non sibi placuit. Non n. sibi ipsi indulsit; non ita bono suo contentus fuit, quamvis ipse esset optimus & beatissimus; ut non etiam curaret aliorum salutem. Nam propter nos homines, & propter nostram salutem descendit de cælis, passus, crucifixus & mortuus est. Flacius in glossa: Primùm præcipit, ut omni studio toleremus, sublevemusque imbecillitates & incommoda proximi: deinde ne tantum nobis, nostrisque commodis serviamus & indulgeamus. Sic etiam initio præcedentis capitis jussit infirmos fratres sumere. Dicit verò id nos debere, nempe divino mandato nos obligante, & quia non nobis tantù nati, & donis à Deo ornati sumus, sed etiam proximo. Nobis placere non significat hic propriè Φιλαυτίαν, qua quis nimium seipsum magnificat ac diligit: sed studium sibi placendi, seu sua tantù commodo ac voluptates quærendi, ac (sicut supra v. 7. locutus est) sibimet vivendi. Effectus placere pro conatu ponitur. Indulgere aut obsequi posses non malè vertere. Et postea: Illustrat & confirmat hic posterius propositionis membrum exemplo Christi, cujus omnis actio est nostra instructio, quemque nos meritò imitari debemus. Is vero non venit, ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ipse aliis serviat, sicut ipsemet inquit. Sic & Philipp. secundo copiose Apostolus ab exemplo Christi argumentatur. Dicit igitur illum non sibi placuisse, aut placere conatum, seu non sibi indulsisse, vacasse aut vixisse, sed Patri, idque sustinendo ejus gratiá summa quæque opprobria & cruces, quod etiam citato Psalmo sexagesimo nono probat. Oratio concisa facilè suppleri potest, hoc modo: sed summo studio nullaque sui habita ratione promovendo gloriam ac voluntatem Patris, attraxit sibi hominum persecutionem & opprobria, sicut scriptum est, &c. Sic enim ibi Dominus testatur suum zelum sibi causam persecutionis esse. Hæc Flacius. Quò faciunt illa Christi Joh. V. 30. Non quæro voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem Patris, qui misit me. Cui sensui etiam antithesis servit: ne nobis ipsis placeamus, sed unusquisque nostrûm proximo placeat, h. e. placere studeat, non in malum sive damni sive vitii, sed in bonum; non ad destructionem, sed ad ædificationem; quà non quævis, sed eximia utilitas notatur, uti ædificia, à quibus metaphora desumta, insigni nobis usui sunt. Quod debitum lex charitatis Christianæ exigit, ut nempe alter alterum non destruat, sed ædificet. Lectioni in prima persona non abnuimus. Nam pauciores legunt ὑμῶν vestrum. Nam & Latina quædam exemplaria MSS. nostrum exhibent, quibus & Syriacus textus & August. hunc locum recitans in l. de morib. Manich. c. 14. consentiunt: eaque lectio respondet parti præcedenti, in qua prima persona expressa fuerat, ut hîc Estius posthabità versione vulgata observavit. In eo autem antiquum obtinet Grotius, quod Psalmum, qui de Christo secundũ contextus συνάφειαν, & explicationis Apostolicæ, aliorumque Scriptorum θεοπνέυσων in N. T. evidentiam totus vaticinatur, secundum literam de Davide explicat: quem confutavimus in Annot. ad lib. Psalmorum. Quæ de opprobriis Patris in Christum recidentibus prædicta, B. Brentius rectè

, explicat in Com̃ent. in Pfal. tùm de blasphemiis, qui- bus Deum impiè suâ doctrinâ, & hypocriticâ suâ religione seu potius superstitione Pharisæi, & reli- qua gentis Judaicæ turba affecerunt, tùm imprimis de opprobriis, quæ in Christum in cruce pendentem jecerunt, apertè in Deum ipsum contumeliosi, di- centes: confidit in Deum, liberet eum nunc, si vult eum: quæ blasphemiæ in Christum ceciderunt, & quamvis urebant, & exedebant eum in animo suo gravissimè, tamen excepit eas summâ obedien- tiâ & patientiâ, & cum potuisset ipsas præsenti fulmine, aut hiatu terræ vindicare, maluit vocatio- ni Dei Patris sui gratificari, quàm sibi placere & majestatem suam importunè ostentare. Alium ad- fert & probat sensum Guilh. Estius: Sic ob illa op- probria indolui, ut pro illis tanquam meis ipsius pec- catis, ad placandam iram tuam in eos, qui hæc admit- tebant, me humiliaverim usque ad mortem crucis: ex- solvens quæ non rapui: (sicut in eodem Psalmo dicitur) qua in re declaravi, quanta mihi cura fuerit salutis eorum. Sed simplicior est prior interpretatio: & lo- quitur Hierossaltes non de dolore Christi ob op- probantium malitiam, hujusque expiatione, sed de patienti opprobriorum toleratione ad implen- dam Patris voluntatem & acquirendam humano generi salutem. B. Lutherus ita interpretatur l. c. Exemplar Christi videte, qui hoc modo nos tractavit, ut non insultaret nostris peccatis, non gloriaretur de forma Dei, nec de omnibus quæ habuit & potuit, sed exinanivit se, & id egit, quo nobis placeret ad provo- cationem boni, dum nostra peccata super se tulit, nec rejecit aut deseruit, tam malos & indignos. Si enim ipse sic fecisset, sicut nos proximis facimus, neminem redemisset; Si autem sic facimus proximis, sicut ipse nobis, nullum hominem contemnemus, quantumlibet peccatorem aut difficilem. Sic etiam Erasmus in h. l. Placet sibi, qui suo servit commodo, & quod agit, ad suum trahit compendium: quod genus hominis Grâ- cis Φίλαυτοὶ dicuntur, non tantùm ob arrogantiam, verum etiam ob privati commodi studium. A quo vitio Christus longissimè abfuit, qui totum sese nobis impendit. Subnotavit & Origenes hîcc damnari vi- tium Φιλαυτίας. Sed sicut scriptum est, Imprope- ria, & cætera) Et hic sermo parum est absolutus, sed contraria pars subaudienda est: Christus non sibi placuit, sed sibi displicuit: hoc est, non inservivit suis commodis, sed suo incommodo nostris consuluit com- modis, quemadmodum scriptum est, opprobria op- probantium, &c.

## 15:4
V. 4. For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning. He meets a tacit objection; these things pertain to David. So it is: but it is agreed among the Jews that all these things are figures of the things of Christ. See 1 Cor. X. 6. προεγράφη written aforetime: and προέγραψα I wrote aforetime Eph. III. 3. just as προηλπικότας we hoped before, above I. 12. for our learning, the same here as πρὸς νυθεσίαν ἡμῶν in the mentioned place 1 Cor. X. 11. that through patience and comfort of the scriptures we might have hope. So that among the evils which we bear, and among the comforts which holy Scripture provides for us, you may perpetually retain hope. See above V. 3. 4. VIII. 25.

There was no doubt about it, that the Psalm pertains not to David, but to Christ, which also the disciples of Christ recalled to their minds at the first cleansing of the temple performed by Christ, John II. 17, and St. Matthew ch. XXVII. 34, 48 has testified: nay, the Rabbis also acknowledge it, as we taught regarding that Psalm. Nor does the Apostle say anything here about a figurative sense: rather, he teaches that those things which are prescribed in the O.T. pertain directly to our instruction, and were delivered and written down also for our sake. Moreover, the Apostle adds this Aphorism on the occasion of the cited Psalm, both that he might teach that the example of Christ, even as it was done in the O.T., serves us, and that every action of Christ is our instruction; and also that he might remind us that the Scripture of the Old Testament is not useless to us in the New Testament, nor written only for the sake of the men under the Old Testament but also for our instruction, and thus commend the Canon of the Old Testament to the faithful in the New Testament, which he does not only only (1.) πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, for information in faith and life, but also (2.) πρὸς ὑπομονὴν, for patience and perseverance in faith: and also (3.) πρὸς παράκλησιν, for consolation, and finally (4.) πρὸς ἐλπίδα, for the hope of eternal life. Lyranus expresses it thus: that these four are the utilities of Scripture: clarity of understanding, solidity of tolerance, sweetness of internal joy, security of obtaining glory. See, if you like, the elenctic use of this aphorism against the Socinians and Papists in the last oracle of the Theol. Apost. Rom. which he also offers against Grotius, who disparages the promises of eternal life in the Old Testament, of which, however, the Apostle testifies that we have hope from the same. Blessed Mylius shows the critical use, namely in judging dogmas and the interpretation of the Scriptures. For whatever doctrine or interpretation cuts the nerves of faith, hope, and consolation, and fosters despair, we know undoubtedly by this Apostolic criterion that it is not analogous to Scripture and faith. Whence it is very easy to perceive what is to be judged concerning the dogma of Papist doubt and the absolute decree of the Sacramentarian predestination. Blessed Luther applies it to the present case in the place cited: Since the tolerance of the weak and the conversation of the morose is not the lightest part of the cross, it is certainly not insignificantly troublesome to the old man, who always strives to please himself and to displease others. Wherefore, through patience, he must be mortified in this part, and through Scripture exhorted to hope in God alone, not in self-pleasing. And thus he rightly applied the general use of Scripture to the part of this cross.

Latin:

V. 4. ὅσα γὰρ προεγράφη, εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν διδασκαλίαν προεγράφη. Occurrit tacitæ objectioni; ad Davidem ista pertinent. Sic ita: at constat inter Judæos omnes istas res figuras esse rerum Christi. Vide 1. Cor. X. 6. προεγράφη ante scriptum: & προέγραψα ante scripsi Eph. III. 3. sicut προηλπικότας ante evicimus, supra III. 9. εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν διδασκαλίαν, idem hic quod πρὸς νυθεσίαν ἡμῶν dicto loco 1. Cor. X. 11. ἵνα διὰ τῆς ὑπομονῆς καὶ διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως τῶν γρα- φῶν τὴν ἐλπίδα ἔχωμεν. Ut inter mala quæ ferimus, & inter solatia quæ nobis præstat sacra Scriptura, spem perpetuò retineas. Vide supra V. 3. 4. VIII. 25.

De eo nullum erat dubium, Psalmum non ad Davidem, sed ad Christum pertinere, quod & di- scipuli Christi in prima templi repurgatione à Christo factâ Joh. II. 17. sibi in mentem revocarunt, & S. Matthæus c. XXVII. 34. 48. testatus est: imò Rabbiui etiam agnoscunt, ut ad Psalmum illum docuimus. Nec quicquam hîc de figurato sensu A- postolus: Directè potius ad nostram doctrinam fa- cere ea, quæ præscripta sunt in V. T. & nostri et- iam causa tradita, & conscripta esse docet. Addit autem hunc Aphorismum occasione adducti Psal- mi Apostolus, tùm ut exemplum Christi etiam prout in V. T. factum, nobis infervire, omnem- que Christi actionem nostram esse institutionem, doceat, tum ut Scripturam V. Test. non inutilem esse nobis in N. T. nec solum ob homines sub V. T. sed etiam ad nostram doctrinam scriptam esse, commonefaciat, adeoque Canonem V. Test. fide- libus in N. T. commendet, quod non tantum fa- ciat (1.) πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, ad informationem in fide, & vita, sed etiam (2.) πρὸς ὑπομονὴν ad patientiam & perseverantiam in fide: nec non (3.) πρὸς παρά- κλησιν, ad consolationem, ac denique (4.) πρὸς ἐλ- πίδα, ad spem vitæ æternæ. Lyranus ita effert: quod hæ quatuor sint Scripturæ utilitates, claritas intelli- gentiæ, soliditas tolerantiæ, suavitas internæ lætitiæ, securitas obtinendæ gloriæ. Aphoristi hujus usum ἐλεγκτικὸν adversus Socinianos & Pontificios vide, si lubet, oraculo ultimo Theol. Apost. Rom. quem etiam adversus Grotium præbet, Veteri Test. pro- missiones vitæ æternæ derogantem, de qua tamen spem nos ex eodem habere testatur Apostolus. Usum κριτικὸν monstrat B. Mylius, in judicandis nempe dogmatibus & interpretatione Scripturarum. Quæcunque enim doctrina, aut interpretatio fidei, spei ac consolationis nervos præcidens, fovet despera- tionem, eam Scripturæ ac fidei analogam non esse, hoc κριτηρίῳ Apostolico indubitanter cognoscimus. Unde quid de dubitationis Pontificiæ dogmate, & prædestinationis Sacramentariæ absoluto decreto sit judicandum, perspicere perfacile est. Ad præsen- tia ita applicat B. Lutherus l. c. Cum tolerantia infirmorum & conversatio morosorum sit non levis- sima pars crucis, certè non mediocriter molesta est veteri homini, qui sibi semper placere studet, & in aliis displicere. Quare per patientiam in hac parte mortificandus est, & per Scripturam exhortandus, ut speret in solo Deo, non in sui placentia. Ac sic re- cte generalem Scripturæ usum ad partem crucis hujus applicavit.

## 15:5
v. 5. And the God of patience and consolation. The God of patience is He whom Christian tolerance regards. Just as below 13, the God of hope. The God of consolation is He from whom comforts come. For the genitive in these books denotes now the object, now the efficient cause.

May He grant you to be of the same mind one toward another. That is, may He grant you all things that can be profitable for mutual concord. See above XII. 18.

according to Christ Jesus. Such a concord, I say, as does not hinder Christian piety. For the name of Jesus Christ is often put for his precepts.

Latin:

v. 5. ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς ὑπομονῆς καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως. θεὸς τῆς ὑπομονῆς est is, quem tolerantia Christiana re- spicit. Sicut infra 13. ὁ θεὸς τῆς ἐλπίδος. θεὸς τῆς παρα- κλήσεως, is à quo solatia veniunt. Genitivus enim in his libris modo objectum, modo causam effectricem denotat.

δώη ὑμῖν τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν ἀλλήλοις. Id est, det vobis omnia, quæ ad concordiam mutuam prodesse possunt. Vide supra XII. 18.

κατὰ χρισὸν Ἰησῦν. Talem, inquam, concordiam, quæ pietati Christianæ non obsitet. Nam Jesu Christi nomen pro præceptis ejus sæpè ponitur.

## 15:6
v. 6. That with one mind you may with one mouth glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. That is, that when you praise God and pour out prayers to Him, you may do it not only with the same sound of words (as doxologies and litanies are wont to be done) but also with a mind full of mutual love, without contempt, without hatred. You have this word ὁμοθυμαδὸν in Acts II. 46, where it is the form of the most perfect Church. Add to the explanation of that word what is in Acts IV. 32. God is called the God of Christ, especially, and God in Eph. I. 17, and Father in Eph. I. 3, and through Him, our God.

The God of patience is not He whom Christian tolerance regards, just as the God of consolation is not He whom Christian consolation regards, but He who is the author and cause of patience and consolation, as noted by Chrysostom and Theophylact. Blessed Luther beautifully says in this place: How diligent a preacher of grace he is, so that, namely, no one may presume to obtain the patience and consolation of Scripture by his own powers, he indicates by his prayer that these gifts of God are to be obtained by humble prayer. Scripture indeed teaches, but grace grants what it teaches. God (he says) is the author and bestower of patience and consolation; may He grant you, because you do not have it of yourselves, to be of the same mind one toward another, that is, that each one may feel the same as the other, that is, that you may be affected, moved, and held by the same things, and that the same things may please all. How? Namely, that the weak may mind the things that the strong do, and again that the strong may not otherwise regard the inconveniences of the weak than their own, so that just as they would wish it to be done to them if they were in the place of the weak, so they themselves may do to them. For this is to be of the same mind, not seeking one's own, but the things of others, as Eph. V teaches. For this spiritual affection is the nerve of the whole Christian religion, without which it cannot subsist, which he calls elsewhere the unity of the Spirit; being diligent (he says) to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. He argues from the sacred letters, says Theophylact, that God bestows both tolerance and consolation together, and therefore he calls Him the God of patience and of consolation, as being the bestower and cause of these. He therefore wishes and prays for them that the same may be exhibited by Him toward one another. For that is the sign of a more certain charity, that what one thinks of himself, he should likewise think of his neighbor. And since there is another kind of love of this age, he added according to Christ Jesus, that is, that you may mind those things which are pleasing to Christ Jesus. Therefore, there is no reason for us to believe that the word Christ is taken for his precepts. There is here an elegant description of true concord from the order of causes, as Blessed Mylius notes: God is established as the efficient cause. Thus it is hinted that this in no way depends on human counsels or powers. The matter of concord is in mutual consent: to which the legitimate form is added when there is consent in Christ Jesus. For the name of peace is indeed a beautiful thing, and the opinion of unity is fair. But who would doubt that the only unity of the Church is that peace which is of Christ, as Hilary speaks. The end of this good is the unanimous celebration of the divine name. Concerning which end B. Luther is to be heard again: That you may unanimously with one mouth honor the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; that is, because there is one God who has called us, you have all obtained the same mercy. He who called the strong, the same also called the weak, and made no distinction between any, so also you, not distracted by these masks into diverse affections, unanimous, acknowledging this grace of God common to all, should glorify God; just as He did not distinguish by the grace of calling, so neither should the diversity of strength or weakness distinguish. Let us also hear Theophylact: What profit do we obtain when we all feel and think as one? Namely, because we ourselves exalt God with praises: and we do this not only with one mouth, but also with one mind. For this is what he intends when he says unanimous. Soon he begins that separately, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. But if you read it thus, namely that He is the God and Father of Christ himself, nor can that seem absurd; for He is God according to the humanity of Christ, and Father according to the divinity. Others take the word καὶ interpretatively, as if to say, God namely the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ 1 Cor. XV. 24. 2 Cor. I. 3. Glorification, however, happens not only when we praise God with hymns or when we pray, but also when we issue a confession of faith, Phil. II. 11.

Latin:

v. 6. ἵνα ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἐν ἑνὶ σόματι δοξάζητε τὸν Θεὸν καὶ πατέρα τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χριστῦ. Id est, ut cum Deum laudatis eique preces funditis, fa- ciatis id non tantùm eodem verborum sono (sicut δοξολο- γίαι & λιτανεῖαι fieri solent) sed & animo pleno mutuæ di- lectionis, sine contemptu, sine odio. Habes hanc vocem ὁμοθυμαδὸν Actor. II. 46. ubi forma est Ecclesiæ perfectissi- mæ. Adde ad ejus vocis explicationem id quod est Act. IV. 32. Deus, eximie Christi, & Deus Eph. I. 17. & pater dici- tur Eph. 1. 3. & per ipsum, noster.

Deus ὑπομονῆς non est quem tolerantia Chri- stiana respicit, sicut nec Deus τῆς παρακλήσεως est, quem respicit Christiana consolatio, sed qui autor est & causa patientiæ & consolationis, ut à Chryso- stomo & Theophylacto notatum. Pulchrè B. Luthe- rus h. l. Quam diligens gratiæ Prædicator, ne vi- delicet quisquam suis viribus patientiam & solatium Scripturæ præsumat obtinere, oratione suâ indicat, hæc dona Dei esse humili prece impetranda. Scriptu- ra quidem docet, sed gratia donat, quod illa docet. Deus (inquit) autor & largitor patientiæ & sola- tii, det vobis, quia non habetis ex vobis, idipsum sapere in alterutrum, hoc est, ut unusquisque sen- tiat idem quod alter, hoc est, eisdem afficiamini, mo- veamini, teneamini, eadem omnibus placeant. Quomodo? Scilicet ut infirmi sapiant ea, quæ firmi, rursus firmi non secus habeant infirmorum incom- moda ac sua propria, ut sicut sibi vellent fieri, si in loco infirmorum essent, ita faciant & ipsi eisdem. Hoc enim est idem sapere, non sua querere, sed qua aliorum, ut Eph. V. docet. Hic enim affectus spiri- tualis, est nervus totius Christianæ religionis, sine quo subsistere nequeat, quem alibi vocat unitatem spiri- tus, foliciti (inquit) servate unitatem spiritus in vincu- lo pacis. Arguit ex sacris literis, inquit Theophyla- ctus, Deum unà & tolerantiam & consolationem largiri, eoque ipsum patientia Deum & consolatio- nis appellat, utpote qui harum sit & largitor & causa. Optat itaque & his comprecatur, idipsum ab eo ad in- vicem sapere exhiberi. Illud enim est certioris cha- ritatis indicium, ut quod de se quispiam sapiat, itidem & de proximo sentiat. Et quoniam est alius quidam hujus seculi amor, intulit secundum Christum Jesum, hoc est, ut illa sapiatis, quæ Christo Jesu sunt placita. Non ergo est, quod vocem Christi pro præceptis ejus accipi credamus. Elegans hîc veræ concordiæ est ex ordine causarum descriptio, notante B. My- lio: Efficiens causa Deus constituitur. Sic istam ab humanis consiliis aut viribus minime pendere innui- tur. Materia concordiæ in mutuo est consensu: cui forma tum legitima accedit, cùm in Christo Jesu con- sentitur. Speciosum enim quidem nomen est pacis, & pulchra opinio unitatis. Sed quis ambigat, eam solam unitatem Ecclesiæ, pacem esse, qua Christi est, ut Hilarius loquitur. Finis boni istius est, unanimiæ divini nominis concelebratio. De quo fine iterum audiendus B. Lutherus: Ut unanimiter uno ore honorificetis Deum & Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi; Hoc est, quia unus est Deus, qui vocavit nos, eandem misericordiam omnes consecuti estis. Qui firmos vocavit, idem & infirmos, nec inter ul- los discrevit, ita & vos, his larvis non distracti in diversos affectus, unanimes, hanc gratiam Dei omni- bus communem agnoscentes, glorificetis Deum; sicut non distinxit vocationis gratia, ita nec distinguere debet, firmitatis infirmitatisve diversitas. Audiamus & Theophylactum: Quidnam lucri consequimur, cùm unum omnes sentimus & sapimus? nempe quia Deum laudibus ipsi efferimus: nec ore duntaxat uno id agimus, sed & animis unis. Hoc enim cum una- nimes ait, prætendit. Mox illud seorsum orditur, & patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Quod si ita per- legas, videlicet ipsius Christi Deum & Patrem esse, neque potest id absurdum videri; est enim secundum humanitatem Christi Deus, & pater secundum di- vinitatem. Vocem καὶ alii ἑρμηνευτικῶς accipiunt, q. d. Deum nempe Patrem Domini nostri JEsu Christi 1. Cor. XV. 24. 2. Cor. I. 3. Glorificatio au- tem non tantùm sit, cum hymnis Deum laudamus aut cum oramus, sed etiam cùm confessionem fi- dei edimus, Phil. II. 11.

## 15:7
v. 7. διὸ προσλαμβάνεσθε ἀλλήλους. Since these things are so, that is, since love is the principal thing in the Gospel, do not, because of such matters, cut one another off from the brotherhood. See above XII. 1.

καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς προσελάβετο ὑμᾶς εἰς δόξαν Θεῦ. That is, just as Christ associated us with Himself, so that we may one day be participants of the divine glory with Him. John XVI. 24.

He not only forbids cutting others off from the brotherhood because of indifferent matters, but also commands that others, even if they are weak in faith and not sufficiently informed regarding the use of adiaphora, be προσλαμβάνεσθαι, which is to receive in a friendly manner, to welcome sweetly those who are voluntarily invited, to cherish benevolently, Philem. v. 12. 17. Acts XXIX. 2. by which is also included a convenient adjustment to the use and customs of one's neighbor in all things: concerning which B. Mylius here explains this word particularly: For while, he says, each person goes off into his own pursuits: there is a kind of dispersion and dissipation of minds, which we see coalesce, while each person adjusts himself not to his own will, but to the use and customs of his neighbor. Theophylact takes it as mutual aid: he repeatedly insists on the previous warnings, and brings forward Christ as an example, saying truly this, that when you have helped one another, it will redound to the glory of God. For such a joining of your souls brings praise to GOD (For in this, he says, all will know that he himself sent me, if you shall come together as one) just as, on the contrary, your dissensions beget blasphemy against GOD. For even the Gentiles, when they see Christian men contending among themselves in factions, accuse and blame the faith itself. The example of Christ, who received us, embraces all the benefits of grace and love: who received us so solidly and sincerely into his care and patronage, that he is not about to desert us until he has brought us safely into eternal life, as Flacius has it here. By the glory of GOD, both Büllinger and Piscator understand a glorious and blessed life, which others explain thus: just as it redounded to the glory of GOD that Christ mercifully received you, so it will redound to the same glory if you receive one another. That former interpretation, however, is to be preferred.

Latin:

v. 7. διὸ προσλαμβάνεσθε ἀλλήλους. Hæc cum ita se habeant, id est, cùm in Evangelio præci- puum sit dilectio, nolite ob res tales, alii alios à fraternita- te abscindere. Vide supra XII. 1.

καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς προσελάβετο ὑμᾶς εἰς δόξαν Θεῦ. Id est, sicut Christus nos sibi sociavit, ut aliquando di- vinæ gloriæ cum ipso simus participes. Joh. XVI. 24.

Non tantùm vetat alios à fraternitate, ob res medias, abscindere, sed jubet etiam alios, etsi infir- mi sint in fide, & circa adiaphororum usum non satis informati, προσλαμβάνεσθαι, quod est, amicè susci- pere, ultrò invitatos suaviter excipere, benevole fo- vere, Philem. v. 12. 17. Act. XXIX. 2. quo etiam comprehenditur commoda ad usum atque mores proximi in rebus omnibus attemperatio: de qua hoc verbum hîc peculiariter explicat B. Mylius: Dum enim, inquit, in sua quisque studia abit: dispersio quasi quædam sit, & dissipatio animorum, quos coalescere videmus, dum non ad suum arbitrium: sed ad usum & mores proximi quisque se attemperat. De mutuo auxilio Theoph. accipit: Superiorib. monitis iteratò insistit, & in exemplum Christum inducit, id sanè in- quiens, cum vobis invicem opem tuleritis, Deo in glo- riam cedet. Istiusmodi namque vestra animorum conjunctio DEO laudem affert (In hoc enim inquit cognituri sunt omnes, quod ipse me miserit, si in unum convenietis.) quemadmodum contra vestra dissidia DEO blasphemiam pariunt. Nam & gentiles cùm Christianos homines viderint factionibus inter se concertare, fidem ipsam criminantur & culpant. Exemplum Christi, qui nos suscepit, omnia com- plectitur gratiæ, & amoris beneficia: qui nos ita solidè sincereque in suam curam & patrocinium recepit, ut qui non sit nos deserturus, donec nos in æternam vitam incolumes perduxerit, ut hìc habet Flacius. Per gloriam DEI vitam gloriosam & beatam intelligunt & Büllinger, ac Piscator, quod alii sic explicant: sicut cessit in DEI gloriam, quòd Christus vos clementer suscepit, ita cedet in ejustem gloriam, si vos alius alium susceperitis. Illa autem prior interpretatio præferenda.

## 15:8
V. 8. λέγω δὲ ἰησῦν χρισὸν διάκονον γεγενῆσθαι περιτο- μῆς ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας Θεῦ.

The manuscript says 'I say for'. He gives the reason for the preceding, and, so that those called from the Gentiles might not despise the Jews in comparison to themselves, he uses an excellent argument, that Christ himself by himself preached the truth of GOD, that is, the Gospel, only to the circumcision, that is, to the circumcised Jews (see above III. 30. IV. 9. 12.). See Matt. XV. 24. Christ, although a son, is rightly called a minister (διάκονος), because he had taken on that role. Matt. XX. 28. John XIII. 14.

εἰς τὸ βεβαιῶσαι τὰς ἐπαγγελίας τῶν πατέρων.

For the Messiah had been promised to the Hebrews, not to the Gentiles, although prophecies concerning the calling of the Gentiles had also preceded. The genitive 'fathers' (πατέρων) here signifies the object. For those promises had been made to the fathers, namely, of the Jews.

Latin:

V. 8. λέγω δὲ ἰησῦν χρισὸν διάκονον γεγενῆσθαι περιτο- μῆς ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας Θεῦ.

Manuscriptus λέγω γὰρ Rationem reddit præcedentium, &, quò minus ex gentibus vocati Judæos præ sese sperne- rent, egregio utitur argumento, quod veritatem DEI, id est, Evangelium, Christus ipse per se non nisi circumcisio- ni, id est, Judæis circumcisis (vide supra III. 30. IV. 9. 12.) prædicaverit. Vide Matth. XV. 24. Christus, quan- quam filius, rectè διάκονος dicitur, quia eam personam susceperat. Matth. XX. 28. Joh. XIII. 14.

εἰς τὸ βεβαιῶσαι τὰς ἐπαγγελίας τῶν πατέρων.

Nam Hebræis promissus erat Messias, non gentibus, quanquam & de gentibus vocandis vaticinia præcesserant. Genitivus πατέρων hìc objectum significat. Patribus enim, nempe Judæorum, facta erant ista promissa.

## 15:9
V. 9. τὰ δὲ ἔθνη ὑπὲρ ἐλέες δοξάσαι τὸν Θεὸν.

And 'I say' (λέγω) is understood from the preceding, and the verb 'to owe' (ὀφείλειν). A similar ellipsis (ἔλλειψις) is above at IV. 13. The Gentiles owe the greatest thanks to GOD for such a benefit shown to them without any obligation of a promise.

The truth of GOD here does not denote the Gospel, but the veracity of GOD in his promises, to which mercy is opposed: that he took the Jews indeed 'for the truth of GOD' (ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας Θεῦ) on account of the truth of the promises made to the fathers, but the Gentiles out of mercy, not indeed by the obligation of a promise, as Grotius himself explains later. Which, however, others explain concerning those special promises made to the Jews, that Christ willed to be born from their stock, and to preach to them in his own person, as one sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, Rom. IX. 5. Matt. XV. 24: because he is called the minister of the circumcision, i.e., of the Jews; since that opposition of truth and mercy seems otherwise to be able to be explained with difficulty; if indeed illustrious predictions concerning the calling of the Gentiles are also found in the Old Testament, some of which the Apostle himself has brought forward here. But although those promises exist in the Holy Scriptures, the oracles of God (τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ) were nevertheless peculiarly entrusted to the Jews, Rom. III. 2, and thus were not published to the Gentiles in such an illustrious manner; and thus far the opinion of Blessed Luther in his explanation of the Epistles and Gospels for Sundays concerning unhoped-for mercy is correct, T. II. Jen. Lat. f. 330. Therefore, nothing differs in Christ between Jew and Gentile, except that Christ was promised to the fathers of the former; therefore the truth of the one fulfilling was owed to them; but to the latter nothing was promised, therefore unhoped-for mercy befell them, which they magnify: although this also renders the Jews equal to the Gentiles, that God promised to their fathers by an equally gratuitous and unhoped-for mercy as he showed to the Gentiles. They were as undeserving of the promise as these were of the exhibition; on both sides it was pure mercy, except that the promise gave the Jews a just cause for expecting the truth, compared to the Gentiles. Since, therefore, Christ is common, and has borne the burdens of all in common, we also ought to become common to one another, to be of the same mind toward one another, to bear one another's burdens, and not to feel differently in Christ on account of any title or respect of persons. To both, says Estius, mercy was promised, but to the Jews it was promised, to the Gentiles it was not promised, but predicted by the Prophets.

as it is written: Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles, O Lord, and will sing to your name. These are the words of the LXX from the Psalm according to the Hebrews 18:50. David says that he will also tell of the benefits of God toward him to neighboring foreigners. These are most excellently applied to the mystical David, Christ.

If David professes these things about himself, that he wishes to commemorate the benefits of God to neighboring foreigners, what does this have to do with proving the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of God, which took place in the time of the New Testament? And therefore, even from this Apostolic proof, it should be manifest that it is not David speaking in that Psalm, but Christ, because the Psalm is brought forward by the Apostle to confirm the calling of the Gentiles under the New Testament. For firm and solid arguments cannot be sought from a mystical sense; not to mention that the claim about a mystical sense has no place, since a single statement has only a single sense. If, therefore, Christ is speaking here, how he is to confess or preach the name of God among the Gentiles in the future, these things are certainly not to be attributed to David. But by the testimony of the Apostle, Christ is speaking here entirely; and indeed about that which did not happen in the time of David, but which was finally to happen in the fullness of time. See what is said about the argument and contents of this Psalm toward the end of Volume I of the Bibl. Illustrations in the Supplements to this passage.

Some wish to say that Christ is said to confess, along with Lyranus and Thomas 1, because he causes those who believe among the Gentiles to confess: since active verbs are sometimes accustomed to be explained in such a way that the action is claimed for the one from whom the power of acting comes: See S. Glassius, Gram. p. 276. But the ordinary meaning can be retained most excellently: for Christ confesses among the Gentiles, and preaches the name of the Lord truly and properly: both in that in the days of his flesh he called all to himself, not excluding the Gentiles, even though he was sent primarily to the Jews; and in that he ordained the Apostles and sent them out to all the Gentiles, and speaks in them and through them: who are his mouth and instruments, as Paul testifies in 2 Cor. 5:20 and here in v. 18.

Latin:

V. 9. τὰ δὲ ἔθνη ὑπὲρ ἐλέες δοξάσαι τὸν Θεὸν.

Subauditur & λέγω ex præcedentibus, & verbum ὀφεί- λειν debere. Similis ἔλλειψις supra IV. 13. Debent Gentes maximas DEO gratias, pro tanto beneficio ipsis exhibito nullâ promissi obligatione.

Veritas DEI hìc non Evangelium notat, sed ve- racitatem DEI in promissis, cui opponitur miseri- cordia: quòd Judæos quidem ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας Θεῦ propter veritatem promissionum Patribus facta- rum, gentes autem ex misericordia, non verò pro- missi obligatione assumserit, ut Grotius ipse post- ea explicat. Quod tamen alii de promissis illis specialibus Judæis factis, quod ex eorum stirpe voluerit Christus nasci, iisque in propria perso- na prædicare, utpote missus non nisi ad perditas oves Israelis Rom. IX. 5. Matth. XV 24. explicant: quia minister circumcisionis, h. e. Judæorum dici- tur: quum videatur ægrè aliàs oppositio illa veri- tatis & misericordiæ expediri posse; siquidem et- iam de gentibus vocandis illustres prædictiones in V. T. reperiantur, quarum nonnullas hìc Aposto- lus ipse adduxit. Sed quanquam promissiones il- læ extent in S. literis, τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ tamen pe- culiariter credita fuêre Judæis, Rom. III. 2. adeo- que non ita illustri ratione publicata gentilibus; & hactenus B. Lutheri in explic. Epist. & Evan- gel. Dominic. sententia de insperata misericordia rectè se habet T. II. Jen. Lat. f. 330. Nihil ergò in Christo differt Judæus & Gentilis, nisi quòd illorum Patribus Christus promissus est; ideò illis debeba- tur veritas exhibentis; his verò nihil promissum est, ideò eis obtigit misericordia insperata, quam magni- ficent: quanquam & hoc Judæos gentibus pares red- dit, quod Deus æquè gratuitâ & insperata misericor- diâ Patribus eorum promisit ætque gentibus exhi- buit. Tam immeriti illi erant promissionis, quàm hi exhibitionis, utrinque pura misericordia, nisi quod promissio fecit Judæis expectandæ veritatis justam causam præ gentibus. Cùm ergò communis sit Chri- stus, omnium communiter tulcrit onera, debemus & nos mutuò communes fieri, idem sapere invicem, alter alterius onera portare, nec ullo titulo, aut per- sone gratia diversa in Christo sentire. Utrisque, inquit Estius, misericordia, sed Judæis promissa, gentibus non promissa, sed à Prophetis prædicta.

καθὼς γέγραπται· διὰ τῦτο ἐξομολογήσομαί σοι ἐν ἔθνεσι Κύριε καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί συ ψαλῶ. Sunt ista verba LXX ex Psalmo secundum Hebræos XVIII. 50. Dicit David se etiam vicinis alienigenis narra- turum DEI in se beneficia. Optimè autem hæc ad mysti- cum Davidem Christum aptantur.

Si David hæc de seipso profitetur, quòd vici- nis alienigenis commemorare velit DEI benefi- cia, quid hoc ad probandam vocationem gentium ad regnum DEI, tempore N. T. factam? Ideoque vel ex hac Apostolica probatione manifestum sit, non Davidem in illo Psalmo loqui, sed Christum, quia confirmandæ vocationi gentium sub N. T. adducitur Psalmus ab Apostolo. Nam è sensu mystico non possunt peti argumenta firma, atque solida; ut taceam, commentum illud de sensu my- stico locum non habere: quum unius dicti unicus tantùm sensus sit. Si ergò Christus hic loquitur, quomodo confessurus, vel prædicaturus olim sit nomen Dei inter gentes, non utique Davidi hæc tribuenda sunt. At Apostolo teste, Christus o- mninò hic loquitur; & quidem de eo, quod non tempore Davidis factum, sed quod in plenitudine temporis fieri demum debuit. Vid. quæ de hujus Psalmi argumento & contentis sub finem T. I. Bibl. Illustrat. in Supplendis ad h. l. dicta.

Confiteri au- tem Christum dici nonnulli volunt cum Lyrano, & Thom. 1, quòd faciat, ut credentes in gentibus confiteantur: cùm verba activa soleant quandoque ita explicari, ut actio vindicetur illi, à quo facul- tas est agendi: Vid. Gram. S. Glassii p. 276. Sed optimè potest ordinaria significatio retineri: nam Christus confitetur in gentibus, & prædicat nomen Domini verè, ac propriè: tùm quà in diebus car- nis ad sese omnes vocavit, ne gentibus exclusis, etsi primum ad Judæos missus fuerit; tùm quà or- dinavit Apostolos & emisit ad gentes universas, & in iis, ac per eosdem loquitur: qui ejus os, & organa sunt, ut Paulus testatur 2. Cor. V. 20. & hic v. 18.

## 15:10
V. 10. And again he says: That is, in another place, as in Matt. 4:7. The Hebrews would say 'and he returned and said', for the LXX are accustomed to translate the verb 'shub' by 'palin'. Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people. It should not be doubted that this is from Deut. 32:43. For there, in the edition of the LXX, the same words exist, and it appears that they read the letters 'am' twice, namely in this way: 'harninu goyim am ammo'.

This did not arise from a double reading of the letters 'am', but from the sense of the words which the LXX interpreters rendered in Deut. 32:43; because they understood those in such a way that the Gentiles are commanded to applaud his people: or as some render it, 'excite, O Gentiles, his people to jubilation', or 'acclaim, O Gentiles, his peoples', as Tirinus and some in Malvenda, or 'sound forth, praise, O Gentiles, his people', as the Chaldean, Samaritan, Syriac, Arabic, Montanus, and some in Malvenda: for when the Gentiles praise the people because of the benefits shown by the Lord, they are certainly celebrating the Lord together with the faithful Jews. Thus, therefore, they did not indeed render the words, yet they did not depart from the sense; and for that reason the Apostle followed them as genuine interpreters of the words of Moses. Not to mention that sometimes the preposition 'im' or 'et' is missing, as in Lev. 26:42, concerning which see Glass. Gramm. S. p. 565, whence Junius and Tremellius explain: Sing, O Gentiles, with his people. Lyranus wishes Isa. XXXV. 1 to be cited here. Thomas, Isa. LXVI. 10. Calvin, Psalm LXVII. But Calvin's reason for leaving the Mosaic passage, in which these very words that the Apostle cites are contained, because Moses there wished rather to terrify the adversaries of Israel with its magnitude than to incite them to magnitude as the supreme ingratitude of the Israelites; therefore Franc. Junius, l. II. Paral. ch. 27, more correctly noted the scope and συνέχειαν in Moses: Moses, having exposed the malice, perfidy, and judgments of GOD upon them under that most grave Canticle, and the future preservation of the remnant according to the election of grace, concludes with that exhortation: Sing, O ye nations, &c. That word ἐπαινέσατε is not without emphasis: for it is properly to praise, to praise together, and thus it is implied that by the same word the faithful from the nations, together with the people of the Lord from the Israelites, would glorify God, and unanimously and with one mouth would celebrate him, as the Apostle had previously prayed v. 6.

Latin:

V. 10. καὶ πάλιν λέγει· Id est, alio loco, ut Matth. IV. 7. Hebræi dicerent וישב ואמר verbum enim שוב per πάλιν solent vertere LXX. ἐυφράνθητε ἔθνη μετὰ τῦ λαῦ ἀυτῦ. Dubitari non debet, quin sit ex Deut. XXXII. 43. Nam ibi in editione LXX. eadem verba exstant, & apparet eos bis legisse litteras עם, nempe hoc modo: הרנינו גוים עם עמו.

Non è gemina literarum עם lectione, sed è sensu verborum, quem Deut. XXXII. 43. reddi- dere LXX. Interpp. hæc orta; quia illa accepêre hoc modo, quòd applaudere jubeantur gentes po- pulo suo: vel ut nonnulli reddunt, excitate ó Gen- tes adjubilum populum ejus, vel acclamate gentes populis ejus, ut Tirinus, & quidam apud Malvend. vel personate, laudate gentes populum ejus, ut Chald. Sam. Syr. Arabs, Montan. & quidam apud Mal- vendam: nam quum gentes populum ob benefi- cia à Domino exhibita laudant, Dominum utique juxta cum fidelibus Judæis celebrant. Ita ergò non quidem verba reddiderunt, à sensu tamen non discesserunt ó; ò eàque de causa Apostolus eosdem sequutus est, ceu interpretes verborum Mosis genuinos. Ut taceam, quod quandoque præpositio עם vel את cùm desit, ut Levit. XXVI. 42. quo de vid. Glass. Gramm. S. p. 565. unde Junius & Tremell. exponunt: Cantate gentes cum populo ejus. Lyranus vult hic citari Esa. XXXV. 1. Thomas Esa. LXVI. 10. Calvinus Psalm. LXVII. Sed Calvini ratio, quare locum Mosaïcum, in quo hæc ipsa verba, quæ adducit Apostolus, habentur, relinquat, quod Moses ibi terrere potius voluerit Israelis adversarios ejus magnitudine, quàm incitare ad communem lætitiam, fundamento destituitur: nam non tàm magnitudinem, quàm ingratitudinem supremam Israelitarum designat; ideò rectius Franc. Junius l. II. Paral. cap. 27. scopum & συνέχειαν in Mose notavit: Moses sub illo Cantico gravissimo expositâ malitiâ, perfidiâ & DEI in ipsos judiciis, venturaque reliquiarum conservatione secundum electionem gratiæ, hortatione illâ concludit: Cantate gentes, &c. Vox illa ἐπαινέσατε emphasin non caret: propriè enim est adlaudate, collaudate, adeoque innuitur eâdem fideles è gentibus una cum populo Domini ex Israelitis Deum glorificaturos, & unanimiter atque uno ore eum celebraturos, ut antea voverat Apostolus v. 6.

## 15:11
V. 11. And again, praise the Lord, all ye nations, and praise him, all ye peoples.

From Psalm CXVII. 1. according to the Hebrew edition: the words here are the same as those among the LXX, except that the conjunction is omitted there, which is also not in the Hebrew, but is understood.

Latin:

V. 11. καὶ πάλιν, αἰνεῖτε τὸν κύριον, πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, καὶ ἐπαινέσατε αὐτὸν, πάντες οἱ λαοὶ.

Ex Psalmo CXVII. 1. juxta Hebraicam editionem: verba hîc eadem quæ apud LXX. nisi quod ibi omittitur copula quæ & in Hebræo non est, sed subauditur.

## 15:12
V. 12. And again Isaiah says, there shall be the root of Jesse and he who rises to rule the nations, in him shall the nations hope.

These are also from the LXX, Isa. XI. 10, where they translated as 'to rule' what is in the Hebrew לנס as 'for a banner of victory,' because a banner is a sign of authority. The passage of the Prophet deals with Hezekiah, but he who was himself no obscure image of Christ. A shoot, he says, will arise from the house of Jesse, which will be set up for the nations as a banner, namely, to this end, that the nations may commit themselves to him with good confidence. These things pertain not only to showing the nations what they owe to GOD, but also to beating back the ferocity of the Jews. What is it? Do you wish to take it ill if God fulfills his promises?

The sentence of the Prophet is perverted against the mind of the Prophet as well as the Apostle. The Apostle accepts the prophecy concerning Christ, not concerning Hezekiah: nor did Hezekiah rule the nations, much less could he have that banner to which the nations should run together, and in which they should hope. That these things sound concerning Christ is manifest: concerning which we have spoken at Isa. XI. Furthermore, what is said in the Hebrew concerning the root of Jesse, that it stands for a banner of the peoples, the Apostle explains with the LXX, that Christ, who is that root of Jesse, arises to rule the nations. Because a banner or trophy is a sign of dominion, just as a people is said to act or serve under the banner of a Prince, and an army under the banner of a General, that is, under his command. What is in the Hebrew, 'to him shall the nations seek,' i.e., they shall flow together to him by seeking, is held in the Greek as 'in him shall the nations hope,' with the same sense. For those who seek and run to the Messiah, they hope in the same: and the hope and expectation of heavenly goods is both the impulsive and the final cause of that seeking and running together, as rightly B. Glassius in Not. ad Epist. Dom. II. Advent. p. 204. Conf. Gen. XLIX, 10. Psalm. XXXIV. 5. 6.

Latin:

V. 12. καὶ πάλιν Ἡσαΐας λέγει, ἔσται ἡ ῥίζα τοῦ Ἰεσσαὶ καὶ ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν, ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσι.

Sunt hæc quoque ex LXX. Esa. XI. 10. ubi quod in Hebræo est לנס in vexillum victoriæ, verterunt ἄρχειν, quia vexillum signum imperii. Locus Prophetæ de Ezechia agit, sed qui & ipse non obscura fuit Christi imago. Orietur, inquit, ex Jesse domo soboles, quæ erigetur Gentibus pro vexillo, nempe in id, ut Gentes ei se committant cum bona fiducia. Hæc pertinent non tantùm ad ostendendum Gentibus quid DEO debeant, verum etiam ad retundendam Judæorum ferociam. Quid est? vultis vos ægrè ferre si Deus promissa præstat?

Pervertitur sententia Prophetæ contra mentem Prophetæ pariter & Apostoli. De Christo, non de Ezechia vaticinium accipit Apostolus: nec Ezechias gentibus imperavit, nedum vexillum illud habere potuit, ad quod concurrerent gentes, & in quo sperare deberent. Quæ de Christo sonare manifestum est: quo de ad Es. XI. diximus. Cæterum quod in Ebræo dicitur de radice Jesse, quod stet in vexillum populorum, explicat cum LXX. Apostolus, quòd exurgat Christus, qui radix illa Jesse est, ut imperet gentibus.
