This explanation is not inappropriate, with which the interpretation of others, that they had an excellent testimony from the Apostles, agrees: which I would prefer to the opinion of Chrysostom and Theodoret, that they were distinguished and illustrious among the Apostles, or that other Evangelists among the Gentiles were also called Apostles, as Corn. à Lapide wishes, or that the name Apostle is taken more generally for fellow-workers of the Apostles, as 2. Cor. VIII. 23. B. Mylius also expounded on the celebrity among the Apostles. Dorotheus records that Andronicus was made Bishop in Pannonia.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἀνδρόνικον) Cùm hic fuerit Judæus, quippe Pauli cognatus, est hoc nomen Græcum expressum de Ju- daico: quod puto fuisse מַצְא־נִצַח Masinissa Pœnis. καὶ Ἰουνίαν) Videtur fuisse uxor Andronici, cui nomen פְּעֵרָה. τοὺς συγγενεῖς μου) quia fortè ἐπίκληρον propinquum duxerat Andronicus. καὶ συναιχμαλώτους μου) Crescit oratio. Major enim ho- nos est passionum ob Christum esse participem, quam san- guinis. Pari honore Aristarchum afficit Coloss. IV. 10. & Epaphram, Philem. 23. sæpè autem in vinculis fuit Pau- lus, ut videre est 2. Cor. VI. 5. Clemens in Epistola ad Corinthios de Paulo: ἑπτάκις δεσμὰ φορέσας. οἵτινές εἰσιν ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις) Id est, qui etiam cæteris Apostolis benè sunt cogniti: quomodo & Syrus videtur accepisse: nec id mirum, cum sequatur: οἳ καὶ πρὸ ἐμοῦ γεγόνασιν ἐν Χριστῷ) Id est, in Eccle- sia Christi: fuere hi aut ex LXX. illis, qui in Penteco- ste Apostolis adfuere, aut ex primis per Petrum conver- sis.

Non inconcinna est hæc explicatio, cui alio- rum interpretatio, quod egregium ab Apostolis habuerint testimonium, consonat: quam præ- tulerim Chrysostomi, & Theodoreti sententiæ, quod inter Apostolos illi insignes fuerint & illustres, vel quod etiam alii Evangelizantes inter gentes Apostoli dicti sint, ut Corn. à Lapide vult, vel quod nomen Apostoli generalius accipiatur pro συνεργοῖς Apostolorum, ut 2. Cor. VIII. 23. De ce- lebritate inter Apostolos etiam B. Mylius expo- suit. Andronicum factum fuisse in Pannonia E- piscopum Dorotheus tradit.

## 16:8
Vers. 8. ἀσπάσασθε Ἀμπλίαν τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ. The manuscript has Ἀμπλιατὸν, just as Origen reads and the Latin. It is a name of the Romans from a passive participle, such as Donatus, Amatus, Præstolatus, Benedictus, the Greek σωζόμενος, the Hebrew Baruch and others.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἀσπάσασθε Ἀμπλίαν τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ. Manuscriptus habet Ἀμπλιατὸν, quomodo & Origenes legit & Latinus. Est id nomen Romanorum ex parti- cipio passivo, qualia Donatus, Amatus, Præstolatus, Benedictus, Græcum σωζόμενος, Hebræum Baruch & alia.

## 16:9
Vers. 9. ἀσπάσασθε Οὐρβανόν. And this is a Roman name, by which several Bishops have been called.

καὶ Στάχυν. The name is Greek.

Baronius says Urban was sent to administer the Byzantine Church. Hippolytus concerning the 72 Disciples implies Urban was created Bishop in Macedonia, and Ampliatus in Odyssa: whom the Apostle calls his most beloved, not because of wealth or singular munificence, but in the Lord, that is, because of one and the same confession, which makes true and solid friendship, joined by the glue of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἀσπάσασθε Οὐρβανόν. Et hoc nomen Romanum, quo appellati sunt Episcopi complures.

καὶ Στάχυν. Nomen est Græcum.

Urbanum ad Byzantinam Ecclesiam admini- strandam missum dicit Baronius. Hippolyt. de 72. Discipul. Urbanum in Macedonia creatum Episcopum, Ampliatum Odyssæ innuit: quem di- lectissimum suum vocat Apostolus, non propter opes aut singularem munificentiam, sed in Do- mino, h. e. propter unam & eandem confessionem, quæ veram solidamque facit amicitiam, Christi glutine copulatam.

## 16:10
Vers. 10. Ἀσπάσασθε Ἀπελλῆν) It is a Laconian name, which belonged both to a philosopher in Plutarch and to a most noble painter. Ἀπέλλη is an assembly: ἀπελλάζειν is to hold an assembly. Origen rightly doubts whether this is not the Apollos named in Acts; for another, who is Ἀπελλῆς in Athenaeus (which is contracted from Ἀπολλόδωρος) is Apelles in the Epitome of Artemidorus of Ephesus, and in Clement of Alexandria. τὸν δόκιμον ἐν Χριστῷ) That is, who by great proofs appeared to be a Christian in good faith. See above IV. 18. ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου) Dead, as I judge: for he speaks in this way also of the family of Onesiphorus 2. Tim. I. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἀσπάσασθε Ἀπελλῆν) Est nomen Laconicum, quod fuit & philosopho apud Plutarchum & nobilissimo pictori. Ἀπέλλη concio: ἀπελλάζειν concionari. Me- ritò dubitat Origenes, an non hic sit Apollos in Actis no- minatus; nam & alius, qui Ἀπελλῆς Athenæo (quod con- tractum ex Ἀπολλόδωρος) est Apelles in Epitome Artemi- dori Ephesii, & apud Clementem Alexandrinum. τὸν δόκιμον ἐν Χριστῷ) Id est, qui magnis experimentis apparuit esse bona fide Christianus. Vide supra IV. 18. ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου) Mortui ut arbitror: nam sic & de Onesiphori familiâ loquitur 2. Tim. I. 16.

## 16:11
V. 11. ἀσπάσασθε Ἡρωδίωνα τὸν συγγενῆ μου) Herodes is an Attic name: Ὑρώδης is Parthian. But I think the Idumeans softened into Greek the name which they had received from the Parthians, who were then powerful, from which they transferred themselves to the Romans: From this name ἡῥωδίων as Καισαρίων & the like.

Greet those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord) I think it is understood to be Narcissus, the freedman of Claudius, in whose house some Christians may have been.

Baronius observes from the Menologium of the Greeks, March 15, that Aristobulus was sent to govern the Church gathered in Britain: and he hands down from Hippolytus that Narcissus took care of the Church of Athens: but he does not prove that opinion which is approved here by Grotius. As regards Narcissus, he says, it is certain that those erred who thought the Apostle meant those who were of the family of Narcissus, the most powerful freedman of the Emperor Claudius, in whose hands (as Suetonius, Tacitus, and Dio testify) the supreme power lay. These things could easily be persuaded, were it not certain that Narcissus himself was killed two years before, namely when Nero was first created Emperor, out of hatred for Agrippina, the mother of the Emperor Nero; for Tacitus recounts his death under the consulship of Asinius and Acilius. B. Balduinus notes: That he made the household of Aristobulus, i.e., his family members, to be greeted, because Aristobulus himself and Narcissus perhaps had not yet come to the knowledge of Christ.

Latin:

V. 11. ἀσπάσασθε Ἡρωδίωνα τὸν συγγενῆ μου) Herodes no- men est Atticum: Ὑρώδης Parthicum. Puto autem Idumæos illos nomen, quod à Parthis tunc potentibus acceperant, in Græcum emolliisse, ex quo ad Romanos se transtule- re: Ab hoc nomine ἡῥωδίων ut Καισαρίων & simi- lia.

ἀσπάσασθε τὺς ἐκ τῶν Ναρκίσσυ τὺς ὄντας ἐν Κυρίῳ) Puto intelligi Narcissum Claudii libertum, in cujus domo ali- qui fuerint Christiani.

Aristobulum missum fuisse ad regendam Eccle- siam in Britannia collectam è Græcorum Meno- logio d. 15. Martii Baronius observat: Narcissum vero Athenarum Ecclesiam curasse ex Hippolito tradit: non autem probat illam, quæ hic Grotio probata, sententiam. Quod ad Narcissum spe- stat, inquit, constat errasse, qui putarunt Aposto- lum intellexisse de his, qui erant ex familia Narcissi potentissimi liberti Claudii Imperatoris, penes quem (ut Suetonius, Tacitus ac Dio testantur) summa rerum erat. Hæc facile suaderi possent, nisi con- staret ipsum Narcissum odio Agrippinæ matris Ne- ronis Imperatoris, ante biennium, cum primum scilicet Nero creatus est Imperator, fuisse necatum, Tacitus enim mortem ejus recenset sub consulatu Asinii & Acilii. B. Balduinus notat: Domum Aristobuli, i. e. familiares fecisse salutari, quod ipse Aristobulus & Narcissus fortè nondum ad agnitionem Christi venerint.

## 16:12
Verse 12. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Whether these names are derived from the Hebrew תרפה & נחמה or whether they were Roman women of unchaste life before they believed in Christ, such as Tryphaena in Petronius, can be doubted.

Grotius could bring forward no cause for this suspicion of his: whom we commit to Baronius, saying that Tryphaena and Tryphosa were noble women of Iconium, converted to Christ at Iconium, but based on the faith of the Acts of Thecla, which is most faithful to him, but of no faith to others.

Greet Persis) She may have been some maidservant or freedwoman born in Persia, and having her name from her homeland, like Mysa, Syrus, Davus.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἀσπάσασθε τρύφαιναν καὶ τρυφῶσαν. Nomina hæc an sint traducta ex Hebræis תרפה & נחמה an verò Romanæ mulieres fuerint vitæ, antequam Christo crediderant, impudicæ, qualis Tryphæna apud Petronium, dubitari potest.

Nullam hujusce suspicionis suæ causam adferre potuit Grotius: quem cum Baronio committimus, Tryphænam & Tryphosam nobiles Iconienses di- cente, Iconii ad Christum conversas, sed ex fide Actorum Theclæ, quæ illi fidelissima, aliis nullius fidei.

ἀσπάσασθε Περσίδα) Fuerit ancilla aut libertina aliqua orta à Perside, & nomen à patria habens, ut Mysa, Syrus, Davus.

## 16:13
Verse 13. Rufus the chosen in the Lord) An excellent son of Simon of Cyrene among the Christians. See Mark XV. 21.

and his mother and mine) Rufus's mother by nature, Paul's by affection: just as the Virgin Mary is the mother of John the Apostle.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ῥῦφον τὸν ἐκλεκτὸν ἐν Κυρίῳ) Eximium inter Christianos filium Simonis Cyrenæi. Vide Marc. XV. 21.

καὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτῶ καὶ ἐμῦ) Rufi matrem natura, Pau- li affectu: quomodo Maria Virgo mater Johannis Apo- stoli.

## 16:14
Verse 14. Asyncritus) A Greek name of good omen, as are many.

Phlegon) And this name is also frequent among the Greeks, which the freedman of the Emperor Hadrian, a Trallian by birth, also had.

It is to be noted here, as B. Mylius warns, the condition of these believers. No one here is named a consul, no one is distinguished as a quaestor or dictator, least of all do the dignities of bishoprics and cardinalates resound here: but most are marked by titles of works, labors, and captivity. Thus it was also true in the Roman Church of old, what the Apostle writes, Not many powerful, not many noble. But the foolish things of the world were chosen by God. However, the Papal Caesarism, such as it prevailed in Rome in later centuries to the ruin of religion with the help of the Devil, did not even have a shadow of it in the age of the Apostles: so far is it from having drawn its origin from the Apostles themselves.

Hermas) It is the name of a freedman, contracted from Hermodorus. See what is in the Prolegomena to Luke. Origen and the ancients who followed him think this is the one who wrote in Greek the book of the Shepherd, which we have in Latin, and certain fragments in Irenaeus and Clement. It is strange that that book once contended for authority with the Epistle to the Hebrews. The Epistle to the Hebrews was used by the rigid defenders of discipline, who did not indeed take away all hope of divine mercy from those who had lapsed after baptism into graver crimes, that is, idolatry, homicide, adultery, yet they did not restore to them the communion of the Church. Hermas, who is said to have himself lapsed after baptism,

, he wished for penance to be granted for one crime, by the authority, as he himself said, of Angels. In the East, Hermas seems to have had approvers of his leniency. But in the West and Africa, severity prevailed, and the first Roman Bishop Zephyrinus admitted to penance—and after the time of it was completed, to communion—not idolaters, nor murderers, but those once convicted or confessed of adultery, with Tertullian contradicting: which dispute later gave Novatus a pretext for splitting the Church. It would not have been a bad thing if that first rigor could have been retained: but for the leaders of the Church, the first concern must be unity, and one must see not only what is best, but also what can be obtained. Ancient rigor and excessive security, to which we are no longer equal, did not want it, says Tacitus.

Not only of the unity of the Church, but also of the salvation of the infirm and of those who have fallen into sins, must account be taken, lest by closing the Church with the Novatians themselves, we provide them with a cause for despair: whence Caelestinus, Roman Bishop, in Epistle 1, disapproved of such rigor in the fifth century in these words: We have learned that penance is denied to the dying, and that the desires of those who, at the time of their passing, wish to be helped by this remedy for their soul, are not granted. We shudder, I confess, that anyone should be found of such impiety as to despair of the mercy of God, as if He could not succor one running to Him at any time, and free a man endangered under the burden of sins by the weight with which he desires to be unburdened. What else is this, I ask, than to add death to the dying, and to kill his soul by one's own cruelty, so that it cannot be absolved: when God, most ready to help, inviting to penance, promises thus: The sinner, He says, on whatever day he shall have turned, his sins shall not be imputed to him. And again: I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he be converted and live. Nor indeed is judgment regarding the opinion or discipline of the early Church safely sought from Tertullian, who was addicted to more than one error. That was the heresy of the Montanists, who barred the doors of the Church to almost every offense. See Jerome, Epistle LIV to Marcella, book II against Jovinian, chapter 2. Ignatius, however, in his Epistle to the Philadelphians I beseech you, he advises, as many as have been led by penance to the unity of the Church, receive them with all meekness, so that through your goodness and patience, those repenting from the snares of the Devil, having now become worthy of Christ, may attain salvation in the kingdom of Christ. And concerning the Ancient Martyrs, Dionysius of Alexandria in the year of the Lord 260: Those divine martyrs, he says, while they were with us, when they perceived the conversion and penance of some of the brethren in whom the crime of sacrificing to idols clung, and who were departing from the faith, and held it sufficiently explored that it could be acceptable to Him who does not at all desire the death of the sinner, they admit them again to themselves, receive them into the Church, celebrate assemblies with them, enter into a society of prayers, and use the communion of feasts together. I pass over Dionysius the Areopagite, whom they call the correction, of Demophilus in Epistle VIII, refuting the same for having cast out and repelled with his heel a sinner and impious man falling before the priest; and the constitution of Clement of Rome, book II of the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 13 and chapter 14, concerning the receiving of penitents: Which, even if they are of no authority among Catholics, would nevertheless be of some authority among the followers of Grotius. But Clement of Alexandria, book II of the Stromata, and Origen, homily VIII on Numbers, as well as homily I on Jeremiah, deserve to be seen. Furthermore, both that the book of the Shepherd is by Hermas, and that it contended among the Ancients with the Epistle to the Hebrews regarding authority, is said rashly: The Scripture of the Shepherd is judged by every gathering of churches, even yours, among the Apocrypha, false and adulterated, he says

ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE R

Tertullian the Montanist, addressing the orthodox in his book on modesty: There is no way to doubt that this book of the Shepherd, as it is currently written, was not composed by Hermas, the disciple of Paul, since it is filled with both heresies and fables: since St. Gelasius in the Roman Council places it among the Apocryphal writings: likewise St. Prosper pronounces it to be of no authority: says Johannes Maria, Master of the Sacred Palace, in the Roman Index of expurgated books, Vol. I, page 171.

Patrobas.

Martial calls a certain freedman of Domitian by this name.

Hermas.

Hermes is a name found in Martial. Such are the names Phoebus, Phoebe, and similar ones.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἀσύγκριτον) Nomen Græcum boni ominis, ut multa.

Φλέγοντα) Et hoc nomen apud Græcos frequens, quod habuit & Adriani Imperatoris libertus ortu Trallia- nus.

Notanda hic, monente B. Mylio, fidelium isto- rum conditio. Nemo hic nominatur consul, nemo quæstor aut dictator insignitur, minime omnium Episcopatuum & Cardinalatuum dignitates hic personant: sed operarum, laborum, captivitatis ti- tulis plerique notantur. Ita verum etiam in Ro- mana Ecclesia fuit olim, quod Apostolus scribit, Non multi potentes, non multi nobiles. Sed stulta mundi electa sunt à Deo. Papatus autem Cæsa- rei, qualis adjuvante Diabolo, in perniciem reli- gionis, posteris seculis Romæ invaluit, ne umbra quidem Apostolorum ætate istic fuit: tantum abest, ut ille originem ab Apostolis ipsis traxe- rit.

ἑρμᾶν) Est nomen libertini hominis, contractum ex ἑρμόδωρος. Vide, quæ in Prolegomenis ad Lucam. Pu- tant Origenes, & eum secuti veteres hunc esse, qui Græce scripsit librum Pastoris, quem habemus Latinè, & fragmenta quædam apud Irenæum & Clementem. Mi- rum est eum librum quondam cum Epistola ad Hebræos certasse de auctoritate. Epistola ad Hebræos utebantur rigidi disciplinæ defensores, qui post baptismum lapsis in graviora crimina, id est, idololatriam, homicidium, adul- terium, misericordiæ quidem divinæ spem omnem non adimebant, non tamen eis reddebant communionem Ec- clesiæ. Hermas, qui ipse post baptismum lapsus dicitur,

, uni crimini poenitentiam volebat dari, Angeli, ut ipse di- cebat, auctoritate. In Oriente videtur Hermas habuisse lenitatis suae approbatores. At in Occidente & Africa prae- valuit severitas, primusque Zephyrinus Episcopus Roma- nus, non idololatras, nec homicidas, sed semel adulterii convictos aut confessos ad poenitentiam, & post ejus ex- actae tempus ad communionem admisit, contradicente Tertulliano: quae disputatio postea Novato scindendi Ec- clesiam praetextum dedit. Non malum fuerat, si retineri potuisset primus ille rigor: sed rectoribus Ecclesiae prima esse debet unitatis cura, & videndum non modo, quid sit optimum, sed & quid obtineri possit. Noluit antiquus rigor & nimia securitas, cui jam pares non sumus, ait Ta- citus.

Non unitatis tantum Ecclesiae, sed & salutis infirmorum, & in peccata prolapsorum habenda est ratio, ne cum Novatianis ipsis Ecclesiam clau- dendo, desperationis causam iis praebeamus: un- de Caelestinus Episcopus Romanus Epist. 1. talem rigorem seculo quinto hisce improbavit: Agnovi- mus poenitentiam morientibus denegari, nec illorum desideriis annui, qui obitus sui tempore hoc animae suae cupiunt remedio subveniri. Horremus, fateor, tantae impietatis aliquem reperiri, ut de Dei pietate desperet, quasi non possit ad se quovis tempore con- currenti succurrere, & periclitantem sub onere pec- catorum hominem pondere, quo se expediri deside- rat, liberare. Quid hoc, rogo, aliud est, quam mo- rienti mortem addere, ejusque animam sua crudeli- tate, ne absoluta esse possit, occidere: cum Deus ad subveniendum paratissimus, invitans ad poeniten- tiam sic promittat: Peccator, inquiens, quacunque die conversus fuerit, peccata ejus non imputa- buntur ei. Et iterum: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed tantum convertatur, & vivat. Nec vero e Tertulliano errori non uni addicto, de Ecclesiae priscae sententia aut disciplina, tuto judicium pe- titur. Montanistarum erat illa haeresis, qui ad omne pene delictum Ecclesiae obserabant fores. Vid. Hieron. Epist. LIV. ad Marcell. lib. II. adv. Jovinian. cap. 2. Ignatius vero Epist. ad Phila- delph. Obsecro vos, monet, quotquot poenitentia ducti fuerint ad unitatem Ecclesiae, recipite illos cum omni mansuetudine, ut per bonitatem & pa- tientiam vestram resipiscentes ex Diaboli laqueis digni jam Christo facti, salutem consequantur in regno Christi. Et de Antiquis Martyribus Dio- nysius Alexandrinus Anno Domini 260. Illi igi- tur, inquit, divini martyres, dum erant apud nos, nonnullos e fratribus, in quibus crimen sacri- ficandi idolis haerebat, quique a fide excedebant, cum conversionem ac poenitentiam eorum perspexe- rent, eamque posse acceptam fore ei, qui omnino non vult mortem peccatoris, satis exploratum ha- berent, ad se denuo admittunt, recipiunt in Eccle- siam, conventus cum illis celebrant, ineunt socie- tatem precum & epularum communione una utun- tur. Taceo Dionysii Areopag. quem vocant, επα- νόρθωσιν, Demophylum Epist. VIII. ad eundem re- darguentis, quod peccatorem atque impium proci- dentem sacerdoti calce abjecerit ac repulerit; & Clementis Romani constitutionem lib. II. Apost. constit. cap. 13. & cap. 14. de recipiendis poeniten- tibus: Quae etsi nullius sint penes Catholicos, penes Grotium tamen alicujus omnino forent authoritatis. Videri autem meretur Clemens Alexandrinus lib. II. Stromat. & Origenes ho- mil. VIII. in Numer. ut & homil. I. in Jere- miam. Caeterum utrumque illud, & quod Pa- storis liber Hermae sit, & quod certarit apud Ve- teres cum Epistola ad Hebraeos de authoritate, temere dicitur: Scriptura Pastoris ab omni co- mitio Ecclesiarum etiam vestrarum inter Apo- crypha falsa & adultera judicatur, inquit

ANNOTATA AD EPIST. AD R

Tertullianus Montanista, orthodoxos alloquens libr. de pudicit. Dubitandum nullo modo est, li- bellum hunc Pastoris, ut modo scriptus habetur, ab Herma Pauli discipulo non esse conscriptum, cum & hæresibus & fabulis sit oppletus: cum S. Gela- sius in Romano Concilio inter Apocrypha scripta sljicit: Item S. Prosper nullius autoritatis esse pronunciat: inquit Johannes Maria. Magi- ster S. Palatii Rom. Indic. libr. expurgat. Tom. I. pag. 171.

Πατρόβαν.

Martialis hoc nomine libertum quendam Domitiani ap- pellat.

Ἑρμῆν.

Hermes nomen est apud Martialem. Talia nomina Phoebus, Phoebe, & similia.

## 16:15
Verse 15. Philologus.

And this is the name of some freedman instructed in letters, and thus named by his master in that hope. Thus the freedman of Attrejus Capito was called Philologus, according to Suetonius, who explains the reason: he seems to have assumed the appellation of Philologus because, just as Aristophanes, who first claimed this surname for himself, he was esteemed for manifold and varied learning.

and Julia.

And she was a freedwoman manumitted by someone from the house of the Caesars.

Nereus.

It is a Sabine name, Neria. See Gellius XIII. 21.

and Olympas.

And this is contracted for Olympiodorus. See the remarks in the prolegomena to Luke.

In such a long catalog it would be strange if St. Peter were not named, if he was at Rome: whom the Apostle would without doubt have greeted before others? Cornelius à Lapide finds nothing to say here, except to invent that Peter was not greeted, or that Paul sent separate letters to Peter: or that Peter, being a Jew expelled from Rome some years before by the Emperor Claudius, was still absent. But whence is either this or that established? And how does this agree with the episcopate held by Peter at Rome for 25 years? Most Papists think Peter was crucified at Rome in the year of Christ 68: yet they refer this Epistle of Paul to the year of Christ 52 or 54: if he was absent from Rome then, how did he sit at Rome for 25 years? Furthermore, they say that Paul came to Rome in the year 59, where he stayed for two years, and from there sent several Epistles, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, and the second to Timothy, in which he indeed makes mention of others, but none of Peter; nay, in Phil. II. 20, 21, he complains that he has no one like-minded, that all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's: and 2 Tim. IV. 15, No one stood with me, but all forsook me. Therefore, it is not likely that Peter was at Rome during that two-year period either: for he would not have forsaken Paul: nor would he have deserved that accusation, that he sought only his own, not the things of Jesus Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Φιλόλογον.

Et hoc nomen libertini alicujus ad literas instituti, atque in eam spem sic a Domino nuncupati. Sic Attrejus libertus Attici Capitonis dictus Philologus teste Suetonio, qui cau- sam explicat: Philologi appellationem assumpsisse videtur, quia sicut Aristophanes, qui primus hoc cognomen sibi vindicavit, multiplici variaque doctrina censebatur.

καὶ Ἰυλίαν.

Et hæc libertina fuit manumissa ab aliqua de Cæsarum domo.

Νηρέαν.

Est nomen Sabinum Neria. Vide Gellium XIII. 21.

καὶ Ὀλυμπᾶν.

Et hoc contractum pro Ὀλυμπιόδωρον. Vide dicta prole- gomenis ad Lucam.

In hoc tam prolixo catalogo mirum foret non nominatum S. Petrum, si is Romæ fuit: quem sine dubio præ aliis salutasset Apostolus? Corne- lius à Lapide non invenit, quid hic dicat, nisi quod fingat, Petrum non salutatum vel quod Paulus pe- culiares ad Petrum dederit literas: vel quod Petrus, utpote Judæus ante aliquot annos Roma pulsus à Claudio Imperatore, etiamnum abesset. Sed un- de vel illud, vel hoc constat? Et quomodo hoc cum Episcopatu per 25. annos Romæ à Petro ge- sto convenit? Plerique Pontificii Petrum Romæ anno Christi 68. crucifixum censent: hanc autem Pauli Epistolam ad annum Christi 52. vel 54. re- ferunt: quo si Romà abfuit, quomodo per 25. annos Romæ sedit? Porrò Paulum Romam an- no 59. venisse ajunt, ubi per biennium substitit, indeque plures Epistolas, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, ad Philippenses, ad Colossenses & posteriorem ad Timotheum misit, in quibus aliorum quidem mentionem facit, nullam autem Petri, quin Phil. II. 20. 21. conqueritur, neminem se habere ἰσόψυχον, omnes, quæ sua sunt, quærere, non quæ sunt Jesu Christi: & 2. Timoth. IV. 15. Nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me dereliquerunt. Proinde nec illo biennio Petrum Romæ fuisse oportet: is enim Paulum non dereliquisset: nec ἔγκλημα il- lud meruisset, quod solum quæ sua sunt, quæreret, non quæ Jesu Christi.

## 16:16
Verse 16. Greet one another with a holy kiss.) Which was a custom for Christians after prayers, as a sign of holy love. See 1 Cor. XVI. 10, 2 Cor. XIII. 12, 1 Thess. V. 26, 1 Pet. V. 14. Justin in his Second Apology: We greet one another with a kiss when we have ceased from prayers. Tertullian on prayer: What prayer is complete if separated from the holy kiss? What kind of duty does the peace hinder? What kind of sacrifice is it, from which one departs without peace? For they called that kiss by the name of peace. Since they withdraw the kiss of peace from the brethren, which is the seal of prayer. Hence to his wife, II: To meet any of the brethren for a kiss. Clement speaks of this kiss in Pædagogus III: The Apostle has called it holy, that we might conduct ourselves worthily of the kingdom, the intention of the soul through a chaste and closed body, through which a gentle manner is especially signified. Origen also mentions this custom in this place, and the Martyrology at II. The Ides of September concerning Sosthenes and Victor. They showed in that way that Christians were all equal among themselves. For among the Persians and other peoples of the East, equals joined their mouths together, while superiors gave their hand to be kissed by inferiors.

Even before the Holy Supper in holy assemblies, the faithful received one another with a kiss, saying, peace be with you, which for those about to communicate was a symbol of reconciliation and of any injury whatsoever being forgiven, and of sincere charity. Blessed Balduinus observes here that kisses were customary (1) Among those departing; examples exist in Ruth I. 9, 1 Kings XIX. 20, 2 Sam. XIX. 39. (2) Among those meeting; examples are Gen. XXX. 11, Exod. XVIII. 7, Tob. VII. 7. (3) Among reconciled friends; examples are 2 Sam. XIV. 33, Luke XV. (4) Among associates of the faith, which kiss was called holy, as is evident from this place, likewise from 1 Cor. XVI, 2 Cor. XIII, and 1 Thess. V; elsewhere it is called the kiss of charity in 1 Pet. V. Concerning greetings, St. Augustine. Sermon XLII de tempore: If anyone, he says, does not greet a man he meets, or does not return a greeting to one who greets him, he will not be considered a man by the traveler, but a trunk, a stone, or a Mercury, who stands in the road showing the way and says nothing. Concerning the idolatrous and superstitious kiss of the heathens, who were accustomed to kiss their hand in honor of their gods, see Job XXXI. 26, 27, 28, and Drusius ibid., 1 Kings XIX. 18, Hos. XIII. 2, and Jerome on that place. But the Apostle calls this a holy kiss. By which name, as Origen warns here, he teaches first, that the kisses which are given in the churches should be chaste. Then, secondly, that they should not be feigned, as was that of Judas, who gave a kiss with his lips and plotted betrayal in his heart. But a faithful kiss should first be chaste, then it should have peace in itself and simplicity in itself that is not feigned.

... the churches of Christ greet you. Which are in Greece. Not that Paul had a command from them, but because their affection was certain, and because there was one spirit in Paul and in all the churches, as Origen says here.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλες ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ.) Qui mos Christianis post orationes, in signum sanctæ dilectio- nis. Vide 1. Cor. XVI. 10. 2. Cor. XIII. 12. 1. Thess. V. 26. 1. Pet. V. 14. Justinus Apologetico II. ἀλλήλες φιλήματι ἀσπαζόμεθα παυσάμενοι τῶν εὐχῶν. Tertullianus de ora- tione: Quæ oratio cum divortio sancti osculi integra? Quem omnino officium facientem impedit pax? Quale sacrificium est, à quo sine pace receditur? Nam osculum illud pacis no- mine appellabant. Cum fratribus subtrahant osculum pacis, quod est signaculum orationis. Hinc ad uxorem II. Alicui fratrum ad osculum convenire. De hoc osculo Clemens Pædag. III. ἅγιον ἀυτὸ κέκληκεν ὁ Ἀπόστολος ἀπογενομέ- νοις ἀξίως τῆς βασιλείας πολιτευόμεθα τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἔννοιαν διὰ σώματος σώφρονος καὶ μεμυκότος δι᾽ ἧς μαλιστα διακοιοῦται τρόπος ἥμερος. Meminit ejus moris & Origenes hoc lo- co, & Martyrologium ad II. Idus Septembris de Sosthene & Victore. Ostendebant eo modo, Christiani se omnes inter se pares esse. Nam apud Persas & alios Orientis po- pulos pares os inter se jungebant, superiores dabant ma- num osculandam inferioribus.

Etiam ante S. Cœnam in Sanctis Conventibus sese osculo excipiebant fideles, dicentes, pax te- cum, quod communicaturis fuit Symbolum re- conciliationis ac injuriæ cujuscunque remissæ & sinceræ charitatis. B. Balduinus observat hic oscula usitata (1.) Inter discedentes, exempla ex- tant Ruth I. 9. 1. Reg. XIX. 20. 2. Sam. XIX. 39. (2.) Inter convenientes : exempla sunt Gen. XXX. 11. Exod. XVIII. 7. Tob. VII. 7. (3.) Inter reconcilia- tos amicos; exempla sunt 2. Sam. XIV. 33. Luc. XV. (4.) Inter socios fidei, quod osculum vocabatur san- ctum, ut patet ex hoc loco, item ex 1. Corinth. XVI. 2. Cor. XIII. & 1. Thess. V. alibi vocatur osculum charitatis in 1. Pet. V. De salutationibus S. Au- gustin. serm. XLII. de tempore: Si quis, inquit, obvium sibi hominem non salutarit, aut salutanti non reddiderit salutem, à viatore non habebitur homo, sed truncus, lapis, aut Mercurius, qui stans in via monstrat iter, & nihil loquitur. De osculo idololatrico & superstitioso Ethnicorum, qui manum deosculari solebant in honorem Deorum suorum, vid. Job. XXXI. 26. 27. 28. & Drusium ibid. 1. Reg. XIX. 18. Os. XIII. 2. & Hie- ronymum ad illum locum. Hoc autem oscu- lum sanctum appellat Apostolus. Quo nomi- ne, monente hic Origene, docet primò, ut ca- stæ sint oscula, quæ in Ecclesiis dantur. Tunc de- inde ut simulata non sint, sicut fuerunt Judæ, qui osculum labiis dabat, & proditionem corde tracta- bat. Osculum verò fidele primo castum sit, tunc deinde pacem habeat in se simplicitatemque in se non fictam.

... ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τοῦ χριστοῦ. Quæ sunt in Græcia. Non quod de ipsis mandatum haberet Paulus, sed quòd de affectu ipsorum constaret, & quod unus spiritus esset in Paulo, atque in omnibus Ecclesiis, ut hic Origenes.

## 16:17
Verse 17. Now I beseech you, brethren, to mark them who cause divisions and offenses contrary to the doctrine which you have learned.

Σκοπεῖν to consider. He has the same word in the same matter in Gal. III. 17. Divisions precede: offenses follow, that is, schisms. See the remarks on Matt. XIII. 41. But he notes here those who, although they were not Jews themselves, wanted to impose the yoke of the Mosaic law upon the called Gentiles, against both the precepts of Christ, who commends peace, and the Apostolic precept, which Paul taught was to be observed everywhere, Acts XVI. 4. Compare the Epistle to the Galatians.

Others wish not only heterodoxy, but also scandals to be noted in this sense, that two types of men are censured, both those who corrupt doctrine and those who corrupt rites, of which the former makes heresies and heretics; the latter begets scandals and makes schismatics: and they are thought to refer primarily to the Pseudo-Apostles, who were corrupting the doctrine concerning justification and salvation.

Moreover, from the words of the Apostle, as Coccejus rightly observes on p. 760, such a rule arises. That which is taught beyond the doctrine which the Romans and all the faithful have learned, causes dissension, and that which is done against it, causes scandal. The little word παρὰ denotes both addition and every change. See 1 John II. 27, 2 Tim. III. 14, 15, Phil. III. 16. Here the blessed Mylius notes four marks of heretics: (1.) It is turbulence, by which the peace and tranquility of well-constituted Churches is disturbed. (2.) Heterodidaskalia, when, beyond that doctrine which was first in the restoring of the Church, new dogmas are introduced. For the first of anything, as Tertullian witnesses, is the most true: whatever is later is adulterated. (3.) Chrestologia and eulogia, when speeches are accommodated to popular favor and the desires of men, and especially things pleasing to reason are said, in such a way that the hearts of the simple may be deceived. (4.) γαστροδουλία, when one serves the belly, and all things are referred to gain, concerning which he says elsewhere that they are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, and that the belly of these is their God, seeking gold and Christ.

and turn away from them) And this argument makes me believe that there were not common assemblies or a presbytery in Rome at that time. Otherwise, he would have wanted such persons to be excommunicated. But where the Church is without such governance, individuals can do nothing else than decline familiar association with those who do not live according to the rule of Christ, as we said in the Commentary on the second epistle to the Thessalonians, where στέλλεσθαι ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντος is the same as ἐκκλίνεσθαι here. See what we said on Matt. 18:17.

Therefore, it is not to be believed that Peter held the episcopate at Rome: because he had no church, nor was there any presbytery or governance in Rome, as Grotius admits, and when Paul came to Rome seven years later, there was still no public church there, no ecclesiastical ministry, let alone an episcopal seat or chair: because the Jews gathered to Paul to learn something about the sect of the Christians. Acts 28. But how could the profession of Christians have been obscure or unknown in Rome if Peter had already held the episcopate there for several years? But the observation of heterodoxy does not pertain only to the clergy, as the Papists wish, but to all the faithful, as is well observed here by Origen: These things, he says on page 360, Paul is to be believed to write through the Holy Spirit both to those who preside over the churches and to all believers, so that they may more diligently consider and perceive who they are that generate dissensions and stumbling blocks in the churches.

Latin:

Vers. 17. παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ, σκοπεῖν τοὺς τὰς δι- χοστασίας, καὶ τὰ σκάνδαλα παρὰ τὴν διδαχὴν ἣν ὑμεῖς ἐμά- θετε ποιοῦντας.

Σκοπεῖν considerare. Idem verbum in eadem re habet Gal. III. 17. διχοστασίας præcedunt : sequuntur σκάνδαλα, id est, schismata. Vide dicta ad Matth. XIII. 41. Notat autem hic eos, qui, cum ipsi Judæi non essent, vocatis gen- tibus imponere volebant legis Mosaicæ jugum contra & præcepta Christi pacem commendantis, & præceptum Apostolicum, quod ubique Paulus servandum docuit, Act. XVI. 4. Confer Epistolam ad Galatas.

Alii non tantum ἑτεροδοξίαν, sed etiam scanda- la notari volunt hoc sensu, quod duo hominum genera perstringantur, & qui doctrinam depra- vant, & qui corrumpunt ritus, quorum illud hæ- reses & hæreticos facit; hoc scandala parit, & schismaticos efficit: & imprimis Pseudo-Aposto- los, qui doctrinam de justificatione & salute cor- rumpebant, respici censent.

Cæterum ex verbis Apostoli, ut recte observat Coccejus p. 760. nascitur talis regula. Quod præ- ter doctrinam, quam Romani & fideles omnes didi- cerunt, docetur, facit dissidium, & quod contra eam fit, facit scandalum. Vocula παρὰ notat & additio- nem & mutationem omnem. Vid. 1. Johan. II. 27. 2. Tim. III. 14. 15. Phil. III. 16. Notat hic B. My- lius quatuor γνωρίσματα hæreticorum: (1.) Est turbulentia, qua Ecclesiis benè constitutis pax & tranquillitas turbatur. (2.) ἑτεροδιδασκαλίαν, cum præter eam doctrinam, quæ in instauranda Ecclesia prima fuit, nova dogmata invehuntur. Primum enim quodque, teste Tertulliano, est verissimum: adulterinum quodcunque posterius. (3.) χρη- στολογία & εὐλογία, cum ad auram popularem, & desideria hominum, sermones accommodan- tur, & præcipuè rationi grata dicuntur, quomodo corda simplicium decipiantur. (4.) γαστροδουλία, cum ventri servitur, & omnia ad quæstum referuntur, de quibus alibi dicit, quod sint Φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον, ἢ Φιλόθεοι, & quod venter istorum sit Deus, χρυσὸν κ' χριστὸν quærentium.

καὶ ἐκκλίνατε ἀπ' αὐτῶν) Et hoc argumentum facit, ut credam non fuisse tunc conventus communes, aut presbyterium Romæ. Alioqui voluisset tales excommunicari. Ubi autem sine tali regimine est Ecclesia, nihil aliud possunt singuli, quam declinare familiarem convictum cum iis, qui non ex regula Christi vivunt, ut diximus in Commentario ad secundam ad Thessalonicenses, ubi στέλλεσθαι ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντος, idem est, quod hic ἐκκλίνεσθαι. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. XVIII. 17.

Non ergò credendum est, Petrum Romæ Episcopatum gessisse: quia nullam habuit Ecclesiam, nec ullum Romæ fuit Presbyterium aut regimen, fatente Grotio, & quum Paulus septennio post Romam venit, nulla adhuc ibi fuit Ecclesia publica, nullum 'ministerium Ecclesiasticum, nedum sedes aut cathedra Episcopalis: quia congregabantur Judæi ad Paulum, ut aliquid cognoscerent de secta Christianorum. Act. XXVIII. Quomodo autem obscura vel ignota potuisset Romæ esse professio Christianorum, si Petrus ibi Episcopatum per aliquot annos jam tum gessisset? Non autem tantum ad Clericos pertinere observationem ἑτεροδοξίας, ut Papistæ volunt, sed ad omnes fideles, hic probè observatum Origeni: Hæc & ad eos, inquit pag. 360. qui Ecclesiis præsunt, & ad omnes credentes per Spiritum Sanctum scribere credendus est Paulus, ut diligentius considerent & perspiciant, qui sint, qui dissensiones & offendicula in Ecclesiis generant.

## 16:18
Verse 18. For such persons do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly) The Apostle describes the same men with the same note in the aforementioned place, Phil. 3:18-19. Indeed, these men looked to two things: first, to free themselves and other Christians from the cross: for the freedom of their religion had been granted to the Jews by the Roman Empire from of old, but not so to Christians: secondly, by that means they prepared for themselves the friendship of the Jews and, from that, advantages. But the Apostle knew this not from conjectures alone, but also by the dictation of the Holy Spirit. Not unlike this is what Plutarch narrates was said about Demades in his book on the study of riches: for he himself was a demagogue for the sake of his belly.

These things, said rashly and by conjecture alone, have no solid foundation. Origen is more correct: For the sake of the belly, he says, that is, of gain and greed. Hence it is that some go around houses speaking with grace, with all adulation and deception, not to build up souls in virtue in the word of God, but to urge them with adulatory and sweet speeches to remain in, or even to progress in, vices, praising and calling good those things which are worthy of correction: putting light for darkness, and darkness for light, the sweet for the bitter, and the bitter for the sweet, and in these things they seduce the hearts of the innocent. Coccejus on this passage, p. 765, has it thus: Indeed, all who cause dissensions serve the belly. For in error there is whoredom with the world and flight from the cross. For truth fights with the wisdom of men and concupiscence: error finds applauders in the world. Therefore, through error they lead disciples after themselves. Which is not done except for the sake of carnal good. What? Do those who profess that they wish to remove from Christian doctrine the things of the Jews and Turks not do this in order to please the Jews and Turks? And indeed, in that in which they err? Thus, do those who seek peace outside the way of peace not seek to please men? The way of peace is unique: to remain in those things which we have learned, and to retain the words taught by the Holy Spirit and the mind of Christ, 1 Cor. 2:13, 16, or the sound words of Christ, and the doctrine which is according to godliness, 1 Tim. 6:3.

and by smooth speech. Smooth-speakers are men who are flattering rather than kind, as those who wrote the life of Pertinax interpret that word. This is a part of obsequiousness, the description of which you have in Theophrastus. Solomon attributes to a strange woman מחלקת לשון, flatteries of the tongue. Some note flatteries both in the manner of doctrine and in the morals of those who teach. But the word itself teaches that doctrine is being referred to here, because they propose the same with a peculiar sweetness: For poisons are not given unless smeared with honey, as Jerome says in Epistle 7 to Laeta: Such as Cyprian notes in his work on the simplicity of prelates, who, namely, while they lie with plausible things, frustrate the truth with subtlety; with the adversary flattering and deceiving, who, according to the word of the Apostle, transforms himself as an angel of light, and suborns his ministers as ministers of righteousness, asserting night for day, destruction for salvation, despair under the pretext of hope, perfidy under the pretext of faith, the Anti-Christ under the name of Christ.

and blessings) To bless, for Isocrates and Aristophanes, is to praise. But those who wish to please others are accustomed to praise them to their face, and even to extenuate their faults. It is about such that 2 Tim. 3:4-7 treats, of whom I wish there were not so many in our own age.

they deceive the hearts of the innocent) Like those who said, Peace, where there was no peace. Jer. 8:10. Innocent here is said by way of irony of men who are easily deceived. Plutarch: The innocent are harmed more by those who speak. Not only praises, but also blessings, good wishes, and magnificent promises. B. Weller wishes to be understood: as things which most easily infatuate minds occupied by hope, fear, and other affections: and he declares this by the example of both those converted from the Jews and the monks: The former, urging works necessary for salvation, put forward an excellent appearance in teaching, but they caused Christ to be denied in this way or his merit to be obscured in great part, Gal. 5:4. Although these men teach many things that are not only false, but also clearly absurd, they nevertheless entice the minds of men into the monstrosities of their opinions by that blandiloquence of theirs, and by magnificent promises, with which they egregiously smear the mouths of the common people: for example, when they promise riches to the worshippers of Anne, when they attribute singular efficacy to the Rosary of Mary, when for the sacrifice of the Mass they promise happiness in all business affairs.

Latin:

Vers. 18. οἱ γὰρ τοιοῦτοι τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστῷ οὐ δουλεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἑαυτῶν κοιλίᾳ) Eadem nota eosdem homines describit Apostolus dicto loco Phil. III. 18. 19. Nimirum isti homines duo spectabant: primum ut semet & alios Christianos liberarent à cruce: nam Judæis ab antiquo permissa erat per Imperium Romanum suæ Religionis libertas, non item Christianis: deinde ea ratione Judæorum sibi amicitiam & inde utilitates parabant. Hoc autem noverat Apostolus non ex conjecturis solis, sed dictante etiam Spiritu Sancto. Non dissimile est, quod de Demade dictum narrat Plutarchus libro de divitiarum studio: αὐτὸς γὰρ εἰς τὴν γαστέρα ἐδημαγώγει.

Hæc temerè & per στοχασμὸν solum dicta nullum solidum habent fundamentum. Rectius Origenes: Ventris, inquit, gratia hoc est quæstus & cupiditatis. Inde est, unde nonnulli circumeunt domos loquentes ad gratiam cum omni adulatione & deceptione, non ut in verbo Dei ædificent animas ad virtutem, sed ut adulatoriis dulcibusque sermonibus permanere, vel etiam proficere eas hortentur in vitiis, laudantes & bona dicentes ea, quæ correptione digna sunt: ponentes lucem tenebras, & tenebras lucem, dulce amarum, & amarum dulce, & in his seducunt corda innocentium. Coccejus in h. l. p. 765. ita habet: Enimverò omnes, qui dissidia faciunt, serviunt ventri. Nam in errore est scortatio cum mundo & fuga crucis. Nam veritas pugnat cum sapientia hominum & concupiscentia: error invenit applausores in mundo. Per errorem igitur abducunt discipulos post se. Quod non fit, nisi propter carnale bonum. Quid? An ii, qui profitentur se velle amovere à doctrina Christiana secunda Judæorum & Turcarum, non hoc agunt, ut placeant Judæis & Turcis? Et quidem in eo, in quo errant? Ita, qui extra viam pacis pacem quærunt, numquid non quærunt hominibus placere? Via pacis unica est, manere in iis, quæ didicimus, & retinere verba docta à Spiritu Sancto & mentem Christi, 1. Cor. II. 13. 16. sive sanos sermones Christi, & doctrinam, quæ est secundum pietatem, 1. Tim. VI. 3.

καὶ διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας. Χρηστόλογοι sunt homines blandi magis quàm benigni, ut interpretantur eam vocem ii, qui Pertinacis vitam scripsere. Est hoc pars ἀρεσκείας, cujus descriptionem habes apud Theophrastum. Mulieri extraneæ tribuit Salomo מחלקת לשון blanditias linguæ. Blanditias notant nonnulli tum in genere doctrinæ, tum in moribus docentium. Sed doctrinam hic respici verbum ipsum docet, quia eandem peculiari suavitate proponunt: Venena enim non dantur, nisi melle circumlita, dicente Hieronymo Epist. VII. ad Lætam: Quales notat Cyprianus de simplicitate prælator, qui scilicet dum verisimilia mentiuntur, veritatem subtilitate frustrantur; blandiente adversario atque fallente, qui secundum Apostoli vocem, transfigurat se velut Angelum lucis, & ministros subornat suos velut ministros justitiæ, asserentes noctem pro die, interitum pro salute, desperationem sub obtentu spei, perfidiam sub prætextu fidei, Anti-Christum sub vocabulo Christi.

καὶ ὐυλογίας) ἐυλογεῖν Isocrati & Aristophani est laudare. Solent autem, qui aliis placere volunt, eos in os laudare, & culpas etiam eorum extenuare. De talibus agitur 2. Timoth. III. 4. 5. 6. 7. quales utinam non tam multi sint nostro etiam seculo.

ἐξαπατῶσι τὰς καρδίας τῶν ἀκάκων) Ut illi, qui dicebant, Pax, ubi non erat pax. Jerem. VIII, 10. Ἄκακοι hic per χαριεντισμὸν dicuntur homines faciles decipi. Plutarchus: ὁι ἄκακοι ὑπὸ τῶν λεγόντων μᾶλλον βλάπτονsų. Non tantum laudationes, sed etiam benedictiones, bonas imprecationes & magnificas promissiones. B. Wellerus se signari vult: utpote quæ facillimè infatuant animos, spe, metu & aliis affectibus occupatos: idque exemplo tum conversorum è Judæis, tum Monachorum declarat: Illi opera urgentes necessaria ad salutem, optimam speciem in docendo præ se ferebant, sed faciebant, ut sic abnegaretur Christus vel meritum ejus magna ex parte obscuraretur Gal. V. 4. Hi etsi multa non solum falsa, sed etiam absurda plane doceant, animos tamen hominum ista sua blandiloquentia, & magnificis promissionibus, quibus egregiè vulgò os oblinunt, in opinionum suarum portenta illiciunt: v. g. cum Annæ cultoribus promittunt divitias, cum Rosario Mariæ singularem tribuunt efficaciam, cum pro sacrificio Missæ promittunt felicitatem in omnibus negotiis.

## 16:19
Vers. 19. For your obedience has reached unto all) Because your faith in Christ is celebrated everywhere, therefore many flock to you from all sides, hoping, of course, that in an opulent city there will be the best hunting-ground for them. Obedience here as above I, 5. XV. 18. The sense is clearly the same as above I. 3. Chrysostom attributes a far different, and altogether more correct, intention to the Apostle here: He preoccupies them with praises, he says, and restrains them with a multitude of witnesses: For he says, I do not bear witness of you alone, but the whole world also. And he does not say your prudence, but your obedience, that is, faithful persuasion: which is to them a testimony of much gentleness of the one giving it. B. Mylius notes here three remedies to be opposed to the evil of dissension and scandals: (1.) It is faith, than which no more present remedy is opposed to disturbers. But faith is not in a question of philosophy: But in the doctrine of the Gospel. Therefore, if there is not the greatest ability to answer all questions: nevertheless, a firm belief in the truth will remain in the heart. In this demonstrative genre, the Apostle extols the Romans with an excellent tribute of praise for this virtue. (2.) Simple prudence, which Christ in Matthew X calls serpentine prudence and columbine simplicity: the Apostle distinguishes each by its objects, so that prudence is toward good, and simplicity toward evil, which he likewise impresses on the Corinthians in 1 Cor. 14:20. (3.) Hope of divine aid, for God, as for the rest, is said to be about to give the effect, in whose judgment, already passed concerning Satan, the pious must firmly rely.

χαίρω ὖν τὸ ἐφ’ ὑμῖν) He congratulates the greater part of the Christians, who had not allowed themselves to be seduced by those money-grubbers, yet because what can happen to anyone can happen to anyone, he adds a warning:

θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς σοφὺς μὲν εἶναι εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀκεραίυς δὲ εἰς τὸ κακόν) So prudent that you may not be deceived, so good that you may not deceive. The same sense, which Matt. X. 16. & 1 Cor. XV. 20. εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, that is, that you may persevere in good.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἡ γὰρ ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ ἐις πάντας ἀφίκετο) Quia ubique celebratur vestra in Christum fides, ideò multi ad vos undique concurrunt, nimirum sperantes in opulenta urbe optimum sibi fore aucupium. ὑπακοὴ hic ut supra I, 5. XV. 18. Idem planè sensus qui supra I. 3. Longè aliam hic mentem, & rectius omninò, Apostoli facit Chrysostomus: Encomiis, inquit, præoccupant, testiumque multitudine continet: Neque enim solus, inquit, testimonium de vobis fero, sed etiam universus orbis. Et non dicit prudentia vestra, sed obedientia vestra, h. e. fidelis persuasio: id quod illis est multæ mansuetudinis testimonium dantis. B. Mylius notat hîc tria remedia, malo τῆς διχοστασίας κ̓ σκανδάλων opponenda: (1.) Est fides, quo nullum præsentius remedium turbatoribus opponitur. Fides verò non est in quæstione Philosophiæ: Sed in doctrina Evangelii. Proinde si non sit maximè ad omnia quæsita respondendi facultas: permanebit tamen in corde firma veritatis credulitas. Hoc in genere demonstrativo effert Apostolus Romanis egregio virtutis istius tributo encomio. (2.) Simplex prudentia, quam Christus Matth. X. serpentinam prudentiam & columbinam simplicitatem appellat: Apostolus ob- jectis utramque distinguit, ut prudentia sit ad bo- num: simplicitas ad malum, quod idem 1. Cor. XIV. 20. inculcat Corinthiis. (3.) Spes divini auxilii, Deus enim, quod reliquum est, effectum daturus esse dicitur, in cujus judicio de Satana jam lato, piis fir- miter recumbendum est.

χαίρω ὖν τὸ ἐφ’ ὑμῖν) Majori parti Christianorum gra- tulatur, quæ se non siverant ab illis lucripetis seduci, at- tamen quia Cvisvis potest accidere quid cuiquam potest, addit monitum:

θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς σοφὺς μὲν εἶναι εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀκεραίυς δὲ εἰς τὸ κακόν) Ita prudentes, ut non fallamini, ita bonos, ut non fallatis. Idem sensus, qui Matth. X. 16. & 1. Cor. XV. 20. εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, id est, ut in bono perseveretis.

## 16:20
Vers. 20. ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης συντρίψει τὸν Σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τὸς πόδας ὑμῶν ἐν τάχει.

The sense of the suspicion of the passage Gen. III. 1 is explained. For there all Hebrews agree that Satan is understood by the serpent: therefore Satan is called by the Hebrews נחש הקדמני, ὄφις ἀρχαῖος Apoc. XII. 9. δράκων often in the same Apocalypse. Satan has craftiness, and strives to harm, like a serpent or dragon. But the Apostle wants to say this: it is Satan who, through those new teachers, began to break that concord which existed among you Christians called from the Jews and from the Gentiles. But his wiles will not last long. The greater and sounder part will easily lead the others back to health. In Genesis it is said to the woman and her posterity תשופנו συντρίψεις, seriously, not evilly. But it is for Christians to refer everything as openly as possible to God's grace, as Paul does here and elsewhere. In the Manuscript it is συντρίψαι, so that it may be a wish, not a prediction. The Syrian, the Latin, and Origen read it no differently.

Grotius perverts the passage of Genesis ch. III. 1. 15. in more than one way: 1. while he understands Satan by the Serpent, if indeed the properly called serpent, which is said there to be craftier than all the beasts of the earth, is noted: even if the Devil hid under the habit of a serpent, as we said regarding that passage in our Commentary on Genesis and in the Illustrated Bibles. 2. while he says that the crushing of the serpentine head is attributed by Moses to both the woman and her posterity: which is not ῥητῶς attributed to either the woman or her posterity, but to the SEED of the woman. 3. He depraves the very word of the promise made in Gen. III. 15, as if it were said to the woman in the second person, thou thyself shalt crush, when in the Hebrew text both the pronoun is of the third person, and the verb is not of the feminine gender, but Masculine, he himself or it (the seed) shall crush. In which part Cornelius à Lapide was more modest and candid here than Grotius. He alludes (he says) to Gen. III. She herself (or as the Hebrew directly has it הוא hu, that is, the seed itself or offspring of the woman, namely Christ) shall crush the head of the serpent. 4. It is feigned; that not everything is referred here by Moses most aptly to the grace of God: because that is Christian: as if Christians ought to refer everything to the grace of God more than Moses? Who indeed uniquely attributes to the grace of God and the merit of Christ all the benefits that happen to us after the fall, as shown at length in the Commentary on Genesis, and constitutes Christ as our sole hyperaspistes and Redeemer, and the crusher of the serpentine head. But there are by no means sufficient causes for us to abandon the more received reading in these words of the Apostle. The Latin and the Syrian cannot prejudice the consensus of the Greek Codices. Origen, however, places here not only a wish, but a promise: as do other Greeks. Chrysostom explains these things especially beautifully: Since he had said, observe those who create dissensions and stumbling blocks: he now says the God of peace, so that they may be confident that they will be freed from them at some time. For he who loves peace will surely dissolve those things which harm it. And he does not say, will subject; but, which is more, will crush: and not only those deceivers, but also him who acts as leader for them in these things, namely Satan. And he will not only crush, but under your feet, so that they themselves might carry off the victory and be rendered illustrious by the trophy obtained. Then again also consolation from the time itself, for he subjoins: Shortly. This, however, was at once both a prayer and a prophecy.

ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν) In this, which I have said, may Christ favor and help us. Here again Paul had proposed to finish, but given the time, he added a few things himself, and his scribe, as is accustomed to be done at the end of epistles.

But whence is it certain that the Apostle proposed to finish here? For could he not have inserted a wish before the conclusion? So that he might seal what he predicts here by wishing, with a special little prayer, and might pray for the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ for them, both for the crushing of Satan and for the communication of benefits, both spiritual and corporal. Nor is it likely that he wished to conclude an epistle concerning the grace of justification and salvation without a δοξολογίᾳ, and only accidentally, given the time, as a postscript, subjoined the same with greetings. Concerning this wish, Origen: The grace of the God of our Lord Jesus Christ is one and the same grace to be received. For just as the Father quickens whom He will: and as the Father has life in Himself, and has given to the Son to have life in Himself, so also the grace which the Father gives, this the Son also gives. It must certainly be known that everything which men have from God is grace. For they have nothing by debt. For who has first given to Him and it shall be repaid to him? Therefore it is grace, whatever he has who was not, and is receiving from Him who always was, and is, and will be forever.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης συντρίψει τὸν Σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τὸς πόδας ὑμῶν ἐν τάχει.

Explicatur sensus ὑπονοίας loci Gen. III. 1. Nam ibi per serpentem intelligi Satanam consentiunt omnes Hebræi: ideò Satan dicitur Hebræis נחש הקדמני, ὄφις ἀρχαῖος Apoc. XII. 9. δράκων sæpè in eadem Apocalypsi. Habet Sa- tanas calliditatem, & studet nocere, ut serpens aut draco. Hoc autem vult dicere Apostolus: Satanas est; qui per no- vos illos doctores eam, quæ inter vos Christianos ex Judæis & ex gentibus vocatos erat, concordiam cœpit rumpere. Sed non diu durabunt ejus astus. Facilè pars major & sa- nior cæteras ad sanitatem reducet. In Genesi dicitur mu- lieri & posteritati ejus תשופנו συντρίψεις, seriòn non ma- lo. Sed Christianorum est quàm apertissimè omnia ad Dei gratiam referre, ut hic & alibi facit Paulus. In Manu- scripto est, συντρίψαι, ut sit votum, non prædictio. Non aliter legêre Syrus, Latinus, & Origenes.

Locum Geneseos c. III. 1. 15. non uno modo per- vertit Grotius: 1. dum per Serpentem intelligit Sa- tanam, siquidem propriè dictus serpens, qui cal- lidior præ omnibus bestiis terræ ibi dicitur, note- tur: etsi sub habitu serpentis latuerit Diabolus, ut ad illum locum in Commentar. in Genesin, & Bi- bliis illustratis diximus. 2. dum & mulieri & poste- ritati à Mose tribui contritionem capitis serpentini, ait: quæ nec mulieri nec posteritati ῥητῶς tribuitur, sed SEMINI mulieris. 3. Verbum ipsum pro- missionis Gen. III. 15. factæ depravat, quasi in se- cunda persona mulieri dictum sit, tu ipsa conteres, quum in textu Ebræo & pronomen tertiæ perso- næ sit, & verbum generis non fœminini, sed Masculini, ipse vel ipsum (semen) conteret. Quà in parte modestior & candidior Grotio hic fuit Cornelius à Lapide. Alludit (inquit) ad Gen. III. Ipsa (vel ut directè habent Hebræa הוא hu, id est, ipsum semen sive proles mulieris, puta Christus) con- teret caput serpentis. 4. Fingitur; non referri hic à Mose omnia aptissimè ad gratiam Dei: eò quod id Christianum sit: quasi Christiani magis ad gratiam Dei referre debeant omnia, quàm Moses? Qui verò unicè gratiæ Dei & Christi merito omnia, quæ nobis post lapsum contingunt beneficia, tri- buit, ut in Comment. ad Genesin prolixè ostensum, & Christum unicum nostrum hyperaspistem & Re- demptorem, & capitis serpentini contritorem con- stituit. Lectionem autem receptiorem ut in his Apostoli verbis deseramus, causæ sufficientes mi- nimè sunt. Codicum Græcorum consensui La- tinus & Syrus præjudicare nequit. Origenes ve- rò hic non votum solum, sed promissionem ponit: ut & alii Græci. Pulchrè imprimis explicat hæc Chrysostomus: Quoniam dixerat, eos, qui dissidia & offendicula gignunt, observate: dicit jam Deum pacis, ut confidant se liberandos aliquando ab illis. Qui enim pacem amat, utique dissolvet, quæ illam lædunt. Et non dicit, subdet; sed, quod magis est, conteret: & non solum deceptores illos, sed & qui ad ista ducem illis agit, nempe Satanam. Et non solum conteret, sed sub pedes vestros, ut & ipsi victoriam auferrent & adepto trophæo illustres redderentur. Deinde rursus & ab ipso tempore consolatio, sub- jungit enim: Brevi. Hoc verò simul erat & precatio & prophetia.

ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν) In hoc, quod dixi, Christus nobis faveat & opituletur. Hic ite- rum finire proposuerat Paulus, sed tempore dato pauca adjecit & ipse, & scriba ejus, ut solet subter epistolas fieri.

Unde verò constat hic finire proposuisse Apo- stolum? Annon enim potuit inserere votum ante conclusionem? ut quod hic vovendo prædicit, peculiari precatiuncula obsignet, & cum ad Sa- tanæ contritionem, tum ad beneficiorum quà spi- ritualium, quà corporalium communicationem gratiam Domini Jesu Christi ipsis appreca- tur. Nec verò simile est, sine δοξολογίᾳ. Epi- stolam de gratia justificationis & salvationis con- cludere voluisse, & tantum per accidens, tempo- re dato, veluti postscriptum eandem cum saluta- tionibus subjunxisse. De hoc voto Origenes; Gratia Dei Domini nostri Jesu Christi, una atque eadem gratia accipienda est. Sicut enim Pater quos vult vivificat: & sicut Pater habet vitam in se, & Filio dedit habere in semetipso vitam, ita & gratiam, quam dat Pater, hanc & Filius dat. Scien- dum sane est, quod omne, quod habent homines à Deo, gratia est. Nihil enim ex debito habent. Quis enim prior dedit illi & retribuetur ei? gratia ergo est, quicquid habet is, qui non fuit, & est acci- piens ab eo, qui semper fuit, & est, & erit in æter- num.

## 16:21
Ver. 21. ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς Τιμόθεος ὁ σύνεργός μου [Timothy my fellow-worker greets you]) See Acts XVI. & following.

The reason why he sends greetings to the Romans in the name of certain individuals specifically, when he had greeted them in the name of the Churches in Greece generally, is not that he wished to reconcile the authority of the Epistle in that way, but that he did it to testify to their mutual affection: concerning which it is pleasing to transcribe the opinion of Origen: It seems to me that concerning those whom he separated from the entire list of those greeting, he sensed something more. Finally, he calls Timothy his helper, and all his kinsmen together. And indeed, it is reported most fully concerning Timothy in the Acts of the Apostles, that he was a citizen of Derbe, the son of a widowed woman, faithful from a Gentile father. Concerning whom Paul himself also says that for this reason he had asked him to remain at Ephesus, so that he might warn certain ones not to teach otherwise, nor to attend to fables and endless genealogies. But some also claim that Lucius is Luke, who wrote the Gospel, because names are accustomed to be pronounced sometimes according to the native declension, and sometimes also according to the Greek and Roman. But that Jason is the one of whom it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles, that at Thessalonica, when crowds were stirring up sedition on behalf of Paul and Silas, he gave himself up so that he might provide the Apostle freedom of speech. Sosipater is also joined to these; I suspect that he is the same one who is written in the Acts of the Apostles as Sosipater son of Pyrrhus of Beroea.

καὶ Λούκιος [and Lucius]) Why we do not think this is the Evangelist Luke, we have said in our Prolegomena to Luke. But this is Lucius of Cyrene, Acts XIII. 1, the brother of Rufus, as some think.

Baronius prefers that it be Luke, because he was joined with the others to Paul. But we easily agree here with Grotius: since the name Lucius, not Luke, is held here: concerning him Chytræus in Onomast. Lucius of Cyrene, a Doctor in the Church at Antioch, Acts XIII. They write that he was the son of Simon of Cyrene, who helped carry the cross for Christ, and after the resurrection of Christ taught the Gospel in Augusta Tiberina, which is now called Ratisbon, as Aventinus in the Annals of the Boii testifies. The same person is thought to be Lucius, who is mentioned in Romans 16.

καὶ Ἰάσων) Paul's host at Thessalonica, Acts 17:5, one of the Jews who believed in Christ, to whom the Epistle to the Thessalonians was written, which is called the second because it became known to the churches later, as we said in our commentary on the second chapter of that Epistle.

Regarding him, Chytræus says thus in the loc. cit.: Jason, host of St. Paul in the city of Thessalonica, Acts 17, is thought by some to be the same person who is mentioned in Romans 16, and that he was afterwards Bishop of Tarsus in Cilicia. Ἰάσων is a physician, from ἰάομαι or from יָשַׁע, salvation. We have discussed the Grotian invention concerning the inverted order of the Epistles to the Thessalonians in the observations on the preface to the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

καὶ Σωσίπατρος) A Berean, Acts 20:4. For it is the same name, and in various dialects Σώπατρος and Σωσίπατρος. And Greek writers give this name to the same person, others that.

οἱ συγγενεῖς μου) They were therefore Jews. Ἰάσων is called in Hebrew יְשׁוּעַ, but Sosipater is אָב יֶשַׁע.

They say that Sosipater was afterwards Bishop of Iconium. Chytræus makes that name Hebrew, not Greek: σωσίπατρος, interpreter of 'savior of a father' or 'of joy,' from שׂוּשׂ, joy, and יָתַר, he interpreted. But it seems rather to be Greek. Origen wishes συγγενεῖς to be said here because of the consanguinity contracted from Baptism: but most others rightly judge them to be so called because they were of the same nation. As for why he does not equally explain Aquila and Priscilla, who are known to have been Jews, by the name of kinsmen, Baronius thinks the reason was that these seemed better known, since they were otherwise living in Rome in the time of Claudius: but perhaps it was necessary to point out the others specifically as visiting Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς Τιμόθεος ὁ σύνεργός μου) Vide Act. XVI. & sequentibus.

Cur nomine quorundam peculiariter salutem dicat Romanis, quum in genere Ecclesiarum in Græcia nomine eos salutarit, causa est, non quod conciliare ita autoritatem Epistolæ voluerit, sed quod testandæ mutuæ compunctioni id fecerit: quo de Origenis adscribere placet sententiam: Vi- detur mihi de istis, quos sequestravit ab omni cata- logo salutantium, plus aliquid sensisse. Denique Timotheum adjutorem suum dicit, & omnes simul cognatos suos. Et quidem de Timotheo plenissimè refertur in Actibus Apostolorum, quod fuerit Der- bæus civis, filius mulieris viduæ, fidelis ex patre gentili. De quo & ipse Paulus dicit, quia propterea rogaverat eum permanere Ephesi, ut denunciet qui- busdam, ne aliter doceant, neque attendant fabu- lis & genealogiis infinitis. Sed & Lucium quidam perhibent esse Lucam, qui Evangelium scripsit, pro eo, quod soleant nomina interdum secundum patriam declinationem, interdum etiam secundum Græcam, Romanamque proferri. Jason verò il- le est, de quo etiam in Actibus Apostolorum scribi- tur, quod Thessalonicæ pro Paulo & Silia sedi- tionem commoventibus turbis, semetipsum dederit, ut Apostolo dicendi faceret libertatem. Sosipater quoque his jungitur, suspicor, quod ipse sit, qui in Actibus Apostolorum scribitur Sosipater Pyrrhi Be- roensis.

καὶ Λούκιος) Cur non esse hunc Evangelistam Lucam pu- temus, diximus in nostris ad Lucam Prolegomenis. Sed est hic Lucius Cyrenæus Act. XIII. 1. frater Rufi, ut qui- dam putant.

Lucam esse mavult Baronius, quòd cum reli- quis Paulo compunctus fuerit. Sed facilè hic annuimus Grotio: quum nomen Lucii, non Lu- cæ, hic habeatur: de eo Chytræus in Onomast. Lucius Cyrenæus, Doctor in Ecclesia Antioche- na, Actor. XIII. scribunt filium fuisse Simonis Cy- renæi, qui Christum in cruce gestanda adjuvit, & post resurrectionem Christi docuisse Evangelion in Augusta Tiberina, quæ nunc Ratisbona di- citur, ut Aventinus in Annalibus Bojorum testatur. Idem Lucius esse putatur, cujus mentio sit Roman. XVI.

καὶ Ἰάσων) Hospes Pauli Thessalonicæ Actor. VII. 5. unus Judæorum in Christum credentium, ad quos scripta est Epistola ad Thessalonicenses, quæ secunda dicitur, ideò quod serius Ecclesiis innotuit, ut diximus in nostro ad se- cundum caput ejus Epistolæ commentario.

De eo Chytræus ita l. c. Jason Hospes S. Pauli in urbe Thessalonica Act. XVII. eundem esse, cujus sit mentio Rom. XVI. eumque postea Tharsi Cilicia Epi- scopum fuisse putant. Ἰάσων Medicus ab ἰάομαι vel à יָשַׁע salus. De inverso Epistolarum ad Thessa- lonicenses ordine commentum Grotianum dis- scussimus in observationibus ad præloquium in E- pist. I. ad Thessalonicenses.

καὶ Σωσίπατρος) Beræus Act. XX. 4. Idem enim nomen & variis dialectis Σώπατρος & Σωσίπατρος. Et Græci ei- dem Scriptori alii hæc, alii illud dant nomen.

οἱ συγγενεῖς μου) Judæi ergo fuere Ἰάσων Hebraicè voca- tur יְשׁוּעַ, Sosipater verò אָב יֶשַׁע.

Sosipatrum dicunt Episcopum postea fuisse Ico- nii. Nomen id Hebræum non Græcum facit Chy- træus: σωσίπατρος servator Patris vel gaudii inter- pres à שׂוּשׂ gaudium, & יָתַר interpretatus est. Sed videtur potius Græcum. Συγγενεῖς Origenes ob consanguinitatem ex Baptismo contractam hic dici vult: Verum rectius ita dictos plerique alii censent, quòd ejusdem gentis essent. Quod autem non æque Aquilam & Priscillam, quos constat fuis- se Judæos, cognatorum nomine exponat, illam Baronius putat fuisse causam, quod hi notiores vi- debantur, quippe qui aliàs tempore Claudii Ro- mæ agebant: cæteros verò fortasse advenas Ju- dæos sic speciatim opus fuerit demonstrasse.

## 16:22
Verse 22. ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἐν Κυρίῳ. The Syriac, Arabic, Origen, Ambrose, and the Greeks read Τέρτιος. Wherefore in the Latin versions which have it otherwise, there is an error of the scribe. Primus, Secundus, Tertius, Quartus, Quintus, Sextus are frequent names among the Romans. ἐν κυρίῳ is to be construed with ἀσπάζομαι as in 1 Corinthians 16:20. Tertius had written this in the margin while he was transcribing this Epistle from Paul's archetype. The Greeks call such persons ὑπογραφέας.

By what witness or document does Grotius hold that these things, which are now read in the text, were written in the margin? Or that this Epistle was transcribed from Paul's autograph by Tertius, whereas most say it was dictated to Tertius by Paul: who certainly could have dictated these words to him as well, so that the Apostle might reveal to the faithful Romans the affection of Tertius, of which he was not ignorant, nay, which he knew from the dictation and inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But Cornelius is injurious to the θεοπνευστίαν of the Epistle, along with Sixtus Senensis, whose words he makes his own here from book II. Bibl. on Tertius: He (Tertius), since he was little skilled in speech and not sufficiently practiced in writing, rendered the Epistle, which is far more obscure than the other Epistles of Paul because of the multitude and sublimity of the questions, most obscure, while he attempted to explain the senses and thoughts of Paul with sometimes confused elocutions, incomplete sentences, and a sometimes transposed order of sequence. The Epistle vindicates itself from such charges. How could Tertius have attempted this, when, as Cornelius the Jesuit confesses from Sixtus, he wrote this Epistle at the dictation of the Apostle? Furthermore, Theodotus, a Presbyter of Coelesyria, reads Terentius in place of Tertius in his exposition of this Epistle: but the Greek Codices and Interpreters, along with the Syriac, Arabic, and other versions, teach that the name Tertius is the genuine one. Diodorus of Tarsus, Sixtus Senensis, and Cornelius à Lapide say he was the same Bishop of Iconium: others say he was appointed Bishop of Berytus in Phoenicia.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἐν Κυρίῳ. Τέρτιος legerunt Syrus, Arabs, Origenes, Ambrosius, & Græci. Quare in Latinis quæ aliter habent, error est ex- scriptoris. Primus, Secundus, Tertius, Quartus, Quintus, Sextus, nomina frequentia apud Romanos. ἐν κυρίῳ con- struendum cum ἀσπάζομαι ut 1.Cor. XVI. 20. Hoc ad mar- ginem adscripserat Tertius, dum hanc Epistolam ex Pauli archetypo describit. Tales Græci ὑπογραφέας vocant.

Quo teste vel documento habet Grotius, hæc ad marginem adscripta fuisse, quæ nunc in textu le- guntur? aut hanc Epistolam ex autographo Pauli descriptam à Tertio, quam plerique dictatam Ter- tio à Paulo ajunt: qui sanè etiam hæc verba ipsi di- ctare potuit, ut Tertii etiam affectum, cujus non ignarus erat, imò quem è dictamine & afflatu Spi- ritus S. noverat Apostolus, fidelibus Romanis aperiret. Injurius autem in θεοπνευστίαν Epistolæ est cum Sixto Senensi Cornelius, cujus verba hic sua facit è lib. II. Bibl. in Tertio: Is (Tertius) cùm esset parum sermone peritus, nec satis in scribendo exercitatus, epistolam, quæ propter multitudinem ac sublimitatem quæstionum, cæteris Pauli Epistolis ob- scurior est, longè reddidit obscurissimam, dum sensus & cogitationes Pauli elocutionibus interdum confu- sis, & inabsolutis sententiis, ac transpositâ nonnun- quam ordinis serie conatus est explicare. Vindicat seipsam Epistola à talibus ἐγκλήμασι. Quomodo hoc conari potuit Tertius, quum dictante Apo- stolo, ut fatetur è Sixto Cornelius Jesuita, hanc Epistolam scripserit? Cæterum Theodotus Cælo- Syriæ Presbyter in expos. hujus Epist. loco Tertii legit Terentium: sed Tertii nomen genuinum esse, Codd. & Interpp. Græci cum Syro, Arabe, aliisque versionibus docent. Eundem Iconii Episcopum Diodorus Tarsensis, Sixtus Senensis, Cornelius à La- pide dicunt: alii Berythi in Phœnicia Episcopum constitutum fuisse ajunt.

## 16:23
Verse 23. ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Γάϊος ὁ ξένος μου) The name was common to many, even Christians of that time, but here the learned well note that the same person is designated who is in 1 Corinthians 1:14. Origen says from tradition that he was afterwards Bishop of the Church of Thessalonica. The Latins wrote Cajus and pronounced it Gajus, because formerly C was γ, as in the Greek Alphabet: hence Γήις for Ceres, and many similar things. As the Greeks pronounced this name, so they wrote Γάϊος. Thus always Polybius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch, Dio, and inscriptions. ξένος means, just as the Latins use hospes, one who receives another.

καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ὅλης) He adds this because, when he was writing this, the assembly of Christians was accustomed to be held in the house of that Gaius.

B. Chytræus observes that Gaius of Macedonia, who is believed to have been born in Thessalonica, mentioned in Acts 19, is one person, and Gaius of Derbe, whom Paul himself baptized, 1 Cor. 1, who accompanied Paul returning from Corinth to Asia, Acts 20, to whom also the third Epistle of John, who ruled the churches in Ephesus and in neighboring Asia, may be inscribed, is another: who is celebrated here as the host of Paul and of the whole church in the city of Corinth.

ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἔραστος ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως) Erastus is a common name among the Greeks, of the same meaning as Agapetus, Pothinus, and similar names. οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως, namely of Corinth. The ancient Romans would have called this a quaestor. But the word οἰκονόμος was transferred from the house to the city, just as the word for treasurer, which the Latin translator used here. For that was anciently the name of a private office, as appears in l. Thais at the end, D. de fidei commissariis libertatibus. You see now from the beginning, although few, there were nevertheless some Christians placed in positions of dignity.

Converted by Paul, he was for some time a companion of Paul's journeys, by whom he was sent ahead from the city of Ephesus into Macedonia, Acts 19. But he remained at Corinth while Paul was a prisoner at Rome, 2 Tim. 4. Ἔραστος, lovable, desirable.

κὶ κούαρτος ὁ ἀδελφός) Quartus is a name like Tertius just now. These Romans were likely merchants in Corinth.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Γάϊος ὁ ξένος μου) Nomen fuit multis, etiam Christianis ejus temporis, commune, sed hic bene notant eruditi designari eundem, qui 1.Cor. I. 4. Hunc postea fuisse Episcopum Thessaloniconsis Ecclesiæ ait ex traditione Origenes. Latini scribebant Cajus, pronuntiabant Gajus, quia olim C fuit γ, ut in Græco Alphabeto: inde Γήις Ceres, multaque similia. Græci ut pronuntiabant hoc nomen, ita scribebant Γάϊος. Ita semper Polybius, Dionysius Halicarnassus, Plutarchus, Dion & inscriptiones. ξένος dicit sicut Latini hospitem, eum qui alterum excipit.

καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ὅλης) Hoc ideò addit, quia cum hæc scriberet, solebat conventus Christianorum haberi in Caji illius ædibus.

B. Chytræus observat, alium esse Cajum Macedonem, qui Thessalonicæ natus creditur, cujus mentio fit Act. IX. alium Cajum Derbensem, quem Paulus ipse baptizavit, 1. Cor. I. qui Paulum ex Corintho in Asiam redeuntem comitatus Act. XX. cui etiam tertia Epistola Johannis, qui Ecclesias Ephesi & in vicina Asia rexit, inscripta sit: qui hic ceu hospes Pauli & totius Ecclesiæ in urbe Corintho celebratur.

ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἔραστος ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως) Erastus frequens apud Græcos nomen paris significatus cum Agapeti, Pothini, similibusque nominibus. οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως nempe Corinthi. Id Romani veteres dixissent quæstorem. Sed οἰκονόμος vox à domo ad urbem translata est, sicut & vox arcarii, quam hic posuit Latinus. Nam id antiquitus nomen fuit privati ministerii, ut apparet l. Thais in fine D. de fidei commissariis libertatibus. Vides jam ab initio, quanquam paucos, aliquos tamen fuisse Christianos in dignitatibus positos.

Hic à Paulo conversus aliquandiu comes fuit profectionum Pauli, à quo ex urbe Epheso præmittitur in Macedoniam, Act. XIX. Sed Paulo Romæ captivo Corinthi mansit, 2. Tim. IV. Ἔραστος amabilis, desiderius.

κὶ κούαρτος ὁ ἀδελφός) Quartus nomen quale modo Tertius. Romani hi fuerint negotiantes Corinthi.

## 16:24
Vers. 24. ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, Ἀμήν.

The same words as above, 20, except that 'all' is absent there. But Paul wrote the same sentiment again with his own hand, as was his custom, 2 Thess. 3:13, 18; 1 Cor. 16:22. Thus also he repeated what he had placed above by the hand of a scribe at the end of chapter 15, here with his own hand.

What was previously inserted through Tertius for the sake of a simple wish, that is repeated here for the sake of a diagnostic wish: and was signed by the Apostle's own hand. Both, however, proceeded from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Yet Tertius himself was not infallibly directed by the Holy Spirit, as Kellet and some Papists maintain. See Voetius, p. 1, disp. Select., p. 46.

PART II. DOXOLOGICAL.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, Ἀμήν.

Eadem verba, quæ supra 20. nisi quod ibi abest πάντων. Sed Paulus eandem sententiam rursus scripsit suâ manu, ut moris ipsi erat 2. Thess. III. 13. 18. 1. Cor. XVI. 22. Sic & quæ suprà posuerat manu scribæ fine cap. XV. repetiit hic suâ manu.

Quod prius voti simplicis causâ per Tertium insertum, id hîc voti diagnosticiergo repetitum : manuque propria Apostoli consignatum fuit. Utrumque autem ex inspiratione S. S. profectum. Non tamen Tertius ipse à S.S. infallibiliter directus fuit, quod Kelletus & Pontificii nonnulli volunt. Vid. Voetius p. 1. disp. Select. p. 46.
