PARS II. Δ Ο Ξ Ο Λ Ο Γ Ι Κ Η.

## 16:25
Vers. 25. τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑμᾶς στηρίξαι.

Paul often attributes this 'to establish' to God, as 1 Thess. 3:13, 2 Thess. 2:17, 3:3, 1 Pet. 5:10. Elsewhere he uses the same word regarding men, in their own degree and order, of course. What men do with words and examples, God does with His Spirit. This is הצליך את־דרך Deut. 25:11, 29.

κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν με. In that doctrine which I teach.

κὶ τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ. The discourse grows, indeed in that which Christ himself preached: for we showed in the Prolegomena to Matthew that 'gospel' and 'preaching' are the same.

ON confirmation in the faith according to the norm of the Gospel here set forth by Paul to the Romans, and of the proclamation of Jesus Christ himself, not that God can only, or of bare power without actual ἐνεργείᾳ, but that he also wills, or concerning the grace of God itself also, he renders the converted faithful certain, because he already glorifies God for their sake. Conf. 1. Corinth. I. 8. 9. 1. Pet. V. 10. 11. Furthermore, this δοξολογία or glorification, which follows, was erased by Marcion, who, as Origen reports, amputated the last two chapters, and thus admitted this Epistle truncated. Certain codices are said to have had this glorification at the end of chapter 14, where Chrysostom places it, as Coccejus has it in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 25. τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑμᾶς στηρίξαι.

Hoc στηρίξαι Deo sæpè tribuit Paulus, ut 1. Thess. III. 13. 2. Thess. II. 17. III. 3. 1. Petr. V. 10. Alibi de hominibus idem verbum usurpat, in suo scilicet gradu atque ordine. Quod homines faciunt verbis, & exemplis, id Deus facit suo Spiritu. Hoc est הצליך את־דרך Deut. XXV. 11. 29.

κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν με. In ea doctrina, quam ego doceo.

κὶ τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ. Crescit oratio, imò in ea, quam prædicavit ipse Christus : nam ἐυαγγέλιον & κήρυγμα idem esse ostendimus in Prolegomenis ad Matthæum.

DE confirmatione in fide juxta normam Evangelii à Paulo hîc Romanis expositi, & præconii ipsius Jesu Christi, non quòd possit tantùm Deus, vel de nuda potentia sine actuali ἐνεργείᾳ, sed quòd etiam velit, seu de ipsa quoque gratia Dei certos reddit fideles conversos, quia Deum jam glorificat ipsorum causa. Conf. 1. Corinth. I. 8. 9. 1. Pet. V. 10. 11. Cæterum δοξολογία hæc sive glorificatio, quæ sequitur, à Marcione erasa fuit, qui, ut refert Origenes, duo postrema capita amputavit, atque ita truncatam hanc Epistolam admisit. Quidam codices dicuntur hanc glorificationem habuisse in fine cap. 14. ubi eam Chrysostomus collocat, ut ha- bet Coccejus h. l.

## 16:26
Verse 26. according to the revelation of the mystery which was kept secret in eternal times, but now is made manifest. That it is not about the calling of the Gentiles alone, but about the whole doctrine of Christ, he will easily believe who has considered the passages Eph. 1.9, 6.19, Col. 1.26, where there are many of the same words as in this place. Likewise 2.2, 1 Pet. 1.10. The Prophets said something about it, as will follow now, but that very thing was never understood except from the event. eternal times, that is, a very long time, as 2 Tim. 1.9; it is the same as hidden from the ages, Col. 1.26, Eph. 3.9, to other generations 16.5. See Is. 42.9, 16.

by the prophetic scriptures according to the commandment of the eternal God made known to all nations for the obedience of faith. Here of the eternal God is put in place of His pronoun. To all nations, that is, among very many nations, that doctrine was made manifest, that is, proved, through the prophetic scriptures, the event, of course, corresponding to the prophecies. See above 1.5, 15.18.

We admit that the mystery concerning Christ is to be understood holistically, not partially only concerning the calling of the Gentiles: but in what sense it is to be accepted that it was silent for a very long time: namely, not by reason of the object; because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13.8, and that Lamb of God slain from the very foundation of the world, Rev. 13.8, but by reason of the circumstances and the mode, and also by reason of a distinct, special, and more manifest proposition; because many things were obscured by the wrappings of words and types, which were made open by the fulfillment: for what was promised concerning Christ through the Prophets, that was finally proven and illustrated by the event in the fullness of time. Grotius himself acknowledges that the Prophets said something about it: but who will admit that it was never understood in the time of the Old Testament? Did the Prophets not understand what they predicted? Which paradox, as Epiphanius testifies in heresy 48, and Jerome, in Eph. 3.5, was that the Prophets spoke in ecstasy and did not know what they were saying, or if they understood it, did they keep it to themselves and not propose it to the people of the Lord? Did they not explain the mind of the Lord themselves? Is it to be believed that the Patriarchs and Abraham himself, the Father of believers, that David, confirmed concerning the Messiah of the God of Jacob, that Isaiah, that Evangelist of the Old Testament as he is called by Jerome, that Daniel, the most enlightened Prophet, the man of the desires of God, did not understand what was revealed to them concerning Christ, but like the ass of Balaam uttered bare sounds without mind and intelligence concerning these things, or that they concealed and kept silent about these things to their own house or to the people of the Lord? Since the Fathers were saved by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ just as we are, Acts 15.11, and there is no other name under heaven in which it is NECESSARY to be saved, Acts 4.12, nor any other way of obtaining salvation than through faith in Christ, which is nothing without the knowledge of Christ and the mysteries concerning Christ; how did the ancients obtain salvation if they were ignorant of these things? Paul testifies that the Scriptures of the Old Testament are able to make one wise unto salvation through faith in Christ, 2 Tim. 3.15, and Peter teaches that all the Prophets bear witness concerning Christ, that all who believe in him receive remission of sins in the name of Jesus, Acts 10.43. And what did St. Paul do more in this Epistle than to construct this mystery of justification through faith in Christ from the Scriptures of the Old Testament? Made manifest, that is, proven, says Grotius, is that doctrine through the prophetic Scriptures. If it is proven by them, it must be contained in them: for either those testimonies were adduced according to the mind of the Prophets, or contrary to it: if the latter, proof could not be sought from them. If the former, it must be that the mind of the Prophets concerning them was the same as that of the Apostles. The escape, which Grotius might perhaps bring forward as usual concerning a mystical sense finally made manifest by the Apostles, has already been refuted often: nor could proof be sought from such a newly delivered mystical sense against those who contradict, without a manifest begging of the question. Therefore, the same doctrine concerning Christ, as to its substance, was proposed in the Old Testament: but that Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of Mary, is the promised Messiah, that was not known except in the fullness of time: this mystery was to be reserved for the New Testament: at the beginning of which John the Proto-Baptist testified concerning him: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, John 1.29; the Apostles testified, the Angels testified, Christ himself testified, indeed those three witnesses in heaven testified, 1 John 5.7. The whole New Testament is occupied in explaining this doctrine more fully and illustrating it more clearly; and thus far that mystery was hidden in ancient times, because it was not so fully delivered, nor so plainly proposed: therefore it is said to be made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures among the nations, with the Apostolic explanation, of course, being added: by which not only proof, but also illustration of the mystery, and a fuller elucidation is designated, in that part and in that manner in which it was hidden or silent.

Concerning which Coccejus not inaptly says on Psalm 78.2: The doctrine concerning Christ was in the Old Testament a riddle, a more obscure speech, not only not known to carnal men, but also not sufficiently perceived by the wise; but in the New it is an interpretation, an explanation, an exegesis, John 1.18. Even children in Christ know where all things tend, which were said and instituted and done in the Old Testament with such effort, such apparatus, in so many ways, and in so many parts. And in this place Coccejus has it thus: But it is said to be silent in secular times, namely until the manifestation. Not that nothing was said about it, but that it was not proclaimed. For the announcement of God concerning Christ the Son is promised, Rom. 1.2, and the mystery is notified through the prophetic Scriptures, here verse 26. None of the Fathers saw and heard what we have seen and heard, Matt. 13.16, 17. 1. 1 Pet. I. 10. 11. 12. that it might be said to the cities of Judah: Behold your God, Is. XL. 9. For the thing itself did not exist: that Jerusalem could be called the Throne of Jehovah, Jer. III. 17. or that the glory of God might be revealed to all flesh, Is. XL. 5. or that they might see eye to eye, Jehovah bringing back Jerusalem, Is. LII. 8. or that it might be proclaimed: Thy God has become King, Is. LII. 7. such as are many things foretold of old to be proclaimed, but which were not proclaimed at that time. Besides the fact that nothing was said before to the Gentiles concerning that ἐπιφανείᾳ Θεῦ; which therefore had need of a new ἀποκαλύψει revelation, Luke II. 32. Whence the Apostle says here, made known to the Gentiles. Finally, not all parts of that mystery were so indicated, that there was not something in the very image of things beyond the hope and expectation of men, Is. LXIV. 3. 1 Cor. II. 9. See also Eph. III. 3. 5. 6. compared with Acts XV. 7. 8. 9. The mystery of salvation, which is of godliness (because godliness is born from the knowledge of it, Tit. I. 1. 1 Tim. VI.) is made manifest in the exhibition of Christ himself and the announcement of those things which he himself did, said, and suffered, and likewise in the proclamation of his kingdom and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. And furthermore: The mystery is not only made manifest in the thing itself, but also made known to the Gentiles. Therefore there is no need for notification any longer. But it has been made known through the Prophetic Scriptures. It is not only manifest in the thing itself, but also furthermore made known, both to those who saw, and to those who did not see the thing itself, so that every scandal of humility and the cross may be removed, and the truth and wisdom of the mystery may be clear even to children, and make them wise. Finally, he gathers into a summary, concerning which things must be kept in mystery: A mystery is a truth which is not known and manifest by itself, but is revealed through the word and Spirit of God. It was first revealed through promise and Prophecy. Then it was made manifest, when the image of things was seen. Then it was known, notified, and preached as good news, and to the nations. Before it was hidden, because it was not seen in the things themselves; and kept silent, because no one said that they had seen those things. Cocceius says these things learnedly. For the sake of opponents, let those things be compared with what we said in the last Oracle of the Roman Apostolic Theology. Briefly: A mystery is called silent 1. by reason of the origin of knowledge, because it was hidden from nature. 2. by reason of fulfillment, because what was promised in the Old Testament was fulfilled in the New: whence the Gospel does not derogate from the Old Testament, it only teaches that it was promised there c. I. 2. which he had promised before through his Prophets in the Holy Scriptures. Some of the ancients not unaptly called the Old Testament the promised Gospel, the New the fulfilled law. 3. by reason of revelation, because it was not so clearly and plainly revealed in the Old Testament as in the New. 4. by reason of promulgation; because it was not made open among the nations; but the promulgation and opening among the nations was reserved for the times of the Messiah. In which way Jerome in this place says the mystery had been silent for eternal times, not among those who promised that it would be, but among all the nations to whom it was afterwards made manifest.

Latin:

Vers. 26. κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσι- γημένου, φανερωθέντος δὲ νῦν. Non de sola vocatione gentium, sed de tota Christi do- ctrina agi facilè credet, qui consideraverit loca Eph. I. 9. VI. 19. Coloss. I. 26. ubi multa verba eadem, quæ hoc lo- co. Ibidem II. 2. 1. Petr. I. 10. Aliquid dixerunt de eo Prophetæ, ut jam sequetur, sed id ipsum nunquam intelle- ctum est, nisi ex eventu. χρόνοις αἰωνίοις, id est, longissimo tempore, ut 2. Tim. I. 9. idem est ἀποκεκρυμμένου ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων. Coloss. I, 26. Eph. III. 9. γενεαῖς ἑτέραις 16. 5. Vide Es. XLII. 9. 16.

διά τε γραφῶν προφητικῶν κατ' ἐπιταγὴν τοῦ αἰωνίου Θεοῦ εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη γνωρισθέντος. Hic τῦ αἰωνίο Θεῦ positum est vice pronominis ejus. In omnes gentes, id est, apud plurimas gentes, patefacta, id est, probata est illa doctrina per Scripturas propheticas, eventu nimirum ad vaticinia respondente. Vide supra I. 5. XV. 18.

Mysterium de Christo, ὁλικῶς, non μερικῶς so- lum de vocatione gentium intelligi,admittimus: sed id tacitum fuisse longissimo tempore, secundum quid accipiendum: sc, non ratione objecti; quia Je- sus Christus heri, hodie idem & in secula Ebr. XIII. 8. & agnus ille Dei occisus ab ipsa mundi origine Apo- cal. XIII. 8. sed ratione circumstantiarum & modi, nec non ratione distincta, specialis, & manifestio- ris propositionis; quia verborum & typorum involucris multa erant obscurata, quæ aperta facta sunt à complemento: quod enim de Christo pro- missum per Prophetas, id in temporum plenitudi- ne demum ab eventu comprobatum & illustratum est. Aliquid dixisse de eo Prophetas agnoscit Gro- tius ipse: id autem nunquam intellectum fuisse tempore Vet. Test. ecquis admittet? Num non intellexerunt Prophetæ, quod prædixerunt? Quod paradoxon Montani teste Epiph. hær. XLVIII. & Hieronym. in Eph. III. 5. fuit, Prophetas in ecstasi loquutos, quid dicerent, nescivisse, aut si intellexe- runt id, num sibi retinuerunt, non proposuerunt populo Domini? non explicarunt ipsi mentem Domini? An credendum, quòd Patriarchæ & Abraham ipse Pater credentium, quod David confirmatus de Messia Dei Jacob, quòd Esaias Evan- gelista ille Veteris Testam. ut ab Hieronymo vocatur, quòd Daniel Propheta illuminatissimus, vir deside- riorum Dei non intellexerint, quæ de Christo ipsis revelata, sed instar asinæ Bileami sonos nudos sine mente & intelligentia de hisce ediderint, aut quòd illæ suæ domui vel populo Domini ista dissimula- rint & reticuerint. Quum gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi æquè Patres, uti nos, salvati sint, Actor. XV. 11. nec aliud sub cælo nomen sit, in quo salvari OPORTEAT, Act. IV. 12. neque ratio alia consequendi salutem, quàm per fidem in Christum, quæ sine notitia Christi & mysteriorum de Christo nulla est; quomodo salutem adepti sunt veteres, si ea ignorarunt? Scripturas certè V. Test. σοφίσαι in- stituere, sapientes reddere ad salutem per fidem in Christum Paulus testatur 2. Tim. III. 15. & de Chri- sto omnes Prophetas testimonium perhibere, quod in nomine Jesu remissionem peccatorum conse- quantur omnes, qui credunt in eum, Petrus docet Act. X. 43. Et quid magis egit in hac Epistola S. Paulus, quàm ut è Script. V. T. hoc mysterium de justificatione per fidem in Christum adstrue- ret? Patefacta, id est, probata est, inquit Grotius, illa doctrina per Scripturas Propheticas. Si proba- ta per easdem, oportet ut iisdem contineatur: nam aut juxta mentem Prophetarum adducta sunt illa testimonia, aut præter eandem: si hoc, ex illis pro- batio peti non potuit. Si illud, Prophetarum ean- dem mentem de illis fuisse oportet, quæ Aposto- lorum. Effugium, quod de mystico sensu ab Apo- stolis demum patefacto forte pro more Grotius adferre posset, jam sæpius profligatum est: nec è tali mystico sensu noviter tradito, probatio peti poterat adversus ἀντιλέγοντας, citra manifestam petitionem principii. Quapropter eadem doctri- na de Christo, quantum ad substantiam, proposi- ta est in Veteri Testamento: sed Jesum Nazare- num Mariæ Filium esse Messiam promissum, id co- gnitum non fuit, nisi in plenitudine temporum: hoc mysterium Nov. Test. reservandum fuit: sub cujus initium Johannes Proto-Baptista de eo te- status est: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccatum mun- di, Joh. I. 29. testati sunt Apostoli, testati sunt An- geli, testatus est Christus ipse, imò testati tres te- stes illi in cœlo, 1. Joh. V. 7. In doctrina etiam hac uberius explicanda, clarius illustranda occupatur totum Nov. Testam. & hactenus antiquis tempo- ribus mysterium illud absconditum fuit, quod non ita plenè traditum, nec adeò plane propositum sit: ideo dicitur patefactum per Scripturas Propheti- cas inter gentes, accedente sc. Apostolica expli- catione: quà non tantum probatio, sed etiam illu- stratio mysterii, & dilucidatio uberior designatur, eâ in parte & eâ ratione, qua absconditum vel taci- tum id fuit.

De quo non inconcinnè ad Psalm. LXXVIII. 2. Coccejus: Doctrina de Christo erat in Veteri Testa- mento חִידָה sermo obscurior, non tantum carnali- bus hominibus non cognitus, sed etiam sapientibus non satis perspectus; at in Novo est מְלִיצָה ἑρμηνεία, explanatio, ἐξήγησις Joh. I. 18. Etiam pueri in Chri- sto sciunt, quò tendant omnia, quæ in Vet. Test. tanta molimine, tanto apparatu, tot modis, tot partibus di- cta & instituta ac gesta sunt. Et in h. l. Coccejus ita habet: Sed dicitur tacitum temporibus secularibus, nempe usq; ad manifestationẽ. Non, quod nihil de eo dictũ sit, sed quod non sit præconiatum. Promissa enim est annunciatio Dei de Christo Filio Rom. I. 2. & my- sterium per Scripturas Propheticas notificatur, hic v. 26. Nemo Patrum vidit & audivit, quod nos vi- dimus & audivimus, Matth. XIII. 16. 17. 1. Pet. I. 10. 11. 12. ut diceretur civitatibus Judæ: Ecce Deus vester, Es. XL. 9. Res enim ipsa non fuit: ut Hiero- solyma posset dici Solium Jehovæ, Jer. III. 17. aut ut revelaretur gloria Dei omni carni, Es. XL. 5. aut ut viderent oculo in oculum, Jehovah reducente Hierosolymam, Es. LII. 8. aut prædicaretur: Rex factus Deus tuus, Es. LII. 7. qualia plurima sunt prænunciata olim præconianda, sed, qua illo tempore præconiata non sunt. Præterquam quod gentibus de illa ἐπιφανείᾳ Θεῦ nihil antea dictũ est: quæ proin- de nova ἀποκαλύψει revelatione opus habuerunt, Luc. II. 32. Unde Apostolus hic dicit, in gentes noti- ficati. Denique non omnes illius mysterii partes ita fuerunt indicatæ, ut non aliquid in ipsa imagine re- rum supra spem & exspectationem hominum esset, Es. LXIV. 3. 1. Cor. II. 9. Vide & Eph. III. 3. 5. 6. col- lato Act. XV. 7. 8. 9. Mysterium salutis, quod est pie- tatis (quia ex ejus cognitione nascitur pietas, Tit. I. 1. 1. Tim. VI.) est manifestum factum in Christi ipsius exhibitione & annunciatione illorum, qua ipse fecit, dixit, passus est, itemque in præconio regni ejus & ef- fusionis Spiritus Sancti. Et porrò: Mysterium non est tantum manifestum factum in re, sed & notifica- tum gentibus. Nulla igitur opus est notificatione amplius. Notificatum verò est per Scripturas Propheticas. Non tantum in re ipsa est manifestum, sed & porro notificatum, tum illis, qui viderunt, tum qui non viderunt rem ipsam, ut tollatur omne scandalum humilitatis & crucis, & veritas ac sa- pientia mysterii etiam pueris liqueat, eosque sapien- tes faciat. Tandem in summam colligit, qua de mysterio retinenda sunt: Μυστήριον est veritas, quæ non per se nota est & manifesta, sed ἀποκαλύπτε]ται per verbum & Spiritum Dei. Id per promissionem & Prophetiam primò revelatum est. Deinde ἐφανερώθη, quando imago rerum visa est. Tunc ἐγνώσθη notificatum est & εὐηγγελίσθη, & gentibus. Antea fuit ἀποκεκρυμμένον occultatum, quia non visum in rebus ipsis; & σεσιγημένον tacitum, quia nemo dixit, se res eas vidisse. Hæc eruditè Coccejus. Quibus propter adversarios conferantur, quæ in Theol. Apost. Roman. diximus Orac. ultimo. Breviter: Tacitum dicitur mysterium 1. ratione originis cognitionis, quia naturæ absconditum. 2. ratione impletionis, quia in Vet. Test. promissum fuit, quod in N. Test. impletum est: unde Evangelium non derogat Veteri Testam. promissum ibi tantum fuisse docet c. I. 2. ὃ προεπηγγείλατο, quod ante promiserat per Prophetas suos in Scripturis S. Veteres quidam non inconcinnè Vetus Testamentum dixere Evangelium promissum, Novum legem impletam. 3. ratione revelationis, quod non tam clarè & planè revelatum in Vet. Test. atque in Novo. 4. ratione promulgationis; quòd non inter gentes patefactum; sed promulgatio ac patefactio inter gentes temporibus Messiæ reservata sit. Quo pacto Hieronymus in h. l. æternis temporibus tacitum fuisse dicit mysterium non apud eos, qui illud futurum pollicebantur, sed apud universas gentes, quibus postea manifestatum est.

## 16:27
Ver. 27. To the only wise God.

Thus he explains that which had been said above, to him who is able. God is called the only wise both here and 1 Tim. I. 17, because he alone is the author of all wisdom, just as he is also said to have immortality alone 1 Tim. VI. 16.

through Jesus Christ to whom be glory for ever.

The added article has the same value as ages of ages, that is, for ever, without end: just as thanksgiving above VII. 24, joy v. 11, so also the doxology is directed through Jesus, as the way to the Father.

God is described and celebrated both by his power and by his wisdom, because both shone forth remarkably in the mystery concerning Christ 1 Cor. I. 24. But while God alone is called wise, either the name God can be understood essentially with Augustine lib. III. against Maxim. Arian. c. 13, because honor is to be deferred to the triune God in Christ the mediator, 1 Tim. II. 5, who is distinguished from God not by reason of essence, but of office: or if God the Father is understood, he is called the only wise, not to exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit who are one with the Father, 1 John V. 7, inasmuch as the Son is the hypostatic Wisdom of God, Prov. VIII. Luke XI. 49. Conf. Matt. XXIII. 34. and the Spirit is the Spirit

Sic explicat id, quod suprà dictum erat τῷ δυναμένῳ. Deus solus sapiens dicitur & hic & 1. Tim. I. 17. quia solus auctor est omnis sapientiæ, sic & solus immortalitatem habere dicitur 1. Tim. VI. 16.

Describitur & celebratur Deus tum à potentia, tum à sapientia, quia utraque in mysterio de Christo illuxit insigniter 1. Cor. I. 24. # 1 Corinthians

## 1:1 Introduction

YEAR TO THE FORMER TO THE EPISTLE

Latin:

ANNO AD PRIOREM AD EPIST

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
GROTIAN PREFACE.

CORINTH, looking out from the narrow border of Achaia on one side to the Ionian Sea, on the other to the Aegean, having acquired great wealth from trade, so that for this reason it is called by Homer wealthy, and by Pindar blessed Corinth, the gateway of Isthmian Poseidon, glorious in youth, arrived from its riches at such luxury that the proverb was born from it: The voyage to Corinth is not for every man. The Corinthians always indulged themselves greatly in harlots, considering it so little a disgrace that harlots were employed in public prayers, and it was in those prayers that they might increase

Wisdom Eph. XI. 1. but to exclude all those who are outside of God, according to the rule of Holy Antiquity: When there is discourse about a thing which belongs to some divine person according to essence, and not according to origin, other divine persons who are of the same divine essence are not excluded, but included. And God is to be glorified through Christ, as the only wise, who made Christ wisdom for us, so that we might glory in God alone, 1 Cor. I. 30, 31. Jer. IX. 24. XVII. 14. Is. XLV. 24. The Father in the Son made a most wise plan concerning our redemption, justification, and glorification; and we have all those things in Christ, and through Christ; therefore glory is owed to the Father in Christ, and through Christ. The Father alone is called wise; because in the Son he does all things wisely through his Spirit. And that in opposition to creatures, Angels no less than men 1 Pet. I. 12. Eph. III. 10. But God is to be glorified through Jesus Christ. And therefore by glorifying Jesus Christ, we glorify God. Which would not be true, if Christ were not one with God: who protests that he will not give his glory to another outside of himself, Is. XLII. 8. whence by glorifying another, God is not glorified, and by glorying in another, we do not glory in God: and God neither wishes, nor can he be glorified, except through Christ, John V. 22, 23. But the article to whom should trouble no one, which indeed is not to be passed over, or expunged with Beza and Grotius: since the Codices agree in it: yet it is rightly judged by B. Glassius in Sacred Grammar p. 206 to be redundant, as in Rev. II. 13. Ludovicus de Dieu in Matt. XXVI. 50. He says that the relative pronoun is used for the demonstrative ἀὐτῷ: thus the sense will be: To him, who is able to establish you, to the only, I say, wise God, through Jesus Christ, to him be glory; so that the pronoun may be referred to God, and it may be indicated that the powerful and only wise God is to be glorified in no other way than through Christ, in whom the Apostle taught that we uniquely have righteousness and blessedness.

πρὸς ῥωμαίυς ἐγράφη. Those annotations, which are accustomed to be attached to the Pauline Epistles, are of no authority, because they do not appear in all copies, and they are different in different ones, and they differ both in the Syriac and Arabic versions. However, I believe that what is said here is true, not because of that annotation, but because the same thing is gathered from the epistle. See what we have said in the Prolegomena to this Epistle.

We agree here with Grotius: and repeating the Apostolic δοξολογίαν for the grace granted to us even in this work of whatever kind, in the name of Jesus; we thus finish this golden Epistle: To the only wise God through Jesus Christ, to him, I say, be glory forever, Amen!

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

CORINTHUS ex angusto Achaiæ limite hinc Ionium, inde Ægæum prospectans mare, ex commerciis magnas adepta divitias, ita ut Homero ob id dicatur ἀφνειὸς, Pindaro verò ὄλβια Κόρινθος, ἰσθμίου πρόθυρον Ποσειδῶνος ἀγλαόκουρον, ex divitiis ad tantum pervenit luxum, ut inde natum sit proverbium: οὐ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς εἰς Κόρινθον ἐσθ' ὁ πλοῦς. Scortis verò plurimum semper indulsere Corinthii, adeo id non turpe habentes, ut publicis precationibus adhiberentur meretrices, essetque in iis precationibus, ut augerent

Sapientia Ef. XI. 1. sed ad excludendum eos omnes, qui extra Deum sunt, juxta S. Antiquitat. regu- lam: Cum sermo est de re, quæ alicui personæ divinæ secundam essentiam, & non secundum originem con- venit, non excluduntur, sed includuntur aliæ personæ divinæ, quæ sunt ejusdem essentiæ divinæ. Et glori- ficandus per Christum est Deus, ut solus sapiens, qui fecit Christum nobis sapientiam, ut ita glorie- mur in solo Deo, 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. Jerem. IX. 24. XVII. 14. Es. XLV. 24. Pater in Filio fecit sapien- tissimum consilium de redemptione, justificatio- ne & glorificatione nostra; & omnia illa habemus in Christo, & per Christum; ideò Patri gloria debe- tur in Christo, & per Christum. Solus Pater dicitur sapiens; quia in Filio facit omnia sapienter per Spi- ritum suum. Idque in oppositione creaturarum, Angelorum non minùs quam hominum 1. Pet. I. 12. Eph. III. 10. Deus autem glorificandus est per Je- sum Christum. Ideoque glorificando Jesum Chri- stum, glorificamus Deum. Quod non esset ve- rum, si Christus non esset unum cum Deo: qui protestatur, alteri extra se non daturum se gloriam suam, Es. XLII. 8. unde glorificando alium non glorificatur Deus, & gloriantes in alio, non glo- riamur in Deo: & nec vult, nec potest Deus glo- rificari, nisi per Christum, Joh. V. 22. 23. Nemi- nem autem turbare debet articulus ὧ́, qui quidem non prætermittendus est, aut expungendus cum Beza & Grotio: quum in eo consonent Codices: redundare tamen rectè censetur à B. Glassio Gram- mat. S. p. 206. uti Apoc. II. 13. Ludovicus de Dieu in Matth. XXVI. 50. Pronomen relativum poni ait, pro demonstrativo ἀὐτῷ: ita sensus erit: Illi, qui potest vos confirmare, soli, inquam, sapienti Deo, per Jesum Christum, ipsi sit gloria; ut pronomen ad Deum referatur, nec aliter, quam per Christum, in quo unicè nos habere justitiam & beatitudinem docuit Apostolus, glorificandum esse potentem illum & solum sapientem Deum indicetur.

πρὸς ῥωμαίυς ἐγράφη. Annotationes istæ, quæ Paulinis Epistolis adjungi solent, nullius sunt auctoritatis, quia nec in omnibus exemplaribus apparent, & aliis sunt alia, discrepantque & in Syriacis & A- rabicis. Hoc tamen, quod hic dicitur, verum esse credo, non ob istam annotationem, sed quia ex epistola idem col- ligitur. Vide, quæ diximus in Prolegomenis ad hanc Epi- stolam.

Annuimus hic Grotio: & Apostolicam δοξολο- γίαν ob gratiam, etiam in hac qualicunque opera nobis præstitam, repetentes, in nomine Jesu; au- ream hanc Epistolam ita finimus: Soli sapienti Deo per Jesum Christum, ipsi, inquam, sit gloria in secula, Amen!

## 1:1 Introduction: Notes by J. On the Epistle to the Corinthians
NOTES BY J. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

gods the number and profit of harlots, some even vowed that they would bring new harlots, which we are taught from Athenaeus and Aelian. There Lais exacted tribute from all of Greece for her lust, indicating the price of her use as ten thousand drachmas, and when she died she had a tomb celebrated by the verses of all the poets. And hence Κορινθιάζεσθαι is commonly used by the Greeks for to fornicate, and Κορινθία κόρη for Plato is one who prostitutes herself. And Suidas mentions the proverb, ἀκροκορινθία ἔοικας χωροπολίσειν. And he adds ἀντὶ τῦ μοιχαρνήσειν ἐν Κορίνθῳ. πολλαὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖ ἑταῖραι. The Scholiast of Nazianzen on the first [invective] against Julian notes that there were always most famous harlots at Corinth. He also says the Corinthians were drunkards. Riches are also accustomed to be accompanied by pride, which Plutarch notes was extraordinary in the Corinthians: it was on their lips: 'The Corinth of Zeus will not be opened.' When this pride had inflated them even to the point of contempt for the Roman name, it brought about their destruction, with Mummius as victor: but the city having been restored by Julius Caesar; as Strabo notes, and Diodorus Siculus in his fragments, those vices returned just as briefly as their opulence did. Studies of philosophy flourished there from ancient times, with Periander, the prince of that city, being numbered among the seven wise men of Greece, and Diogenes, a mocker of the opinions received among men, having spent much time there. How much time and labor the Apostle Paul spent to bring Christianity there, we learn from the Acts. But just as it was easy among ingenious men to overturn the fictitious gods of the Greeks, of whom Venus was the chief at Corinth: so ingrained vices did not yield so easily to a better discipline. And so, just as from other nations, it could with difficulty be obtained from the Corinthians that they should consider fornication a forbidden thing: the opinion of Diogenes was that even the so-called incestuous unions had nothing evil in them; indeed, even those of the Stoics and of Epicurus, as we learn from Sextus the Philosopher, Theophilus of Antioch in book 3, and others. This also clung to them. The Platonists did not believe that bodies would rise again, who judged that bodies were given to souls as a punishment: nor indeed did the Epicureans or the Peripatetics, who taught that there was no care for human affairs by God: the former more openly, the latter indeed in their esoteric discourses. Arrogance, however, was the reason why each preferred to form factions in the Church rather than concede the leadership to another. That these things are so, you may know not only from these epistles of Paul, but also from that which was written some time later by Clement to the same Corinthians. For everywhere he accuses them of arrogance, self-will, boldness, pride, zeal, strife, and contentiousness: whence he says it happened that neither the presbyters nor their leaders were spared, schisms were born, and from there, seditions. He warns, moreover, that they should seriously flee impure and unholy unions, drunkenness, abominable desires, and foul adultery. Clement defends the dogma of the resurrection in many ways in that Epistle. Paul, therefore, having been informed by friends that there were indeed some among those Christians of Corinth who were truly pious, but that there were also others still imbued with philosophical opinions and pride and vices, tempers his speech in such a way that he now applies comforts and praises, now free rebukes, so that each one, according to his own conscience, might apply these or those to himself: just as the Holy Spirit also acts in the Apocalypse with the Church of the Sardians.

OBSERVATIONS ON GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

CORINTH, formerly called Ephyra and Heliopolis, today under the Turkish yoke called Corinda and Hexamiliam, was once the most splendid and noble city of Achaia, which is now Morea, called the city of two seas, the key to the whole Peloponnese, the light and ornament of Greece, as Cicero testifies in his speech for the Manilian Law. Therefore, in such an abundance of wealth and plenty of all things, it is not surprising that pride, gluttony, and filthiness ran rampant, not only among those who, devoid of the true God, served their idols and demigods, but even among the converted themselves, and that the Evangelical doctrine, which the Apostle had scattered there for a year and a half at the warning of God, having converted two leaders of the Jewish synagogue, Crispus and Sosthenes, and others from the Jews and Gentiles, did not remain uncorrupted. For, as Theognis says:

Satiety indeed begets pride, when wealth follows the wicked. Abundance brings arrogance when abundance grows for the wicked.

But when the Apostle, taught by divine oracle and experience that the Lord has a large people in that city, Acts 18:19-20, wished to prepare a remedy for the scandals of doctrine and morals that had arisen there after his departure, about which he had learned through the family of Chloe, he wrote this Epistle to the faithful and saints in that city at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. He does not, however, only refute heterodox opinions about the resurrection and the pride of the Corinthians, but he also inculcates the Evangelical doctrine concerning Christ, and him crucified, through whom salvation was obtained, and he rebukes certain public scandals, such as schisms in the Church, contentions before courts, incest and fornication, the abuse of liberty regarding indifferent matters, concerning celibacy and marriage, concerning the use of things sacrificed to idols, concerning the stipends of the ministers of the Word, concerning the administration of the Holy Supper, and he provides necessary information concerning the difference of gifts; finally, he reproves the neglect of charity. He sets forth at length that the resurrection of the dead was rendered doubtful not so much by the Platonists, Stoics, or Peripatetics, as by the principles of false apostles who were already dreaming that the resurrection had taken place, and by heretical corruptions, and he explains what it will be like. It is evident, therefore, that Grotius touched upon almost only secondary matters, and did not sufficiently observe the primary scope of the Apostolic information and the occasion given to the Apostle, which was twofold, both through the family of Chloe and through the Epistle of the Corinthians: since he exhorts them to concord because of the schisms that had arisen in the Corinthian Church, in such a way that he desires the foundation, which is Christ Jesus, to be kept intact above all: concerning which Blessed Luther warned in his German preface: In this Epistle, he says, St. Paul exhorts the Corinthians to be concordant in faith and doctrine, and to strive above all to diligently learn the principal head of doctrine (namely, that Christ is our salvation), by which indeed all human reason and wisdom is offended. For there had arisen there fanatical and untimely sciolists, tearing apart the consensus of doctrine and stirring up schisms among the believers. One wanted to be of Paul, another of Apollos, another of Peter, another of Christ. One wanted circumcision, another did not. One approved of marriage, another disapproved. One wanted to eat food sacrificed to idols, another did not. Some wanted to be carnally free. Certain little women walked about with bare heads without a veil, and there were very many things of this kind. Until they slipped so far that one of them abused his liberty and took his stepmother as his wife. Some made the resurrection of the dead of absolutely no account, others made the Sacraments of very little account. In sum, there was great confusion, nor was there any order; each one snatched for himself the office of master and teacher, and wanted to act according to his own will with the Gospel, the Sacraments, and the faith. And meanwhile they lazily neglected the principal head, which is that Christ is our salvation, righteousness, and redemption, as if they had long since trampled it under their heels. Therefore, in this place Saint Paul severely censures and condemns this perverse wisdom, and shows these sharp-nosed saints their own foolishness. He says simply that they know nothing about Christ, nor about the Spirit and the gifts of God given to us in Christ: that they still ought to learn, that it is necessary to be spiritual men who wish to understand these things. To be wise and to show off prudence in the Gospel is the truest and greatest scandal and impediment to knowing Christ and God. Our wisdom and intelligence can do something to stir up sects and dissensions, so that all become foolish saints and wild Christians: but they will never be able to know Christ unless they become foolish again, and allow themselves to be humbly instructed and led by the simple word of God. And indeed he inculcates these things in the first four chapters. In the fifth chapter he reproves that abominable incest. In the sixth he censures disputes and lawsuits before the court. In the seventh he delivers precepts concerning chastity and married life. From the eighth to the twelfth he deals with various matters. In the twelfth and thirteenth he treats of how varied the gifts of God are. In the fourteenth he teaches pastors, prophets, and singers how to use their gifts rightly. In the fifteenth he censures those who had wrongly taught and believed concerning the resurrection of the dead. In the sixteenth and last he exhorts them to the brotherly collection of alms, by which the poor and needy are sustained. And thus says B. Luther.

Something must also be said about the Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians: to which Grotius attributes so much that he frequently compares it with this Epistle of St. Paul. Patrick Young, Librarian to the King of Great Britain, published it at Oxford in the year 1632 from, as he says, torn membranes, just as it had been added to the Codex of the books of the Old and New Testament received from Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople, which he says was written out by the hand of Thecla, a noble Egyptian woman, around the times of the first Council: which that same Young not only hawks as genuine and undoubted, nay, as a divine and clearly Apostolic writing, but Grotius also, in his letters to the French, no. CLXII, to Jerome Bignon, judged it to be the same one that Photius read, the same that Jerome read, and before him Clement of Alexandria, the same that Irenaeus had closer to the times of Clement of Rome, and of which Clement of Rome himself was the author; but using less sufficient, less suitable arguments: for whose genuineness a certain Joachim Johannes Mader, Rector of a School, having published it again at Helmstadt, contended not without attacking the name of Hülsemann, yet with no greater success than Young or Grotius, in favor of his Calixtus and Hornejus. For the fact that he says not only that all the passages which are cited by the ancients appear here, but also the very things which Photius observes, has no power of proof, since it is not new that such things are found even in writings that are undoubtedly forged, nor does it agree with the truth in every respect. For it does not occur in the same, what Justin Martyr, or any other author of the Responses to the Orthodox, q. LXXV, reports from that Epistle, nor what Basil, ch. XXIX, to Amphilochius, praises as said by Clement; Conring himself, although he acknowledged boldly enough in letters sent to that Mader that nothing could be produced from all antiquity concerning that genuine Epistle of Clement which might deservedly make one doubt the Junian one: taking refuge in vain at the hiding-place of the loss of four leaves, in which he suspects, though only rashly, that those things of Justin were contained: but he conjectures that Basil perhaps drew his own from other Clementine writings: but what other genuinely Clementine works were praised by antiquity, besides the single Epistle, or the former one to the Corinthians? For he acknowledges that the other, of which Young also published a fragment, even though it was read by Photius, and he thinks it is the one which Eusebius, Jerome, and others mentioned, was wrongly attributed to Clement as author; nay, he expressly confesses that no more than a single Epistle proceeded from Clement, but that all the rest, which pass under the name of the Apostolic Constitutions, or Recognitions, or Epistles, lie about their author, and he affirms that even that single fact is a sufficient argument for him, that St. Irenaeus praises only that one as a testimony of Catholic truth, while he studiously opposes heresies by the consent of the Roman Bishops: how these things can be reconciled with the above Conringian conjecture, I for one do not see.

But what is to be said about the fact that Epiphanius, in heresy XXX against the Ebionites, observed that Clement of Rome extols Samson with praises and teaches virginity in the Epistle which is read in the Holy Churches; or that St. Jerome, book I against Jovinian, noted that Clement of Rome wove almost his entire discourse on the purity of virginity? And that the same man, in ch. IV of the Epistle to the Ephesians, hints that Clement explains the words of the Apostle, Eph. IV. 1, 'I the prisoner in the Lord,' not of material bonds, but of the bond of the love of God: or that Anastasius Sinaita, in the seventh chapter of the Guide, reported that Clement, who is himself called the 'klima,' i.e., the branch of Christ, established some things concerning the two natures in Christ? Or that in the questions attributed to Justin Martyr, in the response to q. 74, certain Sibylline verses are reported to have been found in the Epistle of Clement? which, although Ussher, in the Dissertation prefixed to the Epistles of Polycarp and Ignatius, ch. X, p. 265, refers to the second one inscribed with the same name, which he acknowledges as spurious, are here, in the present edition of the Clementine, referred to the first, among the testimonies of antiquity alleged for its genuineness. For such things are nowhere found in the Clementine Epistle which is hawked as genuine. Is not, therefore, the above pronouncement of Conring clearly convicted of rashness, and is not the genuineness of the Junian Epistle of Clement deservedly called into doubt?

But that argument, which seemed the greatest to Grotius for the same, namely that the character observed by Jerome in the Epistle of Clement approaches that which is in the Epistle to the Hebrews, is most contrary to the same, if one accurately compares the character of the Junian edition with the Epistle of St. Paul to the Hebrews. Eusebius, book III of Ecclesiastical History, ch. 32, says that Clement in his Epistle brings forward many thoughts from the Epistle written to the Hebrews, nay, and that he himself uses certain expressions word for word, and that both Epistles contain a common character of diction, and that they do not differ much from each other in the thoughts themselves. Similarly, Jerome says that the Epistle of Clement not only seems to him to agree in character with the Epistle to the Hebrews, but also that he uses many thoughts from the same, and indeed in the very order of the words; which also Otto of Freising, book III, History, ch. 20, noted, that it is seen to be so similar to Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews that for this reason it is thought by many to be not Paul's, but Clement's; and also Nicephorus, that it uses many sentences from Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews, book III of Ecclesiastical History, ch. 18. But it is a wonder that such a convenience of the character of speech is asserted by modern Critics in this Junian edition: unless it is done by the persuasion of a preconceived opinion and affections. For no one will have shown such and so great a convenience in both Epistles. But the very autopsy refutes that many sentences are found in the same order of words in both: since anyone may discover in this Clementine many passages alleged or indicated from other places of Scripture: whence it is by no means obscure that it is not that Junian Epistle which St. Jerome had in his time, or even the Frisingensis, and Nicephorus, unless perhaps these later ones formed their judgment rather by the faith of Jerome than by their own observation. Some words drawn from Greek writers do not settle the matter: nor do they immediately prove such a great similarity. For the character of the speaking something more is required.

But those signs of non-feigned antiquity, what and how great, I pray, are they, which Grotius observed? First, that this Clement always speaks of Christ, not as later ones πλατωνικώτερον, but singularly plainly, and as the Apostle Paul is accustomed. But who in the time immediately following spoke of Christ πλατωνικώτερον, unless they perhaps disputed κατʼ ἄνθρωπον, ought to have been taught. That was rather desired in the Clementine already in the time of Photius, that he never called Christ God with Paul and other Apostles, in Biblioth. sect. CXXVI. because namely, as that ancient critic speaks, calling our Lord Jesus Christ the high priest and president, does not utter even any words concerning him that are suitable and more sublime for God, although he does not openly blaspheme him anywhere in this. In which, however, it is manifest from those things which we observed before that Photius's copy does not agree with that of Anastasius Sinaita. Next, that Junianus Clemens treats other dogmas, explained more subtly later, more simply here, and uses the words κλήσεως, κλητῶν, ἐκλεκτῶν in the Pauline sense. But what does this latter point have to do with antiquity, since we use those words in the Pauline sense even in the modern age, and what are those dogmas explained more subtly afterwards? They ought to have been named, not passed over in silence, lest there be need for divination. Thirdly, that in the places of the Old Testament he follows the version of the LXX Elders, which is most pure and not yet interpolated: But that also had to be taught, not just baldly stated. Fourthly, that he does not spurn those books of the Hebrews which had authority among the most ancient of Christians according to the Old Testament. But which are those books; perhaps the Apocrypha of the Old Testament? But they never had greater authority than they now have in the Roman Catholic Church? Or perhaps others; but those were to be named, lest words only be given. Fifthly, that he uses words and things taken from those which Paul, Peter, and others wrote to the Hebrews, not also from the Evangelical books which appeared after the Epistles. But the contrary of this is to be seen on page 22 of Mader's edition: where a passage from Luke 6 is adduced. Whence Conringius also corrected Grotius here, because that great man erred in it. Sixthly, that he uses certain sayings not written, but as handed down by hand with recent memory. But which are those? And how will both the genuineness of the Epistle and its great antiquity be solidly established from that? for even pseudonymous writings appeal to traditions, and those published in the second and third century: but whence is it certain that those were recently handed down? Seventhly, that he nowhere mentions that unique authority of bishops, which began to be introduced elsewhere by the custom of the Church after the death of Mark at Alexandria. But the contrary of this is discovered from page 57, because already at that time a contention about the name of bishop had arisen. And our Apostles (so the Pseudo-Clement has it here) knew through Jesus Christ our Lord that a contention about the name of the episcopate would arise, ὅτι ἔρις ἔςαι ἐπὶ τῶ ὀνόματος τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς. Therefore, this Clementine must be more recent than Grotius believed. He refers the time when this Epistle was written to the end of Nero, or certainly to those years which preceded the reign of Vespasian: since he mentions the offerings which were made in the temple according to the law, just as the writer to the Hebrews does, after whose Epistle he believes this was written. Blondellus, in his Apology for the opinion of Jerome concerning Presbyters and Bishops, section II, page 9, says the Epistle of Clement was given between the years of the Lord 68 and 76, the Princes of the Apostles having long since been received into heaven. But Nero is believed to have lived only a year after the slaughter of the Apostles. Moreover, the reign of Vespasian followed a little later, after about a year had elapsed, in the year of Christ 73, and in the following year the city of Jerusalem was captured. That does not agree with the Junian opinion, according to which, in the annotations to the proemium of this Epistle, this Epistle was not written until Clement was relegated into exile, which is said to have happened two years before he ended his life by martyrdom, namely in the year 1. of Trajan, in the hundredth year of the Lord approximately. But how, when he had already spent so many years in exile, could Clement write to the Corinthians in the person of the Roman Church? But we leave these things to be settled by the supporters of the Patrician Clement. Ussher, too addicted to the superiority of bishops over presbyters, and defending it against Beza, in the additions to the aforementioned Dissertation, asserts that when Clement wrote these things, the names of bishops and presbyters still seemed to be common: but it is evident from the words of Clement adduced that the controversy had already begun then, and bishops had arrogated to themselves a certain superiority; whence it may be gathered that this Epistle cannot be referred to the first century, in which that distinction of bishops and presbyters was not yet born.

Certainly it does not befit the first century and an Apostolic man, such as Clement was, that Domaides and Derce, ethnic women, should be counted among the martyrs, which Patricius tries to excuse as a slip of an unskilled scribe: but Grotius not only says this Epistle is genuine, but also recognizes no traces of an adulterous hand in it. Nor are those absurd allegations and proofs of the Scriptures worthy of such a great man as Clement, a disciple of Peter and Paul, as when it is taught from the History of Cain, Genesis 4:3, that death entered into the world through envy, when it is taught that because of zeal, emulation, and contention, which leads to death, which overturns great cities, from which the fratricide of Cain proceeded, holy men have suffered and endured martyrdoms, and when he confirms that the ministers of divine grace, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke about repentance, and the Lord himself spoke about repentance with an oath from the words of Ezekiel: I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, as that he should repent, this the Pseudo-Clement adds, adding also a good opinion, as if the Lord adds this excellent saying, which is truly found in no Biblical Codex, nor even in that manuscript of Thecla, to which this Epistle was sewn, having been written out by the same hand: Repent, O house of Israel, from your iniquity. Say to the sons of my people, if your sins are from the earth to the heaven, and if they are redder than scarlet, and blacker than sackcloth, and you turn to me from your whole heart, and say Father, I will hear you as a holy people. To which the good Patricius had nothing to say, except that several passages of Scripture are joined together into one, and the sense, not the words, is expressed: but which those passages of Scripture are, he could not indicate, at least he promised that he would compensate for this with greater profit, when he is about to bring to light a new edition of the Greek Bible from the manuscript copy of Thecla, which in his own judgment is by far the best and most ancient of all that are in Europe today, which indeed, as far as I know, has not yet been done within these forty years. Whether he found in that Codex also those words of Moses which are attributed to him on p. 24, ἐγὼ δέ εἰμι ἀτμὺς ἀποχύ- τρας, I am the vapor of a pot; or those of I know not what author, which are read under the name of Scripture on page 33. Ταλαίπωροί εἰσιν οἱ δίψυχοι οἱ δισάζοντες τὴν ψυχὴν οἱ λέγοντες, ταῦτα ἠκέσαμεν κᾀ ἀπὸ τῶν πατέρων ὑ- μῶν, κᾀ ἰδὲ γεγηράκαμεν κᾀ ἐδὲν ἡμῖν τέτων συμβέ- βηκεν, Miserable and unhappy are they who are of a double and inconstant mind, saying: We have heard these things from our parents, and behold we have now grown old, yet none of these things has happened to us; we cannot say; in those which have been published in Europe thus far, such things, whether as to words or as to sense, have ever been found, nor would Patricius himself say so; who could not find those anywhere either, which are cited on page 36 as follows: λέγει γὰρ πᾶ: κᾀ ἐξαναστήσεις με κᾀ ἐξομολο- γήσομαί σοι: For he says somewhere, you will raise me up and I will confess to you, which seem to be attributed to David; for a passage is added from Ps. 3:5, 'And I slept and took rest, I rose up, for you are with me.' And: 'I slept and took rest, I rose up, for you are with me': which truly ἀπροσδιονύσως [incongruously], for the sake of proving the resurrection of the dead, in the very age of the Apostles, would not have been easily adduced by an Apostolic man: such an incongruous allegation for the calling of Christians is had not only from Deut. 4:34, p. 38: but also from diverse, but ἀλλοτρίοις [alien] passages, Deut. 5:35, Num. 8:27, with an addition, by I know not what writer, in a manner altogether unworthy of an Apostolic man, compiled under the title of a passage of Scripture, in this way: 'And in another place he says: Behold the Lord takes to himself a nation from the midst of nations, just as a man takes the firstfruits of his threshing floor, and that holy of holies shall go forth from that nation.' And in another place he says: 'Behold the Lord takes to himself a nation from the midst of nations, just as a man takes the firstfruits of his threshing floor, and that holy of holies shall go forth from that nation.' And where, I pray, is it had in the Scriptures, which this Epistle, p. 60, praised as written in the sacred letters: 'For it is written, cleave to the holy, for those who cleave to them shall be sanctified,' Join yourselves to the holy, because those who adhere to them shall be sanctified. In which Bibles are these, produced from Isaiah ch. 60, read in such a way as Pseudo-Clement reads on p. 54, when he proves that the distinction of Bishops and Deacons is not new, but already founded in the Old Testament: 'And this is not new; for it was written long ago concerning bishops and deacons; for thus the Scripture says: I will appoint their bishops in righteousness; and their deacons in faith.' Nor was this indeed a new institution: for many centuries ago it was written concerning Bishops and deacons; for thus the Scripture says somewhere: 'I will appoint their Bishops in righteousness, and their Deacons in faith.' Too simple was that Pseudo-Clement, in that he was persuaded that the distinct offices of Bishops and Deacons had a foundation here, and had been instituted already in the time of Isaiah. Nor is it worthy of an Apostolic man (whom Clement of Alexandria even calls an Apostle), that those things which were most openly said concerning the first coming of Christ by Malachi ch. 3:1, and which Christ himself interpreted concerning it, Matt. 11, and St. Mark ch. 1, should be snatched away to the second coming of Christ, p. 33: 'In truth, quickly and suddenly his will shall be perfected, the Scripture also bearing witness, that the Lord shall come immediately into his temple, and the Holy One, whom you expect, ὅτι ταχὺ ἥξει ὁ Κύριος εἰς τὸν ναὸν ἀυτᾶ, κὶ ὁ ἅγιος ὃν ὑμεῖς προσδοκᾶτε.' Where also the text of the Prophet is found changed, rendered by the 70 Elders thus: 'Suddenly the Lord shall come into his temple whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant, whom you desire.' Now, to be silent about other allegations made wrongly, which with most of those already adduced are not seen in the fragment cited by Clement of Alexandria, book 4 of the Stromata, as an argument not obscure that this Epistle of Clement of Rome, which Patricius edited, was not the one read by Clement of Alexandria: how will those things concerning the High Priest, the Priests, and the Laity, p. 53, be suitable either to a divine and plainly Apostolic writing, or at least to a writer equal in age to the Apostles and a disciple of the Apostles, which Grotius says in vain are spoken not of the Church, but of the Jerusalem temple: because they openly treat of the worship of the New Testament: for to the High Priest his duties are attributed, to the Priests a proper place is assigned, and to the Levites their ministries are incumbent. The layman is bound by lay precepts: 'Let each one of you, brothers, remaining in his own order and station, give thanks to God with a good conscience, and as is fitting, let him contain himself within the prescribed canon of his ministry,' τῆς λειτουργίας κάνονα. Granted, he may allude to the functions of the Old Testament: yet he implies that such also have a place in the New, and commands each to persist in his own station according to the canon of his λειτουργίας [ministry]. Now he also urges (which is likewise less Apostolic) that the Lord commanded all things to be performed at appointed times, namely to perform offerings and other duties (in the original text it is τῆς τε προσφορᾶς κ͵ λειτουργίας ἐπιτελεῖσθε). But where did the Lord ever wish to bind worship to hours, or enjoin sacrifices and the ministries of the Priesthood in the New Testament? Nay, that pseudo-Clement declares those blessed who observe such canonical hours: 'Nor rashly,' he says, 'or inordinately did he wish these things to be done, but at appointed times and hours, where also and by whom he wishes them to be performed, he himself defined by his most exalted will, so that all things religiously fulfilled according to his good pleasure might be pleasing and acceptable to his will.' Therefore, those who make their offerings at appointed times are acceptable and blessed. For following the Lord's commands they do not err: for to the High Priest his duties are attributed, etc. Thus he explains BY WHOM the Lord wishes offerings to be performed: so that there is no doubt that these pertain to the times of the New Testament. But in what place of the New Testament are such things defined, whether regarding hours and times, or regarding persons, and such distinct duties? In what place of Scripture are either the ministries of the Levites designated in the New Testament, or the status of the Laity, not to speak again of the Priests? And concerning Sacrifices, Pseudo-Clement speaks thus, not otherwise than if they were still approved by God in his age, and when he was writing to the Corinthians in the person of the Roman Church. For he says that those who admit anything in the offering of them beyond that which is agreeable to his will are punished with the penalty of death. Which, moreover, are much less consistent if Clement began to preside over the Roman Episcopate, which Maderus in the preface teaches from Anastasius the Librarian, in the year of the first century from the birth of Christ 93: since Jerusalem was overturned in the year 74. How therefore could Clement, writing in the person of the Roman Church, speak of Sacrifices as if they were still accustomed to be offered at Jerusalem, after the city with the temple had already been overturned for nineteen years?

Furthermore, who will believe that the Junian Epistle was held as a great and wonderful epistle, and read publicly in the Churches, as Eusebius affirms of the Clementine in Hist. Eccl. book III, and Jerome in the same place, which, besides the errors we have mentioned, attributes the remission of sins to our charity, contrary to the Apostolic faith set forth primarily in the divine Epistle to the Romans, and derives that energy of charity entirely against the mind and proof of the holy Apostle in Romans IV, from the Davidic Psalm likewise adduced by Paul for the righteousness of faith imputed without works, and adorns, or rather burdens, charity with undue praises: which can be read at length on pages 61, 63, 64, 65. For concerning the chaste and seemly conversation of brotherly love, he says thus: This, he says, is the gate of righteousness opened to life (citing the passage Ps. 118:19) as it is written: Open to me the gates of righteousness, I will enter into them and confess to the Lord, this is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter into it. He who has charity in Christ, let him keep the commandments of Christ. Who can express in words the bond of the love of God? Who is able to recount as is fitting the mighty works of its beauty? The height to which charity raises us is ineffable. (Does charity, by which we love God, truly raise us to an ineffable height?) Charity glues us to God, Charity covers a multitude of sins (this concerning charity Paul indeed teaches of God's grace toward us, but not of our charity toward God, which, to wit, sustains all things, which patiently tolerates all things, does all things in harmony, etc. (as that Clement continues,) in Charity all the elect of GOD have been made perfect, without charity nothing is acceptable to GOD, (but Holy Scripture neither makes them perfect in charity here, nor, when we emerge perfect in the other life, does it attribute it to our charity, but to divine grace. And therefore that also cannot be proven, which is further added) all generations from Adam even to this day have passed away, but those who through the grace of GOD have been perfected in charity οἱ ἐν ἀγάπῃ τελειωθέντες, obtain the place (region) of the pious, & will be manifested in the visitation of the kingdom of Christ, (nowhere is this perfection in charity attributed to the faithful, because just as we know in part, not perfectly in this imperfection, so there is no one who loves perfectly, but much less is this attributed to our love, that we might arrive at the governance of the pious, or the heavenly kingdom: For Christ alone is the way for us, is the truth, & is the life Joh. XIV. 6. Whence those things which are further added here by the Pseudo-Clement are by no means consistent with the analogy of faith: We are blessed, beloved, if we have fulfilled the commandments of the Lord in the harmony of charity (for that is not only ἄγραφον, that we are blessed in it, but also ἀντίγραφον, because not through our charity, or the fulfillment of the law, but solely through the obedience of Christ, just as we are righteous, so also are we blessed, Rom. IV. 6. c. V. 18. 19.) so that through charity our sins may be forgiven us εἰς τὸ ἀφεθῆναι ἡμῖν δι᾽ ἀγάπης, for it is written: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, & whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin, nor is there guile in his mouth. But here David, with the Apostle as interpreter, ascribes blessedness not to our charity, which Clement uniquely celebrates and extols in this place: but he says the blessedness is of that man, ᾧ ὁ Θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων, to whom God imputes righteousness: But which one, pray, his own? By no means, because there is no own righteousness χωρὶς ἔργων without works: but the righteousness of Christ, by which we are constituted righteous c. V. 19. and therefore our charity is excluded here, which is certainly included under the name of the excluded works, but it is not said that blessedness consists in it: nor is charity or any work of ours required in justifying for justification, but God is said to justify the ungodly, who believes in Him, & justification is constituted not in the acceptance of our charity, but in the remission of our sins, the covering of iniquities, the non-imputation of transgressions, nor does the justifying grace of GOD find in us anything except iniquities which it may remit, sins which it may cover, transgressions & offenses which it may not impute. By what right, therefore, Conringius judged that everything in this Epistle refers clearly to Apostolic times, both by the character of the speech, & by THE DOCTRINE ITSELF, let the orthodox judge.

Let those also, by whom these Pseudo-Clementine writings are approved, see how the immoderate praises, with which the Corinthians are burdened on pages 2, 3, 4, agree with Apostolic complaints and rebukes? For thus that Clement rhetorizes, certainly not in the Apostolic manner, or one accepted by Apostolic men at that time, much less consistent with the Epistle to the Hebrews: For who has stayed among you, who has not approved your faith, full of every virtue, firm and stable? Who has not admired your sober and moderate piety in Christ? Who has not praised the splendid and liberal manners of your hospitality? Who has not proclaimed your perfect and certain knowledge blessed? For all things were done by you without regard for persons, & you walked in the laws of GOD, subject to your leaders, & following the elders among you with due honor. And what other immoderate, mostly hyperbolic eulogies follow. Let someone just compare against those, and what follow, YOU WERE ALL of a humble mind, in nothing given to VAIN GLORY, subject to the yoke of others rather than subjecting others to yourselves, giving rather than receiving, content with the provision of GOD, & diligently attending to his word, with the Apostolic ἐπανορθώσει 1. Cor. III. 1. καὶ ἐγὼ, ἀδελφοὶ, ὀυκ ἐδυ- νήθην λαλῆσαι ὑμῖν ὡς πνευματικοῖς, ἀλλ' ὡς σαρκι- κοῖς: which Grotius takes to mean that the greater part of the Corinthian assembly had not progressed much in the doctrine of Christ, which was spiritual; and that they had need of the instillation of the precepts of Christ to subdue the remnants of evil affections: likewise c. III. 18. Let no one deceive himself, if anyone seems among you to be wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may be wise: & c. IV. 8. Now you are full, now you have become rich, you reign without us. And verse 19. 20. I will come to you, & I will know not the speech of those who are PUFFED UP, but the power. What do you want? shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity & a spirit of meekness. Likewise with c. V. 1. 2. 6. It is altogether heard that there is fornication among you, & such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, & you are puffed up, &c. Your boasting is not good; & v. 11. If he who is named a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one do not even eat. Such, therefore, were among them. Let someone also compare these Clementine things, all your labor & contention day and night was for the whole brotherhood, that the number of his elect might be saved with compassion & conscience. You were sincere among yourselves, harmless, & forgetful of every injury. Every sedition & schism was abominable to you, you mourned the faults of your neighbors, you considered their defects your own, led by no repentance because of good deeds, you were prompt & eager for EVERY good work, adorned with a venerable & IN ALL RESPECTS PERFECT conversation, you performed all things in the fear of him, the commands & precepts of the Lord were inscribed more deeply on the tablets of your hearts; with those things which are read in chapters V. & VI. of the Pauline Epistle, & he will confess that they are dissonant δὶς διὰ πασῶν. But it is a wonder if those things which the Apostle reproves in the Corinthians were so amended, that they themselves arrived at such a perfection of piety, that the assembly of the Church, ὄνομα σεμνὸν καὶ περιβόητον, καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις ἀξιαγάπητον, an honorable and illustrious name, and worthy to be loved by all, which had attained it, should have so quickly, as Grotius calculates the years, fallen away, and by the insolence and audacity of a few men should have flared up into such madness, that there arose in it ζῆλος, καὶ ἔρις, καὶ ςάσις διωγμὸς καὶ ἀκαταστασία, πόλεμος καὶ ἀιχμαλωσία, so that with justice and peace exiled far away, each one abandoned the fear of GOD, and was blinded in his faith, and did not walk in the institutions of His precepts, or lead a life worthy of Christ, but walked according to his own depraved lusts etc.

I have not yet spoken of the differences, which anyone can detect, once a comparison has been instituted between the present Clementine Epistle and those excerpts which are produced ἀυτολέξει by Clement of Alexandria in book IV of the Stromata, which ὀφθαλμοφανερῶς show that they differ greatly not only in words and phrases, but also in sentiments and meanings, and in their very ἀκολουθίᾳ and method, so that those who have read this Junian edition must have been led by blind affections, or have been doing something else, if they have read it (they have read at least those who instituted the collation in the margin, were able to notice, who saw the collation that had been instituted) so fearlessly. I have also said nothing yet about that fiction concerning the Phoenix, so prolix and so evidently false, that it is altogether a wonder that learned men could be found who did not hesitate to ascribe these things to Clement of Rome, an Apostolic man, or, as some of them prefer, one absolutely divine, as indeed it is read in the Junian edition. Photius, in Bibliotheca, Chapter 126, warned that this could be criticized in the Clementine [text] read by them, because he used the Phoenix, a unique bird, as a most true argument, ὡς παναληθεσάτῳ ὑποδείγματι: what would he have said if he had read that fiction with such an apparatus of trifles and most inept fables, as it is read in the Junian edition? But for the sake of his Cyril, the Pseudo-Patriarch of Constantinople, and of the fictitious copy of the Clementine Epistle, the overly simple Patricius preferred to believe such prolix fables, nay, to repeat his words, preferred to ERR with his Clement, an Apostolic man, and others, rather than follow Maximus, who indeed solidly refuted it in his own time: praised by the most learned Scholiast of Photius, Andreas Schottus, whose annotation it is helpful to bring in here: Although, he says, before Photius, blessed Clement spoke of this bird with doubt above (Constit. Book V, ch. 8) along with blessed Gregory Nazianzen, Oration on the Holy Spirit, which is the 37th; yet blessed Maximus the martyr also denied the same most plainly in a logical dissertation: there to Peter the Illustrious against the dogmas of Severus, which very place I have decided to append here for you from the Greek Notes, but in Latin: For if, he says, the Phoenix is a bird, it is also absolutely necessary that it be an animal. But if you concede that it is an animal; first, it cannot be entirely unique, at least as far as it is an animal, for no animal is alone. Then, if it is an animal, it is certainly a body, animated and at the same time endowed with sense. Now if it is a body, animated and endowed with sense, it will certainly also be subject to generation and corruption. Consult the wise men themselves, if you like, the inspectors of things that exist, whether it can happen that a body which is subject to generation and corruption, and is likewise animated and endowed with sense, can be of a unique nature (as far as existence is concerned): since the succession of others in these from others is a most evident sign of existing, and a most certain limit. Just as the Holy Scripture itself testifies, showing the certainty of this matter to that just man Noah, where in Gen. 7 it says: Enter you and all, etc. And likewise from all the flying things, etc. in which, if the Phoenix is to be counted, because it is a winged animal, it is certainly not of a unique nature as far as existence is concerned, as GOD himself pronounced. Ulysses Aldrovandus, Book XII, Ornithology, ch. 29, has this to say about the Phoenix: But if, on the contrary, someone were to say that the Phoenix is a true bird, he, if I am not mistaken, having read these things, will never judge, whatever others may say, that it has existed in the nature of things; nay rather, that all things which fabulous antiquity has invented about it are repugnant to the sacred page. For who, unless bereft of his mind, would induce into his own mind that a bird burns itself, and is reduced to ashes, and from the ashes a worm is generated, and from the worm a new bird (and they have feigned such to be the generation of the Phoenix), without any regard for the distinction of sex? For when God blessed the birds, he willed them to be multiplied upon the earth, and when he included them in Noah's ark, he had regard primarily for both sexes: how then does the Phoenix alone out of all living creatures always exist as a unique bird? But it is not only that which lessens belief, that I believe the Phoenix is less likely to be found, but also many other things which writers have trifled about it here and there, which I shall bring forward later, but now pass over for the sake of brevity. And although our age has observed the generation of such a kind in the Barnacle birds, which are born from the putrefaction of ships, as will be said in its place, God willing, and the Ephemeron fly around the river Hypanis bursting forth from a follicle, as Aristotle testifies, demonstrate that they do not exceed the bounds of nature: yet that can by no means be defended, that only one is always found in the whole Hemisphere. Since, as Lucretius rightly wrote:

To this is added that in the sum of things there is no one thing, unique, which is generated, and which grows unique and alone.

But what? If we revolve the writings of the ancients, and of those who are accustomed to be more trifling than the rest, about the Phoenix, is it not evident that they themselves doubt about it? Thus indeed Herodotus, who otherwise is accustomed to foist his own eyewitness faith upon us, asserts that he never saw the Phoenix except in a painting: thus Pliny, would that he were as cautious in other matters; the Ethiopians, he says, and the Indians report birds of most varied colors and indescribable, and before all the noble Phoenix, I know not whether fabulously, one in the whole world, and not much seen. But if indeed Bellonius or another following him should object the authority of the most faithful Historians, and especially of Cornelius Tacitus, who handed down that that bird was sometimes seen in Egypt; let him, I pray, look into it diligently, and consider how well Tacitus is consistent with himself in handing down the History of the Phoenix: for he writes thus: In the consulship of Paulus Fabius and L. Vitellius, after a long circuit of ages, the Phoenix bird came to Egypt, and provided material for the most learned of the natives and of the Greeks to discourse much about that miracle, concerning which they agree, and it is pleasing to bring forward many ambiguous things, but not absurd to know. That animal is sacred to the Sun, and they who have defined its form agree that it is different from other birds in its beak and the distinction of its feathers. Various things are handed down about the number of years, the most common being a space of five hundred. There are those who assert that one thousand four hundred and sixty-one years intervene, and that the former birds flew to the city which is named Heliopolis first under Sesostris, afterwards under Amasis; then under Ptolemy, who reigned third of the Macedonians, with a large company of other birds wondering at the new appearance. But antiquity is indeed obscure. Between Ptolemy and Tiberius there were less than two hundred and fifty years. Whence some have believed this Phoenix to be false, and not from the lands of the Arabs, and that it usurped nothing of those things which ancient memory confirmed. For when the number of years is completed, when death approaches, it builds a nest in its own lands, and pours into it a generative force, from which a young one arises, and the first care for the adult is to bury its father, and not rashly, but having taken up a weight of myrrh, and having tested through a long journey where it is equal to the burden, equal to the passage, it takes up the paternal body, and carries it to the altar of the Sun and burns it. These things are uncertain, and increased by fables. But that this bird is sometimes seen in Egypt is not doubted. Who, I ask, can determine anything certain from these words? Yet there is that which affirms it was seen at some time. But could not something fabulous have been foisted upon him, who does not interpose himself as a witness? And with some things interposed: Let us conclude therefore that the Phoenix is a fabulous bird, and let us say with the most learned Petrarch: When you have had all birds, you will not have the wonderful and most beautiful one. Since these things are so, that is, fabulous, and sought from the fables of the poets, the reader will not wonder if this whole history is almost entirely fashioned from the inventions of the poets. This Ulysses, that most sagacious investigator of nature, who refutes the fable of the Phoenix with many other proofs besides, and shows the disagreement of authors concerning the same, and among other things brings forward the varying accounts of its origin, of Pliny, Of Philostratus, of Oppian. From this, he says p. 824. again Orus Apollo invents a far different birth for the Phoenix, desiring it to be produced from blood poured out from the father's wound, which it inflicts upon itself of its own accord by striking the ground too violently. And these are the things which the ancients have handed down concerning the beginning of its origin, and even a blind man might see how likely they are.
