For the multitude could have made the Savior out of the baptizer, which happened to the Baptist: in which way the boasting of those who gloried in the dignity of the baptizers is tacitly reproved, as if the merit of baptism depended on the baptizer.

Latin:

V. 16. ἐβάπτισα δὲ καὶ τὸν Στεφανᾶ οἶκον. Est ἐπανόρθωσις prioris dicti. Stephanam hunc Graeci purant esse Commentariensem Philippensem, qui conversus Corinthum immigraverit.

λοιπὸν οὐκ οἶδα εἴ τινα ἄλλον ἐβάπτισα Nempe eorum qui nunc Corinthi habitant. Dixit se id nescire, quia fieri poterat, ut alii aliunde eo migrassent.

Gratulatur sibi de ista paucitate baptizatorum:

multitudo enim ex baptizante salvatorem facere potuisset, quod Baptistæ contigit: quo pacto ta- cite reprehenditur jactantia illorum, qui bapti- zantium dignitate gloriabantur, quasi meritum baptismi à baptizante dependeret.

## 1:17
V. 17. For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel.

Compare the saying as many others. Baptism could be performed by anyone: just as those converted by Peter at Pentecost were not all baptized by him: But preaching was a matter most worthy of the Apostles and joined with the greatest danger.

Crellius maintains that Paul here does not only exclude baptism by himself, but also that administered by others under his care: and from there he concludes that the words of Christ in Matt. XXVIII. 19 do not speak of water baptism. But it is manifest that the words of Paul must be taken comparatively, that he was not sent so much to baptize as to preach the Gospel: for if they are understood absolutely and simply, Paul would have acted beyond the parts of his calling and mission when he baptized, or caused baptism to be administered by others. And therefore Schlichting departs here from his Crellius: He does not deny, he says, that he was sent by Christ to have the care of baptism (for we see him drawing an argument from baptism; and from where it happened that all were baptized), but he denies that he was sent to baptize with his own hands as much as he was sent to preach the Gospel with his own mouth.

not in wisdom of speech.

The same is 'wisdom of speech' as 'words of wisdom' (Prov. I. 2), 'cunningly devised fables' (1 Pet. I, 16). Discourses seasoned with much erudition, such as those who were leaders of factions at Corinth sold themselves as. Hence they were called 'sophists'.

lest the cross of Christ be made void.

The power of the death of Christ would appear less if the faith held in the Gospel could be ascribed to learned and artificial words. Regarding the word 'to be made void' (κενῦσθαι), see Rom. IV. 4. Moreover, the word is taken comparatively here.

By 'wisdom of speech,' as the blessed Balduinus says on p. 290, he names that affected eloquence and rhetorical veneer, which boasts of I know not what philosophical acuteness, balanced words, and words sprinkled with sesame, accommodated to soothe the ears of the listeners, although they are entirely empty of substance; that is, it sells smoke for fire. He indicates that the Corinthians looked for such things, but that they were far from his own sermons, and indeed teaches that they ought to be absent, lest the cross of Christ be evacuated, that is, lest, deluded by the blandishments of words, they neglect the matter and the very mystery of Christ crucified. Paul notes, as Selneccerus rightly says, especially those teachers who boasted that they had acquired many disciples by their own work and faithfulness, that they had many listeners, and had baptized and converted many, and in this way claimed for themselves disciples as if snatched from others, and considered them their own church, as if they were gathering it for themselves, not for Christ. The Apostle, wishing to avert this ambition from himself and teaching that he was beyond all suspicion of merit, affirms that it happened by the singular providence of God that he himself baptized very few: not out of contempt for baptism, but because he was occupied primarily in handing down the doctrine concerning Christ, and had committed the administration of baptism to others. This is also supported by the advice of Aristotle himself in his book on Poetics: It is not appropriate, if one must use a more serious sentiment, to apply the splendor of reason, lest the mind be led away from the gravity of the sentiment to the ornamentation of the speech, by which the mind, being soothed and occupied at the very first encounter, cannot easily arrive at the inner meaning.

PART III. Information concerning the Gospel of the cross of Christ.

Latin:

V. 17. ὀὐ γὰρ ἀπέστειλέ με χριστὸς βαπτίζειν, ἀλλ᾽ εὐαγγελίζεσθαι.

Comparate dictum ut multa. Baptismus per quemlibet impleri poterat: sicut illi à Petro conversi in Pentecoste non omnes ab ipso fuerunt baptizati: At prædicatio res erat maxime digna Apostolis & maximo cum periculo con- juncta.

Crellius vult, Paulum hic non tantum excludere baptismum per se, sed etiam per alios, se curante, administratum: atque inde colligit, verba Christi Matth. XXVIII. 19. non loqui de baptismo aquæ. Sed manifestum est, verba Pauli συγκριτικῶς acci- pienda esse, se non tam ad baptizandum, quam ad prædicandum Evangelium missum esse: nam si ἁπλῶς & simpliciter intelligantur, Paulus utique præter vocationis & missionis suæ partes egisset, cum baptizavit, vel per alios baptismum administrari curavit. Ideoque discedit hic à Crellio suo Schlich- tingius: Non negat, inquit, se missum à Christo; ut baptismi curam habeat; (videmus enim illum à ba- ptismo argumentum ducere; & unde factum esset, ut omnes baptizarentur,) sed negat se missum esse, ut tam propriis manibus baptizaret, quam missus erat, ut proprio ore Evangelium prædicaret.

ὐκ ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγου.

Idem σοφία λόγου quod λόγοι σοφίας אמרי בינה Prov. I. 2. σεσοφισμένοι μῦθοι 1. Petr. I, 16. Sermones multa erudi- tione conditi, qualibus se venditabant illi, qui Corinthi partium erant duces. Hinc dicti σοφισταί.

ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ ὁ σταυρὸς τῦ χριστῦ.

Minus appareret virtus mortis Christi, si fides Evangelio habita adscribi potuisset verbis eruditis & artificiosis. De verbo κενῦσθαι vide Rom. IV. 4. Cæterum hic comparate id verbum sumitur.

Σοφίαν λόγου, dicente B. Balduino p. 290. nomi- nat affectatam illam eloquentiam, & fucum Rheto- ricum, qui nescio quod acumen Philosophicum, verba librata, sesamoque sparsa & ad demulcendas audito- rum aures accommodata, licet à rebus prorsus inania jactitat, hoc est, fumum pro igne venditat. Talia Corinthios spectasse, à suis vero concionibus procul abesse indicat, quin & abesse debere docet, ne evacue- tur crux Christi, hoc est, ne blandimentis verborum dementati rem & mysterium ipsum de Christo cru- cifixo negligant. Notat Paulus, ut recte Selnecce- rus, præcipue Doctores, qui gloriabantur, se sua opera & fidelitate multos discipulos acquisivisse, mul- tos auditores habere, ac multos baptizasse & conver- tisse, atque hoc modo discipulos quasi aliis ereptos si- bi vendicabant, & ecclesiam suam esse ducebant, quasi sibi, non Christo, eam congregarent. Hanc am- bitionem à se Apostolus avertere volens, & se extra omnem suspicionem merito esse, docens, affirmat sin- gulari providentia DEI factum esse, quod ipse ad- modum paucos baptizaverit: non comtemtu bapti- smi, sed quod occupatus præcipue esset in tradenda doctrina de Christo, & aliis baptismi administratio- nem commisisset. Quod etiam facit ipsius Aristotelis monitum libro de Poët. Non oportet, si quando graviore sententia utendum est, rationis splendorem adhibere, ne animus abducatur à gravitate senten- tiæ, ad ornatum orationis, quo primo statim congressu delinitus, & occupatus animus ad sensum interiorem haud facile potest pervenire.

PARS III. Informatio de Evangelio de cruce Christi.

## 1:18
Ver. 18. For the word of the cross.

That narrative concerning Christ crucified and resurrected, upon which the authority of Christian doctrine rests. See below II. 2. Gal. VI. 14.

τοῖς μὲν ἀπολλυμένοις μωρία ἐστί.

He denoted the thing by its effect. When he wished to denote the unbelievers, he said those who are perishing, because those who do not believe in the Gospel perish, John 3:18. In like manner men are distinguished into those who are being saved and those who are perishing, 2 Cor. 2:15, 16. It is foolishness, that is, it seems something foolish, unworthy of belief. That indeed happens because they do not turn away from their vices, but dwell in them: therefore they do not want the truths to be seen which are contrary to their vices.

to us who are being saved.

To those who believe; who are the same ones we are on the way to salvation.

Having chastised the schismatic dissension, the Apostle, having recalled them to the unity of doctrine and of phrases, informs them concerning the chief head of doctrine, which is concerning the cross of Christ: and since they had provided the cause of the schism among others, who were so clinging to their teachers because of external gifts, especially also because of eloquence and wisdom, that they despised others: he teaches that the sermon of the Gospel does not need either a pomp of words or foreign wisdom, but if it is proposed sincerely and simply, and is received with true faith, even if it seems mere foolishness to the wise of the world, it is both the power and the wisdom of God unto salvation, and he confirms that with prophetic testimony. Furthermore, the narrative concerning Christ crucified and resurrected not only produces authority for the Evangelical information, which had already obtained authority even before the death of Christ through miracles and other ways: although no mention of refutation is made here: but it is the very nucleus and marrow of Evangelical doctrine, as the Apostle testifies, 1 Cor. 2:6, ch. 3:11, ch. 15:1 ff. For this is the proper object of faith, Rom. 4:24, ch. 10:12. Moral precepts could be had from the law; but the doctrine concerning Christ who died for our sins and was resurrected for our righteousness is proper to the Gospel, indeed the sum of the Gospel consists in that very thing. Furthermore, the cause of unbelief is not established here as perseverance in vices; although that too is in a certain way a cause of unbelief, John 3:19, for the reprobate remain in sins for this reason, that they do not believe in Christ, just as on the contrary faith is effective through love, Gal. 5:6, and those who are born of God do not sin, 1 John 5:9. But the Apostle has designated here as the cause of unbelief that the wisdom of the world does not attain to the divine wisdom, which is above every grasp of reason, nor is it able to submit itself to it, but opposes it and holds it for foolishness.

is the power of God.

The power of God is placed in that sermon, through which we are justified, that is, we are purged from vices, then we are imbued with the Holy Spirit. See Rom. 1:16.

That perverse explanation of justification having been dismissed, that it is situated in the fact that we are purged from vices and imbued with the Holy Spirit, which we refuted in the Epistle to the Romans: the Gospel concerning the cross of Christ is called the power of God, because it is equipped with divine power for our regeneration, conversion, and salvation, John 6:63, 69, Phil. 2:16, Rom. 1:16, Heb. 4:12, James 1:12, nor does it only objectively show the way of salvation, but it also works effectively in us, inasmuch as it is that through which God regenerates us, 1 Pet. 1:23, James 1:18, sanctifies us, John 17:17, saves us, James 1:21. Concerning which see what we said against the fanatics who attribute to the Word of God nothing but an objective power, Tom. 1, System. Theol. ch. 4, Quest. 25, p. 692 ff. Furthermore, he attributes contrary effects to one and the same doctrine concerning Christ crucified, with respect to different objects. One accidentally, the other by itself: one according to appearance, the other according to truth. Accidentally it is foolishness to those who are perishing, that is, to those who savor nothing but human things and judge divine mysteries by the standard of human reason. To these the preaching seems foolish and discordant, nor was it proposed by the Apostles in a showy manner and for the applause of men, and as long as they indulge in these speculations of theirs, they are counted in the number of those who are perishing. By itself it is the power of God to those who believe, that is, a saving instrument and effective medium, by which God works life and salvation in them: as the blessed Balduinus rightly says here.

Latin:

Vers. 18. λόγος γὰρ ὁ τῦ σταυρῦ.

Narratio ista de Christo crucifixo & resuscitato, qua ni- titur Christianæ doctrinæ auctoritas. Vide infra II. 2. Gal. VI. 14.

τοῖς μὲν ἀπολλυμένοις μωρία ἐστί.

Rem denotavit ex effectu. Cum incredulos denotare- vellet, dixit pereuntes, quia, qui Evangelio non credunt, pereunt Joh. III. 18. Pari modo discriminantur homines in σωζομένους & ἀπολλυμένους 2. Cor. II. 15. 16. Est stultitia, id est stultum aliquid videtur, indignum creditu. Id vero evenit quod in vitiis suis non divertantur, sed habitent: ideo nolunt vera videri, quæ vitiis sunt contraria.

τοῖς δὲ σωζομένοις ὑμῖν.

Credentibus; qui iidem in via sumus ad salutem.

Castigata dissensione schismatica Apostolus ad unitatem doctrinæ & phrasewn revocatos infor- mat de præcipuo doctrinæ capite, quod est de cru- ce Christi: & quum causam schismatis præbuerint inter alios, qui doctoribus suis ob dona externa, imprimis etiam ob eloquentiam & sapientiam ita adhærebant, ut alios contemnerent: sermonem Evangelii non indigere sive verborum pompa, sive transmarina sapientia, sed si sincere, ac simpli- citer proponatur, veraque fide suscipiatur, etiamsi stultitia mera sapientibus mundi videatur, & vir- tutem & sapientiam Dei esse ad salutem docet, id- que confirmat testimonio prophetico. Cæte- rum narratio de Christo crucifixo & resuscitato non tantum autoritatem parit informationi Ev- angelicæ, quæ per miracula, aliisque modis auto- ritatem etiam ante mortem Christi jam consequu- ta erat: quamvis hic nulla refutationis mentio fiat: sed est ipse nucleus & medulla doctrinæ Evan- gelicæ, teste Apostolo 1. Cor. II. 6. c. III. 11. c. XV. 1. seqq. Hoc enim proprium fidei objectum est, Rom. IV. 24. c. X. 12. Præcepta Moralia è lege haberi poterant; at doctrina de Christo propter peccata nostra mortuo, & propter justitiam nostram resu- scitato Evangelio propria est, imo in ea ipsa Evan- gelii summa consistit. Porro causa incredulitatis non constituitur hic perseverantia in vitiis; quam- vis & ea causa certo modo sit incredulitatis Joh. III. v. 19. nam ideo in peccatis manēt reprobi, quod non in Christum credant, quemadmodum ex ad- verso fides per charitatem efficax est, Gal. V. 6. & qui ex Deo nati sunt, non peccant 1. Joh. V. 9. Sed eam hic designavit ἀπιστίας causam Apostolus, quod sapientia mundi sapientiam divinam, quæ supra omnem captum rationis est, non assequatur, nec ei sese submittere valeat, sed repugnet eidem, ac pro stultitia eam habeat.

δύναμις Θεῒ ἐςι.

Vis Dei in illo sermone posita est, per quam justifica- mur, id est, a vitiis purgamur, deinde Sancto Spiritu imbui- mur. Vide Rom. I. 16.

Missa illa justificationis perversa explicatione, quod in eo sita sit, quod purgamur à vitiis, & Spi- ritu Sancto imbuimur, quam in Epist. ad Rom. profligavimus: Evangelium de cruce Christi di- citur δύναμις Θεῒ, quia virtute divina instructum est ad nostri regenerationem, conversionem & sa- lutem Joh. VI. 63. 69. Phil. II. 16. Rom. I. 16. Ebr. IV. 12. Jac. I. 12. nec objective tantum monstrat viam salutis, sed operatur etiam efficaciter in nobis, ut- pote per quod Deus nos regenerat 1. Petr. I. 23. Jac. I. 18. sanctificat Joh. XVII. 17. salvat Jac. I. 21. Quo de vid. quæ adversus fanaticos Verbo DEI non nisi objectivam vim tribuentes diximus Tom. I. System. Theol. c. IV. Quæst. XXV. p. 692. seqq. Cæ- terum uni & eidem doctrinæ de Christo crucifixo tribuit contrarios effectus, respectu diversorum obje- ctorum. Unum per accidens, alterum per se: unum κατὰ δόκησιν, alterum per ἀλήθειαν. Per accidens est stultitia pereuntibus, h. e. iis, qui non nisi humana sapiunt, & mysteria divina ad amussim rationis hu- manæ dijudicant. His stulta videtur & absona con- cio, neque ab Apostolis speciose & ad applausum ho- minum proposita fuit & quamdiu his suis speculation nibus indulgent, in numero eorum, qui pereunt, censentur. Per se est virtus DEI credentibus, h. e. salutare organum & efficax medium, quo DEUS in eis vitam & salutem operatur: ut recte hic B. Bal- duinus.

## 1:19
V. 19. For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and will reject the understanding of the understanding ones.

He reads in Isaiah 29:14, אסתך: where we have תסתתר, the LXX also read thus, as Paul does; for they translate it I will hide, I will cause it not to shine: which is the same as I will reject. Justin also, disputing with Trypho, cites the passage of Isaiah three times: first by I will hide: then by I will reject: then again by I will hide. What Isaiah had said concerning the men of his own time, the Apostle with greater right adapts to his own times.

The Prophetic passage itself teaches that Isaiah looks to the times of the N.T., and the Apostle does not merely adapt the words of the Prophet to the men of his own time, but teaches that he looked primarily to them, See Bibl. Illustr. V. T. on the passage Is. XXIX. 14. The reason, however, why God threatens that He will reject the wisdom of the wise of this world is common and general, because, namely, the wisdom of the wise of the world opposes itself to divine wisdom, and holds it for foolishness. Human wisdom is destroyed by GOD, because it despises the divine mysteries themselves: but the wisdom or doctrine revealed in the Gospel saves man. Therefore, God, in procuring our salvation, does not care for the political wisdom of men and similar external gifts.

Latin:

V. 19. γέγραπται γὰρ ἀπολῶ τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν καὶ τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν συνετῶν ἀθετήσω.

Legit in Esaiæ XXIX. 14. אסתך: ubi nos habemus תסתתר, etiam LXX. sic legunt, ut Paulus; vertunt enim κρύψω, abscondam, efficiam ne luceat: quod idem valet cum ἀθετήσω. Justinus quoque cum Tryphone disputans ter lo- cum Esaiæ citat: prius per κρύψω: deinde per ἀθετήσω: deinde rursum per κρύψω. Quod Esaias de sui temporis hominibus dixerat, idem ad sua tempora majori jure aptat Apostolus.

Esaiam respicere tempora N. T. locus ipse Pro- pheticus docet, nec aptat tantum verba Prophetæ ad sui temporis homines Apostolus, sed ea impri- mis respexisse docet, Vid. Bibl. Illustr. V. T. ad locum Es. XXIX. 14. Causa autem cur Deus sapientiam sapientum hujus mundi sese reprobaturum mine- tur, communis & generalis est, quia nempe sapien- tia sapientum mundi opponit se divinæ sapientiæ, eamque pro stultitia habet. Sapientia humana per- ditur à DEO, quia ipsa mysteria divina contemnit: Sapientia vero seu doctrina in Evangelio revelata servat hominem. Idcirco Deus in procuranda salute nostra non curat sapientiam hominum po- liticam & similia externa dona.

## 1:20
V. 20. Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this age?

It is a parody of the passage Is. XXXIII. 18. In which passage likewise where is is found. But there it treats of those who had held the principal duties in the camps of the Assyrians: here, however, of the professors of those arts which the Corinthians valued highly. Wise men were called by the Greeks, חכמים by the Hebrews, by way of excellence those who handed down the precepts of morals, like those seven nobles throughout Greece, then Socrates, and others; scribe ספר in the Hellenistic manner of speaking, both a lawyer and a historian. Disputer of this age, an investigator of the things of nature, which to the Hebrews חוח העולם, that is, a Physicist. That study is wont to be called מחקר: which is properly disputation. Thus in Baruch III. 23. and following, those who seek out understanding on the earth are Physicists, those are mythologists who dictated moral maxims, those who speak proverbs, seekers of understanding, lawyers and historians. But Paul preferred to say disputer rather than seeker, because physical questions were wont to be ventilated by many disputations: which is to dispute. Ignatius to the Ephesians: where is the wise? where is the disputer? where is the boasting of those called mighty? Tertullian translates this passage of Paul thus in his book on idolatry: where is the wise, where is the man of letters, where is the seeker of this age? The sense is: show me Philosophers and Philologists who have led as many men to such probity as we have through the word of the cross. Their disciples are few compared to ours, and they remain fornicators, if not something worse: they remain full of empty conceit, as Timon said: they remain arrogant, litigious, slanderous.

Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world. To make foolish הסכיל here is to convict of foolishness, in which sense words in Hiphil are frequent among the Hebrews. I understand this, however, by comparison with that fruit which the Gospel brought forth. The little word this is not in the Manuscript, nor is there need of it.

No parody of the prophetic passage is instituted here, but a proof is derived from the same: nor does it treat there of diverse offices in the camps of the Assyrians, but of the members of the kingdom of Christ, or even of teachers in the Church; because in it not the wise of this age, not censors, not chancellors, but the humble, simple, and abject especially obtain, as we said regarding that passage. Rightly the blessed Balduinus: It is taught there how few there are in the kingdom of Christ who excel in worldly wisdom in civil affairs, whom he names the lettered, scribes, and seekers of this age, that is, who judge, direct, and compose worldly things by their own wisdom and accurate censure: which wisdom of theirs excludes them from the kingdom of God, if they permit it dominion in divine things. Therefore GOD has made that political wisdom foolish, that is, has shown it to be stupid; not as if the thing in itself were evil and useless, (for it is a singular gift of God,) but because its use was not good in divine things. There is no reason, therefore, why we should say with Crellius that these things were said in Isaiah in a far different sense. Let those things which we said on that passage be compared.

Schlichting's commentary is more suitable here than Grotius's explanation: v. 20. Where is the wise man? That is, what does his wisdom profit the wise man? He trusted in his wisdom, where is it now? He has been made the most foolish of all. Where is the scribe? γραμματεὺς. The learned, the doctor; what does his doctrine profit the learned man? Where is the disputer of this world? That is, he who is held as a disputer in this world, who disputes everything from natural principles, and admits nothing unless he perceives it by the senses or concludes it from natural principles. He opposes this world to the other world. Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? He brings forward the cause of the preceding, namely, because God has made foolish or rendered foolish the wisdom of this world, that is, that which is held for wisdom in this world, while He made those things true and necessary to be believed for salvation which the wisdom of this world judges to be vain and foolish. He opposes this world to the other world, and the wisdom of this world to the wisdom of the other world.

Latin:

V. 20. πῦ σοφὸς; πῦ γραμματεὺς; πῦ συζητητὴς τῶ αἰῶν&gt; τέτε;

Est παρωδία loci Es. XXXIII. 18. In quo loco itidem πῦ sic reperitur. Sed ibi agitur de iis, qui præcipua munia ha- buerant in castris Assyriorum: hic vero de artium professo- ribus earum, quas Corinthii magni faciebant. Σοφοὶ Græ- cis, חכמים Hebræis, per excellentiam dicebantur ii, qui præcepta morum tradebant, ut septem illi per Græciam nobiles, deinde Socrates, & alii γραμματεὺς ספר loquendi genere Hellenistico & legum peritus & historiarum. συζητη- τὴς τῶ αἰῶν&gt;, indagator rerum naturæ, quæ Hebræis חוח העולם, id est, Physicus. Id studium מחקר dicit solet: quod proprie est συζήτησις. Sic apud Baruchum lII. 23. & sequentibus, οἱ ἐκζητῶντες τὴν σύνεσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς sunt Phy- sicἱ, οἱ μυθολογοι sunt, qui γνώμας ἠθικὰς dictabant אומרי משלים ἐκζητηταὶ τῆς συνέσεως legisperiti & historici. Ma- luit autem συζητητὴς quam ἐκζητητὴς dicere Paulus, quia Physicæ quæstiones multis disputationibus ventilari sole- bant: quod est συζητεῖν. Ignatius ad Ephesios: πῦ σοφὸς; πῦ συζητητὴς; πῦ καύχησις τῶν λεγομένων δυνατῶν; Tertul- lianus hunc Pauli locum sic vertit libro de idololatria: ubi sapiens, ubi literator, ubi conquisitor hujus ævi? Sensus est: ostende mihi Philosophos & Philologos, qui tot homines ad tantam probitatem perduxerint, quod & ad quantam nos per sermonem crucis. Pauci sunt illorum discipuli præ no- stris, & manent scortatores, si non pejus aliquid: manent κενεᾶς ὀίησεως ἔμπλεοι ἀσκοὶ, ut dicebat Timon: manent ar- rogantes, litigiosi, maledici.

ἐχὶ ἐμώρανεν ὁ θεὸς τὴν σοφίαν τῶ κόσμε τέτε. Μωραίνειν הסכיל hic est stultitiæ convincere, quo sensu verba in Hiphil frequentia sunt apud Hebræos. Intelligo autem comparatione ejus frugis, quam protulit Evange- lium. Vocula τέτε non est in Manuscripto, nec ea opus.

Non παρωδία loci prophetici hic instituitur, sed probatio ex eodem desumitur: neque ibi agitur de officiis diversis in castris Assyriorum, sed de membris regni Christi, aut etiam de doctoribus in Ecclesia; quod in eo non sapientes hujus seculi, non censo- res, non cancellarii, sed humiles, simplices & abje- cti potissimum obtineant, ut ad illum locum dixi- mus. Recte B. Balduinus: Docetur ibi, quam pau- cisint eorum in regno Christi, qui sapientia mundana pollent in rebus civilibus, quos literatos, scribas & conquisitores hujus seculi nominat, hoc est, qui res mundanas sapientia sua, & accurata censura dijudi- cant, dirigunt ac componunt: qua sua sapientia se regno Dei excludunt, si ei in rebus divinis dominium permittunt. Idcirco infatuavit DEUS sapientiam illam politicam, hoc est, stolidam esse ostendit; non quasi in se res mala sit & inutilis, (est enim singulare donum Dei,) sed quia usus ejus non bonus fuit in rebus divinis. Non ergo est quod cum Crellio dicamus hæc apud Esaiam longe alio sensu dicta esse. Conferantur quæ ad illum locum diximus.

Convenientior autem hic Grotiana explanatione est Commentarius Schlichtingii: v. 20. Ubi sa- piens; Id est, quid juvat sapientem sua sapientia? fi- debat sua sapientia, ubi nunc est? insipientissimus omnium effectus est. Ubi scriba? γραμματεὺς. Li- teratus, doctus; quid juvat doctum sua doctrina? Ubi disputator hujus seculi? Id est, qui in hoc seculo pro disputatore habetur, qui omnia ex principiis na- turalibus disputat, nec quidquam admittit, nisi quod vel sensibus percipit, vel ex principiis naturalibus concludit, Seculum hoc opponit alteri seculo. Non- ne infatuavit Deus sapientiam mundi hujus? Cau- sam affert superiorum, quia scilicet Deus infatuavit seu fatuam reddidit sapientiam mundi hujus, id est, quae in hoc mundo pro sapientia habetur, dum ea ve- ra & ad salutem creditu necessaria fecit qua sapien- tia mundi hujus vana & fatua judicat. Mundum hunc opponit mundo alteri, & sapientiam mundi hujus sapientia mundi alterius.

## 1:21
V. 21. For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom. He calls that knowledge of God here the wisdom of God, which arises from the nature of things. Concerning which we have spoken at Romans 1:20, 21 and Acts 14:16, 17:27. ἔγνω in this place signifies 'revered': which to the Romans is ἐδόξησαν or εὐχαρίστησαν. Thus John also received ἔγνω in 1:10, and explains it by ἔλαβον.

God was pleased. We have a similar construction of the word ἐυδοκεῖν in Luke 12:23, Romans 15:26, Galatians 1:15, Colossians 1:19.

Through the foolishness of preaching. A double trope here: for 'through the foolishness of preaching' is put for 'foolish preaching', and it is called foolish not because it is such, but because it is thought to be such by many learned men. That appears in the following, and soon in 2:14. Thus many things are called according to appearance, not according to being.

to save those who believe. To free from vices for the present, to grant eternal life in the future.

Because after the fall the whole world, even if it still has some wisdom remaining from the light of nature, was by no means able to know God in His wisdom concerning the method of obtaining salvation, or concerning Christ Jesus our life and salvation, through that wisdom; therefore this gracious good pleasure of God was to lead men to salvation through the preaching of His word, even though that may seem mere foolishness to the wise of the world, and to save through the proclamation of the Gospel those who draw faith in Christ from it, and believe. To save, however, is not to free from vices through sanctification, but to remit sins by grace on account of Christ, and to grant eternal life, obtained and acquired for us by his merit: which happens to all who believe in Christ, Acts 10:43, John 20:31. We have therefore here both the truth of natural knowledge about God, because it is honored by the name of wisdom, and indeed its insufficiency for salvation: because through it that saving wisdom, which is exhibited in the Gospel concerning Christ, cannot be known; and also the natural inability of unregenerate men, or of a mind not yet regenerated, to perceive spiritual things, even if they are proposed, by their own powers, without the grace of the Holy Spirit, since it rather holds them for foolishness. Compare 1 Cor. 2:14. Chrysostom in this place: What is, 'in the wisdom of God'? That which appears through works, through which He wished to be known. For He built both it and such things for this reason, that He might be held in admiration from those things which are seen, as the creator... Since therefore he did not wish to know God through this wisdom, He persuaded through the foolishness of what is seen to be preaching: not through reasons, but through faith. Furthermore, where there is the wisdom of God, there is no need for human wisdom. For before, to say that He who created such a great world and in such a way is God, and that it is consistent that He has great and ineffable power, is human wisdom—to reason, and to comprehend Him through these things. Now there is no longer need for reasons, but for faith alone. For to believe in Him who was crucified and buried, and to be persuaded that He both rose again and sits among the heavenly ones, this does not need wisdom, nor reasons, but faith. But these things are not to be taken with Schlichting as if we could arrive at the saving knowledge of God through the most wise works of God (of creation), with wisdom as our guide: because no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him, Matthew 11:27; much less is it to be established with him that God was so offended by the perversity of the world that, because it did not wish to arrive at the knowledge of God through the most wise works of God, with wisdom as guide, so that it might be saved, it has the necessity to believe in a thing foolish according to its own wisdom, if it wishes to be saved. For that economy of salvation ordained by God through the cross and death of Christ is not for that reason, because the world wished to arrive at the knowledge of God through the works of creation: but because the sin of the world had to be expiated through the death of the Son of God, John 1:29, 1 John 2:2. Finally, those things which Schlichting adds are heretical and blasphemous: 'The world found, however, a way and reason, so that it would not believe in a man put on the cross, it said that He was GOD, who joined human nature to Himself. Thus nevertheless it attempted to elude the counsel of GOD.' For we do not elude the counsel of God, who, terrified by the divine curse (Jer. 17:6) in a mere man, and revering the divine prohibition of idolatry, refuse to place our trust, and reverently believe what Scripture teaches, that God redeemed us with His own blood (Acts 20:28), and that the Father did not spare His own and only-begotten Son, who is God blessed forever over all, but that He delivered Him up for us, and that the Lord of glory Himself willed to be put on the cross, Jehovah Himself to be pierced for us, with our reason held captive under the obedience of faith: But the Socinians, who utterly overturn the way and reason of salvation or the counsel of God concerning salvation through the satisfaction of the death of the Son of God, and profess that they do not wish to believe Scripture, even if it were to testify the same expressly not once but often concerning the incarnation and satisfaction of the Son of GOD: which was the unbelief of Smalcius and Socinus. Here B. Selneccerus noted Servetus, who said that nothing comes into his intellect which does not come into the senses: and others asserting that they can embrace nothing by faith which they do not comprehend by their own reason. Which latter point the Socinians still profess, (as we have observed elsewhere from Schlichting,) because they also openly protest that they believe nothing of those things which are expressed in the Holy Scriptures, unless it can be taught by demonstrations that they are so: concerning which in Decad. Dissert. de Mataol. Socin. ortu & progressu.

Latin:

V. 21. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ ἔγνω ὁ κόσμος διὰ τῆς σοφίας τὸν Θεὸν. σοφίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ hic vocat cognitionem illam Dei, quae ex rerum natura oritur. De qua diximus ad Roman. 1, 20. 21. & Act. XIV. 16. XVII. 27. ἔγνω hoc loco significat reveri- tus est: quod ad Romanos ἐδόξησαν vel εὐχαρίστησαν. Sic ἔγνω Johannes etiam accepit I. 10. & exponit per ἔλαβον.

ἐυδόκησεν ὁ Θεὸς. Similem constructionem vocis ἐυδοκεῖν habemus Luc. XII. 23. Rom. XV. 26. Gal. I. 15. Coloss. I. 19.

Διὰ τῆς μωρίας τοῦ κηρύγματος. Duplex hic tropus: nam & Διὰ τῆς μωρίας τοῦ κηρύγμα- τος positum est pro μωροῦ κηρύγματος & stultum dicitur non quod tale est, sed quod tale esse multis eruditis putatur. Ap- paret id in sequentibus, & mox II. 14. Sic multa appellan- tur κατὰ τὸ φαίνεσθαι, non κατὰ τὸ ἔιναι.

σῶσαι τοὺς πισέυοντας. A vitiis liberare in praesens, in posterum donare vita aeterna.

Quia post lapsum mundus universus etsi ali- quam sapientiam e lumine naturae adhuc reliquo habeat, Deum in sua sapientia, de ratione conse- quendi salutem, vel de Christo Jesu vita & salute nostra neutiquam cognoscere per illam sapien- tiam valuit, idcirco gratiosum hoc Dei benepla- citum fuit praedicatione verbi sui, utut illud etiam mera stultitia sapientibus mundi videatur, ad salu- tem perducere homines, & per Evangelii praeco- nium salvare eos, qui inde fidem in Christum hau- riunt, & credunt. Salvare autem non est à vitiis liberare per sanctificationem, sed peccata ex gratia propter Christum remittere, vitamque aeternam do- nare, merito ejus nobis partam & acquisitam: quod contingit omnibus qui credunt in Christum Act. X. 43. Joh. XX. 31. Habemus ergo hic natu- ralis notitiae de Deo tum veritatem, quia sapientiae nomine honoratur, tum vero insufficientiam ad salutem: quia per eam sapientia illa salutifera, quae in Evangelio de Christo exhibetur, cognosci ne- quit; nec non hominum non renatorum, seu men- tis nondum regenitae naturalem ἀνδυναμίαν ad spiritualia, etiamsi proponantur, viribus propriis, sine Spiritus S. gratia percipienda, siquidem ea potius pro stultitia habeat. Conf. 1. Cor. II. 14. Chrysost. in h. l. Quid est, in Dei sapientia? qua apparet per opera, per qua voluit cognosci. Propterea enim & ipsa & talia construxit, ut convenienter ex iis qua cernuntur, in admiratione haberetur effe- ctor -- Quoniam ergo per hanc sapientiam noluit Deum cognoscere, persuasit per stultitiam qua esse videtur praditationis: non per rationes, sed per fidem. De catero, ubi est Dei sapientia, non est opus huma- na. Antea enim dicere, quod qui tantum & sic mun- dum creavit magnum, sit Deus, & quod magnam & ineffabilem potentiam eum habere sit consentaneum, est humana sapientia-ratiocinari, & per hac ipsum comprehendere. Nunc non est amplius opus ratio- nibus, sed sola fide. In eum enim qui fuit crucifixus & sepultus credere, & persuasum habere quod ipse & resurrexit, & sedet apud superos, hoc non eget sa- pientia, neque rationibus, sed fide. Non autem hæc eo accipienda cum Schlichtingio, quasi per sapien- tissima (creationis) Dei opera, sapientia duce, ad Dei notitiam salvificam pervenire possimus: quia nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, & cui Filius vult re- velare Matth. XI. 27. multo minus cum ipso sta- tuendum, Deum in eo ultum esse mundi perversi- tatem, ut quia per sapientissima Dei opera, sapientia duce, ad Dei notitiam pervenire noluit, quo salvus fieret, rei secundum suam sapientiam stultæ, si salvus esse velit, necesse habeat credere. Non enim ideo οἰκονομία illa salutis per Christi crucem & mortem à Deo ordinata, quod mundus per opera creatio- nis ad notitiam Dei pervenire voluit: sed quia pec- catum mundi per mortem Filii Dei expiandum fuit, Joh. I. 29. 1. Joh. II. 2. Hæretica denique & blasphe- ma sunt, quæ addit Schlichtingius: Invenit tamen mundus modum ac rationem, ne in hominem in cru- cem actum, crederet, DEUM esse dixit, qui sibi hu- manam naturam adjunxerit. Ita nihilocminus DEI consilium conatus est eludere. Non enim nos eludi- mus Dei consilium, qui in ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον territi maledictione divina Jer. XVII. 6. & reverentes in- terdictum idololatriæ divinum, fiduciam colloca- re renuimus, & Scripturæ docenti, quod Deus san- guine proprio nos redemerit, Act. XX. 28. quodque Pater Filio proprio & unigenito non pepercerit, qui est Deus benedictus in secula super omnia, quin eun- dem pro nobis traderet, & quod ipse Dominus glo- riæ in crucem agi, Jehovah ipse pro nobis transfigi voluerit, reverenter credimus, ratione sub obse- quium fidei captivatâ: Sed Sociniani, qui modum ac rationem salutis vel consilium Dei de salute per satisfactionem mortis Filii Dei prorsus evertunt, ac Scripturæ, etiamsi non semel sed sæpius eadem expressè testaretur de Filii DEI incarnatione, & satisfactione, se credere non velle profitentur: quæ Smalcii & Socini ἀπιστία fuit. Notavit hic B. Selneccerus Servetum, qui dixit, nihil venire in suum intellectum, quod non veniat in sensum: & alios as- serentes, nihil se posse amplecti fide, quod non ra- tione sua comprehendant. Quod posterius etiam- num profitentur Sociniani, (uti alias è Schlichtin- gio observavimus,) quia etiam nihil sese illorum credere vel palam protestantur, quæ in S. literis expressa, nisi ea per demonstrationes ita se habere doceri possit: quo de in Decad. Dissert. de Mataol. Socin. ortu & progressu.

## 1:22
V. 22. For the Jews also ask for a sign.

Not just any kind, but according to the judgment of their own mind. Matt. XII. 38. namely from heaven Matt. XVI. 1. Mark VIII. 11. just as Moses had made hail descend, and Elijah fire. One must read here ἐπειδὴ καὶ, as it is in most editions, not ἐπειδὴ γὰρ, the coherence of the sense shows. For the Apostle is not arguing, but explaining what has already been said. Furthermore, in the Manuscript it is in the plural σημεῖα.

and Greeks seek wisdom.

The Greeks want what is said to be proven to them by natural causes. In the Manuscript it is, ἐπιζητοῦσι.

Latin:

V. 22. ἐπειδὴ καὶ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι σημεῖον αἰτοῦσι.

Non qualecunque, sed ex animi sui arbitratu. Matth. XII. 38. nempe de cœlo Matth. XVI. 1. Marc. VIII. 11. sicut Moses grandinem fecerat descendere, & Elias ignem. Le- gendum hic ἐπειδὴ καὶ, ut est in plerisque editionibus, non ἐπειδὴ γὰρ, ostendit sensus cohærentia. Non enim argu- mentatur Apostolus, sed jam dicta explicat. Præterea in Manuscripto est pluraliter σημεῖα.

καὶ Ἕλληνες σοφίαν ζητοῦσι.

Volunt Græci quæ dicuntur sibi probari per causas natu- rales. In Manuscripto est, ἐπιζητοῦσι.

## 1:23
V. 23. But we preach Christ crucified.

We do not bring forward reasons, but testimony concerning a thing witnessed.

To the Jews indeed a stumbling block.

Not only because believing in one crucified seemed shameful to them, but because, moreover, this profession of faith dragged the cross along with it: Gal. V. 11.

But to the Greeks foolishness.

It seemed insipid to them that nothing was brought forward concerning the principles of things, concerning ends, concerning the nature of the soul: which are the elements of moral wisdom among the Greeks.

Latin:

V. 23. ἡμεῖς δὲ κηρύσσομεν Χριστὸν ἐσταυρωμένον.

Non rationes adferimus, sed testimonium de re con- specta.

Ἰουδαίοις μὲν σκάνδαλον.

Non tantum quia in crucifixum credere probrosum ipsis videbatur, sed quia insuper hæc fidei professio crucem se- cum trahebat: Gal. V. 11.

Ἕλλησι δὲ μωρίαν.

Insipidurn illis videbatur nihil adferri de rerum princi- piis, de finibus, de animi natura: quæ elementa sunt apud Græcos sapientiæ moralis.

## 1:24
V. 24. but to those who are called.

They are called called here with effect, that is, those who have obeyed the calling, as in Rom. VIII. 28.

Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

These things are to be understood by μετάληψιν: because through Christ God shows both his power for converting men, (see Rom. I. 16.) and his wisdom, concerning which it was treated in Rom. XI. 32. See also below II. 7. and Isaiah LIII. 12.

Christ is called the power and wisdom of God, not because God shows his power and wisdom through him in conversion: for thus the Apostles also could have been called the power and wisdom of God: but because in the cross itself, that is, in his salutary passion and death, because it is a matter of Christ crucified and the cross of Christ, he exerted power by overcoming death, and wisdom by procuring for us eternal salvation through the merit of his active and passive obedience even to the death of the cross, concerning which Isaiah LII. 13. Behold my servant shall act prudently. For it shines forth, if anywhere else, in this business of our redemption and salvation, the power and wisdom of God: the divine power and wisdom of the Son of God himself, our Redeemer and Savior, shines forth in his whole life, which was entirely a passive action and an active passion, for the perfecting of the redemption of the human race, until he should exclaim on the cross, IT IS FINISHED: whence most powerfully and most wisely, as the very power of God Luke I. 35. and the hypostatic wisdom of God Prov. VIII. 22. he performed the work of our redemption, and brought it to an end, and became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him Heb. V. 9. Chrysostom excellently illustrates the present passage again: Great, he says, is the prudence of those things which have been said. For he wishes to say, in what manner God conquered through contraries, and in what manner the preaching is not human. But what he says is of this kind: When we have said to the Jews: Believe, they say: Raise the dead, cast out demons, show us signs. But we, what do we say instead of these? He who is preached was driven to the cross and died. But this is enough, not only not to attract those who do not want it, but even to repel those who do want it: and yet he did not drive them away, but attracts and conquers and overcomes. Again, the Greeks demand from us the force of speaking and the subtleties of sophisms. But we preach the cross to them also: and what in the Jews seems to be weakness, this is foolishness in the Greeks. Since therefore we do not provide not only what they ask, but even the contraries of what they ask: for the cross not only seems not to be a sign if reason is examined, but even the destruction of a sign: and not only does it not seem to be a demonstration of virtue and power, but even a proof of weakness: and not only does it seem not to be a demonstration of wisdom, but even an opinion of foolishness. Since therefore those seeking signs and wisdom not only do not receive what they ask, but even hear the contraries of what they desire, and then are persuaded through contraries, in what manner is the power of that which is preached not infinite? This is Chrysostom.

Moreover, the Socinians do not adhere to the words of the Apostle in explaining the object of the Gospel, when the Apostle calls it Christ crucified, or the cross of Christ, nor do they correctly declare how Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God. For since they deny the satisfaction of Christ, and wish to make the death of Christ a way to demonstrate salvation, but not to merit salvation for us, they wish to look here not so much to the proclamation of the death of Christ as to his resurrection: as if it were shown in the resuscitation of Christ that, through the observation of the precepts of Christ, even if we undergo death, we obtain eternal life. Which end, however, Holy Scripture has nowhere defined for either the death or the resurrection of Christ: just as neither did Christ obtain the resurrection for himself by his obedience, nor can we by our obedience do things equal to Christ, and we are justified and saved solely through the obedience of Christ. John. Crellius in his Commentary on this passage explained the words of the Apostle thus: but we preach Christ crucified: that is, Christ who was crucified: Not that they

preached only the cross of Christ, but that they preached Christ and his doctrine, but in such a way that they would not at all forget the cross of Christ. But truly it is one thing to preach Christ crucified, another to preach Christ who was crucified. For there the cross of Christ, or Christ as he was crucified, is designated as the object, if not the only one, at least the principal one of the evangelical proclamation: here, however, it is implied that Christ is indeed preached, that same one who was crucified, but this is only a specification of the object: it is not taught that it is to be understood reduplicatively, insofar as he was crucified. Then, by Christ, the doctrine of Christ is wrongly understood, when the doctrine concerning Christ is designated peculiarly and explicitly, and indeed concerning the cross, i.e., the passion and death of Christ, as having been endured by Christ in our place and for the expiation of our sins: concerning which Crellius himself at verse 13 had to confess: that by his death Christ procured for us the right to eternal salvation: and Schlichting in his Commentary on this passage v. 13. Was Paul crucified for you? That is, did he allow himself to be driven to the cross for your sins, so that, having been made a victim for them, he might release you from their guilt and punishment, and assert you into the right of eternal life? Christ alone did this, so that he might make you his own, and buy and claim you for himself with his own blood. Thirdly, the Apostle does not only profess that he preaches Christ in such a way that he would not at all forget the cross of Christ, but he constitutes the cross of Christ as the principal object of his proclamation: just as 1. Cor. II. 3. he affirms, I did not judge to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified: which passage Crellius again wrongly perverts thus, that is, except the doctrine of Christ: for it is one thing to be the doctrine of Christ, but another thing to be Christ, and him crucified: the Apostle constitutes Christ, not the doctrine of Christ, as the object of his proclamation, if not the only one, at least the principal one: and Crellius himself admits at v. 18 that the discourse concerning the cross is the announcement of Christ crucified; in which matter, he says, is contained the preaching of the whole Gospel, which rests upon the cross of Christ. Wherefore that gloss of Crellius on the words of the Apostle Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God is foreign: To the called and the faithful, Christ, whom we preach, seems to be the power and wisdom of God, in him they recognize it, they are astonished and marvel, while they think, namely, that he was raised from the dead and exalted by God above all things. For it is of immense power to recall a man extinguished by death to life, and that everlasting, and to confer upon him supreme power over all things. But where such great power appears, there it is necessary that wisdom also be present. For without wisdom so great a thing cannot be accomplished. Add that in this, wisdom shines forth as altogether peculiarly remarkable, that God willed to lead Christ to such great glory through the cross and such an infamous death. To which Schlichtingius has twin points in his Commentary on this passage regarding Christ: Understand it as ἀπὸ κοινοῦ we preach. It includes all things which they preached concerning Christ. The power of God and the wisdom of God. That is, by metonymy of the cause, a thing most full of the power of God and the wisdom of God, or, the greatest work and effect of the power of God and the wisdom of God; of power indeed, because He raised the crucified Christ from the dead and exalted him to heavenly majesty; of wisdom, however, because He suffered him first to be crucified, that is, to be affected by death, and that most ignominious and most bitter. For that was most especially expedient for His divine counsel, by which through death, through afflictions and ignominies, He leads the pious to life and heavenly glory; so that both their faith, constancy, and patience may have that in which to unfold and exercise itself, and the power, wisdom, and goodness of God may become so much the more illustrious, and so much the greater glory may redound to God. What therefore was more fitting than that the greatest leader and prince of the pious or sons of God, the Son, by the same way should be led to the life and glory destined for him before the ages in heaven? That, I say, he should both die, and if he had to die, that he should die for the truth by a violent and bloody death, by which he might at once become a victim for the sins of the world, and if a bloody one, that he should also die by a most ignominious death, from which he might both free his followers from the fear of all these things, and himself having experienced them, might bring to his own a most certain confidence of help, and having been made a victim for the sins of all, might draw all to himself, and at the same time that they might be in him, which things, just as they showed and uncovered upright minds, so also perverse ones, averted from truth and piety. These are the words of Schlichting. But (1.) the Apostle had said that he preached Christ crucified, or the cross of Christ: he had not, however, indicated here everything that he preached concerning Christ. (2.) Why should we admit a metonymy of the cause, when Christ is properly the hypostatic power and wisdom of GOD: and that he showed himself to be such even in the mystery of redemption, so that Schlichting has no reason to wonder here that it could have seemed to Christians that Christ is called in this passage that Wisdom which is celebrated in Solomon: nay, he ought rather to wonder that the Socinians cannot see that, that Solomon designated and understood Christ just as much through wisdom as Paul here called Christ the Wisdom of God: and that Schlichting so perverts the passage of Solomon in Prov. VIII, that Wisdom is understood there as that which is taught and handed down by God to men, but Paul calls it the indwelling wisdom and power of God, insofar as it is his work and effect, as he himself speaks monstrously: (for how is that indwelling in God which is the work and effect of God, i.e., outside of God?) when it is plain that Solomon is dealing with the Wisdom of God, which from eternity, before any man existed, was with God, and existed as the artificer and maker of created things, and thus with the hypostatic Wisdom, the Son of God, through whom all things were created, John I. 1, 2, 3, and that Paul does not call Christ wisdom in any other sense, certainly not understanding wisdom which is the work and effect of God. For that hypostatic power and wisdom, which is truly God, willed to be manifested in the flesh, so that it might powerfully and wisely accomplish our redemption, by overcoming Satan, and destroying sin and death, the works of Satan, 1 Tim. III. 15, 1 John III. 8, Heb. II. 14, and in this the divine force and wisdom shone forth most greatly, that such great things were effected through the cross and death of Christ. (3.) Rashly, therefore, are those things which are said to shine forth in the cross and death of Christ dragged by the Socinians to the resurrection of Christ; as if nothing else is hinted at than the power demonstrated in the resuscitation of Christ, and the wisdom situated in the fact that he willed Christ to be affected by death beforehand. For no mention of the resurrection of Christ is made here. (4.) This enervation of the power of the death of Christ is heretical, and an overturning of the divine economy concerning our salvation, as if Christ only died and was resurrected for the purpose that it might be shown that the pious are led to heavenly life through death and affliction: and that the Son of God was led to eternal life by the same way: whereas Christ died not that he might procure glory for himself, because he was already in the form of God, Phil. II. 6, and whereas he was rich, he willed to become poor for our sake, 2 Cor. 8. 9. and for the joy that was set before him, he endured the cross, despising the shame, Heb. XII. 2, nor to show us the life by which God leads to life, but to merit life for us; for he was given for the life of the world, John VI. 51, nor that he might die for the truth, because his death was not a testimony, but a ransom and a counter-ransom for all, the price of the solution given to God in place of us all, 1 Tim. II. 6, nor is he said to have been made a victim for the world in any other sense than that the sins of the world were transferred onto him, and he himself underwent death in the place of men, just as victims had to be offered in the place of men as a type of that thing 2. Cor. V. 14, 21. Finally, he underwent not only a most ignominious death, but also a cursed one for us, when he was made a curse in our place, so that we might be freed from the curse, Gal. III. 13, without which redemption no one could be freed from the fear of death or eternal curse, nor could anyone have confidence of grace or salvation, Heb. II. 14, nor was there any place for conversion: because we were all under the power and kingdom of Satan, Col. I. 13. Concerning which things more has been said in the assertion of the Catholic dogma, concerning the satisfaction of Christ, in the Socinismo profligato.

Latin:

V. 24. αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς.

Κλητοὶ hic appellantur cum effectu, id est, ii qui voca- tioni paruerunt, ut Rom. IIX. 28.

Χριστὸν Θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ Θεοῦ σοφίαν.

Hæc per μετάληψιν accipienda: quia per Christum Deus ostendit, & potentiam suam ad homines convertendos, (vi- de Rom. I. 16.) & sapientiam, de qua actum Rom. XI. 32. Vide & infra II. 7. & Esaiæ LIII. 12.

Christus DEI virtus & sapientia dicitur, non quòd in conversione Deus virtutem suam & sa- pientiam per ipsum ostendat: sic enim etiam Apo- stoli dici potuissent Dei virtus & sapientia: sed quòd in ipsa cruce, id est, passione & morte suâ salutiferâ, quia de Christo crucifixo, & cruce Chri- sti agitur, virtutem exeruerit, mortem superando, & sapientiam per meritum obedientiæ suæ activæ & passivæ usque ad mortem crucis, nobis æternam sa- lutem conciliando, quo de Es. LII. 13. Ecce servus meus prudenter aget. Elucet enim, si uspiam aliàs, in hoc negotio redemtionis, & salutis nostræ Dei vir- tus, & sapientia: elucet ipsiusmet Filii Dei Redem- toris & Salvatoris nostri divina potentia & sapien- tia in tota vita ejus, quæ tota actio passiva, & passio activa fuit, ad perficiendam redemtionem generis humani, usque dum in cruce exclamaret, CON- SUMMATUM EST: unde potentissimè & sapi- entissimè, ceu ipsa virtus Dei Luc. I. 35. & sapientia Dei hypostatica Prov. IIX. 22. opus redemtionis no- stræ peregit, & ad finem perduxit, ac causa factus o- mnibus ipsi obedientibus æternæ salutis Ebr. V. 9. Eximiè iterum præsentem locum illustrat Chryso- stomus: Magna, inquit, est eorum, quæ dicta sunt, prudentia. Vult enim dicere, quemadmodum Deus vicit per contraria, & quemadmodum non sit hu- mana prædicatio. Quod autem dicit, est ejusmodi: Quando dixerimus Judæis: Credite, dicunt: Mor- tuos excitate, dæmones ejicite, signa nobis ostendite. Nos autem pro iis quid dicimus? In crucem actus est & mortuus qui prædicatur. Hoc autem satis est, non solum ad eos, qui nolunt, non attrahendos, sed & ad eos, qui volunt, repellendos: & tamen non expulit, sed attrahit & vincit, & superat. Rursum Græci à nobis exigunt vim dicendi & sophismatum argutias. Nos autem eis quoque crucem prædicamus: & quod in Judæis videtur esse imbecillitatis, hoc est in Græ- cis stultitia. Quum ergo non solùm quæ petunt non præbeamus, sed etiam eorum quæ petunt contraria: crux enim non solum videtur non esse signum si ratio ne examinetur, sed etiam signi peremtio: & non so- lùm non videtur esse ostensio virtutis ac potentiæ, sed etiam probatio imbecillitatis: & non solùm videtur non esse ostensio sapientiæ, sed etiam opinio stultitiæ. Quum ergo signa quærentes & sapientiam, non so lum non accipiant, quæ petunt, sed etiam contraria audiant eorum, quæ cupiunt, & deinde persuadean- tur per contraria, quemadmodum non est virtus infinita ejus quod prædicatur? Hæc Chrysostomus.

Cætèrùm Sociniani nec in objecto Evangelii explicando Apostoli verbis inhærent, cùm Apo- stolus id Christum crucifixum, vel crucem Christi dicit, nec rectè declarant, quomodo Christus cru- cifixus sit potentia Dei, & sapientia Dei. Nam quum fatisfactionem Christi inficientur, mortemque Chri- sti ad viam salutis demonstrandam, non verò ad sa- lutem nobis promerendam facere velint, non tàm mortis Christi, quàm resurrectionis præconium hîc respici volunt: ac si in resuscitatione Christi monstretur, per observationem præceptorum Chri- sti, etiamsi mortem subeamus, nos consequi æternam vitam. Quem verò finem Scriptura Sacra nuspiam sive morti, sive resurrectioni Christi definivit: quem- admodum nec Christus obedientiâ suâ resurre- ctionem sibi impetravit, neque nos obedientiâ nostrâ Christo paria facere possumus, & unicè per obedientiam Christi justificamur, & salvamur. Joh. Crellius in Commentar. ad h. l. ita exposuit verba Apostoli: nos verò prædicamus Christum crucifixum: id est, Christum qui crucifixus sit: Non quòd solam

Christi crucem prædicarent, sed quod prædicarent Christum & illius doctrinam, sed ita ut crucis Christi minimè obliviscerentur. At verò aliud est Chri- stum crucifixum prædicare, aliud prædicare Chri- stum, qui crucifixus est. Nam ibi objectum si non unicum, saltem præcipuum Evangelici præconii designatur crux Christi, vel Christus quà crucifi- xus: hîc verò Christus quidem prædicari innuitur, idem ille, qui crucifixus est, at specificatio tantùm hæc objecti est: non verò reduplicativè id, qua- tenus crucifixus est, intelligendum esse docetur. Deinde per Christum perperam intelligitur doctri- na Christi, quum designetur peculiariter & exertè doctrina de Christo, & quidem de cruce, h. e. pas- sione & morte Christi, utpote nostri loco, & pro peccatis nostris expiandis à Christo exantlatâ: de qua fateri Crellius ipse ad vers. 13. necessum habuit: quòd suâ morte Christus nobis & jus ad æternam sa- lutem pepererit: & Schlichting. in Commentar. ad h. l. v. 13. An Paulus pro vobis crucifixus est? Id est, an se pro peccatis vestris in crucem agi passus est, ut pro iis victima factus vos eorum reatu & pœnâ solveret, & in æternæ vitæ jus assereret? Hoc solus Christus fecit, ut vos suos faceret, & suo sanguine sibi soli emeret, ac vindicaret. Tertiò non tantùm, ita prædicare se Christum profitetur Apostolus, ut crucis Christi minimè oblivisceretur, sed hûc præci- puum objectum constituit præconii sui crucem Christi: quemadmodum 1. Cor. II. 3. affirmat, non judicavi quicquam scire inter vos, nisi Jesum Chri- stum, & hunc crucifixum: quem locum perperam ita iterum pervertit Crellius, id est, nisi Christi do- ctrinam: aliud enim est doctrina Christi, aliud ve- rò est Christus, isque crucifixus: objectum si non unicum, solum præcipuum præconii sui constituit Apostolus Christum, non verò doctrinam Christi: & fatetur Crellius ipse ad v. 18. Sermonem de cruce esse annunciationem Christi crucifixi; quâ in re, inquit, continetur Totius Evangelii prædicatio, quod Christi cruci innititur. Quapropter aliena est illa Crellii glossa verborum Apostoli Christum Dei po- tentiam & Dei sapientiam: Vocatis & fidelibus Chri- stus, quem nos prædicamus, videtur esse potentia & sapientia Dei, in eo eam agnoscunt, stupent ac miran- tur, dum nimirum cogitant, eum à mortuis resusci- tatum & supra omnia à Deo exaltatum fuisse. Ingen- tis enim est potentiæ hominem morte extinctum, ad vitam, eamque sempiternam revocare, & illi summam in cuncta potestatem conferre. Ubi autem tanta potentia apparet, illic & sapientiam esse necesse est. Sine sapientiâ enim res tanta perfici non potest. Ad- de quod in eo peculiariter insignis prorsus sapientia eluceat, quod per crucem & mortem tam infamem Deus ad tantam gloriam Christum perducere volue- rit. Quibus gemina habet Schlichtingius in Com- mentario ad h. l. Christum: Intellige ἀπὸ κοινοῦ præ- dicamus. Includit omnia, quæ de Christo prædica- bant. Dei potentiam & Dei sapientiam. Id est, per metonym. causæ, rem Dei potentiâ & Dei sapientiâ plenissimam, vel, Dei potentiæ & Dei sapientiæ ma- ximum opus & effectum; potentiæ quidem, quòd Christum crucifixum ex mortuis suscitaverit, & ad cœlestem evexerit majestatem; sapientiæ autem, quòd eum prius crucifigi, id est, morte affici, eaque igno- miniosissimâ & acerbissimâ passus sit. Id enim divino illius consilio vel maximè expedivit, quo per mortem, per afflictiones & ignominias pios ducit ad vitam & gloriam cœlestem; ut & illorum fides, constantia, pa- tientia habeat, in quo se explicet & exerceat, & Dei potentia, sapientia, bonitas tantò fiat illustrior, tanto- que major in Deum gloria redundet. Quid igitur magis conveniebat, quam ut maximus piorum seu filiorum Dei ductor & princeps Filius, eâdem viâ perduceretur ad destinatam sibi ante secula in cœlis vitam & gloriam? ut, inquam, & moreretur, & si moriendum esset, ut moreretur pro veritate morte violentâ & cruentâ, quo simul & victima fieret pro peccatis mundi, & si cruenta, ut etiam morte more- retur ignominiosissimâ, à quo & metu rerum istarum omnium sectatores suos solveret, & ipsemet earum expertus, certissimam auxilii fiduciam suis adfer- ret, & victima pro peccatis omnium factus, omnes ad se traheret, & simul ut in ipso essent, quæ sicut pro- bos, sic & pravos animos, à veritate ac pietate aver- sos, ostenderent & detegerent. Hæc Schlichtingius. At (1.) Apostolus Christum se prædicare dixerat crucifixum, vel crucem Christi: non verò omnia hic indicarat, quæ de Christo prædicavit. (2.) Cur metonymiam causæ admittamus, cum Christus propriè DEI virtus & sapientia sit hypostatica: talemque se etiam in mysterio redemtionis osten- derit, ut mirari hìc non habeat Schlichtingius, Christianis videri potuisse, Christum hoc loco sa- pientiam illam, quæ apud Salomonem celebratur, dici: quin mirari potius oporteat, quòd id Soci- niani videre nequeant, æquè Christum designasse ac per sapientiam intellexisse Salomonem, atque Paulum hîc Christum Sapientiam Dei dixisse: quod- que Schlichtingius locum Salomonis Prov. IIX. ita pervertat, quòd ibi intelligatur Sapientia, quæ docetur & traditur à Deo hominibus, Paulus autem insitam Dei sapientiam & potentiam appellet, qua- tenus illius opus & effectus est, uti monstrofe ipse loquitur: (nam quomodo Deo insitum est, quod Dei opus & effectus, h. e. extra Deum est?) quum planum sit, Salomonem agere de Sapientia Dei, quæ ab æterno, antequam ullus hominum esset, apud Deum fuit, & artifex, ac opifex rerum crea- tarum extitit, adeoque de Sapientia hypostaticâ, Filio Dei, per quem creata sunt omnia Joh. I. 1. 2. 3. nec Paulum Christum alio sensu sapientiam dicere, non certè sapientiam, quæ sit Dei opus & effectus, intelligere. Nam virtus illa, & sapientia hypostati- ca, quæ verè Deus est, manifestari in carne voluit, ut potenter & sapienter redemtionem nostram perageret, vincendo Satanam, ac destruendo pec- catum, & mortem, opera Satanæ, 1. Tim. III. 15. 1. Joh. III. 8. Ebr. II. 14. inque eo eluxit maximè vis & sapientia divina, quòd res tantæ per crucem & mortem Christi effectæ sint. (3.) Temerè ergò quæ in cruce & morte Christi effulgere dicuntur, à Socinianis ad resurrectionem Christi trahuntur; quasi nihil aliud innuatur, quàm potentia in Chri- sti resuscitatione demonstrata, & sapientia in eo sita, quod prius Christum morte affici voluerit. Nam nulla hìc resurrectionis Christi facta est mentio. (4.) Hæretica est hæc virtutis mortis Christi ener- vatio, & œconomias divinæ de salute nostra ever- sio, quasi tantum mortuus Christus & resuscitatus sit eo fine, ut ostenderetur, per mortem & afflictio- nem pios duci ad cœlestem vitam: eâdemque viâ perductus sit Filius Dei ad vitam æternam: quum mortuus Christus sit non ut sibi gloriam concilia- ret, quia in forma Dei jam erat, Phil. II. 6. & quum dives esset pauper nostri causâ fieri voluit 2. Cor. 8. 9. & ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης αὐτῷ χαρᾶς, ὑπέμεινε ςαυ- ρὸν, αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας Ebr. XII. 2. nec ut nobis vitam ostenderet quà Deus ad vitam ducit, sed ut nobis vitam promereretur; datus enim est pro mun- di vita Joh. VI. 51. neque ut moreretur pro veritate, quia mors ejus non fuit μαρτύριον, sed λύτρον & ἀν- τίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, solutionis pretium Deo no- stri omnium loco datum 1. Tim. II. 6. neque victima factus pro mundo alio sensu dicitur, quàm quod peccata mundi in ipsum translata, & ipse loco ho- minum mortem subierit, uti victimæ loco hominu offerri in ejus rei typum debuêre 2. Cor. V. 14. 21. denique mortem non ignominiofissimam tantum, sed etiam maledictam subiit pro nobis, cum nostri lo- co maledictum factus est, ut nos à maledictione libera- remur Gal. III. 13. sine qua redemptione nec à me- tu mortis, aut maledictionis æternæ quisquam sol- vi, nec fiduciam gratiæ, aut salutis habere poterat Ebr. II. 14. nec ullus conversioni locus erat: quia omnes sub potestate & regno Satanæ eramus Col. I. 13. De quibus in assertione dogmatis Catho- lici, de satisfactione Christi, in Socinismo profligato uberiùs dictum.

## 1:25
v. 25. For the foolishness of God) Said comparatively, that is, that which is the least in the Wisdom of God.

is wiser than men.) It is said concisely for wiser than the wisdom of men. Thus in Pliny, having obtained the laurel of all triumphs, the greater. For it is understood, of laurels.

And the weakness of) And this is to be taken comparatively: for it signifies that which is the least in the power of God.

is stronger than men) And here understand than the strong. The sense is the same, which is expressed proverbially in 1 Kings 22. 10.

Latin:

v. 25. ὅτι τὸ μωρὸν τῦ Θεῦ) Comparatè dictum, id est, quod in Sapientia Dei minimum est.

σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐσί.) Est contractè dictum pro σοφώτερον τῦ σοφῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Sic apud Plinium omnium triumphorum lauream adeptæ majorem. Subauditur enim, laureis.

καὶ τὸ ἀσθενὲς τῦ) Et hoc comparatè sumendum: Signi- ficatur enim id, quod in Dei potentia minimum est.

ἰσχυρότερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐσί) Et hic subaudi τῦ ἰσχυρῦ. Idem sensus est, qui proverbialiter exprimitur 1. Reg. 22. 10.

## 1:26
v. 26. For you see your calling, brothers) And here is a metonymy. For he calls the calling the outcome of the calling. Few, such as Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Sergius, had believed the Gospel: many fishermen, many tradesmen: not that the Gospel rejects men of any lot from itself, but because those less burdened enter the narrow way more easily. See Matt. V. 3, XIX. 23, and what is said there. Lactantius VII. 1. No one favors virtue, unless he who can follow it: but to follow is not easy for all: those can, whom poverty and the lack of things have exercised and made capable of virtue. For if virtue is the tolerance of evils, then those who have always been in good things do not grasp virtue: because they have neither experienced evils, nor can they bear them, through habit and the desire for the good things which alone they have known. Hence it happens that the poor and humble believe in God more easily than the rich, who are entangled, nay, chained and fettered by many impediments, and serve at the beck and call of the mistress Greed, who has ensnared them in inextricable bonds: nor can they look up to heaven, because their mind is prone to the earth and fixed upon the ground. Moreover, the way of virtue does not admit those carrying great burdens. The path is very narrow through which righteousness leads a man into heaven. No one can keep to it unless he has been unencumbered and naked. See also what follows there. He says this because among the Corinthians some set themselves before others on account of their learning, others on account of their riches.

Calling, therefore, is taken in a special sense. For calling is spoken of in two ways in Scripture: first, γενικῶς and absolutely, in which manner all who are in the Church are called, whether they be worthy or unworthy, Matt. 22. Then, εἰδικῶς and specially, or with effect: insofar as calling is viewed with its fruit. Which is that of those who receive the calling with true faith and live worthily of it. This was rightly observed against Huber in Confess. brev. p. 22 by the blessed Baldwin, who confuses himself when he makes election broader than calling; for he says the former belongs to all, but the latter to few, or not to many. It is evident, however, from this passage most clearly that election is particular, and not of all: because not many are called with effect, much less are all elected: for there is no doubt that even among these Corinthians who were called with effect and sanctified, some could fall away: whence the Arminians do not indeed observe badly that the word election is sometimes taken without respect to predestination: See also 2 Tim. 1:9, but they wrongly deny for that reason that another meaning of election is given, namely under the condition of the foresight of the perseverance of faith, or that a double predestination must be conceded. Conf. Censura Leidens. on chap. 17 of the Confess. Remonstrant.

ὅ πολλοὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα) supply, have believed. He calls those wise according to the flesh who excel in the wisdom of this world, as he had just said: namely, that which is not from revelation. For the flesh is opposed to divine revelation. Matt. 7:17.

ὅ πολλοὶ δυνατοὶ) Those in political dignities, as in Rev. 6:15. גִּבּוֹרִים.

ὅ πολλοὶ ἐυγενεῖς) noble by birth, such as the Cypselidae and Bacchiadae of Corinth.

Latin:

v. 26. βλέπετε γὰρ τὴν κλῆσιν ὑμῶν ἀδελφοὶ) Et hîc est μετωνυμία. Nam κλῆσιν dicit eventum vocationis. Pauci, qualis Nicodemus, Josephus Arimathensis, Sergius, cre- diderant Evangelio: multi piscatores, multi sellularii: non quod Evangelium ullius sortis homines à se abjiciat, sed quòd arctam viam faciliùs ingrediantur minus sarcinati. Vide Matth. V. 3. XIX. 23. & ibi dicta. Lactantius VII. 1. Nemo virtuti favet, nisi qui sequi potest: Sequi autem non est facile omnibus: ii possunt, quos paupertas & rerum indigentia exercuit & capaces virtutis effecit. Nam si virtus est toleran- tia malorum, non capiunt ergo virtutem, qui semper in bonis fuerunt: quia mala neque experti sunt, neque ferre possunt, assuetudine ac desiderio bonorum quæ sola noverunt. Eo fit ut pauperes & humiles Deo credant facilius, quam divites, qui sunt impedimentis multis implicati, imo catenati & compediti, serviunt ad nutum Dominæ cupiditatis, quæ illos inextricabili- bus vinculis irretivit: neque possunt in cælum aspicere, quo- niam mens eorum in terram prona humique defixa est. Virtutis autem via non capit magna onera portantes. Angustus admodù trames est, per quem justitia hominem deducit in cælum. Hunc tenere non potest, nisi qui fuerit expeditus & nudus. Vide & quæ ibi sequuntur. Hoc ideo dicit, quia inter Corinthios alii ob doctrinam alii ob divitias sese anteponebant aliis.

Vocatio igitur accipitur speciali sensu. Nam duobus modis vocatio dicitur in Scriptura: pri- mùm γενικῶς & absolutè, quo pacto omnes voca- ti dicuntur, qui in Ecclesia sunt, sive digni sint, sive indigni Matth. XXII. Deinde εἰδικῶς & specialiter, vel cum effectu: quatenus vocatio cum fructu suo spectatur. Quæ eorum est, qui verâ fide vocatio- nem accipiunt, eâque dignè vivunt. Quod contra Huberum in Confess. brev. p. 22. rectè observatum à B. Balduino, semetipsum confundentem, quando electionem latiorem facit vocatione; illam n. omnium esse dicit, hanc verò paucorum, vel non multorum. Patet autem ex hoc loco apertissimè, particularem, non verò omnium esse electionem: quia non mul- ti vocati sunt cum effectu, nedum omnes electi: nam & ex his cum effectu vocatis ac sanctificatis Corinthiis quosdam potuisse deficere dubium nõ est: unde Arminiani non male quidem observant, vocem electionis sumi quandoque citra respectum ad prædestinationem: Vide & 2. Tim. I. 9. sed ma- lè ideò negant, aliam dari electionis significationem, sub conditione, prævisione sc. perseverantiæ fidei, aut duplicem prædestinationem concedendam esse. Conf. Censura Leidens. ad cap. XVII. Confess. Remonstrant.

ὅ πολλοὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα) supple, crediderunt. Sapien- tes secundum carnem vocat eos, qui pollent sapientiâ mun- di hujus, ut modò dixerat: eâ scilicet, quæ non est ex reve- latione. Revelationi enim divinæ caro opponitur. Mat. 7, 17.

ὅ πολλοὶ δυνατοὶ) In dignitatibus politi, ut Apoc. VI. 15. גִּבּוֹרִים.

ὅ πολλοὶ ἐυγενεῖς) genere nobiles, quales Corinthi Cypse- lidæ & Bacchiadæ.

## 1:27
vers. 27. ἀλλὰ τὰ μωρὰ τῦ κόσμυ ἐξελέξατο ὁ Θεὸς) τὰ μωρὰ τῦ κόσμυ, that is, τῷ κόσμῳ, such a manner of speaking we have had & Rom. IX. 3. those who are held by the world almost as fools for lack of learning. See Proverbs VIII. 3. Then there is a metonymy: God chose, that is, they believed; for those who believe, God chooses, or approves. And note that the neuter gender is used for the common: as also elsewhere, and in the following.

that he might put to shame the wise) who could never show themselves equal to such a standard.

and the weak things of the world) he understands men of the common people.

that he might put to shame the strong) just as he had said the powerful. Job XII. 19. ואיתנים יסלף he overthrows the mighty of the earth.

Latin:

vers. 27. ἀλλὰ τὰ μωρὰ τῦ κόσμυ ἐξελέξατο ὁ Θεὸς) τὰ μωρὰ τῦ κόσμυ, id est, τῷ κόσμῳ, quale loquendi genus- habuimus & Rom. IX. 3. eos qui à mundo ob eruditionis penuriam penè pro stultis habentur. Vide Proverb. IIX. 3. Deinde est μετωνυμία· elegit Deus, id est, crediderunt; qui enim credunt, eos Deus eligit, sive approbat. Et nota ge- nus neutrum poni pro communi: ut & alibi, & in sequen- tibus.

ἵνα τοὺς σοφοὺς καταισχύνη) qui semet præstare ad talem normam nunquam potuere.

καὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ τοῦ κόσμου) intelligit homines de plebe.

ἵνα καταισχύνη τὰ ἰσχυρά) quomodo dixerat δυνατούς. Job. XII. 19. ואיתנים יסלף δυνάστας δὲ γῆς κατέστρεψε.

## 1:28
v. 28. and the base things of the world) Those who are held by men to be ignoble. Julian in book VI reproaches the Christians, because most of them were menservants and maidservants. You may also learn from Pliny that there were maidservants in the ministry of the Church. Chrysostom below on chapter II says that it was objected to the Christians that the greatest part of them were nurses, midwives, eunuchs.

and the despised things) For such are wont to be despised. Concerning this word see Mark IX. 12. Luke XVIII. 9. Acts IV. 11. Rom. XIV. 3. 10.

and the things that are not, that he might bring to nothing the things that are) a Hebraic hyperbole, which uses אין and אפס concerning things that are very abject. See Isaiah XL. 17. in contrast to the things that are, just as the word is said of that which is of value. Gal. VI. 3. Then indeed take to bring to nothing, as Rom. III. 31. shows it to be of no account. All these things had been prefigured in the times of the exodus from Egypt, and in David's fight against Goliath and his subsequent elevation to the kingdom, and again in the times of Ezra and Nehemiah.

Schlichting explains the word to bring to nothing, and says that those who are not, will be in the future, but those who are, will be brought to nothing: which, if taken simply, imply that the impious will not be resurrected, but will be brought to nothing, about which we have spoken in the Profligated Socinianism: but here the word to bring to nothing denotes not annihilation, but destruction and punishment: or rather confusion, as Grotius rightly says, by which he shows that they are nothing, so that no flesh may glory in his presence. Crellius on this passage says: He uses the word for destroying because of the conciseness of the opposition: God made something out of that which is not, and made nothing out of that which is. But those things are destroyed when they are despised by God, rejected, and not counted in the number of the Church. But it is evident here how vain is the hypothesis of the Papists concerning the Church, that, namely, external glory, happiness, and greatness are proper to it, and that these ought to be recognized as marks of the Church.

Latin:

v. 28. καὶ τὰ ἀγενῆ τοῦ κόσμου) Eos qui apud homines ha- bentur ignobiles. Julianus libro VI. exprobat Christianis, quòd plerique eorum essent servi & ancillæ. Etiam in mi- nisterio Ecclesiæ ancillas fuisse ex Plinio discas. Chrysosto- mus infra ad caput II. objectum ait Christianis, maximam eorum partem fuisse nutrices, obstetrices, eunuchos.

καὶ τὰ ἐξουθενημένα) Solent enim tales despici. De hoc verbo vide Marc. IX. 12. Luc. XIIX. 9. Act. IV. 11. Rom. XIV. 3. 10.

καὶ τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ἵνα τὰ ὄντα καταργήση) ὑπερβολὴ Hebrai- ca, quæ אין & אפס usurpat de rebus valdè abjectis. Vide Es. XL. 17. contrà τὰ ὄντα sicut & τὸ dicitur de eo, quod in pretio est. Gal. VI. 3. Tum vero καταργῆσαι sume, ut Rom. III. 31. ostendit esse nihili. Hæc omnia præfigurata fuerant tem- poribus exitûs ex Aegypto, & in Davidis pugna contra Go- liathum & ejusdem evectione in regnum, & rursus tempo- ribus Esdræ & Nehemiæ.

Schlichtingius vocem καταργεῖν explicat in ni- hilum redigere, & istos quidem qui non sunt, in æternum futuros, illos autem qui sunt, in nihilum re- dactum iri, ait: quæ si simpliciter accipiantur, impios non resuscitatum, sed in nihilum redactum iri, innuunt, quo de in Socinismo profligato dixi- mus: at hîc τὸ καταργεῖν non annihilationem, sed perditionem & pœnam notat: vel potius confusio- nem, ut rectè Grotius, quo ostendat ea nihil esse, ne ulla caro glorietur coram ipso. Crellius ad hunc loc. Utitur, inquit, destruendi verbo propter oppositio- nis concinnitatem: Deus ex eo, quod non est, fecit aliquid, & ex eo quod est, fecit nihil. Destruuntur verò ista, cùm à Deo contemnuntur, repudiantur, in numerum Ecclesiæ non leguntur. Patet autem hîc, quàm vana sit Pontificiorum hypothesis de Ecclesia, quòd nimirum externa gloria, felicitas, & amplitudo ei propria sit, & hæ pro notis Eccle- siæ agnosci debeant.

## 1:29
v. 29. that no flesh should glory in the presence of God) God acted so that man might not attribute anything to himself in this matter. For to glory is to lean upon some thing, to rejoice in some thing. See Rom. II. 17. 23. V. 2. 3. 11. The words not and all are used by the Hebrews to deny universally.
