In the presence of God, that is, where the matter is with God. Where man is called flesh from the viler part, this is done to repress pride.

In the phrase of Scripture, man is called flesh, not synecdochically because of the body: but metonymically, because he is carnal by nature: John III. 5. and all glorying is denied to him, and the cause of the non-election of those things which are great in the world is rendered as the confusion of glorying in carnal things: nor is it poorly noted by Crellius, that it is indicated here that God, in choosing these and spurning those, does not use some absolute will without any fault of men, but is led to it by the pride and arrogance of men: for neither wisdom, nor wealth, nor nobility in themselves stand in the way of God; but the pride and contempt of others which is wont to be born from these and accompany them. But the Apostle also by this very thing beats back all our glorying before God. For since we are all only flesh outside the grace of regeneration, it is clear that no one can glory in any good work or merit, and no one can stand before God by his own righteousness, otherwise he would have something of which he could glory.

Latin:

v. 29. ὅπως μὴ καυχήσηται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Fecit Deus, ne quid in hoc negotio homo sibi tribueret. Nam καυχᾶσθαι est inniti alicui rei, lætari de re aliqua. Vide Rom. II. 17. 23. V. 2. 3. 11. μὴ & πᾶσα Hebræis universaliter negant. ἐνώπιον Θεοῦ, id est, ubi cum Deo res est. Ubi homo ex parte viliore caro appellatur, fit hoc ad fastum repri- mendum.

Caro phrasi Scripturæ homo dicitur, non synec- dochicè ob corpus: sed metonymicè, quia carna- lis est τῇ φύσει: Joh. III. 5. eique derogatur omnis καύχησις, & causa non electionis eorum, quæ ma- gna sunt in mundo, redditur confusio gloriationis in rebus carnalibus: nec malè notatum Crellio, indicari hîc, Deum in his eligendis, illis verò spernendis non absolutâ aliquâ voluntate sine ullâ hominum culpa uti, sed hominum fastu & superbiâ eò adduci: non enim Deo vel sapientia, vel opes, vel nobilitas per se obstant; sed quæ ex his nasci, illaque comitari solet, superbia, & aliorum comtemtus. Sed & retundit Apostolus eo ipso omnem gloriatio- nem nostram coram Deo. Quum enim omnes nos caro tantùm simus extra regenerationis gra- tiam, neminem de ullo bono opere, aut merito gloriari, neminem propriâ justitiâ coram Deo consistere posse, in aprico est, alioquin haberet, de quo gloriaretur.

## 1:30
v. 30. but of him are you in Christ Jesus) of here signifies the primary efficient cause, as Rom. II. 36. when it is used for through as the intermediate cause. And understand are, you are a new creature, you have been made far different than you were.

Although by the particle ἐξ God the Father is established as the fountain and primary origin of salvation, the particle ἐν does not merely denote a mediate or instrumental cause, but is employed for the sake of order and in respect of the mediatorial office of Christ. For we are from the Father, i.e., something, that is, by the grace of the Father. But we are something not of ourselves, because we are nothing but flesh, and are destitute of the glory of GOD, Rom. III. 23, but in Christ Jesus. For the Apostle also used the particle διὰ in v. 9, when he treated of God, through whom you were called, where Schlichtingius has it thus: not as through a mediate cause, but as through a primary and principal cause: For there is no cause superior to GOD, and the particle through has the force of signifying every kind of cause.

v. 30. who was made unto us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption.

There is here a perpetual metonymy of the effect placed for the cause. For Christ, God so providing, was made the cause through which we may be wise, namely divine, through which we may be cleansed from sins, through which we may be gifted with the Holy Spirit, through which we are to be delivered from death at some time: which is called redemption Rom. IIX. 23, Eph. IV. 30.

Because the Apostle instituted the removal of worldly wisdom, and power, and nobility, he now shows the true wisdom, and power, and nobility or dignity, which we have uniquely in Christ: Wisdom indeed, because he alone reveals the Father to us, which is true and solid wisdom Matth. XI. 27, in which eternal life consists, Joh. XIV. 8, ch. XVII. 3. But dignity and power, because in Christ we are children of God Joh. I. 12, victors, and lords of the world 1. Joh. V. 1, and heirs of eternal life Roman. V. 17, in which the highest nobility and glory, virtue and power consists. Therefore Christ was made unto us by GOD righteousness, that in him we might be established as righteous, and have a right to the heavenly kingdom: and sanctification, that we might not fall from that right through the temptations of the world, and of the Prince of the world, but in the kingdom of Christ might serve God in true holiness: and redemption, that finally liberated from every evil, we might be raised to eternal glory. Whence it is taught from Jeremiah, that neither the wise (outside of Christ) ought to glory in his wisdom, because in Christ alone is true wisdom, nor the rich in his riches, which are nothing without Christ, in whom alone we have righteousness and salvation, that true opulence and heavenly treasures; nor the strong in his strength, which is nothing without Christ for overcoming the world, and for obtaining liberation from every evil, and therefore that we ought to glory uniquely in the Lord, and in his grace. Concerning which let those things be compared which we said on Jer. IX. and Esa. XLV. 25. Christ was made unto us by God wisdom in the revelation of the Word Joh. I. 18, and in our conversion to faith, Actor. XXVI. 18. Righteousness in obedience, both active and passive, and its imputation through faith, and justification Rom. VIII. 3, ch. V. 18, 19, ch. IV. 6, holiness in the sanctification of the Spirit, and our renewal, 1. Corinth. I. 2, 5, VI. 11. & redemption, in our liberation from all evils, and eternal glorification, which we hope for from him, in him, and through him, Rom. VII. 14, 15, ch. IIX. 23, 24, 2. Tim. IV. 8, 18.

Crellius here denies the imputation of Righteousness: From wisdom, he says, and redemption it appears that this is not about any imputation of the righteousness and holiness of Christ; for otherwise we would neither be truly wise, nor would we ever be truly redeemed, but only through imputation: But it is not necessary that Christ be said to have been made wisdom and redemption to the Corinthians by the same reason by which he is said to have been made righteousness: just as he was not made redemption by the same reason by which he was made wisdom. For he had already been made wisdom to them actually and in reality through the bestowal of Wisdom; but he had not yet been made redemption to the Corinthians in that way, which they were expecting only in the liberation of the body. Furthermore, it can be conceded that Christ was made all those things for the Corinthians as far as merit or acquisition is concerned: because it is to be attributed to his merits that wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption have been procured for us. For in him and through him every blessing and all salvation comes to us, Eph. 1:4, Acts 4:12. But as far as their actual acquired by the virtue of the merit of Christ in regeneration and conversion, of righteousness in justification, of holiness in renewal, of redemption in our final liberation and glorification. As regards merit, therefore, there is agreement: but not as regards the act of application; for we are converted not through faith, but to faith; but we are justified not to faith, but through faith: we are sanctified, however, when faith exerts itself through love: in which manner, however, we are by no means justified: for this is a consequence of justification. Finally, we are liberated and glorified, having been justified and sanctified, when we persevere in faith and obtain its end, the salvation of souls, 1 Pet. 1:9. And this is that ἀπολύτρωσις τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν, concerning which Rom. 8:23, Luke 21:28, Eph. 4:31, Heb. 11:35, which, however, is not to be confused with the λυτρώσει & ἀπολυτρώσει made by the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:18, Rom. 3:24, Eph. 1:7, 14, Col. 1:14, because the former is the fruit of the latter: but the latter merited the former for us.

Furthermore, as to the order of these benefits, Crellius perverts it when he says that justification partly precedes sanctification and partly follows it; that it is partly the cause of the latter, and partly the effect. Inchoate justification, he says, precedes and produces holiness; but full and absolute justification follows holiness and is derived from it. Whence finally follows redemption, the complement of all our happiness. Therefore, this justification precedes sanctification; nevertheless, sanctification precedes redemption, which, since it happens to no one unless he has first been sanctified, nor does a fuller justification, which redemption necessarily follows, come to anyone unless he has first been sanctified, or has lived holily. Hence it is clear what should be thought of that most trite saying: Good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the justified. For they precede the one to be fully justified: they follow the justified in an inchoate way. Although faith and repentance taken strictly, that is, a firm assent to the doctrine of Christ, and a change of mind and purposes for the better, and a serious and upright detestation of a former life, must always entirely precede justification. Resp. 1. Justification entirely precedes sanctification and is its cause, which Crellius rightly acknowledges: but that justification also follows sanctification and is its effect, we deny, nor has Crellius proved it from the Scriptures: and those things are ἀντιφατικά, because the same thing cannot be both the cause and the effect of the same thing. 2. The distinction between inchoate and absolute justification rests on no foundation of Scripture: Justification is the remission of sins, but is there one remission that is inchoate and another that is consummated? Justification is the imputation of righteousness through faith without works: but is this both full and half-full? 3. That justification, or even salvation, is in any way derived from or depends upon holiness is contrary to Paul: for if it is by works, it is not by grace, otherwise works would not be works, Rom. 11:6. By grace you have been saved, through faith: and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast, Eph. 2:8, 9. If the inheritance were by the law, it would not be given by promise. But God freely gave it to Abraham by promise, κεχάρισαι, Gal. 3:18. 4. That a fuller justification necessarily follows redemption is ἀντίγραφον: for in those who are temporal, even if truly sanctified, that ἀπολύτρωσις does not follow, nor in those who, when they have been enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the mighty works of the age to come, have fallen away, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt, Heb. 6:4, 5, 6. 5. That full justification does not come to anyone unless he has first been sanctified, or has lived holily, the Apostle so far from teaching, that he teaches that Abraham was truly and absolutely justified χωρὶς ἔργων without works, Rom. 4; nay, he convinces us all that we are justified through faith without works, ch. 3, and clearly hands down that a holy life, or the pursuit of good works, does not precede absolute justification, but follows it: whence arose the rule of St. Augustine: Good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the justified: which Crellius in vain weakens by the distinction of inchoate and full justification: because the Apostle in chapters 3 and 4 of Romans does not speak only of the beginning of justification, whether our own or Abraham's, but of the whole or full justification, nowhere distinguishing between the beginning and the consummation of justification in such a way as to attribute the former to faith without works, but the latter to works themselves. 6. Faith is rightly said to precede justification, but faith is not merely a firm assent to the doctrine of Christ: since trust is required above all for faith, or a fiducial application of the righteousness of Christ; but a change of mind and purposes for the better does not by any means precede justification, but follows it, if that trite rule is true, good works follow the justified: and Crellius himself admits, when Christ is said to have been made righteousness and sanctification for us, that the righteousness, which he wishes to be put for justification, while we are justified through faith in Christ, precedes the sanctification by which we are made holy and are led away from sins: So also Schlichtingius: The Apostle, he says, arranged all these things in an elegant and natural order. For first we know the will of God and believe in God, in which matter there is wisdom; then righteousness is imputed to us: this is followed by sanctification with its effect, that is, a holy life, with holy morals; this finally is followed by redemption and eternal life.

Supply 'let it be': A similar ellipsis Rom. XV. 3. elsewhere, and below II. 9 v. 31. 'as it is written, let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.' The sense is concisely drawn from Jeremiah IX. 23, 24. Where in the Greek we have 'but thus says the Lord: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the strong man boast in his strength, and let not the rich man boast in his wealth, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows that I am the Lord, who exercises mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth.' Where in the Hebrew for 'let him boast' is יתהלל which is translated elsewhere by 'to rejoice'.

From this inference likewise and from the preceding, the blessed Hülsemann rightly argues in his unpublished annotations on this passage against the Papists: Michael Baius, Dean of Louvain, and other Papists, whom Bellarmine refutes in book 2 on justification, chapter 1, section 'in the same opinion', and chapter 6, under the name of Calvin, chapter 7, section 'First therefore they teach', that we are justified both by the remission of sins through the imputation of the merit of Christ and by the renewal of the affections, and that this is taught by this saying of the Apostle: And therefore among the propositions of Baius rejected by the Popes Gregory XIII and Pius V, proposition 42 and following, that proposition is rejected, that Christ is called our righteousness both by imputation and by infusion. But that in this passage the boasting of the Jews and Gentiles called to the grace of the Gospel is excluded by this middle term, because not only are they not the authors of their own wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification, but also because their righteousness does not consist in the habitual perfection of righteous works, that is evident both from the mode of inferring which the Apostle uses, and also from the cause or consequence of the inference for which he thus infers in the last verse. From the preceding verses 18, 19, 20 it is evident that he excludes The Apostle [is not] demonstrating whatever merits of the called [there may be], but not in this place, that they have their wisdom, nobility, power, etc., which he mentions in v. 26, from God, for even the Jews who were not yet converted did not deny that: but they did deny this, that that habitual righteousness, which they professed they had by the benefit of God, would profit nothing or does not profit toward the acquisition of salvation; therefore the Apostle wished to deny at least this by excluding every cause of boasting in v. 29, 31, and at Phil. III, v. 3, 4, 5, seq., 2 Cor. XI, 22, from the collation of which places it appears that the Apostle neither refuted that concerning which the Jews did not boast, nor asserted its contrary: But the Jews never boasted that they did not have their holiness from God, but rather they confessed the contrary in the said place at Phil. and at Rom. IX, 1, 2, 3. Therefore, the Apostle did not wish to exclude here that concerning which the Jews did not boast, but that concerning which they did boast, viz., the righteousness of works received from God, just as above he excluded boasting from Abraham, not concerning works done by the power of nature, but concerning works done by the benefit of circumcision, Rom. IV, 2, 10. The same reason for inferring is in this place v. 29, 31. Whence I infer thus: Concerning whatever the Jews could and were accustomed to boast, to exclude this the Apostle said that Christ is our righteousness. The major is evident from the connection of verses 30 and 31, from the conclusive particle ἵνα ὁ καυχώμενος etc. But the Jews were accustomed to and could boast of habitual righteousness of works, from the benefit of God circumcising and sanctifying, not from carnal faculty provided, as is said in Philippians III, 4, 5. Therefore, to exclude habitual righteousness of works, Paul asserted that Christ was made righteousness for us, namely through merit and imputation.

Latin:

v. 30. ἐξ αὐτοῦ δὲ ὑμεῖς ἐστὲ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) ἐξ hîc signifi- cat causam efficientem primariam, ut Rom. II. 36. cùm pro διὰ causam mediam. Et ἐστὲ intellige, estis nova creatura, facti estis longè alii quàm eratis.

Etsi particulâ ἐξ Deus Pater ceu fons & origo prima constituatur salutis, non tamen particula ἐν tantum causam mediam aut instrumentalem no- tat, sed ordinis gratia & officii Christi mediatorii respectu adhibetur. Nam ex patre nos sumus, sc. aliquid, h. e. gratia Patris. Sumus verò aliquid non nobismet ipsis, quia nil nisi caro sumus, & de- stituimur gloria DEI, Rom. III. 23. sed in Christo Jesu. Nam & particulam διὰ v. 9. adhibuit Apo- stolus, cum de Deo egit, per quem vocati estis, ubi Schlichtingius ita habet: non tanquam per causam mediam, sed tanquam per causam primam & prin- cipem: Neque enim est ulla causa DEO superior, & particula per omne genus causæ significandi vim habet.

v. 30. ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία ἀπὸ θεῦ, δικαιοσύνη δὲ καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις.

Est hic perpetua μετωνυμία effecti positi pro causa. Chri- stus enim, Deo ita procurante, factus est causa, per quam sapiamus, divina scilicet, per quam à peccatis purgemur, per quam Spiritu Sancto donemur, per quam à morte quondam vindicandi simus: quod ἀπολύτρωσις dicitur Rom. IIX. 23. Eph. IV. 30.

Quia sapientiæ, & potentiæ, & nobilitatis mun- danæ ἄρσιν instituit Apostolus, jam veram sapien- tiam, & potentiam, & nobilitatem vel dignitatem ostendit, quam in Christo unicè habemus: Sa- pientiam quidem, quia ipse solus nobis revelat Patrem, quæ vera ac solida est sapientia Matth. XI. 27. in qua consistit vita æterna, Joh. XIV. 8. cap. XVII. 3. Dignitatem verò & potentiam, quia in Christo sumus filii Dei Joh. I. 12. victores, & domini mundi 1. Joh. V. 1. & hæredes vitæ æternæ Roman. V. 17. in quibus summa nobilitas & glo- ria, virtus & potentia consistit. Ideò Christus factus nobis à DEO est justitia, ut in ipso justi constituamur, & jus. habeamus ad regnum cœ- leste: & sanctificatio, ne per tentationes mun- di, & Principis mundi jure illo excidamus, sed in regno Christi Deo in vera sanctitate serviamus: & redemptio, ut tandem liberati ab omni malo, ad æternam gloriam evehamur. Unde è Jeremiâ do- cetur, neque sapientem (extra Christum) in sua sapientia, quia in Christo solo vera est sapientia, neque divitem in divitiis suis, quæ nullæ sine Chri- sto, in quo uno justitiam & salutem, veram illam opulentiam & thesauros cœlestem habemus; ne- que fortem in fortitudine sua gloriari debere, quæ nulla sine Christo est ad vincendum mundum, & ad obtinendam liberationem ab omni malo, ad- eoque unicè gloriari nos oportere in Domino, e- jusque gratia. Quo de conferantur, quæ ad Je- rem. IX. & Esa. XLV. 25. diximus. Christus fa- ctus nobis est à Deo sapientia in Verbi revelatio- ne Joh. I. 18. & nostri ad fidem conversione, Actor. XXVI. 18. Justitia in obedientia, tùm activâ tùm passivâ, ejusque per fidem imputatione, ac justifi- catione Rom. VIII. 3. c. V. 18. 19. c. IV. 6. sanctimo- nia in Spiritûs sanctificatione, nostrique renovatio- ne, 1. Corinth. I. 2. 5. VI. 11. & redemtio, in nostri à malis omnibus liberatione, & æternâ glorificatione, quam ab ipso, in ipso, & per ipsum speramus, Rom. VII. 14. 15. cap. IIX. 23. 24. 2. Tim. IV. 8. 18.

Crellius hîc imputationem Justitiæ negat: Ex sapientia, inquit, & redemptione apparet, non agi hîc de aliqua imputatione justitiæ & sanctitatis Chri- stii; nam alioquin nec verè sapientes essemus, nec verè redimeremur aliquando, sed tantum per impu- tationem: Sed non necessum est, ut eâdem ratione dicatur Christus factus Corinthiis sapientia & re- demtio, quâ scilicet ratione factus dicitur justitia: quemadmodum nec eâdem ratione redemtio fa- ctus est, quâ sapientia. Nam sapientia ipsis jam factus erat actu & reipsâ per Sapientiæ largitio- nem; at nondum ita factus Corinthiis tum erat redemptio, quam expectabant demum in libera- tione corporis. Deinde concedi potest Christum illa omnia factum esse Corinthiis quantum ad me- ritum seu acquisitionem: quia meritis ejus tribuen- dum est, quòd nobis parta sapientia, justitia, san- ctitas & redemptio. In ipso enim & propter ipsum omnis benedictio nobis obtingit, & salus universa Ephes. I. 4. Act. IV. 12. Quantum verò ad actua- lem eorum communicationem, sapientiæ acquisitæ virtute meriti Christi participes reddimur in rege- neratione & conversione, justitiæ in justificatione, sanctimoniæ in renovatione, redemptionis in finali nostri liberatione, & glorificatione. Quoad meri- tum ergò convenientia datur: non autem quoad applicationis actum; nam convertimur non per fidem, sed ad fidem; justificamur autem non ad fidem, sed per fidem: sanctificamur verò cum exerit sese fides per charitatem: quo pacto verò neutiquam justificamur: consequens enim hoc est justificationis. Denique liberamur & glorifi- camur justificati & sanctificati, cum perseveramus in fide, ejusque finem animarum salutem reporta- mus 1. Petr. I. 9. Atque hæc est illa ἀπολύτρωσις τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν, de qua Rom. IIX. 23. Luc. XXI. 28. Eph. IV. 31. Ebr. XI. 35. quæ verò confunden- da non est cum λυτρώσει & ἀπολυτρώσει sanguine Christi factâ 1. Petr. I. 18. Rom. III. 24. Eph. I. 7. 14. Col. I. 14. Ebr. IX. 15. quia illa hujus fructus est: hæc verò illam nobis promeruit.

Porrò quod ad ordinem horum beneficiorum, Crellius pervertit eundem, cùm justificationem ait partim antecedere sanctificationem, partim se- qui; partim illius esse causam, partim effectum. Inchoata, inquit, justificatio antecedit & producit sanctitatem; plena verò & absoluta sequitur sancti- tatem, & ab illa deducitur. Unde postremò sequi- tur redemptio, omnis nostræ felicitatis complementum. Itaque hæc justificatio antecedit sanctificationem; nihilominus sanctificatio antecedit redemtionem, quæ cum nemini contingat, nisi prius sanctificatus fuerit, nec plenior justificatio, quam necessario se- quitur redemtio, cuiquam obvenit, nisi prius sancti- ficatus fuerit, seu sanctè vixerit. Hinc patet, quid sentiendum de illo tritissimo dicto: Bona opera non antecedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justifi- catum. Antecedunt enim justificandum plenè: se- quuntur justificatum inchoatè. Quanquam fides & pœnitentia strictè sumtæ, id est, firmus Christi doctrinæ assensus, ac animi & consiliorum in melius mutatio, priorisque vitæ seria ac recta detestatio omninò justificationem semper debet antecedere. Resp. 1. Justificatio omninò antecedit sanctificatio- nem, ejusque causa est, quod rectè agnoscit Crellius: at quod justificatio etiam sanctificatio- nem consequatur, ejusque effectus sit, negamus, nec è Scripturis probavit Crellius: & ἀντίφατι- κὰ illa sunt, quia idem & causa & effectus esse ne- quit ejusdem. 2. Distinctio inter justificationem inchoatam & absolutam nullo nititur Scripturæ fundamento: Justificatio est peccatorum remissio, num verò remissio alia inchoata, alia consummata? Justificatio est Justitiæ per fidem sine operibus im- putatio: num verò hæc & plena est, & semiple- na? 3. Justificationem, aut etiam salutem ullo modo deduci aut dependere à sanctitate, Paulo refragatur: nam si ex operibus, non ex gratia, aliàs opera non essent opera Rom. XI. 6. Gratiâ salvi fa- cti estis, per fidem: & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur Eph. II. 8. 9. Si hæreditas ex lege esset, non daretur per promissio- nem. At Deus Abrahæ eam per promissionem gra- tis donavit, κεχάρισαι. Gal. III. 18. 4. Plenio- rem justificationem necessariò sequi redemtionem, ἀντίγραφον est: nam in προσκαίροις, etsi verè san- ctificatis, non sequitur illa ἀπολύτρωσις, nec in iis, qui cum illuminati fuére, & gustarunt donum cæ- leste, & participes facti sunt Spiritûs S. & gustave- runt bonum Dei verbum, virtutesque venturi seculi, prolapsi sunt, rursum crucifigentes sibi Filium Dei & ostentui habentes, Ebr. VI. v. 4. 5. 6. 5. Justifi- cationem plenam non obvenire cuiquam, nisi prius sanctificatus fuerit, seu sanctè vixerit, adeò non docet Apostolus, ut Abrahamum verè & ab- solutè justificatum doceat χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus Rom. IV. imo omnes nos justificari per fidem sine operibus convincat c. III. & sanctam vitam, vel stu- dium bonorum operum absolutam justificationem non antecedere, sed consequi luculenter tradat: unde S. Augustini regula enata: Bona opera non antecedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justifica- tum: quam nequicquam Crellius enervat distin- ctione justificationis inchoatæ & plenæ: quia non de initio tantùm justificationis, seu nostræ, seu Abrahamicæ Apostolus cap. III. & IV. Rom. lo- quitur, sed de tota vel plena justificatione, nuspiam inter initium & consummationem justificationis ita distinguens, ut illud fidei sine operibus; hanc verò ipsismet operibus tribuat. 6. Fides dicitur rectè justificationem antecedere, sed fides non est firmus tantum doctrinæ Christi assensus: quum imprimis fiducia requiratur ad fidem, vel applicatio Justitiæ Christi fiducialis; mutatio verò animi & consiliorum in melius, justificationem neutiquam antecedit, sed sequitur eandem, si vera sit illa trita regula, bona opera sequuntur justificatum: & fate- tur Crellius ipse, cùm Christus dicitur factus no- bis justitia, & sanctificatio, justitiam, quam pro justificatione poni vult, dum per fidem in Chri- stum justificamur, antecedere sanctificationem, quâ sancti reddimur, & à peccatis abducimur: Ita & Schlichtingius: Eleganti, inquit, & naturali ordine hæc omnia collocavit Apostolus. Nam pri- mò Dei voluntatem cognoscimus & Deo credimus, qua in re sapientia est; deinde justitia nobis impu- tatur: hanc consequitur sanctificatio cum suo effectu, id est sancta vita, sanctis moribus; hanc tandem exci- piet redemtio & vita æterna.

Supple fiat: Similis ἔκλειψις Rom. XV. 3. alibi, & infra II. 9 v. 31. καθὼς γέγραπται, ὁ καυχώμενος ἐν κυρίῳ καυχάσθω. Sensus concisè depromptus ex Jeremiæ IX. 23. 24. Ubi in Græco habemus τὰ δὲ λέγει κύριος. μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ σοφὸς ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ ἀυτᾶ, καὶ μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ ἰσχυρὸς ἐν τῇ ἰσχύϊ ἀυτᾶ, καὶ μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ πλύσιος ἐν τῷ πλύτῳ ἀυτᾶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἢ ἐν τούτῳ καυχάσθω ὁ καυχώμενος, συνιεῖν καὶ γινώσκειν, ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι κύ- ριος, ὁ ποιῶν ἔλεος καὶ κρῖμα καὶ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Ubi in Hebræo pro καυχάσθω est יתהלל quod per ἀγαλλιᾶν alibi vertitur.

Ex hac illatione pariter & ex antecedentibus rectè disputat B. Hülsemann. in annot. ἀνεκδότοις ad h. l. adversus Pontificios: Michael Bajus Deca- nus Lovaniensis aliique Papistæ, quos refutat Bellar- min. l. 2. de justif. c. I. §. in eandem sent. & cap. 6. sub nomine Calvini c. 7. §. Primum igitur docent, & remissione peccatorum per imputationem meriti Christi, & renovatione affectuum nos justificari, idque doceri hoc dicto Apostoli: Ideoque inter propositiones Baji à Pontificibus Gregorio XIII. & Pio V. rejectas propos. 42. seqq. rejicitur ista propositio, Christum dici justitiam nostram & imputatione & infusione. Hoc autem loco Judæorum & Gentium ad gratiam Evangelii vocatorum gloriationem per hunc medium terminum excludi, quòd non solùm ipsi non sint au- thores sapientiæ suæ, justitiæ & sanctificationis, sed quòd etiam justitia eorum non consistat in habituali perfectione operum justorum, id patet cum ex modo inferendi, quo utitur Apostolus; tum etiam ex causa seu consequente illationis propter quod sic infert vers. ult. Ex antecedentibus v. 18. 19. 20. patet, excludere Apostolum vocatorum merita quæcunque, non de- monstrare autem hoc loco, quòd sapientiam, nobilita- tem, potentiam suam &c. quorum meminit v. 26. à Deo habeant, id enim Judæi etiam nondum conversi non negabant: sed hoc negabant, habitualem istam justitiam, quam profitebantur se beneficio DEI babe- re, nihil profuturam aut prodesse ad salutis acquisi- tionem; igitur hoc saltem voluit negare Apostolus excludendo omnem gloriandi causam v. 29. 31. & ad Phil. III. v. 3. 4. 5. seq. 2. Cor. XI. 22. ex quorum locorum collatione apparet, id, de quo non gloriaban- tur Judæi, nec refutasse Apostolum, nec ejus contra- rium asseruisse: Sed nunquam gloriabantur Judæi se sanctitatem suam non habere à Deo, verum contra- rium potius fatebantur dicto loco ad Phil. & ad Rom. IX. 1. 2. 3. E. Apostolus non id, de quo non gloria- bantur, sed id, de quo gloriabantur Judæi, sc. operum justitiam à Deo acceptam hic voluit excludere, ut supra ab Abrahamo excludebat gloriationem, non de operibus vi naturæ factis, sed de operibus ex bene- ficio circumcisionis factis, Rom. IV. 2. 10. Eadem ratio inferendi est hoc loco v. 29. 31. Unde sic infero: De quocunque poterant & soliti erant gloriari Judæi, ad hoc excludendum dixit Apostolus Christum esse no- strum justitiam. . Major patet ex connexione vers. 30. & 31. ex particula conclusiva ἵνα ὁ καυχώμενος &c. Sed de habituali operum justitia, ex beneficio DEI circumcidentis & sanctificantis, non ex car- nali facultate præstita soliti erant & poterant Judæi gloriari, ut dicitur Philipp. III. 4. 5. E. ad exclu- dendam habitualem operum justitiam asseruit Pau- lus Christum esse factum nobis justitiam per meritum scilicet & imputationem.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

The Apostle presents himself as an example, as to why and how he did not preach to the Corinthians with lofty words and lofty wisdom, but announced Christ crucified without the pomp of words: in which, however, he teaches that true wisdom consists, unknown to the wise men of the world, who otherwise would not have crucified the Lord of glory, but ordained by God for salvation; which God revealed through the Spirit who searches all things, sufficient even for the words by which those things are to be proposed: since the natural man does not clearly understand the things which are of the Spirit of God, nor can he know them.

There are two parts of the chapter: The first exhibits the τρόπον παιδείας Apostolicæ, or the manner of teaching the Gospel, both as to words and as to the matter, up to verse 6. The second asserts the wisdom of the Word of the Cross, and distinguishes it from the wisdom of the world, up to the end, v. 16.

PART I. The Apostolic manner of teaching.

v. 1. And I, when I came to you, brethren.

He says this: my manner of speaking and acting also agrees with that ministry of God, both among others, and especially among you.

I came not with excellency of speech.

Paul was not ineloquent: but in Greece there were many more eloquent men, who had added the aids of art and long practice to the resources of nature: therefore he says ὑπεροχὴν, that is גבה.

or of wisdom.

Paul was indeed learned in the law and the writings of the interpreters: but not equally so in that Grecian philosophy.

proclaiming to you the testimony of God.

The Gospel which [is] above in line 6, the testimony of Christ. For God made his will known to us through Christ. In the manuscript it is the mystery of God. See Rom. XVI. 25. and thus the codex had it, which Ambrose used, and that which the Syrian used.

The Apostle teaches that a superiority of speech or wisdom was not lacking to him, but that it was not employed by him in teaching the Gospel: for he did not wish to employ that eloquence which he had, nor that wisdom, but he both used simple speech and truly delivered those things which are greatly alien to worldly wisdom, and that at the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, who gave the Apostles a mouth and wisdom, Luke XXI. 15, so that they might speak, as the Spirit gave them to utter, Acts II. 4. Compare 1 Cor. XII. 7. following. 2 Peter III. 15. But whether Paul could have delivered the testimony of God more eloquently and wisely, as far as his own faculty is concerned, is perhaps a superfluous question: because the Apostles did not speak as they themselves were either wise or eloquent, but from divine inspiration, whatever they spoke, 2 Peter I. 21. 2 Tim. III. 15. Therefore St. Chrysostom: What, tell me, I pray, if you had wished to come in sublimity, would you have been able? I indeed, if I had wished, could not have, but Christ, if he had wished, could have, but he did not wish, so that a more glorious trophy might be made. Therefore, he says, I do not announce the testimony of God by showing off the eloquence of my tongue, nor armed with external arguments.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Exemplum sistit sese Apostolus, quod & cur non sublimibus verbis, & sublimi sapientia præ- dicârit Corinthiis, sed Christum crucifixum citra verborum pompam annunciârit: in quo tamen veram sapientiam, incognitam sapien- tibus mundi, qui aliàs Dominum gloriæ non crucifixissent, at ordinatam à Deo ad salu- tem, consistere docet; quam revelârit Deus per Spiritum omnia scrutantē, verba etiam, quibus illa proponenda, sufficientem: siqui- dem animalis homo ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, plane non intelligat, nec cognoscere possit.

PArtes capitis duæ sunt: Prima τρόπον παιδείας Apostolicæ, seu modum docendi Evangelium, quà verba & quà rem, exhibet, usque ad vers. 6. Altera sapientiam Verbi Crucis adserit, eamque à sapientia mundi distinguit, usque ad finem, v. 16.

PARS I. Modus docendi Apostolicus.

v. 1. Κἀγὼ ἐλθὼν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ.

Hoc dicit: mea quoque loquendi & agendi ratio con- gruit isti Dei ministerio, tum apud alios, tum apud vos maximè.

ἦλθον ὐ καθ' ὑπεροχὴν λόγυ.

Non erat Paulus indifertus: sed in Græcia multi erant di- sertiores, qui ad naturæ opes artis adminicula & longum usum adjecerant: idcò dicit ὑπεροχὴν, id est גבה.

ἢ σοφίας.

Eruditus quidem erat Paulus in lege & scriptis interpre- tum: at non æquè in Philosophia illa Græcanica.

καταγγέλλων ὑμῖν τὸ μαρτύριον τῦ Θεῦ.

Evangelium quod supra l. 6. μαρτύριον τῦ χρισῦ. Deus quippe per Christum voluntatem suam nobis testatam fe- cit. In Manuscripto est τὸ μυσήριον τῦ Θεῦ. Vide Rom. XVI. 25. & sic habuit Codex, quo usus est Ambrosius, & is quo usus Syrus.

Non defuisse sibi ὑπεροχὴν λόγυ, ἢ σοφίας, sed non adhibitam à se fuisse in docendo Evangelio docet Apostolus: nam nec eam, quam habuit elo- quentiam, eamque sapientiam adhibere voluit, sed tum simplici sermone usus est, tum verò ea tradi- dit, quæ à sapientia mundana maximopere aliena sunt, idque suggerente Spiritu S. qui σόμα ᾃ σοφίαν Apostolis dedit Luc. XXI. 25. ut loquerentur, κα- θὼς ἐδίδο τὸ πνεῦμα ἀποφθέγγεσθαι Actor. II. 4. Conf. 1. Cor. XII. 7. seqq. 2. Petr. III. 15. An autem eloquentius & sapientius testimonium Dei tradere, quod ad propriam attinet facultatem, potuerit Paulus, superfluè fortassis quæritur: quia Aposto- li non prout ipsi vel sapientes, vel facundi erant, sed ex inspiratione divina loquebantur, quicquid loquebantur, 2. Petr. I. 21. 2. Tim. III. 15. Ideò S. Chrysost. Quid, dic quæso, si voluisses venire in sublimitate, potuissesne? Ego quidem si voluissem, non potuissem, Christus autem si voluisset, potuisset, sed noluit, ut fieret tropæum præclarius. Non ergò linguæ, inquit, ostentans facundiam, neque exter- nis armatus rationibus annuncio Dei testimonium.

## 2:2
v. 2. For I determined.

I did not make much of it, as in Romans XIV. 5.

To know anything among you except Jesus Christ.

To know the words of the law, and traditions, some languages, to have even read your poets. It is frequent for our writers to place the article before the infinitive, where others would place the [article] that is in you, that is, when I was living among you.

and him crucified.

And indeed crucified, that is, whose example I knew I must follow in enduring all evils for the sake of the Gospel. The following verses show that it is to be taken thus.

Latin:

v. 2. ὁ γὰρ ἔκρινα.

Non magni feci, ut Roman. XIV. 5.

Τῦ εἰδέναι τι ἐν ὑμῖν εἰ μὴ ἰησῦν χρισόν.

Nosse verba legis, & traditiones, linguas aliquas, legisse etiam vestros poëtas. Frequens est nostris scriptoribus τῦ præponere infinitivo, ubi alii ponerent τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, ὧν ἐν ὑμῖν cum apud vos viverem.

καὶ τῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον.

Et quidem crucifixum, id est, cujus exemplum in omnis bus malis Evangelii causa perferendis scirem mihi esse se- quendum. Sic sumendum ostendunt sequentia.

## 2:3
V. 3. And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling.

And here it is for 'for': ἀσθένεια here is sorrow from adverse things, as we said in Rom. VIII. verse 26. Fear and that trembling signify dangers, when Paul was dragged by force by the Jews to the tribunal, Sosthenes was beaten, Paul himself was forced to depart, which you have in Acts XVIII. φόβος & τρόμος are often wont to be joined for the sake of emphasis, as in Psalm II. 11 in the Greek. 2 Cor. VII. 15. Eph. VI. 5. Phil. II. 12. πρὸς ὑμᾶς, that is, παρ᾽ ὑμῖν. See John I. 2.

The word ἔκρινα in the more accepted sense, from which one should not rashly depart, is not 'I magnified' but 'I judged': nor does the Apostle compare the words of the law, much less traditions, or languages, or the sayings of poets, but he simply expresses the object of his Evangelical proclamation, which is Jesus Christ, and him crucified: namely, that he preached to them concerning the person and office of Christ, and especially concerning his crucifixion and saving death, and placed in him solid and supreme wisdom: just as he also protested in Gal. VI. 14: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ: and towards the end of the preceding chapter he warned, he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord: and he taught that the word of the cross is supreme wisdom, v. 18 seqq. Nor indeed does he teach here that he proposed Christ crucified to himself as an example of patience, but he testifies that the cross and death of Christ were the subject matter of his Evangelical proclamation among the Corinthians: although he does not deny his own ἀσθένειαν, in which he performed his office. By which word he does not hint at sorrow from adverse things, but the infirmity of his own powers, which he humbly acknowledges in comparison to the magnitude of the office committed to him: whence he executed it in much fear and trembling, in view of his own inability: which nevertheless he performed not without notable παῥῥησίᾳ in view of divine παραστάσεως. Fear and trembling on account of dangers have nothing to do with this: where the matter concerns the manner of teaching and of carrying out his office, and not indeed the sufferings to be endured on account of the office.

Latin:

V. 3. κὰι ἐγὼ ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, κὰι ἐν φόβῳ, κὰι ἐν τρόμῳ πολλῷ ἐγενόμην πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

κὰι hîc est pro nam: ἀσθένεια hîc est dolor ex rebus ad- versis, ut diximus Rom. IIX. vers. 26. Metus & ille timor pericula significant, cum ab Judæis vi ad tribunal tractus fuit Paulus, Sosthenes pulsatus, Paulus ipse coactus dis- cedere, quæ habes Actor. XVIII. φόβος & τρόμος, sæpe jun- gi solent αὐξήσεως causâ, ut Psalm. II. 11. in Græco. 2. Cor. VII. 15. Eph. VI. 5. Phil. II. 12. πρὸς ὑμᾶς, id est, παρ᾽ ὑμῖν. Vide Joh. I. 2.

Vox ἔκρινα sensu receptiori, à quo temere haud discedendum, non est magnifici sed judicavi: nec comparat Apostolus legis verba, nedum traditio- nes, aut linguas, Poëtarum dicta, sed simpliciter exprimit objectum præconii sui Evangelici, quod est Jesus Christus, isque crucifixus: quod nempe de persona & officio Christi, ac maximè de crucifi- xione & morte ejusdem salutifera ipsis prædicarit, inque eo solidam & summam sapientiam locârit: quemadmodum & Gal. VI. 14. protestatus est: Mihi autem absit gloriari nisi in cruce Domini no- stri Jesu Christi: & sub finem cap. præced. monuit, qui vult gloriari, glorietur in Domino: ac verbum crucis summam sapientiam esse docuit, v. 18. seqq. Nec verò Christum crucifixum sese sibi in exem- plum patientiæ proposuisse hîc docet, sed crucem & mortem Christi materiam fuisse præconii sui Evangelici inter Corinthios, testatur: etsi suam ἀσθένειαν non diffiteatur, in qua suum peregerit of- ficium. Quâ voce non dolorem ex rebus adversis innuit, sed virium suarum infirmitatem, quam in comparatione ad officii sibi commissi magnitu- dinem humiliter agnoscit: unde in timore & tre- more multo, intuitu suæ inhabilitatis id exeque- batur: quod tamen non sine insigni παῥῥησίᾳ intuitu divinæ παραστάσεως peregit. Nihil huc faciunt metus & timor ob pericula: ubi de modo docendi: & officium suum expediundi, non verò de passionibus ob officium sustinendis agitur.

## 2:4
v. 4. And my speech, and my preaching.

My discourses, both private and public. For κηρύσσειν is to speak to many, Matt. X. 27.

not with enticing words of man's wisdom.

Many have noted that Πειθοῖς is not Greek: nor was the Cilician Apostle so [ignorant] as to use a word read nowhere.

Read πιθοῖς as below 13. ἐν διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις. He understands those discourses which human wisdom is accustomed to use. The Syrian reads ἐν πειθοῖ & λόγου with not a bad sense: just as Eusebius also reads; and it seems Origen read it in Philocalia ch. XVI. v. 1. but I prefer what I have said. What Seneca says of Demetrius can be said much more justly of the Apostles, that they were of his eloquence, which is fitting for the most powerful matters, not polished, nor anxious for words, but with a great spirit following its own matters as the impulse carried it. Hippodamus in his book on the Republic: χρῆσθαι δὲ τῷ λόγῳ πολιτικῷ καὶ σεμνῷ καὶ οἰκείῳ τῆς διαθέσιος τῶ λέγοντος, ἀλλὰ μὴ προποιητῷ, ἔτω γὰρ ἡ λέξις ἐσσῖται τὸ ἤθεος τῶ λέγοντος ὁμφαγίσσα.

That criticism is not to be granted to a Philologist in Holy Scripture, that he should invent for himself a new reading without the authority of any Codex, and substitute πεισοῖς for πειθοῖς. Beza, because of the passage of Eusebius at the beginning of the Evangelical Preparation and the Syriac version, prefers that ἐν πειθοῖ: but what stands in the way of the word πειθὸς being used for πειθανὸς by the Apostle, even if it is not read elsewhere in Greek authors?

ἀλλ' ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως. Mathematicians have their ἀποδείξεις: Aristotle has his. But how much greater is that one through so many and such great miracles? The following genitive here denotes the instrument: by the word πνεύματος, he seems to signify prophecies, by the word δυνάμεως, healings.

Latin:

v. 4. κὰι ὁ λόγος με, κὰι τὸ κήρυγμα.

Sermones mei, tùm privati tùm publici. Nam κηρύσσειν est multis dicere Matth. X. 27.

ὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις.

Πειθοῖς Græcum non esse multi notarunt: nec adeò Cilix Apostolus, ut vocem nusquam lectam usurparet.

Legendum πιθοῖς sicut infra 13. ἐν διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις. Intelligit eos sermones, quibus uti solet huma- na sapientia. Syrus legit ἐν πειθοῖ & λόγου sensu non malo: quomodo legit & Eusebius; & videtur legisse Ori, genes Philocalia cap. XVI. v. 1. sed quod dixi præfero. Quod de Demetrio dicit Seneca, multò justius de Aposto. lis dici potest, fuisse eos eloquentiæ ejus, quæ res fortissi- mas deceat, non concinnatæ, nec in verba sollicitæ, sed in- genti animo prout impetus tulit res suas prosequentis. Hippodamus libro de Republica: χρῆσθαι δὲ τῷ λόγῳ πο- λιτικῷ καὶ σεμνῷ καὶ οἰκείῳ τῆς διαθέσιος τῶ λέγοντος, ἀλλὰ μὴ προποιητῷ, ἔτω γὰρ ἡ λέξις ἐσσῖται τὸ ἤθεος τῶ λέγοντος ὁμ- φαγίσσα.

Non concedenda Philologo in S. literis ea cri- sis, ut citra autoritatem ullius Codicis sibi fingat novam lectionem, & pro πειθοῖς substituat πεισοῖς. Beza ob locum Eusebii initio Evangelicæ præ- parationis, & versionem Syriacam præfert illud ἐν πειθοῖ: sed quid obstat vocem πειθὸς adhibitam pro πειθανὸς ab Apostolo, etsi aliàs in Græcis au- toribus non legatur?

ἀλλ' ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως. Habent Mathematici suas ἀποδείξεις: habet Aristoteles suas. At quantò major illa per tot ac tanta miracula? Ge- nitivus subsequens hîc instrumentum denotat: voce πνεύ- ματος, videtur significare prophetias, voce δυνάμεως sa- nationes.

## 2:5
v. 5. ἵνα ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν μὴ ἦ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων. Lest your faith be born of human erudition. ἀλλ' ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ.

But through the excellent power of God, so that, clearly, greater honor and thanks may be given to Him. See above I. 17. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho, speaking of the Prophets: ἀνωτέρω πάσης ἀποδείξεως ὄντες ἀξιόπιστοι μάρτυρες τῆς ἀληθείας. Origen in Philocalia: εἰ γάρ τις καθ'ημαξευμέναι τῶν ἀποδείξεων ὁδοὶ παρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρωποις ἐναποκειμεναι τοῖς βιβλίοις κατίσχυσαν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡ πίσις ἡμῶν ἐνλόγως ἂν ὑπελαμ- βάνετο ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἐκ ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ. &c. By the demonstration of the Spirit and power, neither prophecies, which of themselves bring no demonstration, nor healings or other miracles are designated, which are extrinsic to the word, but the intrinsic force and efficacy of the word: For the Word of God is Spirit and life, John VI. 63. & the power of God, Rom. I. 16. living and effective, Heb. IV. 12. through which He demonstrates that He is the Spirit convincing hearts, and converting them to the Lord, and thus the divine virtue exerts itself: so that whatever fruit redounds from the preaching of the word, it is to be attributed not to the persuasive virtue of human wisdom, but to the demonstration of the Spirit and power, or spiritual virtue, if it is explained by a hendiadys, which is exerted through the word. By which method it is more clearly evident that our faith rests entirely not on human wisdom or eloquence, but on divine virtue, and is to be credited to it, i.e., as the blessed Balduinus rightly says, I therefore abstained from the subtleties of philosophers, as well as the paint of rhetoricians, lest you ascribe the efficacy of the word preached among you to those external things, which is owed entirely to the Holy Spirit.

PART II. The Wisdom of the Evangelical Word, and its distinction from the wisdom of the world.

Latin:

v. 5. ἵνα ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν μὴ ἦ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων. Ne fides vestra nasceretur ex humana eruditione. ἀλλ' ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ.

Sed per eximiam Dei potentiam, quo major scilicet ipfi honor & gratia habeatur. Vide supra I. 17. Justinus in colloquio cum Tryphone de Prophetis loquens: ἀνωτέ- ρω πάσης ἀποδείξεως ὄντες ἀξιόπιστοι μάρτυρες τῆς ἀληθείας. Origenes in Philocalia: εἰ γάρ τις καθ'ημαξευμέναι τῶν ἀπο- δείξεων ὁδοὶ παρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρωποις ἐναποκειμεναι τοῖς βιβλίοις κατίσχυσαν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡ πίσις ἡμῶν ἐνλόγως ἂν ὑπελαμ- βάνετο ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἐκ ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ. &c. Per ἀπόδειξιν πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως non Pro- phetiæ, quæ per se nullam ἀπόδειξιν adferunt, nec sanationes vel alia miracula designantur, quæ ex- trinseca sunt verbo, sed intrinseca verbi vis & ef- ficacia: Verbum enim Dei Spiritus est & vita, Joh. VI. 63. & potentia Dei Roman. I. 16. vivum & efficax, Ebr. IV. 12. per quod demonstrat se Spiri- tus convincens corda, eademque convertens ad Dominum, adeoque virtus divina sese exerit: ut quicquid fructus redundat è verbi præconio, non virtuti suadæ humanæ sapientiæ, sed demonstra- tioni Spiritus & virtutis, aut spiritualis virtutis, si per hendyaden explicetur, quæ per verbum exeri- tur, tribuendum sit. Quo pacto luculentiùs con- stat, fidem nostram non sapientiâ, aut eloquentiâ humanâ, sed virtute divinâ in solidum niti, eique acceptam ferendam esse, q. d. ut rectè B. Baldui- nus, ideò abstinui à Philosophorum argutiis, ut & rhetorum fucis, ne efficaciam verbi inter vos predi- cati adscribatis externis illis rebus, quæ in solidum debetur Spiritui Sancto.

PARS II. Sapientia Verbi Evangelici, ejusque à Sapientia mundi distinctio.

## 2:6
v. 6. σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις. We speak those things which true and upright Christians will judge to be full of wisdom. For those are the perfect, as we said in Matt. V. 48.

The reborn are called perfect not because of legal perfection or probity, but because of Evangelical perfection, not inherent, but imputed: for although we are commanded to strive even for perfect holiness, Matt. V. 48, we do not however attain it in this imperfection, but only there, where that which is in part shall cease, and the perfect shall succeed, 1 Cor. XIII. 10. Cf. Phil. III. 15. The blessed Balduinus says that he calls them perfect, for the state of this age, those who are knowledgeable of the articles of faith, endowed with incorrupt judgment, and having faith in the words of GOD, and thus this word is opposed to the more ignorant, the incredulous, the corrupt, who are still entirely strangers to Christian doctrine: in which sense it is taken in Phil. III. 15, Heb. V. 14. So also Augustine interprets it in tract. 9, quest. 8, in John. He says these are suitable hearers of divine wisdom, who, having become accustomed to the habit of the Holy Spirit, are not moved by the judgment of reason in divine matters.

v. eod. σοφίαν δὲ ὐ τῦ αἰῶνος τύτω. Not that physical wisdom, of which also above I. 20. nor of the rulers of this age. Political, to which jurisprudence and the knowledge of histories adhere.

The Apostle does not here pursue that subtlety of the diction of the disciplines of Physics and Politics, but speaks of the wisdom of the age, and of the prudent of the age, which is valued by the sons of the age, Luke 16:8, and which exists in those who excel in the prudence of the world, which prevails in the world, and are held as Princes in the age. Such is, then, that wisdom which is indeed true, which is had from the light of nature, but which is occupied only with secular things, and perishes with this age; and then also the wisdom ψευδώνυμος, which conforms itself to the world, and to the reason of state, and is held in value among worldlings: both differ greatly from the divine wisdom hidden in a mystery, but the latter is even καδδιάμετρον opposed to the same. Such ἄρχοντες were the Princes of the Pharisees among the Jews, Luke 14:1, and elsewhere.

τῶν καταργυμένων. The empires that now exist will perish no less than those figured by the statue of Daniel 2:44. Virgil, Georgics book 2: 'Not the Roman affairs and kingdoms about to perish.' The Apostle does not treat of the destruction of empires, but of the destruction of the prudent of the age, along with their prudence, and opposes to it the eternal wisdom of the divine word, Isaiah 40:8, through which the faithful are delivered from destruction and attain eternal life, John 17:3, 1 John 2:16.

Latin:

v. 6. σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις. Ea dicimus, quæ plena esse sapientiæ judicabunt veri ac probi Christiani. Ii enim τέλειοι ut diximus Matth. V. 48.

Perfecti dicuntur renati non ob perfectionem legalem vel probitatem, sed ob perfectionem Ev- angelicam, non inhærentem, sed imputatam: nam licet contendere etiam ad sanctitatem perfectam jubeamur, Matth. V. 48. non tamen eam in hac imperfectione assequimur, sed illic demum, ubi id, quod ex parte est, cessabit, & succedet τὸ τέλειον 1. Cor. XIII. 10. Conf. Phil. III. 15. B. Balduinus per- fectos, inquit, vocat, pro statu hujus seculi, gnaros articulorum fidei, incorrupto judicio præditos, & fidem habentes sermonibus DEI, & sic opponitur hæc vox rudioribus, incredulis, corruptis, qui in doctrinâ Christianâ adhuc omnino sunt hospites: quo sensu accipitur Phil. III. 15. Hebr. V. 14. Ita etiam Augustinus interpretatur tract. 9. quæst. 8. in Joh. Hos ait idoneos sapientiæ divinæ auditores esse, qui ad consuetudinem Spiritus Sancti assuefacti, ju- dicio rationis in rebus divinis non moventur.

v. eod. σοφίαν δὲ ὐ τῦ αἰῶνος τύτω. Non illam Physicam, de qua & supra I. 20. ὐδὲ τῶν ἀρχόντων τᾶ αἰῶνος τύτω. Politicam, cui adhærent jurisprudentia & historiarum cognitio.

Illam subtilitatem dictionis disciplinarum Phy- sicæ & Politicæ non sectatur hîc Apostolus, sed sa- pientiam seculi, & prudentum seculi dicit, quæ à fi- liis seculi æstimatur, Luc. XVI, 8. quæque in illis, qui prudentia mundi, quæ in mundo valet, excellunt, ac Principes in seculo habentur. Qualis est tùm vera quidem illa sapientia, quæ ex lumine naturæ habetur, sed quæ circa res seculares tantùm occupa- tur, & cum hoc seculo interit; tùm etiam sapientia ψευδώνυμος, quæ mundo se attemperat, & rationi sta- tus, & in pretio habetur penes mundanos: utraque maximè à sapientia divina in mysterio absconditâ differt, sed hæc eidem etiam καδδιάμετρον adversa est. Ejusmodi ἄρχοντες erant Principes Pharisæo- rum inter Judæos Luc. XIV. 1. & alibi.

τῶν καταργυμένων. Quæ nunc sunt imperia, non minus peribunt, quàm illa figurata per statuam Danielis II. 44. Virgilius l. Georg. II. Non res Romanæ perituraque regna. Non de interitu imperiorum, sed de destructio- ne prudentum seculi, cum sua prudentia, agit Apo- stolus, eique opponit æternam verbi divini sapien- tiam, Es. XL. 8. per quod ab interitu liberantur fideles, & æternam consequuntur vitam Joh. IIX. 51. 1. Joh. II. 16.

## 2:7
v. 7. ἀλλὰ λαλῦμεν σοφίαν Θεῦ ἐν μυστηρίῳ τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην. An inverted phrase for τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην ἐν μυστηρίῳ, which was long kept hidden in secret. See Romans 16:25 and Ephesians 3:4, 5, 9. μυσήριον, רזא and רזין, as in Daniel several times.

ἣν προώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων. Before many times, as is said in the aforementioned place in Romans. Rightly before many times: for this was prefigured not only in Abraham and Melchizedek, but also in Noah, and Enoch, and Abel.

For the wisdom of God in the mystery of Christ, Ephesians 3:4, which is celebrated as the great mystery of godliness, 1 Timothy 3:15, is truly hidden, because it lies outside all reason, nor is it open to anyone apart from divine revelation: nor is it said to be defined only before many times, much less only adumbrated through prefiguration in certain Patriarchs, but indeed predestined πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, that is, before the ages, or from eternity; but it was revealed immediately after the fall in the Proto-Evangelium itself, Genesis 3:15, and furthermore in the exegetical promises of the same, and in the illustrative types under the Old Testament, then especially in the Evangelical sermons in the New Testament: and thus equally through the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, Romans 16:26. Moreover, that mode of salvation, which the Gospel has clearly expounded, was defined by God from eternity.

vers. eod. εἰς δόξαν ἡμῶν. To our greatest honor, whom He willed to adorn with gifts above all the Prophets.

By δόξαν he understands not a certain honor of temporal excellence, which ministering gifts produce, but the glory of eternal life: because this wisdom is truly salvific, and in it eternal life consists, John 17:3. Nor is this glory ours in an exclusive sense, as if it were not the Prophets', but the Apostle calls it ours in an appropriative sense, because anyone can take it as his own and appropriate it to himself, inasmuch as it is divinely proposed to all for that end.

Latin:

v. 7. ἀλλὰ λαλῦμεν σοφίαν Θεῦ ἐν μυστηρίῳ τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην. Inversa locutio pro τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην ἐν μυστηρίῳ quæ diu in arcano recondita fuit. Vide Rom. XVI. 25. & Eph. III. 4. 5. 9. μυσήριον רזא & רזין, ut apud Danielem aliquoties.

ἣν προώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων. Ante multa tempora, ut dicitur dicto Romanorum loco. Rectè ante multa tempora: nam præfiguratum hoc non tantùm in Abrahamo, & Melchisedeco, sed & in Noë, & Enocho, & Abele.

Sapientia enim Dei in mysterio τῦ χρισῦ Eph. III. 4. quod ceu magnum pietatis mysterium cele- bratur 1. Tim. III. 15. verè est abscondita, quòd ra- tionem omnem lateat, nec extra revelationem divinam ulli pateat: nec definita tantùm ante mul- ta tempora dicitur, nedum solùm per præfiguratio- nem in quibusdam Patriarchis adumbrata, sed præ- destinata quidem πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, id est, ante secula, vel ab æterno; patefacta verò statim post lapsum in ipso Prot-Evangelio Gen. III. 15. ac porrò in exegeticis ejusdem promissionibus, typisque illu- stratoriis sub Vet. Test. tùm imprimis in Evange- licis concionibus in Novo Testamento: adeoque per Scripta pariter Prophetica & Apostolica, Rom. XVI. 26. Modus autem ille salutis, quem Evange- lium luculenter exposuit, ab æterno à Deo defini- tus fuit.

vers. eod. εἰς δόξαν ἡμῶν. Ad maximum honorem nostrum, quos donis suprà omnes Prophetas ornare voluit.

Per δόξαν intelligit non honorem quendam ex- cellentiæ temporalis, quem dona ministrantia pa- riunt, sed gloriam vitæ æternæ: quia sapientia hæc verè est salvifica, & in ea vita æterna consi- stit, Joh. XVI. 3. Neque verò nostra est hæc gloria sensu exclusivo, quasi Prophetarum non sit, sed nostram dicit Apostolus sensu appropria- tivo, quia quilibet eam ceu suam sibique propria- re potest, utpote quæ omnibus eo fine divinitùs est proposita.

## 2:8
v. 8. which none of the rulers of this age have known. Namely, wisdom. But when he says rulers, he does not understand those lesser magistrates, such as Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, but those shining ones, such as Pilate and Herod and the Caesars: and among the Jews, Caiaphas and Annas.

That Nicodemus and Joseph are not included here is not because the Apostle designates only the shining magistrates: for even among such, not a few have known the divine wisdom, as is evident from the example of Christian Emperors, Kings, and Princes, but because the Princes of this age, who are devoted only to the present age, have no regard for the age to come. For the Apostle expressly testifies that no Prince of this age, however much he may excel in worldly wisdom or power, knows the saving wisdom of God. However, it appears from the things that follow that Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, and Annas are set forth particularly by way of example.

vers. eod. for if they had known. If they had thoroughly understood God's decrees in this matter.

they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. It is not credible that they would have condemned him to the cross, either by their instigation, as the priests; or by decree, as Pilate; or by consent, as Herod, him whom God wills to be the judge of all. For the glory of Christ looks especially to that day, 1 Pet. IV. 13. Tertullian against Marcion III. The Scripture, which declares Christ to be killable, certainly affirms him to be unknowable: for unless he were unknown, he could surely suffer nothing. Those who gave their assent are also said to have crucified him, Acts II. 36, IV. 10. That ignorance does not excuse them: for Christ had done great enough things that they should have inquired what he brought: if the others had been desirous of learning and doing good, they would have received it from him himself. Christ the Lord of glory is prefigured by the ark, which is the King of glory, Psalm XXIV. 9.

Christ is not called the Lord of glory merely on account of the judgment which he will institute on that glorious day, but on account of his true Deity: just as he is called the God of glory, Acts VII. 2, because he is that God blessed forever over all, Rom. IX. 5, whose is the honor, and glory, and strength, Rev. V. 13, whose divine glory the Angels and Seraphim celebrate and venerate, Isaiah VI. 3, John XII. 41. Christ could by no means exercise this divine glory on the last day in judgment, whether absolving the faithful or condemning the unfaithful, unless he were true God, for which divine omniscience and heart-knowledge, as well as divine virtue and power, are absolutely necessary. But they did not acknowledge Christ as the true God, the Lord of glory, but held him to be a mere, and indeed a very vile and abject man, and they were the ones who affixed him to the cross: because if they had acknowledged him, they would not have dared to attack him, much less kill him. Conf. The disputes which Christ had with the Jews concerning him, John V. and X. Furthermore, we acknowledge that Christ is the Lord of glory not only with respect to his divine nature, but also with respect to his human nature, since the glory which is proper to him as God has been communicated to his human nature: and not only with respect to his person, but also with respect to his office; because he is the King of glory and the Judge, whom we believe will come in the truly immense glory of the Father to the last judgment, Matt. XXV. But that he was prefigured by the ark of the covenant as the Lord of glory is nowhere said, nor is the King of glory, Psalm XXIV. 10, the name of the ark of the covenant, but of the Messiah. Because the Psalmist calls the same person the Lord of glory, whom he calls the Lord of hosts, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle: which things do not befit the ark, but the Lord, who manifested himself at the ark.

Latin:

v. 8. ἣν οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου ἔγνωκεν. nempe σοφίαν. Cùm autem dicit ἄρχοντας non intel- ligit minores illos magistratus, qualis Nicodemus & Jose- phus Arimathensis, sed istos præfulgentes, quales Pilatus & Herodes ac Cæsares: & intra Judæos Caiphas & Annas.

Quòd Nicodemus & Josephus hìc non com- prehendantur, non inde est, quòd solùm præful- gentes Magistratus designet Apostolus: nam etiam inter talès non pauci divinam sapientiam cogno- verunt, ut exemplo Christianorum Imperatorum, Regum, & Principum constat, sed quòd Principes hujus seculi, qui tantùm seculo præsenti dediti sunt, τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος rationem non habent. Nam neminem Principum hujus seculi, quantacunque sapientiâ vel potestate mundanâ etiam polleat, co- gnoscere sapientiam Dei salvificam, Apostolus di- sertè testatur. Exempli tamen loco peculiariter sisti Pilatum, Herodem, Caipham, & Annam, ex iis, quæ subjiciuntur, apparet.

vers. eod. εἰ γὰρ ἔγνωσαν. Si penitus pernossent Dei destinata in hac re.

οὐκ ἂν τὸν Κύριον τῆς δόξης ἐσταύρωσαν. Non credibile est eos cruci addicturos fuisse, aut instiga- tione suâ, ut sacerdotes; aut decreto, ut Pilatus; aut consen- su, ut Herodes, eum quem Deus esse vult omnium judicem. Nam gloria Christi illum diem maximè respicit 1. Petr. IV. 13. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem III. Scriptura, quæ interemptibilem Christum edicentes utique & ignorabilem affir- mant: nisi enim ignoratus, nihil scilicet pati posset. Crucifi- xisse dicuntur etiam qui assensum præbuere Act. II. 36. IV. 10. Non excusat eos illa ignorantia: satis enim res magnas fe- cerat Christus, ut quid afferret inquirerent: cæteræ si discen- di & benè agendi fuissent cupidi, ab ipso percepruri. Chri- stus Κύριος δόξης præfiguratus per arcam, quæ מלך הכבוד Psalm. XXIV. 9.

Christus non dicitur Dominus gloriæ modo ob judicium, quod in glorioso illo die instituet, sed ob veram Deitatem: uti Deus gloriæ vocatur Act. VII. 2. quia est Deus ille benedictus in secula super omnia Rom. IX. 5. cujus est honor, & gloria & for- titudo Ap. V. 13. cujus divinam gloriam celebrant & venerantur Angeli & Seraphim Esaia VI. 3. Joh. XII. 41. Quam divinam gloriam in novissimo die exercere in judicio sive absolutorio fidelium si- ve condemnatorio infidelium minimè posset Chri- stus, nisi verus Deus esset, ad quod omninò divinâ omniscientiâ & καρδιογνωσίᾳ, ut & divinâ virtute ac potestate opus est. Non agnoverunt autem Christum verum Deum, Dominum gloriæ, sed merum, eundemque valdè vilem & abjectum ho- minem habuerunt, qui eundem cruci affixerunt: quia si agnovissent, ausi non fuissent eundem ag- gredi, nedum occidere. Conf. Disputationes, quas Christus cum Judæis de eo habuit Joh. V. & X. cap. De cætero agnoscimus, Christum non solùm respectu naturæ divinæ, sed etiam respectu humanæ naturæ Dominum gloriæ esse, siquidem gloria, quæ ipsi ut Deo propria est, humanæ na- turæ communicata sit: nec solùm respectu perso- næ, sed etiam respectu officii; quia Rex gloriæ est & Judex, quem in gloria Patris verè immensâ venturum credimus ad judicium novissimum Matth. XXV. Præfiguratum autem eundem fuisse per arcam fœderis, ut Dominum gloriæ, nuspiam dicitur, neque מלך הכבוד Psal. XXIV. 10. nomen est arcæ fœderis, sed Messiæ. Quia eundem Do- minum gloriæ, quem Dominum virtutum, Do- minum fortem & potentem, Dominum potentem in prælio vocat Hieropsaltes: quæ arcæ non con- veniunt, sed Domino, qui se ad arcam manife- stabat.

## 2:9
v. 9. but as it is written. It happened, namely: such is the ellipsis above at I, 31, but in the manuscript there is no but, and thus the sense also coheres sufficiently. They did not know, because God does not reveal such things except to those who love him, that is, those who inquire.

things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not ascended into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him. The sense is indeed in Isaiah LXIV. 4, where the Greeks say: from of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides you, and they wait for your works which you will do, showing mercy. Which words the Rabbis also explain concerning the other life in a more mysterious sense: but since Origen, Jerome to Pammachius on the best kind of interpreting, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, and Gregory Syncellus report that the very words which Paul uses here existed in the Apocrypha of Elijah, it is entirely credible that Paul took this from the writings of the Rabbis, who had it from ancient tradition: concerning which kind of sayings, see what we have brought forward at Matt. XXVII. 9. Chrysostom says in this place that many ancient books have perished. The manuscript has as many as he has prepared, instead of which he has prepared. Heart is said by the Hebrews for the whole soul. And to ascend into the heart, Jeremiah III. 16, and elsewhere, is what to the Latins is to come into the mind. Not foreign to this place is that saying of Philo in the book on Abel and Cain: for who would be capable of understanding the transition of a perfect soul to the Being? I do not think that even the one who is waiting knows its improvement, inasmuch as at that time it is becoming divine. For God does not use a counselor who is not suffering regarding the things which he is about to bestow.

What is to be held concerning these Grotian matters, and the Apostolic allegation in general, we have said in the Illustrated Bibles of the O.T. at the place Is. LXIV. 6, which can be compared here. But God is said to have prepared that wisdom and those hidden mysteries, which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which do not ascend into the heart of man, for those waiting for him, Is. LXIV. 4, namely out of love for Christ, and desire for his advent, because he reserved the full revelation of all things for the time of the N.T., or the fullness of times, by which that same one, in whom are all the mysteries of salvation, all that God from eternity according to his infinite wisdom predestined for our glory, our Jesus ought to advance and execute: which admittedly the great mystery of godliness comprises, 1 Tim. III. 6. For although the Lord was found even by those who did not seek him, Is. LXV. 1. as far as the Gentiles are concerned, yet he wished to manifest himself above all among those who from the people of God were awaiting the Savior of the world, and to them was first revealed the γνῶσις σωτηρίας Luke I. 77. ch. II. 25. 38. which the princes of this world could and ought to have known, but who despised the counsel of God proposed to them for their salvation Luke VII. 30. Which was especially made known through the Spirit of God to the Apostles, 1 Cor. II. 10. as those through whom there had to be the Φωτισμὸς τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν προσώπῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ 2 Cor. IV. 6. Concerning which see Estius in his notes on this passage, cited in our annotations on the Isaianic passage.

Latin:

v. 9. ἀλλὰ καθὼς γέγραπται. Evênit scilicet: qualis ἔλλειψις supra I, 31. sed in manu- scripto non est ἀλλὰ, & sic quoque satis cohæret sensus. Illi non noverunt, quia Deus talia non revelat nisi se amanti- bus, id est, inquirentibus.

ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς ὀυκ εἶδε, καὶ ὀυκ ἤκουσε, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώ- που ὀυκ ἀνέβη ἃ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ Θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτόν. Senfus quidem est apud Esaiam LXIV. 4. ubi Græci: ἀπὸ τῶ αἰῶνος ὀυκ ἠκούσαμεν, ὀυδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἡμῶν εἶδον Θεὸν πλὴν σῦ, καὶ τὰ ἔργα σῦ ἃ ποιήσεις ὑπομένεσιν ἔλεον. Quæ verba etiam Rabbini de vita altera exponunt sensu arcanio- re: sed cùm ipsa verba, quibus hîc utitur Paulus, exstitisse in Apocryphis Eliæ tradat Origenes, Hieronymus ad Pam- machium de optimo genere interpretandi, Zacharias Chry- sopolitanus, & Gregorius Syncellus, credibile omnino est, deprompsisse hoc Paulum ex scriptis Rabbinorum, qui ex habuerant ex traditione veteri: de quo genere dictorum vide quæ attulimus ad Matth. XXVII. 9. Multos veteres libros periisse dicit hoc loco Chrysostomus. Manuscriptus pro ἃ ἡτοίμασεν, habet ὅσα ἡτοίμασεν. καρδία Hebræis pro toto animo dicitur. Et ascendere in cor, Jeremiæ III. 16. & alibi, est, quod Latinis in mentem venire. Non alienum ab hoc loco Philonis illud libro de Abele & Caino: τίς γὰρ ἂν γένοιτο ἱκανὸς τὴν πρὸς τὸν ὄντα μετατάστασιν ψυχῆς τελείας κατανοῆσαι; ὀδ᾽ ἀυτὴν οἶμαι τὴν τοῦ ὑπομένοντος εἰδέναι τὴν βελτίωσιν ἀυτῆς, ἅτε κατ' ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον ἐπιθειάζεσαν. τῷ γὰρ ὀυ πάσχοντι συμβούλῳ ὁ Θεὸς περὶ ὧν μέλλει χαρίζεσθαι, ἧ χρῆται.

Quid de his Grotianis, & allegatione Apo- stolica in universum habendum, diximus in Bibliis Illustratis V. T. ad locum Es. LXIV. 6. quæ hîc conferri poterunt. Præparasse autem Deus di- citur sapientiam & mysteria illa abscondita, quæ oculus non vidit, auris non audivit, quæque non ascendunt in cor hominis, expectantibus eum Es. LXIV. 4. ex amore scilicet Christi, & desiderio adventus ejus, quia plenam omnium revelationem N. T. tempori, vel plenitudini temporum refer- vavit, quà idem ille, in quo omnia salutis mysteria, omnia quæ ab æterno Deus pro infinita sua sapien- tia προώρισεν εἰς δόξαν ἡμῶν, Jesus noster ea pro- vehere, & exequi debuit: quæ ὁμολογεμένως μέγα mysterion τῆς ἐυσεβείας complectitur 1. Tim. III. 6. Quanquam enim etiam ab illis, qui non require- bant eum, inventus sit Dominus Es. LXV. 1. quod ad gentes pertinet, tamen inter eos, qui è populo DEI expectabant Servatorem mundi, sese ante omnia manifestare voluit, illisque revelata primum est γνῶσις σωτηρίας Luc. I. 77. c. II. 25. 38. quam cognovisse etiam Principes seculi poterant, ac debebant, qui verò consilium DEI de salute ipsis propositum contemnebant Luc. VII. 30. Quæ im- primis per Spiritum Dei patefacta est Apostolis, 1. Cor. II. 10. utpote per quos fieri debuit Φωτι- σμὸς τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τῆ Θεᾶ ἐν προσώπῳ Ἰη- σᾶ χρισᾶ 2. Cor. IV. 6. Quo de vid. Estius in not. ad h. l. laudatus in annot. nostris ad locum Esaia- num.

## 2:10
v. 10. But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit.

That is, through that spirit which was united to Christ. See what was said on Mark II. 8. & Rom. I. 14. God has opened to us, says the Apostle, through the spirit of Christ, that there will be a universal judgment, which Christ is to exercise, and by what norm, and with what outcome. In the manuscript, there is no ἀυτοῦ.

Why should not the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Most Holy Trinity, to whom the work of revelation pertaining to the third article of faith, which is concerning sanctification, is ascribed, be understood by the more accepted usage of Scripture, rather than the divine nature of the Son of God? For the Holy Spirit is called now the Spirit of God, now the Spirit of the Son of God, inasmuch as he proceeds from both, namely from the Father and the Son. That there is talk here of the universal judgment, and its norm and outcome, is evident from no indication: and therefore these things are commonly referred rather to eternal life, or the good things which have been prepared for the faithful who love God: concerning which, however, see what is in the loc. cit. in the Bibl. Illustr. to be compared.

For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. The same sense as John I. 18. VI. 46. VIII. 19. 38. X. 15. 30. XIV. 7. 9. τὰ βάθη [the depths] are counsels long hidden Rom. XVI. 25. & above 7.

Those passages are foreign here, παράλληλα: for they treat of the ὁμοουσία of the Son with the Father, or of the omniscience of the Son: but here, as we have said, the discourse is of the omniscience of the Holy Spirit, whence from this passage the Fathers proved the Deity of the Holy Spirit against the Pneumatomachi.

Latin:

v. 10. ἡμῖν δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἀπεκάλυψε διὰ τοῦ πνέυματος ἀυτοῦ.

Id est, per illum spiritum, qui Christo fuit adunatus. Vide quæ dicta Marc. II. 8. & Rom. I. 14. Aperuit Deus nobis, inquit Apostolus, per Christi spiritum futurum esse judi- cium universale, quod Christus sit exerciturus, & quà normâ, & quo exitu. In Manuscripto non est ἀυτῦ.

Cur non intelligatur receptiori Scripturæ usu potiùs Spiritus S. tertia persona SS. Trinitatis, cui opus revelationis ad articulum fidei tertium, qui est de sanctificatione, pertinens, adscribitur, quàm divina Filii Dei natura? Nam & Spiritus Sanctus Spiritus modò Dei, modò Filii Dei dicitur, utpote qui ab utroque, Patre scilicet & Filio procedit. De judicio universali, ejusque norma & exitu hîc sermonem esse, nullo indicio constat: ideoque ad vitam potius æternam, vel bona quæ præpara- ta sunt fidelibus Deum diligentibus hæc com- muniter referuntur: de quo verò quæ l. c. in Bibl. Illustr. conferantur.

τὸ γὰρ πνεῦμα πάντα, ἐρευνᾶ καὶ τὰ βάθη τῶ Θεῦ. Idem sensus qui Job. I. 18. VI. 46. VIII. 19. 38 X 15. 30. XIV. 7. 9. τὰ βάθη consilia diu occultata Rom. XVI. 15. & supra 7.

Loca illa aliena hic sunt, παράλληλα: nam de ὁμοουσία Filii cum Patre agunt, aut de omniscentia Filii: hic verò, uti diximus, de omniscientia Spiritus S. sermo est, unde ex hoc loco Deitatem Spiritus S. Patres contra Pneumatomachos evicerunt.

## 2:11
v. 11. τίς γὰρ οἶδεν ἀνθρώπων τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; Who knows the hidden thoughts of princes except the mind of the prince himself? There is no need for that ἀνθρώπων, and it is absent in the Manuscript. οὕτω καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν, εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. No one knows the secrets of God except the Spirit of God himself, who was given to the Prophets in part, but to Christ most perfectly. For οἶδεν in the Manuscript there is ἔγνω, with the same sense.

If the discourse is about that Spirit who was given to the Prophets in part, but to Christ ὀυ κατὰ μέτρον, then it is not about the divine nature, but about the Holy Spirit that is treated here. Grotius is therefore inconsistent with himself.

Latin:

v. 11. τίς γὰρ οἶδεν ἀνθρώπων τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; Principum abditos sensus quis novit nisi ipse Principis animus? Nihil opus illo ἀνθρώπων & abest in Manuscripto. οὕτω καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν, εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. Arcana Dei nemo novit nisi ipse Spiritus Dei, qui Prophetis ex particula, Christo verò perfectissimè datus est. Pro οἶδεν in Manuscripto est ἔγνω, pari sensu.

Si de illo Spiritu, qui Prophetis datus ex parte, Christo autem ὀυ κατὰ μέτρον, sermo est, non ergò de divina natura, sed de Spiritu S. hic agitur. Sibi ipsi itaque adversus est Grotius.

## 2:12
v. 12. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου ἐλάβομεν. Those things which Christ said did not proceed from human ingenuity.

A foreign interpretation. The Apostle is not speaking of those things which Christ said, or what kind of Spirit Christ received, but of himself and other Apostles and disciples of Christ: nor is his purpose to teach that what Christ or the Apostles said did not proceed from human ingenuity, but to explain the difference between the spirit of the world and the Spirit by which the Apostles were governed, just as he had begun to teach that divine wisdom is most distinct from worldly wisdom.

ἀλλὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ. That Spirit, which for our sake was in the man Christ, is as it were a portion and instrument of God himself.

That the Holy Spirit, with whom Christ was anointed according to his human nature for the sake of our redemption, is as it were a portion and instrument of God, is abhorrent to the ὑποτυπώσει τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων. He is said to be ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ, because he proceeds from the essence of God, just as the Son is begotten from the essence of the Father: which is an internal ἐκπόρευσις: just as he is also called the Spirit of God here, in the same way as the spirit which is in man is the spirit of man, with which it is compared in the present passage. He is of the same essence as the Father, the same true and eternal God as the Father: therefore not some portion of God the Father: not an instrument of the same. Which things do not at all agree with the τῇ ὁμοουσία and the divine nature of the Holy Spirit: concerning which [we treat] in our Anti-Crellius.

ἵνα εἰδῶμεν τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ χαρισθέντα ἡμῖν. That we may know with certainty, not by wavering conjecture, those things which God has given us, that is, has decreed to give. For it is a metonymy, such as in Ephesians 1:4, 2:6, 2 Timothy 1:9.

Latin:

v. 12. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου ἐλάβομεν. Non ab humano ingenio profecta sunt ea, quæ dixit Christus.

Aliena interpretatio. Non de iis, quæ Christus dixit, aut qualem Spiritum Christus acceperit, sed de se, aliisque Apostolis, & discipulis Christi loquitur Apostolus: nec in eo est, ut doceat, non ab humano ingenio profecta esse, quæ Christus aut Apostoli dixêre, sed ut discrimen inter Spiritum mundi, & Spiritum quo regebantur Apostoli, explicet, uti divinam sapientiam à mundana distinctissimam esse, docere inceperat.

ἀλλὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Spiritus ille, qui nostri causa in homine Christo fuit, est ipsius Dei velut portio & instrumentum.

Spiritum Sanctum quo Christus secundum humanam naturam nostræ redemtionis causâ unctus est, Dei portionem velut esse, & instrumentum, abhorret ab ὑποτυπώσει τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων. ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ dicitur, quia ex essentia Dei procedit, uti Filius ex essentia Patris genitus est: quæ ἐκπόρευσις interna est: uti etiam Spiritus Dei hic dicitur, quemadmodum spiritus, qui in homine est, hominis spiritus est, cum quo confertur in præsenti. Ejusdem cum Patre est essentiæ, idem cum Patre verus & æternus Deus: Non ergò quædam Dei Patris portio: non instrumentum ejusdem. Quæ τῇ ὁμοουσία & divinæ naturæ Spiritûs S. haud conveniunt: de quo in Anti-Crellio nostro.

ἵνα εἰδῶμεν τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ χαρισθέντα ἡμῖν. Ut certò noscamus, non fluctuante conjecturâ, ea quæ Deus nobis dedit, id est, dare decrevit. Est enim μετωνυμία, qualis Ephes. I. 4. II. 6. 2. Timoth. I. 9.

## 2:13
v. 13. ἃ καὶ λαλοῦμεν. Which we also announce to all peoples according to the precepts of Christ.

οὐκ ἐν διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις. Not in that speech which human learning has taught.

ἀλλὰ ἐν διδακτοῖς πνεύματος ἁγίου. But in that speech which that most holy Spirit of Christ has taught. We have διδακτοῖς here twice with the genitive signifying the cause: such is the locution in John 6:45. In the Manuscript ἁγίου is not expressed, nor is it necessary.

πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες. Explaining those things which the Prophets, moved by the Spirit of God, said, through those things which Christ revealed to us by his Spirit. συγκρίνειν is פתר to explain, Genesis 40:8, 16, 22; 41:12, 13, 15; Daniel 5:13, 17.
