Which is ἐπιλύειν in Gen. 41:12, and thence λύσις in Ecclesiastes 7:30, which is σύγκριμα in Dan. 2:25, 4:15, 5:28, and σύγκρισις in the same, Dan. 2:4, 5, 6, 7, and often elsewhere. For prophecy is not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως. 2 Peter 1:20.

The explanation of τῶν πνευματικῶν is too restricted: for not only those things which the Prophets spoke are to be conveniently explained or judged, but also those things which the Apostles themselves spoke, just as the Berrhoeans are said to have judged those things which the Apostle preached, Acts XVII. 11. examining the scriptures, whether these things are so. If the sense of exposition has a place here at all (which we do not oppose), there is nevertheless a need for the collation and comparison of spiritual things with spiritual: so that they may mutually explain each other

Scriptures, both of the Old and New Testament, so that the former is indeed primarily explained by the latter, though sometimes also, conversely, the latter by the former, and parts of the Old Testament are also explained by other parts of the same (which must similarly be held concerning the New Testament): for all things have proceeded from the same Spirit. The Apostle speaks not only of himself and the Apostles, but of all who have received the Spirit of God. If Grotius had observed that, along with other heterodox searchers of Scripture, he would certainly not have explained the Scriptures from profane authors, but solely from the Scriptures, πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνων. Beza prefers to render that συγκρίνων as joining or adapting, which Pareus says is indeed more obscure, explaining it as: comparing or fitting together spiritual words; since indeed spiritual doctrine ought deservedly to be handed down by a spiritual kind of diction. To which also tends the explanation of B. Balduinus: i.e. It does not befit the doctrine of the Holy Spirit that we persuade listeners in any way whatsoever with an adornment of words and figures, by which authority is won not so much for the doctrine as for the teacher: But that true and good things be proposed also truly and clearly, so that attention is paid not so much to the speech or the speaker as to the things set forth and the strength of the arguments: and this is to attemper spiritual things to spiritual things: Which method of speaking is unusual for secular orators, just as the things themselves are unknown to the wise of this world. Similarly B. Hülsemann, praising to that effect also the explanation of Salmeron, Justinian, Cornelius à Lapide, as well as the Belgians, English, Genevans, Calvin, Musculus, Beza, and even the Photinians who interpret concerning the analogy of things and words.

Latin:

v. 13. ἃ καὶ λαλοῦμεν. Quæ etiam ex Christi præceptis omnibus populis annunciamus.

οὐκ ἐν διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις. Non eo sermone, quem docuit humana eruditio.

ἀλλὰ ἐν διδακτοῖς πνεύματος ἁγίου. Sed eo sermone, quem docuit sanctissimus ille Christi Spiritus. Bis hic habemus διδακτοῖς cum genitivo causam significante: qualis locutio est apud Joh. VI. 45. In Manuscripto non exprimitur ἁγίου, nec opus.

πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες. Exponentes ea, quæ Prophetæ Spiritu Dei acti dixêre, per ea, quæ Christus suo Spiritu nobis aperuit. συγκρίνειν est פתר exponere, Genes. XL. 8. 16. 22. XLI. 12. 13. 15. Daniel. V 13. 17. Quod ἐπιλύειν Gen. XLI. 12. & inde λύσις Ecclesiastæ VII. 30. quod σύγκριμα Dan. II. 25. IV. 15. V. 28. & σύγκρισις in eodem Dan. II. 4. 5. 6. 7. & alibi sæpe. Prophetia enim non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως. 2. Petr. I. 20.

Est nimis restricta τῶν πνευματικῶν explicatio: non enim ea tantùm convenienter seu exponenda sunt, seu dijudicanda, quæ Prophetæ dixêre, sed etiam ea, quæ dixêre ipsi Apostoli, quomodo Berrhoënses ea dijudicasse dicuntur, quæ Apostolus prædicavit, Act. XVII. 11. ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς, εἰ ἔχει ταῦτα οὕτως. Si omninò expositionis sensus hic locum habeat (in quo non repugnamus) collatione tamen & comparatione spiritualium cum spiritualibus opus est: uti mutuò sese explicant

Scripturæ, tùm Veteris & Novi Testam. ut illud quidem imprimis ex hocce, quandoque tamen etiam, vice versà, hoc ex illo declaretur, & partes etiam Veteris Testam. ex aliis ejusdem partibus (quod similiter de Novo Test. haben- dum) exponantur: nam ab eodem omnia profe- cta sunt Spiritu. Non de se & Apostolis solùm lo- quitur Apostolus, sed de omnibus, qui Spiritum Dei accepêre. Id si observasset Grotius, cum aliis heterodoxis Scripturæ scrutatoribus, non sanè Scripturas è profanis autoribus, sed è Scripturis unicè exposuisset, πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγ- κρίνων. Beza illud συγκρίνοντες mavult reddere conjungentes, seu adaptantes, quod verò obscurius esse ait Pareus, exponens: conferentes vel coaptan- tes spiritualia verba; siquidem meritò spiritualis doctrina spirituali dictionis genere tradi debeat. Quò etiam abit B. Balduini explicatio: q. d. Do- ctrinam Spiritûs sancti non decet, ut qualitercunque persuadeamus auditoribus, ornatu verborum & figu- rarum, quibus non tam doctrina quàm doctori auto- ritas conciliatur: Sed ut res veræ & bonæ, verè etiam ac perspicuè proponantur, quo non tam orationi aut oratori, quàm rebus præpositis & argumento- rum robori attendatur: & hoc est spiritualia spiri- tualibus attemperare: Quæ ratio dicendi oratori- bus secularibus insolens est, quemadmodum & ipsæ res sapientibus hujus seculi ignotæ. Similiter B. Hülsemannus, laudans in eam sententiam etiam explicationem Salmeronis, Justiniani, Cornelii à Lapide, ut & Belgarum, Anglorum, Geneven- sium, Calvini, Musculi, Bezæ, etiam Photinia- norum de rerum & verborum analogia interpre- tantium.

## 2:14
v. 14. But the natural man (ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος).

The natural man (ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος) and the carnal man (σαρκικὸς) are not the same. The natural man is he who is led only by the light of human reason: the carnal man is he who is governed by the affections of the body: but for the most part, natural men are in some part carnal, as the Greek philosophers were fornicators, corrupters of boys, seekers of glory, slanderers, envious. But here nothing else is designated than a man relying only on human reason, such as were most of the Jews and the philosophers of the Greeks. Jude in his epistle explains the natural man (ψυχικὸς) as not having the Spirit (πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντας). Hierocles calls it a natural body (ψυχικὸν σῶμα), which he soon explains as the vital (τὸ ζωτικόν).

We readily admit a certain distinction between natural (ψυχικὸν) and carnal (σαρκικὸν) by reason of formal signification, but they agree materially when the discourse is about men in the state of sin: in which all are natural (ψυχικοὶ), not only in part, or some are carnal (σαρκικοὶ): because those who enjoy only the light of human reason, but are not reborn of God, nor led by the Spirit of God, are merely carnal: And such were not only most of the Jews and the philosophers of the Greeks, but such are all men outside the grace of Christ and the illumination of the Holy Spirit by the force of original corruption, which brings with it both the deprivation of true knowledge, with the darkness of errors of the mind, and concupiscence inclining toward sins of every kind. Hierocles does not understand such a natural (ψυχικὸν) state. The Arminians explain the stupidity and impotence of the natural (ψυχικῦ) man as concerning only the sensitive or inferior faculty: in Apol. c. XI. But the intellect does not belong to the sensitive faculty; therefore others, Salmero, Cornel. Justinian, the Belgians, explain it more correctly as concerning those who follow only natural judgment. Conf. Jac. III. 15. Jud. v. 19.

He does not receive the things of the Spirit of God (ὀ δέχεται τὰ τῦ πνεύματος τῦ Θεῦ).

He does not understand those things which were brought forth through the Prophets: since not even the Prophets themselves sufficiently understood them. To receive, here, is what is soon called to know (γνῶναι), to understand.

Τὰ τῦ πνεύματος Θεῦ are divine mysteries, or matters of faith, which were delivered by the Holy Spirit not only through the Prophets, but also through the Apostles. And although the Prophets perhaps did not understand those things which they brought forth as fully as they are understood by us, yet they did not speak like Caiaphas or Balaam's ass, without understanding, or without the true sense of the things said. For the Spirit of Christ, which was in them, searched what things were to come, 1 Pet. 1:11. But the Papists wrongly, as may be seen in Bellarmine, book III, on grace and free will, ch. 3, by of ratifying or assenting, not of the faculty of knowing spiritual things: whereas the Apostle notably uses words of knowledge, οἶδε v. 11, 12, and v. 14 γνῶναι, and v. 15 ἔγνω, and openly contradicts the Pontificians: οὐ δύναται γνῶναι: HE CANNOT understand. Wherefore the Fathers in the Council of Milevis rightly asserted the opinion of the Apostle in the present passage, and among them Augustine, namely concerning both impotencies, both of knowing and of receiving or embracing spiritual things: which Pope Celestine also approves to the Bishops of Gaul, Ep. 6, 10. See Michael Baius on free will, ch. 10, and Vossius, book IV, History of Pelagianism, part 2, p. 449.

for it is foolishness to him.

That is, as if they were the voices of fools signifying nothing. Such was the prophecy of Isaiah to the Ethiopian, Acts 8:31.

The example of the Ethiopian is less fitting. For although he was ignorant of that individual who was the Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth, and was not sufficiently informed about the place in Isaiah ch. 53; yet the words of the Prophet were not foolishness to him, and he had already been pre-catechized about Christ from the Prophets, as a proselyte, as Irenaeus holds concerning him, book IV, ch. 40. But concerning the present Apostolic passage against the Pelagians and those who Pelagianize, especially the Socinians and Arminians, we have spoken more fully in Exeget. Aug. Conf. art. V, ch. 3, th. 5.

because it is spiritually discerned.

In order that their true sense may be judged, there is need of a new and clearer revelation: such as occurs through Christ. Ἀνακρίνεσθαι is a forensic term, Acts 4:9, 12:19. And it is accustomed to be transferred to the examination of doctrine, Acts 17:11, below 14:24. And thus the Hebrew חקר is translated.

For the judging of the sense of Scripture concerning things to be believed or the perception of the mysteries of GOD, there is by no means need of a new revelation, which the Socinians otherwise intend, because Scripture can be explained by Scripture; otherwise, for the perception of those things which have been handed down by Christ and the Apostles, there would be need of a new revelation again. Nor are we sent back to new revelations in matters of faith: but to Holy Scripture, through which GOD informs the Church, but not immediately through visions or illuminations, such as the new Prophets and fanatics boast of.

Latin:

v. 14. ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος.

Non idem est ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος & σαρκικὸς. ψυχικὸς est qui humanæ tantum rationis luce ducitur: σαρκικὸς qui corporis affectibus gubernatur: sed plerumque ψυχικοὶ aliquâ in parte sunt σαρκικοὶ, ut Græcorum Philosophi scortatores, puerorum corruptores, gloriæ aucupes, male- dici, invidi. Verùm hîc nihil aliud designatur, quàm ho- mo humanâ tantùm ratione nitens, quales erant Judæorum plerique & Philosophi Græcorum. Judas in epistola ψυχι- κὺς explicat, πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντας. Hierocles ψυχικὸν σῶμα vocat, quod mox explicat τὸ ζωτικόν.

Discrimen quoddam inter ψυχικὸν & σαρκικὸν faciles admittimus, ratione formalis significatio- nis, sed materialiter conveniunt, cùm de homi- nibus in statu peccati sermo est: in quo omnes ψυχικοὶ, non tantum ex parte, vel nonnulli sunt σαρκικοὶ: quia qui humanæ tantum rationis luce gaudant, non verò ex Deo renati sunt, nec Spi- ritu Dei ducuntur, carnales tantum sunt: Et ta- les non erant Judæorum solum plerique & Philo- sophi Græcorum, sed tales omnes sunt homines extra gratiam Christi, & illuminationem Spiritûs Sancti vi corruptionis originalis, quæ & privatio- nem veræ notitiæ, cum tenebris errorum mentis, & concupiscentiam propendentem in omnis gene- ris peccata infert. Tale ψυχικὸν Hierocles non intelligit. Arminiani stuporem & impotentiam hominis ψυχικῦ de sola parte sensitiva seu inferio- ri facultate exponunt: in Apol. c. XI. Sed intel- lectus non pertinet ad facultatem sensitivam; ideò rectius alii de iis, qui solum naturale judicium se- quuntur, Salmero, Cornel. Justinian. Belga expo- nunt. Conf. Jac. III. 15. Jud. v. 19.

ὀ δέχεται τὰ τῦ πνεύματος τῦ Θεῦ.

Non intelligit ea, quæ per Prophetas sunt prodita: quip- pe quæ ne ipsi quidem Prophetæ satis intellexerint. Ca- pere, hîc est, quod mox γνῶναι intelligere.

Τὰ τῦ πνεύματος Θεῦ sunt mysteria divina, vel res fidei, quæ à Spiritu S. non per Prophetas tan- tum, sed etiam per Apostolos tradita. Etsi autem Prophetæ non adeò plenè fortassis ea, quæ pro- didêre, intellexerint, uti à nobis ea intelliguntur, non tamen instar Cajaphae aut asinae Bileami lo- quuti sunt, citra intelligentiam, aut citra verum dictorum sensum. Spiritus enim Christi, qui in ipsis erat, scrutatus est ea, quae futura erant, 1. Petr. I. 11. perperam autem Papistae, ut apud Bellarmi- num l. III. de grat. & liber. arbitr. c. 3. videre est, haec tantum de assensu explicant, quòd homo ani- malis facultate ratihabendi vel assentiendi destitua- tur, non facultate cognoscendi spiritualia: quum Apostolus notanter verba notitia adhibeat, οἶδε v. 11. 12. & v. 14. γνῶναι, ac v. 15. ἔγνω, ac palàm Pontificiis contradicat: ὀ δύναται γνῶναι: NON POTEST intelligere. Quapropter sententiam Apostoli in praesenti loco rectè asseruere Patres in Concilio Milevitano, & in iis Augustinus, de utraque nempe impotentia, & cognoscendi & sus- cipiendi, vel amplectendi spiritualia: quam etiam approbat Caelestinus Papa ad Episcopos Galliae Ep. 6. 10. Vid. Michaël Bajus de liber. arbitr. c. 10. & Vossius l. IV. Hist. Pelag. part. 2. p. 449.

μωρία γὰρ ἀυτῷ ἐστι.

Id est, quasi stultorum voces nihil significantes. Tale erat Esaiae vaticinium Aethiopi Act. IIX. 31.

Aethiopis exemplum minus congruit. Etsi e- nim is individuum illud, quod erat Messias, Je- sum Nazarenum ignorârit, neque de loco Esai- ae c. LIII. satis informatus fuerit; non tamen μωρία illi erant verba Prophetae, & praecatechisa- tus jam de Christo è Prophetis erat, ceu proselytus, ut Irenaeus de ipso habet l. IV. c. XL. De loco au- tem praesenti Apostolico contra Pelagianos & Pe- lagianizantes, imprimis Socinianos & Arminianos diximus uberius in Exeget. Aug. Conf. artic. V. c. 3. th. 5.

ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται.

Ut dijudicetur verus eorum sensus, opus est nova & apertiori revelatione: qualis per Christum contingit. Ἀνα- κρίνεσθαι est vox forensis Act. IV. 9. XII. 19. Et solet trans- ferri ad examen doctrinae Act. XVII. 11. infra XIV. 24. Et sic vertitur חקר Hebraeum.

Ad dijudicationem sensus Scripturae de rebus credendis vel perceptionem mysteriorum DEI haud opus est nova revelatione, quod aliàs Soci- niani intendunt, quia Scriptura per Scripturam explicari potest; alioquin ad perceptionem eo- rum, quae à Christo & Apostolis tradita sunt, no- vâ iterum revelatione opus foret. Nec ad novas revelationes in rebus fidei remittimur: sed ad Scripturam S. per quam DEUS informat Eccle- siam, non verò ἀμέσως per visiones, aut illuminatio- nes, quales jactitant novelli Prophetae, & fanatici.

## 2:15
V. 15. But the spiritual man discerns all things.

In the Manuscript, ἀνακρίνει τὰ πάντα. He who is imbued with much light from Christ easily judges concerning the sense of the Prophets. It can be said of him with the best right, what Aristotle says in another sense, Eth. III. 15: the man of sound judgment judges each thing correctly.

yet he himself is discerned by no one.

To be judged by no one is to be able to be refuted: as Stephen, Acts 4:10. The reason follows:

Latin:

V. 15. ὁ δὲ πνευματικὸς ἀνακρίνει μετὰ πάντα.

In Manuscripto, ἀνακρίνει τὰ πάντα. Qui multâ à Chri- sto luce imbutus est facile judicat de sensu Prophetarum. Potest de eo optimo jure dici, quod alio sensu dicit Ari- stoteles Eth. III. 15. ὁ σπουδαῖος ἕκαστα κρίνει ὀρθῶς.

ἀυτὸς δὲ ὑπ᾽ ὀὐδενὸς ἀνακρίνεται.

A nemine judicari, est, refelli poteit: ut Stephanus Act. IV. 10. Causa sequitur:

## 2:16
V. 16. For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him?

From Isaiah 40:13, where in the Greek it is: Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who has become his counselor? Just as Paul also cited that passage in Romans 11:34. GOD did not admit anyone before the times of Christ to fully know his secrets, just as kings are accustomed to admit certain counselors. συμβιβάζειν means to instruct, to teach thoroughly, as we saw in Acts 9:22, 16:10; but here, with the meaning not much removed, it is to give counsel, to advise, to become a counselor. Therefore, to advise and to instruct are joined together in Isaiah 40:14.

But we now have the mind of Christ.

But we know the counsels of GOD, which were revealed to Christ. John 15:15. Who can bring more certain things concerning the will of GOD than GOD himself? But he delivered them to Christ. Therefore, he who has them cannot be solidly refuted by any allegations of the Prophets, nor by any petty reasonings of the Philosophers. Ambrose says it best: Whom should I believe more concerning GOD, than GOD?

As we warned before, the Apostle is not dealing only with the judging of Prophetic writings, since spiritual things extend more widely, and the spiritual man is said here to judge all things: nor does it harmonize that no one was admitted to know the secrets of GOD before the times of Christ, nor does Isaiah deny this of himself and other Prophets, but he says that no one was a counselor to GOD in divine decrees, and from that—namely, from the counsel of GOD—he knew the divine mind, so that it might be taught that the decrees of GOD are altogether unutterable and unsearchable apart from divine revelation; which revelation, however, was not reserved until the times of Christ, but happened long ago to the Patriarchs and Prophets; although in the meantime we do not deny that a clearer revelation occurred in the time of the New Testament from Christ and the Apostles, when the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them, whence we also have the mind of Christ from the Apostolic writings. For they did not reserve it for themselves, nor did they receive it for that purpose privately, but so that they might propagate it, as public teachers of the whole world. But these things, which are distinguished by Gratian in Distinction 40, chapter 'Si Papae', and by the Roman Pontiff Boniface VIII himself in the Decretals 'de major. et obed.' concerning the spiritual man who judges all things and is judged by no one, are wrongly restricted to the Roman Pontiff: for thus it would be necessary for all others to be carnal, or merely natural, so that he alone might be held to be spiritual, which is absurd: not to mention that no Roman Pontiff existed in the nature of things when the Apostle wrote these things. But it is well: Gratian himself acknowledges that the Roman Pontiff is not exempt from judgment IF HE DEVIATES FROM THE FAITH: which the same man admits by this limitation can happen, and that it has happened in many cases, as experience, the teacher of fools, has taught abundantly, and as the writings published by our Theologians concerning the Apostasy of the Roman Church have sufficiently confirmed. Moreover, everyone is spiritual who, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, has the true sense of Scripture and a right judgment for discerning the true from the false, or a discerning power: who can be judged by no one, namely, by one who is only natural. For spiritual men can certainly judge one another; and the spirits of the prophets must be subject to the prophets, 1 Corinthians 14:32, and all things must be tested by the faithful, 1 Thessalonians 5:21, so that they do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from GOD, 1 John 4:1.

Latin:

V. 16. τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νῦν Κυρίου, ὃς συμβιβάσει ἀυτόν.

Ex Esa. XL. 13. ubi in Graeco: τίς Κυρίου νῦν ἔγνω, καὶ τίς ἀυτῷ σύμβουλος ἐγένετο; Quomodo & Paulus citavit eum locum Rom. XI. 34. DEUS ante Christi tempora neminem admisit ad arcana sua pernoscenda, sicut reges admittere consiliarios quosdam solent. συμβιβάζειν est in- stituere, edocere, ut vidimus Actor. IX. 22. XVI. 10. hic verò, non multum remoto significatu, est consilium dare, συμβουλέυειν, σύμβουλον γίνεσθαι. Itaque συμβουλέυουσι συμβι- βάζων conjunguntur Esaiae XL. 14.

ἡμεῖς δὲ νῦν χριστῦ ἔχομεν.

Nos autem novimus DEI consilia, quae Christo fuere re- velata. Joh. XV. 15. Quis potest de DEI voluntate cer- tiora adferre quam ipse DEUS? is autem ea Christo tra- didit. Ea igitur qui habet, nullis Prophetarum allegatio- nibus, nullis Philosophorum ratiunculis solide refelli po- test. Optimè Ambrosius: Cui magis de DEO, quàm DEO credam?

Quod antea monuimus, non de solâ Propheti- corum scriptorum dijudicatione agit Apostolus, quùm τὰ πνευματικὰ latius pateant, & τὰ πάντα dijudicare hic dicatur ὁ πνευματικὸς: neque verò consonat, quod ante Christi tempora nemo admis- sus fuerit ad arcana DEI pernoscenda, nec id ne- gat de se aliisque Prophetis Esaias, sed neminem in decretis divinis DEO à consilio fuisse, & inde, è consilio sc. DEI, mentem divinam novisse, ait, ut DEI decreta prorsus esse ἀνεκδιήγητα, καὶ ἀνεξε- ρεύνητα, citra divinam revelationem, doceatur: quæ verò revelatio non reservata est ad Christi usque tempora, sed jam olim Patriarchis & Pro- phetis contigit; etsi interim non diffiteamur, cla- riorem revelationem tempore N. T. à Christo & Apostolis, cum Spiritus Sanctus super eos effusus fuit, contigisse, unde nos etiam mentem Christi ha- bemus è scriptis Apostolicis. Non enim sibi eam reservarunt, nec eâ fini privatim eandem accepe- runt, sed ut propagarent eandem, ceu publici totius orbis doctores. Perperam verò hæc, quæ de spirituali omnia dijudicante, à nemine dijudi- cando à Gratiano distinct. XL. c. Si Papæ, & ab ipso P. R. Bonifacio VIII. extra de major. & obed. restringuntur ad Pontificem Romanum: Sic enim omnes alios oporteret esse σαρκικοὺς, aut merè ψυχικοὺς: ut ipse solus habeatur πνευματικὸς, quod absonum: ut taceam, quòd nullus tunc Romanus Pontifex in rerum natura fuerit, cùm hæc Apo- stolus scriberet. Sed benè est: agnoscit ipse Gra- tianus, Pontificem Rom. judicio exemptum non esse, SI A FIDE deviet: quod verò & posse fieri hac limitatione idem fatetur, & factum esse in plurimis, cùm experientia stultorum magistra edo- cuit abundè, tùm verò scripta de Apostasia Roma- næ Ecclesiæ à Nostris Theologis edita satis con- firmarunt. Cæterum spiritualis est omnis, qui à Spiritu S. illuminatus sensum Scripturæ verum, & rectum judicium habet discernendi verum à fal- so, vel δύναμιν διακριτικὴν: qui à nemine judicari potest, nempe qui animalis tantum sit. Spiritua- les enim sese mutuo dijudicare omninò possunt; & Prophetarum spiritus Prophetis subjecti esse de- bent 1. Cor. XIV. 32. & omnia probanda sunt fideli- bus 1. Thess. V. 21. ne credant omni Spiritui, sed probent Spiritus, num ex DEO sint, 1. Joh. IV. 1.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

By the example of the Corinthians, the Apostle teaches what he had said, that the natural man does not grasp the things that are of the Spirit of GOD; since their schisms convince them that they are still carnal, which they stir up for no reason, when Paul and Apollos are only ministers, and of the same condition, fellow-workers of GOD, even if he himself laid the foundation, and others build upon it, but in different ways, and with a different outcome. He warns them not to destroy the temple of GOD, which they are, not to affect worldly wisdom, and not to boast in any man, but in God alone, and Christ.

There are two parts: The first is didactic, why it was necessary for them to be treated as still very carnal: containing at the same time some correction: because they foster schisms on account of teachers of the Church, who are, however, all ministers and fellow-workers of GOD, both from the exposition of their ministry, in the edification of the Church, and the warning concerning the work of others in the spiritual structure, up to verse 15. The second is hortatory, exhorting that care be taken of the temple of the Holy Spirit, so that it may not be corrupted: which he implies is also done by the persuasion of empty wisdom, and by vain admiration of ministers: up to verse 32 and the end.

PART I. DIDACTIC. To argue against schismatic dissensions as carnal, not distinguishing the principal cause and the ministerial.

V. 1. And I, brethren.

Even I, instructed by such great gifts of GOD.

I could not speak unto you.

I could not, that is, I did not judge it useful, namely when I was among you. Concerning this meaning of the word δύνασθαι we have spoken at Mark VI. 5.

speak unto you as unto spiritual.

Namely, as being. For this particle is accustomed to be understood, as in 2 Cor. XII. 2. Sermons which are held before all are accommodated to the understanding of the greater part. But the greater part of the Corinthian assembly had not yet progressed much in the doctrine of Christ, which was spiritual. Therefore they still had more need of the instillation of the precepts of Christ to subdue the remnants of evil affections, than of the explanation of the figures which lay hidden in ancient history and shadowed forth the things of the new covenant. There is a passage akin to this and explaining it at Hebrews IV. 11, 12, 13, 14, where likewise milk is the elements of the Christian religion, but food is the explanation of the mysteries lying hidden in ancient history. These are suitable for those who have progressed much in piety: those are necessary for beginners.

but as unto carnal.

As if having still within you traces of affections not sufficiently Christian. Comparatively he both denies them to be spiritual and calls them carnal: namely because there were others who had progressed much more in piety.

as unto babes in Christ.

If he uses the word νηπῖοι, as does the writer to the Hebrews V. 13. They are called so, not with regard to time, through which they had known Christ, but of progress. Thus also Homer and Hesiod call men of little wisdom babes. See also Ephes. IV. 14.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Exemplo Corinthiorum docet Apostolus, quod dixerat, animalem hominem non capere ea, quæ Spiritûs DEI sunt; siquidem schi- smata ipsorum eos adhuc carnales esse, con- vincant, quæ ob nullam causam excitent, quum Paulus, & Apollo ministri tantùm sint, ejusdemque conditionis, DEI συνεργοὶ, etsi ipse fundamentum posuerit, alii eidem superstruant, sed diversimodè, & cum di- verso eventu. Monet, templum DEI, quod ipsi sunt, ne destruant, mundanam sapien- tiam ne affectent, nec de ullo hominum glo- rientur, sed de solo Deo, & Christo.

PArtes duæ sunt: Prior διδακτικὴ, cur ipsos ut multùm adhuc carnales tractari oportuerit: aliquid correptionis simul in se continens: quod schismata foveant, ob doctores Ecclesiæ, qui verò omnes ministri & cooperarii DEI sint tum ex- positione ministerii sui, in ædificatione Ecclesiæ, & commonitione de aliorum opere in spirituali structura, ad versum 15. Altera est παραινετικὴ, ex- hortans, ut templi Spiritûs S. ratio habeatur, ne corrumpatur: quo etiam inani sapientiæ persuasio- ne, & vanâ ministrorum admiratione fieri, innuit: ad v. 32. & ultimum.

PARS I. DIDACTICA. Diffidia Schismatica carnales arguere, non dif- cernentes causam principalem, & ministerialem.

V. 1. καὶ ἐγὼ ἀδελφοὶ.

Etiam ego tantis donis DEI instructus.

ἐκ ἠδυνήθην ὑμῖν λαλῆσαι.

Non potui, id est, non ex usu judicavi, nempe cum apud vos essem. De hac significatione vocis δύνασθαι diximus ad Marc. VI. 5.

ὑμῖν λαλῆσαι ὡς πνευματικοῖς.

Nempe ὖσιν. Hæc enim particula subaudiri solet, ut 2. Cor. XII. 2. Sermones qui coram omnibus habentur, accommodantur captui partis majoris. Pars autem major Corinthiaci cœtûs non multum adhuc in doctrina Chri- sti, quæ spiritualis erat, profecerat. Ideò magis adhuc opus habebant instillatione præceptorum Christi ad edo- mandas affectuum malorum reliquias, quàm explicatione figurarum, quæ latebant in veteri historia, & novi fœde- ris res adumbrabant. Est germanus huic locus & hunc explicans ad Hebræos IV. 11. 12. 13. 14. ubi pariter lac sunt elementa Christianæ religionis, cibus verò explicatio mysteriorum in veteri historia latentium. Hæc conve- niunt iis, qui multum profecêre in pietate: illa necessaria sunt incipientibus.

ἀλλ' ὡς σαρκικοῖς.

Tanquam habentes adhuc in vobis vestigia affectuum non satis Christianorum. Comparatè eos & πνευματικὸς negat, & σαρκικὸς appellat: nempe quia alii erant, qui multò plus in pietate profecerant.

ὡς νηπίοις ἐν χρισῷ.

Si vocem νηπῖοι usurpat & scriptor ad Hebræos V. 13. Dicuntur sic, non temporis habitâ ratione, per quod Chri- stum cognoverant, sed τῆς προκοπῆς. Sic & Homerus & Hesiodus homines exiguæ sapientiæ νηπίυς vocant. Vide & Ephes. IV. 14.

## 3:2
V. 2. I have fed you with milk.

Proverbial: still at the nurse's breast. Cicero to Atticus XII. Philo on Agriculture: 'For infants, milk is food; but for the mature, the products of wheat; and the soul's nourishment might be milky in childhood.' Theophilus of Antioch, Book II: 'For when a child is born, it cannot yet eat bread, but is first nourished with milk, then, as its age progresses, it comes to solid food.' Not only infants are accustomed to be nourished with milk, but also the 'hektikoi' (consumptive): for liquids are more easily digested. We have had the verb 'potizein' (to give to drink) in Matt. 10:42, 25:35, 37, 42, 27:48, Mark 9:41, 15:36, Luke 13:15, Romans 12:20. It will also occur in this epistle several times.

and not food.

It is a 'syllepsis' (a figure of speech). For 'epotisa' (I gave to drink) is indeed said of milk, but not of food: therefore, 'I gave' is understood. 'Broma' (food) here is what 'solid food' is in Hebrews 5:12. Philo: 'Do you not see that even our body does not use firm and expensive foods before it uses the varied and milky ones in the age of infancy?'

for you were not yet able.

And here one must understand 'to bear' or 'to digest.' For he kills an infant who gives it bread and meat. Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, book 33. Such ellipses are frequent in Paul, sometimes of nouns, sometimes of verbs: with a similar ellipsis you have the Hebrew 'tukal', that is, 'I shall be able,' in Isaiah 1:13, Psalm 101:5 in the Hebrew.

Because the Apostle had said that spiritual persons are judged by no carnal person, he implies that the Corinthians, being as yet carnal, rashly judge him, the Apostle of Christ, and others: and since they do not yet sufficiently grasp spiritual things, he warns that he had to deal with them as if they were still very carnal: i.e., you blame me because I am a humble teacher among you: but if there is any fault in this, ascribe it to your own ignorance, which compelled me to babble childishly with children, because, however much I might have wished, I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal, or at least as to infants in Christ. He calls them carnal, as not yet sufficiently understanding the foundations of doctrine, hanging only upon men, and indulging in the affections of the flesh regarding judgment: but spiritual, those who have progressed more in the knowledge of the doctrine of the Gospel through the illumination of the Spirit, and in whom the Spirit prevails over the flesh, so that they obey the doctrine and do not hang upon the authority and gifts of men. It is rightly observed, however, that 'carnal' is not used here simply, as are those who are not reborn, but partially, of those who have some light and faith, but in whom the flesh still predominates: carnal, not unbelievers, whom he had previously called 'animal' (natural); but weaker catechumens: for the latter do not understand at all the things that are of the Spirit of God: but the former, although they could not yet grasp more perfect doctrine, were nevertheless capable of the milk of the Gospel. And rightly, as Theophylact notes, the Apostle added that 'I COULD NOT': lest he appear to have been led by envy in not having endowed them with perfection. As far as those things which are of Christ are concerned, he says, you are infants, and therefore I offered you milk to drink, that is, a certain simpler doctrine, not more perfect food. Why? Because you were not yet able. Paul introduced this to repress the arrogance of the Corinthians and remove the insolence of those who rely too much on their own wisdom. These are the words of Theophylact. The drinking of milk is suitable for infants because it tastes of its own sweetness, nourishes with liquid richness, and is easily digested: solid food is for adults, who have stronger organs of mastication, and because of their more vehement labors and movements can take in more solid nourishment. By this metaphorical expression he refers primarily to the manner of presentation, namely, simplicity in teaching as regards little ones: but a greater apparatus of both things and words as regards those who are more adult; he calls them 'nepious' (infants) in Christ, that is, in the knowledge and faith of Christ. The Papists take the nourishment of milk to refer to the ceremonies and rites of the Church; they refer the more solid food to the sanctions of the Church, the Popes, and the Councils. But in the age of the Apostle, nothing was established concerning the decrees of Popes: nor was anything known except the Apostolic Council in Acts 15. Nor ought the simpler ones to be fed only on rites, or the more advanced only on the decrees of Popes and Councils. Therefore, the handed-down interpretation is to be preferred, as having sprung from the text itself. Which is thus proposed by our blessed Mylius: Milk, he says, is provided if not only the general heads of religion are taught in a general way, but also in a simple manner of teaching, that is, a merely catechetical one. Solid food is given when either the arduous mysteries of religion are proposed: or those general and common heads of the same are explained with more solid and exact doctrine, the practice of faith is demanded, and one inquires more accurately into the causes and moments of the mysteries.

but not even yet now are you able.

Not even now, so long after the beginnings of the faith. Knowledge and mighty works ought to have grown with time. Origen against Celsus III. 'The things among you that are most beautiful and divine, we then dare to bring into the midst in public dialogues when we have a supply of intelligent hearers. But we hide and pass over in silence the deeper things from those who come together and are in need of the words figuratively called milk. For it is written by our Paul, sending to the Corinthians, "With milk, indeed, I fed you, not with solid food, for you were not yet able; but not even yet now are you able. For you are still carnal," etc.'

Latin:

V. 2. γάλα ὑμᾶς ἐπότισα.

Proverbiale διὰ τιθήνης ἔτι. Cicero ad Atticum XII. Phi- lo de agricultura: ἐπὶ δὲ νηπίοις μέν ἐσι γάλα τροφή· τε- λείοις δὲ τὰ ἐκ πυρῶν πήμματα, καὶ ψυχῆς γαλακτώδεις μὲν ἄν ἕιεν τροφαὶ κατὰ τὴν παιδικὴν ἡλικίαν. Theophilus Antio- chenus libro II. νὴ γὰρ νῦν ἐπὰν γενηθῇ παιδίον, ἐκ ἤδη δύ- ναται τὸν ἄρτον ἐσθίειν, ἀλλὰ πρῶτον γάλακτι ἀνατρέφεται, ἔπειτα κατὰ πρόβασιν τῆς ἡλικίας, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ςερεὰν τροφὴν ἔρχεται. Lacte nutriri solent non infantes tantum, sed & ἐκτικοί: Facilius enim concoquuntur liquida. Verbum ποτίζειν habuimus Matth. X. 42. XXV. 35. 37. 42. XXVII. 48. Marc. IX. 41. XV. 36. Luc. XIII. 15. Roman. XII. 20. Occurret & in hac epistola aliquoties.

καὶ ἐ βρῶμα.

Est σύλληψις. Nam de lacte quidem dicitur ἐπότισα, non autem de cibis: subauditur ergò, dedi. βρῶμα hic quod ςερεὰ τροφὴ Hebr. V. 12. Philo: ἐχ' ὁρᾷς ὅτι καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἡμῶν ἐ πρότερον πεπηγυίας καὶ πολυτελέσι χρῆται τρο- φαῖς πρὶν ἢ ταῖς ἀποικίλοις καὶ γαλακτώδεσιν ἐν ἡλικίᾳ τῇ βρεφώδει;

ἔπω γὰρ ἠδύνασθε.

Et hic subaudiendum, ferre aut concoquere. Occidit enim infantem, qui ei dat panem & carnes. Maimonides ductore dubitantium l. 33. Frequentes tales in Paulo ἐλλεί- ψεις modò nominum, modò verborum: cum simili ἐλλεί- ψει habes Hebræum תוכל, id est, potero, Esaiæ I. 13. Psalm. CI. 5. in Hebræo.

Quia spirituales à nemine carnali dijudicari di- xerat Apostolus, Corinthios, utpote adhuc car- nales, temerè se, Apostolum Christi, aliosque dijudicare subinfert: & quum spiritualia nondum satis capiant, sese cum ipsis ceu multùm adhuc carnalibus agere debuisse, monet: q. d. vitio mi- hi datis, quòd humilis sim apud vos doctor: At si quæ in hoc culpa, vestræ ruditati eam adscribite, quæ me cum pueris pueriliter balbutire coëgit, quia ut maximè voluerim, non potui vobis loqui ut spiritualibus, sed ut carnalibus, vel saltem ut in- fantibus in Christo. Carnales vocat, nondum sa- tis intelligentes doctrinæ fundamenta, tantùm pen- dentes ex hominibus, & affectibus carnis circa ju- dicium indulgentes: Spirituales verò, qui illumina- tione Spiritûs in cognitione doctrinæ Evangelii plus profecerunt, & in quibus Spiritus prævalet carni, ut doctrinæ obtemperent, neque ex hominum autoritate ac donis pendeant. Rectè autem ob- servatur, carnales non simpliciter hìc dici, quales sunt non renati, sed ex parte, qui aliquid habent lucis & fidei, sed in quibus caro adhuc prædomi- natur: Carnales, non incredulos, quales ante di- xerat animales; sed infirmiores Catechumenos: Illi enim planè non intelligunt ea, quæ sunt Spiritûs DEI: hi verò etsi nondum capere poterant per- fectiorem doctrinam, capaces tamen erant lactis Evangelii. Et rectè, notante Theophylacto, Apo- stolus illud NON POTUI adjecit: ne videatur livore ductus perfections illis nondum præditasse. Quantum ad ea, inquit, quæ Christi sunt, spectat, infantes estis, & ideò lac vobis in potum, hoc est, simpliciorem quandam doctrinam, non cibum vo- bis perfectiorem obtuli. Quamobrem? Quoniam nondum poteratis. Quod eo intulit Paulus, ut Co- rinthiorum reprimat supercilium, & insolentiam tollat, qui suæ plurimùm considerent sapientiæ. Hæc Theophylactus. Lactis potus infantibus convenit, quia dulcedine suâ sapit, liquidâ pinguedine nutrit, facileque digeritur: Cibus solidus adultorum est, qui comestionis organa habent firmiora, & propter labores ac motus vehementiores plus nutrimenti solidi assumere possunt. Respicit hàc metaphorica loquutione imprimis modum propo- nendi, simplicitatem puta in docendo quoad par- vulos: majorem verò tùm rerum tùm verborum apparatum quoad adultiores,νηπίυς autem in Chri- sto dicit, id est, in cognitione & fide Christi. Pon- tificii de ceremoniis & ritibus Ecclesiæ lactis ali- moniam accipiunt; Solidiorem cibum ad Eccle- siæ, Pontificum, & Conciliorum sancita referunt. Sed ætate Apostoli de Pontificum decretis nil con- stabat: nec nisi Apostolicum Concilium Act. XV. notum erat. Neque solis ritibus pasci simplicio- res, aut solis decretis Pontificum & Conciliorum provectiores debent. Præferenda ergò longè tra- dita interpretatio, utpote è textu ipso enata. Quæ ita à B. Mylio nostro proponitur: Lac, inquit, præbetur, si non generalia tantùm religionis capita generatim, sed docendi etiam modo simplice, hoc est, merè Catechetico tradantur. Solidus cibus da- tur, cùm vel ardua religionis mysteria proponun- tur: vel generalia illa, atque vulgaria ejusdem ca- pita, solidiori & exactiori doctrinâ explicantur, fidei praxis exigitur, &, in causas & momenta myste- riorum accuratius inquiritur.

ἀλλ’ ěτε ἔτι νῦν δύνασθε.

Ne nunc quidem tanto tempore post fidei initia. De- buerat cognitio & virtutes crescere cum tempore. Origenes contra Celsum III. Τά ἐν ὑμῖν μάλισα καλὰ κὰι θεῖα τότε τολμῶμεν ἐν τοῖς πρὸς τὸ κοινὸν διαλόγοις φέρειν εἰς μέσον ὅτ’ εὐπορῶμεν συνετῶν ἀκροατῶν. ἀποκρύπτομεν δὲ κὰι παρασιω- πῶμεν τὰ βαθύτερα τὺς συνερχομένοις κὰι δεομένοις λόγων τροπικῶς ὀνομαζομένων γάλα. γέγραπται γὰρ παρὰ τῷ Παύ- λῳ ἡμῶν Κορινθίοις ἀποσέλλοντι, γάλατι μὲν, ὧ καταθερμότοις δίπω τὰ ἔθη γάλα ὑμᾶς ἐπότισα, καὶ ἐ βρῶμα. ἕπω γὰρ ἐδύ- νασθε, ἀλλ’ ἐ δὲ ἔτι νῦν δύνασθε. ἔτι γὰρ σαρκικοί ἐσε &c.

## 3:3
V. 3. For whereas you are still carnal.

Not entirely, but more than enough, comparatively to other Christians, as we have already said.

For whereas there is among you jealousy and strife and divisions.

ὅπε here signifies 'since,' as in 2 Peter 2:11. Xenophon and Plutarch also use this particle in this way. There is, however, a gradation here. For jealousy had produced contention, and contention had produced division. See above 1:10 and below 11:18, 12:25, and add the epistle of Clement. ζῆλος (jealousy) קנא. ἔρις (strife) ריב. διχοσασία (division) מחלקות.

are you not carnal?

For the Apostle counts 'strifes, jealousies, and divisions' among the works of the flesh, Galatians 5:20. By the name of flesh, he is clearly looking at all the effects which do not look primarily to the honor of God and the salvation of one's neighbor, but to those things which are our own and which please us. and you walk according to man. You live as most men are accustomed to live, not according to the prescription of GOD: not according to God, as the Apostle speaks in Rom. VIII. 27. For man in this place is opposed to GOD.

By zeal he understands that foolish emulation of the Corinthians for the authority of their teachers, some of whom favored this one, others that one, not without contempt for the rest and scandal to the weak: he calls contentions the quarrels and wranglings into which this preposterous zeal sometimes erupted. Hence arise dissensions, or partisan leanings and indecorous factions. From these pernicious affections he rightly proves that they themselves are carnal, because zeal and contention are referred to among the works of the flesh, Gal. V. 20, as the blessed Balduinus rightly notes in this place. These vices are attributed to the Corinthians, not because they persisted morosely and pertinaciously in contentions and emulation, but because they exceeded the bounds in these species of vices out of the infirmity of the flesh: on account of which transient and not morose excesses, they could not be excluded from either the kingdom of grace or the kingdom of glory, unless perseverance were added; for under the consideration of habit and perseverance, they are said to exclude from the kingdom of heaven as manifest works of the flesh, Gal. V. 20. Whence, against the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, the blessed Hülsemann observes that it follows that if any of the regenerate should succumb for a time to some vice, yet with a struggle, and that either from insufficient information or from the weakness of the flesh, he is neither to be excluded from the number of the regenerate nor to be judged as not having the indwelling Holy Spirit, which Prosper in Collat. IV. against Cassian, and Augustine in Enchir. c. 114 and tr. 98 in John against the Donatists, deduce. For renewal and sanctification have their own degrees.

Latin:

V. 3. ὅπε ἔτι γὰρ σαρκικοὶ ἐσε.

Non omnino, sed plus satis, comparatè ad alios Chri- stianos, ut jam diximus.

ὅπε γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν ζῆλος κὰι ἔρις κὰι διχοσασίαι.

ὅπε hic valet quandoquidem, ut 2. Petr. II. 11. Utun- tur ita hac particulâ & Xenophon & Plutarchus. Est au- tem hic gradatio. Nam invidia contentionem pepererat, contentio scissuram. Vide supra I. 10. & infra XI. 18. XII. 25. & adde epistolam Clementis. ζῆλος קנא. ἔρις ריב διχοσασία מחלקות.

ὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐσε.

Nam inter opera numerat Apostolus ἔρεις, ζήλους & διχοσασίας Gal. V. 20. Carnis scilicet nomine omnes effe- ctus respiciens, qui non DEI honorem & proximi salu- tem præcipuè respiciunt, sed ea quæ nostra sunt, & nobis placent. καὶ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον περιπατῆτε. Vivitis ut plerique homines solent, non ex DEI præ- scripto: non κατὰ Θεὸν, ut loquitur Apostolus Rom. IIX. 27. Homo enim hoc loco DEO opponitur.

Per zelum intelligit stultam illam æmulationem Corinthiorum pro autoritate suorum doctorum, quo- rum aliqui hunc suspiciebant, alii alium, non sine contemtu cæterorum, & scandalo infirmorum: Con- tentionem vocat lites & jurgia, in quæ præposterus iste zelus nonnunquam crumpebat. Hinc oriuntur διχοστασίαι dissidia seu studia partium & factiones indecoræ. Ex his perniciosis affectibus rectè pro- bat, ipsos carnales esse, quia zelus & contentio inter opera carnis referuntur Gal. V. 20. ut rectè B. Bal- duinus in h. l. Tribuuntur autem Corinthiis hæc vitia, non quòd morosè & pertinaciter perrexe- rint in contentionibus & æmulatione, sed quòd ex infirmitate carnis circa has vitiorum species ex- cesserint: propter quos excessus transitivos & non morosos, neque regno gratiæ neque regno gloriæ excludi poterant, nisi accederet perseverantia; sub intuitu enim habitûs & perseverantiæ dicuntur excludere à regno cœlorum, tanquam manifesta opera carnis, Gal. V. 20. unde adversus Papistas, Socinianos, & Arminianos observat B. Hülseman- nus, consequi, si quis renatorum maximè ad tem- pus succumbat alicui vitio, cum lucta tamen, idque sive ex insufficienti informatione, sive ex imbe- cillitate carnis, neque renatorum numero exclu- dendum esse, neque privatum censendum inhabi- tante Spiritu S. quod Prosper Collat. IV. adversus Cassianum, & Augustinus in Enchir. c. 114. & tr. 98. in Joh. contra Donatistas deducunt. Habet enim suos gradus renovatio & sanctificatio.

## 3:4
V. 4. For when one says, I indeed am of Paul, and another, I of Apollos. They indeed used those names: but the leaders of the sects under this pretext were furthering their own honor and interests, as appears below in IV. 6.

Latin:

V. 4. ὅταν γὰρ λέγῃ τις, ἐγὼ μέν εἰμι Πάυλου, ἕτερος δὲ, ἐγὼ Ἀπολλώ. Illis quidem nominibus illi utebantur: sed principes se- ctarum sub hoc prætextu suo honori & commodis velifica- bantur, ut apparet infra IV. 6.

## 3:5
V. 5. Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos? But ministers through whom you believed. If such a great Apostle and such a great Evangelist wished to think this of himself, how much more ought those to think it who, not being comparable to such great men, nevertheless pursued their own glories to the harm of the Church. Ministers here is not a special name of a function, but a general one corresponding to the Hebrew mshrt, suitable for all who serve the Gospel: as also below in 2 Cor. III. 6, VI. 4, XI. 23, Eph. III. 7, VI. 21, 1 Thess. III. 2, 1 Tim. IV. 6. In a similar way we had ministry in Acts I. 17, VI. 4, XX. 24, XXI. 18. Through whom, that is, by whose work.

The Vulgate is wrong: His ministers, in whom you believed. Since through whom is by whom. The Apostle urges three things:

(1.) that they are only ministers, not Lords;

(2.) that all are ministers of one Lord, and agree in office, although they may perhaps differ in gifts;

(3.) that GOD used them as instruments or ministerial causes for their faith and conversion; therefore they acted here not by their own power, but by the grace and powerful operation of the Lord, and indeed just as the Lord gave to each one, out of the power of GOD, which works even through a weak minister. Nor indeed, as Theophylact paraphrases, have we attained even the slight administration of this duty by our own industry, but we have received even that from GOD, though not in equal measure: both as regards the administering gifts and as regards the effect and fruit of the ministry itself: for all things must be claimed for GOD. It is evident, however, that the Apostle does not here substitute his own name and that of Apollos for the troublemakers, as has seemed to some interpreters: for the Corinthians had not been led to faith through the work and ministry of the troublemakers.

and to each as the Lord gave. There is a transposition here. It would have been correct: and as the Lord gave to each, and to him is understood. They are such as God gave to them, such as God made them by his beneficence: since whatever they have, it has proceeded from him, it ought also by right to serve his honor. We had a similar transposition above in II. 7. And in the same words to each as in Rom. XII. 3.

Latin:

V. 5. τίς ὆ν ἐστι Παῦλος, τίς δὲ Ἀπολλώς; ἀλλ’ ἢ διάκονοι δι’ ὧν ἐπιστεύσατε. Si hoc de se sentire voluit tantus Apostolus & tantus Evangelista, quantò magis id illos cogitare oportuit, qui cum viris tantis comparandi non essent, suas tamen secta- bantur glorias cum Ecclesiæ malo. Διάκονοι hic non spe- ciale nomen est functionis, sed generale respondens He- bræo משרת conveniens omnibus, qui Evangelio inser- viunt: quomodo & infra 2. Cor. III. 6. VI. 4. XI. 23. Eph. III. 7. VI. 21. 1. Thess. III. 2. 1. Tim. IV. 6. Simili modo διακονίαν habuimus Actor. I. 17. VI. 4. XX. 24. XXI. 18. δι’ ὧν, id est, quorum operâ.

Malè Vulgata: Ministri ejus, cui credidistis. Quum δι ὧν sit per quos. Tria urget Apostolus:

(1.) quòd διάκονοι sint tantùm, non Domini:

(2.) quòd omnes ministri sint unius Domini, & officio conveniant, licet fortè donis discrepent:

(3.) quòd ipsis ut organis, vel causis ministerialibus DEUS usus sit ad fidem ipsorum & conversionem; non ergò propriâ virtute, sed gratiâ & potenti operatione Domini, & quidem prout unicuique Dominus dedit, hic egerunt, ex virtute DEI, quæ operatur etiam per infirmum Diaconum. Nec sanè, ut παραφράζει Theophyl. vel tenue administrandi hoc munus nostrâ sumus industriâ consecuti, quin vel idipsum à DEO, etsi haud pari mensurâ, accepimus: utpote tùm quà dona administrantia, tùm quà effectum & fructum ipsum ministerii: omnia enim DEO vindicanda sunt. Patet autem hîc non subrogare Apostolum suum & Apollo nomen turbatoribus, quod nonnullis interpretibus visum: non enim per turbatorum operam & ministerium ad fidem perducti erant Corinthii.

καὶ ἑκάστῳ ὡς ὁ Κύριος ἔδωκεν. Est hic trajectio. Rectum fuerat: καὶ ὡς ἑκάστῳ ὁ Κύριος ἔδωκεν, & subauditur τούτῳ. Tales sunt prout eis Deus dedit, quales eos Deus sua beneficentia effecit: cum quic- quid habent, ab ipso profectum sit, merito etiam ejus ho- nori inservire debeat. Similem trajectionem habuimus supra II. 7. Et in iisdem vocibus ἑκάστῳ ὡς Rom. XII. 3.

## 3:6
V. 6. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. He said watered figuratively for irrigated, which is a word proper to farmers: but the translation is well touched upon, because what is to be irrigated for plants, that is to provide drink for animals. And therefore, conversely, those who have drunk well are said to be irrigated: for such are reciprocal metaphors. And let this be said concerning this word. Furthermore, there is again another translation in all those things from plants to human talent. God is here compared to the earth, from which planted things are nourished. He who plants inserts a shoot into the earth: he who waters opens the paths of the earth: but the increase is in reality from the earth itself, the mother and nurse of all. Thus in the business of the Gospel, the entire yield of faith, justice, and holiness is owed to GOD, from whom is the revelation, and the testimonies of revelation, and the gifts of the spirit. He gave the increase, he caused to sprout, Isaiah LV. 10, LXI. 11.

God, who grants the increase, is more rightly compared to the Sun than to the earth; or the increase is derived from the internal power and life of the plant rather than from the earth: just as there is an inherent power in the seed of the divine Word to bring forth fruit, not in the human heart itself, which is compared to the earth and the field, Luke VIII.

Latin:

V. 6. ἐγὼ ἐφύτευσα, Ἀπολλὼς ἐπότισεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Θεὸς ηὔξανεν. ἐπότισεν dixit figurate pro ἤρδευσε, quæ vox propria agri- colis: sed bene tacta est translatio, quia quod plantis est irrigari, id animalibus est potum præbere. Et ideo vicis- sim qui bene potarunt, irrigati dicuntur: sunt enim tales μεταφοραὶ ἀντίστροφοι. Et hoc quidem dictum sit de hac voce. Cæterum alia rursus est in omnibus illis translatio a plantis ad humanum ingenium. Deus hic comparatur terræ, unde aluntur insita. Qui plantat, surculum infigit terræ: qui rigat, vias terræ aperit: incrementum autem revera ab ipsa est terra, matre ac nutrice omnium. Ita in Evangelii negotio, fidei, justitiæ, sanctitatis proventus o- mnis DEO debetur, a quo est revelatio, & revelationis testimonia & spiritus dona. ηὔξανεν הצמיח Esaia LV. 10. LXI. 11.

Rectius Deus, qui incrementum largitur, Soli comparatur, quam terræ; vel incrementum a plan- tæ interna vi & vita derivatum potius quam a ter- ra: quomodo semini Verbi divini insita est vis, ut fructus proferat, non ipsi cordi humano, quod terræ comparatur & agro Luc. VIII.

## 3:7
V. 7. So that neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth. They are nothing, namely if you look to God. They are nothing great. For thus τί is used in Gal. VI. 3, 2 Cor. III. 5.

but God that giveth the increase. The similitude is somewhat different, tending to the same point and likewise taken from agriculture, but in another way. In Philo: 'The mind is self-loving and godless, thinking itself to be equal to God, seeming to act while being examined in suffering. But when God is sowing and planting good things in the soul, the mind that says that I am planting is impious. You shall not plant when God is the planter.'

But the Calvinists wrongly derogate all operation and power from the ministry in these matters, approaching the Schwenkfeldians: since GOD works faith and conversion not immediately, but through διακόνους or ministers: and they are subordinated to GOD as a ministerial cause to the principal, just as the Apostle called them ministers through whom the Corinthians believed: and a little later v. 9, For we are, he says, Θεοῦ συνεργοί. Wherefore, either the ministers are viewed in themselves, and thus they are nothing, regarding spiritual operation: or by reason of their διακονία, and as they are subordinated to GOD, and thus they are not entirely nothing, but fellow-workers of GOD: Naturally, in themselves and of themselves they have no power, but whatever power they have in their ministry, they have from GOD, and by the grace of GOD they are what they are. 1 Cor. XV. 10.

Latin:

V. 7. ὥστε ὔτε ὁ φυτεύων ἐστί τι, ὔτε ὁ ποτίζων. Nihil sunt, nempe si Deum respicias. Nihil magni sunt. Sic enim τί sumtum Gal. VI. 3. 2. Cor. III. 5.

ἀλλ᾽ ὁ ἀυξάνων Θεός. Paulo alia est similitudo eodem tendens & itidem ab agricultura desumta, sed alio modo. Apud Philonem: Φίλαυτοι δὲ καὶ ἄθεοι ὁ νῦς, οἰόμενος ἴσος εἶναι Θεῷ, ποιεῖν δοκῶν ἐν τῷ πάσχειν ἐξεταζόμενος. Θεῷ δὲ σπείροντι καὶ φυτεύοντι ἐν ψυχῇ τὰ καλὰ, ὁ λέγων νοῦς ὅτι ἐγὼ φυτεύω, ἀσεβεῖ. Οὐ φυτεύσεις ἐν ὅταν ὁ Θεὸς φυτεργῇ.

Male autem ministerio omnem in hisce ope- rationem & vim derogant Calviniani, Schvvenk- feldianis appropinquantes: quum DEUS non immediate, sed per διακόνους vel ministros fidem & conversionem operetur: illique DEO subor- dinentur ceu causa ministerialis principali, quem- admodum Apostolus eos ministros dixit, per quos crediderint Corinthii: & paulo post v. 9. Θεᾶ γάρ, inquit, ἐσμεν συνεργοί. Quapropter vel in se spe- ctantur ministri, atque ita nihil sunt, quoad ope- rationem spiritualem: vel ratione διακονίας suæ, & prout DEO subordinantur, & ita non sunt omnino nihil, sed DEI cooperarii: Nimirum in se & ex se nullam habent virtutem, sed quicquid habent virtutis in ministerio suo, ex DEO ha- bent, & gratia DEI sunt quod sunt. 1. Cor. XV. 10.

## 3:8
V. 8. Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one. They perform the same business: just as those in agriculture bring the plant to the earth and the earth to the plant, so these in the Gospel bring men to GOD and GOD to men. Those who apply themselves to the same business ought not to make factions. Concerning this manner of speaking, see John X. 30, XVII. 11, 12, 1 John V. 7, 8.

Those passages which treat of substantial unity in the divine essence, such as John X. 30, 1 John V. 7, are very poorly compared. For they who plant and who water, Paul and Apollos, are not one in substance or individual: just as they are not one in degree, nor in gifts, nor in calling, nor in authority, nor in time, nor in labor, nor in reward; but they are one in ministry, faith, charity, and intention and scope: laborers of one Lord, defenders of one faith, planters of one heaven: they are one, as Theodoret says, insofar as they serve one another: for both serve the divine majesty.

V. On the same. Each one will receive his own reward according to his own labor.

According to the magnitude of the labor will be the magnitude of the reward: but the reward is immensely greater than the labor.

Reward in general is understood both as that which happens in this age, and that which happens in the future: where the just judge will multiply the glory of eternal blessedness for those who have labored more than others: ACCORDING TO the labor, not BECAUSE OF THE LABOR. For we merit nothing before GOD. Therefore the reward is unowed, a reward of grace: from the gratuitous promise of GOD, Matt. V. 12.

For we are God's fellow workers.

We Apostles and other teachers: whom he had cast down, by comparing them to GOD, and comparing them to men, he greatly lifts up: for he says they work with God, in their own way, of course. They are likewise said to cooperate with the truth, III John v. 8. Conversely, God is said to be a fellow worker with the Apostles, Mark XVI. 20.

Latin:

V. 8. ὁ φυτεύων δὲ καὶ ὁ ποτίζων ἕν εἰσιν. Idem agunt negotium: sicut illi in agricultura plan- tam terræ & terram plantæ admovent, sic hi in Evange- lio homines ad DEUM, DEUM ad homines perducunt. Qui eidem negotio incumbunt, non debent partes face- re. De hoc loquendi genere vide Joh. X. 30. XVII. 11. 12. 1. Joh. V. 7. 8.

Pessime conferuntur ea loca, quæ de substan- tiali unitate in essentia divina agunt, utpote Joh. X. 30. 1. Joh. V. 7. Non enim unum sunt, qui plan- tat, & qui rigat, Paulus & Apollo, substantia, aut individuo: uti nec gradu nec donis, nec voca- tione, nec autoritate, nec tempore, nec labore, nec mercede; sed unum sunt ministerio, fide, cha- ritate, & intentione ac scopo: unius Domini ope- rarii, unius fidei propugnatores, unius cœli plantatores: unum sunt, dicente Theodoreto, quatenus alteri subserviunt: ambo enim serviunt divinæ altitudini.

V. eod. ἕκαστος δὲ τὸν ἴδιον μισθὸν λήψεται κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον κόπον.

Pro magnitudine laboris erit magnitudo mercedis: sed immenso major labore merces.

Merces in genere intelligitur tum quae in hoc seculo contingit, tum quae in futuro: ubi justus judex gloriam aeternae beatitudinis multiplicabit iis, qui plus caeteris laborarunt: SECUNDUM laborem, non PROPTER LABOREM. Ni- hil enim meremur penes DEUM. Ideo merces est indebita, merces gratiae: ex gratuito DEI pro- misso Matth. V. 12.

Θεῦ γάρ ἐσμεν συνεργοί.

Nos Apostoli & doctores alii: quos dejecerat, DEO comparans, eos hominibus comparans multum attollit: dicit enim eos cum Deo operari, suo scilicet modo. Iidem & veritati cooperari dicuntur III. Joh. v. 8. Vicissim Deus συνεργῶν dicitur Apostolis Marc. XVI. 20.

## 3:9
V. 9. You are God's field, God's building.

He addresses the common people here, and by employing two similes, he finishes the former discourse taken from agriculture, and begins a new one from architecture. γεώργιον is everything that is cultivated by a farmer. It is read in the Greek books of the Old Testament, as Gen. XXVI. 14, Jerem. LIII. 23, Prov. VI. 7, XXIV. 30, XXXI. 16. In a similar sense, the people in Isaiah LXI. 5 are called φύτευμα Κυρίου.

Theophylact applies these things to the goal thus: If therefore you are the cultivation and building of GOD, you ought to derive your name from the Lord himself, not from farmers or stonemasons. It will therefore be necessary that, as a cultivation and field, you be covered with the hedges and ramparts of concord, and that you come together as one, differing in nothing, just like some building covered with walls.

Latin:

V. 9. Θεῦ γεώργιον, Θεῦ οἰκοδομή ἐστε.

Plebem hic alloquitur, & duas adhibens similitudines, priorem sermonem ab agricultura desumtum finit, & no- vum ab architectura orditur. γεώργιον est omne quod ab agricola excolitur. Legitur in Graecis libris Veteris Testa- menti, ut Genes. XXVI. 14. Jerem. LIII. 23. Proverb. VI. 7. XXIV. 30. XXXI. 16. Pari sensu populus Esaiae LXI. 5. φύτευμα Κυρίου.

Ad scopum haec ita applicat Theophylactus: Si itaque DEI estis cultura & aedificatio, ab ipso Domi- no, non ab agricolis seu fabris murariis, ducere nomen debetis. Necesse itaque erit, ut tanquam cultio & ager concordiae septis & vallo obducamini, & in unum ut nihil discrepantes, haud secus ac aedificium aliquod muris obductum, conveniatis.

## 3:10
V. 10. According to the grace of God which was given to me.

He refers everything to the honor of GOD, so that he may teach others to do the same.

As a wise master builder I have laid the foundation.

Σοφὸς is an adjective for all craftsmen among the Greeks. And so we read σοφὸς ἄραρε τέκτων even in Homer. Thus in Exodus XXXIV in the Greek: The wise men who do the works of the holy place. And in Isaiah III. 2, חכם חרשים is translated as wise master builder. He lays a foundation who gives a beginning to some thing. The Apostle uses it regarding the Gospel, Rom. XV. 20, and the writer to the Hebrews VI. 1. With the translation carried a little further, the Apostles themselves, as princes in preaching, are called foundations, Apoc. XXI. 14.

The Apostles are called foundations in Apoc. XXI. 14, not so much as Princes in the preaching of the word by reason of their person, as by reason of the doctrine which they delivered by voice and writings, inasmuch as it is the foundation of faith and salvation in the Church: the principle and norm of all dogmas which are to be delivered in the Church; since indeed ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίω φερόμενοι they preached and wrote, and their doctrine was truly θεόπνευστος, to whom therefore the Holy Spirit was promised by Christ, as the Spirit of truth, to lead them into all truth Joh. XVI. 13. and given at the feast of Pentecost, so that their doctrine might be the foundation, principle, and rule of the faith of all believers, by which name we are also said to be built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets Ephes. II. 20. which are the Apostolic and Prophetic writings, not indeed materially by reason of the words or letters; but formally considered by reason of the sense and dogmas, in which foundation the cornerstone is Jesus Christ. Naturally, it is called a foundation by an architectural phrase with respect to the building which is built upon it, and because either the faithful are said to be built upon the foundation, both individually and collectively, which Eph. II. 21. 22. or the heads of doctrine that are not fundamental, inasmuch as they lean upon the fundamental ones, which Ebr. V. VI. is also observed in the present passage: Therefore, in the former respect indeed, the whole Prophetic and Apostolic scripture obtains the name of the foundation, because all scripture is God-breathed, and

profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness, 2. Tim. III. 16. In the latter respect, however, that is called a foundation primarily, which the Apostle here professes to have laid, which is Jesus Christ. That most fundamental dogma, upon which the others lean. Grotius acknowledges the different relation of the foundation in this place also, regarding the following words.

but another builds upon it.

Because he had made mention of a building, he institutes a comparison different from the building. Before, he had called the faithful the building of GOD; now he calls those things which are taught by teachers in the Christian Church a building. You have similar transitions, with part of the similitude retained and part changed, in Matth. XIII. Marc. IV. Joh. X. and elsewhere.

but let each one see how he builds upon it.

He shows that the matter is full of danger.

Latin:

V. 10. κατὰ τὴν χάριν τῦ Θεῦ τὴν δοθεῖ- σαν μοι.

Omnia refert ad honorem DEI, ut alios doceat idem facere.

Ὡς σοφὸς ἀρχιτέκτων θεμέλιον τέθεικα.

Σοφὸς Graecis Adjectivum est omnium artificum. Itaque σοφὸς ἄραρε τέκτων etiam apud Homerum legimus. Sic Exodi XXXIV. in Graeco: Οἱ σοφοὶ οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰ ἔργα τῶ ἁγίω. Et Esaiae III. 2. חכם חרשים vertitur σοφὸν ἀρχιτέκτονα. Fundamentum jacit, qui rei alicui initium dat. De Evangelio id usurpat Apostolus Rom. XV. 20. & scriptor Ebr. VI. 1. Paulo longius provecta translatione ipsi Apostoli, ut in praedicatione Principes fundamenta di- cuntur Apoc. XXI. 14.

Non tam ut Principes in praedicatione verbi ratione personae fundamenta dicuntur Apostoli Apoc. XXI. 14. quam ratione doctrinae, quam voce ac scriptis tradidere, utpote quae fundamentum est fidei, & salutis in Ecclesia: Principium & nor- ma dogmatum omnium, quae in Ecclesia traden- da; siquidem ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίω φερόμενοι prae- dicarint atque scripserint, & doctrina ipsorum ve- re fuerit θεόπνευστος, quibus ideo S. S. & promis- sus a Christo, ceu Spiritus veritatis, ducturus eos in omnem veritatem Joh. XVI. 13. & datus in festo Pentecostes, ut doctrina ipsorum fundamentum, principium, & regula esset fidei omnium creden- tium, quo nomine etiam aedificati dicimur super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum Ephes. II. 20. quod sunt scripta Apostolica, & Propheti- ca, non quidem materialiter ratione vocum, vel literarum; sed formaliter ratione sensus & dogma- tum considerata, in quo fundamento lapis ἀκρο- γωνιαῖος est Jesus Christus. Nimirum fundamen- tum dicitur phrasi architectonica respectu aedificii, quod ei superflruitur, & quia vel fideles super- strui fundamento dicuntur, tum singuli, tum uni- versi, quod Eph. II. 21. 22. vel capita doctrinae non fundamentalia, utpote quae innituntur fundamen- talibus, quod Ebr. V. VI. nec non in loco praesenti observatur: Ideo priori quidem respectu univer- sa scriptura Prophetica, & Apostolica, nomen τοῦ θεμελίου obtinet, quia πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, καὶ

ὠφέλιμ@ πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, πρὸς ἔλεγχον, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, 2. Tim. III. 16. Posteriori autem respectu fundamentum imprimis dicitur, id quod posuisse se hic profite- tur Apostolus, quod est Jesus Christus. Dogma illud maximè fundamentale, cui cætera innitun- tur. Quam diversam σχέσιν fundamenti etiam in hoc loco agnoscit Grotius ad verba sequentia.

ἄλλ@ δ' ἐποικοδομεῖ.

Quia ædificii mentionem fecerat, aliam instituit ab ædi- ficio comparationem. Ante fideles dixerat ædificium DEI, nunc ædificium vocat ea, quæ in Ecclesia Christiana à Do- ctoribus docentur. Similes transitiones parte similitudi- nis retentâ, parte mutatâ habes Matth. XIII. Marc. IV. Joh. X. & alibi.

ἕκαστος δὲ βλεπέτω, πῶς ἐποικοδομεῖ.

Ostendit rem esse periculi plenam.

## 3:11
V. 11. For no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid.

It is not permitted to lay another foundation than that which I have laid, that is, it is not permitted to teach otherwise. 'Can' here signifies the right of acting; see Matth. IX. 15. Luc. V. 21. Thus also the Jurisconsults use the word 'to be able' and the name of power.

Who is Jesus the Christ.

That is, the history, precepts, and promises of Christ. Thus, that God exists, that the world was created by him and is governed, and that a law was given by him, the Hebrews call עיקרים, that is, foundations.

We admit all these things, that the history, precepts, and promises of Christ are called the foundation, but not as regards all and individual parts and circumstances, and certainly not in the Grotian sense, as if the reason for salvation consisted in the observation of the precepts and the knowledge of the promises of Christ—which even the Socinians desire—but that that dogma concerning Jesus Christ is the foundation upon which the other heads of religion and faith lean, and upon which whatever is taught in the Church must be built or constructed, so that it remains entirely safe and unmoved, and is not overturned. For those who overturn it do not build upon the foundation, but destroy the foundation; whether this is done through the ἀναίρεσιν (denial) of that dogma, or through the θέσιν (positing) of a foreign foundation. For this is the principal dogma: that Jesus is the Christ, sent by the Father as the Savior of the world; this is that head of the corner upon which whatever is of sacred doctrine leans; this is the foundation upon which it is necessary that all doctrine be superstructed, by which being safe, faith is safe, and eternal salvation is safe and secure, because in no other name is there salvation (Acts 4:12), and in the fact that Jesus was sent by GOD for the sake of our salvation, eternal life is situated (John 17:3), and by the knowledge of this we are rendered righteous (Isaiah 53:11). This is that λόγος πιστὸς, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος (faithful word, and worthy of all acceptance), that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). And this is the end of sacred scripture, namely, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of GOD, and that believing we may have faith in his name (John 20:31). This foundation is sometimes accustomed to be called dogmatic, for the sake of distinction, so that it may be distinguished from the essential or personal foundation; since Christ, by reason of his person, is the foundation of the Church, upon whom as a rock the faithful lean, and the universal Church as the house of the living GOD (1 Timothy 3:15), sustaining and preserving the entire building of the Church, which not even the gates of hell are able to overturn (Matthew 16:17). That dogmatic foundation has it a little more fully thus: Namely, that Jesus is the Son of GOD sent into the world by the Father for the sake of the salvation of the human race, having put on our flesh or human nature, so that he might both expiate our sins and fulfill the divine law for us, so that through faith in him we might obtain the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal salvation. In which fundamental dogma, or dogmatic foundation these special doctrines are comprised, both concerning God the author of our salvation, by reason of his essence and gracious will, or divine grace, and the same universal towards the whole human race, and concerning Christ the Mediator between God and men and his person, and mediatorial office, for whose sake he also took our sins upon himself, that he might satisfy for us by his passion and death, and might obtain for us the remission of them, and he subjected himself to the law for us, that he might fulfill the same in our stead, and his righteousness, or obedience, might be given to us: then concerning justifying faith, by which we place trust in the grace of God in view of the mediation of Christ, because God wills to remit all sins to us out of grace, provided we believe in Christ, that is, that we apprehend and apply to ourselves both his satisfaction for our sins and his righteousness or fulfillment of the law performed for us, so that by his active and passive obedience alike we may be constituted righteous, and attain eternal salvation. Which faith it is necessary to preserve, lest by heresy, or mortal sins, we fall from the same, and perish.

Latin:

V. 11. Θεμέλιον γὰρ ἄλλον ἐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸν κείμενον.

Non licet aliud ponere fundamentum, quàm quod ego posui, id est, non licet contra docere. Δύναται hic signifi- cat jus agendi, vide Matth. IX. 15. Luc. V. 21. Sic & Juris- consulti verbum posse & nomen potestatis usurpant.

Ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ χριστός.

Id est Christi historia, præcepta & promissa. Sic Deum esse, mundum ab eo conditum, ac regi, datam ab eo legem עיקרים id est fundamenta vocant Hebræi.

Admittimus hæc omnia, fundamentum dici historiam, præcepta, & promissa Christi, sed non quoad omnes, & singulas partes, ac circumstantias, necdum sensu Grotiano, quasi in observatione præ- ceptorum, & notitiâ promissorum Christi, quod vo- lunt etiam Sociniani, salutis ratio consistat, sed quod dogma illud de Jesu Christo fundamentum sit, cui innituntur cætera religionis, & fidei capita supra quod ædificanda, seu extruenda sunt, quæ- cunque traduntur in Ecclesia, ita ut id omninò salvum, & immotum maneat, non verò evertatur. Nam qui id evertunt, non ædificant super funda- mentum, sed destruunt fundamentum; sive id fiat per dogmatis illius ἀναίρεσιν, sive per alieni funda- menti θέσιν. Nam hoc præcipuum dogma est Jesum esse Christum, missum à Patre Salvatorem mundi: hoc est caput illud anguli, cui innititur, quicquid est doctrinarum sacrarum; hoc est fun- damentum, cui omnem doctrinam superstrui o- portet, quô salvo salva est fides, salva est & in tuto salus æterna, quia in alio nomine salus non est Act. IV. 12. & in eo, quod Jesus sit à DEO missus no- stræ salutis causâ, vita æterna sita est. Joh. XVII. 3. hujusque cognitione nos justi reddimur, Es. LIII. 11. Hic est λόγος ille πιστὸς, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος, quod Christus Jesus in mundum venerit, salvos fa- cere peccatores 1. Tim. I. 15. Atque hic est finis scri- pturæ sacræ, ut nempe credamus, Jesum esse Chri- stum Filium DEI, & ut credentes fidem habeamus in nomine ejus. Joh. XX. 31. Hoc fundamentum vocari solet quandoque dogmaticum, distinctio- nis gratiâ, ut nempe discernatur à fundamento essentiali, vel personali; siquidem Christus ratione personæ suæ fundamentum Ecclesiæ sit, cui tan- quam petræ innituntur fideles, atque Ecclesia uni- versa ceu domus DEI viventis 1. Tim. III. 15. sus- tentans & conservans universum Ecclesiæ ædifi- cium, quam ne portæ inferorum quidem evertere valent. Matth. XVI. 17. Dogmaticum illud fun- damentum ita paulo plenius habet: Quod nem- pe Jesus sit Filius DEI à Patre salutis generis hu- mani causâ missus in mundum, carnem nostram vel naturam humanam indutus, ut & peccata no- stra expiaret, & legem divinam pro nobis imple- ret, ut per fidem in ipsum remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & salutem æternam consequamur. In quo fundamentali dogmate, vel dogmatico fundamento hæ speciales doctrinæ comprehenduntur, tum de Deo salutis nostræ autore, ratione essentiæ & volun- tatis gratiosæ, seu gratiæ divinæ, ejusdemque uni- versalis erga totum genus humanum, tum de Christo Mediatore inter Deum & homines ejusdemque & persona, & officio mediatorio, cujus ergo & peccata nostra in se suscepit, ut passione ac morte sua pro nobis satisfaceret, eorumque remissionem nobis impetraret, & legi pro nobis se subjecit, ut eandem vice nostra impleret, ejusque justitia, vel obedien- tia nobis donari posset: tum de fide justificante, qua fiduciam in Dei gratiam collocamus intuitu μεσι- τείας Christi, quod Deus velit nobis ex gratia re- mittere peccata omnia, modo in Christum creda- mus, hoc est, ejus tum satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris, tum justitiam vel impletionem legis pro nobis præstitam apprehendamus, nobisque applicemus, ut obedientia ejus activâ pariter & passivâ justi con- stituamur, & æternam salutem consequamur. Quam fidem servare oportet, ne per hæresin, aut peccata mortalia eâdem excidamus, & per- eamus.

## 3:12
Ver. 12. εἰ δέ τις ἐποικοδομεῖ ἐπὶ τὸν θεμέλιον τῦτον χρυσὸν, ἄργυρον, λίθες τιμίας, ξύλα, χόρτον, καλάμην.

Paul imagines for himself a building partly Royal, partly Rustic: Because although it is not the custom for such to be made, yet it is not repugnant to nature, and the rendering requires it. He proposes therefore to us a house, whose walls are of marble, the columns partly of gold and partly of silver, the beams of wood: but the roof of straw and stubble, whence it is called a culmen (top). Precious stones or choice ones are also called marbles, as the passage of Isaiah LIV. 11 shows, compared with 1 Chronicles XXI. 12, in the Greek, and with Josephus. See what we have said on that passage of Isaiah. In the structure of the tabernacle there were gold, silver, stones, woods, Exodus XXV. 4, 5.

Such a building, which in part, as regards the lower parts, namely the walls and columns, is royal: but in part as regards the upper parts, namely the beams and the roof, is rustic, as imagined here by the Apostle, is a monstrous figment of the Grotian brain, unheard of in the Church before him.

On the contrary, the Apostle makes a twofold building rather upon the same foundation, which each building is entirely different, not by reason of the architects only, but also by reason of the material and structure, of which if one pleases to call the one Royal, constructed entirely as to the base and the top from gold, silver, and precious stones: and the other rustic, compacted from wood, hay, and stubble, as to the entire structure placed upon the foundation, we do not object.

But what the Apostle designates by this twofold building, interpreters vary concerning it: inasmuch as some of the Fathers take these to be good and evil acts, Origen Homily VI on Exodus, Jerome book II against Jovinian, Augustine on Faith and Works ch. 16, who complains that this passage is one of the most difficult, as also Chrysostom and Theophylact on this passage. The Papists, by the name of gold, silver, and precious stones, understand the works of monks, the vows of religious, as they call them, of perpetual celibacy, voluntary poverty, and monastic obedience, in which they constitute spiritual perfection, alms, canonical hours, and other inventions of their own; but by the name of wood, hay, and stubble, political and economic works. Which explanation, however, does not in any way agree with the Apostolic mind, since the Apostle is dealing here with doctrine, not with life; nor is it consistent with the analogy of faith. Others take them to be about different hearers. By the name of gold, silver, and precious stones they posit grave and constant hearers, who in the heat of the cross and persecutions do not desist, but stand unmoved. But by the name of wood, hay, and stubble they understand such as indeed receive the doctrine of the Gospel with a certain alacrity of mind; but in the time of persecution do not sustain the test of fire. Which opinion also pleased Brentius, not indeed alien to the analogy of faith, but not convenient to the scope and mind of the Apostle: which they attain more correctly who take the words of the Apostle to be about doctrine, which however is not done in the same way. For most understand by gold, silver, and precious stones dogmas different from the foundation, but homogeneous to the same, not adverse. There are, however, those who wish not different, but the very same dogmas, which were also expressed by the name of the foundation, to be designated, which they say are built upon by the successors of the Apostles, not by reason of different material, but by reason of another labor, because namely they repeat, continue, and confirm all and singular the same fundamental dogmas concerning Christ preached by the Apostles in the beginning from the same Prophetic and Apostolic scripture, to which Pareus's explanation of this passage tends: It is not the foundation of other doctors, says Paul, to lay, but to build upon that which is laid, the scriptures of the Prophets and Apostles, that is, to hold faithfully, explain, dilate, apply, and to treat and illustrate for the perfecting of the building, that is, for the building up of the Church, the Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine concerning Christ with doctrines and reasons consonant with the foundation. The Lord D. Haberkorn also praises and approves this sense from Flacius in his faithful and solid admonition against Syncretism, p. 347. By wood, hay, and stubble, he understands not only erroneous, vain, and unnecessary things built upon fundamental matters, which however do not overturn the same; but also dogmas that are plainly heretical, impious, blasphemous, and conflicting with the foundation.
