But the common explanation of our Doctors, the blessed Hunnius, Hesbusius, Weinrichius, Balduinus, and others, seems more suitable; they distinguish the dogmas which are built upon the foundation, which is Christ Jesus, from the foundation itself, just as the Apostle here openly distinguishes, not by reason of the labor of another, but of the material; and the nature of the metaphor requires this. For the foundation in a building is one thing, and that which is built upon the foundation is another; these are distinguished not only by reason of labor, derivation, or corroboration, but by reason of the work and the structure itself, since no house is built by the expansion and corroboration of the foundation, but it is necessary to build walls, columns, beams, and a roof upon the foundation so that a building may be made. Rightly, therefore, the blessed Hunnius: As regards the foundation once laid, no one can lay another foundation besides that which has already been laid, which is the true, solid, and unshaken doctrine concerning Jesus Christ, upon whom, as the firmest rock, the whole mass of salvation and justification rests and leans. And furthermore: The Apostle persists in the trope of the metaphor; by gold, silver, and precious stones, which are built upon the doctrine of Jesus Christ, he understands those things that are in agreement with the word of God. But by wood, hay, and stubble built upon the foundation, he denotes erroneous opinions, traditions, and doctrines of men, namely those which indeed do not overturn the foundation of the doctrine concerning God, His essence and will, concerning Christ and His person, office, and the benefit of justification: meanwhile, however, they are deviant from the word and alien to the sincerity of Christian doctrine. Similarly our blessed Mylius: It is to be noted that those things are not understood which are openly impious and superstitious, conflicting with both the foundation and the substance of the Christian faith: But those things which add somewhat from alien matters to Christ and faith and either obscure somewhat the sincerity of faith and worship, or delay them. Nor indeed are dogmas conflicting with the foundation built upon the foundation, but they overturn the foundation, for the reason that they conflict with the foundation; nor do those who overturn the foundation of faith stand in the fire of testing, or obtain salvation as if through fire: But since faith has no place, the foundation of faith being overturned, neither can the end of faith, the salvation of souls, be obtained; those, however, who build wood, hay, and stubble upon it, the foundation being retained, can still be saved, even if the dogmas which they build upon it are erroneous and useless, which do not sustain the fire of testing, but are consumed by the same. But those things which do not stand in the way of the salvation of the teachers themselves, provided they do not obstinately contradict the Holy Scripture with a resisting conscience, in which case they fall short of salvation not because of the quality and condition of the dogmas themselves, that they are per se destructive and overturn the foundation of faith, but because of a stubborn and obstinate reluctance against the truth demonstrated from the scriptures.

Latin:

Vers. 12. εἰ δέ τις ἐποικοδομεῖ ἐπὶ τὸν θεμέλιον τῦτον χρυσὸν, ἄργυρον, λίθες τιμίας, ξύλα, χόρτον, καλάμην.

Fingit sibi ædificium Paulus partim Regale, partim Ru- sticum: Quia quanquam tale fieri moris non est, tamen naturæ non repugnat, & id requirit ἀπόδοσις. Proponit ergo nobis domum, cujus parietes sint ex marmore, colu- mnæ partim ex auro & partim ex argento, trabes ex ligno: fastigium vero ex stramine & culmo, unde culmen dicitur. Λίθοι τίμιοι aut ἔκλεκτοὶ etiam marmora dicuntur, ut osten- dit locus Esaiæ LIV. 11. collatus cum 1. Paralip. XXI. 12. in Græco, & cum Josepho. Vide, quæ ad illum locum Esaiæ diximus. In tabernaculi structura erant aurum, argen- tum, lapides, ligna, Exod. XXV. 4 5.

Tale ædificium, quod ex parte, quoad sc. infe- riora utpote parietes & columnas, regale sit: Ex parte verò quoad superiora, trabes nempe ac fasti- gium sit rusticum ab Apostolo hic fingi cerebri Grotiani figmentum est monstrosum, ante ipsum in Ecclesia inauditum.

Ex adverso geminam po- tius οἰκοδομὴν facit Apostolus super idem θεμέλιον, quod utrumq; ædificium totum diversum est, non ratione architectorum tantum, sed etiam ratione materiæ & structuræ, quorum alterum si dicere lu- beat Regale, ex auro, argento, & lapidibus pre- tiosis totum quoad ima, & summa constructum: Alterum verò rusticum ex ligno, fœno & stipulis, quoad universam structuram, fundamento impo- sitam, coagmentatum, non repugnamus.

Quid- nam vero per hanc utramque οἰκοδομὴν designet Apostolus, de eo variant interpretes: utpote quod è Patribus quidam de bonis atque malis actibus hæc accipiant, Orig. Homil VI. in Exodum, Hieron. lib. II. contra Jovinianum, Augustinus de Fide & operibus l. 16. qui queritur, hunc locum esse unum ex difficillimis, ut & Chrysostomus & Theophylactus in h. l. Pontificii auri, argenti & lapidum pretioso- rum nomine, monachorum opera, religiosorum vo- ta, ut vocant, cælibatus perpetui, paupertatis spon- taneæ, & obedientiæ monasticæ, in quibus perfectio- nem spiritualem constituunt, eleemosynas, horas canonicas, ac alia suorum adinventa, intelligunt; nomine autem lignorum, fæni & stipularum opera politica & œconomica. Quæ verò explicatio nec menti Apostolicæ ullatenus congruit, cum de do- ctrina hic agat Apostolus, non de vita; nec analo- giæ fidei consentanea est. Alii de diversis audito- ribus ea accipiunt. Nomine auri, argenti, & pre- tiosorum lapidum auditores ponunt graves & con- stantes, qui in ardore crucis, & persecutionum non desistunt, sed immoti consistunt. Nomine autem lignorum, fæni & stipularum intelligunt ta- les, qui quidem Evangelii doctrinam animi qua- dam alacritate accipiunt; sed persecutionis tem- pore examen ignis non sustinent. Quæ senten- tia Brentio etiam placuit, non aliena quidem ab analogia fidei, at non conveniens scopo, & menti Apostoli: Quam rectius assequuntur, qui de do- ctrina verba Apostoli accipiunt, quod verò non eodem modo fit. Nam plerique per aurum, ar- gentum, & lapides pretiosos dogmata à fundamen- to diversa, sed eidem homogenea, non adversa in- telligunt. Sunt tamen, qui non diversa, sed ea- dem omnino dogmata, quæ fundamenti nomine etiam expressa erant, designari velint, quæ di- cantur à successoribus Apostolorum superstrui, non ratione diversæ materiæ, sed ratione alterius laboris, quod nempe eadem de Christo funda- mentalia dogmata omnia & singula ab Apostolis initio prædicata ex eadem scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica repetant, continuent & confirment, quo abit Parei explicatio in hunc locum: Alio- rum doctorum, inquit Paulus, non est fundamen- tum ponere, sed super id, quod positum est, Propheta- rum & Apostolorum scripturis superstruere, hoc est, Propheticam & Apostolicam doctrinam de Christo fideliter tenere, explicare, dilatare, applicare, & ad ædificium perficiendum, hoc est, ad Ecclesiam ædifi- candam doctrinis & rationibus fundamento consen- taneis pertractare atque illustrare. Quem sensum è Flacio etiam laudat & approbat Dominus D. Ha- berkorn in fideli & solida admonitione contra Syn- cretismum p. 347. Per lignum, fœnum & stipulas non tantum erronea, vana, non necessaria de rebus fundamentalibus superstructa, eadem autem non evertentia; sed etiam dogmata plane hæretica, im- pia, blasphema, cum fundamento pugnantia intel- ligens. Magis autem conveniens videtur com- munis Doctorum nostrorum B. Hunnii, Hesbusii, Weinrichii, Balduini & aliorum explicatio, qui distinguunt dogmata, quæ superstruuntur funda- mento, quod est Christus Jesus, ab ipso fundamento, quemadmodum hic Apostolus aperte distinguit, non ratione laboris alterius, sed materiæ; idque Metaphoræ ratio requirit. Aliud siquidem est fundamentum in ædificio, aliud, quod fundamento superstruitur, quæ non tantum ratione laboris, di- ductionis vel corroborationis distinguuntur, sed ra- tione operis, & structuræ ipsius, quum dilatatione & corroboratione fundamenti nulla domus ædificetur, sed necessum sit fundamento superstruere parietes, columnas, trabes & fastigium, ut fiat ædificium. Recte itaque B. Hunnius: Quod attinet funda- mentum semel positum non valeat quisquam aliud fundamentum ponere præter id, quod jam ante ja- ctum est, quod est doctrina vera, solida & inconcussa de Jesu Christo, cui ut firmissimæ petræ tota moles sa- lutis ac justificationis incumbit & innititur. Et porrò: Perseverat Apostolus in Metaphoræ tro- po; Per aurum, argentum, & lapides pretiosos, quæ doctrinæ de Jesu Christo superstruuntur, intelli- gens cum Dei verbo consentientia. Per ligna ve- rò, fœnum & stipulas fundamento superstructas notans opiniones erroneas, traditiones & doctri- nas hominum, eas videlicet, quæ quidem non evertunt fundamentum doctrinæ de Deo, essentiâ ejus & voluntate, de Christo ejusque persona, of- ficio, ac justificationis beneficio: Interim tamen à verbo deviæ sunt, & à doctrinæ Christianæ sin- ceritate alienæ. Similiter B. Mylius noster: No- tandum, non illa intelligi, quæ palam impia sunt & superstitiosa, cum & fundamento & substantia fidei Christianæ pugnantia: Sed ea, quæ Christo & fidei nonnihil ex rebus alienis affuunt & sincerita- tem fidei & cultus vel obscurant nonnihil, vel remo- rantur. Nec verò dogmata cum fundamento pugnantia super fundamentum extruuntur, sed fundamentum evertunt, ideo, quia cum funda- mento pugnant, neq; illi, qui evertunt fundamen- tum fidei, in igne probationis consistunt, aut salutem veluti per ignem consequuntur: Sed cum fides lo- cum non habeat, fundamento fidei everso, neque finis fidei salus animarum obtineri potest, qui ve- rò ligna, fœnum & stipulas superstruunt, retento fundamento, adhuc salvari possunt, etsi dogmata, quæ superstruunt, erronea & inutilia sint, quæ ignem probationis non sustinent, sed eodem comburuntur. Quæ verò saluti Doctorum ipso- rum non obstant, modo non præfractè Scripturæ Sacræ renitente conscientia contradicant, quo casu non ob dogmatum ipsorum qualitatem & condi- tionem, quod ea per se exitiosa sint, & fundamen- tum fidei evertant, sed ob contumacem & præfra- ctam adversus veritatem è scripturis demonstra- tam reluctantiarn, salute excidunt.

## 3:13
Verse 13. ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον φανερὸν γενήσεται. The outcome will show which material is firm, which is weak. ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει, ὅτι ἐν πυρὶ ἀποκαλύπτεται. A long time is accustomed to bring fires, whether by accidental chance, or by heavenly fire, or by the force of war, ἡμέρα, that is, a long time: Long day also to the Latins. Thus the LXX often translate יום as χρόνον. See what we said at Num. III. 13. Add Is. III. 24. ἡμέρα δηλώσει is the same as what Sophocles says: Ἄπανθ' ὁ μακρὸς κᫀναρίθμητος χρόνος Φύει τ' ἄδηλα. And what Simonides says: Οὐκ ἔστι μείζων βάσανος χρόνου οὐδενὸς ἔργου. And here ἀποκαλύπτεται, understand ἔργον ἐν πυρὶ by means of a conflagration.

καὶ ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον, ὁποῖόν ἐστι, τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει. Rightly. For gold is invincible to fires: Silver and marbles resist fire for a long time: Wood less: Straw and stubble least of all: ἐν πυρὶ δοκιμάζεται χρυσὸς, Eccl. II. 5.

By the day is not understood an indefinitely long time, but a certain day, according to the common and more received usage of the word. Nor yet is the day of the Lord or of the final judgment designated, which most Roman Catholics wish, since the word 'Lord' has crept into the old version, which is not found in the Greek codices; but the day of tribulation, because it is not a matter of the manifestation of all hidden things, which will happen on the last day, but of the explanation of dogmas which are built upon the foundation; and that manifestation is said to take place in the fire of exploration, i.e., of both the scriptures and of temptations, whether in the danger of persecutions and of life, or in the final article of the struggle, whereby the faith of the scriptures is proven true, and is perfected like gold, but the false and erroneous is consumed like hay. For scripture also is compared to fire, Ps. XII. 7, Jer. XXIII. 29, Luke XXIV. 32, and the temptation of the cross, 1 Peter I. 7. On the last day there will not be a time of testing, but of judgment, by which everyone will receive according to how he was found in his departure from this life. And the day of God's judgment is indeed like a burning fire, but to the impious: to the pious, however, it is the day of redemption, of refreshing, and of the restoration of all things, Luke XXI. 28, Acts III. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον φανερὸν γενήσεται. Eventus ostendet, quæ materia firma sit, quæ infirma. ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει, ὅτι ἐν πυρὶ ἀποκαλύπτεται. Longum tempus afferre solet incendia, sive casu fortui- to, sive igne cœlesti, sive vi bellica, ἡμέρα, id est, longum tempus: Longa dies etiam Latinis. Sic יום sæpè χρόνον vertunt LXX. vide, quæ diximus Num. III. 13. Adde Es. III. 24. ἡμέρα δηλώσει idem est, quod dicit Sophocles: Ἄπανθ' ὁ μακρὸς κᾀναρίθμητος χρόνος Φύει τ' ἄδηλα. Et quod Simonides: Οὐκ ἔστι μείζων βάσανος χρόνου οὐδενὸς ἔργου. Et hic ἀποκαλύπτεται, intellige ἔργον ἐν πυρὶ per incen- dium.

καὶ ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον, ὁποῖόν ἐστι, τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει. Rectè. Nam aurum ignibus invictum est: Argentum & marmora diu igni resistunt: Minus lignum: Minime stra- men & culmus: ἐν πυρὶ δοκιμάζεται χρυσὸς, Eccl. II. 5.

Per diem non indefinitè longum tempus, sed cer- ta dies intelligitur, usu vocis communi & receptio- ri. Nec tamen dies Domini vel judicii novissimi designatur, quod Pontificii plerique volunt, quum in veterem versionem vox Domini irrepserit, quæ in Græcis codicibus non invenitur; sed dies tribu- lationis, quia non de manifestatione omnium oc- cultorum agitur, quæ fiet in novissimo die, sed de explicatione dogmatum, quæ fundamento super- struuntur; & manifestatio illa fieri dicitur in igne explorationis sc. tum scripturarum, tum tentatio- num, sive in persecutionum & vitæ periculo, sive in extremo agonis articulo, quò fides scriptura- rum vera probatur, & perficitur quasi aurum, fal- sa verò, & erronea consumitur ut fœnum. Nam & scriptura igni comparatur Ps. XII. 7. Jer. XXIII. 29. Luc. XXIV. 32. & tentatio crucis, 1. Petri I. 7. In novissimo die non erit tempus probationis, sed judicii, quo unusquisque suscipiet, prout in suo ex hac vita excessu repertus fuit. Et dies judicii Dei est quidem instar ignis ardentis, sed impiis: Piis verò est dies redemptionis, refrigerii, & restitu- tionis omnium, Luc. XXI. 28. Act. III. 21.

## 3:14
Verse 14. εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον μένει, ὃ ἐπῳκοδόμησε, μισθὸν λήψεται. Now he comes to the ἀπόδοσιν. If any teacher has given special precepts which, when the matter, time, place, and circumstances are considered, agree with the general precepts of Christ, he will obtain honor among all the Churches. Clement, Stromata VII: 'Faith, therefore, is, so to speak, a concise knowledge of urgent matters; but knowledge is a strong and certain demonstration of those things received through faith, built upon faith through the Lord's teaching unto that which is unchangeable, and leading one after knowledge to that which is graspable. And it seems to me that there is a first saving change, that from the nations to faith, as I said before. But the second is that from faith to knowledge. And that which is perfected unto love, from then on already presents the knowing friend to the known friend.' Plato says that for magistrates the reward is honor. And that honor which is held for a teacher by all the Churches is a presage of the honor to be obtained from God according to the promise, Matt. XVI. 19. Therefore, to the conflagration corresponds the light which shines from all the Churches to one laboring Church. Thus the judgments of God are compared to fire, Is. IV. 4, LXVI. 16. And the Spirit was first given to the Church in the form of fire.

We find two things lacking in this explanation. One is that the works built upon the foundation are referred only to precepts, which ought entirely to be referred also to other dogmas, concerning both teaching and exhortation. For whatever of dogmas is built upon the foundation is understood by the Apostle: when, namely, useful and in a certain way necessary dogmas, analogous to Holy Scripture, and wholesome consolations and exhortations, which go by the name of gold, silver, and precious stones, are built upon the fundamental doctrine concerning the person and office of Christ; or vain, useless, and curious doctrines, which, even if they do not overturn the foundation, are nevertheless alien to it, of no use, and do not harmonize with Holy Scripture, such as immediately arose in the primitive Church, because ceremonies and traditions or erroneous opinions and vain questions were introduced. And thus afterwards Jerome, while he extolled monasteries and virginity too much, so that he even heaped insults upon marriage and condemned even second nuptials, built hay and stubble upon the foundation, which did not tolerate the fire of temptation, but were consumed: Augustine likewise, when he denied that the baptism of John conferred the remission of sins, and sometimes confused renewal with justification, etc. The other is that he wishes the light, which shines from all the Churches to one laboring Church, to correspond here to the conflagration. For to understand this light as the fire by which each one's work is tested is inconvenient: since there is no need for the light of various Churches to examine the work of any one person. And the judgments of God are manifested not by the light of Churches, but by the fire of tribulations, if we close our eyes to the light of scripture, and they are accustomed to consume the stubble of errors.

Latin:

Vers. 14. εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον μένει, ὃ ἐπῳκοδόμησε, μισθὸν λήψεται. Jam venit ad ἀπόδοσιν. Si quis doctor præcepta specia- lia dederit, quæ considerata re, tempore, loco, circum- stantiis, conveniant cum generalibus Christi præceptis, is honorem apud Ecclesias omnes consequetur. Clemens Stromatum VII. ἡ μὲν οὖν πίστις σύντομός ἐστιν, ὡς εἰπεῖν, τῶν κα- τεπειγόντων γνῶσις, Ἡ γνῶσις δὲ ἀπόδειξις τῶν διὰ πίσεως πα- ρειλημμένων ἰσχυρὰ καὶ βέβαιος, διὰ τῆς κυριακῆς διδασκα- λίας, ἐποικοδομουμένη τῇ πίστει εἰς τὸ ἀμετάπτωτον, καὶ μετ' ἐπι- στήμην καταληπτὸν παραπέμπουσα. Καί μοι δοκεῖ πρώτη τις εἶ- ναι μεταβολὴ σωτήριος, ἡ ἐξ ἐθνῶν εἰς πίσιν, ὡς προεῖπον. Δευ- τέρα δὲ ἡ ἐκ πίστεως εἰς γνῶσιν. Ἡ δὲ εἰς ἀγάπην περαιουμένη, ἐνθένδε ἤδη φίλον φίλῳ τὸ γιγνῶσκον τῷ γιγνωσκομένῳ παρί- στησι. Plato magistratibus mercedem dicit esse honorem. Et honor is, qui habetur Doctori ab Ecclesiis omnibus præsagium est honoris a Deo consequendi ex promisso Matth. XVI. 19. Incendio igitur respondet lux, quæ ab Ecclesiis omnibus uni Ecclesiæ laboranti allucet. Sic Dei judicia igni comparantur Es. IV. 4. LXVI. 16. Et Spiritus Ecclesiæ primum in ignis forma datus.

Duo in hac explicatione desideramus. Unum est, quod ad Præcepta tantum referantur opera su- perstructa fundamento, quæ ad alia etiam dogma- ta, tum διδασκαλίαν, tum παράκλησιν concernen- tia referenda omninò sunt. Nam quicquid funda- mento superstruitur dogmatum, ab Apostolo in- telligitur: Cum scil. doctrinæ fundamentali de persona & officio Christi superstruuntur dogmata utilia & certo modo necessaria, Scripturæ S. ana- loga, ac consolationes & exhortationes salubres, quæ auri, argenti & lapidum pretiosorum nomine veniunt; Aut doctrinæ vanæ, inutiles & curiosæ, quæ etsi fundamentum non evertant, ab eo tamen alienæ sunt, nullius usus, nec Scripturæ S. conso- nant, quales in primitiva Ecclesia statim multæ oriebantur, quia ceremoniæ & traditiones vel opiniones erroneæ ac quæstiones vanæ invehe- bantur. Atque ita postmodum Hieronymus, dum nimium extulit monasteria, & virginitatem, ut contumeliis etiam affecerit conjugium, & secun- das etiam damnarit nuptias, fœnum & stipulas ædi- ficavit super fundamentum, quæ ignem tentatio- nis non tolerarunt, sed consumptæ sunt: Augusti- nus item, cum negavit baptismum Johannis con- tulisse remissionem peccatorum, ac renovationem cum justificatione quandoque confudit, &c. Al- terum est, quod incendio hic respondere vult lu- cem, quæ ab Ecclesiis omnibus uni Ecclesiæ allucet la- boranti. Hanc enim lucem intelligere per ignem, quo uniuscujusque opus probatur, inconveniens est: Cum non ad cujusvis opus explorandum di- versarum Ecclesiarum luce opus sit. Et judicia Dei non per Ecclesiarum lucem, sed per tribula- tionum ignem, si ad lucem scripturæ oculos clau- damus, manifestentur, atque stipulas errorum ab- sumere soleant.

## 3:15
Vers. 15. Εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον κατακαήσεται.

If it is detected by other Churches that the doctrine of someone is repugnant to the doctrine of Christ, either directly, as that it is lawful to have intercourse with a stepmother, as that the resurrection is not to be expected; or when circumstances are considered, as that it is lawful to feast in an idol's temple, that it is lawful to litigate before profane Magistrates. For such things cannot stand in the judgment of sound Churches. Justin, disputing with Trypho, denies that those who deny the future resurrection are to be held as Christians. Tertullian against Marcion V. Because your superstructure is judged by fire, beams are accustomed to perish in a fire: the letter called Jeremiah's 55.

Ζημιωθήσεται.

He will be cast down by the judgment of all from the office of Teacher, or will even be deprived of communion, as happened to that incestuous man.

Αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται, ὕτω δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός.

That is, he will be in the greatest danger of his salvation: Even if he obtains it, (which the Apostle prefers to hope for the sake of a good omen,) it will not happen without grave sadness and pain. See 2 Cor. II. 7. This is the ὄλεθρος σαρκὸς below verse 5. Σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς is proverbial for the signification of extreme danger: Thus Judas 23 said ἐκ τῦ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες. Aristides on Apelles: ἐκ μέσε, φασὶ, πυρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σώζειν. Cyprian, epistle LXVI. The burden must be quickly taken out of the fire, before it is consumed by the flames coming upon it. No one is safe for long who is near danger.

Doctrine directly repugnant to the fundamental doctrine of Christ, such as this is: That the resurrection of the dead is not to be expected Heb. VI. 1. 2. is not built upon the foundation, but overturns the foundation, and concerning such a one, who namely defends such doctrine, we can neither hope, nor is it permitted to augur, that he will obtain salvation. If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen: If Christ has not risen, your faith is vain, 2 Cor. XV. 16. 17. If those who deny the future resurrection, how can they obtain eternal salvation? For that κατακαήσεται, it will be burned, is not said of the erring person, but of the erroneous doctrine. But that, even if it is said that it will suffer loss ζημιωθήσεται, which does not sound of removal from the office of Doctor, but of the deprivation or loss of the honor which they obtain from God, who build upon gold, silver, and precious stones, σωθήσεται will be saved, yet as if through fire, by which is regarded not so much excommunication, such as was that of the incestuous man, which was done not on account of heresy or erroneous doctrine, but on account of a most grave moral sin; but generally an exploration or testing, which is done through scripture or temptation. For as Doctors, who build upon the foundation of Christian Doctrine things that are salutary, useful, and analogous to the faith, whose work remains through the fire of tribulations, and has the use of both information and consolation, will receive their reward before others, Dan. XII. 3. Matt. V. 12. So those who build upon the foundation dogmas that are not analogous and are useless, will suffer the losses of their labor, experiencing at length that they have served no one with them, yet they will not suffer the loss of salvation, because they retain the foundation: But they will be saved, yet as if through fire, as if snatched from a dangerous conflagration, with the stubble of errors also burned up. And then they will experience with how much danger they taught those things which they previously held in great esteem.

Whence it is entirely manifest that the present passage has nothing at all to do with the fire of purgatory; because this conflagration, of which the Apostle speaks, is in this age, not in the other, to which the Papists refer their purgatory, it is of the testing of doctrine, but not indeed of the expiation of sin, and it is done not by fire properly so called, but ὡς διὰ πυρὸς, as if through the fire of the cross and exploration, as Grotius himself acknowledges, that fire properly so called is not noted here, but that σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς is proverbial for the signification of extreme danger, comparing Jude verse 23. Add that the Apostle speaks of such a fire, through which pass both those who build upon gold and those who build upon stubble, although the latter suffer only loss. Which does not suit the purgatory fire of the Papists. And this gloss on purgatory of Bellarmine, Salmeron, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, and Menochius is refuted not only by B. Luther Tom. V. Jen. Germ. fol. 166. Wiederruff vom Fegfeuer. Reinoldus on the Apocryphal books part II. 166. and others, but also from among the Papists Roffensis Art. XVIII. controv. Luther. fol. 602. Cajetan, Justinian, Estius in this place and in IV. sentent. distinct. 17. Sixtus Senensis lib. VI. Biblioth. annot. 249. and Vasquez in I. secundae Tom. I. disp. 147.

PART II. PARÆNETIC.

Exhorting that regard be had for the temple of the Holy Spirit, lest it be corrupted.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον κατακαήσεται.

Si ab aliis Ecclesiis deprehendatur doctrina alicujus re- pugnare Christi doctrinæ, aut directè, ut licitum esse cum noverca concubitum, ut non expectandam resurrectio- nem; aut spectatis circumstantiis, ut licere epulari in ido- lio, licere litigare apud profanos Magistratus. Talia enim judicio sanarum Ecclesiarum stare non possunt. Justinus cum Tryphone disputans negat, pro Christianis habendos, qui resurrectionem futuram negant. Tertullianus adver- sus Marcionem V. Quia per ignem judicatur vestra superædi- ficatio, trabes incendio solent perire: epistola dicta Jere- miæ 55.

Ζημιωθήσεται.

Dejicietur omnium judicio de Doctoris munere, aut etiam communione privabitur, ut illi incesto accidit.

Αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται, ὕτω δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός.

Id est, in summo erit salutis suæ periculo: Etsi eam adi- piscetur, (quod boni ominis causa sperare mavult Aposto- lus,) non fiet id sine gravi mœstitia & dolore. Vid. 2. Cor. II. 7. Hic est ὄλεθρος σαρκὸς infra vers. 5. Σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς est proverbiale ad significationem summi periculi: Sic ἐκ τῦ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες dixit Judas 23. Aristides in Apel- lem: ἐκ μέσε, φασὶ, πυρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σώζειν. Cyprianus epi- stola LXVI. Exuenda est velociter de incendio sarcina, prius- quam flammis supervenientibus concremetur. Nemo diu tu- tus est periculo proximus.

Doctrina directè repugnans doctrinæ funda- mentali Christi, qualis hæc est: Non esse expectan- dam mortuorum resurrectionem Ebr. VI. 1. 2. non superstruitur fundamento, sed evertit fundamen- tum, & de tali, qui scil. ejusmodi doctrinam pro- pugnat, nec sperare possumus, nec ominari licet, eum salutem adepturum. Si non resurgunt mor- tui, nec Christus resurrexit: Si Christus non resur- rexit, vana est fides vestra, 2. Cor. XV. 16. 17. Si pro Christianis non habendi, qui resurrectionem futuram negant, quomodo salutem æternam adi- pisci possunt? Nec enim illud κατακαήσεται, ar- ferit, de persona errante dicitur, sed de doctrina er- ronea. Illa autem etsi detrimentum passura dica- tur ζημιωθήσεται, quod non de remotione ab officio Doctoris, sed honoris, quem à Deo consequuntur, qui aurum, argentum, & lapides pretiosos super- struunt, privatione, vel damno sonat, σωθήσεται servabitur adhuc, sed quasi per ignem, quà non tam excommunicatio, qualis incestuosi erat, quæ non ob hæresin vel doctrinam erroneam facta, sed ob peccatum morale gravissimum; quàm generatim exploratio vel probatio, quæ per scripturam vel tentationem fit, respicitur. Ut enim Doctores, qui salutaria, & utilia, fidei analoga superstruunt fundamento Doctrinæ Christianæ, quorum opus igne tribulationum manet, usumque cum infor- mationis tum consolationis habet, mercedem suam reportabunt præ aliis, Dan. XII. 3. Matth. V. 12. Sic illi, qui non analoga fundamento dogmata & inutilia superstruunt, detrimenta patientur labo- ris sui, experientes tandem, se illis nemini infer- viisse, non tamen jacturam salutis patientur, quia fundamentum retinent: Sed salvi fient, at quasi per ignem, tanquam ex periculoso incendio, confla- gratis etiam errorum stipulis, erepti. Et tunc ex- perientur, quanto cum periculo ea docuerint, quæ prius in magno habuere pretio.

Unde manifestum oppidò est, locum præsen- tem nihil omninò facere ad ignem purgatorii; quia hoc incendium, de quo Apostolus, in hoc seculo, non in altero est, ad quod referunt Papistæ suum purgatorium, probationis est doctrinæ, non verò expiationis peccati, & fit non per ignem propriè dictum, sed ὡς διὰ πυρὸς, quasi per ignem crucis & explorationis, ut agnoscit ipse Grotius, non ignem propriè dictum hic notari, sed σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς proverbiale esse ad significationem summi periculi, conferens Judæ vers. 23. Adde, quod Apostolus de tali igne loquatur, per quem trans- eunt, tam qui aurum, quam qui stipulas superstru- unt, licet hi tantum damnum patiantur. Quod non convenit purgatorio Papistarum igni. Et re- fellit hanc de purgatorio Bellarmini, Salmeronis, Cornelii à Lapide, Tirini & Menochii glossam non solùm B. Lutherus Tom. V. Jen. Germ. fol. 166. Wiederruff vom Fegfeuer. Reinoldus de libris A- pocryphis parte II. 166. alii, sed etiam è Papistis Roffensis Art. XVIII. controv. Luther. fol. 602. Cajetanus, Justinianus, Estius in h. l. & in IV. sentent. distinct. 17. Sixtus Senensis lib. VI. Bi- blioth. annot. 249. & Vasquez in I. secundæ Tom. I. disp. 147.

PARS II. PARÆNETICA.

Exhortans, ut templi Sp. S. ratio habeatur, ne corrumpatur.

## 3:16
Vers. 16. Do you not know that you are the temple of God. He returns to the comparison begun above, from which he had deflected to certain other things, though related. Philo compares the family of Abraham to a temple. Rabbi Alscheck on Haggai II. says the Israelitic people are called the temple of GOD. But much more justly are Christians, both individually and collectively, [called the temple] because of the Spirit of God dwelling in them. See below VI. 19. 2. Corinth. VI. 16. Salvianus to his sister: Blessed therefore is our God, who was always the guardian of your spirit, now especially also of your flesh, and remaining in you and guarding you, stretched out his hand from your interior parts even to the exterior: He preserved not only the holy of holies, but also the vestibules of his temple and the enclosures, and spreading his protection more widely, caused the salvation of your soul to reach even to the salvation of your body.

and the Spirit of God dwells in you. That is, because. This indwelling is much more august than that by the radiance near the Ark.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Οὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι ναὸς Θεῦ ἐστε. Redit ad comparationem cœptam supra, à qua ad alia quædam, affinia tamen, deflexerat. Philo familiam Abrahami templo comparat. Rabbi Alscheck ad Ag- gæum II. ait populum Israëlïticum dici templum DEI. Multò justius vero Christiani & singuli & collecti ob Spiri- tum Dei in ipsis habitantem. Vide infra VI. 19. 2. Co- rinth. VI. 16. Salvianus ad sororem : Benedictus itaque Deus noster, qui semper Spiritus tui custos nunc præcipue etiam carnis fuit, & in te manens teque custodiens manum suam ex interioribus tuis usque ad exteriora porrexit: Non solum sancta sanctorum, sed etiam vestibula templi sui & circumsepta serva- vit, protectionemque suam latius pandens fecit salutem animæ tuæ usque ad salutem corporis pervenire.

καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν. id est quia. Multo augustior hæc inhabitatio, quàm illa per fulgorem apud Arcam.

## 3:17
Vers. 17. If anyone destroys the temple of God. He destroys, which is accustomed to be done by evil doctrines and evil examples, Rom. XIV. 15. Here below VIII. 11.

God will destroy him. That is, he will punish most gravely, unless indeed he repents when warned. Φθερεῖ here is what ἀπολέσει, Matt. XXI. 41. Thus God destroyed Athaliah, thus Balthasar, the former because she had [profaned] the temple; the latter because he had profaned the gifts of the temple.

For the temple of God is holy. Holy things must not be violated.

Οἵτινές ἐστε ὑμεῖς. That is, that you are the temple. For a relative pronoun placed between two nouns sometimes takes the gender and number of the preceding one, sometimes of the following one.

How the Apostle returns to the previous exhortation, Grotius did not explain, saying only that he returns to the comparison begun; but the blessed Balduinus taught this not badly: In this part, the Apostle returns to his exhortation, by which he joins together teachers and learners alike in the Corinthian Church, and he does not want them to be admirers of human wisdom, from which arose party spirit, contentions, and schisms. In the teachers, the Apostle noted an admiration for their own wisdom in divine matters, from which it is necessary that self-love and contempt for colleagues arise. In the hearers, however, he noted a preposterous love of persons because of those singular gifts, from which it happened that they boasted more of one teacher than of another: when nevertheless they ought to have attended to the common duty of all, and to have granted glory to God alone. Both, therefore, are corrected jointly in this part. If you ask how the Church is violated or polluted by those vices which Paul noted in the Corinthians? The blessed Balduinus answers: It is certain that in those vices a stumbling block is placed for others, not only because those rivalries of teachers and altercations of hearers are scandalous in themselves: but also because a depraved opinion is easily born from them, as if those things which the Spirit of God works in the Church were to be ascribed to human wisdom. And thus the honor due to God alone is attributed to creatures, than which violation indeed nothing more foul can be conceived. Therefore, the Apostle asserts that the Holy Spirit is also driven out by this means, and that it is contrary to the holiness of the Church, and that they incur the most just punishment of God. Therefore, the Apostle teaches that those empty artifices, in which they so greatly pleased themselves, are just as many illusions of the Holy doctrine and of the purity of the Churches.

Moreover, the Fathers have noted here an argument for the deity of the Holy Spirit, which we have set forth at length in our Anti-Crellius, and that in various ways. First, from his omnipresence. For he who dwells in all and each of the faithful must be omnipresent, or certainly divided from himself. Second, from his grace. He who dwells in the faithful by his grace is the true God. But the Holy Spirit dwells in the faithful by his grace. Therefore. Third, from divine worship. For it is fitting for no one to have a temple except God alone, and we venerate with religious worship him to whom we consecrate ourselves as a temple. Fourth, from a comparison of passages. He whose temple the faithful are is God, 2 Cor. VI. 16. But the Holy Spirit is he whose temple the faithful are, 1 Cor. VI. 19. Os. I. 5. E. Likewise: He who dwells in our bodies as in his own temple, him we ought to glorify as God, or he is called God to be glorified by us, 1 Cor. VI. 19. 20. But the Holy Spirit dwells in our bodies as in his temple. Whence Theophylact rightly says: If we are the temple of God because the Holy Spirit dwells in us. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is God.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Εἴ τις τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φθείρει. Destruit, quod fieri solet malis doctrinis & malis exem- plis, Rom. XIV. 15. Hic infra VIII. 11.

Φθερεῖ τοῦτον ὁ Θεός. Id est, gravissimè puniet, nisi nempe monitus resipiscat. Φθερεῖ hic quod ἀπολέσει, Matth. XXI. 41. Sic Atholiam, sic Balthasarem perdidit Deus, illam quod templum; hunc quod templi donaria profanasset.

Ὁ γὰρ ναὸς Θεοῦ ἅγιός ἐστι. Sancta violari non debent.

Οἵτινές ἐστε ὑμεῖς. Id est, quod templum vos estis. Nam Relativum inter duo substantiva positum modo recipit genus & numerum præcedentis, modo subsequentis.

Quomodo ad exhortationem priorem redeat Apostolus, non exposuit Grotius, solum ad com- parationem cœptam rediri ait; non malè autem id docuit B. Balduinus: Redit hac parte Apostolus ad exhortationem suam, qua docentes pariter & discen- tes in Ecclesia Corinthiaca conjungit, eosque non vult esse humanæ sapientiæ admiratores, unde studia par- tium, contentiones & schismata oriebantur. In do- centibus notavit Apostolus admirationem pro- priæ sapientiæ in rebus divinis, unde Φιλαυτίαν & contemptum collegarum oriri necesse est. In au- ditoribus autem præposterum personarum amo- rem ob dona illa singularia, unde factum, quod de uno Doctore plus gloriabantur, quàm de alte- ro: Cum tamen omnium commune officium at- tendere, & Deo soli gloriam concedere debuis- sent. Utrumque ergo conjunctim hac parte cor- rigitur. Si quæras, quomodo vitiis illis, quæ Pau- lus in Corinthiis notavit, violetur vel polluatur Ec- clesia? Respondet B. Balduinus: Certum est in vi- tiis illis offendiculum poni aliis non saltem, quia æmulationes illæ Doctorum, & altercationes audito- rum in sese scandalosæ sunt: Sed etiam quia prava opinio facile inde nascitur, quasi ea, quæ in Ecclesia operatur Dei Spiritus, humanæ sapientiæ sint adscri- benda. Et sic honor soli Deo debitus creaturis tri- buitur, qua quidem violatione nihil fœdius excogi- tari potest. Idcirco & Spiritum Sanctum hoc pa- cto exturbari, & contra sanctitatem Ecclesiæ id esse, & justissimam Dei pœnam incurrere, asserit Apostolus. Inania ergo illa artificia, in quibus tan- topere sibi placebant, Apostolus docet esse totidē doctrinæ S. & puritatis Ecclesiarum illusiones.

Cæterum notarunt hic Patres argumentum Dei- tatis Sp. S. quod pluribus exequuti sumus in Anti- Crellio nostro, idque diversimodum. Primum ab omnipræsentia. Qui enim in fidelibus universis & singulis habitat, eum omnipræsentem esse opor- tet, aut certè à semetipso divisum. Alterum à gratia ejusdem. Qui inhabitat in fidelibus gratia sua, is est verus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. habitat in fidelibus gratia sua. Ergò. Tertium à cultu di- vino. Nulli enim templum habere convenit, nisi soli Deo, & cui nosmetipsos in templum consecra- mus, eum cultu religioso veneramur. Quartum è collatione locorum. Is, cujus templum sunt fide- les, est Deus, 2. Cor. VI. 16. Atqui Sp. S. est is, cu- jus templum sunt fideles, 1. Cor. VI. 19. Os. I. 5. E. Item: Qui inhabitat in corporibus nostris, ut in " templo suo, eum glorificare debemus, ut Deum, " vel is dicitur Deus à nobis glorificandus, 1. Cor. " VI. 19. 20. Atqui Sp. S. habitat in corporibus " nostris, ut in templo suo. Unde rectè Theo-"" phylactus: Si Dei templum nos sumus, quia in " nobis inhabitat Sp. S. Ergo Sp. S. est Deus. "

## 3:18
Verse 18. Μηδεὶς ἑαυτὸν ἐξαπατάτω. אל־תשאו נפשתיכם Jer. 37:9. All human philosophy, repugnant to the Gospel, is deception, 2 Thess. 2:3.

If any one seems to be wise among you in this age. Wise in this age is wise according to the wisdom of the world, as follows. If anyone pleases himself in this, that he knows the opinions and arguments of all the Philosophers.

Let him become a fool. Let him hold to the Gospel, which those Philosophers think foolish, see above I. 18. 20.

That he may become wise. That he may be wise in those things which can certainly lead him to eternal life.

The Apostle does not understand 'foolish' only according to man, as the Gospel seemed to the wise of the world, but he wants them to become fools, that is, to acknowledge their own foolishness, and to count all wisdom of the flesh in divine matters as nothing, so they will truly begin to be wise from God, even if before the world they are held as fools: let them renounce the wisdom of this world, so that divine wisdom may be able to rule among them. He therefore dissuades from the vain persuasion and admiration of wisdom, by which the Doctors proposed divine matters to the grasp of human reason, and pleased themselves in it, and the hearers admired that in them, which was not true wisdom, but mere persuasion and opinion. Since carnal wisdom is foolishness before God in matters, namely, of faith, or divine things. For this persuasion of wisdom was the source of all dissensions among the Corinthians.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Μηδεὶς ἑαυτὸν ἐξαπατάτω. אל־תשאו נפשתיכם Jer. XXXVII. 9. Omnis phi- losophia humana, Evangelio repugnans, deceptio est, 2. Thess. II. 3.

Εἴ τις δοκεῖ σοφὸς εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ. Σοφὸς ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ est σοφὸς κατὰ σοφίαν κόσμυ, ut se- quitur. Si quis in eo sibi placet, quod novit omnium Phi- losophorum sententias & rationes.

Μωρὸς γενέσθω. Evangelio se teneat, quod illi Philosophi stultum pu- tant, supra I. 18. 20.

Ἵνα γένηται σοφὸς. Ut ea sapiat, quæ ad vitam æternam certo eum possunt perducere.

Non κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον tantum stultum intelligit Apostolus, quale Evangelium videbatur sapienti- bus mundi, sed vult, ut stulti fiant, id est, stultitiam suam agnoscant, omnemque sapientiam carnis in rebus divinis pro nihilo reputent, ita verè & ex Deo sapere incipient, utut coram mundo pro fa- tuis habeantur : Sapientiæ mundi hujus renun- cient, ut dominari inter eos possit divina sapientia. Dehortatur ergò à vana persuasione & admiratio- ne sapientiæ, qua res divinas ad captum rationis humanæ proponebant, & in eo sibi placebant Do- ctores, idque admirabantur in iis auditores, quæ verò non vera sapientia erat, sed persuasio & opi- nio mera. Siquidem sapientia carnalis stultitia sit apud Deum in rebus scil. fidei, vel divinis. Hæc enim persuasio sapientiæ fons erat omnium dissi- diorum penes Corinthios.

## 3:19
Vers. 19. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. It does not please God any more than total foolishness, because it does not exhibit that purity of mind which God requires, see above I. 21. And foolishness, that is, it is worth no more than foolishness. A similar expression Rom. I. 14. & 25. Thus in Isaiah XLIV. 56. רעהם יסכל he makes their counsel foolish, & 2. Samuel XV. 32. סכל־נא את עצת אחיתפל where some translate 'make foolish', others 'make foolish the counsel of Ahithophel'.

The reason why the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God is not that which Grotius gives, that it does not exhibit the purity of mind which God requires, nor is there any word of that in 1 Cor. I. 21. But because it mocks the mysteries of faith concerning Christ crucified, in which is the highest wisdom of God, as the Apostle teaches there.

For it is written: He who catches the wise in their craftiness. It is from the words of Eliphaz in Job V. 13. Where the LXX have: He who catches the wise in their prudence. To catch is properly to enclose in the fist, Lev. II. 2. Num. V. 26. Taken more broadly it means the same as to seize. As Ps. III. 12. in the Greek. And craftiness is a neutral word, here meaning the same as prudence. See Proverbs I. 4. VIII. 5. Sir. XIX. 21. XXXIV. 10. God did this remarkably, when he set the Philosophers against one another, so that one affirmed nothing for certain which another equally ingenious did not overturn.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἡ γὰρ σοφία τῶ κόσμυ τούτω μωρία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ ἐστι. Deo non magis placet, quam summa stultitia, quia puri- tatem illam animi, quam Deus requirit, non exhibet, supra I. 21. Et stultitia, id est, non pluris sit, quam stultitia. Si- milis loquutio Rom. I. 14. & 25. Sic Esaiæ XLIV. 56. רעהם יסכל τὴν βυλὴν αὐτῶν μωραίνει, & 2. Samuel. XV. 32. סכל־נא את עצת אחיתפל Ubi alii μα- ταιῶσον, alii ἀφρόνησον τὴν βυλὴν Ἀχιτοφέλ.

Causa, cur sapientia mundi hujus stultitia coram Deo sit, non est illa, quam reddit Grotius, quod puritatem animi, quam Deus requirit, non exhi- beat, nec de eo verbum ullum 1. Cor. I. 21. Sed quod mysteria fidei de Christo crucifixo rideat, in quibus summa Dei sapientia, docente illic Apo- stolo.

Γέγραπται γὰρ· ὁ δρασσόμενος τὺς σοφὲς ἐν τῇ πανεργίᾳ αὐτῶν. Est ex verbis Eliphazi apud Job. V. 13. Ubi LXX. ha- bent: Ὁ καταλαμβάνων σοφὺς ἐν τῇ φρονήσει. Est δράσσειν propriè pugno includere, Lev. II. 2. Num. V. 26. Laxius sumptum idem valet, quod καταλαμβάνειν. Ut Ps. III. 12. in Græco. Et πανεργία vox est media, hic idem valens, quod φρονήσει. Vide Proverb. I. 4. VIII. 5. Sir. XIX. 21. XXXIV. 10. Fecit hoc Deus egregiè, cum Philosophos inter se commisit, ut nihil alter pro certo affirmaverit, quod non alter æquè ingenuosus everfum eat.

## 3:20
Vers. 20. And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. From Ps. XCIV. 11. Where in the Greek: The Lord knows the thoughts of men that they are vain. Paul put 'wise' instead of 'men', because it suited his purpose: and undoubtedly the Psalmist deals especially with those who seemed to themselves to be very wise.

God knows how to catch the wise of this world in various ways, not only by setting them against one another, but also by as it were ensnaring and confounding each one in his own wisdom by his own thoughts, so that they may be convinced that their wisdom is nothing, especially in comparison with divine wisdom, because the foolishness of God is wiser than men 1 Cor. I. 25. which is stated generally in Job VII. 3., that God catches the wise of this age in wisdom or rather craftiness, as the Apostle rendered it above. Because worldly wisdom, on account of the adhering vice of original sin, is craftiness when it is compared to divine wisdom, which it attacks, nor can it grasp it: But it is confounded by God, so that it may be understood that divine wisdom is far superior to the vain things of men, and the wise of the world themselves, when they oppose divine wisdom, are caught in their own wisdom. Since God not only knows intimately the most cunning counsels of profane men, but can easily dissipate and overturn them, as is held in Ps. XCIII. 11. In which place the Theological rule is rightly to be observed: Words of knowledge do not only imply knowledge and affection, but sometimes also effect. Therefore it is not about the wisdom of natural things, or of those things which human reason can attain, such as all things which are held in Theoretical and practical Philosophy, which wisdom is not disapproved of in itself, but is commended as a gift of God, Exodus XXXI. 3. XXXIV. 16. 1 Kings IV. 34. V. 12. Prov. II. 6. Dan. I. 21. But about the wisdom of the flesh, by which man left to himself, because of the corruption of original sin, opposes divine wisdom and the mind of the flesh is enmity against God, Rom. VIII. 7. James III. 15. For both testimonies, as B. Hunnius posits, are directed to the Apostle's scope, that one should not trust at all in the wisdom of the world and human reason, but should lower its swollen sails, especially in those things which are of faith, and are placed above every grasp of earthly wisdom and knowledge.

Latin:

Vers. 20. καὶ πάλιν· Κύριος γινώσκει τὺς διαλογισμὸς τῶν σοφῶν, οτι εἰσὶ μάταιοι. Ex Ps. XCIV. 11. Ubi in Græco: Ὁ Κύριος γινώσκει τὺς διαλογισμὸς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὅτι εἰσὶ μάταιοι. Paulus pro ἀν- θρώπων posuit σοφῶν, quia id instituto ipsius conveniebat: & haud dubie de iis maximè agit Psalmographus, qui sibi sapere plurimum videbantur.

Variis modis capere Deus novit sapientes hujus mundi, non tantum eos inter se committendo, sed etiam propriis cogitationibus quemque in sua sa- pientia velut irretiendo & confundendo, ut con- vincantur, nullam esse sapientiam suam, imprimis ἐν συγκρίσει divinæ sapientiæ, quia τὸ μωρὸν τῶΘεῶ σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων 1. Cor. I. 25. quod genera- tim Jobi VII. 3. effertur, capere Deum sapientes hu- jus seculi in sapientia vel potius πανεργίᾳ, uti Apo- stolus reddidit supra. Quia sapientia mundana, propter adhærens labis originalis vitium πανερ- γία est, cum confertur divinæ sapientiæ, quam im- pugnat, nec capere potest : Sed à Deo confundi- tur, ut intelligatur, divinam sapientiam longe su- periorem esse vanis hominum rebus, & ipsimet sapientes mundi, cum sapientiæ divinæ adversan- tur, in sapientia sua capiantur. Siquidem Deus astutissima consilia hominum profanorum, non tantum intimè norit, sed dissipare & evertere facile possit, ut habetur Ps. XCIII. 11. Quo in loco ritè observanda regula Theologica: Verba notitiæ non saltem scientiam & affectum, sed etiam effectum quandoque inferunt. Non ergo de sapientia re- rum naturalium, aut eorum, quæ ratio humana assequi potest, qualia universa sunt, quæ in Philo- sophia Theoretica & practica habentur, quæ sa- pientia per se non improbatur, sed ceu donum Dei commendatur, Exodi XXXI. 3. XXXIV. 16. 1. Reg. IV. 34. V. 12. Prov. II. 6. Dan. I. 21. Sed de sapientia carnis, qua homo sibi relictus ob corru- ptionem mali originalis divinæ sapientiæ adversa- tur & Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς est ἐχθρὰ εἰς τὸν Θεόν, Rom. VIII. 7. Jac. III. 15. Utrumque enim testi- monium, ponente B. Hunnio, dirigitur ad Apo- stoli scopum, ne quicquam sapientiæ mundi & humanæ rationis fidat, sed illius turgida vela con- trahat, in his præcipuè, quæ sunt fidei, & supra omnem terrenæ sapientiæ scientiæque captum posita.

## 3:21
Vers. 21. So let no one boast in men. Let him rejoice that he has had this or that teacher, so as to dedicate himself to him, as among the Jews the disciples of Hillel and Shammai: Among the Greeks the Pythagoreans, Platonists, Aristotelians, Epicureans.

For all things are yours. You are not for the sake of the teachers: But they are for your sake, God gives gifts to them for your use.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ὥστε μηδεὶς καυχάσθω ἐν ἀνθρώποις. Lætetur, quod hunc aut illum doctorem habuerit, ut ei se addicat, ut apud Judæos Hillelis & Sammæi discipuli: Apud Græcos Pythagorici, Platonici, Aristotelici, Epi, curei.

Πάντα γὰρ ὑμῶν ἐστιν. Non vos doctorum causa estis: Sed illi vestrum causa, Deus illis dona dat in usum vestrum.

## 3:22
Vers. 22. Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas. Because they were putting forward these names, he uses those names. But if the Apostles are for the sake of those whom they instruct, how much more so those who were making themselves leaders of sects?

The argument is drawn from what is unseemly. It is unseemly for a master to boast of his servants. For we are accustomed to boast of a more excellent thing. Now, indeed, the teachers of the Church, with all their gifts, are your ministers and the guardians of your souls given to you by God. Therefore, there is no reason why you should boast greatly of their gifts, but rather give glory to God, who procures your salvation through these instruments. This argument stands in verse 21, where a special proposition directed to the hearers is included at the same time. Therefore, let no one boast in men: For all things are yours.

Whether the world. They boast of their knowledge of natural things. And yet the whole universe was created for this, that God might be known. Those very people truly possess the universe, use the universe, and enjoy it, who know God.

Whether life. If God prolongs life for the teachers, He does it so that they may benefit the Church, Phil. 1:24.

Whether death. If they meet death for the sake of the Gospel, it happens so that others may become stronger through their constancy.

Whether things present. If they have the gifts of tongues and healings, they have them for this purpose, that the faithful may grow from them both in number and in strength.

Whether things to come. The same is true of the revelations of future things.

all things are yours. All these things are not for their sake only, but for the sake of others, such as you are.

but you are Christ's. A creature of Christ, so that you may obey Him.

and Christ is God's. Just as Christ obeyed His Father, below 11:3.

Too arbitrary glosses concerning the knowledge of natural things, the longevity of life, the martyrdom of Doctors, the gifts of tongues, of healings, and of the revelations of future things. The Apostle implies rather this, that not only are Doctors for the sake of the faithful, but the whole world; and not only Doctors, but the whole world, and that the world does not serve for their good outside of themselves, but even as regards themselves, both life and death are not to be ordered except for their own salvation. Nor only present things are to be of service to their salvation, but also all future things. Because to those who love God all things work together for good, Rom. VIII. 28. But that they themselves are sanctified by the grace of Christ and for Christ: but Christ by the grace of God and therefore sanctified, because He is the Mediator of God and men, and thus for men He sanctified Himself, and offered Himself to God, having become obedient to Him even unto death, even the death of the cross, John X. 30. ch. XVII. 9. Eph. VI. 2. Phil. II. 8. Therefore, a peculiar argument is included in this induction, which is that since all teachers are ministers of the Church, all are servants of Christ: but Christ is the one Lord of them, there ought to be no schism among them on account of the diversity of gifts, nor ought the hearers to depend upon any man as a Lord: And that, having cast aside a preposterous admiration of human wisdom, and having omitted the study of parties, they may henceforth glory in Christ alone, not in men, however distinguished and excellent. And thus the Apostle connects the Church, as the mistress of all things in the world, with Christ and God, as her head and Lord, and this to this end: That she may not too much cast herself down to the services of others, however excellent, nor yet too much exalt herself, but may depend entirely upon her Emperor Christ. Wherefore not all glorying in men is forbidden, when, for instance, the gifts of God in them are acknowledged with a grateful mind. But that glorying is vicious, when it is directed not to the gifts of God, or to God, the author of the gifts, but to the person endowed with the gifts, so that one might praise him while leaving the former, which is here forbidden by the Apostle. But Christ is not in the same way of God as the faithful are of Christ. For these were not only created by Christ, but also redeemed through His blood, and are justified, sanctified, and saved through the merit of Christ, and thus are Christ's by reason of creation, redemption, as also by reason of justification, or the remission of sins, renewal, and salvation by the virtue of the meritorious redemption of Christ, apprehended by true faith. By which reason no one would say that Christ is of God: although He depends on God, as a creature by reason of His human nature, just as He was sent by God for the sake of His office, namely for the salvation of the human race, not His own. Therefore, the Socinians obtain nothing for their unbelief and denial of the Deity of Christ by this gradation.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Εἴτε Παῦλος, εἴτε Ἀπολλὼς, εἴτε Κηφᾶς. Quia illi hæc nomina prætendebant, utitur illis nomi- nibus. Quod si Apostoli sunt illorum causa, quos insti- tuunt, quanto magis illi, qui se faciebant sectarum Prin- cipes?

Ab indecoro argumentum petitum est. Inde- corum est, gloriari dominum de servis suis. Nam de re præstantiori gloriari solemus. Jam verò Doctores Ecclesiæ, cum omnibus donis suis sunt ministri vestri & curatores animarum divinitus vobis donati. Ergo non est, quod de donis ipso- rum magnopere gloriemini, sed gloriam potius date Deo, qui per ista organa salutem vestram procurat. Extat hoc argumentum vers. 21. ubi propositio specialis ad auditores directa simul in- clusa est. Nemo itaque glorietur in hominibus: Omnia enim vestra sunt.

Εἴτε κόσμος. Jactant se rerum naturalium scientia. Atqui totum universum in hoc conditum est, ut Deus cognoscatur. Illi ipsi verè universum possident, universo utuntur, ac fruun- tur, qui Deum norunt.

Εἴτε ζωὴ. Si vitam Doctoribus protrahit Deus, id facit, ut prosint Ecclesiæ, Phil. I. 24.

Εἴτε θάνατος. Si ob Evangelium mortem obeunt, id fit, ut alii ipsorum constantia firmiores fiant.

Εἴτε ἐνεστῶτα. Si linguarum & sanationum dona habent, in id habent, ut fideles inde & numero & viribus crescant.

Εἴτε μέλλοντα. Idem est de rerum futurarum revelationibus.

πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν. Omnia hæc non sunt ipsorum tantum, sed aliorum, qua- les vos estis, causa.

ὑμεῖς δὲ Χριστοῦ. Christi creatura, ut ipsi obediatis.

Χριστὸς δὲ Θεοῦ. Sicut Christus Patri suo obedivit, infra XI. 3.

Glossæ nimis arbitrariæ de rerum naturalium scientia, longævitate vitæ, martyrio Doctorum, lin- guarum, sanationum donis, rerum futurarum reve- lationibus. Id potius innuit Apostolus, non Docto- res modo fidelium causa esse, sed totum mundum; Nec Doctores solum, sed totum mundum, neque mundum tantum bono ipsorum inservire extra ipsos, sed quoad ipsosmet, vitam etiam ac mortem propriam non nisi saluti ipsorum ordinari. Nec præsentia tantum: saluti ipsorum velificari, sed & futura quæque. Quia diligentibus Deum omnia cedunt in bonum, Rom. VIII. 28. Ipfos verò esse Christi gratia & sanctificatos Christo: Christum au- tem Dei gratia eoque sanctificatum, quia Mediator est Dei & hominum, adeoque pro hominibus se sanctificavit, & obtulit Deo, obediens eidem fa- ctus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Jo- hann. X. 30. cap. XVII. 9. Eph. VI. 2. Phil. II. 8. Includitur ergo huic inductioni argumentum pe- culiare, quod quoniam omnes Doctores ministri Ecclesiæ, omnes servi Christi sint: Christus verò unus eorum Dominus sit, nulla debeat ob dono- rum diversitatem inter ipsos esse scissio, nec ab ho- mine ullo tanquam Domino pendere debeant au- ditores: Utque abjectâ præposterâ admiratione sapientiæ humanæ, & omissis partium studiis, posthac in solo Christo, non in hominibus, quam- libet eximiis, & excellentibus, glorientur. Atque sic connectit Apostolus Ecclesiam, tanquam Do- minam rerum omnium in mundo cum Christo & Deo, tanquam capite Dominoque suo, idque hunc in finem: Ne nimium se abjiciat ad aliorum, utut excellentissimorum, servitia, nec tamen nimium se extollat, sed ab Imperatore suo Christo in soli- dum pendeat. Quare non omnis prohibita glo- riatio est in hominibus, cum nempe dona Dei in ipsis gratâ mente agnoscuntur. Vitiosa autem est illa gloriatio, quando ea non ad dona Dei, vel Deum, autorem donorum, sed ad personam donis ditatam, dirigitur, ita ut eam illo relicto quis præ- dicet, quod hic prohibitum ab Apostolo. Non autem eadem ratione Christus Dei, quâ fideles Christi sunt. Hi enim à Christo non tantum crea- ti, sed & redempti sunt per sanguinem ejus, & per Christi meritum justificantur, sanctificantur, & salvantur, adeoque Christi sunt ratione creatio- nis, redemptionis, ut & ratione justificatio- nis, seu remissionis peccatorum, renovationis & salvationis virtute redemptionis Christi merito- riæ, verâ fide apprehensæ. Qua ratione Christum Dei esse nemo dixerit: etsi dependeat à Deo, ut creatura ratione humanæ naturæ, uti missus est à Deo officii gratia, ob salutem scil. generis humani non suam. Nihil ergo pro ἀπισίᾳ sua, & inficia- tione Deitatis Christi hac gradatione obtinent Sociniani.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He explains what the teachers of the word are, namely ministers and stewards, in whom faith alone is required, which, however it may be judged by the human day, he has approved with his conscience as witness, expecting praise one day from God; warning that one should not be exalted against another, since we receive all things from God; and reproaching the Corinthians, because they carry themselves as if they were already reigning, and so that by the example of the Apostles, who are held by all as the offscouring of the world, they may study humility as their children, he sends Timothy to them for their imitation, and promises his own arrival, to the end that he may test the virtue of the puffed up, seeking whether they wish him to come with a rod, or indeed with a spirit of meekness.

There are three parts, I. Information concerning the office of the teachers of the word, to verse 5. II. Dehortation from elation, to verse 14. III. Mitigation of the rebuke, to verse 21.

PART I. Information concerning the office of the teachers of the word.

Vers. 1. Let a man so account of us. איש that is, ἕκαστος, everyone. A Hebraism. Thus below VI. 18. VII. 1. 26. XI. 27. Gal. II. 6. III. 15. VI. 1. 7. and often elsewhere.

As ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Again he raises up those whom he might have seemed to have cast down for the sake of the faithful. It is a great thing to be a minister of the Messiah, and a dispenser of God to distribute those things which were hidden for a long time. You have ὑπηρέτας in this sense also at the beginning of Luke. By the word mysteries he understands the Evangelical dogmas. See Rom. XVI. 25. above II. 17. The Latin rightly translates οἰκονόμως here as stewards. Thus also in the glossary: οἰκονόμος, steward. This name pertains first to the treasurers of private affairs, then also to those of public affairs, as was said in Luke XII. 41. 1 Cor. IV. 1.

These things are said not so much to raise up those whom he might not have seemed to have cast down, but whom he had altogether cast down on account of the contentions stirred up; as for the estimation of the Apostolic office, so that, its dignity being acknowledged, both with faith and joined humility, they might neither be puffed up themselves, nor follow the speech of the puffed up, but rather the word and example of their Fathers in Christ. Whence Lyranus rightly notes the connection: After the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians for this, that they attributed too much to some ministers, here he argues against them for this, that they despised some too much. And Musculus in this place: Whatever you may think of your Pseudo-Apostles, this is what must be thought of us, however despised, that we are ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. And let no one think anything above this, nor below this, concerning us. For either will result in the ignominy of Christ. We are ministers and stewards; therefore we are not to be worshipped as Lords. But again we are ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God, and by this name we are not to be cast away; but to be heard on account of Christ. Furthermore, since he has rebuked two vices in the Corinthians, in the hearers rashness in judging concerning teachers, in the teachers arrogance and swelling, now he teaches what kind of teachers ought to be held, and opposes his own humility to the arrogance of the teachers. He calls himself a minister of Christ, where the little word as is not of comparison but of truth. Moreover, the word minister is a word of labor and hardships, as Aretius notes. For it is from the verb to row. Hence rowers, and service of any kind. Wherefore the ministers of Christ confess that they sit at the oars, where they must row with tireless labor at the nod of the master of the ship, Christ, which thought will break the eyebrow of glory and dignity, etc. Others, however, prefer that the Biblical usage has a place here, by which ὑπηρέται signify not just any common servant, but a public and Royal minister, Prov. XIV. 35. Wisd. VI. 5. John VII. 45.

The word οἰκονόμος, arising from νόμος (law), implies skill in administration, so that all things may be done legitimately, decently, and in order, and it presupposes an οἰκοδεσπότην, which word Forster explains from the Hebrew אָמָן in his Lexicon, page 37, which signifies a steward, a nourisher, and is derived from faith. But it is certain that by μυστήρια the mysteries of the Gospel are signified, which ministers of the word dispense along with all its heavenly treasures, not excluding the sacraments, which are the σφραγῖδες of the Gospel, and are likewise entrusted to the faith of the ministers of the word, Matt. 28:9. And yet the Popish Mass does not contribute to this, as Thomas wishes: for this belongs to the μυςήρια of Papal iniquity. Furthermore, blessed Luther rightly notes here how the Papists dispense those mysteries: dispensations, he says, are numerous enough, but of prebends, fasts, possessions, marriages, and similar things, a new kind of dispensation, to wit, unknown to the Apostle. For no one knows or teaches the Word of God and the sacrament of the cross. Moreover, the right of that οἰκονομία does not imply any power of dispensing by divine law, or of remitting anything concerning it, which the Popes claim for themselves, but it denotes the distribution and administration of divine rights and of the benefits or gifts entrusted to the Church, as is evident from a comparison of Luke 12:42, 16:2, Rom. 16:15, 2 Cor. 2:7. Which, with Bernard, lib. 1, consider. to Eugenius, Cajetan, Salmero, Estius, Saa, and Justinianus acknowledge in this place. Therefore, it is a mere abuse when Bellarmine, Book IV on the Eucharist, ch. 28, and indeed even the Council of Trent itself, Sess. XXI, can. 2, usurps this right of dispensation for the license to dispense concerning the Eucharistic Chalice, so that it is not distributed to the Laity, which is sacrilege, not an οἰκονομία τῶν μυςηρίων Θεοῦ. For this ought to be done according to the prescription of the divine word, not against it. Pareus also rightly noted here the mysteries of Antichrist: Satan also had and still has his mysteries. For the heathens, I ask, to whom did they once celebrate the mysteries of Dionysus or Bacchus, of Ceres, the great and small Eleusinian mysteries? To the Devil, says the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10. Antichrist also has his mysteries. For the Babylonian harlot will bear written on her forehead, mystery, because her kingdom will be full of mysteries. Just as today in the Papacy there is no little ceremony so trifling, so frivolously devised and introduced, to which a huge mystery is not attached. Concerning which, see the Rationale of Durandus. The ministers of Christ ought not to be stewards of such mysteries, but of the mysteries of God. But the same Pareus acts wrongly, when he acknowledges that the sacraments are simultaneously included here, which the Greeks for that reason particularly called μυςήρια, he draws this word to such a point that whatever is of mystery in the sacraments is emptied out, and a mystery is feigned in a mere analogy or signification, and nothing else is left to the ministers of the word than the dispensation of bare signs and external elements, and not indeed of whole sacraments, to which certainly, besides the earthly matter, belongs the heavenly matter, without which the sacraments are neither mysteries nor have divine power, unless you wish to ascribe this to bare elements. But because the ministers of the word are stewards of the mysteries of God and of the sacraments, it behooves them to dispense not only the earthly matter, but also the whole sacraments.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Explicat, quid Doctores verbi sint, ministri nempe & œconomi, in quibus fides solum re- quiritur, quam, utcunque ab humano die ju- dicetur, teste conscientia probarit, laudem olim à Deo expectans; monens, ne alter ad- versus alterum extollatur, cum omnia à Deo accipiamus; & exprobrans, quod Co- rinthii, quasi jam dominentur, se efferant, utque exemplo Apostolorum, qui ab omni- bus tanquam purgamenta mundi habean- tur, ceu liberi ipsorum, humilitati studeant, ad sui imitationem mittit ipsis Timotheum, & promittit adventum suum, eo fine, ut ex- periatur turgidorum virtutem, quærens an nè cum virga, velint, veniat, anne vero cum spiritu mansuetudinis.

Partes sunt tres, I. Informatio de doctorum verbi munere, ad vers. 5. II. Dehortatio ab ela- tione, ad vers. 14. III. Reprehensionis mitigatio, ad v. 21.

PARS I. Informatio de doctorum verbi munere.

Vers. 1. Οὕτως ἡμᾶς λογιζέσθω ἄνθρωπος. איש id est, ἕκαστος, quilibet. Hebraïsmus. Sic infrà VI. 18. VII. 1. 26. XI. 27. Gal. II. 6. III. 15. VI. 1. 7. & ali- bi sæpè.

Ὡς ὑπηρέτας χριστῦ καὶ οἰκονόμως μυστηρίων Θεῦ. Rursum erigit quos, ut fidelium causa institutos, dejecis- se videri poterat. Magnum est, Messiæ esse ministrum, & Dei dispensatorem ad elargienda ea, quæ diu condita fue- re. Ὑπηρέτας hoc sensu habes & Lucæ initio. Μυστηρίων voce intelligit dogmata Evangelica. Vid. Rom. XVI. 25. supra II. 17. Οἰκονόμως dispensatores rectè hic vertit La- tinus. Sic & in glossario: Οἰκονόμος, dispensator. Per- tinet hoc nomen primum ad privatorum, deinde & ad publicæ rei arcarios, ut dictum Luc. XII. 41. 1. Co- rinth. IV. 1.

NOn tam ad erigendos, quos non dejecisse vi- deri poterat, sed omninò ob contentiones excitatas dejecerat; quam ad officii Apostolici æsti- mationem hæc dicuntur, ut agnita ejus cum digni- tate, tùm fide, & conjunctâ humilitate nec esse- rantur ipsi, nec inflatorum sermonem, sed ver- bum potius & exemplum Patrum suorum in Chri- sto sequantur. Unde Lyranus rectè συνέχειαν no- tat: Postquam Apostolus reprehendit Corinthios de hoc, quod aliquibus ministris nimis attribuebant, hic contra arguit eos de hoc, quod aliquos nimis con- temnerent. Et Musculus in h. l. Quicquid de Pseudo-Apostolis vestris sentiatis, de nobis utut con- temptis hoc est sentiendum, quod sumus Christi mi- nistri, dispensatoresque mysteriorum Dei. Nec suprà hoc quispiam, nec infra de nobis sentiat. Nam utrumque cedet ad ignominiam Christi. Mi- nistri sumus & dispensatores; igitur non adoran- di, velut Domini. At rursus sumus Christi mini- stri, & mysteriorum Dei dispensatores, & hoc no- mine non abjiciendi; sed propter Christum audien- di. Porrò cum duo in Corinthiis reprehenderit vitia, in auditoribus judicandi de doctoribus te- meritatem, in doctoribus arrogantiam & tumo- rem, jam quales doctores haberi debeant, do- cet, & doctorum arrogantiæ suam opponit hu- militatem. Vocat autem se ὑπηρέτην χριςῦ, ubi vocula ὡς non comparationis sed veritatis est. Vox autem ὑπηρέτης vox laboris & ærumnarum est, annotante Aretio. Est enim verbum ἐρέσσω remigo. Hinc ἐρετμοὶ remiges, & ὑπηρεσία servi- tium qualecunque. Quare Christi ministri con- fitentur, se ad remos sedere, ubi ad nutum nau- cleri Christi indefesso labore sit remigandum, quæ cogitatio franget supercilium gloriæ & dignita- tis, &c. Alii tamen malunt, hic usum Biblicum locum habere, quo ὑπηρέται non servum quem- vis gregarium, sed publicum & Regium mini- strum significant, Proverb. XIV. 35. Sap. VI. 5. Joh. VII. 45.

Vox οἰκονόμος à νόμῳ lege oriunda infert dex- teritatem administrationis, ut omnia legitimè, de- center, atque ordine fiant, ac præsupponit οἰκο- δεσπότην, quam vocem ex Ebræo אָמָן explicat Forsterus in Lex. pag. 37. quod dispensatorem, nutritium significat, & à fide deducitur. Per μυστήρια verò arcana Evangelii significari, cer- tum est, quæ cum omnibus ejus thesauris cœ- lestibus dispensant ministri verbi, non exclusis sacramentis, quæ Evangelii σφραγῖδες sunt, & fidei ministrorum verbi itidem credita sunt, Matth. XXVIII. v. 9. nec tamen Missa Papistica huc facit, ut Thomas vult: Hæc enim ad μυςή- ρια Papalis iniquitatis pertinet. Papistas de cæ- tero hic rectè notat B. Lutherus, quomodo di- spensent illi mysteria: dispensationes, inquit, sa- tis multæ sunt, sed præbendarum, jejuniorum, pos- sessionum, matrimoniorum, & his similium, novum scil. genus dispensationis Apostolo incognitum. Ver- bum enim Dei & sacramentum crucis nullus neque novit, neque docet. Porrò οἰκονομίας illius jus non infert potestatem aliquam dispensandi de jure divino, vel aliquid de eo remittendi, quam Papæ vendicant, sed distributionem notat, & admini- strationem jurium divinorum, ac beneficiorum, vel munerum Ecclesiæ creditorum, quemadmo- dum patet è collatione Luc. XII. 42. c. XVI. 2. Rom. XVI. 15. 2. Cor. II. 7. Quod cum Bern- hardo lib. 1. consider. ad Eugenium agnoscunt Ca- jetanus, Salmero, Estius, Saa & Justinianus in h. l. Merus itaque abusus est, cum hoc dispensationis jus Bellarm. L. IV. de Eucharist. cap. 28. imo & ipsum Concilium Tridentinum Sess. XXI. can. 2. abripit ad licentiam dispensandi de Calice Euchari- stico, ut non distribuatur Laicis, quod sacrilegium est, non οἰκονομία τῶν μυςηρίων Θεẽ. Hæc enim fieri debet juxta præscriptum verbi divini, non contra illud. Rectè etiam hic notavit Pareus my- steria Antichristi: Habuit & habet etiam Satan sua mysteria. Ethnici enim mysteria Dionysii seu Bacchi, Cereris, Eleusinia magna & parva olim cui quæso celebrabant? Diabolo, inquit Apostolus 1. Co- rinth. X. Habet etiam Anti-Christus sua mysteria. Nam meretrix Babylonica in fronte scriptum geret, mysterium, quia regnum ejus plenum erit myste- riorum. Sicut hodie in Papatu nulla cæremoniola est tam nugax tam frivolè excogitata, invecta, cui non ingens affingatur mysterium. De quo Ratio- nale Durandi videatur. Non talium mysteriorum æconomi esse debent ministri Christi, sed myste- riorum Dei. Male autem idem Pareus, quum agnoscat sacramenta hic simul comprehendi, quæ Græci peculiariter ideo vocarint μυςήρια, vocem hanc eo trahit, ut evacuetur, quicquid est mysterii in sacramentis, & in nudâ analogia vel significa- tione fingatur mysterium, nec ministris verbi quicquam aliud relinquatur, quam nudorum signorum, & externorum elementorum dispen- satio, non vero integrorum sacramentorum, ad quæ utique præter materiam terrestrem pertinet cælestis materia, sine qua sacramenta nec mysteria sunt, nec vim divinam habent, nisi hanc nudis ele- mentis adscribere velis. Quia vero ministri ver- bi dispensatores mysteriorum Dei ac sacramen- torum sunt, oportet eosdem non tantum rem ter- renam, sed & sacramenta integra dispensare.

## 4:2
Verse 2. Ὁ δὲ λοιπόν.

It has the same value as what is more frequently said, λοιπὸν, above 1:16, Acts 27:20, 2 Cor. 13:11, 2 Tim. 4:8, or τὸ λοιπὸν, as Matt. 26:45, Mark 14:41, Eph. 6:10, Phil. 3:1, 1 Thess. 4:8, 5:1, 2 Thess. 3:1, Heb. 10:13. It is used both of things and of remaining times. But often, as here, it connects the discourse and has the force which the Latin word 'cæterum' (furthermore/as for the rest) has.

Ζητεῖται ἐν τοῖς οἰκονόμοις.

Ζητεῖται approaches a Latinism: It is required. He pursues the translation of the word οἰκονόμος.

Ἵνα πιςός τις εὑρεθῇ.

He placed the singular after the plural, because these are used indiscriminately in distributive senses. To be faithful is the chief praise in a steward, Matt. 14. Therefore it is attributed to Moses, Heb. 3:5, to Samuel, 1 Sam. 3:20, to the ministers of the Gospel, John 6:21, Col. 1:7, 4:7. But those leaders of sects at Corinth were certainly not such.

Aretius, following Aristotle, Book V, Politics, ch. 12, requires four things in these faithful stewards

(1.) ἐμπειρίαν, skill in affairs, (2.) εὐφυΐαν, good natural ability, (3.) Φιλοπονίαν, assiduity in labor, (4.) δικαιοσύνην, justice. These especially suit the stewards of Christ. For it is necessary that they be skilled in scripture, from whose storehouse they bring forth food. It is also necessary that they be endowed with good natural ability, that is, not to be malicious and hypocrites, so that they may act candidly and seriously, because what they do must always be taught, always read. Φιλοπονία is also necessary for them, one must always be occupied with letters, scripture must be handled by day and by night. Finally, justice is very necessary, so that he may express in life and morals what he teaches, lest with one hand he destroys what he builds with the other. From this passage, three things can be noted in a steward: (1.) diligence or faithfulness, cf. 1 Cor. 4:17, 2 Tim. 3:2, in the dispensation of heavenly food, John 12:42, and the winning of souls, Matt. 25:14. (2.) Tolerance, or equanimity, v. 3, cf. 2. 1 Cor. VI. 8. 9. X. 2. (3.) A good conscience i.e. true piety. See 2 Cor. I. 12. Acts XXIII. 1. XXIV. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὁ δὲ λοιπόν.

Idem valet, quod frequentius dicitur λοιπὸν supra I. 16. Act. XXVII. 20. 2. Cor. XIII. 11. 2. Tim. IV. 8. aut τὸ λοιπὸν, ut Matth. XXVI. 45. Marci. XIV. 41. Eph. VI. 10. Phil. III. 1. 1. Thess. IV. 8. V. 1. 2. Thess. III. 1. Ebr. X. 13. Usurpatur & de rebus & de temporibus restantibus. Sed sæpè, ut hic, orationem connectit & vim habet eam, quam Latina vox cæterum.

Ζητεῖται ἐν τοῖς οἰκονόμοις.

Ζητεῖται ad Latinismum accedit: Requiritur. Vocis οἰκονόμꙋ translationem persequitur.

Ἵνα πιςός τις εὑρεθῇ.

Plurali subjecit singulare, quia ista in distributivis pro- miscuè usurpantur. Fidelem esse præcipua laus in dispen- satore, Matth. XIV. Itaque tribuitur Mosi, Hebr. III. 5. Samueli, 1. Sam. III. 20. Ministris Evangelii, Joh. VI. 21. Col. I. 7. IV. 7. Tales autem certe non erant illi secta- rum duces Corinthi.

Quatuor in fidelibus æconomis his, præeunte Aristotele lib. V. Polit. cap. 12. requirit Aretius

(1.) ἐμπειρίαν peritiam rerum, (2.) εὐφυΐαν bonam indolem, (3.) Φιλοπονίαν laboris assiduitatem, (4.) δικαιοσύνην justitiam. Hæc œconomis Christi im- primis quadrant. Oportet enim peritos esse scri- pturæ, ex cujus penu proferant cibaria. Oportet etiam bona indole esse præditos, hoc est, non esse malitiosos & hypocritas, ut candidè & seriò agant, quia semper docendum est, semper legendum est, quod agunt. Φιλοπονία etiam illis est necessaria, semper versandum in literis, diurna nocturnaque manu versanda scriptura. Denique justitia per- necessaria est, ut vitâ & moribus exprimat id quod docet, ne una manu destruat, quod altera ædificat. Ex hoc loco notari possunt in œcono- mo tria: (1.) diligentia s. fidelitas, conf. 1. Cor. IV. 17. 2. Tim. III. 2. in cibi cœlestis dispensatione, Johan. XII. 42. & animarum lucratione, Matth. XXV. 14. (2.) Tolerantia, seu æquanimitas, v. 3. conf. 2. Co- rinth. VI. 8. 9. X. 2. (3.) Bona conscientia s. veræ pietas. Vid. 2. Cor. I. 12. Act. XXIII. 1. XXIV. 16.

## 4:3
Verse 3. But to me it is a very small thing.

It is a Hebraism: For to them attributes, which in Greek would be expressed by the Nominative, are expressed by ל, which is equivalent to εἰς. See what we have said at Matt. XIX. 5.

That I should be judged by you.

Ἵνα here is equivalent to if. It matters little to me what you judge concerning me, compared to that which God is about to judge concerning me. He wishes those whom he does not name, but marks, to think of this.

Or by man's day.

Jerome thinks this and certain other things are from the idiom of the Cilicians, where Paul had first learned the Greek language. For among them a day is accustomed to be said for a judgment: Nor is it a wonder since we also say in Latin 'dicere diem' [to appoint a day], and the word in German signifying to cite to judgment is derived from 'day'. But the Hebrews interpret יום and יומי in Job XXIV. 1 as judgment.

Some take this judgment in a good sense, even Blessed Luther, as if he were saying, I care for no one, nor does it move me in the slightest that I am preferred to others by your judgment: If it happens to be judged by the Lord, that is, to be approved, I shall be truly praised. Others, however, interpret it in a bad sense, the interlinear Gloss, Bullinger, Aretius, and most others, as if he were saying: It matters little that I am judged by you as an evil steward. But those opinions are well reconciled if it is understood in both directions with Blessed Jerome Weller, in this way: It is a small thing to me whether you exalt me by your judgment, or indeed depress me. Some wish to note by 'man's day' proclamations and applause, from Jer. XVII. 16, where, however, in the source it is not 'day of man', but 'day of destruction'. But it is called a human day when judgment is passed not from truth, or according to God's word, but from lust or rashness, as men are wont to do for the most part.
