Therefore it is contradistinguished from the judgment of God. But an illegitimate judgment is understood, whether encomiastic or detracting, concerning the industry, gifts, and qualities of teachers, and therefore it is wrongly distorted by the Anabaptists, certain English troublemakers, and Thom. Erastus in argument 4 against excommunication, to prohibit Ecclesiastical judgments. For neither does the object fit, which is such here that certainty cannot be had concerning it in this life, and which only the day of the Lord will manifest: Nor the subject, which are not so much the Teachers as the Hearers, who presumed to judge their teachers.

But neither do I judge myself.

I do not take upon myself full parts of judging concerning myself, Juvenal having spoken concerning the Gods: A man is better known to them than to himself.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐμοὶ δὲ εἰς ἐλάχισόν ἐστι.

Est Hebraïsmus: Nam illis attributa, quæ Græce No- minativo exprimerentur, exprimuntur per ל, quod valet εἰς. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. XIX. 5.

Ἵνα ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν ἀνακριθῶ.

Ἵνα hic valet si. Parum mea refert, quid vos de me ju- dicetis, præ eo, quod Deus de me judicaturus est. Hoc vult cogitare illos, quos non nominat, sed notat.

Ἢ ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνης ἡμέρας.

Hieronymus putat hoc & alia quædam esse è Cilicum, ubi Græcam linguam didicerat primum Paulus, idiomate. Illis enim diem solitum dici pro judicio: Nec mirum cum & Latinè dicamus dicere diem, & Germanis verbum signi- ficans citare ad judicium, à die deducatur. Sed יום & יומי Jo- bi XXIV. 1. Hebræi interpretantur judicium.

Nonnulli hoc judicium in bonam partem acci- piunt, etiam B. Lutherus, quasi dicat, nullius fa- cio, neque tantillum me movet, vestro judicio me aliis preferri: Si à Domino contigerit judicari, hoc est, probari, ero verè laudatus. Alii verò malam in partem interpretantur, Glossa interlinear. Bul- lingerus, Aretius, & plerique cæteri, quasi dicat: Parum refert, quod à vobis judicer, ut malus dispen- sator. Sed probè consistunt illæ sententiæ, si cum B. Hier. Wellero in utramque partem intel- ligatur, hoc modo: Pro minimo mihi est, utrum vos judicio vestro me extollatis, án verò depri- matis. Diem humanum notare præconia, & ap- plausus, nonnulli è Jer. XVII. 16. volunt, ubi ta- men in fonte non est dies hominis, sed dies contri- tionis. Dicitur autem humanus dies, cum non ex veritate, vel juxta Dei verbum, sed ex libidine vel temeritate, ut solent plerumque homines, judi- cium fertur. Ideò judicio Dei contradistinguitur. Intelligitur autem judicium illegitimum sive enco- miasticum, sive detractorium, circa industriam, dona, & qualitates doctorum, ideoque perperam id ab Anabaptistis, Anglicanis quibusdam turba- toribus, & Thom. Erasto argum. 4. contra excom- munic. detorquetur ad prohibenda judicia Eccle- siastica. Nam nec objectum convenit, quod tale hic est, de quo non potest haberi certitudo in hac vita, quodque solum dies Domini manifestabit: Nec subjectum, quod non tam Doctores sunt, quam Auditores, qui præsumebant judicare do- ctores suos.

Ἀλλʼ ὀυδὲ ἐμαυτὸν ἀνακρίνω.

Non mihi sumo plenas de memet judicandi partes, Ju- venalis de Diis locutus: Notior est illis homo, quàm sibi.

## 4:4
For I know nothing against myself, yet I am not hereby justified.

The construction is rather involved in the Hebrew manner: which you may explain thus: Although it does not come to my mind that I have done anything otherwise in the ministry entrusted to me, yet not thereby it follows that I am clearly free from all blame. For that is what δικαιοῦσθαι signifies, Acts VIII. 38. Rom. VI. 7. See also the Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans. Chrysostom grasped the sense well: 'And what then, if he is conscious of nothing in himself, has he been justified?' Because it happened that he had committed some sins, but he did not know them to be sins. To this pertains especially what James says, III. 2: 'We all stumble in many things,' and what we are all and always commanded to say: 'Forgive us our debts.' Clement in his epistle: 'Stretch out your hands to the sovereign God, beseeching him to be merciful, if you have sinned unwillingly.' In the so-called Ignatian epistle to the Romans we have: 'But in their misdeeds (the soldiers, by whom he was being dragged) I am rather being discipled, but I am not thereby justified.' Jerome, in the second dialogue against the Pelagians, mentioning this passage of Paul, adds: 'He says this, lest he might have committed some fault through ignorance.' Possidius on Augustine: 'He used to say that after receiving baptism, even praised Christian priests ought not to depart from the body without worthy and competent penance.' This is the truest interpretation of this passage, and no other is to be sought. Compare Ps. XIX. 13.

But he who judges me is the Lord. He is the one who, with not only actions but also thoughts revealed, will bring the most exact judgment both of me and of others. אלהים חקר Ps. XLIV. 22.

Here we easily agree with Grotius, and Dr. Selneccer excellently to the same effect in his explanation of this passage, p. 137. Conscience is useful not for justification before God, but for testifying to innocence toward one's neighbor, with God as witness. And as charity is the testimony of faith, so conscience is the internal testimony of charity. But as often as we boast of a good conscience, as Paul does in 1 Cor. I. 12, we must always attribute every good to God, as it is written, 'He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord' (1 Cor. I. 31), and retain the foundation, namely, that the confidence and certainty of our salvation is situated in the mercy of God alone, not in our conscience, Luke XVII. 10. From this, however, it is gathered that our justification is not situated in the infusion of righteousness or charity: for regarding that, the testimony of conscience would suffice; but in the gracious remission of sins, which is forgiven us for Christ's sake out of mere mercy, not because of our works. And although the faithful sometimes appeal to a good conscience, that is done either regarding the righteousness of the cause, but not regarding the righteousness of the person; or it is done only in a certain respect, not absolutely, regarding innocence as far as more serious, voluntary sins are concerned, but not regarding all-encompassing perfection. For we all stumble in many things, James III. 2, and conscience, however good it may seem, is nevertheless polluted by sins, Prov. XX. 9. Nor is anyone at all innocent before God, Exod. XXXIV. 7. All saints are bound to seek the remission of sins, Psalm XXXII. 6. One must also distinguish between a good conscience as it is considered before God and as it is before one's neighbor. For before one's neighbor, a good conscience is taken to mean when someone harms no one and strives to be useful to all, and lives in such a way that he is not ashamed to live. But before God, such a conscience is not yet good, for He searches the innermost parts of our heart; but it is necessary that the conscience be purified by the blood of Christ through faith.

From which, however, with the Papists, the uncertainty of grace is not to be concluded, because the grace of justification does not depend on our holiness or innocence, but on the righteousness of Christ, apprehended by true faith, Rom. IV. 6, ch. V. 18. For Paul did not doubt, but was certain of his own justification, Rom. VIII. v. last. Even if he does not wish to deduce that certainty here from the goodness of conscience, and denies that he is righteous by the purity of his conscience. Furthermore, Paul here acts only against the judgments of other men, but he does not derogate from himself the judgment concerning his own faith and justification, since he commands everyone to test himself, whether he is in the faith, 1. Cor. XIII. 5. He indeed says, 'I do not judge myself, but he who judges me is God,' but this is to be understood concerning the judgment of faithful administration, not concerning the judgment of the testing of faith: concerning the judgment of one's own praise, because he expects praise from God, not concerning the judgment of divine grace and love in Christ: concerning the judgment of deeds, not concerning the judgment of reception into grace. Blessed Balduinus thinks one must distinguish between the judgment of decree, by which someone is absolved or condemned through a judicial sentence, which belongs to God alone, and the judgment of testing, which everyone can institute concerning himself, whether he is in the faith, 2 Cor. XIII. 8. Pareus says that no one can establish anything legally from works, because when and to what extent the merits of works suffice in the judgment of God can be known by no mortal: The reason is because, as Christ pronounces, when we have done all things, we are unprofitable servants. But he says that it belongs to faith not to merit salvation, but to receive righteousness freely, Acts XXVI. 18. And he who believes, he says, does not not know nor doubt, but knows, feels, and sees that he believes, according to August. Book XIII de Trinit. ch. 1. Because faith is a movement of the heart and πληροφορία, 1 John III. 21, Rom. VIII. 16. Blessed Hülsemann judges that, by the force of the subject matter, the discourse is about justification or the absolving sentence not before God, but before human judgment; but 'in this I am not justified,' i.e., that the conscience of innocence does not give assurance to himself or others: but the former explanation seems simpler, that the Apostle was indeed conscious of nothing in himself regarding neglected or wrongly administered duty: Yet since no one knows how often he sins; but all have need to ask with David: 'Deliver me from hidden things, O Lord,' Psalm XIX. 13, by that very fact he is not yet justified before God. But if the Apostle did not even have to determine concerning all things which were to be performed in his office, whether he might have failed somewhere even unknowingly, and therefore because he knowingly and prudently, with his conscience as witness, did nothing against the faith of his office, he was not in the least justified before God, how much less could he so judge concerning his whole life, or determine that he was justified by the innocence of his life. For we are not justified by the certainty of conscience, but by faith. Since conscience tells us all that we are sinners, and lack the glory of God: Faith on the contrary knows that we are justified freely by the blood of Christ.

Latin:

Ὀυδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἀλλʼ ὀυκ ἐν τόυτῳ δεδι- καίωμαι.

Constructio est involutior more Hebræo: Quam sic ex- plices: Quanquam non in mentem mihi venit, me in mini- sterio mihi credito secus quicquam fecisse, tamen non inde sequitur, me plane ab omni culpa esse liberum. Id enim significat δικαιοῦσθαι, Act. VIII. 38. Rom. VI. 7. Vide & Pro- legomena in Epistolam ad Romanos. Chrysostomus sen- sum bene assecutus est: καὶ τί δηποῖ;, εἰ μηδὲν ἑαυτῷ σύνοι- δεν, ὀ δεδικαίωται; ὅτι συνέβαινεν ἁμαρτῆσθαι μὲν ἀυτῷ τινα ἁμαρτήματα, μὴ μὴν ἀυτὸν εἰδέναι ταῦτα ἁμαρτήματα. Huc præcipue pertinet, quod dicit Jac. III, 2. πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαν- τες, & quod omnes & semper jubemur dicere: Dimitte no- bis debita nostra. Clemens in epistola: ἐξετείνατε τὰς χεῖ- ρας ὑμῶν πρὸς τὸν ἀυτοκράτορα θεὸν, ἱκετεύοντες ἀυτὸν ἵλεων γενέσθαι, εἴτι ἄκοντες ἡμάρτεθε. In Ignatiana, quæ dicitur, epistola ad Romanos habemus: ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἀδικήμασιν ἀυτῶν (militum, à quibus trahebatur) μᾶλλον μαθητέυομαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐ παρὰ τῦτο δεδικαίωμαι. Hieronymus dialogo adversus Pelagium secundo hunc Pauli locum commemorans ad- dit: Hoc dicit, ne quid forte per ignorantiam deliquisset. Po- sidius de Augustino: Dicebat post perceptum baptismum et- iam laudatos Christianorum sacerdotes absque digna & com- petente pœnitentia exire de corpore non debere. Hæc verissima est hujus loci interpretatio, nec quærenda est alia. Confer. Ps. XIX. 13.

ὁ δὲ ἀνακρίνων με Κύριός ἐστιν. Is est, qui detectis non actibus tantum, sed & cogitatio- nibus exactissimum & de me & aliis judicium feret. אלהים חקר Pf. XLIV. 22.

Facile hic annuimus Grotio, & eximiè in ean- dem sententiam D. Selneccerus in explicatione hu- jus loci p. 137. Conscientia prodest non ad justifica- tionem coram Deo, sed ad innocentiam testandam erga proximum teste Deo. Et ut charitas est testi- monium fidei; ita conscientia est internum testimo- nium charitatis. Quoties autem gloriamur de bona conscientia, ut Paulus 1. Cor. I. 12. semper debemus omne bonum Deo ferre acceptum, ut scriptum est, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, (1. Cor. I. 31.) & retinere fundamentum, videli- cet in sola Dei misericordia sitam esse nostræ salu- tis fiduciam & certitudinem, non in nostra con- scientia, Luc. XVII. 10. Colligitur autem hinc, Ju- stificationem nostram non sitam esse in justitiæ vel charitatis infusione: Nam de illa conscientiæ testi- ficatio sufficeret; sed in gratiosa peccatorum re- missione, quæ ob Christum nobis condonatur ex mera misericordia, non ob nostra opera. Et quanquam fideles nonnunquam ad bonam con- scientiam provocent; id tamen aut fit, quà justitiam causæ, non verò quà justitiam personæ; aut fit se- cundum quid solum, non simpliciter, qua innocen- tiam, quantum ad peccata graviora, voluntaria, non verò quoad perfectionem omnimodam. Nam in multis labimur omnes, Jac. III. 2. & conscientia, utut optima videatur, peccatis tamen polluta est, Prov. XX. 9. Neque ullus apud Deum omninò innocens est, Exod. XXXIV. 7. Omnes Sancti te- nentur petere remissionem peccatorum, Psalm. XXXII. 6. Distinguendum etiam inter conscien- tiam bonam, quà consideratur coram Deo, & quà coram proximo. Nam coram proximo bona con- scientia sumitur, cum quis neminem lædit, atque omnibus prodesse studet, & ita vivit, ut vivere eum non pudeat. Coram Deo autem talis con- scientia bona nondum est, qui intima cordis no- stri scrutatur; sed opus est, ut conscientia purifi- cetur sanguine Christi per fidem.

Ex quo tamen cum Pontificiis non est conclu- denda incertitudo gratiæ, quia justificationis gratia non dependet à nostra sanctitate, vel innocentia, sed à Christi justitia, vera fide apprehensa, Rom. IV. 6. c. V. 18. Non dubitavit enim Paulus, sed certus fuit de justificatione sua, Rom. VIII. v. ult. Etsi eam certitudinem hic non deducere velit è con- scientiæ bonitate, negetque se puritate conscientiæ suæ justum esse. Agit præterea hic Paulus solum adversus hominum aliorum judicia, non verò de- rogat sibi judicium de fide & justificatione pro- pria, cum quemque justum probare jubeat, num qui in fide sit, 1. Cor. XIII. 5. dicit quidem, ego meipsum non judico, sed, qui me judicat, Deus est, sed hoc de judicio administrationis fidelis, non de judicio pro- bationis fidei: de judicio propriæ laudis, quia à Deo laudem expectet, non de judicio divinæ in Christo gratiæ & dilectionis: de judicio factorum, non de judicio receptionis in gratiam, intelligendum. B. Balduinus distinguendum censet inter judicium decreti, quo per sententiam judiciariam quis absol- vitur, vel damnatur, quod soli Deo competit, & judicium probationis, quod unusquisque de se in- stituere possit, utrum in fide sit, 2. Cor. XIII. 8. Pareus ex operibus, ait, nemo statuere potest legali- ter, quia quando & in quantum sufficiant in Dei judicio operum merita, cognosci à nullo morta- lium potest: Ratio est, quia, pronunciante Chri- sto, cum omnia fecimus, servi inutiles sumus. Fi- dei verò esse ait idem, non mereri salutem, sed justi- tiam gratis accipere, Act. XXVI. 18. Et qui cre- dit, eum non nescire nec dubitare, sed novisse sentire, ac videre se credere, secundum August. L. XIII. de Trinit. cap. 1. Quia fides motus cor- dis est & πληροφορία, 1. Joh. III. 21. Rom. VIII. 16. B. Hülsemannus judicat, vi subjectæ materiæ ser- monem esse de justificatione seu sententia absolu- toria non coram Deo, sed coram die humano; sed in hoc justificatus non sum, q. d. conscientiam inno- cetiæ sibi non aliis fidem facere: sed simplicior vi- detur prior explicatio, quod sibi quidem nil con- scius fuerit Apostolus de neglecto vel perperam administrato officio: Tamen cum nemo sciat quoties peccat; sed rogare opus habeant omnes cum Davide: Ab occultis libera me, Domine, Psal. XIX. 13. eo ipso nondum justificatus sit co- ram Deo. Si autem ne statuere quidem habuit Apostolus de omnibus, quæ in officio suo exequen- da erant annè alicubi vel nescius defecerit, atq; id- eo quod sciens prudens, teste conscientia, nihil ad- versus fidem muneris egerit, se minime justificari coram Deo, quanto minus ita judicare de vita sua universa potuit, aut statuere se per innocentiam vitæ suæ justificari. Nec enim per conscientiæ cer- titudinem, sed per fidem justificamur. Cum con- scientia omnibus nobis dicat, nos esse peccatores, & carere gloria Dei: Fides contra norit, nos gra- tis justificari sanguine Christi.

## 4:5
Vers. 5. ὥστε μὴ πρὸ καιρᾶ τι κρίνετε. He directs this especially against those who, while calling themselves disciples of Christ and Peter, accused Paul as an enemy of the Jewish nation: which fault Paul everywhere removes from himself with great zeal. But it appears by no evidence that Paul institutes such an apology here, lest he appear an enemy of the Jewish nation. He rejected in general the judgments of the Corinthians concerning himself, both because of their futility, because they are vain and human or carnal; and because of their rashness, because not even he, who knows himself more rightly than others, dares to judge himself in his deeds, before God, even though before men he has so conducted himself that he has, with God as witness, a good conscience: and because of their impiety, because they sacrilegiously take upon themselves the parts of judging that belong to God, and place themselves on the tribunal of divine judgment, and anticipate the divine judgment, which He has reserved for Himself on the day of universal judgment; because it is an injury to the judge if a sentence proceeds from a servant before His judgment.

Ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ Κύριος, ὃς καὶ φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆ σκότους, καὶ φανερώσει τὰς βελὰς τῶν καρδιῶν. One who lives flagitiously can indeed be safely condemned for his present state. For the works of the flesh are manifest. But to ascribe an evil mind to acts that are in themselves good or indifferent is against the rule of love. Those secrets must be left to Christ the Judge: Τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆ σκότους מְגַלֶּה־עֲמֻקּוֹת מִנִּי־חשֶׁךְ Job. XII. 22. what he had said obscurely before φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ, that by ἐξάγουσι he explains תעלמות לב, the counsels of the hearts, the hidden things of the heart, in the passage Ps. 44:22. For to know these is the prerogative of God alone and of Christ, Acts 1:24, 15:8. φωτίσει here is 'will bring to light'. κὰι τότε ἔπαινος γενήσεται ἑκάστῳ ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ. Namely, if he has done good things with a good mind: whence the contrary is also understood to be given: but he prefers ἐυφημεῖν.

By the hidden things of darkness, some understand hidden hypocrisy; others, secret intentions, which they distinguish from the counsels of the hearts, that is, from decrees, opinions, and judgments. But generally, the hidden things of darkness are explained by the ordinary gloss as sins, which love darkness and are done in secret, John 3. And God is going to bring to light not only those things which have already been perpetrated and actually committed in secret: but also the very counsels of the hearts, intentions, thoughts, desires, decrees, pleasures, affections, hatred, anger, and the like, which no one knows, except the spirit of man which is in man. Others interpret it even more generally, because ἔπαινος does not befit the works of darkness (which word Heinsius warns is rashly and ἄτερ γραφῆς used to denote punishments and disgrace), concerning the hidden thoughts and counsels of the hearts, which here are mere darkness to us and cannot be discerned by us, but will one day be placed and exposed in the open light, or, as they say, on the disk of the sun. That is to say: You now, O Corinthians, like judges of the games, rashly crown some, and dismiss others with ignominy. But there will be a day when Christ, to whom this uniquely belongs as the searcher of hearts, will make manifest who are worthy of praise and a crown. Furthermore, by this Apostolic doctrine, the teachers of the word are by no means constituted ἀνυπεύθυνοι, or exempted from all censure. For not even Paul himself refused the judgment of the Church concerning his doctrine, 2 Cor. 10:15; judge for yourselves what I say. But only rash judgments are reproved, by which, if sincere teachers are unjustly oppressed, they deservedly despise them and hold them for nothing, to be judged by the human day, such as, for example, are the Tridentine anathemas, and other merely human and carnal judgments. Stapleton is therefore mistaken when he says that pastors and Bishops are simply to be obeyed, and not to be judged, if they have been legitimately called. For although those who are sound in doctrine, even if depraved in morals, are to be heard, nevertheless one must test the spirits to see whether they are from God, 1 John 4:1.

PART II. Dehortation from elation.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὥστε μὴ πρὸ καιρᾶ τι κρίνετε. Hoc maximè adversus eos torquet, qui cum Christi & Petri discipulos se dicerent, Paulum accusabant tanquam inimicum Judaicæ gentis: Quam culpam magno ubique studio à se amolitur Paulus. Id verò nullo apparet indicio, quod talem apo- logiam hic instituat Paulus, ne videatur Judaicæ gentis inimicus. Reprobavit in genere judicia Corinthiorum de sese, tum ob futilitatem, quia vana & humana vel carnalia sint; tum ob temerita- tem, quia ne quidem ipse, qui rectius se novit, quàm alii, sese judicare ausit in factis suis, coram Deo, etsi coram hominibus ita sese gesserit, ut bonam, teste Deo, habeat conscientiam: tum ob impietatem, quod partes judicandi Deo compe- tentes sacrilegè sibi sumant, & in tribunali judicii divini sese collocent, ac judicium divinum, quod sibi in die pantocritico reservavit, anticipent; quia judicis injuria est, si ante judicium ejus à servo pro- cedat sententia.

Ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ Κύριος, ὃς καὶ φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆ σκό- τους, καὶ φανερώσει τὰς βελὰς τῶν καρδιῶν. Tuto quidem damnari potest pro statu præsenti, qui fla- gitiose vivit. Manifesta enim sunt opera carnis. At acti- bus per se bonis aut mediis malum animum adscribere con- tra dilectionis est regulam. Christo Judici relinquenda ista arcana: Τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆ σκότους מְגַלֶּה־עֲמֻקּוֹת מִנִּי־חשֶׁךְ Job. XII. 22. quod prius obscure dixerat φωτίσει τὰ κρυπτὰ, id per ἐξάγουσι explicat תעלמות לב τὰς βυλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν τὰ κρύφια τῆς καρδίας dicto Pf. XLIV. 22. Hæc enim nosse solius Dei & Christi est, Act. I. 24. XV. 8. φωτίσει hic est in lucem protrahet. κὰι τότε ἔπαινος γενήσεται ἑκάστῳ ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ. Nempe si bona egerit bono animo: Unde & contrarium datur intelligi: Sed mavult ἐυφημεῖν.

Per occulta tenebrarum alii hypocrisin occultam intelligunt; alii intentiones abditas, quas à consiliis cordium, hoc est, decretis sententiis ac judiciis discernunt. Sed generatim occulta tenebrarum, à glossa ordinaria de peccatis, quæ tenebras amant, & in abscondito fiunt, Joh. III. explicantur. Nec illa tantum illustraturus est Deus, quæ jam patrata sunt, & actu commissa in occulto: Sed etiam ipsa cordium consilia, intentiones, cogitationes, desideria, decreta, voluptates, affectus, odium, iram, & similia, quæ nemo novit, nisi spiritus hominis, qui in homine est. Alii adhuc generalius interpretantur, quia ἔπαινος non convenit operibus tenebrarum, (quam vocem temere & ἄτερ γραφῆς Heinsius supplicia & opprobrium notare monet:) de cogitationibus & consiliis cordium occultis, quæ hic nobis meræ tenebræ sunt, & à nobis dignosci nequeunt, olim in aperta luce, vel solis, quod ajunt, disco ponendis atque exponendis. Q. d. Vos nunc, ô Corinthii, tanquam agnonothetæ temerè coronatis alios, alios cum ignominia dimittitis. Erit autem dies, quo Christus, cui hoc unicè competit, ceu cordium scrutatori, palam faciet, quinam laude & coronâ digni. Cæterum per hanc doctrinam Apostolicam nequaquam constituuntur Doctores verbi ἀνυπεύθυνοι, vel omni eximuntur censuræ. Nam nec ipse Paulus refugit judicium Ecclesiæ de doctrina sua, 2. Corinth. X. 15. judicate vos ipsi, quod dico. Sed temeraria tantum judicia reprobantur, quibus si iniquè premantur sinceri Doctores, meritò ea contemnunt, ac pro minimo habent, judicari ab humano die, qualia, exempli gratiâ, sunt anathemata Tridentina, & alia merè humana, & carnalia judicia. Fallitur ergò Stapletonus, cum ait, pastoribus & Episcopis simpliciter esse obediendum, non verò eos judicandos, si legitimè vocati sint. Nam quamvis audiendi sint, qui doctrina sani sunt, licet moribus pravi, Spiritus tamen probare oportet num ex Deo sint, 1. Joh. IV. 1.

PARS II. Debortatio ab elatione.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. Ταῦτα δὲ ἀδελφοὶ μετεσχημάτισα εἰς ἐμαυτὸν κὰι Ἀπολλῶ δι ὑμᾶς. The Syrian rightly translates: I have proposed these things in my own person, and Apollo's. Because these teachers of yours abuse my name and Apollo's also, in our person I showed them how modestly they ought to judge concerning themselves and others, and how much care they ought to have for you and for peace. Μετασχηματίζειν properly is to change one's habit, as can be seen in 1 Sam. 28:8. Thence it is transferred to speech, which seems to say one thing but hints at another: which kind of locutions are wont to be called by the Greeks λόγοι ἐσχηματισμένοι, which Quintilian 9.11 called figured controversies, and Suetonius called figures in Vespasian and Domitian: Jerome Epist. 66 to Rufinus. Philostratus on Herodes Atticus: Σχηματίσας τὸν λόγον. Chrysostom, dealing with this passage in his sermon on not divulging sins: συνεσκίασε τὴν κατηγορίαν. Concerning the accusative Ἀπολλῶ, see what we have said on Acts 19:1.

Most of the ancients understand that μετασχηματισμὸν as a fiction, by which the Apostle transferred the ambition of false teachers onto himself and Apollo, either because he considered them unworthy to be named, or so as to affect or move them less. But the Apostle had said nothing about false teachers before, nor does any reason for such a fiction appear. Nor do ταῦτα fit, such as that they are ministers, that they are stewards, and other things which Paul had said about himself and Apollo: I planted, Apollo watered, to the false teachers. However, he uses the word μετεσχημάτισα, not so much because he spoke figuratively, as because he figured in his own person and Apollo's things which befit all ministers, but not false teachers. For when we figure in our own person specifically, or transfer to ourselves things which are common to others, this word is rightly employed. It is one thing when this word is transferred to speech, which is not the case here, where μετασχηματισμὸς is of the person, not by way of fiction, but by way of figuration: These things I have transfigured into myself and Apollo for your sake: So that you may feel that I and Apollo are nothing else than ministers, and that we do not justify ourselves by our own integrity and innocence, so that you may not establish that even we, who planted and watered there, let alone others, are anything in respect to God, who gave the increase, and that you may learn true humility from our example. So also our blessed Hunnius, Paræus, and others: and also Crellius among the Socinians: Paul uses the word μετεσχημάτισα to show that he has used a certain manner and figure of speaking when he introduced himself and Apollo: Namely, because he wanted to teach not only what they ought to think about himself and Apollo; but something further, namely, what ought to be thought about all other teachers: Therefore he names himself and Apollo, but besides himself and Apollo he also understands others: which he who does, uses a certain form and figure of speech. Schlichtingius also well, page 16: I have transfigured into myself and Apollo, that is, I have proposed to you in my own and Apollo's person, I have not spoken in general, which I could have done. For your sake, that is, on your account. So that in us, that is, in our example, who seem to you to be such great men, of such dignity, that you make names for yourselves from us and are split into factions: You may learn not to think above what is written, namely in the preceding chapter 3:5 and following, and in this very chapter verse 1. Namely, whether concerning yourselves, or concerning any other teacher in the Church of Christ, even concerning Peter himself: So that one may not be puffed up for one against another, that is, one for another, namely one for the praise and glory of another: that is, by a metonymy of the cause, that you may not contend in studies and factions against another, which proceeds from a vain swelling of the mind, desiring to stand out above the rest. For those who contend in studies and factions for the glory of another, they themselves privately sail for their own glory; they seek another's praise in appearance, but in reality they are grasping for their own.

That in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written. That in our person, in those things which I wrote concerning myself and Apollos, you may learn not to adopt other sentiments than such as God requires in scripture. Γέγραπται in these books always refers to the books of the Old Testament.

That you may not be puffed up one for one against another. It seems it should have been written φυσιοῖσθε. That you may not be arrogant one against another for this or that teacher. By these words he shows that, when he said γέγραπται, he had regard to some place of scripture, not word for word, but in sense. That place is Deut. 17, 20. For if it is commanded to a King not to exalt himself haughtily above others, how much more to others. It is common to all nations to say to inflate for to be arrogant: Hence an inflated man in Cicero. To inflate a wineskin, in the Satire, to make proud. Thus to bear great spirits is to be arrogant. Chrysostom aptly to this place: For one part does not become higher than another, except when a swelling occurs. Then: he who is inflamed, this is the one who is sick.

That some place of the Old Testament is regarded is not sufficiently clear, much less that one about the King; since in general those things which occur in scripture concerning modesty and humility can be regarded, namely that we should not be wise beyond what is fitting. Just as some [regard] those things which Solomon has concerning humility Prov. 11, 2. c. 29, 25. others, who wish for what occurs in the Gospel, Mark X. 44, Luke XVIII. 14. Others wish for what was written above in ch. III. 21 to be looked at. For what kind of warning is Rom. XII. 3? But perhaps this can be understood as if we were warned that no one should presume to be wise about divine matters beyond what God has revealed in the scriptures; since the Apostle himself protested that he had said nothing outside of what was written in Moses and the Prophets, Acts XXV. 22. Which was Beza's interpretation: he opens the ulcer: For whence these evils, except that they did not contain themselves within the measure prescribed by the word of God? Yet the explanation of the blessed Luther seems simpler, that no one should think more highly of himself than is now written. To this also goes the paraphrase of the blessed Hunnius: What I warned, that you should not contend about me and Apollos, and at the same time I preached our humility, I indeed conferred that upon us through a figure of translation or κοινοποίησις, but let it be commended to you as an example, so that you Corinthians, and especially you teachers in that Church, may learn from our example, that no one should think more ambitiously of himself than what has been written by us, lest from this root of evils those harmful and factious contentions be born. Beza also worried about the word Φυσιοῦσθαι, and Erasmus before him, as did Grotius here. But Erasmus Schmid rightly warns that the indicative is put for the subjunctive, observing similar things from Budaeus, who also rightly noted Camerarius in this place, as if for one to be puffed up above another is the same as against another, unless it is believed that ὑπὲρ τῦ ἑνός is neuter, so that it is ὑπὲρ τῦ ἑνός πράγματος, so that indeed one is puffed up about that matter against another. For there are three persons here, which was also observed by Erasmus: He who is puffed up, suppose one of the Corinthians; He for whom he is puffed up, such as Paul, Apollos, or Cephas; And he against whom he is puffed up in the assembly of the Corinthians, that is, swelling with the persuasion of wisdom and dexterity of judgment, he carries himself and exalts himself against another, while he extols this teacher above another, as if he possessed a singular prudence in judging divine gifts, and therefore he also excites contentions and quarrels and schisms. The metaphor is taken from swollen bladders, which nevertheless are accustomed to subside suddenly with a single prick of a needle. Chrysostom deduces it from a phlegmon, an inflammation, through which an ὄιδημα or tumor is made. For what is puffed up has a tumor of spirit, filled with corrupt humor. Others say the metaphor is taken from toads, because Φύσαλος signifies a toad. A toad is puffed up with poison, which is most harmful, and therefore it is avoided with great prudence, as here the blessed Weinrich.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ταῦτα δὲ ἀδελφοὶ μετεσχημάτισα εἰς ἐμαυτὸν κὰι Ἀπολλῶ δι ὑμᾶς. Rectè Syrus vertit: Proposui hæc in persona mea, & Apollo. Quia hi vestri doctores meo etiam & Apollo nomine abutuntur, in nostra persona ipsis ostendi, quàm modestè de se ac de aliis judicare debeant, quantamque curam gerere vestri & pacis. Μετασχηματίζειν propriè est mutare habitum, ut videre est 1. Sam. XXVIII. 8. Inde transfertur ad orationem, quæ aliud videtur dicere, aliud innuit: Cujusmodi locutiones à Græcis vocari solent λόγοι ἐσχηματισμένοι, quas controversias figuratas dixit Quintilianus IX. 11. & figuras Suetonius Vespasiano & Domitiano: Hieronymus Epist. LXVI. ad Rufinum. Philostratus de Herode Attico: Σχηματίσας τὸν λόγον. Chrysostomus de hoc loco agens in sermone de non vulgandis peccatis: συνεσκίασε τὴν κατηγορίαν. De Accusativo Ἀπολλῶ vide, quæ diximus ad Act. XIX. 1.

PLerique veteres illum μετασχηματισμὸν de fictione intelligunt, qua Apostolus ambitionem falsorum Doctorum in se, & Apollo transtulerit, seu quod indignos existimaret, quos nominaret, seu ut minus eos afficeret, aut commoveret. Sed de falsis Doctoribus nihil antea Apostolus, nec ulla ratio apparet ejusmodi fictionis. Neque con- veniunt ταῦτα, utpote quod ministri sint, quod oeconomi, & quæ alia de se, & Apollo dixerat Pau- lus: Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit, falsis Doctori- bus. Voce autem μετεσχημάτισα utitur, non tam, quod figuratè loquutus sit, quam quod in suâ per- sonâ & Apollo figurarit, quæ omnibus ministris, non verò Doctoribus falsis conveniunt. Nam cum in nostra persona peculiariter figuramus, vel in nos transferimus, quæ aliis communia sunt, rectè hoc verbum adhibetur. Aliud est, cum hoc ver- bum ad orationem transfertur, quod hic non sit, ubi μετασχηματισμὸς est personæ, non per fictio- nis, sed per figurationis modum: Hæc transfiguravi in me & Apollo propter vos: Ut cum me & Apollo nihil aliud esse, quam ministros, nosque haud ju- stificare nosmetipsos ex integritate & innocentia nostra sentiatis, ne nos quidem, qui plantavimus & rigavimus illic, nedum alios quicquam esse re- spectu Dei, qui incrementum dedit, statuatis, no- stroque exemplo veram humilitatem addiscatis. Sic etiam B. Hunnius noster, Paræus & alii: nec non è Socinianis Crellius: Utitur Paulus verbo μετεσχημάτισα, ut ostendat, se modo ac figura qua- dam loquendi usum esse, cum se & Apollo induxit: Nempe quia non id tantum, quid de se & Apollo sentire debeant, docere voluit; sed quiddam am- plius, quid videlicet de omnibus aliis Doctoribus sentiendum sit: Itaque se quidem & Apollo nomi- nat, sed præter se & Apollo etiam alios intelligit: quod qui facit, certa quadam dicendi forma & fi- gura utitur. Bene etiam Schlichtingius pag. 16. Transfiguravi in me ipsum & Apollo, id est, in mea ipsius & Apollo persona vobis proposui, non in genere loquutus sum, quod poteram. Propter vos, id est, vestri causa. Ut in nobis, id est, in exemplo nostro, qui vobis tanti viri, tantæ digni- tatis videmur, ut à nobis nomina vobis faciatis & in partes scindamini: Discatis non supra, quam scriptum est, in superioribus videl. cap. III. 5. & seqq. & hoc ipso capite vers. 1. sentire. Nempe si- ve de vobis ipsis, sive de ullo alio in Ecclesia Chri- sti Doctore, etiam de Petro ipso: Ut non unus pro uno, id est, alter pro altero, alter videlicet pro al- terius laude & gloria: Inflemini adversus alte- rum, id est, per Metonymiam causæ, adversus al- terum studiis & factionibus certetis, quod ex va- no animi tumore, supra cæteros eminere volentis, proficiscitur. Nam qui pro alterius gloria, stu- diis & factionibus certant, & ipsi privatim suæ glo- riæ in eo velificantur; alienam in speciem laudem quærunt, revera captant suam.

Ἵνα ἐν ὑμῖν μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν. Ut in nostra persona in iis, quæ de me & Apollo scripsi, discatis, non alios sumere affectus, quam quales Deus in scriptura exigit. Γέγραπται in his libris semper ad libros Veteris Testamenti refertur.

Ἵνα μὴ εἷς ὑπὲρ ἑνὸς φυσιοῦσθε κατὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου. Videtur scriptum fuisse φυσιοῖσθε. Ne superbietis alter contra alterum pro hoc vel illo doctore. His verbis osten- dit se, cum dixit γέγραπται, locum aliquem respexisse scri- pturæ non verbotenus, sed sensu. Is locus est Deut. 17, 20. Nam si Regi præceptum, ne se supra alios efferat fastuosè, quanto magis aliis. Commune est omnibus gentibus, ut inflare dicant pro superbire: Hinc homo inflatus apud Ci- ceronem. Inflare utrem, in Satyra, superbum facere. Sic spiritus magnos gerere, est superbire. Chrysostomus ap- positè ad hunc locum: Ἄλλως γὰρ οὐ γίνεται ὑψηλότερον ἕτε- ρον ἑτέρου μέρος, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ὅταν οἴδημα γένηται. Deinde: ὁ φλεγμαίνων, οὗτος ὁ νοσῶν.

Locum aliquem respici Vet. Testam. non satis liquet, nedum illum de Rege; Cum in genere respici possint ea, quæ de modestia & humilitate in scriptura occurrunt dicta, ne scilicet ultra sapia- mus, quam oportet. Quomodo nonnulli ea, quæ Salomo habet de humilitate Prov. 11, 2. c. 29, 25. alii, quæ in Evangelio occurrunt Marc. X. 44. Luc. XVIII. 14. Alii quod supra scriptum c. III. 21. respici volunt. Qualis enim monitio Rom. XII. 3. Sed intelligi hoc forsan ita poterit, quasi moneamur, ne quis de rebus divinis sapere præsumat super ea, quæ Deus in scripturis revelavit; Siquidem Apostolus ipse protestatus sit, se nihil dixisse extra ea, quæ scripta sint in Mose & Prophetis, Act. XXV. 22. Quæ Bezæ fuit interpretatio: ulcus aperit: Unde enim hæc mala, nisi quod intra modum à verbo Dei præscriptum sese non continebant? Simplicior tamen B. Lutheri videtur explicatio, daß niemand höher von sich halte, denn ietzt geschrieben ist. Quo etiam abit B. Hunnii paraphrasis: Quod monui, ne de me & Apollo contenderetis, simulque nostram humilitatem prædicavi, id per figuram translationis sive κοινοποιήσεως in nos quidem contuli, vobis autem id exempli vice commendatum esto, ut vos Corinthii, & maximè vos in ea Ecclesia doctores ab exemplo nostro discatis, ne quis supra id, quod scriptum à nobis est, de se sentiat ambitiosius, ne ex hac radice malorum nascantur infesta illa & factiosa contentiones. Verbū Φυσιοῦσθαι solicitavit etiam Beza, & ante eum Erasmus, uti hic Grotius. Sed rectè Erasmus Schmidius monet, Indicativum pro Conjunctivo poni, similia observans è Budæo, qui etiam Camerarium meritò hoc loco notavit, quasi inflari unum supra alterum idem sit, quod contra alterum, nisi ὑπὲρ τῦ ἑνός neutrum esse creditur, ut sit ὑπὲρ τῦ ἑνός πράγματος, ut nempe de illa re infletur contra alterum. Nam tres hic sunt personæ, quod etiam observatum Erasmo: Ejus, qui inflatur, puta alicujus è Corinthiis; Ejus, pro quo inflatur, utpote Pauli, Apollo, vel Cephæ; Et ejus, adversus quem in cœtu Corinthiorum inflatur, id est, persuasione sapientiæ & dexteritatis judicandi turgens sese effert, & extollit adversus alium, dum hunc doctorem præ alio extollit, quasi singulari polleat de donis divinis censendi prudentia, ideo etiam contentiones & rixas ac schismata excitat. Metaphora petita est à vesicis turgidis, quæ tamen unico ictu acus læfæ subitò detumere solent. Chrysostomus à phlegmone, inflammatione, per quam ὄιδημα seu tumor fit, deducit. Nam quod est inflatum, habet tumorem spiritus, repletum humore corrupto. Alii à bufonibus metaphoram petitam dicunt, quia Φύσαλος bufonem significat. Bufo veneno inflatur, quod maximè noxium est, ideo magna prudentia devitatur, ut hic B. Weinrichius.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. For who makes you differ.

He first touches those whom the people admired so much for their extraordinary gifts that they vied with each other in dedicating themselves to them. Which, when they ought to have hindered, they did not hinder, pleasing themselves in it. God makes the difference, when he gives more to this one, less to another. Hence the discernings of spirits below in XII. 10. You have this sense treated at length at the beginning of book VIII of the constitutions, which are called Clement's.

And what do you have that you did not receive.

In every matter, the honor belongs to the giver, not to the receiver. Moreover, they are and are rightly called gifts of grace. Even if you had Apostolic gifts, (but that is far from the case) yet the very name of the gifts ought to have made you modest. God gave them for his own uses, not for yours.

But if you also received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

Why do you please yourself in it, as if you had acquired it for yourself by your own labor? He touches the teachers most of all.

Thus also some others think these things are said against the teachers who were the cause of the schism. Theophylact, with Chrysostom leading the way: He inveighs again against the teachers of the Corinthians, saying, who makes you differ, and judged you worthy of praise? Or is it man? But human judgment is deceived. Let it be granted that there is something praiseworthy in you, yet I would by no means say that it is yours, but granted by the gift of God. And you did not receive that by any merit or duty of your own. If therefore you received it, why do you boast, and swell up boastfully, as if you had received nothing, and believe rather that you produced it from yourself and your own labors? Nor does it befit anyone to become insolent in those things which he has received, since they are foreign, and brought together by others, not produced by himself. Whom our blessed Hunnius followed, as did the blessed Weinrich. But no indication of a change of persons appears. For he addresses the same ones whom he reproves because they say some are of Paul, others of Apollos: And when they, puffed up with wisdom, arrogated judgment to themselves, he recalls them to humility: Supposing as it were that they possessed the faculty of judging above others, just as they seemed to themselves to be wise above others, and one carried himself against another. Whence neither does the sense of Erasmus deserve assent, as if he were disputing against those who preferred themselves to others because they had been baptized by the principal Apostles. Nor the interpretation of Beza: Who makes you differ, that is, separates, or exempts from the flock of colleagues, as if you were something else in the Church than your colleagues in the same function. For he was in a way expunging the other pastors, who carried himself against them, so that he alone might stand out. Therefore Pareus deserted Beza, warning that this apostrophe is not directed to false teachers (as some think) but to the puffed-up Corinthians generally. So also the blessed Balduinus, and not least the blessed Hülsemann; who also notes: the subjects distinguished from one another are not viewed here as the elect and the reprobate, but as disciples of different masters, who nevertheless were all striving for eternal life, all believed to be satisfied, enriched, and to have already attained the kingdom, certainly they were presumptively already in a state of grace, verse 10, 11, they were all beloved children, v. 14, all begotten through the Gospel, verse 15, and so these things can only be applied by a certain analogy to the discretion of the faithful from the unfaithful, the elect from the reprobate, by Augustine throughout Tom. VII. lib. 1. de praedest. sanct. cap. 6. l. 1. de Peccator. Merit. & Remiss. c. 18. by the blessed Chemnitz, and others. But if God alone gratuitously makes us differ; if all things which we have, we have from his grace, and have received freely from him, there can be no place for our merits or works, by which God would be moved to choose us over others. And this even most of the Papists acknowledge, namely that whatever makes for salvation is referred by the Apostle among things received through grace: What hast thou that thou didst not receive? By nature there is no difference; who made thee to differ? See Suarez, lib. 11 de concursu Dei cum natura cap. 2. Franc. Zumel, Tom. II in Thomam disc. V. Sect. I. concl. 4. & 5. Alvarez de auxiliis gratis disp. IV. IX. LXII. &c. Who are therefore sounder than the Arminians, and among these Corvinus against Molin. cap. 36, against Tilen. pag. 136, contending that a certain natural faculty is in man, by which he may at least occasionally distinguish himself from the reprobate, by doing what is in him.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Τίς γάρ σε διακρίνει.

Eos primum attingit, quos plebs ita ob eximia dona admirabatur, ut eis se certatim addiceret. Quod illi cum impedire debuissent, non impediebant, sibi in eo placentes. Discernit Deus, cum huic plus dat, alii minus. Hinc διακρίσεις πνευμάτων infra XII. 10. Habes hunc sensum fusè tractatum initio lib. VIII. constitutionum, quæ dicuntur Clementis.

Τί δὲ ἔχεις, ὃ ὐκ ἔλαβες.

In omni re honos penes dantem, non penes accipientem. Sunt autem & merito dicuntur χαρίσματα. Etiamsi dona haberetis Apostolica, (multum autem id abest) tamen ipsorum donorum nomen, modestos vos facere debuit. Deus dedit in suos usus, non in tuos.

Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἔλαβες, τί καυχᾶσαι ὡς μὴ λαβών;

Quid in eo tibi places, tanquam tuo labore tibi parasses? Doctores maxime tangit.

Sic etiam alii nonnulli censent hæc adversus doctores dici, qui schismatis causa fuerint. Theophylactus, præeunte Chrysostomo: Rursum in Corinthiorum doctores invehitur, inquiens, quis te discernit, & dignum laude judicavit? an num homo? At fallitur humanum judicium. Concedatur, ut in te sit aliquid laudabile, id tamen haud qua- quam dixerim tuum esse, sed Dei dono concessum. Idque non tuo aliquo vel merito, vel officio accepisti. Si itaque accepisti, quid gloriaris, & jactabundus intumescis, quasi nihil acceperis, & credis potius, ex te illud, & propriis laboribus peperisse? Non etiam quempiam decet, ut in his, quæ acceperit, insolescat, quippe quæ aliena sunt, & ab aliis collata, non per se parta. Quos sequutus est B. Hunnius noster, ut & B. Weinrichius. At nullum apparet variatio- nis personarum indicium. Eosdem enim, quos reprehendit, quod dicant se alii Pauli, alii Apol- lo, compellat: Et cum inflati sapientia, judicium sibi arrogarint, ad humilitatem eosdem revocat: Ponens veluti, præ aliis eos judicandi facultate pollere, ut sibi præ aliis sapere videbantur, & al- ter adversus alterum sese efferebat. Unde nec Erasmi sensus assensum meretur, quasi disputet adversus illos, qui se cæteris præferebant, quod essent à præcipuis Apostolis baptizati. Nec Bezæ inter- pretatio: Quis te διακρίνει, id est, segregat, aut eximit à collegarum grege, quasi sis tu quodpiam aliud in Ecclesia, quam tui in eadem functione col- lega. Expungebat enim quodammodo cæteros pa- stores, qui sese adversus eos efferebat, ut solus emi- neret. Ideo Bezam deseruit Pareus monens, hanc apostrophen non ad falsos doctores, (ut aliqui pu- tant) sed ad inflatos Corinthios generatim esse dire- ctam. Ita & B. Balduinus, nec non B. Hülseman- nus; Qui etiam notat: subjecta ab invicem discre- ta non spectari hic tanquam electos & reprobos, sed tanquam diversorum magistrorum discipulos, qui tamen omnes ad vitam æternam contendebant, omnes saturati, ditati, & regnum jam adepti crede- bantur, certè præsumptivè jam in statu gratiæ erant, vers. 10. 11. filii dilecti omnes erant, v. 14. omnes ge- niti per Evangelium, vers. 15. adeoque hæc nonnisi per analogiam quandam applicari ad discretionem fidelis ab infideli, electi à reprobo, ab Augustino passim Tom. VII. lib. 1. de prædest. sanct. cap. 6. l. 1. de Peccator. Merit. & Remiss. c. 18. B. Chemnitio, & aliis. Quod si solus Deus nos gratuito discer- nit; Si omnia, quæ habemus, ex ipsius habemus gratia, & ab ipso gratis accepimus, nullus esse po- test locus meritis vel operibus nostris, quibus nos præ aliis eligendos Deus moveretur. Atque hoc agnoscunt etiam plerique Pontificiorum, nimirum quicquid ad salutem facit, ab Apostolo referri in- ter accepta per gratiam: Quid habes, quod non ac- cepisti? Per naturam nullum est discrimen; quis te discrevit? Vid. Suarez. lib. 11. de concursu Dei cum natura cap. 2. Franc. Zumel. Tom. II. in Tho- mam disc. V. Sect. I. concl. 4. & 5. Alvarez de au- xiliis gratis disp. IV. IX. LXII. &c. Qui proinde saniores sunt Arminianis, & inter hos Corvino con- tra Molin. cap. 36. contra Tilen. pag. 136. conten- dentibus, naturalem quandam facultatem inesse ho- mini, qua se occasionaliter saltem discernat à repro- bis, faciendo quod in se est.

## 4:8
Vers. 8. Ἤδη κεκορεσμένοι ἐστέ.

A long and grave irony, as I see you think, there remains nothing for you to seek, no more than for those who have become full from a feast.

Ἤδη ἐπλουτήσατε.

You have obtained, that is, such an abundance of gifts that you surpass any other Apostles as well. You speak like Ephraim, Hos. XII. 19. Πεπλούτηκα, εὕρηκα, ἀναψυχὴν ἐμαυτῷ.

Χωρὶς ἡμῶν ἐβασιλεύσατε.

From the time I have been away from you, you have been in safety, like Kings whom no one can harm. You speak like Babylon, Isaiah XLVII. 7. 8.

καὶ ὄφελόν γε ἐβασιλεύσατε.

I do not indeed envy you: I wonder more.

ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεν.

If your affairs were thus in tranquility and out of danger, it would be a safe refuge for me.

This is to be understood of that satiety and abundance of heavenly goods, which they had persuaded themselves they possessed solely from the instruction of their Rabbis. Therefore he adds 'without us,' to note their ingratitude, because they glory that they had attained those things without the Apostles and true teachers, e.g., Paul and Sosthenes, through whom, however, the Corinthians had been enriched with all knowledge and all speech, 1 Cor. 1, and the greatest pride, as if they no longer even needed the work of the Apostles. Moreover, the discourse grows in this irony; to be rich is more than to be satiated, and to reign is more than to be rich. A similar boasting was that of the Bishop of Laodicea, of whom Apoc. 3:17. But the kingdom is understood not so much of glory—for this would have been too great a folly if the Corinthians had boasted that they were already living in it—as of grace, because they were already ruling over the whole world and sin, not only satiated fully with the delights of all knowledge and enriched with any treasures of grace, but also reigning over spiritual enemies with great power. Moreover, the consequence of that: 'And I would to God that you did reign, that we also might reign with you,' seems to be the nerve of it: That if the Corinthians, converted to the faith by the Apostles and enriched with knowledge of every kind, were already reigning, the Apostles, as their teachers θεοπνεύστως, who are ruled by the immediate impulse of the Holy Spirit, and their spiritual fathers—not common ones, but the first and principal ones in the Church, appointed by Christ to propagate and govern the whole Church—would be reigning much more already.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἤδη κεκορεσμένοι ἐστέ.

Ironia longa & gravis, ut vos existimare video, nihil re- stat vobis expetendum, non magis, quam iis, qui de epulis facti sunt saturi.

Ἤδη ἐπλουτήσατε.

Tantam scil. copiam donorum consecuti estis, ut quosvis alios etiam Apostolos vincatis. Loquimini ut Ephraim Os. XII. 19. Πεπλούτηκα, εὕρηκα, ἀναψυχὴν ἐμαυτῷ.

Χωρὶς ἡμῶν ἐβασιλεύσατε.

Ex quo ego à vobis absum, vos in tuto estis, sicut Re- ges, quibus nemo potest nocere. Loquimini ut Babylon, Esaix XLVII. 7. 8.

καὶ ὄφελόν γε ἐβασιλεύσατε.

Non equidem invideo: Miror magis.

ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεν.

Si ita in tranquillo essent, & extra periculum res vestræ, tutum mihi esset eò confugium.

Accipienda haec de illa saturitate, & abundan- tia caelestium bonorum, quam ex suorum Rabbi- norum informatione unicè sese habere persuasi erant. Ideo addit sine nobis, ut notet ingratitudi- nem eorum, quod illa sine Apostolis verisque do- ctoribus, e. g. Paulo, & Sosthene consecutos esse glorientur, per quos tamen ditati erant Corinthii omni cognitione omniq; sermone, 1. Cor. I. summam- que superbiam, quasi ne Apostoli quidem amplius egeant operâ. Crescit autem oratio in hac ironia, divitem esse plus est, quam saturatum esse, & regna- re plus est, quam divitem esse. Similis gloriatio erat Episcopi Laodicensis, de quo Apoc. III. 17. Regnum autem non tam gloriae intelligitur; haec enim ni- mia fuisset stultitia, si in eo sese jam versari Corin- thii gloriati essent; quàm gratiae, quod jam super universum mundum & peccatum dominarentur, non tantum saturati plene delitiis omnis cognitio- nis & ditati thesauris quibusvis gratiae, sed regna- rent etiam super hostes spirituales magna potesta- te. Consequentiae autem illius: Atque utinam regnaretis, ut & nos vobiscum regnaremus, nervus ille videtur: Quod si Corinthii ab Apostolis ad fi- dem conversi, & omnis generis cognitione ditati jam regnarent, Apostolos ceu magistros ipsorum θεοπνεύστως, qui immediato Spiritus S. nutu regun- tur & patres eorum spirituales, non vulgares, sed primos & principales in Ecclesia à Christo propa- gandae & gubernandae universae Ecclesiae praefe- ctos, multo magis jam regnaturos.

## 4:9
Vers. 9. For I think that God has set forth us the Apostles last, as it were appointed to death. 'Ὅτι' is missing in the Manuscript. 'Δοκῶ,' as is often the case among the Latins, is 'credo' [I believe], and is ironical; if God's favor is gathered from prosperous things, as you seem to think, we Apostles will have been placed by God in the lowest place, like those who fight with beasts. For thus Tertullian translates this passage in his book 'De Pudicitia': 'And I think God has chosen us Apostles last, as it were bestiarii.' Below all men was the lot of those condemned to the beasts, who are here called κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence] 'appointed to death.' To the Hebrews this would be בני מות. 'Ἀπέδειξεν' [set forth] means 'constituted,' which Tertullian translates 'chose,' is מנה.

Rightly the word 'last' is ascribed to the predicates rather than the subject. And therefore there is no reason for interpreters to torture themselves as to how Paul calls himself the last of the Apostles, since he professes that he is placed in the lowest place not regarding the Apostleship, but regarding his miserable lot and state. Therefore that word is not to be compared with the Apostleship. Thus Schlichting's gloss is to be rejected: 'Us the Apostles last, that is, me who am last in respect of Peter and the other Apostles, since I was called to the Apostolic office after all.' For he is not speaking of himself alone. Regarding the word 'appointed to death,' Camerarius reports diverse but inconvenient expositions: Just as this name was made in a singular manner, so also others have interpreted it differently, and it is indicated that some referred it to the death of Christ, after the office and function of the Apostles was usurped, and that Paul counted himself with others. Or it will be a metaphor, says another, so that it is understood that no further Apostles are to be expected, but that those are the last and inviolable. Just as 'appointed to death' [ἐπιθανάτιοι] are 'sure' or 'unmovable' covenants. Others interpreted 'appointed to death' more simply as 'subject to death.' Which explanation approaches the word more than that which is added from Tertullian. For that one is more special: but this one is general, since it does not express the species of death, but only brings in death in general.

For we have been made a spectacle to the world, and to Angels, and to men. He insists on the simile begun; and he said 'spectacle' [θέατρον] for those who are watched, just as those who are heard are called 'audience' [ἀκρόαμα]. Not unlike this, to be in a theater according to Cicero is to be watched by all. It is a usage of the container for the contained. Properly, an amphitheater was called the place in which one fought with beasts: But an amphitheater is also a species of theater, consisting of two as it were concurrent theaters. Job said of himself תפת לפנים XVII. 6. The Greeks translate that: 'laughter has come upon them.' When Paul had introduced the world as a spectator of the Apostolic struggle, he added 'and to Angels and to men,' where that first 'world' is put for, that is, for the world, this is, he distributes the most powerful 'intellectual things' of the world into Angels and men: the Hebrews call that the upper and lower family.

Camerarius brings forward yet another interpretation, yet he prefers this one, which makes for exaggerating the unhappy lot of the Apostle: Of which there is properly talk here: Chrysostom, he says, interprets 'We have been made a spectacle to the world, or to the Angels,' not that the deed was done in some corner, but that the constancy of the Apostles in enduring adversities was already watched by the world, and that the struggles were worthy of Angelic contemplation. Others preferred 'spectacle' in this place to signify the sad show of mockery and affliction of Christians in this world, before men and Angels. Which certainly do not seem to abhor from those things which follow. Therefore Paul says this: that the Apostles are the last, or men of extreme lot, such as those are whom a judge has already adjudged to death. For God, when He was about to make a spectacle to the world, brought forth the Apostles, whose misery both Angels and men watch with admiration, not otherwise than once the miserable in theatrical spectacles, exposed to lions, bears, and other beasts, moved some to laughter, others to commiseration; Thus those faithful ministers of the churches, exposed to the lust of tyrants and the mockery of the world, excite laughter among many among men, but certainly commiseration among good Angels, and men who are pious and imitate their nature; as Baldwin has it here. He seems to speak of evil Angels, because in this theater we have a struggle with evil spirits. To some, however, it pleases to understand it of good ones, because they are spectators of the struggle, and witnesses of our constancy, over which they themselves also rejoice.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Δοκῶ γὰρ ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ἡμᾶς τοὺς Ἀποστόλους τοὺς ἐσχάτους ἀπέδειξεν, ὡς ἐπιθανατίους. Ὅτι deest in Manuscripto. Δοκῶ ut saepe apud Latinos credo est εἰρωνικὸν, si ex rebus secundis, ut vos videmini existimare, colligitur Dei favor, nos Apostoli à Deo collo- cati erimus infimo loco, tanquam bestiarii. Sic enim Ter- tullianus hunc locum transfert libro de pudicitia: Et puto, nos Deus Apostolos novissimos elegit veluti bestiarios. Infra omnes homines fors erat damnatorum ad bestias, qui hic κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicuntur ἐπιθανάτιοι. Id Hebraeis esset בני מות Ἀπέδειξεν constituit, quod Tertullianus vertit, elegit, est מנה.

Rectè vox ἐσχάτους praedicatis potius adscribi- tur, quàm subjecto. Ideoque non est, quod se tor- queant interpretes, quomodo se Paulus Aposto- lorum ultimum dicat, cum infimo loco se non quoad Apostolatum, sed quoad miserabilem sortem & statum collocatum esse, profiteatur. Non ergò cum Apostolata vox illa componenda est. Repro- banda itaq; Schlichtingii glossa: Nos Apostolus ul- timos, id est, me qui Petri & Apostolorum caeterorum respectu sum ultimus, quippe post omnes ad Apostoli- cum munus vocatus. Non enim de se solo loqui- tur. De voce ἐπιθανατίους diversas sed inconve- nientes expositiones refert Camerarius: Quem- admodum hoc nomen singularem in modum factum est; ita etiam alii aliter fuerunt interpretati, ac in- dicatur aliquos ad mortem Christi retulisse, post- quam Apostolorum munus & functio usurpata sit, & se numerare Paulum cum aliis. Vel Metaphora erit, inquit alius, ut intelligatur, nullos praeterea Aposto- los jam expectandos, sed illos esse ultimos & inviola- biles. Sicut ἐπιθανάτιοι διαθῆκαι βέβαιοί εἰσι, ἠ ἀμετακίνητοι. Alii ἐπιθανατίως interpretati fuere simplicius morti obnoxios. Quae explicatio voci ma- gis accedit, quam illa, quae ex Tertulliano additur. Nam illa magis specialis est: Haec autem generalis, cum speciem mortis non exprimat, sed tantum mortem in genere inferat.

Ὅτι θέατρον ἐγενήθημεν τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ Ἀγγέλοις, καὶ ἀνθρώποις. Instat coeptae similitudini; Et θέατρον dixit pro iis, qui spectantur, sicut ἀκρόαμα dicuntur ii, qui audiuntur. Non dissimiliter, versari in theatro apud Ciceronem est spectari ab omnibus. Est usurpatio continentis pro contento. Pro- priè amphitheatrum dicebatur locus, in quo pugnabatur cum bestiis : Sed & amphitheatrum theatri est species, ex duobus constans velut concurrentibus theatris. Job se dixit תפת לפנים XVII. 6. Id Græci vertunt : γέλως αὐτοῖς ἐπέβη. Cum mundum velut spectatorem Apostolici certaminis Paulus introduxisset, addidit καὶ Ἀγγέλοις κὶ ἀνθρώποις, ubi illud prius κόσ́μος ponitur pro, id est, Mundum enim, hoc est, mundi potissima τὰ νοερὰ dispertit in Angelos & homines : id Hebræi vocant familiam superiorem & inferiorem.

Camerarius confert adhuc aliam interpretationem, hanc tamen præfert, quæ ad exaggerandam infelicem sortem Apostoli facit: De qua propriè hic sermo est: Chrysostomus, inquit, Θέατρον ἐγενήθημεν τῷ κόσμῳ, ἡ τοῖς Ἀγγέλοις interpretatur, non in angulo aliquo rem gestam, sed jam spectatam esse mundo constantiam Apostolorum in perpetiendis adversis, ē εἶναι τὰ παλαίσματα ἄξια Ἀγγελικῆς θεωρίας. Alii θέατρον maluerunt hoc loco significare spectaculum triste ludibrii & afflictionis Christianorum in hoc mundo, coram hominibus & Angelis. Quæ sane ab his, quæ sequuntur, non videntur abhorrere. Id Paulus ergo dicit: Apostolos esse novissimos, seu extremæ sortis homines, quales ii sunt, quos judex morti jam adjudicavit. Deum enim, cum spectaculum facturus esset mundo, Apostolos produxisse, quorum miseriam & Angeli & homines cum admiratione adspiciunt, non secus ac olim miseri in theatricis spectaculis leonibus, ursis, aliisque bestiis objecti, ad risum nonnullos, ad commiserationem alios commovebant; Ita fideles illi Ecclesiarum ministri tyrannorum libidini & mundi ludibrio expositi risum excitant apud multos inter homines, commiserationem certè apud Angelos bonos, & qui naturam eorum imitantur, homines pios; ut hic habet Balduinus. De Angelis malis videtur loqui, quia in hoc theatro cum spiritibus malis lucta nobis est. Nonnullis tamen placet de bonis intelligere, quia illi spectatores sunt certaminis, & constantiæ nostræ testes, de qua etiam ipsi lætantur.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. We are fools for Christ's sake.

We are seen daily as fools for the sake of the Gospel. See Acts 26:24, above 1:25.

But you are wise in Christ.

You boast of yourselves in the name of learning, and that in Christ, that is, in His Church. See what is said in Rom. 9:3.

The voice of Christ is not to be taken metonymically for the Church, but properly. For the prudence which they boasted of was, according to their own persuasion, in Christ, or spiritual.

We are weak.

Wretched, afflicted: חלשים. See above I. 27. II. 3. Rom. VIII. 27. and what is said there.

But you are strong.

Powerful. See above I. 27.

You are glorious, and we are dishonored.

You are magnificent. See Luke VII. 25. It is usually translated thus for כבדים and נכבדים. We are despised as in Matthew XIII. 57. Mark VI. 4. נקלים. Which is opposed to honorable ones in Isaiah III. 4. and glorious ones, I Samuel XVIII. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἡμεῖς μωροὶ διὰ χρισόν.

Nos Evangelii causa quotidie ut stulti videmur. V. Act. XXVI. 24. supra I. 25.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ φρόνιμοι ἐν χρισῷ.

Vos eruditionis nomine vosmet jactatis, idque in Christo, id est, in ejus Ecclesia. Vide, quæ dicta Rom. IX. 3.

Vox Christi non Metonymicè pro Ecclesia, sed propriè accipienda. Prudentia enim, quam jactabant, in Christo, seu spiritualis erat secundum ipsorum persuasionem.

Ἡμεῖς ἀσθενεῖς.

Miseri afflicti : חלשים Vide supra I. 27. II. 3. Rom. VIII. 27. & ibi dicta.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἰσχυροί

Potentes. Vide supra I. 27.

Ὑμεῖς ἔνδοξοι, ἡμεῖς τε ἄτιμοι.

Vos magnifici. Vide Luc. VII. 25. Verti sic solet כבדים & נכבדים. Nos despecti ut Matth. XIII. 57. Marci VI. 4. נקלים. Quod opponitur ἐντίμοις Es. III. 4. & ἐνδόξοις, I. Sam. XVIII. 23.

## 4:11
Verse 11. Until this hour.

Even now: Lest you think that I am speaking only of past things.

and we hunger, and we thirst, and we are naked.

He recites the principal inconveniences of life, from which the rest of the same kind are to be understood. See Acts XX. 19. Philippians IV. 12. 2 Corinthians IV. 8. and following VI. 4. 5. 6. Γυμνῆται are light-armed soldiers, whence γυμνητέυειν means to act as a light-armed soldier. But it is used catachrestically of all who are naked, that is, thinly clothed. See Mark XIV. 52. John XXI. 7.

and we are buffeted.

What colaphizein properly means, see Matt. XXVI. 67. But by catachresis it is used for any grievous vexation, as can be seen in 2 Cor. XII. 7, 1 Pet. II. A similar manner of speaking is in 2 Cor. XI. 20.

and we are tossed about.

We are tossed about נרנו. This makes our poverty sadder, that we are not able to hide it even with a humble hearth; but everywhere we carry it about from place to place. We are homeless, without a hearth. We are driven as fugitives, outcasts of the earth.

Some wish it to be reproached to the Corinthians that they called Paul and his colleagues fools because they taught discordant things and suffered dire things, but held themselves to be wise in Christ. That they attributed weakness of the Spirit to them, but strength to themselves. That they boasted that they struggled with poverty and ignominy, but that they themselves flowed with riches and glory. But that they boasted these things about themselves, we easily admit. On the other hand, however, that they so despised the Apostles does not appear, nor is it indeed likely, since they rather exalted themselves in their name, saying that they were of Paul or of Cephas. Nor does the Apostle complain that such Apostles are so only κατὰ δόκησιν, but that they are truly such in the world. Just as it is agreed among all that they were not beaten with rods or affected by blasphemies by the Corinthians, but by others.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἄχρι τῆς ἄτι ὥρας.

Etiam nunc: Ne me de præteritis tantum agere existimetis.

καὶ πεινῶμεν, καὶ διψῶμεν, καὶ γυμνητεύομεν.

Præcipua vitæ incommoda recitat, unde intelligenda cætera ejusdem generis. Vid. Actor. XX. 19. Philipp. IV. 12. 2. Cor. IV. 8. & sequentibus VI. 4. 5. 6. Γυμνῆται sunt velites, unde γυμνητέυειν velitem agere. Sed καταχρησικῶς dicitur de omnibus nudis, id est, tenuiter vestitis. Vide Marc. XIV. 52. Joh. XXI. 7.

καὶ κολαφιζόμεθα.

Κολαφίζειν proprie quid sit, vide Matth. XXVI. 67. Sed per κατάχρησιν ponitur pro quavis gravi vexatione, ut videre est 2. Cor. XII. 7. 1. Petr. II. Simile loquendi genus 2. Cor. XI. 20.

καὶ ἀσατῦμεν.

Jactamur נרנו. Hoc tristior est nostra paupertas, quod nec tenui lare eam abscondere valemus ; sed ubique licorum eam circumferimus. Sumus ἄοικοι, ἀνέστιοι. Ἐλαυ- νόμεσθα φυγάδες ἔξεδροι χθονός. '

Nonnulli exprobrari Corinthiis volunt, quod Paulum cum collegis stultos, quod absona doce- rent, & dira paterentur, se autem prudentes habue- rint in Christo. Illis infirmitatem Spiritus, sibi robur tribuerint. Illos cum paupertie, & ignomi- nia conflictari, se verò divitiis & gloria fluere ja- ctitarrint. Sed quod de sese haec gloriati sint, faci- lè admittimus. Ex adverso autem ipsos ita de- spexisse Apostolos, non apparet, neque vero est simile, quum sese potius ipsorum nomine extule- rint, dicentes se Pauli vel Cephae esse. Neque quod tales Apostoli sint κατὰ δόκησιν tantum, sed quod revera tales sint in mundo, queritur Aposto- lus. Quemadmodum nec à Corinthiis, sed ab aliis colaphis cœsos, aut blasphemiis affectos dici, inter omnes constat.

## 4:12
Verse 12. And we toil, working with our own hands. We labor to the point of weariness, see Acts 17:3, 2 Thess. 3:8. All these things, by a silent opposition, note the Corinthian teachers, opulent, inflated, for whom the Gospel was a source of gain.

You would find here neither open nor hidden traces of that contrast. And the Apostle labored with his own hands before such teachers, if the Corinthians had any converted to the faith, had arisen.

Being reviled, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure. Being defamed, we entreat.

By Christ's precept, Matt. 5:10, 44. We entreat, namely, God. We pray to God for them. In Matthew: Pray for those who despitefully use you. For βλασφημούμενοι in the manuscript is δυσφημούμενοι. You have that word often among Greek writers and 1 Macc. 7:4, as also the noun δυσφημίας 1 Macc. 2:38.

Latin:

Vers. 12. καὶ κοπιῶμεν ἐργαζόμενοι ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσί. Laboramus ad lassitudinem, Vide Act. XVII. 3. 2. Thess. III. 18. Hæc omnia tacita oppositione notant doctores Corinthios, opulentos, inflatos, quibus quæstuosum erat Evangelium.

Illius ἀντιθέσεως nec aperta, nec operta hic re- perias vestigia. Et laboravit manibus suis Apo- stolus, antequam tales, si Corinthii habuere ad fi- dem conversi, exorti sunt Doctores.

Λοιδορούμενοι, εὐλογῶμεν. Διωκόμενοι, ἀνεχόμεθα. Βλασφημέμενοι, παρακαλῶμεν.

Ex Christi præcepto Matth. V. 10. 44. Παρακαλῶμεν nempe Deum. Deum pro ipsis precamur. In Matthæo Προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς. Pro βλασφη- μούμενοι in Manuscripto est δυσφημούμενοι. Habes id ver- bum apud Græcos scriptores sæpe & 1. Macc. VII. 4. ut & nomen δυσφημίας 1. Macc. II. 38.

## 4:13
Verse 13. As the offscouring of the world we have become. This word περικαθάρματα is found in Prov. 21:18 and signifies a lustration. Thus also Ambrose cites this passage: We have been made as the lustrations of this world. Just as περικαθαίρειν is the same as καθαίρειν, John 5:4, Deut. 18:10. So περικαθαρμα is the same as κάθαρμα. Vile men were accustomed to be used for this. The mother of Menoeceus in Papinius, Thebaid X.

Shall I, a vile mother, nourish you, wicked boy, as a lustration for the beasts of Thebes, and as a devoted head?

To which passage the Scholiast: It is a Gallic custom to lustrate the city with a human sacrifice. For someone from the most destitute was enticed with rewards, so that he would offer himself for this, who was fed for a whole year at public expense with purer foods: Finally, on a certain and solemn day, led through the city, he was killed by the people outside the city walls with stones. Caesar also mentions this custom of the Gauls in book VI, and Servius on that line of Virgil: The accursed hunger for gold. Such men, not only those who devoted themselves to death but also to the lash, are called by the Greeks καθάρματα. The Scholiast on the Plutus of Aristophanes: They were called καθάρματα, who were sacrificed to the gods for the cleansing of some plague or some other disease. And this custom also prevailed among the Romans. And on the Knights: For the Athenians used to carry very ignoble and useless men, and at the time of some calamity befalling the city, I mean a plague or something similar, they sacrificed them for the sake of being cleansed of the pollution, whom they also named καθάρματα. And because they were vile, as we said, thence it was born, as Eustathius testifies, that those who are base and cast-off are called καθάρματα. When Curtius said the offscourings of their cities, he had that Greek word καθάρματα in mind. And Tertullian in his book on modesty correctly translates what is here περικαθάρματα as offscourings. Plautus called it a piacular offering.

The offscouring of all things until now.

Jer. 22:28. Is he a despised offscouring? Thus Symmachus translates: Jerome interprets it as refuse. Eustathius interprets περίψημα as a sponge, that with which one is wiped clean. Others, dung. In the glossary it is refuse, dung. I prefer that here to interpreting it as a towel, although grammarians report that it is also signified by the same name. You would not translate it badly here as dross. Tob. 5:24, But may he be the offscouring of our child, where see what is said. Barnabas: The offscouring of your love, that is, nothing, if compared with you.

Budaeus has already proved this from the authors of both languages, that those were called καθάρματα whom the Latins called sacred men, by whose head all the crimes of a city or some nation were expiated, and who were sacrificed to avert the anger of the Gods. This does not please Beza; but his reasoning is nothing, because it is not likely that either that common custom was then known everywhere to the Greeks, or that Paul referred to it. It was certainly known everywhere, and therefore it is entirely likely that the Apostle referred to it. For as to what he says, that he took these from Lam. III. 45, it does not appear: since neither are those things held there, nor are the words synonymous, whether you look at the LXX interpreters or the text. Pareus more correctly: Men were called καθάρματα who were most vile and abject, likewise wicked and destructive, likewise sacred or expiatory, by whose death and destruction public calamities were expiated, just as the Gentiles then regarded Christians, as if they were the authors of all evils; Tertull. apol. cap. 2. Hence Ambrose: We have been made lustramenta. The word is from καθαίρω, I purge, I cleanse: Whence καθάρματα are purgaments, excrements, from which the world is to be purged. The preposition περὶ increases the foulness of the thing: Just as filth is swept together from all sides with brooms to be cast out: So wherever we have come, we are swept out as most pestilential men. Περίψημα is sawdust, shavings, or dross, which is purged from any thing: Or also a cloth, by which the dirt of shoes is wiped off, from περιψᾶν to wipe off. He therefore indicates the extreme abjection, contempt, and misery of the Apostles in the world, because they are commonly held to be expiatory victims and abominable, who stink to the world like purgaments.

PART III. Mitigation of the rebuke.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ὡς περικαθάρματα τῶ κόσμῳ ἐγενήθημεν. Reperitur hæc vox περικαθαρμα Prov. XXI. 18. & signi- ficat lustramen. Sic & Ambrosius hunc locum citat; Tan- quam lustramenta hujus mundi facti sumus. Sicut περικα- θαίρειν, idem quod καθαίρειν Joh. V. 4. Deuter. XVIII. 10. Ita περικαθαρμα idem quod κάθαρμα, Solebant ad id viles homines adhiberi. Mater Menœcei apud Papinium Thebaidis. X.

Lustrafemne feris ego te puer improbe Thebis. Devotumque caput, vilis ceu mater, alebam.

Ad quem locum Scholiastes : Lustrare civitatem humana hostia Gallicus mos est. Nam aliquis de egentissimis pellice- batur præmiis, ut se ad hoc senderet, qui anno toto publicis sumptibus alebatur purioribus cibis : Denique certo & solenni die per civitatem ductus ex urbe extra pomœria saxis occideba- tur à populo. Meminit ejus moris Gallorum & Cæsar li- bro VI. & Servius ad illud Virgilii : Auri sacra fames. Ta- les homines non modo qui morti, sed & qui flagris se devo- vebant, Græcis dicuntur καθάρματα. Scholiaites ad Plu- tum Aristophanis : Καθάρματα ἐλέγοντο, οἱ ἐπὶ καθάρσει λοιμᾶ τινος, ἤ τινος ἑτέρας νόσε θυόμενοι τοῖς θεοῖς. Τετὶ δὲ τὸ ἔθος καὶ παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις ἐπεκράτησε. Et ad equites: Ἔφε- ρον γάρ τε τῷ Ἀθηναῖοι λίαν ἀγενεῖς κὶ ἀχρήσως, κὶ ἐν καιρῷ συμ- φορᾶς τινος ἐπελθέσης τῇ πόλει, λοιμῶ λέγω, ἤ τοιέτω τινὸς, ἔθυον τάτες ἕνεκα τῶ καθαρθῆναι τῶ μιάσματος ὕς κὶ ἐπωνόμα- ζον καθάρματα. Et quia illi viles erant, ut diximus, inde natum teste Eustathio, ut καθάρματα dicantur οἱ ἐντερεῖς κὶ ἀπόβλητοι. Curtius cum dixit purgamenta urbium sua- rum, Græcum illud καθάρματα in mente habuit. Et Ter- tullianus libro de pudicitia, quod hic est περικαθάρματα re- cte vertit purgamenta. Piacularem dixit Plautus.

Πάντων περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι.

Jer. XXII. 28. μὴ περίψημα Φαῦλον. Ita vertit Sym- machus : Hieronymus interpretatur quisquilias. Eusta- thius περίψημα interpretatur σπόγγισμα id quod spongia abstergitur. Alii σκύβαλον. In glossario est quisquilia σκύ- βαλον. Id malo hic quam sabanum interpretari, quanquam id quoque eodem nomine fignificari tradant Grammatici. Non male hic verteris retrimentum Tob. V. 24. Ἀλλὰ περί- ψημα τῶ παιδίε ἡμῶν γένοιτο, ubi dicta vide. Barnabas : Περίψημα τῆς ἀγάπης ὑμῶν, id est, nihil, si vobiscum com- parer.

Id etiam Budæus ex utriusque linguæ autoribus jam probavit, καθάρματα dictos fuisse, quos La- tini sacros homines dicebant, quorum capite omnia civitatis aut gentis alicujus scelera luebantur, qui- que avertendæ Deorum iræ mactabantur. Non id placet Bezæ; sed ratio ejus nulla est, quod non sit verisimile, vel communem illam consuetudinem tum fuisse passim Græcis notam, vel Paulum ad eam respexisse. Notissimum certe undiquaque erat, atque ideo verisimile omnino est, eo respexisse Apostolum. Nam quod ait, eum hæc è Thr. III. 4. desumpsisse, non apparet: Quum nec illa ibi ha- beantur, nec synonyma verba, sive LXX. interpre- tes respicias, seu textum. Rectius Pareus: Ka- θάρματα dicebantur homines vilissimi & abjectissi- mi, item scelerati & exitiales, item sacri seu piacu- lares, quorum nece & exitio publicæ calamitates expiabantur, quomodo gentiles tunc habebant Christianos, quasi omnium malorum autores; Tertull. apol. cap. 2. Hinc Ambrosius: Facti su- mus lustramenta. Vox est à καθαίρω, expurgo, mundo: Unde καθάρματα purgamenta, excre- menta, à quibus mundus sit purgandus. Præpo- sitio περὶ auget rei fœditatem: Sicut sordes cir- cumquaque scopis converruntur ad ejiciendum: Ita quocunque locorum venerimus, everrimur ut pestilentissimi homines. Περίψημα est scobs, ra- mentum, vel scoria, quæ depurgatur à quacunque re: Vel etiam peniculum, quo sordes calceorum absterguntur, à περιψᾶν abstergere. Extremam igitur abjectionem, contemptum, miseriam Apo- stolorum in mundo indicat, quod vulgo piacula- res habeantur atque abominabiles, qui purga- mentorum instar mundo fœteant.

PARS III. Reprehensionis mitigatio.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. I do not write these things to shame you. Ἐντρέπειν is to make ashamed in Plutarch and other good Greek writers. Among the Interpreters it corresponds to the Hebrew כלם and other words of equal meaning. He says this, that he does not write these things to traduce the Corinthians before other Churches. Having spoken about the Teachers, he now turns his words to the individual believers.

Such a change of persons does not appear from the text. The Apostle always addresses the same people: Nor does he deal with the Teachers; but with the hearers, who were mutually exalting themselves against one another because of diverse judgments about their Teachers, indeed about the Apostles themselves, and their colleagues.

But as my beloved children I admonish you. In the Manuscript νουθετῶν, correctly, so that it may cohere with that ἑντρέπων. Νουθετεῖν is to chastise so that the other may become better. This name is especially suitable for parents, as can be seen in Wis. XI. 11, XII. 26. It corresponds to the Hebrew יסר and בין.

Latin:
