Vers. 14. Οὐκ ἐντρέπων ὑμᾶς γράφω ταῦτα· Ἐντρέπειν est pudefacere Plutarcho, & aliis bene Græ- cis. Apud Interpretes respondet Hebræo כלם & aliis verbis, paris significatus. Hoc dicit non se hæc scribe- re, ut Corinthios apud alias Ecclesias traducat. De Do- ctoribus loquutus, nunc verba ad fidelium singulos vertit.

Talis mutatio personarum non apparet è textu. Eosdem semper alloquitur Apostolus: Nec cum Doctoribus agit; sed cum auditoribus, qui mutuò se efferebant alii adversus alios ob judicia diversa de Doctoribus suis, imò de ipsis Apostolis, eorum- que collegis.

Ἀλλ' ὡς τέκνα μου ἀγαπητὰ νυθετῶ. In Manuscripto νουθετῶν, rectè, ut cohæreat cum illo ἑντρέπων Νουθετεῖν est castigare in id, ut alter melior fiat. Parenti- bus maximè id convenit nomen, ut videre est Sap. XI, 11, XII. 26. Respondet Hebræo יסר & בין.

## 4:15
Vers. 15. For if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ. Columella and Cicero rightly called παιδαγωγὸν in Latin a pedagogue: Horace called him a guardian. He is called such who is present to a boy or adolescent to form his morals. Thus Sophocles introduces Orestes with a pedagogue in Electra, and Leonidas is called the pedagogue of Alexander. See Gal. III. 25.

But not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus through the gospel I have begotten you. He says advisedly in Christ Jesus, that is, through the gifts given by Christ. The first honor in this matter is of the Father, Matt. XXIII. 9. 1 Pet. I. 3. 1 John III. 9. The next is of Christ, as appears here, and in the cited place of Matthew: The third is of the Apostles, as here, Philem. 10. Gal. IV. 19. To all these both the title of Father and the word of begetting is suitable, but each in its own degree. Thus Christ is the foundation and the Apostles are the foundations: Christ saves men, and the Apostles save them. The Father in this place is he who first instructs someone in the Gospel.

The sense is, you ought to obey me above others, as your spiritual Father: And to hear others also, if any walk according to my doctrine, as your tutors. For although I am not a little despised in the world: Yet this The Lord granted me honor above others, in that I begat you through my ministry. For the Father alone is He who has begotten children; those who instruct the begotten are pedagogues. They are called fathers, by whose ministry and labor either some entire Church, or individual persons, are first converted to the faith of the Gospel: but pedagogues are those who further confirm and edify men already converted to the faith by the preaching of others, by teaching, admonishing, correcting, consoling, and performing other parts and works of the Ecclesiastical office. Paul, therefore, calling himself the Father of the Corinthians, shows that they were first called and led to the communion of faith by his ministry, Acts XVIII. And therefore he adds, 'for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through my Gospel,' that is, the Lord Jesus has begotten you through my Gospel preached among you, so that from Gentiles you might be born Christians, from infidels believers, from children of wrath children of grace, and heirs of the heavenly kingdom, as the blessed Hunnius rightly says here. But while the Apostle claims this title of Father for himself, he does not exclude his associates Apollos, Sosthenes, etc., as faithful fellow-workers, but those who, through perverse ambition, were attempting to destroy the glory of the Apostle and seize it for themselves. We also learn from this that the power of regeneration is attributed not only to the Gospel as the means of salvation, but also to the teachers of the Word as the ministerial cause, not improperly, or for the sake of honoring them, as the Calvinists cavil, but properly, since they are true causes of regeneration, albeit ministerial, subordinate to the principal cause, through which God as the principal cause regenerates us. Therefore he called Timothy his son. But he begat the Corinthians in Christ Jesus, that is, by the merit and efficacy of Christ, as Mediator and Redeemer, through and because of whom we are regenerated to spiritual and eternal life. 1 Pet. I. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἐὰν γὰρ μυρίους παιδαγωγὸς ἔχητε ἐν χριστῷ. Παιδαγωγὸν Latinè pædagogum rectè dixere Columella & Cicero: Custodem Horatius. Ita dicitur is, qui puero aut adolescenti adest, ad mores ejus formandos. Sic Ore- sten cum pædagogo introducit Sophocles Electra, & Leo- nidas Alexandri dicitur παιδαγωγός. Vide Gal. III. 25.

Ἀλλ' ὐ πολλὺς πατέρας· Ἐν γὰρ χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ διὰ τῦ ἐυαγγελίε ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς ἐγέννησα. Provide ait ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησῦ, id est, per dona à Christo data. Primus in hac re honor est Patris, Matth. XXIII. 9. 1. Pet. I. 3. 1. Joh. III. 9. Proximus Christi, ut hic apparet, & dicto Matthæi loco: Tertius Apostolorum, ut hîc, Philem. 10. Gal. IV. 19. His omnibus & titulus Patris, & gignendi verbum convenit, sed suo cuique gradu. Sic Christus fun- damentum & Apostoli fundamenta: Christus servat homi- nes, & Apostoli eos servant. Pater hoc loco is est, qui primus in Evangelio aliquem instituit.

Sensus est, mihi præ cæteris obedire debeba- tis, tanquam Patri vestro spirituali: Cæteros etiam, si qui secundum doctrinam meam ince- dunt, audire, ut pædagogos vestros. Etsi enim in mundo non parum contemnor: Tamen hunc honorem mihi præ aliis conceffit Dominus, quod per minifterium meum vos regenui. Solus enim Pater est, qui liberos genuit, qui genitos erudiunt, pædagogi sunt. Patres dicuntur, quorum ministe- rio & labore sive integra aliqua Ecclesia, sive perso- næ singulæ primitus ad fidem Evangelii convertun- tur: Pædagogi vero, qui homines aliorum predica- tione jam ad fidem conversos in eadem amplius con- firmant, & ædificant, docendo, admonendo, corrigen- do, consolando, aliasque muneris Ecclesiastici par- tes & operas obeundo. Paulus itaque se Patrem Corinthiorum nuncupans, ostendit, suo ministerio illos ad fidei communionem primo esse vocatos & per- ductos, Act. XVIII. Ideoque subjungit, siquidem in Christo Jesu per Evangelium meum vos genui, hoc est, Dominus Jesus vos per Evangelium meum inter vos prædicatum regenuit, ut ex Ethnicis Christiani, ex infidelibus fideles, ex filiis iræ nasceremini filii gra- tiæ, & regni cælestis hæredes, ut recte hîc B. Hun- nius. Dum autem vendicat sibi hunc Patris titu- lum Apostolus, non excludit socios Apollo, Sosthe- nem, &c. ceu fideles συνεργὺς, sed eos, qui perver- sa ambitione gloriam Apostoli destruere & ad se rapere conabantur. Discimus etiam hinc, non tantum Evangelio, ceu medio salutis vim regene- rationis tribui, sed etiam verbi Doctoribus ceu cau- sæ ministeriali, non impropriè, vel cohonestandi causa, ut Calviniani cavillantur, sed propriè, cùm veræ causæ sint regenerationis, etsi ministeriales, subordinatæ causæ principali, per quas Deus ceu causa principalis nos regenerat. Ideo Timo- theum filium suum dixit. In Christo Jesu autem ge- nuit Corinthios, id est, merito & efficacia Christi, ceu Mediatoris & Redemptoris, per & propter quem regeneramur ad vitam spiritualem, & æter- nam. 1. Petr. I. 3.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. I beseech you therefore, be ye followers of me. Why should it not be possible, since Paul himself has imitated Christ? Below XI. 1. But he requires imitation here especially in the care of protecting both unity and soundness in the Church.

He exhorts properly to humility, that they may follow and approve it by his example. At the same time, however, he excites them to other virtues, and also to concord. This exhortation serves not only to mitigate the correction, because he presents himself as a Father for imitation, but also to assert the right and authority over them which a father has over children in preference to pedagogues. That this may be more fruitful, he sends to them Timothy, his son, uniquely genuine and faithful, as a living example and a most worthy teacher, and presents and commends him to them.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Παρακαλῶ ὖν ὑμᾶς, μιμηταί με γίνεσθε. Quid ni fieri possit, cum Paulus Christum ipsum sit imitatus? Infra XI. 1. Imitationem autem præcipuè hîc requirit in cura tutandæ in Ecclesia tum unitatis, tum san- ætitatis.

Ad humilitatem propriè hortatur, ut eam sui exemplo sectentur & probent. Simul autem ad alias virtutes, etiam ad concordiam excitat. Facit hæc exhortatio non saltem ad mitigandam cor- reptionem, quia se Patrem ad imitationem sistit, sed etiam ad asserendum jus & autoritatem in ipsos, quam pater habet in liberos præ pædago- gis. Quæ ut fructuosior sit, Timotheum filium suum singulariter γνήσιον & fidelem, ceu vivum exemplar, & dignissimum doctorem ad ipsos mit- tit, iisque sistit & commendat.

## 4:17
Vers. 17. For this cause have I sent unto you Timothy. Namely, that he may explain more broadly in words those things which this epistle briefly comprehends. Who is my beloved son and faithful in the Lord. For from a boy he had clung to the Apostle as a companion. See 2 Tim. I. 5. 1 Tim. IV. 6. See what we have said in the Appendix concerning the Antichrist. Therefore the Apostle was accustomed to call Timothy son, not in that common sense, but in a more special sense, 1 Tim. I. 2, 18. 2 Tim. I. 2, II. 1. Who shall bring you into remembrance of my ways, which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church. He will bring back to your memory how I both live myself according to the precepts of Christ, and teach that one must live. He will remind.

They were to be warned not only concerning life, but also to be informed in doctrine. For both of these pertained to the ways of the Apostle in Christ, which both the Apostle also taught everywhere in all the Churches. He commends Timothy to them (1.) by spiritual kinship. For he is Paul's spiritual son, therefore let them receive him as a brother in the Lord. For also

he had named them his own children. (2.) By faithfulness in office, because he is faithful in the Lord, that is, in the work of the Lord, which has been committed to him among them. (3.) By the office itself. For he will remind you of my ways, that is, he will narrate to you my institutes, my doctrine and life, which by the grace of God I have led blameless, and will all but present them. (4.) By the excellence of his doctrine. For he will not propose to you his own dreams or anything new, but that catholic doctrine which already sounds in every Church, and is sufficient for salvation. Therefore, in hearing Timothy, you will hear me, as the blessed Balduinus says here. Thus he binds Timothy and the Corinthians to the Apostolic doctrine, so that they may not wish to obtrude or receive anything into the Church besides it: But much less is it permitted to other teachers, who wish to be considered ministers of Christ, to deflect from the ways of the Apostles, or to introduce another kind of doctrine besides that which Paul taught in all the Churches. And we have that comprehended in the Apostolic Epistles: because what Gospel they preached, that they also comprehended in writings, as Irenaeus testifies.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Δία τῦτο ἔπεμψα ὑμῖν τὸν Τιμόθεον. Nempe qui verbis latius explicet ea, quæ breviter hæc epistola comprehendit. Ὅς ἐσι τέκνον με ἀγαπητὸν καὶ πισὸν ἐν Κυρίῳ. Nam à puero comes Apostolo hæserat. Vide 2. Ti- moth. I. 5. 1. Tim. IV. 6. Vide, quæ diximus in Appendi- ce de Antichristo. Ideo Timotheum non communi illo, sed specialiari sensu τέκνον vocare consueverat Apostolus 1. Tim. I. 2. 18. 2. Tim. I. 2. II. 1. Ὅς ὑμᾶς ἀναμνήσει τὰς ὁδύς με, τὰς ἐν χρισῷ, καθὼς πανταχ῱ ἐν πάσῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ διδάσκω. In memoriam vobis reducet, quomodo ego & vivam ipse secundum Christi præcepta, & vivendum esse doceam. Ἀναμνήσει יזכיר.

Non de vita tantum monendi, sed in doctrina etiam informandi erant. Hæc enim ambo ad vias Apostoli in Christo pertinebant, quæ utraq; etiam Apostolus ubique in omnibus Ecclesiis docuit. Commendat ipsis Timotheum (1.) à cognatione spirituali. Est enim Pauli filius spiritualis, ergò recipiant ipsum ut fratrem in Domino. Nam &

ipsos filios suos nominaverat. (2.) A fidelitate in officio, quia fidelis est in Domino, hoc est, in opere Domini, quod ipsi commissum est apud ipsos. (3.) Ab officio ipso. Commonefaciet enim vos vias meas, hoc est, instituta mea, doctrinam atque vi- tam meam, quam per Dei gratiam gessi inculpa- tam, vobis enarrabit, & tantum non præsentabit (4.) à præstantia doctrinæ suæ. Non enim sua somnia aut novi aliquid vobis proponet, sed eam, quæ sonat jam in omni Ecclesia, doctrinam catho- licam, & ad salutem sufficientem. Timotheum igitur audituri, meipsum audietis, ut hic B. Bal- duinus. Sic Timotheum & Corinthios ad doctri- nam Apostolicam adstringit, ne quid præter eam Ec- clesiæ obtrudere, aut recipere velint: Multo autem minus aliis doctoribus, qui ministri Christi haberi volunt, à viis Apostolorum deflectere, aliudve doctri- næ genus invehere licet, præter id, quod Paulus in omnibus Ecclesiis docuit. Id verò Epistolis Apostolicis comprehensum habemus: quia quod Evangelium prædicarunt, id scriptis etiam com- prehenderunt, teste Irenæo.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you.

That is, they behave themselves proudly, as above IV. 17. For from thence arose factions, because one teacher despised another, and was the author of doing the same to the common people. But many faulty things of this kind happened in the Churches in the absence of Paul, which his presence would have easily repressed. See Phil. II. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ὡς μὴ ἐρχομένου δέ με πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐφυ- σιώθησάν τινες.

Id est, superbè se gerunt, ut supra IV. 17. Inde enim natæ partes, quod Doctorum alius alium sperneret, idem- que faciendi autor esset plebi. Multa autem mendosa hu- jusmodi eveniebant in Ecclesiis absente Paulo, quæ facile præsentia ejus repressisset. Vide Phil. II. 22.

## 4:19
Vers. 19. But I will come to you shortly.

So indeed Paul hoped, but he was compelled to defer this journey longer, so that he wrote a second letter after some interval, before he returned there, 2 Cor. 1:23.

If the Lord wills.

It is fitting for Christians to speak thus, James 4:13, 14, 15. See Rom. 1:10. The Hebrews say אם ירצה השם If God wills; or בגבורת השם by the power of God.

and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power.

It will appear by experience, not whether they are more eloquent than I (for this is nothing to the point), but whether God works more powerfully through them or through me.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἐλεύσομαι δὲ ταχέως πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Ita quidem sperabat Paulus, sed diutiùs differre hoc iter coactus fuit, ita ut & alteram epistolam ex aliquo in- tervallo scripserit, priusquam eo rediret, 2. Cor. I. 23.

Ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θελήσῃ.

Ita convenit loqui Christianis Jacob. II. 13. 14. 15. Vide Rom. I. 10. Hebræi dicunt אם ירצה השם Si Deus voluerit; aut בגבורת השם per Dei potentiam.

καὶ γνώσομαι ὀυ λόγον τῶν πεφυσιωμένων, ἀλλὰ τὴν δύναμιν.

Experimento apparebit, non illine me sint disertiores, (nihil enim hoc ad rem) sed an Deus per eos, an per me po- tentius operetur.

## 4:20
Vers. 20. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.

The kingdom of God, that is, Majesty, appears not in words curled with a curling iron, but in the force of miracles, such as cannot proceed from human aid. See above 2:1. Just as the Latins say to Kings: Your Majesty: So the Greeks: Βασιλεία σε.

They are puffed up, namely, with an opinion of wisdom. Which seems to pertain primarily to the Teachers. Others explain it concerning carnal security; given to luxury, they exalted themselves and showed themselves proudly refractory. He wishes therefore to come, that he may know and beat back their insolence, and make it manifest that they are swollen and puffed up with the empty boasting of words, but that in reality nothing of substance or virtue underlies it. By power, therefore, it is manifest that not so much signs and miracles are to be understood, as Chrysostom wishes, as the efficacy of doctrine. Moreover, not only the Teachers are puffed up, but also others sinning with a high hand. Therefore, not content with words, he requires work and truth, as Saint John in the charity of the neighbor, 1 Epist. 3:18. According to Blessed Balduinus, the Apostle distinguishes the grandiloquence of words from the solid knowledge of spiritual things, of which those proud and clamorous teachers boasted. In this, however, they were more than children, which he says he will show, God helping, once the examination is instituted. At the same time, he censures the Corinthian gullibility, because they depend on those external things and think that the very virtue, force, and efficacy of the kingdom of God consists in those trappings of words. The kingdom of God is not in speech; but in power v. 20. He teaches therefore that the Church is not built by that babbling of empty words, which contributes nothing either to a pious and happy life in this age, or to eternal salvation; but by the true knowledge of God, by a pious and burning zeal of confession, by true faith, patience, and similar virtues, by which the power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit exerts itself. Where, therefore, that is found, there you have a taste of the kingdom of God, even if that external splendor and ornament of words is absent.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Οὐ γὰρ ἐν λόγῳ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν δυνάμει.

Dei regnum, id est, Majestas, apparet non in verbis ca- lamistro inustis, sed in vi miraculorum, qualia ab huma- na ope proficisci nequeunt. Vide supra II. 1. Sicut Lati- ni dicunt Regibus: Tua Majestas: Ita Græci: Βασι- λεία σε.

Inflati sunt nempe sapientiæ opinione. Quod ad Doctores imprimis pertinere videtur. Alii de securitate carnali explicant, luxui dediti semet- ipsos efferebant, & fastuosè refractarios se præbe- bant. Venire ergo vult, ut cognoscat & retun- dat insolentiam eorum, & palam faciat eos inani jactantia verborum, & securitate inflatos tume- re, nihil verò rerum virtutisque subesse. Per δύναμιν ergò non tam signa & miracula, ut Chry- sostomus vult, quam doctrinæ efficaciam intelligi manifestum est. Inflati autem non solum Docto- res sunt, sed & alii elato brachio peccantes. Pro- inde non verbis contentus ἔργον & ἀλήθειαν re- quirit, ut Sanctus Johannes in charitate proximi 1. Epist. III. 18. Secundum B. Balduinum distin- guit Apostolus grandiloquentiam verborum à so- lida cognitione rerum spiritualium, quarum il- lam jactabant fastuosi illi, & clamosi docto- res. In hac autem plus quam pueri erant, id quod se, instituto examine, ostensurum, Deo juvante, ait. Perstringit autem simul Corin- thiorum facilitatem, quod ab externis illis pen- deant, & ipsam virtutem, vim ac efficaciam regni Dei in istis phaleris verborum consi- stere putent. Non in sermone est regnum Dei; sed in virtute v. 20. Docet itaque Ecclesiam non ædificari isto vaniloquiorum garritu, qui neque ad vitam piã & felicem in hoc seculo, neque ad salutem æternam quidquam facit; sed verâ cognitione Dei, pio ardenteque zelo confessionis, verâ fide, patientia, & similibus virtutibus, quibus Spiritûs S. virtus atque efficacia se exerit. Ubi ergo ista invenitur, ibi gustum habetis regni Dei, utut externus ille verborum splendor & ornatus absit.

## 4:21
V. 21. What do you wish?

Τί for πότερον. Thus Livy: Two most celebrated leaders, which of them had conquered first. And the writer of the Spanish war: Let there be a contention between two, which of them should occupy the bridge first.

Shall I come to you with a rod?

Ἐν here has the force of 'with' according to the custom of the Hebrews. By 'rod' he understands metaphorically the power of inflicting either death, as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira; or blindness, as in the case of Elymas; or diseases. Thus God then supplied that which the magistrates of the Church ought to perform, and at that time were not performing. מטה, which is accustomed to be translated as ῥάβδος, is translated as πληγὴ in Isaiah 10:24. We have noted a similar use of the word μάστιγος in Mark 3:10.

Or in love, and in a spirit of gentleness?

Or rather full of love, and of a mild and kind spirit.

He opposes the rod and charity. Not that the rod of a parent is without charity; for whom the Father loves, he chastens, Prov. 3:12, Heb. 12:6. But because charity exerts itself more in benefits than in punishments and chastisements. If they persist in despising him, let them know that he has a rod at hand, and that he has the authority and power by which he can coerce them. A specimen of which severity he produced in the case of the incestuous man: but if they give place to his fatherly admonitions, they will also experience his gentleness. Regarding what he adds, 'in a spirit of gentleness,' says Augustine, lib. 3 adv. Parm. cap. 1, he warns us to understand that the rod also has charity: but the charity of gentleness is one thing, the charity of severity is another. It is indeed one charity; but it works differently in different cases. But it is a violent distortion when the rod is snatched by the Papists, Bellarmine lib. 4 de Rom. Pontif., Suarez in def. fid. Cath. lib. 3, cap. 23, for the removal of rights and temporal possessions, which the Apostles certainly did not have in hand, from which Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Nazianzen, orat. 1 de pace, explain it as concerning rebuke and severe correction; even among the Pontificals, Cardinal Cajetan, Salmero, Justinianus, and Saa explain it. Estius expressly names the rod, not the sword, Conf. 2 Cor. 7:15, Cap. 10:6. St. Augustine indeed brings forward this passage against the epistle of Parmenianus the Donatist, lib. 3, 1, when he teaches that there exists in the Church the power of coercing heretics even with civil punishments. But that this power belongs to Bishops, by virtue of the key of binding and loosing of excommunicating, are Jesuitical ravings, not indeed Apostolic dogmas.

Latin:

V. 21. Τί θέλετε.

Τί pro πότερον Sic Livius: Duo & celeberrimi duces, quis prior eorum vicisset. Et scriptor belli Hispanici: Inter duos sit contentio, quis prior pontem occuparet.

Ἐν ῥάβδῳ ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς·

Ἐν hic valet cum more Hebræorum. Per virgam μεταφορικῶς intelligit potestatem immittendi aut mortem, ut Ananiæ & Sapphiræ; aut cæcitatem, ut Elymæ; aut morbos. Ita tunc Deus supplebat id, quod magistratus Ecclesiæ præstare debent, & tunc non præstabant. מטה, quod ῥάβδος verti solet, vertitur, πληγὴ Es. X. 24. Similem usum vocis μάστιγος annotavimus Marci III. 10.

Ἢ ἐν ἀγάπῃ, πνεύματί τε πραότητος·

An potius plenum amoris, & animi lenis, ac benigni.

Opponit virgam, & charitatem. Non quod virga parentis absque charitate sit; quem enim amat Pater, castigat, Prov. III. 12. Ebr. XII. 6. Sed quia charitas sese magis exerit in benefactis, quam in pœnis & castigationibus. Si contemnere se pergant, sciant, sibi virgam ad manum esse, seque habere autoritatem & potestatem, qua ipsos coërcere possit. Cujusmodi severitatis specimen in incestuoso edidit: Sin vero paternis suis monitis locum dederint, suam quoque lenitatem experientur. Quod addit spiritu mansuetudinis, inquit August. l. III. adv. Parm. cap. 1. admonet intelligi, quia & virga charitatem habet: Sed aliud est charitas mansuetudinis, aliud charitas severitatis. Una quidem charitas est; sed diversa in diversis operatur. Violenta vero detorsio est, cum virga à Papistis, Bellarm. l. IV. de Rom. Pontif. Svarez in def. fid. Cath. l: 3. c. 23. abripitur ad ablationem jurium, & possessionum temporalium, quam utique Apostoli non habebant in manu, unde de objurgatione & correptione severa Chrys. Theophyl. & Nazianz. orat. I. de pace; etiam è Pontificiis Cardin. Cajanus, Salmero, Justinianus, & Saa explicant. Estius diserte virgam nominat, non gladium Conf. 2. Cor. VII. 15. Cap. X. 6. Adducit quidem S. Augustinus hunc locum adversus epistolam Parm. Donatistæ l. III. 1. cum docet, extare in Ecclesia potestatem coërcendi hæreticos pœnis etiam civilibus. Sed quod hæc potestas competat Episcopis, vigore clavis ligantis & solventis excommunicandi, Jesuitica deliria sunt, non vero Apostolicadogmata.

## 5:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE CORRECTIVE EPISTLE. CHAPTER V.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians on account of the incest tolerated with a stepmother, and decrees that the man is to be excommunicated, so that the leaven, of which even a small part corrupts the whole lump, may be purged out, and the passover may be celebrated in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. He repeats that one must not associate with fornicators, which is to be understood not of those or similar wicked men who are in the world, but of those who wish to be brothers; but he teaches that God will judge those who are outside.

There are three parts: I. Concerning the excommunication of the incestuous man, to v. 5. II. Concerning the purging out of the old leaven, to v. 8. III. Concerning avoiding communion with the wicked, to v. 13.

PART I. Concerning the excommunication of the incestuous man.

V. 1. It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you.

First, it is unworthy that any filthiness should be heard of among you who profess Christ: Then, indeed, such a one: Ὅλως, that is, at all: as μὴ ὀμνύναι ὅλως in Justin and Chrysostom, which elsewhere is καθόλꙋ. See on Matt. V. 33. By the name of fornication, not only whoredom is signified, but all Venus against divine law, rights, and good morals. We have also noted on Matt. V. 32 that adulteries come under that name. Thus among the Prophets תזנות & זנות is very often used. Illegitimate marriages also come under that name. Tertullian on modesty: Therefore, among us, secret unions also, that is, not previously declared to the Church, are in danger of being judged according to adultery and fornication. Thus in Basil: The maidens who followed against the will of the father commit fornication: And: She who gave herself to a man against the will of the master committed fornication. Likewise: If anyone, overcome by impurity, should fall into an unlawful union of two sisters, let this not be considered a marriage.

And such fornication as is not even named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.

To have here is as it were to use as a wife, as the Syrian understood. See what was said on Matt. XIV. 4, where we also noted this, that she is called the wife of someone who was a wife, even with the husband now deceased. In the manuscript, ὀνομάζεται is missing, which the Latin also did not have in his codex. The Apostle says such a disgrace is not even found among the Gentiles, that is, is hardly found. Truly, Plutarch relates of Seleucus, when he wished to grant his wife Stratonice to his son Antiochus, that he feared lest she herself might be offended τῷ μὴ νενομισμένῳ, as by an illicit thing. And Cicero in a similar matter says: A crime unheard of in all life.

In the rebuke, we note first the crime of incest: Second, the guilt of the Corinthians: Third, the remedy for the public scandal. The Apostle exaggerates the crime first as notorious, by the word ὅλως, which is not to be drawn to the word πορνείας with Grotius, nor to be taken as a particle of connection with Crellius, as if the Apostle, after he had threatened the rod, should say: That I may not use many circumlocutions, I will explain what the matter is. Such a use of the word is nowhere found in the N.T.; but it is for expressing the truth of the rumors and the notoriety: Which sense even Crellius himself did not deny, and Schlichtingius adopted. Then as most grievous, that fornication, whoredom, should be heard of among them, which wickedness should by no means be heard of among Christians, Eph. V. 3, and indeed not simple whoredom, but such as should not even be named among the Gentiles, according to the judgment of the sounder ones among them, among whom, therefore, Christianity is most basely prostituted. And finally, that from which nature itself peculiarly abhors, that one should have his father's wife, because incestuous cohabitation is admitted among them with a stepmother, the wife of his father. But whether he was joined to her by marriage, which Grotius does not collect firmly enough from the word ἔχειν, or whether he used her company without the bond of marriage, most leave in the middle. Yet the latter seems more likely, both from the more famous meaning of the word fornication, and from the fact that the incestuous marriage would have to be dissolved, not only the incestuous person excommunicated, of which, however, the Apostle gave no warning. Nor is it clear that the stepfather had already sufficiently conceded the incest, and therefore it is to be held a more grievous crime, and this kind of whoredom most foul, because adultery concurred with incest. Cornelius à Lapide, with certain others, concludes that she was the wife of a living father rather than the concubine whom he had in incest. For this is properly called the wife of a dead father and a widow. And from Anselm he refers the words of 2 Cor. VII. v. 12 hither: I wrote this not for his sake that did the wrong, nor for his sake that suffered. At least this is undoubted, that it was not done secretly, but, with the Church aware, the stepmother was abused, inasmuch as she is blamed for this reason, that by her connivance she participated in the crime. That indeed ὀὐδὲ ὀνομάζεται is explained less conveniently: it is scarcely found; because many examples of those who married stepmothers, of Antiochus Soter, and of Darius, as Plutarch testifies, of Menephontes in Ovid, Book VII of the Metamorphoses, of Antonius Caracalla, of Spartianus, of the Emperor Claudius, of Sextus Aurelius, and of others are extant, which were not unknown to the Holy Scriptures. And therefore it is more correctly said that it is not so much a matter of the fact, as of the approval, namely that even the saner and more honest nations did not approve of such things, and did not even name such foul crimes, except with detestation, inasmuch as the delinquents themselves even detested them; just as Antiochus Soter, the son of Seleucus, preferred to die than to reveal his incest, as Valerius Maximus testifies, Book V, chapter on parental love. and Phoenix in Homer, Iliad IX, complained that he was cursed because he had relations with his father's concubine.

Latin:

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ ΕΠΑΝΟΡΘΩΤΙΚΗ. CAPUT V.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Reprehendit Corinthios Apostolus ob incestum cum noverca toleratum, hominemque decernit excommunicandum, ut fermentum, cujus vel exigua pars totam massam corrumpit, expurgetur, & pascha in azymis sinceritatis & veritatis celebretur. Repetit, scortatoribus non esse communicandum, quod non de illis aut similibus facinorosis, qui in mundo sunt, sed qui fratres esse volunt, accipiendum; illos vero, qui foris sunt, Deum judicaturum esse docet.

PArtes tres sunt I. De incestuosi excommunica- tione ad v. 5. II. De fermenti veteris expurga- tione ad v. 8. III. De vitanda communione cum flagitiosis ad v. 13.

PARS I. De incestuosi excommunicatione.

V. 1. Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία.

Primum indignum, quod apud vos Christum professos ulla audiatur turpitudo: Deinde vero talis: Ὅλως, id est ulla omnino: ut μὴ ὀμνύναι ὅλως apud Justinum & Chryso- stomum, quod alibi καθόλꙋ. Vide ad Matth. V. 33. πορνείας nomine non sola scortatio significatur, sed omnis Venus contra fas, jura, bonosque mores. Etiam adulteria eo no- mine venire annotavimus ad Matth. V. 32. Sic apud Pro- phetas תזנות & זנות saepissime sumitur. Veniunt eo nomine etiam conjugia illegitima. Tertullianus de pudi- citia: Ideo penes nos occulta quoque conjunctiones, id est, non prius ad Ecclesiam professa, juxta mochiam & fornicationem judicari periclitantur. Sic Basilio Αἱ κόραι, αἳ παρὰ γνώμην τῦ πατρὸς ἀκολꙋθήσασαι πορνεύꙋσι: Et: Ἡ παρὰ γνώμην τᾶ δεσπότε ἀνδρὶ ἑαυτὴν ἐκδῶσα ἐπόρνευσεν. Item: Ἐάν τις πά- θη ἀκαθαρσίας κρατηθεὶς ἐκπέσοι πρὸς δυοῖν ἀδελφῶν ἄθε- σμον κοινωνίαν, μὴ γάμον ἡγεῖσθαι τῦτο.

Καὶ τοιαύτη πορνεία, ἥτις ὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ὀνομάζε- ται, ὥστε γυναῖκά τινὰ τᾶ πατρὸς ἔχειν.

Ἔχειν hic est quasi conjuge uti quomodo intellexit Syrus. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XIV. 4. ubi & hoc notavimus, uxorem alicujus dici eam, quæ uxor fuit, etiam marito jam defuncto. In manuscripto deest ὀνομάζεται, quod nec La- tinus in suo habuit codice. Tale probrum dicit Aposto- lus etiam in gentibus non reperiri, id est, vix reperiri. Vere Plutarchus Seleucum narrat, cum vellet Stratonicen uxo- rem suam filio suo Antiocho concedere, veritum ne ipsa of- fenderetur τῷ μὴ νενομισμένῳ ut re illicita. Et Cicero in re simili dicit: Scelus in omni vita inauditum.

In reprehensione notamus primo incestus deli- ctum: Secundo Corinthiorum reatum: Tertio scan- dali publici remedium. Delictum exaggerat Apo- stolus primum ceu notorium, voce ὅλως, quæ non ad vocem πορνείας cum Grotio trahenda, nec cum Crellio ut connexionis particula accipienda, quasi Apostolus postquam virgam minatus fuerat, di- cat: Ne multis utar ambagibus, id quod res est, ex- ponam. Qualis vocis usus nuspiam in N. T. reperi- tur; sed ad veritatem rumorum, & notorietatem exprimendam: Quem sensum nec ipse Crellius negavit, & affumpsit Schlichtingius. Deinde ut gravissimum, quod πορνεία scortatio inter ipsos audiatur, quod flagitium inter Christianos audi- ri minime debeat Eph. V. 3. & quidem scortatio non simplex sed talis, quæ nec inter Ethnicos, se- cundum saniorum ex ipsis judicium nominari de- beat, apud quos proinde ideo Christianismus turpissime prostituitur. Ac denique ea, à qua na- tura ipsa peculiariter abhorreat, ὥστε γυναῖκα τᾶ πατρὸς ἔχειν, quod incestuosus concubitus inter ipsos cum noverca, uxore patris sui admittatur. An vero conjugio ipsi junctus fuerit, quod ex voce ἔχειν Grotius non satis firmiter colligit, num con- suetudine ejus usus sit citra conjugii vinculum, plerique in medio relinquunt. Videtur tamen posterius vero similius, tum ex vocis πορνείας fa- mosiori significatu, tum ex eo quod dissolvendum fuerit conjugium incestuosum, non tantum ex- communicanda incestuosa persona, de quo vero nihil monuit Apostolus. Nec id liquet, vitricum incesti jam satis concessisse, atque ideo gravius delictum habendum, maximeque fœdum hoc scortationis genus, quod adulterium cum incestu concurrerit. Cornelius à Lapide cum quibusdam aliis colligit, uxorem viventis potius patris fuisse, quam concubinam incestus habuit. Hæc enim di- citur proprie uxor Patris mortui & vidua. Et ex Anshelmo verba 2. Cor. VII. v. 12. huc refert: Hæc scripsi non propter eum, qui fecit injuriam, nec propter eum, qui passus est. Saltem id indubium, quod non clam, sed, conscia Ecclesia, noverca abu- fus fuerit, utpote quæ ideo reprehenditur, quod conniventia sua sceleri participaverit. Illud vero ὀὐδὲ ὀνομάζεται minus commode explicatur: vix reperitur; quia exempla plura eorum, qui duxêre novercas, Antiochi Soteris, & Dariı, teste Plutar- cho, Menephontis apud Ovidium 1. VII. Metam. Antonii Caracallæ, Spartiani, Imperatoris Claudii, Sexti Aurelii, & aliorum prostant, quæ S. S. igno- ta non erant. Ideoque rectius dicitur non tam de re, quam approbatione agi, quod nempe et- iam gentes saniores & honestiores talia haud ap- probarint, ac ne quidem nominarint tam fœda scelera, nisi cum detestatione, utpote quæ etiam delinquentes ipsimet detestati sunt; quemadmo- dum Antiochus Soter, Seleuci filius mori maluit, quam incestum suum aperire, perhibente Vale- rio M. l. V. c. de par. am. & Phœnix apud Home- rum Iliad. IX. conquestus est, se maledictum esse, quod cum concubina Patris rem habuit.

## 5:2
V. 2. And you are puffed up.

You are puffed up with the opinion of a certain greater wisdom, which considers such things indifferent. For so the Cynics and Stoics also thought. But if Christians are bound by the civil laws of every people, as Paul teaches in chapter XIII to the Romans, much more are they bound by those which are accepted among all well-mannered peoples, not without a weightier reason, and especially those which agree with the law given by GOD to the Hebrews through Moses. See Lev. XVIII. 8. Perhaps someone will wonder that the Roman Proconsul did not exact penalties for such incest. But undoubtedly an accuser was lacking, nor were Roman magistrates accustomed to inquire solicitously into those things that did not directly touch the public state.

And have you not rather mourned?

Metonymy of the Adjunct. For because the Church, when it was about to exclude someone from its fellowship, used to take on the habit of mourners, it came about that it is said to mourn, instead of to excommunicate. Thus the ancients interpret πενθήσω, 2 Cor. XII. 21. Clement in the Constitutions II: 'With grief and mourning, send away him who is behaving improperly from the Church.' Tertullian on Modesty: 'The Church does not bring joy to the one who has found it, but mourning.' Origen against Celsus III: 'These (Christians) mourn for those who have perished, or who have fallen into some absurdity, as if they were dead.' The bishops of the Synod of Ephesus to the Church of Constantinople, narrating the deposition of Nestorius: 'Having first wept over what had happened.' Thus also Theodoret in his twelfth sermon against the Greeks: 'or we shall mourn for those who are living and will live like beasts in a shameful manner,' etc.

That he who has done this deed might be removed from among you.

Not by death, as Tertullian seems to have understood, but by כרוי. For the Apostles retained all the praiseworthy institutions of the Synagogue. And if anyone compares what the Hebrews wrote about that matter with the customs of the ancient Church, he will find a wonderful agreement. ἐξαίρειν ἐκ μέσου is to exclude from the Church, as Cyprian speaks. You ought to have prayed that the whole Church, consenting, would excommunicate such people. 'And in discord, even the most wicked shares in honor.'

The guilt of the Corinthians is threefold: (1.) That they were still puffed up with the persuasion of wisdom and excellence, when they tolerated so foul a crime in their midst, which the saner and more honest Gentiles would not have tolerated at all. (2.) That they did not mourn because of that stain on their Church, which ought to have been entirely deplored. (3.) That they did not even think about a remedy and the removal of the wicked man, so that the author of such a great scandal might be taken from their midst, and the public scandal itself might cease. Thus the Apostle hints at what the parts of the Church are in more atrocious sins, namely that the Church should mourn and think about remedies. Mourning has a cause when one sins enormously, and therefore the name of the Lord is blasphemed among the nations. For when it does not mourn, but connives, not only does the whole Church get a bad name, and many are affected by the scandal; but the wrath of GOD is stirred up against the whole assembly, and guilt is drawn upon the entire body. Therefore public offenses were to be expiated publicly by the Israelite Church, Deut. XXI. But there is no reason for us to understand mourning either as a public fast with some, or as a ceremony of mourning joined to excommunication, or as excommunication itself with Grotius, nor is mourning taken in that sense in 2 Cor. XII. 21. But it holds its proper meaning there. However, it is rightly denied that this ἵνα ἐξαρθῇ deals with capital punishment, which the law dictates for the incestuous. Because the Apostle does not say simply, that he might be taken from the midst; but from the midst of you, that is, of the Church: and to inflict capital punishment does not pertain to the Church, but to the civil magistrate: the Apostle prescribes the reason for taking him from the midst of the Church, not killing, but excommunication.

Latin:

V. 2. Καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐσί.

Inflati estis majori cujusdam sapientiæ opinione, quæ talia censet ἀδιάφορα. Ita enim censebant & Cynici & Stoi- ci. Atqui si legibus civilibus cujusque populi tenentur Christiani, ut Paulus docet cap. XIII. ad Romanos, multo magis iis, quæ apud omnes bene moratos populos rece- ptæ sunt, non sine graviori ratione, & iis maxime, quæ cum lege à DEO per Mosen Hebræis data consentiunt Vide Lev. XVIII. 8. Mirabitur forte aliquis Romanum Proconsulem pœnas non exegisse de tali incēstu. Sed ni- mirum defuit accusator, neque solebant Romani Magistra- tus in ista statum publicum non directe tangentia solicite inquirere.

Καὶ ὀὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἐπενθήσατε.

Metonymia Adjuncti. Nam quia Ecclesia, cum aliquem esset à suo consortio exclusura, lugentium sumebat habi- tum, eo factum, ut lugere dicatur, pro excommunicare. Sic πενθήσω interpretantur veteres, 2. Cor. XII. 21. Clemens Constitutionum II. Μετὰ λύπης καὶ πένθυς ἀπάτως ἔχοντα τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἀποπέμπετε. Tertullianus de pudicitia: Nec gaudium confert repertrici Ecclesia, sed luctum. Origenes contra Celsum III. Ου̗τοι δὲ (Christiani) ἀπολωλότας, ἡ̓ τινος ἀτόπῳ γενημένους ὡς νεκρὺς πενθοῦσι. Episcopi Synodi Ephesinæ ad Ecclesiam Constantinopolitanam narrantes depositionem Nestorii : Πρότερον μὲν ἐπὶ τῷ γεγονότι δακρύ- σαντες. Sic & Theodoretus sermone duodecimo adversus Græcos: ἡ̓τι ἐπιμώμωι θηριώδως βιώσοντες, κα̖ι περίοντας θρηνήσομεν &c.

Ἴνα ἐξαρθῇ ἐκ μέσυ ὑμῶν ὁ τὸ ἔργον τῦτο ποιήσας.

Non per mortem, ut videtur intellexisse Tertullianus, sed per כרוי. Nam omnia laudabilia instituta Synagogæ retinuere Apostoli. Et si quis, quæ Hebræi de ea re scri- psere, cum moribus antiquæ Ecclesiæ comparet, miram inveniet congruentiam. ἐξαίρειν ἐκ μέσου est ex Ecclesia ex- cludere, quomodo loquitur Cyprianus. Orasse debuera- tis, ut tota Ecclesia consentiens tales excommunicaret. Ἐν δὲ διχοστασία̕ καὶ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς.

Reatus Corinthiorum triplex est (1.) quod sa- pientiæ, & excellentiæ persuasione adhuc inflati fuerint, cum scelus tam fœdum in medio sui to- lerarint, quod saniores & honestiores gentiles minime tolerassent. (2.) Quod ob istam Eccle- siæ suæ maculam haud luxerint, quæ omnino de- ploranda fuerat. (3.) Quod ne quidem cogita- rint de remedio, & remotione scelerati, ut de me- dio tolleretur tanti scandali autor, ipsumque pu- blicum scandalum cessaret. Ita quæ sint Ecclesiæ partes in peccatis atrocioribus subinnuit Apo- stolus, ut nempe lugeat Ecclesia, & de remediis cogitet. Luctus causam habet, quando unus enor- miter delinquit, & ideo nomen Domini blasphe- matur inter gentes. Ea enim non lugente, sed connivente non modo tota Ecclesia male audit, plurimique scandalo afficiuntur; sed ira DEI in totum cœtum concitatur, ac reatus universitati attrahitur. Ideo publica delicta publice ab Ec- clesia Israëlitica erant expianda Deut. XXI. Ut vero luctum vel de jejunio publico cum nonnul- lis, vel de ceremonia luctus adjuncta excommuni- cationi, aut de ipsa excommunicatione cum Grotio intelligamus, causa nulla est, nec eo sensu luctus accipitur 2. Cor. XII. 21. Sed propria ibi obtinet significatio. Recte autem negatur, ista ἵνα ἐξαρθῇ de supplicio capitali agere, quod lex incestuosis dictitat. Quia non simpliciter ait Apostolus, ut tolleretur e medio; sed è medio vestri, hoc est, Ecclesiæ: & capitis supplicium, irrogare non ad Ecclesiam pertinet, sed ad magistratum civilem: rationem tollendi e medio Ecclesiæ præscri- bit Apostolus non occisionem; sed excommu- nicationem.

## 5:3
V. 3. For I indeed, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have already judged as though present, him who has so done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan.

In the manuscript, ὡς is missing: Not bad. It was the duty of the Apostles, if anything was neglected in the Church, to supply it by their authority, with miracles often accompanying. He says he is absent in body, but present in spirit, that is, in mind, for the reason that he saw all things which were being done there, just as Elisha did when he was absent from Gehazi, 2 Kings 5:26. Where 'my heart' is, for that which is 'my spirit' here. Chrysostom rightly connects that 'in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ' with the following 'when you are gathered together.' For as often as the faithful assemble, they assemble in the name of Christ. But when he says 'you,' he does not mean all the Corinthians who wished to be called Christians (for they were divided among themselves), but the best. But what he adds, 'and my spirit,' by that he signifies: just as he now knew all things that were happening there, so he would also see what they were about to do then. Furthermore, he says that the very miraculous power, namely of Christ, would be present with him. But to deliver to Satan is to pray to God that He may deliver him into the power of Satan, namely, that he may be vexed by him with diseases. So also 1 Tim. 1:20. For just as Satan sometimes receives that power specially to tempt the pious, as Job 1:4, 5, 6, 7 and Paul 2 Cor. 12:7, so he generally obtains it against those who, although they are profane, yet wish to be reckoned among the pious.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἐγὼ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ἀπὼν τῷ σώματι, παρὼν δὲ τῷ πνεύ- ματι, ἤδη κέκρικα ὡς παρὼν, τὸν ὕτω τῦτο κατεργασάμε- νον, ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, συναχθέντων ὑμῶν, καὶ τῦ ἐμῦ πνεύματος, σὺν τῇ δυνάμει τῦ κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, παραδῦναι τὸν τοιῦτον Σατανᾷ.

In Manuscripto deest ὡς : Non male. Apostolorum erat munus, si quid in Ecclesia negligebatur, id supplere sua autoritate, accedentibus sæpe & miraculis. Absentem se dicit corpore, præsentem vero spiritu, id est, animo, ideo, quod omnia videret, quæ ibi gerebantur, ut Elisæus qua- se absente faciebat Giezi 2. Reg. V. 26. Ubi est cor meum, pro eo, quod hic est Spiritus. Illud ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ κύ- ριυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ recte conjungit Chrysostomus cum sequentibus συναχθέντων ὑμῶν. Nam fideles quoties con- veniunt, conveniunt in Christi nomine. Vos autem cum dicit, non omnes Corinthios, qui Christiani dici volebant, intelligit (erant enim scissi inter se) sed optimos. Quod autem addit, καὶ τῦ ἐμῦ πνεύματος, eo significat, Sicut nunc cognoscebat omnia, quæ ibi fierent, ita tunc etiam, quæ facturi essent, se visurum. Præterea dicit ipsam virtutem mirificam, nempe Christi, ipsi adfuturam. Tradere au- tem Satanæ est precari Deum, ut eum tradat in potesta- tem Satanæ, nempe ut per eum morbis vexetur. Sic & 1. Tim. I. 20. Nam eam potestatem sicut interdum specia- liter Satanas accipit ad tentandos pios, ut Jobum II. 4. 5. 6. 7. & Paulum 2. Cor. XII. 7. Ita plerumque eam obti- net in eos, qui profani cum sint, piis tamen accenseri vo- lunt.

## 5:5
V. 5. For the destruction of the flesh.

So that by the sense of divine wrath, carnal affections may be extinguished in him. Thus 'flesh' is taken in Rom. 7:5, 8:9. 'Destruction of the flesh' is said in a similar way to 'mortifying the deeds of the body,' Rom. 8:13.

That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ.

That the spirit, that is, the soul deposited with God (see Luke 23:46, Acts 7:59), may not perish, but be saved for Him, to be restored, of course, to the body on the day of the resurrection, 2 Tim. 1:12. Temporary evil heals many, Ps. 83:17.

The remedy for scandal, therefore, is excommunication; of which, as is manifest from this passage, if you attend to the principal efficient cause, the Lord Jesus Christ is named, in whose name the faithful are gathered, and excommunication is instituted. Therefore, the one to be excommunicated is said to be delivered 'with the power' of our Lord Jesus Christ into the power of Satan. This sacred act, therefore, is not to be undertaken except by divine authority, and in the fear of the Lord, with the imploring of divine assistance. If you look to the ministerial cause, it ought not to be done either by the ministers of the word alone, or by the Church alone: but by the ministry and the assembly of the Church together: just as the Apostle names both himself as absent indeed in body, but present in spirit, and the Church gathered in the name of Jesus Christ together with his spirit, where Grotius rashly understands not all Christians, but the best. For who were to be gathered in this way, or who were to be considered the best, would have been in obscurity. Nor is it noted there by 'and my spirit' only that Paul would see by the Spirit what things are to come, but presence and authority are implied, because if not corporally, yet in spirit, the minister of the Church and the Bishop, whom the Apostle was referring to, ought to be present, conscious, and consenting, and by his authority excommunication is to be instituted. To the form of ex- excommunication pertains the delivery into the power of Satan, which brings with it the exclusion from the kingdom of GOD, inasmuch as the kingdom, that is, the power of Satan, is opposed to it: By which such a person is removed from the fellowship of the Church and the communion of saints, not only as a public assembly of the Church and admission to hearing the word of GOD in that particular Church and to using the sacraments: but also as private familiar conversation with the faithful, unless the reason of political or economic necessity demands it, as is to be gathered from v. 11: You shall not eat with him: and also the peculiar power of Satan, which God wills to permit to the same over such persons. Whence those cast out outside the society of the Church, and deprived of its goods, are so exposed to the tyranny of the Devil, whose power is outside the Church, that he rages against them more than before, and drives them into every evil. Rightly Theodoret on this passage: He assembled a court full of horror. He established a judgment full of horror. For first he gathered everyone in the name of the Lord. Then he also introduced himself through the grace of the spirit, and showed that the Lord himself presides and pronounces sentence, and delivers to the lictor, and prescribes the end, so that he may chastise the body alone. For he prepares a medicine for the soul from salutary discipline. From this, however, we are taught that the Devil invades those who are segregated and separated from the Ecclesiastical body, finding them destitute of grace. And in 1 Tim. I. 20. For those separated from the Ecclesiastical body and stripped of divine grace were cruelly scourged by the adversary, fell into diseases, and difficult afflictions. They are delivered, however, to Satan, not so that they may be fully committed to Diabolical power, which is joined with eternal destruction, but for the destruction of the flesh, which Chrysostom, Theophylact, Anselm, and the author of the interlinear gloss understand indeed as the death and affliction of the body: Others more generally as scourges to be sent by Satan, whether through external affliction of the body, or through internal anxieties, horrors, and terrors of conscience, such as Hymenaeus and Philetus experienced 1 Tim. I. 20, and not unless rashly

Thomas Erastus denied that such power is given in the Church, by which it can so eject stubborn criminals from Ecclesiastical communion that they are even delivered to Satan to afflict the soul with anxiety; against whom this matter has been treated by Bellarmine and Suarez u. s. and Sander on the key of David and particularly by Theodore Beza. The end of this excommunication and sifting by Satan is partly subtractive, so that the flesh may perish, when it is said to be for the destruction of the flesh, namely the destruction of the lustful flesh, which ought to be so tamed by new contrition and the crucifixion of the old man that it may perish, in which manner Augustine explains it in book III, ch. 1 against Parmenianus, to the destruction of the flesh, that is, so that through repentance, since he had been delivered to Satan, he might destroy the wicked concupiscence of the flesh, just as a similar end is expressed when Hymenaeus and Alexander were delivered to Satan, namely so that they might learn not to blaspheme: Partly positive, so that the spirit may be saved: Which, with the flesh mortified, is raised up, and with the old man corrupted, the new one comes forth, who finally attains salvation: That the spirit may be saved, that is, so that the miserable sinner may finally be saved in spirit, or according to the spirit, or according to the new spiritual man, as it is said in Gal. VI. 8, he who sows in the spirit, will reap eternal life from the spirit: And just as flesh and blood or our nature, as it is corruptible, cannot possess the kingdom of GOD 1 Cor. XV. 50. So neither as it is subject to sin: And therefore it is necessary for the flesh to perish, so that the spirit may be saved, and for our outward man to be corrupted, so that he who is within may be renewed day by day 2 Cor. IV. 16, and that we may be transformed into the image of Christ from glory to glory ch. III. 18, until we pass from this imperfection to perfection, when that which is in part shall be done away, and that which is perfect shall come, or succeed 1 Cor. XIII. 10. Whence the Apostle warns that, having these promises, we should cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of GOD 2 Cor. VII. 1. For if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live. Rom. VIII. 13. And being freed from sin, and having become servants to righteousness, we have our fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life Rom. VI. 22. The end therefore of this delivery into the power of Satan is not that the wicked person should perish either in soul or body, but that he may be brought back from sin to repentance and eternal life. And while the lust of the flesh is tamed, the old man is crucified, mortified, and corrupted; but the spirit escapes saved. And in that sense Ambrose and Anselm explain it, as well as Augustine in book III against Parmenianus, ch. 2. destruction of the flesh, that carnal pleasure may perish, which however, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Cornelius à Lapide etc., they accept as concerning the sickness of the body, wounds, or plagues, by which he ought to have been macerated by the Devil, so that the flesh might be worn down, and the vigor of the flesh might perish, so that being thus humbled he might repent, so that the spirit might be saved, that is, so that the soul and mind, repenting and renewed by this punishment, might be saved in the day of judgment. Which, however, is not to be taken exclusively concerning the soul alone, even if it is the proper subject of repentance and renewal. Our blessed Hunnius says, the effect of this work is a temporal punishment, by which the excommunicated man is harassed by Satan with temptations, and is afflicted with terrors of conscience, or other calamities sent by GOD, by which his flesh is subdued and tamed, so that there may be a place for the Holy Spirit to elicit a salutary conversion in the mind, so that the spirit, and consequently with the spirit the body also, may be saved in the day of the Lord. To which explanation the blessed Hülsemann also adds his approval, alleging for the same Tertullian lib. IV contra Marc. ch. 6, Cyprian Ep. XXIX and XL, and Augustine in the aforementioned book. Hugo, Thomas, Salmeron, Estius, Melanchthon, and Hemmingius, but they seem to be hindered both by the opposition of flesh and spirit, which in the sense familiar to Paul must be accepted not as body and soul, but as the exterior or new man, as it is also accepted by Christ in John 3:5, and by the fact that this does not so much contribute to the end of the delivery into the power of Satan by the intention of Paul and the Church, so that a man may be afflicted in body and soul by Satan, as it does to the formal aspect of that power, to which he is committed for the destruction of the flesh and the salvation of the spirit, and by the fact that that opposition is with difficulty reconciled or explained, since not only the spirit, that is, the soul, ought to obtain plenary salvation on the day of the Lord, but the body also along with the spirit: Nor are those afflictions to be referred to the body only, but primarily to the soul, which is to be harassed by terrors and horrors, so that the wrath of God may be felt in the conscience, and it may be miserably tormented. Which will then be more fully established from the discussion of the Socinian ψευδερμηνείας [false interpretation].

The end, therefore, is not damnation, but the salvation of the evildoers, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of Jesus Christ. And therefore excommunication does not bring about total excision, such as that of Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5. For to this Peter did not use the delivery to Satan, but the power of Christ: Not the deprivation of goods, possessions, and dominion, such as the Papists Bellarmine, Suarez, and Sanders on the key of David derive from the power of excommunication, by virtue of which they strip Kings themselves and Princes of their kingdoms, dominions, and possessions: But the suspension and deprivation of the powers and benefits of the Church, and anxiety of soul, with which those who are in his power are agitated by Satan, then also at times affliction of the body. However, this punishment is Ecclesiastical, not political; therefore, it is not permitted to conclude from it that heretics, as excommunicated persons, are to be subjected to capital punishment, which is done by Bellarmine, book 3, on the laity, chapter 21, proceeding from the greater to the less, but not in the same, rather a different kind of punishment. Whence an ἀσυλλογισία (non-sequitur) arises, namely from an Ecclesiastical punishment to a political one. See B. Gerhard on the Magistrate, § 362.

Furthermore, regarding the object of excommunication, it must be observed that the object of the greater excommunication is not Kings and Princes. For the greater excommunication, as B. Hülsemann warns in his work on fraternal correction, p. 302, which forbids Christians from free and voluntary commerce of eating, drinking, and conversing with the excommunicated, has no place in Kings, just as it does not in spouses, lest they deny the conjugal debt, or in children, lest they perform due duties to their parents; or in servants and subjects, lest they show services to their Lords. For a spiritual punishment of the soul does not dissolve the bonds which the divine law, the law of nature, and the law of nations have bound; but only those which have been contracted by the communion of baptism and the sacrament of the Supper: which has not been conferred by the benefit of the Church, nor can it be taken away from anyone by the censure of the Church. Compare also B. Luther on the Ban, Vol. I, Jena, German. & in the admonition to the Ecclesiastics gathered at Augsburg in the year 1530, Vol. V, Jena, German. B. Dannhauer praises this opinion of B. Hülsemann in his book, The Conscience Opened, part II, p. 1133. If the question is about positive, extreme, greater excommunication, and yet one to be inflicted upon an unwilling and refractory person, whether such rigor ought to be extended to a King? He also praises a similar opinion of M. Antonio de Dominis in book VI, On the Ecclesiastical Republic, ch. 9, p. 751. If we take excommunication for that ordinary, rigorous punishment by which we are accustomed to exclude someone from the society of our faithful, so that he is to us as a Gentile and a tax collector, with a prohibition that the faithful should not use his custom and company, certainly a supreme prince neither can nor ought to be excommunicated. He cannot, because for the same reason that this excommunication works nothing in children with respect to a father, in Lords with respect to their family, in a wife with respect to her husband, because, as the Scholastics and Sumists teach everywhere, this excommunication can do nothing against the law of nature, by the same right, surely, as a father must perpetually take care of his children and family, so also every king must take care of his whole people, and the people of necessity need the care and government of their king. But neither ought he, even if a king could be excommunicated by such an excommunication, out of prudence, according to the excellent rule of Augustine. M. Antonio concludes: Morally speaking, therefore, the counsel of such a separation, according to Augustine's rule, will always be both vain and pernicious, nay, as the same asserts, both impious, and proud, and sacrilegious. B. Hülsemann adds notably: furthermore, one must proceed cautiously and slowly even to the lesser excommunication of Kings and Princes on account of the inseparable danger of schism and to avert a greater evil from the Church, if they are stubborn and unwilling to be corrected. And this is also to be observed in other persons, when the danger of schism and the ruin of the Church is to be feared. The excommunication of the guilty is to be suspended or even omitted if it appears that a schism in the whole community, or a greater evil than the toleration of sins, would arise from it. Nor, because certain sinners are not excommunicated, should the external communion with the innocent, among whom they live, be abandoned. Where, regarding the precept of the Apostle in this chapter, last verse. “Remove the evil from among you,” St. Augustine responds thus: In this, as it were, narrowness of the question, do not say anything new or unusual, but what the health of the Church observes, that when any of the brothers, that is, of the Christians established within the society of the Church, has been caught in any such sin that he is held worthy of anathema, let this be done, WHERE THERE IS NO DANGER OF SCHISM, and that, with that love, about which he himself commands elsewhere, saying, do not consider him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother. For you are not [there] to eradicate, but to correct. The things which St. Augustine adds there are worthy to be read here as well. But if he does not acknowledge himself, nor correct himself by repenting, he himself will go out, and by his own will will be severed from the unity of the Church. For the Lord himself also, with the servants wishing to gather the tares, said: let both grow until the harvest; he prefaced the cause, saying, lest perhaps, when you wish to gather the tares, you eradicate the wheat along with them. Where he sufficiently shows that, when that fear is not present, but rather a certain security remains regarding the certain stability of the grains; that is, when the crime of each one is so known to all, and appears execrable to all, that it has either no defenders at all, or not such ones through whom a schism could arise; let not the severity of discipline sleep, in which the correction of depravity is so much more effective, as the preservation of charity is more diligent. But then this can be done without the stain of peace and unity, and without the injury of the grains, when the multitude of the congregation of the Church is alien to that crime which has been anathematized. Ivo of Chartres, Ep. 144, to Paschal: You should temper the cause of Kings, he says, lest that of Solomon happen regarding him: “He who wrings the nose brings forth blood.” And Ep. 132, to the Bishop of Sens: And because the dispensations of temporal things are attributed to Kings, and they are the Basileus, that is, the foundation of the people, and its head, if they sometimes abuse the power granted to them, they are not to be gravely exasperated by us. But where they have not acquiesced to the admonitions of the Priests, they are to be reserved for divine judgment.

Crellius the Socinian denies that simple excommunication is designated here: "He wishes something more to be signified, for which, namely, the singular power of the Lord Jesus and Apostolic authority is needed. Nor can it be said rightly of those who are only temporarily barred from the fellowship of the Church that they are delivered to the power of Satan, since no right over them is therefore given to Satan, neither according to the flesh nor according to the spirit. Therefore, it does not seem doubtful to him that various afflictions of the body to be inflicted by Satan are signified by these words, no differently than if someone were delivered to Satan as if to some executioner to be vexed and punished. By the destruction of the flesh, however, he wishes not a certain metaphorical death of carnal appetite to be signified, but the true and proper death and destruction of the body itself, although brought about not suddenly, but gradually through various afflictions and pains." Since neither is Satan a suitable minister of a good thing by himself, and not a life lived according to the judgment of the spirit, but salvation in the day of our Lord is opposed to the destruction of the flesh: And finally, the Greek word ὄλεθρος seems too harsh to designate this spiritual death of the flesh, nor is it used by the Apostle in this sense anywhere. To this also tend the commentaries of Jonas Schlichting in his Commentary on this passage. But these things do not hinder the common opinion of the Fathers and our own theologians and other interpreters, who agree on this, that the discourse here is about excommunication. For although the δύναμις or power of Jesus is required for this, that someone be delivered to Satan, it is not, however, an extraordinary or miraculous power: Although the Apostle joins himself to the ecclesiastical assembly in this act, he is viewed here not as an Apostle, but as a minister of the Church, from 1 Cor. IV. 1, nor is this a property of Apostolic authority. That this pertains to miracles, and therefore the Church ought not to arrogate to itself that it should deliver someone to Satan, Schlichtingius rashly assumes. For in that way, binding sins would also have to be considered a miracle. Schlichtingius admits that the Church can pour out prayers to Christ, that he may deliver the unclean, especially apostates, blasphemers, and persecutors, to Satan. And since Christ is willing to hear, and does hear, the prayers of the Church: Can the Church not, by its prayers, deliver such people into the power of Satan? For Schlichtingius acknowledges here that excommunication has such prayers attached to it, and is therefore called Anathema Maran Atha, ch. XVI. 22. Wherefore there is no doubt that those who are excommunicated in this way are delivered to Satan, which was also done here. Whom he is accustomed to torment with anxieties of conscience, and sometimes also with afflictions, having received power over them. Which was observed before from Theodoret; yet I would not altogether deny that there could have been something extraordinary in the present example, when the singular afflictions of soul and body, through the efficacy of the Apostle's prayers to lead the soul away from eternal destruction through serious repentance, intervened, which the Apostle brings forward only so that the man might finally be freed from his unusual wickedness and snatched from the jaws of Satan through those very Satanic afflictions. Nor does the Church only pour out prayers to God, but it carries out a judicial sentence, ratified in heaven, concerning which our B. Hunnius says: We are warned that legitimate excommunication is not an empty scarecrow, or a flash of lightning from a chamber pot, but an action and sentence ratified and effective before God, and thus pregnant with the judgment of temporal and eternal punishments. For such people are truly delivered to Satan according to the immovable sentence of Christ in Matt. 16 and 18, as also in John 20. And why should not the destruction of the flesh indicate the improper death of carnal appetite? If indeed the end of these afflictions, according to the intention of God and the Church (though not of Satan), is true repentance, which brings about the recognition of sin, which is followed by the mortification of the flesh, so that concupiscences are extinguished and the old man is abolished. Nor indeed is the death and destruction of the body itself signified by the destruction of the flesh, for thus he would rather have said the destruction of the body, nor is it established by the examples of this incestuous man, or Hymenaeus, or Alexander in 1 Tim. I. 20, or others, that they were so struck by the Apostle, or delivered to Satan to be struck, that they were afflicted with a slow death by bodily afflictions, so that they might prepare themselves for repentance, that the spirit might be saved; there is deep silence in the scriptures concerning such a miraculous striking. On the contrary, it is clear that this criminal was preserved even in temporal life, from 2 Cor. VII. 7. What also was the point of the Church praying that it might grant pardon to the repentant adulterer, unless he had been delivered to the power of Satan by the Church and the Apostle at the same time? For he had to be freed from Satan in turn by those by whom he had been delivered to him. Then if he was to be afflicted by Satan even unto death, and was delivered to Satan by the Apostle for that reason and intention, by an authority not pastoral but Apostolic, why does the Apostle beseech the Corinthians to grant him pardon?

The arguments of Crellius against the more accepted meaning of the destruction of the flesh have no strength. For although Satan by himself and from his own intention is not a minister of such a good thing: it can nevertheless be that it pertains to him, accidentally and beyond his intention, according to divine ordination and direction, since God knows how to direct temptations, even Diabolical ones, to a good end: as is clear here, that the afflictions of Satan are directed to the salvation of the soul, which Crellius cannot deny: Furthermore, he says, by these words, as also by the following ones, in which the end of the delivery to Satan is indicated, limits are indeed placed on the power of Satan, not that he should only afflict the body and have no right over the soul; nor that he should extinguish the man with sudden death, but consume him with slow blows, so that he might perform repentance, and correct his life, and consequently obtain eternal salvation at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Not otherwise than the power of that Satan to whom Job had been permitted was circumscribed, although not in the same way: There indeed, so that he would not harm Job's life, but here, so that he would not harm the heavenly salvation of this man. Furthermore, salvation on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ is indeed opposed to the destruction of the flesh; but the ultimate positive end is named in this way, the intermediate one is not excluded, but included, as being the vivification of the spirit, which is directly and immediately opposed to the mortification of the flesh, which finally is followed by salvation on the day of the Lord. That he says thirdly that the Greek word ὄλεθρον is too harsh to designate the spiritual death of the flesh is vain and frivolous. For are not other words of this kind used by the Apostle? As for example, you put to death in Rom. VIII. 13, Put to death your members which are on the earth in Col. III. 5, They crucified the flesh in Gal. V. 24, The outer man is perishing in 2 Cor. IV. 16, Having died to sins in 1 Pet. II. 24, etc. Nor does the word ὄλεθρος always denote total destruction: it often designates only affliction, as can be seen from the usage of the LXX Interpreters and the concordances of Kircher. It nowhere implies total annihilation, not even when the punishment of the damned themselves is being discussed. And are not the putting to death and the corruption of the flesh sufficient for destruction or perdition? For crucifixion and mortification and corruption tend toward the destruction of the flesh; which, if an altogether total destruction is urged in this word ὄλεθρος, it is manifest that it is more fitting for the flesh or the old man in the extirpation of sin than for our body in its reduction to ashes. For the former ceases to be entirely, the latter does not cease, nor does it go into nothingness, because it will be resurrected gloriously one day on the last day.

As to the fourth, that the term ὀλέθρου τῆς σαρκὸς is nowhere used by the Apostle concerning the mortification of the flesh, I answer: Nor is it used anywhere concerning the total annihilation of the human body; indeed, this is diametrically opposed to the analogy of faith concerning the resurrection of the dead. And it suffices that the synonymous terms which we have adduced are employed by the Apostle. The term ὀλέθρου nowhere occurs with the term τῆς σαρκὸς; indeed, it is used in the New Testament only twice, but concerning destruction in hell, which is of most grievous affliction, not of annihilation. However, there is enough affliction for our flesh and the old man when he is crucified, corrupted, and finally brought to destruction. Finally, one must observe the sophism of the Socinians, by which Crellius, as well as Schlichtingius, attempt to carve out their own entirely atheological and heretical hypothesis here, from the opposition of flesh and spirit, because the flesh is said to be destroyed, but the spirit to be saved, namely that the body of man should perish entirely and be annihilated: but that the spirit alone, that is, the soul, should remain surviving until the day of Jesus Christ. That death will be the total abolition of the body and annihilation, because the term ὀλέθρου denotes destruction, is falsely inferred. For that term does not imply total destruction; nor, when it denotes destruction, does it entail abolition through annihilation, as can be seen in 2 Thessalonians 1:9.

1. Tim. VI. 9. For Scripture teaches that the impious are not to be annihilated on the last day, but are to be cast into eternal fire, and the Socinians do not dare to deny this. For although only the spirit is said to be saved, it is not therefore denied to the body itself, inasmuch as it is one day to be resurrected to eternal salvation, because the spirit is not opposed to the body, so that a division of man into soul and body is insinuated, but flesh and spirit, as is frequently done elsewhere, Rom. VII. 14. seqq. Gal. V. 17. &c. are opposed to each other, and thus destruction, nay even total abolition, is appropriate for the flesh. But the spirit is said to be saved, because only the new and spiritual man arrives at eternal life. The Apostle does not therefore divide man, as if he wished him to be partly destroyed, partly saved. For neither can the body perish without separation from the soul, nor can the soul be saved without the salvation of the body, that is, with the body left in perpetual death: But here occurs that antithesis of flesh and spirit familiar to Paul for the old and new man. Nor is there any question here of miraculous punishment and excommunication. For the Corinthians are rebuked because they had not long ago removed the incestuous person from their midst; who indeed could not be rebuked for not having performed a miracle: it is commanded that they remove him: to whom certainly a miracle could not be commanded. For the miracles of the Apostles there was no need of a solemn assembly of the Church. But for the removal of this man, the congregation of the Church in the name of Jesus was required. The end of the delivery into the power of Satan was not that the incestuous person should be killed, but that he might repent in spirit, with the flesh mortified, and not finally perish. Just as for the same end those were delivered to Satan 1. Tim. I. 20. not that they should be killed and removed from the midst, but that they might repent and learn not to blaspheme. Therefore the incestuous person is ordered to be removed, not so that he should not exist, or be removed from the midst of men; but that he should not be tolerated in the midst of the Church, should not be mixed with the brethren, and that food should not be taken with him v. 11. Nor indeed did the Corinthians remove him by a miracle, who nevertheless without doubt executed the command of the Apostle; but by public rebuke they cast him out of the Church, as is evident from 2. Cor. II. 6. ἐπιτιμίαν ὑπὸ πλειόνων, that the rebuke made by the many sufficed for him. Whence Ambrose and Augustine explain this passage in no other way than as referring to his excommunication. Chrysostom indeed and Jerome think that a miraculous punishment was added, but that cannot be gathered from the text, and it is clear that the man remained in life and did not perish by a miracle, nor does Crellius deny this.

He uses a most vain evasion, that this was done because he repented, and that the decree of the Apostle was not absolute, but hypothetical. In which way the decree will be thus: I have now decreed that he who, to wit, has committed this, when you are gathered in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in my name, together with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, i.e., that he be delivered by me and you to Satan to be afflicted, so that, unless he repents, the body may perish: but the spirit may be saved. If, however, he repents, the body may perish. But who will admit that gloss, and where, I pray, is that hypothesis in the text? Do not all things savor of a simple decree? Just as it is simply commanded that they should not mix with him, that they should remove him from their midst. Is not the end, why he is to be delivered to Satan, both that the flesh may perish and that the spirit may be saved? If, however, he was to be afflicted by Satan so that he might be consumed by slow blows, by which he could repent, and the spirit be saved while the body perished, as Crellius interprets, will not repentance in that way be a certain means of saving the spirit, but not of freeing the body from destruction and ruin? But let us finally dismiss those distortions of the Socinians, in which Grotius was certainly sounder here, understanding ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός as the extinction of carnal affections, which is the sense of divine wrath. To whom, however, we cannot add our vote in this, that he explains πνεῦμα as the soul deposited with God, because the spirit, when it is opposed to the flesh, does not denote the soul itself considered in its essence, nor is there anything here about the soul deposited with God, but about the salvation of the flesh of the man who is penitent and mortified, and consequently of the spirit vivified, for whose sake excommunication was to be instituted here as a medicinal remedy.

PART II. Concerning the purging of leaven.

Latin:

V. 5. Εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς.

Ut iræ divinæ sensu carnales affectus in illo extinguan- tur. Ita σὰρξ sumitur Rom. VII. 5. VIII. 9. ὄλεθρος σαρ- κὸς pari modo dicitur quo θανατῦν τὰς πράξεις τῦ σώματος. Rom. VIII. 13.

Ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῦ κυρίυ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ.

Ut Spiritus, id est animus apud Deum depositus (Vide Luc. XIII. 46. Act. VII. 59.) non intereat, sed salvus ei fit, restituendus nimirum corpori in die resurrectionis 2. Tim. I. 12. Multos sanat malum temporarium Ps. LXXXIII. 17.

Remedium itaque scandali est excommunica- tio; cujus, ut ex hoc loco manifestum est, si cau- sam efficientem principalem attendas, Dominus Je- sus Christus nominatur, in cujus nomine congre- gantur fideles, & instituitur excommunicatio. Ideo tradi excommunicandus dicitur σὺν τῇ δυ- νάμει cum virtute Domini nostri Jesu Christi in pote- statem Satanæ. Est itaque hic actus sacer non nisi autoritate divina, & in timore Domini, cum imploratione assistentiæ divinæ suscipiendus.
