In the place of excommunication, where there is either no presbytery or the Church is torn apart, there succeeds a flight from private familiar association: whence that saying of Charondas does not depart far: 'Let no one associate with an unjust man or woman, lest he be reproached as being like them.'

With such a one not even to eat. With such, that is, so vicious and usurping the name of Christians, not even to have common meals, which is the least among the signs of friendship. See Galatians 2:12. You have συνεσθίειν in Genesis 43:32, Psalm 101:5 in the Greek; it was the custom of the Hebrews not to take common food with him who was in נדוי.

He prohibits familiar conversation, such as is wont to be between brothers, not civil dealings: as far as concerns life and ecclesiastical society, not as far as concerns political life. For man in this life leads a double life, as it were; ecclesiastical, insofar as he is a Christian and devotes effort to things conducive to divine worship, and political in human conversation, because man is a ζῶον πολιτικὸν, in which, however, as conversation with the impious is not to be altogether declined if there be hope of conversion; so it is not to be sought after rashly and affected, since he who touches pitch is defiled, and evil communications corrupt good manners, 1 Cor. 15. But especially the participation in evil works is to be fled. With those men who are only disgraces to the Church, there is to be no commerce, but they are to be fled as if they were ἀλάστορες and pollutions, both for the sake of God, lest his name be ill-spoken of if such are tolerated in the Church; and for the sake of the wicked themselves, lest they be confirmed in their impiety, but rather be recalled by severe discipline to serious repentance; and for the sake of others, lest the examples of crimes creep further, offend the minds of the pious, and be a scandal to us ourselves. Nor is the warning of Chrysostom, Homily 56 on John, to be unobserved: If we can make them better, and do not harm ourselves, all things must be done. But when we cannot profit them, if, that is, they are incorrigible, and we harm ourselves, they are to be altogether cut off. We must therefore take care altogether not to connive at such crimes and errors: not to dissemble their sins; not to approve their blasphemies by our silence: not to frequent the houses and tables of the impious for the sake of our own belly rather than for the sake of winning our neighbor; not to offend the weak of Christ by our wicked example: not to confirm the impious in error, and not to let the zeal for piety be broken in us by the company of the wicked, as Heshusius rightly warned here. See Phil. 2:15, 1 Peter 2:12. But when conversation is necessary for the sake of bringing glory to God, or promoting the salvation of a neighbor, or performing our duty, then let us know that to the pure all things are pure. We cannot indeed always refuse political dealings with the impious; but to contract familiarity, which consists in social life, cohabitation, friendly conversation, and similar parts of more intimate friendship, is not fitting, because of scandals and the danger of seduction.

Latin:

Νυνὶ δὲ ἔγραψα ὑμῖν.

Nuni hic non est ad temporis discriminationem additum, quasi nunc aliud scriberet Paulus, quam ante scripserat, sed habet vim adversativæ, quomodo νῦν sumitur infra VII. 14. & XII. 20. & νυνὶ infra XII. 18. & XV. 20. Ita apud Cicero- nem sæpe ponitur: nunc vero.

Μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι, ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζό- μενος ἦ πόρνος, Ἢ λοίδορος, ἢ πλεονέκτης, ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης, ἢ μέθυσος, ἢ ἅρπαξ,

Si quis frater dictus, id est, Christianus dici volens. Vid. Act. VI. 3. Amicitia cum talibus peccatoribus dehonestabat Ecclesiam, cum iis qui extra Ecclesiam erant non item. Ad modo dicta vitiosorum nomina addit hic pari jure λοίδορος & ebriosos. Λοιδορία respondet Hebræis vocibus ריב & רבה : Illa jurgium, hæc ψόγον & ὀνείδισμα significat. Vide Joh. IX. 8. Act. XXIII, 4. supra IV. 12. 1. Petr. II. 23. Habes ergo hic præcipuas excommunicationis causas. In excom- municationis locum ubi aut presbyterium non est, aut Ec- clesia est lacerata, succedit privata familiaris commercii fuga : Unde non longe abit Charondæ illud: Ἀδίκῳ ἀνδρὶ ἢ γυναικὶ μὴ ὁμιλεῖν μηδένα, ἢ ὀνειδίζεσθαι ὡς ὄντας ὁμοίους.

Τῷ τοιούτῳ μηδὲ συνεσθίειν. ι Cum talibus id est adeo vitiosis, & Christianorum no- men usurpantibus, nec epulas quidem habere communes, quod minimum est inter amicitiæ signa. Vid. Gal. II. 12. Συνεσθίειν habes Gen. XLIII. 32. Ps. CI. 5. in Græco, He- bræis mos erat cibum communem non sumere cum eo, qui erant in נדוי.

Familiarem conversationem prohibet, qualis es- se solet inter fratres, non commercia civilia : Quã- tum ad vitam & societatem Ecclesiasticam, non quantum ad vitam politicam. Homo enim in hac vita duplicem quasi vitam agit; Ecclesiasticam, qua- tenus Christianus est & rebus ad cultum divinum proficientibus operam dat, & politicam in conver- satione humana, quia homo est ζῶον πολιτικὸν, in qua tamen, uti non omnino declinanda est con- versatio cum impiis, si spes sit conversionis; ita non ambienda temere & affectanda, cum qui pi- cem tangit, commaculetur, & corrumpant mores consortia prava 1. Cor. XV. Maxime vero partitipa- tio malignorum operum fugienda. Cum illis ho- minibus, qui tantum sunt dedecora Ecclesiæ, non est habendum commercium, sed velut ἀλάστορες κὴ μιάσματα sunt fugiendi, tum ob Deum, ne nomẽ ejus male audiat, si tales in Ecclesia tolerentur; tum ob ipsosmet flagitiosos, ne in impietate sua con- firmentur, sed severa potius disciplina ad seriam pœnitentiam revocentur, tum ob alios, ne scele- rum exempla serpant latius, piorum animos offen- dant, nobisque ipsis scandolo sint. Nec monitum Chrysost. Hom. LVI. in Johan. observandum : Si eos meliores possimus reddere, ac nobis ipsis non officia- mus, omnia facienda sunt. Sed cum illis prodesse non possumus, si scilicet incorrigibiles sint, & nos ipsos lædimus, omnino abscindendi sunt. Cavendum er- go omnino, ne ad talia scelera & errores conni- veamus: Ne peccata illorum dissimulemus; ne silentio nostro illorum blasphemias approbemus: Ne potius nostri ventris causa, quam lucrandi proximi gratia domos & mensas impiorum fre- quentemus; ne imbecilles Christi pravo nostro 'exemplo offendamus: ne impios in errore con- 'firmemus, & ne in nobis studium pietatis malorum 'consortio frangatur, ut hic recte monuit Heshusius. Vide Phil. II. 15. 1. Petri II. 12. Quando vero vel gloriæ Dei afferendæ, vel salutis proximi prove- hendæ, vel muneris nostri obeundi causa necessa- ria est conversatio, tunc sciamus, mundis omnia es- se munda. Politica sane commercia non semper detrectare possumus cum impiis; familiaritatem vero contrahere, quæ in convictu, cohabitatione, colloquio amico, similibusque intimioris amici- tiæ partibus consistit, non convenit, propter scan- dala & seductionis periculum.

## 5:12
V. 12. For what have I to do to judge those who are outside. This is not so necessary for me or for you, for preserving the purity of the Church. Καὶ is absent in the Manuscript, rightly. Do you not judge those who are inside? That is, ought you not to judge? Is it not your duty, either to punish them with certain penalties, if they accept them, or if they do not wish that, to separate those living in such a way from your company? In this you ought all to have agreed and consented.

Latin:

V. 12. Τί γάρ μοι καὶ τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν. Non adeo hoc mihi aut vobis necesse est, ad servandam Ecclesiæ puritatem. Καὶ abest in Manuscripto recte. Οὐχὶ τοὺς ἔσω ὑμεῖς κρίνετε. Id est, debetis judicare? Nonne vestri est officii, aut pœ- nis quibusdam, si suscipiant eas, castigare, aut si id nolint, à vestra consuetudine segregare ita viventes? In hoc conve- nire omnes & consentire debueratis.

## 5:13
V. 13. But those who are outside God will judge. More correctly κρινεῖ, he will punish them, that is, in his own time. Τὺς ἔξω, the outsiders, as the LXX translate; this is to be read as a parenthesis.

The Apostle distinguishes between those who are outside the Church and those who are within the same, whether they be true Christians or hypocrites. It is not for us to judge the former, but they are to be committed to the judgment of God. But over the latter the Church has right, and can judge them. The saints will indeed one day judge the world, but when the judgment of GOD is revealed, through the approval of the same, 1 Cor. 6:2. And here they can indeed pass judgment on him by way of cognition, but not by way of condemnation, because those who are outside the Church are not subject to their power and care in that way. And the Apostle here treats primarily of the judgment of excommunication, which has nothing to do with those outside. In those matters also which are curiously inquired into concerning the salvation of the infants of the Gentiles, or the condemnation of these or those nations, we are accustomed to use that saying: What have we to do with those who are outside? Since we ought to be more solicitous about our own salvation and that of those who are committed to us or are our brothers, than to judge concerning strangers, as far as concerns those things which have not been judged in the Holy Scriptures.

And put away the wicked person from among yourselves. In the manuscript ἐξάρατε. Other codices are better: ἐξαίρετε. Just as κρίνετε preceded. For those things cohere, with the parenthesis, as we have said, interposed, so that the sense may be: Ought you not to remove him from you? Just as κρίνετε means you ought to judge. For often such verbs signify not so much an act as a duty. Therefore the Syrian translated both this interrogation and the preceding one by the Imperative. This expression is taken from Deut. 24:17, where in the Greek it is 'you shall put away the wicked person from among yourselves.' So also Deut. 13:5, 17:7, 21:21, 22:21.

It is rather a commandment, ἡ, ἐξαιρεῖτε, cast out that wicked person from among yourselves. The Apostle admonishes and commands concerning the wicked person himself, not merely concerning the casting out of the vice. For he says τὸν πονηρὸν, not τὸ πονηρόν. Moreover, when he says from among yourselves, he indicates that this will bring very much benefit to them themselves, as Theophylact admonishes.

Latin:

V. 13. Τὺς δὲ ἔξω ὁ Θεὸς κρίνει. Rectius κρινεῖ, puniet eos suo scilicet tempore. Τὺς ἔξω חיצונים, ἀλοτρίυς ut vertunt LXX. hoc per parenthesin le- gendum est.

Distinguit Apostolus inter eos, qui extra Eccle- siam, & qui intra eandem sunt, sive veri sint Chri- stiani, sive hypocritæ. Illos nostrum non est, ju- dicare, sed judicio Dei committendi sunt. In hos vero Ecclesia jus habet, eosque judicare potest. Judicabunt quidem olim sancti mundum, sed cum patefiet DEI judicium, per approbationem ejus- dem 1. Cor. VI. 2. Et hic judicium de eo ferre qui- dem possunt per modum cognitionis, non autem per modum condemnationis, quia sic eorum pote- stati & curæ non sunt subjecti qui extra Ecclesiam sunt. Et agit hic imprimis Apostolus de judicio excommunicationis, quod nihil attinet τὺς ἔξω. In iis etiam, quæ curiose disquiruntur de salute infantum gentilium, vel condemnatione harum aut illarum gentium, solemus usurpare illud: Quid nobis cum iis, qui foris sunt? Siquidem magis de no- stra & eorum, qui commissi nobis sunt, vel fratres nostri sunt, salute debeamus esse soliciti, quam judicare de extraneis, quantum ad ea, quæ in sa- cris literis dijudicata non sunt.

Καὶ ἐξαιρεῖτε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν. In manuscripto ἐξάρατε. Melius alii Codices: ἐξαίρετε. Sicut præcessit κρίνετε. Nam ista cohærent, parenthesi, ut diximus, interposita, ut sensus sit: Nonne debetis eum à vobis amovere? Sicut κρίνετε est debetis judicare. Sæpe enim verba talia non tam actum, quam officium signifi- cant. Ideo Syrus & hanc interrogationem & præcedentem per Imperativum transtulit. Sumpta autem hæc loquutio ex Deut. XXIV. 17. ubi in Græco ἐξαρεῖς τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν. Ita & Deut. XIII. 5. XVII. 7. XXI. 21. XXII. 21.

Præceptum potius est, ἡ, ἐξαιρεῖτε extraprosli- gate malum istum ex vobis ipsis. De scelerato ipso, non de vitio solum ejiciendo monet ac præcipit Apostolus. Dicit enim τὸν πονηρὸν, non τὸ πονηρόν. Ex vobis ipsis autem, cum inquit, indicat utilita- tis plurimum id ipsis allaturum, monente Theo- phylacto.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

ARGUMENT & DIVISION.

The Apostle reproves the Corinthians because they drag the faithful to the tribunals of unbelievers, [those who are] to judge the world, nay even the Angels one day, as if no one among them possessed the prudence to judge, whereas they ought not to litigate rashly, but rather suffer injury and loss; and because they themselves even inflict injury and loss upon their brothers, warning that the unjust shall not inherit the kingdom of GOD, just as neither idolaters nor fornicators, the covetous, drunkards, revilers, [and] such as some of them had been, yet now that they are justified such things do not befit them; and setting himself as an example, who abstains even in lawful things, such as in the use of foods, lest he be in any way captivated: Gravely also reproving fornication; since our bodies are members of Christ, and it is not fitting to be one body with harlots, who are one spirit with the Lord: And fornicators, otherwise than other sinners, sin against their own body, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit, and they are not their own, but the portion of the Lord, bought by Him, and therefore they ought to glorify GOD in body and Spirit alike. There are three parts: I. Reproof of those litigating before a profane tribunal to v. 8. II. Admonition concerning the unjust and other wicked persons who will not inherit the kingdom of GOD, from which vices the Apostle dissuades the justified, to v. 13. III. Invective against fornication to v. 20.

PART I. Reproof of those litigating before a profane judgment.

V. 1. Does any of you dare, having a matter against another. Having a matter, ריב לו אשר יהיה לו ריב 2 Sam. XV. 10. Such a person is called by the Hebrews בעל משפט. πρὸς here means κατὰ, which you have in Matthew V. 23.

To be judged before the unjust.

Κρίνεσθαι is to litigate, רוב, as in Matthew V. 39, and in the Old Testament often the verb נשפט, which corresponds exactly to the Greek itself. The unjust are called here idolaters, who do not render to GOD what they owe, who will soon be called ἄπιστοι (unbelievers). This is what Paul commands from the praiseworthy institutions of the synagogue. The Hebrews used to say: He who brings an Israelite to the tribunal of the Gentiles profanes the name of God. For those who do this give the outsiders an occasion to say: Behold how harmonious are those who worship one God. Ἐπὶ is taken here as in Acts XXV. 9, 10, 1 Timothy VI. 13. This matter is treated in the Constitutions of Clement II. 4, 5.

And not before the saints.

Rather than among Christians, namely, arbitrators, διατητάς. Even where there is no diversity in sacred matters, it is the part of a good man to go to an arbitrator rather than to a judge, because of the delays and expenses of lawsuits, and the craftiness of legal practitioners who increase them: And because a criminal judgment often arises from a civil lawsuit.

Salmero, Cornelius, and other Papists claim this connection with the preceding chapter, that they ventilated a matrimonial cause, such as that of the incestuous person, before a secular forum, and for this purpose, that such cognizance might be entirely taken away from seculars. But it is false that that cause was referred to a secular forum. Nor does Paul forbid processes to be instituted before a secular forum, because at that time Christians had no secular forum there; but [he forbids them] before Gentile judges. Three things, however, occur concerning this reproof: I. Correction because of litigations before infidels, v. 1, 2, 3, 4. II. The amendment and remedy of this scandal is partly the appointment of arbitrators among the believers themselves, v. 4, partly the intermission of litigations as far as possible, since they ought rather to suffer injury and loss than to litigate with a brother before infidels, v. 6, 7, partly the avoidance or cutting off of such causes, as is added III. Reproof of those who provide causes by inflicting injury and causing loss to their brothers, v. 8, to whom he threatens exclusion from the kingdom of GOD because of injustice. In the correction, first the fault is expressed, then the reasons are indicated. The fault lies in the fact that they dare κρίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων, καὶ υ̐χὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων, to call brothers into court and contend or litigate not under the saints, but under the unjust or infidels, which the Apostle exaggerates (1) because it was an act of audacity, implying the shamefulness of the thing. For we dare things that are either difficult, or not entirely lawful, or less decent for a plaintiff. Therefore he objects shame to them, v. 5. (2) Because it is about things not even of great moment; whence he calls it not a controversy, but a matter (negotium), which could be settled in another way: such are those things which concern βιωτικὰ (the things of this life), which pertain to the use of this life. (3) Because a brother litigates with a brother, which does not befit fraternal love if it is done under the unjust and infidels, to whom they reveal this shame not without scandal, and therefore he says in v. 6, ἤδη, and that under infidels. Moreover, since the judgment of the Gentiles did not at all befit the faithful, and causes could not always be defined without arbitrators, Christians ought to appoint their own arbitrators by compromise, and to act in all ways so that the matter might be settled rather than devolved to the tribunal of infidels. The Syrian rendered 'to judge' as רברון, to try something by judgment, as it is taken in ישפוט 1 Sam. XII. 7, Jer. II. 35, Ezech. XX. 35.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Reprehendit Apostolus Corinthios, quod ad infi- delium tribunalia fideles, mundum, imo etiã Angelos olim judicaturos abripiant, quasi nemo inter ipsos prudentia ad judicandum polleat, cum non temere litigare, sed potius injuriam & damnum pati debeant; quodq́ etiam injuriam ac damnum fratribus ipsi- met inferant, monens, quod injusti regnum DEI consequuturi non sint, ut nec idolola- træ nec scortatores, avari, ebriosi, calumnia- tores, quales etsi nonnulli ex ipsis fuerint, jam tamen justificatis talia non convenire; & exemplum se sistens, qui etiam in licitis, utpote in usu ciborum, abstineat, ne ullate- nus captivetur: Graviter etiam redarguens scortationem; Siquidem corpora nostra Christi membra sint, nec cum scortis unum corpus esse deceat, qui unus spiritus cum Do- mino sunt: Et scortatores, secus, atque alii peccatores, in proprio peccent corpore, quod templum est Spiritus sancti, ipsique non sui sint, sed Domini portio, ab ipso empti, ideo- que DEUM in corpore pariter & Spiritu glorificare debeant. PArtes sunt tres: I. Reprehensio litigantium co- ram profano tribunali ad v. 8. II. Monitum de injustis, aliisque facinorosis, regnum DEI non hære- ditaturis, à quibus vitiis dehortatur justificatos Apostolus, ad v. 13. III. Invectiva adversus scorta- tionem ad v. 20.

PARS I. Reprehensio litigantium coram profano judicio.

V. 1. Τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν πρᾶγμα ἔχων πρὸς τὸν ἕτερον. Πρᾶγμα ἔχων ריב לו אשר יהיה לו ריב 2. Sam. XV. 10. Dicitur talis Hebræis בעל משפט . πρὸς hic valet κατὰ, quod habes Matth. V. 23.

Κρίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων.

Κρίνεσθαι est litigare רוב ut Matth. V. 39. & in Veteri Testamento sæpe verbum נשפט, quod exacte Græco ipsi respondet. Ἄδικοι hic dicuntur idololatræ, qui DEO non exhibent, quod debent, qui mox dicentur ἄπιστοι. Est hoc quod Paulus præcipit ex laudabilibus institutis synago- gæ. Dicebant Hebræi: Qui adducit Israëlitam ad tribunal gentium, is profanat nomen Dei. Occasionem enim dant, qui id faciunt, extraneis dicendi: Ecce quam concordes sunt illi, qui unum Deum colunt. Ἐπὶ hic sumitur, ut Act. XXV. 9. 10. 1. Timoth. VI. 13. Tractatur hæc res Clementis con- stitutionum II. 4. 5.

Καὶ υ̐χὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων.

Potius, quam apud Christianos, arbitros scilicet διατη- τάς. Etiam ubi non est in sacris diversitas, viri boni est, ad arbitrum potius ire, quam ad judicem, ob litium moras & impensas, & pragmaticorum ea augentium versutias: Et quia sæpe ex lite civili nascitur judicium criminale.

Nexum cum præcedenti capite Salmero, Corne- lius, aliique Papistæ tradunt hunc, quod causam matrimonialem, qualis fuerit incestuosi, coram se- culari foro ventilarint, idq; eo fine, ut talis cogni- tio secularibus plane adimatur. Sed falsum est, illam causam ad forum seculare relatam. Nec pro- hibet Paulus coram seculari foro processus institui, quia tunc temporis Christiani ibi nullum forum seculare habuere; sed coram judicibus gentilibus. Tria autem circa hanc reprehensionem occurrunt I. Correptio ob litigia coram infidelibus, v. 1. 2. 3. 4. II. Emendatio & remediũ hujus scandali est partim arbitrorum inter ipsos fideles constitutio v. 4. par- tim litigiorum, quoad fieri potest, intermissio, cum potius injuriam & damnum pati debeant, quam coram infidelibus cum fratre litigare, v. 6. 7. par- tim causarum talium vitatio, vel præcisio, uti ad- ditur III. Eorum reprehensio, qui causas præbent, injuriam inferendo, & damno afficiendo fratres suos v. 8. quibus ob injustitiam minatur exclusio- nem è regno DEI. In correptione primum culpa ex- primitur, tum rationes indicantur. Culpa in eo est, quod audeant κρίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων, καὶ υ̐χὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων in jus vocare fratres, & contendere, vel li- tigare non sub sanctis, sed sub injustis vel infideli- bus, quod exaggerat Apostolus (1.) quod audacia fuerit, innuens rei turpitudinem. Audemus enim vel difficilia, vel non omnino licita, vel minus decentia actorem. Ideo pudorem ipsis objicit v. 5. (2.) quod de rebus etiam non magni momenti; Unde non controversiam, sed negotium vocat, quod & alia ratione transigi possit: quales sunt, quæ βιωτικὰ concernunt, quæ ad usum vitæ hujus faciunt. (3.) quod frater cum fratre litiget, quod fraternæ dilectioni non convenit, si id fiat sub in- justis & infidelibus, quibus turpitudinem hanc nõ sine scandalo produnt, ideoque ait v. 6. ή τὶτο, id- que sub infidelibus. Cæterum, cum judicium gen- tilium fidelibus minime convenerit, neque causæ sine arbitris semper definiri potuerint, Christiani arbitros proprios constituere ex compromisso debebant, idque omnibus modis agere, ut nego- tium componeretur potius, quam ad tribunal infi- delium devolveretur. Judicare Syrus רברון judicio experiri aliquid reddidit, ut ישפוט 1. Sam. XII. 7. Jer. II. 35. Ezech. XX. 35. accipitur.

## 6:2
V. 2. Do you not know that the saints will judge the world. They themselves, having first been judged by Christ, will then be assessors to Christ, who is judging others. Which is said of the Apostles in Matthew XIX. 28, Luke XXII. 30. Cyprian: As friends of the Lord, and subsequently to judge with him.

The Apostle brings the causes of his reproof and dissuasion partly from the dignity of the faithful, that they themselves are judges, and indeed far more eminent ones, as they are to judge both the world and the angels, and indeed concerning far graver matters: Who therefore are unworthy to be judged concerning fleeting things, and those pertaining to the use of life, as if they were the least? Partly from the contempt of infidels, who in the Church are deservedly held as the most abject and are considered in contempt. Why therefore do they commit judgment to such people concerning those contentions which they happen to have among themselves about fleeting things, as if Gentile judges were wiser than the whole Church, whom they otherwise hold in contempt in the Church, and no one of the faithful is found of such wisdom that he can judge or perform the role of an arbitrator to settle such matters. That judgment of the world, which is attributed to the saints, B. Balduinus here understands of the faithful, who condemn the works and pursuits of the world by the Word: But it is a question of the future judgment of the world, and since it is added that even the angels will be judged by the saints, there is no doubt that it refers to the judgment which will take place on the last day, which Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Ambrose, Anselm, and most other Doctors acknowledge. Concerning which in aphorism II, B. Balduinus confesses: That Christ will then be the universal, ordinary, and primary Judge, to whom the Father has given all judgment, John 5:22. Nevertheless, the saints will judge, by approving the sentence of the Judge, and by their faith convicting the infidelity of the world. Matt. 12:41, ch. 19:28. Although indeed some claim this prerogative for the Apostles above other saints from Matt. 19:28, it is nevertheless certain that all the saints will judge the world from Matt. 12:40, 41, Luke 11:31, 32, and from Rev. 2:26, 27. Ch. 3:21, ch. 20:4, as also Dan. 7:9, is not obscurely gathered. The Israelite Church also believed the same, Wisd. 3:8, ch. 5:1. Which will take place not so much by the testimony which they will render concerning the good works of the pious, concerning beneficence, and the example of faith, as Remigius explains the present passage: For these things pertain not to the judge, but to the witnesses, by sitting beside Christ the judge, and by ratifying or approving his sentence, Rev. 19:1, 2, with which honor Christ will deem his saints and faithful worthy, who, although they themselves also must first be placed before the tribunal of Christ at his right hand, yet after they themselves have received a joyful sentence from Christ, they will be raised to judicial thrones, constituted as Kings by Christ and judges of the world, and will judge the infidels and the impious, in the stated manner, with Christ, sitting on the throne of Christ, which indeed Christ has assigned to each, Rev. 3:21, ch. 4:4, ch. 20:4, in which session, however, a more eminent degree, both of glory and of thrones, will be granted to the Apostles, as universal teachers and fathers of the faithful of the New Testament throughout the whole world, Matt. 19:28. But these things are not to be understood of material thrones, nor is it for us to explain how that dignity of session or degree of glory will be, as they are ἀνεκδιήγητα, ἡ ἀνεξερέυνητα (ineffable and unsearchable). Salmero, however, is foolish when he determines that the seats of the Apostles, in which they will judge, will be aerial and notable for some splendor.

And by you the world is judged. By you as assessors of Christ. The world, the greatest part of men. The majority are evil. And is judged is present for future, as above 3:7, 14.

But why this should not be taken in the present without enallage does not appear. For not only in On the last day the saints will judge the world justly, by whom they have been judged unjustly here, but they also judge the world in the present age, and they disapprove of its evil works from the Word of God, and condemn its customs and pursuits; inasmuch as by these the world is crucified, and they who are crucified to the world Gal. VI. 16.

Are you unworthy of the smallest tribunals?

Are you unworthy to judge concerning perishable things? Kriterion here is not a tribunal, but krisis a judgment מִדִין, as in Jud. V. 9. Daniel VI. 10. 26.

Latin:

V. 2. ὒκ οἴδατε, ὅτι οἱ ἅγιοι τὸν κόσμον κρινοῦσιν. Ipfi primum à Chrifto judicati, erunt deinde Christo assessores, judicanti alios. Quod de Apostolis dicitur Matth. XIX, 28. Luc. XXII. 30. Cyprianus: Utpote amici Domini, & cum ipso postmodum judicaturi.

Causas correptionis & dehortationis suæ affert Apostolus partim à dignitate fidelium, quod ipsi- met judices, & quidem longe eminentiores sint, utpote & mundum, & Angelos judicaturi, & quidem de longe gravioribus: Qui ergo indigni, de rebus caducis, & ad vitæ usum pertinentibus, ceu mini- mis, judicari? Partim à contemptu infidelium, qui in Ecclesia merito pro abjectissimis habeantur, & despicatui ducantur. Cur ergo talibus judicium, de iis contentionibus, quas forte inter se de rebus caducis habent, committant, ac si Ethnici Judi- ces præ tota Ecclesia saperent, quos abjectim alias in Ecclesia habent, nec ullus fidelium reperiatur ejus sapientiæ, ut judicare possit, vel arbitri partes obire ad negotia talia componenda. Judicium illud mundi, quod sanctis tribuitur, B. Balduinus de fidelibus hic accipit, qui opera, & studia mundi damnant ex verbo: Sed agitur de futuro mundi ju- dicio & cum addatur, etiam Angelos judicatum iri à sanctis, dubium nullum est, judiciů respici, quod fiet in novissimo die, quod agnoscunt Chrysost. Theodor. Theophyl. Ambros. Anselmus, & pleri- que alii Doctores. De quo in aphorismo II. fate- tur B. Balduinus: Judicem tum universalem, ordi- narium, & primarium futurum Christum, cui Pa- ter dedit omne judicium Job. V. 22. Sanctos tamen nihilominus judicaturos, approbando sententiam Judicis, & fide sua infidelitatem mundi arguendo. Matth. XII. 41. c. XIX. 28. Quanquam vero hanc prærogativam Apostolis præ aliis sanctis vendi- cent nonnulli è Matth. XIX, 28. omnes tamen san- ctos mundum judicaturos è Matth. XII. 40. 41. Luc. XI. 31. 32. constat, & ex Apoc. II. 26. 27. Cap. III. 21. C. XX. 4. ut & Dan. VII. 9. non obscure colligitur. Credidit idem & Isrælitica Ecclesia Sap. III. 8. Cap. V. 1. Quod fiet non tam testimonio, quod reddent de piorum bonis operibus, de bene- ficentia, & exemplo fidei, ut Remigius præsentem locum explicat: Hæc enim non ad judicem, sed ad testes pertinent, quam Christo judici assidendo, ejusque sententiam ratihabendo, vel approban- do, Ap. XIX. 1. 2. quo honore dignabitur Christus sanctos & fideles suos, qui, etsi ipsi quoque coram tribunali Christi primum ad dextram ejus statuen- di, tamen postquam ipsi lætam à Christo sententia acceperint, in thronos judiciarios, ceu Reges à Chri- sto, & judices mundi constituti, evecti, infideles & impios, dicta ratione, cum Christo judicabunt, sessuri in throno Christi, quem nempe cuique Chri- stus assignavit Ap. III. 21. c. IV. 4. c. XX. 4. in quo consessu tamen eminentior gradus ut gloriæ ita & thronorum Apostolis, ceu doctoribus universalibus, & patribus fidelium N. Testamenti per totum ter- rarum orbem concedetur Matth. XIX. 28. Quæ vero nec de materialibus thronis intelligenda, nec quo pacto sessionis dignitas illa, aut gradus gloriæ sese habebunt, nobis ἀνεκδιήγητα, ἡ ἀνεξερέυνητα sunt. Ineptus autem est Salmero, cum statuit, sedes Apostolorum, in quibus judicabunt, aëreas futuras, & aliquo splendore notabiles.

Καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν κρίνεται ὁ κόσμος. Per vos tanquam adsessores Christi. ὁ κόσμος maxi- ma hominum pars. Οἱ πλείους κακόι. Et κρίνεται præsens pro futuro, ut supra III. 7. 14.

Id vero, cur non in præsenti accipiendum sit ci- tra enallagen, non apparet. Nam non tantum in novissimo die judicabunt sancti mundum juste, à quo hic judicati sunt injuste, sed judicant etiam in præsente seculo mundum, ejusque opera mala ex Verbo Dei improbant, & damnant ejus mores & studia; utpote quibus crucifigitur mundus, & qui mundo crucifiguntur Gal. VI. 16.

Ἀνάξιοί ἐστε κριτηρίων ἐλαχίστων;

Indigni estis, qui cognoscatis de rebus caducis? Κριτήριον hic non est tribunale, sed κρίσις judicium מִדִין, ut Jud. V. 9. Danielis VI. 10. 26.

## 6:3
V. 3. Do you not know that we shall judge angels?

For even the angels who sinned will receive their sentence at that time, Jude 6. Tertullian on the apparel of women: These are the angels whom we are to judge: These are the angels whom we renounce in the bath. Perhaps good angels also will receive greater honors.

How much more things of this life?

Much less the things of this life. Thus with the cares of this life Luke XXI. 34. Mēti ge here signifies אַף כִּי.

Concerning good angels, who are to be affected with greater honors on the last day, scripture hands down nothing. But the wicked, no otherwise than impious men, will be judged by the faithful; namely, by an approbative judgment. For since the saints have been victors over the devil in this life, in the last judgment they will expose his malice and pride before the whole world, and will condemn him for his cunning and tyranny. But what that judgment is, and how it is to be brought against the devil and his angels, it is not for us to explain. Just as we do not dare to define that good angels are also to judge. For in scripture that is not found defined. Where a most obscure matter is disputed, without the aid of certain and clear documents of the divine scriptures, human presumption ought to restrain itself, doing nothing by inclining to either side, advises Blessed Augustine, Book II, on the Merits and Remission of Sins, last chapter.

Latin:

V. 3. Οὐκ ὄιδατε, ὅτι Ἀγγέλους κρινοῦμεν.

Nam & qui peccarunt Angeli, eo tempore sententiam accipient, Judæ 6. Tertullianus de cultu fœminarum: Hi sunt Angeli, quos judicaturi sumus: Hi sunt Angeli, quibus in lavacro renuntiamus. Forte & boni Angeli majores honores accipient.

Μήτι γε βιωτικά;

Nedum res hujus vitæ. Sic μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς Luc. XXI. 34. Μήτι γε valet hic אַף כִּי.

De Angelis bonis, majoribus honoribus in novissimo die afficiendis, nihil tradit scriptura. Mali vero non aliter, quam homines impii, à fidelibus judicabuntur; judicio scil. approbativo. Quum enim sancti victores diaboli in hac vita fuerint, in judicio novissimo malitiam & superbiam ejus coram toto mundo traducent, eumque ob astutias & tyrannidem condemnabunt. Quod vero judicium, quomodo ferendum adversus diabolum, ejusque Angelos sit, nostrum non est explicare. Quemadmodum nec id definire audemus, quod Angeli boni etiam judicaturi sint. In scriptura enim id definitum non reperitur. Ubi de re obscurissima disputatur, non adjuvantibus divinarum scripturarum certis clarisque documentis, cohibere se debet humana præsumptio, nihil faciens in alteram partem declinando, monet B. August. L. II. de Peccat. Merit. & remif. cap. ult.

## 6:4
V. 4. If then you have tribunals concerning the things of this life.

It is a metonymy. For he calls the things to be judged kriteria here.

Set those who are of no account in the Church to judge.

If those great Doctors of yours have no time for it, take even the least from the common people of the pious. Exouthenēmenoi נְבָזִים. Thus they are to be understood as compared, who are held below the rest. And kathizein here is hōshīv which, having been said first of Judges who are placed in magnificent seats 1 Sam. II. 8. Sir. X. 17. XI. 1, began then to be transferred to arbitrators and to other offices.

Latin:

V. 4. Βιωτικὰ μὲν ὖν κριτήρια ἐὰν ἔχητε.

Est Μετωνυμία. Nam κριτηρια hic vocat res dijudicandas.

Τὺς ἐξυθενημένους ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τύτυς καθίζετε.

Si magnis illis vestris Doctoribus id non vacat, vel minimos de piorum plebe sumite. Ἐξυθενημένοι נְבָזִים. Sic comparate intelligendi, qui infra cæteros habentur. Et καθίζειν hic est הושִׁיב quod primo de Judicibus dictum, qui in magnificis sedibus collocantur 1. Sam. II. 8. Sir. X. 17. XI. 1. cœpit deinde ad arbitros, & ad alia munera transferri.

## 6:5
I say this to your shame.

That you may be ashamed of this matter, as also below XV. 54. above IV. 14. I do not write to shame you. But signifying in another sense that he is not writing for this purpose, that he might traduce the Corinthians before others. Ἐντροπή is כְּלִמָּה Job, XX. 3. Psalm XLIV, 1. 6. LXXI. 13. & CIX. 29.

We have previously indicated another sense, that those who are despised in the Church were not those who were of an inferior order among the believers, but unbelievers, who were held in contempt in the Church. And that the word καθίζετε is not to be taken in the imperative mood but in the indicative mood; as Chrysostom, Jerome, Bucer, Drusius, Heinsius, Valla, Faber Stapulensis & others take it; so that the reason for the rebuke is new, taken from the indecency that they should enter into judgment before those who are abject and held of no account in the Church, as if there were not among the believers themselves many far more worthy, who could be chosen as arbiters, men abounding in wisdom and prudence. Thus Ambrose says the Corinthians do wrong, because they make Gentiles, whom they themselves hold in contempt, the judges of their affairs. Which the sense favors, because it is added: I say this to your shame. If, however, one prefers with Grotius, Augustine, & Gregory the Great, book XIX. Moral. chap. 21. If one prefers to take it as an imperative with the Vulgate, Beza, Tremellius, the Dutch, Remigius, Bucer, Martyr &c., it will pertain to this remedy, namely that judges should rather be consulted who are of less account in the Church, than that one should litigate under unbelievers; whence Papists seek in vain here for a foundation for Ecclesiastical judgment, whether concerning Ecclesiastical matters, which are not looked at here, or concerning secular ones, which is forbidden to them Luke XII. 13. 2 Thess. II. 4. But if he wishes abject ones to be chosen, to what end does the Apostle add: Is there not a wise man among you, who can judge? Ambrose's explanation is therefore better.

Is there thus no wise man among you, not even one, who will be able to judge between his brothers? Is there really no one among you learned, who can judge, that is, who has the leisure. This should have been especially the duty of those who sell themselves among you under the name of wisdom. But if they avoid that, it should have been gone to even the unskilled. It appears from the Syriac that it was written here formerly: Between the brothers, and his brothers. For ἀνὰ μέσον is not said of one. See Gen. XVI. 5. Deut. I. 16. The repetition of the same words, as often, gave the occasion for omitting the later ones.

Latin:

Πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λέγω.

Ut vos pudeat hujus rei, ut & infra XV. 54. supra IV. 14. Οὐκ ἐντρέπων ὑμᾶς γράφω. Sed alio sensu significans non in hoc se scribere, ut Corinthios apud alios traducat. Ἐντροπή est כְּלִמָּה Job, XX. 3. Psalmo XLIV, 1. 6. LXXI. 13. & CIX. 29.

Alium sensum antea indicavimus, τὺς ἐξυθενημένους ἐν Ἐκκλησίᾳ non qui inferioris ordinis erant inter fideles, sed infideles, qui contemptim in Ecclesia habebantur, esse. Nec verbum καθίζετε modo imperandi sed modo indicandi accipi; ut accipiunt Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Bucerus, Drusius, Heinsius, Valla, Faber Stapulensis & alii; ut ratio reprehensionis nova sit ab indecoro petita, quod judicium ineant coram iis, qui abjecti, & nullius æstimii habeantur in Ecclesia, quasi non sint inter ipsos fideles multis parasangis digniores, qui arbitri eligi possint, viri sapientia & prudentia pollentes. Ita Ambrosius male facere Corinthios dicit, quod Ethnicos, quos ipsi contemptim habeant, negotiorum suorum judices faciant. Cui sensus favet, quod additur: Ad verecundiam vestram dico. Si tamen cum Grotio, Augustino, & Gregorio M. l. XIX. Moral. cap. 21. Vulgata, Beza, Tremellio, Belgis, Remigio, Bucero, Martyre &c. imperative accipere quis malit, ad remedium hoc pertinebit, ut nempe judices potius consulantur, qui in Ecclesia minoris sunt æstimii, quam sub infidelibus litigetur; unde frustra hic quærunt Papistæ fundamentum judicii Ecclesiastici, sive de rebus Ecclesiasticis, quæ hic non respiciuntur, sive de secularibus, quod ipsis interdictum est Luc. XII. 13. 2. Thess. II. 4. Quod si abjectos eligi vult, ad quid ad- dit Apostolus: Annon est inter vos sapiens, qui judi- care possit? Præstat ergo Ambrosii explicatio.

Οὕτως ὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ὑμῖν σοφὸς, ὐδὲ ἗ις, ὃς δυνήσεται δια- κρῖναι ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ἀδελφῶν αὐτῦ; Adeone nemo est inter vos eruditus, qui possit judicare, id est, cui vacet. Fuerat hoc illorum potissimum, qui se sa- pientiæ nomine inter vos venditant. At si illi id defugiunt, vel ad imperitos iri oportuit. Apparet ex Syro, scriptum hic olim fuisse: Διὰ μέσον τῶν ἀδελφῶν, καὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν αὑτῦ. Nam ἀνὰ μέσον de uno non dicitur. Vide Gen. XVI. 5. Deuter. I. 16. Repetitio earundem vocum, ut sæpe, occasio- nem dedit posteriores omittendi.

## 6:6
V. 6. But brother goes to law with brother. That is, litigates with a brother, as we have often said.

and this before unbelievers. See above 1.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἀλλὰ ἀδελφὸς μετὰ ἀδελφῶ κρίνεται. Id est cum fratre litigat, ut sæpe diximus.

καὶ τῦτο ἐπὶ ἀπίσων. Vide supra 1.

## 6:7
V. 7. Now therefore it is altogether a defeat for you, that you have lawsuits with one another. He said κρίματα, because above he said πρᾶγμα, which is מדין, which we said in the same place. He who litigates over things that can easily be done without, acts against the precept of Christ, which we explained in Matt. V. 40. Those who have made great progress in Christianity & in contempt of the world, suffer any loss rather than litigate, which Clement teaches in the aforementioned place of the constitutions. Those who have not yet arrived at that, in them it is not a transgression, but a defeat, that is, something less than the highest. For it is called a defeat comparatively to something greater, as Rom. XI. 21. Thus also it has ἐλάττωμα and ἐλάττωσιν in Sirach and Tobit. Chrysostom: He is righteous, he is merciful, he is a lover of the poor. But he has some defect.

The Apostle proceeds to the remedies for this scandal, of which the first is the choice of arbiters from among the believers. For it cannot be that in the midst of the Church there are not at least some prudent men, whom they can choose as arbiters in such least matters. To the evidence of which thing he uses the schema of an interrogation: Is there not a wise man among you? The other is the intermission of lawsuits between brothers, as being those for whom it is not fitting to litigate, since this very thing is easily a defeat & a sin. But ἥττημα by the force of the word is properly such a disaster and defect, by which one is overcome and as it were subjugated, Is. LIV. 17. Although indeed ἥττημα and παράπτωμα can be distinguished, it is not however free from sin. For ἥττημα is a defect. But what else is sin than a defect from the law, or lawlessness 1 John III. 4. because no other than a moral defect is noted here? Who will deny that sin was committed in this, that a brother should litigate against a brother, that he allowed himself to be overcome by the emotion of anger, vengeance, and bile, when he ought rather to have observed the admonition of Christ in Matthew 5:40? And St. Augustine, Enchiridion ch. 78, teaches that even just lawsuits are scarcely undertaken without sin, because they almost always proceed from an excessive love of temporal things, and are scarcely free from the danger of hatred, malevolence, and calumny, and are joined with the loss of temporal peace and eternal tranquility. However, judicial proceedings are not altogether prohibited here, as the Anabaptists wish; but by the Apostle, as well as by Christ, it is only taught that Christians ought to be prepared for patience; and that a mind tenacious of the things of this age, and greedy and itching for lawsuits to approach tribunals over trivial matters, and to pursue any injuries whatsoever with rigor, ought to be absent from the faithful; that one must take care lest, through a desire for vengeance, patience be lost, which is to be valued more highly than what anyone can take away from another against his will. And Augustine warns in Epistle 5 that it is not judicial proceedings that are reprehended here, but the rashness of contending over the smallest matters, the indignity of contention before unbelievers, and the triviality of the causes of contentions, which he wishes rather to be removed through the tolerance of injuries and some loss, and mutual forgiveness. Judicial proceedings are divine ordinances; but contentions are called ἥττημα (a defeat) of this kind, because they are human failings, since we, carried away by emotions, for an easy reason drag our brothers to the tribunal. Nor indeed, if lawsuits are a certain ἥττημα (as it cannot be doubted; for if all Christians were such as they ought to be, there would be no cause for lawsuits, no lawsuits), does it follow that the remedies for lawsuits are evil, such as judgments; just as judicial processes are not evil in themselves; but only by reason of those by whom the lawsuits were born, or those who pursue them badly.

Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? It seems that ἀδικεῖσθαι (to be wronged) pertains to wounded dignity, and ἀποστερεῖσθαι (to be defrauded) to the loss of things. For from these two causes lawsuits are born.

Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be wronged? Lysias against Diagiton: 'Knowing that not only do those who do wrong seem worse to you, but also if any who, having less than they should from their relatives, are unable to endure it.' What Lysias says about relatives, Paul says here about companions of the same faith. And ἀδικεῖσθαι here, as in Plato and Menander, is to endure injuries with a calm mind.

Thirdly, the provision and avoidance of the causes of lawsuits pertain to the remedies of this scandal, so that a brother may not easily seize upon a cause for litigating against a brother, but rather endure loss or injury, and the other may take care not to inflict injury or loss upon a brother, since the former is contrary to Christian patience, and the latter is wicked and unjust, which latter, as a graver crime, he exaggerates and on that occasion condemns other crimes also, which exclude one from the kingdom of God. Those two causes are assigned: the former by the word ἀδικεῖσθαι (to be wronged) brings in injury; the latter by the verb ἀποστερεῖσθαι (to be defrauded) brings in loss of things. Wherefore we are commanded to swallow an injury rather, and to suffer some loss of things, than to contend with a brother in judgment. Where, however, it is permitted to distinguish between light and grave offenses or injuries, verbal and real, those which can be neglected with a safe conscience and reputation, and those which cannot; and similarly between small and great losses, which cannot be sustained without our significant inconvenience. And to a needy brother, who cannot restore the loss, one ought rather to remit and donate something than to contend in judgment with his further impoverishment; and whatever other things of this kind Christian charity, the regulator of such things, dictates.

PART II. The threatening concerning the unjust and other wicked persons, who are to be excluded from the inheritance of the kingdom of God.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἤδη μὲν ὖν ὅλως ἥττημα ὑμῖν ἐστιν, ὅτι κρίματα ἔχετε μεθ' ἑαυτῶν. Κρίματα dixit, quod supra πρᾶγμα מדין quod ibidem diximus. Qui ob res, quibus facile caretur, litigat, facit contra Christi præceptum, quod Matth. V. 40. explica- vimus. Qui magnum profectum in Christianismo & mun- di contemptu fecere, damnum quodvis faciunt potius, quam ut litigent, quod docet Clemens dicto modo consti- tutionum loco. Qui nondum eo pervenere, in iis non est παράπτωμα, sed ἥττημα, id est, minus aliquid summo. Dicitur enim ἥττημα comparatè ad aliquid majus, ut Rom. XI. 21. Sic & ἐλάττωμα & ἐλάττωσιν habet apud Siracidem & Tobiam. Chrysostomus: Δίκαιός ἐστιν, ἐλεήμων ἐσὶ, φι- λόπτωχός ἐστιν. Ἀλλ' ἔχει τι ἐλάττωμα.

Ad remedia hujus scandali progreditur Apo- stolus, è quibus primum est arbitrorum è fidelibus electio. Fieri enim non potest, quin in medio Ec- clesiæ aliqui saltem sint prudentes, quos ceu arbi- tros eligere possint in rebus ejusmodi ἐλαχίστοις. Ad cujus rei evidentiam schemate interrogatio- nis utitur: Adeone inter vos non est sapiens quis- piam? Alterum est litigiorum inter fratres inter- missio, utpote, quibus non convenit litigare, cum hoc ipsum facile ἥττημα & peccatum sit. Est au- tem ἥττημα vi vocis propriè ejusmodi clades, & de- fectus, quo quis superatur, & quasi subjugatur Es. LIV. 17. Quanquam vero ἥττημα & παράπτωμα distingui possint, non tamen illud peccato vacat. Ἤττημα enim defectus est. Quid autem peccatum aliud est, quã defectus à lege, vel ἀνομία 1. Joh. III. 4. quia nullus alius hic notatur quam moralis defe- ctus? Quis inficias ibit, in eo peccatum commis- sum, quod frater contra fratrem litigarit, quod ira, vindicta, & bilis affectu se vinci passus sit, cum po- tius monitum Christi Matth. V. 40. observare de- buerit? Et S. August. Enchir. c. 78. doceat, lites etiam justas vix suscipi sine peccato, quia fere pro- cedunt ex nimio amore rerum temporalium, & vix carent periculo odii, malevolentiæ, calumniæ, & conjunctæ sunt cum dispendio temporalis pacis, & tranquillitatis æternæ. Non autem prohibentur hic omnino judicia, ut Anabaptistæ volunt; sed ab Apostolo pariter, & Christo id tantum docetur, paratos debere esse Christianos ad patientiam; & ani- mum rerum hujus seculi tenacem, litiumque avi- dum ac pruritum ob res leves tribunalia adeundi, & injurias quasvis cum rigore persequendi, à fide- libus abesse debere; cavendum esse, ne vindican- di cupiditate amittatur patientia, quæ pluris ha- benda, quam quod potest quis invito aliquid au- ferre. Et monet August. epistola V. Non judicia hic reprehendi, sed contendendi de rebus ἐλαχίστοις temeritatem, contentionis coram infidelibus in- dignitatem, & causarum contentionum levitatem, quas removeri potius vult, per injuriarũ & damni alicujus tolerantiam, mutuamque condonationẽ. Judicia divinæ ordinationes sunt; at contentiones ejusmodi ἥττημα dicuntur, quia defectus sunt hu- mani, cum affectibus abrepti fratres facili de cau- sa abripimus ad tribunal. Neque verò, si lites ἥττη- μα quoddam sunt (uti ambigi de eo nequit; nam si omnes Christiani tales essent, quales esse de- beant, nulla litium causa esset, nullæ lites) Con- sequens est, litium remedia mala esse qualia sunt judicia; uti processus judiciarii per se mali non sunt; sed tantùm ratione eorum, à quibus natæ lites, vel eorum, qui eas malè prosequuntur.

Διὰ τί ὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἀποστερεῖσθε; Videtur ἀδικεῖσθαι ad dignitatem læsam, ἀποστερεῖσθαι ad rerum damnum pertinere. Nam ex his duabus causis na- scuntur lites.

Διὰ τί ὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἀδικεῖσθε; Lysias adversus Diagitonem: Εἰδὼς ὅτι ὀὐ μόνον οἱ ἀδικοῦν- τες χείρυς ὑμῖν εἶναι δοκοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴ τινες ὢν ἔλαττον ὑπὸ τῶν προσηκόντων ἔχοντες, ἀνέχεσθαι μὴ δύνανται. Quod Ly- sias de propinquis dicit, hìc de ejusdem fidei consortibus Paulus. Et ἀδικεῖσθαι hìc, ut apud Platonem & Menan- drum, est æquo animo injurias perpeti.

Ad remedia hujus scandali pertinet tertiò, cau- sarum litium tum pravisio, tum vitatio, ut nempe frater adversus fratrem litigandi causam non faci- lè arripiat, quin potius damnum aut injuriam per- ferat, alter vero caveat, ne injuriam aut damnum fratri inferat, cum illud adversus Christianam pa- tientiam, hoc verò iniquum & injustum sit, quod posterius, ceu gravius crimen, exaggerat eaque occasione alia etiam crimina, è regno Dei exclu- dentia, damnat. Causæ illæ assignantur geminæ: Prior voce ἀδικεῖσθαι injuriam; posterior verbo ἀποστερεῖσθαι rerum damnum infert. Quapropter injuriam potius devorare, & rerum aliquod da- mnum pati jubemur, quam judicio cum fratre contendere. Ubi tamen distinguere licet inter of- fensas vel injurias leves, & graves, verbales & reales, eas, quæ salvâ conscientia & fama negligi possunt, & quæ non possunt; ac similiter inter damna exi- gua & magna, quæ citra nostrum insigne incom- modum sustineri nequeunt. Et fratri egeno, qui restituere damnum non possit, remittendum po- tius, ac donandum aliquid est, quam judicio con- tendendum cum ejus ulteriori depauperatione; Et quæ alia hujusmodi charitas Christiana talium moderatrix dictitat.

PARS II. Comminatio de injustis aliisque facinorosis, à regni Dei hæreditate excludendis.

## 6:8
verse 8. But you do wrong and defraud, and that to your brothers. Not only do you not endure, but you yourselves inflict injury. He said this to those whose cause was worse.

Chrysostom notes here a varied crime in the Corinthian Church, noted by the Apostle: again a double crime perhaps, or even triple, and quadruple. One is not to know how to endure injury, another to inflict it, a third to permit judgment about these unjust things, a fourth to affect a brother with injury. For sins are not judged similarly when they are committed against others and when they are committed against one's own member. For the daring here is of greater rashness. For in the former case only the nature of the thing is trampled upon, in the latter also the quality of the person.

Latin:

vers. 8. Ἀλλὰ ὑμεῖς ἀδικεῖτε καὶ ἀποστερεῖτε καὶ ταῦτα ἀδελφούς. Non modo non fertis, sed ipsi infertsis injuriam. Hoc eis dixit, quorum pejor erat causa.

Varium hic crimen notat Chrysostomus in Eccle- sia Corinthiaca, notatum ab Apostolo: Rursum duplex crimen fortasse, aut etiam triplex, & quadru- plex. Unum quidem nescire injuriam perferre, al- terum inferre, tertium injustis de his judicium per- mittere, quartum injuria afficere fratrem. Neque enim similiter peccata judicantur, quando in alios, & quando in proprium membrum committuntur. Majoris enim temeritatis hic ausus est. Nam illic natura rei sola conculcatur, hic etiam persona qua- litas.

## 6:9
v. 9. Or do you not know that the unjust shall not inherit the kingdom of God? And this name 'unjust,' and what follows, are not to be referred to the habit alone, but to any deliberate act, as long as it is not washed away through serious repentance and amendment. Thus in law we call him a thief and an adulterer who has once stolen or committed adultery: for these are sins that devastate the conscience, deadly, which kill with one blow, as Augustine speaks. There are other daily incursions, as Tertullian speaks, not consisting according to purpose, as Clement. From these must be distinguished those graver ones, about which Paul treats here, and Galatians 5:19, 20, 21, 1 Timothy 1:9, 10, which he who has been born of God will not admit at all, not being about to be a son of God if he should admit them, as Tertullian speaks. The word 'unjust' here includes those who will be called below 'thieves and covetous'.

By the word 'do you not know' he indicates that this is most known and explored, and is evident to all Christians, indeed that it is evident even by the light of nature, as the Apostle taught in Romans 1:32. But he is rightly warned here about certain deliberate acts, that they also exclude one from the kingdom of God, not habits only. Which is to be observed against the Socinians, who, when they sin in defect, say that not just any acts of such sins, but only habits, are to be condemned, against the open judgment of the law in Deuteronomy 27: last verse, Galatians 3:10, and other clear testimonies in Matthew 5:19, Romans 1:last, Chapter 6:last, Chapter 8:12, 1 John 3:8, Chapter 5:18, James 1:15, Chapter 2:9; when they sin in excess, with those who have been converted, contracting the habit of some mortal sin, they completely shut the kingdom of God, concerning which matter it was acted upon in Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Art. 12, c. 2, th. 11, seqq. Compare also B. Meisner's Theological Considerations on the Photinians, chapter 1, 11. Which, however, when we assert that any reigning sins exclude one from the kingdom of God, are to be understood with the exception of repentance, which, just as it is not closed to any sinner, so neither is forgiveness denied to any who repent. Ezekiel 18:31, Chapter 33:11. And therefore neither is repentance for graver sins impossible or fruitless for the converted.

Do not be deceived. Christ is accustomed to use this preface, as in Luke 21:8, and Paul, as below in 15:33, Galatians 6:7, James also 1:17, as often as they are about to say something which, if ignored or not observed, will cost one the greatest evil.

Indeed, the inclination of the flesh toward such an error is simultaneously hinted at, as if such vices would not be very harmful to us, and God would easily forgive the same for us. By which παραλογισμοῖς (fallacies) we not rarely seduce ourselves into fulfilling any desires whatsoever, since each one is tempted by his own desire, James 1:14. See Sirach 5:2 ff. Chrysostom, on these words: 'Do not be deceived,' says in this place, it signifies many saying, what many also say now, that God is kind and merciful, and does not avenge sins. For it is the ultimate error and fraud that one who hopes for the best should obtain the contrary, and have such an opinion of God as no one would think even of a man. Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς ἀπατάτω καινοῖς λόγοις (Let no one deceive you with empty words), says the Apostle, occupied with this very matter, Eph. 5:6.

Οὔτε πόρνοι (Nor fornicators). That is, fornicators, who mingle themselves with harlots, as we said above, verse 19, and it may be manifest below, verse 15.

Οὔτε εἰδωλολάτραι (Nor idolaters). Who worship false gods.

Latin:

v. 9. Ἦ ὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι ἄδικοι βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ ὐ κληρονομᾶσιν; Et hoc nomen ἄδικοι, & quæ sequuntur, non ad ἕξιν so- lam referenda sunt, sed ad quemvis actum deliberatum, quamdiu is non per seriam pœnitentiam emendationemque eluitur. Sic in jure furem & adulterum dicimus, qui semel furatus est, aut adulterium fecit: Sunt enim hæc peccata vastantia conscientiam, mortifera, quæ uno ictu perimunt, ut loquitur Augustinus. Sunt aliæ quotidianæ incursatio- nes, ut Tertullianus loquitur, μὴ κατὰ προαίρεσιν συνιστάμενα, ut Clemens. Ab his distinguenda illa graviora, de quibus hic agit Paulus, & Galat. V. 19. 20. 21. 1. Timoth. I. 9. 10. quæ non admittet omnino, qui natus ex Deo fuerit, non futurus Dei filius, si admiserit, ut loquitur Tertullianus. Vox ἀδίκων hic complectitur eos, qui infra dicentur κλέ- πται καὶ πλεονέκται.

Verbo οὐκ οἴδατε indicat maximè hoc notum & exploratum esse, ac constare omnibus Christia- nis, imò id naturæ etiam lumine constare, Apo- stolus Rom. I. 32. docuit. Recte autem monetur hic de actibus quibusdam deliberatis, quod illi etiam à regno Dei excludant, non habitus tantum. Quod contra Socinianos observandum, qui modo in de- fectu peccant, cum non actus quoslibet talium pec- catorum, sed habitus solum damnare ajunt, con- tra sententiam legis apertam Deut. XXVII. v. ult. Gal. III. 10. & luculenta testimonia alia Matth. V. 19. Rom. I. ult. Cap. VI. ult. Cap. IIX. 12. 1. Joh. III. 8. cap. V. 18. Jac. I. 15. Cap. II. 9. modò in excessu, cum conversis, peccati alicujus mortalis habitum contrahentibus, regnum Dei penitus occludunt, qua de re actum in Exeg. Aug. Conf. Art. XII. c. 2. th. 11. seqq. Conf. & B. Meisneri Consider. Theolog. Photin. cap. I. 11. Quæ tamen cum peccata regnan- tia quævis à regno Dei excludere asserimus, cum exceptione pœnitentiæ intelligenda, quæ uti non præclusa est ulli peccatori; ita nec pœnitentibus ullis venia denegatur. Ez. XIIX. 31. Cap. XXXIII 11. Ideoque nec pro gravioribus peccatis pœnitentia vel impossibilis conversis est vel frustranea.

Μὴ πλανᾶσθε. Solet hac præfatione uti Christus, ut Luc. XXI. 8. & Pau- lus, ut infra XV. 33. Gal. VI. 7. Jacobus quoque I. 17. quo- ties aliquid dicturi sunt, quod ignoratum aut non observa- tum maximo stabit malo.

Innuitur verò simul proclivitas carnis ad ejus- modi errorem, quasi non multùm nocitura nobis sint ejusmodi vitia, nobisque Deus facile eadem condonaturus sit. Quibus παραλογισμοῖς nos ipsos non rarò seducimus ad quasvis concupiscen- tias perficiendas, cum unusquisque tentatur à pro- pria concupiscentia sua Jac. I. 14. Vide Sir. V. 2. seqq. Chrysostomus ad hæc verba: Nolite errare, hoc in loco, inquit, significat multos dicentes, quod & nunc multi dicunt, quod benignus est Deus, & clemens; & non ulciscatur peccata. Erroris namque & frau- dis ultima est, ut qui optima speret, contraria conse- quatur, & talem de Deo habeat opinionem, quam nec de homine quisquam arbitretur. Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς ἀπα- τάτω καινοῖς λόγοις ait Apostolus, in hac ipsa ma- teria occupatus, Eph. V. 6.

Οὔτε πόρνοι. Id est πορνευταὶ, qui cum scortis se miscent, ut diximus supra V. 19. & manifestum sit infra 15.

Οὔτε εἰδωλολάτραι. Qui falsos Deos colunt.

## 6:10
v. 10. Οὔτε μοιχοί (Nor adulterers). Who defile the marriages of others.

Οὔτε μαλακοί (Nor the effeminate). That is, the passive. The scholiast on the first book of Thucydides: 'Philoctetes, having contracted a feminine disease on account of the death of Paris, and not bearing the shame, departed from his fatherland and built a city, which, because of the affliction, he called Malakia.' Regarding the same matter, Ausonius: 'The Paeantian hero was soft and easy for men.' Catullus: 'O you catamite Thallus, softer than a rabbit's hair.' Phaedrus spoke of 'soft males' in this sense. In Petronius, in the same sense: 'The soft ones of old.' Vibius Sequester: 'Mollescit (he becomes soft), that is, he is obscene.' Pliny, book XXVIII: 'of shameful softness.' Arnobius: 'Fabius is burned in his soft parts.' Augustine also uses the word 'mollium' (of the soft) in this way in The City of God, book VI. Claudian concerning Eutropius: '-- -- For what will shame a slave and a soft man?' Philo also uses μαλακίαν (softness) in this sense in On the Special Laws. Chrysostom also uses μαλακοὺς (the effeminate) in this sense above in chapter four, and in this place explains it as 'those who have played the harlot'. The Syrian here translates it as מחבלא, that is, those who corrupt themselves.

Οὔτε ἀρσενοκοῖται (Nor sodomites). That is, those who lie with males. It is the counterpart of that which preceded.

Nor thieves.

A thief is, as the jurists define it, one who fraudulently, for the sake of gain, handles a thing, or the use, or the possession of another's property.

A covetous person.

He is so called who breaks faith in contracts, or in any way circumvents another. Both Xenophon and Aristotle use the word in this way. See above V. 10. 12. Eph. IV. 19. C. V. 3. 5. Mark VII. 22. Rom. I. 24. Coloss. III. 9. In Hebrew בצע.

Nor drunkards.

Consider those to be such who deliberately gorge themselves with wine, so that they even deprive themselves of the use of reason.

Nor revilers.

See above V. 11.

Nor extortioners.

They differ from thieves in that thieves use guile, while robbers use force. See above V. 11.

Shall not inherit the kingdom of God.

That is, as long as they are such, they ought not to hope for a part in heavenly blessedness. However, the guilt remains until the serious performance of repentance, if indeed God grants it. For He does not grant it to all, but blinds and hardens some. But upon whom that severity is to be used, He alone knows, who looks into the innermost parts of men and knows what measure of His patience is appropriate.

First, he excludes from the kingdom of God the wicked of a triple kind: (1.) τοὺς ἀδίκους, the unjust, of whom the Apostle had treated in the preceding words, v. 8 & 9, who sin against their neighbor. (2.) τοὺς πόρνους, the fornicators, on the occasion of the fornicator of whom [he spoke] above, who sin against their own body. (3.) Idolaters, who transgress immediately against God. Afterwards, he pursues specifically the twins of fornicators, adulterers, the effeminate, and sodomites: also certain classes of the unjust, thieves, and defrauders. And since drunkenness contributes greatly to fornication, and the itch for slandering is not unlike the crimes of thieves and defrauders, and these are grave sins in themselves, he commemorates them particularly, and immediately subjoins them in the present catalog, which he finally concludes with the crime of extortioners: which is almost transcendent. For both those who steal glory from God are idolaters; and those who [steal] goods and reputation from their neighbor are thieves, defrauders, and slanderers; and those who [steal] the debt and body from a spouse, whose dominion they have handed over to them (1 Cor. VII. 4), are adulterers; or [those who steal] from the Lord His temple and His members (1 Cor. VI. 15, 19, 20), are fornicators, the effeminate, and sodomites; and those who [steal] health and life from themselves can be called drunkards and extortioners, though primarily and particularly the violent stealers of goods are so called. And concerning all these, the Apostle pronounces that they shall not inherit the kingdom of God, the heavenly kingdom, which, as the inheritance of the blessed Father, prepared for true believers from the foundation of the world, they obtain (Matt. XXV. 34, 1 Pet. I. 4, 5). For such are destitute of true faith, which can in no way consist with these sins, without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI. 6), and thus the inheritance of God cannot be entered. Those works are not doubtful, but manifest and known to all, of the flesh, which those who do shall not inherit the kingdom of God (Gal. V. 19, 20, 21. Cf. Eph. V. 3, 4, 5, 6, Col. III. 5, 6, Rev. XXI. 8, Ch. XXII. 15). Concerning the unjust and similar [sins], see particularly Deut. 27:17, Is. V. 8, Jer. XXII. 13, Ez. XI: X. 12, 13, Amos VIII. 7, Mic. II. 1, Hab. II. 6, Mal. III. 5, 1 Thess. IV. 6. Concerning fornicators, see Job XXIV. 18, 19, ch. XXXI. 9, 12, Prov. V. 5, VII. 27, IX. 18, XXII. 14, XXIII. 25. Concerning idolaters, Deut. XXVII. 15, Ez. XVIII. 12. Here Cornelius à Lapide notes the politicians in the papacy: Our politicians err more shamefully, who deny that fornication was forbidden by the law of Moses: to whom, besides the decalogue in Ex. XX, he opposes Deut. XXII. 21, Num. XXV. 9, Prov. XIX. 3. Tob. I. He also notes the opinion of Thomas: Drunkenness is not a mortal sin because of ignorance of the strength of the wine, or the weakness of one's own head, by which, however, the excuse is removed by frequent experience. Therefore, the Apostle significantly says, a drunkard, not drunk. This opinion, I say, he rejects, and deservedly. The Greek μέθυσος, he says, denotes as much a drunkard as one who is drunk. Wherefore the word for drunkard here does not properly denote the frequency or custom of getting drunk, but the act. For thus also the others here, such as a slanderer or an adulterer, signify the act. For one act of them excludes them from the kingdom of heaven.

And such were some of you.

You were these things, that is, some of you were such. The neuter is used for the common [gender]. No past crime excludes anyone from baptism. But the faults of many, contrary to previously received knowledge, are such that they are not fit for faith, and therefore not τεταγμένοι πρὸς τὴν ζωὴν αἰώνιον (ordained to eternal life). There lies hidden here a Socinian-Arminian trick, which they have from Pelagius. For Grotius is accustomed to sail with the wind for this [view] also, as if some disposition were required in man for faith. Truly, no one is fit for faith unless God makes him fit, from whom also all ἱκανότης (sufficiency) and faith itself, as the work of God, comes (2 Cor. III. 5, John VI. 29).

But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.

You were baptized, and then you received the Holy Spirit, and you made greater progress daily in righteousness. For the order persuades that the word ἐδικαιώθητε (you were justified) is taken in this place in this way, and the same sense [is found] in Rev. XXII. 11. In the name of Christ, that is, through the doctrine of Christ, which doctrine is sealed by the Spirit.

That meaning of justification can certainly be admitted, but in such a sense that it denotes the continuation of justification, not indeed the progress of holiness, which contributes nothing to justification, inasmuch as it consists solely of the grace of God and faith in the righteousness and obedience of Christ, and not indeed in our own holiness or righteousness. And thus the blessed Balduinus in his Analysis p. 351 expresses the present state after regeneration with three words: (1.) is washing, by which he understands baptism, as the first door into the Church. (2.) sanctification, which is the fruit of regeneration, by which a Christian is recognized from the outside and discerned from infidels. (3.) Justification, which is the daily purging and remission of sins, which bestows all these benefits upon them in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of God, that is, through the invocation of the name of Christ and the operation of the Holy Spirit. For he joins the meritorious and efficient cause of our redemption. Since the operation and efficacy of the holy ministry, in which the benefits of Christ are conferred upon us, is attributed to the Holy Spirit. However, the gradation holds very well according to the common interpretation, if it is understood to be made not by ascending, but by descending, in this way: Such you were; but you were washed through baptism, and sanctified, nay even justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of your God. For the first is justification, which is done in the name of, or on account of the merit of, and through the obedience of the Lord Jesus, which is imputed to us for righteousness. There follows through the Spirit of God our sanctification: And finally, as regards the Corinthians, washing through baptism, inasmuch as they, having been converted to the faith as adults and having become believers, were washed in baptism from their sins for the sealing of the righteousness of faith (Rom. IV. 11). But when infants are washed from sins by the laver of regeneration through the blood of Christ the Savior, this is their very justification, inasmuch as it consists in the remission of sins, and to it is connected sanctification, which also comes to pass by the virtue of baptism, as a λύτρoν not only of παλιγγενεσίας, but also of ἀνακαινώσεως πνέυματος ἁγίυ Tit. III. 5. For the washing in baptism, by which we are bathed and cleansed from the filth of our sins, occurs not physically, by purging away filth, as the Papists imagine; but by the removal of them, not by their imputation, by their remission Rom. IV. 7. 8. so that we do not appear impure in the eyes of the Lord, nor be judged as such by God, but by the imputation of the justice and innocence of Christ, so that we may be reckoned pure in the judgment of God, and thus not be condemned, but justified.

But the Crellian gloss is not to be admitted, as being alien to the analogy of faith: But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified, that is, but you are cleansed from those vices and sins. We are cleansed from sins in a twofold manner, both as we are freed from the sins themselves, and as we are freed from their guilt and punishments. He seems to have designated the former cleansing with a double verb, one metaphorical, of being washed; the other more proper, of being sanctified: The latter he expressed with the verb of being justified. Moreover, Paul preserved in his words the order that exists in the things themselves, for the washing from the filth of sins precedes, and the sanctification of man, and consecration to God; Justification and liberation from the guilt of sins follows, and by how much the former is fuller and more certain, by so much is the latter firmer and more perfect. Twin to these are the things which Schlichtingius has on this passage. But justification is not a consequence of purity from vices and sanctification, as these men wish; but according to the Apostle it is the cause, since those who are justified abstain from vices and strive for holiness, but not those who are to be justified. B. Balduinus page 35 notes these things against

Bellarmine, book 2 on Justification, chapter 3, who infers from this passage that justification is washing and sanctification: The word sanctification is sometimes taken for the imputation of the holiness of Christ. In which sense we easily concede that Justification comprises these two things: (1) the remission of the evil that is in us, and this is called the remission of sins; (2) the conferring of good outside of us, and this is commonly called internal sanctification of hearts, when the holiness and justice of Christ is imputed to us through faith. And the word Sanctification being taken in this meaning, Bellarmine's argument does nothing against us. The late lamented one warns in Aphorisms, page 354. There are three things in sin from which Christ has perfectly freed us: first, that filth and uncleanness which makes us abominable before God; that is washed away in baptism: Then, the contamination arising from that filth, which makes us useless for good: But this too has been removed through the benefit of sanctification, while Christ has gifted us with the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies our thoughts, words, and actions, and renders us fit for those things which are pleasing to God. Finally, the guilt or punishment owed for sins, from which we have been freed through justification, which is nothing other than absolution from sins in the judgment of God. D. Paul embraces all these things in this place, which is to be noted against the Papists. Furthermore, one must observe here the testimony of the Holy Trinity, concerning which Theodoret writes on this passage. He openly shows the equality of the Son and the Spirit, and he also joined the mention of God and the Father. For through the invocation of the Holy Trinity the nature of the waters is sanctified, and the remission of sins is exhibited.

All things are lawful for me. He repeats the words used by those Corinthian teachers who sought after the sumptuous tables of the rich. They used to say: All things are lawful for me, that is, God created all these things for our sake; wherefore there is no evil if we use them.

But not all things are expedient. Paul responds that a limit must be applied. For not every use of such things is conducive either to health, which a wise man should not neglect, or to the right use of reason. For the body, burdened with yesterday's vices, weighs down the mind as well.

Latin:

v. 10. Οὔτε μοιχοί. Qui aliena matrimonia polluunt.

Οὔτε μαλακοί. Id est Pathici. Scholiastes ad primum Thucydidis: Φιλοκτήτης διὰ τὸν Πάριδος θάνατον θήλειαν νόσον νοσήσας, καὶ μὴ φέρων τὴν αἰσχύνην ἀπελθὼν ἐκ τῆς πατρίδος, ἔκτισε πόλιν, ἣν διὰ τὸ πάθος μαλακίαν ἐκάλεσε. De eadem re Au- sonius: Mollis erat facilísque viris Pæantius heros. Catullus: Cinæde Thalle mollior cuniculi capillo. Phædrus hoc sensu dixit molles mares. Apud Petronium eodem sensu: Molles veteres. Vibius Sequester: Mollescit, id est, obscænus sit. Plinius lib. XXVIII. probrosa mollitiei. Arnobius: In partibus Fabius aduritur mollibus. Utitur vo- ce mollium sic & Augustinus de civitate Dei lib. VI. Clau- dianus de Eutropio: -- -- Quid enim servum mollemque pudebit? μαλακίαν hoc sensu usurpat & Philo de legibus speciali- bus. Chrysostomus quoque μαλακοὺς hoc sensu usurpat supra capite quarto, & hoc loco exponit ἑταιρηκότας. Sy- rus hic vertit מחבלא id est qui se corrumpunt.

Οὔτε ἀρσενοκοῖται. Id est drauci. Est Ἀντίστροφος ejus, quod præcessit.

Οὔτε κλέπται.

Fur est, Jurisconsultis definientibus, qui fraudulosè lu- cri causâ rem, usumve, aut possessionem rei alienae con- trectat.

Πλεονέκτης.

Ita dicitur, qui in contractibus fidem fallit, aut quovis modo alium circumvenit. Sumunt ita hanc vocem & Xe- nophon, & Aristoteles. Vide supra V. 10. 12. Eph. IV. 19. C. V. 3. 5. Marci VII. 22. Rom. I. 24. Coloss. III. 9. He- braice בצע.

Οὔτε μέθυσοι.

Eos puta, qui de studio vino se ingurgitant, ita ut & usum rationis sibi adimant.

Ου λοίδοροι.

Vide supra V. 11.

Οὐχ ἅρπαγες.

Distant à furibus, quod fures dolo, raptores vi utantur. Vide supra V. 11.

Βασιλείαν Θεῦ ὐ κληρονομήσουσιν.

Id est, quamdiu tales sunt, non debent sperare partem in beatitudine caelesti. Manet autem reatus usque ad seriam poenitentiae functionem, si tamen eam Deus concedit. Ne- que enim concedit omnibus, sed quosdam occaecat & ob- durat. In quos autem eâ severitate utendum sit, ipse solus novit, qui intima hominum introspicit & novit, quae men- sura patientiae ipsius conveniat.

Triplicis primum generis flagitiosos à regno Dei excludit (1.) τὲς ἀδίκυς injustos, de qualibus in ver- bis praecedentibus v. 8. & 9. egerat Apostolus, qui delinquunt adversus proximum. (2.) Τὲς πόρνες scortatores, occasione scortatoris, de quo supra V. qui peccant in proprium corpus. (3.) Εἰδωλολάτρας qui adversus Deum immediatè praevaricantur. Post speciatim persequitur scortatoribus geminos, maechos, molles, draucos: Nec non injustorum quasdam classes, fures, defraudatores. Et quum ebriositas ad scortationem plurimum adminicu- letur, calumniandi Cacoëthes verò non absimile sit furum & defraudatorum criminibus, eaque per se gravia peccata sint, commemorat eadem pecu- liariter, illisque immediate subjungit in praesenti catalogo, quem denique raptorum crimine con- cludit: Quod fere transcendens est. Nam & qui Deo rapiunt gloriam, idololatrae; & qui proximo bona & famam, fures, defraudatores & calumnia- tores; Et conjugi debitum & corpus, cujus domi- nium ipsi tradidere 1. Cor. VII. 4. adulteri; aut Domino templum suum & membra sua, scor- tatores, molles, & drauci 1. Cor. VI. 15. 19. 20. & qui sibi ipsis sanitatem & vitam, ebriosi raptores dici possunt, imprimis tamen ac peculiariter violenti bonorum raptores dicuntur. Et de his omnibus pronuntiat Apostolus, quod regnum Dei haere- ditaturi non sint, regnum caeleste, quod ceu haere- ditatem, benedicti Patris, veri fideles, à consti- tutione mundi sibi paratum, consequuntur Matth. XXV. 34. 1. Petr. I. 4. 5. Tales enim vera fide, quae cum his peccatis nullatenus consistere potest, de- stituuntur, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere Ebr. XI. 6. adeoque haereditas Dei adiri non po- test. Opera illa sunt non dubia, sed manifesta, omnibusque nota τῆς σαρκὸς, qua qui faciunt, re- gnum Dei non haereditabunt Gal. V. 19. 20. 21. Conf. E b. V. 3. 4. 5. 6. Col. III. 5. 6. Ap. XXI. 8. C. XXII. 15. de injustis & similibus peculiariter vide Deut. 27, 17. Es. V. 8. Jer. XXII. 13. Ez. XI: X. 12. 13. Amos. IIX. 7. Mich. II. 1. Hab. II. 6. Mal. III. 5. 1. Thess. IV. 6. De scortatoribus vide Jobi XXIV. 18. 19. c. XXXI. 9. 12. Prov. V. 5. VII. 27. IX. 18. XXII. 14. XXIII. 25. De idololastris Deut. XXVII. 15. Ez. XIIX. 12. Notat hic Cornelius à Lapide Politicos in papatu: Errant turpius nostri Politici, qui fornicationem lege Mo- sis vetitam esse negant: Quibus praeter decalogum Ex. XX. opponit Deut. XXII. 21. Num. XXV. 9. Prov. XIX. 3. Tob. I. Notat & Thomae sententiam: Ebrietas non est peccatum mortale ob ignorantiam fortitudinis vini, vel debilitatem proprii capitis, qua tamen excusatio tollitur per frequentem experientiam. Ideo signanter ait Apostolus, ebriosus, non ebrius. Hanc, inquam, sententiam reprobat, & merito. Græcum μέθυσος, inquit, tam ebrium notat, quam ebriosum. Quare vox ebriosi hic non proprie fre- quentiam vel consuetudinem se inebriandi, sed a- ctum denotat. Sic enim & cætera hic, ut sunt male- dicus, adulter, actum significant. Unus enim eo- rum actus eos à regno cœlorum excludit.

Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε.

Hæc fuistis, id est, tales fuistis vestrum quidam. Posi- tum est neutrum pro communi. Nullum anteactum faci- nus baptismo quemquam excludit. Sed multorum culpæ contra acceptas prius notitias sunt tales, ut ii ad fidem non sint idonei, ac proinde non τεταγμένοι πρὸς τὴν ζωὴν αἰώνιον. Latet hic ὕπουλον Sociniano-Arminianum, quod à Pelagio habent. Huic enim & aliàs velificari so- let Grotius, quasi aliqua in homine requiratur ad fi- dem dispositio. Nemo profectò est ad fidem ido- neus, nisi quem Deus idoneum facit, à quo & ἱκα- νότης omnis, & fides ipsa, ceu ἔργον Θεῦ est. 2. Cor. III. 5. Joh. VI. 29.

Ἀλλ’ ἀπελύσασθε, ἀλλ’ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλ’ ἐδικαιώ- θητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ κυρίυ Ἰησῦ, καὶ ἐν τῷ πνέυματι τῦ Θεῦ ἡμῶν.

Baptizati estis, ac deinde accepistis Spiritum Sanctum, & majores quotidie in justitia profectus fecistis. Nam ita illud ἐδικαιώθητε hoc loco sumi suadet ordo, & idem sensus in Apoc. XXII. 11. In nomine Christi, id est, per doctrinam Christi, quæ doctrina per Spiritum obsignatur.
