Admitti sanè potest illa justificationis signifi- catio, sed eo sensu, ut continuatio justificationis, non vero progressus sanctitatis, quæ ad justificatio- nem nihil facit, utpote, quæ sola Dei gratia & fide in Christi justitiam & obedientiam, non verò no- stra sanctitate vel justitia propria constat, denote- tur. Atque ita B. Balduinus in Analysi p. 351. sta- tum præsentem post regenerationem tribus exprimit vocabulis: (1.) est ablutio, qua intelligit bapti- smum, tanquam primam januam in Ecclesiam. (2.) sanctificatio, quæ est fructus regenerationis, quo Christianus ab extra agnoscitur, & ab infide- libus discernitur. (3.) Justificatio, quæ quotidiana est peccatorum purgatio & remissio, quæ benefi- cia omnia tribuit istis in nomine Jesu Christi, & in Spiritu Dei, hoc est, per invocationem nominis Christi, & operationem Spiritus Sancti. Conjungit enim causam meritoriam & efficientem redemtio- nis nostræ. Siquidem Spiritui sancto tribuitur operatio & efficacia sacrosancti ministerii, in quo beneficia Christi nobis conferuntur. Optimè tamen se habet gradatio juxta communem inter- pretationem, si non adscendendo, sed descendendo facta intelligatur, hoc modo: Tales fuistis; sed abluti estis per baptismum, & sanctificati, imò & justificati, in nomine Domini Jesu, & in Spiritu Dei vestri. Prior enim est justificatio, quæ fit in nomine, vel propter meritum, & per obedientiam Domini Jesu, quæ nobis imputatur ad justitiam. Sequitur per Spiritum Dei sanctificatio nostra: Ac denique, quod ad Corinthios, ablutio per baptismum, utpote, qui adulti ad fidem conversi, & fideles facti, in ba- ptismo abluti sunt à peccatis ad obsignationem ju- stitiæ fidei Rom. IV. 11. Cum verò infantes per la- vacrum regenerationis à peccatis abluuntur Chri- sti Servatoris sanguine, hæc est ipsa eorundem justificatio, utpote, quæ in peccatorum remissione consistit, eique connexa est sanctificatio, quæ etiam virtute baptismi fit, ceu λύτρoν non παλιγγενεσίας tantùm, sed etiam ἀνακαινώσεως πνέυματος ἁγίυ Tit. III. 5. Ablutio enim in baptismo, quà à pec- catorum nostrorum sordibus lavamur & munda- mur, fit non physicè, sordes purgando, ut Papistæ fingunt; sed earum tediione, non imputatione, re- missione Rom. IV. 7. 8. ut non impuri in oculis Do- mini compareamus, nec à Deo tales cenfeamur, sed justitiá ac innocentiá Christi imputatione, ut puri in judicio DEI reputemur, adeoque non con- demnemur, fed justificemur.

Non autem glossa Crelliana admittenda est, ut- pote aliena ab analogia fidei: Sed abluti, sed san- ctificati, sed justificati estis, id est, sed à vitiis & peccatis istis repurgati estis. Duplici ratione à pec- catis purgamur, tum quatenus ab ipsis peccatis, tum quatenus ab eorum reatu ac pœnis liberamur. Priorem purgationem duplici verbo designasse vide- tur, unô Metaphorico abluendi; altero magis pro- prio sanctificandi: Alteram verbo justificandi ex- pressit. Ordinem autem, qui in rebus ipsis est, serva- vit etiam Paulus in verbis, Præcedit enim ablutio à peccatorum sordibus, & hominis sanctificatio, ac Deo consecratio; Justificatio & à peccatorum reatu liberatio sequitur, quantoque illa plenior est ac cer- tior; tanto & hæc firmior est, & perfectior. Gemel- la istis sunt, quæ habet Schlichtingius in hunc lo- cum. Sed justificatio non est consequens puritatis à vitiis & sanctificationis, ut hi volunt; sed secun- dum Apostolum est causa, cum justificati à vitiis abstineant, & sanctitati studeant, non autem ju- stificandi. B. Balduinus pag. 35. hæc notat adversus

Bell. l. 2. de Just. cap. 3. qui ex h. l. infert, justificatio- nem esse ablutionem & sanctificationem: Vocabulum sanctificationis interdum accipitur de imputatione sanctitatis Christi. Quo sensu facile concedimus, Justificationem ista duo complecti (1.) remissionem mali, quod in nobis est, & hæc vocatur remissio pec- catorum (2.) collationem boni extra nos, & hæc vul- go vocatur sanctificatio interna cordium, quando sanctitas & justitia Christi per fidem nobis impu- tatur. Atque hæc significatione accepto vocabulo Sanctificationis, nihil contra nos facit argumen- tum Bellarmini. Monet ὁ μακαρίτης in Aphor. pag. 354. Tria sunt in peccato, à quibus perfectè nos liberavit Christus: primum sordes & immun- dities illa, quæ facit nos abominabiles coram DEO; illa abluitur in baptismo: Deinde contaminatio ex sordibus illis oriunda, quæ nos facit inutiles ad bo- num: Sed & hæc sublata est per sanctificationis be- neficium, dum Christus nos Spiritu S. donavit, qui cogitationes, sermones & actiones nostras sanctificat, & ad ea, quæ Deo grata sunt, nos idoneos reddit. Denique reatus seu pœna peccatis debita, à qua libe- rati sumus per justificationem, quæ nihil aliud est, quam absolutio à peccatis in judicio Dei. Hæc o- mnia complectitur D. Paulus hoc loco, quod contra Pontificios notandum est. Cæterum observandum hic testimonium SS. Trinitatis, de quo Theodor. ad h. l. Aperte ostendit æqualitatem Filii & Spiri- tus, conjunxit etiam Dei & Patris mentionem. Per S. enim Trinitatis invocationem aquarum natura sanctificatur, & exhibetur peccatorum remissio.

Πάντα μοι ἔξεσι. Repetit verba usitata Doctoribus illis Corinthiis, qui opiparas divitum mensas sectabantur. Dicebant illi: Omnia mihi licent, id est, Deus ista omnia nostri causa condidit; quare nihil est mali, si eis utamur.

Ἀλλ’ ὐ πάντα συμφέρει. Respondet Paulus adhibendum modum. Non enim omnem usum talium conducere aut valetudini, quæ sapien- ti negligenda non est, aut recto usui rationis. Nam Corpus onustum. Hesternis vitiis animum quoque degravat.

## 6:12
V. 12. All things are lawful for me. He repeats their words again, so that he may respond more pointedly. Such repetition of objections is frequent in Seneca.

But I will not be brought under the power of any. There is a paronomasia in 'are lawful' (ἔξεσι), which preceded, and 'be brought under power' (ἐξυσιασθήσομαι). To have power (ἐξυσιάζειν) is to have authority, Luke XXII. 25, below VII. 4. He responds to the Hebrew 'mashal' (משׁל), as can be seen in Nehemiah IX. 37, Ecclesiastes IX. 17, X. 4, and 'shalat' (שׁלט) in Nehemiah V. 15, and

in Ecclesiastes several times. Hence the passive ἐξουσιάζεσθαι is to be reduced into slavery. He who fills himself with feasts beyond measure, who pursues the delicacies of foods, is a slave of foods, not a master.

Latin:

V. 12. Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν. Iterum repetit illorum verba, ut pressius respondeat. Frequens talis objectionum repetitio apud Senecam.

Ἀλλ’ ὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξυσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος. Est παρονομασία in ἔξεσι, quod præcessit, & ἐξυσιασθήσο- μαι. Ἐξυσιάζειν est imperium habere, Luc. XXII. 25. in- fra VII. 4. Respondet Hebræo משׁל, ut videre est Nehem. IX. 37. Ecclesiastæ IX. 17. X. 4. & שׁלט in Neh. V. 15. &

in Ecclesiaste aliquoties. Hinc passivum ἐξουσιάζεσθαι est in servitutem redigi. Qui ultra modum epulis se implet, qui ciborum delicias sectatur, servus est ciborum, non Do- minus.

## 6:13
Τὰ βρώματα τῇ κοιλίᾳ, καὶ ἡ κοιλία τοῖς βρώμασι) The datives here correspond to the Hebrew particle ל, which often signifies 'on account of': Foods are for the sake of filling the belly, and the belly is for receiving and digesting foods. Understand the belly here as the stomach and intestines.

Ὁ δὲ θεὸς καὶ ταύτην, καὶ ταῦτα καταργήσει) He will cause the bodies to cease when they will be like the angelic ones; they will not need food. (For they ate no grain, nor drank sparkling wine) those who lead a heavenly life, as we said in Matt. XXII. 30. But what is said here that God is about to do, so that the belly also may cease, some understand this regarding the use of the belly. But from the writings of the ancients on this passage, it appears they believed that men would indeed recover their bodies, but it does not follow that in that body there would be those parts whose functions are then to cease. Plutarch, or whoever is the author of the Banquet of the Seven Sages: 'Would it have been worthy for the stomach and the liver to perish along with the injustice, which provide no perception of anything, nor desire.' But this discourse also pertains to this, that we should care for eternal things rather than temporal ones, which are soon to end.

No trace of such imitation or objection appears in the text. The Apostle rather presents himself as an example of submission in indifferent matters, and those by no means prohibited by the law of God, not as to what is lawful, but what is expedient, yet in such a way that he does not suffer himself to be reduced into slavery, he observes, e.g., in the use of foods, as they serve only the necessity of the belly: just as the belly is destined for the use of foods; but with respect to whose use, not less the belly than the food will be destroyed, or will cease at last, nor will there be a place for it in the other life. Since he does this in those things which are indifferent, so that he does not allow himself to be carried away by the whim of his own will; but attends to what is expedient, how much less should we yield to our lust and depraved concupiscence in those things which are prohibited by divine law, and the kingdom of God, which is not situated in food and drink, Rom. XIV. 17? The Apostle perhaps also slipped into this on the occasion of drunkenness being censured, so that he might warn that one should not only abstain from the illicit drink of the cup, which they call drunkenness; but also from the licit one, namely the cup of cheerfulness, as it is accustomed to be called, and that what is expedient here, both for us and for others, so that we may not be a scandal to them, must be properly observed. Thus Chrysostom: He hints here at gluttons, and those who are addicted to the belly. For since he is about to return again to the fornicator, and fornication arises from delicacies and intemperance, he strongly chastises that affection. For he does not say this about prohibited things, for those are not lawful, but about those which seem to be indifferent: Of what kind is that which I say? It is lawful, he says, to eat, to drink, which is his admirable and unexpected way, which he is indeed often accustomed to do, that which he says turning into the contrary, here too he accomplished that; and he shows that to do what is in one's power is not only not expedient, but it is not even a matter of power, but rather of slavery. And first indeed he turns away and dissuades from it from the fact that it is not expedient, saying: They are not expedient. But secondly, also from the contrary, saying: I will be brought under the power of none. But this is what he says. It is in your power, he says, to eat. Remain therefore having this power and see, lest you become a slave to this affection. For he who uses it for that which is proper, he himself has it in his power. But he who goes out to excess and intemperance is no longer the master, but its slave, with voracity and gluttony exercising tyranny over him. Cornelius à Lapide also praises this sense; as if he were to say: It is lawful for me to eat all foods, but I will not allow the gluttony of any food to dominate me, so that I become a slave of the belly. Ambrose and Thomas, however, refer it to expenses, as if he were to say: It is lawful for me, evangelizing, to receive expenses and sustenance from you, but I will not receive them, lest I be beholden to anyone, and lose my liberty. But this is foreign to the context.

Cornelius thinks it most appropriate to refer Anselm, as well as Thomas, to the preceding remarks about lawsuits, as if he were saying: I have said these things against lawsuits, not as if it were illicit in itself to seek one's own in a lawsuit, but because I would not have you reduced to the power of others, namely judges, advocates, and procurators, especially those who are infidels.

However, the use of indifferent things degenerates into abuse in two ways: (1) when utility, or edification, and the advantage of one's neighbor is neglected, for then it is not expedient for him, and when it is joined with scandal, or even when it is not expedient for us ourselves; (2) when we are reduced into servitude, or for the sake of the danger to our liberty, or of subjection under sin. The Apostle warns that both of these abuses are to be avoided by his example. Those statements can also be understood through meiosis: Not all things are beneficial; that is: There are some things, even sometimes harmful, if you use them, inasmuch as they are joined with the scandal of a neighbor or our own loss. And in those words, 'I will not be brought under the power of any,' the person can be understood, that no mortal will bring himself into servitude in matters that are free; or the thing can be understood, as if he were saying: The use of all things is free to me, but I will not give myself into servitude to any thing, so that it is not permitted for me to abstain even from that, if I should wish and it should seem expedient. God certainly created both food and drink for the use of man and the sustenance of the belly: He also made the belly, which might crave, digest, and convert and contribute food and drink to the use of the whole human body, so that food is destined for the belly, and the belly for food. But He does not want the belly to become a seminary of lust and pleasure from the use of foods, nor did He create the belly only for the sake of food, much less that we should serve the belly, Phil. 3:19. Since He willed it to contribute to the integrity of the human body, therefore, when food ceases, the belly is nevertheless not destroyed, and some have been preserved for a time, although extraordinarily, as is evident from the examples of Moses and Elijah, nor is there any doubt that they could be preserved perpetually without food, if God willed it: Just as in the other life there will be neither food, nor appetite, nor the use of food, and by reason of that the belly will be abolished. Although by reason of substance it is the same, inasmuch as it pertains to the integrity of the human body, it is not to be abolished, just as Christ, rising gloriously, whose body ours will be conformed to, Phil. 3:21, did not lack a belly, Luke 24:43. This is to be observed against the distortion of the Socinians, who commonly understand here an all-encompassing abolition of the belly, as was also done here by Crellius, who says from these words of Paul: It is for anyone to gather that in the future age there will be no place for the belly, any more than for foods. The same is to be thought concerning the other members of our body, which are destined for the uses of this mortal life. This inference is no less illogical than it is a miscopying. For the discourse here is about the destruction of the belly not by reason of substance, but by reason of the use of foods, and the Apostle sufficiently teaches that we will have the belly, along with the other members of our body, in the glorious resurrection, when he says that 'this corruptible,' by which name our whole body is indicated, is not to be abolished or annihilated, but says it must 'put on,' that is, it will put on 'incorruption,' 1 Cor. 15:53. It will remain, therefore, by reason of substance, but not by reason of corruptibility: But this same body, which is corruptible here, will put on incorruptibility. Nothing is held here concerning the abolition of the substance of the belly. And Crellius himself does not deny that the use is being referred to: 'But God will abolish both this and these.' As if he were saying, even if it is free for Christians, in themselves, to eat any foods; they ought nevertheless to use this liberty sparingly, thinking that both the belly and foods are to be abolished by God. For it is by no means fitting that Christians should be more than is right addicted to perishing things, and should place any part of their happiness in them. Hence it is that in the epistle to the Rom. 14:17.

he left it written: The kingdom of God is not food and drink, that is, to gorge oneself with food and drink, and to use them without discrimination: But righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. In these things consists the true happiness of Christians, and that which is proper to them in this age. What? That Paul, a little later, is about to call our bodies members of Christ, and temples of the Holy Spirit, and of God Himself, flesh bought with a price: Shall we believe, however, that these bodies, which are flesh bought with the price of the blood of Christ, which are members of Christ, which are temples of the Holy Spirit, which are God's just as much as our Spirit, are to be utterly destroyed, and annihilated, and deprived of heavenly beatitude?

But Grotius brings aid here also to the Socinians, namely that it appears from the writings of the ancients on this passage that they believed that men would indeed recover their bodies, but that it does not follow that there would be in that body those parts whose functions are then to cease. But what, pray, will thus remain, and what kind of human bodies will they be then, with all those parts failing whose functions will then cease? Nor indeed did he name the ancients who might agree with him. Theophylact certainly contradicts him: He says, (He will destroy) not the belly, but the gluttony of the belly. For he thinks that the belly is called gluttony itself, not the stomach, a member of our body. For he also praises others who say that the condition of the future age is being foretold here, where neither can food be taken, nor drink be consumed. But he does not admit the abolition of the stomach. Theophylact here, as in other things, has followed Chrysostom, who holds as follows: He does not call the belly the belly here, but gluttony, as when he says: 'Whose god is the belly': Not speaking of the member, but of voracity. For that it is so, hear what follows: 'And the belly for foods: but the body not for fornication, but for the Lord.' And yet the belly is also a body. But he placed two pairings, foods and gluttony, which indeed he called the belly. Christ and the body. But what is 'foods for the belly'? Food, he says, enters into friendship with gluttony, and they with them. They cannot, therefore, he says, lead us to Christ, but they draw us to themselves. For it is a heavy and beastly affection, and it makes us servants, and causes us to serve it. Chrysostom likewise added our explanation concerning the future state: But he did not assert what Grotius attributes to the ancients; indeed, he taught the contrary: Some say that what was said is a prophecy, but that it signifies the state which is in the future age: And that it is not permitted there either to eat or to drink. But if it is to have an end, consistent in proportion and symmetry, it is much more necessary to abstain from immoderation. Then, lest you think it is a reproach of the body, nor suspect that he reproached the whole from a part, nor say that the nature of the body is the cause of fornication, hear what follows. For I do not accuse, he says, the nature of the body, but the immoderate luxury of the soul. But the Saint confirmed our faith concerning the resurrection of the same bodies in number from the following words of the Apostle. Chrysostom: For if our body is a member of Christ, and Christ has risen, the body also will altogether follow the head. Thus also Athanasius (or whoever the author is) explains the belly regarding gluttony and drunkenness, Quæst. ad Antioch. p. 133. We acknowledge, however, that the belly itself is understood here, not gluttony, and that it is said to be destroyed by reason of the underlying matter, so that, namely, it may no longer be a belly of foods, which is fed by foods, nor that foods may be of the belly, so that they may bait and fill the belly.

v. 13. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα ὐ τῇ πορνείᾳ, ἀλλὰ τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ ὁ Κύριθ- τῷ σώματι. Lest anyone, because of what had been said about foods, should drag it also to fornication, as if its use also were permitted along with foods, as those philosophers rather than Christians taught, he opposes himself to this error, and shows that not in the same way does this matter stand. For we have a body, not that we may commit fornication, but that we may serve the Lord, namely through continence or marriage. For the Lord also, having been raised to that highest power, [did so] for this, that he might grant our bodies, after the course of obedience is finished, the fellowship of his glory.

The Apostle prepared for himself an approach by the mention of the belly, to act further against fornication, which the Corinthians had tolerated even when joined with incest, and which was reckoned among the Gentiles as almost indifferent, so that the whole Apostolic council had to specifically decree in Acts 15:29 that they should abstain from fornication. But this abomination did not proceed from Philosophy, as it is equally opposed to it, but from depraved concupiscence, which in the unregenerate unfolds its full powers, with the distinction even between honest and base things being not a little obscured by Original sin. For this is the fountain and origin, as of all errors, so also of depraved lusts.

Regarding the phrase ὁ Κύριος τῷ σώματι, although Grotius has the agreement of Ambrose and Anselm, as if the intention were that Christ will be the reward for a chaste and pure body, and will grant it incorruption and immortality; yet this is not a discourse about the remuneration of chastity, but it is taught that the body is not destined for fornication, as the belly is for foods, and that the use of the body is not to be considered equally indifferent for any intercourse whatsoever, as the use of the belly is for any food whatsoever, but that the body is dedicated to God as its Creator, Redeemer, and Savior, and therefore these things are referred to each other: our body to the service of God; but Christ to the lordship of the body. So that nothing is to be admitted into our body which does not agree with that holy service owed to the Lord. Just as we are not the lords of our body, but Christ is its Lord. Therefore the body is referred to the Lord, that it may serve him: but the Lord to the body, that he may rule over it, and use it unblemished for his own purposes, for he certainly does not want it to be an instrument of fornication: But he wants it to be his member, as he is our head and one with us, by a mystical union, as our bridegroom and husband, and the temple of the Holy Spirit whom he gives to us, as the Lord of the temple, in which he wants to dwell with God the Father and the Holy Spirit and be glorified, which therefore ought to be holy and inviolable. For in these ways he explains that the Lord is for the body, and the body for the Lord, and by these reasons he recalls Christians from the vice of fornication. Theophylact says, the body, he says, was by no means made so that it might be in luxury and delights, and fall into fornication, but that it might follow God, as the head itself, since God presides over it like a head. And before him Chrysostom: The body is not constructed so that you may be prodigal and luxurious, and commit fornication, but that it may follow Christ as the head, and the Lord be placed over the head. For not, as Theodoret has it, as the belly is a receptacle for food: so the body was created for the sake of fornication.

But God both raised the Lord, and will raise us up through his power.

This particle δὲ is explanatory of the preceding. Concerning this power of God, revealed in the resurrection of Christ, see Rom. 1:19-20.

The particle δὲ very well retains its proper sense, which is adversative. For the body is for the Lord, and the Lord is for the body. But just as God raised the Lord; so he will also raise us to eternal life. Wherefore our body is to be consecrated solely not to fornication or sins, but to the Lord and his honor. And the Lord solely wants to rule over our body. But those who are not raised to a fleeting life, much less to the pleasures of the flesh, but to another heavenly life, in which holiness and justice dwell, and who therefore died for our sins, was raised from the dead, so that he might also raise us through his power to a heavenly life. Those who are given to fornication and other sins do not think of nor acknowledge

Christ delivered for our sins, and raised for our justification, so that he might be our Lord, and our body also might be sacred to him, and that he might also raise us, even as regards this very body, one day to that life where no carnal pleasure, no sin has a place. Therefore he does not want to exclude here this body of ours, whose chastity he claims for the Lord, from the glorious resurrection; but by the argument of a future raising he teaches that it must be consecrated to the Lord, not permitted to fornication, because it is likewise to be raised, when we shall be raised, just as the Lord was raised: who certainly was not raised without a body. And how could we be said to be raised, if our body, which pertains to the integrity of man, and without which man is not man, without which we are not we, that is, those very men who are commanded here to serve God with a chaste mind and body? The Socinians clearly cut the nerve of this Apostolic argument, when they deny the raising of our body, nay, they contend it is denied here. We see, says Crellius on this passage, that Paul changed the terms on purpose, when he speaks of the resurrection, and substituted 'us' for 'our body'; lest if he said our bodies were to be raised, he might seem to have forgotten himself, and urge the resurrection of the belly, which he had said a little before was to be abolished. But yet we are not we, if our bodies do not exist at all, but have ceased to be, or have been reduced entirely to nothing. Nor did the Apostle say our belly was to be destroyed otherwise than in respect of USE. Nor does Crellius deny, the Apostle. Rom. 8, 11. to call our MORTAL bodies to be vivified: To which he says it is indeed sufficient if we are to have other bodies (which may succeed into the place of these), for the reason that those which thus succeed one another are in a certain way one, and the others are as it were reborn in the others. But if bodies substantially other were to succeed into the place of these bodies, and these were indeed clearly reduced to nothing; then neither would these mortal bodies be vivified, nor would we ourselves be raised, and the force of the Apostolic argument would perish: Because he is dealing with that body to be consecrated to the Lord, and not to be dedicated to fornication, which will be eternal to the Lord, and therefore will be raised from death, and will be vivified, but not indeed concerning a new body substantially different from this one of ours. The matter is in the open. Those things which succeed one another in turn are not one, but diverse, since that one perishes completely, while this one finally arises, that one goes into nothing, this one is created from nothing. These words contain, says Crellius, an argument why we ought to dedicate and preserve OUR BODIES entirely for the Lord, because, forsooth, we are to carry away a great reward for this thing (certainly in those very bodies of ours, not in other bodies, but in those which we are commanded to consecrate here to God, not to sins), namely such a one, by which, no otherwise than the Lord himself, we also are to be affected by God. Which will by no means happen without bodies, as Schlichtingius admits here. But he adds: Although with matter and form much more excellent. That, however, contradicts the Apostle. For if they are different in both matter and form, they will certainly not be the same which are to be consecrated here to the Lord, which nevertheless the Apostle intends, when he teaches that these bodies of ours, which we now dedicate to God alone, are to be raised. For as to what Schlichtingius says, that we see in our very mortal bodies themselves that they are the same, which are the same by succession: For this we concede concerning those things which remain according to substantial parts, even if they suffer alteration, just as our mortal bodies here remain as to substantial parts, even if they are subject to alteration, nutrition, augmentation, etc. For members and other parts do not succeed those which nature has granted. But when bodies clearly, as to all members and parts, into nothing are reduced, and substances entirely different are created anew, and produced from nothing, he would not be in possession of his reason who would say that those bodies, newly produced from nothing, different in matter and form, or in number, nay in species and genus, such as the Socinians imagine, are the same on account of succession. On account of succession alone, I say. Which if it be sufficient, the soul also would be the same, if another succeeded in its place, and why not also the same man, who is substituted in the place of another?

Concerning the power of God, manifested in the resurrection of Christ, Rom. I. 19. 20. nothing is held. For it is treated there of the power manifested in the work of creation. But in Eph. I. 19. 20. the divine power, manifested in the resurrection of Christ, is exhibited. Which also, a thing we should observe against the Socinians, is the power of Christ himself, John V. 29. For the essence and power of the Father and the Son are one, John X. 30. Therefore also Christ was powerfully declared the Son of God by the resurrection, Rom. I. 4. because he raised himself, John II. 19. C. X. 19. and he will demonstrate the same divine power, by which he is able to subject all things to himself, in our resurrection, when he will transfigure this humble body of ours, that it may be σύμμορ- φον (conformed) to his glorious body, Phil. III. 21. Conf. Anti-Crellius §. 293.

Latin:

Τὰ βρώματα τῇ κοιλίᾳ, καὶ ἡ κοιλία τοῖς βρώμασι) Dativi hic respondent Hebrææ particulæ ל, quæ sæpe propter si- gnificat: Cibi sunt ventris implendi causa & venter ad ci- bos accipiendos & digerendos. Ventrem intellige hic ventriculum & intestina.

Ὁ δὲ θεὸς καὶ ταύτην, καὶ ταῦτα καταργήσει) Efficiet, ut ces- sent corpora ubi Angelicis erunt similia, non egebunt cibi. (ἐ γὰρ σῖτον ἔδυσ', ὐ πίνυσ' αἴθοπα οἶνον) ii, qui cæle- stem vitam degunt, ut diximus Matth. XXII. 30. Quod autem dicitur hic Deus facturus, ut & venter cesset, id qui- dam de usu ventris intelligunt. Sed ex veterum scriptis ad hunc locum apparet eos credidisse homines quidem corpora recuperaturos, at non sequi, in eo corpore fore eas partes, quarum tunc officia sunt cessatura. Plutar- chus, aut quisquis est Scriptor convivii Sapientum: Ἀρ' ἦν ἄξιον συνεκπεσεῖν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ καὶ στόμαχον, καὶ ἧπαρ, οἱ καλᾶ ὐ- δενὸς αἴσθησιν,ὐδὲ ὄρεξιν ἐνδίδωσι. Pertinet autem & hic ser- mo, ut æterna potius curemus, quàm temporaria, ac brevi defitura.

Talis μιμήσεως vel ἀνθυποφορᾶς nullum in tex- tu apparet vestigium. Exemplum potius se sistit Apostolus submissionis in adiaphoris, ac lege Dei minime prohibitis, quod non quid liceat, sed quid conducat, ita tamen, ut non patiatur, se in servitutem redigi, observet, e. g. in usu ciborum, utpote qui ventris tantùm necessitati serviunt: uti venter usui ciborum destinatus est; Cujus verò usus respectu non minus venter quàm cibus de- struetur, vel cessabit tandem, nec in altera vita ei locus erit. Hoc cum faciat in iis, quæ indifferen- tia sunt, ut se non à libitu voluntatis suæ abripi patiatur; sed τὸ συμφέρον attendat, quantò minus in iis, quæ lege divinâ prohibita sunt, & regno Dei, quod non situm est in cibo & potu, Rom. XIV. 17. libidini & concupiscentiæ nostræ pravæ obsequen- dum est? Dilapsus etiam forsan hûc est Apostolus occasione taxatæ ebrietatis, ut moneret, non tan- tum abstinendum à potu illicito poculi, quod vo- cant, ebrietatis; sed à licito quoque, poculo nempe hilaritatis; quemadmodum nuncupari solet, & quid hic conducat tum nobis, tum aliis, ne scan- dalo ipsis simus, probe observandum esse. Ita Chrysostomus: Helluones, & eos, qui ventri sunt de- diti, hic innuit. Nam quoniam ad fornicatorem rursus est rediturus, oritur autem fornicatio à deli- ciis & immoderatione, affectionem eam valdè ca- stigat. Non enim de prohibitis hoc dicit, illa enim non licent, sed de iis, quæ videntur esse indifferen- tia: Cujusmodi est quod dico? Licet, inquit, edere, bibere, quod est ejus admirabile & præter opinio- nem, quod quidem sæpe solet facere, id quod dicit con- vertens in contrarium, hic quoque id effecit; & osten- dit, quod in potestate facere non solùm non expedit, sed nec potestatis quidem est, imò verò servitutis. Et primum quidem ex eo, quod non expediat, avertit, & dehortatur dicens: Non expediunt. Secundo autem etiam ex contrario, dicens: Ego sub nullius redigar potestate. Hoc est autem quod dicit. Est in potestate tua, inquit, comedere. Mane ergo hanc habens potestatem & vide, ne hujus affectionis fias servus. Nam qui ad id, quod oportet, ea utitur, ipse eam habet in potestate. Qui autem exit ad exuperationem, & immoderationem, non est am- plius Dominus, sed ejus servus, voracitate & in- gluvie tyrannidem in eo exercente. Quem sensum etiam laudat Cornelius à Lapide; quasi dicat: Licet mihi omnibus cibis vesci, sed non sinam gulam alicujus cibi mihi dominari, ut fiam mancipium ventris. Ambrosius tamen & Thomas referunt ad sumptus, quasi dicat: Licet mihi evangelizanti à vobis accipere sumptus & victum, sed ego eos non accipiam, ne ulli siam obnoxius, & meam liber- tatem perdam. Sed hoc alienum est à contextu.

Aptissimè autem Anshelmum ut & Thomam referre ad superiora de judiciis putat Cornelius, quasi di- cat: Hæc contra judicia dixi, non quasi illicitum sit ex se, in judicio sua repetere, sed quod nolim sub alio- rum, scilicet judicum, advocatorum, procuratorum, maximè infidelium, potestatem vos redigi.

Duobus autem modis usus Indifferentium in abusum degenerat; (1.) quando negligitur utili- tas, seu ædificatio, & commodum proximi, tum enim non expedit eidem, & cum conjunctus est cú scandalo, aut etiam cum nobis ipsis non expedit (2.) quando in servitutem seu libertatis nostræ pe- riculi, seu subjectionis sub peccatum causa redigi- mur. Quem utrumque abusum exemplo suo de- clinandum monet Apostolus. Dicta etiam illa per μείωσιν intelligi possunt: Non omnia conducunt; id est: Sunt nonnulla, etiam aliquando noxia, si iis uta- ris, utpote cum scandalo proximi, aut damno nostro conjuncta. Et in illis, non ego in servitutem redigar ab ullo, tùm persona intelligi potest, nullum mortalium se in rebus liberis in servitutem adducturum; tum res, quasi dicat: Omnium usus mihi liber est, sed non ego me in servitutem dabo ulli rei, ut mihi etiam ab illa abstinere, si velim, & expedire videam, non liceat. Condidit sanè Deus, ut escam, ita & potum in usum hominis, & sustentationem ventris: Fecit & ventrem, qui cibum & potum appetat, digerat, & in usum totius corporis humani convertat & con- ferat, ut cibus ventri destinatus sit, & venter cibo. Non autem vult ex usu ciborum ventrem fieri li- bidinis & voluptatis seminarium, neque ventrem solum propter escam condidit, nedum ut ventri serviamus, Phil. III. 19. Siquidem ad integritatem corporis humani eundem facere voluerit, ideò cessante cibo venter destructus tamen non est, ac conservati sunt nonnulli ad tempus, licet extraor- dinarie, ut exemplis Mosis, & Eliæ constat, nec du- bium est, quin perpetuo conservari sine cibo pos- sint, si Deus velit: Uti in altera vita nec cibus, nec appetitus, vel usus cibi erit, ejusque ratione venter abolebitur. Etsi substantiæ ratione idem, utpote ad integritatem corporis humani pertinens, abolen- dus non sit, quemadmodum Christus gloriose re- surgens, cujus corpori nostrum σύμμορφον erit Phil. III. 21. ventre non caruit Luc. XXIV. 43. Quod contra detorsionem Socinianorum observandum, qui ventris omnimodam abolitionem hic commu- niter intelligunt, uti hic etiam à Crellio factum, qui ex his Pauli verbis, inquit: Cuivis colligere est, in futuro seculo nullum futurum locum cùm ventri, quàm cibis. Idem de aliis corporis nostri membris existimandum est, quæ hujus mortalis vitæ usibus sunt destinata. Est hæc collectio non minùs ἀσυλ- λόγιστος, quam ἀντίγραφoς. Nam de ventris de- structione hic sermo est non ratione substantiæ, sed ratione usus ciborum, & ventrem, cum aliis corporis nostri membris, in resurrectione gloriosa nos ha- bituros, Apostolus satis docet, cum τὸ φθαρτὸν τõ- το, quo nomine totum corpus nostrum indigitatur, non abolendum vel annihilandum dicit, sed ἐνδύ- σασθαι inquit, hoc est, induet ἀφθαρσίαν 1. Cor. XV. 53. Manebit ergò substantiæ ratione, non autem ra- tione corruptibilitatis: Sed idem hoc corpus, quod hic corruptibile est, induet incorruptibilitatem. De substantiæ ventris abolitione nihil hic habetur. Usum autem respici, nec ipse Grellius diffitetur: Deus autem & hunc & has abolebit. Quasi dicat, etiamsi Christianis liberum sit, per se quibusvis escis vesci; parcè tamen hac libertate uti debent, cogitan- tes & ventrem & escas à Deo abolendas esse. Mini- me enim convenit, ut Christiani rebus perituris plus æquo sint addicti, & in iis aliquam felicitatis partem collocent. Hinc est, quod in epistola ad Rom. XIV. 17.

scriptum reliquit: Regnum Dei non est cibus & po- tus, id est, cibis & potu sese ingurgitare, iisque sine discrimine uti: Sed justitia, & pax, & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto. His in rebus vera, & Christiano- rum in hoc seculo propria felicitas consistit. Quid? quod Paulus paulo post corpora nostra membra Christi dicturus est, & templa Spiritus Sancti, ac Dei ipsius, caro redempta pretio: Num autem cor- pora ista, quæ caro sanguinis Christi pretio empta, quæ membra Christi, quæ templa Spiritus sancti, quæ Dei sunt æque, ut Spiritus noster, credemus penitus destruenda, & annihilanda, & beatitudine cœlesti privanda?

At suppetias hic quoque fert Socinianis Grotius, nimirum quod ex veterum scriptis ad hunc locum appareat, eos credidisse homines quidem corpora re- cuperaturos, at non sequi in eo corpore fore eas partes, quarum tunc officia sunt cessatura. Sed quænam tandem ita superabunt, & qualia tum erunt huma- na corpora, omnibus illis partibus deficientibus, quorum officia tunc cessabunt? Nec verò nomina- vit veteres, qui cum ipso faciant. Contrariatur uti- que Theophylactus: Non ventrem, inquit, (destruet) sed ventris ingluviem. Nam ventrem ingluviem ipsam appellari censet, non stomachum, corporis nostri membrum. Laudat enim & alios, qui futuri seculi conditionem hic prænuntiari dicant, ubi nec capi poterit cibus, nec potus hauriri. Sed non admittit stomachi abolitionem. Theophylactus hic, ut in aliis, sequutus Chrysostomum est, qui sic ha- bet: Ventrem hic non dicit ventrem, sed ingluviem, ut quando dicit: Quorum Deus venter est: Non de membro dicens, sed de voracitate. Nam quod ita sit, audi quæ sequuntur: Et venter escis: Corpus autem non fornicationi, sed Domino. Atqui venter quoque est corpus. Sed duas posuit conjugationes, escas & ingluviem, quam quidem vocavit ventrem. Chri- stum & corpus. Quid est autem escæ ventri? Cibus, inquit, cum ingluvie intercedit amicitia, & ipsi cum eis. Non possunt ergo, inquit, nos ducere ad Christum, sed ad se trahunt. Est enim gravis & belluina affe- ctio, & servos reddit, & ut ei serviant, efficit. Addi- dit Chrysostomus pariter nostram de statu futuro explicationem: Sed non asseruit, quod Grotius veteribus tribuit; imò contrarium docuit: Qui- dam dicunt, quod dictum est, esse prophetiam, signi- ficare autem statum, qui est in futuro seculo: Et quod illic non liceat nec comedere, nec bibere. Si autem est habiturus finem, proportione & symmetria conveni- entem, multò magis oportet abstinere ab immode- ratione. Deinde ne existimes, esse reprehensionem corporis, neque suspiceris, quod à parte totum reprehen- derit, neque dicas naturam corporis esse causam for- nicationis, audi quæ sequuntur. Non accuso enim, inquit, naturam corporis, sed immoderatum ani- mi luxum. Nostram vero fidem de resurrectio- ne corporum eorundem numero è sequenti- bus verbis Apostoli confirmavit Sanct. Chryso- stomus: Si enim corpus nostrum est Christi mem- brum, resurrexit autem Christus, corpus quoque omninò sequetur caput. Sic etiam ventrem de ingluvie & crapula explicat Athanasius (vel quis- quis est autor) quæst. ad Antioch. p. 133. Agnosci- mus tamen ventrem ipsum, non ingluviem hic in- telligi, & destruendum dici substrata materiæ ratio- ne, ut scil. non sit amplius venter escarum, qui escis pascatur, nec escæ sint ventris, ut ventrem inescent & impleant.

v. 13. Τὸ δὲ σῶμα ὐ τῇ πορνείᾳ, ἀλλὰ τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ ὁ Κύριθ- τῷ σώματι. Ne quis, quod de cibis dictum erat, ad scortationem quoque pertraheret, quasi ejus quoque usus cum cibis esset permissus, ut docebant isti Philosophi magis, quam Christia- ni, opponit se huic errori, ostenditque non eodem modo hanc rem se habere. Corpus enim habere nos, non ut scor- temur, sed ut Domino serviamus, nempe per continentiam aut conjugium. Nam & Dominum evectum in summam illam potestatem in hoc, ut corpora nostra post peractum obedientiæ cursum suæ gloriæ consortio donet.

Præparavit sibi Apostolus mentione ventris aditum, ulterius agendi adversus scortationem, quâ etiam cum incestu conjunctam tolerarant Corin- thii, quæque inter gentiles ferè indifferentibus ac- censebatur, ut opus haberet totum concilium A- postolicum Act. XV. 29. peculiariter sancire, ut abstineant à scortatione. Quæ verò abominatio non è Philosophia,utpote cui itidem ea refragatur, sed è prava concupiscentia profecta, quæ in non re- natis vires integras explicat discrimine etiam ho- nestorum & turpium, non parum per peccatum Originis obscurato. Nam hoc fons est & origo, ut errorum omnium, ita & pravarum libidinum.

De phrasi ὁ Κύριος τῷ σώματι, etsi Grotius ὁμοψή- φος habeat Ambrosium & Anshelmum, quasi id intendatur, Christum corpori casto & puro præmium fore,illique incorruptionem & immortalitatem dona- turum; Non tamen de castitatis remuneratione hic sermo est,sed docetur, non ita fornicationi corpus, uti escis venter, destinatum,non pariter ἀδιάφορον usum corporis ad quamvis συνυσίαν, uti ventris u- sum ad escam quamlibet censendum esse, sed cor- pus Deo, ceu Creatori, Redemptori & Salvatori suo dicatum esse, ideoque referri hæc ad sese mutuò: Corpus nostrum ad servitium Dei; Christum verò ad corporis Dominium. Ut non admittendum quic- quam in nostro corpore, quod cùm illo sancto ser- vitio,Domino debito, non conveniat. Quemad- modum nec sumus Domini corporis nostri,sed Chri- stusDominus ejus est.Refertur ergo corpus adDo- minum, ut ei serviat: Dominus verò ad corpus, ut ei dominetur, illudque illibatum usibus suis adhi- beat, qui utique illud scortationis instrumentum esse non vult: Sed membrum suum,ut caput ipsius & unum nobiscum esse vult, unione mystica, ceu sponsus & maritus noster, & templum Spiritus S. quem donat nobis,ceu Dominus templi,in quo ha- bitare cum Deo Patre ac Spiritu sancto vult & glo- rificari, quod proinde sanctum & inviolabile esse debet. His enim modis Dominum esse corpori,& cor- pus esse Domino deinceps explicat, & his rationibus à scortationis vitioChristianos revocat. Theophyla- ctus,corpus,inquit,haudquaquam ideò est effectum,ut in luxu sit & deliciis, & in fornicationem labatur, sed Deum, ut caput ipsum, sectetur, cum Deus ipsi capitis instar præsideat. Et ante eum Chrysostomus: Non est ideò constructum corpus, ut sis prodigus & luxurio- sus, & forniceris, sed ut Christum sequatur tanquam caput, & Dominus imponatur capiti. Non enim, ut Theodoretus habet,sicut venter est cibi receptaculum: Ita corpus propter scortationem creatum est.

ὁ δὲ Θεὸς καὶ τὸν Κύριον ἤγειρε, καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐξεγερεῖ διὰ δυνά- μεως ὁυτῶ.

Hæc particula δὲ est ἐξηγητικὴ præcedentium. De hac Dei potentia,inChristi resuscitatione patefacta,vid.Rom.I.19.20.

Particula δὲ optimè retinet sensum proprium, qui adversativus est. Corpus enim Domino,& Domi- nus est corpori. Ut vero Deus Dominum excitavit; ita & nos excitabit ad vitam æternam. Quapropter cor- pus nostrum non fornicationi aut peccatis, sed Domino ejusque honori unicè sacrandum est. Et Dominus unicè corpori nostro dominari vult.Qui verò non ad caducam vitam,nedum ad voluptates carnis, sed ad alteram cœlestem vitam, in qua san- ctitas & justitia habitat, nos excitavit, atque ideò mortuus propter peccata nostra, excitatus est à mortuis, ut nos etiam per potentiam suam excita- ret ad vitam cœlestem. Qui fornicationi aliisque peccatis dediti sunt,non cogitant neque agnoscunt

Christum propter peccata nostra traditum, & pro- pter justitiam nostram resuscitatum, ut noster Do- minus esset, & corpus nostrum quoque ipsi sacrum esset, nosque etiam quoad hoc ipsum corpus ali- quando excitaret ad eam vitam, ubi nulla voluptas carnalis, nullum peccatum locum habet. Non ergo exclusum hic vult corpus hoc nostrum, cujus casti- tatem Domino vendicat, a gloriosa resurrectione; sed argumento futuræ excitationis id Dno. conse- crandum esse docet, non fornicationi permitten- dum, quod pariter id excitandum sit, cum nos ex- citabimur, quemadmodum excitatus est Dominus: Qui certè non sine corpore excitatus est. Et quo- modo excitari nos diceremur, si corpus nostrum, quod ad hominis integritatem pertinet, & sine quo homo non est homo, sine quo nos non sumus nos, hoc est, illi ipsi homines, qui Deo servire hic casto animo & corpore jubemur? Cui Apostolico argu- mento nervum planè incidunt Sociniani, cum cor- poris nostri suscitationem negant, Imò hic negari contendunt. Videmus, inquit Crellius in hunc lo- cum, de industria Paulum terminos mutasse, cum de resuscitatione loquitur, & pro corpore nostro nos repo- suisse; Ne si diceret corpora nostra resuscitanda esse, sui quasi oblitus videretur, & ventris resuscitationem, quem paulo ante abolendum dixerat, urgere. Atqui nos non sumus nos, si corpora nostra omninò non sint, sed esse desierint, vel in nihilum plane redacta sint. Neque ventrem nostrum aliter, quàm ratione USUS, destruendum dixit Apostolus. Nec diffite- tur Crellius, Apostol. Rom. 8, 11. corpora nostra MOR- TALIA vivificanda dicere: Ad quod quidem suffi- cere ait, si corpora alia (quæ in locum istorum succe- dant) habituri simus, eo quod, quæ sibi sic succedunt, unum quodammodo sint, aliique in aliis veluti rena- scantur. At si corpora substantialiter alia in horum corporum locum fuccederent, hæc verò planè in nihilum redigerentur; nec corpora isthæc morta- lia vivificarentur, neque nos ipsimet excitaremur, & periret argumento Apostolico vis sua: Quia de illo corpore Domino consecrando, nec scortationi dicando, agit, quod Dno. erit æternum, atque ideò excitabitur à morte, & vivificabitur, non verò de novo corpore substantialiter ab hoc nostro diver- so. Res est in aprico. Quæ sibi invicem succedunt, non unum sunt, sed diversa, cùm illud pereat planè, hoc verò demum oriatur, illud in nihilum abeat, hoc è nihilo creetur. Continent hæc verba, in- quit Crellius, argumentum, cur CORPORA NOSTRA Domino dedere & conservare peni- tus debeamus, quia nimirum magnum istius rei præmium (utique in illis ipsis corporibus nostris, non in aliis corporibus, sed in illis, quæ Deo hic, non peccatis consecrare jubemur) reportaturi su- mus, nempe tale, quo non secus ac Dominus ipse, nos quoque à Deo afficiendi sumus. Quod sine corporibus haudquaquam fiet, ut Schlichtingius hic fatetur. Sed addit: Licet materia & forma multo præstantio- ribus. Id verò Apostolo refragatur. Nam si & ma- teriâ & formâ diversa sint corpora, utiq; non erunt eadem, quæ hic Domino consecranda sunt, quod tamen Apostolus vult, cum hæc corpora nostra, quæ jam Deo uni dicamus, excitanda docet. Nam quod Schlichtingius ait, in ipsis etiam mortalibus nostris corporibus nos videre, quod & illa eadem sint, quæ successione sunt eadem: Nam hoc de iis, quæ se- cundum partes substantiales manent, etsi alteratio- nem patiantur, concedimus, uti corpora nostra mortalia hic quoad partes substantiales manent, et- si alterationi, nutritioni, augmentationi &c. obno- xia sint. Membra n. & partes aliæ non succedunt illis, quas natura concessit. Cum verò corpora pla- nè, quoad omnia membra, & partes, in nihilum redigantur, & substantiæ prorsus diversæ de novo creentur, atq; è nihilo producantur, rationis com- pos non fuerit, qui corpora illa, noviter è nihilo producta, materiâ & formâ, vel numero, imo specie, & genere diversa, qualia fingunt Sociniani, eadem esse ob successionem dixerit. Ob solam, inquam, suc- cessionem. Quæ si sufficiat, etiam anima eadem fue- rit, si alia in ejus locum successerit, & cur non etiam homo idem, qui in alterius locum surrogatur?

De potentia Dei, in Christi resuscitatione pate- factâ, Rom. I. 19. 20. nihil habetur. Agitur enim il- lic de potentia, in opere creationis manifestata. At Eph. I. 19. 20. potentia divina, in Christi resuscita- tione patefacta, exhibetur. Quæ etiam, id quod contra Socinianos observemus, est ipsius Christi potentia Joh. V. 29. Una enim Patris & Filii & essen- tia & potentia Joh. X. 30. Ideò etiam Christus poten- ter declaratus est Filius Dei resurrectione Rom. I. 4. quia seipsum excitavit Joh. II. 19. C. X. 19. eandem- que divinam potentiam, qua omnia sibi subjicere valet, demonstrabit in nostri excitatione, cum hoc corpus nostrum humile transfigurabit, ut σύμμορ- φον sit glorioso suo corpori Phil. III. 21. Conf. Anti- Crellius §. 293.

## 6:16
v. 16. Do you not know that your bodies are the members of Christ? For the Church is a mystical body, whose head is Christ, but the individual Christians are the members, both in soul and in body. For Christ must be served with the body also. See below XI. 3. Eph. I. 22. IV. 15. V. 23. 30. Col. I. 18. See also Rom. XII. 4. and below XII. 12. and the following up to 27.

Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them the members of a harlot? Shall I take them away from Christ, that they may serve a harlot? For as Ambrose says on this passage, members adhering to a harlot cease to be members of Christ.

God forbid. That is by no means fitting for those called to chastity.

That which is a member of Christ ought not to become a member of a harlot. But the body of a faithful man is a member of Christ. Therefore it ought not to become a member of a harlot. But it becomes a member of a harlot through fornication: Because it is said, nay, it is even mingled, and by such carnal copulation it becomes one with her, as the Apostle will now teach. Who hearing this, says Theophylact, would not shudder, that the members of Christ, torn away from Christ, are converted into the members of a harlot? Which is surely much more atrocious than all sacrileges. The body of each one is composed of many members, all of which are no less members of Christ than the body itself is a member of Christ in the whole Church. That statement of Ambrose, therefore, is most true: Members adhering to a harlot cannot be members of Christ. Whence it is most false, what is here from the mind of the Council of Trent held by Cornelius à Lapide: The fornicator remains a member of Christ and the Church, when he retains the true faith, or can retain knowledge concerning matters of faith. He cannot retain true faith. For faith, if it does not have works, is not true faith, but νεκρά ἐσι καθ’ ἑαυτὴν, it is dead in itself.

Or do you not know that he who is joined to a harlot is one body? For they shall be, he says, the two into one flesh. He says, namely, the Scripture, as in Rom. IV. 3. and elsewhere. What had been said of a wife in Gen. II. 24. he adapts to a harlot, who is as it were a usurious wife, and performs those things which it was lawful for a wife to perform. Εἰς σάρκα μίαν is a Hebraism for σὰρξ μία. He uses דבק in the cited passage of Genesis concerning a wife. Thus Apuleius spoke of the glue of Venus. Lucretius.

And they cling so greedily to the bonds of Venus.

The Apostle proves what he said. For since those who are glued to a harlot through fornication become one body with her, just as spouses, according to the sentence and ordinance of God, are one flesh; it follows that he also makes his members the members of a harlot, as they are those of which the body consists. From the commerce of lust, says Theophylact, the fornicator and the harlot become one. Thus it happens that the members of a man, which are Christ's, are turned into the members of a common woman. What is said of spouses is transferred to fornicators, because the external acts, whether of spouses or of fornicators, do not differ according to the species of nature, although they differ in the genus of morality, nay, in genus. For the acts of the latter are of base lust and vice, those of the former are of chastity and virtue. But while they are said to be one flesh, the unity of affection and of the carnal spirit is not excluded, which is evident from the consent to such carnal commixture, which is no less vicious than the commixture itself. And the Apostle is intent on rendering this sin as abominable as possible, because it so disgraces the person who, while he ought to be entirely one with Christ and transformed into Christ, becomes one with a harlot, and as it were transforms himself into a harlot: one body with a harlot, one soul, and as it were one person, just as a husband and wife are accustomed to be considered one civil person, or are civilly one.

Latin:

v. 16. Οὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν μέλη χρισῦ ἐστι; Est enim Ecclesia corpus mysticum, cujus caput Christus, membra autem singuli Christiani, tum animo, tum corpore. Nam & corpore Christo serviendum est. Vide infra XI. 3. Eph. I. 22. IV. 15. V. 23. 30. Col. I. 18. Vide & Rom. XII. 4. & infra XII. 12. & sequentibus usque ad 27.

Ἄρας ὖν τὰ μέλη τῦ χρισῦ ποιήσω πόρνης μέλη; Christo ea auferam, ut serviant scorto? Nam ut ait Am- brosius ad hunc locum, membra adhærentia meretrici de- sinunt esse membra Christi.

Μὴ γένοιτο. Minime id decet ad castitatem vocatos.

Quod est Christi membrum, non debet fieri membrum meretricis. At hominis fidelis corpus est Christi membrum. Non ergò membrum mere- tricis fieri debet. Fit autem meretricis membrum per scortationem: Quia & dicatur, imò & commi- scetur, & copula ejusmodi carnali unum fit cum ea- dem, ut jam docebit Apostolus. Quis audiens id, inquit Theophylactus, non contremiscat, Christi mem- bra, à Christo divulsa, in meretricis membra conver- ti? Quod utique omnibus sacrilegiis multò atro- cius venit. Corpus cujusque ex multis membris est compositum, quæ omnia non minus sunt Christi membra, quam ipsum corpus est Christi membrum in tota Ecclesia. Illud ergò Ambrosii est verissimum: Membra adhærentia meretrici, non possunt esse mem- bra Christi. Unde falsissimum est, quod hic ex mente Concilii Trident. habet Cornelius à Lapide: Chri- sti & Ecclesiæ membrum manet fornicator, quando veram fidem retinet, seu cognitionem de rebus fidei retinere potest. Fidem veram retinere non potest. Fides enim, si opera non habeat, non est fides vera, sed νεκρά ἐσι καθ’ ἑαυτὴν, mortua est in semetipsa.

Ἤ ἐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν. Ἔσον- ται γὰρ, φησὶν, ὁι δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν. Φησὶ nempe ἡ γραφὴ, ut Rom. IV. 3. & alibi. Quod de uxore dictum erat Gen. II. 24. aptat meretrici, quæ est velut uxor usuraria, & iis fungitur, quibus uxorem fungi jus fuit. Εἰς σάρκα μίαν Hebraismus est pro σὰρξ μία. Komãdai דבק in dicto Geneseos de uxore. Sic Veneris glutinum dixit Apulejus. Lucretius.

Iisque adeo cupide Veneris compagibus hærent.

Probat, quod dixit, Apostolus. Quum enim, qui meretrici conglutinantur per scortationem, unum corpus cum ea fit, ut conjuges, juxta Dei sententiam & ordinationem, una sunt caro; mem- bra etiam sua faciat meretricis membra, utpote ex quibus corpus constat, oportet. Ex libidinis com- mercio, ait Theophylactus, unum fiunt fornicator & meretrix. Ita fit ut viri membra, quæ Christi sunt, in vulgatæ fæminæ membra vertantur. Quæ de conjugibus dicuntur, ad scortatores transferun- tur, quia actus externi seu conjugum, seu scortan- tium, secundum speciem naturæ non differunt, licet in genere moris specie, imò genere differant. Horum enim actus sunt pravæ libidinis, & vitii, illorum sunt castitatis & virtutis. Dum autem una caro esse dicuntur, non excluditur unitas affectus & spiritus carnalis, quod è consensu in ejusmodi carnalem commixtionem, qui non minus vitiosus est, quàm ipsa commixtio, patet. Et in eo est Apo- stolus, ut quàm maximè abominabile reddat hoc peccatum, quod eo ita se infamet, ut qui cum Chri- sto totus, quantus est, unum esse & in Christum transformari debeat, unum cum scorto fiat, & in scortum se quasi transformet: unum cum scorto corpus, una anima, & velut una persona, uti vir & fœmina una persona civilis censeri solent, vel civi- liter unum sunt.

## 6:17
v. 17. ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν. This is an Antanaklasis, and it refers to the passage in Deut. X, 20. Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σε φοβηθήσῃ, καὶ αὐτῷ λατρεύσεις, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν κολληθήσῃ. But here Κύριος seems to be taken rather of Christ, just as things said of God in the Old Testament are often applied to Christ in the New. Ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν, that is, he is animated in the same way that Christ was animated. Thus friends are called ψυχὴ μία. A metonymy in which the cause is named for the effect. A similar expression is found in John III. 6.

It is not only implied that through edification and conglutination with the Lord the believer becomes so animated as Christ was animated; that is, not only is a conformation of morals and mind indicated exclusively, but a mystical unity is signified, which imports something more, by which those who are united to Christ through faith, adhere, and are conglutinated, and are thus one with Christ, just as spouses are one both in body and soul, when they become one flesh and there ought to be one mind and will for them, and there is a mutual communion and mutual right of the other. For we are also one spirit in this way, since we are flesh of the flesh of Christ, and not only is our soul united to Christ and to be conformed to him, but Christ also dwells in our body, and is united to it spiritually, and wishes to render it conformable to himself, which, since it does not happen here, we hope for in the other life, Phil. III. 21. And therefore this mystical union brings about a mutual communion of Christ and the faithful, by which both the faithful participate in those things which are Christ's, and Christ claims for himself those things which are the faithful's, since we are said to be made partakers even of his divine nature, 1 Pet. I. 4. Nor should our body be excluded from this communion of grace and glory; just as, conversely, the Lord claims for himself not only our soul, but also our body in its entirety. It must therefore be taken cumulatively, not exclusively, as if he were saying, for example, we adhere to the Lord through faith, we are not only one with him as regards the communion of flesh, because he willed to be a partaker of our flesh, and we are flesh of his flesh: We not only enjoy his flesh both spiritually and sacramentally, and are one mystical body with him, but we are also ἓν πνεῦμα one spirit with the Lord, as if transformed into the spirit of Christ, just as 2. Cor. III. 18. we are said to be transformed into the same image, not indeed by a substantial metamorphosis, as the fanatics wish, but by a mystical and spiritual one, so that every believer is not only of the Lord, but is one with the Lord, as if he himself were the Lord, as if he had passed into Christ. For just as they participate in the righteousness of Christ, and shine with it before the very face of God, and his satisfaction is imputed to them, so that since one died for all, it is the same as if all had died, 2 Cor. V. 14. now Christ lives in them, and they live in Christ, and are animated by the Spirit of Christ, so that they may consecrate themselves entirely, body and soul, to God, and may be ruled by the power of the spirit against the devil, the world, and the flesh, so that the Lord may work all things in them, with whom they are one, and they may be able to do all things by the power of the Lord, Rom. XV. 18. Phil. IV. 13. here partakers of the divine nature through grace, and in the future to be like the Lord in the state of glory, both in soul, by which they have wisdom and holiness, and in body, by which they have incorruptibility and glory. 1. Joh. III. 2. Thus Christ prayed for the faithful, Joh. XVII. 11. that they might not only be one among themselves; but also, that they might be one in GOD himself, that is, as Hilary interprets in book VIII de Trin., among themselves, in concord and peace from the unity of faith and unfeigned charity: In GOD, by participation of grace and the operation of the Spirit. For he who adheres to GOD is made one spirit with Him, which, according to the blessed Hunnius, means being partakers of the same Spirit, and spiritually incorporated into the Lord, as members to their head, from whom they have life and salvation. The blessed Balduinus has this to say about this: The faithful adheres to Christ through faith in Him, which apprehends His merit and applies it all to itself, as if it had been performed by itself. But through that adherence, one becomes one spirit with Christ, that is, one spiritual body, a partaker of divine goodness, holiness, and all virtues: For which reason St. Peter called the faithful partakers of the divine nature, 2. Pet. I. 4. It is therefore a sacrilege for a man of this kind to be joined with a harlot, whom Christ has deigned to receive into the fellowship of His mystical body and into the participation of His Spirit. And afterwards: The highest conjunction of GOD and man is that which occurs through mutual adhesion: For that makes one spirit out of both, that is, it communicates to man the goodness and happiness of GOD. Now GOD adheres to us through the communication of His grace, and we adhere to Him through the trust of the heart, which apprehends the grace of GOD. But that Apostolic expression is more emphatic, ἓν πνεῦμά ἐςι, and its power can neither be sufficiently comprehended by the mind nor expressed. The blessed Luther is accustomed to theologize sweetly about these things. Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. fol. 42. in Comm. ad Gal. on chapter II, he has this: This faith must be taught purely, namely, that you are so glued to Christ through it, that out of you and Him there is made, as it were, one person, which cannot be separated; but perpetually adheres to Him, so that you can say with confidence: I am Christ; That is: Christ's righteousness, victory, and life are mine: And conversely, Christ says: I am that sinner, that is, his sins, death, etc., are mine; because he adheres to me, and I to him, for we are joined into one flesh and bone, Eph. V. We are members of the body of Christ, and flesh of his flesh, and bone of his bones. So that this faith couples Christ and me more tightly than a husband is coupled to his wife, etc. And concerning Christian liberty, Tom. II. Witteb. Lat. fol. 5. 6. The third incomparable grace of faith is this, that it couples the soul with Christ, as a bride with a bridegroom. By which sacrament (as the Apostle teaches in Eph. V.) Christ and the soul are made one flesh. But if they are one flesh, a true marriage between them, indeed the most perfect of all by far, is consummated; (since human marriages are but faint figures of this unique one) it follows that all their things become common, as well the good as the bad, so that the faithful soul can presume and boast of whatever Christ has as if it were its own, and Christ claims for Himself whatever belongs to the soul, as if it were His own. Let us compare these things, and we shall see inestimable ones: Christ is full of grace, life, and salvation; the soul is full of sins, death, and damnation. Now let faith intervene, and it will come to pass that the sins, death, and hell will be Christ's, but the grace, life, and salvation will be the soul's. For it is necessary that He, if He is the bridegroom, should accept at the same time those things which the bride has, and impart those things which are His own to the bride. For he who gives his body and himself to her, how does he not give all that is his? And he who receives the body of the bride, how does he not receive all that is the bride's? Here now a most sweet spectacle emerges, not only of communion, but of a saving war, and of victory, and of salvation, and of redemption. For since Christ is God and Man, and that person who neither sinned, nor dies, nor is damned, but neither can sin, die, or be damned: And His righteousness, life, and salvation are insuperable and eternal and omnipotent. When, I say, such a person makes the sin, death, and hell of the bride common to Himself, indeed His own, because of the ring of faith, and in them He behaves no differently than if they were His own, and He Himself had sinned, laboring, dying, and descending into hell, so that He might overcome all things, and sin, death, and hell could not swallow Him up, they were necessarily swallowed up in Him in a stupendous duel. For His righteousness is superior to all sins, His life more powerful than all death, His salvation more invincible than all hell. Thus the faithful soul, through the pledge of its faith, becomes in Christ its bridegroom, free from all sins, secure from death, and safe from hell, endowed with the eternal righteousness, life, and salvation of its bridegroom Christ. Thus He presents to Himself the bride, without spot or wrinkle, glorious, cleansing her with the washing of water by the word of life, Eph. V. that is, through the faith of the word, of life, of righteousness, and of salvation. Thus He betroths her to Himself in faith, in mercy, in compassions, in righteousness and in judgment, as Hosea II says. Shortly after, fol. 6. b. Who then can comprehend the height of Christian dignity, which through its royal power dominates all things, death, life, sin, etc.? But through priestly glory before God, it can do all things, because God does what he himself asks and desires, as it is written: He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him, and will hear their cry, and will save them, Psalm CXLV. To this glory, certainly, no one arrives by works, but by faith alone. And no less sweetly did the blessed Meisner discourse on these things, in his Oration on the Christian, delivered at the promotion of Doctors in the year 1622: Every one of the faithful consists not of one, but of two natures, both his own human one, which he has by nature, and the divine one of Christ, which is united to him through grace. As therefore the human and divine nature are united personally in Christ the head: so they are united spiritually in Christian members. As there the assumed flesh subsists in the Λόγῳ through participation of the ὑποςάσεως: so here our nature subsists in Christ through fellowship of grace and of the θείας Φύσεως. As there from two natures one σύνθετος person is made: so here from the same is made one mystical composite, and a close and mutual περιχώρησις, or circumincession, as Galatinus translates, is given between the natures: since Christ is so in the Christian, and the Christian in Christ, that they remain always coupled, nor is the Christian able to be thought of without Christ even for a moment of time; but where the Christian exists, there Christ coexists: when the Christian is seen, Christ is beheld in him: when the Christian speaks, Christ speaks, when he suffers he suffers, when he works he works. For just as the soul vivifies, moves, and vegetates the body, so that the whole is rendered animated: so Christ through his union and gracious indwelling so animates and moves the Christian, that he becomes entirely spiritual, and clearly a new creature. Just as furthermore from soul and body, through physical union, one human suppositum is made: so from Christ the Christian, through hyperphysical union, becomes a certain mystical one: indeed as it were one person, and one man, whence the Apostle does not hesitate to affirm in Galatians 3:28: You are all εἷς ἐςε one in Christ Jesus. This therefore is that divine mode of subsisting, by which the Christian subsists not in himself, but in Christ, just as a branch in a tree, a shoot in a vine, a scion in an olive tree, and from Christ life, and motion, power, and light it receives everything, as a member from the head, the body from the soul, iron from fire, etc. And afterwards: Furthermore, just as from the hypostatic union flow three kinds of communication of idioms; namely, idiopoieia, or the appropriation of properties; koinopoieia, or the communion of offices; and metapoieia, or the communication of infinite gifts, the assumed flesh having been made: So similarly from our spiritual union with Christ flows idiopoiesis, or appropriation; because the Savior imputes his actions and passions to us, and in turn appropriates ours to himself, and koinopoiesis, or the communion of offices, because we are all rendered together prophets, priests, kings, and judges of the world; and finally metapoiesis, or the communication of divine charisms, such as wisdom, justice, holiness, the power of performing miracles, and of converting and regenerating others, all of which, if they are weighed piously, contain a most sweet foretaste of eternal life, and provide most effective comfort. These are the words of the blessed Meisner.

Latin:

v. 17. ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν. Est Ἀντανάκλασις, & respicitur locus Deut. X, 20. Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σε φοβηθήσῃ, καὶ αὐτῷ λατρεύσεις, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν κολ- ληθήσῃ. Sed hic Κύριος de Christo potius sumendum vide- tur, ut sæpe quæ de Deo dicta sunt in Vetere Testamento, Christo applicantur in Novo. Ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν, id est, ita animatus est, quomodo Christus fuit animatus. Sic amici dicuntur ψυχὴ μία. Metonymia in qua causa nominatur pro effectu. Similis est locutio Joh. III. 6.

Non id tantùm innuitur, per ædificationem & conglutinationem cum Domino fidelem ita ani- matum fieri, ut Christus animatus fuit; hoc est, non tantùm morum & animi conformatio indicatur ex- clusivè, sed unitas mystica significatur, quæ aliquid amplius importat, quâ ii, qui Christo per fidem uniuntur, adhærent, & conglutinantur, ita unum sunt cum Christo, uti conjuges unum sunt & cor- pore & anima, quum fiant una caro & una ipsis mens ac voluntas esse debeat, mutua communio, mutuum jus alterius sit. Nam & nos ita sumus unus spiritus, cum caro simus de carne Christi, nec anima nostra tantùm unitur Christo, eique con- formanda est, sed habitat Christus etiam in corpore nostro,, eidemque unitur spiritualiter, & vult sibi conforme reddere, quod cum hic non fiat, in altera vita speramus, Phil. III. 21. Ideoque hæc unio my- stica mutuam communionem Christi, & fidelium infert, quâ & fideles participant ea, quæ Christi sunt, & Christus sibi vendicat ea, quæ fidelium sunt, cum divinæ etiam naturæ ejus participes reddi di- camur, 1. Pet. I. 4. Nec ab hac gratiæ & gloriæ com- munione corpus nostrum excludi debeat; uti vicis- sim non tantum animam nostram, sed etiam corpus nostrum sibi in solidum vendicat Dominus. Acci- piendum ergò id cumulativè, non exclusivè, quasi dicat, verbi gratia, nos adhæremus Domino per fidem, non modo unum cum eo sumus, quoad car- nis communionem, quia carnis nostræ particeps es- se voluit, nosque sumus caro de carne ejus: Non so- lum carne ejusdem fruimur cum spiritualiter, tum sacramentaliter, & unum cum ipso sumus corpus my- sticum, sed etiam ἓν πνεῦμα unus spiritus cum Do- mino sumus, quasi in Christi spiritum transformati, quemadmodum 2. Cor. III. 18. in ejusdem transfor- mandi dicimur imaginem, non quidem substan- tiali μεταμορφώσει, quod fanatici volunt, sed my- sticâ & spirituali, quod unusquisque fidelis non Domini tantùm sit, sed unum cum Domino sit, ipse veluti Dominus, quasi in Christum transierit. Nam uti Christi justitiam participant, eâque coru- scant coram ipsa Dei facie, & satisfactio ejus ipsis imputatur, ut cum unus pro omnibus mortuus sit, idem id sit, ac si omnes mortui essent, 2. Cor. V. 14. nunc vivit Christus in ipsis, & ipsi vivunt in Christo, & Christi Spiritu animantur, ut se totos corpore & anima Deo consecrent, dominētur, virtute spiritus, diabolo, mundo & carni, ut omnia in ipsis Dominus operetur, cum quo unum sunt, & omnia ipsi virtute Domini possint, Rom. XV. 18. Phil. IV. 13. hîc divinæ naturæ per gratiam participes, olim similes Domino in statu gloriæ futuri, & animâ, qua sapientiam & sanctitatem, & corpore, qua incorruptibilitatem & gloriam. 1. Joh. III. 2. Sic Christus oravit pro fidelibus Joh. XVII. 11. ut non tantum unum sint inter se; sed etiam, ut unum sint in DEO ipso, hoc est, Interprete Hilario l. IIX. de Trin. inter se, concordia & pace ex fidei unitate & charitate non simulatâ: In DEO, participatione gratiæ & spiritus operatione. Qui enim adhæret DEO, unus spiritus cum ipso efficitur, quod B. Hunnio est, ejusdem Spiritus participes, & Domino spiritualiter incorporati, tanquam membra suo capiti, à quo vitam & salutem habent. B. Balduinus ita de hoc habet; Adhæret fidelis Christo per fidem in ipsum, quæ meritum ejus apprehendit, sibique totum applicat, tanquam à seipso præstitum. Per illam verò adhærentiam unus fit cum Christo spiritus, hoc est, unum spirituale corpus, divinæ bonitatis, sanctitatis ac virtutum omnium particeps: Quam ob causam D. Petrus fideles vocavit divinæ consortes naturæ 2. Pet. I. 4. Nefas igitur est, hujusmodi hominem commisceri cum scorto, quem Christus in corporis sui mystici consortium recipere, spiritusque sui participatione dignatus fuit. Et postmodum: Summa conjunctio DEI & hominis est, quæ fit per adhæsionem mutuam: Ea enim facit unum ex utroque spiritum, hoc est, communicat homini bonitatem & felicitatem DEI. Adhæret autem nobis DEUS per communicationem suæ gratiæ, nos adhæremus ipsi per cordis fiduciam, quæ gratiam DEI apprehendit. Sed ἐμφατικώτερον est illud Apostolicum, ἓν πνεῦμά ἐςι, nec mente satis comprehendi, nec efferri vis ejus satis potest. B. Lutherus suaviter de hisce solet θεολογεῖν. Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. fol. 42. in Comm. ad Gal. ad cap. II. ita habet: Hæc fides purè est docenda, quod sc. sic per eam conglutineris Christo, ut ex te & ipso fiat quasi una persona, quæ non possit segregari; sed perpetuò adhærescat ei, ut cum fiducia dicere possis: Ego sum Christus; Hoc est: Christi justitia, victoria, vita est mea: Et vicissim Christus dicat: Ego sum ille peccator, hoc est, ejus peccata, mors &c. sunt mea; quia adhæret mihi, & ego illi, conjuncti enim sumus in unam carnem & os, Eph. V. Membra sumus corporis Christi, & caro de carne ejus, & os de ossibus ejus. Ita ut hæc fides Christum & me arctius copulet, quam maritus est uxori copulatus &c. Et de libertate Christiana Tom. II. Witteb. Lat. fol. 5. 6. Tertia fidei gratia incomparabilis est hæc, quod animam copulat cum Christo, sicut sponsam cum sponso. Quo sacramento, (ut Apostolus docet Eph. V.) Christus & anima efficiuntur una caro. Quod si una caro sunt, verum inter eos matrimonium, imò omnium longè perfectissimum, consummatur; (cum humana matrimonia hujus unici figuræ sint tenues) sequitur, & omnia eorum communia fieri, tam bona, quam mala, ut, quæcunque Christus habet, de iis tanquam suis præsumere, & gloriari possit fidelis anima, & quæcunque animæ sunt, ea sibi arroget Christus, tanquam sua. Conferamus ista, & videbimus inæstimabilia: Christus plenus est gratiâ, vitâ & salute, anima plena est peccatis, morte & damnatione. Intercedat jam fides, & fiet, ut Christi sint peccata, mors & infernus, animæ verò gratia, vita, & salus. Oportet enim eum, si sponsus est, ea simul, quæ sponsa habet, acceptare, & ea, quæ sua sunt, sponsæ impertire. Qui enim corpus suum & seipsum illi do- nat, quomodo non omnia sua donat? Et qui corpus sponsae accipit, quomodo non omnia, quae sponsae sunt, accipit? Hic jam dulcissimum spectaculum prodit, non solum communionis, sed salutaris belli, & vi- ctoriae, & salutis, & redemptionis. Cum enim Chri- stus sit Deus & Homo, eaque persona, quae nec pecca- vit, nec moritur, nec damnatur, sed nec peccare, mori, damnari potest: Ejusque justitia, vita, salus insuperabilis, aeterna, omnipotens est. Cum, inquam, talis persona peccatum, mortem, infernum sponsae propter annulum fidei, sibi communia, imo propria facit, & in iis non aliter se habet, quam si sua essent, ipseque peccasset, laborans, moriens, & ad infernum descendens, ut omnia superaret, peccatumque, mors & infernus eum absorbere non possent, necessario in ipso absorpta sunt stupendo duello. Nam justitia sua omnium peccatis superior, vita sua omni morte potentior, salus sua omni inferno invictior. Ita fia anima fidelis, per arrham fidei suae, in Christo sponsa suo, omnibus peccatis libera, a morte secura, & ab inferno tuta, donata aeterna justitia, vita, salute sponsi sui Christi. Sic exhibet sibi sponsam, sine ma- cula & ruga, gloriosam, mundans eum lavacro in verbo vitae, Eph. V. id est, per fidem verbi, vitae, ju- stitiae & salutis. Sic sponsat eam sibi in fide, in mi- sericordia, in miserationibus, in justitia & judicio, ut Hos. II. dicit. Paulo post fol. 6. b. Quis ergo comprehendere potest altitudinem dignitatis Chri- stianae, qui per regalem suam potentiam omnium dominatur, mortis, vitae, peccati &c.? Per sacerdo- talem vero gloriam apud Deum omnia potest, quia Deus facit, quae ipse petit & optat, sicut scriptum est: Voluntatem timentium se faciet, & depreca- tionem eorum exaudiet, & salvos faciet illos Psal. CXLV. Ad hanc gloriam certe nullus operibus, sed sola fide pervenit. Nec minus suaviter disseruit de his B. Meisnerus, in Oratione de Christiano, in promot. Doctor. Anno 1622. habita: Quili- bet fidelium non una, sed duabus naturis constat, tum sua humana, quam habet per naturam, tum divina Christi, quae ipsi adunatur per gratiam. Ut igitur humana & divina natura in Christo capite uniuntur personaliter: Ita in Christianis membris uniuntur spiritualiter. Ut ibi assumpta caro sub- sistit in Λόγῳ per participationem ὑποςάσεως: Ita hic nostra natura subsistit in Christo per consortium gratiae & θείας Φύσεως. Ut ibi ex duabus naturis fit una persona σύνθετος: Ita hic ex iisdem fit unum compositum mysticum, daturque arcta & mutua inter naturas περιχώρησις, vel circumincessio, ut Galatinus vertit: Siquidem ita Christus est in Christiano, & Christianus in Christo, ut semper co- pulati maneant, nec Christianus sine Christo vel co- gitari saltem ad temporis momentum valet; sed ubi Christianus existit, ibi Christus coëxistit: Christia- no viso, Christus in ipso conspicitur: Christiano lo- quente, Christus loquitur, patiente patitur, operan- te operatur. Sicut enim anima corpus vivificat, movet, vegetat, ut totum reddatur animatum: Ita Christus per suam ἔνωσιν & inhabitationem gratio- sam sic animat, movetque Christianum, ut totus fiat spiritualis, & nova plane creatura. Velut insuper ex anima & corpore, per unionem physicam, fit unum suppositum humanum: Ita ex Christo Chri- stianus, per unionem hyperphysicam, fit unum quod- dam mysticum: Imo una quasi persona, & unus vir, unde Apostolus affirmare non ambigit Galat. III. 28. Omnes vos εἷς ἐςε unus estis in Christo Jesu. Hic ergo est divinus ille subsistendi modus, quo Christianus non in sese, sed in Christo subsistit, veluti ramus in arbore, palmes in vite, surculus in olea, & a Christo vitam, motumque, vim, lucemque omnem accipit, ceu membrum à capite, corpus ab anima, ferrum ab igne, &c.
