Et postmodum: Porrò sicut ex unione ὑποστατικῇ dimanant tria generœ communicationis Idiomatum; nempe ἰδιοποιΐα, vel proprietatum appropriatio; κοινοποιΐα vel officiorum communio; & μεταποιΐα vel infinitorum munerum, carnis assumta facta communicatio: Ita similiter ex unione nostri cum Christo πνευματικῇ fluit ἰδιοποίησις, vel appropriatio; quia Salvator suas actiones & passiones nobis imputat, nostrasque sibi vicissim appropriat, & κοινοποίησις, vel officiorum communio, quia nos omnes una reddimur Prophetæ, Sacerdotes, Reges, & judices mundi; tandemque μεταποίησις, vel divinorum charismatum communicatio, ut sunt sapientia, justitia, sanctimonia, potestas miracula edendi, aliosque convertendi & regenerandi, quæ omnia, si expendantur pie, suavissimum vitæ æternæ prægustum continent, & efficacissimum solamen suppeditant. Hæc B. Meisnerus.

## 6:18
V. 18. Flee fornication.

That is, be as far away as possible, even from the extreme edges.

Because, as Anselm, Cassian, and the Fathers teach everywhere, other vices are conquered by fighting, but lust alone by fleeing, namely by fleeing women, objects, and occasions of lust, by turning away the eyes and the mind so that it may see and think of other things. For if you oppose yourself to a base temptation and resist the thought, by thinking you stir up the imagination of those same things more, and from that you inflame the flesh and innate concupiscence more into profuse lust, as noted here by Cornelius à Lapide. No differently, as Theophylact warns, than some female pursuer who always urges us, he exhorts that lust must be fled, and persuades us that we should earnestly abstain from it.

Every sin that a man commits is outside the body.

He shows that there is something in which fornication surpasses other crimes: Not that other external sins are not also performed through the body: But that they do not bring insult to the body of the one performing them. Anthropos here is equivalent to aner, a man. By equal right, however, all these things are to be understood regarding women, from the nature of relative terms.

but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.

Indeed because it plunges it into a sewer. Nor were they themselves ignorant of this. For they had the custom, when coming from such intercourse, of washing themselves entirely, which Chrysostom notes here.

Some understand these things regarding bodily filthiness and the enervation of strength, because although other crimes also harm the body, none nevertheless inflicts such force upon it as fornication, by which the limbs are enervated, and peculiar, often also contagious diseases, and those incurable, are summoned. But more correctly these things are accepted regarding the insult to one's own body, which is the more grave among Christians, the greater the dignity of their bodies is, as members of Christ, to whom spiritual communion and unity with Christ intervenes, and as temples of the Holy Spirit. For it is not the consequences of sin that are said to be either outside the body or to concern one's own body; but the sins themselves; so that in that respect we do not inflict insult upon our own body with other sins, in the way we do with fornication, by which we sacrilegiously render the members of Christ the members of a harlot, and those who are one spirit with Christ, most wretchedly become one with a harlot, and we corrupt the temple of the Holy Spirit in a profane manner. Since other sins, says our blessed Hunnius, proceed outward, to harm the neighbor's body, life, honor, and faculties: This sin of fornication is committed against one's own body, and although it is also carried to the harlot, nevertheless it is reflected from her into one's own members, not without horrible filthiness. The whole man is indeed polluted by other sins as well, Matt. XV. But not in such a way as by fornication, which inflames the body of man with the impure flame of shameful lust, and brands it with a mark of turpitude, and sprinkles upon the limbs a foul stain of most filthy pollution, and not rarely, by abominable diseases, as if by branded stigmata, it betrays and brings into the open the impurity of the previous life. Nor does Cornelius à Lapide speak ill: The fornicator sins against his own body, and is injurious: Because he excites foul and shameful lust in the body, which so absorbs the mind that in the act of it a man can think of nothing else. Therefore the fornicator makes his body a slave of lust and concupiscence, so that foul lust may rule in it, and claim it all for itself, nor does gluttony or any other vice excite such shameful and such vehement concupiscence in the body, which so enslaves the body to itself, as lust. Lust alone, therefore, dominates the body, and infects, subjugates, and corrupts it with its own concupiscence and sin. Other sins, says Jerome, are external, which have repentance after the deed, and although gain may invite, conscience bites; lust alone, even in the very time of repenting, suffers the goads of the past, and the titillation of the flesh and the incentives of sin, so that by thinking through these things which we desire to correct, it becomes again the material for sinning. To these is added also the foul pollution, by which the very members are infected through whoredom. Which does not happen in marriage, because of the word by which the act of cohabitation is sanctified.

Ἦ οὐκ οἴδατε.) Do you not consider? V. 19. Ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τꭣ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίꭣ Πνεύματός ἐσι. The Holy Spirit is here what the שכינה is in the temple. The whole man is a temple of GOD, see above III. 16. 17. But the דביר, that is, the adytum, is the mind of man: the other parts of the soul are the היכל, the basilica of the temple: the body, indeed, is the אולם, the portico with its open courts. Tertullian explains this passage well in his second book on the apparel of women: Since we are all a temple of GOD, with the Holy Spirit brought into us and consecrated, the sacristan and priestess of that temple is modesty, which allows nothing unclean or profane to be brought in, lest that God who dwells within, offended, should abandon the defiled seat. Οὗ ἔχετε ἀπὸ Θεꭣ. That Spirit is from GOD, much more than that splendor which appeared at times between the Cherubim. The construction is Greek, which gives the preceding case to the relative pronoun.

These things are to be understood concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, no less than concerning grace. For He dwells in the faithful not only by power and grace, as in His own temple, both in the soul and in the body of the faithful, because He claims the whole man for Himself, as a temple, just as He regenerates, renews, and sanctifies the whole man, but also by reason of substance He is closer to us by a special presence, proper to the faithful, than to all creatures and other men, for whom the presence is general, as we taught in part II of the System of Theology, chapter XII, question III, page 630. It must be confessed, says Augustine in Epistle LVII to Dardanus: that GOD is everywhere by the presence of His divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of indwelling. But that is much more wonderful, that, although GOD is everywhere in His entirety, He does not, however, dwell in all. For it cannot be said to all, what the Apostle says: Do you not know that you are the temple of GOD, for the Spirit of GOD dwells in you. Although what follows afterwards, in whom He dwells, they have Him according to the diversity of their capacity, some more, some less, whom He Himself builds for Himself as a most beloved temple by the grace of His goodness. A twofold argument is found here, as Theophylact notes: This, he says, terrifies all the more, both because of the magnitude of the gift, that is, the Holy Spirit, and the dignity of the giver, that is, GOD. You are, he says, a temple, and a holy one: for it is established that it is from the Holy Spirit. Do not, therefore, make this temple, which has been endowed with holiness, impure and filthy. Nor render this gift of GOD useless. For you have received this Spirit from GOD. Schlichting, however, rashly twists these words, which you have from GOD, to his own heresy, as if it were said that he, although he is not GOD himself, is nevertheless the Spirit and holy breath of GOD, and is had from no other source than from GOD himself. For these things are not opposed in the Apostolic school, to be from GOD, and to be GOD, just as the Son of GOD is from GOD, and is GOD himself, blessed forevermore over all. By the former, the origin from the Father is noted, but by the latter, the homousia of the person, or identity of essence with the Father, which is certainly to be believed in a holy manner. For the Holy Spirit proceeds from GOD the Father in such a way that He is of the same essence as the Father, 1 John V. 7. The Apostle did not here keep silent that He is GOD, when he claimed for the Holy Spirit that which is proper to GOD, the temple, and commanded us to glorify GOD in our body, namely Him who dwells in our body as His own temple, which is no less the temple of the Holy Spirit than of the Father and the Son, John XIV. 23, 26.

And you are not your own. Furthermore, you are not under your own power, Rom. XIV. 7, 8. For you were bought with a price.

He omitted the right from creation, because the other was more recent and more special. You have the same words below in VII. 23, and the sense in 1 Pet. I. 18. For you were bought with a price, you will rightly translate, you have been acquired or purchased for a price. For qanah, which is to receive, is translated as to acquire, to buy, and has in Hebrew after it bimchir, for a price. And Isa. LV. 1. shibru belo-kesef ubelo-mechir in Greek: Buy without silver and price. And qanah, which is properly to possess, is translated by to buy, 2 Chron. XXXIV. 2, Prov. XX. 17, Isa. XXI. 2, and for the sake of distinction, as with silver is added, 2 Chron. XXI. 24. Therefore, to buy has the same value as to acquire, Acts XX. 28, whence acquisition, Eph. I. 4, 1 Thess. V. 9, 2 Thess. II. 14, 1 Pet. II. 9. Thus also for the ancient Latins, to buy was to take, whence to take away, and to remove, and a reward. The sense is: Christ has claimed you for Himself, redeemed from sins, but you cost Him much, by His own bloody death.

That the Apostle did not omit the right of creation, the blessed Balduinus notes, observing these arguments from the present text: (1) from the article of creation, v. 13; (2) from the article of redemption, v. 14; (3) from the article of resurrection, v. 15, 16, 17; (4) from a comparison of fornication with other sins, v. 18; (5) from the article of sanctification, v. 19; (6) finally from the article of redemption. You are not your own, for you were bought with a great price, v. 20, as if he were saying, it is not permitted for you to use, or rather to abuse, your bodies at your own pleasure: For you are not of your own right, but you live at the will of Him who bought you with the price of His own blood: That one is indeed Christ Jesus, that GOD of chastity, and man born of a chaste virgin, who redeemed you from all impurity, under which that spirit of impurity sold you. Grotius rightly unfolds the emphasis of the word to buy, from which we have asserted the satisfaction of Christ against the Socinians in our work 'Socinismus profligatus,' which he who wishes may consult here. The force of the argument is, since we have been bought with such a price, namely the blood of GOD Himself, Christ the God-man, who is that GOD who acquired us with His own blood, Acts XX. 21, GOD blessed over all forevermore, Rom. IX. 5, both in soul and body, it is necessary to value our bodies highly, since the demon bargains for them with the base and brief pleasure of the body. You are, with Theophylact as interpreter, established under a Lord, and you have nothing that is of your own right, not even the body itself. Since you have been bought with a great price, that is, with the blood of Christ. Whence it happens that your members are not bound to you, but to the Lord in servitude, and must necessarily be moved according to His will.

In vain does Schlichting snarl that we have sold no one to GOD, and that the life and blood of the Son of GOD, speaking properly, is not a price, but exceeds and surpasses every price. For we had been sold under the power of the Devil, to whom, through divine justice which man had offended, he had been handed over through sin. There was need, therefore, of satisfaction, not to be rendered to the Devil, as a bailiff, but to GOD the judge, and of our redemption, which was indeed not rendered with a material price of gold or silver, yet with a price far surpassing all gold and silver, namely the blood of Christ, that is, the price of not a mere man, but of the great and true GOD, most precious. And although GOD forgives us all sins, and does not demand a price from us, nor are we able to pay it to Him, our redemption was nevertheless not made without a price, but through the intervention of the payment of a price rendered by Christ our Mediator, in our place, 2 Cor. V. 14, 1 Tim. II. 5. Schlichting himself confesses that God, among other things, willed the blood of His Son to be shed for this very purpose, that He might sanction the remission of sins, and bind Himself to us to forgive them. But He could not sanction it, while preserving justice, unless satisfaction had been rendered, which the Son of GOD rendered in our stead, when He paid what He did not steal, Ps. LXIX. 5. Nor could or would GOD forgive sins, much less bind Himself to forgive them through His truth and justice, without the ransom of that most precious blood, which is abundantly asserted in the cited passage. And what kind of obligation is this through the shedding of Christ's blood, if we weigh the force of the Socinian opinion? They believe, forsooth, that a mere man, though innocent, was handed over to death, who was devoid of all sin, so that GOD might bind Himself to us to forgive sins. What sign or bond of obligation to forgive sins to the guilty is there in the death of an innocent man, if he is both a mere man, and was not handed over in our place, nor satisfied for us and for our sins, but died so that by his obedience he might acquire a reward not for us, but for himself.

Latin:

V. 18. Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.

Id est, quam longissimè abeste, etiam ab extremis lineis.

Quia, ut Anshelmus, Cassianus & passim Patres docent, alia vitia pugnando, sola libido fugiendo vincitur, scilicet fugiendo fœminas, objecta, occasiones libidinis, divertendo oculos & mentem, ut alia videat & cogitet. Si enim turpi tentationi te opponas, & cogitationi repugnes, cogitando magis commoves imaginationem eorundem indeque carnem & concupiscentiam innatam, & in libidinem profusam magis accendis, ut hic notatum Cornelio à Lapide. Haud secus, monente Theophylacto, quam insectatricem aliquam, quæ semper nos urgeat, fugiendam hortatur libidinem, suadetque ut ab ea enixè abstineamus.

Πᾶν ἁμάρτημα, ὃ ἐὰν ποιήσῃ ἄνθρωπος, ἐκτὸς τῦ σώματός ἐσιν.

Ostendit esse aliquid, in quo scortatio alia crimina superet: Non quod non & alia peccata exteriora per corpus peragantur: Sed quod ipsi corpori peragentis contumeliam non afferant. Ἄνθρωπος hic valet ἀνὴρ vir. Pari autem jure hæc omnia de fœminis intelligenda, ex natura τῶν πρός τι.

ὁ δὲ πορνεύων εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἁμαρτάνει.

Nimirum quia id immergit in cloacam. Nec id ipsi nesciebant. Morem enim habebant, à tali concubitu venientes, totos se abluendi, quod hic notat Chrysostomus.

De fœditate corporali, ac enervatione virium nonnulli hæc intelligunt, quod etsi alia quoque scelera lædant corpus; nullum tamen tantam vim eidem inferat, atque scortatio, qua membra enervantur, & peculiares, sæpe quoque contagiosi morbi, iique incurabiles, accersuntur. Sed rectius de contumelia in proprium corpus hæc accipiuntur, quæ eò gravior est penes Christianos, quo major est dignitas corporum ipsorum, ceu membrorum Christi, quibus communio & unitas spiritualis cum Christo intercedit, ac templorum Spiritus Sancti. Nam non consequentia peccati dicuntur, vel ἐκτὸς τῦ σώματος esse, vel τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα concernere; sed peccata ipsa; ita ut ea ratione contumelia proprium corpus non afficiamus aliis peccatis, quemadmodum scortatione, quà membra Christi sacrilegè reddimus membra meretricis, & qui unus cum Christo spiritus sunt, pessime cum scorto unum evadunt, templumque Spiritus Sancti corrumpimus profanum in morem. Quum peccata cætera, inquit B. Hunnius noster, progrediantur foras, ad lædendum proximi corpus, vitam, honorem, facultates: Hoc peccatum scortationis in proprium corpus committitur, & licet feratur etiam ad scortum, tamen ab eodem in membra propria, non sine horribili fœditate, re- flectitur. Polluitur quidem homo totus cæteris quo- que peccatis, Matth. XV. Sed non ita, ut scorta- tione, quæ flagitiosæ libidinis flamma impura cor- pus hominis accendit, eique notam turpitudinis inu- rit, & membris tetram maculam fœdissimæ pollu- tionis aspergit, quin haud raro morbis abominabi- libus, ceu stigmatibus inustis, antegressæ vitæ impu- ritatem prodit, & in apertum profert. Nec malè Cornelius à Lapide: Fornicator in corpus suum peccat, & injurius est: Quia in corpore fœdam & pudendam libidinem excitat, quæ ita mentem absorbet, ut in illius actu homo nihil aliud cogitare possit. Facit ergò fornicator corpus suum man- cipium libidinis & concupiscentiæ, ut in eo fœ- da libido dominetur, illudque totum sibi vendi- cet, nec gula, nec aliud vitium in corpore tam pudendam & tam vehementem concupiscentiam excitat, quæ ita sibi corpus mancipet, ut libido. Sola ergo libido dominatur corpori, illudque suâ concupiscentia & peccato inficit, subjugat & cor- rumpit. Alia peccata, inquit Hieronymus, forin- secus sunt, quæ post factum pœnitudinem habent, & licet invitet lucrum, mordet conscientia; sola libido, etiam in ipso tempore pœnitendi præteritos stimulos patitur, & titillationem carnis & incen- tiva peccati, ut per hæc, quæ corrigi cupimus, co- gitantes, rursum sit materia peccandi. His acce- dit etiam tetra pollutio, qua ipsa membra infi- ciuntur per scortationem. Quod non fit in ma- trimonio, ob verbum, quo actus concubialis sanctificatur.

Ἦ οὐκ οἴδατε.) Annon cogitatis. V. 19. Ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τꭣ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίꭣ Πνεύματός ἐσι. Spiritus Sanctus hic quod שכינה in templo. Totus homo templum DEI, supra III. 16. 17. Sed דביר, id est, adytum est mens hominis: Animi cæteræ partes היכל basilica templi: Corpus vero אולם porticus cum subdialibus. Bene hunc locum explicat Tertullianus libro de cultu fœminarum altero: Cum omnes templum simus DEI, illato in nos & consecrato Spiritu Sancto, ejus templi œditua & antistita pudicitia est, quæ nihil immundum ac profanum inferri sinat, ne Deus ille, qui inhabitat, inquina- tam sedem offensus derelinquat. Οὗ ἔχετε ἀπὸ Θεꭣ. Spiritus ille à DEO est, multo magis, quam splendor ille, qui apparebat interdum inter Cherubinos. Con- structio est Græca, quæ relativo pronomini dat casum præcedentem.

De persona Spiritus Sancti hæc intelligenda, non minus quàm de gratia. Non enim tantùm virtute & gratiâ in fidelibus habitat, tanquam in templo suo, tum in anima, tum in corpore fide- lium, quia totum hominem sibi, ceu templum, vendicat, quemadmodum totum hominem rege- nerat, renovat, sanctificat, sed etiam substantiæ ratione proximior nobis est specialis præsentia, fidelium propria, quam universis creaturis, ali- isque hominibus, quæ generalis est præsentia, ut part. II. Syst. Theol. docuimus cap. XII. quæst. III. pag. 630. Fatendum est, inquit Augustinus Epist. LVII. ad Dardan: ubique esse DEUM, per divinitatis præsentiam, sed non ubique, per inhabitationis gratiam. Verum illud est multo mi- rabilius, quod, cum DEUS ubique sit totus, non tamen in omnibus habitat. Non enim omnibus di- ci potest, quod dicit Apostolus: Nescitis, quod templum DEI estis, Spiritus enim DEI habitat in vobis. Quamvis quod postea sequitur, in qui- bus habitat, habeant eum pro suæ capacitatis diver- sitate, alii amplius, alii minus, quos ipse sibi dilectissi- mum templum gratia suæ bonitatis ædificat. Gemi- num hic argumentum est, monente Theophyla- cto: Hoc magis, inquit, territat cum ob muneris, hoc est, Spiritus Sancti, magnitudinem, tum lar- gientis, hoc est, DEI dignitatem. Templum, in- quit, estis, & sanctum: quippe quod ex sancto Spiritu esse constat. Nolite ergo hoc templum, quod sanctitate donatum est, impurum & sordidum effi- cere. Neque DEI hoc donum inutile reddite. A DEO namque accepistis hunc Spiritum. Temere autem haec verba, quam habetis a DEO, ad haere- sin suam torquet Schlichtingius, quasi dicatur, qui etsi DEUS ipse non est, tamen DEI Spiritus & afflatus sanctus est, & non aliunde, quam ab ipso DEO, habetur. Nam haec in schola Apostolica non sunt opposita, esse a DEO, & esse Deum, ut Filius DEI a DEO est, & ipse Deus est, bene- dictus in secula super omnia. Illo origo a Patre, hoc autem ὁμουσία personae, seu identitas essen- tiae cum Patre, notatur, quae utique sancte cre- denda est. Nam ita a DEO Patre procedit Spiri- tus Sanctus, ut ejusdem cum Patre sit essentiae, 1. Joh. V. 7. quem Deum esse hic non subticuit Apostolus, cum id, quod DEI proprium est, tem- plum Spiritui Sancto vindicavit, & glorificare DEUM in corpore nostro jussit, eum scilicet, qui in corpore nostro, ceu templo suo, habitat, quod non minus est Spiritus Sancti, quam Patris & Filii, Joh. XIV. 23. 26.

Καὶ ὐκ ἐσὲ ἑαυτῶν. Praeterea non estis vestrae potestatis, Rom. XIV. 7. 8. Ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.

Omisit jus ex creatione, quia alterum erat recentius, & magis speciale. Habes eadem verba infra VII. 23. & sen- sum 1. Petr. I. 18. ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς, recte verteris, ac- quisiti sive comparati estis pretio. Nam קנה, quod est accipere, acquirere vertitur ἀγοράζειν & habet in Hebraeo post se במחיר τιμῇ pretio. Et Es. LV. 1. שברו בלוא- כסף ובלוא מחיר Graece: Ἀγοράσατε ἄνευ ἀργυρίε καὶ τιμῆς. Et קנה, quod est proprie κτᾶσθαι, vertitur per ἀγοράζειν 2. Paral. XXXIV. 2. Prov. XX. 17. Esa. XXI''. 2. & discriminis causa additur ὡς ἀργυρίω 2. Paral. XXI 24. Valet ergo ἀγοράζειν idem, quod περιποιεῖν Act. XX. 28. unde περιποίησις Eph. I. 4. 1. Thess. V. 9. 2. Thess. II. 14. 1. Petr. II. 9. Sic & Latinis veteribus emere erat sumere, unde demo, & adimo, & praemium. Sensus est: Christus vos a peccatis redemptos sibi mancipavit, sed magno ei statis, morte ipsius cruenta.

Non omisisse Apostolum jus creationis, B. Bal- duinus notat, haec observans e praesenti textu ar- gumenta (1.) ex articulo creationis v. 13. (2.) ex articulo redemptionis v. 14. (3.) ex articulo re- surrectionis v. 15. 16. 17. (4.) a comparatione scor- tationis cum aliis peccatis v. 18. (5.) Ex articulo sanctificationis. v. 19. (6.) denique ex articulo re- demtionis. Non estis vestri, empti enim estis pretio magno, v. 20. quasi dicat, non licet vobis vestris corporibus uti, vel abuti potius, pro libitu vestro: Non enim vestri juris estis, sed ad arbitrium ejus vivitis, qui caro pretio sanguinis sui vos redemit: Is vero est Christus Jesus, Deus ille castitatis, & homo de casta natus virgine, qui ab omni im- munditie vos redemit, sub qua vos vendidit spi- ritus ille impuritatis. Recte autem emphasin ver- bi ἀγοράζειν evolvit Grotius, e qua satisfactionem Christi, adversus Socinianos, in Socinismo profli- gato asseruimus, quem hic conferet, cui libuerit. Vis argumenti est, cum tanto pretio, sanguinis nimirum ipsius DEI Christi θεανθρώπε, qui est DEUS ille, qui sanguine suo nos acquisi- vit, Act. XX. 21. DEUS super omnia benedi- ctus in secula, Rom. IX. 5. empti simus, & anima & corpore, magnifacere oportet corpora no- stra, cum ea licetur daemon turpi & brevi cor- poris voluptate. Estis, inquit, Theophylacto inter- prete, sub Domino constituti, neque quicquam ha- betis, quod vestri sit juris, nec corpus ipsum. Quippe qui pretio empti magno sitis, hoc est, Christi san- guine. Quo fit, ut membra vestra non vobis, sed Do- mino obstricta sint servitute, & pro illius arbitrio ferantur necesse est.

Nequicquam oggannit Schlichtingius, nemi- nem nos DEO vendidisse, & vitam ac sanguinem Filii DEI proprie loquendo pretium non esse, sed superare & excedere omne pretium. Nam venditi eramus sub Diaboli potestatem, cui per justi- tiam divinam, quam offenderat homo, per pec- catum traditus erat. Opus erat ergo satisfactio- ne, non Diabolo, ceu lictori, sed DEO judici præstanda, & redemtione nostri, quæ non qui- dem pretio materiali auri vel argenti, caro tamen pretio omne aurum & argentum largissime superante, sanguinis nempe Christi, hoc est, non nudi hominis, sed magni & veri DEI pretio- sissimi est præstita. Et quamvis DEUS nobis condonet peccata omnia, & à nobis pretium non poscat, nec ei solvendo simus, non tamen sine pretio facta est nostra redemptio, sed inter- ventu solutionis pretii à Christo Mediatore no- stro, nostri loco, præstitæ, 2. Cor. V. 14. 1. Tim. II. 5. Fatetur Schlichtingius ipse, Deum inter alia in hoc ipsum Filii sui sanguinem effundi voluisse, ut remissionem peccatorum sanciret, & se nobis ad ea condonanda penitus obstringeret. Atqui sancire non poterat eam salvâ justitia, nisi præstitâ satis- factione, quam nostri vice Filius DEI præstitit, cum solvit, quæ non rapuit. Psal. LXIX. 5. Nec condonare peccata, nedum ad ea condonanda se obstringere per veritatem & justitiam suam vel valuit, vel voluit DEUS, citra λύτρον sanguinis istius pretiosissimi, quod loco citato assertum ab- unde. Et qualis hæc est obligatio per sanguinis Christi effusionem, si vim sententiæ Socinianæ ex- pendamus? Nimirum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, innocen- tem tamen in mortem traditum, credunt, qui omnis peccati expers fuit, ut DEUS se nobis ad condonanda peccata obstringeret. Quodnam vel indicium vel vinculum est obligationis ad con- donanda nocentibus peccata, in morte hominis innocentis, si ille & purus homo, nec nostri loco traditus est, neque pro nobis & pro pecca- tis nostris satisfecit, sed mortuus, ut obedientiâ suâ non nobis, sed sibi, præmium acquireret.

## 6:20
Glorify therefore GOD.

Honor God, which is done chiefly by obeying. But some manuscripts had δοξάσατε ἄρα τὸν Θεὸν. Whence unskilled scribes made ἄρατε.

In your body.

Not with the soul alone. For it is also His body, and it ought to serve Him.

And in your Spirit.

Nor with the body alone: For that is the way of hypocrites, but with the soul as well.

We add here only the observation of Theophylact, that it is shown here that we must decline from adultery not only in body, but also in soul. In human servitude the soul is free, even though the body serves. Although we ought to prove ourselves to them not only by external services before the eyes of masters, but from the heart, Col. III. 22. But in the servitude which we owe to GOD, the soul ought to serve just as much as the body; because GOD has saved the soul just as much as the body, and has therefore claimed it for His own service. Which, as Schlichtingius also observed in this place, why therefore does he exclude the body, which GOD has saved just as much as the soul, from eternal salvation, while to eternal life does he deny that he will rise again? For we have surely been preserved by the Lord for eternal life. Ἢ τινά ἐσι τῷ Θεῷ.

Not only by right of creation, but also by the aforementioned redemption, which Christ performed in such a way that He acquired us not only for Himself, but also for GOD, Ap. V. 9. Indeed, God Himself is also said to have acquired us, Acts XX. 28. See Rom. III. 23, 24. Truly, this particle and that καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ὑμῶν are absent in the Manuscript, just as they were absent from the Codices used by the Latins.

The Greeks, however, and the Syrian, and the Arab read these. The passage in Acts XX. 28 is wrongly snatched away to GOD the Father, whereas it clearly treats of Christ; for He who διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος περιεποιήσατο τὴν ἐκκλησίαν (acquired the church through His own blood) is not the Father, but Christ. The Father does not have blood, nor is He ever said to have shed His own blood, or to have redeemed us with His own blood; but this is proper to Christ Himself, that great GOD and our Savior, who gave Himself for us, that He might redeem us from all iniquity, Tit. II. 13, 14.

PART III. OF THE EPISTLE DIDACTIC. MEMBER I. Concerning morals and practical cases regarding the questions raised by the epistle.

SECTION I. Concerning those things which pertain to marriage and celibacy.

Latin:

Δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν.

Honorate Deum, quod præcipuè fit obsequendo. At quidam codices habuere δοξάσατε ἄρα τὸν Θεὸν. Unde im- periti scribæ fecerunt ἄρατε.

Ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.

Non solo animo. Nam & corpus ejus est, & ei ser- vire debet.

Καὶ ἐν τῷ Πνέυματι ὑμῶν.

Neque solo corpore: Id enim est ὑποκριτῶν, sed animo simul.

Addimus hic tantum observationem Theophy- lacti, quod ostendatur hic, non modo corpore esse ab adulterio declinandum, sed etiam animo. In humana servitute animus est liber, quamvis cor- pus serviat. Tametsi non tantùm externis ser- vitiis, coram oculis Dominorum, nos probare ipfis debeamus, sed cordicitus, Col. III. 22. In servitute autem, quam DEO debemus, ani- mus æquè servire debet, ac corpus; quia animam æquè DEUS servavit, ac corpus, adeoque ser- vituti suæ vindicavit. Quod uti etiam observa- vit Schlichtingius in hoc loco, quid ergo corpus, quod DEUS servavit, æquè ut animam, ab æter- na salute excludit, dum ad vitam æternam resurrecturum negat? Nam servati utique sumus à Domino ad vitam æternam. Ἢ τινά ἐσι τῷ Θεῷ.

Non folò creationis jure, verum etiam jam dictæ redemptionis, quam ita fecit Christus, ut non sibi nos tantùm, sed & DEO acquisiverit, Ap. V. 9. Imo & Deus ipse nos dicitur acquisivisse, Act. XX. 28. Vide Rom. III. 23. 34. Verum hæc particula & illa καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ὑμῶν abest in Manuscripto, sicut & abfuit à Codicibus, quibus usi Latini.

Græci verò, & Syrus, & Arabs hæc legerunt. Locus Actor. XX. 28. perperam abripitur, ad DEUM Patrem, qui luculenter agit de Christo; siquidem is, qui διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος περιεποιήσατο τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, non Pater fit, sed Christus. Pater sanguinem non habet, neque fudisse proprium sanguinem, vel proprio sanguine nos redemisse uspiam dicitur; sed proprium hoc est ipsius Christi, magni illius DEI & Servatoris nostri, qui semetipsum dedit pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, Tit. II. 13. 14.

PARS III. EPISTOLÆ ΔΙΔΑΚΤΙΚΗ. M E M B R U M I. Mores, & casus practicos de quæfitis per epistolam concernens.

SECTIO I. De iis, quæ conjugium, & calibatum attinent.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. ARGUMENT & PARTITION

He teaches that marriage is to be entered into for the sake of avoiding fornication, and that the conjugal debt is to be mutually rendered within marriage, and he counsels how long one should abstain from it, so that it may be good for both the unmarried and the widows: Then he urges the Lord’s precept concerning divorces, and reveals his own counsel regarding an unbelieving spouse, and on that occasion explains whether the state is to be changed on account of Christianity, as regards circumcision and uncircumcision, as regards servitude and liberty? Finally, he resolves three questions concerning the unmarried: whether and to what extent it is expedient to remain in celibacy? Whether and to what extent parents ought to give their daughters in marriage? And whether it is lawful for widows to marry again? There are, therefore, two parts.

The first is concerning marriage and divorce, up to verse 17. A general epembolē (digression) is subjoined concerning everyone’s calling, up to verse 24. The second is concerning the solitary state of virgins up to verse 38, and of widows up to verse 40.

PART I. Concerning Marriage and Divorce.

Verse 1. Περὶ ὧν ἐγράψατέ μοι, καλὸν γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι, διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω. It was a frequent question among the philosophers: whether a wise man should take a wife?

Those who referred everything to themselves, considering how little convenient the dispositions of women often are, how troublesome the education of children is, and to how many dangers it is exposed, judged that one should abstain from nuptials. There is a passage to this effect from the philosopher Antiphanes in Stobaeus, and the sayings of Lycurgus, Thales, Socrates, and others. On the contrary, those who looked to public utilities said that it was owed to the republic, just like other tributes, and the sowing of children.

And you have illustrious sayings of Musonius and Hierocles to this effect in Stobaeus. Menander says thus: To marry, if one considers the truth, Is an evil, but a necessary evil. Metellus Numidicus in the oration which he delivered as Censor: If we could be without a wife, Quirites, we would all be free from that annoyance. But since nature has so ordained that one can neither live with them conveniently enough, nor in any way without them, one must consult for perpetual safety rather than for brief pleasure. Therefore, when at Corinth, under the name of Christians, philosophers—or rather, those who were more philosophers than Christians—had variously treated this controversy, certain pious men, who preferred the Apostle to those teachers, judged that he should be consulted on this matter.

He, however, as one looking [to the end], indeed prefers a life without nuptials, because in this way one can more readily serve God and the Church and each of the saints. But to those who either could not or would not restrain themselves from women, he says that nuptials are not only expedient, but also ex hypothesi (by hypothesis) necessary, because God is vehemently offended by fornication. The Christians were not so solicitous about bearing children that they would impose upon themselves the necessity of taking a wife for that reason alone, because they suspected that the end of the ages was imminent. Tertullian on monogamy: "Increase and multiply," he has emptied of the end of times.

If, however, any were to enter into marriage, they judged that this end also ought to be set before them. Ἄπτωδαι is said σεμνῶς as in Prov. VI. 27. Gen. XX. 6. Terence in the Hecyra: "That first night he did not touch the virgin." Catullus: "So the virgin, while she remains untouched, grows old untouched." This therefore Paul says: that it is best, when no woman married or unmarried has intercourse with him. Ἀπτωδαι here means a man, as above VI. 18. So in law: "If a man or woman." Διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας, namely to be avoided.

He seems to have spoken in the plural, porneias, to include all kinds of impurity. Let each have his own woman, not a public one, that is.

And let the woman, content with her own husband, not know another. See Heb. XIII. 4. ἔχειν (to have), where it treats of marriage and is attributed to the husband and the wife, as we said at Matt. XIV. 4. Lactantius: "Whoever cannot curb those affections, let him restrain them within the prescribed limit, then of the legitimate bed."

Chrysostom: "Marriage is the safeguard of chastity."

The information concerning matrimony follows conveniently, after the Apostle has thundered against fornication.

But that those doubtful cases were raised by the philosophers, I do not see from where it can be gathered. Nor is it ours to examine now the opinions of the philosophers, where the mind of the Apostle is to be weighed. But that the Christians were not so solicitous in marriage about bearing children, or that they did not have the principal end of marriage, seems a rash suspicion.

For surely we shall believe that the same men were ignorant of the matrimonial law, or of the necessity of procreating children, which is established by the law of nature? Therefore the Apostle does not touch upon this end; hence it must be judged that this is because there was no doubt about it, since the world cannot subsist without the generation of children. Nor would that saying of Christ have been unknown to them, Matth. XXIV. 39, concerning marriages being entered into up to the advent of the Son of Man. But a scruple had been raised by the Pseudo-Apostles, as Ambrose and Ansbelm note, who, that they might seem holier, taught that nuptials were to be despised, abusing the words of Christ, Matth. XIX. 12: There are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Corinthians proposed such a case to the holy Apostle by letter, not simply, whether it is lawful to enter into marriage? But whether one ought in this way to devote oneself to prayer, piety, &c. Cornelius states the case thus: Whether Christians ought to be so holy that they are bound to abstain entirely from the use of marriage, even those who are married?

For that saying, καλὸν ἄνθρωπον γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι (it is good for a man not to touch a woman), does not agree; which when Estius and Cornelius assume, they openly contradict verses 3 and 4 concerning rendering the conjugal debt, and they have contradicting them Erasmus, Cajetan, Justinian, Gerson, and others: Therefore, by πορνείαν [fornication] in v. 2, it is not the fornication of married persons that is understood, as Salmero wishes; but the whoredom of the unmarried. And how would it not be good to exercise the act of marriage, which God himself sanctioned and instituted, and that for the reason that it is not good for man to be alone? Gen. II. 15. Cornelius a Lapide objects, not indeed that it is a sin to touch a woman; yet it is an evil, because this touching is an act of carnal concupiscence and depraved delight, which, however, is excused by the good of marriage, but is clearly removed by the good of celibacy. But that distinction is inept: For whatever in the category of morals is not good but evil, that is sin and ἀνομία [lawlessness]. But how is that against the law of GOD, which is conformable to the divine matrimonial law, and in which we comply with the divine law? Those things are different: It is an evil for a man to touch a woman, and it is a good for a man not to touch a woman. The Apostle says the latter, not the former. For by the former, the having of relations with a woman is disapproved, as being evil in itself, in the Jesuit sense, which, while it is not amended if it happens in marriage, is nevertheless intrinsically evil, as a carnal act and one of depraved delight: But by the latter, the having of relations with a woman is not disapproved; but it is judged to be good when a woman is not touched, which is not to be understood concerning abstinence from relations with a woman, whether lawful and honest, or illicit and dishonest: Because the law of nature dictates that illicit relations, such as that of whoremongers, is in itself an evil and a sin, and the Apostle had already taught this sufficiently. Therefore it did not pertain to teach now that it is good to abstain from whoredom; nor is this to be taken concerning abstinence from a woman taken into matrimony, because a husband is bound to render the debt to his wife, by the command of the Lord. How therefore would it be good in the category of morals not to touch a wife? And therefore St. Augustine, Epist. XIX, rightly teaches that the Apostle is speaking not of abstinence from a marriage already contracted, but one to be contracted. Who, however, wrongly designates a middle ground between good and evil (moral), which is what is useful and convenient, which is indeed understood in this place, but it is not a middle ground between good and moral evil, but a good of a different kind, which it may be permitted to call civil, or of common life for the more convenient conducting of the same, and that not absolutely; but relatively, according to the reason of a certain time, such as that was on account of τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην [the present necessity] v. 26. and on account of θλίψιν [tribulation] to be avoided v. 28, and also regarding the avoiding of secular cares, so that we may care solely for τὰ τῦ Κυρίε [the things of the Lord] v. 34, where τὸ καλόν [the good] is the same as συμ- φέρον [expedient] Matt. XXVI. 24 and Luke IX. 33. Wrongly, therefore, does Cornelius a Lapide deny that 'good' here means useful or convenient, and understands it as moral and spiritual good, which of itself contributes to the victory over concupiscence, piety, and salvation. For if abstinence from marriage were a moral good, it would follow that non-abstinence from marriage, or when someone enters into matrimony, would be a moral evil, and thus a sin. If abstinence from the act of marriage or relations with a woman of itself contributes to the victory over concupiscence, piety, and salvation; why is abstinence, for the sake of devoting oneself to prayers, not enjoined, but permitted by the Apostle in liberty?

Therefore Grotius does not interpret correctly, as if the Apostle were saying: It is best to have no relations with any woman, married or unmarried, because this gloss does not reach the proposed case, which is not about relations of any kind, or that which is outside of matrimony, which the Apostle had already condemned under whoredoms; but about entering into matrimony, which is thus expedited: that it is indeed done better for a certain reason, if one is endowed with the gift of continence, not to take a wife: But since this is not given to all, on account of avoiding fornication for those who cannot contain themselves, matrimony is to be entered into. Where τὸ ἔχειν [to have] does not denote the continuation of a possessed thing, as if the discourse were about a marriage already entered into, that it is good not to use one's spouse, which Cornelius a Lapide contends, and Jerome wished in lib. 1. contra Jovin. (more unfair to marriage, as Virvesius admits in Philippica 18. in Harm. Fabric. f. 378. Marco Ant. de Dom. l. V. de Rep. Eccl. c. 11.) since τὸ ἔχειν [to have] occurs not rarely even concerning a thing not yet had, as Matt. XIX. 21, Mark XI. 22, Rom. XIII. 3. The Apostle therefore expressly distinguishes the unmarried and widows from the married v. 10 seqq., v. 27, 28, 32, 33, so that he is blind who does not see that the unmarried and virgins are also being discussed in this chapter. This, therefore, is what the Apostle gives here in place of a response: that in his own judgment, then primarily on account of the present state of time, then also on account of other causes, it is more useful not to enter into matrimony, if one can abstain; but if stimuli are felt, and it cannot be otherwise, matrimony is to be used as a remedy for lusts.

Wherefore this decision does not conflict with the words of the Lord in Genesis II. verse 18: It is not good for man to be alone. For this was not good with respect to the preservation of the species; indeed, marriage viewed in itself is simply good. Which the Protoplasts would have experienced in the state of integrity, free from all trouble. But this is by accident, that now after the fall, with calamities having arisen, it is sometimes better not to enter into marriage. Therefore, God speaks in the institution about marriage viewed in itself: the Apostle speaks here about that which happens to marriage.

Therefore, by this precept of the Apostle, διὰ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω [because of fornications, let each man have his own wife], the law of celibacy prescribed for priests in the Papacy is utterly overthrown, which Cassander, Clichtoveus, and Espencaeus, among the Papists, also attacked; which Bellarmine, in his book de Cleric. c. 21, tries to refute in vain in this way: as if the question had been about married men, whether after conversion they ought to use their wives, about which there could be no doubt. Let Thomas answer Bellarmine, while he explains this expression of the Apostle: The Apostle first instructs those who are not joined in matrimony, whether they ought to contract matrimony? Concerning this he manifests two things: First, that it is good in itself, then that it is necessary. Thomas also observes there that, in the avoidance of fornication, against which the Apostle had written, certain persons not having zeal according to knowledge proceeded so far that they even condemned marriage, and that because this seemed harsh to the Corinthians, they wrote to the Apostle about this, to whom the Apostle replies. Thomas observes that the Apostle here sets forth an argument concerning the contract of marriage, but then finally in verse 33 instructs those who have contracted marriage. Let Bellarmine and Lyra, who likewise teaches that the Apostle in these words instructs the Corinthians concerning contracting marriage, reply. Let Arias Montanus also reply, giving this explanation of verse 2: It is good and desirable above all not to touch a woman, but if a woman is to be touched, one must abstain entirely from whoredom. But legitimate marriages are to be entered into, and they are to be cultivated with the utmost fidelity, purity, and simplicity. Furthermore, Bellarmine objects in vain that only counsel is being delivered, not a precept, because the discourse is about everyone; yet not everyone is suited for marriage. For the universality is restricted by the added reason, on account of fornication: that he prescribes this remedy to all who feel the flames of lust, and it is understood entirely that condition, unless they are inept, whether by nature or by some chance for marriage, just as the Papists likewise restrict the universal term, to those who do not have the gift of continence, but whether anyone is going to have it perpetually, no one can be certain, nor that the whole order of priests has it in the Papacy, the Papists themselves have admitted, Claud. Espensæus digress. II. in cap. I. ad Tit. And so that the license of marriage might be permitted to priests, the Roman Emperor & the Duke of Bavaria, the Cardinal of Lorraine, the Bishops of France &c. solicited in public contentions, as witnessed by Sleidanus l. ult. Hist. and Petrus Suavis in the Hist. Conc. Trid. c. 1. lib. IIX. Which the speeches delivered in the Council of Trent itself also speak of. And an obligation from a vow of human law cannot prejudice an obligation from divine and natural law, such as the law of entering into matrimony. On which matter let B. Hülsemannus be consulted in the Manual of the Augsburg Confession, Disp. XXI. p. 1261.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO

Conjugium propter stupra vitanda ineundum, & in conjugio debitum conjugale mutuò reddendum docet, & quousque illo abstinendum, consulit, ut & solutis, & viduis bonum fit: Tum de divortiis præceptum Domini urget, suumque consilium quoad conjugem infidelem aperit, eaque occasione explicat, an ob Christianismum status mutandus fit, utpote quoad circumcisionem & præputium, quoad servitutem & libertatem? Tandem de solutis tres quæstiones resolvit, an & quatenus expediat in calibatu manere? An & quatenus parentes filias elocare debeant? Et an viduis iterum nubere liceat? Partes ergò duæ sunt.

Prima de conjugio, & divortio, usque ad v. 17. Subjuncta ἐπεμβολὴ generali de cujusque vocatione ad v. 24. Altera de statu solitario virginum usque ad vers. 38. & viduarum ad v. 40.

PARS I. De Conjugio & Divortio.

Vers. 1. Περὶ ὧν ἐγράψατέ μοι, καλὸν γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι, διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω. Frequens erat apud Philosophos quæstio, an sapienti ducenda uxor?

Qui omnia ad se referebant, confiderantes, quàm parùm commoda sæpe sint mulierum ingenia, educatio liberorum quàm molesta, quot periculis obnoxia, abstinendum à nuptiis censebant. Est in eam sententiam Antiphanis Philosophi locus apud Stobæum, & dicta Lycurgi, Thaletis, Socratis & aliorum. Contrà qui publicas spectabant utilitates, dicebant, reipublicæ, sicut alia tributa, & liberûm fationem deberi.

Et in eam partem habes apud Stobæum dicta illustria Musonii & Hieroclis. Menander sic ait: Γαμεῖν, ἐάν τις τὴν ἀλήθειαν σκοπῇ Κακὸν μέν ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ἀναγκαῖον κακόν. Metellus Numidicus in oratione, quam Censor habuit: Si fine uxore possemus, Quirites, esse, omnes eâ molestia careremus. Sed quoniam ita natura tradidit, ut nec cum illis satis commodè, nec fine illis ullo modo sibi possit, saluti perpetua potius, quàm brevi voluptati confulendum. Itaque cum Corinthi sub Christianorum nomine Philosophi verius quàm Christiani variè tractassent hanc controversiam, pii quidam homines, qui Apostolum illis doctoribus præferrent, confulendum eum hac de re censuerunt.

Is verò, ut spectans, vitam quidem fine nuptiis præfert, quod sic expeditius quis Deo & Ecclesiæ & sanctorum singulis inservire possit. Cæterum iis, qui temperare sibi a fœminis aut non possent, aut etiam nollent, nuptias dicit, non conducibiles modò, sed & ἐκ ὑποθέσεως necessarias, ideò quod Deus scortatione vehementer offendatur. De liberis ferendis non ita soliciti erant Christiani, ut ob id solum ducendæ uxoris necessitatem sibi imponerent, ideò quod finem seculorum de proximo instare suspicarentur. Tertullianus de monogamia: Crescite & redundate, evacuavit extrema temporum.

Si qui tamen inirent conjugium, iis hunc etiam finem propositum esse debere sentiebant. Ἄπτωδαι est dictum σεμνῶς ut Prov. VI. 27. Gen. XX. 6. Terentius Hecyra: Nocte illa prima virginem non attigit. Catullus: Sic virgo dum intacta manet, dum intacta senescit. Hoc ergò dicit Paulus: Optimum esse, cum nulla fœmina nupta aut innupta consuetudinem habere. Ἀπτωδαι hic est vir, ut supra VI. 18. Sic in jure: Si homo, vel mulier. Διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας vitandas scilicet.

Pluraliter videtur dixisse πορνείας, ut omnia impuritatis genera includeret. Suam quisque mulierem habeat, non publicam scilicet.

Et mulier suo viro contenta alterum non norit. Vide Ebr. XIII. 4. ἴχεν ubi de conjugio agitur & viro tribuitur & mulieri, ut diximus ad Matth. XIV. 4. Lactantius: Quisque affectus illos frenare non potest, cohibeat intra præscriptum, tum legitimi thori.

Chrysostomus: Γάμος ἀσφάλεια σωφροσύνης.

Commode sequitur informatio de matrimonio, postquam adversus scortationem detonavit Apostolus.

Cafus autem illos dubios motos esse à Philosophis, non video, unde colligi queat. Nec nostrum est dispicere jam de Philosophorum sententiis, ubi mens Apostoli expendenda. Christianos autem non adeò solicitos fuisse in conjugio de ferendis liberis, vel eosdem non habuisse finem conjugii præcipuum, temeraria videtur suspicio.

Num enim credemus, iisdem ignotam fuisse legem matrimonialem, aut necessitatem procreationis liberorum, quæ naturæ lege constat? ergò hunc finem non tangit Apostolus, ideo fieri censendum, quod de eo nullum fuerit dubium, cùm fine fatione liberorum mundus consistere nequeat: Nec ignotum fuerit illud Christi, Matth. XXIV. 39. de conjugiis ineundis usque ad adventum Filii hominis. Scrupulus autem erat à Pseu-Apostolis motus, notante Ambrosio & Ans-belmo, qui, ut sanctiores viderentur, nuptias spernendas esse docebant, abusi verbis Christi Matth. XIX. 12. Sunt eunuchi, qui seipsos castraverunt propter regnum cælorum. Unde casum ejusmodi per literas proponebant Corinthii S. Apostolo, non simpliciter, anne liceat matrimonium inire? Sed annon ita vacandum orationi, pietati, & ca. statum pervertit Cornelius hoc modo: Utrum Christiani tam sancti esse debeant, ut à re uxoria prorsus abstinere teneantur, etiam conjugati?

Nam non convenit illud, καλὸν ἄνθρωπον γυναικὸς μὴ ἅπτεσθαι; quod cùm assumunt Estius, & Cornelius, apertè repugnant versui 3. & 4. de reddendo debito conjugali, & contradicentes habent bent Erasmum, Cajetanum, Justinianum, Ger- sonem, aliosque: Ideò per πορνείαν v. 2. non fornicatio maritorum, ut Salmero vult; sed soluto- rum scortatio intelligitur. Et quo modo non esset bonum exercere actum conjugii, quod Deus ipse sanxivit, & instruxit, idque ea de causa, quod non sit bonum, hominem esse solum? Gen. II. 15. Obver- tit Cornelius à Lapide, non quidem peccatum id esse, mulierem tangere; esse tamen malum, quia hoc tan- gere actus est concupiscentis carnalis, pravaeque de- lectationis, quae tamen excusetur per bonum conju- gii, sed planè tollatur per bonum calibatus. Sed inepta est illa distinctio: Quicquid enim in gene- re morum non bonum sed malum est, id pecca- tum est & ἀνομία. Quî autem contra legem DEI est, quod legi divinae matrimoniali conforme est, & in quo morem gerimus divinae legi? Diversa illa sunt: Malum homini mulierem tangere, & bo- num est homini, mulierem non tangere. Posterius Apostolus dicit, non prius. Nam illo improbatur τὸ consuescere cum muliere, ceu per se malum, sensu Jesuitico, quod non quidem emendetur, si in conjugio fiat, intrinsecè tamen malum sit, tan- quam actus carnalis, & pravae delectationis: Hôc verò non improbatur τὸ consuescere cum mulie- re; sed bonum esse judicatur, cum non tangitur mulier, quod non de abstinentia à consuetudine cum muliere seu licita & honesta, sive illicita & inhonesta intelligendum: Quia illicitam consue- tudinem, qualis scortatorum est, per se esse ma- lum & peccatum & naturae lex dictitat, & satis jam docuerat Apostolus. Non ergò attinebat jam docere bonum esse, abstinere à scortatione; neque id accipiendum de abstinentia à muliere in matri- monium acceptà, quia tenetur vir uxori debitum reddere, ex praecepto Domini. Quì ergò bonum esset in genere morum, uxorem non tangere? Ideo- que S. Augustinus Epist. XIX. rectè docet, non de abstinentia à conjugio jam contracto, sed contra- bendo loqui Apostolum. Qui tamen malè inter bonum & malum (morale) medium designat, quod utile est & commodum, quod hoc in loco quidem intelligitur, non autem medium est inter bonum & malum morale, sed diversi generis bonum, quod ita vocare liceat, civile, seu vitae communis ad eandem commodius traducendam, idque non ab- solutè; sed secundum quid pro ratione temporis certi, quale illud erat ob τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην v. 26. & ob θλίψιν evitandam v. 28. nec non quoad fugiendas curas seculares, ut unicè τὰ τῦ Κυρίε curemus v. 34. ubi τὸ καλόν idem est quod συμ- φέρον Matth. XXVI. 24. & Luc. IX. 33. Perperam ergò Cornelius à Lapide negat bonum hic esse uti- le vel commodum, & bonum morale ac spirituale intelligit, quod per se faciat ad concupiscentia vi- ctoriam, pietatem & salutem. Nam si abstinentia à conjugio bonum morale esset, oporteret non abstinentiam à conjugio, vel cum quis init matri- monium, malum morale esse, adeoque peccatum. Si abstinentia ab actu conjugii vel consuetudine cum muliere per se facit ad concupiscentiae vi- ctoriam, pietatem & salutem; Cur abstinentia ad vacandum precibus non injuncta, sed in liber- tate permissa est ab Apostolo?

Non ergò rectè Grotius interpretatur, quasi dicat Apostolus: Optimum esse, cum nulla faemi- na nupta aut innupta consuetudinem habere, quia non attingit haec glossa casum propositum, qui non est de consuetudine quacunque, aut eâ, quae extra matrimonium est, quam sub scortationibus jam damnavat Apostolus; sed de ineundo matri- monio, qui ita expeditur: quod melius quidem fit certà ratione, si dono continentiae quis praeditus fit, uxorem non ducere: Sed cùm hoc omnibus non detur, propter fornicationem devitandam illis, qui se continere nequeunt, ineundum esse matri- monium. Ubi τὸ ἔχειν non continuationem rei pos- sessæ notat, quasi de matrimonio jam initò sermo fit, quod bonum sit conjuge non uti, quod Corne- lius à Lapide contendit, & Hieronymus voluit lib. 1. contra Jovin. (iniquior conjugio, fatente Virve- sio Philippica 18. in Harm. Fabric. f. 378. Marco Ant. de Dom. l. V. de Rep. Eccl. c. 11.) quum τὸ ἔχειν etiam de re nondum habita occurrat non rarò, ut Matth. XIX. 21. Marci XI. 22. Rom. XIII. 3. Distinguit itaque Apostolus expressè cœlibes & viduos à conjugatis v. 10. seqq. vers. 27. 28. 32. 33. ut cæcus sit, qui non videat, de solutis & virgini- bus etiam in hoc capite disquiri. Hoc ergò est, quod Apostolus hic respondi loco reddit: suo qui- dem judicio, tum imprimis ob præsentem temporis rationem, tum ob alias etiam causas utilius esse, non inire matrimonium, si quis abstinere possit; at si stimuli fentiantur, nec fieri aliter possit, matri- mo utendum esse ceu remedio libidinum.

Quapro- pter non pugnat hæc decisio cum verbis Domi- ni Genes. II. vers. 18. Non est bonum homini, esse solum. Non enim bonum hoc erat respectu spe- ciei conservandæ; imò conjugium in se spectatum simpliciter bonum est. Quod in statu integrita- tis experti fuissent Protoplasti, omnis molestiæ expertes. Hoc verò ex accidenti est, quod nunc post lapsum, calamitatibus exortis, quandoque præstet non inire conjugium. De conjugio ergò per se spectato Deus in institutione loquitur: de eo, quod accidit conjugio, hic loquitur Apo- stolus.

Hoc itaque præcepto Apostoli διὰ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω lex cœlibatus sa- cerdotibus in Papatu præscripta penitus proster- nitur, quam eodem etiam impugnarunt è Papi- stis Cassander, Cblictovæus, Espensæus; quod ne- quicquam elidere conatur Bellarminus lib. de Cleric. c. 21. hoc modo: quasi quæstio fuerit de con- jugatis, an post conversionem debeant uxoribus uti, quo de nullum poterat esse dubium. Respondeat Bellarmino Thomas, dum hanc Apostoli locutio- nem explanat: Apostolus primo instituit eos, qui non sunt matrimonio juncti, utrum scilicet debeant matrimonium contrahere? Circa hoc duo manife- stat: Primùm quod per se bonum, deinde quod sit necessarium. Observat etiam ibi Thomas, quod in devitatione fornicationis, contra quam scripserat Apostolus, quidam non habentes zelum, secundum scientiam, in tantum processerint, quod etiam ma- trimonium condemnarent, quodque ideò, quia hoc Corinthiis durum videbatur, super hoc ad Aposto- lum scripserint, quibus Apostolus respondeat. Ob- servat Thomas, Apostolum hic ponere argumentum de contractu matrimonii, deinde verò versu 33. de- mum instruere eos, qui matrimonium contraxe- runt. Respondeat Bellarmino & Lyranus, qui pa- riter docet, Apostolum his verbis instruere Corin- thios de matrimonio contrahendo. Respondeat & Ariasmontanus, hanc reddens explicationem v. 2. Bonum & optandum est cumprimís fæminam non tangere, sed si tangenda est mulier, à scortatione omninò abstinendum. Sed conjugia ineunda legiti- ma, eaque summa fide, puritate, ac simplicitate sunt colenda. Frustra obvertit porrò Bellarminus, quod consilium tantùm tradatur, non præceptum, quia de omnibus sermo sit; non autem omnes ad conjugium sint idonei. Nam restringitur univer- salitas, addità ratione, propter fornicationem: quod omnibus, qui libidinum flammas sentiunt, hoc præscribat remedium, & subintelligitur omnino illa conditio, nisi inepti sint, sive naturâ, sive casu aliquo ad conjugium, quemadmodum Papistæ iti- dem restringunt vocem universalem, ad eos, qui donum continentiæ non habent, quod vero an quis perpetuò habiturus sit, nemo certus esse potest, nec totum sacerdotum ordinem habere in Papa- tu ipsimet Papistæ fassi sunt Claud. Espensæus di- gress. II. in cap. I. ad Tit. Adeoque ut licentia con- jugii permittatur sacerdotibus, publicis conten- tionibus solicitarunt Imperator Romanus & Dux Bavariæ, Cardinalis Lotharingius, Episcopi Gal- liæ &c. teste Sleidano l. ult. Hist. Petro Suavi Hist. Conc. Trid. c. 1. lib. IIX. Quod orationes etiam in ipso Concilio Tridentino habitæ loquuntur. Et obligatio ex voto juris humani præjudicare non potest obligationi ex jure divino & naturali, qua- lis est matrimonii lex ineundi. Quo de confera- tur B. Hülsemannus in Manuali Augustanæ Confes- sionis Disp. XXI. p. 1261.

## 7:3
V. 3. Let the husband render to the wife the affection that is due, and likewise also the wife to the husband.

There was another question, whether, once a wife had been taken, it would not be more correct to use her for the management of the house, not for intercourse. Paul denies that this is safe for such people as he knew the Corinthians to be. עונת which is Exodus XXI. 10. and is translated by the LXX as ὁμιλία. Paul calls it quite modestly ἔυνοιαν, just as Homer calls it φιλότητα, and Plutarch φιλοφροσύνην. In his Amatorius: In such friendliness. In his Solon: This is a certain honor of a man toward a chaste wife and friendliness. But that Manuscript and others have ὀφειλὴν here in the same sense, so that the other one seems to be an interpretation of this one. This precept, which Paul places here, is among the one hundred and twenty-first precepts commanding the law.

Latin:

V. 3. Τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλομένην ἔυνοιαν ἀποδιδό- τω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.

Altera erat quæstio, an ducta jam uxore rectius non fo- ret, uti ea ad domus regimen, non ad concubitum. Id Pau- lus tutum negat talibus, quales norat esse Corinthios. עונת quod est Exodi XXI. 10. & à LXX. vertitur ὁμιλία. Paulus σεμνῶς admodum vocat ἔυνοιαν, quomodo Home- rus φιλότητα, Plutarchus φιλοφροσύνην. In Amatorio: Ἐν τῇ τοιάυτῃ φιλοφροσύνῃ. In Solone: Τιμή τις ἀνδρὸς αὕτη πρὸς σώφρονα γυναῖκα καὶ φιλοφροσύνη. Sed Manuscriptus ille & alii hic habent ὀφειλὴν eodem sensu, ita ut videatur alterum illud esse hujus interpretamentum. Est hoc præ- ceptum, quod hic ponit Paulus, inter præcepta jubentia le- gis centesimum primum & vigesimum.

## 7:4
V. 4. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. And likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.

Οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει here means, does not have full and complete right. For a partnership has been entered into not only of life, but also of bodies. But in a social matter, no one of the partners has full right.

Do not deprive one another) of that right.

Latin:

V. 4. Ἡ γυνὴ τῦ ἰδίε σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἀνὴρ. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τῦ ἰδίε σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιά- ζει, ἀλλ’ ἡ γυνή.

Οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει hic est, non habet jus plenum & integrum. Nam non vitæ tantum, sed & corporum inita est κοινωνία. In re autem sociali nemo sociorum jus plenum habet.

Μὴ ἀποσερεῖτε ἀλλήλυς) isto jure.

## 7:5
V. 5. Unless it be by consent for a time, that you may have leisure for fasting and prayer.

Εἰ μή τι is if not. By consent one can always abstain, as far as the right of spouses is concerned: For to one who is willing, no injury is done: And we learn from Salvianus and others that some Christians imposed this continence upon themselves. But that, as I said, Paul judged not sufficiently safe for the Corinthians. And so he wants them to sleep apart, or to be in a chaste state, as the Romans used to say, for a short time, and this also according to Jewish custom. For the Jews observed chastity either for the sake of mourning, as the Chaldean Paraphrast teaches us on Ecclesiastes III. 5. and Matthew IX. 15. Or in order to prepare themselves for a sacred solemnity, which can be understood from the passages in Exodus XIX. 15. and 1 Samuel XXI. 4., where see what was said by us: Tertullian in his second book to his wife, dissuading Christian women from marrying Pagans, among other inconveniences brings forward this one: Who, finally, will calmly endure a wife staying out all night during the solemnities of Easter? Prayers love the company of fasting, Matthew XVII. 21. Mark IX. 29. Luke II. 37. Acts XIV. 23.

And again come together to the same place. For ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ is to the same place, as in Acts II. 1. and below XI. 20.

That Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

For Satan stirs up the sparks of vices. Those are called ἀκρατεῖς by Aristotle who are not constant in a good purpose, but succumb to the allurements of vices. That disease is called by him ἀκρασία. Now there were many such Corinthians, even among those who professed Christianity; but they had not yet grown enough in it.

The state of the question is poorly formed, which was not: Whether, having taken a wife, it would be more right to use her for the management of the house, not for sexual intercourse? Nor is the decision of the Apostle directed to this, that for such as he knew the Corinthians to be, that is in no way safe; but that a new question is not even formed here: The Apostle continues by explaining the former case more fully: That although it is better not to enter into marriage, yet it is necessary on account of fornication, nor does its use hinder piety; nay, the conjugal debt must be rendered, by virtue of divine law, nor should conjugal use be interrupted except by mutual agreement, since a spouse does not have power over their own body; yet for a time, if it so pleases, by the mutual consent of the spouses, for the sake of prayer and supplication, it may be interrupted; which, however, the Apostle does not command; but proposes to them κατὰ συγγνώμην. All of which are as clear as possible from the very words of the Apostle. But that counsel is not to be snatched at with Jerome, as if one cannot pray unless one abstains from the use of marriage. For the order of GOD does not hinder one praying, nor could the Apostle have urged the conjugal debt in such a way; or only counselled abstinence for a time, so that afterwards the spouses might come together again ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, if the use of marriage hindered piety and prayer. Certainly, the common and daily custom of prayer is not seen here, which can well consist with the use of marriage, but the customary fasts and solemn prayers are noted, which Christians were accustomed to observe, setting aside not only connubial, but also other political and economic business; as the word νηστεία added to the word προσευχῆς teaches, from a comparison of the passages Matt. XVII. 21. Mark IX. 29. Luke II. 37. Acts XIV. 20, ch. XI. 1, ch. XIII. 2, 3. Which Chrysostom, Augustine, Cajetan, and Espencaeus de contin. sacerd. l. I. c. 6 acknowledge. That a temporary suspension of connubial use is designated here on account of fixed prayers joined with fasts, as it shines forth from the text clearer than the midday sun. Therefore the Apostle used the word σχολάζειν, which is to be free for solemn rites. Guilhelmus Estius on this passage says: Paul, he says, does not speak there of any prayer whatsoever; but of the prayer to which the faithful gathered publicly, such as on Sundays and solemn days. For that was to be free for prayer. For the Apostle does not say, that you may pray, but that you may be free for prayer, as Theophylact observes and urges. Salmero on this passage: It does not seem to be a discourse about private fasts and daily prayers, but public and solemnly undertaken ones, such as when some calamity looms, from which the judgment of the wrath of GOD against us appears, or when something must be done which is of great moment. Lorinus on 1. Pet. III. 8. The discourse, he says, seems to be (1. Cor. VII. 5.) about public fasts and prayers, and when a more serious common calamity or necessity looms. And so also the Roman Pontiff Nicholas I accepts it, cap. 570, in his response to the questions of the Bulgarians, warning that they should abstain from the use of wives during the whole of Lent.

Some indeed extend that εὔνοιαν ὀφειλομένην to support, defense, and tolerance of infirmity, which a husband absolutely owes to his wife; but from the following verse, that the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife, it is clear that the conjugal debt is understood here, which, because it proceeds from intimate love, comes here under the name of εὐνοίας, benevolence, concerning which Theophylact beautifully says on this passage, that the wife is both servant and mistress of the husband, and the husband reciprocally both servant and master of the wife, namely as far as the bed is concerned; since otherwise lordship is to be left to the husband, as the head of the wife 1. Cor. XI. 3. But that, he says, mutual charity is to be demanded in place of the debt, he now reveals, when he asserts that neither of them has power over their own bodies, but that the woman bears the appearance of a servant and of a mistress: Of a servant, because she is subject to her husband, nor may she claim any power over her body, so that she might be able to satisfy that common lust for whomever she pleases: Of a mistress, because on the contrary it is the husband's body, over which he has no power, so that he could, at his own whim, hand it over to adulteresses and harlots. Therefore, by no dissimilar reasoning, the husband is also the servant and master of the wife. Therefore St. Chrysostom warns, hom. XIX. When therefore a harlot approaches to tempt you, you should say, it is not your body, but your wife's: Likewise let the wife also say to those who wish to storm her chastity, my body is not my own, but my husband's.

Latin:

V. 5. Εἰ μή τι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνε πρὸς καιρὸν, ἵνα σχολάζητε τῇ νησείᾳ, καὶ τῇ προσευχῇ.

Εἰ μή τι אם לא. Ex consensu semper abstineri po- test, quantum jus conjugum attinet: Volenti enim non fit injuria: Et eam continentiam sibi indixisse Christianos nonnullos, ex Salviano & aliis discimus. Sed id, ut dixi, Corinthiis non satis tutum judicavit Paulus. Itaque vult eos secubare, aut in casto esse, ut Romani loquebantur, ad tempus breve, & hoc quoque ex more Judaico. Nam Judæi castimoniam servabant aut luctus causa, ut nos do- cet Paraphrastes Chaldæus Ecclesiastæ III. 5. & Matthæus IX. 15. Aut ut ad sacrum solenne se pararent, quod intel- ligi potest ex locis Exod. XIX. 15. 1. Sam. XXI. 4. ubi dicta à nobis vide: Tertullianus libro ad uxorem secundo, diffua- dens fœminis Christianis, ne Paganis nubant, inter alia in- commoda & hoc affert: Quis denique solennibus Paschæ ab- noctantem securus sustinebit? Preces amant comitatum je- junii Matth. XVII. 21. Marc. IX. 29. Luc. II. 37. Act. XIV. 23.

Καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέρχεσθε. In eundem lectum convenite. Nam ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ est in eundem locum ut Act. II. 1. & infra XI. 20.

Ἱνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀκρα- σίαν ὑμῶν.

Nam Satanas vitiorum scintillas excitat. Ἀκρατεῖς Ari- stoteli dicuntur, qui in bono proposito constantes non sunt, sed illecebris vitiorum succumbunt. Is morbus ei dicitur ἀκρασία. Tales autem multi erant Corinthii, et- iam inter eos, qui Christianismum profitebantur; sed non- dum satis in eo adoleverant.

Malè formatur status quæstionis, qui non fuit: An ducta uxore rectius foret ea ad domus regimen uti, non ad concubitum? Neque decisio Apostoli eò directa est, quod talibus, quales norat esse Co- rinthios, id tutum minimè sit; sed ne nova qui- dem hic formetur quæstio: Pergit Apostolus in priori casu plenius explicando: Quod etsi præstet non inire conjugium, necessarium tamen id ob for- nicationem sit, nec ejus usus obstet pietati; imò de- bitum conjugale reddendum sit, vi legis divinæ, nec nisi ex mutuâ conventione usus conjugalis intermit- tendus sit, quum conjux non habeat potestatem sui corporis; ad tempus tamen, si ita placeat, ex con- sensu mutuo conjugum, precum & orationis cau- sa, intermitti possit; quod verò non præcipit Apo- stolus; sed κατὰ συγγνώμην ipsis proponit. Quæ omnia ex ipsis Apostoli verbis quàm maximè lu- culenta sunt. Quod verò consilium non eò abri- piendum cum Hieronymo, quasi orari non possit, nisi abstineatur ab usu conjugii. Ordo enim DEI non obstat precanti, neque Apostolus ita urgere potuisset debitum conjugale; vel tantum ad tem- pus consulere abstinentiam, ita, ut postmodum vicissim ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ conveniant conjuges, si con- jugii usus obstaret pietati & orationi. Non uti- que hic communis, & quotidiana orationis con- suetudo conspicitur, quæ cum usu conjugii pro- bè consistere potest, sed notantur solita jejunia, & solennes preces, quibus vacare solebant Chri- stiani, sepositis non modò connubialibus, sed et- iam aliis, politicis & œconomicis negotiis; Uti vox νηστεία voci προσευχῆς addita docet, è collatione locorum Matth. XVII. 21. Marci IX. 29. Luc. II. 37. Act. XIV. 20 cap. XI. 1. cap. XIII. 2. 3. Quod agnoscunt Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Cajetanus, Espensæus de contin. sacerd. l. I. c. 6. Ob stativas preces, jejuniis conjunctas, temporalem solùm usus connubialis suspensionem hic designari, quemadmo- dum è textu id sole meridiano clarius effulget. Ideò adhibuit Apostolus verbum σχολάζειν, quod est solennibus ritibus vacare. Guilhelmus Estius in h. l. Paulus, inquit, ibi non loquitur de quacunque oratione; sed de oratione, ad quam fideles convenie- bant publicè, velut Dominicis ac solennibus diebus. Nam id erat orationi vacare. Non enim dicit Apo- stolus, ut oretis, sed ut orationi vacetis, ut observat & urget Theophylactus. Salmero, in h. l. Non vi- detur esse sermo de privatis jejuniis, & precibus quotidianis, sed publicis, & solenniter susceptis, ut cum ingruit aliqua calamitas, ex qua apparet ju- dicium iræ DEI adversus nos, vel quando aliquid agendum, quod magni sit momenti. Lorinus in 1. Petr. III. 8. Sermo, inquit, videtur esse (1. Cor. VII. 5.) de publicis jejuniis & orationibus, & quan- do ingruit gravior communis calamitas, aut neces- sitas. Atque ita etiam accipit Pontifex Romanus Nicolaus I. cap. 570. respons. ad quæstiones Bul- garor. monens, ut totâ quadragesimâ usu uxorum abstineant.

Istam εὔνοιαν ὀφειλομένην extendunt quidem nonnulli ad sustentationem, defensionem, tolerantiam infirmitatis, quam omninò vir debet uxori; sed è versu sequenti, quod vir non habeat sui corporis potestatem, sed mulier, liquet, debitum conjugale hic intelligi, quod, quia ex intimo amore profi- ciscitur, εὐνοίας benevolentia nomine hic venit, de quo Theophylactus pulchrè in hunc locum, quod uxor & serva & domina mariti sit, & maritus re- ciprocè & servus & dominus uxoris, scilicet quan- tum ad thorum; cum de cætero relinquendum sit marito dominium, ceu uxoris capiti 1. Cor. XI. 3. Quod autem, inquit, mutua charitas debiti loco ab his sit exigenda, nunc patefacit, cum nullam hos afferit suorum habere corporum potestatem, sed mu- lierem servæ speciem præ se ferre, & dominæ: Servæ, quia subjecta sit viro, nec ullum vendicet corporis sui potestatem, ut vulgare illud ad libidinem, qui- bus libeat, queat: Dominæ, quia contrà suum viri sit corpus, in quo nullum habeat ille imperium, ut possit pro ejus arbitrio adulteratis illud & meretri- cibus demandare. Non itaque absimili ratione & vir uxoris est servus, & dominus. Ideò monet S. Chry- sostomus hom. XIX. Cum ergo ad tentandum me- retrix accesserit, dicas, non tuum esse corpus, sed uxoris: Itidem & uxor dicat iis, qui volunt ex- pugnare pudicitiam, corpus meum non est meum, sed viri.

## 7:6
Vers. 6. But I say this by way of concession, and not by commandment) That is, what I said, let each one have his own husband or wife, I did not command, but advised. This is an אזהרה לא מצוה (admonition, not a commandment). Precepts touch everyone, but warnings are given according to what is expedient for each. συγγνώμη here does not signify the forgiveness of a sin, but a fair concession, just as we said the Hebrew סלח is sometimes taken, at Luke IV. 27. The Apostle said this indulging, not commanding, says Tertullian in his work On Monogamy.

Grotius wrongly drags this, along with the Papists, to the preceding words, let each one have his own husband or wife; for there a commandment is held to be given to all who cannot contain themselves, not merely a counsel. Εχέτω, which word, as Erasmus notes here, is clearly in the imperative mood among the Greeks, nor is there any reason why you should interpret it as 'let him have' or 'it is permitted to have,' since it is said to those who cannot restrain themselves from the company of women, not to everyone. And indeed, to those who would otherwise permit themselves fornication or some fouler kind of lust, he commands that they should rather take a wife. Thus Erasmus. Thomas notes that the Apostle is teaching what is necessary, because not all are suited for this good, not to touch a wife. Nor indeed, with Cornelius a Lapide and other Papists, should these words κατὰ συγγνώμην be referred to the preceding ἐπὶ τὸ συνέρχεσθε (to come together): for although it may seem more plausible, and is even done by Origen, Tertullian, and Jerome, as if the return to conjugal use after prayers is not commanded but permitted or merely indulged, it is nevertheless repugnant to the Apostle, who had given a commandment about entering into marriage on account of fornication, and that a spouse should not withdraw from a spouse forever, and he cannot be at odds with himself: and therefore he advises abstinence from conjugal relations at least for a time, and by mutual consent: And he adds expressly that he says this κατὰ συγγνώμην, and not κατ᾿ ἐπιταγήν. He does not think it safe, as Justinian has it in his annotations, to abstain from the use of marriage too often or too long, wherefore, thinking it should be moderately permitted, he adds, unless perhaps by consent. Claudius Espencaeus on continence. lib. 1. c. 13. notes that the decency of virginity is held here, not a law, and that Paul, out of his modesty, adds that he only wishes to attempt this, not to compel. With whom Faber Stapulensis and Cajetan agree: And among the ancients, Cyprian Epist. XIV, Aug. de haeres. c. 7, 8, Chrysost. Nor indeed does συγγνώμη denote an indulgence of such a kind by which a dispensation is granted regarding the omission or transgression of any commandment: but a counsel or what is fitting. For γνώμη is said of the judgment of the intellect, not of the power of the will, 1 Cor. I. 10, chap. VII. 21, 40, 2 Cor. VIII. 10, Philem. vers. 14, Apoc. XVII. 13, 17, as B. Hülsemann observes in this place, that it indicates a vote and counsel, not a certain authoritative indulgence and remission.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω κατὰ συγγνώμην, 8 κατ᾿ ἐπιταγήν) Hoc est, id quod dixi, habeat quisque suum aut suam con- jugem,non præcepi,sed suasi. Est hoc אזהרה לא מצוה Præcepta omnes tangunt, monita dantur, prout cuique ex- pedit. συγγνώμη hic non veniam delicti significat, sed æquam concessionem, quomodo & סלח Hebræorum in- terdum sumi diximus ad Luc. IV. 27. dixit hoc Apostolus indulgens, non præcipiens, ait Tertullianus de Mono- gamia.

Perperam id abripit Grotius, cum Papistis, ad superiora,habeat quisque suum aut suam conjugem; ibi enim habetur præceptum omnibus datum, qui continere non possunt, non tantum consilium. Εχέτω, quod verbum, notante hic Erasmo, apud Græcos plane est Imperativi modi, nec est, cur inter- preteris habeat, habere liceat, cumq; id dicatur istis, qui sese non possunt à consuetudine mulierum cohibe- re, non omnibus. Atque his sanè, qui sibi permissu- ri essent scortationem, aut fædius aliquod libidinis genus, imperat, ut potius ducant uxorem. Hæc Erasmus. Thomas notat, docere Apostolum, quod sit necessarium, quia ad hoc bonum, non tangere uxo- rem, non omnes sunt idonei. Neque verò cum Cor- nelio à Lapide, aliisq; Papistis hæc verba κατὰ συγ- γνώμην ad præcedentia ἐπὶ τὸ συνέρχεσθε traden- da: quod, etsi speciosius sit, & ab Origene, Tertul- liano, & Hieronymo etiam fiat, quasi reditus ad usum conjugalem post preces non præcipiatur, sed per- mittatur, vel indulgeatur tantum, repugnat ta- men Apostolo, qui præceptum de ineundo, pro- pter scortationem, conjugio, & ne se conjux sub- ducat conjugi in perpetuum, dederat, & sibi ipsi adversus esse non potest: ideoque ad tempus sal- tim, & ex consensu mutuo abstinentiam à consuetu- dine connubiali suadet: Additque disertè, hoc se dicere κατὰ συγγνώμην, 8κατ᾿ ἐπιταγήν. Non pu- tat esse tutum, ut habet Justinian. in annot. sæpius aut diutius ab usu conjugii abstinere, quocirca id moderatè permittendum ratus, addit, nisi forte ex consensu. Claudius Espensæus de contin. lib. 1. c. 13. notat, decentiam tantum virginitatis, non ve- rò legem hic haberi, & Paulum pro modestia sua ad- dere, se illa tentare solùm velle, non impellere. Qui- bus & Faber Stapulensis & Cajetanus consonat: Et è veteribus Cyprianus Epist. XIV. Aug. de hæref. c. 7. 8. Chrysost. Nec verò συγΓνώμη indulgentiam ejusmodi notat, quâ dispensetur circa omissionem, aut transgressionem alicujus præcepti: sed consi- lium vel congruum.
