Γνώμη enim de judicio intelle- Ctus dicitur, non de voluntatis potestate, 1. Cor. I. 10. cap. VII. 21. 40. 2. Cor. VIII. 10. Philem. vers. 14. Apoc. XVII. 13. 17. ut observat, hoc in loco B. Hül- semannus, suffragium & consilium, non potestati- vam quandam indulgentiam & remissionem indi- cari.

## 7:7
Vers. 7. For I would) See what was said at Matt. XXVI. 39, Mark X. 35, Rom. VII. 15.

That all men were even as myself) Paul, when he exhorts to great things, brings forward his own example.

But each one has his own gift, one in this way, another in that) Not only those gifts of the spirit which are obtained without any labor can be called χαρίσματα (gifts), but also those which are obtained with much labor. For every good gift is from God, James I. 17. How, however, continence is a gift, see Matt. XIX. 11 and what was said there. We see, however, that here even conjugal chastity is called a gift of God. For there are some gifts of God that are greater, others that are lesser.

The Apostle therefore teaches this: Although he wishes that he would like all men to be as he himself was, he does not, however, command that they abstain forever, because the gift of continence does not fall to everyone. Whence it is again manifest that the preceding words, 'I say this according to indulgence,' cannot be taken as if he only indulges that spouses should come together again, but by no means commands it, because he had commanded the cohabitation of spouses entirely, and he only advises abstinence for a time, on account of prayers and fastings. He does not sanction divorce; but he commands expressly a return to the use of marriage, lest they be tempted by Satan through intemperance. Just as he had commanded before, μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλες, do not defraud one another: Which he also inculcates again v. 10, Let not the wife be separated from the husband.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Θέλω γάρ) Vellem. Vide, quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 39. Marc. X. 35. Rom. VII. 15.

Πάντας ἀνθρώπες εἶναι ὡς ἐμαυτὸν) Paulus, ubi ad magna hortatur, suum adducit exemplum.

Αλλ᾿ ἕκαστος ἴδιον χάρισμα ἔχει, ὃς μὲν ὕτως, ὃς δὲ ὕτως) Non tantum illa spiritus dona, quæ nullo labore obținen- tur, dici χαρίσματα possunt, sed & illa, quæ multo labore obtinentur. Omne enim bonum datum à Deo, Jac. I. 17. Quomodo autem continentia donum sit, Vide Matth. XIX. 11. & ibi dicta. Videmus vero hic etiam conjugalem ca- stitatem donum Dei dici. Sunt enim Dei alia majora, alia minora dona.

Hoc ergo docet Apostolus: Etsi optet, se velle omnes homines esse, qualis ipse erat, non tamen id se præcipere, ut in perpetuum abstineant, quia non omnibus donum continentiæ obtingit. Unde iterum manifestum est, verba præcedentia: Hoc dico secundum indulgentiam, non posse eo accipi, quasi indulgeat tantum, ut conjuges rursum in unum conveniant, minimè verò præcipiat, quia cohabitationem conjugum omnino præceperat, nec nisi ad tempus suadet, ob preces & jejunia, abstinentiam. Non sancit divortium; sed præcipit expresse reditum ad usum conjugii, ne tententur à Satana per intemperantiam. Quemadmodum præceperat ante, μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλες, ne frau- detis vos invicem: Quod etiam inculcat denuò v. 10. Uxor à viro ne separetur.

## 7:8
Vers. 8. But I say to the unmarried and to the widows) The Hebrews say אלמן and אלמנה. The Greeks call a woman who has lost her spouse χήραν: That a man who has lost his spouse should be called χῆρος, analogy permits, but popular usage does not receive it. Wherefore Paul sought another word, and said ἀγάμοις (unmarried), using the name of the genus for the species. For ἄγαμος by the force of the word is as much one who has never been in marriage as one whose spouse has perished. But Paul uses it here in the latter sense, as the added mention of widows teaches us, and the word ἄγαμος repeated below in verse 11.

It is good for them if they remain as I am) From this place it is not implausibly gathered that Paul had a wife, which Clement of Alexandria also thinks, but that she was dead when these things were written. Καλὸν, that is, κάλλιον, better. See what has been said by us and others at Luke II. 36.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Λέγω δὲ τοῖς ἀγάμοις, καὶ ταῖς χήραις) Hebræi di- cunt אלמן & אלמנה. Græci mulierem amisso conju- gio χήραν vocant: Ut vir amisso conjugio χῆρος dicatur, ἀναλογία permittit, usus popularis non recipit. Quare aliam vocem quæsivit Paulus, & ἀγάμως dixit, generis nomen pro specie usurpans. Nam ἄγαμος ex vi vocis est tam qui nunquam in conjugio fuit, quam cui periit conju- gium. Sed in posteriore sensu hîc usurpat Paulus, ut vidua- rum addita mentio nos docet, & vox ἄγαμος repetita in- fra 11.

Καλὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστιν, ἐὰν μείνωσιν ὡς κἀγώ) Ex hoc loco non improbabiliter colligitur, Paulo fuisse uxorem, quod & Clemens Alexandrinus putat, sed cum hæc scriberentur, mortuam. Καλὸν, id est, κάλλιον, melius. Vide, quæ à nobis & aliis dicta ad Lucam II. 36.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. If they do not exercise self-control) If they do not wish to persevere, or cannot, as Cyprian speaks. To exercise self-control is the same as to endure, to restrain oneself from some thing, to abstain. The Hebrew פקד is translated in both ways. And to Aristotle, he is self-controlled who is constant in the purpose of doing good.

Let them marry) Let them contract marriages. For that is common to males and females. For in Latin, 'nubere' is said only of females, or of effeminate men in mockery. But Christian writers do not always observe those proprieties.

For it is better to marry than to burn) בער is translated as to burn in Prov. 4:21. But to desire in Isaiah 1:29. And צרף is translated both as to burn and to test, to be inflamed with desires, and Cicero in the Tusculans spoke of being inflamed with lust. Virgil: Unhappy Dido is burned. In the Glossary, I am burned means I grow hot. This agrees with that which he said above, 'because of sexual immorality'.

Now therefore the Apostle extends his discourse to widowers and widows. In which we do not disagree with Grotius, that by 'unmarried' are understood not just any unmarried persons, but widowers, since he had already dealt with the celibate: And therefore this second case concerns remarriages: What is fitting for widows, whether they should remain in the state of widowhood, or indeed whether they should enter into marriage again, where he decides concerning widows in the same way as he had settled the matter regarding the celibate, namely that it is good or better that they live outside of marriage by his example, if indeed they are likewise endowed with the gift of continence; but if indeed they do not contain themselves, or are destitute of that gift, it is better that they contract marriage anew than be burned by the flames of lust, where the comparison is improper, as the Logicians call it. 'Better is it to marry than to burn.' Because to burn is clearly not good, so that the comparison might not have a place, that to burn is indeed good; but it is better to enter into marriage than to burn. Nor are two evils compared, as if marriage were an evil, but that lusts are a worse evil. For marriage is not an evil, but a good, to be applied as a remedy for an evil, namely for depraved lusts. Nor indeed does the Apostle here denote only the external act of fornication, as Bellarmine explains in Book II of 'On Monks', chapter 30, and Cornelius à Lapide, according to whom 'to burn' does not signify to be hot or to be tempted by the ardors of lust; but to be overcome by them, whom the interior heats of lust themselves do not hold as fornication. But the Apostle wishes any burning whatsoever to be excluded here, since even the mere look at another woman, joined with illicit desire, is fornication, Matt. 5:28, and rightly observes B. Balduinus: That the remedy of marriage is shown here primarily for internal temptations; not likewise for external ones. For if those who are tempted overcome external temptations, there is no need for that remedy; if they are overcome, the remedy is prepared too late. Nevertheless, B. Mylius rightly distinguishes between heat and burning: By the term burning, he says, not just any heat is noted, which can arise from the stubble of the flesh and concupiscence (for he who feels heat is not immediately burning, as the ancients said), but the impetus of flames and the heat of a conflagration is signified, which can in no way be overcome by struggle and effort, or extinguished by exercises and study. For under this burning, although the body may be kept unpolluted: yet the spirit is not kept pure: by the violation of the sixth commandment the conscience is wounded, prayer is disturbed, the exercises of piety are hindered, the works of charity are contaminated, not to mention the danger of fornication, which is finally avoided with difficulty, and even then barely. And by that word Paul already shows what he called not containing, namely, the burning itself. If, therefore, incontinence is defined by the description of burning: then continence cannot be joined with burning, so that it is clearly frivolous and ἀντιφατικὸν (contradictory) to demand continence from some, whether they are burning and tempted by lust, or not: which the Papists require of their Clerics, which is just as if they were to comprehend and involve continence within the definition of its opposite, incontinence. Moreover, from this Apostolic distinction, the error of those is evident who condemn the repetition of marriage, whether in general, which was done by Montanus, Tertullian, the Montanist, and the Novatians; or in Bishops, and mark it with the odious name of bigamy or polygamy, which is done so much by the Papists that Bellarmine, even in his book on the Clergy, ch. 24, does not fear to decree that such successive bigamy is a greater obstacle in choosing a Bishop than concubinage and adultery. How this may agree with the Apostolic definition, if they do not contain themselves let them marry (γαμησάτωσαν); for it is better to marry than to burn, let the Papists see to that. Let them also see how they can free themselves from the error of the Montanists, which Bellarmine himself condemned in his treatise on marriage, ch. 9. For if a second marriage, and indeed a third, and a fourth, and others thereafter are in themselves lawful and true marriages (and are therefore Sacraments), as the Cardinal says, and is consistent with Canon Law, Cause 31, Question 9, from Jerome and Augustine, ch. 'concerning these', and ch. 'what if' in the same place, how are they illicit for Bishops and ministers of the Church, to whom they are not prohibited by divine or Apostolic law; but are commanded for the sake of avoiding fornication? But it will also be necessary for the Papists to examine here how truly and piously Campegius, Piggias, Hosius, the Cardinals, Eccius, Costerus in his Enchiridion, ch. on the celibacy of priests, prop. 9, and others have taught that a priest sins more gravely if he takes a wife than if he fornicates or keeps a concubine. Cornelius à Lapide is not alien to this impiety in his annotations to this place: saying, for those bound by a vow of chastity, and who have professed it, just as for married men, it is better to burn and fornicate than to marry a second time. For these marriages are a permanent sacrilege, or adultery, which is worse than fornication, or a passing sacrilege. Thus, a marriage which the Papists hold as a sacrament will be a sacrilege: a sacrilege which was commanded by the Apostle to all as a remedy for lusts, and is forbidden to no one by divine law. What Grotius conjectures about Paul being in a widowed state when he wrote this, the Papists, whose cause he mostly pleaded, are by no means going to concede; nor is it firmly concluded from the present passage. For he could have set himself as an example even to widows, even if he had been a celibate; so that, namely, widows might remain as he did, by not entering into marriage, just as he did not enter into it; even if they thus contain themselves from a second marriage, since Paul clearly abstained from marriage, which is the opinion of the Ancients, Ambrose, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Anselm on this passage, Epiphanius, heresy LXXVIII, Jerome, Ep. XXII to Eustochium, which seems not obscurely gathered from verse 7.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται) Si perseverare nolunt, aut non possunt, ut loquitur Cyprianus. Ἐγκρατεύεσθαι idem est, quod ἀνέχεσθαι, ab aliqua re sibi temperare, abstinere. Utroque modo vertitur פקד Hebræum. Et Aristoteli est ἐγκρατὴς, qui constans est in bene agendi proposito.

Γαμησάτωσαν) Nuptias faciant. Id enim commune maribus & fœminis. Nubant enim Latine de fœminis tantum dicitur, aut de effœminatis per irrisum. Sed Chri- stiani Scriptores non semper proprietates istas observant.

Κρεῖσσον γάρ ἐστι γαμῆσαι, ἢ πυροῦσθαι) בהר vertitur πυ- ρῦσθαι Prov. IV. 21. Ἐπιθυμεῖν verò Esaiæ I. 29. צרף ve- ro vertitur & πυροῦν, & πειράζειν inflammari ad cupidita- tes, & inflammatum libidinis dixit in Tusculanis Cicero. Virgilius: Uritur infelix Dido. In Glossario πυροῦμαι ca- lesco. Convenit hoc cum eo, quod dixit supra διὰ τὰς πορ- νείας.

Jam ergo ad viduos & viduas extendit oratio- nem suam Apostolus. In quo non abnuimus Grotio, per ἀγάμυς non innuptos quosvis, sed viduos intelligi, cum cælibes jam expedierit: Ideoque alter hic casus concernit iterata matri- monia: Quid viduis conveniat, an ut in statu vi- duitatis maneant, an verò, ut iterum conjugium ineant, ubi ad eundem modum definit de viduis, uti rem quoad cælibes expedierat, quod scilicet bonum vel melius sit, ut extra conjugium agant suo exemplo, si scilicet pariter etiam dono conti- nentiæ præditi sint; quod si verò se non conti- neant, vel dono illo destituti sint, satius esse, ut matrimonium denuò contrahant, quam libidi- num flammis urantur, ubi impropria, ut Logici vocant, est comparatio. Κρεῖσσον, melius est nu- bere, quàm uri. Quia uri planè non est bonum, ut sic comparatio locum non habeat, bonum qui- dem esse uri; sed melius matrimonium inire, quàm uri. Nec etiam duo mala comparantur, quasi conjugium malum sit, sed pejus malum sint libidines. Nam conjugium non malum est, sed bonum, in remedium mali, libidinum nempe pravarum, ad- hibendum. Neque vero tantum hic fornicatio- nis externum actum notat Apostolus, uti Bel- larm. explicat lib. II. de Monach. cap. 30. & Cor- nelius à Lapide, juxta quem τὸ uri non significat calere, aut tentari libidinis ardoribus; sed vinci iisdem, quos interiores libidinis æstus ipsi pro for- nicatione non habent. Sed quamlibet ustulatio- nem hic exclusam vult Apostolus, siquidem etiam solus aspectus alienæ mulieris, cum illicito desiderio conjunctus, fornicatio sit, Matth. V. 28. & rectè observat B. Balduinus: Internis tentationibus po- tissimum conjugii medicinam hic monstrari; exter- nis non item. Nam si tentati tentationes externas vincunt, non opus est medicina ista; si vincuntur, nimis sero medicina parata est. Recte tamen B. Mylius distinguit inter calorem & ustionem: Ustionis, inquit, vocabulo non calor quivis notatur, qui ex stipulis carnis & concupiscentia oboriri potest, (non enim statim uritur, qui calorem sentit, ut di- xerunt veteres) sed impetus flammarum, atque aestus incendii significatur, qui lucta, conatuque supe- rari, aut exercitiis studioque extingui nullus possit. Sub hac enim ustione, licet corpus impollutum serve- tur: spiritus tamen purus non retinetur: Sexti prae- cepti violatione conscientia sauciatur, turbatur in- vocatio, impediuntur exercitia pietatis, charitatis opera contaminantur, ut taceam scortationis peri- culum, quod vix, ac ne vix quidem tandem evitatur. Et vocabulo isto jam ostendit Paulus, quid antea vo- carit, non contineri, ipsam nimirum ustionem. Si igitur incontinentia ustionis descriptione finitur: continentia cum ustione conjuncta esse nulla poterit, ut frivolum plane & ἀντιφατικὸν sit, continentiam flagitare ab aliquibus, sive urantur & libidine ten- tentur, sive non: quod Pontificii requirunt à suis Clericis, quod perinde est, ac si continentiam inconti- nentia, & si contrarii sui finitione comprehendant, atque involvant. Patet autem ex hac distinctione Apostolica eo- rum error, qui iterationem matrimonii, sive in ge- nere, quod à Montano, Tertulliano, Montanista, & Novatianis factum; sive in Episcopis damnant, & odioso bigamia, vel polygamia nomine notant, quod à Pontificiis adeo fit, ut Bellarminus etiam libro de Cler. c. 24. non vereatur decernere, biga- miam illam successivam magis obstare in deligendo Episcopo, quam concubinatum & adulteria. Quod quomodo Apostolici definitioni, si se non continent γαμησάτωσαν, conveniat; Melius enim est nubere, quam uri, Papistae viderint. Viderint etiam, quo- modo se à Montanistarum errore, Bellarmino ipsi in tract. de matrimonio cap. 9. damnato, liberare possint. Nam si secunda nuptia, imo & tertia, & quarta, & alia deinceps per se licita, & vera matri- monia, (atque adeo Sacramenta sunt) quod ait Cardinalis, & Juri Canonico consentaneum est causa 31. C. Articulo 9. ex Hieronymo & Augustino c. de iis, & c. quod si ibidem, quomodo illicitae sint Episcopis, & Ecclesiae ministris, quibus jure divi- no aut Apostolico prohibitae non sunt; sed ob vi- tandam scortationem mandatae. Sed & de eo dispiciendum hic erit Papistis, quam vere ac pie Campegius, Piggias, Hosius, Cardinales, Eccius, Costerus in Enchir. cap. de caetib. Sacerd. pro- pos. 9. & alii docuerint, gravius peccare sacerdo- tem, si uxorem ducat, quam si scortetur, aut concu- binam alat. A qua impietate alienus non est in annot. ad hunc locum Cornelius à Lapide: Voto ca- stitatis, inquiens, constrictis, eamque professis, aeque ut maritis, satius est uri, & fornicari, quam secundo nubere. Nuptia enim ha permanens sacrilegium sunt, vel adulterium, quod pejus est scortatione, vel sacrilegio transeunte. Ita sacrilegium erit conju- gium, quod pro sacramento habent Papistae: Sa- crilegium, quod ab Apostolo in medicinam libidi- num omnibus praeceptum, nemini interdictum est jure divino. Quod de Paulo in statu viduo, cum haec scribe- ret, constituto, Grotius conjectat, Papistae, quo- rum causam plerumque egit, ipsi concessuri haud sunt; nec id firmiter concluditur e loco praesenti. Nam se ipsum etiam viduis in exemplum sistere potuisset, etiamsi cælebs fuisset; ut nempe vidui sic maneant, sicut ipse, non ineundo conjugium, quemadmodum ipse non iniit; etsi illi sic conti- neant se à secundo matrimonio, quum Paulus pla- nè à conjugio abstinuerit, quæ sententia Veterum est Ambrosii, Theodoreti, Chrysostomi, Theophyla- cti, Oecumenii, Anshelmi in hunc locum, Epipha- nii hær. LXXVIII. Hieron. Ep. XXII. ad Eustach. quæ è vers. 7. non obscure colligi videtur.

## 7:10
Verse 10. To those who are married I command) I do not now advise, but I order.

Not I, but the Lord) Said by way of comparison, not I of myself, but by the authority of Christ. Similar to Matthew 10:20.

Let not the wife be separated from the husband) He rightly says this is commanded by Christ, by an argument from the lesser, that is, the less credible. The Law of Moses had allowed a husband to dismiss his wife: Christ, calling us to greater love and patience, forbids this to be done where unchastity is absent. If Christ said this to the man, to whom the Law of Moses had given so much right, how much more must the same be understood of the woman, to whom the Law of Moses had granted nothing of the sort? Therefore, the same tolerance which Christ had prescribed to men in exercising the Law of Moses was much more justly to be observed by women, to whom not the Law of Moses, but Roman and Greek laws, adapted to the temperaments of those peoples, gave the right of departing from a husband. Paul speaks accurately here, when he says of the woman, μὴ χωρισθῆναι, that is, let her not separate herself. For the passive here, as elsewhere, is for the reciprocal: concerning the man, μὴ ἀφιέναι. For to dismiss from the house, which Paul called ἀφιέναι, and the Attics called ἀποπέμπειν, is the act of the husband, as master of the house: Χωρίζεσθαι or ἀποχωρίζεσθαι, although in some sense it can be applied to both, nevertheless more properly suits the woman, as with the Attics ἀπολείπειν, to desert. Thus Josephus: 'Is it permitted for a woman, even if separated, to marry on her own?' And Justin in his first Apology, speaking of a woman, says ἐχωρίσθη, which the Romans would say 'departed' or 'divorced'.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Τοῖς δὲ γεγαμηκόσι παραγγέλλω) Non jam moneo, sed jubeo.

Οὐκ ἐγὼ, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ κύριος) Comparatè dictum, non ego ex me, sed ex Christi autoritate. Simile Matth. X. 20.

Γυναῖκα ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς μὴ χωρισθῆναι) Rectè dicit hoc à Christo præceptum, argumento à minori, id est, minus cre- dibili. Lex Mosis indulserat Marito uxorem dimittere: Christus ad majorem dilectionem & patientiam nos vo- cans vetat id fieri, ubi abest impudicitia. Si hoc Christus viro dixit, cui tantum juris dederat lex Mosis, quantò ma- gis idem intelligi debet de foemina, cui lex Mosis nihil tale concesserat? Eadem ergo tolerantia, quam in exercenda le- ge Mosis Christus viris præscripserat, multo justius erat ob- servanda foeminis, quibus jus à marito dabat discedendi, non lex Mosis, sed Romanæ & Græcæ leges, illorum populorum ingeniiis aptatæ. Accuratè autem hic loquitur Paulus, cum de muliere dicit, μὴ χωρισθῆναι, id est, ne se separet. Nam passivum hic, ut alibi, est pro reciproco: de viro, μὴ ἀφιέ- ναι. Nam dimittere à domo, quod Paulus dixit ἀφιέναι, Attici ἀποπέμπειν, est mariti, ut domini domus: Χωρίζε- σθαι vel ἀποχωρίζεσθαι, quanquam aliquo sensu utrique aptari potest, magis tamen propriè convenit foeminæ, ut apud Atticos ἀπολείπειν deferere. Sic Josephus: Γυναικὶ οὐδὲ διαχωρισθείσῃ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν ἔξεστι γαμηθῆναι; Et Justinus in Apologetico priore de foemina loquens ἐχωρίσθη, quod Romani dicerent discessit, aut divertit.

## 7:11
But if she also separates) If some little coldness has intervened, and for that reason the wife has betaken herself elsewhere from the husband's house.

Let her remain unmarried) Let her remain celibate, in the hope of repairing the love.

Ἤ τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγήτω) If she does not wish to wait until the husband himself seeks ways of restoring himself to her favor, which he also ought to do if there was any fault in him. See the general precept, which ought also to be referred here, prescribed in Matt. V. 24. But when Paul was writing these things, it was kept in memory and handed down by word of mouth.

Καὶ ἄνδρα γυναῖκα μὴ ἀφιέναι) The Attics would say Μὴ ἀποπέμψειν: Let him not repudiate, let him not cast out. The Hebrews would say לֹא יְגָרֵשׁ, let him not cast out. For that word is usually translated by the interpreters in that way in Lev. XXI, 7, 14; XXII, 13; Num. XXX, 10; Ez. XLIV, v. 22. However, Christ's precept, briefly indicated here, is to be understood in the sense which Christ had explained.

From marriage the Apostle passes to divorce, where he determines both in general, whether it is lawful for Christians, and specifically, whether it is on account of an unbelieving spouse?

But that divorces are not lawful (outside the case of fornication) is not defined by some special law of Christ, who prohibited them, even though they were granted by Moses, because he calls us to greater love and patience, Grotius affirms with not one, but a triple error. First, that divorces were granted by Moses. We demonstrated the contrary at Matt. V and XIX. Second, that Christ prohibited them by some peculiar law, whereas on the contrary Christ did not hand down a new law, but recalled his own from Pharisaical corruptions to the primordial law of marriage. Third, that he calls us to greater love and patience. Since Christ merely repeated the law concerning the love of God and neighbor from Moses, than which no greater could be required. For what greater thing concerning the love of God did he either command, or could he command, than that we love God with our whole heart, whole mind, whole soul, and all our strength? What is greater concerning the love of neighbor than that we love our neighbor as ourselves? In which precepts, just as the sum of love, so also the perfection of patience, which ought to proceed from love, shines forth: love and patience prescribed divinely could have been illustrated more by Christ, which was done especially by the example of Christ, that law could not be further perfected, because to it, which is the highest in its kind, nothing greater or more perfect can be added. But just as the law of Moses gave husbands no right of abdicating or dismissing wives, even though because of the σκληροκαρδίαν (hardness of heart) of the people, prone to dismissing wives, it prescribed a law concerning a bill of divorce, to restrain that wicked lust to some extent, for the sake of the polity of Israel: So neither could it give women the right of departing from their husbands. Because, whom God has joined, man cannot separate, but by the very primeval matrimonial law he taught that two are already one flesh, and therefore, while they live, are inseparable. Which Christ urged from Moses against divorces, establishing the rights of marriage Matth. XIX. The Apostle therefore repeats this from the mouth of the Lord, παραγγέλλων, not advising, but commanding, γυναῖκα ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς μὴ χωρισθῆναι, that a wife should not be separated from her husband, or depart. Which is similarly to be understood reciprocally concerning the man, namely, that a husband should not dismiss or desert his wife. Which the Apostle teaches does not need to be defined; but has already been defined by the Lord, and therefore he warns from that, if a woman has departed from her husband at all, (the reason for the husband is the same) she cannot marry another; but ἄγαμον, must remain unmarried, until she is reconciled with her husband; or that the husband may in turn reconcile her love to himself, or that she herself may seek reconciliation with her husband, and obtain it, which the latter is only commemorated here; but that the former is not excluded from the general law of reconciliation, is evident from Matth. V. 23. 24., which Paul did not need to repeat from memory, if indeed he wrote whatever he wrote by divine inspiration.

Latin:

Ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ) Si frigufculum aliquod intercesserit, & ob id de domo viri uxor aliò se contulerit.

Μενέτω ἄγαμος) Maneat cælebs, in spem resarciendi amoris.

Ἤ τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγήτω) Si expectare non vult, donec maritus ipse quærat vias se restituendi in ipsius gratiam, quod etiam facere debet, si in ipso fuit aliquid culpæ. Vi- de præceptum generale, quod huc etiam referri debet, per- scriptum Matth. V. 24. Sed cum hæc Paulus scriberet, me- moria servatum, ac voce traditum.

Καὶ ἄνδρα γυναῖκα μὴ ἀφιέναι) Μὴ ἀποπέμψειν dice- rent Attici: Ne repudiet, ne exigat. Hebræi dicerent לֹא יְגָרֵשׁ μὴ ἐκβαλῃ. Ita enim ea vox ab interpretibus verti solet Lev. XXI, 7. 14. XXII, 13. Num. XXX. 10. Ez. XLIV. v. 22. Intelligendum autem Christi præceptum, hic brevi- ter indicatum in eo sensu, quem Christus explicaverat.

A conjugio transit ad divortium Apostolus, ubi tum in genere determinat, an id Christianis li- citum sit? tum specialiter, an ob infidelem conjugem?

Non autem licita esse divortia (extra casum forni- cationis) non ex speciali quadam lege Christi de- finit, quem ea prohibuisse, etsi à Mose indulta fue- rint, quia ad majorem dilectionem & patientiam nos vocat, non uno, sed triplici errore affirmat Grotius. Primò, quod à Mose concessa fuerint di- vortia. Contrarium ad Matth. V. & XIX. de- monstravimus. Secundò, quod Christus peculiari quadam lege ea prohibuerit, cum ex adverso Chri- stus non legem novam tradiderit, sed ad legem pri- mordialem matrimonii suos à Pharisæicis corrupte- lis revocârit: Tertiò, quod ad majorem dilectionem & patientiam nos vocet. Siquidem Christus le- gem de dilectione Dei & proximi è Mose solum repetierit, qua major requiri non poterat. Quid enim de dilectione Dei majus aut præcepit, aut præcipere potuit, quàm, ut Deum ex toto corde, to- ta mente, tota anima, omnibusq́; viribus diligamus? Quid majus de dilectione proximi, quam, ut proximum diligamus, sicut nos ipsos? In quibus præceptis uti Summa dilectionis, ita & patientiæ, quæ ex dilectione proficisci debet, perfectio relu- cet: Illustrari potuit magis à Christo dilectio, & patientia divinitus præscripta, quod factum im- primis exemplo Christi, perfici ulterius lex illa non potuit, quia ei, quod fummum est in suo ge- nere, nihil majus, aut perfectius accedere potest. Uti autem maritis nullum jus abdicandi, vel dimit- tendi conjuges lex Mosis dedit, etsi ob σκληροκαρ- δίαν populi, proni ad dimittendum conjuges, le- gem de libello repudii, ad quadantenus coercen- dam pravam illam libidinem, politiæ Israelis causa, præscripserit: Ita nec fœminis jus à maritis disce- dendi dare potuit. Quia, quos Deus conjunxit, homo separare non potest, sed lege ipsâ matrimo- niali primæva jam duos in carnem unam esse, adeoque, dum vivunt, inseparabiles esse, docuit. Quod è Mose Christus adversus divortia ursit, jura conjugii stabiliens Matth. XIX. Repetit ergò hoc Apostolus ex ore Domini, παραγγέλλων, non monens, sed præcipiens, γυναῖκα ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς μὴ χωρισθῆναι, ne uxor à viro separetur, vel discedat. Quod similiter de viro accipiendum reciprocè, ne scilicet maritus uxorem dimittat vel deserat. Quod non opus habere definiri; sed à Domino jam definitum esse, docet Apostolus, adeoque mo- net inde, si omninò mulier à viro discesserit, (par ra- tio est mariti) eam non posse alteri nubere; sed ἄγα- μον, innuptam manere debere, donec cum viro re- concilietur; sive ut vir amorem ipsius vicissim sibi conciliet, seu ut ipsa reconciliationem cum viro quærat, & impetret, quod posterius hic tantum commemoratur; sed è generali reconciliationis lege prius non excludi, è Matth. V. 23. 24. con- stat, quam Paulus non opus habuit è memoria re- petere, siquidem ex inspiratione divina scripserit, quæcunque scripsit.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. But to the rest I say, not the Lord.) Christ had given a commandment to those who were to be of his discipline. Concerning those marriages in which one was a Christian and the other was not, he had said nothing. It remained therefore to derive from the general precepts, concerning the love of all men, admonitions, which nevertheless cannot be so perpetual that they are not restricted by circumstances, as must be done in sayings indeed καθόλου (universally), but to be applied πρὸς τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον (to the individual case).

The Apostle digresses to a special scruple concerning the marriages of infidels: Whether the bond of marriage is dissolved, or whether marriage ought to be dissolved, on account of the infidelity of one of the spouses? Or, whether a believer can cohabit with an infidel without a wound to the conscience? He denies the former, namely, that neither should a husband dismiss his spouse, even if she is an infidel, if she wishes to cohabit with him, nor in turn should a believing woman depart from her husband, even if he is a Pagan and an infidel, if it has pleased him, notwithstanding the discrepancy of religion, to adhere to the woman. Which, just as it is evident from the matrimonial law, so he confirms it further by a singular reason

Apostle v. 14. But that opposition, ἐγὼ λέγω, ὀχ ὁ Κύριος, is not to be understood as if the matrimonial law, repeated and inculcated by Christ, only concerns Christians, since the matrimonial law was prescribed for all living in marriage in the primeval institution of marriage, and is the same law of nations and of nature: But that that case had not been so expressly stated by the Lord, even though it is implicitly comprehended in that law: Whence, a scruple having arisen, the Apostle deemed it to be decided. For some things are and are said in the Scriptures, some things are not said, but are: some things are not had κατὰ γράμμα (according to the letter), yet they are in the Scriptures κατὰ πράγμα (according to the matter), as the note has the rule of Nazianzen. It is not therefore for us to say with Valla, Erasmus, Cajetan, Heinsio, that the Apostle speaks not from divine institution, but human, which openly contradicts v. 40; since the Apostle designates the Holy Spirit as the principle of his γνώμης (opinion) there, whence the diversity is not in the revealing principle, but in the mode of revelation; not indeed for the reason that one is of strict mandate; namely, that married persons should not separate themselves, Matth. V. 32. XIX. 9. and the other can be dispensed according to its circumstances, if, namely, the infidel spouse wishes, or does not wish, to cohabit with the believing spouse. But that one is general and implicit, while the other is special and explicitly directed to the proposed case. He determines the proposed question therefore according to the reason of the double case. For either the infidel consents to cohabit with the believer, or he does not consent: If he does not consent, the believer, on account of the diversity of religion, ought not to dismiss the spouse, vers. 12. 13. But if the infidel departs, and does not wish to cohabit any longer, he teaches that he can be left, verse 15.

Εἴ τις ἀδελφὸς (If any brother) Christian. Γυναῖκα ἔχει ἄπιστον (has an unbelieving wife) Idolater. See above VI. 6. So below 13. 14. 15. X. 27. XIV. 22. 23. 24. 2. Cor. IV. 14. 15. 1. Tim. V. 8. Tit. I, 15. Apoc. XXI. 8. Has, that is, believed in Christ having been caught in such a marriage. For after the faith it was not at all permitted to enter into such marriages. See Tertullian to his wife IV.

Grotius poorly explains that ἔχει: Has, that is, believed in Christ, having been caught in such a marriage, following Bellarmine, who with Salmeron and most other Papists in book II on marriage, understands by τοὺς λοιποὺς (the rest) those spouses who had both contracted in infidelity, so that afterwards one or the other of them was converted. But the Apostle speaks indefinitely, if any brother has an infidel wife, whether he married her an infidel, or she afterwards fell away from the faith. For, that infidelity is an impediment to marriage, Grotius did not prove, even if from a positive and peculiar law it was necessary for the Jews to abstain from marriage with the Canaanite nations, as being devoted to destruction, Exod. XXXIV. 16. Deuter. VII. 3. but then, if that were at all an impediment to contracting marriage, the question nevertheless remained here concerning one already contracted, whether it ought to be torn apart on account of infidelity? Nor, however, does the Apostle give them the faculty of contracting marriage with infidels, which marriages, even if not simply forbidden, are unsafe on account of the danger of seduction; but he prohibits the dissolution of a marriage already contracted, on account of disparity of worship. Augustine also explained the REST concerning those who contracted marriage before the faith, lib. 1 de adulter. conjugiis ad Pollent. cap. 1, concerning whom the Lord commanded nothing: but Paul gives counsel that a husband should not dismiss an infidel wife, if she is willing to cohabit without injury to the Creator. But because this is counsel, not a command, therefore it is permitted to dismiss an infidel wife, and, at that time especially, if she is unwilling to cohabit. Which opinion Bellarmine embraced, lib. de matrimon. cap. 12, contending that the marriage of infidels can be dissolved, even as to the bond, if one of the spouses is converted to the faith, and the other is unwilling to cohabit with him without injury to the Creator. But the marriages of the faithful, contracted after Baptism, cannot be dissolved as to the bond, even if one is converted from heresy, and the other is unwilling to cohabit, without injury to the Creator: with this reason for the diversity rendered, that the former, even if they are ratified and firm, are not by their nature Sacraments, and therefore the most powerful reason for indissolubility is lacking to them; but the latter are indeed Sacraments, and therefore have a double reason for indissolubility. But that opinion proceeds from a false hypothesis concerning marriage: that it is a Sacrament in the Church, and for that reason more indissoluble, when it is by its nature absolutely indissoluble, nor does that accident, that it is performed in the Church or outside the Church, contribute anything to its indissolubility. And although the same is asserted by Lombard lib. IV. sent. dist. 3, Gratian in quæst. 1, Hervæus, Thomas, Lyranus, the Carthusian, most of the Sententiaries, and Dominicus Soto: nevertheless, Haymo, Cajetan, Gagneius, Justinian, and Estius disapprove of it, who says that it was never in the Church permitted for a believer to dismiss from himself an unbelieving spouse, to whom he had been joined in paganism, willing to remain without injury to religion, and that if this had been permitted, in the judgment of Theophylact and Oecumenius, the Christian religion would have come into great reproach, through which marriages legitimately contracted not without grave disturbance of human society. Nor does Augustine obscurely derogate from his own opinion in 2 Retract. c. 57, confessing that in that work on Adulterous Marriages he had not arrived at a perfect clarification of the question which he treated there. And although the Greek interpreters, as also Jerome, Haymo, Cajetan, and Gagney, do not accede to the aforementioned opinion of Augustine: yet they explain the others, τοὺς λοιπὺς, of whom the Apostle speaks, similarly concerning Christians having unbelieving spouses to whom they had been joined before conversion. But Estius refutes them from this, because neither did the Apostle by any indication in the preceding signify that he was speaking only of those who are both Christians, nor is there any reason why the Apostle's discourse should be restricted to them alone.

∵ What then do those words mean: But to the rest I say? Estius and Cornelius à Lapide hold that they refer to the preceding, and are to be understood as not the married. For he had just dealt with the married, says Estius (v. 10), saying: To those who are joined in matrimony, not I, but the Lord. Therefore, what he says here: To the rest I say, not the Lord, ought to be taken concerning the not married, so that it is as if it were an adversative discourse. They allege to the same opinion Tertullian, lib. de exhortat. cast. cap. 3 and libr. conjug. cap. 3, Ambrosius Catharinus, and Joh. Hesselius, and Cornelius clarifies it thus, that these words are to be separated from the following and referred to the preceding, as if he were saying: To the rest not joined in matrimony the Lord does not command, but I say, and I advise, that which I said a little before, and established v. 8, namely, it is good if they remain, namely unmarried, as he repeats that in v. 25. But in truth, these cannot be separated from the following and snatched away to the preceding: And a new decision of a case is begun here concerning the marriage of unbelievers, which pertains to the questions about divorce. Moreover, the condition and duty of those already married, which B. Hülsem. in Brev. extenso cap. XXI. §. 10. admits (although he previously did so with Estius in the unpublished Annotations), is expressly opposed in verses 8 and 10 to the condition of those not yet married: To the unmarried and widows I say, etc. But to those who are joined in matrimony, I command, etc. Among these, however, those are recounted, concerning whom he disposes in v. 12, 13. Therefore, what the Apostle says under the Adversative: Τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς, but to the rest, Osiander in his paraphrase refers to the words immediately preceding in this way: But to the rest, who have not yet made a separation from each other. It can also be said that the rest are called with respect had to the letters of the Corinthians: But to the rest in your Church, concerning whom you wrote specifically, and concerning whom it remains to be said, thus I explain my opinion. Beza says that by the appellation of the rest are understood those who were living bound in an unequal marriage, and thought themselves as it were polluted by the company of an unbeliever, which the Apostle denies.

And she consents to dwell with him) Who does not give cause for divorce first, content with his character, although not persuaded of the same things concerning divine matters. He said consents (συνευδοκεῖ) rather than is willing (εὐδοκεῖ), to signify the will of the woman concordant with the will of the husband.

Concord is noted, not regarding character, but regarding cohabitation, for the underlying matter, because it is not simply said she consents (συνευδοκεῖ): but it is added, to dwell with him (οἰκεῖν μετ’ αὐτῇ). For such a one, who wishes to cohabit with a believing husband; even if she is not only an unbeliever, and differing in religion, but also in character, and not otherwise much in concord with the will and mind of the husband, is not to be dismissed; because the consent of cohabitation makes for the substance of marriage, but not the consent of minds and characters.

Let him not dismiss her) let him not send away. Let him not, being the first to be well in concord, dissolve the marriage. It can be objected: But Nehemiah wished the marriages of the Jews with women of an alien cult to be dissolved. Let the answer be: This precept was given to the Hebrew people alone, Exod. XXXIV. 16, as those who at that time had to be separated as far as possible from other peoples. To other peoples that law was not given, nor was it expedient for it to be given after the mystery concerning the calling of the Gentiles was revealed.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἐγὼ λέγω, ὀχ' ὁ κύριος.) Chri- stus præceptum dederat iis, qui suæ futuri essent disciplinæ. De iis conjugiis, in quibus alter esset Christianus, alter non esset, nihil dixerat. Restabat ergo è præceptis generali- bus, de dilectione omnium hominum, derivare monita, quæ tamen non possunt ita esse perpetua, ut non ex circum- stantiis restringantur, ut debet fieri in dictis quidem καθό- λου, sed πρὸς τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον applicandis.

Digreditur Apostolus ad specialem scrupulum de conjugiis infidelium: Anne ob infidelitatem al- terius conjugum dirimatur conjugii vinculum, vel dirimendum sit conjugium? Vel, anne fidelis cum infideli sine vulnere conscientiæ cohabitare possit? Prius negat, nempe, nec maritum debere conju- gem dimittere, etsi infidelis sit, si cum ipso velit cohabitare, nec vicissim mulieri fideli disceden- dum esse à viro, etsi Pagano, & infideli, si huic placuerit, non obstante discrepantia religionis, mulieri adhærere. Quod uti ex lege matrimo- niali constat, ita ratione singulari adhuc confirmat

Apostolus v. 14. Non autem illa oppositio, ἐγὼ λέγω, ὀχ ὁ Κύριος, eò accipienda, ac si lex matri- monialis, à Christo repetita & inculcata, solum concernat Christianos, cum omnibus in conjugio viventibus lex matrimonialis in primævâ conjugii institutione præscripta sit, eademque juris gen- tium & naturæ sit: Sed quod casus ille adeò disertè expressus non fuerit à Domino, etsi implicitè in lege illa comprehendatur: Unde scrupulo suborto eundem decidendum duxit Apostolus. Quædam enim in Scripturis sunt & dicuntur, quædam non dicuntur, sed sunt: quædam κατὰ γράμμα non ha- bentur, sunt tamen in Scripturis κατὰ πράγμα, uti nota habet Nazianzeni regula. Non ergo est, ut cum Valla, Erasmo, Cajetano, Heinsio dicamus, Apostolum non ex instituto divino, sed humano lo- qui, quod apertè v. 40. repugnat; siquidem prin- cipium ibi γνώμης suæ Spiritum Sanctum Aposto- lus designet, unde diversitas non est in principio re- velante, sed modo revelationis; non quidem ea ra- tione, quod alter sit stricti mandati; videlicet ne conjugati sese separent, Matth. V. 32. XIX. 9. alter secundum circumstantias suas dispensari possit, si scil. infidelis conjux velit, aut nolit cohabitare conjugi fideli. Sed quod alter generalis sit, & implicitus, alter verò specialis, & explicitè ad casum propositum directus. Quæstionem ergo propositam determinat pro ratione duplicis casus. Nam aut infidelis consentit cohabitare cum fideli, aut non consentit: Si non consentiat fidelis, ob religionis diversitatem, conjugem dimittere non debet, vers. 12. 13. Si vero discedat infidelis, nec cohabitare amplius velit, relinqui eum posse docet vers. 15.

Εἴ τις ἀδελφὸς) Christianus. Γυναῖκα ἔχει ἄπιστον) Idololatrida. Vide supra VI. 6. Sic infra 13. 14. 15. X. 27. XIV. 22. 23. 24. 2. Cor. IV. 14. 15. 1. Tim. V. 8. Tit. I, 15. Apoc. XXI. 8. Habet, id est, Christo credidit in tali matrimonio deprehensus. Nam post fidem talia matrimonia inire omnino non licebat. Vide Tertullianum ad uxorem IV.

Malè illud ἔχει exponit Grotius: Habet, id est, credidit Christo, in tali matrimonio deprehensus, sequutus Bellarminum, qui cum Salmerone & aliis plerisque Pontificiis per τοὺς λοιποὺς lib. II. de matrimonio, eos intelligit conjuges, qui uterque in infidelitate contraxerant, ita, ut postmodum alteruter eorum conversus fuerit. Sed Apostolus loquitur indefinitè, si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem, sive eam duxerit infidelem, sive postmodum desciverit à fide. Nam, quod infidelitas sit impedimentum conjugii, non probavit Grotius, etsi ex lege positiva & peculiari de causa Judæis à conjugio cum gentibus Cananæis, utpote internecioni dicatis, abstinendum fuerit, Exod. XXXIV. 16. Deuter. VII. 3. tum verò, si omninò impedimentum illud foret contrahendi conjugii, quæstio tamen hic restabat de contracto, anne illud ob infidelitatem distrahendum sit? Neque tamen Apostolus his facultatem dat contrahendi cum infidelibus, quæ conjugia etsi non simpliciter interdicta, ob seductionis periculum intuta sunt; sed prohibet matrimonii jam contracti, ob cultus disparitatem, dissolutionem. Exposuit & Augustinus CÆTEROS de iis, qui matrimonium ante fidem contraxerunt, lib. 1. de adulter. conjugiis ad Pollent. cap. 1. de quibus Dominus nihil præceperit: Paulus verò consilium det, ut vir non dimittat uxorem infidelem, si velit ea cohabitare sine injuria Creatoris. Sed quia hoc consilium est, non præceptum, ideo licere dimittere uxorem infidelem, & s, tunc maximè, si illa nolit cohabitare. Quam sententiam amplexus Bellarminus lib. de matrimon. cap. 12. contendit, conjugium infidelium solvi posse, etiam quoad vinculum, si alter conjugum convertatur ad fidem, & alter nolit ei cohabitare sine injuria Creatoris. Conjugia verò fidelium, post Baptismum contracta, non posse solvi quoad vinculum, etiamsi alter convertatur ab hæresi, & alter nolit cohabitare, sine injuria Creatoris: Ratione diversitatis hac redditâ, quod priora, etsi rata, & firma sint, ex natura sua non sint Sacramenta, ac proinde potissima insolubilitatis ratio ipsis desit; posteriora verò sint Sacramenta, ac proinde duplicem habeant insolubilitatis rationem. Sed ea sententia ex hypothesi falsa de conjugio procedit: quod in Ecclesia Sacramentum sit, & ob id magis insolubile, cum prorsus insolubile sua natura sit, nec accidens illud, quod in Ecclesia fiat, vel extra Ecclesiam, ad insolubilitatem quicquam faciat. Et tametsi à Lombardo lib. IV. sent. dist. 3. Gratiano in quæst. 1. Hervæo, Thoma, Lyrano, Carthusiano, sententiariis plerisque, & Dominico Soto idem asseratur: Improbant tamen id, Hayno, Cajetanus, Gagnejus, Justin. & Estius, qui nunquam in Ecclesia per- missum ait, ut fidelis conjugem infidelem, cui in Pa- ganismo conjunctus fuerat, absque religionis injuria commanere volentem abs se dimittere, quodque si id licuisset, judicio Theophylacti, & Oecumenii in magnam reprehensionem ventura fuisset reli- gio Christiana, per quam conjugia legitimè con- tracta tam facile dirimerentur, non sine gravi per- turbatione societatis humanae. Nec obscurè de- rogat Augustinus propriae sententiae in 2. retract. c. 57. confessus: se in illo opere de Adulterinis con- jugiis non pervenisse ad perfectam enodationem quae- stionis, quam ibi tractavit. Etsi verò Graeci In- terpretes, ut & Hieronymus, Hayno; Cajetanus & Gagnejus sententiae praedictae Augustini non acce- dunt: Caeteros tamen τὺς λοιπὺς, de quibus Apo- stolus, similiter de Christianis, habentibus conjuges infideles, quibus ante conversionem fuerint con- juncti, explicant. Quos verò inde refellit Estius, quod nec Apostolus ullo indicio in superioribus si- gnificavit, se de iis tantum loqui, qui ambo Christiani sunt, neque ratio ulla sit, cur Apostoli sermo ad eos solos restringatur.

∵ Quid ergò illa sibi volunt: Caeteris verò ego di- co? Estius, & Cornelius à Lapide volunt, ea refer- ri ad superiora, & intelligi non conjugatos. Nam de conjugatis proximè egerat, inquit Estius (v. 10.) dicens: Iis, qui matrimonio juncti sunt, de quo non ego, sed Dominus. Quod ergò hic dicit: Caeteris Ego dico, non Dominus, accipi debet de non con- jugatis, ut quasi sit adversativus sermo. Allegant in eandem sententiam Tertullianum lib. de ex- hortat. cast. cap. 3. & libr. conjug. cap. 3. Ambro- sium Catharinum, & Joh. Hesselium, eamq; ita di- lucidat Cornelius, quod haec verba à sequentibus se- jungenda sint, & referenda ad superiora, quasi dicat: Caeteris matrimonio non junctis Dominus non praecipit, sed ego dico, & consulo, id quod paulo ante dixi, & constitui v. 8. scil. bonum est, si perma- neant, scilicet innupti, ut repetit id v. 25. Verùm enim verò, nec sejungi haec à sequentibus possunt, & ad praecedentia abripi: Et nova hic casus deci- sio inchoatur de conjugio infidelium, quod ad quae- stiones de divortio. Conditio autem, & officium jam conjugatorum, quod B. Hülsem. in Brev. ex- tenso cap. XXI. §. 10. fatetur (etsi prius cum Estio fecerit in Annotatis ἀνεκδότοις) diserte opponitur versibus 8. & 10. conditioni nondum conjugatorum: Non nuptis & viduis dico &c. Iis autem, qui ma- trimonio juncti sunt, praecipio &c. Inter hos au- tem illi recensentur, de quibus v. 12. 13. disponit. Quod ergò dicit Apostolus sub Adversativa: Τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς de caeteris verò, Osiander in paraphrasi re- fert ad verba immediatè praecedentia hoc modo: Sed caeteris, qui adhuc à se invicem non fecerunt discessionem. Dici etiam potest, reliquos vocari respectu habito ad literas Corinthiorum: Caeteris autem in vestra Ecclesia, de quibus scripsistis peculia- riter, & de quibus dicendum adhuc restat, ita meam explico sententiam. Beza reliquorum appellatio- ne eos intelligi ait, qui impari matrimonio constri- cti degebant, ac veluti sese pollui infidelis consor- tio putabant, quod negat Apostolus.

Καὶ αὐτὴ συνευδοκεῖ οἰκεῖν μετ’ αὐτῦ) Quæ prior causam non det divortio, contenta ipsius moribus, quanquam de rebus divinis non idem persuasa. Συνευδοκεῖ dixit potius, quam εὐδοκεῖ, ut significaret voluntatem foeminae cum mariti voluntate concordantem.

Concordia notatur, non quoad mores, sed quo- ad cohabitationem, pro substrata materia, quia non simpliciter dicitur συνευδοκεῖ: sed additur, οἰκεῖν μετ’ αὐτῇ. Talis enim, quae vult marito fideli cohabitare; etsi non infidelis tantum, & religione, sed etiam moribus discrepans, nec de caetero ad- modum cum voluntate & animo mariti concor- dans, dimittenda non est; quia ad substantiam ma- trimonii consensus cohabitationis, non verò consen- sus animorum & morum facit.

Μὴ ἀφιέτω ἀυτὴν) μὴ ἀποπεμπῃ. Ne ipse prior benè concordans matrimonium dissolvat. Objici potest: At Nehemias conjugia Judæorum cum fœminis alieni cultus dissolvi voluit. Responsum esto: Hoc præceptum datum fuisse soli populo Hebræo Exod. XXXIV. 16. ut qui illo tempore quam longissimè ab aliis populis debebat separari. Aliis populis ea lex non fuit data, nec expediebat eam dari post revelatum mysterium de vocatione gentium.

## 7:13
Vers. 13. And the woman who has an unbelieving husband) He gives equal admonitions to both sexes. An example in the mother of Timothy. And he himself consents to dwell with her, let her not dismiss him) To dismiss (ἀφιέναι) is used here concerning the woman, not by a very harsh catachresis, because even she who leaves (ἡ ἀπολείπουσα) can be said to dismiss (ἀφιέναι). Thus שלח is translated by to dismiss (ἀφιέναι) and to leave (ינח) and others, which have the signification of deserting.

Therefore, the dissolution of marriage is not granted on account of infidelity, which is granted on account of fornication, even if the former is a graver sin than the latter; because fornication by its nature fights against marriage, through which a spouse adheres to a spouse, and they are two in one flesh. Infidelity, however, does not fight against the nature of marriage. For the fornicator, as Theophylact warns, has separated himself. For taking away his members from his wife, he makes them the members of a harlot. The unbeliever, however, has sinned nothing against the carnal union; nay rather, perhaps through it he will be united, and joined even according to the faith. Therefore, Bellarmine falsely asserts that marriage can be dissolved regarding cohabitation on account of subsequent infidelity, if either of the spouses departs from the Catholic faith. That it can also be dissolved on account of prior infidelity, when both spouses are first infidels, and afterwards one is converted to the faith, with whom the other is unwilling to cohabit without injury to the Creator. This opinion is refuted by the Apostle's precept, μὴ ἀφιέτω ἀυτήν. It is refuted by Christ's decision, Matt. XIX. 6. What God has joined, let not man separate; and Luke VI. 32. He who dismisses his wife, except for fornication, commits adultery. Let Blessed Gerhard on marriage §. 665 be consulted. Cornelius admitted here that infidelity in the time of the Apostle was neither an impediment dissolving a marriage contracted with a believer, nor an impediment to contracting or to one already contracted, if there was no danger of perversion for the believer, but the infidel consented to dwell peaceably with the believer, while the believer remained a believer, as the Apostle teaches here. He adds: But now it has been introduced by custom in the Church, that not heresy, but infidelity, not only impedes, but also dissolves a marriage which a believer, while remaining a believer, might wish to contract with an infidel. What is this other than that the Roman Catholic custom is contrary to the Apostolic doctrine? But what if the infidel person attempts to lead the believing spouse to his impiety? Resp. The believer cannot seek a divorce or desert the infidel spouse on account of that danger: Because that danger is not invincible, and therefore there is a different reason for the danger to life, which is inevitable. For someone can be killed corporally by superior force or by treachery; but the soul cannot be seduced, whether by violence or by fraud; provided it constantly adheres to the divine word; and we have remedies prepared against the danger to the soul, not likewise against the danger to the body; and therefore the argument does not proceed: If it is permitted to depart from a violent husband because of snares laid for one's life; much more will it be permitted to depart from him who attempts to destroy the soul. If, however, the spouse attempts to force the spouse to infidelity not only by threats and force; but also if the infidel magistrate exposes one to persecutions, in a safer place the faithful spouse may withdraw; since it seems to be the same thing, whether someone maliciously deserts a spouse, or drives them away by force, threats, and persecutions, and in that case the spouse, as far as in them lies, seems to have broken the marriage bond by their own betrayal. Here, however, one departs not because of the infidelity of the spouse, but because of snares laid for one's life. Nor, however, can one pass to other vows, unless a very long time has intervened, and after reconciliation and secure cohabitation have been attempted in vain by the spouse, and the danger is established as inevitable. It would be safer for the conscience, however, if one can contain oneself, not to pass to other marriages. That Ezra and Nehemiah dismissed their unfaithful wives was done out of spontaneous liberty in honor of the divine law, not out of a legitimate precept of God, notes Blessed Baldwin p. 368, because otherwise the others, Solomon, Booz, Joram, David, etc., would have acknowledged themselves to be obligated.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Καὶ γυνὴ ἥτις ἔχει ἄνδρα ἄπισον) Paria dat mo- nita utrique sexui. Exemplum in matre Timothei. Καὶ ἀυτὸς συνευδοκεῖ οἰκεῖν μετ᾿ ἀυτῆς, μὴ ἀφιέτω ἀυτόν) Ἀφιέναι hic usurpat de muliere, non admodum dura κατα- χρήσει, quia etiam ἡ ἀπολείπουσα potest dici ἀφιέναι. Sic שלח vertitur per ἀφιέναι & ינח & alia, quæ deserendi habent significationem.

Non ergo propter infidelitatem conceditur matrimonii dissolutio, quæ concessa est, propter scortationem, etsi illa gravius peccatum sit, quam hæc; quia scortatio naturâ suâ pugnat cum matri- monio, per quod conjux adhæret conjugi, & sunt duo in carnem unam. Infidelitas autem non pugnat cum natura matrimonii. Fornicator enim, Theo- phylacto monente, seipsum separavit. Auferens enim membra sua ab uxore efficit membra meretri- cis. Infidelis autem nihil in carnalem unionem pec- cavit; imo potius per ipsam fortasse unietur, & con- jungetur etiam secundum fidem. Falso ergò Bel- larminus asserit, conjugium dissolvi posse quoad co- habitationem propter infidelitatem sequentem, si al- teruter conjugum à fide Catholica discedat. Dissol- vi etiam posse propter infidelitatem præcedentem, quando uterque conjux primò infidelis est, & postea alter ad fidem convertitur, cui alter cohabitare nolit sine injuria Creatoris. Quam sententiam profli- gat Apostoli præceptum, μὴ ἀφιέτω ἀυτήν. Profli- gat Christi decisio, Matth. XIX. 6. Quod Deus con- junxit, homo non separet; & Luc. VI. 32. Qui di- miserit uxorem, nisi ob fornicationem, mœchatur. Conferatur B. Gerhardus de conjugio §. 665. Fas- sus hîc fuit Cornelius, infidelitatem tempore Aposto- li nec fuisse impedimentum dirimens matrimonium, cum fideli contractum, nec impediens contrahendum aut contractum, si fideli non erat periculum perver- sionis, sed infidelis consentiret, cum fideli, manente fideli, pacificè habitare, ut hic docet Apostolus. Ad- dit: Jam autem consuetudine inductum est in Eccle- sia, ut non hæresis; sed infidelitas, non tantum impe- diat; sed & dirimat matrimonium, quod fidelis exi- stens fidelis contrahere vellet cum infideli. Quod quid aliud est, quam Romanam Catholicam con- suetudinem contrariam esse Apostolicæ doctrinæ? Quid si autem persona infidelis conetur fidelem con- jugem ad impietatem suam deducere? Resp. fidelis ob periculum illud divortium petere, aut infide- lem conjugem deserere non potest: Quia pericu- lum illud non est invincibile, ideoque est dispar ra- tio periculi vitæ, quod est inevitabile. Nam occi- di aliquis potest corporaliter per vim majorem, aut per insidias; Anima vero seduci non potest, sive per violentiam, sive per fraudulentiam; modò con- stanter adhærescat verbo divino; & parata habe- mus contra animæ periculum remedia, non item contra periculum corporis; Ideoque non proce- dit argumentum: Si propter insidias vitæ structas licet discedere à violento marito; multò magis discedere licebit ab eo, qui animam perdere cona- tur. Si tamen non tantum minis & vi conjux con- jugem ad infidelitatem adigere conetur; sed etiam magistratus infidelis persequutionibus objiciat, in tutiorem locum secedere potest conjux fidelis; cùm perinde videatur, sive aliquis conjugem malitiose deferat, sive vi, minis, & persecutionibus à se abi- gat, atque eo casu conjux, quantum in se est, vin- culum conjugale proditione suâ diremisse videa- tur. Hic verò non ob infidelitatem conjugis, sed ob insidias vitæ structas discedit. Nec tamen ad alia vota transire potest, nisi tempus bene longum intercesserit, ac frustra à conjuge tentata reconci- liatione, & securâ cohabitatione, periculum con- stet inevitabile. Tutius tamen fuerit conscientiæ, si continere sese possit, ad alias nuptias non transire. Quod Esdras, & Nehemias uxores infideles dimi- serunt, ex spontanea libertate in honorem legis di- vinæ factum esse, non ex legitimo præcepto Dei, monet B. Balduinus p. 368. quia alias etiam cæteri Solmon, Booz, Joram, David &c. obligatos sese agnovissent.

## 7:14
Vers. 14. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband) Here the husband and the wife are spoken of metonymically, for the use of the husband or wife, that is, conjugal intimacy. And in the wife, and in the husband, means on account of the Christian woman, on account of the Christian man. In the manuscript, however, for in the husband it is in the brother, according to the custom of Christian spouses, who called each other brothers and sisters. See Tertullian to his wife. What he wishes to say is this: Whoever is a Christian, man or woman, knows the limits of their duty even in that intimacy. See the history of the Christian woman in Justin's Apology. Tertullian II to his wife: Not as if the duties of the sex among the saints, with the honor of the necessity itself, as if under the eyes of God, were transacted modestly and moderately. See Clement of Alexandria, Pedagogue II. 10. The same, Stromata III. Of those who have been sanctified, the seed also is holy. Wherefore, just as food, that is, the use of foods, is sanctified through prayers and thanksgivings, 1 Tim. IV. 5, that is, is pleasing to God: So also is that use of marriage on account of piety, which the better of the spouses observes even in that matter. The reason why Paul wrote these things, Tertullian notes: They feared that it might not be lawful for them to use their marriage, who had believed in the holy flesh of Christ. Among the Hebrews, a wife is said to be sanctified to a husband through a pledge, a writing, and intercourse, that is, to become a legitimate spouse. See Moses of Kotzi, commanding precept 48, and regarding the honesty of women, the Chaldean Paraphrast on Cant. IV. 12.

Else your children are unclean. But now they are holy) Else here is otherwise, as is frequent among the Greeks: And then is redundant. Thus the Syrian and the Latin rightly interpret it here: If you were both idolaters, your children would be unclean, that is, profane, because they would be educated in the worship of idols, which is displeasing to God.

But now they are holy) But now your children are righteous, clean, pleasing to God, because God assists the better part for the education of the children: Of which we have an example in Timothy: And there is no doubt that many others of this kind existed when Paul wrote these things. Tertullian on the soul: For hence also the Apostle says that holy children are procreated from one sanctified sex, as much from the prerogative of the seed as from the discipline of instruction. Otherwise, he says, they would be born unclean, wishing to be understood, however, as if they were designated for holiness, and through this also for the salvation of the children of the faithful, so that by the pledge of this hope, he might patronize the marriages which he had judged should be retained. The same to his wife II. If therefore such a marriage is valid before God, why should it not also turn out prosperously, so that it is not so harassed by pressures, and straits, and impediments, and defilements, having already from the divine side the patronage of grace? Jerome also, to the Pauline questions, understands that children are called holy for the reason that they are candidates for the faith, born and educated outside the defilements of idolatry. The same to Laeta: A holy and faithful house sanctifies the unbeliever. He is already a candidate for the faith, whom a believing crowd of children and grandchildren surrounds: That is, concerning such a man, there is reason to hope well.

The unbeliever is therefore said to be sanctified through marriage with a believer, not as regards the person, who is not sanctified except by faith; but as regards the use, and conjugal intimacy, which is sanctified through the prayers of the believing spouse. Others say that he is sanctified, not as regards internal holiness, which is nothing without faith; but as regards a certain external holiness, by which they are said to be sanctified, because they are not unclean, but clean, lawful, and approved by God. But because the holiness of renewal, and internal, is not of anything but a person, whereas the external is not of a person, but of the marriage, the former distinction is more convenient. The latter, however, is more aptly applied to the holiness of children, which here is not internal, or of faith, or federal, as the Calvinists please. For this is not from generation, but from regeneration: But external, or of the communion of sacraments, and access to the privileges of the Church; which some call ecclesiastical holiness, others political: But it is not properly ecclesiastical, because the privilege of access to the Church does not yet make one a citizen of the Church; nor political, because it does not arise from civil society, nor does it concern civil benefits, which have no holiness. That holiness, however, is merely relative, and is so called only according to an external denomination; concerning which Blessed Baldwin has it thus: Since the holiness of children born of the faithful is to be understood as neither merely civil, nor merely ecclesiastical or spiritual, we interpret the passage as concerning an intermediate holiness, which we can call Levitical or legal, that is, concerning that right and power of obtaining the privileges of the citizens of the Church. For just as not anyone among the people of God could perform sacred rites in the temple or tabernacle, but only the Levites, who according to the law were sanctified by certain ceremonies, 1 Chron. 15:14. And just as not all vessels were called holy, but those which were applied to sacred things and for this were sanctified by certain rites, while the others were unclean: So not all indiscriminately are to be admitted to Baptism and the benefits annexed to it, but those who are born of citizens of the Church, or faithful parents. These, therefore, are holy, because they have access to the privileges of the Church, which are not granted to others who are outside. For which reason Tertullian named such holy ones candidates for the faith, in his book on monogamy, and Augustine interprets this holiness, of which the Apostle speaks, not as the holiness of faith, but as the communion of the Sacraments and a similarity of profession, Epist. 106. But this access and that privilege does not yet make one a citizen of the Church or a partaker of the covenant of God, but this benefit is finally obtained in baptism. Others say that the unbelieving husband is sanctified by a certain denomination and a certain as it were sprinkling of holiness (which was also Anselm's formula). It certainly cannot be denied that that sanctification of the unbelieving spouse can be extended to the person in a certain way, because it brings about some communion of ecclesiastical goods, such as: mutual communication regarding divine things, the prayer or intercession of the faithful party before God for the unbelieving one, the calling back of the unbelieving party from the purpose of sinning, and others of that kind, which are not given among unbelievers alone outside of association with the faithful. Cf. 1 Pet. 3:11, 12. For the discussion here is about a communion of such holiness as depends upon marital association, as Chrysostom teaches; and which faithful and unbelieving spouses commonly and ordinarily have between themselves. Whence these things are rashly snatched away by Calvin, Beza, Pareus, and others to the natural or original holiness of children born of faithful parents.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἡγίασται γὰρ ὁ ἀνὴρ ὁ ἄπιστος ἐν τῇ γυναικὶ, καὶ ἡγίασται ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄπιστος ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ) Hic ὁ ἀνὴρ & ἡ γυνὴ dicuntur μετωνυμικῶς, pro usu viri aut uxoris, id est, con- suetudine conjugali. Et ἐν τῇ γυναικὶ, & ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ, valet propter mulierem Christianam, propter virum Christia- num. In Manuscripto verò pro τῷ ἀνδρὶ est ἀδελφῷ, ex more Christianorum conjugum, qui se mutuo fratres & so- rores vocabant. Vide Tertullianum ad uxorem. Quod vult dicere, hoc est: Qui Christianus est, quæve Christia- na, novit etiam in consuetudine illa officii sui limites. Vi- de historiam de fœmina Christiana apud Justinum Apolo- getico. Tertullianus II. ad uxorem: Non ut penes sanctos officia sexus, cum honore ipsius necessitatis, tanquam sub oculis Dei, modeste, & moderate transigantur. Vide Clementem Alexandrinum pædagogi II. 10. Idem Stromat. III. Τῶν ἁγιασθέντων ἅγιον καὶ τὸ σπέρμα. Quare sicut cibus, id est, ciborum usus, sanctificatur per preces & gratiarum actio- nes, 1. Tim. IV. 5. hoc est, Deo gratus est: Ita & ille con- jugii usus propter pietatem, quam etiam in ea re conjugum melior observat. Causam, cur hæc scripserit Paulus, Ter- tullianus annotat: Verebantur, ne non liceret eis matrimonio suo uti, qui in carnem sanctam Christi credidissent. Apud He- bræos dicitur uxor viro sanctificari per arrham, scripturam, concubitum, id est, fieri legitima conjux. Vide Mosen de Kotzi præcepto jubente 48. & de honestate fœminarum Pa- raphrasten Chaldæum ad Cant. IV. 12.

Ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτά ἐστι. Νῦν δὲ ἁγιά ἐστιν) Ἐπεὶ hic est alioqui, ut apud Græcos sæpius: Et ἄρα πλεο- νάζον. Ita rectè hic interpretantur & Syrus, & Latinus: Si uterque essetis Idololatræ, liberi vestri essent immundi, id est, פסולים profani, quia educarentur in cultum idolo- rum Deo displicentem.

Νῦν δὲ ἁγιά ἐστι) Jam verò liberi vestri sunt כשרים recti, mundi, Deo grati, quia Deus ad educationem libe- rum opitulatur parti meliori: Cujus exemplum habemus in Timotheo: Et haud dubium, quin multa extiterint alia hujusmodi, cum hæc Paulus scriberet. Tertullianus de anima: Hinc enim & Apostolus ex sanctificato altero sexu sanctos procreari ait, tam ex seminis prærogativa, quam ex in- stitutionis disciplina. Cæterum, inquit, immundi nascerentur, quasi designatos tamen sanctitati, & per hoc etiam saluti intel- ligi volens fidelium filios, ut hujus spei pignore, matrimoniis, quæ retinenda censuerat, patrocinaretur. Idem ad uxorem II. Si ergo ratum est apud Deum matrimonium ejusmodi, cur non & prosperè cedat, ut pressuris, & angustiis, & impedimentis, & inquinamentis non ita lacessatur, habens jam ex parte divina gratiæ patrocinium? Hieronymus quoque ad quæsita Pau- lina intelligit Sanctos dici liberos ideo, quod Candidati sint fidei, nati & educati extra inquinamenta idololatriæ. Idem ad Lætam: Sancta & fidelis domus utrum sanctificat infidelem. Jam Candidatus est fidei, quem filiorum & nepo- tum credens turba circumdat: Id est, de tali viro est, cur be- nè speretur.

Sanctificari ergò ἄπιστος dicitur per conju- gium cum fideli, non quoad personam, quæ non- nisi fide sanctificatur; sed quoad usum, & conju- galem consuetudinem, quæ sanctificatur per preces fidelis conjugis. Alii dicunt, ipsum sanctificari, non quoad sanctitatem internam, quæ nulla est si- ne fide; sed quoad externam quandam sanctita- tem, qua sanctificata dicuntur, quod non immun- da sint, sed munda, licita, & Deo probata. Sed quia sanctitas renovationis, & interna, non est, nisi personæ, externa autem non persona est, sed conjugii, prior distinctio commodior est. Poste- rior autem aptius applicatur liberorum sanctitati, quæ hic non est interna, vel fidei, vel fœderalis, ut Calvinianis placet. Hæc enim non ex generatio- ne, sed regeneratione est: Sed externa, vel com- munionis sacramentorum, & aditus ad privilegia Ecclesiæ; quam nonnulli Ecclesiasticam sanctita- tem vocant, alii politicam: Sed nec Ecclesiastica propriè est, quia privilegium aditus ad Ecclesiam nondum facit civem Ecclesiæ; nec politica, quia non oritur è societate civili, nec civilia beneficia concernit, quæ nihil sanctitatis habent. Sancti- tas autem illa est merè relativa, & secundum ex- ternam tantum denominationem ita vocatur; de qua B. Balduinus ita habet: Cum neque de merè civili, neque de merè Ecclesiastica, vel spirituali sanctitate intelligenda sit sanctitas liberorum, ex fidelibus prognatorum, nos locum de intermediâ sanctitate interpretamur, quam Leviticam, seu legalem appellare possumus, hoc est, de jure isto, & potestate consequendi privilegia civium Eccle- siæ. Quemadmodum enim non quilibet in po- pulo Dei sacra facere in templo, vel tabernaculo poterat; sed Levitæ saltem, qui juxta legem cer- tis ceremoniis sanctificabantur, 1. Paralip. XV. vers. 14. Et quemadmodum non omnia vasa di- cebantur sancta, sed quæ ad res sacras adhibeban- tur, & ad hoc certis ritibus sanctificabantur, cæ- tera immunda erant: Ita non omnes promiscuè admittendi sunt ad Baptismum, & ei adjuncta be- neficia, sed qui ex civibus Ecclesiæ, seu fidelibus parentibus nati sunt. Hi ergò sancti sunt, quia habent aditum ad privilegia Ecclesiæ, quæ aliis, qui foris sunt, non conceduntur. Quam ob cau- sam Tertullianus ejusmodi sanctos fidei Candida- tos nominavit, libro de monogamia, & Augusti- nus hanc sanctitatem, de qua Apostolus loquitur, non de sanctitate fidei; sed de communione Sacra- mentorum, & similitudine professionis interpreta- tur, Epist. 106. Hic verò aditus, & privilegium illud nondum facit civem Ecclesiæ, aut fœderis Dei consortem, sed hoc beneficium demum in baptismo impetratur. Alii dicunt, infidelem maritum qua- dam denominatione, & quadam quasi sanctitatis aspergine (quæ etiam Anshelmi fuit formula) in- de sanctificari. Non sanè negari potest, illam etiam conjugis infidelis sanctificationem ad per- sonam certâ ratione extendi posse, quod aliquam inferat bonorum Ecclesiasticorum communio- nem, qualia sunt: mutua communicatio de rebus divinis, precatio seu intercessio apud Deum partis fi- delis pro infideli, revocatio partis infidelis à propo- sito peccandi, & alia ejus generis, quæ extra con- versationem cum fidelibus inter solos infideles non dantur. Conf. 1. Pet. III. 11. 12. Agitur enim hic de communione talis sanctitatis, quæ è con- suetudine conjugali dependet, ut Chrysostomus docet; & quam fidelis & infidelis conjuges inter se communiter & ordinariè habent. Unde te- merè hæc à Calvino, Beza, Pareo, aliisque abri- piuntur ad sanctitatem liberorum, à fidelibus pa- rentibus prognatorum, naturalem, vel origi- nariam.

## 7:15
Vers. 15. Εἰ δὲ ὁ ἄπιστος χωρίζεται) If he withdraws himself, that is, if the pagan party dissolves the marriage. χωρίζεται is said here of both spouses. The passive for the reciprocal.

χωριζέσθω) Let him be allowed to do what he wants. An idolater is like an adulterer: Hermas II. 4.

Οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις) He is not obligated to remain unmarried and to await or procure reconciliation. The law of Christ and of Christian discipline deals with those who are fellow-members: those whom a closer bond connects, and among whom, if anything has gone astray, healing is easy through the authority of the Church. See what we have said at Matt. V. Every obligation is similar to servitude, and therefore it takes that name from a neighbor.

God has called us in peace,) that is, to peace, so that we may preserve peace even with pagans, as far as it is possible. See Rom. XII. 18. We have been called to this, that is, this is our duty.

But the bond of marriage is not dissolved, except through malicious desertion. But whether that separation is to be considered a malicious and stubborn desertion or not, that must finally be tested through an attempt at reconciliation. Nor does that law, that what God has joined, let no man separate, concern only those who are partners in Christian discipline: For it must be believed that God has joined even infidels, whether they were such before the union, or finally failed in the marriage. Meanwhile, we easily admit that the party who is deserted is not bound to perpetual celibacy, and that this is the meaning of the Apostle's words. But if the deserting party cannot be reconciled, the innocent party is finally absolved, even from the bond, if indeed the infidel cannot be brought to cohabit, then the believer is not tied to the deserting infidel party, but is free, not for the reason that idolatry is like adultery, and idolatry is a kind of fornication; but because the infidel has broken the faith of marriage, and has deserted the believing spouse. Therefore, the Apostle's Rule applies not only to idolaters, but to any malicious deserters, by parity of reason. Because desertion is a violation of the bond, and thus removes marriage as to its substance, of whose essence it is to adhere to one's spouse, and to be one flesh with the spouse. But that Christ in Matt. V. 32 assigns only one cause for divorce, namely fornication, is because he is dealing with divorce, to be made by the innocent party for a just cause, as Gerhard teaches with the blessed Chemnitz and Menzer §. 607. concerning marriage, but Paul here speaks of divorce, rashly and unjustly made by the guilty party. When it is asked, for what cause a spouse may repudiate a spouse, it is rightly answered that it is permitted solely on account of adultery: For from that the Pharisees were asking, whether it is permitted to dismiss a wife for any cause whatsoever? But here it was asked, whether divorce should be made on account of infidelity? Which, just as the Apostle denies, so a doubt arose, what then should be done if the infidel does not wish to cohabit, but separates himself? The Apostle answers that the party unjustly deserted is not to be held under servitude on account of the infidel's illegitimate act. Therefore, it is not a question of the causes for making a divorce: but, the divorce having been made illegitimately, the conscience of the innocent person is here consulted. The infidel departs, let him depart. A brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such a case. What that servitude is, appears from the servitude of the deserting party, verse 11. Let not a wife depart from her husband; but if she has departed, let her remain unmarried. Therefore, the innocent party is not held by the servitude or duty of not entering into another marriage, by which the deserting party is held: Which servitude is called a bond in verse 39, and subjection, Rom. VII. 2. And although desertion is not adultery, yet in those who are not innocent it is equated by the Apostle to adultery, both because of the presumption of adultery in the deserter; and because of the danger of adultery in the deserted party; to which also the stubborn and incorrigible denial of the conjugal debt is not unlike, and implacable cruelty; because they stubbornly and incorrigibly injure the conjugal faith and the use of the marriage bed, whence also these, after the observed degrees of separation from bed and board, finally dissolve the bond itself. But what some Papists argue in Henriquez, lib. II. de matrim. c. 8. from verse 11. and 12. that a believer, whose infidel spouse does not wish to be converted, although he wishes to cohabit with the believer without insult to the Creator, has by this very fact the right of entering into another marriage, that Henriquez himself acknowledges to be contrary to Paul. Sanchez also says that the Church now everywhere forbids a believer to remain with an infidel. But Navarrus and others deny this. See Cornel. a Lapide on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Εἰ δὲ ὁ ἄπιστος χωρίζεται) Si se subtrahit, id est, dirimit conjugium pars pagana. χωρίζεται hîc de utroque conjuge dicitur. Passivum pro reciproco.

χωριζέσθω) Sinatur facere, quod vult. Idololatra mœ- cho similis: Hermas II. 4.

Οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις) Non obligatur, ut cælebs maneat, & reconciliationem expe- ctet, aut procuret.
