Lex Christi & Christianæ disciplinæ confortibus agit: Quos propius vinculum nectit, & apud quos, si quid aberratum est, facilis est sanatio per Eccle- siæ autoritatem. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. V. Omnis obligatio servituti est similis, & ideo ex vicino id nomen arripit.

Ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς,) id est, εἰς εἰρήνην, ut pacem servemus etiam cum paganis, quoad fieri potest. Vide Rom. XII. 18. In id vocati sumus, id est, hoc est offi- cii nostri.

At conjugii vinculum non solvitur, nisi per malitiosam desertionem. An vero separatio illa pro malitiosa & pertinaci desertione habenda sit, necne, id demum per reconciliationis tentationem experiri oportet. Neque lex illa, quod Deus con- junxit, homo ne separet, Christianæ tantum disci- plinæ consortes concernit: Nam & infideles Deum conjunxisse credendum est, seu ante conjunctio- nem tales fuerint, seu in conjugio demum defe- cerint. Interim non obligari eam partem, quæ deseritur, ad cælibatum perpetuum, eumque ver- borum Apostoli sensum esse, facile admittimus. Sed si reconciliari nequeat pars deserens, inno- cens pars tandem absolvitur, etiam à vinculo, si nempe infidelis eò adduci nequeat, ut cohabitet, tum fidelis non est parti deserenti infideli alligata, sed libera, non ex ea causa, quod idololatria moecho similis, & idololatria fornicatio quædam sit; sed quod infidelis fidem conjugii fregerit, & fidelem conjugem deseruerit. Ideo non tantum idolo- latris, sed in quibusvis malitiosis desertoribus, ex paritate causæ, militat Apostoli Regula. Quia desertio est violatio vinculi, adeoque tollit quoad substantiam matrimonium, de cujus essentia est adhærere conjugi, & esse cum conjuge in carnem unam. Quod autem Christus Matth. V. 32. uni- cam causam tantum divortii assignat τὴν πορνείαν, inde est, quod de divortio agat, à parte innocente ex justa causa faciendo, ut cum B. Chemnitio, & Menzero Gerhardus §. 607. de conjugio docet, Paulus verò hic de divortio loquatur, à parte no- centi temerariè & injustè facto. Cum quæritur, ob quam causam conjux repudiare possit conjugem, re- cte respondetur, id unicè propter adulterium li- cere: Ex eo enim quærebant Pharisæi, an ex qua- cunque causa liceat uxorem dimittere? At hic quæ- rebatur, an ob infidelitatem faciendum sit divor- tium? Quod uti negat Apostolus; ita dubium oriebatur, quid tum faciendum, si infidelis coha- bitare nolit; sed se separet? Respondet Aposto- lus, partem injustè desertam non esse sub servitute detinendam propter illegitimum infidelis factum. Non ergò de causis faciendi divortii agitur: sed, facto illegitimo divortio, personæ innocentis con- scientiæ hic consulitur. Infidelis discedit, disce- dat. Non est servituti subjectus frater aut soror hujusmodi. Servitus illa qualis sit, è servitute partis deserentis apparet, vers. 11. Uxor à viro non discedat; quod si discesserit, maneat innupta. Pars ergo innocens servitute vel debito non in- eundi alterius conjugii non tenetur, quo tenetur pars deserens: Quæ servitus δεσμὸς vocatur v. 39. & subjectio, Rom. VII. 2. Etsi autem desertio adul- terium non sit, in non innocentibus tamen ab Apostolo æquiparatur adulterio, tum ob præ- sumptionem adulterii in desertore; tum ob peri- culum adulterii in parte deserta; Cui etiam non absimilis est pertinax & incorrigibilis debiti conju- galis denegatio, & sævitia implacabilis; ed quod fidem conjugalem, & usum doria talia pervicaci- ter, & incorrigibiliter lædant, unde & illa post observatos gradus separationis à mensa & thoro ipsum tandem vinculum dirimunt. Quod verò Papistæ nonnulli apud Henriquez. lib. II. de ma- trim. c. 8. disputant è vers. 11. & 12. fidelem, cujus conjux infidelis non vult converti, licet sine contume- lia Creatoris velit fideli cohabitare, hoc ipso jus ha- bere ineundi aliud matrimonium, id Henriquez ipse Paulo contrarium esse agnoscit. Sanchez etiam Ecclesiam ait jam passim vetare, ne maneat fidelis cum infideli. Sed id negant Navarrus & alii. Vi- de Cornel. à Lapide ad hunc locum.

## 7:16
Vers. 16. For what do you know, O wife, whether you will save your husband, or what do you know, O husband, whether you will save your wife?) This pertains to that which was said above 12. 13. 14. For that 15 was only inserted as a parenthesis. We had a similar one above 6. and elsewhere. But he does not say this in vain, because there were examples of husbands gained by wives, and wives by husbands, which would give good hope. For the holy conversation of a husband or wife had great power over souls. They are said to save one another who lead them to Christ, below IX. 21. 1 Tim. IV. 16. Jas. V. 20. Thus Joseph the son of Jacob, thus Moses transferred their own wives to their own piety, says the writer of the responses to the orthodox in response X. Clement Strom. IV. A wise woman would choose, first of all, to persuade her husband to become a partner with her in those things that lead to happiness. But if she should be unable, let her alone hasten toward virtue, obeying her husband in all things, so that she may never be heard to do anything against him, except for those things which are considered to pertain to virtue and salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Τί γὰρ οἶδας γύναι εἰ τὸν ἄνδρα σώσεις, ἢ τί οἶδας ἄνερ εἰ τὴν γυναῖκα σώσεις;) Pertinet hoc ad id, quod di- ctum supra 12. 13. 14. Nam illud 15. per παρενθήκην tan- tum interjectum fuit. Simile habuimus supra 6. & alibi. Non frustra autem hoc dicit, quia lucrifactorum per inu- lieres virorum, & mulierum per viros, erant exempla, quæ bonam spem facerent. Magnam enim vim habebat in ani- mos sancta viri aut mulieris conversatio. Σώζειν dicun- tur alii alios quos ad Christum perducunt infra IX. 21. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Jac. V. 20. Sic Josephus Jacobi filius, sic Moses τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας εἰς τὴν ἑαυτῶν μετέφερον εὐσέβειαν, ait scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos responsione X. Clemens Strom. IV. Ἐλοιτ’ ἂν ἐν ἡ σώφρων, πρῶτον μὲν πεί- θειν τὸν ἄνδρα κοινωνὸν ἁυτῇ γίνεσθαι τῶν πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν φε- ρόντων. Εἰ δ᾽ ἀδυνάτως ἔχοι, μόνη σπευδέτω ἐπ᾽ ἀρετὴν, πάν- τα μὲν τῷ ἀνδρὶ πειθομένη, ὡς μηδὲν ἀκούσῃ ἐκείνῳ πρᾶξαί ποτε, πλὴν ὅσα ἐπ᾽ ἀρετήν τε, καὶ σωτηρίαν διαφέρειν νομί- ζεται.

## 7:17
Vers. 17. But as God has distributed to each one, as the Lord has called each one, so let him walk) That indeed, which I said, you do not know; but this you ought to know, that such things do not stand in the way of salvation. Eminent men have noted that 'unless' is put for 'but'. Such is that Plautine phrase: And of children, unless riches, there was nothing. That is, he had no children, but there were riches. See Gal. I. 7. and II. 16. Then indeed in inverted order 'as' is placed twice here, just as also above III. 5. and in the Manuscript it is: To each as the Lord has distributed. God is said to distribute, when he assigns to someone some lot of birth, fortune, or marriage. But he adds well, as God has called each one, explaining that 'distributed'. From the time God called you to the Gospel, and you, of course, obeyed the caller, from that time he bears a fatherly and special care for you. But if he had thought it harmful to your salvation to live with a pagan, to be born from an Israelite or a pagan, to be by status free or a slave, he would have dispensed those things otherwise. Now, since he has not dispensed them otherwise, conclude from that that nothing of this stands in the way of your salvation, so that, indeed,

— — whatever lot, whether reason has given it to you or chance has cast it your way, live content with it.

Περιπατεῖν here, as הלך is among the Hebrews, is to persist in a way of life or practice. They are mistaken who think that a transposition was made here by the copyists against Paul's intention. It is Paul's custom to interject certain things in passing that are not foreign to the subject, and then to resume the discourse he had begun. And so, from the occasion of those things which he had said about unequal marriage, he enters upon a common topic concerning the various conditions of this life, which stand in no way in the path of salvation. He returns, however, to the subject at verse 25.

Some, even among our own, understand the question negatively, concerning the doubtful and uncertain conversion of an unbelieving spouse, so that this verse is a second reason why the separation of the unbelieving party should be patiently tolerated by the believing party, namely because the believing party has been called to peace, not to contradiction, verse 15; furthermore, because the conversion of the unbelieving party is not a matter of human power, but of divine. Εἰ μὴ UNLESS God has granted this success, according to the diverse distribution of grace which He has distributed to each: both for patiently tolerating adverse things and for converting unbelievers. But most explain it affirmatively: What do you know, whether perhaps you will convert and save your spouse? That this phrase, who knows, has the force among the Hebrews of making the affirmative part of the interrogation hopeful, is shown from Joel II, Jonah III. 2, 2 Samuel XII. Estius urges Eccl. III, and admits that most, both Greeks and Latins, understand it in this way: that a new reason is provided for not separating oneself from an unbelieving spouse. For the first was from the external sanctification of the unbeliever, as long as he wishes to cohabit with the believer, v. 14, because not only is that marriage not unclean, inasmuch as it is sanctified through the prayers of a faithful spouse; but also the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through cohabitation with the faithful one, since he becomes a participant in sacred discourses, and can be stirred by the example of holy conversation, and thus can enjoy a certain external communion of the benefits which are held in the Church alone. The second is from the divine calling to peace. For since the unbelieving spouse wishes to cohabit, the faithful one is not to provide a cause for separation, but to foster harmony. The third is taken from the possible conversion of the unbelieving spouse. For who knows whether the unbelieving spouse might be converted to the faith by divine grace through cohabitation with the faithful one? Except that (this is the ordinary sense of the particle εἰ μὴ, 1. Cor. II. 2. 11. chap. IIX. 4. chap. X. 1. chap. XII. 3.) God has distributed to each: What do you know about the conversion of a spouse, through your prayers, exhortations, and holy conversation, except this, that God distributes grace to each as He wills; where, however, there is also an opposing sense, and εἰ μὴ can have the place of ἀλλὰ, as if he were saying: You are not indeed certain of this, that you are going to save your spouse; which, however, could entirely happen. But you ought to know this, that God distributes grace to each, as if by measure, according to His pleasure; whence He can also distribute the same grace to you, so that the unbelieving spouse may be saved through you. Which sense B. Luther renders in the explanation of this chapter, Tom. II. Jen. Germ. fol. 311. Since you do not know whether GOD wishes to save them through you or not, you should have peace with them, and no husband should urge his unchristian wife, or quarrel with her for the sake of faith, nor a wife with her unchristian husband. But if GOD wishes to convert them through you, He will help you, and distribute grace and gifts among you thereafter, which serve for this purpose. This seems to me to be the right understanding of St. Paul in this place, that he does not want anyone to be forced to faith or piety, but to live peacefully with everyone, until GOD through us with His grace converts whom He wishes to convert, as St. Peter also teaches 1. Petr. II. Others render εἰ μὴ as 'what if not'. Erasmus explains it as 'however it may be', etc. See Estius on this place.

And so in all the churches I ordain) I burden you with nothing more than the others. I teach the same things everywhere, both precepts and admonitions.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Εἰ μὴ ἑκάστῳ ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἑκαστοι ὡς κέκλη- κεν ὁ Κύριος, ὕτω περιπατείτω) Illud quidem, quod dixi, non scis; sed hoc debes scire, talia non obstare saluti. Εἰ μὴ pro ἀλλὰ poni notarunt viri egregii. Tale est Plauti- num illud: Et liberorum, nisi divitia, nihil erat. Id est, nihil ei erat liberorum, sed erant divitiæ. Vide Gal. I. 7. & II. 16. Tum vero inverso ordine bis hic ὡς positum, quomodo & supra III. 5. & in Manuscripto est: Ἑκάσῳ ὡς ὁ Κύριος ἐμέρισεν. חלק id est μερίζειν dicitur Deus, cum alicui sortem aliquam assignat natalium, fortunæ, conjugii. Bene autem addit, ut quemque vocavit Deus, explicans illud ἐμέρισεν. Ex quo Deus te vocavit ad Evangelium, & tu scilicet vocanti paruisti, ex eo paternam & peculiarem tui gestat curam. Quod si putasset saluti tuæ esse noxium, vivere cum pagano, natum esse ex Israelita aut pagano, sta- tu liberum esse aut servum, aliter ea dispensasset. Nunc cum non aliter dispensaverit, inde collige, nihil hoc saluti tuæ obstare, ut nimirum,

— — quam tibi sortem, Seu ratio dederit, seu fors objecerit, illà Contentus vivas.

Περιπατεῖν hic, ut הלך apud Hebræos est vitæ genus sive institutum insistere. Errant, qui putant ab exscriptoribus hîc transpositionem factam contra Pauli mentem. Mos est Pauli, obiter quædam à re non aliena interjicere, ac de- inde cœptum sermonem repetere. Itaque ex occasione eorum, quæ de conjugio dispari dixerat, locum ingreditur communem, de variis hujus vitæ conditionibus, quæ sa- luti nihil obstent. Redit verò ad propositum comma- te 25.

Nonnulli, etiam è nostris, negativè quæstionem intelligunt, de dubia & incerta conversione con- jugis infidelis, ita, ut hic versus sit ratio altera, ob quam separatio partis infidelis patienter tole- randa sit à parte fideli, quia nempe ad pacem, non ad contradictionem vocata sit pars fidelis vers. 15. deinde, quia partis infidelis conversio non sit res humanæ opis, sed divinæ. Εἰ μὴ NISI Deus hunc successum largitus fuerit, pro diversa parti- tione gratiæ, quam cuique partitus est: cum ad res adversas patienter tolerandas, tum ad infideles convertendos. Sed affirmativè plerique expli- cant: Quid scis, annon fortè convertes & salvabis conjugem? Quam vim habere phrasin, quis scit, apud Hebræos, ut sperabilem faciat affirmantem interrogationis partem, è Joel. II. Jon. III. 2. Sa- mvel. XII. Eccl. III. urget Estius, atque ita plerosque tam Græcos, quam Latinos intelligere, fatetur: Ut nova ratio non separandi se à conjuge infideli tra- datur. Prima enim erat ab infidelis externa san- ctificatione, quousque cohabitare vult fideli, v. 14. quod non tantum conjugium illud non sit immun- dum, utpote per preces fidelis conjugis sanctifi- catum; sed etiam sanctificetur conjux infidelis per cohabitationem fideli, quum consors fiat sacro- rum sermonum, & excitari exemplo sanctae con- versationis, adeoque externa quadam communio- ne beneficiorum, quae in Ecclesia sola habentur, frui possit. Altera est, à divina ad pacem vocatio- ne. Cum enim conjux infidelis cohabitare velit, fidelis est, non causam praebere separationi, sed concordiam fovere. Tertia ab infidelis conjugis possibili conversione desumpta est. Quis enim scit, anne conjux infidelis divina gratia per cohabitatio- nem cum fideli ad fidem converti possit? Nisi quod (hic est ordinarius particulae εἰ μὴ sensus, 1. Cor. II. 2. 11. cap. IIX. 4. cap. X. 1. cap. XII. 3.) Deus unicuique partitus est: Quid scis de conversione conjugis, per tuas preces, cohortationes & san- ctam conversationem, nisi hoc, quod Deus gratiam cuique distribuit, prout vult; ubi tamen etiam ad- versarius sensus est, & εἰ μὴ pro ἀλλὰ locum ha- bere potest, quasi dicat: Id certus quidem non es, quod tu salvaturus sis conjugem; quod verò fieri omnind posset. Sed id tamen scire debes, quod dis- tribuat Deus cuique gratiam, veluti ad mensuram, ex placito; Unde & tibi potest eandem distribue- re gratiam, ut salvari per te possit conjux infide- lis. Quem sensum reddit B. Lutherus in expli- catione hujus capitis Tom. II. Jen. Germ. fol. 311. Weil ihr denn nicht wisset, ob GOTT durch euch sie will selig machen oder nicht, so sollet ihr Friede mit ihnen haben, und kein Mann sein unchristlich Weib dringen, oder mit ihr zancken umbs Glau- bens willen, noch ein Weib mit ihrem unchristli- chen Mann. Will sie aber GOTT durch euch bekehren, so wird Er euch helffen, und Gnade und Gaben darnach unter euch austheilen, die darzu dienen. Diss düncket mich der rechte Verstand seyn St. Pauli an diesem Orte, dass er will nieman- den zum Glauben oder Frömmigkeit gezwungen haben, sondern friedlich mit jedermann leben, biss dass GOTT durch uns mit seiner Gnade bekehre, welche er bekehren will, wie auch St. Petrus lehret 1. Petr. II. Alii εἰ μὴ reddunt, quod si non. Era- smus exponit, utcunque fuerit &c. Vid. Estius in hunc locum.

Καὶ ὕτως ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις πάσαις διατάσσομαι) Nihi- lo plus vos, quam caeteros onero. Paria doceo ubique tum praecepta, tùm monita.

## 7:18
V. 18. Was anyone called while circumcised?) Was anyone called to the faith when he had been circumcised by his parents, in the Jewish manner.

Let him not draw it over) 'the foreskin' is understood. אל ימשך ערלה let him not cover the glans by extending the skin: For thus Celsus speaks. VII. 27. Josephus calls it 'to cover the circumcision'. Some did this out of hatred for Judaism, concerning which we spoke 1. Maccab. I. 17. He by whom this was done was called a 'spaster', according to Epiphanius.

Was anyone called in uncircumcision?) Born, of course, from the Gentiles. Ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ, that is, having uncircumcision, as Rom. IV. 10.

Let him not be circumcised) There is no reason for you to take up a burden not imposed by GOD. For you are not from the descendants of Abraham.

Latin:

V. 18. Περιτετμημένος τις ἐκλήθη) Vocatus quis est ad fidem, cum à parentibus esset circumcisus, more Judaico.

Μὴ ἐπισπάσθω) subauditur τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν. אל ימשך ערלה ne glandem tegat, cutem extendendo: Ita enim loquitur Celsus. VII. 27. Josephus id vocat τὴν περιτομὴν ἐπικαλύπτειν. Faciebant hoc quidam odio Judaismi, qua de re diximus 1. Maccab. I. 17. quo id fiebat, spaster dice- batur, teste Epiphanio.

Ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ τις ἐκλήθη) Natus scilicet ex gentibus. Ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ, id est, ἀκροβυστίαν ἔχων, ut Rom. IV. 10.

Μὴ περιτεμνέσθω) Non est, quod suscipias onus à DEO non impositum. Neque enim es ex Abrahami posteris.

## 7:19
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing) It is nothing, that is, it is of no moment, in the business of salvation, with which we are dealing here.

But the keeping of the commandments of God) Supply: has the greatest moment. From this place, compared with that which is in Gal. V. 6. & VI. 15., we learn that it comes to the same thing, whether you say the observation of the commandments of GOD (namely in the Gospel), or faith which works through love, or a new creature. The first expression signifies the thing, the second assigns parts to that thing, the third indicates the primary cause. Since, therefore, salvation depends on this thing, let us refer all our efforts to this.

Although it hinders salvation in no way to have been born of Jews and to have received circumcision, or from pagans and in uncircumcision, provided one is converted to the faith: yet those things from which our salvation depends are not explained here. Much less, in the Grotius sense, is the observation of the commandments of God either prescribed in the Gospel or does it contribute to obtaining salvation, in such a way that eternal salvation depends both on faith and on love. For this is diametrically opposed to Apostolic doctrine. It is one thing to be valid and to have great moment, just as piety is said to be useful for all things 1. Timoth. IV. 8., but it is another thing to be valid for obtaining or acquiring eternal salvation. Piety and religion do not consist in circumcision or in uncircumcision, but in the obedience of the heart, which can exist in any state. But the observation of the commandments of GOD is pleasing to GOD, only through faith, Heb. XI. 6., not because it is perfect, but because it proceeds from faith, which is the apprehension of the perfect obedience of Christ.

Latin:

Ἡ περιτομὴ ὀὐδέν ἐστι, καὶἡ ἀκροβυστία ὀὐδέν ἐστι) Οὐδέν ἐστι, id est, nullius est momenti, in salutis negotio, de quo hic agimus.

Ἀλλὰ τήρησις ἐντολῶν θεῶ) Supple momentum habet maximum. Ex hoc loco collato cum eo, qui est Gal. V. 6. & VI. 15. discimus in idem recidere, sive dicas observa- tionem praeceptorum DEI (nempe in Evangelio) sive fidem, quae per dilectionem operatur, sive novam crea- turam. Prima loquutio rem significat, secunda partes ei rei assignat, tertia causam primariam indicat. Quando igitur ab hac re pendet salus, ad hanc studia omnia nostra referamus.

Etsi saluti nihil officiat, natum esse à Judaeis, ac circumcisionem suscepisse, aut è paganis & in praeputio, dummodo conversus quis sit ad fidem: Non tamen hic explicantur ea, unde salus nostra pendeat? Nedum, Grotiano sensu, vel in Evangelio præscribitur, vel ad salutem consequendam facit observatio præceptorum Dei, ita, ut tùm à fide, tùm à dilectione pendeat salus æterna. Hoc enim doctrinæ Apostolicæ καδδιάμετρον adversatur. A- liud est valere, ac momentum magnum habere, uti pietas ad omnia utilis esse dicitur 1. Timoth. IV. 8. aliud verò valere ad salutem æternam obtinendam vel impetrandam. Non consistit pietas & religio in circumcisione, vel in præputio, sed in cordis ob- sequio, quod in quo libet statu esse potest. Grata autem est DEO observatio mandatorum DEI, non nisi per fidem, Ebr. XI. 6. non quod illa perfecta sit, sed quod ex fide, quæ est apprehensio perfectæ obedientiæ Christi, proficiscatur.

## 7:20
V. 20. Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called) This is a paronomasia. For κλῆσις signifies one thing, and ἐκλήθη another. Κλῆσις is an appellation, that is, the condition of a man, from which he is called a Jew, a Greek, a freeman, a slave, by a metonymy frequent among the Hebrews, to whom נקרא signifies to be called, or the state or condition of someone. But the verb ἐκλήθης pertains to the designation of the time at which one arrived at the faith. Let him remain in this, that is, let him be content with this, as we have already said. For μένειν stands for ὑπομένειν, to tolerate. And the Hebrew חנה & יחר is translated in both ways.

Latin:

V. 20. Ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ κλήσει ἐν ᾗ ἐκλήθη, ἐν ταύτῃ μενέ- τω) Est παρονομασία. Nam aliud significat κλῆσις, aliud ἐκλήθη. Κλῆσις est appellatio, id est, conditio hominis, ex qua appellatur Judæus, Græcus, liber, servus, per μετωνο- μίαν Ebræis frequentem, quibus נקרא καλεῖσθαι statum alicujus, aut conditionem significat. Verbum autem ἐκλή- θης pertinet ad designationem temporis, quo quis ad fidem pervenit. In hac maneat, id est, hac contentus sit, ut jam diximus. Nam μένειν pro ὑπομένειν tolerare. Et utroque modo vertitur Hebræum חנה & יחר.

## 7:21
V. 21. Were you called being a slave) when you were a slave, you attained the knowledge of the Gospel.

Let it not be a care to you) Do not let that move you to such an extent that you flee from your Master on account of it. For under the guise of the liberty which Christ prepared for his own, some were despising the authority of both magistrates and masters. Thus the Stoic sect, which said that the wise man is King, when poorly understood, made men arrogant and turbulent, as Tacitus notes in Annals XIV. Some were also troublesome to the Church, so that they might obtain liberty at its expense, which the epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, mentioned above, rebukes. Every one of the Christians who was of a similar condition ought to think that which Epictetus thought: I was born Epictetus, a slave and maimed in body, and Iros in poverty, and a friend to the immortals. Aristonymus recounts this among the benefits of Philosophy: You will live content with present things, not desiring those that are absent.

But if you are also able to become free, use it rather) If you can obtain liberty with the Lord's will, take it, not as a good, but as a preferred thing, as the Stoics say. But do this for no other reason than that you may be able to serve God and the Church more readily. For slaves could not become Bishops or Presbyters without the Lord's will. See Apostolic Canon LXXXII. He does not persuade us to imitate those Hebrews who allowed their ears to be pierced, Exodus XXI. 6.

Latin:

V. 21. Δοῦλος ἐκλήθης) cum servus esses, Evangelii co- gnitionem es adeptus.

Μή σοι μελέτω) Ne id te eousque commoveat, ut pro- pterea à Domino fugias. Nam specie libertatis, quam Chri- stus suis paravit, quidam & magistratuum & Dominorum imperia spernebant. Sic Stoica secta, quæ sapientem esse Regem dicebat, malè intellecta arrogantes faciebat & tur- bidos, notante Tacito Annal. XIV. Quidam etiam molesti erant Ecclesiæ, ut ejus sumptu libertatem adipiscerentur, quod reprehendit Ignatii dicta epistola ad Polycarpum. Debebat quisque Christianorum, qui similis esset conditio- nis, id cogitare, quod Epictetus: Δοῦλος Ἐπίκτητος γενόμην καὶ σώματι πηρὸς, Καὶ πενίην Ἶρος, καὶ φίλος ἀθανάτοις. Aristonymus inter Philosophiæ beneficia hoc recitat: Βιώσῃ ἀρκούμενος τοῖς παροῦσι, τῶν ἀπόντων ἐκ ἐπιθυμῶν.

Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ δύνασαι ἐλεύθερος γενέσθαι, μᾶλλον χρῆσαι) Si potes volente Domino libertatem obtinere, sume hoc, non tanquam ἀγαθὸν, sed tanquam προηγμένον, ut loquuntur Stoici. Fac autem hoc non aliam ob causam, quam ut ex- peditius Deo & Ecclesiæ servire possis. Nam servi non po- terant Episcopi aut Presbyteri fieri nolente Domino. Vide Canonem Apostolicum LXXXII. Non suadet, ut illos He- bræos imitemur, qui aures sibi perforari sinebant, Exod. XXI. 6.

## 7:22
V. 22. For he who was called in the Lord, being a slave, is the Lord's freedman. Likewise also he who was called being free, is a slave of Christ) There is here both an antithesis and an oxymoron, Rom. VI. 20, 21, 22. A slave brought to the faith through Christ is a freedman of Christ, and indeed an Orcinus, having been liberated by Him from troublesome masters, desires, and vices. Conversely, a freeborn man ought nevertheless to be a slave, namely, of Christ. See with what brief argumentation Paul has equaled slaves to the free; Ignatius: let them serve more for the glory of God, that they may obtain a better liberty from God. Tertullian on the crown: Secular liberty also crowns, but you have already been redeemed by Christ, and indeed at a great price. How does the world manumit another's slave? And if it seems like liberty, it also seemed like slavery. All things in the world are imaginary and nothing is true. For you were then a free man of Christ, having been redeemed by Christ, and now you are a slave of Christ, even though manumitted by a man. Ἀπελεύθερος, פטור among the Rabbis and Chaldeans. The Syrian here has placed מחררא which is ἐλευθερωθείς.

Latin:

V. 22. Ὁ γὰρ ἐν Κυρίῳ κληθεὶς δοῦλος, ἀπελεύθερος Κυ- ρίου ἐστίν. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἐλεύθερος κληθεὶς, δοῦλός ἐστι Χριστοῦ) Est hic & ἀντίθετον & ὀξύμωρον, Rom. VI. 20. 21. 22. Servus per Christum ad fidem perductus, libertus est Christi, & quidem Orcinus, per ipsum scilicet liberatus à molestis Dominis, cupiditatibus ac vitiis. Vicissim homo ingenuus, servus nihilominus esse debet, nempe Christi. Vide quam brevi argumentatione Paulus servos liberis æquaverit Ignatius: εἰς δόξαν Θεοῦ πλέον δουλευέτωσαν, ἵνα κρείττονος ἐλευθερίας τύχωσιν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ. Tertullianus de corona: Co- ronat & libertas secularis, sed tu jam redemptus es à Chri- sto, & quidem magno. Servum alienum quomodo seculum manumittit? Et si libertas videtur, sed & servitus videba- tur. Omnia imaginaria in seculo & nihil veri. Nam & tunc liber hominis eras redemptus à Christo, & nunc servus es Christi, licet manumissus ab homine. Ἀπελεύθερος, פטור Rabbinis & Chaldæis. Syrus hic posuit מחררא quod est ἐλευθερωθείς.

## 7:23
Vers. 23. You were bought with a price) He repeats what he had said above VI. 20, because it could not be said too often.

Do not become slaves of men) You are Christ's: do not voluntarily bring upon yourselves a slavery that is not necessary, which those teachers wish to impose upon you according to their own pleasure. As if he were to say: If that slavery, introduced by laws, is burdensome to you, why do you draw another upon yourselves of your own accord?

Latin:

Vers. 23. Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε) Repetit, quod supra dixerat VI. 20. quia nimis sæpe id dici non poterat.

Μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων) Christi estis: nolite in vos ultro accersere servitutem non necessariam, quam vobis imponere volunt isti Doctores pro suo lubitu. Quasi di- cat: Si servitus illa, legibus introducta, vobis est gravis, cur aliam sponte vestra in vos attrahitis?

## 7:24
V. 24. Let each one in that in which he was called, in this remain before God) Let each one tolerate the state in which he arrived at the faith, as if GOD were looking on: לפני יהוה.

It is in the open that the Apostle is transferring the hypothesis to the thesis. For since he said that it is not contrary to the Christian profession if someone is joined with an unbelieving spouse, this he added a common doctrine, that each one, in whatever kind of life, should do what is of his own duty: And let him not think that his kind of life, condition, or lot, whatever it may be, is a hindrance to the Christian profession. But the Apostolic method is to be observed above all: He who is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman; likewise he who is called, being free, is Christ's servant. For this, just as it excellently relieves the troubles of servants, so it effectively restrains the liberty of masters within limits. For servants in this world are free before God, as being liberated from the spiritual servitude of sin and the wrath of God. But those who are free in this world, having been converted to Christ, are bound to serve God in justice and holiness. Which pious and holy servitude consists well with civil liberty. Both are truly free, in that they have been liberated by Christ, John VIII. 36. If the Son has liberated you, you are truly free. Therefore they ought to care for nothing more than that they may enjoy this liberty of theirs, and not become servants of men by submitting themselves to a yoke contrary to Christian liberty, so that they do anything at the nod of another against their conscience, who have been redeemed at a great price, namely, by the precious blood of the Son of God.

Moreover, Estius not unreasonably warns that the Apostle is speaking here not of the state to which one is called—let each one walk as God has called him—but in what state he was called, namely, to the faith of Christ, at verse 18. He who is called, being circumcised: That is, if anyone was previously circumcised, as a Jew or a proselyte, and is called to the faith of Christ, let him not draw on the foreskin; as the Vulgate has correctly expressed the sense: which indeed, if it be understood literally, Cajetan considers impossible, along with Origen in his book De Principiis, Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian, chapter 6, and in his commentary on Isaiah 52, and Augustine in his book De Mendacio, chapter 5. But Epiphanius teaches otherwise in his book De Ponderibus et Mensuris, being skilled in Jewish matters, by the example of Symmachus, who was circumcised a second time. Nor does Cajetan's gloss hold: Let him persevere in circumcising his sons. For it is a very different thing to make foreskins for oneself and to leave sons uncircumcised. But the Apostle indicates this, that one should not be ashamed of circumcision, nor affect to be uncircumcised, according to Estius. Indeed, that he should not, beyond this, because he is a Christian, cease to observe Mosaic institutions, provided he knows that the law is dead, which is to be buried with honor. Blessed Luther renders the sense beautifully in the place cited before: It is all the same whether you are a Jew or a Gentile: If you are circumcised and under the Jewish law, do not think that it is a sin or wrong, and that you must get out of it. For faith is above circumcision and all law, so that you may be circumcised or uncircumcised, and there is no necessity for salvation. But both are free to remain in. Just as there is no necessity to be married or to remain without marriage, but both are free. So also if you are a Gentile, uncircumcised, and without Jewish law, you must not think that it is wrong and that you must be circumcised: but it is free. Faith alone makes you righteous, which also alone fulfills the commandments of God. Therefore, the utility of circumcision is not simply denied, when the Apostle says that it profits nothing, which was entirely profitable to the Jews themselves as a sacrament of regeneration, but that in the time of the New Testament, when circumcision and other ceremonial laws of the Old Testament were dead, they avail nothing. He also hints at the same thing by the example of servants and the free, that it is the same in the eyes of God whether one is called a servant in the Lord or free. One is not better than the other before God: As Paul says in Galatians III. 28. Here there is not

Jew, not Gentile, not servant, not free, not male, nor female: But all are one in Christ Jesus. Whence the parabolic sense of Jerome, which does not deserve to be brought forward, falls to the ground.

PART II. ON THE SOLITARY STATE.

Latin:

V. 24. Ἕκαστος ἐν ᾧ ἐκλήθη, ἐν τούτῳ μενέτω παρὰ Θεῷ) Quisque in quo statu ad fidem pervenit, eum toleret, tanquam DEO inspectante: לפני יהוה.

In aprico est, quod hypothesin ad thesin transferat Apostolus. Quum enim dixerit, non repugnare id professioni Christianæ, si quis cum infideli conjuge junctus sit, hanc communem doctrinam adjunxit, unusquisque, in quocunque genere vitæ, faciat, quod sui est mune- ris: Nec vita genus, conditionem aut sortem, qua- cunque illa sit, officere Christianæ professioni existi- met. Observanda autem imprimis ratio Apo- stolica: Qui in Domino vocatus est servus, liber- tus est Domino, similiter qui liber vocatus est, ser- vus est Christi. Hæc enim uti molestias servo- rum egregie sublevat, ita libertatem Domino- rum intra limites efficaciter coercet. Servi enim in hoc mundo liberi sunt coram Deo, utpote à spiri- tuali servitute peccati, & ira Dei liberati. Liberi autem in hoc mundo, ad Christum conversi, ad serviendum Deo in justitia & sanctitate obstricti sunt. Quæ servitus pia & sancta cum libertate ci- vili probè consistit. Utrique verè liberi sunt, quâ à Christo liberati, Joh. VIII. 36. Si Filius vos libe- ravit, verè liberi estis. Ideo nihil magis curare de- bent, quàm ut hac libertate suâ fruantur, nec ser- vi hominum fiant, jugo se submittendo, libertati Christianæ adverso, ut ad nutum alterius quic- quam contra conscientiam faciant, qui magno pretio redempti sunt, pretioso nempe sanguine Filii Dei.

Cæterum non abs re monet Estius, Aposto- lum hic loqui non de statu, ad quem quis vocatus est, unumquemque sicut vocavit Deus, ita ambulet: Sed in quo vocatus, scilicet ad fidem Christi, ad vers. 18. Circumcisus qui vocatus est: Id est, si quispiam prius circumcisus, utpote Judæus, aut proselytus, vocatus est ad fidem Christi, ne at- trahat præputium; uti sensum rectè expressit Vul- gatus: quod quidem si propriè intelligatur, pro impossibili habet Cajetanus cum Origene lib. de princip. Hieronymo lib. 1. contra Jovin. cap. 6. & in comm. Es. LII. Augustino l. de mendac. cap. 5. Sed aliud docet Epiphanius lib. de ponder. & men- sur. rerum Judaicarum peritus, Symmachi exem- plo, qui secundò circumcisus fuerit. Neque glossa Cajetani locum habet: Perseveret circumci- dendo filios. Nam longe diversa sunt, facere sibi præputia, & relinquere filios incircumcisos. Id au- tem indicat Apostolus, ne pudeat circumcisionis, nec affectet esse præputiatus, secundum Estium. Imo, ne præter hoc, quia Christianus est, desinat instituta Mosaica servare, modo sciat legem mor- tuam esse, quæ cum honore sepelienda sit. Sen- sum pulchrè reddit B. Lutherus loco antea citato: Es gilt gleich viel, du seyst Jud oder Heyde: Bist du beschnitten, und im Jüdischen Gesetze, so laß dichs nicht düncken, es sey Sünde, oder Unrecht, und müssest heraus. Denn der Glaube ist über Beschneidung und alle Gesetz, daß du magst be- schnitten oder unbeschnitten seyn, und keinerley noth ist zur Seligkeit. Sondern beydes ist frey drinnen zu bleiben. Gleichwie nicht noth ist ehelich zu werden, oder ohne Ehe zu bleiben, son- dern beydes frey. Also auch bist du ein Heyde, un- beschnitten, und ohn Jüdisch Gesetz, darffst du nicht dencken, es sey Unrecht, und müssest beschnitten seyn: sondern ist frey. Der Glaube allein machet dich gerecht, welcher auch allein die Gebott GOttes erfüllt. Non ergò simpliciter negatur utilitas cir- cumcisionis, cùm eam nihil prodesse dicit Aposto- lus, quæ omnino profuit ipsis Judæis, ceu sacra- mentum regenerationis, sed quod tempore Novi Testamenti, quo circumcisio, & alia ceremonialia Vet. Test. mortua erant, nihil valeant. Idem etiam exemplo servorum & liberorum innuit, perinde esse in Dei oculis sive servus quis vocatus sit in Domino, seu liber. Non hic illo melior est coram Deo: Uti Paulus Gal. III. 28. Hic non

Judæus, non gentilis, non servus, non liber, non mas, nec fæmina: Sed omnes unum sunt in Christo Jesu. Unde sensus parabolicus Hieronymi, qui adduci non meretur, in spongiam incumbit.

PARS II. DE STATU SOLITARIO.

## 7:25
Ver. 25. Now concerning virgins.

He returns to the subject. For since he had dealt with married people and widows, it was right that he should also say something about virgins.

I have no commandment of the Lord.

Interpret as above 6 and 10. I have no commandment of the Lord suitable for all.

But I give my judgment.

I give advice; and if you follow it, I will praise you: but if not, I will not condemn you. See what we said at Matt. XIX. 12. Γνώμη is advice, as in 2 Cor. VIII. 10. Thucydides and others use it thus. And the Syriac translator took it so here. For מלכא is advice. It occurs often among the Chaldean paraphrasts.

As one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful.

As one who is a faithful servant to the Lord; but having obtained this very thing by the benefit of God. Thus Paul always refers whatever virtue is in himself and others to the mercy of God, which indeed never failed men, but was most openly revealed in the Gospel. ἠλεημένος, from ἐλεεῖσθαι, which is to obtain a benefit, which passive verb we have in Matt. V. 7, Rom. II. 30, 31, 2 Cor. IV. 1, 1 Tim. I. 13, 16, 1 Pet. II. 10. ἠλεημένος is the same as κεχαριτωμένος, מוחנן. For with our writers ἔλεος signifies every benefit. See what we said at Luke I. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Περὶ δὲ τῶν παρθένων.

Redit ad propositum. Nam cum de conjugibus & vi- duis egisset, æquum erat, eum aliquid dicere & de virgi- nibus.

Ἐπιταγὴν Κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω.

Interpretare ut supra 6. & 10. Nullum habeo Domini præceptum omnibus conveniens.

Γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι.

Consilium do; quod si secuti eritis, laudabo vos: Sin minus, non damnabo. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. XIX. 12. Γνώμη est consilium, ut 2. Cor. VIII. 10. Utitur sic Thu- cydides & alii. Et ita hic accepit Syrus. Nam מלכא est consilium. Occurrit apud paraphrastas Chaldæos sæpe.

Ὡς ἠλεημένος ὑπὸ Κυρίου πιστὸς εἶναι.

Ut qui Domino fidelis sim servus; sed hoc ipsum con- secutus Dei beneficio. Ita semper Paulus, quicquid in se & aliis est virtutis, refert ad Dei misericordiam, quæ nun- quam quidem hominibus defuit, sed in Evangelio aper- tissime patefacta est. ἠλεημένος, ab ἐλεεῖσθαι, quod est bene- ficium consequi, quod verbum passivum habemus Matth. V. 7. Rom. II. 30, 31. 2. Cor. IV. 1. 1. Tim. I. 13. 16. 1. Pet. II. 10. Idem est ἠλεημένος, quod κεχαριτωμένος, מוחנן. Nam nostris scriptoribus ἔλεος omne beneficium signifi- cat. Vide, quæ diximus ad Luc. I. 28.

## 7:26
Ver. 26. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity.

Καλὸν, that is, κάλλιον, better, as above in 1, because of the present distresses. For ἐνεστὼς is opposed to μέλλοντι, Rom. VIII. 38, above III. 2, Gal. I. 4. But ἀνάγκη signifies distresses and miseries, as we said at Luke XXI. 23. Now what Paul says about his own times applies to all times after Christ. For those who wish to live according to Christ will never lack vexations, sometimes smaller, sometimes greater: but even suddenly the greatest can rush in. And how much better is it to expose one head than many to such evils?

For one soul for which to grieve is a moderate burden, says Euripides. But Philippides:

It is a good thing, dearest friend, to feign not to take a wife, nor to expose oneself to fortune through more affairs.

See Matt. XXIV. 19.

To be so.

He had proposed a question about the female sex, and he answers concerning both. For the reason is almost the same. Τὸ οὕτως εἶναι, that is, as the virgins, namely, without marriage.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Νομίζω οὖν τοῦτο καλὸν ὑπάρχειν διὰ τὴν ἐνε- στῶσαν ἀνάγκην.

Καλὸν, id est, κάλλιον melius, ut supra 1. ob præsentes angustias. Nam ἐνεστὼς opponitur μέλλοντι, Rom. VIII. 38. supra III. 2. Galat. I. 4. Ἀνάγκη vero angustias atque ærumnas significat, ut diximus ad Luc. XXI. 23. Quod autem de suis temporibus dicit Paulus, id omnibus tempo- ribus post Christum convenit. Nam secundum Christum vivere volentibus nunquam deerunt vexationes, modo mi- nores tamen, modo majores: Sed etiam subito maximæ ingruere possunt. Et quanto est satius unum caput quam multa objicere talibus malis?

Μία γὰρ ψυχὴ ἧς ὕπερ ἀλγεῖν Μέτριον ἄχθος, ait Euripides. Philippides vero:

Τὸ πλάττεσθαι ἀγαθόν ἐστι τοῦτο φίλτατε Μὴ λαμβάνειν γυναῖκα, μηδὲ τῇ τύχῃ Διὰ πλειόνων αὑτὸν προβάλλειν πραγμάτων.

Vide Matth. XXIV. 19.

Τὸ οὕτως εἶναι.

Quæstionem proposuerat de fœminino sexu, & respon- det de utroque. Par enim ferme est ratio. Τὸ οὕτως εἶναι, id est, sicut Virgines, sine conjugio scilicet.

## 7:27
Ver. 27. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release.

He so prefers the celibate life that he does not want a divorce to begin from a believer. Δέδεσαι, that is, you are obligated. For marriage is a bond. Thus Rom. VII. 2. Λύσις is separation. Thus in the digests: Marriage being dissolved.

You are loosed from a wife.

That is, you are free. For he is now speaking especially of those who have never experienced marriage. Thus among the Hebrews, passive forms are often used for neuter verbs.

Do not seek a wife.

This is now a matter of counsel, as he said above.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Δέδεσαι γυναικὶ; μὴ ζήτει λύσιν.

Ita cælibem vitam præfert, ut à fideli nolit incipere di- vortium. Δέδεσαι, id est, obligatus es. Nam matrimo- nium vinculum est. Sic Rom. VII. 2. Λύσις est χωρισμός. Sic in digestis: Soluto matrimonio.

Λέλυσαι ἀπὸ γυναικός.

Id est, liber es. Nam præcipue de nunquam nuptias expertis nunc loquitur. Sic apud Hebræos sæpe passiva su- muntur pro verbis neutris.

Μὴ ζήτει γυναῖκα.

Hoc jam consilii est, ut supra dixit.

## 7:28
Vers. 28. But if you also marry, you have not sinned.

You have not violated the covenant, as Clement of Alexandria speaks in this matter.

But such will have trouble in the flesh.

Marriage itself has indeed always had many troubles, but it cannot but have very many, where one has proposed to live against the custom of the age. For the world loves its own, and hates those who are contrary.

But I spare you.

That is, I am led by pity for you. See Acts XX. verse 9.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ἐὰν δὲ καὶ γήμῃς, οὐχ ἥμαρτες.

Non violasti fœdus, ut loquitur in hac re Clemens Ale- xandrinus.

Θλίψιν δὲ τῇ σαρκὶ ἕξουσιν οἱ τοιοῦτοι.

Ipsum quidem matrimonium semper per se multas ha- buit molestias, sed non potest non plurimas habere, ubi quis vivere proposuit contra seculi morem. Mundus enim suos amat, odit contrarios.

Ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῶν φείδομαι.

Id est, vestrum miseratione ducor. Vide Actor. XX. vers. 9.

## 7:29
Ver. 29. Now this I say, brethren.

He commends the utility of his counsel, which is always good, based on future things revealed to him by God, that is, by the persecution about to come through Nero. You have a similar prediction made to the Ephesians by Paul in Acts XX. 29.

He calls not every thing that he delivers here a counsel, but a γνώμην, an opinion; for what he says in v. 27: Art thou bound unto a wife? seek not a release or divorce, is of divine precept, not of a singular opinion or counsel, as is evident from verse 10. But that which he suggested here to the Corinthians regarding a peculiar question, namely, concerning virgins or unmarried persons, and that not concerning all, but those who have the gift of continence. For the Lord had already given a precept to the rest: Let every man have his own wife because of fornication, and let every woman have her own husband, verse 2. Nor does this so-called counsel of the Apostle concerning celibacy look so much to all times as primarily to those which were then prevailing. Which were so constituted that he judged it more advisable, if anyone is free, not to seek a wife, because of the present necessity. That a prediction is being made here concerning some imminent necessity is clear from no document. The Apostle expressly designated the present [necessity] by the phrase 'because of the present distress.' And although by parity of reason these things may in their own way suit all times, yet here the special condition of those times is noted, and therefore some things occur which are not to be applied in the same way to all times. But they do not grasp the mind of the Apostle who, with Corn. à Lapide, explain the 'instant necessity' as the brevity of our life, which therefore should be given not to the world, not to a wife, but to the soul and to God: As if the Apostle were explaining it thus;

This therefore I say, brethren: The time is short. Nor does what is delivered here by way of counsel for the time being contribute anything to the counsels of evangelical monastic perfection, so falsely named: of which neither Paul nor Christ knows anything at all, inculcating our imperfection everywhere, and not permitting a snare to be cast upon the conscience on account of such external things, which contribute not a whit to interior perfection. Nay, the Apostle does not call that doctrine concerning virginity, as we have already hinted, βυλὴν, a counsel, but γνώμην, an opinion. But βυλὴ and γνώμη differ: the former is of the will, the latter of the mind. And in Aristotle in the Ethics, book 6, chapter 11, γνώμη and συγγνώμη are used concerning that which is not judged rigidly in the same way for all, but according to equity and goodness, having regard for circumstances, in certain cases ἐπιεικῶς, yet rightly. In the same way this word is accepted here also. Furthermore, the Papists maintain that a counsel is above the precept of God. But now our Apostle does not even dare to call this doctrine of his concerning virginity a precept of God: therefore it can much less be a counsel of God, such as the Papists imagine. For a counsel, they say, is more than a precept, as the blessed Balduinus rightly warned here on page 380. Nor can the Papists by any art elicit from this passage, even if they were to use ten alembics, that celibacy is in our power, so that anyone can live celibate without a spouse if he wishes, however much he may be inclined to lust by nature or habit: which Cornelius à Lapide contends here. That this is otherwise is evident from the fact that Christ expressly denies that this is given to all, Matt. XIX. 11. Common gifts, indeed, necessary for all and promised by God, can be obtained through prayers: but the gift of continence is a peculiar gift, concerning which there is no promise that He is willing to give it to all. Tertullian in his book on monogamy handed this down; but he drew it from the Montanist spirit. Origen also thought that this gift is given to all who ask; but when he experienced otherwise, he is believed to have done violence to himself. Other ancients say that this gift does not befall the idle, but those who strive and ask; but they do not say it is given to all who ask: but they inculcate that saying of Christ: All men do not receive this word.

The time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none.

These things are to be read in one breath. For the sense is, that the time hereafter will be short, when those who have wives will be in the same position as those who do not have them, namely, because they will daily be in danger, lest one be snatched away from the other by the cruelty of judges or enemies. Καιρὸς ἐσταλμένος, the time is contracted, that is, short. Τὸ λοιπὸν is hereafter, as in Matt. XXV. 45, Mark XIV. 41, Heb. X. 13. Demosthenes and others also use it. In the Glossary, λοιπὸν, an adverb, after, otherwise, now. Moreover, this is a prophecy shadowed forth with a certain liberty from that of Isaiah XXIV. To which is a similar passage in Ezekiel VII. 12, 13. And ἵνα is for ὥστε, as in John III. 4. So it is often placed for אֶל among the Hebrews, as in Gen. XXXVIII. 9.

And those who weep, as though they were not weeping,

It will not be possible for those who will be in mourning to take up mourning clothes; Ezek. XXIX. 16. 22. Jer. XVI. 4. XXII. 18. Moreover, there will be reason for them to rejoice because friends have been snatched away from calamities Jer. XXII. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Τῦτο δέ φημι ἀδελφοὶ.

Utilitatem sui consilii, semper boni, commendat ex re- bus futuris sibi à Deo revelatis, id est, à superventura per- sequutione per Neronem. Similem prædictionem Ephesiis factam à Paulo habes Act. XX. 29.

Non consilium, sed γνώμην sententiam vocat non omne illud, quod hic tradit; Nam quod v. 27. ait: Alligatus es uxori; ne quære solutionem vel divor- tium, præcepti est divini, non singularis sententiæ aut consilii, ut è vers. 10. constat: Sed illud, quod hic ad peculiare quæsitum suggessit Corinthiis, ni- mirum de virginibus vel solutis personis, idque non de omnibus; sed quæ continentiæ donum habeant. Nam cæteris jam præceptum dederat Dominus: Quisque propter scortationem propriam fæminam habeat, & unaquæque proprium maritum, vers. 2. Nec hoc Apostoli, quod vocant, consilium de cæli- batu tam omnia respicit tempora, quam imprimis ea, quæ tunc vigebant. Quæ ita comparata erant, ut consultius censeret, non quærere uxorem, si quis liber sit, propter necessitatem præsentem. De immi- nente quâdam necessitate hic prædictionem fieri, nullo documento liquet. Præsentem Apostolus διαῤῥήδην designavit διὰ τὴν ἐνεςῶσαν ἀνάγκην. Etsi autem ex paritate rationis hæc omnibus tempori- bus suo modo conveniant; hic tamen specialis conditio istorum temporum notatur, ideoque nonnulla occurrunt, quæ non ita omnibus tem- poribus aptanda. Non autem assequuntur men- tem Apostoli, qui cum Corn. à Lapide instantem necessitatem de brevitate vitæ nostræ explicant, quæ proinde non mundo, non conjugi; sed animæ & Deo danda sit: Quasi explicet ita Apostolus;

Hoc itaque dico, fratres: Tempus breve est. Nec quæ hic consilii instar pro tempore tradita, quic- quam ad consilia, ψευδωνύμως ita dicta, perfectionis Evangelicæ monastica faciunt: De qua nihil omni- nò vel Paulus, vel Christus novit, imperfectionem nostram undique inculcantes, nec conscientiæ la- queum, ob talia externa, injici permittentes, quæ ad interiorem perfectionem nec gry nec my con- ferunt. Imò Apostolus illam de virginitate do- ctrinam, ut jam innuimus, non vocat βυλὴν consi- lium, sed γνώμην sententiam. Differunt autem βυλὴ & γνώμη: Illa voluntatis, hæc mentis est. Et apud Aristotelem in Ethicis l. 6. c. 11. γνώμη & συγ- γνώμη de eo usurpatur, quando non rigidè eodem modo de omnibus; sed ex æquo & bono, habita ra- tione circumstantiarum, in certis casibus ἐπιεικῶς, rectè tamen judicatur. Eodem pacto hic etiam accipitur hoc vocabulum. Porrò Pontificii sta- tuunt, consilium supra præceptum Dei esse. Jam ve- rò Apostolus noster hanc suam de virginitate do- ctrinam ne quidem præceptum Dei nominare au- det: Ergo multò minus consilium Dei esse potest, quale fingunt Pontificii. Plus enim est consilium, inquiunt, quam præceptum, ut rectè B. Balduinus hic pag. 380. monuit. Nulla etiam arte ex hoc loco elicere, si vel decem alembicos adhibeant, Pontificii possunt, cælibatum in nostra potestate esse, ita ut quilibet sine conjuge cælebs vivere possit, si velit; quantumvis à natura, vel habitu proclivis sit in libidinem: Quod hic contendit Cornelius à Lapide. Id verò secus se habere, hinc constat, quod omnibus hoc datum esse Christus disertè ne- gat Matth. XIX. 11. Dona quidem communia, omnibus necessaria, & à Deo promissa per preces obtineri possunt: At donum continentiæ pecu- liare est donum, de quo nulla habetur promissio, quod id omnibus dare velit. Tertullianus lib. de monogamia id tradidit; sed à Spiritu montanistico id hausit. Origenes etiam putavit, donum hoc pe- tentibus omnibus dari; sed cum aliud experiretur, sibi ipsi vim intulisse creditur. Alii veteres donum illud non otiosis; sed contendentibus & petentibus obtingere dicunt; omnibus autem, qui petunt, dari non dicunt: Sed illud Christi inculcant: Non omnes capiunt verbum hoc.

Ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος τὸ λοιπόν ἐστιν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσι.

Legenda hæc uno spiritu. Sensus enim est, breve posthac tempus futurum, cum ii, qui uxores habent, pares futuri sint non habentibus, nempe quia quotidie in periculis erunt, ne alter alteri abripiatur per sævitiam judicum aut inimicorum. Καιρὸς ἐσταλμένος, tempus contractum, id est, breve. Τὸ λοιπὸν est posthac, ut Matth. XXV. 45. Marci XIV. 41. Ebr. X. 13. Utitur & Demosthenes & alii. In Glossario λοιπὸν, ἐπίῤῥημα post, secus, jam. Est autem hæc prophetia cum libertate quadam adumbrata ex illa Esaiæ XXIV. Cui similis locus Ezech. VII. 12. 13. Et ἵνα est pro ὥστε, ut Johan. III. 4. Ita sæpe ponitur אֶל apud Ebræos, ut Gen. XXXVIII. 9.

Καὶ οἱ κλαίοντες, ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες,

Non vacabit iis, qui in luctu erunt, sumere lugubria; Ezech. XXIX. 16. 22. Jer. XVI. 4. XXII. 18. Insuper erit, cur gaudeant ob ereptos amicos calamitatibus Jeremiæ XXII. 4.

## 7:30
Vers. 30. And those who rejoice, as though they were not rejoicing,

Bridegrooms and brides will bear equal evils with the rest, nor will joy remain for them. Joel II. 16.

And those who buy, as though they were not possessing,

Those who have bought land will be equal to those possessing nothing. You have this sense in the stated passages Ezek. VII. 12. 13. & Isaiah XXIV. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Καὶ οἱ χαίροντες, ὡς μὴ χαίροντες,

Sponsi & sponsæ paria cum cæteris mala ferent, nec manebit eis gaudium. Joel. II. 16.

Καὶ οἱ ἀγοράζοντες, ὡς μὴ κατέχοντες,

Qui fundum emerunt, pares erunt nihil possidentibus. Hunc sensum habes dictis locis Ezech. VII. 12. 13. & Esaiæ XXIV. 2.

## 7:31
Vers. 31. And those who use this world, as though they were not using it to the full.

Καταχρᾶσθαι is the same as χρᾶσθαι, except that it seems to signify something fuller. Plato: Οὐκ ὀρθῶς κατακέχρηται δωρεᾷ; he has not used the gift rightly. Lysias: Αἰγύπτιον κατεχρήσατο he consumed an Egyptian, just as the Romans also say to abuse a thing, for to consume by using. Thus σχολὴν καταχρᾶσθαι to spend time. He understands the world here as the things of this life. Those who have used them abundantly before will be equal to those who have used them sparingly.

Thus Grotius explains these things concerning the brevity of a tranquil and peaceful time. But the Apostle had indicated in verse 26 that the times were already grievous then. Understanding present, not future, distresses by 'the present necessity,' with Grotius himself as interpreter. Others therefore understand it concerning the brevity of this life; as if we were warned by the same that one should rather abstain from marriage; since a short time is given to us for the acquisition of eternity, which therefore should not be given to a spouse, not to the world, but to the soul and to God. But in that way, no one should enter into matrimony. Nor indeed can we acquire eternal life by our works, even if we were to choose virginity; nor does marriage hinder eternal salvation in any way, as it is ordained by God, and if you believe the Papists, a peculiar Sacrament (which the state of virginity is not) entered into by the most holy persons. Estius prefers to understand it concerning the brevity of this age, as if we think about taking a wife and about taking care of the things of this age, by which the mind might be distracted from God, we will think less; but to take a wife, and to do those things which are required for sustaining this life, do not in themselves distract from God; but can well consist with the pursuit of piety. And since it would have been necessary for all time and for all people to think about how quickly this age passes, no one would ever have had to think about marriage. The Apostle, however, does not forbid, but commands that each one take a wife on account of fornication, he only warns that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them. Others wish for καιρὸν χαλεπὸν, as it is called in 2 Tim. III. 1, to be understood through συνεσταλμένον, and thus they take this word not concerning a short, but a difficult and hard time, as in Sir. IV. 36, a parsimonious hand διεσφαλμένη is opposed to a liberal one. Which explanation, in the judgment of the blessed Hülsemann, agrees most with verses 30 and 31.

For the times are hard and difficult, and the Apostle seems to warn that wives and other worldly things must be used so that no one, under the pressure of persecutions, allows himself to be led away from the confession of the Evangelical doctrine, lest the Corinthians sin for the sake of their wives, out of a desire to retain this temporal life and secular comforts; or lest they shamefully fall away and recoil from the profession of faith through ἀποστασίαν, as the blessed Hunnius thinks. We admit, however, that the Apostle is easily speaking about the brevity of this life, not to dissuade from marriage, but to provide a most necessary caution regarding spouses and other things of this life; namely, that our whole heart ought not to be occupied by the cares of worldly things; but because this life is quite fleeting, we must live in the world as if we were not in the world, so that our mind and πολίτευμα may be in heaven, and in whatever circumstance—whether in marriage or outside of marriage, whether in mourning or in joy, whether we possess something or lose our possessions—each of the faithful may in the same way sustain himself in all things with the hope of eternal life. If they have spouses, let them be as though they had none; let them not place their highest happiness in the fact that they have convenient companions of life; let them consider that they can be deprived of them, or that they themselves must someday depart from their spouse, and thus let them serve the Lord as promptly as if they did not have spouses; let them prefer the love of God to the love of a spouse; let them not think too solicitously about those things which are of this world, how they may please their wives; but rather about those which are of the Lord, how they may please the Lord, as is explained here in verse 31. And let them not be too dejected in adversity, nor too elated in prosperity, nor establish the end of their desire and the substance of their joy in earthly things: let them possess earthly things, but let them beware lest they be possessed by them, etc.

For the fashion of this world passes away. The sense is the same as in those words of Isaiah 24:4, 'The earth mourns and fades away, the world languishes.' But the expression is taken from the theater. It is said that the fashion of the scene passes away, where the scene is inverted and shows a completely different face. This is what it means: tranquil things will not remain as they are now, but will be changed into turbulent ones. Thus 1 John 2:17, 'The world is passing away.'

These words do not sound of the inversion of the scene of this world, but of the total passing and destruction of this world's schism. The Apostle does not prophesy that tranquil things are to be changed into turbulent ones, but indicates that the world is eventually to cease entirely, which is also done by John in 1 Epist. 2:17 and Revelation 21:1. 'The first heaven and the first earth passed away,' or went by, 'and the sea is no more,' by which it is taught what kind of passing this is, namely, that the world is to pass in such a way that it is no longer. The sense of the Apostle is clear from the preceding words: 'Those who use the world, as not abusing it,' that is, not setting their heart upon it by adhering to it with excessive and immoderate love, since the whole world and whatever is in the world is passing away. Augustine, Book V against Julian the Pelagian: 'What is it, as if they do not use, unless that they do not love what they use, since it is such that they do not use it well otherwise,' and Book XV of the City of God, chapter 7. The good use the world for this purpose, that they may enjoy God. The wicked, on the contrary, use it so that they may enjoy the world, as they wish to use God. Gregory, part 3 of the Pastoral Care, admonition 82: 'The fashion of this world passes away,' says the Apostle, as if he were saying openly: 'Do not love the world constantly, when even he whom you love cannot stand; you fix your heart in vain, as if remaining, while he whom you love flees.' And Homily 36 on the Gospels: 'Let us hold those things which are of this world in such a way that we are not held by them; let the temporal thing be in use, the eternal in desire,' etc. Gregory Nazianzen on the life of travelers.

Therefore it is ordained that all things of this life should be uncertain and unstable, so that we may burn with love and desire for firm and stable things. Philo rightly warned in his book On the Cherubim that we use the possessions of others, and that we do not possess glory, nor riches, nor honors, nor empires, nor anything else proper to the body or soul as if these were of our own right and dominion; but we have only the usufruct of them while we live here. By 'the fashion of this world' some understand the conversation of this age, the life in this world, which is eventually to cease, Luke 20:34. Some understand the appearance and beauty of the world, whatever is specious, pleasant, and agreeable in the world. But it is signified that the world itself with all its fashion is to pass away. Whence, since the Calvinists, expecting only an accidental change of the world and not its substantial destruction, conclude from this passage: 'the fashion of the world passes away, therefore the matter [does not],' we rightly invert this with Justin in Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, question 45: 'If the habit of this world passes away, it is certain that at the same time all other things which were made because of the habit of the world must necessarily pass away with the habit of the world.' And Ambrose on this passage: 'If the form of the world will perish, there is no doubt that all things which are in the world will perish.' The word παράγει occurs in the sense of passing away in Psalm 144:4, 'His days pass away like a shadow,' and 1 John 2:17, 'the world is passing away.' Just as when a comedy is finished, the curtains and the things that served the comic act are removed from the middle so that they are nowhere visible to the eyes of the beholders, so when the span of this age has run its course, the world, like a certain curtain that served the comedy of this life, will be removed from the middle and will be seen no more. And so, that the Apostle may call us away from the excessive love of the world, he sets two things before us: both the brevity of our life and the corruptibility of the whole world, so that we may not adhere to the world greedily, because we must soon emigrate from the world, and the world itself is not to remain eternally, but is eventually to perish.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Καὶ οἱ χρώμενοι τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ, ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι.

Καταχρᾶσθαι idem est, quod χρᾶσθαι, nisi quod videtur plenius quiddam significare. Plato: Οὐκ ὀρθῶς κατακέχρηται δωρεᾷ; dono non recte est usus. Lysias: Αἰγύπτιον κατεχρήσατο absumpsit, sicut & Romani abuti rem dicunt, pro utendo consumere. Sic σχολὴν καταχρᾶσθαι tempus insumere. Mundum hic intelligit res hujus vitæ. Qui large eis usi sunt antea, pares erunt eis, qui parce usi sunt.

Ita de brevitate temporis tranquilli & placati hæc explicat Grotius. Sed tempora tum jam fuisse ærumnosa vers. 26. indicarat Apostolus. Præsentes, non futuras angustias per τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην, interprete ipsomet Grotio, intelligens. Alii ergò de brevitate vitæ hujus intelligunt; ac si eadem moneremur, à conjugio abstinendum esse potius; cum breve tempus nobis detur ad æternitatis acquisitionem, quod proinde non conjugi, non mundo; sed animæ & Deo dandum sit. Sed ita nemini esset matrimonium ineundum. Neque vero nos operibus nostris vitam æternam acquirere possumus, etiamsi virginitatem eligeremus; nec saluti æternæ quicquam officit conjugium, utpote à Deo ordinatum, & si Pontificiis credas, Sacramentum peculiare (quod virginitatis status non est) à sanctissimis quibusvis initum. Estius mavult de brevitate hujus seculi intelligere, quam si cogitemus, de uxore ducenda, deque rebus hujus seculi curandis, quibus animus à Deo avocetur, minus cogitabimus; sed uxorem ducere, ac ea, quæ ad sustentandam hanc vitam requiruntur, agere, per se non avocant à Deo; sed cum studio pietatis probè consistere possunt. Et quum omni tempori, omnibusque cogitandum fuerit, quàm citò transeat hoc seculum, nullis unquam de matrimonio cogitandum fuisset. Apostolus verò non prohibet, sed jubet, ut quisque uxorem ducat propter scortationem, monet tantum, ut, qui uxorem habent, sint, quasi non habeant. Alii καιρὸν χαλεπὸν, uti 2. Tim. III. 1. vocatur per συνεσταλμένον intelligi volunt, adeoque vocem hanc non de brevi; sed difficili ac duro tempore accipiunt, ut Sir. IV. 36. parca manus διεσφαλμένη opponitur liberali. Quæ explicatio judicio Beati Hülsemanni vers. 30. 31. maximè convenit.

enim tempora sunt dura ac difficilia, uxoribus, aliisq; rebus mundanis utendum, ne nimio talium amore à confessione doctrinæ Evangelicæ abduci se quis pa- tiatur, persecutionibus urgentibus, monere vide- tur Apostolus, ne quid in gratiam uxorum Corin- thii, studio retinendæ hujus vitæ temporalis, & com- moditatum secularium peccent; aut à fidei professio- ne per ἀποστασίαν turpiter desciscant, & resiliant, uti censet B. Hunnius. Admittimus tamen faci- les, de brevitate vitæ hujus agere Apostolum, non ut conjugium dissuadeat; sed ut cautelam de con- jugibus, aliisque hujus vitæ rebus, maximè ne- cessariam tradat; quod scilicet totum cor nostrum non debeat occupari curis rerum mundanarum; sed quia hæc vita caduca admodum est, ita in mundo vivendum sit, tanquam non essemus in mundo, ut animus noster & πολίτευμα in cœlis sit, ac quo- cunque casu, seu in conjugio, seu extra conju- gium; sive in luctu, sive in gaudio; sive possidea- mus quid; sive amittamus possessiones, eodem modo erga religionem affectus fidelium quisque in omnibus se vitæ æternæ spe sustentet. Si con- juges habent, sint tanquam non habentes, non ponant in eo summam felicitatem, quod habeant commodas vitæ socias; cogitent se iis privari pos- se, aut sibi aliquando à conjuge discedendum esse, atque ita promptè serviant Domino, ac si non ha- berent conjuges, dilectionem Dei amori conju- gis præponant, non nimis solicitè cogitent de illis, quæ sunt hujus mundi, quomodo placeant uxoribus; sed potius, quæ sint Domini, quomodo Domino pla- ceant, ut hic exponitur vers. 31. Nec in adversis animo sint nimium demisso; nec in prosperis ni- mium elato, nec finem desiderii & substantiarn gaudii sui in terrenis constituant: Res terrenas possideant; sed caveant, ne ab iis possidean- tur, &c.

Παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα τῦ κόσμε τύτε. Idem sensus est, qui in illis Esaiæ XXIV. 4. הארץ אמללה נבלה תבל Sed locutio desumpta est à the- atro. Dicitur παράγειν τὸ σχῆμα τῆς σκηνῆς, ubi scena inver- titur, aliamque plane ostendit faciem. Hoc vult: Non ma- nebunt,ut nunc sunt,res tranquillæ, sed mutabuntur in tur- bidas. Sic 1. Joh. II. 17. Ὁ κόσμος παράγεται.

Non de scenæ hujus mundi inversione; sed de totali schismatis hujus mundi transitu & interitu hæc sonant. Non quod res tranquillæ in turbidas mutandæ sint, vaticinatur Apostolus, sed quod mundus plane destiturus aliquando sit, indicat, quod & à Johanne fit 1. Epist. II. 17. & Apoc. XXI.1. Primum cælum & prima terra παρῆλθε transiit, vel præteriit, & mare ὐκ ἔσιν ἔτι, non est amplius, quo docetur, qualis sit transitus, quod nempe ita transiturus sit mundus, ut non amplius sit. Sen- sus Apostoli luculentus est verbis præcedentibus: Qui utuntur mundo, tanquam non abutentes, cor scilicet ei non apponant, nimio & immoderato amore ei adhærendo, quum mundus totus, & quicquid in mundo est, transeat. Augustinus l. V. contra Julian. Pelag. Quid est, quasi non utantur, nisi non diligant, quo utuntur, quoniam tale est, ut bene aliter non utantur, & lib. XV. de Civit. Dei cap. 7. Boni ad hoc utuntur mundo, ut fruantur Deo. Mali contra, ut fruantur mundo, uti volunt Deo. Gregorius part. 3. curæ pastor. admon. 82. Præterit figura hujus mundi, dicit Apostolus, ac si patenter dicat: Nolite constanter mundum diligere, quando & ipse non potest, quem diligitis, stare, in- cassum cor, quasi manentes, figitis, dum fugit ipse, quem amatis. Et homil. XXXVI. in Evangelia: Sic teneamus ea, quæ sunt hujus mundi, ut tamen per ea non teneamur; sit res temporalis in usu, æter- na in desiderio &c. Greg. Nazianz. de vit. itiner.

Ideo constitutum est, ut res omnes hujus vitæ incertæ sint ac instabiles, ut rerum firmarum stabiliumque amore ac desiderio exardescamus. Rectè Philo li- bro de Cherubim monuit, nos alienis uti possessio- nibus, nec gloriam, nec divitias, nec honores, nec imperia, nec aliud quippiam vel corporis vel animi proprium, quasi hæc juris & dominii nostri sint, possideamus; sed eorum usumfructum, dum hic vi- vimus, habemus solum. Per τὸ σχῆμα τῶ κόσμꙋ nonnulli conversationem hujus seculi, vitam in hoc mundo intelligunt, quæ aliquando cessatura est, Luc. XX. 34. Aliqui speciem ac pulchritudinem mundi, quicquid in mundo speciosum, jucundum & gratum est, intelligunt. Sed mundus ipse cum omni suo schemate præteriturus significatur. Unde cum Calviniani accidentalem tantum mun- di mutationem, non substantialem ejusdem de- structionem expectantes, concludunt ex hoc lo- co, figura mundi præterit, ergo materia, merito in- vertimus cum Justino in qq. & resp. ad orthod. q. 45. Si præterit habitus hujus mundi, certum est, simul necessario alia omnia, quæ propter habitum mundi sunt effecta, cum mundi habitu esse præteri- tura. Et Ambrosius in hunc locum : Si forma mundi peribit, dubium non est, omnia, quæ sunt in mundo, interire. Verbum παράγει deces- satione occurrit Ps. CXLIV. 4. Ἡμέραι ἀυτῶ ὡσεὶ σκιὰ παράγꙋσι 1. Joh. II. 17. ὁ κόσμος παράγεται: Sicut finita comœdia, aulæa, & quæ comico actui inservierunt, è medio tolluntur, ut nuspiam am- plius oculis intuentium sint obvia: Sic decurso hujus seculi spatio, mundus instar cujusdam aulæi, quod hujus vitæ Comœdiæ inserviit, è medio tol- letur, nec amplius conspicietur. Ut itaque à ni- mio amore mundi nos avocet Apostolus, duo no- bis sistit, tum vitæ nostræ brevitatem, tum mundi totius corruptibilitatem, ut mundo non adhæresca- mus avidè, quia brevi nobis è mundo emigran- dum, & mundus ipse non æternum mansurus, sed tandem interiturus est.

## 7:32
Vers. 32. Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνες εἶναι. Θέλω here again is 'I would wish' or 'I would prefer,' as above in 7. And ἀμερίμνες is to be understood comparatively. For he who cares for himself, not his whole family, has fewer cares. This is the second reason, besides that concerning persecution, why celibacy is to be preferred to marriage. But this holds place especially in those who have given themselves wholly to the ministry of the Church. Ὁ ἄγαμ© μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ Κυρίꙋ, πῶς ἀρέσει Κυρίῳ. He is occupied chiefly with this, he has scarcely anything else to do. Ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ κόσμꙋ, πῶς ἀρέσει τῇ γυναικί. He is solicitous in the care of the body, in the decoration of houses, and of himself and his wife, such things as wives are accustomed to love. See Plautus, Aulularia III. 5.

These things seem to be said in favor of monasticism and the celibacy of priests. For Grotius frequently pleads the cause of the Papists. Although indeed celibates have fewer domestic cares, and those who have given themselves to the sacred ministry can more easily care for those things which are the Lord's, since they are ἄγαμοι: nevertheless, the Apostle does not here specifically look to the sacred order; but he answers in general concerning celibacy, and therefore it is equally true of all, that this ἄγαμ©, whether he be a minister of the word or not, can especially do and care for those things which are the Lord's. Which things also ministers of the word may especially do, since it is not good to be alone, and for man, in whatever state God has made a helpmate, and for all in every state, marriage ought to be τίμιον, precious and honorable, Heb. XIII. 4. Faithful life-partners can be of great use and assistance in many things necessary for life and health: but to those who do not have the gift of continence, also are also necessary, by virtue of a divine precept, spouses: wherefore they can in no way be forbidden to them, on the argument of the greater utility of the Church. For all things which God has ordained and commanded are without doubt most wisely ordained. But it must be observed that the Apostle is speaking primarily of unequal marriages, such as were not rare at that time, where believers were joined to unbelievers, in which much hindrance is wont easily to intervene in caring for those things which are the Lord's, which is objected by the unbelieving party. If the believer wishes to please him, or not to displease him, he is certainly drawn away not a little from divine worship, and many things must be feigned and dissembled for the sake of peace. Which also happens in the marriages of Christians and believers, since rarely is an equal zeal for piety and devotion found in both. Finally, these things are to be taken not in an exclusive sense, as if in marriage those things which are the Lord's cannot be cared for, as is fitting, especially those which are required by the law of sacred duty; but in a comparative sense, and indeed in a certain respect. Rightly Claudius Espencæus, comm. on Tit. II: What the Apostle says, that the unmarried woman thinks of the things of God, that she may be holy in body and spirit, is not to be taken in such a way that we think a chaste Christian spouse is not holy in body, for it is said to all believers that their bodies are members of Christ, of the living God, and temples of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνες εἶναι. Θέλω hic rursus est velim, aut malim, ut supra 7. Et ἀμερίμνες intelligendum comparate. Minus enim curarum habet, qui se, non totam familiam curat. Hæc altera est ratio præter illam de persecutione, cur cælibatus conjugio præferendus. Maxime autem hoc locum habet in iis, qui se totos Ecclesiæ ministerio dederunt. Ὁ ἄγαμ© μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ Κυρίꙋ, πῶς ἀρέσει Κυρίῳ. Hoc præcipue agit, vix aliud habet, quod agat. Ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῶ κόσμꙋ, πῶς ἀρέσει τῇ γυναικί. Solicitus est in cultu corporis, in ornatu ædium, suique & uxoris, qualia amare solent uxores. Vide Plautum Au- lularia III. 5.

Hæc in gratiam monachatus ac cælibatus sacer- dotum dicta videntur. Pontificiorum enim causam frequenter agit Grotius. Quanquam verò mi- nus curæ domesticæ habeant cælibes, & illi, qui se sacro ministerio dederunt, magis possint curare ea, quæ sunt Domini, cum ἄγαμοι sunt: Non ta- men Apostolus hic sacrum ordinem speciatim re- spicit; sed in genere de cælibatu respondet, adeoq; de omnibus id ex æquo verum est, quod nempe hæc præcipuè ἄγαμ©, sive minister verbi sit, seu non, agere & curare possit, quæ sunt Domini. Quæ etiam verbi ministri præcipuè agant, cum bonum non sit, esse solum, & homini, in quo- cunque statu Deus fecerit adjutorium, omnibusq; in omni statu, τίμιον pretiosum & honorabile de- beat esse conjugium, Ebr. XIII. 4. magno usui & adjumento in multis, ad vitam & valetudinem necessariis, esse possunt fideles vitæ consortes: Il- lis autem, qui donum continentiæ non habent, etiam etiam necessariæ sunt, vi divini præcepti, conju- ges: quapropter interdici illis, argumento majo- ris utilitatis Ecclesiæ, nullo modo possunt. Omnia enim, quæ Deus ordinávit & præcepit, si- ne dubio sapientissimè ordinata sunt. Tum ve- ro observandum, quod imprimis loquatur Apo- stolus de conjugiis imparibus, qualia illo tempore non rara fuerunt, ubi fidelibus juncti fuerunt infi- deles, in quibus multum impedimenti facilè inter- venire solet, in curandis iis, quæ Domini sunt, quod à parte infideli objicitur. Cui si fidelis pla- cere velit, aut non displicere, abstrahitur utique à cultu divino non parum, ac multa pacis studio si- mulanda, & dissimulanda sunt. Quod etiam sit in Christianorum ac fidelium conjugiis, cum rarò æquale studium pietatis & devotionis in utrisque reperiatur. Denique accipienda hæc non sensu exclusivo, quasi in conjugio curari ea non possint, quæ Domini sunt, prout par est, imprimis quæ ex lege officii sacri requiruntur; sed in sensu compa- rato, & quidem secundum quid, ac certo respectu. Rectè Claudius Espensæus comm. in Tit. II. Quod Apostolus dicit, innuptam cogitare, quæ sint Dei, ut sit sancta corpore & spiritu, non sic accipiendum est, ut putemus, non esse sanctam corpore Christianam conjugem castam, omnibus quippe fidelibus dicitur, eorum corpora esse membra Christi, Dei vivi, & Spi- ritus S. templa.

## 7:34
Vers. 34. Μεμέρισται καὶ ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος. There is here also a passive for a neuter verb, as above 27. μεμέρισαι, that is, differs: Because those things which are divided, differ. Thus the Hebrews and Syrians use נפרד. There is much difference between a married woman and a virgin.

Ἡ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῦ κυρίυ, ἵνα ᾖ ἁγία καὶ σώματι καὶ πνεύματι. Understand ἁγία here as preeminently. For she has both a body untouched by pleasures, and a mind more fully vacant for Christ. Well Naumachius: It is good to keep the body chaste, and to remain an untouched maiden, and always to rejoice in pure meditations, neither carrying the burden of heavy-laden loins, nor trembling at a husband, fearing the marriage bed. But to sit as a queen of unseen women, pouring the bright eye of the soul beyond life, where marriages are noble and true, where the greatest mind brings forth bright thoughts in divine words. Ἡ δὲ γαμήσασα μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῦ κόσμε, πῶς ἀρέσει τῷ ἀνδρὶ. She accompanies herself with the eyes of her husband, she adapts her manners to him.

But what accommodation, if the husband be pious, makes for his manners, so that it may be with piety preserved, and for piety, thus they are not opposed to each other, except in a certain respect, to please the husband and to please the Lord, when the husband calls away from those things which are the Lord's, and interferes with the piety of the spouse. For the rest, Nazianzen, occupied in explaining the utility of spouses, sang thus among other things in poem II, which is in praise of virginity: Κληῖς δ' ἀμφοτέροισι σωφροσύνης τε πόθων τε Συζυγίη, καὶ σφρηγὶς ἀναγκαίης Φιλότητος &c. Συμφυέες σάρκεσσιν ὁμόφρονες, εὐσεβίης τε Κέντρον ἐν ἀλλήλοισι πόθῳ θήγοντες ὁμοῖον &c. Χρειοῖ πλειοτέρη, πλέον θεὸν ἀμφαγαπάζει: Nay, marriage closes desire within a granted limit, and as a guardian seals loves eternally.
