They are joined together in flesh; thus they cohere in mind, and mix fires among themselves with pious flames, and because there is need of protection, and of things, here is greater want; the woman and the man trust in God with a greater heart.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Μεμέρισται καὶ ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος. Est & hic passivum pro verbo Neutro, ut supra 27. με- μέρισαι, id est, distat: Quia, quæ dividuntur, distant. Sic נפרד usurpant Hebræi & Syri. Multum interest nu- pta & virgo.

Ἡ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῦ κυρίυ, ἵνα ᾖ ἁγία καὶ σώματι καὶ πνεύματι. Ἁγία hic intellige eximie. Nam & corpus habet inta- ctum voluptatibus, & animum Christo plenius vacantem. Bene Naumachius: Καλὸν μὲν δέμας ἁγνὸν ἔχειν, ἀδμῆτά τε μίμνειν Παρθενικὴν, καθαροῖσι τ' ἀεὶ μελεδήμασι χαίρειν, Μήτε βαρυλήτων λαγόνων περὶ Φόρτον ἄγουσαν, Μήτε πόσιν τρομέουσαν ἀγάσσον εἰλεάθυσι. Ἀλλ' ἧσαι βασιλεῖαν ἀφανρῶν θηλυτεράων Ψυχῆς ὄμμα Φαεινὸν ὑπὲρ βιότοιο χέουσαν, ἔνθα γάμοι κεδνοὶ καὶ ἀληθέες, ἔνθα μεγίστα Θεσπεσίοις ἐπέεσσι νοήματα φαίδιμα τίκτει. Ἡ δὲ γαμήσασα μεριμνᾷ τὰ τῦ κόσμε, πῶς ἀρέσει τῷ ἀνδρὶ. Comit se oculis mariti, ei mores suos accommo- dat.

Quæ vero accommodatio, si maritus pius sit, ad mores ejusdem, uti salva pietate sit, & ad pieta- tem facit, ita non, nisi secundum quid, illa sibi op- ponuntur, placere viro, & placere Domino, cum vir avocat ab illis, quæ Domini sunt, & pietati conjugis intercedit. De cætero præclarè Na- zianzenus, in explicanda utilitate conjugum oc- cupatus, ita inter alia cecinit carmine II. quod est in laudem virginitatis: Κληῖς δ' ἀμφοτέροισι σωφροσύνης τε πόθων τε Συζυγίη, καὶ σφρηγὶς ἀναγκαίης Φιλότητος &c. Συμφυέες σάρκεσσιν ὁμόφρονες, εὐσεβίης τε Κέντρον ἐν ἀλλήλοισι πόθῳ θήγοντες ὁμοῖον &c. Χρειοῖ πλειοτέρη, πλέον θεὸν ἀμφαγαπάζει: Quin desiderium, concesso limite, claudit Conjugium, custosque æternum obsignat amores. Illi sunt carne simul juncti; sic mente cohærent, Inter seque piis miscent incendia flammis, Et quia præsidii est, rerumƣ, hic major egestas; Fæmina virƣ, Deo majori pectore fidunt.

## 7:35
Vers. 35. Τῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον λέγω. It is the counsel of one giving it, to look at what is expedient for him to whom the counsel is given. The manuscript has σύμφορον in the same sense. Οὐχ ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω. Βρόχος is מוקש, Prov. VI. 5. XXII. 25. elsewhere παγίς. Not that I may cast a snare upon you, that is, that I may dictate to you precepts which Christ did not give. For the Hebrews call that אסר, that is, to bind. The same is said to be ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν, Acts XV. 10. and βάρος, Acts XV. 28. φορτία, Matt. XXIII. 4. The translation is plain enough. For an opinion about some thing, as if it were illicit, holds a man pressed, bound, and as it were ensnared. Thus Prov. VI. 2. נוקשת you are bound.

Therefore he calls the Apostle's precept of celibacy a snare, which he does not wish to impose, because he does not command, but only advises celibacy, leaving it free to each what he wishes to do with a safe conscience. The Papists therefore act very badly, and against the mind of the holy Apostle, while they cast a snare upon the whole order of priests; nay, they even shut up monks and nuns in cloisters with a perpetual vow of celibacy, burdening them as with a yoke, and those persons who do not have the gift of continence. For Bellarmine acknowledges, lib. de Monach. c. 29. §. 10, that the necessity which detains one against his will is called a snare by the Apostle; and that vows are snares of those who have vowed rashly, or who have been forced by others to vow, when they themselves desired nothing of the sort. That this is likewise done all day in the Papacy, experience teaches. Nor does Cassander deny it in consult. art. 23. Many in the Papacy complain of it, Alvatus de planctu Ecclesiæ art. 27. the Author of the Oneris Ecclesiæ, and others.

Α'λλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον. Comparatively. For marriage is honorable, but chaste celibacy is more honorable. Thus εὐσχημοσύνη is decorum, below XII 23. and εὐσχημόνως decorously, Rom. XIII. 13. below XIV. 40. 1 Thess. IV. 2. In the Glossary εὐσχήμων, honorable.

καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως. He is said to be παρεδρεύειν, who sits by, Prov. VIII. 3. And by translation, who serves, below IX. 13. Thus 1 Sam. II. 12. הִצֵּב אוֹת. Symmachus had translated προσεδρεύσουσι. He who is vacant for someone is said to be πάρεδρος to him, or to have him as a πάρεδρος, Wisd. VI. 14. IX. 4. Εὐπάρεδρον, in the Greek manner, where they use a neuter adjective for a denominated substantive, is ease in being vacant for someone. For εὖ has that force in compositions. We have the adjective ἀπερισπάστῳ also in Wisd. XVI. 11. and Sirach XLI. 2. Περισπᾶσθαι is to be occupied, to be distracted, Eccl. I. 13. V. 19. Luke X. 40. Ἀπερισπάστως so that you may not be distracted, just as domestic care distracts those who live in marriage from pious meditations and deeds. Athenæus uses this word.

Holy Scripture nowhere teaches that chaste celibacy is more honorable than matrimony. Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσι, the Apostle admonishes in Heb. XIII. 4. The Vulgate is therefore to be corrected here, rendering it 'Honorable': since it is that which is becoming. For marriage is not marked as a dishonorable, or less honorable, way of life; but he commends celibacy as, in a certain respect, a more becoming and more expeditious way of life for the exercises of piety. And that εὐσχήμων is to be explained from the verb ἀσχημονεῖν in the following verse, by which he denotes that it is unbecoming when a virgin is ὑπέρακμος, exceeding the time for marrying, which is only said to be so in a relative sense, from which it may be gathered that these things are accepted only κατὰ δόξαν, and that in the judgment of the Apostle there is a distinction between τὸ συμφέρον, which is what is expedient, which he said comparatively concerning celibacy, on account of the present distress, the various tribulation of the flesh in marriage, and its calamity, and the greater convenience for serving God, and τὸ εὔσχημον, which he committed to their own judgment, being unwilling in any way to cast a snare upon them, whether to marry or indeed to remain ἄγαμοι, and whether they acknowledge it to be equally εὔσχημον, καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ? In that case, however, where it might at least seem unbecoming not to marry, he persuades and counsels that they be joined in matrimony.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Τῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον λέγω. Consilium dantis est, spectare, quod ei expedit, cui con- silium datur. Manuscriptus habet σύμφορον pari sensu. Οὐχ ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω. Βρόχος est מוקש, Prov. VI. 5. XXII. 25. alibi παγίς. Non ut vobis laqueum injiciam, id est, vobis præcepta dictem, quæ Christus non dedit. Id enim אסר, id est, legare dicunt Hebræi. Idem dicitur ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν, Acto. XV. 10. & βάρος, Act. XV. 28. φορτία, Matth. XXIII. 4. Translatio satis plana. Nam opinio de re aliqua, ut illici- ta, hominem pressum, adstrictum & quasi illaqueatum te- net. Sic Prov. VI. 2. נוקשת obligatus es.

Laqueum itaq; dicit Apostoli præceptum cæli- batus, quod ferre non vult, quia non præcipit, sed suadet tantum cælibatum, liberum cuique relin- quens, quid salva conscientia facere velit. Pessi- me ergo Papistæ agunt, & contra S. Apostoli γνώ- μην, dum toti ordini sacerdotum laqueum injiciunt; imò & claustris includunt monachos, & moniales perpetuo cælibatus voto, ceu jugo, onerantes, & personas illas, quæ donum continentiæ non habent. Agnofcit enim Bellarminus lib. de Monach. c. 29. §. 10. laqueum ab Apostolo nominari necessitatem, quæ detinet invitum; Ac vota esse laqueos illorum, qui temerè voverunt, vel qui coacti sunt ab aliis vo- vere, cum ipsi nihil tale cuperent. Quod itidem tota die in Papatu fieri, experientia docet. Nec diffitetur Cassander in consult. art. 23. Conque- runtur de eo plurimi in Papatu, Alvatus de planctu Ecclesiæ art. 27. Autor oneris Ecclesiæ, aliique.

Α'λλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον. Comparate. Est enim honestum matrimonium, sed honestior castus cælibatus. Sic εὐσχημοσύνη est decor, in- fra XII 23. & εὐσχημόνως decore, Rom. XIII. 13. infr. XIV. 40. 1. Thess. IV. 2. In Glossario εὐσχήμων, honestus.

καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως. Παρεδρεύειν dicitur, qui assidet, Prov. VIII. 3. Et per translationem, qui inservit, infra IX. 13. Sic 1. Sam. II. 12. הִצֵּב אוֹת. Symmachus verterat προσεδρεύσουσι. Qui alicui vacat, dicitur ei esse πάρεδρος, aut eum habere πάρε- δρον, Sap. VI. 14. IX. 4. Εὐπάρεδρον, Græco more, qui Adje- ctivum neutrum pro substantivo denominato usurpant, est facilitas ad vacandum alicui. Nam eam vim habet εὖ in compositionibus. Ἀπερισπάστῳ adjectivum habemus & Sap. XVI. 11. & Sirach. XLI. 2. Περισπᾶσθαι est occupari, distrahi, Eccl. I. 13. V. 19. Luc. X. 40. Ἀπερισπάστως ita ut non distraharis, sicut cura familiaris distrahit eos, qui in conjugio vivunt, à piis meditationibus & factis. Utitur hac voce Athenæus.

Castum cælibatum honestiorem esse matrimo- nio, Scriptura S. nuspiam docet. Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσι, monet Apostolus Ebr. XIII. 4. Corrigen- da ergo hic vulgata reddens, Honestum: quum sit id, quod decens est. Non enim conjugium nota- tur, ut inhonestum, vel minus honestum vitæ genus; sed cælibatum commendat, ut certo respectu ma- gis decens, & expeditius vitæ genus ad pietatis exercitia. Et explicandum illud εὐσχήμων è versus sequentis verbo ἀσχημονεῖν, quo indecorum id no- tat, cum virgo ὑπέρακμος est, nubendi tempus exce- dens, quod nonnisi secundum quid ita dicitur, unde colligere liceat κατὰ δόξαν solum ista accipi, & di- stingui in γνώμῃ Apostoli τὸ συμφέρον, quod con- ducibile est, quod συγκριτικῶς de cælibatu dixit, ob præsentem calamitatem, variam in conjugio carnis tribulationem, & calamitatem ejus, & Deo fervien- di majorem commoditatem, & τὸ εὔσχημον, quod judicio ipsorum commisit, nolens ullatenus ipsis la- queum injicere, an nubere, an verò ἄγαμοι mane- re, & utrum εὔσχημον pariter, καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ agnoscant? In illo vero casu, ubi saltem in- decorum id videatur non nubere, matrimonio ut jungantur, suadens, atque consulens.

## 7:36
Vers. 36. Εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν παρθένον αὑτοῦ νομίζει, ἐὰν ᾖ ὑπέρακμος, καὶ οὕτως ὀφείλει γίνεσθαι, ὃ θέλει, ποιείτω. If anyone thinks he is ἀσχημονεῖν, that is, ἀσχημονήσειν, the present for the future, as often, that he will undergo some disgrace through the virgin, because she is more than sufficiently mature. He has regard for the temperaments of the Corinthian girls. The masters seem to have thought the same concerning Hebrew girls, whose opinion is: If your daughter is בוגרת ὑπέρακμος, manumit your servant, so that you may make him a husband to her. This is the reason why Justinian did not want a daughter to be able to be disinherited, if she has sinned in any way against her own body, after she has reached twenty-five years of age, and the parents have delayed giving her in marriage, Nov. CXV. 3. Menander: A marriageable daughter, even if she says nothing at all, by her silence says very much about herself. Akme is the very flower of age. Those who have passed it show more of what kind of character they have, and if they are carried toward that, they are more eager. Nature does not grant these goods to early youth, which is accustomed to come soon after thirty-five years. Aschemosyne is accustomed to be said of a shameful thing, as in Rom. I. 27. But the shame of children redounds upon the parents, Prov. XIX. 13. Ei houtos opheilei genesthai: If necessity urges from the body or the mind of the girl. Opposed to this is me echon ananken, upon whom no such necessity is imposed. Ho thelei, poieito. Let him give her in marriage. For that matter, according to the custom of the Jews, which even now prevails, depended upon the authority of the fathers: and no less according to the custom of the Greeks: 'But as for my marriage, it will be the father's concern.' It is in Euripides. And in Sophocles a woman speaks thus: 'But when we reach the age of discretion, we are pushed out and sold off.' Gameitosan. Namely, she herself, and he who desires her. He had begun in the singular: He concludes in the dual; because this matter, unless between two, cannot be accomplished. Therefore, such a one who has passed the flower of age is said to be a disgrace here, not in truth, but in reputation. Therefore, 'he thinks' is added, since she who has exceeded the flower of age, being kept at home too long, seems a disgrace to her parents; as if she were either not worthy to be married; or for whose sake the parents and the whole family are despised by others: As B. Luther and also the Syriac Interpreter rendered: If anyone thinks that he is despised because of his virgin, in which sense Deut. XXV. 3. Aschemonein is said of one who is struck with more than forty stripes. Some wish for the shame to be feared from a lascivious daughter, who is not endowed with the gift of continence, to be indicated by aschemonein: Because aschemosyne is used of foul actions and pollutions, Rom. II. 16. Gen. XXXIV. 7. Exod. XXVIII. 12. Lev. XVIII. 6. Ezek. XVI. 7. 1 Cor. XI. 23. Sir. XXVI. 30. But the opposition to to euschymo is more correctly urged, so that by that word indeed every kind of decorum, greater and lesser, is implied; but by this (aschemon) every kind of indecorum, whether political and civil, or moral, is implied; but not the highest degree of ignominy or shame, cf. ch. XIII. 5. Which was observed here by B. Hülsemann against the Papists, Salmeron, Justinian, Cornelius à Lapide, who gather from this passage that, if the fear of public ignominy is absent, to be expected from a virgin daughter, unless extreme necessity urges, it is meritorious for parents to persuade their daughters to a vow of celibacy. And the late lamented one warns that the same reason exists in those words, 'and so it ought to be,' refuting the Heinsian interpretation, that it does not always signify physical necessity, or the extreme degree of moral necessity, but any civil congruity whatsoever, and one customary among neighbors, or one appropriate to good morals and custom, as a little later in ch. IX. 5. ch. XI. 7. 10. where it concerns the congruity of female attire with the quality of the sex, 2 Cor. XII. 11. 14. Heb. II. 17. ch. V. 3. 12. Therefore Luther rightly explains that indecorum of the virgin as concerning only the contempt among the common people, because the young woman is not yet betrothed, 'only that it is considered that one mocks him with his virgin, as one who has gone too long,' etc. Therefore it is false that only a case of extreme necessity allows parents to give their daughter in marriage, which Estius acknowledged, saying of the corruption of his accomplices: 'Some explain this OPORTET because of the danger of the virgin's continence.' But if the Apostle meant that, he would rather say, as above v. 9. (If she does not contain herself, let her marry) but he would not say: 'Let him do what he wants.' Which B. Luth. rightly explains: 'Then let him do what he wants, let him give her to a man, or despise the shame,' if it is in the mouth of all the common people concerning the adult age of the virgin, and he consecrates her to God, to preserve continence. Furthermore, even if it is admitted that that opheilei simultaneously looks to the danger of the virgin, if she does not have the gift of continence, as B. Hunnius, Gerhard in his book on marriage §. 536, Balduinus, Heshusius and others explained. If a parent has noticed that the daughter cannot be without marriage without danger to her modesty, let him by all means give her in marriage, and let him know that he does not sin: Yet this has nothing to do with a vow of celibacy, much less with merit. Since the discussion is only about a purpose, not a vow of preserving virginity, and a purpose can easily be changed; indeed, it ought to be, when the necessity of danger urges.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν παρθένον αὑτοῦ νομίζει, ἐὰν ᾖ ὑπέρακμος, καὶ οὕτως ὀφείλει γίνεσθαι, ὃ θέλει, ποιείτω. Si quis putat ἀσχημονεῖν, id est, ἀσχημονήσειν, Præsens pro futuro, ut sæpe, subiturum se dedecoris aliquid per vir- ginem, eo quod sit plus satis matura. Respicit Corinthia- rum puellarum ingenia. Idem de Hebræis puellis viden- tur existimasse magistri, quorum est sententia: Si filia tua sit בוגרת ὑπέρακμος, manumitte servum tuum, ut ipsi eam facias maritum. Hæc est causa, cur Justinianus noluerit exhæredari posse filiam, si quid in corpus suum peccaverit, postquam ad viginti quinque annos ætatis ve- nerit, & parentes eam nuptum dare distulerint Nov. CXV. 3. Menander: Θυγάτηρ ἐπίγαμος, κἂν ὅλως μηδὲν λαλῇ, Διὰ τὸ σιωπᾷν πλεῖστα περὶ αὑτῆς λέγει. Ἀκμὴ est flos ipse ætatis. Eam quæ supergressæ sunt, magis oftendunt, cujus sunt ingenii, & si eò ferantur, ma- gis ὀργῶσι. Hæc bona non primæ tribuit natura juventæ, Quæ cito post septem lustra venire solet. Ἀσχημοσύνη solet dici de re turpi, ut Rom. I. 27. turpi- tudo autem liberûm ad parentes redundat, Prov. XIX. 13. Εἰ ὕτως ὀφείλει γενέσθαι: Si urget necessitas ex corpore aut animo puellæ. Huic opponitur μὴ ἔχων ἀνάγκην, cui nul- la talis imponitur necessitas. Ὃ θέλει, ποιείτω. Det eam nuptum. Ea enim res more Judæorum, qui & nunc obti- net, ex autoritate patrum dependebat : nec minus more Græcorum : Τῶν δ᾽ ἐμῶν νυμφευμάτων Πατέρι μελήσει. Est apud Euripidem. Et apud Sophoclem mulier sic lo- quitur: Ὅταν δ᾽ ἐς ἥβην ἐξικώμεθ᾽ ἔμφρονες Ὠθύμεθ᾽ ἔξω καὶ διομπολούμεθα. Γαμείτωσαν. Nempe ipsa, & qui ipsam desiderat. In singulari cœ- perat: Concludit in duali; Quia res hæc, nisi inter duos, peragi non potest. Dedecori ergo esse hic dicitur talis ὑπέρακμος non κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν, sed κατὰ δόξαν. Ideo additur νομίζει, cum ea, quæ florem ætatis excessit, diu- tius domi detenta, videtur dedecori parentibus; quasi vel non digna sit, quæ ducatur; vel cujus gratia parentes & tota familia ab aliis contemnan- tur: Ut B. Lutherus nec non Syrus Interpres red- didit: Si quis putat, quod despectus sit propter vir- ginem suam, quo sensu Deut. XXV. 3. ἀσχημονεῖν dicitur, qui plagis pluribus, quam quadraginta, percutitur. Nonnulli turpitudinem à lascivien- te filia metuendam, quæ dono continentiæ præ- dita non sit, per ἀσχημονεῖν indigitari volunt: Quia ἀσχημοσύνη de fœdis actionibus & pollutionibus adhibetur, Rom. II. 16. Genes. XXXIV. 7. Exod. XXVIII. 12. Levit. XVIII. 6. Ezech. XVI. 7. 1. Co- rinth. XI. 23. Sir. XXVI. 30. Sed rectius urgetur oppositio τῶ εὐσχήμῳ, uti per illud quidem omnis generis decorum, majus & minus; per hoc verò (ἄσχημον) omnis generis indecorum, sive politicum & civile, sive morale innuatur; non verò supre- mus ignominiæ vel turpitudinis gradus, conf. cap. XIII. 5. Quod observatum hic à B. Hülse- manno ob Papistas, Salmeronem, Justinianum, Cornelium à Lapide, ex hoc loco colligentes, si absit metus publicæ ignominiæ, à filia virgine ex- pectandæ, nisi extrema necessitas urgeat, merito- rium esse parentibus, persuadere filias ad cælibatus votum. Atque eandem rationem esse monet ὁ Μα- καρίτης in illis, καὶ ὕτως ὀφείλει γενέσθαι, refellens Heinsianam interpretationem, quod non semper significet necessitatem physicam, vel extremum gra- dum necessitatis moralis, sed quamcunque congruen- tiam civilem, & inter vicinos usitatam, seu bonis moribus & consuetudini competentem, ut paulo post cap. IX. 5. c. XI. 7. 10. ubi de congruentia habi- tus fœminini cum qualitate sexus, 2. Cor. XII. 11. 14. Ebr. II. 17. c. V. 3. 12. Igitur Lutherus illud in- decorum virginis rectè exponit de solo vilipendio apud vulgus, quod juvencula nondum sit despon- sata, allein das angesehen, daß man seiner spottet mit seiner Jungfrauen, als die zu lang gegangen sey &c. Proinde falsum est, quod solus extremæ ne- cessitatis casus indulgeat parentibus elocationem filiæ in matrimonium, quod agnovit Estius, dicens de suorum complicum corruptela: Quidam istud OPORTET exponunt, ob periculum continentiæ virginis. Sed si id vellet Apostolus, potius diceret, ut supra v. 9. (Si se non continet, nubat) non autem diceret: Quod vult faciat. Quod B. Luth. rectè exponit: So thue er, was er will, er gebe sie hin ei- nem Mann, oder veracht das schämen, si in ore to- tius vulgi est de adulta virginis ætate, eamque Deo consecret, ad servandam continentiam. Porrò etsi admittatur, illud ὀφείλει simul respicere peri- culum virginis, si donum continentiæ non habeat, uti B. Hunnius, Gerhardus L. de conjugio §. 536. Balduinus, Heshusius & alii explicarunt. Si animadverterit parens, filiam sine pudicitiæ pericu- lo matrimonio carere non posse, omnino elocet eam, & sciat, se non peccare: Nihil tamen hæc ad vo- tum cælibatus, nedum ad meritum. Cum de pro- posito tantum, non voto servandæ virginitatis ser- mo sit, & propositum mutari facile possit; imò debeat, urgente necessitate periculi.

## 7:37
Vers. 37. Hos de hesteken hedraios en te kardia. He who first himself is tenacious of his own purpose, to keep his daughter a virgin. Hedraios is tenacious of purpose, below XV. 58. Col. I. 23. In the Glossary: Hedraios, firm, stable.

Me echon ananken. That is, if besides that, neither the body nor the mind of the daughter opposes such a purpose.

Exousian de echei peri tou idiou thelematos. He executes the same matter in many words, because he does not want the necessity of virginity to be imposed upon an unwilling daughter. If he has the liberty of doing what he wants, that is, if it does not depend on the daughter. For the right in this matter is great for parents, but the will of the daughter must also be regarded. Virginity is not entirely yours, it is in part the parents'.

Καὶ τοῦτο κέκρικεν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτοῦ, τοῦ τηρεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ παρθένον. Philosophers use the word κέκρικα when they have clearly determined something. See Rom. XIV. 13. And the τοῦ here, as elsewhere, is often placed before the infinitive, for which others would use τὸ. Τὴν ἑαυτοῦ, namely his daughter, for the articles serve in place of nouns, which are easily understood from the subject matter.

Kalos poiei) He does a very praiseworthy thing. He wishes to give to his daughter what is by far the best.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Ὃς δὲ ἕστηκεν ἑδραῖος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ. Qui primum ipse tenax est sui propositi, filiam servandi virginem. Ἑδραῖος est tenax propositi infra XV. 58. Col. I. 23. In Glossario: Ἑδραῖος, firmus, stabilis.

Μὴ ἔχων ἀνάγκην. Id est, si præterea tali proposito nec corpus nec animus filiæ obsistit.

Ἐξουσίαν δὲ ἔχει περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος. Multis verbis rem eandem exequitur, quia non vult no- lenti filiæ necessitatem virginitatis imponi. Si libertatem habet faciendi, quod vult, id est, si per filiam non stat. Nam jus hac in re magnum est parentum, sed & spectanda filiæ voluntas. Virginitas non tota tua est, ex parte parentum est.

Καὶ τοῦτο κέκρικεν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτοῦ, τοῦ τηρεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ παρθένον. Κέκρικα dicunt Philosophi, ubi aliquid planè decreve- runt. Vide Rom. XIV. 13. Et τοῦ hic, ut alibi, sæpe præ- ponitur Infinitivo, pro quo alii τὸ ponerent. Τὴν ἑαυτοῦ filiam scilicet, nam articuli sunt vice nominum, quæ ex subjecta materia facile intelliguntur.

Καλῶς ποιεῖ) Rem facit valde laudabilem. Dare vult filiæ, quod longe est optimum.

## 7:38
Vers. 38. Ὥστε καὶ ὁ ἐκγαμίζων, καλῶς ποιεῖ. Ἐκγαμίζειν means to betroth or to give in marriage. See Matth. XXII. 30. XXIV. 38. Luc. XVII. 27. XX. 34. 35. In the manuscript, it is γαμίζων twice.

He who does not give her in marriage does better. For there is something better than what is lawful. See what we have said in book III of the Law of War and Peace, IV. 12.

These things are rightly said by Grotius. The discourse is about the parent of a virgin who is past her prime, who has firmly resolved within himself, and is not urged by any necessity on account of his daughter, but is able to use the power of his own will freely through her, and has well weighed and judged this in his heart, to keep his daughter a virgin; the Apostle judges that he does well in this way, so that he does not do badly, but also does well, who gives his virgin daughter in marriage. If, however, a comparison is instituted between these, he judges that he does better if she is endowed with the gift of continence, and it pleases her to remain in the state of virginity, when he does not give her away, for the reasons previously adduced. The Papists think here that they have found something for the vow of celibacy, namely that the Apostle approved of it. But it is one thing, as the Papists themselves admit, to have a purpose of virginity, and another to have a vow of virginity. For it is often permitted to change a purpose without any fault, according to Bellarmine, book on Monks, chapter 24. But a vow excludes all power of entering into matrimony according to their own doctrine. Nor does the Apostle speak about the virgin herself, but about the parent of the virgin. But parents cannot make a vow for their sons or daughters, but the free consent of the one vowing is required. Jerome, book I against Jovinian, understands virginity by the word virgin, which false interpretation I have already refuted in heresy 61, which is that of the Apostolici. Epiphanius: Paul said, if anyone wishes to keep his virgin, he did not say his own virginity. He did not speak of his own body; but of the father, preserving the daughter's virginity. It is evident, however, from this, that it is the father's right to give his daughters in marriage; and that they must not marry without paternal consent, which Cornelius à Lapide rashly, and contrary to the express opinion of the Apostle, denies in this place, teaching that the Apostle does not mean that the consent of the daughter to a husband is not sufficient for marriage, unless the Father consents to it. The Apostle's words concerning the parent are clear: Let him do what he wishes.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Ὥστε καὶ ὁ ἐκγαμίζων, καλῶς ποιεῖ. Ἐκγαμίζειν est spondere, nuptum collocare. Vide Matth. XXII. 30. XXIV. 38. Luc. XVII. 27. XX. 34. 35. In Manuscripto bis est γαμίζων.

Ὁ δὲ μὴ ἐκγαμίζων κρεῖσσον ποιεῖ. Est enim aliquid licito melius. Vide, quæ diximus lib. III. de jure belli & pacis, IV. 12.

Rectè hæc dicuntur à Grotio. Sermo est de parente virginis ὑπεράκμῳ, qui firmiter penes se constituit, nec necessitate aliqua, ratione filiæ, ur- getur, sed potestate suæ voluntatis per ipsam libe- re uti valet, & hoc in corde suo probè expendit, ac dijudicavit, servare filiam suam virginem, eum bene facere ita censet Apostolus, ut non male, sed bene etiam faciat, qui nuptum elocat virginem fi- liam. Si tamen comparatio inter hæc instituatur, melius eum facere judicat, si dono continentiæ prædita sit, & placeat ipsi, in statu virginitatis ma- nere, cum eam non elocat, ob rationes antea ad- ductas. Pontificii hic putant, se invenisse aliquid pro voto cælibatus, quod nempe id approbarit Apostolus. Sed aliud est, fatentibus ipsismet Pa- pistis, propositum virginitatis, aliud virginitatis vo- tum. Propositum enim sine ulla culpa mutare sæpe li- cet, juxta Bellarm. l. de Mon. c. 24. Sed votum omnem ineundi matrimonii potestatem juxta ipsorum doctrinam excludit. Neque de virgine ipsa loquitur Apostolus, sed de parente virginita- tis. At parentes non possunt emittere votum pro filiis vel filiabus suis, sed requiritur liber consen- sus voventis. Hieron. lib. I. contra Jovin. per vir- ginem intelligit virginitatem, quam ψευδερμηνείαν refutavit jam in hæresi LXI. quæ Apostolicorum est. Epiphanius: dixit Paulus, si quis suam virgi- nem vult servare, non dixit propriam virginita- tem. Non de proprio corpore dixit; sed de patre, filiæ virginitatem asfervante. Patet verò hinc, patris esfe, nuptui dare filias; nec sine paterno consensu illis nubendum esfe, quod temere, & contra disertam Apostoli sententiam negat hoc loco Cornelius à Lapide, tradens, Apostolum non significare consensum filiæ in maritum non sufficere ad matrimonium, nisi Pater in illud consentiat. Luculenta sunt Apostoli de parente verba: Quod vult, faciat.

## 7:39
V. 39. Γυνὴ δέδεται νόμῳ ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς.

She is bound by the law of marriage. Thus we have had the word νόμος and the verb δεδέδαι also in Rom. VII. 2. But there it is according to the law of Moses. Here it is according to the law given by Christ.

The law of marriage given by Christ is not different from that which was given by Moses. It is one and the same law. And Christ recalled the Pharisees to the primeval law of marriage, but he did not deliver a new law concerning marriage.

Ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ.

We have spoken about this expression at Matt. IX. 24, XXVII. 52, John XI. 11, Acts XIII. 36. See also below XI. 30, XV. 6, 18, 20, 51, 1 Thess. IV. 13, 14, 15, 2 Pet. III. 4. In the manuscript, however, it is ἀποθάνῃ.

Ἐλευθέρα ἐσὶν, ὧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι.

That is, she has the right to decide for herself. By marrying she does nothing against Christ, she does not offend God.

Μόνον ἐν Κυρίῳ.

That is, within the Church, with a Christian, of course. See what has been said about this expression at Rom. IX. 3. Concerning the matter itself, see below 2 Cor. VI. 14. And Tertullian's book to his wife, the second. Thus the Arab understood it here.

The Apostle teaches that it is lawful for widows to marry again; otherwise than Tertullian, the Montanists, and the Novatians contended; provided that it be done in the Lord, that is, in the fear of the Lord, and therefore not precisely with a Christian, because even if she marries someone other than a Christian, or an infidel, in the fear of the Lord, she can marry, or with the invocation of the divine name. For the Apostle had previously taught that marriage with an infidel is not contrary to GOD. Therefore, Cornelius à Lapide does not rightly prove from this place the Roman Catholic Church's interdict on marriage with an infidel, and the invalidation of a Christian marriage with a pagan, and that it is a mortal sin to contract a marriage with a heretical man or woman. Where, however, he excepts Germany, Poland, and France, because there heretics are mixed with Catholics. Thus in Italy and Spain it will be a mortal sin, which in Germany, Poland, and France is not at all. But Bellarmine contradicts Cornelius, whose proposition is this: Marriage between a believer and an infidel is not invalid by divine, natural, or positive law, or by any certain law of the Church.

Latin:

V. 39. Γυνὴ δέδεται νόμῳ ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς.

Vincta est lege conjugii. Sic vocem νόμος & verbum δεδέδαι habuimus & Rom. VII. 2. Sed ibi secundum jus Mosis. Hic secundum jus à Christo datum.

Diversum non est conjugii jus à Christo datum, ab eo, quod est à Mose datum. Unum est, idemque jus. Et revocavit Christus Pharisæos ad primævam matrimonii legem, non verò novam legem tradidit de matrimonio.

Ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθῇ ὁ ἀνὴρ.

De hac loquutione diximus ad Matth. IX. 24. XXVII. 52. Joh. XI. 11. Actor. XIII. 36. Vide & infra XI. 30. XV. 6. 18. 20. 51. 1. Thess. IV. 13. 14. 15. 2. Petr. III. 4. In manuscripto tamen est ἀποθάνῃ.

Ἐλευθέρα ἐσὶν, ὧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι.

Id est, jus habet de se statuendi. Nubendo nihil facit contra Christum, Deum non offendit.

Μόνον ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Id est, intra Ecclesiam, cum Christiano scilicet. Vide quæ de hac locutione dicta ad Rom. IX. 3. De re ipsa vide infra 2. Cor. VI. 14. Et Tertulliani librum ad uxorem secundum. Ita hic accepit Arabs.

Docet Apostolus, viduis licitum esse iterum nubere; secus atque Tertullianus, Montanistæ & Novatiani contenderunt; modo id fiat in Domino, id est, in timore Domini, adeoque non præcise Christiano, quia etiamsi alii, quam Christiano, vel infideli nubat in timore Domini, nubere potest, vel cum invocatione nominis divini. Nam & conjugium cum infideli DEO adversum non esse, antea docuerat Apostolus. Non rectè ergò ex hoc loco Cornelius à Lapide probat, Romano-Catholicæ Ecclesiæ interdictum, conjugium cum infideli, & irritationem matrimonii Christiani cum pagana, & quod peccatum mortale sit, contrahere cum hæretico, vel hæretica conjugium. Ubi tamen excipit Germaniam, Poloniam, & Galliam, quod illic cum Catholicis permixti sint hæretici. Sic in Italia & Hispania peccatum mortale erit, quod in Germania, Polonia, & Gallia minime est. Cornelio autem contrariatur Bellarminus, cujus hæc est propositio: Matrimonium inter fidelem & infidelem non est irritum, jure divino, naturali, vel positivo, vel certa aliqua lege Ecclesiæ.

## 7:40
V. 40. But she is more blessed, if she so remain.

Happier, more tranquil, more secure, if she should so remain, that is, such as she is, namely unmarried. Thus οὕτως we also had above 27.

According to my judgment.

According to that counsel which I gave above 25.

The Papists take these things concerning the blessedness of the future age, and draw hither that saying of Ambrose: It is better that he should contain himself, that he may be more worthy in the future, as is to be seen from Bellarmine. But Ambrose has nothing there concerning the future age; rather he persuades widows to abstain from second marriages, that they may be more fit for the future time, to endure the calamities of this life. Nor does the Apostle speak of anything but the happiness or blessedness or tranquility of this life, which is clear from the whole context; and not indeed of the blessedness of the other world. In vain, therefore, do the Papists gather from hence a more perfect merit of celibacy over marriage, following Jerome, who was seduced by Tatian. But St. Augustine rightly, in On Holy Virginity ch. 26, says that eternal life and the kingdom of heaven are given commonly and equally to all, both to the married and to virgins, who are justified by faith freely through the redemption of Christ; for Scripture knows nothing of any human merit of that state.

And I also think that I have the Spirit of God. He does not mean revelation; but a sincere affection to serve God and the pious. See above IV. 21.

The Spirit of God is not sincerity of affection. For it is nowhere taken in that way: But it is that Spirit, by which being moved the holy men of God spoke, 2 Pet. I. 21. Therefore he joins himself with the other Apostles with the particle καὶ; κἀγὼ and I, as if to say, interpreting with Cornelius: Just as the other Apostles; so also I have the Spirit of God. That word δοκῶ I think is accepted, not as a conjectural opinion, but as a certain assertion, even by Papist interpreters, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, etc. And Augustine observes, tract. 32 in John, that it is not the word of one doubting; but of one asserting. It is used by the holy Apostle, however, for the sake of modesty and humility.

Latin:

V. 40. Μακαριωτέρα δέ ἐστιν, ἐὰν οὕτω μένῃ.

Felicior, tranquillior, securior, si ita maneat, id est, qualis est, innupta nimirum. Ita οὕτως & supra habuimus 27.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην.

Secundum id consilium, quod dedi supra 25.

Pontificii hæc de beatitudine futuri seculi accipiunt, & huc trahunt illud Ambrosii: Melius est, ut se contineat, ut dignior sit in futuro, ut è Bellarm. videre est. Sed ibi Ambrosius de seculo futuro nihil habet; sed abstinentiam à secundis nuptiis suadet viduis, ut aptiores sint in tempus futurum, ad sufferendas hujus vitæ calamitates. Nec nisi de felicitate vel beatitudine aut tranquillitate hujus vitæ loquitur Apostolus, quod è toto contextu liquet; non verò de beatitudine alterius seculi. Frustrà ergo perfectius meritum cælibatus præ conjugio cum Hieronymo, à Tatia- no seducto, hinc colligunt Pontificii. Recte au- tem S. Augustinus de Sancta virginitate c. 26. vitam æternam & regnum cælorum ait communiter & ex æquo dari omnibus & conjugibus & virginibus, qui fide gratis per redemptionem Christi justificati; De merito enim humano illius status nihil novit scriptura.

Δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα Θεῶ ἔχειν. Non intelligit revelationem; sed sincerum affectum DEO & piis serviendi. Vide supra IV. 21.

Πνεῦμα Θεῶ non est sinceritas affectus. Sic enim nuspiam sumitur: Sed est Spiritus ille; quo φερό- μενοι loquuti sunt sancti DEI homines, 2. Pet. I. 21. Ideo se cum aliis Apostolis particulâ καὶ conjun- git: κἀγὼ & ego, q. d. interprete Cornelio: Sic- ut alii Apostoli; Ita & ego Spiritum DEI habeo. Illud δοκῶ puto, non de opinione conjecturali, sed certâ sententiâ etiam Pontificii Interpp. Estius, Cornelius à Lapide &c. accipiunt. Et observat August. tract. 32. in Joh. Illud non dubitantis esse; sed asseverantis. Modestiæ autem & humilitatis causa adhibetur à S. Apostolo.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

The Apostle, being informed concerning things sacrificed to idols, requires not only knowledge, but love; he teaches that an idol is nothing in itself, since there is but one God; and concerning those who make a conscience for themselves about the eating of things sacrificed to idols, he warns that they pollute their conscience, and asserts liberty in the eating of food, provided it be not done with the scandal of the weak, which he commands to be guarded against, lest the brother perish, for whom Christ died, and sin be committed against Christ himself.

There are two parts: I. Concerning the nullity of idols v. 6. II. Concerning the liberty of those eating things sacrificed to idols, with the condition of avoiding scandal.

PART I. Concerning the nullity of idols.

Vers. 1. Now concerning things sacrificed to idols. Concerning pollutions, of meats offered in sacrifice. We said at chapter XV of Acts that things sacrificed to idols, insofar as they were forbidden by the Apostolic decree, which Paul also preached everywhere, as is to be known from Acts XVI. 4, are of two kinds. For either the portions were given upon the altar, and the rest of the entrails returned to him who had offered the victims, who then signified that he had sacrificed to his friends, and that he prayed them to come to the returned entrails: Or the portions were given at a table before the guests in a place which served in the stead of an altar, and then the banquet was begun in the same place. Another custom had also prevailed at Corinth, that those who had won at the Isthmian games would give a banquet to the people in the very temple after the public sacrifice. I believe others did the same among themselves as fellow-initiates or fellow-members of a religious guild. All these things; but above the rest this third one could hardly receive any other interpretation from common sense than that the worship of idols was approved by those who ate of such sacrificial offerings. See Num. XIV. 2. But those Corinthians, Christians in name, Greek philosophers at heart, just as they did with the matter of the incestuous man, so too they dragged this into certain dialectical disputes. An idol does not exist in reality, which was true of those Corinthian gods: for Jupiter, Apollo, Venus, Leucothea, and Palaemon had been men who had long since perished. Therefore εἰδωλόθυτα are to the Hebrews זבחי מתים. That which does not exist cannot contaminate the soul. Therefore there is no sin in it if I feast in a temple: if I go when called to the entrails; if after the portions have been given to the fire I recline at the table. Thus those men, of whom Trypho also says: And indeed I inquire of many of those who profess to acknowledge Jesus, and are called Christians, that they eat of things sacrificed to idols, and say that they are in no way harmed. Paul, who had the Spirit of Christ, and referred all things not to the subtleties of disputes, but to use, to the honor of GOD, to drawing away the greatest number from paganism, and to retaining in Christianity those who had already begun to be Christians, treated such matters both more sincerely and, as usually follows, more perspicaciously. And so, with Apostolic prudence, he answers the pious from Corinth who had consulted him on this matter. Agreeing with whom, Justin replies to Trypho these things: 'And from the fact that these men confess themselves to be Christians, and confess the crucified Jesus to be both Lord and Christ, and not teaching his teachings, but those from the spirits of error, we, the disciples of the true, pure teaching of Jesus Christ, become more faithful and more certain.' Valeria, when those who were deposing her from the pack-animal were urging her to eat of the idol-offerings, and she testified that it was not at all permitted to her, because she was a Christian, was slaughtered. Thus Ado on the 28th of April in the Martyrology.

The occasion and summary of this information concerning idol-offerings is not quite correctly handed down by Grotius. For it stands thus: Since some of the Corinthians were accustomed to attend the banquets and idol-offerings prepared by the Gentiles, but others were affected by scandal from this, who, led by conscience, considered the eating of idol-offerings as some participation in idolatry: Therefore, information was sought from the Apostle concerning it. Who at the beginning premises, as if for the sake of preparation, the doctrine concerning knowledge regarding the use of indifferent things, that when it is destitute of love, and not joined with practice, looking to the honor of God and the edification of the neighbor, it only renders men puffed up; Because although all acknowledge that idols are nothing in the world, but that there is only one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, from whom are all things, and to whom all ought to tend; Only one Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom all uniquely arrive at God; however many gods and lords and saviors may be believed and worshipped both in heaven and on earth; Yet they were not sufficiently informed concerning those indifferent things; nor was the knowledge of all joined with the love owed both to God and to the neighbor, and thus both the glory of God is sinned against and the neighbor is affected by scandal. Furthermore, the Apostle warns that primarily the conscience must be taken into account. For although any food is in itself lawful, and there is no difference to be sought in it; If, however, anyone doubtful about idol-offerings participates in them at the banquets of the Gentiles, he teaches that his own weak conscience is contaminated. That this, therefore, must be looked into, lest a stumbling block be placed for other weak ones. For if any of the weaker ones sees another, who has knowledge, participating in the eating of idol-offerings with the Gentiles, he can easily be affected by scandal and thus be destroyed, he who was redeemed by Christ: In which way it will be acted against the love of the neighbor, and it will be sinned against Christ himself, to whose glory all things ought to serve.

That those who provided the occasion for the question were Christians in name, but Greek philosophers within, is more easily said than proved. The contrary rather appears from the fact that the Apostle joins himself with those by whom the occasion was provided, by reason of his knowledge and profession, and desires not so much knowledge, but love in them. For he says, verse 1, concerning idol-offerings, 'that we all have knowledge,' and further v. 4, concerning the eating of idol-offerings, v. 4, 'we know that no idol is in the world': Making that knowledge common to himself and them, and pronouncing concerning himself and them v. 6, 'To us there is one God and one Lord.' Nor is it established that a scruple remained for the Corinthians from this, that since an idol does not exist in reality, and idol-offerings are nothing, no sin is committed if one feasts with the Gentiles in a temple; if he goes when called to the entrails, if he reclines at a table after the portions have been given to the forum. These things were not proposed for the sake of an objection, or by way of counter-objection, to remove a doubt (which Grotius wants). For that was beyond doubt among all who were converted to the faith of Christ, that there were no gods of the Gentiles, and no saviors whom they worshipped, that there was only one God, only one Savior Christ: Nor was there any doubt about this, that one must not communicate in the idolatry of the Gentiles, or that no sin is committed in the participation of the same, so far is it from being the case that they were induced by that reasoning, because idols do not exist in reality, that idolatry also is in reality nothing, even if one should communicate with idolatrous Gentiles in idol-temples: Because what does not exist cannot contaminate the mind. Such a method of philosophizing would have been very crude and inept; and it cannot be presumed even of the sounder philosophers, let alone of those who had been converted to the faith of Christ. But a doubt had arisen, whether it is sinned by the frequenting of an idolatrous table, and the eating of idol-offerings, since those things seem to be entirely indifferent, just as also abstinence from blood and things strangled. Whence the Corinthians erred here concerning the use of indifferent things, and were to be more correctly informed about it by the Apostle: Since those things are indifferent. The use of idol-offerings was indeed forbidden by the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15. But that prohibition was temporary. Nor is the use of them prohibited here; but a tempering is applied, lest there be doubtful consciences, and it be done with the scandal of the weaker ones. And therefore that is not condemned, as if it were in itself idolatrous, but it is guarded against, lest the weak conscience be harmed. Nothing in the present chapter yet concerning what they call participated idolatry, which is entirely prohibited, and is a most grave sin, since it is at least concerning the use of a thing not prohibited, namely of the remains of foods which had been offered to idols, when they were prepared at the banquets of the Gentiles to which Christians were invited as neighbors. For concerning that, chapter 10:29, the Apostle warns: If any of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat everything that is set before you, asking no questions for conscience' sake. But if anyone says to you, this is an idol-offering, do not eat for the sake of him who pointed it out, and for conscience' sake: I say conscience, not ONE'S OWN, but that of the other. If the eating of them were prohibited in itself, everyone would be bound to abstain from them for the sake of their own conscience. But when infidels require the eating of them as a symbol of communion with their idolatry, which happened to Valeria, their enjoyment is entirely prohibited, and there is μετοχὴ καὶ κοινωνία with the infidels and their idols. Which is also to be observed in the examples and opinions of the Martyrs and other ancients, who rigidly abstained from things sacrificed to idols, and taught that one must abstain, brought forward by Voetius in part IV, diss. sel. p. 249, which he drags to that point in vain, as if every eating of things sacrificed to idols were prohibited. Alleging also for that opinion on p. 256 B. Balduinus in cases of conscience book II, ch. XIV, case VII, where the plain contrary is held, namely that it was formerly permitted for Christians to eat at the banquets of the Gentiles on things sacrificed to idols, which B. Balduinus confirms in the same place from 1 Cor. 10:27. And in Comm. on this passage p. 392. This, he says, is the nature of all things indifferent, that the use of them cannot harm a rightly informed conscience. It does, however, harm the conscience of a neighbor not yet rightly instructed. Thus the eating of things sacrificed to idols, as Paul admits in this chapter, v. 8, commends no one to GOD, and thus it is FREE, and is left as INDIFFERENT to anyone, and yet it is added in v. 13, If food shall scandalize my brother, I will not eat flesh forever. Although indeed it was prohibited by divine law that the Israelites should eat things sacrificed to idols, so that they might be the more drawn away from impious cults, to which they were very prone, and the Apostles prohibited the same at the beginnings of the Church: nevertheless afterwards by various cases that arose, where Gentiles converted to the Christian faith were invited by their relatives to banquets, at which idol-meats were also served, the Apostle instructed the Corinthians concerning Christian liberty, that the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof, and that to the pure all things are pure, so that no scruple that liberty to the rule of charity, lest a weak neighbor be affected by scandal through the abuse of the same. Therefore, interpreters assign such a theme to the Apostle in this place: Idol-meats do not defile, except for him who eats them under the opinion of some divinity inherent either in the image or in the thing signified by the image to which those things offered were dedicated, and with a hesitation of conscience whether it is lawful to eat the same or not? For even he who eats while thus hesitating is defiled.

We know that we all have knowledge.

Lest those puffed up ones think that they alone are wise, we understand no less than they what an idol or a fictitious god is. All, that is, the greatest part of us, as in Romans 3:12. How that which follows is also to be taken.

There is no need for the universal particle to be restricted. For although the knowledge of all was not equal, yet all knew this, that idols are nothing, and that idol-meats have no peculiar efficacy, even if perhaps not all were fully informed about the use of these. Nor did all use their knowledge rightly. But they were rather puffed up by it, instead of using it for the glory of God and the edification of their neighbor. Whence he notes that knowledge separated from practice is what puffs up, but does not edify. Indeed, that Grotius-style restriction of the passage in Romans 3:12 is false. For not only did the greatest part of men fall away from God, but we all fell away, without any exception.

Knowledge puffs up.

It is accustomed to do this: it does so in many things.

But love edifies.

Love dictates that in all things one must see what is expedient for the common good. See Romans 14:19, 15:2. Where there is a noun corresponding to this verb, edification. Paul often uses both this noun and the verb.

Knowledge does not edify; but only puffs up, if it is without charity: conversely, if charity is sincere, it does not puff up, but edifies, as the opposition demands.

Latin:

CAPUT IIX. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

De idolothytis informatus Apostolus, non sci- entiam solùm, sed dilectionem requirit, idolum per se nihil esse docet, cum non sit nisi unus DEUS, deque iis, qui sibi super idolothytorum esu conscientiam faciunt, monet, quod conscientiam polluant, & li- bertatem in escæ esu asserit, modo non fiat cum infirmorum scandalo, quod præ- cavere jubet, ne pereat frater, pro quo Christus mortuus est, & in Christum ipsum peccetur.

Partes duæ sunt I. De idolorum nullitate v. 6. II. De idolothytis vescentium libertate, cum conditione vitandi scandali.

PARS I. De idolorum nullitate.

Vers. 1. Περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων. Περὶ τῶν ἀλισγημάτων, de immolatitiis carnibus. Di- ximus ad caput XV. Actorum εἰδωλόθυτα quatenus Apo- stolico decreto, quod ubique prædicavit etiam Paulus, ut cognoscere est Act. XVI. 4. vetita sunt, esse duûm ge- nerum. Nam aut in aram data prosecta, & cætera exta reddita ei, qui victimas obtulerat, qui deinde significabat, amicis se sacrificasse, & orare se eos, ut ad reddita exta venirent: Aut apud mensam coram convivis in locum, qui erat vice aræ data prosecta, ac deinde cœptum ibi- dem convivium. Corinthi & alius mos invaluerat, ut qui Isthemiis vicerant populo in ipso templo post sacrificium publicum darent epulum. Idem credo fecisse inter se alios συμμύσας sive συνθιασιώτας. Hæc omnia; sed supra cætera tertium hoc ex sensu communi aliam interpretationem vix poterat recipere, quam ab iis, qui talibus immolati- tiis vescebantur approbari cultum idolorum. Vide Num. XIV. 2. At isti Corinthii, nomine Christiani, intus Græ- canici philosophi, sicut illud de incestis, ita & hoc ad dialecticas quasdam disputationes trahebant. Idolum re ipsa non subsistit, quod verum erat de Diis illis Corin- thiis: Nam Jupiter, Apollo, Venus, Leucothea, Palæmon homines fuerant, qui jam olim interierant. Ideo εἰδωλό- θυτα Hebræis זבחי מתים. Quod non est, contami- nare animum non potest. Nihil ergò in eo peccati, si in templo epuler: si ad exta vocatus eam; si post prosecta in focum data mensæ accumbam. Sic illi, de quibus & Tryphon: καὶ μὴν πολλοὺς τῶν τὸν ἰησοῦν λεγόντων ὁμολο- γεῖν, καὶ λεγομένων χρισιανῶν, πυνθάνομαι ἐσθίοντά εἰδωλό- θυτα, καὶ μηδὲν βλάπτεσθαι λέγειν. Paulus qui Christi ha- bebat Spiritum, & omnia non ad disputationum subtilita- tes, sed ad usum, ad DEI honorem, ad plurimos à pa- ganismo abstrahendos, ad retinendos in Christianismo, qui jam Christiani esse cœperant, referebat, & sincerius, & quod sequi solet perspicacius talia tractabat. Itaque piis ex Corintho, qui ipsum hac de re consuluerant, Apostolica prudentia respondet. Cui consentiens Justinus Tryphoni hæc reponit: καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τούτους εἶναι ἄνδρας ὁμολογεῖται ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι χριστιανοὺς, καὶ τὸν σταυρωθέντα Ἰησοῦν ὁμολογεῖν καὶ κύριον, καὶ χριστὸν, καὶ μὴ τὰ ἐκείνου διδάγματα διδάσκοντας, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῶν τῆς πλάνης πνευμάτων, ἡμεῖς οἱ τῆς ἀλη- θινῆς Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ καθαρᾶς διδασκαλίας μαθηταὶ, πιστότεροι καὶ βεβαιότεροι γινόμεθα. Valeria cum eam deponentes de sa- gmario hortarentur de idolothytis manducare, nec sibi omnino licitum testaretur, quia esset Christiana, mactata est. Sic Ado ad IV. Calendas Maji in Martyrologio.

Occasio, & summa hujus de idolothytis infor- mationis non satis rectè à Grotio traditur. Ita verò habet: Quum è Corinthiis nonnulli con- viviis & idolothytis gentilium apparatis interesse consueverint, alii verò inde scandalo affecti fue- rint, qui conscientiâ ducti esum idolothytorum pro idololatrias aliquâ communicatione habe- bant: Idcircò de eo expetita fuit ab Apostolo in- formatio. Qui initio præmittit, veluti παρασκευῆς ἕνεκα, doctrinam de γνώσει de usu rerum indiffe- rentium, quod ea charitate destitutâ, nec cum praxi, honorem DEI & ædificationem proximi respiciente conjuncta, inflatos modo reddat; Quod etsi agnoscant omnes, idola nihil esse in mundo, sed unum tantùm Deum esse, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, ex quo omnia, & ad quem omnes tendere oporteat; Unum tantùm Dominum & Salvatorem, Jesum Christum, per quem omnia & per quem omnes unicè ad Deum perveniant; utut plures credantur & colantur Dii & Domini ac Salvatores tùm in cœlo tum in ter- ra; Non tamen satis de illis indifferentibus infor- mati sint; nec omnium notitia conjuncta sit cum charitate debita tùm DEO, tùm proximo, adeo- que & adversus DEI gloriam peccetur & proxi- mus scandalo afficiatur. Porrò autem monet A- postolus, quod imprimis conscientia ratio habenda sit. Etsi enim esca qualibet per se licita sit, nec in ea quærenda aliqua differentia; Si tamèn quis dubius de idolothytis in conviviis Ethnicorum de illis participet, conscientiam infirmam ipsius con- taminari docet. Hoc itaque dispiciendum esse, ne aliis infirmis offendiculum ponatur. Siqui- dem si viderit infirmiorum quis alium, qui co- gnitionem habet, de idolis, de esu τῶν εἰδωλοθύ- των cum gentilibus participare, facilè scandalo affici adeoque ita perdi possit, qui à Christo re- demptus est: Quo pacto contra proximi chari- tatem agetur, & in Christum ipsum peccabitur, cujus gloriæ debebant inservire omnia.

Qui autem quæstioni occasionem præbuêre, nomine Christianos, intus Græcanicos Philosophos fuisse facilius dicitur, quàm probatur. Contra- rium potius ex eo apparet, quod se scientiæ & professionis suæ ratione, cum illis, à quibus oc- casio præbita fuit, conjungat Apostolus, nec γνῶσιν adeò, sed ἀγάπην in eis desideret. Nam οἴδαμεν, inquit, versu 1. de idolothytis, ὅτι πάν- τες γνῶσιν ἔχομεν & porrò v. 4. de esu τῶν εἰδωλο- θύτων v. 4. οἴδαμεν ὅτι οὐδὲν εἴδωλον ἐν κόσμῳ: No- titiam illam sibi & ipsis communem faciens, & de se & ipsis pronuncians v. 6. Nobis unus est Deus & unus Dominus. Neque constat scrupu- lum inde Corinthiis hæsisse, quod quum idolum reipsâ non subsistat, neque idolothyta quicquam sint, nihil peccetur, si in templo quis cum genti- libus epuletur; si ad exta vocatus eat, si post pro- secta in forum data mensæ accumbat. Hæc non objectionis causa, vel κατ' ἀνθυποφορὰν proposita, ut dubium, (quod vult Grotius) eximat. Nam id extra dubium erat penes omnes ad fidem Christi conversos, nullos esse gentilium Deos, nullos & Sospitatores, quos ipsi colebant, unum tantùm esse Deum, unum tantùm Salvatorem Christum: Neque de eo dubium erat, non esse idololatriæ gentilium communicandum, aut nullum pecca- tum in participatione ejusdem committi, tantum abest, ut illâ ratione inducerentur, quia idola reipsâ non subsistant, idololatriam etiam reverâ nullam esse, si maximè quis cum gentibus ido- lolatricis in idoleis communicet: . Quia quod non est, animum contaminare non potest. Qualis phi- losophandi ratio admodum crassa, & inepta fuis- set; ac ne de Philosophis quidem sanioribus, ne- dum de iis, qui ad fidem Christi conversi erant, præsumi potest. Sed dubium subortum erat, an- ne adeò peccetur frequentatione mensæ idololatricæ, & esu idolothytorum, cum illa ἀδιάφορα omninò videantur vel indifferentia, quemadmodum etiam abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato. Unde circa usum indifferentium hic aberrarunt Corinthii, & de eo rectius informandi erant ab Apostolo: Quum illa sint ἀδιάφορα. Vetitus quidem erat εἰδωλοθύτων usus Concilio Hierosolymitano Act. XV. Sed interdictum illud temporale erat. Nec pro- hibetur hic usus illorum; sed temperamentum ad- hibetur, ne dubiæ conscientiæ sint, & cum scan- dalo infirmiorum is fiat. Ideoque non damnatur ille, ceu per se idololatricus, sed cavetur, ne con- scientia infirma lædatur. Nihil in præsenti adhuc capite de idololatria participata quam vocant, quæ omnino prohibita, & peccatum gravissimum est, quum saltem de usu rei non prohibitæ, cibo- rum nempe ab iis, qui oblati erant idolis, reli- quorum, cum in conviviis Ethnicorum Christia- nis propinquis ad ea invitatis appararentur. De eo enim cap. X. 29. monet Apostolus: Si quis infidelium invitaverit vos & vultis accedere, omne quod vobis apponitur, edite, nihil disputantes pro- pter conscientiam. Si quis verò dixerit vobis, hoc est idolothytum, ne edatis propter eum, qui indica- vit, & conscientiam: Conscientiam dico non PRO- PRIAM, sed alterius. Si per se prohibitus esset esus illorum, ob conscientiam propriam quisque ab eis abstinere teneretur. Quum verò infideles esum eorum requirant in symbolum communio- nis cum idololatria ipsorum, quod Valeriæ ac- cidit, omnino prohibita est eorum fruitio, & cum infidelibus, & idolis eorum μετοχὴ καὶ κοινωνία. Quod etiam observandum in exemplis & senten- tiis Martyrum & aliorum veterum, qui rigidè ab idolothytis abstinebant, & abstinendum esse do- cebant, à Voëtio parte IV. diss. sel. p. 249. addu- ctis, quæ nequicquam eò abripit, quasi omnis ido- lothytorum esus prohibitus sit. Allegans etiam in eam sententiam p. 256. B. Balduinum in casibus conscientiæ l. II. c. XIV. casu VII. ubi planè con- trarium habetur, nimirum Christianis olim vesci licuisse inEthnicorum conviviis idolothytis,quod B. Balduinus è 1. Cor. X. 27. ibidem confirmat. Et in Comm. ad h. l. p. 392. Est hac, inquit, adia- phororum omnium natura, ut usus eorum consci- entiam rectè informati lædere non possit. Lædit ta- men conscientiam proximi nondum rectè instructi. Ita esus Idolothytorum, fatente Paulo, in hoc capite, v. 8. neminem comm DEO commendat, atque sic LIBER, atque INDIFFERENS cuivis relinqui- tur, & tamen additur v. 13. Si esca scandalizave- rit fratrem meum, non vescar carnibus in æter- num. Quanquam verò lege divinâ prohibitum fuerit, ne Israëlitæ ederent idolothyta, ut eò ma- gis ab impiis cultibus, ad quos valdè proni erant, avocarentur, & sub primordia Ecclesiæ idem pro- hibuerint Apostoli: Postmodum tamen variis incidentibus casibus, ubi conversis ad fidem Chri- stianam gentilibus à cognatis invitatis ad convi- via, in quibus etiam idolothyta apponebantur, Apostolus de libertate Christiana Corinthios in- formavit, quod Domini sit terra, & omnis pleni- tudo ejus, quod mundis omnia sint munda, ne scru- pulus conscientiis injiciatur. Restringit tamen li- bertatem ad regulam charitatis, ne proximus in- firmus scandalo per abusum ejusdem afficiatur. Ideo thema Apostoli hoc loco tale Interpp. assi- gnant: Idolothyta non inquinant, nisi eum, qui ista comedit, sub opinione alicujus divinitatis inhæren- tis seu simulacro, seu rei per simulacrum signatæ, cui oblata illa fuère, & hæsitatione conscientiæ, anne liceat iisdem vesci, nec ne? Nam & ille, qui ita hæsitans vescitur, inquinatur.

Οἴδαμεν, ὅτι πάντες γνῶσιν ἔχομεν.

Ne isti πεφυσιωμένοι putent, se solos sapere, non minus & nos intelligimus, quid sit idolum sive Deus commen- titius. Πάντες id est, pars maxima nostrum ut Rom. III. 12. Quomodo sumendum & quod sequitur.

Non opus est, ut restringatur particula uni- versalis. Nam etsi non omnium æqualis fuerit notitia, omnes tamen hoc norant, quod idola nihil sint, & idolothyta nullam peculiarem ha- beant efficaciam, utut fortè non omnes plenè de usu horum informati essent. Neque omnes utebantur notitiâ suâ recte. Sed superbiebant po- tius eadem, quam ut eadem ad gloriam DEI & ædificationem proximi uterentur. Unde notat γνῶσιν à praxi sejunctam, quod inflet, non verò ædi- ficet. Illa vero loci Rom. III. 12. restrictio Gro- tiana falsa est. Non enim tantùm pars maxima hominum à DEO defecit, sed defecimus omnes, sine ullius exceptione.

Ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ.

Solet hoc facere: facit in multis.

Ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ.

Dilectio dictat in rebus omnibus videndum quid in commune expediat. Vide Rom. XIV. 19. XV. 2. Ubi no- men est huic verbo respondens οἰκοδομῆ. Sæpe & nomine hoc & verbo Paulus utitur.

Notitia non ædificat; sed tantum inflat, si sine charitate sit: Vicissim charitas si sincera sit, non inflat, sed ædificat, ut postulat oppositio.

## 8:2
V. 2. But if anyone thinks that he knows anything.

That is, if anyone pleases himself in this one thing, that he is clever, that he is learned, that he knows dialectical disputes. Concerning this meaning of the word to think, see what we have said at Matthew 3:9 and Mark 10:42. So also below in 11:16. In the manuscript it is to have known, so that one word is repeated three times.

He has not yet known anything as he ought to know.

He is ignorant of this, which is the principal thing, that knowledge in itself is not saving, but only insofar as it leads to love. To know, as one ought, is to use knowledge rightly for one's own salvation and that of others.

Latin:

V. 2. Εἰ δέ τις δοκεῖ εἰδέναι τι.

Id est, si quis in hoc uno sibi placeat, quod ingeniosus, quod eruditus sit, quod dialecticas disputationes norit. De hac significatione vocis δοκεῖν vide quæ diximus ad Matth. III. 9. & Marc. X. 42. Sic & infra XI. 16. In ma- nuscripto est ἐγνωκέναι, ut una vox ter repetatur.

Οὐδέπω οὐδὲν ἔγνωκε καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι.

Hoc, quod præcipuum est, ignorat, cognitionem per se non esse salutiferam, sed quatenus ad dilectionem ducit. Scire, ut oportet, est scientia recte uti ad suam & aliorum salutem.

## 8:3
Εἰ δέ τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν Θεὸν.

Connected to this is also that, that one's neighbor should be loved for the sake of God.

Οὗτος ἔγνωσται ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.

Again, Antanaklasis. For he had used ἔγνωκεν in one sense, and in another sense he says ἔγνωσται, Matt. VII. 27: οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς. So also Rom. VII. 15, VIII. 29, XI. 2, 2 Tim. II. 19, 1 Thess. V. 12, 19, John XVII. 3, Psalm I. 6: γινώσκει κύριος ὁδὸν δικαίων, that is, he approves, he loves. Thus wisdom, Prov. VIII. 7: ἐγὼ τὺς ἐμὲ φιλῦντας ἀγαπῶ. Similar is the antanaklasis in the verb of knowing in Gal. IV. 9, and here below in XIII. 12.

Thus the Apostle reproves the empty persuasion of wisdom, which is vain without love, and calls back those who are puffed up to the knowledge of their own infirmity, and warns that the knowledge of oneself is also acquired for the sake of charity, so that we may be rightly occupied in matters of indifference. It is not enough to know something in a general way;

-but at the same time all circumstances must be perceived. And the fall of human intellect is very easy. Therefore, nothing is safer or better than to think humbly of oneself, and always to pray to the Lord that He may rule us by His Holy Spirit and suggest salutary counsels. But then we ought to glory in this rather, that we are known by GOD through Christ, as his household and friends, than that we know many things.

Latin:

Εἰ δέ τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν Θεὸν.

Cui connexum est & illud, ut proximus diligatur pro- pter Deum.

Οὗτος ἔγνωσται ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.

Rursum Ἀντανάκλασις. Nam alio sensu dixerat ἔγνωκεν, alio sensu dicit ἔγνωσται Matth. VII. 27. οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς. Sic & Rom. VII. 15. IIX. 29. XI. 2. 2. Tim. II. 19. 1. Thess. V. 12. 19. Joh. XVII. 3. Psal. I. 6. γινώσκει κύριος ὁδὸν δικαίων, id est, approbat ἀγαπᾷ. Sic sapientia Prov. VIII. 7. ἐγὼ τὺς ἐμὲ φιλῦντας ἀγαπῶ. Similis est ἀντανά- κλασις in verbo noscendi Gal. IV. 9. & hic infra XIII. 12.

Ita Inanem sapientiæ persuasionem, quæ vana est sine dilectione, reprehendit Apostolus, & τὺς πε- φυσιωμένυς revocat ad cognitionem propriæ in- firmitatis, ac suam solam notitiam ad charitatem etiam acquiri, ut recte in adiaphoris occupemur, monet. Non satis est nosse aliquid in genere;

-fed simul omnes circumstantiæ perspiciendæ sunt. Et facillimus est lapsus humani ingenii. Ideo ni- hil est tutius aut melius, quàm submissè de se sen- tire, & semper orare Dominum, ut nos regat suo Spiritu Sancto, & salutaria suggerat consilia. Tum verò in eo potius gloriari debemus, quod nos no- ti simus DEO per Christum, tanquam domesti- ci & amici ejus, quam quod nos multa cogno- scamus.

## 8:4
V. 4. Περὶ τῆς βρώσεως ὖν τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων.

Having prefaced certain very necessary generalities, he returns to the specific chapter.

Οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἐδὲν εἴδωλον ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.

Those gods are imaginary things. Therefore they are called אלילים or הבלים, μάταια, and שקרים, ψευδῆ. An idol is nothing. Thus Origen in Exodus, and Cedrenus following him in the life of Theodorus. Theophilus, book 1: the names of the gods you say you worship are the names of dead men. Arnobius, book VI: It is easy to worship dead men instead of immortal gods. See what follows there, and Clement in his Exhortation to the Gentiles, and Lactantius II. 14 and following. Therefore the Jews [call them] sons of the ever-living GOD in the additions to Esther.

Idol here does not mean only statues or images, as the Papists wish, but also fictitious gods, whose statues and images they are, and thus it includes whatever is falsely worshipped as GOD, which honor is also referred to the images and statues themselves by certain idolaters. For although some gods in the world were something, just as statues are something in the world materially, they are nevertheless nothing formally, in that they are worshipped as gods; because there is no God but one.

And that there is no other God except one. Not many Gods.

This must be opposed to the Socinians, who contend that more than one GOD are to be religiously worshipped, against whom, because we have disputed at length in natural and revealed Theology, we do not wish to do the work already done here.

Latin:

V. 4. Περὶ τῆς βρώσεως ὖν τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων.

Generalia quædam admodum necessaria præfatus, redit πρὸς τὸ εἰδικὸν κεφάλαιον.

Οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἐδὲν εἴδωλον ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.

Dii isti res sunt imaginariæ. Ideo vocantur אלילים vel הבלים, μάταια & שקרים ψευδῆ. Idolum est ἐκ ὄν. Ita Origenes in Exodum, & eum sequutus in vita Theodori Cedrenus. Theophilus libro 1. τὰ ὀνόματα ὧν φὴς σέβεσθαι θεῶν ὀνόματά ἐσι νεκρῶν ἀνθρώπων. Arnobius libro VI. Promptum est, pro Diis immortalibus mortuos sos colere. Vide quæ ibi sequuntur, & Clementem Admoni- tione ad Gentes, & Lactantium II. 14. & sequentibus. Ideò Judæi filii semper viventis DEI in additionibus ad Estherem.

Idolum hic non statuas solùm vel imagines, quod Papistæ volunt, sed Deos etiam fictitios, quorum statuæ & imagines sunt, adeoque quic- quid falsò pro DEO colitur, qui honor ipsis quo- que imaginibus & statuis ab idololatris quibus- dam refertur, complectitur. Nam quanquam non- nulli Dii in mundo aliquid fuerint, uti & statuæ aliquid in mundo sunt materialitèr, ἐδὲν tamen sunt formaliter, qua coluntur ut Dii; quia non est, nisi unus Deus.

Καὶ ὅτι ἐδεὶς Θεὸς ἕτερος εἰ μὴ εἷς. Non plures Dii.

Hoc Socinianis opponendum, qui plures uno DEO religiose colendos contendunt, adversus quos quia prolixè disputavimus in Theologia na- turali & revelata, nolumus hic actum agere.

## 8:5
V. 5. For even if there are so-called gods.

Even if some exist, who in reality have the name of Gods, and are called אלהים. As in 2 Thess. II. 4. 'above every one that is called God'.

Whether in heaven.

As the Sun, moon, stars.

Whether on the earth.

As living Kings. But if those stars and those Kings are not Gods to us, much less are those who do not exist.

As there are many gods.

Namely, according to the manner of speaking accepted among the nations: 'so-called' as he said just now.

And many lords.

בעלים For thus in the east the Gods of the nations were called.

Crellius wishes to designate by θεὸς λεγομένως & κυρίως angels and magistrates, the former in heaven, the latter on earth. But more correctly, with Irenaeus, book III, ch. 6, Chrysostom, and Theophylact on this passage, they are understood as the gods and lords of the Gentiles, and the idols which were worshipped by the Gentiles as gods and lords, whether of all things or as heroes and servants of GOD, whom they likewise worshipped religiously. We confirmed this sense in Theol. natur. & revel. p. 461, and Faustus Socinus acknowledged it in Anti-Wuj. page 25. The subject there is the divinity to be worshipped and the gods of the Gentiles, and the idols which were worshipped by them. First, that one God is opposed, then also Christ, as our one Lord. Moreover, an opposition is instituted between idols and the gods of the Gentiles and the true God; idols are said to be nothing in the world, namely, in truth of fact, and one God is asserted to be the true God, where the Apostle seems to allude to Ps. XCVI. 5, since the gods of the Gentiles are said there to be אלילים (Conf. Lev. XIX. 4. Es. IX. 10.) that is, ἐδὲν or ἐδαμινοὶ, just as they are also called μηδὲν ὄντες by the Hellenists in 1 Sam. XII. 21. Since, therefore, idols are nothing, And since the Apostle asserted that God alone is the true God, he explains in turn each member of the opposition, in that by idols he understands the gods and lords of the Gentiles, who are many and various; but by the one true God and Lord, the Father, from whom are all things, and Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, he designates. There is no trace of angels and magistrates in this text; nor could there be any doubt that they are called gods in a far different sense than the one who is truly God by nature himself; but the idols of the heathens, whose feasts the Christians were eating from the remains of the sacrifices, were to be annihilated, and the distinction between Christians and heathens was to be clearly inculcated. Therefore, Crellius and Smalcius prove in vain from this passage that men and even angels are truly gods; for if he were speaking of them at all, he is openly dealing with gods so-called, but not indeed those who are truly and properly so called, as we have taught more fully in the cited passage and on page 545 of the same work.

Latin:

V. 5. Καὶ γὰρ εἴπερ εἰσὶ λεγόμενοι θεοὶ.

Etiamsi aliqui existant, revera qui Deorum habeant nomen, & dicantur אלהים. Sicut 2. Thess. II. 4. ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν.

Εἴτε ἐν ἐρανῷ.

Ut Sol, luna, astra.

Εἴτε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.

Ut Reges viventes. Quod si illa astra & illi Reges Dii nobis non sunt, multò minus ii, qui non existunt.

Ὥσπερ εἰσὶ θεοὶ πολλοὶ.

Nempe more loquendi apud gentes recepto: λεγόμενοι ut dixit modo.

Καὶ κύριοι πολλοὶ.

בעלים Sic enim in oriente Dii gentium vocabantur.

Crellius per θεὸς λεγομένως & κυρίως Angelos & magistratus designare vult, illos in cœlo; hos in terra. Sed rectius cum Irenæo l. III. c. 6. Chrysost. & Theophyl. in h. l. intelliguntur Dii, & Domini gentilium, & idola, quæ à gentilibus colebantur, ut Dii & Domini sive rerum omnium; sive heroës & servi DEI, quos itidem religiose colebant. Quem sensum confirmavimus Theol. natur. & revel. p. 461. & agnovit Faust. Socinus in Anti- Wuj. pag. 25. Agitur ibi de divinitate colenda & Diis gentium, atque idolis, quæ ab illis colebantur. Opponitur primùm ille unus Deus, deinde etiam Christus, ut unus noster Dominus. Instituitur autem oppositio inter idola, & Deos gentium & Deum verum, idola dicuntur nihil esse in mundo, scil. in rei veritate, Deusque unus asseritur verus Deus, ubi alludere videtur Apostolus ad Pf. XCVI. 5. cum Dii gentium ibidem dicantur אלילים (Conf. Lev. XIX. 4. Es. IX. 10.) id est ἐδὲν vel ἐδαμινοὶ, uti quoque ab Hellenistis 1. Sam. XII. 21. μηδὲν ὄντες dicuntur. Quum ergo nihil esse idola, solumque Deum esse verum Deum asseruerit Apo- stolus, explicat deinceps utrumque oppositionis membrum, quod per idola Deos, Dominosque gen- tium, qui multi ac varii sunt, intelligat; per unum autem verum Deum atque Dominum, Patrem, ex quo omnia, & Jesum Christum, per quem omnia de- signet. De Angelis & Magistratibus nullum in hoc textu vestigium; nec dubium esse poterat, illos longè aliâ ratione Deos vocari, quam ipsum- met verum naturâ Deum; sed Ethnicorum idola, quorum epulis è reliquiis sacrificiorum vesceban- tur Christiani, erant annihilanda, & discrimen Christianorum & Ethnicorum luculenter incul- candum. Nequicquam igitur ex hoc loco Crellius & Smalcius homines etiam & Angelos verè Deos esse, probant; Qui si maximè de illis loqueretur, apertè agit de Diis λεγομένοις, non verò ὄντως & propriè ita dictis, ut loco citato, & pag. 545. ibidem plenius docuimus.

## 8:6
V. 6. But to us there is one God, the Father. Namely, the Father of Christ and through him our Father, John XVII. 3. From whom are all things. This preposition signifies the primary cause of things. And we to him. To his glory. For he created us so that we might be honored by us. See Rom. XI. 36. And this is a Hebraism, and we are for his sake. For whose sake we are. And one Lord Jesus Christ. He is indeed called God; but never in this Apostle, where there is mention of the Father. Therefore, Lord signifies excellence above all things, except the Father, below XV. 27, Acts II. 36. Through whom are all things. Which pertain to the new creation, 1 Tim. II. 5. And we through him. Through him we are what we are, namely Christians, 1 Pet. I. 21.

The Christian faith is here expounded concerning God and Christ. To us one God the Father: which name is here taken commonly, as it is common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because to us, that is, in respect to us, and thus by way of excellence he is called Father, and indeed by reason of creation, which is a common work, because it is added: From whom are all things, which, when Grotius restricts it to the Father of the only-begotten Son, because he is here established as the primary cause of things, and is understood exclusively, he detracts from the honor of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, who with the Father are that one primary cause of created things, to whose glory all things are directed, and to whom we all must strive; and who therefore is both the supreme efficient cause and the ultimate end of all things. It is necessary that Grotius, unless he has defected from the Catholics and the Athanasian Creed, has acknowledged that the predicates apply not only to the first person, the Father, but also to the second, the Son, and the third, the Holy Spirit. But to the Socinians, who conclude from this that the Son is different in essence and inferior in dignity, and therefore that the Father is indeed called God, but Christ is called Lord, we have opposed a just refutation in Natural and Revealed Theology, p. 762, and in the Examination of the books of Crellius on the one God the Father, § 26 seqq. If there is only one God who is to be worshipped by Christians as a deity, or religiously adored, it follows of necessity and infallibly, either that Christ is not God, who is to be worshipped by Christians as a deity and religiously adored; or that he is truly that one God, or the same God by nature and essence, who alone is to be worshipped as a deity. But the adversaries acknowledge that Christ is altogether God, to be worshipped by Christians as a deity and religiously adored. Therefore, it is a consequence that Christ is truly that one God, or the same God by nature and essence, who alone is to be worshipped as a deity. Again, if only one God is to be worshipped by Christians, then certainly Christ is not to be worshipped as another God different in nature. Furthermore: If it is heathen to have and worship many gods, and not Christian, then the Socinians should not be counted among Christians; but among the heathens, who have and worship two gods, one supreme, the other not supreme, one God by nature, the other by gift or grace. If only one Lord is to be worshipped, either the Father will not be the Lord to be worshipped by Christians, or he will be one Lord with Christ. But it is undoubted that the Father is the Lord to be worshipped by Christians. Therefore, the Father will be one Lord with Christ, and consequently Christ will not be, as a Lord other than the Father, dependent on him and subordinate to him, to be acknowledged and worshipped. Likewise: If it is heathen to have and worship many lords, then the Socinians are to be numbered among the heathens, who have and worship two lords. But let these things be read there. But concerning Christ, the Apostle professes our faith thus: To us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. The heathens worshipped many lords and saviors with religious worship: but to us Christians there is no one but one Lord, who obtains dominion over all things by right of creation: Through whom are all things: Because through him all things were created. Which are rashly restricted by Grotius to those things which pertain to the new creation: Because they are said to be through whom are all things, just as they are said to be from whom are all things. But that these are taken universally concerning all things, the Socinians have not denied, and Grotius has conceded. Compare what we have said in the cited book, page 769 seqq. But it seems the Apostle added we through him distinctly, so that just as we tend toward one true God as the ultimate end, so we may aspire to the same and enjoy him only through Christ the unique Savior. Theophylact expressed this sense in this way: But when he says, and we in him, he expresses the reason of faith, by which we are joined to God in familiarity; just as if he were saying, and we are turned to him and we hang upon him. And concerning Christ: Through the Son all things were brought into being, and thus we also were brought into this life. And not only this; but we also through him were brought to this, that it might go well with us, and having been made faithful, we might pass from errors to the truth. So that that double article, namely both concerning the Holy Trinity, that one and true God, and concerning Christ the unique Mediator and Savior, may be expressed. Which was also done in John XVI. 3. Both of which passages we have expressly defended in our Anti-Crellius against the Socinians, which the inept apostate of Danzig indeed barked at, but was repelled by the blessed D. Maukisius, our successor in Danzig: But to refute within these XXX. & which for years no one from among the Socinians has been able, nor indeed has dared, to do.
