That the name κυρίᾳ is to be understood as denoting excellence above all things, the Father excepted, if the excellence and lordship of the one GOD is to be established in a more eminent degree, is by no means to be admitted. For the same lordship and the same majesty belong equally to the Son and to the Father, since they are of the same essence, and likewise of the same glory: nor are there two distinct Lords, or beings diverse in nature, God and Lord, Father and Son; but the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the same God and Lord, as Grotius could have known even from the Athanasian Creed, unless perhaps he renounced it together with the Socinians. Thus God the Father (so the creed has it), God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and yet there are not three Gods, but one God: thus Lord Father, Lord Son, Lord Holy Spirit, and yet there are not three Lords; but one is Lord. For just as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person individually as God or Lord; so we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to say there are three Gods or Lords.

PART II. Concerning the liberty of eating things sacrificed to idols.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἀλλ' ἡμῖν εἷς Θεὸς ὁ Πατὴρ. Pater nempe Christi & per eum noster Joh. XVII. 3. Ἐξ ὗ τὰ πάντα. Hæc præpositio causam significat primariam rerum. Καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς ἀυτὸν. Ad ejus gloriam. Creavit enim nos, ut à nobis hono- retur. Vide Rom. XI. 36. Et est hic Hebraïsmus, & nos ipsius causa. Pro cujus causa nos sumus. Καὶ εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς χριστὸς. Dicitur quidem is & Deus; Sed nunquam apud hunc Apostolum, ubi Patris est mentio. Itaque κύριος signifi- cat excellentiam supra res omnes, excepto Patre infra XV. 27. Act. II. 36. Δἰ ὗ τὰ πάντα. Quæ ad novam creationem pertinent 1. Tim. II. 5. Καὶ ἡμεῖς δἰ ἀυτῶ. Per ipsum sumus quod sumus, nempe Christiani 1. Petr. I. 21.

Fides Christiana hic exponitur de Deo & Chri- sto. Nobis unus Deus Pater : Quod nomen hic κοινῶς accipitur, ut est commune Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto, quia nobis, id est respectu nostri, adeoque κατ' ἔξω Pater dicitur, & quidem ratione creationis, quod opus commune est, quia additur: Ex quo sunt omnia, quod quum ad Patrem Filii unigeniti restringit Grotius, quod hic constitua- tur causa primaria rerum, atque exclusivè intelli- gatur, honori Filii DEI & Spiritus Sancti derogat, qui cum Patre una illa causa rerum creatarum sunt primaria, ad cujus gloriam omnia dirigi, & ad quem omnes contendere debemus; quique proinde & causa Efficiens suprema, & finis rerum omnium ultimus est. Prædicata non solùm primæ personæ Patri, sed etiam secundæ Filio, & tertiæ Spiritui S. convenire, nisi à Catholicis & Symbolo Athanasiano defecerit, necessum est, agnoverit Grotius. Socinianis autem inde Filium essentia diversum & dignitate inferiorem concludentibus, & ideò Patrem quidem DEUM, Christum verò Dominum dici, justum elenchum opposuimus in Theol. Naturali & Revel. p. 762. & in Exa- mine librorum Crellii de uno DEO Patre §. 26. seqq. Si unus tantùm est Deus, qui Christianis pro nu- mine colendus, vel religiosè adorandus, sequitur ἐξ ἀνάγκης & infallibiliter, aut Christum non esse Deum, qui Christianis pro numine colendus, & religiosè adorandus sit; aut eundem verè esse unum illum Deum, vel eundem naturâ & essentiâ Deum, qui unus tantùm colendus est pro numi- ne. At agnoscunt adversarii, Christum omninò Deum esse à Christianis pro numine colendum, & religiosè adorandum. Proinde consequens est, Christum esse verè unum illum Deum, vel eun- dem naturâ & essentiâ Deum, qui unus tantum colendus est pro numine. Rursus si unus tan- tùm Deus colendus est Christianis, utique Christus non est colendus, ut alius naturâ diversus Deus. Porrò : Si multos habere & colere Deos Ethni- cum est, non Christianum; utique Christianis haud accensendi erunt Sociniani; sed Ethnicis, qui duos habent & colunt Deos, unum summum, alterum non summum, unum naturâ Deum; alterum do- no vel gratiâ. Si unus tantùm est colendus Do- minus, aut Pater non erit Dominus, colendus à Christianis, aut unus erit cum Christo Dominus. At indubium est, Patrem esse Dominum colen- dum à Christianis. Quocirca Pater unus erit cum Christo Dominus, & per consequens non erit Christus, ut alius à Patre Dominus ab eo depen- dens, eique subordinatus agnoscendus & colen- dus. Item: Si Ethnicum est, multos habere & co- lere Dominos, utique Sociniani Ethnicis annume- randi, qui duos habent coluntque Dominos. Sed hæc ibi legantur. De Christo autem ita fidem nostram profite- tur Apostolus: Nobis unus est Dominus Jesus Chri- stus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Dominos & sospitatores multos venerabantur Ethnici cul- tu religioso : Nobis autem Christianis non est nisi unus Dominus, qui rerum omnium domini- um obtinet jure creationis: Δι' ὗ τὰ πάντα: Quia per ipsum condita sunt omnia. Quæ temerè à Gro- tio restringuntur ad ea, quæ ad novam creationem pertinent: Quia æquè δι' ὗ τὰ πάντα, atque ἐξ ὗ τὰ πάντα dicuntur. Hæc autem universaliter de rebus omnibus accipi, non disseffi sunt Sociniani, & concessit Grotius. Confer quæ libro citato di- ximus pag. 769. seqq. Distinctè autem addidisse Apostolum ἡμεῖς δι ἀυτῦ videtur, ut quemad- modum nos εἰς ἕνα θεὸν ad unum verum Deum, ceu ultimum finem tendimus, ita non nisi δι ἀυτῦ per Christum Salvatorem unicum ad eundem ad- spiremus, eoque fruamur. Quem sensum expres- sit hoc modo Theophylactus: Cum verò, & nos in ipso, inquit, fidei exprimit rationem, quâ Deo jun- cti familiaritate nos sumus; perinde ac si dicat, & ad ipsum conversi sumus & in ipsum pendemus. Et de Christo: PER FILIUM ad aliquid esse per- ducta sunt universa, adeoque etiam nos ad hanc vi- tam inducti. Neque hoc solum; sed & NOS PER IPSUM eo producti, ut bene nobiscum ageretur, & fideles effecti ad veritatem ab erroribus transire- mus. Ut ita geminus ille articulus nimirum tùm de SS. Trinitate, uno illo & vero DEO, tùm de Christo Mediatore & Salvatore unico exprimatur. Quod etiam Joh. XVI. 3. factum. Quem utrumque locum in Anti-Crellio nostro ex professo adversus Socinianos vindicavimus, quem allatrare quidem ineptus apostata Danzvickensis, à B. D. Maukisio successore nostro Dantiscano repulsus: Confu- tare autem intra hosce XXX. & quod excurrit annos è Socinianis nemo potuit, & ne ausus qui- dem fuit. Nomen κυρίᾳ de excellentia supra res omnes, excepto Patre, intelligendum esse si excel- lentiam & dominium unius DEI in gradu emi- nentiori constituatur, nequaquam admittendum. Nam idem Dominium, eadem majestas ex æquo convenit Filio, ac Patri, quum ejusdem sint, ut essentiæ; ita & gloriæ: Nec duo sint distincti Do- mini, aut naturâ diversi, Deus & Dominus, Pater & Filius; sed Filius cum Patre, & Spiritu Sancto idem Deus sit atque Dominus, ut vel è symbolo Athanasiano novisse potuit Grotius, nisi eidem forte cum Socinianis renunciavit, Ita Deus Pater, (sic habet symbolum) Deus Filius, Deus Spiritus Sanctus, & tamen non tres Dii, sed unus est Deus: Ita Dominus Pater, Dominus Filius, Dominus Spi- ritus S. & tamen non tres Domini; sed unus est Dominus. Quia sicut singulatim unamquamque personam Deum aut, Dominum confiteri Christia- na veritate compellimur; Ita tres Deos aut Domi- nos dicere Catholicâ religione prohibemur.

PARS II. De esus idolothytorum libertate.

## 8:7
V. 7. But knowledge is not in all.

Not all have that knowledge, that those idols are nothing; that there is one God, one Lord.

We admit the former, that not all equally have that knowledge concerning idols, according to the underlying subject matter, regarding the use of things sacrificed to idols. Not so the latter. For Christians can be ignorant of something concerning Christian liberty. But they cannot be Christians who are ignorant that there is one God and one Lord. And ἡ γνῶσις can be understood as that knowledge which the Apostle was requiring, that is, which is not separated from charity. For not all had sufficient knowledge concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, consistent with the doctrine of Christian liberty, and if some did have it, yet charity was not joined to that knowledge in all, where it was to be brought down to practice.

But some, with conscience of the idol, unto this hour eat it as a thing sacrificed to an idol.

He calls it 'conscience of the idol' here, meaning an opinion about the idol as if it had some power. It is a translation from a neighboring thing to a neighboring thing. For that opinion has something similar to conscience. Those who are such eat of the sacrificial meats as sacrificial, that is, they think that they have actually received some holiness from that deity to whom the altar was dedicated. The Syrian seems to have correctly grasped this sense. He says 'unto this hour' correctly, because paganism was still very vigorous even at Corinth. But in the Manuscript it is: Τῇ συνηθείᾳ τῶ εἰδώλε, so that it may be a metonymy.

And their conscience being weak is defiled.

Ἀσθενὴς here is morbid, poorly instructed. Μολύνεται, is contaminated, because by such acts a perverse opinion grows more and more. But every perverse opinion, especially concerning divine things, is a certain defilement of the mind.

Grotius explains those things both concerning the perverse opinion about idols regarding the subject; and concerning the communion of the pagan sacrificial flesh regarding the predicate. Neither of which was fitting for Christians; nor could any doubt arise for the Corinthians converted to the Christian faith regarding either the former or the latter, because those things imply idolatry. For that opinion about idols, as if they have some divine power, is contrary to the profession already made in the name of Christians, 'we know that an idol is nothing in the world.' And the participation of sacrificial meats, as sacrificial, or as if they had received some holiness from the idol, what is it but participated idolatry; which would not have been a certain weakness of conscience; but a disease close to destruction. But here the Apostle speaks only of a weak conscience. But what kind of infirmity the Apostle wishes to be understood, he himself explains in v. 9: Namely, of those who were still tender in faith, with Grotius as interpreter of that passage, not those to whom pagan idolatry clung, which cannot consist with faith. But Grotius seems to have drawn his explanation from the Papists. For it is that of Estius, as also of Cornelius à Lapide, although the latter cuts his own vines here, arguing against the Libertines in this place. Who does not see that the Apostle is speaking here not of sins or illicit things, but of adiaphora, such as eating things sacrificed to idols? For what? Is this an adiaphoron, to eat things sacrificed to idols in such a way with such a conscience, that the things sacrificed to idols are changed by the idol, and physically breathed upon by the Devil, just as if they were infected with a Diabolical breath, or certainly as if they were morally vitiated or polluted, from the fact that they are now considered to be things of the Devil and food of a demon, as Cornelius explains. Pareus in this place has it thus: The thing itself speaks, that some do not yet have knowledge, because they still have a conscience of the idol, that is, they are touched within by a certain reverence for the idol, as if it were not entirely a log: But that some deity underlies it: And they eat, as a thing sacrificed to an idol, i.e., as food consecrated, which has some holiness from the immolation. Which infirmity Pareus calls, not indeed excusable; but yet not damnable. But how is it not damnable, when it is in reality idolatry? Nor are the Socinians alien to this gloss. Crellius explains conscience of the idol through a conscience subject to idols, when they think that some divinity underlies the idols; but which it is a sin to worship, and therefore things offered and consecrated to them become impure, and it is a certain wickedness for him who dares to touch them to bind himself. Which agree with those previously brought forward by the Papists and the Calvinist Pareus, except that a divinity of such a kind is thrust in, which it is a sin to worship, so that idolatry may be excused. Without doubt, however, the interpretation of the blessed Hunnius and other orthodox men holds itself more correctly here: Knowledge is not in all, because some stumble concerning the use of indifferent things, thinking themselves to sin if they eat of things sacrificed to idols. Whence the Apostle writes concerning the same: That some eat with a singular conscience; calling that erroneous conscience the conscience of an idol, because they did not indeed think that any divinity was in the idols to signify it: Meanwhile they ascribed to them the power of polluting by themselves. Therefore he declares their conscience, if they eat, since it is weak, to be polluted and contaminated before GOD.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἀλλ’ ἐκ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡ γνῶσις.

Non omnes eam cognitionem habent, idola ista nihil esse; unum esse Deum, unum Dominum.

Prius admittimus, non omnes ex æquo eam habere de idolis, pro substrata materia, quoad usum εἰδωλοθύτων cognitionem. Non item poste- rius. Nam ignorare aliquid circa libertatem Chri- stianam possunt Christiani. At Christiani esse non possunt, qui ignorant unum esse Deum & unum esse Dominum. Et potest ἡ γνῶσις de illa cognitione intelligi, quam requirebat Apostolus, hoc est, quæ non sejuncta est à charitate. Nam neque cogni- tionem sufficientem, de esu idolothytorum, do- ctrinæ de libertate Christiana convenientem, ha- bebant omnes, & si qui eam habebant, non ta- men cognitioni illi juncta erat in omnibus cha- ritas, ubi ad praxin ea deducenda erat.

Τινὲς δὲ συνειδήσει τῶ εἰδώλε ἕως ἄρτι ὡς εἰδωλό- θυτον ἐσθίεσι.

Συνείδησιν εἰδώλε hic vocat opinionem de idolo quasi vim aliquam haberet. Est translatio à re vicina ad vici- nam. Nam opinio illa habet aliquid simile conscientiæ. Qui tales sunt, carnibus immolatitiis vescuntur, tanquam immolatitiis, id est, putant ex profectis aliquid illas acce- pisse sanctimoniæ à numine illo, cui ara fuit dicata. Hunc sensum rectè videtur assecuutus Syrus. Ἕως ἄρτι rectè di- cit, quia multum adhuc vigebat paganismus etiam Co- rinthi. At in Manuscripto est: Τῇ συνηθείᾳ τῶ εἰδώλε, ut sit μετωνυμία.

Καὶ ἡ συνείδησις ἀυτῶν ἀσθενὴς ὖσα μολύνεται.

Ἀσθενὴς hic est morbida, malè instituta. Μολύνεται, con- taminatur, quia talibus actibus magis magisque inolescit prava opinio. Omnis autem prava opinio, præsertim circa res divinas, inquinamentum quoddam est animi.

Explicat illa Grotius tùm de perversa opinione de idolis quoad subjectum; tùm de communione carnis immolatitiæ paganæ circa prædicatum. Quo- rum neutrum Christianis conveniebat; neque vel de priori, vel posteriori dubium suboriri Corin- thiis ad fidem Christianam conversis poterat, quia idololatrism illa inferunt. Nam & opinio illa de idolis, quasi vim aliquam divinam habeant, con- traria est professioni, nomine Christianorum jam factæ, scimus, quod idolum nihil est in mundo. Et participatio carnium immolatitiarum, ut immo- latitiarum, vel quasi aliquid sanctimoniæ ex idolo acceperint, quid est nisi idololatria participata; quod non infirmitas quædam conscientiæ fuisset; sed morbus exitio proximus. At hic de infirma tantùm conscientia loquitur Apostolus. Qualem autem infirmitatem intellectam velit Apostolus, ipse v. 9. explicat: Eorum nempe, qui fidei ad- huc teneræ erant, interprete ad illum locum Gro- tio, non quibus hærebat idololatria pagana, quæ cum fide consistere nequit. Explicationem autem suam è Papistis hausisse videtur Grotius. Est enim ea Estii, ut & Cornelii à Lapide, tametsi hic propria vineta cædat, contra Libertinos hoc loco disputans. Quis non videt, Apostolum hîc loqui non de peccatis, rebusve illicitis, sed adiaphoris, quale est manducare idolothyta? Quid enim? An hoc adiaphorum est, manducare ita idolothyta cum ejusmodi conscientia, quod idolothyta ab idolo sunt immutata, & physicè à Diabolo afflata, perinde ac si halitu Diabolico infecta essent, vel certè ac si moraliter vitiata aut polluta essent, ex eo quod censeantur jam esse res Diaboli & cibus dæmonis, ut explicat Cornelius. Pareus in h. l. ita habet: Res ipsa loquitur, quosdam nondum habere scientiam, quia adhuc habent conscientiam idoli, id est intus tanguntur quadam idoli reverentia, quasi non sit omnino truncus: Sed aliquid numinis subsit: Et edunt, ut idolothytum, h. e. ut cibum consecra- tum, qui aliquid sanctitatis ex immolatione habeat. Quam infirmitatem vocat Pareus, non quidem ex- cusabilem; sed non tamen damnabilem. At quo- modo non damnabilis, quum revera sit idolola- tria? Nec alieni sunt ab hac glossa Sociniani. Crel- lius conscientiam idoli explicat per conscientiam idolis obnoxiam, quum putant, idolis aliquid divi- nitatis subesse; sed quam colere sit nefas, ideoque iis oblata ac consecrata fieri impura, & sit scelere quo- dam se alligare eum, qui attingere audeat. Quæ prioribus è Papistis & Pareo Calviniano adductis consonant, nisi quod ingeratur divinitas ejusmodi, quam colere sit nefas, ut idololatria excusetur. Sine dubio autem rectius sese hic habet B. Hunnii & aliorum orthodoxorum interpretatio: Non in omnibus est scientia, quia titubant circa usum rerum indifferentium nonnulli, arbitrantes se pec- care si vescantur idolothytis. Unde scribit Apo- stolus de iisdem: Nonnullos cum conscientia singu- lari edere; Conscientiam simulacri nominans con- scientiam illam erroneam, quod simulacris non quidem aliquam divinitatem ad significandum eam inesse putarint: Interim adscripserint illis vim polluendi per se. Ideò pronunciat conscien- tiam illorum, si vescantur, cum sit infirma, pollui & contaminari coram DEO.

## 8:8
V. 8. Βρῶμα δὲ ἡμᾶς οὐ παρίστησι τῷ Θεῷ. That is, meals shared with infidels. Those who entered such banquets without scruple wished to be believed wiser than the rest: But Paul says, they are not on that account more acceptable to GOD. Παρίστησι, that is, commends: Because those who commend someone to a King are accustomed to bring him into the King's sight, which is παριστάναι.

Οὔτε γὰρ ἐὰν φάγωμεν.

If we are present at the banquets of infidels.

Περισσεύομεν.

We shall be none the more pleasing to God on that account. Concerning the word περισσεύειν see Rom. III. 7. V. 15.

Οὔτε ἐὰν μὴ ὑστερούμεθα.

Nor if we abstain, shall we have any the less of the Lord's benevolence. Concerning the meaning of the word ὑστερεῖσθαι see above I. 7. In the Manuscript there is an inverted order: Οὔτε γὰρ ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν περισσεύομεν, οὔτε ἐὰν φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα.

These things refer to food in general, not to food offered to idols; even if they look toward this, and are to be applied specifically, just as in general it is also said in Rom. XIV. 17, The kingdom of God is not food or drink. And therefore we rightly use this passage against the choice of foods and the fasts of the Papists, who seek merit in abstinence from food, or from a certain kind of food. But Cornelius ineptly retorts: Food does not commend us to God, because it is not a virtue; but abstinence from forbidden food is an act of temperance, obedience, and religion. Because Paul is not speaking about food itself, but about the use of food. And the prohibition and distinction of foods is not from GOD, which the Papists observe; but it is a demonic doctrine 1 Tim. IV. 13, and therefore there is no act here of either virtue or obedience; much less of religion. Not to mention that Monastic religion is a pure and simple Papistic invention, and an abominable ἐθελοθρησκεία. Nor did Paul warn without reason that we should not allow ourselves to be deceived in food and drink, Col. II. 16. For the Levitical law concerning the distinction of foods has been abolished. Therefore now nothing that enters the mouth defiles a man, Matth. XV. 11. And it is said to Peter, Acts X. 15, What God has purified, do not call unclean. But in the Ebionites, Montanists, Tatianists, and Encratites, the Papists themselves condemn that they condemned foods which God proposed to the human race, and that they abhorred meats. See Prateolus l. XVI. hæref. 32. Baronius around the year of Christ 174, n. 4. Erasmus in Paraphras. 1 Cor. 8. Food, he says, does not commend us to GOD. For since God created all things for human use, and requires nothing from us except piety of life, why then do we ask whether we eat the flesh of fish, or of quadrupeds, or of birds? For the choice of these neither adds anything to piety, nor takes anything away. It can make one superstitious, but by no means pious.

Latin:

V. 8. Βρῶμα δὲ ἡμᾶς ὀ παρίστησι τῷ Θεῷ. Id est, epulæ cum infidelibus communes. Qui sine scru- pulo talia inibant convivia, volebant credi sapientiores cæteris: At ait Paulus, non ob id DEO esse acceptiores. Παρίστησι, id est commendat: Quia qui aliquem Regi com- mendant, solent eum in Regis conspectum adducere, quod est παριστάναι.

Οὔτε γὰρ ἐὰν φάγωμεν.

Si interfumus infidelium conviviis.

Περισσεύομεν.

Nihilo ob id erimus Deo gratiores. De verbo περισσεύ- ειν Vide Rom. III. 7. V. 15.

Οὔτε ἐὰν μὴ ὑστερούμεθα.

Neque si abstineamus, eò minus habebimus de Domini benevolentia. De significatione verbi ὑστερεῖσθαι vide supra I. 7. In Manuscripto est inversus ordo: Οὔτε γὰρ ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν περισσεύομεν, οὔτε ἐὰν φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα.

Hæc de esca in genere sonant, non de esca ido- lothytorum; etsi ad hanc respiciant, & speciatim applicanda sint, uti in genere etiam Rom. XIV. 17. dicitur, Regnum Dei non est cibus vel potus. Ideoque rectè hoc loco utimur contra delectum ciborum & jejunia Papistarum, qui meritum in abstinen- tiâ à cibis, vel certo genere ciborum quærunt. Ineptè verò Cornelius regerit: Esca non commen- dat nec Deo, quia non est virtus; sed abstinentia ab esca vetitâ est actus temperantiæ, obedientiæ & religionis. Quia Paulus non de esca ipsa loquitur; sed de usu escæ. Et prohibitio ac discrimen cibo- rum non est à DEO, quod observant Papistæ; sed dæmoniaca est doctrina 1. Tim. IV. 13. ideoque nul- lus hîc actus est aut virtutis aut obedientiæ; ne- dum religionis. Ut taceam, quod Monastica reli- gio purum putum sit commentum Papisticum, & abominanda ἐθελοθρησκεία. Nec abs re monuit Paulus, ne decipi nos patiamur in cibo & potu, Col. II. 16. Sublata enim est lex Levitica de discrimine ciborum. Idcirco jam nihil, quod ingreditur os, polluit hominem Matth. XV. 11. Et Petro dicitur Act. X. 15. Quæ Deus purificavit, tu immunda ne dixeris. In Ebionitis verò, Montanistis, Tatianis, Encratitis Papistæ ipsi reprobant, quod cibos damnarint, quos Deus humano generi proposuit, & quod carnes fuerint abominati. Vid. Prateolus l. XVI. hæref. 32. Baronius circa annum Chr. 174. n. 4. Erasmus in Paraphras. 1. Cor. 8. Esca, inquit, nos non commendat DEO. Cum enim Deus uni- versa creaverit ad usum humanum, neque quicquam à nobis exigat, præter vitæ pietatem. Quid ergò querimus, an piscium, an quadrupedum, an vola- tilium carnibus vescamur? Nihil enim pietati quisquam vel addit, vel demit horum delectus. Su- perstitiosum facere potest, pium nequaquam.

## 8:9
V. 9. Βλέπετε δὲ. Again and again see, that is, beware.

Μήπως ἡ ἐξυσία ὑμῶν αὕτη. A metonymy. For he said liberty, when he wished to be understood as the usurpation of liberty. The word ἐξυσίας signifies the right of acting, as Rom. IX. 21, above VII. 27. See also above VI. 12.

Πρόσκομμα γένηται. Πρόσκομμα here is מכשול, that by which someone is impelled into ruin. See what [is said] regarding Matt. V. 29 and the prohibitive precept CLXVIII. But understand ruin here as departure from Christianity.

Τοῖς ἀσθενῦσιν. In the manuscript ἀσθενέσιν. This is not to be understood absolutely here, as just now; but comparatively concerning those who, when they had recently added themselves to the Christian assembly, were of tender faith, and which could easily be overturned by bad teachings or examples.

Those who were certain that they could eat idol-meats without offense to conscience ought to have used their liberty in eating them in such a way that they placed no stumbling block before the weak, who were doubtful whether one could eat them without participation in idolatry. For that reason, indifferent things are free, so that in their use, however, we must take the greatest care that by either adopting or omitting them, a scandal is not created for the weaker ones. Concerning which the Formula of Concord, solid declaration, art. X, p. 793, warned gravely.

Latin:

V. 9. Βλέπετε δὲ. Etiam atque etiam videte, id est cavete.

Μήπως ἡ ἐξυσία ὑμῶν αὕτη. Μετωνυμία. Nam libertatem dixit, cum vellet intelli- gere libertatis usurpationem. Ἐξυσίας vox jus agendi signi- ficat, ut Rom. IX. 21. supra VII. 27. Vidè & supra VI. 12.

Πρόσκομμα γένηται. Πρόσκομμα hic est מכשול, id per quod quis in rui- nam impellitur. Vide quæ ad Matth. V. 29. & præceptum vetans CLXVIII. Ruinam autem hic intellige discessio- nem a Christianismo.

Τοῖς ἀσθενῦσιν. In Manuscripto ἀσθενέσιν. Id hic non absolutè intelli- gendum, ut modò; sed comparate de iis, qui, cum recens Christiano cœtui se addidissent, fidei erant teneræ, & quæ facilè malis documentis aut exemplis convelli posset.

Ita libertate uti debebant in comedendis ido- lothytis illi, qui citra offensam conscientiæ iis se vesci posse, certi erant, ut offendiculum nullum infirmis, qui, anne iis vesci quis possit citra idolola- triæ participationem, ambigui erant, ponant. Eà ergò ratione libera sunt adiaphora, ut in eorum usu tamen maxime id nobis cavendum sit, ne ea- dem vel adhibendo, vel intermittendo infirmio- ribus scandalum creetur. Quo de graviter monuit Formula Concordiæ solid. declar. art. X. p. 793.

## 8:10
V. 10. Ἐὰν γάρ τις ἴδῃ σε τὸν ἔχοντα γνῶσιν. You who are learned and seem so to yourself and are believed to be so by others. For they called themselves Γνωσικὺς as if seeing more than the rest. See 1 Tim. VI. 20, and Clement of Alexandria calls those who have knowledge πεφυσιωμένος, Pædagog. I. 6.

As for those who are noted here by the Apostle, who had that knowledge that idol-meats could be eaten without idolatry, provided that spiritual communion with idolaters is not held, I ask, from where will it be taught that they were of the number of the Gnostics? That knowledge is not reproved here by the Apostle, but those endowed with it are merely commanded to beware of scandal.

Ἐν εἰδωλείῳ. Εἰδωλεῖον is the temple of an idol, as we said 1 Maccab. I. 50, X. 83. Thus we have ἀσαρτεῖον 1 Sam. XXXI. 10. Thus Ἀτεργατεῖον 2 Maccab. XII. 26. Thus also Ποσειδώνιον to the Greeks is the temple of Neptune, Μυσεῖον, of the Muses, Νυμφαῖον, of the Nymphs.

Κατακείμενον. Reclining; that is, feasting in the Greek manner. Thus Plato in the second book of the Republic, ἐπὶ κλινῶν κατακεῖsθαι. Virgil: You grant to recline at the feasts of the gods. See Matt. XXVI. 20.

Οὐχὶ ἡ συνείδησις αὐτῶ ἀσθενῦς ὄντος οἰκοδομηθήσεται εἰς τὸ τὰ εἰδωλόθυτα ἐσθίειν; Συνείδησις again [means] opinion. Οἰκοδομηθήσεται will be confirmed, in the way Paul is accustomed to use this word. Εἰς τὸ τὰ εἰδωλόθυτα ἐσθίειν, namely in honor of the idol just as he thinks you are doing. And so he is led to the point that he judges there is nothing evil in ἐν εἰδωλολατρείᾳ.

This sense has no difficulty. Namely, the Apostle declares in what way a stumbling block can be placed before weak brothers. For if any weak person, not yet having the knowledge of evangelical liberty, sees you reclining and eating idol-meats at a feast or banquet where the remains of idol-meats are served; then the weak person will be invited by your example to eat as well, but with a conscience either hesitating whether he is doing right or otherwise, or clearly resisting, as one who is still persuaded that the eating of idol-meats is joined with sin, as Hunnius has in this place. Συνείδησις is conscience, not knowledge, as will be warned at verse 12.

Little by little he will cease to be a Christian, thinking to himself, why do I endure persecutions, if these things are ἀδιάφορα (matters of indifference). In the manuscript it is slightly different: ἀπόλυται ἐν ἐν τῇ σῇ γνώσει ἀδελφὸς δι ὃν, &c.

Latin:

V. 10. Ἐὰν γάρ τις ἴδῃ σε τὸν ἔχοντα γνῶσιν. Te qui eruditus & tibi videris & aliis crederis. Voca- bant enim illi se Γνωσικὺς tanquam plus videntes cæteris. Vide 1. Tim. VI. 20. & Clemens Alexandrinus πεφυσιωμέ- νος οἱς γνῶσιν vocat Pædagog. I. 6.

Hos, qui ab Apostolo hic notantur, qui cogni- tionem illam habebant, quod idolothyta citra idololatriam comedi possint, modo non habea- tur spiritualis cum idololatris communio, è Gno- sticorum numero fuisse, quæso, unde docebitur? Non hic ea γνῶσις reprehenditur ab Apostolo, sed cavere tantùm illà præditi jubentur scandalum.

Ἐν εἰδωλείῳ. Εἰδωλεῖον est templum idoli, ut diximus 1. Maccab. I. 50. X. 83. Sic ἀσαρτεῖον habemus 1. Sam. XXXI. 10. Sic Ἀτεργατεῖον 2. Maccab. XII. 26. Sic & Ποσειδώνιον Græcis est templum Neptuni, Μυσεῖον, Musarum, Νυμφαῖον, Nym- pharum.

Κατακείμενον. Accumbentem; id est epulantem more Græco. Sic Plato de Republica secundo, ἐπὶ κλινῶν κατακεῖsθαι. Virgilius: Tu das epulis accumbere divûm Vide Matth. XXVI. 20.

Οὐχὶ ἡ συνείδησις αὐτῶ ἀσθενῦς ὄντος οἰκοδομηθήσεται εἰς τὸ τὰ εἰδωλόθυτα ἐσθίειν; Συνείδησις rursum opinio. Οἰκοδομηθήσεται confirmabi- tur, quomodo Paulus hâc voce uti solet. Εἰς τὸ τὰ εἰδωλό- θυτα ἐσθίειν, nempe in honorem idoli sicut & te facere existimat. Itaque eò perducitur, ut ἐν εἰδωλολατρείᾳ nihil mali esse arbitretur.

Sensus hic nullam habet difficultatem. Nimi- rum declarat Apostolus, quà ratione poni queat offendiculum fratribus infirmis. Etenim si quis infirmus, nondum habens scientiam libertatis Ev- angelicæ, videat te in epulo seu convivio, quo ido- lothytorum àpponuntur reliquiæ, accumbentem & vescentem idolothytis; tùm exemplo tuo invita- bitur infirmus, ut & ipse edat, sed conscientiâ vel hasitante, rectè ne faciat vel secus, aut plane re- pugnante, ut qui hoc sibi adhuc persuasum habet, esum idolothytorum esse cum peccato conjun- stum, ut hoc loco habet Hunnius. Συνείδησις con- scientia est, non scientia, ut ad vers. 12. monebitur.

Paulatim definet esse Christianus, ita secum cogitans, cur persecutiones sustineam, si ita sunt ἀδιάφορα. In manuscripto paulo aliter ἀπόλυται ἐν ἐν τῇ σῇ γνώσει ἀδελφὸς δι ὃν, &c.

## 8:11
Ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ γνώσει (By thy knowledge).

By the occasion of your knowledge, under the pretext of which you defend these things.

Δι ὃν χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν (For whom Christ died).

Christ died for all men whatsoever, so that they might be able to be converted through the Gospel. Therefore also for those who perish Rom. XIV. 15. 2. Pet. II. 1. Hebr. X. 29.

These things are to be observed against the Calvinists, who deny that Christ died for all men; concerning whose error, as it is embellished by more recent writers, one may compare our writing published in the name of the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg under the title Gründtlicher Beweiß, daß der Reformirten Lehre der Seligkeit nachtheilig sey, chap. 11, part 11. Ludovicus Crocius urges this Apostolic testimony to his associates in the faith in his duodecimo dissertations, p. 646, in this manner: He who died not only for those who are saved, but also for those who can perish and do perish, he died for all men. But Christ died not only for those who are saved, but also for those who can perish and do perish. Therefore. The major premise is conceded on both sides, and by the force of the terms is so evident that the opponents have required no proof of it. The minor is proved by the passages already cited. (Rom. XIV. 16. 1. Cor. VIII. 11. 2. Petr. II. 1. Ebr. VI. 6. chap. X. 29.) Concerning those who seek an escape in the present passage in the word perdition, he adds this: I wonder that some interpret the word ἀπωλείας so coldly, that it denotes not a grave and total injury to faith and conscience, but only an incipient one, caused by the communication of a sacrifice offered to idols, which nevertheless the Apostle greatly exaggerates in chap. X. 20, 21. Thus Crocius. For such weak persons, who do not consider that communication a lawful thing, but as participating in idolatry, if they are induced by the example of the stronger in knowledge to eat even of things sacrificed to idols notwithstanding that persuasion, they both sin against conscience; and they can thus perish eternally, and are precipitated into the ruin of damnation by such an abuse of the knowledge of him by whose example they are enticed to eat, even though their conscience may be wavering or reluctant. And ἀπώλεια is commonly used for eternal ruin in Matth. VII. 13. Joh. XVII. 13. Act. IIX. 20. Roman. IX. 22. Phil. I. 28. chap. III. 19. 2. Thess. II. 3. 1. Tim. VI. 9. Ebr. X. 39. 2. Pet. II. 1. 2. 3. chap. III. 7. 16. Apocal. XVII. 8. 11. and it occurs nowhere only for an incipient ruin of the soul; and it is used only once for temporal ruin, where the discourse is about a secular judgment, and that in the speech of Festus, Act. XXV. 16. Otherwise, whenever it occurs regarding persons, it denotes eternal ruin. Nor can this be denied regarding the parallel passage 2. Petr. II. 1. 2. 3. Then indeed it is explained in a passage that is entirely similar, Rom. XIV. 16, where ἀπώλεια is explained by καταλύειν, destruction bringing about eternal ruin. Where indeed there are not lacking (among the Reformed) those who, as Crocius says in the cited passage, think they can enervate the force of that passage through the sophism of homonymy in the word perdition, because not every perdition is perfect and eternal, but some is incipient and temporal, as in Luke XIV. 17, and 14, and 6. & 9. but that which the Apostle is speaking of is only the offense of a weak brother, v. 13, and an injury to justice and mutual charity because of the imprudent use of foods formerly forbidden, v. 15, and thus an occasion of cursing, v. 16. To which Crocius gives this response in book 1, p. 649. But in truth this perdition signifies not only an incipient injury to the work of God, but also destruction, v. 20. Do not for the sake of food destroy the work of God; Μὴ ἕνεκεν βρώματος κατάλυε ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Καταλύειν for Homer, Thucydides, Xenophon, and others is to dissolve, cut down, destroy, abolish, finish. And for Isocrates, καταλύειν βίον means to end life, to die, for which καταλύειν is also read simply in Gregory. But the object, the work of God, also intends the force of this καταλύσεως. The corruption of the temple, φθορὰ 1 Cor. 3:17, points this way. And the λύσις τοῦ ναοῦ, John 2:19, the dissolution of the temple, which denotes not just any violation, but a full destruction, to which is opposed there ἔγερσις, the raising up, and οἰκοδομὴ, the building up, Matthew 26:61. This is Ludovicus Crocius. These things easily suffice for refuting the sophistry of the Calvinists and others.

Latin:

Ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ γνώσει.

Occasione scientiæ tuæ, cujus obtentu ista defendis.

Δι ὃν χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν.

Christus pro omnibus omninò hominibus mortuus est, ut per Evangelium converti possent. Ergò & pro iis, qui pereunt Rom. XIV. 15. 2. Pet. II. 1. Hebr. X. 29.

Observanda hæc contra Calvinianos, qui Christum pro omnibus hominibus mortuum esse negant; de quorum errore, prout à recentioribus incrustatur, conferri poterit Nostrum facultatis Theologicæ Wittenberg. nomine editum scriptum sub titulo Gründtlicher Beweiß, daß der Reformirten Lehre der Seligkeit nachtheilig sey, cap. 11. part, 11. Urget fidei suæ socios hoc Apostolico testimonio Ludovic. Crocius in duodec. dissert. p. 646. h. m. Qui non tantùm pro iis, qui servantur, verum etiam pro iis, qui perire possunt, ac pereunt, mortuus est, is pro omnibus hominibus mortuus est. Atqui Christus non tantùm pro iis, qui servantur, sed & pro iis, qui perire possunt ac pereunt, mortuus est. Ergo. Major utrinque concessa est, & vi terminorum adeò evidens, ut contradictores nullam ejus probationem requisiverint. Minor probatur locis jam prolatis. (Rom. XIV. 16. 1. Cor. VIII. 11. 2. Petr. II. 1. Ebr. VI. 6. cap. X. 29.) De illis, qui in loco præsenti effugium quærunt in voce perditionis, hæc subjicit: Miror, vocem ἀπωλείας tam frigide quosdam interpretari, ut notet non gravem & totalem, sed inchoatam duntaxat fidei & conscientiæ læsionem, factam sacrificii idolis immolati communicatione, quam tamen Apostolus magnopere exaggerat cap. X. 20. 21. Hæc Crocius. Nam tales infirmi, qui non habent communicationem illam pro re licita, sed pro idolatria participata, si exemplo firmiorum in cognitione inducantur, ut non obstante illa persuasione etiam de idolothytis comedant, & peccant contra conscientiam; & perire ita æternum possunt, & in damnationis exitium præcipitantur tali abusu scientiæ ejus, cujus exemplo illecti edunt, titubante vel reluctante licet conscientiâ. Et ἀπώλεια de æterno exitio communiter usurpatur Matth. VII. 13. Joh. XVII. 13. Act. IIX. 20. Roman. IX. 22. Phil. I. 28. cap. III. 19. 2. Thess. II. 3. 1. Tim. VI. 9. Ebr. X. 39. 2. Pet. II. 1. 2. 3. cap. III. 7. 16. Apocal. XVII. 8. 11. nec uspiam de inchoato solùm animæ exitio occurrit; ac semel tantùm de temporali exitio, ubi de judicio seculari sermo est, adhibetur, idque in sermone Festi, Act. XXV. 16. Cæteroquin semper, cum de personis occurrit, æternum exitium notat. Neque id negari potest circa locum parallelum 2. Petr. II. 1. 2. 3. Tum verò explicatur in loco prorsus simili, Rom. XIV. 16. ἀπώλεια per καταλύειν, destructionem æternum exitium inferentem. Ubi quidem non desunt (è Reformatis) qui, dicente Crocio, loco citato, vim loci istius enervare se posse putent per sophisma homonymicè in voce perditionis, quia non omnis perditio perfecta & æterna est, sed quædam inchoata ac temporalis, ut Luc. XIV. 17. & 14. & 6. & 9. ea verò, quâ de Apostolus, est tantùm offensio infirmi fratris, v. 13. ac justitiæ & mutuæ charitatis læsio ob imprudentem ciborum olim vetitorum usum v. 15. atque ita maledictionis occasio v. 16. Quibus hoc responsum reddit Crocius l. 1. p. 649. Verum enim verò hæc perditio non inchoatam tantum læsionem operis Dei significat, sed & destructionem v. 20. Ne cibi causâ destrue opus Domini; Μὴ ἕνεκεν βρώματος κατάλυε ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Καταλύειν Homero, Thucydidi, Xenophonti, & aliis est dissolvere, excidere, destruere, abolere, finire. Et Isocrati καταλύειν βίον vitam finire, mori, pro quo etiam καταλύειν simpliciter apud Gregorium legitur. Intendit verò etiam vim hujus καταλύσεως objectum τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Horsum facit corruptio templi φθορὰ 1. Cor. III. 17. Et λύσις τοῦ ναοῦ Joh. II. 19. solutio templi, quæ non violationem quantulam- cunque, sed & plenam notat destructionem, cui ibi opponitur ἔγερσις exstructio & οἰκοδομὴ ædifica- tio Matth. XXVI. 61. Hæc Ludovicus Crocius. Quæ facilè sophismati Calvinianorum aliorum refel- lendo sufficiunt.

## 8:12
v. 12. And thus sinning against the brethren, and wounding their weak conscience. Τύπτειν here is to inflict a wound, Proverbs 26:22. He calls conscience here the persuasion concerning the truth and necessity of the Gospel, which, since it is still tender, is destroyed by a light wound.

You sin against Christ. For you snatch away from him a disciple, the fruit of the death of Christ, as much as in you lies, you hinder. This is a great injury against Christ.

But why should we not take the word συνείδησιν ἀσθενοῦσαν as 'weak conscience,' as it sounds, just as other interpreters commonly take it? For that word is perpetually used in the sacred writings: which is evident from an induction of passages: Job 8:9; Acts 23:1, 24:16; Romans 6:15, 9:1, 13:5; 2 Corinthians 1:12, 4:2, 5:11; 1 Timothy 1:5, 19, 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:3, 4:2; Titus 1:16; Hebrews 9:9, 14, 10:2. Nor does it have any other sense in this chapter, v. 7, 10, or in the parallel place, chapter 10:28, 29. We note here, for the sake of the Syncretists, especially Calixtus, the opinion of the blessed Balduinus: are Papists, hearing the Mass, rightly called idolaters, when they do this not out of malice, but out of simplicity, and are so persuaded in their conscience? Idolatry in the office of the Mass is sufficiently manifest, while they invoke the saints, and adore the blessed bread, and fall down before a creature, saying it is the Creator. And although there is a distinction here between those who defend this idolatry against their conscience, and others who do it out of a simple persuasion of the error in which they were born: nevertheless, the Mass-worship does not put off its nature, and because it is itself idolatrous, it therefore renders its worshippers idolaters, with whatever affection or intention this may be done by them. I would wish the Calixtines to observe this, who absolve from idolatry the Papists, not only the simple ones, but even the stubborn defenders of the Mass.

Wherefore if food causes my brother to stumble, I will by no means eat meat forever, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble. It is an exaggeration. Rather than give an occasion to any Christian to return to idolatry, I would prefer to abstain not only from those sacrificial feasts, but from all meat or living things entirely, and to live on bread alone and herbs, as some do. He does not, however, say this because it is necessary in any case, but to show that things much more serious than those which are treated here must be sustained for the salvation of our neighbors. We have observed a similar manner of speaking in Matthew 5:29.

He therefore commends his own example to them, from which they may learn what sort of people they ought to be toward the weak; for he writes that he is so affected that if he knows that the eating of meats sacrificed to idols is a stumbling block placed before a weak brother, he would not want to eat meat forever; not that it is not permitted before God, but that it is not expedient on account of the conscience of the weak, whom, in a matter concerning their salvation, one must deservedly spare, as the blessed Hunnius says here. Let Christian love, therefore, be the rule and standard of our conversation with the weak, so that in the use of liberty we may lower ourselves entirely to their infirmity, so that they may be confirmed in the faith by both salutary instruction and prudent conversation, and be fully gained for Christ the Lord. In which matter the Apostle Paul is a living example to us, who, just as he did not yield even for a moment in indifferent matters to the stubborn enemies of the Evangelical truth, Galatians 2, so conversely, for the sake of the weak, he circumcised Timothy, Acts 16. He fulfilled the vow of the Nazarites, Acts 21, and to the Jews he became as a Jew, that he might gain the Jews; to the Gentiles as a Gentile, that he might gain the Gentiles, 1 Corinthians 9. Chrysostom is beautiful on this passage: It is the height of madness that we should consider those things which are most precious to Christ, and such that he did not refuse to undergo death for their sake, to be so despicable that we will not abstain from foods for their sake.

Latin:

v. 12. Οὕτω δὲ ἁμαρτάνοντες εἰς ἀδελφοὺς, καὶ τύπτοντες αὐτῶν τὴν συνείδησιν ἀσθενοῦσαν. Τύπτειν hic est vulnus infligere Prov. XXVI. 22. Συνεί- δησιν hic vocat persuasionem de veritate & necessitate Evan- gelii, quæ cum adhuc sit tenera, levi vulnere interimitur.

Εἰς χριστὸν ἁμαρτάνετε. Eripitis enim ei discipulum, fructum mortis Christi, quantum in vobis est, impeditis. Magna hæc est in Chri- stum injuria.

Cur verò vocem συνείδησιν ἀσθενοῦσαν de con- scientia infirma, uti sonat, non accipiamus, quem- admodum cæteri communiter Interpretes ac- cipiunt? Nam vox illa perpetuò adhibetur in sacris: Quod ex inductione locorum constat Job. IIX. 9. Act: XXIII. 1. c. XXIV. 16. Rom. VI. 15. c. IX. 1. cap. XIII. 5. 2. Cor. I. 12. cap. IV. 2. cap. V. 11. 1. Tim. I. 5. 19. Cap. III. 9. 2. Tim. I. 3. cap. IV. 2. Tit. I. 16. Ebr. IX. 9. 14. cap. X. 2. Neque alium sensum habet in hoc capite, v. 7. 10. locove parallelo c. X. 28. 29. Notamus hic in gratiam Syncretistarum, Calixti imprimis, B. Balduini sententiam, anne Pontificii, missam audientes, idololatræ rectè di- cantur, cum non ex malitia, sed ex simplicitate, & in conscientia ita persuasi hoc faciant? Idolola- tria in officio missæ satis manifesta est, dum san- ctos invocant, & benedictum panem adorant, & coram creatura procidunt, dicentes eam Creato- rem. Et quamvis hic discrimen sit inter eos, qui contra conscientiam hanc idololatriam defendunt, & alios, qui ex simplici persuasione erroris, in quo nati sunt, id faciunt: Attamen cultus Missaticus naturam suam non exuit, & quia ipse idololatri- cus est, idcirco & cultores suos reddit idololatras, qualicunque affectu aut intentione hoc ab ipsis fiat. Hoc observent velim Calixtini, Pontificios non simplices tantùm, sed pertinaces etiam Missæ pro- pugnatores, ab idololatria absolventes.

Διόπερ εἰ βρῶμα σκανδαλίζει τὸν ἀδελφόν μου, οὐ μὴ φάγω κρέα εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, ἵνα μὴ τὸν ἀδελφόν μου σκανδαλίσω. Est exaggeratio. Potius quam occasionem dem alicui Christiano redeundi ad idololatriam, malim non epulis tantùm illis immolatitiis, sed omni omnino carne sive animato abstinere, & pane solo, atque oleribus, ut nonnulli faciunt, victitare. Non autem hoc dicit, quod hoc aliquo casu opus sit, sed ut ostendat multo graviora quam de qui- bus hic agitur, sustinenda pro proximorum salute. Simile loquendi genus observavimus Matth. V. 29.

Suum ergo eis commendat exemplum, è quo discant, quales erga infirmos esse oporteat; se enim ita scribit affectum, ut si sciat, esu carnium idolis immolatarum poni fratri infirmo offendicu- lum, nolit vesci carnibus in æternum; non quod non liceat coram DEO, sed quod non expediat propter conscientiam infirmorum, quibus in re, salutem illorum attinente, meritò parcendum est, ut hic B. Hunnius. Sit ergò Christiana dilectio regula & amussis nostræ cum infirmis conversa- tionis, ut in usu libertatis nos totos demittamus ad illorum imbecillitatem, ut & institutione salu- tari, & prudenti conversatione confirmentur in fide, & Christo Domino ad plenum lucrifient. Qua in re Paulus Apostolus vivum nobis exemplar est, qui ut in rebus adiaphoris ne ad momentum quidem cessit pertinacibus Evangelicae veritatis hostibus, Gal. II. Sic è converso in gratiam infir- morum circumcidit Timotheum, Act. XVI. Ex- plevit votum Nazaraeorum, Act. XXI. & Judaeis factus est tanquam Judaeus, ut Judaeos lucrifaceret, gentibus tanquam gentilis, ut gentiles lucrifaceret. 1. Cor. IX. Pulchrè Chrysostomus in h. l. Summa amentia est, quae Christo pretiosissima sunt, & talia, ut eorum gratia mortem obire non recusavit; ita nos despicatissima arbitrari, ut escis propterea non abstineamus.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER 9.

ARGUMENT & DIVISION.

The Apostle continues to set himself as an example regarding the use of indifferent things, that he himself, as an Apostle—whose seal of apostolic office they were—did not use his power in leading about a wife and in receiving a stipend, which he excellently teaches from Scripture and nature to be just, and that he preached the Gospel for free, and made himself a servant to all, and accommodated himself so that he might gain more, to the Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles, and thus became weak to the weak, indeed became all things to all men for the sake of the Gospel; and he warns them to run in such a way that they may carry off the prize, and to fight in such a way that they may carry off the incorruptible crown, again proposing himself to them as an example.

There are two parts: The former is the Apostle's example regarding the use of indifferent things in acquiring the means of support, up to v. 23. The latter is the Apostolic admonition regarding the course and the sacred contest, illustrated by example, up to v. 27.

PART I. The Apostolic example regarding the use of indifferent things.

v. 1. Am I not an Apostle?

He continues to argue against those teachers who, puffed up by the name of erudition, attributed more to philosophical disputations than to the utility of the faithful. He urges them, however, with his own example, saying this: If I am an Apostle, as I am, I am in no way inferior to those teachers.

Am I not free?

Liberty is certainly equal for all, and it belongs to me no less than to them. In the manuscript, the speech grows better: Am I not free, am I not an Apostle? And it appears that the Syriac and the Arab read it thus.

Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

If Greek erudition confers some authority upon them, so do divine revelations upon me.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Pergit Apostolus se in exemplum sistere, quoad usum rerum mediarum, quod ipse ceu Apo- stolus, cujus muneris Apostolici sigillum ipsi erant, potestate in circumducenda uxore, & accipiendo stipendio, quod aequum esse è Scriptura & natura egregiè docet, usus non sit, quodque Evangelium gratis praedicârit, & se omnibus servum fecerit, atque attem- perârit, ut plures lucrifaceret, Judaeis pro- selytis & gentibus, adeoque infirmis infir- mus, imò omnibus omnia factus sit propter Evangelium; monetque, ut ita currant, quo brabeum, ita pugnent, ut immarcesci- bilem coronam reportent, se iterum in ex- emplum iisdem proponens.

PArtes duae sunt: Prior Apostoli quoad usum rerum indifferentium in acquirendis sustenta- tionis mediis exemplum ad v. 23. Posterior Apo- stolicum quoad cursum & certamen sacrum moni- tum exemplo illustratum ad v. 27.

PARS I. Apostolicum quoad usum rerum indifferentium exemplum.

v. 1. Οὐκ εἰμὶ Ἀπόστολος;

Pergit arguere doctores illos, qui eruditionis nomine inflati plus Philosophicis disputationibus quàm utilitati fi- delium tribuebant. Urget autem eos suo exemplo, hoc dicit: Si Apostolus sum, ut sum, nihilo minor sum illis Doctoribus.

Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐλεύθερος;

Libertas certè omnibus aequalis est, nec mihi minus, quàm illis competit. In Manuscripto melius crescit oratio: Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ εἰμὶ Ἀπόστολος. Et sic legisse Syrum & Arabem apparet.

Οὐχὶ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν ἑώρακα;

Si illis autoritatis aliquid confert Graecanica eruditio, ac mihi divinae revelationes.

## 9:2
v. 2. Are not you my work in the Lord?

I formed you for Christ. Thus also that great work of the great Caesar. Concerning him who had been instituted by Caesar.

If I am not an Apostle to others, yet doubtless I am to you.

If others were to doubt whether I were an Apostle, you certainly ought not to doubt because of the signs of an Apostle which I produced among you.

For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

Just as it is evident through the affixed signs that some instrument is genuine, so it is evident through your conversion that I am an Apostle. Regarding the word σφραγίδος, see what has been said at John 3:3 and Romans 4:11. Ἀποστολὴ is the Apostolic office, Acts 2:5, Galatians 2:8.

That these things were said on account of false teachers, although it can easily be admitted, does not, however, appear to be a sufficient indication. In general, Paul had warned the Corinthians, whom he had admonished by his own example concerning not usurping liberty in food and drink with scandal; he finished admonishing them in such a paradigmatic way, which, so that it might penetrate more, he first sets forth his own Apostolic authority, and that under the scheme of an interrogation, on account of the energy of the speech: Am I not an Apostle? Am I not free? Which two interrogations the Vulgate transposed rashly, and against the original codices. It is rather: that he was an Apostle: He adds, however, am I not free? Lest anyone should believe that the Apostolic office, because Apostles and teachers are ministers of the Church, and he himself had made himself a servant to all v. 19, derogates anything from liberty. And when he called himself an Apostle, lest there be doubt about it, or at least he himself be considered inferior to other Apostles, who saw Christ in the flesh, he asks further: Have I not seen Christ? Concerning which one must read Act. IX. 5. Chap. XXII. 18. Finally, he insists by asking: Are you not my work in the Lord? Because from that he could confirm his Apostleship by their own testimony, who had both received him as an Apostle, and had experienced the power of his Apostolic office and doctrine. For which reason he adds: If I am not an Apostle to others; yet at least I am to you. For you are the seal of my Apostleship in the Lord. Which shone forth especially in the virtue of his preaching, miracles, labors, and dangers among them, and in their conversion, by which as divine seals he had consigned and corroborated his Apostolic office. However, the Apostle does not boast of these things out of a certain ambition; but he wishes the mouth to be stopped of those who were attacking his office with calumnies, so that they might derogate from the faith and authority of the doctrine preached by the Apostles. Theophylact, handing down this continuity, has it thus: As if he were to say: Although Christ himself commands that he who preaches the Gospel should take his living from the Gospel, that is, from those who were to be instructed in the faith. I myself, however, if the option is given, would indeed prefer to be consumed by hunger than to seem to have received anything from you, but I procure the sustenance of life for myself by the help of my own hands. There were also (as it seems) among the Corinthians some teachers, very rich and opulent, who considered it a glory to instruct others for free, and were striving so that the food sought from doctrine might result in ignominy for the Apostle. Having noticed this, he himself took care not to take sustenance from his disciples, even though it was permitted to him. Thus it is dealt with me, he says; you, however, do not abstain from things sacrificed to idols in the meantime. Yet the whole sense of this speech is reduced to this: Am I not, he says, an Apostle? Lest anyone perhaps occurring might say: You take no food from your disciples because it is not permitted to you to do this. Whence he infers: What is that? Do not the other Apostles also take sustenance from their disciples? Yes, he says. What then? Am I not also an Apostle, as they are? Certainly. Am I not free? That is, having no one who prohibits me from taking this sustenance. And lest that be objected besides: But in that the others surpass you, because they saw the Lord, he thus infers: Have I not seen the Lord Jesus, and last of all, as to one born out of due time, he was seen by me? What then, someone will say, if you are an Apostle, and perform the office of an Apostle, and yet have not brought forth any deed of an Apostle? For Judas was also an Apostle, and had seen the Lord. Therefore Paul, to meet this objector, says thus: Are you not my work? I have therefore performed the ministry of an Apostle. And since he had boasted of a truly great thing, he added, in the Lord, that is, I did not do that by my own virtue, but by the power of the Lord.

Latin:

v. 2. Οὐ τὸ ἔργον μου ὑμεῖς ἐστε ἐν Κυρίῳ;

Ego vos Christo formavi. Sic Et magnum magni Caesaris illud opus. De eo, qui à Caesare institutus fuerat.

Εἰ ἄλλοις οὐκ εἰμὶ Ἀπόστολος, ἀλλ' ὑμῖν εἰμί.

Si alii dubitarent, an Apostolus essem, vos certe dubi- tare non deberetis propter signa Apostolatus, quae apud vos edidi.

Ἡ γὰρ σφραγὶς τῆς ἐμῆς ἀποστολῆς ὑμεῖς ἐστε ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Sicut per signa apposita constat instrumentum aliquod sincerum esse, ita per vestram conversionem constat, me esse Apostolum. De voce σφραγίδος vide, quae dicta ad Joh. 3, 3. & Rom. 4, 11. Ἀποστολὴ munus Apostolicum Act. 2, 5. Gal. 2, 8.

Haec ob falsos Doctores dicta esse, quamvis ad- mitti facile possit, non tamen sufficiens indicium apparet. In genere Paulus Corinthios, quos de libertate in cibo & potu non usurpanda cum scandalo suo exemplo monuerat; ita παραδειγμα- τικῶς monere peregit, quod ut magis penetret, autoritatem suam Apostolicam primum sistit, id- que sub schemate interrogationis, ob orationis ἐνέργειαν: Non sum Apostolus? Non sum liber? Quas duas interrogationes temere, & invitis Codicibus Originalibus, transposuit Vulagatus. Potius est: quod fuerit Apostolus: Addit tamen, nonne sum liber? Ne Apostolicum munus quis credat, quia Apostoli & Doctores mi- nistri sunt Ecclesiae, & ipse servum se fecerat omni- bus v. 19. libertati quicquam derogare. Et cum Apostolum se dixit, ne dubium de eo sit, aut saltim ipse inferior censeatur aliis Apostolis, qui Chri- stum in carne viderunt, quaerit porro: Nonne Christum vidi? Quo de legere est Act. IX. 5. Cap. XXII. 18. Denique instat quaerendo: Nonne opus meum vos estis in Domino? Quia inde Apostolatum suum confirmare poterat proprio ipsorum testi- monio, qui & tanquam Apostolum eum suscepe- rant, & vim Apostolici muneris & doctrinae ejus experti erant. Quo nomine addit: Etsi aliis non sum Apostolus; Sed tamen vobis sum. Nam signaculum Apostolatus mei vos estis in Domino. Quod in virtute praeconii, miraculorum, laborum, & periculorum inter ipsos, & conversione ipsorum imprimis effulgebat, quibus ceu sigillis divinis consignarat & corroborarat munus Apostolicum. Non autem hisce se jactat Apostolus e quadam ambitione; sed os obturatum vult illis, qui calu- mniis officium illius impetebant, ut doctrinae per Apostolos praedicatae fidem, ac autoritatem dero- garent. Theophylactus συνέχειαν hanc tradens ita habet: Quasi dicat: Quamvis Christus ipse jubeat, ut is, qui Evangelium praedicaret, de Evangelio, hoc est, ab iis, qui ad fidem instruerentur, sumeret vi- ctum. Ipse tamen, si optio detur, malim equidem ine- dia confici, quam ut videar a vobis quidpiam acce- pisse, sed mearum manuum opem vitae mihi alimoni- am comparo. Erant etiam (ut videtur) apud Corin- thios praeceptores nonulli, praedivites & opulenti, qui gloriae ducerent, alios gratis instruere, molirentur- que, ut Apostolo ad ignominiam cederet quaesitus ex doctrina cibus. Qua re ipse animadversa cavebat, ne victum a discipulis sumeret, tametsi esset id ei per- missum. Mecum itaque sic agitur, inquit; Vos ta- men nec idolothytis interea abstinetis. Huc tamen omnis orationis hujusce sensus redigitur: Non sum, inquit, Apostolus? Ne quis forte occurrens inquiat: Propterea nulla sumis a discipulis alimen- ta, quia tibi, ut agas hoc, non licet. Unde id infert: Quid illud? Nonne & Apostoli caeteri victum a discipulis capiunt? Etiam inquit. Quid igitur? Nonne & ipse Apostolus sum, ut illi sunt? Scilicet. Nonne liber sum? hoc est, neminem habens, qui me capere hunc victum prohibeat. Et ne illud praeterea objiceretur: At in eo te superant caeteri, quia vide- runt Dominum, sic infert: Nonne Dominum Je- sum conspexi, & omnium postremo, ut abortivo visus est mihi? Quid tum, inquiet aliquis, si Apostolus es, & Apostoli officio fungeris, nec dum tamen Apostoli aliquod prae te tuleris facinus? Erat namque & Judas Apostolus, & Dominum viderat. Propterea Paulus, ut hac objicienti occurrat, sic ait: Nonne opus meum vos estis? Sum itaque Apostoli ministerio functus. Et quoniam rem sane ingentem jactaverat, adjecit, in Domino, hoc est, nec mea id quidem virtute; sed Domini potentia egi.

## 9:3
v. 3. My defense to those who examine me is this. I think these things are better referred to what follows than to what precedes. To those who arrogate to themselves the right to judge my actions, I answer with what follows. Some teachers of the Corinthians, those Gnostics, of course, were slandering Paul, as if he were less understanding of how great the liberty of a wise man is. But Paul shows that he understands this correctly, and teaches it with many arguments. But that he circumscribes the use of liberty within the bounds of prudence and love. Anselm and Theophylact refer it to what precedes, as if he were to say: To those who inquire about my calling and Apostleship, my apology is among them, which exists in you. But these things are altogether more conveniently referred to what follows by Chrysostom and Ambrose.

Latin:

v. 3. Ἡ ἐμὴ ἀπολογία τοῖς ἐμὲ ἀνακρίνουσιν αὕτη ἐστί. Melius haec putem ad sequentia quam ad praecedentia referri. Qui sibi arrogant, ut de meis actionibus judicent, eis respondeo, quae sequuntur. Doctores nonnulli Corinthiorum, γνωστικοὶ illi scilicet, Paulum obtrectabant, tanquam minus intelligentem, quanta esset hominis sapientis libertas. Ostendit vero Paulus, se id recte intelligere, & id multis argumentis docet. Sed se usum libertatis circumscribere prudentiae & dilectionis finibus. Ad praecedentia refert Anshelmus & Theophylactus, quasi dicat: Qui inquirunt de mea vocatione & Apostolatu, apud eos apologia mea est, quae in vobis extat. Sed omnino commodius haec ad sequentia referuntur a Chrysostomo, & Ambrosio.

## 9:4
V. 4. Have we not power to eat and to drink? Which power concerning food and drink promiscuously, with the distinction removed, which was once commanded in the law, some, and among these B. Hunnius and Heshusius, understand: Others, with Cornelius a Lapide, restrict it to the power of eating and drinking at the expense of the Church, or of demanding sustenance from those among whom he was teaching. B. Balduinus leaves the matter in the middle. But the Apostle had already dealt sufficiently with the indifference of food and drink before, and in this chapter he denotes something peculiar, nor does he make mention of the distinction of foods anymore, he pursues only the matter concerning the means of sustaining, and in that way he introduces the power of leading about a woman, because both for himself and his wife, if he wished to lead about a spouse, provision would have to be made for sustenance at the expense of those whose teacher he was. Concerning marriage itself, he had already taught sufficiently in the preceding. And therefore it did not pertain here to commemorate the liberty of taking a wife: Much less, however, is it to be conceded to the Papists, Salmeron and others, who snatch these things away to the excellence of the contemplative life and to the greater perfection of the Monastic orders. For Paul is not dealing here with that which must always and everywhere be avoided, but only with that which must be avoided in the case of the harmful scandal of weak brothers, as is evident from the determination of the case in the last verse. But not concerning a comparison, which state is more perfect, or not? For which reason this argument must rather be inverted: From which state more scandals arise for the weaker, that is to be avoided: For this is the major premise of Paul; From the state of celibacy, abstinence from meats, money, etc., more scandals arise toward the weak according to civil custom, Therefore, etc., as here B. Hulsemannus.

Latin:

V. 4. Μὴ οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν φάγειν καὶ πιεῖν; Quam potestatem de cibo & potu promiscuo, sublato discrimine, olim in lege praecepto nonnulli, & inter hos B. Hunnius & Heshusius intelligunt: Alii ad potestatem manducandi & bibendi de sumptibus Ecclesiae, vel victum ab iis, apud quos docebat, exigendi, restringunt, cum Cornelio a Lapide. B. Balduinus rem in medio relinquit. Sed de cibi & potus ἀδιαφορίᾳ jam ante satis egerat Apostolus, & hoc capite peculiare quid denotat, nec amplius discriminis ciborum mentionem facit, materiam solum de mediis sustentandi persequitur, illaque ratione potestatem circumducendi mulierem ingerit, quod & sibi & uxori, si vellet conjugem circumducere, prospiciendum de victu foret sumptibus eorum, quorum Doctor erat. De ipso conjugio jam satis docuerat in superioribus. Ideoque non attinebat hic libertatem ducendae uxoris commemorare: Multo vero minus Papistis, Salmeroni & aliis annuendum, haec ad praestantiam vitae speculativae, & ad majorem perfectionem ordinum Monasticorum abripienti. Non enim Paulus hic agit de eo, quod semper & ubique vitari oporteat, sed de eo tantum, quod in casu noxii scandali infirmorum fratrum vitandum est, ut patet ex determinatione casus v. ult. Non vero de comparatione, uter status sit perfectior, nec ne? Quam ob rem invertendum est potius hoc argumentum: Ex quo statu infirmiori plura oriuntur scandala, ille vitandus est: Nam haec Major est Pauli; Ex statu caelibatus, abstinentia a carnibus, nummis &c. consuetudini civili oriuntur erga infirmos plura scandala, Ergo &c. ut hic B. Hulsemannus.

## 9:5
v. 5. Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other Apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas. The discourse grows. For first he names the Apostles, then the brethren, that is the kinsmen of the Lord: Lastly Cephas himself, the Prince of the Apostolic assembly. Cephas or Peter had his wife as a companion of his journeys, who was also led to death in his presence, as Clement of Alexandria reports from tradition in book VII. The other Apostles did the same and made use of the services of their wives for converting matrons, as the same author narrates in book III. Although he adds, not as wives, but as sisters leading about women, as if wishing to signify that the Apostles did not use their wives as wives, when nevertheless he had said before that children were born to both Peter and Philip, and that daughters were given in marriage by Philip. It seems therefore more correct to take γυναῖκα here not as referring to such matrons as had once accompanied Christ. For the Jews were accustomed to call their wives sisters, on account of their common origin. Tob. V. 18. in the Greek. Christians, however, did so on account of their common faith, as we said above VII. 14. For a like reason Tertullian calls his most beloved wife a fellow-servant in the Lord. Περιάγειν is to lead about with one, wherever one goes. Thus περιήγαγε is used in Ezech. XLV. 1. 2. Ἄγεσθαι means this very thing in Justin, where he treats of the Jews at the end of his dialogue with Trypho: That women might not be drawn into alliances or foreign nations, says Tacitus, Annals III. 2. Understand, however, that περιάγειν is at the expense of the Churches, as was the custom.

Latin:

v. 5. Μὴ οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα περιάγειν, ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἀπόστολοι, καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ τοῦ Κυρίου, καὶ Κηφᾶς. Crescit oratio. Nam primum Apostolos nominat, deinde fratres, id est cognatos Domini: Postremo Cepham ipsum Principem Apostolici coetus. Cephas sive Petrus uxorem suam comitem habuit itinerum, quae & coram ipso ad mortem ducta est, ut ex traditione refert Clemens Alexandrinus libro VII. Idem fecere & alii Apostoli & uxorum opera usi sunt ad matronas convertendas, ut idem narrat libro III. Quanquam addit, οὐχ ὡς γαμετάς, ἀλλ' ὡς ἀδελφὰς περιήγοντας γυναῖκας, quasi significare volens, non usos Apostolos uxoribus, ut uxoribus, cum tamen ante dixisset & Petro & Philippo natos filios, & a Philippo filias nuptum datas. Videtur ergo rectius, γυναῖκα hic accipere non de matronis talibus, quales Christum comitatae olim fuerant. Solebant enim Judaei uxores suas appellare sorores, ob communem originem. Tob. V. 18. in Graeco. Christiani autem ob communem fidem, ut diximus supra VII. 14. Pari de causa Tertullianus uxorem suam dilectissimam in Domino conservam vocat. Περιάγειν est secum ducere, quoquo quis eat. Sic περιήγαγε sumitur Ezech. XLV. 1. 2. Ἄγεσθαι hoc ipsum Justino, ubi de Judaeis agit fine colloquii cum Tryphone: Ne foeminae in socios aut gentes externas traherentur, ait Tacitus, annalium III. 2. Intellige autem περιάγειν sumptu Ecclesiarum, ut fieri solebat.

## 9:6
v. 6. Or I only and Barnabas. Barnabas, long a companion of Paul, had drawn much from his example.

Just as the preeminence of Peter, let alone his primacy over the remaining Apostles, cannot be concluded by Papists from a certain order, which is evident even from Galatians 2:9; so Grotius rightly departs from those who understand γυναῖκα here as merely a matron serving, and not truly a wife. Concerning which see Bellarmine, book 1, On Clerics, ch. 20; Gregor. de Valent., book 2, On Celibacy, ch. 6; Salmero, Justinianus, Tirinus, Corn. a Lapide on this passage. The example of Christ, which they themselves allege, is ἀλόγιστον (irrational). For he himself did not lead women around, but they followed him for the sake of piety and religion, drawn by the efficacy of his teaching and the excellence of his miracles. These are celebrated for their munificence, which does not fit this woman, whom the Apostle had the power to lead around, and whom the Churches ought to have supported together with the Apostle, trusting in her ministry. Therefore, the discussion is about that woman whom the Churches ought to have supported first, along with the Apostle, trusting in her ministry. Secondly, the Apostle could have led her around at his own pleasure, and thirdly, without scandal, and fourthly, by the example of Peter and the brothers of Christ; add fifthly, that each one had the ἐξουσίαν (authority) to lead around no more than one; however, for the sake of service, several could have been at the disposal of one. Nor would there have been a need for a woman for service, since that could have been performed by persons of his own sex, both more conveniently and without scandal or grounds for detraction. For the Apostle teaches that one must abstain even from the appearance of evil, 1 Thess. 5:22. Unless those were wives, says Andr. Dudithius, Bishop of Pécs, in his Demonstration for the Marriage of Clerics, a suspicion could have arisen that harlots were being led around by the Apostles, which it is likely they avoided with the greatest zeal, lest the authority of the Gospel which they taught be wounded by insults and accusations through their own lives. Moreover, it was fitting that the house and family of the Apostles, and their entire society, be free not only from crime but from the suspicion of crime. Furthermore, the discussion is about such a woman whom the Apostle indeed had the power to lead around, but did not lead around. Yet the Apostle did not shun the honest conversation and ministries of pious women (Acts 16:14, 18:2, 18, Rom. 16:1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 13, 15, 1 Cor. 16:19, 2 Tim. 4:19). Besides, that woman is understood, for the designation of whom the word ἀδελφὴ (sister) was not sufficient, but the mention of γυναικὸς (wife/woman) was also required, which is used by the Apostle everywhere for a wife, most frequently in 1 Cor. 7, and often elsewhere. To signify the sex, the word ἀδελφὴ alone suffices, just as the word γυναικὸς is omitted elsewhere (Rom. 16:12, 1 Tim. 5:2, Tit. 2:3, Phil. 2:1). Finally, [the discussion is] about such a woman over whom the Apostles had marital ἐξουσίαν (authority), so that by virtue of the same they could lead them around with them everywhere, and they were bound to follow them. And the verb περιάγειν (to lead around) implies the authority of the one who leads over the person who is led. But who gave the Apostles the power to lead around other men's wives? Clement is the authority that Peter and the other Apostles had their wives as companions on their journeys. Nor must it be conceded to the Papists that the conjugal duty ceased between them and their wives during their Apostleship; that which the ancients established, according to Vasquez in his commentary on Thomas, disp. 89, on the sacrament of matrimony, is a begging of the question; Clement nowhere holds this, only hinting that in the pilgrimage of the Apostles they served the kingdom of heaven more than private and domestic duties. But how does that gloss of Cornelius fit the Apostle's scope: I could lead around a matron who would support me, when his purpose is to assert the power of leading around a wife, not one who would support him, but one who would be supported with him at the expense of the Church.

Therefore, after Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian (Exhortation to Chastity, ch. 8), Eusebius (book 3, Eccl. Hist., ch. 3), and Ambrose (on 2 Cor. 11), not only Valla and Vatablus, but also the Roman Pontiff Leo IX, against the letter of Nicetas, and from him the Canon Law (Distinction 31), accepted this passage as being about the wives of the Apostles. The aforementioned Bishop of Pécs, in his Demonstration for the Marriage of Clerics, p. 85, urges these points for our explanation of this passage: What else can be understood by 'sister woman'? Or any other woman? Why then does he add the word 'woman'? For it would be a trifling, and to exclude a man, it was enough to have named 'sister'. The Greek context has ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα. That the first is equivalent to the same, it appears sufficiently, as if he had said πιστὴν, that is, faithful or Christian. For thus the Apostles, and all that antiquity, used to call brothers and sisters those who worshipped the same God the Father and believed in his Son Christ, etc. Wherefore it ought not to seem new, nor unusual, that he honored a wife also with the title of sister. These are his words. B. Luther, on 1 Cor. 8:8, in the explanation of that passage (Vol. II, Jena, fol. 303b) and on Phil. 4:3, concludes that Paul had a wife, and was a widower at that time, and had the power to take and lead around a wife, which Espensaeus teaches (book 1, On Continence, ch. 9) that most of the ancients also established, namely that Paul was once married; whether he was a widower then, or did not wish to take with him the wife whom he could lead around, he holds that opinion as the better one.

Οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν τῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι.

That is, the right of sparing our labor and living at the expense of the Churches. You perhaps think that we two do not understand our right. We understand it indeed; but we also understand when it is more useful not to use that right. See Acts 18:3.

This interpretation of Theophylact and others, which receives light from the following verse, does not displease. Some interpret it as the power of seeking sustenance for oneself by the work of one's own hands: but they are misled, as it appears, by the Vulgate version, which omitted the negative in the words ἐξουσίαν τῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι, rendering it as the power of working, instead of not working.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἢ μόνος ἐγὼ καὶ Βαρνάβας. Barnabas Pauli diu comes multum ab exemplo ipsius traxerat.

Ut ex ordine certo non potest praeminentia Petri, nedum principatus in reliquos Apostolos tum Papistis concludi, quod vel e Gal. II. 9. patet; ita recte ab illis discedit Grotius, qui hic per γυναῖκα matronam solum inservientem, non vero uxorem intelligant. Quo de vid. Bellarm. l. 1. de Cleric. c. 20. Gregor. de Valent. l. 2. de caeb. c. 6. Salmero, Justinianus, Tirinus, Corn. a Lapide in hunc locum. Exemplum Christi, quod ipsi allegant, ἀλόγιστον est. Non enim ipse circumduxit foeminas, sed ipsae secutae eum pietatis & religionis causa sunt, allectae doctrinae efficacia & miraculorum praestantia. Quae a munificentia celebrantur, quod huic mulieri, cujus circumducendae potestatem habuit Apostolus, non convenit. De ea ergo muliere sermo est, quam primo alere una cum Apostolo debuissent Ecclesiae, ministerio ejus fidentes. Secundo circumducere pro lubitu suo potuisset Apostolus, idque tertio sine scandalo, & quarto exemplo Petri, & fratrum Christi, adde quinto, quam quisque non nisi unicam circumducendi ἐξουσίαν habuit; servitii autem causa plures uni praesto esse potuissent. Nec ad servitium muliere opus fuisset, cum id a personis sui sexus, & commodius, & citra scandalum, ac obtrectationis materiam praestari potuerit. Nam a specie etiam mali abstinendum esse docet Apostolus 1. Thess. V. 22. Nisi illa uxores fuissent, inquit Andr. Dudithius Episcopus Quinque-Ecclesiensis in Demonstratione pro Conjugio Clericorum, suspicio oriri potuisset, scorta ab Apostolis circumduci, quod summo studio illos cavisse, verisimile est, ne per ipsorum vitam Evangelii, quod docebant, autoritas convitiis & criminationibus vulneraretur. Decebat autem Apostolorum domum & familiam, atque universam societatem non crimine solum, sed criminis suspicione vacare. Porro de tali muliere sermo est, quam potestatem quidem circumducendi habuerit Apostolus; sed non circumduxerit. At piarum mulierum honestam conversationem, & ministeria non aversatus est Apostolus Act. XVI. 14. C. XIIX. 2. 18. Rom. XVI. 1. 2. 3. 6. 12. 13. 15. 1. Cor. XVI. 19. 2. Tim. IV. 19. Adhaec ea intelligitur mulier, ad quam designandam non sufficiebat vox ἀδελφὴ; sed etiam γυναικὸς mentio requirebatur, quae passim pro uxore ab Apostolo sumitur, 1. Cor. VII. saepissime, & alias frequenter. Ad sexum significandum sola vox ἀδελφὴ sufficit, uti alias omissa est vox γυναικὸς Rom. XVI. 12. 1. Timoth. V. 2. Tit. II. 3. Phil. II. 1. Denique de tali muliere, in quam ἐξουσίαν maritalem habuere Apostoli, ut vi ejusdem ipsas secum ubique circumducere potuerint, illaeque eosdem sequi debuerint. Et verbum περιάγειν autoritatem ejusdem, qui circumducit, in personam, quae circumducitur, infert. Quis vero Apostolis potestatem dedit, alienas mulieres circumducendi? Quemadmodum Petrum, & alios Apostolos comites habuisse suorum itinerum, autor Clemens est. Neque vero concedendum est Pontificiis, quod cessarit inter ipsos & uxores conjugale officium in Apostolatu, quod veteres statuisse secundum Vasquezium in Thom. disp. 89. de sacram. matrimon. petitio principii est; nuspiam habet Clemens, id solum innuens, quod in peregrinatione Apostolorum magis administraverint regno coelorum, quam privatis & domesticis officiis. Sed quomodo scopo Apostoli convenit glossa illa Cornelii: Possem matronam, quae me aleret, circumducere, cum propositum ipsi sit, asserere potestatem circumducendae uxoris, non quae ipsum aleret; sed quae sumptibus Ecclesiae aleretur cum illo.

Idcirco post Clementem Alex. & Tertull. exhort. ad castitatem c. 8. Euseb. l. 3. A. Eccl. l. 3. c. 3. Ambrosium in 2. Cor. XI. non tantum Valla, & Vatablus, sed etiam ita Pontifex Romanus Leo IX. contra Epistolam Nicetae, & ex eo Jus Canonicum nec omnino distinct. XXXI. locum hunc de uxoribus Apostolorum accepere. Praedictus QuinqueEccles. Episcopus in demonstr. pro conjug. Cleric. p. 85. haec pro nostra hujus loci explicatione urget: Quid aliud per sororem mulierem intelligi potest? An alia quaevis foemina? Cur ergo addit vocem mulierem? Nugatio enim esset, & ad excludendum virum satis erat sororem nominasse. Graecus contextus habet ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα. Primum illud idem valere, satis apparet, quam si dixisset πιστὴν, id est, fidelem seu Christianam. Ita enim fratres & sorores Apostoli, & tota illa antiquitas vocare solebat eos, qui eundem Deum Patrem colerent, inque ejus Filium Christum crederent &c. Quare novum videri non debet, neque inusitatum, quod uxorem sororis quoque vocabulo cohonestaverit. Haec ille. B. Luth. d 1. Cor. VIII. 8. in expl. istius loci T. II. Jen. f. 303. b. & d Phil. IV 3. colligit, Paulum uxorem habuisse, ac viduum tum fuisse, & potestatem habuisse, uxorem ducere ac circumducere, quod etiam plerosque veterum statuisse, Paulum nempe aliquando conjugatum fuisse, Espensaeus docet lib. 1. de contin. c. 9. sive viduus tum fuerit, sive uxorem, quam circumducere poterat, secum ducere noluerit, ac sententiam illam pro potiori habet.

Οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν τῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι.

Id est jus parcendi operae nostrae & vivendi impensis Ecclesiarum. Putatis forte, nos duos jus nostrum non intelligere. Intelligimus sane; sed & intelligimus, quando utilius sit eo jure non uti. Vide Act. XVIII. 3.

Non displicet haec interpretatio Theophylacti, & aliorum, quae e versu sequenti lucem accipit. Nonnulli de potestate victum sibi opera manuum suarum quaerendi interpretantur: Sed seducti, ut apparet, per vulgatam versionem, quae negativam in verbis ἐξουσίαν τῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι omisit, ea reddens potestatem hoc operandi, pro non operandi.

## 9:7
v. 7. Τίς στρατεύεται τοῖς ἰδίοις ὀψωνίοις ποτέ.

To show that he understands his own right, he brings forward arguments for that right, first from the consensus of nations, then also from the law of Moses. Ὀψώνια [wages] stipends, Luke III. 15. To serve at one's own stipends, that is, at one's own expense, at one's own cost.

Who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof?

It is permitted for vinedressers to eat grapes.

Or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?
