Shepherds are accustomed, if any necessity urges, to sustain themselves with the milk of the flocks. Milk is said to be both drunk, as above III. 2, and eaten, as here, namely with bread, which shepherds carried in a wallet, II Kings IV. 24, Judith X. 5, XIII. 11.

Paul therefore shows by how much right he yielded for the sake of the newly planted Church, so that he might the more entice the Corinthians to the Christian faith.

Latin:

v. 7. Τίς στρατεύεται τοῖς ἰδίοις ὀψωνίοις ποτέ.

Ut ostendat, se jus suum intelligere, argumenta ejus juris affert, primum ex consensu gentium, deinde etiam ex lege Mosis. Ὀψώνια stipendia Luc. III. 15. suis stipendiis militare, id est, suo aere, suo sumptu.

Τίς φυτεύει ἀμπελῶνα, καὶ ἐκ τῦ καρπῦ ἀυτῦ ἐκ ἐσθίει.

Vinitoribus licet uvas edere.

Ἢ τίς ποιμαίνει ποίμνην, καὶ ἐκ τῦ γάλακτος τῆς ποίμνης μὴ ἐσθίει;

Solent pastores, si qua necessitas urgeat, lacte pecudum se sustentare. Lac & bibi dicitur, ut supra III. 2. & edi, ut hic, nimirum cum pane, quem in pera ferebant pastores II. Reg. IV. 24. Judith. X. 5. XIII. 11.

Ostendit ergo Paulus, quanto jure cesserit in gratiam Ecclesiae recens plantatae, ut Corinthios eo magis pelliceret ad fidem Christianam.

## 9:8
v. 8. Do I say these things according to man?

Do you think that I construct what I say by human authority alone, that is to say, from customs? See Rom. VI. 19.

Or does not the law say these things?

The law itself given by God, in which there is nothing unjust.

Latin:

v. 8. Μὴ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ταῦτα λέγω.

An putatis me, quae dico, sola humana autoritate adstruere, ex moribus scilicet. Vide Rom. VI. 19.

Ἢ ὀυχὶ ὁ νόμος ταῦτα λαλεῖ;

Lex ipsa a Deo data, in qua nihil est iniqui.

## 9:9
For in the law of Moses it is written: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn.

The words of the LXX, Deut. XXV. 4. Φιμοῦν [to muzzle], to halter, as Pliny and Columella speak: To bridle, as Ambrose translates. Ἐπιστομίζειν, as Hesychius, to close the mouth, whence by metaphor it signifies to impose silence, Matt. XXII. 12, 34, Mark I. 25, IV. 39, Luke IV. 35, 1 Pet. II. 15. Oxen are said Ἀλοᾷν [to thresh] when they extract grains from the ears with their feet: which is the custom of the East, but also of Greece, as we learn from Theophrastus and others. See on this matter Moses of Coucy, in the commanding precept XCI and the forbidding precept CLXXXIV.

Regarding this, B. Balduinus has it thus: What is done today with flails was formerly done by the benefit of oxen, which, enclosed in the threshing floor, trampled the ears of corn with their feet; they were called Triones and Teriones. Sometimes beams or boards weighted with stones were also added, which the oxen dragged around, so that the stalks might be better crushed and the grains shaken from the ears, of which custom mention is made in Is. XXIX. 28. Therefore, some who were more attentive to the matter while these were working would muzzle their mouths, or pass ropes around their necks in the manner of a wheel with an instrument (which they called παυσικάπην), or smear their nostrils with cow dung, so that they could not snatch anything from the ears, as Cato notes in chapter 54 of his work on agriculture: Which inhumanity God rebukes in that law. Compare what we have said about this passage at Deut. XXV. 4, where we also refuted the twofold sense of the Mosaic saying fabricated by the Papists. Balduinus does indeed also say that Paul openly teaches here that that law does not pertain properly to oxen, but figuratively denotes something else in the house of the Lord. But he only means that in sanctioning this law, God did not primarily or solely have regard for oxen; but primarily wished to teach, by that paradigm as it were, what man owes to man. For that he does not deny that the law pertains to oxen, the argument which he makes here from the mind of the Apostle testifies. If a man is bound by divine sanction to provide food for the beasts whose ministry he uses in economic matters: much more does he owe the same duty to men, especially those whose ministry he uses for the salvation of his soul. But the former is established from the cited law of Deuteronomy. Therefore, the latter cannot be denied either.

Does God care for oxen?

Not primarily, but we are commanded to exercise mercy even toward beasts for this reason, that we may the more recognize that it must be exercised toward men. Quintilian V. 9: Nor does it seem to me that the Areopagites, when they condemned the boy who was plucking out the eyes of quails, judged anything other than that this was a sign of a most pernicious mind, and one that would be a bane to many if it had grown up. Men whom God has abandoned from his protection are said to be held like fish and insects, because God cares only for the very genera of living things, and for men also as individuals, if they are of such worth. See what Maimonides discusses philosophically about this matter in The Guide for the Perplexed III. 17. Philo in his book on those who sacrifice: For the law is not for the sake of irrational creatures, but for the sake of those who have mind and reason, so that the concern is not for the victims, but for those who sacrifice, that they may not contract any passion. Philostratus, Life of Apollonius VIII. 9: This is not for the sake of the lions. For we are not concerned with the leading of wild beasts, but we are giving a bridle to tyrants. Not unlike that of Aeschines against Timarchus: For the lawgiver was not concerned for the sake of the servants, but wishing to accustom us to keep far from the insolence toward free men.

Latin:

Ἐν γὰρ τῷ νόμῳ Μωσέως γέγραπται· Οὐ φιμώσεις βοῦν ἀλοῶντα.

Verba LXX. Deut. XXV. 4. Φιμοῦν capistrare, ut loquuntur Plinius & Columella: Infrenare, ut vertit Ambrosius. Ἐπιστομίζειν, ut Hesychius, os occludere, unde per translationem significat silentium indicere Matth. XXII. 12. 34. Marci I. 25. IV. 39. Luc. IV. 35. 1. Pet. II. 15. Ἀλοᾷν dicuntur boves cum grana ex aristis exterunt pedibus: Qui mos Orientis, sed & Graeciae, ut ex Theophrasto & aliis discimus. Vide de hac re Mosen de Kotzi praecepto jubente XCI. vetante CLXXXIV.

De hoc ita habet B. Balduinus : Quod hodie fit paxillis, olim beneficio boum fiebat, qui areæ in- clusi pedibus proterebant spicas, Triones & Terio- nes dicebantur. Interdum etiam addebantur trabes, vel tabula lapidibus gravatæ, quas boves circumtrahebant, ut eò melius culmi comminue- rentur, & grana à spicis discuterentur, cujus consuetudinis mentio fit Es. XXIX. 28. His ergò laborantibus nonnulli attentiores ad rem ora ca- pistrabant, vel instrumento, (quod παυσικάπην vocabant,) ad modum rotæ, rotundo colla trans- mittebant, vel nares fimo bubulo illinebant, ne quid de spicis præcerpere possent, notante Catone c. 54. de re rustica: Quam inhumanitatem Deus ista lege reprehendit. Confer quæ de hoc loco diximus ad Deut. XXV. 4. ubi etiam geminum dicti Mosaici sensum à Papistis confictum profli- gavimus. Dicit quidem etiam Balduinus, apertè Paulum hic docere, legem illam non propriè ad boves pertinere, sed figuratè aliud quid notare in do- mo Domini. Sed id tantùm vult,quod in sancien- da hac lege Deus non primariò, nec unicè respe- xerit boves; sed imprimis, quid homo homini debeat, illo veluti paradigmate docere voluerit. Non enim negare ipsum, quod ad boves lex illa spectet, argumentum, quod ex mente Apostoli hic facit, testatur. Si homo ex sanctione divina tenetur alimenta suppeditare pecudibus, quarum ministerio in rebus œconomicis utitur : Multo ma- gis idem officium debet hominibus, iis imprimis, quorum ministerio utitur ad salutem animæ. Sed prius constat ex allegata lege Deuteronomii. Ergo & posterius negari nequit.

Μὴ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ Θεῷ.

Non præcipuè, sed ideo jubemur misericordiam etiam in jumentis exercere, ut eò magis eam noscamus in homi- nes exercendam. Quintilianus v. 9. Nec mihi videntur Areopagitæ cum damnaverunt puerum coturnicum oculos eji- cientem, aliud judicasse, quam id fignum esse perniciosissimæ mentis multisque malo futuræ si adolevisset. Homines, quos Deus à tutela sua destituit, dicitur habere velut pisces & in- secta, quia Deus animantium ipsa tantum genera curat, homines etiam singulos, si tanti sint. Vide quæ hac de re φιλοσοφικῶς differit Maimonides duce dubitantium III. 17. Philo libro de sacrificantibus : Οὐ γὰρ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλογῶν ὁ νό- μος, ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ τῶν νῦν καὶ λόγον ἐχόντων, ὥστε ὡ τῶν θυομέ- νων φροντίς ἐστιν ἀλλὰ τῶν θυόντων, ἵνα μηδὲν πάθος χαραμώσι. Philostratus vita Apollonii VIII. 9. Τῦτο δὲ ἐχ ὑπερ τῶν λεόντων ἔπει. Οὐ γὰρ ὑπὲρ θηρίων ἀγωγῆς σπυδάζομεν,ἀλλὰ ἡνίαν ἐπὶ τὺς τυράννυς διδύς. Non dissimile illud Æschinis contra Timocratem: Οὐ γὰρ ὑπὲρ τῶν οἰκετῶν ἐσπύδασεν ὁ νομοθέτης, ἀλλὰ βυλόμενος ἡμᾶς ἐθίζειν πολὺ ἀπέχειν τῆς τῶν ἐλευθέρων ὕβρεως.

## 9:10
Or does he say it altogether for our sake?

Πάντως is primarily: just as πάντες is for the most part.

Wicked are the things which Grotius inserts here, that God cares only for the very genera of living things, and for men also as individuals, if they are of such worth. For it is the certain opinion of the Scriptures that every individual of living things, and much more of men, whatever they may be, is cared for, Job XXXVIII. 10, Ps. XXXVI. 6, Ps. CIV. 27, 28, Ps. CXLVII. 9, Matt. VI. 26, ch. X. 29, Luke XII. 6. To deny this, indeed, is the mark of atheists, who deny God's providence and the universal sustenance of things. The opinion of Moses Maimonides, that no corruptible individuals are subject to divine providence except men, on account of the intellect, which is incorruptible—which is akin to the atheism of the Arabs, e.g., Algazel, book III of Metaphysics, ch. 5, 'The First Cause does not know particulars except through universal knowledge'—not even the Jews themselves approved. For the well-known saying of R. Manahem, cited by Drosius, book 1, p. 27, is omitted. The providence of the blessed God is also particularly concerned with wild beasts and animals. But Grotius is even worse than Maimonides, denying that even the single individuals of men are cared for, perhaps following those philosophers about whom Justin speaks in his Dialogue with Trypho: 'Certain philosophers wish to persuade us that God indeed takes care of this universe and of the genera and species themselves, but not likewise of me and of you, and of that body individually.' From which atheism, however, sounder philosophers even in the midst of paganism recoiled. See Plato in the Epinomis, Plotinus in Augustine, book X of The City of God, chapter 14. But Origen embraced the opinion of the Christians, Homily III on Genesis: 'We profess as a certain and immovable dogma that God cares for mortal things, and that nothing is done without his providence, neither in heaven nor on earth.'

For it was written for our sake, that he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope of partaking of his hope. The books vary here, as has been noted by others. That manuscript: That he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope of partaking. In which reading two things are to be noted; first, after he who threshes, one must understand to thresh, and that from the similar to plow which preceded. Then, to partake is to be referred, not only to the latter, but also to the former in hope. He who wished to provide for beasts of burden, much more for men who labor, so that hope of reward may soothe the labor, whether it be given in a portion of the thing itself in which one labors, as is the case with sharecropping farmers, or in money, which takes the place of all things.

Latin:

Ἢ δι’ ἡμᾶς πάντως λέγει.

Πάντως est præcipuè: Sicut πάντες plerique.

Improba sunt, quæ hic ingerit Grotius, Deum animantium ipsa genera tantùm curare, homines etiam singulos, si tanti sint. Nam individua etiam quæque animantium ac multo magis hominum, qualescunque illi sint, curari, scripturæ certa est sententia Job. XXXIIX. 10. Psal. XXXVI. 6. Psal. CIV. 27. 28. Ps. CXLVII. 9. Matth. VI. 26. c. X. 29. Luc. XII. 6. Id vero negare atheorum est, qui Dei providentiam & universalem rerum sustentationem inficiantur. Mosis Maimonidis sententiam, nulla individua corruptibilia subjacere providentiæ di- vinæ, nisi homines, propter intellectum, qui est incorruptibilis, quæ Arabum Atheismo e. g. Al- gazelis l. III. Metaph. c. 5. Prima causa non scit particularia nisi per notitiam universalem gemina est, ne Judæi ipsi quidem probarunt. Notum enim dictum R. Manahem laudatum Drosio l. 1. præterit. f. 27. Providentia Dei benedicti est etiam particulariter circa feras & bestias. Deterior autem adhuc Maimonide Grotius etiam homi- st num singula individua curari negans, sequutus forte Philosophos illos, de quibus Justinus in Dial. cum Tryph. Quidam Philosophi cupiunt nobis persuadere, universitatis quidem hujus ac generum specierumque ipsarum curam gerere DEUM, meique autem atque tui, & illius cor- poris sigillatim non itidem. A quo tamen atheismo saniores Philosophi etiam in medio gentilismo abhorruere. Vid. Plato in Epinomide, Plotinus apud August. l. X. de Civitate Dei cap. 14. Chri- stianorum vero sententiam complexus est Orige- nes homil. III. in Genesin: Deum curare mortalia, & nihil absque ejus providentia geri, neque in cœlo, neque in terra, certo & immobili dogmate profite- mur.

Δἱ ἡ̃μα̃ς γὰρ ἐγράφη, ύ̨τι ἐπ̓ ἐλπίδι ὀφείλει ὁ ἀροτριω̃ν ἀροτρια̃ν, καὶ ὁ ἀλοω̃ν τἠ̃ς ἐλπίδος αὐτου̃ μετέχων ἐπ̓ ἐλπίδι. Libri hic variant, ut est ab aliis annotatum. Manuscri- ptus ille : Ότι ὀφείλει ἐπ̓ ἐλπίδι ὁ ἀροτριω̃ν ἀροτρια̃ν, καὶ ὁ ἀλοω̃ν ἐπ̓ ἐλπίδι του̃ μετέχειν. In qua lectione duo notanda ; pri- mum post ὁ ἀλοω̃ν subaudiendum ἀλοα̃ν, idque ex simili ἀροτρια̃ν quod præcessit. Deinde μετέχειν referendum, non ad posterius tantum, sed & ad prius ἐπ̓ ἐλπίδι. Qui ju- mentis consultum voluit, multo magis hominibus labo- rantibus, ut laborem soletur spes mercedis, sive ea detur in parte rei ipsius in qua laboratur, ut sit colonis partiariis, sive in pecunia, quæ omnium rerum vicem subit.

## 9:11
v. 11. If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things? He draws the argument twice from the lesser: First from beasts of burden to men: Then from men laboring in things that pertain to this life, to men laboring in things leading to a better life. If those are worthy to be fed, how much more these. To sow and to reap are frequent in the Proverbs, as we have noted at Matt. XXV. 22, John IV. 37. In this place, to sow is to perform labor, to reap is to receive something for the labor. Great, that is, is it a wonder? Thus, is it a great thing, not a wonder at all. 2 Cor. XI. 15.

Those who plow, plow in the hope of a future harvest. Hope nourishes farmers, as Ovid says in book 1 of the Pontic Epistles. Those who thresh, thresh in the hope of obtaining a reward. It is just, therefore, that those who are occupied in the spiritual plow and threshing should not be frustrated in the hope of fruit and reward. Which, however, Cornelius wrongly draws to the hope of eternal reward. For it is not about an eternal reward, but about the stipend owed to the ministers of the Church. Nor indeed is one to work with the intention of the reward of eternal life. For that is a grace, Rom. VI. last verse. And rightly St. Bernard in his treatise on loving God: God is not loved except for a reward, even though he is to be loved without the intention of a reward: True charity is not mercenary, although a reward follows it.

If others partake of your authority, do not we more? If others enjoy a right over you, how much more we, supply, was it just to enjoy an equal right? Authority of you over you, just as authority over all flesh. John XVII. 2. Authority over spirits, Matt. X. 1.

By others, some understand the false Apostles. But they believe more correctly that the true Doctors of the Churches are designated, not precisely of the Corinthian Church. For these took stipends by right: Those in fact. And the argument is sought from right and authority.

But we have not used this authority. He who has a right can also abstain from the use of that right. Otherwise, the Lord would not be the master of that right.

But we endure all things. We bear. Thus we have endure below XIII. 7, 2 Thess. III. 1. 5.

Lest we give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ. To hinder is to impede, Rom. XV. 22, Gal. V. 7, 1 Thess. II. 18. Hence hindrance, an impediment, as where a road is cut off.

This impediment could easily arise from the acceptance of a reward or necessary expenses, even if in itself it were lawful and just; therefore the Apostle did not wish to use his right, lest he should in any way delay it. the Gospel, lest it should have the appearance as if the preaching of the Gospel were done for the sake of the belly, and not for the salvation of the hearers; which scandal the Apostle also wished to avoid, for the better promotion of the course of the Gospel at that time in planting the Church. Nor, however, let anyone conclude from this that he is hindered by the acceptance of a stipend, or that by the example of the Apostle the Church must be served for free. For the Apostle sufficiently asserted the right of receiving stipends by examples, comparisons, arguments, and divine commands.

Nor does the command of the Lord in Matt. X. 8 stand in the way of that. For that deals with the gift of miracles, not with the proclamation of the word, concerning which in Luke X. 7 the Lord ordained that the laborer is worthy of his hire, which however is not given for the doctrine, inasmuch as that cannot be repaid by any treasures of the world; but for the labor of the ministry, and so that they may be able to be free from care and anxiety for their livelihood Sir. XXXIX. Gal. VI. 6. Meanwhile, we must sometimes remit our right, and endure deficiencies, lest an obstacle and detriment to the preaching of the Gospel should arise.

Latin:

v. 11. Εἰ ἡ̃μει̃ς ὑμι̃ν τὰ πνευματικὰ ἐσπείραμεν, μέγα εἰ ἡ̃μει̃ς ὑμω̃ν τὰ σαρκικὰ θερίζομεν; Bis a Minori ducit argumentum : Primum a jumentis ad homines: Deinde ab hominibus laborantibus in iis, quæ ad hanc vitam attinent, ad homines laborantes in rebus du- centibus ad vitam meliorem. Si illi digni sunt qui alantur, quanto magis hi. Serere & metere frequentia in Prover- biis, ut notavimus ad Matth. XXV. 22. Johan. IV. 37. Hoc loco serere est operam præstare, metere pro opera aliquid accipere. Μέγα, id est, an mirum est? Sic ἐ̉ μέγα minime mirum. 2. Cor. XI. 15.

Qui arant, in spe arant messis sequuturæ. Spes alit agricolas ut Ovidius l. 1. de Ponto. Qui tri- turant, in spe mercedis consequendæ triturant. Æquum ergo, ut qui in aratro & tritura spiritua- li occupantur, spe fructus & mercedis non fru- strentur. Quæ tamen perperam trahit Cornelius ad spem mercedis æternæ. Non enim de æterna mer- cede, sed de stipendio ministris Ecclesiæ debito agitur. Nec vero mercedis vitæ æternæ intuitu operandum est. Illa enim χάρισμα est Rom. VI. v. ult. Et recte S. Bernhardus tr. de dilig. Deo: Non nisi præmio diligitur Deus, etsi absque præmii intuitu diligendus est : Vera charitas mercenaria non est, quamvis merces eam sequatur.

Εἰ ἁ̃λλοι τἠ̃ς ἐξουσίας ὑμω̃ν μετέχουσιν, οὐ μα̃λλον ἡ̃μει̃ς. Si alii fruuntur jure in vos, quanto magis nos, supple, æquum fuit pari frui jure? Ἐξουσία ὑμω̃ν εἰς ὑμα̃ς, quomo- do ἐξουσία πάσης σαρκός. Joh. XVII. 2. Ἐξουσίαν πνευμάτων Matth. X. 1.

Per alios nonnulli Pseudo-Apostolos intelligunt. Sed rectius veros Doctores Ecclesiarum, non præ- cisè Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ designari credunt. Hi enim jure stipendia capiebant: Illi de facto. Et argumentum à jure & ἐξυσίᾳ petitum est.

Ἀλλ̓ οὐκ ἐχρησάμεθα τἠ̃ ἐξουσία̨ ταύτῃ. Qui jus habet, potest & ejus juris usu abstinere. Alio- qui Dominus ejus juris non esset.

Ἀλλὰ πάντα στέγομεν. Perferimus. Sic στέγον habemus infra XIII. 7. 2. Thess. III. 1. 5.

Ἱνα μὴ ἐγκοπήν τινα δω̃μεν τὠ̃ Εὐαγγελίω̨ του̃ χριστου̃. Ἐγκόπτειν est impedire, Roman. XV. 22. Galat. V. 7. 1. Thess. II. 18. Hinc ἐγκοπὴ impedimentum, ut ubi via intercisa est.

Hoc impedimentum facilè oriri poterat è mer- cedis vel sumptuum necessariorum acceptione, etsi per se licita & justa; Ideo jure suo Apo- stolus uti noluit, ne ulla ratione remoraretur. Evangelium, neve speciem id haberet, quasi præ- dicatio Evangelii ventris causa fiat, non ob salu- tem Auditorum; quod scandalum declinare etiam voluit Apostolus, ad cursum Evangelii melius isto tempore in Ecclesia plantanda promovendum. Nec tamen inde colligat quis, illum per se impediri acceptione stipendii, vel exemplo Apostoli gratis esse serviendum Ecclesiæ. Nam satis Apostolus jus accipiendorum stipendiorum asseruit exemplis, similitudinibus, argumentis, & mandatis divinis.

Nec illi obstat præceptum Domini Matth. X. 8. Nam illud agit de dono miraculorum, non de præconio verbi, de quo Luc. X. 7. Dominus or- dinavit, quod operarius dignus sit mercede sua, quæ tamen non datur pro doctrina, utpote quæ nullis mundi thesauris rependi potest; sed pro labore ministerii, & ut illi sine cura & solicitudine victus vacare possint Sir. XXXIX. Gal. VI. 6. Interim re- mittendum quandoque de jure nostro, & susti- nendi defectus, ne offendiculum & detrimentum præconii Evangelici oriatur.

## 9:13
v. 13. Do you not know that those who perform the sacred rites eat from the temple.

The Levites, of course, whose task it was to slaughter the cattle. These lived from the sacred, that is, from the tithes,

Those who attend to the altar share with the altar.

This manuscript has παρεδρεύοντες, concerning which word we spoke above VII. 35. Understand the priests, whose task it was to place the entrails on the altars, but to retain parts for themselves Lev. VII. 6. Therefore they are rightly said here to share with the altar itself, as much of the priests as of the Levites. See the passage Deut. XVII. 1. Thus Ion in Euripides: the altars fed me. The former concerning the sanctuary is more rightly referred to the priests and Levites together: for both served the sanctuary, and they used those things which God had assigned to the sanctuary, such as sacrifices, firstfruits, and tithes. The latter is to be understood specifically of the priests, who alone participated in those things which were offered on the altar, and in expiatory sacrifices the whole flesh of the victim, unless when the bodies were to be burned outside the camp; but in peace offerings a certain part fell to the priest, the blood of the victims was owed to the altar, as was the fat. The former was sprinkled, the latter was burned on the altar.

Latin:

v. 13. Οὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι οἱ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζόμενοι, ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐσθίουσιν.

Levitæ nimirum, quorum erat mactare pecudes. Hi de sacro vivebant, id est de decimis,

Οἱ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντες, τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζονται.

Manuscriptus hic habet παρεδρεύοντες, de qua voce dixi- mus supra VII. 35. Intellige sacerdotes, quorum erat exta aris imponere, partes autem sibi retinere Lev. VII. 6. Ideò rectè hic dicuntur partiri cum ipso altari tam de sacerdoti- bus quàm de Levitis. Vide locum Deut. XVII. 1. Sic Jon apud Euripidem: βωμοὶ μ’ ἔφερβον. Prius de sacrario rectius ad Sacerdotes & Levi- tas simul refertur: Utrique enim sacrario inservie- bant, & illis, quæ sacrario Deus assignaverat, ut- pote sacrificiis, primitiis, decimis utebantur. Po- sterius speciatim de sacerdotibus intelligendum, qui soli de iis, quæ in altari offerebantur, partici- pabant,atque in sacrificiis expiatoriis tota victimæ caro, nisi cum comburenda erant corpora extra castra; in pacificis autem certa pars sacerdoti ce- debat, sanguis victimarum altari debebatur, ut & adeps. Ille spargebatur, hic accendebatur in altari.

## 9:14
Even so the Lord has ordained for those who proclaim the Gospel to live from the Gospel.

Namely, from the saying which was then handed down by word of mouth. Furthermore, now it is written down in Matt. X. 10. Luke X. 8.

Latin:

Οὕτως καὶ ὁ Κύριος διέταξε τοῖς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον καταγγέλ- λουσιν ἐκ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου ζῆν.

Nimirum ex dicto quod tunc per manus tradebatur. Cæterum nunc perscriptum est Matth. X. 10. Luc. X. 8.

## 9:15
v. 15. But I have used none of these.

I have not accepted food, nor gifts.

But I have not written these things, that it might be so in my case,

That is for me. I did not write so that those things which are for others might be provided to me.

For it is better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void.

We have already often said that καύχημα is ἀγαυλίαμα, joy. I would rather die than have that joy which my conscience brings me from the Gospel preached at my own expense taken away. Abraham once showed a great spirit, desiring nothing for himself from the spoils obtained in war, Gen. XIV. 22, 23. Paul showed a much greater one, not even taking sustenance for his heavy and life-giving labor. We have had Καλὸν with the dative in a similar sense in Matt. XVIII. 8, 9, XXVI. 24, Mark IX. 42, 43, 45, 47. But we have had the verb κενῦν in Rom. IV. 14 and above in I. 17.

Latin:

v. 15. Ἐγὼ δὲ οὐδενὶ ἐχρησάμην τούτων.

Non alimenta accepi non munera.

Οὐκ ἔγραψα δὲ ταῦτα, ἵνα οὕτω γένηται ἐν ἐμοί,

Id est mihi. Non ideo scripsi ut mihi præstentur quæ aliis.

Καλὸν γάρ μοι μᾶλλον ἀποθανεῖν, ἢ τὸ καύχημά μου ἵνα τις κενώσῃ.

Κάυχημα jam sæpe diximus esse ἀγαυλίαμα gaudium. Malim mori quam gaudium illud quod mihi parit conscien- tia meo sumptu prædicati Evangelii auferri. Magnum ani- mum olim ostendit Abrahamus nihil de præda bello parta sibi cupiens Gen. XIV. 22. 23. Multo majorem Paulus pro gravi & salutifero labore ne alimenta quidem sibi sumens. Καλὸν cum dativo pari sensu habuimus Matth. XVIII. 8. 9. XXVI. 24. Marci IX. 42. 43. 45. 47. Verbum verò κενῦν habuimus Rom. IV. 14. supra I. 17.

## 9:16
For if I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of.

Understand this comparatively. For the conscience is more uplifted by those things which it has done excellently out of no obligation.

Therefore Cornelius wrongly twists καύχημα to the glory of a work of supererogation and to an evangelical counsel. For the Apostle does not boast of a work of supererogation, but wishes his joy to be kept safe for himself. He does not suggest an evangelical counsel, but confirms by his own example the free use of indifferent things, that it is expedient at times to remit the right of one's own power for the sake of the weak. Nor indeed is there any reason why Bellarmine, book II on Monks, chapter [X], should say that Paul professes that he did more than was commanded him, and therefore earned singular glory before God: for although it was simply free to abstain from a salary or to accept it, yet because of the reasons of circumstances, which we are taught to evaluate in matters indifferent according to the law of charity, so that no hindrance or stumbling block is placed in the way of doctrine, that abstinence was not without a command, because the Lord certainly commanded not to abuse a right, even if it is free, and not to place a stumbling block. It was therefore a certain debt from the law of charity, and consequently neither a merit nor above the command.

For woe is unto me if I preach not the gospel.

Amos III. 8, VII. 15, 16, 17, Jer. XX. 8. He who has been enlightened by God for this purpose ought to instruct others even at the peril of his own life, says Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed II, 31, and Rabbi Israel on the soul, chapter 6. If anyone flees, that which happened to Jonah, or something worse, will happen to him.

Cornelius rightly warns here that it was commanded to the Apostles by a grave command that they should evangelize, Matt. XXVIII. 20, and that Bishops and Archbishops are also held by the same command. But how do they execute it in the Papacy? Therefore the Apostle denounces woe upon them.

Latin:

Ἐὰν γὰρ εὐαγγελίζωμαι, οὐκ ἔστι μοι κάυχημα.

Comparate intellige. Magis enim erigitur conscientia de iis, quæ ex nulla obligatione egregia fecit.

Κάυχημα ergò malè detorquet Cornelius ad glo- riam operis supererogationis, & ad consilium Evange- licum. Nam Apostolus non jactat opus superero- gationis,sed gaudium suum sibi salvum vult. Non suggerit consilium Evangelicum, sed liberum re- rum mediarum usum exemplo suo confirmat, quod expediat quandoque de potestatis suæ jure, in gratiam infirmorum remittere. Nec verò est, quod Bellarm. l. II. de Monach. cap. dicat Paulum profiteri, se plus fecisse, quàm sibi esset præceptum, atque ideò singularem gloriam apud Deum promeritum esse: Nam etsi simpliciter libe- rum erat, abstinere à salario, vel id accipere, ta- men ob rationes circumstantiarum, quas in adia- phoris juxta legem charitatis æstimare docemur, ne remora doctrinæ ponatur, aut offendiculum, non erat ea abstinentia sine præcepto, quia utique præcepit Dominus, non abuti jure, etsi libero, & non ponere offendiculum. Fuit ergò debitum quoddam ex lege charitatis, ac proinde nec meri- tum, nec supra præceptum.

Οὐαὶ δέ μοί ἐσιν ἐὰν μὴ εὐαγγελίζωμαι.

Amos. III. 8. VII. 15. 16. 17. Jer. XX. 8. Qui à Deo in hoc illuminatus est, debet alios instruere etiam cum vitæ suæ periculo, ait Maimonides ducis dubitantium II, 31. & Rabbi Israel de anima cap. 6. Si quis defugiat, eveniet ei, quod Jonæ aut pejus aliquid.

Recte hic monet Cornelius, gravi præcepto Apostolis præceptum fuisse, ut evangelizent Matth. XXIX. 20. eodemque præcepto teneri etiam Episcopos & Archi-Episcopos. Sed quomodo exe- quuntur illi in Papatu? Væ ergò ipsis denunciat Apostolus.

## 9:17
For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward.

If I had done this of my own accord, not commanded, as Frumentius and certain others. Μισθὸν ἔχω, I could hope from it for a reward, not just any, but an exceptional one. Ἃ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐντολὴν γίνεται, πολὺν ἔχει τὸν μισθὸν κατὰ τῦτο. Ἃ δὲ ἐν ἐντολῆς τάξει ἐ τοσῦ- τον. See the things said by us at Luke XVII. 10, where we also touched upon this passage of Paul.

But if unwillingly.

Ἄκων here does not mean unwilling, but commanded, not by my own judgment.

I have been entrusted with a stewardship.

I must render an account of the office imposed upon me. Οἰκονομία is פְקֻדָּה, which elsewhere is ἐπισκοπή. See above IV. 1. Πετίςευμαι with the Accusative as in Rom. III. 2. It can be said to me: render an account of your stewardship. Luke XVI. 2.

These things hold better than the Cornelian gloss; If I preach voluntarily, liberally, and freely, I have abundant glory for an unowed work. But if I do not preach of my own accord, nor liberally or freely, then I do not have that singular glory, but neither do I sin, because I am performing my duty, and doing what I am commanded. For this work is not unowed, but owed, to preach the Gospel. However, to remit one's right of receiving a stipend is a use of power that is voluntary, not proceeding from a desire for one's own glory, but from a love of divine glory and the propagation of the Church.

Latin:

Εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν τῦτο πράσσω, μισθὸν ἔχω.

Si id sponte fecissem, non jussus, ut Frumentius & alii quidam. Μισθὸν ἔχω, sperare inde possem præmium non quodvis sed eximium. Ἃ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐντολὴν γίνεται, πολὺν ἔχει τὸν μισθὸν κατὰ τῦτο. Ἃ δὲ ἐν ἐντολῆς τάξει ἐ τοσῦ- τον. Vide dicta à nobis ad Luc. XVII. 10. ubi & hunc Pau- li locum attigimus.

Εἰ δὲ ἄκων.

Ἄκων hic non est invitus sed jussus, non meopte arbi- tratu.

Οἰκονομίαν πεπίςευμαι.

Ratio mihi reddenda est impositi muneris. Οἰκονομία פְקֻדָּה quod alibi ἐπισκοπή. Vide supra IV. 1. Πετίςευμαι cum Accusativo ut Rom. III. 2. Potest mihi dici: redde ra- tionem villicationis tuæ. Luc. XVI. 2.

Rectius hæc sese habent, quàm Corneliana glossa; Si voluntarius, liberaliter, & gratis prædi- cem, copiosam habeo gloriam operis indebiti. Si autem non ultroneus, nec liberaliter aut gratis præ- dicem, tunc non habeo gloriam illam singularem, sed neque pecco, quia officio fungor meo, & facio, quod jubeor. Nam opus hoc non indebitum est, sed debitum, Evangelium prædicare. Remittere autem de jure suo accipiendi stipendii, usus est potestatis libera voluntarius, non è studio gloriæ propriæ, sed ex amore gloriæ divinæ & propaga- tionis Ecclesiæ profectus.

## 9:18
v. 18. What then is my reward?

That is, whence then the hope of some exceptional reward? Augustine: Blessed Paul could have sought his living from the Gospel. Because he preferred to work, he was bestowing more.

That in preaching the gospel I may make the gospel of Christ without charge.

Ἵνα here is 'if'. Thus above VII. 27 we had ἵνα for 'when'. Θήσω here is said in the way that τιθέναι χάριν is often used among the Greeks, to place or bestow a benefit among the Latins. Ἀδάπανον, namely for those receiving it: So that it costs them nothing. In the Glossary, ἀδάπανον, obtained without expense.

So as not to make full use of my authority in the Gospel.

It is not καταχρήσασθαι to use badly, as some have thought, but to use, or to use fully, as above 7, 31, in preaching the Gospel, that is.

To abuse here is to use one’s own right with offense to others. For the Corinthians could have thought that the Gospel was a kind of new merchandise, from which men might grow rich. Therefore, the Apostle preferred to abstain entirely from demanding his own right, rather than either to connive at such opinions or to provide an occasion for them, as our blessed Balduinus rightly says. There is, therefore, no reason for us to think that the compound is used for the simple, or "abuse" for "use": since the proper sense should have place, from which one must not depart. Grotius, however, seems to be sailing with the wind for Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide, and other Papists, who, in order to maintain that the Apostle did more than was commanded, [argue] that he did not abuse his right itself, or that he would have placed a stumbling block if he had by all means accepted a stipend, as if he were saying, 'lest I use my power as much as I am able.' But that neither suits the word, unless it be said with the Socinian Crellius that the Apostle used the word 'abuse' as an abuse; nor does it touch the nerve of the argument. For he wished to abstain from a salary, not lest he should use his power vehemently, or demand it strongly (for he could have demanded this by the best of rights); but lest he should do anything against the propagation of the Gospel, which, by demanding a reward, would easily have been hindered and checked in some, who could have been offended by the fact that the Apostle, as one sent divinely, extraordinarily, and immediately, was accepting a stipend; and thus he would be abusing his power with some stumbling block. Nor is ἐγκοπὴ correctly explained by Bellarmine as an interruption made by another; but it is to be taken as an impediment by which an interruption could be made by himself. For he does not say that he fears lest others place a delay, but lest he himself should place it, v. 11. Which Thomas acknowledged in his commentary on this passage. This, however, he was doing according to the gloss, lest the Gospel should appear venal. Furthermore, 'that I may not abuse my power,' that is, [the power] committed to me in preaching the Gospel. Which would be the case if I were to accept it indiscriminately, because I would lose the authority of rebuking freely. And Salmero: 'It would have been abusing power if he had exacted expenses, and in that matter had stripped his authority from the Gospel.' Justinianus: 'That I may not abuse my power.' But who would say that he avoided the abuse of this power without being compelled by the necessity of a command? For the Corinthians, as this Cornelius [says], although rich, were nevertheless rather stingy; therefore, lest they should think that Paul was seeking not them but their goods, for this reason Paul preached to them for free. From the Thessalonians and Philippians, however, as being more liberal, he accepted sustenance.

Latin:

v. 18. Τίς ὖν μοί ἐσιν ὁ μισθὸς;

Id est, unde ergò spes eximii cujusdam præmii? Au- gustinus: Potuit B. Paulus ex Evangelio sibi victum quærere. Quod maluit operari amplius erogabat.

Ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος ἀδάπανον θήσω τὸ εὐαγγέ- λιον τῦ χρισῦ.

Ἵνα hic est si. Sic supra VII. 27. habuimus ἵνα pro quando. Θήσω hic est dictum quomodo τιθέναι χάριν apud Græcos sæpe, locare aut collocare beneficium apud La- tinos. Ἀδάπανον, nempe accipientibus: Ita ut ipsis nihilo constet. In Glossario ἀδάπανον, sine impensa partu.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ καταχρήσασθαι τῇ ἐξωσίᾳ μὲ ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ.

Non est καταχρήσασθαι malè uti, ut quidam putarunt, sed uti, aut peruti, ut supra 7, 31. in Evangelio prædicando scilicet.

Abuti hic est jure suo uti cum offensione alio- rum. Existimare enim poterant Corinthii, Evan- gelium esse quasi novum quoddam mercimonium, unde ditescerent homines. Maluit ergò abstinere prorsus Apostolus ab exigendo jure suo, quàm ad ejusmodi opiniones vel connivere, vel earum occasio nem præbere, ut rectè B. Balduinus no- ster. Non ergò est, quod Compositum pro simpli- ci, abuti pro uti adhibitum censeamus: Quum proprius sensus locum habeat, à quo discedendum non est. Velificari autem videtur Grotius Bellar- mino, Cornel. à Lapide, aliisque Pontificiis, qui ut obtineant fecisse Apostolum plùs, quàm præce- ptum fuerit, non abusum ipsum jure suo fuisse, aut offendiculum positurum, si maximè stipendium accepisset, quasi dicat, ne, quantum possum, utar potestate meâ. Sed id nec voci convenit, nisi cum Crellio Sociniano dicatur, Apostolum voce abusus abusum esse; nec nervum argumenti attingit. Nam abstinere voluit à salario, non, ne vehementer uteretur potestate sua, aut valde id exigeret, (hoc enim jure optimo exigere poterat;) sed ne aliquid contra propagationem Evangelii faceret, quæ exigen- do mercedem facile in quibusdam præpedita, & sufflaminata fuisset, qui ex eo, quod Apostolus, ut divinitus, extraordinarie & immediate missus sti- pendium accipiat, oftendi poterant; & ita potesta- te sua cum aliquo offendiculo abuteretur. Neque ἐγκοπὴ rectè à Bellarmino de interruptione ab alio facta explicatur;sed accipienda est de impedimen- to, quo interruptio à seipso fieri potuerit. Non enim ait, se metuere, ne alii ponant remoram, sed ne ipse ponat v. 11. Quod agnovit Thomas Comm. in h. l. Hoc autem faciebat secundum glossam, ne Ev- angelium videretur venale. Adhæc ut non abutar potestate meâ, id est, commissa mihi in Evangelio prædicando. Quod esset, si acciperem indistinctè, quia perderem autoritatem libere arguendi. Et Sal- mero: Fuisset id abuti potestate, si sumtus exegisset, & in ea re suam Evangelio autoritatem ademisset. Justinianus: Ut non abutar potestate mea. Quis autem dicat, nullâ cum præcepti necessitate compul- sum hujus potestatis abusum vitasse? Corinthii enim, ut hic Cornelius,licet divites,tenaciores tamen erant; Ne ergo illi putarent, Paulum non se sed sua bona quærere, hac de causa Paulus eis gratis prædicavit. A Thessalonicensibus verò & Philippensibus, ut- pote liberalioribus alimoniam accepit.

## 9:19
v. 19. For being free from all.

That is, free from all men: I am beholden to no one.

I made myself a slave to all.

I voluntarily behaved as the servant of all, shunning no labor, no inconveniences for their sake.

That I might gain the more.

That I may gain the more, that is, save. See Matt. XVIII. 15: For that which is saved is gained. Therefore, for the same thing he will soon say, 'I will save'.

Latin:

v. 19. Ἐλεύθερος γὰρ ὢν ἐκ πάντων.

Id est ab hominibus omnibus liber: Nemini sum obno- xius.

Πᾶσιν ἐμαυτὸν ἐδύλωσα.

Sponte me ut omnium servum gessi, nullum laborem, nulla incommoda ipsorum causa defugiens.

Ἵνα τὲς πλείονας κερδήσω.

Ut eo plures lucrifaciam, id est servem. Vide Matth. XVIII. 15: Lucrifit enim quod servatur. Itaque pro eodem mox dicet, σώσω.

## 9:20
v. 20. And I became to the Jews as a Jew.

As if I were a Jew, namely in religion. See the example in Acts XXI. 23, 24, 25, 26.

To those under the law as under the law.

As if I were a proselyte. For proselytes subjected themselves to the law. See an example of this matter in Acts 16:3.

Latin:

v. 20. Καὶ ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἰεδαίοις ὡς ἰεδαῖος.

Quasi Judæus essem, nempe religione. Exemplum vide Act. XXI. 23, 24. 25. 26.

Τοῖς ὑπὸ νόμον ὡς ὑπὸ νόμον.

Quasi proselytus essem. Proselyti enim legi se subjicie- bant. Exemplum hujus rei vide Act. XVI. 3.

## 9:21
To those without law as without law.

Those without law are called here those not having the law, Rom. 2:14, that is, those to whom the law of Moses was not given, such as all who were outside the Israelites and proselytes. See an example of this matter in Acts 17:22, Gal. 2:3, 14.

(Not being without law to God, but under the law to Christ)

He added this parenthesis, lest anyone interpret the word 'without law' wrongly. For in another sense, those who live according to the pleasure of their own mind are called 'without law'. Mark 15:28, Luke 22:37, Acts 2:13, 2 Thess. 2:18, 1 Tim. 1:9, 2 Pet. 2:8. He says, therefore, that he has a law, namely Christ's, and lives according to it. Thus the son of Sirach said 'living under the law'. In the manuscript, 'God' and 'Christ' are in the genitive with the same sense. And so the Greeks read, who wrote on this passage.

Latin:

Τοῖς ἀνόμοις ὡς ἄνομος.

Ἄνομοι hic dicuntur οἱ νόμον μὴ ἔχοντες Rom. II. 14. id est, quibus lex Mosis data non est, quales erant omnes extra Israelitas & proselytos. Exemplum hujus rei vide Act. XVII. 22. Gal. II. 3. 14.

(Μὴ ὢν ἄνομος Θεῷ, ἀλλ' ἔννομος χριστῷ)

Hanc parenthesin addidit, ne quis vocem ἄνομος male interpretaretur. Nam alio sensu dicuntur ἄνομοι qui pro ani- mi lubitu vivunt. Marci XV. 28. Luc. XXII. 37. Act. II. 13. 2. Thess. II. 18. 1. Tim. I. 9. 2. Petr. II. 8. Dicit ergo se legem habere,nempe Christi & secundum eam vivere. Sic ἔννομος βίωνων dixit Sirachides. In Manuscripto θεῶ & χριστῶ in Ge- nitivo pari sensu. Et sic legere Græci, qui ad hunc locum scripsere.

## 9:22
I became to the weak as weak.

As a novice and tender in the faith.

To all I have become all things.

I turned myself into all forms as the utility of those with whom I had dealings required. It is the mark of a prudent man not to cling to universal principles, but to look to particular cases.

And this I do for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a partaker of it.

A metonymy, that I may become a partaker of the Gospel, that is, of its reward, which is promised in the Gospel. Thus 'the prize'; the Syrian here said 'victory'.

Augustine, in epistles 9 and 19, explains that in verse 19, when he says he became all things to all men, he does not mean by conforming himself to the will of all, but by condescending to their infirmity as much as piety permitted; not by lying, but by sympathizing; not with the cunning of a dissembler, but with the affection of one who feels for them, Paul became all things to all men. He became as a Jew to the Jews regarding the observation of ceremonies, so that they would not abhor his conversation or become more alienated from the Gospel, although he himself was freed from the ceremonial law by Christian liberty. Conversely, to the Gentiles not having the law, he became as if he did not have the law, so that he would not deter them by the rigor of the ceremonial law. Whence, although he circumcised Timothy for the sake of those who had the law, Acts 16:3, he did not allow Titus to be circumcised for the sake of the Gentiles, Tit. 2:3. Finally, he became weak to the weak among Christians, who, to be sure, were not yet rightly informed about the use of Christian liberty, for whose sake he freely abstained from those things which it was lawful to enjoy. But why did Paul resist Peter, who was conforming himself to the Jews? Gal. II. 14. This was done because Peter, certain about the removal of the yoke and burden of the ceremonial laws from the Council of Jerusalem, at which he himself had been present, nevertheless wished to impose it upon the Gentiles, lest he be ill-spoken of among the Jews, not without scandal to the weak, as if the observance of the ceremonial law were necessary, and with the danger of the corruption of the Apostolic article concerning justification. It was no light cause for rebuke, says Thomas in the Catena on Gal. II. For there was a danger that the truth of the Gospel would perish if men were compelled to observe legal requirements, which Peter was inducing, not indeed by command, but by example. This was not to serve the weak, but to place a stumbling block. If you listen to Bellarmine, l. 1. de Rom. Pontif. c. 27. Peter, he says, because he was especially the Apostle of the Jews, wished to offend the Gentiles rather than the Jews. Paul, however, disapproved of that choice and rebuked Peter quite sharply.

PART II. The Apostolic admonition concerning the course and the sacred contest.

Latin:

Ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἀσθενέσιν ὡς ἀσθενὴς.

Tanquam novitius ac tener in fide.

Τοῖς πᾶσι γέγονα τὰ πάντα.

In omnes formas me verti prout ferebat utilitas eorum, quibuscum mihi res erat. Prudentis est non inhærere τοῖς καθ' ὅλε, sed spectare τὰ καθ' ἕκασα.

Τῦτο δὲ ποιῶ διὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, ἵνα συγκοινωνὸς αὐτῶ γένωμαι.

Μετωνυμία ut particeps Evangelii fiam, id est, præmii ejus, quod in Evangelio promittitur. Sic βραβεῖον, Syrus hic dixit victoriam.

Quod v. 19. omnibus omnia factus sit, non at- temperando se omnium voluntati, sed condescen- dendo infirmitati, quantum pietas permittebat, explicat Augustinus ep. IX. & XIX. non mentiendo, sed compatiendo; non simulantis astu; sed commise- rentis affectu omnibus omnia factus est Paulus, Judæis factus quasi Judæus quoad observationem ceremoniarum, ne à conversatione sua abhorre- rent, aut alieniores ab Evangelio fierent, licet ipse pro libertate Christiana à lege ceremoniali solu- tus esset. Vicissim gentilibus legem non habenti- bus factus quasi legem non haberet, ne legis cere- monialis rigore eosdem absterreret. Unde quum Timotheum in gratiam eorum, qui legem habe- bant, circumciderit Act. XVI. 3. Titum in gratiam gentium non passus est circumcidi Tit. II. 3. De- nique infirmis è Christianis infirmus factus est, qui scilicet nondum rectè informati erant de usu libertatis Christianæ, in quorum gratiam libere abstinuit ab iis, quibus frui licebat. Sed cur restitit Paulus Petro Judæis se attemperanti? Gal. II. 14. Factum hoc, quia Petrus de sublato jugo & one- re legum ceremonialium è concilio Hierosolymi- tano, cui ipse interfuerat, certus, id tamen gentili- bus imponere volebat, ne malè apud Judæos audiret, non absque scandalo infirmorum, quasi necessaria esset legis ceremonialis observatio, & periculo corruptelæ articuli de justificatione Apo- stolica. Non levis causa reprehensionis erat, inquit Thomas in Caten. ad Gal. II. Periculum enim erat, ne periisset veritas Evangelii, si cogerentur homines servare legalia, quod inducebat Petrus, non quidem imperio, sed exemplo. Non hoc erat infirmis in- servire, sed offendiculum ponere. Bellarminus si audias l. 1. de Rom. Pontif. c. 27. Petrus, inquit, quia Judæorum præcipuè Apostolus erat, gentiles po- tius, quam Judæos offendere voluit. Paulus au- tem electionem illam improbavit, & Petrum satis acriter reprehendit.

PARS II. Apostolicum de cursu & certamine sacro monitum.

## 9:24
v. 24. Do you not know that those who run in a race, all indeed run, but one receives the prize.

A transposition for 'all those who run in a race run.' And that former 'running' is a participle for the noun 'stadium-runners,' in the Hebrew manner. 'Stadion' is a racecourse in the Glossary. 'Brabeion' is a palm in the same Glossary. And in citing this passage where there is 'brabeion,' Cyprian and Ambrose have said 'palm.' You have the same word in the sense toward which this comparison tends in Philippians III. 14.

Concerning the connection with the preceding, B. Glassius says thus in Part II, Exeg. Text. Evang. & Epist. p. 228. He seems altogether to hint by this similitude that those Corinthians, who, for the sake of weak brothers, were unwilling to abstain from the eating of things sacrificed to idols and from the banquets of idolaters, were the cause of that evil because they were addicted to gluttony, and therefore he calls them by this similitude and his own example to sobriety and the mortification of the flesh, so that the cause being removed, the effect might also be removed.

Οὕτω τρέχετε, ἵνα καταλάβητε.

Run in such a way that you may be first in the race, and thus may be able to attain the prize.

Chrysostom took the particle 'houto' as a mark of the apodosis: As runners do not cease to run until they have reached the goal: So we also ought to persevere, and not make an end of running as long as we live. Moreover, in a worldly race indeed the first only one receives the prize, but in this spiritual race he wishes all to receive it; therefore he says, one receives the prize. Concerning this, however, he warns all: So run, that you may obtain, because the contest is not held to leave those running with us behind in our zeal, but to excite them entirely by examples and to help them with warnings, which must be instituted against our enemies, the malignant spirits, the flesh, and the world. Our judge of the games is not envious, says Jerome to Lucinus, T. 1, f. 87, nor does the palm of one bring ignominy to another. He desires all his athletes to be crowned. The particle 'thus' can, however, be taken not inconveniently regarding the manner of the race, so that the particle is not one of comparison, but of quality, as if he were to say: Run in such a way that you may receive the palm or prize. Which sense seems simpler. The requirements of a runner can be applied here to Christians, which are enumerated as six: 1. To choose the right path. 2. Not to stand still, nor to turn back. 3. 3. To avoid all detours. 4. To neglect the judgments of the spectators. 5. To lay aside the pressing burden. 6. To tolerate sweats and annoyances.

And everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things. Horace: He who strives to reach the desired goal in a race, has suffered and done much as a boy, has sweated and shivered, has abstained from Venus and wine.

Epictetus: Do you wish to win the Olympics? And I, by God, do; for it is elegant. But consider the antecedents and the consequences, and thus set your hand to the work. You must keep order, follow a diet, abstain from pastries, exercise under compulsion at a set time, in heat, in cold, not drink cold water, not wine, as it happens. Simply, as to a physician, give yourself over to the trainer. Chrysostom executes the same thing at length in his 21st homily on the statues. Others have produced a passage of Tertullian on this matter. See Aristotle, Politics VIII. 4, and Hesychius on 'anagkophagein'. He uses this argument drawn from theatrical, gymnastic, and equestrian contests to the contest of virtue. Philo also in his book against Flaccus.

They indeed, that they may receive a corruptible crown. Suppose of olive, or pine, or laurel. Philo: But indeed, for the sake of wild olives and parsley, the end is glorious. But to the wise, and much more for the sake of liberty, the desire for which is implanted in souls alone, if one must tell the truth. Basil: And since I have mentioned crowns and athletes, those men, having suffered ten thousand things upon ten thousand, and having increased their strength for themselves from many sources, having sweated much in gymnastic exercises, and having received many blows from the trainer, and choosing not the sweetest diet, but that which is prescribed by the trainers, and other things—so that I may not waste time speaking—living thus, as if their life before the contest were a practice for the contest, they then strip for the stadium, and do everything, and risk everything, so as to receive a crown of wild olive, or parsley, or some other such thing. Eumenius: Or if the bravest men in sacred contests, with the greatest labor and even danger to life, think only of the voice of the herald and the testimony of the crown, etc. And note this for the Corinthians, among whom the Isthmian games were held.

But we an incorruptible one. 'That we may receive' is understood from the preceding. He calls eternal and heavenly life metaphorically an 'incorruptible' crown, just as Peter calls it an 'unfading' crown, 1 Ep. V. 4.

Musculus, which we repeat for the sake of continuity, holds it thus: with an argument taken from the distinction between the heavenly and earthly prizes, he puts them to shame, because in the zeal of competing they were surpassed by those who, competing for the sake of a perishing crown, show such great self-control and at the same time patience, are able to bear such great inconveniences, and to refrain from delicacies, even lawful ones, led by the single hope of winning, when meanwhile they have sustained themselves from refraining from things sacrificed to idols for the sake of the Gospel. But 'all things' is said for 'in all things'. The Vulgate has 'abstains from all things', and so does the Syriac: Understand this of those things which can impede or delay a runner, which refers primarily to a frugal diet, which the diet of athletes is accustomed to be called in a proverb. Athletes, says Tertullian, are segregated to a stricter discipline, so that they may be free to build up their strength: They are restrained from luxury, from richer foods, from more pleasant drink. They are compelled, they are tortured, they are fatigued; the more they have labored in their exercises, the more they hope for victory. And they, says the Apostle, so that they may obtain a corruptible crown, we, about to obtain an eternal one, let us interpret the prison as our wrestling school.

Latin:

v. 24. Οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι οἱ ἐν σταδίῳ τρέχοντες, πάντες μὲν τρέ- χουσι, εἷς δὲ λαμβάνει τὸ βραβεῖον.

Trajectio pro πάντες μὲν οἱ ἐν σταδίῳ τρέχοντες τρέχουσι. Et prius illud τρέχοντες est participium pro nomine σταδιο- δρόμοι, more Hebræo. Στάδιον curriculum in Glossario. Βρα- βεῖον palma in eodem Glossario. Et in hoc loco citando ubi est βραβεῖον, palmam dixere Cyprianus & Ambrosius. Ean- dem vocem in sensu ad quem tendit hæc comparatio habes Philipp. III. 14.

De nexu cum præcedentibus ita B. Glassius par- te II. Exeg. Text. Evang. & Epist. p. 228. Videtur omnino hac similitudine innuere, quod Corinthii isti, qui in gratiam infirmorum fratrum ab esu idolo- thytorum, & conviviis idololatrarum abstinere nol- lent, ejus mali causam esse, quod gulæ essent dediti, ac proinde eos hac similitudine & suo exemplo ad so- brietatem & carnis mortificationem vocat, ut causa sublata effectus quoque tollatur.

Οὕτω τρέχετε, ἵνα καταλάβητε.

Ita currite, ut primi sitis in cursu, & sic præmium possi- tis assequi.

Chrysostomus particulam ὅτω pro ἀποδόσεως no- ta accepit: Uti cursores currere non desinunt, do- nec ad metam pertigerint: Ita & nos perseverare debere, nec finem currendi facere, quamdiu vi- vimus. Cæterum in terreno quidem cursu primus- tantum accipit brabeum, at in hoc spirituali cursu omnes vult accipiant; ideò de illo unus, inquit, accipit brabeum. De hoc vero omnes monet: Sic currite, ut comprehendatis, quia non ad συντρέ- χοντας post nos in studio relinquendos, sed ex- emplis omnino excitandos, monitisque juvandos, certamen fit, quod contra hostes nostros, spiritus malignos, carnem & mundum instituendum. Non est invidus agonotheta noster, inquit Hieron. ad Lu- cin. T. 1. f. 87. nec ulterius palma alteri parit ignomi- niam. Omnes athletas suos desiderat coronari. Ac- cipi tamen particula ὕτως non incommodè potest de modo cursus, ut particula non sit similitudinis, sed qualitatis, quasi dicat: Ita currite, ut palmam vel brabeum accipiatis. Qui sensus simplicior videtur. Requisita cursoris hic applicari possunt Christia- nis, quæ sex recensentur: 1. Rectam viam eligere. 2. Non consistere, nec retrocedere. 3. Omnes ambages vitare. 4. Judicia spectatorum negligere. 5. Onus premens deponere. 6. Sudores & molestias tolerare.

Πᾶς δὲ ὁ ἀγωνιζόμενος ἐγκρατεύεται πάντα. Horatius: Qui studet optatam cursu contingere metam, Multa tulit fecitque puer, sudavit & alsit, Abstinuit Venere & vino.

Epictetus : Μέλεις σοι ὀλύμπια νικῆσαι; Κἀγὼ νὴ τὸν θεόν· Κομψὸν γάρ ἐστι. Ἀλλὰ σκόπει τὰ καθηγούμενα καὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα, καὶ ὕτως ἅπτω τῶ ἔργε. Δεῖ σ’ εὐτακτεῖν, ἀναγκοτροφεῖν, ἀπέχε- σθαι πεμμάτων, γυμνάζεσθαι πρὸς ἀνάγκην ἐν ὥρᾳ τεταγμένῃ, ἐν καύματι, ἐν ψύχει, μὴ ψυχρὸν πίνειν, μὴ οἶνον, ὡς ἔτυχεν. Ἁπλῶς ὡς ἰατρῷ ἐπιδιδόναι σεαυτὸν τῷ ἐπιστάτῃ. Late idem exequi- tur Chrysostomus XXI. de statuis. Locum Tertulliani hac de re alii produxere. Vide Aristotelem Polit. VIII. 4. & Hesy- chium in ἀναγκοφαγεῖν. Utitur hoc argumento à certamini- bus scenicis, gymnicis & equestribus ad certamen virtutis ducto. Philo quoque contra Flaccum libro.

Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν ἓν ἵνα φθαρτὸν στέφανον λάβωσιν. Puta ex Oleastro aut picea, aut lauru. Philo: Ἁλλὰ γὰρ ὑπὲρ κοτίνων καὶ σελίνων εὐκλεὴς ἡ τελευτή. Σοφοῖς δὲ κ’ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἐλευθερίας, ἧς ὁ πόθος ψυχαῖς μόνον, εἰ δεῖ τ’ ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, ἐνίδρυται. Basilius : Ἐπεὶ δὲ στεφάνων κὴ ἀθλητῶν ἐμνήσθην, ἐκεῖνοι μυρία παθόντες ἐπὶ μυρίοις, κὴ πολλαχόθεν τὴν ῥώμην ἑαυτοῖς συναυξήσαντες, πολλὰ μὲν γυμνασικοῖς ἐνιδρώσαντες. Πόσοις πολλαὶ δὲ πληγὰς ἐκ παιδοτρίβε λαβόντες δίαιταν δὲ ὀ τὴν ἡδίστην, ἀλλὰ τὴν παρὰ τ̃ γυμναστῶν αἱρέμενοι κὴ τἆλλα, ἵνα μὴ διατρί- βω λέγων, ὕτω διάγοντες ὡς τῶ πρὸ τῆς ἀγωνίας βίον, μελέτην εἶναι τῆς ἀγωνίας τηνικαῦτα ἀποδύδονται πρὸς τὸ στάδιον, κὴ πάντα ποιῶσι, κὴ κινδυνεύουσιν, ὥστε κοτίνου λαβεῖν στέφανον, ἢ σελίνου, ἢ ἄλ- λε τινὸς τῶν τοιούτων. Eumenius : An si fortissimi viri in sacris certaminibus summo labore atque etiam vitæ periculo solam vocem præconis, & coronæ testimonium putant &c. Et nota hæc Corinthiis apud quos Isthmia agebantur.

Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἄφθαρτον. Subauditur ἵνα λάβωμεν ex superioribus. Vitam æternam atque cœlestem vocat μεταφορικῶς coronam ἄφθαρτον, sicut Petrus στέφανον ἀμαράντινον 1. Ep. V. 4.

Musculus quod συνεχείας causa repetimus, ita ha- bet, argumento à brabeorum cœlestis & terreni di- scrimine sumpto, pudefacit eos, quod in studio certan- di superarentur ab illis, qui perituræ coronæ gratia certantes tantam ostendunt continentiam simul & patientiam, tanta possunt ferre incommoda, & à de- licatis sese continere, etiam licitis, una vincendi spe inducti, cum interea istine ab idolothytis quidem sese continere sustinuerint Evangelii gratia. Dicitur au- tem πάντα pro κατὰ πάντα. Vulgatus habet ab omnibus se abstinet, sic & Syrus: Intellige de iis, quæ currentem impedire vel remorari possint, quod respicit imprimis frugalem victum, qui victus ath- letarum in proverbio dici solet. Athletæ, inquit Tertullianus, segregantur ad strictiorem discipli- nam, ut robori ædificando vacent: Continentur à luxuria, à cibis lætioribus, à potu jucundiore. Coguntur, cruciantur, fatigantur, quanto plus in exercitationibus laboraverint, tanto plus de victo- ria sperant. Et illi, inquit Apostolus, ut coronam corruptibilem consequantur, nos æternam consequu- turi carcerem nobis pro palæstra interpretemur.

## 9:26
Verse 26. I so run, not as uncertainly. That is, so that it may appear that I am making progress; not like him of whom the epigram is: Whether Pericles ran the stadium or sat, no one knows at all. A divine slowness. Others explain that 'not uncertainly', which the Vulgate renders 'not in uncertainty', as not in uncertain hope, or so that I may be certain that I will bring back the prize. Others take it concerning the certain goal of the race of the faithful. For he runs 'uncertainly' who wanders and does not aim at a certain mark. But the Grotius sense does not seem inconvenient.

So I box, not as beating the air. In the glossary, 'pykteuo' means to box. Boxers or 'pyctae', before they competed, used to throw their hands and arms into the wind, as Seneca speaks. Others call this 'ventilating'. Virgil concerning Dares: And he throws his arms alternately, stretching them out, and beats the air with blows. Theophilus of Antioch in book III: Those who write about uncertain things beat the air. Eustathius on that of Homer, Iliad I: 'And thrice he struck the deep air.' And see 'to strike the air', from which the proverb seems to have been taken, 'to beat the air', used of those who attempt things in vain. Some, however, think such a proverb was said from boxers, who often, not hitting the mark, move their hands in vain. The same Eustathius on the Psi of the Iliad: And their art is sometimes to wear out frequent hours to the detriment of their opponents with the raising and striking down of hands, as if one were also beating the air, which is called 'skiamachein' or fighting in a warlike manner. Seneca, Natural Questions VII. 13. To solve these things, what else is it than to exercise the hand and to throw the arms into the wind.

Πυκτεύειν is to contend with cestus, says Aretius in this place, which kind of contest is between Dares and Entellus in Virgil. Among Homer, Achilles also instituted a contest of boxers at the tomb of Patroclus, in which Epeus won. Erasmus, attending precisely to the origin of the word (πὺξ an adverb, with the fist or with fists; πυγμὴ a fist, the hand contracted into a fist), translates it as to contend with fists in his annotation. And while the Vulgate interpreter translates πυκτεύω as I fight, he says he did not allude to fist-fights. However it is understood, it is certain that the Apostle is speaking of a spiritual struggle against various enemies. Those who play without an adversary, and tire themselves more than they exercise, are said to beat the air. But the struggle of Christians is not a shadow-boxing match; but is directed against the most atrocious and crafty enemies: Satan, the world, the flesh, and depraved affections. These are to be attacked, struck, and conquered, as B. Glassius holds here.

But I buffet my body and bring it into bondage. The true reading is this, ὑπωπιάζω, not ὑποπιέζω nor ὑποπιάζω. For he pursues the last simile taken from a boxer. It is the way of boxers to ὑπωπιάζειν an adversary. ὑπώπια are properly the marks of blows under the eyes, as Pollux says; but they began to be called more broadly wounds from any blow whatsoever, as the Scholiast on the Acharnians of Aristophanes says. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations II: Boxers bruised with cestus, that is, ὑπωπιαζόμενοι. We have had the metaphorical use of this word in Luke 18:5. When Paul had compared himself to a boxer, it could be asked who the adversary was: My own body, he says; I buffet this, he says, that is, I afflict it with many inconveniences, concerning which see above 4:11. אצער אני אתגופי as Maimonides says concerning the same matter. Also δυλαγωγεῖν is taken from boxers. For he who had won would drag the defeated adversary as if he were a slave. Thus Paul triumphed over his body as if it were subdued. Thus Seneca in epistle 8 said that the body must be treated more harshly, lest it obey the mind poorly. Josephus calls this σκληραγωγίαν in the history of Daniel. Paul calls it bodily exercise in 1 Timothy 4:8. The Apostolic Canon 51 calls it ἄσκησιν. Basil, on reading Greek books: 'But in speech one must despise the body, not as one intending to wallow in the mire of pleasures, or one must touch it only so much, as Plato says, as one who acquires service for wisdom, similar to Paul, who advises that one ought to have no provision for the body to fulfill its desires.' See Ambrose in epistle 7, Nazianzen in oration 6, Augustine on the work of monks, chapters 1, 9, and 10. Athenagoras also uses the word δυλαγωγῶν in this sense. By a silent comparison, he lashes those gluttonous Corinthians.

We add what B. Chemnitius has concerning this passage from the Council of Trent, part 4, on fasting, p. 749.

Paul in 1 Cor. 9 uses the example of athletes, whose regimen of diet was most exquisite. For they did not indiscriminately gorge themselves on just anything, and they abstained from many things, so that neither would the body be burdened, nor the power of the mind be overwhelmed, but so that both the body might be rendered agile, and the power of the mind present, alert, and vigorous, for the circumspection of delivering, receiving, and warding off blows. Thus also I, says Paul, subdue, coerce, restrain, buffet, and blunt my body. For there is a very illustrious metaphor in the word ὑπωπιάζω. For just as a boxer observes his adversary, and restrains, buffets, and subdues him with blows and strikes: So, says Paul, I observe my body, and lest the flesh, by its adversarial resistance, cast the spirit down from its state, and render it, once subjugated, a slave or captive to the flesh, I subdue, blunt, tame, and subjugate my body, so that it may be reduced to the servitude of the soul or spirit, lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway. But that subjection or subjugation of the body, or mortification of the flesh, is accomplished either by temperance, or abstinence, or fasting, or studies, labors, business, occupations, cares, the cross, afflictions, terrors, the sense of the wrath of God, etc. With this end: that the intemperance, petulance, and sloth of the flesh might not impede the intention of the mind in meditations and exercises of piety, and that leisure and luxury might not beget sins, which drive out the Holy Spirit. These are the words of the blessed Chemnitius. Basil, in his homily on reading Gentile writings, with the praise of Cornelius a Lapide, has it thus: The body is to be chastised, and restrained like some wild beast, and the tumults arising from it against the soul are to be checked by reason as if by a whip, lest by loosening the rein entirely to pleasure, the mind, like a charioteer, be carried and snatched away by stubborn and disobedient horses; and among other things, it is fitting to remember the saying of Pythagoras, who, seeing a certain man taking care of and fattening himself with exercises and daintily prepared foods, said: 'Hey, wretch, do you not cease to prepare a harder prison for yourself?' The blessed Hülsemann in his unpublished notes warns: that ὑπωπιάζειν denotes an indefinite subjection of the body, yet one to be determined to abstinence from those species which Paul had hitherto mentioned he could lawfully use, from verse 1 up to 20, which the reason of the object and the connections teach and demonstrate. Espensaeus in Comm. on Chapter 4 of the Epistle to Timothy, verse 8. this word is to be understood concerning bodily exercises, such as strictly called fasts, vigils, sleeping on the ground, and generally concerning deprivation and abstinence from those comforts enumerated here: Such abstinence as Paul indeed extenuates in the cited place to Timothy in comparison to more useful exercises, namely the preaching of alms, but does not disapprove. Therefore, it is vain what Bellarmine in Book II de Monach. c. 30, and others, such as Salmeron and Cornelius, imagine, and Gretser in de discip. c. 8, concerning the chastisement of Paul's body by rods to extinguish venereal ardor. On the contrary, Justinianus and Estius say this conjecture is inept. Salmeron, disp. 16, although he understands the means of bruising as a hairshirt, nevertheless denies that the end was the suppression of venereal concupiscence. Chrysostom understood that τὸ ὑπωπιάζειν as abstinence from the eating of things sacrificed to idols, because this was the adequate object of Pauline abstinence. However, we judge that this similitude of buffeting—that is, of bruising until black and blue, and of reducing the body into servitude—extends more broadly than to look only at abstinence from those indifferent things about which he had treated above. Because here it is taught generally how we ought to check and subdue the body, that is, the old man resisting the spirit, who comes under the name of the body in Rom. 6:6, ch. 7:14, Col. 2:11, whose members are enumerated in Col. 3:5, namely, just as athletes were accustomed to both buffet their antagonists, which is to inflict a notable mark on the face, and to trip them up or cast them to the ground. What the Apostle mystically performed in his flesh resisting the spirit, not only by abstinence, temperance, and fasts, but primarily by pious prayers, sacred meditations on the Word, studies, labor, holy occupations, mortification of the flesh, etc. Therefore, the Papists prove their buffetings in vain in this place from this word ὑπωπιάζειν, since it is not always used concerning blows inflicted on the body, as is evident from Luke 18:5, nor is the body to be understood here substantially; but accidentally concerning the body of sin, where it is a matter of the coercion of the flesh, lest it dominate the spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἐγὼ εὖ ὅτω τρέχω, ὡς ἐκ ἀδήλως. Id est ut appareat, me promovere; Non ut ille de quo est Epigramma: Τὸ σάδιον Περικλῆς εἶτ' ἔδραμεν, εἴτ' ἐκάθητο Οὐδεὶς οἶδεν ὅλως. Δαιμόνιον βραδύτης. Alii illud ἐκ ἀδήλως, quod vulgata reddit non in incertum exponunt, non in incertam spem, vel ut certo confidam me præmium reportaturum. Alii de certa cursus fidelium meta accipiunt. Ἀδήλως enim currit, qui vagatur, nec ad certum collimat scopum. Non incommodus autem videtur Gro- tianus sensus.

Οὕτω πυκτεύω, ὡς ἐκ ἀέρα δαίρων. In Glossario πυκτεύω pugilo. Pugiles sive pyctæ prius- quam certarent, manum & brachia in ventum jactabant, ut Seneca loquitur. Ventilare id dicunt alii. Virgilius de Darete: - - - Alternaque jactat Brachia protendens & verberat ictibus auras. Theophilus Antiochenus libro III. Οἱ τὰ ἄδηλα συγγρά- φοντες ἀέρα δέρκσι. Eustathius ad illud Homeri Iliados I. Τρὶς δ' ἠέρα τύψε βαθεῖαν. Καὶ ὅρα τὸν ἀέρα, τύψει, ἐξ ἧς ἐλῆ- φθαι παροιμία δοκεῖ, ἀέρα δαίρειν, ἐπὶ τῶν ἀπράκτοις ἐγχειρέν- των. Τινὲς μέντοι ἀπὸ τῶν πυγμάχων τὴν τοιαύτην παροιμίαν εἰρῆσθαι δοκῦσιν, οἳ πολλάκις ἐκ ἐυςοχῆντες μάτην κινῦσι τὰς χεῖρας. Idem Eustathius ad ψ Iliados: Ἡ δὲ ποτὲ αὐτοῖς τέ- χνη κὶ τρίβειν συχνὰς ὥρας ἐπὶ κακῷ ἳ ἀντιπάλων ἀνατάσεσι κὶ κα- ταφορᾷ χειρῶν, ὡς εἰ καὶ ἀέρα ὃ δὴ λέγεται ὕδαιρον ἢ κὶ ἐσκιαμά- χεν πολεμικῶς. Seneca Naturalium quæstionum VII. 13. Solvere ista quid aliud est, quam manum exercere, & in ventum jactare brachia.

Πυκτεύειν est cæstibus certare, inquit Aretius in h. l. quale certamen est inter Daretem & Entellum apud Virgilium. Apud Homerum Achilles ad Pa- trocli tumulum quoque instituit agonem pugilum, quo vicit Epeus. Erasmus verbi originem præci- se attendens (πὺξ adverbium pugno vel pugnis; πυ- γμὴ pugnus manus in pugnum contracta) pugnis certare vertit in annotation. Dumque vulgatus In- terpres πυκτεύω pugno vertit ad pugnos, non pugnas eum allusisse ait. Quomodocunque autem intel- ligatur, certum est, de lucta spirituali, contra varios hostes, Apostolum loqui. Aërem verberare di- cuntur, qui sine adversario ludunt, seque magis fati- gant, quam exercent. Christianorum autem lucta non umbratilis est; sed contra atrocissimos & subdo- los hostes Satanam, mundum, carnem, pravosque affe- ctus, directa. Hi adoriendi, feriendi, vincendi sunt, ut hic habet B. Glassius.

Ἀλλ' ὑπωπιάζω με τὸ σῶμα κὰ δυλαγωγῶ. Vera lectio hæc ὑπωπιάζω, non ὑποπιέζω nec ὑποπιάζω. Persequitur enim postremam similitudinem à pycta desum- ptam. Pyctarum est adversarium ὑπωπιάζειν. Sunt ὑπώ- πια proprie τὰ ὑπὸ τὲς ὦπας τῶν πληγῶν ἴχνη, ut ait Pol lux; sed latius dici sic cœpere ἀφ' οἱασεδηποτῶν πληγῆς τραύ- ματα, ut ait Scholiastes ad Acharnenses Aristophanis. Ci- cero Tusculanarum II. Pugiles cæstibus contusi, id est ὑπωπια- ζόμενοι. Usum μεταφορικὸν hujus vocis habuimus Luc. XVIII. 5. Cum Paulus pyctæ se comparasset, quæri poterat, quis esset adversarius: Ipsum, inquit, corpus meum; Hoc ego obtundo, inquit, id est multis afficio incommodis, de quibus vide supra IV. 11. אצער אני אתגופי ut de ea- dem reMaimonides. Etiam δυλαγωγεῖν à pyctis desumptum est. Nam qui vicerat, victum trahebat adversarium, quasi ser- vum. Sic Paulus de corpore suo velut edomito triumpha- bat. Sic Seneca epistola VIII. dixit durius tractandum cor- pus, ne animo male pareat. Σκληραγωγίαν hoc vocat Jose- phus in Danielis historia. Σωματικὴν γυμνασίαν Paulus 1. Tim. IV. 8. Ἄσκησιν Canon Apostolicus LI. Basilius de le- gendis Græcorum libris: Ἐπὶ δὲ λόγῳ ὑπεροπτέον τὲ σώματος τῷ μὴ ὡς ἐν βορβόρῳ ταῖς ἡδοναῖς αὐτὸ καταρεμβύχθαι μέλ- λοντι, ἢ τοσῦτον αἰθίκτεον αὐτῷ, ὅσοι Φησὶ Πλάτων, ὑπηρε- σίαν σοφίᾳ κτωμένῳ ἐοικότα πε τῷ Παύλῳ, ὃς παραινεῖ μη- δεμίαν χρῆναι τῷ σώματος προνοίαν ἔχειν εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν ἀφορ- μῆς. Vide Ambrosium epistola VII. Nazianzenum ora- tione VI. Augustinum de operibus Monachorum cap. 1. 9. & 10. voce δυλαγωγῶν hoc sensu etiam Athenagoras uti- tur. Tacita comparatione perstringit illos epulatores Co- rinthios.

Addimus quæ habet de hoc loco B. Chemni- tius ex Concil. Trid. parte IV. de jejunio p. 749.

Paulus 1. Cor. IX. utitur exemplo athletarum, quo- rum victus ratio exquisitissima erat. Non enim pro- miscue quidvis ingurgitabant, & a multis abstine- bant, ut nec corpus gravaretur, nec animi vis obru- eretur, sed ut & corpus agile, & vis mentis praesens, alacris, & vegeta redderetur, ad circumspectionem inferendi, excipiendi, & praecavendi ictus. Ita & ego, inquit Paulus, corpus meum subigo, coërceo, co- hibeo, sugillo, obtundo. Est enim valde illustris Me- taphora in verbo ὑπωπιάζω. Sicut enim pugil ad- versarium suum observat, & ictibus ac plagis cohi- bet, sugillat & subigit: Ita, inquit Paulus, ego corpus meum observo, & ne caro adversaria sua relucta- tione spiritum de statu suo dejiciat, & subjugatum carni servum seu captivum reddat, subigo, obtundo, edomo & subjugo corpus meum, ut in servitutem ani- mae seu spiritus redigatur, ne aliis praedicans, ipse reprobus efficiar. Illa autem subactio seu subjuga- tio corporis, vel mortificatio carnis fit vel temperan- tia, vel abstinentia, vel jejunio, vel studiis, laboribus, negotiis, occupationibus, curis, cruce, afflictionibus, pavoribus, sensu irae Dei &c. Hoc fine ne intempe- rantia, petulantia & desidia carnis impediat inten- tionem animi, in meditationibus & exercitiis pieta- tis, neve otium & luxus pariant peccata, excutien- tia Spiritum Sanctum. Haec B. Chemnitius. Ba- silius homilia de legendis Gentil. scriptis laudante Cornelio a Lapide ita habet: Est corpus castigan- dum, ac ferae cujusdam instar cohibendum, & ab ipso adversus animam tumultus orientes ratione veluti flagello compescendi, ne frenum voluptati omnino laxando mens velut auriga ab equis contumacibus & minime obtemperantibus feratur ac rapiatur, ac inter caetera Pythagorae meminisse dicti oportet, qui videns quendam exercitationibus ac cibis laute ap- positeque sese curantem ac saginantem: Heus, inquit, miser non desinis continuo duriorem tibi carcerem praeparare! B. Hülsemannus in notis ἀνεκδότοις mo- net: Τὸ ὑπωπιάζειν indefinitam subactionem cor- poris notare, determinandam tamen esse ad abstinen- tiam ab illis speciebus, quibus licite quem uti posse commemoraverat hactenus Paulus a v. 1. usque ad 20. quod ratio objecti & connexiones docent, demon- strantque. Espensaeus in Comm. Cap. 4. epist. 1. ad Tim. v. 8. hoc verbum de corporalibus exercitiis, qualia sunt stricte dicta jejunia, vigiliae, humicuba- tiones, esse intelligendum, & communiter de pri- vatione & abstinentia ab illis commodis hic enume- ratis: Qualem abstinentiam dicto loco ad Tim. Paulus extenuet quidem in comparatione ad utilio- ra exercitia praedicationis scilicet eleemosynarum, non autem improbet. Proinde inane est, quo l. II. de Monach. c. 30. ad Utum Bellarm. aliique, ut Salmeron, & Cornelius fingunt Gretserus de discip. c. 8. de castigatione corporis Pauli per virgas ad ex- tinguendum ardorem Venereum. Contra Justinia- nus & Estius conjecturam hanc dicunt esse in- eptam. Salmer. disp. 16. etsi contundendi medium de cilicio intelligit, finem tamen negat fuisse sup- pressionem concupiscentiae Venereae. Chrysostomus illud τὸ ὑπωπιάζειν intellexit de abstinentia a com- estione idolothytorum, quia hoc fuerit objectum adaequatum abstinentiae Paulinae. Latius tamen hanc patere similitudinem de sugillando, hoc est, ad livorem usque contundendo, & de redigendo in ser- vitutem corpore, quam ut abstinentiam solum ab illis rebus indifferentibus, de quibus supra egerat, respiciat, censemus. Quia hic generatim, quo- modo corpus, id est, veterem hominem spiritui re- luctantem, qui corporis nomine venit Rom. VI. 6. cap. VII. 14. Col. II, 11. cujus membra Col. III. 5. enumerantur, compescere ac subigere debea- mus, doceatur, scilicet, uti athletae suos antago- nistas solebant tum sugillare, quod est notam in- signem faciei infligere, tum supplantare, vel in humum posternere. Quod mystice in carne sua spiritui reluctante præstabat Apostolus, non absti- nentia modo, temperantia, jejuniis, sed imprimis piis precibus, sacris verbi meditationibus, studiis, la- bore, occupationibus sanctis, mortificatione carnis &c. Nequicquam ergo hoc loco è verbo hoc ὑπωπιά- ζειν sugillationes suas probant Pontificii, quum ne- que de ictibus corpori inflictis id semper adhibea- tur, ut è Luc. XIIX. 57. constat, neque corpus hic substantialiter intelligendum sit; sed accidenta- liter de corpore peccati, ubi de coërcitione carnis agitur, ne dominetur in spiritum.

## 9:27
Lest perhaps having preached to others. Who have taught others the way of salvation.

I myself should become a castaway. I myself should become unworthy of that salvation.

Ἀδόκιμος to the Rabbis is פסול, rejected to Cato and Varro. It is opposed to ἀδόκιμον γενέσθαι to that which we had above, συγκοινωνὸν γενέσθαι εὐαγγελίου, to be a partaker of the reward proposed in the Gospel. Chrysostom in this place: 'But if Paul fears this, he who has taught so many, and fears after having preached, and having become an angel, and having demonstrated the guardianship of the world, what should we say? For do not think, he says, because you have believed, that this suffices for your salvation. For if for me, to preach, to teach, to bring thousands, does not suffice for salvation, unless I also keep my own affairs blameless, much more so for you.' Concerning the word ἀδόκιμος we have spoken at Rom. 1:28.

To the blessed Hülsemann it seems that Paul here does not properly treat of ἀδοκιμία or reprobation from the grace of justification, or eternal glory, which would otherwise follow that Peter and others, using those things from which Paul abstained, were ἀδόκιμοι, but that he speaks of comparative fitness for the office of the Apostolate, to be executed with respect to the weak. In which sense δοκιμὴ is taken in 2 Cor. 9:13, and δόκιμος and ἀδόκιμος signify, by reason of the objects about which they are predicated, aptitude and ineptitude for a certain office, 2 Tim. 2:15, 2 Cor. 10:8. Thus Apelles is called δόκιμος ἐν χριστῷ in Rom. 16:10. One abstaining from the scandal of a brother is called δόκιμος in Rom. 14:18. Thus ἀδόκιμος in 2 Cor. 13:7, land inept and unable for the crop, Heb. 6:8. But it does not seem admissible that the late blessed one [ὁ Μακαρίτης] supposed in that same place that the Apostle, in these comparisons, was using only the matter of things sacrificed to idols [εἰδωλοθύτων] or indifferent things, when he is rather defining in general the course and struggle of Christians, which is sufficiently evident from the continuity [συνεχεία] of the following chapter. Therefore, the blessed Hunnius, the blessed Balduinus, the blessed Weinrichius, and others of our side rightly prove from this passage against the Calvinists that the regenerate can fall from the grace of God and become reprobate.

The Papists, however, rashly seek here the merit of good works, as if we obtain or merit the prize of eternal life by our course and fight.
