For eternal life is a gratuitous gift (Rom. 6:23), nor does it depend in any way upon our course, labor, or fight (Rom. 9:16), whence the goal and reward are destined for us before we enter the course: and thus it is not indicated as a means of obtaining salvation, but only as a manner or order destined, by which we are led to heavenly glory only through struggles, labors, and tribulations.

Latin:

Μήπως ἄλλοις κηρύξας. Qui alios docui viam salutis.

Αὐτὸς ἀδόκιμος γένωμαι. Ipse ea salute indignus fiam.

Ἀδόκιμος Rabbinis est פסול Rejiculus Catoni & Varroni. Opponitur ἀδόκιμον γενέσθαι ei quod supra habuimus συγκοινωνὸν γενέσθαι εὐαγ- γελίου, participem esse præmii in Evangelio propositi. Chry- sostomus hoc loco: Εἰ δὲ Παῦλος τοῦτο δέδοικεν ὁ τοσούτους δι- δάξας, καὶ δέδοικε μετὰ τὸ κηρύξαι, καὶ γενέσθαι ἄγγελος, καὶ τῆς οἰκου- μένης τὴν προστασίαν ἐπιδείξασθαι, τί ἂν εἴποιμεν ἡμεῖς; Μὴ γὰρ δὴ νομίσητε φησιν, ἐπειδὴ ἐπιστεύσατε, ὅτι ἀρκεῖ τοῦτο εἰς σωτηρίαν ὑμῖν. Εἰ γὰρ ἐμοὶ τὸ κηρύξαι, τὸ διδάξαι, τὸ μυρίους προσαγαγεῖν οὐκ ἀρκεῖ εἰς σωτηρίαν, εἰ μὴ καὶ τὰ κατʼ ἐμαυτὸν παραθοίμην ἄ- ληπτα, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμῖν. De voce ἀδόκιμος diximus ad Rom. I. v. 28.

B. Hülsemanno videtur Paulus proprie hic non agere de ἀδοκιμίᾳ seu reprobatione à gratia justifi- cationis, aut gloria æterna, quod alias sequeretur, Pe- trum aliosque, utentes iis, quibus abstinebat Paulus, fuisse ἀδοκίμους, sed loqui de comparativa idoneita- te ad Apostolatus officium, respectu infirmorum exe- quendum. Quo sensu δοκιμὴ sumitur 2. Cor. IX. 13. & δόκιμος atque ἀδόκιμος significant ratione obje- ctorum, de quibus prædicantur, aptitudinem & ine- ptitudinem ad certum quoddam officium 2. Tim. II. 15. 2. Cor. X. 8. Sic Apelles vocatur δόκιμος ἐν χριστῷ Rom. XVI. 10. Abstinens à scandalo fratris dicitur δόκιμος Rom. XIV. 18. Sic ἀδόκιμος 2. Cor. XIII. 7. terra inepta & inhabilis ad segetem Ebr. VI. 8. Sed non videtur admittendum, quod ὁ Μακαρίτης ibi- dem supposuit, Apostolum in hisce similitudini- bus unice adhuc usum εἰδωλοθύτων, vel rerum me- diarum respicere, quum potius in genere cursum & certamen Christianorum definiat, quod è capi- tis sequentis συνεχεία satis constat. Quapropter recte B. Hunnius, B. Balduinus, B. Weinrichius, aliique nostrates ex hoc loco contra Calvinianos probant, renatos excidere posse gratia Dei & repro- bos fieri.

Papistæ autem temere hic quærunt meri- tum bonorum operum, quasi brabeum vitæ æternæ cursu & pugna nostra impetremus, aut mereamur. Vita enim æterna donum est gratuitum Rom. VI. v. ult. nec à nostro cursu, labore aut pugna depen- det ullatenus Rom. IX. 6. unde meta & præmium nobis destinatur, antequam cursum ingrediamur: Adeoque non medium consequendi salutem, sed modus tantum, seu ordo destinatus indicatur, quo non nisi per certamina, labores & tribulationes ad cœlestem gloriam traducimur.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

ARGUMENT & DIVISION.

The Apostle continues to exhort that they should studiously beware lest they become reprobate, since the Fathers, all baptized from the cloud and the Red Sea, and all having had the same spiritual food and drink, nevertheless displeased God for the most part and were slain in the desert, as an example to us, lest by desires of idolatry, we indulge in fornication, nor let us tempt Christ, nor let us murmur, as was done by the Fathers, to their own great harm; but, let him who stands, see that he does not fall; especially if a temptation arises that is more than human, which however God, being faithful, does not permit among his own beyond their strength. Furthermore, he teaches that the worship of idols must be fled because of the communication of the body and blood of Christ, and the spiritual communion of those who become partakers of the blessed bread in one mystical body, so that we may not come into the communion of the sacrifices of the Gentiles made to demons, and together with the cup of the Lord drink also the cup of demons. He teaches further, even if all things are lawful, that those things must nevertheless be fled which are not expedient for one's neighbor. And if it is lawful to eat all things that are sold or set before one, without scruple, yet for the sake of a neighbor's conscience, while our own remains free, one must abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and all things must be done for the honor of God, with the avoidance of scandal and the edification of one's neighbor, in imitation of the Apostolic example.

There are three parts: I. A dehortation from security to verse 13. II. An exhortation to flee the communion of the worship of idols to verse 22. III. A repeated admonition concerning things lawful, to be used so freely that the conscience of one's neighbor is nevertheless spared, and all things are done for the glory of God, to the last verse, where an objection is resolved concerning Christian liberty, the true and legitimate use of which the Apostle distinguishes from the illegitimate abuse.

PART I. Dehortation from security.

Verse 1. I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren. Better in the Manuscript: For I do not want you to be ignorant, as the Latin also reads, and Ambrose, and others. This coheres well with the preceding. He had said in the preceding that he himself treats his body harshly, lest he fall short of the hoped-for prize. He warns the Corinthians to do the same, and not to flatter themselves, as many were doing then, and are doing now, because they had received many gifts from God. For by those things they are not placed outside of danger, but are all the more obligated to take heed to themselves. Which very thing he shows to be foreshadowed by the affairs of the ancient Hebrew people, in which the wisest of the Hebrews agreed there was a figure of the times of the Messiah. To be ignorant here means to be unmindful. For those Corinthians had read the books of the Old Testament; but they did not retain everything in their memory, they did not understand the more recondite sense of everything. Thus to be ignorant is taken in Romans 6:3, 7:1.

The reason for the coherence is rightly sought in the preceding admonition about beating down the body (but of sin) and bringing it into subjection, lest we fall short of the hoped-for prize, because from there the Apostle descends to this exhortation concerning fleeing security. Others provide the connection here with Pareus, that whereas he had indeed discoursed before about the use of things sacrificed to idols as a matter in itself free, and to be avoided only because of scandal, now he rejects and prohibits it as a matter altogether unworthy of Christians, under the threat of divine wrath, which they are to experience after the example of the Israelites. But because the proposition or conclusion of the Pauline exhortation in verse 12 is general: Let him who stands see that he does not fall, and the Apostle prohibits not only idolatry, but also wicked concupiscence, fornication, the tempting of Christ, and murmuring against the Ministers of God, under the commination of divine wrath, and a general warning about curbing the flesh had intervened, the former reason for the connection is to be preferred. There is a digression toward certain things in the first part on the occasion of the contest, concerning which the Apostle had treated toward the end of the preceding chapter, from where he returns further in the second and third parts to the matter concerning things sacrificed to idols, and completes the same, which was begun in chapter 8.

For our fathers. Of the Hebrews, whose Paul was.

Spiritual Fathers or faithful Elders are not being referred to, because even if Abraham is called the Father of believers with respect to faith, yet simply and without an addition, I believe, Elders will not easily be found called Fathers who were of the same faith with respect to the children of the faithful. Indeed, those who have begotten us spiritually are called Fathers, just as Paul is called the Father of the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 4:15. But this meaning is foreign here, for the Corinthians were not begotten spiritually by those who were under the cloud. Nor is there any reason to depart from the proper meaning of the word our fathers. Although indeed the fathers of the Corinthians or of the Gentiles were not Hebrews: yet they were the fathers of Paul and of other Hebrews, according to the flesh: therefore the Apostle understands himself with others through a figure of communication, just as in verse 8 such a communion is had. And there were not a few converted from among the Hebrews among the Corinthians. Therefore our fathers, that is, of the Jews, from whom I am, and many of you, B. Hunnius thinks they are called Fathers regarding the series of succession in the Church; but the proper sense is simpler, that the Fathers are designated not by reason of holiness, but of procreation and age. Certainly, faithful elders cannot be understood. For not only the faithful were under the cloud. Nor were all those who crossed the sea faithful, but many of them did not please the Lord.

They were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea.

They were protected by a cloud against the heat of the sun, Ezek. VIII. 21. Christ thus defends us from divine wrath, so that He may show us the way to salvation. They passed through the sea, Exod. XIV. We have begun to despise the world. But there remains a vast desert to be crossed.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Pergit cohortari Apostolus, ut studiose sibi ca- veant, ne reprobi fiant, quum Patres ex nube atque mari rubro baptizati omnes, & cibum ac potum Spiritualem eundem habuerint o- mnes, plerique tamē Deo displicuerint, in de- serto casi, nobis in exemplū, ne cupiditatibus idolatria, scortationi indulgeamus, nec Christum tentemus, nec murmuremus, que- admodum a Patribus, malo ipsorum maxi- mo, factum; sed, qui stat, videat, ne cadat; si praesertim tentatio plus quam humana oria- tur, quam tamen Deus fidelis penes suos su- pravires non permittat. Porro fugiendum idolorum cultum docet ob communicatio- nem corporis & sanguinis Christi, & eorum, qui panis benedicti participes fiunt, spiritua- lem communionem in uno mystico corpore, ut ne in communionem sacrificiorum gentilium daemonibus factorum veniamus, & una cum calice Domini etiam calicem daemoniorum bibamus. Docet adhuc, etsi liceant omnia, fugienda tamen esse ea, quae non expediunt proximo. Et si omnibus vesci liceat, quae venduntur, vel apponuntur, sine scrupulo, ob proximi tamen conscientiam, nostra et- iam libera manente, abstinendum esse idolo- thytis, omniaque facienda esse ad Dei hono- rem, cum scandali evitatione, & proximi aedificatione ad imitationem exempli Apo- stolici.

Partes tres sunt I. Dehortatio a securitate ad v. II. Adhortatio ad fugiendam communionem cultus idolorum ad v. 22. III. Commonefactio itera- ta de rebus licitis ita libere usurpandis, ut con- scientiae tamen proximi parcatur, & omnia ad glo- riam Dei fiant v. ult. ubi objectio dirimitur de li- bertate Christiana, cujus verum & legitimum usum Apostolus ab illegitimo abusu distermi- nat.

PARS I. Dehortatio a securitate.

Vers. 1. Οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν ἀδελφοὶ. Melius in Manuscripto: Οὐ θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, quo- modo & Latinus legit & Ambrosius, aliique. Bene cohæ- ret id cum superioribus. Dixerat in præcedentibus, se ipsum corpus suum male tractare, ne sperato præmio excidat. Monet Corinthios idem ut faciant, ac ne sibi blandiantur, ut multi tunc faciebant, & nunc faciunt, quod multa dona a Deo accepissent. Per ea enim eos non constitui extra pericu- lum, sed eo magis obligari, ut sibi caveant. Quod ipsum ostendit adumbratum rebus antiqui populi Hebraici, in qui- bus figuram fuisse temporum Messiæ sapientissimi Hebræo- rum consentiebant. Ἀγνοεῖν hic valet esse immemorem. Nam legerant isti Corinthii libros Veteris Testamenti; sed non omnia memoria retinebant, non omnium sensum re- conditiorem intelligebant. Sic ἀγνοεῖν sumitur Rom. VI. 3. VII. 1.

Recte cohærentiæ ratio quæritur in admoni- tione præcedanea de corpore (sed peccati) obtun- dendo, & sub servitutem redigendo, ne præmio sperato excidamus, quia inde ad hanc παραίνεσιν de fugienda securitate descendit Apostolus. Alii huc cum Pareo nexum tradunt, quod quidem ante de usu idolothytorum, tanquam de re, in se libera, & propter scandalum tantum vitanda disseruisset, jam tanquam rem omnino indignam Christianis re- jiciat & prohibeat, sub interminatione iræ divinæ, quam ad exemplum Israëlitarum experturi sint. Sed quia propositio vel conclusio exhortationis Pau- linæ v. 12. generalis est: Qui stat videat, ne cadat, nec tantum idololatriam, sed etiam concupiscen- tiam pravam, stupra, tentationem Christi & mur- mur adversus Ministros Dei prohibet Apostolus, sub iræ divinæ comminatione, ac intervenerat mo- nitum generale de carne compescenda, prior συν- εχείας ratio præferenda. Digressio erga quædam est in parte prima occafione agonis, de quo sub fi- nem capitis præcedentis egerat Apostolus, unde porro in secunda & tertia parte ad materiam de idolothytis redit, eandemque capite IIX. inchoa- tam absolvit.

Ὅτι πατέρες ἡμῶν. Hebræorum quorum erat Paulus.

Non respiciuntur Patres spirituales vel Majo- res fideles, quia etsi Abraham Pater credentium di- catur fidei respectu, simpliciter tamen & sine addi- to Patres non facile, credo, reperientur dicti ma- jores, qui ejusdem fidei fuerint respectu libero- rum fidelium. Dicuntur quidem Patres, qui nos spiritualiter genuêre, uti Paulus Corinthiorum Pater dicitur 1. Cor. IV. 15. Sed hæc significatio hic aliena est, non enim ab iis, qui sub nube fuerunt, spiritualiter geniti sunt Corinthii. Neque citra causam à propria vocis πατέρες ἡμῶν significatione discedendum est. Quanquam vero Corinthiorum seu gentilium Patres non fuerint Ebræi: Pauli ta- men, & aliorum Ebræorum Patres erant, secundum carnem: Se ergo cum aliis per communicationis fi- guram intelligit Apostolus, uti versu 8. talis κοίνω- σις habetur. Et erant non pauci ex Ebræis con- versi inter Corinthios. Patres ergo nostri, id est Ju- dæorum, è quibus ego, & multi ex vobis, B. Hunnius Patres dici putat quoad seriem successionis in Ec- clesia; sed simplicior est sensus proprius, quod Pa- tres designentur, non ratione sanctitatis, sed pro- creationis & ætatis. Fideles certe majores in- telligi nequeunt. Nec enim soli fideles sub nube fuerunt. Nec omnes illi, qui mare transierunt, fide- les fuêre, sed multi eorum Domino haud placuerunt,

Ὑπὸ τὴν νεφέλην ἦσαν, καὶ πάντες διά ἐ θαλάσσης διῆλθον.

Illi nube protecti fuêre contra calorem solis Ezech. VIII. 21. Nos Christus ita defendit ab ira divina, ut viam nobis ad salutem monstret. Illi per mare transiêre, Exod. XIV. Nos mundum cœpimus contemnere. Sed restat transeundum ingens desertum.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. And all were baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea.

They were baptized, that is, they were as if baptized. He uses this word so that he may the more show the shadow of our things. For the reality of baptism is in those two things which we have already mentioned: liberation from divine wrath, and liberation from the world. Then in that which is seen and something similar. The cloud hung over their heads: so also the water over those who are baptized. The sea surrounded their sides: so also the water those who are baptized. To be baptized into Moses is to believe in Moses, and through that confidence to begin the journey under the cloud, then also through the sea, with Moses himself going before. Just as Christ went before us, see Exod. XIV. 31. and what was said by us at Matth. XXVIII. 19. Tertullian in his book on baptism: 'First indeed, when the people, having been freed from Egypt, escaped the force of the King of Egypt by passing through the water, the water extinguished the King himself with all his forces.' What figure is more manifest in the sacrament of baptism? The nations are liberated from the world, namely through water, and they leave behind the Devil, their former master, drowned in the water.

Latin:

Vers. 2. καὶ πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ καὶ τῇ θαλάσσῃ.

Baptizati sunt, id est quasi baptizati sunt. Usurpat istam vocem, ut eo magis ostendat umbram rerum nostrarum. Res enim baptismi est in illis duobus, quæ jam diximus, li- beratione ab ira divina, & liberatione à mundo. Deinde in eo quod conspicitur & aliquid simile. Nubes impendebat illorum capitii: Sic & aqua iis, qui baptizantur. Mare circum- dabat eorum latera: sic & aqua eos qui baptizantur. In Mo- sen baptizari est Mosi credere, & per eam fiduciam iter inci- pere sub nube, deinde & per mare, ipso Mose præeunte. Sic- ut Christus nobis præivit, vide Exod. XIV. 31. & quæ à nobis dicta ad Matth. XXVIII. 19. Tertullianus libro de baptismo: Primo quidem cum populus de Ægypto expeditus, vim Regis Æ- gypti per aquam transgressus evasit, ipsum Regem cum totis co- piis aqua exstinxit. Quæ figura manifestior in baptismi sacra- mento? Liberantur de seculo nationes, per aquam scilicet, & Dia- bolum dominatorem pristinum in aqua depressum derelin- quunt.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. And all ate the same spiritual food.

He calls Manna spiritual food because God worked various tastes in it, as we said at Exod. XVI. Thus the law is spiritual, Rom. VII. 14, that is, given by God. For GOD is also by excellence spirit, John IV. 14. When he says 'the same,' he does not mean the same as us, but the same who were then saved, like Joshua and Caleb, and those who perished. This parity does not prevent the difference in outcome. Truly, in the Manuscript it is not 'the same,' neither here nor in the following member. But 'they ate spiritual food, and drank spiritual drink.' Manna given from heaven figures Christ sent to us from heaven for the nourishment of the soul with various mighty works. Philo interprets Manna as the divine word twice, in the book 'The Worse Attacks the Better,' and in the book 'Who is the Heir of Divine Things.'

Regarding the body and blood of Christ, Dr. Sebastian Schmid explains in a special disputation held on this passage, and in his later biblical collection, p. 335, that they ate the body and drank the blood of Christ through faith, namely in the type of the manna and the water from the rock: even though they did not have the body or blood of Christ present, as we do in the Holy Supper, but only typically, since our sacraments are antitypical. But we deservedly persist in the common interpretation of our theologians and the ancients, where spiritual food and spiritual drink is understood here not of the body and blood of Christ; but of the Manna and water from the rock: and it is called πνευματικὸν both because of its divine origin and because of its spiritual signification. For it is not necessary that the same signification of the word occur when it is applied to food and drink, and when it is applied to the rock. On which argument, and a less firm one, that opinion rests. And indeed did all the fathers, all the Israelites, who all passed through the sea, and were under the cloud, eat the body and blood of Christ by faith? That certainly cannot be said. And therefore the explanation concerning the body and blood of Christ is not suitable. But that the fathers of the Hebrews, whose Paul was, are called the only believers, does not fit this passage any more than the speech of Stephen Acts VII. 2. 11. 39. 44. 45. and Acts XIII. 32. ch. XXIX. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 3. καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ βρῶμα πνευματικὸν ἔφαγον.

Manna vocat βρῶμα πνευματικὸν quia Deus in eo opera- batur gustus varios, ut diximus ad Exod. XVI. Sic νόμος πνευ- ματικὸς Rom. VII. 14. id est à Deo datus. Nam DEUS & per excellentiam spiritus Joh IV. 14. Cum dicit τὸ αὐτὸ non vult dicere idem nobiscum, sed idem qui tunc servati sunt, ut Josue & Caleb, & qui periêre. Hæc paritas non impedit eventus discrimen. Verum in Manuscripto non est τὸ αὐτὸ, neque hic neque in sequente membro. Sed τὸ πνευματικὸν ἔφαγον βρῶμα, & τὸ πνευματικὸν ἔπιον πόμα. Manna de cœlo datum figurat Christum nobis cœlitus missum ad animi ali- mentum cum variis virtutibus. Μάννα θεῖον λόγον bis inter- pretatur Philo libro, Pejorem insidiari meliori, & libro, quis sit rerum diversarum hæres.

De corpore & sanguine Christi exponit Dn. D. Sebastian. Schmid disput. peculiari de h. l. habita, & in Coll. bibl. poster. p. 335. quod ederint per fidem corpus, & biberint sanguinem Christi scilicet in typo mannæ & aquæ è petra: Etsinon habuerint corpus Christi præsens aut sanguinem, ut nos in sacra cœna, sed tantum typice, cum sacramenta nostra sint anti- typica. Sed persistimus merito in communi Theo- logorum nostrorum & veterum interpretatione, qua cibus spiritualis, & potus spiritualis hic non d corpore & sanguine Christi; sed de Manna & aqua è petra intelligitur: & πνευματικὸν tum ob originem divinam, tum ob spiritualem significationem dici- tur. Neque enim necessum est, eandem vocis signi- ficationem occurrere, cum de cibo & potu, & cun de petra eadem adhibetur. Quo argumento, sec minus firmo, nititur illa sententia. Et num omnes patres, omnes Israëlitæ, qui omnes per mare trans- ierunt, & sub nube fuerunt, fide comederunt cor- pus & sanguinem Christi? Id utique dici non potest. Ideoque non convenit explicatio de cor- pore & sanguine Christi. Patres vero Ebræorum, quorum erat Paulus, solos fideles dici, non magis huic loco congruit, quam orationi Stephani Act. VII. 2. 11. 39. 44. 45. & Act. XIII. 32. c. XXIX. 25.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. And all drank the same spiritual drink.

Explain as the former. As well those who were safe as those who perished used the same drink given divinely.

These things are rightly said concerning the fathers compared among themselves, but not indeed with us. For all those, both believers and unbelievers, ate the same food, namely the heavenly Manna, but they did not all have the same food with us. For although the believers also participated in the true Christ by faith through the Manna, just as we do in the N. T. Acts XV. 10, yet the unbelievers, who are included under the word πάντες, repeated five times, did not at all enjoy that spiritual food of the body of Christ at the same time, which is perceived only through faith. But the Reformed err, and do not stand in the scope of Paul, when they extend the communion of the Fathers concerning their sacraments not only to a communion of the Fathers in species the same as the communion of our sacraments (as can be seen in Calvin, Beza, Marloratus, Pareus) but also to an identity of the Israelitic sacraments with our sacraments: nor do they assert that the body and blood of Christ are present to those enjoying the Holy Supper in any other way than the Passover was present to those celebrating in the O. T., or eating the Paschal lamb, so that they may take away and snatch from us the true, real, and substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ from the Holy Supper. Moreover, five benefits are recounted here, in which the favor of God exercised itself toward the Israelites, and which at the same time exhibited symbols and figures of future things. Which all the Israelites in general, with no one excluded at that time, experienced. The first is that all the Fathers were under the cloud, which led them by day; it defended them against the heat, and by night it shone before them like a torch, because it was then fiery Exod. XIII. Which was a symbol of the perpetual grace of Christ, of which Is. IV. 4. 5. Second, that all passed through the Red Sea Ex. XIV. Which foreshadowed our passage through the Red Sea of the blood of Christ in baptism, and the destruction of the infernal Pharaoh in the wave of baptism, and the drowning of the old man with all his lusts. Third, that all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea Ex. XIV. Which some explain causally concerning baptism by the hand of Moses, as the Syrian also translates, that is, by his ministry, done in the passage through the Red Sea, or with Moses going before, as Junius explained, explaining that by an ellipsis of the word εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν, i.e., coming to Moses, running to him, and following him Parall. II. 36. others however interpret it more conveniently as final, which also pleased Grotius, concerning a baptism done to win faith for Moses, so that they might believe in Moses, and consequently in GOD speaking and working through Moses, and thus place their trust in GOD, which Moses especially inculcated Exod. XIV. 31. B. Hülsemann urges the induction, that βαπτισθῆναι is taken either properly or even improperly; if it is established with the preposition εἰς, it always denotes baptism received into the profession or ratification of that doctrine which he professed, into whom one is said to be baptized Matth. XXVIII. 19. Acts II. 39. ch. XIX. 3. Rom. VI. 3. 1. Cor. I. 13. 15. thus below ch. XV. 29. into the faith which the dead professed, having been baptized in Christ. Gal. III. 27. He wonders at the rashness of Heinsius, who chastises his accomplices, as if they were ignorant of the force of this phrase and that to be baptized into Moses is the same as not even Moses being excepted: of which exposition he brings forward no suitable example. But by the word of baptism, our baptism is indeed alluded to, yet there is not an exact collation of the sacramental rites of the O. and N. T., as the Calvinists wish: just as that Βαπτισμὸς under the cloud and in the Red Sea was not a sacrament, but only some sign or type of our baptism. As the cloud was of heavenly origin; but the Sea was on earth: So in our baptism there are also two things, the heavenly Thing, the Most Holy Trinity; and the earthly, water, by which we are washed in the name of the most holy Trinity. To the Israelites the divided sea and the clouds were a visible testimony of the gracious divine presence and help: So our baptism is an effective symbol of the present divine grace, and a washing of our regeneration and renewal, Tit. III. 5. The Israelites were obligated by that typical baptism to faith in God through Moses; So we, through baptism, the sacrament of the New Testament, are bound to faith in God through Christ the Mediator. The fourth benefit of the Fathers is that they all ate the same spiritual food, namely Manna rained down from heaven, which is called πνευματικὸν βρῶμα, not because of an intrinsic power of exhibiting various tastes: Nor as the law is called spiritual because of the spiritual perfection and obedience which it demands not only externally, but especially of our spirit and soul: Nor because of a spiritual libation, because the food was only material and bodily; but because of its divine origin and typical reason, because it foreshadowed the body of Christ, or rather Christ, as that bread of life, which descended from heaven, by the interpretation of Christ himself John VI. 33. Therefore the Calvinian argument is sand without lime, that we do not eat the substantial body of Christ itself in the Holy Supper, because the Fathers in the Old Testament, who did not yet have the substantial body of Christ present, ate the same food with us. For that word NOBISCUM (with us) is rashly inserted into the text by Calvin, Inst. Book IV, ch. 14, § 23, since it is too clear that the Fathers are not being compared with us, but among themselves, because while all indeed ate the spiritual food, not all pleased God, or were faithful, but very few. If that word 'with us' is to be added here, it must also be thrust into the preceding clauses, that the Fathers were WITH US under the cloud, passed WITH US through the Red Sea, were baptized WITH US into Moses, which are absurd. And the Apostle's scope is not to compare the Israelites with Christians as equals: But to prefer them to these, as in prerogatives, so also in punishments: Conf. Heb. 11. 3. Whence Oecolampadius himself, citing B. Chemnitius on the fundamentals of the Supper, ch. 12. There is not, he says, to be made a comparison with us, as some explain, that they ate the same food as we; but the comparison is made among themselves, so that the food which Moses ate was not denied to Korah, nor to Abiram, nor to the women. The fifth benefit is that all drank the same spiritual drink; namely, the water flowing from the rock, which is likewise called spiritual drink, both on account of its divine production, because it was not brought into act by the virtue of the rock, but was produced in the rock and thus drawn from the rock by the miraculous power of GOD: and on account of its spiritual signification, by which the water, which CHRIST offers [it] springing up into eternal life John IV. 14. [it] foreshadowed, just as also in both those symbols, namely food and drink miraculously provided to the Israelites, the mystery of the body and blood of Christ, instituted by Christ himself for us to eat and drink sacramentally, was figured.

For they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them.

That rock is called spiritual, because God had put water into it: 'Then first water flowed into it through invisible channels,' as Philo explains in the Life of Moses. Moreover, the rock is said to have followed the Israelites, in effect, that is; the water following them, which flowed from the rock. Tertullian in the said book on baptism: 'This is the water which flowed to the people from the accompanying rock.' Philo in the said book, 'The worse lying in wait for the better,' explains the rock as 'the solid and unbroken wisdom of God.' God is צוּר in the Old Testament, Christ in the New.

And the rock was Christ.

That is, it prefigured Christ. They did not understand this, but we understand it, for whom all those things were prepared. The struck rock gave water; Christ, struck unto death, obtained the Holy Spirit for his own. See below XII. 13. Through that very water the rock accompanied the Hebrews. And Christ is with us through the Spirit to the end of the age, Matt. XXVIII. 20. As the seven cows and ears of corn are seven years, Gen. XLI. 26, that is, they prefigure seven years. See also Apocal. XVII. 15.

Now the discourse is not about a material rock, but about Christ, who is the spiritual rock, and is so called not only in the New Testament, but also in the Old, Ps. CXIIX. 22, Zach. III. 9, so that Philo's interpretation is not inappropriate here. This is taught both by the proper meaning of the word πνευματικῆς, from which one should not depart without cause; and by the description of the rock, which is said to have 'followed' the Israelites, which is absurd to say of a material rock. Moreover, to have recourse to metonymy is contrary to the laws of good interpretation and highly inconvenient, since it is said of the rock from which they drank that it followed or accompanied them: but they did not drink from spiritual water, but from the spiritual rock. With Grotius himself as interpreter; then the Apostle's clear interpretation, who, lest we should doubt which rock he understands, adds expressly: 'And that rock was Christ,' where Grotius in vain feigns a trope in the substantive verb ἦν WAS with the Calvinists; which I have clearly refuted as being plainly incapable of a trope in 'Stereom. verbor. Testam. Jesu Christi' against Mr. Johann Berg. Nor indeed is there any reason why we should understand these things tropically, since in reality the rock from which the Israelites were given to drink, and which accompanied them everywhere, was Christ, whom they are said to have tempted in the desert, v. 9. For they drank not so much from a material rock, because that was by no means naturally suited to pour forth water, as from the spiritual rock, as from a fountain abundantly springing forth, from whose fullness we all receive, John I. 16, of which rock, if that material rock be said to have been a figure, we shall not gainsay. For water was elicited from the material rock for this reason, and not from another thing, because Christ, designated by the material rock, was our rock to be struck and cleft for us, Zach. III. 9, just as the blood of Christ, which was abundantly poured out from his struck side, was foreshadowed by the water, by which we are spiritually and sacramentally given to drink unto eternal life. B. Glassius observes in 'Gramm. S.' p. 504, that the preposition ἐκ denotes not the material, but the efficient cause, as it sometimes does elsewhere. See John VI. 65, Matt. I. 20, Rom. XI. 36. Nor is there any doubt that the word ἀκολυθούσης more correctly applies to Christ, who accompanied the Israelites everywhere. The Syrian translated it: 'which was coming or going with them,' rather than to a material rock, which to be noted by that word as having followed them does not at all accord with the usage of the word in the Lord's saying. But that it followed them everywhere, which Thomas wishes, is foreign to history. Which Musculus acknowledges in this passage, when he says: 'They drank from the spiritual rock; he calls the minds of the readers away from the bodily rock to Christ the spiritual rock.' Whence he also adds: 'And the rock was Christ.' A bodily rock can also be called spiritual, because it was a figure of the spiritual rock. But since he adds, 'which followed,' I think it must be understood of Christ himself, for He was following the people in the desert, and was supplying them with water by a miraculous spring. Goclenius: 'Christ,' he says, 'is truly our rock, not by essence, but by excellence, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, that is, by likeness, solidity, and certainty he is above every bodily rock.' A bodily rock certainly did not follow the Israelites, nor did the water itself flowing from the rock, as Beza and Pareus wish. For we are taught that the water vanished and failed, Ex. XVII. 6, as also Num. XX. 21. But it would not have failed if the rocky water had followed them everywhere. To say nothing of the fact that the stream of that one rock could not naturally have followed the Israelites for so many years, wandering through various winding paths. But if such a thing happened by a miracle, how is it that it was not commemorated by Moses, the most diligent of historians? Therefore, the spiritual rock, which accompanied them everywhere, was Christ. Concerning which see B. Dannhavver in 'Mysteriosoph.' Sect. 1. Art. VIII. §. 51. What rock was that? A stony one? But that was not accompanying, but remained perpetually fixed and immovable. The Hebrews indeed imagine that the waters flowing from the rock followed the camps, wherever they might set out, through channels or conduits, which the Princes made with their staffs, dragged on the ground behind them, and hence the rock, that is, the water flowing from the rock, is said to be accompanying. They confirm their opinion from Num. XXI. 17, Ps. LXXVIII. 20, and Ps. CV. 41. But how will they prove this fable to us? There was certainly a time, when water failed the thirsty, Num. XX. 21, after the rock had already been struck before, Ex. XVII. 4, nor is it credible that the Israelites, wandering through winding detours and not going in a straight line, had waters as companions for themselves through those same detours. Numbers XXI. v. 17, עלי באר is not necessarily explained vocatively as 'descend, O well!', but 'over the well' (über den Brunnen); in the cited Psalms the flowing forth of waters is handed down, nothing about winding ambages. It remains, therefore, that by the accompanying rock Christ is to be understood: So that τὸ ἀκολυθεῖν is enunciated in a congregative sense, not a consecutive one, as Mr. Dr. Glassius explains most excellently from the parallels of Franc. Junius, l. 3. Philol. tr. 6. p. m. 551. And Junius also acknowledged that the word ἀκολυθεῖν does not stand in the way, l. 11. parall. 36. For the word ἀκολυθεῖν means not only to follow one going before (as it is commonly accustomed to be taken), but it also signifies generally to make a journey together with another, whether you go before, or follow, or have joined yourself as a companion to the side of one going. For it is made from the particle α, which among the Greeks not infrequently has the meaning of τοῦ ὁμοῦ (together), and the noun κέλευθος (way, journey). Whence this primary and general meaning has proceeded. The Syrian rendered it emphatically: But that rock itself was Christ. Therefore it ought not to be taken concerning the meaning only. Truly the spiritual rock was Christ: the spiritual rock did not merely signify Christ.

No example can truly be brought forward, which is taken significatively or figuratively in a proposition of the third adjacent, or when it is to be joined, and which signifies that it ought to be explained. In that Gen. XLI. 26, the word IS is not had, and therefore it cannot be explained σημαντικῶς (significatively). It is said simply: The seven cows, seven years. That which is not, cannot be modified. Why might it not be permitted to understand, 'seven cows are understood', if anything is to be understood? Such an ellipsis is also in the place Apoc. XVII. 15. The many waters are many peoples (to be understood), so that there is no need for the word εἰσί to be vexed against its nature, since it is a copula.

If you say that not all who enjoyed the water from the rock believed in Christ and held him for the rock of salvation: one must distinguish between the drinking itself and the intention of drinking. For although the infidels did not have the actual intention of drinking typically from the water of the rock, yet because they truly drank from the rock, which was a type of Christ, they can rightly be said to have all drunk a spiritual drink, and, as the blessed Hülfemann holds, all the Israelites without exception participated in the spiritual rock, Christ, as far as the communion of preventing grace is concerned, which is by no means denied by the fact that most did not believe, Heb. IV. 2, and that in most God did not have pleasure, here v. 5. For that all guests are called to the wedding, and that the same spiritual food is proposed to all, Matt. XXII. 4, this is certainly a benefit of the grace of Christ, the communion of which can by no means be denied to those not clothed in a wedding garment, v. 11. Mylius brings forward yet another meaning of the word ἀκολυθῦσα. If, however, he says, it should please anyone to refer this to the rock in a transferred sense, so that it is called ἀκολυθῦσα because it was obedient to the word of the Lord and showed itself compliant in pouring forth waters: we for our part will not peevishly object, provided only that the Pauline sentiment remains intact, that all the Israelites, in whatever difference they were placed, yet by promise ate the same spiritual food, at least in an analogical and typical manner, not unlike our mysteries, and drank the same spiritual drink, and from the same spiritual rock, that is, that they did not lack the most brilliant types of the highest mysteries, and thus of the highest good itself, namely Christ, so that provided true faith and piety had been present, nothing would have been lacking to them either for dignity or for supreme happiness, and thus in the dignity of the mysteries they were very close to us. But the former explanation is better. For the blessed Mylius himself admits, f. 221, that the Apostle is not speaking of a simple or natural rock (of which it certainly could not be said that it was or had been Christ: but he only noted the same) but of a spiritual rock.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ πόμα πνευματικὸν ἔπιον.

Expone ut priora. Tam qui sospites fuêre, quam qui perierunt, eodem usi sunt potu divinitus dato.

Recte hæc de patribus inter se comparatis, non vero nobiscum. Cibum enim eundem omnes illi tum fideles tum infideles manducarunt, Manna nempe cœleste, non vero nobiscum eundem ci- bum omnes habuêre. Etsi enim fideles etiam Chri- stum verum Manna fide participarint, quemad- modum nos in N. T. Act. XV. 10. infideles tamen qui sub voce πάντες, quinquies repetita, compre- henduntur, simul esca illa spirituali corporis Christi minime fruiti sunt, quæ non nisi per fidem percipi- tur. Errant autem Reformati, nec in scopo Pauli consistunt, cum communionem Patrum circa sua sacra extendunt non solum ad communionem Pa- trum specie eandem cum comunione nostrorum sacrorum (ut apud Calvinum, Bezam, Marlora- tum, Pareum videre est) sed etiam ad identitatem sacrorum Israëliticorum cum sacris nostris: nec alia ratione præsto esse corpus & sanguinem Chri- sti Sacra Eucharistia fruentibus, quam adfuerit Pa- scha in V. T. celebrantibus, vel agnum Paschalem comedentibus, asserunt, ut veram, realem ac sub- stantialem præsentiam corporis, & sanguinis Chri- sti è S. Cœna tollant, nobisque eripiant. Cæterum quinq; hic recensentur beneficia, in quibus Dei fa- vor erga Israëlitas se exeruit, quæque simul rerum futurarum symbola, & figuras exhibuêre. Quæ omnes in universum Israëlitæ, nullo eo tempore ex- cluso, experti sunt. Primum quod omnes Patres sub nube fuerint, quæ illos duxit interdiu; adversus æstum defendit, noctu facis instar, quia ignea tum erat, illis præluxit Exod. XIII Quæ symbolum fuit gratia Christi perpetua, de qua Es. IV. 4. 5. Se- cundo quod omnes per mare rubrum transierint Ex. XIV. Quod adumbrabat nostram per mare ru- brum sanguinis Christi in baptismo traductionem, & Pharaonis infernalis in baptismi unda deletio- nem, veterisque hominis cum omnibus concupi- scentis submersione m. Tertio quod omnes in Mo- sen baptizati sint in nube & in mari Ex. XIV. Quod nonnulli causaliter de baptismo per manum Mosis, ut Syrus etiam vertit, id est per ministerium ejus, in transitu per mare rubrum facto, vel Mose prœeunte, ut Junius exposuit, id per ellipsin verbi explicans εἰς τὸν Μωσῆν ad Mosen scil. venientes, accurrentes, eumque sequentes Parall. II. 36. alii autem commo- dius interpretantur finaliter, quod Grotio etiam placuit de baptismo facto ad fidem Mosi concili- andam, ut crederent Mosi, & consequenter DEO per Mosen loquenti & operanti, adeoque in DEUM fiduciam collocarent, quod Moses im- primis inculcabat Exod. XIV. 31. B. Hülsemannus urget inductionem, quod βαπτισθῆναι seu proprie seu etiam improprie sumatur; si constituatur cum præpositione eis semper notet baptismum acceptum in professionem seu ratihabitionem ejus doctrinæ, quam professus est is, in quem quis dicitur baptizari Matth. XXVIII. 19. Act. II. 39. cap. XIX. 3. Rom. VI. 3. 1. Cor. I. 13. 15. sic infra cap. XV. 29. in fidem, quam professi sunt defuncti in Christo baptizati. Gal. III. 27. Miratur Heinsii temeritatem castigantis suos complices, quasi ignorarent vim hujus phraseos & baptizari in Mosen idem sit, quod ne Mose quidem excepto: Cujus expositionis nullum idoneum exemplum ille profert. Verbo autem baptismi ad nostrum baptismum alluditur quidem, non tamen exacta, ut Calviniani volunt, sit rituum sacramen- talium V. & N. T. collatio: Quemadmodum nec Βαπτισμὸς ille sub nube & in mari rubro sacramen- tum fuit, sed tantum signum aliquod vel typus ba- ptismi nostri. Ut nubes cælestis originis erat; Mare vero erat in terris: Ita in baptismo nostro duo etiam sunt, Res cælestis SS. Trinitas; & terrestris, aqua, qua abluimur in nomine sacrosanctæ Trini- tatis. Israëlitis mare divisum, & nubes erant visi- bile divinæ præsentiæ gratiosæ & auxilii testimo- nium: Ita baptismus noster est efficax gratiæ divi- næ præsentis symbolum, & regenerationis ac renova- tionis nostræ lavacrum, Tit. III. 5. Israëlitæ illo typi- co baptismo ad fidem in Deum per Mosen obli- gabantur; Ita nos per baptismum, Nov. Testam. Sa- cramentum, adstringimur ad fidem in Deum per Christum Mediatorem. Quartum beneficium Pa- trum est, quod omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederint, Manna scil. cœlitus deplutum, quod πνευματικὸν βρῶμα dicitur, non ob vim intrinse- cam gustus varios exhibendi: Nec uti lex spiritua- lis dicitur ob spiritualem perfectionem & obedien- tiam, quam postulat non externam modo, sed im- primis spiritùs & animæ nostræ: Neque ob spiri- tualem libationem, quia cibus erat materialis tan- tum & corporalis; sed ob originem divinam & ra- tionem typicam, quia adumbrabat corpus Christi, vel Christum potius, ceu panem istum vitæ, qui de cælo descendit, interprete ipsomet Christo Joh. VI 33. Arena ergo fine calce est argumentum Cal- vinianum, quod non edamus in S. Cœna ipsum substantiale corpus Christi, quia eandem nobiscum escam comederent in Veteri Testamento Patres, qui substantiale Christi corpus præsens nondum ha- buêre. Nam illud NOBISCUM temere inseritur textui à Calvino l. IV. Instit. cap. 14. §. 23. quum nimis clarum sit, non conferri Patres nobiscum, sed inter se, quod omnes quidem comederint escam spiritualem, non autem omnes Deo placuerint, vel fi- deles fuerint, sed paucissimi. Si hic illud nobiscum addendum, etiam in prioribus illud ingerendum, Patres NOBISCUM sub nube fuisse, NOBIS- CUM per mare rubrum transiisse, NOBISCUM in Mosen baptizatos esse, quæ absurda sunt. Et Apostoli scopus non est, Israëlitas conferre Chri- stianis, ut pares: Sed hoc illis anteferre, ut in præro- gativis, ita & in pœnis: Conf. Ebr. 11. 3. Unde Oe- colampadius ipse, citante B. Chemnitio de fundam. cœnæ cap. 12. Non est, inquit, facienda collatio cum nobis, sicut quidam exponunt, quod eandem, quam nos escam comederint; sed inter ipsos fit comparatio, ut esca, quam Moses manducavit, nec Core, nec Abiram, nec mulieribus sit dene- gata. Quintum beneficium est, quod omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberint; Aquam scilicet è petra fluentem, quæ itidem spiritua- lis potus dicitur, tum ob productionem divi- nam, quia non è virtute petræ causa'i in actum deducta, sed miraculosa DEI virtute in petra pro- ducta & ita è petra educta fuit: tum ob spiritua- lem significationem, qua aquam, quam CHRISTUS præbet scaturientem in vitam æternam Joh. IV. 14. adumbrabat, uti etiam in utroque illo symbolo cibo nempe, & potu Israëlitıs miraculose præbito figuratum fuit corporis & sanguinis Christi, ad eden- dum & bibendum sacramentaliter ab ipso Christo nobis instituto mysterium.

Ἔπινον γὰρ ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας.

Rupes illa spiritualis dicitur, quia Deus ei aquam indide- rat : Τότε πρῶτον ὕδατος ἀφανέσι ὑπονόμοις εἰς ἀυτὴν ἀτρέκ συῤῥοόντων ut Philo exponit de vita Mosis. Dicitur autem Israëlitas sequuta rupes, effectu scilicet; aqua ipsos sequente, quæ è rupe manabat. Tertullianus dicto libro de baptismo: Hæc est aqua, quæ de comite petra populo defluebat: Philo dicto libro, Pejorem insidiari meliori, petram explicat τὴν στεῤῥὰν καὶ ἀδιάκοπτον σοφίαν Θεὒ. Deus צוּר in Veteri Te- stamento, Christus in Novo.

Ἡ δὲ πέτρα ἦν ὁ χριστὸς.

Id est Christum præfigurabat. Non illi hoc intelligebant, sed nos intelligimus, quibus omnia ista præstruebantur. Ru- pes percussa aquam dedit, Christus ad mortem percussus Spiritum Sanctum suis obtinuit. Vide infra XII. 13. Per ipsam aquam rupes Hebræos comitabatur. Et Christus per spiri- tum nobiscum est ad finem seculi Matth. XXVIII. 20. Ut se- ptem boves & spicæ sunt septem anni Gen. XLI. 26. id est septem annos præfigurant. Vide & Apocal. XVII. 15.

Jam non de materiali rupe sermo est, sed de Christo, qui spiritualis petra est, & ita dicitur non in Novo tantum Testamento, sed etiam in Veteri Ps. CXIIX. 22. Zach. III. 9. ut hic non incommoda sit Philonis interpretatio. Quod docet tum vocis πνευματικῆς propria significatio, à qua citra causam discedendum non est; tum petræ descriptio, quæ ἀκολυθούση sequuta dicitur Israëlitas, quod de petra materiali dicere absurdum est. Ad Metonymiam autem recurrere, legibus bonæ interpretationis contrarium & valde inconveniens, quum de rupe, ex qua bibebant, dicatur, quod sequuta, vel comi- tata ipsos fuerit: Non autem bibebant ex aqua spirituali, sed ex rupe spirituali. Interprete ipso Gro- tio; tum diserta Apostoli interpretatio, qui ne ambi- geremus, quamnam petram intelligat, addit ex- presse: Petra autem illa erat Christus, ubi nequic- quam cum Calvinianis tropum in verbo substan- tivo ἦν ERAT fingit Grotius; quod plane incapax esse tropi in Stereom. verbor. Testam. Jesu Christi contra D. Johannem Bergium luculenter evicimus. Neque vero est, quod tropice hæc intelligamus, quum revera petra, è qua potabantur Israëlitæ, quæque illos ubique comitabatur, fuerit Chri- stus, quem in deserto tentasse dicuntur v. 9. Bibe- runt enim non tam ex materiali petra, quia illa mi- nime apta nata erat fundere aquam, quam è petra spirituali, tanquam è fonte largiter scaturiente, ex cujus plenitudine accipimus omnes, Joh. I. 16. cujus petræ figuram, si rupes illa materialis fuisse dicatur, non refragabimur. Nam ideo è petra ma- teriali eliciebatur aqua, non vero ex alia re, quod designatus per petram materialem Christus fuerit petra nostra pro nobis percutienda & scindenda, Zach. III. 9. quemadmodum per aquam sanguis Christi, qui è percusso ejus latere lagiter effusus est, adumbratus est, quo spiritualiter, & sacramen- taliter potamur ad vitam æternam. B. Glassius ob- servat in Gramm. S. p. 504. præpositionem ἐκ non materiam, sed causam efficientem denotare, uti alias nonnunquam. Vid. Joh. VI. 65. Matth. I. 20. Rom. XI. 36. Neq; dubium est, rectius vocem ἀκο- λυθούσης convenire Christo, qui comitatus est ubiq; Israëlitas. Syrus exposuit: quæ veniebat seu ibat cum ipsis, quam petræ materiali, quam ea voce no- tari, obsequentem fuisse, dicto Domini vocis usui haud congruit. Eandem vero, quod Thomas vult, ubique ipsos sequutam esse, ab historia alienum est. Quod agnoscit Musculus in hunc locum, cum di- cit: Biberunt de spirituali petra; avocat mentes le- gentium à petra corporali ad Christum petram spiritualem. Vnde & subdit: Petra autem erat Christus. Potest & corporea petra spiritualis vocari, propterea, quod figura fuerit spiritualis petræ. Verum quoniam addit, quæ sequebatur, intelligendum esse puto de ipso Christo, Is enim consequebatur populum in deserto, & aquas illi miraculosa scaturigine subministrabat. Goclenius: Christus, inquit, est vere petra nostra non per essentiam, sed per excellentiam κατ' ἐξοχὴν hoc est similitudine, soliditate & certitudine est supra omnem petram corpoream. Petra utique corporalis Israëlitas sequuta non est, nec aqua ipsa è petra fluens, ut Beza & Pareus volunt. Nam evanisse aquam & defecisse Ex. XVII. 6. docemur, ut & Num. XX. 21. Non autem defecisset, si aqua petrosa ubiq; sequuta eosdem fuisset. Vt taceam, quod unius illius petræ rivus per tot annos Israëlitas, per varios anfractus oberrantes sequi non potuerit naturaliter. Si autem per miraculum tale quid evenit, qui factum, quod id à Mose, Historicorum diligentissimo, commemoratum non sit. Petra ergo spiritualis, quæ ipsos comitata ubivis est, Christus erat. Quo de B. Dannhavver. in Mysteriosoph. Sect. 1. Art. VIII. §. 51. Quænam petra illa? An lapidea? At illa concomitans non fuit, sed perpetuo fixa & immobilis mansit. Fingunt quidem Hebræi aquas è petra promanantes, castra, quocunque proficiscerentur, subsequutas fuisse per canales sive ductus, quos Principes baculis suis, in terra post se tractis, fecerint, atque hinc petram, id est aquam petra promanantem, dici concomitantem. Confirmant suam opinionem ex Num. XXI. 17. Ps. LXXVIII. 20. & Ps. CV. 41. Quomodo vero hanc nobis fabulam probabunt? Fuit certe, cum defecit aqua sitientes Num. XX. 21. postquam jam ante petra percussa esset Ex. XVII. 4. nec credibile est, Israëlitas sinuosos anfractus pererrantes, non linea recta euntes, habuisse sibi aquas, per eosdem anfractus comites. Numer. XXI. v. 17. עלי באר non necessario exponitur vocative per descende puteè! Sed super puteo über den Brunnen, in Psalmis citatis aquarum effluxus traditur, nihil de anfractuosis ambagibus. Relinquitur itaque per petram concomitantem intelligi Christum: Vt τὸ ἀκολυθεῖν in sensu congregativo, non consecutivo enuncietur, ut optime è Franc. Junii parallel. exponit Dn. D. Glassius l. 3. Philol. tr. 6. p. m. 551. Neque obstare verbum ἀκολυθεῖν agnovit etiam Junius l. 11. parall. 36. Est enim verbum ἀκολυθεῖν non solum sequi præeuntem, (ut vulgo solet accipi) verum etiam generaliter significat simul iter facere cum altero sive præeas, sive sequaris, sive te comitem ad latus euntis adjunxeris. Factum enim est ex particula α quæ apud Græcos non infrequenter significationem habet τοῦ ὁμοῦ simul & nomine κέλευθος via, iter. Vnde primaria hæc & generalis significatio profecta est. Syrus emphatice reddidit: Petra autem illa ipse erat Christus. Non ergo de significatione tantum accipi debet. Vere erat Christus petra spiritualis: Non vero tantum significabat petra spiritualis Christum.

Nullum profecto exemplum proferri potest, quod EST significative vel figurative in propositione tertii adjecti, vel cum copulandum est, accipiatur, & quod significat exponi debeat. In illo Genes. XLI. 26. non habetur verbum EST, ideoque non potest σημαντικῶς explicari. Simpliciter dicitur: Vaccæ septem, septem anni. Quod non est, id modificari nequit. Cur non subaudire liceat, septem vaccæ intelliguntur, si quid subaudiendum? Qualis ellipsis etiam est in loco Apoc. XVII. 15. Aquæ multæ populi multi (intelligendæ) sunt, ut ita opus non sit, ut verbum εἰσί contra naturam suam, quum copula sit, vexetur.

Si dicas, non omnes, qui aqua e petra fruebantur, in Christum credidisse, eumque pro petra salutis habuisse: Distinguendum inter bibitionem ipsam, & bibendi intentionem. Etsi enim infideles ipsam intentionem typice bibendi ex aqua petræ non habuerint; tamen quia revera biberunt è petra, quæ typus Christi erat, omnes bibisse potum spiritualem recte dici possunt, &, uti B. Hülfemannus habet, participarunt omnes omnino Israëlitæ de petra spirituali Christo, quantum ad communionem gratiæ prævenientis, quæ nequaquam exinde negatur, quod plerique non crediderint Ebr. IV. 2. in plerisque Deus beneplacitum non habuerit, hic v. 5. Nam quod convivæ omnes ad nuptias vocantur, quod omnibus eadem edulia spiritualia proponuntur Matth. XXII. 4. hoc utique beneficium est gratiæ Christi, cujus quidem communio nequaquam denegari potest non indutis veste nuptiali, v. 11. Mylius aliam adhuc vocis ἀκολυθῦσα adfert significationem. Si tamen, inquit, translato sensu hoc ad petram referre cuipiam libuerit, ut ἀκολυθῦσα vocetur, quæ dicto Domini fuit obsequens, & ad fundendas aquas obedientem sese præbuit: equidem non morose refragabimur, duntaxat illibata constet sententia Paulina, Israëlitas omnes, in quali differentia positos, promissue tamen eandem spiritualem ex mysteriis nostris, analogica saltem & typica ratione, haud absimilem escam manducasse, eundem spiritualem potum, & de eadem spirituali petra bibisse, hoc est, summorum mysteriorum, adeoque summi ipsius boni, Christi videlicet, typis luculentissimis non caruisse, ita, ut dummodo vera fides ac pietas accessisset, nihil ipsis vel ad dignitatem, vel felicitatem summam defuturum fuerit, adeoque mysteriorum dignitate nobis fuerint vicinissimi. Præstat autem superior explicatio. Apostolum enim non loqui fatetur ipse B. Mylius f. 221. de simplici aut naturali petra (de qua utique dici non poterat, quod esset aut fuerit Christus: sed eundem duntaxat notavit) sed de spirituali petra.

## 10:5
Vers. 5. Ἀλλ’ ἐν τοῖς πλείοσιν αὐτῶν οὐκ εὐδόκησεν ὁ Θεός. Εὐδόκησεν רצה. GOD did not have pleasure in the very greatest part of them. The same will happen to many Christians who do not make good use of great gifts given to them.

Κατεστρώθησαν γὰρ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ. He used the very word which is in the Greek of Num. XIV. 16. Κατέσρωσεν αὐτὸς ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, see the same there 29:32. XXVI. 64. 65. Ps. LXXVIII. 33. This destruction of theirs is an image of eternal destruction.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἀλλ’ ἐν τοῖς πλείοσιν αὐτῶν οὐκ εὐδόκησεν ὁ Θεός. Εὐδόκησεν רצה Multo maximam eorum partem DEUS gratam non habuit. Idem eveniet multis Christianis, qui magnis datis bene non utuntur.

Κατεστρώθησαν γὰρ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ. Vocem ipsam usurpavit, quæ est in Græco Num. XIV. 16. Κατέσρωσεν αὐτὸς ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, Vide ibidem 29:32. XXVI. 64. 65. Ps. LXXVIII. 33. Hoc illorum exitium æterni exitii imago est.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. Ταῦτα δὲ τύποι ἡμῶν ἐγενήθησαν. A type is a rough delineation of a thing, from which a more perfect image is made. Hence ἐν τύπῳ among Aristotle, in a rough mode of teaching. Opposed to it is τὸ ἀκριβὲς, τὸ λεπτομερές. See Rom. V. 14. Justin also uses the word τύποι in this sense in his dialogue with Trypho.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἐπιθυμητὰς κακῶν, καθὼς κἀκεῖνοι ἐπεθύμησαν. Ἐπιθυμηταὶ κακῶν are those who, not content with necessities, ardently desire more, like those Israelites Num. XI. 4. Ps. LXXVII. 29. Ἐπιθυμηταὶ מתאוים. This again touches the Corinthian revelers.

So also the blessed Balduinus holds: He refers to the history of Num. XI. and Exod. XVI. where it is read how the Israelites, weary of Manna, that heavenly bread, began to cry: Who will give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish which we used to eat in Egypt, etc. Where indeed the appetite in itself is not evil, nor is the thing which they desired evil: but concupiscence of evil things happens by accident, because of ingratitude and nausea for the divine benefit which God had provided for them through the ministration of the bread of Angels. The Apostle aptly applies this example to the Corinthians, who desired idolatrous feasts, and in this kind betrayed their character, that they wished to serve their gluttony and belly, the luxuries of foods, more than GOD and the studies of religion and the exercises of piety.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ταῦτα δὲ τύποι ἡμῶν ἐγενήθησαν. Typus est rudis rei delineatio, de qua fit imago perfectior. Inde ἐν τύπῳ apud Aristotelem, rudi docendi modo. Opponitur ei τὸ ἀκριβὲς, τὸ λεπτομερές. Vide Rom. V. 14. Utitur voce τύποι in hoc sensu & Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἐπιθυμητὰς κακῶν, καθὼς κἀκεῖνοι ἐπεθύμησαν. Ἐπιθυμηταὶ κακῶν sunt, qui necessariis non contenti plura ardenter desiderant, ut illi Israëlitæ Num. XI. 4. Ps. LXXVII. 29. Ἐπιθυμηταὶ מתאוים. Hoc rursum tangit Corinthios epulatores.

Sic etiam habet B. Balduinus: Respicit ad historiam Num. XI. & Exod. XVI. ubi legitur, quomodo Israëlitæ Mannæ, panis illius cœlestis pertæsi cœperint clamare: Quis dabit nobis ad vescendum carnes? Recordamur piscium, quos comedebamus in Ægypto &c. Ubi non quidem appetitus in se malus est, neque res quam appetebant, mala: Fit autem concupiscentia malarum rerum per Accidens, propter ingratitudinem & nauseam divini beneficii, quod Deus ipsis per ministrationem panis Angelorum præstiterat. Apposite hoc exemplum applicat Apostolus ad Corinthios, qui convivia idolatrica appetebant, & hoc in genere prodebant ingenium suum, quod magis gulæ & ventri, lauti- tiis ciborum, quam DEO & religionis studiis exercitiisque pietatis inservire vellent.

## 10:7
Vers. 7. Μηδὲ εἰδωλολάτραι γίνεσθε, καθώς τινες αὐτῶν.

Hence he touches those who ate of things sacrificed to idols, which was either the worship of an idol, or a step toward the worship of an idol.

Ὥσπερ γέγραπται, ἐκάθισεν ὁ λαὸς τῷ φαγεῖν κὶ πιεῖν, καὶ ἀνέστησαν παίζειν.

The very words of the LXX. of Exodus XXXII. where we said that παίζειν is to salute, for which Virgil also said to play; εὐφραίνεσθαι Acts VII. 41. The people sat down, namely just as you recline. To dance, as you also do.

Since idolaters are expressly named by the Apostle, the idolatrous act in Ex. XXXII, by which they worshipped the golden calf, is looked back upon, even though those words only concerning the banquet prepared from things sacrificed to idols were brought in from the Mosaic text because of the analogous transgression among the Corinthians. Calvin rightly executes this in his Commentary on this place: This passage is rightly explained by few; for they understand that intemperance was the cause of the people's lasciviousness: Just as we say in the common proverb: After a full belly, dancing follows. But Moses speaks of a sacred banquet, that is, one which they celebrated in the worship of an idol. A feast, therefore, and games will be two appendages of idolatry. For it was customary for the people of God, as well as for the superstitious, to add a feast to the immolation, as a part of divine worship: At which it was permitted for no profane or unclean person to be present. The nations also instituted sacred games for their idols, by the rite of which the Israelites undoubtedly worshipped their calf. For this is the perversity of human nature, to attribute to God whatever pleases itself. And so the Gentiles fell into such madness that they believed their gods were delighted by the foulest spectacles, by unchaste dances, by the filthiness of words, and by every kind of obscenity; consequently, in imitation of them, the Israelite people, after the solemn feast was finished, rose up to celebrate games, so that nothing might be lacking for the worship of the idol. This is the genuine and simple sense. But it is asked here, why the Apostle mentions the feast and the games rather than the adoration? For this idolatry was the head: but those former things were only accessories. Indeed, he chooses what was most appropriate for the Corinthians, for it is not likely that they frequented the assemblies of the impious in order to prostrate themselves before idols; but they participated in their banquets, instituted in honor of demons, nor did they flee from the impious ceremonies which were symbols of idolatry: Not without cause, therefore, does the Apostle testify that that in which they were sinning is expressly condemned by God, etc. Junius has similar things in his parallels, ch. XXXVII: Paul took pains on purpose to extract those words from the whole history which would most agree with the argument and the question that is being dealt with here. Now, the matter concerns things sacrificed to idols, the use of which was mostly such that they were not only consumed in public feasting, but were also joined with revelries, games, choruses, and dances: Just as the Israelites had done at that time. Which things are more appropriate than the ordinary gloss; To play, that is to adore, which is similar to the play of children. For childhood is easily inclined to play. But what is so similar to childish play as to adore idols.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Μηδὲ εἰδωλολάτραι γίνεσθε, καθώς τινες αὐτῶν.

Hinc tangit eos, qui idolothytis vescebantur, quod aut idoli cultus erat, aut gradus ad cultum idoli.

Ὥσπερ γέγραπται, ἐκάθισεν ὁ λαὸς τῷ φαγεῖν κὶ πιεῖν, καὶ ἀνέστησαν παίζειν.

Ipsa verba LXX. Exodi XXXII. ubi παίζειν esse diximus salutare, pro quo & Virgilius dixit ludere; εὐφραίνεσθαι Actor. VII. 41. Sedit populus, nempe sicut vos accumbitis. Ad saltandum, ut & vos facitis.

Quum idololatrae expresse nominentur ab Apostolo, actus idololatricus Ex. XXXII. quo colebant vitulum aureum respicitur, etsi verba tantum illa de convivio ex idolothytis apparato, ob analogam inter Corinthios praevaricationem e textu Mosaico adducta sint. Recte haec exequitur Calvinus in Comm. ad hunc locum : Locus hic a paucis rite exponitur; intelligunt enim, intemperantiam populo causam lasciviendi fuisse: Sicuti vulgari proverbio dicimus: Alvo bene referta succedere choreas. At Moses de sacro convivio loquitur, hoc est, quod in idoli cultum celebrabant. Epulum ergo & lusus duae erunt idololatriae appendices. Fuit enim tam populo Dei, quam superstitiosis usitatum, adjungere immolationi epulum, tanquam partem divini cultus: Cui interesse nullis profanis aut immundis liceret. Sacros etiam ludos gentes idolis suis instituebant, quorum ritu procul dubio Israëlitae vitulum suum coluerunt. Haec enim est humani ingenii protervia, quicquid sibi arridet, Deo affingere. Itaq; huc prolapsi sunt dementiae gentiles, ut foedissimis spectaculis, ut impudicis saltationibus, ut verborum spurcitia, & omne genus obscoenitatibus, Deos suos oblectari crederent, eorum proinde imitatione populus Israëliti- cus, peracto solenni epulo surrexit ad ludos celebrandos, ne quid deesset ad idoli cultum. Hic genuinus & simplex est sensus. Sed quaeritur hic, cur epuli potius & ludorum meminerit Apostolus, quam adorationis? Hac enim idololatria caput erat: Priora autem illa tantum accessiones. Nempe eligit, quod maxime Corinthiis congruebat, neque enim verisimile est, conventus impiorum frequentasse, ut coram idolis se prosternerent; sed communicabant eorum conviviis, in Daemonum honorem institutis, nec fugiebant impias ceremonias, qua idololatriae symbola erant: Non ergo absque causa testatur Apostolus, id, in quo peccabant, a Deo nominatim damnari &c. Similia habet Junius in parallelis c. XXXVII. de industria operam dedit Paulus, ut ea verba ex tota historia excerperet, quae cum argumento & quaestione ea, qua hic agitur, maxime convenirent. Agitur autem de idolothytis, quorum usus fuit maxime, ut non solum convivatione publica consumerentur, sed etiam biteriis, ludis, choreis, & saltationibus conjungerentur: Prout in illo tempore Israëlitae fecerant. Quae magis congruunt, quam gloffa ordinaria; Ludere, id est adorare, quod ludo puerorum simile. Facilis namque est ad lusum pueritia. Quid autem lusui puerili tam simile est, quam idola adorare.

## 10:8
Verse 8. Μηδὲ πορνέυωμεν. Thus Paul is accustomed, when he says something odious, to use the first person plural by way of communion.

Καθώς τινες ἀυτῶν ἐπόρνευσαν. Πορνέυειν here clearly means to have relations with women outside of marriage. In the Greek of Num. XXV. 1. Ἐβεβηλώθη ὁ λαὸς ἐκπορνεῦσαι εἰς τὰς θυγατέρας Μωάβ. לִזְנוֹת This refers to that man contaminated by incest.

Καὶ ἔπεσον ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ εἰκοσιτρεῖς χιλιάδες. In the Hebrew and Greek of Numbers, chapter XXV, verse 9, it is twenty-four thousand. But understand a thousand killed by Phinehas and his companions; but twenty-three thousand by a plague sent divinely.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Μηδὲ πορνέυωμεν. Sic solet Paulus, ubi aliquid odiosum dicit, uti plurali primae personae κατὰ κοίνωσιν.

Καθώς τινες ἀυτῶν ἐπόρνευσαν. Πορνέυειν manifeste hic est cum foeminis extra nuptias rem habere. In Graeco Num. XXV. 1. Ἐβεβηλώθη ὁ λαὸς ἐκπορνεῦσαι εἰς τὰς θυγατέρας Μωάβ. לִזְנוֹת Tangitur hic ille incestu contaminatus.

Καὶ ἔπεσον ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ εἰκοσιτρεῖς χιλιάδες. In Hebraeo & Graeco Numer. cap. XXV. vers. 9. εἴκοσι τέσσαρες χιλιάδες. Sed intellige mille occisos a Phinee & sodalibus ejus; viginti vero & tria millia plaga divinitus immissa.

## 10:9
Vers. 9. Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted.

It must by all means be read, μηδὲ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν θεὸν, as it is in that most ancient Manuscript. The error was committed from the abbreviations for θεὸν & χριστὸν. Christ is the name of a man. Exπειράζειν is נסה Deut. VI. 16. The Hebrews did this often; but especially at that time, of which the narrative is, Num. XXI. 5. & following. To tempt God is to make an experiment, how far his patience will go. The authors of schisms are touched upon here.

A rash emendation of all the Codices from a single Manuscript, and a mere conjecture or suspicion, which was neither proven—namely, that the names were expressed only by abbreviations—nor, if it were proven, does it avail to teach that a change of abbreviations was made. Although indeed the name of Christ is not merely the name of a man, yet it includes his humanity at the same time, because τὸ συναμφότερον is understood, as Damascenus says: Yet it is the same person who was tempted by the Israelites; whether he comes under the name of the Son of God, or of wisdom, or of the Word, or of the Angel, in whom is the name of the Lord, or is called Christ, or Jesus Christ, as the Apostle testifies Heb. XIII. 8. yesterday, today, the same also for ever. Christ was acknowledged and believed in before he was made man, and he is anointed, because by his knowledge he justified even the faithful of the Old Testament Is. LIII. 11. ch. XLI. 23. 24. 25. Jer. XXIII. 6. Although indeed the pronoun αὐτὸν is not repeated, which the Socinians urge, (except that Faber Stapulensis, Cajetan, and Erasmus testify that they saw copies which have Καθὼς καί τινες αὐτὸν ἐπείρασαν) yet the reason of ordinary grammatical construction teaches that the subject tempted is to be repeated ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, since the pronoun αὐτὸν was omitted on account of the concurrence of the genitive plural αὐτῶν. And that he who led them through Moses was tempted by the Israelites is most well-known from the scriptures. But that the people spoke of Christ is evident from ch. III. & IV. Exod. & ch. XIII. 19. ch. XXIII. 20. and also Is. LXIV. v. 9. Moreover, temptation is not only of patience and goodness; but also a trial of divine power and truth Num. XI. 23. ch. XIV. v. 22.

And were destroyed by the serpents.

By those fiery serpents; thus also those who irritate God become the prey of the Devil.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Μηδὲ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν χριστὸν, καθὼς καί τινες αὐτῶν ἐπείρασαν.

Omnino legendum est, μηδὲ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν θεὸν, quo- modo est in vetustissimo illo Manuscripto. Error commis- sus ex notis θεὸν & χριστὸν. Christus nomen est hominis. Ex- πειράζειν est נסה Deut. VI. 16. fecere id sæpe Hebræi; sed eximie eo tempore, cujus narratio est, Num. XXI. 5. & se- quentibus. Tentare Deum est experimentum capere, quo- usque itura sit ejus patientia. Tanguntur hic schismatum autores.

Temeraria emendatio Codicum omnium ex unico Manuscripto, meraque conjectura vel su- spicione, quæ nec probata fuit, per notas scil. tan- tum nomina expressa fuisse, nec si probetur, nota- rum commutationem factam esse, docere valet. Etsi vero Christi nomen non quidem tantum hominis nomen sit, humanitatem tamen simul includat, quia τὸ συναμφότερον νοεῖται, dicente Damasceno: Eadem tamen persona est, quæ tentata ab Israëlitis fuit; sive Filii Dei, aut sapientiæ, aut Verbi, aut An- geli, in quo est nomen Domini, nomine veniat, sive Christus vocetur, aut Jesus Christus, teste Aposto- lo Ebr. XIII. 8. heri, hodie, idem & in secula. Agni- tus & creditus fuit Christus, antequam homo fa- ctus, & unctus est, quia per cognitionem suam justi- ficavit etiam veteris Testamenti fideles Es. LIII. 11. cap. XLI. 23. 24. 25. Jer. XXIII. 6. Quanquam vero Pronomen αὐτὸν non repetatur, quod urgent So- ciniani, (nisi quod Faber Stapul. Cajetanus & E- rasmus testentur sibi visa exemplaria, quæ habeant Καθὼς καί τινες αὐτὸν ἐπείρασαν) Ordinariæ tamen constructionis Grammaticæ ratio docet, subje- ctum tentatum ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repetendum esse, cum Pronomen αὐτὸν propter concursum Genit. plura- lis αὐτῶν omissum sit. Et tentatum esse ab Israëlitis eum, qui per Mosen eos duxit, notissimum est è scripturis. Christum autem populum dixisse ex cap. III. & IV. Exod. & cap. XIII. 19. cap. XXIII. 20. nec non Es. LXIV. v. 9. constat. Tentatio autem non est tantum patientiæ & bonitatis; sed etiam poten- tiæ & veritatis divinæ probatio Num. XI. 23. cap. XIV. v. 22.

Καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ὄφεων ἀπώλοντο.

Ab illis ignitis serpentibus; sic & qui Deum irritant, præ- da fiunt Diaboli.

## 10:10
Vers. 10. Neither murmur ye.

Γογγύζειν is to speak against superiors, as can be seen in Num. XIV. 1. Those who were speaking less than decently about this Apostle are touched upon here.

And were destroyed by the destroyer.

In the book of Num. XIV. 33. they are said to be struck and slaughtered before God: But it is the custom of God to execute his judgments through Angels, as can be seen 2. Sam. XXIV. 16. 1. Kings XIX. 35. Eccles. V. 5. Thus also he dispenses certain benefits through Angels John V. 4. The Angel ὀλοθρευτὴς, or ὁ ὀλοθρεύων Hebr. XI. 28. & Sap. XVIII. 22. 25. It is he who in the book of Tobit is אשמודו, from שמר is ὀλοθρεύων: משחית Ezech. XII. 23. Jer. II. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Μηδὲ γογγύζετε.

Γογγύζειν est obloqui superioribus, ut videre est Num. XIV. 1. Tanguntur hic illi, qui de Apostolo hoc minus de- center loquebantur.

Καὶ ἀπώλοντο ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀλοθρευτοῦ.

In libro Num. XIV. 33. dicuntur percussi & mactati coram Deo: Sed Dei mos est judicia sua per Angelos exequi, ut videre est 2. Sam. XXIV. 16. 1. Reg. XIX. 35. Eccles. V. 5. Sic & beneficia quædam per Angelos dispensat Joh. V. 4. Angelus ὀλοθρευτὴς, aut ὁ ὀλοθρεύων Hebr. XI. 28. & Sap. XVIII. 22. 25. Est qui in Tobiæ libro אשמודו, à שמר est ὀλοθρεύων: משחית Ezech. XII. 23. Jer. II. 30.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples.

The Manuscript has τυπικῶς instead of τύποι. They were prefigurations, rough outlines, of what happened to them. There, temporary things; here, eternal. The Hebrews say אבות סימן לבני The fathers are a sign for the children.

It was written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

For in all the actions of the ancient age, God always had before His eyes the times of the Messiah, in which not only prophecies, but also all figures were to be fulfilled. See what we have brought to this matter from Justin, Tertullian, and others on Matt. I. 22. τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων is the same as πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου Gal. IV. 4. πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν Eph. I. 10. that is, that time after which no new law or greater prophecy was to be expected. Νουθεσία אזהרה.

Others commonly take it concerning the nearness of the end of the ages or of the universe. Therefore, the fullness of time and of the seasons seems to be one thing; but the ends of the ages is another. We allow, however, that one may abound in his own sense here too. Grotius's explanation appears not inappropriate on account of the preceding words: And others also explain it thus, that the ends of the

ages are spoken of concerning the time which was to follow the coming of Christ in the flesh, because Christ fulfilled all things formerly predicted by the Prophets, and nothing remains to be expected except His return for judgment, according to Peter saying in 1 Epist. IV. 7 that the end of all things is at hand, and John in 1 Epist. ch. II. 18 that it is the last hour, and James ch. V. 8 that the coming of the Lord draws near: See also Acts II. 17, Heb. I. 1, ch. IX. 26, ch. X. 25, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τύποι συνέβαινον ἐκείνοις.

Manuscriptus pro τύποι habet τυπικῶς. Erant, quæ ipsis evenêre præfigurationes, rudia lineamenta. Ibi res tempo- rariæ, hic æternæ. Dicunt Hebræi אבות סימן לבני Patres documentum filiis.

Ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν εἰς ὃς τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντησεν.

Nam in omnibus actionibus prisci seculi Deus semper ob oculos habebat tempora Messiæ, in quibus non vaticinia tantum, sed & figuræ omnes implerentur. Vide quæ ad hanc rem attulimus ex Justino, Tertulliano, & aliis ad Matt. I. 22. τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων est idem quod πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου Gal. IV. 4. πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν Eph. I. 10. id est tempus il- lud, post quod nulla nova lex aut major Prophetia erat ex- pectanda. Νουθεσία אזהרה.

Alii communiter de propinquitate finis seculo- rum vel universi accipiunt. Aliud itaque videtur esse πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου & τῶν καιρῶν; Aliud vero τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων. Permittimus tamen hic que- que abundare sensu suo. Non inconcinna ob verba præcedentia apparet Grotiana explicatio: Et exponunt alii quoque ita, quod τὰ τέλη τῶν

αἰώνων dicantur de tempore, quod sequuturum adventum Christi in carnem, quia Christus omnia complevit, per Prophetas olim prædicta, neque quicquam expectandum restat, nisi reditus ipsius ad judicium juxta Petrum dicentem 1. Epist. IV. 7. rerum omnium finem imminere, ac Johannem 1. Epist. cap. II. 18. esse horam novissimam, & Jacobum cap. V. 8. adventum Domini appropinquare: Vide etiam Actor. II. 17. Ebr. I. 1. cap. IX. 26. cap. X. 25. 37.

## 10:12
Ver. 12. Wherefore let him who thinks he stands.

The present for the future, that is, he who thinks he will always stand.

Let him take heed lest he fall.

Let him see to it that he does not fall, that is, let him beware for himself, fearing whatever can happen, Rom. XI. 20.

Most take it as a general exhortation, by which they present the immediate sense, or one deduced as a corollary from the preceding; or as a proposition by way of conclusion, since the Apostle wished to dissuade from carnal security by the example of the Israelites, lest we fall from the grace of God. Since even those who stand by faith ought to take heed solicitously lest they fall, and work out their salvation with fear and trembling, Phil. II. 12, Prov. XXVIII. 1, Job IX. 28. Which possibility of falling, and caution, does not conflict with the certainty of divine promises, or the full assurance of our faith: Because the promises are not absolute; but include the hypothesis of means, of diligent meditation on the divine word, of devout prayer, and of perpetual vigilance: Nor does full assurance exclude filial fear, but rather doubt concerning the grace of God, and servile fear. Which is to be observed both against the Papists' dogma of the desperation of the uncertainty of grace, and against the absolute decrees of the Calvinists, the absolute certainty and the indefectibility of the faithful. More specifically, however, the blessed Hülsemann takes it, as if these things were said to those wanton and bold eaters of idols: he who thinks he stands firmly, let him take heed lest he fall.

Who also explains those things which follow concerning human temptation in this way. Although this maxim may be extended even to more serious temptations sent by GOD or the Devil: yet it speaks properly and adequately of the temptation arising from the use of things sacrificed to idols, and the usurpation of similar indifferent things, which are indeed lawful, but sometimes dangerous. But we acquiesce in the common explanation, which the blessed Hunnius handed down as follows: He infers from the premises that the Corinthians must take pains not to be secure, as if the war were already won, or as if less danger and fewer struggles remained under the kingdom of the exhibited Messiah. For the greater the grace that has been obtained under the Gospel, the more certain and atrocious are the punishments that threaten profane despisers, and the closer they have come to the boundaries of eternity, the more they should remember that Satan rages more horribly and lays snares for the eternal salvation of men.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὥστε ὁ δοκῶν ἑστάναι.

Præsens pro futuro, id est, qui se semper staturum putat.

Βλεπέτω μὴ πέσῃ.

Videat, ne cadat, id est, caveat sibi, timendo quicquid evenire potest, Rom. XI. 20.

Plerique accipiunt ceu generalem adhortationem, qua sensum immediatum, seu πορισματικῶς deductam è præcedentibus; seu per συμ- πέρασμα propositionem exhibentem, cum à securitate carnali dehortatri voluerit Apostolus exemplo Israëlitarum, ne gratia Dei excidamus. Siquidem etiam qui per fidem stant, solicite debeant cavere, ne cadant, & cum timore ac tre- more salutem operari, Phil. II. 12. Prov. XXVIII. 1. Job. IX. 28. Quæ possibilitas casus, & cautio non pugnat cum certitudine promissionum divinarum, aut πληροφορίᾳ fidei nostræ: Quia promissiones non absolute sunt; sed hypothesin mediorum includunt, sedulæ meditationis verbi divini, devotæ orationis, & perpetuæ vigilantiæ: Nec πληροφορία excludit timorem filialem, sed dubitationem de gratia DEI, & timorem servilem. Quod tum contra Pontificiorum desperationem incertitudinis gratiæ dogma, tum contra absoluta Calvinianorum decreta, absolutam certitudinem & ἀναποστασίαν fidelium, observandum. Specialius tamen accipit B. Hülsemannus, quasi hæc protervis & audacibus illis idolorum comestoribus dicta sint: qui sibi videtur firmiter consistere, videat, ne cadat.

Qui etiam ea, quæ sequuntur, de tentatione humana ita explicat. Quanquam hæc gnome ad graviores etiam tentatione à DEO vel Diabolo immissas extendi possit: Proprie tamen & adæquate loquitur de tentatione nascente ex usu idolothytorum, & usurpatione similium adiaphororum, quæ licita quidem sunt, sed periculosa quandoque. Sed acquiescimus communi explicationi, quam ita tradidit B. Hunnius: Infert ex præmissis, dandam esse operam Corinthiis, ut non sint securi, quasi debellatum jam sit, aut quasi minus periculi, minus etiam certaminum restet sub regno exhibiti Messiæ.
