Quo enim major obtigerit gratia sub Evangelio, eo certiores & atrociores imminere pœnas profanis contemptoribus, & quo propius ad æternitatum terminos devenerint, eo meminerint horribilius sævire Satanam, & insidias struere sempiternæ hominum saluti.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. Πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος.

Because they could think that they had already had a test of their own strength, because they had endured certain inconveniences on account of the Gospel; he shows that those things are light compared to the evils which could come upon them hereafter. Πειρασμὸς ἀνθρώπινος is a common temptation, frequent among men. Thus ῥάβδος ἀνδρῶν and ἁφαὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων are common, frequent chastisements, 2 Sam. VII. 14. Thus γραφὴ ἀνθρώπου is a style which is in use, Isa. VIII. 1. Thus ἀνθρώπινον λέγω is I speak in the manner of the common people, Rom. VI. 19. Thus Levit. VI. 3. ὧν ἐὰν ποιήσῃ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, that is, of those things which are frequently done. You have not yet resisted unto blood, says the writer to the Hebrews XII. 4. εἴληφε you have caught.

Human temptation is rightly explained as common and lighter, so that it may be more easily overcome by man. Such as they were, which they had perhaps sustained on account of the Gospel. Some wish it to be called human in opposition to divine and diabolical; because the human arises from the weakness of the flesh; the Divine comes to pass through the sending of a cross; the Diabolical through seduction to a fault. But here temptation is not understood as that which is a fault toward evil, since it is rather probationary, and is sent by God. And therefore it cannot be explained concerning temptation to such crimes, which can easily be overcome or declined. Therefore Cornelius à Lapide does not rightly explain: Be, O Corinthians, tempted and solicited to schisms, to litigations, to luxury and Venus, to idols and idol-meats; yet be constant: Because these temptations, which seize and occupy you, are common and human, which you will easily overcome, if you wish. For this temptation is not from God, but from the Devil: Therefore Cornelius corrects (but rashly) the Greek text, although he acknowledges it to agree with the Syriac and the reading of Chrysostom, and in place of εἴληφε he substitutes εἰληφέτω in the Imperative: as if he were to say: when some such temptation creeps into the mind, do not cherish it, and seize it so that it gradually increases, and becomes insuperable. But we here commit Cornelius to Estius, who has it thus: In the Complutensian and Royal books, and some others as well ancient as recent, and in the Roman Missal it is read apprehendit, with the third vowel. Which reading is more sincere. For the Greek codices read εἴληφε, he has taken, a verb of the past tense. The Greek commentators and the Syriac version also agree. But also in Cyprian lib. 3. testim. c. 91. for the verb apprehendit is read occupavit. Ambrosiaster and Primasius in their Commentaries do indeed read it in the hortatory or optative mode, apprehendat: Likewise Augustine lib. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte cap. 9. and the author of the questions of the Old and New Testament quest. 99. But Sedulius criticizes and corrects that reading, writing thus: Because some, not understanding the Apostle's testimony, have placed the Optative mode for the Indicative. Otherwise, his exposition sufficiently argues that Pelagius also read the Indicative. This is Estius on the reading. As for the sense of the words, Estius easily agrees with Cornelius. For although he acknowledges as probable that one concerning persecutions and inconveniences to be endured for the faith, which is Cajetan's, he nevertheless prefers the opinion of those who think Paul is speaking of temptation which is from the flesh, e.g., of gluttony tempting one to eat idol-meats. B. Hieronymus Wellerus, with B. Glassius praising him in Exeg. Epist. supra Dom. IX. Trinit. page 65. properly calls those human temptations which arise from human infirmity, such as temptations against the second table, such as being inflamed with hatred, envy, anger, desire for vengeance, etc. But spiritual ones, which are placed above and outside the intellect of the human mind, namely those internal fears and terrors, such as the temptation concerning the rejection and denial of Christ and the Gospel; likewise concerning the affectation of divinity and the like. For there are very few who understand these temptations; fewer who have tasted them; very few who have truly felt them. For they do not fall upon the common people, but only upon those who are endowed with singular gifts and have most tender consciences. This is B. Wellerus. Which distinction, however much it may not be lacking in its foundation. Nevertheless, I doubt whether it fits this place. B. Glassius indeed seems to apply the same here l. c. page 58. Temptation has not taken you except human, as if he were to say, you are so languid, tepid, weak, and incurious about spiritual things, that you can scarcely suffer and overcome a human and easily surmountable temptation and solicitation to sins, being altogether about to be overcome and to fall, as far as in you lies, if a more than human, that is, a Diabolical temptation were sent to you. He adds however later on page 65. It can also be said that the word humana alludes antithetically to Diabolical temptations, which God in his holy counsel allows certain children of his grace to be exercised by, which Paul calls the fiery darts of the wicked one Eph. VI. 16. and which he himself had more than sufficiently experienced 2. Cor. XII. 17. And the same observes that the argument is treated in Heb. XII. 3. seqq. where indeed it is a matter of temptations of the cross sent by God, but not of the temptation of the flesh. You have not yet resisted unto blood. Paul seems to look to temptations of this kind also in this place, which are indeed sent by God, but are human, that is, not above the strength of the faithful, and easy to bear, such as were among the Israelites the lack of desired foods, of flesh and fish, for which cause they became impatient Num. XI. 4. and ate of idol-meats with the Midianites Num. XXV. 1. whence they fell into fornication: The lack of bread and water, and other foods besides Manna, and the leading through long and difficult ways. Num. XXI. 5. on account of which they were rebellious against God: The terrors of the explorers of the land of Canaan concerning the giant sons of Enakim, on account of which they murmured against Moses and Aaron Num. XIV. 1. seqq. The longer absence of Moses from the people, on account of which they erected a golden calf for themselves Exod. XXXII. Since therefore only such human temptations have occurred to the Corinthians, and far graver ones could happen to them, the Apostle warns that those who stand should carefully beware, lest by chance they fall, when the same temptations press in. He comforts the faithful at the same time with divine goodness, assistance, and readiness of deliverance.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος.

Quia putare poterant, se jam virium suarum habuisse experimentum, quod incommoda quædam ob Evangelium pertulerant; ostendit levia illa esse præ iis malis, quæ posthac ipsis supervenire possent. Πειρασμὸς ἀνθρώπινος est vulgaris tentatio, frequens inter homines. Sic ῥάβδος ἀνδρῶν & ἁφαὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων sunt castigationes communes, frequentes 2. Sam. VII. 1. Sic γραφὴ ἀνθρώπου stylus, qui in usu est Esa. VIII. 14. Sic ἀνθρώπινον λέγω loquor vulgi more Rom. VI. 19. Sic Levit. VI. 3. ὧν ἐὰν ποιήσῃ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, id est, eorum quæ frequenter fiunt. Nondum ad sanguinem restitistis, ait scriptor ad Hebræos XII. 4. εἴληφε deprehendis.

Tentatio humana recte explicatur vulgaris ac levior, ut ab homine facilius superari possit. Quales erant, quas ob Evangelium forte sustinuerant. Nonnulli humanam dici volunt in oppositione ad divinam & diabolicam; quod humana ex imbe- cillitate carnis oriatur; Divina per immissio- nem crucis fiat; Diabolica per seductionem ad delictum. Sed hic tentatio non intelligitur, quæ ad malum culpa est, quum potius probatoria sit, & à Deo immittatur. Ideoque non potest expli- cari de tentatione ad talia crimina, quæ facile su- perari queant, vel declinari. Non ergo recte Cornelius à Lapide exponit: Esto, ô Corinthii, ten- temini & solicitemini ad schismata, ad litigia, ad luxum & Venerem, ad idola & idolothyta; constan- tes tamen estote: Quia hæ tentationes, quæ vos ap- prehendunt & occupant, communes sunt & huma- næ, quas facile, si velitis, vincetis. Hæc enim ten- tatio à Deo non est, sed à Diabolo: Ideo corrigit Cornelius, (sed temere) textum Græcum, etsi cum Syriaco & Chrysostomi lectione convenire agno- scat, & loco εἴληφε substituit εἰληφέτω in Impe- rativo: quasi dicat: cum tentatio talis aliqua in animum irrepit, nolite eam fovere, & a: pre- hendere ita ut sensim increscat, fiatque insupera- bilis. Sed committimus hic Cornelium cum Estio, qui sic habet: In libris Complutensibus, ac Regiis, aliisque nonnullis tam vetustis, quam re- centioribus, atque in Missali Romano legitur ap- prehendit, cum tertia vocali. Quæ lectio sincerior est. Nam Græci codices legunt εἴληφε cepit ver- bo præteriti temporis. Consentiunt & Græci tra- ctatores, & versio Syriaca. Sed & apud Cyprianum lib. 3. testim. c. 91. pro verbo apprehendit legitur oc- cupavit. Legunt quidem exhortandi sive optan- di modo apprehendat Ambrosiafter & Primasius in Commentariis: Item Augustinus lib. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte cap. 9. & autor quæstionum veteris & Novi Testamenti quæst. 99. Verum reprehen- dit & corrigit eam lectionem Sedulius, ita scri- bens: Quod Apostoli testimonium non intelligentes quidam posuerunt pro Indicativo Optativum mo- dum. Alioqui Pelagium quoque Indicativum legisse, satis arguit ejus expositio. Hæc Estius de lectione. Quantum vero ad sensum verborum, Cornelio facile consentit Estius. Quanquam enim probabilem agnoscat illam de persecutionibus & in- commodis ob fidem exantlandis, quæ Cajetani est, præfert tamen illorum sententiam, qui putant Paulum loqui de tentatione, quæ à carne est v. c. de gula tentante ad comedenda idolothyta. B. Hierony- mus Wellerus, laudante B. Glassio in Exeg. Epist. supra Dom. IX. Trinit. pag. 65. humanas tenta- tiones proprie dicit eas esse, quæ ab infirmitate hu- mana oriuntur, utpote tentationes contra secundam tabulam, quales sunt accendi odio, invidia, ira, cu- piditate vindictæ &c. Spirituales vero, quæ supra & extra intellectum humanæ mentis positæ sunt, videlicet illos internos pavores ac terrores, ut est tentatio de abjectione & abnegatione Christi & Evangelii; item de affectatione divinitatis & si- miles. Perpauci enim sunt, qui has tentationes intelligunt; pauciores, qui degustarunt; paucis- simi, qui vere illas senserunt. Non enim cadunt in vulgus hominum, sed tantum in eos, qui singu- laribus donis præditi sunt, ac tenerrimas habent conscientias. Hæc B. Wellerus. Quæ distinctio utut fundamento suo non destituatur. Atta- men huic loco conveniat, dubito. Videtur quidem eandem hic applicare B. Glassius l. c. pag. 58. Tentatio vos non cepit nisi humana, qua- si dicat, tam languidi, tepidi, imbecilles & spi- ritualium incuriosi estis, ut vix humanam, facile- que superabilem tentationem ac solicitationem ad peccata possitis sufferre ac vincere, superandi superandi omnino & casuri, quantum in vobis est, si plus quam humana, hoc est Diabolica vobis tentatio immitteretur. Addit tamen postea pag. 65. Po- test etiam dici, vocem humana ἀντιθετικῶς allu- dere tentationibus Diabolicis, quibus Deus con- silio sancto quosdam gratiæ suæ filios exercere si- nit, quas ignita spicula maligni Paulus appellat Eph. VI. 16. quasque ipse expertus plus satis fuerat 2. Cor. XII. 17. Et observat idem argumentum tra- ctari Ebr. XII. 3. seqq. ubi vero de tentationibus crucis à Deo immissis, non vero de tentatione car- nis agitur. Nondum usque ad sanguinem restitistis. Ejusmodi tentationes videtur respicere Paulus hoc etiam in loco, quæ à Deo immissæ quidem, sed humanæ, id est, non supra fidelium vires, por- tatuque faciles sint, quales nempe fuerunt penes Israelitas defectus ciborum desideratorum, carnis & piscium, cujus causa impatientes fiebant Num. XI. 4. & idolothytis cum Madianitis vescebantur Num. XXV. 1. unde in fornicationem incidebant: Carentia panis & aquæ, aliorumque ciborum præ- ter Manna, & deductio per vias longinquas, & diffi- ciles. Num. XXI. 5. ob quas adversus Deum rebe- les erant: Terrores exploratorum terræ Canaan de gigantibus filiis Enakim, ob quos murmurabant adversus Mosen & Aaron Num. XIV. 1. seqq. Absen- tia diuturnior Mosis à populo, ob quam vitulum aureum sibi erigebant Exod. XXXII. Quum ergo non nisi tales humanæ tentationes obvenerint Corinthiis, & longe graviores ipsis contingere possint, monet Apostolus, ut, qui stant, accurate si- bi caveant, ne forte cadant, tentationibus iisdem ingruentibus. Solatur autem simul fideles di- vina bonitate, assistentia, & ereptionis prompti- tudine.

## 10:14
Vers. 14. God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that you are able. But will make with the temptation also the issue that you may be able to bear it.

He had said that greater evils could happen, so as to render them the more cautious. Now, lest they be too dismayed, he adds comfort, signifying that God, provided they themselves are not negligent, will give strength equal to the temptation. Ἔκβασις, which elsewhere is δίεξοδος, תוצאה. Thus the issues of death, Ps. 68, 21, is an escape. He falls into temptation who succumbs, as we said on Matt. VI. 13. He goes out who overcomes temptation. Cyprian, in Testimonies III. 9, interprets Ἔκβασιν as the faculty of escaping, so that you may be able to bear it, where he also sets forth this sentiment: That each one is tempted only as much as he can sustain. He does not say that you may endure it altogether, but that you may be able to endure: That you may be able to bear, as Tertullian says in the cited place. God will give arms, through which you will be able to conquer, if you are not ῥαθυμότατοι. Moreover, he says πιστὸς, ὁ Θεὸς, because God has promised His aid in such a state, Matt. VII. 11, Luke XI, 13. See above I, 9. 2. Corinth. I. 18. 1. Thess. V. 24. 2. Thess. III. 3.

Blessed Baldwin teaches that God exhibits His assistance in four ways: 1. By exploring our strengths before He sends in any adversity. 2. By not imposing more than anyone can bear. And thus He makes the cross and temptation surmountable: In which sense St. Paul writes elsewhere: God is faithful, who will establish you and keep you from evil, 2. Thess. III. Therefore He awaits a suitable time, and does not impose the heaviest burdens on those weaker in faith, but exercises them with lighter ones, until they have made greater progress in faith and patience. 3. By bestowing the desired and often unexpected liberation from evil, which Paul calls ἔκβασιν, an escape or exit, which happens unexpectedly, often when they are thinking of no such thing. 4. By supplying strength, so that we may be able to suffer, even if such an escape does not appear in dangers. However, this promise is wrongly restricted to the elect alone. For they are promised to all in general in the Corinthian Church, in which there were many not elect: And especially to the faithful, to whom the grace and assistance of GOD is not lacking, unless you render yourselves unworthy of it, by the force of the promises in 1 Thess. 5, 2 Thess. 3. The providence of God, says Leo in Epistle XXVII, always provides necessary help to its own.

Therefore, my beloved brothers, flee from idolatry.

Flee, that is, be as far away as possible. This coheres well with what was said a little before: If you accustom yourselves to banquets in an idol temple, easily, when a more serious persecution settles in, you will devolve into the fullest idolatry.

These things come by numbers and their own degrees. And: No one suddenly becomes most base.

He now returns from the digression to the path and subject matter concerning idolatry, which he had begun in chapter VIII, and pursues it. He teaches that it must be fled in every way, and that one must abstain even from participation in a meal of food offered to idols in honor of an idol, for which sacrifices were offered and prepared in an idolatrous temple. For if, through communion at the table of food offered to idols, they come into communion with idolatry—if they participate in it knowingly and prudently—they consequently come into communion with demons. He notes, therefore, as B. Hunnius rightly does, especially that impious collusion which had then prevailed among them, because some were both using the sacraments of the Christians and nevertheless, under the empty pretext of Evangelical liberty, were not obscurely rendering themselves participants in the worship of images in the chapels of idols and at their banquets, contaminating their own conscience and not lightly striking against the rule of charity toward one's neighbor because of the offense given. Which he confirms both by the example of Eucharistic communion and by the example of the Levitical sacraments.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Πιστὸς ὁ Θεὸς, ὃς ὀυκ ἐάσει ὑμᾶς πειρασθῆναι, ὑπὲρ ὃ δύνασθε. Ἀλλὰ ποιήσει σὺν τῷ πειρασμῷ καὶ τὴν ἔκβα- σιν τοῦ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς ὑπενεγκεῖν.

Dixerat majora mala posse evenire, ut eo magis cautos redderet. Nunc ne nimium consternarentur, solatium ad- dit significans, Deum, modo ipsi negligentes non sint, datu- rum vires pares tentationi. Ἔκβασις quod alibi δίεξοδος תוצאה. Sic exitus mortis Ps. 68, 21. est evasio. Incidit in tentationem qui succumbit, ut diximus Matth. VI. 13. Exit, qui tentationem vincit. Ἔκβασιν evadendi facultatem, ut pos- sitis tolerare, interpretatur Cyprianus Testimoniorum III. 9. ubi & hanc ponit sententiam: Tantum unumquemque tenta- ri, quantum potest sustinere. Non dicit ut omnino perferatis, sed ut possitis perferre: Ut possitis tolerare, quomodo dicto loco Tertullianus. Arma Deus dabit, per quæ valebitis vin- cere, si non sitis ῥαθυμότατοι. Ideo autem dicit πιστὸς, ὁ Θεὸς, quia Deus in tali statu opem suam promisit Matth. VII. 11. Luc. XI, 13. Vide supra I, 9. 2. Corinth. I. 18. 1. Thess. V. 24. 2. Thess. III. 3.

Quadrifariam Deum assistentiam suam exhi- bere B. Balduinus docet 1. explorando vires nostras, antequam adversi quid immittat. 2. Non imponen- do plus, quam quilibet ferendo. Atque sic crucem & tentationem facit superabilem: Quo sensu S. Pau- lus alibi scribit: Fidelis Deus, qui stabiliet vos & cu- stodiet à malo 2. Thess. III. Idcirco tempus ido- neum expectat, nec infirmioribus in fide gravissi- ma imponit onera, sed levioribus exercet, donec majores in fide ac patientia progressus fecerint. 3. Largiendo exoptatam & inopinatam sæpe libera- tionem à malo, quam Paulus vocat ἔκβασιν evasio- nem sive exitum, qui ex improviso sit, sæpe nil tale cogitantibus. 4. Subministrando vires, ut sufferre valeamus, si maxime ejusmodi evasio in periculis non appareat. Perperam autem restringitur hæc promissio ad solos electos. Nam omnibus in gene- re promittuntur in Ecclesia Corinthiaca, in qua erant multi non electi: Et imprimis fidelibus, quibus gratia & assistentia DEI non deest, nisi teipsos ea indignos reddant, vi promissionum- 1. Thess. V. 2. Thess. III. Providentia Dei, ait Leo Epist. XXVII. semper suis necessarium praestat auxi- lium.

Διὸ ἀδελφοί με ἀγαπητοὶ, φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας.

Fugite, id est, quam longissime abeste. Bene hoc cohæ- ret cum paulo ante dictis : Si vosmet ipsos assuefaciatis epu- lis in idolio, facile, ubi gravior persecutio incubuerit, ad plenissimam idololatriam devolvemini.

Per numeros veniunt ista, gradusque suos. Et: Nemo repente fit turpissimus.

Redit jam e diverticulo in viam & materiam de idololatria, quam cap. VIII. ceperat, persequi- tur. Quam fugiendam omnibus modis, etiam participatione mensæ ex idolothytis in honorem idoli, cui sacrificia oblata, in templo idolola- trico paratæ, abstinendum esse docet. Siqui- dem per communionem mensæ idolothytorum in communionem idololatriæ, si scientes prudentes illi participent, veniant; & consequenter in com- munionem dæmoniorum. Notat ergo, ut re- cte B. Hunnius, imprimis eam, quæ tum inter illos invaluerat, collusionem impiam, quod aliqui & sacris utebantur Christianorum, & nihilominus in sacellis idolorum atque epulis sub inani præ- textu libertatis Evangelicæ non obscure se parti- cipes reddebant cultus simulachrorum, contami- nantes conscientiam propriam, & in regulam charitatis proximi propter datum offendiculum non leviter impingentes. Quod confirmat tum ab exemplo communionis Eucharisticæ, tum ab exem- plo sacrorum Leviticorum.

## 10:15
Vers. 15. I speak as to wise men. He excites the attention of the Corinthians, since he attributes intelligence to them. Φρόνιμος here is he who is Φρεσήρης in Homer.

Judge for yourselves what I say. As if he were to say: I will bring forward things so fair that I will take none other than yourselves as judges.

The cup of blessing which we bless. We have said at Matt. XXVI. 25 that ἐυλογεῖν and ἐυχαριστεῖν are used for the same thing, as are ἐυλογίαν and ἐυχαριστίαν. However, it is not a common blessing or thanksgiving that is understood here, but that which is proper to this business, through which the faithful rejoice, so that that bread and that wine become, as they were soon called in XI. 27, 29, the body and blood of Christ and the nourishment of the new creation.

Is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? A metonymy such as above I. 18, Rom. I. 16. He calls that communion through which the communion itself is made. Thus also Irenaeus, verse 7, arguing against those who denied that the world was created by God. Thus, however, according to these things, clearly, neither did the Lord redeem us with his blood, nor is the cup of the Eucharist a communion of his blood. Which he soon interprets: When therefore both the mixed cup and the broken bread receives the word of God, it becomes the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ. There is a not dissimilar expression in Valerius Maximus VI. 2, where Scipio is said to have shared concord with Gracchus at the banquet of Jupiter.

The bread which we break. For the bread which we break. Thus: These whom you see standing here, these two captives, for these whom. And: The city which I am establishing is yours, for the city. A similar kind of speaking is in Matt. XXI. 14. The breaking signifies both the breaking performed on the cross and the communion itself.

The argument from the example of Eucharistic communion is this: As whoever approaches the table of the Lord becomes a participant by the Lord's institution, through the medium of the blessed bread and wine of the body and blood of Christ, and thus comes into communion with Christ; so those who approach the table sacred to idols become participants by the institution of demons, through the medium of the use of cursed food offered to idols, of communion with idolatry, and thus come into communion with demons. He therefore applies those things which he had said about the idolatry of the fathers in the desert: If those who enjoyed typical sacraments, and which were only a shadow and figure, were destroyed because of communion with idolaters and idolatry, how could they escape the judgment of God who enjoy the holy Supper, in which there is not a figure but a communion of the body and blood of Christ, and nevertheless come into communion with the worship of idols. In vain do the Calvinists and Papists contend (as B. Hülsemann observes here) that the mode of communion or connection between the Eucharistic symbols and the body of Christ, and between the partakers and the body of Christ, must be the same as the mode of communion between things sacrificed to idols and the demon to whom the things sacrificed to idols are consecrated, and between the partaker of things sacrificed to idols and the demon himself, which union is only moral and denominative. Likewise, that whatever the mode of offering things sacrificed to idols or sacrificial was, such also is the mode of offering the Eucharistic symbols, or sacrificial, or pertaining to the Mass. See Bellarm. book on the Mass, ch. 14. If this hypothesis stands, countless absurdities would follow, indeed regarding the sacrificial Mass, just as when things are sacrificed to idols, the demon himself was not sacrificed; so if the Eucharistic symbols were sacrificed in the highest degree, the body of Christ itself, or Christ himself, who in the terms of the comparison corresponds to the demon in v. 21, would not be sacrificed. Again, just as through the libation of things sacrificed to idols, the things sacrificed to idols are not transubstantiated into the demon: so in the consecration of the Eucharistic symbols, these symbols are not transubstantiated into Christ. Which, however, Bellarm. lib. 12 de Euchar. c. 2, attempts to elicit by the force of this inference. It remains, therefore, from the communion or comparison of these communions among themselves, concerning which Paul treats from v. 16 to 22, that nothing more ought to be gathered than what was necessary for Paul's purpose regarding not abusing lawful things and indifferent matters, and for demonstrating the dangers of abuse, namely, just as those eating things sacrificed to idols are united in a certain way both with the things sacrificed to idols and with the demons to whom the things sacrificed to idols are consecrated: And just as things sacrificed to idols are united in a certain way with the demons to whom they are consecrated: So those eating the Eucharistic bread and wine are united in a certain way both with these very symbols and with that term with which the symbols are united, namely the body and blood of Christ. However, the mode of union is in neither case equal, nor the same in species; nor is this required for demonstrating Paul's scope, or for the danger and harm to be contracted from the eating of things sacrificed to idols, that there be a univocal or the same and equal ratio of union between things sacrificed to idols and the Demon; between the bread and the body of Christ, which Estius also noted here. See also Vasquez, T. II. in the third part of Thomas, Disp. 147, n. 20 seq., T. III. Disp. 168, n. 15 seq., Disp. 254, n. 1 and seq.

Furthermore, εὐλογία and εὐχαριστία are not simply the same, which although they seem to be interchanged in Matth. XXVI. 26. 27., in reality, however, they are not interchanged, but are hinted to be taken conjunctively, because in the first part of the Supper, εὐχαριστία was joined with εὐλογία, and in the other part, εὐλογία with εὐχαριστία. For Christ both gave thanks to God in both instances and blessed not only the Eucharistic bread, but also the wine, so that the cup is named from thence τῆς εὐλογίας or of blessing, which we also bless by the example of Christ. That this εὐλογία is a prayer, that that bread may become a communication of the body of Christ, and that that cup or Eucharistic wine may become a communication of the blood of Christ, is most correctly said: But such a prayer is not the εὐχαριστία itself, inasmuch as it brings in thanksgiving, not indeed a common one, but one proper to this sacred action, for divine hearing, and for the performance of that which Christ prays for in the real blessing, just as he was accustomed

Christ gives thanks, when he has sought something by prayers, certain of being heard. See John 11:41, 42. But the Calvinists (John Bergius in Pseudo-Stereom. & others) wrongly deny that εὐλογίαν is to be taken for the blessing of the body and blood of Christ for the use of sacramental eating and drinking, and they say it implies nothing else than εὐχαρισίαν and thanksgiving for the passion and death of Christ, and is described by the Apostle through ἀνάμνησιν: Because not even εὐχαρισία in the act of the Holy Supper performed by the Lord was a bare thanksgiving intended only for the redemption of the human race through the passion and death of the Lord; but it looks at the same time to the prayer of the consecration of the sacrament, by which thanks were given for the same, as a means of salvation, which it pleased the divine goodness to establish. But this εὐλογία implies the consecration of the bread and wine for the sacramental office. Whence Oecumenius interprets ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν as ὃ εὐλογοῦντες κατασκευάζομεν, which we prepare by blessing, so that, namely, the bread may be the communion of the body, the wine may be the communion of the blood of Christ; which everyone understands to be distinct from the ἀνάμνησις. For the ἀνάμνησις of the Lord's death does not contribute to the essence of the Holy Supper, and can be absent from it, although the latter cannot profit without the former. But if the divine εὐλογία is taken away, what will be had besides bare elements, bread and wine? The ἀνάμνησις is an act of faith commended to us: the εὐλογία is an act of Christ, and of the ministers who are in the place of Christ. On which matter see the Stereoma of the words of Christ's Testament opposed to Bergius, p. 75 seqq.

Now as to the Apostolic propositions: The cup of blessing, which we bless, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? The bread, which we break, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? In the subject it is manifest that by the bread, which we break, is understood the blessed bread, just as the cup of blessing is called that which we bless, and indeed not as it is broken by comminution or cutting into parts; but as it is distributed, because to break, in the Hebrew phrase, is to distribute, Is. 58, and therefore the Eucharistic bread is to be viewed in the use and act of distribution, not outside the use and act of distribution, for instance, when it is stored in a pyx, or lies on a paten, or is carried around with pomp; but when it is distributed for eating, and is eaten, as is manifest from the words of institution; where Christ says: Take, eat, then at last he testifies: This is my body. Similarly the cup of blessing, (by which God blesses us) which we bless, namely the Pastors and ministers of the word (as ministers and legates of Christ) by consecrating, but the Church at the same time by praying, approving, and celebrating and dispensing the whole sacred act, because the sacraments are goods of the Church, not insofar as it is placed on the altar or table, nor insofar as it is viewed materially, but insofar as it is established in its sacramental office; so that it may be distributed, and drunk from, and thus the wine itself, which is in the cup, insofar as it is offered to the guests in the Holy Supper after the blessing, and is distributed, is received and drunk by them, just as Christ in the institution itself offered and distributed the wine to the Apostles, and thus at last testified: Drink: this is my blood.

Therefore as to the predicate, κοινωνία or communion of the body of Christ is asserted of the bread which is broken, or distributed, and eaten in the Eucharist. That in this distribution and eating the Eucharistic bread is the communion of the body of Christ, and thus not only bread is distributed and perceived, but with the bread the body of Christ is distributed and perceived. For the Apostle wishes this, which he says, to be judged

by the Corinthians themselves, who could not judge it from elsewhere than from the words of Christ's institution. Since these exhibit such a κοινωνίαν, which consists in giving and receiving, it is in the open that the bread is also called the κοινωνία of the body of Christ for no other reason than that by means of this bread the body of Christ is given, received, and eaten in the Holy Eucharist. Whence this simplest sense emerges, that with the bread taken and eaten, the body of Christ is taken and eaten, in one indeed undivided eating, which is done by the mouth, which however does not behave in the same way toward the bread and the body of Christ. For the earthly thing, namely the bread, is taken in an earthly manner; but the heavenly, namely the body of Christ, is taken and eaten in a manner congruent to it, that is, a heavenly or mystical one, which squares with the mode of union by which the bread and the body are united or coupled. Since that union is Sacramental, and takes place in a mystery and is therefore called mystical, certainly the mode of eating depending on this with respect to the body of Christ is plainly mystical, is Sacramental, and incomprehensible to human reason; as the blessed Hunnius rightly says. Which must be held likewise concerning the distribution of the cup or blessed wine. And Grotius's explanation can be admitted on that account, that by κοινωνίαν the medium of communication is understood. For the sense returns to the same thing, that, namely, the Eucharistic bread in its sacramental use is the medium of the communication of the body of Christ. But the sacramental metonymy, which the Calvinists invent, that the bread is a κοινωνία, that is, a sign of the body of Christ, overturns the nature of the sacrament, which ought to consist of an earthly and a heavenly thing, and does not consist in a bare relation and signification, and perverts the sense of the Apostle's words: Who delivers a true and real communication of the body of Christ, not a bare signification, and teaches that the Eucharistic bread is the medium of communication, and an exhibitive symbol of the heavenly thing, the body of Christ, and does not propose here a bare sign only. However, the example which Grotius brings by reason of the word is foreign, that, namely, Scipio is said to have communicated concord with Gracchus at the feast of Jove: Nor does it fit, he says, to signify the breaking and the breaking performed on the cross, and the communion itself. For breaking here signifies not a crumbling into particles, but a distribution, much less the breaking or crumbling of the body of Christ, which ought by no means to have been broken or crumbled on the cross, John 19:33, 36. But the distribution of the Eucharistic bread among the guests; yet we are certain from the institution of Christ that when this is distributed, the body of Christ is distributed, and therefore the Apostle called the bread which we break, or distribute, the communion of the body of Christ. Whence it is necessary that the body of Christ be united with the Eucharistic bread, and constitute one sacramental thing. Otherwise, indeed, when the bread was distributed, the body of Christ would not be received, nor would the Eucharistic bread be the communion of the body of Christ. Therefore, by the body of Christ is not understood the efficacy of the body of Christ, but the substantial body itself, even though it is entirely living, and is not destitute of spiritual and saving efficacy, which, however, not all who partake of the body of Christ in the Holy Supper with the Eucharistic bread—inasmuch as it is for all a communion of the body of Christ—actually receive in a saving manner, but only the faithful.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ὡς φρονίμοις λέγω. Attentionem Corinthiorum excitat, cum ipsis ingenium tribuit. Φρόνιμος hic qui Homero Φρεσήρης.

Κρίνατε ὑμεῖς ὃ φημι. Quasi dicat: Adeo æqua adferam, ut non alios quam vosmet ipsos sumam judices.

Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς ἐυλογίας, ὃ ἐυλογῶμεν. Pro eodem poni ἐυλογεῖν & ἐυχαριστεῖν: Item ἐυλογίαν & ἐυχαριστίαν diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 25. Intelligitur autem hic non ἐυλογία aut ἐυχαριστία communis; sed illa huic ne- gotio propria, per quam ovant fideles, ut panis ille, & vinum illud fiant, sicut mox appellabantur XI. 27. 29. corpus & sanguis Christi, & alimentum novæ creationis.

Οὐχὶ κοινωνία τῆ αἵματος τῆ χριστᾶ. Μετωνυμία qualis supra I. 18. Rom. I. 16. Κοινωνίαν vo- cat id, per quod fit ipsa communio. Sic & Irenæus vers. 7. contra eos disputans, qui mundum negabant a Deo condi- tum. Sic autem secundum hæc videlicet, nec Dominus san- guine suo redemit nos, neque calix Eucharistiæ communicatio sanguinis ejus est. Quod mox interpretatur: Quando ergo & mixtus calix & fractus panis percepit verbum DEI, fit Eu- charistia sanguinis & corporis Christi. Est loquutio non dissimilis apud Valerium Maximum VI. 2. Ubi Scipio Jovis epulo cum Graccho concordiam communicasse dicitur.

Τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν. Pro ὁ ἄρτος ὃν κλῶμεν. Sic. Hos quos videtis stare hic captivos duos pro hi, quos. Et urbem quam statuo vestra est pro urbs. Simile loquendi ge- nus Matth. XXI. 14. Fractio & fractionem in cruce pera- ctam significat & ipsam communionem.

Argumentum ab exemplo communionis Eucha- risticæ hoc est: Ut quicunque mensam Domini accedunt, participes ex institutione Dominica fiunt, mediante pane & vino benedicto corporis & sanguinis Christi, & ita in communionem Chri- sti veniunt; sic qui mensam idolis sacram acce- dunt, participes ex institutione Dæmonum fiunt, mediante usu idolothytorum maledictorum, communionis idololatriæ, adeoque in commu- nionem Dæmoniorum veniunt. Applicat ergo ea, quæ de idololatria patrum in deserto dixerat: Si illi qui sacris typicis, & quæ umbra tantum & fi- gura fuêre, fruebantur, ob communionem cum idololatris & idololatriam interempti funt; Quo- modo judicium Dei possent effugere, qui sacra Cœna, in qua non figura, sed communicatio cor- poris & sanguinis Christi est, fruuntur, & nihilo fecius in cultus idolorum communionem veniunt. Nequicquam Calviniani & Pontificii contendunt, (quod hic observat B. Hülsemannus) oportere eun- dem esse modum communionis seu connexionis inter symbola Eucharistica, & corpus Christi, inter come- dentes & corpus Christi, qualis communionis modus est inter idolothyta & dæmonem, cui sacrantur ido- lothyta, inter comedentem idolothyta & dæmonem ipsum, quæ unio tantum moralis & denominativa. Item, qualis fuerit modus libandi idolothyta sive sacrificialis, talem etiam esse modum libandi Eu- charistica symbola, sive sacrificialem, vel missati- cum. Vid. Bellarm. l. de Missa cap. 14. Qua hypo- thesi stante innumera absurda sequerentur, quoad sacrificium missaticum quidem, quemadmodum sacrificatis idolothytis, dæmon tamen ipse non fuit sacrificatus; Ita si maxime sacrificarentur symbola Eucharistica, ipsum tamen Christi cor- pus, seu ipse Christus, qui in comparationis ter- minis respondet dæmoni v. 21. non sacrificaretur. Rursus quomodo per libationem idolothytorum idolothyta non transubstantiantur in dæmonem : Ita in consecratione symbolorum Eucharistico- rum symbola hæc non transubstantiari in Chri- stum. Id quod tamen Bellarm. lib. 12. de Euchar. c. 2. ex vi hujus illationis conatur elicere. Relinquitur ergo ex communione seu comparatione commu- nionum harum inter se, de quibus Paulus a v. 16. ad 22. agit, nihil amplius oportere colligi, quam ad propositum Pauli de non abutendo licitis re- bus & adiaphoris, & ad abusum pericula demon- stranda erat necessarium, videlicet, quemadmo- dum vescentes idolothytis certo modo uniuntur, & cum idolothytis & cum dæmonibus, quibus sacra- ta sunt idolothyta : Et quemadmodum idolothyta certo modo uniuntur cum dæmonibus quibus sa- crata sunt : Ita vescentes pane & vino Eucharistico certo modo uniuntur & cum his ipsis symbolis, & cum illo termino, cum quo symbola unita sunt, sive corpore & sanguine Christi. Modus autem unionis neutrubi æqualis est, nec idem specie ; ne- que hoc requiritur ad scopum Pauli demon- strandum, sive ad periculum & noxam ex idolo- thytorum esu contrahendum, ut univoca seu ea- dem & æqualis ratio unionis sit inter idolothyta & Dæmonem ; inter panem & corpus Christi, quod etiam Estius hic monuit. Vid. etiam Vas- quez. T. II. in tert. part. Thomæ Disp. 147. n. 20. seq. T. III. Disp. 168. n. 15. seq. Disp. 254. n. 1. & seq.

Porro non simpliciter idem sunt εὐλογία, & εὐχαρισία, quæ etsi permutari Matth. XXVI. 26. 27. videantur, revera tamen non permutantur, sed conjunctim accipienda esse innuuntur, quod & in prima Cœnæ parte cum εὐλογίᾳ conjuncta fue- rit εὐχαρισία, & in altera parte cum εὐχαρισίᾳ εὐλογία. Nam & Deo gratias egit Christus utrobi- que & benedixit non pani solum Eucharistico, sed etiam vino, uti inde poculum τῆς εὐλογίας vel benedictionis nominatur, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, cui & nos exemplo Christi benedicimus. Quam εὐλο- γίαν precationem esse, ut panis ille fiat communica- tio corporis Christi, & ut poculum illud vel vinum Eucharisticum communicatio fiat sanguinis Chri- sti, rectissime dicitur : Sed talis precatio non est propria ipsa εὐχαρισία, utpote quæ gratiarum actionem non quidem communem; sed huic sa- cræ actioni propriam infert, pro divina exauditio- ne, & ejus, quod precatur Christus in benedictio- ne reali præstatione, quemadmodum consuevit

Christus gratias agere, cum aliquid precibus expe- tiit, certus de exauditione. Vid. Joh. XI. 41. 42. Per- peram vero Calviniani (Joh. Bergius in Pseudo- Stereom. & alii) εὐλογίαν negant pro corporis & sanguinis Christi ad usum manducationis & bibi- tionis sacramentalis benedictione accipiendam esse, ac nihil aliud inferre ajunt, quam εὐχαρισίαν & gratiarum actionem pro passione & morte Christi, atque ab Apostolo per ἀνάμνησιν describi: Quia ne εὐχαρισία quidem in actu S. Cœnæ à Domino fa- cta nuda solum gratiarum actio fuit pro redem- ptione generis humani per passionem & mortem Domini destinata; sed respicit simul precationem ordinationis sacramenti, qua pro eadem, ceu me- dio salutis, quod placuit divinæ bonitati sancire, gratiæ actæ sunt. Εὐλογία vero hæc infert con- secrationem panis atque vini ad officium sacramen- tale. Unde Oecumenius ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν interpretatur ὃ εὐλογοῦντες κατασκευάζομεν, quod benedicentes adornamus, ut scilicet panis κοινωνία sit corporis, vinum κοινωνία sit sanguinis Christi; quam ab ἀνα- μνήσει distinctam esse nemo non intelligit. Ἀνά- μνησις enim mortis Dominicæ non facit ad essen- tiam S. Cœnæ, & ab ea abesse potest, licet hæc fine illa prodesse non possit. Si vero tollatur εὐλογία divina, quid habebitur præter nuda elementa, pa- nem & vinum. Ἀνάμνησις est actus fidei nobis commendatus: εὐλογία Christi actus est, & mi- nistrorum qui vice Christi sunt. Qua de re vi- deatur Stereoma verborum Testamenti Christi Bergio oppositum p. 75. seqq.

Jam quod ad propositiones Apostolicas: Calix benedictionis, quem benedicimus nonne est commu- nicatio corporis Christi? Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communicatio sanguinis Christi? In sub- jecto manifestum est, per panem, quem frangi- mus, intelligi panem benedictum, sicut calix bene- dictionis dicitur, quem benedicimus, & quidem non qua frangitur per comminutionem vel scissionem in partes; sed qua distribuitur, quia frangere, Ebræa phrasi, est distribuere Es. LIIX. ideoque in usu & actu distributionis spectari panem Eucharisticum, non extra usum & actum distributionis, puta, quando reconditur in pyxide, vel jacet in patina, vel circumfertur cum pompa; sed cum ad edendum distribuitur, & editur, prout è verbis institutio- nis manifestum est; ubi Christus ait: Accipite, edite, tum demum testatur: Hoc est corpus meum. Si- militer calix benedictionis, (per quem Deus nobis benedicit) cui benedicimus Pastores scil. & verbi ministri (ceu ministri & legati Christi) consecran- do, Ecclesia vero simul precando, approbando, to- tumque actum sacrum, quia sacramenta sunt bona Ecclesiæ, celebrando & dispensando, non quatenus in altari vel mensa collocatur, nec qua- tenus materialiter spectatur, sed quatenus in of- ficio suo sacramentali constituitur; ita ut distribua- tur, & ex eodem bibatur, adeoque vinum ipsum, quod est in calice, quatenus in S. cœna post be- nedictionem, convivis præbetur, ac distribuitur, ab iisdem accipitur, & bibitur, uti Christus in ipsa institutione Apostolis vinum præbuit, ac distri- buit, & ita demum testatus est: Bibite: hoc est san- guis meus.

Quod ergo ad prædicatum, κοινωνία vel commu- nicatio corporis Christi effertur depane qui frangi- tur, vel distribuitur, & manducatur in Eucharistia. Quod in distributione hac & manducatione panis Eucharisticus sit communicatio corporis Christi, adeoque non distribuitur & percipiatur solum pa- nis, sed cum pane distribuatur & percipiatur cor- pus Christi. Dijudicari enim hoc, quod dicit, vult

Apostolus, ab ipsis Corinthiis, qui aliunde id non poterant dijudicare, quam ex verbis institutionis Christi. Quae quum ejusmodi κοινωνίαν exhi- beant, quae in δόσει & λήψει consistit, non alia ra- tione etiam panem κοινωνίαν corporis Christi di- ci, in aprico est, quam quod mediante hoc pane corpus Christi detur, accipiatur, & edatur in S. Eucharistia. Unde simplicissimus iste emergit sensus, quod pane sumpto & manducato sumatur & edatur corpus Christi, una quidem indivisa man- ducatione, quae fit ore, quae tamen non pariter sese habeat ad panem & corpus Christi. Nam res terrena, nempe panis, terreno sumitur modo; coelestis vero, nempe corpus Christi congruente sibi sumitur & manducatur modo, hoc est coelesti, sive mystico, qui quadret ad modum unionis, qua panis & corpus unita seu copulata sunt. Ea unio cum sit Sacramentalis, & in mysterio fiat adeoque mystica nuncupetur, utique & manducationis hinc dependentis modus respectu corporis Christi plane mysticus est, Sacramentalis est, & humana rationi incomprehensibilis; ut recte B. Hunnius. Quod pariter habendum de distri- butione calicis vel vini benedicti. Et admitti ea ratione potest Grotiana explicatio, quod per κοινωνίαν medium communicationis intelligatur. Nam eodem sensus redit, quod nempe panis Eu- charisticus in usu suo sacramentali medium sit communicationis corporis Christi. Metonymia vero sacramentaria, quam Calviniani fingunt, quod panis sit κοινωνία, id est signum corporis Christi, evertit naturam sacramenti, quod con- stare oportet re terrena & coelesti, non vero in nuda relatione & significatione consistit, & pervertit sensum verborum Apostoli: Qui veram & realem communicationem corporis Christi, non nudam significationem tradit, & panem Eu- charisticum medium esse communicationis, ac symbolum exhibitivum rei coelestis, corporis Christi, docet, non vero nudum tantum signum hic proponit. Alienum tamen est exemplum, quod ratione λέξεως confert Grotius, quod nempe Scipio dicatur Jovis epulo cum Graccho concordiam communicasse: Nec congruit, quo fractionem & fractionem in cruce peractam significare, & ipsam communionem, ait. Nam fractio significat hic non comminutionem in particulas, sed distributionem, nedum fractionem vel comminutionem corporis Christi, qui frangi nullatenus vel comminui de- buit in cruce Joh. XIX. 33. 36. Sed panis Euchari- stici inter convivas distributionem; quo distri- buto tamen corpus Christi distribui ex institu- tione Christi certi sumus, adque idcirco panem, quem frangimus, vel distribuimus, communica- tionem corporis Christi dixit Apostolus. Unde oportet cum pane Eucharistico unitum esse cor- pus Christi, & unum sacramentale constituere. Alioquin enim pane distributo non percipere- tur corpus Christi, nec panis Eucharisticus esset communicatio corporis Christi. Non ergo per corpus Christi efficacia corporis Christi, sed ipsum substantiale corpus intelligitur, etsi id omnino vi- vum sit, & efficacia spirituali, ac salutari non de- stituatur, quam vero actu ipso non omnes, qui participant corpus Christi in S. Coena cum pane Eucharistico, utpote qui omnibus est communi- catio corporis Christi, sed soli fideles salutariter percipiunt.

## 10:17
Verse 17. Ὅτι εἷς ἄρτος. Supply ἐστὶ, as the Syrian took it here. That, however, is to be understood by zeugma from that which follows, ἑσμέν. Just as that which was dispersed, after it has been gathered, has become one bread, says Clement in the Constitutions VII. 26.

We the many are one body.

We are one body, that is, members of Christ, who is the head. Rom. XII. 4. 5. supra VI. 15. infra XII. 12. 14. 18. 19. 20. 22. 25. 26. 27. Eph. I. 22. IV. 15. 25. V. 30. Coloss. I. 18.

For we all partake of the one bread.

All, namely those who sit together at the same sacred table, and make one φρατρίαν (brotherhood), which φρατρία bears the image of the whole Church. The loaves were large among the Syrians and Greeks, so that ten or more could easily eat from the same bread, Diogenes Laërtius in the life of Pythagoras: 'The friends of old used to go to one bread, just as the barbarians do even now.'

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὅτι εἷς ἄρτος. Supple ἐστὶ, ut hic accepit Syrus. Id autem subintelli- gendum per ὑπόζευγμα ex eo quod sequitur ἑσμέν. Sicut hoc quod dispersum fuit, postquam est congregatum, factus est unus panis ait Clemens Constitutionum VII. 26.

Ἓν σῶμα οἱ πολλοί ἐσμεν.

Unum sumus corpus, id est membra Christi, qui est ca- put. Rom. XII. 4. 5. supra VI. 15. infra XII. 12. 14. 18. 19. 20. 22. 25. 26. 27. Eph. I. 22. IV. 15. 25. V. 30. Coloss. I. 18.

Οἱ γὰρ πάντες ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἄρτου μετέχομεν.

Omnes, nempe qui eidem mensae sacrae pariter accumbi- mus, & unam facimus φρατρίαν, quae φρατρία totius Eccle- siae gerit imaginem. Magni erant panes apud Syros & Grae- cos, ita ut facile deni aut plures eodem pane vescerentur, Diogenes Laërtius in vita Pythagorae : ἐφ' ἕνα ἄρτον οἱ πάλαι τῶν φίλων ἐφοίτων, καθάπερ καὶ νῦν οἱ βάρβαροι.

## 10:18
Vers. 18. Behold Israel according to the flesh.

For we are Israelites according to the spirit Rom. IX. 6. Gal. VI. v. 16.

Are not those who eat the sacrifices

שלמים (peace offerings), the saving sacrifices, from which those who had offered them used to eat.

Partakers of the altar?

By that they show that they worship that God whose altar it is, upon which the victims have been placed.

One body cannot here be understood in the proper sense of Christ's own substantial body, as it seemed to some (as Estius wished to signify in the sign of this unity, that the bread is not one thing and the body of Christ another; but one and the same, because the bread itself is the body of Christ): But as Grotius and most interpreters rightly and commonly [hold], the mystical body of Christ, because the faithful, when they partake of the one Eucharistic bread, which as regards the specific unity of the sacramental office is the same for all, and is compacted into one from many, so to speak, atoms of flour, also have their own unity mystically, because all are compacted into one body: of which unity, therefore, there is a symbol in the participation of the same Eucharistic bread. Because as the glossator, according to the opinion of Augustine, tract. XXVI. on John has: As one bread is made from many grains, and one body is composed of many members: So the Church is connected from many faithful, joined by charity. But Thomas, not as Estius judges, ineptly, but sublimely and subtly observes a double unity in these words: The first of incorporation, by which we are transformed into Christ: When he says: One bread: The second of life and sense, which we receive from Christ, when he adds: One body. For by the word, one bread, the body of Christ is not noted; but the Eucharistic bread, which is offered to all as one, viz., which is the communion of the body of Christ. Nothing here about the unity of incorporation. For not all who partake of that one bread, even though for all of them there is a communion of the body of Christ, are incorporated or grafted into Christ, which is the property of the faithful: Again, we are said to be one body, many as we are, on account of that participation of the Eucharistic bread, because we are mystically united among ourselves mutually. Where there is no express mention of the influx of life and sense from Christ the head, but only of the mutual union of Christians among themselves. Which unity in this place is properly Ecclesiastical, and has a place among all those who partake of the Eucharistic bread, even if they are not all faithful. Therefore he adds: We all partake of one bread. There is therefore no reason why Estius and other Papists should explain the one bread as the body of Christ. One bread, he says, according to the sense and exposition of all the orthodox, he understands as the body of the Lord itself. Nor indeed can it be explained otherwise without manifest falsehood. For it is evident that it is most false concerning material bread that all the faithful partake of one bread. But how is this evident? Do not all partake of that one bread, which is the communion of the body of Christ? Which is manifest to be one on account of the specific unity of the sacramental office, even though it is manifold in number, quantity, and quality of the matter of the bread. However, the opinion of the Papists is not consistent with itself. For if by bread the body of the Lord itself is to be understood, how does the Apostle say, the bread which we break, (that is, the body of Christ) is it not the communion of the body of Christ? How can he call the body of Christ bread, when those things are most distinct, bread and the body of Christ? Estius answers: The body of the Lord is called bread, both because it is made from bread, by which reasoning man is called dust or earth, Gen. III, and most especially because it retains the species of bread and its entire operation. But the Apostle does not say: Bread is the body of Christ: But, it is the communion of the body of Christ. But that which is the communion of the body of Christ cannot be the body of Christ itself, or be transubstantiated into the body of Christ; because thus the body of Christ could not be communicated through it. For that through which the body of Christ is communicated is one thing; but the body of Christ itself, which is communicated, is another. Nor does the Apostle say that only the bare species of bread is the κοινωνίαν of the body of Christ, but the bread itself; it is said not of the bare species, but of the bread itself, one bread: He says not of the bare species, but of the bread itself: We all partake of one bread. Therefore the Apostle has nothing to do with the fiction of transubstantiation, but is everywhere opposed to it. It is manifest from the scope

of Paul, that the subject is the union of the profession of the same faith and religion among those who observe the same sacred rites, which is evident from v. 18 immediately following, where he infers from the Israelites eating of the same victims of the same altar: Just as they are considered to profess that faith which the priests are accustomed to profess by their action concerning that altar: So those eating of the victims sacrificed to a demon testify by this eating that they profess that idolatry which the idolatrous priests were professing by their action concerning that altar. Hence it is clear that the communion of which Paul speaks in v. 16 properly and formally denotes that communion which is between the eaters and Christ; just as the participation of which he speaks in v. 20, 21 properly and formally denotes the communion which is between the eater of things sacrificed to idols and the demon to whom the things sacrificed to idols are consecrated. Yet it is rightly inferred from this communion which is between the eater of the Eucharist and Christ, and between the eater of things sacrificed to idols and the demon: That there is given a still closer communion and union between the Eucharistic bread and wine, which are eaten and drunk in the Eucharist, and Christ: A closer union between the thing sacrificed to idols and the demon. The reason is because by means of the thing sacrificed to idols the eater is united with the demon. Therefore, for that reason the eater is called such or a partner of demons in v. 20, that thing is more such: And for that reason the Eucharistic guest is said to have union with Christ, that thing is more such, or has a greater union with Christ. Just as in truth the sacramental symbols are sacramentally united with the body and blood of Christ, so that by one denomination they can be called the body and blood of Christ; yet the Eucharistic guest is not united sacramentally, but spiritually with Christ. Nor is it permitted to say by one denomination of the guest and Christ in common: This guest is the body of Christ, as it is rightly said: This bread is the body of CHRIST. From which it appears, although the third term of comparison between the eater of things sacrificed to idols and the demon, and between the thing sacrificed to idols and the demon is common, and to be applied to the union which is between the one eating bread and wine, and the body and blood of Christ: Likewise regarding the union which is between the bread and the body of Christ; yet the modes of union on both sides are not parts. This indeed they have in common, that each mode of union, both of things sacrificed to idols with the demon, and of sacramental symbols with the body of Christ, is by institution: The former indeed by human institution, and the opinion of the common people, to which Paul expressly appeals v. 19, 20, 28, 29, with the words for the sake of another's conscience; but this mode of union is by divine institution. That mode is merely imaginary, and modal, regarding the union of victims or things sacrificed to idols with the demon v. 20. This one, over and above a moral congruence, adds also a supernatural mode of union, and in the union of Eucharistic guests with Christ, it is far closer, and the union is of a different species from that mode of union by which the demon and things sacrificed to idols are joined. Therefore these modes of union are not to be equated with one another, but only compared ἐν πλάτει (in a broad sense), insofar as some mode of uniting is granted on both sides, as here B. Hülsemann.

This can also be taken as a new argument with B. Hunnius p. 313. He brings another argument of dissuasion from the worship of idolatrous sacred rites and a profane life, in this sense: It is altogether unworthy for those who are, as it were, bound together into one assembly and body by the fellowship of the same sacred rites, to mix themselves with the worshippers of images. But those who become partakers of one and the same Eucharistic bread, of the same cup, of the same body and blood, these are joined into one and the same body of an external congregation. Therefore let them abstain from the contrary congregation of the church of the malignant and those who follow idols. He proves the minor premise from the fact that because they partake of one and the same bread, they therefore come into the society of the same body by this common participation. And so, just as he previously drew an argument of proof from the substance of the Supper, so now he does so from its end and effect. For among other ends and effects of the Lord's Supper is also this, that just as one bread is kneaded from many grains of wheat or rye; so we all together, whoever use the sacrament of the Eucharist, coalesce into one bread and one mystical body. Where, however, we do not at all think that bread is taken in a different sense than in the preceding, and that by one bread one mystical bread is understood, but we understand bread properly; nor do we judge it to be said that we coalesce into one bread, but into one mystical body.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Βλέπετε τὸν Ἰσραὴλ κατὰ σάρκα.

Nos enim κατὰ πνεῦμα Israëlitae sumus Rom. IX. 6. Gal. VI. v. 16.

Οὐχὶ οἱ ἐσθίοντες τὰς θυσίας.

שלמים τὰς σωτηρίους θυσίας, unde qui eas obtulerant vescebantur.

Κοινωνοὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου εἰσί.

Per id ostendunt, se eum Deum colere, cujus est altare, in quod profecta victimae data sunt.

Non hic corpus unum sensu proprio de corpore Christi proprio & substantiali, quod nonnullis vi- sum, (quomodo Estius voluit significare in signo hujus unitatis, non aliud esse panem, aliud corpus Christi; sed unum & idem, quia panis ipse est cor- pus Christi) intelligi potest: Sed ut recte Grotius & plerique Interpp. communiter, corpus Christi mysticum, quia fideles, cum de uno pane Euchari- stico participant, qui quoad specificam unitatem officij sacramentalis penes omnes idem est, & ex multis, ut ita dicam, farinae atomis coagmentatur in unum, unitatem etiam suam habeat mystice, quia ad unum corpus omnes coagmentantur: Cu- jus proinde unitatis symbolum est in participatio- ne ejusdem panis Eucharistici. Quia ut glossa- tor ex Augustini sententia tract. XXVI. super Jo- han. habet: Sicut unus panis ex multis granis con- ficitur, & unum corpus ex multis membris compo- nitur: Sic Ecclesia ex multis fidelibus, charitate co- pulante, connectitur. Inepte vero, non, ut Estius judicat, sublimiter & subtiliter Thomas in his ver- bis duplicem observat unitatem: Primam incorpo- rationis, qua in Christum transformemur: Cum dicit: Unus panis: Alteram vitae, & sensus, quam a Christo accipimus, cum addit: Unum corpus. Nam verbo, panis unus, non Christi corpus no- tatur; sed panis Eucharisticus, qui unus omni- bus praebetur, scil. qui communicatio corporis Christi est. Nihil hic de incorporationis uni- tate. Nam non omnes, qui panem illum unum participant, etsi omnibus illis sit communica- tio corporis Christi, incorporantur, vel inse- runtur Christo, quod est proprium fidelium: Rursus unum corpus multi esse dicimur, ob parti- cipationem istam panis Eucharistici, quod my- stice uniti simus inter nos omnes mutuo. Ubi nulla expressa mentio est influxus vitae, & sensus a Christo capite, sed mutuae tantum unionis Chri- stianorum inter sese. Quae unitas hoc loco pro- prie Ecclesiastica est, atque inter omnes illos, qui participant panem Eucharisticum, locum habet, etsi fideles non sint omnes. Ideo addit: Omnes de uno pane participamus. Non ergo est, quod Estius aliique Papistae unum panem de corpore Christi exponant. Unum panem, inquit ille, juxta sensum & expositionem omnium orthodoxo- rum intelligit ipsum corpus Domini. Nec vero aliter absque manifesta falsitate exponi potest. Nam de pane materiali falsissimum esse constat, omnes fideles de uno pane participare. Qui vero hoc constat? Annon omnes de uno illo pane, qui est communicatio corporis Christi, parti- cipant? quem unum esse ob specificam unita- tem officii sacramentalis, etsi multivarius sit nu- mero, quantitate, ac qualitate materia panis ma- nifestum est. Non constat autem sibi Papistarum sententia. Nam si per panem ipsum corpus Do- mini intelligendum, quomodo dicit Apostolus, panis quem frangimus, (hoc est, corpus Christi) nonne est communicatio corporis Christi? Quo- modo corpus Christi panem vocare potest, quum illa distinctissima sint, panis & corpus Chri- sti? Respondet Estius: Corpus Domini vocari pa- nem, tum quia ex pane factum, qua ratione homo pulvis seu terra vocatur, Gen. III. tum potissime, quia speciem panis, totamque ejus operationem reti- net. At Apostolus non ait: Panis est corpus Chri- sti: Sed, est communicatio corporis Christi. Quod autem est communicatio corporis Christi, id non potest esse ipsummet corpus Christi, vel transsubstantiari in corpus Christi; quia sic per illud non posset communicari corpus Christi. Aliud enim est id, per quod corpus Christi com- municatur; aliud autem est corpus ipsum Christi, quod communicatur. Nec tantum speciem nu- dam panis dicit Apostolus κοινωνίαν esse corporis Christi, sed panem ipsum; non de specie nuda, sed de pane ipso dicitur, unus panis: Non de nuda specie, sed de pane ipso ait: Omnes de uno pane participamus. Nihil ergo commercii habet Apo- stolus cum commento transsubstantiationis, sed ubique ei adversus est. Manifestum est ex scopo

Pauli, de unione professionis ejusdem fidei & reli- gionis inter eos, qui eadem sacra colunt, agi, quod patet ex v. 18. immediate sequente, ubi ab Israëli- tis de iisdem victimis ejusdem altaris comedentibus infert: Quemadmodum illi censentur profiteri illam fidem, quam sacerdotes solent profiteri a- ctione sua circa illud altare: Ita comedentes de vi- ctimis immolatis dæmoni testari hac comestione, se profiteri illam idololatriam, quam profiteban- tur sacerdotes idololatrici actione sua circa illud altare. Hinc patet, communionem, de qua lo- quitur Paulus v. 16. proprie & formaliter notare illam communionem, quæ est inter comedentes & Christum; quomodo participatio, de qua v. 20. 21. proprie & formaliter notat communionem, quæ est inter comestorem idolothytorum & dæmonem, cui sacrata sunt idolothyta. Recte tamen ex com- munione hac, quæ est inter comestorem Eucha- ristiæ, & Christum, inter comestorem idolothy- torum & dæmonem infertur: Dari propiorem ad- huc communionem & unionem inter panem & vi- num Eucharisticum, qui eduntur & bibuntur in Eucharistia & Christum: Propiorem unionem in- ter idolothytum & dæmonem. Ratio est, quia mediante idolothyto comestor unitur cum dæ- mone. Ergo propter quod comestor dicitur talis seu consors dæmoniorum v. 20. illud magis est tale: Et propter quod conviva Eucharisticus dicitur unionem habere cum Christo, illud ma- gis est tale, seu majorem unionem habet cum Christo. Quomodo revera symbola sacramen- talia sacramentaliter uniuntur cum corpore & sanguine Christi, ut una denominatione dici pos- sint corpus & sanguis Christi; conviva tamen Eu- charisticus non unitur sacramentaliter, sed spiri- tualiter cum Christo. Nec licet una denomi- natione conviva & Christo communi dice- re: Hic conviva est corpus Christi, quomodo recte dicitur: Hic panis est corpus CHRISTI. Ex quibus apparet, quanquam compara- tionis tertium inter comedentem idolothyta & dæmonem, inter idolothytum & dæmonem com- mune sit, & applicandum ad unionem, quæ est inter comedentem panem & vinum, & corpus & sanguinem Christi: Ad unionem item, quæ est inter panem & corpus Christi; modos tamen unionis utrinque non esse partes. Hoc quidem habent commune, quod uterque modus unionis, & idolothytorum cum dæmone, & symbolorum sacramentalium cum corpore Christi ex instituto est: Ille quidem ex instituto humano, & opinione vulgi, ad quam Paulus expresse provocat v. 19. 20. 28. 29. verbis propter conscientiam alterius; hic autem unionis modus ex instituto divino. Ille modus mere imaginarius est, & modalis, quoad unionem victimarum seu idolothytorum cum dæmone v. 20. Hic super congruentiam moralem superaddit etiam supernaturalem unionis modum, & in unione convivarum Eucharisticorum, cum Christo longe propior, atque alia specie est unio ab illa modo unionis, quæ dæmon & idolothyta conjunguntur. Ergo hi modi unionis non sunt coæquandi invicem, sed ἐν πλάτει tantum comparandi, quoad utrinque detur aliquis uniendi modus, ut hic B. Hülseman- nus.

Potest hoc etiam ut novum argumentum accipi cum B. Hunnio p. 313. Aliud argumentum affert dehortationis à cultu sacrorum idololatricorum & vita profanitate, hoc sensu: Indignum prorsus est, eos, qui eorundem sacrorum consortio in unum cœtum & corpus quasi devinciuntur, admiscere sese simulacrorum cultoribus. At qui unius ejusdemque panis Eucharistici, ejusdem poculi, ejusdem corporis, & sanguinis fiunt participes, hi junguntur in unum idemq; congregationis externæ corpus. Ergo abstineant à contraria congregatione Ecclesiæ malignantium, & idola sectantium. Minorem probat inde, quia de uno, eodemque pane participent, idcirco hac communi participatione venire in societatem ejusdem corporis. Itaque ut prius à substantia cœnæ probationis argumentum deduxit, ita nunc à fine & effectu. Inter alios namque fines & effecta Cœnæ Dominicæ est & hoc quod quemadmodum ex multis granis tritici vel siliginis panis unus pinsitur; Ita nos simul omnes, quicunque utimur Eucharistiæ sacramento, coalescimus in unum panem, unumque corpus mysticum. Ubi tamen panem alio sensu, quam in præcedentibus accipi, & per unum panem unum mysticum panem intelligi minime arbitramur, sed panem proprie intelligimus; nec nos in unum panem, sed in unum corpus mysticum coalescere dici censemus.

## 10:19
Vers. 19. Τί ὖν φημι ὅτι ἔιδωλόν τί ἐςι.

Because the Corinthians were easily going to see where that comparison was tending, namely that those who ate things sacrificed in the Greek manner would be considered to worship those gods to whose altars the things had been offered, he does not express this, but meets that which he knew the philosophers would say, that an idol is nothing, as above VIII. 4. He therefore concedes this to them, that they are nothing beyond Jupiter, Neptune, Ceres: that they had perished long ago.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τί ὖν φημι ὅτι ἔιδωλόν τί ἐςι.

Quia facile visuri erant Corinthii, quo tenderet ista comparatio, nempe ut qui immolatitia Græcania ederent, cen- ferentur eos Deos colere, quorum aris data erant profecta, ideo hoc non exprimit, sed occurrit ei quod sciebat dicturos philosophos, idolum nihil esse ut supra VIII. 4. Concedit ergo hoc illis non esse ultra Jovem, Neptunum, Cererem: periisse eos pridem.

## 10:20
Vers. 20. Ἀλλ' ὅτι ἃ θύει τὰ ἔθνη δαιμονίοις θύει.

That is, evil demons through those names, which are nothing, lead men away from the true God. He proves it from Deut. XXXII. 17. Where in the Greek it is ἔθυσαν δαιμονίοις κ, ὐ Θεῷ, where for δαιμονίοις in the Hebrew it is לשדים, that is, goat-formed demons. Tertullian on spectacles: We know that they are nothing but the names of the dead, just as the images themselves are not, but we are not ignorant of who work and rejoice under these names and instituted images, and feign divinity—the wicked spirits, that is, demons.

Οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς κοινωνὸς τῶν δαιμονίων γίνεσθαι. Not even in appearance would I wish you to be associated with those worst Spirits, enemies of God and human salvation: Κοινωνὸς γίνεσθαι is צמד, which the Greeks translate as τελεῖσθαι, that is, to be initiated, Num. XXIV. v. 9, Ps. CVI. 28.

The objection arose from this, that the Apostle himself wrote above that an idol is nothing; should it be judged that there is in images either power to do good or value to pollute consciences, or that meats offered to images and idols are in themselves polluted, so that it is not lawful to eat them for any reason? If indeed he had previously forbidden eating them only in the sanctuary and at a solemn feast instituted for idolatrous worship, but not at common banquets, provided scandal is absent, does he now seem to forbid all eating of things sacrificed to idols, as if it were participation in idolatry? But the holy Apostle answers: Although idols are in reality nothing in the world; because, however, they are worshipped by men as Gods, and thus demons are truly served when they are served, and, as the Psalmist testifies, the Gods of the gentiles, whoever they may be, are demons Ps. XCVI. 5, because demons lurk under the idols, and this worship is derived from them, therefore those things which are sacrificed to idols are in reality sacrificed to demons. Yet it is not in itself and simply forbidden to eat things sacrificed to idols, provided it does not happen in idolatrous chapels and banquets instituted in honor of idols, and provided regard is had for the weak, as will be clear from what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἀλλ' ὅτι ἃ θύει τὰ ἔθνη δαιμονίοις θύει.

Id est dæmones mali per ista nomina, quæ nihil sunt, homines à vero Deo abducunt. Probat ex Deut, XXXII. 17. Ubi in Græco ἔθυσαν δαιμονίοις κ, ὐ Θεῷ, ubi pro δαιμονίοις in Hebræo est לשדים id est dæmonibus τραγομόρφοις. Tertullianus de spectaculis: Scimus nihil esse nisi nomina mortuorum, sicut nec ipsa simulacra eorum, sed non ignoramus qui sub istis nominibus & institutis simulacris operentur & gaudeant, & divinitatem mentiantur nequam spiritus scilicet dæmones.

Οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς κοινωνὸς τῶν δαιμονίων γίνεσθαι. Ne in speciem quidem velim vos sociari pessimis illis Spiritibus Dei, & salutis humanæ inimicis: Κοινωνὸς γίνεσθαι צמד quod τελεῖσθαι, id est initiari vertunt Græci Num. XXIV. v. 9. Pf. CVI. 28.

Objectio inde nata est, quod ipse Apostolus supra scripserit, idolum nihil esse, anne simulacris vel potestatis ad benefaciendum, vel valoris quid ad polluendas conscientias inesse, aut carnes simu- lacris & idolis oblatas per se pollutas esse, ut nulla ratione iis vesci liceat, censendum sit? siquidem su- pra solum iisdem in sacrario & epulo solenni ob cul- tus idololatricos instituto vesci prohibuerit, non au- tem in conviviis vulgaribus, modo scandalizatio absit, jam vero videatur cuncto esui idolothytorum, ceu participationi idololatriæ, interdicere? Re- spondet autem sanctus Apostolus: Tametsi idola revera nihil sint in mundo; quia tamen ut Dii co- luntur ab hominibus, & ita dæmoniis revera ser- vitur, cum illis servitur, &, teste Psalte, Dii gen- tium; quicunque sint, dæmonia sunt Pf. XCVI. 5. eo quod sub idolis latitantur dæmonia, & ab iis profe- ctus hic cultus sit, ideo quæ immolantur idolis, re- vera immolari dæmoniis. Non tamen per se, ac simpliciter prohibitum esse idolothytorum esum, dummodo non in sacellis idololatricis & convi- viis in honorem idolorum institutis fiat, & in- firmorum habeatur ratio, ut è sequentibus pate- bit.

## 10:21
Vers. 21. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.

You cannot does not mean it is not fitting, it is not becoming. Above III. 10. Matt. IX. 15. He calls the cup of demons the wine offered to gods, which for the Hebrews is יין עבודה זרה; see what we have brought forward on this matter at Matt. XXVI. 27.

And of the table of demons.

Were tables also set before idols for the people, the tribes, the guilds? You have Ἱερὰν τραπέζην in the Scholiast on the Plutus.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Οὐ δύνασθε ποτήριον Κυρίου πίνειν, καὶ ποτήριον δαιμονίων.

Οὐ δύνασθε non convenit, non decet. Supra III. 10. Matth. IX. 15. ποτήριον δαιμονίων vocat vinum Diis libatum, quod Hebræis יין עבודה זרה vide quæ de ea re at- tulimus ad Matth. XXVI. 27.

Καὶ τραπέζης δαιμονίων.

Num & in idolis mensæ ponebantur populo tribubus, sodalitatibus. Ἱερὰν τραπέζην habes in Scholiafte Pluti.

## 10:22
Vers. 22. Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?

That is, we provoke to anger. For thus often קנא ζηλῶ, whence also the verb קנא or הקניא, which is translated παραζηλῶ, παροξύνω, παροργίζω. It is usually said emphatically of those who show honor to idols, as can be seen in Deut. XXXII. 21.

Are we stronger than he?

So that, indeed, we might be able to escape the punishments which an angry GOD might wish to inflict upon us. The sense is drawn from Job X. v. 18, ch. XXXVII. 23.

This impossibility is what they call moral, or of right, not of fact, and therefore it is rashly snatched up by the Calvinists to mean that the wicked cannot participate in the body of the Lord in the Holy Supper, because this is a matter of fact, that the wicked and those who have communion with the Devil approach the holy Eucharist; the Apostle testifies that they partake of the body and blood of the Lord entirely, but to their judgment, and become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἢ παραζηλῶμεν τὸν Κύριον.

Id est ad iram provocamus. Ita enim sæpe קנא ζηλῶ unde & verbum קנא sive הקניא, quod vertitur παραζη- λῶ, παροξύνω, παροργίζω. Eminenter autem dici solet de iis, qui idolis honorem exhibent, ut videre est Deuter. XXXII. 21.

Μὴ ἰσχυρότεροι ἀυτῦ ἐσμεν.

Ut nempe pœnas evadere possimus, quas iratus DEUS nobis velit infligere. Sensus depromptus ex Jobi X. v. 18. c. XXXVII. 23.

Hæc impossibilitas est moralis, quam vocant, vel juris, non facti, adeoque temere à Calvinianis eo abripitur, quod impii non possint participare corpus Domini in S. Cœna, quia hoc facti est, quod impii & qui cum Diabolo communionem habent, ad sacram Eucharistiam accedant; Quos omnino frui corpore & sanguine Domini, sed ad judicium, & reos fieri corporis & sanguinis Domini, testatur Apostolus.

## 10:23
Vers. 23. All things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable.

Namely, things of that kind about which he also treated above in VI. 12, where the same is said. In general, to eat food sacrificed to idols is not illicit, as if someone were alone and had nothing else to eat: in certain circumstances, it becomes illicit because it can make others worse. Paul transitions here, as he often does, from the second person to the first: for it is the same thing when it concerns any person whatsoever. Thus also above 6, 7, 8, 9, 20. A similar change happens sometimes.

But not all things edify.

He said less; he felt more. These things do not so much make men better, as they even impel them to ruin.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' ὐ πάντα συμφέρει.

Ejus scilicet generis res de quibus & supra egit VI. 12. ubi idem dictum. In genere edere εἰδωλόθυτον non est illicitum, ut si quis solus sit, nec aliud habeat, quod edat: In circum- stantiis certis, ideo fit illicitum, quia alios id potest pejores reddere. Transit hic Paulus, ut sæpe à secunda persona ad primam: Id enim perinde est, ubi de quovis homine agitur Sic & supra 6. 7. 8. 9. 20. Similis mutatio fit aliquoties.

Ἀλλ' ὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ.

Minus dixit; plus sensit. Illa adeo homines meliores non faciunt, ut etiam ad ruinam impellant.

## 10:24
Vers. 24. Μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτῦ ζητείτω.

Let no one look only to that which, from such a thing, may be good or evil for himself.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ τῦ ἑτέρω ἕκαστος.

For among Christians, one's neighbor claims a great part of us for himself. He who loves his neighbor, loves God.

All things are lawful for me, that is to say, things indifferent, and subject to liberty in the kingdom of Christ. Paul's sentiment is indeed consistent, with both concession and correction at once. The concession is that which he grants, that all things are lawful in matters by their own nature intermediate and indifferent. Furthermore, he adds a correction to his concession, showing that the free use of those indifferent things does not always conduce to or build up. Therefore, he prescribes this rule: Let no one seek what is his own; but each one what is another's. Namely, as the moderator of Christian liberty he wishes there to be charity toward one's neighbor, the property of which is this, that it seeks not what is its own, but what is the neighbor's, to whose edification and utility it refers everything, as the blessed Hunnius has vigorously explained this.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτῦ ζητείτω.

Ne quis id unum spectet, quod ex tali re ipsi esse boni aut mali possit.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ τῦ ἑτέρω ἕκαστος.

Nam inter Christianos partem nostri magnam sibi proxi- mus vendicat. Qui proximum amat, Deum amat.

Omnia mihi licent, scilicet adiaphora, & li- bertati in regno Christi subjecta. Constat vero sententia Pauli, concessione simul & correctione. Concessio est, quod largitur, omnia licere in rebus suapte natura mediis & indifferentibus. Con- cessioni porro suæ correctionem subdit, osten- dens non semper conducere vel ædificare libe- rum illum rerum indifferentium usum. Pro- inde regulam præscribit hanc: Nemo, quod suum est, quærat; sed quisque quod alterius est. Nimirum moderatricem libertatis Christianæ vult esse charitatem erga proximum, cujus proprietas haec est, quod quaerit non quod suum est, sed quod proximi, ad cujus aedificationem & utilitatem universa refert, ut haec nervose exposuit B. Hunnius.

## 10:25
v. 25. 'Eat everything that is sold in the meat market.' Μάκελλον is a Greek word from the Latin, like Φλαγελλεῖν, κουστωδία, and similar ones. Plutarch also uses it, explaining it as κρεωπώλιον, as do the Greek-Latin lexicons. The Syriac also retained it. The Rabbis write מקולין. It takes its name from a place that was in Rome: that place, however, was named after the man to whom that ground had belonged. It could happen that a butcher, ὁ ὀψοπώλης, before he brought meat to the market, had given some of it to the altar. 'May the goods in the market be polluted by libations.' Eusebius, book VIII. It could also happen, as Augustine noted, that priests would sell the portions that fell to them. He does not wish for this to be inquired into anxiously, even if one is ignorant of such things, and says that he was ignorant. Tertullian on fasting: 'He handed the keys of the market to you, permitting the eating of everything to establish an exception for things sacrificed to idols.'

'Asking no questions for conscience' sake.' Ἀνακρίνειν here is to condemn, in the way that κρίνειν is also often used.
