To condemn here, however, is to hold as impure διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν, that is, on account of your own persuasion. See above VIII. 7. Understand, however, that persuasion to be that which follows, that nothing is in itself impure in foods. See what we have said on Matt. XV. 11.

The simpler and more common interpretation is that of INQUIRY and judging, which the word ἀνακρίνειν properly brings in, Acts XVII. 11, 1 Cor. II. 4, 1 Tim. IV. 3, 4, that they may buy whatever is sold in the market without hesitation, and have no need to ask scrupulously for the sake of conscience whether those meats were previously sacrificed to idols or not? Because nothing is unclean in itself, and not even such meats are unclean in themselves; and the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. But if one is to buy and eat whatever is sold in the market, how does that agree with the Jerusalem decree, Acts XV. 29, XVI. 4, concerning not eating blood, things strangled, and things sacrificed to idols? Answer. That decree was particular, both by reason of the time at the beginning of the gathering of the Christian Church from the Jews, whose infirmity had to be consulted; because the Jews, addicted to Levitical ceremonies, such as these were, Lev. XVII. 12, could not lay them aside so suddenly until Christian liberty became more fully known, and thus the Jewish synagogue might be buried with honor: and also by reason of the place; it did not concern all churches, but, as the synodical epistle has it, those which were in Antioch, and in Syria, and Cilicia.

Latin:

v. 25. Πᾶν τὸ ἐν μακέλλῳ πωλούμενον, ἐσθίετε. Μάκελλον vox est Graeca ex Latino, ut Φλαγελλεῖν, κουστωδία & similia. Utitur & Plutarchus exponens κρεωπώλιον & Lexica Graeco-Latina. Retinuit & eam Syrus. Rabbini scribunt מקולין. Nomen habet a loco, qui erat Romae: Is autem ab homine, cujus id fuerat solum. Fieri poterat, ut macellarius ὁ ὀψοπώλης antequam ad macellum carnes ferret, aliquid de iis in aram dedisset. Τὰ κατ' ἀγορὰν ὤνια ταῖς σπονδαῖς κατακολύοιτο. Eusebius l. VIII. Fieri etiam poterat, quod Augustinus notavit, ut sacerdotes partes, quae ipsis cedebant, venderent. De eo non vult solicite inquiri, licet nescire talia, & nescisse se dicere. Tertullianus de jejuniis: Claves macelli tibi tradidit, permittens esui omnia ad constituendam idolothytorum exceptionem.

Μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν. Ἀνακρίνειν hic est damnare, quomodo & κρίνειν saepe ponitur. Damnare autem hic est pro impuro habere διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν propter persuasionem nempe vestram. Vide supra VIII. 7. Persuasionem autem intellige eam, de qua sequitur, nihil esse in cibis per se impurum. Vide, quae diximus ad Matth. XV. 11.

Simplicior est, & communior interpretatio INQUISITIONIS & dijudicationis, quam proprie verbum ἀνακρίνειν infert Act. XVII. 11. 1. Cor. II. 4. 1. Tim. IV. 3. 4. quod emere possint, quicquid in macello venditur, absque haesitatione, nec interrogare scrupulose opus habeant ob conscientiam, an carnes illae prius immolatae sint simulacris, vel non? Quia per se nihil immundum est, ac ne carnes quidem tales immundae per se sint; Et Domini sit terra, ac plenitudo ejus. Sed si emendum & edendum, quicquid in macello venditur, quomodo id convenit decreto Hierosolymitano Act. XV. 29. XVI. 4. de non edendo sanguine, suffocato & idolothyto? Resp. Decretum illud particulare fuit, tum ratione temporis sub initium collectionis Ecclesiae Christianae e Judaeis, quorum infirmitati consulendum erat; Quia Judaei ceremoniis Leviticis addicti, quales hae erant Lev. XVII. 12. non tam subito easdem deponere potuerunt, donec libertas Christiana uberius innotesceret, & ita Judaica synagoga cum honore sepeliretur: Tum ratione loci; Non omnes Ecclesias, sed, ut habet epistola synodica, eas, quae Antiochiae, & in Syria, & Cilicia erant, concernens.

## 10:26
V. 26. 'For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof.' It is from Psalm XXIV. 1. מלוא or πλήρωμα is everything that moves upon the earth, just as πλήρωμα θαλάσσης is everything that is in the sea, Ps. XCVI. 11, 1 Chron. XVI. 32. Κυρίου here is ליהוה. For when the Apostles cite passages of the Old Testament, they often call God the Lord, whereas otherwise, when speaking of their own Christ, they are accustomed to give the name of Lord.

Latin:

V. 26. Τοῦ γὰρ Κυρίου ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς. Est ex Psalm. XXIV. 1. מלוא sive πλήρωμα est omne id, quod super terram versatur, sicut πλήρωμα θαλάσσης, omne id, quod in mari est, Ps. XCVI. 11. 1. Paral. XVI. 32. Κυρίου hic est ליהוה. Nam cum Apostoli citant loca veteris Testamenti, saepe Deum Dominum vocant, cum alioqui de suo loquentes Christo soleant dare Domini nomen.

## 10:27
v. 27. 'If any of the unbelievers invite you.' Not signifying, of course, that he has sacrificed. Καλεῖν is to call to a banquet. The servants who were sent to this were called κλήτορες by the Greeks, and vocatores by the Latins.

'And you are disposed to go.' If you wish to go at all, he tacitly admonishes that perhaps you would do better if you did not go. He does not, however, forbid going. Above V. 10.

'Eat everything that is set before you.' That is, eat of the things set before you, whatever you like. Παρατίθεσθαι is a word proper to the table, Mark VIII. 6, 7, Luke IV. 16, X. 18, XI. 6, Acts XVI. 34.

'Asking no questions for conscience' sake.' The same sense as above, 25.

This verse, therefore, pertains to banquets that are not sacred to idols, nor religious, but civil: if anyone is invited to them by unbelievers, that one should eat, without scrupulous inquiry, whatever is set on the table. Let no one consider it a matter of religion in his conscience to take whatever he likes, without disquisition, as to whether the foods are consecrated to idols or not. It is evident from this, however, that it is not illicit to frequent the banquets of unbelievers, much less any civil conversation whatsoever, just as Christ himself did not shrink from the banquets of the Pharisees.

Latin:

v. 27. Εἰ δέ τις ὑμᾶς καλεῖ τῶν ἀπίστων. Non significans scilicet, se sacrificasse. Καλεῖν est ad convivium vocare. Qui ad id mittebantur servi, κλήτορες Graecis, Latinis vocatores.

Καὶ θέλετε πορεύεσθαι. Si omnino ire vultis, admonet tacite, forte melius facturos, si non eant. Ire tamen non prohibet. Supra V. 10.

Πᾶν τὸ παρατιθέμενον ὑμῖν, ἐσθίετε. Id est, edite de appositis, quod lubet. Παρατίθεσθαι vox propria mensae, Marci VIII. 6. 7. Luc. IV. 16. X. 18. XI. 6. Act. XVI. 34.

Μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν. Idem sensus, qui supra 25.

Hic ergo versus ad convivia non idolis sacra, vel religiosa, sed civilia pertinet: Si quis ab infidelibus ad ea invitatur, quod, citra inquisitionem scrupulosam, comedendum sit, quicquid apponitur in mensa. Ne quis religioni sibi ducat in conscientia de cibis, citra disquisitionem, sintne consecrati idolis, vel non, capere quicquid lubet. Patet autem hinc, non illicitum esse, frequentare convivia infidelium, nedum conversationem ci- vilem quamcunque, quemadmodum nec ipse Christus à conviviis Pharisæorum abhorruit.

## 10:28
v. 28. But if anyone says to you, 'This is food offered to idols.' If someone, namely the host, says to you: 'I have sacrificed to Ceres, and for this reason I have invited you to these entrails.' In the manuscript, here for εἰδωλόθυτον (food offered to idols) there is ἱερόθυτον (food offered to a sacred rite). That word is in the Oeconomica, which are attributed to Aristotle. Phrynichus prefers ϑεόθυτον (food offered to a god) to be said rather than ἱερόθυτον.

Do not eat for the sake of that one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience. Namely, because he believes that Ceres is something, and he is confirmed in that opinion by your eating of the things sacrificed. Thus we had συνείδησιν (conscience) regarding a pagan above at VII. 17. Here the καὶ (and) has an explanatory force, as it often does.

Latin:

v. 28. Ἐὰν δέ τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ, τῦτο εἰδωλόθυτόν ἐστι Si quis, nempe convivator, vobis dixerit: Sacrificavi Cereri, & ad hæc exta vos vocavi. In Manuscripto hic pro εἰδωλόθυτον est ἱερόθυτον. Est ea vox in Oeconomicis, quæ Aristoteli tribuuntur. Phrynichus mavult dici ϑεόθυτον quam ἱερόθυτον.

Μὴ ἐσθίετε δι ἐκεῖνον τὸν μηνύσαντα, καὶ τὴν συνείδησιν. Nempe quia ille Cererem esse aliquid credit, & in ea opi- nione confirmatur, te de immolatitiis edente. Sic συνεί- δησιν de pagano habuimus supra VII. 17. Habet hîc καὶ vim ἐξηγητικὴν, ut sæpe.

## 10:29
V. 29. For the earth and its fullness are the Lord's. The earth and the fruits are God's, not Ceres'; do not therefore nourish false opinions: Thus these words can be explained in this place: But perhaps they will be more correctly omitted as having been poorly repeated: For the manuscript does not have them in this place. The Syriac also, the Latin, and the Arabic did not read them.

These things are not to be taken precisely concerning the rites of Ceres; but concerning the idols of anyone whatsoever: And not only concerning the host, but also concerning any other guest, who, moved by a scruple of conscience, warns about the things offered to idols, lest, for instance, either an unbelieving host, believing that an idol is something, when he sees a believer, even though warned, eating the same things, be confirmed in his idolatry, or some weak guest be offended, as if it does not matter much, even if someone, how, and where he pleases, participates in sacrificed foods, and not knowing how to judge the circumstances, sins in the eating of things offered to idols, and even frequents the very feasts sacred to idols; or also lest, thinking that sacrificed meats are entirely illicit, he suffers scandal from the eating of the same. He understands, therefore, the conscience of the one giving the warning, who, if he is an unbeliever, is confirmed in his error: If he is a weak Christian, he will not see it without offense. Nor indeed is there a need for that sentence of the Psalm to be eliminated, which is not read among certain interpreters. Since the Greek codices, which alone are authentic, consistently have it; nor is it inappropriately repeated, even if with a different application. Namely, if one must abstain from those things which have been sacrificed to idols for the sake of the weak conscience of a neighbor out of charity, there will nevertheless not be a lack of other foods in that fullness of the Lord, to whom the whole earth belongs.

But I mean not your own conscience. That is, yours, who know that Ceres is nothing, and that all those things are under the dominion of the Creator.

But that of the other. Of that one who had invited you, ἕτερος (the other), הָרֵעַ (the neighbor), he with whom you have business.

For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? ἕτερος (the other) is one thing, ἄλλος (another) is another. Ἕτερος is, as I said, the one with whom there is business; ἄλλος is any other person with whom there is no business. If some guest knows that those things are sacrificed; but I do not know it, I use my just liberty: if he, on that account, considers me an idolater, he judges me unjustly.

Latin:

V. 29. Τῦ γὰρ κυρίε ἡ γῆ καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς. Terra & fruges Dei sunt, non Cereris; Noli ergò alere falsas opiniones: Ita possunt hæc verba hoc loco exponi: Sed rectius forte omittentur ut malè repetita: Neque enim habet ea hoc loco Manuscriptus. Syrus quoque, Latinus, Arabs, non legerunt.

Non præcise hæc de Cereris sacris; sed quo- rumcunque idolorum accipienda: Nec tantùm de convivatore, sed etiam de conviva quovis alio, qui scrupulo conscientiæ motus id de idolothytis mo- neat, ne scilicet vel infidelis convivator, idolum ali- quod esse credens, ubi viderit fidelem etsi monitum, iisdem vesci, in idolatria sua confirmetur, vel conviva aliquis infirmus offendatur, quasi non mul- tum referat, etiamsi quis, quomodo, & ubi lubeat de cibis immolatitiis participet, & circumstantias dijudicare nesciens, in esu idolothytorum peccet, ac vel ipsas etiam epulas idolis sacras frequentet; aut etiam ne illicitas planè esse carnes immolati- tias existimans ex esu earundem scandalum patia- tur. Conscientiam ergo monitoris intelligit, qui si infidelis est, in errore suo confirmatur: Si infir- mus Christianus, non sine offensione id videbit. Nec verò opus est, eliminetur illa sententia Psal- mi, quæ apud interpretes quosdam haud legitur. Siquidem constanter eam habent codices Græ- ci, qui soli authentici sunt; Nec inconvenien- ter, etsi alia applicatione, ea repetatur. Nimirum si maximè ab his, quæ idolis immolata sunt ob in- firmam proximi conscientiam ex charitate abstinen- dum sit, non defore tamen alios cibos in illa Domini plenitudine, cujus est universa terra.

Συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω ὐχὶ τὴν ἑαυτῦ. Id est, tuam, qui nosti Cererem nihil esse, & omnia ista in dominio esse Creatoris.

Ἀλλὰ τὴν τῦ ἑτέρε. Illius, qui te vocaverat, ἕτερος, הָרֵעַ is, quicum tibi negotium est.

Ἱνα τί γὰρ ἡ ἐλευθερία με κρίνεται ὑπὸ ἄλλης συνειδήσεως; Aliud est ἕτερος, aliud ἄλλος. Ἕτερος is, ut dixi, qui- cum negotium est, ἄλλος quivis alius, quicum negotium non est. Si quis conviva norit, eas res esse immolatitias; ego autem id nesciam, ego libertate justa utor: ille, si me propterea pro idololatra habeat, iniquè me damnat.

## 10:30
v. 30. But if I partake with thanksgiving. If I, not knowing it, of course, through the benefit of God, that is, God giving and granting it, partake of the foods, namely, those set before me. In the manuscript, this εἰ ἐγὼ χάριτι μετέχω (if I partake with thanksgiving) without the δὲ (but) coheres with the preceding.

Why am I slandered? For that for which I give thanks to God. See 1 Tim. IV. 4. There is here an antithesis, such as are many in Paul.

That more subtle distinction between ἕτερον (the other) and ἄλλον (another), I do not know whether it suits Paul's mind. For why should ἕτερος not be the same as ἄλλος, when the reasoning proving it must be appropriate to the thing being proved? For the Apostle says not your own conscience, but that of another, whoever he may be, whether of the host or of the guest: For as far as your own conscience is concerned, it would be safe, with you rightly informed about indifferent matters, and using your liberty, even if it were perhaps judged by another.

For what harm is it that your liberty is judged by another's conscience? It does not harm you, but it can harm a weak neighbor. And therefore I do not say this for your sake, but for your neighbor's, whose weakness must be consulted out of charity. Yet you suffer calumny by no right if you partake of any food whatsoever with thanksgiving. For all are sanctified through prayers, 1 Tim. IV. 4.

Latin:

v. 30. Εἰ δὲ ἐγὼ χάριτι μετέχω. Si ego, id ignorans scilicet, per Dei beneficium, id est, Deo dante & id concedente participo cibos scilicet appo- sitos. In Manuscripto hoc εἰ ἐγὼ χάριτι μετέχω sine δὲ co- hæret cum superioribus.

Τί βλασφημῦμαι; Cur calumniam patior? Ὑπὲρ ὗ ἐγὼ εὐχαρισῶ. Pro re, de qua Deo gratias ago. Vide 1. Tim. IV. 4. Est hic ἀντίθετον, qualia multa apud Paulum.

Subtilior illa inter ἕτερον & ἄλλον distinctio, ne- scio, an Pauli menti conveniat. Cur enim non idem sit ἕτερος ἡ ἄλλος, quum ratio probans con- venire debeat rei probandæ? Dicit enim Apo- stolus non tuam ipsius conscientiam, sed alterius, quicunque ille sit, sive convivatoris, sive convi- væ: Tuam enim conscientiam quod attinet, salva ea foret, te rectè informato de adiaphoris, & liber- tate tuâ utente, etiamsi ab alio forte judicaretur.

Quid enim nocet, ab alterius conscientia tuam ju- dicari libertatem? Tibi id non nocet, sed proxi- mo infirmo nocere potest. Ideoque non tui causa id dico, sed proximi, cujus infirmitati ex charitate debita est consulendum. Nullo tamen jure ca- lumniam pateris, si cum gratiarum actione cibum quemcunque participaris. Omnes enim per preces sanctificantur, 1. Tim. III. 14.

## 10:31
v. 31. Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatsoever you do, do all to the glory of God. That is, take care that by no act of yours, because of circumstances, the honor of God is injured. It is a saying of the Hebrews: Let all your works be for the sake of heaven. It is in Pirke Aboth and in Maimonides.

Latin:

v. 31. Εἴτε ὖν ἐσθίετε, εἴτε πίνετε, εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν Θεῦ ποιεῖτε. Id est, cavete, ne ullo vestro facto ἐκ περιστάσεως Dei ho- nor lædatur. Dictum est Hebræorum כל מעשיך יהוך לשם שמים Est id in Pircke Aboth & apud Maimoni- dem.

## 10:32
v. 32. Be without offense, both to the Jews, and to the Gentiles, and to the church of God. Ἀπρόσκοποι is taken here actively, for one who offends no one, that is, makes no one worse, without a stumbling block. See the prohibitive precept CLXVIII. Acts XXVI. 26, where we dealt with this word. The Jews, if any Christian ate in an idol's temple, or went when called to things sacrificed, used to say: See how truly they say that they worship one God: The Greeks used to say, if they do this, they judge there is nothing evil in idolatry: The Christians, still being held, were easily impelled to defection by some impending evils.

Latin:

v. 32. Ἀπρόσκοποι γίνεσθε καὶ ἰκδαίοις, καὶ Ἕλλησι, καὶ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τῦ Θεῦ. Ἀπρόσκοποι hîc active sumitur, pro eo, qui neminem offendit, id est, deteriorem facit בלא מכשול. Vide præceptum vetans CLXVIII. Act. XXVI. 26. ubi de hac vo- ce egimus. Judæi, si quis Christianus in idoleo ederet, aut ad immolatitia vocatus iret, dicebant: Ecce quam vere illi dicant, se unum Deum colere: Græci dicebant, si illi hoc faciunt, nihil in idololatria mali esse censent: Christiani ad- huc teneri, impendentibus malis aliquibus facilè ad defe- ctionem impellebantur.

## 10:33
v. 33. As I also please all men in all things. Ἀρέσκω here is used metonymically for 'I benefit'. See Rom. XV. 1, 2. Ἀρέσκειν corresponds to the Hebrew words ישר and טוב. The sense is the same as above in IX. 19.

Not seeking my own profit, but that of the many, that they may be saved. See above 24. The eternal salvation of another far outweighs our own conveniences.

He concludes the present subject with general rules, that all things must be done to the glory of God, even in indifferent matters, in eating and drinking, and for the edification of the neighbor, so that, namely, regard is had for the neighbor's salvation, lest any stumbling block be placed before him in such indifferent things. In which matter the Apostle sets himself as an example, because he strives to please all, not through illicit men-pleasing by conniving at sins or by flattering the neighbor, but by adapting himself in free matters to everyone as far as can be done out of Christian liberty, or rather by serving all, as Grotius rightly says, so that the salvation of all may be sought, even with one's own inconvenience; not seeking what is useful to himself, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved: which he taught below in chapter XIII. 5 is the mark of charity. Not only our own conscience, but also that of the neighbor must be considered, lest it be disturbed by words or deeds. Therefore, in food also, something must be subtracted from our liberty if it could not be used without the injury of the weak: Which, however, must always be understood concerning weak brothers, associates of the same religion, and not yet rightly informed in that chapter: on account of others our liberty is not to be disturbed. And that must always be weighed in all other indifferent matters: For it must be seen not only what our own conscience can bear, but what the neighbor's can; as the blessed Balduinus rightly warned.

Latin:

v. 33. Καθὼς κἀγὼ πάντα πᾶσιν ἀρέσκω. Ἀρέσκω hîc est prosum μετωνυμικῶς. Vide Rom. XV. 1. 2. Ἀρέσκειν respondet verbis Hebræis ישר & טוב. Sensus idem, qui supra IX. 19.

Μὴ ζητῶν τὸ ἐμαυτῦ συμφέρον, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν πολλῶν, ἵνα σωθῶσι. Vide supra 24. Æterna salus alterius nostris commodis multum præponderat.

Generalibus regulis materiam præsentem con- cludit, omnia facienda esse ad gloriam Dei, etiam in adiaphoris, in edendo & bibendo, & ad proxi- mi ædificationem, ut nempe salutis proximi habea- tur ratio, ne eidem in ejusmodi indifferentibus ponatur aliquod offendiculum. Quâ in re exem- plum sese sistit Apostolus, quod placere studeat omnibus non per ἀνθρωπαρεσκείαν illicitam, con- nivendo ad peccata, vel abblandiendo proximo, sed in rebus liberis se quibusvis è libertate Christia- na, quoad ejus fieri potest, attemperando, vel po- tius omnibus inserviendo, ut rectè Grotius, ut omni- um salus quæratur, etiam cum proprio incommodo; non quod sibi utile, sed quod multis, ut salvi fiant: quod charitatis esse c. XIII. 5. infra docuit. Non nostræ saltem, sed & proximi conscientiæ ratio ha- benda est, ne ea dictis aut factis turbetur. Idcir- cò in cibis etiam detrahendum est aliquid liberta- ti nostræ, si ea non sine læsione infirmorum usur- pari posset: Quod tamen semper de infirmis fra- tribus, ejusdem religionis sociis, & nondum rectè in isto capite informatis intelligendum est: propter cæteros non est turbanda libertas nostra. Idque in omnibus aliis adiaphoris semper pensi haben- dum est: Non enim saltem quid nostra, sed quid proximi ferat conscientia, videndum est; ut rectè monuit B. Balduinus.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having exhorted them to his imitation, the Apostle praises the observance of his tradition, and warns that, because Christ is the head of the man, and the man the head of the woman, the former should pray with his head uncovered, but the woman with her head covered, which he shows that nature itself teaches; dissuading from contradiction, and rebuking the fact that schisms show themselves in sacred assemblies, and that when the Lord's Supper is to be celebrated, each one snatches his own supper, and some approach it with a full belly, not without contempt for the Church; and having repeated the institution of the Holy Supper, namely, of the bread, and with it the body of Christ, and also the cup, which is the New Testament in the blood of Christ, and the distribution thereof, and having added a reminder concerning the proclamation of the Lord's death, and that unworthy participation should be avoided, and the guilt of the body and blood of the Lord, by one's own due self-examination; since indeed because of unworthy communion the judgments of the Lord are already being felt; finally, he wishes abuses to be abandoned, reserving the disposition of the rest until his arrival.

There are two parts: The former concerning the covering of the woman's head and the uncovering of the man's in prayer, up to verse 17. The latter concerning other things in public assemblies, such as contentions and other things that were happening regarding the celebration of the Holy Supper; for the sake of which the institution of the Holy Supper, as it was received from the Lord, is presented with an exhortation concerning worthy participation in it, up to verse 34.

PART I. Concerning the veiling and uncovering of the head.

v. 1. Be ye followers of me.

The conclusion of the preceding chapter, by which the Apostle had proposed himself as an example of charity, in how he strives to please all, that is, to be profitable to them, is connected in this way with the present chapter, by a general exhortation to the Corinthians to imitate him, whence he praises the observation of his traditions; but with a grain of salt, noting indeed at the same time certain abuses of their assemblies and of the communion of the Holy Supper. And therefore there is no need that this verse be referred to the preceding chapter, but it can conveniently be left to this one according to the Greek Codices. Whence Theophylact exhibits the connection and sense of this passage thus: For if I myself (he says) have followed Christ, who, that He might bestow life upon you, neglected His own; I am by far more to be imitated by you, even if I have not myself rendered you as much as He, who surpasses both me in a certain incomparable goodness, and the others.

Even as I also of Christ.

The Corinthians ought not to despair that they can imitate Paul, if he himself could imitate Christ the Son of God. Not unlike that of Cyrus in Xenophon, book VIII: 'Just as I command you to imitate me, so do you teach those who have authority under you to imitate you.'

The imitation of Christ is to be understood, not insofar as He is set before us as a merit, which no one can imitate; for He trod the winepress alone, Is. LXIII. 3, nor is there any Savior besides Him, Is. XLV. 21, Acts IV. 12. But it is to be understood as an example, 1 Pet. II. 21; which, however, was not done out of fact, or was absolute and perfect in all parts and ways, as Theophylact has already warned, as far as the outcome and completion, even though a constant and sincere purpose and a serious endeavor to imitate Christ in all things were not lacking. For the Apostle himself also complained that he does not always do what he wills, but does what he hates, Rom. VII. 15, and that the flesh lusts against the spirit, Gal. V. 17. The Apostle understands imitation, however, primarily in love. For nothing can make one an imitator of Christ as much as love for one's neighbor, as Chrysostom says here.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Adhortatus ad sui imitationem Apostolus lau- dat observationem traditionis suæ, & monet, ut quia Christus viri, vir autem mulieris caput, is quidem aperto, mulier autem oper- to capite oret, quod naturam ipsam docere, ostendit; A contradictione dehortans, & redarguens, quod in conventibus sacris schi- smata se prodant, quodque cum Cœna Do- mini celebranda, quisque suam cœnam præ- ripiat, ac nonnulli pleno ventre ad eam accedant, non sine comtemtu Ecclesiæ; ac repetita S. Coenae institutione, panis nempe, & cum eo corporis Christi, nec non calicis, qui est N.T. in sanguine Christi, distributio- ne, additaque commonefactione de mortis Domini annunciatione, atque ut evitetur in- digna participatio, & reatus corporis & sanguinis Domini, debita sua ipsius proba- tione; siquidem ob indignam communio- nem jam judicia Domini sentiantur; deni- que abusus abdicari vult, caeterorum dispo- sitionem ad adventum suum reservans.

Partes duae sunt: Prior de capite mulieris ve- lando, viri detegendo in oratione ad v. 17. Po- sterior de aliis in conventibus publicis, quales erant contentiones, & alia, quae circa celebrationem S. Coenae fiebant; quorum causa sacrae Coenae in- stitutio, prout a Domino accepta est, cum adhor- tatione de digna ejusdem participatione, exhi- betur, ad v. 34.

PARS I. De capitis velamine ac detectione.

v. 1. Μιμηταί με γίνεσθε.

Connectitur ita capitis praecedentis conclusio, qua se in exemplum charitatis proposuerat Apo- stolus, quomodo omnibus studeat placere, id est, prodesse, cum praesente capite, adhortatione gene- rali Corinthiorum ad sui imitationem, unde lau- dat observationem traditionum suarum; sed cum grano salis, notans nempe simul abusus quosdam conventuum, & communionis S. Coenae. Ideoque non opus est, ut hic versus ad praecedens caput re- feratur, sed commode juxta Graecos Codd. huic re- linqui potest. Unde Theophyl. hujus loci nexum & sensum ita exhibet: Nam si ipse (inquit) sum Christum sectatus, qui, ut vobis vitam largiretur, suam neglexit; longe magis sum a vobis imitandus, etsi quidem non adeo vos ipse praestiterim, quan- tum ille, qui tum me bonitate quadam incompara- bili, tum caeteros antecedit.

Καθὼς κἀγὼ Χριστᾶ.

Desperare non debent Corinthii, Paulum se posse imita- ri, si ipse Christum Dei Filium imitari potuit. Non dissi- mile illud Cyri apud Xenophontem libro VIII. Ὥσπερ δ᾽ ὑμᾶς κελεύω ἐμὲ μιμεῖσθαι, ὕτως ὑμεῖς τὲς ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν ἀρχὰς ἔχοντας μιμεῖσθαι ὑμᾶς διδάσκετε.

Imitatio Christi, non quatenus sistitur nobis in meritum, quod nemo imitari potest; Torcular enim calcavit Solus, Es. LXIII. 3. nec est praeter ipsum Salvator ullus, Es. XLV. 21. Act. IV. 2. Sed in exemplum 1. Pet. II. 21. intelligenda est; quae tamen non ex affe facta est, aut omnibus partibus & modis absoluta & perfecta fuit, ut jam monuit Theophylactus, quantum ad eventum & comple- mentum, utut propositum constans & sincerum, ac conatus serius haud defuerit Christum per omnia imitandi. Nam & Apostolus ipse questus est, se non agere semper id, quod vult, sed id, quod odio habet, facere, Rom. VII. 15. carnemque concupiscere adversus spiritum, Gal. V. 17. Imitationem autem in dilectione imprimis intelligit Apostolus. Nihil enim aeque potest facere imitatorem Christi, atque dilectio proximi, ut hic Chrysostomus.

## 11:2
v. 2. Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things. Here the discourse turns to those pious ones who had written to him.

Paul is accustomed to soften with milder words those whom he hopes to lead from vices to good, says Theophylact in this place. Providing an example for preachers, that they should either prefix or intermix true praises with sharper rebukes, and approve in their hearers what can be approved, and blame what deserves the severity of correction. This alternation of praise and blame makes the rebuke itself both more acceptable and more wholesome.

And as I delivered to you the traditions, you keep them. We said at Matt. XV. 2 that everything that is taught is called by the name of tradition. But here it signifies certain precepts of that kind which Christ had permitted to the prudence of the Apostles and leaders, pertaining to good order and propriety, such as were not all written down, because it sufficed that they had been brought into use by the authority of the Apostles. Mention is made of some not by design, but incidentally and when the occasion was given in the Epistles. See 1 Thess. II. 2, 15. There were many things in this category not in themselves of such great moment for piety, but in which it was useful for something to be established in common, lest a differing practice should disgrace the Church and sow disputes, and from disputes, as happens, schisms. As for example, it was asked in the assembly of the Church, whether men ought to be with head uncovered or covered, and especially at the time of prayer, or where revelations received from GOD were being expounded to the people? Here, first, as regards women, the matter did not have much difficulty. It appeared sufficiently that it was more becoming for women to have the head covered on account of the modesty of their sex; concerning men, it could be argued in either direction. Just as among the Greeks it is said to be done with a bare head, which is to be in public without fear or shame, so also among the Hebrews. Wherefore, because in Exodus XIV. 8 the Israelites are said to have gone out with a high hand, the Chaldean said with an uncovered head. And Ben Arama says that Moses spoke with God with an uncovered head. And when Moses addressed the people in the name of God, as one prophesying, he did not have a covering on his head, but only a veil spread over his face, lest the brightness should dazzle the eyes of those standing by, Exod. XXXIV, 33. But the Levites in the temple were with covered head, as if fearing that they, being less worthy, might behold the Majesty of GOD. This, however, like other things of the temple, the Jews transferred to the Synagogue. Among the Greeks it was the custom to perform sacred rites with an uncovered head. For one must read in Macrobius I. Sat. 8. That there divine service is performed with an uncovered head according to the Greek rite appears from a passage in the 10th chapter of the same book, where it is likewise treated of Saturn, and it is said that a sacrifice is made to him with an uncovered head, by a foreign rite, that is, a Greek one. And from the passage III. 8, where he says that Varro states that this is the custom of the Greeks, to sacrifice with an uncovered head: Plutarch, dealing with the same rites of Saturn in his Roman Questions, says with an uncovered head. Festus testifies that it was customary to say that this makes for light. In the same way, that is, with an uncovered head, it is also testified that it was customary to sacrifice to Hercules at the great altar, besides Macrobius in the said book III. 61, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 1. Doubtless because that sacred rite had been instituted by Evander, a Greek man. But Aeneas brought the contrary custom into Italy, of performing sacred rites with a veiled head, lest any evil omen should meet the eyes or ears, as Virgil teaches us in Aeneid III. and Servius to him, and Aurelius Victor in the Breviary, but also Plutarch in his Roman Questions. And Plautus also mentions this custom in certain Comedies, as he is wont to mix Roman things with Greek. Paul, writing to the Greek Corinthians, prefers the Greek custom and brings forward reasons such as the nature of the business required: From Paul's prescription, the ancient Christians kept this custom perpetually. Tertullian in the Apology: Looking up to heaven, we Christians with hands outstretched, because we are harmless, with head bare, because we do not blush, finally without a prompter, because we pray from the heart, etc. The custom of the north of uncovering heads as a sign of reverence has no relevance here, which, although it spread widely through the German nations, was nevertheless unknown to the Jews, and to the Greeks, and to ancient Italy.

Therefore the Papists, Salmero and Stapleton, rashly strive to prove their dogmatic traditions from this passage. For the matter of the treatment testifies that the Apostle is looking only to ceremonial ones, such as were those concerning praying with head uncovered or covered, and other middle and indifferent things, as Grotius acknowledges, that these traditions concern only those things which pertained to good order and propriety. Nor could Justinian deny it. Not to mention that those traditions could have been delivered in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, which we have already said is lost: And that no Papist can teach, if it were admitted that there were some dogmatic ones, that they are not contained in the Canonical Scripture of the New Testament, or that they are those which the Tridentine synod defined as Apostolic, not written, to be received with equal affection of piety as the Sacred Scriptures. Moreover, that there was doubt concerning the attire of women no less than of men in prayer and prophecy appears sufficiently from the Apostolic decision, and will be established in the progress. Concerning the Greek custom, the Greek Fathers [say] otherwise than Grotius, not indeed regarding sacrifices, but regarding prayers and prophecies. Namely, that it was either a constitution of the Greek law, or the ancestral custom of that nation, and an ancient habit, that men should let their hair grow long while supplicating and prophesying, as Theophylact has it; women, says Chrysostom, indeed prayed and prophesied with head uncovered and bare. For women also prophesied then, but men let their hair grow, as those who were engaged in Philosophy, and covered their head while praying and prophesying: Which indeed was both the law of the Greeks. Since therefore he admonished them concerning all these things when he was present: And perhaps some had heard, but others had not obeyed, therefore also through an epistle, pouring words into them again like a good and wise physician, he corrects the sin.

Latin:

v. 2. Ἐπαινῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ, ὅτι πάντα με μέμνησθε. Hic sermo ad illos pios se vertit, qui ad ipsum scripserant.

Solet Paulus mitioribus verbis lenire, quos a vi- tiis sperat ad bonum traducere, inquit h. l. Theo- phylactus. Exemplum praebens concionatoribus, ut objurgationibus acrioribus laudes veras vel praemittant vel intermisceant, & probent in suis auditoribus, quæ probari posfunt, culpent, quæ correptionis severitatem merentur. Facit hæc al- ternatio laudis & vituperii objurgationem ipsam acceptiorem juxtà & salubriorem.

Καὶ καθὼς παρέδωκα ὑμῖν τὰς παραδόσεις κατέχετε. Παραδόσεως nomine vocari omne id, quod docetur di- ximus ad Matth. XV. 2. Hîc verò significat præcepta quæ- dam ejus generis, quæ Christus Apostolorum & ἡγεμόνων prudentiæ permiserat, pertinentia ad ἐυταξίαν & τὸ πρέπον, qualia non omnia perscripta sunt, quia sufficiebat ea au- toritate Apostolorum in usum esse perducta. Quorundam non ex proposito, sed obiter & occasione data in Epistolis fit mentio. Vide 1. Thess. II. 2. 15. Multa erant in hoc genere per se non ita magni ad pietatem momenti, sed in quibus utile erat aliquid in commune constitui, ne discre- pans usus dedecoraret Ecclesiam, disputationes & ex dis- putationibus, ut sit, schismata sereret. Ut ecce quære- batur in Ecclesiæ conventu, homines aperto esse deberent an operto capite, & specialiter precum tempore, aut ubi revelationes à DEO acceptæ exponebantur populo? Hic primum fœminas quod attinet, res non multum habebat difficultatis. Satis apparebat, magis decere fœminas operto esse capite ob pudorem sexus, de viris poterat in utramque partem disferi. Sicut apud Græcos γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ fieri di- citur, quod palam sit sine metu aut pudore, ita & Hebræis. Quare quod Exodi XIV. 8. Israelitæ dicuntur egressi ma- nu elata, Chaldæus dixit בריש גלי. Et Ben Arama Mo- sem dicit cum Deo collocutum בראש גלוי capite aper- to. Et cum populum alloqueretur Moses Dei nomine, ὡς προφητεύων, non tegmen habuit in capite, sed velum tantum oppansum vultui, ne fulgor præftingueret adstantium oculos, Exod. XXXIV, 33. At Levitæ in templo tecto erant capite, quasi metuentes, ne ipsi minus digni DEI Maje- statem conspicerent. Hoc verò, sicut alia templi, ad Syn- agogam transtulere Judæi. Apud Græcos mos fuit, sacra facere capite aperto. Legendum enim apud Macrobiurn I. Sat. 8. Illic Græco ritu capite aperto res divina fit, apparet ex loco ejusdem libri capite 10. ubi itidem de Saturno agi- tur, & sacrum ei fieri dicitur aperto capite, ritu peregrino, id est, Græco. Et ex loco III. 8. ubi Varronem ait dicere, Græci hoc esse moris, aperto capite sacrificare : Ἀπαρακα- λύπτῳ κεφαλῇ ait de iisdem Saturni sacris agens Plutarchus in Romanis quæstionibus. Lucem facere id dici solitum Festus testatur. Eodem modo, id est, aperto capite, etiam Herculi in ara maxima sacrum fieri solere testatur præter Macrobiurn dicto libro III. 61. Dionysius Halicarnassen- sis libro 1. Nimirum quia id sacrum institutum erat ab Evandro homine Græco. Sed Æneas contrarium morem in Italiam intulit, sacra faciendi velato capite, ne quod ma- lum omen oculis aut auribus obveniret, ut Virgilius nos docet Æneidos III. & ad eum Servius, & in Breviatio Au- relius Victor, sed & Plutarchus in Romanis quæstionibus. Et ejus moris etiam Plautus meminit in Comœdiis quibus- dam, ut solet admiscere Romana Græcis. Paulus Græcis Corinthiis scribens, Græcum præfert morem, & causas affert, quales ferebat negotii natura: Ex Pauli præscripto perpetuo hunc morem tenuere Christiani veteres. Ter- tullianus Apologetico : Illuc suspicientes Christiani mani- bus expansis, quia innocui, capite nudo, quia non erubescimus, denique sine monitore, quia de pectore oramus &c. Nihil huc pertinet mos septentrionis in reverentiæ signum capita nudandi, qui quanquam per Germanicas nationes latè ma- navit, & Judæis tamen, & Græcis, & veteri Italiæ fuit in- cognitus.

Temerè ergò Papistæ, Salmero & Stapletonus ex hoc loco traditiones suas dogmaticas probare satagunt. Nam ceremoniales tantum respicere Apostolum, tractationis materia testatur, quales scilicet erant de orando aperto vel operto capite, aliisque rebus mediis & indifferentibus, ut agno- scit Grotius, has παραδόσεις tantum ea concer- nere, quæ pertinebant ad ἐυταξίαν & τὸ πρέπον. Nec diffiteri potuit Justinianus. Ne de eo di- cam, quod traditiones illæ traditæ esse potue- rint in prima Epistola ad Corinthios, quam deper- ditam esse jam diximus : Quodque nemo Papi- starum docere queat, si dogmaticas nonnullas fuisse admitteretur, non contineri eas in Scriptu- ra Canonica N. Testamenti, vel eas esse, quas ceu Apostolicas, non scriptas pari pietatis affectu cum Scripturis Sacris suscipiendas esse definivit Tri- dentina synodus. Cæterum de mulieris habitu non minus quam virorum in oratione, & prophetiâ dubium fuisse e decisione Apostolica satis apparet, & in progressu constabit. De Græco more aliter, quam Grotius, Patres Græci, non quidem quoad sacrificia, sed quoad preces & prophetias. Quod nempe Græcæ legis vel constitutio, vel ejus gentis mos patrius fuerit, & prisca consuetudo, ut viri comam supplicando & vaticinando promitterent, ut habet Theophylactus, mulieres quidem, inquit Chrysostomus, aperto & nudo capite orabant, & prophetabant. Etenim prophetabant & tunc mu- lieres, viri autem comam alebant, ut qui in Philo- sophia versarentur, & caput operiebant orantes & prophetantes : Quod quidem erat utrumque legis Græcorum. Quoniam ergo de his omnibus eos, quum adeffet, admonuit : Et forte alii quidem audierant, alii vero non paruerant, propterea etiam per episto- lam eis rursus tanquam bonus & sapiens medicus verba infundens, peccatum corrigit.

## 11:3
v. 3. But I want you to know, that of every man.

Namely, the Christian.

the head is Christ.

Commanding him and influencing through the Spirit. See what was brought forward above X. 17.

But the head of the woman is the man.

This ought not to be understood only of married women, but of the whole sex, as Tertullian interprets in the book where he shows that even virgins must be veiled in the Church, and he says that this was observed perpetually at Corinth from this prescription of Paul. Our ancestors, says M. Porcius Cato in Livy XXXIV, wished women to conduct no business, not even private, without an author. To be in the hand of parents, brothers, husbands. The same custom was honorable among Hebrew women. Therefore a harlot is called שלטת in Deut. XVI. 30, that is, commanding herself. This is inserted by way of parenthesis. For the discourse returns to that which had preceded.

But the head of Christ is God.

Thus Christ commands the Christian man, just as God commands Christ. See above III. 23.

Head is not taken here according to physical analogy: how the members of the human body, as if from a source, draw spirit and vigor from the head to which they are subject: but according to political signification, just as a magistrate is the head of his subjects by reason of power and eminence, which, as it shines forth, and is above every mode and measure of comparison in Christ over men, however supreme and most refined: so a certain image of power and eminence shines forth in men over the female sex in its own way and degree. But God is called the head of Christ not by reason of his divine nature, because the Father and the Son are one, John X. 11, but by reason of his human nature, according to which the Father is greater, John XIV. 28. And therefore the Son is also to be subjected to the Father, 1 Cor. XV. 28. Which the blessed Hunnius observes against the Eutychians and Schwenckfeldians in the cited passages, no. V.

Latin:

v. 3. Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς εἰδέναι, ὅτι παντὸς ἀνδρὸς.

Nempe Christiani.

ἡ κεφαλὴ ὁ χριστός ἐστι.

Imperans ipsi & per Spiritum influens. Vide adducta supra X. 17.

Κεφαλὴ δὲ γυναικὸς ὁ ἀνήρ.

Hoc non de nuptis tantum debet intelligi, sed de toto sexu, quomodo interpretatur Tertullianus libro, quo ostendit, etiam virgines in Ecclesia velandas, & id obser- vatum ait perpetuo Corinthi ex hoc Pauli præscripto. Majores nostri, ait M. Porcius Cato apud Livium XXXIV. nullam, ne privatam quidem, rem agere fœminas sine autore voluerunt. In manu effe parentum, fratrum, virorum. Idem mos honestis apud Hebræos fœminis. Ideo meretrix dicitur שלטת Deut. XVI. 30. id est, sibimet imperans. Hoc per παρένθεσιν interjectum est. Nam redit oratio ad id, quod antecesserat.

Κεφαλὴ δὲ χριστοῦ ὁ Θεός.

Ita viro Christiano Christus imperat, sicut Christo Deus. Vide supra III. 23.

Caput hic non accipitur secundum analogiam physicam : Quomodo ex capite tanquam fonte membra humani corporis subjecta spiritum & vigorem hauriunt : Sed juxta significationem politicam, prouti magistratus subditorum caput est ratione potestatis & eminentiæ, quæ ut reful- get, & supra omnem comparationis modum & mensuram in Christo præ viris utut summis, ac politissimis : Ita potestatis & eminentiæ quoddam quasi simulacrum in viris præ fœmineo sexu suo quodam modo atque gradu refulget. Caput au- tem Christi Deus dicitur non ratione divinæ na- turæ, quia Pater & Filius unum sunt, Joh. X. 11. sed ratione naturæ humanæ, juxta quam Pater major est, Joh. XIV. 28. Atque ideo etiam Patri subjiciendus Filius, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Quod contra Eutychianos, & Schwenckfeldianos observat B. Hunnius in LL. CC. n. V.

## 11:4
v. 4. Every man praying or prophesying.

That is, even then when he prays or expounds the revelations of God. In public, Hebrew men were always with covered head, Musar. 6. So also among the Greeks and Romans.

Having [something] down from his head.

So also Mark said κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς XIV. 3. Where Matthew says ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν XXVI. 7. A cap or hat is understood.

He dishonors his own head.

That is, he does an injury to himself. Thus to your head, that is, to yourself among the Latins.

More correctly, Christ is understood by the head, who was just now called the head of the man. For Christ himself is in a certain way affected by ignominy from this. For since the man by reason of his authority is the image of Christ, certainly if he so little esteems the symbol of liberty and dominion, namely a free and unencumbered and uncovered head, this redounds indirectly to the contempt

of Christ, whose image he ought to be by the usurpation of a symbol, which signifies liberty and power, as B. Hunnius has well observed here. Theophylact has both senses: But in what way is his head dishonored? Namely, when a Prince, born a man and powerful, subjects himself to the dominion of another. For to cover the head is to impose a yoke upon the head. That veil of the head is also a sign of servitude, not of power. Or otherwise: Someone dishonors the head, that is, Christ, who is his head, and disgraces him, when he diminishes himself.

Latin:

v. 4. Πᾶς ἀνὴρ προσευχόμενος ἢ προφητεύων.

Id est, etiam tunc cum precatur, aut revelationes Dei ex- ponit. In publico viri Hebræi semper tecto erant capite, Musar. 6. Sic & apud Græcos & Romanos.

Κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων.

Sic & κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς dixit Marcus XIV. 3. Ubi Mat- thæus ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν XXVI. 7. subauditur pileum vel ga- lerum.

Καταισχύνει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κεφαλήν.

Id est, sibi ipsi injuriam facit. Sic capiti tuo, id est, tibi apud Latinos.

Rectius per caput intelligitur Christus, qui mo- do viri caput dicebatur. Christus enim ipse hinc quodammodo ignominia afficitur. Nam cum vir ratione potestatis sit imago Christi, utique si symbolum libertatis & Dominii, nempe libe- rum & expeditum, apertumque caput tam flocci- pendit, per indirectum cedit hoc in despectum-

Christi, cujus imago esse debebat ufurpatione symboli, quod libertatem potestatemque significat, ut probè hic observavit B. Hunnius. Theophylactus utrumque sensum habet: Verum quo pacto caput ejus deturpat? Nempe cum Princeps natus sit vir & potens, alterius se ditioni addicat. Caput namque obtegere, capiti est jugum imponere. Capitis etiam velamen illud servitutis est signum, non potestatis. Vel aliter: Deturpat aliquis caput, id est, Christum, qui suum caput est, & dehonesta t, cum se imminuit.

## 11:5
v. 5. But every woman praying or prophesying.

Just as in the Old Testament there were prophetesses, such as Miriam the sister of Moses, Exod. XV. 20, Deborah, Judg. V, the wife of Isaiah, ch. VIII. 3, Huldah, 2 Kings XXII. 14. So also in the New; as the daughters of Philip, Acts XXI. 9, and others afterwards. Now such women were accustomed to expound sacred prophecies even publicly, as appears from the cited passages of the Old Testament. Wherefore, what Paul forbids, that women should perform the office of teaching in 1 Cor. XIV. 28, is to be understood with an exception, unless they have a special command from God.

With uncovered head.

Plutarch speaks in this way too, for that which the Latins call 'with open head.' A woman among the Hebrews was not seen in public unless with covered head, Musar. 37. See Gen. XXIV. 65. Hence to uncover a woman's head is to treat her contumeliously, as a most learned man has noted from Phesichtha on Lev. XXIV. 19 and from Rabbi Solomon on Num. V. 18. Among the Greeks, the attire of women in public seems to have been various, just as Plutarch teaches us in his Roman Questions that it was various among the Romans. Paul preferred that which was most consistent with modesty.

She dishonors her own head.

Interpret as above in 4.

Nay, it is not the woman's own head, but the husband, whom the Apostle had called the head of the wife, that is understood. For he would be dishonored if the woman appeared with uncovered head, as if she did not acknowledge the husband as head, nor wished to be subject to him. For the veil of the head was a sign of that.

Latin:

v. 5. Πᾶσα δὲ γυνὴ προσευχομένη ἢ προφητεύουσα.

Sicut in Veteri Testamento fuere fœminæ προφήτιδες, ut Maria soror Mosis Exod. XV. 20. Debora, Judic. V. Uxor Esaiæ, c. VIII. 3. Holda, 2. Reg. XXII. 14. Ita & in Novo; Ut filiæ Philippi, Act. XXI. 9. & aliæ postea. Solebant autem tales etiam publicè prophetias sacras exponere, ut apparet dictis Veteris Testamenti locis. Quare quod Paulus vetat fœminas docendi munere fungi intra XIV. 28. Id intelligendum cum exceptione, nisi speciale Dei mandatum habeant.

Ἀκατακαλύπτῳ τῇ κεφαλῇ.

Sic & Plutarchus loquitur, pro eo, quod Latini dicunt aperto capite. Fœmina Hebræis in publico non aspiciebatur nisi operto capite, Musar. 37. Vide Genes. XXIV. 65. Inde caput mulieris nudare est eam contumeliose tractare, ut ex Phesichtha ad Levit. XXIV. 19. & ex Rabbi Salomone ad Num. V. 18. notavit vir eruditissimus. Apud Græcos videtur varius fuisse in publico fœminarum habitus, ut & apud Romanos fuisse varium, Plutarchus in Romanis nos docet. Paulus id prætulit, quod maximè conveniebat verecundiæ.

Καταισχύνει τὴν κεφαλὴν ἑαυτῆς.

Interpretare, ut supra 4.

Imo non mulieris caput proprium, sed vir, quem caput uxoris dixerat Apostolus, intelligitur. Hic enim dehonestaretur, si mulier capite operto compareret, quasi virum caput non agnosceret, nec ei subjici vellet. Nam ejus signum erat capitis velamen.

## 11:6
v. 6. For if she is shorn.

Which was not accustomed to be done to women, unless when they wished to appear shameful, as in mourning, Deut. XXI. 12. Suetonius in Caligula: That certain petty kings had laid aside their beards and shaved the heads of their wives as a sign of extreme mourning. It is more to be shaved than to be shorn.

But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved.

The beauty of form is hair, according to Petronius. Servius on Aen. 1: 'Cæsaries' (hair) is said to be from 'cadendo' (falling). Therefore it belongs only to men.

Let her be covered.

Let her be with covered head: in the Church, of course, which custom is retained according to the prescription of Paul. Clement, Constitutions, books 27. Let women pray with their heads covered (for so it befits the order of women).

From this Chrysostom and Theophylact gather that a woman must always be veiled. He shows that it is necessary for her to have her head covered not only at the time of prayer, but also perpetually. In the case of a man, however, the discourse treats not of a head covering, but of hair. For he commands him to cover his head only when he prays. But he forbids him to grow his hair long at all times. Therefore, just as he said of the woman, 'but if she is not veiled, let her be shorn,' so also of the man, 'if he grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him.' He did not say, 'if he covers himself,' but 'if he grows his hair long.'

Latin:

v. 6. Εἰ γάρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐξυρημένη.

Quod fœminis fieri non solebat, nisi cum turpes videri vellent, ut in luctu, Deut. XXI. 12. Suetonius in Caligula: Regulos quosdam barbam posuisse & uxorum capita rasisse ad indicium ultimi luctus. Plus est radi, quam tonderi.

Εἰ δὲ αἰσχρὸν γυναικὶ τὸ κείρασθαι ἢ ξυρᾶσθαι.

Formæ decus capilli apud Petronium. Servius ad Æn. 1. A cadendo dicta cæsaries. Ergo tantum virorum est.

Κατακαλυπτέσθω.

Operto sit capite: In Ecclesia scilicet, qui mos ex præscripto Pauli retentus. Clemens constitutionum ll. 27. Αἱ γυναῖκες κατακεκαλυμμέναι τὴν κεφαλὴν (ὡς γὰρ ἁρμόζει γυναικῶν τάξει) προσευχέτωσαν.

Ex eo colligit Chrysost. & Theophyl. fœminam semper vèlandam esse. Ostendit, quod non solum tempore orationis, sed etiam perpetuo eam oportet habere caput opertum. In viro autem, non de capitis tegumento, sed de coma tractat oratio. Nam tunc solum jubet caput operire, quando orat. Comam autem alere semper prohibet. Propterea sicut dixit de muliere, si autem non velatur, tondeatur: Ita etiam de viro, si comam nutriat, ignominia est illi. Non dixit, si operiatur, sed si comam nutriat.

## 11:7
v. 7. For a man indeed.

Man here is spoken of regarding the whole sex, as is woman.

He ought not to cover his head.

It does not befit a man to be with a covered head.

Being the image and glory of God.

Man is made to the likeness of God, namely, having authority even over his wife, as Isidore rightly explains this, saying that it is for this reason that it is not said of the woman that she was created to the image of God. Gen. 1:26, 27. Rightly, therefore, is man called the glory of God, that is, the brightness, the effulgence, the radiation. It is a Hebrew idiom. For the Hebrews called the effulgence of the divine Majesty the ray כבוד, and the Hellenists called it δόξα, as in Exod. 16:10, 33:18, 22, 40:34, 35, Num. 14:11, 16:20, 42, Ezech. 2:1, 3:23, 8:4, 10:4. Augustine, in Sermon 4 in the octave of Easter: 'Their heads are to be uncovered, which is a sign of liberty.'

But the woman is the glory of the man. Something less than the man, as the moon is a light less than the sun. 'The female is an imperfect male,' according to the philosophers. The mistress of the house commands her household, but in the name of her husband.

To others, 'image and glory' is, through hendiadys, the image of glory or the glorious image of God, in which the greater majesty of God and His glory shine forth. B. Hunnius concludes from this that these things concern not virgins, but married women. It pertains to decorum, he says, that a woman be veiled, as being subject to her husband: whereas it is not so precisely required of virgins that they be veiled, because they still enjoy their liberty, nor are they subject to husbands as wives are, and therefore it is permitted to them to use a garland, the symbol of their virginity. Although this may be lawful, and the Apostle did not wish to cast shackles upon Christian liberty here, yet in opening his mind to the Corinthians concerning decorum, he includes virgins no less than unmarried women, the noun designating the sex, not the status. Just as these things pertain equally to men outside of marriage as well as in marriage. The reasons indeed seem to be more appropriate to those married regarding the authority of the husband and the subjection of the wife: But others, however, are general: and those living outside of marriage, yet are ordained by divine ordinance to marriage, so that they may pass to its vows. And therefore, in a similar position, as far as the present matter is concerned, they are held to be like those married.

Theophylact makes this the nerve of the argument, that man is the glory of God and the image of God. It is necessary, therefore, that the prince of the greatest Emperor should appear in the presence of the Emperor with the insignia of his office, that is, with his head free and uncovered. For that is an indication that this man is subject to the dominion of no human thing, but just like the image of GOD, he commands all.

But how is the woman the glory of the man? Theophylact interprets it thus: That is, under the power of the man. It is necessary, therefore, that she herself should appear with the insignia of servitude, which consist in the veiling of the head. Our blessed Hunnius explains this more clearly: He says that the woman is the glory of the man, since in the subjection of the wife appears, from the nature of correlatives, the glory, eminence, and power of the man over the woman, since the woman herself also receives her honor and ornament from the man, shining with the rays of her husband. Therefore, let her be subject to the man, and let her not be ashamed to testify to her subjection by the veiling of her head. Others tighten the nerve thus: The glory of God is to be revealed; but the glory of man is to be hidden. And therefore, since the woman is the glory of the man, but the man is the glory of GOD, it follows that the woman should be veiled, not the man. But the former connection of the Apostolic reasoning is more appropriate and is more elegant. By some, the woman is called the glory of the man, that is, a glorious image, because the woman was made for the glory of the man from the man, as his image, whence she is subject to him. But the Apostle subsequently urges this reason. Therefore, the explanation of Theophylact is to be preferred. Salmero says that the woman is a notable ornament of the man, inasmuch as she was given to the man both as a help for procreating children and for propagating the family, and as a subject matter, and as it were a domain, in which the man may exercise his jurisdiction and dominion.

But it is absurd that Anacletus, in his Epistle to the Bishops of Gaul, restricts the opinion of the Apostle to the Clergy (which Cornelius admits he speaks not of Clerics alone, but of all men in general).

It is more absurd what Cornelius brings forward concerning the head of priests in the New Testament not being covered, since a priest in the Old Testament had to be covered with a tiara, that the Messiah, our head, was covered and hidden in the Old Testament, and is conspicuous and manifest in the New Testament. The high priest in the Old Testament was a type of Christ, the only priest of the New Testament, not of the Mass-sacrificers, whom Scripture does not know, nay, rejects, acknowledging only the one priest of the New Testament. Finally, it is most absurd what he says about his sacrificers, that they do not cover their head while they sacrifice; but, as Rupertus says, they roll it over the mouth of the chasuble. For they do not uncover the head entirely everywhere.

Latin:

v. 7. Ἀνὴρ μὲν γὰρ.

Vir hic de toto sexu dicitur, ut & mulier.

Οὐκ ὀφείλει κατακαλύπτεσθαι τὴν κεφαλήν.

Non decet virum esse velato capite.

Εἰκὼν καὶ δόξα Θεῦ ὑπάρχων.

Vir ad Dei effigiem factus, nempe imperio etiam in uxorem, ut rectè hoc explicat Isidorus, dicens, ideò de muliere non dici, conditam eam ad Dei imaginem. Gen. I. 26. 27. Merito ergo vir vocatur Θεῦ δόξα, id est, ἀπαύγασμα, effulgentia, radiatio. Est Hebraica loquutio. Nam Hebræi effulgentiam divinæ Majestatis radium vocabant כבוד Hellenistæ δόξαν, ut Exod. XVI. 10. XXXIII. 18. 22. XL. 34. 35. Num. XIV. 11. XVI. 20. 42. Ezech. II. 1. III. 23. VIII. 4, X. 4. Augustinus sermone IV. in octava Paschæ : Revelanda sunt capita eorum, quod est indicium liber- tatis.

Γυνὴ δὲ δόξα ἀνδρός ἐστι. Minus aliquid viro, ut luna lumen minus sole. Τὸ θῆ- λυ, ἄῤῥεν ἀτελὲς Philosophis. Imperat materfamilias suæ familiæ, sed viri nomine.

Aliis imago & gloria per hendyaden imago glo- riæ vel gloriosa Dei, in qua major elacet Dei ma- jestas & gloria ejus. B. Hunnius inde concludit, hæc non virgines, sed mulieres concernere. Ad decorum, inquit, pertinet, ut mulier velata sit, tanquam viro suo subdita : Cum quidem à virgi- nibus non ita præcise exigatur, ut velentur, quia etiamnum libertate sua gaudent, nec ut uxores vi- ris subditæ sunt, ideoque licet eis uti serto, virgini- tatis suæ symbolo. Quod etsi licitum sit, neque enim libertati Christianæ hic compedes injicere voluit Apostolus, hîc tamen Corinthiis suam mentem de decoro aperiens, non minus virgines, quàm mulieres non maritatas complectitur, no- mine sexum, non statum designante. Uti viros non minus extra conjugium, quàm in conjugio æqualiter hæc attinent. Rationes quidem viden- tur magis convenire conjugatis de imperio mari- ti & subjectione conjugis : Sed aliæ tamen genera- les sunt : & extra conjugium viventes, ordinati tamen sunt, divinâ ordinatione ad conjugium, ut ad ejus vota transire possint. Ideoque parili lo- co, quantum ad rem præsentem, cum conjugatis habentur.

Nervum argumenti, quod vir Dei gloria sit, & Dei imago, hunc facit Theophyl. Oportet itaque Imperatoris maximi Principem in Imperatoris con- spectu, cum magistratus insignibus apparere, id est, capite libero & expedito. Id enim indicio est, rei nullius humanæ ditioni subesse hunc virum, sed per- inde ac DEI imaginem cunctis imperitare.

Sed quomodo mulier gloria viri? Theophyla- ctus ita interpretatur : Id est, sub viri potestate. Necesse itaque est, hanc ipsam cum servitutis insi- gnibus comparere, quæ in capitis velamento consi- stunt. Luculentius autem hoc exponit B. Hun- nius noster : Mulierem gloriam esse viri ait, quandoquidem in subjectione uxoris apparet, ex natura correlatorum, gloria, eminentia & po- testas viri super mulierem, quin à viro ipsa quo- que mulier decus suum & ornamentum accipit, coruscans radiis mariti. Ergò sit subjecta viro, suamque subjectionem non pudeat illam testari capitis sui velamine. Alii nervum sic constrin- gunt : Gloria Dei revelanda est; hominis verò gloria occultanda. Ideoque cum mulier sit glo- ria viri; vir vero DEI, sequitur, quod mulier velanda sit, non vir. Sed prior nexus consequen- tiæ Apostolicæ tractationi magis convenit, estque concinnior. Quibusdam mulier dicitur gloria vi- ri, id est, imago gloriosa, quod mulier facta sit ad gloriam viri ex viro, velut ejus imago, unde illi subjecta sit. Sed hanc rationem deinde urget Apostolus. Explicatio ergò Theophylacti præ- ferenda. Salmero dicit, mulierem esse insigne or- namentum viri, utpote viro datam tùm in adjuto- rium ad procreandum liberos & ad propagandam familiam, tùm in materiam, & quasi ditionem, in quam vir exerceat suam jurisdictionem & do- minium.

Ineptum verò est, quod Anacletus Epist. ad Episc. Galliæ Apostoli sententiam ad Clerum restringit (quem vero non de solis Clericis, sed omnibus viris in genere loqui, fatetur Cornelius)

Ineptius est, quod Cornelius, de capite sacerdotum in N. T. non velando, cum sacerdos in V. Testamento tiará tegi debuerit, adfert, quod Messias caput nostrum in V. T. velatus fuerit & absconditus, in Novo Testamento conspicuus sit & manifestus. Summus sacerdos in V. T. Christi typus fuit, unici sacerdotis N. T. non sacrificulorum Missaticorum, quos ignorat, imò reprobat, unicum sacerdotem tantùm agnoscens N.T. scriptura. Ineptissimum denique est, quod de sacrificulis suis ait, eos non tegere caput, dum sacrificant; sed, ut Rupertus ait, super os casulæ revolvere. Non enim ubique retegunt omninò caput.

## 11:8
v. 8. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. And this is from Moses, Gen. II. 21.

Latin:

v. 8. Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἀνὴρ ἐκ γυναικὸς, ἀλλὰ γυνὴ ἐξ ἀνδρός. Et hoc ex Mose Gen. II. 21.

## 11:9
v. 9. For indeed man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man. If God had wished there to be one human, it should have been a man, not a woman: Since man is more apt for human actions, as he has less moisture, but more heat. But because of that: Increase and multiply, a woman was also needed.

That argument, that a man has less moisture but more heat, does not fit a perfect temperament, such as both had in the state of integrity. A twofold cause for the preeminence of the man is given by the Apostle: The one from the origin of the woman; that the first man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man: The other from the end for which the woman was created; namely, that the man was not created for the woman. For he already existed in his own perfection; but the woman was created for the man, as being for the help of the man.

Latin:

v. 9. Καὶ γὰρ ὐκ ἐκτίσθη ἀνὴρ διὰ τὴν γυναῖκα, ἀλλὰ γυνὴ διὰ τὸν ἄνδρα. Si unum Deus esse hominem voluisset, vir is esse debuit, non mulier: Quin vir aptior ad actiones humanas, quippe humoris minus habens, plus autem caloris. Sed propter illud: Crescite & multiplicamini, fœmina quoque opus fuit.

Ratio illa, quod vir humoris minus habeat, plus autem caloris, perfecto temperamento, quale erat utrique in statu integritatis, non congruit. Causa præcellentiæ viri gemina redditur ab Apostolo: Altera ab origine fœminæ; Quod non ex muliere vir primus sit; sed mulier ex viro: Altera à fine conditæ mulieris; quod nempe non vir propter mulierem conditus. Ille enim jam sua perfectione constabat; sed mulier propter virum, utpote in adjutorium viri.

## 11:10
v. 10. For this reason the woman ought to have authority on her head. A metonymy frequent among the Hebrews, where the sign receives the name of the thing signified. For the veil is a sign of the authority under which the woman is. And conversely, the man, who has authority over the woman, is for that reason called her veil, as some think, Genesis XX. 16. The Greek sentiment is: Nature has not given to woman to rule.

Therefore, because of modesty and decency, not only were Jewish women accustomed to be veiled; as Tertullian says in De corona militis, ch. 4, that for Jewish women the veil of the head is so customary that they are known by it, but also Gentile women, as the same author observes in the book De velandis virginibus, ch. XVII, which book he wrote to teach that all women, not only married but also unmarried, must be veiled, notwithstanding any custom whatsoever, in which, however, he does not deserve assent, because the Apostle does not impose this upon all women by way of a precept; but he explains what is fitting, and that primarily because of the state of the Corinthians, where wives were addicted not only to luxury but also to the worship of Venus, enticers of lovers and shameless, walking about with open face and head and showing off their curls, which custom some of the converts imitated as if it were ancestral, elegant, and decent. Such uncovering of the head, therefore, by which curls are displayed, is noted here, and for that reason a veil for the head is required by the arguments brought forward by the Apostle. For he desires this in them, as the blessed Balduinus notes here, that they were prophesying with hair let down, not without a sign of lasciviousness, and in imitation of the Gentiles, whose pythonesses uttered their prophecies with these gestures and this adornment of the body. The Apostle speaks according to the custom of that place, where the uncovering of the head was a sign of liberty, but the covering a sign of servitude, whereas with us now, conversely, the uncovering of the head is a sign of humility, just as standing with covered head is a sign of authority. The Apostle certainly does not prescribe a fixed and immutable rite for all churches, but teaches what is most fitting for the Corinthians and what appears more decorous in itself. He does not prejudice a received custom that is free from scandal, and therefore he does not wish a contention to be stirred up about these things, v. 6. Finally, there is no doubt that necessity and reasons of health are also excepted, provided that the suspicion of pride, luxury, and singularity is avoided as far as possible.

Because of the Angels.

If women wish to be veiled elsewhere, they certainly ought to be such in the Church, where it is right that all things be done with the utmost modesty, and that order and decorum be preserved, since not only are men present there, but the Angels of God themselves: Just as there were Cherubim in the temple to signify the presence of Angels, to which Agrippa looks in his speech to the Jews in book II of the Jewish War, ch. 28, in Josephus: I call to witness your holy things and the holy angels. Thus also in the synagogue, Angels were believed to be present. See Deut. XXXIII. 2 and the Hebrew interpreters at the beginning of Ps. 82. Philo in the book De humanitate concerning Moses: He performed hymns through every kind of harmony and symphony, which both men and angels, the ministers, listen to. The former as acquaintances for the instruction of a similar grateful disposition; the latter as overseers according to the wise commerce. Having observed whether there is anything discordant in the song, etc. The Hebrew book called Chasidin names the Angel of prayer. Tertullian also in De oratione: With the Angel of prayer still standing by. Chrysostom also mentions these Angels in De Eleemosyna, homily I. See also 1 Tim. v. 21. Plutarch also, in the book Why Oracles have ceased, says there are certain demons who are overseers of divine rites and initiators of mysteries. And Iamblichus V. 26, that every temple has its own guardians. See also what is said at Ecclesiastes V. 2. Athenagoras attributes particular providence to Angels. Sarah sinned because she laughed in the presence of the Angels, Gen. XVIII. 12. Everything in the sight of the Angels ought to be serious.

Most interpreters take this BECAUSE OF THE ANGELS as a new reason, that women, if they do not wish to be veiled to maintain decency among men, should nevertheless do so out of reverence for the holy Angels, who are present at sacred assemblies and are most studious of divine order and modesty. In the judgment of B. Hülsemann, however, no new argument is proposed here, whose opinion, because his Annotations have not yet seen the light of day, I am pleased to transcribe in its entirety, for it does not seem inelegant: Just as the male is said to be the glory of God passively, because he receives glory immediately from God, not through the mediation of another creature as a principle of order or intermediate cause: So the female is said to be the glory of the man passively, because she receives glory from the man, which sense appears from the attribute of the image and divine glory, that these are to be taken passively. Whence the exposition of the word ἐξουσίας in verse 10 is easy, namely, that this is to be taken passively for the recognition of a superior power, not for a sign of active power, which is directly against the scope of the Apostle. Likewise, the exposition of the cause is easy, for which women ought to wear a sign of subjection because of the Angels, namely, as being superior in order and dignity, not because they are censors or witnesses of morals and modesty, and consequently conscious of all our actions, and therefore to be invoked, as Bellarmine lib. 5 de cultu sanct. cap. 5, Becanus opusc. de invocat. sanct. cap. 6. §. 5. §. 6, the Rheims translators in their annotations to this place, Salmero disp. 18. dub. 6, and others trifle. For although the antecedent is true, namely that the Angels are spectators of our actions, which Hemmingius, Hunnius, and Balduinus repeatedly observe here: I deny, however, that this was said or intended by the Apostle here. The reason is that the middle term of the Apostle, by which he proves the duty of women to wear some sign of subjection on their head, is continuously drawn from the superiority of order established in the first creation, in which order the female is not the image of God, namely immediate, verse 5. And which is the cause of recognizing the man as superior on account of the priority of order in creation established, the same is the cause of revering the Angels, as being still superior in order and dignity of creation. Which sense is most simple and homogeneous to the Apostolic argument. And Estius is mistaken here, who contends that the reason brought forward concerning the Angels is different from the previous ones. It is not a different reason, but a stronger one in the same genus that is brought forward, which Chrysostom clearly noted in this place. Those who take the Angels metaphorically here are clearly far from the Apostle's scope, who even after this reason concerning the superiority of the Angels has been alleged, remains nevertheless in the method of arguing taken from creation in verses 11 and 12. (The woman is from the man, both from God.) So that you may see the middle term is perpetually drawn from the order of creation. See also the annotations of Heinsius.

Latin:

v. 10. Διὰ τῦτο ὀφείλει ἡ γυνὴ ἐξυσίαν ἔχειν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς. Μετωνυμία frequens Hebræis, ubi signum rei significatæ nomen accipit. Velamen enim signum est imperii, sub quo est mulier. Et vicissim vir, qui mulieri imperat, velamen ejus ob id, ut quidam putant, dicitur Genes. XX. 16. Sententia est Græca: Γυναικὶ δ᾽ ἄρχειν ὐ δίδωκεν ἡ φύσις.

Idcircò ob pudorem & honestatem non tantùm Judææ mulieres velari solebant; uti Tertull. de cor. milit. c. 4. Judæis fœminis tàm solennè est velamen capitis, ut inde cognoscantur, sed etiam gentiles, observante eodem libr. de velandis virginibus cap. XVII. quem librum scripsit, ut doceret, omnes, non tantum nuptas, sed etiam innuptas mulieres velandas esse, non obstante quacunque consuetudine, in quo tamen assensum non meretur, quia non per modum præcepti hoc imponit Apostolus omnibus mulieribus; sed quod conveniens sit, explicat, idque imprimis ob Corinthiorum statum, ubi uxores non tantum luxui, sed etiam cultui Veneris erant addictissimæ, amasiorum illices & impudentes, aperto vultu & capite incedentes, & cincinnos suos ostentantes, quem morem quasi patrium, atque elegantem & decentem etiam è conversis nonnullæ imitatæ sunt. Ejusmodi ergo capitis denudatio, quà cincinni ostentantur, hic notatur, eaque ratione capitis velamen per eas, quæ ab Apostolo adductæ sunt, rationes requiritur. Id enim in iis desiderat, ut notat hìc B. Balduinus, quod passis capillis, non sine indicio lasciviæ, prophetarent, & ad imitationem gentilium, quorum pythonissæ his gestibus, atque hoc ornatu corporis vaticinia sua edebant. Loquitur autem Apostolus pro loci istius consuetudine, ubi apertio capitis signum libertatis; tectio verò servitutis erat, quum vice versá nunc penes nos capitis apertio humilitatis signum sit, uti tecto stare capite autoritatis est. Non præscribit sanè Apostolus certum & immutabilem ritum omni- bus Ecclefiis, sed quid Corinthiis maxime conve- niat, & in se magis decorum videatur, docet. Con- suetudini autem receptae scandali experti non praeiudicat, ideoque etiam contentionem de hisce moveri non vult, v. 6. Denique necessitatem, & valetudinis rationes etiam excipi, dubium non est, modo superbiae, luxuriei, & singularitatis suspicio, quoad fieri potest, evitetur.

Διὰ τοὺς Ἀγγέλους.

Si alibi velatae esse volunt mulieres, certe in Ecclesia tales esse debent, ubi par est geri omnia summa cum verecundia, ordinemque & decorem servari, quippe ubi non tantum adsint homines, sed & ipsi Dei Angeli: Sicut Cherubini erant in templo, ad significandam Angelorum praesentiam, quo respiciens Agrippa in oratione ad Judaeos libro II. belli Judaici cap. 28. apud Josephum: Μαρτύρομαι δὲ ἐγὼ μὲν τὰ ὑμῶν τὰ ἅγια, καὶ τοὺς ἱεροὺς ἀγγέλους. Sic & in synagoga Angeli adesse crediti. Vide Deuter. XXXIII. 2. & Interpre- tes Hebraeos ad initium Ps. 82. Philo libro περὶ φιλανθρω- πίας de Mose: Ὑμνῳδίας ἐποιεῖτο διὰ πᾶν συμφωνίας κᾀ ἁρμο- νίας εἶδος, ἣν κατακούουσι ἄνθρωποί τε κᾀ ἄγγελοι λειτουργοί. Οἱ μὲν ὡς γνώριμοι πρὸς τὴν τῆς ὁμοίας εὐχαρίστου διαθέσεως διδα- σκαλίαν; οἱ δ᾽ ὡς ἔφοροι κατὰ τὴν σοφὴν ἐμπορίαν. Θεασάμε- νοι μήτι τῆς ᾠδῆς ἐκμελές, &c. Angelum orationis nominat liber Hebraeus Chasidin dictus. Tertullianus quoque de oratione: Angelo orationis adhuc adstante. Meminit & ho- rum Angelorum Chrysost. de Eleemosyna oratione I. Vide & 1. Tim. v. 21. Etiam Plutarchus libro cur oracula defe- cerint, quosdam ait esse δαίμονας ἐπισκόπους θείων ἱερῶν καὶ μυστηρίων ὀργιαστάς. Et Jamblichius V. 26. cuique templo suos esse custodes. Vide & quae ad Ecclesiasten V. 2. Athe- nagoras τὴν ἐπὶ μέρους πρόνοιαν Angelis tribuit. Peccavit Sa- ra, quod apud Angelos risit, Gen. XVIII. 12. Omnia in An- gelorum conspectu seria esse debent.

Interpp. plerique hoc PROPTER ANGE- LOS ceu novam rationem accipiunt, quod mu- lieres, si non ad honestatem inter homines tuen- dam velari velint, id tamen propter reverentiam sanctorum Angelorum facere debeant, qui sacris coetibus intersunt, & ordinis divini ac modestiae sunt studiosissimi. B. Hülsemanni tamen judicio non hic novum argumentum proponitur, cujus sententiam, quia Annotata lucem nondum aspe- xerunt, integram adscribere placet, non enim inconcinna videtur: Quemadmodum masculus dicitur gloria Dei passive, quod gloriam immediate a Deo accipiat, non mediante alia creatura, tan- quam principio ordinis seu causa intermedia: Ita foemina dicitur gloria viri passive, quod gloriam a viro accipiat, qui sensus apparet ex attributo imaginis & gloriae divinae, haec passive esse ca- pienda. Unde facilis expositio est vocabuli ἐξυ- σίας v. 10. scil. hanc passive esse accipiendam pro recognitione potestatis superioris, non pro signo potestatis activae, quod directe est contra scopum Apostoli. Facilis item expositio causae, propter quam foeminas oporteat signum subjectionis portare propter Angelos, scil. tanquam ordine & dignitate superiores, non quod censores aut testes morum & pudicitiae, & consequenter conscii omnium actionum nostrarum, adeoque invocan- di sint, quomodo Bellarm. lib. 5. de cultu sanct. cap. 5. Becanus opusc. de invocat. sanct. cap. 6. §. 5. §. 6. Remenses in annotat. ad hunc locum, Salmero disp. 18. dub. 6. aliique nugantur. Quan- quam enim antecedens verum sit, Angelos scilicet esse spectatores actionum nostrarum, quod Hem- mingius, Hunnius, Balduinus identidem hic observant: Nego tamen ab Apostolo id hic di- ctum, aut intentum fuisse. Ratio est, quia Apostoli medius terminus, quo probet foemina- rum debitum deportando in capite aliquo subje- ctionis signo, continue ducitur a superioritate ordi- nis in prima creatione constituti, quo ordine foemi- na non est imago Dei, scilicet immediata, vers. 5. Et quae est causa recognoscendi virum tanquam superiorem ob prioritatem ordinis in creatione constitutum, eadem est causa reverendi Angelos, tanquam adhuc superiores ordine, & dignitate creationis. Qui sensus simplicissimus & argumen- to Apostolico homogeneus est. Falliturque Estius hîc, qui rationem de Angelis allatam, diversam à superioribus esse contendit. Non diversa, sed fortior in eodem genere affertur ratio, quod Chrysostomus clare in h. l. notavit. Qui Angelos metaphoricè hic sumunt, planè absunt à scopo Apostoli, qui etiam post allegatam hanc ratio- nem de superioritate Angelorum, manet tamen in argumentandi ratione, à creatione desumpta vers. 11. 12. (Mulier ex viro est, uterque ex Deo.) Ut videas medium terminum perpetuum duci ex creationis ordine. Vide etiam Heinsii annotata.

## 11:11
v. 11. Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man in the Lord.

That is, the Lord redeemed neither men with women excluded, nor women with men excluded. The sexes are unequal in creation and duties, equal in the business of salvation, Gal. III. 28.

Latin:

v. 11. Πλὴν ὔτε ἀνὴρ χωρὶς γυναικὸς, ὔτε γυνὴ χωρὶς ἀνδρὸς ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Id est, Dominus neque viros exclusis fœminis, neque fœminas exclusis viris redemit. Dispares sunt sexus in creatione & officiis, pares in salutis negotio, Gal. III. 28.

## 11:12
12. For as the woman is from the man.

He repeats what he had said above in verse 7, so that by the addition he may mitigate that very thing.

So also is the man through the woman.

This article, as elsewhere, indicates the whole genus of men, except Adam. For all are brought into the light through women. Concerning this use of the article, see what is said at Matt. XII. 32 and Mark III. 26.

But all things are from God.
