Even the first man, Luke III. 2, and consequently all his descendants. The preposition ἐκ signifies the Efficient cause here. See Rom. XI. 36, above I. 30. And here it refers to creation; elsewhere it is referred to the new creation.

Others do not take verse 11 concerning the redemption of Christ, but concerning the divine ordination. Because he had said, says the blessed Balduinus, that the woman is from the man and created for the sake of the man, husbands could easily have seized upon that to excuse their moroseness and to cloak tyranny over their wives: Therefore he now adds a correction: Although by reason of domestic and economic affairs such is the order between spouses, yet let no one on that account despise the other, because neither can lack the work of the other. The man is the head of the wife, and the wife is the helper of the man, both in the Lord, that is, by the law and ordination of the Lord. To which also the interpretation of the blessed Hunnius and Cornelius à Lapide tends, with Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Theophylact preceding. Which explanation is more convenient. For the following things teach that he is looking to the primal ordination of creatures: For just as the woman is from the man, so is the man through the woman. The former of which is to be understood concerning the creation of Eve, the latter concerning the procreation of all men, except Adam. It also teaches the common origin of men and women: Concerning which it is added: But all things are from God. By these it is taught that God is the cause of both sexes, by whose intuition and reverence the man may remember to moderate his rule, and the woman to comply and subject herself equanimously.

Latin:

12. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ γυνὴ ἐκ τῦ ἀνδρὸς.

Repetit, quod dixerat supra 7. ut adjectione id ipsum mitiget.

Οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ διὰ τῆς γυναικὸς.

Articulus hic ut & alibi totum genus virorum indicat, excepto Adamo. Omnes enim per fœminas in lucem e- duntur. De hoc usu articuli vide, quæ ad Matth. XII. 32. & Marci III. 26.

Τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ.

Etiam primus homo Luc. III. 2. ac proinde & omnes ejus posteri. Præpositio ἐκ causam hic Efficientem signifi- cat. Vide Rom. XI. 36. supra I. 30. Et hic ad creationem; alibi ad novam creationem refertur.

Alii non de redemtione Christi, sed de ordinatio- ne divina versum 11. accipiunt. Quia dixerat, in- quit B. Balduinus, mulierem esse ex viro, & pro- pter virum conditam, potuissent facile mariti id ad excusandam suam morositatem arripere, & ty- rannidem in uxores palliare: Idcircò correctio- nem jam addit: Licet ratione rei familiaris & œconomicæ talis sit ordo inter conjuges, nemo tamen alterum propterea contemnat, quia neuter alterius operâ carere potest. Vir est caput uxoris, & uxor adjutorium viri, utrumque in Domino, id est, ex lege atque ordinatione Domini. Quo etiam abit B. Hunnii interpretatio, & Cornelii à Lapide, præeunte Ambrosio, Chrysostomo, Theophylacto. Quæ explicatio convenientior est. Nam primæ- vam creaturarum ordinationem respici sequentia docent: Nam quemadmodum mulier ex viro est, sic vir per mulierem. Quorum illud de creatione Evæ, hoc de procreatione virorum omnium, præ- ter Adamum intelligendum. Docet & commu- nis virorum & fœminarum origo: De qua additur: Omnia verò ex Deo. Iis docetur, Deum esse cau- sam utriusque sexus, cujus intuitu & reverentia tum vir imperium suum moderari, tum mulier æquanimiter obsecundare seque subjicere memi- nerit.

## 11:13
v. 13. Judge among yourselves.

Similar above X. 15.

It is fitting for a woman to pray with her head uncovered.

In that act, which most requires what is fitting, the force of which word, see Cicero, De Officiis, Book I.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἐν ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς κρίνατε.

Simile supra X. 15.

Πρέπον ἐςὶ γυναῖκα ἀκατάλυπτον τῷ Θεῷ προσεύχεσθαι.

In eo actu, qui maxime requirit τὸ πρέπον, cujus vocis quæ sit vis, vide Ciceronem de officiis primo.

## 11:14
v. 14. Does not nature itself teach you.

This is not strictly natural: But just as jurists often give the name of natural law to the law of nations, so also those things are called natural which have been widely and broadly accepted not without probable reason, as we said in Book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis, XII. 28. Tertullian, De Corona: Do you seek, therefore, the law of God? You have that common one in the public sphere of the world, and in the natural tablets, to which the Apostle is also accustomed to appeal, as when he says, does not nature itself teach you regarding the covering of the face?

That if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him. For it is commonly said.

There is no long-haired man who is not counted. Understand this regarding long hair, which is forbidden to clerics by the canons.

But if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her. God made woman naturally endowed with hair alone, just as a horse with a mane, glorying in it, says Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II. Plutarch, Roman Questions: For men, to be shorn, and for women, to have long hair, is customary. The Hebrews interpret the word פאר, which properly signifies glory, Ezek. 24:17, as curls.

Latin:

v. 14. Ἡ ἐδὲ αὐτὴ ἡ φύσις διδάσκει ὑμᾶς.

Non est hoc plane naturale: Sed sicut Jurisconsulti juri gentium sæpe dant nomen juris naturæ, ita & natu- ralia dicuntur, quæ non sine probabili ratione longè & late recepta sunt, ut diximus lib. II. de jure belli ac pacis XII. 28. Tertullianus de corona: Quæris igitur Dei legem? Habes communem istam in publico mundi, & in naturalibus tabulis, ad quas & Apostolus solet provocare, ut cum in vela- mine faciei non natura vos, inquit, docet?

Ὄτι ἀνὴρ μὲν ἐὰν κομᾷ, ἀτιμία αὐτῷ ἐστι. Solet enim dici.

Οὐδεὶς κομήτης ὅστις οὐ ψηφίζεται. Quod intellige de longa coma, quæ Clericis per ca- nones interdicta.

Γυνὴ δὲ ἐὰν κομᾷ, δόξα αὐτῇ ἐστι. Deus fœminam fecit αὐτοφυῆ τῇ κόμῃ μόνῃ, ὥσπερ ἵππον τῇ χαίτῃ, γαυρομένην ait Alexandrinus Clemens Strom. II. Plutarchus quæstionibus Romanis: Τοῖς μὲν (ἀνδράσι) τὸ κείρεσθαι, ταῖς δὲ (γυναιξὶ) τὸ κομᾷν σύνηθές ἐστιν. Hebræi פאר, quod proprie δόξαν fignificat, Ezech. XXIV. 17. in- terpretantur cincinnos.

## 11:15
v. 15. That hair is given to her instead of a covering. Musonius, in Stobaeus under the title On Intemperance, calls hair a covering provided by Nature.

Others also take nature for the custom of that time and place. But why could it not be taken properly? Since natural reason itself and the constitution of the body so dictate, that women grow longer hair than men, which the interpreters acknowledge: Therefore, by this reasoning, it is less in accordance with nature when men grow longer hair. To which it is no objection (what Cornelius à Lapide urges) that some nations formerly held long hair in men to be for beauty, such as the Gauls, from whom Gaul was called 'long-haired,' and the Achaeans, whom Homer called 'long-haired Achaeans,' that is, curly-haired Achaeans; and also the ancient Romans. Regarding those nations, Schlichtingius says: That they overcame nature by custom, and do not recognize that shame, and the disgrace and reproach of their own male sex. Nor indeed should it be judged that this is entirely beyond or against nature, even if it is more in accordance with nature not to grow long hair: And this may be a natural sign of authority, by which the Apostle seems to look primarily to the name of 'nature,' namely, that the woman is by nature subject to the man; and that nature has marked this, when it gave the woman more abundant hair as a natural veil. But as for the beard, it was not given to man as a covering, but for dignity and majesty. For it is itself a not ignoble symbol of the man's authority over the woman: Which Estius admits here: And B. Balduinus acknowledges that hair is, as it were, a natural veil and ornament for a woman, and therefore, in that respect, the argument is drawn not only from custom, but also from natural reason. The law concerning the Nazarites was singular and extraordinary, on account of its mystical significance, for which there would have been no need if it were ordinary for men to grow their hair long, and not to allow a razor to touch their head. But why, says Theophylact, is long hair considered a disgrace to a man? Because he puts on the appearance of a woman, and he who was created to rule has admitted the badges of servitude. But to a woman, that thicker hair yields glory, since she also preserves her own proper institution. For the observance of one's own condition is honorable for everyone. Someone will ask: Why then is it necessary to put a cloth over the head, for the sake of veiling, if hair has been given as a veil? Doubtless, so that the woman may profess her servitude not only through faith, but also by her own will. These are the words of Theophylact. Chrysostom explains this latter point more clearly: But if they were given as a veil, he says, for what reason is it necessary to add another veil and covering? So that she may acknowledge it not only by nature, but also by a free resolution of the mind. For that you ought to cover your head, even prior nature established as a law. Add therefore also what is yours, so that you may not seem to overturn even the laws of nature, which is indeed a matter of great impudence, to fight not only with us, but also with nature.

Latin:

v. 15. Ὄτι ἡ κόμη ἀντὶ περιβολαίυ δέδοται αὐτῇ. Musonius apud Stobæum titulo περὶ ἀκολασίας comam vocat σκέπην ὑπὸ τῆς Φύσεως πεπορισμένην.

Naturam & alii pro consuetudine istius tem- poris ac loci accipiunt. Sed cur non accipi pro- priè possit? Quum ipsa naturalis ratio, & con- stitutio corporis ita ferat, ut longiorem comam alant fœminæ, quàm viri, quod agnoscunt In- terpretes: Hâc ergò ratione naturæ minus con- venit, cum viri promissiorem comam alunt. Cui non obstat, (quod Cornelius à Lapide urget) quod gentes nonnullæ olim comam in viris pro decore habuerint, ut Galli, à quibus Gallia comata nun- cupata, & Achivi, quos Homerus καρηκομόον- τας Ἀχαίους, id est, cinnatos Achæos dixit; Nec non Romani prisci. De gentibus istis Schlichtingius dicit: Quod consuetudine naturam vicerint, & turpitudinem istam, sexusque sui virilis dedecus & contumeliam non agnoscant. Nec verò prorsus id præter vel contra naturam esse censeri debet, etsi magis naturæ conveniat, comam non alere: Idque naturale potestatis veluti signum sit, quo cumpri- mis nomine Φύσεως respicere videtur Apostolus naturâ scilicet subjectam esse viro fœminam; id- que naturam ita signasse, cum largiorem comam ceu velamentum naturale fœminæ dedit. Quod verò ad barbam, ea non pro tegumento viro da- ta est, sed ad dignitatem & majestatem. Est enim & ipsa symbolum non ignobile potestatis viri su- pra mulierem: Quod hic fatetur Estius: Et B. Balduinus agnoscit, naturale quasi velamentum & ornamentum mulieri esse comam, adeoque eo respectu argumentum non tantùm a consue- tudine, sed & à naturali ratione petitum esse. Lex de Nasiræis singularis & extraordinaria erat, ob mysticam significationem, qua opus non fuis- set, si hoc ordinarium foret viris promissam co- mam alere, nec, ut novacula caput ascendant, com- mittere. Cur vero, inquit Theophylactus, viro coma prolixior ignominia datur? Quoniam mu- lieris speciem induit, & qui, ut dominetur, est con- ditus, insignia servitutis admiserit. Mulieri autem gloria cedit densior ille capillus, quoniam proprium servat & hæc institutum. Est enim honorabilis cui- que suæ conditionis observatio. Quæret aliquis: Quid ergò necessarium est, linteum capiti, velandi gratia, superinducere, si pro velamine coma tributa est? Nimirum, ut non solum per fidem, sed volun- tate etiam suam profiteatur mulier servitutem. Hæc Theophylactus. Quod posterius luculentius edisserit Chrysostomus: At si pro velamine, inquit, dati sunt, quanam de causa oportet aliud reddere velum & amiculum? Ut non ex natura solum, sed etiam ex libero animi instituto fateatur. Nam quod te oporteat caput operire, etiam prior natura legem statuit. Adde ergò & quæ sunt tua ne vi- dearis etiam leges naturæ evertere, quod quidem magnæ est impudentiæ, non solùm nobiscum, sed et- iam cum natura pugnare.

## 11:16
v. 16. Εἰ δέ τις δοκεῖ φιλόνεικος εἶναι. If it pleases anyone to dispute against these things with that freedom of a younger Academy. Concerning this use of the word δοκεῖν we have spoken at Matt. III. 1.

We have no such custom. We do not use the Apostolic manner, namely, that we should permit women in the Churches to be with head uncovered.

Neither do the Churches of God. Nor do those Churches, which are everywhere in the world, do so. He cuts off disputes with two axes: by Apostolic institution and by the custom of the Churches. To wish to call into controversy that which is received through all the Churches is the mark of those who are contentious.

The Apostle speaks more of the custom not of uncovering the head in prayers, but of covering it, or of the contention, as Chrysostom and Ambrose explain, i.e., We do not have the custom of contending, but of obeying the precepts of the masters without contention. Theophylact and Oecumenius also do not disagree with this sense. The blessed Hunnius and the blessed Balduinus, etc., prove the same. In this way, the Apostle prepares for himself an approach to the correction concerning contentions and schisms.

PART II. Concerning schisms and abuses regarding the use of the Holy Supper.

Latin:

v. 16. Εἰ δέ τις δοκεῖ φιλόνεικος εἶναι. Si cui libeat contra hæc disputare libertate illa adolescentioris Academiæ. De hoc usu vocis δοκεῖν dixi- mus ad Matth. III. 1.

Ἡμεῖς τοιαύτην συνήθειαν οὐκ ἔχομεν. Nos Apostolico more non utimur, ut scilicet in Ecclesiis mulieres sinamus esse capite aperto.

Οὐδὲ αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τοῦ Θεοῦ. Neque Ecclesiæ illæ, quæ ubique sunt terrarum, ita fa- ciunt. Duabus securibus disputationes amputat instituto Apostolico, & consuetudine Ecclesiarum. Quod per omnes Ecclesias receptum est, disputando velle in contro- versiam vocare, est φιλονείκων.

De consuetudine non capitis aperiendi in preci- bus, sed contegendi, vel τῆς φιλονεικίας magis loquitur Apostolus, ut Chrysostomus & Ambro- sius explicant, q. d. Nos consuetudinem non ha- bemus contendendi, sed magistrorum præceptis abs- que contentione obtemperandi. Cui sensui etiam non repugnat Theophylactus, nec Oecumenius. Probant eundem B. Hunnius, & B. Balduinus &c. Hoc pacto aditum sibi parat Apostolus ad ἐπα- νόρθωσιν de contentionibus & schismatibus.

PARS II. De schismatibus & abusibus circa usum S. Cœnæ.

## 11:17
v. 17. Now in giving this instruction I do not praise you.

In the Manuscript [it is] 'Now I instruct you, not praising,' just as the Latin appears to have read, and the Syriac. That I may proceed, he says, to give precepts concerning good order, there are the deeds of some which I cannot praise. He had praised the deeds of others, and those better ones, above at XI. 2. Thus, often in this epistle and others, he tempers his speech to the various minds of those who lived in the same Church.

Augustine in 'On the Work of Monks', both Glosses, and Lombard refer these things to the preceding: Grotius, however, more correctly referred them with the Greek interpreters to the following. For he expresses this, which he does not praise, first in general, that they come together not for the better, but for the worse, that is, not for spiritual progress, but rather for spiritual detriment, so that from that assembly you bring back not the fruit of piety, but loss: Then in particular, that schisms among them break out into a nerve, and that they do not treat the Holy Eucharist with the reverence that is due. They also refer these things to v. 2. 'I do not praise you,' etc., as if he were saying: Although I praised you because you hold the traditions, you are not nevertheless devoid of fault, but I have something which I must rebuke even in you.

That you come together not for the better, but for the worse.

That your assemblies proceed not for the better, but for the worse. It was an old custom in Greece that the rich would offer certain things to the gods, which then went to the use of the poor, or that a public feast was held, where one contributed more, another less, according to his means: but all feasted on all things by equal right. The Scholiast of Aristophanes mentions both customs, the former in 'Plutus', the latter indeed in 'Peace': Plutarch in 'Lycurgus', where he describes the Laconian common meals, 'walking to the same dinner, the poor man with the rich.' Those first Christians in Achaia had not only imitated this custom but had greatly surpassed it, which Paul had instituted, and there is no doubt that he had also kindled them by the example of that common life which the Christians had instituted at Jerusalem, so that they might approach that very thing as much as possible. And so on the Lord's days, banquets were held at the expense of the rich, from which both the poor and the rich ate by equal right, and the poor carried away the leftovers. But when Paul had departed, the rich, who did not wish to be held by a stricter discipline, had taken to themselves teachers suited to their own inclinations, and with them, having spurned the poor, they had banquets more sumptuous than was fitting. This, however, was now not to progress, but to go backward. Paul therefore denies that he can praise this in terms of moderation: signifying that this is very much disapproved of by him.

These things are to be understood concerning the banquets which were accustomed to be instituted in sacred assemblies before the use of the Holy Eucharist, as appears from v. 20, 21, and that according to the example not only of the faithful in the Apostolic Church, but also of Christ himself, who celebrated a common supper before the institution of the Holy Eucharist. Which custom lasted until the time of Sozomen, as can be seen in chapter VII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 29, and from the Council of Carthage III, canon 29. However, that the Corinthians imitated the custom of the Gentiles, although it seemed so to Primasius and Sedulius, is not likely. For the Apostle would have undoubtedly disapproved of this, nay, would have abolished it, who, however, here rebukes not the custom of such solemn banquets itself, but only the abuse regarding the same. Interpreters, however, inquire about this: whether they instituted the banquets before the reception of the Holy Eucharist, or indeed after it was finished? Cornelius a Lapide says that this agape was held in the time of Paul before the holy communion, but that after these first times of the Church, the Church decreed that the Eucharist, out of reverence, should be received only by those who were fasting. And therefore, the agape was accustomed to be celebrated after the Eucharist. Estius attributes this decree to the Apostles themselves in this place at verse 21. And for this matter he cites Augustine, Epist. 135. But yet before that, namely before it was decreed by the Apostles that the Eucharist should be received only by those who were fasting, he gathers from the same Father, St. Augustine, Epist. 118 to Januarius, that it was customary for the same to be celebrated after a common meal, following the example of Christ: However much he may grant that the Greeks, Chrysostom, and others, and indeed even Pelagius among the Latins, made the reception of the Eucharist prior to the meal: he prefers the opinion of these others, because in the beginning it was the custom that a common meal should be held first, and afterwards the participation of the Holy Eucharist should take place. But that the Apostles decreed that the Eucharist should be received by those who were fasting is by no means to be admitted. For evidence of this matter can be brought forward neither from the scriptures nor from the earlier centuries; indeed, the exact opposite is gathered from verse 34. Moreover, that it was the custom in the Corinthian Church for a meal to be instituted first appears from the fact that the Apostle used the word προλαμβάνει in verse 21: Namely, that when they came together for the Holy Eucharist, each one would take or receive his own supper, of which more later.

Latin:

v. 17. Τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλων οὐκ ἐπαινῶ.

In Manuscripto Τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω οὐκ ἐπαινῶν, quo- modo & Latinum legisse apparet, & Syrum. Ut pergam, inquit, dare præcepta περὶ εὐταξίας, sunt quorundam fa- cta, quæ laudare non possum. Aliorum eorumque melio- rum facta supra laudaverat XI. 2. Ita sæpe in hac epistola & aliis sermonem variis eorum, qui in eadem vivebant Ecclesia, animis attemperat.

Ad præcedentia hæc referunt Augustinus de Opere Monach. Glossa utraque, & Lombardus: Rectius tamen illa cum Græcis interpretibus Grotius ad sequentia retulit. Τοῦτο enim, quod non laudat, exprimit tum in genere, quod nempe non in melius, sed in deterius conveniant, hoc est, non ad profectum spiritualem; sed potius ad spirituale detrrimentum, ut ex eo conventu non fructum pietatis; sed dispendium referatis: Tum in spe- cie, quod schismata inter ipsos in nervum erum- pant, quodque non eâ, qua par est, reverentiâ S. Eucharistiam tractent. Referunt etiam hæc ad v. 2. Non laudo vos &c. quasi dicat: Quanquam vos laudarim, quod traditiones teneatis, non ta- men expertes estis culpæ, sed habeo, quod repre- hendam etiam in vobis.

Ὅτι οὐκ εἰς τὸ κρεῖττον, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὸ ἧττον συνέρχεσθε.

Quod conventus vestri non in melius, sed in pejus procedunt. Mos vetus erat in Græcia, ut divites quædam offerrent diis, quæ deinde in usum cedebant pauperum, aut ut fieret πανδαισία, ubi alius plus, alius minus confere- bat pro suis opibus: Omnes autem de omnibus pari jure epulabantur. Meminit Scholiastes Aristophanis utriusque moris, illius quidem ad Plutum, hujus verò ad Pacem: Plutarchus Lycurgo, ubi συσσίτια Laconica describit ἐπὶ ταυτὸ δεῖπνον τῷ πένητι τῶ πλουσίῳ βαδίζοντες. Hunc morem non imitati tantum erant, sed multum superaverant primi illi in Achaia Christiani, quod Paulus instituerat, & non dubium quin & exemplo illius κοινοβίε, quod Hierosoly- mis instituerant Christiani, accenderat, ut ad illud ipsum quantum fieri posset, accederent. Itaque Dominicis die- bus divitum sumptu fiebant convivia, de quibus pari jure & pauperes & divites vescebantur, & pauperes auferebant ἀποφόρητα. At Paulo digresso divites, qui arctiore disci- plina teneri nolebant, doctores sibi adsciverant aptos suis ingenijs, cumque illis, spretis pauperibus, epulas habe- bant lautiores, quam deceret. Hoc verò jam non erat pro- gredi, sed retrocedere. Negat igitur Paulus, se lauda- re hoc posse κατὰ λιτότητα: Significans valdè hoc sibi im- probari.

De conviviis hæc accipienda, quæ in conven- tibus sacris ante usum sacræ Eucharistiæ institui consueverant, ut è v. 20. 21. apparet, idque ad exemplum non modo fidelium in Ecclesia Apostolica, sed etiam ipsius Christi, qui cœnam vulgarem ante S. Eucharistiæ institutionem celebravit. Quæ consuetudo Sozomeni tempore adhuc duravit, ut videre est cap. VII. Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ cap. 29. & è Concilii Carthag. III. can. 29. Imitatos autem esse Corinthios gentium morem, etsi Primafio, & Sedulio ita visum, non est verisimile. Hoc enim improbasset sine dubio Apostolus, imo sustulisset, qui verò hîc non ipsum conviviorum ejusmodi solennium morem, sed abusum solùm circa eundem reprehendit. De eo tamen, utrum ante S. Eucharistiæ perceptionem convivia instituerint, an vero finitâ eâdem? disquirunt Interpretes. Cornelius à Lapide ante sacram synaxin agapen hanc tempore Pauli factam esse, post prima autem hæc Ecclesiæ tempora Ecclesiam sanxisse, ait, ut Eucharistia, ob reverentiam, nonnisi à jejunis sumeretur. Ideoque agapen post Eucharistiam celebrari consuevisse. Hanc sanctionem Apostolis ipsis tribuit Estius in h. l. ad v. 21. Et in eam rem allegat Augustinum Epist. CXXXV. Sed antea tamen priusquam scilicet illud sanciretur ab Apostolis, ut non nisi à jejunis accipiatur Eucharistia, eandem post convivium commune, exemplo Christi, celebrari consuevisse, ex eodem Patre S. Augustino ep. CXIIX. ad Jan. colligit Estius: Utut largiatur, Græcos, Chrysostomum, & alios, imò etiam è Latinis Pelagium perceptionem Eucharistiæ fecisse convivio priorem: Horum vero sententiæ illam præfert, quod initio mos fuerit, ut prius haberetur convivium commune, postea fieret participatio S. Eucharistiæ. Cæterum Apostolos id sancivisse, ut Eucharistia à jejunis accipiatur, nequaquam admittendum. Ejus enim rei documentum nec è scripturis, nec è prioribus seculis proferri potest, imò contrarium prorsus è v. 34. colligitur. In Ecclesia autem Corinthiaca morem illum fuisse, ut prius convivium institueretur, ex eo apparet, quod Apostolus voce προλαμβάνει v. 21. usus est: Quod nempe, cum convenirent ad S. Eucharistiam, unusquisque propriam cœnam presumeret vel acciperet, quo de posteà.

## 11:18
v. 18. Πρῶτον δὲ συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. That is, in that house in which meetings are held. For just as συναγωγὴ is properly the meeting itself, and improperly the place into which one meets, so also the name Ἐκκλησία has both meanings. That the word is to be taken in this way here is shown by what follows in verse 22. Moreover, that Christians, when times were peaceful, had certain buildings into which they would meet is manifest from Eusebius, where he comes to the times of Diocletian.

John Camero, in his lectures on the Church, Vol. I of his Works, page 219, argues against the Papists, who contend that the word Ἐκκλησία necessarily means a house or sacred building here, asserting that the term Church never signifies a place in the New Testament. But to that which Bellarmine urges, that to meet in the Church is not to meet in a gathering, but in a place, he replies: Although it is not usually said to meet in a gathering, it is nevertheless said to meet in a senate or a synod; nor is it said to have met in the Church in any other way than to designate the nature of the gathering, that it was an Ecclesiastical gathering, and to insinuate an argument from the holiness not of the place, but of the gathering. For in every gathering, dissensions are to be avoided, but they are to be detested much more vehemently in an Ecclesiastical gathering, which is instituted for the sake of religion. Thus ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ in verse 20 does not signify a place, but a conjunction of persons, and it is the same as 'together', and although the Church is opposed later to private buildings, 'do you not have houses', or

You despise the Church; (from which Bellarmine almost triumphs, because one passage is opposed to another: But before victory) he proves nothing solidly. For cannot the Church be opposed to private houses, even if by this is not understood a place or temple, but an ecclesiastical assembly? Which the following words teach is understood here, where they explain themselves mutually, do you despise the Church, and confound those who have not, that is, the poor? Namely, that the Church is despised, to which the poor belong.

I hear that there are divisions among you.

It was already happening in those times, as happens much more in ours, that a thing instituted for incorporating the faithful was turned into a banner of schism.

And I believe a part.

That is, I believe that the fault is in some, not in all. See above 1.11. Thus ἀπὸ μέρους is taken in Rom. XI. 25.

Grotius establishes the Eucharist as the subject matter of the schism, just as Estius also thinks that the schisms were debated there either about the place of reclining, or about the time of beginning the Supper, or about the foods and drinks themselves and other things of that kind, especially between the rich and the poor, of whom the former were despised by the latter. But others think that those schisms, which had arisen on account of the diverse gifts of teachers, about which chapter 1, had prevailed in ecclesiastical assemblies. The Apostle expresses nothing. Schisms of both this and that kind could have flourished in those assemblies, according to the diversity of time and occasion. Aretius extends these schisms not only to sects from the names of teachers, and the violation of concord, when the richer, without regard for the poor, anticipated the feasts out of ambition, but also to litigations before the Gentiles. But here the discourse is about ecclesiastical schisms, not judicial contentions. But that he says, I believe in some part, that can be referred both to the object, because he does not believe the report to be true in all respects; and to the manner of assent, because he does not have faith in it entirely and plainly.

For there must be heresies among you.

That matter has some use, and therefore God judges that it should not be hindered by His omnipotent power. See what we said on Matt. VIII. 7. and Luke XVII. 1. We saw above I. 10. and XVI. 17. that σχίσματα and διχοστασίας are the same. Nor does it signify anything else by the force of the word αἱρέσεως, although usage has prevailed that αἵρεσις is called that split which differs by some dogma. And it was once a neutral word, as appears in Acts XXIV. 5, 14, XXVI. 5, and from the writings of philosophers and physicians, just as the Latin word secta is used in a good sense both by philosophers and by Latin jurists. But the more frequent usage of Christians has prevailed so that it is placed in the category of fault, as here and Gal. V. 20. But for the most part, as one of the ancients says, schism erupts into heresy. Because those who are leaders of sects, in order to make them immortal, innovate something popularly in dogmas, such as that whoredoms and incests are indifferent things, and do no harm to the wise if they eat things sacrificed to idols, and other things of that kind.

Latin:

v. 18. Πρῶτον δὲ συνερχομένων ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. Id est, in ea domo, in qua conventus habentur. Nam sicut συναγωγὴ propriè est ipse conventus, improprie locus, in quem convenitur, ita & nomen Ἐκκλησίας utrumque habet significatum. Ita hîc sumendam vocem ostendit, quod sequitur 22. Fuisse autem Christianis, cum pacata essent tempora, certas ædes, in quas convenirent, ex Eusebio, ubi ad Diocletiani venit tempora, manifestum est.

Non hic necessariò per vocem ἐκκλησίας domum vel ædes sacras intelligi, contra Pontificios, id contendentes, disputat Jo. Camero in prælect. de Eccl. T. I. Oper. pag. 219. in Novo Testamento nunquam Ecclesiæ vocabulum locum significare, afferens. Ad illud verò, quod urget Bellarminus, convenire in Ecclesiam non esse convenire in conventum, sed in locum, respondet: Etsi non soleat dici convenire in conventum, dici tamen convenire in senatum vel synodum; neque dici aliter in Ecclesiam convenisse, quàm ad designandam conventus rationem, quod fuerit conventus Ecclesiasticus, & ut argumentum insinuaret à sanctitate non loci, sed conventus. Nam in omni sane conventu dissidia fugienda sunt, at detestanda in conventu Ecclesiastico, qui instituitur religionis causâ multo vehementius. Sic ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ v. 20. non locum significat, sed personarum conjunctionem, & idem est, quod unà, Ecclesia autem etsi opponatur postea ædibus privatis, non domos habetis, aut

Ecclesiam contemnitis; (ex quo penè triumphat Bellarminus, quod locus opponatur loco: Sed ante victoriam) nihil solidè probat. Annon enim ædibus privatis opponi potest Ecclesia, etiamsi per hanc non intelligatur locus vel templum, sed con- ventus Ecclesiasticus? Quem hic intelligi sequen- tia docent, ubi illa mutuo se explicant, an conte- mnitis Ecclesiam, & confunditis eos, qui non habent, id est, pauperes? Eam nempe Ecclesiam conte- mni, ad quam pertinent pauperes.

Ἀκούω σχίσματα ἐν ὑμῖν ὑπάρχειν.

Accidebat jam illis temporibus, quod nostris multo magis evenit, ut res instituta ad concorporandos fideles in vexillum schismatis vertéretur.

Καὶ μέρος τι πισέυω.

Id est, credo in aliquibus eam esse culpam, non in omnibus. Vide supra 1.11. Sic ἀπὸ μέρους sumitur Rom. XI. 25.

Materiam schismatis constituit Grotius Eucha- ristiam, quemadmodum etiam Estius schismata vel de loco recumbendi,vel de tempore Cænæ inchoan- dæ, vel de cibis ipsis ac potibus aliisvè ejusmodi dis- ceptatum illic fuisse, maximè inter divites & pau- peres, quorum illi ab illis comtemti sint, existimat. Alii vero schismata ista, quæ ob doctorum dona diversa extiterant, de quibus cap. 1. in conven- tibus Ecclesiasticis invaluisse putant. Aposto- lus nihil exprimit. Potuêre & istius & hujus ge- neris schismata in conventibus illis viguisse, pro diversitate temporis & occasionis. Aretius ex- tendit hæc schismata non ad sectas tantùm ex no- minibus Doctorum, & violationem concordiæ, cum ex ambitione ditiores, non habita paupe- rum ratione, epulas præoccuparunt, sed ad liti- gia etiam coram gentilibus. Sed hic de schisma- tibus Ecclesiasticis, non contentionibus judiciali- bus sermo est. Quod autem aliquâ ex parte, in- quit, credo, id tum ad objectum, quod non per omnia veram esse famam credat; tum ad modum assensus, quod non omninò, & plane ei fidem ha- beat, referri potest.

Δεῖ γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν αἱρέσεις εἶναι.

Habet ea res usum aliquem, ideoque judicat Deus, eam non esse vi sua omnipotente impediendam. Vide, quod di- ximus Matth. VIII. 7. & Luc. XVII. 1. Idem esse σχίσματα & διχοστασίας vidimus supra I. 10. & XVI. 17. Nec aliud ex vi vocis αἱρέσεως significat, quanquam usus obtinuit, ut αἵρεσις dicatur ea scissura, quæ dogmate aliquo discrepat. Fuitque olim vox media, ut apparet Actor. XXIV. 5. 14. XXVI. 5. & ex Philosophorum & Medicorum scriptis, quomodo & Latina vox sectæ in bonum sensum usurpatur & à Philosophis & à Jurisconsultis Latinis. Sed frequen- tior Christianorum usus evicit, ut in culpæ parte ponere- tur, velut hic & Gal. V. 20. Plerumque autem, ut veterum quidam loquitur, schisma in hæresin eructat. Quia qui sectarum sunt Principes, ut eas faciant immortales, aliquid in dogmatibus populariter innovant, quale erat, scorta- tiones & incestus esse res medias, sapientibus nihil nocere, si vescantur immolatitiis, & alia ejusmodi.

## 11:19
v. 19. That those who are approved may be made manifest among you.

Those who are constant in faith and morals. Οἱ δόκιμοι are the בחרים to the Rabbis. Opposed to these are the ἀδόκιμοι, 2 Cor. XIII. 5. Where such things happen, the dross departs from the body, the gold remains. Chrysostom well says on this passage, which also agrees with other places: For this 'that' is not everywhere of causality, but in many places also of the outcome of things.

That necessity is not absolute, but hypothetical, of the consequence, as they call it, not of the consequent: Arising from the supposition both of human blindness and ignorance, which adheres to us in perceiving and admitting divine matters after the fall, 1 Cor. II. 14. regarding the intellect, as well as malice, ambition, desire for novelty, and gain, regarding the will: and both of Diabolical perversity and cunning, which obscures heavenly truth, and blinds the minds of the infidels, 2 Cor. IV. 4. and ensnares men entangled in various desires into heresies, which partly immediately, partly mediately through false

prophets, the Spirit of lying works, 1 Kings XXII. 22. 2 Cor. XI. 14. 15. 2 Peter II. 1. 2. 3. Those terms, schism and heresy, if you look to Biblical usage, behave themselves as a broader and a stricter term. For schism signifies any division in sacred matters, whether on account of dogmas or ceremonies, since schism is called both that division which arose on account of a primary dogma, namely concerning the person and office of Christ, John VII. 43. ch. IX. 16. X. 19. Acts XIV. 2. 2 Peter II. 1. likewise concerning the hope of the resurrection, ch. XXIII. 7. and also when contention arises from a lighter cause, not concerning the dogmas of religion, or at least secondary dogmas, such as the schism that occurs in this place, and 1 Cor. I. 10. Heresy, however, denotes a sect, in the phrase of scripture, erring in a primary article of faith, or καθ᾽ ἀλήθειαν, such as were the sects of the Sadducees, denying the resurrection, Acts V. 17. and of the Pharisees perverting various heads of faith, Acts XV. 5. whence also a man is called heretical in that sense Tit. III. 10. or κατὰ δόξαν: in which way the sect or heresy of the Nazarenes or Christians was called Acts XXIV. 5. XXVIII. 22. ἣν λέγουσιν αἵρεσιν, Acts XXVI. 5. But in Ecclesiastical phrase, as Grotius rightly observed, schism is called a division of the Church on account of ceremonies or slight controversies, secondary doctrines, with the unity of faith preserved, when namely no article of faith is overturned, yet charity is dissolved, and the unity of the Church: Heresy, however, when the truth of the articles of faith is undermined. This passage also confirms that diversity. For the Apostle hints that heresy is something graver than schism by the particle καὶ, which is intensive here: I hear that there are schisms among you. For there must also be heresies among you. For thus the Greek codices have it: Δεῖ γὰρ καὶ αἱρέσεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι: But not as Grotius: Δεῖ γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν αἱρέσεις εἶναι. Doubtless the Apostle says he easily believes that there are schisms or contentions among them, concerning matters of no great moment, since there must also be contentions or heresies among them concerning the very articles of faith. From which it is clear that the terms schism and heresy are not taken in this place καθ᾽ ἰσοδυναμίαν, which seemed so to some, but are distinguished, and thus in sacred matters the term schism is either general, as we have already observed concerning other places; Or special, which sense obtains here in ch. I. 10. The end of divine permission, not of heresy, which being evil in itself has no end, but is permitted by God, so that God may elicit good from it according to His infinite wisdom, and is directed to a good outcome by immense divine goodness, is δοκιμασία or the testing τῶν δοκίμων, so that they may be tempted by heresies, and rendered approved, Deut. XIII. 1. 2. 3. For God judged it better to do good from evils, than to permit no evils to exist, as Augustine says, Enchir. ch. XXVII. For although God is ἀπείραστος κακῶν, James I. 14. and thus tempts no one, so as to impel or seduce them to sin, yet He is not an idle spectator, but deliberately permits heresies, and calls the faithful to examination, so that it may be publicly known who are sincere in faith and constant, who would prefer to lose not only wealth and honors, but life itself, rather than the faith, Heb. X. v. last, ch. XI. 36. 37. Cf. Matt. X. 32. 33. James I. 13. But God does not tempt in such a way that by tempting He learns what men cherish in their hearts, as He is the one who intimately knows hearts and reins: But because He makes men, both those who are approved and others, know those things which lie hidden in the heart. For even οἱ δόκιμοι do not know themselves and their own strengths, and how much they value God, more rightly than when such a test is instituted. See August. quest. LIIX. in Genesis. Chrysost. Hom. XLVII. in Genesis. Gregor. M. l. XXIII. Moral.

Add that God himself knows [it] thus by experience, and sees in the very work what he previously perceived clearly in his closed heart, but which had not yet been brought forth by the evidence of an external deed. Conf. Gen. XXII. 12. 2 Chron. XXXII. 31.

Latin:

v. 19. Ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι φανεροὶ γένωνται ἐν ὑμῖν.

Ii, qui constantes sunt in fide & moribus. Οἱ δόκιμοι בחרים Rabbinis. His opponuntur ἀδόκιμοι, 2. Cor. XIII. 5. Ubi talia eveniunt, discedit scoria à corpore, manet au- rum. Chrysostomus bene ad hunc locum, quod & aliis locis convenit: Τὸ γὰρ ἵνα τῦτο, ὐ πανταχῦ αἰτιολογίας ἐςὶν, ἀλλὰ πολλαχῦ καὶ τῆς τῶν πραγμάτων ἐκβάσεως.

Necessitas illa non absoluta est, sed hypothetica, consequentiæ, quam vocant, non consequentis: Exurgens è suppositione tùm humanæ cæcitatis & ignorantiæ, quæ in rebus divinis percipiendis & admittendis post lapsum nobis adhæret, 1. Cor. II. 14. quoad intellectum, ut & malitiæ, ambi- tionis, studii novitatis, & lucri, quoad vo- luntatem: tùm Diabolicæ perversitatis & astutiæ, quæ veritatem cœlestem obscurat, & mentes infidelium excæcat, 2. Cor. IV. 4. hominesque va- riis cupiditatibus inescatos ad hæreses seducit, quæ partim immediatè, partim mediatè per falsos

Prophetas operatur Spiritus mendacii, 1. Reg. XXII. 22. 2. Cor. XI. 14. 15. 2. Petr. II. 1. 2. 3. Voces illæ, schisma, & hæresis, si usum Biblicum respicias, habent sese, ut terminus latior, & strictior. Nam schisma in sacris quamvis scissionem significat, sive ob dogmata, sive ob ceremonias, quum schisma di- catur tùm illa divisio, quæ ob dogma præcipuum, de Christi nempe persona & officio, Joh. VII. 43. cap. IX. 16. X. 19. Act. XIV. 2. 2. Petr. II. 1. item de spe resurrectionis, cap. XXIII. 7. oboriebatur, tum quoque cum contentio ex causa leviori, dogma- ta religionis non concernente, aut saltem dogma- ta secundaria exurgit, quale schisma hoc loco, & 1. Cor. I. 10. occurrit. Hæresis autem sectam no- tat, phrasi scripturæ, in primario fidei articulo errantem, vel καθ᾽ ἀλήθειαν, quales sectæ erant Sadducæorum, resurrectionem negantium, Act. V. 17. & Pharisæorum varia fidei capita perverten- tium, Act. XV. 5. unde & homo hæreticus eo sen- su dictus Tit. III. 10. vel κατὰ δόξαν: quomodo secta vel hæresis Nazaræorum vel Christianorum dicta Act. XXIV. 5. XXVIII. 22. ἣν λέγουσιν αἵρε- σιν, Act. XXVI. 5. Phrasi autem Ecclesiastica ple- rumque, ut rectè observavit Grotius, schisma di- citur scissio Ecclesiæ ob ceremonias vel exiguas con- troversias, doctrinas secundarias, servata fidei unitate, cùm scilicet nullus fidei articulus ever- titur, charitas tamen solvitur, & unitas Ecclesiæ: Hæresis autem, cum veritas articulorum fidei labe- factatur. Diversitatem istam hic locus etiam com- probat. Nam gravius quid schismate esse hæresin Apostolus particula καὶ, quæ hic intensiva est, innuit: Audio schismata inter vos esse. Nam etiam hæreses oportet inter vos esse. Ita enim codices Græci habent: Δεῖ γὰρ καὶ αἱρέσεις ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι: Non vero ut Grotius: Δεῖ γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν αἱρέσεις εἶναι. Nimirum facile se credere ait Apostolus, quod inter ipsos schismata vel contentiones sint, de rebus non magni momenti, cum etiam de ipsis articulis fidei contentiones vel hæreses inter ipsos esse oporteat. Ex quo patet, non καθ᾽ ἰσο- δυναμίαν hoc loco voces schismatis & hæreseos accipi, quod quibusdam visum, sed distingui eas- dem, adeoque in sacris vocem schismatis vel generalem esse, ut de aliis locis jamjam observa- vimus; Vel specialem, qui sensus hic cap. I. 10. obtinet. Finis permissionis divinæ, non hæreseos, quæ per se mala nullum finem habet, sed à Deo & permittitur, ut bonum inde pro sapientia sua in- finita eliciat Deus, & dirigitur ad exitum bonum immensâ bonitate divinâ, est δοκιμασία vel pro- batio τῶν δοκίμων, ut illi per hæreses tententur, ac probati reddantur, Deut. XIII. 1. 2. 3. Nam me- lius judicavit Deus de malis benefacere, quam ma- la nulla esse permittere, ut ait Augustin. Enchir. cap. XXVII. Quanquam enim Deus ἀπείρασ- τος κακῶν sit, Jac. I. 14. adeoque neminem tentet, ut ad peccandum impellat aut seducat, non tamen otiosus spectator est, sed consulto permittit hære- ses, & ad examen vocat fideles, ut publicè in- notescat, quinam sinceri in fide ac constantes, qui non opes modo & honores, sed ipsam vitam ma- lint perdere, quàm fidem, Ebr. X. v. ult. cap. XI. 36. 37. Conf. Matth. X. 32. 33. Jac. I. 13. Non autem ita tentat Deus, ut tentando cognoscat, quod corde foveant homines, utpote corda & renes intime cognoscens: Sed quod homines tum qui probantur, tum alios ea cognoscere fa- ciat, quæ in corde latent. Nam & οἱ δόκιμοι se viresque suas, & quanti Deum faciant, non rectius cognoscunt, quàm cum talis instituitur probatio. Vide August. quæst. LIIX. in Genes. Chrysost. Hom. XLVII. in Genesin. Gregor. M. l. XXIII. Moral.

Adde, Deum ipsummet experimento ita cogno- scere, & in opere ipso videre, quod antea clarè cernebat clauso pectore, sed indicio externi fa- cti nondum proditum. Conf. Genes. XXII. 12. 2. Chron. XXXII. 31.

## 11:20
v. 20. Συνερχομένων ὖν ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ. ] יַחַד Ps. II. 2. elsewhere יַחְדָּו. See Acts II. 1.

Οὐκ ἔστι κυριακὸν δεῖπνον φαγεῖν. The Lord's supper is the agape, of which the sacred mysteries were a part. Chrysostom and others think the mysteries preceded, and the banquet followed. And indeed that suited the customs of the Greeks, among whom the banquet preceded and the feast followed, as we said above. But in the East, consistently with the Jewish custom, the banquet preceded, and at its end followed the distribution of bread and wine, which we showed was long observed in Egypt at Matt. XXVI. 25. He therefore calls the whole of that banquet the Lord's supper, of which they made the mysteries either the first or the last part. This, says Paul, is not to celebrate the Lord's banquet. For that makes all equal, just as Christ died equally for all. Nor in this matter should there be any distinction between rich or poor.

Latin:

v. 20. Συνερχομένων ὖν ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ. ] יַחַד Pf. II. 2. alibi יַחְדָּו. Vide Act. II. 1.

Οὐκ ἔστι κυριακὸν δεῖπνον φαγεῖν. Κυριακὸν δεῖπνον est ἀγάπη, cujus pars erant sacra my- steria. Chrysostomus & alii putant præcessisse mysteria, se- cutum convivium. Et sane conveniebat id Græcorum mo- ribus, apud quos præcedebat convivium, sequebantur epu læ, ut supra diximus. At in Oriente congruenter Judaico more præcedebat convivium, in fine ejus sequebatur panis & vini distributio, quod diu servatum in Ægypto osten- dimus ad Matth. XXVI. 25. Vocat igitur δεῖπνον κυριακὸν totum illud convivium, cujus partem aut primam aut po- stremam faciebant mysteria. Hoc vero, inquit Paulus, non est celebrare convivium Domini. Id enim omnes æquat, sicut Christus pro omnibus pariter est mortuus Nec in hac re ullum discrimen esse debet divitis aut pauperis.

## 11:21
v. 21. Ἑκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον δεῖπνον προλαμβάνει ἐν τῷ φαγεῖν. He means this: the rich first feasted among themselves at separate tables. Then they gave their leftovers to the poor. Ἑκαστος is also used of many, as above.

Καὶ ὃς μὲν πεινᾷ. The poor meanwhile go hungry.

ὃς δὲ μεθύει. He drinks more than enough, in the way the Hebrews use their שׁכר and as we had μεθύειν in John II. 10.

Latin:

v. 21. Ἑκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον δεῖπνον προλαμβάνει ἐν τῷ φαγεῖν. Hoc vult: divites primum inter se mensis diversis epu- labantur. Deinde reliquias suas dabant pauperibus. Ἑκαστος etiam de multis dicitur, ut supra.

Καὶ ὃς μὲν πεινᾷ. Pauperes interim esuriunt.

ὃς δὲ μεθύει. Plus satis bibit, quomodo Hebræi usurpant suum שׁכר & quomodo habuimus μεθύειν Joh. II. 10.

## 11:22
v. 22. Μὴ γὰρ οἰκίας ὐκ ἔχετε εἰς τὸ ἐσθίειν κὶ πίνειν; As much as you please and with whom you please. Domestic banquets are for whom you wish; these are common to the faithful, as the Lord himself [intended].

Ἢ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τῦ Θεῦ καταφρονεῖτε. Reference is made to the passage which is Lev. XIX. 30, 'Reverence my sanctuary'.

Καὶ καταισχύνετε τὺς μὴ ἔχοντας. This, he says, is to reproach the poor for their poverty. It is harsh that they go hungry in the meantime. They feel themselves to be despised.

Unhappy poverty has nothing harder in itself than that it makes men ridiculous.

Τί ὑμῖν εἴπω; ἐπαινέσω ὑμᾶς ἐν τύτῳ; ὐκ ἐπαινῶ. It is a figure which the ancients call erotesis, which Isidore of Pelusium noted in book III, epistle 183, that this Apostle often used.

The Papists in particular raise a doubt as to whether the Holy Eucharist is understood here by the κυριακὸν δεῖπνον, or rather the ἀγάπη. The Dillingen Jesuits, Estius, and others prefer the latter. Grotius, as he does elsewhere, loves a compromise, acting as a moderator and conciliator of parties; he seems to propose this: that the whole of that banquet, of which the mysteries formed either the first or the last part, is being designated. But the reason does not appear why we should deny that the Holy Eucharist itself is understood. When you come together, says the Apostle, it is not to eat the Lord's Supper. He gives the reason why he judges that they are doing something else rather than celebrating the Holy Eucharist; as if he were saying, you are so far from celebrating the Eucharist as it was instituted by the Lord, that you are doing everything else instead, since you hasten to the feast before you have all gathered, and each one takes his own supper, the food prepared at home, and those things which they ought to have contributed in common, so that, while some are still fasting and hungry, others are already full, indeed drunk; Estius acknowledges that this sense—that what you are doing is not to eat the Lord's Supper, but something far different—is held by the Greek interpreters and, among the Latins, by Herveus and Cajetan, and that it is very convenient. This is certainly simpler than if you were to translate ἐσὶ with Erasmus, the interlinear Gloss, Lombard, Thomas, and Lyranus, in this way: You act in such a way that it is not permitted to celebrate the Lord's Supper as is fitting. Nor does it truly stand in the way of this interpretation, as Estius believed it did, that it is in no way likely that these things which are reported by Paul happened in the communion of the Holy Eucharist. For even if we grant that, it is not necessary, even if we take δεῖπνον κυριακὸν to mean the Holy Eucharist. For we do not think that those things happened in that supper, but around the agape or common banquet, which was joined with the Holy Eucharist in the same ecclesiastical assembly, since indeed due preparation was required before the reception of the sacrament, and holy conduct after it, and such things as the Apostle reproves were in no way becoming to these assemblies. And by the Lord's Supper here, St. Augustine (Epist. CXIIX to Januarius), Ambrose (in this place), Pelagius, Bede, Anselm, the Gloss, Lombard, Thomas, Lyranus, Claudius of Turin, Herveus, and Dionysius the Carthusian understand the sacred feast itself, in which the body and blood of the Lord are taken. and among the Greeks, Theodoret and Oecumenius, whose words are: He calls the Lord's sacrament the Lord's supper. It seems that this understanding is also favored by the fact that the Apostle, repeating the Lord's tradition a little later, says: I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you, etc. Where he commemorates no other supper besides that in which the body and blood of the Lord were taken; Estius admits this. Nor do Chrysostom and Tertullian, to whom Estius appeals, deny it to us. The former, in Homily XXVII on this passage, says of the Holy Eucharist: Extend your heart to this Lord's supper. And although Chrysostom reproves the rich because they did not sit with the poor in the assemblies of ἀγάπης καὶ Φιλαδελφίας, he nevertheless adds that the Apostle, by these words δεῖπνον κυριακὸν Φαγεῖν, directs the Corinthians to that evening in which Christ delivered the venerable sacraments. But the latter, namely Tertullian, in his book De Spectaculis. We cannot, he says, eat the supper of the Lord and the supper of demons. These testimonies are to be opposed not only to the interpretation of Estius, but also to the impudence of Galen (Catech. 124) and Maldonatus (on Matthew ch. 26), who proclaim the folly and ridiculous ignorance of the Calvinists and Lutherans, and also their heretical novelty, because they call the sacrament of the body and blood a supper, and the Lord's Supper. But it is necessary that they argue against not only the aforementioned authors, but many other Fathers and Papist Doctors besides, who likewise name the Holy Eucharist in this way, such as Origen (in Ex. Hom. IV), Basil of Caesarea (reg. brev. n. 210), Gregory of Nyssa (orat. II on the resurrection of Christ), Anastasius Sinaita (in Hexaem. lib. V), Germanus of Constantinople (in Theoria), Rabanus (de inst. Cleric. lib. I, c. 31), Nilus (in Paraenesib. n. 120), Hesychius (in Lev.), Procopius (in c. XIV Lev.), Photius (in Biblioth. cod. 215), Sedulius, and Haymo (in this place). Cabasilas (Exposit. Liturg. c. 42), and indeed the Pope himself, Leo I (sermon VII on the passion), as well as the Catechism published by the authority of the Council of Trent, which in the chapter on the Eucharist has this: The most ancient Fathers, following the authority of the Apostles, sometimes called the Holy Eucharist by the name of supper, because it was instituted by Christ the Lord in that last supper as a saving mystery. It refers without doubt to the present passage, outside of which you would look in vain for another where the Apostle has called it so. Concerning which, one should also hear Johannes Stephanus Durandus, President of the Theological Curia (lib. I, c. 1): Paul, he says, in 1 Cor. XI, calls the mystical banquet of Christ, in which the faithful become partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, not a common supper, but the Lord's Supper. Estius himself, even if he is for himself with Cajetan, Gagny, and Hofmeister, Chrysostom and Theophylact, as well as Primasius and Sedulius, he does not deny, however, that some of them include the very communion of the Eucharist under the name of the Lord's Supper together with the banquet, although he thinks it more likely that only that banquet of the faithful, as it was distinct from the participation of the Eucharist, is called the Lord's Supper by the Apostle. But whom does D. Thomas refute here; it is not permitted or it is not fitting for you to eat the Lord's Supper, that is, to take the sacrament of the Eucharist. And Lyranus: Here the Apostle argues a third time, that they will behave badly regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist, as far as food is concerned, because some of them were taking the body of Christ after having eaten: Dionysius the Carthusian: To eat the Lord's supper, that is, to take the Eucharist, which had been instituted at the last supper. Cornelius à Lapide refutes this, explaining this verse thus: When you come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper. As if he were saying, while you come together in such a way for the Eucharist and the supper of Christ the Lord, your supper is no longer the Lord's supper, as it used to be: And your eating is no longer to eat the Lord's supper, as it once was; you do not institute the supper of the Lord (who invited all the Apostles, and even Judas, to his sober and pious supper), but that of Bacchus or Mars. For you come together to get yourselves drunk, and to exclude the poor: Therefore, each one is drunk in himself, but violent toward the poor: Thus Anselm, Chrysostom, Theophylact. Secondly, with Vatablus and Erasmus, the Greek ὐκ ἔςι can be taken for ὐκ ἔξεςι, it is not, that is, it is not permitted for you to eat the Lord's supper for the reason which he adds; but the former sense is deeper, and more vigorous, and stings the Corinthians more. These things are there in Cornelius: Who furthermore has this to say regarding the following verse: For every one taketh before other his own supper: St. Augustine in his one hundred and eighteenth epistle says, he takes before, that is, he takes before the synaxis. For this is properly to take before: And because to remove this presumption, he commands in verse 33 that they wait for one another, namely at the supper before the holy synaxis. For in the holy synaxis itself or after it, there does not seem to have been a need for waiting, since it was not celebrated until after all had gathered, and they took it indiscriminately, the poor mixed with the rich. Which are entirely conformable to our opinion, and confirm it sufficiently. Jerome illustrates the whole passage thus: It is no longer the Lord's, but human, when each one seizes it alone as his own supper, and does not share with another who has not offered; so that you seem to come together more for the sake of satiety than for the sake of the mystery. Moreover, the Lord's supper ought to have been common to all, because he delivered the sacraments equally to all his disciples who were present. Anselm explains it thus: Now you cannot receive the sacrament of the Redeemer, nor do you any longer make a banquet there in the likeness of the Lord's supper, etc., and thus you are not fit to eat the Lord's supper, that is, to receive the holy Eucharist, which is to be received by those who are fasting and in harmony. Regarding the abuse in the agapes, Aretius has this to say: The scope of the institution of the agapes was to refresh the poor; moderate satiety. They observe neither; they send the poor away hungry; they themselves depart not satisfied but drunk. To leave the poor hungry was a great inhumanity: But to depart drunk is a great impudence.

Latin:

v. 22. Μὴ γὰρ οἰκίας ὐκ ἔχετε εἰς τὸ ἐσθίειν κὶ πίνειν; Quantum lubet & quibuscum lubet. Domestıcæ epulæ sunt, quorum vultis, istæ communes fidelibus, ut ipse Do- minus.

Ἢ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τῦ Θεῦ καταφρονεῖτε. Respicitur locus, qui est Levit. XIX. 30. Sanctuarium meum reveremini,

Καὶ καταισχύνετε τὺς μὴ ἔχοντας. Hoc vero est, inquit, pauperibus exprobrare pauperta- tem. Durum est, quod interim esuriant. Sentiant se con- temni.

Nil habet infelix paupertas durius in se, Quam quod ridiculos homines facit.

Τί ὑμῖν εἴπω; ἐπαινέσω ὑμᾶς ἐν τύτῳ; ὐκ ἐπαινῶ. Est schema, quod ἐρώτησιν vocant veteres, quo sæpè uti hunc Apostolum notavit Isidorus Pelusiota libro III. epi- stola 183.

Dubium reddunt imprimis Pontificii, anne per κυριακὸν δεῖπνον hic S. Eucharistia, an vero ἀγάπη intelligatur. Quod posterius malunt Jesuita Dil- lingenses, Estius & alii. Temperamentum, ut alias, ceu moderator & conciliator partium amat Grotius; hoc proponere videtur : totum illud convivium, cujus partem aut primam aut postre- mam faciebant mysteria, designari. Sed non ap- paret causa, cur negemus ipsam Eucharistiam S. intelligi? Convenientibus vobis, non est, inquit Apostolus, Cœnam Dominicam edere. Causam, cur aliud quid agere potius eos judicet, quam sa- cram Eucharistiam celebrare, reddit; quasi dicat, tantum abest, ut Eucharistiam, prout à Domi- no instituta est, celebretis, ut alia omnia potius agatis, quandoquidem properetis ad epulum, antequam conveneritis omnes, & quisque suam cœnam occupet cibos domi præparatos, & illos quos in commune conferre debebant, adeo, ut, dum nonnulli jejuni adhuc sunt, & esuriunt, alii jam saturi sint, imo ebrii; quem sensum, id, quod agitis, non est edere Dominicam cœnam, sed longe aliud, Græcos Interpp. & è Latinis Herveum & Cajetanum tradere, ac percommodum esse agno- scit Estius. Simplicius certè hoc est, quam si ἐσὶ cum Erasmo, Glossa interlineari, Lombardo, Thoma, & Lyrano vertas licet; hoc modo: Ita agitis, ut non liceat Dominicam cœnam celebrare, quemadmodum oportet. Nec vero huic inter- pretationi obstat, quod Estius obstare credidit, quod nullo modo verisimile sit, hæc, quæ à Paulo referuntur, in communione S. Eucharistiæ conti- gisse. Nam id ut afferamus, necessum non est, etsi δεῖπνον κυριακὸν de S. Eucharistia accipiamus. Non enim in illa cœna ea accidisse, sed circa aga- pam seu commune convivium censemus, quod cum S. Eucharistia conjunctum fuit in eodem conventu Ecclesiastico, cum nempe ante per- ceptionem sacramenti debita præparatio, & post eandem sancta conversatio requirebatur, nec ul- latenus istos conventus talia, quæ reprehendit Apostolus, decebant. Et per cœnam Domi- nicam hic ipsum epulum sacrum, in quo sumun- tur corpus & sanguis Domini, intelligunt S. Au- gustinus Epist. CXIIX. ad Januar. Ambrosius in h. l. Pelagius, Beda, Anshelmus, Glossa, Lombar- dus, Thomas, Lyranus, Claudius Taurinensis, Hervæus, Dionysius Carthus. & inter Græcos Theo- doretus, & Oecumenius, quorum verba sunt : Dominicam cænam vocat Dominicum sacramen- tum. Huic etiam intellectui favere videri, quod Apostolus traditionem Dominicam paulò post repetens, dicat: Ego sic accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi vobis &c. Ubi non aliam cœnam præter eam, in qua corpus & sanguis Domini sumebantur, commemorat; fatetur Estius. Nec verò abnuunt nobis Chrysostomus, & Tertullia- nus, ad quos provocat Estius. Ille Hom. XXVII. in h. l. de S. Eucharistia: Ad hanc cænam Domi- nicam, inquit, cor tuum extende. Et quanquam Chrysostomus divites redarguat, quod cum paupe- ribus non accumberent in conventibus ἀγάπης καὶ Φιλαδελφίας. Addit tamen, Apostolum his ver- bis δεῖπνον κυριακὸν Φαγεῖν ad illam Corinthios transmittere vesperam, in qua Christus reverenda tradidit sacramenta. Hic verò, Tertullianus nem- pe, libro de spectac. Non possumus, ait, cænam Dei edere, & cænam dæmoniorum. Quæ testimo- nia non tantum interpretationi Estiana, sed etiam impudentiæ Galeni Catech. 124. & Maldonati in Matth. c. 26. opponenda sunt, qui stultitiam & ridiculam inscitiam Calvinianorum & Lutherano- rum, nec non hæreticam novitatem proclamant, quod sacramentum corporis & sanguinis cœnam, & cœnam Dominicam nuncupent. Cujus vero ne- cessum est, ut arguant non solum prædictos auto- res, sed multos præterea alios Patres & Doctores Pontificios, qui pariter ita S. Eucharistiam nomi- nant, ceu sunt Origenes in Ex. Hom. IV. Basil. Cæs. regul. brev. n. 210. Greg. Nyssenus orat. II. in resur- rect. Christi, Anastas. Sinait. in Hexaem. l. V. Ger- man. Constantin. in Theoria, Raban. de inst. Cleric. lib. I. c. 31. Nilus in Parænesib. n. 120. Hesych. in Lev. Procopius in c. XIV. Lev. Photius in Biblioth. cod. 215. Sedul. & Haymo in h. l. Cabasila Expo- sit. Liturg. c. 42. imo Pontifex ipse Leo I. sermone VII. de passione, ut & Catechismus, Concilii Tri- dentini autoritate editus, qui capite de Euchari- stia ita habet: Vetustissimi Patres, Apostoli autori- tatem sequuti, cæna etiam nomine S. Eucharistiam interdum appellarunt, quod in illo novissima cæna salutari mysterio à Christo Domino sit instituta. Respicit sine dubio præsentem locum, extra quem alium, ubi ita appellarit Apostolus, temere quæ- res. De quo etiam audiendus Johannes Stephanus Durandus Theolog. Cur. Præses l. I. c. 1. Paulus, inquit, 1. Cor. XI. mysticum Christi convivium, in quo fideles satri corporis & sanguinis Domini par- ticipes fiunt, non cænam communem, sed cænam Dominicam appellat. Estius ipse, etsi pro sese cum Cajetano, Gagnao & Hofmeistero Chrysostomum & Theophylactum, nec non Primasium & Sedulium laudet, non diffitetur tamen, illorum nonnullos nomine cœnæ Dominicæ cum convivio simul compre- bendere ipsam Eucharistiæ communionem, quan- quam verosimilius putet, solum illud convivium fidelium, ut erat ab Eucharistiæ participatione diversum, Apostolo dici cœnam Dominicam. Quem verò redarguat hic D. Thomas; non licet vel non competit vobis cœnam Dominicam manducare, id est, sumere Eucharistiæ sacramentum. Et Lyranus: Hic tertio arguit Apostolus, quod male se habebunt circa sacramentum Eucharistiæ, quantùm ad ci- bum, quia aliqui eorum pransi sumebant corpus Christi: Dionysius Carthusianus: Dominicam cœnam manducare, id est, Eucharistiam sumere, quæ in cœna novissima fuerat instituta. Redarguat Cornelius à Lapide, hunc versum ita explicans: Convenientibus ergo vobis in unum, jam non est Do- minicam cœnam manducare. Quasi dicat, dùm convenitis tali modo ad Eucharistiam, & cœnam Christi Domini, jam vestra cœna non est cœna Dominica, uti esse solebat: Et vestrum mandu- care jam non est Dominicam cœnam manduca- re, uti olim erat; non instituitis cœnam Domini, (qui omnes Apostolos, quin & Judam cœnæ suæ sobriæ & piæ adhibuit) sed Bacchi aut Martis. Convenitis enim ad vos inebriendum, & paupe- res excludendum: Itaque quilibet in se ebrius, in pauperes verò violentus est: Ita Anshelmus, Chry- sostomus, Theophylactus. Potest secundo cum Vatablo & Erasmo Græcum ὐκ ἔςι sumi pro ὐκ ἔξεςι, non est, hoc est, non licet vobis Domini- cam cœnam manducare ob rationem, quam subdit; sed prior sensus penitior est, & nervosior magisque pungit Corinthios. Hæc ibi Cornelius: Qui porrò ad versum sequentem ita habet: Unus- quisque enim suam cœnam presumit: S. Augusti- nus epistola centesima decima octava presumit, inquit, hoc est, sumit ante synaxin. Hoc enim proprie est presumere: Et quia ad hanc præsum- tionem tollendam, jubet vers. 33. ut invicem sese expectent, scilicet in cœna ante S. synaxin. Nam in ipsa sacra synaxi vel post eam, non videtur opus fuisse expectatione, cum ea non celebraretur, nisi postquam omnes convenissent, eamque pro- miscue sumebant pauperes misti divitibus. Quæ nostræ sententiæ prorsus conformia sunt, eam- que satis confirmant. Hieronymus totum locum ita illustrat: Jam non est Dominica, sed humana, quando unusquisque tanquam cœnam propriam solus invadit, & alii, qui non obtulerit, non imper- tit; ita ut magis propter saturitatem, quam propter mysterium videamini convenire. Cæterùm cœna Dominica omnibus debebat esse communis, quia ille omnibus discipulis suis, qui aderant, æqualiter tradidit sacramenta. Anshelmus ita explicat: Jam non potestis sacramentum Redemptoris accipere, nec jam ad similitudinem cœnæ Domini facitis ibi con- vivium &c. & ita non estis idonei Dominicam cœnam manducare, id est, sacram Eucharistiam percipere, quæ à jejunis & concordantibus est acci- pienda. De abusu in agapis Aretius ita habet: Scopus institutionis τῶν ἀγαπῶν erat reficere pau- peres; moderata saturitas. Neutrum illi servant; Pauperes dimittunt famelicos; ipsi non saturati sed ebrii discedunt. Famelicos relinquere pauperes, magna erat inhumanitas: At ebrium discedere magna impudentia.

## 11:23
v. 23. For I have received of the Lord.

It can be doubted whether Paul learned these things from the other Apostles narrating them, or additionally from revelation, just as it is credible that Moses learned certain things of past time.

I taught you. There cannot be any doubt that Paul received it from divine revelation, who expressly says he received it from the Lord, who professes that he received his Gospel from no man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, Gal. I. 12. and in general 2 Tim. III. 16. All, he says, scripture is God-breathed. But the Papists are impious when they argue against this divine tradition, even if this were an Apostolic precept, that the Church and the supreme Pontiff could have abrogated this precept, which is done by Vasquez, Part III. Thom. disput. 216. n. 60. But they are rash who say that the tradition is indeed described, but not the precept, with Andradius and Bellarmine. Certainly, Eck himself had to admit in Homily 36 on the sacraments that Paul commanded the Corinthians the use of both kinds, and that Cyprian and Jerome testify to this. And the Jesuit Gregory of Valencia concedes in his book on the legitimate use of the Eucharist, that the Apostle here does not merely narrate the history of the institution; but also adapts to the Church itself the precepts of the Lord, which are either contained in that institution or are deduced from it.

That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed.

When death was as if present before his eyes. And you, when the memory of such a thing is celebrated, do you growl because of your riches?

He took bread.

See what we have said regarding Matthew on this matter. He broke the bread for the sake of distribution. Therefore the Evangelists add that he distributed the broken bread. But how he broke the same is not certain. However, that a peculiar manner was used by Christ in the breaking of even common bread, from which he himself could be recognized, as being proper to him, is gathered from Luke XXIV. 35. Which, because we are ignorant of it, it is not necessary that we use the breaking itself in the administration of the Holy Supper according to the example of Christ, provided it is true bread, and so prepared that it can be distributed. Otherwise than has seemed to most Calvinists, who make the breaking of bread in the Holy Supper simply necessary, and some part of it, whether essential or integral. And said take. For He did not wish so holy an action to be some mute spectacle, from which each person might conjecture what He himself intends: But He Himself wished to indicate in sufficiently clear and perspicuous words what kind of banquet He institutes here, and what kind of food is to be expected there. He said therefore: Take, He did not say, look, just as in the Papacy the blessed bread in the sacrifice of the Mass is offered to be looked at by those standing by, and is feigned to be the body of the Lord. Christ, however, did not wish to institute a spectacle here, but a divine feast, in which the guests are satisfied not by seeing, but by taking. Therefore He soon adds, and eat, He does not say, sacrifice, put back the bread, carry it around, adore. For the sacrament was not instituted for this; but He commands to eat: By what instrument, indeed? Certainly by that by which bread could be eaten, which is done by the mouth, which the Adversaries themselves call the organ of mastication, and that is clear from the other part of the sacrament, where Mark says of the disciples: That they all drank from the cup: Where to drink cannot be the same as to believe. For Judas also drank from the cup, who nevertheless did not have faith. But what that is, which they ought to eat, is expressed in explicit words: This is my body, as the blessed Balduinus succinctly refuted the errors of both the Papists and the Calvinists with these words. We, on the other hand, have dealt by design against the Calvinist Sacramentarians in the Stereoma of the words of the Testament of Christ; Against

But let those who wish compare the Papists on the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Article X, here.

Latin:

v. 23. Ἐγὼ γὰρ παρέλαβον ἀπὸ τῦ κυρίυ.

Dubitari potest didicerit hæc Paulus narrantibus Apo- stolis aliis, an insuper ex revelatione, quomodo credibile est, Mosen quædam didicisse præteriti temporis.

Vos docui. Non potest esse dubium, quin ex revelatione divina acceperit Paulus, qui diserte se accepisse ait ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, qui Evangelium suum à nullo ho- minum, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi se accepisse profitetur Gal. I. 12. & in genere 2. Tim. III. 16. Πᾶσα, inquit, γραφὴ θεόπνευστος. Impii autem sunt Papistæ, cum disputant adversus hanc tradi- tionem divinam, etiamsi Apostolicum præceptum hic foret, Ecclesiam & summum Pontificem præ- ceptum hoc abrogare potuisse, quod à Vasquio fit Part. III. Thom. disput. 216. n. 60. Temerarii au- tem sunt, qui traditionem quidem describi, non au- tem præceptum ajunt cum Andradio, & Bellarmino. Fateri certe Eccius ipse debuit Homil. 36. de sacr: Paulum præcepisse Corinthiis utriusque speciei usum, idque testari Cyprianum ac Hieronymum. Et con- cedit Gregorius de Valentia Jesuita libr. de legit. usu Eucharistiæ, Apostolum hic non nudam tan- tùm narrare historiam institutionis; sed etiam ad ipsam Ecclesiam accommodare præcepta Domini, quæ vel in illa institutione continentur, vel ex ea dedu- cuntur.

Ὅτι ὁ κύριος Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῇ νυκτὶ, ᾗ παρεδίδοτο.

Cum ei mors velut præsens esset ante oculos. Et vos cum memoria talis rei celebratur, ob divitias vestras ingu- mescitis ?

Ἔλαβεν ἄρτον.

Vide, quæ ad Matthæum hac de re diximus. Fregit panem propter distributionem. Ideo ad- dunt Evangelistæ, quod panem fractum distribue- rit. Quomodo autem eundem fregerit, non constat. Peculiarem autem modum adhibitum fuisse à Christo in fractione panis etiam commu- nis, è quo dignosci ipse potuerit, utpote ei pro- prio, è Luc. XXIV. 35. colligitur. Quem quia ignoramus, necessum non est, ut fractionem ipsam in S. Cœnæ dispensatione ad exemplum Christi adhibeamus, modo verus panis sit, & ita compa- ratus, ut distribui possit. Secus atque Calvinianis plerisque visum est, qui ἀρτοκλασίαν in S. cœna simpliciter necessariam, ejusque partem aliquam sive essentialem, sive integralem faciunt. Καὶ εἰπὲ λάβετε. Hoc fracto pane dixit. Noluit enim tam sanctam actionem esse mutum aliquod spectacu- lum, de quo unusquisque conjicere possit, quid ipse velit: Sed ipse verbis satis claris ac perspicuis indicare voluit, quale hic instituat convivium, & qualis ibi cibus expectandus sit. Dixit igitur: Ac- cipite, non dixit, aspicite, quemadmodum in Pa- patu panis benedictus in sacrificio Missæ spectan- dus præbetur adstantibus, & corpus Domini esse fingitur. Christus autem hic non spectaculum instituere voluit, sed divinum epulum, in quo con- vivæ non videndo, sed accipiendo saturantur. Id- circò mox addit, & manducate, non ait, sacrifica- te, reponite panem, circumgestate, adorate. Ad hoc enim sacramentum institutum non est; sed manducare jubet: Quo vero instrumento? Certe eo, quo panis manducari poterat, quod ore fit, quod manducationis organum vocant ipsi Adver- sarii, idque ex altera parte sacramenti liquet, ubi Marcus de discipulis dicit: Bibisse eos ex ca- lice omnes: Ubi bibere non potest idem esse, ac credere. Nam & Judas è calice bibit, qui ta- men fidem non habuit. Quid autem illud sit, quod manducare debeant, disertis exprimitur verbis: Hoc est corpus meum, uti succinctè B. Bal- duinus hisce tum Pontificiorum, tum Calviniano- rum errores profligavit. Nos contra Sacra- mentarios Calvinianos ex instituto egimus in Stereom. verborum Testamenti Christi; Contra

Pontificios verò in Exegem. A. C. art. X. quæ hic conferat, cui libuerit.

## 11:24
v. 24. Τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον. Some manuscripts have θρυπτόμενον, not badly.

One or another manuscript Codex cannot prejudice the others, whose total consensus Erasmus asserts. Nor is that θρυπτόμενον appropriate. For it is broken into minute parts: which is the proper meaning of the word θρύπτω. But was the body of Christ broken into minute parts on the cross? Was it not to be preserved from breaking in such a way that, by divine caution, already made in the type of the paschal lamb, Ex. XII, not even a bone of it should be broken, John XIX? Wherefore neither can that κλώμενον be taken properly concerning the breaking of the body: But the Pauline phrase must be explained from the words of institution τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον. Which is given for you, as Luke has it in chapter XXII. 19. Which phrases are not exchanged without cause. Because the gravity of Christ's passion is indicated: That the body of Christ was so delivered into death that, although it was not broken, much less crushed, but had to be preserved whole by the holy counsel of God; yet it felt such great passions, such great torments, as if it had been broken or crushed. There are indeed those who refer that κλώμενον to the breaking in the Holy Eucharist κατ' ἀναλογίαν, because it is done by the Sacramentarians, who here seek the sacramental analogy of broken bread and broken body of Christ, which they imagine. But there is no place for this, since the body of Christ cannot be said to be broken on the cross in that sense, or even according to mere likeness, in the way that the Eucharistic bread is broken in the celebration of the Holy Supper: However, there ought to be an agreement and likeness between the sign and the thing signified. There are also some among the orthodox who understand the breaking of the body of Christ as taken in the sense of distribution, which sense the blessed Luther proposed in the Major Confession, Vol. III, Jena, German, page 497, and the blessed Hülsemann agrees with him, understanding the breaking or distribution of both the earthly and heavenly thing in the Eucharist. There is no doubt for me, says the blessed Luther, that the text of Paul: This is the body, which is broken for you, is to be understood simply of the breaking and distributing at the table, as he also says in 1 Cor. X. The bread that we break is the distributed body of Christ. Since then the text in Paul, which speaks of the bread or body of Christ, is understood of the distribution at the table, and not of the giving on the cross, so the text of the cup can certainly have the very same meaning. And thus Matthew and Mark would also be found to agree. Namely, this is my body, concerning which they say nothing of giving: As if it were otherwise well to be noted that He gives His body to them when He says: This is my body, there you have my body. So also of the cup: This is my blood, poured out for you, that is, distributed at the table, and set forth for the forgiveness of sins. I see nothing yet in the words that strongly contradicts such a meaning. For also Saint Paul leaves out at the cup (which is poured out for you), as if he wished to have said enough, because the bread is broken for them, so also the cup is distributed for them. These are the words of the blessed Hülsemann: We explain Τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον with Luther in the Major Confession rather as the breaking of bread or the distribution of earthly and heavenly things in the Eucharist than as the dissolution of Christ's life on the cross. Whence it is also a consequence that ποτή- ριον, ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν properly and immediately signifies the pouring into the mouths of the communicants, which very pouring is for the remission of sins, otherwise than Bellarmine, book 1, on the sacraments, chapter 24, contends from that, that the promise concerning the remission of sins was not made for the use of the Eucharist, because that pouring, to which the remission of sins is annexed, signifies the pouring of the blood of Christ on the cross, not in the Eucharist. Although indeed this explanation has no inconvenience, whence it was also approved by the blessed Balduinus: But he who explains τὸ διδόμενον concerning the giving into death made for us, and deems it likely that the Lord said both concerning His body in the first institution, because both were taken from the mouth of Christ, and the body of Christ is given for us in death, but is broken or distributed among us in the Holy Supper: Yet some things intervene, so that it seems less possible to subscribe to the same: 1. because Saint Luke uses τὸ δεδόμενον, which must be taken not concerning the giving or distribution in the Holy Eucharist, but concerning the giving or delivery into death, as the blessed Balduinus himself admits. 2. because it is added besides that the body of Christ is given ὑπὲρ for us. But when Christ or the body of Christ is said to be given for us, His merit is signified. Nowhere, however, is this the same as being given before us, or in our sight. Nor does this sense obtain in the word ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν 1 Cor. XV. 29. For there it does not denote in the sight of the dead, or among the dead; but over the dead according to the explanation of the blessed Luther, Vol. VI, Jena, f. 246, concerning which in its own place. Nor perhaps will another example of the same be able to be brought forth from the scriptures. 3. Because in the other part of the Holy Supper τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον does not denote the pouring into the mouths of those drinking, but the pouring of the blood of Christ made on the altar of the cross, because it is said that the cup is poured out ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, for us, Luke XXII. 20, on account of the blood of Christ, which it exhibits, since it is κοινωνία τῦ αἵματος, the communion of the blood of Christ, 1 Cor. X. 16. But not so; there ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν is before you, or in your sight, because it is one thing to be poured out in the sight of the Apostles, another to be poured out into the mouths of the Apostles, and it is most clear from Matthew and Mark that the pouring out is understood to have taken place in the passion of Christ, by these words τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν. Which Blessed Luther acknowledges. For that explanation, in the sight of many, has no place here, as it does not suit the use of the preposition περὶ with the genitive, which brings with it advantage, or even the substitution for many believers, or in the place of many, not a place, or sight before many, or in the sight of many, see Acts VIII. 15. Col. IV. 3. 1. Pet. III. 18. 4.
