Even if Christ had used both phrases, the τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν δεδόμενον which Luke has, and the τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον which Paul has, he would nevertheless have done so without doubt to explain the giving into death and his most grievous passion, endured in our stead: He would not, however, have explained both, namely both the delivery into death and the distribution in the Supper, so clearly, nor would the analogy then correspond in the other part, where τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν and τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν occurs. Blessed Luther certainly explains Luke and Paul as speaking of the same pouring out at the table, but says that Matthew and Mark deal with the pouring out on the cross. 5. Blessed Luther does not sell his opinion as certain: I do not say this, that I stand certain upon it, etc. And he acknowledges that the ancients explained it otherwise: Although this understanding has not been held until now, but everyone has understood the text as referring to the giving into suffering, and the pouring out on the cross. But why one should depart from the common interpretation, I see no solid reason? To say nothing of the fact that the sense would be inconvenient if it were explained in this way: This is the body my, which is broken for you, that is, in, with, and under this bread, which analysis we proved that such propositions, which exhibit it, require in the Stereoma, composed 40 and more years ago, is my body, that is, earthly and heavenly matter. For is there not with the bread and under the bread both the body of Christ and the bread itself? Nor, as Flacius said (l. 2. de sacr. c. 14.), can it be said that the breaking is attributed to the body of Christ on account of the breaking of the bread, because of the sacramental union of the bread and the body of Christ, as the blessed Gerhard taught (de cœna §. 163). Erasmus indeed prefers that explanation concerning the distribution of the body of Christ: The wheaten bread is broken, he says, so that it may confer life upon many: The body of Christ is also said to be broken, because it confers life equally upon all who worthily receive it. The same bread distributed among many is a symbol of concord: The same body immolated for all is a sign of friendship. Moreover, Erasmus admonishes the reader to examine it more diligently: Which was also done not obscurely by the blessed Luther.

As for St. Ignatius, whom they praise for that opinion from the Epistle to the Philadelphians, he has nothing except this: ἔις ἄρτος τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐθρύφθη, One bread broken for all. But what is this to the present phrase, by which the body of Christ is considered to be said to have been broken for us? The whole passage (so that the matter may be clear) is as follows: Μία γάρ ἐστιν ἡ σάρξ τῦ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ, ἰ̓ ἓν ἀυτῦ τὸ αἷμα, τὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐκχυθέν. ἑἷς ἰ̓ ἄρτος τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐθρύφθη, ἰ̓ ἓν ποτήριον τοῖς ὅλοις διενεμήθη: That is: For there is one flesh of the Lord Jesus, and one blood of his, which was poured out for us, and one bread broken for all. Nor does Chrysostom help that opinion. He says nothing else than that Christ was broken for all, namely on the cross, and was made body, that is, man in the incarnation for all. Καὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ὁμοίως ἐκλάσθη, καὶ σῶμα γέγονεν ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ἐξίσης. The whole passage serves to illustrate the present passage of the Apostle: If you therefore, he says, approach for the Eucharist, that is, thanksgiving, you also should do nothing unworthy of the eucharist or thanksgiving: Neither put your brother to shame, nor despise the hungry; do not get drunk, do not treat the Church with contumely. For you approach giving thanks for those things which you have obtained, and you therefore should return like for like, and not cut yourself off from your neighbor. For Christ gave to all equally, saying: Take, eat. He gave the body equally. But you do not even give common bread equally. For he was broken similarly for all and was made body equally for all. Nothing also can be carved out on this matter from Theophylact, whose words are these: Remember, he says, how he gave you this mystery at the last, and on that night, when he was about to be killed shortly after, and had a traitor as a guest. But you consider your brother worthy of any things, especially when you have been instructed to give thanks, such as Christ himself gave, so that he might both form and instruct us for that matter. You do, therefore, what is less worthy of these thanks, when you confound the Church itself, and while another is starving, you revel. And he indeed commanded this commonly to all: Take and eat, namely his body, which he had destined to die while distributing it equally to all, etc. Therefore, he explained τὸ κλώμενον as the dissolution of life or death rather than the breaking in the Eucharist. Finally, no one else can be brought forward who understood it as the breaking in the Eucharist, so that the blessed Luther rightly said that they all explained it as the delivery unto death and the passion.

Latin:

v. 24. Τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον. Manuscripti quidam habent θρυπτόμενον non male.

Non potest unus aut alter manuscriptus Codex cæteris, quorum summum consensum Erasmus af- ferit, præjudicare. Neque convenit illud θρυ- πτόμενον. Est enim in partes minutas fractum: quæ propria vocis θρύπτω significatio est. Num autem corpus Christi in cruce fractum est in minu- tas partes? Annon ita à fractione præservandum fuit, ut divina cautione, jam in typo agni paschalis factà, Ex. XII. ne ullum quidem os eidem frangi debuerit, Joh. XIX. Quapropter nec illud κλώμε- νον propriè de fractione corporis accipi potest: Sed explicanda phrasis Paulina est, è verbis institutio- nis τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον. Quod pro vobis tra- ditum est, ut Lucas habet cap. XXII. 19. Quæ phrases non sine causa permutantur. Quia in- dicatur gravitas passionis Christi: Quod corpus Christi ita traditum in mortem sit, ut quamvis non fractum, nedum comminutum sit, sed integrum servari, sancto Dei consilio, debuerit; tantas tamen passiones, tormenta tanta senserit, ac si con- fractum aut comminutum fuerit. Sunt quidem, qui illud κλώμενον ad fractionem in S. Eucharistia referunt κατ' ἀναλογίαν, quod sit à Sacramenta- riis, hic sacramentalem, quam fingunt, fracti panis & fracti corporis Christi analogiam quæren- tibus. Cui verò locus nullus est, siquidem cor- pus Christi non possit eo sensu, vel secundum simi- litudinem tantùm fractum dici in cruce, quem- admodum panis Eucharisticus frangitur in S. Cœnæ celebratione: Inter signum autem & signa- tum convenientiam & similitudinem intercedere oporteat. Sunt etiam ex orthodoxis quidam, qui fractionem corporis Christi, sensu distributionis acceptam intelligant, quem sensum proposuit B. Lutherus in Confess. Major. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. pag. 497. eique annuit B. Hülsemannus, fractionem seu distributionem rei & terrenæ & cælestis in Eu- charistia intelligens. Es ist bey mir kein Zweiffel, inquit B. Lutherus, daß der Text Pauli: Das ist der Leib, der für euch gebrochen wird, sey schlechts zu verstehen von dem Brechen und Austheilen über Tische, wie er auch saget 1. Cor. X. Das Brod, das wir brechen, ist der ausgetheilete Leib Christi. Weil dann der Text im Paulo, so vom Brod oder Leibe Christi redet, von der Austheilung über Tische, und nicht von dem Hingeben am Creutz verstan- den wird, so kan freylich der Text vom Becher auch eben denselbigen Verstand haben. Und so würden Matthäus und Marcus dann auch sich fin- den. Nemlich, das ist mein Leib, bey welchem sie nichts sagen vom Geben: Als sey es sonst wohl zu mercken, daß Er seinen Leib ihnen gebe, wenn Er spricht: Das ist mein Leib, da habet ihr meinen Leib. Also auch vom Becher: Das ist mein Blut, für euch ausgegossen, das ist, über Tische ausgetheilet, und fürgesetzet zur Vergebung der Sünden. Ich sehe noch nichts in Worten, das wider solchen Verstand fast streite. Dann auch Sanct Pau- lus bey dem Becher aussen läst, (der für euch ver- gossen wird) als wolle Er genug gesagt haben, weil das Brod für sie gebrochen wird, also werde auch der Becher für sie ausgetheilet. B. Hülsemanni hæc sunt: Τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον cum Luthero in Conf. Major. potius de panifragio seu distributio- ne rerum terrestrium & cælestium in Euchari- stia, quam de dissolutione vitæ Christi in cruce exponimus. Unde consequens est etiam ποτή- ριον, ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν proprie & proxime significare effusionem in ora communicantium, quæ ipsa effusio sit in remissio- nem peccatorum, secus quam Bellarminus lib. 1. de sacram. cap. 24. exinde contendit, promissionem de remissione peccatorum non factam esse usui Eucha- ristiæ, quia effusio illa, cui annexa est remissio pec- catorum, dicat effusionem sanguinis Christi in cru- ce, non in Eucharistia. Quanquam verò hæc ex- plicatio nihil incommodi habeat, unde etiam B. Balduino probata fuit: Qui vero τὸ διδόμενον de datione in mortem pro nobis facta explicat, & verisimile censet, Dominum de suo corpore utrumque dixisse in prima institutione, quia utrum- que ex ore Christi sumptum est, & corpus Christi pro nobis in morte datur, frangitur autem vel dis- tribuitur inter nos in S. Cœna: Nonnulla tamen intercedunt, quo minus subscribendum eidem videatur: 1. quod S. Lucas τὸ δεδόμενον adhibeat, quod non de datione vel distributione in S. Eu- charistia, sed de datione vel traditione in mortem, fatente ipsomet B. Balduino, accipiendum. 2. quod addatur prætereà dari corpus Christi ὑπὲρ pro no- bis. At cum Christus vel Christi corpus pro no- bis dari dicitur, meritum ejus significatur. Nu- spiam autem hoc idem est, quod ante nos, vel in conspectu nostri dari. Neque hic sensus in voce ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν 1. Cor. XV. 29. obtinet. Nam illic non notat in conspectu mortuorum, vel inter mor- tuos; sed super mortuos secundum explicationem B. Lutheri Tom. VI. Jen. f. 246. de quo suo loco. Nec fortè aliud ejusdem exemplum proferri po- terit è sacris. 3. Quia in altera S. Cœnæ parte τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον non notat effusionem in ora bibentium, sed effusionem sanguinis Christi in ara crucis factam, quia ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, pro nobis effundi dicitur τὸ ποτή- ριον Luc. XXII. 20. propter sanguinem Christi, quem exhibet, cum sit κοινωνία τῦ αἵματος com- municatio sanguinis Christi, 1. Cor. X. 16. Non autem; illic ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν est ante vos, vel in conspectu vestri, quia aliud est in conspectu Apostolorum ef- fundi, aliud in ora Apostolorum fundi, & è Matthæo & Marco luculentissimum est, effusionem in pas- sione Christi factam intelligi, vocibus istis τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν. Quod, agnoscit B. Lutherus. Nam hic locum non habet illa explicatio, in conspectu multorum, utpote non conveniens usui Præpositionis περὶ cum Genitivo, quæ commodum infert, aut etiam vicariatum fi- delium multorum, vel vice multorum, non lo- cum, vel conspectum ante multos, vel in conspe- ctu multorum, vid. Act. IIX. 15. Col. IV. 3. 1. Pet. III. 18. 4. Etiamsi utramque phrasin Christus ad- hibuisset, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν δεδόμενον quod Lucas, & τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον, quod Paulus habet, id ta- men sine dubio ad dationem in mortem & passio- nem ejus gravissimam, nostra vice exantlatam, ex- plicandam fecisset: Non vero utrumque, puta & traditionem in mortem, & distributionem in Cœna ita satis luculenter exposuisset, neque tùm ana- logia in altera parte, ubi τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμε- νον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν & τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν occurrit, responderet. B. Lutherus certe Lu- cam & Paulum de eadem fusione in mensa expli- cat, Matthæum autem & Marcum de effusione in cruce agere ait. 5. B. Lutherus non venditat suam sententiam pro certa: Solches sage ich nicht, daß ich gewiß darauff stehe, &c. & agnoscit, aliter exposuisse veteres: Ob nun wohl dieser Verstand bisßher nicht gehalten, sondern vom geben ins Lei- den, und vom vergiessen am Creutz jedermann den Text verstanden hat. Cur autem à communi in- terpretatione recedendum sit, nullam video so- lidam rationem? Ut taceam inconvenientem fore sensum, si hoc modo explicetur: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur, id est, in, cum, ac sub pane hoc, quam analysin exhibitivas ejusmo- di propositiones postulare in Stereomate, ante hos 40. & quod excurrit, annos concinnato, evicimus, est corpus meum, h. e. materia terrena & cælestis. Num n. cum pane & sub pane est & corpus Christi, & panis ipse? Neque cum Flacio dici posse l. 2. de sacr. c. 14. corpori Christi fractionem tribui propter fractionem panis, propter sacramentalem panis & corporis Christi unionem, docuit B. Gerhardus de cœna §. 163. Erasmus quidem præfert illam expli- cationem de distributione corporis Christi: Fran- gitur, inquit, panis triticeus, ut multis vitam con- ferat: Frangi dicitur & corpus Christi, quod vitam ex æquo conferat omnibus dignè sumentibus. Idem panis inter multos distributus concordiæ est symbo- lum: Idem corpus pro omnibus immolatum amici- tiæ signum est. Cæterum admonet lectorem Era- smus, quo diligentius excutiat: Quod etiam haud obscurè à B. Luthero factum.

Quod ad S. Ignatium, quem pro ista sententia laudant ex Epist. ad Philadelphenses, nihil ille habet, nisi hoc: ἔις ἄρτος τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐθρύφθη, Unus panis omnibus confractus. Quid verò hoc ad præsentem phrasin, quà corpus Christi pro nobis fractum, dici censetur. Integer locus (ut res constet) ita ha- bet: Μία γάρ ἐστιν ἡ σάρξ τῦ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ, ἰ̓ ἓν ἀυτῦ τὸ αἷμα, τὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐκχυθέν. ἑἷς ἰ̓ ἄρτος τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐθρύφθη, ἰ̓ ἓν ποτήριον τοῖς ὅλοις διενεμήθη: Id est: Una enim est caro Domini Jesu, & unus ejus sanguis, qui pro nobis effusus est, & unus panis, pro omnibus confractus. Nec Chrysostomus eam juvat sententiam. Nihil aliud dicit, quam quod Chri- stus pro omnibus fractus sit, scilicet in cruce, & ex æquo factus corpus, id est, homo in incarnatione pro omnibus. Καὶ γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ὁμοίως ἐκλάσθη, καὶ σῶμα γέγονεν ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ἐξίσης. Totus locus ad præsentem Apostoli locum illu- strandum facit: Si tu igitur, inquit, accedas pro- pter Eucharistiam, id est, gratiarum actionem, tu quoque nihil facias indignum eucharistia seu gra- tiarum actione: Neque fratrem pudore afficias, ne- que esurientem despicias; ne inebrieris, ne Ecclesiam afficias contumelia. Accedis enim gratias agens pro iis, quæ es adeptus, & tu ergo par pari referas, & ne te abscindas à proximo. Etenim Christus omnibus ex æquo dedit, dicens: Accipite, comedite. Ille cor- pus ex æquo dedit. Tu autem ne panem quidem com- munem das ex æquo. Etenim pro omnibus similiter est fractus & ex æquo factus est corpus pro omnibus. Nihil quoque eam in rem è Theophylacto exsculpi potest, cujus ista sunt: Reminiscere, inquit, quem- admodum postremum id vobis mysterium dederit, & eâ nocte, quæ erat paulo post occidendus, & pro- ditorem haberet convivam. Tu verò fratrem qui- busvis rebus ducis dignum, præsertim cum instru- ctus sis gratias agere, quales & Christus ipse agebat, ut nos ad eam rem & formaret & instrueret. Facis ergo, quod minus est his gratiis dignum, cum Eccle- siam ipsam confundis, & alio famescente, tu debac- charis. Et id quidem communiter cunctis præcepit: Accipite & manducate, corpus scilicet suum, quod omnibus æque dispertiens mori destinasset &c. De dissolutione ergo vitæ vel morte potius, quam de fractione in Eucharistia τὸ κλώμενον exposuit. Nullus denique alius afferri potest, qui de fractio- ne in Eucharistia acceperit, ut recte B. Lutherus quosvis de traditione in mortem & passione expo- suisse dixerit.

## 11:25
v. 25. After supper.

He adds this so that he may distinguish the mystical people from those preceding things, which Luke mentions. See what was said on Matt. XXVI. 25.

This cup is the new testament in my blood. These are the words of Luke in this history. Whence it is credible that Paul took these from his Commentaries, although, as I think, they were not yet published at that time.

He did not take these from Luke, but received them from the Lord, v. 23. The whole words of Luke are as follows: Τῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί με, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον. Which predicate is not brought forth concerning the blood, because the construction is repugnant, but concerning the cup: But how concerning the cup? Certainly not by reason of the pouring out of the cup, which was happening at the supper: for that does not admit that 'for you', which is not 'before you' or 'in your presence', but 'for your sake', and is explained concerning the shedding of blood, Matt. XXVI. 28, done for us for the remission of sins: for this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. But this shedding of blood was done on the altar of the cross. What then does that predicate mean here, when the cup is said to be poured out for us? Resp. It is not brought forth concerning this cup in itself, and by itself, or taken materially, but in this sacramental use, for thus the cup, as one was drinking from it, was the new testament not by reason of that wine contained in it simply, but as it was the communication of the blood of Christ, which was offered with the wine in the cup of blessing, and so in the blood, and on account of the blood of Christ, which they were receiving from the cup with the wine, as it was the blood of the New Testament shed for the remission of sins. Wherefore the cup is also said to be poured out for the remission of sins, on account of the blood, which it contains, and offers to be drunk for us for the remission of sins. The container for the thing contained: The cup, that is, the blood, contained in the cup. Concerning which we have spoken to Luke, and in the Stereoma of the words of the Testament of Christ.

Latin:

v. 25. Μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι.

Hoc addit, ut mysticum populum ab illis antecedenti- bus, quorum Lucas meminit, distinguat. Vide, quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 25.

Τῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ αἵματι. Sunt verba Lucæ in hac historia. Unde credibile est ex ejus Commentariis, quanquam tunc, ut puto, nondum editis, Paulum hæc sumpsisse.

Non è Luca hæc sumpsit, sed à Domino accepit, v. 23. Verba Lucæ integra ita habent: Τῦτο τὸ πο- τήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί με, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑ- μῶν ἐκχυνόμενον. Quod prædicatum non de san- guine effertur, quia repugnat constructio, sed de τῷ ποτηρίῳ: Quomodo autem de poculo? Non utique ratione effusionis poculi, quæ in cœna fie- bat: id enim non admittit illud ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, quod non est ante vos vel coram vobis, sed pro vobis, & ex- plicatur de sanguinis effusione, Matth. XXVI. 28. pro nobis factâ in remissionem peccatorum τῦτο γάρ ἐςι τὸ αἷμά με τὸ τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης, τὸ πε- ρὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν. Hæc autem effusio sanguinis facta est in ara crucis. Quid ergò sibi hic vult illud prædicatum, cum po- culum pro nobis dicitur effusum? Resp. Non de poculo hoc effertur in se, & per se, aut materialiter accepto, sed in usu hoc sacramentali, sic enim pocu- lum, qua bibebatur ex eodem, erat ἡ καινὴ διαθή- κη non ratione vini illius in eodem contenti sim- pliciter, sed qua erat communicatio sanguinis Chri- sti, qui cum vino præbebatur in poculo benedi- ctionis, adeoque ἐν τῷ αἵματι, in sanguine, & pro- pter sanguinem Christi, quem è poculo cum vino percipiebant, utpote qui erat sanguis N. Testa- menti effusus in remissionem peccatorum. Qua- propter poculum effusum etiam dicitur in remis- sionem peccatorum, ob sanguinem, quem continet, & bibendum præbet pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum. Continens pro contento: Poculum, id est, sanguis, in poculo contentus. Quo de ad Lucam, & in Stereomate verborum Testamenti Chri- sti diximus.

## 11:26
v. 26. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup. These are the words of Paul showing to what these mysteries pertain.

You proclaim the death of the Lord. You proclaim, that is, you ought to proclaim.

Until he comes. To judgment, that is. See Acts 1:11.

That word ὁσάκις implies that this sacrament is to be used more frequently, and because it is subjoined καὶ (ὁσάκις) τὸ ποτήριον τῦ τὸ πίνητε, it is taught that the use of the chalice is not to be separated from the reception of the Eucharistic bread, but that whoever and as often as they ought to partake of the Eucharistic bread, the same persons ought then also to drink the blessed chalice, and since the end of this sacred action is added, the proclamation of the death of Christ, what is clearer than that those who in the reception of the Holy Eucharist are commanded to proclaim the death of the Lord are commanded not only to eat this bread, but also to drink this cup, for the proclaiming of the death of the Lord, and that this is to be observed so, not only for one or two ages, but ἄχρις ὗ ἂν ἔλθῃ, until the Lord shall have come to judgment, that is, until the consummation of the age. Which things are utterly repugnant to the Papal chalice-theft. For what the Apostle commanded here, that the Pope, NOTWITHSTANDING the institution of Christ and the Apostolic precept, in the Council of Constance, deservedly called from thence the OBSTANTIAN [Council], ordained otherwise, while he decreed that the chalice was not to be offered to the Laity, but only the Eucharistic bread. And that very Council of Constance itself confesses that in the primitive Church this sacrament was received by the faithful under both kinds. Cassander in his book on communion under one kind, fol. 17, says that it cannot be demonstrated that for a full thousand years and more in any part of the Catholic Church this most holy sacrament of the Eucharist has been administered to the faithful people in the holy assembly from the Lord's table otherwise than under both the symbol of bread and of wine. What? That Gelasius wished all to be bound to the reception of the chalice, and defined it to be sacrilege if the chalice is not distributed with the Eucharistic bread. C. Comperimus, distinct. II. de consecrat. We find that some, having taken only a portion of the sacred body, abstain from the chalice of the sacred blood. Who without doubt (since I know not by what SUPERSTITION they are taught to be bound) should either receive the entire sacraments, or be kept from the entire ones, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot come about without GREAT SACRILEGE. Therefore, by the judgment of this Pontiff, the Council of Constance made itself guilty of great sacrilege. Thomas Aquinas in this place, lecture 5, teaches that this sacrament is handed down under a double species for three reasons: First, indeed, because of its perfection: Because since it is a spiritual refreshment, it ought to have spiritual food and drink. For even bodily refreshment is not perfected without food and drink. Secondly, because of its signification. For it is a memorial of the Lord's passion, through which the blood of Christ was separated from the body, and therefore in this sacrament the blood is offered separately from the body. Thirdly, because of the salutary effect of this sacrament. For it avails for the health of the body, and therefore the body is offered; it avails for the health of the soul, and therefore the blood is offered.

§. 51. Reason from the preceding.

Latin:

v. 26. Ὁσάκις γὰρ ἂν ἐσθίητε τὸν ἄρτον τῦτον καὶ τὸ ποτήριον τῦτο πίνητε. Sunt verba Pauli ostendentis, quo pertineant hæc my- steria.

Τὸν θάνατον τῦ κυρίε καταγγέλλετε. Annunciatis, id est, annunciare debetis.

Ἄχρις ὗ ἂν ἔλθῃ. Ad judicium scilicet. Vide Act. I. 11.

Illud ὁσάκις innuit frequentius esse usurpan- dum hoc sacramentum, & quia subjungitur καὶ (ὁσάκις) τὸ ποτήριον τῦ τὸ πίνητε docetur, non di- vellendum esse usum calicis à panis Eucharistici perceptione, sed quicunque & quoties participare debent panem Eucharisticum, eosdem tum etiam bibere debere calicem benedictum, & quum fi- nis addatur hujus actionis sacræ, annunciatio mor- tis Christi, quid luculentius est, quam eos, qui in S. Eucharistiæ perceptione jubentur annunciare mortem Domini, juberi non tantum panem hunc edere, sed etiam poculum hoc bibere, ad an- nunciandam mortem Domini, idque ita obser- vandum esse, non unâ alterave ætate tantùm, sed ἄχρις ὗ ἂν ἔλθῃ, usque dum venerit Dominus ad judicium, hoc est, usque ad consummationem se- culi. Quæ τῇ ποτηριοκλεψίᾳ Papali penitus repu- gnant. Quod enim Apostolus hic præcepit, id Papa, NON OBSTANTE institutione Chri- sti & præcepto Apostolico, in Concilio Constantiensi, meritò inde OBSTANTIENSI nuncupato, se- cus ordinavit, dum calicem Laicis præbendum non esse, sed solum panem Eucharisticum sancivit. Et fatetur ipsum illud Constantiense concilium, in primitiva Ecclesia sacramentum hoc à fidelibus sub utraque specie acceptum fuisse. Cassander in libro de communione sub una specie fol. 17. ait, demonstrari non posse, totis mille amplius annis in ulla Ecclesiæ Catholicæ parte sacrosanctum hoc Eu- charistiæ sacramentum aliter in sacræ synaxi è men- sa Dominicâ fideli populo, quàm sub utroque panis & vini symbolo administratum fuisse. Quid? quod Gelasius omnes obstrictos voluerit ad perceptio- nem calicis, & sacrilegium esse definiverit, si ca- lix non distribuatur cum pane Eucharistico. C. Comperimus, distinct. II. de consecrat. Compe- rimus, quod quidam sumpta tantummodo corporis sacri portione à calice sacri sanguinis abstineant. Qui procul dubio (quoniam nescio, quæ SUPER- STITIONE docentur obstringi) aut integra sa- cramenta percipiant, aut ab integris arceantur, quia divisio unius ejusdemque mysterii sine GRAN- DI SACRILEGIO non potest provenire. Gran- dis ergò sacrilegii reum, judicio hujus Pontificis, se fecit Constantiænse concilium. Thomas de Aquin. in h. l. lect. 5. tradi, docet, hoc sacramentum sub duplici specie propter tria: Primò quidem propter ejus perfectionem: Quia cum sit spiritualis refectio, debet habere cibum & potum spiritualem. Nam & corporalis refectio non perficitur sine cibo & po- tu. Secundo propter ejus significationem. Est enim memoriale Dominicæ passionis, per quam sanguis Christi fuit separatus à corpore, & ideo in hoc sa- cramento sanguis seorsim à corpore offertur. Tertiò propter hujus sacramenti effectum salutarem. Va- let enim ad salutem corporis, & ideo offertur corpus, valet ad salutem animæ, & ideò offertur sanguis.

§. 51. Ratio ex præcedentibus.

## 11:27
V. 27. Whoever eats this bread, or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily.

Jurisconsults note that just as joined things are sometimes put for disjoined, so disjoined are put for joined, as when it is said 'concerning money or his guardianship' L. Sæpe, in the Digest, On the signification of words. And the Syriac in this place has put a conjunctive for a disjunctive particle. Nevertheless, the disjunctive can here be taken in its own property, because it could happen that a rich man might drink separately from the poor, and not eat; or might eat, but not drink separately. Furthermore, Ambrose and Chrysostom in this place, according to certain editions, teach us that many ancient books had 'of the Lord' here after 'unworthily': Oecumenius also here: Basil in the last chapter of book I and in the third question of book II. Augustine against the Donatists book V, c. 8, and book IX against Fulgentius: He eats or drinks unworthily of the Lord, who in this act cares for what is his own, not what is the Lord's. And let them not seem to have played with the Lord's communion, says Canon III of the Council of Elvira.

Grotius rightly observes that disjunctive particles are sometimes put for conjunctive. Whence not only the Syriac, but also Thomas, Lyranus, Cajetan, and others, indeed most copies of the Vulgate version itself, prove a conjunctive here, which in Latin codices, before the Sixtine edition, they constantly had, not 'or', but 'and'. Nor indeed can it be gathered from the particle 'or' that the species of bread is sufficient, otherwise it would also be gathered from there that the species of wine is sufficient. But that conjecture of Grotius, concerning separate eating, has no foundation. Moreover, he does not only eat and drink unworthily who in this act cares for what is his own, not what is the Lord's; but everyone who enjoys this sacred feast without repentance, without faith, without a purpose of amendment of life: For for the due commemoration of the Lord's death, repentance, faith, and holiness of life are needed. A memory of the death of Christ is required not only theoretical, but also practical, which is done by way of contrition, when the passion and death of Christ is recalled, with respect to the legal, just as an evident document of divine wrath against sins is exhibited in the passion of the Lord; by way of faith, when we rest in the obedience of Christ with true faith, as having been performed for us according to the divine law: By way of new obedience, when the passion of the Lord is regarded as an example of various virtues, that we may crucify our flesh, and die to sin and live to righteousness. And such an 'anamnesis' or remembrance of the death of Christ is needed in the use of the Eucharist, which the Apostle required in v. 24 and 25, to which also the 'proclaiming' pertains, or the commemoration of the Lord's death, which he demands here, that we may also celebrate the merit of Christ with worthy words, and stir up others to its meditation and celebration. As often as we approach to receive the sacrament of the eternal gift (Haymo warns in this chapter XI to the Corinthians), which the Lord, being about to suffer, left for us to be held in memory of himself, we ought to approach with fear and compunction of heart, and all reverence, remembering with how much love he loved us, who offered himself for us, that he might redeem us. To which the prayer of the Greek Church in the Horologion Ecclesiasticum contributes, which it uses in the usurpation of this sacrament: Do not observe my iniquities, O Lord, and cleanse my heart, making it a temple of thy immaculate body and blood: Do not cast me away entirely from thy face, thou who hast immense mercy. To the reception of thy sanctifications, how shall I, unworthy, approach unashamedly? For if I have dared to approach thee with the worthy, the garment convicts me, that it is not of the (nuptial) supper, and I shall have procured condemnation for my much-sinning soul. Cleanse therefore, O Lord, the uncleanness of my soul, and save me, thou lover of mankind! Likewise: Establishing me on the rock of faith, thou hast dilated, O Lord, my mouth over my enemies. For my spirit has exulted, while it sings: There is no holy one except our God, and there is no just one besides thee, O Lord. Give me, O Christ, drops of tears, cleansing the filth of my heart, that cleansed with a good conscience, I may approach with faith, and with fear to the reception of thy divine gifts, etc. May the fountain of good things, O Christ, the reception of thy immortal mysteries, become for me light and life, and a voiding of vicious affections, and may it confer the progress and increase of more divine virtue, O thou who alone art good, that I may glorify thee! Therefore, the unworthy are not to be understood by reason of legal dignity: For thus we are all unworthy Rom. III. 21. Matt. VIII. 8. Luke XVII. 10. 11. But by reason of Evangelical dignity, those who are destitute of true faith: Not those who are weak in faith: For to these the S. supper serves for the confirmation of faith: But the unfaithful, the impenitent, and hypocrites, who do not examine themselves. Therefore, they are worthy who examine themselves, search their own conscience, acknowledge their sins, seriously pray for forgiveness, and have a purpose of a better life: they distinguish this sacred banquet from others, ponder the mystery in it, and receive it with due devotion and reverence. Therefore, they are called worthy, not because they are worthy of this supper in themselves, but because they use it worthily, as B. Balduinus rightly says here.

Ἔνοχος ἔσαι τῶ σώματος κὰι τῷ αἵματος τῦ κυρίε.

He made it equal, as if he were slaughtering Christ. Heb. VI. 6. X. 19. Ἔνοχος ἔσται here has the same value as the Hebrew נכר חיב which they are accustomed to use when they compare sins with sins.

That likeness indeed with the slayers of Christ has a place here: But the immediate sense of the words Ἔνοχος ἔσαι τῶ σώματος κὰι τῷ ἐίματος τῦ κυρίε does not consist in it. For this is the meaning: that such a one, who unworthily eats this bread, which is the communion of the body of Christ, and drinks this cup, which is the communion of the blood of Christ, commits guilt against the very body and blood of the Lord through the unworthy eating and drinking of the same. And therefore the object of the sin and the guilt of that fault is constituted here as the body of Christ, when it is eaten unworthily, and the blood of Christ, when it is drunk unworthily, whence the body and blood of Christ must also be received by the unworthy, because otherwise guilt and sin against the body and blood of Christ would not be committed. For the object against which the unworthy sin by eating and drinking must be the object around which the eating and drinking of the unworthy revolves. blood of the Lord. For when something is added in construction to the word ἔvoxῶ, either a type of punishment is expressed, as Deut. XIX. 6, Matth. V. 22, or the object against which one sins, Exod. XXIII, Deut. XXI. 1, Num. XXX. Since, therefore, it is not the punishment itself that is noted here, but the object of the guilt in which those participating unworthily sin; and that is the body and blood of Christ, it is necessary that the unworthy participate in the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, and sin by an unworthy enjoyment of the same. Which is to be observed against the Calvinists. And in this consists that similarity, that just as the Jews sinned gravely by treating Christ unworthily: so also do those who participate in the holy Eucharist unworthily. While those indeed afflicted the body of Christ with various injuries and shed his blood: these truly handle the body of Christ unworthily and take his blood without true repentance. This very similarity is more fully developed by Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and others, that unworthy guests are no less guilty of the body and blood of the Lord than the Jews who crucified Christ. Oecumenius in this place has it thus: What he says, he will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, this indicates that just as when Judas betrayed him, and the Jews raged and raved against him, so they treat him with contumely who receive his most holy body with impure hands, as the Jews held him then, and offer it to a cursing and wicked mouth. Chrysostom explained that ἀξίως as ὡς χρὴ, as it is fitting and convenient, namely, both for the one receiving and for the dignity of the thing to be received, just as that word is accepted in Rom. XVI. 2, 1 Thess. II. 2. And upon the words, whoever shall eat unworthily, shall be guilty of the body of Christ. Wherefore? Because he sheds blood, and presents not a sacrifice, but a slaughter. For just as those who pierced Christ at that time, not so that they might drink his blood, but so that they might shed it, the same thing certainly does he who drinks the blood of Christ unworthily, and receives no fruit from his drinking. And homily XX to the people of Antioch: No small punishment is proposed for those who receive unworthily. Consider how much indignation there is against traitors, against those who crucified him. Therefore consider, lest you also be guilty of the body and blood of Christ. They slaughtered the most holy body, but you receive it with a polluted soul after so many benefits. Cyprian, Sermon V on the lapsed, teaches from this passage that the contumacious and obstinate offer violence to the body and blood of the Lord, and sin more now against the Lord with their hands and mouth than when they killed the Lord.

Latin:

V. 27. Ὅς ἂν ἐσθίῃ τὸν ἄρτον τῦτον, ἢ πίνῃ τὸ ποτήριον τῦ κυρίε ἀναξίως.

Notant Jurisconsulti sicut conjuncta pro disjunctis, ita disjuncta pro conjunctis interdum poni, ut cùm dicitur super pecunia tutelave sua L. Sæpe ita verbor. signific. Et Syrus hoc loco pro disjunctiva particula conjunctivam posuit. Potest tamen disjunctiva hic in sua proprietate sumi, quia fieri poterat, ut dives seorsim à pauperibus bi- beret, non ederet; aut ederet, non autem biberet seorsim. Cæterum veteres libros multos hî post ἀναξίως habuisse τῦ κυρίε docent nos Ambrosius & Chrysostomus h. l. secun- dum quasdam editiones: Oecumenius quoque hîc: Basi- lius capite ultimo libri I. & quæstione tertia libri II. Au- gustinus contra Donatistas libro V. c. 8. & libro IX. con- tra Fulgentium: Indigne Domino edit vel bibit, qui in hoc actu curat, quæ sua sunt, non quæ Domini. Nec lu- sisse de Dominica communione videantur ait Canon III. Concilii Elibertini.

Recte observat Grotius, disjunctivas particulas quandoque pro conjunctis poni. Unde conjuncti- vam hic non solùm Syrus, sed etiam Thomas, Ly- ranus, Cajetanus & alii, imò ipsius Vulgatæ versio- nis pleraque exemplaria probant, quæ non aut: sed & in Latinis Codicibus, ante editionem Sixti- nam constanter habuere. Nec verò è particula ἢ colligi potest, speciem panis sufficere, alioquin etiam colligeretur inde, vini speciem sufficere. Con- jectura autem illa Grotiana, de seorsivâ manduca- tione, nullum fundamentum habet. Non autem indigne tantum edit & bibit, qui quæ sua sunt, non quæ Domini, in hoc actu curat; sed quisque, qui sine pœnitentia, sine fide, sine proposito emendatio- nis vitæ sacro hoc epulo fruitur: Nam ad com- memorationem debitam mortis Dominicæ, pœ- nitentia, fide, ac vitæ sanctitate opus est. Memo- ria mortis Christi non tantum theoretica, sed & practica requiritur, quæ ratione contritionis fit, cum recolitur passio & mors Christi, respectu le- gali, prout iræ divinæ adversus peccata evidens documentum in passione Domini exhibetur, ra- tione fidei, cum in obedientia Christi vera fide recumbimus, ceu divinæ legi pro nobis præstita: Ratione novæ obedientiæ, quando passio Domini respicitur ut exemplum variarum virtutum, ut carnem nostram crucifigamus, ac peccato moria- mur & justitiæ vivamus. Atque tali ἀναμνήσει seu recordatione mortis Christi opus est in usu Eu- charistiæ, quam v. 24. & 25. requisivit Aposto- lus, ad quam etiam τὸ ἀναγγέλλειν pertinet, seu commemoratio mortis Dominicæ, quam hic postu- lat, ut dignis quoque sermonibus celebremus me- ritum Christi, aliosque ad ejus meditationem & celebrationem excitemus. Quotiescunque acce- dimus ad percipiendum sacramentum muneris æterni (monet Haymo in hoc caput XI. ad Corinth.) quod nobis Dominus passurus in memoriam sui di- misit tenendum, cum timore & compunctione cor- dis, omnique reverentia debemus accedere, recor- dantes, quanto amore dilexerit nos, qui pro nobis seipsum obtulit, ut nos redimeret. Quo facit pre- catio Ecclesiæ Græcæ in horologio Ecclesiasti- co, qua utitur in sacramenti hujus usurpatione: Iniquitates meas ne observa Domine, & cor meum munda, templum id efficiens immaculati corporis & sanguinis tui: Ne me totum abjicias à facie tua, qui misericordiam habes immensam. Ad perce- ptionem sanctificationum tuarum, quomodo indi- gnus inverecunde accedam? Si enim ausus fuero accedere ad te, cum dignis, vestis me arguit, quod non sit cœnæ (nuptialis) & condemnationem con- ciliavero multum peccanti animæ meæ. Purga er- go Domine immunditiem animæ meæ, & salva me tu hominum amantissime! Item: In petra fidei firmans me dilatasti, Domine, os meum, super ini- micos meos. Exultavit enim spiritus meus, dum psallit: Non est sanctus nisi Deus noster, & non est justus præter te, Domine. Da mihi, Christe, lacry- marum guttas, sordes cordis mei detergentes, ut bona conscientia mundatus, fide accedam, & cum timore ad perceptionem divinorum tuorum mune- rum &c. Fons bonorum, Christe, perceptio immor- talium tuorum mysteriorum, fiat mihi lux & vita, & vitiosorum affectuum vacuitas, atque virtutis divinioris profectum & augmentum conferat, ô so- lus bone, ut te glorificem! Indigni igitur non in- telligendi sunt ratione legalis dignitatis: Sic enim omnes indigni sumus Rom. III. 21. Matth. IIX. 8. Luc. XVII. 10. 11. Sed ratione Evangelicæ digni- tatis, qui verâ fide destituti sunt: Non qui infir- mi sunt in fide: His quippe inservit S. cœna ad fidei confirmationem: Sed infideles, impœniten- tes, & hypocritæ, qui seipsos non probant. Digni ergo sunt, qui seipsos probant, conscientiam suam excutiunt, peccata agnoscunt, seriò deprecantur, propositum melioris vitæ habent: sacrum hoc convivium à cæteris discernunt, mysterium in eo expendunt, & debita cum devotione ac reveren- tia accipiunt. Digni ergo vocantur, non qui se- ipsis hac cœna digni sunt, sed qui ea digne utuntur, ut hic recte B. Balduinus.

Ἔνοχος ἔσαι τῶ σώματος κὰι τῷ αἵματος τῦ κυρίε.

Par fecit, quasi Christum trucidaret. Hebr. VI. 6. X. 19. Ἔνοχος ἔσται hic idem valet, quod apud Hebræos נכר חיב quo uti solent, ubi peccata peccatis comparant.

Similitudo illa quidem cum occisoribus Chri- sti locum hic habet: Sed non in ea sensus verbo- rum Ἔνοχος ἔσαι τῶ σώματος κὰι τῷ ἐίματος τῦ κυρίε immediatus consistit. Hic enim est, talem, qui indigne edit panem hunc, qui est communica- tio corporis Christi, & bibit poculum hoc, quod est communicatio sanguinis Christi, reatum in ipsum corpus & sanguinem Domini per ejusdem indignam manducationem & bibitionem committere. Ideoque objectum peccati & reatus culpæ istius constitui- tur hic corpus Christi, quum indigne manducatur, & sanguis Christi, quum indignè bibitur, unde corpus & sanguinem Christi oportet etiam ab indignis percipi, quia aliàs culpa & peccatum in corpus & sanguinem Christi non committeretur. In quod enim objectum indigni peccant manducatione & bibitione, circa illud objectum versari oportet manducationem & bibitionem indignorum. At in corpus & sanguinem Domini peccant. Quando enim vocabulo ἔvoxῶ in constructione aliquid additur, vel genus supplicii exprimitur, ut Deut. XIX. 6. Matth. V. 22. vel objectum, in quod peccatur Exod. XXIII. Deut. XXI.1. Num. XXX. Quum ergo hic non ipsa pœna, sed culpæ objectum notetur, in quo peccent indigne participantes; id autem sit corpus & sanguis Christi, necessum est, indignos corpus & sanguinem Christi in S. cœna participare, atque indigna ejusdem fruitione peccare. Quod contra Calvinianos observandum. Et in eo consistit illa similitudo, quod uti Judæi graviter peccarunt indigne Christum tractando: Ita & hi, qui indigne sacram Eucharistiam participant. Quum illi quidem corpus Christi variis injuriis affecerint, sanguinemque ejus effuderint: Hi verò indignè corpus Christi contrectent, sanguinemque ejus sumant absque vera pœnitentia. Quam ipsam similitudinem plenius Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, aliique exequuntur, quod indigni convivæ non minus rei sint corporis & sanguinis Domini, quàm Judæi, qui Christum crucifixerunt. Oecumenius in hoc loco ita habet: Quod ait reus erit corporis & sanguinis Domini, hoc indicat, ut cum Judas tradidit, grassati verò in eum ac debacchati fuere Judæi, ita ipsum contumelia afficiunt, qui sanctissimum illius corpus impuris manibus, uti tunc tenuere Judæi, suscipiunt, & execrando nefandoque offerunt ori. Illud ἀξίως Chrysostomus exposuit ὡς χρὴ ut decet ac convenit scil. tùm sumenti, tùm rei sumendæ dignitati, uti vox ea accipitur Rom. XVI. 2. 1. Thessal. II. 2. Et super verba, quicunque comederit indignè, reus erit corporis Christi. Quamobrem? Quia effundit sanguinem, & non sacrificium, sed jugulationem præ se fert. Quemadmodum enim hi, qui eo tempore Christum pupugere, non ut biberent ejus sanguinem, sed ut effunderent, idem sane facit, qui Christi sanguinem bibit indigne, & nullum ex ejus potione fructum accipit. Et homil. XX. ad populum Antiochenum: Non parva pœna proponitur indignè sumentibus. Considera, quantum adversus proditores indignationis, contra eos, qui crucifixerunt eum. Itaque considera, ne tu quoque sis reus corporis & sanguinis Christi. Illi sanctissimum corpus jugularunt, tu verò pollutâ suscipis animâ post tot beneficia. Cyprianus Serm. V. de lapsis, contumaces & pervicaces vim corpori & sanguini Domini inferre ex hoc loco docet, ac plus modo in Dominum manibus atque ore delinquere, quam cum Dominum necaverunt.

## 11:28
V. 28. Δοκιμαζέτω δὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτὸν. He says this because church discipline had been prostrated through schisms, as we saw above VI. Do not believe, he says, even if the judgments of the Church cease, that you will bear the contempt of the mysteries with impunity.

Δοκιμάζειν is to explore, to recognize, whether something is such as it ought to be, Rom. XII. 2, Eph. V. 11, 1 Thess. V. 21, just as δοκίμιον is the experiment which is taken of some thing, and δοκιμὴ is experimental knowledge, Jac. I. 3, 1 Petr. I. 7, Rom. V. 4. The Apostle requires a probation of oneself, lest anyone eat and drink unworthily, so that he may examine himself in his heart, whether he has duly prepared himself for this holy feast, so that he may be a worthy guest. For this preparation is required both the discernment of the body and blood of the Lord, and a serious conversion to God, to which pertains the admonition of the Apostle 1 Cor. XIII. 5. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith? See B. Luth. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. sermon on Monday of Easter, on the worthy reception of the sacrament. T. V. in the second part, exhortation to the use of the Lord's Supper, and B. Höpfner, Isagoge to the salutary use of the Lord's Supper, tract. p. 159 seqq.

Latin:

V. 28. Δοκιμαζέτω δὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτὸν. Hoc dicit quia per schismata prostrata erat Ecclesiæ disciplina, ut vidimus supra VI. Ne credite, inquit, etiamsi Ecclesiæ judicia cessent, impune vos laturos contemptum mysteriorum.

Δοκιμάζειν est explorare, recognoscere, an aliquid sit tale, quale esse debeat Rom. XII. 2. Eph. V. 11. 1. Thess. V. 21. uti δοκίμιον est experimentum, quod de re aliqua capitur, & δοκιμὴ notitia experimentalis Jac. I. 3. 1. Petr. I. 7. Rom. V. 4. Probationem autem sui ipsius requirit Apostolus, ne scilicet indignè quis manducet ac bibat, ut se exploret in corde suo, an rite se ad hoc sacrum epu- um præparaverit, ut dignus hospes esse possit. Ad quam præparationem requiritur tùm discre- tio corporis & sanguinis Domini, tùm seria ad De- um conversio, quo pertinet monitum Apostoli 1. Cor. XIII. 5. Tentate vos ipsos, an sitis in fide? Vid. B. Luth. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. serm. in Fer. II. Paschat. de digna sumtione sacramenti. T. V. in part. secund. adhort. ad usum cæn. Domin. & B. Höpfner. Isagoge ad salut. usum cænæ Domin. tract. p. 159. seqq.

## 11:29
V. 29. Ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων ἀναξίως, κρῖμα ἑαυτῷ ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει.

That is, by eating and drinking he procures condemnation for himself. What is of itself salutary is turned into poison for him. He participated for punishment, says Clement in the Constitutions VII. 26.

And therefore Origen gravely warns in Psalm XXXVII. When your soul is sick, and is urged by the languors of sins, you are secure, you contract hell, etc. You do not fear to communicate the body of Christ, to approach the Eucharist, as if clean and pure, as if there were nothing unworthy in you, and in all these things do you think that you escape the judgment of GOD?

Μὴ διακρίνων τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Κυρίου.

That is, because he does not discern this bread made by the sacrament the body of the Lord from common bread. Justin in Apologetic II. For we do not receive these as common bread, nor common drink, but in the manner in which Jesus Christ our Savior, having been made flesh through the word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so also we have been taught that the food which has been made eucharistic by the prayer of the word from him, from which our blood and flesh are nourished by transformation, is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh.

From this, therefore, we demonstrate again, invincibly, against the Calvinists, that even the unworthy receive the body and blood of the Lord in the holy supper, albeit to their judgment. He who eats and drinks judgment to himself, when he eats and drinks unworthily, for the reason that he does not discern the body of the Lord, it must be that he receives the body of the Lord, even if unworthily, because he does not receive it with greater reverence than common foods, and thus treats the body of the Lord irreligiously. Hilary on Psalm 127: We obtain the living bread, the heavenly bread from Him who said: I am the living bread from heaven, which he who receives unworthily according to the command of the Apostle, acquires judgment for himself. Augustine, Book V against the Donatists, chapter 8. Just as Judas, to whom the Lord hands the morsel, did not by receiving an evil thing, but by receiving it evilly, provide a place for the Devil within himself; so let no one who takes the Lord's sacrament unworthily cause it to be that, because he himself is evil, the thing is evil, or because he did not receive it for salvation, he received nothing. For the body of the Lord and the blood of the Lord was nonetheless theirs also, of whom the Apostle was saying: He who eats unworthily, eats judgment to himself. Anselm on this passage: The body of the Lord is nonetheless [the body of the Lord]. But he receives this not to life, but to judgment, because he does not judge the body of the Lord, that is, he does not discern how much more worthy this body is than all creatures.

Latin:

V. 29. Ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων ἀναξίως, κρῖμα ἑαυτῷ ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει.

Id est, edendo & bibendo damnationem in se acærit. Quod per se salutare est, in venenum ipsi vertitur. Adsup- plicium participavit, ait Clemens Constitutionum VII. 26.

Ideoque graviter monet Origenes in Psalm. XXXVII. Cum anima tua ægrotet, & peccatorum languoribus urgeatur, securus es, contrahis gehen- nam &c. Communicare non times corpus Christi, accedere ad Eucharistiam, quasi mundus & purus, quasi in te nihil sit indignum, & in his omnibus putas, quod effugias DEI judicium?

Μὴ διακρίνων τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Κυρίου.

Id est, propterea quod panem istum factum sacramen- to corpus Domini à pane communi non discernat. Justi- nus Apologetico II. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς κοινὸν ἄρτον, οὐδὲ κοινὸν πό- μα ταῦτα λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὃν τρόπον διὰ λόγου Θεοῦ σαρκο- ποιηθεὶς Ἰησοῦς χριστὸς ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν καὶ σάρκα καὶ αἷμα ὑπὲρ τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν ἔσχεν, οὕτω καὶ τὴν δι᾿ εὐχῆς λόγου τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐχαριστηθεῖσαν τροφὴν, ἐξ ἧς αἷμα καὶ σάρκες κατὰ μετα- βολὴν τρέφονται ἡμῶν, ἐκείνου τοῦ σαρκοποιηθέντος Ἰησοῦ καὶ σάρκα καὶ αἷμα ἐδιδάχθημεν εἶναι.

Ex eo ergò iterum invictè contra Calvinia- nos demonstramus, etiam indignos percipere cor- pus & sanguinem Domini in sacra cœna, licet ad judicium. Qui manducat & bibit sibi judicium, cum indigne manducat & bibit, ex ea causa, quod non discernat corpus Domini, eum oportet cor- pus Domini percipere, etsi indigne, quod non majori reverentia id suscipiat, ac vulgares cibos, & ita irreligiosè corpus Domini tractet. Hila- rius in Psal. CXXVII. Obtinemus panem vivum, panem cœlestem ab eo, qui dixit: Ego sum panis vivus de cœlo, quem qui indigne secundum man- datum Apostoli acceperit, judicium sibi acquirit. August. l. V. contra Donatist. cap. IIX. Sicut Judas, cui buccellam tradit Dominus, non malum accipiendo, sed male accipiendo, locum in se Dia- bolo præbuit; Sit indigne quisque sumens Domini- cum sacramentum non efficit, ut, quia ipse malus est, malum sit, aut quia non ad salutem accepit, nihil acceperit. Corpus enim Domini & sanguis Domini nihilo minus erat illis etiam, de quibus dicebat Apostolus: Qui manducat indigne, judi- cium sibi manducat. Anshelmus in hunc locum: Corpus Domini nihilo minus est. Sed ille accipit hoc non ad vitam, sed ad judicium, quia non diju- dicat corpus Domini, id est, non discernit; quam sit dignius omnibus creaturis hoc corpus.

## 11:30
V. 30. Διὰ τοῦτο.

On account of these, and similar things.

Ἐν ὑμῖν πολλοὶ ἀσθενεῖς καὶ ἄῤῥωστοι

The discourse grows. For ἀσθενὴς is one who is languid, דל or רפה: Ἄῤῥωστος is one who is sick, חלה. See Leviticus 26:16, 25; Deuteronomy 28:21, 22.

Καὶ κοιμῶνται ἱκανοί.

By an untimely death, which in the law is signified by כרת ἐξολοθρευθήσεται, which you have in Exodus 12:15, 19 concerning those who celebrate the Passover with leaven. When he says κοιμῶνται, he shows that he is speaking of those who, touched by repentance, were dying. Doubtless, God has the right to afflict even the repentant with the loss of this life. Clement, Stromata IV: Ἰστέον μέν τοι τοὺς μετὰ τὸ λύτρον τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι περιπίπτοντας, τούτους εἶναι τοὺς παιδευομένους : Τὰ μὲν γὰρ προενεργηθέντα ἀφέθη· Τὰ δὲ ἐπιγινόμενα, ἐκκαθαίρεται.

We add what Theophylact has here: Let the things that happen to you be an argument. For indeed, both premature deaths and long-lasting diseases arise, because many do not receive that mystery with merit; what about those who maintain excellent and unoffended health even until old age? Are not these also bound by crimes? But not only do these present torments, but even more serious ones, and future ones await those who have approached that mystery unworthily. We, however, would not be afflicted with punishments at all if we were not subject to sins. Some understand these things concerning the plague, or another contagious disease, sent divinely on account of the profanation of this sacrament. Which opinion is not improbable.

Latin:

V. 30. Διὰ τοῦτο.

Propter hæc, & similia.

Ἐν ὑμῖν πολλοὶ ἀσθενεῖς καὶ ἄῤῥωστοι

Crescit oratio. Nam ἀσθενὴς est qui languet דל vel רפה: Ἄῤῥωστος qui ægrotat חלה. Vide Levitic XXVI. 16. 25. Deut. XXVIII, 21. 22.

Καὶ κοιμῶνται ἱκανοί.

Morte immatura, quæ in lege significatur per כרת ἐξολοθρευθήσεται, quod habes Exodi XII. 15. 19. de his qui pascha celebrant cum fermento. Cum dicit κοιμῶνται ostendit se loqui de iis, qui pœnitentia tacti moriebantur, Nimirum Deus jus habet etiam pœnitentes afficiendi hujus vitæ damno. Clemens Strom. IV. Ἰστέον μέν τοι τοὺς μετὰ τὸ λύτρον τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι περιπίπτοντας, τούτους εἶναι τοὺς παι- δευομένους : Τὰ μὲν γὰρ προενεργηθέντα ἀφέθη· Τὰ δὲ ἐπι- γινόμενα, ἐκκαθαίρεται.

Adjicimus, quæ hic habet Theophylactus: Argumento sint, quæ vobis contingunt. Eo namque & mortes jam immaturæ, & diuturni morbi oboriuntur, quia haudquaquam merito id mysterium sumunt multi, quid de iis, qui ad usque senectam ipsam optimam & inoffensam valetudinem servant? Nonne & hi criminibus obstringuntur? At non modo præsentia ista tormenta, quin & graviora ista, & futura hos manent, qui indignè mysterium illud adierint. Nos autem baudquaquam pœnis afficeremur, nisi essemus peccatis obnoxii. Nonnulli de peste, aut alio contagioso morbo hæc intelligunt, divinitus, ob profanationem hujus sacramenti, immisso. Quæ sententia non improbabilis est.

## 11:31
V. 31. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged.

The manuscript often mentioned to us has Εἰ δὲ ἑαυτὺς. And Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact have ἐκρίνομεν. If we were to exact from ourselves the punishments for our deeds, with a contrite and humbled heart, with tears, fasts, and other σκληραγωγίαις (hardships), God would have no need to send punishments upon us. Simplicius to Epictetus: If someone becomes a judge to himself, perhaps he succeeds all the sooner in this way because he punishes himself of his own free will. This passage can also be understood: If judgments were exercised in the Church as they ought to be.

Why should that διακρίνομεν not be accepted in the same sense in which διακρίνει was used in v. 24, because it certainly looks back to the preceding verse? There, however, it had the meaning of judging through discernment. And therefore, in that sense, we here prove, judge, and properly discern the condition of our life and actions, so that hypocrisy and simulation may not underlie them, and the deception of self-love may not deceive us, so that we may not be παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτὺς (deceiving ourselves) as in James 1:22, just as Cajetan, Gagnejus, and Cornelius à Lapide explain by 'we would prove, examine, discuss': So that whatever sin is found may be cast off by true repentance. For nothing is accomplished by one's own affliction and destruction, and it is not scourging and one's own bodily affliction, but only the mercy of God among the truly penitent that averts the punishments deserved, Luke 18:7. Nor does contrition alone suffice for the averting of punishments, but true repentance and faith are needed, without which it is impossible to please GOD. The judicial power of the Church and its judging has nothing to do with this, since the discussion is about avoiding the judgment of GOD. For most things that come into the judgment of GOD are hidden from men. But the Church does not judge concerning hidden things. Men look at those things which are exposed to the eyes: but God looks at the hearts, 1 Sam. 16:7. Theophylact has it thus: For he did not say, if we were to afflict ourselves with tortures, but if we were only to judge, that is, if we ourselves were to condemn ourselves for wicked deeds, we would not indeed be condemned by God in earthly matters, but we would perhaps escape both present and future punishments. Chrysostom, whom Benedictus Justinianus praises here, paraphrases in this way: He did not say, he says, if we were to castigate ourselves, if we were to punish; but only: if we were willing to acknowledge our sins, if we were to condemn ourselves; if we were to pass sentence on our offenses, we would be freed from the punishment that is both here and there. Similarly, Salmero also explained it concerning the judgment of discussion at this place: If anyone were to discuss his conscience well and diligently, and by accusing himself and condemning himself as worthy of death, were to implore divine mercy, this person would certainly not be judged, that is, punished, by God. Wilhelmus Estius indeed brings forward various interpretations, but he prefers ours, and he explicitly rejects and refutes that one from which Bailius in Catech. controvers. tract. 3. 9. 12. strives to prove our satisfactions from this place. To judge is explained in three ways by interpreters in this place. First, that it is the same as to judge in the latter place, that is, to punish, as many Latins understand it, in this sense: If we were to punish ourselves for our sins, namely by voluntary afflictions and satisfactions, anticipating the hand of the Lord: We would not, at any rate, be more severely scourged by Him, whether in this age or in the future. Which sense manifestly confirms the Catholic doctrine concerning the satisfaction of the faithful for sins. In another way, that to judge is to condemn even without punishment. Thus the Greeks understood it, among whom is Theophylact: He did not say, he says, if we were to punish ourselves, but only, if we were to judge and condemn ourselves: We would not now be condemned by God here, but we would escape both present and future punishments. Thirdly, that to judge is to examine, to discuss. Thus the sense is: That if we were to examine ourselves, that is, to prove ourselves, and would not approach that holy table unless proved, as he said before; but let a man prove himself and so of the bread, etc., we would not at any rate be judged, that is, punished by GOD on account of the unworthy reception of the body and blood of the Lord. Thus Haymo, Lyranus, Cajetanus, and others among the Latins explain it, indeed quite probably and consistently with the preceding, and the commentator Ambrose favors it, who reads and explains it as 'we would discern'. For what the first exposition held is openly rejected by the Greeks, and deservedly so. Since neither the Greek διακρίνειν nor the Latin dijudicare means to punish: But its most common meaning is that which we brought forward in the third place: according to which it was also said a little before, 'not judging the body of the Lord'. This is Estius.

But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world.

He spoke of Κρίνεσθαι (being judged) concerning the evils of this life and premature death: of κατακρίνεσθαι (being condemned) concerning eternal punishments. All evils that happen in this life become νυθεσίαι (admonitions) or παιδεύσεις (chastisements), מוסרים, if serious repentance and amendment follow. To such, the Hebrews say: May your death be an expiation for all your sins. By the world here, understand those who are alien to Christ, as in John 18:4 and elsewhere.

Therefore, these things seem to have been added for the sake of consolation for those who had been seized by diseases, so that they might understand that those chastisements are at least paternal, by which they are recalled to repentance, lest they be condemned with the world. Cf. Job XIII. 15. He who spares himself in fault now, will not be spared in punishment later, according to Gregor. lib. XI. Mor. cap. 19. B. Chemnitius writes beautifully about these words, Concil. Trid. part. 2. p. 245. The Apostle delights in the paronomasia of forensic words: κρίνειν, διακρίνειν, κατακρίνεσθαι. Κρίνειν denotes temporary punishments, because it is explained by παιδεύεσθαι, by which God, as a pedagogue, warns us of sin with scourges, so that He may bend us to repentance. Κατακρίνεσθαι comprises the final and eternal punishments of the damned. Διακρίνειν is the investigation of a cause, as in 1 Cor. XVI. and among the LXX, Exod. XVII. Lev. XXIV. 1 Reg. III. Psal. LXXXI. The meaning is: If, having shaken off security, we were to inquire with perpetual repentance into our nature and life, mortifying the root of sin, repressing depraved desires, etc. Then there would be no need for God to warn us of these things through scourges: but when we, secure, neglect the sin that dwells within us, and gradually indulge it ourselves, then God recalls us to repentance through chastisements, lest we be condemned in our sins with the world.

Latin:

V. 31. Εἰ γὰρ ἑαυτὺς διεκρίνομεν, ὐκ ἂν ἐκρινόμεθα.

Εἰ δὲ ἑαυτὺς habet Manuscriptus sæpe nobis dictus. Et ἐκρίνομεν habent Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus. Si inde factorum pœnas de nobis ipsis exigeremus, animo contrito & humiliato, lachrymis, jejuniis, & aliis σκληραγωγίαις, non opus haberet Deus pœnas nobis immittere. Simplicius ad Epictetum : Ἐάν τις ἑαυτῷ γίνηται δίκη, τάχα κὰι θᾷττον οὕτω κατορθεῖ διὰ τὸ αὐτοπροαιρέτως κολάζεσθαι. Potest etiam hic locus intelligi : Si in Ecclesia judicia, ita ut oportet, exercerenter.

Cur non accipiatur illud διακρίνομεν eodem sensu, quo διακρίνει v. 24. adhibitum est, quia respicit utique versus præsens superiorem? Ibi autem dijudicandi per discretionem significatum habebat. Ideoque ea ratione hic nos ipsos probare, dijudicare, ac probe discernere vitæ actionumque nostrarum conditionem, ne hypocrisis ac simulatio subsit, propriique amoris fucus nos fallat, ne simus παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτὺς Jac. I. 22. quemadmodum Cajetanus, Gagnejus, Cornelius à Lapide per probaremus, examinaremus, discuteremus, exponunt: Ut quicquid peccati invenitur, verà pœnitentià exuatur. Propria enim afflictione & perditione nihil efficitur, pœnasque promeritas non flagellatio, ac propria corporis afflictio, sed sola Dei miseratio penes verè pœnitentes avertit Luc. XIIX. 7. Nec sola contritio sufficit ad pœnarum aversionem, sed vera opus est pœnitentia & fide, sine qua DEO placere impossibile est. Judicialis Ecclesiæ potestas, ejusque dijudicatio huc nihil facit, quum de evitando DEI judicio sermo sit. Nam pleraque, quæ in judicium DEI veniunt, hominibus occulta sunt. De occultis autem non judicat Ecclesia. Homines ea, quæ oculis exposita sunt, respiciunt: Deus autem corda intuetur 1. Sam. XVI. 7. Theophylactus ita habet: Non enim si nos ipsos cruciatibus dixit afficeremus, sed si dijudicaremus duntaxat, hoc est, ipsi nos ob prava facinora damnaremus, baud quidem in terrenis à Deo damnationi addiceremur, sed evaderemus forsitan ut præsentia, ita & futura supplicia. Chrysostomus quem hic laudat Benedictus Justinianus, hoc modo παραφράζει: Non dixit, inquit, si castigaremus nos ipsos, si puniremus; sed solum: si agnoscere vellemus peccata, si nos ipsos condemnare; si delictis ferre sententiam, liberaremur ab eo, quod & bic & illic est, supplicio. Similiter etiam de judicio discussionis exposuit Salmero ad hunc locum: Si quis bene ac diligenter discuteret suam conscientiam, & semetipsum accusando, & morte se dignum consuendo, divinam misericordiam imploraret, hic profecto à Deo non judicaretur, hoc est, puniretur. Wilhelmus Estius affert quidem varias interpretationes, sed nostram præfert, illam verò, è qua Bailius in Catech. controvers. tract. 3. 9. 12. ex hoc loco satisfactiones nostras probare satagit, disertè reprobat & refellit. Dijudicare hoc loco trifariam ab interpretibus exponitur. Primum ut idem sit, quod judicare posteriori loco, id est punire, quomodo multi Latini intelligunt, hoc sensu: Si nosmetipsos pro peccatis nostris puniremus, scilicet per voluntarias afflictiones & satisfactiones manum Domini præveniendo: Non utique ab eo gravius flagellaremur, sive in hoc seculo, sive in futuro. Qui sensus manifeste confirmat doctrinam catholicam de satisfactione fidelium pro peccatis. Alio modo ut dijudicare sit condemnare etiam citra punitionem. Sic Græci intellexerunt, inter quos Theophylactus: Non dixit, inquit, si nos ipsos puniremus, sed tantum, si judicaremus & condemnaremus nos ipsos: Non jam bic condemnaremur à Deo, verum & præsentia & futura supplicia effugeremus. Tertiò ut dijudicare sit examinare, discutere. Ita sensus est: Quod si nosmetipsos examinaremus, id est, probaremus, ac non nisi probati mensam illam sacram accederemus, prout ante dixit; probet autem seipsum homo & sic de pane &c. non utique judicaremur, id est, puniremur à DEO ob indignam corporis & sanguinis Dominici sumptionem. Sic exponunt Haymo, Lyranus, Cajetanus, & alii ex Latinis nonnulli, sanè quam probabiliter & præcedentibus congruenter, favetque Commentator Ambr. qui legit, & exponit discerneremus. Nam quod prima habebat expositio, id à Græcis apertè rejicitur, ac merito. Siquidem nec Græcum διακρίνειν, nec Latinum dijudicare, significat punire: Sed usitatissima ejus significatio est, quam attulimus tertio loco: juxta quam paulo ante etiam dictum est, non dijudicans corpus Domini. Hæc Estius.

Κρινόμενοι δὲ ὑπὸ τῦ κυρίε παιδευόμεθα, ἵνα μὴ σὺν τῷ κόσμῳ κατακριθῶμεν.

Κρίνεσθαι dixit de malis hujus vitæ & morte immatura: κατακρίνεσθαι de pœnis æternis. Omnia mala, quæ in hac vita eveniunt, fiunt νυθεσίαι sive παιδεύσεις, מוסרים si sequatur seria pœnitentia & emendatio. Talibus dicunt Hebræi: Sit tibi mors tua in expiationem omnium peccatorum tuorum. Mundum hic intellige eos, qui à Christo sunt alieni, ut Joh. XVIII. 4. & alibi.

Consolationis igitur causa hæc addita videntur pro iis, qui morbis correpti erant, ut intelligant, istas castigationes saltem esse paternas, quibus ad pœnitentiam revocentur, ne cum mundo condemnentur. Conf. Job. XIII. 15. Qui vero sibi nunc in culpa parcit, ei postmodum in pœna non parcitur juxta Gregor. lib. XI. Mor. cap. 19. Pulchre de his verbis B. Chemnitius, Concil. Trid. part. 2. p. 245. Delectatur Apostolus παρονομασία verborum forensium: κρίνειν, διακρίνειν, κατακρίνεσθαι. Κρίνειν notat pœnas temporarias, quia explicatur per παιδεύεσθαι, quibus tanquam pædagogus flagellis Deus nos admonet de peccato, ut flectat ad pœnitentiam. Κατακρίνεσθαι complectitur ultimas & æternas pœnas damnatorum. Διακρίνειν est inquisitio causæ, ut 1. Cor. XVI. & apud LXX. Exod. XVII. Lev. XXIV. 1. Reg. III. Psal. LXXXI. Sensus est: Si excussa securitate, perpetua pœnitentia inquireremus in naturam & vitam nostram, mortificantes radicem peccati, reprimentes pravas cupiditates &c. Tunc opus non esset, Deum per flagella nos admonere horum: Quando vero securi peccatum inhabitans negligimus, & sensim ipsi indulgemus, tunc Deus per castigationes nos revocat ad pœnitentiam, ne cum mundo in peccatis damnemur.

## 11:33
V. 33. Ὡστε ἀδελφοί μυ.

He consoles those who were terrified again with this gentle form of address.

Συνερχόμενοι ἐις τὸ φαγεῖν. Namely, the Lord's Supper, which is understood here from what precedes.

Ἀλλήλους ἐκδέχεσθαι. So that the table may be common to both rich and poor.

Some refer these things to the agape, William Estius and others, concerning which, when brought together in common, some here, others there, and thus in different corners of the temple they partook of the sacred supper, not without contempt for the poor, who could bring nothing, or arrived later, whence the Apostle commands that they wait for one another, until all come together. But we do not here disagree with Grotius, who understands τὸ φαγεῖν of the Lord's Supper, that is, the Eucharist. For although the Corinthians were accustomed to celebrate a first feast, and then the sacred Eucharist, which some approached sober, others already drunk from that feast: yet the Apostle corrects that custom, and commands that all come together, and first celebrate the sacred Eucharist, so that this may be the common synaxis. But he does not touch upon the banquet from the agape, nor did he forbid those who might wish to frequent it after the sacred synaxis was performed, provided it be celebrated in charity only without luxury, gluttony, contentions, and other abuses, and that all things be done κατὰ τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην, which he was about to advise later. Therefore, the Apostle does not here command, as some wish, that after the synaxis all should wait for one another for the agape to be celebrated, nor that they should wait for one another for the supper prior to the synaxis, which Cornelius à Lapide prefers, but that they should wait for one another for the synaxis, and that all should celebrate it together, and afterwards approach the agape in common charity, refreshed by the feast of the Lord's body and blood, and strengthened by faith. The meaning therefore is, as interpreted by B. Hunnius, when you come together in the assembly of the Church for the solemn action of the sacred supper, do not any longer occupy yourselves with different suppers, in different corners, with such great ἀταξίᾳ, to the offense of the Church and the contempt of the poor: But wait for one another, so that there may be one certain solemn action, and that one grave, and worthy of so great a mystery.

Latin:

V. 33. Ὡστε ἀδελφοί μυ.

Perterrefactos rursum hac blanda compellatione solatur.

Συνερχόμενοι ἐις τὸ φαγεῖν. Nempe τὸ κυριακὸν δεῖπνον, quod hic ex superioribus subauditur.

Ἀλλήλους ἐκδέχεσθαι. Ut communis sit mensa divitum & pauperum.

Ad agapas referunt nonnulli hæc Guilielmus Estius, aliique, de quibus in commune collatis seorsim hic aliqui, ibi alii, & sic in diversis templi angulis cœnam sacram sumserint, non sine despe- ctu pauperum, qui nihil afferre potuerint, vel tar- dius advenerint, unde jubeat Apostolus, ut alii alios expectent, donec omnes conveniant. Sed non abnuimus hic Grotio, τὸ φαγεῖν de Cæna Domi- nicâ, hoc est, Eucharistiâ intelligenti. Nam quam- vis epulum primum celebrare consueverint Co- rinthii, dehinc sacram Eucharistiam, quam alii sobrii accedebant, alii jam ex epulo isto ebrii: Morem tamen illum emendat Apostolus, jubet- que, ut omnes conveniant, & prius sacram Eu- charistiam celebrent, ut hæc sit communis synaxis. Convivium verò ex agapis non tangit, nec illis, qui peracta sacra synaxi id frequentare velint, dum solum citra luxum, crapulam, contentiones, & alios abusus in charitate id celebretur, & κατὰ τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην, quod deinde moniturus erat, pera- gantur omnia, prohibuit. Non ergo, quod non- nulli volunt, jubet hic Apostolus, ut post synaxin omnes invicem expectent pro agape celebranda, nec ut invicem expectent pro cœna prævia syna- xi, quod mavult Cornelius à Lapide, sed ut expe- ctent sese invicem ad synaxin, eamque conjunctim omnes celebrent, ac postea communi charitate ad agapen accedant Dominici corporis & sanguinis epulo refecti, fideque roborati. Sensus igitur est, interprete B. Hunnio, cum convenitis in cœtu Ecclesiæ ad solennem actionem cœnæ sacræ, no- lite amplius diversas occupare cœnas, diversis in angulis, tanta cum ἀταξίᾳ, offendiculo Ecclesiæ & despectu pauperum: Sed alius alium expectate, ut una quædam sit actio solennis, eaque gravis, & tanto mysterio digna.

## 11:34
V. 34. Εἰ δέ τις πεινᾷ.

It is χλευασμὸς. For he speaks as if to children, who are accustomed to be so ὀξύπεινοι, that they snatch at anything, and do not call others to a share, nor do they wish to σῦκα μερίζειν.

Ἐν οἴκῳ ἐσθιέτω.

Whatever he wants and as much as he wants, and with whom he wants, or alone, if it so pleases. For everyone is King in his own home.

Which is not to be extended to gluttony or a more generous drink to the point of drunkenness, by which the S. synaxis may be reverently frequented, and the agape celebrated. From which it appears that a fast is not prescribed here for one about to approach the S. synaxis, or that they must approach entirely sober; but it is left free, if anyone is hungry, that he may eat at home first, but soberly. To B. Hunnius it seems that those solemn feasts, which were held either before or after the Lord's supper, were here entirely abrogated, lest having relapsed into their former profanity, they cause the venerable action to turn to judgment and condemnation for themselves. But because the agape was still in use among the faithful in subsequent times, it is not probable that it was entirely abrogated here.

Ἵνα μὴ εἰς κρῖμα συνέρχησθε.

Lest those things which are done wrongly in your assemblies be a cause of evil for you.

Τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ, ὡς ἂν ἔλθω, διατάξομαι.

The Apostles had the right of establishing what pertained to the ἐυταξίαν of the assemblies and to the λειτουργίαν. See above VII. 17. below XVI. 1. where the same word is used. This is the origin of the canons which are called Apostolic, which were not indeed written by them but were introduced into use by them.

While Grotius affirms in the former [part] that the Apostolic canons, though not indeed written by the Apostles, were nevertheless introduced into use by them, and that they embrace those remaining things, τὰ λοιπὰ, so as to aid the Papists,

He contradicts Lindanus, who in the chronicle prefixed to the Panoplia says that the canons of the Apostles are certainly of the Apostles, and Franciscus Turrianus, who contends for this in a special work, and Albertus Pighius in book II of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, ch. 10, and Alphonsus de Castro in book 1 against heresies, ch. 5, who adheres to the same, although this Alphonsus is doubtful in ch. 11 and says they were either collected or translated by Clement: And also Salmeron, who maintains that those canons were established by the Apostles in the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15. Which Lorinus says was also the opinion of Sophronius on Acts 15:29, although he notes that Pamphilus the Martyr judged them to have been written at Antioch, which Pope Innocent does not deny in Epistle 118. But in the latter [part] Grotius opposes those who make the use of the Apostolic canons far later than the Apostolic age, as Baronius acknowledges at the year 92, no. 15, that these canons scarcely became known in the Church before the end of the seventh century, having been received by the sixth general council (which council, however, he teaches at the year 656, no. 40, was rejected by the Roman Church), and who confess that they are not observed by the modern Church, and thus [are opposed] to the very practice of the Church (which certainly would not neglect a use ordained by the Apostles themselves if it believed it to be from the Apostles), as Michael Medina on the continent of sacred homilies, book V, ch. 105, Ex. 84. From the Apostolic canons, he says, which Clement, the Roman Pontiff and his disciple, gathered into one, the Latin Church now observes scarcely six or eight; how, for example, the 9th canon, commanding that all the faithful who are present at the sacred rites should communicate sacramentally, is notorious for being contrary to the decree of the Council of Trent, sess. 22, ch. 6, and the practice of the Roman Church. And by Gelasius himself with 70 Bishops, C. sancta dist. 15, the book of Apostolic canons is constituted Apocryphal. Now, Apocryphal books are those which the Catholic and Apostolic Church in no way receives, but rather judges that they should be avoided by Catholics. And in Canon law, it is defined thus from Isidore, C. Canones dist. 16. The canons which are called of the Apostles, but because neither the Apostolic see received them, nor did the holy Fathers provide their assent to them, for the reason that they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, although useful things may be found in them, nevertheless it is established that their deeds are removed from the authority of the canons and the Apostolic [writings] and are reckoned among the Apocrypha. There would have been no place for these decrees, definitions, and practice of the Church if those things which are contained in the canons of the Apostles had been introduced into use by the Apostles themselves. Finally, not even the Papists themselves understand the τὰ λοιπὰ concerning those things which are exhibited in those canons. Estius on those things pertaining to the worthy, honest, and orderly celebration of mysteries: Pazmannus, book IV, hodeg., on the decent words pertaining to the administration of the Eucharistic sacrament, on the honorable ordination of the Lord's supper, and its consumption before food: Which pertain to rites. But those are free, and they are not the same everywhere in the Church.

Moreover, although Cornelius à Lapide boasts that this is an illustrious place for traditions, and Bellarmine, book IV on the Word of God, ch. 5, [boasts] that Catholics rightly judge that the Apostle not only disposed of those things which pertained to rites and ceremonies, but also delivered other more serious things, such as the ordination of ministers, the sacrifice of the altar, and the matter and form of other sacraments, and that heretics cannot show the contrary, yet they can demonstrate nothing (1.) with firm proof regarding their traditions, this or that one, in particular, disposed by the Apostle. With the same ease that they assert it, with that same ease we reject it. But it is ridiculous that by us (whom they falsely [call] heretics & calumniously name the worst of heretics) demand contrary arguments, or for the negative, since a simple denial is sufficient. But the burden of proof lies upon those who affirm (2.) It is asked, did Paul come to Corinth afterwards? That fact, which he promises here, cannot be certainly gathered from the Acts of the Apostles, as Estius says in this place. Compare what he has on that 2 Cor. XII. Behold, the third time I am now ready to come to you. But what he adds: If the Apostle did not do by himself what he promises here, that he could have done it through his disciples, is frivolous. The consequence from possibility to actuality is not valid. (3.) Nor does Augustine have anything about this in the place cited by Estius from the letter to Januarius, who gathers from our passage that something was ordained here by the Apostle not concerning those weightier matters, which Bellarmine calls dogmas, but concerning rites, which Estius does not deny. Whence it is given to be understood, (says Augustine) because it was certainly a great matter that he should insinuate in a letter that whole order of acting which the universal Church throughout the world observes, to have been ordained by him, which is varied by no diversity of customs. What have these to do with those weightier matters of Cardinal Bellarmine? (4.) What? That Bellarmine strives to demonstrate those weightier matters, each in its own place, from the scriptures.
