Therefore they cannot be understood here by τὰ λοιπά. For he judges that these are nowhere to be found in the scriptures. The rest, when I come, I will set in order. What he set in order is never found written. (5.) I pass over that Cardinal Cajetan understands by the rest those things which had been treated of before, namely that the Apostle wished to ordain and set them in order then, when he should arrive. The rest, he says, namely the things previously narrated. For he had narrated besides the abuse of the anticipation of the supper another abuse, namely and one indeed is hungry, and another is drunk. He had narrated that, when they came together, there were dissensions among them, and he had applied a remedy to neither of these. Therefore he says: The rest previously narrated, when I come, I will set in order. (6.) But however we may admit that that disposition and τὰ λοιπά speak of other things, it will not yet be proven ever that other new dogmas are understood. Those Διατάξεις look only to order: Whence Thomas expounds τὰ λοιπά as those things which were not of such great danger. Theophylact, although he does not deny that sense which Cajetan embraced, yet observes that it can also be accepted concerning the amending of other abuses: For he says, either he discourses in this place about some other things among these delinquents, who might be in need of a way of living, or he makes mention of the same thing now, just as if he were to say, it is right that some should use this excuse, I wish however in the meantime those things which I have reported to be observed, but if anyone has anything else which is to be said, let him defer it to my arrival to you. But he terrifies them, when he asserts that he is coming, so that being repressed and curbed they may soon be corrected: But if not, that they may at least behave rightly toward one another. Chrysostom understands those other things, as does Thomas, ὁ σφόδρα κατεπέγοντα, who thus preceded Theophylact: Either to certain other things, or to this very thing. For since it was likely that they would both state some causes, and it was not permitted to correct everything by letter. What I have admonished, he says, let them be observed in the meantime. But if you have anything else which you may say, let that be reserved for my arrival, either speaking about this matter as I have said, or about some other things not very urgent. But he does this, so that he may render them better from it. For thinking of his arrival and being anxious, they were about to correct what they had sinned. For it was not a light thing that Paul was about to be among them, and showing that he said, as if I am not coming to you, so some are puffed up. Truly it is not to be said that those dogmas were necessary, τὰ λοιπά; since indeed

the Corinthians had already been sufficiently instructed about those things, whom the Apostle declares that they are rich ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει, and simply ἐν παντὶ in every thing, necessary namely for salvation 1 Cor. I. 5. Therefore τὰ λοιπά is to be understood concerning rites, concerning those things which are only of the same kind with those which he had treated hitherto, the reason of συνεχείας in the preceding demands. Furthermore the word διατάσσειν here looks to ceremonies, pertaining to εὐταξίαν, concerning which Theodoret and Ambrose also explain.

Latin:

V. 34. Εἰ δέ τις πεινᾷ.

Est χλευασμὸς. Loquitur enim tanquam pueris, qui ita solent esse ὀξύπεινοι, ut quidvis arripiant, nec alios ad partem vocent, neque velint σῦκα μερίζειν.

Ἐν οἴκῳ ἐσθιέτω.

Quod volet & quantum volet, & quibus cum volet, vel solus, si ita lubet. Est enim quisque Rex domi suæ.

Quod non ad commessationem vel largiorem potum ad ebrietatem usque extendendum, quo reverenter S. synaxis frequentetur, & agape cele- bretur. Ex quo apparet, non præscriptum hic esse jejunium accessurus ad S. synaxin, vel ut sobrii prorsus accedant; sed liberum relictum, si quis esurit, ut domi prius manducet, sed sobriè. B. Hun- nio videtur hic penitus epulas illas solennes, quæ vel ante vel post cœnam Dominicam agitatæ fue- rint, abrogatas esse, ne in pristinam prophanita- tem relapsi efficiant, ut venerabilis actio ad ju- dicium & condemnationem ipsis vergat. Sed quia agape sequentibus temporibus penes fideles ad- huc in usu fuit, non est probabile, eam hic peni- tus abrogatam fuisse.

Ἵνα μὴ εἰς κρῖμα συνέρχησθε.

Ne ea, quæ in conventibus vestris perperam fiunt, causa vobis sint mali.

Τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ, ὡς ἂν ἔλθω, διατάξομαι.

Apostoli jus habebant constituendi quæ ad conventuum ἐυταξίαν & ad λειτουργίαν pertinebant. Vide supra VII. 17. infra XVI. 1. ubi idem est verbum. Hæc origo est cano- num, qui dicuntur Apostolici, qui ab ipsis non quidem conscripti sed in usum introducti fuêre.

Dum canones Apostolicos non quidem ab Apo- stolis conscriptos, in usum tamen ab iisdem in- troductos, eosque τὰ λοιπὰ cætera illa comple- cti, ut Papistas juvet, affirmat Grotius, in priori,

Lindano, qui in Chronico præfix: Panopl. Apo- stolorum canones certe, inquit, sunt Apostolorum, & Franc. Turriano peculiari opere id contendenti, Alberto Piggio l. II. Hist. Eccles. Hierarch. c. 10. Alphonso de Castro libro 1. advers. hæres. c. 5. idem adhærenti contradicit, quamvis hic Alphonsus du- bius sit cap. II. eosque à Glemente aut collectos aut translatos dicat: Nec non Salmeroni, qui canones illos in Concilio Hierosolymitano Act. XV. ab Apo- stolis conditos esse statuit. Quam etiam Sephro- nii fuisse sententiam Lorinus ad Act. XV. 29. ait, etsi Pamphiliam Martyrem Antiochiæ eosdem scriptos esse censuisse notet, non abnuente Inno- centio Papa Epist. CXIIX. In altero verò refraga- tur Grotius istis, qui Canonum Apostolicorum usum longe inferiorem ætate Apostolica faciunt, uti Ba- ronius ad annum 92. n. 15. agnoscit, canones hos vix ante finem seculi septimi innotuisse in Ecclesia, receptos à Concilio generali sexto (quod tamen concilium ad annum 656. num. 40. docet repro- batum esse ab Ecclesia Romana) quique à moder- na Ecclesia eosdem haud observari fatentur, adeo- que ipsimet praxi Ecclesiæ (quæ sanè usum ab ipsis Apostolis ordinatum haud negligeret, si ab Apostolis esse crederet) ut Michael Medina de sacr. homin. continent. l. V. c. 105. Ex. 84. Ex Apostolicis canonibus, inquit, quos Clemens Roma- nus Pontifex, & ejusdem discipulus in unum coë- git, vix sex aut octo Latina Ecclesia nunc observat, quomodo, verbi gratia, canonem IX. præcipien- tem, ut fideles omnes sacramentaliter communicent, qui intersunt sacris; & decreto synodi Trident. sess. 22. cap. 6. & praxi Ecclesiæ Romanæ contrariari notorium est. Et à Gelasio ipso cum LXX. Epi- scopis C. sancta dist. XV. liber canonum Aposto- licorum Apocryphus constituitur. Jam libri Apo- cryphi sunt, quos nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia, sed à Catholicis potius vitan- dos esse censet. Inque jure Canonico ex Isidoro ita definitur C. Canones dist. XVI. Canones qui dicun- tur Apostolorum, sed quia eosdem nec sedes Aposto- lica recepit, nec sancti Patres illis assensum præbue- runt, pro eo, quod ab hæreticis sub nomine Aposto- lorum compositi dignoscuntur, quamvis in eis utilia inveniantur, tamen ab autoritate canonum atque Apostolica eorum gesta constat esse remota atque in- ter Apocrypha deputata. Quibus decretis, defini- tionibus & praxi Ecclesiæ minime locus fuisset, si in usum introducta ab ipsis Apostolis fuissent, quæ in canonibus Apostolorum continentur. Τὰ λοιπὰ denique ne ipsi Papistæ quidem de his, quæ canonibus illis exhibentur, intelligunt. Estius de spectantibus ad dignam, honestam & ordinatam mysteriorum celebrationem: Pazmannus l. IV. hodeg. de decentibus verbis ad sacramenti Eucha- ristici administrationem pertinentibus, de honori- fica cænæ Dominicæ ordinatione, ejus ante cibum sumptione: Quæ ad ritus spectant. Illi verò liberi sunt, nec ubique in Ecclesia iidem.

Cæterum etsi hic illustrem haberi locum pro traditionibus Cornelius à Lapide glorietur & Bel- larm. l. IV. de V. D. c. 5. merito Catholicos censere, censent, Apostolum non solum disposuisse, quæ ad ritus & ceremonias pertinebant, sed etiam tradi- disse alia graviora, ut de ordinatione ministrorum, de sacrificio altaris, de aliorum sacramentorum materia & forma, nec hæreticos contrarium posse ostendere, nullo tamen illi (1.) documento fir- mo, quod asserunt de traditionibus suis, hâc, vel illa, in specie, ab Apostolo dispositis, de- monstrare possunt. Qua ergo facilitate id asse- runt, eadem facilitate id rejicimus. Ridiculum vero est, quod à nobis (quos hæreticos falso & calumniosè nominant hæreticorum pessimi) argumenta postulent contraria, vel pro negativa, cum sola sufficiat negatio. Affirmantibus autem ipsis incumbat probatio (2.) Quæritur, an Pau- lus adhuc postea Corinthum venerit? Factum id, quod hic pollicetur, ex actis Apostolorum certò col- ligi non potest, dicente hoc loco Estio. Conf. quæ habet ad illud 2. Cor. XII. Ecce tertio nunc para- tus sum ad vos venire. Quod verò subjicit : Si per se non fecit, quod hic promittit Apostolus, per discipulos suos facere potuisse, frivolum est. A posse ad esse non valet consequentia. (3.) Nec de eo quicquam Augustinus habet loco Estio adducto ex epistola ad Januar. qui non de gravioribus illis, quæ vocat Bellarminus, vel dogmatibus, sed de ri- tibus hic aliquid ab Apostolo ordinatum esse, è nostro loco colligit, quod non diffitetur Estius. Unde intelligi datur, (inquit Augustinus) quia utique multum erat, ut in epistola totum illum agen- di ordinem insinuaret, quem universa per orbem servat Ecclesia, ab ipso ordinatum esse, quod nulla morum diversitate variatur. Quid hæc ad gra- viora illa Cardinalis Bellarmini? (4.) Quid? quod Bellarminus ista graviora suo quæque loco, è scri- pturis demonstrare satagat. Non ergo illa hic in- telligi possunt per τὰ λοιπά. Hæc enim nuspiam in scripturis haberi censet. Cætera, cum venero, disponam. Quod disposuerit, nunquam scriptum invenitur. (5.) Taceo, quod Cajetanus Cardina- lis per cætera intelligat ea, de quibus antea actum erat, scilicet quod ea tum ordinare & disponere voluerit Apostolus,cum advenerit. Cætera, inquit, scil. prænarrata. Narraverat autem præter abu- sum anticipationis cœnæ alium abusum, scilicet & alius quidem esurit, & alius ebrius est. Nar- raverat, quod, cum convenirent, dissidia erant inter eos, & neutri horum remedium adhibuerat. Propterea dicit: Cætera prænarra- ta, cum venero, disponam. (6.) Utut verò admittamus de aliis dispositionem illam & τὰ λοι- πὰ loqui, non tamen probabitur unquam, alia nova dogmata intelligi. Διατάξεις illæ solum ad ordinem spectant: Unde Thomas de iis τὰ λοιπὰ exponit, quæ non erant tanti periculi. Theophyla- ctus, etsi non abnuat illi sensui, quem Cajetanus amplexus est, de aliis tamen abusibus emendan- dis etiam accipi posse observat: Aut enim, inquit, hoc loco de aliis nonnullis apud hos delinquentibus differit, qui vivendi modo indigeant, aut eadem de re mentionem nunc facit, perinde ac si dicat, par esse nonnullos ad hac excusatione usuros, velim ta- men interea servanda esse quæ retuli, quod si quis aliud quidpiam habeat, quod sit dicendum, in meum differat ad vos adventum. Terret autem eos, cum se asserit venturum, ut repressi ac frenati mox cor- rigantur: Sin autem, recte saltem se invicem ge- rant. Alia illa Chrysostomus intelligit, uti Thomas ὁ σφόδρα κατεπέγοντα, qui ita præivit Theophy- lacto: Aut ad quædam alia, aut ad hoc ipsum.. Nam quoniam verisimile erat, eos & dicere causas aliquas, & non licebat omnia corrigere per literas. Quæ admonui, inquit, interim serventur. Si quid autem habetis aliud, quod dicatis, illud reservetur ad meum adventum, aut de hac re dicens ut dixi, aut de aliquibus aliis non valde urgentibus. Hoc autem facit, ut eos ex eo reddat meliores. Nam de ejus adventu cogitantes & soliciti, quod pecca- rant, erant correcturi. Non enim leve quid erat, quod Paulus apud eos erat versaturus, idque osten- dens dicebat, tanquam non veniam ad vos, sic in- flati sunt quidam. Sanè dogmata illa necessaria fuisse, τὰ λοιπὰ, dicendum non est; siquidem

| de illis jam instructi affatim fuerant Corinthii, quos Apostolus prædicat, quod divites sint ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει, & simpliciter ἐν παν- τὶ in omni re, necessaria scilicet ad salutem 1. Cor. I. 5. Ergò τὰ λοιπὰ intelligi de ritibus, de iis, quæ ejusdem generis tantùm cum illis, quæ tractave- rat hactenus, συνεχείας ratio in præcedentibus postulat. Cæterum verbum διατάσσειν hic cere- monias respicit, ad εὐταξίαν pertinentes, de qui- bus etiam explicant Theodoretius & Ambrosius.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

Having premised a distinction of those who are inspired by an impure spirit, or by a holy one, that the former curse Christ, but the latter profess the Lord Jesus; he teaches that the Holy Spirit is the one author of all gifts in the Church, which offices and virtues therefore vary indeed for the use of the Church, but arise from the same, the same distributing, as he wills. Thence he treats of the diverse members in the mystical body of Christ, into which we are baptized, by one Spirit, and are made to drink into one Spirit, having applied a comparison of the human body, in which there is no discord between the feet, hands, ears, eyes, and the members seen to be weaker are most necessary, the less honest and comely are affected with the greatest honor and comeliness, and one suffering or rejoicing the others suffer and rejoice with it, admonishing toward concord and bringing in the orders of the ecclesiastical hierarchy according to the diversity of gifts constituted in the primitive Church, with a subjoined exhortation, that they should strive for the more excellent gifts, and a promise of a more excellent way.

There are two parts I. Didactic concerning the one author of the gifts although various in the Church to v. 11. II. Didactic-Parænetic concerning the unity of the mystical body of Christ and the necessity of concord. To the end v. 31.

PART I. DIDACTIC.

On the one author of gifts, although various in the Church.

V. 1. Περὶ δὲ τῶν πνευματικῶν ἀδελφοὶ) that is, περὶ τῶν πνευματοφόρων, concerning those who are inspired by a spirit, whether impure or holy. For the noun πνεύματος is common to both, as can be seen in 1 John IV. 1, 2, 3, 6. Thus also below you have the masculine noun πνευματικὲ XIV. 37.

The more common meaning of the word πνευματικῶν is concerning spiritual gifts, and the explanation of these words is common among interpreters. That novel and singular one, concerning those inspired by a spirit, is a usage of the word that is nowhere to be found. And therefore we prefer the explanation of Chrysostom and Theophylact; concerning spiritual things, says Theophylact, that is, concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For those among the leaders of Corinth who had been bathed in the water of baptism were abundantly imbued with the Holy Spirit. Although this was less apparent to human eyes, it nevertheless produced some visible evidence of its operation, so that these people would either speak in a variety of tongues, or confirm by prophecies and miracles that they had obtained the Holy Spirit. There were therefore among the Christians on account of this kind of spirit's grace, some dissensions arose. For those who were endowed with greater gifts were carried away by pride: but those with lesser ones envied those who had received more of the Spirit. There were, moreover, many soothsayers and prophets who were less truthful, because they could not easily be distinguished from the true or divine ones. All of which the Apostle corrects, and especially those things which pertain to those soothsayers and prophets. We are taught in verses 2 and 3 that this concerns not only ministering gifts, but also sanctifying ones, which was also observed by Philippus, Hunnius, Hesfusius, and the Belgian Interpreters.

I do not want you to be ignorant) That is, to be unmindful, as above in X. 1.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Præmissa discretione eorum qui spiritu impuro, quive sancto afflantur, quod illi Christum execrentur, hi vero Dominum Jesum profiteantur; donorum omnium in Eccle- sia autorem unum esse Spiritum Sanctum docet, quæ proinde officia atque virtutes varient quidem ad usum Ecclesiæ, sed ab eodem oriantur, eodem distribuente, sic- ut vult. Inde de diversis membris in cor- pore Christi mystico, ad quod baptizá- mur, per unum Spiritum, & potamur in unum Spiritum agit, adhibita compara- tione corporis humani, in quo inter pe- des, manus, aures, oculos nulla discordia est, & membra infirmiora visa maximè necessaria sunt, minus honesta & decora maximo afficiuntur honore, & decore, uno- que patiente aut gaudente alia compatiun- tur ac congaudent, commonefaciens ad concordiam & hierarchia Ecclesiasticæ or- dines pro diversitate donorum in Ecclesia primitiva constitutos adducens, subjuncta parænesi, ut ad præstantiora contendant dona, ac promissione viæ excellentioris.

PArtes duæ sunt I. Didactica de uno autore donorum etsi variorum in Ecclesia ad v. 11. II. Didactico - Parænetica de unitate corporis Christi mystici & concordiæ necessitate. Ad finem v. 31.

PARS I. DIDACTICA.

De uno autore donorum, etsi variorum in Ecclesia.

V. 1. Περὶ δὲ τῶν πνευματικῶν ἀδελφοὶ) id est, περὶ τῶν πνευματοφόρων, de iis, qui Spiritu afflantur sive impuro sive sancto. Est enim nomen πνεύματος ad utrumque com- mune, ut videre est 1. Joh. IV. 1. 2. 3. 6. Sic & infra habes nomen Masculinum πνευματικὲ XIV. 37.

Usitatior vocis πνευματικῶν significatio est de donis spiritualibus, & de illis communis est Interpp. horum verborum explicatio. Novella & singularis illa περὶ τῶν πνευματοφόρων, qualis vocis usus nuspiam deprehenditur. Ideoque præ- ferimus explicationem Chrysostomi, & Theophy- lacti, de spiritualibus, inquit Theophylactus, hoc est, de Spiritus Sancti donis. Nam qui ex pri- matibus Corinthi essent baptismi aqua perfusi, af- fatim Spiritu Sancto imbuebantur. Qui etsi hu- manis oculis minus pateret, sua tamen operationis visibile aliquod edebat indicium, ita ut aut lin- guarum varietate hi loquerentur, aut vaticiniis & miraculis confirmarent Spiritum Sanctum se esse adeptos. Erant itaque inter Christianos ob hujuscemodi spiritus gratiam dissensiones obor- tæ nonnullæ. Nam qui majoribus essent donis affecti, superbia efferebantur: Qui verò minori- bus, his invidebant, qui plus Spiritus accepissent. Erant præterea vaticinatores plerique & Prophe- tæ minus veridici, quia veris aut divinis haud fa- cile discernerentur. Quæ omnia castigat Apo- stolus, & ea imprimis, quæ ad vates illos pertinent & prophetas. Non autem de donis tantum mi- nistrantibus, sed etiam sanctificantibus hic agi v. 2. & 3. docemur, quod Philippo, Hunnio, Hesfusio, Belgis Interpretibus etiam observatum.

Οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν) Id est immemores esse ut su- pra X. 1.

## 12:2
V. 2. You know that when you were Gentiles) גוים that is, idolaters. That ὅτε is noted by some as another reading, but the τῷ ὅτι is not added. B. Glassius says the best reading of all is ὅτι, with which the participle ἀπαγόμενοι coheres well, which otherwise would have to be changed in meaning to the verb ἀπάγεσθαι. But since the Greek Interpreters read both, and the Complutensian edition does so as well, as does the Vulgate Latin, and the sense is clear, we easily agree that both particles should be retained, and that this is the genuine reading: You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to mute idols, however you were being led.

To mute idols, however you were being led, being carried away) How you were being led to mute idols, namely, led away from GOD. You were being led by the hope of learning future things to mute idols, that is, to the soothsayers who were present at them, as in the temple of Pythius, Amphiaraus, or Trophonius. He significantly called them mute idols, from Habakkuk II. 18, where in the Greek it is εἴδωλα κωφὰ, which is the same as ἄφωνα, so that he might give to understand that that way by which those soothsayers, whether male or female, predicted certain things which the outcome then confirmed, or performed certain things exceeding human power, was not from the image, which is as devoid of understanding as it is of voice, Psalm CXV. 4. But from demons, who by that false persuasion were leading the people away from GOD. See above X. 20. It is no wonder, however, if those evil demons predict many things that come to pass, and perform other stupendous things, with GOD permitting it, for the reason that besides the sharpness of their intellect, they also have long experience of things, and since they are incredible in number, they easily discover the hidden signs of future events. See what we have said in the annotations to book IV of the truth of the Christian religion. Think that what happened to you then, when you were idolaters, can also happen now. For such python-diviners, Bacchic-possessed, and nymph-possessed can also approach your assemblies at the Devil's instigation: and predict certain things to which the outcome corresponds. You will learn that this has happened at times from Eusebius, History IV. 16.

The distinction here in the Greek Interpreters of divination is handed down between the soothsayers of the Gentiles and true Prophets. By the former, they were led away to mute idols, which were truly ἄφωνα by themselves, even if they were believed to be animated by a demon to teach and give answers: whose answers, however, were also ἄφωνα; because they rendered no certain sense, but were ambiguous, and sometimes did not even produce an intelligible sound, but an inarticulate murmur of no meaning. The emphasis is on the word ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε ἀπαγόμενοι, as if you were led away abducted, because they followed those things with a certain frenzy. For Satan makes his worshippers frenzied. Theophylact has this to say about these words: The Apostle brings forth the distinction between a soothsayer and a Prophet, saying, in the time of idols, if anyone predicted the future while struck and possessed by an impure spirit, he was drawn in such a way that he was led and instigated by it, ignorant of nothing of what he was saying, but was carried away in a frenzy: but a Prophet is not so, but speaks everything with a vigilant mind: Thus it happens that this is found to be the distinction between a soothsayer and a Prophet. But the Apostle seems rather to speak generally about the converted, and the miserable condition of their former state, as Estius, B. Balduinus, and others observe. Their state as Gentiles was indeed extremely miserable. For just as they were led as if devoid of reason to idols, and the living desired to be taught by the dead, those who speak by the mute, men by stones, and craftsmen by their own works, in matters of the greatest importance, than which nothing was more foolish. The condition of men was far more unhappy and miserable when those mute images gave forth a sound: for then they were harassed by the illusions and lies of Satan, than which nothing was more miserable. And not without reason does B. Hunnius note that the Apostle wished to depress the pride and boasting of those who were proud because of miraculous gifts; first by recalling to their mind their former sad and miserable state, that they were Gentiles ignorant of the true GOD, and therefore entirely alien and exiled from eternal life, which is placed in the knowledge of the true GOD. He contends, therefore, he says, between a Gentile man cursing the Lord Jesus, and then a Christian man, who confesses Jesus as his Lord. He denies that that Gentile is governed by the Spirit of GOD, and indicates that such were the Corinthians formerly, when, with the fame of the preaching about JESUS of Nazareth increasing, they were still alien to the knowledge of Him. But this one, namely the Christian, who from a faithful heart confesses Jesus as his Lord and God, he shows to be so certainly ruled by the Holy Spirit, that he asserts evidently that no one can say Lord Jesus (namely with a sincere heart and true trust) except through the Holy Spirit, since He is the proper spirit of Christ, who does not pronounce the Lord Jesus anathema or accursed, but illuminates and glorifies the same, John XVI.

Latin:

V. 2. Οἴδατε ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦτε) גוים id est, idololatræ. Illud ὅτε ceu alia lectio notatur ab aliis, non verò τῷ ὅτι additur. B. Glassius omnium optima, inquit, lectio est, ὅτι quo cum bene cohæret Partici- pium ἀπαγόμενοι, quod alioquin in verbum ἀπή- γεσθαι significatione mutandum foret. Sed quum Græci Interpretes utrumque legant, atque ita et- iam Complutensis editio, ut & vulgata Latina ha- bent, sensusque luculentus sit, facile annuimus, utramque particulam retinendam esse, eamque esse germanam lectionem: Scitis, quod quum gen- tes essetis ad simulachra muta prout euntes duceba- mini.

Πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ ἄφωνα, ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε, ἀπαγόμενοι) Quomodo ageremini ad idola muta, abducti nempe à DEO. Ageremini spe discendi futura ad idola muta, id est, ad vates, qui illis aderant, ut in templo Pythio, Amphiarai, Trephonii. Significanter autem dixit muta idola, ex Abac. II. 18. ubi in Græco εἴδωλα κωφὰ, quod idem est, cum ἄφωνα, ut daret intelligi, illam viam, qua vates isti sive mares sive fœminæ prædicebant quædam, quæ deinde eventus comprobabat, aut quædam humanam vim supe- rantia efficiebant, non fuisse à simulacro, ut vocis ita in- tellectus experte Psal. CXV. 4. Sed à dæmonibus, qui fal- sa ista persuasione populum à DEO abducebant. Vide supra X. 20. Non mirum autem, si mali isti dæmones multa prædicunt, quæ eveniunt, & alia quædam stupenda, DEO sinente, edunt, ideo quod præter ingenii perspicaciam, longam quoque habent rerum experientiam, & cum in- credibili sint numero, facile latentia rerum futurarum in- dicia explorant. Vide quæ diximus in annotatis ad librum IV. de veritate religionis Christianæ. Hoc quod tunc, cum idololatræ essetis, vobis evenit, putate etiam nunc evenire posse. Nam & tales πυθομάντεις, Βακχόληπτοι, νυμφόλη- πτοι, Diabolo instigante ad vestros cœtus possunt accede- re: & quædam prædicere, quibus exitus respondeat. In- terdum id accidisse disces ex Eusebio historiæ IV. 16.

Discrimen hic in Græcis Interpp. μαντίας tra- ditur inter vates Gentilium, & veros Prophetas. Per illos abducebantur ad muta idola, quæ per se verè ἄφωνα erant, etsi animata à dæmone docere & responsa reddere crederentur: Cujus verò re- sponsa etiam ἄφωνα; quia nullum certum sensum reddebant, sed ambigua erant, & quandoque ne sonum quidem intelligibilem, sed murmur incon- ditum nulliusque significationis edebant. Empha- sis est in voce ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε ἀπαγόμενοι quasi ab- repti ducebamini, quod illa furore quodam sequu- ti sint. Furiosos namque suos cultores facit Sa- tan. Theophylactus de his verbis ita habet: Va- ticinatoris & Prophetæ discrimen profert Apostolus, inquiens, idolorum tempore, si quis cum futura præ- diceret spiritu impuro percitus & detentus sic tra- hebatur, ut ab eo erat deductus & instigatus, nihil eorum gnarus quæ diceret, sed furens efferebatur: Propheta verò haud ita se habet, sed mente pervi- gili cuncta proloquitur: Ita fit, ut id esse comperia- tur inter vatem & Prophetam discrimen. Sed vi- detur potius Apostolus generaliter loqui de con- versis, & status eorum pristini miserabili condi- tione, ut Estius, B. Balduinus, aliique observant. Summè utique miser erat status gentilium. Nam sicut rationis expertes agebantur ad idola, & vivi a mortuis, loquentes a mutis, homines a lapidi- bus, opifices ab operibus suis edoceri cupiebant, in rebus longe maximis, quo nihil erat stolidius. Longe infelicior erat miseriorque hominum con- ditio, cum muta illa simulacra sonum edebant: Tum enim illusionibus & mendaciis Satanæ exa- gitabantur, quo nihil erat miserius. Nec abs re notat B. Hunnius, voluisse Apostolum eorum, qui propter dona miraculosa superbiebant, fastum & jactantiam deprimere; Primum ad animum eis revocando pristinum illorum statum tristem & miserum, quod gentes fuerint ignaræ veri DEI, ideoque a vita æterna, quæ in notitia veri DEI posita est, prorsus alienæ & extorres. Contendit itaque, inquit, inter se hominem Ethnicum execran- tem Dominum Jesum, & deinde hominem Christia- num, qui Jesum confitetur Dominum suum. Eth- nicum quidem illum a DEI Spiritu gubernari ne- gat, & tales subindicat olim fuisse Corinthios, cum increbrescente fama prædicationis de JESU Nazare- no adhuc alieni essent ab ipsius notitia. Hunc ve- ro, nempe Christianum, qui ex fideli corde confite- tur Jesum Dominum & Deum suum, ostendit tam certo regi Spiritu Sancto, ut evidenter asserat, ne- minem posse dicere Dominum Jesum (scilicet sin- cero corde, veraque fiducia) nisi per Spiritum Sanctum, quandoquidem is est Christi proprius spiritus, qui Dominum Jesum non anathema seu maledictum pronuntiat, sed eundem illustrat & glorificat Joh. XVI.

## 12:3
V. 3. Therefore I make known to you) I teach you. The Corinthians could ask, since the matter is such that they can predict the future, and be inspired by GOD and by a demon, how shall we distinguish them? Paul teaches them about this matter, applying those things which are of the law κατ' ἀναλογίαν to the times of the Gospel.

That no one speaking by the Spirit of God says 'Jesus is accursed') Just as in the old law, for someone to be ascribed to the Prophets, it was not sufficient that the event corresponded with the predictions, but besides that it was required that he should not lead men away from the true GOD, as the comparison of the passages Deut. XIII. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. & XVIII. 21. 22. shows. So also under the new Testament, besides the agreement of the event with the predictions, it is required that he does not lead men away from Jesus. For just as God and the providence of God was the foundation in those times, so now Jesus, or God known through Jesus, is the foundation of the whole religion. See above III. 11. The meaning is clearly the same in 1 John IV. 3. to say 'Jesus is accursed', concerning Jesus [Hebrew: חרף] to say is to execrate his name: To blaspheme as it is in Acts XXVI. 11. & among Justin: To curse Christ, as it is in the letter of Pliny. In the Manuscript it is, 'Jesus is accursed' so that it may be a mimetic speech.

And no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit) That is, he who has the inspiration, if he constantly professes Jesus to be his Lord, whom he wishes to obey in all things, do not doubt but that he is inspired by a Divine, not a Satanic, Spirit. John says clearly the same in the place already mentioned & Polycarp in the letter to the Philippians.

This is the other, according to the Greek Interpreters, distinction between the prophets of the gentiles & the true Prophets. Theophylact says this again, that for distinguishing a prophet, let this be an indication to you, when he has cursed Jesus, & execrates him. But on the contrary, concerning a Prophet, that is an argument when he follows the name of Jesus with blessings. Indeed, when afterwards it is treated concerning true Teachers in the Church, and their distinct classes as it were, that interpretation concerning the prophets of the gentiles, from whom the Apostle distinguishes the duties of true Teachers in the Church, and the gifts of the same, may not seem inappropriate. But since he has addressed the Corinthians generally 'that when you were gentiles', and has made no mention of any prophets among them, the opposition of the state of the Corinthians in former pagan idolatry, and ignorance of the true GOD, nay rather execration and blasphemy; and their modern state in the worship of the one true GOD, and the acknowledgment of Jesus our Lord in the Church is instituted here. But in general of all the faithful it is to call Jesus Lord, not anathema.

If you look at the usage of the word, according to common opinion, it is said in both a good and a bad sense, because חרם denotes a thing separated and devoted to GOD. That it is used of good things, when they were consecrated to GOD, or were hung up for the sake of memory: but of bad things and persons, when on account of singular sins they were remitted to GOD as a just Judge, unworthy to be held or to dwell among men any longer.

The learned Salmasius does not like that homonymy of the word ἀναθέματ@. He warns that ἀνάθημα & ἀνάθεμα should not be confused. He takes the former for a votive offering, and a thing consecrated to temples, and indeed that it is not used by the Greeks for every thing consecrated to the Gods, but only for that kind of gift which could be hung up, or set in a high and sublime place, so that they might be an ornament to the temples. Hesychius says ἀνάθημα is an ornament. Pollux says: 'Votive offerings are for the most part crowns, bowls, drinking cups, censers, etc.' And he thinks that Luke ch. XXI. 5 clearly and distinctly testifies that those things are called ἀναθήματα only, by which a temple would properly be adorned. But ἀνάθεμα, to Salmasius, is properly a thing separated and removed from the rest of the body and number, or exempted from the use of any private person, so that it might be dedicated to GOD. But nowhere, he says, is ἀνάθημα taken in a bad sense among the Greeks, nor did they ever say ἀνάθημα for ἀνάθεμα, so that it is clear from this that ἀνάθημα is one thing, and ἀνάθεμα another, although men most learned in these letters think otherwise. In the thing itself, τὸ ἀνάθεμα can indeed signify a devoted and cursed man; but the notion of the word is different, which properly signifies separated and removed, as is evident from the words of Paul in Rom. IX. Rightly, therefore, did Hesychius explain it as 'uncommunicated,' which property does not fall upon the word ἀνάθημα, when it is taken for a votive offering and a thing dedicated to temples. Salmasius derives that from the different notion of ἀναθεῖναι, to dedicate, whence comes ἀνάθημα, and of ἀναθέσθαι, to take back a vote, and to move a pebble from its seat, whence comes ἀνάθεμα. But he says that the word itself does not make this difference, which is the same. But the preposition, because just as the ἀνὰ in the verb ἀναβάλλειν, which is to throw and send upwards, signifies one thing, and in the verb ἀνακαλεῖν, which is to recall, it signifies another; so the notion of ἀνὰ in the verb ἀναθεῖναι and in the verb ἀναθέσθαι is altogether different.

But that distinction of words is not observed among the Hellenists. For even ἀνάθημα is taken in a bad sense in Deut. XXVII. 29: 'And every ἀνάθημα, whatever is set apart from men, shall not be redeemed, but shall surely be put to death.' And ἀνάθεμα occurs in the sense in which Salmasius wants ἀνάθημα to be said, in Judith XVI. 17: 'He gave it as an ἀνάθεμα to the Lord,' and 2 Macc. VI. 11, 13: 'and letters of the kings concerning ἀναθέματα.' In which way also τὸ ἀναθεματισμένον is used in Numbers XVIII. 14, where this word is used for the Hebrew חרם among the LXX Interpreters, which is properly to excommunicate, to devote from common use and to cut off entirely, but figuratively to consecrate, because everything that was killed was consecrated to the Lord, or rather because what was consecrated was separated from common use.

Nor is the verb καταναθεματίζειν in Matth. XXVI. 74 taken otherwise. Where Salmasius again criticizes the Vulgate version: 'They translate wrongly,' he says, 'Then he began to devote himself': There is no signification of devotion or consecration in this word at all, as I see has been persuaded to most learned men until now. But because it is considered a great evil to be cast out and to be an exile from that body and society of which you desire to be a participant, it has been used from that as a form of imprecation; for just as those who want to be believed, when affirming something, are accustomed to say, 'May I not live,' instead of 'May I be detestable, unless this is so': So for the Jews and ancient

Christians, the solemn formula in an oath was, 'let it be anathema,' that is, excluded from the Synagogue and the Church. Whence also καταναθεματίζειν is to imprecate such an anathema upon oneself. Thus here Peter was imprecating an anathema upon himself, if he had seen the man. These are the words of Salmasius. But he only quibbles there on the word 'to devote': which, when used by Beza, denotes nothing other than that Peter bound himself with curses. And ἀνάθεμα is perpetually used by the LXX Interpreters for חרם, excision, or cursing, for a cursed and excommunicated person in Numbers XXI. 3, Deut. VII. 26, ch. XIII. 15, 17, ch. XX. 17, Josh. VI. 17, ch. VII. 15, 18, 1 Chron. II. 7, Zech. XIV. 11. Nor does it occur in the New Testament in any other sense than of an excommunicated or cursed person, Rom. IX. 3, 1 Cor. XVI. 22, Gal. I. 8, 9, or for a devotion or execration, Acts XXIII. 14. And even in this sense. In this place, to say anathema is the same as to devote and to execrate; in which manner the Gentiles are noted, who used to curse Christ, and strove to compel Christians by threats and torments to curse Him as well. See Pliny, Epistle to Trajan.

The Apostle therefore denies that anyone who is moved by the Spirit of God and speaks in the Spirit of God curses or execrates Christ, which was done by the Gentiles, who were inspired by an evil spirit; and he thus warns that the gifts of the Holy Spirit must be used in such a way that Jesus is not called anathema or blasphemed. By that very fact, he requires a constant confession of Jesus, so that one may not, with the Gentiles or Jews, blaspheme the name or doctrine of Christ (Acts 13:48), which is also done by heretics, who are said to blaspheme the way of truth (2 Peter 2:2), and [he warns against] the holy usurpation of the name of Jesus, so that they may not abuse the name of Jesus in execrations, or, while boasting of the name of Jesus, cause it to be blasphemed by their own life (Romans 2:23-24; 2 Timothy 2:19), but rather that they may refer all things to the acknowledgment, glory, and honor of Jesus (Colossians 3:17). Conversely, to call Jesus Lord is to acknowledge Jesus as Lord, to believe in Him, to invoke, celebrate, and glorify His name with a true confession of faith, holy obedience, and subjection. For all these things, the gift of the Holy Spirit is required, which the holy Apostle wished here to promise as something general and common to all Christians and believers, distinguishing true Christians from Gentiles before he proceeds to the special gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which he primarily enriches the ministers of the Church for the public utility of the Church. Here is a beautiful paraphrase by our blessed Balduinus: 'Furthermore, most beloved, regarding those spiritual gifts about which you also consulted me, I would like you at the beginning to consider diligently your former state, when you were still Gentiles, and, as you well remember, you followed idols in the manner of brute beasts, consulted oracles, inspected entrails, and by these means desired to be instructed about future things, just as each one was seized by a certain blind impulse of reason or even by the persuasion of others. At that time, you had certainly received nothing yet from the Spirit of God. For it cannot be that anyone led by the Holy Spirit would blaspheme or persecute Christ Jesus, which it is evident you did. But those who are led by the Holy Spirit invoke God, acknowledge, and confess that He is the Lord, who has the right of life and death over them.' Such, however, are all Christians, equal in this in all respects: otherwise, there are certainly differences of gifts, although all things proceed from and are effected by one Spirit. Therefore, it is not just any naming of the Lord that is understood here, since even hypocrites say 'Lord, Lord' (Matthew 7:21), but that which comes from true faith and has holy obedience as its companion, which consists solely in this: those who do the will of the heavenly Father. For in divine matters, not by words, but by action is there need, and it is not the pronunciation of the tongue, but the affection of the heart that profits. Moreover, it is manifest from this sentence, no one can say that Jesus is Lord, except by the Holy Spirit, the weakness of the powers of free will, that we are capable of nothing in spiritual matters without the Holy Spirit, by whose illumination, regeneration, and conversion there is need, so that we may believe in Christ, and call upon him as our Lord. For faith is the work of God John VI. 29. and it is given to us by GOD, that we may believe in Christ Phil. I. 29.

Latin:

V. 3. Διὸ γνωρίζω ὑμῖν) [Hebrew: הודעתיכם] doceo vos. Quærere poterant Corinthii, cum res ita se habeat, ut fu- tura prædicere possint, & a DEO, & a dæmone afflati, quomodo eos dignoscemus? Hac de re eos edocet Pau- lus, ea quæ sunt legis κατ' ἀναλογίαν applicans ad Evan- gelii tempora.

Ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἐν πνεύματι Θεοῦ λαλῶν λέγει ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦν) Sicut in veteri lege, ut quis Prophetis adscriberetur, non sufficiebat eventus cum prædictis respondens, sed præter- ea requirebatur, ne a vero DEO homines abduceret, ut ostendit collatio locorum Deut. XIII. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. & XVIII. 21. 22. Sic & sub novo Testamento præter convenien- tiam eventus cum prædictis requiritur, ne homines a Jesu abducat. Nam sicut Deus & Dei providentia fundamen- tum fuit illis temporibus, ita nunc Jesus, sive Deus per Jesum cognitus fundamentum est totius religionis. Vide supra III. 11. Idem plane sensus 1. Joh. IV. 3. λέγειν ἀνά- θεμα Ἰησοῦν, de Jesu [Hebrew: חרף] dicere est ejus nomen execrari: Βλασφημεῖν ut est Act. XXVI. 11. & apud Justinum: Male- dicere Christo, ut est in epistola Plinii. In Manuscripto est, λέγει ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦς ut sit oratio μιμητική.

Καὶ οὐδεὶς δύναται εἰπεῖν Ἰησοῦν Κύριον εἰ μὴ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ) Id est, qui afflatum habet, is si constanter Jesum profiteatur suum esse Dominum, cui per omnia parere ve- lit, ne dubitate, quin Divino non Satanico afflatus sit Spi- ritu. Plane idem dicit Johannes dicto jam loco & Poly- carpus in epistola ad Philippenses.

Alterum hoc est, juxta Græcos Interpretes, va- tum gentilium & verorum Prophetarum discri- men. Hoc præterea inquit iterum Theophylactus, ad vatem internoscendum, tibi indicio sit, cum Jesu is maledixerit, & execretur. Contra verò de Pro- pheta illud est argumento cum Jesu nomen benedi- ctis prosequitur. Sanè quum postea de veris Do- ctoribus in Ecclesia, eorumque distinctis veluti classibus agatur, non inconcinna videri potest illa de vatibus gentilium interpretatio, a quibus dis- cernat Apostolus munia verorum in Ecclesia Doctorum, & dona earundem. Sed quum com- muniter alloquutus sit Corinthios ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦσθε, nec ullam vatum apud eosdem mentionem fecerit, oppositio status Corinthiorum pristini in pagana idololatria, verique DEI ignorantia, imo execratione ac blasphemia; & moderni in unius veri DEI cultu, & Jesu Domini nostri agnitione in Ecclesia hic instituitur. In genere verò omnium fidelium est Jesum dicere Dominum, non ana- thema.

Si vocis usum spectes, ex communi sententia, dictum tum in bonam, tum in malam partem, quia חרם notat rem separatam ac Deo addictam. Quod de rebus bonis adhibeatur, cum DEO consecra- bantur, aut memoriae causa suspendebantur: De malis vero rebus ac personis, cum ob singularia piacula DEO ceu justo Judici remittebantur, in- digna, quae inter homines amplius haberentur vel versarentur.

Cl. Salmasio non placet illa vo- cis ἀναθέματ@ ὁμωνυμία. Monet confunden- dum non esse ἀνάθημα & ἀνάθεμα. Illud pro dona- rio, ac re templis consecrata sumi, & quidem non de re omni Diis consecrata a Graecis adhiberi, sed de illo tantum genere donorum, quae suspendi poterant, aut in excelso & sublimi loco statui, ut essent templis ornamento. Hesychius ἀνάθημα inquit κόσμημα. Pollux Τὰ δὲ ἀναθήματα ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στέφανοι, Φιάλαι ἐκπώματα, θυμιατήρια &c. Idque Lucam cap. XXI. 5. clare ac diferte testari, putat ἀναθήματα ea tantum dici, quibus templum proprie ornaretur. At ἀνάθεμα Salmasio proprie res separata & semota a reliquo corpore & nume- ro, aut ab usu privati alicujus exempta, ut DEO dicaretur. Nusquam autem, inquit, ἀνάθημα apud Graecos in malam partem accipitur, nec illi unquam ἀνάθημα dixere pro ἀνάθεμα, ut hinc liqueat, aliud esse ἀνάθημα, aliud ἀνάθεμα, licet contra sen- tiant viri in his literis doctissimi. Re quidem ipsa devotum & maledictum hominem significare po- test τὸ ἀνάθεμα; sed verbi notio alia est, quae pro- prie separatum ac semotum significat, ut ex verbis Pauli Rom. IX. constat. Recte itaque Hesychius ἀκοινώνητον exposuit, quae proprietas non cadit in vocabulum ἀνάθημα, cum pro donario ac re tem- plis dicata sumitur. Deducit id Salmasius e di- versa notione τοῦ ἀναθεῖναι, dedicare, unde ἀνάθη- μα & τοῦ ἀναθέσθαι, ψῆφον ἀναθέσθαι, calculum re- ducere, ac sede sua movere, unde ἀνάθεμα. Quam vero differentiam non verbum ipsum facere ait, quod idem est. Sed Praepositionem, quia ut aliud signifi- cat τὸ ἀνὰ in verbo ἀναβάλλειν, quod est sursum jacere ac mittere, aliud in verbo ἀνακαλεῖν, quod est revocare; Ita aliam omnino esse notionem τοῦ ἀνὰ in verbo ἀναθεῖναι & in verbo ἀναθέσθαι.

Sed ea vocum distinctio apud Hellenistas non observatur. Nam & ἀνάθημα in malam partem sumitur Deut. XXVII. 29. καὶ πᾶν ἀνάθημα, ὃ ἐὰν τεθῇ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὐ λυτρωθήσεται, ἀλλὰ θα- νάτῳ θανατωθήσεται. Et ἀνάθεμα eo sensu, quo ἀνάθημα dici vult Salmasius, occurrit Judith. XVI. 17. εἰς ἀνάθεμα τῷ Κυρίῳ ἔδωκε & 2. Macc. VI. 11. 13. καὶ ἐπιστολὰς βασιλείων περὶ ἀναθεμάτων. Quo- modo & τὸ ἀναθεματισμένον adhibetur Numer. XIIX. 14. ubi haec vox pro Hebraeo חרם apud LXX. Interpp. usurpata, quae proprie est excommu- nicare, ab usu communi devovere ac porro excidere, tralatitiè vero consecrare, quia omne, quod oc- cidebatur, consecrabatur Domino, vel potius quia quod consecrabatur, ab usu communi separaba- tur.

Nec aliter verbum καταναθεματίζειν Matth. XXVI. 74. accipitur. Ubi Salmasius iterum re- prehendit vulgatam versionem: Male, inquit, vertunt: Tunc coepit se devovere: Nulla prorsus devotionis aut consecrationis in hac voce significa- tio, ut persuasum hactenus fuisse video doctissimis viris. Quia vero pro magno malo ducitur extor- resieri & exulare ab eo corpore & societate, cujus te cupis esse participem, ex eo vice imprecationis usurpatum est; ut enim qui sibi credi volunt, ali- quid affirmantibus, solent dicere, ne vivam, pro eo intestabilis sim, nisi hoc sit: Ita Judaeis & antiquis

Christianis solennis in jurejurando formula, ana- thema sit, hoc est, a Synagoga & Ecclesia exclusus. Unde & καταναθεματίζειν sibi tale anathema im- precari. Ita hic Petrus anathema sibi ipsi impreca- batur, si hominem vidisset. Hæc Salmasius. Sed tricatur tantum ibi in voce devovere: Quæ verò Bezæ eam adhibenti nihil aliud notat, quàm quod Petrus diris se obligarit. Et ἀνάθεμα perpetuo à LXX. Interpp. pro חרם excisione, vel maledictio- ne, pro maledicto & excommunicato adhibetur Numer. XXI. 3. Deuter. VII. 26. cap XIII. 15. 17. cap. XX. 17. Jos. VI. 17. cap. VII. 15. 18. 1. Paral, II. 7. Zach. XIV. 11. Neque alio sensu in N. Testa- mento occurrit, quam de excommunicato, vel ma- ledicto Rom. IX. 3. 1. Cor. XVI. 22. Gal. I. 8. 9. vel pro devotione, aut execratione Act. XXIII. 14. At- que etiam in hoc sensu. Hoc loco anathema dicere, idem est ac devovere, & execrari; quo pacto gen- tiles notantur, qui Christo maledicebant, & Chri- stianos minis & tormentis, ut eidem maledice- rent, adigere satagebant. Vide Plinium Epist. ad Trajan.

Negat ergò Apostolus, quenquam, qui Spiritu DEI agitatur, & in Spiritu DEI loquitur, Christum maledicere aut execrari, quod à gentilibus fiebat, Spiritu maligno afflatis, adeoque monet, ita uten- dum esse donis Spiritus Sancti, ut ne Jesus ana- thema dicatur, vel blasphemetur. Requirens eo ipso constantem Jesu confessionem, ne cum Genti- libus aut Judæis Christi nomen vel doctrinam bla- sphement Act. XIII. 48. quod ab hæreticis etiam fit, qui viam veritatis blasphemare dicuntur 2. Petr. II. 2. sanctamque nominis Jesu usurpationem, ne in execrationibus nomine Jesu abutantur, vel no- men Jesu jactantes, vitâ sua ut id blasphemetur, efficiant: Rom. II. 23. 24. 2. Tim. II. 19. quin ad Jesu agnitionem, gloriam, & honorem omnia re- ferant. Col. III. 17. Ex adverso Jesum dicere Do- minum est Jesum agnoscere Dominum, in eum credere, nomen ejus invocare, celebrare, ac glo- rificare, vera fidei confessione, sanctâ obedientia, & subjectione. Ad quæ omnia requiritur Spiri- tus Sancti donum, quod hic ceu generale & com- mune omnibus Christianis & fidelibus promittere voluit S. Apostolus, discernens veros Christianos à gentilibus, antequam ad specialia dona Spiritus Sancti, quibus imprimis ministros Ecclesiæ ditat ad utilitatem Ecclesiæ publicam accedat. Pulchra hic est B. Balduini nostri παράφρασις: Cæterum, charissimi, quod attinet spiritualia illa dona, de qui- bus me etiam consuluistis, velim vos principio dili- genter considerare pristinum statum vestrum, cum gentiles adhuc essetis, & ut probe meministis, bru- torum in modum sectabamini idola, consulebatis oracula, inspiciebatis exta, & his modis de futuris rebus erudiri cupiebatis, prout unusquisque cæco quodam rationis impetu, vel etiam persuasione alio- rum capiebatur. Tunc temporis sane de Spiritu DEI nihil adhuc acceperatis. Fieri enim non potest, ut quis Spiritu Sancto ductus Christum Jesum blasphe- maret aut persequeretur, quod vos fecisse constat: Sed qui Spiritu Sancto ducuntur, invocant Deum, agnoscunt atque confitentur, ipsum esse Dominum, qui in ipsos habeat jus vitæ & necis. Tales autem sunt omnes Christiani, in hoc per omnia æqua- les: Alias certè sunt discrimina donorum, licet ab uno Spiritu proficiscantur & efficiantur omnia. Non ergo hic qualiscunque nuncupatio Domini intelligitur, siquidem & hypocritæ dicant Domi- ne, Domine Matth. VII. 21. sed quæ ex vera fide fit, sanctamque obedientiam comitem habet, quæ in eo solum sita est: Qui faciunt voluntatem Pa- tris cœlestis. Nam in rebus divinis non verbis, sed facto opus est, nec pronunciatio linguæ, sed ani- mi affectus prodest. Manifesta autem est ex hac sententia, nemo potest Jesum dicere Dominum, nisi per Spiritum Sanctum, ἀδυναμία virium li- beri arbitrii, quod in spiritualibus nihil valeamus sine Spiritu Sancto, cujus illuminatione, regenera- tione ac conversione opus est, ut in Christum cre- damus, eumque ceu Dominum nostrum invoce- mus. Fides enim est ἔργον τῦ Θεῦ Joh. VI. 29. & datur id nobis à DEO, ut in Christum credamus Phil. I. 29.

## 12:4
V. 4. Now there are diversities of gifts) After the distinction given, which is very necessary to know, between those inspired by the divine spirit and those inspired by the spirit of Satan, he proceeds to say that there are also distinctions of the divine inspiration, not because all things are not good, but because not all things are given to all: And all things are given not to adorn individuals, but for the utility of the Churches. Which pertains to this, that both pride may be taken away and envy. Moreover, let modesty be inculcated, and a zeal for serving all the faithful.

The same Spirit) These do not differ in origin, as divine things do from Diabolical ones, but they differ in effect. The same Spirit here in the beginning, but one and another in operation.

Latin:

V. 4. Διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσὶ) Post datum discri- men, perquam necessarium cognitu, inter afflatos divino & afflatos Satanæ spiritu, pergit dicere etiam afflatus di- vini esse discrimina, non quod non omnia bona sint, sed quod non omnia omnibus data: Et omnia data non ad ornandos singulos, sed ad utilitatem Ecclesiarum. Quod eo pertinet, ut & superbia auferatur & invidia. Inculce- tur autem modestia, & studium fidelibus omnibus inser- viendi.

Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα) Non distant hæc origine, ut divina à Diabolicis, sed distant effectu. Idem hic Spiritus primor- dio, sed alius atque alius opere.

## 12:5
And there are diversities of ministries and the same Lord) There are various ministries in the Church: There are the faithful, there are deacons, there are presbyters, there are princes of the presbyters, and of these there are princes. Diakonia is sometimes the name of the lowest species, as Acts VI. 1, sometimes the name of the genus as Acts VI. 4, Rom. XI. 13, and elsewhere. The same Lord, that is, to the same Christ all these ought to serve.

Latin:

Καὶ διαιρέσεις διακονιῶν εἰσὶ κὰι ὁ αὐτὸς Κύριος) Varia sunt ministeria in Ecclesia: Sunt fideles, sunt diaconi, sunt presbyteri, sunt principes presbyterorum, & horum sunt principes. Διακονία modo nomen est speciei infimæ, ut Act. VI. 1. modo nomen generis ut Act. VI. 4. Rom. XI. 13. & alibi. Idem Dominus, id est, eidem Christo omnia hæc servire debent.

## 12:6
V. 6. And there are diversities of operations) For different ministries God gave different gifts: Yet not the same to all, nor always: But to whom and when it seemed good to him, for reasons known to him, not to men. Energon is proper to that thing, of which it is treated here Matth. XIV. 2, Mark VI. 14, Gal. II. 8, III. 7, Eph. II. 2, III. 20, concerning this distinction of gifts thus Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: Who also receive gifts each as they are worthy, being enlightened through the name of this Christ. For one indeed receives the spirit of understanding, another of counsel, another of strength, another of healing, another of foreknowledge, another of teaching, another of the fear of God.

But it is the same God who works all in all) All these things, in those who have Christ for Lord, proceed from one Lord.

The Apostle recalls the Corinthians from the gods of the Gentiles to the one true God, to whom they had given their name in baptism, of whom also v. 13 he makes tacit mention, and to whom they themselves had been converted, from the worship of those who by nature are not gods, when previously they had not known God, as is said of the Galatians chap. IV. 8, 9, but they had been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the one true GOD. This one therefore, the only true God, he presents to them, when he speaks of one Spirit, one Lord (Jesus the Son of GOD), one God working all in all, not only in those who have Christ for Lord; But whosoever and whatsoever things there are at all. Concerning which in Anti-Crellius page 918 and Tom. III. System. Theol. page 71. we spoke for the asserting and vindicating of our Catholic faith, and in the former place indeed we asserted the opinion of those who take this whole passage concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, to whom the Blessed Glassius adds his support, and who wish him to come here under the name of one Spirit, one Lord, and one GOD, against Crellius at least, so that we might discern whether those things which he opposed to him are sufficiently valid, but in the latter we took from thence an argument for the Most Holy Trinity. For although the Crellian exceptions opposed to the Catholics are less firm, we do not doubt that their explanation, which establishes that all three persons of the divinity are exhibited here, stands on a firmer footing: Because the Apostle recalls the Corinthians to the adequate object of worship and faith, which is the triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by that one Lord he understands the same one whom he had called kurion in v. 3, and by the one GOD he designates the same one, concerning whom he had spoken in v. 3, likewise naming the Spirit of GOD: In which very verse he had likewise expressed all three persons of the Deity, God and his Spirit, and the Lord Jesus. But as for those diversities, when making distinct mention of the gifts, the ministries, and the operations, he assigns the same to distinct persons in the Holy Trinity, no partition or division of works is made between the divine persons. For the works of the Trinity to the outside, such as those are, are undivided: those diversities are called so, both because the gifts themselves were divided and various from one another; and because they were divided by reason of the subjects, while some things were distributed to some and others to others: And because the divisions are only of graces in the ministers, in Christ alone is the fullness of grace. Concerning which Thomas: To Christ alone the Spirit is given, not by measure as is said in John III, but as far as others are concerned there are divisions of graces because some abound in one, some in another. For just as in the natural body the head has all the senses, but other members do not: So in the Church alone Christ has all the graces, which are divided among the other members.

How, however, χαρίσματα, διακονίαι, and ἐνεργήματα differ is not explained in the same way. Some make χαρίσματα the genus, and διακονίαι and ἐνεργήματα the species: But as these are attributed to the three persons distinctly, not separately, so also they are of a triple order: to the Holy Spirit are assigned χαρίσματα, both the ministering gifts, as they are called, and the sanctifying ones, according to the third article of the Apostolic Creed concerning sanctification: to Christ the Lord, as our Arch-Bishop, are attributed διακονίαι or ministries: to God the Father, from whom originally is all efficacy, from whom are all things, are claimed τὰ ἐνεργήματα. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are granted not immediately but through the mediation of the ministry, therefore the Apostle subjects διακονίαι to them. But since the Holy Spirit distributes gifts through the ministry, ἐνεργήματα or salutary effects are ascribed to GOD the Father, who through the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the ministers of the word is efficacious in the Church.

That some understand by charismata here the gifts which are called ministering is taught by the enumeration of most of them which is subjoined. However, it is sufficiently clear that sanctifying gifts are not excluded from verse 3, where faith in Christ is attributed to the Holy Spirit as the author. These χαρίσματα, however, are so assigned to the Holy Spirit that the Lord (Christ Jesus) is not excluded, from whom and through whom all χαρίσματα redound: Because of his fullness we all receive grace for grace, John 1:16, in whom χάρις grace, and χαρίσματα all gifts of grace befall us, 1 Cor. 1:4, nor is God the Father excluded, from whom each one has his own χάρισμα, 1 Cor. 7:7, Rom. 11:28, 1 Cor. 1:4, 2 Tim. 1:6. Furthermore, διακονίαι are sacred offices in general of whatever kind, which, however, are less correctly enumerated here by Grotius. There are various ministries in the Church: there are the faithful, there are Deacons, there are Presbyters, there are Princes of the Presbyters, and there are also Princes of these. The name of the faithful is not of an office, but a common appellation of those who truly believe. Concerning the Princes of the Presbyters, by whom he undoubtedly understands Bishops with the Papists, the scripture knows nothing, by which they are considered distinct from Presbyters, whether for the sake of order, or of authority and jurisdiction, concerning which Blondellus and Salmasius had treated at length. Nor does the Holy Scripture know anything of the Princes of the Princes of the Presbyters or Bishops, whether they be understood as Arch-Bishops, or even Cardinals, or finally Pontiffs. For these names and offices have no foundation in the scriptures, no jot is found concerning them. But again, διακονίαι are attributed to the Son of God, the Lord, not divisively or exclusively: For the same are also referred to the Holy Spirit 2 Cor. 3:5, and to God the Father 2 Cor. 5:18, ch. 6:4, 1 Thess. 3:2, but through a special relation of the Ministers to the Lord. For they are ὑπηρέται τῶ Χριςῶ [servants of Christ] 1 Cor. 4:1, διάκονοι τῶ Χριςῶ [deacons of Christ] Col. 1:7, 1 Tim. 4:6, who is that one Lord 1 Cor. 8:6, Eph. 4:5. Finally, all ἐνεργήματα [workings] are the works and effects of grace, which GOD ordinarily works in the Church through sacred ministries, for which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are granted to the Ministers. Nor should any division be thought of here. For they are so attributed to the Father that neither the Holy Spirit is excluded, 1 Cor. 12:10, 11, nor the Son. For my Father, says Christ, John 5:17, ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται [is working until now], κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι [and I am working], and v. 19, Whatever the Father does, that the Son also does likewise.

But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good) Φανερῶν [to make manifest] is to give, so that it may appear, נתון [given] Jer. 33:6. Hence φανέρωσις [manifestation] is a conspicuous gift. They are given, he says, not for their own sake, but for the Church's.

Latin:

V. 6. Καὶ διαιρέσεις ἐνεργημάτων εἰσὶν) Pro diversis mi- nisteriis Deus diversa dabat dona: Non tamen omnibus eadem, nec semper: Sed quibus & quando ipsi visum, ob causas ipsi, non hominibus cognitas. Ἐνεργῶν proprium ei rei, de qua hic agitur Matth. XIV. 2. Marci VI. 14. Gal. II. 8. III. 7. Eph. II. 2. III. 20. de hoc donorum discrimine sic Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: Οἳ κὰι λαμβάνεσι δόματα ἕκαστος ὡς ἄξιοί εἰσι, φωτιζόμενοι διὰ τῦ ὀνόματος τῦ χριστῦ τύτυ. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ λαμβάνει συνέσεως πνεῦμα, ὁ δὲ βυλῆς, ὁ δὲ ἰσχύος, ὁ δὲ ἰάσεως, ὁ δὲ προγνώσεως, ὁ δὲ διδα- σκαλίας, ὁ δὲ φόβυ Θεῦ.

Ὁ δὲ αὐτός ἐσι Θεὸς ὁ ἐνεργῶν τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι) Hæc omnia in iis, qui Christum pro Domino habent, ab uno procedunt Domino.

A Diis Gentilium revocat Apostolus Corin- thios ad unum verum Deum, cui nomen dede- rant in baptismo, cujus & v. 13. mentionem te- ctam facit, & ad quem ipsi conversi erant, ab eo- rum cultu, qui naturâ non sunt Dii, cum antea Deum non cognossent, ut de Galatis dicitur cap. IV. 8. 9. baptizati autem erant in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, ceu unius veri DEI. Hunc ergo solum verum Deum sistit iisdem, cum unum Spiritum, unum Dominum (Jesum DEI Filium) unum Deum omnia in omnibus, non tantum iis, qui Christum pro Domino habent; Sed quicunque & quæcunque omnino sunt, operantem. Quo de in Anti-Crellio pag. 918. & Tom. III. System. Theol. pag. 71. ad asserendam & vindicandam fidem no- stram Catholicam diximus, & in priori quidem loco eorum sententiam, qui totum hunc locum de persona Spiritus S. accipiunt, quibus B. Glassius calculum addit, eumque nomine unius Spiritus, unius Domini, & unius DEI hic venire volunt, adversus Crellium faltim, ut dispiceremus, an va- lida satis sint, quæ ei opposuit, asseruimus, in po- steriori autem argumentum inde SS. Trinitatis desumpsimus. Etsi enim minus firmæ sint exce- ptiones Crellianæ Catholicis oppositæ, firmiori tamen talo stare illorum explicationem, quæ omnes tres personas divinitatis hic exhiberi statuit, non dubitamus: Quia ad objectum adæquatum cultus & fidei revocat Corinthios Apostolus, quod est trinunus Deus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus San- ctus, & per unum illum Dominum eundem, quem v. 3. dixerat κύριον, intelligit, per unum DEUM eundem, quo de v. 3. itidem nominato Spiritu DEI loquutus erat, designat: In quo ipso versu pariter omnes tres Deitatis personas expresserat, Deum ejusque Spiritum, & Dominum Jesum. Quod autem ad illas διαιρέσεις, quum τῶν χαρισμάτων, τῶν διακονιῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐνεργημάτων distinctam mentionem faciens, easdem distinctis personis in S. Trinitate assignat, nulla operum fit seu parti- tio, seu divisio inter personas divinas. Ope- ra enim ad extra Trinitatis, qualia illa sunt, indivisa sunt: διαιρέσεις illæ dicuntur, tum quod dona ipsa à se invicem divisa & varia fuerint; tum quod dividebantur ratione subjectorum, dum aliis alia distribuebantur: Tum quod divisiones tantùm in ministris sint gratiarum, in Christo so- lo sit gratiæ plenitudo. Quo de Thomas: Chri- sto soli datus est Spiritus, non ad mensuram ut di- citur Job. III. sed quantum ad alios sunt divisiones gratiarum quia quidam abundant in una, quidam in alia. Sicut enim in corpore naturali caput ha- bet omnes sensus, non autem alia membra: Ita in sola Ecclesia Christus habet omnes gratias, quæ in aliis membris dividuntur.

Quomodo autem differant χαρίσματα, δια- κονίαι, & ἐνεργήματα, non eodem modo explica- tur. Nonnulli χαρίσματα genus, διακονίας & ἐνερ- γήματα species faciunt: Sed ut hæc tribus perso- nis distinctè, non seorsim tribuuntur, ita etiam triplicis ordinis sunt: Spiritui Sancto χαρίσματα dona cùm ministrantia, quæ vocant, tùm sancti- ficantia, secundum tertium symboli Apostolici articulum de sanctificatione, assignantur: Chri- sto Domino ceu Archi-Episcopo nostro διακονίαι vel ministeria tribuuntur: Deo Patri, à quo ori- ginaliter omnis efficacia est, ex quo omnia sunt, τὰ ἐνεργήματα vendicantur. Dona Spiritus S. non immediatè sed mediante ministerio conce- duntur, ideo subjicit iisdem Apostolus διακονίας. Cum autem per ministerium Spiritus Sanctus do- na distribuat, ἐνεργήματα seu effecta salutaria DEO Patri adseruntur, qui per dona Spiritus Sancti, & ministros verbi efficax est in Ecclesia.

Per charismata hic dona quidam, quæ vocan- tur ministrantia peculiariter intelligi, ἐξαρίθμησις plerorumque subjuncta docet. Non excludi ta- men sanctificantia dona è versu 3. satis liquet, ubi Spiritui Sancto autori tribuitur fides in Christum. Hæc autem χαρίσματα ita Spiritui Sancto assi- gnantur, ut non excludatur Dominus, (Christus Jesus) à quo & per quem omnia χαρίσματα red- undant: Quia de ejus plenitudine accipimus o- mnes gratiam pro gratia Joh. I. 16. in quo nobis χάρις gratia, & χαρίσματα gratiæ dona omnia obtingunt 1. Cor. I. 4. nec Deus Pater, ex quo quisque habet suum χάρισμα 1. Cor. VII. 7. Rom. XI. 28. 1. Cor. I. 4. 2. Tim. I. 6. Porrò διακονίαι sunt officia sacra in genere quæcunque, quæ verò minus rectè hic recensentur à Grotio. Varia sunt ministeria in Ecclesia: Sunt fideles, sunt Diaconi, sunt Presbyteri, sunt Principes Presbyterorum, sunt & horum Principes. Fidelium nomen non officii est, sed communis verè credentium appellatio. De Principibus Presbyterorum, per quos sine dubio Episcopos cum Papistis intelligit, nihil novit scri- ptura, quâ distincti illi censetur à Presbyteris, sive ordinis, sive autoritatis & jurisdictionis causa, de quo Blondellus & Salmasius fusè egerant. Neque de Principibus Principum Presbyterorum vel Episco- porum, sive Archi-Episcopi, sive etiam Cardinales, sive denique Pontifices intelligantur, quicquam S. S. novit. Hæc enim nomina & officia in scri- pturis nullum habent fundamentum, nullus de illis reperitur apex. Tribuuntur autem iterum διακονίαι Filio Dei, Domino, non divisim, vel ex- clusive: Nam & ad Spiritum Sanctum eadem re- feruntur 2. Cor. III. 5. & ad Deum Patrem 2. Cor. V. 18. c. VI. 4. 1. Theff. III. 2. sed per peculiarem relationem Ministrorum ad Dominum. Sunt enim ὑπηρέται τῶ Χριςῶ 1. Cor. IV. 1. διάκονοι τῶ Χριςῶ Col. I. 7. 1. Tim. IV. 6. qui est unus ille Dominus 1. Cor. IIX. 6. Eph. IV. 5. Denique ἐνεργήματα omnia sunt opera & effecta gratiæ, quæ ordinariè per ministeria sacra operatur in Ecclesia DEUS, ob quæ Ministris conceduntur Spiritus Sancti charismata. Neque hic cogitanda ulla divisio. Nam ita Patri tribuuntur, ut nec Spiritus Sanctus excludatur 1. Cor. XII. 10. 11. nec Filius. Pater enim meus, inquit Christus, Joh. V. 17. ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται usque nunc operatur, κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι & ego operor, & v. 19. Quæcunque Pater facit, illa & Filius similiter facit.

Ἑκάςῳ δὲ δίδοται ἡ φανέρωσις τῶ πνεύματος πρὸς τὸ συμ- φέρον) Φανερῶν est dare, ita, ut appareat נתון Jer. XXXIII. 6. Hinc φανέρωσις donum conspicuum. Data sunt, inquit, non ipsorum causa, sed Ecclesiæ.

## 12:8
V. 8. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom) Of speaking grave sentences, such as are in the books of Solomon. This gift, like others following, others acquired with much labor: Christians, God willing, by inspiration alone, ἀκοπεί [without labor]. Here is σοφία [wisdom], which in the books of Solomon is חכמה [wisdom]. See above 1:20.

And to another the word of knowledge) γνῶσις [knowledge] [דעת [knowledge] is γραμματεία [learning], knowledge of histories. See the cited place 1:20. In the books of Solomon it is often taken thus.

According to the same Spirit) κατὰ [according to] here has the same value as ἐν [in] in the following. Thus also the Greeks say: Αἱ κατὰ τὸ σῶμα ἀδοναὶ [the pleasures according to the body].

The Apostle deliberately interchanges those particles διὰ [through], κατὰ [according to], and ἐν [in], so that in those particles one might not seek any diversity and inequality of causation, or dependence and inferiority. Therefore he says not only that all those things are done through the Spirit and in the Spirit, but also that the Spirit himself works all those things as he wills, v. 11. Which is to be noted against the Pneumatomachi. Furthermore, φανέρωσις τῶ πνέυματος [manifestation of the Spirit] is understood concerning the manifestation of the Spirit regarding all things that appear in the Church, not only concerning that which is evident to the external senses. For there is also an interior φανέρωσις [manifestation] which does not strike the eyes or sense: but the word of wisdom seems more correctly to be distinguished from the word of knowledge, because the former concerns the wisdom of the mysteries of the faith, which are necessary for us to know for salvation, 1 Cor. 2:7. But the latter concerns the knowledge of other things which are contained in the scriptures, to which also the knowledge of histories pertains, how the Apostle distinguishes those in 1 Cor. 13:2, if he knows all mysteries and all γνῶσιν [knowledge]; or with the blessed Hunnius, Theophylact, and Chrysostom, it must be said that knowledge is understood, such as most of the faithful attain: but wisdom, which is for the more perfect, such as John the son of thunder had obtained, such as Paul had also attained. To the blessed Baldwin, the word of wisdom is the accurate knowledge of the articles of faith with the dexterity of explaining those things which otherwise, as mysteries of GOD, are more obscure to human reason: but the word of knowledge denotes speech of knowledge, ready counsels in perplexed and obscure cases, which pertain to practice in theological matters. To Estius, knowledge is the skill of discoursing about sacred matters from those things which are of human science or experience, which is done, in his opinion, when secular philosophy is applied to explain and illustrate the doctrine of faith: Who makes the word of knowledge, however, the milk of the unrefined, but the word of wisdom the solid food of the more perfect.

Latin:

V. 8. Ὦ μὲν γὰρ διὰ τῶ πνέυματος δίδοται λόγος σοφίας) Dicendi graves sententias, quales sunt in Salomonis libris. Hoc donum, ut alia fequentia, alii acquirebant multo la- bore: Christiani, DEO volente, solo afflatu, ἀκοπεί. Est hic σοφία, quod in libris Salomonis חכמה. Vide su- pra I. 20.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ λόγος γνώσεως) γνῶσις [דעת est γραμματεία cognitio historiarum. Vide dictum locum I. 20. In libris Salomonis sæpe sic sumitur.

Κατὰ τὸ ἀυτὸ πνέυμα) Idem hic valet κατὰ, quod ἐν in sequentibus. Sic & Græci dicunt: Αἱ κατὰ τὸ σῶμα ἀδοναὶ.

De industria Apostolus particulas illas διὰ, κατὰ & ἐν permutat, ne in particulis illis quæratur ali- qua causandi diversitas & inæqualitas, aut depen- dentia, & inferioritas. Ideo non tantum per Spi- ritum & in Spiritum omnia illa fieri dicit, sed et- iam omnia illa ipsum Spiritum operari prout vult v. 11. Quod contra Pneumatamachos observan- dum. Porro Φανέρωσις τῶ πνέυματος de manife- statione Spiritus, quoad omnia, quæ in Ecclesia apparent, accipitur, non tantùm de ea, quæ ex- ternis sensibus patet. Nam & interior est φανέρω- σις quæ non in oculos incurrit vel sensum: λόγος verò σοφίας rectius à λόγῳ γνώσεως videtur dis- cerni, quod ille sapientiam mysteriorum fidei, quæ ad salutem cognitu necessaria nobis sunt, con- cernat 1. Cor. II, 7. Hic verò notitiam rerum alia- rum, quæ in scripturis habentur, ad quem etiam historiarum cognitio pertinet, quomodo distin- guit illa Apostolus 1. Cor. XIII, 2. si noverit omnia mysteria, & omnem γνῶσιν; aut cum B. Hunnio, Theophylacto & Chrysostomo dicendum, fcientiam intelligi, qualem plerique fidelium adipiscuntur: Sa- pientiam vero, quæ perfectiorum est, qualem vide- licet Johannes tonitrui filius erat fortitus, qua- lem & Paulus erat consequutus. B. Balduino λό- γος σοφίας est accurata notitia articulorum fidei cum dexteritate explicandi ea, quæ aliàs, ut my- steria DEI, rationi humanæ obscuriora sunt: λό- γος γνώσεως verò sermo scientia notat expedita consilia in causis perplexis & obscuris, quæ per- tineant ad praxin in rebus Theologicis. Estio γνῶσις est notitia differendi de rebus sacris, ex iis, quæ sunt humanæ scientiæ, vel experientiæ, quod fit ipsius sententiâ, cum Philosophia fæcula- ris adhibetur ad explicandam & illustrandam fidei doctrinam: Qui sermonem scientiæ tamen lac rudium, sapientiæ verò cibum solidum perfectio- rum facit.

## 12:9
V. 9. And to another faith in the same Spirit) Faith is understood here not that which is required in all Christians, but that by which one believes that God wills to do something miraculous through himself, as below 12:2, Matt. 17:20. To this pertains the power of casting out demons. God was accustomed to give this reward to mature and well-preserved faith, Mark 16:17.

And to another gifts of healings in the same Spirit) This gift of healing diseases was given especially to Presbyters governing the Church. See what we have said on Mark 16:18.

Latin:

V. 9. Ἑτέρῳ δὲ πίσις ἐν τῷ ἀυτῷ πνέυματι) Fides hic in- telligitur non ea, quæ in omnibus Christianis requiritur, sed ea, per quam quis credit, per se Deum aliquid miri velle facere, ut infra XII. 2. Matth. XVII. 20. Huc perti- net potestas dæmones ejiciendi. Solebat Deus hoc præ- mium dare adultæ & bene conservatæ fidei Marci XVI. 17.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων ἐν τῷ ἀυτῷ πνέυματι) Hoc donum sanandi morbos Presbyteris Ecclesiam guber- nantibus maximè dabatur. Vide quæ diximus ad Marci XVI. 18.

## 12:10
V. 10. And to another workings of powers) The power of punishing the wicked, such as was exercised against Ananias and Sapphira, against Bar-Jesus, against Hymenaeus and Philetus. Δύναμις [power] is the general name of these gifts, as appears in Matt. 11:21, 23, and elsewhere. But because others have a special name, therefore the common name adhered to this gift, above 4:20, 5:4.

Most Greeks, Cajetan, and Estius explain the word πίςεως [faith] with Theophylact as the faith of miracles. Which opinion is to be declared thus: that for this reason, in this place, special mention is made of the gift of healings, and ἐνεργημάτων [workings] or operations and effects, and δυνάμεων [powers] of faculties and virtues, because to some indeed the gift of performing miracles was granted in the primitive Church, but to others the gift of healings was proper, and finally to some the ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων [workings of powers] were proper, where Grotius not badly refers the power of punishing to the sources. It is also not inconveniently included the power of the ἐνεργυμένης [being worked] to free the possessed from a demon. However, it pleases me here, with B. Hunnius, to understand by faith that heroic impulse by which men, incited not by rash daring or private whim, but by the secret agitation of the divine Spirit, undertake admirable things, and bring them to the desired ends with happy and ready success, beyond the expectation of all men, and in doubtful matters firmly adhere to GOD: Where others, who do not have this faith, tremble from anxiety and do not dare to promise or hope for the desired success for themselves. But Whittaker wrongly explains it as justifying faith, chapter 3 on Holy Scripture, p. 554, against Calvin, Martyr, Pelican, Pareus, Marlorat, and the Belgian Interpreters.

To faith is subjoined the gift of miraculous healing, when they cured the sick either by word alone, or by anointing with oil, or by the laying on of hands and other rites, as also the efficacy of powers exerting themselves with miracles, such as were: to be able to recall the dead to life, to illuminate the blind, to restore gait to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, to cast demons out of possessed bodies, which are deservedly designated by the name of δυνάμεων [powers] κατ' ἐξοχὴν [pre-eminently]; which are more notable than the healing of the sick, even if miraculous. For the curing of the infirm is done also by human art, although not equally quickly and easily. Estius observes that this explanation is that of most Latins, and he embraces it. This diversity of gifts, however, was not so much in the Apostles, to whom all things seem to have been granted, as teachers of the whole world, illuminating the world with various miracles; as it was conspicuous in other teachers of the word in the primitive Church, some of whom were distinguished by these gifts, others by those.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ προφητεία [And to another prophecy]) Prediction of future events, such as Agabus had, Acts 11:28, 12:11, and many others in those times. A register of these, once well-examined, was made: and theirs was the first dignity after the Apostles. Below 12:28, Eph. 3:5 and 4:11.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ διακρίσεις πνευμάτων [And to another discerning of spirits]) Discernment, who were true Prophets, who false, below 14:29. But that was done in this way. If they did not lead men away from Christ, what they had said was noted, the outcome was awaited: If it agreed with the words, it was ascribed to the order of Prophets. In like manner, judgment was made concerning miracles. For those were held as divine which professed Jesus as their author. This gift seems to have been given especially to the presidents of the Presbyters, who gathered together to recognize that matter. To this pertains that which is below 14:34, ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων [he is convicted by all, he is judged by all]. Tertullian, in his book on the soul, when he had dealt with visions: They are most diligently sorted, so that they may also be tested. You have an example of such a meeting, as I said, for examining prophecies in the cited place of Eusebius, v. 16, 17, where Apollinaris uses the words ἐξετασάντων [examining] and ἀποδοκιμασάντων [rejecting], as also the word ἐξελέγχειν [to convict]. These were parts of the Sanhedrin in the Jewish Republic.

By some, prophecy is explained as the prediction of future events; by others, as the interpretation of scripture. Blessed Balduinus agrees with the former sense, Blessed Hunnius with the latter. It is permitted, however, perhaps to join both, because Prophecy is understood as being from the revelation of GOD and immediate concerning future and unknown things, and mediate, made through the holy Scriptures, because it is a singular gift of GOD to open the mind of God, whether by holy Scripture, for the understanding of which there is need of the hermeneutical gift of the Holy Spirit, which is not granted to all. But because under λόγῳ σοφίας, καὶ γνώσεως is also included the gift of explaining from the scriptures the mysteries of the faith, and other things handed down in the sacred writings, the gift of Prophecy here seems rather to be taken concerning the faculty of predicting the future: whence the name of Prophet is applied to those who predicted the future by divine inspiration, v. 28, 29, when diverse offices are enumerated, which illustrates this gift of προφητείας.

The discernment of spirits does not only regard Prophets predicting the future, but also those instructed by the preceding gifts of wisdom, knowledge, faith, grace, healings, and the working of mighty works: of all of whom the Spirits are to be tested and discerned, both from the Scriptures and from their fruits. Since not all who performed miracles in the name of Jesus are to be counted among the true teachers and ministers of Christ. Conf. 1 Cor. XIV. 29, 1 Thess. V. 19, 20, 21, 1 John IV. 1, Matt. VII. 16, 22, 23.
