Those things which Grotius brings forward concerning the register of Prophets, and concerning the Presidents of the Presbyters, who were accustomed to meet for the discernment of Spirits, are conjectures rather than finding a foundation in the Acts of the Apostles or the history of the earlier centuries. For neither were the Presidents of the Presbyters instructed with a faculty for διακρίσεις πνευμάτων distinguished above others, nor was this gift restricted to certain orders. But it seems that here too Grotius wished to gratify his Papist Bishops, who boast themselves to be Presidents and Superiors by divine authority in respect to the jurisdiction of Presbyters. In the Apostolic Council certainly, which was convened at Jerusalem for the discernment of spirits, more specifically of the false Apostles and their dogmas, not only the Apostles and Bishops, but also the Presbyters are read to have come together, Acts XV. 6. Concerning which we spoke in Tom. I. in August. Confess. in the treatise on Councils.

To another, kinds of tongues) Various kinds of languages for the men with whom there was business. This was a gift given especially to the Apostles and Evangelists.

To another, the interpretation of tongues) Because it could happen that not all to whom the Apostles or Evangelists were speaking were of the same language, therefore there were those in the Church who, by a gift given to them divinely, would interpret the same to others, for which matter there was need of a great memory. See below XIV. 5.

The interpretation of languages is more correctly translated with the Syrian (as the Latin text is also cited by Tertullian lib. V. contr. Marc. c. 8, Augustine lib. XIV. contra Faust. cap. 8, and is read in the Ambrosian commentary) than the interpretation of speeches, as the vulgate has it; the gifts of speaking in tongues and of interpreting tongues were different. For there were those who spoke in tongues, yet could not conveniently interpret those things which they were saying. And conversely there were those who had the gift of interpreting those things which others brought forth in a foreign language, and they were not so much instructed for teaching as for interpreting those things which were taught by others. To which gift of interpretation the office of those who are called Professors of languages succeeded in later centuries.

Latin:

V. 10. Ἄλλῳ δὲ ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων) Potestas punien- di fontes, qualis exercita in Ananiam & Sapphiram, in Bar- jesum, in Hymenæum & Philetem. Δύναμις nomen est generale istorum donorum, ut apparet Matth. XI. 21. 23. & alibi. Sed quia alia speciale nomen habent, ideo no- men commune huic dono adhæsit, supra IV. 20. V. 4.

Græci plerique, Cajetanus, Estius explicant cum Theophylacto de fide miraculorum vocem πίςεως. Quæ sententia ita declaranda, quod ideo h. 1. spe- cialis mentio doni fanationum, & ἐνεργημάτων vel operationum & effectuum, δυνάμεων faculta- tum ac virtutum fiat, quod aliis quidem alia mi- racula faciendi donum in primitiva Ecclesia con- cessum sit, aliis verò proprium fuerit donum sa- nationum, nonnullis denique propria fuerint ἐνερ- γήματα δυνάμεων, ubi potestatem puniendi fontes non male refert Grotius. Comprehenditur, et- iam non incommode potestas ἐνεργυμένης obses- sos liberandi à dæmone. Placet autem per fidem hic cum B. Hunnio intelligere heroicum illum im- petum, quo incitati homines non ausu temerario, vel privato libitu, sed divini Spiritus arcanâ agi- tatione admiranda suscipiunt, eaque felici, & ex- pedito successu ad optatos fines, supra omnium hominum expectationem perducunt, inque rebus dubiis DEO firmiter adhærent: Ubi alii, qui hanc fidem non habent, præ angustia & trepidant, & exoptatum successum sibi polliceri, aut sperare non audent. Perperam autem de fide justificante explicat Wittakerus cap. 3. de Scriptura S. p. 554. contra Calvin. Martyr. Pelican. Pareum, Marlo- ratum, Belgicos Interpretes.

Fidei subjungitur fanationis miraculosæ donum, cum vel solo verbo, vel unctione olei, vel manu- um impositione aliisque ritibus ægrotos cura- runt, ut & efficacia potentiarum cum miraculis sese exeremtium, ut erant: posse mortuos ad vitam revocare, cæcos illuminare, claudis gressum, sur- dis auditum, mutis loquelam restituere, dæmo- nes è corporibus obsessis ejicere, quæ δυνάμεων nomine κατ' ἐξοχὴν meritò designantur; Quæ in- signiora sunt ægrotorum sanatione etsi miracu- losâ. Nam infirmorum curatio fit etiam arte hu- mana, licet non æque cito ac facile. Quam ex- plicationem Latinorum plerorumque esse obser- vat, & amplectitur Estius. Hæc autem donorum diversitas, non tam in Apostolis, quibus omnia concessa videntur, ceu mundi totius doctoribus, variis miraculis orbem illustrantibus; quàm aliis in primitiva Ecclesia conspicua fuit verbi docto- ribus, quorum alii his, alii aliis donis claruere.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ προφητεία) Prædictio futurorum, qualem ha- buit Agabus Actor. XI. 28. XII. 11. & multi alii illis tem- poribus. Horum autem bene exploratorum fiebat matri- cula: & illorum erat post Apostolos prima dignitas. In- fra XII. 28. Eph. III. 5. & IV. 11.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ διακρίσεις πνευμάτων) Dijudicatio, qui Prophe- tæ veri effent, qui falsi infra XIV. 29. Id autem fiebat hoc modo. Si à Christo homines non abduceret, annotaban- tur quæ dixerat, expectabatur eventus: Is si dictis con- grueret, ascribebatur ordini Prophetarum. Pari modo de miraculis judicabatur. Nam pro divinis habebantur, quæ Jesum profitebantur autorem. Hoc donum videtur ma- xime datum præsidibus Presbyterorum, qui plures ad eam rem cognoscendam coibant. Huc illud pertinet infra XIV. 34. ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων. Ter- tullianus libro de anima, cum de visionibus egisset: Dili- gentissime digeruntur, ut etiam probentur. Exemplum talis conventus, qualem dixi ad examinandas prophetias ha- bes dicto Eusebii loco v. 16. 17. ubi voces ἐξετασάντων & ἀποδοκιμασάντων usurpat Apollinaris, ut & vocem ἐξελέγ χειν. Ex partes in Judaica Republica fuerant Synedrii.

Prophetiâ à quibusdam de futurorum prædi- ctione, ab aliis de fcriptura interpretatione expli- catur. Priori sensui B. Balduinus, posteriori B. Hunnius accedit. Licet autem fortassis utrum- que conjungere, quod Prophetia e revelatione DEI & immediata de rebus futuris atque incogni- tis, & mediata per Scripturas sacras facta intelli- gatur, quia donum DEI singulare est, mentem Dei aperire, sive ex singulari inspiratione divina, sive per Scriptura sacra instructionem, ad cujus intel- ligentiam opus est dono hermeneutico Spiritus Sancti, quod non concessum est omnibus. Sed quia sub λόγῳ σοφίας, καὶ γνώσεως etiam compre- henditur donum explicandi e scripturis mysteria fidei, aliaque in sacris literis tradita, Prophetia do- num videtur hic potius de facultate futura prædi- cendi accipiendum: unde Prophetæ nomen de iis, qui ex inspiratione divina futura prædicebant v. 28. 29. adhibitum, cum diversa munia recensen- tur, quod hoc προφητείας donum illustrat.

Discretio spirituum non tantum respicit Pro- phetas futura prædicentes, sed etiam præcedenti- bus donis sapientiæ, scientiæ, fidei, gratiæ, sani- tatum & operationis virtutum instructos: Quo- rum omnium Spiritus probandi, & discernendi sunt tum e Scripturis, tum e fructibus ipsorum. Quum nec omnes, qui miracula patrarunt, in no- mine Jesu, veris doctoribus & ministris Christi accensendi sint. Conf. 1. Cor. XIV. 29. 1. Thess. V. 19. 20. 21. 1. Joh. IV. 1. Matth. VII. 16. 22. 23. Illa quæ affert Grotius de matricula Prophetarum, de- que Præsidibus Presbyterorum, ad discretionem Spi- rituum coire solitis, conjecturæ potius sunt, quam fundamentum in Actis Apostolicis aut historia priorum seculorum inveniunt. Neque enim in- signi præ aliis ad διακρίσεις πνευμάτων facultate instructi fuere Præsides Presbyterorum, aut ad- strictum hoc donum erat ad certos ordines. Sed videtur & hic gratificari voluisse Grotius Ponti- ficiis suis Episcopis, qui se Præsides & Superiores ju- risdictione, autoritate divina jactitant Presbytero- rum respectu. In Concilio certe Apostolico, quod Hierosolymis ad discretionem spirituum falsorum magis Apostolorum eorumque dogmatum coa- ctum fuit, non solum Apostoli & Episcopi, sed etiam Presbyteri convenisse leguntur Act. XV. 6. Quo de Tom. I. in August. Confess. tract. de Con- ciliis diximus.

Ἑτέρῳ δὲ γένη γλωσσῶν) Varia linguarum genera pro hominibus, quibuscum res erat. Hoc erat donum Apo- stolis maxime & Evangelistis datum.

Ἄλλῳ δὲ ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν) Quia fieri poterat, ut non omnes, quibus Apostoli aut Evangelistæ loquebantur, es- sent ejusdem linguæ, ideo erant in Ecclesia, qui dono sibi divinitus dato eadem aliis interpretarentur, quam ad rem magna opus erat memoria. Vide infra XIV. 5.

Rectius interpretatio linguarum vertitur cum Syro (ut etiam citatur textus Latinus a Tertullia- no lib. V. contr. Marc. c. 8. Augustino lib. XIV. contra Faust. cap. 8. & legitur in Ambrosiano commentario) quam interpretatio sermonum, uti vulgata habet, diversa erant dona linguis loquendi, & linguas interpretandi. Fuere enim, qui linguis loquebantur, nec tamen ea, quæ dicerent, inter- pretari commode poterant. Et vicissim fuerunt, qui donum habebant interpretandi ea, quæ alii lingua peregrina proferebant, nec tam ad docen- dum instructi erant, quam ad interpretandum ea, quæ ab aliis docebantur. Cui interpretationis dono posterioribus seculis officium eorum, qui Professores linguarum vocantur, successit.

## 12:11
V. 11. But all these things works the one and the same Spirit) of GOD, not of the Devil. For he treats here of those who profess Christ. See above IV.

Dividing to each one individually as he wills) By the most free will of GOD. For he is bound to give such things to no one. Nor did he promise it to anyone individually. ἰδίᾳ here is worth what בפרט is to the Rabbis.

Those words 'as he wills' are referred to the Holy Spirit, not to God the Father, and by this it is taught that the Holy Spirit is truly a person, inasmuch as a will is attributed to him, and the granting of gifts, and the effecting of works in the Church. For it is of a person to have a will, and it is asserted by a common canon that the actions are of the supposita. See T. III. Syst. Theol. p. And not only the personality of the Holy Spirit against the Sabellians, but also his true Deity against the Macedonians is firmly constructed from this passage: Because he who works all the χαρίσματα in the Church, and distributes the same to individuals as he wills, is the true GOD. For this does not befit a creature, but the one true GOD, v. 6.

PART II. DIDACTIC-PARAENETIC. Concerning the unity of the mystical body, and the necessity of concord in the same.

Latin:

V. 11. Πάντα δὲ ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα) DEI, non Diaboli. Agit enim hic de Christum profiten- tibus. Vide supra IV.

Διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ καθὼς βόλεται) Liberrimo DEI arbitratu. Nemini enim dare talia tenetur. Nec cuiquam fingulatim id promisit. ἰδίᾳ hic valet, quod Rabbinis בפרט.

Illa καθὼς βύλεται ad Spiritum Sanctum refe- runtur, non ad Deum Patrem, eoque docetur Spi- ritum Sanctum vere personam esse, utpote, cui vo- luntas tribuitur, & donorum concessio, atque ope- rum effectio in Ecclesia. Nam personæ est volun- tas, & suppositorum actiones esse vulgato cano- ne asseritur. Vide T. III. Syst. Theol. p. Nec tan- tum personalitas Spiritus Sancti contra Sabellia- nos, sed etiam vera ejus Deitas contra Macedonia- nos ex hoc loco firmiter adstruitur: Quia is, qui operatur χαρίσματα omnia in Ecclesia, eadem- que singulis distribuit, prout vult, verus DEUS est. Non enim hoc creaturæ convenit, sed uni vero DEO, v. 6.

PARS II. DIDACTICO-PARÆNETICA. De unitate corporis mystici, & concordia in eo- dem necessitate.

## 12:12
V. 12. For just as the body is one) The physical body, for example, of a man.

And has many members) Each one destined for its own uses. See Galen on the use of parts. See also Romans XII. 14 and above VI. 12.

Πάντα δὲ τὰ μέλη τῦ σώματος τῦ ἑνὸς πολλὰ ὄντα ἕν ἐσι σῶμα) Subtly stated: For all parts do not differ from their whole in reality, but in reason.

Οὕτω καὶ ὁ χρισός) Namely with his Church, which itself also comes under the name of Christ. Rom. IX. 13. The kingdom is in the King and the subjects.

By this simile the Apostle wishes to teach that those who have received more spiritual gifts ought not to grow proud, or hold others in contempt: Nor should those who have less be saddened, and envy others: But that all ought to contribute their gifts to the common utility of the whole body. Then indeed it would be incongruous if each one of the faithful had all the gifts, just as it would be absurd if, in a natural body, all functions were attributed to the same members. The Gloss on this passage says Christ is called head and body on account of the ineffable unity of the head and members. Augustine, book on the unity of the Church, chapter IV: The whole Christ is head and body: The head is the only-begotten Son of GOD and his body is the Church, Bridegroom and Bride, two in one flesh. Now therefore it is not only a question of the variety of gifts or functions regarding the Ministers of the Church: But regarding all the faithful, because all pertain to the mystical body of Christ.

Latin:

V. 12. Καθάπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἕν ἐσι) Corpus φυσικὸν, puta hominis.

Καὶ μέλη ἔχει πολλά) Singula suis usibus destinata. Vi- de Galenum de usu partium. Vide & Roman. XII. 14. & supra VI. 12.

Πάντα δὲ τὰ μέλη τῦ σώματος τῦ ἑνὸς πολλὰ ὄντα ἕν ἐσι σῶμα) Subtiliter dictum: Nam cunctæ partes à suo toto non re differunt, sed ratione.

Οὕτω καὶ ὁ χρισός) Nempe cum sua Ecclesia, quæ & ipsa venit sub Christi nomine. Rom. IX. 13. Regnum est in Rege & subditis.

Hac similitudine id docere vult Apostolus, nec eos, qui plus acceperunt donorum spiritualium, infolescere debere, aliosve despicatui habere: Nec eos, qui minus habent, contristari, & aliis invide- re: Sed omnes sua dona conferre debere ad com- munem totius corporis utilitatem. Tum vero in- congruum id fore, si unusquisque fidelium omnia haberet dona, sicut absurdum foret, in corpore naturali omnia officia iisdem membris attributa esse. Glossa in h. l. caput & corpus dicitur Chri- stus propter ineffabilem unitatem capitis & mem- brorum. Augustinus lib. de unitate Ecclesiæ cap. IV. Totus Christus caput & corpus est: Caput uni- genitus DEI Filius & corpus ejus Ecclesia, Sponsus & Sponsa, duo in carne una. Jam ergò non tan- tum de donorum vel functionum quoad Mini- stros Ecclesiæ varietate agitur: Sed quoad fideles universos, quia omnes pertinent ad corpus Chri- sti mysticum.

## 12:13
V. 13. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ πνέυματι ἡμεῖς πάντες εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν.) In one Spirit, that is, in the hope of the same Spirit, or of spiritual gifts, which all come from the same origin, as was said above 4. Baptism is the sealing of faith. But God gives those gifts to believers, and to those professing it, Mark XVI. 16. 17. Εἰς ἓν σῶμα, so that we might all together become one body.

Εἴτε Ἰυδαῖοι, εἴτε ἕλληνες, εἴτε δῦλοι, εἴτε ἐλεύθεροι) In the eyes of the world these distinctions are worth something, in the eyes of Christ they are worth nothing. See above VII. 12, and following. Gal. III. 28.

Καὶ πάντες εἰς ἓν πνῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν) We also drink the cup of the Lord in this hope. Baptism washes the exterior of the body: The cup irrigates the interior: Thus the Spirit of GOD works both inside and outside. It is for honey and oil. But in the Manuscript it is for these words: Καὶ πάντες ἓν σῶμα ἐσμέν.

Chrysostom on this passage is excellent: This is what he says: That which brought it about that we were one body, and regenerated us, is one Spirit. For one was not baptized in one Spirit, and another in another. Moreover, not only is he one who baptized us, but also that into which he baptized is one, that is, that for the sake of which he baptized is one. For we were not baptized so that diverse bodies might be made, but so that we might all preserve the unity of the body among ourselves. That is, so that we might all become one body, we were baptized. Wherefore both he who built is one, and that to which it is built is one. And he did not say, that we may become one body, but that we may all be one body. For he always takes pains to use expressions which have greater emphasis. Therefore the discourse is not about the unity of hope, but about the cause of the unity of the mystical body of Christ, and how the faithful have become one body, namely through the Holy Spirit as the principal cause and through baptism as the medium divinely ordained, through which we are inserted into Christ and become members of that mystical body, whose head is Christ. And likewise how we are sustained in that one body, namely through the sacrament of the Eucharist: In which we are all made to drink into one Spirit, not into one hope: But that we are made to drink and are watered by the blood of Christ, which is offered to us in the Eucharistic cup, for the drawing of the same Spirit that enlivens, sanctifies, and sustains us. Some explain the drinking as the draught or drinking of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which in Scripture are compared to rivers and waters, John VII. 38, and Estius observes that this is the commentary of many. But he acknowledges a more genuine explanation concerning the draught of the blood of Christ, which he says is that of Thomas, Lyranus, and Cajetan. He could have added Salmeron and Justinianus, to whom Cornelius à Lapide also agrees. Cf. 1 Cor. X. 2, 3; 1 John V. 6. Nor indeed does the Apostle say, we have been made to drink in one Spirit; but into one Spirit. And therefore he does not mean that we are made to drink by the Spirit, or by the gifts of the Spirit, nor does he treat of the cause, whether material or efficient, of the drinking, but of the end; as he had said we are baptized into one body: so he now affirms that we are made to drink into one spirit. Therefore two sacraments of the New Testament are asserted here, not more; and it is taught concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist: That all who have been baptized into one body, without distinction of nations and states, are to be admitted to the drink of the blood of Christ, and no one is to be excluded, so that, namely, all may coalesce more and more and be strengthened by spiritual virtue. We are all, he says, made to drink into one Spirit. Since indeed through the sacrament of the Supper, the members of Christ, grafted in through baptism, ought to be enlivened, so that they may remain in him spiritually and enjoy his virtue and efficacy. For the Spirit of Christ wishes to penetrate, strengthen, and confirm all the members who participate in this drink, so that they may be rendered more and more fit for their various functions. Baptism and the Supper are that sacred glue through which we coalesce into one body of Christ and are rendered participants of his holy vigor and spiritual efficacy.

But that Grotius says baptism washes the exterior of the body, and the cup washes the interior, is not entirely true. For St. Peter denies, 1 Epist. III. 21, that baptism is the putting away of the filth of the flesh, and it is foreign to this place. Because it is not a question here of the external washing or internal irrigation of our body, but of the cause and end of baptism with respect to the mystical body of Christ, into which we are implanted through baptism, Rom. VI. 5, and in which we are made to drink through the blood of Christ into a more abundant perception of the virtue of the Spirit of Christ. Where we note besides that this εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα can be accepted concerning the unity of the Spirit either taken hypostatically, that we are made to drink in the Lord's Supper into a more abundant fruition of one Spirit, from whom all gifts are both sanctifying and ministering, or as the Spirit is understood energetically, or metonymically, so that we may coalesce more and more into one spirit through the holy Supper, just as we have coalesced through baptism into one body; and that it is not the Holy Spirit himself, but our spirit, which is from him, that is designated.

For whatever is born of the Spirit is spirit, John III. 6. But because τὸ ἓν πνεῦμα always designates the Holy Spirit himself in this chapter, and we are said to be baptized into one mystical body in that one Spirit, without doubt we are understood here also to be made to drink into the same Spirit, so that we may draw the Holy Spirit himself and be strengthened by his efficacy in the holy Eucharist. Theophylact with Chrysostom prefers to refer this latter also to baptism, by which we are made to drink, no otherwise than trees are accustomed to be irrigated by some fountain. But one must not depart from the proper meaning of the word ἐποτίσθημεν. Nor do those Greek Fathers disapprove of the explanation concerning the holy supper. Chrysostom provides this paraphrase: We have come to the same imitation of mysteries, we enjoy the same table. And why did he not say, we are nourished by the same body, and drink the same blood? Because when he said Spirit, he signified both flesh and blood. For through both we are made to drink in one Spirit.

Schlichtingius the Socinian in the former member concerning baptism understands the words ἐν ἑνὶ πνέυματι materially, not of the efficient cause, so that he destroys the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, as if it were said: God has poured such a quantity of the Holy Spirit upon us through Christ, that we have been baptized and immersed in him as in a river: But thus the gifts of the Holy Spirit are confounded with the author of the gifts: It is not taught that he poured out his gifts in baptism, but that we have been received into the mystical body of Christ through baptism, and that in one Spirit: by the virtue of that one Spirit, of which it is expressly treated there. Furthermore, in the latter member Schlichtingius perverts the words εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα thus: In one Spirit, εἰς for ἐν is used, and it is redundant: Finally, he repeats those from the common into one body: But he wishes to extort this sense: Not only have we all been baptized in one Spirit, and thus most abundantly poured out with him, and immersed in him, but we have all been made to drink of him. This heavenly water has passed thoroughly into our souls, it has not stuck only to the exterior bodies, by which our souls have been made to drink and are filled, so that this water has become in our souls a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. John IV. 14. But the Apostle deliberately employed the particle εἰς, and just as we were baptized εἰς ἓν σῶμα according to the Apostle: so we were made to drink εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα, so that that εἰς ἓν σῶμα is not to be repeated, but that opposition or distinction of the one mystical body, into which we are received through baptism, and of the one Spirit, into which we are made to drink not through baptism, but through the Eucharistic cup, remains intact, as the Apostle teaches. Which sense, although even among the Papists Cardinal Bellarmine wished to pervert in favor of the Papal ποτηριοκλεψία (cup-theft), contending in book IV de Euchar. c. 17 that the discourse here is not about the drinking of the blood of the Lord in the Holy Supper, but about the drinking of the Spirit in the baptism of Christ. But in vain. For besides the fact that parallel passages, above chapter X. 2. 3. and 1 John V. 6. and the reason concerning the communion of one drink compared among themselves teach that both sacraments are joined here, they acknowledged it after Augustine, book 1 contra Faust. chapter 8. Thomas Aquinas, Erasmus, Faber Stapulensis, Cajetan, Salmero, Estius, Justinianus, Cornelius à Lapide, and other Papists, compelled by the force of truth, with whom let the patrons of Bellarmine settle the matter.

Latin:

V. 13. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ πνέυματι ἡμεῖς πάντες εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν.) In uno Spiritu, id est, in spem Spiritus ejus- dem, sive spiritualium donorum, quæ ab eadem omnia origine veniunt, ut dictum est supra 4. Baptismus fidei est consignatio. Deus autem dat ista dona credentibus, & id profitentibus, Marci XVI. 16. 17. Εἰς ἓν σῶμα, ut omnes simul unum fieremus corpus.

Εἴτε Ἰυδαῖοι, εἴτε ἕλληνες, εἴτε δῦλοι, εἴτε ἐλεύθεροι) Apud mundum aliquid, apud Christum nihil valent hæc discri- mina. Vide supra VII. 12, & feqq. Gal. III. 28.

Καὶ πάντες εἰς ἓν πνῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν) Calicem quoque Domini in hanc spem bibimus. Baptismus exteriora cor- poris lavat: Calix irrigat interiora: Sic Spiritus DEI & intus & extra operatur. Est pro melle & oleo. Sed in Manuscripto est pro his verbis: Καὶ πάντες ἓν σῶμα ἐσμέν.

Egregie de hoc loco Chrysostomus: Hoc est quod dicit: Quod effecit, ut essemus unum corpus, & nos regeneravit, unus est Spiritus. Non enim alius quidem in altero, alius vero in altero bapti- zatus fuit Spiritu. Non solum autem unus est, qui nos baptizavit, sed & unum est, in quod baptiza- vit, hoc est propter quod baptizavit, unum est. Non enim ut diversa fiant corpora, sed ut omnes corporis unitatem inter nos conservemus baptizati sumus. Hoc est, ut omnes unum corpus fimus, ba- ptizati sumus. Quamobrem & qui construxit unus, & ad quod constructum est, unum est. Et non di- xit, ut fiamus unius corpus, sed ut omnes simus unum corpus. Semper enim dat operam, ut ponat dictiones, quæ majorem habent emphasin. Non ergo de spei unitate, sed de causâ unitatis corporis Chri- sti mystici sermo est, & quomodo fideles unum facti sunt corpus, videlicet per Spiritum Sanctum, tanquam causam Principalem & per baptismum, tanquam medium divinitus ordinatum, per quod inserimur Christo, & membra evadimus corpo- ris illius mystici, cujus caput est Christus. Quo- modo item in uno illo corpore sustentemur per sacramentum scilicet Eucharistiæ: In quo omnes in unum Spiritum potamur, non in spem unam: Sed ut sanguine Christi, qui præbetur nobis in calice Eucharistico, ad hauriendum eundem Spi- ritum nos vegetantem, sanctificantem, & susten- tantem potemur & rigemur. Potationem nonnulli explicant de haustu seu potatione donorum Spiri- tus Sancti, quæ in scriptura fluminibus & aquis comparantur Joh. VII. 38. eumque multorum esse commentarium, observat Estius. Sed magis ger- manam agnoscit explicationem de haustu sangui- nis Christi, quam Thomæ, Lyrani, & Cajetani esse ait. Addere poterat Salmeronem, & Justinianum, quibus etiam accedit Cornelius à Lapide. Conf. 1. Cor. X. 2. 3. 1. Joh. V. 6. Nec verò dicit Aposto- lus, in uno Spiritu potati sumus; sed in unum Spi- ritum. Ideoque non spiritu, seu donis Spiritus nos potari vult, nec de causâ, seu materiali, seu Efficiente potationis, sed de fine agit; Uti in unum corpus nos baptizari dixerat: Ita in unum spiritum nos potari jam affirmat. Duo ergò hic sacramen- ta Novi Testamenti adseruntur, non plura; Et de sacramento Eucharistiæ docetur: Quod omnes, qui baptizati in unum corpus sunt, sine discrimi- ne nationum, & statuum ad potum sanguinis Christi admittendi sint, nemò verò excludendus, ut sc. omnes magis magisque coalescant, & robo- rentur virtute spirituali. Omnes, inquit, in unum Spiritum potati sumus. Siquidem per sacramen- tum cœnæ membra Christi, per baptismum insi- ta vegetari debeant, ut in illo maneant spirituali- ter, ejusque virtute & efficacia perfruantur. Spi- ritus enim Christi omnia membra, quæ de ista potione participant, vult penetrare, roborare, confirmare, ut ad quasvis functiones suas red- dantur magis magisque idonea. Baptismus & Cœ- na sunt sacrum illud gluten, per quod in unum corpus Christi coalescimus, ejusque sancti vigo- ris & spiritualis efficaciæ participes reddimur.

Quod verò Grotius baptismum exteriora cor- poris lavare, calicem lavare interiora ait, neque omninò verum est. Negat enim sanctus Petrus 1. Epist. III. 21. Baptismum esse σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσιν ῥύ- που, & alienum hoc loco. Quia non de corporis nostri sive externa ablutione, sive interna irriga- tione, sed de causâ & fine baptismi, respectu cor- poris Christi mystici hic agitur, in quod implanta- mur per baptismum Rom. VI. 5. & in quo per san- guinem Christi potamur in virtutis Spiritus Chri- sti uberiorem perceptionem. Ubi id præterea no- tamus, illud εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα accipi posse de unitate Spiritus vel ὑποστατικῶς accepti, quod in unius Spiritus, à quo dona omnia sunt cùm sanctifican- tia, tùm ministrantia, uberiorem perfruitionem in Cœna Domini potemur, vel prout Spiritus in- telligitur ἐνεργητικῶς, aut Metonymicè, ut nos ma- gis magisque coalescamus in unum Spiritum, per sanctam Cœnam, quemadmodum per baptismum in unum corpus coaluimus; Nec ipse Spiritus S. sed spiritus noster, qui ab illo est, designetur.

Quicquid enim ex Spiritu natum est, Spiritus est Joh. III. 6. Sed quia τὸ ἓν πνεῦμα semper ipsum- met Spiritum Sanctum designat in hoc capite, & in uno illo Spiritu nos in unum corpus mysticum baptizari dicimur, sine dubio hic etiam in eun- dem Spiritum nos potari, ut hauriamus ipsummet Spiritum Sanctum, ejusque efficaciâ corrobore- mur in sacra Eucharistia intelligimur. Theophy- lactus cum Chrysostomo hoc posterius mavult ad baptismum itidem referre, quo potemur non ali- ter, quàm arbores solent à fonte aliquo irrigari. Sed non est discedendum à proprio verbi ἐποτί- σθημεν significatu. Neque improbant illi Græci Patres explicationem de sacra cœna. Chrysosto- mus hanc paraphrasin tradit: Venimus ad eandem mysteriorum imitationem, eadem mensa fruimur. Et cur non dixit, eodem corpore nutrimur, eun- demque bibimus sanguinem? Quoniam cum di- xit Spiritu, utrumque significavit & carnem & sanguinem. Per utrumque enim uno Spiritu pota- mur.

Schlichtingius Socinianus in priori membro de baptismo verba ἐν ἑνὶ πνέυματι materialiter in- telligit, non de causa Efficiente, ut Spiritus San- ctus ὑπόςασιν destruat, quasi dicatur: Tantæm copiam Deus per Christum Spiritus Sancti in nos perfudit, ut in illo tanquam in flumine baptizati & mersi fuerimus: Sed ita Spiritus Sancti dona confunduntur cum autore donorum: Non doce- tur, quod dona sua in baptismo effuderit, sed quod nos in corpus Christi mysticum per baptismum recepti simus, idque in uno Spiritu: Virtute unius illius Spiritus, de quo ex professo ibi agitur. Por- rò in posteriori membro Schlichtingius verba εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα sic pervertit: In uno Spiritu εἰς pro ἐν usitatè, idque REDUNDAT: Repetit denique illa ἀπὸ κοινᾶ in unum corpus: Sensum autem hunc extorquere vult: Non tantùm omnes in una Spiritu baptizati, & sic illo largissimè profusi, in eoque mersi sumus, sed omnes illo potati sumus. Trans- ivit hæc cœlestis aqua penitùs ad animas nostras, non in solis exterius hæsit corporibus, qua animæ nostræ potatæ & repletæ sunt, adeo ut hæc aqua facta sit in animis nostris fons aqua salientis in vi- tam æternam. Joh. IV. 14. At Apostolus de in- dustria adhibuit particulam εἰς, & quemadmo- dum εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν secundum Aposto- lum: Ita εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν, ut non repe- tendum sit illud εἰς ἓν σῶμα, sed oppositio vel distinctio illa salva maneat corporis unius mystici, in quod per baptismum recipimur, & Spiritus unius, in quem non per baptismum, sed per cali- cem Eucharisticum potamur, docente Apostolo. Quem sensum, etsi inter Papistas etiam Cardina- lis Bellarminus in gratiam ποτηριοκλεψίας Papalis intervertere voluit, hic non de potu sanguinis Do- mini in S. cœna, sed de potu Spiritus in baptismo Christi sermonem esse, contendens l. IV. de Eu- charist. c. 17. Sed frustra. Nam præterquam, quod loca parallela, supra cap. X. 2. 3. & 1. Joh. V. 6. & ratio de communione unius potus inter se col- lata utrumque sacramentum hic conjungi doce- ant, agnovêre id post Augustinum l. 1. contra Faust. cap. 8. Thomas Aquinas, Erasmus, Faber Stapulensis, Cajetanus, Salmero, Estius, Justinianus, Cornelius à Lapide, aliique Papistæ, vi veritatis coacti, cum quibus patroni Bellarmini transigant.

## 12:14
V. 14. Καὶ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἐκ ἔσιν ἓν μέλος, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ.) Not any one member, however excellent, makes a body, but all together: as above 12. Dionysius Longinus: For no one of the members, when cut off from another, possesses any significance. But all together with one another fulfill a perfect system embodied by communion, and because it is enclosed by the bond of harmony. Maximus Tyrius in his dissertation for active life. The need of the body, being manifold and various, is preserved by the contribution of the parts to the service of the whole; feet carry, hands work, eyes see, ears hear. And the rest, so that I do not waste time with words.

Latin:

V. 14. Καὶ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἐκ ἔσιν ἓν μέλος, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ.) Non unum aliquod membrum, quamvis excellens, facit corpus, sed cuncta simul: ut supra 12. Dionysius Longi- nus: Τῶν γὰρ μελῶν ἓν μὲν ἐδὲν τμηθὲν ἀφ᾿ ἑτέρε τὸ ἀξιόλογ γον ἔχει. Πάντα δὲ μετ᾿ ἀλλήλων ἐκπληροῖ τέλειον σύστημα σωματοποιούμενον τῇ κοινωνίᾳ, καὶ ὅτι τῷ δεσμῷ τῆς ἁρμο- νίας περικλειόμενον. Maximus Tyrius in dissertatione pro vita activa. Ἡ τῶ σώματος χρεία πολυμερής τε ὖσα καὶ πο- λυειδὴς, σώζεται τῇ συντελείᾳ τῶν μερῶν πρὸς τὴν ὑπηρεσίαν τῶ ὅλω· φέρεσι πόδες, ἐργάζονται χεῖρες, ὁρῶσιν ὀφθαλμοὶ, ἀκέεσιν ἀκοαὶ. καὶ τὰ ἄλλα, ἵνα μὴ διατρίβω λόγοις.

## 12:15
V. 15. If the foot shall say, because I am not the hand) With similar festivity, Menenius in Livy, Book II, attributes speech to human limbs, which passage is to be compared with this: And Aesop, in the cited passage of Maximus Tyrius, introduces the foot complaining about the burden and wishing to abandon it. It signifies, however, that those of lower rank ought not to envy those of higher rank.

Latin:

V. 15. Ἐὰν εἴπῃ ὁ πῦς, ὅτι ἐκ εἰμὶ χεὶρ) Pari festivitate membris humanis sermonem tribuit Menenius apud Li- vium libro II. qui locus cum hoc conferendus est: Et Aeso- pus apud Maximum Tyrium dicto loco pedem inducit que- rentem de onere, & id destituere volentem. Significat au- tem, non debere minores invidere majoribus.

## 12:17
V. 17. If the whole body were an eye) Quintilian VIII. 5. But I would not want there to be eyes in the whole body, lest the other limbs lose their own function.

Where is the hearing) Not unlike Plotinus: For seeing is not of the fingers.

Latin:

V. 17. Εἰ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ὀφθαλμὸς) Quintilianus VIII. 5. Sed neque oculos esse toto corpore velim, ne caetera membra suum officium perdant.

Πᾶ ἡ ἀκοὴ) Non dissimiliter Plotinus: Οὐδὲ γὰρ δακτύ- λων τὸ βλέπειν.

## 12:18
V. 18. But now God has set the members, each one of them in the body, as He willed) In a suitable place, not by the force of the material, but for the use of the whole by providence, as the Stoics say. See Eph. IV. 15. Plato, Book X of the Laws: For a part is fashioned for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for the sake of the part.

Latin:

V. 18. Νυνὶ δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἔθετο τὰ μέλη, ἓν ἕκαστον ἀυτῶν ἐν τῷ σώματι, καθὼς ἠθέλησεν) Loco conveniente, non ex vi materiae, sed ad usum totius ἐκ προνοίας ut loquuntur Stoi- ci. Vide Eph. IV. 15. Plato X. de legibus: Μέρος μὲν γὰρ ἕνεκα ὅλω, καὶ ἐκ ὅλον ἕνεκα μέρες κατεργάζεται.

## 12:19
And if all were one member, where is the body) For the human body is a composite thing, consisting of connected parts.

Most Papist interpreters apply this to the ministers of the word, or if they extend it further, they have their own interpretation. To them, the feet are those who are established in a lower, contemptible ministry, the hands those in a more honorable one: Or according to Thomas, the feet are the subjects, the hands the prelates: By eyes and ears, they understand those in the Church who are occupied with the actions of the contemplative life, so that the eyes denote the teachers, the ears the disciples: The head to them is the Roman Pontiff: The weaker but necessary members are the old, the ignoble are servants and the poor; the uncomely are the married, or those who are infamous because of some crime committed, or worthy of infamy. Concerning which, see Estius. But there is no need for a more subtle discussion of each and every one in allegories, unless the Holy Spirit shows the application: Nor does the Church know any other head than Christ. Gregory the Great, Book XXI of the Morals, chapter 6, hands down such an interpretation: For what is the holy Church, if not the body of its heavenly head, in which one is an eye by seeing high things, another a hand by doing right things, another a foot by running to what is enjoined, another an ear by understanding the voice of the precepts, another a nose by discerning the stench of evils and the fragrance of good things. We omit other things here by design. But (setting aside a more special application) the Apostle means this: that there is a sweet harmony of members in the body, and that each member has its own function, its own use, and that the diverse members were established to that end, that they might need one another, or succor one another with their services, that the more noble members should not despise the less noble, whether because they are not necessary or because they are unworthy of the body, and that each should be content with its own place, state, and duty, and that God has placed all things in the body as He willed. The interpretation is both certain and clear in the mystical body of Christ. But all things tend to this, that unity may be preserved and mutual charity fostered in the Church.

Latin:

Εἰ δὲ ἦν τὰ πάντα ἓν μέλος, πᾶ τὸ σῶμα) Est enim cor- pus humanum συνθετόν τι, constans ἐκ συνημμένων.

Pontificii Interpretes plerique trahunt ad mi- nistros verbi, aut si ulterius extendant, ἰδίαν ha- bent ἐπίλυσιν. Pedes illis sunt, qui in inferiori con- temptibili ministerio, manus qui in honoratiori constituti sunt: Vel juxta Thomam pedes subdi- ti, manus praelati: Per oculos & aures, qui in Ec- clesia vacant actionibus vitae contemplativae, in- telligunt, ut oculi doctores, aures discipulos no- tent: Caput ipsis est Romanus Pontifex: Mem- bra infirmiora, sed necessaria senes, ignobiliora ser- vi & pauperes; inhonesta, conjugati, vel qui pro- pter crimen aliquod commissum infames sunt, aut infamia digni. De quo videatur Estius. Sed non opus est in Allegoriis omnium & singulo- rum subtiliori discussione, nisi Spiritus Sanctus applicationem monstret: Neque ullum aliud ca- put Ecclesia novit, quam Christum. Gregorius M. l. XXI IX. moralium cap. 6. talem tradit ἀπόδοσιν: Quid enim sancta Ecclesia, nisi superni sui capitis corpus est, in qua alius alta videndo, oculus, alius recta operando manus, alius ad injuncta discurren- do pes, alius praeceptorum vocem intelligendo auris, alius malorum faetorem, bonorumque fragrantiam discernendo naris est. Alia consulto hic praeteri- mus. Id autem (missa specialiori applicatione) vult Apostolus, in corpore suavem esse membro- rum concordiam, quodque membrum suum ha- bere officium, suum usum, membra diversa eo fine constituta esse, ut mutuis egeant, sive invi- cem succurrant officiis, nobiliora membra non despicere minus nobilia, sive quod non necessa- ria, sive quod corpore indigna, quaeque conten- ta esse suo loco, statu, & munere, Deum omnia in corpore posuisse, sicut voluit. ἀπόδοσις & cer- ta & luculenta est in corpore Christi mystico. Omnia autem eo tendunt, ut servetur unitas, & foveatur charitas mutua in Ecclesia.

## 12:21
V. 21. And the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you) Just as Menenius fables that the members complained to the belly that they had withdrawn their service. The hand provides nourishment to the body, in which the eye is.

Latin:

V. 21. Οὐ δύναται δὲ ὀφθαλμὸς εἰπεῖν τῇ χειρὶ, χρείαν σε ἐκ ἔχω) Sicut membra ventri indignata subtraxisse suum officium fabulatur Menenius. Manus alimenta praebet corpori, in quo est oculus.

## 12:22
V. 22. Or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you) Those who are lesser ought not to be despised by those who are greater.

Two most eminent and excellent members are named, the eye and the head, which, although they far precede the middle and lowest, e.g., the hands and feet, do not however despise them as less necessary: For just as the hand needs the direction of the eye when it performs its own function, so that it may work rightly, so in turn the eye needs the protection of the hand, lest it be harmed. The head itself, although it holds the highest place, yet cannot say to the feet, though placed in the lowest position, I have no need of you, but it needs them, so that it may move from place to place together with the rest of the body, as much to avoid harmful things as to pursue convenient ones. But beware lest you conclude from this with Estius in this place: There is therefore in the Church some head which cannot say to the feet, that is, to the subjects: You are not necessary to me. But this head is certainly not Christ, who can say to all, great and small: I have no need of your ministry. Therefore it must be admitted that there is some other head in the Church, by the ministry of the feet, for the government of the whole body, as if for spiritual movement. For it must be considered that parabolic Theology is not argumentative. For, as Estius himself later adds, the metaphorical body ought not to square with the human body in all things, but only in those respects for which the translation or comparison was taken from it. Nor does the Apostle know any head in the Church except Christ, Eph. IV. 15, Col. I. 18. And Christ in the Church absolutely has need of feet or ministry, not indeed absolutely, but by the hypothesis of the ordination, because He has thus constituted His mystical body. But who are those feet which Estius points out, which the head of the Church needs for the government of the whole body, as if for spiritual movement? If they are subjects of the Pope, all men must be feet, because according to them it is of the necessity of salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff, as Boniface VIII declares, says, and defines, C. unam sanctam, extra de Majorit. & obed. What then are his hands, what are his eyes, what are his ears, etc.? Wherefore this similitude ought not to be extended beyond its scope, which is: just as that which is chief among the members of the human body ought not to despise the lower ones, so neither ought those who are in the chief place in the Church to hold the mystical members of a lower order in contempt or disdain. But it is not necessary that there be some one visible head of the whole body of the Oecumenical Church, which is also among the impossibilities; or if the comparison holds in all things, will not the Church be monstrous, which besides that undoubted head, Christ, still has another head, the Roman Pontiff, just as a man would necessarily be altogether monstrous if he had two heads?

Latin:

V. 22. Ἡ πάλιν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῖς ποσὶ χρείαν ὑμῶν ἐκ ἔχω) Non debent, qui minores sunt, a majoribus contemni.

Nominantur duo membra eminentissima & praestantissima oculus & caput, quae etsi multum antecedant mediis, & infimis e. g. manibus & pe- dibus, non tamen ea, tanquam minus necessaria, despiciunt: Nam uti manus directione oculi indi- get, cum suo fungitur officio, ut rite operetur, ita vicissim oculus manus indiget protectione, ne laedatur. Caput ipsum etsi summum obtineat lo- cum, pedibus tamen, quamvis infimo loco posi- tis dicere non potest, non est mihi opus vobis, sed indiget iisdem, ut una cum reliquo corpore mo- veatur de loco in locum, tam ut evitet noxia, quam ut commoda prosequatur. Cave autem ne hinc concludas cum Estio in h. l. Est igitur in Ecclesia caput aliquod, quod pedibus, id est subdi- tis dicere non possit: Non estis mihi necessarii. Hoc autem caput Christus utique non est, qui omnibus ita dicere potest, magnis, & parvis: Ministerio ve- stro mihi non est opus. Ergo fatendum est, aliquod aliud esse in Ecclesia caput, pedum ministerio, ad totius corporis regimen, tanquam ad motum spiri- tualem. Cogitandum enim Theologiam parabo- licam non esse argumentativam. Non enim, ut Estius ipse postea subdit, humano corpori debet per omnia quadrare corpus metaphoricum, sed in his duntaxat, propter quæ desumpta est inde trans- latio vel comparatio. Neque ullum caput in Ec- clesia, nisi Christum novit Apostolus Eph. IV. 15. Col. I. 18. Et omnino Christus in Ecclesia opus habet pedibus vel ministerio, non quidem absolu- te, sed ex hypothesi ordinationis, quod ita corpus suum mysticum constituerit. Quinam autem pe- des illi sunt, quos indigitat Estius, quibus caput Ecclesiæ indiget ad totius corporis regimen, tan- quam ad motum spiritualem? Si sunt subditi Pa- pæ, omnes homines pedes esse oportet, quod secun- dum eos de necessitate salutis sit, omnem creatu- ram humanam subesse Pontifici Romano, ut decla- rat, dicit & definit Bonifacius VIII. C. unam san- ctam extra de Majorit. & obed. Quæ ergo ejus manus, qui oculi, quæ aures? &c. Quapropter extendi non debet ultra scopum hæc similitudo, qui est, quemadmodum quod est præcipuum in- ter membra corporis humani, inferiora despicere non debet, ita nec illi, qui præcipuo loco sunt in Ecclesia, inferioris ordinis mystica membra con- temtui aut despicatui habere debent. Non vero necessum est, ut totius corporis Ecclesiæ Oecu- menicæ unicum aliquod caput sit visibile, quod etiam est ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων; aut si per omnia mi- litat comparatio, annon monstrosa erit Ecclesia, quæ præter caput illud indubitatum Christum ad- huc aliud habeat caput Pontificem Romanum, quemadmodum omnino monstrosum oporteret esse hominem, si duo capita haberet?

## 12:23
V. 23. But much more those members of the body which seem to be more feeble are necessary. What is either more delicate or more useful than the eye?

Estius here, and deservedly, criticizes the Vulgate for a solecism, which renders it 'more necessary'. And certainly, he says, 'more necessary' is not Latin. The ancient Latins read 'necessary', Ambrose in his book on Noah and the Ark, ch. 8, and Augustine in book XXI against Faustus, ch. 8, and book XXIX, ch. 4, and again in book IV against Julian, ch. 6, likewise Bede, Lombard, Hervaeus, and the ancient concordances. That 'much more' is here that of one correcting, according to Chrysostom and Theophylact, i.e., rather those things which are thought to be weaker commend themselves by necessity and use. Estius takes it in a comparative sense, and says that almost all the Latins, as well as Theodoret and Oecumenius, take it in this way: But the members which seem weaker are more necessary than other stronger ones. Such are the brain, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the bladder, which although they are weak and easily injured, are nevertheless more necessary to the life of the whole body than many others, and to these he compares the old men, who although they are feeble through age, are yet so necessary that the Church cannot lack their instruction and counsel. But Chrysostom's explanation is deservedly to be preferred, which the adversative particle 'but' and the lack of a comparison of the other member favor: whence they sound positively rather than comparatively. * Others also include the eye under these weaker [members]. But this does not please Estius. Because everywhere the eye is placed by the Apostle among those members which are held in the highest regard. But the Apostle is not dealing here with dignity or estimation, but now with necessity.

And those which we think to be less honorable of the body, to these we bestow more abundant honor) As to the belly and those things which are under the belly we give coverings. For many peoples walk about with arms and feet naked, or partially naked. He called clothing here honor. Thus we give a case to rings, leather to a bow, for the sake of more diligent protection: Which is a certain honor.

Some make feet and those things which serve for excretion members of this kind. But most people walk about with naked feet. And therefore the belly, with those things which are under the belly, is more correctly referred to here.

and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness) ערוה The Greek interpreters call those parts uncomeliness, which we name from shame. We remove them like mysteries from the sight of the common people.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἀλλὰ πολῷ μᾶλλον τὰ δοκοῦντα μέλη τῦ σώματος ἀσθενέστερα ὑπάρχοντα ἀναγκαῖά ἐστι) Oculo quid aut tene- rius, aut utilius.

Vulgatam hic, & merito, ob Solæcismum re- prehendit Estius, quæ reddit necessariora sunt. Nec certe Latinum est, inquit, necessariora. Ne- cessaria legunt Latini veteres Ambrosius libr. de Noe, & arca cap. 8. Et Augustinus lib. XXI. con- tra Faust. c. 8. & l. XXIX. cap. 4. rursumque lib. IV. contra Julian. c. 6. item Beda, Lombardus, Her- væus & veteres concordantiæ. Illud πολλῷ μᾶλ- λον corrigentis hic est secundum Chrysost. & Theo- phyl. l. d. quin potius ea, quæ putantur infirmiora, necessitate & usu se commendant. Sensu com- parativo accipit Estius, qui omnes Latinos fere, nec non Theodorectum & Oecumenium sumere hoc mo- do, ait: Sed membra, quæ videntur infirmiora, ma- gis necessaria sunt aliis firmioribus. Talia ipsi sunt cerebrum, venter, hepar, splen, vesica, quæ licet in- valida sint, facileque lædantur, ad vitam tamen corporis totius præ aliis multis necessaria sunt, iisque senes comparat, qui etsi per ætatem debi- les, adeo tamen necessarii sunt, ut eorum instru- ctione, & consiliis Ecclesia carere non possit. Præferenda autem merito Chrysostomi explicatio, cui favet particula adversativa ἀλλὰ & defectus comparationis membri alterius: Unde positive potius, quàm comparative illa sonant. * Oculum sub his infirmioribus alii etiam complectuntur. Non autem id placet Estio. Quia ubique oculus ab Apostolo inter ea membra ponitur, quæ maximi fiunt. Ast non hic de dignitate vel æstimio, sed de necessi- tate jam agit Apostolus.

Καὶ ἃ δοκῦμεν ἀτιμότερα εἶναι τῦ σώματος, τύτοις τιμὴν περισσοτέραν περιτίθεμεν) Ut ventri & iis, quæ sub ventre damus tegmina. Nam multi populi brachiis & pedibus nudis, aut ex parte nudis incedunt. Vestitum hic dixit τι- μήν. Sic annulis damus dactylothecam, arcui corium, custodiæ diligentioris causa: Qui honos quidam.

Hujusmodi membra, pedes, & quæ inserviunt egestioni, nonnulli faciunt. Sed pedibus nudis plurimi incedunt. Ideoque rectius huc refertur venter cum iis, quæ sub ventre sunt.

καὶ τὰ ἀσχήμονα ἡμῶν εὐσχημοσύνην περισσοτέραν ἔχει) ערוה Interpretes Græci ἀσχημοσύνην vocant eas partes, quas à pudore nominamus. Eas tanquam mysteria à vulgi conspectu amovemus.

## 12:24
V. 24. But our comely parts have no need) The face, which is most beautiful in man, is not covered, is not hidden, it is open to all, like the exterior of a temple.

Augustine, book XXIX against Faustus, chapter 4, warned that they are called unhonest, because they do not have that appearance of beauty which the members that are placed in public have. He corrected these things, however, in book VI, tractate II, chapter 7, but a more probable reason for the name was rendered in other things written afterwards (as in the book on the sin of Origin, c. 34, and the book on marriage and concupiscence, c. 6, and book II, c. 4, book XIV on the City of God, c. 26), why the Apostle also called them unhonest, namely on account of the law in the members resisting the law of the mind, which happened from sin, not from the first nature of creation. Compare book IV against Julian, c. 16.

But God tempered the body) There is need of temperament in placing the members of the body.

To that which lacks) To those things which have less of dignity, such as those through which excretion is done. See what ὑστερεῖν is, Rom. III, verse 23, above I, verse 7, VIII, verse 8. In the manuscript it is τῷ ὑστερημένῳ.

Giving more abundant honor) Cicero, On Duties I. In the beginning, nature herself seems to have had great regard for our body, which placed our form and the rest of our figure, in which there was an honest appearance, in plain view: But those parts of the body which were to have an appearance deformed and shameful for the necessity of nature, these she covered and hid.

Chrysostom and Theophylact understand that mixture and temperament with respect to mutual necessity and mutual aid, but those things which immediately precede and those which follow teach that dignity is being looked at here. God bestows honor, however, both because GOD prepared clothing for the protoplasts to cover their uncomely parts, Gen. III, and because God himself is the author of that which men do by the instinct of nature.

Latin:

V. 24. Τὰ δὲ εὐσχήμονα ὐ χρείαν ἔχει) Facies quæ in ho- mine pulcherrima non tegitur, non absconditur, patet omni- bus, sicut templi extima.

Augustinus l. XXIX. contra Faust. cap. 4. inho- nesta dici monuit, quia non habent eam speciem decoris, quam membra, quæ in propatulo locata sunt. Correxit autem hæc in libro VI. tract. II. cap. 7. sed probabilior in aliis postea scriptis (ut po- tel. de peccato Orig. c. 34. & l. de nupt. & Concu- pisc. c. 6. & l. II. c. 4. Libr. XIV. de Civitate DEI c. 26.) nominis reddita est ratio, cur ea dixerit etiam Apostolus inhonesta propter legem scilicet in membris repugnantem legi mentis, quæ de peccato accidit, non de prima institutionis natura. Confer lib. IV. contra Julian. c. 16.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ Θεὸς συνέκρασε τὸ σῶμα) Temperamento opus est in corporis membris collocandis.

Τῷ ὑστερῦντι) Iis, quæ minus habent dignitatis, qualia sunt, per quæ fit egestio. ὑστερεῖν quid sit, vide Rom. III. vers. 23. supra I. vers. 7. VIII. vers. 8. In Manuscripto est τῷ ὑστερημένῳ.

Περισσοτέραν δὺς τιμὴν) Cicero de officiis I. Principio, corporis nostri magnam natura ipsa videtur habuisse rationem, quæ formam nostram, reliquamque figuram, in qua esset spe- cies honesta, eam posuit in promptu : Quæ partes autem cor- poris ad naturæ necessitatem aspectum essent deformem habi- turæ atque turpem, eas contexit atque abdidit.

Κρᾶσιν & temperaturam illam respectu mutuæ necessitatis, mutuique auxilii Chrysost. & Theo- phylactus intelligunt, sed respici hic dignitatem, quæ proxime antecedũt, & quæ sequunttur docẽt. Tribuit autem honorem Deus, tum quod DEUS Protoplastis ad tegendum τᾶ ἀσχήμονα vestitus paravit Gen. III. tum quia ejus, quod homines faciunt instinctu naturæ, Deus ipse autor est.

## 12:25
That there might be no schism in the body) It is a figurative expression, meaning that no parts should be neglected by the body. Thus also in the body of the Church, those to whom less illustrious gifts have fallen, such as casting out demons or interpreting, ought not to be despised.

Why the gift of casting out demons is referred to among the less illustrious, I do not see. The disciples of Christ certainly boast greatly of that, that even the demons were subject to them, Luke X. 17.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη) That all members may agree in one, just as Menenius speaks:

- - - - - Thus the one demands the help of the other, and the matter conspires in a friendly way.

V. 25. κό εἴτε πάσχει ἐν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη) Pliny spoke of the consensus of members. Celsus of their fellowship. Plutarch to Brutus: Correctly accustoming the citizens by law to feel and suffer with one another just as if they were one body. Chrysostom on Repentance X. For we are bound together like a body and its members. And in the body, even if the foot receives a wound, we see the head bowing down; and yet what is more noble than this? But it does not look to its dignity in the time of calamity.

Concerning that compassion, Augustine in his commentary on Psalm CXXX. Does it happen because the foot in the body seems as if far from the eyes, that when by chance it has stepped on a thorn, the eyes abandon it? And do we not see the whole body contract, and the man sits bent, the spine of the back, so that he may seek the thorn which has stuck in the sole: All the members do whatever they can, so that the thorn which had stuck in the lowest and smallest place may be drawn out. But that the συμπάθεια or compassion of the mystical members yields to solace and relief, concerning that in epistle CXXXIII, Augustine: I do not know how that which one member suffers becomes less, if the other members suffer with it. Nor does the relief itself happen through the sharing of the disaster, but through the solace of charity.

Latin:

Ἵνα μὴ ᾖ σχίσμα ἐν τῷ σώματι) Est figurata loquutio, pro ne ullæ partes negligerentur à corpore. Sic etiam in Ecclesiæ corpore contemni non debent, quibus minus illustria dona contigere, ut expellendi dæmonas, interpre- tandi.

Cur donum expellendi dæmones inter minus illustria referatur, non video. Discipuli certe Christi plurimum de illo gloriantur, quod & dæ- mones ipsis subjecti essent Luc. X. 17.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη) Ut omnia membra in unum consentiant, quemadmodum Menenius loquitur:

- - - - - Alterius sic Altera poscit opem, res & conspirat amice.

V. 25. κό εἴτε πάσχει ἐν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη) Consensum membrorum dixit Plinius. Celsus consor- tium. Plutarchus Bruto: Ὀρθῶς ἐθίζοντος τῦ νόμε τὺς πο- λίτας ὥσπερ ἑνὸς μέρες συναισθάνεσθαι κὰι συναλγεῖν ἀλλήλοις. Chrysostomus de Pœnitentia X. Σώματος γὰρ κὰι μελῶν δί- κην ἀλλήλοις ἐσμὲν συνδεδεμένοι. Ἐπὶ δὲ τῦ σώματος κἂν ὁ πῦς δέξηται τραῦμα, τὴν κεφαλὴν ἐπικόπτυσαν ὁρῶμεν· Καὶ τοι τί ταύτης σεμνότερον ; ἀλλ’ ὐχ ὁρᾷ τὴν ἀξίαν ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τῆς συμφορᾶς.

De illa compassione August. in comm. Psalm. CXXX. Numquid quia in corpore pes quasi longe videtur ab oculis, quando forte per spinam calcaverit, deferunt oculi? Et non sicut videmus totum corpus contrahitur, & sedet homo curva- tus, spina dorsi, ut queratur spina, quæ hæsit in planta: Omnia membra quicquid possunt, fa- ciunt, ut de infimo & exiguo loco spina, quæ inhæ- serat, educatur. Quod vero συμπάθεια vel com- passio membrorum mysticorum solatio ac leva- mini cedat, de eo in epist. CXXXIII. Augusti- nus: Nescio quomodo minus fit, quod patitur unum membrum, si compatiuntur alia membra. Nec ipsa revelatio fit per communionem cladis, sed per sola- tium charitatis.

## 12:26
Εἴτε δοξάζεται ἓν μέλος, συγχαίρει πάντα τὰ μέλη) Δοξάζεται here is to be affected by some good, just as is accustomed to happen to those whom we honor. Therefore Cyprian translated δοξάζεται, which is here, as rejoices.

Latin:

Εἴτε δοξάζεται ἓν μέλος, συγχαίρει πάντα τὰ μέλη) Δοξά- ζεται hic est bono aliquo afficitur, sicut fieri solet eis, quos honoramus. Ideo Cyprianus δοξάζεται quod hic est ver- tit lætatur.

## 12:27
V. 27. Ὑμεῖς δέ ἐστε σῶμα χριστῦ) All together the mystical body of Christ, as the head. Eph. I. 23. Coloss. V. 18.

καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους) that is, you are members individually, ἐκ μέρους for οἱ ἐξ μέρος with the articles suppressed.

Perperam interpres Latinus legit ἐκ μέλης ex membro, whereas the Greek texts consistently have ἐκ μέρους ex parte.

Latin:

V. 27. Ὑμεῖς δέ ἐστε σῶμα χριστῦ) Omnes simul corpus mysticum Christi, ut capitis. Eph. I. 23. Coloss. V. 18.

καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους) id est singuli membra estis, ἐκ μέρους pro οἱ ἐξ μέρος suppressis articulis.

Perperam interpres Latinus legit ἐκ μέλης ex membro, quum Græca constanter habeant ἐκ μέ- ρους ex parte.

## 12:28
V. 28. Καὶ ἓς μὲν ἔθετο ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ πρῶτον Ἀποσόλες) Those indeed eminently so called, called by Christ to that end, that they might lay the first foundations of the Churches.

Δεύτερον Προφήτας) Prophets next in honor to the Apostles Eph. IV. 11.

Τρίτον διδασκάλες) Διδάσκαλοι here and Acts XIII. 1. and Eph. IV. 11. διδάσκοντες Rom. XII. 7. are those who, eminent in learning, presided over the establishing of many Churches, such as Titus in Greece. See what was said at that place in Romans.

Ἔπειτα δυνάμεις) In the Hebrew manner, the abstract for the concrete, as in the following. For Δυνάμεις are called here those who have ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων, the power of punishing sources. See above 10. Thus גברת for the Hebrews is to be established in power.

Εἶτα χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων) Those who received the power of healing diseases.

Ἀντιλήψεις) Ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι means to take care of someone, as we said at Luke 1:54. Since that word is quite general, in this place it seems to signify the presidents of the presbytery, who were accustomed to remind the people of their duty. And therefore they are called παρακαλοῦντες in Romans 12:8, where see what is said. For these things also GOD gave peculiar gifts. Many Greeks explain what is here ἀντιλήψεις as προστασίας.

Κυβερνήσεις) These are they who are the ποιμένες in Ephesians 4:11, from the Syriac פרנסים, the οἱ προϊστάμενοι in Romans 12:8, and elsewhere the πρεσβύτεροι, who governed individual churches.

Γένη γλωσσῶν) Not all spoke in all languages, as the Apostles did for the use of the nations, but one in this, another in that, and indeed in such a one as he had never learned.

The Apostles hold the chief place, as being called immediately by Christ either in the days of his flesh, such as the eleven were; Judas the traitor having been made a devil; or by heavenly revelation, which happened to St. Paul by a voice from heaven, through the medium of the lot of Matthias in Acts 1, because the Apostles laid the foundations of the churches among the nations. Therefore, twelve foundations are established in Revelation 21:14, marked with the names of the twelve Apostles, as they were plainly infallible in teaching, and were led by the Holy Spirit into all truth, John 16:13. To whom St. Paul was added out of the ordinary course. Barnabas is also called an Apostle in Acts 14:14, and is joined to Paul by this communion of the name, concerning which it is so doubtful whether he belonged to the first order? But because it is by no means certain that Barnabas taught by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit and was infallible in teaching (as the other Apostles were), he can scarcely be referred to the first order, but seems to belong to the third. And therefore they are either called Apostles in the strict sense, who were both infallible and at the same time teachers of the whole world called immediately; or in a broad sense: thus Barnabas is reckoned among the Prophets or Teachers in Acts 13:1, and because by the immediate command of God he was set apart with Paul and sent by the Holy Spirit into the world, also comes under the name of Apostle Acts XIV. verse 14.

In the second order are established the Prophets, who taught concerning future or abstruse matters, such as were the Prophets in the Antiochene Churches Acts XI. 27. Chap. XVIII. Judas & Silas chap. XIV. verse 32. Agabus c. XXI. 10. and also the daughters of Philip Acts XXI. verse 9. Estius understands those who by divine inspiration either predicted some future things: or expounded the scriptures. But these latter belong to the following order. The preeminence of the Apostles over the Prophets is also evident partly from the gift of tongues, with which the latter were not endowed, partly from the mode of inspiration, because in the Apostles the Holy Spirit dwelt perpetually, and led them into all truth; in the Prophets only at a certain time. In the former it resided as if by an immanent habit, in the latter it happened by way of a transient act Num. XI. 25. 2. Kings III. 15. 18. 27. partly from the object, about which they were occupied, because the Prophets were sent to certain peoples, or certain persons, the Apostles were sent into the whole world. Wherefore with much greater right they are preferred to the Prophets of the New Testament, who alone are understood here: Not as Paulinus thought, also the Prophets of the Old Testament, who prophesied until John Matt. XI. 13. Luke XVI. 16.

In the third order are commonly placed the teachers, who although they did not teach from immediate revelation, were nevertheless divinely instructed with a peculiar gift of teaching. And as the Apostles spoke from divine inspiration, and were instructed with all gifts v. 8. seqq., at least those more eminent twelve with St. Paul, the Prophets predicted future things from immediate revelation: So these teachers of the third order had the word of wisdom & knowledge, & the discerning of spirits, but they were not unaccountable & infallible, as the Apostles & Prophets. It was also by accident that they presided over many Churches. But why did the Apostle omit in this catalogue the Evangelists & pastors, who in Eph. IV. 11. are in the third and fourth order, with the fifth place assigned to Teachers. I think the cause of that matter is this, that the Evangelists are included here partly under the Prophets, partly under the Teachers, since some of them were also inspired by God, as Mark, & Luke in writing the Gospel: Others were not infallible, who are to be reckoned in the order of Teachers, to whom also Pastors are reckoned. But in the place to the Ephesians they are distinctly recounted in a lower order as teachers, where specifically are to be understood Teachers not performing the pastorate. To Grotius Eph. IV. the Evangelists are helpers of the Apostles Acts XXI. 8. 2. Tim. IV. 5. such as were Titus, Timothy, Apollo, Silas, Mark, Luke. Of these the latter two were inspired by God, who were employed for writing the Gospel. For the rest, neither they seem to have been inspired by God, nor the remaining Teachers.

In the fourth order are placed the mighty works or by mighty works, that is, those endowed with the more illustrious gift of performing miracles: In the fifth the gifts of healings, or rather, those who were instructed with those gifts of healings, of which above. In the sixth Grotius thinks that by helps are to be understood the presidents of the presbytery.

In the seventh [place], by governments [are meant] Presbyters or Pastors. But why those who excelled in the gifts of miracles and healings should be postponed to such [people], the reason does not appear. If it be said that in that place also those endowed with such gifts are to be understood as being in charge of such a pastoral and Episcopal office, and because those gifts were added in that way, they were deservedly designated for that more eminent place! What then will become of the Metropolitans? Why are they simply preferred, whether they are endowed with extraordinary gifts or not? Although that [point] about the Metropolitans has little to do with this matter: where the discussion is about those orders which were in existence at the time when the Apostle was writing these things to the Corinthians. It seems, therefore, that Grotius wished to gratify the Papists in this catalogue, in which, however, he could not find a Pope, who therefore must have had no place in the primitive hierarchy of the Apostolic Church and was a mere non-entity. Otherwise, the Apostles would not have been the first in that series: but Peter alone would have obtained the first place, and the remaining Apostles would have been placed as inferiors and only in the second order. Paul, however, knows of no disparity among the Apostles, no superiority, but makes them all equally peers with Peter, and assigns the first place to the Apostles without distinction, just as he refers all the Prophets to the second order.

But having dismissed the fictions, both Papal and Grotian, the distribution in that Apostolic Hierarchy seems to be this: that there were in the Church those who were teaching, those who were performing miracles, and finally those who were administering other duties. Those teaching were either those who preached by the immediate calling and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, or those who taught without immediate inspiration and impulse. Of the former kind were, first of all, the Apostles, who were also appointed as Teachers of the whole world, and also the Prophets, who predicted future events through the Holy Spirit or revealed other abstruse things; to which order belong the Evangelists, who were endowed with the gift of infallibility, which is evident concerning Mark and Luke, who consigned to writing those things which were abstruse and unknown, if not entirely, yet as far as certain circumstances were concerned, being carried along by the Holy Spirit: but it is not evident that they were otherwise perpetually infallible in teaching outside of their Gospel-writing. Of the latter kind were the teachers, whether they performed a pastorate, who were more important because of their holier office, or not: whom the Apostle places after the Pastors in Ephesians 4:11, who simply taught, just as today there are Academic and Scholastic Doctors not ordained to the pastoral office by the laying on of hands. Pastors, therefore, are comprehended generally and in this place under the name of teachers. To this pertains that statement of Paul in Augustine, Epistle 58: "In all these diverse names, I see that a similar and almost single office of doctrine was treated." In the other place, however, which is in the Epistle to the Ephesians, the name of teachers is taken specifically for those Doctors who do not perform a pastorate. The reason for this is because there the Apostle designates all who have been called, or are still called, for the information of the Church—which is the consequence and effect of the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ into heaven, as David testifies in Psalm 68 and the Apostle in Ephesians 4—by five appellations, namely: Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors, and Doctors. Of these, the Apostles are Teachers of the whole world. The Prophets of the Old Testament were not indeed Teachers of the whole world by their proclamation, yet some, whose writings have been inserted into the canon of the Holy Scriptures, teach the whole world by their writings: besides whom, there were not a few in both the Old and New Testaments who were inspired by the Prophetic Spirit, but here the Prophets of the New Testament are designated. Among the Evangelists, those are eminent who, with those two Apostles Matthew and John, described the Evangelical Acts of Christ and the Apostles by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, Spirit, those writings being likewise divinely consecrated for the informing of the whole world. Besides whom, Philip is mentioned in Acts 21:8, who had once been one of the seven Deacons and had become an Evangelist, that is, according to Grotius on that passage, a traveling Presbyter not attached to any certain Church, who with what success he preached the Gospel in Samaria and elsewhere is taught in Acts 8:5. Thus Timothy is commanded in 2 Timothy 4:5 to perform the work of a good Evangelist. Most of the Seventy make such Evangelists.

disciples, and the like, who served the Apostles in preaching the Gospel, and who did not preach everywhere as the Apostles did, but here and there, such as were Priscilla and Aquila, as also St. Stephen and Apollo. B. Hunnius, along with Chrysostom, says that besides the four Evangelists, the writers of the Gospel history, the companions of the Apostles come under the name of Evangelists, whom they joined to themselves to lighten their labors, such as were Timothy, Philip, Titus, Sosthenes, Sylvanus, Tychicus, Erastus, Epaphras. 2 Tim. 4, 12. Acts 19, 22. How Timothy is called Paul's fellow-worker in the Gospel 1 Thess. 3, 2. Rom. 16, 21. 1 Cor. 16, 10. Pastors are called generally all those to whom the care of souls has been committed by a special vocation in a certain Church, or diocese, or entire province. Doctors, however, as we have said, are distinguished there from Pastors, and those are understood who have not been ordained to the office of pastor. Mr. Dr. Sebastian Schmid, in his later Biblical College, p. 279, thinks that the Apostle had some regard for the Jewish Church, in which the teachers were not priests, but Doctors, who taught in schools or synagogues, just as priests performed their duty in their temple, and thus he calls those Doctors who taught outside the Church congregation and its ordinary place. But Pastors, who succeeded into the place of the priests of the Old Testament, performed their duty in those things which concerned teaching the word and administering the sacraments in the Church: Thus also B. Hunnius explains that Pastors are those who were neither sent immediately by Christ or the Holy Spirit into the universal world, as the Apostles, nor were they sent here and there to the Churches to lighten the labors of these, as the Evangelists, but Churches were assigned and committed to each one of them. But Doctors are those who, from the word of God, delivered the foundations of Christian doctrine, which office is performed today by those who teach sacred subjects in public schools, such Doctors as were Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, etc. And this is concerning the first class, namely, of those teaching in the Church, of whom the first three were suitable for planting the Church, namely, Apostles, Prophets, and Evangelists, the rest, Pastors and Doctors, for the planted Church. Tit. 1, 5.

In the second class are established those performing miracles, both those who produce mighty works and those who are endowed with the gift of healings, which is lower in the order of dignity. But the office of Doctors excels both of these, which the Church can in no way lack, and which therefore is perpetual in the Church, whereas those were only temporary, necessary only for the planting of the Church, but not for the planted Church.

To the third kind belong (1.) Helps, by which name the Papists themselves understand those who assist the poor and the sick, and not the presidents of the presbyters, not those who remind the people of their duty, which is the task of Doctors. Let us hear Estius. The Latins, he says, generally explain it as those who cooperate with and assist the Bishops in instructing and ruling the flock of the faithful. Such as are Parish Priests, Deacons, whom some call the assistants of the Bishops. But if you understand these, the order of dignity will no longer be preserved in that enumeration of gifts. For it is certain that these ministries are more worthy than the gifts of miracles. Add that such assistances pertain to the number of doctors, whom the Apostle placed in the third position. To which the Bishops themselves also pertain. For which reason Eph. 4 joined Pastors and Prophets. Cajetan thinks that by the word for helps is signified the order of those who in the Church of God are occupied with works of mercy. But this office ought to be common to all the faithful: Paul, however, deals with those things which neither are, nor ought to be, common to all. Wherefore others interpret this gift better as that by which, having received it divinely, one is apt for fostering the sick and the weak, and ministering to them, as is done in hospitals. For not all good faithful people are apt for such a ministry. But this is less than the gift of healing the infirm through a miracle. This is the commentary of Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius; and the same is consistent with Scripture, in which the Greek word to take hold of is frequently taken for to take up, just as the infirm, whether in body or in soul, are taken up as if by an outstretched hand, as in Acts 20. Thus it is necessary to support the weak, Luke 1. He has supported Israel his servant. Ps. 3. The Lord has supported me. Hence the supporter, helper, a frequent expression in the Psalms. Therefore this gift of helping seems to me to be the same as that which the Apostle signified by those words: He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

These are the words of Estius, with whom agree Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, Menochius, and others, as well as our own B. Hunnius: Paul understands the ministry of those who, from the goods of the Church, helped and relieved.

(2.) Governments. Which word does not designate pastors and presbyters, as Grotius wishes, but as the order kept by the Apostle teaches, they are inferior to any doctors, as also to the helpers of the poor and the sick, namely, those who preside over the dispensation of temporal things. Estius could have taught Grotius that again: By this word, he says, some think is signified parochial presbyters, to whom the government of particular flocks is committed. But how little probable this is, we have already shown. Therefore, the opinion of Theophylact and Cajetan is more pleasing, who explain this as the ministry of those who preside over the administration and dispensation of temporal things which have been offered to the Church by the faithful. For this also was a peculiar gift, not fitting for all, and perhaps the same as that which in Rom. 12 is signified by that part, He who gives, in simplicity. For to give there is to dispense and distribute. But it is placed after helps in this passage, because it was concerned only with external things. Cornelius à Lapide does not deny it, and notes that such were those who served the tables, Acts VI. B. Hunnius interprets it as those who were ordained to rule ecclesiastical discipline, which was the task of the elders in the primitive Church. Cf. 1 Tim. 5, 17.

(3.) Γένη γλωσσῶν. With the abstract again substituted for the concrete, those endowed with the gift of speaking in a different kind of languages are understood. Which gift is mentioned in the last place, because it brings less utility than the others, if it be alone, and was only for a certain time. For what the Latins append, INTERPRETATIONES SERMONUM, is found neither in the Greek, nor Syriac, nor Arabic, nor among the Greek interpreters, nor in the Glossa Ordinaria, nor among most other Latin interpreters, Pelagius, Primasius, Sedulius, Haymo, Lombard, Hervaeus, nor finally in very many Latin codices, as Estius admits. The Latin Vulgate ought therefore deservedly to have been emended here, which was neglected by the Roman Pontiffs.

From this order, moreover, the subordination of the ministers of the Church is evident, and the blessed Hülseman proves that it is both of divine right and necessary from the harmonic constitution of the mystical body, and that it also differs in degrees of dignity, against Saravia, who had contended that all ministers of the Church ought to be equal in respect of dignity (whom Beza, in book VI against the Belgian Saravia on the government of the Church, ch. 9, 12, and Marc. Ant. de Dominis, in book 2 on the Republic, ch. 7, refuted, from which αἰθήματι the cause of rebellion first arose in England and Ireland) 1. from the word for appointing, which is used likewise of the natural ordering of the members of a natural body from the pure will of God, v. 18, and the application of this will to the constitution of ministers in the Church, especially if this word τιθέναι is explained by parallel passages, as Acts XX. 28.

Rom. IV. 17. ch. IX. 33. 2. Cor. V. 19. 1. Thess. V. 9. 1. Tim. I. 12. ch. II. 7. 2. Tim. I. 11. II. Because the same natural necessity of subordination is altogether posited in the harmony of the natural and Ecclesiastical body in the protasis v. 13. 14. and the apodosis of the comparison v. 15. compared with v. 27. 28. 29. III. Also the diversity of dignity is evident from the words bringing in dignity and indignity, which occur v. 22. 23. 24. It is evident IV. from the diversity of dignity, which is between the eye and the toe v. 17. and 22. which dignity the Apostle applies in the comparison v. 17. and 29. It is evident V. from the numbers, signifying the precedence of order and dignity v. 28. Finally VI. from the comparison of the offices among themselves. For teaching and prophecy, as it excels in the abstract in dignity over bodily and extrinsic ministries, Acts VI. 2. 3. 1. Cor. XIV 39. 1. Tim. V. 17. so also in the concrete, ministers occupied with these diverse offices are more worthy than others in the said place to Timothy and here v. 28. 29. and lastly, where certain things are called χαρίσματα κρείττονα (greater gifts).

Latin:

V. 28. Καὶ ἓς μὲν ἔθετο ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ πρῶτον Ἀποσόλες) Illos nempe eminenter sic dictos, à Christo in id vocatos, ut prima Ecclesiarum fundamenta ja- cerent.
