Δεύτερον Προφήτας) Prophetæ Apostolis honore proximi Eph. IV. 11.

Τρίτον διδασκάλες) Διδάσκαλοι hic & Act. XIII. 1. & Eph. IV. 11. διδάσκοντες Rom. XII. 7. sunt illi, qui eruditione eminentes multis Ecclesiis instituendis præerant, qualis Ti- tus in Græcia. Vide quæ dicta ad illum ad Romanos locum.

Ἔπειτα δυνάμεις) More Hebræo abstractum pro concreto, ut in sequentibus. Δυνάμεις enim hic dicuntur, qui ha- bent ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων, jus plectendi fontes. Vide su- pra 10. Sic גברת Hebræis in potestate constitui.

Εἶτα χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων) Eos qui morbos sanandi po- testatem accepere.

Ἀντιλήψεις) Ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι est curam alicujus gerere ut diximus ad Luc. I, 54. Ea vox cum satis sit generalis hoc loco videtur significare præsides presbyterii, qui popu- lum commonefacere officii sui solebant. Ideoque παρακα- λῦντες dicuntur Rom. XII. 8. ubi dicta vide. Ad hæc quo- que DEUS dabat dona peculiaria. Græci complures quod hic est ἀντιλήψεις, explicant προστασίας.

Κυβερνήσεις) Hi sunt, qui ποιμένες Eph. IV. 1. ex Syriaco פרנסים οἱ προϊστάμενοι Rom. XII. 8. alibi πρεσβύτεροι, qui singulas regebant Ecclesias.

Γένη γλωσσῶν) Non omnes omnibus linguis loqueban- tur, ut Apostoli ex usu gentium, sed alius hac, alius illa, & quidem tali, quam nunquam didicerat.

Principem locum obtinent Apostoli, utpote à Christo immediate vocati vel in diebus carnis, quales erant undecim; Juda proditore Diabolo facto; vel per cœlestem revelationem, quæ median- te forte Matthiæ Act. I. per vocem de cœlo S. Paulo contigit Act. IX. quia Apostoli fundamenta jece- runt Ecclesiarum inter gentes. Ideo XII. funda- menta constituuntur Ap. XXI. 14. XII. Apostolo- rum nominibus insignita, utpote qui plane infalli- biles erant in docendo, & à Spir. Sanct. in omnem veritatem ducebantur. Joh. XVI. 13. Quibus extra ordinem accessit S. Paulus. Vocatur & Barnabas Act. XIV. 14. Apostolus, jungiturque Paulo hac nominis communione, quo de adeo dubium, anne ad primum ordinem pertineret? Sed quia Barna- bam immediato Spiritus Sancti afflatu docuisse, & in docendo infallibilem fuisse, (uti cæteros Apo- stolos) minime constat, vix ad primum ordinem ipse referri potest, sed ad tertium pertinere vide- tur. Ideoque vel Apostoli dicuntur ἐξοχικῶς, qui & infallibiles fuere, & simul orbis totius docto- res immediate vocati; Vel ὡς ἐν πλάτει: Sic Bar- nabas & Prophetis vel Doctoribus accensetur Act. XIII. 11. & quia immediato Dei jussu cum Paulo segregatus à Spiritu Sancto missus fuit in orbem, Apostoli nomine quoque venit Actor. XIV. vers. 14.

In secundo ordine constituuntur Prophetæ, qui de rebus futuris aut abstrusis tradebant, quales erant Prophetæ in Antiochenis Ecclesiis Act. XI. 27. Cap. XVIII. Judas & Silas cap. XIV. vers. 32. Agabus c. XXI. 10. nec non filiæ Philippi Act. XXI. vers. 9. Estius intelligit eos, qui ex inspiratione divina vel futura aliqua prædicebant: vel scriptu- ras exponebant. Sed bi posteriores ad sequentem ordinem pertinent. Apostolorum ἐξοχὴ præ Pro- phetis etiam patet partim ex dono linguarum, quo hi præditi non erat, partim ex modo afflatus, quia in Apostolis Spiritus Sanctus perpetuo habitabat, eosque in omnem veritatem ducebat; in Prophe- tis certo tantum tempore. Illis per habitum veluti immanentem inerat, his per modum actus trans- euntis contigit Num. XI. 25. 2. Reg. III. 15. 18. 27. partim ex objecto, circa quod occupabantur, quia Prophetæ ad certos populos, vel personas certas emissi sunt, Apostoli in totum terrarum orbem emissi sunt. Quapropter multo majore jure Pro- phetis N. Testamenti præferuntur, quales hic unice intelliguntur: Non ut Paulinus existimavit, etiam Veteris Testamenti Prophetæ, qui usque ad Johan- nem prophetarunt Matth. XI. 13. Luc. XVI. 16.

In ordine tertio locantur communiter διδάσκα- λοι, qui etsi ex immediata revelatione non docebāt, Dono tamen peculiari docendi divinitus instructi erant. Atque ut Apostoli ex inspiratione divina lo- quebantur, omnibusque donis v. 8. seqq. instructi fuêre, ad minimum eminentiores illi XII. cum S. Paulo, Prophetæ ex immediata revelatione futura prædicebant: Ita hi tertii ordinis doctores sermonem sapientiæ & scientiæ, & discretionis spirituum habe- bant, sed non erant ἀνυπεύθυνοι & infallibiles, ut A- postoli & Prophetæ. Id etiā ex accidenti erat quod multis præessent Ecclesiis. Cur vero prætermisit Apostolus in hoc catalogo Evangelistas & pasto- res, qui Eph. IV. 11. tertii & quarti sunt in ordine, quinto loco assignato Doctoribus. Causam ejus rei, arbitror hanc esse, quod Evangelistæ comprehensi hic sint partim sub Prophetis, partim sub Doctoribus, quum & illorum nonnulli θεόπνευςοι fuerint, uti Marcus, & Lucas in conscribendo Evangelio: Alii infallibiles haud fuere, qui ordini Doctorum accen- sendi sunt, quibus etiam accensentur Pastores. In loco a. ad Ephes. distinctim & inferiori ordine re- censiti sunt doctores, ubi speciatim intelligendi sunt Doctores pastoratu non fungentes. Grotio Eph. IV. Evangelistæ sunt adjutores Apostolorum Act. XXI. 8. 2. Tim. IV. 5. quales fuerint Titus, Ti- motheus, Apollo, Silas, Marcus, Lucas. Ex his po- steriores duo θεόπνευςοι fuere, qui ad Evangelium scribendum adhibiti. De cætero nec illi viden- tur θεόπνευςοι fuisse, nec reliqui Doctores.

In quarto ordine virtutes vel virtutibus, id est dono illustriora miracula edendi præditi collocā- tur: In quinto χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων dona sanationis, vel potius, qui illis donis sanationum instructi erant, de quibus supra. In sexto Grotius per ἀντι- λήψεις intelligendos censet Præsides presbyterii.

In septimo per κυβερνήσεις Presbyteros, vel Pastores. Sed cur talibus, qui donis miraculorum & sanatio- num pollebant illi postponendi sint, causa non ap- paret. Si dicatur, quod & istic talibus donis præditi officio ejusmodi pastorali & Episcopali præfecti intelligendi sint, & quia ita accessere illa dona, me- rito etiam eminētiori illi loco designati sint! Quid tum fiet Metropolitanis? Cur illi simpliciter præ- feruntur, sive donis extraordinariis præditi, sive non? Quamvis illud de Metropolitanis huc mini- me faciat: Ubi de iis ordinibus, qui tum temporis, cum hæc ad Corinthios perscriberet Apostolus, sermo est. Videtur itaque Pontificiis in hoc cata- logo gratificari voluisse Grotius, in quo tamen non potuit invenire Pontificem, quem proinde in hie- rarchia primitiva Apostolocæ Ecclesiæ oportet nullum habuisse locum ac merum non ens fuisse. Alioquin primi in ista serie non fuissent Apostoli: Sed Petrus solus primum locum obtinuisset, atque inferiores, & secundo ordine demum collocandi fuissent Apostoli reliqui. Paulus vero nullam no- vit inter Apostolos disparitatem, nullam superio- ritatem, sed illos pariter omnes juxta cum Petro pares facit, ac primum locum assignat Apostolis sine discrimine omnibus, uti ad secundum ordinem Prophetas omnes refert.

Missis autem commentis tum Papalibus, tum Grotianis distributio in Hierarchia illa Apostolica hæc videtur, quod nempe fuerint in Ecclesia tum docentes, tum miracula patrantes, tum denique alia munia administrantes. Docentes erant vel qui immediata Spiritus S. vocatione & afflatu prædica- runt, vel qui citra immediatū afflatum & impulsum docebant. Prioris generis erant Apostoli impri- mis, qui & totius orbis Doctores constituti erant, nec non Prophetæ, qui per Spiritum Sanctum futura prædicebant, vel abstrusa alia revelabant, ad quem ordinem pertinent Evangelistæ, qui scilicet infalli- bilitatis dono ditati erant, quod de Marco & Luca constat, qui ea, quæ abstrusa & incognita, si non ex toto, tamen quoad certos περιστάσεις erant, scriptis consignarunt, Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου: quos vero cæteroquin extra ἐυαγγελιογραφίαν, in do- cendo perpetuo fuisse infallibiles, non constat. Po- sterioris generis erant διδάσκαλοι, sive pastoratu fū- gerētur, qui potiores fuere ob sanctius munus, sive non: Quos Apostolus post Pastores locat Eph. IV. 11. qui scilicet simpliciter tantum docebant, uti hodie Doctores Academici & Scholastici sunt ad officium pastorale per χειροθεσίαν non ordinati. Pastores ergo sub τῶν διδασκάλων nomine generatim acce- pto in h. l. cōprehenduntur. Quo facit illud Paulini apud August. epist. 58. In omnibus his diversis nomi- nibus simile, & prope unum doctrinæ officium video fuisse tractatum. In altero vero, qui est in Epistola ad Ephesios loco τῶν διδασκάλων nomē specialiter accipitur pro iis Doctoribus, qui pastoratu non funguntur. Ratio hæc est, quia illic Apostolus omnes, qui vocati sunt, aut etiamnum vocantur, ad informationem Ecclesiæ, quæ consequens & effectus est passionis, mortis, & resurrectionis atq; ascensionis Christi in cœlū, teste Davide Ps. LXIIX. & Apostolo Eph. 4. quinque appellationibus desi- gnati sunt Apostolorum nempe, Prophetarum, Evan- gelistarum, Pastorum & Doctorum. E quibus Apo- stoli totius orbis Doctores sunt. Prophetæ Veteris Testam. non quidem orbis totius Doctores præ- conio suo fuere, nonnulli tamen, quorum scripta canoni sacrarum literarum inserta sunt, scriptis suis totum orbem docent: Præter quos & in V. Test. & in novo Spiritu Prophetico afflati non pauci fuere, sed hic Novi Testam. Prophetæ designantur. Inter Evangelistas eminent, qui cum duobus illis Apostolis Matthæo & Johanne Evangelica Acta Christi & Apostolorum instinctu Spir. S. descri- psêre, scriptis illis ad totum orbem informandum divinitus itidem consecratis. Præter quos comme- moratur Act. XXI. 8. Philippus, qui quondam è VII. Diaconis fuerat post Εὐαγγελιστὴς factus, hoc est, juxta Grotium ad illum locum Presbyter περιοδευς nulli certæ Ecclesiæ affixus, qui quo successu Evangelium prædicarit in Samaria & alibi, docetur Act. 8, 5. Sic Timotheus jubetur 2. Tim. 4, 5. opus boni Evange- listæ exequi. Tales Evāgelistas faciunt pleriq; LXX.

discipulos, & similes, qui servierunt Apostolis in prædicando Evangelio, quique non ubique ut A- postoli, sed hinc inde prædicabant, quales fuerint Priscilla & Aquila, ut & S. Stephanus & Apollo. B. Hunnius cum Chrysost. præter IV. Evangelistas, historiæ Evangelicæ scriptores, comites Apostolorum dicit Evangelistarum nomine venire, quos illi sibi ad levandos labores adjunxerint, cujusmodi fue- rint Timotheus, Philippus, Titus, Sosthenes, Sylva- nus, Tychicus, Erastus, Epaphras. 2. Tim. 4, 12. Act. 19, 22. quomodo Timoth. Pauli συνεργος in Evan- gelio dicitur 1. Thess. 3, 2. Rom. 16, 21. 1. Cor. 16, 10. Pastores dicuntur generatim omnes, quibus cura a- nimarum per specialem vocationem commissa est in certa Ecclesia, aut diœcesi, aut integra provincia. Doctores vero, ut diximus, à Pastoribus ibi discrimi- nantur, iiq; intelliguntur, qui ad munus pastoratus ordinati non sunt. Dn. D. Sebastiano Schmid. Col- leg. Bibl. poster. p. 279. videtur, Apostolum respe- ctum aliquem habuisse ad Ecclesiam Judaicam, in qua διδάσκαλοι nō erant sacerdotes, sed Doctores, qui in scholis, vel synagogis docebant, uti sacerdo- tes in templo suo fungebantur officio, atque ita Doctores dicere eos, qui extra Eccles. congregatio- nem & locum ejus ordinarium docebant. Pastores vero, qui in locum sacerdotum Vet. Test. succe- dentes in iis, quæ in Ecclesia docendo verbum, & administrando sacramēta suo fungebātur officio: Sic etiam B. Hunnius explicat, Pastores esse, qui ne- que imediate per Christum aut Spir. S. emitteban- tur in orbem universum, ut Apostoli, neq; ad levan- dos horum labores ad Ecclesias mittebantur pas- sim, ut Evangelistæ, sed suæ cuique assignatæ, com- missæque erant Ecclesiæ. Doctores vero eos, qui ex verbo Dei tradidere fundamenta doctrinæ Chri- stianæ, quo munere hodie funguntur, qui in scho- lis publicis sacra profitētur, quales Doctores fuere Justinus Martyr, Athenagoras, Pantænus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes &c. Atque hæc de classe prima, docentium nempè in Ecclesia, quorum tres priores Ecclesiæ plantandæ conveniebant, Apostoli nempe, Prophetæ, & Evangelistæ, reliqui Pastores & Doctores Ecclesiæ plantatæ. Tit. 1, 5.

In altera classe miracula patrantes constituun- tur, tum qui virtutes insignes edunt, tum qui dono sanationū pollent, quod ordine dignitatis inferius est. Quibus vero utrisque præstat Doctorum mu- nus, quo carere nullo modo potest Ecclesia, quod- que proinde perpetuum in Ecclesia est, quum illa temporaria tantum fuerint, Ecclesiæ plantandæ solum necessaria, non autem Ecclesiæ plantatæ.

Ad tertium genus spectant (1.) Ἀντιλήψεις, quo nomine Papistæ ipsi eos, qui pauperibus & ægrotis opitulantur, intelligunt, non vero presbyterorum præsides, non qui populum officii sui commonefa- ciunt, quod Doctorum est. Audiamus Estium. La- tini fere, inquit, exponunt de iis, qui cooperantur & opitulantur Episcopis, in instituenda ac regenda plebe fidelium. Ut sunt Parochi, Diaconi, quos Epi- scoporum adminicularios quidam appellant. Verum si hos intelligas, jam non servabitur ordo dignitatis in ista donorum enumeratione. Constat n. hæc ministe- ria digniora esse miraculorum donis. Adde quod hu- jusmodi opitulationes pertinent ad numerum docto- rū, quos tertiō loco posuit Apostolus. Quo pertinēt ipsi quoque Episcopi. Propter quod Eph. 4. conjunxit Pa- stores & Prophetas. Cajetanus opitulationum voca- bulo significari putat ordinem eorum, qui in Ecclesia Dei operibus misericordiæ vacant. At hoc munus debet omnibus fidelibus esse commune: Paulus autem de iis agit, quæ nec sunt, nec esse debent omnibus com- munia. Quocirca melius hoc donum interpretantur alii de eo, per quod divinitus acceptum, quis aptus est ad fovendum ægrotos ac debiles, iisque ministran- dum, ut fit in nosocomiis. Non enim omnes boni fide- les ad hujusmodi ministerium apti sunt. Hoc autem minus est, quam donum sanandi infirmos per mira- culum. Hic commentarius est Chrysostomi, Theophy- lacti, & Oecumenii; idemque scripturæ consentaneus, in qua Græcum verbum ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι frequenter accipitur pro suscipere, quomodo velut manu porre- cta suscipiuntur infirmi seu corpore, seu animo, ut Act.20. Sic laborantes oportet infirmos suscipere Luc. 1. Suscepit Israël puerum suum.Ps.3. Dominus suscepit me. Hinc ἀναλήπτωρ susceptor, adjutor, dictio fre- quens in Psalmis. Igitur hoc donum opitulandi mihi videtur idem esse cum eo, quod Apostolus significavit illis verbis : Qui miseretur, in hilaritate.

Hæc Estius, cui consonant Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, Menochius, alii, nec non è nostris B. Hun- nius: Intelligit Paulus ministerium eorum, qui ex Ecclesiæ bonis opitulabantur, & subveniebant.

(2.) Κυβερνήσεις. Quæ vox non pastores & presby- teros designat, uti Grotius vult, sed quod ordo ab Apostolo servatus docet, inferiores doctoribus qui- busvis, ut & opitulatoribus pauperum & ægrotorum, illos scil. qui rerum temporalium dispensationi præ- sunt. Docere id Grotium iterum poterat Estius: Hac voce, inquiens, quidam existimant significari parochiales presbyteros, quibus gubernatio commit- titur particularium plebium. Sed hoc quam parum sit probabile, jam ostendimus. Itaque magis placet Theophylacti, & Cajetani sententia, qui hoc exponunt de ministerio eorum, qui præsunt administrationi ac dispensationi rerum temporalium, quæ à fidelibus oblatæ sunt Ecclesiæ. Erat enim & hoc peculiare do- num, non omnibus congruens, ac forsitan idem cum eo, quod Rom. 12. significatum est illa parte, Qui tribuit in simplicitate. Nam tribuere illic dis- pensare & impertire est. Opitulationibus autem h. l. postpositum est, quia versabatur in rebus tantum externis. Cornelius à Lapide non abnuit, talesque fuisse, qui mensis inserviebant, Act. VI. monet. B. Hunnius interpretatur de iis, qui ordinati fuerunt, ut Ecclesiasticam disciplinam regerent, id quod se- niorum fuerit in primitiva Eccl. Conf. 1. Tim. 5,17.

(3.) Γένη γλωσσῶν. Abstracto iterum posito pro Concreto, dono loquendi diverso genere linguarum præditi intelliguntur. Quod donum ultimo nomi- natur loco, quod minorem cæteris utilitatem affe- rat, si solum sit,& certi tantum temporis fuerit. Quod n. attexunt Latini, INTERPRETATIONES SERMO- NUM, nec in Græcis, nec Syriacis, nec Arabicis, nec apud Interpp. Græcos, nec in glossa ordinaria, nec apud alios Interpp. plerosque Latinos, Pelagium, Primasium, Sedulium, Haymonem, Lombardum, Hervæum, nec denique in Codicibus plurimis Latinis reperitur, fatente Estio. Emendari ergo merito de- buisset hic Vulgata Latina, quod à Romanis Pon- tificibus neglectum est.

Ex hoc autem ordine luculenta est subordinatio ministrorum Ecclesiæ, eamque & juris divini esse, & necessaria ex constitutione corporis mystici har- monica, ac differre etiam gradib. dignitatis probat B. Hülseman. contra Saraviam, qui contenderat, ministros Ecclesiæ omnes pares esse debere dignitatis ratione (quem Beza l. VI. contra Saraviam Belgam de gubernatione Eccl. c. 9, 12. Marc. Ant. de Do- minis l. 2. de Pec. c. 7. refutarunt, ex quo αἰθήματι causa rebellionis primum in Anglia & Hybernia enata est) 1. ex vocabulo constituendi, quæ pariter usurpantur de naturali ordinatione membrorum corporis naturalis ex pura voluntate Dei, v. 18. & applicatione hujus voluntatis ad constitutionem ministrorum in Ecclesia, præsertim si hoc vocabu- lū τιθέναι explicetur locis parallelis, ut Act. XX. 28.

Rom. IV. 17. cap. IX. 33. 2. Cor. V. 19. 1. Thess. V. 9. 1. Tim. I. 12. cap. II. 7. 2. Tim. I. 11. II. Quia eadem necessitas naturalis subordinationis omnino ponitur in harmonia corporis naturalis & Ecclesiastici in προτάσει v. 13. 14. & ἀποδόσει comparationis v. 15. collato cum v. 27. 28. 29. III. Etiam dignitatis diversitas patet ex vocabulis dignitatem & indignitatem inferentibus, quæ occurrunt v. 22. 23. 24. Patet IV. ex diversitate dignitatis, quæ est inter oculum & digitum pedis v. 17. & 22. quam dignitatem applicat Apostolus in collatione v. 17. & 29. Patet V. ex numeris, prælationem ordinis & dignitatis significantibus v. 28. Denique VI. ex collatione munerum inter se. Doctrina enim & Prophetia, uti in abstracto dignitate præstat ministeriis corporalibus & extrinsecis, Act. VI. 2. 3. 1. Cor. XIV 39. 1. Tim. V. 17. ita etiam in concreto ministri versantes circa diversa hæc officia digniores sunt alii aliis dicto loco ad Timoth. & hic v. 28. 29. & ultimo, ubi quædam dicuntur χαρίσματα κρείττονα.

## 12:29
Vers. 29. Are all Apostles?) We cannot all do everything.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Μὴ πάντες Ἀπόστολοι) Non omnia possumus omnes.

## 12:30
Do all interpret?) Interpret as above 10.

Latin:

Μὴ πάντες διερμηνεύουσι) Interpretare ut supra 10.

## 12:31
Vers. 31. But covet the greater gifts) Deal with God in prayers, that you may receive from God the best gifts, that is, the most useful. For ζηλῦν (to covet) here is to seek after, as below XIV. 39. Thus also Wisd. I. 12. In the Manuscript for κρείττονα (greater) there is μείζονα (greater).

As if he were to say: I by no means forbid that you should seek after the most excellent gifts, from which the most abundant fruit may redound to the Church of God, provided that this be done without pride and elation of mind, and without contempt for others, to the praise of one GOD and the utility of the Church, as rightly the blessed Hunnius. The commentary of Cornelius à Lapide is inept: Seek after the more useful, that is, ask of God the Apostleship, Prophecy. For the Apostle commands not only to ask, but to emulate and seek after with zeal and fervor, nor is the Apostleship among those things which can be sought by prayers. Nor is the gift of prophecy promised to our prayers. Others read by way of interrogation (Chrysostom, Theophylact, Photius) and in the present tense: Emulate, that is, if you emulate the better things, behold I show you a more excellent way. But the common interpretation in the sense of commanding is simpler. Nor indeed did the Corinthians truly aspire to the better gifts, since they proposed the gift of tongues, which was truly the last, to other more excellent ones. Therefore Theodoret indeed brings up that sense, but does not approve it. But Estius rightly notes that it is not an absolute precept, because the Spirit distributes gifts as He wills, but that the sense is of this kind: Since you emulate charisms, which I do not forbid, strive to attain the better ones, that is, those more useful to the Church of God.

And yet I show you a more excellent way) I will show you a way by which you may know which are the most useful. Although perhaps there is no need for that, because experience itself teaches you that. Therefore he said κατὰ ὑπερβολήν (by way of excellence), that is, as the Jurisconsults speak, ex superabundanti (superabundantly). יותרן (more) as the Rabbis.

Here is a preparation for the following treatise on charity, when it is taught that charity is more excellent than all these ministering gifts, which he had recounted in a long series, because those gifts can exist without saving faith. But charity can no more exist without faith than an effect can exist without a cause, or fruit without a tree. Gal. V. 6. Matt. XII. 33. 1. Tim. I. 5. Jas. II. 18. Certain Greeks make the beginning of the following body here: but some Latins from that part: But emulate the better charisms. That καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν (by way of excellence) is not from abundance. But if it is referred to the word δείκνυμι (I show), it should be rendered rather most diligently. Moreover, by most, and more conveniently, it is referred to the way, as also

The Vulgate rendered it a more excellent way, as if it said excessively better. Augustine, tr. 6 in John, citing Bede, has supereminent. Cassian, and I show you a way still more excellent beyond measure. There is no need to be warned that 'way' is taken for a kind of life or a mode and manner of living. For the use of Scripture is known.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Ζηλῦτε δὲ τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα) Agite cum Deo precibus, ut à Deo accipiatis dona optima, id est, maxime utilia. Nam ζηλῦν hic est expetere, ut infra XIV. 39. Sic & Sap. I. 12. In Manuscripto pro κρείττονα est μείζονα.

Quasi dicat: Neutiquam prohibeo, quin dona sectemini quam præstantissima, ex quibus uberrimus ad Ecclesiam Dei redundet fructus, dummodo id fiat citra superbiam, & elationem animi, & absque aliorum contemptu in unius DEI laudem & Ecclesiæ utilitatem, ut recte B. Hunnius. Ineptus est commentarius Cornelii à Lapide: Sectamini utiliora, id est petite à Deo Apostolatum, Prophetiam. Nam non petere tantum, sed æmulari & sectari cum zelo & fervore jubet Apostolus, nec Apostolatus est inter ea, quæ precibus expeti possunt. Nec prophetiæ donum promissum est precibus nostris. Alii per interrogationem legunt (Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Photius) & in tempore præsenti: Æmulamini, hoc est, si æmulamini meliora ecce ostendo vobis viam excellentiorem. Sed simplicior est communis interpretatio sensu imperandi. Nec vero Corinthii revera adspirabant ad dona meliora, siquidem donum linguarum, quod probe extremum erat, aliis præstantioribus proponebant. Ideo Theodoretius sensum illum adducit quidem, non autem probat. Recte autem notat Estius non esse absolutum præceptum, quia Spiritus dona distribuit, sicut vult, sed sensum esse ejusmodi: Quoniam æmulamini charismata, quod non prohibeo, studete consequi meliora, id est Ecclesiæ Dei utiliora.

Καὶ ἔτι κατὰ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι) Viam vobis ostendam, qua nosse possitis quæ sint utilissima. Quanquam id forte opus non est, quia ipsa experientia id vos docet. Ideo dixit κατὰ ὑπερβολήν, id est, ut Jurisconsulti loquuntur ex superabundanti. יותרן ut Rabbini.

Hic παρασκευή est ad sequentem tractatum de charitate, quum docetur, charitatem omnibus istis donis ministrantibus, quæ longa serie recensuerat, esse præstantiorem, quia dona illa fine fide salvifica esse possunt. Charitas vero tam non potest esse sine fide, quam effectus esse nequit sine causa, fructus sine arbore. Gal. V. 6. Matth. XII. 33. 1. Tim. I. 5. Jac. II. 18. Græci quidam faciunt hic initium corporis sequentis: Latini autem nonnulli à parte illa: Æmulamini autem charismata meliora. Illud καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν, non est ex abundanti. Sed si ad verbum δείκνυμι referatur, potius reddendum quam diligentissime. Cæterum à plerisque, & commodius, refertur ad viam, uti etiam

Vulgatus reddidit excellentiorem viam, quasi dice- ret excessive meliorem. Augustinus tr. in 6. in Jo- hannem, citante Beda, habet supereminentem. Cas- sianus & adhuc excellentiorem supra modum viam vobis demonstro. Viam pro genere vitæ seu modo & ratione vivendi sumi, non opus est, ut moneatur. Notus enim est scripturæ usus.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

The excellence of charity is taught, that without it other gifts of tongues, prophecy, knowledge, miraculous faith, are nothing, nor are martyrdoms. Its properties, and acts both negative and positive; Also its duration, while other gifts of prophecy, tongues, and this childish and specular cognition cease: And finally its prerogative over faith and hope is handed down.

There are three parts. I. The excellence of charity above other ministering gifts to v. 3. II. The attributes and proper works of charity to v. 7. III. The duration of charity, and by reason of it, its prerogative above faith and hope to v. 13.

PART I. The excellence of charity above ministering gifts.

Vers. 1 Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ.

That is, in the languages of all nations. He says this because many who had received that gift were not using it modestly: they were too pleased with themselves above others, even though that gift was not given for the sake of ostentation, but for the benefit of others. There were no such gifts of grace by which men could not make bad use, and which they could not lose by using them badly. For when discipline departs, as Cyprian says, grace also departs.

Καὶ τῶν Ἀγγέλων.

There is also in angels something analogous to languages, through which they convey concepts to one another: however, analogous things are accustomed to receive the communication of words among themselves. See Daniel VIII. 13. Nazianzen doubts whether angels even use external voices among themselves.

Ἀγάπην μὴ ἔχω.

For this too is what faith leads to and by which we are judged. Those gifts of grace are sometimes given, sometimes not given, as the use of others requires. Love is also that which imitates God, it can be perpetually present, and can commend us to God forever.

Γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν.

That is, a bell sounding for the sake of the mind, but signifying nothing. Bells were made of bronze.

Ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον.

He distinguishes cymbals from bronze, because most were made of silver. Ἀλαλάζειν is an onomatopoeia, and signifies any unrefined sound. See what is at Mark V. 36. A cymbal is named from its sound צלצל 2 Sam. VI. 5. and often in the Psalms and Chronicles.

That they should pursue charity above all, which was to be the most effective medicine for the pride and also the schisms and contentions of the Corinthians, the Apostle adorns it with distinguished praises and sets forth its properties, preferring it in a certain manner also to faith and hope, so that he may inflame the Corinthians toward charity: He begins, however, with the gift of tongues, because they valued that most highly. If I speak with the tongues of Angels, is not said by Hyperbole, as Beza wishes, who says that he sometimes assumes those things which neither are, nor can be, as in Gal. I. 8. Nor is the Hebrew language to be understood here with some, which they say GOD, the Angels, and Adam in Paradise used. But the Apostle thus points out that there is a language peculiar to Angels, concerning which Theodoret says that the languages of Angels are not those which are perceived by sense, but by intelligence: Through which they both praise the God of all things and differ among themselves. Where it is to be observed that angels speak with humans in one way, and among themselves in another. The former must necessarily take place by an external and sensible sign, or by a voice generally formed externally. The latter, however, occurs in a spiritual manner proper to angels. By this method they define the speech of angels, as being the thought of an intelligent nature brought to the notice of another by a certain indication. As Theophylact says on this passage: Angels, he says, have an intellectual tongue, that power, namely, by which they impart to one another the understanding of divine things and divine thoughts, concerning which speech Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and other Greeks also speak here. But when the Apostle posits humans speaking with the tongue of angels, this is not to be understood as a mutual conversation of angels among themselves, but as an address made to humans; as if he were to say: If I could even speak with the tongues and speech of angels, such as they used when they appeared to humans, or which they use among the blessed heavenly beings, or which I heard in the third heaven, when I perceived ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα there. 2 Cor. XI. Others do not understand this as the gift of tongues, but as eloquence; if I were even the most eloquent of humans, or possessed an eloquence that is above humans and is angelic. But because the gifts previously recounted are here compared with charity, the gift of tongues is more correctly understood here than eloquence: although that too was given not without, but with the eloquence and fluency becoming to men of God, and therefore both can be understood together. If I were to speak most elegantly with any tongues of humans, or even with angelic tongues and angelic eloquence, and did not have charity, I would be as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal, which only fills the ears and has no use. Because from that, fruit would redound neither to God nor to one's neighbor, but rather a speech destitute of the affection of charity would tend toward any other end. A cymbal, as Cajetan notes, was among the ancients an instrument of sound rather than a musical one, which women used, as if the Apostle were saying: Brass indeed resounds, but by its tinkling it signifies nothing certain: a cymbal, however, delights only by its tinkling, but neither contributes anything to the use of human life, unless it is played with art. Thus, tongues are of no benefit unless they are directed by charity. What art provides for inanimate instruments, that charity provides for tongues, namely, utility and edification. For if charity does not direct and moderate them toward edification, so that tongues may be understood and lead to utility, what will they be but tinkling brass? Therefore, they are not only of no benefit to themselves, as the Papist interpreters explain, who are destitute of charity; but neither to others, even if they are skilled in many various tongues, while they do not apply them to the use of the Church, but only so that they may be heard without understanding, as is accustomed to be done in the Papal Mass.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Docetur excellentia charitatis, quod sine illa alia dona linguarum, prophetiæ, scientiæ, fidei mi- raculosæ, nihil sint, nec martyria. Ejusdē pro- prietates, & actus tum negativi, tū positivi; Nec non duratio, cessantibus aliis donis pro- phetiæ, linguarum, & cognitionis hujusce infantilis & specularis: Ac denique præro- gativa ejusdem præ fide ac spe traditur.

PArtes sunt tres. I. Charitatis præ aliis donis ministrantibus excellentia ad v. 3. II. Charitatis attributa, & opera propria ad v. 7. III. Charitatis duratio, ejusque ratione, præ fide ac spe, præroga- tiva ad v. 13.

PARS I. Charitatis præ donis ministrantibus excellentia.

Vers. 1 Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ.

Id est, omnium gentium linguis. Hoc ideo dicit, quia multi, qui id donum acceperant, non modeste utebantur: Nimium sibi placebant præ cæteris, cum tamen id donum non sit datum ostentationis causa, sed ad utilitatem alio- rum. Nulla erant ejusmodi χαρίσματα, quibus non male uti homines possent, & quæ non possent male utendo per- dere. Recedente enim disciplina, ut loquitur Cyprianus, recedebat & gratia.

Καὶ τῶν Ἀγγέλων.

Est & in Angelis aliquid ἀνάλογον linguis, per quod con- ceptus sibi mutuo tradunt: Solent autem ἀνάλογα inter se recipere communicationem vocabulorum. Vide Daniel VIII. 13. Dubitat Nazianzenus, an Angeli inter se etiam externis vocibus utantur.

Ἀγάπην μὴ ἔχω.

Nam & hoc est quo fides ducit & ex quo censemur. Χα- ρίσματα illa modo dantur, modo non dantur, prout aliorum usus exigit. Dilectio est & quæ Deum imitatur, perpe- tuo adesse potest, & nos in perpetuum Deo commendare.

Γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν.

Id est, tintinnabulum animi causa sonans, nihil autem significans. Tintinnabula erant ex ære.

Ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον.

Cymbala distinguit ab ære, quia erant pleraque ex ar- gento. Ἀλαλάζειν est ὀνοματοποιΐα, & quemvis sonum in- conditum significat. Vide quæ ad Marcum V. 36. κύμβα- λον à sono dicitur צלצל 2. Sam. VI. 5. & in Psalmis & Paralipomenis sæpe.

Ut charitatem maxime consectentur, quæ fa- stus etiam ac scismatum & contentionum medi- cina efficacissima Corinthiis futura, insignibus eam mactat elogiis, ejusque proprietates sistit Apo- stolus, certa ratione fidei quoque ac spei eandem præferens, ut ad charitatem Corinthios inflam- met: A dono autem linguarum incipit, quia id maximi æstimabant. Si linguis Angelorum loque- rer, non per Hyperbolen dictum, ut Beza vult, quam interdum assumere dicit ea, qua neque sunt, nec esse possunt, ut Gal. I. 8. Nec intelligenda hic cum nonnullis est lingua Hebræa, qua DEUM, Angelos, & Adam in Paradiso usos esse ajunt. Sed indigitat ita Apostolus, peculiarem Angelis esse linguam, de qua Theodoretus, Angelorum linguas esse, ait, non quæ sensu, sed quæ intelligentia perci- piuntur: Per quas & universorum Deum laudant & inter se differunt. Ubi observandum, aliter Ange- los cum hominibus, aliter inter se loqui. Illud ex- terno & sensibili signo, seu formata plerumque extrinsecus voce fieri necesse est. Hoc v. sit spiri- tuali & Angelis proprio modo. Quo pacto loquu- tionem Angelorum definiunt, quod sit intelligentis naturæ cogitatio ad notitiam alterius certo indicio producta. Uti Theophyl. in hunc locum: Angelis, inquit, lingua est intellectiva, vis nimirum illa, qua sibi mutuo divinarum rerum intellectum, ac divinas cogitationes impertiunt, de qua loquutione hic et- iam Chrysostomus, Oecumenius aliique Græci. Sed cum Apostolus homines lingua Angelorum loquentes ponit, non de mutuo Angelorum ad se invicem colloquio id accipiendum, sed de alloquio ad homines facto; Quasi dicat: Si vel Angelorum linguis & locutione possem loqui quali usi sunt illi, cum hominibus apparuêre, aut qua utuntur penes cœlites beatos, vel quam audivi in tertio cœlo, cum ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα ibi perciperem. 2. Cor. XI. Alii non de dono linguarum, sed de facundia id ac- cipiunt; si vel eloquentissimus hominum essem, vel eloquentia, quæ super homines, & Angelica sit, pollerem. Sed quia dona prius recensita hic componuntur cum charitate, donum linguarum rectius hic intelligitur, quam facundia: Quan- quam & illud non absque, sed cum facundia & elo- quentia, viros Dei decente, datum fuerit, ideoque conjunctim utrumque comprehendi queat, Si lin- guis quibuscunque hominum elegantissime loque- rer, imo linguis Angelicis, & facundia Angelica, & charitatem non haberem, essem velut æs reso- nans & cymbalum tinniens, quod aures implet tantum, nullumque usum habet. Quia neque ad Deum, neque ad proximum inde fructus redun- daret, quin charitatis affectu destituta oratio in quemvis alium potius finem tenderet. Cymbalum, notante Cajetano, apud veteres instrumentum erat sonorum magis, quam Musicum, quo mulieres ute- bantur, quasi dicat Apostolus: Æs resonat quidem, sed suo tinnitu nihil certi significat: Cymbalum autem tinnitu tantum delectat, neutrum vero quicquam confert ad usum vitæ humanæ, nisi arte pulsetur. Ita nihil prosunt linguæ, nisi charitate dirigantur. Quod ars præstat instrumentis inani- matis, id charitas linguis, utilitatem scilicet & ædificationem. Si enim charitas non dirigat & moderetur ad ædificationem, ut intelligantur lin- guæ, & ad utilitatem cedant, quid nisi æs tinniens erunt? Non ergo tantum sibi non prosunt, ut ex- plicant Pontificii Interpretes, qui charitate desti- tuuntur; sed nec aliis, etiamsi multivarias linguas calleant, dum non adhibent ad usum Ecclesiæ, sed ut audiantur solum sine intellectu, ut in Missa Pa- pali fieri solet.

## 13:2
Vers. 2. And if I have prophecy

For some can have even this and yet lose piety and salvation. Matt. VII. 22.

And I know all mysteries. If I understand toward what all these figures of the Old Testament tend.

Not only figures, but also oracles are called mysteries, not by reason of the mode of proposing, or by reason of things which are hidden from us and exceed the capacity of our reason, and are above the mind, above reason, and above all comprehension,

And all knowledge. All knowledge of histories

In the scriptures, besides the mysteries of faith, not only histories and examples of faith and charity and other virtues are exhibited, but legal matters also and many other things of various sciences occur; the knowledge of all of which, and not only of those things which are contained in the sacred letters, but also those which are contained in exotic and profane ones, and thus the Apostle embraces all knowledge of divine and human things, because however great that may be, without charity it is nothing, that is, of no use and fruit. The word I have must be repeated here: If I had all knowledge, or if I understood all knowledge.

And if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains. For that was the reward of adult faith, to perform wondrous things, as we said above in 9. Moreover, to move mountains is a proverbial expression, that is, to perform things that are clearly stupendous, as can be seen in Matt. XVII. 20, where see the things said. Add Revelation VIII. 8.

This miraculous faith does not always presuppose saving faith, much less is it only some degree of saving faith: since it can exist without saving faith, and exists in others who have miraculous faith and do not have charity, Matt. VII. 22. Therefore Bellarmine is vain, who strives to prove from this passage that saving faith can exist without charity. Salmero and Estius acknowledge that this is not dealing with saving faith here, with Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius preceding.

But I have not love.

Faith has many promises, because it is the way to love. But love itself is that which produces works more admirable than those which are called miracles, and if the time or opportunity for working is lacking, it makes those who have been made partakers of divine goodness also partakers of divine blessedness. To know this and to do this is to be a Christian.

I am nothing.

I will be of no value before God for obtaining eternal life. This manuscript has: Οὐδὲν ὠφελῦμαι. See Pf. L. 15.

Faith is not mere knowledge, but trust, nor is it a way to love, but the cause and mother, or parent of charity. Nor does our love make us partakers of divine goodness or divine blessedness. For this is the property of faith, which apprehends divine grace and goodness, and renders us partakers of salvation and eternal blessedness, without which it is impossible to please God. Heb. XI. 6. Take 'all faith' as the whole faith, just as πᾶς is taken as ὅλος in Matthew 27:45, Col. II. 9. That 'I am nothing' is to be understood regarding the use and fruit redounding to God (to the glory of God) and to one's neighbor, but not regarding our own salvation and eternal blessedness: because here the Apostle is not treating of the method of obtaining salvation, but of the use and fruit of spiritual gifts. Therefore it is soon explained by 'I am profited nothing'.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω προφητείαν

Nam & hanc habuisse quidam possunt & tamen pietatem & salutem amittere. Matth. VII. 22.

Καὶ εἰδῶ τὰ μυσήρια πάντα. Si intelligam quo tendant omnes istæ figuræ Veteris Te- stamenti.

Non figuræ tantum, sed etiam oracula μυσήρια dicuntur, non ratione modi proponendi, seu ratio- ne rerum, quæ nobis absconditæ, nostrumque ca- ptum rationis excedunt, & sunt ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λό- γον, καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν,

Καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γνῶσιν. Omnem historiarum cognitionem

In scripturis præter fidei mysteria non tantum historiæ, & exempla fidei, ac charitatis, aliarumque virtutum exhibentur, sed legalia quoque & multa alia variarum scientiarum occurrunt; Quorum omnium cognitionem, nec eorum solum, quæ in sacris literis, sed etiam, quæ in Exoticis & profanis continentur, adeoque omnem rerum divinarum & humanarum notitiam complectitur Apostolus, quod quantacunque illa sit, sine charitate nulla sit, hoc est, nullius usus & fructus. Repetendum hic verbum ἔχω: Si omnem scientiam haberem, aut il- lud εἰδῶ sinoverim omnem scientiam.

Καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω πᾶσαν τὴν πίσιν, ὥστε ὄρη μεθισάνειν. Fidei enim adultæ id erat præmium, res miras efficere, ut diximus supra 9. Est autem proverbialis loquutio montes transferre, id est, res plane stupendas efficere, ut videre est Matth. XVII. 20. ubi dicta vide. Adde Apocalypsin. VIII. 8.

Fides hæc miraculosa non supponit semper sal- vificam fidem, nedum gradus tantum est aliquis fidei salvificæ: Siquidem sine fide salvifica esse possit, & in aliis sit, qui fidem miraculosam habent, & charitatem non habent, Matth. VII. 22. Ideo vanus est Bellarminus, qui ex hoc loco probare satagit, fidem salvificam esse posse sine charitate. Non hic de salvifica fide agi agnoscunt Salmero & Estius, præeunte Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Theophylacto, Oecumenio.

Ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω.

Fides multa promissa habet, quia via est ad dilectionem. Ipsa autem dilectio est, quæ opera edit magis admiranda, quam ea, quæ miracula vocantur, & si operandi tempus de- sit aut occasio, participes factos divinæ bonitatis, participes etiam facit divinæ beatitatis. Hoc scire & hoc agere est esse Christianum.

Οὐδέν εἰμι.

Nullo apud Deum ero in pretio ad consequendum vitam æternam. Manuscriptus hic habet: Οὐδὲν ὠφελῦμαι. Vide Pf. L. 15.

Fides nec nudum scire est, sed fiducia, nec via est ad dilectionem, sed causa & mater, vel genitrix charitatis. Neque dilectio nostra vel divinæ boni- tatis nos participes facit, vel beatitatis divinæ. Hoc enim proprium est fidei, quæ apprehendit divinam gratiam & bonitatem, nosque salutis & æternæ beatitatis participes reddit, sine qua im- possibile est Deo placere. Ebr. XI. 6. Omnem fidem ac- cipe de tota fide, uti πᾶς accipitur ὅλος Matth. 27, 45. Col. II. 9. Illud ἰδέν εἰμι nihil sum de usu & fru- ctu ad Deum (ad Dei gloriam) & proximum redun- dante, non vero de nostra ipsorummet salute & beatitudine æterna accipiendum: Quia hic non agit Apostolus de ratione consequendi salutem, sed de usu & fructu donorum spiritualium. Ideo mox explicatur per ἰδὲν ὠφελῦμαι.

## 13:3
Vers. 3. And if I bestow all my goods. This also can be done for the sake of glory, just as Origen records was done by a certain Theban in Matthew XIX. ψωμίζειν properly means to give for eating, Num. XI. 4, 18, Deut. VIII. 3, 16; figuratively, to spend for someone's use, Is. LVIII. 14.

And if I deliver my body, that I may be burned. For Calanus did this, and long after, the philosopher Peregrinus, for the sake of fame, not for the love of God, like the companions of Daniel. Thus, before God, these things are estimated more by the purpose than by the deed. See what we have said at Matthew VI. 1 and following.

But I have not love.

That which truly makes us children of God. See Matthew V. 48.

I am profited nothing.

Namely, regarding the heavenly reward.

That handing over of all goods or faculties might seem a mere act of liberality and munificence, but since it is without charity, it is mere ostentation and a testimony of ambition, not of virtue. Likewise, whatever sufferings are undertaken and endured without faith and charity: thus, even if someone with an unconquered and intrepid spirit sustains any most exquisite tortures and martyrdoms, such as burning, for the sake of religion, but is destitute of charity, he has no profit from it. For when charity is lacking, faith is lacking, justice is lacking. before GOD, eternal salvation fails, and the fruit of all martyrdoms vanishes into nothing. I fear to say, says St. Jerome on Ephesians 5, that martyrdom itself, if it is done so that we may be held in admiration and praise by our brothers, the blood has been shed in vain. Nor yet does our charity make us sons of GOD, nor is that held in Matthew 5:48, but faith in Christ John 1:12, Galatians 3:26.

PART II. CHAPTER XIII.

The attributes and proper works of charity.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ ἐὰν ψωμίσω πάντα τὰ ὑπάρχοντά μυ. Hoc etiam gloriæ causa fieri potest, sicut à Thebano quo- dam factum commemorat Origenes ad Matth. XIX. ψωμί- ζειν proprie est ad vescendum dare Num. XI. 4. 18. Deut. IIX. 3. 16. figurate in alicujus usus impendere Es. LVIII. 14.

Καὶ ἐὰν παραδῶ τὸ σῶμά μυ, ἵνα καυθήσομαι. Nam hoc fecit Calanus, & multo post peregrinus Philo- sophus, ὑπεροφημίας causa, non Dei amore, ut socii Danie- lis. Adeo apud Deum res istæ ex proposito magis quam ex facto æstimantur. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. VI. 1. & sequent.

Ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω.

Illam quæ vere nos filios Dei facit. Vide Matth. V. 48.

Οὐδὲν ὠφελῦμαι.

Nempe ad præmium cœleste.

Illa traditio omnium τῶν ὑπαρχόντων vel facul- tatum merus liberalitatis, & munificentiæ actus videri queat, sed cum sine charitate sit, mera est ostentatio, & ambitionis, non virtutis testimo- nium. Similiter & passiones quæcunque sine fide, & charitate suscipiuntur & exantlantur: Ita suma- xime quis invicto & intrepido animo quavis sup- plicia & martyria exquisissisima, qualis est ustu- latio, religionis causa sustineat, charitate autem destitutus sit, nihil inde utilitatis habet. Defi- ciente enim charitate deficit fides, deficit justitia coram DEO, deficit æterna salus, & in nihilum evanescit fructus omnis martyriorum. Timeo dicere, inquit S. Hieronymus in Ephes. V. marty- rium ipsum, si ideo fiat, ut admirationi & laudi ha- beamur à fratribus, frustra effusus est sanguis. Nec tamen charitas nostra nos facit DEI Filios, nec id Matth. V. 48. habetur, sed fides in Christum Joh. I. 12. Gal. III. 26.

PARS II. CAPUT XIII.

Charitatis attributa & opera propria.

## 13:4
Verse 4. Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ.

A clearly divine description of charity proceeding from his full breast. Μακροθυμεῖ האריך אפו Proverbs 19:11.

χρηστεύεται.

It shows kindness. Thus χρηστεύεσθαι is used in canon 11 of the Council of Nicaea. The Hebrews would say עשה בחסד.

The principal attributes of charity are two: 1. μακροθυμία, long-suffering in enduring evils, and 2. χρηστότης, kindness in conferring goods. Which, as they shine forth in the most eminent manner in the charity of GOD, who is charity itself 1 John 4:16, as the archetype and prototype of true charity Romans 2:4, 2 Timothy 1:15, 1 Peter 3:20, 2 Peter 3:15, Romans 11:22, Ephesians 2:7, Titus 3:4, so in our charity, which is like some ray of divine charity and a certain copy of it, they ought to shine forth Galatians 5:22, Ephesians 4:2, Colossians 1:11, chapter 3:12, 2 Timothy 3:10, chapter 4:2, Hebrews 6:12, 2 Corinthians 6:6. Augustine, Manual, chapter 19, says: God the Father is Charity, God the Son is love, God the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son. This charity and this love requires something similar in us, namely charity, by which we may be associated and joined to Him as if by a certain affinity of consanguinity Luke 6:36, 1 John 4:16.

Ἡ ἀγάπη ὀυ ζηλοῖ.

It does not envy. In which sense we have this word in Genesis 31, 27:10. Thus Theodoret: Ζηλωτὸς μὲν ὑμῖν ὁ τὸν ἄτροπον ὕπνον ἰάνων Εὐδυμίων.

Love is boastful.

I act perperam (wrongly) in the Glossary. This word is not found in the ancient Greeks, and what is read in Cicero to Atticus I. 11, ἐνεπερπερευσάμην, is entirely corrupt. Whence it is to be conjectured that this word was born from the Latin. For in Latium it is an old word, Accius: 'To describe in the theater the perperos (foolish) commoners.' Likewise: 'And the poets are punished for it, more often by their own fault, by your excessive Duclability, or perperitudine (foolishness).' Now these are opposites, to do rightly, and perperam (wrongly), as appears from Cicero pro Caecina. But the Greeks accepted it a little more strictly in the meaning of simulation. For perpereia, kallōpismos (adornment) is in Clement, Pædagogi III. 1. So also Basil in his definitions: 'What is it to be boastful? Everything which is taken up not for need, but for adornment.' The custom of love is not that of ambition, to have one thing locked in the breast, another thing ready on the tongue. The Hebrews would say לא יליץ.

The Apostle now pursues the works of charity partly negatively, partly positively, according to those two attributes, and that in a reverse order, and thus (1.) by reason of kindness, how it may be kind, charity may exercise kindness, and because he is called kind who easily offers the use of himself to others, or who is available for the uses of all: and not only courtesy and humanity of manners, but also a ready zeal to serve others, ought to shine forth in him who is truly kind: By reason of this, there is removed from charity both zeal, that is, envy or emulation. Charity does not envy, because envy does not consist with the zeal of doing good to one's neighbor, and is almost diametrically opposed to charity, whose nature it is to wish good to the neighbor, as a neighbor, and if it has it, to rejoice: and also to be boastful, that is, to act wrongly and perversely, to lie in wait for the neighbor, or to proceed importunately with him. Which does not befit beneficence. The Syrian interprets: Charity does not tumultuate, does not stir up motions and disturbances. Some explain it concerning adulation, others concerning ostentation. Chrysostom also interprets it as propeteuetai (to act rashly), which according to Musculus is to snatch at and presume something before it is timely. But these do not so well agree with the ambition to be excluded. The following member agrees better.

It is not puffed up.

It does not swell up. See above IV. 6. 18. 19. V. 2. VIII. 1. It has joined to itself a huge retinue of virtues, among them also humility.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ.

Divina plane ἀγάπης descriptio profecta ex pectore ejus pleno. Μακροθυμεῖ האריך אפו Prov. XIX. 11.

χρηστεύεται.

Humanitatem ostendit. Sic χρηστεύεσθαι sumitur canone XI. Synodi Nicenæ. Hebræi dicerent עשה בחסד.

Attributa charitatis præcipua sunt duo 1. μα- κροθυμία longanimitas in malis perferendis & 2. χρησότης benignitas in bonis conferendis. Quæ ut eminentissima ratione in charitate DEI, qui ipsa charitas est 1. Joh. IV. vers. 6. ceu archetypo & prototypo veræ charitatis effulgent Rom. II. 4. 2. Tim. I. 15. 1. Petr. III. 20. 2. Petr. III. 15. Rom. XI. 22. Eph. II. 7. Tit. III. 4. Ita in nostra chari- tate, quæ tanquam radius aliquis est divinæ charita tis, ejusque ἔκτυπον quoddam, resplendescere de- bent Gal. V. 22. Eph. IV. 2. Col. I. 11. cap. III. 12. 2. Tim. III. 10. cap. IV. 2. Ebr. VI. 12. 2. Cor. VI. 6. Augustin. Manual. cap. XIX. Deus Pater, inquit, Charitas est, DEUS Filius dilectio est, Deus Spiritus Sanctus amor Patris & Filii est. Hæc charitas & hæc dilectio aliquid simile in nobis requirit, sci- licet charitatem, qua velut quadam affinitate con- sanguinitatis ei sociemur & conjungamur Luc. VI. 36. 1. Joh. IV. 16.

Ἡ ἀγάπη ὀυ ζηλοῖ.

Non invidet. Quo sensu hanc vocem habemus Genes. XXXI. XXVII. 10. Sic Theodoretus: Ζηλωτὸς μὲν ὑμῖν ὁ τὸν ἄτροπον ὕπνον ἰάνων Εὐδυμίων.

Ἡ ἀγάπη περπερεύεται.

Περπερεύομαι perperam ago in Glossario. Vox hæc in Vete- ribus Græcis non reperitur & quod in Cicerone ad Atti- cum I. 11. legitur ἐνεπερπερευσάμην omnino corruptum est. Unde conjicere est natam hanc vocem ex Latina. Nam in Latio vetus vox, Accius: Describere in theatro perperos populares. Item: Et eo plectuntur Poëtæ quam suo vitio sæpius Duclabilitate nimia vestra, aut perperitudine. Sunt autem hæc contraria, recte facere, & perperam, ut ex Cicerone pro Cecina apparet. Sed Græci paulo strictius accepêre in significatione simulationis. Nam περ- περεία, καλλωπισμὸς apud Clementem Pædagogi III. 1. Sic & Basilius in definitionibus : Τί ἐστι τὸ περπερεύεσθαι; πᾶν ὃ μὴ διὰ χρείαν, ἀλλὰ διὰ καλλωπισμὸν παραλαμβάνεται. Dilectionis mos non est is qui ambitionis, aliud clausum in pectore, aliud in lingua promptum habere. Hebræi di- cerent לא יליץ.

Persequitur jam Apostolus opera charitatis partim ἀρνητικῶς; partim θετικῶς, juxta illa duo attributa, idque καθ’ ὕστερον πρότερον, adeoque (1.) ratione χρηστότητος, quomodo χρησεύηται benignitatem exerceat charitas, & quia χρηστὸς be- nignus dicitur, qui facile sui usum aliis præbet, seu qui omnium usibus obvius est: ac non tan- tum comitatem & humanitatem morum, sed etiam promptum aliis inserviendi studium, in eo, qui vere χρηστὸς sit, effulgere oportet: Ratione hujus removetur à charitate tum ζῆλος invidia feu æmulatio. Charitas non invidet, quia invidia cum studio benefaciendi proximo non consistit, & è diametro fere charitati opponitur, cujus est velle bonum proximo, tanquam proximo, & si habeat, gaudere : tum περπερεύεσθαι hoc est perperam & perverse agere, insidiari proximo, vel importune cum illo procedere. Quod beneficentiæ non convenit. Syrus interpretatur : Charitas non tumultuatur, non ciet motus & turbas. Nonnulli de adulatione, alii de ostentatione exponunt. Chrysostomus & προπετεύεται interpretatur, quod juxta Musculum est, priusquam tempestivum sit, aliquid præripere & præsumere. Sed hæc non adeo congruunt ambitioni excludendæ. Magis sequens membrum convenit.

Οὐ φυσιοῦται.

Non intumescit. Vide supra IV. 6. 18. 19. V. 2. VIII. 1. Habet sibi adjunctum ingentem comitatum virtutum, inter eas & ταπεινοφροσύνην.

## 13:5
Verse 5. It does not behave unseemly.

It takes care to do nothing that might be considered shameful even in the opinion of men. It does not act the Cynic. See Cicero, De Officiis, Book I.

The following things look to courtesy and humanity of manners by way of negation. (1.) It is not puffed up, it is not proud, it does not despise others. (2.) It does not behave unseemly, it does not act indecorously; it pursues those things which belong to seemliness, observing a manner befitting persons and times, Phil. IV. 8. Col. IV. 5. 6. 1 Thess. IV. verses 11. 12. To Chrysostom it means not to disdain any thing that might serve the neighbor's convenience. The Vulgate is wrong: 'It is not ambitious.' Which could not please Estius either. In Greek, he says, it is not 'it is ambitious,' but 'it behaves unseemly,' which word signifies to do something dishonestly and beyond what is decorous, or to be ashamed, which is the effect of a dishonest action.

It does not seek its own.

In all things it conducts the public business more than its own. See above X. 24. 33.

This may be referred to both duties of kindness, namely beneficence and humanity, or affability, because it seeks not only its own in advantages or honors, but also those things which are of the neighbor, or which benefit the public good. For that it must be accepted in this sense is evident from the fact that ordered charity begins with itself, and therefore it is not contrary to it, but consistent with it, to seek what is its own. Concerning which Augustine says in his rule: Charity, he says, of which it is written that it does not seek its own, is understood in this way, because it prefers common things to private ones, not private to common, and therefore, by how much more you have cared for the common thing than for your own, by so much more know that you have progressed, so that in all things which a passing necessity uses, the charity which remains may superabound.

It is not provoked.

It is difficult never to be angry, which is παροξύνεσθαι חרה. But this is the disposition of those who love men, that they not only do not become angry without cause, but also keep moderation in a just agitation. See what has been said at Matt. V. 22 and at Acts XV. 39.

It thinks no evil.

That is, it does not easily suspect anything evil. It takes doubtful matters in the better part. Λογίζεσθαι is often to think, to estimate.

These things pertain to long-suffering, not to be exasperated (1.) to avoid quick-temperedness, not to permit the affection of anger to pour itself out into evil (2.) Not to think evil, or not to plot revenge. Others, however, with Grotius explain it not as thinking ill of one's neighbor, but as interpreting all things in the better part.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ.

Cavet quicquam agere quod vel opinione hominum turpe sit. Non agit Cynicum. Vide Ciceronem de officiis primo.

Ad comitatem, & humanitatem morum spectant κατ' ἄρσιν quæ sequuntur. (1.) Οὐ φυσιοῦται, non inflatur, non superbit, non contemnit alios. (2.) Οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ, non indecore agit, quæ τῆς εὐσχημοσύνης sunt, persequitur rationem decentem personarum, & temporum observans Phil. IV. 8. Col. IV. 5. 6. 1. Thess. IV. vers. 11. 12. Chrysostomo est, non fastidire rem ullam, quæ proximi commodis serviat. Perperam vulgata : Non est ambitiosa. Quod nec Estio placere potuit. Græce, inquit, non est φιλοτιμεῖται, sed ἀσχημονεῖ, quod verbum significat inboneste ac præter decorum agere quippiam aut pudesieri, qui inbonestæ actionis effectus est.

Οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς.

In omnibus rebus magis publicum quam suum agit negotium. Vide supra X. 24. 33.

Hoc referri queat ad utrumque benignitatis officium, beneficentiæ scilicet & humanitatis, vel comitatis, quia nec in commodis nec in honoribus unice quærit, quæ sua sunt, sed etiam quæ proximi sunt, vel bono publico prosunt. Nam hoc sensu hoc accipiendum esse, inde constat, quod charitas ordinata incipiat à seipsa, ideoque ei adversum non sit sed consentaneum, quærere, quæ sua sunt. Quo de Augustinus in regula : Charitas, inquit, de qua scriptum est, quod non quærit, quæ sua sunt, sic intelligitur, quia communia propriis, non propria communibus anteponit, & ideo, quanto plus rem communem, quam propria vestra curaveritis : tanto vos amplius profecisse noveritis, ut in omnibus, quibus utitur transitura necessitas, superemineat quæ permanet charitas.

Οὐ παροξύνεται.

Difficile est nunquam irasci quod est παροξύνεσθαι חרה Sed hoc ingenium est eorum, qui homines diligunt, ut non modo sine causa non irascantur, sed & in justa commotione modum servent. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. V. 22. ad Act. XV. 39.

Οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακὸν.

Id est, non facile mali quicquam suspicatur. Dubia in partem accipit meliorem. Λογίζεσθαι sæpe est cogitare, æstimare.

Hæc ad μακροθυμίαν spectant, non exasperari (1.) ὀξυχολίαν vitare, non affectui iræ permittere, ut se in malum effundat (2.) Malum non cogitare, vel non moliri vindictam. Alii tamen cum Grotio explicant non male de proximo cogi- tare, sed omnia in meliorem partem interpretari.

## 13:6
Vers. 6. Οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ.

It does not applaud those doing evil. Χαίρει is a metonymy.

Συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.

It loves integrity, straight paths. For ἀλήθεια extends widely, as does the Hebrew אמונה. Not to rejoice in injustice, but to rejoice together with the truth, is of goodness, not of one approving evil, much less rejoicing in it, from which kindness overflows, and which is joined to sincere charity. Which, as it desires justice and truth to rule: So it testifies against injustice, which is expressed here by μείωσιν, it does not rejoice, but for the sake of truth it is praised.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ.

Non applaudit male agentibus. Χαίρει est μετωνυ- μία.

Συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.

Amat integritatem, vias rectas. Nam ἀλήθεια late pa- tet, ut & Hebræum אמונה. Non gaudere de injustitia, sed congaudere veri- tati, bonitatis est, non probantis malum, nedum de eo gaudentis, ex qua benignitas redundat, quæ- que charitati sinceræ conjuncta est. Quæ uti ju- stitiam & veritatem dominari optat: Sic ob inju- stitiam testatur, quod per μείωσιν hic effertur, non gaudet, ob veritatem vero laudatur.

## 13:7
Vers. 7. Πάντα στέγει.

It bears what can be borne in any way. See above IX. 12. Universal terms are accustomed to be restricted by the underlying subject matter. Thus Gen. III. 20. Of every living thing, the Chaldean interprets as of all the sons of man.

Πάντα πιστεύει.

It prefers to believe things which, when believed, do no harm, rather than rashly to condemn someone of a lie.

Πάντα ἐλπίζει.

It does not easily despair of anyone that they might be able to come to a better way of life. Euripides: Οὕτως δ᾽ ἀνὴρ ἄριστος ὅστις ἐλπίσι Πέποιθεν αἰεί.

Πάντα ὑπομένει.

From those who are in progress, he expects better things daily. It is a Greek maxim. Περιστέλλει τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἡ ἔννοια. Add Prov. X. 12.

Charity, on account of long-suffering and kindness, which are proper to those who truly love, as far as positive acts are concerned: 1. It bears all things: For charity covers all transgressions, Prov. X. 12. It placidly tolerates the infirmities of one's neighbor, and labors to restore him with meekness, Gal. VI. 1. 2. Or as some explain: It covers all things with the cloak of charity, hiding them as with a banner, as far as can be done honestly, those things which happen that are less right and just, which is also the meaning of the word στέγει. 2. It believes all things. For the candid person thinks others are of the same candor as himself. Yet it is one thing to believe every word out of simplicity, which is not of prudence, Prov. XIV, 17, and another out of charity. 3. It hopes all things concerning one's neighbor, and does not cast away hope of his amendment, but promises itself good things concerning him. 4. It endures all things, ὑπομένει, it brings in perseverance in the hope conceived; if amendment does not follow immediately, it nevertheless endures by hoping, and long-sufferingly seeks and promotes the neighbor's conversion. Estius: It endures all things, that is, evils, whatever are inflicted by men, such as curses, insults, slanders, exiles, chains, torments, death itself, it bears with an even mind, as much for the sake of the salvation of those by whom it suffers these things, as for others: Among these, it even prays to GOD for its enemies, that He may grant them repentance, which is surely of great charity. Paul declares this sense to us by his own example, 2 Tim. II, when speaking of his persecutions he says: I endure all things for the elect's sake, that they also may obtain salvation, where it is read similarly as here: Πάντα ὑπομένω. But Musculus rightly: These are not to be referred indiscriminately to all things in general, but only to those which a pious man, loving sincerely not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, can suffer, believe, hope, and endure. He can, however, do all things which neither displease GOD, nor are repugnant to piety, nor harm the salvation of the brother whom he loves. Thomas and Lyranus refer these three, it believes all things, it hopes all things, it endures all things, to the three Theological virtues, to faith, hope, and patience. But these are foreign. Lombard, Hervaeus, and others take these as concerning the duty of charity toward GOD, in whom one must believe, in whom one must hope, for whom all things must be endured: But the former [are] concerning duties toward one's neighbor. But more correctly, and more conveniently to the scope of the Apostle, Pelagius, Primasius, and Sedulius refer these three also to one's neighbor.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Πάντα στέγει.

Fert quæ fieri ullo modo possunt. Vide supra IX. 12. So- lent voces universales restringi ex materia subjacente. Sic Gen. III. 20. Omnis viventis Chaldæus interpretatur omnium filiorum hominis.

Πάντα πιστεύει.

Mavult credere quæ credita nihil nocent, quam temere aliquem mendacii damnare.

Πάντα ἐλπίζει.

Non facile de quoquam desperat quin ad meliorem fru- gem venire possit. Euripides: Οὕτως δ᾽ ἀνὴρ ἄριστος ὅστις ἐλπίσι Πέποιθεν αἰεί.

Πάντα ὑπομένει.

Ab iis qui in profectu sunt, indies meliora expectat. Græca est sententia. Περιστέλλει τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἡ ἔννοια. Adde Prov. X. 12.

Charitas ob μακροθυμίαν & χρηστότητα, quæ pro- pria sunt vere amantibus, quantum ad actus po- sitivos 1. Omnia suffert : Nam omnes prævarica- tiones operit charitas, Prov. X. 12. Infirmitates proximi placide tolerat, & eum καταρτίζειν με- τὰ πραότητος laborat Gal. VI. 1. 2. Vel ut non- nulli exponunt : Omnia tegit pallio charitatis, veluti vexillo occultans, quantum honeste fieri potest, quæ minus recta & justa accidunt, quæ etiam vocis στέγει significatio est. 2. Omnia credit. Nam candidus alios ejusdem secum candoris esse existimat. Aliud tamen ex simplicitate omni ver- bo credere, quod non est prudentiæ, Prov. XIV, 17. aliud ex charitate. 3. Omnia sperat de proximo, & de emendatione spem non abjicit, sed bona de eo sibi pollicetur. 4. Omnia sustinet, ὑπομένει perseverantiam in spe concepta infert, si non statim sequatur emendatio, sustinet tamen spe- rando & μακροθύμως proximi conversionem quærit & promovet. Estius: Omnia sustinet, id est mala, quæcunque ab hominibus inferuntur, ut maledicta, contumelias, obtrectationes, exilia, vincula, tormenta, mortem ipsam æquo fert ani- mo, tam propter ipsorum salutem, à quibus hæc patitur, quam aliorum : Inter hæc etiam DEUM pro inimicis orans, ut det illis pœni- tentiam, quod profecto magnæ charitatis est. Hunc sensum Paulus suo ipsius exemplo nobis declarat, 2. Tim. II. cum de persecutionibus suis loquens ait: Omnia sustineo propter electos, ut & ipsi salutem consequantur, ubi similiter ut hic legitur: Πάντα ὑπομένω. Recte autem Mu- sculus : Non sunt hæc citra discretionem in uni- versum ad omnia referenda, sed ad ea tantum, quæ homo pius & sincere non secundum car- nem, sed secundum Spiritum diligens, sufferre, credere, sperare, ac sustinere potest. Potest autem omnia, quæ nec DEO displiceant, nec pietati repugnent, neque fratris, quem diligit, salutem incommodent. Thomas & Lyranus hæc tria, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet, ad tres virtutes Theologicas refert, ad fidem, spem & patientiam. Sed haec aliena sunt. Lombardus, Hervaeus & alii de officio charitatis erga DEUM, cui credendum, in quem sperandum, ob quem sustinenda omnia, haec accipiunt: Superiora autem de officiis erga proximum. Sed rectius, & scopo Apostoli convenientius, Pelagius, Primasius, Sedulius haec tria etiam ad proximum referunt.

## 13:8
Vers. 8. Love never fails.

לא נבל It never lacks use.

Whether there be prophecies, they shall be done away; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall be done away.

In that better age, neither foretellings of the future nor the commemoration of the past will have use. For there will be there a most present knowledge of all things which it will be expedient to know for that state. And here is the failure, if prophecies, namely, happen to anyone.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει.

לא נבל Nunquam usu caret.

Εἴτε δὲ προφητεῖαι καταργηθήσονται, εἴτε γλῶσσαι παύσονται, εἴτε γνῶσις καταργηθήσεται.

In seculo illo meliore neque praesagia futurorum, neque commemoratio praeteritorum usum habebit. Erit enim ibi cognitio praesentissima omnium quae cognoscere pro illo statu expediet. Et hic ἔκπτωσις, si prophetiae, nempe alicui obtigere.

## 13:9
Vers. 9. For we know in part.

He explains what he had said: Knowledge will not be lacking, but it will not be such as it is now. For if we look at present things, how much is it that even those who have obtained the greatest gifts in that matter are ignorant?

And we prophesy in part.

There are few things about which prophecies are given: And not even the Prophets themselves fully understand them, except after the event.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐκ μέρους δὲ γινώσκομεν.

Explicat quae dixerat: Non deerit cognitio, sed non talis erit qualis nunc est. Nam si res praesentes spectamus, quantum est quod ignorant etiam qui maxima ea in re dona sunt consequuti?

Καὶ ἐκ μέρους προφητεύομεν.

Pauca sunt de quibus dantur prophetiae: Et eas ne Prophetae quidem ipsi plene intelligunt, nisi post eventum.

## 13:10
Ver. 10. But when that which is perfect is come.

That more perfect life, which is αἰὼν τετελειωμένος, Heb. VII. ver. 28.

Then that which is in part shall be done away.

Those gifts shall cease, because the knowledge of all will be the same.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον.

Vita illa perfectior, quae αἰὼν τετελειωμένος, Hebr. VII. vers. 28.

Τότε τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται.

Dona illa cessabunt, quia omnibus eadem erit cognitio.

## 13:11
Ver. 11. When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child.

He illustrates the matter with a comparison, which Maimonides also uses. There is one kind of speech, other pursuits, and other concepts of things for children, and these things are different for men. But the difference between this time and that heavenly life will be much greater: The boy who now knows how to utter words and marks the ground with a steady foot, delights to play with his peers, and gathers and lays aside his anger rashly, and changes from hour to hour.

Concerning the word νηπίου see Matt. XXI. 16.

But when I became a man.

A man of full age Eph. IV. 13. Thus in Horace: The age and spirit of a man.

I have put away childish things.

That is, I have corrected the faults of speech, I have devoted myself to greater matters, I have understood the things themselves more clearly. Thus I have obliterated those former things.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὅτε ἤμην νήπιος, ὡς νήπιος ἐλάλουν, ὡς νήπιος ἐφρόνουν, ὡς νήπιος ἐλογιζόμην.

Similitudine rem illustrat, qua & Maimonides utitur. Alius est sermo, alia studia, alii rerum conceptus pueris, alia haec viris. Multo autem major erit differentia temporis hujus & illius caelestis vitae: Reddere qui voces jam scit puer & pede certo Signat humum, gestit paribus colludere, & iram Colligit ac ponit temere & mutatur in horas.

De voce νηπίου vide Matth. XXI. 16.

Ὅτε δὲ γέγονα ἀνήρ.

Vir plenae aetatis Eph. IV. 13. Sic apud Horatium: Aetas animusque virilis.

Κατήργηκα τὰ τοῦ νηπίου.

Id est, sermonis vitia correxi, studui rebus majoribus, res ipsas intellexi clarius. Ita priora illa obliteravi.

## 13:12
Ver. 12. For now we see through a glass, in a riddle. But then face to face.

This appears to be taken from Num. XII, where Moses is preferred over other Prophets in that he understood things to be done and future things not through shadowing figures, but by open indications, as if through the conversation of a friend. But the difference between the knowledge that Moses had and the knowledge of the future age will be much greater than that which then existed between Moses and the other Prophets. Paul added that διʼ ἐσόπτρου, because the things we see in a mirror cannot be touched: it is a certain image of a thing, not the thing itself. What he said here πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον, he said פנים בפנים. 2 Cor. V. 7, that is, to the Hebrews תמונה.

Not only the use and fruit of charity is regarded. For as we love primarily with spirit and heart; so charity remains, even if it does not proceed outwardly. For it cannot always exert itself through works, and yet it does not ἐκπίπτει. Blessed Luther explains charity as not growing weary in doing good. Thus also Chrysostom [says it does] not fail in this life, and Erasmus, it never falls away, that is, it ceases, it is useful everywhere, where it is of use. But the comparison of prophecies teaches that the perpetuity and duration of charity is regarded not only in this, but also in the future age. There is no place there for prophecies, because nothing will be future there, but mere eternity. And therefore in the future age prophecies will cease entirely. Their use, however, will be conspicuous even then, especially: The commemoration of past things, indeed, will be among the chief works of the blessed for the eternal glorification of GOD: Therefore, when the saints pray for something in this age, they promise the eternal celebration of the divine name. Tongues will cease in the future life, because there will be no variety of tongues there, just as there was none before the confusion of tongues, nor did it have a place in the state of integrity. Rightly, therefore, Estius here: He does not say that language will cease, but tongues. For the use of bodily language, that is, sensible speech, will not cease after the resurrection, but there will not be kinds of tongues there. For there will be no need for a gift of this kind there, where all the elect will be of one lip and the same speech, much more than men were from the beginning of their kind until the building of the tower of Babel, Gen. XI. Knowledge, which pertains to this life, will be done away with, such as is had from the revealed word or the book of nature. For then clear and intuitive cognition will succeed in the blessed vision of GOD, and situated in glorious illumination, that partial, imperfect, and inadequate knowledge will cease, which is merely childish; but total, perfect, and adequate knowledge will succeed, truly manly, absolute and consummated in all ways and respects. According to which we will also be ἰσάγγελοι. Speculative and enigmatic knowledge will cease, the knowledge of vision and immediate knowledge will follow, which is face to face, where it is not just a species as in a mirror, but we will gaze upon the object itself, GOD himself, as he is. 1 John III. verse 2. That abolition and cessation, according to some, is not to be understood through annihilation, or alteration, or temporal rest, in the way that things that rest for a time cease, but as regards completion and consummation, just as the light of dawn ceases while it is completed and perfected by the rising of the sun. Just as that λογικὸν which children have in themselves is not abolished by manly age, but is rather completed and rendered more perfect, while its imperfection is abolished: So also the knowledge of GOD itself remaining in itself, its imperfection being abolished, says Musculus. But Estius raises a doubt, whether it should not also be said that charity will cease, because it will become perfect from the imperfect, such as it is now? Some, therefore, say that the sciences acquired in this age perish at death along with the senses of the body. But Thomas refutes this in this place and I. q. 98. art. 5, because knowledge is in the intellect, not in the sense, from which it does not depend even according to the species of the act in the separated soul. Cajetan says that knowledge will cease because it includes something imperfect in its definition, like faith and hope. But if knowledge formally includes imperfection, how is it attributed to GOD himself? It is more convenient, because others with Thomas judge that the mode of present cognition will cease, because the separated soul contemplates without a phantasm, nor does it need revelation of the word made through the scriptures. It pleases Estius more that the gift of scripture, by reason of its use for informing one's neighbor, will cease, because there all will be perfectly taught by GOD, and no one will have need of the information of another. When, therefore, it is asked how charity is not also to be abolished in the future, since, just as we know and prophesy in part; so also we love in part. For all our love in this state of the way is imperfect. Estius answers: Prophecy, tongues, and knowledge will not cease because they are imperfect in themselves, but because they were given only on account of the imperfection of others. But charity is not given solely, nor properly, for the utility of others. For in truth the Apostle clearly teaches that our knowledge, which is of this life, as also prophecy, is to be destroyed for this reason: that here we know only in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away with. Which things teach most clearly that it is a question here of the imperfection of those in whom those gifts reside, not of others for whose instruction they served. Which is also confirmed by the similitude taken from childish and manly age, since in it the imperfection and perfection of him in whom the gifts and qualities are, of which there is speech, is regarded, and not in others. For he who speaks, thinks, and reasons as a little child; the same man, having become a man, puts off childish speech, sense, and thought, and does all things manfully, that is, perfectly. Nor does the other similitude of specular and obscure vision, compared with clear and direct vision, prove that opinion any less. Because the same people who here know in part, since they see only through a mirror in an enigma, will one day know fully by clear, direct, and intuitive vision. Nor can that ἐκ μέρους, in part, be accepted with the partiality of the subject, that some of the faithful have knowledge and prophecy only in the kingdom of grace, but in the kingdom of glory all the elect will have it. But concerning the partiality of knowledge, because it is opposed to τὸ τέλειον itself, or perfect knowledge. Wherefore it must be said that knowledge is to be done away with, which is on the way by reason of its principle and mode of existing, because it arises from Prophetic and Apostolic scripture, because the oἰκονομία of the kingdom of grace, which is administered through the word and sacraments, will cease in the kingdom of glory, or the spiritual fatherland; And at death all knowledge, which is in this life, is to be lacking through phantasms. Concerning our Theological knowledge, which deduces conclusions from the principles of faith, Cornelius à Lapide explains with Cajetan, Molina, and Vasquez, because there theology will be of another species, as being from the vision of GOD and most evident principles, most evident. He adds, however, other interpretations as well. Photius, he says, explains not badly that γνῶσις, that doctrine and learning, will be done away with. For in heaven we will neither teach nor learn. Others say that knowledge, that is, the use of the language of knowledge, by which matters of faith are here explained and illustrated through natural sciences, will cease in heaven. B. Hunnius: Knowledge also shall be abolished, that is, that mode of knowing which consists in teaching and learning, and which strives from the lowest degree to a higher one by successive increments, yet does not reach the pinnacle of perfection in this life. This habit of successive knowledge, this mode of knowing, this incomplete and imperfect awareness will have no place in that light of eternity. Of this Paul writes: We know in part and we prophesy in part. Indeed, insofar as the whole counsel of GOD is revealed to us by the benefit of scripture, Acts 20. and insofar as nothing is lacking to our knowledge that pertains to the attainment of eternal salvation: thus far our knowledge itself is also called perfect: But if it be compared with the absolute wisdom of the other life, it is not without reason said that our knowledge is ἐκ μέρους in part, or imperfect. Prophecy also shall be done away, because in itself it includes imperfection, insofar as it is a prediction of future things. For there nothing will be future, but a perpetual νῦν. Charity, however, will not be abolished; because he who dies in charity, his charity is not destroyed with death in the soul separated from the body, but the soul, irradiated by the light of glory, emerges far more perfect from a more imperfect state: for God is charity, and he who remains in charity, remains in GOD 1 John IV. 16.
