The Apostle v. 12 explained the difference between this knowledge and the future life thus: Now I know in part, but then I shall know, even as I have been known; Namely, just as I am known by God intimately both as to essence and as to all things that are in me, a priori and by intuitive knowledge; so also I shall know God, and other things whatsoever that befit the elect ἰσαγγέλοις, not by gathering them a posteriori, but a priori, through the beatific vision of GOD, and intuitive knowledge, not only as to attributes, but as to the very essence itself. In the simile concerning different age, some note a preposterous order of speech, because the first thing is to think or reason, then to feel something, and thirdly, as it were, to conclude what you feel. But there is no need to admit a preposterous order. That order is correct, and one ascends by degrees according to Grotius's explanation. Nor does Thomas inappropriately refer those things to the gifts reviewed above: He says, it can be referred, what he says: I spoke as a child, to the gift of tongues. When he says, I understood as a child, to the gift of prophecy: But what he adds, I thought as a child, to the gift of knowledge. Aretinus beautifully here: What else is the gift of tongues than the babbling of this life? And the wisdom of this life, than childish nuts? And the power of gathering Dialectics (as an infant ἐλογιζόμην) seems something nervous and splendid: But that Dialectic is childish: They ride on a long reed. B. Hülsemann refers those things concerning the different progress of childish and manly age to the different progress of catechumens and the perfect in the state of grace; as Gal. IV. 13, Chap. III. 24, 1 Cor. I. 2, Rom. II. 10, Eph. IV. 14, Heb. V. 13, 1 Cor. XIV. 20, but not to a diversity of grace. And he explains that ἐκ μέρους as to time: And from there he seeks an argument for the cessation of miracles in the Church, which the Apostle predicted here. But since the Apostle opposed τὸ τέλειον to τῷ ἐκ μέρους, not a part of time, but partial knowledge is regarded, to which a more perfect one is opposed. Nor can these be torn away from v. 12 as to sense, where it is granted that a comparison is instituted between the state of grace and glory; and therefore we judge that one must adhere to the common interpretation received by all. In the words δι᾽ ἐσόπτρου, B. Glassius notes in Grammat. S. p. 506 that the particle διά is taken ἐνυπαρτικῶς and signifies IN.

Now I know in part.

The things which I myself, who am an Apostle, have known from the gifts, are small compared to the knowledge of the better age. This tends to this end, that those who have received such gifts here may not grow insolent.

But then I shall know fully.

I shall know exactly every way by which God governed the world and procured the salvation of men, and the causes of the dispensations. See 1 John III. 2. Ἐπιγινώσκειν is more than γινώσκειν. For ἐπὶ increases it. See Rom. III. 20, X. 2. Philo on Allegories: Those who thus reason through a shadow grasp God, through works, understanding the craftsman. But there is a certain more perfect and more purified idea, having been initiated into the great mysteries, who does not know the cause from the things that have come to be, as if from a shadow the remaining thing, but having looked beyond the generated, receives a clear impression of the ungenerated, so as to grasp him from himself, and his shadow just as both the word and this world. Hebrews and Plato in the Philosopher also posit that knowledge will be perfect in the other life.

Even as I have been known.

That is, just as God knows my counsels and thoughts exactly. Juvenal concerning the Gods: Man is better known to them than to himself. See also above IV. 4, 1 John III. 20.

Some explain that καϑὼς causally, because I have been known by God. But the Apostle is occupied here in explaining the manner. Nor should one depart from the proper meaning. Moreover, the compound verb ἐπιγνώσομαι is used for the sake of emphasis concerning the knowledge of the other life, whereas for the knowledge of this life the simple verb alone has been used. And it is to know above or more, so that the eminence of the future knowledge may be indicated. The Apostle says he is known, however, not by reason of the first conservation, where he is known by GOD through heavenly vision, as Drusius lib. VI. praeter p. 235 explains. For that was personal, and proper to Paul. Here, however, the discourse is about the common lot of the elect faithful, and not only by reason of knowledge, election, or predestination to eternal life, for although I do not deny that this knowledge is included, yet just as God knows his own as to faith, which lies hidden in the heart: 2 Tim. II. 19. Thus he knows all things that are in them intimately, he also knows and beholds our very essence immediately: Because in him we live, and move, and have our being Acts 17, 28. c. XV. 18. Then in heaven, says Cornelius à Lapide, I shall perfectly know and behold God, as he is in his essence, and the remaining mysteries of GOD and faith, just as he himself knows and beholds me, this which I am through my essence. Thus Anselm, Theophylact, Cajetan, Ambrose; and Theodorecus: I shall know, he says, even as I have been known, that is, as one known and familiar, who clearly beholds the face of a friend. B. Hunnius explains it thus: Just as God acknowledges us most perfectly: So in turn we shall know GOD most perfectly, he indeed with divine and infinite perfection, we however not with infinite, but finite, and nevertheless complete in its own kind, as much as can indeed fall to a rational creature.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι διʼ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι. Τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον.

Apparet haec sumpta ex Num. XII. ubi Moses aliis Prophetis profertur eo quod non per figuras adumbrantes, sed apertis indiciis velut per amici colloquium sibi facienda & futura alia intelligeret. Multo autem majus erit discrimen inter cognitionem quam habuit Moses & cognitionem futuri aevi quam tunc fait inter Mosen & Prophetas alios. Addidit Paulus illud διʼ ἐσόπτρου, quia quae in speculo videmus, ea palpari nequeunt: Imago quaedam est rei, non res ipsa. Quod hic dixit πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον id dixit פנים בפנים. 2. Cor. V. 7. id est Hebraeis תמונה.

Non tantum usus & fructus charitatis respicitur. Nam ut spiritu & corde cumprimis diligimus; ita manet charitas, etiamsi ad extra non prodeat. Non enim semper sese per opera exerere potest, nec tamen ἐκπίπτει. B. Lutherus non fatigari benefaciendo charitatem exponit. Sic etiam Chrysostomus non deficere in hac vita, & Erasmus, nunquam excidit, hoc est cessat, ubique prodest, ubi est usui. Sed collatio prophetiarum docet perennitatem & durationem charitatis respici non tantum in hoc, sed & in futuro seculo. Ibi nullus prophetiis locus, quia nihil ibi futurum, sed mera æternitas. Ideoque in seculo futuro desinent plane prophetiæ. Usus autem earum conspicuus vel maxime tum erit: Præteritorum vero commemoratio ad æternam DEI glorificationem inter præcipua beatorum opera erit: Ideo cum aliquid precantur in hoc seculo, æternam nominis divini pollicentur cele- brationem sancti. Linguæ cessabunt in futura vita, quia ibi linguarum varietas nulla erit, quem- admodum ante linguarum confusionem nulla fuit, nec in statu integritatis locum habuit. Recte ergo hic Estius: Non dicit linguam ces- saturam, sed linguas. Non enim post resurre- ctionem cessabit usus linguæ corporeæ, id est loquutio sensibilis, sed non erunt ibi genera linguarum. Neque enim hujusmodi dono illic opus erit, ubi electi omnes erunt labii unius & sermonem eorundem, multo magis quam fue- runt homines ab exordio sui generis usque ad extructionem turris Babel, Genes. XI. Scien- tia, quæ ad hanc vitam pertinet, evacuabitur, qualis scilicet è verbo revelato, vel libro na- turæ habetur. Tum enim clara & intuitiva cognitio succedet in visione DEI beata, & il- luminatione gloriosa sita, cessabit partialis, im- perfecta & inæquata illa cognitio, quæ mere puerilis, succedet vero totalis, perfecta & ad- æquata, vere virilis, omnibus modis & nume- ris absoluta ac consummata. Juxta quam etiam ἰσάγγελοι erimus. Desinet specularis & ænig- matica notitia, sequetur cognitio visionis & imme- diata, quæ est à facie ad faciem, ubi non spe- ciem tantum velut in speculo fit, sed objectum ipsum intuebimur, DEUM ipsum, sicuti est. 1. Johan. III. vers. 2. Abolitio illa & cessatio secundum quosdam non per annihilationem, aut alterationem, aut quietem temporalem, quomodo cessant, quæ ad tempus quiescunt, intelligenda, sed quoad complementum & consummationem, uti lux auroræ cessat, dum ex ortu solis com- pletur & perficitur. Quemadmodum λογικὸν illud, quod habent pueri in se, non aboletur per virilem ætatem, sed magis completur, atque perfectius redditur, aboletur vero illius imper- fectio: Sic & ipsa scientia DEI in se manente abolita illius imperfectio, ait Musculus. Sed dubium movet Estius, annon ita etiam charita- tem cessaturam dicendum sit, quia ex imperfe- cta, qualis nunc est, perfecta fiet? Nonnulli er- go scientias in hoc seculo acquisitas cum sensi- bus corporis perire in morte ajunt. Quod vero refellit Thomas in hunc locum & I. q. 98. art. 5. quia scientia est in intellectu, non in sensu, à quo nec secundum speciem actus dependet in anima separata. Cajetanus cessaturam scientiam ait, quod in sua ratione aliquid imperfecti includat, sicut fides & spes. Sed si scientia formaliter imperfe- ctionem includit, quomodo DEO ipsi tribui- tur? Convenientius est, quia alii cum Thoma modum cognitionis præsentis cessaturum censent, quod anima separata sine phantasmate contem- pletur, neque verbi revelatione per scripturas facta indigeat. Estio magis placet, quod do- num scripturæ ratione usus ad proximum infor- matorii cessaturum sit, quia ibi omnes à DEO perfecte docti erunt, nullaque informatione alterius quisquam opus habebit. Cum ergo quæritur, quomodo charitas non etiam abo- lenda sit in futuro, quandoquidem, uti cognosci- mus & prophetamus ex parte; ita etiam diligi- mus ex parte. Omnis enim dilectio nostra in hoc statu viæ imperfecta est. Respondet Estius: Prophetia, linguæ, scientia non ideo cessabunt, quod in seipsis imperfecta sunt, sed quia tantum propter aliorum imperfectionem data. At charitas nec solum, nec proprie datur ob utilitatem aliorum. Verum enim vero Apostolus aperte docet, scientiam nostram, quæ hujus vitæ, ut & prophetiam ea ratione destruendam; quod hic ex parte tantum cognoscamus & ex parte prophetemus, seu partialis tantum sit nostra cognitio & prophetia. Cum autem venerit id, quod perfectum est, evacuatum iri, quod ex parte est. Quæ luculentissime docent de imperfectione eorum, quibus insunt illa dona, non aliorum, quibus erudiendis servierunt, hic agi. Quod etiam confirmat similitudo ab ætate puerili & virili desumpta, quum in ea respiciatur imperfectio & perfectio ejus, cui insunt dona, & qualitates illæ, de quibus sermo est, non vero in aliis. Qui enim ut parvulus puer loquitur, sapit, cogitat; idem ipse vir factus puerilem sermonem, sensum, cogitationem exuit, ac viriliter, id est, perfecte omnia agit. Nec minus comprobat eam sententiam altera similitudo visionis specularis & obscuræ, collatæ cum visione clara & directa. Quia iidem, qui hic ex parte cognoscunt, quum videant solum per speculum in ænigmate, olim plene agnoscent visione clara, directa & intuitiva. Neque vero illud ἐκ μέρους ex parte cum partialitate subjecti, quod nonnulli fidelium in regno gratiæ tantum cognitionem & prophetiam habeant, in regno autem gloriæ omnes electi habituri sint, accipi potest. Sed de partialitate cognitionis, quia opponitur ipsi τὸ τέλειον, seu perfecta cognitio. Quapropter evacuatum iri scientiam dicendum est, quæ in via est ratione principii & modi existendi, quod ea oriatur è scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica, quia oἰκονομία regni gratiæ, quod per verbum & sacramenta administratur, cessabit in regno gloriæ, vel spiritualis patriæ; Et in morte omnis scientia, quæ in hac vita est, per phantasmata defutura est. De cognitione nostra Theologica, quæ ex principiis fidei conclusiones deducit, explicat Cornelius à Lapide cum Cajetano, Molina, Vasquezio, quia ibi alia specie Theologia futura est, utpote ex visione DEI, & principiis evidentissimis, evidentissima. Addit tamen & alias interpretationes. Photius non male, inquit, explicat, quod γνῶσις ea doctrina & discentia evacuabitur. In cœlo enim nec docebimus, nec discemus. Alii, scientia, inquiunt, id est usus sermonis scientiæ, quo hic res fidei per scientias naturales explicantur & illustrantur, in cœlo cessabit. B. Hunnius: Abolebitur & scientia, hoc est ille sciendi modus, qui in docendo, discendoque consistit, & ab infimo gradu ad altiorem subinde per incrementa contendit, nec tamen ad perfectionis fastigium in hac vita pertingit. Hic successivæ scientiæ habitus, hic cognoscendi modus, hæc manca & imperfecta notitia in illa æternitatis luce locum habebit nullum. De hoc scribit Paulus: Ex parte cognoscimus & ex parte prophetamus. Equidem quatenus scripturæ beneficio nobis revelatur omne consilium DEI Actor. XX. & quatenus cognitioni nostræ nihil deest, quod ad consecutionem salutis æternæ pertinet: Hactenus ipsa quoque notitia nostra perfecta dicitur: At si conferatur cum absoluta sapientia vitæ alterius, haud abs re dicitur cognitio nostra esse ἐκ μέρους ex parte, sive imperfecta. Evacuabitur & prophetia, quia in se imperfectionem includit, quatenus est futurorum prædictio. Ibi enim nihil futurum erit, sed perpe- tuum νῦν. Charitas autem non evacnabitur; quia qui in charitate decedit, ejus charitas cum morte non aboletur in anima à corpore separata, sed ex imperfectiori longe perfectior evadit anima per lumen gloriæ irradiata: Deus enim est charitas, & qui in charitate manet, manet in DEO 1. Joh. IV. 16. Cognitionis hujus & futuræ vitæ diversitatem A- postolus v. 12. sic exposuit: Nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc autem cognoscam, sicut & cognitus sum; Uti nempe à Deo intime & quoad essentiam, & quoad omnia, quæ in me, cognitus sum à priori, & intui- tiva notitia; ita & ego cognoscam Deum, & alia, quæcunque electis ἰσαγγέλοις conveniunt, non à posteriori modo ea colligendo, sed à priori, per visionem DEI beatificam, & cognitionem intuiti- vam, non tātum quoad attributa, sed quoad ipsam- met essentiam. In similitudine de diversa ætate nonnulli orationem præposteram notant, quod pri- mum sit cogitare seu ratiocinari, deinde sentire ali- quid, ac veluti concludere tertio, quod sentias. Sed nō opus est admittere ordinem præposterum. Recte se ille ordo habet, & ascenditur per gradus juxta explicationem Grotii. Nec incommode Thomas illa refert ad dona superius recensita: Po test, inquit, referri, quod dicit: Loquebar, ut par- vulus, ad donum linguarum. Cum dicit, sapiebam ut parvulus, ad donum prophetiæ: Quod autem subdit, cogitabam ut parvulus, ad donum scientiæ. Pulchre hic Aretins: Quid linguarum donum aliud est, quam balbuties hujus vitæ? Et sapientia hujus vitæ, quam pueriles nuces? Et vis colligendi Dia- lectica (ut infans ἐλογιζόμην) nervosū quiddam & splendidum videtur: Sed puerilis est illa Dialecti- ca: Equitant in arundine longa. B. Hülsemannus illa de diversis profectibus ætatis puerilis & virilis refert ad profectus diversos catechumenorum & per fectorum in statu gratiæ; ut Gal. IV. 13 Cap. III. 24. 1. Cor. I. 2. Rom. II. 10. Eph. IV. 14. Ebr. V. 13. 1. Cor. XIV. 20. non vero ad diversitatem gratiæ. Illudque ἐκ μέρυς exponit ad tempus: Atque inde argumen- tum petit cessationis miraculorum in Ecclesia, quam hic prædixerit Apostolus. Sed quum Apo- stolus τῷ ἐκ μέρυς opposuerit τὸ τέλειον, non pars temporis, sed partialis cognitio respicitur, cui per- fectior opposita est. Neque divelli possunt hæc à v. 12. quoad sensum, ubi conceditur collationem institui status gratiæ & gloriæ; ideoque communi & penes omnes receptæ interpretationi inhæren- dum censemus. In verbis δι᾽ ἐσόπτρε particulam διὰ ἐνυπαρτικῶς accipi, & IN significare, notat B. Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 506.

Ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρυς.

Quæ ipse ego qui sum Apostolus ex donis cognovi, exi- gua sunt præ cognitione seculi melioris. Hoc eo tendit, ne insolescant qui talia dona hic acccepere.

Τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι.

Exacte novero omnem modum, per quem Deus mun- dum gubernavit & salutem hominum procuravit, & dispen- sationum causas. Vide 1. Joh. III. 2. Ἐπιγινώσκειν plus est quam γινώσκειν. Nam ἐπὶ auget. Vide Rom. III. 20. X. 2. Philo de Allegoriis: Οἱ δὲ οὕτως ἐπιλεγιζόμενοι διὰ σκιᾶς τὸν Θεὸν καταλαμβάνουσι, διὰ τῶν ἔργων, τὸν τεχνίτην κατα- νοοῦντες. Ἐστί δέ τις τελεώτερος, καὶ μᾶλλον κεκαθαρμένος ἰδέα, τὰ μεγάλα μυστήρια μυηθεὶς, ὅς τις ἐκ ἀπὸ τῶν γεγονότων τὸ αἴτιον γνωρίζει, ὡς ἂν ἀπὸ σκιᾶς τὸ μένον, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπερκύψας τὸ γενητὸν, ἔμφασιν ἐναργῆ τοῦ ἀγενήτου λαμβάνει, ὡς ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ αὐτὸν καταλαμβάνειν, κὰι τὴν σκιὰν αὐτοῦ ὥσπερ ἐν τόν τε λό- γον κὰι τόνδε τὸν κόσμον. Perfectam fore in vita altera cogni- tionem etiam Hebræi statuunt & Plato in Philosopho.

Καθὼς κὰι ἐπεγνώσθην.

Id est, sicut Deus mea consilia & cogitata exacte novit. Juvenalis de Diis: Notior est illis homo quam sibi. Vide & supra IV. 4. 1. Joh. III. 20.

Illud καϑὼς nonnulli explicant causaliter, quia à Deo cognitus sum. Sed Apostolus versatur hic in explicando modo. Nec à propria significatione dis- cedendum est. Adhibetur autem emphaseos cau- sa verbum compositum ἐπιγνώσομαι de cognitione alterius vitæ, quum de cognitione hujus vitæ sim- plex verbum solum adhibitum sit. Estque illud su- per vel amplius cognoscere, ut eminentia futuræ co- gnitionis indicetur. Cognitum autem se dicit Apo- stolus non ratione prima conservationis, ubi per visionem cælestem à DEO cognitus, ut Drusius lib. VI. præter p. 235. explicat. Id enim personale erat, & proprium Paulo. Hic vero de communi sorte electorum fidelium est sermo, neque solum ratione cognitionis, electionis vel prædestinationis ad vitam æternam, nam ut hanc cognitionem in- cludi non negem, tamen uti quoad fidem, quæ la- tet in corde, Deus novit suos: 2. Tim. II.19. Ita novit omnia, quæ in ipsis sunt, intime, novit etiam atque intuetur ipsammet essentiam nostram immediate: Quia in ipso vivimus, movemur & sumus Actor. 17, 28. c. XV. 18. Tum in cælo, inquit Cornelius à La- pide, perfecte cognoscam & intuebor Deum, sicuti est in sua essentia, & reliqua DEI & fidei mysteria, si ut ipse me novit & intuetur hoc quod sum per meam essentiam. Ità Anselmus, Theophylactus, Cajeta- nus, Ambrosius; & Theodorecus: Cognoscam, inquit, sicut & cognitus sum, id est, sicut notus & familiaris, qui vultum amici clare intuetur. B. Hun- nius ita explicat: Sicut Deus nos agnoscit perfe- čtissime: Ita vicissim nos cognoscemus DEUM perfectissime, ille quidem perfectione divina & infinita, nos vero non infinita, sed finita, atque ni- hilominus in suo genere completa, quanta qui- dem in creaturam rationalem cadere potest.

## 13:13
Vers. 13. But now there remain faith, hope, charity, these three.

Νυνὶ here is not of time, but of opposition, for at vero as in Rom. III. 21. VII. 16. above V. 11. Mένει is opposed to that which he said καταργηθήσεται. But how will they remain (for the present here has the signification of the future, as below XV. 32. XVI. 3.) in the other age? Namely, in that way in which the rock followed the Israelites by its effect. Above X. 4. Thus works follow the dead. Apoc. XIV. 13. Faith, hope, love will have a reward, 2. Tim. IV. 7. 8. not prophecy Matth. VIII. 22. Balaam acted the Prophet, and was hateful to GOD, Judas v. 11. He adds τρία ταῦτα which ternary number is sacred to God.

These three sanctifying gifts, faith, hope, charity, are said to remain νυνὶ now, that is, as long as the present age lasts, which, since it is not said of other ministering gifts, it is implied that those gifts of miracles, prophecy, and tongues are to cease even here in the Church, as most think. Whether this can be firmly concluded from this, however, may be doubtful, since they also reckon knowledge among the ministering gifts, which remains in the Church at all times. Calvin says that τὸ μένειν to remain in this place is the same as saying that when all things are subtracted, as in a calculating ledger, this sum remains, so that the sense is: There are indeed many and various things, but all tend toward and look to this goal (of faith, hope, and charity). But this is foreign and twisted. The common interpretation is concerning the preservation and perpetual permanence of these gifts in the Church: Because the Church, which is the assembly of the faithful, cannot exist without faith, hope, and charity: Since hope is joined to faith. Charity, however, as the effect of the cause, is procreated from the mother, from faith. Grotius's gloss is singular: that Νυνὶ here is not a mark of time, but of opposition, which openly contradicts the text, inasmuch as μένει is to be taken in the Future, not as the present sounds: likewise the remaining in the other age is to be denoted, but by reason of the effect (the example concerning the rock does not fit; for the Rock did not follow them merely by its effect, but καθ' ὑπόστασιν: for it was Christ) faith, hope, and love to be considered by reason of the reward, since their permanence is in question here, not the reward: Finally, that the prophecies of the False Prophets are attended to here; which, however, does not appear in the least from the text.

Μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη.

Μείζων is also said of many things, as can be seen in Matt. 13:23, Luke 9:46. It is the greatest among these three: Because faith and hope lead to love. Love joins us to God and makes us like Him, 1 John 4:8. Without this, faith and hope themselves also remain fruitless, as can be understood from what was said at the beginning of this chapter. Gal. 5:6, James 2:10, and the following. Ignatius in his epistle to the Ephesians: Ἀρχὴ ζωῆς πίσις, τέλος δὲ ἀγάπη.

That charity is greater than faith and hope, because the latter lead to love, and the former joins us to God and makes us like Him, is repugnant to the analogy of faith. Faith does not so much lead to love as it is the cause of love according to Scripture: Nor is it taught anywhere that hope leads us to love. Nor does love join us to God, but faith, Eph. 1:12, Gal. 3:26, Mark 16:16, Heb. 11:6. According to St. Ignatius, faith is the causal principle of salvation, but the end is love, which in the other life not only endures but attains perfection. And in this sense most interpreters make love greater than hope and faith, because faith and hope look to this age, not to the future, where we shall walk not by faith, but by sight, 2 Cor. 5:7. Thus Chrysostom, Homily 24 on this passage: Charity is greater than faith and hope, because these pass away, that endures: Theodoret on this passage: Because gifts will cease, charity alone will remain. Augustine, Book I, De doctrina Christiana, ch. 38. To faith succeeds the thing which we shall see, and to hope succeeds the very blessedness to which we are to arrive. Charity, however, will be increased more strongly even when these pass away. For if we love by believing what we do not yet see, how much more when we have begun to see? And if we love by hoping for what we have not yet reached, how much more when we have reached it? Anselm on this passage: Because faith will cease when the future things which are believed have arrived, and hope will have received its blessedness, which each one awaits. But charity alone will persevere forever, and will rejoice without end in the vision of the Creator and the blessedness of the saints. The Roman Catholics also agree. Cornelius à Lapide; He says, Paul clearly teaches in this chapter that hope, faith, and charity remain here, but in the fatherland charity alone. Thus the Fathers. See Gregor. de Valentia, disp. I, q. 5, on the subject of faith, point II. Thus also Estius: Charity alone never fails, but remains in the fatherland, when faith will be changed into vision and hope into apprehension.

However, some others bring forward other reasons for the excellence of love, which it is pleasing to repeat here from B. Glassius's Exegetical Annotations on Quinquagesima Sunday, namely (1) because of the breadth of the object. Faith looks only at Christ, and has to do with God alone. Hope looks only at future goods and expects them: But charity is referred to God and to one's neighbor, and furthermore, it will most tranquilly enjoy future goods already obtained forever. (2) Because of manifestation. Other virtues hide themselves in the recesses of the human heart: But charity renders itself conspicuous in external works, and is the virtue through which faith itself exerts itself; and as Paul says, it is effective, Gal. 5:6. (3) Because of operation. Because it provides the greatest utility in the government of the Church and in preserving peace among men, which reason B. Mylius observed was attended to here.

But the inference of the Papists is vain, that love justifies, not faith, because love is said to be greater than faith. Because the comparison is instituted here not by reason of justification, concerning which article not even a jot is held here, but by reason of duration, or if you prefer, for other reasons of prerogative, as not a few, even Roman Catholics, acknowledge. Therefore again, says B. Mylius, the Roman Catholics commit the fallacy of 'in a certain respect and simply' and 'of the non-cause as a cause,' arguing thus: Charity is superior to faith: Therefore it justifies, or at least contributes more to justification than faith: Just as if someone were to conclude from the fact that gold is superior to bread, that gold also nourishes. Dr. Sebastian Schmid denies that justifying faith is understood here, and explains it as faith by which, without rash and evil suspicion, one believes the words, promises, and any signs of the mind of another (God and man): Just as hope, according to the same author, is that which always hopes for good or better things about another, and does not rashly distrust what kind of person he will have him to be in the future: But he makes charity the mother and origin of both, so that it may beget faith and hope from itself, and charity believes and hopes all things. See the Disputation on 1 Cor. 13:13 concerning the excellence of charity. Which opinion we leave in its place, easily, and without detriment to Evangelical orthodoxy, conceding that justifying faith is designated. This faith, which believes the words and promises of GOD, does not seem to be separable from miraculous faith: But here the 'better' or more excellent gifts are shown.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Νυνὶ δὲ μένει πίςις, ἐλπὶς, ἀγάπη, τὰ τρία ταῦτα.

Νυνὶ hic non est temporis, sed oppositionis pro at vero ut Rom. III. 21. VII. 16. supra V. 11. Mένει oppositum est ei quod dixit καταργηθήσεται. Sed quomodo manebunt (præsens enim hic futuri habet significationem, ut infra XV. 32. XVI. 3.) in altero ævo? Nempe eo modo; quo rupes Israëlitas sequebatur effectu suo. Supra X. 4. Sic mortuos sequuntur opera. Apoc. XIV. 13. Fides, spes, di- lectio præmium habebunt, 2. Tim. IV. 7. 8. non prophetia Matth. VIII. 22. Balaam Prophetam egit, & DEO invisus fuit, Judas v. 11. Addit τρία ταῦτα qui ternarius numerus Deo sacer.

Hæc tria dona sanctificantia fides, spes, charitas νυνὶ nunc, hoc est, quoad durat præsens seculum, manere dicuntur, quod cum de aliis donis mini- strantibus non dicatur, dona illa miraculorum, prophetiæ, & linguarum etiam hic in Ecclesia de- situra esse, innuitur, ut plerique censent. Id tamen, an firmiter hinc concludatur, dubium esse queat, siquidem & cognitionem inter dona ministrantia recensuerint, quæ omni tempore in Ecclesia manet. Calvinus τὸ μένειν manere hoc loco idem esse ait, ac omnibus subductis tanquam in calculo supputatorio summam hanc restare, ut sit sensus: Complura quidem sunt, & varia, sed in hunc scopum (fidei, spei, & charitatis) tendunt omnia, & respiciunt. Sed hoc alie- num, & contortum. Communis interpretatio est de conservatione & permanentia horum donorum perpetua in Ecclesia: Quia Ecclesia, quæ est cœ- tus fidelium, sine fide, spe & charitate esse nequit: Cum fidei spes conjuncta sit. Charitas autem ceu effectus causæ proles è matre, ex fide procreetur. Singularis est Grotii glossa: Νυνὶ hic non esse tem- poris, sed oppositionis notam, quæ textui aperte repugnat, utpote μένει in Futuro, non præsenti uti sonat accipiendũ esse: Mansionẽ item in altero ævo denotari, sed ratione effectus (exemplum de rupe non quadrat; Rupes enim non effectu suo tan- tum sequebatur, sed καθ' ὑπόστασιν: Erat enim Chri- stus) fidem, spem, & dilectionem ratione præmii spe- ctari, quum de eorum permanentia hic agatur, non de præmio: Denique prophetias Pseudo - Pro- phetarum hic attendi; quod vero è textu minime apparet.

Μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη.

Μείζων etiam de pluribus dicitur, ut videre est Matth. 13, 23. Luc. 9, 46. Maxima est inter has tres: Quia fides & spes ad dilectionem ducunt. Dilectio nos Deo conjungit & similes facit 1. Joh. 4, 8. Sine hac ipsæ quoque spes & fides manent infructuosæ, ut intelligi potest ex dictis initio capitis hujus. Gal. 5, 6. Jac. 2, 10. & sequentibus. Ignatius in epistola ad Ephesios: Ἀρχὴ ζωῆς πίσις, τέλος δὲ ἀγάπη.

Majorem esse charitatem fide ac spe, quod illa ad dilectionem ducant, hæc Deo nos conjungat, & similes faciat, analogiæ fidei repugnat. Fides non tam du- cit ad dilectionem, quam causa dilectionis est secu- dum scripturam: Nec uspiam docetur, spem nos ad dilectionem ducere. Neque dilectio nos conjungit Deo, sed fides Eph. 1, 12. Gal. 3, 26. Marc. 16, 16. Ebr. 11, 6. Secundum S. Ignatium fides est principium causale salutis, finis vero est dilectio, quæ in altera vita non tantum durat, sed perfectionem assequi- tur. Atque hoc sensu majorem faciunt spe ac fide dilectionem pleriq; Interpretes, quia fides ac spes ad hoc seculum spectant, non ad futurum, ubi am- bulabimus non per fidem, sed per speciem 2. Cor. V. 7. Ita Chrysostomus Homil. 24. in hunc locum: Chari- tas major fide & spe, quia transeunt hæ, illa durat: Theodoretus in hunc locum: Quia cessabunt dona, sola manebit charitas. Augustinus lib. I. de doctrina Christian. c. XXXIIX. Fidei succedit res, quam vi- debimus, & spei succedit beatitudo ipsa, ad quam per- venturi sumus. Charitas autem istis etiam deceden- tibus augebitur fortius. Si enim credendo diligimus, quod nondum videmus, quanto magis, cum videre cœpimus? Et si sperando diligimus, quo nondum per- venimus, quanto magis cum pervenerimus? Anshel- mus in hunc locum: Quia fides cessabit, dum futu- ra, quæ creduntur, advenerint, & spes suam habebit beatitudinem, quam quisque præstolatur, acceperit. Sola vero charitas in æternum perseverabit, & de visione Conditoris ac beatitudine sanctorum fine fi- ne gaudebit. Annuunt & Pontificii. Cornelius à Lapide; Clare, inquit, hoc capite docet Paulus spem, fidem & charitatem hic manere, sed in patria solam charitatem. Ita Patres. Vid. Gregor. de Valentia disp. I. q 5. de subjecto fidei puncto II. Sic & Estius: Chari- tas sola nunquam excidit, sed permanet in patria, quando & fides in visionem & spes in apprehensio- nem commutabitur.

Alii tamen nonnulli alias τῆς ἐξοχῆς dilectionis rationes adducunt, quas è B. Glassii Exeget. An- not. in Domin. Quinquag. huc repetere placet, ut- pote (1) ob objecti latitudinem. Fides intuetur solum Christum, & ipsi cum solo Deo res est. Spes futura solum bona respicit expectatque: Charitas vero refertur ad Deum & ad proximum, & insuper fu- turis bonis jam impetratis, tranquillissime iis in æternum fruetur. (2.) Ob manifestationem. Aliæ virtutes abdunt se in latebras cordis humani: At charitas reddit se in externis operibus conspicua, & est virtus, per quam ipsa fides se exerit; & ut Pau- lus ait, ἐνεργεῖθαι efficax est, Gal. 5, 6. (3.) Ob opera- tionem. Quia in Ecclesiæ gubernatione, & pace in- ter homines conservanda, maximam utilitatem bræstat, quam rationem hic attendi observavit B. Mylius.

Vana vero est Papistarum illatio, dilectionem, non fidem justificare, quia dilectio major fide dicitur. Quia non ratione justificationis, de quo articulo ne apex quidem hic habetur, sed ratione duratio- nis, aut si ita mavis, ob alias prærogativæ rationes, σύγκρισις hic instituitur, agnoscentibus non pau- cis, etiam Pontificiis. Iterum ergo, inquit B. My- lius, paralogismum τẽ πῆ ϰὶ ἁπλῶς, καὶ τẽ μὴ αἰτίε ὡς αἰτίε committunt Pontificii, sic argumentantes: Charitas præstat fidei: Ergo justificat, aut saltem plus ad justificationem confert, quam fides: Per- inde ac si quis ex eo, quia aurum pane præstantius est, colligat, aurum etiam nutrire. Dn. D. Sebastian Schmid per fidem hic justifi- cantem fidem intelligi negat, eamque explicat de fi- de, quâ sine suspicione temeraria & mala crediur alterius (Dei & hominis) verbis, promissis, & qui- buscunque animi signis: Sicut spes, eodem autore, est, quæ bona aut meliora de altero semper sperat, nec temere, qualem imposterum eum habiturâ, diffidit: Charitatem vero utriusque matrem facit, & origi- nem, ut ex se gignat fidem & spem, & charitas credat, speretque omnia. Vid. Disp. è 1. Cor. XIII. 13. de cha- ritatis præstantia. Quam sententiam suo loco re- linquimus, facile, & sine detrimento orthodoxias Evangelicæ, concedentes, fidem justificantem de- signari. Fides hæc, quæ creditur DEI verbis & promissis, à fide miraculosa non videtur disseparan- da: Hic vero τὰ κρείττονα præstantiora seu meliora dona monstrantur.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

With a previous admonition to charity and the pursuit of ministering gifts, he inculcates prophecy above all, and institutes a comparison of it with the gift of tongues, because foreign languages do not contribute to information, as prophecy does, and therefore the Apostle prefers that they be able to interpret the scriptures, which he illustrates with the simile of instruments, which emit no significant sound, and that we are barbarians to those whose language we do not understand, and he warns that if anyone speaks in tongues, he should explain it, so that it may bear fruit, and thus he should pray and sing with both spirit and mind, so that those present may be able to say Amen, and he proves this by his own example. Furthermore, he warns that tongues are a sign to the unbelievers from the Law (Old Testament Isa. 28. 11.) he confirms, since prophecies are not for the unbelieving, but for the believing, and he shows how discordant it would be if all in the assembly spoke in tongues, with the Church perceiving nothing, and finally he teaches that all things ought to be done for edification. So that, therefore, the meaning of those speaking in tongues may be declared by interpreters: but those interpreting the Scriptures should submit themselves to the judgment of others, and those having revelations should propose them in order and distinctly: Because God is a God of order, not of confusion. Women, however, are commanded to be silent in the Church: And it is advised that all things be done according to decency and order.

There are two parts: I. A comparison of the gift of tongues with the gift of prophecy, up to v. 25. II. An admonition concerning the edification of the Church, and the order to be observed in the same, up to verse 40.

PART I. A comparison of the gift of tongues with the gift of prophecy.

Vers. 1. Διώκεθε τὴν ἀγάπην) It coheres with the preceding, since love is of such great value, strive by all means to have it. Concerning the word διώκειν see Rom. 9. 31. 12. 13. 14. 19. Ζηλῦθε δὲ τὰ πνευματικὰ) Understand χαρίσματα. Seek to have them if it is possible. For they are not altogether necessary for salvation.

Μᾶλλον δὲ ) That is, especially. For here μᾶλλον stands for the superlative; as just now μείζων.

Ἵνα προφητεύητε ) He prefers prophecy to other gifts, because that matter provided the greatest authority to the Gospel, convinced the incredulous, and strengthened the believers. For prediction is believed by all men to be divine, and for that reason it is called divination.

This is not to be understood as prophecy, which is the revelation of future or otherwise hidden things. For no one can attain that gift by striving, but such things are immediately of divine inspiration: But by the name of prophecy is signified the interpretation of the scriptures, as it is in 1 Thess. 5:19, 'Do not despise prophecies.' 2 Pet. 1:21, 'Every prophecy or exposition of scripture does not come by private interpretation.' Rom. 12:6, 'If anyone has prophecy, let it be according to the analogy of faith,' which teaches that the office of interpreting serves for exhortation and consolation, v. 3, with no mention made of the prediction of future things; for which reason he teaches that prophecy is a sign not for the unbelieving, but for the believing. These have no need of miracles, but easily assent to scripture. But how can we emulate spiritual gifts, for example, the gift of miracles or of tongues? Answer. The sense here is, since you are emulators of spiritual gifts, strive especially that you may obtain the gift of prophecy, that is, of interpreting scripture.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Prævia admonitione ad charitatem & studium donorũ ministrantiũ inculcat imprimis pro- phetiam, ejusq; comparationẽ instituit, cum linguarũ dono, quod peregrinæ linguæ nõ fa- ciant ad informationem, ut Prophetia, ideoq; magis optet Apostolus, ut scripturas inter- pretari possint, quod illustrat simili instru- mentorũ, nullum sonum significativum eden- tium, & quod barbari illis simus, quorum lin- guam non intelligimus, monetque, ut si quis linguis loquatur, id explicet, quo fructum fe- rat, atque ita & spiritu & sensu oret ac psal- lat, ut assistentes Amen dicere possint, suoque ipsius exemplo comprobat. Linguas insuper signa esse incredulis è lege (Veteri Testam. Es. XXIIX. 11.) confirmat, quum prophetiæ non incredulorum, sed credentium sint, & quam absonum futurum sit, si omnes in conventu linguis loquantur, Ecclesia nihil percipiente, ostendit, omnia denique ad ædificationem fieri debere, tradit. Ut proinde linguis loquẽ- tiũ sensus per interpretes declaretur: Scri- pturas vero interpretantes aliorum judicio se submittant, revelationes habentes ordine & distincte eas proponant: Quia Deus ordi- nis Deus est, non confusionis. Mulieres au- tem tacere jubentur in Ecclesia: Et ut omnia secundum honestatem & ordinem fiant, monetur.

PArtes sunt duæ I. Comparatio doni linguarum cum prophetias dono ad v. 25. II. Commonefactio de ædificatione Ecclesiæ, & ordine in eadem obser- vando ad vers. 40.

PARS I. Comparatio doni linguarum cum dono prophetiæ.

Vers. 1. Διώκεθε τὴν ἀγάπην) Cohæret cum superioribus, cum tanti sit dilectio, omnino efficite, ut eam habeatis. De voce διώκειν vide Rom. IX. 31. XII. 13. XIV. 19. Ζηλῦθε δὲ τὰ πνευματικὰ) Subaudi χαρίσματα. Expe- tite ut ea habeatis si fieri potest. Neque enim omnino illa ad salutem sunt necessaria.

Μᾶλλον δὲ ) Id est, maxime. Est enim hic μᾶλλον pro su- perlativo; ut modo μείζων.

Ἵνα προφητεύητε ) Prophetiam caeteris donis praefert, quia maximam ea res autoritatem praestabat Evangelio, con- vincebat incredulos, firmabat credentes. Divinum enim ab omnibus hominibus creditur esse praedictio, dicta ob id divinatio.

Non de Prophetia, quae est futurorum, aut alio- quin abditorum revelatio, haec accipienda. Nam illud donum sectando assequi nemo potest, sed im- mediatae talia sunt divinae inspirationis: Sed prophe- tias nomine interpretatio scripturarum significa- tur, ut est 1. Thess. V. 19. Prophetias nolite spernere. 2. Petr. I. 21. Omnis prophetia seu expositio scri- pturae propria interpretatione non fit. Rom. XII. 6. Si quis prophetiam habet, fidei sit analoga, quod in- terpretandi munus ad exhortationem & consola- tionem facere docet v. 3. nulla mentione facta prae- dictionis futurorum; quapropter prophetiam non infidelibus, sed fidelibus, signum esse docet. Hi opus non habent miraculis, sed scripturae facile assentiuntur. Quomodo autem aemulari spiritua- lia v. g. donum miraculorum aut linguarum pos- sumus? Resp. Sensus hic est, quoniam aemulatores estis donorum spiritualium, studete praecipue, ut donum consequamini prophetiae, hoc est interpre- tandi scripturam.

## 14:2
Vers. 2. Ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ ) He especially restrains those who did not use the gift of tongues modestly among those who knew that language, but in the Church where there were either none or few who could understand: And trusting in that gift, they despised others. Indeed, those gifts did not come divinely after Christ, except to those believing in Christ. But those who had believed could, by losing love or even faith, extinguish those gifts in themselves, 1 Thess. 5:19. For as discipline receded, grace also receded, as Cyprian says,

Οὐκ ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ ) Namely, unless men of such a language are present,

Ἀλλὰ Θεῷ ) He has God alone as a witness.

Οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει ) Namely in the Church. He speaks of that which usually happened. It was rare for foreigners to be present. Ἀκούειν here is to understand, as שָׁמַע often is for the Hebrews. See Gen. 11:7, Is. 36:11, Rom. 11:8.

Πνεύματι δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια ) He speaks indeed by the breathing of the Spirit, but things which are not manifest. For whatever lies hidden, whether it is future or present, is called a mystery, Rom. 11:25, 16:25, 2 Thess. 2:17.

By spirit is not understood the Holy Spirit, but the spirit of man, or the mind renewed by the Holy Spirit. Job 3:6. And he is said to speak hidden things, not because he does not understand himself while speaking, as Estius wishes, but because he sometimes brings forth mysteries, which are truly hidden, and is not understood by others who do not understand the language, and thus he does not speak to men, but to God. And that happens just as if he were speaking those things by spirit and mind alone.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ ) Maxime eos compescit qui linguarum dono non modeste utebantur apud ejus lin- guae gnaros, sed in Ecclesia ubi aut nulli aut pauci erant, qui intelligerent: Et eo dono confisi spernebant caeteros. Non contingere quidem divinitus dona ista post Christum, nisi in Christum credentibus. Sed poterant, qui crediderant, amit- tendo dilectionem aut etiam fidem, dona ista in sese extin- guere 1. Thess. V. 19. Recedente enim disciplina recedebat & gratia, ut loquitur Cyprianus,

Οὐκ ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ ) Nempe nisi adsint ejusmodi linguae homines,

Ἀλλὰ Θεῷ ) Deum solum habet conscium.

Οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει ) Nempe in Ecclesia. Loquitur de eo quod plerumque fiebat. Rarum erat ut adessent peregrini. Ἀκούειν hic est intelligere ut שָׁמַע saepe Hebraeis. Vide Gen. XI. 7. Es. XXXVI. 11. Rom. XI. 8.

Πνεύματι δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια ) Spiritu quidem afflante lo- quitur, sed res quae non pateant. Nam quicquid latet, sive id futurum est, sive praesens, μυστήριον dicitur Rom. XI. 25. XVI. 25. 2. Thess. II. 17.

Per spiritum non intelligitur Spiritus S. sed spi- ritus hominis, vel mens renovata per Spir. S. Job 3, 6. Occulta autem loqui dicitur, non quod seipsum lo- quens non intelligat, ut Estius vult, sed quod myste- ria, quae vere occulta, quandoque proferat, ab aliis non intelligentibus linguam non intelligatur, adeoque non hominibus loquatur, sed Deo. Idque perinde fit ac si solo spiritu, ac mente ea loquatur.

## 14:3
Vers. 3. Ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν) He benefits others, for that is what οἰκοδομεῖν means for Paul, as we have often said.

And exhortation and consolation ) He divides the genus name into species, it is useful by warning the fragile, by consoling the afflicted: the former by the prediction of dangers, the latter by the prediction of liberation. Both with circumstances which could not be foreseen by human means.

It is treated here of admonition or consolation in general, which is had from the interpretation of scripture, and is its application to use, not that which is sought from predictions alone.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν) Prodest aliis, id enim οἰκοδομεῖν Paulo ut saepius diximus.

Καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παραμυθίαν ) Generis nomen in spe- cies dispertit, prodest monendo fragiles, solando afflictos: illos periculorum, hos liberationis praedictione. Utrumq; cu circumstantiis quae humanitus prospectari non poterant.

De admonitione vel consolatione in genere hic agitur, quae e scripturae interpretatione habetur, ejusque est ad usum applicatio, non quae e praedi- ctionibus solum petitur.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. He who speaks with a tongue, edifies himself ) For he feels within himself the power of Christ.

But he who prophesies edifies the Church ) Both those present and those absent. For prophecies were accustomed to be transmitted from Churches to Churches.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ, ἑαυτὸν οἰκοδομεῖ ) Sentit enim intra se vim Christi.

Ὁ δὲ προφητεύων Ἐκκλησίαν οἰκοδομεῖ ) Et praesentes & absentes. Solebant enim prophetiae ab Ecclesiis ad Eccle- sias transmitti.

## 14:5
Vers. 5. I wish ) I would like, as in Rom. VII. 16 and elsewhere.

That you all speak with tongues ) Namely if it were to please God in such a way. He shows himself to be affected in the same way as Moses once was, Num. 11, 29.

But rather that you may prophesy ) Because that is more conducive to many, as he has already said.

For greater is he who prophesies, than he who speaks with tongues.) Greater, that is, more useful to the Church as above XIII. 13.

Unless he interprets ) It is a double negation for one, in the Hebrew manner עַד אִם־לֹא. The sense is, unless the same person who has the gift of tongues, also has the gift of interpreting, that is, a faithful memory.

By the gift of interpreting is not meant a faithful memory, but a hermeneutical power, the faculty of explaining the thoughts of the mind, whether one's own or another's, in a language known to the hearers. Estius thinks that those who were endowed only with the gift of tongues could not render what they spoke in a foreign language into their own known and common language, which is to interpret, because they did not understand what they were saying. But who would believe that they either did not understand what they were speaking, or could not utter and express in their own common language what they had conceived in their mind? That is not what those words of the Apostle in chapter 12 mean: 'Others the interpretation of speeches' and 'do all interpret?' But the meaning of these words is this, that some translate and interpret speeches uttered in an exotic language by others into a known and common one, where those who uttered them could not propose them to the people in the same language due to a lack of the common language.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Θέλω ) velim, ut Rom. VII. 16 & alibi.

Πάντας ὑμᾶς λαλεῖν γλώσσαις ) Nempe si ita Deo place- ret. Ostendit se pariter affectum ut olim Moyses Num. 11, 29.

Μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε ) Quia id pluribus conducit, ut jam dixit.

Μείζων γὰρ ὁ προφητεύων, ἢ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσαις.) Major, id est, Ecclesiae utilior ut supra XIII. 13.

Ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ διερμηνεύῃ ) Est duplex negatio pro una, more Hebraeo עַד אִם־לֹא. Sensus est, nisi idem qui linguae donum habet, habeat & donum interpretandi, id est, fide- lem memoriam.

Per donum interpretandi non memoria fidelis, sed δύναμις ἑρμηνευτικὴ facultas sensa animi sive proprii, sive alterius, lingua auditoribus nota, explicandi. Estius putat eos, qui solo præditi erant dono linguarum, non potuisse ea, quæ peregrina lingua loquebantur, nota ac vulgari sua lingua reddere, quod est interpretari, propterea quod non intelligerent ea, quæ dicerent. Sed quis credat, vel non intellexisse ea quæ loquerentur, vel lingua sibi vulgari non potuisse ea eloqui & efferre, quæ mente conceperant. Non id sibi volunt illa Apost. c. 12. Alii interpretatio sermonum & nunquid omnes interpretantur? Sed hæc est istorum verborum sententia, quod nonnulli sermones, exotica lingua prolatos ab aliis, in notam & vulgarem transfundant, & interpretentur, ubi illi, qui protulerunt eosdem, ob defectum vulgaris linguæ populo proponere in eadem non potuerunt.

## 14:6
V. 6. But now brothers) Nuni is placed here also for 'But truly', as above XIII. 13.

Ἐὰν ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς γλώσσαις λαλῶν) Paul is often accustomed to place the first person hypothetically.

Τί ὑμῖν ὠφελήσω ἐὰν μὴ ὑμῖν λαλήσω) Here ἐὰν μὴ stands for 'but'. For he is dealing with another kind of addressing. We spoke of this use of these particles above at VII. 17.

Ἢ ἐν ἀποκαλύψει) Ἀποκάλυψις here is the exposition of figures lying hidden in the Old Testament, such as he has many in the Pauline epistles, and in that to the Hebrews. It is sometimes taken more generally, as below at 30.

Ἢ ἐν γνώσει) γνῶσις is the knowledge of histories, as we said above at XII. 8. XIII. 28.

Ἢ ἐν προφητείᾳ) By predicting what is about to happen.

Ἢ ἐν διδαχῇ) διδαχὴ here calls for excellent maxims such as are in the books of Solomon. Which above [he called] σοφίαν,

There appears no reason why that ἐὰν μὴ should not be taken in its ordinary meaning of UNLESS. For the sense is plain: If I come to you speaking in (foreign) tongues, what shall I profit you, unless I speak to YOU (so that the voice may be understood, or in your own language). By ἀποκάλυψιν is understood not an exposition of figures lying hidden in the Old Testament, but a new revelation, such as was the Johannine ἀποκάλυψις, which sense is clear from v. 30. By γνῶσιν is meant the knowledge not only of histories, but of any things whatsoever, especially divine ones. By προφητείαν the interpretation of the sacred scriptures: By διδαχὴν instruction or information, for which the faculty of teaching is required. For there are those who indeed have knowledge of things, but cannot communicate it to others, being destitute of the faculty of teaching: there are those who, even if their knowledge is small, can nevertheless transmit what they do know excellently, being, that is to say, good teachers. The four mystical senses, which Sedulius and Primasius carve out from there, are not insinuated here, as even the Papists themselves, Estius and Cornelius à Lapide, acknowledge this to be forced; nor is it necessary, however, that that revelation and prophecy, knowledge and doctrine be taken relatively, so that doctrine corresponds to revelation, that is, for the sake of teaching, through which we communicate to others that which we know. For new revelations were also given in the primitive Church, nor was it the task of the Prophets only to interpret revelations, but any interpretation of scripture was called prophecy. Estius observes that many agree that revelation is understood as the mysteries of God, concerning which the gift of wisdom is occupied, but knowledge as that which makes divine things credible by means of human reasoning, and that prophecy is spoken of generally both regarding the prediction of future events and the explanation of the hidden senses of scripture, while doctrine is that which concerns morals. Sed prior explicatio convenientior est.

Latin:

V. 6. Νυνὶ δὲ ἀδελφοὶ) Nuni hic quoque positum pro At vero, ut supra XIII. 13.

Ἐὰν ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς γλώσσαις λαλῶν) solet sæpe Paulus personam primam ponere ὑποθετικῶς.

Τί ὑμῖν ὠφελήσω ἐὰν μὴ ὑμῖν λαλήσω) Est hic ἐὰν μὴ pro sed. Nam agit de alio genere alloquendi. Diximus de hoc usu istarum particularum supra VII. 17.

Ἢ ἐν ἀποκαλύψει) Ἀποκάλυψις hic est expositio figurarum latentium in veteri Testamento, qualia multa habet in Paulinis epistolis, & in illa ad Hebræos. Sumitur interdum generalius ut infra 30.

Ἢ ἐν γνώσει) γνῶσις est historiarum cognitio, ut diximus supra XII. 8. XIII. 28.

Ἢ ἐν προφητείᾳ) Prædicendo quæ eventura sunt.

Ἢ ἐν διδαχῇ) διδαχὴ hic vocat præclaras sententias quales sunt in libris Salomonis. Quod supra σοφίαν,

Non apparet ratio, cur illud ἐὰν μὴ non accipiatur ordinario significatu NISI. Nam sensus apertus est: Si venero ad vos, linguis (peregrinis) loquens, quid vobis prodero, nisi VOBIS (ut vox intelligatur, vel vestra lingua) loquar. Per ἀποκάλυψιν non expositio figurarum latentium in Veteri Testamento, sed nova revelatio intelligitur, qualis erat ἀποκάλυψις Johannea, qui sensus è v. 30. patet. Per γνῶσιν non historiarum tantum, sed rerum quarumvis, imprimis divinarum cognitio. Per προφητείαν sacrarum literarum interpretatio: Per διδαχὴν doctrina seu informatio, ad quam requiritur facultas docendi. Sunt enim qui rerum quidem notitiam habent, sed eam cum aliis communicare nequeunt, docendi facultate destituti: Sut qui etsi exiguæ sint notitiæ, ea tamen, quæ noverunt, præclare possunt tradere, boni scilicet didactici. Non hic quatuor sensus mystici, quos inde exsculpunt Sedulius & Primasius, insinuatur, uti coactum hoc esse agnoscunt ipsimet Papistæ Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, nec necessum tamen est, ut illa revelatio & prophetia, scientia & doctrina relative accipiantur, ut revelationi respondeat doctrina, id est, docendi gratia, per quam id, quod scimus, aliis communicamus. Nam & novæ revelationes dabantur in primitiva Ecclesia, nec Prophetarum erat tantum revelationes interpretari, sed prophetia dicebatur quæcunque scripturæ interpretatio. Estius observat inter multos convenire, revelationem intelligi mysteriorum Dei, circa quæ versetur sapientiæ donum, scientiam vero eam, quæ ex humanis rationibus divina credibilia facit, prophetiam generaliter dici & de prædictione futurorum, & de explicatione occultorum scripturæ sensuum, doctrinam vero eam esse, quæ est de moribus. Sed prior explicatio convenientior est.

## 14:7
V. 7. Ὅμως) Atqui ut Gal. III. 5. Τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα) Ἄψυχα vocat instrumenta sensu carentia.

Εἴτε ἀυλὸς, εἴτε κιθάρα, ἐὰν διαστολὴν τοῖς φθόγγοις μὴ δῷ, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ ἀυλόμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον; If instruments sound something unheard, nothing can be understood. For this reason, the Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian modes are accustomed to be distinguished. The city of Thebes was built to the flute, and to the flute it was destroyed. There is use of the flute in joyful occasions, Matt. 11:17, and also in mourning, Matt. 9:23. The same lyre sings of the deeds of heroes and of loves.

Καὶ γὰρ) similarly.

Latin:

V. 7. Ὅμως) Atqui ut Gal. III. 5. Τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα) Ἄψυχα vocat instrumenta sensu carentia.

Εἴτε ἀυλὸς, εἴτε κιθάρα, ἐὰν διαστολὴν τοῖς φθόγγοις μὴ δῷ, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ ἀυλόμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον) Si inauditum quid sonent instrumenta nihil intelligi potest. Ideo distingui solent modi Dorii, Phrygii, Lydii. Thebarum urbs ad tibiam structa, ad tibiam est diruta. Est tibiæ u- sus in lætis Matth. XI. 17. est & in luctu Matth. IX. 23. Eadem cithara canit res heroum, & amores.

Καὶ γὰρ) similiter.

## 14:9
V. 9. If the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? Formerly there was one sound of the trumpet for battle, another for retreat. Procopius, Gothic Wars II: 'Those who in ancient times used trumpets in the Roman army knew certain signals, two in number; by one, when it was sounded, the greater part of the soldiers were urged to rush into battle; by the other, they were recalled to the camp when it seemed best to the general. In this way, the generals always commanded the duties to the soldiers, and they were able to perform the tasks ordered; for a shout in the clashes of battle is by no means naturally suited to signal anything clearly.' Procopius says in the same place that this was interrupted to his own times with great harm. Thus among the Hebrews, there is one sound of the pipe for civil assemblies, another for a journey. Num. 10:1. Φωνὴ is תרועה in the same place, Num. 10:6.

V. 9. So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood) Namely, to those who are present or to the majority of them.

How shall it be known what is spoken) τὸ λαλούμενον, the word.

For ye shall speak into the air) A locution similar to that which is above, 9:26, 'as one that beateth the air.' For he who is understood by no one speaks to the winds.

Latin:

V. 9. Ἐὰν ἄδηλον φωνὴν σάλπιγξ δῷ, τίς παρασκευάσεται εἰς πόλεμον;) Olim alius erat tubæ sonus ad pugnam, alius ad receptum. Procopius Gothicorum II. Οἱ ταῖς σάλπιγξι τὸ παλαιὸν ἐν τῷ Ῥωμαίων στρατῷ χρώμενοι. Νό- μους τινὰς ἠπίσταντο δύο, ὧν ἑτέρῳ μὲν ἐγκελευομένῳ τὸ πλεῖ- σον ὄγκον ἐς τὰς στρατιώτας εἰς μάχην ὁρμῶντι· ὁ δὲ ἄλλῳ ἐπὶ τὸ στρατόπεδον ἀνεκαλοῦντο μαχομένους, ἡνίκα ταῦτα ἐδό- κει τῷ στρατηγῷ ὡς ἄριστα ἔχειν· Ταύτῃ δὲ ἀεὶ οἱ μὲν στρατη- γοὶ τὰ καθήκοντα τοῖς στρατιώταις ἐκέλευον, ἐκεῖνοι δὲ τὰ πα- ραγγελλόμενα ἔργα ἐπιτελεῖν ἴσχυον· Κραυγὴ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ξυμ- βολαῖς σημῆναί τι σαφὲς οὐδαμῶς πέφυκε. Id magno malo in- termissum ad sua tempora ait Procopius ibidem. Sic apud Hebræos alius tibiæ sonus ad conventus civiles, alius ad iter. Num. X. 1. Φωνὴ est תרועה ibidem Num. X. 6.

V. 9. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς γλώσσης ἐὰν μὴ εὔσημον λόγον δῶτε) Nempe iis qui adsunt aut eorum plurimis.

Πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ λαλούμενον) τὸ λαλούμενον המילה.

Ἔσεσθε γὰρ εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες) Similis loquutio illi quæ supra IX. 26. ὡς ἀέρα δέρων. Nam qui à nemine intelligitur, is ventis loquitur.

## 14:10
V. 10. There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices) He said 'so many' as if pointing with his finger to the number seventy. For the Hebrews say there are that many languages. But he adds 'it may be,' because there can also be more, of which the Hebrews had heard nothing.

And none of them is without signification) Here 'of them' (αὐτῶν) does not refer to 'voices' (φωνὰς), but to the men themselves, although they are not named, but are easily understood from the preceding. We have noted the equal use of the name 'of them' elsewhere. Here the name is understood from above, Num. 8:9, Esther 5:9. But in the manuscript 'of them' is missing, so that the neuter singular stands for the masculine plural. They are peoples: As varied in languages, habit, as in dress and arms. How the number seventy is pointed out here with the finger, I confess I cannot see, nor is it established by certain proof that there are precisely that many languages. It is said in general that there are many kinds of languages among men, which, however, some take to refer to many kinds of instruments, i.e., why should I count individual sounding instruments, since they are almost innumerable? But the following verse shows it is more correctly understood of languages, with Chrysostom and Theophylact.

Latin:

V. 10. Τοσαῦτα, εἰ τύχοι, γένη φωνῶν ἐστι) Τοσαῦτα dixit quasi digito monstrans numerum septuagenarium. Tot enim linguas esse ajunt Hebræi. Sed addit, si forte, quia possunt esse & plures de quibus Hebræi nihil audierant.

Καὶ οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ἄφωνον) Hic αὐτῶν non refertur ad φωνὰς, sed ad ipsos homines quanquam ii nominati non sunt, sed facile ex præcedentibus intelliguntur. Parem usum nomi- nis αὐτῶν & alibi notavimus. Hic nomen ex superioribus subauditur Num VIII. 9. Esther. V. 9. Sed in manuscripto deest αὐτῶν, ut Neutrum singulare sit pro plurali Masculino. Sunt populi: Tam varii linguis, habitu, quam vestis & armis. Quomodo hic digito monstretur numerus se- ptuagenarius, fateor, me videre non posse, ne- que totidem præcise linguas esse, certo documen- to constat. In genere dicitur, multa esse inter homi- nes linguarum genera, quod tamen nonnulli de multis instrumentorum generibus accipiunt, q. d. quid singula numerem instrumenta sonantia, cum sint pene innumera? Sed rectius de linguis cum Chry- sostomo & Theophylacto accipi sequens versus docet.

## 14:11
V. 11. Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice) He calls the signification of the voices 'power' (δύναμιν).

I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me) He used the word 'barbarian,' which corresponds to the Hebrew לעז, Psalm 114:1, in the sense of 'relative to something,' just as Ovid also: 'I am a barbarian here, because I am not understood by anyone.' Thus to Homer, the Carians are 'barbarian-speaking.' Anacharsis: 'To me, all Greeks are Scythian-speaking.' Here 'in me' (ἐν ἐμοὶ) is for 'to me' (ἐμοὶ), as 'in' (ἐν) often abounds in these writings.

Barbarians were first called by the Greeks whoever sounded a language different from the Greek, because the Greek language sounded in almost the whole world, or because, as others prefer, the Greeks considered their own language the purest. The Romans, however, later called those barbarians who used a language other than Greek or Latin. Finally, they were called by that name who speak a language which another does not understand. Whence Cajetan notes that the name 'barbarian' is relative, and that no man is absolutely a barbarian. The sense, therefore, and the connection is such: since there are so many kinds of languages to sanctify the senses of the mind, he who speaks in a foreign language speaks in vain, or if he is not understood, he is a barbarian to the other who does not understand.

Latin:

V. 11. Ἐὰν οὖν εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς) Δύναμιν appellat vocum significationem.

Ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβα- ρος) Usurpavit vocem barbari quæ respondet Hebrææ לעז Psalm. CXIV. 1. in sensu τῶν πρός τι, quomodo & Ovidius: Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli. Sic Homero Cares βαρβαρόφωνοι. Anacharsis: Ἐμοὶ δὲ πάν- τες ἕλληνες σκυθίζουσι. Est ἐν ἐμοὶ hic pro ἐμοὶ, quomodo sæpe ἐν in his scriptis πλεονάζει.

Barbari primum Græcis dicti, quicunque di- versam à Græca sonabant linguam, quia lingua Græca fere in toto orbe sonabat, vel quod alii ma- lunt, quia Græci suam linguam reputarunt purissi- mam. Romani autem postea barbaros dixere, qui alia quam Græca, aut Latina lingua uterentur. Denique eo nomine appellati, qui lingua loquun- tur, quam alius non intelligit. Unde Cajetanus notat, nomen barbarus esse relativum, ac nullum hominem esse absolute barbarum. Sensus ergo & connexio talis est, cum tam multa sint linguarum genera, ad sanctificanda sensa animi, frustra utique loquitur, qui aliena lingua loquitur, vel si non in- telligatur, estque alteri non intelligenti barbarus.

## 14:12
Vers. 12. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς) Οὕτω here means therefore, לכן. Πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ζητεῖτε, ἵνα περισσεύητε) A transposition: For ζητεῖτε ἵνα περισσεύητε πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας. Desire that you may abound in those gifts especially, from which the greatest utility may return to the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς) Οὕτω hic valet propterea, לכן. Πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ζητεῖτε, ἵνα περισσεύητε) Trajectio: Pro ζητεῖτε ἵνα περισσεύητε πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας. Optate, ut abundetis iis maxime donis, unde plu- rimam utilitatis ad Ecclesiam redeat.

## 14:13
V. 13. Διόπερ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω, ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ.) Let him also pray that he may retain with a mindful heart what he said in a foreign tongue, so that he may thus be able to explain the same in Greek.

Latin:

V. 13. Διόπερ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω, ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ.) Etiam oret ut memori animo retineat quæ lingua externa dixit, ut sic eadem Græce possit exponere.

## 14:14
Vers. 14. Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ) Otherwise, if I should utter prayers to God in a foreign tongue, even if they are the best.

Τὸ πνεῦμά με προσεύχεται) He calls that motion which is from inspiration πνεῦμα.

Ὁ δὲ νοῦς με ἄκαρπός ἐστι) My mind brings forth nothing well thought out by itself.

Νοῦς here, according to Cornelius, is the same as sense, as in v. 19 and ch. II, last verse; in what way the Apostle accepts it: τίς ἐπι τούτων τῶν ῥημάτων νους: This mind, therefore, that is, the sense, meaning, and intelligence of my tongues is without fruit, because no one grasps or understands it, so as to be stirred to piety thereby. Thus Cornelius à Lapide. The mind is called ἄκαρπος not by reason of the speaker, but of the hearer. Estius, on the contrary, so that he may favor the most unlearned clerics and laymen who hear prayers without understanding them, applies these things to those who, ignorant of Latin, recite prayers in the Latin language, who indeed are moved by the spirit and affection of devotion toward God, if they truly pray: But because they do not understand the words, their mind is without fruit, namely, of understanding. Where he is vain, when he says: Those who pray thus, even if they do not perceive the fruit of understanding, and therefore are not nourished by the senses through the signifying words, yet have the fruit of a mind elevated to God. For what kind of elevation of the mind to God is this, when the mind understands nothing of what is said? That devotion is brutish, not a prayer pleasing to God. And thus the Apostle is openly contradicted, who simply calls such a mind and prayer ἄκαρπον, which is without understanding.

It is therefore a paradox that Estius adds, that it happens that someone praying without understanding may merit and obtain more before God than another who attains the sense of the prayer by understanding. But that ἄκαρπον is said here by reason of the hearers, to whom no fruit redounds, the whole discourse of Paul teaches, to whom he is also a Barbarian who speaks in a tongue (i.e., an exotic one). Compare especially v. 19. Which sense the Rheims translators, Cornelius, and Justinianus acknowledge, that it is not said that the words and the mind of the prayer are not understood by the one praying, but it is said that they are not understood by those hearing the one praying publicly, so that the paraphrase of B. Hunnius is correct here: For if I pray in a tongue unknown to other men, then my spirit indeed prays, meanwhile my mind, that is, the sense of the words of my prayer, escapes and lies hidden from the hearers, and therefore it is void of fruit, namely, that fruit which a prayer said and understood in a common language otherwise brings to one's neighbor. By this whole doctrine of Paul, the worship of the Roman Church in an exotic language, which is not understood by the common people, is utterly overthrown, just as Justinianus himself, at v. 4 and 5, explained these things concerning sacred offices being performed with the Church in the common language: whom Cajetan preceded in Sixtus Senensis, lib. VI, annot. 263, Faber Stapulensis, and Erasmus, to which opinion Cassander brought many Fathers and Papists in 'De officiis pii viri' in the defense of his Works, fol. 865, and Espencaeus on 1 Timothy, f. 12 seq. Nor does the passage Romans 8:26 contribute anything for prayers void of sense. For there it is not a matter of ignorance of the object that is sought, or of the words by which something is sought, but of the insufficiency of just devotion, and the manner in which something is to be sought from GOD, which that 'καθὼς δεῖ' sufficiently indicates.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ) Alioqui si vel optima ad Deum preces lingua externa eloquar.

Τὸ πνεῦμά με προσεύχεται) πνεῦμα vocat motum illum qui est ab afflatu.

Ὁ δὲ νοῦς με ἄκαρπός ἐστι) Mens mea nihil bene à se exco- gitatum profert.

Νοῦς hic secundum Cornelium est idem, quod sensus ut v. 19. & c. II. v. ult. quo pacto id Apostolus accipit: τίς ἐπι τούτων τῶν ῥημάτων νους: Hæc ergo mens, id est sensus, significatio, intelligentia lingua- rum mearum est sine fructu, quia nemo eam capit, intelligitve, ut inde ad pietatem excitetur. Ita Cor- nelius à Lapide. Ἄκαρπος dicitur mens non ratione loquentis, sed audientis. Estius contra ut indoctissi- mis clericis, & laicis preces audientibus non intel- ligentibus velificetur, hæc illis applicat, qui Lati- nitatis ignari, Latino sermone preces recitant, qui quidem spiritu & affectu devotionis in Deum fe- runtur, si vere orent: Quia vero verba non intelli- gunt, mens eorum sine fructu est videlicet intelli- gentiæ. Ubi vanus est, cum ait: Qui sic orant, etsi fructum intelligentiæ non percipiant, ideoque nec pa- scantur sensibus per verba significantia, habent tamen fructum mentis elevatæ in Deum. Qualis n. hæc est mentis in Deum elevatio, cum eorum, quæ dicun- tur, mēs nihil intelligit. Bruta est illa devotio, non grata Deo oratio. Et aperte ita contradicitur Apo- stolo, qui simpliciter ἄκαρπον talem mentem & orationem dicit, quæ est sine intelligentia.

Para- doxum ergo est, quod addit Estius, contingere, ut quispiam sine intelligentia orans plus apud Deum me- reatur & impetret, quam alius, intellectu sensum as- sequūs orationis. Ἄκαρπον autem dici hic audientiū ratione, ad quos nullus fructus redundat, tota ora- tio Pauli docet, quibus etiam Barbarus est, qui lin- gua (scil. exotica) loquitur. Conf. imprimis v. 19. Quem sensum agnoscunt Remenses, Cornelius; Ju- stinianus, non dici, quod verba & mens preca- tionis non intelligantur à precante, sed dici, quod nō intelligantur ab audientibus precantē publice, ut recte hic se habeat paraphrasis B. Hunnii: Nam si lingua orem aliis hominibus ignota, tum spiritus sane meus orat, interim mens mea, hoc est verborū precationis meæ sensus fugit & latet audientes, ideoque fructu vacat, fructu nimirum eo, quem alias precatio vulgato sermone dicta & intellecta profert ad proximum. Hac vero universa Pauli doctrina prosternitur penitus cultus Romanæ Ec- clesiæ in lingua exotica, quæ à plebe non intelligitur, quemadmodum Justinianus ipse ad v. 4. & 5. hæc de sacris officiis cum Ecclesia, vulgari lingua peragen- dis exposuit: Cui præiverunt Cajetanus apud Sixt. Senens. l. VI. annot. 263. Faber Stapulensis & Era- smus, in quam sententiam Patres, & Pontificios plu- res adduxit Cassander de officiis pii viri in defen- sione Operum fol. 865. Espensæus in priorem ad Ti- moth. 1. f. 12. seq. Nec pro precibus sensu cassis quic- quam facit locus Rom. IIX. 26. Ibi n. non agitur de ignorantia objecti quod petitur, aut verborum, quibus aliquid petitur, sed de insufficientia justæ de- votionis, & modi, quo quid à DEO petendum est, quod indicat satis illud καθὼς δεῖ.

## 14:15
V. 15. Τί οὖν ἐστι) What therefore is it, namely that which is to be desired. Προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοῒ) Ἵνα is understood. This is to be desired, that I may pray, that is, that someone may pray, not only by that inspired motion, but also by those things which he himself has devised.

Ψαλῶ δὲ τῷ πνεύματι, ψαλῶ δὲ τῷ νοῒ) What he said concerning prayers to God, the same [he says] concerning the praises of God תהלים which were accustomed to be pronounced by singing. See what we have said at Matt. XXVI. 30. Add Mark XIV. 26. Acts XVI. 25. Eph. V. 19. Coloss. III. 16.

Not an inspired motion is understood by πνεῦμα, but the spirit, which in man is opposed to the flesh. Νοῦς, however, is added, so that the intelligence of the prayer and hymn, with respect to those among whom the prayer and hymns are instituted, may be simultaneously intimated. I will pray in the spirit for my own edification, so that I may worship my GOD in the spirit: Meanwhile I will pray also with the mind, that is, I will pray in such a way that I may be understood for the benefit of others. For the mind in this place signifies the sense and intelligence of the recited discourse, as B. Hunnius rightly does here. This sense is continued by those things which follow further.

Latin:

V. 15. Τί οὖν ἐστι) Quid igitur est, nempe quod optandū sit. Προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοῒ) Ἵνα subauditur. Hoc optandum est ut orem, id est, oret aliquis, non tantum motu illo afflatitio, verum etiam iis quæ ipse excogitavit.

Ψαλῶ δὲ τῷ πνεύματι, ψαλῶ δὲ τῷ νοῒ) Quod de preci- bus ad Deum dixit, idem de laudibus Dei תהלים quæ solebant canendo pronuntiari. Vide quæ diximus Matth. XXVI. 30. Adde Marci XIV. 26. Act. XVI. 25. Eph. V. 19. Coloss. III. 16.

Non motus afflatitius per πνεῦμα intelligitur, sed spiritus, qui in homine carni opponitur. Νοῦς vero additur, ut intelligentia orationis, & hymni respe- ctu eorum, apud quos oratio & hymni instituun- tur, simul innuatur. Orabo spiritu in mei ædi- ficationem, ut spiritu colam DEUM meum: Interim orabo, & mente, hoc est, sic precabor, ut intelligar ad aliorum utilitatem. Mens enim hoc loco recitati sermonis sensum & intelligentiam fignificat, ut hic recte B. Hunnius. Quem sensum continuant ea, quæ porro sequuntur.

## 14:16
V. 16. Ἐπεὶ) Ἐπεὶ here is 'otherwise', as in Rom. XI. 6. 16. Ἐὰν εὐλογήσῃς τῷ πνεύματι) If you praise God only while that motion of a foreign tongue lasts. Εὐλογεῖν is the same as that which follows immediately, εὐχαριστεῖν. See what we have said on Matt. XXVI. 26.

It is a new thing for Πνεῦμα to be explained as the inspiration of a foreign tongue: To speak in a foreign tongue is expressed otherwise by the Apostle, namely γλώσσῃ λαλεῖν, or γλώσσαις, v. 18, 19. But why should not πνεῦμα be taken simply, as it sounds, for the spirit? For even to him who gives thanks only in the spirit, Amen cannot be sung, because others do not perceive it, since we bless only with the spirit, not with the mouth, just as they do not perceive it when we bless in a language unknown to them. We do not, however, deny that these things may also be referred to an exotic language, as was done by B. Hunnius. Again, from the antithesis, he teaches that thanksgiving is fruitless if it is either recited or chanted in an exotic idiom, if you refer it so to your own spirit and understanding alone, that he who is an idiot neither perceives what you are singing or chanting, nor is able to add his Amen to your song and thanksgiving, and declare his assent. In this way you indeed give thanks well, if that blessing or thanksgiving of yours flows from a faithful heart. But meanwhile you are frustrated of that most beautiful fruit, which is the edification of brothers and sisters. To bless in the spirit, says B. Balduinus, is to perform a sacred duty in the Church in a foreign tongue, which you have from a singular gift of the Holy Spirit. For here, a blessing is any sacred action instituted in a public assembly, whether by speech, or by prayers to the people, or in any other way.

ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου) ἰδιώτης, the unlearned, [says] the Scholiast on the Frogs. In the Glossary: ἰδιώτης, he who is not learned in the law, rustic, rude. Alexis uses it thus. The Hebrew Rabbis made their הדיוט from it. See Acts IV. 13. And ἀναπληρῶν τόπον, מַלֵּא מָקוֹם, is likewise a Hebraism, for being in some state.

There is, therefore, no reason why you should understand it, as some Papists do, of a certain cleric who answers Amen in place of the people. For τόπος is nowhere the same as 'in place of', and ἀναπληροῦν is not to be in the place of someone, but to fill and occupy a place. And thus Bellarmine also refuted his own associates in book 2, de verbo DEI, cap. 1, and acknowledges our interpretation to be true, as B. Balduinus observes. And thus the Greeks, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, also explained it, that it was the custom of the ancients that the people themselves would acclaim the prayers of the priests, which sense Cajetan, Guilliandus, and Gagnæus also embrace. Cf. Ps. CVI. 48. Cornelius à Lapide: I say, he says, that 'idiot' here does not signify a minister of sacred things, but anyone from the laity: For in Greek it is ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου, who fills or occupies the place of an idiot, that is, who sits among the idiots, who is an idiot (for the Prophets and Doctors sat in one place, the idiots and the people in another), as is every commoner, and the whole unlearned populace. Thus Chrysostom and Theophylact; for the whole populace, and consequently any idiot, formerly answered Amen in sacred assemblies, as is evident from Justin, Apol. 2, at the end. Whence Jerome, at the end of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, says that in the Roman Church, it resounds like heavenly thunder, Amen.

Πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμὴν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ) In the ancient Church, the people would sing Amen to the Bishop or any other person praying or praising God, whence that [verse]: 'And the ether strikes the heavens with the resounding Amen.' By that word, they approved what was said, and that according to the Hebrew custom, according to which Amen is called an ἐφύμνιον by Philo. See Deut. XXVIII. 22, and what [is said] on Matt. V. 18 in Aruc: אין עונים אמן יתומה. When someone says Amen to prayers which he does not understand, that is called by the Hebrews אמן יתומה, an orphan Amen. Therefore, prayers and praises were celebrated in the popular language both among the Jews and the Christians. Origen against Celsus VIII: 'The rest of the Christians do not even use the names found in the divine scriptures, even if they are ordained by God, in their prayers, but the Greeks use Greek [names], and the Romans use Roman [names]; and thus each prays to God according to his own dialect, and praises Him as he is able.' And the Lord of every dialect hears those who pray in every dialect, hearing as one (if I may so name it) voice that which is according to the meanings, manifested from the varied dialects. For the God who is over all is not like one of those who have been allotted some barbarian or Greek dialect, and who no longer know the others, or no longer care for those who speak in other dialects.

Ἐπειδὴ τί λέγεις, ὐκ οἶδε) He does not understand, having been taught only the Greek language.

Latin:

V. 16. Ἐπεὶ) ἐπεὶ hic est alioqui, ut Rom. XI. 6. 16. Ἐὰν εὐλογήσῃς τῷ πνεύματι) Si Deum laudes tantum dum durat ille motus linguæ peregrinæ. Εὐλογεῖν idem cum eo, quod mox sequitur, εὐχαριστεῖν. Vide, quæ diximus Matth. XXVI. 26..

Πνεῦμα de afflatu linguæ peregrinæ explicari novum est: Linguâ peregrinâ loqui aliter effer- tur ab Apostolo, nimirum γλώσσῃ λαλεῖν, vel γλώσσαις, v. 18. 19. Cur non verò πνεῦμα simpli- citer, ut sonat, de spiritu accipiatur. Nam & illi, qui spiritu tantum gratias agit, non potest acci- ni Amen, quia non percipiunt alii, cum spiritu tantum benedicimus, non ore, æquè uti nec tum percipiant, cum ignotâ ipsis linguâ benedicimus. Non tamen repugnamus, ut hæc etiam ad lin- guam exoticam referantur, quemadmodum à B. Hunnio factum. Rursum ex antithesi frustraneam esse docet gratiarum actionem exotico idiomate, vel recitatam vel decantatam, si ad tuum solius spiritum & intelligentiam sic eam referas, ut qui idiota est, nec percipiat, quid canas aut psallas, nec ad cantionem tuam & gratiarum actionem suum Amen adjungere, & assensum declarare queat. Quâ ratione tu quidem bene gratias agis, si ex fideli corde promanet tua illa benedictio, seu gratiarum actio. Verum frustraris interim pulcherrimo illo fructu, qui est fratrum & soro- rum ædificatio. Benedicere spiritu, inquit B. Bal- duinus, est officium sacrum in Ecclesia expedire lingua peregrina, quam habes ex singulari dono Spiritus Sancti. Est enim hic benedictio quævis sacra actio in publico cœtu instituta, sive sermo- ne, sive precibus ad populum, sive alio quovis modo.

ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου) ἰδιώτης, ὁ ἀμαθὴς, Scholiastes ad Ranas. In Glossario: ἰδιώτης, ὁ μὴ νομικων, rusticus, rudis. Utitur sic Alexis. Rabbini Hebræi inde fe- cerunt suum הדיוט Vide Act. IV. 13. Et ἀναπληρῶι τόπον מַלֵּא מָקוֹם itidem Hebraismus, pro in statu ali- quo esse.

Non ergo est, quod cum Pontificiis quibus- dam id de clerico quodam intelligas, qui vice po- puli respondeat Amen. Nam τόπος nuspiam idem est, quod vice, & ἀναπληροῦν non est loco alicujus esse, sed locum implere, & occupare. Et ita Bellar- minus etiam suos sociennos refutavit lib. 2. de ver- bo DEI cap. 1. nostramque interpretationem ve- ram agnoscit, ut observat B. Balduinus. Atque ita exposuere etiam Græci Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus, Oecumenius, quod mos fuerit antiquis, ut precibus sacerdotum ipse populus acclamaret, quem sensum etiam amplectitur Cajetanus, Guil- liandus, & Gagnæjus. Conf. Ps. CVI. 48.
