Corne- lius à Lapide: Dico, inquit, Idiotam hic non signi- ficare ministrum sacrorum, sed quemvis è plebe: Græce enim est ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου, qui implet vel occupat locum idiotæ, id est, qui se- det inter idiotas, qui est idiota, (alio enim loco sedebant Prophetæ & Doctores, alio idiotæ & populus.) uti est plebejus quisque, & tota plebs indocta. Ita Chrysostomus & Theophylactus; to- ta enim plebs, & consequenter quivis idiota olim in sacris conventibus respondebat Amen, ut pa- tet ex Justin. apol. 2. in fine. Unde Hieronymus in fine commentarii in epistolam ad Galatas, in Ecclesia Romana, ait, ad instar cœlestis tonitru re- boat, Amen.

Πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμὴν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ) In veteri Eccle- sia Episcopo aut alio quovis Deum precante vel laudante plebs accinebat Amen, unde illud: Et resonaturis ferit æthera Sobis Amen. Ea voce dicta approbans, idque ex more Hebræo, secun- dum quem Amen dicitur ἐφύμνιον Philoni. Vide Deut. XXVIII. 22. & quæ ad Matth. V. 18. in Aruc אין עונים אמן יתומה cum quis Amen dicit ad preces, quas non intelligit, id vocatur Hebræis אמן יתומה Amen pupillum. Ideo preces & laudes celebrabantur lingua po- pulari tàm apud Judæos, quam Christianos. Origenes adversus Celsum VIII. Οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν χρισιανῶν ἐδὲ τοῖς ἐν ταῖς θείαις γραφαῖς κειμένοις ὀνόμασι, κᾀν τεταγμένοις ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ, χρῶνται ἐν ταῖς ἐυχαῖς, ἀλλ' οἱ μὲν Ἕλληνες Ἑλληνικοῖς, οἱ δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι Ῥωμαϊκοῖς· Καὶ ὕτως ἕκασος κα- τὰ τὴν ἑαυτῦ διάλεκτον ἔυχεται τῷ Θεῷ, κᾀι ὑμνεῖ ἀυτὸν ὡς δύναται. Καὶ ὁ πάσης διαλέκτε Κυρίος τῶν ἀπὸ πάσης δια- λέκτε ἐυχομένων ἀκύει, ὡς μῖας (ἴ' ὕτως ὀνομάσω) φωνῆς τῆς κατὰ τὰ σημαινόμενα ἀκέων, δηλωμένης ἐκ τῶν ποικίλων διαλέκτων. Οὐ γάρ ἐσιν ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι Θεὸς ὥς τις τῶν κεκλη- ρωμένων διάλεκτόν τινα βάρβαρον ἢ Ἕλληνα, κᾀι μηκέτι τὰς λοιπὰς ἐπισαμένων, ἢ μηκέτι τῶν ἐν ἄλλαις διαλέκτοις λεγό- των φροντίζων.

Ἐπειδὴ τί λέγεις, ὐκ οἶδε) Non intelligit, Græcam tan- tum linguam edoctus.

## 14:17
V. 17. Σὺ μὲν γὰρ καλῶς ἐυχαριστεῖς) מברך. Ἀλλ' ὁ ἕτερος ὐκ οἰκοδομεῖται) He profits nothing from it.

Latin:

V. 17. Σὺ μὲν γὰρ καλῶς ἐυχαριστεῖς) מברך. Ἀλλ' ὁ ἕτερος ὐκ οἰκοδομεῖται) Nihil inde proficit.

## 14:18
V. 18. Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ με πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶν) The Apostles had a group of all the gifts.

Latin:

V. 18. Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ με πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶν) Apostoli omnium donorum habebant ὀμάδα.

## 14:19
V. 19. 'Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.' In the manuscript it is: Tῷ νοΐ μυ. In the church, that is, where few are very knowledgeable in languages, I would rather speak five, that is, a few words, thought out by myself, than many through the inspiration of a foreign tongue, and one not understood by most. Κατηχήσω אשמיע, I will cause to hear, that is, to understand, μυρίους רבבות that is, numberless.

Latin:

V. 19. Ἀλλ' ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ θέλω πέντε λόγες διὰ τῦ νοός με λαλῆσαι, ἵνα κᾀι ἄλλες κατηχήσω, ἢ μυρίυς λόγες ἐν γλώσσῃ) In Manuscripto est: Tῷ νοΐ μυ. In Ecclesia, id est, ubi pauci sunt plurimi linguarum gnari, malim quinque, id est, pauca verba loqui, à me ipso cogitata, quam multa per afflatum linguæ peregrinæ, & plerisque non intellectæ. Κατηχήσω אשמיע, faciam audire, id est, intelligere, μυρίους רבבות id est, innumera.

## 14:20
V. 20. 'Brethren, be not children in understanding.' It is the way of children to show off in useless matters.

'But in malice be ye children.' I do not forbid you to imitate children in innocence, just as Christ did not forbid it, Matt. XVIII. 3.

'But in understanding be men.' Similar to adult men, Eph. IV. 14.

Latin:

V. 20. Ἀδελφοὶ, μὴ παιδία γίνεσθε ταῖς φρεσί) Puero- rum est, se oftentare in rebus inutilibus.

Ἀλλὰ τῇ κακίᾳ νηπιάζετε) Innocentia pueros vos imi- tari non veto, ut nec Christus vetuit Matth. XVIII. 3.

Ταῖς δὲ φρεσὶ τέλειοι γίνεσθε) similes viris adultis Eph. IV. 14.

## 14:21
V. 21. 'In the law it is written.' By the word νόμυ here he signifies all writings given divinely, as in John X. 34, XV. 25.

'With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me.' Origen teaches us in Philocalia VII that these are cited by Paul from the passage of Isaiah XXVIII. 11 & 12, yet not from the LXX version, but from the version of Aquila. There are, however, certain words which the Prophet placed in the middle, omitted as not pertaining to this matter. It is a punishment to be among men of a foreign tongue. And do you impose that upon the Church? 'Lip' among the Hebrews signifies speech no less than 'tongue'. Gen. XI. 1.

Latin:

V. 21. Ἐν δὲ νόμῳ γέγραπται) Νόμυ vocabulo hic signifi- cat omnia scripta divinitus data, ut Joh. X. 34. XV. 25.

Ὅτι ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις, κᾀι ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέροις λαλήσω τῷ λαῷ τύτῳ, κᾀ ἐδὲ ὕτως εἰσακέσονταί με) Hæc citari à Pau- lo ex loco quidem Esaia XXVIII. 11. & 12. non tamen ex versione LXX. sed ex versione Aquilæ docet nos Orige- nes Philocaliæ VII. Sunt autem verba quædam, quæ Pro- pheta in medio posuit, omissa, ut ad rem hanc non perti- nentia. Pœna est versari inter homines linguæ extraneæ. Et vos id Ecclesiæ imponitis? Labium apud Hebræos non minus quam lingua loquelam significat. Gen. XI. 1.

## 14:22
'Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not.' They are given especially to convert foreigners, those still infidels: spoken comparatively.

'But prophesying [serveth not] for them which believe not.' Namely, only.

Latin:

Ὥστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖόν εἰσιν, ὐ τοῖς πισέυεσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοῖς) Præcipue dantur ad convertendos extraneos, infideles adhuc: comparatè dictum.

Ἡ δὲ προφητεία ὐ τοῖς ἀπίστοις) Nempe tantum.

## 14:24
If all prophesy) Greek language. If an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters) In Greek, a Christian or pagan who understands.

He is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and thus the secrets of his heart become manifest) We have said elsewhere that to prophesy is also said of things past or present, but so hidden that they can be known by no power of human ingenuity. See Matt. XXVI. 68. Therefore, the prophets, when people entered, said such things as Christ said to the Samaritan woman, John IV. 29, or as Elisha said to Gehazi, 2 Kings V. 26. Irenaeus says in I. 6 that he knew many, and had heard the brothers themselves, who brought the hidden things of men into the open.

Latin:

Ἐὰν δὲ πάντες προφητεύωσιν) Lingua Græca Εἰσέλθῃ δὲ ἄπιστος ἡ ἰδιώτης) Græce intelligens Christia- nus aut paganus.

Ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων, καὶ οὕτω τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας αὐτοῦ φανερὰ γίνεται) Diximus alibi προφητεύειν dici etiam de rebus præteritis aut præsentibus, sed ita arcanis, ut nulla vi humani ingenii cognosci possint. Vide Matth. XXVI. 68. Prophetæ ergo intrantibus talia dicebant, qualia Christus Samaritidi Joh. IV. 29. qualia Elisæus Giezi 2. Reg. V. 26. Dicit Irenæus I. 6. se multos novisse, & audisse ipsum fratres, qui occulta hominum in apertum proferrent.

## 14:25
V. 25. And thus falling on his face he will worship God) He will venerate God, and indeed with prostrate body. Just as in the Books of Kings, so in the honor of GOD there were various gestures: but the highest submission was shown by a prostrate body, as we said at Matt. VIII. 2, and in the larger Annotations on the Decalogue. Thus Job I. 20: Falling to the ground he worshipped.

Proclaiming that God is truly among you) Just as the Egyptian magicians said: The finger of GOD is here, Exod. VIII. 19. God is said to be where He works the most wondrous things.

These things do not pertain to the miraculous manifestation of hidden things, but to the ordinary power of the divine word, by which the unfaithful are struck when they hear it. For it is the power of GOD unto salvation, Rom. I. 16, living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, it judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, Heb. IV. 12. Rightly, therefore, the blessed Hunnius explained these things thus: He demonstrates more abundantly that that ambitious display of foreign languages does not achieve any fruit, not even among the unfaithful (for whose sake those were otherwise given). For if in a solemn assembly all those who are gifted with the gift of tongues begin to speak at once in languages commonly unknown, and meanwhile the known and vernacular language falls silent: But if unlearned men, rude and ignorant of those languages, and not yet converted to the faith of the Gospel, enter, they will judge from that confusion that you are insane, rather than perceive any fruit from it. But if you all prophesy. The sense is, if you prophesy in a familiar language and interpret the scriptures, and an unbeliever and unlearned person enters, who is nevertheless well-versed in the language in which you prophesy: He will hear his idolatry, unbelief, injustice, and other sins argued and judged by all, and thus the secrets of his heart become manifest, when you bring forth the scriptures, which are powerful for discussing his silent thoughts and for bringing his sins out of darkness into the light and condemning them. Hence it happens that, falling on his face, he gives glory to GOD and acknowledges that God truly is present in your sacred assemblies by His Spirit, inasmuch as His word reigns there opulently and strikes the souls of men with such an effective sense, and bends them toward conversion. Here Cornelius à Lapide notes eight exercises of the ancient Church assemblies, which, if the Canon is correctly explained regarding the words of institution, we easily admit. But ah! how they differ from the assemblies of the Papists. From this place note: In the primitive Church this was the rite and order of sacred things in the sacred assemblies of Christians (as is evident from Justin's apology to Antoninus at the end, and Tertullian in Apologeticus ch. 39, and others) instituted by Paul and the Apostles: 1. They sang psalms, even the people. 2. Prophecies and sacred scripture were read. 3. The Bishop preached. 4. The supper and the sacrament were performed, which then consisted almost only of the oblation, consecration, communion, the canon, and the Lord's Prayer, and some prayer to which the people responded: Amen. 5. All communicated. 6. Some, as if inspired by the Spirit, dictated and sang psalms and hymns to the praise of GOD in various languages, others prophesied. 7. Others, in the manner of the Jews, interpreted the sacred scriptures or exhorted, and those were two or three, especially Prophets or spiritual men: Others listened and occasionally asked questions, even women (but through an abuse which Paul corrects here) about something concerning what was being said, and when something good and pious was said beautifully, they all shouted together: Amen, amen. 8. An agape, or feast common to all, closed everything as a symbol of charity, after which hymns and prayers followed again.

PART II. Admonition concerning the edification of the Church, and the order to be observed in the same.

Latin:

V. 25. Καὶ οὕτω πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον προσκυνήσει τῷ Θεῷ) Deum venerabitur, & quidem prostrato corpore. Sicut in Regum, ita in DEI honore varii erant gestus: Summa au- tem demissio ostendebatur projecto corpore, ut diximus ad Matth. VIII. 2. & in majoribus Annotatis ad Decalogum. Sic Jobi I. 20. Πεσὼν χαμαὶ προσεκύνησεν.

Ἀπαγγέλλων, ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς ὄντως ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστι) Sicut Ægyptii magi dicebant: Digitus DEI est hic, Exod. VIII. 19. Deus esse dicitur, ubi maximè mira operatur.

Hæc non ad miraculosam occultorum manife- stationem, sed ad vim verbi divini ordinariam fa- ciunt, quo percelluntur infideles, cum id audiunt. Est enim potentia DEI ad salutem, Rom. I. 16. vi- vum ac efficax ac penetrantius quovis gladio anci- piti, & pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ & spiritus, compagumque & medullarum, dijudi- cat cogitationes & intentiones cordis, Ebr. IV. 12. Recte itaque B. Hunnius hæc ita exposuit: Ex abundanti demonstrat amplius, ambitiosam illam ostentationem peregrinarum linguarum, ne quidem apud infideles, (quorum causa alias datæ illæ sunt) fructum aliquem consequi. Etenim si in solenni cœtu ii simul omnes, qui dono lingua- rum pollent, loqui incipiant linguis vulgo igno- tis, atque interim contiăescat lingua nota & ver- nacula: Ingrediantur vero homines idiotæ lin- guarum illarum rudes & ignari, nec dum ad Ev- angelii fidem conversi, hi potius ex ista confu- sione judicabunt, vos insanire, quàm ut ullum in- de fructum percipiant. Quod si omnes prophetetis. Sensus est, si lingua familiari prophetetis, & scri- pturas interpretemini, ingrediatur autem incredu- lus & indoctus, ejus tamen linguæ, qua vos pro- phetatis, probe gnarus: Is audiet argui & dijudi- cari ab omnibus suam idololatriam, incredulita- tem, injustitiam, cæteraque peccata, atque sic oc- culta cordis ejus manifesta fieri, quando scripturas proferetis, quæ ad tacitas ipsius cogitationes dis- cutiendas, & peccata ejus velut ex tenebris in lucem eruenda & condemnanda valent. Hinc sit, ut in faciem procidens det DEO gloriam, & agno- scat Deum suo Spiritu verè interesse sacris vestris cœtibus, utpote in quibus verbum ejus opulen- ter regnet, tamque efficaci sensu animos homi- num percellat, & ad conversionem flectat. No- tat hic Cornelius à Lapide octo conventuum Ec- clesiæ antiquorum exercitia, quæ si Canon recte explicetur de verbis nempe institutionis, facilè ad- mittimus. Sed ah! quantum à Papicolarum con- ventibus differunt. Ex hoc loco nota: In Ecclesia primæva hic erat ritus & ordo sacrorum in sacris Christianorum conventibus (ut patet ex Justino apologia ad Antoninum in fine, & Tertul- liano in Apologetico cap. 39. & aliis) à Paulo & Apostolis institutis: 1. canebant psalmos, etiam po- pulus. 2. Legebantur prophetiæ & sacra scriptura. 3. Episcopus prædicabat. 4. fiebat cœna & sacrum, quod tunc fere tantum oblatione, consecratione, communione, canone, & Pater noster, ac oratione aliqua, cui populus respondebat: Amen, constabat. 5. omnes communicabant. 6. quidam psalmos & hymnos in laudem DEI variis linguis quasi afflati Spiritu dictabant & canebant, alii prophetabant. 7. Alii more Judæorum sacras scripturas inter- pretabantur vel exhortabantur, iique duo, vel tres, præsertim Prophetæ aut viri spirituales: Alii au- diebant & subinde interrogabant, etiam fæminæ, (sed per abusum, quem Paulus hic corrigit) ali- quid circa id, quod dicebatur, cumque aliquid boni & pii pulchre dicebatur simul inclamabant: Amen, amen. 8. claudebat omnia agape, sive convivium omnibus commune in symbolum charitatis, post quod rursum succedebant hymni & orationes.

PARS II. Commonefactio de ædificatione Ecclesiæ, & ordine in eadem observando.

## 14:26
V. 26. What then is it?) What then is to be done? He takes the person of the questioner, so that he may answer. When you come together) as above 23. Each of you has a psalm) these members are to be read with a question. Even those extemporaneous hymns were often from inspiration. Such was the hymn of Simeon: and of Anna the widow: and, as is credible, of Moses and his sister Miriam, and another of Moses and Deborah, and of Anna who was married to Elkanah, and of Deborah, and of Isaiah 5. All things, which once came either from talent or from labor, were then given to many suddenly and divinely, so that from this the supreme beneficence of GOD might be understood. Has a teaching) excellent sentences, above XIV. 6. Has a tongue) The gift of some language, which he has not learned. Has a revelation) The gift of explaining those things which lie hidden under the figures of the Old Testament. Has an interpretation) The gift of saying in Greek, in order, all things which another said in a foreign language. In the manuscript these are all written a little differently: ψαλμὸν ἔχει, ἀποκάλυψιν ἔχει, γλῶσσαν ἔχει, ἑρμηνείαν ἔχει. Πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γενέσθω) Our glory is not looked to, but the utility of the Church. V. 27. Εἴτε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, κατὰ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος) Because there were many at that time who had the gift of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle, the greatest guardian of εὐταξίας (good order), does not want all who had the gift of foreign languages to use it at one time in the assembly, lest the people be detained more than is necessary: nor indeed that some address those in this part of the basilica, and others those in that, and as it were distract the people, as charlatans do in the forum, but he commands that on one day no more than two or three should demand a hearing for themselves, and that in divided intervals of time, so that first this one, then that one, and soon another might be heard. Here κατὰ signifies καθ᾽ ἡμέραν (daily). For κατὰ is accustomed to be used in distributions, Matt. XXIV. 7, below XVI. 2. Ἀνὰ μέρος, that is, not simultaneously, but each in his own order. Καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω) Let one person, who has that gift and understands both languages, explain what was said in the foreign tongue in the Greek language, omitting or changing nothing. 28. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ᾖ διερμηνευτὴς) If no one is present who has that gift. Σιγάτω ἐν Ἐκκλησίᾳ) If anyone has the gift of a tongue, let him reserve it for other places where foreigners are to be converted. But let him not disturb public assemblies of those who do not understand that language. Ἑαυτῷ δὲ λαλείτω καὶ τῷ Θεῷ) At his own home, if he wishes, with God as his witness. Grotius seems to refer all these things to the extraordinary gifts which flourished in the primitive Church. But those things which were delivered generally by the Apostle are suitable for all times. For that common and catholic rule: πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γενέσθω, and the reason brought forward by the Apostle is universal: God is not a God of confusion, but of peace.

Latin:

V. 26. Τί ὖν ἐστι) Quid ergo faciendum est? Sumit in- terrogantis personam, ut respondeat. Ὅταν συνέρχησθε) ut supra 23. Ἕκαστῶν ὑμῶν ψαλμὸν ἔχει) cum interrogatione legen- da hæc membra. Etiam extemporales isti hymni sæpe ab afflatu erant. Talis fuit hymnus Simeonis: & Annæ vi- duæ: &, ut credibile est, Mosis & Mariæ sororis ejus, & al- ter Mosis & Deboræ, & Annæ, quæ nupta Elcanæ, & Debo- ræ, & Esaiæ 5. Omnia, quæ olim aut ex ingenio aut ex la- bore veniebant, tunc multis dabantur subito & divinitus, ut ex eo intelligeretur DEI summa beneficentia. Διδαχὴν ἔχει) sententias eximias, supra XIV. 6. Γλῶσσαν ἔχει) Donum linguæ alicujus, quam non di- dicit. Ἀποκάλυψιν ἔχει) Donum explicandi ea, quæ latent sub figuris Veteris Testamenti. Ἑρμηνείαν ἔχει). Donum omnia ordine dicendi Græce, quæ alter dixit lingua peregrina. In manuscripto hæc omnia paulò aliter scripta sunt: ψαλμὸν ἔχει, ἀποκάλυψιν ἔχει, γλῶσσαν ἔχει, ἑρμηνείαν ἔχει. Πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γενέσθω) Non nostra spectatur gloria, sed utilitas Ecclesiæ. V. 27. Εἴτε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, κατὰ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος) Quia multi erant illo tempore, qui donum Spiritus Sancti habebant, maximus εὐταξίας custos Apo- stolus, non vult omnes, qui donum linguarum extranea- rum habebant, in uno conventus tempore eo uti, ne plus quam oportet plebs detineretur: neque vero alios in hac parte basilicæ, alios in ista adfari, & quasi distrahere ple- bem, ut in foro Agyrtæ faciunt, sed præcipit, ut uno die non plures duobus aut tribus audientiam sibi poscant, idque divisis temporum spatiis, ut primum hic, deinde iste, mox alius audiretur. Κατὰ hic valet καθ᾽ ἡμέραν. Solet enim κατὰ in distributionibus usurpari Matth. XXIV. 7. in- fra XVI. 2. Ἀνὰ μέρος, id est, non simul, sed suo quisque ordine. Καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω) Unus aliquis, qui id donum ha- beat, & linguam utramque intelligat, dicta peregrino ser- mone explicet sermone Græco, nihil prætermittens, aut immutans. 28. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ᾖ διερμηνευτὴς) Si nemo adsit id donum habens. Σιγάτω ἐν Ἐκκλησίᾳ) Si quis donum linguæ habet, re- servet id aliis locis, ubi peregrini sint convertendi. Publi- cos autem cœtus linguam illam non intelligentium ne obturbet. Ἑαυτῷ δὲ λαλείτω καὶ τῷ Θεῷ) Domi suæ, si vult, Deo teste. Omnia hæc Grotius ad extraordinaria dona, quæ in primitiva Ecclesia vigebant, referre vide- tur. Quæ verò generatim ab Apostolo tradita, omnibus temporibus conveniunt. Regula enim illa communis & catholica: πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γενέσθω, & causa ab Apostolo adducta universa- lis est: Deus non confusionis Deus, sed pacis.

## 14:29
V. 29. Προφῆται δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν) Namely on one day, just as he said concerning those having the gift of tongues. Καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν) The president of the Church, having also called in, if the matter is more difficult, the presidents of neighboring Churches. See above XII. 10. Judgment is permitted not concerning predictions made by immediate revelation, but concerning the ordinary interpretation of scripture, not only to the presidents of Churches, nor to Pastors or Teachers alone, but also to laymen, just as the Bereans judged concerning the doctrine of Paul, Acts XVII. 11, and everyone is commanded δοκιμάζειν τὰ

spirits, 1 John 4:1. Furthermore, that prophecy is not taken here as the prediction of future events from immediate divine revelation is also taught by the fact that he commands women to be silent in the Church. For those who were moved by a prophetic spirit to manifest future or hidden things were certainly not forbidden to propose them publicly, just as we know was done by the prophetesses of the Old and New Testaments, whence Grotius admits this exception at verse 34.

Latin:

V. 29. Προφῆται δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν) Nempe uno die, sicut de linguæ donum habentibus dixit. Καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν) Præses Ecclesiæ, advocatis etiam, si res sit difficilior, vicinarum Ecclesiarum præsidi- bus. Vide supra XII. 10. Judicium non de Propheticis per immediatam revelationem factis predictionibus, sed de ordina- ria scripturæ interpretatione permittitur aliis, non tantum præsidibus Ecclesiarum, nec Pastoribus aut Doctoribus solum, sed etiam laicis, quemadmo- dum Berrhoënses de doctrina Pauli judicabant, Act. XVII. 11. & quisque jubetur δοκιμάζειν τὰ

πνεύματα, 1. Joh. IV. 1. Porrò prophetiam non ac- cipi hîc de futurorum prædictione ex immediata Dei revelatione, id etiam docet, quod mulieres in Ecclesia tacere jubeat. Quæ enim Prophetico spiritu agitatæ fuêre ad futura aut abdita manife- standa, illis utique non interdictum erat, publicè illa proponere, quemadmodum à Prophetissis Ve- teris & Novi Testamenti id factum novimus, un- de hanc exceptionem admittit Grotius ad v. 34.

## 14:30
V. 30. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting) For they were accustomed to propose prophecies while standing, Jer. 26:2, which position they also took when praying, as we said at Matt. 6:5. If, while one person is speaking, God inspires another, let him not interrupt the other, or deal with the people separately, but wait until the former has finished. Regarding the custom of sitting, see Acts 22:3.

Latin:

V. 30. Ἐὰν δὲ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ καθημένῳ) Nam stantes solebant prophetias proponere, Jerem. XXVI. 2. quo po- sito etiam precabantur, ut diximus ad Matth. VI. 5. Si uno aliquo loquente Deus alium afflaverit, ne is alium interpellet, aut seorsim cum populo agat, sed expectet, do- nec prior ille desierit. De sedendi more vide Act. XXII. 3.

## 14:31
V. 31. For you can all prophesy one by one) On different days, or at different hours.

So that all may learn, and all may be encouraged) Which would not happen if at the same time one person were addressing the people in this corner, and another in that.

Latin:

V. 31. Δύνασθε γὰρ καθ᾽ ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν) Di- versis aut diebus, aut horis.

Ἵνα πάντες μανθάνωσι, καὶ πάντες παρακαλῶνται) Quod non fieret, si eodem tempore alius in hoc angulo, alius in illo plebem affaretur.

## 14:32
V. 32. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets) And here is for 'for', and that is 'causally'. Someone might say: 'But I am so urged that I cannot delay.' Paul answers that the matter is not so with men inspired by God as it is with those possessed by Pythonic spirits. These are so seized and driven that they are not in control of themselves. But the gifts of GOD, although they do not proceed from the human will, easily allow themselves to be governed by his will regarding the act, the time, and the delay necessary for order. Regarding the Sibyl, Virgil says: 'But the seer, not yet enduring Phoebus, raves wildly in the cave, if she might be able to shake the great God from her breast; so much the more he fatigues her rabid mouth, taming her wild heart.' Lucan in the fifth book concerning the Pythia: '—she raves madly, bearing the neck of another through the cave, and the fillets of the God, and the Phoebean garlands, with hair standing on end, she tosses her head with a double neck, and scatters the tripods that stand in her way as she wanders, and seethes with a great fire, bearing you, Phoebus, in your anger.' Not so were Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other Prophets driven by the inspiration of GOD, but gently and with moderation. They were so able not to obey that Jonah refused the task. There is no compulsion here except from the fear of punishment. This meaning was rightly perceived by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. But they wander far from it who think that prophetic gifts are subject to other Prophets. The gifts of GOD do not fight among themselves: nor are opinions to be sought where it is certain that God is speaking.

This explanation, that the Spirit of the Prophets is subject to those very Prophets who are governed by the Spirit, seems foreign: because the discourse here is not about the same Prophets, but different ones; namely, about those who prophesy or interpret scripture, and about those who judge such Prophets or interpreters, as is manifest from verse 29 compared. And thus it is gathered that 'spirits of the prophets' is to be taken from 1 John 4:1. Lest perhaps through emulation, says the blessed Hunnius, the former person tries to defend his own opinion, even if it is inconvenient and causes offense to the Church, and to refute the interpretation of his colleague: Paul prescribes this rule, that the spirits of the Prophets be subject to the prophets, that is, that he who prophesies should not hesitate to submit his speech and sermon to the censure and judgment of the remaining preachers, nor consider it a disgrace to himself if anything is corrected by his colleagues, and proposed either more conveniently or more clearly. For unless this equanimity is applied, he shows that quarrels will arise, and confusion will be born in the sacred place and assembly. Similarly, the blessed Balduinus, rendering this meaning: 'He who has the prophetic gift is not therefore unaccountable, so that he cannot err, but it may happen that another Prophet brings forward something better, by which the opinion of the former is corrected.' Therefore, it is necessary that the former person take his censure in good part, lest the truth suffer violence on account of the authority of a person. Estius brings these things forward against the former explanation and in favor of this latter one: 'And indeed he seems to want to say something peculiar about the Prophets, which would not pertain to those who spoke in tongues. Otherwise, he would have brought forward a general opinion about both, that their spirits were subject to them, especially because confusion arose more from those who spoke in tongues than from those who prophesied. But he does not do that.' Indeed, in this whole exhortation he assumes that all those who had the gift of either tongues or prophecy could be silent and wait for an opportune time to speak. This was also known by experience. Furthermore, he says specifically about the Prophets that their spirits are subject to the Prophets, that is, to be judged by other prophets: which could not be said similarly about those who had the gift of tongues. For those who possessed only that gift were not fit to judge others who had a similar gift, but the Prophets could and ought to judge them, that is, judge their speech, if they understood the language. But if an interpreter were lacking, they had to be silent. And he notes that the commentaries of the ancients, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Pelagius, favor this latter interpretation; as well as Theophylact in the former passage, and that certain moderns also follow it, Johann Hofmeister and others.

Latin:

V. 32. Καὶ πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται) Καὶ hîc est pro nam, idque καὶ αἰτιολογικῶς. Poterat ali- quis dicere: Atqui ita urgeor, ut differre nequeam. Re- spondet Paulus, rem non ita se habere in divinitus afflatis hominibus, quomodo se habet in Pythonicis. Hos ita arripi atque agi, ut suæ potestatis non sint. At DEI dona, quan- quam non ab hominis voluntate profecta, voluntate ta- men ejus regi quoad actum, tempus & moram ordini ne- cessariam facilè pati. De Sibylla Virgilius: At Phœbi nondum patiens immanis in antro Bacchatur vates, magnum si pectore possit Excussisse Deum, tanto magis ille fatigat Os rabidum, fera corda domans. Lucanus quinto de Phœbade: —— bacchatur demens aliena per antrum Colla ferens, vittasque Dei, Phœbeaque serta Erectas discussa comas, per inania templi Ancipiti cerbice rotat, spargitque vaganti Obstantes tripodas, magnoque exæstuat igne Iratum te Phœbe ferens. Non sic Esaias, Jeremias & Prophetæ alii afflatu DEI age- bantur, sed leniter & cum modo. Adeo poterant non ob- sequi, ut Jonas munus detrectaverit. Nulla hic coactio nisi ex pœnæ metu. Hunc sensum recte perviderunt Chry- sostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius. Multum autem ab eo aberrant, qui putant, dona Prophetica aliis Prophetis esse subjecta. Non pugnant inter se DEI dona: Nec sen- tentiæ exquirendæ sunt, ubi Deum loqui constat.

Explicatio hæc, quod Spiritus Prophetarum illis ipsis Prophetis, qui à Spiritu reguntur, sub- jectus sit, aliena videtur: Quia hîc non de iisdem Prophetis, sed diversis sermo est; de illis nempe, qui prophetant vel interpretantur scripturam, & de illis, qui tales Prophetas vel interpretes diju- dicant, ut è v. 29. collato manifestum est. Atque ita πνεύματα προφητῶν accipi è Joh. IV. 1. colligi- tur. Ne fortè per æmulationem, inquit B. Hunnius, prior ille sententiam suam, licet incommodam cum offendiculo Ecclesiæ conetur defendere, & collega sui interpretationem refellere: Paulus hanc regulam præscribit, ut spiritus Prophetarum prophetis sub- jiciantur, id est, ut is, qui prophetat, non dubitet, sermonem & concionem suam censuræ judicioque reliquorum concionatorum subjicere, nec dedeco- ri sibi ducat, si quid à collegis emendetur, & pro- ponatur vel commodius, vel dilucidius. Hæc enim æquanimitas nisi adhibeatur, exorituras ostendit lites, & nascituram confusionem in loco & cœtu sacro. Similiter & B. Balduinus hunc reddiens sensum: Qui donum habet propheticum, non propterea est ἀνυπεύθυνος, ut errare non possit, sed fieri potest, ut alius Propheta melius aliquid afferat, quo prioris illius sententia corrigatur. Ejus itaque censuram, ut prior ille boni consulat, ne- cesse est, ne veritas vim patiatur, ob autoritatem personæ. Estius adversus priorem explicationem, & pro hac posteriori hæc affert: Ac sane vide- tur, aliquid peculiare dicere velle de Prophetis, quod ad eos, qui linguis loquebantur, non pertineret. Alio- qui generalem attulisset de utrisque sententiam, spi- ritus eorum eis subjectos esse, præsertim quia confusio magis nascebatur ab iis, qui loquebantur linguis, quàm à prophetantibus. Atqui non id fa- cit. Imò verò in tota hac adhortatione supponit omnes eos, qui donum vel linguarum vel prophetiæ habebant, posse tacere, tempusque ad loquendum opportunum expectare. Id quod etiam experientia notum erat. Cæterum de Prophetis peculiariter di- cit, eorum spiritus esse Prophetis subjectos, id est, ab aliis prophetis dijudicandos: Quod de iis, qui donum linguarum habebant, consimiliter dici non poterat. Nam qui illo solo dono potiebantur, idonei non erant, qui judicarent de aliis donum si- mile habentibus, sed de illis, hoc est, de sermone eo- rum judicare poterant & debebant Prophetæ, si lin- guam intelligerent. Quod si interpres deesset, ta- cendum illis erat. Atque huic posteriori inter- pretationi favere notat Commentarios veterum Chrysostomi, Theodoreti, Pelagii; nec non Theo- phylacti priori loco, eamque neotericos quosdam etiam sequi Johannem Hofmeisterum & alios.

## 14:33
V. 33. For God is not a God of confusion, but of peace.) Unclean spirits are violent; GOD is peaceful and gentle. See 2 Kings 19:12. This is to be read as a parenthesis: 'Akastasia' is 'arbubia' to the Rabbis. You have this word also in 2 Cor. 12:20 and James 3:16.

Estius rendered the meaning and connection more correctly: 'God is not the author of contention or confusion, but of peace: Therefore, the Prophets ought not to contend, each for his own opinion, but willingly and spontaneously submit themselves to the judgment of others.' 'Akastasia' is confusion and disturbed order, such as is usually present in tumult and sedition.

(Ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐκκλησίαις τῶν ἁγίων.) This must be referred to what he said, that the gifts of GOD are subject to the free uses of men; see a similar passage above XI. 16.

The Vulgate incorrectly adds the word 'I teach,' which is found neither in the Greek nor the Syriac copies, nor indeed in certain Latin manuscripts, nor in Primasius and Sedulius. Cajetan, however, refers this sentence to what follows regarding women. But it is more correctly referred to the preceding: That the same should be observed regarding the use of gifts, even in the other churches of the saints.

Latin:

V. 33. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι ἀκαταστασίας ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλ' εἰρήνης.) Spi- ritus impuri violenti sunt, DEUS pacificus & lenis. Vide 2. Reg. XIX. 12. Hoc per parenthesin legendum est: Ἀκα- ταστασία est עַרְבּוּבְיָא Rabbinis. Habes hanc vocem & 2. Cor. XII. 20. Jac. III 16.

Rectius sensum & connexionem reddidit Esti- us : Deus non est autor contentionis, vel confusionis, sed pacis: Igitur non debent Prophetæ pro sua quis- que sententia certare, sed aliorum judicio libenter ac sponte sese submittere. Ἀκαταστασία est confusio, & ordo turbatus, qualis esse solet in tumultu & seditione.

Ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐκκλησίαις τῶν ἁγίων.) Referendum ad id, quod dixit hominum liberis usibus subjici DEI dona, Vide simile supra XI. 16.

Perperam adjicit Vulgata verbum doceo, quod nec in Græcis, nec Syriacis exemplaribus repe- ritur, imò nec in quibusdam Manuscriptis Lati- nis, neque apud Primasium & Sedulium. Refert autem hanc sententiam Cajetanus ad id, quod se- quitur de mulieribus. Sed rectius refertur ad præcedentia: Quod idem observetur quoad usum donorum, etiam in aliis sanctorum Ecclesiis.

## 14:34
V. 34. Let your women keep silence in the church.) Let them not teach the people, or interrupt those speaking. Tyrraeus:

To speak much is a shame for a woman, but silence brings grace to all. - Sophocles: Woman, silence brings ornament to a woman. Which is most to be observed in public. Valerius Maximus III. 8. What have women to do with a public assembly? If ancestral custom is observed, nothing. See also L. 1. §. secundo D. de postulando and L. fœminæ D. de regulis juris, and what we have said there. In the manuscript it is ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις, but it is to be understood with the exception of prophetic inspiration, as we said above XI. 5.

For it is not permitted unto them to speak.) It is not allowed, as in 1 Tim. II. 12.

But to be under obedience.) To revere the stronger sex, which is done also by silence. But it is not 'is permitted' that is understood, but 'is commanded,' and that from the contrary, as in 1 Tim. IV. 3. But in the manuscript it is simpler: But let them be subject to their husbands.

As also saith the law.) Gen. III. 16. See above XI. 7. and what was said there.

Latin:

V. 34. Αἱ γυναῖκες ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ σιγάτωσαν.) Ne doceant populum, aut interrumpant loquentes. Tyr- ræus:

Πολλὰ λέγειν ἐνυμ' αἰδὼς γυναικὶ δὲ πᾶσι χαρίζεται. - Sophocles : Γυνὴ, γυναικὶ κόσμον ἡ σιγὴ φέρει. Quod ma- ximè servandum in publico. Valerius Maximus III. 8. Quid fœminæ cum concione? Si patrius mos servatur, nihil. Vide & L. 1. §. secundo D. de postulando & L. fœminæ D. de regulis juris, & ibi à nobis dicta. In Manuscripto est ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις, intelligendum vero cum exceptione af- flatus prophetici, diximus supra XI. 5.

Οὐ γὰρ ἐπιτέτραπται αὐταῖς λαλεῖν.) Non permissum est, ut 1. Tim. II. 12.

Ἀλλ' ὑποτάσσεσθαι.) Revereri sexum potiorem, quod fit etiam silentio. Subauditur autem non ἐπιτρέπεται, sed κελεύεται jubetur, idque ex contrario, ut 1 Tim. IV. 3. Sed in Manuscripto est simplicius : Ἀλλ' ὑποτασσέσθωσαν τοῖς ἀνδράσι.

Καθὼς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει.) Gen. III. 16. Vide supra XI. 7. & ibi dicta.

## 14:35
V. 35. And if they will learn any thing.) If they have not sufficiently understood something said by the teacher.

Let them ask their own husbands at home.) Let them ask the males of their own house, who will either answer from themselves or consult those more learned. The unbridled boldness of women has always caused much evil to the churches.

For it is a shame for women to speak in the church.) Of their own, that is to say. And 'shameful' is that which is not becoming. See above XI. 13.

Estius does not permit women to teach in the church, not even if they are endowed with the gift of prophecy or have received a revelation. But why would it be given to them from God the prophetic Spirit, or revelation, if it were not entirely within their power to bring forth prophecies or revelations?

Latin:

V. 35. Εἰ δέ τι μαθεῖν θέλουσιν.) Si quid à Doctore dictum non satis intellexerint.

Ἐν οἴκῳ τοὺς ἰδίους ἄνδρας ἐπερωτάτωσαν.) Mares domus suæ interrogent, qui aut respondebunt ex se, aut consulent peritiores. Multum semper Ecclesiis mali dedit effrenis mulierum audacia.

Αἰσχρὸν γάρ ἐστιν ἐν Ἐκκλησίᾳ γυναιξὶν λαλεῖν.) De suo sci- licet. Et αἰσχρὸν est, ὃ πρέπον. Vide supra XI. 13.

Estius mulieres, ne quidem, si dono prophetiæ præditæ sint, aut revelationem acceperint, doce- re non permittit in Ecclesia, Sed cur illis daretur à Deo Spiritus propheticus, aut revelatio, si non proferre vaticinia aut revelationes ipsis integrum foret?

## 14:36
V. 36. Or did the word of God come out from you? He says this because those Corinthian teachers had introduced a custom contrary to the institutions of all the Churches, that women should both teach and ask questions. But the word of the Gospel had gone out from Jerusalem. There it was done otherwise.

or did it reach you only? Just as you are not the first who believed, so neither are you the only ones. So many other Churches have equal right with you, and it is fair that the part should yield to the whole, not the whole to the part.

Latin:

V. 36. Ἢ ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ ἐξῆλθεν; ) Hoc ideo dicit, quia Corinthii illi Doctores morem introduxerant contrarium omnium Ecclesiarum institutis, ut fœminæ & docerent & interrogarent. At Hierosolymis exierat ser- mo Evangelii. Ibi aliter fiebat.

ἢ εἰς ὑμᾶς μόνυς κατήντησεν; ) Sicut primi non estis, qui credidistis, ita nec soli. Par vobiscum jus habent tot aliæ Ecclesiæ, & æquum est partem toti, non totum parti ce- dere.

## 14:37
V. 37. If any man thinks himself to be a prophet) If any man among you is believed to be a Prophet.

or spiritual) Or instructed by other gifts of the spirit. See above XII. 1.

Let him acknowledge the things that I write unto you) I desire this to be shown to him. For if he truly has an inspiration from God, he will not be able to contradict these things which I have said.

That they are the commandments of the Lord) I do not say these things of my own accord, but commanded by God.

The Apostle brings forward this argument, the strongest of all, as Theophylact says, in the last place, taken namely from the authority of Christ, as if to say: Christ commands these things to you through me, and true Prophets and spiritual men ought not to be ignorant of this. They can certainly know that these things are not contrary to the will and word of God, but consistent with them. However, it is not necessary that these things be understood of Prophets moved by the immediate inspiration of God. For who would doubt that such things can be judged from the scriptures, namely that they are consistent with the divine will? And the Apostle himself proved most of those things from the scriptures.

Latin:

V. 37. Εἴτις δοκεῖ προφήτης εἶναι) Si quis apud vos cre- ditur esse Propheta.

ἢ πνευματικός) Aut aliis donis spiritus instructus. Vi- de supra XII. 1.

Ἐπιγινωσκέτω ἃ γράφω ὑμῖν) Cupio hoc ei ostendi. Nam si verè à Deo afflatum habet, his quæ dixi contra- dicere non poterit.

Ὄτι κυρίε εἰσὶν αἱ ἐντολαὶ) Non meæ sponte, sed à Deo jussus hæc dico.

Argumentum hoc omnium fortissimum, ut Theo- phylactus ait, ultimo loco profert Apostolus, sum- ptum videlicet ab autoritate Christi, q. d. Hæc per me vobis præcipit Christus, idque veri Prophetæ & spirituales ignorare non debent. Nosse certè possunt, ea voluntati & verbo Dei non adversa esse, sed consentanea. Non autem necesse est, hæc de Prophetis immediato Dei afflatu actis in- telligi. Nam è scripturis dijudicari talia posse, quod nempe consentanea sint divinæ voluntati et quis ambigat? Et probavit pleraque illa Apo- stolus ipse è scripturis.

## 14:38
V. 38. But if any man is ignorant) If any man should say that he doubts whether this has been commanded to me. In the Manuscript: that it is a commandment of the Lord.

Let him be ignorant) Let him doubt by all means, but at his own peril. For the Apostolic authority, when spurned, has God as its avenger.

The words sound not of one doubting, but of one being ignorant. Which Estius rightly renders: But if any are ignorant of this, and are not easily persuaded to receive those things as the commands of the Lord, I judge that they should be left to themselves and their own ignorance. He is similarly anxious about the Latin reading, which has: But if any man is ignorant, he shall be ignored. But since he acknowledges that the Greek and Syriac Codices, as well as the Greek commentators and Cajetan, agree on this Greek reading, he would have done better if he had rejected the Vulgate as erroneous. Which, however, being deterred by the authority of the Council of Trent, both in this text and in others, he did not dare to do at all.

Latin:

V. 38. Εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ) Si quis dicat se dubitare, an mihi hoc imperatum sit. In Manuscripto: ὅτι θεῦ ἐστιν ἐντολή.

Ἀγνοείτω) Dubitet sane, sed suo periculo. Nam spreta auctoritas Apostolica Deum habet vindicem.

Non de dubitante, sed ignorante verba sonant. Quæ recte Estius reddit: Si qui verò id ignorant, nec facilè persuadentur, ut illa tanquam Domini mandata recipiant, eos sibi, suæque ignorantiæ relin- quendos esse censeo. De Latina lectione idem so- licitus est, quæ habet: Si quis autem ignorat, igno- rabitur. Sed quum Græcos, & Syriacos Codices, nec non tractatores Græcos & Cajetanum conspirare in hac Græca lectione agnoscat, rectius fecisset, si vulgatam ceu erroneam reprobasset. Quod tamen facere, Concilii Tridentini autoritate, tum in hoc textu, tum in aliis, abster转变atus, minime ausus est.

## 14:39
V. 39. Wherefore, brethren) From the digression about women he returns to the things said before, and he is not reluctant to repeat what is most necessary.

Zealously desire to prophesy) Especially seek from God the prophetic gift above 1.

And do not forbid speaking in tongues) Do not prohibit anyone gifted with that gift from using it, provided he uses it in the way I just said.

Latin:

V. 39. Ὡστε ἀδελφοί με) Ex diverticulo de fœminis redit ad prius dicta, & quod maximè necessarium est, repe- tēre non gravatur.

Ζηλῦτε τὸ προφητεύειν) Præcipue à Deo expetite do- num propheticum supra 1.

Καὶ τὸ λαλεῖν γλώσσαις μὴ κωλύετε) Neminem eo do- no præditum prohibete uti eo, modo utatur ita, ut modo dixi.

## 14:40
Let all things be done decently and in order) Better in the Manuscript and certain other books is πάντα δέ. For it is a restriction of what preceded. Εὐσχημόνως is the same as above πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον VII. 35. But κατὰ τάξιν is the same as just now ἀνὰ μέρος. At divided times, each in his own order.

Not only that order of speaking, but generally any good order is required here. And these are two limits and ends to be properly observed regarding sacred Ecclesiastical matters and ceremonies. Εὐσχημοσύνη or honesty or decorum and ἐυταξία or good order.

OF THE THIRD PART, Which is DIDACTIC, MEMBER II. Setting forth the doctrine concerning the truth and the quality of the resurrection from the dead.

The Apostle, about to deliver teaching concerning the resurrection from the dead, repeats the summary of the Gospel concerning Christ having died for our sins and having been raised, and proves the resurrection of Christ from various appearances, refuting with absurd consequences those who denied the resurrection of the dead. Furthermore, he builds up our resurrection from the faith of those who have fallen asleep in Christ, and from the resurrection of Christ, because he himself became the firstfruits of those who sleep, and as through Adam came death, so through him came the resurrection of the dead; and on that occasion he teaches how the firstfruits will follow, pertaining to Christ at the coming of Christ, when he will deliver the kingdom to his Father, the last enemy, death, having been conquered. He further confirms the resurrection also from baptism for the dead, and the martyrdoms of Christians, and also the most certain danger of atheism (Is. XXII. 13.) thence he answers concerning the qualities of bodies in the resurrection from the likeness of seed, and the diversity of flesh, and of bodies, celestial and terrestrial, and teaches that bodies will be incorruptible and glorious, illustrating this from a comparison of the first and second Adam, and confirming from thence that corruptible flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of GOD. He also opens the mystery concerning the order of the resurrection, regarding the living and the dead, when the last trumpet shall sound, and all are to be clothed with incorruptibility, so that a song of victory may be sung over death swallowed up in victory (Is. XXV. Hos. XIII. 14.), exhorting the Corinthians to stand firm in the faith, and to abound in the work of the Lord.

There are four parts, I. Epitomic, a repetition of the summary of the Gospel, to v. 4. II. Demonstrative, partly a proof of the resurrection of the dead from the resurrection of Christ, to v. 17, partly a confirmation of our resurrection from the resurrection of Christ and other arguments, to v. 24. III. Didactic, exhibiting information both concerning the qualities of bodies in the resurrection, to v. 50, and concerning the transformation not only of the dead, but also of the living, to v. 57. IV. Exhortatory, containing an exhortation to perseverance in the faith, and progress in the work of the Lord, to v. 58.

PART I. Epitomic, Summary repetition of the Gospel. V. 1. Now I make known to you, brethren.

Paul attacks the greatest evil, but not so widely diffused through the Church of the Corinthians, in the last place to remedy it. For because the dogma of the resurrection was accustomed to be opposed by certain philosophical arguments, as is to be known from Acts XVII. 18, from Athenagoras, from the objections concerning the resurrection which are in the works of Justin, and from the book of Tertullian on the resurrection, it had come to pass that some, having indeed become Christians, but not sufficiently freed from the opinions of certain Philosophers, of whom were Hymenaeus and Philetus, were turning that dogma into an allegory, and saying that they were already now in possession of the resurrection, which Clement of Alexandria testifies the Gnostics did, Strom. III. Therefore they thought that the resurrection did not exclude the things of this life, among which is marriage, but only meditation after the example of the celibate Essenes. For since this was considered by them to be a certain new life, compared to which the prior life was death, they therefore called that death and this resurrection, as is to be understood from the passage of Paul 2 Tim. II. 17, 18, and the cited passage of Clement, and from those things which both Irenaeus and Tertullian have concerning Saturninus. And both to this and to certain other dogmas pertains also that saying of Tertullian in the Apologeticum: Certain men have adulterated this new little preparation of ours from the seed of these men with their own opinions according to philosophical sentiments, and from one way they have cut many oblique and inexplicable paths. Since this was in truth nothing other than to tear up the very foundations of Christian doctrine, the Apostle judged that it must be solicitously refuted by him.

Since very many among the Corinthians denied the resurrection from the dead, because in no matter is the Christian faith contradicted as it is in the resurrection of the dead, as Tertullian says, the Apostle recalls to the memory of the Corinthians before all things the faith entrusted to them; saying (as Theophylact interprets), I preach to you nothing either new or foreign, but what is known to you. For I make known to you the Gospel, that is, I repeat and bring back to memory. However, by the name of brothers, those who denied the resurrection of the dead among the Corinthians are not addressed, as the Syncretists today wish. For how could they be called brothers who deny an article of faith that is most fundamental, such as the resurrection of the dead is, as the Apostle demonstrates here? But those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, even if there were such heretics among them, were called by this name, because the denomination is made from the stronger and better part. By the fraternal appellation he both softens them and at the same time admonishes them, says Theophylact, and reminds them whence they receive that name of brotherhood, just as, namely, when they have that name both from the very coming of Christ into the flesh, from which they are in danger of falling away (those who approach that heresy), and from baptism, which is indeed a figure of Christ's burial and resurrection. Whether that heresy of the Gnostics, which Grotius describes here, found a place among the Corinthians, we leave in the middle. He tacitly censures, as observed by the blessed Baldwin, their negligence and carelessness, that they did not more diligently guard so excellent a treasure, and at the same time he commends his Gospel as a thing to be fixed in deep minds and never to be let go from memory. Which he says is done by three reasons brought forward: 1. from the certainty of this doctrine, in which you also stand. 2. from the principal end, which is the salvation of souls. 3. from the danger, unless you have believed in vain.

Τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον, ὃ ἐυαγγελισάμην ὑμῖν.

The word Gospel first indeed signifies the preaching of Christ, then also those things by which that preaching was confirmed, that is, the history concerning the life, miracles, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of Christ, as we said in the Prolegomena to the Gospels.

ὃ καὶ παρελάβετε.

Which you received as true. Thus לקח is used among the Hebrews. Whence also the noun לקח for doctrine is frequent.

Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἑστήκατε.

In whose profession the greatest part have persisted until now.

Latin:

Πάντα εὐσχημόνως κ̓ κατὰ τάξιν γινέσθω) Melius in Manu- scripto & aliis quibusdam libris πάντα δέ. Est enim re- stricto ejus, quod præcessit. Εὐσχημόνως idem est, quod supra πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον VII. 35. κατὰ τάξιν vero idem, quod modo ἀνὰ μέρος. Partitis temporibus, suo quisque ordine.

Non tantùm ordo ille loquendi, sed generaliter quivis bonus ordo hic requiritur. Suntque hi duo limites & fines probe observandi quoad sacra Ecclesiastica & ceremonias. Εὐσχημοσύνη seu ho- nestas vel decorum & ἐυταξία seu bonus ordo.

PARTIS TERTIÆ, Quæ est Δ Ι Δ Α Κ Τ Ι Κ Ή, MEMBRUM II. Expediens doctrinam de Resurrectionis à mor- tuis tùm veritate, tùm qualitate.

Traditurus de resurrectione à mortuis Apostolus, summam Evangelii de mortuo Christo propter peccata nostra, & resuscitato, repetit, ac resurrectionem Christi ex apparitionibus variis probat, absurdis consequentibus refellens eos, qui negabant resurrectionem mortuorum. Porrò resurrectionem nostram adstruit è fide eorum, qui obdormivêre in Christo, & è resurrectione Christi, quia ipse primitiæ factus dormientium, & ut per Adamum mors, ita per ipsum resurrectio mortuorum; eâque occasione docet, quomodo primitiæ sequuturæ sint, ad Christum attinentes sub adventum Christi, quando regnum Patri suo tradet, hoste novissimo, morte devictâ. Ulterius resurrectionem confirmat etiam è baptismo ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, & Christianorum martyriis, nec non periculo certissimo atheismi (Es. XXII. 13.) dehinc respondet de qualitatibus corporum in resurrectione è simili seminis, & diversitate carnis, & corporum, cælestium & terrenorum, ac docet incorruptibilia, & gloriosa fore corpora, illustrans hoc è collatione primi & secundi Adami, & confirmans inde, quod caro & sanguis corruptibilis regnum DEI possidere nequeant. Aperit etiam mysterium de ordine resurrectionis, quoad vivos & mortuos, cum tuba novissima sonuerit, omnibusque incorruptibilitate vestiendis, ut epinicium canatur de morte in victoriam absorptâ (Esa. XXV. Os. XIII. 14.) adhortans, ut immoti perstent in fide Corinthii, & proficiant in opere Domini.

PArtes sunt quatuor, I. Ἐπιτομικὴ, Summæ Evangelii repetitio, ad v. 4. II. Ἀποδεικτικὴ, partim resurrectionis mortuorum è resurrectione Christi probatio, ad v. 17. partim resurrectionis nostræ è resurrectione Christi aliisque argumentis confirmatio, ad v. 24. III. Διδακτικὴ, exhibens tum de corporum in resurrectione qualitatibus, ad v. 50. tum de transmutatione non solùm mortuorum, sed etiam viventium informationem, ad v. 57. IV. παραινετικὴ, adhortationem continens ad perseverantiam in fide, & profectum in opere Domini, ad v. 58.

PARS I. Ἐπιτομικὴ, Summaria Evangelii repetitio. V. 1. Γνωρίζω δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοὶ.

Maximum malum, sed non ita late diffusum per Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, ultimo loco aggreditur medicari Paulus. Nam quia resurrectionis dogma philosophicis quibusdam ratiunculis oppugnari solebat, ut cognoscere est Act. XVII. 18. ex Athenagora, ex objectis de resurrectione, quæ sunt in Justini operibus, & ex libro Tertulliani de resurrectione eo evenerat, ut quidam facti quidem Christiani, sed Philosophorum quorundam opinionibus non satis liberati, quorum fuêre Hymenæus & Philetas, dogma illud in ἀλληγορίαν verterent, seque jam nunc resurrectionis esse compotes dicerent, quod Gnosticos fecisse testatur Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. III. Resurrectionem itaque arbitrabantur, non vacare rebus hujus vitæ, inter quas est matrimonium, sed soli meditationi ad exemplum Cælibum Essenorum. Hoc enim cum nova quædam ipsis vita esse censeretur, cui comparata prior vita mors erat, ideo & illud mortem & hoc resurrectionem vocabant, ut ex loco Pauli 2. Tim. II. 17. 18. & dicto Clementis loco, & ex iis, quæ de Saturnino habent tum Irenæus, tum Tertullianus, darur intelligi. Et ad hoc & ad alia quædam dogmata per- tinet & illud Tertulliani in Apologetico: Ex horum semine istam nostram hanc novitiolam paraturam viri quidam suis opinionibus ad philosophicas sententias adulteraverunt, & de una via obliques multos & inexplicabiles tramites sciderunt. Hoc vero cum revera nihil esset aliud, quam ipsa doctrinæ Christianæ fundamenta convellere, solicite refutandum sibi censuit Apostolus.

Quüm apud Corinthios plurimi resurrectio- nem à mortuis negarent, quia nulla in re sic con- tradicitur fidei Christianæ, quàm in resurrectione mortuorum, dicente Tertulliano, Apostolus Co- rinthiis ante omnia in memoriam revocat fidem ipsis creditam; Nihil inquiens (Theophylacto in- terprete) vobis vel novi vel peregrinum prædico, sed quod vobis cognitum est. Vobis enim Evange- lium notum facio, h. e. repeto & ad memoriam redi- go. Fratrum autem nomine non illi, qui resurre- ctionem mortuorum negabant inter Corinthios, ut Syncretistæ hodiè volunt, nuncupantur. Quo- modo enim fratres dicerentur, qui articulum fidei maximè fundamentalem, qualis, demonstrante hic Apostolo, est resurrectio mortuorum, infician- tur? Sed sanctificati in Christo Jesu, sancti vocati, etsi inter eos etiam ejusmodi hæretici essent, hoc nomine appellati, quia à potiori & meliori parte fit denominatio. Fraterna illos appellatione & mi- tigat simul, inquit Theophylactus, & commonefa- cit, unde id fraternitatis accipiunt nomen, quemad- modum vid. cùm ex ipso Christi in carnem adven- tu, à quo ne desciscant periclitantur (qui hæresi illi accedunt) tùm à baptismo, qui profectò Christi est sepulturæ & resurrectionis figura, nomen illud ha- beant. An autem illa Gnosticorum hæresis, quam hic describit Grotius, apud Corinthios locum in- venerit, in medio relinquimus. Tacitè autem per- stringit, quod observatum B. Balduino, ipsorum negligentiam & oscitantiam, quod thesaurum tam præclarum non diligentius adservaverint, simulq; commendat Evangelium suum, ut rem altis men- tibus infigendam, & nunquam ex memoria di- mittendam. Quod rationibus tribus adductis fieri ait, 1. ab ἀσφαλείᾳ hujus doctrinæ, in quo & sta- tis. 2. à fine præcipuo, qui est salus animarum. 3. à periculo, nisi frustra credidistis.

Τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον, ὃ ἐυαγγελισάμην ὑμῖν.

Vox Evangelii primum quidem τὸ κήρυγμα Christi signi- ficat, deinde & illa, per quæ κήρυγμα illud confirmatum est, id est, historiam de vita, miraculis, morte, resurrectio- ne & in cœlum evectione Christi, ut diximus in Prolego- menis ad Evangelia.

ὃ καὶ παρελάβετε.

Quod tanquam verum recepistis. Sic לקח sumitur apud Hebræos. Unde & nomen לקח pro doctrina frequens.

Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἑστήκατε.

In cujus professione perstitistis hactenus pars maxima.

## 15:2
V. 2. Δι’ ὗ καὶ σώζεσθε.

There is also here a present for a future, as above XIII. below XVI. 5. 1 Pet. III. 11. by which you will obtain salvation.

By what word I preached the gospel to you, if you hold fast.

There is also here a transposition, and λόγῳ is placed for mode. If you remember correctly, how I announced that to you, that is, both the history with its circumstances, and the dogmas with their explanation. For thus you will easily see how much these differ from those things which those badly Christian men from the philosophers keep saying.

Unless you believed in vain.

There is also here a double negation for one, as above XIV. 5. when he says, unless you believed in vain, he means this, unless all those things previously believed have slipped away from you.

These things follow one another: the announcement of the Gospel, the reception of the announced [Gospel] through faith, the preservation of the received [Gospel] in perseverance in faith, and through that which was received and preserved by faith, eternal salvation. For he who believes and perseveres in faith is saved, Mark XVI. 16. John III. 16. Rom. X. 14. 1 Pet. I. 5. Therefore he exhorts here to standing in faith v. 58. and chap. XVI. 13. Christ warns about retaining and keeping the word in the heart, Luke VIII. 15. That τίνι λόγῳ, which the Vulgate renders 'by what reason', Hentenius and others 'by what speech', the Syriac 'by what words', implies that the depositum must be holily held and guarded in the same way in which it was delivered, so that nothing may be added to it or taken away from it, 1 Tim. I. Gal. I. 7. Rev. XXII. 18. 19. and that it may not in any way be violated or perverted 2 Pet. III. 16. 1 Tim. VI. 3. and that the very pattern of sound words may be more holily guarded. The words, 'unless you believed in vain', can be referred both to the standing or perseverance in faith, and to the word immediately preceding, 'you are saved'. For it is believed in vain if one does not persevere in faith. Those who take it in the latter way wish to infer an absurdity from the Apostle: namely, as blessed Glassius has in his Homily on the Epistle for the 12th Sunday after Trinity, either that they believed the Gospel in vain (which the Apostle assumes as an absurdity, inasmuch as he is writing to believers v. 58, whose faith the divine goodness and faithfulness does not permit to be in vain) or that their salvation is placed in the Gospel, which is most true. There is therefore no reason why we should think the words, 'in which also you stand', were spoken by simulation with Chrysostom, as if Paul were feigning that he is ignorant of the inconstancy of the Corinthians, or why we should explain them with others as concerning only an external profession, because those things concern believers, and those who have been constant up to this point, whom the Apostle therefore solicitously warns not to allow themselves to be led away from the faith by heretics: Since none but those who persevere obtain salvation, and faith will have been in vain if perseverance is lacking, Rev. II. 8. for he says, 'you are being saved' in the present: Because the salvation of Christians, which they receive through faith in the Gospel, begins in this life, but is perfected in the future, as Estius says here.

Latin:

V. 2. Δι’ ὗ καὶ σώζεσθε.

Est & hic Præsens pro Futuro, ut supra XIII. infra XVI. 5. 1. Pet. III. 11. per quod salutem consequemini.

Τίνι λόγῳ ἐυαγγελισάμην ὑμῖν, εἰ κατέχετε.

Est & hic trajectio, & λόγῳ positum est pro modo. Si rectè meministis, quomodo id vobis annunciaverim, id est, & historiam cum suis circumstantiis, & dogmata cum sua explicatione. Ita enim facile videbitis, quantum hæc distent ab iis, quæ isti ex Philosophis malè Christiani dictitant.

Ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ εἰκῆ ἐπισεύσατε.

Est & hic duplex negatio pro una, ut supra XIV. 5. cum dicit, nisi frustra credidistis, hoc vult, nisi illa omnia prius credita vobis exciderunt.

Sequuntur hæc se invicem Evangelii annuncia- tio, annunciati per fidem susceptio, suscepti in fide perseveranti conservatio, perque illud fide susce- ptum, & conservatum æterna salvatio. Qui enim credit & in fide perseverat, salvatur, Marci XVI. 16. Joh. III. 16. Rom. X. 14. 1. Pet. I. 5. Ideo ad statio- nem in fide hortatur hic v. 58. & cap. XVI. 13. De verbo retinendo & conservando in corde monet Christus Luc. IIX. 15. Illud τίνι λόγῳ, quod Vul- gata reddit, qua ratione, Hentenius & alii quo ser- mone, Syrus quibusnam verbis, innuit, τὴν παρα- καταθήκην sancte eodem modo, quo tradita est, tenendam & custodiendam esse, ne quid ei adda- tur, vel detrahatur, 1. Tim. I. Gal. I. 7. Apoc. XXII. 18. 19. neve ullo modo temeretur, aut pervertatur 2. Pet. III. 16. 1. Tim. VI. 3. utque etiam ipsa verbo- rum sanarum ὑποτύπωσις sanctius custodietur. Verba, nisi frustra credidistis, & ad stationem vel perseverantiam in fide, & ad verbum proximum σώζεσθε referri possunt. Frustra enim creditur, si in fide non perseveratur. Qui posteriori modo accipiunt, ab absurdo colligere volunt Aposto- lum: nimirum ut B. Glassius in Dom. XII. post Trin. Homil. Epist. habet, vel frustra ipsos cre- didisse Evangelio (quod pro absurdo assumat A- postolus, utpote ad fideles scribens v. 58. quorum fidem frustraneam esse divina bonitas & fidelitas non permittit) vel eorum salutem in Evangelio esse positam, id quod verissimum. Non ergo est, quod verba, in quo & statis, vel per simulationem dicta cum Chrysostomo existimemus, quasi Paulus simulet, se ignorare Corinthiorum inconstantiam vel de externa tantùm professione cum aliis expli- cemus, quia concernunt illa fideles, & hactenus constantes, quos proinde sollicitè monet Aposto- lus, ne per hæreticos se patiantur à fide abduci: Quum non nisi perseverantes salutem consequan- tur, & fides frustra fuerit, si perseverantia defue- rit, Apoc. II. 8. dicit enim, salvamini in præsenti: Quia salus Christianorum, quam accipiunt per fidem Evangelii, incipit in hac vita, perficitur au- tem in futura, ut hic Estius.

## 15:3
V. 3. For I delivered to you among the first. Among the chief things which you ought to have believed.

Which I also received. Which I myself had received from Ananias first, then also from the Apostles, with perhaps a special revelation being added, as we said above XI. 22.

That Christ died. Truly, not imaginarily. Therefore all things which pertain to the death and resurrection have been so accurately observed, delivered, and finally written down.

For our sins. Thus 'for our offenses', Rom. IV. 25. where see what is said.

Latin:

V. 3. Παρέδωκα γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐν πρώτοις. Inter præcipua, quæ credere debebatis.

Ὃ καὶ παρέλαβον. Quod ego ipse acceperam ab Anania primum, deinde & ab Apostolis, accedente forte & speciali revelatione, ut diximus supra XI. 22.

Ὅτι χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν. Verè non imaginariè. Ideo omnia, quæ ad mortem & resurrectionem pertinent, tam accuratè observata, tra- dita, ac postremum conscripta sunt.

ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Sic διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν, Rom. IV. 25. ubi dicta vide.

## 15:4
V. 4. And that he was buried. Just as Isaiah, Daniel, and others had predicted, see what is said at Luke 24:26, 27; Acts 26:23.

And that he was buried. Lifeless, he was placed in a tomb that was still empty. See what is said regarding the Gospel of Matthew.

And that he has been raised on the third day. The return of Christ to life is signified sometimes by resurrection, sometimes by rising: because, clearly, death is compared both to a fall and to sleep.

According to the scriptures. For Isaiah and Daniel had predicted this too, and Jonah had prefigured it.

From a tradition made by an unwritten word, which preceded the epistles sent to the Corinthians themselves, the Papists seek patronage for their own traditions. But even if they did not have the epistles, when the Gospel was being handed down by word of mouth, could they not have had other writings of the New Testament? And how will it be taught that there were others which were handed down to them than those which were written to them? Indeed, the Apostle adds what those things are, and Lyranus acknowledges this: What those things are, says Lyranus, he adds: That Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the scriptures. What, therefore, does this do for unwritten traditions? Salmeron notes on this passage that the word tradition encompasses everything which they had received from Christ, whether they were written or unwritten. These certainly are written, because they were both handed down from the scriptures of the Old Testament and are here summarized in writing. But when the Apostle says among the first he means that this is the principal doctrine; and most fundamental, which is to be believed, in which one must persevere, through which salvation is to be obtained, concerning Christ having died for sins, buried and resurrected, that it is the core and marrow of the Gospel: Which doctrine being overturned, faith would be overturned, one must remain in sins, and have no hope of a blessed resurrection. Which primarily concerns those articles about the satisfactory death of Christ, for us, and our sins, and also about the life-giving resurrection of the same, as is also taught in Rom. IV. 24: Consequently, however, because the burial confirms the truth of the death of Christ, and the burial and putting away of our sins, the article about the burial is also referred to that. But when the Apostle says that he delivered what he received from the Lord, he asserts the divine authority of his doctrine, and that he delivered nothing other than what he warns was revealed to him by God, just as in Gal. I. 12 he testifies that he did not receive or learn the Gospel from men, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. Rashly, therefore, does Grotius doubt here about the revelation made to Paul, perhaps injecting his own. Furthermore, from this passage, both the satisfaction of Christ for our sins, and the necessity of this doctrine (both of which heads we have expressly shown elsewhere) are proved against the Socinians, and also the corruption of all men through sin, from which, therefore, perhaps not even Mary the Θεοτόκος will be exempt. Thus Estius paraphrases: This, he says, I delivered to you first and taught, that Christ, promised in the law and the Prophets, sustained death, which is the penalty of sin, not for his own sins, which he had none, but for ours, that is, to redeem the penalties owed for our sins. This passage shows that, except for Christ, no man is free from sin, because Christ died for all. But because Paul, with those things which he delivered, and which the Corinthians had received through faith, says that Christ died for our sins, and was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures, he teaches by that very fact that all things which are delivered and are to be believed must be proved from the Scriptures: it is handed down that ὀυδὲν ἄτερ γραφῆς was the symbol of Peter. The Apostle protested that he delivered nothing outside of those things which were written by Moses and the Prophets, Acts XXVI. 2. And Christ said from Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets that he ought to die, and conversely to rise again from the dead, Luke XXIV. 44. Moreover, the testimonies which deal with the death of Christ and the satisfaction for our sins in the O.T. pertain here, not only oracles or Prophetic predictions, but also types and figures. Gen. III. 15. Ps. IIX. Ps. XVI. Ps. XXII. Ps. XL. Ps. XLV. Ps. LXIX. Ps. CXVIII. Es. LIII. & XLIII. Dan. XII. Zach. IX. & XII. Add Gen. XXII. Lev. XVI. &c. and those by which the burial of Christ was predicted and prefigured, Ps. XVI. Es. XI. cap. LIII. Jon. II. and also the resurrection of Christ, Gen. III. 15. Ps. XVI. Ps. LXIIX. Es. LIII. LXIII. Os. VI. c. XIII. Jon. II. &c. That he says Christ rose again on the third day according to the scriptures, it is certain that it looks to the oracle of Os. VI. 12. and the type of Jonah cap. II., as also the type of Isaac, Gen. XXII. Heb. XI. 3. Theophylact in h. l. b. brought forward two types. It is also evident from this that the σκοπὸν σκοπιμώτατον of the scriptures of the Old Testament is also Christ, delivered for our sins, and resurrected for our justification, Rom. IV. 24. John V. 39. Apoc. XIX. 10.

PART II. ᾿Αποδεικτική. ARTICLE I. By which the resurrection from the dead is proved from the resurrection of Christ.

A matter of such great moment, and not easy to believe, needed many witnesses. What is touched upon here is the same as that which Luke has in XXIV. 34.

Latin:

V. 4. Καὶ ὅτι ἐτάφη. Sicut Esaias, Daniel & alii prædixerant, Vide, quæ dicta ad Luc. XXIV. 26. 27. Act. XXVI. 23.

Καὶ ὅτι ἐτάφη. Exanimis repositus fuit in monumento adhuc vacuo. Vide, quæ ad Evangelium Matthæi.

Καὶ ὅτι ἐγήγερται τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ. Reditus Christi in vitam, modo per ἀνάστασιν, modo per ἐγέρσεως significatur: Quia scilicet mors & casui & so- mno comparatur.

Κατὰ τὰς γραφάς. Nam & hoc Esaias & Daniel prædixerant, & præfigu- raverat Jonas.

E traditione verbo non scripto facta, quæ præ- cessit apud Corinthios epistolas ad ipsos missas, suis traditionibus patrocinium quærunt Papistæ. Sed etsi epistolas non habuêre, cum viva voce Evangelium traderetur, annon potuêre alia scri- pta N. Testamenti habere? Et quomodo doce- bitur, alia fuisse, quæ illis tradita ab his, quæ ad ipsos scripta? Imò quæ sint illa, Apostolus sub- jicit, idque Lyrano agnoscente: Quæ sint, inquit Lyranus, illa subdit: Quoniam Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris secundum scripturas, & quod sepultus est, & quod resurrexit tertiâ die secundum scripturas. Quid ergò hoc facit pro traditionibus ἀγράφοις? Salmero in hunc locum notat traditio- nis vocabulum omnia complecti, qua à Christo ac- ceperant, sive scripta essent, sive non scripta. Hæc certè scripta sunt, quia & è scripturis V. Testa- menti tradita, & hic summatim scripto compre- hensa sunt. Cum autem Apostolus ait ἐν πρώτοις hanc præcipuam doctrinam esse; maximèq́; funda- mentalem, quæ credenda, in quâ perseverandum, per quam salus obtinenda sit, de Christo pro pec- catis mortuo, sepulto & resuscitato, nucleum esse & medullam Evangelii: Qua doctrina eversa fi- des evértatur, in peccatis manere oportet, & nul- lam spem habere beatæ resurrectionis. Quod primario quidem articulos illos de morte Christi satisfactoriâ, pro nobis, & peccatis nostris, nec non de resurrectione ejusdem salutiferâ, uti etiam Rom. IV. 24. docetur, concernit: Consequenter au- tem, quia sepultura veritatem mortis Christi, & sepelitionem ac abdicationem nostrorum peccato- rum confirmat, articulus etiam de sepultura eò refertur. Quum autem Apostolus se tradidisse ait, ut accepit à Domino scil. doctrinæ suæ divinam autoritatem asserit, nec aliud se tradidisse, quàm quod divinitus sibi revelatum esse monet, uti Gal. I. 12. se non ab hominibus accepisse, aut didicisse Evangelium, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi te- statur. Temerè ergò hic dubitat Grotius de re- velatione Paulo factâ, suum forte ingerens. Ex hoc porrò loco tùm satisfactio Christi pro pecca- tis nostris, tùm doctrinæ hujus necessitas, (quod utrumque caput alibi ex professo ostendimus) contrà Socinianos probatur, tùm etiam omnium hominum per peccatum corruptio, à quâ proindè forte ne quidem Maria Θεοτόκος eximenda erit. Ita παραφράζει Estius: Hoc, inquit, imprimis tra- didi vobis & docui, quod Christus in lege & Prophetis promissus, mortem, quæ peccati pœna est, sustinuit non propter sua peccata, quæ nulla habuit, sed pro- pter nostra, id est, ad redimendas pœnas peccatis no- stris debitas. Ostendit hic locus, excepto Christo, nullum hominem expertem esse peccati, quia Chri- stus pro omnibus est mortuus. Quod vero Paulus cum ea, quæ tradidit, quæque Corinthii per fidem susceperant, ait, Christum pro peccatis nostris mortuum, & sepultum esse, & resurrexisse tertiâ die secundum Scripturas, eo ipso è scripturis pro- banda esse omnia, quæ traduntur, & credenda sunt docet: ὀυδὲν ἄτερ γραφῆς Petri symbolum fuisse traditur. Nihil extrà ea, quæ à Mose & Pro- phetis scripta sunt, se tradidisse protestatus est Apo- stolus Act. XXVI. 2. Et Christus è Mose, Psalmis, & Prophetis mori se debuisse, ac vicissim resur- gere à mortuis dixit Luc. XXIV. 44. Pertinent autem huc testimonia, quæ de morte Christi ac de satisfactione pro peccatis nostris in V. T. agunt, non solùm oracula vel prædictiones Propheticæ, sed etiam typi, & figuræ. Gen. III. 15. Ps. IIX. Ps. XVI. Ps. XXII. Ps. XL. Ps. XLV. Ps. LXIX. Ps. CXVIII. Es. LIII. & XLIII. Dan. XII. Zach. IX. & XII. Ad- de Gen. XXII. Lev. XVI. &c. & quibus sepultura Christi prædicta & præfigurata est Psal. XVI. Es. XI. cap. LIII. Jon. II. nec non resurrectio Christi, Gen. III. 15. Ps. XVI. Ps. LXIIX. Es. LIII. LXIII. Os. VI. c. XIII. Jon. II. &c. Quod secundum scri- pturas tertio die resurrexisse Christum dicit, eo & oraculum Os. VI. 12. & typum Jonæ cap. II. respi- cere certum est, ut & Isaaci typum, Genes. XXII. Ebr. XI. 3. Theophylactus in h. l. b. duos typos ad- duxit. Patet etiam hinc, scripturarum quoque Ve- teris Testamenti σκοπὸν σκοπιμώτατον esse Chri- stum, propter peccata nostra traditum, & propter justitiam nostram resuscitatum, Rom. IV. 24. Joh. V. 39. Apoc. XIX. 10.

PARS II. ᾿Αποδεικτική. ARTICULUS I. Quo resurrectio à mortuis è resurrectione Christi probatur.

Res tanti momenti, neque facilis creditu multis egebat teftibus. Quod hic tangitur, idem est cum eo, quod habet Lucas XXIV. 34.

## 15:5
Εἶτα τοῖς δώδεκα.

This looks to the history which is in Luke XXIV. 36. The Apostles are called οἱ δώδεκα, not because there were that many, with Judas dead and Thomas absent, but because their college was instituted with that number. See what is said in John XX. 24.

The Apostle appeals not only to scripture in v. 5 concerning the resurrection of Christ, but also to its fulfillment in the New Testament, which he confirms primarily from the appearances of Christ, recounting only those which were made to men, not those which were made to women, and thus bringing forward only male witnesses, lest, as the blessed Hunnius observes, there should be material for the mockery of evasion, especially among the Gentiles, whom histories teach to have been too scrupulous in rejecting the testimonies of women. The first appearance among men, therefore, was made to Peter, which is nowhere historically described, but only touched upon in the cited passage: Christ truly rose, and appeared to Simon. The second happened to the twelve Apostles. He acknowledges Judas here as already dead, whom Grotius elsewhere rashly judged to have still been alive at Matth. XXIX. 16. But here the Apostle joins those two appearances, made in the absence and presence of Thomas, because the latter was made as a supplement to the former, on account of Thomas, who had been absent. The Vulgate here wrongly reads eleven. For the Greek codices consistently have τοῖς δώδεκα, with which the Syriac version agrees.

Latin:

Εἶτα τοῖς δώδεκα.

Spectat hoc ad historiam, quæ est Luc. XXIV. 36. Vo- cantur autem Apostoli οἱ δώδεκα, non quod tot effent, mortuo Juda, & Thoma absente, sed quia eo numero insti- tutum erat eorum collegium. Vide, quæ dicta apud Jo- hannem XX. 24.

Non tantùm ad scripturam v. 5. provocat Apo- stolus, circa resurrectionem Christi, sed etiam ad ejus complementum in Novo Testamento, quod confirmat imprimis ex apparitionibus Christi, eas solùm recensens, quæ viris factæ sunt, non quæ mulieribus, adeoque testes solùm masculos adducens, ne, quod B. Hunnius observat, empæ- ctis elusionis esset materia, præcipuè inter gen- tes, quas in repudiandis mulierum testimoniis ni- mis fuisse scrupulosas, historiæ docent. Prima er- gò apparitio inter viros Petro facta, quæ nuspiam historicè descripta, sed tantùm loco citato tacta est: Verè Christus resurrexit, & Simoni apparuit. Altera Apostolis XII. obtigit. Judam hîc agno- scit jam mortuum, quem aliàs vixisse adhuc Gro- tius temerè censuit ad Matth. XXIX. 16. Hic autem conjungit Apostolus binas illas apparitio- nes, absente ac præsente Thomâ factas, quia poste- rior in supplementum prioris, ob Thomam, qui absens fuerat, facta est. Vulgata hic perperam legit undecim. Græci enim codices constanter ha- bent τοῖς δώδεκα, quibus consonat Syriaca versio.

## 15:6
V. 6. Ἔπειτα ὤφθη ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐφάπαξ.

This appearance took place in Galilee, Matt. XXVIII. 7. on the mountain, as tradition holds, Tabor or Itabyrium. ἐφάπαξ כּאַחַד at the same time. Ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις is a Greek construction, just as we say in Latin: He kills more than three hundred.

Of whom the majority remain until now.

From whom, whoever wishes, will be able to seek out testimony.

But some have fallen asleep.

Whose children and acquaintances can still testify what they heard from their own mouths regarding this matter.

Some, with Chrysostom, explain ἐπάνω by reason of the place as ἄνω ἐκ τῶν ὀρανῶν, from above from the heavens, as if he did not appear walking on the earth, but in the air above their heads. But because he willed to be visibly lifted into the air only at his own time, that interpretation is not probable, but the common explanation, which also pleased Grotius, is to be preferred. Some explain that ἐπάνω as πάλιν, again, just as in the glossary of Stephanus ἐπάνω is rendered as moreover, over, above. But thus this would be superfluous. For that ἔπειτα had already been used. Regarding this appearance, which Ambrose thinks is not commemorated in the other scriptures, we observed in the Harmony that it was the same one in which he appeared to the Apostles on a certain mountain in Galilee, Matt. XXIX. 16. Which opinion Grotius also approves here.
