Estius says that this is the consensus of almost everyone, and he does not doubt that besides the eleven Apostles, the LXX disciples were also present, and among them Matthias and Barnabas, and that Christ chose a place remote from Jerusalem, as being safer, to which the faithful might gather freely and without danger. If a doubt is raised as to how such a great number of five hundred brethren could gather in the place of Acts I. 15, where only 120 disciples are said to have gathered, Thomas responds that these were in Jerusalem, but that there were many other disciples besides in Galilee, and perhaps all were gathered together when the Lord appeared. Beautiful here is the paraphrase of Theophylact: I have, he says, also some witnesses surviving, but some have already finished their life. But when he says they have fallen asleep, he set forth the beginning of the resurrection. For he who sleeps and has departed from life is one who is going to rise again.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἔπειτα ὤφθη ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐφάπαξ.

Hæc apparitio contigit in Galilæa, Matth. XXVIII. 7. in monte, ut traditio habet, Thabor sive Itabyrio. ἐφάπαξ כּאַחַד eodem tempore. Ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις constructio est Ἑλληνικὴ, sicut Latinè dicimus: Interficit plus trecentos.

Ἐξ ὧν οἱ πλείες μένεσιν ἕως ἄρτι.

Ex quibus, qui volet, poterit testimonium exquirere.

Τινὲς δὲ ἐκοιμήθησαν.

Quorum liberi & familiares testari adhuc possunt, quid ex ipsorum ore istâ de re audiverint.

Nonnulli cum Chrysostomo ἐπάνω ratione loci explicant ἄνω ἐκ τῶν ὀρανῶν supernè ex cælis, quasi non in terra ingrediens, sed in aëre supra ipsorum capita apparuerit. Sed quia in aërem suo demum tempore visibiliter evehi voluit, non est probabi- lis illa interpretatio, sed præferenda communis, quæ etiam Grotio placuit, explicatio. Quidam illud ἐπάνω explicant πάλιν rursum, quemadmo- dum in glossario Stephani ἐπάνω redditur insu- per, super, supra. Sed ita superfluum hoc foret. Adhibitum enim jam erat illud ἔπειτα. De hac apparitione, quam in reliquis scripturis non com- memorari putat Ambrosius, observavimus in Har- moniâ, quod eadem illa fuerit, quâ in Galilæa in monte quodam apparuit Apostolis, Matt. XXIX. 16. Quam sententiam hîc approbat quoque Gro- tius. Estius omnium fermè hunc consensum esse ait, nec dubitat, præter undecim Apostolos etiam LXX. discipulos adfuisse, & inter eos Matthiam, & Barnabam, ac Christum elegisse locum ab Hiero- solyma remotum, ceu tutiorem, ad quem liberè, & sine periculo fideles congregarentur. Si du- bium moveatur, quomodo tantus quingentorum fratrum numerus conveniat loco Act. I. 15. ubi tantùm 120. discipuli congregati dicuntur, respon- det Thomas, hosce fuisse in Jerusalem, at multos alios præterea discipulos fuisse in Galilæa, & fortè omnes congregatos simul, cum Dominus appa- ruit. Pulchra hic est paraphrasis Theophylacti: Habeo, inquit, & testes nonnullos superstites, quos- dam verò vitâ jam functos. Cum autem dormie- runt, (inquit) initium resurrectionis proposuit. Est enim, qui dormit, & vitâ excessit, resurrecturus.

## 15:7
V. 7. Then he appeared to James.

It seems that ἔπειτα here means not 'afterwards', but 'furthermore', as above in XII. 28 and Heb. III. 17. For the appearance of Christ to James took place immediately after the resurrection, as tradition holds, which we have commemorated from Jerome in the prolegomena to Matthew.

There is no need for us to depart from the common meaning of the word, nor does that agree with the preceding v. 5, Eἶτα; and if ἔπειτα in v. 6 were taken as 'afterwards', the word ἔσχατον in v. 8 would show that the Apostle wished to observe the order here. That tradition in Jerome is considered by him himself to be among those things which were stitched onto the Gospel of Matthew by the Nazarenes, and it lacks every appearance of probability. And Estius, along with John Hessels, rejects that narrative as fabulous, or rather, contrary to the faith of the sacred Gospels.

Then to all the apostles.

Concerning which see John XX. 25 and the following, and XXI.

This is not that which is read as described by John, either in chapter XX or XXI. For the Apostle had already included in v. 5 that which happened to Thomas and the other Apostles. But that which took place at the Sea of Tiberias happened to a few, not all, and not only to the Apostles, John XXI. 2, and therefore it is omitted here. Wherefore the last appearance on earth, which took place on the day of the ascension, is to be understood. Concerning which, let the Harmony be compared.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἔπειτα ὤφθη Ἰακώβῳ.

Videtur ἔπειτα hic esse non postea, sed præterea, ut supra XII. 28. Hebr. III. 17. Nam apparitio Christi Jacobo fa- cta est statim post resurrectionem, ut habet traditio, quam ex Hieronymo commemoravimus in prolegomenis ad Matthæum.

Non opus est, ut à communi vocis significa- tione discedamus, nec id convenit cum antece- denti v. 5. Eἶτα; & v. 6. si ἔπειτα acceptum fuerit pro postea, & ordinem hic observare voluisse A- postolum vox ἔσχατον v. 8. doceat. Traditio illa apud Hieronymum ab ipso censetur inter ea, quæ assuta sunt à Nazaræis Evangelio Matthæi, omni- que specie probabilitatis carent. Et narrationem istam ceu fabulosam, imo fidei sacrorum Evange- liorum contrariam cum Johanne Hesselio rejicit Estius.

Ἔπειτα τοῖς ἀποστόλοις πᾶσιν.

De quo vide Joh. XX. 25. & sequentibus & XXI.

Hæc non illa est, quæ à Johanne descripta legi- tur sive cap. XX. sive XXI. Nam illam, quæ Tho- mæ & aliis Apostolis contigit, jam ante comple- xus erat Apostolus v. 5. Quæ verò ad mare Tibe- riadis facta est, paucis quibusdam, non omnibus, nec solis Apostolis contigit, Joh. XXI. 2. ideoque hic prætermittitur. Quapropter intelligenda est postrema in terris apparitio in die ascensionis fa- cta. De qua conferatur Harmonia.

## 15:8
V. 8. And last of all he appeared to me also, as to one untimely born.

There is a transposition here as well. For the direct phrasing would have been 'he appeared to me, as to one untimely born', נפל Job III. 16, Eccl. VI. 3. He says this, however, because he was not brought to Christianity by long instruction, by which he might be as a natural birth, but by a sudden force, in the way that immature births are wont to be cast out. Ignatius, or whoever is the writer of the epistle to the Romans among the Ignatian letters, imitated this: 'For I am not worthy, being the last of them, and an untimely birth.'

Aretius explains it in almost the same way. He calls himself ἔκτρωμα, that is, an immature fetus, because his conversion was sudden, and he was converted in a moment, to which manner a just fetus is not brought to completion, but has need of a certain duration and delay. Thus the remaining Apostles conversed with Christ for a long time, so that they might be rendered fit. Compared to these, Paul, an ἔκτρωμα, was formed suddenly. Others, however, because there are two things in an abortive fetus: 1. that it is born, but outside the due time, and is cast out with a certain force; 2. that it is imperfect, dead, unpleasant to look at, and sometimes even monstrous and foul-smelling; they wish for the latter to be looked at here, not so much the former, and as the following things show, that he called himself an Apostle in this way for the sake of self-abasement, and to indicate his impurity and unworthiness. Thus, after the Greek commentators, Thomas and Estius, and Baronius and Lorinus, who reject the opinion that he is called an abortive because he was a supernumerary among the Apostles. Conf. Num. XII. 12. Ps. LIIX. 9. Estius warns that concerning this appearance, as also concerning the preceding ones, it must be held without doubt that it was such that Christ showed himself to Paul to be seen corporally and with bodily eyes. For if it had not been such a vision, he says, even that of which Paul now speaks, how could he bring himself forward as an eyewitness just like the others to prove the truth of the resurrection of Christ? For a vision of a body formed and assumed by an Angel, which would represent the appearance of Christ as a man, would by no means suffice for Paul to bear eyewitness testimony to his resurrection, by which, after other witnesses had been brought forward who had seen the Lord, he himself could also say: 'He was seen by me also.' Nor, if such a body had been offered to the eyes of the Apostles, would they have believed on that account that he had risen, which is sufficiently evident from the Evangelical history. How much less would other men have believed it from the testimony of the Apostles, if they knew that they had seen nothing else. Whence he teaches that that opinion of Ansbertus Ambrosius in Haimo, book 1, Commentary on the Apocalypse, is to be rejected entirely: 'It can be believed that the Lord did not appear to the blessed Apostle Paul after his ascension in his own nature, but rather through an Angel in the form in which he is wont to be recognized by men.' But what Thomas gathers from that, that Christ after his ascension into the heavens sometimes descended corporally to the earth, that even Estius himself does not assume; indeed, he notes that it seems not impossible to many (among the Papists) that Christ, remaining in heaven, also showed himself on earth as simultaneously present locally. Therefore, the fabrication of Musculus, Marloratus, and Pareus is deservedly to be rejected, who say that not Christ, but only some phantom was seen by Paul on the road to Damascus, Acts IX, or that the appearance was not corporal, but intellectual. For thus, from the testimony of Paul, the truth of the resurrection of the body of Christ could not be established with the same firmness as it was established from the vision of Peter, James, and the other Apostles. For witnesses who see a phantom of a thing, who see in a way other than sensible and ocular, do not deserve the same faith as those who saw the object itself with their own eyes, not through a dream or any other analogical mode of seeing.

Latin:

V. 8. Ἔσχατον δὲ πάντων ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί.

Est & hic trajectio. Recta enim elocutio fuerat ὤφθη κἀμοὶ, ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι. Conspectus est mihi, qui sum velut partus ex abortione נפל Job. III. 16. Eccl. VI. 3. Hoc autem ideò dicit, quia non longâ institutione ad Christianismum perductus fuit, quo esset velut naturalis partio, sed vi subita, quomodo immaturi partus ejici so- lent. Imitatus hoc est Ignatius, aut quisquis est scriptor epistolæ ad Romanos inter Ignatianas: Οὐ γάρ εἰμι ἄξιος, ὢν ἔσχατος αὐτῶν, καὶ ἔκτρωμα.

Eodem ferè modo explicat Aretius. Ἔκτρωμα se vocat, hoc est, fœtum immaturum, quia subita- nea fuit sua conversio, & in momento conversus, ad quem morem non perficitur justus fœtus, sed diuturnitate quâdam & morâ illi opus est. Sic re- liqui Apostoli diu cum Christo sunt conversati, ut idonei redderentur. His collatus Paulus ἔκτρωμα est subito formatus. Alii tamen, quia in fœtu ab- ortivo duo sunt, 1. quod nascitur, sed extra tempus debitum, & cum vi quadam ejicitur. 2. quod imper- fectus, mortuus, aspectu gravis, quandoque etiam monstrosus & fœtidus est; Non tam prius, quàm posterius respici hic volunt, & ut sequentia osten- dunt, extenuationis gratia, & ad indicandam im- puritatem & indignitatem suam se ita Apostolum vocasse. Ita post Græcos tractatores Thomas & Estius, Baronii & Lorini, qui abortivum dici, quod supernumerarius fuerit inter Apostolos, senten- tiam reprobant. Conf. Num. XII. 12. Ps. LIIX. 9. De hàc apparitione, ut & de præcedentibus in- dubitatò tenendum esse monet Estius, talem fuis- se, quâ Christus semetipsum corporaliter atque oculis corporeis videndum Paulo ostenderit. Nam nisi talis; inquit, visio fuisset, etiam de quâ nunc Paulus loquitur, quomodo se perinde ut cæteros te- stem adduceret oculatam ad probandam veritatem resurrectionis Christi. Nam visio corporis ab An- gelo formati & assumpti, quod Christi hominis spe- ciem repræsentaret, haudquaquam Paulo sufficeret, ad ferendum oculare testimonium resurrectionis ejus, quo post alios testes adhibitos, qui Dominum viderant, ipse etiam dicere posset: Visus est & mi- hi. Neque si tale corpus Apostolorum oculis oblatum fuisset, idcircò credidissent eum resurrexisse, quod satis ex Evangelica historia patet. Quanto minus id credidissent ex Apostolorum testimonio cæ- teri homines, si scirent, illos non aliud vidisse. Unde rejiciendam omninò docet istam Ansberti Ambrosii apud Haimonem l. 1. Comm. in Apocal. sententiam: Credi posse, quod B. Paulo Apostolo Dominus post suam ascensionem non in sua natu- ra apparuerit, sed potius per Angelum in ea forma, in qua recognosci ab hominibus solet. Quod autem Thomas inde colligit, Christum post ascensionem in cœlos aliquando corporaliter in terram descen- disse, id nec ipse Estius assumit, imo multis non impossibile videri notat (inter Pontificios) Chri- stump in cœlo manentem, se etiam in terra exhi- buisse simul præsentem localiter. Rejiciendum pro- inde meritò commentum Musculi, Marlorati, Parei, qui non Christum, sed simulacrum tantùm aliquod Paulo in via Damascena visum ajunt, Act. IX. aut apparitionem fuisse non corporalem, sed intellectualem. Sic enim ex Pauli testimonio non posset pari firmitate veritas resurrectionis corpo- ris Christi stabiliri, quæ stabilita est ex visione Petri, Jacobi, & aliorum Apostolorum. Testes enim, qui simulacrum rei vident, qui modo alio vident, quàm sensibili & oculari, non merentur parem fidem cum iis, qui oculis suis ipsum obje- ctum viderunt, non per somnium, aut alium ali- quem analogicum videndi modum.

## 15:9
V. 9. For I am the least of the Apostles. To increase the credibility of his testimony, about to proclaim great things concerning himself, he first humbles himself as much as he can, lest he might seem to be seeking glory.

We add the words of Theophylact: The Apostle passed judgment upon himself, inasmuch as he says he is inferior not only to the twelve, but also to all the others. Observe, however, how he makes mention of these errors now, from which he was afterwards freed through baptism, in order to show with how many gifts God has endowed him. Someone will ask, why does Paul produce himself as a witness of the Lord's resurrection, and then recount his own errors? Truly, so that greater faith may be placed in him. For he will not spare the transgressions of others, who brings forth his own.

who am not fit to be called an Apostle. ἱκανὸς is ἄξιος, as appears by a comparison of the passage in Matt. III. 11 and John II. 7. He affirms that he is unworthy of such great honor on account of his former life. And yet elsewhere he said that he had obtained mercy, because he had done what he had done in ignorance, 1 Tim. I. 13. It is true. But that diminishes the guilt, it does not remove it. And he who commits such things, if one acts by strict right, is not worthy of Apostolic honor.

Because I persecuted the Church of God. God had already forgiven this, and he himself remembers it.

Latin:

V. 9. Ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ ἐλάχιστος τῶν Ἀποστόλων. Ad augendam testimonii fidem, magna de se prædica- turus primum quantum potest se dejicit, ne glorias stare videretur.

Addimus verba Theophylacti: Sententiam in se tulit Apostolus, quippe qui non modo duodenis se dicit inferiorem, sed & cæterorum omnium. Ad- verte autem, quemadmodum idcircò de his faciat erratis nunc mentionem, è quibus per baptismum sit postmodum liberatus, ut ostendat, quantis se do- nis Deus affecerit. Quæret aliquis, cur seipsum Paulus resurrectionis Dominicæ testem producit, deinceps & sua errata commemorat? Nempe, ut fides ei major adhibeatur. Haud enim parcet alie- nis commissis, qui sua expromit.

ὃς οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς, καλεῖσθαι Ἀπόστολος. ἱκανὸς est ἄξιος, ut apparet collatione loci Matth. III. 11. & Joh. II. 7. Indignum se affirmat tanto honore ob vi- tam priorem. Atqui alibi dixit, miserationem sibi obti- gisse, ideò quod quæ fecerat, ea fecisset per ignorantiam, 1. Tim. I. 13. Verum est. Sed id culpam minuit, non de- trahit. Et qui talia peccat, si summo jure agatur, Aposto- lico honore non est dignus.

Διότι ἐδίωξα τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν τῦ Θεῦ. Deus id jam condonaverat, & ipse meminit.

## 15:10
V. 10. But by the grace of God I am what I am. By the mercy of God I am an Apostle.

And His grace, which was bestowed upon me, was not in vain. The honor conferred upon me did not lack its fruit.

But I labored more abundantly than them all. Περισσότερον, more, abundantly, it effected. See Rom. XV. 19, 20.

Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me. This is also said comparatively, not to exclude himself, but to attribute the most powerful parts to divine power. A similar expression is in Matt. X. 20. The grace of GOD is said to be with someone, whom He favors and helps. See Matt. XXVII. 20. What is explained here by σὺν, is elsewhere by ἐπὶ, Acts IV. 33, and by μετὰ, 2 Tim. VI. 21. This is an explanation of the word Immanuel. The preposition is correctly explained: if you except the comparison with Immanuel, which we said brings something more to Is. VII and Matt. I. But the Apostle does not here establish himself or his own free will as being granted, as Eccius gathers from the Vulgate, which, having omitted the article, wrongly translates ἡ σὺν ἐμοὶ as 'the grace of God with me': But he proclaims solely the grace of GOD, and specifies it as such, which is mine, or which is present with me, but he by no means divides the works between himself and the grace of God. That this is said comparatively, as Grotius wishes, appears by no evidence. Alvarez, as noted by B. Hülsemann, book 9, on the aids of grace, disp. 71, to the third, and disp. 96, in the 9th question, whether free will of itself also works something? He denies this proposition. If that is taken of itself actively from an innate and natural principle, and he proves at length the explanation of this saying from Pope Gelasius, Augustine, Book 1 of Retractations, chapter 9, of the same book on the grace of Christ, chapter 13, and the testimonies of other Fathers, that it is with me merely subjective, but not an operating principle, of itself and by natural faculties, which he rightly demonstrates by the parallels of the Apostle, Gal. II. 20 and others, besides that most Greek copies, which Luther also followed, read not σὺν ἐμοὶ, but εἰς ἐμέ. By which phrase the passive subject is more clearly denoted.

Latin:

V. 10. χάριτι δὲ Θεῦ εἰμὶ, ὅ εἰμι. Dei miseratione sum Apostolus.

Καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτῦ, ἡ εἰς ἐμὲ ὐ κενὴ ἐγενήθη. Collatus mihi honor fructu suo non caruit.

Ἀλλὰ περισσότερον πάντων αὐτῶν ἐκοπίασα. Περισσότερον יותר מן plus amplius effecit. Vide Rom. XV. 19. 20.

Οὐκ ἐγὼ δὲ ἀλλ’ ἡ χάρις τῦ Θεῦ, ἡ σὺν ἐμοί. Comparatè & hoc dictum, non ut se excludat, sed ut potentiæ divinæ potissimas tribuat partes. Similis locu- tio Matth. X. 20. Gratia DEI cum aliquo esse dicitur, cui favet atque opitulatur. Vide Matth. XXVII. 20. Quod hic per σὺν explicatur, id alibi per ἐπὶ, Act. IV. 33. per μετὰ 2. Tim. VI. 21. Est hæc explicatio vocabuli עמנואל. Rectè præpositio explicatur: Si collationem עמנואל excipias, quod amplius aliquid infer- re ad Es. VII. & Matth. I. diximus. Non autem hic se, vel liberum arbitrium suum concessum Apo- stolus constituit, ut Eccius è vulgata, quæ omisso articulo ἡ σὺν ἐμοὶ perperam vertit gratia Deime- cum, colligit: Sed unicè gratiam DEI prædicat, eamq; ita specificat, quæ est meum, vel quæ mihi ad- est, minimè verò operas inter se & gratiam Dei di- vidit. Comparatè autem hoc dictũ, uti Grotius vult, nullo indicio apparet. Alvarez, notante B. Hülse- manno, l. 9. de auxil. gratiæ disp. 71. ad tert. & disp. 96. in 9. quæst. utrum liberum arbitrium ex se etiam aliquid operetur? negat hanc propositio- nem. Si illud ex se sumatur activè ex innato & naturali principio, & dicti hujus explicationem ex Gelasio Papa August. l. 1. Retract. c. 9. ejusdem libri de gratiâ Christi cap. 13. aliorumque Patrum testimoniis prolixe probat, illud mecum esse me- rè subjectivum, non autem principium operans, ex se, & naturalibus facultatibus, quod parallelis Apostoli rectè demonstrat, Gal. II. 20. & aliis, præterquam quod pleraq; Græca exemplaria, quæ Lutherus quoq; sequutus est, legant non σὺν ἐμοὶ, sed εἰς ἐμέ. Quâ phrasi subjectum passum clarius denotatur.

## 15:11
V. 11. Whether therefore I.

I, who have built so many churches.

Whether they.

Other apostles, supply are referred to. A similar locution above XIII. 8.

So we preach.

And that Christ in reality according to the literal sense has risen, and we shall rise.

And so you believed.

The rule of Christ, into which you were baptized, contains both.

Latin:

V. 11. Εἴτε ὖν ἐγὼ.

Ego, qui tot struxi Ecclesias.

Εἴτε ἐκεῖνοι

Apostoli alii, supple respiciuntur. Similis loquutio su- pra XIII. 8.

Οὕτω κηρύσσομεν.

Et Christum reipsa κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν resurrexisse, & nos re- surrecturos.

Καὶ ὕτως ἐπιστεύσατε.

Regula Christi, in quam baptizati estis, utrumque continet.

## 15:12
V. 12. But if Christ is preached that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead.

That is, to be of those things that are simply impossible, which are things that are not, things that are not possible. For certainly, what has been done, can be done. Abarbanel argues against such persons on the first of Isaiah.

Latin:

V. 12. Εἰ δὲ χριστὸς κηρύσσεται, ὅτι ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγήγερται, πῶς λέγουσί τινες ἐν ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν.

Id est, esse τῶν ἁπλῶς ἀδυνάτων, quæ sunt οὐκ ὄντα, οὐκ ἐνδεχόμενα. Nam certè, quod factum est, fieri potest. Con- tra tales disputat Abarbanel ad prima Esaiæ.

## 15:13
V. 13. But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.

When the genus is removed, the species is also removed. This is an argument, as the schools say, in Ferio, brought forward for this reason: that by convicting the inference of falsehood and the assumption of being manifest—namely, that Christ had died—the proposition, which is that no dead person rises again, might be destroyed.

Latin:

V. 13. Εἰ δὲ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ χριστὸς ἐγήγερται.

Sublato genere tollitur & species. Est argumentum, ut scholæ dicunt in Ferio, ideo adductum, ut convictâ fal- sitatis illatione & assumptione manifestâ, nempe Christum fuisse mortuum, perimatur propositio, quæ est, nullum mortuum resurgere.

## 15:14
V. 14. Εἰ δὲ χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, κενὸν ἄρα τὸ κήρυγμα ἡμῶν, κενὴ δὲ καὶ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν.

And therefore, because the Apostles had used this argument principally to prove that the doctrine of Christ was true, which God would not have raised him from the dead if he had taught falsely. See Acts 1:22, 2:32, 4:10, 33, 13:37, Rom. 1:4, 18, 24.

That the Apostles intended this principally will not be taught, because Christ did not undergo death merely as a martyr and for the sake of confirming the truth of his doctrine. And therefore, neither is his resurrection said to have been done to confirm the truth of Christ's doctrine, much less said to have been done principally for that; but since he was delivered for our sins and raised for our justification, the more important end of the resurrection is the grace obtained for us in our justification and the application of our salvation. This is also the principal argument of the Gospel, namely concerning the cause and end of the death and resurrection of Christ, and the testimony of all the Prophets, Acts 10:43. If this is overturned, our faith is κενὴ, empty, vain, and void, since the delivery of Christ into death for us and his resurrection from the dead must be apprehended by faith as the proper object of saving faith, Rom. 4:24, 25. Rightly, therefore, Theophylact: For if he had been unable to rise again while dying, neither would sin have been removed, nor would death itself have been destroyed, and finally our preaching would have been empty and superfluous, and your faith would be proven even emptier.

Latin:

V. 14. Εἰ δὲ χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, κενὸν ἄρα τὸ κήρυγμα ἡμῶν, κενὴ δὲ καὶ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν.

Et ideo, quia hoc præcipuè argumento usi erant Apo- stoli, ut evincerent verum esse Christi dogma, quod Deus eum, si falsa docuisset, non resuscitasset è mortuis. Vide Act. I. 22. II. 32. IV. 10. 33. XIII. 37. Rom. I. 4. 18. 24.

Id præcipuè intendisse Apostolos haud doce- bitur, quia Christus non ut martyr tantùm, & confirmandæ veritatis doctrinæ suæ gratia mor- tem subiit. Ideoque nec resuscitatio ejus ad con- firmandam doctrinæ Christi veritatem facta, ne- dum præcipuè facta traditur, sed cum traditus sit propter peccata nostra, resuscitatus propter justifi- cationem nostram, potior finis resuscitationis est gratia nobis parta in justificatione & salvatione no- stri applicatio. Quod etiam præcipuum argumen- tum Evangelii est, de causa nempe ac fine mor- tis & resurrectionis Christi, & testimonium Pro- phetarum omnium, Act. X. 43. Quo everso fides nostra κενὴ vacua, vana, & irrita est, quum fide apprehendenda sit Christi pro nobis in mortem traditio, & à mortuis resuscitatio, ceu proprium objectum fidei salvificæ, Rom. IV. 24. 25. Rectè er- go Theophylactus: Si enim moriens resurgere ne- quivisset, neq; peccatum fuisset sublatum, neq; mors ipsa deleta, & nostra demum inanis fuisset & super- vacana prædicatio, & fides vestra inanior argue- retur.

## 15:14
Man was made into a living soul, that is, he was made a living animal.

For it is the abstract for the concrete. It is of animals to live for a time.

ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδὰμ. Christ. Εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν.

He was made through the resurrection and ascension into heaven a man plainly divine, who has the power even of giving life to others, and indeed eternal life, John VI. 33. 40. 47. 50. 57. and above 22. In Adam there was ἐπὶπνεύματος a certain thing for living.

But in Christ there is ἐπίγνωσις, says Cyril. The sense is: As through the insufflation of the breath of life the first man was made into a living soul, the life of the soul being communicated to the body truly and really, whence by the force of the natural union of soul and body, a truly living body proceeded from the clay: So the second Adam through the assumption of the Son of GOD, and the communication of the divine nature, was made into a life-giving spirit, with spiritual life and δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ, with life-giving power, truly and really communicated to the human nature of Christ, so that thence it might be truly life-giving, and endowed with the spiritual power of giving life, and the second man becomes for us the cause of eternal and blessed life, that in him all may be made alive, just as the Apostle taught in v. 22.

But Christ is not here called a life-giving spirit by reason of his divine nature, which Beza wishes, because the Son of GOD is not called a life-giving Spirit in the nominative case, which belongs to the Son of GOD κατ' αὐτὸ, and ὀσιωδῶς or essentially, but most recently Adam is said to be MADE into a life-giving spirit, which belongs to Christ the man, according to human nature, by force of the union, and the hypostatic communication, or ἀλλ' ἄλλο, because human nature is united to the Word, or to the life-giving spirit, that is, to the divine nature, and to it has been communicated the same divine power of giving life, just as the Father has life in himself, Job V. 25. ὅτι because or in as much as he is the Son of man, which is added in v. 27. just as also he gave to him the power of raising the dead to life, and of performing judgment, as is taught in the same place.

Concerning which Cyril, book 2 on John c. 14. Do not marvel, if, when you see me to be a man, I nevertheless promise that I will raise the dead, and will bring them into judgment. For the Father gave me the power of giving life, he gave the power of judging. Wherefore the cause, why he said this was given to him by the Father, he immediately subjoined, saying: Because he is the Son of man, so that we may understand, all things are given to him, as to a man, who although he is a creature, has nothing from himself, but the only-begotten Son, not a partaker of life, but life naturally, as the Father is.

And in book III. on John cap. 21.

The nature of flesh itself cannot give life BY ITSELF. For what greater thing could it have than the nature of Deity? When therefore Christ calls his flesh life-giving, he does not attribute to it the power of giving life as to himself, or to his own Spirit. FOR THE Spirit gives life BECAUSE OF HIMSELF, to whose VIRTUE the flesh ascends through conjunction. But how that is done, we can neither understand with the mind, nor speak with the tongue, but we receive it in silence and firm faith.

Therefore the last Adam was not finally made into a life-giving Spirit through the resurrection and ascension into heaven, but through the hypostatic union and communication. As the first Adam was made into a living soul immediately in his first creation, so the second Adam was made into a life-giving spirit in the first conception, when the power of the Highest took up the corporeal mass in the virginal womb. For as the pious ancients said: ἅμα σὰρξ, ἅμα Θεοῦ λόγῳ σάρξ. For by the resurrection human nature was not changed, or the soul of Christ into an immutable Spirit, which fiction Grotius seems to foster here, nor did Christ through his ascension into heaven, which the Socinians imagine, to whom he appears to approach, lay aside the truth of human body, and was transubstantiated into a spirit, or having put off the body was made entirely spirit: But what the Son of GOD once assumed, he does not lay aside for eternity.

Nor is it to be understood with Estius, that in the resurrection he received his spirit, without the subsidy of food, to supply perpetual life to the body. The Apostle ascends to the very cause of our glory, which we are about to attain by reason of the body, and primarily what this is, which is not only an incorruptible body in glory, and in power not -ptible, such as is sown here in dishonor and in weakness, such as Adam had after the fall, will rise, but also a spiritual (πνευματικὸν) body, and not indeed a natural (ψυχικὸν) body, not such as the first man had before the fall and received when he was made into a living soul, but of far more excellent qualities: which is certainly to be credited to the second Adam, who, having been made a life-giving spirit for our sake, will make us alive, v. 22, through whose life-giving flesh we have life and salvation, both by reason of merit and by reason of efficacy. For he was enriched with life-giving power (δυνάμει ζωοποιικῇ), so that through the merit of his obedience, active and passive, he could free us from death and merit life for us, John VI. 33, 50, 51, 54. Concerning which Cyril in Defense of Anathema XI against the Orientals: "Since, however, the Word which is from the Father is life according to nature, he makes his flesh life-giving." And further: "Since, however, it is the body of life, it is life-giving. For on that account he grants life to our mortal bodies, and destroys the dominion of death." v. 46. Ἀλλ' οὐ πρῶτον πνευματικόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικόν, ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν.

Namely the body, which is to be understood from the preceding v. 44. God promised the more imperfect things, so that more perfect things might follow.

Sic ante pueri sumus, quàm viri. Sic prius lex, deinde Evangelium. Prius cœlum & terra, quæ cernimus, posterius cœlum & terra, id est, universum multò pulchrius.

Theophylact here: Lest anyone should happen to ask, Why then do we now possess this animal body, which is inferior, while he possesses the spiritual one, which is superior? He answers that the principles of each were so disposed: Adam first, Christ last. Thus it comes about that our affairs are advanced for the better. August. in Ench. cap. 91. Just as now it is called an animal body, because it is a body of seed, not a soul: so then it will be a spiritual body, yet it will be a body, not a spirit. Irenaeus against heresies, book V, cap. 10. Our bodies in this life are animal, that is, participating in a soul, and when they have lost it, they are mortified: then, rising through the Spirit, they become spiritual bodies, or have life through the Spirit remaining forever. v. 47. The first man is from the earth, earthy. He spoke of soul and Spirit. Now he speaks of the body. choikos, limaceus to Tertullian, from slime, in the Latin of Irenaeus V. 11. He refers to that in Gen. II. 7. God formed man taking dust. It is the Hebrew word which you also have in Gen. III. 19. It signifies any particle of earth. Philo: The human race. For the one is from the earth, the other is earthly. The one from the earth is from heaven; inasmuch as he was made in the image of God, he is partaker of no corruptible or composite generation. But the earthly one was compacted from scattered matter, which he has called dust. Theophilus, where Adam was taken from, interprets it not as of dry land, but as a part of manifold and varied matter.

The Apostle spoke not only of the soul and spirit, but primarily of the body, and that both animal and spiritual, although he taught that the animal draws its origin from the inspiration of a living soul, and the spiritual from the vivifying spiritual virtue of the human nature of Christ. For we have the former from the first Adam, by the power of natural generation, and we shall obtain the latter from the second by the power of spiritual regeneration, in the blessed palingenesis, Matt. XIX. 28. The second man, the Lord from heaven. This is called from heaven in the Hebrew manner for heavenly, that is, celestial, already possessing a celestial body. v. 48. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy. Such a body as Adam had, such he also sowed in his descendants; in the person of Adam the human race is described. Origen against Celsus IV. And as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. Thus also Christ, who has regenerated us, will give us a body like his own. But when he said heavenly, he wishes it to be understood that the body will be worthy of a supercelestial dwelling. See Heb. VI. 4. Concerning the word heavenly see Eph. I. 3. The third seat, in which is the Majesty of God and the Angels, is indeed called heaven, namely the third, more excellent than the others, and therefore it is called the heaven of heavens and heavens, in the plural. But it is no less supercelestial, with respect had to the visible heaven. Origen Philocalia XVIII. How is it possible for the flesh also to change its qualities and become such as that which possesses the heavenly, and to live in their places?

There is no reason for us to depart from the customary meaning of the expression, ex ouranou, from heaven: nor is the body said to have a heavenly nature, but the Lord himself is said to be from heaven. Therefore, the predicate Lord from heaven expresses his divine nature.

For he is not said to be, nor can be said to be, from heaven by reason of his flesh, as the Anabaptists and fanatics dream together with Valentinus and Apollinarius; but because the Son of GOD for our sake and for our salvation descended from heaven, as is contained in the Nicene Creed. No one ascends into heaven except he who descended, namely the Son of man, John III. 13. Therefore the second man is called GOD from heaven on account of the communication of idioms. On which Theophylactus: Nor therefore is the man, or the very assumption of humanity, from heaven, as that madman Apollinaris raved, but because there is one person of the one Christ. And he is said to be a man from heaven on account of the unity, and GOD is asserted to have been crucified for the same cause. The reason is therefore given why ὁ πρῶτον τὸ πνευματικὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικὸν, because ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, and therefore the body was not first spiritual, but animal, because the first man, brought forth from earth with respect to origin, was therefore earthly, with respect to nature and earthly constitution, and the affections suitable to an earthly body: Not yet indeed spiritual, and heavenly. Conversely the reason is also given, whence does the spiritual body come? Because the second man is not from earth and earthly only, as the first was: He is not a mere man, but true GOD, since with respect to nature he is ὁ κύριος, JEHOVAH, (which essential name is rendered by the word κύριος) of the divine essence, with respect to divine origin, from heaven; because he came forth from the bosom of the heavenly Father, as μονογενὴς παρὰ Πατρὸς Job I. 12. The Son begotten from eternity by the Father, who descended from heaven, and ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, λόγῳ ἐνεσαρκωθείς. What came from things above, Job I. 14. 15. cap. III. 16. & 13. When he is in the heavens, he descended from heaven, Johan. I. 31. he went out from the Father, and came into the world Johan. XVI. 28. For just as the first man, as having sprung from earth, and of an earthly nature and condition, was first made into a living soul, after the manner of earth: So the second man was made not only into a living soul, but also into a life-giving spirit, because he was not only from earth, but also from heaven, not ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, but κύριος. Now the first man is said to be of earth, earthly, not on account of mortality, or because his body is resolved into earth, because he is of earth. For after the fall this was at last said to him, and it pertains to the punishments of sin: Earth thou art, and into earth shalt thou be converted; here however it regards Adam partly with respect to origin, because he was formed from the clay of the earth before sin, partly with respect to state, because placed in earth he was subject to earthly affections, just as also the animal body was attributed to him, not on account of sin or corruptibility, but on account of condition, and actions pertaining to this earthly life, to which namely the soul grants life, sense and motion, according to what suits this temporal state, which has need of refreshment, preservation of radical moisture, food, and drink. Therefore in this place the earthly animal body is not opposed to an immortal and incorruptible body, but to a heavenly and spiritual one, which will no longer be furnished with the proper affections of this life, but with heavenly and spiritual endowments, and therefore will have no need of food and drink, digestion, refreshment &c.

the Lord, true God by nature. For let it not be, as Cyril has it in his epistle to Nestorius, that we should receive the human flesh of Christ as common flesh, far be this: nor again as that of some sanctified man, or associated with the WORD only by equality of dignity, or having obtained divine inhabitation, but as TRULY LIFE-GIVING, proper to the WORD himself. For since it is LIFE, so that God according to nature, at the same time and one certain thing (the WORD) was made with his own flesh, he immediately conferred upon it the virtue of giving life. These things, therefore, concerning Christ, as the cause of our vivification and glorious resurrection, which is to be in a body not animal, but spiritual, by reason of affections and qualities, in kinship with Adam, from whom we receive a body not spiritual, but animal. Now he renders the reason of the consequence. For such as the earthly one is, from whom we draw our origin through natural generation, such also are we earthly ones. If he had an animal and earthly body, we also have such a one: being of the same origin, the same nature, constitution, and affection as he. Again, such as the heavenly one is, from whom we draw our origin through spiritual regeneration, such also are we heavenly ones, who are like him not by nature, but by grace: both as to origin from above, because reborn from above, and as to spiritual communion, because partakers of the divine nature. And therefore, as he himself after the resurrection had no longer an animal and earthly body, as far as qualities go, but a spiritual and heavenly body, so also we are to have such a body, when he shall transform the body of our humiliation into its becoming conformed to the body of his glory.

Phil. III. 21. Therefore, the false interpretation of Crellius is not to be admitted, to which Grotian's is akin in his explanation of 1 Cor. XV, that in those words, the second man the Lord from heaven, the discourse is not about the Deity of Christ, but about the nature of the body, which Christ now has and we are one day to have. For in the verse immediately following, it is about the nature or rather the quality of the body, both of Christ and of the faithful of Christ, but in these words there is nothing about the body of Christ and its nature, much less of the elect. And therefore Crellius, with the Calvinist Mustulus, prefers to suspect that the word ὁ κύριος was put there by the carelessness of scribes, instead of οὐράνιος, so that it might obtain that the nature of the body is regarded, because the matter of the body of Christ is indeed expressed by the words from heaven: but the nature, consonant to the matter, is expressed by the word heavenly. But in what place this is to be held is evident from the fact that Crellius himself did not dare, without the faith of copies, to rely on his own conjecture, and acknowledges the truth of the Greek reading. But that Crellius, while he invents that the nature of the body, since it is different in reason of origin and substance, which, to wit, is taken from heaven or from heavenly bodies, and has a nature consonant to heavenly matter, contradicts the Apostle openly with his Socinus. Who does not speak of the οὐσία or substance of the body, but of the ποιότης or quality. Ποίω δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται v. 35. and here v. 48. διον & τοῖτοι. And that body of humiliation does the same thing as substance, with τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης, admitting only by the μετασχηματισμός of some transformation a diversity of qualities, by which from the state of humiliation that same body shall be raised to the state of glory: As he is about to say here a little later, τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο this corruptible itself, (not another body) shall put on incorruptibility, and τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο this mortal (body) shall put on immortality, v. 53. Nor did Christ ever lay aside the body which he once assumed, which was conceived by the Holy Spirit in Mary and overshadowed by the power of the Most High; but in the same body he suffered and was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of GOD; he was seen by Stephen and Paul, he is to come to judgment, to be beheld by those who pierced him, and by the elect in heaven, as the Son of man coming in the clouds, and as the lamb slain in the midst of the throne, to be celebrated without end for ever and ever.

Nor do they concern the substance of the body, but qualities, which Crellius himself adduces, in explaining the difference of the heavenly and earthly nature of the body. The earthly one, he says, is gross, this heavenly one, subtle: that hard and unmanageable; that unpleasing, and of itself unfit for motion upward; this subject to no motion of itself, most ready to be taken up into any motion at the will of the vital Spirit: that cold of itself; this endowed with none of such vile qualities, nor subject to them: that corruptible, and easily dissipated; this incorruptible, and most tenacious of its integrity, especially since it must be that it receive some quality against the assault of its nature, and suffer forms repugnant to its own character, which it always strives to shake off, just as the earthly mass in the human body and universally in the animal; but if anything of qualities is still impressed upon it, it entirely agrees excellently with its nature, he says, so that it never wishes to shake off any of them. These things, I say, all argue diverse qualities, not diverse substances: since, the same substance remaining, those diverse qualities can have place. Concerning the seat in which glorious bodies shall be with the Angels, of what nature it is made, is not certain, nor must the seat in which the Majesty of GOD is be figured as bodies, even though most subtle, since GOD is an infinite Spirit, φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον, 1 Tim. VI. 16. whom the heavens of heavens do not contain. 1 Kings VIII. Verse 49. Καὶ καθὼς ἐφορέσαμεν τὴν εἰκόνα χοϊκοῦ. A body like the body of Adam, and on that account subject to diseases, evils and death. Φορέσωμεν καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ ἐπουρανίου. Φορέσωμεν other Codices have, and thus read the Syriac, Arabic, and thus Origen cites it against Celsus: We shall have a body like the body of Jesus, yet in its own degree.

Thus the word image is taken Rom. VIII. 29. These things now pertain to the remaining attributes or predicates of the animal and earthly body, and of the spiritual and heavenly, concerning their differences, inasmuch as to the former are assigned corruption, dishonor, weakness, but to the latter incorruption, glory, and power, vers. 42. and 43. For those do not regard any longer the earthly origin and the primeval condition of the body of Adam, in the state before sin, but that condition which belonged to him and his posterity after the fall. For before the fall, although there was not that incorruptibility or glory or power which is expected in the other life, yet corruption had no place, nor ignominy, nor infirmity, but these are consequences and punishment of sin, whence diseases, all evils, and death drew their origin, Rom. V. 12. Sap. II. We bear therefore the image of the earthly Adam, such as he was after the fall, because not after the image of GOD, which was lost through the fall, but after his own image (which he had procured for himself through sin) he begot children, Gen. V. vers. 2. But we shall bear the image of the heavenly (Adam, Christ, since we shall be perfectly renewed not only in respect of the soul to the image of GOD, as to wisdom and holiness, and righteousness, but also in respect of the body, as to incorruptibility and immortality, being entirely free from all things, as of sin, so also of disease and death, which are the consequences of sin, and we shall be like the angels, even in respect of incorruptibility and immortality. The image indeed, says Theod. Theophylact, of the earthly, like that, because it is, and into dust you shall return: But the heavenly image is the resurrection of the dead and incorruptibility itself: So that it must be understood that these things were said as if concerning the resurrection, not concerning a way of living. And you will understand that "we shall bear the image of the heavenly" was not said as a piece of advice, but as an indication of a future thing, that is, that we are going to bear the heavenly image.

Hence Estius's explanation is to be rejected, as if the Apostle were intermixing an exhortation of doctrine, admonishing that just as we have exhibited in ourselves by sinning the image, that is, the very express likeness of the earthly Adam, who first sinned: So henceforth we should exhibit in ourselves the image of the heavenly man, that is, of Christ, through holy conversion and newness of life, imitating him, so that we may be able to arrive at a glory similar to his. For the Vulgate wrongly reads PORTEMUS (let us bear), when in the Future it is held as portabimus (we shall bear), so that the Syriac may agree with the Greeks, and they have also interpreted it in such a way as a continuation of the doctrine concerning the resurrection. The Greek interpreters, Theodoret, Theophylact, Methodius, Oecumenius, admit this, with Estius confessing that the Greek reading agrees not only with the preceding, but also with what follows immediately.

Ver.

50. Now I say this, brethren.

He explains his own words more clearly.

Thus also above VII.

29. That flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

Here it appears that by flesh and blood, בשר ודם, is understood such a body as we have here, fragile, perishable, Sir.

XIV. 19.

Heb.

15. consisting of the smallest particles which perish daily and in whose place others arrive from the outside, as Alfenus says in L. proponebatur D. de judiciis. Such bodies do not befit that immutable kingdom. Κληρονομῆσαι (to inherit) to hold, to possess by certain right.

Thus Augustine is to be softened by interpretation, when he says in the book against Adimantus XII. that in the resurrection there will be neither flesh nor blood.

Basil indeed explains these things, as Theophylact notes, as having been brought forth by the Apostle in such a way as to exhort the Corinthians to live rightly, because flesh and blood, that is, carnal actions and corruption, that is, wickedness corrupting the nobility of the mind, shall not possess that glory. But these things are foreign to the mind and scope of the Apostle.

There are not wanting those who would have them said by way of doctrine and information concerning glorious bodies, so that they take flesh and blood metonymically for the works of the flesh and blood, because they shall not attain the heavenly inheritance, Gal.

19. just as they observe that by the name of corruption sin is noted, from 2.

Pet.

19. or concerning men who are addicted to the works of the flesh and the corruption of sin, or concerning flesh subject to sin. Tertullian de resurr.

By the name of flesh and blood, guilt, not substance, is barred from the kingdom of God.

S.

Augustine, however, even if he favors both senses, both concerning the flesh, by which he notes the allurements of secular pleasures, and by which he signifies the corruption of the flesh, where sin becomes the punishment of sin, book

II. against the diverse laws and Prophets, chap.

6.; yet elsewhere, namely in epist.

146. to Consentius, he says the Apostle was not speaking of works, but of the mode of resurrection, when he wrote this.

Conf. l.

1. cap.

17. lib.

II. c.

And therefore he seems to take it concerning the flesh, which is corruptible, not going to attain the kingdom of GOD.

But this is indicated in the following member; Neither shall corruption possess incorruptibility.

Whence a tautology would thus be committed, if man, as mortal and corruptible, is also understood in the prior words; not to mention that flesh and blood existed even in man before the fall, who indeed was not then mortal and corruptible.

Wherefore others understand flesh and blood, not metonymically for the works of the flesh, or metaphorically for the corrupt qualities of flesh and blood: Nor synecdochically or complexly, for the substance with its qualities, or as it is subject to sin, corruption, or death, but concerning flesh and blood simply, or as they befit man as an animal, or as made into a living soul: Which opinion Estius notes to be that of certain Latin Fathers and of Cajetan, and it does not seem alien to the mind of Justinian and Estius himself, so that indeed by flesh and blood is understood such as it is in animal life, which requires the use of food and the procreation of children.

And Theophylact also interprets it in that way, that in the future age this body will not be so concrete with flesh and blood that it will have need of drink and food by which it may be nourished.

Nor in any other sense did Augustine deny that there would be flesh and blood in the resurrection, which is rightly observed here by Grotius.

But B. Hülsemann proves this interpretation primarily,

that by flesh and blood here are not understood vices, but the substance itself, not with vicious qualities, but with vicious qualities merely abstracted, in this sense: Such a body, as Adam received, and we from him, will not possess the kingdom of heaven, but one far more glorious; and he wonders that neither the Weimar nor the Belgian interpreters noticed this.

The proposition, he says to v.

of the Apostle, concerning the present imperfection and future perfection of the animal body, does not indeed require that we understand the animal and dusty (v.

48.) complexly with the attendant infirmities contracted after the fall: Especially since he seems to have taken the animal according to that condition with which man was first created, v.

But it suffices if the animal and dusty be taken precisely with natural qualities, and with the exclusion of supernatural axioms.

For the Apostle wishes to show that our bodies in the heavens are to acquire a condition far better than they had from the first creation, just as there is no doubt that the body of the Protoplasts, even if they had persisted in their innate perfection, would have been endowed in the state of glorification with more distinguished axioms than they had received in the first condition, and therefore nothing stands in the way of flesh and blood (v. 50) being understood purely and precisely concerning the substance of man, even the protoplast, regarding the respect to infirmities contracted through the fall, or at least taken regarding the respect, or with the exclusion of the gifts of glory to be superadded to the qualities of the first creation.

For this is what the Apostle intends to demonstrate, how even before the fall the grain springing from the earth rose more gloriously than the bare grain sown: Thus the glory of our bodies will be even greater than the glory of the body of the Adamic protoplast. But the opinion of the Socinians is to be rejected entirely, that the very substance of flesh and blood is understood here and excluded from the kingdom of GOD, which is diametrically opposed to the opinion of the Apostle, as he teaches at length that the body, in respect of substance, which is sown here, will rise again, and not another different in substance; and he assigns a difference of qualities only, not of substance, which the Greek and Latin Fathers bring forward with great consensus, and is most clear from the text itself. Οὐδὲ ἡ φθορά (Neither corruption).

And here is the abstract for the concrete.

For by corruption (φθοράν) he wishes to be understood the corruptible (φθαρτόν).

And thus he explains what he meant by flesh and blood. Incorruptibility inherits.

It cannot reach that immutable state.

These things were not said by way of explanation (κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν) of the antecedents, but as there flesh and blood are excluded from the kingdom of GOD nakedly, without glorious axioms, or as they are held in this age, here in this place the Apostle excludes corruptible bodies, and therefore to the state that immutable one, he does not even admit flesh and blood so simply, such as it was before the fall, much less φθορὰν (corruption) or a corruptible body, such as it was made after the fall.

ARTICLE II. INFORMATION CONCERNING THE TRANSMUTATION OF THE DEAD AND THE LIVING.

Verf. 51. ἰδὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω. (Behold, I tell you a mystery.)

Something hitherto unknown to you and others. See Rom. XI. 25. XVI. 25. above II. 7. IV. 1. XIII. 2. XIV. 2. Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα. (We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.) The books vary here. That Manuscript is best: οἱ πάντες οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα οὐ πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα. Neither shall we all sleep, that is, die. Nor shall we all be changed.

The following words show this to be the true reading. The same sentiment is in the commentary on the book Aboth. LIII. 2. and in the notes to chapter I of the Rabbis of Israel on the soul. The passage in Acts 42 and the words of the creed look to the same thing. It is by no means convenient to reject the other codices because of a single MS.

For the Greek reading is very consistent with itself: We shall not all indeed sleep, (because the day of the Lord will find some alive) but we shall all be changed, those indeed who are dead, by receiving in the resurrection a body endowed with other qualities: But these, who will be alive at the coming of the Lord, by undergoing in the twinkling of an eye an ἀλλαγὴν (change), because it is altogether necessary for this corruptible to put on incorruptibility. Which explanation is also that of Chrysostom, hom. XLII. He is about to say something venerable and arcane, and which not all know: Which also shows the great honor with which he affects them, namely, to speak of arcana. But what is this? We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed. But this is what he says, we shall not all indeed die, but we shall all be changed, even those who do not die.

For they also are mortal. Therefore, do not fear, he says, because you will die, as if you were not going to rise again. For there are, there are even some who will escape this, and yet this is not enough for them for that resurrection, but those bodies also, which do not die, must be changed, and pass over to incorruption. But the reading of the Vulgate does not agree, which is neither found in those Greek codices, as Jerome testifies, nor is it held today in any Greek ones, as Estius admits; We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed, because not all rise again, but only those who are dead.

But on the contrary, all will be changed, as we have said. Therefore, neither is the reading of some consistent: We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed, which Pelagius, Jerome, and Augustine indeed report, as does Oecumenius, but found in few Latin and Greek Codices. But the modern common Greek reading is found in most Greek Codices as well as in the Syriac and Arabic text. But that which is written in the margin of the Complutensian, and from those of the Royal [Polyglot]: πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντες ἀλλαγησόμεθα, that is, we shall all indeed therefore sleep, but we shall not all be changed, with that mutual ἣν in ἣν, is rightly suspended, in the judgment of Estius. For after those words: Behold I tell you a mystery, the ILLATIVE discourse does not fit in any way. We shall all indeed THEREFORE sleep.

We shall all indeed THEREFORE sleep. The modern reading is also proved by the testimony of Acacius in Jerome, that most Codices read it thus, from Origen in vol. 3. Epist. to the Thess. and the book against Marc. (produced from the Vatican by Estius) still unpublished, Theodore, and Apollinaris, whom Jerome praises, Justin, or whoever that author may be, quaest. to the orthod. num. 61. and 107. Theodoret, Chrysostom, Basil, Jerome, Epist. to Marc. II. num. 148. Theophylact, Oecumenius and others. Which Estius recognizes as true and genuine, and proves primarily by six reasons, that the Apostle here treats only of the resurrection of the good.

Finally, he adds that the change of the Greek reading into Latin is easier and more prone, or at first sight more apparent and likely, than the reverse of the Latin reading into Greek. Which is to be observed against Papal infallibility in canonizing the Vulgate.

Grotius's reading, found nowhere by others. To be compared with this passage is what is found in 1 Thess. IV. 15., to which the modern Greek reading agrees better than the Latin, as also Acts X. 42. Rom. XIV. 9. 1 Petr. IV. 5. See B. Gerh. de resurr. Mort. §. 116. seqq. But as to why not all are said to be about to fall asleep, most understand it of the faithful, whose death is called sleep.

It should be compared with this place, which is held in 1 Thess. IV. 15. to which the modern Greek reading is more suitable than the Latin, as also Acts X. 42. Rom. XIV. 9. 1 Pet. IV. 5. See B. Gerh. on the resurrection of the dead § 116. seqq. But that not all are said to be about to sleep, most understand of the faithful, whose death is called sleep.

But how do these agree with the universal testimonies concerning the death of all men, Rom. V. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 22. Ebr. IX. Answer: That all are said to die, either because GOD will extinguish them by his power, and in turn raise them again immediately (we leave to its own place the opinion of certain Papists, that they will be extinguished by the conflagrating fire of the world; Augustine indeed places the world's later conflagration before the resurrection itself), or because something analogous to death and resurrection intervenes here, as in the book de Ecclesiast. dogm. c. 7., which some wish to be by Gennadius the presbyter (not Augustine); it is reported that this is explained thus by some: It is helpful to transcribe the whole passage: The resurrection, he says, shall be of all.

If there will be of all, therefore all will die, so that death brought in by Adam may rule over all his sons, and that privilege may remain to the Lord, which is specially said of him, you will not give your holy one to see corruption. This reason, handed down by the greatest crowd of the Fathers, we have accepted. But because there are also other equally Catholic and learned men, who believe that the soul remaining in the body (that is, without the dissolution of soul and body, which is death properly so called) those who are found alive at the coming of the Lord are to be changed to incorruption and immortality, and this is counted to them for a resurrection from the dead, because they explain mortality by change, not by death, anyone who may acquiesce in this is not a heretic, unless he becomes a heretic out of contention. This is Gennadius.

Death to them, says Theophylact, is a change, for corruption dies in the pious, finally changed into innocence. Sparetz brings the suffrages of others Tom. II. Comm. in part. 3. Thom. q. 56. Disp. 50. sect. 2. pag. 571. This opinion (which denies that those just men, who will have lived at the time of judgment, are either to die or to be raised up, but only to be changed or transformed) seems to be that expressed by Paul.

And thus they judge by explaining these places (1 Corinth. XV. and 1 Thess. IV.) Chrysostom homil. 42. in 1 Corinth. and homil. 7. in Thess. Theodoret, Theophylact and Oecumenius ibid. Origen in book V. against Celsus not far from the beginning and Hie rome, Epist. 52 to Minervius, refers to this opinion of Theodore of Heraclea and Apollinaris, which he himself does not judge improbable, and upon Isaiah ch. 51 he follows that reading of Paul: We shall not all sleep, but epistle 148, q. 3, interpreting the passage of Paul 1 Thess. 4, he teaches this opinion absolutely.

Augustine also, q. 3 to Dulcitius, although he reads the passage 1 Cor. 15 differently, and therefore seems to be doubtful about the whole opinion, yet because of another testimony to the Thessalonians he is strongly inclined to this opinion, and plainly confesses that he is ignorant in what other sense the passage can be explained.

And Gennadius, De Eccl. Dogm. ch. 7 and 8, leaves this opinion as probable.

Furthermore, Tertullian, lib. De Resurr. Carnis ch. 41 and 42, although he reads the passage 1 Cor. 15 differently, nevertheless openly teaches this opinion and accommodates to it the Vulgate reading, which has it thus: We shall all indeed rise again, saying that that change, which will happen in the just then living, is counted for a resurrection.

The observation of Oecumenius is more subtle than solid. That 'we shall not all sleep' must be understood in this way, that we shall not sleep with a long sleep, so that there is need of a sepulcher and dissolution unto corruption, but they who are found then will endure a brief death.

For to sleep is not to be held by sleep, but to die. He sleeps according to the idiom of the scriptures, says Didymus of Alexandria, who is dead, in the hope of a future resurrection. See Hieron. Epist. 53, who brings forward another or alien explanation of this text: It is better to think spiritually of what is written, and not to take sleep in the present passage as death, by which the soul is separated from the body.

But sin after baptism, and the offense of GOD, and sleep after baptism, etc. For it is the sleep of sin, which leads to death, and there is another sleep of transgression, which is not bound by death, etc. Since therefore some do not sleep, who always live and watch in Christ, it follows that by no means do all sleep, and on the contrary all are changed, not by the change of glory, which is properly owed to the saints, but by that commutation, by which this corruptible is rendered incorruptible, so that it may receive either eternal punishments or rewards, etc.

But that there is no need for this gloss, the things said above show. But what Jerome, preferring the Latin Vulgate, urges with Didymus against the Greek text: It must be considered whether what follows can agree with what was premised, 'we shall all be changed.' The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

For if we shall all be changed, and this is common with the others, it was superfluous to say: And we shall be changed. Wherefore it must be read thus: We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed. For if in Adam all die, and in death there is sleep, therefore we shall all sleep, or we shall die: This moves us little. For it is not superfluous, but the Apostle is already speaking particularly of those who will be survivors on the last day, in the twinkling of an eye, and the dead shall rise, and we (namely, those existing alive) shall be changed.

That 'we,' says Chrysostom, he does not say of himself, but of those who will then be found living. Socinians weave a rope from sand, when from this ἀλλαγῇ (change) they gather a substantial diversity of the resurrected bodies, because not only a substantial, but also an accidental ἀλλαγῇ is given, and this is described by qualities, and by induction, which changes nothing in substance, but change is one thing, and destruction is another, says Tertullian lib. De Resurr.

Mort. ch. 55. For to have perished is in total not to be, what one had been; to have been changed is to be otherwise. Moreover, while it is otherwise, it can be the same being. For it has a being, which does not perish. Verf. 52. ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ σάλπιγγι (in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet).

This must be brought to the next thing which preceded. He says that this change of the corruptible body into an immortal body will be so sudden that the time cannot be perceived. ἐν ἀτόμῳ (in a moment), the same as elsewhere ἐν στιγμῇ (in a point), Ef. 29. 5. ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ (in the twinkling of an eye) among the Rabbis. רגע עין (twinkling of an eye) Syrus here, that ἐν ἀτόμῳ even the Philosophers use, the other, in the twinkling of an eye, many nations.

In the last trumpet, that is, at the sound of the last trumpet: or at the last signal, such as is accustomed to be given by a trumpet in the military.

Salientes γὰρ (For they shall leap). For it will give a signal.

See Matt. 24. 31 where these things are said, and 1 Thess. 5. 16.

The mystical sense of the passage Zech. 9. 14. Καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται (And the dead shall rise). Καὶ (And) here denotes then.

In the Manuscript for ἐγερθήσονται (shall rise) is ἀναστήσονται (shall stand up). Ἄφθαρτοι (Incorruptible).

See above 50. That which is said in 1 Thess. 4: The dead, who are in Christ shall rise first, then we, who are living, shall be caught up together with them, etc., does not conflict with this passage.

For although all, as well the living as the dead, having been resurrected (which resurrection, as far as the conjunction of the soul with the body is concerned, will happen in an instant) will be changed together, and that in a moment, nevertheless the resurrection of the dead precedes, the rapture of all to meet the Lord will follow. Theodore of Heraclea in Comm. apud Jerome in Epist. ad Minor. & Alexand. Tom. 3. n. 152. They who shall have risen from the dead, and shall have been caught up living into the clouds, shall pass to incorruption, and shall be changed from mortality into immortality, not in time, not even in a brief space, but in an atom, in a point of time, and a moment, in which the eyelid can be moved, at the last trumpet. For with such speed will the resurrection of the dead happen, that the living, whom the time of consummation shall have found in their bodies, shall not be able to forestall the dead rising from the underworld, namely, in the rapture to meet the Lord, as Apollinaris and Diodorus explain in the same place (apud Jerome).

Anselm: The dead, in Christ shall rise πρῶτον (first), before namely they are caught up to meet Christ in the air, then we, who are living, together with them, who shall have risen from the dead, shall be caught up to meet Christ. For the order is placed here not of those rising, nor of the resurrection to the resurrection, but the order of the resurrection to the rapture and meeting of the Lord, namely, that those first, who were dead, shall rise, then that the same with others then living shall be caught up together to meet Christ, as B.

Gerardus has in De Resurr. Mortuorum §. 120. As to the last trumpet, which is called the trumpet of the Angels, Matt. 24. 31, the trumpet of GOD 2 Thess. 4. 16, and with the added voice of the Archangel.

Theophylact by it wishes nothing else to be understood than the nod of GOD. By the trumpet, he says, than which there will be none at all in the future judgment of GOD, he makes manifest the nod and command, which is about to reach all. Gregory the Great, as also Flacius, by the trumpet understand the voice and command of Christ, by which he will call the dead, John 5. 28. Others however distinguish the trumpet from the voice, because that is of the Son of GOD, this is attributed to the Angels, and the Apostle joins the voice of the Archangel and the trumpet of GOD, he does not hold them for the same.

In which opinion B. Gerardus brings forward many arguments §. 66.

He leaves the matter in the middle, however, which is better than to contend idly about these things, not expressly defined, with the Scholastics, (ad diffin. 43. lib. 4. sentent.) or even to ask ineptly whether that trumpet is to be made of silver or brass, or of cloud and meteors.

Let us rather be solicitous, that we may hear the trumpet of the Archangel with hilarity. than we should discuss with rashness.

Our B. Hunnius explains the trumpet of GOD through the voice of the thundering Almighty GOD: But he compares it with that sonorous trumpet, which sounded from Mount Sinai in the promulgation of the law, at whose force the earth trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were shaken, which he says was nothing else than that horrible and unheard-of tempest, in which the Lord willed to promulgate his law. And he judges that the last trumpet will be the last tempest, by whose majesty and power not only will the elements in the sublunary region melt away, but the very hinges and columns of the heavens will be shaken in an inexplicable manner, until by the final lightning of all, this machine of the created world, utterly overturned, shall fall, and the heavens, with an incredible crash, shall pass away in the manner of a storm.

But as we have said, it is better here to choose the τὸ ἐπέχειν. That οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται ἄφθαρτοι, most understand of the elect only, and of their incorruption, and not inconveniently, because the Apostle treated of this by design, and this also will happen in one moment with the transformation of the living, nor are those things which follow in verses 53 and 54 to be understood otherwise, because death will be swallowed up into victory as regards the elect, and theirs alone will be the victory, and the epinicion, which is sung here.

Acacius, Bishop of Caesarea, in the IV. συλλεκτῶν ζητημάτων apud Hieronym. epist. 152, says that the transformation is glorification, and proper to the saints: But that incorruption is the communion of all, because in it sinners will be more miserable, so that they may be perpetual for torments, and not be dissolved in a mortal and corruptible body.

And thus Didymus in the same place says that incorruption is of all who rise again, but glory and transformation are properly of the saints. But although these things can be distinguished thus (if transformation into glory be understood: For the wicked also who are living are seen to be transformed, but to ignominy, not to glory), yet here it is treated properly only of the resurrection of the elect. Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα.

Namely, those whom God shall find living there, among whom Paul thought it possible that he himself might be, and many others who were living with him.

Thus Paul said ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες concerning the same matter in 1 Thess. IV. v. 17. It happens for this reason, because Christ had revealed nothing to his own concerning the last day, when it would be, so that it might always be expected. And the Apostles and those who followed them were closer to the Christians, so as to believe that it would happen shortly. See, if you please, what we have noted on this matter in the III. book on the truth of the Christian religion, and in the Appendix to our work on the Antichrist.

That the Apostle thought this, must not be said. For he wrote by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, and he rightly understood the things which he wrote: nay, in the later epistle to the Thessalonians, he refuted those who, from the former epistle, concluded that the day of the Lord was near. Therefore Theophylact is more correct: Paul by no means asserts this of himself, but of those who will then be survivors and will be acting in human affairs.

The Apostle speaks, as above, in the person of the just and the elect, whom the coming of the Lord will find living: just as he speaks, and indeed more expressly, in 1 Thess.

IV, saying: We who are living, who are left unto the coming of the Lord, shall not prevent those who have fallen asleep. And again: Then we who are living, who are left, shall be caught up together with them, etc., as Estius here. Which is to be noted against Salmeron, who rashly and against the manifest text denies that Paul, either here or in 1 Thess. IV, is dealing with those who will be living at the coming of the Lord, as above of the just and the elect, whom the coming of the Lord will find living. Therefore St. Augustine, l. XX. de civitate DEI cap. 10, says that the Apostle transfigured the person of those whom Christ is to find living here, into himself and others who were then living with him. Vers. 53.

Δεῖ γὰρ τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν. Tertullian in his book on the resurrection of the flesh explains this passage thus: For it behooves this corruptible to put on incorruptibility.

This will be that dwelling from heaven, which we, groaning in this flesh, desire to put on over the flesh in which we shall be found: because he says that we who are in the tabernacle are burdened, not that we wish to be unclothed, but rather to be clothed upon, that the mortal may be swallowed up, happy from life, while that which is from heaven is changed by being clothed upon. For what will he not desire, while he is in the flesh, to put on immortality and to continue life, to gain by death through a blessed transformation, etc.

Again in the same book: For it behooves this corruptible to put on incorruption and this mortal to put on immortality: What is mortal, if not flesh? What is corruptible, if not blood? But do not think that the Apostle is still feeling, providing for you and that you may understand it as said of the flesh, laboring.

When he says this corruptible and this mortal, he could not have pronounced the skin itself. It is a word of bodily demonstration.

And against Marcion thus: For it behooves this corruptible, holding its own flesh, said the Apostle. Justin has a fatherland [citation] to the Symbol.

Plutarch to Brutus concerning Exfare: Τῇ χειρὶ τὸ σῶμα, ἀυτόματον εἶπε τὶν ἐξ ὧν ἁμὶν δοκεῖ. Βρεῖν, ἀμύναι τινὶ τὸ σάκιον; Ἐνδύσασθαι is valid, חלש, which the Hebrews use when it is treated of an immortal body. Καὶ τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν. A mortal body can also be that which does not die.

The Apostle does not speak only of those whom he said were to be changed while living, as Estius wishes, but in general of the bodies that are to enter into glory, even if he entirely includes those living, because in them this mortal and corruptible body must also put on incorruption and immortality, even if properly neither dead nor corrupted, but mortality is to be swallowed up by life.

Crellius indeed, τῇ ὑποθέσει δέλευων, in 1 ad Corinth. XV. v. wishes that Paul here looks especially to those who are survivors at the coming of the Lord, and to the dead, not except consequently and less properly. But the assertion of Paul is contrary, and from these demonstrative pronouns, τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο, τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο, they are rightly urged, who deny that the same body in number will rise again, which is also done by the Socinians.

Note, says Theophylact, that these things are brought forward against those who assert that the bodies which will rise again are not the same ones that were in this life, but certain others.

For the Apostle says, this corruptible, and this mortal, not some other thing, but designates this body alone, whereby it happens that the body indeed remains the same, but not that which is put on. But mortality and corruption are removed by immortality and incorruption prevailing. But corruption differs from mortality, since mortality falls only upon that which is animated, but corruption even upon those things which lack a soul: Nor does the word of putting on any less refer to the substance, which is to be put on with some novelty, the identity.

Therefore also they are said to be clothed upon, who will be found living on the last day, 1 Cor.

V. 4. For he, Crellius admitting l. c., is only clothed upon, who is already another like a garment, he is clothed upon not indeed with another body (for, as Crellius again admits, it cannot happen that a man is simultaneously and constantly endowed with two bodies) but with immortality: Because τὸ θνητὸν, or the mortal, must put on immortality.

But it is a fiction, not the sentiment of the Holy Spirit, which Crellius brings forward here at length.

Thus indeed (he says) this clothing upon will happen, so that this celestial body may descend to the faithful themselves, while they are still dwelling in this lower air, yet already beginning to be carried on high, and may embrace their mortal bodies, and by that reason the faithful themselves may be clothed upon as with a new garment, cast over the old.

But because that incorruptible body cannot consist together with the corruptible, and cannot receive our spirit: it will consume it by its own hidden virtue, yet entirely heavenly and admirable, in a moment and in the twinkling of an eye, and will reduce this mortal body as it were to nothing, no otherwise than if it were endowed with a certain fiery force, and would absorb our body more quickly than a moment. But having dismissed such figments, Jerome in his epistle to Marcellus rightly teaches from that place what the bodies of the resurrected dead will be, that the bodies of the living will also be transmuted into such a substance, we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, that this mortal may be swallowed up by life, so that the body is not forsaken by the soul, but the soul, dwelling in the body, becomes glorious, which before was inglorious.

Rufinus in his exposition of the Symbol has it thus: This, which is now a corruptible body, will be incorruptible by the grace of the resurrection, and that which is now mortal will be clothed with the virtues of immortality, not by the nature of the flesh being cast away, but by its condition and quality being changed.

But above all, Theophylact is to be heard here in 2 Cor. V.
