Since it appeared harsher and grave, what he had said, that we groan and take it heavily, being desirous to be freed from this body, when it is established that the affection of the mind toward the body is ineffable, therefore he says: We do not groan for this reason, that we are simply to depart from the body, but because the desire has seized us to be clothed upon with incorruption, just as if it were not enough to be clothed with this, or we wish to be empty of corruption, so that it is not consumed and perishes as a body from life.

Nor are we burdened only for the sake of the body, but because it becomes corruptible, we take it heavily. Hence the mouths of the Heretics are obstructed, since no mention is made here of the diversity of bodies, when it is discussed only concerning corruptibility and incorruptibility.

Add that the Apostle brings forward only the mutation, and not the total destruction of this mortal body.

Where indeed Crellius (in 1 Cor. XV. p. 250 of the separate edition) says that the mutation consists in this, that other bodies will be substituted in the place of others.

But it is one thing entirely to be a mutation of a thing, and another to be a surrogacy or substitution of another in the place of the same. Which Crellius himself ought to have acknowledged, writing on this place: It had been said of all the faithful, that they were to be changed in a moment, and so also those who rise again. But if you look at the common manner of speaking, it is not so properly called a mutation, when he who had already ceased to be, and that even long ago, afterwards becomes another than he had been before he ceased to be.

But they are more properly said to be changed, who, while they still exist in reality, begin to be others than they were a little before, or put on another body.

Vers. 54. Τότε γενήσεται ὁ λόγος ὁ γεγραμμένος. Λόγος the thing itself. Then shall come to pass that which is written.

This is wont to be said when the words of the Prophets are drawn into a more eminent sense.

The place is Is. XXV. 8. We deny that the words are drawn into a more eminent sense.

For the literal and proper sense obtains.

Nor is there need that we refer all the words to Is. XXV, or that we betake ourselves with Cornelius to the place of Hos. XIII, from which the following things are rather taken. Κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος. בִּלַע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח which the LXX indeed translate as κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος. בִּלַע is very often translated as εἰς νῖκος according to etymology, as 2 Sam.

II. 26, Jer. III. ver. 5, Lam.

V. 20, Amos I. 11, VIII. 7, Prov. XXI. 28, where Symmachus, Aquila, Theodotion, all translate as εἰς νῖκος. But the sense is: forever.

And so it is translated as εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, εἰς νῖκος , Is. XIII. 20, and the Chaldean often translates as לְעָלַם

we have been vindicated and asserted into liberty; this is not of human virtue, not of human dignity or merit, but the benefit of one and only God. He is the one who has bestowed that illustrious and everlasting victory, and that through Christ Jesus our Lord, who blotted out sin with his blood, consumed death by his death, and cut down and destroyed hell by his descent to the dead, as the blessed Hunnius holds here. The struggle, says Theophylact, is the Lord's; he waged it. But the victory has been conferred upon us, by no vicissitude of our own benefits, but through the clemency of God the Father, who made us superior through the most intense work of the Son. Moreover, not only habitual sin or the custom of sinning and voluntary sin, but any sin whatsoever is the sting of death, and brings condemnation, as we have elsewhere proven against the Socinians. This sentiment contains a tacit proof of the resurrection of the dead, and a most firm one at that. For if victory over sin and death is given to us through Christ, then just as sin, so also death must at length be utterly destroyed. But death is not destroyed unless life is restored, and that perpetual: which does not happen except through the resurrection promised to the just, as Eftius holds here.

PART IV. PARENETIC, ON PERSEVERANCE IN FAITH. Ver. 58. ὥστε Therefore. For it is a note of inference, as above III. 21. IV. 5. XIV. 20. ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε, ἀμετακίνητοι. He said the same thing twice, to show that great constancy is required in performing one's duty. Thus τετραγωνισμένοι, ἰδέαοι .

See also above VII. 37. and Abac. II. 3. 4. Simonides calls a good man χερσίν τε καὶ ποσὶ καὶ νόῳ τετράγωνον. Περισσεύοντες ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ τοῦ Κυρίου πάντοτε. Doing all things that are pleasing to God abundantly, even more than anyone might dare to demand, as Paul does, announcing the Gospel at his own expense. He exhorts primarily to constancy in faith, according to the norm of the Gospel which they had received; and thus also in the faith of the resurrection of the dead, without which all faith in Christ is void.

Nor is it that we should hold these for the same things, which the blessed Hunnius more rightly distinguishes: He warns, he says, that by the expectation of the blessed resurrection, they may be stable in faith of perpetual victory, founded indeed upon the one rock of salvation, Jesus Christ: Let them be immovable in hope, lest they allow themselves to be moved by any storms of adversity from the hope demonstrated in the word of the Lord: Let them be abundant in the work of the Lord, progressing in piety, and prepared for every good work. Εἰδότες, ὅτι ὁ κόπος ὑμῶν οὐκ ἔστι κενὸς ἐν Κυρίῳ Αἰτιῶς.

For he wishes to say that the rewards of labor will be great. ὁ κόπος ἐν Κυρίῳ is labor according to the Lord, according to Christ's precept.

He has well woven this admonition with the discourse on the resurrection. For if the dogma of the resurrection is true, no labor ought to seem burdensome. For what is sweeter than life, and that immortal and most blessed? He assigns therefore the reason, taken from the article of the resurrection, already explained, and drawn from the fountain of utility, because indeed our labor, undertaken in the Lord and proceeding from faith, will by no means be futurely void or empty, but will one day have an inestimable retribution and compensation in eternal life, as the blessed Hunnius says here again. The words in the Lord do not refer to κόπον labor, as Oecumenius does by hyperbaton with Grotius, although he explains it as labor undertaken for the Lord's sake, but to the word κενὸς empty, as was also done by Theophylact: But he contributed in the Lord, either because we then labor in the Lord when we receive help from above and from heaven, which usually happens freely from God for works: Or because any labor expended will not be in vain through him, but rather from the same he is about to receive rewards. It seems that hyperbaton should not be admitted without necessity.

PART IV. OF THE EPISTLE. CONCLUDING PORTION. ON THE COLLECTION, AND CERTAIN PRIVATE EXHORTATIONS. AND SALUTATIONS. CHAPTER XVI. ARGUMENT & DIVISION. He commands that on every sabbath each one deposit something for the saints; he promises that he will convey the collections to Jerusalem either through others or even with others; that he will come to the Corinthians when he passes through Macedonia, and there perhaps will spend the winter; but now at Ephesus, where a great door has been opened to him, he will remain until Pentecost. He commends Timothy to them, & promises the coming of Apollos: admonishing them to vigilance & constancy in faith, & to the charity and service of the house of Stephanas and of other fellow-workers (συνεργῶν). He greets them in the name of others, & in his own, & concludes the epistle with a warning of anathema upon him who does not love JESUS, and with a vow. The parts are IV. I. Admonition concerning the collection, to v. 4. II. Promise of his own coming, of Timothy's, & of Apollos's, to v. 12. III. Exhortation to vigilance & constancy, & to the honor to be rendered to those who serve them, to v. 18. IV. Salutation made in the name of others & his own, together with a final warning & vow, to v. 24. PART I. Admonition concerning the Collection.

Latin:

V. 14. & supra 22. Factus est homo in animam viventem, id est, factus est vivens animal.

Et enim abstractum pro concreto. Animalium est vivere ad tempus.

ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδὰμ. Christus. Εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν.

Factus est per resurrectionem & evectionem in coelum homo plane divinus, qui potestatem habeat etiam aliis dandi vitam & quidem aeternam, Joh. VI. 33. 40. 47. 50. 57. fur pra 22.

In Adam fuit ἐπὶπνεύματος quaedam ad vivendum. In Christo autem ἐπίγνωσις, ait Cyrillus. Sensus est: Ut per insufflationem spiraculi vitae homo primus factus est in animam viventem, vita animae communicata corpori verè ac realiter, unde vi unionis naturalis animae & corporis, è luto formati corpus verè vivum prodiit: Ita secundus Adam per Filii DEI ἐπίληψιν, & naturae divinae communicationem, factus est in spiritum vivificantem, vita spirituali & δυνάμει ζωοποιητικῇ, virtute vivificante, verè ac realiter humanae Christi naturae communicata, ut inde illa serè sit vivifica, ac virtute spirituali vivificandi praedita, & causa vitae aeternae ac beatae nobis fit secundus homo, ut in ipso omnes vivificemur, quemadmodum v. 22. docuit Apostolus.

Non autem hic Christus spiritus vivificans dicitur, ratione divina natura, quod Beza vult, quia non in casu recto Filius DEI dicitur Spiritus vivificans, quod convenit Filio DEI κατ' αὐτὸ, & ὀσιωδῶς vel essentialiter, sed novissime Adam dicitur FACTUS in spiritum vivificantem, quod convenit Christo homini, secundum humanam naturam, vi unionis, & communicationis hypostaticae, vel ἀλλ' ἄλλο, quia humana natura unita est λόγῳ, seu spiritui vivificanti, hoc est divinae naturae, eique communicata est ejusdem divina vis vivificandi, sicut Pater vitam habet in semetipso, Job. V. 25. ὅτι quia vel quatenus Filius hominis, quod aditur v. 27. quemadmodum etiam ei dedit potestatem resuscitandi mortuos ad vitam, & faciendi judicium, ut ibidem docetur.

Quo de Cyrillus lib. 2. in Johannem c. 14. Nolue mirari, si, cum me hominem esse videatis, resuscitaturum tamen mortuos me pollicear, & in judicium deducturum. Dedit enim mihi vivificandi virtutem Pater, dedit judicandi potestatem. Quapropter causam, quare hac sibi à Patre dato dixerit, illico subjecit, dicens: Quia Filius hominis est, ut intelligamus, omnia ipsi data, ut homini, qui cum creatura sit, nihil habet à seipso, unigenitus vero Filius, non vitae particeps, sed vita naturaliter, ut Pater est.

Et libro III. in Johannem cap. 21.

Natura carnis ipsa per SE vivificare non potest. Quid enim majus natura Deitatis haberet? Quando igitur vivificam suam carnem Christus appellat, non ita illi, ut sibi, sive proprio Spiritui, vim vivificandi attribuit. NAM PROPTER SEIPSUM Spiritus vivificat, ad cujus VIRTUTEM caro per conjunctio nem conscendit. Quomodo autem id fiat, nec mento intelligere, nec lingua eloqui possumus, sed silentio & firma fide id recipimus.

Non ergo novissimus Adam demum per resurrectionem & evectionem in coelum factus est in Spiritum vivificantem, sed per unionem & communicationem hypostaticam. Ut primus Adam in prima statim creatione factus est in animam viventem, ita secundus Adam in conceptione prima, cum virtus Altissimi suscepit massam corpoream in utero virginali, factus est in spiritum vivificantem. Nam ut pii veteres dixerunt: ἅμα σὰρξ, ἅμα Θεοῦ λόγῳ σάρξ. Resurrectione enim non mutata est natura humana, aut anima Christi in Spiritum immutabilem, quod commentum fovere hic videtur Grotius, nec Christus per evectionem in coelum, quod Sociniani fingunt, quibus ipsum accedere apparet, deposuit veritatem corporis humanae, & in spiritum transsubstantiatus, aut corpore exuto spiritus factus est totus: Sed quod semel Filius DEI assumsit, in aeternum non deponit.

Neque id ita accipiendum cum Eflio, quod in resurrectione susceperit spiritus ejus, absque subsidio alimenti, perpetuam vitam corpori subministrare. Ascendit Apostolus ad ipsam causam nostrae gloriae, quam corporis ratione consequuturi sumus, & imprimis quale hoc fit, quod non tantum corpus incorruptibile in gloria, & in virtute non corruptibili, ptibili, quale ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ καὶ ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ hic feritur, quale post lapsum habuit Adam, resurrecturum fit, sed etiam corpus πνευματικὸν vel spirituale, non verò ψυχικὸν animale, non quale ante lapsum primus homo habuit, & accepit, cum in animam viventem factus est, sed longè præstantiorum qualitatum: quod scilicet alteri Adamo, hoc accepto ferendum fit, qui, factus in spiritum vivificantem nostri gratia, nos vivificaturus est, v. 22. per cujus carnem vivificam nos habemus vitam & salutem, cùm ratione meriti, tùm ratione efficaciæ. Idem enim δυνάμει ζωοποιικῇ ditatus est, ut nos per meritum obedientiæ suæ, activa & passiva, morte liberare, & vitam nobis promereri posset, Job. VI. 33. 50. 51. 54. Quo de Cyrillus in defens. anathem. XI. contra Orientales: Quia autem vita secundum naturam est verbum, quod ex Patre est, vivificatricem efficit carnem suam. Et porro: Quoniam autem est corpus vita, vivificum est. Propterea namque mortalibus nostris corporibus largitur vitam, & mortis imperium evacuat. v. 46. Ἀλλ' οὐ πρῶτον πνευματικόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικόν, ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν.

Nempe corpus, quod subaudiendum ex superiori v. 44. Promisit DEUS imperfectiora, ut perfectiora sequerentur.

Sic ante pueri sumus, quàm viri. Sic prius lex, deinde Evangelium. Prius cœlum & terra, quæ cernimus, posterius cœlum & terra, id est, universum multò pulchrius.

Theophylactus hic: Ne quis forte quærat; Cur ergo corpore hoc animali, quod deterius est, nunc ipsi potimur, spirituali vero, quod satius est, potitur? Respondet utriusque principia sic fuisse disposita: Adam primò, postremo Christum. Ita fit, ut in melius provehantur res nostræ. August. in Ench. cap. 91. Sicut nunc corpus animale dicitur, quod semen corpus, non anima est: Ita nunc spiritua. le corpus erit, corpus tamen, non spiritus erit. Irenæus adversus hæref. lib. V. cap. 10. Corpora no- stra in hac vita sunt animalia, id est, participantia animam, quam cum amiserint, mortificantur: deinde per Spiritum surgentia fiunt corpora spiritua- lia, aut per Spiritum semper manentem habeant vitam. v. 47. Ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς, χοϊκός. Dixit de anima & Spiritu. Nunc de corpore loquitur. χοϊκός, limaceus Tertulliano, ex limo, in Latino Irenæi V. 11. Respicit illud Gen. II. 7. ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον χοῦν λαβών. Hebræum est עפר quod habes & Gen. III. 19. Significat autem quamvis terræ particulam. Philo: Ἀνθρώπινον γένη. Ὁ μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἐκ γῆς, ὁ δὲ γήϊνος. ὁ δὲ γήϊνος. ὁ ἐκ γῆς ἐστιν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ· ἄτε καὶ εἰκόνα Θεοῦ γεγονώς, φθαρτῆς καὶ συνόλου γενέσεως ἀμέτοχος. Ὁ δὲ γήϊνος ἐκ σποράδος ὕλης ἧς χοῦν κέκληκεν, ἐπάγη. Theophilus, ube dendemptus est Adam interpretatur ὁ τῆς ξηρᾶς, ἀλλὰ τῆς πολυμεροῦς καὶ ποι- κίλης ὕλης μέρος.

Non de anima & Spiritu tantùm dixit Apostolus, sed imprimis de corpore, eoque tùm animali, tùm spirituali, etsi animale ab animæ viventis inspiratione, spirituale a vivifica virtute spirituali humanæ Christi naturæ originem trahere docuerit. Illud enim habemus ab Adamo primo, vi naturalis generationis, hoc a secundo virtute spiritualis regenerationis consequemur, in beata παλιγγενεσία, Mattb. XIX. 28. Ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος, ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. Hic ἐξ οὐρανοῦ dicitur Hebræo more pro οὐράνιος, id est, cœlestis, habens jam corpus cœleste. v. 48. Οἷος ὁ χοϊκός, τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ χοϊκοί. Quale corpus Adamus habuit, tale & sevit in posteros, in Adami persona genus humanum describitur. Origenes contra Celsum IV. Καὶ οἷος ὁ ἐπουράνιος, τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ ἐπουράνιοι. Sic & Christus, qui nos regenuit, nobis corpus dabit suo simile. Cum autem dixit ἐπουράνιοι, intelligi vult corpus fore dignum habitaculo supercœlesti. Vide Hebr. VI. 4. de voce ἐπουράνιον vide Eph. I. 3. Sedes III. in qua est DEI MAJESTAS & Angeli dicitur quidem cœlum, nimirum tertium excellentius cœteris, ideoque dictum שמי שמים & οὐρανοὶ, pluraliter. Sed id nec minus ἐπουράνιοι supercœlestis, respectu habato ad cœlum spectabile. Origenes Philocalia XVIII. πῶς ὁ δυνατὸν καὶ τὴν σάρκα τὰ ἰντὰ ἀμείψασαι ποιότητας γεγονέναι ταύτην ὁ ποῖος ἔχειν, ὡς τὰ οὐράνια, καὶ τὰς αὐτῶν ἀντὶ τόποις πολιτευομένη;

Non est quod discedamus ab usitata significatione vocis, ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, ἐ cœlo: neque corpus dicitur habere cœleste, sed κύριος Dominus esse è cœlo. Prædicatum ergò Dominus è cœlo, naturam ejus dividam exprimit.

Non enim de cœlo esse dicitur, aut dici potest, ratione carnis, ut Anabaptistæ & fanatici cum Valentin. & Apollinar. somniant; sed quia filius DEI propter nos, & nostram salutem de cœlo descendit, ut in Symbolo Niceno habetur. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit, Filius nempe hominis, Johan. III. 13. Ideoque secundus homo ob communicationem idiomatum DEUS de cœlo dicitur. Quo de Theophylactus: Neque propterea homo sive ipsa humanitatis assumptio, è cœlo esset, quemadmodum demens ille Apollinaris delirabat, sed quod una sit unius Christi persona. Et homo de cœlo esse propter unitatem dicitur, & DEUS fuisse eandem ob causam crucifixus asseritur. Causa itaque redditur, cur ὁ πρῶτον τὸ πνευματικὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικὸν, quia ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ideoque corpus non prius spirituale, sed animale fuerit, quia primus homo, è terra productus ratione originis, adeoque terrenus fuerit, ratione natura & constitutionis terrenæ, & affectionum terreno corpori convenientium: Nondum verò spiritualis, & cœlestis. Vice versa ratio etiam reddita, unde spirituale corpus fit? Quia secundus homo non ex terra & terrenus tantùm est, uti primus erat: Non est merus homo, sed verus DEUS, quum ratione naturæ fit ὁ κύριος, JEHOVAH, (quod essentiale nomen redditur per vocem κυρίος) divinæ essentiæ, ratione ortus divini, è cœlo; quia venerit ex sinu Patris cœlestis, ut μονογενὴς παρὰ Πατρὸς Job. I. 12. Filius ab æterno à Patre genitus, qui de cœlo descendit, & ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, λόγῳ ἐνεσαρκωθείς. Quid è supernis venit, Job. I. 14. 15. cap. III. 16. & 13. Quum in cœlis sit, è cœlo descendit, Johan. I. 31. à Patre exiit, & in mundum venit Johan. XVI. 28. Nam uti primus homo, utpote è terra ortus, & terrenæ naturæ & conditionis, primùm in animam viventem, moretreno, factus est: Ita secundus homo non in animam modo viventem factus est, sed etiam in spiritum vivificantem, quia non fuit solùm è terra, sed etiam è cœlo, non ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, sed κύριος. Dicitur autem primus homo de terra terrenus, non ob mortalitatem, vel quod in terram resolva- tur corpus ejus, quia de terra est. Nam post lapsum hoc demum ipsi dictum, & ad pœnas peccati pertinet: Termes, & in terram converteris, hîc verò respicit Adam partim ratione ortus, quia de terræ limo formatus est ante peccatum, partim ratione status, quia in terra constitutus terrenis affectionibus obnoxius fuit, quemadmodum & corpus animale ipsi tributum, non ratione peccati aut corruptibilitatis, sed ratione conditionis, & actionum ad hanc vitam terrenam pertinentium, cui scilicet vitam, sensum ac motum, more huic temporali statui conveniente, præstat anima, ad quem opus est refectione, humidi radicalis conservatione, cibo, ac potu. Non ergo opponitur hoc loco corpus terrenum animale corpori im-morali & incorruptibili, sed cœlesti & spirituali, quod non amplius affectionibus hujus vitæ propriis, sed cœlestibus & spiritualibus dotibus instructum erit, ideoque cibo & potu, concoctione, refectione &c. opus non habebit.

ὁ κύριος, verus natura Deus. Neque enim, ut Cyrillus habet in epistola ad Nestor. carnem humanam Christi naturam ut carnem communem suscipiamus, absit hoc: neque rursum tanquam viri cujuspiam sanctificati, aut dignitatis tantum aequalitate VERBO consociati, aut divinam inhabitationem fortiti, sed tanquam VERE VIVIFICAM, ipsius VERBI propriam. Nam cum VITA fit, ut Deus secundum naturam, simul atque unum quoddam (VERBUM) cum ipsa sua carne effectum est, mox vivificandi virtutem ipsi contulit. Haec ergo de Christo, ceu causa nostrae vivificationis & gloriosae resurrectionis, quae in corpore non animali; sed spirituali, ratione affectionum & qualitatum, futura est, in συγγένειες cum Adamo, à quo accipimus corpus non spirituale, sed animale. Jam rationem consequentiae reddit. Qualis enim terrenus est, à quo ortum trahimus per naturalem generationem, tales & nos terreni sumus. Si ille corpus habuit animale, & terrenum, etiam nos tale habemus: utpote ejusdem cum illo originis, ejusdem naturae, constitutionis & affectionis. Rursus qualis est ὁ ἐπουράνιος, à quo ortum trahimus per spiritualem regenerationem, tales etiam nos sumus οἱ ἐπουράνιοι, qui illi similes sumus non per naturam, sed per gratiam: Tum quoad originem e supernis, quia ἄνωθεν renati, tum quoad communionem spiritualem, quia θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως . ideoque ut ipse post resurrectionem habuit non corpus animale & terrenum amplius, quantum ad qualitates, sed corpus spirituale & caeleste, ita etiam nos tale corpus habituri sumus, cum μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸ σύμμορson τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτῦ .

Phil. III. 21. Non ergo admittenda Crellii ψευδερμηνεία , cui Grotiana affinis est in explic. 1. Cor. XV. quod in verbis illis, secundus homo Dominus ex caelo, non de Deitate Christi, sed de natura corporis, quod Christus nunc habeat & nos aliquando habituri sumus, sermo fit. Nam in versu demum sequenti de natura vel potius qualitate corporis agitur, tum Christi, tum fidelium Christi, in verbis autem istis nihil de corpore Christi, ejusque natura habetur, nedum electorum. Ideoque Crellius cum Mustulo Calviniano suspicari mavult, vocem ὁ κύριος librariorum incuria esse repositam, pro οὐράνιος, ut naturam corporis respici obtineat, quod materia quidem corporis Christi verbis ex caelo: Natura autem, materiae consentanea, voce caelestis exprimitur. Quod vero quo loco habendum sit, vel inde patet, quod Crellius ipse non ausus sit, sine exemplarium fide, conjectura sua niti, & veritatem lectionis Graecae agnoscat. Naturam autem corporis, dum & originis & substantiae ratione diversam, quae scil. ex caelo, vel corporibus caelestibus transsumpta fit, & naturam materiae caelesti consentaneam habeat, comminiscitur cum Socino suo Crellius, palam Apostolo contradicit. Qui non de οὐσία vel substantia corporis loquitur, sed de ποιότητι vel qualitate. Ποίω δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται v. 35. & hic v. 48. διον & τοῖτοι. Et corpus illud ταπεινώσεως idem facit, quod substantiam, cum τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης, solum μετασχηματισμῷ transformationis alicujus qualitatum diversitatem admittens, qua è statu ταπεινώσεως idem illud corpus ad statum τῆς δόξης evehetur: Quomodo hic paulo post dicturus est, τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο hoc ipsum corruptibile, (non aliud corpus) induturum ἀφθαρσίαν incorruptibilitatem, & τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο, hoc ipsum mortale (corpus) induturum ἀθανασίαν immortalitatem, v. 53. Neque unquam deposuit Christus corpus, quod semel assumpsit, quod a Spiritu Sancto conceptum est in Maria & obumbratum virtute Altissimi; sed in eodem corpore passus & sepultus, resurrexit, ascendit in caelum, sedet ad dextram DEI; visus est Stephano & Paulo, venturus est ad judicium conspiciendus ab iis, qui pupugerunt, & ab electis in caelo, ceu Filius hominis venturus in nubibus, & ut agnus occisus in medio throni, fine fine celebrandus in secula seculorum.

Nec substantiam corporis concernunt, sed qualitates, quas ipse Crellius affert, in explicanda naturae corporis caelestis & terreni differentia. Terrenum, inquit, crassum est, hoc caeleste, subtile: Illud durum ac intractabile; illud gratum, & ad motum in sublime per se ineptum; hoc nulli per se motui obnoxium, ad quemvis pro arbitrio Spiritus vitalis suscipiendum babilissimum: Illud se frigidum; hoc nullis ejusmodi vilibus qualitatibus preditum, vel obnoxium: Illud corruptibile, & dissipari facile; hoc incorruptibile, & integritatis suae tenacissimum, praesertim cum necesse sit, id qualitatem aliquam contra naturae suae impetum recipere, & formas aliquas pati suo ingenio repugnantes, quas excutere semper nitatur, quemadmodum terrena moles in corpore humano atque in universum in animali, sed si quid adhuc qualitatum imprimitur, id totum cum ejus natura egregie consentit, ait ut nunquam earum quicquam velit excutere. Haec, inquam, omnia qualitates diversas arguunt, non diversas substantias: Quum, manente eadem substantia, diversae istae qualitates locum habere possint. De sede, in qua corpora gloriosa futura sunt cum Angelis, cujusnam naturae fit, non constat, neque sedes, in qua DEI Majestas est, corpora fingenda est, etsi subtilissima, cum DEUS Spiritus infinitus fit, φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον , 1. Tim. VI. 16. quem caeli coelorum non capiunt. 1. Reg. VIII. Vers. 49. Καὶ καθὼς ἐφορέσαμεν τὴν εἰκόνα χοϊκοῦ. Corpus simile corpori Adami, & ob id morbis, malis & mortio obnoxium. Φορέσωμεν καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα τῦ ἐπουρανίυ. Φορέσωμεν habent alii Codices & sic legerunt Syrus, Arabs & sic citat Origenes contra Celsum: Corpus habebimus simile corpori Jesu, in suo tamen gradu.

Sic vox εἰκόνος sumitur Rom. VIII. 29. Haec jam ad reliqua attributa vel praedicata corporis animalis & terreni, ac spiritualis & caelestis differentias concernentia pertinent, utpote quod illi φθορά, ἀτιμία, ἀσθένεια affignata, huic vero ἀφθαρσία, δόξα, & δύναμις vers. 42. & 43. Nam illa non respiciunt amplius originem terrenam, & primigeniam conditionem corporis Adami, in statu ante peccatum, sed eam conditionem, quae ipsi & posteris ejus post lapsum conveniebat. Ante lapsum enim, etsi non ea fuerit incorruptibilitas vel gloria vel virtus, quae in altera vita expectatur, non tamen locum habebat corruptio, non ignominia, non infirmitas, sed haec consequentia sunt & poena peccati, unde morbi, mala quae vis, & mors originem traxere, Rom. V. 12. Sap. II. Imaginem ergo portamus terreni Adami, qualis ille erat post lapsum, quia non ad imaginem DEI, quae per lapsum deperdita, sed ad imaginem suam (quam per peccatum sibi conciliarat) genuit liberos, Gen. V. vers. 2. Portabimus autem imaginem caelestis (Adami, Christi, cum non modo ratione animae perfecte renovabimur ad imaginem DEI, quoad sapientiam & sanctitatem, ac justitiam, sed etiam ratione corporis, quoad incorruptibilitatem & immortalitatem, omnes ut peccati, ita & morbi ac mortis, quae consequentia peccati, prorsus expertes, & ἰσάγγελοι futuri, etiam ratione ἀφθαρσίας καὶ ἀθανασίας. Imago quidem, inquit Theod. Theophylactus, terreni, ut illud, quia est, & in cinerem reverteris: Imago autem caelestis est mortuorum resurrectio & incorruptibilitas ipsa: Ita ut tanquam de resurrectione, non de modo vivendi dicta haec fuisse intelligendum sit. Et illud portabimus imaginem caelestis, non consulentes esse dictum intelliges, sed rei futurae indicium, hoc est, quod caelestem sumus imaginem portaturi.

Unde reprobanda & Estii explicatio, quasi Apostolus doctrinae exhortationem intermisceat, admonens, ut sicut in nobis peccando exhibuimus imaginem, id est, expressam valde similitudinem terreni Adam, qui primus peccavit: Ita deinceps exhibeamus in nobis imaginem hominis caelestis, id est, Christi per sanctam conversionem, ac vitae novitatem eum imitantes, ut ad similem cum eo gloriam pervenire possimus. Nam perperam Vulgata legit PORTEMUS, cum in Futuro habeatur portabimus, ut Graecis Syra consonent, atque ita etiam interpretati sint, ut continuationem doctrinae de resurrectione. Graeci interpretes, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Methodius, Oecumenius, fatente Estio, qui Graecam lectionem non modo praecedentibus, sed etiam quae proxime sequuntur, convenire, agnoscit.

Sed hoc sequenti membro; Neque corruptio incorruptibilitatem possidebit, indicatur.

Unde ταυτολογία sic committeretur, si etiam in prioribus verbis homo, qua mortalis & corruptibilis, intelligatur; ne dicam, quod caro & sanguis etiam in homine ante lapsum fuerunt, qui vero tum mortalis & corruptibilis non fuit.

Quapropter alii carnem & sanguinem intelligunt, non Metonymice de operibus carnis, vel Metaphorice de carnis & sanguinis corruptis qualitatibus: Nec Synecdochice vel complexe, pro substantia cum qualitatibus suis, aut prout peccato corruptioni aut morti obnoxia est, sed de carne & sanguine simpliciter, vel prout hominis animali, vel in animam viventem facto, conveniunt: Quam sententiam Latinorum quorundam Patrum & Cajetani esse notat Estius, neque ea à mente Justiniani ipsiusque Estii, aliena esse videtur, ut nempe per carnem & sanguinem intelligatur, qualis est in vita animali, quae requirit usum ciborum, & procreationem filiorum.

Atque eo interpretatur quoque Theophylactus, quod in futuro seculo corpus hoc carne & sanguine non ita concretum futurum sit, ut potu & cibo opus habiturum sit, quo nutriatur.

Neq alio sensu negavit Augustinus, in resurrectione carnem & sanguinem fore, quod hic recte observatum Grotio.

Probat autem hanc interpretationem imprimis B.

Hülsemannus, per carnem & sanguinem hic non intelligi vitia, sed ipsam substantiam, non cum qualitatibus vitiosis, sed abstractis tantum qualitatibus vitiosis, hoc sensu: Tale corpus, quale Adam accepit, & nos ab eo, non possidebit regnum caelorum, sed longe gloriosius; miraturque, nec Vinarienses, nec Belgicos interpretes id animadvertisse.

Propositio, inquit ad v.

Apostoli, qua praesentem imperfectionem & futuram perfectionem corporis animalis, non quidem requirit, ut τὸ animale & pulvereum vers.

48. complexe cum adjunctis infirmitatibus, post lapsum contractis, intelligamus: Praesertim cum τὸ animale videatur sumpsisse secundum illam conditionem, cum qua homo primum conditus est, vers.

Sed sufficit, si animale & pulvereum sumatur praecise cum qualitatibus naturalibus, & exclusionibus axiomatum supernaturalium.

Vult enim Apostolus ostendere corpora nostra in coelis acquisitura esse conditionem longe meliorem, quam à prima creatione habuerunt, quomodo dubium non est, etiam Protoplastorum corpus, si maxime in congenita perfectione perstitissent, in statu glorificationis insignioribus axiomatibus fuisse donandum, quam in prima conditione accepissent, ac proinde nihil obesse, quo minus caro & sanguis v. 50. pure & praecise de substantia hominis, etiam protoplasti, circa respectum ad infirmitates, per lapsum contractas intelligatur, saltem sumatur circa respectum, sive cum exclusione donorum gloriae superaddendorum primae creationis qualitatibus.

Hoc enim intendit Apostolus demonstrare, quomodo etiam ante lapsum frumentum nascens ex terra, gloriosius surgebat, quam nudum granum insitum: Ita gloriam corporum nostrorum majorem etiam fore gloria corporis Adamitici protoplasti. Reprobanda autem omnino Socinianorum sententia, quod ipsa carnis & sanguinis substantia hic intelligatur, & à regno DEI excludatur, quae diametro adversa est sententiae Apostoli, utpote qui prolixe docet, corpus idem substantiae ratione, quod hic seminatur, resurrecturum, non vero aliud substantia diversum; & qualitatum tantum, non vero substantiae differentiam assignat, quod magno consensu Patres Graeci & Latini afferunt, & è textu ipso luculentissimum est. ARTICULUS II. DE TRANSMUTATIONE MORTUORUM ET VIVENTIUM INFORMATIO.

Vers. 51. ἰδὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω.

Rem hactenus vobis aliisque incognitam. Vide Rom. XI. 25. XVI. 25. supra II. 7. IV. 1. XIII. 2. XIV. 2. Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα. Variant hic libri. Optime Manuscriptus ille: οἱ πάντες οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα οὐ πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα. Neque omnes obdormiemus, id est, moriemur. Neque omnes mutabimur.

Veram hanc lectionem ostendunt sequentia. Eadem sententia in commentario ad libr. Aboth. LIII. 2. & notis ad caput I. Rabbini Israelis de anima. Eodem spectat locus Act. 42. & verba symboli. Ob unicum MS. cæteros codices dejicere minime conveniens est.

Nam optime sibi constat Græca lectio: Omnes quidem non dormiemus, (quia vivos nonnullos offendet dies Domini) omnes autem immutabimur, illi quidem, qui mortui sunt in resurrectione, corpus aliis qualitatibus præditum accipiendo: Hi vero, qui vivi erunt in adventu Domini, in ἰδὺ oculi ἀλλαγὴν subeundo, quia omnino oportet hoc corruptibile induere incorruptibilitatem. Quæ explicatio etiam Chrysostomi est hom. XLII. Venerandum quippiam & arcanum, & quod non omnes norunt est dicturus: Quod etiam ostendit magnum bonorem, quo eos afficit, nempe dicere arcana. Quid hoc autem est? Omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur. Hoc est autem, quod dicit, non omnes quidem moriemur, omnes autem immutabimur, etiam qui non moriuntur.

Nam illi quoque sunt mortales. Ne ergo, quoniam morieris, propterea, inquit, timeas, tanquam non resurrecturus. Sunt enim, sunt etiam aliqui, qui hoc effugient, & tamen hoc eis non sufficit ad illam resurrectionem, sed oportet illa quoque corpora, que non moriuntur, immutari, & transire ad incorruptionem. Non autem congruit lectio Vulgatæ, quæ nec in illis Græcis codicibus reperta, teste Hieronymo, nec hodie in ullis Græcis habetur, fatente Estio; Omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur, quia non resurgunt omnes, sed solum qui mortui sunt.

Ex adverso autem immutabuntur omnes, ut diximus. Proinde neque illa quorundam lectio consentanea est: Omnes quidem dormiemus, non autem omnes immutabimur, quam refert quidem Pelagius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, ut & Oecumenius, sed in paucis Latinis & Græcis Codibus repertam. Moderna autem usitata Græca lectio in Codicibus Græcis plerisque ut & in textu Syriaco & Arabico reperitur. Ea autem, quæ scripta est ad marginem Complutensium, & ex iis Regiorum: πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντες ἀλλαγησόμεθα, hoc est, omnes quidem igitur dormiemus, sed non omnes immutabimur, mutuo illo ἣν in ἣν, merito suspensa est, judice Estio. Nam post illa verba: Ecce mysterium vobis dico, nullo modo convenit ILLATIVUS sermo. omnes quidem IGITUR dormiemus.

Probatur etiam moderna lectio ex Acacii testimonio apud Hieron. quod plerique Codd. sic legerint, ex Origene in vol. 3. Epist. ad Thessal. & libr. advers. Marc. (apud Estium è Vaticano producto) adhuc ἀνεκδότῳ, Theodoro, & Apollinario, quos laudat Hieronymus, Justino, vel quisquis ille auctor sit, quæst. ad orthod. num. 61. & 107. Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, Basilio, Hieronymo, Epist. ad Marc. II. num. 148. Theophylacto, Oecumenio & aliis.

Quam vera & germana agnoscit Estius, probatque imprimis sex rationibus, quod hic de sola bonorum resurrectione agat Apostolus. Addit denique, quod facilior sit & proclivior mutatio Græcæ lectionis in Latinam, vel prima facie magis apparentem & verisimilem, quam contra lectionis Latinæ in Græcam. Qua contra Papalem infallibilitatem in Canonizanda Vulgata observanda.

Grotii lectio nusquam reperta ab aliis. Conferendum cum hoc loco, quod habetur 1. Thess. IV. 15. cui magis convenit Græca moderna lectio, quam Latina, ut & Act. X. 42. Rom. XIV. 9. 1. Petr. IV. 5. Vid. B. Gerh. de resurr. Mort. §. 116. seqq. Quod autem non omnes dicuntur obdormituri, de fidelibus plerique intelligunt, quorum mors somnus dicitur.

Non adstrinxit sermonem ad homines sui temporis, ac si innuat, imminere adventum Domini, quem sensum è similibus verbis 1. Thess. IV. acceptum corrigit Apostolus 2. Thess. II. sed comprehendit quoque electos postea futuros, & qui non obdormierant, adeoque sensus hic est verborum Apostoli: Non omnes electi dormient somno mortis, omnes tamen immutabuntur in statum beatæ immortalitatis, ita ut pro corpore animali spirituale, atque pro corruptibili incorruptibile consequantur.

At quomodo hæc consonant testimoniis universalibus de omnium hominum morte Rom. V. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 22. Ebr. IX. Resp. Omnes morituros dici sive quod DEUS sua virtute extincturus, ac vicissim excitaturus statim fit (Pontificiorum nonnullorum sententiam, quod per ignem mundi conflagratorium extinguendi, suo loco relinqui-mus, Augustinus. sane mundi conflagrationem posteriorem facit ipsa resurrectione) sive quod analogum quid morti & resurrectioni hic interveniat, quemadmodum in libro de Ecclesiast. dogm. c. 7. quem Gennadii presbyteri (non Augustini) esse nonnulli volunt, hoc à quibusdam explicari refertur: Locum integrum adscribere juvat: Omnium, inquit, erit resurrectio.

Si omnium erit, ergo omnes morientur, ut mors ab Adam ducta omnibus ejus filiis dominetur, & maneat illud privilegium Domino, quod de eo specialiter dicitur, non dabis sanctum tuum, videre corruptionem. Hanc rationem, maxima Patrum turba tradente, suscepimus. Verum quia sunt & alii æque Catholici, & eruditi viri, qui credunt, anima in corpore manente (hoc est, citra dissolutionem animæ & corporis, quæ est mors proprie dicta) immutandos ad incorruptionem & immortalitatem eos, qui in adventu Domini vivi invenientur, & hoc eis repuari pro resurrectione è mortuis, quod mortalitatem immutatione exponant, non morte, quilibet, qui acquiescat modo, non est hæreticus, nisi ex contentione hæreticus fiat. Hæc Gennadius.

Mors illis, inquit Theophylactus, est immutatio, moritur namque in piis corruptio, in innocentiam denique commutata. Aliorum suffragia affert Sparetz Tom. II. Comm. in part. 3. Thom. q. 56. Disp. 50. sect. 2. pag. 571. Hæc sententia (quæ negat illos homines justos, qui tempore judicii vixerint, esse aut morituros aut resuscitandos, sed solum immutandos, vel transformandos) videtur esse expressa Pauli.

Et ita censent exponendo hæc loca (1. Corinth. XV. & 1. Thess. IV.) Chrysostomus homil. 42. in 1. Corinth. & homil. 7. in Thess. Theodore-tus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius ibid. Origenes libro V. contra Celsum non longe ab initio & Hie- Et Hieronymus epist. 52. ad Minervium refert in hanc sententiam Theodorum Heracleotem, & Apollinarium, quam ipse non judicat improbabilem, & super Esaiam cap. LI. illam lectionem Pauli sequitur: Non omnes dormiemus, epistola vero 148. q. 3. interpretans locum Pauli 1. Thess. IV. absolute docet hanc sententiam.

Augustinus etiam q. 3. ad Dulcitium, licet locum 1. Cor. XV. aliter legat, & ideo dubius de tota sententia esse videatur, tamen propter aliud testimonium ad Thess. valde est propensus ad hanc sententiam, & plane fatetur, se ignorare, in quo alio sensu locus exponi possit.

Et Gennadius de Eccl. dogm. cap. 7. & 8. hanc sententiam ut probabilem relinquit.

Praeterea Tertull. lib. de resurr. carnis cap. 41. & 42. licet locum 1. Cor. XV. aliter legat, & hanc nihilominus sententiam aperte docet, & ad illam accommodat vulgatam lectionem, qua sic habet: Omnes quidem resurgemus, dicens illam immutationem, quae fiet in justis tunc viventibus, pro resurrectione computari.

Oecumenii observatio subtilior magis est, quam solida. Illud non omnes obdormiemus hoc modo oportet accipere, quod non dormiemus diuturna dormitione, ut opus sit sepulchro ac solutione ad corruptionem, sed brevem mortem sustinebunt, qui tunc reperientur.

Nam obdormire non est somno teneri, sed mori. Dormit juxta idioma scripturarum, inquit Didymus Alexandr. qui mortuus est, spe resurrectionis futurae. Vid. Hieron. Epist. LIII. qui aliam seu alienam hujus textus affert explicationem: Melius est spiritualiter sentire, quod scriptum est, & dormitionem in praesenti loco non mortem accipere, per quam anima e corpore separatur.

Sed peccatum post baptismum, & offensam DEI, dormitionemque post baptismum &c. Est enim somnus peccati, qui ducit ad mortem, & est alia delicti dormitio, quae morte non stringitur &c. Cum igitur quidam non dormiant, qui semper in Christo vivunt & vigilant, sequitur, ut nequaquam omnes dormiant, & e contrario omnes immutentur, non immutatione gloriae, quae proprie debetur sanctis, sed ea commutatione, qua corruptivum hoc redditur incorruptivum, ut vel paenas vel praemia recipiat sempiterna &c.

Sed non opus esse isto glossamate, superius dicta docent. Quod autem Hieronymus, Vulgatam Latinam, praeferens, cum Didymo, adversus Graecum textum urget: Considerandum, an ei, quod praemissum est, omnes immutabimur, possit convenire, quod sequitur. Mortui surgent incorrupti, & nos immutabimur.

Si enim omnes immutabimur, & hoc commune cum caeteris est, superfluum fuit dicere: Et nos immutabimur. Quamobrem ita legendum est: Omnes quidem dormiemus, non omnes autem immutabimur. Si enim in Adam omnes moriuntur, & in morte dormitio est, omnes ergo dormiemus, sive moriemur: Hoc parum nos movet. Non enim id superfluum, sed loquitur jam Apostolus particulariter de illis, qui superstites erunt die novissimo, in ictu oculi, & mortui resurgent, & nos (vivi scilicet existentes) immutabimur.

Illud nos, inquit Chrysostomus, non dicit de ipso, sed de iis, qui tunc invenientur viventes. Sociniani funiculum ex arena nectunt, cum ex hac ἀλλαγῇ substantialem corporum resuscitorum diversitatem colligunt, quia non tantum substantialis, sed etiam accidentalis datur ἀλλαγὴ, & haec à qualitatibus describitur, ac per inductionem, quae nihil in substantia immutat, sed aliud immutatio, aliud perditio est, inquit Tertullianus lib. de Resurr.

Mort. cap. 55. Perisse enim est in totum non esse, quod fuerit, Mutatum esse aliter esse est. Porro dum aliter est, id ipsum esse potest. Habet enim esse, quod non perit. Vers. 52. ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ σάλπιγγι.

Hac inferenda ad proximum quod praecessit. Dicit mutationem istam corporis caduci in corpus immortale ita subitam fore, ut tempus percipi non possit. ἐν ἀτόμῳ, idem quod alibi ἐν στιγμῇ, Es. XXIX. 5. ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ apud Rabbinos. רגע עין Syrus hic, illud ἐν ἄτομῳ etiam Philosophi usurpant, alterum, in ictu oculi, multa gentes.

In ultima tuba, id est, ad sonum tubae ultimae: sive ad signum ultimum, quale per tubam in militia dari solet.

Vide Matth. XXIV. 31. ubi dicta, Et 1. Thess. V. 16.

Καὶ hic notat tunc. In Manuscripro pro ἐγερθήσονται est ἀναστήσονται. Ἄφθαρτοι. Vide fupra 50.

Quod 1. Thess. IV. dicitur: Mortui, qui in Christo sunt, resurgent primi, deinde nos, qui vivimus, simul cum ipsis rapiemur &c. huic loco non refragatur.

Nam etsi omnes tam vivi, quam mortui resuscitati, (quae resurrectio, quantum ad animas cum corpore conjunctionem, in instanti fiet) simul, idque in momento, immutabuntur, praecedit tamen resurrectio mortuorum, sequetur omnium raptus in occursum Domini. Theodorus Heracleotes in Comm. apud Hieronymum in Epist. ad Minor. & Alexand. Tom. III. n. 152. Qui ex mortuis resurrexerint, & in nubibus viventes rapti fuerint, transibunt ad incorruptionem, & à mortalitate in immortalitatem mutabuntur, non in tempore, non saltem in brevi spatio, sed in atomo, in puncto temporis, atque momento, quo palpebra oculi commoveri potest, in novissima tuba. Tanta enim fiet celeritate resurrectio mortuorum, ut vivi, quos in corporibus suis consummationis tempus invenerit, mortuos de inferis resurgentes praevenire non valeant, scilicet, in raptu in occursum Domini, ut cum Theodoro Apollinarius & Diadorus ibidem (apud Hieronymum) explicant.

Anselmus: Mortui, in Christo resurgent πρῶτον primum, antequam scilicet Christo obviam in aere rapiantur, deinde nos, qui vivimus, simul cum illis, qui ex mortuis resurrexerint, rapiemur obviam Christo. Ponitur enim hic ordo non resurgentium, nec resurrectionis ad resurrectionem, sed ordo resurrectionis ad raptum & occursum Domini, videlicet, quod illi primi, qui mortui erant, resurgent, deinde quod iidem cum aliis tum viventibus simul rapientur in occursum Christi, ut habet B.

Gerardus de Resurr. mortuorum §. 120. Quod ad tubam ultimam, quae tuba Angelorum, De tuba Matth. XXIV. 31. tuba DEI 2. Thess. IV. 16. & addita voce Archangeli, dicitur.

Theophylactus per eam nihil aliud intelligi vult, quam nutum DEI. Per tubam, inquit, qua nulla omnino erit in futuro judicio DEI, nutum & imperium patefacit, quod ad omnes fit perventurus. Gregorius M. ut & Flacius, per tubam intelligunt vocem & mandatum Christi, quo vocabit mortuos, Joh. V. 28.

Alli tamen voce distinguunt tuba sonitum, quia illa est Filii DEI, haec Angelis tribuitur, & vocem Archangeli & tubam DEI conjungit Apostolus, non pro iisdem habet. In quam sententiam plura affert argumenta B. Gerardus §. 66.

Hunnius noster tubam DEI explicat per vocem tonantis Omnipotentis DEI: Sed comparat eamen cum sonora illa tuba, quæ clangebat è monte Sinai in promulgatione legis, à cujus impetu contremiscebat terra, & fundamenta montium concutiebantur, quam nihil aliud fuisse dicit, quam horribilem & inauditam illam tempestatem, in qua Dominus legem suam promulgare voluit. Idemque censet, ultimam tubam ultimam tempestatem fore, cujus majestate atque vi non tantum in sublunari regione elementa colliquescent, sed ipsi cælorum cardines & columna inexplicabilem in modum concutientur, donec fulmine omnium novissimo hæc creati mundi machina, penitus eversa, concidat, & cæli incredibili cum fragore, procella in morem, transeant.

IV. dicens: Nos qui vivimus, qui residui sumus in adventum Domini, non præveniemus eos, qui dormierunt. IV. de residuis in adventu Domini victuris agere, notandum, uti superius justorum atque electorum, quos vivos adventus Domini deprehendet. Ideo S. Augustinus l. XX. de civitate DEI cap. 10. quod Apostolus personam eorum, quos hic viventes Christus inventurus est, in se atque alios, qui tunc secum vivebant, transfiguravit. Vers.

53. Δεῖ γὰρ τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν. Tertullianus libro de resurrectione carnis ita hunc locum explicat: Oportet enim corruptibilem istud induere incorruptibilitatem. Hoc erit illud domicilium de cælo, quod gementes in hac carne superinduere desideramus utique super carnem in qua deprehendemur: quia gravari nos ait qui sumus in tabernaculo, quod nolimus exui, sed potius superindui, ut devoretur mortale, à vita felices, dum demutatur superinduendo quod est de cælo.

Quid enim non desiderabit, dam in carne est, superinduere immortalitatem & continuare vitam, lucrifacere morte per beatam demutationem &c. Rursus eodem libro: Oportet enim corruptibilem istud induere incorruptionem & mortale istud induere immortalitatem: Quid mortale, nisi caro?

Quid corruptibile, nisi sanguis? At ne putes adhuc sentire Apostolum, providentem tibi & ut de carne dictum intelligas, laborantem.

Quum dicit istud corruptibilem & istud mortale cutem ipsam pronuntiasse non potuit. Demonstrationis corporalis est verbum.

Et adversus Marcionem ita: Oportet enim corruptibilem hoc, suam tenens carnem dicebat Apostolus.

Patria habet Justinus ad Symbolum. Plutarchus Bruto de Exfare: Τῇ χειρὶ τὸ σῶμα, ἀυτόματον εἶπε τὶν ἐξ ὧν ἁμὶν δοκεῖ. Βρεῖν, ἀμύναι τινὶ τὸ σάκιον; Ἐνδύσασθαι valet, חלש, quod Hebræi usurpant cum de corpore immortali agitur. Καὶ τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν. Potest esse corpus mortale etiam quod non moritur.

Non loquitur Apostolus tantum de his, quos vivos immutandos dixit, ut Estius vult, sed in genere de corporibus gloriam ingressuris, etsi omnino ipse viventes includat, quod in eis corpus hoc mortale & corruptibile etiam induere oporteat incorruptionem & immortalitatem, etsi proprie nec mortuum nec corruptum, sed mortalitas absorbenda sit à vita.

Crellius sane, τῇ ὑποθέσει δέλευων, in 1. ad Corinth. XV. vult, Paulum hic ad eos potissimum respicere, qui superstites sunt in adventu Domini, ad mortuos vero, non nisi consequenter ac minus proprie. Sed contraria est Pauli assertio, & ex istis pronominibus δευτικoῖς, τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο, τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο recte urgentur, qui idem numero corpus resurrecturum negant, quod etiam à Socinianis fit.

Nota, inquit Theophylactus, hæc dicta in eos proferri, qui afferant corpora non eadem illa resurrectura esse, quæ in hac vita fuere, sed alia quædam.

Inquit enim Apostolus, corruptibile hoc, & mortale hoc, non aliud quippiam, sed hoc duntaxat corpus designat, quo fit, ut corpus quidem id ipsum maneat, non autem quod induitur. Mortalitas autem & corruptio tollitur immortalitate & incorruptione superante. Differt autem corruptio à mortalitate, siquidem in animata duntaxat cadit mortalitas, corruptio autem vel in ea, quæ anima carent: Nec minus quoque verbum indutionis refert substantiam, quæ aliqua novate indutenda, identitatem.

Ideo etiam superindui dicuntur, qui vivi in novissimo die deprehendentur, 1.

Cor. V. 4. Is enim, fatente Crellio l. c. tantum superinduitur, qui jam alia instar vestis est, superinduitur non quidem aliud corpus (nam, ut iterum Crellius fatetur, fieri non potest, ut duobus corporibus homo simul & constanter sit præditus) sed immortalitas: Quia τὸ θνητὸν, seu mortale, oportet induere immortalitatem.

Commentum autem est, non Spiritus Sancti sententia, quod prolixe hic affert Crellius.

Ita nimirum (inquit) fiet hæc superinduitio, ut cœleste corpus hoc ad ipsos fideles, inferiori hoc aere adhuc versantes, in sublime tamen jam ferri incipientes, descendat, eorumque mortalia corpora amplectatur, eaque ratione ipsi fideles superinduantur veluti nova veste, veteri superiniecta.

Sed quia corpus illud incorruptibile cum corruptibili simul consistere, & spiritum nostrum excipere non potest: id virtute sua occulta, caelesti eamen prorsus at admiranda, in momento atque in ictu oculi absumet, & veluti in nihilum rediget hoc mortale corpus, non secus, atque si ignea quadam vi esset preditum, & corpus nostrum amplexum monentio citius absorberet. Missis autem talibus figmentis, recte ex illo loco Hieronymus epistol. ad Marcel. futurum docet, ut qualia corpora mortuorum resurrectorum sint, in talem substantiam etiam vivorum corpora transmutentur, nolumus expofiali, sed supervestiri, ut absorbeatur mortale hoc à vita, ne scilicet corpus ab anima deferatur, sed anima, habitante in corpore, fiat inclytum, quod ante inglorium fuit.

Ruffinus in exposit. Symb. ita habet: Hoc, quod nunc corruptibile corpus est, resurrectionis gratia incorruptibile erit, & quod nunc mortale est, immortalitatis virtutibus induetur, non natura carnis abjecta, sed conditione ejus & qualitate mutata.

Sed imprimis hic audiendus Theophylactus in 2. ad Cor. V. Cum durius esse, & grave, quod dixerat, appareret ingemiscere nos & graviter ferre, percupidos hoc corpore liberari, cum constet ineffabilem esse animi erga corpus affectum, idcirco inquit: Haudquaquam propterea ingemiscimus, quod è corpore simpliciter sit abeundum, sed quia nos libido incefferit, incorruptionem superinduere, perinde ac si haud fat fuerit, hanc ipsam induere, vel corruptionis volumus vacui esse, ut illa non corpus à vita consumatur & pereat.

Nec corporis gratia solum gravemur, sed quia corruptibile fit, moleste ferimus. Hinc obstruuntur Haereticorum ora, quippe cum de corporum diversitate nulla fiat hic mentio, quando de corruptibilitate duntaxat & incorruptibilitate disseritur.

Adde quod Apostolus mutationem solum, non vero totalem destructionem corporis hujus mortalis afferat.

Ubi quidem Crellius (in 1. Cor. XV. pag. 250. separatae editionis) mutatio, inquit, in eo consistit, quod alia corpora aliorum loco substituentur.

Sed aliud omnino est mutatio rei, aliud vero alterius, loco ejusdem, surrogatio, aut substitutio. Quod agnoscere debuit ipse Crellius, in hunc locum scribens: De omnibus fidelibus dictum erat, eos in momento mutatum iri, atque adeo etiam eos, qui resurgunt. Atqui haec si communem loquendi rationem spectes, non ita proprie dicitur mutatio, cum is, qui jam esse desierat, idque etiam jam pridem, postea alius fiat, quam fuerat, antequam esse desineret.

Magis autem proprie illi dicuntur mutari, qui cum adhuc reipsa existant, alii quam paulo ante fuerant, esse incipiant, seu aliud corpus induant.

libertatem vindicati & asserti sumus; non id humanae virtutis, non humanae dignitatis aut meriti, sed unius ac solius Dei beneficium. Hic est, qui victoriae praeclaram illam & sempiternam largitus est, idque per Christum Jesum Dominum nostrum, qui peccatum suo sanguine delevit, mortem sua morte absumpsit, infernum suo ad inferos descensu excidit ac destruxit, ut hic habet B. Hunnius. Domini Jesu, inquit Theophylacti, certamen est, hoc ille gessit. Nobis vero collata victoria est, nulla beneficiorum nostrorum vicissitudine, sed per Dei Patris clementiam, qui nos per Filii intensissimam operam superiores effecit. Non autem tantum peccatum habituale seu consuetudo peccandi & peccatum voluntarium, sed quodvis omnino peccatum est aculeas mortis, & damnationem infert, ut alias contra Socinianos evicimus. Continet autem haec sententia tacitam probationem resurrectionis mortuorum, eamque firmissimam. Si enim per Christum victoria nobis datur de peccato & morte, ergo sicut peccatum; ita & mortem penitus tandem destrui oportet. Mors autem non destruitur, nisi vita reddatur, & quidem perpetua: Quod non contingit, nisi per resurrectionem justis promissam, ut hic habet Estius.

Vult enim dicere magna fore laboris praemia. ὁ κόπος ἐν Κυρίῳ labor secundum Dominum, secundum Christi praeceptum.

Bene hanc admonitionem contexuit cum sermone de resurrectione. Nam si verum est dogma de resurrectione, nullus labor gravis videri debet. Quid enim suavius vita, eaque immortali, ac beatissima? Assignat ergo rationem, ex articulo resurrectionis, jam explicato, desumptam, & ex fonte utilitatis haustam, quia nimirum noster, in Domino susceptus, & ex fide profectus, labor nequaquam fit futurus irritus aut inanis, sed habiturus olim inaestimabilem retributionem & compensationem in vita aeterna, ut hic iterum B. Hunnius. Praecipit, ut quovis sabbato quisque aliquid pro sanctis deponat, collectas Hierosolymam vel per alios, vel etiam cum aliis se transportaturum promittit, ad Corintbios cum per Macedoniam transiturus est, venturum, ibique forte hyemem exacturum, jam autem Ephese, ubi magna sibi janua aperta, usque ad Pentecosten mansurum. ## 15:15
V. 15. Εὑρισκόμεθα καὶ ἡμεῖς ψευδομάρτυρες τῦ Θεῦ.

We are caught having borne false witness in the name of God, having abused the name of God, against the commandment of Exodus 20:7. Which, of course, is least to be believed of us, whom a life so amended easily frees from every suspicion of false testimony.

ὅτι ἐμαρτυρήσαμεν κατὰ Θεῦ, ὅτι ἤγειρε τὸν χριστόν.

For every testimony is against God which says that God did that which He did not do. If it is a great crime to speak falsely about a man, how much more so about God? If anyone counterfeits the King's coin, he is punished most severely; how much more so he who counterfeits God's. For miracles are the coin of God.

ὃν οὐκ ἤγειρεν, εἴπερ ἄρα νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται.

It is the same connection as above in 13.

ARTICLE II. Proof of the resurrection of the faithful from the resurrection of Christ.

Latin:

V. 15. Εὑρισκόμεθα καὶ ἡμεῖς ψευδομάρτυρες τῦ Θεῦ.

Deprehendimur nomine Dei falsum tulisse testimoni- um, abusi Dei nomine, contra præceptum Exodi XX. 7. Quod scilicet de nobis minimè credendum est, quos vita tàm emendata facilè ab omni falsimoniæ suspicione libe- rat.

ὅτι ἐμαρτυρήσαμεν κατὰ Θεῦ, ὅτι ἤγειρε τὸν χριστόν.

Contra Deum enim est testimonium omne, quod Deum fecisse dicit id, quod non fecit. Si de homine falsum di- cere magnum est scelus, quantò magis de Deo? Si quis Regis monetam adulterat, gravissime punitur, quantò ma- gis, qui Dei. Miracula enim moneta Dei.

ὃν οὐκ ἤγειρεν, εἴπερ ἄρα νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται.

Est eadem connexio, quæ supra 13.

ARTICULUS II. Probatio Resurrectionis fidelium è Christi resurrectione.

## 15:17
V. 17. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain.

The same as above 14. For the Apostles often repeat what is very necessary.

You are still in your sins.

You are not certain of the remission of your sins, which Christ promised by God's command: of which command nothing gives more assurance than his own resurrection from death, Rom. IV. 25.

These words convey nothing other than that the resurrection of Christ is a confirmation of the doctrine proposed by Christ. But at Rom. IV. 25, that is not taught; rather, our δικαίωσις or justification is established as the cause of Christ's resurrection, not the βεβαίωσις or confirmation of Christ's doctrine. Those things smell of the Socinian lamp of Grotius. Theophylact's paraphrase, with Chrysostom leading the way, is far more correct: For if Christ has not risen, then he has not undergone death either. If he has not suffered death, he has not dissolved sins either. For his death is the resolution of sins. For he says, Behold the Lamb of God, behold, who takes away the sins of the world. He calls him the Lamb who was slain and sacrificed for our sake. But if the offense has not been removed by the death of Christ, you are indeed subject to the offense, and you remain in it. Why then do you think that you have been freed from this crime? Up to this point, however, the Apostle has mainly proved that some resurrection must be admitted: inasmuch as Christ, who in reality was dead, has altogether risen. Whence that dispute has no proper place here, by what argument the resurrection of the rest of the dead follows from the resurrection of Christ, whether from a likeness, or from a meritorious cause, or from an exemplary cause. For as Grotius rightly says, he has not yet deduced our resurrection from Christ's, but has only formed it generally, that it is possible, nay, that it cannot be denied that there is a resurrection from the dead, because it is most certain that Christ has in reality risen from the dead. Now, however, the Apostle proceeds to demonstrate the resurrection of the faithful, v. 17. But if Christ, etc. This is not a bare repetition, but a digression to another member of the proof, namely, concerning the truth of the resurrection of the faithful. Before, he called the dogmatic faith by which we believe that Christ was raised vain, if Christ has not in reality risen, v. 14. Now, however, he calls the very saving faith in Christ vain, both as regards the living, so that they are still in their sins; and as regards those sleeping in Christ, who must have perished, as if they were never to be raised to glory, Christ not having been raised.

Latin:

V. 17. Εἰ δὲ χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, ματαία ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν.

Idem quod supra 14. Nam valdè necessaria Apostoli sæpe repetunt.

Ἔτι ἐστὲ ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν.

Non estis certi de remissione peccatorum vestrorum, quam Christus promisit Dei mandato: cujus mandati fidem non alia magis facit res, quàm ipsius ex morte resuscitatio, Rom. IV. 25.

Nihil aliud hæc præ se ferunt, quàm resurrectionem Christi confirmationem esse doctrinæ à Christo propositæ. At Rom. IV. 25. id non docetur; Sed causa resurrectionis Christi constituitur nostra δικαίωσις vel justificatio, non doctrina Christi βεβαίωσις, vel confirmatio. Socinianam illa Grotiana olent lucernam. Rectius longe habet Theophylacti paraphrasis, præeunte Chrysostomo: Si enim Christus non resurrexit, ergò nec mortem subiit. Si minus est ille mortem perpessus, neque peccata dissolvit. Mors quippe illius peccatorum est resolutio. Inquit enim, Ecce agnus DEI, ecce, qui tollit peccata mundi. Agnum verò eum appellat, qui fuerit occisus, & nostri gratia immolatus. Quod si baudquaquam est Christi morte delictum sublatum, estis sanè delicto obnoxii, in eoque permanetis. Cur ergò existimatis fuisse vos crimine hoc liberatos? Hactenus autem id maxime probavit Apostolus, resurrectionem aliquam admittendam esse: Siquidem Christus, qui reverâ mortuus fuit, omninò resurrexerit. Unde hic locum propriè non habet illa disputatio, quo argumento ex Christi resurrectione sequatur cæterorum mortuorũ resurrectio, an à simili, an à causâ meritoria, an à causa exemplari. Nam ut rectè Grotius, nondum è Christi resurrectione nostram deduxit, sed tantum γενικῶς formavit possibilem esse, imo negari non posse, quod detur resurrectio à mortuis, quia Christum reverà à mortuis resurrexisse certissimum est. Jam verò pergit Apostolus ad demonstrandam fidelium resurrectionem, v. 17. Εἰ δὲ χριστὸς &c. Non est hæc nuda repetitio, sed digressio ad alterum probationis membrum, de veritate nempe resurrectionis fidelium. Antea vanam dixit fidem dogmaticam, quâ credimus, Christum resuscitatum esse, si Christus reverâ non resurrexit, v. 14. Jam verò vanam dicit ipsam fidem salvificam in Christum, tùm quà viventes, ut illi adhuc in peccatis sint; tùm quà dormientes in Christo, quos periisse oportuit, ceu nunquam resuscitandos ad gloriam, Christo haud resuscitato.

## 15:18
V. 18. Then also those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.

They have perished, therefore, without hope of a better life, who died for the sake of Christ, that is, of the Gospel, like Stephen and others. 'In' here is placed for 'on account of', and what is 'in Christ' here is said the same as 'through Jesus', 1 Thess. IV. 14.

These things concern not only Stephen and the Martyrs of the New Testament, but all the faithful of the Old and New Testaments, Adam, Abel, Abraham, etc., who all, like us, hoped that they would obtain eternal salvation by the grace of Jesus Christ, John VIII. 58, Acts XV. 11, Heb. XI. 6. For they too fell asleep in Christ. But the Apostle seems to have said emphatically, 'who have fallen asleep in Christ', that is, who are called by us Christians 'those sleeping in Christ', because of the certain hope of the resurrection. Which consideration increases the absurdity: namely, that they have perished whom we call 'sleeping' by the Christian custom of speaking, and by this we testify that they will be awakened at some time, as Estius says here.

Latin:

V. 18. Ἄρα καὶ οἱ κοιμηθέντες ἐν χριστῷ ἀπώλοντο.

Perierunt igitur sine spe vitæ melioris, qui Christi, id est, Evangelii causa mortem obierunt, ut Stephanus & alii. Ἐν hic positum est pro propter & quod hic est ἐν χριστῷ, idem dicitur διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, 1. Thess. IV. 14.

Non tantùm hæc Stephanum, & Martyres Novi Testamenti, sed omnes fideles Veteris & Novi Testamenti, Adamum, Abelem, Abrahamum &c. concernunt, qui omnes gratiâ Jesu Christi, uti nos, sperârunt æternam se adepturos salutem, Job. IIX. 58. Act. XV. 11. Ebr. XI. 6. Nam & illi obdormierunt in Christo. Videtur autem emphaticè Apostolus dixisse, qui dormierunt in Christo, hoc est, qui nobis Christianis vocantur dormientes in Christo, ob spem certam resurrectionis. Quæ consideratio auget absurdum: Scilicet eos periisse, quos ita loquendi Christianâ consuetudine vocamus dormientes, & per hoc excitandos aliquando testamur, ut hic Estius.

## 15:19
V. 19. If in this life we have hope in Christ only, we are of all men most miserable. An argument of the greatest weight, which the Apostle also develops more broadly below in verse 30. That the Apostles were not madmen was sufficiently evident from their life, their sayings, and their writings. Yet it would have been the act of madmen to expose themselves to so many hatreds, inconveniences, dangers, and death itself, unless they expected some reward after this life. No thing had given them more assurance of this reward than the resurrection of Christ. Truly, therefore, the Apostles were to be pitied if they were so insane. For what could they hope for from Christ in this life that could be compared with such great evils? Μόνον is to be construed with τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ. Ἐλεεινότεροι πάντων is a construction like that above in XIII. 13.

Theophylact has it thus here: If all our hope is advanced only as far as this life, and we are occupied in it and it alone, and we desire nothing beyond this, we who hope in Christ—that is, those whose hope is placed in Christ—and await no other life in heaven, we undoubtedly surpass other men in miseries and calamities: for we neither enjoy present things, as we said above, and we shall lack future things, because, as some among you think, we are not to rise again. Someone will say that the soul alone is to have the use of heavenly goods. But what of that? For it is not this alone that has undertaken labor, but the body also has sweated in good deeds. By what logic, therefore, should that pair be seen as such that the body, which has undergone greater labors, should have nothing at all in the future and be devoid of rewards, and the soul alone be crowned?

This is a new proof, or a confirmation of the preceding, that if the faithful are not to be resurrected to another life, they must be the most miserable among mortals, as being in this life more afflicted than others, and having no hope of another life. To this pertains that which is brought forward from Pamphilus the Martyr in his Apology for Origen from book 1 of his work on the resurrection: How does it not seem absurd that this body, which for Christ bore scars, and equally with the soul endured the cruel torments of persecutions, and also bore the punishments of prisons and chains and lashes, was even tortured by fire, cut by iron, and furthermore suffered the bloody bites of beasts, the crosses of the gallows, and diverse kinds of punishments, should be defrauded of the rewards of such great struggles? It seems to be against all reason that the soul alone, which had not struggled alone, should be crowned, and that the vessel of its body, which served it with great labor, should obtain no rewards of the contest and victory, etc.

Latin:

V. 19. Εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν ἐν χριστῷ μόνον, ἐλεεινότεροι πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἐσμὲν. Argumentum maximi ponderis, quod etiam latius de- ducit Apostolus infra 30. Non amentes esse Apostolos sa- tis constabat ex vita ipsorum, dictis, & scriptis. Atqui amentium fuerat objicere se tot odiis, incommodis, peri- culis, morti ipsi, nisi præmium aliquod post hanc vitam ex- spectarent. Cujus præmii fidem nulla magis illis res fece- rat, quàm Christi resurrectio. Verè ergò miserandi erant Apostoli, si eò usque insanirent. Quid enim à Christo in hac vita sperare poterant, quod cum tantis malis compa- raretur? Μόνον construendum cum τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ. Ἐλεει- νότεροι πάντων constructio, qualis supra XIII. 13.

Theophylactus hic ita habet: Si ad usque hanc vitam spes omnis nostra provehitur, in eaque & sola versamur, neque hanc præter quicquam ultra cupi- mus, nos qui in Christo speramus, hoc est, quorum est in Christo spes sita, neque ullam aliam opperimur in cælo vitam, miseriis haud dubiè & calamitati- bus cæteros homines anteimus: Quippe, qui neque præsentibus fruimur, ut diximus supra, & futuris carebimus: quia ut inter vos quidam existimant, resurrecturi non sumus. Dicet aliquis, solam ani- mam usum esse bonorum cælestium habituram. Ve- rùm quid illud? Neque enim hæc sola laborem sus- cepit, sed corpus etiam bonis actibus insudavit. Quo ergò pacto par illud videri debet, ut corpus, quod majores labores subierit, nil prorsus futurum ha- beat, & præmiorum sit expers, solaque anima co- ronetur?

Nova hæc est probatio, aut præcedentis con- firmatio, si fideles non resuscitandi sunt ad alte- ram vitam, miserrimos eos esse oportet inter mor- tales, utpote in hac vita præ aliis afflictissimos, nullamque alterius vitæ spem habentes. Quo facit illud è Pamphilo Martyre Apolog. pro Origene ex l. 1. ejusdem de resurrectione addu- ctum: Quomodo non videtur absurdum, ut hoc corpus, quod pro Christo pertulit cicatrices, & pa- riter cum anima persecutionum toleravit sæva tor- menta, carcerum quoque ac vinculorum & verbe- rum supplicia pertulit, igne etiam cruciatum, ferro cæsum est, insuper & bestiarum cruentos morsus, crucis patibula, ac diversa pœnarum genera per- pessum est, tantorum certaminum præmiis defrau- detur? Contra omnem rationem esse videtur, quod sola anima, quæ sola non certaverat, coronetur, & corporis sui vasculum, quod ei cum magno labore servivit, nulla agonis & victoriæ præmia conse- quatur &c.

## 15:20
V. 20. But now Christ is risen from the dead. Νυνὶ is used here also as in Rom. III. 21, VII. 10, and above in V. 11, VII. 24, XII. 20, XIV. 6.

He became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Clement follows in his Epistle: Let us consider, beloved, how the Lord continually shows us that there will be a future resurrection, of which He made the Lord Jesus Christ the firstfruits, having raised Him from the dead. Concerning the use of the word ἀπαρχῆς, see Rom. VIII. 23, XI. 16, XVI. 5. Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, however, not because of death, but because of the immortal life, which He was the first of all men to obtain after death. I am speaking now according to the Hebrews, to whom it is said that not the soul alone lives, but the whole man. In the same sense Christ is called in Coloss. I. 18 and Apoc. I. 5, the firstborn from the dead.

This argument is taken from the Levitical type, Lev. XXIII. 10, 11, Exod. XXIII. 19, chap. XXIV. 26, Deut. XXVI. 2. For just as the harvest immediately followed the offering of the firstfruits, made on the second day of the Jewish Passover, so Christ, on the day following the Jewish paschal Sabbath—that is, on the Lord's Day—was raised on high from the sepulcher through the resurrection, as the firstfruits of those who sleep. From there, therefore, the full harvest will certainly follow at the consummation of the age, which harvest is mentioned in Matt. XIII. 39. Concerning which Augustine says in Psalm CXXIX: Christ our priest in His resurrection renewed that which was slain (His body) and gave it as His firstfruits to GOD and says to you: All your things are already preserved, when such firstfruits of yours have been given to GOD from you. Hope, therefore, that what preceded in your firstfruits will also happen in you.

He is not called the firstfruits so much by reason of order, because Enoch and Elijah had already obtained immortal life not only through the change, which is like death, but Moses had also obtained it through true death; as by reason of sanctification, because through these firstfruits we have all been consecrated to a blessed life, just as in the firstfruits the whole mass was consecrated to the harvest: Or by reason of causality: Concerning which the blessed Luther, Tom. VI. on 1 Cor. XV. f. 234, 235: Therefore, although some saints before Christ, such as Enoch and Elijah, went to heaven, or were raised by Him, or rose with Him, that does not apply here, since one is not dealing with a private resurrection, as when one or two have risen, but with the general resurrection, and with the Head or Cause of the same, which is Christ. For although some have risen individually, that is of no concern to me, but it is of great concern that we know that Christ has risen, and how we also through Him are to come to that place, and remain where He is. The Lord D. Sebastian Schmid, in a special disputation on this passage, has it thus: There was a threefold kind of fruits: 1. The fruits of the second earth, which ripened after the first. 2. The first, or those ripening before all others. 3. The firstfruits of the first, Deut. XXVI. 2. These alone, when brought into the temple, were holy to the Lord, and through them the remaining fruits were sanctified, so that they could be eaten by all. Christ, therefore, is the firstfruits; the second fruits are the whole human race, from which Christ assumed human nature. The first are those who have a prerogative from the human race, the Church of GOD, because just as Christ the Savior reaches the human race remotely, so He reaches the Church proximately, in which He was both born and educated. Wherefore the Holy Spirit calls the Church ἀπαρχὴν, Jas. I. 18. Rev. XIV. 4. God gave Him to us that Christ might be the firstfruits, John III. 16. But He could not be, unless He were offered to God the Father in His passion, and thus made satisfaction for us. Nor can this accrue to us for righteousness and sanctification, unless we present these firstfruits to God the Father in the due manner, acknowledging our misery, and committing ourselves solely to the grace of GOD in Christ in true faith. Just as was done in the offering of the firstfruits, Deut. XXVI. 5. To the type of the firstfruits also pertains this: That the firstfruits were to be designated and separated before anything was gathered from the fruits of the earth, but those who were further from Jerusalem, so that they could not carry them there separated, were accustomed to dry them and carry them at their own time, although more rarely. Thus Christ was separated and destined as Redeemer before any man gathered any spiritual goods or was transferred to eternal life. Nevertheless, it came to pass that men gathered fruit from the spiritual goods to be acquired by Christ, and some even, like Enoch and Elijah, were translated into heaven. Whence also Christ remains the firstfruits of those who sleep, even if it could be proven that some were resurrected to eternal life before Him, provided that Christ was destined and separated for this, that He might acquire for them the resurrection to eternal life; that, however, would have been extraordinary. But among those who rise in the ordinary way, no one rose before the resurrection of Christ.

Latin:

V. 20. Νυνὶ δὲ χριστὸς ἐγήγερται ἐκ νεκρῶν. Νυνὶ etiam hic ut Rom. III. 21. VII. 10. supra V. 11. VII. 24. XII, 20. XIV. 6.

Ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων ἐγένετο. Sequitur Clemens in Epistola κατανοήσωμεν ἀγαπητοὶ, πῶς ὁ δεσπότης ἐπιδείκνυται διηνεκῶς ἡμῖν τὴν μέλλουσαν ἀνά- στασιν ἔσεσθαι, ἧς τὴν ἀπαρχὴν ἐποιήσατο τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστήσας. De usu vocis ἀπαρχῆς vide Rom. VIII. 23. XI. 16. XVI. 5. Dicitur autem χριστὸς ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, non ob mortem, sed ob vitam immortalem, quam omnium hominum primus post mor- tem est consequutus. Loquor jam secundum Hebræos, quibus vivere dicitur non animus solus, sed homo totus. Eodem sensu Christus dicitur Coloss. I. 18. & Apoc. I. 2. πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν.

Argumentum hoc ex typo Levitico petitum, Lev. XXIII. 10. 11. Exodi XXIII. 19. cap. XXIV. 26. Deut. XXVI. 2. Ut enim primitiarum oblationem, altera Paschatis Judaici feria factam, statim se- quuta est messis: Ita Christus feria, sabbatum paschale Judaicum sequente, die scilicet Domi- nica, è sepulchro in sublime elevatus per resur- rectionem, ceu primitiæ dormientium. Inde er- go plena messis certò sequutura est in consum- matione seculi, quæ messis dicitur Matth. XIII. 39. De quo Augustinus in Psal. CXXIX. Christus sacerdos noster in resurrectione innovavit illud, quod occisum est, (corpus suum) & tanquam primi- tias suas dedit DEO & ait tibi: Conservata sunt jam omnia tua, quando tales primitiæ tuæ de te datæ sunt DEO. Spera ergò, & in te futurum, quod præcessit in primitiis tuis.

Non autem ἀπαρχὴ dicitur tàm ratione ordinis, quia vitam immortalem non per ἀλλαγὴν tantùm, quæ instar mortis est, Enoch & Elias, sed etiam per veram mortem Moses jam consecuti erant; quàm ratione sanctificationis, quia per hanc ἀπαρχὴν consecrati sumus omnes ad beatam vitam, ut in primitiis tota massa consecrabatur ad messem: Vel ratione causalitatis: Quo de B. Lutherus Tom. VI. in 1. ad Cor. XV. f. 234. 235. Darumb ob etliche Heiligen vor Christo, als Enoch und Elias, gen Himmel gefahren, oder durch ihn aufferweckt, oder mit ihm aufferstanden sind, das gehet dieses nicht an da man handelt nicht de privata resurrectione, wie einer oder zween aufferstanden sind, sondern von der gemeinen Aufferstehung, und von dem Haupt oder Ursach derselben, welches ist Christus. Denn ob etliche sonderlich aufferstanden sind, da liegt mir nichts an, aber da liegt viel an, daß wir wissen, daß Christus aufferstanden ist, und wie auch wir durch Ihn darzu kommen sollen, und bleiben, da er ist. Dominus D. Sebastian Schmid. disput. peculiari de hoc loco sic habet: Triplex fructuum erat genus, 1. Fructus terræ secundi, qui post primos maturescebant. 2. Primi seu primo omnium maturescentes. 3. Primitiæ primorum, Deut. XXVI. 2. Hæ sole in templum allatæ sanctæ erant Domino, & per eas reliqui fructus sacrificabantur, ut ab omnibus edi possent. Christus ergò primitiæ, fructus secundi sunt totum genus humanum, ex quo Christus humanam naturam assumsit. Primi sunt, qui ex humano genere prærogativam habent, Ecclesia DEI, quia sicut Christus Salvator genus humanum remotè, ita Ecclesiam proximè attingit, in qua & natus & educatus est. Quare Ecclesiam vocat Spiritus S. ἀπαρχὴν, Jac. I. 18. Apoc. XIV. 4. Christus primitiæ ut esset, dedit eum nobis Deus, Joh. III. 16. Sed esse non potuit, nisi Deo Patri offerretur in passione, & ita satisfaceret pro nobis. Nec nobis in justitiam & sanctificationem id cedere potest, nisi has primitias debito modo Deo Patri sistamus, miseriam nostram agnoscentes, & in vera fide gratiæ DEI in Christo nos unicè committentes. Quemadmodum in oblatione primitiarum factum, Deut. XXVI. 5. Ad typum primitiarum etiam hoc pertinet: Quod primitiæ definandæ & separandæ fuerint, antequam de fructibus terræ quicquam perciperetur, illi verò, qui remotiores erant ab Hierosolymis, ut separatas eò non possent deportare, arefacere illas & suo tempore deportare, quanquam rarius, solebant. Ita Christus separatus & destinatus in Redemptorem, priusquam ullus hominum quicquam bonorum spiritualium perciperet, aut ad vitam æternam transferretur. Factum nihilominus, ut homines de bonis spiritualibus à Christo acquirendis, fructum perceperint, & nonnulli etiam, ut Enoch & Elias, in cœlum translati sint. Unde etiam Christus primitiæ dormientium manet, etiamsi probari posset, quod quidam ante ipsum ad vitam æternam resuscitati sint, modò Christus ad hoc destinatus ac separatus fuerit, ut resuscitationem ad vitam æternam illis acquireret; id tamen extraordinarium fuisset. Inter eos vero, qui ordinario modo resurgunt, nemo ante Christi resurrectionem resurrexit.

## 15:21
V. 21. For since by man came death) The sense is the same as in Rom. V. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. Just as through one Adam death reached, to wit, all who participated in his nature,

And by man came the resurrection of the dead.

And here signifies 'so', in the Hebrew manner. And the resurrection of the dead here is תְחִיַּת, a blessed resurrection, the word being taken in the better sense.

The blessed resurrection happens to all who are participants in the nature of Christ, which properly pertains indeed to those who have believed in Christ, who promised it: Nevertheless, it will also happen without a promise to the pious who were before Christ, because they followed the τοῦ λόγου, who was ἐσαρκώθη in Christ. For there were given to them, as it were by way of loan, certain gifts from the gifts destined for Christ, which they used rightly according to the measure of the times. V. 22. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνήσκουσι. That is, through Adam, because of the life given by him. Ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ here is the same as δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου, Rom. V. 12. Οὕτω καὶ ἐν τῷ χριστῷ πάντες ζωοποιηθήσονται. In Christ, that is, through Christ, all namely who are participants in the nature of Christ. Thus the word all is taken also in Rom. V. 18. Ἐν τῷ χριστῷ is the same as ἐν χάριτι τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, Rom. V. 15. and διὰ τοῦ ἑνὸς Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, Rom. V. 17. διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνός v. 16. 19. where see the stated passages. The word ζωοποιεῖν in the sense of the blessed resurrection we have had in John V. 21. VI. 13. Rom. IV. 17. VIII. 11. It properly corresponds to the Hebrew החיה.

Dismissing that Pelagian error concerning the pious before Christ, who were destitute of the promise of heavenly blessedness and the blessed resurrection, which has now been often refuted, to which David's Psalm XVII, Job ch. XIX, Dan. ch. XII, and other oracles of the Old Testament, and the testimonies of Christ himself John V. 39, and the Holy Apostle 2 Tim. III. 16, openly cry out: the connection of the Apostolic inference, from the meritorious cause of death, Adam's disobedience, to the meritorious cause of life, Christ's obedience, and thus from death, which is inflicted upon all by force of justice because of sin, to the resuscitation to life, which will be obtained by the faithful by the grace of God because of Christ's meritorious obedience, is by no means obscure. Especially because Christ, by his obedience which he performed, by sanctifying himself wholly in body and soul for us, procured and merited not only that blessedness of our soul, but also the resuscitation of the body to life. And not only the soul, but the whole body is made alive in Christ.
