Otherwise, the sin and demerit of Adam, by which death was brought upon soul and body, would have had greater efficacy than the obedience and merit of Christ.

Therefore, the resurrection of the body procured through Christ must be no less than the death brought in through Adam: Because we die on account of Adam, and we are made alive on account of Christ, not only in part, or in respect of the soul, but in whole, and thus also in respect of the body. Adam was made the cause and source of injustice and death for the whole human race, because these are derived through him into the whole posterity by carnal generation. But Christ was made the source of justice and life for believers, which he communicates through spiritual generation. Concerning which Ambrose says: Because death was brought in by the sin of man, the justice of Christ merited the resurrection of the dead. Just as Adam, sinning, brought in death and held all from his origin so that they are dissolved: So also Christ, not sinning, and by this conquering death—because he who does not sin conquers death, since death is from sin—acquired life for all from his body, that is, the resurrection. Theophylact on this passage: He brings in the cause, he says, by which he confirms his statements. For it was necessary that nature itself, which had clearly succumbed, should emerge victorious, and that he should carry off the palm of victory who had been prostrated. For as in Adam (that is, in Adam's transgression) all are subject to death, so also in Christ all are to be resurrected, because that one was found without sin, and not subject to death, and he died intending to rise again a little later. For it could not be that the Author of life should be subjected to that corruption.

Some take the resurrection of the dead generally, so that it extends even to the wicked, among whom is Pseudo-Ambrose among the ancients, and among the more recent, after Calvin, l. III. instit. cap. XV.

sect. 9. 10. and Scarpium in Conf. Theol. l. 20. cap. 1173. is Dr. Henricus Boëthius, Professor at Helmstedt, who, in the promotion of candidates of philosophy, responding to the question concerning the resurrection of the wicked, contends that the resurrection of the wicked also depends on the virtue of the merits and resurrection of Christ, and he published those pages at Magdeburg in the year 1613, and when our blessed Balduinus was publicly setting forth his opinion on that question here in his lectures on this passage, [he argued that] the wicked will not rise again by the virtue of the resurrection of Christ, but because of the immutable decree of God, by which it is appointed for man to die once, and after that the judgment, Heb. IX. 27. and the opinion of Boëthius, without however any mention of his name, the same Boëthius did not hesitate in the year 1614 to oppose a brief pericope, as he calls it, to B. Balduinus, with a Lycambean style, to which indeed our late blessed one prepared an Apology, both of which treatments of his are read in the commentary on this passage, p. 570. Indeed, the blessed Caspar Erasmus Brochmand also asserts in System. Theol. de Serv. Christo chap. XV. q. VI. that the resurrection of the wicked also depends upon the resurrection of Christ, by the argument that the power of Christ's resurrection extends as widely to raising the dead from the dust as death, which invaded the human race through the fall of Adam, extends itself, as the Apostle testifies in 1 Cor. XV. 21. But without doubt the blessed Brochmand did not see or weigh those things which were disputed with Boëthius, nor did he hand down anything concerning the power of the merits of Christ in this question, but only concerning the dependence upon the resurrection of Christ: Where indeed, as we already warned 37 years ago in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession Art. XVII. §. III. Th. IIX., we must distinguish entirely between the dependence of the raising of the wicked upon the resurrection of Christ, which is an effect, and the meritorious cause; and a dependence of such a kind which is that of a consequent from an antecedent; and we taught that the restoration of the bodily life of the wicked is neither a fruit nor an effect of the merit of Christ's resurrection, because the fruits of Christ's merits are benefits, pertaining to the mercy of GOD, and are always in themselves salutary, and are not obtained except through faith: Nor does it depend upon the resurrection of Christ, as a consequent from an antecedent, because even if Christ had never died and been resurrected, the wicked would still have been to be raised from the dead. But that this Apostolic treatment is not concerned with the resurrection of the wicked to judgment, which depends upon justice, but with that of the blessed to life, which is to be attributed to the merit of Christ, is clear from the text. For although in v. 12 he proves generally from Christ's resurrection that which is falsely denied, that there is a resurrection from the dead, inasmuch as it is established by the example of Christ, he does not however stop at the fact that a resurrection is possible, but discusses particularly the resurrection to eternal life, and proves it among other things from the merit of Christ, because he concludes from the necessary connection of a proper and sufficient cause with its effect, such a connection as does not exist between Christ and the resurrection of the dead, and he treats of such a resurrection as Christ's was, which indeed was a resurrection to glory: And according to which Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep, namely, of those who have fallen asleep in Christ, v. 18, 19. But not of the wicked; for Christ is not the firstfruits of these, because he is not of their mass. Moreover, he treats of that resurrection which is followed by the glory of bodies and the possession of the kingdom of God, verses 43, 50, and which is the victory of death, v. 45, such as the resurrection of the wicked is not, for whom the restoration of life is not so much the destruction of death as its renewal, nay, its duplication, because it is the delivery of the body into eternal death, where death is not swallowed up, but revives for eternal torments of body and soul. Therefore, that all are said to be made alive in Christ must be understood of all those who are in Christ through faith, and who fall asleep in Christ, as far as the actual participation of life acquired through Christ is concerned, for which faith is necessary: But not indeed of all men generally, except as far as the acquisition of salvation and life is concerned, which has been obtained by the merit of Christ for all, even if they do not actually possess and enjoy the same, except for the believers alone. The Apostle is dealing with the universal cause of life, not with the fruit actually redounding to all men, because those who are destitute of faith, by which alone that fruit of life obtained through Christ's merit is obtained, do not possess that fruit, Rom. V. 18. But conversely, v. 19, when he deals with the application, he taught that not all men, but only believers, are actually justified through the righteousness of Christ. Therefore, in this place, since these things pertain to actual vivification: As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive, a comparison is instituted, partly by reason of the origin of death and life, because Adam and his sin is the cause of death, but Christ and his merit is the cause of life; partly by reason of the universality of the subjects, but in this way, that all reach God, whoever have been procreated from Adam through carnal generation, and so likewise all who derive their origin from Christ, through spiritual regeneration, are to attain blessed life and vivification. Concerning which Augustine, Epist. LVII. to Dardanus. He said all and all for this reason; because into death no one, except through him (Adam), into life no one, except through this one (Christ). In the first it was evident that the will of man availed for death. But in Christ, that the help of GOD availed for life. And book II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 30. He said therefore that the death of the body of all was made through one man, and he promised that the resurrection of the body of all into eternal life would be through one Christ. How therefore did he harm us more by sinning, than this one profited by redeeming, since through the sin of the former we die temporally, but through the redemption of the latter we rise again not to temporal life, but to perpetual? Add also Epist. XXIX. to Hieron. to Hilar. LXXXIX. quest. 3. Epist. CLVII. to Optatus, book XIII. de Civit. DEI cap. 33. Book XX. c. 20. Leo M. epist. XXXII. referring to these words: So also in Christ shall all be made alive: These again all, he says, who although they were born in Adam, are nevertheless found reborn in Christ. Add homil. XV. de pass. Domini. To which are added the interlinear gloss, Dionysius the Carthusian, Hofmeisterus, Hervæus, Estius, and other Papists: Most of the Reformed, Martyr, Ursinus, Bucanus, Polanus, etc. And also B. Luther, Tom. VI. Jenens. on the first to the Corinthians XV. on this place. B. Ægidius Hunnius, He is dealing here, he says, with vivification to blessed life, the following member of the Apostolic text argues, in which he says that those who are made alive through Christ are Christ's, which is a not unknown periphrasis for the pious or believers. B. David Rungius disp. XVI. on 1. to the Corinthians, part III. By the force of this argument it is clear that the Apostle is not dealing in general with the resurrection of the dead both to life and to damnation, but specifically with the resurrection to eternal life, which happens only to those who believe in Christ. And for these the Apostle's reasoning is most true. Otherwise, if Paul's argument is accommodated to all men in general, then it will not proceed from cause to effect, but only from example. Nor will it conclude anything more than that the dead can rise again, because Christ rose again. But Paul does not stop at the consideration of what can happen, but necessarily concludes that the dead will certainly rise again, because Christ rose again. Which method of arguing pertains only to those who are to be believed and saved. For it is not to be ascribed to the resurrection of Christ that the impious are to rise again to eternal punishments, Dan. XII. John V. Add also Tilemann Heshusius on this place p. 328. and D. Gerhard. de resurrectione mortuorum §. 19. & 55.

Latin:

V. 21. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ δι ἀνθρώπε ὁ θάνατος) Idem est sensus, qui Rom. VI. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. Sicut per unum Adamum mors pertigit sc. ad omnes, qui naturam ejus participabant,

Καὶ δὶ ἀνθρώπε ἀνάσασις νεκρῶν.

Kαὶ hîc valet ita, more Hebræo. Et ἀνάσασις νεκρῶν hîc est תְחִיַּת resurrectio beatà, sumptâ voce in partem meliorem.

Resurrectio beata omnibus contingit, qui naturæ Christi sunt participes, quod propriè quidem pertinet ad eos, qui Christo crediderunt, eam pollicenti: Attamen etiam sine pollicitatione continget piis, qui ante Christum fuêre, quia τοῦ λόγου sunt sequuti, qui in Christo ἐσαρκώθη. Data enim illis sunt velut pro mutuo dona quædam, de donis Christo destinatis, quibus pro temporum ratione rectè sunt usi. V. 22. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνήσκουσι. Id est, per Adamum, ob vitam ab ipso datam. Ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ hic idem est, quod δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου, Rom. V. 12. Οὕτω καὶ ἐν τῷ χριστῷ πάντες ζωοποιηθήσονται. In Christo, id est, per Christum, omnes nempe, qui par- ticipes sunt naturæ Christi. Sic vox omnes sumitur & Rom. V. 18. Ἐν τῷ χριστῷ idem, quod ἐν χάριτι τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, Rom. V. 15. & διὰ τοῦ ἑνὸς Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, Rom. V. 17. διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνός v. 16. 19. ubi dicta vide. Ver- bum ζωοποιεῖν in sensu beatæ resurrectionis habuimus Joh. V. 21. VI. 13. Rom. IV. 17. VIII. 11. Propriè respondet Hebræo החיה.

Misso errore illo Pelagiano, de piis ante Chri- stum, promissione beatitudinis cœlestis, & beatæ resurrectionis destitutis, jam sæpè profligato, cui Davidis Psalm. XVII. Jobi cap. XIX. Dan. c. XII. aliaque oracula Veteris Testamenti, & testimo- nia ipsius Christi Johan. V. 39. & Sancti Apostoli 2. Tim. III. 16. palàm reclamant: Nexus Aposto- licæ illationis est, à causa meritoria mortis Ada- mi, inobedientia, ad causam meritoriam vitæ Chri- sti, obedientiam, adeoque à morte, quæ omnibus, vi justitiæ, ob peccatum infligitur, ad resuscitation- nem ad vitam, quæ DEI gratiâ, ob Christi meri- toriam obedientiam, fidelibus obtinget, minimè obscurus est. Imprimis, quia Christus obedientia suâ, quam præstitit, sese totum corpore, & animâ pro nobis sanctificando, non modò illam animæ nostræ beatitudinem, sed etiam corpori resuscita- tionem ad vitam peperit, ac promeruit. Nec ani- ma tantùm, sed totum corpus vivificatur in Chri- sto. Alioqui majoris efficaciæ fuisset peccatum, & demeritum Adami, quo animæ & corpori mors conciliata, quàm obedientia & meritum Christi.

Resurrectionem itaque corporis per Christum partam oportet esse, non minùs quàm mors cor- poris per Adamum invecta est: Quia propter Ada- mum morimur, & propter Christum vivificamur, non ex semisse tantùm, vel ratione animæ, sed ex asse, adeoque etiam ratione corporis. Adam factus est toti humano generi causa & fons injustitiæ & mortis, quia hæc per ipsum in totam posteritatem per carnalem generationem derivantur. Christus autem fons justitiæ & vitæ factus est credentibus, quam per spiritualem generationem communi- cat. Quo de Ambrosius: Quia peccato hominis mors invecta est, Christi justitia resurrectionem meruit mortuorum. Sicut Adam peccans mortem invexit, & omnes ex ejus origine tenuit, ut dissol- vantur: Ita & Christus non peccans, & per hoc vin- cens mortem, quia, qui non peccat, vincit mortem, cum mors ex peccato sit, omnibus ex ejus corpore acquisivit vitam, hoc est, resurrectionem. Theo- phylactus in hunc locum: Causam, inquit, infert, qua sua dicta confirmet. Erat enim necesse, ut na- tura ipsa, quæ planè succubuit, victrix evaderet, & ille victoriæ palmam referret, qui fuerat prostratus. Nam ut in Adam, (hoc est in Adæ delicto) omnes sunt morti obnoxii, sic & in Christo resurrecturi sunt omnes, quia sine peccato sit unus ille inventus, nec morti obnoxius, & volens paulò post resurre- cturus obierit. Fieri enim non poterat, ut vitæ Dux illi corruptioni subjiceretur.

Nonnulli mortuorum resurrectionem genera- liter accipiunt, ut ad malos etiam sese porrigat, inter quos est à Veteribus Pseudo-Ambrosius, è recentioribus post Calvinum l. III. instit. cap. XV.

sect. 9. 10. & Scarpium in Conf. Theol. l. 20. cap. 1173. est D. Henricus Boëthius, Professor Helm- stadiensis, qui in promotione Candidatorum Phi- losophiæ, ad quæstionem de impiorum resurre- ctione respondens, contendit, etiam impiorum re- surrectionem à virtute meritorum & resurrectio- nis Christi dependere, easque pagellas Magdebur- gi Anno 1613. publicavit, & quum de illa quæ- stione sententiam suam hic publicè in prælectio- nibus ad hunc locum exponeret B. Balduinus noster, impios non virtute resurrectionis Christi re- surrecturos, sed propter immutabile DEI decretum, quo statutum est homini semel mori, & postea ju- dicium, Ebr. IX. 27. & opinionem Boëthii, sine tamen nominis ejus mentione, expenderet, non dubitavit idem Boëthius Anno 1614. brevem pe- ricopam, ut vocat, B. Balduino, stylo Lycambeo, opponere, ad quam verò noster ὁ Μακαρίτης Apo- logiam adornavit, quæ utraque ejus tractatio le- gitur in comm. ad h. l. p. 570. Adserit quidem & B. Caspar Erasmus Brochmand. in System. Theol. de Serv. Christo cap. XV. q. VI. resurrectionem impiorum etiam pendere à resurrectione Christi, eò argumento, quod tàm latè fundat se virtus resur- rectionis Christi, ad excitandum è pulvere mortuos, quàm latè se extendat mors, quæ per lapsum Ada- mi invasit genus humanum, teste Apostolo 1. Cor. XV. 21. Sed procul dubio non vidit, aut expendit B. Brochman. ea,quæ disputata cum Boëthio sunt, neque de virtute meritorum Christi quicquam tradidit in hac quæstione, sed tantùm de depen- dentia à resurrectione Christi: Ubi verò, ut jam ante 37. annos in Exegef. Augustanæ Confessio- nis Art. XVII. §. III. Th. IIX. monuimus, di- stinguendum omninò inter dependentiam excita- tionis impiorum à resurrectione Christi, quæ effe- ctus est, à causa meritoria; & dependentiam ejus- modi, quæ consequentis est ab Antecedenti; ac re- stitutionem vitæ corporalis impiorum neque fru- ctum aut effectum esse meriti resurrectionis Chri- sti docuimus, quia fructus meritorum Christi be- neficia sunt, ad misericordiam DEI pertinentia, & in se semper sunt salutaria, nec nisi per fidem obtinentur: Neque à resurrectione Christi depen- dere, tanquam Consequens ab Antecedenti, quia etiamsi Christus nunquam mortuus & resuscita- tus esset, impii tamen è mortuis resuscitandi fo- rent. Quod verò ad hanc Apostolicam tracta- tionem, non de impiorum resurrectione ad judi- cium, quæ à justitia dependet, sed beatorum ad vitam, quæ merito Christi tribuenda est, hic agi, è textu luculentum est. Quanquam enim v. 12. ge- neratim è Christi resurrectione id probet, quod falsò negetur, dari resurrectionem à mortuis, utpo- te quæ exemplo Christi constet,non tamen in eo sub- sistit, quod possibilis sit resurrectio, sed peculiariter disserit de resurrectione ad æternam vitam,eamque probat inter alia è Christi merito, quia concludit à nexu necessario causæ propriæ & sufficientis cum suo effectu, qualis nexus inter Christum & mor- tuorum resurrectionem non est, agitque de tali re- surrectione, qualis Christi erat, quæ verò erat re- surrectio ad gloriam:Et juxta quam Christus ἀπαρ- χὴ est dormientium, eorum scilicet, qui in Christo obdormierunt,v.18.19. Non autem impiorum; Ho- rum enim ἀπαρχὴ non est Christus, quia non est de ipsorum massâ. De eâ insuper resurrectione agit, quam sequitur corporum gloria, & regni Dei possessio, vers. 43. 50. quæque mortis est victoria, v. 45. qualis non est impiorum resurrectio, penes quos vitæ restitutio non tàm est mortis destru- ctio, quàm ejusdem instauratio, imò duplicatio, quia est corporis in æternam mortem traditio, ubi non absorbetur mors, sed reviviscit ad æter- nos corporis, animique cruciatus. Quod ergò in Christo omnes vivificari dicuntur, intelligen- dum est de iis omnibus, qui per fidem sunt in Christo, & in Christo obdormiunt, quantum ad actu- alem vitæ per Christum acquisitæ participationem, ad quam fide opus est : Non verò de omnibus hominibus generatim, nisi quantum ad salutis & vitæ acquisitionem, quæ merito Christi parta est omnibus, utut eadem actu non potiantur & fru- antur, nisi soli fideles. De causá quidem vitæ uni- versali, non de fructu ad omnes homines actu red- undante, quia qui fide destituuntur, quâ solâ fru- ctus ille vitæ per Christi meritum partæ obtine- tur, fructu illo non potiuntur, agit Apostolus, Rom. V. 18. At vicissim v. 19. cum de applicatio- ne agit, non omnes homines, sed solùm fideles actu justificari per Christi justitiam docuit. Itaque hoc loco cum ad actualem vivificationem hæc attine- ant: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Chri- sto vivificabuntur, collatio instituitur, partim ra- tione originis mortis & vitæ, quod Adam ejusque peccatum causa sit mortis, Christus verò ejusque meritum causa sit vitæ; partim ratione universa- litatis subjectorum, sed hoc pacto, quod ad Deum omnes perveniant, quicunque ab Adamo procre- ati sunt per carnalem generationem, & ita simili- ter omnes, qui à Christo originem ducunt, per spiritualem regenerationem, vitam beatam & vivi- ficationem consequuturi sint. Quo de Augusti- nus Epist. LVII. ad Dardan. Omnes & omnes ideò dixit; quia in mortem nemo, nisi per illum (Ada- mum) in vitam nemo, nisi per istum (Christum.) In primo patuit, quod hominis arbitrium valeret ad mortem. In Christo autem, quod DEI adjuto- rium valeret ad vitam. Et lib. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 30. Omnium ergò corporis mortem factam per unum hominem dixit, & omnium cor- poris resurrectionem in vitam æternam per unum Christum futuram esse promisit. Quomodo ergò plus nobis nocuit ille peccando, quàm iste profuit redi- mendo, cum per illius peccatum temporaliter mo- riamur, per istius autem redemptionem non ad tem- poralem vitam, sed ad perpetuam resurgamus? Ad- de & Epist. XXIX. ad Hieron. ad Hilar. LXXXIX. quæst. 3. Epist. CLVII. ad Optat. l. XIII. de Civit. DEI cap. 33. Lib. XX. c. 20. Leo M. epist. XXXII. referens hæc verba: Ita & in Christo omnes vivi- ficabuntur: Hi iterum omnes, ait, qui licet in Adam sint nati, in Christo tamen inveniuntur renati. Ad- de homil. XV. de pass. Domini. Quibus accedunt glossa interlinearis, Dionysius Carthusianus, Hof- meisterus, Hervæus, Estius, aliique Pontificii : Re- formati plerique omnes Martyr, Ursinus, Buca- nus, Polanus &c. Nec non B. Lutherus Tom. VI. Jenens. in priorem ad Corinth. XV. ad h. l. B. Ægidius Hunnius, Agi hic, inquit, de vivificatione ad vitam beatam, sequens membrum textus Apo- stolici arguit, in quo eos, qui per Christum vivifican- tur, dicit esse Christi, quæ piorum seu credentium non ignota periphrasis est. B. David Rungius disp. XVI. in 1. ad Corinth. parte III. Ex vi hujus ar- gumenti patet, Apostolum non in genere de mortuo- rum resurrectione tàm ad vitam, quàm ad damna- tionem agere, sed speciatim de resurrectione ad vi- tam æternam, quæ solis contingit in Christum creden- tibus. Et de his verissima est Apostoli ratio. Alioqui si accommodetur argumentum Pauli ad omnes in uni- versum homines, tùm non procedet à causa ad effe- ctum, sed ab exemplo tantùm. Neque amplius con- cludet, quàm posse mortuos resurgere, quia Christus resurrexit. Sed Paulus non subsistit in consideratio- ne ejus, quod fieri potest, sed necessario concludit, certò mortuos resurrecturos, quia Christus resurre- xit. Quæ ratio argumentandi tantùm ad creden- tes & salvandos pertinet. Neque enim adscriben- dum est resurrectioni Christi, quod impii resurre- cturi sunt ad æterna supplicia, Dan. XII. Joh. V. Adde & Tilemann. Heshusium in h. l. p. 328. & D. Gerhard. de resurrectione mortuorum §. 19. & 55.

## 15:23
V. 23. Ἕκαστῷ δὲ ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ τάγματι. Tertullian III. against Marcion understands within the thousand years, which are mentioned in the Apocalypse XX. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. that some will rise again sooner, others later, according to their merits. Nor does he seem to mean anything else in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, when he says: But each in his own order, namely because also in his own body. For the order is nothing other than the disposer of merits. But to me that matter concerning the first resurrection of the martyrs, which is in the Apocalypse, is held as certain, that it was known neither to Paul nor to Christians before the publication of the Apocalypse. But it is credible that Paul both knew and indicated here that individuals would rise again earlier in such a way as they had more closely expressed the image of Christ. In a similar sense we had τὸ τάξιν above XIV. 48. Ἀπαρχὴ χρισός) He has already risen. Ἔπειτα οἱ τῦ χρισῦ. Those who have faithfully served Christ. Ἐν τῇ παρεσίᾳ ἀυτῦ. Namely ζωοποιηθήσονται. Concerning the diverse readings of the Latin Codices, let Estius be consulted. It suffices for us that the Greeks agree, whom the Syrian also favors, indeed even some Latin MSS. and ancient concordances, as also the Glossa Ordinaria, and Lyranus, with Estius admitting that they read: Then those who are Christ's at his coming. But those words, and each in his own order, look to an order not of time, as Cajetan wants, but of dignity, which Estius observes that most, both Greeks and Latins, feel will be according to the diversity of the degrees of glory, and that the things said below v. 40. 41. 42. favor that sense. Others establish four orders: 1. the firstfruits Christ, 2. those who have fallen asleep in Christ, 3. those surviving until the day of judgment, 4. the other deceased. But Christ is not in this τάγματι [order], because this passage treats of those who will be made alive; Christ, however, has long since risen and now [is] as the Ἀπαρχὴ [firstfruits], by whose power οἱ τῦ χρισῦ [those who are Christ's] will rise, destined to follow Christ who was raised long ago, but finally ἐν τῇ παρεσίᾳ ἀυτῦ [at his coming], lest anyone dream of some resurrection, which was done by the Chiliasts, before the last day, or the advent of Christ. Therefore it is added: Εἶτα τὸ τέλῷ [Then the end]. Concerning which blessed Luther [writes] on this passage, fol. 235: 'For such is required by the order, that he should be the first to break the path and bring life, thereafter to gather together one after another all who are his members and belong to the resurrection, so that they all come forth together on one day which He has determined for this purpose, and live eternally with him.' But the Papists are foolish when they thrust Monastic orders into this passage. Suarez in I. Thom. tr. lib. II. c. 20. Cornelius à Lapide, etc. so that the older orders are to rise first, then the more recent ones. But in this way the Jesuits will easily rise in the last place, which seems less fitting for the Society of Jesus.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἕκαστῷ δὲ ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ τάγματι. Tertullianus III. adversus Marcionem intelligit intra mille annos, quorum mentio fit in Apocalypsi XX. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. pro meritis alios maturius, alios tardius resurrectu- ros. Nec aliud videtur velle libro de resurrectione carnis, cum dicit: Unusquisque autem in suo ordine, scilicet quia & in suo corpore. Ordo enim non alius quàm meritorum dispo- sitor. Sed mihi certum habetur illud de resurrectione priore martyrum, quod est in Apocalypsi, neque Paulo, neque Christianis ante Apocalypsis editionem fuisse cognitum. Sed illud credibile est & scivisse & hic indicasse Paulum, resurrecturos ita prius singulos, prout Christi imaginem propius expresserint. Simili quodammodo sensu habuimus τὸ τάξιν supra XIV. 48. Ἀπαρχὴ χρισός) Is jam surrexit. Ἔπειτα οἱ τῦ χρισῦ. Qui Christo fideliter servierunt. Ἐν τῇ παρεσίᾳ ἀυτῦ. Nempè ζωοποιηθήσονται. De lectionibus diversis Codicum Latinorum vi- deatur Estius. Nobis sufficit, quod Græci consen- tiant, quibus etiam Syrus favet, imò etiam Latini nonnulli MSS. & concordantiæ antiquæ, ut & Glossa Ordinaria, & Lyranus, fatente Estio legentes: De- inde qui sunt Christi in adventu ejus. Ordinem autem non temporis, ut Cajetanus vult, sed digni- tatis respiciunt illa, & unusquisque in suo ordine, quem secundum diversitatem graduum gloriæ fu- turum, plerosque cùm Græcos, quàm Latinos senti- re, eique sensui, quæ infra dicuntur v. 40. 41. 42. favere, observat Estius. Alii quatuor ordines sta- tuunt 1. primitiæ Christus, 2. qui in Christo obdor- mierunt, 3. Superstites ad diem judicii, 4. Cæteri de- functi. Sed Christus in hoc τάγματι non est, quia hic de illis, qui vivificabuntur, agitur; Christus ve- rò jam pridem resurrexit & modo ceu Ἀπαρχὴ, cu- jus virtute resurgent οἱ τῦ χρισῦ, sequuturi Chri- stum olim resuscitatum, sed demum ἐν τῇ παρε- σίᾳ ἀυτῦ, ne quis resurrectionem aliquam somniet, quod à Chiliastis factum, ante diem novissimum, vel adventum Christi. Ideo additur: Εἶτα τὸ τέ- λῷ. Quo de B. Lutherus in hunc locum fol. 235. Denn solches fordert die Ordnung, daß er der er- ste wäre, der die Bahn breche, und das Leben bräch- te, darnach alle nach einander zusammen sammlete, die seine Glieder sind, und zur Aufferstehung gehö- ren, daß sie alle zugleich herfür kommen auf einen Tag, den Er darzu bestimmt hat, und ewiglich mit ihm leben. Inepti autem sunt Papistæ, cum hic ordines Mo- nasticos ingerunt. Suarez. in I. Thom. tr. lib. II. c. 20. Cornelius à Lapide &c. ita ut antiquiores or- dines primò resurrecturi sint, deinde recentiores. Ita verò Jesuitæ facilè postremo loco resurgent, quod societati Jesu minus congruum videtur.

## 15:24
V. 24. Εἶτα τὸ τέλῷ [Then the end]. Namely, of that kingdom which Christ administered in the place and name of God the Father, as follows. Ὅταν παραδῶ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ Θεῷ κὶ Πατρὶ [When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father]. Namely, just as governors sent into provinces used to return the power received to the Caesars.

That Christ administered the kingdom of grace in the place and stead of God the Father is a phrase of the Socinians, not of Scripture, which makes Christ not a vicar, but σύνθρονον [co-enthroned] with the Father. For the Father did not divest Himself of authority when He gave to the Son according to the flesh all judgment and all power in heaven and on earth, John V. 22, Matt. XXVIII. 18. For all things whatsoever the Father does, the Son also does likewise, on account of which communication of power made to Christ as man, Christ will in turn deliver up the kingdom to the Father at the end of the world. This handing over of the kingdom, however, which he received from the Father, who gave him power over all flesh, John 17:2, is not merely a presentation of the elect, as some understand the elect through the kingdom, as Hilary lib. 11 de Trin., Augustine lib. 1 de Trin. cap. 8, Hugo Victor in this place explain, i.e., When he shall have brought his elect, in whom he now reigns while they live by faith, to the contemplation of GOD and the Father. And Heshusius: Christ will hand over the kingdom, that is, the Church, gathered by the Gospel from the whole human race, he will bring into the sight of GOD and the Father: That the Church may behold the Father face to face, in whom it believed, and now joyfully triumph over all enemies, having been overcome through Christ, and may enjoy the sweetest fellowship of GOD for all eternity. Then God will no longer deal with us through the word, through the sacraments: Then there will be no need to believe what we do not see. But we shall immediately behold the divinity, immediately God will suffuse us with his light, wisdom, justice, life, and joy: We shall see God, as he is, face to face, without any covering: then we shall experience, and truly possess, what we here believe according to the word of GOD. This is to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, namely, to set the triumphant Church before the sight of the Father, free from all its enemies. To which the passage Eph. 5:27 could be referred. These things, I say, even if they are correct, yet the handing over of the kingdom is not to be defined solely by the presentation of the elect, but it is also a resignation of the government which Christ exercised in this age, which, how it will come to pass, no one will easily explain. Some explain it as a public and solemn profession, by which he is to testify that he attributes the entire glory of his kingdom to GOD the Father, not only before the Angels and the elect, but also before the reprobate, so that all may acknowledge that power and glory belong to GOD alone. But this will not happen through an absolute abdication of the kingdom, because we know from Isa. 9:6, Dan. 7:14, Luke 1:33 that his kingdom will be eternal and will have no end. But as to the form of government, or quality, namely the communion of administration, that which had a place in this age, as being through the word and sacraments, and their ministry, and not without battle and warfare, since he must now rule in the midst of his enemies, Psalm 110:2, then the enemies will have been placed as a footstool for his feet. Christ will nevertheless reign in another mode of government, befitting the kingdom of glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as God in the unity of essence, as man at the right hand of glory for all eternity. The Apostle is not speaking (these are the words of the blessed Balduinus) of the kingdom of Christ in himself, which he is never to lay down, but of the state of his government, which he will change after the end of the world: Where he will no longer rule the elect with the scepter of the preached word, nor will they have any infirmities, by which Satan exercises them here: Nor will he any longer permit persecutions of his kingdom, but all the subjects of his kingdom will enjoy perfect holiness, and intuitive knowledge, and the joy of Christ the King, and all his enemies will be a footstool for his feet. Theophylact illustrates this with an example: An Emperor entrusts to his Son the waging of war against the most remote nations. And so, those nations having been subdued, and the war finished, the son can then indeed be said to have handed over the war to the father, that is, to have completed the task entrusted to him by the father. Paul therefore says that all things have then already reached an end and are terminated, when the Son has subjected them to his dominion. For Christ is then to have perfect empire in all things, when we shall no longer disagree among ourselves, nor shall we have obeyed GOD in part, and in part

the Demons. Whence it happens that Christ hands over to the Father the empire, snatched no differently than from a tyrant (the Devil), made ready and free. The blessed Dan. Cramerus, on the kingdom of Christ, Part II, chap. IV, page 339, teaches that the kingdom of power, which extends to all creatures, is also to be handed over by Christ: Because with the objects of Christ's power changed, inanimate and irrational things, which will cease, the mode of the kingdom of Christ's power will also be changed. But whether the handing over and resignation of the government of those things which no longer exist, but cease with the world itself, has a place here, might seem doubtful. Therefore, the cessation of government over irrational and inanimate creatures, which is nothing once they are destroyed, is one thing; the handing over and resignation of a certain form of government, by which he rules subjects who must indeed survive if only the mode of government changes, and not the government itself, is another. The kingdom of grace, therefore, will cease in such a way by reason of the economy, when it is handed over to GOD, that the kingdom of glory follows, as regards the elect, resurrected to eternal life, and as regards the Angels. But as for the reprobate, resurrected to eternal punishment, they will be subject to Christ, along with the Devils, indeed placed as a footstool for his feet. Furthermore, that kingdom and dominion will be common to Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as GOD, because of the homoousion, as man, because of the grace of the communicated divine Majesty, which is to be distinguished from the kingly office of Christ, which looks to the present age, or the economy of the kingdom of grace. The blessed Luther on this passage: He speaks of the kingdom of Christ now on earth, which is a kingdom of faith, wherein He reigns, through the Word, not in a visible public state, but it is just as one sees the sun through a cloud; one sees the light well, but the sun itself one does not see. But when the clouds are gone, then one sees both light and sun together in one state: Thus Christ now reigns with the Father undivided, and it is one kingdom. The only difference is that it is now dark and hidden, or veiled and covered, entirely grasped in faith and in the Word, so that one sees nothing more of it than Baptism, Sacrament, nor hears anything of it than the external Word, which is all his power and might, through which He reigns, and accomplishes everything. And in that way Megalander distinguishes the kingdom of Christ and of GOD: That means St. Paul, when he says that Christ will deliver the kingdom of God to the Father, that is, he will put aside faith and the hidden essence, and present his own before God the Father, and thus set us openly into the kingdom which He has established, and now daily drives forward, so that we shall see Him without veil and dark words, most clearly, and it will then be called not a kingdom of faith, but of clarity and public essence. And although it is one and the same kingdom, both of Christ (who became man for the sake of it, that He might establish faith in Him) and of God (for whoever hears Christ, hears God the Father Himself), yet it is now properly called the Lord Christ's kingdom, because God is now hidden in His majesty, and has given everything to Christ, that He might bring us to Him through His Word and Baptism, and also hidden Himself in Christ, that we should seek and recognize God nowhere but in Him. There, however, it will properly be called God's kingdom, after Christ will have accomplished everything that He is to accomplish, and will no longer rule under our weakness and adversity, but death and sin, and everything that is against

That we shall see Him with the Father in the Divine Majesty, and shall no longer need to pursue His Gospel, Baptism, and forgiveness of sin, nor learn to know Him, nor fear ourselves for any kind of misfortune, but rather pure God, eternal righteousness, blessedness, and life shall be with us in the present visible being, and shall share all such things with us, so that we shall be as He is.

When He shall have abolished all rule and all authority and power.

That καταργήσῃ, which is an aorist, has here the significance of a pluperfect. For what is said here precedes the παρουσίαν. But those names, rule, authority, power, signify all the empires and kingdoms of the world and lesser governments. For it refers, though in a more sublime sense, to that which is in Daniel VII. 14, 27. Then indeed Christ will be the ruler of the kings of the earth and King of kings, as He is called in Rev. I. 5, 1 Tim. VI. 15, when, with all that power destroyed, He will pass judgment on kings no less than on the lowest of all.

Grotius, as far as it appears, understands this of secular powers; Cajetan of all Magistrates, as he calls them, even Ecclesiastical and Angelic, to which he assigns certain prefectures in this age: but the sacred scriptures are ignorant of what these perpetual prefectures, differing by reason of provinces, are. Augustine in De Trinitate, book 1, chapter 8, and other Latins restrict these to the angelic orders. But how is it said that they will be evacuated? The Greek Interpreters, as also the ancient Latins, Ambrose, Pelagius, Primasius, and Sedulius, interpret these as referring to the opposing powers or demons, who are called by these names in Eph. VI and Rom. VIII, which sense Estius judges to be clearly required by those things which follow in verse 25. Blessed Hunnius takes this to refer both to spiritual powers and to worldly empires. And therefore Christ will also then deliver the kingdom to GOD and His Father, when He has first, by His glorious advent, abolished every principality, and power, and virtue, that is, when those spiritual enemies, Satan, Death, and hell, have already been crushed under the feet of the faithful by the power of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the empires of this world, which had been adverse and hostile to the kingdom of Christ, have been reduced to nothing. To which view the commentary of Blessed Balduinus also seems to incline. Heshusius adds to these, with Blessed Luther, the ministries and offices of the Church, as well as the Principalities and ministries of the Angels. But although the Angelic ministries, which now flourish with regard to the faithful, for whose sake they are sent forth as ministering spirits, Heb. I. 12, as well as the ecclesiastical offices, are to have an end, yet this is not the evacuation of powers, that is: of Angelic virtues and ecclesiastical principalities, which scripture certainly does not admit, assigning to Bishops not rule, but the ministry of teaching, Luke XXII. 25, 26. And therefore these seem rather to be referred to the opposing powers, both Diabolical and worldly, under which the Pope is entirely comprehended, with his Cardinals and Bishops, as the chief enemies of Christ and His kingdom, provided those enemies are understood in whose midst Christ reigns, and whom He makes the footstool of His feet. Whence the kingdom of Christ is said to be about to destroy the kingdoms of the world, Daniel II. 44. If, however, we look to the proper scope of the Apostle, which is the confirmation of the resurrection of the dead, perhaps the Diabolical powers are more correctly understood. For the destruction of the kingdoms of the world does not contribute to that, which also are nowhere comprehended under the same title with the Diabolical powers, just as in Eph. VI. 12, by rules and authorities the spirits of wickedness are understood, and so also in Rom. VIII. 38, rules and powers are explained as referring to Diabolical powers. Add also 1 Pet. III. 22, where they are said to be subject to Christ sitting at the right hand of God, after He went into heaven, as authorities and powers. These, therefore, although subject to the rule of Christ, can do no harm to the faithful: yet they dominate in the world until they are evacuated by Christ, whether with regard to power, because they could no longer lie in wait for the faithful, and with the unfaithful they will certainly be cast into the infernal fire, whence the Prince of this world will no longer be the Devil, a title he now enjoys; whence, however, it cannot be certainly gathered that Demons will exercise no power at all after the time of the last judgment over the damned, but only that the principality of the world and of this age will cease. For there they will not torment the damned as Princes, but as executioners, if indeed after the judgment Demons will preside over the punishments of these, which point Blessed Gerhard leaves in the middle in his work on hell, § 73, and Estius clearly denies in his commentary on book IV of the Sentences, distinction. XXIX. And so he wishes that men, as well as the Demons themselves, are to be tormented by eternal fires solely by the power of God without the ministry of Demons: Or with regard to that subordination also of rule, authority, and power, which flourishes in this world; but at the end of the age and in eternity is to cease. Although indeed the empires of the world are also to cease, that is designated by the general name of the end, by which the consummation of the age is expressed, then the end. But here the kingdom and power of the Devil is opposed to the kingdom of Christ, because the consummation of the age is to be, or the end of the world, when Christ will deliver His kingdom to God the Father, but the kingdom of the Devil will be destroyed, or evacuated. For both the delivery of the kingdom of God and the evacuation of the Diabolical kingdom confirm the resurrection of the dead. For he could not deliver the kingdom to God and the Father, unless the elect had been resurrected from death, who are to be presented to God: Nor is it a true evacuation of the Diabolical kingdom and of the ἐξυσίας κὶ δυνάμεως of Satan, with the elect established under the power of death, because the Devil is described as having τὸ κράτος, the empire of death, Heb. II. 14. As for the confirmation sought from Psalm CX. 1, that holds correctly, even if it treats only of the evacuation of the Diabolical power in v. 24. For if all enemies are to be placed as a footstool for the feet of the Lord, it is necessary that the Diabolical powers also be evacuated, and that death itself must be evacuated, from which the Apostle gathers this, inasmuch as it also pertains to those enemies, and is described as a Tyrant dominating over all enemies, Rom. V. 14. The passage of Daniel ch. VII. 14. 27. has been dealt with in its proper place. It is not a question there of the subjection of the empires of the world at the consummation of the age, but in the kingdom of grace, not of the evacuation of kingdoms, but of the conversion of peoples to the kingdom of Christ.

Latin:

V. 24. Εἶτα τὸ τέλῷ. Nempe regni illius, quod DEI patris vice ac nomine Christus administravit, ut sequitur. Ὅταν παραδῶ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ Θεῷ κὶ Πατρὶ. Nempe sicut præsides in provincias missi reddebant Cæsaribus acceptam potestatem.

Dei Patris vice ac loco Christum administrasse regnum gratiæ, phrasis est Socinianorum, non scri- pturæ, quæ Christum non vicarium, sed σύνθρονον Patri facit. Neque enim Pater sese exuit imperio, cum Filio secundum carnem dedit omne judicium omnemque potestatem in cælo & in terra, Joh. V. 22. Matth. XXVIII. 18. Nam omnia quæcunque facit Pater, similiter facit & Filius, ob quam pote- statis communicationem, Christo, ut homini, fa- ctam, Christus Patri vicissim tradet regnum in fine mundi. Hæc autem regni, quod à Patre accepit, qui ei potestatem dedit omnis carnis, Joh. XVII. 2. traditio non est electorum tantum præsentatio, quemad- modum electos per regnum nonnulli intelligunt, ut Hilarius lib. XI. de Trin. August. l. 1. de Trin. cap. 8. Hugo Victor in h. l. exponunt, q. d. Cum perduxerit electos suos, in quibus nunc ex fide vi- ventibus regnat ad contemplationem DEI & Pa- tris. Et Heshusius: Tradet Christus regnum, id est Ecclesiam, collectam Evangelio, ex toto genere humano, adducet in conspectum DEI & Patris: Ut Ecclesia coram intueatur Patrem, in quem credi- dit, & jam læta triumphet de omnibus hostibus, per Christum devictis, & dulcissima consuetudine DEI in omni æternitate fruatur. Tum non am- plius aget nobiscum Deus per verbum, per sacra- menta: Tum non opus erit credere, quæ non vide- mus. Sed immediatè intuebimur divinitatem, im- mediatè Deus perfundet nos suâ luce, sapientiâ, justitiâ, vitâ, & lætitiâ: Videbimus Deum, sicuti est, à facie ad faciem, sine omni involucro: tum experiemur, & reverâ possidebimus, quæ hic secun- dum DEI verbum credimus. Hoc est regnum Deo & Patri tradere, nimirum triumphantem Eccle- siam de omnibus hostibus suis statuere in conspectum Patris. Quo referri posset locus Eph. V. 27. Hæc, inquam, etsi rectè se habeant, non tamen solâ præsentatione electorum definienda est regni tra- ditio, sed etiam est resignatio regiminis, quod ges- sit Christus in hoc seculo, quæ, quomodo futura sit, nemo facilè explicabit. De professione publi- câ & solenni explicant nonnulli, quâ testaturus sit, se universam regni sui gloriam DEO Patri ac- ceptam referre, non coram Angelis & electis tantùm, sed etiam coram reprobis, ut omnes agno- scant, potentiam & gloriam esse solius DEI. Non autem id fiet per abdicationem omnimodam regni, quia regnum ejus fore æternum, nec habiturum finem, novimus ex Es. IX. 6. Dan. VII. 14. Luc. I. 33. Sed quà regiminis formam, seu qualitatem, com- munionem nempe administrationis eam, quæ lo- cum habuit in hoc seculo, utpote per verbum & sacramenta, eorumque ministerium, nec sine pugnâ & militiâ, quum dominari eum jam oporteat in medio inimicorum suorum, Psalm. CX. 2. tum inimici positi erunt in scabellum pedum ejus. Re- gnabit tamen Christus alio regiminis modo, con- veniente regno gloriæ, cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto, quà Deus in unitate essentiæ, quà homo in dextra gloriæ in omnem æternitatem. Non agit Aposto- lus (verba B. Balduini sunt) de regno Christi in se, quod nunquam depositurus est, sed de statu guber- nationis suæ, quem mutabit post finem mundi: Ubi non amplius reget electos sceptro verbi prædicati, nec infirmitates aliquas habebunt, quibus hic eos exercet Satan: Nec persequutiones regni sui amplius permittet, sed omnes regni sui subditi fruentur per- fectâ sanctitate, & intuitivâ notitiâ, lætitiâque Christi Regis, & omnes ipsius hostes erunt scabellum pedum suorum. Illustrat id exemplo Theophy- lactus: Imperator quispiam Filio bellum, adversus remotissimas nationes procurandum, demandat. Subactis itaque gentibus illis, & bello finito, dici tunc quidem filius potest, bellum patri tradidisse, hoc est, demandatum sibi à patre negotium absol- visse. Dicit itaque Paulus, tunc omnia finem esse jam nacta & terminata, cum ea suæ ditioni sub- jecerit Filius. Christus namque in omnibus tunc perfectè est imperium habiturus, cum non amplius inter nos dissidebimus, nec DEO partim, partim

Dæmonibus paruerimus. Quo fit, ut Patri Christus, haud secus, quam tyranno (Diabolo) ereptum im- perium, expeditum & liberum tradat. B. Dan. Cra- merus de regno Christi parte II. cap. IV. pag. 339. regnum potentiæ, quod se extendit ad omnes crea- turas, etiam à Christo tradendum docet: Quia variatis objectis potentiæ Christi, rebus inanimatis & irrationalibus, quæ desinent, variabitur quoque modus regni potentiæ Christi. Sed an hic locum habeat traditio & resignatio regiminis illorum, quæ non amplius supersunt, sed cum mundo ipso desinunt, dubium videri queat. Aliud ergo est cessatio regiminis super creaturas irrationales & in- animatas, quod destructis iisdem nullum est, aliud traditio & resignatio certæ formæ regiminis, qua sub- ditos, quos utique superesse oportet, si modus tan- tum regiminis variet, non ipsum regimen desinat. Regnum itaque gratiæ ita ratione œconomias ces- saturum, cum tradetur DEO, ut subsequatur, quoad electos, ad æternam vitam resuscitatos, & quoad Angelos, regnum gloriæ. Quod autem ad reprobos, ad æternam pœnam resuscictatos, subjecti illi Christo erunt, cum Diabolis, imo positi in sca- bellum pedum ipsius. Cæterum regnum & domi- nium illud Christo erit commune cum Patre ac Spiritu Sancto, ut DEO, ob ὁμοουσίαν ut homini, ob communicatæ divinæ Majestatis gratiam, quod distinguendum ab officio Christi Regio, quod ad præsens seculum spectat, vel œconomiâ regni gratiæ. B. Lutherus in hunc locum: Er redet von dem Reich Christi jetzt auff Erden, welches ist ein Reich des Glaubens, darinnen Er regieret, durch das Wort, nicht im sichtlichen offentlichen Wesen, son- dern ist gleich wie man die Sonne siehet durch eine Wolcke, da siehet man wohl das Licht, aber die Son- ne selbst siehet man nicht. Wenn aber die Wolcken hinweg sind, so siehet man beyde Licht und Son- ne zugleich in einerley Wesen: Also regieret jetzt Christus mit dem Vater ungetheilet, und ist einer- ley Reich. Allein ist der Unterscheid, daß es jetzt dunckel und verborgen ist, oder verhüllet und zuge- decket, gar im Glauben und ins Wort gefasset, daß man nicht mehr davon siehet, denn die Tauffe, Sa- crament, noch davon höret, denn das äusserliche Wort, das ist alle seine Krafft und Macht, dadurch Er regieret, und alles ausrichtet. Atque eâ ra- tione distinguit regnum Christi & DEI Mega- lander: Das meynet St. Paulus, als er spricht, daß Christus das Reich GOttes dein Vater über- antworten wird, das ist, er wird den Glauben und das verborgene Wesen beyseit thun, und die Seine darstellen für GOtt dem Vater, und uns also offent- bahrlich setzen in das Reich, das Er angerichtet hat, und jetzt täglich treibet, daß wir Ihn sehen wer- den ohn Deckel und dunckel Wort, auffs allerklä- reste, und wird denn heissen nicht ein Reich des Glaubens, sondern der Klarheit und offentlichen Wesens. Und wiewohl es einerley Reich ist, beyde Christi, (welcher um desselben willen ist Mensch worden, daß Er den Glauben an ihn auffrichtete) und GOttes, (denn wer Christum höret, der höret GOtt den Vater selbst) doch heisset es jetzt eigent- lich des HErrn Christi Reich, weil GOtt jetzt in seiner Majestät verborgen ist, und Christo alles ge- geben hat, daß Er durch sein Wort und Tauffe uns zu Ihm bringe, darzu auch sich selbst in Chri- stum verborgen, daß wir GOtt nirgend, denn in Ihm suchen und erkennen sollen. Dort aber wird es eigentlich GOttes Reich heissen, nachdem Christus alles wird ausgerichtet haben, was Er ausrichten soll, und nicht mehr regieren unter unser Schwachheit und Widerwärtigkeit, son- dern Tod und Sünde, und alles, was wider

Dass wir Ihn mit dem Vater in der Göttlichen Ma- jestät sehen, und nicht mehr werden bedürffen sein Evangelium, Tausse und Vergebung der Sünde zu treiben, noch Ihn erkennen lernen, oder uns für einigerley Unglück mehr fürchten, sondern wird eitel GOtt, ewige Gerechtigkeit, Seligkeit und Le- ben bey uns seyn in gegenwärtigem sichtbaren We- sen, und uns solches alles mittheilen, daß wir seyn werden, wie Er ist.

Ὅταν καταργήσῃ πᾶσαν ἀρχὴν καὶ πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν καὶ δύναμιν.

Illud καταργήσῃ quod est ἀόριστον hic plusquam per- fecti habet significationem. Nam quod hic dicitur, præce- dit παρουσίαν. Illa autem nomina ἀρχὴν, ἐξουσίαν, δύναμιν, significant omnia imperia & regna mundi ac regimina mi- nora. Respicitur enim, sed sublimiore sensu id, quod est apud Danielem VII. 14. 27. Tunc verò Christus erit ἄρχων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς & βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων, quomo- do vocatur Apoc. I. 5. 1. Tim. VI. 15. cum destructo omni illo potentatu de Regibus non minus quàm de infimis qui- busque sententiam feret.

De potestatibus secularibus, quantum apparet, intelligit Grotius; Cajetanus de omnibus Magi- stratibus, quos vocat, etiam Ecclesiasticis & An- gelicis, quæ hisce præfecturæ certæ assignatæ in hoc seculo: quas verò præfecturas perpetuas, pro- vinciarum ratione differentes, ignorant scriptu- ræ sacræ. Augustinus de Trinitate lib. 1. cap. 8. alii- que Latini ad Angelicos ordines hæc restringunt. Sed quomodo dicitur, illos evacuatum iri? Græci Interpretes, ut & veteres Latini, Ambrosius, Pe- lagius, Primasius & Sedulius de potestatibus ad- versariis vel dæmonibus hæc interpretantur, qui hisce nominibus vocantur Eph. VI. Roman. VIII. quem sensum planè exigere ea, quæ v 25. sequun- tur, censet Estius. B. Hunnius tum de potestatibus spiritualibus, tum de imperiis mundanis hæc acci- pit. Ideoque etiam tum tradet Christus regnum DEO & Patri suo, quando prius per adventum suum gloriosum aboleverit omnem principatum, & potestatem & virtutem, hoc est, quando jam spiri- tuales illi hostes Satanas, Mors & infernus, virtute Domini Jesu Christi, sub pedes fidelium contriti, & imperia hujus mundi, quæ Christi regno fuerant adversa & infesta, in nihilum redacta fuerint. Quo etiam abire B. Balduini commentarius videtur. Heshusius addit ad hæc, cum B. Luthero, ministe- ria & officia Ecclesiastica, ut & Principatus & mi- nisteria Angelorum. Sed quamvis Angelica mini- steria, quæ nunc vigent quoad fideles, ob quos e- mittuntur πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ, Ebr. I. 12. ut & officia Ecclesiastica finem habitura sint, non tamen hoc est evacuatio potestatum, id est: & virtutum Angelicarum, & principatuum Ecclesiasticorum, quos utique scriptura non admittit, Episcopis non imperium, sed docendi ministerium affi- gnans, Luc. XXII. 25. 26. Ideoque ad adversarias potestates tùm Diabolicas, tùm mundanas, sub qui- bus omninò comprehenditur Papa, cum Cardi- nalibus ac Episcopis suis, ceu præcipui hostes Chri- sti & regni ejus, hæc videntur potiùs referenda, siquidem illi hostes intelligantur, in quorum me- dio dominatur Christus, quosque scabellum pe- dum suorum ponit. Unde regna mundi destru- cturum dicitur regnum Christi, Daniel. II. 44. Si tamen scopum proprium Apostoli, qui est confir- matio resurrectionis mortuorum, respiciamus, fortè rectiùs potestates Diabolicæ intelligentur. Nam destructio regnorum mundi eò non facit, quæ et- iam nuspiam cum Diabolicis potestatibus sub eo- dem titulo comprehenduntur, quemadmodum Eph. VI. 12. per ἀρχὰς κὶ ἐξουσίας τὰ πνεύματα τῆς πονηρίας intelliguntur, atque ita etiam Rom. VIII. 38. ἀρχαὶ καὶ δυνάμεις de Diabolicis potestatibus explicantur. Adde & 1. Petr. III. 22. ubi subjectæ Christo ad dextram Dei sedenti, postquam pro- fectus est in cœlum, dicuntur ἐξυσίαι καὶ δυνάμεις. Hæ ergò, etsi Christi imperio subjectæ, fideli- bus nihil nocere possint: In mundo tamen domi- nantur, donec à Christo evacuabuntur, sive quod ad potestatem, quia nec fidelibus insidiari amplius potuerunt, & cum infidelibus certè in ignem infernalem detrudentur, unde Princeps mundi non amplius tùm erit Diabolus, quo titulo nunc gaudet; Unde tamen certò colligi nequit, Dæ- mones nullam amplius potestatem post tempus no- vissimi judicii exercituros in homines damnatos, sed principatum mundi, hujusque seculi tantùm defiturum. Ibi enim non ut Principes, sed ut licto- res damnatos torquebunt, si omninò post jud́- cium Dæmones præerunt suppliciis horum, quod verò in medio relinquit B. Gerhard. de in- ferno §. 73. ac planè inficiatur Estius ad lib. IV. sen- tent. distinct. XXIX. adeoque vult, solâ tunc Dei virtute absque Dæmonum ministerio homines, ut & ipsos Dæmones æternis ignibus esse cruciandos: Si- ve quod ad subordinationem etiam illam ἀρχῆς, ἐξυσίας καὶ δυνάμεως, quæ in hoc mundo viget; in fine autem seculi & æternitate desitura sit. Quan- quam verò imperia mundi etiam cessatura sint, id tamen generali finis nomine, quo consummatio se- culi exprimitur, designatum est, εἶτα τὸ τέλος. Hic autem opponitur regno Christi regnum & potestas Diaboli, quod nempe consummatio seculi futura sit, vel finis mundi, cum Christus regnum suum Deo Patri tradet, regnum verò Diaboli de- struetur, vel evacuabitur. Nam & traditio regni Dei, & evacuatio regni Diabolici resurrectionem mortuorum comprobat. Non enim regnum tra- dere Deo & Patri posset, nisi electi à morte resu- scitati essent, qui Deo præsentandi sunt: Nec ve- ra & regni Diabolici & ἐξυσίας κὶ δυνάμεως Sata- næ evacuatio est, electis sub mortis potestate con- stitutis, quia Diabolus describitur, quod τὸ κρά- τος imperium mortis habeat, Ebr. II. 14. Confir- mationem autem, è Psal. CX. 1. petitam, quod at- tinet, ea recte se habet, etiamsi solùm de evacua- tione potestatis Diabolicæ v. 24. agatur. Nam si omnes hostes ponendi sunt scabellum pedum Do- mini, evacuari utique oportet etiam potestates Diabolicas, & mortem ipsam evacuari debere, in- de colligit Apostolus, utpote quæ etiam ad hostes illos pertinet, & instar Tyranni dominantis in o- mnes hostes, describitur Rom. V. 14. De loco Da- nielis cap. VII. 14. 27. actum est in sede propria. Non ibi de subjectione imperiorum mundi in con- summatione seculi, sed in regno gratiæ, non de eva- cuatione regnorum, sed de conversione populorum ad regnum Christi agitur.

## 15:25
v. 25. Δεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν βασιλεύειν ἄχρις ᾗ ἂν θῇ πάντας τὺς ἐχθρὺς ὑπὸ τὺς πόδας αὑτῦ. In the Manuscript τὺς ἐχθρὺς αὑτῦ. Until he subjects all his enemies to him. From Psalm CX. understood in the way Christ explains it in Matt. XXII. 44. That ὁ Θεὸς ought to be understood for that θῇ, appears both from the Psalm and from that which follows in v. 27.

Concerning the literal sense of Ps. CX. 1. we have spoken to the same effect. Commonly that ἄχρι, until, is explained indeterminately, so that the sense may be, sit always and forever at my right hand, and reign with me, even until I place your enemies under your feet, even at that time which seems opposed and contrary to your kingdom, as B. Glassius explains from Genebrardus, Gramm. S. page 430. But the more customary sense of the word can be retained, indeed it is more conveniently retained, if we weigh the matter more accurately, so that the limit of the kingdom, not indeed of the kingdom simply, but as the Apostle speaks of it, with respect to the mode, namely, that is considered, and as he now reigns in the midst of his enemies, be designated. For the Apostle goes on to prove this term from David, not that he is about to cease sitting at the right hand of God at the end of the age, or to rule, because his kingdom is eternal and has no end, of his enemies, and reigning through the word and sacraments: Because then the enemies will be fully subjected, which that phrase designates, until his enemies are placed under his feet. What it is to reign in this place, it is necessary that he himself reign, Oecumenius declares, Reigning is not taken in the common way, but so that it is to exercise the works of one reigning, for example, to defeat enemies, to assist his own, to overthrow the former, but to liberate the latter.

Latin:

v. 25. Δεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν βασιλεύειν ἄχρις ᾗ ἂν θῇ πάντας τὺς ἐχθρὺς ὑπὸ τὺς πόδας αὑτῦ. In Manuscripto τὺς ἐχθρὺς αὑτῦ. Donec ejus inimicos omnes ei subjiciat. Ex Psalmo CX. sic intellecto quomo- do Christus eum explicat Matth. XXII. 44. Ad illud θῇ subaudiri debere ὁ Θεὸς, tùm ex Psalmo apparet, tùm ex eo, quod sequitur v. 27.

De sensu literali Ps. CX. 1. ad eundem diximus. Communiter illud ἄχρι donec explicatur, indeter- minate, ut sensus sit, sede semper & in perpetuum ad dextram meam, & regna mecum, etiam donec inimicos tuos supponam pedibus, etiam eo tempo- re, quod tuo regno videtur oppositum & contra- rium, ut B. Glassius è Genebrardo exponit, Gramm. S. pag. 430. Sed retineri potest, imò commodius retinetur, si rem accuratius expen- damus, usitatior vocis sensus, ut terminus τῆς βασιλείας regni non quidem regni simpliciter, sed prout de eo loquitur Apostolus, ratione modi scil. spectati, & prout nunc regnat in medio inimico- rum, designetur. Hunc enim terminum probatum it Apostolus e Davide, non quod in fine seculi cessaturus sit sedere ad dextram Dei, vel domina- ri, quia regnum ejus æternum est, nullumque fi- nem habet, sed quod desiturus sit in medio inimi- corum dominari, & per verbum & sacramenta re- gnare: Quia tum plene subjecti erunt inimici, quod phrasis illa designat, donec ponantur inimi- ci ejus sub pedes ipsius. Regnare quid sit hoc loco, oportet ipsum regnare, Oecumenius declarat, Re- gnare non vulgari modo capitur, sed ut sit regnantis opera exercere, puta inimicos debellare, suis auxi- liari, illos quidem evertere, hos vero liberare.

## 15:26
V. 26. The last enemy is destroyed, death) Death is called the last enemy, through a certain personification, which also occurs in Rom. V. 14. Although indeed death does not rule over the blessed, nor is it a punishment, but a gateway into heaven, by which it is considered evangelically, yet when viewed legally on account of sin, it rules in the world as a tyrant, until the evacuation of the Diabolical power, and since death by itself is the destruction of nature, it fully deserves the name of enemy, even if by accident, on account of the intervening victory of faith, it does not so much harm us as benefit us. Moreover, it will exercise hostility primarily until the consummation of the age, if indeed it is about to swallow up countless numbers of those whom the day of the Lord will find surviving, who namely will have been found in unbelief, whereas the elect will experience only something analogous to death. But then (on the last day) that last enemy will be destroyed. For although the reprobate must perish by eternal death, yet that death will have no right over the unfaithful to swallow them up, but it itself will be swallowed up into victory, and will be bound to give back those whom it had killed and reduced to the dust of the earth, and thus had held as it were under its power until that time. Whence the Apostle again deduces the resurrection of the dead. For if death itself is to be evacuated, it will not be able to retain the elect in its power, when they are raised from the dead to life and possess life. For death would not be perfectly destroyed if we were still to remain in death, nor were we to be excited to life. It is clear, says Theophylact, that he is about to send death under the yoke by his own works. But in what way will the servitude of this death appear, and will it be established that this very thing has been subdued, unless it gives up the bodies which it had once received? For then we shall say that this has been properly overcome, when its spoils are plundered.

Latin:

V. 26. Ἔσχατος ἐχθρὸς καταργεῖται ὁ θάνατος) Novissimus hostis dicitur mors, per quandam Pro- sopopæiam, quæ etiam Rom. V. 14. occurrit. Quan- quam vero beatis mors non dominetur, nec pœ- na sit, sed janua in cælum, qua consideratur Ev- angelice, legaliter tamen spectata ob peccatum, ceu tyrannus, dominatur in mundo, usque ad e- vacuationem potestatis Diabolicæ, & quum mors per se sit destructio naturæ, ἐχθρῶ nomen omnino meretur, etsi ex Accidenti, ob intervenientem victoriam fidei, nobis non tam noceat, quam pro- sit. Hostilitatem autem imprimis exercebit, usque ad consummationem seculi, siquidem innumeros ex iis, quos superstites offendet dies Domini, ab- sorptura sit, qui scilicet in ἀπιστίᾳ inventi fuerint, electi vero aliquid solum analogi morti experturi sint. Tum autem (in die novissima) hostis ille no- vissimus destruetur. Nam licet æterna morte per- eundum sit reprobis, infideles tamen nullum jus habebit illa mors, eosdem absorbendi, sed ab- sorbebitur ipsa in victoriam, & reddere tenebitur eos, quos interfecerat, & in pulverem terræ rede- gerat, adeoque eo usque veluti sub potestate sua habuerat. Unde Apostolus iterum deducit resur- rectionem mortuorum. Nam si mors ipsa eva- cuanda est, non poterit in potestate sua retinere electos, quum illi e mortuis ad vitam resusciten- tur, & vita potiantur. Non enim perfecte destrue- retur mors, si adhuc in morte maneremus, nec ad vitam excitaremur. Perspicuum est, inquit Theo- phylactus, uti vel sua opera mortem sit sub jugum missurus. At quo pacto mortis hujusce servitus appa- rebit, & hanc ipsam constabit fuisse subactam, nisi evemat, quæ olim exceperat, corpora? Tunc enim hanc proprie devictam fuisse dicemus, cum ejus exu- viæ diripientur.

## 15:27
V. 27. For he has subjected all things under his feet. This is from Psalm VIII, mystically understood, as the writer to the Hebrews II. 8 receives it. For Christ is the other Adam, in whom are all greater and eternal things.

When he says that all things are subjected, it is clear that it is outside of him who subjected all things to him. Lest it be believed that he does injury to GOD, the maker of all things, whom both the Jews and the pious among the Gentiles worshipped, if he were to say that all things would be subject to Christ, he meets the perverse interpretation and from the very word שתה which is in Psalm VIII, he shows that it is sufficiently open to all that he who subjected the rest to Christ is excepted. Irenaeus used to say that he would not have believed even in Christ, if he had preached another God than the maker of the world. Moreover, this interpretation is of that kind which the Greeks call an exception, which necessity often compels one to use: As when we say: And what the heaven covers, all things. When he says, namely the scripture as in Heb. I. 7.

We also showed in the annotations to the eighth Psalm that it treats of Christ according to the letter. The force of the Apostolic argument is this: If death were not to be destroyed by the resurrection of the dead, not all things would be subjected under the feet of Christ. But all things are subjected, even the Devil, who has the empire of death, even death itself, as the last enemy, will be subjected to him. Therefore it is necessary that he no longer have power, but be destroyed. But what he adds about him who subjected all things to Christ, he adds not because of the fables of the Greeks about Jove, who subdued Saturn his father, but to signify the universal subjection of all things under Christ, as Estius notes with Thomas and Cajetan, so that while the Father alone performs the rest, we may understand that all things without exception will be subject to Christ, and thus even death itself. Compare Heb. II.

Latin:

V. 27. Πάντα γὰρ ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ. Hoc est ex Psalmo VIII. mystice intellecto quomodo eum accipit scriptor ad Hebræos II. 8. Nam Christus alter Adam, in quo omnia majora & æterna.

Ὅταν δὲ εἴπῃ, ὅτι πάντα ὑποτέτακται, δῆλον ὅτι ἐκτὸς τοῦ ὑποτάξαντος αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα. Ne DEO rerum omnium opifici, quem & Judæi & pii in gentibus colebant, credatur facere injuriam, si diceret, Christo fore omnia subjecta, occurrit pravæ interpretatio- ni & ex ipso verbo שתה quod est in Psalm. VIII. ostendit, satis apertum esse omnibus eum, qui cætera Christo subje- cit excipi. Irenæus dicebat, se ne Christo quidem creditu- rum fuisse, si alium Deum quam mundi opificem prædi- casset. Est autem hæc interpretatio ejus generis, quod Græ- ci vocant ὑπεξαίρεσιν, quo sæpe uti cogit necessitas: Ut cum dicimus: Et quod tegit omnia cælum. Ὅταν εἴπῃ, nem- pe scriptura ut Hebr. I. 7.

Etiam Psalmum octavum quoad literam de Christo agere, in annotatis ad eundem oftendi- mus. Vis argumenti Apostolici hæc est: Si mors non destrueretur per resurrectionem mortuo- rum, non omnia sub pedes Christi essent subjecta. At omnia subjecta sunt, etiam Diabolus, qui im- perium mortis habet, etiam ipsa mors, ceu novissi- mus hostis, ei subjicietur. Oportet ergò eum am- plius non habere potestatem, sed destrui. Quod autem de eo addit, qui subjecit Christo omnia, non ob Græcorum fabulas de Jove, qui Saturnum pa- trem subegerit, sed ad significandam universalem subjectionem omnium sub Christo addit, ut cum Thoma & Cajetano monet Estius, ut dum solus cætera exequitur Pater, intelligamus omnia sine exceptione Christo fore subjecta, adeoque etiam mortem ipsam. Conf. Ebr. II.

## 15:28
v. 28. But when all things are subjected to him, then also the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him.

He will be like an ambassador, who, having laid down the burden of his embassy, retains his dignity.

This passive subjection is to be explained in such a way that neither is the divine nature of Christ derogated with the Arians, since he himself is of one power with the Father, concerning which in the Anti-Crellius, nor is the reflux of the Son into the Father designated with the Sabellians and Marcionites in Ambrose lib. V. de fide c. 7, to which monstrosity we have refuted the twin dogma of Heinrich Nicolai in Tom. III. System. Theol.; nor is the eternity of the dominion or kingdom of Christ according to his human nature derogated, because of his kingdom there will be no end, Luke II. 33. For that empire extends itself to all things which are subject to him. But subjection is with respect to him who subjected all things to him. And therefore these things can properly consist: To be subject to GOD, which befits Christ according to his human nature, and to rule over all things which are outside and beyond GOD, which the eternity of the empire, granted to Christ according to his human nature, requires. Therefore in heaven the lamb was seen in the midst of the throne in the Apocalypse, and sitting on the throne of GOD. But that is to be observed, although he is even now subject to GOD, according to his human nature, here however on the last day his majesty will be otherwise conspicuous to all, when he himself is about to appear in the glory of GOD, and sitting on the throne of his glory, Matth. XXV. 31. in the appearing of the glory of the great God, and our savior Jesus Christ, Tit. II. 13. the holy Apostle teaches openly that he will still be subject to him who subjected all things to him, lest anyone invent an equalization of the human nature of Christ, or that the same will be absorbed by the divine Majesty and converted into the divine essence, as the fiction of Marcellus has it according to Basil, and of some fanatics, Schvvenckfeld and others; nay rather, that that subjection of the human nature of Christ, or of the Son of GOD according to his human nature, will be even then most especially conspicuous. For things are said to come to pass in Holy Scripture when they are manifested. And therefore the gloss of those whom Augustine mentions in book contra sermon. Arianorum chapter 37, that the subjection of the Son at that time will be the conversion of his human nature into the divine substance, is diametrically opposed to the Apostle. But the interpretation of Athanasius de hum. nat. suscepta, Theodoret in h. l., and Augustine quæst. 69 among 83, by which these words of the Apostle are understood of the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church, is foreign. For that is subject to Christ. But here the Son of God (according to his human nature) is said to be about to be subjected to the Father. For the Apostle says emphatically: Then the Son himself also shall be subjected. And therefore Jerome in book 1 Dial. adv. Pelag. c. 6 teaches: these things are to be understood according to the disposition of the flesh assumed. Which sense Augustine also approved in book III contra Max. chapter 18, along with most other Latins. Such therefore is what the Apostle says, says Estius: The Son will not for that reason cease to be subject to the Father, because all things are subject to him. Nay, it is most just that he should remain he is subject to him who subjected all things to himself. Furthermore, he will be subject in reality and confession, because he will acknowledge and confess GOD the Father as greater than himself, as he says in the Gospel, The Father is greater than I . And he will refer his kingdom and all good things back to the Father with thanksgiving.

However, in Petavius, book III on the Trinity, ch. 5, n. 2, the twofold interpretation of Gregory of Nazianzus, Orat. II on the Son, is highly approved: As long as I am not subject, but still seditious and rebellious, both by denying GOD and by the perturbations of my own mind, Christ himself is not yet subject, as far as I am concerned.

And Ambrose, book V on the faith, ch. 6: Is Christ therefore already subject, because many have believed? By no means, because the subjection of Christ is not in the few, but in all.

For just as, if I look at myself, while I am still flesh, against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, I do not seem to be subject, even if I am subject in part: So because the whole Church is his body, Christ, as long as the human race dissents, we divide Christ.

Therefore Christ is not yet subject, whose members are not yet subject. But when we are many members, but one Spirit, then he himself will also be subject, so that through his subjection GOD may be all in all.

Gregory, orat. on these words: The subjection of GOD is a perfect and in every part absolute alienation from evil, because in him all the faithful and elect of Christ will be removed from all evil, and then they will receive the principate in good, and will be most closely joined with the Deity, and his immortality, kingdom, and happiness: And then GOD will be all in all, when there will be no evil in those things which are.

For GOD cannot be in evil, but is necessarily in all good. Christ therefore will be subjected to the Father, when the Church of Christ will be subjected to the Father, and thus it will be liberated from all evil.

For the subjection of the Church is called the subjection of Christ. See Cornelius à Lapide.

But the explanation given earlier is simpler.

Which Luther, for his divine art of speaking and rhetoric, so adorns in I Cor. xv, fol. 242. He comes back to it again, and concludes what he has said, how Christ will deliver up the kingdom to GOD the Father, there it will become quite another thing, from faith a clear face, from the Word the essence, from the dark understanding a bright light-giving sun, where we will presently see all our enemies, both those we now have on earth, and death besides, utterly destroyed and exterminated, and he drives the Word ever forward, that the Father has put all things under Christ, and draws so much from it, that He is indeed excepted, who has put all things under him, and that the Son, when he will have put all things under him, will also himself be subject.

These seem like empty dark words, but it is all, as I have said, spoken to the end that he makes a distinction between the kingdom of GOD and of Christ, although it is in itself one and the same kingdom, but it is called Christ's now, because we here still see and hear, as one sees a worldly King sitting securely before one's eyes in his kingdom, with the Royal Crown, and great glorious Splendor, for it is not yet manifest what we have in Him, and what we should obtain through the Gospel, Sacrament and Faith.

But afterwards it will be called GOD's kingdom, when it is no longer hidden, but has become manifest before all creatures, and faith is to cease, which He calls delivering the kingdom to the Father, that is, to present us and his whole Christendom manifest before the Father in eternal clarity and glory, so that He himself may rule without any veil, yet nevertheless Christ will remain in his Majesty and dominion.

For He is the same God and Lord, eternal and almighty with the Father. But because He now rules through his Word, Sacrament etc., so that the world does not see, it is called Christ's kingdom, and all must be subject to Him (yet excepted he who makes all things subject to Him) until the last day, when he will lift up all things, and then submit himself with his kingdom to the Father, and say to him: I have hitherto ruled with thee in faith, this I deliver over to thee, that they may now see, how I am in thee, and thou in me, together with the Holy Spirit, in a Divine Majesty, and have and enjoy all things manifest in thee, which they have hitherto believed and waited for.

Nor is it inconveniently said by Augustine, book I on the Trinity, ch. 8: Christ, in so far as he is GOD, has us subject with him; in so far as he is priest, he himself is subject with us. ἵνα ᾖ ὁ Θεὸς τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι.

All things will be full of GOD.

There, everything is related to everything, says Seneca to Marcia on the heavenly life, speaking according to his own measure, Angels and the pious will be united with GOD just as a spark with the sun, says R.

Solomon in the book Keter Malchut, and the Hebrews draw the place in Seph. III. 9 here in a mystical sense. This is, says Theophylact, that all things may depend on the Father, lest anyone perchance suspect two free principalities divided and torn from each other: Since indeed the enemies lie prostrate at the feet of the Son, but the Son does not differ from the Father.

But rather, as befits the Son, he is made subject to GOD the Father.

Thus GOD will be entirely and the Father will be all in all.

Beza's gloss has, that it will then finally be, that it is fully acknowledged that GOD has the perfections of all things, because Scripture then signifies that a thing is or is becoming, when it is fully known.

Now where the Devil resists GOD, the impious pervert the order instituted by GOD, many scandals are presented to the eyes etc., it does not clearly appear that GOD is all in all.

But after Christ, having executed the judgment commanded by GOD, has prostrated Satan and all the impious into destruction, the glory of GOD will be conspicuous to all.

The sense is, says Estius: Thus finally it is made plain to all that GOD is the Principle, even of Christ the man, and the author of all good things, both of him and of the whole kingdom, which is the Church, which will then consist of all and only the elect.

Then it will be manifested, says St. Thomas, that whatever good we have is from GOD.

But how GOD will be all in all to the elect, we only understand in part here.

We can scarcely stammer about it, and that more by way of a wish, than by way of a thesis: That he will be all in all to us: then because he will act with us immediately, not, as here, mediately, not through the Word and Sacraments: For this economy of the kingdom will cease, he will not rule us through Political magistrates, or defend us through the ministries of Angels, he will not sustain us through benefactors, but will immediately provide all things that are necessary for us.

He himself will be our Doctor, our King, our salvation, our food, in a word, all in all; then by reason of the object, because we will not be occupied with other things, as here we are distracted by various things, but GOD will be all in all to us, both in our mind, and in our will, and in our affections, and in all our actions.

Our mind will be fixed on him, our will will rest in him, our affections will be carried into him, in knowing, loving, and celebrating him we will be occupied wholly and uniquely.

Augustine, sermon XVI on the time:

What is all things?

Whatever you were seeking here, whatever you held as great, He Himself will be to you. Whatever you wanted, whatever you loved to eat and drink here, He Himself will be food to you, He Himself will be drink to you, He Himself will be immortality to you.

The same in book 1 against the sermon of the Arians, ch. 27.
