The Apostle says: Then the Son will be subject to the Father, so that GOD may be all things, not only in the form of that one man (Christ) but in all, that is, so that for the having of life, for the satisfying of our desire, the divine Nature will suffice; For then GOD will be all things in all, and besides Him we shall desire to want nothing at all.

For He will be all things to us, when, He being sufficient, nothing will be lacking.

B.

Luther on this passage: Whatever must be begged by us piecemeal from all creatures in this age, He alone will be to us in the place of all these things, we shall never labor under any want.

Let us hear him speaking αὐτοσομάτως [in his own person], fol. 243. Then (he says) GOD will be all in all, that is, each one will have in GOD Himself everything that he now has in all things, so that when He reveals Himself, we shall all have enough, in soul and body, and will no longer need such various things as we now must have on earth, firstly for necessity and for the preservation of body and life, father and mother, food and drink, house and home, clothes and shoes, in addition to princes and lords, who protect us and create peace, then in the spiritual Regiment, pastors and preachers, who teach there and administer the Sacrament, comfort in distress, and advise in matters of conscience, etc. Likewise sun and moon, air, fire and water for the whole world. And who can recount everything that a man here on earth must have for the necessity of the body alone? But there it will all be finished, and none of these things will be of any value, but we shall have so much in GOD, that no food, no drink or Malmsey is so delicious, nor can one eat or drink as well as GOD Himself will do with one glance, so that you will always be stronger and fresher, healthier and happier, and also brighter and more beautiful than sun and moon, so that all the clothes and golden pieces that a prince or king wears will be mere mud compared to that, when we shall be illuminated by one divine glance alone. So we shall also need no protector nor any authority, money nor goods, house nor home, nor other bodily goods, but have everything in Him alone. Thus also we shall have all spiritual goods, eternal righteousness, comfort and joy of conscience, so that no one will frighten us anymore, nor make us err or restless. In sum, what we now must take here and there individually and piecemeal from all creatures, although it also comes from Him and is given, for that we shall have Him alone without intermediary, without any lack and ceasing.

Which, however, is to be understood in such a way that the inequality of the degrees of glory in the elect is not denied, He will be all in all to each, but in an unequal degree.

Bernard, sermon IV. On all saints. God, he says, will fill our rational soul with the light of wisdom, the concupiscible with justice, the irascible with perfect tranquility. That this filling of the soul can consist in different degrees for different people, there is no doubt.

But some fanatics, whom Cornelius à Lapide calls Contemplatives, (who have pursued a certain excessive and impossible union with GOD,) ineptly gather from this passage that in the resurrection all men, and all created things, are to return to their ideal and divine being, which they have had from eternity in GOD, and so are to be converted into GOD Himself.

Cornelius himself also concludes wrongly: If in the resurrection GOD will be all in all. Therefore all things, that is, all created things, will be and will remain. The contrary rather follows from it: Therefore other creatures will not be, because we shall not need them. GOD alone will suffice for us.

Nothing will be lacking to you, GOD will become all things to all. v.

Latin:

v. 28. Ὅταν δὲ ὑποταγῇ αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, τότε καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ υἱὸς ὑποταγήσεται τῷ ὑποτάξαντι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα.

Erit sicut legatus, qui deposito legationis onere digni- tatem retinet.

Hæc ὑποταγὴ passiva ita explicanda est, ut nec cum Arianis derogetur divinæ Christi natu- ræ, siquidem ipse unius est cum Patre potentiæ, de quo in Anti-Crellio, nec cum Sabellianis, & Marcionitis apud Ambrosium lib. V. de fide c. 7. Fi- lii in Patrem refusio designetur, cui portento ge- minum dogma Heinrici Nicolai Tom. III. System. Theol. profligavimus; nec dominii vel regni Chri- sti secundum humanam naturam æternitati, quia regni ejus non erit finis, Luc. II. 33. Nam impe- rium illud extendit se ad omnia, quæ ipsi subdita sunt. ὑποταγὴ autem est respectu ejus, qui omnia ei subjecit. Ideoque hæc probe consistere possunt: Subjectum esse DEO, quod Christo convenit, se- cundum humanam naturam, & dominari omni- bus, quæ sunt extra & præter DEUM, quod im- perii, Christo secundum humanam naturam con- cessi, æternitas requirit. Ideò in cœlo agnus visus est in medio throni in Apocalypsi, & sedere in thro- no DEI. Id verò observandum, cum etiamnum subjectus DEO sit, secundum humanam naturam, hic tamen in novissimo die aliter conspicua erit majestas ejus omnibus, comparituro ipso in glo- ria DEI, & sedente in throno gloriæ suæ, Matth. XXV. 31. ἐν ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς δόξης τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, Tit. II. 13. adhuc subje- ctum fore illi, qui subjecit ei omnia, docet apertè sanctus Apostolus, ne quis fingat exæquationem humanæ Christi naturæ, vel eandem à Majestate divinâ absorptum, & in essentiam divinam con- versum iri, uti habet commentum Marcelli a- pud Basilium, & fanaticorum nonnullorum, Schvvenckfeldii & aliorum; imò conspicuam et- iam tùm maximè futuram illam ὑποταγὴν, vel subjectionem humanæ Christi naturæ, seu Filii DEI secundum humanam naturam. Nam res tùm fieri dicuntur in S. literis, cum manifestantur. Id- eoque è diametro adversatur Apostolo illorum glossa, quorum meminit Augustinus libr. contra sermon. Arianorum cap. 37. illam tunc Filii subje- ctionem fore ipsius humanæ naturæ in divinam sub- stantiam commutationem. Aliena autem est inter- pretatio Athanasii de hum. nat. suscepta, Theodor. in h. l. August. quæst. 69. inter 83. qua hæc Apo- stoli accipiuntur de corpore Christi mystico, quod est Ecclesia. Nam illa Christo subjecta. Hic verò Filius DEI (secundum humanam naturam) Pa- tri subjiciendus dicitur. Emphaticè enim Aposto- lus: Tunc & ipse Filius subjicietur. Ideoque Hie- ronymus lib. 1. Dial. adv. Pelag. c. 6. docet: hæc ac- cipienda esse juxta dispositionem carnis assumtæ. Quem sensum etiam Augustinus probavit libr. III. contra Max. cap. 18. cum aliis Latinis plerisque. Tale igitur est, quod dicit Apostolus, inquit Estius: Non idcirco Filius desinet subjectus esse Patri, quod subjecta ei sint omnia. Imò justissimum est, ut maneat ei subjectus, qui ipsi omnia subjecit. Porro subjectus erit re & confessione, quia agnoscet & confitebitur, DEUM Patrem se majorem, sicut in Evangelio dicit, Pater major me est . suumque regnum & omnia bona cum gratiarum actione Patri referet accepta.

Petavio tamen libr. III. de Trin. c. 5. n. 2. maximopere probatur gemina Gregorii Nazianzeni, Orat. II. de Filio, interpretatio: Quamdiu ego non sum subjectus, sed adhuc seditiosus & rebellis, tum negando DEUM, tum animi mei perturbationibus, nondum, quod ad me spectat, subjectus est & ipse Christus.

Et Ambrosii lib. V. de fide cap. 6. Ergo jam subjectus est Christus, quia plurimi crediderunt?

Minimè, quia non in pauci est Christi subjectio, sed in omnibus. Sicut enim, si in me conspiciens adhuo caro fit, adversus Spiritum. Spiritus autem adversus carnem, non videor esse subjectus, etsi ex parte sim subditus: Ita quia omnis Ecclesia suum corpus est Christi, quamdiu genus dissentit humanum, Christum dividimus.

Nondum ergo subjectus est Christus, cujus non sunt adhuc membra subjecta. Cum autem fuerimus nos multa membra, sed unus Spiritus, tunc etiam ipse subjectus erit, ut per ipsius subjectionem DEUS sit omnia in omnibus.

Gregor. orat. in hæc verba: DEI subjectio est perfecta & omni ex parte absoluta à malo abalienatio, quia in eo omnes fideles & electi Christi semoti erunt ab omni malo, tuncque suscipient bono principatum, & arctissime conjungentur cum Deitate, ejusque immortalitate, regno, & felicitate: Atque tunc DEUS erit omnia in omnibus, quando nullum erit malum in iis, quæ sunt.

Non potest enim DEUS esse in malo, sed necessario est in omni bono. Christus ergo subjicietur Patri, cum Ecclesia Christi Patri subjicietur, itaque liberabitur ab omni malo.

Ecclesiæ enim subjectio dicitur Christi subjectio. Vide Cornel. à Lapide.

Sed simplicior est explicatio prius tradita.

Quam Lutherus pro divina sua dicendi & rhetoricandi arte ita exornat in I. ad Cor. xv. fol. 242. Da kömmt er wieder drauf, und beschliesset, das er gefaget hat, wie Christus das Reich GOTT dem Vater wird überantworten, da wird es gar ein ander Ding werden, aus dem Glauben ein klar Angesicht, aus dem Wort das Wesen, aus dem dunklen Verstand eine helle lichte Sonne, da wir werden gegenwärtig sehen alle unsere Feinde, beide die wir iezt auf Erden haben, und den Tod darzu, gank hingerichtet und vertilgei, und treibt immer das Wort, daß der Vater Christo alles unterthan habe, zeucht so viel draus, daß Er freylich ausgenommen sey, der ihm alles unterthan hat, und daß ihm der Sohn, wenn er ihm alles wird unterthan gemacht haben, auch selbst wird unterthan seyn.

Das scheinen eitel dunkele Worte, ist aber alles, wie ich gesagt habe, dahin geredet, daß er einen Unterschied setze des Reiches GOTTes und Christi, wiewohl es doch an ihm selbst einerley Reich ist, aber darum heisset es itzt Christi, daß wir hier doch sehen noch hören, wie man einen weltlichen König sicher für Augen sitzen in seinem Reich, mit der Königlichen Crone, und grossem herrlichen Pracht, dennes ist noch nicht offenbahr, wes wir an Ihm haben, und durch das Evangelium, Sacrament und Glauben erlangen sollen.

Darnach aber wirds heissen GOTTes Reich, wenn es nicht mehr verborgen, sondern für allen Creaturen offenbahr worden, und der Glaube aufhören soll, welches Er heisset das Reich dem Vater überantworten, das ist, uns und seine ganze Christenheit offenbahrlich darstellen für dem Vater in die ewige Klarheit und Herrlichkeit, daß Er selbst regiere ohn alle Deckel, doch nichts destoweniger wird Christus in seiner Majestät und Herrschaft bleiben.

Denn Er ist derselbige GOtt und HErr, ewig und allmächtig mit dem Vater. Aber weil Er ixt so regieret durch sein Wort, Sacrament 2c. daß die Welt nicht siehet, so heisset es Christi Reich, und muß alles Ihm unterthan seyn (doch ausgenommen den, der Ihm alles unterthan machet) bis an den jüngsten Tag, da ers alles wird auffheben, und sich alsdenn mit seinem Reich dem Vater untergeben, und zu ihm sagen: Ich hab bisher mit dir regieret im Glauben, das gebe ich dir über, daß sie nun sehen, wie ich in dir, und du in mir seyest, samt dem Heiligen Geist, in einer Göttlichen Majestät, und alles in dir offenbahrlich haben und genießen, was sie bisher geglaubt und gewartet haben.

Nec incom- modè Augustinus libr. I. de Trinit. cap. 8. Christus, in quantum DEUS est, cum illo nos subjectos habet, in quantum sacerdos, nobicum ipse subjectus est. ἵνα ᾖ ὁ Θεὸς τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι.

Omnia erunt DEI plena.

Illic omnibus omne cognatum, ait Seneca ad Marciam de vita cœlesti, pro suo modulo loquens, Angeli & pii adunabuntur cum DEO sicut scintilla cum sole, ait R.

Salomo in libro Keter Mal-chut, & huc mystico sensu trahunt Hebræi locum Seph. III. 9. Hoc est, inquit Theophylactus, ut omnia à Patre dependeant, ne quis fortè duos liberos principatus divulso & discissos ab invicem suspicetur: Siquidem inimici Filii pedibus prostrati subjaceant, Filius verò nihil à Patre dissideat.

Quin potius, ut Filium decet, DEO subjecitus fit Patri.

Sic DEUS omnino & Pater erit omnia in omnibus.

Glossa Beza habet, iùm demum fore, ut plenè agnoscatur, DEUM habere omnium rerum perfectiones, quia Scriptura iùm rem esse vel fieri significat, cum plene cognoscitur.

Nunc ubi reluctatur Diabolus DEO, impii ordinem à DEO institutum pervertunt, scandala multa oculis obversantur &c. non liquido apparet, DEUM esse omnia in omnibus.

Sed postquam Christus judicium à DEO mandatum exequutus, Satanam & omnes impios in exitium prostraverit, gloria DEI omnibus erit conspicua.

Sensus est, inquit Estius: Ita denique palam omnibus fit, DEUM esse Princip.m, etiam Christi hominis, & auctorem omnium bonorum, tam ipsius, quam totius regni, quod est Ecclesiæ, quæ tunc omnibus & solu constabit electis.

Tunc manifestabitur, ait S. Thomas, quod, quidquid boni habemus, est à DEO.

Quomodo autem electis DEUS omnia futurus sit in omnibus, id ex parte hic tantum intelligimus.

Vix balbutire de eo possumus, idque magis κατ' ἄγωω, quàm κατὰ θέσιν: Quod omnia in omnibus nobis futurus fit: tum quia immediate nobiscum ager, non, ut hic, mediate, non per verbum & Sacramenta: Hæc enim œconomia regni cessabit, nos reget non per magistratus Politicos, aut per Angelorum ministeria nos defendet, non per benefactores nos sustentabit, sed immediate omnia, quæ nobis, et necessaria sunt, præstabit.

Ipse erit Doctor noster, Rex noster, salus nostra, cibus noster, uno verbo, omnia in omnibus; tum ratione objecti, quod non circa alia occupabimur, uti hic variis distrahimur, sed DEUS nobis futurus sit omnia in omnibus, qua nostram mentem, qua voluntatem, qua affectus, qua actiones omnes.

In ipsum mens nostra defixa erit, in ipso voluntas nostra acquiescet, in ipso ferentur affectus nostri, in ipso cognoscendo, amando, celebrando toti unicè occupabimur.

Augustinus sermone XVI. de tempore:

Quid est omnia?

Quicquid hic quarebas, quicquid pro magno habebas, ipse tibi erit. Quicquid volebas, quicquid hic amabas manducare & bibere, ipse tibi cibus, ipse tibi erit potus, ipse ille erit tibi immortalitas.

Idem libro 1. contra serm.

Arianorum cap. 27. Apostolus dicit: Tunc Patri Filium subjectum futurum, ut sit DEUS omnia, non tantùm in illius unius forma hominis (Christi) sed in omnibus, id est, ut ad habendam vitam, ad satiandum desiderium nostrum, Natura divina sufficiet; Tunc enim DEUS erit omnia in omnibus, & præter ipsum nihil omninò velle cupiemus.

Omnia quippe nobis erit, quando ipso sufficiente nihil deerit.

B.

Lutherus in h. l. Quicquid frustratim ab omnibus creaturis nobis mendicandum est in hoc seculo, ille unus omnium horum instar nobis erit, nulla inopiâ unquam laborabimus.

Audiamus eum αὐτοσομάτως loquentem fol. 243. Alsdenn (spricht er) wird GOtt senn alles in allen, das ist, ein teglicher wird an GOtt selbst alles haben, was er ieht an allen Dingen hat, dass wenn Er sich offenbahret, werden wir alle genug haben, an Seel und Leib, und nicht mehr so mancherley dürffen, wie wir ieht auf Erden müssen haben, erstlich zur Nothdursst und zur Erhaltung des leibes und lebens, Vater und Mutter, Essen und Trinken, Haus und Hos, Kleider und Schuh, darzu Fürsten und Herren, die uns schützen und Friede schaffen, dårnach im Geistlichen Regiment Pfarrer und Prediger, die da lehren und Sacrament reichen, trösten in Nöthen, et rathen in Sachen des Gewissens &c. Item Sonn und Mond, lusst, Feuer und Wasser für die ganze Welt. Und wer an alles erzehlen, was ein Mensch hier auf Erden allein zu des leibes Noth haben muss? Aber dort wird es alles aus seyn, und derselben keines mehr gelten, sondern werden an GOtt so viel haben, dass kein Essen, kein Tranck oder Malvasier so köstlich ist, noch sowohl Speisen oder träncken kan, als GOtt selbst mit einem Anblick thun wird, dass du immer starck und frisch, gesund und fröhlich, darzu heller und schöner seyn wirst, denn Sonn und Mond, also, dass alle Kleider und gülden Stück, die ein Känfer oder König trägt, lauter Koth seyn wird gegen dem, da wir werden allein von einem Göttlichen Augenblick durchleuchtet werden. So werden wir auch keines Schutz-Herrn noch einiger Obrigkeit, Geldes noch Gutes, Haus noch Hos, noch anderer leiblichen Güter dürffen, sondern alles an ihm allein haben. Also auch alle geistliche Güter, ewige Gerechtigkeit, Trost und Freude des Gewissens haben, dass uns niemand mehr wird schrecken, noch irr oder unruhig machen. Summa, was wir ieht bey allen Creaturen hin und her einzeln und stücklicht müssen nehmen, wiewohl es auch von Ihm herkömmt und gegeben wird, dasür werden wir ohn Mittel Ihn allein haben, ohn allen Mangel und Auffhören.

Quæ tamen ita accipienda, ut non negetur inæqualitas graduum gloriæ in electis, omnia in omnibus erit singulis, sed dispari gradu.

Bernardus serm. IV. Omn. sanct. Deus, inquit, implebit animam nostram rationalem luce sapientia, concupiscibilem justitia, irascibilem perfecta tranquillitate. Quam impletionem animæ diversis gradibus penes diversos constare posse, dubium nullum est.

Ineptè verò fanatici nonnulli, quos Contemplativos dicit Cornelius à Lapide, (qui nimiam quandam & impossibilem cum DEO unionem consectati sunt,) colligunt ex hoc loco, quod in resurrectione omnes homines, omnesque res create redituræ sint ad suum esse ideale, & divinum, quod ab æterno habuerint in DEO, adeoque convertendæ sint in ipsum DEUM.

Perperam etiam Cornelius ipse concludit: Si in resurrectione DEUS erit omnia in omnibus. Ergò omnia, id est, omnes res create, erunt & permanebunt. Contrarium potius inde sequitur: Ergò creaturæ aliæ non erunt, quia illis non indigebimus. DEUS solus nobis sufficiet.

Nil tibi deficiet, DEUS omnibus omnia fiet. v.

## 15:29
29. Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται; Τί καὶ βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; Here inì is besides: & νῦν, is therefore. Τί ποιήσουσιν; What will they effect? It is a new argument from the rite then received through the Churches, whence it might appear that the resurrection was believed by all.

For if anyone had died in the state of the catechumens, there was someone who was baptized in his place and name, thus sealing the faith of the dead man before the Church.

Tertullian on the resurrection of the flesh: But if some are baptized for the dead, we shall see whether with reason. Certainly he contends that they instituted this by that presumption, because they thought that it would be profitable even to the flesh, as a vicarious baptism, for the hope of the resurrection, which unless it were bodily would not otherwise be bound by bodily baptism. What, he says, of them being baptized themselves, if the bodies for which they are baptized do not rise?

The same against Marcion: What, he says, will they do, who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?

Let that institution look to itself. The Kalends, if by chance, of February, (they used to answer) they would ask for the dead. Do not therefore [blame] the apostle or his confirmers, so that he might the more establish the resurrection of the flesh, the more those who were variously baptized for the dead did this for the sake of the resurrection.

Ambrose, or whoever it is who is read under his name on this passage: He wishes to show the resurrection of the dead to be so stable and firm, that he uses the example of those who were so secure about the future resurrection that they were even baptized for the dead, if death had forestalled anyone, fearing that he might either badly or not rise, who had not been baptized, he was baptized alive in the name of the dead. Whence he subjoined: Why are they even baptized for them? By this example he does not prove their deed, but shows the fixed faith in the resurrection.

That the Marcionites used this custom is understood both from the words of Tertullian, and Chrysostom openly says it, and after him others. But the Marcionites wanted to appear as diligent followers of all things that Paul either instituted or approved. We should wonder at this rite, because in some places the very bodies of the dead were baptized, as appears from the canon which is XVIII to some, XIX to others, of the Council of Carthage, and no less was the Eucharist given to dead bodies, as the same canon of Carthage teaches us, and LXXXIII of the synod held in Trullo.

I believe, however, that among other things that vicarious baptism was used, so that the Church might pray for the dead. For public prayers were not accustomed to be made for the Catechumens, although it was lawful to give alms for them.

This passage indeed has not received as many interpretations as it has interpreters, as Calixtus [says] on this passage and in his book on Purgatory. Nevertheless, many expositions of it occur.

Some (1.) seek a trope in the word baptism, and interpret it of the first baptism of blood or affliction, as e.g. Alexand. Morus on this passage, who besides invents an enallage, and contortedly explains being baptized for the dead as being baptized with the baptism of Christ, in this way: Or what can be more foolish for us, who do not undergo death for that dead one, but nevertheless undergo as it were so many deaths, daily in danger of our head.

(2.) To which especially the Papists incline, who explain it of voluntary afflictions, undertaken for the dead, for them by praying, fasting, groaning, and afflicting themselves. Bellarm. l. 1. de Purg. Salmero, Stapleton, Mcnochius, Saa, Tirinus, Estius in IV. sent. distinct. 3. §. 2. Tannerus and others.

(3.) of martyrdoms, Claudius Grillaudus on this passage, 3. of martyrdoms.

Gagneus, and Bence, Doctors of the Sorbonne, on this passage. Maldon. on Luc. XII. 50. They are baptized, he says, for the dead, the martyrs, who suffer and are afflicted for the faith and the article of the resurrection of the dead: to whom (although the Papists themselves, even Estius himself on this passage, ἑαυτο- ) ἑαυτομαχῶν, and Gabriel Vasquez the Jesuit in 3. Thomas t. 2. disp. 157. num. 45, let them refute his mouth) from the Calvinists Franc. Jun. in Bellarm. de Purg. does not deny: From the Arminians Daniel Tilenus Part II. disp. cap. 5. to whom indeed ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν is over, beyond, and above those who already before for the sake of faith, or in the faith of Christ have died.

B. Job also agrees. (4.) Jerome explains it thus: What does it profit the world to die, if eternal life does not follow this contempt of pleasures? (5.) In Brochmand in System. βαπτίζεσθαι is to grieve and to weep, so that the sense may be: What do they do, what comfort have they, who more bitterly weep for their own, and are washed with their tears for the dead, which interpretation in Job. Tob. Major's oration for the deceased against Grot. cap. II, §. 140. seems the simplest of all.

(6.) Anna Maria Schurman in Cloppenburg. Disput. Select.

XIV. §. 14. explains it thus: In vain are so many labors undergone for the dead, for the faithful and the elect, who for that reason are plainly to be held as dead, if there is no resurrection of the dead.

But to these interpretations one descends rashly to the tropical acceptance of the word βαπτίζεσθαι, used twice: Neither to fast, to groan, to afflict oneself, is to be baptized, nor is to be baptized anywhere the same as to grieve, or to undergo labors.

Furthermore, that one must pray and fast for the dead is ἄγαφον, nor can ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν be explained, either for the faith of the dead, or beyond the dead, or for the faithful in the habit of the dead, or τί ποιήσουσι, what comfort will they have.

Others therefore understand baptism as ὕδατοβαπτισμῷ, and that again in diverse ways.

For (7.) some prefer that the locutions refer to those who were rendered unclean by contact with the dead, Num. XIX. because those signified the resurrection of the dead: Comparing Simc. c. XXXIV. 30. As Vasquez Tom. II. part 3. disp. 157. num. 49. seqq. and Johan. Coccejus in Comm. on Hebrews IX. 13. 14. But which contorted and circuitous explanation hardly deserves to be mentioned, which even Benedictus Justinianus rightly called forced and violent.

(8.) More expeditious seems the ἔκθεσις of Mr. D. Sebastian Schmid disp. on baptism over the dead §. III. and on Luke VI. 1. concerning the sabbath δευτεροπρώτῳ which holds thus: because the resurrection of the dead is certainly to be, those who touched the dead became unclean, and were baptized over them, so that by that rite they might profess that they believed on account of the resurrection of the dead that they were rendered altogether unclean by the most grievous sin, whoever treated the dead less piously and honestly, and had need of ablution from sin.

To which explanation indeed, with the authority of the best Theologian, and one most friendly to me, we cannot subscribe: because it is not easily to be said that those who touched the dead were rendered unclean, for the reason that they treated the dead less piously and honestly; those who were one day to rise again, for they were also rendered unclean from the carcasses of beasts: Nay, that Levitical uncleanness was contracted from carcasses for the reason that the carcasses polluted them, not that the carcasses were treated less honestly by them, conf.

Hagg. II. 14. and that signification was a certain curse of death and corruption, which was brought in through sin. Therefore it seems to contribute nothing to the resurrection of the dead.

Not to mention that it is not established from antiquity that those who had touched the dead, or even who had treated them less honestly, were washed with water for the profession of the faith of the resurrection of the dead. (9.)

If to some indeed the explanation of Beza and the Belgic annotations on the ablutions of the dead, which are done in the faith of the resurrection of the dead, seems perhaps more convenient, which Chamier prefers to all others Tom. III. Panstrat. lib. XXVI. cap. XIX. num. 35. the words of the Apostle will stand against them, who does not speak actively, but passively, βαπτιζόμενοι, nor does the phrase to be baptized over the dead agree, which certainly does not denote to wash the dead.

(10.) But that interpretation of Turrianus, which from some person dying in legal uncleanness they washed another in his name with lustral water, whence the Papists derive a similar use of their holy water, is more worthy of the Masters of Jewish fables than of Christian interpreters.

Furthermore (11.) that baptism is to be understood in the more famous signification, which is proper to the New Testament for the sacrament of baptism, most interpreters easily admit: But they explain the other words in diverse ways, as for instance the word νεκρῶν, through which Sedulius understands dead works, who are baptized for the dead works to be abolished, having obtained, to wit, their remission: Whom Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Aquinas and Contarenus follow.

But although sins are called ἔργα νεκρὰ, Ebr. IX. 14. yet they nowhere come absolutely under the name of τῶν νεκρῶν, and it is too manifest that the discourse here is about persons, not about works.

Others (12.) and indeed Johan. Gerhard.

Vossius disp. XII. on baptism and Guilielmus Estius explain it for the dead, for the breath of the dead, or that it may go well for them after death. Akin to this is the explanation of Isidore of Pelusium l. I. epist. CXXII: They are baptized for bodies dead and extinct by nature, believing them to be changed into immortality and a breath alien from corruption; And of Sebastian Castellio: This is Paul's argument: While Christians are baptized, they are baptized in this, that they may die with Christ, then rise again.

This is to be baptized for the dead, that is for themselves, in the hope of the thing which they are to attain after death, namely the resurrection, that which would be supported, if there were no future resurrection.

A certain Italian taught me this opinion.

But the Apostle treats of other persons, for whom baptism is undertaken, not of those undertaking it themselves: Nor is the breath of the dead ever noted by the name of νεκρῶν.

Others (13.) take νεκρῶν of those who are like the dead, the dying, and thus explain it of the baptism of the Clinics to Epiphanius, as for instance Calvin, Marlot, Hemmingius, Flacius in this way: What do they do, who are baptized for the dead? that is, who are baptized, when they are held more for dead than for living, and when it is certain that they are not baptized for any convenience of this life, since they are held for dead. Vid. Epiphan. ber.

XXIX. But how can to be baptized ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν be as the dying? Where is the force of the Preposition ὑπὲρ left?

It is certainly one thing to be baptized for the sake of death, another for the dead (14.) Some with Oecumenius and Theophylact wish to define dead flesh, with Jerome preceding on this place: What is the need to baptize flesh, if it does not rise again? But neither is flesh indicated by the name of τῶν νεκρῶν, nor can to be baptized ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν be the same as to be baptized flesh.

(15.) Chrysostom explains the word ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν for faith concerning the dead, and their resurrection, over the dead bodies to wit, because they are to rise again from the dead. But this sense cannot be understood or had from the words of the Apostle.

What do they do, who are baptized for the dead? that is, so that they may testify by the profession of the Apostolic symbol, which will never be taught to have been in use then, the resurrection of the same.

(16.) Cloppenburg does not choose certain dead, those to wit, who are from the dead.

from five hundred brethren in the Lord had fallen asleep, in whose memory and testimony concerning Christ's resurrection baptism was accustomed to be sought: But that custom cannot be taught from the history of that time. (17) Heinfius's explanation is related, that the living are said to be baptized for the dead, because the names of the dead were imposed upon them. But who does not see that these are very different, and do not mutually explain each other? Not to mention that nothing solid can be adduced concerning that custom.

Furthermore, from the diversely interpreted meaning of the word ὑπὲρ, a diversity of exposition has arisen for this passage (18) in the notes of Junius and Tremellius on the New Testament. Beza's note explains it thus: That those who are baptized, are baptized for the dead, that is, that they may have a remedy against death, that death itself may be extinguished, or for the resurrection of the dead, of which baptism is a symbol.

But is this ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, against death?

(19) The notes of Tremellius on the translation of the Syriac text explain ὑπὲρ as 'beyond', likewise in an unusual sense, in this way: That if those holy men, who have hitherto undergone death, have been deluded in their expectation and hope, why then is the same thing done any further by the survivors, why is it still continued in the Church, and why do those who now live pursue the dead in the same office, if all things are in vain? Why, if the dead have fallen from their hope, do the living fail, by imitating the miserable dead, and make their own faith void over the void faith of others?

Sense: We understand those baptized ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν as those washed by Holy baptism, which was a symbol and profession of the future resurrection, Rom. VI. 3. seqq. Heb. VI. 2. after other deceased persons. But a similar example of the meaning of the word ὑπὲρ, joined with the Genitive, will hardly be found. Those things which are brought forward from Rom. I. 3. are foreign.

(20) Ludovicus de Dieu renders this ἔκθεσιν: As many as are baptized in the Church, are baptized not only for themselves, but for the faithful dead: Not to aid or liberate or relieve them, or in their place, but to establish incessantly the promises of the covenant made to them, and still to be fulfilled, so that as long as and as often as baptism is administered in the Church, so long and so often is the promise made to the dead renewed, that GOD is the GOD of them. And because GOD is not the GOD of the dead, but of the living, that they themselves live by the promise of GOD; wherefore it is necessary that they themselves should at some time live in act. Whence it is firmly concluded that the living are baptized for the dead in vain, if they are not to rise again. But in truth, since baptism is a means of salvation, with respect to those who use it, it is administered solely for the living, not for the dead. Therefore it is not dispensed on that reasoning, that the divine promise should be renewed regarding the dead, and if this is supposed in this place, it will not be a proof of the article of the resurrection of the dead , but a mere begging of the question.

(21) Deminus D. Henricus Moller wishes ὑπὲρ to be taken defensively for 'for', he differs. Theol. Hist. on baptism for the dead p. 49. so that they are said to be baptized for the dead who have fallen asleep in Christ, who by their baptism defend the dead in the faith of a blessed resurrection, and the nerve of the argument becomes: If you do not believe that those who have fallen asleep in Christ are to be raised to life, why do you defend them with your baptism, while you are baptized to this end, that the promise of life, apprehended by them through faith, may also be applied to you through faith. But this interpretation is hindered among other things, by the fact that it seems to encounter ἄπτησις τὲ ἐν ἀρχῇ.

For if the Corinthians had believed that those who had died in the faith had attained eternal life through baptism, the resurrection would not have needed to be confirmed by arguments for the sake of raising them up at some time (22) B. Luther wishes to refer to the custom by which Christians were accustomed to baptize in cemeteries over the sepulchres of the dead, and therefore it is the same as ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν: or that by the very fact they testified that the dead would one day be raised, or that they declared they would rather die than deny the Christian religion, whence it is consequently gathered that they believed in the resurrection of the dead, which is held earlier in Luther's notes on 1. Cor. XV. and later in Andreas Osiander.

Hunnius on this passage, as also D. Tilcm. Heshusius in h. l., B. Polycarpus Lyserus, comm. on Genesis chapter XXIII. p. 169., has it thus: At length it was introduced by custom that the dead are buried either in temples or beside temples.

Nor was this done at the beginning out of superstition, as if one place were more effective than another: But it was a testimony of one faith.

For when any one of the Bishops or Martyrs was impiously and wickedly killed somewhere on account of the confession of the truth, the pious built a chapel in his memory: and afterwards others also who had died in the same faith wished to be buried there, to testify to the hope of a broad resurrection.

There afterwards the survivors gathered together, prayed, read and heard the word of GOD, thought upon the resurrection, and received consolation over their dead. Indeed, even still in the time of the Apostles some wished to be baptized over the dead, that is, in that place where the saints had died, to testify the same faith, and hope of eternal life, 1. Cor. XV. 29. B.

D. Mylius on this passage has it thus concerning this matter: We follow the safer footsteps of Luther, who is certain to have been instructed by the Spirit of Prophecy. He retains the other interpretation (namely that ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν means over the dead), and he judges that because the Sacrament of Baptism in the time of the Apostles, especially among the Gentiles, for whom the article of resurrection was as it were incredible, was conferred in cemeteries and at the tombs of the dead, it had been established as a custom.

He retains the other interpretation (that namely ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν means 'over the dead'), and thinks that the Sacrament of Baptism in the time of the Apostles, especially among the Gentiles, to whom the article of the resurrection was as it were incredible, was accustomed to be conferred in cemeteries and at the sepulchres of the dead. Therefore, from this argument taken in the present case, he concludes that this rite would be frivolous if there were no resurrection. But since this is posited as an absurdity, he feels that the rite itself was invented for a salutary purpose and for the greatest use. Therefore he concludes from this that the resurrection is also most certain. To which B. Hutter in LL. de morte §. 268. B. Menzerus l. II. disp. Giessenf. disp. XIV. B. Meisnerus on Papist purgatory, conf. V. The authors of the Vinavien notes. B. Walther in his Harmony. B. Glassius l. III. Gram. Sacræ tr. VI. B. Dorcheus in Mysar. Miss. p. 31. B. Cundisius in Tyskivoz. elench. dn. D. Gejer disp. on prayers for the dead, as also Job Gerhard. Vossius disput. on the resurrection of the flesh th. 18. and Casp. Barthius in advers. L. XIV. c. 2. agree, and to support that opinion Dn. D. Müller l. c. brings forward that the most beloved of the faithful were accustomed to be buried in private houses, since because of persecutions they did not have public cemeteries and baptisteries, and that baptism was instituted over those sepulchres in domestic assemblies, although he himself confesses that he can scarcely prove what he timidly conjectures about these things.

Finally, and (23) by not a few, the explanation of Ambrose in his Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul is proven by a certain reason. He subjoins the example of those who were so secure about the future resurrection, that they even baptized for the dead, if by chance death had anticipated anyone, fearing that he might either badly, or not at all, rise again, who had not been baptized, the living was dipped in the name of the dead. By which example the Apostle does not approve of their deed, but builds up a firm faith in the resurrection. For by saying in the words immediately following, 'and why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour', he distinguished the persons, showing that it is not the Catholics, who were baptized for the dead.

Which custom Epiphanius attributes to the Corinthians, haer. XXVIII. & Chrysostom to the Marcionites, hom. XI. in ad Cor., as does Tertullian, l. de resurr. carnis & l. V. adversus Marc. cap. 10. See Pamelius on this passage, and in the same place Latinus Latinus.

Anselm and Haymo approve of this explanation, as does Chrysostom above on the Codex.

Eccl. univers. can. V. Andr. Hyperius Comm. in h.l. Camero in Myrothec. Jacob Laurentius in h.l.

Grotius here. D. Danhavv. Act. I. Dram. p. 447. Which we have also followed in the tract de Meib. doc. & Diff. p.

557. & D. Calixtus defended it l. c., as also in de immortalitate animarum pag. 57. Joseph Scaliger also assents to this interpretation, and among the Papists, Baronius ad ann.

Christi LVII. num. 168. Among the Socinians, Johannes Crellius in Comm. ad Corinth. XV. asserts it at length, as does Jonas Schlichtingius in h.l. And the properties of the words favor it, where each retains its usual meaning: βαπτίζεσθαι (to be baptized) are said of those who are baptized, νεκροὶ (dead) are truly such, and ὑπὲρ (for) is used in the customary sense, for ἀντὶ (instead of), just as it is also explained by Emmanuel Saa: What will they do, who are baptized in the place of the deceased? since it is consistent with history: Which some call into doubt in vain with Cloppenburg, since the very ancient Doctors of the Church testify to the antiquity of that rite (even if it is by no means to be approved): Nor does it stand in the way that it was perhaps a particular rite, because the Apostle also speaks only of some, and deals with καὶ ἀνθρώπων (and men): What will they do, who are baptized for the dead?

Or that the Apostle did not rebuke it. For there is no need for that in the disputes of καὶ ἀνθρώπων (and men). Add that no other explanations, if they are correctly weighed, are sufficiently convenient, as you can trust from that.

We leave the interpretation of the letter of the Apostle by the blessed Luther alone in the middle, not without merit, whether this last one of Ambrose, or the explanation of some of the blessed Luther, which, if anyone wishes, may be read in Tom. VI. Jenenf. Germ. fol. 246. But that which cannot be approved in Grotius is that Tertullian attributes to it that heterodoxy concerning care for the salvation of the dead, and prayers for the deceased, or that they were not done publicly for ceremonies, and therefore were accustomed to be done in such a vicarious baptism; because the Ancients, Tertullian, Epiphanius, Ambrose, disapprove of that insane rite of baptism, they do not praise it: To whom, therefore, Grotius rashly attributes a contrary mind, just as he did an injury to Scaliger in animadvert. ad Callandr. p.

93, as if he considers this custom to be good, when he rather considers it not good. The Ancients teach that this custom was used by heretics: Grotius inverts this, and says it was used by the Catholic Church, and therefore also draws without, who had crept in, of baptizing the deceased, and of offering the Eucharist even to their bodies, and thus he imagines that that vicarious baptism was used among other things, so that the Church might pray for the deceased.

Which he could by no means prove from the custom of the Church. V.

Latin:

29. Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται; Τί καὶ βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; Hic inì est præterea: & νῦν, est ergò. Τί ποιήσουσιν; Quid efficient? Est novum argumentum ex ritu tunc per Ecclesias recepto, unde appareat ab omnibus creditam resurrectionem.

Nam si quis in statu κατηχουμένων esset mortuus, erat qui ipsius vice ac nomine baptizabatur, sic mortui fidem apud Ecclesiam obsignans.

Tertullianus de resurrectione carnis: Si autem baptizantur quidam pro mortuis, sidebimus an ratione. Certe illa præsumptione hoc instituisse contendit, quia alii etiam carni, ut sicarium baptisma, profuturum existimarunt ad spem resurrectionis, quæ nisi corporalis non alias sic baptismate corporali obligaretur. Quid & ipsos baptizari, ait, si non qua baptizantur corpora resurgunt?

Idem adversus Marcionem: Quid, ait, facient, qui pro mortuis baptizantur, si mortui non resurgunt?

Viderit institutio ista. Kalendæ, si forte, Februaria, (respondebant illi) pro mortuis peterent. Noli ergò apostolum aut confirmatorum ejus ut denotare, ut tanto magis sisteret carnis resurrectionem, quanto illi, qui varie pro mortuis baptizarentur esse resurrectionis hoc facerent.

Ambrosius aut quisquis est, qui sub ejus nomine ad hunc locum legitur: In tantum stabilem & ratam vult ostendere mortuorum resurrectionem, ut exemplum eorum, qui tam securi erant de futura resurrectione, ut etiam pro mortuis baptizarentur, si quem mors prævenisset, timentes ne aut male aut non resurgeret, qui baptizatus non fuerat, vivus nomine mortui tingebatur. Unde subjecit: Quid & baptizantur pro illis? Exemplo hoc non factum illorum probat, sed fixam fidem in resurrectione ostendit.

Marcionitas hoc mores usos tùm è Tertulliani verbis intelligitur, tùm apertè id dicit Chrysostomus & post eum alii. Volebant autem videri Marcionitæ omnium, quæ Paulus aut instituerat aut probaverat, seduli sectatores. Mirari hunc ritum debemus, quod nonnullis in locis ipsa mortuorum corpora sint baptizata, ut apparet ex canone, qui aliis est XVIII. aliis XIX. concilii Carthaginensis, nec minus mortuis corporibus data Eucharistia, ut nos docet idem canon Carthaginensis & LXXXIII. synodi in Trullo habitæ.

Credo autem inter alia usurpatum illum vicarium baptismum, ut Ecclesia pro defunctis oraret. Non solebant enim publicæ preces fieri pro Catechumenis, quamquam eleemosynas pro eis licebat dare.

Locus hic quidem non tot interpretationes nactus est, quot habet interpretes, ut Calixtus ad hunc locum & libr. de Purgat. Benè tamen multæ occurrunt ejusdem expositiones.

Nonnulli (1.) in voce baptismi tropum quærunt, & de baptismi prismo sanguinis vel afflictionis interpretantur, utpote Alexand. Morus in hunc locum, qui præterea Enallagen fingit, & baptizari pro mortuis contortè explicat, baptizari baptismo Christi, hoc modo: Aut quid nobis fieri poterit stultius, qui pro illo mortuo quidem non oppetimus mortem, sed tamen totidem quasi mortes, quotidie discrimine capitis adimus.

(2.) Quo faciunt imprimis Papistæ, qui de sponsaneis afflictionibus, suscipietis de sponsaneis pro mortuis, pro illis orando, jejunando, gementes, do, sese affligendo exponunt. Bellarm. l. 1. de Purg. Salmero, Stapleton, Mcnochius, Saa, Tirinus, Estius in IV. sent. distinct. 3. §. 2. Tannerus aliique.

(3.) de martyriis Claudius Grillaudus in h. l. 3. de martyriis.

Gagneus, & Bence DD. Sorbonici hoc loco Maldon. ad Luc. XII. 50. baptizantur, inquit, pro mortuis martyres, qui patiuntur & affliguntur pro fide & articulo resurrectionis mortuorum: quibus (etsi Papistæ ipsi, etiam Estius ipse in hoc locoἑαυτο- ) ἑαυτομαχῶν, & Gabriel Vasquez Jesuita in 3. Thomæ t. 2. disp. 157. num. 45, ei os refellant) è Calvinianis Franc. Jun. in Bellarm. de Purg. non abnuit: Ex Arminianis Daniel Tilenus Parte II. disp. cap. 5. cui verò ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν est super, præter, & ultra illos, qui jam ante propter fidem, vel in fide Christi mortui sunt.

Annuit etiam B. Job. (4.) Hieronymus ita explicat: Quid prodest mundo mori, si hunc contemptum voluptatum non sequitur vita æterna? (5.) Brochmando in System. βαπτίζεσθαι est dolere & deflere, ut sensus sit: Quid faciunt, quodnam solamen habent, qui acerbius suos deflent, & lacrymis suis abluuntur pro mortuis, quæ interpretatio Job. Tob. Majori orat. pro defunctis contra Grot. cap. II, §. 140. simplicissima omnium videtur.

(6.) Anna Maria Seburmannia apud Cloppenburg. Disput.

Select. XIV. §. 14. ita explicat: Frustra tot labores subiri pro mortuis, pro fidelibus & electis, qui ea ratione pro mortuis planè habendi, si nulla est mortuorum resurrectio.

Sed istis interpretationibus temerè ad tropicam acceptionem vocis βαπτίζεσθαι, binis vicibus adhibitæ, descenditur: Neque jejunare, gemere, seipsum affligere, est baptizari, nec uspiam baptizari idem est, quod dolere, aut labores subire.

Porrò pro mortuis orandum & jejunandum esse, ἄγαφον est, neque ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν explicari potest, vel pro fide mortuorum, vel præter mortuos, vel pro fidelibus pro mortuis habitu, aut τί ποιήσουσι, quodnam habebunt solamen.

Alii itaque baptismum intelligunt de ὕδατοβαπτισμῷ, atque id iterum diversimodè.

Nam (7.) quidam loquutiones respici. malunt eorum, qui ex contactu mortuorum immundi reddebantur, Num. XIX. quod illæ significarint resurrectionem mortuorum: Conferentes Simc. c. XXXIV. 30. Utpote Vasquez Tom. II. parte 3. disp. 157. num. 49. seqq. & Johan. Coccejus in Comm. in Ebræos IX. 13. 14. Quæ verò contorta & anfractuosa explicatio vix referri meretur, quam etiam Benedictus Justinianus meritò coactam ac violentam dixit.

(8.) Expeditior videtur Dn. D. Sebastiani Schmidii ἔκθεσις disp. de bapt. super mortuos §. III. & ad Luc. VI. 1. de sabbato δευτεροπρώτῳ quæ ita habet: quia resurrectio mortuorum certò futura est, immundi fiebant, qui tangebant mortuos, atque baptizabantur super illos, ut ritu illo profiterentur, se propter resurrectionem mortuorum credere omnino immundos peccato gravissimo reddi, quicunque minus piè & honestè mortuos tractarent, & ablutione à peccato opus habere.

Cui vero explicationi, salvâ autoritate Theologi optimi, mihique amicissimi, subscribere non possumus: quia non facile dicendum, immundos redditos esse, qui tangebant mortuos, ideò quod minus piè & honestè mortuos; olim resurrecturos, tractârunt, nam & immundi redditi sunt è cadaveribus bestiarum: Imò immundities illa Levitica à cadaveribus ideò contracta fuit, quod cadavera ipsos polluerint, non quod cadavera ab ipsis minus honestè tractarentur, conf.

Hagg. II. 14. eratque ea significatio quædam maledictionis mortis & corruptionis, quæ per peccatum invecta. Nihil ergò videtur facere ad resurrectionem mortuorum.

Ut taceamus, quod ex antiquitate non constet, eos, qui mortuos attigerant, aut etiam, qui minus honestè tractarant, ablutos fuisse aqua ad professionem fidei resurrectionis mortuorum.

(9.) Si quibus verd commodior videtur fortè Bezæ & annot. Belgic. de ablutionibus mortuorum, qua fiunt in fidem resurrectionis mortuorum, explicatio, quam omnibus aliis præfert Chamier Tom. III. Panstrat. lib. XXVI. cap. XIX. num. 35. iis verba Apostoli obstabunt, qui non activè loquitur, sed passivè, βαπτιζόμενοι, neque congruit phrasis baptizari super mortuis, quæ certè non notat abluere mortuos.

(10.) Illa verò interpretatio Turriani, quæ à Bedecente aliquo in immunditie legali alium ejus nomine aqua lustrali abluerint, unde Papistæ aquæ suæ benedictæ usum similem deducunt, Judais fabellarum Magistris dignior est, quàm interpretibus Christianis.

Porrò (11.) baptismum famofiore significatione intelligendum esse, quæ Novi Testamenti propria est pro sacramento baptismi pleraque interpretis facile admittunt: Cætera verò verba diversimodè explicant, utpote vocem νεκρῶν, per quam mortua opera intelligit Sedulius, qui baptizantur pro mortuis operibus abolendis, impetrata scil. eorum remissione: Quem sequuntur Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Aquinas & Contarenus.

Sed quamvis peccata ἔργα νεκρὰ dicantur, Ebr. IX. 14. nuspiam tamen τῶν νεκρῶν nomine absolutè veniunt, & nimis manifestum est, de personis hic sermonem esse, non de operibus.

Alii (12.) & quidem Johan. Gerhard.

Vossius disp. XII. de bapt. & Guilielmus Estius pro mortuis exponunt, pro flatu mortuorum, vel ut sibi post mortem benè fit. Affinis est Isdori Pelusiotæ l. I. epist. CXXII. explicatio: Pro corporibus natura mortuis & extinctis baptizantur ea in immortalitatem ac flatum à corruptione alienum mutari credentes; Et Sebastiani Castallionis: Pauli argumentum hoc est: Christiani dum baptizantur, in hoc baptizantur, ut cum Christo moriantur, deinde resurgant.

Hoc est baptizari pro mortuis, id est pro seipsis, in spem rei, quam post mortem assequuturi sint, videlicet resurrectionis, id quod fultum esset, si nulla futura esset resurrectio.

Hanc sententiam me docuit quidam Italus.

Sed de aliis personis, pro quibus baptismus suscipitur, non de ipsis suscipientibus agit Apostolus: Neque uspiam nomine νεκρῶν flatus mortuorum notatur.

Alii (13.) νεκρῶν accipiunt de iis, qui mortuis similes sunt, moribundi, adeoque de baptismo Clinicorum Epiphanio explicant, ut puta Calvinus, Marlot. Hemmingius, Flacius hoc modo: Quid faciunt, qui baptizantur pro mortuis? id est, qui baptizantur, quando habentur magis pro mortuis, quàm viventibus, & quando certum est, eos non baptizari pro ullo commodo hujus vitæ, cum pro mortuis habeantur. Vid. Epiphan. ber. XXIX. At ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, quomodo esse potest baptizari, ceu moribundos?

Ubi vis Præpositionis ὑπὲρ relinquitur?

Aliud certè est baptizari mortis causa, aliud pro mortuis (14.) Nonnulli cum Oecumenio & Theophylacto carnem mortuam definire volunt, præeunte Hieronymo in hunc locum: Quid baptizare opus est carnem, si non resurgat? Sed nec caro τῶν νεκρῶν nomine indigitatur, neque ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν baptizari idem esse potest, quod baptizari carnem.

(15.) Chrysostomus vocem ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν exponit pro fide de mortuis, eorumque resurrectione, super mortuis scilicet corporibus, quod de mortuis resurrectura sint. At hic sensus è verbis Apostoli intelligi vel haberi non potest.

Quid faciunt illi, qui pro mortuis baptizantur? id est, ita ut testentur symboli Apostolici professione, quod tùm in usu fuisse nunquam docebitur, eorumdem resurrectionem.

(16.) Cloppenburgius pro mortuis non eligit certos quosdam mortuos, eos nimirum, qui ex mortuis.

ex quingentis fratribus in Domino obdormierant, in quorum memoriam & testimonium de Christi resurrectione baptismus peti consueverit: Sed illa consuetudo ex historia istius temporis haud doceri potest. (17) Affinis est Heinfiana explicatio, vivos pro mortuis baptizatos dici, quod nomina mortuorum ipsis imposita sint. Sed hæc maximè diversa esse, non verò mutuo se explicare, ecquis non videt? ut taceam, nec de illa consuetudine quicquam adduci solidè posse.

Ulterius è vocis etiam ὑπὲρ diverimodâ interpretatione diversitas exorta est expositionis hujus loci (18) in notis Junio-Trevellianis ad N. Testam. Adversione Bezæ Junius ita exposuit: Quod, qui baptizantur, pro mortuis baptizentur, id est, ut adversus mortem remedium habeant, ut mors ipsa extinguatur, sive in resurrectionem mortuorum, cujus baptismus est symbolum.

Sed num hoc est ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, adversus mortem?

(19) Tre-mellianæ notæ ad Syriaci textus translationem ὑπὲρ explicant præter, insolito itidem sensu, hoc modo: Quod si sancti illi viri, qui hactenus obiverunt mortem, sua expectatione & spe delusi sunt, quid ergò à superstitibus idem amplius agitur, cur ita adhuc pergitur in Ecclesia, & qui nunc vivunt, mortuos in eodem officio persequuntur, si inani sunt omnia? Cur si mortui spe fui exciderunt, viventes deficiunt, mortuos miseros imitando, & super irrita illorum fide irritam faciunt suam?

Sensus: Baptizatos ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν intelligimus de ablutis S. baptismo, quod erat symbolum & professio futuræ resurrectionis, Rom. VI. 3. seqq. Ebr. VI. 2. post alios demortuos. Sed significationis vocis ὑπὲρ, conjunctæ cum Genitivo, confimilem exemplum vix reperietur. Aliena sunt, quæ è Rom. I. 3. afferuntur.

(20) Ludovicus de Dieu ἔκθεσιν hanc reddit: Quotquot in Ecclesia baptizantur, non modo pro se, sed pro mortuis fidelibus baptizantur: Non ad eos juvandos aut liberandos, aut sublevandos, aut eorum loco, sed ad stabiliendas indefinenter promissiones fœderis ipsis factas, & adhuc implendas, adeò, ut quamdiu & quoties baptismus administratur in Ecclesia, tamdiu & toties renovetur facta mortuis promissio, DEUM esse DEUM ipsorum. Et quia DEUS non est DEUS mortuorum, sed viventium, vivere ipsos DEI promissione; quocirca necesse esse, ut aliquando ipsi vivant actu. Unde firmiter concluditur, frustra vivos pro mortuis baptizari, si non sint resurrecturi. Verum enimverò, cum baptismus sit medium salutis, respectu eorum, qui utuntur eodem, non pro mortuis, sed vivis administratur unicè. Non itaque eâ ratione dispensatur, ut renovetur, quoad mortuos, divina promissio, & si hoc supponatur hoc loco, erit sic non articuli resurrectionis mortuorum probatio, sed mera principii petitio.

(21) De-minus D. Henricus Moller ὑπὲρ, pro, accipi defensè vult differt. Theol. Hist. de baptismo pro mortuis p. 49. ut illi dicti sint pro mortuis, qui in Christo obdormierunt, baptizari, qui baptismo suo defendunt mortuos in fide beatæ resurrectionis, & nervus argumenti fit: Si non creditis eos, qui in Christo obdormierunt, resuscitatum iri ad vitam, cur defenditis eos baptismo vestro, dum eum in finem baptizamini, at promissio vita, ab ipsis fide apprehensa, etiam vobis per fidem applicetur. Obstat autem huic interpretationi inter alia pariter, quod ita videatur occurrere ἄπτησις τὲ ἐν ἀρχῇ.

Nam si credidissent Corinthii, per baptismum eos, qui in fide deceffere, vitam æternam adeptos, olim ad eos resuscitandos, argumentis firmanda non fuisset resuscitatio (22) B Lutherus respici vult consuetudinem, qua Christiani in cemeteriis solebant baptizare super sepulchris mortuorum, ideoque idem est, quod ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν: seu quod ipso facto ita testarentur, mortuos olim resuscitatum iri, seu quod mori malle declarent, quam religionem Christianam abnegare, unde consequenter colligitur, eos resurrectionem mortuorum credidisse, quorum prius habetur apud Lutherum in notis ad 1. Cor. XV. posterius apud Andream Osiandrum. Cui sententiæ favet B.

Hunnius ad hunc locum, ut & D. Tilcm. Heshusius in h. l. B. Polycarpus Lyserus comm. in Genetin cap. XXIII. p. 169. ita habet: Tandem usu introductum est, ut mortui sepeliantur vel in templis, vel juxta templa.

Neque hoc initio ex superstitione factum est, quasi unus locus plus faceret, quam alter: Sed fuit id testimonium unius fidei.

Nam quando aliquis Episcoporum vel Martyrum ob confessionem veritatis impiè & nefariè alicubi occisus est, pii in memoriam ejus ædificaverunt, vel sacellum: Ibidemque postea & alii in eadem fide defuncti sepeliri voluerunt ad testificandam spem latæ resurrectionis.

Ibi postea superstites convenerunt, orarunt, verbum DEI legerunt & audierunt, de resurrectione cogitarunt, atque consolationem super mortuis suis receperunt. Imò adhuc Apostolorum tempore aliqui super mortuos baptizari voluerunt, hoc est, in eo loco, abi sancti mortui essent, ad testificandam eandem fidem, & spem vitæ æternæ, 1. Cor. XV. 29. B.

D. Mylius in h. l. de eo ita habet: Nos Lutheri tutius sequimur vestigia, quem Spiritu Prophetia instructum fuisse certum est. Is alteram interpretationem (quod nempe ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν sit super mortuis) retinet, & quod Baptismi Sacramentum tempore Apostolorum, præcipue inter gentes, quibus articulus resurrectionis erat quasi incredibilis, in cemeteriis, & ad sepulchra mortuorum collatum fuerit, in more positum fuisse existimat.

Huic ergo argumento in præsenti causa petito, ritum istum frivolum fore colligit, si non fit resurrectio. Atqui hoc pro absurdo posito, salutari consilio & usu maximo ritum ipsum inventum esse sentit. Ergo resurrectionem hinc etiam certissimam esse colligit. Quibus & B. Hutterus in LL. de morte §. 268. B. Menzerus l. II. disp. Giessens. disp. XIV. B. Meisnerus de purgat. Papist. cvf. V. Autores notarum Vinavienfium. B. Waltherus in Harmonia. B. Glassius l. III. Gram. Sacræ tr. VI. B. Dorcheus in Mysar. Miss. p. 31. B. Cundisius in Tyskivoz. elench. dn. D. Gejer disp. de precibus pro defunct. ut & Job Gerhard. Vossius disput. de resurr. carnis th. 18. & Casp. Barthius in advers. L. XIV. c. 2. annuunt, eique sententiæ juvandæ affert Dn. D. Müllerus l. c. quod in ædibus privatis fidelium charissimi sepeliri consueverint, cum ob persecutiones cemeteria & baptisteria publica non haberentur, & fuper illa sepulchra, in ædibus baptizatus, in congressibus domesticis institutus fit, quum ipse fatetur, se vix probare, quæ timide de his conjicit.

Postremo denique & (23) non paucis certâ ratione probatur Ambrosii explicatio tuorum in Comment. in Epist. Paulin. Exemplum eorum subjicit, qui tam securi erant de futuræ resurrectione, ut etiam pro mortuis baptizarent, si quem forte mors prævenisset, timentes, ne aut male, aut non resurgeret, qui baptizatus non fuesset, vivus nomine mortui tingebatur. Quo quidem exemplo non illorum factum probat Apostolus, sed fixam in resurrectione fidem adstruit. Dicendo enim verbis immediatè sequentibus, quid & nos omni hora periclitamur, discrevit personas, ostendens, non visse Catholicos, qui pro mortuis baptizabantur.

Quam consuetudinem Corinthianis tribuit Epiphanius hær. XXVIII. & Marcionitis Chryfostomus hom. XI. in. ad Cor. ut & Tertull. l. de refurr. carnis & l. V. adversus Marc. cap. 10. Vidcatur Pamelius ad hunc locum, & ibidem Latinus Latinus.

Probant hanc explicationem Anselmus & Haymo, ut & Chryfostomus fuperius ad Codicc.

Ecclef. univers. can. V. Andr. Hyperius Comm. in h.l. Camero in Myrothec. Jacob Laurentius in h.l.

Grotius bic. D. Danhavv. Act. I. Dram. p. 447. Quam etiam fequuti fumus tract. de Meib. doc. & Diff. p.

557. & propugnavit D. Calixtus l. c. ut & de immortalitate animarum pag. 57. Annuit etiam huic interpretationi Jofephus Scaliger, & è Pontificiis Baronius ad ann.

Christi LVII. num. 168. E Socinianis Johannes Crellius in Comm. ad Corinth. XV. prolixè eam afferens, ut & Jonas Sublichtingius in h.l. Et favent illi tum verborum proprietates, quæ singula ita redinent suam usitatam fignificationem, βαπτίζεσθαι dicuntur, qui baptizantur, νεκροὶ mortui, revera tales, & ὑπὲρ sensu confueto, pro avrì vice adhibetur, quemadmodum etiam ab Emanuele Saa exponitur: Quid facient illi, qui loco defunctorum baptizantur? cùm hisoria consonantia: Quam nequicquam nonnulli in dubium vocant cum Cloppenburgio, siquidem antiquitatem istius ritus (etfi minimè probandi) Doctores Ecclesiastici perantiqui testentur: Neque obstat, vel quod particularis fortè ille ritus fuerit, quia etiam de quibusdam tantùm loquitur, & καὶ ἀνθρώπων agit Apostolus: Quid facient illi, qui baptizantur pro mortuis?

Vel quod non reprehenderit illum Apostolus. Id enim in disputationibus καὶ ἀνθρώπων non opus est. Adde quod nullæ aliæ explicationes, fi rectè expenddantur, fatis conveniant, ut ex eam confidere potes.

Sola B. Lutheri interpretatio litera Apostoli, de non immeritò in medio relinquimus, five hanc postremam Ambrofii, five nonnullorum B. Lutheri explicationem, qui fiqui velit, de qua legatur Tom. VI. Jenenf. Germ. fol. 246. Id verò in Grotius ne probari nequit, quod Tertullius affricet inde heterodoxiam illam, de cura pro salute mortuorum, & orationes pro defunctis, five pro cæremoniis publicè facta non sint, ideoque in tali vitario baptismo fieri confueverunt; quia ritum istum baptismi vesanum improbat, non laudant Veteres, Tertullianus, Epiphanius, Ambrofius: Quibus proinde Grotius temerè affingit contrariam mentem, quemadmodum & Scaligero in animadvert. ad Callandr. p.

93. injuriam fecit, quasi morum hunc pro probo habeat, quem potius pro non probo habet. Scaligeri Veteres ab hæreticis, & usurpatam hanc consuetudinem docent: Invertit hoc Grotius, & usurpatam ait ab Ecclesia Catholica, ideoque etiam trahit absque, qui irrepserat, baptizandi defunctos, & præbendi eorum corporibus etiam Eucharistiam, adeoque fingit, baptismum illum vicarium inter alia usurpatum, ut Ecclesia pro defunctis oraret.

Quod probare ex Ecclesiæ consuetudine minimè potuit. V.

## 15:30
30. Τί καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν πᾶσαν ὥραν; Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour? We, the Apostles, and our fellow-workers the Evangelists, if there is no resurrection of the dead to be hoped for, we are the most foolish of men.

See above 19. / καὶ ἀνθρώπω ἀποθνήσκω.

That is, I am prepared to die daily. See 2. Cor. IV. 11. Thus Paul died daily, just as he is said to have committed adultery who desired it.

403 V. 31. Νὴ τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, ἣν ἔχω ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν. By your rejoicing, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The possessive pronoun here, which is in place of the Genitive, just as the genitive elsewhere, designates the efficient cause. For he wants to say this: As truly as I rejoice (for that is what καύχησις is) in your progress in Christ, so true it is that I am prepared to die daily: So far is it from the case that I doubt whether there is a resurrection.

A response to the objections of the Greeks, which is in the works of Justin: Even if the doctrine concerning the resurrection is not true to you, how do the witnesses of their own Savior, from others, endure the most severe tortures and deaths for the doctrine of their own resurrection, or of their own knowledge of God, I mean the Christians concerning the resurrection of the dead. Εἰ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ. If I fought with beasts at Ephesus after the manner of men.

Some think that Paul was actually forced to fight with beasts at Ephesus and escaped safe by the help of GOD, just as we read that Ignatius was thrown to the beasts, and Christians were condemned to the lion, according to Tertullian.

But first, Luke would not have passed over such a remarkable thing, who notes even lesser things of Paul, and indeed of those times. Wherefore it will be more correct to understand that he had to contend at Ephesus with beastly men, just as Plutarch says in Lycurgus θηριομάχης τρέφειν (to raise a beast-fighter).

Thus also Deut.

XXIII. 33. they are compared to impious beasts, and kings are everywhere in the writings of the Prophets, and 2. Tim. IV. 17. For it was commonly accepted that those who had business with savage men were called θηριομάχοι (beast-fighters). However, I agree with Tertullian, who thinks that the same thing is touched upon here that is touched upon in 2.

Cor. I. 8. For thus he says concerning the resurrection: Through which he will also fight against the beasts at Ephesus. Τί μοι τὸ ὄφελος, εἰ νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται. What is the profit to me, if the dead are not raised?

It would have been easy for me to appease their minds, had not the confidence of the resurrection caused me to despise all dangers. Τί τὸ ὄφελος; מה בצע (What is the profit?).

Ambrosiaster, Theodoret, Primasius, Cajetan, Cornelius, and the blessed Luther take θηριομαχίαν (fighting with beasts) properly concerning beasts, and that Paul was truly thrown to the beasts at Ephesus, but was divinely delivered. But because that is nowhere read either in scripture or in Ecclesiastical history, nor is Paul said here to have been thrown to the beasts, but to have fought with beasts, whereas when martyrs were thrown to the beasts, they did not fight with them, it is more correctly understood metaphorically, that he says he fought with beasts, that is, with men of beastly minds and manners.

Ignatius in his epistle to the Romans.

From Syria to Rome, by land and sea, I fight with beasts; so that not only Tertullian, but also the Greeks Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, as well as Pelagius, Haymo, Herveus, and Thomas refer it to the contention with Demetrius, Act.

XIX. 2. Cor. I. But since that pressure of 2.

Cor. I. is mentioned as recent, indeed it is evident from the Acts that it happened at the final time when Paul stayed at Ephesus, it could not yet be brought forward here, and therefore this must be another fight, not mentioned in the Acts, in which no other is mentioned. See

2. Cor. XI. Oecumenius does not explain that καὶ ἀνθρώπων (and men) from Photius, as much as was possible for me.

Cajetan renders it interrogatively: Did I fight with beasts according to man and not according to GOD?

Estius by a parenthesis in this way from the collation of Rom.

III. 5. I Cor. III. 8. Gal.

III. 15. 2. Cor. XI. That (to speak after the manner of men, who are wont to talk freely about their fights, from which they have emerged gloriously) I met with my adversaries as if with beasts, and fought at Ephesus, and sustained their attack, what does it profit me?

Perhaps it is not inconveniently explained: If I fought with beasts according to the (external) man, exposing my body and this human life to extreme dangers, what does this profit me?

And Tertullian seems to go away: Namely, that Paul insinuates the hope of the resurrection of his own body, because he had suffered such things in the body.

Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die. An imitation depicting the Epicureans and others of that kind in their own words. The words are taken from the Greek of Isaiah XXII. 13. Horace has many such things. Strato: "And let us drink and enjoy ourselves, Diophantus. For we shall not drink forever, nor shall we always be enjoying ourselves." And another: "Drink and be merry, for what tomorrow or what the future holds, no one knows." But Zalladus: "Death is owed to all mortals, nor is there any mortal who knows if he will live tomorrow."

Both in Isaiah and here, "tomorrow we die" means we shall die shortly. Life is short. The present is used here again for the future, as above in XIII. 13. Therefore, the Apostle means to say: If there is no future resurrection, what prevents everyone from leading an Epicurean life, and filling themselves with delights and pleasures, and saying: Let us eat and drink, let us live genially, while we may.

Let Wisdom II. v. 33 be compared. "Do not be deceived." A form of warning as above in VI. 9. Gal. VI. 7. "Evil communications corrupt good manners." This is a verse from Menander's Thais, as Jerome teaches us, written thus by Menander himself: "Evil communications corrupt good manners." For it is a Trimeter made of Spondees and Iambs: but with the Spondee in its own place. Tertullian translated it in a freer Trimeter, such as Latin Comedies use, thus: "Evil gatherings corrupt good manners."

Not unlike this sentiment: "Every evil man is born from evil associations." And that of Theognis: "For from the noble you will learn noble things, but if you mingle with the base, you will destroy even the mind that you possess." Donatus on Eunuchus II. 2. See how he demonstrates sententiously that the bad are made from the good by contagion, with examples prevailing toward the base.

Paul signifies that the conversations of those who take away the hope of another life are most dangerous. If, therefore, as Tertullian has it in the cited place, what was written by Menander was the word of a man, the same thing later, dictated by the Holy Spirit, written by Paul, became the word of GOD. The Apostle implies, however, that there were among the Corinthians those who, with arguments taken from Philosophy, as is likely, tried to undermine the faith of the resurrection among the faithful in private conversations. v. 34. "Awake to righteousness." Eknephsein is properly said of those who return to themselves from drunkenness, as in Gen. IX. 24, 1 Sam. XXV. 37, Joel I. 5. It is transferred to all those who are freed from error, as in Hab. II. 19. "Righteously," however, is briefly said for "living righteously," to live justly in the future. "And do not sin."

Do not give yourselves to pleasures, as those Epicureans do. "For some have an ignorance of GOD." There are hidden among you certain atheists, asher lo yade'u El, as the Hebrews say. "Without understanding" and the despair of a better life are neighbors. "I speak to your shame." As above in VI. 5. He chastises them because they do not flee the company of such men. Estius here disapproves of the Latin Vulgate, which has "awake, ye just."

In Greek dikaios, literally "justly": with the Syriac text agreeing. Some Latin MSS also read "justly," and with them the ancient concordances, as well as Ambrose in his commentary on Psalm 118, section 10. Nor was there such a need for the Apostle to exhort the just to awake, as those about whom it follows immediately: "For some have an ignorance of GOD." It is no wonder, however, if "justly" was changed to "just," which is read in most Latin texts: For the slip of the scribes in one letter was easy, especially when they did not understand what it is to "awake justly."

These are the words of Estius. He signifies, however, that some among the Corinthians had already been seduced by evil conversations, whom he recalls to a sound and sober mind. Eknephate is rendered: "And be sober" by Ambrose, Augustine in epistle 137 and in his commentary on Psalm 128, and Sedulius in this place. These can be joined for a fuller sense of the Greek word in this way: That, having digested the drunkenness of errors and pleasures, they may awaken from sleep, devoted to sobriety, wise in those things which are just and right. "Do not sin" is added, lest by the despair of a future life they immerse themselves in pleasures, because what follows applies to such people: "For some have an ignorance of GOD," who, namely, immerse themselves entirely in the pleasures of this world, so that they do not even think about GOD. The Vulgate wrongly renders pros entropen as "to reverence."

For it is "to shame," that is, so that I may inflict shame upon you. PART III. DIDACTIC. ARTICLE I. Concerning the Qualities of Bodies in the Resurrection. v. 35. "But someone will say, how are the dead raised?" That is, how can it be that the dead come to life again?

For after Paul had established his own points, he refutes the objections of the Philosophers. "And with what body do they come?" Namely, into life. Thus those Philosophers argued. If they return in the same body, whose will it be? For they will neither eat, nor drink, nor beget. If in another, they will not be the same. Paul answers that it will be in some way the same, and in some way not the same, and he illustrates this through similarities. "Fool."

He rightly calls them so, who do not believe that miracles can happen, when nature itself is full of miracles, but which, by their frequency, migrate into another name. v. 36. "You, what you sow, what is made alive, unless it dies." It was an old custom among the Rabbis to compare a buried body to a grain. Rabbi Meir uses this similarity regarding Cleopatra, as we read in the Gemara on the Sanhedrin, chapter XI; Rabbi Hya also uses it. Clement V. 6 explains this similarity quite diligently. Theophilus of Antioch, book 1: "For if it happens to be a grain of wheat or of the remaining seeds, if it is cast into the earth, it first dies and is dissolved, then it is raised and becomes an ear of corn." And book II: "See the earth becoming that which exists in dissolution. He fashioned it within, and various and many things, and that through them the resurrection is shown as a sign of the resurrection of all men that is to be."

A grain is said to die when, snatched from the air, it is hidden in the earth. In the manuscript it is zoopoieitai. The Hebrew chayah is translated now this way, now that. Pliny says of the seed that it "vivifies." No objection is moved here by the adversaries against the resurrection, but information is provided regarding a Theological doubt, how bodies will behave themselves in the resurrection: Or as Theophylact: Two things come into doubt, namely the mode of rising, by what means the body, once collapsed into ashes and resolved, is lifted up, and with what body, this one or some other?

But he dissolves both of these with a weighty example. Yet he uses a similarity of this kind, which exhibits the figure of the resurrection.

To prove and illustrate it in a certain way, that it is not incredible that putrid bodies be reformed and resurrected, just as putrefied and dead seed germinates as it is reborn: Compare Job XII. 24. Whom Saint Augustine makes the Apostle to be gathering in Epistle 146. If GOD can add what was not in the new seed, much more in the resurrection can He repair what was in the body of man.

Therefore, death does not stand in the way of the resurrection, so that the death of bodies is, as it were, a certain sowing toward life, as the Apostle teaches. Augustine, Sermon 34 on the words of the Apostle: The whole administration of this world, he says, is a testimony of the future resurrection. We see trees stripped of fruit and leaves in the winter time or at its arrival: But they [are restored] also in the spring time. to express the appearance of the resurrection, which first indeed begin to swell in the buds, then to be adorned in flowers, to be clothed in leaves, and afterwards to be weighed down with fruits. Question, O faithless man, you who doubt the resurrection, where are these things, which are produced at the time that GOD has ordained? Tell me, where do they hide before they are produced? Which are nowhere indeed seen. But yet GOD, who is omnipotent, and created them from nothing, produces them by His secret power. Hence now look back to the fields and meadows, which, when summer has passed, are despoiled of their herbs and flowers, and the very spaces of the lands remain bare. But again in the spring time they are revealed, and the farmer rejoices everywhere as the new sprout begins. Certainly the herb, which lived before and dies, revives again from the seed: Thus also our body revives from the dust. v.

Latin:

30. Τί καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν πᾶσαν ὥραν; Nos Apostoli, & Evangelistæ coadjutores nostri, fi nulla est refurrectio mortuorum speranda, stultissimi nos hominum fumus.

Vide supra 19. / καὶ ἀνθρώπω ἀποθνήσκω.

Id est, quotidie paratus fum mori. Vide 2. Cor. IV. 11. In Sic Paulus quotidie moriebatur, quomodo dicitur adulterium feciffe, qui id voluit.

403 V. 31. Νὴ τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, ἣν ἔχω ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.

Pronomen hic possessivum, quod vice Genitivi est, sicut alibi genitivus, defignat causam efficientem. Hoc enim vult dicere: Quàm verè ego gaudeo (id enim est καύχησις) de vestro profectu in Christo, ita verum est, me quotidie paratum mori: Tantum abest, ut dubitem an fit refurrectio.

Responfio ad objecta Græcorum, quæ ost in Justini operibus: Εἰ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἐκ ὄντο ἀληθὲς τὸ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως δόγμα, ὑπὲρ τῆς τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἀναστάσεως οἱ μάρτυρες τοῦ ἐαυτῶν Σωτῆρος πῶς δὴ ἐξ ἄλλων δεινοτάτους βασάνους τε καὶ θανάτους ὑπομένειν τὸ δόγμα, ἢ τῆς ἑαυτῶν Θεογνωσίας, λέγω δὴ τῶν χριστιανῶν περὶ τῆς τοῦ νεκρῶν ἀναστάσεως. Εἰ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ.

Quidam putant, Paulum revera cum bestiis coactum depugnare Ephefi & DEI ope salvum evasisse, quomodo Ignatium feris objectum legimus, & Christianos ad Leonem damnatos apud Tertullianum.

Sed primùm non erat rem tam infignem præteriturus Lucas, qui & minora Pauli, & quidem illorum temporum, annotat. Quare rectius erit intelligere, concertandum sibi fuisse Ephefi cum hominibus feris, quoinodo θηριομάχης τρέφειν dicit in Lycurgo Plutarchus.

Sic & Deut.

XXIII. 33. impiis feris comparantur, & paffim Reges in literis Prophetarum, & 2. Tim. IV. 17. Erat enim vulgo receptum, ut quibus negotium erat cum hominibus efferatis, ii dicerentur θηριομάχοι. Assentior autem Tertulliano, qui eandem rem hic tangi putat, quæ tangitur 2.

Cor. I. 8. Ita enim ille de refurrectione: Per quam & repugnabit ad bestias Ephefi. Τί μοι τὸ ὄφελος, εἰ νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται.

Facile mihi fuisset placare illorum animos, nisi fiducia refurrectionis effecisset, ut omnia pericula contemnerem. Τί τὸ ὄφελος; מה בצע.

Mam θηριομαχίαν accipiunt propriè de feris Ambrosiaster, Theodoretus, Primafius, Cajetanus, Cornelius, B. Lutherus, verèque Paulum Ephefi feris objectum fuisse, sed divinitus liberatum. Sed quia id nuspiam legitur five in scriptura, five in historia Ecclesiastica, nec objectus hic bestiis dicitur Paulus, sed pugnasse cum bestiis, quum verò martyres bestiis objicerentur, non pugnârunt cum illis, rectius Metaphoricè intelligitur, quod cum bestiis, id est hominibus, ferinis animis & moribus etiam se pugnasse dicit.

Ignatiis in epist. ad Rom.

A Syria Romam usque terrâ marique cum bestiis depugno; ut non Tertullianus tantum, sed etiam Græci Chryfostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius, nec non Pelagius, Haymo, Herveus, Thomas referunt ad contentionem cum Demetrio, Act.

XIX. 2. Cor. I. Sed quum illa pressura 2.

Cor. I. ut recens commemoretur, imd ex Actis constet, extremo tempore, quo Paulus Ephefi moratus est, factam esse, hic eadem adduci nondum potuit, ideoque aliam hanc esse oportet pugnam, in Actis non commemoratam, in quibus nec alia commemorata. Vid.

2. Cor. XI. Illud καὶ ἀνθρώπων non exponit Oecumenius ex Photio, quantum mihi erat poffibile.

Cajetanus interrogativè reddit: Numquid fecundum hominem & non fecundum DEUM pugnavi cum bestiis?

Estius per parenthesin hoc modo è collatione Rom.

III. 5. I Cor. III. 8. Gal.

III. 15. 2. Cor. XI. Quod (ut hominum more loquar, qui commorare liberter folent pugnas suas, è quibus gloriofè evaserunt) cum adversariis meis velut cum feris congreffus, depugnavi Ephefi, & impetum eorum sustinui, quid mihi prodest?

Fortè non incommodè exponitur: Si fecundum (externum) hominem ad bestias pugnavi, corpus meum & vitam hanc humanam periculis extremis objiciens, quid mihi hoc prodest?

Ed abire videtur Tertullianus: Paulum nempe infinuare spem refurrectionis corporis sui, quod in corpore talia passus esset

Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν· Αὔριον ἀποθνήσκομεν. Μίμησις Epicureos & ejus generis alios ipforum verbis depingens. Verba sunt deprompta ex Græco Efaiz XXII. 13. Multa talia habet Horatius. Strato: Καὶ πίνω κἀὶ τέρπω Διόφαντε. Οὐ γὰρ εἰς αἰὼ Πιόμεθ', οὐδ' αἰεὶ τερψιό μεθ' ἐσόμεθα. Et alius: Πῖνε καὶ εὐφραίνου, τί γὰρ αὔριον, ἢ τί τὸ μέλλον, Οὐδεὶς γινώσκει. Zalladus verò: Πᾶσι θανεῖν μερόπεσσιν ὀφείλεται, ὐδέ τις ἐστὶ Αὔριον οἷ ζήσει θνητὸς ἐπιστάμενος.

Tam in Efaia quam hic αὔριον ἀποθνήσκομεν est brevi moriemur. Brevis est vita. Præfens hic iterum pro futu. ro ut supra XIII. 13. Id ergò vult dicere Apostolus: Si non est futura refurrectio, quid vetat, quo minus Epicuream ducant omnes vitam, & delitiis ac voluptatibus fefe expleant, dicantque: Comedamus & bibamus, ge-nialiter vivamus, dum licet.

Conferatur Sap. II. v. 33. Μὴ πλανᾶσθε. Monendi forma supra VI. 9. Gal. VI. 7. Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί.
