Est verfus ex Thaide Menandri, ut Hieronymus nos docet, ita scriptus ab ipso Menandro. φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρῆστ' ὁμιλίαι κακαί. Est enim Trimeter ex Spondzis & Jambis: Sed Spon-dzis in sua fede. Tertullianus Trimetro liberiore, qualem Comœdiæ Latinæ ufurpant, sic transtulit: Bonos corrumpunt mores congreffus mali.

Sententiæ huic non diffimilis: Κακαῖς ὁμιλίαι παντὸς ἐκθύση κακός. Et Theognidis: Ἐσθλῶν μὲν γὰρ ἀπ' ἐσθλὰ μαθήσεαι, ἦν δὲ κακοῖσι. Συμμιχθῇς, ἀπολεῖς καὶ τὸν ἐόντα νόον. Donatus ad Eunuchum II. 2. Vide ut sententiose demonstret, malos ex bonis contagione fieri, exemplis in pravum præ-falentibus.

Significat Paulus periculofa maximè esse alloquia eorum, qui spem tollunt vitæ alterius. Si ergò, ut Tertullianus loco citato habet, quod à Menandro scriptum erat verbum hominis, idem postea, dictante Spiritu Sancto, scriptum à Paulo factum est verbum DEI. Innuit autem ita Apostolus, fuisse inter Corinthios, qui ratiunculis ex Philofophia, ut verifimile est, petitis, fidem refurrectionis in privatis colloquiis labefactare apud fideles conati sint. v. 34. Ἐκνήψατε δικαίως. Ἐκνήφειν propriè dicuntur, qui ex vinolentia ad fe redeunt, ut Gen. IX. 24. 1. Sam. XXXV. 37. Joel. I. 5. transfertur ad eos omnes, qui ab errore liberantur, ut Hab. 11.19. Δικαίως autem breviter dictum est pro ζήσοντες δικαίως, in posterum juste victuri. Καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε.

Ne vos date voluptatibus, ut faciunt isti Epicurei. Ἀγνωσίαν γὰρ θεοῦ τινες ἔχουσι. Latent inter vos quidam athei אשר לא ידעו אל ut loquuntur Hebræi. Vicina sunt ἀσύνετος & desperatio vitæ melioris. Πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λέγω. Ut supra VI. 5. Castigat eos, quod talium hominum commercia non fugiant. Latinam vulgatam, quæ habet, evigilate justi, hic improbat Estius.

Gracè δικαίως, ad verbum justè: Syro textu annuente. Quadam etiam Lati-næ MSS. justè legunt, & cum iis veteres concordan-tiæ, nec non Ambrof. in enarr. Pfal. 118. oflon. 10. Nec tam opus erat, ut justos bortaretur Apostolus ad evigilandum, quam illos, de quibus statim fequitur: Ignorantiam enim DEI quidam habent. Non mirum autem, fi justè mutatum fit injusti, quod apud plerosque Latinos legitur: Facilis enim fuit scribarum lapsus in una litera, cum præfertim, quid fit evigilare justè, non intelligerent.

Hæc Estius. Significat autem ex Corinthiis seductos aliquos jam fuisse pravis colloquiis, quos ad fanam & fo-briam mentem revocat. Ἐκνήψατε redditur: Et sobrii estote ab Ambrofio, Augustino, in epist. 137. & in enarr. Pfal. 128. & Sedulio in hunc locum. Conjungi ad pleniorem sensum verbi Græci hæc poffunt hoc modo: Ut ebrietate errorum & vo-luptatum digesta è fomno expergiscantur, sobrietati dediti, ea sapientes, quæ justa & recta sunt. Ad-ditur nolite peccare, ne desperatione vitæ futuræ voluptatibus fe immergant, quia in tales convenit, quod fequitur, ignorantiam enim DEI quidam babent, qui scilicet totos fe immergunt mundi hujus voluptatibus, ut ne cogitent quidem de DEO. πρὸς ἐντροπὴν perperam vulgata reddit, adreverentiam.

Est enim ad pudorem, id est, ut pudorem vobis injiciam. PARS III. ΔΙΔΑΚΤΙΚΗ. ARTICULUS I. De corporum in Refurrectione Qualitatibus. v. 35. Ἀλλ' ἐρεῖ τις πῶς ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροί. Id est, quomodo fieri potest, ut mortui reviviscant?

Nam postquam sua adstruxerat Paulus, refellit Philofo-phorum objecta. Ποίω δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται. Nempe in vitam. Ita argumentabantur Philofophi isti. Si in eodem corpore redibunt, quorum hoc? Ne-que enim edent, neque bibent, neque gignent. Si in alio, non iidem erunt. Respondet Paulus fore aliquatenus idem, aliquatenus non idem, idque per fimilitudines illustrat. Κάρον.

Meritò sic eos vocat, qui miracula fieri non credunt, cum natura ipsa plena fit miraculis, sed quæ sui frequentia migrant in nomen aliud. v. 36. Σὺ ὃ σπείρεις, ὃ ζωοποιεῖται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ. Vetus erat apud Rabbinos mos, corpus sepultum grano comparare. Ufus eâ fimilitudine ad Cleopatram Rab-binus Meir, ut legimus in Gemara de synedrio cap. XI. utitur & Rabbi Hya. Satis diligenter hanc fimilitudinem explicat Clemens V. 6. Theophilus Antiochenus lib. 1. ἐὰν γὰρ τύχοι σῖτον κάκκον σίτου, ἢ τῶν λοιπῶν σπερμάτων, ἐὰν βληθῇ εἰς τὴν γῆν, πρῶτον ἀποθνήσκει λυται, ὅτα ἐγείρεται καὶ γίνεται στάχυς. Et libr. II. ὁρᾶτα ἀνὰ γῆ γι-νομίτη ὅτι ὑπάρχει ἀνασκευάς. Κατεσκεύασεν ἐν ἀν-τὴν, καὶ διάφοροι καθοτὴν καὶ πλεθὺν, καὶ ὅτι δι' αὐτῶν δέ-κυται ἡ ἀνάστασις εἰς δεῖγμα τῆς μελλούσης ἔσεσθαι ἀνάστασις ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων.

Granum mori dicitur cum aeri ereptum terrâ occultatur. In manuscripto est ζωοποιεῖται. Hebræum הוחה modo hoc, modo illo vertitur. Vivificit dicit de femine Plinius. Non objectio hic ab adversariis contra refur-rectionem movetur, sed informatio de dubio Theologico, quomodo corpore fefe habitura sint in refurrectione, traditur: Vel ut Theophyla-qus: Duo quædam in dubitationem veniunt, modus scilicet refurgendi, quo pacto corpus, in cineres semel collapsum & resolutum, sublevetur, & quo corpore, bocne an alio quopiam?

Utraque autem hac gravi exemplo dissolvit. Simili tamen ejusmodi utitur, quod figuram refurrectionis exhibet.

Ad eam quodammodo probandam & illustrandam, quod non incredibile fit, putrida corpora reformari & resuscitari, uti femen putrefactum & mortuum renascens germinat: Confer Job. XII. 24. Quemadmodum sanctus Augustinus colligentem facit Apostolum Epist. 146. Si DEUS potest addere, quod non erat in novo femine, multò magis in refurrectione potest reparare, quod erat in hominis corpore.

Mortem ergò non obstare resurrectioni, ut mors corporum fit aded seminatio quædam ad vitam, ut docet Apostolus. Augustinus Serm. 34. de verbis Apostoli: Totæ, inquit, hujus mundi admi-nistratio testimonium est refurrectionis futuræ. Vi-demus cerid byemis tempore vel adventu, arbores foliari pomis, nudari foliis: Sed eas etiam verno tempore. speciem resurrectionis exprimere, que primo quidem incipiunt turgere in gemmis, tunc ornari in floribus, vestiri e foliis, & postmodum pomis gravari. Interrogate, infidelis homo, qui de resurrectione dubitas, ubi sunt ista, qua tempore, quo DEUS disposuit, producuntur? Dic mibi, ubi latitant, antequam producuntur? Que nusquam quidem videntur. Sed tamen DEUS, qui omnipotens est, & ea ex nihilo condidit, secreta sua virtute producit. Hinc jam ad campos & prata respicite, que estate transacta herbis suis spoliantur, ac floribus, & nuda remanent ipsa spatia terrarum. Sed iterum verno tempore revelantur, & novo ubique germine incipiente letatur agricola. Certe herba, qua ante vixit & moritur, rursus reviviscit ex semine: Sic etiam & nostrum corpus reviviscit ex pulvere. v.

## 15:37
37. And that which you sow, you do not sow the body that shall be.

For many things proceed from it. Minutius: Seeds do not revive unless they have rotted. Tertullian in his Apologeticus: Seeds do not rise unless they have rotted and dissolved accordingly. But a bare grain. A grain without a stalk, without an ear. If it happens to be wheat. You will translate correctly in Latin, pure wheat. Or some of the others.

Of barley, of spelt, of millet. v. 38. But GOD gives it a body, as He has willed. For the works of nature are also from GOD, who established nature. Theophylact on this passage has it thus: Since he said two things, it could be doubted, namely, how the dead are raised, and with what body they are to rise again. Now, however, explaining how the dead are to rise, he also reveals the rest, about which there was doubt. He says, therefore, that that body is raised, that is, that it becomes of the same substance, yet it is rendered more splendid and more refined. Heretics, however, say that the same thing that had been is not raised. For that, they say, the Apostle pretends when he says: You do not sow the body that will be, when he by no means thinks so, but he undoubtedly expresses this, that he himself does not sow it as it will be: more shining, that is, and more adorned, but bare, and rather the likeness of a grain of wheat, from which the ear itself, more beautiful, is born in such a way that the grain and the ear are by no means the same. Nor is that form in the ear fated, namely, covered with stalk and ears, but bare. Nor was anything else sown for it, since it is certain that the ear itself did not come from the grain of other crops, but from that bare grain of wheat. These are the words of Theophylact.

Just as a bare grain is sown, without the garment of a husk, without the foundation of an ear, without the protection of an awn, the pride of a stalk, but it rises up gifted with abundance, built up with structure, in the order of fruits, protected by cultivation and clothed on every side, and that is the body which GOD gives to it, indeed far more excellent than what was fated: so also to the dead and putrefied men GOD is about to give much more adorned bodies, of the same substance indeed, but in quality and condition far different and more excellent; as Tertullian elegantly says. But as every likeness is a dissimilarity, so heretics wrongly conclude from this passage that bodies will not rise again in the same number. For the Apostle intends nothing else by this simile than that what is born is not such as what is sown: Because a bare grain is sown, but a grain is born, clothed with herb and awns: Mark IV. v. 28. and thus also the body does not rise again such as it is sown in death or burial, because it is sown mortal and inglorious, but it will rise clothed with immortality and glory.

Here the diversity of the thing is not considered, but of quality and condition, as to each seed a proper body is given by GOD; so GOD is about to give to each in the resurrection a body, such as He Himself wills. The ear, says Chrysostom on this passage, is the same, and not the same. The same indeed in this, because the substance is the same; not the same, because it is better. Tertullian on the resurrection of the flesh, ch. 2. This therefore is already certain from the example of the seed, that no other flesh is made alive than that very one which was dead. The Apostle's question also was not about the substance, but about the quality of the body: With what body do they come? Theophylact also urges the rest of the Apostle's words: If GOD, he says, is about to give a body, why do you yourself so curiously inquire with what body we are to rise again, and doubt the resurrection, when you hear of GOD's power and will? GOD indeed raises the dissolved body, yet rendered more excellent in beauty and spirit, which can clearly be understood even in the seeds themselves. For since the seed is committed to the earth, that which sprouts and is produced from it rises far more beautiful.

To each of the seeds its own body. That completely stops the mouths of the heretics, who assert that it is not this same body, but some other that is to be raised at the final resurrection. Behold now you hear that a proper body is granted to each. Concerning which see what has been said at length in Socinismo profligato. v.

Latin:

37. Καὶ ὃ σπείρεις οὐ τὸ σῶμα τὸ γενησόμενον σπείρεις.

Multa enim ex eo prodeunt. Minutius: Semina non nisi corrupta reviviscunt. Tertullianus in Apologetico: Semina non nisi corrupta & dissoluta secundum surgunt. Ἀλλὰ γυμνὸν κόκκον. Granum sine culmo, sine arista. Εἰ τύχοι σίτου. Latine recte vertes, pura tritici. Ἢ τινος τῶν λοιπῶν.

Hordei, farris, milii. v. 38. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς αὐτῷ δίδωσι σῶμα, καθὼς ἠθέλησε. Nam & opera naturæ a DEO sunt, qui naturam instituit. Theophylactus in hunc locum ita habet: Cum duo dixerit, subdubitari posset, quemadmodum scilicet mortui excitentur, & quo sint corpore resurrecturi. Nunc autem explicans, quomodo resurrecturi sint mortui, & reliquum aperit, quo de ambigebatur. Inquit itaque, quod corpus illud suscitatur, hoc est, quod eiusdem substantiæ fit, splendidius tamen & comptius redditur. Heretici vero non idem illud, quod fuerat, dicitant suscitari. Id enim, inquiunt, prætendit Apostolus, cum dicit: Non corpus, quod futurum est, seminas, cum ille haudquaquam sic sentiat, sed id haud dubie exprimit, non feminas ipse, quale futurum est: fulgentius scilicet & ornatius, sed nudum, & tritici grani potius similitudinem, e quo spica ipsa pulchrior ita enascitur, ut nequaquam idem sint granum & spica. Neque etiam in spica formam illud est fatum, culmo videlicet & aristis obductum, sed nudum. Neque pro eo aliud quippiam profeminatum, quippe non ex frugum aliarum cocco, sed ex nudo illo frumenti grano spicam ipsam prodiisse constat. Hæc Theophylact.

Quemadmodum nudum granum seritur, sine folliculi veste, fine fundamento spicæ, sine munimento aristæ, superbia culmi, exsurgit autem copia feneratum, compagine ædificatum, ordine fructuum, cultu munitum & usque quaque vestitum, atque istud est corpus, quod illi DEUS dat longe quidem præstantius, quam fatum fuit: sic etiam mortuis & putrefactis hominibus multo ornatiora corpora DEUS daturus est, eadem scilicet substantia, sed qualitate & conditione longe diversa & præstantiora; ut eleganter Tertullianus. Ut vero omne simile est dissimile, ita hæretici perperam ex hoc loco colligunt, non eodem numero corpora olim resurrectura. Nihil enim aliud hac similitudine vult Apostolus, quam quod non tale sit, quod seminatur, quale nascitur: Quia seminatur nudum granum, nascitur vero granum, herba & aristis vestitum: Marc. IV. v. 28. atque ita etiam corpus tale non resurgat, quale in morte vel sepultura seminatur, quia seminatur mortale & inglorium, resurget vero vestitum immortalitate & gloria.

Non hic spectatur diversitas rei, sed qualitatis & conditionis, ut unicuique semini datur proprium corpus a DEO; ita DEUS cuique in resurrectione daturus est corpus, quale ipse vult. Spica, inquit Chrysostomus in huic locum, eadem est, & non eadem. Eadem quidem hac, quia substantia eadem; non eadem, quia melior. Tertullianus de resurr. carnis c. 2. Hoc ergo jam de exemplo feminis constat, non aliam vivificari carnem, quam ipsam, quæ erat mortua. Apostoli etiam quæstio non erat de substantia, sed de qualitate corporis: Ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται; QUALI CORPORE venient. Urget & Theophylactus cætera Apostoli verba: Si DEUS, inquit, daturus est corpus, quid ipse tam curiose inquis, quali sumus corpore resurrecturi, & resurrectioni diffidis, cum DEI potentiam audis & voluntatem? DEUS quidem resolutum suscitat corpus, præstantius tamen pulchritudine & spiritu redditum, quod plane potest vel in seminibus ipsis comprehendi. Siquidem mandato terræ semine, formosius longe surgit, quod pullulat ex eo & procreatur.

Unicuique seminum proprium corpus. Id prorsus hæreticorum obstrutit ora, afferentium, non idem hoc corpus, sed aliud quoddam esse in resurrectione denique suscitandum. Ecce jam audis, proprium esse cuique corpus concessum. Quo de vide, quæ in Socinismo profligato fuse dicta. v.

## 15:39
39. Not all flesh is the same flesh.

Flesh is a species of body. Just as meats, although differing much among themselves, do not cease to be meats: So also bodies, although differing much among themselves, are nevertheless bodies. Flesh to the Hebrews is not said, except of a mortal body. But one of men, another of beasts, another of fish, another of birds. The word ktēnōn here corresponds to the Hebrew [בהמה], by which name come all mute living things walking on the earth with feet. But Pliny also called the flesh of fish in more than one place, just as the Hebrews in Leviticus.

XIV. v. 40. And celestial bodies, and terrestrial bodies. But the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. He calls the appearance of things doxan here, the eidos. Luke IX. 29. which is the idea in Matt. XXVIII. 3. [מראה] to the Hebrews. One glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. Not only is the appearance different for terrestrial and celestial bodies, but the celestial bodies themselves also differ among themselves in appearance, or in that which is seen.

The sun hides the brightness of all the stars. The sun differs much from the moon in power and glory, says Theophilus of Antioch. But truly ---- The moon shines among the lesser fires. Among the other stars there are wandering ones, there are fixed ones; and among these there are other excellent ones, Arcturus, Sirius, the ear of the virgin, others smaller, and that by many degrees. See Daniel XII. 4. and Psalm XLVIII. 3. v.

Latin:

39. Οὐ πᾶσα σὰρξ ἡ αὐτὴ σάρξ.

Caro species est corporis. Sicut carnes quanquam multum inter se differentes, non definiunt esse carnes: Sic & corpora multum inter se distantia, tamen corpora sunt. Caro Hebræis non dicitur, nisi de corpore mortali. Ἀλλὰ ἄλλη μὲν ἀνθρώπων, ἄλλη δὲ κτηνῶν, ἄλλη δὲ ἰχθύων, ἄλλη δὲ πτηνῶν. Vox κτηνῶν respondet hic Hebræo , quo nomine veniunt omnia animantia muta super terram pedibus gradientia. Carnem autem piscium dixit etiam Plinius non uno loco, sicut Hebræi Levit.

XIV. v. 40. Καὶ σώματα ἐπουράνια, καὶ σώματα ἐπίγεια. Ἀλλ’ ἑτέρα μὲν ἡ τῶν ἐπουρανίων δόξα, ἑτέρα δὲ ἡ τῶν ἐπιγείων. Δόξαν hic vocat rerum speciem, τὸ εἶδος. Luc. IX. 29. quæ idea Matth. XXVIII. 3. מראה Hebræis. Ἄλλη δόξα ἡλίου, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα σελήνης, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα ἀστέρων. Ἀστὴρ γὰρ ἀστέρος διαφέρει ἐν δόξῃ. Non tantum alia est species terrenis, alia cœlestibus corporibus, sed & ipsa inter se corpora cœlestia differens specie, sive eo quod conspicitur.

Sol omnium fiderum fulgorem abscondit. Ὁ ἥλιος πολὺ διαφέρει τῆς σελήνης δυνάμει καὶ δόξῃ, ait Theophilus Antiochenus. At vero ---- Micat inter ignes Luna minores. Inter stellas alias sunt errantes, sunt fixæ; & inter has aliæ eximiæ, Arcturus, Sirus, spica virginis, aliæ minores, idque per multos gradus. Vide Danielis XII. 4. & Psalmo XLVIII. 3. v.

## 15:40
v. 40. & 41. And therefore Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Primasius, Jerome, and Bede rightly prove here the disparity of rewards in glory.

Theophylact: Lest perhaps, when you have understood that the grain grows in a similar way everywhere and in every place, you might likewise think in the resurrection that all will be equal in honor; he strives to show from dignity, or that there will be a distinction among those rising again.

Which he reveals beforehand, when he said: Each in his own order.

He added besides, not all flesh is the same flesh, that is, by no means will all rise with equal honor; See.

Dan. XII. 1.

However, some, even Theophylact, refer that comparison of celestial and terrestrial bodies to the distinction between the blessed and the reprobate, because celestial bodies are compared with the former, but terrestrial bodies with the latter.

But it is sound, says Theophylact, that the bodies of the just differ from the bodies of the impious, as much as celestial bodies do from terrestrial ones.

So also Chrysostom and Oecumenius.

Which opinion we leave in the middle.

Yet both the name δόξης (glory) and the treatment of the Apostle, who deals only with the glorious resurrection of the blessed, seem to stand against it.

But that [part] about one flesh of men, another of cattle, another of birds, another of fish, is more clever than true, because by men are to be understood the good, who live according to reason.

But by cattle the luxurious, by birds the proud, by fish the greedy, as also that of Tertull. lib. de resurr. carn. cap. 52.

Another flesh of man, that is, of the servants of God, another of a beast of burden, that is, of the Heathen, another of birds, that is, of the martyrs, another of fish, that is, of those for whom the water of baptism is sufficient. It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption.

As if he were saying: that whole comparison which I have brought forward tends here, that it may be understood that the species of a mortal body is far different from that of an immortal one.

E φθορᾷ from grain, & φθορᾷ, which flows away and is thus corrupted. Εν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, that is, ἀφθαρ-τε, which cannot be corrupted.

See above XI. 5.

In the golden verses of Pythagoras: You shall be an immortal God, deathless, no longer mortal. It is sown in dishonor.

Cast away by men, lest the stench cause harm.

For it concerns the living that the dead be buried.

The appearance of a corpse is spoken of as a contempt in Terence. It is raised in glory.

Here δόξα does not signify just any appearance, but a beautiful and venerable one כבוד. v.

Latin:

v. 40. & 41. Ideoque rectè hic Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Oecumenius, Primasius, Hieronymus, Beda probant disparitatem præmiorum in gloria.

Theophylactus: Ne fortè, cum intellexisset granum pari modo omne & passim crescere, sic etiam in resurrectione existimes, honore similes fore omnes, de dignitate ostendere nititur, vel resurgentium fore discrimen.

Quod præveniens patefacit, cum dixit: Unusquisque in suo ordine.

Adjecit præterea, non omnis caro eadem caro, hoc est nequaquam omnes pari honore resurgent; Vid.

Dan. XII. 1.

Illam tamen corporum cœlestium & terrestrium comparationem nonnulli, etiam Theophylactus, referunt ad discrimen beatorum & reproborum, quod cum illis componantur cœlestia, cum his verò terrena corpora.

Sed sanum, inquit Theophylactus, justorum differunt corpora ab impiorum corporibus, quantum à terrenis cœlestia.

Sic etiam Chrysostomus & Oecumenius.

Quam sententiam in medio relinquimus.

Obstare tamen ei videtur tùm nomen δόξης gloria, tùm tractatio Apostoli, qui solum de resurrectione gloriosa beatorum agit.

Ista verò de alia carne hominum, alia pecudum, alia volucrum, alia piscium argutior est, quam verior, quod per homines intelligendi sint boni, qui secundum rationem vivunt.

Per pecora verò luxuriosi, per volucres superbi, per pisces avari, ut & illa Tertull. lib. de resurr. carn. cap. 52.

Alia caro hominis, id est servi Dei, alia jumenti, id est Ethnici, alia volucrum, id est martyrum, alia piscium, id est quibus aqua baptismi satis sufficit. Σπείρεται ἐν φθορᾷ, ἐγείρεται ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ.

Quasi dicat, tota illa quam attuli, comparatio hic tendit, ut intelligatur longè alia esse species mortalis, alia immortalis corporis.

E φθορᾷ de grano, & φθορᾷ, quod diffluit & sic corrumpitur. Εν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, id est, ἀφθαρ-τε, quod corrumpi nequit.

Vide supra XI. 5.

In aureo carmine Pythagoræ: Ἔσσεαι ἀθάνατος Θεός, ἄμβροτος, οὐκ ἔτι θνητός. Σπείρεται ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ.

Abjectum ab hominibus, ne foetor noceat.

Nam mortuos sepeliri, viventium interest.

Cadaveris facies, in contemptu dicitur apud Terentium. Ἐγείρεται ἐν δόξῃ.

Hic δόξα non quamvis speciem, sed pulchram atque venerabilem significat כבוד. v.

## 15:42
42. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

So also the matter stands in the resurrection of the dead. A similar way of speaking in Matt. XIII. 24. Let this be noted against the Papists, who oppose fish to meats in their fasts, without fasts.

For Estius also admits the same thing here: There is no doubt that there is also the flesh of fish, just as of cattle and birds, and that according to the proper signification of flesh. He also adds the passage, Num. XI. But whether by this simile it is noted that the different quality of the body in death and in the resurrection does not stand in the way of the truth of the resurrected bodies, because meats, even if very different, are truly meats: Or whether the Apostle intends this rather: As there is different flesh for different living things; so there will be different bodies for different men in the resurrection, as regards the degrees of glory? It could be a matter of doubt. The latter, however, seems more convenient, and is approved by Augustine in his Epistle to Consentius, Bede, Lombard, and Herveus.

For in the former conclusion it must be supposed There is a numerical identity of the bodies which are sown here, and which will one day rise again. And he confesses the latter is more v.

Latin:

42. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ ἀνάστασις τῶν νεκρῶν.

Sic etiam se res habet in resurrectione mortuorum. Si: mile loquendi genus Matth. XIII. 24. Notetur hoc adversus Papistas, pisces carnibus in jejuniis suis, sine jejuniis, opponentes.

Nam & Estius hic idem fatetur: Non dubium, quin piscium quoque sit caro, sicut pecudum & volucrum, idque secundum propriam carnis significationem. Addit & locum, Num. XI. Utrum vero hac similitudine notetur, corporis qualitatem diversam in morte & in resurrectione non obstare corporum resuscitatorum veritati, quia carnes, etsi diversissimæ, verè carnes sint: An verò id velit potius Apostolus: Sicut diversorum animantium diversa caro est; ita diversorum hominum in resurrectione fore diversa corpora, quod ad gradus gloriæ? dubium esse queat. Posterius tamen convenientius videtur, & Augustino in Epistola ad Consent. Bede, Lombardo, Herveo probatur.

Nam in priori collectione supponenda est identitas numerica corporum, quæ hic seminantur, & quæ olim resurgent. Et posteriori fatetur magis v.

## 15:43
43. It is sown in weakness.

Without sense, without the power of enduring in that state. It is raised in power.

Vigorous, firm, with many senses, which we do not now understand. v.

Latin:

43. Σπείρεται ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ.

Sine sensu, fine potestate durandi in eo statu. Ἐγείρεται ἐν δυνάμει.

Vegetum, firmum, cum sensibus multis, quos nunc non intelligimus. v.

## 15:44
44. It is sown a natural body.

That is, which was ψυχικόν (natural); you have a similar manner of speaking in Matt. XXII. 23, Rom. IV. 5.

But σῶμα ψυχικόν (natural body) is called that which lives for a time, while the soul is present.

The soul is the voice of this life.

Afterwards it is not called so except improperly.

And so Maimonides says that the soul in this life is spirit in potentiality, and in the other life will be spirit in act. It is raised a spiritual body.

Having in itself in place of the soul an immutable spirit that will never depart, and as the leader of the body, which spirit Peter calls the divine nature II.

1. 4. Irenaeus V.

12. & it is called the spirit surrounding the man inside and out.

Such a body is called כוס של חיים (cup of life) by Akiva in the book on the letters.

The earnest of this spirit is the spirit which is given to Christians in this life.

See Irenaeus V. 11. And Tertull. de resurrectione carnis.

Tatian calls that Spirit the wing of the soul. There is a natural body and there is a spiritual body.

As if he were saying: Those things differ much among themselves.

That difference is 1. regarding the passible and spiritual qualities, corruptibility and incorruptibility.

2. External form.

A dead body is a deformed, pale, ignominious corpse: A rising body is glorious, shining, translucent, glittering.

3. Powers.

A dead body is weak, destitute of sense, motion, and all faculties.

But it will rise powerful, and not subject to any need or defect.

4. Internal reason: That which was subject in this life to animal affections and operations, to generation, nutrition, augmentation, motion, needing food, drink, clothing, air, external heat, etc., which is governed by the soul, as an internal principle, in natural, moral, and civil actions, is sown: A spiritual body will rise, which will be free for spiritual operations, and will be moved by the Spirit of GOD, not that the soul will then cease to move, but that it itself, full of spiritual light, will become one that will move the body spiritually, and finally it will not need food or drink, and will not perform other external animal actions proper to this life, but will be devoted to celestial things.

Which things, however, are all so arranged that they do not take away the substance of this body and flesh of ours, because most of them rather presuppose the same.

But it is not correctly said that the spirit is in place of the soul, because the soul does not cease, so that the Spirit might take its place, but as the body is the same, so also the same soul remains. But the body becomes spiritual, not because it is no longer governed by the soul: But because it is not governed by the soul as it is in this age, since it lives by a spiritual life.

It is called animal, says B.

It is called animal, says B. Hunnius, in this age, because it is vegetated, governed, and led by the soul, so that it is both generated, and generates, and needs food, drink, motion, rest, sleep, and other aids and supports of this animal life.

And such indeed is the body in this age, which is sown, and sent into the sepulcher: But it will rise spiritual, so called, not because it is turned into spirit in this respect (for the body will truly be a body) but because it acquires and provides the virtues and properties of a spirit, and being exempt from this animal life, and having abdicated the use of food, drink, sleep, rest, marriage, and other things pertaining to the future of this life, it will henceforth depend on and be governed by the Spirit of GOD alone, without those lower powers of the soul, especially the vegetative, and other affections of the terrestrial bodies of this age, so much so that in eternity it will not lead an animal life, but a spiritual one, namely the life of celestial spirits and blessed Angels Matth.

XXII. Let also the explanation of B. be seen.

Luther on 1.

Cor.

XV.

B.

Chemnit. on the two natures in Christ c. 30. p.

457. as also Gerhard on eternal life §.

84. Some add that the body is called spiritual because it will be most perfectly subject to the guidance of the spirit without any resistance, and they think the first man is to be considered, not as he was before the fall without any struggle of Spirit and flesh, but as he was made after the fall.

But here we accept B.

Luther's and B.

But here we accept the explanation of B. Luther and B. Hunnius, since it has been said that the Apostle looks not to Adam after the fall, but before the fall, Gen.

II. Regarding the creation of Adam, it sufficiently teaches that Adam was made into a living soul.

To which pertains that of Augustine l.

XIII. on the City of GOD ch.

To which pertains that of Augustine l. XIII. on the City of GOD ch. 20. Not only will the body of the blessed not be such as it is now in any best state of health, but not even such as it was in the first men before sin.

Who, although they would not have died unless they had sinned, nevertheless used food, as men, not yet bearing spiritual, but still animal terrestrial bodies.

Thomas part 1. q. 97. artic.

3. In the first state the rational soul communicated to the body that which is appropriate to it, in so far as it is a soul: And therefore that body was called animal, in so far as it had life from the soul.

But the first principle of life in these lower things, as is said, in the book on of the soul, is the soul: vegetable, whose works are to use food, and to generate, and to grow. And therefore these works belonged to man in the first state. In the last state, however, after the resurrection, the soul will communicate in a certain way to the body those things which are proper to itself, in as much as it is also spirit. Immortality indeed, as regards all, but impassibility and glory and power, as regards the good, whose bodies shall be called spiritual. Whence after the resurrection men will not have need of food. But in the state of innocence they had need of them.

But indeed by the divine nature the spirit, which is made in place of the soul, is not understood: But we are said to become partakers of the divine nature, because the same is not communicated to us κατ' ἐνοίκησιν, according to a bare indwelling, but also κατ' ἐνέργειαν, according to an efficacious operation, so that, namely, we may be rendered partakers of divine wisdom, justice, and holiness, through the irradiation of divine glory. We shall be θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως, that is, partakers of divine wisdom, truth, justice, goodness, life, joy, immortality, and the rest of the highest goods in GOD, as interpreted by B. Luther.

Grotius imagines a new spirit, I know not what, different from the soul, different from the Holy Spirit, different also from the spirit according to which we are renewed, which is wont to be opposed to the flesh; and indeed a certain substantial Spirit, of which spirit the Spirit, which is given to Christians in this life, becomes the earnest, who is none other than the Holy Spirit himself. Yet Estius here observes that it does not follow from this word 'spiritual' that through the resurrection our bodies will be turned into spirits, as certain erring ones have opined: of whom Augustine makes mention in the letter written to Consentius. For besides that that would not be a resurrection of bodies, but an abolition: The Apostle quite evidently excludes the intellect, while he expressly repeated the word 'body', saying: a spiritual body shall rise.

Augustine, book XIII. of the City of GOD, chap. 20, notes that some have thought that the body is to be converted into Spirit, because it is held here concerning a spiritual body: Which Ludovicus Vives in his scholia judges to concern Origen, who in his book περὶ ἀρχῶν says that it will come to pass that all corporeal creature is changed into spiritual bodies, and all substance is converted into one most pure body, and purer in splendor, and such as the human mind cannot now conceive; and afterwards, he says, GOD will be all in all, so that the universal nature may be reduced into that substance which is better than all, namely into the divine, than which there is none better.

The opinion of Proclus the Platonic Philosopher, who said that glorified bodies are spiritual, because they are to be changed into air, or wind, or ether, which are called spirits, can be read as refuted in Epiphanius, book II, Tom. I. against heresies, by whoever wishes.

Latin:

44. Σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν.

Id est, quod fuit ψυχικόν, simile loquendi genus habes Matth. XXII. 23, Rom. IV. 5.

Dicitur autem σωμα ψυχικόν id quod ad tempus vivit, dum anima adest.

Anima est vox hujus vitæ.

Postea non nisi improprie sic dicitur.

Itaque Maimonides animam in hac vita ait potentia esse spiritum, in altera vita actu fore. Ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν.

Habens in se vice animæ spiritum immutabilem nunquam abcessurum, & ducem corporis, quem spiritum naturam divinam appellat Petrus II.

1. 4. Irenæus V.

12. & dicitur spiritus circumdans intus & foris hominem.

Tale corpus כוס של חיים dicitur Aquibæ in libro supra literas.

Hujus spiritus arrhabo est spiritus, qui in hac vita Christianis datur.

Vide Irenæum V. 11. Et Tertull. de resurrectione carnis.

Eum Spiritum Tatianus animæ alam vocat. Ἔστι σῶμα ψυχικὸν καὶ ἔστι σῶμα πνευματικόν.

Quasi dicat: Distant multum illa inter se.

Differentia illa est 1. quoad qualitates passibiles & spirituales, corruptibilitatem & incorruptibilitatem.

2. Formam externam.

Corpus mortuum est cadaver deforme, pallidum, ignominiosum: Corpus resurgens est gloriosum, fulgidum, pellucidum, coruscum.

3. Vires.

Corpus mortuum est infirmum sensu, motu, & facultatibus omnibus destitutum.

At resurget potens, nec indigentiæ aut defectui ulli obnoxium.

4. Rationem internam: Seminatur quod fuerit in hac vita animalibus subjectum affectionibus & operationibus, generationi, nutritioni, augmentationi, motui, indigens cibo, potu, vestitu, aere, calore externo &c. quod ab anima, ut principio interno, regitur in actionibus naturalibus, moralibus, civilibus: Resurget corpus spirituale, quod operationibus spiritualibus vacabit, & movebitur Spiritu DEI, non quod anima tunc cessabit movere, sed quod ipsa quoque, plena luce spirituali, corpus spiritualiter motura fit, nec denique cibo aut potu indigebit, aliisque aut externas actiones animales hujus vitæ proprias expediet, sed cœlestibus deditum erit.

Quæ tamen omnia ita comparata sunt, ut substantiam corporis & carnis hujus nostræ non tollant, quia potius supponant eandem pleraque.

Non autem rectè dicitur spiritus vice animæ esse, quia anima non definit, ut vicem ejus subeat Spiritus, sed ut idem corpus, ita & eadem anima manet. Πνευματικὸν autem evadit corpus, non quod non regatur amplius ab anima: Sed quod non ita ab anima regatur, ut in hoc seculo, quum vitâ spirituali vivat.

Animale dicitur, inquit B.

Animale dicitur, inquit B. Hunnius, in hoc seculo, quia vegetatur, regitur & ducitur ab anima, ita ut & generetur, & generet, indigeat cibo, potu, motu, quiete, somno, aliisque vitæ hujus animalis præsidiis & adminiculis.

Et tale quidem est in hoc seculo corpus, quod seminatur, ac in sepulcrum mittitur: Resurget autem spirituale, sic dictum, non quod hoc ratione vertatur in spiritum (corpus enim erit verè corpus) sed quod virtutes & proprietates acquirat atque præstet spiritum, & exemptum hac animali vita, abdicatoque usu cibi, potus, somni, quietis, matrimonii, aliarumque rerum, ad futuram hujus vitæ pertinentium, posthac secundum DEUM à solo pendet & regatur spiritu, citra inferiores illas anime potentias, vegetativam præsertim, aliasque affectiones terrenorum corporum hujus seculi, adeo ut in æternitate ψυχικὴν agat vitam, sed πνευματικὴν, vitam nimirum spirituum cœlestium, & beatorum Angelorum Matth.

XXII. Videatur & explicatio B.

Lutheri in 1.

Cor.

XV.

B.

Chemnit. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 30. p.

457. ut & Gerhard. de vita æterna §.

84. Addunt quidam, spirituale dici corpus, quod perfectissimè fine ulla repugnantia subjectum sit futurum ductui spiritus, & considerari censent primum hominem, non qualis ante lapsum fuit absque omni Spiritus & carnis lucta, sed qualis factus est post lapsum.

Verum hic accipicimus B.

Lutheri & B.

Verum hic accipicimus B. Lutheri & B. Hunnii explicationi, quandoquidem Apostolum non Adamum post lapsum, sed ante lapsum respicere, dictum est Gen.

II. De creatione Adami adductum, quod Adam factus fit in animam viventem, satis doceat.

Quo pertinet illud Augustini l.

XIII. de civitate DEI c.

Quo pertinet illud Augustini l. XIII. de civitate DEI c. 20. Non solum non erit tale beatorum corpus, quale nunc est in quavis optima valetudine, sed nec tale quidem, quale fuit in primis hominibus ante peccatum.

Qui licet morituri non essent, nisi peccassent, alimentis tamen, ut homines, utebantur, nondum spiritualia, sed adhuc animalia corpora terrena geflantes.

Thomas parte 1. q. 97. artic.

3. In primo statu anima rationalis communicabat corpori, id quod competit ei, in quantum est anima: Et ideo corpus illud dicebatur animale, in quantum scilicet habebat vitam ab anima.

Primum autem principium vitæ in istis inferioribus, ut dicitur, in libro de anima, est anima: vegetabilis, cuius opera sint alimento uti, & generare, & augeri. Et ideò haec operam homini in primo statu competebant. In ultimo vero statu post resurrectionem anima communicabit quodammodo corpori ea, quae sunt sibi propria, in quantum & spiritus. Immortalitatem quidem, quantum ad omnes, impassibilitatem verò & gloriam & virtutem, quantum ad bonos, quorum corpora spiritualia dicentur. Unde post resurrectionem homines cibis non indigebunt. Sed in statu innocentiae eis indigebant.

Nec verò per divinam naturam spiritus, qui vice animae fit, intelligitur: Sed divinae naturae consortes fieri dicimur, quia non communicatur nobis eadem κατ' ἐνοίκησιν, secundum nudam inhabitationem, sed etiam κατ' ἐνέργειαν, secundum efficacem operationem, ut scilicet participes reddamur divinae sapientiae, justitiae, & sanctitatis, per gloriae divinae irradiationem. Erimus θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως, hoc est, divina sapientia, veritatis, justitiae, bonitatis, vitae, laetitiae, immortalitatis, & reliquorum summorum in DEO bonorum, interprete B. Lutheri.

Grotius fingit novum, nescio quem, spiritum, diversum ab anima, diversum à Spiritu Sancto, diversum etiam à spiritu, secundum quem renovamur, qui carni opponi solet; & quidem substantialem quendam Spiritum, cuius spiritus arrhabo fit Spiritus, qui Christianis in hac vita datur, qui alius non est, quam ipse Spiritus Sanctus. Redde tamen hic observat Estius, ex hac voce spirituale consequens non esse, quod per resurrectionem corpora nostra vertentur in spiritus, ut quidam errantes opinati sunt: quorum meminit Augustinus in epistola commemorata ad Consentium. Nam praeterquam quod illa non esset resurrectio corporum, sed abolitio: Satis evidenter illumin tellectum excludit Apostolus, dum expresse repetivit vocabulum corporis, dicendo: surget corpus spirituale.

Augustinus l. XIII. de civitate DEI, cap. 20. notat, nonnullos putasse, corpus in Spiritum convertendum esse, quod hic habeatur de corpore spirituali: Quod Origenem concernere Ludovicus Vives in scholiis censet, qui libro περὶ ἀρχῶν ait, fore, ut omnia creatura corporea in spiritualia corpora mutetur, & cuncta substantia in unum corpus mundissimum, & splendore purius convertatur, ac tale, quale nunc humana mens cogitare non potest; & post, inquit, erit DEUS omnia in omnibus, ut universa natura redigatur in eam substantiam, quae omnibus melior est, in divinam scilicet, qua nulla est melior.

Procli Philosophi Platonici opinionem, qui corpora glorificata spiritualia dixerit, quod in aërem, vel ventum, vel aethera, quae spiritus dicuntur, sint commutanda, refutatam apud Epiphanium libr. II, Tom. I. adv. haerel. qui volet, legere poterit.

## 15:45
v. 45. Οὕτω καὶ γέγραπται· Ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Paul adds the name Adam from the preceding in Moses, and the name first so that he might better compose Christ to him, See Rom. V. 14. and above 22.

Latin:

v. 45. Οὕτω καὶ γέγραπται· Ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Paulus addit nomen Ἀδὰμ ex praecedentibus apud Mosen, & nomen πρῶτον ut melius Christum ei componeret, Vide Rom.

## 16:1 Argument
Ver. 1. Περὶ δὲ τῆς λογίας τῆς εἰς ἁγίους) Unless the consensus of the Codices restrained me, I would gladly read εὐλογίας here. For Paul uses that word in the sense of liberality, 2 Cor. IX. 6. Thus the Hebrew בְּרָכָה is accustomed to be taken, by a translation from words to things. He understands, however, the collection of money for relieving the poverty of the faithful in Judea Rom. XV. 16. ὥστε διέταξα ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Γαλατίας) The Apostles loved to introduce the same customs everywhere. And these are the Apostolic traditions related, as we said in ὡς καίαι. This is the journey through Galatia, the mention of which is in Acts XVI. ver. 6. That the Greeks also use the word λογίας, has been observed not only by Erasmus Schmidius on this passage, but also by Suidas, who adduces Chrysostom explaining λογίαν here as συλλογὴν. To Erasmus it seems a metaphor drawn from the fruits of herbs and the earth, which are said to be gathered, whence also the word for legumes. It was called otherwise διακονία εἰς τὰς ἁγίους 2 Cor. IX. ver. 1. and in verse 12. διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας and χάρις 2 Cor. IX. v. 4. and in this place ver. 3. But the discourse here is not about the collection, of which mention is made in Acts XI. ver. 28. and XII., but about another later one, concerning which 2 Cor. IX. 19. We said above that the Apostolic Canons, as they are called, are by no means of Apostolic authority. Ver. 2. Κατὰ μίαν σαββάτου) The agreements of the Jews, says Philo, ἅπαξαν ὄντα καὶ τῆς ἀλλῆς οὐσίας, namely even outside the Sabbaths. Christians especially on Sabbaths and Lord's days, which are μία σαββάτων Matth. XXVIII. ver. 1. con they were meeting. But because these people, who having been made Christians from among the Jews, retained Jewish customs and did not handle money on the Sabbath, for that reason the following day was more suitable for that matter. Tertullian in his Apology: Each one deposits a small contribution on the monthly day, or when he wishes, and if only he wishes, and if only he can. For no one is compelled, but contributes of his own accord. These are, as it were, deposits of piety. For it is not dispensed from there for feasts, nor drinking bouts, nor ungrateful gluttony, but for feeding and burying the needy, and for boys and girls destitute of property and parents. And likewise for those in domestic service: likewise for the shipwrecked, and if any are in the mines: and if any are in the islands or in prisons, provided they are there for the sake of the cause of God, they become foster-children of their own confession.

The first of the Sabbaths is the first of the Sabbaths, or that day which is the first in the week of days, which comes under the name of σάββατον (Sabbath) in Luke 18, verse 12. See Augustine’s epistle 86 to Casulanus. Which day was the Lord’s Day, which therefore there is no doubt was of Apostolic institution, on which the offerings of the faithful were made at the altar. To which day also the collections of alms properly belong, so that we may be excited to munificence and the showing of mercy by grateful memory of the grace of GOD exhibited on this day in the beginning of creation, the resurrection of Christ for our justification, and the mission of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, the Teachers of the world.

Which causes are more fitting than the Grotian one. For it is not likely that that ἐθελοθρησκεία (will-worship) of not handling money on the Sabbath flourished among the converted Jews. Jerome against Vigilantius: The Apostle Paul commanded, he says, that everyone should contribute money on the Sabbath, that is, on the Lord’s Day, so that it might be sent to Jerusalem for relief. Cf. Acts 20, verse 7. Rev. 1, verse 10. ἕκαστος ὑμῶν παρ ἑαυτῷ τιθέτω θησαυρίζων (let each of you lay by him, storing up) Let him set aside for himself, making some heap little by little.

For that is אצר (to store) which is translated sometimes by θησαυρίζειν (to store up), sometimes by συνάγειν (to gather). That succeeded into the place of tithes. Estius does not want the money, which each person intended to contribute, to have been stored privately, but collected in public on the Lord’s Day: And so he draws the words of verse 2, "by the first of the Sabbath," to verse 1, where the mention of collections was made; but it is manifest that whatever had been established regarding alms and collections and the treasury, and the command for individuals to set aside something with themselves every Lord’s Day, that it was to be kept in a domestic treasury.

Whence it is gathered that the communion of goods no longer flourished, which had obtained in the primitive Jerusalem Church. For he did not say "contribute immediately," lest perhaps someone, whose means were then slender, might have been ashamed to contribute a tiny amount, but "let each one," he says, "store up with himself and heap up," and let him bring it forward later, heaped up, as Theophylact has it here. ὅ, τι ἐὰν εὐοδῶται (whatever he may prosper). In the Manuscript more clearly, ὅτι ἐὰν ἰωο-δῶς; it is, however, a brief expression: Whatever GOD shall have prospered, for "whatever GOD prospering shall have given to him." The Hebrews express this sense of εὐοδῶ (to prosper) thus: אשר מצא ויר (that which he found and...). It is not the case that it should be amended from one codex of the others. Theophylact explains: ὅ, τι ἂν ὁ θεὸς εὐο-δώσῃ καὶ πέμψῃ, ἃ ὃ ἐυχαρασέξη. Whatever God shall have well-fortuned, and sent, and what shall have been in private. Nor does Chrysostom observe otherwise, that it was not said "whatever he shall have earned," but "whatever shall have happened prosperously," so that it might be understood that means are also supplied by GOD, and for this very purpose, that the needy might be relieved from there. Which sense it pleased B. Luther also to render: "Nach Vermögen" (According to means). For the proper meaning of the Greek verb is: To be prospered on the way, that is, in one’s actions, to act prosperously. And that this is more suitable to the present exhortation than what Erasmus conjectures the ancient interpreter to have read, who rendered it "what pleased him well," Estius recognizes εὐδοκήσας (having been well-pleased). ἵνα μή ὅταν ἔλθω, τότε λογίαι γίνωνται (that there be no collections when I come) that is, then for the first time.

But if that were the case, the collections would have been more slender than those which would have grown from a long time. Ὅταν δὲ παραγένωμαι, οὓς δοκιμάσητε, δι ἐπιστολῶν, τούτους πέμψω ἀπενεγκεῖν τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν εἰς ἱεροσόλυμα (And when I arrive, whomsoever you shall approve by letters, them will I send to carry your grace to Jerusalem). Theophylact rightly advises that a punctuation mark should be placed after δοκιμάσητε (you shall approve). And again it is a brief expression: "I will send by letters," that is, sending by letters I will commend them, I will follow them with my testimony. See how such a great man did not want to open any crack for suspicion. He called the benefit χάριν (grace/gift): See above chapter 10, verse 30. See 18, verse 18. Verse 4. Ἐὰν δὲ ἄξιον ᾖ κἀμὲ πορεύεσθαι, σὺν ἐμοὶ πορεύσονται (And if it be worthy that I also go, they shall go with me). See how he excites them, so that they might give as much as possible.

If the sum collected shall be of such value, I will accompany them instead of a letter. Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius observe that the word for "grace" is used rather than "blessing" and "communication," because those are more civil and honorable than "alms"; because that is a miserable word, and unworthy of the healthy, to whom the subsidy was to be sent, as Oecumenius has it. But the Apostle was not ashamed of this word before Felix the Governor, when he said he had come to Jerusalem to bring alms to his nation, Acts 24, verse 17. Nor was it otherwise unusual to the Holy Spirit, Acts 9, verse 36, chapter 10, verses 2, 4, 31. Therefore it is called "grace" rather, because it ought to proceed from a benevolent and gracious mind, and the λογία (collection) ought to be purely gratuitous. Moreover, he called the thing itself "grace," that is, liberality and munificence, so that he might argue that they are doing a great thing, not with an unwilling mind, or compelled by any necessity.

For this indeed ought to be called grace, which is offered voluntarily, as Theophylact has it here. PART II. The promise of the arrival of the Apostle, Timothy, and Apollo. Verse 5. ἐλεύσομαι δὲ πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ὅταν Μακεδονίαν διέλθω (But I will come to you, when I shall have passed through Macedonia). He did indeed pass through Macedonia, Acts 20, verse 3. But excluded by the straits of time, he did not go to Ephesus, but called the presbyters to himself, ibid. 16 and following. Μακεδονίαν γὰρ διέρχομαι (For I am passing through Macedonia). Again here the Present for the Future. See what was said at Matthew 26, 28. But when he was writing these things, it appears from verse 8 that Paul was at Ephesus, from where he could easily come by ship into Macedonia, and from here by land journey to the Corinthians. For when he was at Ephesus, says Theophylact, he was about to depart from there into Macedonia, and to pass through it very quickly, and to go soon also to the Corinthians.

Therefore, by many arguments, he reveals his benevolence toward the Corinthians, both because he by no means wanted to revisit them in passing, and because he desires very much to be escorted by them. Verse 6. Πρὸς ὑμᾶς δὲ τυχὸν παραμενῶ, ἢ καὶ παραχειμάσω, ἵνα ὑμεῖς με προπέμψητε οὗ ἐὰν πορεύωμαι (But with you it may be that I will abide, or even winter, that you may bring me on my journey whithersoever I go). From this purpose, mention of which is also in Acts 19, verse 21, other more serious matters diverted the Apostle, as we have already said.

Moreover, some from the Churches were accustomed to add themselves to the Apostle for the journey and some companions, as can be seen in Acts 15, verse 7, 17, verses 4, 15, 20, verse 38, 21, verse 5. Whither I shall go, that is, into Judea, 2.

Cor. 1, 16. That Paul was diverted from this purpose does not appear from Acts 20. And since he had determined this for himself ἐν Πνεύματι (in the Spirit), to go to Jerusalem through Macedonia and Achaia, in which Corinth was situated, Acts

19, verse 21, it is in no way credible that it did not succeed. What? Because it is evident from Acts 20, verse 3, that in Greece, to which it looked

Corinth remained for three months. But those who think with Thomas that Paul is speaking here of that journey into Macedonia which is designated in Acts XVI, are hallucinating without a doubt. Because that first journey into Macedonia happened before he had preached the Gospel to the Corinthians. Acts XVIII. Ver. 7. Οὐ θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἐν παρόδῳ ἰδεῖν) Here θέλω signifies a wish and desire. Ἄρτι, that is, now.

But this now here signifies the imminent future. Ἐν παρόδῳ, in passing, by the way. Ἐλπίζω δὲ χρόνον τινὰ ἐπιμεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος ἐπιτρέψῃ) Better in the Manuscript: Ἐλπίζω γὰρ. He explains what had preceded. And speaking of an uncertain Future, he uses the caution customary to Christians. Thus Rom. I. ver. 10, above IV. ver. 19, Jas. IV. ver. 15.

If GOD wills, Tertullian in his 'On the Testimony of the Soul' shows it was customary even for Pagans. Others of the ruder sort among them used to say: If the gods will, as Plautus in the last scene of the fourth act of the 'Penulus', Cicero in the fourth 'Verrine', Suetonius in 'Caligula' 9, or, when it is about those willing, which is in Ennius, Plautus several times, and Cato in 'De Re Rustica'. Ἐπιμενῶ δὲ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ ἕως τῆς πεντηκοστῆς) Afterwards other occasions made it so that he should hasten more, and that he should wish to be in Jerusalem at Pentecost itself, that is, at the end of the fifty days from Passover, Acts XX.

16. Thus the wills of men are ambulatory. He was therefore at Ephesus at that time, where he still wishes to remain, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius observe, to make the Corinthians more certain of where he is staying and how long he is to remain there.

By Pentecost, Erasmus understands the fiftieth day, because the Apostle wishes to remain at Ephesus for so many days; others understand the feast of Pentecost of the Christians. But it is more correctly understood of the Pentecost of the Jews.

Because the Apostle was not accustomed to neglect it for the sake of the Jews, until at length the Synagogue should be buried with honor, especially because in the confluence of men an opportunity was at hand for propagating the Gospel. For the same feast of Pentecost is undoubtedly understood here as that in Acts XIX. ver. 21, even if not of the same year, because there (in the Acts) it is a matter of the Pentecost of the following year; but there the Pentecost of the Jews is denoted.

For it was for the sake of this, not because of the Pentecost of the Christians, that there was a need to go to Jerusalem, outside of which the Jews did not celebrate it. Ver. 9. Θύρα γὰρ μοι ἀνέῳγε μεγάλη, καὶ ἐνεργής) A door signifies hope, as can be seen in Hosea II.

15. Because just as a door gives access into a house, so hope [gives access] to a matter. Thus also Acts XIV. ver. 26, 2 Cor. II. ver. 12. Better in other Codices ἐνεργής. A conspicuous hope; in the Glossary, ἐνεργής is 'liquid', 'evident'. Thus it appears that Ambrose read it here. Why is that reading ἐνεργής, though less used, to be preferred? The Greek commentators certainly followed the received reading.

A door brings in not so much hope as opportunity and access, just as to open a window for the Latins is to give an opportunity. For Ephesus was the metropolis of all Asia Minor, most famous for the study of the arts, to which very many flocked from all places. But the opening of this door, so that access might be open, must be attributed solely to GOD, Acts XIV. ver.

27, Col. IV. ver. 3, 2 Thess. III. ver. 1, both in that liberty of preaching the Gospel freely, which was divinely granted, and in the efficacy of the Gospel, by which GOD introduced very many, as if through an open door, into His kingdom. Καὶ ἀντικείμενοι πολλοί) What would have terrified another, this invites Paul. There are many enemies of the Gospel there, therefore I desire to be there, that I may oppose myself to them.

Solet sic fumi Hebraeum בְּרָכָה à verbis ad res ducta translatione. Intelligit autem collationem pecuniarum ad sublevandam paupertatem fidelium in Judaea Rom. XV. 16. ὥστε διέταξα ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Γαλατίας) Amabant Apostoli easdem consuetudines ubique introducere. Et hae sunt traditiones Apostolicae relatae, ut diximus in ὡς καίαι. Hoc est iter per Galatiam, cujus mentio Act. XVI. vers. 6. IX. vers. 1. & versu 12. διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας & χάρις 2. Cor. IX. v. 4. & hoc loco vers. 3. Non autem hic de collecta sermo est, cujus Act. XI. vers. 28. & XII. mentio facta, sed de alia posteriori, de qua 2. Cor. IX. 19. Canones Apostolicos quos vocant, minime esse auctoritatis Apostolicae supra diximus. Vers. 2. Κατὰ μίαν σαββάτου) Συμφωνήσεις Ἰουδαίων, ait Philo, ἅπαξαν ὄντα καὶ τῆς ἀλλῆς οὐσίας, nempe etiam extra sabbata. Christiani maxime sabbatis & diebus Dominicis, qui sunt μία σαββάτων Matth. XXVIII. vers. 1. conveniebant. Sed quia hi, quæ ex Judæis facti Christiani moris Judaici retinentes sabbatis pecunias non tractabant, ideo ad eam rem aptior erat dies sequens. Tertullianus Apologetico: Modicam unusquisque stipem menstrua die, vel cum velit, & si modo velit, & si modo possit, apponit. Nam nemo compellitur, sed sponte confert. Hæc quasi deposita pietatis sunt. Nam inde non epulis nec potaculis nec ingratis voratrinis dispensatur, sed egenis alentis dumandusque, & pueris ac puellis re ac parentibus destitutis. Itemque domesticis sensibus: item naufragis, & si qui in metallis: & si qui in insulis vel in custodiis duntaxat ex causa Dei sectæ, alumni confessionis suæ fiunt.

Una sabbatorum est prima sabbatorum, vel dies illa, quæ prima est in hebdomade dierum, quæ σάββατον nomine venit Luc. XIIX, vers. 12. Vid. Augustini epist. LXXXVI. ad Casulan. Quæ dies Dominica erat, quam proinde Apostolicæ institutionis fuisse, dubium nullum est, qua oblationes fidelium ad altare fiebant. Cui diei & proprie conveniunt eleemosynarum collectæ, quo gratiæ DEI hoc die exhibitæ in creationis auspicio, resurrectionis Christi propter nostram justitiam, & missionis Spiritus Sancti super Apostolos, orbis Doctores, beneficio grata memoria ad munificentiam, & misericordiam exhibendam excitemur.

Quæ causæ magis congruunt, quam Grotiana. Nam illam ἐθελοθρησκείαν non tractandæ in sabbato pecuniæ penudæos conversos viguisse non est verisimile. Hieronymus contra vigilant: Pecuniam sabbati, inquit, hoc est, in Dominica omnes conferre qua Hierosolymam in solatia dirigantur, Apostolus Paulus præcepit. Conf. Actor. XX. vers. 7. Apoc. I. vers. 10. ἕκαστος ὑμῶν παρ ἑαυτῷ τιθέτω θησαυρίζων Sibi seponat, paulatim cumulum aliquem faciens.

Id enim est אצר quod modo per θησαυρίζειν; modo per συνάγειν vertitur. Id successit in locum decimarum. Estius non vult, pecuniam, quam quisque conferre cogitabat, privatim reconditam, sed in publicum in die Dominico collatam fuisse: Adeoque trahit verba vers. 2. per unam sabbati ad vers. 1. ubi collectarum mentio facta; sed manifestum est, quæcumque constitui fuerat eleemosynarum & collectarum & thesaurarium & juberi singulos dies Dominicos aliquid apud se seponere, idque in thesauro domestico asservari.

Unde colligitur communionem bonorum non amplius viguisse, quæ in primitiva Hierosolymitana Ecclesia obtinuerat. Neque enim dixit statim conferte, ne quem forte, cujus tenues tune essent facultates, pusillum quippiam tribuere puduisset, sed recondat, inquit, apud seipsum quisque & cumulet, aculumque deinceps & cumulatum deferat, ut hic habet Theophylactus. ὅ, τι ἐὰν εὐοδῶται In Manuscripto clarius, ὅτι ἐὰν ἰωο-δῶς; est autem brevis loquutio: Quodcunque DEUS prosperaverit, pro quodcunque DEUS prosperans ei dederit. Εὐοδῶ Hebræi hunc sensum sic exprimunt: אשר מצא ויר Non est quod emendetur ex uno codice cæteri. Theophylactus exponit: ὅ, τι ἂν ὁ θεὸς εὐο-δώσῃ καὶ πέμψῃ, ἃ ὃ ἐυχαρασέξη. Quicquid Deus bene fortunaverit, & miserit, & quod in privatam fuerit. Nec aliter Chrysostomus observans, non esse dictum, quicquid lucratus fuerit, sed quicquid prospere obtigerit, ut intelligeretur facultates etiam a DEO suppeditari, & in hoc ipsum, ut inde subleventur egeni. Qui sensus etiam B. Lutheri reddere placuit: Nach Vermögen. Nam Græci verbi propria significatio est: Prosperari in via, id est, actionibus suis, prospere agere. Idque magis aptum esse exhortationi præsenti, quam quod legisse interpretem veterem, qui reddidit, quod ei bene placuerit, Erasmus auguratur, εὐδοκήσας agnoscit Estius. ἵνα μή ὅταν ἔλθω, τότε λογίαι γίνωνται id est, tunc primum.

Quod si esset, tenuiores futuræ erant collationes quam quæ ex longo tempore primum crevisent. Ὅταν δὲ παραγένωμαι, οὓς δοκιμάσητε, δι ἐπιστολῶν, τούτους πέμψω ἀπενεγκεῖν τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν εἰς ἱεροσόλυμα Notam interpungentem ponendam post δοκιμάσητε recte monet Theophylactus. Et rursum brevis est loquutio: Mittam per literas, id est, mittens per literas eas commendabo, testimonio meo eos prosequar. Vide quomodo vir tantus nullam suspicioni rimam aperire voluerit. χάριν dixit beneficium: Vide supra cap. X. vers. 30. Sin XVIII. vers. 18. Vers. 4. Ἐὰν δὲ ἄξιον ᾖ κἀμὲ πορεύεσθαι, σὺν ἐμοὶ πορεύσονται Vide quomodo eos excitat, ut dent quam plurimum.

Si summa collecta tanti erit, ego pro epistola eos comitabor. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius observant vocem gratiæ potius, & benedictionis, & communicationis adhibitam, quod civiles & honorifice magis illæ sint, quam eleemosynæ; quod illud miserum fit vocabulum, & indignum sanis, quibus mittendum erat subsidium, ut habet Oecumenius. Sed non puduit Apostolum, hujus vocis apud Felicem Præsidem, cum se venisse Hierosolymas dixit, eleemosynas facturum in gentem suam Actor. XXIV. vers. 17. Nec inusitata ea fuit alias Spiritui Sancto Actor. IX. vers. 36. cap. X. vers. 2. 4. 31. Gratia igitur potius dicta, quod ex animo benevolo & gratioso proficici, & mere gratuita esse debet λογία. Gratiam autem rem ipsam appellavit, hoc est, liberalitatem & munificentiam, ut arguat eos rem grandem facitare, non animo iniquo, vel ulla coactos necessitate.

Hac quippe dici gratia debet, quæ ultro offeratur, ut Theophylactus hic habet. PARS II. Promissio adventus Apostoli, Timothei & Apollo. Vers. 5. ἐλεύσομαι δὲ πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ὅταν Μακεδονίαν διέλθω Macedoniam quidem transiit Actor. XX. vers. 3. Sed angustiis temporis exclusus non adiit Ephesum, sed presbyteros ad se accivit ibid. 16. & sequentibus. Μακεδονίαν γὰρ διέρχομαι Rursum hic Præsens pro Futuro. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 28. At cum hæc scriberet, Ephesi fuisse Paulum è vers. 8. apparet, unde in Macedoniam facile navigio venire potuit, & hinc itinere terrestri ad Corinthios. Ephesi enim cum esset, inquit Theophylactus, concessurus inde in Macedoniam erat, eamque celerrime præteriturus, aditurusque mox & Corinthios.

Multis itaque argumentis, suam in Corinthios benevolentiam aperit, cum quia nequaquam eos vellet transeunde revisere, tum quia se ab iisdem deduci percupiat. Vers. 6. Πρὸς ὑμᾶς δὲ τυχὸν παραμενῶ, ἢ καὶ παραχειμάσω, ἵνα ὑμεῖς με προπέμψητε οὗ ἐὰν πορεύωμαι Ab hoc proposito, cujus mentio & Actor. XIX. vers. 21. alia graviora Apostolum diverterunt, ut jam diximus.

Solebant autem quidam ex Ecclesiis Apostolo se itineris aliquosque comites addere, ut videre est Actor. XV. vers. 7. XVII. vers. 4. 15. XX. vers. 38. XXI. vers. 5. Quo ibo, id est, in Judæam, 2.

Cor. I. 16. Paulum ab hoc proposito divertisse ex Actor. XX. haud constat. Et cum ἐν Πνεύματι id sibi constituerit, per Macedoniam & Achaiam, in qua sita erat Corinthus, adire Hierosolymam Act.

XIX. vers. 21. nullo modo credibile est, id non successisse. Quid? quod ex Actor. XX. vers. 3. pateat, quod in Græcia, ad quam spectabat

Corinthus per tres menses substiterit. Qui vero cum Thoma putant, Paulum hic de ea profectione in Macedoniam loqui, quae Actor. XVI. designata, hallucinantur procul ambiguo. Quia illa prima in Macedoniam profectio contigit antequam Corinthiis praedicasset Evangelium. Actor. XVIII. Vers. 7. Οὐ θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἐν παρόδῳ ἰδεῖν) Hic θέλω votum & desiderium significat. Ἄρτι, id est, nunc.

Hoc vero nunc hic significat futurum imminens. Ἐν παρόδῳ, in transcursu, obiter. Ἐλπίζω δὲ χρόνον τινὰ ἐπιμεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος ἐπιτρέψῃ) Melius in Manuscripto: Ἐλπίζω γὰρ. Explicat quod praecesserat. Et de Futuro incerto loquens usurpat solitam Christianis cautionem.

Sic Rom. I. vers. 10. supra IV. vers. 19. Iac. IV. vers. 15. Si DEUS voluerit, etiam Paganis usitatum ostendit Tertullianus de testimonio Animae. Alii rudiores eorum dicebant: Si dii volent, ut Plautus Penulo IV. scena ultima, Cicero IV. Verina, Suetonius Caligula 9. aut, cum de iis volentibus quod est apud Ennium, Plautum aliquoties & Catonem de re Rustica. Ἐπιμενῶ δὲ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ ἕως τῆς πεντηκοστῆς) Postea aliae occasiones fecere, ut magis properaret, velletque in ipsa Pentecoste, id est, fine dierum quinquaginta a Paschate esse Hierosolymis, Actor.

XX. 16. Ita ambulatoriae sunt hominum voluntates. Fuit itaque tum Ephesi, ubi permanere adhuc vult, quomodo Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius observant, Apostolum certiores facere Corinthios, ubi degat, & quamdiu illic commoraturus sit.

Per Pentecosten Erasmus diem quinquagesimam, quod tot dies Ephesi manere velit Apostolus, intelligit, alii festum Pentecostes Christianorum. Sed rectius de Pentecoste Judaeorum intelligitur.

Quia non solebat in gratiam Judaeorum ea negligere Apostolus, donec tandem cum honore sepeliretur Synagoga, imprimis, quod in confluxu hominum occasio suppeteret propagandi Evangelium. Nam idem fine dubio Pentecostes festum hic intelligitur, quod Actor. XIX. vers. 21. etsi non ejusdem anni, quia ibi (in Actis) de Pentecoste sequentes anni agitur; at illic Judaeorum Pentecoste denotatur.

Hujus enim gratia, non ob Pentecosten Christianorum opus erat Hierosolymam tendere, extra quam Judaei eam non celebrabant. Vers. 9. Θύρα γὰρ μοι ἀνέῳγε μεγάλη, καὶ ἐνεργής) Ostium spem significat, ut videre est Osee II. 15. Quia sicut ostium aditum dat in domum, ita spes ad rem.

Sic & Actor. XIV. vers. 26. 2. Cor. II. vers. 12. Melius in aliis Codicibus ἐνεργής. Spes conspicua, in Glossario ἐνεργής liquidus, evidens. Ita apparet legisse hic Ambrosium. Cur illa lectio ἐνεργής minus usitata praeferenda? Graeci certe commentatores receptam lectionem secuti sunt.

Ostium non tam spem, quam occasionem & aditum infert, ut Latinis fenestram aperire est occasionem dare. Nam Ephesius totius Asiae minoris metropolis erat ob artium studia celeberrima, ad quam ex omnibus locis plurimi confluebant. Sed ostii hujus apertio, ut pateret aditus DEO tribuenda unice Actor. Καὶ ἀντικείμενοι πολλοί) Quod alium terruisset, hoc Paulum invitat. Multi ibi sunt hostes Evangelii, ideo desidero ibi esse, ut me iis opponam.

## 16:10
Ver. 10. Ἐὰν δὲ ἔλθῃ Τιμόθεος) Paul had indeed sent Timothy, faithful to himself and to the Lord, as appears above IV. 17. But in such a way that he had many Churches to visit on the journey. Therefore, foreseeing the dangers, he says, if he shall come to you. Βλέπετε ἵνα ἀφόβως γένηται πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Take care that those men among you, puffed up with riches or learning, the authors of schisms, whose faults he will rebuke, may not be able to harm him in any way.

Take care as much as is in you, for not all dangers could be avoided at that time. But it is the part of good men to try everything, lest the evil harm other good men. Τὸ γὰρ ἔργον κυρίου ἐργάζεται, ὡς κἀγώ) A great commendation.

For what had Paul not done? The work of the Lord is the promotion of the Gospel, Acts XII. ver. 2, XIV. 25, XV. 38. See also Matt. XXI. 28. Μήτις οὖν αὐτὸν ἐξουθενήσῃ) He warns the pious to revere him according to his merits. See 1 Tim. IV. 12. Προπέμψατε δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν εἰρήνῃ, ἵνα ἔλθῃ πρός με) That is, see to it that he may depart from you to return to me, with that friendship which ought to be among you. Ἐνδέχομαι γὰρ αὐτὸν μετὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν) I desire his return, and that of his companions (for others also had entered Corinth with Timothy, as the following also show), intending to use their work.

Theophylact has it thus here: Since it was fitting that Timothy should offend by his intervention those who had done wrong, and should rebuke their crimes, he makes them more certain, and warns them not to rise up against Timothy, who were considered wise and rich among themselves: not because of what was about to happen, lest he should succumb through fear, but because a calamity was about to befall the Corinthians from that.

Timothy indeed had been admonished and was prepared and ready to undergo dangers. But he says 'among you' rightly, just as if he were saying: I would by no means demand this from any Gentiles, but it is a deposit from you, that he may remain safer among you.

For I am working the work of the Lord here: let no one therefore despise him, that is, no differently than he himself is about to preach, and he is establishing others in the faith, which indeed redounds to the great praise of Timothy.

Since therefore he is of such a kind, I would not have anyone hold him in low esteem. For he was not of great age, but younger, and alone destined for so arduous a matter, since the care of an elated and proud people had been permitted to him. Whence it could not seem a wonder if he were held in low esteem by them. But conduct him in peace, that he may come to me. For I am expecting him with the brethren.

Nay rather, he says, honor him, which certainly, when he says 'conduct him', is intended. In peace, however, that is, in safety; without any fear, with altercation removed, and obedience rendered. But I say 'I send him forth' to terrify these, just as if Timothy were about to report to him on his arrival everything as it has been done: And therefore he warns them not to show themselves troublesome to them: At the same time also, that reverence may make him more worthy: Inasmuch as he is so necessary to himself, that when he shall have decided he must be expected.

Cf. 1 Tim. IV. ver. 11. That 'with the brethren', which Grotius refers to the companions of Timothy, others prefer to refer to those who were desiring and expecting the return of Timothy with Paul.

To whom also the Blessed Hunnius is added. Ver. 12. Περὶ δὲ Ἀπολλῶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ) The Corinthians knew him. For he had been among them, Acts XVIII. ver. 17. And since the pious men who were at Corinth knew both his piety and his learning, they had greatly desired that he himself, above all others, should be sent to correct the affairs at Corinth. Καὶ πάντως οὐκ ἦν θέλημα ἵνα νῦν ἔλθῃ) I could not obtain that from him, namely because other more urgent matters were detaining him at that time. Ἐλεύσεται δὲ, ὅτε εὐκαιρήσῃ) That is, when he shall have extricated himself from those affairs. Εὐκαιρεῖν is to be free from other matters, as in Mark VI. ver.

31, Acts XVII. ver. 21. Hence εὐκαιρία. Sir. XXXVIII. 36, 1 Macc. XI. 48.

The Apostle seems to excuse himself, when he sent Timothy and not rather Apollo, as the Greeks have noted. Theophylactus: Apollo was older than Timothy in age, and a man sufficiently eloquent. Therefore, lest the Corinthians should complain that this man was not rather sent to them, but one who was younger, he says thus: I have greatly entreated him, and exhorted him, that he might come to you. Nor does he say that he had already resisted him, but that he might render him free from blame, that it was not his will, he added, that is, it did not please God. In the Greek, there is not 'his will', which some Latins have, nor in the Syriac, nor indeed in the more corrected Latin texts. Therefore, with Oecumenius and Theodoret, Theophylactus refers it to the will of God. Others, however, especially the Latins, more correctly refer it to the will of Apollo, that he himself for certain reasons had no mind to go to Corinth at that time: nor did the Apostle think it expedient to urge him with commands. But it is not relevant what Jerome in his Commentary on Titus III reports about Apollo, that he was Bishop of the Corinthians, and because of the dissensions that were in Corinth, he sailed to the neighboring island of Crete with Zenas the lawyer. For Bishops are of such piety and vigilance, that they would not desert their flock because of dissensions, especially one that is new, and not yet sufficiently informed.

PART III. Exhortation to vigilance and constancy.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἐὰν δὲ ἔλθῃ Τιμόθεος) Timotheum sibi & Domino fidum miserat quidem Paulus, ut apparet supra IV. 17. Sed ita, ut in itinere multas Ecclesias haberet invisendas. Quare pericula prospiciens dicit, si ad vos venerit. Βλέπετε ἵνα ἀφόβως γένηται πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Curate, ne illi homines inter vos divitiis aut eruditione turgidi, schismatum autores, quorum culpas arguet, quicquam nocere ei possint.

Curate quantum in vobis est, non enim omnia pericula illo tempore vitari poterant. Sed bonorum est omnia experiri, ne mali bonis aliis noceant. Τὸ γὰρ ἔργον κυρίου ἐργάζεται, ὡς κἀγώ) Magnum praeconium. Nam quid non fecerat Paulus?

Opus Domini est Evangelii promotio Actor. XII. vers. 2. XIV. 25. XV. 38. Vide & Matth. XXI. 28. Μήτις οὖν αὐτὸν ἐξουθενήσῃ) Monet pios ut eum pro meritis revereantur. Vide 1. Tim. IV. 12. Προπέμψατε δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν εἰρήνῃ, ἵνα ἔλθῃ πρός με) Id est, facite ut ad me rediturus a vobis discedat opsite ea quae inter vos esse debet amicitia. Ἐνδέχομαι γὰρ αὐτὸν μετὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν) Multum ejus comitemque ejus (Nam & alii cum Timotheo Corinthum inierant, ut & sequentia ostendunt) reditum desidero, opera eorum usurus.

Theophylactus hic ita habet: Quoniam par erat, ut Timotheus suo interventu offenderet, qui deliquissent, objurgaretque eorum facinora, certiores hos reddit, & commonefacit, ne Timotheo insurgant, qui apud se sapientes haberentur & divites: neque eo, quod futurum esset, ne pra timore ille succumberet, sed quia Corinthiis ex eo obventura esset calamitas.

Timotheus quidem admonitus erat ad pericula subeunda paratus & promptus. Recte autem apud vos dicit, perinde ac finquiat: Nequaquam id a gentibus ullis exigerem, sed a vobis depositum, ut tutior ille apud vos maneat.

Opus enim Domini operatur hic ego: Nequis ergo illum spernat, hoc est baud secus, atque ipse, praedicaturus est ille, & alios instauras ad fidem, quod sane magnam cedit Timothei in laudem. Cum itaque istiusmodi sit, nemo hunc parvi duxerit velim.

Erat namque is non grandis natu, sed junior, & solus ad eam rem tam arduam destinatus, quippe cui elati & superbi entis populi cura erat permissa. Unde nec mirum videri poterat, si ab illis parvifieret. Deducite autem illum in pace, ut veniat ad me. Exspecto enim illum cum fratribus.

Quin potius, inquit, honore hunc prosequamini, quod certe, cum deducite inquit, praetenditur. In pace autem hoc est in tuto; fine ulla formidine, altercatione sublata, & obedientia praestita. Expello autem illum ad territandos hos dixit, perinde ac si cuncta, quemadmodum gesta sint, in ejus adventu sibi fit Timotheus renuntiaturus: Eoque ne illi molestos se praebeant, commonefacit: Simul etiam, ut reverentia cum efficiat digniorem: Utpote, qui adeo sibi fit necessarius, ut cum duxerit exspectandum.

Conf. 1. Tim. IV. vers. 11. Illud μετὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν, quod ad comites Timothei refert Grotius, alii ad eos, qui cum Paulo desiderabant & exspectabant Timothei reditum, referri malunt.

Quibus accedit etiam Beat. Hunnius. Vers. 12. Περὶ δὲ Ἀπολλῶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ) Noverant hunc Corinthii. Nam apud ipsos fuerat Actor. XVIII. vers. 17. Et cum viri & pietatem & eruditionem haberent cognitam, multum optaverant pii, qui erant Corinthi, ipsum potissimum ad res Corinthi corrigendas mitti. Καὶ πάντως οὐκ ἦν θέλημα ἵνα νῦν ἔλθῃ) Non potui id ab eo obtinere, nempe quia alia magis urgentia tum distinebant. Ἐλεύσεται δὲ, ὅτε εὐκαιρήσῃ) Id est, ubi ab illis negotiis se expedierit. Εὐκαιρεῖν est vacare ab aliis rebus, ut Marci VI. vers.

31. Actor. XVII. v. 21. Hinc εὐκαιρία. Sir. XXXVIII. 36. 1. Macc. XI. 48.

Excusare se videtur Apostolus, cum Timotheum & non potius Apollo miserit, ut Graeci notarunt. Theophylactus: Erat Apollo Timotheo aetate provectior, & vir fatis facundus. Ne itaque quererentur Corinthii, non hunc potius ad se fuisse transmissum, sed cum, qui junior esset, sic inquit: Multum rogavi eum, & cohortatus sum, ad vos se conferret. Neque hunc dicit, sibi jam obsistisse, quin ut culpa liberum reddat, utique non fuit voluntas ejus, subjecit, hoc est, Deo non libuit. In Graeco non est voluntas ejus, quod nonnulli Latini habent, nec in Syro, imo nec in emendatioribus Latinis. Ideo cum Oecumenio & Theodoreto ad voluntatem Dei refert Theophylactus. Alii tamen, imprimis Latini, rectius ad voluntatem Apollo referunt, quod ipsi ob certas causas animus non fuerit tum Corinthum eundi: Nec expedire censuerit Apostolus, ut eum praeceptis urgeret. Non est vero affine, quod Hieronymus in Comm. ad Tit. III. de Apollo refert, eum Corinthiorum Episcopum fuisse, & propter diffensiones, quae in Corintho erant ad vicinam insulam Cretam cum Zena legis doctore transfretaffe. Episcopi enim tantae pietatis & vigilantiae sunt, gregem ob dissensiones deferere, maxime novellum, nec adeo fatis informatum.

PARS III. Adhortatio ad vigilantiam & constantiam.

## 16:13
Ver. 13. Γρηγορεῖτε) See Matth. XXIV. 42. XXV. 13. XXVI. 41. Acts XX. 31. Στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει) Stand, that is, persevere. See above XV. ver. 5. He has the verb νίκην for ἴσα, and Mark XI. ver. 15. Rom. XIV. 4. Gal. V. 1. Phil. I. 7. IV. 1. 1. Thess. III. 8. 2. Thess. II. 15. Ἀνδρίζεσθε) Now be men, as the old Latin poet speaks, and Homer: Ἀνδρίζεσθε ἴδεν ἀνδρεῖοι 2. Paral. XXXII. ver. 7. Moses often encourages Joshua with this verb. Jos. I. ver. 6. 7. 9. 18. David encourages Solomon 1. Paral. XXVIII. ver. 20. Κραταιοῦσθε) Here also it is passive for reciprocal, show yourselves strong. For 1. Sam. IV. ver. 9. where in the Greek it is παραταυτᾶσθε, in the Hebrew it is הִתְחַזְקוּ and elsewhere. Ver. 14. Πάντα ὑμῶν ἐν ἀγάπῃ γινέσθω) Where this is, there are no schisms. Therefore Paul commends it so often to the Corinthians VIII. 1. XIII. 1. 3. 4. 8. 13. XIV. 1. 2. Cor. II. 4. 8. VI. 6. He warns that in the meantime, until he arrives, 1. they should watch against the snares of both spiritual and corporal enemies, that they may take care of their salvation not sleepily, Rom. XIV. ver. 17. 1. Petr. V. ver. 8. 2. they should persist in the faith; and that with a manly, or strong spirit, and below Ἀνδρίζεσθε, κραταιοῦσθε. 3. Let them do all things in charity, which is the bond of perfection Col. III. ver. 14. ἐν ἀγάπῃ, which is not 'with charity', as Erasmus rendered it; but 'in charity', which is more effective, so that not only by the dictate of charity, but also in sincere and constant charity, without hypocrisy, all things may be done.

Theophylactus thought that this particularly concerned those who were tearing the Church apart with dissensions and factions; but it is a general warning. Ver. 15. Παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί, οἴδατε τὴν οἰκίαν Στεφανᾶ, ὅτι ἐστὶν ἀπαρχὴ τῆς Ἀχαΐας, καὶ εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἔταξαν ἑαυτούς) Concerning this Stephanas, see what we said above 16. But concerning the meaning of the word ἀπαρχὴ Rom. XVI. He says, you know that Stephanas with his own and among the first are those who believed, and that they have served the other faithful much. He implies that they did not intrude themselves into the ecclesiastical ministry, which would be against Heb. V. ver. 4. but that they devoted themselves with voluntary charity to ministering to the saints in those things which pertain to τὰ βιωτικά (the necessities of life): That is, that they constituted themselves to receive the needy faithful, and to minister to them, and to bring aid, not unwillingly and forced, but they do it voluntarily, as Theophylactus has it. Nor are the Grotian interpretations alien to this sense.

Latin:

Verf. 13. Γρηγορεῖτε) Vide Matth. XXIV. 42. XXV. 13. XXVI. 41. Act. XX. 31. Στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει) State, id est, perffate. Vide supra XV. verf. 5. Verbum νίκην pro ἴσα habet & Marci XI. verf. 15.
