Rom. XIV. 4. Gal. V. 1. Phil. I. 7. IV. 1. 1. Thess. III. 8. 2. Thess. II. 15. Ἀνδρίζεσθε) Nunc fite viri, ut loquitur vetus Poëta Latinus, & Homerus: Ἀνδρίζεσθε ἴδεν ἀνδρεῖοι 2. Paral. XXXII. verf. 7. Mofes Josuam saepe hoc verbo animat. Jos. I. verf. 6. 7. 9. 18. David Salomonem 1. Paral. XXVIII. verf. 20. Κραταιοῦσθε) Est & hic passivum pro Reciproco, fortes vosmet praestatis. Nam 1. Sam. IV. verf. 9. ubi in Graeco est παραταυτᾶσθε in Hebrzo est הִתְחַזְקוּ & alibi. Verf. 14. Πάντα ὑμῶν ἐν ἀγάπῃ γινέσθω) Quae ubi est, ibi non sunt schismata. Ideo toties eam Corinthiis Paulus commendat VIII. 1. XIII. 1. 3. 4. 8. 13. XIV. 1. 2. Cor. II. 4. 8. VI. 6. Monet, ut interea, dum advenerit, 1. vigilent adversus insidias tum spiritualium, tum corporalium hostium, ut salutis curam gerant haud somnolenter, Rom. XIV. verf. 17. 1. Petr. V. Verf. 8. 2. in fide persistant; idque animo virili, seu forti, & infra Ἀνδρίζεσθε, κραταιοῦσθε. 3. In charitate omnia faciant, quae vinculum est perfectionis Col. III. verf. 14. ἐν ἀγάπῃ, quod non est cum charitate, ut Erasmus reddidit; sed in charitate, quod efficacius, ut non modo ex charitatis dictamine, fed etiam in sincera & constanti charitate, cita fucum, omnia fiant.

Haec peculiariter concernere eos, qui discerpebant Ecclesiam diffidiis & factionibus, Theophylactus autumavit; fed monitum est generale. Verf. 15. Παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί, οἴδατε τὴν οἰκίαν Στεφανᾶ, ὅτι ἐστὶν ἀπαρχὴ τῆς Ἀχαΐας, καὶ εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἔταξαν ἑαυτούς) de hoc Stephana vide quae diximus supra 16. De significatu autem vocis ἀπαρχὴ Rom. XVI. Scitis ait Stephanam cum suis & inter primos esse qui crediderunt, & multum eos inservisse fidelibus aliis. Non seipsos in ministerium Ecclesiasticum in-gessisse, quod esset contra Ebr. V. verf. 4. sed ad ministrandum sanctis in iis, quae ad τὰ βιωτικά spectant, ultronea charitate sese addixisse innuit: Ut fideles videlicet egenos excipiant, eisdemque ut ministrent, & opem ferant, seipsos constituerunt, non inviti & coacti, sed ultro id agunt, ut Theophylactus habet. Nec ab hoc sensu aliena sunt Grotiana.

## 16:16
Ver. 16. Ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ὑποτάσσεσθε τοῖς τοιούτοις) ὑποτάσσεσθαι in this place is indeed to revere, to defer honor and obedience, as Eph. V. 21. 1. Petr. V. 5. Καὶ παντὶ τῷ συνεργοῦντι καὶ κοπιῶντι) Those who cooperate for the propagation of the Gospel and labor to support the faithful, he shows that what he said is not to defer to persons, but to merits. It signifies not a legal ὑποταγὴ (submission), which we owe to Bishops and teachers of the word, but a moral one, by which we show ourselves reverent and obedient to those who excel in virtue, as Eftius observes with Cajetan.

Latin:

Verf. 16. Ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ὑποτάσσεσθε τοῖς τοιούτοις) ὑποτάσσεσθαι hoc quidem loco est revereri, honorem & obsequia deferre, ut Eph. V. 21. 1. Petr. V. 5. Καὶ παντὶ τῷ συνεργοῦντι καὶ κοπιῶντι) Qui cooperantur ad propagationem Evangelii & laborant ad sublevandos fideles, ostendit, quod dixit non personis se deferre, sed meritis. Significatur non ὑποταγὴ legali, quam Episcopis & verbi doctoribus debemus, sed morali, qua reverentes & obsequentes nos praebemus iis, qui virtute praestant, ut cum Cajetano observat Eftius.

## 16:17
Ver. 17. Χαίρω δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ Στεφανᾶ καὶ Φορτουνάτου καὶ Ἀχαϊκοῦ) Fortunatus is a Roman name. Achaicus is a Greek name. But Roman names were also frequent among the Greeks at that time. And it seems to me that this Fortunatus and Achaicus were children of Chloe. See above 1. 11. Ὅτι τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα ὗτοι ἀναπληρώσαν) What you all ought to have done, they did. They made me certain of your troubles. In a similar way he said προσαναπληρῶ τὸ ὑστέρημα 2. Cor. IX. 12. הִלְא הִתְחַזְקוּ. Ver. 18. Ἀνέπαυσαν γὰρ τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα τὸ ὑμῶν) Ἀνέπαυσαν הִנִּיחוּ that is, they refreshed Zach. VI. ver. 8. 2. Cor. VII. v. 13. Philem. 7. 20. See also Matth. XI. ver. 29. They refreshed Paul, when he understood that there were many in the Corinthian Church who held to true dogmas: who cultivated piety and peace. They in turn refreshed those pious ones, when they signified to them with what love Paul pursued them. Τὸ πνεῦμα, for 'my spirit' or 'me', is a frequent expression: Ignatius in his epistle to the Romans Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα, and indeed with the verb ἀναπαύειν it is repeated in the cited places of Zechariah and to Philemon.

Others interpret this ἀναπλήρωσιν differently, that they were present to Paul in place of all the absent ones, as if sent by the Corinthians with a letter, to bring back an answer concerning their doubts. Ἐπιγινώσκετε ἐν τοῖς τούτοις) That is, esteem highly. Μνημονεύω is frequent among the Hebrews.

The Greeks, especially the Interpreters, as also the Latins, have observed this force of the verb ἐπιγινώσκετε here, namely that knowledge is implied with affection and reverence. Know them, that is, hold them in honor, says Theophylactus. So 1. Thess. V. 12. We ask that you know those who labor among you; where however the verb is εἰδέναι.

PART IV. Salutations with a warning and final wish.

Latin:

Verf. 17. Χαίρω δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ Στεφανᾶ καὶ Φορτουνάτου καὶ Ἀχαϊκοῦ) Fortunatus nomen est Romanum. Achai-cus nomen Graecum. Sed nomina Romana etiam apud Graecos eo tempore erant frequentia. Et mihi videntur Fortunatus iste & Achaicus liberi fuisse Chloës. Vide supra 1. 11. Ὅτι τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα ὗτοι ἀναπληρώσαν) Quod vos omnes facere oportuit, id illi fecerunt. Certiorem me fecere de vestris morbis. Simili modo προσαναπληρῶ τὸ ὑστέρημα dixit 2. Cor. IX. 12. הִלְא הִתְחַזְקוּ. Verf. 18. Ἀνέπαυσαν γὰρ τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα τὸ ὑμῶν) ἀνέπαυσαν הִנִּיחוּ id est, recrearunt Zach. VI. verf. 8. 2. Cor. VII. v. 13. Philem. 7. 20. Vide & Matth. XI. verf. 29. Recrearunt Paulum, cum intellexit multos in Ecclesia Corinthiaca esse, qui vera dogmata retinerent: pietatem & pacem colerent. Recrearunt vicissim pios illos, cum eis significarunt, quo amore eos Paulus prosequeretur. Τὸ πνεῦμα, pro animum meum aut me, loquutio frequens: Ignatius in epistola ad Romanos Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα & quidem cum verbo ἀναπαύειν repetitur dictis Zachariae & ad Philemonem locis.

Aliter interpretantur hanc ἀναπλήρωσιν alii, quod nempe Paulo praesentes fuerint instar absentium omnium, ceu missi a Corinthiis cum epistola, ut responsum de dubiis referrent. Ἐπιγινώσκετε ἐν τοῖς τούτοις) Id est, magnifacite. Μνημονεύω frequens apud Hebraeos.

Hanc vim verbi ἐπιγινώσκετε observarunt hic Graeci imprimis Interpretes, ut & Latini, notitiam nempe innui cum affectu & reverentialem. Cognoscite, id est in honore habetote, ait Theophylactus. Ita 1. Thess. V. 12. Rogamus, ut noveritis eos, qui laborant inter vos; ubi tamen est verbum εἰδέναι,

PARS IV. Salutationes cum monito & voto finali.

## 16:19
Ver. 19. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ Ἐκκλησίαι τῆς Ἀσίας) From this a probable conjecture is drawn that this epistle was written from Ephesus rather, as the Syriac and Arabic books have it, than from Philippi in Macedonia, as the Greek books have it. That which we had above 6. and 8., which is 2. Cor. II. ver. 12, favors this opinion. Some wish that it was written at Ephesus but sent away from Philippi. More probable, however, is that it was written at Ephesus and sent also from there, from ver. 8. and the present passage, by which name he salutes the Corinthians on behalf of the Churches of Asia. Philippi, moreover, is a city of Macedonia. B. Gerhard teaches, in Exeg. de Script. S. § 258, that this epistle was written before the passage through Macedonia 1. Corinth. XVI. ver. 5. Then the Apostle had stayed at Ephesus Acts XI. ver. 19. 20, because he salutes the Corinthians in the name of Aquila and Priscilla, and he left them at Ephesus when he went down into Macedonia Acts XIX. ver. 20; nor did the subscriptions proceed from the Apostle, but were added by later hands. Which do not always agree: Thus while in the present to the subscription let it be added that the letter was sent through Stephanus and Fortunatus and Achaicus and Timotheus; regarding the first three, indeed, that could be admitted, but not regarding Timotheus. For that he was absent when this letter was written, and was not actually with Paul, is gathered from chapter IV, verse 17. To which place Theodoret: Through these (Stephanus, Fortunatus, and Achaicus) the Corinthians had written, and questioned the Apostle about those who had contracted marriage. Through them he also sent this letter. For not, as some have supposed, did the blessed Timotheus carry the letters to them: But it was indeed sent to them; however, it is likely that, since he had performed some duty in another city, he thus approached them. For this is signified by those things which are written about him: "If, however, Timotheus comes, see that he is among you without fear."

We add Flacius’s suffrage and observation: That this letter was written not from Philippi, as the Greek copies have it, but from Ephesus, is clearly seen from this last chapter: But perhaps someone was deceived by ascribing this to that Hebraism: "Now I am passing through Macedonia," verse 5, where the present is put for the future.

The same can be proven also from the next letter, chapter 2, verse 12, where he narrates that he only later came to Troas, and from there departed into Macedonia. Verse

20. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ Κυρίῳ. That is, they wish you all good things from Christ. Ἀκύλας καὶ Πρίσκιλλα. Who had followed Paul from Corinth to Ephesus, Acts XVIII, verse 19. Σὺν τῇ κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν Ἐκκλησίᾳ.

That is, with his whole family which was Christian. See Rom. XVI, verse 5. Wherever they went, they carried the Church with them.

In the Vulgate is added: "With whom I also lodge." But Estius says at this place that neither the Greek nor the Syriac codices have this, nor the ancient Concordances, and finally, neither the better and more ancient Latin Codices. He says that it is a gloss written between the lines, and that this is the argument that it was not in the text. Furthermore, it does not appear from the Acts of the Apostles that Paul lodged with Aquila and Priscilla at Ephesus, but only at Corinth. Which things militate against the authenticity of the Vulgate.

Latin:

Verf. 19. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ Ἐκκλησίαι τῆς Ἀσίας) Hinc probabilis conjectura sumitur Ephesi potius, ut habent Syriaci, & Arabici libri quam Philippis in Macedonia, ut habent Graeci, scriptam hanc epistolam. Favet huic fententid id quod supra habuimus 6. & 8. quod est 2. Cor. II. verf. 12. Volunt nonnulli Ephesi scriptam, Philippis vero ablegatam esse. Verisimilius autem Ephesi scriptam, & inde quoque missam e verf. 8. & praesenti, quo nomine Ecclesiarum Asiae salutat Corinthios. Philippi autem urbs est Macedoniae. Docet B. Gerhard. in Exeg. de Script. S. § 258. quod scripta fit haec epistola ante transitum per Macedoniam 1. Corinth. XVI. verf. 5. Tunc autem substiterit Apostolus Ephesi Actor. XI. verf. 19. 20. quod falutet Corinthios nomine Aquila & Priscilla, eos autem Ephesi reliquerit, cum descenderet in Macedoniam Actor. XIX. verf. 20. neque profectae sint subscriptionis ab Apostolo, sed a posterioribus additae. Quae neque semper congruunt: Ita cum in praesenti subscriptione addatur, missam esse epistolam per Stephanum & Fortunatum & Achaicum & Timotheum, de tribus prioribus quidem id admitti posset, sed non de Timotheo. Nam quod absens ille fuerit, cum hæc epistola scriberetur, non vero adfuerit ...Paulo, colligitur e cap. IV. vers. 17. Ad quem locum Theodoretus: Per hos (Stephanum, Fortunatum & Achaicum) scripserant Corinthii, & Apostolum interrogauerunt de iis, qui matrimonium contraxerant. Per eos hanc quoque misit epistolam. Non enim, ut quidam existimarunt, beatus Timotheus literas ad eos tulit: Sed ad eos quidem missa est; est autem verisimile, quod cam aliquo officio in alia civitate functus esset, ita ad ipsos accessit. Hoc enim significant ea, quæ deeo scripta sunt: Si autem venerit Timotheus, cure, ut sine timore sit apud vos.

Addimus Flacii suffragium & observationem: Quod bac epistola non ex Philippis, sicut Græca exemplaria habent, sed ex Epheso scripta sit, ex hoc ultimo capite liquido cernitur: Sed deceptus forte est aliquis hoc adscribens illo Hebraismo: Nunc Macedoniam transeo vers. 5. ubi Præsens pro futuro ponitur.

Idem probari potest & ex sequentis epistolæ cap. 2. vers. 12. ubi narrat se postea demum venisse Troada, & inde abiisse in Macedoniam. Vers.

20. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ Κυρίῳ. Id est, à Christo omnia bona vobis apprecantur. Ἀκύλας καὶ Πρίσκιλλα . Qui Paulum Corintho Ephesum erant sequuti Actor. XVIII. vers. 19. Σὺν τῇ κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν Ἐκκλησίᾳ.

Id est, cum tota familia sua quæ erat Christiana. Vide Rom. XVI. vers. 5. Quocunque illi ibant, secum ferebant Ecclesiam.

In vulgata additur: Apud quos & hospitor. Quod vero nec Græcos, nec Syriacos codices habere, nec veteres Concordantias, denique nec Latinos Codices meliores & antiquiores. Glossam vero scriptum habere inter lineas, idque argumentum esse, in textu non fuisse, ait hoc loco Estius. Quin neque ex actis Apostolorum apparere, paulum Ephesi apud Aquilam & Priscillam hospitatum fuisse, sed Corinthi tantum. Quæ contra authentiam Vulgatæ militant.

## 16:20
Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες) Namely, those who are in this region. Similar to Rom. XVI. Ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλους ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ) See Rom. XVI, verse 16. And he rightly commands the kiss of peace to those who were in danger of being torn away by schisms. Thus also Theophylact added: "in a holy kiss" because of the various dissensions of the Corinthians.

For he had generally exhorted them to be of one mind: But he says "with a holy kiss" because it lacks deceit, it is not feigned. Theodoret says he expelled the dissension and bound them together through the holy kiss. Verse 21. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου) The previous parts had been written down from the autograph of Paul by Tertius or Timotheus or someone else.

The rest Paul added with his own hand. See 2 Thess. III. 12. Verse 22. Εἴ τις οὐ φιλεῖ τὸν κύριον ἰησοῦν χριστὸν, ἤτω ἀνάθεμα μαρανάθα.

With his own hand he adds the sentence which he most wanted them to remember, just as Augustus sometimes did to the governors of the provinces. Ἀνάθεμα μαρανάθα is most grave, with the addition of a prayer that GOD may take vengeance on him as soon as possible. See what we said at Luke VI, verse 22. To the Syrians it is "Lord," whence the Syrian Maronites, because they call Christ and the Kings in ancient Latium "Murrani," about which at Aeneid XI: And Marnas is the God of the Gazarenes to Epiphanius, and the virgins to the Cretans are "magan," just as elsewhere "kyrian." Hence in Spain it used to be said, as histories narrate: "Let him be anathema Marana and excommunicated."

The Arab in this place: "He is entirely made excommunicate from the hope of the Lord." That is, from that hope which the Lord gave us. Similar to Gal. I. 8, 9. Whoever loves the Lord keeps his word, John

XIV, verse 23. But he who does not keep the word of GOD, does not hold his word reverently, nor adheres to the doctrine of the Lord, but diverges from it, or does not obey the precepts of the Lord, he does not love GOD. By this very fact, therefore, heretics who contumaciously oppose the doctrine of the Lord are excommunicated or pronounced anathema, as well as malignant sinners who voluntarily transgress the commandments of the Lord. Thomas explains: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ," that is, the faith of Christ, and these are heretics; the Greek interpreters wish them to be struck by this anathema, whom the Apostle chastised in this letter for grave sins, such as the drunkards, fornicators, those eating idol-sacrifices with offense to the brethren, those eating the sacred mysteries unworthily, as well as those not believing in the resurrection of the dead.

But some wrongly explain the foreign words here as "you are cursed," since they are read otherwise in the authentic text, and that word does not signify "cursed," but "cursing." (For it is the Participle Benoni) it signifies. More correctly, Beza constitutes Maranatha as a species of extreme anathema, and thus distributes anathema into [parts], and this latter he makes both simple and Maratha or Schamatha: about which Drusius, book

VI. of the Praeterita on this place, page 246. Anathema is a noun of the genus sometimes, which is called in Hebrew. Its three species are Niddui, Cherem, and Samata, which is thus called Maranatha. Both words sound: "The Lord comes," Maran "Lord," and Atha "comes."

It is a Syriac fem[inine] noun. It is used for the Tetragrammaton. Whence Samatha "The Lord comes." For "Lord." Others etymologize, "mittha" is death.

Hence they strike the word with the final excommunication, which they call Samatha in the book of precepts 28. 3. "Far be that from us," says Elias. With which agree those things which Erasmus has from Jerome in the Epistle to Marcellus: Maranatha is more Syrian than Hebrew, although from the border of both languages it sounds somewhat Hebrew and is interpreted "Our Lord comes."

Therefore Cornelius à Lapide does an injury to Erasmus and Beza, while he says they think it should be read not Maranatha, but Macharam Motha, so that it is the same as the Hebrew, that is, anathema and a thing devoted to death. Although we do not deny that B.

Luther and Bullinger cherished that opinion: Yet the explanation of Jerome does not agree, because the sense is: "If anyone does not love the Lord JESUS, let him be anathema," and with that completed, let it be inferred thereafter, "Our Lord comes." Which is superfluous, to want to contend with persistent hatreds against him who is already known to have come. Although one may easily yield to Jerome with Chrysostom and Theophylact: Maranatha, that is, "The Lord comes," which he brought in so that he might also confirm the mystery of the incarnation, and through that very thing assert the resurrection, or so that he might affect them with shame, just as if he were saying: "He endured all things no less for our sake, but you hold him in hatred: Inasmuch as you have partly acquired names for yourselves from men, and partly you will incite yourselves to wicked crimes."

Others take it concerning the future advent, i.e., "Let him be delivered to eternal destruction, on the day on which the Lord will come to judgment," as this exposition is reported in Augustine's Epistle CLXXIIX, "until the Lord returns." Thus Titelmanus explains:

Let him be anathema, that is, execrated Maranatha at the coming of the Lord, or when the Lord shall come to judgment. Anselm seems to refer it to both comings: If anyone, he says, does not love the LORD JESUS, as if His coming, which is already completed, were of no use to him. Thus, a second coming, which is still to be, becomes for him a condemnation. Although we readily admit that this execration, made from the coming of the Lord or the contestation of divine judgment, which is expressed in the past tense because of the certainty of the Lord's coming, is taken technically, we do not deny it, to designate the extreme species of anathema: But so that it is not held as a single word with Beza, when it is clear that there are two, whether it be rendered as מָרָן, the Lord of the Syrians, or מָרָא with the suffix Nun, our Lord, to which is added the Hebrew אָתָא, he comes, whence Beza's opinion is corrected in the Tremellius-Junius notes: Thus it is written separately in the Syriac codex, nor do I see why the faith of the scribes should be suspected in this part by some. For nothing occurs to me thus far more consistent, or apt, than that by these words the formula of extreme anathema is touched upon, because the sinner was condemned to the extreme condemnation of Christ the Judge of the world without hope of pardon. To this, indeed, the reason for the name could be accommodated in some way, by which the Talmudists call an anathema of this kind מָרָנָתָא, which seems to have coalesced from two because of its frequent use, namely from מָרָן & אָתָא, which is the same as, Lord come. Although I am not unaware that it is explained otherwise in three ways by the expositors of the Talmud. By this solemn formula, therefore, Maranatha, the Lord comes, the ancient Church taught that it had fulfilled all parts of its duty toward a man of this kind: Henceforth to abstain from him by common counsel, and to commit him to the judgment & coming of GOD, as one whose hope among men is lost.

Latin:

Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες) Nempe qui in hoc sunt tractu. Simile Rom. XVI. Ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλους ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ) Vide Rom. XVI. vers. 16. Et recte osculum pacis iis imperat qui in periculo erant ne per schismata abriperentur. Ita & Theophylactus adjecit in osculo sancto propter varias Corinthiorum dissensiones.

Commonfecerat enim eos plerumque, ut unum ferent omnes: Osculo autem sancto dicit, quod dolo careat, non fictum sit. Theodor. dissensionem, inquit, expulit, & per osculum sanctum eos colligavit. Vers. 21. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου) Priora ex autographo Pauli descripserat Tertius aut Timotheus aut alius quis.

Cætera adscripsit Paulus sua manu. Vide 2. Thessal. III. 12. Vers. 22. Εἴ τις οὐ φιλεῖ τὸν κύριον ἰησοῦν χριστὸν, ἤτω ἀνάθεμα μαρανάθα.

Sua manu adscribit sententiam, cujus maxime eos meminisse volebat, ut Augustus aliquando faciebat ad provinciarum præsides. Ἀνάθεμα μαρανάθα est gravissimum, addita precatione, ut DEUS quamprimum in eum vindicet. Vide quæ diximus ad Luc. VI. vers. 22. Syris est Dominus, unde Syri Maronitæ, quia Christum vocant & Murrani Reges in Veteri Latio, de quibus ad XI. Æneidos: Et Marnas Gazarorum Deus Epiphanio, & virgines Cretenfibus μάγαν, sicut alibi κυρίαν. Hinc in Hispania solebat dici ut historiæ narrant: Sit anathema Marana & excommunicatus.

Arabs hoc loco: Is omnie fit excommunicatus à spe Domini. Id est, ab ea spe quam Dominus nobis dedit. Simile Gal. I. 8. 9. Quisquis Dominum diligit, sermonem ejus servat Iob.

XIV. vers. 23. Qui vero sermonem DEI non servat, verbum ejus non reverenter habet, nec doctrinæ Domini adhærescit, sed ab ea divaricatur, aut præceptis Domini non paret, is DEUM non diligit. Hoc ipso ergo excommunicantur, vel anathemate pronuntiantur, hæretici, qui doctrinæ Domini contumaciter adversantur, tum peccatores maligni, qui mandata Domini voluntarie transgrediuntur. Thomas exponit: Si quis non amat Dominum Iesum Christum, id est fidem Christi, & isti sunt hæretici, Græci Interpp. eos hoc anathemate percelli volunt, quos Apostolus ob gravia peccata in hac epistola castigavit, utpote ebrios, fornicarios, idolothytis cum offendiculo fratrum vescentes, sacra mysteria indigne comedentes, ut & resurrectionem mortuorum non credentes.

Perperam autem nonnulli hic voces peregrinas sic exponunt tu fis maledictus, quum & legantur aliter in textu authentico, nec vox ista maledictum, sed maledicentem significat. (Est enim Participium Benoni) significat. Rectius Beza Maranatha speciem constituit extremi anathematis, adeoque anathema distribuit in & & hoc posterius tum simplex facit tum Maratha vel Schamatha: de quo Drusius libr.

VI. Præteritorum ad hunc locum pag. 246. Anathema nomen est generis aliquando, quod Ebraice dicitur. Ejus tres species Niddui, Cherem & Samata, quæ sic dicitur Maranatha. Utraque vox sonat: Dominus venit, Maran Dominus, & Atha venit.

Syriacum est fem nomen. Id pro Tetragrammato usurpatur. Unde Samatha Dominus venit. Nam Dominus. Alii ἐτυμολογοῦσι, jam ibi mittha mors.

Hinc verbum feriunt cum ultima excommunicatione, quam Samatha vocant in libro præceptorum 28. 3. Absit ea à nobis, inquit Elias. Quibus congruunt, quæ habet Erasmus ex Hieronymo in Epist. ad Marcellum: Maranatha magis Syrum est, quam Hebræum, tametsi ex confinio utrarumque linguarum aliquid & Hebræum sonat & interpretatur Dominus noster venit.

Injuriam ergo Erasmo & Bezæ facit Cornelius à Lapide, dum ait eos putare, legendum esse non Maranatha, sed Macharam Motha, ut fit idem, quod Hebræum id est anathema sit & res addicta morti. Quanquam non diffiteamur B.

Lutherum & Bullingerum istam sententiam fovisse: Explicatio tamen Hieronymi non convenit, quod sensus fit: Si quis non amat Dominum IESUM, anathema fit, & illo completo deinceps inferatur, Dominus noster venit. Quod superfluum fit odiis pertinacibus adversus eum velle contendere, quem venisse jam constet. Etsi facile Hieronymo annuat cum Chrysostomo Theophylactum: Maranatha, hoc est Dominus venit, quod eo intulit, ut & incarnationis mysterium confirmaret, affereretque per idipsum & resurrectionem, vel ut illos pudore afficiat, perinde ac si dicat: Cuncta non minus nostri causa toleravit, vos vero illum odio habetis: Quippe qui partim nomina vobis ab hominibus consciveritis, partim pravis incibitis facinoribus.

Alii de futuro adventu accipiunt, q. d. Æterno tradatur exitio, in die, quo Dominus veniet ad judicium, ut in epist. CLXXIIX. Augustin. refertur hæc expositio, donec Dominus redeat. Sic exponit Titelmanus:

Sit anathema, id est execratus Maranatha in adventum Domini, vel cum veniet Dominus ad judicium. Anselmus ad utrumque adventum referre videtur: Si quis, inquit, non diligit DOMINUM JESUM, sicut ei non utilis est adventus ejus, qui jam completus est. Sic ad damnationem fit ei secundus, qui adhuc futurus est. Quanquam vero facile admittamus, execrationem illam ab adventu Domini, seu contestatione judicii divini factam, quæ in Præterito effertur propter certitudinem adventus Domini, τεχνικῶς accipi, non abnuimus, ad designandam scilicet extremam anathematis speciem: Sed ita ut non unica tantum vox cum Beza habeatur, quam duas esse apertum sit, sive מָרָן Syrorum Dominus, sive מָרָא cum Suffixo Nun Dominus noster, reddatur, cui additur Hebræum אָתָא venit, unde castigatur in eo Beza sententia in notis Tremellio-Julianis: Ita divisim in codice Syro scribitur, neque video, cur fides librariorum quibusdam hac in parte suspecta sit. Nihil enim mihi occurrit hactenus magis consentaneum, aut aptam, quam ut his verbis extremi anathematis formula attingatur, quia extrema Christi mundi Judicis condemnationi absque spe veniæ addicebatur peccator. Huc vero accommodari utcunque posset ratio nominis, quo hujusmodi anathema vocant Thalmudistæ מָרָנָתָא quod ex duobus propter frequentem ejus usum videtur coaluisse, nempe ex מָרָן & אָתָא, quod idem est, quod Domine veni. Quanquam non ignoro, ab expositoribus Thalmud tribus modis aliter exponi. Hac igitur solemni formula Maranatha Dominus venit, prisca Ecclesia docuit se omnibus officii sui partibus erga virum ejusmodi perfunctam esse: Deinceps ab eo de communi consilio abstinere, eumque DEI judicio & adventui, ut deplorata inter homines spei, permittere.

## 16:23
Ver. 23. Ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ κυρίῳ ἰησοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν) Rom. XVI. ver. 24. Ver. 24. Ἡ ἀγάπη μου μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ) That is: I, for Christ's sake, love you all sincerely. And that phrase, μεθ' ὑμῶν, has force. Friendships are said to be dissolved by intervals of places. He denies that this happens in his case: That he is present to them in spirit, and cares for their affairs. Which Indicative sense we prefer to the Optative, which is held by the Ephesian. I wish my charity, with which I love you, to be & to remain with you all. Which indeed will happen, if you remain in the faith & love of Christ. The Ephesian also adds the passive ἔκθεον: My charity, that is, which is loved by you in turn by you in Christ, this is sincere & Christian love.

For concerning the fact that he was less loved by the Corinthians, he himself had explained in 2 Epist. XII. 15. Nay, rather, the Ephesian suspects that the Apostle wrote the charity of GOD, because in Greek μῦ & ὀξ do not differ much, and at the end of the second epistle it is written thus: The original text is to be burdened with charges and the wish for the grace of Jesus Christ had already preceded. But Theodoret agrees with Grotius: He prayed for the grace of the Lord JESUS for them, as he was accustomed: But he added his own love not without reason: But teaching that, incited by love toward them, he used somewhat harsher words, imitating paternal benevolence and desiring their salvation; as also with Chrysostom, whom he loves to follow. Thus Theophylact, with whose exposition and wish we conclude this epistle: I myself am present to you all, and I am here, even if absent. For, if I seem to be distant from you in place, I am not far in spirit. Thus he makes it clear that what he had written to them, even if they showed a certain bitterness, did not proceed from hatred or anger, but from the charity and care which he had for them: And lest he subjected it to JESU, that is, nothing of this charity of mine has in itself, and we prefer nothing hateful. For thus we shall be deemed worthy of the most pleasant habitations of GOD in Christ JESU, who has pursued us with such great love. To whom be glory for ever and ever!

A M E N.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ κυρίῳ ἰησοῦ μεθ' ὑμῶν) Rom. XVI. vers. 24. Vers. 24. Ἡ ἀγάπη μου μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ) Id est: Ego propter Christum vos omnes fincere diligo. Et vim habet illa loquutio, μεθ' ὑμῶν. Dicuntur amicitiæ dissolvi intervallis locorum. Hoc negat apud se fieri: Se animo ipsis esse præsentem, res eorum curare. Quem sensum Indicativum præferimus Optativo, qui habetur apud Ephesium. Opto meam charitatem, qua vos diligo, esse & permanere cum omnibus vobis. Quod quidem fiet, si vos in fide & dilectione Christi permanseritis. Addit Ephes & passivum ἔκθεον: Charitas mea, id est, quæ a vobis vicissim a vobis diligitur in Christo, hoc est sincera & Christiana dilectione.

Nam de eo, quod minus a Corinthiis diligeretur, ipse cum exposuerat 2. epist. XII. 15. Quin imo suspicatur Ephes, Apostolum scripsisse charitas DEI, quod in Græco μῦ & ὀξ non multum differant, & in fine secundæ epistolæ ita scriptum legatur: Chacionibus gravandus textus originalis & præcesferat jam votum gratiæ Jesu Christi. Grotio autem consentit Theodoretus: Domini quidem JESU gratiam eis, ut consuevit, precatus est: Suam autem dilectionem non abs re adjecit: Sed docens quod ab amore in ipsos incitatus, verbis paulo acerbioribus usus est, patriæ benevolentiæ imitans & eorum salutem desiderans; ut & cum Chrysostomo, quem sequi amat. Sic Theophylacus cujus expositione & voto hanc epistolam concludimus: Omnibus vobis præsto sum ipse, & adsum, vel absens. Neque enim, si loco videor a vobis distare, animo procul sum. His itaque patefacit, qua ad eos scripsisset, & si acrimoniam quandam præferrent, nequaquam ab odio vel ira prodire, sed a charitate & cura quam de bis gesserit: Et ne JESU subjecit, hoc est, nihil mea hac charitas in se habet, & odiosum nil preferamus. Sic enim juncundissimie DEI dignabimur habitaculis in Christo JESU, qui nos tanto est prosequutus amore. Cui gloria in secula seculorum!

A M E N.

# 2 Corinthians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
GROTIAN PROEM.

Paul did not write this epistle to the Corinthians immediately after the former, nor long after. For there was only so much interval as was needed for Timothy, sent by Paul, to be able to go to Corinth, explain Paul's mandates, and labor that they might be obeyed, and to return to Paul. His labor, however, had succeeded well among most at Corinth, whence this epistle is somewhat milder than the prior one. Yet there remained some who envied Paul, to whose detractions this epistle responds in various places.

Observations on the Grotian Proem, with other Prolegomena.

§. I. Grotius advises on three things: 1. On the time of writing: 2. On the occasion and cause: 3. On the scope and purpose. But other things seem to be added. For concerning the circumstance of time, it is not irrelevant to inquire also about the circumstance of place, so that both may be established, when and whence this epistle was written. Concerning the occasion and cause, it must be explained not only with what mind the prior epistle was received by the faithful, but also how the infidels, both the Pseudo-Apostles and other malevolent detractors, behaved themselves. Concerning the scope, not only the state of the epistle, but also its argument and partition are deservedly set forth.

§. II. As to the time of writing, the interval between the first and second epistle does not seem to be so restricted. For there would already be need of an excuse for the delayed arrival, or what cause the detractors would have had to easily accuse the Apostle of fickleness, if this had been written immediately upon the return of Timothy, the bearer of the prior epistle. Nor is it indeed consistent that Timothy was sent with the first epistle, as we warned around chapter XVI. 19 of the preceding epistle. B. Gerhard in Exeg. de Script. S. §. 259 judges this epistle to have been written in the 18th or 19th year of Paul's conversion.

§. III. The place from whence this epistle was sent is designated at its end in this manner: πρὸς κορινθίους δευτέρα ἐγράφη ἀπὸ φιλίππων ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας (The second to the Corinthians was written from Philippi in Macedonia). Although these subscriptions are of little authority, it is nevertheless likely that the present epistle was written at Philippi, when, having left Ephesus, he had betaken himself thither, Acts. XX. 1. In the summary of the Epistle prefixed to Latin Codices, it is said to have been sent from Troas, but because it is commemorated that Paul had already departed from there in chapter II. 12, 13, Estius rightly refutes this regarding the argument of the epistle, although he doubts whether it was written in Macedonia or in the city of Nicopolis, situated in Epirus, near Greece, after Paul's return from Macedonia, as Baronius thinks: Nor did Cornelius a Lapide dare to contradict Baronius: He admits, however, that the Apostle could easily have gone, while traveling through Asia, and returned to Philippi, and stayed there for a while, while he wrote this epistle: Since Luke does not narrate all the comings and goings of the Apostle in Acts XX. The Syriac and the Latin Complutensian agree with the Greek Codices at the end of the Epistle.

§. IV. As to the occasion of this epistle, it was seized upon primarily from the prior epistle by the Adversaries of the Apostle, such as were especially the false teachers, and others, who interpreted all the words and deeds of the Apostle for the worse. Hence they traduced Paul under the name of fickleness, because he had not kept his promise, nor arrived at Corinth; and because of the excessive rigor with which he had delivered the incestuous man to Satan in chapter V, and because of the overturning and trampling of the Law and the undermining of piety through the doctrine of the Gospel, which they slandered as making men carnal and filthy. For when the Apostle delayed his arrival at Corinth somewhat longer, and the false teachers had more easily insinuated themselves into the Church itself, they did not fear to traduce both the person and the doctrine of the Apostle himself, and sought from every side an occasion to cavil at it.

Since, therefore, the Apostle could not hasten immediately, he wished by these letters to meet the machinations of the false teachers, who were striving to disseminate their dogmas through contempt and the accusation of the Apostle.

Although indeed most in the Corinthian Church held the Apostle in esteem and reverently received the prior epistle, and had complied in excommunicating the incestuous man and amending those things which the Apostle had reproved: yet they still needed spurs to sincerely conserve the doctrine of the faith, and also to kindly exhibit grace to needy brothers.

And therefore the Corinthians are warned about the doctrine of faith and the holiness of life to be sought, and the society and communion of infidels to be fled, and are provoked by the example of the faithful in Macedonia and other arguments to a further large collection of money for the poor.

§. V. The state of the epistle, therefore, is Apologetic against the accusations (ἐγκλήματα) of the false teachers. For most things that occur in it can be recalled to the same, even the exhortations to holiness, of which beneficence toward the needy is a part. For their slanders were stopped, that the doctrine of the Apostle makes men carnal and hinders the pursuit of piety.

§. VI. The sum and argument of the epistle consists in this: that he excuses the delay of his arrival, shows favor to the penitent fornicator, testifies to his sincerity, teaches that the doctrine of the Gospel indeed brings greater clarity than the Law, yet does not overturn the Law, or the holiness commanded in the Law, but teaches that it makes for raising up the same, and excites beneficence, defends his gift, tears off the mask from the Pseudo-Apostles, asserts the authority of his apostleship from the perils and labors endured for Christ, and from revelations and miracles, and terrifies them with the threat of his coming.

§. VII. Interpreters of this epistle, besides those who have written on all the Pauline epistles, or on both to the Corinthians specifically, are from among the Pontificians Johannes Hayton the Englishman, Johannes Hoffmeierus the Swabian; from among the Reformed Andreas Hyperius and Wolfgang Musculus; from among our own B. Weinrichius and B. Hilfemannus.

§. VIII. It can be distributed, with the inscription premised, into three parts: (I.) A personal apology, or against the accusations of personal vices, especially of fickleness, chapter I., and of excessive rigor, chapter II. 16. (II.) A doctrinal apology against the accusations concerning the trafficking of doctrine and the evacuation of the Law through the Gospel, where (1.) he explains the clarity of the Gospel, chapter III. (2.) he treats of the confession of the same, to which the cross brings, and explains the utility of the cross in chapter IV and chapter V to verse 1, 2, 3. (3.) He further declares the evangelical grace, which we have in the merit of Christ, and the end of His righteousness, namely that we should live not for ourselves, but for Christ, in the remainder of chapter V, (4.) he warns them in chapter VI not to receive the grace of GOD in vain, but to show themselves in all things as ministers of GOD, even in persecutions, and to have no commerce with injustice. Furthermore (5.) he praises the Corinthians, because through Titus he had received much comfort in afflictions, having known their godly sorrow and holy obedience, in chapter VII. Finally (6.) he excites the same to show grace liberally to the brethren in chapters VIII and IX. In this part, therefore, although it is apologetic, both the principal doctrines are contained, concerning the distinction between the law and the Gospel, concerning confession, concerning the cross, concerning the state after this life, concerning the last things, concerning the satisfaction of Christ, and our justification, concerning renewal, etc., and exhortations to the study of liberality, and those indeed in the three first chapters III, IV, and V, but these in the following four chapters, namely VI, VII, VIII, and IX. (III.) The Ministerial Apology, in which he deals with the accusations concerning the abuse of Apostolic power in chapter X, concerning the indignity of the Apostle, where he proclaims both his labors and sufferings or cares in chapter XI, and his sacred revelations, and his miracles, and his solicitude for the Corinthians in chapter XII, for whose sake he makes them more certain of his arrival, so that he may not have need to use severity when he arrives, with a short exhortation subjoined for the perfecting and mutual consent of minds, with a final prayer in chapter XIII.

Latin:

PROOEMIUM GROTIANUM.

Neque statim post priorem, neque multò post scripsit hanc ad Corinthios Paulus epistolam. Tantum enim intervalli fuit, quo Timotheus à Paulo missus, ire Corinthum potuit, mandata Pauli explicare, &, ut eis pareretur laborare, & ad Paulum redire. Labor autem ejus Corinthi apud plerosque bene successerat, unde & lenior aliquanto haec est epistola, quàm prior. Manebant tamen Paulo quidam invidentes, quorum obrectationibus passim haec epistola respondet.

Observationes ad Grotii Prooemium, cum Prolegomenis aliis.

§. I. De tribus monet Grotius, 1. De scriptionis tempore: 2. De occasione & causa: 3. De scopo & instituto. Addenda autem videntur alia. Nam circa temporis circumstantiam etiam non abs re quaeritur de circumstantia loci, ut utrumque constet, quando, & unde exarata sit haec epistola. Circa occasionem & causam non modo quo animo suscepta prior epistola fuerit a fidelibus, sed etiam quales sese infideles cùm Pseudo-Apostoli, tùm alii malevoli & obtrectatores gesserint, explicandum. Circa scopum non tantum status epistolae, sed argumentum etiam, & partitio ejus merito expeditur.

§. II. Quod ad tempus scriptionis, non ita coarctandum videtur intervallum prima, & secunda epistolae. Quidem enim opus jam foret excusatione dilati adventus, aut quam causam obtrectatores etiam habuissent, tam facilè levitatis arguendi Apostolum, si illico poët reducem Timotheum prioris epistolae latorem haec exarata. Neque verò consentaneum est, Timotheum missum fuisse cum prima epistola, ut circa cap. XVI. 19. praecedentis epistolae monuimus. B. Gerhard. in Exeg. de Script. S. §. 259. scriptam hanc epistolam censet Anno conversionis Pauli 18. vel 19.

§. III. Locus, unde missa haec epistola est, designatur sub calcem ejus hoc modo πρὸς κορινθίους δευτέρα ἐγράφη ἀπὸ φιλίππων ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας. Quanquam vero hae subscriptionis exiguae sint autoritatis, verisimile tamen est, epistolam praesentem Philippis scriptam, cum, Epheso relicta, ed se contulisset, Act. XX. 1. In summario quidem Epistolae Codicibus Latinis prefixo dicitur è Troade missa, sed quia inde jam Paulum discessisse cap. II. 12. 13. commemoratur, rectè id reprobat Estius circa argumentum epistolae, etsi ambigat, utrum in Macedonia num vero in urbe Nicopoli, in Epiro sita, Graeciae vicina, post reditum Pauli è Macedonia, ut Baronius existimat, scripta sit: Neque Cornelius a Lapide ausus est contradicere Baronio: Fatetur tamen, potuisse facile Apostolum per Asiam cursitantem ire, & redire Philippos, ibique haerere tantisper, dum scriberet hanc epistolam: Siquidem non omnes Apostoli cursus & recursus narret Lucas Act. XX. Graecis Codicibus consonant Syri, & Latina Complut. in fine Epistolae.

§. IV. Quod ad occasionem hujus epistolae, arrepta ea potissimum è priori epistola ab Adversariis Apostoli, quales maxime falsi doctores erant, & aliis, omnia dicta & facta Apostoli in deterius interpretantibus. Inde levitatis nomine Paulum traducebant, quod promissum non fer-vaverit, neque ad Corinthios pervenerit; nimis rigor is quod incestuosum cap. V. Satanae tradiderit, Legis everse, & conculcatae & pietatis labefactate per doctrinam Evangelii, quam homines carnales & fecuos reddere calumniabantur. Quum enim differret aliquanto diutius suum ad Corinthios adventum Apostolus, falsique doctores eò facilius sese insinuassent ipsi Ecclesiae, non veriti etiam sunt Apostoli ipsius tùm personam, tùm doctrinam traducere, & undique occasione illam cavillandi conquirere.

Quum ergò statim accurrere non posset Apostolus, hisce literis falsorum doctorum molitionibus, qui per contemptum, & accusationem Apostoli sua disseminare dogmata fatagebant, occurrere voluit.

Quanquam vero plerique in Corinthiaca Ecclesia & in pretio haberent Apostolum, & reverenter susciperent priorem epistolam, cui in abdicando incestuoso, & emendandis iis, quae reprehenderat Apostolus morem gesserat: Calcaribus tamen adhuc indigebant in fidei doctrina sincerè conservanda, nec non in gratia fratribus egenis benigne exhibenda.

Ideoque Corinthii graviter de doctrina fidei & sanctitate vitae quaerenda, fugiendaeque infidelium societate & communione monentur, & exemplo fidelium in Macedonia, aliisque argumentis ulterius ad largam pecuniae collationem in pauperes provocantur.

§. V. Status ergo epistolae est Apologeticus adversus falsorum doctorum ἐγκλήματα. Nam ad eundem revocari pleraque possunt, quae in ea occurrunt, etiam exhortationes ad sanctitatem, cujus pars ipsa beneficentia in egenos est. Nam illis ora obstruebantur calumniae, quod doctrina Apostoli carnales reddat, & studio pietatis officiat.

§. VI. Summa & argumentum epistolae in eo consistit, quod excuset dilationem adventus, gratiam fornicario poenitenti faciat, sinceritatem suam testetur, Evangelii doctrinam claritatem quidem majorem afferre quam legis, non tamen legem, aut sanctitatem in lege praeceptam evertere, sed ad eandem erigendam facere doceat, ac beneficentiam excitet, munus suum defendat, Pseudo-Apostolis larvam detrahat, Apostolatus sui autoritatem e periculis & laboribus pro Christo exantlatis, ac revelationibus & miraculis asserat, ac comminatione adventus sui eosdem terreat.

§. VII. Interpretes hujus epistolae, praeter illos, qui in omnes Paulinas epistolas, aut in utramque ad Corinthios specialiter scripsere sunt è Pontificiis Johannes Hayton Anglus, Johannes Hoffmeierus Suevus, è Reformatis Andreas Hyperius & Wolfgang Musculus, è nostris B. Weinrichius & B. Hilfemannus.

§. VIII. Distribui potest, praemissa inscriptio-ne, in tres partes (I.) Apologia personalis est, vel adversus ἐγκλήματα vitiorum personalium, imprimis levitatis, cap. I. nimique rigoris, cap. II. 16. (II.) Apologia doctrinalis adversus ἐγκλήματα de doctrina cauponatione, ac legis per Evangelium evacuatione, ubi (1.) Evangelii claritatem exponit cap. III. (2.) de confessione ejusdem agit, ad quam affert crucem, & crucis utilitatem explicat cap. IV. & cap. V. ad v. 1. 2. 3. (3.) Evangelicam gratiam, quam habemus in Christi merito, ac ju- stitia ejus finem, ut nempe non nobis, sed Christo vivamus, c. V. reliquo declarat ulterius, (4.) ne gratiam DEI frustra accipiant, sed in omnibus, ut ministros DEI, etiam in persequutionibus se exhibeant, nullumque cum injustitia commer- cium habeant, monet cap. VI. Porrò (5.) lau- dat Corinthios, quod per Titum multum solatii in afflictionibus, cognita ipsorum divina tristitia, sancta obedientia acceperit cap. VII. Denique (6.) excitat eosdem ad gratiam fratribus liberali- ter exhibendam cap. IIX. IX. In hac ergò parte, etsi apologetica sit, tùm doctrinæ præcipuæ conti- nentur, de discrimine legis & Evangelii, de confes- sione, de cruce, de statu post hanc vitam, de novissi- mis, de satisfactione Christi, ac justificatione nostri, de renovatione &c. tùm adhortationes ad studium liberalitatis, & illæ quidem tribus imprimis capiti- bus III. IV. & V. hæ verò sequentibus quatuor capitibus, nimirum VI. VII. VIII. & IX. (III.) Apologia Ministerialis, qua ἐγκλήματα de abusu potestatis Apostolicæ cap. X. de indignitate Apostoli, ubi prædicat tùm labores & passiones vel curas suas cap. XI. tùm revelationes sibi sacras, & miracula sua, tùm solictudinem pro Corinthiis cap. XII. cu- jus gratia de adventu suo certiores ipsos reddit, ut ne adveniens severitate uti opus habeat, sub- junctâ brevi ad καταρτισμόν & consensum ani- morum mutuum cohortatiuncula, cum voto finali cap. XIII.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. OF THE EPISTLE. PERSONAL APOLOGY. CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The inscription and votive prayer having been premised, he celebrates God for the consolation in calamities, which he testifies he experienced in Asia with danger, to sharpen confidence in God and living hope, provoking them concerning his sincerity to his own conscience and the experience of the Corinthians, and purging himself from the crime of levity and inconstancy because of the delay of his arrival: And asserting the truth of his word concerning Christ Jesus, which is sealed by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the faithful, and explaining the cause why he did not arrive, namely that he might consult their infirmity.

There are IV parts. I. The inscription of the epistle with the prayer of greeting, verses 1 and 2. II. The eucharistic exordium or preparation for declining the crime of levity, to verse 7. III. The narrative of the affliction in Asia, as the cause of the delayed arrival, to verse 11. IV. The refutation of the crime of levity, that he had not arrived until now contrary to the faith given, by which he also asserts his sincerity in conversation and word to verse 22, and invokes God as a witness, that he wished to spare them, verses 23, 24.

PART I. The inscription of the epistle.

V. 1. Paul an Apostle of Jesus Christ) In the former epistle 'called Apostle' is added. But the sense is the same, namely that he is an ambassador of Christ, and of no less authority than the other Apostles were.

Timothy had been sent to the Corinthians, although not as a letter-carrier, 1 Cor. IV. 17, c. XVI. 10, 11, who having returned had reported concerning their state and the machinations of the Pseudo-Apostles. Wherefore he joins him to himself in the frontispiece of the epistle, for the sake of honor, unanimity, and testimony, whom he deems worthy of the name of brother, not so much because of communion in faith, as because of cooperation in the ministry, as if he were not unworthy of that name of Apostle. Whom he also did not hesitate to join to himself in other epistles, namely to the Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, as also to Philemon, just as in the former he had joined Sosthenes to himself. Elsewhere he calls him son, 'genuine in faith', 1 Tim. I. 2, and 'beloved', 2 Tim. I. 2, and 'faithful in the Lord' 1 Cor. IV. 17, because he had begotten him in Christ through the Gospel.

With all the saints, who are in all Achaia) Paul wished copies of this epistle to be sent to other Churches in Achaia, as was the custom to be done then.

Corinth was the metropolis of Achaia. But he calls it the Church of GOD, which was at Corinth, and the saints, who were in all Achaia; interchanging these, namely the congregation of GOD, and the saints, because the Church is properly the communion of saints, even if hypocrites are mixed in, such as there were very many in the Corinthian Church, and the other Churches of all Achaia, which we have asserted against the Cathari, Donatists, and Anabaptists in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, articles VII and VIII.

Latin:

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ. APOLOGIA PERSONALIS. CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissâ inscriptione, & votivâ precatione, Deum celebrat ob consolationem in cala- mitatibus, quas se in Asia cum discrimi- ne expertum esse, ad acuendam fiduciam in Deum & spem vivam, testatur, de sin- ceritate ad propriam conscientiam & Co- rinthiorum experientiam provocans, & sese ob dilationem adventus sui à levita- tis & inconstantiæ crimine purgans: Ac verbi sui de Christo Jesu veritatem, quæ per Spiritum Sanctum in cordibus fide- lium obsignetur, adstruens, causamque cur non advenerit, exponens, ut nempe ipsorum infirmitati consuleret.

PArtes sunt IV. I. Epistolæ inscriptio cum salu- tationis voto, v. 1. & 2. II. Exordium ἐυχα- ρισικὸν seu preparatio ad declinandum levitatis crimen, ad v. 7. III. Narratio afflictionis in Asia, ceu causa dilati adventus, ad v. 11. IV. Profliga- tio criminis levitatis, quod præter fidem datam hactenus non advenerit, qua & sinceritatem suam in conversatione & verbo asserit ad v. 22. & Deum teste invocat, quod ipsis parcere voluerit, v. 23.24.

PARS I. Epistolæ inscriptio.

V. 1. Παῦλος Ἀπόστολος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ) In prio- ri epistola additur κλητὸς Ἀπόστολος. Sensus au- tem idem est, quod nempe legatus Christi sit, ne- que minoris autoritatis, quàm erant cæteri Apo- stoli.

Missus erat ad Corinthios Timotheus, etsi non ceu γραμματοφόρος, 1. Cor. IV. 17. c. XVI. 10. 11. qui reversus de ipsorum statu, & Pseudo-Apostolorum moliminibus retulerat. Quapropter ipsum sibi conjungit in frontispicio epistolæ, honoris ὁμοψηφίας & testimonii causâ, quem dignatur fratris nomine, non tam ob communionem in fide, quàm ob συνέργειαν in ministerio, veluti eo Apostoli nomine non indignum. Quem etiam in aliis epistolis sibi adjungere non dubitavit, utpote ad Philippenses, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses, ut & ad Philemonem, quemadmodum in priori sibi Sosthenem junxerat. Alias ipsum filium, γνήσιον ἐν πίστει, 1. Tim. I. 2. & ἀγαπητὸν, 2. Tim. I. 2. καὶ πιστὸν ἐν Κυρίῳ 1. Cor. IV. 17. vocat, quia per Evangelium ipsum in Christo genuerat.

Σὺν τοῖς ἁγίοις πᾶσι, τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἀχαΐᾳ) Voluit Paulus exempla hujus epistolæ mitti ad alias in Achaia Ecclesias, ut tùm fieri solebat.

Erat Achaia metropolis Corinthus. Appellat autem Ecclesiam DEI, quæ Corinthi erat, & sanctos, qui in tota Achaia; commutans hæc, congregationem scilicet DEI, & sanctos, quia Ecclesia est proprie communio sanctorum, etsi admixti sint hypocritæ, quales plurimi erant in Ecclesia Corinthiaca, cæterisque universæ Achaiæ Ecclesiis, quæ contra Catharos, Donatistas & Anabaptistas in Exeg. A. C. artic. VII. & VIII. asseruimus.

## 1:2
V. 2. Grace to you and peace) See Rom. I. 7. 1. Cor. I. 3. This was a solemn vow for Paul in all the epistles given to entire Churches, and also the one which is inscribed to Philemon, which embraces both the gratuitous favor of GOD, with which He pursues the faithful, as a Father his children, not only by remitting their sins, but also by exhibiting benefits of every kind: and peace, both internal with GOD, which is the tranquility of conscience, and external with men, as a chief gift of grace and a consequence of the gratuitous remission of sins, Rom. V. 1. chap. VIII. 6. chap. XIV. 17. Phil. IV. 7. 2. Tim. II. 22. The Apostle prays for both from GOD our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ: the name of the Father being taken essentially, or regarding the paternity κατ' ἔξω with respect to regeneration, which is common to the most holy Trinity, Jesus Christ being named peculiarly, because in Him consists the οἰκονομία of grace, peace, and salvation, who is called our Lord by a singular title, inasmuch as by reason of redemption, because He acquired us with His blood, Acts XX. 28. so that thus the cause of salvation, both the original, the triune God, and the meritorious, Christ Jesus, may be expressed, outside of whom neither grace nor peace can be obtained by us. Therefore, it is not as the Socinians teach, that either the Son of GOD as begotten by the Father κατ' ἔσω within the embrace of the Deity, or the Holy Spirit is excluded when the Father is named; since these three are one, 1. Joh. V. 7. or that Jesus Christ the Lord is constituted of an inferior order, when there is but one Lord, but one divine power, which belongs to Christ as GOD οὐσιωδῶς, and as true man by virtue of union and hypostatic communication. Nor indeed could the Apostle pray for grace and peace from Christ the Lord, as from GOD the Father, if He were a Lord of an inferior order, since divine grace is an essential attribute of GOD, peace of conscience is a divine gift and effect, and religious invocation is a divine axiom, and all these things are proper to the supreme Lord. But concerning these matters, see expressly in System. Theol. Tom. III. and the Anti-Crellius and other Anti-Socinian works. But as to what is objected that it should be read from GOD our Father, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, from the Syriac interpretation, which repeats the particle Min and the collation of 2. Tim. I. 2. χάρις,

Mercy, peace from God the Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ, & 2. Joh. v. 3. is refuted by from God the Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ the Son of the Father. Add Rom. XVI. 24. 1. Cor. XVI. 29. Philipp. IV. 23. 2. Thess. III. 18. Gal. VI. 18. Philem. v. 25. 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Aretius refers grace to God the Father, but peace to the Lord Jesus Christ. Zanchius wishes for grace to be understood as only spiritual goods, and by peace only temporal ones: Joh. Crocius in Ephes. I. 2. rejects both. He says, not individual things to individuals, that is, grace to the Father, and peace to Christ, but he refers both to both: The Father is the fountain: Christ is the Mediator of grace and peace. By grace, however, he understands the fountain of all salutary gifts, namely the gratuitous favor and benevolence of GOD. By the name of peace he does not wish only temporal things to be comprehended, but also eternal ones, and for that reason he says the Apostle uses it, both because the Jews were accustomed to signify every happiness by it, and because there is nothing more excellent than it in human affairs and it is almost the compendium of all blessings itself, just as war is a certain deluge of curses. Although this is true, the name of peace is nevertheless accepted here specifically: Which Aretius acknowledges in 1. Cor. I. 2. Peace is the tranquility of conscience born from the grace of GOD. For after we feel that God is pacified toward us, we begin to be pacified, so that the conscience may not be in turmoil from the fear of divine judgment; but may invoke God as a Father reconciled in Christ. Therefore peace is the effect of grace. And as in grace there are also the gifts of the Holy Spirit: So with that internal peace is had external peace, that is, the zeal for living peaceably. It was customary for the Greeks to prefix their χαίρειν, εὐπράττειν, & ὑγιαίνειν. By which they wished for joy, health, and success in the actions of life. The Latins said greetings, but they understood no other salutary things than those which would both endure in this life and at the same time end with it; we have more ample goods.

PART II. An eucharistic exordium.

Latin:

V. 2. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη) Vide Rom. I. 7. 1. Cor. I. 3. Erat solenne hoc votum Paulo in omnibus epistolis, ad integras Ecclesias datis, nec non ea, quæ Philemoni est inscripta, quod complectitur tùm gratuitum DEI favorem, quo fideles, ceu Pater filios, prosequitur, non modo remittendo ipsis peccata, sed etiam omnis generis beneficia exhibendo: tùm pacem & internam cum DEO, quæ tranquillitas est conscientiæ, & externam cum hominibus, ceu donum præcipuum gratiæ & consequens gratuitæ remissionis peccatorum, Rom. V. 1. cap. VIII. 6. cap. XIV. 17. Phil. IV. 7. 2. Tim. II. 22. Precatur autem Apostolus utrumque à DEO Patre nostro, & Domino Jesu Christo: Patris nomine essentialiter accepto, vel quoad paternitatem κατ' ἔξω respectu regenerationis, quæ communis est sacrosanctæ Trinitati, Jesu Christo peculiariter nominato, quia in eo consistit οἰκονομία gratiæ, pacis, & salutis, qui Dominus noster dicitur titulo singulari, utpote ratione redemptionis, quia acquisivit nos sanguine suo, Act. XX. 28. ut ita causa salutis tùm originaria Deus triunus, tùm meritoria, Christus Jesus exprimatur, extra quem nec gratia, nec pax obtingere nobis potest. Non ergò est, quod docent Sociniani, vel Filium DEI qua genitum à Patre κατ' ἔσω intra amplexum Deitatis, vel Spiritum Sanctum excludi Patre nominato; cum hi tres unum sint, 1. Joh. V. 7. vel Jesum Christum Dominum inferioris ordinis constitui, quum non sit nisi unus Dominus, non nisi unica divina potestas, quæ Christo ut DEO οὐσιωδῶς competit, ut homini vero vi unionis & communicationis hypostaticæ. Neque verò gratiam & pacem à Christo Domino precari posset Apostolus, ut à DEO Patre, si Dominus inferioris ordinis esset, cum gratia divina attributum DEI essentiale, pax conscientiæ donum & effectum divinum, & invocatio religiosa axioma divinum sit, atque hæc omnia Domino summo propria sint. Sed de his in System. Theol. Tom. III. & Anti-Crellio aliisque Anti-Socinianis operibus ex professo. Quod verò obvertitur legendum esse à DEO Patre nostro, & Domini Jesu Christi, è Syra interpretatione, quæ repetit particulam Min & collatione 2. Tim. I. 2. χάρις,

ἔλεος, εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ χρισῦ Ἰησῦ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν, & 2. Joh. v. 3. παρὰ Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ παρὰ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ τῦ υἱᾶ τῦ Πατρὸς refelli- tur. Adde Rom. XVI. 24. 1. Cor. XVI. 29. Philipp. IV. 23. 2. Thess. III. 18. Gal. VI. 18. Philem. v. 25. 2. Cor. XIII. 13. Aretius gratiam ad Deum Patrem refert, pacem verò ad Dominum Jesum Christum. Zanchius per gratiam solum spiritualia bona, per pacem solum temporalia intelligi vult: utrumque rejicit Joh. Crocius in Ephes. I. 2. Non singula, in- quit, ad singulos, id est, gratiam ad Patrem, & pa- cem ad Christum, sed ambo ad utrumq́; refert: Pa- ter fons est: Christus est Mediator gratiæ & pacis. Per gratiam autem intelligit fontem omnium do- norum salutarium, nempe gratuitum favorem ac benevolentiam DEI. Pacis nomine non sola tem- poralia comprehendi vult, sed etiam æterna, eo- que nomine uti Apostolum, tùm quia Judæi eo felicitatem omnem solebant significare, tùm quia illâ nihil est præstabilius in humanis atque ipsa fere est compendium omnium benedictionum, sicut bellum quoddam maledictionum diluvium. Quod etsi verum, pacis nomen tamen hic εἰδικῶς accipitur: Quod agnoscit Aretius in 1. Cor. I. 2. Pax est tranquillitas conscientiæ nata ex gratia DEI. Postquam enim sentimus, pacatum nobis esse Deum, incipimus pacari, ne tumultuetur conscientia ju- dicii divini metu; sed Deum ut Patrem in Christo placatum invocet. Itaque pax effectus est gratiæ. Et ut in gratia etiam sunt dona Spiritus Sancti: Sic cum pace illa interna habetur pax externa, hoc est, studium pacate vivendi. Græcis consuetum erat præfigere suum χαίρειν, εὐπράττειν, & ὑγιαί- νειν. Quibus lætitiam, sanitatem, successum in actio- nibus vitæ comprecebantur. Latini salutem plu- rimam dicebant, sed non alia salutaria intellige- bant, quam quæ in hac vita & durarent, & simul cum illa finirentur; nos ampliora habemus bona.

PARS II. Exordium εὐχαρισικόν.

## 1:3
V. 3. Blessed be God) A solemn formula of giving thanks, Rom. I. 25. IX. 5.

In the exordium, the Apostle wishes both to win benevolence for himself, giving thanks for their consolations which result in good, and promising that they will be participants in the consolations, and he prepares a way for himself to the narrative about his afflictions, prefixing to them the due thanksgiving for divine consolation. But that God and Father must be separated with respect to our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore they place a comma at the word God, and Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Theophylactus advise that it should be placed. For it is not said that he is both the God of Christ and his Father, but he is the same God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The name of God is taken personally concerning God the Father, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, because this Son of his is eternally begotten by him, Ps. II. 7. Therefore heretics wrongly conclude from this that the Son is inferior in Deity to the Father, as one who acknowledges God the Father, and a superior Lord, from whom he himself received divinity. For the Father and the Son are of the same nature, therefore nothing inferior is to be thought of here. Even if the name of GOD is also referred entirely to the Lord or Christ, God of Christ will have to be understood by reason of human nature: but his Father by reason of divine nature, as Theophylactus advises. However, it must not be said with Aretius that God is the Father of Christ according to humanity through conception from the Holy Spirit. For there is only one person, God and man, one Son, one sonship with respect to God the Father: Not a double sonship, lest the person of Christ be doubled. For the name of Son is the name of a person, and it brings about generation from the essence, nor can the word Father be taken simultaneously and properly concerning the Father because of generation, and improperly concerning the Father so called because of creation. And although the humanity of Christ is from GOD the Father through creation, because it is not without a person, and subsists only in the person of the Son of GOD, it cannot come under the name of Son, or claim sonship for itself in itself and by itself, but it is assumed into the hypostasis of the Son of GOD, so that there is one Son of GOD, consisting of divine and human nature, one sonship of God, belonging to the divine nature through eternal generation from the Father, but to the human nature through assumption into the hypostasis of the Son of GOD. Although the mode of attribution of the sonship is different: Yet there is only one sonship, and therefore he is called the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ not because of a different sonship, but because of that one true and natural one, because our Lord Jesus Christ is that true and natural Son of GOD.

The Father of mercies) A genitive for an adjective, as also in the subsequent words, he says, the Father who is supremely merciful. See Exodus XXXIV, 6. God merciful and gracious in Syriac and Arabic.

And the God of all consolation. Is this therefore also to be understood for that reason, that GOD is the supreme comforter or most consolable, so that I may use that word actively with Crellius? It does not seem so. For it is known that God is called the God of consolation, as well as of patience and hope. But who will understand God of hope in such a way that he hopes the most? Or of patience, that he is the most patient? And not rather, that he is the author of hope and patience. And therefore he is also the God of all consolation, because he is the author of all true consolation. Thus both the affection in GOD, mercy, and the effect, consolation, are noted. These epithets agree very well with the argument. Because he shows himself as a Father supremely merciful in tempering and ending afflictions, as also the God of all consolation, for overcoming and enduring them, where there is need of divine help and consolation.

Latin:

V. 3. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς) Formula solennis gratias agen- di, Rom. I. 25. IX. 5.

In exordio tùm benevolentiam sibi conciliare vult Apostolus, gratias agens pro consolationi- bus ipsorum bono cedentibus, eosque participes fore consolationum spondens, tùm viam sibi ad narrationem de afflictionibus suis parat, præmit- tens illis debitam pro παρακλήσει divina εὐχαρι- σίαν. Sejungenda autem illa Deus, & Pater re- spectu Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Ideo hyposti- gma figunt in voce Deus, & figendum monent Theodoretus, Oecumenius, & Theophylactus. Non enim & Deus Pater Christi & Pater ejus dicitur, sed idem est Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi est. Nomen Θεῦ personaliter accipitur de Deo Patre, qui Pater est Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quia hic Filius ejus est ab æterno genitus ab ipso, Ps. II. 7. Perperàm ergò hæretici inde colligunt, Filium Deitate inferiorem esse Patre, ut qui Deum Patrem agnoscat, & Dominum superiorem, à quo ipse divinitatem acceperit. Pater enim & Filius ejusdem sunt naturæ, ideo nihil inferius hic co- gitandum. Etsi omninò referatur etiam nomen DEI ad Dominum vel Christum, Deus Christi in- telligendus erit ratione humanæ naturæ: Pater verò ejus ratione divinæ naturæ, ut Theophyla- ctus monet. Non autem cum Aretio dicendum, quod Deus Pater Christi sit quoad humanitatem per conceptionem è Spiritu S. Nam unica tantum est persona Deus & homo, unus Filius, una υἱότης respectu Dei Patris: Non gemina υἱότης, ne gemi- netur persona Christi. Nomen enim Filii est no- men personæ, & generationem infert ex essentia, nec potest simul & propriè vox Patris accipi de Patre ob generationem, & impropriè de Patre ob creationem ita dicto. Et quamvis humanitas Chri- sti à DEO Patre per creationem sit, quia tamen non ἀνυπόστατος est, ac subsistit solum in per- sona Filii DEI, non potest ipsa venire Filii no- mine, vel in se ac per se υἱότητα sibi vendicare, sed assumpta est in hypostasin Filii DEI, ut unus sit DEI Filius, divina & humana natura constans, una υἱότης τοῦ θεοῦ, divinæ naturæ per æternam ge- nerationem à Patre conveniens, humanæ verò na- turæ per assumptionem in hypostasin Filii DEI. Quanquam verò modus attributionis τῆς υἱότητος diversus sit: Una tamen est tantum υἱότης, ideoque Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi non ob diversam υἱότητα, sed ob unicam veram illam ac naturalem dicitur, quia Dominus noster Jesus Christus est verus ille & naturalis DEI Filius.

Ὁ πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν) Genitivus pro Adjectivo, ut & in verbis subsequentibus Pater, inquit, summe miseri- cors. Vide Exodi XXXIV, 6. Deus רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן Syris & Arabibus.

Καὶ θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως. Num ergo & hoc ea ratione intelligendum, quod DEUS sit consola- tor summus vel maximè consolabilis, ut cum Crellio voce illa utar activè? Non videtur. Notum enim est, quod ut consolationis, ita & patientiæ & spei Deus dicatur. Ecquis vero Deum spei ita intel- liget, quod maxime speret? aut patientiæ, quod maxime patiens sit: Et non potius, quod autor sit spei & patientiæ. Ideoque & Deus omnis con- solationis est, quia omnis veræ consolationis au- tor. Notatur itaque & affectus in DEO miseri- cordia, & effectus consolatio. Conveniunt ap- prime argumento hæc Epitheta. Quia se Patrem summè misericordem in afflictionibus temperan- dis & finiendis, ut & Deum omnis consolationis, ad easdem superandas & exantlandas, exhibet, ubi auxilio & consolatione divina opus est.

## 1:4
V. 4. Who comforts us in all our affliction) He did not say this without cause against those who think that those who are involved in many inconveniences are hated by GOD. Compare Rom. V. 3. VIII. 35.

He by no means said, who permits us to be pressed or distressed, but when we are urged and pressed, he comforts us, as Theophylactus here, who also observes that the verb of the present tense brings in perpetuity. Therefore Paul by no means added that he comforted us once, but added who comforts, to show the perpetuity of consolation. Nor only in this or that pressure, but in every tribulation, whatever that may be. So that the universality of both time and tribulation is noted, that in every affliction he comforts them continuously and perpetually.

Εἰς τὸ δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς παρακαλεῖν τοὺς ἐν πάσῃ θλίψει) Paul refers all his own things to the utility of the Church.

Διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως, ἧς παρακαλούμεθα αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ) That is, through those gifts of the spirit by which God consoles me. See Acts IV. 36. IX. 31. XIII. 15.

Not only through those gifts, but also through the example, concerning which Theophylact says: GOD consoles us, he says, not because we ourselves are worthy of this consolation, but so that we may be able to console others, on account of this example of consolation which has been set forth in us, and the rest who are accustomed to be pressed by various diseases. Aretius brings forward these causes why GOD exercises his ministers with various calamities: 1. That he may establish examples of the profession, in which they yield to no threats of tyrants. 2. That they may be examples of constancy. 3. That they may learn to despair of their own strength. 4. To trust in GOD alone. 5. That they may be able to confirm others, and to sympathize with those being exercised in a similar arena. The warnings which we have learned by experience are excellent. The Vulgate translates badly and barbarously: 'by the exhortation, by which we ourselves are exhorted by GOD.' For the discourse is about consolation in adversities, not about exhortation, as Estius acknowledges along with Ambrosiaster, Primasius, and Sedulius, observing that this passage was therefore corrected by Jerome in the Vulgate, but that this correction, like many others, had perished through the inveterate use of the old edition. How excellently, therefore, does the emendation of the two Pontiffs, Sixtus V and Clement VIII, stand.

Latin:

V. 4. Ὁ παρακαλῶν ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει ἡμῶν) Non sine causa hoc dixit adversus eos, qui DEO exosOS putant eos, qui in multis incommodis versantur. Confer- Rom. V. 3. VIII. 35.

Haud quaquam dixit, qui nos premi aut angi permittit, sed cum urgemur & premimur, nos consolatur, ut hic Theophylactus, qui observat et- iam verbum præsentis temporis inferre perpe- tuitatem. Propterea Paulus nequaquam illud, quod semel nos consolatus est, intulit, sed qui consolatur adjecit, ut perpetuitatem consolationis ostendat. Ne- que in hac solum aut illa pressura, sed in omni tri- bulatione, quæcunque sit illa. Ut ita universalitas tùm temporis, tùm tribulationis notetur, quod in omni afflictione & jugiter ac perpetuo ipsos con- soletur.

Εἰς τὸ δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς παρακαλεῖν τοὺς ἐν πάσῃ θλίψει) Omnia sua Paulus ad Ecclesiæ utilitatem refert.

Διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως, ἧς παρακαλούμεθα αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Id est, per dona illa spiritus, quibus Deus me sola- tur. Vide Act. IV. 36. IX. 31. XIII. 15.

Non tantum per dona illa, sed etiam per exem- plum, de quo Theophylactus: Non eo, inquit, quia & digni ipsi consolatione hac sumus, solatur nos DEUS, sed ut cæteros, pro hujusce consolationis exemplo, quod in nos editum est, & reliquos, qui urgeri variis morbis solent, consolari possimus. Causas, cur DEUS suos ministros exerceat variis calamitatibus, has adfert Aretius: 1. Ut statuat exempla professionis, in qua nullis cedant Tyran- norum minis. 2. Sint exempla constantiæ. 3. Di- scant de suis viribus desperare. 4. In solo DEO confidere. 5. Alios confirmare possint, & condolere in simili palæstra exercendis. Optime sunt moni- ta, quæ experimento didicimus. Vulgata male vertit & barbare: per exhortationem, qua & ipsi exhortamur a DEO. De consolatione enim in ad- versis, non de exhortatione sermo est, ut agnoscit cum Ambrosiaftro, Primafio, & Sedulio Estius, ob- servans locum hunc ideo in Vulgata ab Hierony- mo correctum, sed correctionem hanc, ut alias multas per usum inveteratum editionis veteris excidisse. Tam præclare ergo se habet Pontificum duorum Sixti V. & Clementis IIX. emendatio.

## 1:5
V. 5. Περισσεύει) They are many and great. See Rom. III. 7. V. 15. XV. 13.

Our sufferings are not compared with the sufferings of Christ, as if the latter were more abundant, which seemed to be the view of Theophylact: But our sufferings are called the sufferings of Christ, when the abundance of our consolation through Christ is composed of the abundance of those [sufferings], Ps. XCIV. 19. Which sense Theophylact also embraced: Whither are you tending, (he says) O hearer, when you hear of sufferings and torments? For the more they have flowed in, the more abundant will the consolation also be. Nor did he express sufferings simply, but Christ's, so that from these he might also console the Corinthians. For such sufferings as we endure are indeed Christ's. Whence it happens that in bearing these we are made participants of Christ. Therefore, that you have undergone the sufferings of Christ ought to be a great consolation to you. He brings together opposites such as sufferings and consolations, and says that as one increases, it is fitting that the other also increases. Just as if a physician were to say that, as a disease grows stronger, the medicines also become sharper. Moreover, the sufferings of Christ are those which we suffer, both because we are the mystical members of Christ, in whom Christ suffers, Acts IX. 5, and because we sustain the same for the sake of Christ's glory and his name.

Latin:

V. 5. Περισσεύει) Multa sunt & magna. Vide Rom. III. 7. V. 15. XV. 13.

Non comparantur passiones nostræ cum pas- sionibus Christi, quasi istæ abundantiores sint, quod Theophylacto visum: Sed passiones nostræ dicuntur Christi passiones, cum illarum abundan- tia componitur abundantia consolationis nostræ per Christum, Ps. XCIV. 19. Quem sensum etiam amplexus est Theophylactus: Quo tendis, (inquit) o auditor, passiones cum audis & cruciatus? Quan- to enim magis affluxerint, tanto abundantior erit & consolatio. Nec simpliciter passiones expressit, sed Christi, ut ex his & Corinthios consoletur. Christi quippe sunt hujusmodi passiones, quas nos toleramus. Quo fit, ut in his ferendis Christi simus effecti par- ticipes. Debet ergo magnum in modum vel illud tibi consolationi esse, quod Christi subieris passiones. Contraria confert ut παθήματα & παρακλήσεις, ac ait, uno crescente, par esse alterum etiam cresce- re. Quemadmodum si Medicus dicat, morbo in- valescente, medicamenta quoque acutiora fieri. Christi autem passiones sunt, quas nos patimur, tum quia Christi membra mystica sumus, in qui- bus Christus patitur Act. IX. 5. tum quia pro Chri- sti gloria ac ejus nomine easdem sustinemus.

## 1:6
Εἴτε δὲ θλιβόμεθα) In the Manuscript: Εἴτε παρακαλούμεθα, so that this depends on the preceding verb περισσεύει, which was used of both afflictions and consolations. He says that afflictions happen to him for the sake of their salvation, that is, because of the Gospel, whence he said above 'the sufferings of Christ,' that is, those which are borne for the sake of Christ. See 1 Pet. IV. 16.

V. 6. Καὶ σωτηρίας) It is missing in the Manuscript.

Τῆς ἐνεργουμένης) That is, κατεργαζομένης. See Rom. VI. 3. ἐνεργεῖσθαι is sometimes taken deponentially, sometimes, as here, passively.

Τῶν αὐτῶν παθημάτων) Those are called the same which are suffered for the same reason.

The meaning of the Apostle is plain: That all things which happen to the Apostle, or to the ministers of the word, are for the benefit of the Corinthians, for instance, whether afflictions or consolations. For afflictions also make for their consolation, which they can draw from the example of the ministers of the word in adversities, and from their consolatory words, inasmuch as temptation has made them perfect theologians. Indeed, the afflictions of the Doctors make for the salvation of the hearers, not by way of merit, since they do not arrive at salvation except through the merit of Christ, Acts IV. 12. But because, looking at their example, they are stirred up to faith and a similar constancy of faith, Heb. XIII. 7, Jas. V. 10, 11, especially by the most efficacious consolations of their Word, the power of which the Doctors have experienced in afflictions, being strengthened, Ps. CXIX. 50, 92. Moreover, the end of faith is salvation, 1 Pet. I. 9, Heb. X. 38, 39. The preposition ὑπὲρ therefore denotes here not merit, but advantage, or the event alone: For your salvation, that is, for the advantage and use of your salvation. The word ἐνεργουμένης is wrongly taken actively by Cornelius a Lapide, explaining the Vulgate thus: 'which works in the enduring,' that is, endurance, as the Hebrews speak, 'I touch in the staff,' that is, the staff, which [endurance] namely both exhortation and salvation work, i.e., Exhortation excites and animates you to the hope of salvation, so that because of it you may bravely endure all adversities with us for the faith of Christ. Exhortation, therefore, works endurance effectively by exciting you to it. But salvation hoped for from thence works endurance objectively, just as the intention of an end works the embrace and execution of the means. What, I ask, do these things have to do with the matter? The Apostle is not discoursing about the fruits of the exhortation, or indeed even of the consolation of the Corinthians, but about the fruits of the tribulation or θλίψεως of the Doctors; that those things make for the salvation of the Corinthians or the hearers: Nor about the hope of salvation moving them to sustain sufferings, as a means of obtaining the hoped-for salvation: But about the salvation of the hearers, which is effected or obtained by divine grace in the endurance of similar sufferings which the Doctors have sustained, when indeed they endure the same with similar faith and perseverance. Erasmus indeed renders it actively, but reading τῆς ἐνεργύσης, and explaining it thus: 'It works and acts, and unfolds and opens its power in endurance,' and warns that Chrysostom reads ἐνεργομένης passively, so that there may be a place for the grace of GOD, to whom the chief praise of our salvation is due, and that he interprets ἐνεργεῖται as δείκνυται αὔξεται ἐκτείνεται, it is shown, it grows, and is extended, and becomes greater. For in the scriptures, things are said to be done which are manifested.
