And Estius rejects the reading of Erasmus, as one which hardly appears anywhere, nor was it annotated by Robert Stephanus, and he says that in the Greek it is a passive participle, and for that reason the interpreters of Oecumenius and Theophylact translated it well and clearly. Yet Estius did not properly render the sense in this way: 'Which salvation is effected, generated, and prepared, to be obtained at length by you through the endurance of such afflictions as we suffer,' that is, by this, that you sustain similar afflictions. For our patience is not established as the cause of salvation, but the affliction of the Doctors is taught to result in our salvation through the tolerance of sufferings, not by the tolerance, but by faith, if, namely, we persevere in the faith in the same way as the Doctors, whose faith we ought to imitate, Apoc. II. 10; and even if tolerance were said to effect salvation, it is not to be understood causally or meritoriously, but only morally or occasionally, just as danger teaches one to pray. But we must acquiesce in the explanation of Chrysostom, praised by Estius, that salvation is shown in tolerance: to which also the version of B. Luther tends: Welches Heyl beweiset sich, so ihr leidet mit Gedult. And therefore the Socinians are in vain, establishing from this the work as the cause of salvation along with the Papists, since it is not taught here of set purpose what the sufferings of the hearers work in themselves, but to what end the θλίψεις endured by the Doctors conduce for the hearers.

Furthermore, Estius, not undeservedly, recalls the Vulgate version to censorship, even though it was pronounced authentic in the Council of Trent and fortified by the bulls of two Popes, because it departs from the more excellent and more ancient Latin translation books of the Old Testament, especially those which the Louvain scholars used in correcting the bibles, and from the ancient Concordances, as noted by Fr. Lucas, since it has three members in this place—the first of tribulation, the second of consolation, the third of exhortation—whereas there are only two in the Greek and Syriac Codices, and one word παρακλήσεως εἴτε παρακαλόμεθα ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως, which, rendered in two ways by others, whether we are comforted (passive) for your consolation, or by others, whether we are exhorted (likewise passive) for your exhortation, is read in the Vulgate according to both versions, with both translations joined together. But as for the fact that he excuses the Roman correctors in any way whatsoever, what else does it testify to, other than that the infallibility of the Roman Pontiffs, who [authorized] that correction by their own authority in the Church, failed here. But the consolation which the Doctors receive makes for the consolation and salvation of the hearers, especially the real one, which comes about through an admirable deliverance from dangers, because it is a help to others for supporting hope and patience in afflictions, and for strengthening

Latin:

Εἴτε δὲ θλιβόμεθα) In Manuscripto: Εἴτε παρακαλού- μεθα, ut pendeat hoc a verbo præcedente περισσεύει, quod & de afflictionibus & solatiis positum fuit. Afflictiones sibi evenire dicit ipsorum salutis causa, id est, propter Ev- angelium, unde supra dixit παθήματα Χριστῦ, id est, quæ Christi causa feruntur. Vide 1. Pet. IV. 16.

V. 6. Καὶ σωτηρίας) Deest in Manuscripto.

Τῆς ἐνεργουμένης) Id est, κατεργαζομένης. Vide Rom. VI. 3. ἐνεργεῖσθαι modo deponentialiter sumitur, modo, ut hic, passive.

Τῶν αὐτῶν παθημάτων) Eadem dicuntur, quæ eandem ob causam sufferuntur.

Sententia Apostoli plana est: Omnia ad utili- tatem Corinthiorum facere, quæ Apostolo, vel verbi ministris eveniunt, puta sive afflictiones, sive consolationes. Nam & afflictiones facere ad ipsorum consolationem, quam & ab exemplo mi- nistrorum verbi haurire possunt in adversis, & e verbis eorum consolatoriis, utpote quos Theo- logos perfectos effecit tentatio. Imo facere afflictio- nes Doctorum ad salutem auditorum, non per modum meriti, quum non nisi Christi merito ad salutem perveniant, Act. IV. 12. Sed quia intuen- tes exemplum eorum ad fidem & constantiam fidei similem excitantur, Ebr. XIII. 7. Jac. V. 10. 11. imprimis Verbi ipsorum consolationibus effica- cissimis, quarum vim experti Doctores in afflictio- nibus sunt, roborati, Ps. CXIX. 50. 92. Finis autem fidei salus est, 1. Petr. I. 9. Ebr. X. 38. 39. Præposi- tio ergo ὑπὲρ hic non meritum, sed commodum, vel eventum solum notat: Pro salute vestra, id est, in commodum & usum vestræ salutis. Vox ἐνερ- γομένης perperam active accipitur a Cornelio a La- pide explicante ita Vulgatam, quæ operatur in to- lerantia, id est, tolerantiam, ut Ebræi loquuntur, tango in baculo, id est, baculum, quæ scilicet tum exhortatio, tum salus operatur tolerantiam, q. d. Exhortatio excitat & animat vos ad spem salutis, ut propter eam nobiscum pro fide Christi adversa quæque fortiter toleretis. Exhortatio ergo opera- tur tolerantiam effectivè ad eam excitando. Sa- lus vero inde sperata operatur tolerantiam obje- ctivè, perinde ac intentio finis operatur ample- xum & exequutionem mediorum. Quid, obse- cro, hæc ad rem faciunt? Non de exhortationis, imò nec de consolationis Corinthiorum, sed de tribulationis vel θλίψεως Doctorum fructibus dis- serit Apostolus; quod illæ faciant pro salute Co- rinthiorum vel auditorum: Nec de spe salutis mo- vente ad sustinendas passiones, ceu medio con- sequendi salutem speratam: Sed de salute Audi- torum, quæ efficitur vel obtinetur divinâ gratiâ in tolerantia similium passionum, quas sustinuere Doctores, cum nempe simili fide & perseveran- tia easdem tolerant. Erasmus reddit quidem Activè, sed legens τῆς ἐνεργύσης, & ita expo- nens: Operatur & agit, ac vim suam explicat & aperit in tolerantia, monetque, Chrysostomum legere ἐνεργομένης passivè, ut locus sit gratiæ DEI, cui præcipua laus nostræ salutis debetur, & ἐνεργεῖ- ται interpretari δείκνυται αὔξεται ἐκτείνεται osten- ditur, crescit & intenditur, sitque major. In scri- pturis enim fieri dicuntur, quæ manifestantur. Et rejicit Estius lectionem Erasmi, ut quæ vix us- quam appareat, nec à Roberto Stephano annotata sit, aitque in Græco esse Participium passivum, eaque ratione bene & dilucide vertisse Oecume- nii & Theophylacti interpretes. Sensum tamen non probe reddidit Estius hoc modo: Quæ salus efficitur, gignitur, & paratur, obtinenda tandem à vobis per tolerantiam talium afflictionum, quales nos patimur, id est per hoc, quod similes afflictiones sustinetis. Non enim patientia nostra salutis cau- sa constituitur, sed afflictio Doctorum in salutem nostram cedere docetur in tolerantia passionum, non per tolerantiam, sed per fidem, si scil. æquè ut Doctores, quorum fidem imitari debemus, in iisdem in fide perseveremus, Apoc. II. 10. ac si ma- xime tolerantia diceretur efficere salutem, non tamen id causaliter vel meritoriè, sed moraliter tantum vel occasionaliter intelligendum, quomo- do periculum docet orare. Sed acquiescendum Chrysostomi explicationi ab Estio laudatæ, quod salus ostendatur in tolerantia: Quo etiam abit B. Lutheri versio: Welches Heyl beweiset sich, so ihr leidet mit Gedult. Ideoque frustra sunt So- ciniani, hinc opera causam salutis constituentes cum Papistis, siquidem non quid operentur pas- siones auditorum in ipsismet, sed ad quid θλίψεις à Doctoribus exantlare, penes auditores condu- cant, hic ex instituto doceatur.

De cætero vulgatam versionem etsi authenti- cam pronunciatam in Concilio Tridentino, & à duobus Pontificibus bullis munitam ad censu- ram, nec immerito, revocat Estius, quod à præ- stantioribus & antiquioribus Veter. libris Lati- næ translationis, iis maximè, qui in castigandis bibliis usi fuere Lovavienses, & à veteribus Con- cordantiis discedat, ut notatum Fr. Lucæ, cum tria membra primum tribulationis, secundum con- solationis, tertium exhortationis hoc loco habet, siquidem duo solum sint in Græcis, & Syriacis Codicibus, & verbum unum παρακλήσεως εἴτε παρακαλόμεθα ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως, quod duobus modis redditum ab aliis, sive conso- lamur (passive) pro vestra consolatione, ab aliis, sive exhortamur (passive itidem) pro vestra exhorta- tione secundum utramque versionem in vulgata legatur, conjuncta utraque translatione. Quod verò qualitercunque excusat Romanos correcto- res, quid aliud testatur, quam quod infallibilitas Romanorum Pontificum, qui correctionem illam suo diplomate in Ecclesia sancivere, hic defece- rit. Consolatio autem, quam Doctores accipiunt, facit ad consolationem & salutem auditorum, im- primis realis, quæ per admirandam è periculis li- berationem fit, quia adjumento aliis est, ad fulci- endam spem & patientiam in afflictionibus, & ad firmandam fiduciam liberationis.

## 1:7
V. 7. And our hope is firm for you) These ought to be read as a parenthesis. For what follows, whether we are comforted, responds to that which preceded, whether we are afflicted. But he says this here, that he has a firm hope concerning their constancy even in suffering evils. Moreover, I did not think I should pass over in that Manuscript, of which I have spoken so often, the preceding words placed in another order, in this manner: of consolation and salvation, whether we are comforted for your consolation which is worked out in the patience of the same sufferings which we also suffer, and our hope &c.

There is no need for a parenthesis if the more accepted reading is retained. For according to the same, that whether we are comforted does not follow, but these words precede, and our hope &c.

Knowing) This is not referred to the Corinthians, but to Paul and Timothy. And he says that he knows the Corinthians are touched by the sense of both the adversities and the good things which were happening to them by the gift of God.

It is rightly referred to Paul and Timothy: but the sense here is that they know that the Corinthians, just as they experience passions by the will of GOD, will also be partakers of a similar consolation. Which comparison is not to be referred here to Christ, so that they may be rendered conformable to his image; but to Paul and Timothy. Theophylact brings forward both senses: For just as, when we ourselves are afflicted, it by no means escapes me that you take that ill, and are tormented no otherwise than if you yourselves were suffering. So indeed I have it as certain that you consider our consolation as your own. Or otherwise: Just as you have suffered evil things with me in this life, so in the future life you will be affected with good things together with me forever. But the latter is simpler and more convenient.

PART III.

Narrative of the affliction endured in Asia.

Latin:

V. 7. Καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡμῶν βεβαία ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) Hæc per parenthesin legi debent. Nam quod sequitur, εἴτε παρα- καλόμεθα, respondet ei, quod præcessit, εἴτε θλιβόμεθα. Hoc autem dicit hic, firmam se habere spem de constan- tia etiam in sufferendis malis. Cæterum non prætereun- dum duxi in illo Manuscripto, de quo dixi toties, verba præcedentia alio posita ordine, hunc in modum: παρακλή- σεως καὶ σωτηρίας, εἴτε παρακαλόμεθα ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρα- κλήσεως τῆς ἐνεργουμένης ἐν ὑπομονῇ τῶν αὐτῶν παθημάτων, ὧν καὶ ἡμεῖς πάσχομεν, καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς &c.

Non opus est parenthesi, si receptior lectio retineatur. Nam juxta eandem illud εἴτε παρα- καλόμεθα non sequitur, sed præcedit ista, καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς &c.

Εἰδότες) Hoc non ad Corinthios refertur, sed ad Pau- lum & Timotheum. Et scire se dicit Corinthios tangi sensu ut adversorum, ita & bonorum, quæ ipsi dante Deo contingebant.

Recte ad Paulum & Timotheum refertur: Sen- sus autem hic est, quod sciant, Corinthios, sicut DEO volente passiones experiantur, etiam simi- lis consolationis participes fore. Quæ compa- ratio non ad Christum, ut imagini ejus confor- mes reddantur, hic referenda; sed ad Paulum & Timotheum. Theophylactus affert utrumque sen- sum: Quemadmodum enim, cum ipsi nos afflicta- mur, baudquaquam me fugit, id moleste vos ferre, angique baud secus, atque ipsimet pateremini. Sic sa- ne compertum habeo, nostram vos consolationem pro vestra ducere. Vel aliter: Sicuti enim mecum estis in hac vita mala perpessi, sic in vita futura bonis mecum una sempiternis afficiemini. Sed posterior simplicior est & convenientior.

PARS III.

Narratio afflictionis in Asia exantlatæ.

## 1:8
V. 8. For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning the affliction) There is here peri for hyper, indeed the Manuscript has here peri, and agnoein for agnoontas einai.

That which happened to us in Asia) Those dangers seem to be indicated, concerning which Acts XX. 19.

Asia Minor is signified, in which Ephesus is; in Acts XX. 19 no affliction is commemorated. But in the preceding chapter the tumult against Paul excited at Ephesus by Demetrius is related, which Theodoret and most of the Latins take these words to refer to. Chrysostom indeed and Theophylact, as also Oecumenius, refer them to those things which are held in 1 Cor. XVI. 9 concerning many adversaries. But these things, which he does not want them to be ignorant of, are more recent and not yet known to them. Nor indeed is this one affliction alone looked to, even if the word affliction is used in the singular, because under that singular any affliction endured in Asia can be understood, just as in v. 4 he celebrated God on account of the consolation in all our affliction. For the Apostle undoubtedly sustained many afflictions which were not mentioned by Luke, and however that may have been the most grievous, to which the sentence of death, of which v. 9, is not inconsistent. He could, however, experience more of that kind, in which he was in danger of his life, just as in he delivers v. 10 he testifies that he is still exposed to dangers of death, and is snatched from them. Therefore there is no reason why we should restrict affliction to only that affliction which was brought about by Demetrius, and therefore Estius in vain denies that the delay of Paul's arrival is excused here (which most interpreters establish) from the fact that that tumult was not so much a cause for the Apostle to stay longer, as to depart from there more hastily, since the Apostle was not subject to one affliction in Asia.

That we were burdened beyond measure beyond strength) kath' hyperbolen, exceedingly, as Rom. VII. 13, 1 Cor. XII. 31. ebarethemen, we were pressed, as below v. 4. hyper dynamin, beyond what human strength could sustain, it was a temptation not human, 1 Cor. X. 13.

So that we despaired even of life, ἐξαπορεῖsθαι, Psalm LXXXVIII. v. 15. below IV. 8.

Latin:

V. 8. Οὐ γὰρ θέλομεν ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, ὑπὲρ τῆς θλίψεως) Est hic περὶ pro ὑπὲρ, imo Manuscriptus habet hic περὶ, & ἀγνοεῖν pro ἀγνώτας εἶναι.

Τῆς γενομένης ἡμῖν ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ) Videntur indicari illa pericula, de quibus Act. XX. 19.

Significatur Asia minor, in qua Ephesus est, Act. XX. 19. nulla commemoratur afflictio. Sed capite præcedenti relatus est tumultus adversus Paulum per Demetrium Ephesi excitatus, de quo hæc accipiunt Theodoretius & Latini plerique. Chrysostomus quidem & Theophylactus, ut & Oe- cumenius ad ea, quæ 1. Cor. XVI. 9. de adversariis multis habentur, referunt. Sed hæc, quæ ipsos non vult ignorare, recentiora sunt, & nondum cognita ipsis. Nec verò hæc unica tantum affli- ctio respicitur, etsi in singulari vox θλίψεως ad- hibeatur, quia sub isto singulari quævis afflictio in Asia exantlata intelligi potest, quemadmodum v. 4. Deum celebravit ob consolationem ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει. Nam multas sine dubio sustinuit affli- ctiones Apostolus, quæ non memoratæ sunt à Luca, & utut illa gravissima fuerit, cui non discon- veniat responsum mortis, de quo v. 9. Plures tamen ejusmodi experiri potuit, in quibus de vita peri- clitatus est, quemadmodum ί ῥύεται v. 10. se ad- huc periculis mortis exponi, & ex iis eripi testa- tur. Non ergo est, quod ad solam illam afflictio- nem, quæ per Demetrium illata est, restringamus θλίψιν, ideoque frustra negat Estius moram ad- ventus Paulini hic excusari (quod plerique In- interpretes statuunt) ex eo, quod tumultus ille non tàm fuerit Apostolo causa morandi diutius, quàm festinatius inde discedendi, quum non uni θλίψει in Asia obnoxius fuerit Apostolus.

Ὅτι καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ἐβαρήθημεν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν) καθ’ ὑπερ- βολὴν valde, ut Rom. VII. 13. 1. Cor. XII. 31. ἐβαρήθημεν, pressi sumus, ut infra v. 4. ὑπὲρ δύναμιν, supra quam vi- res humanæ sustinerent, fuit πειρασμὸς ὁυκ ἀνθρώπινος, 1. Cor. X. 13.

Ὢστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τῶ ζῇν) Ita ut spem vitæ ab- jicerem, ἐξαπορεῖsθαι, Psalm. LXXXVIII. v. 15. in- fra IV. 8.

## 1:9
Vers. 9. But we ourselves have had the sentence of death in ourselves) Ἀπόκριμα θανάτυ גְזַרַת הַמּוּת the sentence of death. That is, we were affected in the same way as those upon whom a sentence of death has been pronounced. A locution similar to that in 1 Cor. XV. 32.

Others, to reconcile the passage in 1 Cor. X., prefer to say that the Apostle is speaking there of more than human temptations, which God does not impose beyond the strength granted; but here, indeed, of human, yet most grievous afflictions, which have exceeded the ordinary powers of grace, which the Apostle only overcame, strengthened by more powerful grace. B. Walther, in his Harmony, from B. Balduin's Commentary on this passage, has it thus: There is, he says, a twofold reconciliation of these passages: 1. By reason of the object or the Pauline afflictions. For he treats here of bodily afflictions, of sickness or other persecutions, where the strength even of pious men sometimes fails, Is. XXXVIII. 13. But in the former epistle he speaks of spiritual temptations, in which none of the pious are overcome, GOD bestowing virtue and faith, which is the victory of the world. 2. By reason of the subject, for if you wish to understand both passages as referring to spiritual temptations, it is manifest that Paul in the 1st to the Corinthians treats of powers divinely granted, which no temptation overcomes, but here he treats of merely human powers, which cannot subsist in temptations, nay, even in sicknesses, in dangers, and especially in death, they finally fail, for the virtue of GOD must be perfected in our infirmity. But the former reconciliation seems to be preferred. The Vulgate wrongly rendered it, so that we were weary of life itself. To which Tertullian agrees in his book on the Resurrection of the Flesh, chap. 48, that we despaired of life. And the Syriac interpreter, so that our life was near, so that it might be cast away. Which sense the Greek scholia and Theophylact also render, and Estius admits that it is favored by what follows concerning the sentence of death. He calls it a response, according to the interpretation of Theophylact, because the thing itself had almost given forth a voice, just as if he were saying, this expectation of death has proceeded so far, and is now so confirmed in my mind, that we were undoubtedly awaiting it.

That we should not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead) He brings forward the cause why God willed Paul to come into such great dangers. Among the Hebrews, those are sometimes called dead who are as if dead, and those resurrected who are delivered, as can be seen in Ezek. XXXVII.

Again he reminds the Corinthians, as Theophylact has it here, to take account of the resurrection. Which he discussed so much in the former epistle, confirming it even from present things, and for that reason he added that, who delivered us from so great a death. For he did not say from a danger, but from death. For since the resurrection itself was something future, and uncertain to many, he shows how it happens that we are raised from the dead every day. For when GOD has drawn a man back from the very gates of hell, he presents nothing else than the resurrection itself. Whence we are accustomed to use such a saying for that matter, we see this or that person raised from the dead.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἀλλ’ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὸ ἀπόκριμα τῦ θανάτυ ἐσχήκαμεν) Ἀπόκριμα θανάτυ גְזַרַת הַמּוּת sententiam mortis. Id est, ita affecti fuimus, quomodo ii, de quibus sententia ad mortem pronuntiata est. Locutio similis illi 1. Cor. XV. 32.

Alii ad conciliandum locum 1. Cor. X. malunt dicere, ibi Apostolum de plus quam humanis ten- tationibus loqui, quas non ultra vires concessas Deus imponit: hic verò de humanis, sed gravis- simis afflictionibus, quæ vires gratiæ ordinarias excesserint, quas tantum superarit Apostolus, gratia potentiori roboratus. B. Waltherus in Harm. è B. Balduini Comment. in hunc locum ita habet: Duplex, inquit, est locorum horum con- ciliatio, 1. Ratione objecti seu afflictionum Paulina- rum. Agit enim hic de afflictionibus corporalibus, de morbo aut persecutionibus aliis, ubi vires etiam piorum hominum interdum deficiunt, Es. XXXIIX. 13. In priori verò epistola loquitur de tentationi- bus spiritualibus, in quibus nemo piorum vincitur, DEO largiente virtutem & fidem, quæ est victoria mundi. 2. Ratione subjecti, quod si enim utrum- que locum de spiritualibus tentationibus intelligere velis, manifestum est, Paulum in 1. ad Corinthios agere de viribus divinitus concessis, quas nulla supe- rat tentatio, hic verò agit de viribus mere humanis, quæ in tentationibus subsistere non possunt, quin & in morbis, in periculis & cumprimis in morte tan- dem deficiunt, oportet enim virtutem DEI infir- mitate nostra perfici. Sed prior conciliatio præ- ferenda videtur. Vulgata perperam reddidit, ita ut tæderet, nos etiam vivere. Cui accinit Ter- tullianus libr. de Resurr. Carn. cap. 48. ut de vita hæsitaremus. Et Syrus interpres, adeo ut pro- pinqua esset vita nostra, ut projiceretur. Quem sensum etiam reddunt scholia Græca & Theophy- lactus, favetque illi, fatente Estio, quod sequitur de responso mortis. Responsum vero dicit, inter- prete Theophylacto, quod res ipsa vocem pene eden- tes reddiderant, perinde, ac si inquiat, eo usque mortis expectatio ista processit, & adeo est animo meo jam obfirmata, ut eam baud dubie opperiremur.

Ἱνα μὴ πεποιθότες ὦμεν ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς, ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ, τῷ ἐγείροντι τὺς νεκρύς) Causam adfert, cur Deus in tan- ta pericula Paulum pervenire voluerit. Hebræis interdum mortui dicuntur, qui quasi mortui sunt, & resuscitati, qui liberantur, ut videre est Ezech. XXXVII.

Rursum Corinthios, ut hic Theophylactus habet, de resurrectionis ratione habenda commonefacit. Quæ de in superiori epistola tàm multa disseruit, eam vel ex præsentibus rebus confirmans, eoque & illud adjecit, qui ex tantà nos morte exemit. Neque enim discrimine dixit, sed morte. Nam'cum esset resurrectio ipsa futurum aliquid, & multis incer- tum, ostendit, quemadmodum in dies singulos à mor- tuis excitari contingat. Nam cum hominem ab ipsis inferni foribus retraxerit DEUS, nihil aliud, quam resurrectionem ipsam prætendit. Unde & usurpare ejusmodi re id dictum solemus, à mortuis videmus hunc illumve excitatum.

## 1:10
V. 10. Who delivered us from so great a death) We are said to be delivered not only from the evils which we feel, but also from those which are imminent. See Proverbs 10:2, 11:4, and compare 24:2. See also the Song of the companions of Daniel near the end. Τηλικόυτο from so sad a death, by the hands of countrymen, by the hands of those who profess to worship one God.

And will deliver) Neither the Greek Commentators nor the Syrian read this.

Whether the Greek Commentators read it or not is doubtful. For although they pass over it in interpretation as if it were easy and not at all obscure, it is not to be concluded from that that they did not read it. It is found, therefore, in all the Codices: and the Apostle hints, as Estius admits, that he is nevertheless still involved in continuous dangers, of which some always succeed others, even if they are not all of equal gravity. For the word 'deliver' is not to be referred to so great a death, but to deaths simply, that is, the dangers of death: according to that which he said in 1 Cor. 4: 'Even unto this present hour we suffer persecution.'

In whom we have hoped, that he will also deliver) He says this, not because he feared death, but because he knew that his longer life was of great importance to the Churches. See Philippians 1:24.

Salmero and Estius, as well as Petrus Cotonus in his Institutes, Book IV, rashly infer here the invocation of saints living in heaven. For the consequence from the state of souls in these lands having knowledge of our needs to the state of souls triumphant in heaven, who are ignorant of our particular needs, and from the petition of intercessions, which the living mutually seek from the living, to the invocation of saints is not valid, since the former is consistent with Scripture and brotherly love, while the latter neither accords with Holy Scripture, nor is it an affection of someone pertaining to the second table of the law concerning love of neighbor, but introduces a religious worship of the first table, which ought not to be directed toward a neighbor, but only toward God. Therefore, Cajetan rightly judged that neither the invocation of souls living in heaven, nor their intercession for us who survive in this life, can be established from this passage.

Latin:

V. 10. ὄς ἐκ τηλικόυτου θανάτου ἐῥῥύσατο ἡμᾶς) Liberari dicimur non tantum è malis, quæ sentimus, sed etiam ab iis, quæ imminent. Vide Proverb. X. 2. XI. 4. & confer XXIV. 2. Vide & Canticum sodalium Danielis circa finem. Τηλικόυτο à morte tàm tristi, per manus popularium, per manus eorum, qui unum Deum colere se profitentur.

Καὶ ῥύεται) Hoc neque Commentatores Græci lege- runt, neque Syrus.

An legerint Græci Commentatores, necne, dubium est. Nam etsi in interpretatione ceu facile minimeque obscurum prætereant, non ta- men inde colligendum, id non legisse. Reperi- tur itaque in omnibus Codicibus: Innuitque ita, fatente Estio, Apostolus, se nihilominus adhuc ver- sari in continuis periculis, quorum semper alia aliis succedant, etsi non omnia paris gravitatis. Nec enim verbum eripit referendum ad tantam mortem, sed ad mortes simpliciter, id est, mortis pericula: se- cundum illud, quod dixit 1. Cor. IV. Usque in hanc horam persequutionem patimur.

Εἰς ὃν ἠλπίκαμεν, ὅτι καὶ ῥύσεται) Dicit hoc, non quod mortem metueret, sed quod longiorem suam vitam sciret è magna re esse Ecclesiarum. Vide Philipp. I. 24.

Temerè hic Salmero, Estius, ut & Petrus Coto- nus instit. lib. IV. colligunt invocationem sancto- rum viventium in cœlis. Nam à statu animarum in his terris notitiam nostrarum necessitatum ha- bentium ad statum animarum triumphantium in cœlis, quæ particulares nostras necessitates igno- rant, à petitione intercessionum, quas viventes à viventibus mutuò expetunt, ad invocationem san- ctorum non valet consequentia, siquidem illa scri- pturæ & amori fraterno consentanea sit, hæc nec Scripturæ S. consonet, nec affectus sit cujusdam ad tabulam secundam legis de amore proximi per- tinentis, sed cultum religiosum tabulæ primæ in- ferat, qui non erga proximum, sed solum erga Deum ferri debet. Ideo rectè Cajetanus censuit, neque invocationem animarum in cœlis viventium, neque harum intercessionem pro nobis in hac vita superstitibus ex hoc loco confici posse.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. You also helping together by prayer for us) There is also here a transposition for τῇ δεήσει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Paul confers great honor upon the Corinthians when he wishes to be helped by their prayers.

That the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf) Most codices have ὁ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, and the Syrian and many Greeks read it thus. There is also a transposition here. The discourse is more correctly τὸ εἰς ὑμᾶς χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων, that is, the gift of GOD given to me in respect of many men, namely, the safety granted for the sake of many believers. פנה is to look upon, hence פנים which is translated πρόσωπον, is respect. So also below II. 10. Hence מפני is because of. Εὐχαριστηθῇ may be celebrated with thanksgiving: ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν in my stead, in my name.

In most codices it is read ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. However, with that transposition admitted, the sense is obvious if you take the word πρόσωπον concerning persons. You also helping together, for us by prayer, so that that which from many persons (redounded) into us as a gift (for the word GIVEN is included in the word χάρισμα) may be celebrated by many with thanksgiving, not in our stead (for the Apostle himself gave thanks to GOD entirely, he did not wish to give them only through proxies), but for us. Theophylact explained these things excellently in this way: God (he says) delivered us from dangers, and will deliver us, you praying for me. So that what is of the donation in us, that is, the grace which was bestowed upon me, may be given thanks for by many, that is, by you, who are many praying for me, from the persons of many faces, that is, by you. For God has bestowed upon all of you the safety which is already prepared for me by your prayers, so that many pious people may give thanks for my sake. Furthermore, you will have to become accustomed not only to pray for one another, but to give thanks. Note, however, how he says that he was rendered safe by the clemency of GOD, and soon also ascribes the received safety to the prayers of these people. For it is necessary that after divine mercy, we ourselves also contribute some help for our own part so that we may be safe. Therefore, from these things Paul neither attributes the sum of the duties to the Corinthians, lest he give them a cause for pride, nor does he make them entirely alien to this kind of duty, lest he make them lazier and sluggish. For God will deliver (he says) me, you helping by praying, that is, you contributing vows according to your strength. The sense, I say, Theophylact rendered very well, even if that διὰ πολλῶν is more correctly referred to εὐχαρισίαν. The interpretation that it means among many, that is, in a great crowd of people, is more alien. For the words διὰ πολλῶν ought not to be rendered as 'among', but 'by' many. However, the judgment of Estius here is less pious: that Paul did not have much regard for properly placing articles, he who confesses himself unskilled in speech. For the Holy Spirit inspired Paul in what he wrote, dictating not only the thoughts, but also the very words, who certainly is not unskilled in speech, but the supreme Master of speaking.

PART IV. The refutation of the accusation of fickleness, because Paul had not arrived thus far contrary to the faith pledged.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Συνυπουργούντων καὶ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τῇ δεήσει) Est & hîc trajectio pro τῇ δεήσει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Magno ho- nore Corinthios afficit Paulus, cum vult eorum precibus adjuvari.

Ἱνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων τὸ εἰς ὑμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολ- λῶν ἐυχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) Plurimi codices habent ὁ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, & sic Syrus, Græcique multi legerunt. Est & hîc trajectio. Rectius sermo τὸ εἰς ὑμᾶς χάρισμα ἐκ πολ- λῶν προσώπων, id est, donum DEI respectu multorum ho- minum mihi datum, incolumitas nempe concessa in gra- tiam multorum fidelium. פנה est respicere, inde פנים quod πρόσωπον vertitur, est respectus. Sic & infra II. 10. Hinc מפני est propter. Εὐχαριστηθῇ gratiarum actione celebretur: ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν mea vice, meo nomine.

In plurimis codicibus legitur ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Tra- jectione autem illa admissà sensus obvius est, si vocem πρόσωπον de personis accipias. Cooperan- tibus & vobis, pro nobis per precationem, ut id, quod ex multis personis in nos donum (scilicet red- undavit, nam verbum DONATUM EST in ver- bo χάρισμα includitur) per multos gratiarum actione celebretur, non vice nostri, (ipse enim Apostolus DEO gratias omninò egit, non per vicarios tantum agere voluit) sed pro nobis. Exi- miè hæc Theophylactus exposuit hoc modo: Eri- puit nos (inquit) à periculis Deus, erepturussœ est, pro me vobis precantibus. Ut quod in nobis est donationis, hoc est, quæ in me collata est gra- tia per multos, hoc est, per vos, qui plurimi estis pro me orantes, ex multarum personis facierum gratia habeantur, hoc est, à vobis. Nam salutem, quæ mihi vestris precibus jam parata est, univer- sis vobis largitus est Deus, ut multi pii mei ob gra- tiam grates dicant. Erit præterea vobis insue- scendum non solum precari pro invicem, sed gra- tias agere. Adverte autem, quemadmodum DEI clementia salvum, dixerit fuisse se redditum, mox- que & horum precibus acceptam salutem adscri- bat. Oportet namque post divinam misericordi- am, & ipsi ut salvi simus pro nostra virili aliquid opis conferamus. Ex his itaque Paulus neque offi- ciorum summam Corinthiis tribuit, ne superbiendi his causam præbeat, neque prorsus ab hoc officii ge- nere alienos effecit, ne pigriores reddat & torpidos. Liberabit enim (inquit) me Deus vobis orando juvantibus, hoc est, conferentibus vobis pro vestris viribus vota. Sensum, inquam, optimè reddidit Theophylactus, etsi illud διὰ πολλῶν rectiùs ad εὐχαρισίαν referatur. Alienior est interpretatio, ut inter multos, id est, in magna hominum frequen- tia. Non enim inter, sed per multos verba διὰ πολλῶν reddi debent. Κρίσις autem Estiana mi- nus pia hic est : Articuli rite collocandi, non ita magnam rationem habuisse Paulum, qui se fate- tur imperitum sermone. Quæ enim scripsit Pau- lus, inspiravit ei Spiritus Sanctus, non tantum sententias, sed etiam ipsa verba dictando, qui certe non est imperitus sermone, sed summus dicendi Magister.

PARS IV. Profligatio accusationis levitatis, quod præter fidem datam hactenus non advenerit Paulus.

## 1:12
V. 12. For our rejoicing is this) Our joy, as we have already often explained this name καύχησις, and καύχημα, and the verb καυχᾶσθαι.

The testimony of the conscience. See Rom. II. 15. IX. 1.

That in simplicity and sincerity of God. With a sincere mind as if God were looking on. See 1 Cor. V. 8. He says this because some were accusing him, as if he had promised a return while intending nothing of the sort. He says, therefore, that he is now the same as he was in Corinth, of the best faith, but that guaranteeing the outcome is not his own. Many things intervene which compel one to change a plan. All things must be the same as they were when you promised, so that you may keep the faith of the one promising, says Seneca in his work on benefits, where you have many examples similar to the matter being discussed here. In the manuscript, for simplicity there is holiness.

The reason for the confidence concerning divine deliverance, of which v. 10 speaks, is thus rendered: in whom we hope, or rather, the confidence concerning the intercession of the Corinthians before God, by which the charge of fickleness is simultaneously refuted. For he who walks among the faithful in the simplicity of heart and sincerity of God is accused of fickleness toward them only falsely. Simplicity is opposed to duplicity, while someone does one thing and intends another. Sincerity, however, rectifies the intention itself. Therefore, that hypocrisy is excluded, and this wicked intention. Theophylact says: In simplicity, he says, of heart, that is, with a mind not wicked, and sincerity, that is, with a purer mind, and void of any deceit or fraud, which has nothing in itself shadowed or feigned: and let him exist such that he is both pleasing and more acceptable to God. He introduced these things for the sake of certain apostles who were deceitful among them and full of guile.

Not in fleshly wisdom. It is an indirect statement. For he lashes out at his detractors, who were swollen with Grecian learning. Compare 1 Cor. II. 1. 4.

But in the grace of God. 'In' for 'with'. With many spiritual gifts.

We have behaved in the world. Wherever we have been. We have behaved (Hebrew: we walked).

But more abundantly toward you. Especially among you. See the cited passage 1 Cor. II.

Latin:

V. 12. Ἡ γὰρ καύχησις ἡμῶν ἅυτη ἐςὶ) Gaudium no- strum, ut jam sæpe nomen hoc καύχησις, & καύχημα, & verbum καυχᾶσθαι exposuimus.

Τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως με) Vide Rom. II. 15. IX. 1.

Ὅτι ἐν ἁπλότητι καὶ εἰλικρινείᾳ Θεῦ) Sincero animo tanquam DEO inspectante. Vide 1. Cor. V. 8. Hoc ideo dicit, quia quidam ipsum incusabant, quasi reditum pol- licitus esset, nihil tale cogitans. Dicit igitur, se qualis fuit Corinthi, & nunc esse, fidei optimæ, sed eventum præ- stare non esse suum. Multa intervenire, quæ cogant mu- tare consilium. Omnia debent eadem esse, quæ fuerint cum promitteres, ut promittentis fidem teneas, ait Se- neca de beneficiis, ubi multa habes exempla, ei rei, de qua hîc agitur, similia. In Manuscripto pro ἁπλότητι est ἁγιότητι.

Ratio ita redditur fiduciæ de divinâ liberatione, de qua v. 10. in quem speramus, vel potius confi- dentiæ de intercessione Corinthiorum apud De- um, qua simul profligatur ἔγκλημα levitatis. Qui enim in simplicitate cordis, & sinceritate DEI inter fideles ambulat, levitatis erga eosdem non nisi falsò arguitur. Simplicitas opponitur dupli- citati, dum quis aliud agit, aliud intendit. Sin- ceritas autem ipsam intentionem rectificat. Ex- cluditur ergo illa hypocrisis, hæc prava intentio. Theophylactus: In simplicitate, inquit, cordis, hoc est, mente non improba, & sinceritate, id est, animo puriore, & quovis dolo vel fraude vacuo, qui nihil in se habeat adumbratum fictumve: & talis existat, ut DEO & gratus sit, & acceptior. Hæc autem Apostolorum quorundam gratia intulit, qui fallaces essent inter eos, & dolo pleni.

Οὐκ ἐν σοφίᾳ σαρκικῇ) Est obliqua oratio. Perstringit enim obtrestatores suos, eruditione Græcania turgentes. Conf. 1. Cor. II. 1. 4.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἐν χάριτι Θεῦ) ἐν pro cum. Cum multis donis spiritualibus.

Ἀνεστράφημεν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ) Ubicunque fuimus. Ἀνε- στράφημεν התהלכנו.

Περισσοτέρως δὲ πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Maximè apud vos. Vide dictum locum 1. Cor. II.

## 1:13
V. 13. For we do not write other things to you, but what you read, or even acknowledge. Manuscript: But you read and acknowledge. I judge the true reading to be that which the Syriac followed: But what you read, and acknowledge. We do not write other things to you (than what are true, that is), but what you read here, those things you acknowledge as having been done thus.

There is no reason to depart from the received reading. For ἀλλ’ ἢ is the same as ἢ in Plato in the Apology: Τίνα ἄλλον λόγον ἔχεσι βοηθῦντες ἐμοὶ ἀλλ’ ἢ τὸν ὀρθόν τε κὶ δίκαιον. Estius trifles with Calvin concerning the words: Οὐ γὰρ ἄλλα γράφομεν ὑμῖν, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε: For we do not write other things to you than what you read, in which way the Apostle rightly teaches those things which are clearly true from his own writings, which the Corinthians might be able to read. Therefore he prefers that ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε be translated as, you recognize, that is, which you can easily remember. But against Calvin, Beza observed that Paul gracefully says he writes nothing other than what is read, that is, he writes candidly, sincerely, and without any deceit: so that he might prove that sincere simplicity which he had attributed to himself in the previous verse. For he who uses covered or disguised speech is deservedly said to write other things than what are read: Just as if some honest woman were to say that she brings no other face than that which is seen: Which cannot be attributed to her who smears herself with paint, and with whom (as he says) her face does not sleep. Although indeed the Greeks also explain it in the sense of recognizing, just as we recognize those things which we know by remembering, whence Macrobius interprets ἀνάγνωσιν as repeated cognition, but he takes ἐπιγινώσκειν as simple cognition, as if the Apostle were saying that he writes nothing other than what the Corinthians themselves were able to recall, or even what they might know and understand of their own accord, even if he did not suggest them: Yet that interpretation of Beza seems forced, and does not sufficiently cohere with what precedes and follows. However, in our judgment, those two seem to be more simply joined in this way, what you now read, but also have known, since they are rendered thus by Beza: For we do not write other things than what you read, or even recognize. In which manner Ambrosiaster: He says, he writes those things which they might not only perceive by letters, but also have manifest by his works. And Erasmus notes that Paul expressed this sentiment in his own manner, we do not write other things to you than those which you not only read written by us, but also recognize expressed by us in deed and actions. Beza on those words καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε, that is, you already know sufficiently, and have persuaded, as the Syrian interpreter translates, so that the Apostle makes not now the letter, but their very souls the witnesses of that perpetual candor of his, which he had used toward them: which exposition seems to cohere best with those things which are subjoined. For otherwise, although speech is the interpreter of the mind: Yet it is not so difficult to simulate candor in writing. Or you recognize, namely as things already known to you before, or at least entirely corresponding to those things which you once heard from me when I was present, just as Basil in his 1st epistle testifies, but ἐπιγνῶναι, that is, to have recognized a letter as having proceeded from Gregory, just as, he says, we recognize certain people to be the children of certain others from the fact that they bear the countenance of their parents.

Ἐλπίζω δὲ κὶ ἕως τέλυς ἐπιγνώσεσθε) He shows that he has not cast away all hope of coming to them. You will recognize me, so I hope, perpetually as such. Namely when I shall have come to you.

Latin:

V. 13. Οὐ γὰρ ἄλλα γράφομεν ὑμῖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἢ ἃ ἀναγινώσκε- τε, ἢ καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε) Manuscriptus : Ἀλλ᾿ ἀναγινώσκετε καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε. Veram lectionem esse arbitror, quam se- quutus est Syrus: Ἀλλ᾿ ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε, καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε. Non alia vobis scribimus, (quàm quæ vera sunt scilicet) sed quæ hîc legitis, ea sic gesta agnoscitis.

Non est causa discedendi a recepta lectione. Nam ἀλλ’ ἢ idem est, quod ἢ apud Platonem in Apolog. Τίνα ἄλλον λόγον ἔχεσι βοηθῦντες ἐμοὶ ἀλλ’ ἢ τὸν ὀρθόν τε κὶ δίκαιον. Estius tricatur cum Cal- vino de verbis: Οὐ γὰρ ἄλλα γράφομεν ὑμῖν, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε: Non enim alia scribimus vo- bis, quam quae legitis, quomodo recte doceat A- postolus ea, quae scilicet vera esse ex suis ipsius scri- ptis, quae legere possint Corinthii. Proinde ma- vult, ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε vertendum esse, vos reco- gnoscitis, id est, quorum facile meminisse potestis. Sed adversus Calvinum observavit Beza, venuste Paulum dicere, se non aliud scribere, quam quod le- geretur, id est, candide, sincere, & absque ullo fuco scribere: ut eam sinceram simplicitatem probaret, quam sibi tribuerat superiore versu. Nam qui te- cta aut fucata oratione utitur, merito sane alia di- citur scribere, quam quae leguntur: Veluti si qua honesta mulier dicat, se non aliam faciem afferre, quam quae spectatur: Quod non possit ei tribui, quae sese fuco illinit, & quicum (ut dicit ille) fa- cies sua non dormiat. Quanquam vero Graeci etiam ita exponant sensu recognoscendi, uti re- cognoscimus, quae reminiscendo cognoscimus, unde ἀνάγνωσιν Macrobius repetitam cognitionem in- terpretatur, ἐπιγινώσκειν autem accipit de sim- plici cognitione, q. d. Apostolus, se non alia scribe- re, quam quorum ipsi poterant recordari Corinthii, aut etiam quae sponte ipsi scirent & intelligerent, et- iamsi non ea suggereret: Ea tamen interpretatio Bezae violenta videtur, nec satis cum praecedenti- bus & sequentibus cohaerere. Videntur autem no- stro judicio simplicius illa duo conjungi hoc mo- do, quae modo legitis, sed & cognovistis, quum κα- τὰ πόδα ita reddantur a Beza: Non enim alia scribimus, quam quae legitis, aut etiam agnoscitis. Quo pacto Ambrosiaster: Ea, inquit, se dicit scri- bere, quae non solum literis cernerent, sed & ope- ribus ejus manifesta haberent. Et notat Era- smus, Paulum suo more expressisse hanc senten- tiam, non alia scribimus vobis, quam ea, quae non solum legitis a nobis scripta, verum etiam agno- scitis a nobis expressa re factisque. Beza ad illa καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε, id est, jam satis nostis, & persua- sa habetis, ut Syrus interpres vertit, ut non jam epistolam, sed ipsos eorum animos faciat Apostolus sui illius perpetui candoris testes, quo erga ipsos usus fuerat: quae expositio videtur optime cohaerere cum iis, quae subjiciuntur. Nam alioqui quamvis ora- tio sit animi interpres: Tamen non ita difficile est, candorem scribendo simulare. Aut agnoscitis, nem- pe ut jam ante vobis nota, vel saltem iis prorsus respondentia, quae olim ex me praesente audivistis, sicut Basil. 1. epist. testatur, sed ἐπιγνῶναι, id est, agnovisse epistolam a Gregorio profectam, sicut, in- quit, quosdam agnoscimus esse quorundam filios ex eo, quod parentum vultum referant.

Ἐλπίζω δὲ κὶ ἕως τέλυς ἐπιγνώσεσθε) Ostendit, se non omnem spem abjecisse ad ipsos veniendi. Agnoscetis me, ita spero, perpetuo talem. Nempe ubi ad vos venero.

## 1:14
V. 14. Καθὼς κὶ ἐπέγνωτε ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ μέρες) ἀπὸ μέρες, that is, some of you, just as in Rom. XI. 25. such as some of you have known me, that is, you have shown that you recognize me as such, when you received Timothy so kindly, and followed his admonitions.

He does not yet make an indication of a future arrival here, but says that he hopes that they will always recognize him as such even unto the end. I hope, he says, that it will be that you will continue to know me to be the same, so that the end may correspond to the beginning, as Beza has it here. Who nevertheless explains ἕως τέλυς as perfectly, and wishes τὸ ἀπὸ μέρες to be opposed to it as in part. You, says Paul, have known who I am in some part, as one who has been so long conversant among you, and have even written to you before.

But the former explanation is more convenient. Nor yet is in part opposed to a more perfect future cognition, nor are only some people looked at here, but the Apostle rather thus reproves the Corinthians, because, listening more than enough to rivals and detractors, they still felt less well and honorably about their Apostle. For it is better to refer that to the thing known than to the persons knowing. Theophylactus: But in part you have known me, this is, you have experienced me in part, and have made a trial of me, showing forth some signs of living well.

Ὅτι καύχημα ὑμῶν ἐσμέν) For you rejoice that I am your teacher. Καθάπερ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ) For you will be a joy to me, that is, a cause of joy, when I shall see you participants of the same salvation and glory.

Most people take the word ὅτι causally. Estius, however, referring it to the immediately preceding in a specific sense, in this way: Just as you have already known of me in part and are persuaded that I am your glory or boasting, that is, that from me there is for you matter for boasting, namely that you have obtained such an Apostle, and so sincere a preacher of the Gospel, who does not seek his own things, but only those which are of Jesus Christ and of your salvation. Concerning joy, no one will easily be found who has explained it. Yet so that this may not seem to have been said too arrogantly, he adds, just as you also will be our boasting in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, as if he were to say that he in turn will boast at the coming of the Lord to judgment concerning the Corinthians, among whom he will not have labored without copious fruit. Cf. Matt. XXV. 22. Concerning this καύχημα[τι] in time, Theophylactus beautifully: But when will that place of boasting be given to us? Certainly, even if it were permitted for us to boast at this time, yet especially in the day of the Lord Jesus, that is, at the time of judgment. For in the present, very many, when they notice the insults and mockeries which we tolerate, will perhaps accuse us, and bring forward calumnies. But then, with all things lying open, I shall appear, and I myself by no means such as those who are not true Apostles slander. Nay, you are even to yield to me for glory, because by instructing you I led you to the faith, and made you safe.

Latin:

V. 14. Καθὼς κὶ ἐπέγνωτε ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ μέρες) ἀπὸ μέρες, id est, quidam vestrum, quomodo Rom. XI. 25. qualem me novistis quidam, id est, ostendistis vos me talem agnoscere, cum Timotheum tam benigne excepistis, ejus- que monita sequuti estis.

Nondum hic adventus futuri indicium facit, sed sperare se ait, quod usq; in finem semper ipsum talem agnituri sint. Spero, inquit, fore, ut eundem esse me porro cognoscatis, ut finis respondeat princi- pio, ut Beza hic habet. Qui tamen ἕως τέλυς ex- ponit perfecte, eique τὸ ἀπὸ μέρες ex parte op- poni vult. Vos, inquit Paulus, quis sim, cognovi- stis aliqua ex parte, ut qui apud vos fuerim tam diu versatus, & ad vos etiam antea scripserim.

Sed prior explicatio convenientior est. Neque tamen ex parte opponitur futura perfectiori cognitioni, nec etiam hic aliqui tantum respiciuntur, sed perstringit ita potius Apostolus Corinthios, quod, plus satis auscultantes æmulis, & obtrectatoribus, minus adhuc benè & honorifice de suo Apostolo sentirent. Præstat enim id ad rem cognitam referre, quàm ad personas cognoscentes. Theophylactus: Ex parte autem me cognovistis, hoc est, in partem me experti jam estis, & fecistis mei periculum, signa nonnulla bene vivendi præferentes.

Ὅτι καύχημα ὑμῶν ἐσμέν) Gaudetis enim me Doctore. Καθάπερ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ) Eritis enim gaudium mihi, id est, causa gaudii, cum videbo vos ejusdem salutis & gloriæ participes.

Vocem ὅτι plerique causaliter accipiunt. Estius tamen referens ad immediatè præcedentia sensu specifico, hoc modo: Quemadmodum & jam ex parte de me cognovistis & persuasum habetis, quod sim gloria sive gloriatio vestra, hoc est, quod ex me vobis sit gloriandi materia, nempe quod nacti sitis talem Apostolum, tamque sincerum Evangelii prædicatorem, qui non sua quærat, sed tantum ea, quæ sunt Jesu Christi ac vestræ salutis. De gaudio nemo facile invenietur, quă exposuerit. Ne tamen arrogantius hoc videatur dixisse, addit, sicut & vos nostra eritis gloriatio in die Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quasi dicat, se vicissim in adventu Domini ad judicium de Corinthiis gloriaturum, apud quos non sine copioso fructu laboraverit. Conf. Matth. XXV. 22. De hoc καύχημα[τι] tempore pulchre Theophylactus: At quando dabitur nobis is gloriandi locus? Certe etsi hoc tempore gloriari nobis liceret, præcipue tamen in Domini Jesu die, hoc est, judicii tempore. In præsentia namque permulti, ubi contumelias & ludibria, quæ toleramus, adverterint, criminabuntur nos forsitan, & calumnias ingerent. Tunc verò universis patentibus videbor, & ipse haud quaquam talis, qualem non veri Apostoli calumniantur. Quin etiam estis mihi ad gloriam concessuri, quia vos instruendo ad fidem perduxi, & salvos feci.

## 1:15
Vers. 15. Καὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πεποιθήσει) Confident that I am dear to most of you. πεποίθησις is בטון 2 Kings XVIII. 20.

Ἐβυλόμην ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς τὸ πρότερον) Here also there is a transposition. For τὸ πρότερον is to be construed with ἐβυλόμην. I had wished to come to you before, namely when I was writing the former epistle, which see XVI. 5. and following. I did not feign that I wished, but in reality I did wish. I said what I felt.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πεποιθήσει) Confisus me vobis plerisque esse cordi. πεποίθησις est בטון 2. Regum XVIII. 20.

Ἐβυλόμην ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς τὸ πρότερον) Hîc quoque trajectio est. Nam τὸ πρότερον constituendum est cum ἐβυλόμην. Volueram antehac ad vos venire, nempe cum priorem epistolam scriberem, quam vide XVI. 5. & sequentibus. Non finxi me velle, sed reipsa volui. Dixi, quod sentiebam.

## 1:16
V. 16. Ἱνα δευτέραν χάριν ἔχητε) That you might have this second benefit from me, as 1 Cor. XVI. 3.

Καὶ δι' ὑμῶν ἐλθεῖν εἰς Μακεδονίαν, καὶ πάλιν ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) The word με is understood: As if he were to say, the first benefit was that I stayed with you intending to go to Macedonia, the second I hoped would be that I would betake myself to you from Macedonia. It is a construction according to the sense. For in the word δευτέραν there is tacitly contained a double benefit, which he explains what kind it is.

Καὶ ὑφ' ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι εἰς τὴν Ἰεδαίαν) That is, that I might take some of you as companions of my journey into Judea, if by chance I were to go there. See 1 Corinth. XVI. 4. 5. 6. 7. and what is said there.

Grotius’s explanation, by which he explains the first and second benefit, is pleasing. But because the latter had to be deferred, the delay is therefore excused here by the Apostle. Moreover, his arrival is promised anew in ch. XII. 14 and ch. XIII. 1. It was not, however, entirely abandoned, as it seemed to Grotius at 1 Cor. XVI. 6. The Greek interpreters, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Oecumenius, understand these things in this way: I wished to come to you not only after the Macedonian journey, as I wrote (in the former epistle), but also before it. I intended more than I wrote. But Estius objects: If Paul intended so much, he did not write it: What need was there for him to excuse himself concerning such an unfulfilled intention, and he inquires whether in that very first epistle, which is lost, he revealed that intention of his to the Corinthians? But there is no need for those, according to this explanation of Grotius. For these do not refer to a different intention, but to a twofold arrival of Paul.

Latin:

V. 16. Ἱνα δευτέραν χάριν ἔχητε) Ut alterum hoc à me habeatis beneficium, ut 1. Cor. XVI. 3.

Καὶ δι' ὑμῶν ἐλθεῖν εἰς Μακεδονίαν, καὶ πάλιν ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Subauditur με: Quasi dicat, primum beneficium fuit, quod apud vos substiti in Macedoniam iturus, alterum sperabam fore, quod ex Macedonia ad vos me reciperem. Est constructio πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. Nam in voce δευτέραν tacitè inest duplex beneficium, quod quale sit explicat.

Καὶ ὑφ' ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι εἰς τὴν Ἰεδαίαν) Id est, ut quosdam de vobis comites sumerem mei in Judæam itineris, si forte eò irem. Vide 1. Corinth. XVI. 4. 5. 6. 7. & ibi dicta.

Placet Grotiana explicatio, qua primum & alterum beneficium explicat. Quod posterius vero differendum fuit, ideoque excusatur hic dilatio ab Apostolo. Promittitur autem denuo adventus cap. XII. 14. cap. XIII. 1. Non verò planè intermissus est, ut ad 1. Cor. XVI. 6. visum fuit Grotio. Interpretes Græci, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, & Oecumenius hæc accipiunt hoc modo: Volui non modo post iter Macedonicum, uti scripsi, (priori epistola) sed & ante illud ad vos venire. Plus volui quàm scripsi. Ast objicit Estius : Si Paulus voluit tantum, non scripsit : Quid opus erat, ut de ejusmodi voluntate non impleta se excusaret, ac disquirit, annè in illa omnium prima epistola, quæ deperdita, Corinthiis istam voluntatem suam aperuerit ? sed illis opus non est, secundum hanc Grotii explicationem. Non enim diversam vo- luntatem, sed geminum adventum Pauli hæc re- ferunt.

## 1:17
V. 17. Did I then, when I was thus minded) Since in truth that was my plan at that time.

Did I use lightness?) Can I be accused because I said something different then than what I had in mind? Ἐλαφρία here is the same as κυφότης, that is, vanity, as the glossary explains. We are accustomed to call those vain who are liars: Because their words lack weight: Virgil called the vain and the liar joined together.

Or the things I plan, do I plan according to the flesh?) But someone will say, did you change your plan? Paul answers, did I change it for my own advantage? If I had done that, there could be some appearance of accusing me.

That there might be with me yes, yes, no, no?) It must be read here entirely as the Syriac reads here, and it follows immediately: that there might be with me yes, and no, that is, so that for that reason I say one thing and do another. For yes, likewise no, sometimes signify that promissory affirmation, but this one signifies the abnegative, sometimes the very implementation of such a promise: Therefore, from this double meaning, a knot has been made here, as we said in Book II of the Law of War and Peace XXX. 21. and on Matthew V. 37. Festus, where he explains the word nauci: Some say it is from the Greek, because it is yes and no, wishing to signify a light man. Light, ἐλαφρὸν, thus that passage of Festus explains this one of Paul most excellently.

The Syriac is not foreign to this sense, rendering it thus: This therefore which I thought, did I think it as a light man? Ἐλαφρία is lightness of mind. For nothing is more mobile than deer; they are excited to motion by any noise. Thus, characters that are easy to change their plans are called light, ἐλαφρά. To consult according to the flesh is a custom born in men, who do not persist in a plan longer than it seems useful and proper to them. The sense is in the open: Am I light, am I carnal? so that for that reason there is with me, it is, and it is not, now to affirm, now to deny, now to will, now to not will, which is carnal and familiar to light men. Weinrichius has it thus: My plans do not proceed from the flesh, but from the guidance of the Holy Spirit, who according to His most free will rules the events of human plans and actions, so that it is not in man to direct his way, nor in a man to direct his steps, as the Prophet Jeremiah says in chapter X. Therefore, a man can propose something to himself, which nevertheless God Himself disposes according to His own will. Thus in Acts chapter XVI, Paul and Silas had entirely determined to go into Bithynia, but they are forced to change their mind, because the Spirit does not permit this to them. Nor is there need for the Estian suspicion that the negative particle NOT has fallen out, which being added it might be read: That there might not be with me yes yes and no no. For no codex has had that same reading, approved by Grotius; not the Syriac indeed, in which he himself is mistaken. The Greek codices, however, have it, concerning which let Beza be consulted on this passage. Camerarius has it thus: Others have punctuated these things differently. We shall relate what we have deemed most true. It is, however, ἐν πάθει, that is, with singular intention and zeal toward the Corinthians, when he wished to defend why the promise had not been fulfilled, thus therefore the speech is changed by the figure of interrogation. He also said κατὰ σάρκα by a Hebrew phrase, in the human manner. This therefore is the sense: When that was my plan, did I use lightness in it? Or are my plans carnal? that is, human, so that it is the case that I can affirm or deny out of myself? Or so that affirmations and negations are in my power? For he wishes this to be understood, that his plans are governed divinely by the Holy Spirit, so that he himself can determine nothing by human judgment, but has a necessity to obey the will of the Holy Spirit. Thus this defense is excellent. The intention was to come to you long ago. This I did not change, but it seemed otherwise to GOD, to whom it behooves me to yield. For I do not deliberate anything in such a way that I wish it to be done or not done, which is approved by human judgment, but my will serves the decision of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

V. 17. Τῦτο ὖν βυλευσάμενος) Cum revera id meum consilium fuerit eô tempore.

Μήτι ἄρα τῇ ἐλαφρίᾳ ἐχρησάμην;) Possumne accusari, quod aliud tunc dixissem, quam haberem in animo ? Ἐλα- φρία hic idem, quod κυφότης, id est, vanitas, ut exponit glossarium. Vanos vocare solemus eos, qui mendaces sunt : Quia verba eorum carent pondere : Vanum mendacem- que conjunctum dixit Virgilius.

Ἡ ἃ βυλεύομαι, κατὰ σάρκα βυλεύομαι;) At dicet aliquis, mutasti consilium ? Respondet Paulus, mutavine ob mea commoda ? Id si fecissem, poterat aliqua species esse me accusandi.

Ἱνα ἦ παρ᾽ ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, τὸ ὔ, ὔ;) Omnino legendum hic est, quomodo hic legit Syrus, & mox sequitur : ἵνα ἦ παρ᾽ ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ, κὰι τὸ ὔ, id est, ut propterea aliud dicam, aliud faciam. Nam ναὶ, item ὔ modo promissum illud addictivum, hoc verò abnuitivum significant, modo ipsum promissi talis implementum : Itaque ex duplici hoc signi- ficatu facta hic est πλοκὴ, ut diximus libro II. de jure Bel- li & Pacis XXX. 21. & ad Matth. V. 37. Festus ubi expli- cat vocem nauci : Quidam ex Græco quod sit ναὶ κὰι ὐχὶ le- vem hominem significari volente. Levem ἐλαφρὸν, ita opti- me Festi ille locus hunc Pauli explicat.

Non alienus est ab hoc sensu Syrus, reddens ita : Hoc igitur quod cogitavi, nunquid tanquam levis cogitavi. Ἐλαφρία levitas est animi. Cervis enim nihil mobilius est, quovis strepitu excitan- tur ad motum. Sic ingenia, quæ facilia sunt ad mutanda consilia, levia dicuntur, ἐλαφρά. Secun- dum carnem consultare est more hominibus con- nato, qui non diutius in consilio persistunt, quàm ipsis utile & decorum videtur. Sensus in aprico est : Num levis, num carnalis sum ? ut propterea apud me sit, est, & non est, modo affirmare, mo- do negare, modo velle, modo nolle, quod car- nale est, & levibus hominibus familiare. Weinri- chius ita habet: Consilia mea non à carne profici- scuntur, sed à Spiritus Sancti moderamine, qui pro suâ liberrima voluntate consiliorum & actionum humanarum eventus regit, ita, ut non sit hominis via ejus, neque viri, dirigere gressus suos, ut Jere- mias Propheta ait cap. X. Potest itaque homo ali- quid sibi proponere, quod tamen Deus ipse pro sua voluntate disponit. Sic Act. XVI. capite Paulus & Silas omnino constituerant ire in Bithyniam, sed animi sententiam mutare coguntur, propterea, quod Spiritus hoc ipsis non permittit. Nec opus est su- spicione Estianâ, quod exciderit particula negan- di NON, qua addita legatur : Ut non sit apud me est est & non non. Nullus enim codex eandem habuit lectionem, Grotio probatam; Non Syrus quidem, in quo ipse falsus. Græci tamen Codi- ces habent, de quo videatur Beza in hunc lo- cum. Camerarius ita habet : Hæc alii aliter di- stinxerunt. Nos quod verissimum duximus, refe- remus. Est autem ἐν πάθει, id est, singulari volun- tate & studio erga Corinthios, cum defendere vel- let, quod promissum non factum esset, ita igitur mutata est oratio interrogationum figurâ. Etiam κατὰ σάρκα dixit phrasi Hebraica, humano more. Hic igitur sensus est : Cum istud consilium meum esset, nunquid levitate in eo usus sum ? Aut suntne consilia mea carnalia ? id est, humana, ut sit, quod ego ex me ipso affirmare aut negare possim. Vel ut sint affirmationes & negationes penes me. Hoc enim vult intelligi, sua consilia gubernari divinitus à Spiritu Sancto, ut ipse sententia humana nihil possit statuere, sed necesse habeat obsequi voluntati Sancti Spiritus. Ita est præclara hæc defensio. Ani- mus erat, dudum venire ad vos. Hunc non mu- tavi ego, sed aliud visum fuit DEO, cui me morem gerere oportet. Non enim sic delibero quicquam, ut fieri aut non fieri id velim, quod humano judicio probatur, sed mea voluntas inservit arbitrio Spi- ritus Sancti.

## 1:18
V. 18. But God is faithful, that our word, which was toward you, was not yes and no) That is, as true as God is, so true it is, and you know, that I have used no fraud among you. A similar expression: The Lord lives, that is, as truly as the Lord lives.

From those human sayings and promises, in which the Apostle purged himself of lightness and inconstancy, he turns himself to the divine sayings and promises, which he had announced in the proclamation of the word: because for that reason the false Apostles were accusing Paul of lightness in that promise, so that they might render his entire doctrine suspect. Whence Theophylactus thinks that the Apostle is answering that objection, as if the Apostle's preaching could not be safely believed, who did not keep faith in the promise which he made, in such a way that in that promise of arrival the opinion itself deceived him, but the preaching is the work of GOD, and therefore it cannot happen that divine mysteries deceive anyone. But those words God is faithful are to be taken by way of asseveration. For in order to refute the accusation of his doctrine more validly, he appeals to the faithfulness of GOD, or employs the testimony of GOD: Which Aretius prefers to be a certain congratulation, God be praised. Although indeed some still explain the word as the word of the promise of arrival, it is nevertheless clear from what follows that the Apostle is now looking at the word of his Evangelical proclamation. Which was also noted by the blessed Balduinus: This solemn protestation pertains not only to the civil life of Paul, but also to his Apostolic office. For to this end the adversaries were accusing him of lightness, so that his entire doctrine might be rendered suspect of lightness and inconstancy, as if, like Vertumnus, he would affirm this article of faith today, and deny the same tomorrow. He affirms therefore under oath that a notable injury is being done to him, for his own words, whether sermons or epistles, are as far as possible from such lightness and inconstancy.

Latin:

V. 18. Πιστὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς, ὅτι ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν, ὁ πρὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ ἐγένετο ναὶ καὶ οὐ) Id est, quam verus est Deus, tam verum est, & vos scitis, me nulla apud vos fraude usum. Similis loquutio: Vivit Dominus, id est, quam verè vivit Dominus.

A dictis illis & promissis humanis, in quibus se à levitate, & inconstantia purgavit Apostolus ad dicta & promissa divina, quæ in præconio ver- bi annunciarat, se convertit: quia ideò in illa promissione levitatis accusabant Paulum falsi A- postoli, ut ejus universam doctrinam suspectam redderent. Unde putat Theophylactus, objectioni illi, quasi & prædicationi Apostoli tutò non cre- di posset, qui in promisso, quod fecit, non fidem præstitit, sic respondere Apostolum, quod in illa adventus promissione quidem opinio ipsa ipsum fefellerit, prædicatio verò DEI opus sit, & ideo nec fieri possit, ut quempiam fallant divina my- steria. Sed verba illa πιστὸς ὁ Θεὸς accipienda per modum asseverationis. Ut enim eò validius cri- minationem doctrinæ suæ reprobet, ad DEI fidem provocat, vel DEI adhibet testimonium: Quod Aretius mavult congratulationem quan- dam esse, Gott sey Lob. Quanquam verò non- nulli λόγον de verbo promissi adventus adhuc ex- plicent, è sequentibus tamen patet, Apostolum jam respicere verbum præconii sui Evangelici. Quod notatum etiam B. Balduino: Pertinet au- tem hæc solennis protestatio non saltem ad civilem vitam Pauli, sed & ad Apostolicum ejus officium. Nam hunc in finem levitatis eum accusabant ad- versarii, ut universa ejus doctrina levitatis & in- constantiæ suspecta redderetur, quasi Vertumni in- star hodie hunc articulum fidei affirmaret, cras eun- dem negaret. Affirmat itaque sub juramento, in- signem sibi fieri injuriam, suos enim sive sermones, sive epistolas ab ejusmodi levitate & inconstantia quam maximè alienas esse.

## 1:19
V. 19. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy) He explains what is meant by 'by us.' And Silvanus here, as Jerome rightly noted, is none other than he who is Silas in the Acts, by a variation in pronunciation.

He was not yes and no, but in him it has become yes) Christ himself did not hold our words to be void, but confirmed them with many miracles.

There is nothing here about the confirmation of the Apostle's words through miracles performed. He says that Christ, who was preached through them, was not and did not become yes and no. And therefore, the proclamation concerning Christ made to them cannot be considered yes and no: inasmuch as it was made to them by them as ambassadors of Christ. Moreover, he adds Timothy and Silvanus to himself, as witnesses of his preaching and for the sake of declaring mutual agreement, and finally so that he might teach humility by his own example, as Theophylact notes.

Latin:

V. 19. Ὁ γὰρ τῦ Θεῦ ὑιὸς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν δι᾽ ἡμῶν κηρυχθεὶς δι᾽ ἐμᾶ καὶ Σιλουανοῦ καὶ Τιμοθέου) Explicat, quid sit δι᾽ ἡμῶν. Et Silvanus hic, ut rectè notavit Hieronymus, non alius est, quam qui Silas in Actis, varia pronuntiatione.

Οὐκ ἐγένετο ναὶ καὶ οὐ, ἀλλὰ ναὶ ἐν ἀυτῷ γέγονεν) Chri- stus ipse non irrita habuit verba nostra, sed multis mira- culis ea confirmavit.

De confirmatione verborum Apostoli per mi- racula factâ hîc nihil. Christum ait non fuisse aut factum esse na & non, qui prædicatus est per ipsos. Ideoque nec præconium de Christo ad ipsos factum censeri non posse na & non: utpo- te quod per ipsos ceu legatos Christi ad eosdem factum. Addit autem sibi Timotheum & Silva- num, ceu testes prædicationis suæ & mutui con- sensus declarandi gratia, denique ut humilitatem suo exemplo doceat, notante Theophylacto.

## 1:20
V. 20. For as many as are the promises of GOD in the Old Testament, pertaining to the new creation.

In him is the yes, and in him the amen) These have their fulfillment through Christ; yes and amen mean the same thing, and therefore they are also accustomed to be joined together. See the stated passage on the law of war and peace. The one word is Greek, the other Hebrew, similar to Abba, the Father. In the Manuscript: In him is the yes, wherefore also through him is the Amen. That is, because God fulfills the promises through Christ, therefore also for his honor is amen sung in the Churches. And thus the Syrian reads and interprets it.

To God for glory) A transposition for for the glory of God, so that there may be praise to GOD. But if the reading of the Manuscript in these, what precedes, we follow, to God will rightly cohere with that Amen.

Through us) by our ministry. It refers especially to the conversion of the Gentiles.

The Apostle teaches that there was so far from being any variety, uncertainty, or inconstancy in Christ and in the prophetic proclamation concerning Christ, that there is held even through Christ a certainty and fulfillment of all the promises of grace, inasmuch as they are in Christ yes and Amen, and obtain their truth and complement to the glory of God, and that through the ministry of the Apostle, Silvanus, and Timothy. But in whom and through whom all promises have truth and complement, the proclamation of him, whether made immediately by him or mediately and through the Apostles, must by all means not be fallacious and doubtful, but true and certain. For all the promises of the Gospel are yes and Amen in Christ, both because they were made concerning Christ as the principal object of Scripture, and because they are performed and attain their truth through and on account of Christ and his merit and intercession: since outside of Christ no grace comes to us.

Latin:

V. 20. Ὅσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι τῦ Θεῦ) Quotquot sunt promissa DEI in Veteri Testamento, ad novam creationem pertinentia.

Ἐν ἀυτῷ τὸ ναὶ, καὶ ἐν ἀυτῷ τὸ ἀμὴν) Ea per Christum habent suum implementum, ναὶ & ἀμὴν idem valent, ideo- que & conjungi solent. Vide dictum locum de jure belli & pacis. Altera vox Græca est, altera Hebræa, simile Ab- ba ὁ πατὴρ. In Manuscripto: Ἐν ἀυτῷ τὸ ναὶ, διὸ καὶ δι᾽ ἀυ- τῦ τὸ Ἀμήν. Id est, quia Deus promissa per Christum im- plet, ideo etiam ejus honori canitur amen in Ecclesiis. Et sic legit & interpretatus est Syrus.

Τῷ Θεῷ πρὸς δόξαν) Trajectio pro πρὸς δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ, ut DEO laus sit. At si Manuscripti lectionem in iis, quæ præcedunt, sequimur, τῷ Θεῷ rectè cohærebit cum illo Ἀμὴν.

Δι' ἡμῶν) nostro ministerio. Spectat præcipuè gentium conversionem.

In Christo, & Prophetico de Christo præconio adeo non fuisse varietatem, incertitudinem aut in- constantiam, Apostolus docet, ut habeatur etiam per Christum certitudo, & impletio omnium pro- missionum gratiæ, utpote quæ in Christo sunt næ & Amen, veritatem & complementum suum nan- ciscuntur ad DEI gloriam, idque per ministerium Apostoli, Sylvani, & Timothei. In quo autem & per quem omnes promissiones veritatem & com- plementum habent, illius præconium sive ab ipso immediatè, seu mediatè ac per Apostolos factum omninò oportet non fallax & dubium, sed verum & certum esse. Sunt enim næ & Amen in Chri- sto omnes promissiones Evangelicæ, tum quia de Christo ceu præcipuo objecto scripturæ factæ sunt, tum quia per & propter Christum ejusque meritum & intercessionem præstantur & verita- tem suam consequuntur: quum extra Christum nulla nobis obtingat gratia.

## 1:21
V. 21. But he who confirms us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, is God) Supply 'is', and 'but' here means 'for'. For he gives the reason why all these things redound to the honor of God, because this power proceeds from the Father. From him proceeds this anointing, that is, the interior operation of the Spirit, supporting and strengthening faith in Christ. This anointing is also mentioned in 1 John II. 20, namely because it was mystically signified by that anointing which Kings and priests received, as can be seen in the passage Ps. XLV. 8, compared with that which is in Heb. I. Christians are priests because they offer their soul and body and goods to God; they are Kings because they are destined for a kingdom.

Latin:

V. 21. Ὁ δὲ βεβαιῶν ὑμᾶς σὺν ἡμῖν εἰς χριστὸν, καὶ χρίσας ἡμᾶς, Θεὸς) Supple est, & δὲ hîc valet nam. Causam enim reddit, cur ista omnia cedant ad honorem DEI, quia à Pa- tre ista potestas proficiscitur. Ab eo procedit ista unctio, id est, spiritus operatio interior, fidem in Christum fulciens & roborans. Hæc unctio dicitur etiam 1. Joh. II. 20. nem- pe quia mysticè significabatur per illam unctionem, quam accipiebant Reges & sacerdotes, ut videre est loco Ps. XLV. 8. collato eo, qui est Hebr. I. Christiani sacerdotes, quia animum & corpus & bona DEO offerunt, Reges, quia ad regnum destinantur.

## 1:22
V. 22. Who also has sealed us) Who also willed that the power and nature of that Spirit should appear by external signs of testimony. See Eph. I. 13. Faith is added to instruments by the signs of witnesses. See Rom. IV. 11, 1 Cor. IX. 2.

And has given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts) He makes us conscious of those spiritual gifts, which spiritual gifts are an earnest of future spiritual life, below V. 5, Eph. I. 14. The word 'earnest' (arrhabo) is originally Hebrew, and consequently Phoenician, and came into Greek from the Phoenicians, who were excellent merchants. The origin of the word is from 'arab, which is to guarantee or pledge. See Gen. XXXVIII. 18. An earnest is a part of the price, and it pledges for the whole price. See what we said on 1 Corinthians XV. 46. The Latins, cutting off the end of the word, call an earnest 'arrha'. But the word 'arrhabo' is also found in Plautus, Terence, and Varro.

There is no need for us to depart from the ordinary meaning of the word 'but': But he who confirms us. For he teaches, not why all these things redound to the honor of God, but what is the principal point in this discussion, whence both he himself with his colleagues and the faithful Corinthians have certainty regarding the doctrine of the Gospel and the divine promises, so that they may place an undoubted and firm trust in Christ, in whom all promises have their truth, namely not from some human tradition or authority, which cannot generate divine faith and the certainty of faith, but from God himself, who confirms our hearts while he anoints us with that most precious ointment of gladness, or of a most tranquil and joyful conscience, namely with the oil of the Holy Spirit. That there is an allusion to the typical anointing of the Old Testament is manifest; so it cannot be doubted that they refer primarily to the anointing of Christ, in whom we are confirmed, inasmuch as he was anointed for our sake, his companions, with the immense gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that he might be our Prophet, Priest, and King, and might make us prophets, priests, and kings, Apoc. I and V. Concerning which Theophylact says here: 'He himself both anointed us and sealed us, that is, he made us prophets and priests and kings.' For such is he who has been washed in baptism. Prophets indeed, because we perceive and hear what the eye cannot see, and what the ear has never heard. Priests truly, because it is necessary that we offer ourselves to God as a sacrifice, living, holy, and acceptable to him. Finally, he constituted us Kings, because he adopted us as his sons, he in whose dominion are all things, and made us heirs of the future and heavenly empire. But as in the Old Testament the priests themselves and Kings were anointed with oil, so also at this time we are anointed with the Spirit, and we receive his pledge, which God has sent into our hearts. And just as he has bestowed this pledge, so without a doubt he is going to bestow the rest upon us. By 'pledge' in this place he means the gifts of the Spirit. Blessed Balduinus says beautifully: 'Just as athletes were once anointed so that their limbs might be rendered more solid and more capable of enduring the conflict: so that oil of gladness fortifies our heart against the temptations of Satan, the world, and our own flesh, by which the promises of God are attacked.' This anointing of the Holy Spirit therefore accomplishes three things: first, it recreates and exhilarates spiritually, just as ointment and oil recreate corporally, Ps. XLV. 8. Then, it makes us prophets, priests, and kings; just as the prophets, priests, and kings of old were anointed with sacred oil. See 1 Kings XIX. 16 concerning Elisha the Prophet, Ez. XXIX concerning the priest, 1 Sam. X. 1, C. XVI. 13 concerning the King to be anointed. Third, it causes us to struggle bravely against the world, sin, and Satan, just as wrestlers of old were accustomed to be anointed before engaging. Furthermore, God is said to have 'sealed' the Corinthians, not 'signed' them, as the Vulgate has it, as Cajetan, Justinian, and Cornelius a Lapide admit; not because he made the miracles of the Apostolic doctrine appear in them. For God had sealed the Apostle himself and his associates Silvanus and Timothy through the miracles performed by the Apostle among the Corinthians: But because he sealed the certainty of faith in them, just as sacraments are called seals of faith in Rom. IV. 11. And since 'seal' is said even of things, as are letters, Esth. III. 12, ch. VIII. 8, 1 Kings XXI. 8, which are sealed; the stone of Daniel VII. 17. Matth. XXVII. or concerning the truth, which is sealed, Joh. III. 33. concerning sins sealed by GOD, Dan. IX. 24. &c. or concerning persons, both those who are sealed for the sake of others, so that they may be known by them, as the Son is said to be sealed by the Father for our sake Joh. VI. 27. and those who themselves are confirmed concerning some benefit being conferred or conferred: Here the discourse is not concerning a seal as regards manifestation with respect to others, but as regards the confirmation of the person who is sealed. Since a seal is spoken of either concerning an instrument or a signet, by which we seal something, or concerning the image expressed therefrom, or a signature, here the Holy Spirit himself, however, as a signet, cannot be separated from the image which he expresses in us, because the Holy Spirit himself is communicated to us, not only the gifts of the Sp. H. faith, certainty of grace, peace of conscience, and similar things, which are effects of the Holy Spirit; nor is he absent, but graciously present he seals us, and renders us certain of grace, then he cries in our hearts Abba Father, and bears witness to us that we are children of God, Rom. VIII. 16. Gal. IV. 6. Joh. Crocius thus has in his Comment. on Eph. p. 114 concerning this sealing: Lombard and Hugo understand the image of GOD reformed in us. That pleases. By sealing, the image of the seal is imprinted. Thus the image of the H. Spirit is imprinted on the faithful. What is that? Wisdom and holiness, the principal part of which is charity. That is imprinted in sanctification.
