Aristotle in the first book of his Rhetoric calls earlier agreements ἄκυρα, and later ones κύρια, because the earlier agreement is rendered void and ineffective by the later: whence is derived κυρόω, as if I approve by votes and make valid. He therefore exhorts them, as Estius interprets and observes, to make their charity toward him firm and valid by public consent and decree, namely by receiving him into the peace of the Church. This sense is demanded by the Greek verb κυρῶσαι, which does not mean just any kind of confirmation, or (as Tertullian and Pacianus read) to constitute, but to decree with authority and to transact legitimately. Let one also compare Beza on this passage. Some think that by this confirmation of charity, participation in the Eucharist is properly signified, as it was the symbol of restored communion. Certainly this commentary would be welcome and worthy of acceptance, if it were found to have a foundation in the scriptures or the fathers, as Estius says here again.

Vers. 19. For this I wrote) Namely, those things which are in the first epistle, chapter V. This aorist has the meaning of a pluperfect.

That I might know your proof, whether you are obedient in all things) δοκιμὴ is an experiment, as in Rom. V. verse 4, below VIII. v. 2, IX. 13, XIII. 3, Philipp. II. 22. Here, however, by metonymy, it is the very disposition which is revealed by the trial. That I might know by experience whether you would be willing to obey me in all things as an Apostle of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Διὸ παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς κυρῶσαι εἰς αὐτὸν ἀγάπην) Κυρῶσαι proprie est alicui rei formam suam legitimam dare ac sic eam ratam firmamque facere, hic per transla- tionem est facto ostendere. Nam qui hoc facit, is aliquo modo ratum facit, quod in animo habebat. Factum autem quod hic requiritur, sunt preces totius Ecclesiæ, pro illo graviter afflicto.

De voce κυρῶσαι rectius Erasmus: Quod pro- pemodum valeat, ac si dicas, facite ut pondus & au- toritatem habeat charitas erga illum. Loquitur enim velut ad judices & concionem, quorum suffragiis velit absolvi eum, qui traditus fuerat Satanæ. Nam κυρία concionem significat, in qua creantur magi- stratus, quam Latini vocant comitia & diem ali- cujus rei causa præstitutum, & jus aliquid agendi. Quin & κύριον Græci dicunt scriptum authenticum autoribus Hesychio & Suida. Mihi videtur & ea sententia, quæ vicisset in suffragiis dicta fuisse κυρία, unde proverbium, αὕτη κυρία. Κῦρος item significat efficacem probationem seu pondus, & autoritatem sententiæ, quæ κύρωσις dicitur. Aristoteles libro Rhetoricorum primo pacta priora vocat ἄκυρα, po- steriora κύρια, quod prius pactum posteriore redda- tur irritum & inefficax: Unde ductum κυρόω veluti suffragiis comprobo & ratum facio. Hortatur ergo eos, Estio interprete, & observat, ut publico con- sensu ac decreto firmam ratamque faciant suam erga eum charitatem, recipiendo videlicet eum ad pacem Ecclesiæ. Quem sensum exposcit Græcum verbum κυρῶσαι, quod non significat utcunque confirmare, sive (quemadmodum legunt Tertullianus & Pacianus) constituere, sed cum authoritate decernere & legiti- merem transigere. Conferat etiam Beza in hunc locum. Quidam per hanc charitatis confirmatio- nem proprie significari putat Eucharistiæ participa- tionem, ut quæ erat symbolum redditæ communionis. Sane gratus esset hic Commentarius & acceptione dignus, si in scripturis aut patribus inveniretur ha- bere fundamentum, ut hic iterum Estius.

Vers. 19. Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἔγραψα) Nempe ea, quæ sunt in prima epistola cap. V. Aoristus hic significationem habet plusquamperfecti.

Ἵνα γνῶ τὴν δοκιμὴν ὑμῶν, εἰ εἰς πάντα ὑπήκοοί ἐστε) δο- κιμὴ est experimentum, ut Rom. V. vers. 4. infra VIII. v. 2. IX. 13. XIII. 3. Philipp. II. 22. Hic vero per μετωνυμίαν ipse animus, qui ex periculo patescit. Ut nossem experiendo an mihi ut Christi Apostolo per omnia obedire velletis.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

And to whom you forgive anything) If anything is pardoned to anyone according to the rules of equity and leniency.

And I) As if present in spirit, just as I had been in that delivering over to Satan, 1 Cor. V. v. 4.

For if I have forgiven anything for your sakes in the person of Christ) In the manuscript it is as the Latin also reads: For indeed what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, for your sakes, so that after 'for your sakes' the word 'forgiven' is again to be understood from what precedes. The Arab reads more simply: what I have forgiven, I have forgiven for your sakes. He shows that he had already led the way in pardoning, just as he had previously led the way in condemning. For your sake, he says, I did this, for your good, so that by my example you might learn to use leniency no less than severity; 'In the person of Christ', that is, in this matter looking to Christ, so that I may save men in the faith of Christ. Thus above ch. v. 11, 'From many persons', in respect of many.

Chrysostom interprets the words 'in the person of Christ' as 'that which is according to God or for the glory of Christ, and this by the command of Christ', that is, either according to God, or for the glory of Christ, or even as this by the command of Christ. The Ambrosiaster renders it 'in the person of Christ', that is, in the place of Christ. For he who bears the person of Christ pardons in the place of Christ. Erasmus renders it 'in the person or in the face or sight of Christ', as if before Christ. Which sense is also found in the Greek scholia. But 'in the sight of' and 'before' is never rendered by 'en prosopo', but by 'enanti', 'enantion', 'enopion', or 'kata prosopon' (Luke II. v. 31, Acts III. v. 13, Gal. II. v. 11, 2 Cor. X. v. 1, 7) or 'eis prosopon' (2 Cor. II. v. 21). And therefore the ancient Latin commentators more correctly explained it as 'in the person of Christ', that is, in the name, place, and authority of Christ: just as he had also delivered the man to Satan in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians. V. Which the Greek text of Theophylact also has: 'as if being in his person', as if representing his person.

Estius and other Papists attempt to establish their indulgences from this passage, because it is asserted here that there is a power of relaxing the temporal punishment still remaining for one who has done penance for a sin. But what temporal punishment still remained for the fornicator, which the Apostle ascribes to the Corinthians the power of relaxing? But it is a Papistic misinterpretation. 'It is sufficient for him', that is, he has already paid enough of the penalties, let the rest be pardoned to him: in which Estius falsely appeals to the agreement of Chrysostom and Theophylact. For they interpret that far otherwise. 'Not only', say the words of Theophylact, 'is all your rebuke begun against him to be dissolved, and reproaches to be taken away, but even more some pardon is to be granted to him, and you should comfort him', that is, restore him by consoling. And do not act otherwise than someone is accustomed to do, who after blows have been inflicted, allows them to be healed.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

ᾧ δέ τι χαρίζεσθε) Si cui aliquid condonatur ex æqui- tatjs & lenitatis regulis.

Καὶ ἐγὼ) Tanquam animo præfens, sicut in illo Satanæ tradendo fueram, 1. Cor. V. v. 4.

Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι δι' ὑμᾶς ἐν προσώπῳ χριστῶ) In Manuscripto est quomodo & Latinus legit: Καὶ γὰρ ὅ κεχάρισμαι, εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι, δι'ὑμᾶς, ut post δι' ὑμᾶς ite- rum subaudiatur κεχάρισμαι ex superioribus. Simplicius legit Arabs: ὃ κεχάρισμαι, κεχάρισμαι δι'ὑμᾶς. Ostendit se jam præivisse condonando, sicut ante præiverat con- demnando. Propter vos, inquit, hoc feci, vestro bono, ut meo exemplo discerctis lenitate non minus, quam se- veritate uti; Ἐν προσώπῳ χριστῦ, id est, in hac re Christum respiciens, ut homines servem in fide Christi. Sic supra l. v. 11. Ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων, respectu multorum.

Chrysostomus verba ἐν προσώπῳ χριστῦ inter- pretatur ἡ κατὰ Θεὸν ἢ εἰς δόξαν τῦ χριστ, καὶ τῦτο κελέυοντος, id est, vel secundum Deum, vel in glo- riam Christi, aut velut & hoc jubente Christo. Am- brosianus reddit, in persona Christi, id est, vice Chri- sti. Nam qui personam Christi gerit, vice Chri- sti condonat. Erasmus reddit, in persona vel in facie aut conspectu Christi, quasi coram Christo. Qui sensus etiam habetur in scholiis Græcorum. Sed in conspectu & coram nunquam redditur ἐν προσ- ώπῳ, sed ἐνάντι, ἐναντίον, ἐνώπιον, aut κατὰ πρόσ- ωπον Luc. II. v. 31. Actor. III. vers. 13. Gal. II. v. 11. 2. Cor. X. v. 1. 7. vel εἰς πρόσωπον 2. Cor. II. v. 21. Ideoque rectius Latini Commentatores veteres in persona Christi exposuere, id est, nomine, vice, & autoritate Christi: uti etiam in nomine Domini nostri JESU Christi hominem Satanæ tradiderat 1. Corinth. V. Quod etiam habet Græcus textus Theophylact. ὡς ἀντὶ πρόσωπον ὢν ἐκείνε, velut il- lius personam referens.

Estius, aliique Pontificii ex hoc loco indulgen- tias suas stabilire conantur, quod asseratur hic potestas relaxandi pœnam temporalem ei, qui pro peccato pœnitentiam egit, adhuc restantem. Sed quæ pœna temporalis adhuc restabat fornicatori, quam relaxandi potestatem Corinthiis adscribat Apostolus? Ψευδερμηνεία autem Papistica est. Sufficit illi, id est, satis jam pœnarum dedit, reli- quum ei condonetur: In qua falso ad consensum Chrysostomi & Theophylacti provocat Estius. Lon- ge aliter enim illud interpretantur. Non modo, (inquit), verba sunt Theophylacti, solvenda est omnis vestra in eum cœpta objurgatio, & tollenda convitia, quin & plus illi aliquid veniæ conceden- dum, & consolemini, hoc est, solando reficite. Nec secus agite, quam solet quispiam, qui post plagas in- gestas curari illas permiserit.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

Lest we should be circumvented by Satan) Lest we be circumvented by Satan, as this Latin has it: lest we be defrauded, as Tertullian. There is a metonymy here also. For those who circumvent others are accustomed to have more than their own. In a similar way 'ashaq', which is properly 'pleonektein', also signifies to wound and to injure in any way. Thus also this word is used below, 2 Cor. XII. v. 17 and 18. He speaks in the plural, however, because the ruin of even one is a loss to Christ and the Church.

For we are not ignorant of his devices) 'noemata', 'mezimmoth', 'methodeias' (Ephes. VI. v. 11). Satan does this in diverse ways, so that he may lead men away from God, either by allurements or by injecting despair. See below XI. v. 3, 1 Pet. V. v. 8. The ancient Christians also, even those whom they never admitted to communion because of grave crimes, nevertheless did not wish to despair of God's mercy. Tertullian on Modesty: 'This will be the penance, which we also acknowledge is indeed owed much more, but we reserve the pardon for God.' Much more did they command those who were abstaining for a time to hope for good.

There is no reason why the proper force of the plural expression should be neglected. For not only that fornicator, but also others, who indeed could be offended by too much severity toward him, were easily exposed to such danger, or were precipitating themselves also into peril through mercy. Here that 'for your sakes' is explained. For by too much austerity an occasion is offered to Satan of seizing us into his power, as those who, forgetful of all mercy and charity, neglect him who is already sticking in the jaws of the Devil, whom we could have snatched away by our commiseration. The thoughts & cogitations of Satan are his counsels & intentions of seducing men from true piety toward God, and charity toward their neighbor, a thing which can sometimes be done by excessive leniency, by which the souls of men are suffocated in the mire of malice, sometimes by excessive harshness, by which others are precipitated into the abyss of despair, and the rest who could have rescued them from there rush into their own destruction through their inhumanity and ἀστοργίᾳ, as the blessed Balduinus holds here.

THE LATTER PART. A celebration of divine grace for the manifestation of the fragrance of saving knowledge.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ἱνα μὴ πλεονεκτηθῶμεν ὑπὸ τῦ Σατανᾶ) Ne circumve- niamur a Satana, ut hic Latinus: ne fraudemur, ut Tertul- lianus. Est & hic Metonymia. Nam qui alios circumve niunt, plus suo habere solent. Pari modo עשׁק quod pro- prie est πλεονεκτεῖν, etiam vulnerare & quovis modo lædere significat. Sic & infra hoc verbum sumitur 2. Cor. XII. v. 17. & 18. Pluraliter autem loquitur, quia etiam unius exitium damnum est Christi & Ecclesiæ.

Οὐ γὰρ αὐτῦ τὰ νοήματα ἀγνοῦμεν) νοήματα מְזִמּוֹת με- θοδείας Ephes. VI. vers. 11. diversis modis hoc agit Satanas, ut homines à Deo abducat, aut illecebris, aut injecta de- speratione. Vide infra XI. v. 3. 1. Petr. V. v. 8. Christiani veteres etiam eos, quos ob gravia crimina ad communio- nem nunquam admittebant, nolebant tamen desperare de Dei misericordia. Tertullianus de pudicitia: Hæc erit pœnitentia, quam & nos deberi quidem agnoscimus multo magis, sed de venia Deo reservamus. Multo magis ad tem- pus abstentis jubebant bene sperare.

Pluralis loquutionis propria vis cur negliga- tur, nulla causa est. Nam non solus ille fornica- tor, sed etiam alii, qui scilicet nimia erga ipsum se- veritate offendi poterant, periculo tali facile ex- ponebantur, aut semetipsos quoque per miseri- cordiam in discrimen præcipitabant. Explicatur hic illud δι᾽ ὑμᾶς. Nimia enim austeritate occasio præbetur Satanæ rapiendi nos in suam potestatem, ut qui misericordiæ & charitatis omnis obliti negligimus eum in faucibus Diaboli jam hærentem, quem nostra commiseratione eripere poteramus. Νοήματα & cogitationes Satanæ sunt ejus consilia & intentiones seducendi homines à vera pietate in Deum, & charitate in proximum, id quod interdum nimia lenitate fieri potest, qua suffocantur hominum animi in cæno malitiæ, interdum asperitate nimia, qua præcipitantur alii in desperationis abyssum & cæteri qui eos inde eripere poterant inhumanitate & ἀστοργίᾳ sua proprium ruunt in exitium, ut hic habet B. Balduinus.

PARS POSTERIOR. Gratiæ divinæ pro manifestatione odoris cognitionis salutiferæ celebratio.

## 2:12
Ver. 12. But when I came to Troas, for the gospel of Christ) This looks to the history which we have in Acts 16. v. 2. Tim. IV. 13.

To others it seems that this arrival of Paul at Troas is not found, but is omitted in the history of Luke, and is intermediate between the first, of which Acts XVI, and the third, which is in Acts XX. ver. 6, and that it happened when Paul set out to go into Macedonia, Acts XX. v. 1.

And a door being opened to me in the Lord) Great hope having been given to me of acquiring many for Christ. See 1. Corinth. XVI. 9. and here it is although.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἐλθὼν δὲ εἰς τὴν Τρῳάδα, εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ) Spectat hoc ad historiam, quam habemus Actor. 16. v. 2. Tim. IV. 13.

Aliis videtur, hunc Pauli ad Troadem accessum non reperiri, sed prætermitti in historia Lucæ, & medium esse inter primum, de quo Actor. XVI. & tertium, quem Actor. XX. vers. 6. ac contigisse, quando profectus est Paulus, ut iret in Macedoniam Act. XX. v. 1.

Καὶ θύρας μοι ἀνεῳγμένης ἐν Κυρίῳ) Magna spe mihi data multos Christo acquirendi. Vide 1. Corinth. XVI. 9. καὶ hic est quamvis.

## 2:13
Ver. 13. I had no rest in my spirit) Ἄνεσις signifies rest of mind, Acts XXIV. ver. 23. below VII. 5. VIII. 13. 2. Thess. I. 7.

In the Lord and the power of the Lord, or through the Lord, as the Syrian and others interpret, or because God opened the hearts of those to whom he was preaching. Compare 1. Cor. XVI. 9. Act. XVI.

Because I did not find Titus my brother) Because Titus had been at Corinth on some occasion, and was well received, below VII. ver. 7. 13 14. Therefore Paul shows both here and elsewhere how pleasing that is to him. For he valued Titus highly, so that he bore the absence of so good a helper most heavily.

Jerome in epistle 150 to Hedibia, q. 11, warns that Titus was an interpreter for Paul, and therefore he was saddened because he had not found the pipe and instrument of his preaching at that time, through which he might sing of Christ. But this cause is nothing, since Paul, being endowed with the gift of tongues, had no need of an interpreter. Others therefore seek other causes. The Greek interpreters in general think that the absence of Titus, as an excellent co-worker, was the cause that the Apostle could not finish what he had begun at Troas in the business of preaching the Gospel, as Theophylact says, because the Apostle could by no means instruct the faithful alone, with the unbelievers clamoring. Which cause also Ambrosiaster, Haymo, Lombard, Thomas, Lyranus, and Dionysius the Carthusian bring forward. But the cause of Pelagius, Primasius, Sedulius, and among the Greeks, Theodoret, is altogether to be preferred, which flows from the text itself, as it is that in which the Apostle is occupied, to demonstrate his affection for the Corinthians, that because he did not find Titus he had no rest, because he had anxiously awaited through Titus, whom he had sent to Corinth, in what state the Corinthian Church was, and whether the Corinthians had amended themselves according to the admonition of the former epistle, so that they might understand, as Primasius teaches, that he did everything for the sake of charity, and although he was not present with the Corinthians in body, he was nevertheless not absent in spirit and solicitude. Which reason is approved by Arias Montanus, Joh. Hofmeister, Estius, among our own by the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, the blessed Balduinus, and receives light from chapter VII. 6; but God, who comforts the humble, comforted us in the coming of Titus. Add ver. 12 seqq.

Ἀλλ’ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς) And here the word αὐτοῖς does not have an expressed noun to which it refers, but a noun is understood from the word Troas. For those who were in Troas are understood.

The Vulgate is barbaric, but 'bidding them farewell I went on into Macedonia.' Ambrose: 'Having said farewell to them.' Erasmus: 'having dismissed them,' which Beza does not approve: for he says, we dismiss those to whom we give the opportunity of departing: but here Paul himself departs. See Mark 6, verse 46. Furthermore, it seems that from this word it can be elicited that Paul did not depart from Troas until the Church was established or certain mandates had been added. The sense, therefore, is: but when I had given mandates, and thus had first ordered and arranged the affairs of the Church, I departed, thence ἐξῆλθον, I went out, or I went on into Macedonia; not indeed as Estius wishes, but when I had dismissed the brothers staying there, having given mandates.

Ἐξῆλθον εἰς Μακεδονίαν) That I might be nearer to Titus, and might call him to me, below 8. 6. 16.

Here it seemed to some that another impediment to Paul's arrival was being insinuated, or the reason for his changed plan regarding visiting the Corinthians before he went into Macedonia. But already before he departed from Ephesus, it had been decided by him to go first into Macedonia, 1 Corinthians 16, verse 5, namely for the sake of collecting the subsidy which he would carry to the needy brothers in Jerusalem. Some make the vision of the Macedonian man, Acts 16, verse 9, the occasion of this journey, with Haymo, Thomas, and Dionysius leading the way. But they are mistaken. For when that vision occurred, Paul had not yet preached the Gospel to the Corinthians, which is most manifest from the series of the acts and journeys of Paul. Therefore, he seems to have gone from Ephesus through Troas, which are two cities of Asia, into Macedonia, Acts 20. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οὐκ ἔσχηκα ἄνεσιν τῷ πνεύματί μου) Ἄνεσις requiem animi significat, Actor. XXIV. vers. 23. infra VII. 5. VIII. 13. 2. Thess. I. 7.

In Domino & virtute Domini, vel per Dominum, ut Syrus & alii interpretantur, vel quia corda eorum aperuit Deus, quibus ille prædicabat. Conf. 1. Cor. XVI. 9. Act. XVI.

Τῷ μὴ εὑρεῖν με Τίτον τὸν ἀδελφόν μου) Quia Titus ex occasione aliqua Corinthi fuerat, & bene exceptus infra VII. vers. 7. 13 14. Ideo ostendit Paulus & hic, & alibi, quam id sibi gratum sit. Plurimi enim à se Titum fieri, ita ut absentiam tam boni adjutoris gravissimè tulerit.

Hieronymus epistola CL. ad Hedibiam q. 11. Titum interpretem Pauli fuisse monet, ideoque eum contristatum fuisse, quia prædicationis suæ impræsentiarum fistulam organumque, per quod Christum caneret, non invenerat. Sed hæc causa nulla est, cum Paulus dono linguarum instructus, nullo opus habuerit interprete. Alii ergo alias causas quærunt. Græci Interpp. in genere absentiam Titi velut egregii multum cooperatoris in causa fuisse putant, quo minus Apostolus, quod cœperat Troade in negotio prædicandi Evangelii posset absolvere, ut Theophylactus, quia haudquaquam solus Apostolus posset fideles instituere, incredulis obstrepentibus. Quam causam & Ambrosiasier, Haymo, Lombardus, Thomas, Lyranus & Dionysius Carthusianus adferunt. Sed præferenda omnino Pelagii, Primafii, Sedulii & è Græcis Theodoreti causa, quæ è textu ipso fluit, utpote in quo occupatur Apostolus, ut demonstret affectum suum Corinthiis, quod Tito non invento requiem non habuerit, quod per Titum, quem Corinthum miserat, anxiè expectarat, quo loco res Corinthiacæ Ecclesiæ esset, & an Corinthii se juxta monitum prioris epistolæ emendarint, ut intelligant, docente Primafio, ipsum omnia propter charitatem fecisse, & quamvis Corinthiis corpore non adfuerit, spiritu tamen & solicitudine non defuisse. Quæ ratio probatur Ariæmontano, Joh. Hofmeistero, Estio, è nostris B. Ægid. Hunnio, B. Balduino, & è cap. VII. 6. lucem accipit; sed qui consolatur humiles, consolatus est nos Deus in adventu Titi. Adde vers. 12. seqq.

Ἀλλ’ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς) Et hic αὐτοῖς nomen non ha- bet expressum quo referatur, sed subintelligitur no- men ex voce Troadis. Intelliguntur enim, qui erant Troade.

Vulgata barbare, sed valefaciens eis profectus sum in Macedoniam. Ambros. Vale illis facto. Erasmus dimissis illis, quod non probatur Beza: dimittimus enim, inquit, eos, quibus abeundi fa- cultatem facimus: Hic vero Paulus ipse discedit. Vide Marci VI. vers. 46. Deinde videtur ex hoc verbo elici posse Paulum nonnisi constituta Eccle- sia aut certę additis mandatis Troade discessisse. Sen- sus ergo est, sed cum datis mandatis, adeoque rebus Ecclesię prius ordinatis & dispositis discessissem, inde ἐξῆλθον, exivi, vel profectus sum in Mace- doniam; non vero ut Estius vult, sed cum fratres illic morantes, datis mandatis, dimisissem.

Ἐξῆλθον εἰς Μακεδονίαν) Ut proprior essem Tito, & eum ad me vocarem, infr. VIII. 6. 16.

Hic impedimentum aliud adventus Pauli insi- nuari nonnullis visum est, vel rationem mutati consilii de Corinthiis prius visendis quam iret in Macedoniam. Sed jam ante, quam Epheso disce- deret, constitutum erat ipsi, prius in Macedo- niam proficisci 1. Corinth. XVI. vers. 5. colligendi nempe subsidii causa, quod ad fratres egenos Hierosolymam perferret. Occasionem hujus iti- neris faciunt quidam visionem viri Macedonici, Actor. XVI. vers. 9. præeunte Haymone, Thoma, Dionysio. Sed falluntur. Cum enim visio illa contigit, nondum prædicaverat Paulus Corinthiis Evangelium, quod è serie actorum & itinerum Pauli manifestissimum est. Epheso ergò per Troa- dem, quæ duæ civitates Asiæ sunt, profectus vide- tur in Macedoniam, Act. XX. 1.

## 2:14
V. 14. Τῷ δὲ Θεῷ χάρις, τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ) It is true what learned men have noted, that θριαμβεύειν here is used for the Hiphil, just as βασιλεύειν is to make someone reign, 1 Samuel 9, verse 22, 12, verse 1, 15, verse 35, and ἐπισπεύδειν is to incite to haste: Esther 6, verse 14. Moreover, θριαμβεύειν corresponds to the Hebrew תגביר. God through Christ causes us to overcome all adverse things. Thus both the Syrian and Ambrose seem to have understood this word.

Jerome, in the place cited, renders it thus: 'He leads his triumph through us.' So also most Greeks and Latins, both ancient and recent, 'He makes us triumph,' not only does He make us victors, but He also renders us glorious and conspicuous from our victories, as if publicly celebrating a triumph. Thus also Erasmus: 'Who triumphs through us.' But Beza and Estius rightly observe that the Apostle is Hebraizing and that the word θριαμβεύω is to be taken in the Hiphil form, whom Grotius has not undeservedly followed here. In Christ, that is, through and because of Christ.

Καὶ τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς γνώσεως αὐτῦ, φανερῦντι δι’ ἡμῶν ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ) He alludes to that perfumed ointment with which the high priest was anointed, Exodus 30, verse 23, Psalm 133, verse 2. By a good odor here, however, is signified a good reputation, Hosea 14, verse 7, Jeremiah 45, verse 11, just as by a bad odor a bad reputation, Genesis 34, verse 30, Exodus 5, verse 21.

The Belgian Interpreters explain it as the odor of the incense of sacrifices diffusing through the temple. Beza wishes both the anointing of the priests and the incense of the sacrifices to be regarded; both can be admitted. Camerarius here not unaptly wishes χρίσμα, which was mentioned above, to be regarded as well. The Gospel, therefore, is a spiritual anointing. This indeed remains such, nor does it admit its own fragrance, although, just as ointments kill beetles, so the divine odor of the Gospel is wont to be destructive to the impious, because of their contumacy. Estius explains it thus: 'He spreads the knowledge and fame of Himself, like a certain odor, everywhere through me and the partners of my labor in the Gospel: while we not only preach Christ among all, but are also ground down as if by pestles by persecutions and pressures, so that the odor of the knowledge of God, that is, His fame, may be diffused from us as far as possible.' For if odoriferous things are ground, just as they smell more vehemently, so they spread their odor further. Moreover, in the Greek it is not 'His knowledge,' as the Vulgate has it, but αὐτῦ, that is, of Christ, whose name is 'oil poured out,' Canticles 1, verses 2, 3. Ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ, Aretius notes that this is to be understood appropriately, namely, where the Apostle had come, just as in Romans 15, verse 19, he says that he had filled all things with the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem in a circuit as far as Illyricum; yet it is not to be denied that the odor of the knowledge of Christ was also spread there where the Apostle did not come. For where the foot of the Apostles did not come, there their sound came. Romans 10, verse 18, Colossians 1, verse 24.

Latin:

V. 14. Τῷ δὲ Θεῷ χάρις, τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ) Verum est quod viri eruditi notarunt θριαμβεύειν hic esse pro Hiphil, sicut βασιλεύειν est facere ut quis regnet, 1. Samuel. IX. vers. 22. XII. vers. 1. XV. vers. 35. & ἐπισπεύδειν ad festinandum incitare: Esther. VI. vers. 14. Respondet autem θριαμβεύειν Hebræo תגביר Deus per Christum facit, ut omnia adversa superemus. Ita videntur accepisse hoc verbum tum Syrus, tum Am- brosius.

Hieronymus u.s. ita reddit: Triumphum suum agit per nos. Ita etiam Græci & Latini plerique tam veteres quam recentiores triumphare nos facit, non solum victores nos efficit, sed etiam ex victoriis reddit gloriosos & conspicuos, velut publicè triumphum agentes. Sic etiam Erasmus: Qui triumphat per nos. Sed rectè observant Beza & Estius, Apostolum Hebraizare & verbum θριαμβεύω forma Hiphilica accipi, quos hic non immerito sequutus est Grotius. In Christo, id est, per & propter Christum.

Καὶ τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς γνώσεως αὐτῦ, φανερῦντι δι’ ἡμῶν ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ) Alludit ad unguentum illud odoratum, quo ungebatur summus sacerdos, Exod. XXX. vers. 23. Psalm. CXXXIII. vers. 2. Per bonum odorem autem hic significatur bona fama, Oseæ XIV. vers. 7. Jer. XLV. v. 11. sicut per malum odorem mala fama, Gen. XXXIV. vers. 30. Exod. V. vers. 21.

Belgici Interpretes suffitus sacrificiorum odo- rem per templum diffundentes explicant. Beza & unctionem sacerdotum, & sacrificiorum suffi- tus respici vult; utrumque admitti potest. Ca- merarius hic non inconcinne etiam respici vult χρίσμα, cujus supra mentio facta est. Evange- lium igitur unctio spiritualis est. Hæc manet illa quidem talis, neque admittit fragrantiam suam, quamvis, ut unguenta scarabeos necant, ita Ev- angelii divinus odor impiis exitiosus esse soleat, propter contumaciam ipsorum. Estius ita expo- nit: Sui notitiam ac famam, velut odorem quen- dam, spargit quaquaversum per me & socios labo- ris mei in Evangelio: Dum non modo prædicamus Christum apud omnes, sed etiam persecutionibus & pressuris quasi pistillis conterimur, ut odor noti- tiæ Dei, id est, fama ejus, à nobis quam longissime diffundatur. Res enim odoriferæ si conterantur, ut vehementius olent, ita longius odorem spargunt. Cæterum in Græco non est notitia sua, ut Vulga- ta habet, sed αὐτῦ ejus scilicet Christi, cujus no- men oleum effusum est Cant. I. vers. 2. 3. Ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ id accommodè intelligendum notat Aretius, quo scilicet venerat Apostolus quomodo Rom. XV. versu 19. ait, se ab Hierosolymis per circuitum usque ad Illyricum omnia replevisse Evangelio Christi; non tamen negandum, etiam odorem cognitionis de Christo sparsum illic, quo non venit Apostolus. Nam quo non venit pes Aposto- lorum, eò venit sonus eorum. Roman. X. versu 18. Coloss. I. v. 24.

## 2:15
Vers. 15.

Ὅτι χριστῦ εὐωδία ἐσμὲν τῷ Θεῷ ἐν τοῖς σωζομένοις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις) One must understand here in the second member κακωδία by the force of opposites. A similar ellipsis of an opposite is in 1 Timothy 4, verse 3, 1 Corinthians 14, verse 44, 1 Timothy 2, verse 12. The pious speak well of the Apostles and the Gospel, and the impious speak ill. Moreover, the pious are called σωζόμενοι from the outcome, Acts 3, verse 47, conversely the impious are οἱ ἀπολλύμενοι, 2 Corinthians 1, verse 18. Θεῷ, that is, to the honor of GOD.

There is no reason why we should understand κακωδίαν here: Nor is it possible to find a similar argument for an ellipsis in the cited passages. Nor is the discourse about how men receive the Gospel, well or ill: but about the internal power of the Gospel and the divine intention. That the ministers of the Gospel of Christ are a good odor, pleasing to God, not only regarding those who are saved, but also regarding those who perish by their own fault. Jerome: 'We are a good odor of the name of Christ to GOD in every place, and the fragrance of our preaching breathes far and wide.' On which Theophylact elegantly says: 'What he says is such, whether they attain salvation and the reward, or destruction and perdition, the Gospel nevertheless prevails by its own virtue and strength: and we remain in the same state in which we are.' And just as light itself and radiance, darkening all that is weak, otherwise persists in its own splendor: honey likewise, even if it seems bitter to those who have a depraved taste, nevertheless preserves its own sweetness; thus the Gospel is fragrant and sweet, even though some unbelievers perish and are scattered. Nor does Estius deny this: For although not all receive the faith of Christ, we nevertheless, like some fragrant ointment or flowers or herbs, spread the fame of his name, as a good and sweet odor, and most pleasing to God (for it is an allusion to the odor of incense burned) among all, not only those who believe and are saved, but also those who, unwilling to believe, perish. These are the words of Estius: Who has already noted the Grotian gloss anonymously in another place: There is one who thinks that part, and in those who perish, should be supplied by the contrary in this way: And we are a bad odor in those who perish. But far be it that we should admit that good ministers of Christ are or spread a bad odor to God on account of the malice of those who do not believe. It is known, however, that a good odor is salutary to some, and lethal to others.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ὅτι χριστῦ εὐωδία ἐσμὲν τῷ Θεῷ ἐν τοῖς σωζομένοις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις) Subaudiendum hic est in secundo membro κακωδία ex vi contrariorum. Similis ἔλλειψις contrarii 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 3. 1. Corinth. XIV. vers. 44. 1. Timoth. II. vers. 12. Pii bene de Apostolis & Evange- lio loquuntur, & impii male. Vocantur autem ex even- tu pii σωζόμενοι, Actor. III. vers. 47. contra impii οἱ ἀπολ λύμενοι, 2. Corinth. I. vers. 18. Θεῷ, id est, in honorem DEI.

Non est, quod hic subaudiamus κακωδίαν: Nec simile Ἐλλείψεως argumentum reperire est lo- cis allegatis. Neque de eo sermo est, quomo- do accipiant homines Evangelium, benè, an male: sed de interna Evangelii vi, & intentione divina. Quod ministri Evangelii Christi bonus odor sint, Deo gratus, non tantùm quoad eos, qui salvantur, sed etiam quoad eos, qui culpa sua pereunt. Hieronymus: Nominis Christi in omni loco bonus odor sumus DEO, & prædicationis no- stræ longe lateque spirat fragrantia. Quo de ele- ganter Theophylactus: Quod autem dicit, tale est, sive salutem assequantur, præmiumque, sive inter- itum & perditionem, præstat tamen sua virtute & robore Evangelium: nosque eodem, quo sumus statu, consistimus. Et quemadmodum lux ipsa & ful- gor, imbecilliom quæque obtenebrans, in suo splendo- re alioqui perseverat: Mel item, etsi his, qui de- pravato sunt gustu, amarius videatur, suam ta- men servat dulcedinem; sic Evangelium odorum est & suave, tametsi increduli nonnulli intereant & dißerdantur. Neque abnuit Estius: Quamvis enim fidem Christi non omnes recipiant, nos tamen instar fragrantis cujusdam unguenti seu florum aut herbarum famam nominis ejus, velut bonum ac suavem odorem, Deoque gratissimum (est enim allu- sio ad odorem thymiamatis incensi) spargimus apud omnes, non eos solum, qui credunt & salvi fiunt, ve- rum etiam qui credere nolentes pereunt. Hæc Estius: Qui Grotianam glossam in alio ἀνωνύμως jam no- tavit: Est qui partem illam, & in iis, qui pereunt, supplendam putet per contrarium hoc modo: Et ma- lus odor sumus in iis, qui pereunt. Sed absit, ut fa- teamur, bonos Christi ministros esse aut spargere malum odorem Deo propter malitiam eorum, qui non credunt. Notum est autem, bonum odorem aliis esse salutarem, aliis lethalem.

## 2:16
Verse 16.

To some a savor of death unto death) Here the former word θανάτυ signifies quality, as in 2 Kings IV, verse 40. The latter signifies the outcome. There are certain odors so bad that they even bring destruction, such as the exhalations of Avernus and the Asphaltite lake. That bad reputation believed concerning the Gospel brings eternal ruin to many. In the Manuscript it is, ἐκ θανάτυ εἰς θάνατον doubtless because that evil report has as its authors men dead in sins.

But to whom a savor of life unto life) Just as certain odors restore those who are deficient in spirit as if to life; so a good report about the Gospel leads those who drink it in to eternal life. And this Manuscript has, ἐκ ζωῆς. Doubtless because that good report is from God, the author of life. A similar manner of speaking is ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν, Rom. I. 17. and below III. 18. ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, and Clement of Alexandria reads this and the preceding member in this way.

There is nothing here about a report, evil or good, believed about the Gospel, but about the εὐωδία τῶ χρισῷ [fragrance in Christ] which is of itself pleasing to God, just as the τῇ ὀσμῇ τῆς γνώσεως τῶ χρισῷ [savor of the knowledge of Christ] spread everywhere by the Apostles is the sole subject; the predicates, however, are diverse. But the subject is not to be doubled, as if the discourse were about both a good report and an evil report, or even as if odors by their own nature, and according to their own quality, were some lethal and bringing destruction, others life. Nor is the report of the Gospel as believed noted here, but the preaching of the Gospel performed by the ministers of God: Therefore, that which says that an evil report has as its authors men dead in sins is also foreign. That preaching is indeed ὀσμὴ τῆς γνώσεως χρισῦ, a savor of the saving knowledge of Christ, and a εὐωδία, a sweet and pleasing odor to God, and thus a ὀσμὴ ζωῆς, a savor of life: And indeed from the intention of God not εἰς θάνατον, unto death; but εἰς ζωὴν, unto life, Ezek. XVIII. v. 32. chap. XXXIII. v. 11. II Tim. ch. 2, v. 4, but from the outcome of certain persons, namely those who are perishing, it is by their own fault and vice ὀσμὴ θανάτου εἰς θάνατον, a savor of death unto death. Estius acknowledges this: Again, he calls himself a savor causally, insofar as by his preaching he spread the fame of the name of Christ far and wide like a sweet savor. This savor was lethal to the wicked and reprobate, not by its own fault, but by theirs; because, on the occasion of the Gospel being preached to them, while they are unwilling to believe, they are more severely condemned: since that savor is always good in itself, even then, when to some it is a savor of death unto death. For thus also the fragrance of a good ointment invigorates a dove, but kills a beetle, as Oecumenius says. Thus also the light of the sun refreshes healthy eyes, but offends weak ones: and fire purges gold, but consumes stubble: and Christ himself is set for the ruin of some, and for the resurrection of others, Luke II. For which reason the Church also sings concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord: It is death to the wicked, life to the good. Nor could Beza deny this sense: It must be known, he says, that the Gospel does not destroy anyone, but the contempt of the Gospel, and he praises the opinion of Nyssen on this matter as excellent: Οἷον μύρος τῇ περιστερᾷ ῥώμη, τῷ δὲ κανθάρῳ φθορά [Like ointment, strength to the dove, but destruction to the beetle]. But B. Hülsemann rightly observes: If it were even most true that the preaching of the Gospel, even with respect to the same effect which it obtains in the damned, is called εὐωδίαν Θεῷ [a fragrance to God], it would not follow that the cause of this fragrance, or the divine complacency, is an absolute good pleasure of God in the perdition of the impious, or a different nature of the medium, by which from a peculiar influence of God it is indeed wholesome to the elect, but as if infected and poisonous to the reprobate, as Calvin explains. For the fact that the reprobate are killed by the same remedy by which the elect are refreshed does not arise from a different quality of the remedy, which GOD, because of a different affection toward the subjects suffering, as if inspires into the medicine or the preached word. But the same fatted calves, the same feasts are, and the same wines have an intrinsic nutritive power toward the elect and the reprobate, Matt. XXII. verse 4. but the diverse effect arises from the added vice—not indeed that innate and natural one, but the acquired and stubbornly kept and preserved one, John IX. verses 39, 41—of the stomach or the receiving subject, to which vice, and the consequent destruction of the suffering subject, GOD does not concur with any will other than judicial and decreeing that He does not wish 1. to apply other remedies to this sufferer than the ordinary ones. 2. also to withdraw the ordinary ones after long-standing contempt and 3. not to leave that contempt unpunished. For which reason the Belgians at verse 16 translated very poorly when they say that ὀσμὴν θανάτε in German is the same as intrinsically deadly, since it appears quite evidently from the text, especially from verse 17, where the Apostle declares his sincerity in teaching and his charity toward all hearers as a subordinate and ministerial cause of the supreme agent, that the discourse is only about the outcome, not about the primary cause of the outcome, residing in the good odor of God, as Calvin and Beza wish from verse 15. The authors of the Belgian notes, even though they call the odor of the Gospel lethal, nevertheless ought to have confessed that this happens only with respect to the outcome, and by the fault of the reprobate, which they rendered thus, those who placed German notes under the Bibles of Tossanus: To the words Geruch des Todes, that is, which is deadly. Not that the Gospel in and of itself, and by its nature, causes death, for it is the ministry of life 1. Cor. III. verse 6, 7. and a power of God unto salvation to all who believe in it, Rom. I. verse 16. but because the unbelievers willfully oppose it, and thus by their own fault draw a more severe judgment of God upon themselves, S. John III. verse 36, 1 Pet. II. verse 7, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Οἷς μὲν ὀσμὴ θανάτυ εἰς θάνατον) Hic prior vox θανάτυ qualitatem significat, ut 2. Reg. IV. vers. 40. Altera eventum significat. Sunt odores quidam tam mali, ut etiam exitium afferant, ut Averni & Asphaltitæ halitus. Fama illa mala de Evangelio credita, multis affert perni- ciem æternam. In Manuscripto est, ἐκ θανάτυ εἰς θάνατον nimirum quia mala illa fama autores habet homines in peccatis mortuos.

Οἷς δὲ ὀσμὴ ζωῆς εἰς ζωὴν) Sicut odores quidam animo defectos velut in vitam restituunt; ita bona de Evangelio fama eos, qui eam hauriunt, perducit ad vitam æternam. Et hic Manuscriptus habet, ἐκ ζωῆς. Nimirum quia bona illa fama est à Deo autore vitæ. Simile loquendi genus ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν, Rom. I. 17. & infra III. 18. ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, & ita hoc & præcedens membrum legit Clemens Alexandrinus.

Non hic quicquam de famà mala vel bona de Evangelio credita, sed de εὐωδία τῶ χρισῷ per se Deo grata, ut τῇ ὀσμῇ τῆς γνώσεως τῶ χρισῷ ubi- que sparsa per Apostolos, subjectum unicum est; prædicata vero diversa sunt. Non verò gemi- nandum subjectum, quasi & de fama bona, & de fama mala sermo sit, aut etiam odores suâ naturâ, & secundum qualitatem propriam alii lethales sint & exitium adferant, alii vitam. Neque fama Ev- angelii ut credita hic notata, sed prædicatio Evan- gelii à ministris Dei facta: Alienum ergò etiam il- lud est, quod mala fama autores habeat homines in peccatis mortuos. Prædicatio sanè illa est ὀσμὴ τῆς γνώσεως χρισῦ, odor salutaris cognitionis Christi, & εὐωδία suavis & gratus Deo odor, adeoque ὀσμὴ ζωῆς, odor vitæ: Et quidem ex intentione Dei non εἰς θάνατον, ad mortem; sed εἰς ζωὴν, ad vitam E- zech. XIIX. v. 32. cap. XXXIII. v. 11. 1. Timoth. II. v. 4. sed ex eventu quorundam, eorum nempe, qui pereunt, culpa & vitio sit ὀσμὴ θανάτε εἰς θά- νατον mortis ad mortem. Agnoscit id Estius: Rur- sum causaliter odorem se vocat, quatenus sua prædi- catione famam nominis Christi tanquam bonum odo- rem latè dispergebat. Qui odor malis ac reprobis le- thalis erat, non suo, sed illorum vitio; propterea quod occasione Evangelii sibi prædicati, dum credere no- lunt, gravius condemnantur: Quum odor ille se- cundum se semper bonus sit, etiam tunc, quando qui- busdam est odor mortis ad mortem. Sic enim & fra- grantia boni unguenti columbam vegetat, scarabæum necat, ut ait Oecumenius. Sic & lumen solis oculos sanos recreat, debiles offendit: Et ignis aurum pur- gat, stipulas absumit: Et ipse Christus aliis in rui- nam, aliis in resurrectionem positus est Luc. II. Qua ratione etiam de sacramento corporis & sanguinis Domini canit Ecclesia: Mors est malis, vita bonis. Nec sensum hunc diffiteri potuit Beza: Sciendum est, inquit, Evangelium non perimere quenquam, sed Evangelii contemptum, laudatque Nysseni hac de re sententiam ceu egregiam: Οἷον μύρος τῇ πε- ριστερᾷ ῥώμη, τῷ δὲ κανθάρῳ φθορά. Recte autem B. Hülsemannus observat: Si maxime verum esset, prædicationem Evangelii etiam respectu ejusdem effectus, quem in damnatis sortitur, dici εὐωδίαν Θεῷ, non sequuturum tamen causam εὐωδίας hujus, seu complacentia divina, in perditione impiorum absolutum esse Dei beneplacitum, vel diversam me- dii indolem, qua ex peculiari Dei influentia electis quidem salubris, reprobis autem quasi infecta & venenata sit, quomodo Calvinus explicat. Quod enim eodem remedio enecantur reprobi, quo recre- antur electi, non oritur ex diversa qualitate reme- dii, quam DEUS pro diverso affectu erga subjecta passa, quasi inspiret medicinæ seu verbo prædicato. Eadem autem altilia, eadem dapes sunt, eandem vina intrinsecam nutritivam habent erga electos & reprobos Matth. XXII. vers. 4. diversuas autem ef- fectus oritur ex accedente vitio, non quidem conna- to illo & naturali sed adscitio & præfracte soto ser- vatoque Johan. IX. versu 39. 41. stomachi seu subjecti recipientis, ad quod vitium, atque inde consequentem interitum subjecti patientis DEUS non concurrit voluntate alia, quam judiciali & de- cernente quod non velit 1. huic patienti alia adhibe- re remedia, quàm ordinaria. 2. etiam ordinaria subtrahere post diutinum contemptum & 3. Con- temptum illum non dimittere impunem. Quamob- rem Belgæ ad vers. 16. pessimè verterunt, quando ὀσμὴν θανάτε Germanìcè idem esse ajunt, quod in- trinsecè mortiferum, cum ex textu satis evidenter appareat, præcipue ex versu 17. ubi Apostolus suam in docendo sinceritatem & charitatem erga omnes Auditores, tanquam subordinata & ministra cau- sa supremi agentis declarat tantum sermonem esse de eventu, non autem de prima causa eventus, resi- dente in bono odore Dei, ut Calvinus & Beza vo- lunt ex versu 15. Belgicarum notarum autores etsi lethalem dicant odorem Evangelii, fateri tamen debuère, id tantùm respectu eventus fieri, & cul- pa reproborum, quas ita reddidere, qui Bibliis Tossani notas Germanicas subjecerunt: Ad ver- ba Geruch des Todes, das ist, der tödtlich ist. Nicht daß das Evangelium an und für sich selbst, und seiner Natur nach den Tod verur- sache, denn es ist das Amt des Lebens 1. Cor. III. vers. 6. 7. und eine Krafft GOttes zur Se- ligkeit allen, die daran gläuben Roman. I. vers. 16. sondern weil die Ungläubigen demselben sich muthwillig widersetzen, und also durch ihre eigene Schuld ein desto schwerer Gericht GOttes über sich ziehen, S. Johan. III. vers. 36. 1. Petr. II. versu 7. 8.

## 2:17
Verse 17. Καὶ πρὸς ταῦτά τις ἱκανός) that is; how difficult is this, which we perform, who also despise so many adversities and the worst rumors about us for the sake of Christ. The answer to this question will be placed below III. 5. For the things that intervene are an explanation of the difficulty.

The Vulgate is noted here again (although canonized by Papal authority) by Estius rendering: And for these things who is so sufficient? The little word SO is not added in the Greek and Syriac, just as it is not in the text of Ambrose and Sedulius, and Augustine reads it without it throughout, as in tract 50 on John and in the enarrations of Psalm 7 and other places in Bede. Erasmus suspects the interpreter translated: Who then is sufficient? Certainly reason shows that that SO ought to be absent, lest the sentence be too arrogant. However, neither did Grotius correctly express the sense, because the Apostle teaches not only that this is difficult for us, but that we are plainly insufficient for it: Nor did Estius; understanding sufficient as one who in reality shows himself to be such, and affirming that very few are such. For the discourse is about ἱκανότητι, aptitude, not about the act or the work itself: and the Apostle denies that anyone is ἱκανὸν, sufficient, fully by his own powers. Aretius removes, he says, the charge of arrogance, as if he were saying: It is a great thing that I have said, that I am the good odor of Christ, as much in the good as in the reprobate, but all this is a benefit of God, it is not my dignity, who is sufficient? as if he were saying, no one: the sufficiency is of God alone, it is not of our dignity. And I refer these things to the contrary effects of the ministry. But the contrary effect is also referred to God in such a way that, namely, the Gospel and the preaching of the same is to the reprobate an odor of death unto death, which is the Calvinist error noted before. The gloss of Pelagius, which Sedulius also made his own, is plainly foreign to the context, nor does it suit the modesty of the Apostle: For doing these things who can be so sufficient as we, who have been chosen for this?

PART II. EPISTLES. Doctrinal Apology. SECTION I. Concerning the chief heads of faith.

Vers. 17. For we are not as the rest, peddling the word of God) He touches upon the remnants of evils still remaining at Corinth in the teachers rather than in the people. A huckster (κάπηλος) is one who sells food and drink, as we have said at Sirach XXVI, 24. Hence it began to be transferred to all things which are held for gain. Thus Herodotus said 'to peddle affairs' (καπηλεύειν τὰ πράγματα), Herodian 'to peddle peace' (καπηλεύειν εἰρήνην), Ennius 'to huckster war' (cauponari bellum). In a similar way, Ignatius to the Trallians calls those who have the Gospel for gain 'merchants of Christ' (χριστεμπόρους). See also below IV. 2.

Let the approach in this manner be for the purpose of repelling the accusation and crime of the adulteration of doctrine, which the Apostle declines from himself in such a way that he quite clearly makes the Pseudo-Apostles guilty of it. This was also noted by Aretius: The third place is concerning the integrity of the Apostle, which he opposes to the deceits of his calumniators. A proposition must be established here: The Apostle Paul always and everywhere sincerely taught the Gospel without deceit. Matthias Flacius touched the matter to the quick, especially in his gloss. In the second, he says, main part of this epistle, although the Apostle may seem to wish to defend himself and his office, nevertheless he properly celebrates the ministry of the Gospel and its effects, and prefers it by far to the ministry of the law. And thus he discourses most especially concerning the distinction between the law and the Gospel, and concerning the article of justification, showing that the Gospel, which is the power of God, saves freely and effectively, not that the law, which is ineffective, saves men by merits: at the same time, however, he also amplifies his own effort and office in promoting the Gospel, and conversely covertly censures the fruitless inculcation of the law by the Pseudo-Apostles: Which doctrine will be duly reckoned to the article of justification. Moreover, the causal particle is to be connected, as Beza rightly observes, not with the immediate epiphonema, which had been as it were an interjection, but with those things which he had said about himself in verses 14 and 15. It seemed otherwise, however, to Camerarius, who refers the explanation (αἰτιολογίαν) to the immediately preceding words, and to Theophylact. Jerome also thinks that the word 'to peddle' (καπηλεύειν) looks to gain, explaining it as those who sell the Word of God, that is, those who think that gain is godliness, and do everything for the sake of base lucre. But the Apostle looks rather to the vitiation of doctrine, which is evident from the opposite, 'sincerity' (εἰλικρινείας), those who vitiate the word of God by the admixture of falsehood: Such were the Pseudo-Apostles, vitiating the doctrine of the Gospel by the admixture of the law, mixing faith and works, adulterating, as Theophylact has it here, the grace of God. For since the chief study of those who sell food or drink is to sell vitiated things as sincere. Erasmus observes here that the ancients called anything that was insincere and vitiated by deceit and fraud 'huckstered' (κάπηλον). And thus those are called 'peddlers' (καπηλεύοντες) who are in the habit of corrupting wine with water, Isaiah I, 22, where the LXX have: 'Your hucksters (οἱ κάπηλοί σου) mix wine with water,' and the Greeks interpret 'to peddle' (καπηλεύειν) as 'to huckster wine' (καπεύειν τὸν οἶνον), and note that 'clay' (πῆλον) once signified 'wine' (οἶνον). However, both can be joined: both the vitiation of doctrine and gain. For as innkeepers, out of a desire for gain, vitiate food and drink: so the Pseudo-Apostles did the same, vitiating the Evangelical doctrine for the sake of profit and gain; therefore the Apostle marked them both as false Doctors and as lovers of gain in 2 Cor. XI. And Chrysostom looks to both here, from which, however, the chief thing is the adulteration of doctrine, in which way the Vulgate translates it, although it uses a different metaphor. Camerarius says that 'to peddle' (καπηλεύειν), that is, to act as an innkeeper, signifies as much seeking something for oneself from the boasting of doctrine as also corrupting it, which is 'huckster-like' (καπηλικὸν), and that for the sake of gain. Beza is singular here, to whom it seems that the Apostle persists in the metaphor taken from precious ointments: which, because they were precious and brought from distant regions, the impostures of merchants in adulterating them were great and lucrative.

But as of sincerity) Sincerely. See 1 Cor. V. 8. above I. 2. Phil. I. 10. 'as' (ὡς) here is 'for truth' (לאמתת כה) as the Hebrews say.

The Vulgate omits the particle 'as' (ὡς), which, however, in the judgment of Beza, is by no means idle, but refers to the Caph of truth, which the Hebrews call so, whom Grotius followed here.

But as of God) commanded by God.

No otherwise than as commanded by God, just as Ambrose elegantly translates: As it proceeded from God. Which is more suitable to the text than if it were referred with Aretius to a legitimate calling. For the Apostle is engaged in vindicating the sincerity of his doctrine, as Aretius himself admits.

Before God) having God before our eyes.

Whom no one can deceive, whatever wiles he may use. I teach as if always having an inspector present, so sincere is my doctrine, or reverence for God; as this Aretius says.

Εν χρισῷ λαλῦμεν) We say these things in Christ, that is, in the name of Christ, as his ambassadors, below V. 20. We simply rebuke sins, we raise up the penitent. Not like those who, that they may pursue their own gain, promise God's pardon even to those not amending their lives, God not approving of it, 2 Tim. III. verse 6.

In Christ, says the Apostle, not as Beza renders it, concerning Christ, although we do not deny that ב is sometimes taken for על as in Psalm LXXVII. 13. But what reason is there for departing from the proper meaning? I speak in Christ. Christ is truth: Therefore I cannot lie in Christ, says Aretius: Whose things, however, which follow, are foreign here. And it seems, he says, to be the form of one swearing, or certainly of one asserting by the testimony of Christ, in whom it is not right to deceive. Others more correctly [say] in Christ; that is, through Christ, or by the authority of Christ: or as vicars of Christ, from whom all deceit and πλεονεξία is far absent.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Καὶ πρὸς ταῦτά τις ἱκανός) id est; quam dif- ficile est hoc, quod nos præstamus, qui & tot adversa & pessimos de nobis rumores Christi causa contemnimus. Huic quæstioni responsio subjicietur infra III. 5. Nam quæ intercedunt, explicatio sunt difficultatis.

Notatur hic iterum Vulgata (etsi autoritate Papali canonizata) ab Estio reddens: Et ad hæc quis tam idoneus? Vocula TAM in Græco, & Sy- riaco non additur, ut nec in textu Ambrosii, & Se- dulii, legitque sine ea passim Augustinus, ut tract. 50. super Joan. & in enarr. Psalmi 7. & aliis locis apud Bedam. Suspicatur Erasmus interpretem vertisse: Quisnam idoneus? Certe ratio ostendit, illud TAM abesse debere, ne sit sententia arrogan- tior. Sensum autem nec Grotius recte expressit, quia non solum, quod difficile hoc nobis sit, sed quod plane inidonei ad id simus, docet Apostolus: Nec Estius; idoneum intelligens, qui reipsa talem se præbet, & perpaucos tales esse, affirmans. Nam de ἱκανότητι, aptitudine, sermo est, non de actu vel opere ipso: & negat Apostolus, plenè quan- quam propriis viribus ἱκανὸν idoneum esse. Are- tius removet, inquit, crimen arrogantiæ, quasi dicat: Magnum est, quod dixi, me esse Christi bonum odo- rem, tam in bonis, quam reprobis, sed totum hoc est Dei beneficium, non mea est dignitas, quis idoneus? quasi dicat, nemo: ἱκανότης solius Dei est, non nostræ est dignitatis. Et ταῦτα refero ad contrarios effe- ctus ministerii. Sed ad Deum ita refertur etiam effectus contrarius, quod nempe Evangelium & prædicatio ejusdem reprobis odor mortis sit ad mortem, qui Calvinianus error ante notatus est. Glossæma Pelagii, quod suum etiam fecit Sedu- lius, plane alienum est à contextu, nec modestiæ Apostoli convenit: Ad hæc facienda quis potest tam idoneus esse, quam nos, qui ad hoc sumus electi?

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ. Apologia Doctrinalis. SECTIO I. De capitibus fidei præcipuis.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

Having declined from self-boasting, the Apostle proceeds to the sincerity of his doctrine, appealing to the letters of recommendation of the hearts of the Corinthians by the Spirit of God, and claiming all ἱκανότητα not for himself, but for God alone. Teaching that his ministry, which is of the New Testament, as regards form, efficacy, and glory of doctrine, excels the ministry and doctrine of Moses by infinite parasangs, and that he openly and without a veil displays the brightness of the Lord, whereas on the contrary the Mosaic veil still lies upon the hearts of the Jews, so that they do not see it, whereas on the contrary those converted to the Lord, beholding with unveiled face, are transformed into the image of the Lord by the Spirit of the Lord.

There are three parts: I. The epistle of the sincerity of the Apostolic doctrine as a recommendation to v. 3. II. The sole cause of the ἱκανότητος of the ministry to the middle of v. 6. III. The contention of the ministry of the New and Old Testament of the Apostle to v. 18. Flacius thus exhibits the οἰκονομίαν and proper scope of this chapter: First, in the first three verses he (the Apostle) commends himself and his ministry by the effect or conversion of the Corinthians: secondly, by comparison he treats of the glory and efficacy of his

of the Gospel, against the obscurity and inefficacy of the law, up to the beginning of v. 12. Finally, concerning the veil of the law and its removal, which will be brought about through the Gospel and Christ: which two parts also contribute greatly to the commendation of his ministry. For the sum and primary praise of a Teacher is that he spreads abroad saving doctrine. Therefore, this whole chapter primarily aims at this, that all, having despaired of the justice and salvation of the law as impossible, may flee to the ready and prepared justice and life of Christ.

PART I. An epistle establishing the sincerity of Apostolic doctrine.

Vers. 1. Are we beginning again to commend ourselves) These things cohere with the preceding, and therefore a new section should not be made here. For since he had begun to show how difficult it was to fulfill all the parts of a truly and solidly Christian man, and for that reason had mentioned certain things about himself as if compelled, restraining himself lest he continue this discourse longer, he says there is no need for it among the Corinthians, who had been witnesses of his integrity, labor, and constancy. That πάλιν looks to those things which are in the first to the Corinthians, ch. V, IX, XIV; I think also to those which were in the epistles that have now perished. Moreover, ἀρχόμεθα is put for 'is there any need that we begin?' And the interrogation is for a negative: as if he were to say, there is no need for it at all, with which sense the following things cohere well.

Εἰ μὴ χρήζομεν) that εἰ μὴ is a formula of one objecting to himself that which is most easily solved. Cicero and others often use the word 'nisi' in this way.

Ὥς τινες) as others less known.

Συστατικῶν ἐπιστολῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἢ ἐξ ὑμῶν συστατικῶν) Commendatory letters are needed on both sides among strangers. There are many examples of such epistles. Not a few in Cicero, and in Nazianzen and Isidore.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Declinata περιαυτολογίᾳ ad doctrinæ suæ since- ritatem pergit Apostolus, ad systatica cordis Corinthiacarum provocans scripta Spiri- tu Dei, omnemque ἱκανότητα non sibi, sed Deo uni vendicat. Ministerium suum, quod Novi Testamenti est, quoad for- mam, efficaciam & gloriam doctrinæ in- finitis parassangis antecellere Mosis mini- sterium & doctrinam, docens, seque aper- te ac sine velo claritatem Domini præferre, quum contra Judæorum cordibus adhuc incumbat velum Mosaicum, ut illam non videant, quum contra conversi ad Domi- num retecta facie intuentes in imaginem Domini transformentur à Domini Spi- ritu.

PArtes tres sunt I. Epistola sinceritatis doctrinæ Apostolicæ systatica ad v. 3. II. Unica ἱκανότητος ministerii causa ad v. 6. medium. III. Contentio ministerii Novi & Veteris Testamenti Apostolicæ ad v. 18. Flacius ita capitis hujus οἰκονομίαν & sco- pum proprium exhibet: Primò tribus primis ver- sibus commendat (Apostolus) se suumque ministe- rium ab effectu seu conversione Corinthiorum: se- cundò per collationem agit de gloria ac efficacia sui

Evangelii, contra legis obscuritatem & inefficaciam, usque ad initium v. 12. postremo de velamine legis & ejus detractione, quæ fiet per Evangelium & Chri- stum: Quæ duæ particulæ etiam ad commendatio- nem ministerii ejus plurimum faciunt. Summa e- nim & primaria laus Doctoris est, quod salutiferam doctrinam circumferat. Totum igitur hoc caput po- tissimum id agit, ut omnes desperata justitia ac salute legis tanquam impossibili ad obviam paratamque ju- stitiam & vitam Christi confugiant.

PARS I. Epistola sinceritatis doctrinæ Apostolicæ systatica.

Vers. 1. Ἀρχόμεθα πάλιν ἑαυτοὺς συνιστάνειν) Cohærent hæc cum superioribus, itaque nova sectio hic non erit fa- cienda. Cum enim cœpisset ostendere quam esset difficile omnes partes implere hominis verè & solidè Christiani, & ob id quædam de se quasi coactus commemorasset, re- primens se ne diutius hunc sermonem continuet, ait, non opus eo esse apud Corinthios, qui testes fuissent suæ inte- gritatis, laboris & constantiæ. Illud πάλιν spectat ad ea, quæ sunt in priore ad Corinthios cap. V. IX. XIV. puto etiam ad ea, quæ erant in epistolis quæ nunc periere. Est autem positum ἀρχόμεθα, pro opus ne est ut incipiamus? Et interrogatio pro negativa: quasi dicat, minime id opus, cum quo sensu bene cohærent sequentia.

Εἰ μὴ χρήζομεν) illud εἰ μὴ est formula objicientis sibi- met id quod facillime solvitur. Utitur sic voce nisi sæpe Cicero, & alii.

Ὥς τινες) ut alii minus noti.

Συστατικῶν ἐπιστολῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἢ ἐξ ὑμῶν συστατικῶν) Commendatitiis literis utrinque opus inter ignotos. Multa talium epistolarum exempla. Apud Ciceronem non pau- ca, & apud Nazianzenum & Isidorum.

## 3:2
Vers. 2. Ἡ ἐπιστολὴ ἡμῶν ὑμεῖς ἐστε) Paul is accustomed to seize the occasion from preceding words to transfer them to something more elevated: You are my epistle; as Rom. XIII. 9. and elsewhere. You are my epistle, that is, I have inscribed the Gospel upon your souls. And he gives the name of the whole to the part. For he spoke of them themselves, and shows that he is speaking of their zeal and affection.

Γινωσκομένη καὶ ἀναγινωσκομένη ὑπὸ πάντων ἀνθρώπων) Paul also loves paronomasia, as below IV. 8. First the hand is recognized, then the epistle is read. Thus all knew the Christian Corinthians to be disciples of the Apostle Paul. Then they saw his own sentiments expressed in their life.

Concerning the several epistles to the Corinthians which may have perished, no evidence remains. Here, however, the Apostle defends his ministry, so that he may gradually proceed from the commendation of his person to the commendation of the dignity of Evangelical doctrine. That he proves by the own testimony of the Corinthians, who themselves were a living commendatory epistle. He uses the name of epistle by metaphor for a thing effective like a commendatory epistle. For what commendation would provide to others, this the conversion of the Corinthians provides to Paul. A double commendatory is designated: Do we have need of commendatory letters either from others to you, or from you to others? For the adversaries, the false Apostles, noted by the words ὥς τινες, both needed and used both. The Apostle needed neither. Compare 1 Cor. IX. 2. He shows, however, as Theophylact notes, some crafty and fictitious Apostles, whose fame being more obscure, because they were famous for no proper works, would carry about for their own commendation, wherever they pleased, and from these had acquired both praise and a name for themselves among outsiders. But what Paul says, not without bitterness of spirit, is such as this: has someone perhaps said that commendatory epistles must be carried about by us to you, or from you to others, so that through them we may be made better known? But he says they are written in our hearts, not as Grotius here seems to hint, and Aretius wishes in your hearts, ὑμῶν.

For all the Codices have ἡμῶν. He understands the inscription through love and memory made. Cf. Is. XLIX. 16. But that the same is evident to others, the following things insinuate: Which is known and read, or which is recognized and acknowledged by all men. For the fame of the Corinthians was spread far and wide. Thus the testimony of the Corinthians is established by the consensus of other Churches. Similarly, Theophylact explains these things thus: That, he says, you had acted as an epistle for my commendation and praise, you do that yourselves through you. For when we are either watched by others, or heard, or wherever we have gone, we carry you about: since we have you inscribed on our heart and we proclaim your virtues openly to all. Since, therefore, I hold you in the place of an epistle, who commend me to others and extol me with highest praises, I have demanded no other letters from you, so that I might become known to those who do not know me. It is added, moreover, that I do not need the commendation of others among you, since you are implanted in my mind and heart. For commendatory letters are necessary to those to whom we are unknown. But you are inscribed on my soul, so that you can in no way fall away. By which words he not only proves their charity by his own testimony, but also extols their virtues. Since indeed they seemed to have enough strength to manifest the dignity of the Teacher to other men. For the virtue of the disciples is an ornament to the Master.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἡ ἐπιστολὴ ἡμῶν ὑμεῖς ἐστε) Solet Paulus ex vocibus præcedentibus occasionem captare eas transfe- rendi ad aliquid ἀνεπιότερον Vos estis mea epistola; ut Rom. XIII. 9. & alibi. Vos estis mea epistola, id est, Ego Evangelium vestris inscripsi animis. Et dat totius nomen parti. Nam ipsos dixit, & ostendit se loqui de eorum stu- dio & affectu.

Γινωσκομένη καὶ ἀναγινωσκομένη ὑπὸ πάντων ἀνθρώπων) Amat & παρονομασίας Paulus, ut infra IV. 8. Prius agno- scitur manus, deinde legitur epistola. Sic Corinthios Christianos omnes sciebant esse Apostoli Pauli discipulos. Deinde videbant sensus ipsius in illorum vita expressos.

De epistolis pluribus ad Corinthios, quæ per- ierint, nihil superat indicii. Hic autem suum tue- tur ministerium Apostolus, ut sensim à personæ commendatione procedat ad doctrinæ Evangelicæ dignitatem commendandam. Illud & proprio Co- rinthiorum testimonio comprobat, qui ipsi viva erant epistola systatica. Epistolæ nomen usurpat per Metaphoram pro re efficaci instar epistolæ com- mendatoriæ. Quod enim commendatio aliis præ- staret, hoc conversio Corinthiorum Paulo præ- stat. Gemina autem systatica designatur: Num opus habemus literis commendatitiis vel ab aliis ad vos, vel à vobis ad alios. Utrisque enim indigebant & utebantur adversarii falsi Apostoli, notati ver- bis ὥς τινες. Neutris indigebat Apostolus. Confer 1. Cor. IX. 2. Ostendit autem, notante Theophylacto, subdolos & fictitios nonnullos Apostolos, quorum fa- ma cum esset obscurior, quia nullis essent propriis o- peribus clari, in suam commendationem, quocunque liberet, deferrent, ex hisque & laudem sibi & nomen apud exteros comparasse. Quod vero Paulus non fine animi acerbitate loquitur, tale est, num for- san dixerit quispiam circumferendas esse & nobis commendatitias ad vos epistolas, vel ex vobis ad alios, ut per eas notiores efficiamur. Scripta autem inquit in cordibus nostris, non ut hic Grotius videtur in- nuere, & Aretius vult in cordibus vestris ὑμῶν.

Nam omnes Codd. habent ἡμῶν. Inscriptionem intelligit per amorem & memoriam factam. Conf. Es. XLIX. 16. Quod vero aliis eadem pateat, se- quentia insinuant: Quæ scitur & legitur, vel quæ cognoscitur & recognoscitur ab omnibus homini- bus. Fama enim Corinthiorum longe lateque dif- fusa erat. Ita Corinthiorum testimonium alia- rum Ecclesiarum consensu stabilitur. Similiter Theophylactus hæc ita explicat: Quod, inquit, epi- stola in meam commendationem egissent & laudem, id ipsi per vos agitis. Nam cum ab aliis vel specta- mur, vel audimur, vel quocunque profectum est, vos circumferimus: quippe quos cordi habemus inscri- ptos & vestras virtutes omnibus propalamus. Cum itaque epistola loco vos habeam, qui me apud alios commendatis, & laudibus summis effertis, nullas alias à vobis exegerim literas, ut me nescientibus in- notescam. Accedit præterea, ut neque aliorum apud vos commendatione indigeam, quandoquidem insiti mihi menti & cordi sitis. Sunt namque ad eos necessa- ria commendatitiæ literæ, quibus ipsi incogniti su- mus. Vos autem mihi animo estis inscripti, ita ut excidere nullo pacto possitis. Quibus dictis non modo illorum suo testimonio comprobat charitatem, ve- rum & virtutes extollit. Siquidem & Præceptoris manifestandam cæteris hominibus dignitatem satis habere virium videbantur. Magistro namque disci- puli virtus decori est.

## 3:3
Vers. 3. Φανερούμενοι ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐπιστολὴ χριστοῦ). This refers to that ὑμεῖς ἐστε. Here also φανερούμενοι is a passive for a reciprocal, which the Hebrews call Hithpael. Thus φανερῶθητε is התראו. At the same time, there is here a certain correction such as above XV. 10: For when he had said that the Corinthians were his letter, in order to mitigate the envy of the statement, he says they are the letter of Christ, but written by his ministry.

Διακονηθεῖσα ὑφ' ἡμῶν) And this is a concise expression: For he said it was ministered by himself and his helpers, meaning written through his ministry: Christ had dictated the letter, Paul had been the scribe.

Ἐγγεγραμμένη ὀ μέλανι). In the way that the letters of men are accustomed to be written: Μέλαν is ink, more often gore.

Ἀλλὰ πνέυματι Θεοῦ ζῶντος) By the sight of miracles. The letter of Christ, not so much because it was written by Christ, as because Christ is written in it, as is explained by the Greeks. But the former is included in the following καθ' ὑπόνοιαν: Διακονηθεῖσα ὑφ' ἡμῶν, as if he were to say, Christ is the principal author of this writing, we were only his amanuenses. Cf. 1 Cor. IV. 1. And therefore it is not rendered sufficiently aptly by Erasmus as 'subministrata' (supplied). For he who provides and offers something also supplies it, even if he is not the minister of the one to whom he offers it. But it is not said to be written by the Spirit of God because the letter of Christ was manifested by the sight of miracles. For it is one thing to be manifested, another to be written: this was done through the power of the Spirit, by which reference is made to Jer. XXXI. 33.

Οὐκ ἐν πλαξὶ λιθίναις) The Gospel prefers not only human letters, but also divine ones of an older time. לוחות Exod. XXXI. 18. πλάκες. Whence also the writer of the Orphics said δίπλακα θεσμόν.

Ἀλλ' ἐν πλαξὶ καρδίας σαρκίναις) That σαρκίναις alludes here indeed to the material of the heart, which is fleshy, but it properly signifies minds that are ductile, and not stony. He shows that what Jeremiah had predicted in XXXI. 33 is fulfilled. A similar opposition is found in Plutarch on Lycurgus: 'The former, the most authoritative and greatest things for the happiness and virtue of a city, are in the customs, so that they remain immovable, ingrained in the habits of the citizens, and having a firm choice as a very strong bond of necessity, and which education made for the young, producing a lawgiver's disposition regarding each of them.' But Dion of Prusa in that discourse, in which he prefers custom to law: 'Those (the laws) are kept on tablets or pillars, but each of them is in our souls. And such a guard is safer and better.' In the old law, the written is the principal thing: vocal instruction serves it. In the Gospel, vocal instruction is the principal thing; Scripture serves to guard it.

Not on stone tablets like the law of Moses, which the Pseudo-Apostles were reading, and mixing with the Gospel: But on tablets of flesh. Cf. Ezek. 36:26. This is now to be understood concerning the hearts of the Corinthians. Hearts no longer stony, such as they were by nature, in which the image of God had been erased by sin: but fleshy or renewed, in which the true knowledge of Christ and new impulses pleasing to God, as if inscribed through the exercises of piety, exerted themselves and offered themselves to be viewed by others, as the blessed Balduinus notes here, because Paul does not say ἐν πλαξὶ σαρκικαῖς in carnal tablets, but ἐν πλαξὶ σαρκίναις, noting not the qualities, but the substance of the heart. Where a fleshy heart is taken in a good sense for a heart that is soft and admits the rule of the Holy Spirit, just as it is used in Ezek. 11:19, ch. 36:26. In Jeremiah it is called the inward parts, and the heart, into which it can be written, Jer. 31:33, to which places the Apostle undoubtedly looked. Augustine explains it thus in book 15 against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 4. For neither there (in the Prophet) does what is said, a fleshy heart, nor here, fleshy tablets, mean that we should think carnally: But because in comparison to a stone, which is without sense, flesh feels, by the insensibility of the stone is signified a heart not understanding, and by the sensuality of the flesh is signified a heart understanding. Theophylact, he says, seizing the occasion of comparing the Law with the Gospel, begins from it, saying thus: Just as Moses was once the minister of the Law, so we also, for the spreading and preaching of this faith of ours, perform a ministry: And as he inscribed tablets, so we also hearts. But the Law was inscribed with ink, whereas in us the Gospel is engraved by the Spirit. Therefore, as much as the Spirit differs from ink, and the heart itself from a stone, so much does the new testament differ from the old Law. He also adds another reason for the allusion. That saying can also be taken in another sense. For since it is certain that, while the Jews and others alien to the faith were tormenting themselves, they possessed stony hearts, he introduced the fleshy hearts of the faithful, as being those which both admit reason and are governed by this same thing. Grotius, however, seems here to favor unwritten traditions, which might already be principal in the Gospel, as Cornelius a Lapide does with Bellarmine, book 4, On the Word of God, ch. 3, from which they strive to carve out traditions not written, but kept in the heart, and subsequently propagated by the pen of historians. But Vasquez, Tom. 2, in part 1, of Thomas, disp. 82, judges this as inept as if those things which God promises He will inscribe on a fleshy heart, Ezek. 36:26, were drawn to unwritten traditions.

PART II. The sole cause of the sufficiency of the Ministry of the New Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Φανερούμενοι ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐπιστολὴ χριστοῦ). Refertur hoc ad illud ὑμεῖς ἐστε. Est & hic φανερούμενοι Passivum pro Reciproco, quod Hithpaël Hebræi vocant. Sic φανερῶθητε est התראו. Simul est hic ἐπανόρθωσις quædam qualis su- pra XV. 10: Nam cum Corinthios dixisset suam esse episto- lam, ut invidiam dicti mitiget, dicit eos esse epistolam Christi, sed suo scriptam ministerio.

Ἀλλ' ἐν πλαξὶ καρδίας σαρκίναις) Illud σαρκίναις alludit hic quidem ad materiam cordis, quæ est carnea, sed proprie significat animos ductiles, & non saxeos. Ostendit imple- tum, quod prædixerat Jeremias XXXI. 33. Similis oppo- sitio apud Plutarchum de Lycurgo: τὰ μὲν ἓν, κυριώτατα καὶ μέγιστα πρὸς ἐνδαιμονίαν πόλεως καὶ ἀρετὴν ἐν τοῖς ἤθεσιν, ὥστε καὶ ταῖς ἀγωγαῖς τῶν πολιτῶν ἐγκατεστοιχειωμένα μένειν ἀκίνητα, καὶ βεβαίαν ἔχοντα τὴν προαίρεσιν δεσμὸν ἰσχυρότατον τῆς ἀνάγκης, καὶ ἣν παίδευσις ἐποιεῖτο τοῖς νέοις νομοθέτου διά- θεσιν ἀπεργαζομένη περὶ ἕκαστον ἀυτῶν. Dion autem Prusiæn- sis eo sermone, quo consuetudinem legi præfert: Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν (ὀι νόμοι) ἐν σανίσιν ἤ στήλαις φυλάττονται, τῶν δὲ ἕκαστον ἐν ταῖς ἡμετέραις ψυχαῖς. Ἀσφαλεστέρα δὲ κὴ κρείττων ἡ τοιαύτη φυλακή. In lege veteri scriptum præcipuum est: Vocalis in- stitutio ei servit. In Evangelio vocalis institutio præcipua, Scriptura ei custodiendæ servit.

Non in tabulis lapideis ut lex Moysis, quam Pseudo-Apostoli legebant, & commiscebant Ev- angelio: Sed in carneis tabulis. Conf. Ezech. XXXVI. 26. Haec jam de cordibus Corinthiorum accipienda. Corda non lapidea amplius, quales erant natura, in quibus imago Dei per peccatum erat deleta: sed carnea seu renovata, in quibus verus Christi agnitio, novique motus Deo placentes quasi inscripti per exercitia pietatis sese exerebant aliisque spectandos praebebant, ut B. Balduinus hic notat, quod Paulus non dicat ἐν πλαξὶ σαρκικαῖς in tabulis carnalibus, sed ἐν πλαξὶ σαρκίναις, notans non qualitates, sed substantiam cordis. Ubi carneum cor in bonam partem accipitur de corde molli & regimen Spiritus sancti admittente, quemadmodum usurpatur Ezech. XI. 19. cap. XXXVI. 26. apud Jeremiam vocatur viscera, & cor, in quod scribi potest Jerem. XXXI. 33. ad quae loca haud dubie respexit Apostolus. Ita exponit Augustinus libr. XV. contra Faustum Manich. cap. 4. Nam neque ibi (apud Prophetam) quod dictum est cor carneum, neque hic tabulae carnales hoc volunt, ut carnaliter sapiamus: Sed quia in comparatione lapidis, qui sine sensu est, caro sentit, per lapidis insensibilitatem signatum est cor non intelligens, & per carnis sensualitatem signatum est cor intelligens. Theophylactus, occasionem, inquit, arripiens legem cum Evangelio conferendi, ex ea sic inquiens initium sumit: Quemadmodum legis Moyses olim fuit minister, sic & nos ad fidem hanc nostram vulgandam, & praedicandam ministerio fungimur: Utque & tabulas ille insculpsit, sic & nos corda. Atqui & lex erat atramento inscripta, in nobis vero Evangelium spiritu est exaratum. Quantum itaque differt ab atramento Spiritus, & cor ipsum a lapide; tantundem novum a lege veteri testamentum. Addit & aliam allusionis rationem. Potest & in alium sensum id dictum capi. Nam cum constet, se cruciantibus Judaeis, & aliis a fide alienis, corda inesse lapidea, eo fidelium corda carnalia intulit, utpote quae & rationem admittant, & eadem hac gubernentur. Favere autem hic videtur Grotius traditionibus non scriptis, quae in Evangelio jam praecipuae sint, uti Cornelius a Lapide cum Bellarm. libr. IV. de V. D. c. 3. hinc traditiones non scriptas, sed in corde servatas, & deinceps Historicorum calamo propagatas, exsculpere nituntur. Quod verò tam ineptum Vasquez Tom. II. in part. 1. Thom. disp. 82. judicat, quàm si ea, quae se cordi carneo inscripturum promittit DEUS, Ezech. XXXVI. 26. ad traditiones non scriptas trahantur.
