## 3:4
Verse 4. And such confidence we have through Christ toward God) Here after the parenthesis he repeats the discourse which we had above at 2:17. What I said was hardly to be performed, that I nevertheless perform, and trust that I will perform hereafter, not by native strengths, but by those which God promised to believers through Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Πεποίθησιν δὲ τοιαύτην ἔχομεν διὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν) Hic post παρενθήκην repetit sermonem, quem habuimus supra II. 17. Quod dixi vix esse ut praestetur, id tamen praesto, & praestiturum me deinceps confido, non viribus nativis, sed iis, quas Deus per Christum promisit credentibus.

## 3:5
Verse 5. Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves) Those things which God revealed through the Gospel, unknown for so many centuries, from which arise strengths for performing such excellent works, are of such a kind that they could not have come into the mind of anyone, however ingenious. But because he had said 'from ourselves,' he repeats 'as from ourselves,' because a man can indeed grasp these things, but not discover them from himself. Such are the incarnation of the Word, the cross of the Son of God, and the resurrection of the same who died.

He refers everything to God when it is a matter of sufficiency or aptitude concerning divine things, and when he has said that no one is apt and suitable for his work of ministry, he now explains his confidence toward God, from whom alone he professes with a grateful mind that he has every spiritual aptitude, and likewise every sufficiency for the ministry, and he makes Him the author of his conversion, and of his ministry, and of all the works and

fruits of the same. He does not, however, simply say: We are suitable, but not through ourselves, but through God, when he answers the question: Who is sufficient for these things? But we have such confidence toward God, since he speaks of the continuation of sufficiency, and just as he celebrated the victory in Christ with due thanksgiving as the fruit of his ministry hitherto accomplished with God; so he testifies that he places all his confidence in God, in his ministry, who alone made him worthy or apt, and is going to make him so further for such a great work. Nor does he refer only the aptitude for the work of the ministry as accepted from God, but he attributes whatever good is in him at all to God: he acknowledges that he cannot even think of anything good from himself, let alone execute it, nor does he have any faculty for good in his own strengths, but that all aptitude is from GOD. Through Christ, he says, that is, on account of the merit of Christ, which is the foundation of all our confidence: Because outside of Christ there is no grace, nor do we have access to God, except through faith in Him, Eph. 3:12. Regarding the corruption of the words of the preceding chapter, v. 17, which he here brings up again, what I said was HARDLY to be performed, it was said there; that not difficulty, but our inability is indicated, and this is confirmed here also, when all sufficiency is removed from us, and ascribed solely to God the author. Nor indeed are we only inept at thinking of those things which have been revealed through the Gospel (for who of us was persuaded that those things could be thought of?), but in general to think anything, that is, of good, so that all good thoughts also are referred not to our strengths, but to God the author. For this is a general sentiment, by which all sufficiency is taken away from our strengths, and is derived solely from God, whence further specifically the sufficiency for the ministry of the New Testament is asserted to be solely from God, v. 6. Therefore Augustine, book on the gift of perseverance, ch. 13, accepts those words concerning the knowledge of Him, as it pertains to the way of piety, and the true worship of God: The Synod of Orange, canon 7, as it pertains to the salvation of eternal life. Which Estius wrongly restricts to the thought affecting the will: that a man can think of something good and pious by the sole apprehension of the mind from himself and the sole strengths of nature. For that is entirely contrary to the Apostle, who clearly denies that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything good: which, in rendering the sense of the words, not even Estius himself could deny, thus paraphrasing the same: We claim nothing for ourselves, as those who are not able to think, much less to do and execute, any good thing that pertains to the Evangelical matter or at all to piety from the proper powers of our nature? But that we are sufficient to think or do any good thing, and whatever good we can at any time, that whole thing is from GOD through Christ. Let Estius therefore retract his words: A man can think some good and pious thing by the sole apprehension of the mind from himself, nor does he have need of the grace of God through Christ for a thought of this kind. As these things can in no way consist with that paraphrase, so neither can they with the commentaries of the Greeks, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, who, with Estius approving, explain the mind of the Apostle thus: That nothing is ours, and something else God's, and therefore that nothing at all is ours, not even the least thing (and consequently not even to think by the sole apprehension of the mind), but that the whole is to be ascribed to God. For every figment of the human heart is only evil, all the days, Gen. 6:5. Thoughts pertain primarily to the figment of our heart. And since the tablets of our heart are by nature stony, not fleshy, such as they finally become through the Holy Spirit, so it is not possible for any to think anything good of ourselves, as the stone tablets have need of the inscription of the Holy Spirit, by the gracious illumination, regeneration, and conversion of the same, and how there is need that the heart of stone be taken away from our flesh, and a heart of flesh be given to us: a new heart and a new spirit Ez. XXXVI. 26. that we may know the Lord, and the law of the Lord be written in our inward parts and in our heart Jer. XXXI. 33. 34. that not only our will, but also our mind may be renewed, so that we may be able both to understand and to think what is good, and to will the same. Τὸ λογίζεσθαι therefore is not to conclude and to decide, which signification Estius acknowledges does not fit this place: not to think with the deliberate judgment of reason and the affection of the will, as Estius wishes, but simply to think, as 1. Corinth. XIII. 5. Charity 8 λογίζεται does not think evil, whence Anselm on this place: Let those attend to these words who think that the beginning of faith is from us, and the completion of faith is from God. For who does not see that to think is prior to believing? For no one believes anything unless he has first thought that it is to be believed. If, therefore, we are not sufficient to think anything good of ourselves, surely we are not sufficient to believe, which we cannot do without thinking. But our sufficiency, by which we also begin to believe, is from God. Thinking we believe, thinking we speak, thinking we do whatever we do. But as it pertains to the way of piety and the true worship of God, we are not sufficient even to think anything from ourselves, as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power. And in the Council of Orange, chapter 7, it is defined that heretics are deceived by the spirit, and do not understand that saying of the Apostle, are we sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as if from ourselves, who said that a man by the vigor of nature can think anything good pertaining to salvation and eternal life, (Estius adds, as is expedient, but Surius thinks those words are superfluous,) etc. And chapter 9. We deviate from the path when we both think rightly and keep our feet from falsehood and injustice; and chapter 22. No one has anything of his own, except falsehood and sin. But if any man has truth and justice, it is from that fountain, since we ought to thirst in this desert, so that, sprinkled from it as if by certain drops, we may not fail on the way. Author of the books on the calling of the Gentiles, book 1, c. 3. The heart being changed, he says, it is granted to know what is right, and to will what is right.

But our sufficiency is from God) It is God who, by those reasons discovered by Himself, implants such great strength in us.

The Vulgate has our sufficiency, which the sophists abuse, as if there were some faculty in unregenerate man for good: but so weak that, unless it is helped by God, it is not sufficient. It is truly a wonder (to make Beza's words here my own) not only of ignorance, but also of impudence, to dare to usurp this very thing to snatch away from God a part of His glory: Which the Apostle wrote for this reason, lest he should seem not to attribute all things to the grace of God. But to them we answer in one word with the Apostle: What do you have that you did not receive? If they hear that saying and transfer it to the gifts of nature, I refer them (as openly Pelagian) to Augustine.

Vers. 5. Οὐχ ὅτι ἱκανοί ἐσμεν, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν λογίσασθαί τι, ὡς ἐξ ἑαυτῶν) Ea, quae tot seculis incognita, per Evangelium Deus patefecit, unde nascuntur vires tam eximia edendi opera, ejusmodi sunt ut nemini quamvis ingeniosissimo in mentem venire potuerint. Ideo autem cum dixisset ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν, repetit ὡς ἐξ ἑαυτῶν, quia potest quidem homo ista capere, sed non ex se reperire. Talia sunt Verbi ἐυσάρκωσις, crux Filii Dei, ejusdem mortui resurrectio.

Omnia ad Deum refert, cum de ἱκανότητι vel aptitudine agitur circa res divinas, & quum neminem aptum & idoneum esse dixerit ad opus suum ministerii, jam fiduciam suam explicat erga Deum, ex quo uno uti omnem spiritualem aptitudinem; ita & ἱκανότητα omnem ad ministerium se habere grata mente profitetur, quem & conversionis suae, & ministerii, omniumque operum &

fructuum ejusdem autorem facit. Non autem simpliciter dicit: Idonei nos sumus, sed non per nos- metipsos, sed per Deum, cum ad quæstionem re- spondet: Ecquis adhæc idoneus est? Sed fiduciam talem habemus ad Deum, quandoquidem de ἱκα- νότητος continuatione loquatur, & uti ministerii sui hactenus cum Deo expediti fructum, victoriam in Christo cum debita gratiarum actione cele- bravit; ita se fiduciam omnem in Deum colloca- re testatur, in ministerio suo, qui unice dignum vel aptum se fecit, ac porro facturus sit tanto o- pere. Nec aptitudinem tantum ad opus ministerii Deo acceptam refert, sed quicquid omnino boni est in se, Deo tribuit: ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ sese ne quidem boni quid cogitare, nedum exequi posse, nec ul- lam ad bonum habere in viribus suis facultatem, sed aptitudinem omnem ex DEO esse agnoscit. Per Christum, inquit, id est, propter Christi meri- tum, quod omnis fiduciæ nostræ est fundamen- tum: Quia extra Christum nulla est gratia nec ac- cessum habemus ad Deum, nisi per fidem in ipsum Eph. III. 12. De verborum præcedentis capitis v. 17. corruptela, quam hic iterum ingerit, quod dixi VIX esse, ut præstetur, dictum illic est; non difficultatem, sed ἀδυναμίαν nostram indicari, id- que hic etiam confirmatur, quum omnis ἱκανότης à nobis removetur, solique Deo autori transcri- bitur. Nec vero tantum nos ineptos esse ad ea c- togitanda, quæ per Evangelium revelata sunt (Ec- quis enim à nobis illa excogitari posse persuasus fuit? sed in genere λογίσασθαί τι cogitandi aliquid, boni scilicet, ut omnes etiam bonæ cogitationes non ad vires nostras, sed ad Deum autorem refe- rantur. Est enim hæc sententia generalis, qua vi- ribus nostris omnis ἱκανότης derogatur, & à Deo unicè deducitur, unde porro speciatim ἱκανότης ad ministerium N. Testamenti à Deo unicè esse asse- ritur v. 6. Ideò Augustinus l. de dono persev. cap. 13. accipit illa de cognitione ejus, quod attinet ad pie- tatis viam, & verum Dei cultum: Synodus Arausi- cana can. 7. quod ad salutem pertinet vitæ æternæ. Quod perperam Estius restringit ad cogitationem voluntatem afficientem: quod bonum aliquid & pium cogitare sola mentis apprehensione homo ex se- ipso & solis naturæ viribus possit. Id enim Aposto- lo prorsus contrarium est, qui plane negat, nos ad cogitandum quicquam boni ex nobismetipsis idoneos esse: quod in sensu verborum reddendo nec ipse Estius diffiteri potuit, ita eadem παραφράζων: Ni- hil nobis vendicamus, ut qui non valeamus boni quippiam, quod ad rem Evangelicam vel omnino ad pietatem pertinet ex propriis naturæ nostræ viribus vel cogitare, quanto minus agere & exequi? Sed quod idonei sumus ad aliquid boni cogitandum vel agendum & semel quicquid boni possumus, id totum ex DEO est per Christum. Revocet ergo Estius verba sua: Bonum aliquid & pium cogitare sola mentis apprehensione ex seipso potest homo, neque ad hujusmodi cogitationem opus habet gratiâ Dei per Christum. Quæ ut cum illa παραφράσει nullatenus consistere possunt: ita nec cum Græcorum, Chry- sostomi, Theophylacti, & Oecumenii commenta- riis, Apostoli mentem, Estio probante, ita expli- cantibus: Non aliud esse nostrum, aliud Dei, adeoque nihil plane nostrum esse, ne minimum quidem (ac proinde nec cogitare sola mentis apprehensione) sed totum Deo adscribendum. Omne enim figmen- tum cordis humani tantum malum est, omnibus die- bus Gen. VI. 5. Ad figmentum cordis nostri imprimis cogitationes pertinent. Et quum tabulæ cordis nostri lapideæ sint natura, non carneæ, quales eva- dunt demum per Spiritum S. tam non potest ali- aliquid boni ex seipso cor nostrum cogitare, quam lapideæ tabulæ opus habent inscriptione Spiritus sancti, ejusdem gratiosâ illuminatione, regeneratione, & conversione, & quàm opus est, ut lapideum cor de carne nostra auferatur, & detur nobis cor carneum: cor novum & spiritus novus Ez. XXXVI. 26. ut cognoscamus Dominum, & lex Domini in visceribus nostris & in corde nostro scribatur Jer. XXXI. 33. 34. ut non voluntas tantum, sed etiam mens nostra renovetur, ut & intelligere ac cogitare bonum, & velle idipsum queamus. Τὸ λογίζεσθαι ergo non est concludere & decernere, quam significationem non quadrare huic loco agnoscit Estius: non cogitare cum deliberato rationis judicio, & voluntatis affectu, ut Estius vult, sed simpliciter cogitare, ut 1. Corinth. XIII. 5. Charitas 8 λογίζεται non cogitat malum, unde Anshelmus in hunc locum: Attendant hæc verba, qui putant ex nobis esse fidei cœptum, & ex Deo esse fidei complementum. Quis enim non videat, prius esse cogitare, quam credere? Nullus quippe credit aliquid, nisi prius cogitaverit, esse credendum. Si ergo non sufficimus cogitare aliquid boni ex nobis, profecto nec credere sufficimus, quod sine cogitatione non possumus. Sed sufficientia nostra, qua & credere incipiamus, à Deo est. Cogitantes credimus, cogitantes loquimur, cogitantes agimus quicquid agimus. Quod autem attinet ad pietatis viam, & verum Dei cultum, non sufficimus vel cogitare aliquid à nobis, quasi ex nobis ipsis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Non enim est ex potestate nostra cor nostrum & cogitationes nostræ. Et in Concilio Arausicano cap. 7. definitum est, hæreticos falli spiritu, nec intelligere illud Apostoli, nunquid idonei sumus cogitare aliquid à nobis, quasi ex nobis, qui dixerit hominem per naturæ vigorem bonum aliquid ad salutem pertinens vitæ æternæ cogitare, (Estius addit, ut expedit, sed Surius censet eas voces superfluas esse,) &c. Et cap. 9. Deviamus ab itinere, cum & recte cogitamus, & pedes nostros à falsitate & injustitia tenemus & cap. 22. Nemo habet de suo, nisi mendacium & peccatum. Si quis autem habet homo veritatem atque justitiam, ab illo fonte est, quum sitire debemus in hac eremo, ut ex eo quasi guttis quibusdam irrorati non deficiamus in via. Autor. libror. de vocat. gent. libr. 1. c. 3. Corde mutato, inquit, recta sapere, & recta velle donatur.

Ἀλλ’ ἡ ἱκανότης ἡμῶν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Deus est, qui illis rationibus à se repertis nobis vires tantas indit.

Vulgata habet sufficientia nostra, quo abutuntur sophistæ, quasi aliqua in homine irregenerato facultas sit ad bonum: sed ita infirma, ut nisi à Deo adjuvetur, non sufficiat. Mirum vero (ut verba Bezæ hic mea faciam) non tantum ignorantiæ, sed etiam impudentiæ, hoc ipsum audere usurpare ad eripiendam Deo gloriæ suæ partem: Quod idcirco scripsit Apostolus, ne non omnia Dei gratiæ tribuere videretur. Illis vero uno verbo respondemus cum Apostolo: Quid habes, quod non receperis? Quod dictum si audiant ad naturæ dotes transferre, illos ego (ut aperte Pelagianos) ad Augustinum relego.

## 3:6
Verse 6. Who also made us sufficient) You have ἱκανὸν also in Col. I. 2. responding to the Hebrew הֵכִין, and even more to the Rabbinic הִסְפִּיק. God did not find us fit for such a great ministry, but made us so. Thus Paul was here made into another man, as once another of the same name was, 1. Sam. X. 6.

Ministers of the new testament) The word minister is taken here generally, as in 1. Cor. III. 5. So also ministry in Acts I. 17. and often elsewhere. Concerning the name of the new testament, see our prolegomena to the Gospels.

By the new testament is understood the new covenant, which God established with us in Christ concerning grace, justice, and salvation to be conferred upon us through faith in Christ, which, with respect to God, was sanctioned in the passion and death of Christ by the blood of the Son of God; on our part, it is sanctioned and applied to us through the sacred ministry, so that we may be received into this covenant through the word and sacraments. The Old Testament was the old covenant or pact concerning justice and salvation to be obtained through the observance of the law, which was solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai and sanctioned by the blood of calves, Exod. XXIV. Therefore, he does not want these covenants and testaments, which are by their nature most different, to be confused, as was done by the false Apostles, but to be left distinct, and therefore he teaches that he is not a minister of the old covenant, as Moses was, nor even of both the old and the new, as the Pseudo-Apostles were, mixing law and Gospel, patching together and confusing the old covenant with the new, when they contended that a man is justified and saved both by faith in Christ and by the observance of the law; but that he is a minister of the new covenant, which preached grace, justice, and salvation to be obtained solely through faith in Christ, who among the Corinthians judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, 1. Cor. II. 2. And by this reasoning the Apostle prepares for himself a transition to the comparison and distinction of both Testaments, so that he may meet the confusion of the Pseudo-Apostles and assert the sincerity of his own doctrine, who was a herald of the Evangelical doctrine concerning Christ, so that through faith in Him, in whom the shadows and figures, as well as the predictions and promises of Moses and the Prophets, have their fulfillment, they who believe in His name may obtain the remission of sins, Acts X. 43. chapter XXVI. 38. 39.

PART III. The Apostolic contention of the ministry of the New and Old Testament.

Not of the letter but of the spirit) Moses brought the writing on stone tablets to the people: the Apostles gave the word accompanied by more illustrious signs than Moses had given, such as tongues, healings, the resuscitation of the dead, and even the power of conferring such gifts upon others, which had never been seen.

By the letter he does not understand the writing, but the law itself, both material and formal, the words or the writing and the sense. By the spirit, which is opposed to the letter, he does not understand the power of performing miracles, or any similar faculty of extraordinary gifts, by which the doctrine of the Apostles was confirmed: But by metonymy, the doctrine of the Gospel, which is animated by the Spirit and divine power, is living and efficacious, John VI. v. 63. Heb. IV. 12. The law demands only things to be done, and brings no strength for doing, and thus is nothing but γράμμα or letter, contributing nothing to salvation. The Gospel, however, brings the Spirit, by whose power the faith which it requires in us is kindled, and it is thus called Spirit, because it is instructed by the Holy Spirit, who, graciously uniting himself with the word of the Gospel, bestows upon it spiritual power and efficacy to convert, illuminate, regenerate, and renew our hearts, and to justify and save us. The Spirit, therefore, is not to be separated from the word of the Gospel, inasmuch as he is intimately and inseparably united with it, so that it may be the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Romans I. v. 16. Concerning which see what was said against the fanatics in Tom. I. System. Theol. cap. IV. qu. XXV. Theophylact, with Chrysostom leading the way: The law was indeed spiritual, that is, granted by and proceeding from the Spirit; yet that old law did not confer the Spirit as the new one does. He says therefore: By no means were letters alone entrusted to us, as they were to Moses: But the Spirit itself was granted. Cf. Gal. III. v. 2. We add that the law was also spiritual, because it required not only external, but internal and spiritual obedience Rom. VII. v. 14. The law is spiritual, but I am carnal. It is not, however, called the Spirit as the Gospel is: because it demanded only obedience, but did not confer the spirit and the power to perform that obedience, and although the law also had spiritual force, it acted only to crush hearts, not to vivify them, and therefore the Apostle denies that a law was given which could vivify a man after the fall Gal. III. 21. If a law had been given which could vivify, righteousness would truly be from the law. Moreover, the law is called the letter, because it was written and engraved by GOD in letters on stone tablets, which letter or written law was to be kept in the ark of the covenant Exod. XXXIV. v. 1. 28. 1 Kings VIII. v. 3. And therefore, by synecdoche, the law is called the letter, that is, the external writing on stone tablets containing the law. To minister or teach the letter is to teach the law alone in its rigor, by which it requires perfect obedience, and accuses those destitute of it, strikes them with a curse, and condemns them. To teach the letter, says B. Luther in a marginal gloss, is to teach the bare law and works, without the knowledge of the grace of GOD, by which everything that man is and does is condemned and recognized as guilty of death, for he can do nothing good without the grace of GOD. The Gospel, however, is called the Spirit metonymically, because it exhibits the Spirit, who through it insinuates himself into the hearts of men, and works in them, which is also attributed to the Holy Spirit in a peculiar way, as from the most benevolent Paraclete, the Comforter and effector of eternal salvation, and therefore B. Luther explains teaching the Spirit thus: To teach the Spirit is to teach grace without law and merit, by which man becomes alive and blessed. Add Tom. I. Jenens. Germ. fol. 138. b. The letter causes that no one can remain before the wrath of GOD; the Spirit causes that no one can perish before His grace.

But the fanatics, the Schvvenckfeldians, ineptly understand the written word by the letter, and divine motions and enthusiasms by the spirit: because the Apostles did not refer men to enthusiasms, but to scripture. No less ineptly do the Papists say that the scripture of the Old and New Testament is designated by the letter, but the unwritten word or preaching done by living voice by the Spirit: Because they contradict Paul, who says that scripture is not destitute of the power of vivifying and saving 2. Timoth. III. v. 15. seq. nor did the Apostles preach anything outside of those things which were written in Moses and the Prophets Acts XXVI. v. 22. and the word which they preached, they also consigned to the monuments of letters, as Irenaeus testifies; finally, the written and unwritten word was defined by the Council of Trent to be received with equal affection of piety. Whence the proof of Becanus l. 1 is ridiculous. Manual. c. 5. that Scripture cannot be the judge of controversies, because the letter kills. Origen also wrongly understood the literal sense by the letter, and the allegorical and spiritual sense by the spirit, in book VI. against Celsus near the end. He called the literal sense a certain sensible understanding of divine letters, but the intellectual sense the spirit. Thence, since the letter is said to kill, but the spirit to vivify, he attempts to transform almost everything into Allegories, the literal sense being set aside. For the literal sense is the very meaning of the Holy Spirit signified through words by the force of the context, whether understood properly or figuratively. Innocent III. in cap. solicite extr. de majorit. & obedient. understands by the letter the scriptures of the Old Testament, to prove that what is written in the histories of the Old Testament, concerning Moses and Joshua commanding the Priests, not only does not bind in the New, but is even harmful, because the letter kills. Finally, some dull monks ignorantly understand by the letter knowledge and erudition, because, forsooth, a learned man is said to know letters; which brothers of ignorance the Poet rightly mocks wittily: Take good care, lest by chance any letter be able to kill you, for no letter is known to you.

But when the Apostle denies that he is a minister of the letter, or of the moral law, this is to be understood not simply, but comparatively, as 1. Cor. I. v. 17. he says he was sent not to baptize (namely primarily) but to evangelize, that he was constituted not primarily to teach the law, but the Gospel, which B. Hunnius warns is to be opposed to the Jews and the Judaizing Pseudo-Apostles at the same time in this sense: We Apostles were not placed into the ministry by God primarily so that we might preach the law, just as the Pseudo-Apostles urge the law principally, and perniciously mix it with the Gospel, and much less so that we might persist in the manner of the Jews in the preaching of the law, with the Gospel of grace concerning Christ omitted and struck out: But the doctrine of the Gospel is enjoined upon us altogether principally, lest by urging the law alone we seem to kill men rather than to instruct them in the reasons for salvation, when yet the end and scope of our ministry is the perpetual salvation of men.

For the letter kills) Just as חָיָה וְהֶחֱיָה is said in Hebrew to ζωοποιεῖν [make alive] concerning him who has not killed someone, as in Exodus 1:17 and Judges 8:19. Thus, he is said to kill who leaves a man to death and does not free him from it. This, however, the law of Moses does, having no promises of new life for those living according to it, John 6:49, Galatians 3:21. Furthermore, it kills, that is, it punishes sinners with violent death.

But the Spirit makes alive) It is the Spirit of God who provides eternal life.

As he previously set forth the different nature of the law and the Gospel, that the former is letter only, but the latter is spirit: so now he shows the distinction of both from their effect, that the law kills, but the Gospel makes alive. Grotius diminishes both the effect of the law and the Gospel, and perverts the very nature of both. For he attributes to the law, not what the Apostle does, τὸ ἀποκτείνειν [to kill], although the Apostle teaches that it expressly brings death, nay, condemnation: but only to leave to death, not to free from death, which can also be said of philosophy and any other things (outside of the Gospel, Christ, and divine grace); and consequently he must attribute to the Gospel, not what the Apostle does, τὸ ζωοποιεῖν [to make alive], that it truly makes alive, but only that it does not leave a man to death. But what he further says about the law, that it kills, that is, according to Grotius's interpretation, that it punishes sinners with violent death, that cannot be accepted of the law in general, but only of certain commands of the law which, when violated, demanded a violent death, which is ἀλλότριον [foreign] in this place: because it looked to the Mosaic polity, and that pertained to forensic laws: but it does not prescribe judgments or punishments for Christians; concerning which it was not Paul's purpose to treat here either. Nor does that contribute anything to the opposition of letter and spirit. For does the letter kill, that is, punish sinners with violent death, and the Spirit make alive by freeing transgressors, who have deserved it, from violent death? But that Grotius perverts the nature of the law is by no means obscure, since it leaves no promises of eternal life to those living according to it. Which openly contradicts Paul in Galatians 3:12, who teaches that the law promises eternal life, provided it is kept: He who shall do these things shall live in them. But how it perverts the Gospel has been observed elsewhere, because its preaching is not about the free remission of sins and the righteousness of Christ, which is apprehended through faith, but about an obedience from us far more perfect than the law of Moses requires, according to Grotius, so that we may be righteous before God and be saved. Which things approach and are akin to the doctrines not of the Apostles, but of the Pseudo-Apostles: since according to the Apostolic doctrine the law demands perfect obedience from us, which is impossible for us to perform. But the Gospel shows the way by which the τὸ ἀδύνατον of our nature is compensated, namely by the obedience of Christ, both active and passive, by which the law and divine justice have been satisfied. The letter, therefore, that is, the law, is said to kill, not indeed of itself. For thus ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐἰς ζωὴν is spoken of in Romans 7:10, but because its power ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς was weakened through the flesh, that is, our corrupt nature, so that it cannot make us alive, Romans 8:3; nay, it cannot but convict us of sin, work wrath, denounce the curse upon us, kill us or adjudge us to death and condemn us, Rom. 3:20, ch. 4:16, and thus ἑυρέθη ἡμῖν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐἰς ζωὴν, αὕτη ἐἰς θάνατον, ch. 7:10. Wherefore the law kills not so much by way of a physical cause as a moral cause; not so much by destroying us as by adjudging and condemning us to death, although it may also be said to kill in that manner as a physical cause, because it crushes our hearts and mortifies them, so that they feel nothing but death, and we must eternally perish, prostrated by the blow and thunderbolt of the law, unless grace comes to our aid. But the Spirit of God is said to make alive, not that the Spirit of God immediately provides eternal life, but that the Gospel is metonymically called Spirit in contrast to the letter, that is, the law, through which the Holy Spirit is conferred upon us and works life in us; and thus the Gospel is said to make us alive when we are otherwise prostrated and perishing by the thunderbolt of the law, both as a moral cause, which lifts us up with the promises of grace; and as a physical cause, which confers the remission of sins, righteousness, and salvation organically, and effects spiritual life in us, since through the Gospel we are regenerated and obtain the life of grace. Gal. 2:2. Some understand by Spirit the Holy Spirit: But in the same sense. For the Holy Spirit does not make alive immediately, but through the Gospel, insofar as, united to the word of the Gospel, He exerts His power into our hearts, which glides in with the word and through the word. Nor is the word of the Gospel separated from the Holy Spirit, who is inseparable from it, and as it were its soul, rendering it living and effective through a mystical union with the word, so that the word may be spirit and life, whence Christ in John 6:63: The words that I speak, they are spirit and they are life.

Wherefore the misinterpretation and distortion is by no means to be tolerated, when the Schwenkfeldians and other fanatics call the preached or written word of God a dead letter, and claim the life-giving power only for their internal word and their enthusiasms; whereas divine power is ascribed here to the law and the preaching of the law, not indeed of making alive, but of killing, whence the law is not a dead letter but a most living one, killing men or the whole human race outside of grace. For that which is dead does not act, nor does it kill. But the Spirit is the Gospel or the doctrine of the Gospel, whether comprised in Holy Scripture or preached by living voice, which makes alive and has the power of making alive through the Holy Spirit united to the word of the Gospel, who is therefore given through the preaching of the Gospel (not through immediate enthusiasm) and is effective for conversion, faith, and salvation. The reason, therefore, is rendered here, indicated by the causal particle, why the Apostles were not sent primarily for the sake of preaching the law, sought from the ultimate end and supreme scope of the ministry of the holy Apostles, which is not to kill or condemn, but to save and make alive: because indeed the law by its nature kills transgressors spiritually and adjudges them to eternal death: certainly from the property of the law and the Apostolic preaching compared with one another, it becomes clear regarding the scope and end, that they are not ministers of killing or death in their office, which the letter or voice of the law effects, but of making alive, which the preaching of the Gospel concerning the grace of Christ works, as the blessed Hunnius aptly notes here. To which also the paraphrase of Theophylact contributes, even though he refers it to baptism, which is a visible word, and the washing of the Spirit in the word, Eph. 5:26, and thus is also a medium of regeneration and of the renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. 3:5. The law, he says, that older one, if it catches anyone delinquent even in the smallest matters, it kills them no differently than it did the one gathering sticks on the Sabbath. But the Holy Spirit, if He receives a man bound by even a thousand crimes, through the washing of baptism, both renders him righteous and makes him alive from the death of sin.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ὃς καὶ ἱκάνωσεν ἡμᾶς) ἱκανὸν habes & Col. I. 2. respondens Hebræo הֵכִין, & magis etiam Rabbinico הִסְפִּיק. Deus nos ministerio tanto aptos non reperit, sed fecit. Sic Paulus hic factus est in virum alium, ut olim alius ejusdem nominis, 1. Sam. X. 6.

Διακόνους καινῆς διαθήκης) Vox διακόνος hic generaliter sumitur, ut 1. Cor. III. 5. Sic & διακονία Act. I. 17. & alibi sæpius. De nomine καινῆς διαθήκης vide prolegomena nostra ad Evangelia.

Per novum testamentum fœdus novum intelligitur, quod pepegit nobiscum Deus in Christo de gratia, justitia & salute per fidem in Christum nobis conferenda, quod respectu Dei, in passione & mor- te Christi sancitum est sanguine Filii Dei; ex parte nostri, ut scilicet in fœdus istud recipiamur per verbum & sacramenta sancitur, nobisque appli- catur per sacrum ministerium. Vetus Testamentum vetus erat fœdus vel pactum de justitia & salute per legis observantiam consequenda, quod in monte Sinai solemniter promulgatum, & san- guine vitulorum sancitum est Exod. XXIV. Hæc ergò fœdera atque testamenta naturà suà diversis- sima non vult confundi, quemadmodum à falsis Apostolis fiebat, sed distincta relinqui, ideoque se non fœderis antiqui, ut Moses erat, nec etiam tum antiqui, tum novi Ministrum esse, quales e- rant Pseudo-Apostoli legem & Evangelium commi- scentes, fœdus antiquum cum novo consarcinan- tes & confundentes, quando & per fidem in Chri- stum & per observantiam legis hominem justificari ac salvari contendebant; sed novi fœderis, quod gratiam, justitiam & salutem unicè per fidem in Christum consequendam prædicabat, ministrum esse docet, qui inter Corinthios nil se scire judi- cavit, nisi Jesum crucifixum 1. Cor. II. 2. Atque hac ratione transitum sibi parat Apostolus ad collatio- nem & discrimen utriusque Testamenti, ut confusio- ni Pseudo-Apostolorum occurrat, doctrinæque suæ sinceritatem asserat, qui præco erat doctrinæ Evangelicæ de Christo, ut per fidem in ipsum, in quo umbræ & figuræ, nec non prædictiones & promissiones Mosis & Prophetarum suum ha- bent complementum, remissionem peccatorum consequantur, qui in nomen ejus credunt Act. X. 43. cap. XXVI. 38. 39.

PARS III. Contentio ministerii Novi & Veteris Testa- menti Apostolica.

Ὀὐ γράμματος ἀλλὰ πνέυματος) Moses scripturam in ta- bulis lapideis populo attulit: Apostoli verbum comitatum illustrioribus signis quam Moses dederat, ut linguis, sana- tionibus, mortuorum resuscitatione, quin & potestate dona talia aliis conferendi, quod nunquam visum fuerat.

Per Literam non intelligit scripturam, sed le- gem ipsam, qua materiale & formale, verba vel scripturam & sensum. Per Spiritum, qui oppo- nitur literæ, non intelligit virtutem miracula pa- trandi, aut similem aliquam facultatem donorum extraordinariorum, quibus doctrina Apostolo- rum confirmabatur: Sed per metonymiam, Evan- gelii doctrinam, quæ Spiritu & virtute divina ani- mata est viva & efficax Johan. VI. v. 63. Ebr. IV. 12. Lex poscit tantum agenda, nullasque vires affert agendi, adeoque nil nisi γράμμα vel litera est, ad salutem nihil conferens. Evangelium vero Spiri- tum affert, cujus virtute fides, quam requirit in nobis, accenditur, & ita Spiritus dicitur, quia Spi- ritu sancto instructum est, qui sese gratiose uni- entlo cum verbo Evangelii, largitur ei vim & effi- caciam spiritualem corda nostra convertendi, il- luminandi, regenerandi, ac renovandi, nosque justificandi ac salvandi. Spiritus ergò non seque- strandus est à verbo Evangelii, utpote intime cum eodem unitus ac inseparabiliter, ut potentia Dei sit ad salutem omni credenti Roman. I. v. 16. Quo de vide, quæ contra fanaticos Tom. I. Sy- stem. Theol. cap. IV. qu. XXV. dicta Theophyla- ctus, præeunte Chrysostomo: Lex spiritualis qui- dem erat, hoc est à Spiritu concessa & prodiens; nec tamen ut nova, vetus illa Spiritum conferebat. Ait igitur: Haudquaquam nobis, quemadmodum Mo- si, literæ duntaxat credita sunt: Sed Spiritus ipse concessus. Conf. Gal. III. vers. 2. Addimus spi- ritalem etiam legem fuisse, quod obedientiam non externam tantum, sed internam & spiritualem requisiverit Rom. VII. v. 14. Lex spiritualis est, ego vero carnalis sum. Non tamen, ut Evangelium Spiritus dicitur: quia postulabat solum obedien- tiam, non verò spiritum & facultatem conferebat ad præstandam obedientiam, & licet vim spiritua- lem quoque habuerit lex, ea tamen ad conteran- dum tantum corda faciebat, non verò ad eadem vi- vificanda, ideoque datam negat Apostolus legem, quæ hominem post lapsum vivificare posset Gal. III. 21. Si data lex, quæ vivificare posset, revera è lege esset justitia. Vocatur autem lex litera, quia literis à DEO inscripta & insculpta fuit tabulis lapideis, quæ litera vel lex scripta in arca fœderis asservan- da erat Exod. XXXIV. vers. 1. 28. 1 Reg. VIII. v. 3. Ideoque Synecdochice lex dicta est litera, hoc est, externa scriptura in tabulis lapideis legem conti- nens. Ministrare autem seu docere literam est so- lam legem in suo rigore, quo perfectam obedien- tiam requirit, eaque destitutos accusat, maledi- cione ferit & condemnat, docere. Buchstaben lehren, inquit B. Lutherus in glossa marginali, ist das blosse Gesetz und Werck lehren, ohne der Gnade GOttes Erkänntniß, dadurch wird alles verdammt, und des Todes schuldig erkannt, was der Mensch ist und thut, denn er kan ohne GOttes Gnade nichts gutes thun. Evangelium verò vo- catur Spiritus Metonymicè, quia Spiritum exhi- bet, qui per illud sese cordibus hominum insinuat, inque iisdem operatur, quod etiam à Spiritu sancto peculiari ratione est, ut à benevolentissimo Para- cleto, Consolatore & salutis æternæ effectore, ideoque Spiritum docere ita explicat B. Lutherus: Geist lehren, ist die Gnade ohne Gesetz und Ver- dienst lehren, dadurch wird der Mensch lebendig und selig. Adde Tom. I. Jenens. Germ. fol. 138. b. Der Buchstab machet, daß niemand für GOt- tes Zorn bleiben kan; der Geist machet, daß nie- mand für seiner Gnade verderben kan.

Ineptè autem fanatici, Schvvenckfeldiani per literam verbum scriptum, per spiritum divinos motus & enthusiasmos intelligunt: quia Apostoli non ad Enthusiasmos, sed ad scripturam remitte- bant homines. Nec minus ineptè Papistæ per literam scripturam Veteris & Novi Testamenti, per Spiritum autem verbum non scriptum vel præ- dicationem vivâ voce factam designari ajunt: Quia scripturam destitui virtute vivificandi & salvandi, Paulo repugnant 2. Timoth. III. v. 15. seq. neque quicquam prædicarunt Apostoli, extra ea, quæ in Mose & Prophetis scripta erant Actor. XXVI. v. 22. & verbum quod prædicarunt, litera- rum quoque monumentis consignarunt, Irenæo teste; denique verbum scriptum & non scriptum per Concilium Tridentinum definitum est pari pie- tatis affectu suscipiendum. Unde ridicula est pro- batio Becani l. 1. Manual. c. 5. quod Scriptura ju- dex controversiarum esse non possit, quia litera occidit. Perperam etiam Origenes per literam sen- sum literalem, per spiritum sensum allegoricum & spiritualem intellexit libr. VI. contra Celsum sub finem. Literam sensibilem quandam dixit divina- rum literarum intelligentiam, spiritum verò intelle- ctualem. Inde quum litera occidere, spiritus au- tem vivificare dicatur, literali sensu posthabito, omnia fermè in Allegorias transformare conatur. Sensus enim literalis est ipsa Spiritus sancti sen- tentia per verba vi contextus sive propriè, sive figu- ratè intellecta, significata. Innocentius III. in cap. solicite extr. de majorit. & obedient. per lite- ram intelligit scripturas Veteris Testamenti, ut probet, quod in historiis Veteris Testamenti, de Mose & Josua imperantibus Sacerdotibus scri- ptum est, non solum non obligare in Novo, sed etiam noxium esse, quia litera occidit. Imperite denique per literam Monachi nonnulli insulsi scientiam & eruditionem intelligunt, quia scilicet scire literas eruditus dicitur; quales ignorantiæ fratres meritò Poëta salse irridet: Cavisli bene, ne fors te ulla occidere possit Litera, nam nulla est litera nota tibi.

Cum autem negat Apostolus, se esse ministrum literæ, vel legis moralis, intelligendum hoc non simpliciter, sed comparatè, uti 1. Cor. I. vers. 17. se non ad baptizandum (scilicet primario) sed ad evangelizandum missum ait, quod non πρώτως ad docendum legem, sed Evangelium constitutus sit, quod opponi Judæis simul & Pseudo-Aposto- lis Judaizantibus monet B. Hunnius hoc sensu: Nos Apostoli non ideo potissimum in ministerium à Deo collocati sumus, ut legem prædicemus, quem- admodum Pseudo-Apostoli legem principaliter ur- gent, & cum Evangelio perniciose commiscent, multo vero minus, ut in concione legis Judaorum in modum subsistamus, omisso & dispuncto Evangelio gratia de Christo: Sed omnino principaliter injuncta nobis est Evangelii doctrina, ne solam urgendo legem homines occidere potius, quam ad salutis rationes erudire videamur, cum tamen ministerii nostri finis atque scopus sit perpetua hominum salus.

Τὸ γὰρ γράμμα ἀποκτείνει) Sicut חָיָה וְהֶחֱיָה Hebræis ζωο- ποιεῖν dicitur de eo, qui aliquem non interfecit, ut Exod. I. v. 17. & Judic. VIII. v. 19. Sic interficere dicitur, qui ho- minem morti relinquit, nec ab ea liberat. Hoc autem fa- cit lex Mosis, nulla habens promissa novæ vitæ, secundum ipsam viventibus Joh. VI. 49. Gal. III. 21. Præterea oc- cidit, id est, morte violenta punit peccantes.

Τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ζωοποιεῖ) Spiritus Dei est, qui vitam præ- stat æternam.

Ut prius naturam diversam legis & Evangelii tradidit, quod illa litera tantum, hoc vero spiri- tus sit: Ita nunc discrimen utriusque ab effectu ostendit, quod lex occidat, Evangelium verò vi- vificet. Grotius & effectum legis & Evangelii ex- tenuat, & naturam ipsam utriusque pervertit. Legi enim tribuit, non quod Apostolus, τὸ ἀποκτείνειν occidere, cum Apostolus eam expres- se mortem imò damnationem afferre doceat: Sed tantum morti relinquere, à morte non liberare, quod etiam de Philosophia & quibusvis aliis dici potest (extra Evangelium, Christum, & gratiam divinam) ac proinde Evangelio tribuat oportet, non quod Apostolus τὸ ζωοποιεῖν, quod verè vivi- ficet, sed tantum, quod hominem non relinquat morti. Quod autem de lege porrò dicit, quod ea- dem occidat, id est, interprete Grotio, morte vio- lenta puniat peccantes, id nec in universum de lege accipi potest, sed de quibusdam tantùm mandatis legis, quæ violata mortem postulabant violen- tam, quod ἀλλότριον hoc loco est: quia respicie- bat politiam Mosaicam, & ad forenses leges id pertinebat: Non vero Christianis judicia vel sup- plicia præscribit; de quibus etiam hic agere Pau- lo non erat propositum. Neque vero ad opposi- tionem literæ & spiritus id quicquam facit. Num enim litera occidit, id est morte violentâ punit pec- cantes, Spiritus vivificat, à morte violenta trans- gressores, eam promeritos, liberando? Natu- ram autem legis pervertere Grotium minimè ob- scurum est, siquidem legi nulla promissa vitæ æter- næ relinquit, secundum eam viventibus. Quod aperte refragatur Paulo Galat. III. v. 12. legem vi- tam æternam promittere docenti, si modo serve- tur: Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis. Evangelium verò quomodo pervertat, alias observatum, quod non concio ipsi est de remissione peccatorum gratuita, & justitiâ Christi, quæ per fidem apprehenditur, sed obedientiam à nobis longè perfectiorem, quàm lex Mosis requirit, secundum Grotium, ut justi co- ram Deo simus & salvemur. Quæ non Aposto- lorum, sed Pseudo-Apostolorum doctrinæ accedunt & affinia sunt: siquidem juxta Apostolicam do- ctrinam lex perfectam obedientiam à nobis exi- gat, quæ præstitu nobis impossibilis est. Evange- lium verò viam monstret, quà naturæ nostræ τὸ ἀδύνατον compensetur, nimirum obedientiâ Chri- sti tam activâ, quàm passivâ, qua legi & justitiæ divinæ satisfactum est. Litera ergò, hoc est, lex occidere dicitur non quidem per se. Sic enim ἡ ἐν- τολὴ ἡ ἐἰς ζωὴν dicitur Roman. VII. v. 10. sed quia vis ejus ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς infirmata est per car- nem, id est, naturam nostram corruptam, ut non possit nos vivificare Roman. 8. v. 3. imò non possit non arguere in nobis peccatum, operari iram, de- nunciare nobis maledictionem, occidere nos vel adjudicare morti & condemnare Rom. III. 20. cap. IV. 16. & ita ἑυρέθη ἡμῖν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐἰς ζωὴν, αὕτη ἐἰς θάνατον cap. VII. 10. Quapropter occidit lex non tam per modum causæ physicæ, quàm ut causæ mo- ralis; non tam nos perimendo, quam morti adju- dicando & condemnando, quanquam & ea ratio- ne occidere, ut causa physica dicatur, quod corda nostra conterat, & mortificet, ut nil nisi mortem sentiant, & æternum pereundum sit nobis ictu & fulmine legis prostratis, nisi gratia succurrat. Spi- ritus autem Dei vivificare dicitur, non quod Spi- ritus Dei immediatè vitam æternam præstet, sed quod Evangelium Metonymicè Spiritus vocetur in ἀντιθέσει ad literam, hoc est, legem, per quod Spiritus sanctus nobis confertur, & in nobis vitam operatur, adeoque Evangelium dicitur nos legis fulmine prostratos & perituros alioquin vivifica- re, tum ut causa moralis, quæ promissionibus gra- tiæ erigit; tum ut causa physica, quæ remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & salutem ὀργανικῶς con- fert, & vitam spiritualem in nobis efficit, siquidem per Evangelium regeneremur & vitam gratiæ consequamur. Gal. II. 2. Nonnulli intelligunt per Spiritum Spiritum sanctum: Sed eodem sensu. Nam Spiritus sanctus non vivificat ἀμέσως, sed per Evangelium, quatenus verbo Evangelii unitus suam vim in corda nostra exerit, quæ cum verbo, & per verbum illabitur. Neque verbo Evangelii à Spiritu sancto sejuncto, qui ab eo inseparabilis est, ejusque veluti anima, vivum id reddens, & efficax per unionem mysticam cum verbo, ut ver- bum spiritus sit & vita, unde Christus Joh. VI. 63. Verba quæ ego loquor, spiritus sunt & vita.

Quapropter ψευδερμηνεία & στρεβλότης minime toleranda est, cum Schwenkfeldiani, aliique fa- natici literam mortuam dicunt verbum Dei prædi- catum aut scriptum, & vim vivificantem suo tan- tùm interno verbo & enthusiasmis suis vendicant; quum legi & legis concioni vis divina hîc adscriba- tur non quidem vivificandi, sed occidendi, unde non mortua litera sed maxime viva lex est, homi- nes vel totum genus humanum extra gratiam oc- cidens. Quod enim mortuum est, non agit, nec occidit. Spiritus autem sit Evangelium vel doctri- na Evangelii sive scripturâ sacrâ comprehenssa, sive viva voce prædicata, quæ vivificat, & vim vivifi- candi habet per Spiritum sanctum verbo Evange- lii unitum, qui proinde per Evangelii concionem, (non per immediatum Enthusiasmum) datur, & ad conversionem, fidem ac salutem efficax est. Ra- tio itaque hic, particula causali indicata, redditur, cur non principaliter legis prædicandæ gratia missi sunt Apostoli, petita ab ultimo fine & supremo sco- po ministerii sanctorum Apostolorum, qui non est occidere seu damnare, sed salvare & vivificare: quia vero lex sua natura transgressores spiritualiter occi- dit, ac sempiternæ morti addicit: utique ex collata inter se proprietate ista legis & prædicationis Apo- stolicæ scopo atque fine perspicuum evadit, ut in suo munere non occisionis sive mortis sint administri, quam litera seu vox legis efficit, sed vivificationis, quam Evangelii concio de gratia Christi operatur, ut commode hic B. Hunnius. Quo etiam facit pa- raphrasis Theophylacti, etsi ad baptismum, qui ver- bum est ὁρατὸν, & lavacrum Spiritus in verbo Ephes. V. 26. adeoque medium etiam regenerationis est & renovationis Spiritus sancti Tit. III 5. id referat. Lex, inquit, illa vetustior, si quem deprehendat vel rebus in minimis delinquentem, non secus officit morte, quam ligna sabbato legentem effecerit. Spiri- tus autem sanctus, si vel mille hominem facinoribus obstrictum exceperit, baptismi lavacro, & justum reddit, & peccato vivificat mortuum.

## 3:7
Verse 7.

If the ministration of death) that is, of the law, all of whose promises were terminated by death, without any hope of restitution, see Lev. 26, Deut. 5 and 28.

It is false that all the promises of the law are terminated in death without hope of restitution. For the law had not only temporal promises, but also those of eternal life, as Christ himself taught in Luke 10:25 et seqq., Leviticus 19:5.

Ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις) He says that the ministry of Moses was inscribed on stone tablets, because those tablets showed that he, to whom God had delivered them, was the mediator of that covenant; it is therefore a metonymy of the cause for the effect. Ἐντυπῶι is חָרַת, to engrave. Exodus 30:1, verse 15, where it treats of the same tablets.

But how did the stone tablets show that Moses was the mediator of the covenant? Nay, not Moses, but Christ alone is the mediator of God and men, Galatians 3:20, 1 Timothy 2:5. We admit a metonymy, but in the fact that the law is called the ministry of death, which was inscribed on stone tablets, because the law is not properly a ministry or a ministry of death or bringing death, but as it was dispensed or promulgated through the ministry of Moses: and that deadly ministry had as its object the law inscribed on stone tablets as the killing letter, which by proposing death threatened, denounced a curse, and brought condemnation. Therefore it is called the ministry of death and condemnation in verses 7 and 8, the ministry of Moses concerning the law as such. Regarding the version of the word ἐντετυπωμένη in the Vulgate as DEFORMATA, the Erasmian censure of Hugo is to be noted, because Hugo of Saint-Cher interprets it as shamefully deformed, and afterwards, very well formed. Erasmus says it is most impudent, indeed, to wish to interpret the New Testament written in Greek by the Apostles if you are entirely ignorant of Greek. Paul, he says, wrote ἐντετυπωμένη, that is, informed, to render it word for word, that is, inscribed. Although the interpreter elegantly said deformata for formata. For he does not increase it here (perhaps he meant to say he diminishes it) any more than in deambulare and deosculari. And Quintilian: Marbles first deformed by the hand. Ambrose reads formata, not deformata.

The Apostle now for the third time compares the law with the Gospel, or the ministry of the law and the Gospel, in respect of glory; and he teaches that the glory of the latter is far greater from those things which have been said: For if the Mosaic and legal ministry, which is of death, and engraved in letters on stones, had glory, which the Israelites could not bear, how much more shall the Evangelical and Apostolic ministry, which is life, and inscribed on the tables of the heart (preserving the metonymical expression), have glory. This serves not only to extol the glory of the Apostolic doctrine and the Evangelical ministry, but primarily to explain and exhibit in that συγκρίσει (comparison) that which was designated or adumbrated there by the glory and radiance of the law, which the Israelites could not look upon, if it is compared with the glory which is not merely adumbrated, but clearly manifested in the Gospel. For why did Moses shine with such radiance in that διακονίᾳ (ministry) of his, unless it was because he had conversed immediately with God, and because he carried with him the divine law, which is a type of divine justice? How much more eminent, therefore, must the glory of the Evangelical doctrine be considered, which is preached by the Apostles, when in it the very radiance of divine glory, the Son of God, is exhibited, He who has been made both our justice and the fountain of divine grace, from whose fullness we draw grace for grace? The force of this argument is intensified by adding another difference, namely, that that glory with which the law shone, and the very διακονία (ministry) of the law or its administrator, was καταργουμένη (being brought to an end), that is, such as was easily evacuated and ceased, not only at the death of Moses (as Grotius doubtfully conjectures), but shortly after his return from the mountain. But this glory of the Gospel and of its διακονία (ministry) is by no means evacuated. For in the Gospel and the Evangelical ministry, that ἀπαύγασμα (effulgence) τῆς δόξης (of the glory) and the most brilliant splendor of divine justice and grace always shine forth. The Apostle proposes that difference and his argument more fully through elaboration; and indeed regarding different parts: first, regarding the comparison of the ministry of life and death: For if the ministration of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of justice abound in glory, as Estius has not poorly expressed the sense: For if the ministry of the law, which renders men liable to eternal condemnation and death, was glory, that is, a glorious thing, therefore a much greater and more excellent glory is due to the ministry of the new law (more correctly, the Gospel), which brings justice, by which condemnation is escaped and life is acquired. Secondly, regarding the comparison of partial and total glory, v. 10. For that which shone in that part (namely, the face) was not glorified, because of the excellent glory, or in comparison to the same, which is by no means so partial that only the face shines, but is truly total, by which we are rendered shining in both soul and body: Nor does it render only the face of the minister shining; but it also renders us all shining and glorious. For the Israelites not only did not participate in that (Moses') glory, but could not even look upon it: But this (Gospel) glory is so constituted that it is altogether our glory, and the splendor of the Gospel shines forth in us all: and that ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης (because of the surpassing glory), because this glory is superabundant, which is not only sufficient for illuminating all, but superabounds. Thirdly, regarding the comparison of the temporary and the perpetual thing, v. 11. For if that which is being evacuated is through glory, much more is that which remains in glory. He previously called τὴν δόξαν (the glory) or the radiation of the Mosaic face καταργουμένην (being brought to an end) in v. 7. But now the legal ministry itself, which was διὰ δόξης (through glory) when Moses brought forth the law, is called τὸ καταργού- μενον (that which is being brought to an end), that which is to be destroyed; but the Evangelical ministry is called τὸ μένον (that which remains), that which abides: because that transitory brightness of the Mosaic face was a symbol of the evacuation of the legal ministry. But how was the legal ministry evacuated? Not by its own fault and in itself, but by our fault and as far as we are concerned. For since the law cannot be fulfilled by us, the διακονία τοῦ γράμματος (ministry of the letter) is evacuated thus far, as to its power of justifying and saving, because the law was weakened through the flesh, and there is need of the διακονία τοῦ πνεύματος (ministry of the Spirit) and the Evangelical doctrine concerning Christ, who is our justice and the salvation of God, and it is necessary that the same remain perpetual. Therefore the law does not cease absolutely, but as to a certain use, which it does not perform not by its own fault, but by ours: because its power is weakened by our corrupt nature, by which the yoke of the law is plainly ἀβάστακτον (unbearable) to us, so that consequently it can contribute nothing to our justification and salvation, but it is necessary that those who are saved be saved solely by the grace of Christ our Lord apprehended through faith, Acts XV. v. 10, 11.

Therefore, both the law and the Mosaic ministry of the law are compared with the Gospel and its Apostolic ministry, and that of the Apostolic successors, in a triple respect: (1) regarding nature, because the former exhibits only the letter, the latter the spirit; (2) regarding efficacy, because the former kills and the latter gives life; and (3) regarding glory, which is far more eminent here than there, whether we contend between the nature of the law and the Gospel themselves, or look at the subject which is glorified, or the use and the end.

Theophylact says this concerning those three: Having laid open the difference between the New and Old Testaments above, he asserts that the one was written with ink, the other with the Spirit, and that the former was engraved on stones, but the latter on hearts: and likewise that death is compared from the one, and life from the other. Now indeed he strives to show that the glory of the Gospel is far greater than that of the law was. For the old law obtained a certain sensible glory, namely, the more shining face of Moses, but the new one, that which is conceived by the mind. Since it is no longer permitted for anyone to look upon this same thing sensibly with the eyes. He therefore shows that the excellence of the Gospel itself can be comprehended by a certain concept of the mind, and says that the former law was a minister of death. For he did not say it was the producer, so that he might not provide any occasion for the error of heretics, but a minister. For indeed sin had brought forth death, but death brought the punishment. Furthermore, the letter of the Old Testament itself stood alone, nor did it bring any help to those struggling, which certainly does not happen in baptism. Therefore Theophylact concludes: If the law, therefore, when it was such, was brought about in glory, how much more so the grace, which excels to such a degree that nothing can be compared to its excellence. Now let us also hear Grotius on these matters.

Ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι ἀτενίσαι τοὺς ὑιοὺς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον Μωυσέως διὰ τὴν δόξαν τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ) He explains well what is in Exodus XXXIV, verse 30. They were afraid to approach him. For they did not dare to approach because they could not look directly at him, which is ἀτενίζειν; Luke II, verse 20, XXII, 56, Acts III, 4, 12, VI, 15, VII, 55, XI, 6, XIII, 9, XIV, 9. And he rightly called the radiance of the face of Moses δόξαν, because the Seventy also translate the Hebrew word קרן as ἦν δεδοξασμένη and δεδόξασται. See what has been said by us on that passage of Exodus, and 1 Cor. XI, 7.

The Vulgate, therefore, in Exod. XXXIV. verse 36, making the face of Moses horned, although pronounced authentic by the Council of Trent and two Roman Pontiffs, must here be amended, as Grotius admits, who acknowledges that the Hebrew word should be translated as δεδοξασμένην with the LXX, to whom the Apostle himself has given his approval. For they did not dare to approach Moses because of horns, but because of the δόξαν, the glory or splendor of his face.

Τὴν καταργουμένην) Because, he says, the splendor was to cease with death, if not even before. See 1 Cor. II. 6, VI. 13, XIII. 8, 10.

It was noted before that that conjecture rests on no evidence, that Moses shone throughout his whole life from the time the law was received from God. That, therefore, as an ἄγραφον, or rather an ἀντίγραφον, is deservedly to be rejected.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Εἰ δὲ ἡ διακονία τοῦ θανάτου) id est legis, cujus omnia promissa morte terminabantur, sine ulla spe restitutionis, Vide Lev. XXVI. Deut. V. & XXVIII.

Falsum est legis promissa omnia terminata in morte esse sine spe restitutionis. Nam non tan- tum promissiones temporales lex habebat; sed etiam æternæ vitæ, uti Christus ipse docuit Luc. X. vers. 25. seqq. Levit. XIX. vers. 5.

Ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις) Dicit ministerium Mosis inscri- ptum fuisse saxeis tabulis, quia illæ tabulæ ostendebant, ipsum, cui Deus eas tradiderat, esse μεσίτην illius fœderis, est ergo μετωνυμία causæ pro effectu. Εντυπῶι est חָרַת κε- λάπτει. Exod. XXX. I. v. 15. ubi de iisdem tabulis agitur.

Quomodo vero tabulæ lapideæ ostendebant Mosen esse μεσίτην fœderis? Imò non Moses, sed Christus unicè μεσίτης est Dei & hominum Gal. III. vers. 20. 1. Timoth. II. vers. 5. Metonymiam admittimus, sed in eo, quod ministerium mortis lex dicatur, quæ in tabulis lapideis insculpta fuit, quia lex non propriè est διακονία aut διακονία τοῦ θανάτου vel mortem afferens, sed ut per ministerium Mosis dispensata vel promulgata est : & ministe- rium illud mortiferum pro objecto habuit legem in tabulis lapideis insculptam ceu literam occiden- tem, quam proponendo mortem minabatur, ma- ledictionem denunciabat, & condemnationem afferebat. Ideò ministerium mortis & condemna- tionis dicitur vers. 7. & 8. Mosis circa legem mini- sterium qua tale. Circa vocis ἐντετυπωμένη ver- sionem in Vulgata DEFORMATA obser- vanda censura Hugonis Erasmica, quia Hugo Carrensis interpretatur turpiter deformata, & postea, valde bene formata. Impudentissimum nem- pe dicit Erasmus, novum Testamentum Græce scri- ptum ab Apostolis interpretari velle, si Græce prorsus nescias. Paulus, inquit, scripsit ἐντετυπωμένη, id est informata, ut ad verbum reddam, hoc est insculpta. Quanquam eleganter interpres dixit deformata pro Formata. Nec enim hic auget (minuit fors dicere voluit) non magis quam in deambulare ac deoscu- lari. Et Quintilianus: Marmora primà deforma- ta manu. Ambrosius formata legit, non defor- mata.

Comparat jam tertiò Apostolus legem cum Evangelio vel ministerium legis & Evangelii ratione gloriæ; & hujus longe majorem gloriam esse docet ex iis, quæ dicta sunt: Si enim ministerium Mosaïcum & legale, quod mortis, & in lapidibus literis insculptum, gloriam habuit, quam ferre non potuere Israëlitæ, quantò magis ministerium Evangelicum & Apostolicum, quod vita est, & in tabulis cordis inscriptum (servata Metonymica loquutione) habiturum est gloriam. Quod facit non tantum ad gloriam doctrinæ Apostolicæ & ministerii Evangelici extollendam, sed imprimis ad id, quod ibi per gloriam & fulgorem legis, quem Israëlitæ intueri non poterant, designatum vel adumbratum fuit, si cum gloria, quæ non adumbratur tantùm, sed luculenter manifestatur in Evangelio, comparetur, explicandum, & in συγκρίσει illa exhibendum. Cur enim Moses in sua illa διακονίᾳ tanto fulgore coruscabat, nisi quod immediate cum Deo conversatus fuerat, quodque legem divinam, quæ typus justitiæ divinæ, secum ferebat. Quanto ergo eminentior gloria Evangelicæ doctrinæ censenda, quæ ab Apostolis prædicatur, quum in illa ipse fulgor divinæ gloriæ Filius DEI exhibeatur, is, qui & justitia nobis factus est, & gratiæ divinæ fons, ex cujus plenitudine gratiam pro gratia haurimus? Cujus argumenti vis intenditur, additâ aliâ differentiâ, quod nempe gloria illa, qua lex fulsit & ipsa διακονία legis vel administer ejusdem, καταργουμένη fuerit, hoc est talis, quæ facile evacuabatur & cessabat, non cum morte demum Mosis, (uti Grotius dubiè conjectat) sed paulo post reditum è monte. Hæc autem Evangelii, & διακονίας ejusdem gloria minimè evacuetur. Siquidem in Evangelio, & Evangelico ministerio semper effulgeat ἀπαύγασμα illud τῆς δόξης, & justitiæ ac gratiæ divinæ splendor nitidissimus. Differentiam illam & argumentum suum uberius proponit Apostolus per expolitionem; & quidem quoad diversas partes: primò quoad ministerii vitæ & mortis comparationem: Nam si ministratio damnationis gloria est, multò magis abundat ministerium justitiæ in gloria hujus, uti sensum non male expressit Estius: Quod si ministerium legis, quæ reddit homines æternæ damnationi & morti obnoxios, gloria fuit, id est, res gloriosa, igitur multo major & excellentior debetur gloria ministerio novæ legis (rectius Evangelii) quæ justitiam affert, qua damnatio evaditur, & vita acquiritur. Secundo quoad comparationem gloriæ partialis & totalis v. 10. Nam nec glorificatum est, quod claruit in illa parte, (faciei scilicet) propter excellentem gloriam, vel in comparatione ad eandem, quæ neutiquam ita partialis est, ut facies solum coruscet, sed verè totalis, qua coruscantes reddimur & animâ & corpore: Nec tantum faciem ministri reddit splendentem; sed etiam splendentes & gloriosos reddit nos omnes. Illam enim (Mosis) gloriam Israëlitæ non modo non participabant, sed nec intueri poterant: Hæc verò (Evangelii) gloria ita comparata est, ut omnino nostra gloria sit, in nobis omnibus splendor Evangelii effulgeat: idque ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης, quia superabundans est hæc gloria, quæ non sufficiat modo illuminandis omnibus, sed superabundet. Tertio quoad comparationem rei temporariæ & perpetuæ vers. 11. Si enim, quod evacuatur, per gloriam est, multo magis, quod manet, in gloria est. Prius τὴν δόξαν gloriam vel radiationem fa- ciei Mosaicae dixit καταργουμένην vers. 7. Jam ve- rò ministerium ipsum legale, quod διὰ δόξης erat, cum Moses legem proferret, dicitur τὸ καταργού- μενον illud quod destruendum est; Ministerium verò Evangelicum dicitur τὸ μένον illud, quod manet: quia illa transitoria faciei Mosaicae cla- ritas evacuationis ministerii legalis symbolum erat. Quomodo verò evacuatum ministerium legale? Non proprio vitio & per se, sed culpâ nostrâ & quoad nos. Quum enim à nobis præ- stari lex nequeat, evacuatur hactenus διακονία τοῦ γράμματος, quantum ad vim justificandi & salvandi, quia lex infirmata est per carnem, at- que opus est διακονίᾳ τοῦ πνεύματος & doctrina Evangelica de Christo, qui nostra est justitia & salutare DEI, eandemque oportet manere perpetuam. Non ergò lex cessat absolutè, sed quoad certum usum, quem non præstat non vi- tio proprio, sed nostro: quia virtus ejus infir- mata per corruptam nostram naturam, qua ju- gum legis nobis planè est ἀβάστακτον, ut proinde nihil conferre possit ad nostram justificationem & salutem, sed gratiâ Christi Domini nostri per fidem apprehensâ unicè salvari necessum sit, qui salvantur Act. XV. v. 10. 11.

Confertur ergò tum lex, tum ministerium Mo- saicum legis cum Evangelio, ejusque ministerio A- postolico, & successuum Apostolicorum triplici ratione (1) quoad naturam, quod illa tantùm li- teram, hæc spiritum exhibeant; (2) quoad effica- ciam, quod illa occidant & hæc vivificent; & (3) quoad gloriam, quæ hic longe est eminen- tior, quam illic, sive naturam legis & Evange- lii inter se contendamus, sive subjectum, quod glorificatur, sive usum & terminum respiciamus.

De tribus istis ita Theophylactus: Patefacta su- perius novi & veteris Testamenti differentia asse- rit alterum atramento, alterum spiritu esse conscri- ptum, & insculptum lapidibus illud, hoc vero cordibus: itemque ex altero mortem, vitam ex alte- ro comparari. Nunc quidem ostendere nititur, longe majorem esse Evangelii gloriam, quam legis fuerit. Lex quippe vetus sensibilem quandam na- cta est gloriam, Mosis scilicet faciem fulgentiorem, nova vero eam videlicet, quæ mente concipitur. Quandoquidem hanc ipsam nemini jam sensibiliter licet oculis intueri. Ostendit itaque Evangelii excellentiam ipsam animi conceptu quodam com- prehendi posse, inquitque priorem legem fuisse mor- tis ministram. Neque enim effectricem dixit, ne ullam præbeat hæreticorum errori occasionem, sed ministram. Enimvero peccatum mortem pepere- rat, mors vero supplicium afferebat. Litera præ- terea ipsa Veteris Testamenti sola constabat, neque ullam afferebat opem certantibus, quod sane in ba- ptismo non accidit. Concludit ergò Theophyla- ctus: Si lex itaque, cum talis extiterit, in gloria est effecta, quanto magis & gratia, qua adeo præstat, ut nihil queat ejus excellentiæ comparari. Jam & Grotium de his audiamus.

Ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι ἀτενίσαι τοὺς ὑιοὺς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον Μωυσέως διὰ τὴν δόξαν τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ) Bene explicat, quod est Exodi XXXIV. vers. 30. Metuebant accedere ad eum. Ideo enim non audebant accedere, quia non pote- rant eum contra tueri, quod est ἀτενίζειν; Luc. II. vers. 20. XXII. 56. Act. III. 4. 12. VI. 15. VII. 55. XI. 6. XIII. 9. XIV. 9. & fulgorem faciei Mosis recte δόξαν dixit, quia & LXX. verbum Hebræum קרן vertunt ἦν δεδοξασμένη & δεδόξασται. Vide quæ à nobis dicta ad illum Exodi locum, & 1. Cor. XI. 7.

Vulgata ergo Exod. XXXIV. vers. 36. faciem Mosis cornutam faciens, utut à concilio Tridentino binisque Pontificibus Romanis authentica pronunciata, hic emendanda, fatente Grotio, qui δεδοξασμένην vertendam esse vocem Hebræam cum LXX. agnoscit, quibus Apostolus ipse calculum adjecit. Non enim propter cornua accedere Mosen haud ausi sunt, sed propter δόξαν, gloriam, vel splendorem faciei ejus.

Τὴν καταργουμένην) Quia, inquit, splendor cum morte, si non & ante, erat cessaturus. Vide 1. Cor. II. 6. VI. 13. XIII. 8. 10.

Monitum ante, nullo documento niti conjecturam illam, quod à tempore acceptæ legis à Deo per totam vitam Moses coruscarit. Id ergò ceu ἄγραφον, imò, ἀντίγραφον meritò reprobandum.

## 3:8
v. 8. Πῶς ὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἡ διακονία τῦ Πνεύματος ἔsαι ἐν δόξῃ;) How much more honorable is the ministry of that Spirit, which is the earnest of eternal life?

The Grotian hypothesis, which he seems to hide here, must not be passed over in silence, namely, that the Spirit as an earnest of eternal life was not given in the Old Testament; which, however, we amend thus: that it was not given through the law or the Old Testament, yet it was given under the law and the time of the Old Testament. For the faithful of the Old Testament were no less children of God than those of the New: and therefore, as children of GOD, they were by no means destitute of the hope of eternal life and the Holy Spirit, the earnest of life; just as a long catalog of the faithful of the Old Testament is woven in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter XI, who sustained themselves with the hope of eternal life.

Latin:

v. 8. Πῶς ὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἡ διακονία τῦ Πνεύματος ἔsαι ἐν δόξῃ;) Quanto honoratius est ministerium illius spiritus, qui arrhabo est vitæ æternæ?

Hypothesis Grotiana, quam hic occultare videtur, non tacenda, quod nempe Spiritus ceu arrhabo æternæ vitæ in Veteri Testamento non datus fuerit; quam verò ita emendamus, quod non datus fuerit per legem vel Vetus Testamentum, datus tamen sub lege ac tempore Veteris Testamenti. Non minus enim filii Dei fuerunt fideles Veteris Testamenti, quàm Novi: ideoque ut filii DEI, destituti spe vitæ æternæ, & arrhabone vitæ Spiritu Sancto, minimè fuere: quemadmodum prolixus catalogus fidelium Veteris Testamenti texitur in Epistola ad Hebræos cap. XI. qui se vitæ æternæ spe sustentarunt.

## 3:9
vers. 9. Εἰ γὰρ ἡ διακονία τῆς διακρίσεως δόξα. For the law, destroyed by those things which had been before the law and are traditional in the law, did nothing else than condemn sin, that is, it made its foulness more manifest, Rom. V: 1. 7. 8. Gal. III. 19. and following; and it gave more occasions for sinning.

What those traditional things are, Grotius does not explain. But the law did not only condemn formerly, but even now it condemns sin, nor was that condemnation brought about, nor is it, solely by rendering the foulness of sin more manifest, but by subjecting man to the guilt and punishment of condemnation on account of sin, because it works wrath, it kills, it denounces a curse, just as it is therefore called the διακονία τῦ θανάτε καὶ τῆς κατακρίσεως. Compare Rom. IV. verse 11, chapter III. verse 19, Gal. III. verse 32. Those are different effects of the law, that it uncovers sin and its foulness, Rom. III. verse 21, and that it works wrath and condemnation. Nor does it contribute to this that it gives more occasions for sinning, which is by accident, because, namely, we strive for what is forbidden: because the Apostle is not discussing this effect of the law at present, and punishment is one thing, guilt another, even if the latter draws the former with it.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον περισσεύσει ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐν δόξῃ. Here that δόξῃ is to be construed with περισσεύσει. The ministry of righteousness will be much more glorious; namely, of that internal righteousness, and so pleasing to GOD, that it also promises to it another life, and that everlasting. Concerning which righteousness, see the Epistle to the Romans.

Grotius understands inherent righteousness with the Papists, which looks to the law and the works of the law. But the Apostle understands imputed righteousness, which is exhibited in the Gospel and comes from faith and through faith, which we have shown more fully in the golden Epistle to the Romans. The paraphrase of Theodoret is as follows: The law condemned those who sinned, but grace, receiving them, justifies them through faith, for it leads to divine baptism and grants remission. If, therefore, he who served that was a partaker of glory, much more do those who have served this, namely grace, attain a greater one.

Latin:

vers. 9. Εἰ γὰρ ἡ διακονία τῆς διακρίσεως δόξα. Lex enim destructa ab iis, quæ ante legem fuerant & in lege sunt tralatitia, nihil aliud, quam damnabat peccatum, id est, fœditatem ejus faciebat apertiorem, Rom. V : l. 7. 8. Gal. III. 19. & sequentibus; & plures occasiones peccandi dabat.

Quænam illa tralatitia sint, non explicat Grotius. Non autem lex tantum damnabat quondam, sed etiamnum damnat peccatum, nec damnatio ista facta est, ac sit solum fœditatem peccati reddendo apertiorem, sed reatui & pœnæ condemnationis hominem ob peccatum subjiciendo, quia iram operatur, occidit, maledictionem denunciat, sicut & ideo διακονία τῦ θανάτε καὶ τῆς κατακρίσεως dicitur. Confer Rom. IV. vers. 11. cap. III. vers. 19. Gal. III. vers. 32. Diversa illa sunt legis effecta, quod peccatum & fœditatem ejus detegat, Rom. III. vers. 21. & quod iram ac condemnationem operetur. Neque huc illud facit, quod plures occasiones peccandi det, quod ex accidenti est, quia scilicet nitimur in vetitum: quia de hoc legis effectu impræsentiarum non disserit Apostolus, & aliud est pœna, aliud culpa, etsi hæc illam secum trahat.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον περισσεύσει ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐν δόξῃ. Hic illud δόξῃ construendum est cum περισσεύσει. Multo gloriosius erit ministerium justitiæ; nempe illius internæ, & ita DEO gratæ, ut & ei vitam alteram eamque sempiternam polliceatur. De qua justitia vide epistolam ad Romanos.

Justitiam inhærentem intelligit Grotius cum Papistis, quæ legem respicit, & opera legis. At Apostolus justitiam imputatam, quæ in Evangelio exhibetur, & ex fide ac per fidem venit, quod in aurea ad Romanos epistola uberius ostendimus. Paraphrasis Theodoreti ita habet: Lex eos, qui peccabant, condemnabat, gratia autem eos suscipiens, per fidem justificat, ad divinum enim baptismum adducit, & donat remissionem. Si ergo qui illi serviit, fuit gloriæ particeps, multo ma- gis qui huic, nempe gratiae servierunt, majorem assequuntur.

## 3:10
v. 10. Καὶ γὰρ οὐ δεδόξασται τὸ δεδοξασμένον ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης.

The Syriac interpreter does not translate that δεδόξασται badly: it was not right for that ministry to be honored (although honored in itself) thus far, if account is taken of the more eminent glory reserved for the Gospel, namely, through so many spiritual gifts and eternal promises. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει here and below in IX. 13 and 1 Pet. IV. 16 is 'thus far': 'in this'. Thus ἐν μέρει in Coloss. II. 16, 'as far as it concerns', just as Greek writers also say, τὸ ἐμὸν μέρος, 'as far as I am concerned'. But that Ἕνεκεν is placed in the sense of comparison has been rightly noted by others.

Latin:

v. 10. Καὶ γὰρ οὐ δεδόξασται τὸ δεδοξασμένον ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης.

Illud δεδόξασται Syrus interpres non male vertit : aequum non fuit honorari illud ministeriū (quamvis per se honoratum) hactenus si ratio habeatur eminentioris gloriae Evangelio sc. reservatae, per tot dona spiritualia, & promissa aeterna. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει hic & infra IX. 13. & 1. Pet. IV. 16. est hactenus : in hoc. Sic ἐν μέρει Coloss. II. 16. quod attinet, quomodo & Graeci scriptores dicunt, τὸ ἐμὸν μέρος, me quod attinet. Ἕνεκεν autem in significatu comparationis poni recte ab aliis notatum est..

## 3:11
Εἰ γὰρ τὸ καταργούμενον) That ministry, all the fruit of which perished with this life. Διακονία is indeed feminine: but the construction is according to the sense: as: Triste lupus stabulis.

Διὰ δόξης) Here too διὰ is for μετὰ, as above II. 4.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὸ μένον ἐν δόξῃ) The ministry which remains, that is, which has a perpetual fruit that will never cease.

The word δεδόξασται must not be moved from that meaning of τῆς δόξης, which the Apostle has used more than once in this elaboration, which indeed brings in brightness and splendor, not honor; nor is there any doubt that, in the comparison made with the Evangelical ministry, its own honor is left to the legal ministry, both of which are always needed in the Church, unless we wish to have the law eliminated from the Christian Church with the Antinomians, and deprive it of due honor. Although indeed that explanation can be admitted, that ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει or in this part of the comparison, and thus far, with respect to a more eminent glory, what shone in Moses cannot even be considered glory or brightness: yet the preceding context, where mention is made only of the Mosaic face, conspicuous for its brightness, leads to that declaration of the Apostolic comparison, namely, that not even in that part, which alone shone, does the brightness count ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης: But that supereminent glory is not to be established in the promises of eternal life, as these are not to be denied to the law, or the Old Testament, but in other things, as we have said: and therefore it is said less correctly, in the Grotius sense, that the fruit of the legal ministry perished with this life, because it brought only temporal goods, since it did promise eternal life, albeit under the condition of perfect observance of the Lord's commandments, which, however, can be performed by no mortal. Hunnius executes the present comparison thus: That which is eternal incomparably excels that which is abolished.
