Moreover, the doctrine of the Gospel lasts forever, since the benefits preached in the Gospel accompany us even into the other, everlasting life: whereas, on the contrary, the law is abolished for believers, and they themselves are dead to the law, Rom. VII, being freed both from its servile obedience, which was most rigidly demanded in all its details, and from the curse, by which it adjudges transgressors to the underworld through a condemnatory sentence.

Latin:

Εἰ γὰρ τὸ καταργούμενον) Illud ministerium, cujus omnis fructus cum vita hac interibat. Διακονία quidem est Foemininum : Sed constructio est ad rem : ut: Triste lupus stabulis.

Διὰ δόξης) Etiam hic διὰ est pro μετὰ, ut supra II. 4.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὸ μένον ἐν δόξῃ) Ministerium, quod manet, id est, quod fructum habet perpetuum nunquam desiturum.

Verbum δεδόξασται non dimovendum ab ea τῆς δόξης significatione, quam in hac ἐξεργασίᾳ Apostolus plus vice simplici adhibuit, quae vero infert claritatem & splendorem, non honorem; neque dubium est, in contentione, facta cum ministerio Evangelico, honorem suum relinqui ministerio legali, quo utroque opus semper est in Ecclesia, nisi cum Antinomis legem ex Ecclesia Christiana eliminatam velimus, & honore debito privemus. Quanquam vero admitti possit ista explicatio, quod ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει sive in hac comparationis parte, & hactenus, respectu scil. gloriae eminentioris, ne gloria vel fulgor quidem censeri possit, quod in Mose refulsit: antecedentia tamen, ubi solius faciei Mosaicae, fulgore conspicuae, mentio facta, ad declarationem illam comparationis Apostolicae, faciunt, quod scilicet, ne in illa quidem parte, quae fulgebat unice, fulgor in censum veniat ἕνεκεν τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης δόξης: Quae vero supereminens gloria non in vitae aeternae promissis, utpote quae haud neganda legi, vel Veteri Testamento, sed in aliis, uti diximus, constituenda est: ideoque ministerii legalis fructus cum hac vita periisse, sensu Grotiano, minus recte dicitur, quod nempe bona tantum attulerit temporalia, siquidem contra aeternam vitam promiserit, etsi sub conditione perfectae observationis mandatorum Domini, quae vero a nemine mortalium praestari potest. Comparationem praesentem ita exequitur Hunnius: Id quod aeternū est, incomparabiliter antecellit ei, quod aboletur. Caeterum Evangelii doctrina durat in aeternum, quandoquidē beneficia in Evangelio praedicata, in alteram usque sempiternam vitam nos comitantur: Cum econtra lex credentibus abolita, ipsique legi sint mortui, Rom. VII. liberati quippe tum a servili ejus obsequio, quod cunctis absolutum numeris exigebatur rigidissime: tum a maledictione, qua transgressores per sententiam condemnatoriam inferis adjudicat.

## 3:12
v. 12. Ἔχοντες οὖν τοιαύτην ἐλπίδα) Which reaches into eternity.

Πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ χρώμεθα) We both act and speak openly. For both are the Syrian פוחסיא as we have said elsewhere.

Latin:

v. 12. Ἔχοντες οὖν τοιαύτην ἐλπίδα) Quae in aeternum prominet.

Πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ χρώμεθα) Aperte & agimus & loquimur. Nam utrumque Syris פוחסיא ut alibi diximus.

## 3:13
v. 13. Καὶ οὐ καθάπερ Μωϋσῆς ἐτίθει κάλυμμα ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσωπον αὑτοῦ) It is an ἔκθλιψις. For the sense is full. Our affairs are not so situated as when Moses put a veil upon his face. He translates κάλυμμα, as do the LXX, the Hebrew מסוה Exod. XXXIV. 33.

Now the Apostle discourses concerning the clarity of his proclamation, persisting in the comparison of the Mosaic veil, which is not that he speaks with the people with a veil imposed, as Moses did, but without a veil, in open speech, using πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ. Τoιαύτην ἐλπίδα may be referred to πεποίθησιν τοιαύτην, verse 4. For the ministers of the Gospel use παῤῥησίᾳ in the confidence of the sufficiency to be granted by GOD, and it is not in their own native powers, but in the grace of Him who makes them fit for the ministry of the Spirit. Conf. chap. IIX. 13. Yet the meaning of the hope of salvation is no different, if these things are explained skillfully: Which was done by the blessed Hunnius: Since we are not ministers of the letter, so that we might acquiesce entirely in the preaching of the law: but since, as ministers of the spirit, we lead men from the law to the joyful preaching of the Gospel concerning the clemency of GOD toward us through Christ, and to the hope of salvation shown to us in the Gospel: Act with much boldness on both sides, both we Apostles in bringing and propagating such a salutary doctrine, and you Corinthians in gladly embracing it and constantly retaining it to the end.

So that the children of Israel might not look steadfastly to the end of that which is abolished.

Here Paul begins to explain the root, that is, mystically, the radiance of Moses and the veil. That radiance of Moses prefigured the radiance of the Messiah, which it was not given to know in those times. Christ is the end of the law, Romans X. verse 4, and consequently also of the legal ministry, which is abolished, as we have already explained above 7, 11, in 'so that they might not look steadfastly,' so that they might not gaze upon it.

Latin:

v. 13. Καὶ οὐ καθάπερ Μωϋσῆς ἐτίθει κάλυμμα ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσωπον αὑτοῦ) Est ἔκθλιψις. Sensus enim plenus est. Non ita se res nostrae habent, ut cum Moses faciei suae velum imposuit. κάλυμμα vertit, ut & LXX. Hebraeum מסוה Exod. XXXIV. 33.

Jam de praeconii sui perspicuitate differit Apostolus, persistens in comparatione Mosaici velaminis, quod non imposito, ut Moses velamine cum populo loquatur, sed sine velamine, aperto sermone, πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ utens. Τoιαύτην ἐλπίδα referre licet ad πεποίθησιν τοιαύτην, vers. 4. Nam fiducia τῆς ἱκανότητος a DEO concedendae παῤῥησίᾳ utuntur ministri Evangelii, nec ea est in viribus ipsis nativis, sed in gratia ejus, qui ipsos idoneos reddit ad ministerium Spiritus. Conf. cap. IIX. 13. Non alia tamen est significatio spei salutis, si dextre hæc explicentur: Quod à B. Hunnio factum: Cum non simus ministri litera, ut in concione legis in solidum acquiescamus: sed cum, ut ministri spiritus, à lege deducamus ho- mines ad lætam prædicationem Evangelii de DEI erga nos per Christum clementia, & ad spem salutis in Evangelio nobis commonstratam: Agite multa utrinque παῤῥησίᾳ utamur, & nos Apostoli in af- ferenda & propaganda tàm salutari doctrina, & vos Corinthii in eadem libenter amplexanda, & ad finem usque constanter retinenda.

Πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίσαι τὺς ψὸς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ τέλῷ τῆ καταργημένε.

Hic Paulus incipit שׁרשׁ, id est, mystice explicare fulgorem Mosis & velum. Fulgor ille Mosis præfigurabat fulgorem Messiæ, quem cognoscere illis temporibus non dabatur. Christus finis est legis, Roman. X. vers. 4. ac proinde & legalis ministerii, quod καταργῆται, ut jam exposuimus supra 7, 11. in πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίζειν, ita ut non inspectarent.

## 3:14
But their minds were hardened) That is, although they ought now to acknowledge Him, so clearly revealed, yet they do not acknowledge Him. Thus, through the neglect of internal righteousness, the minds of many have hardened. They desire eternal life through the law, which is nowhere promised in the law. ἐπωρώθη כהר.

Setting aside the error of the Vulgate version, which has 'into the face' instead of 'into the end' (which Estius acknowledges and notes with just censure), the cause of the veil being imposed was not that it was not given in those times to know the radiance of the Messiah, for JESUS Christ is the same today, yesterday, and forever, Heb. XIII. 8. And how could they have had faith in the Messiah without knowledge of the Messiah, or salvation without faith in the Messiah? But because they were not able to gaze upon the open face of Moses with unswerving eyes on account of its radiance and glory, much less, being intent only on the moral law, could they penetrate or gaze upon the end of that which is abolished, that is, Christ, to gaze upon whose glory and radiance there is need of the Evangelical ministry and the grace promised in the Gospel, and to be conferred through the Gospel, and by the life-giving Spirit. Those things were also given in those times, although not through the law, but through the promise, just as even at this time they do not happen through the law, but through the Gospel, Gal. III. 2. It is not a question here of the distance or negation or concealment of the object of living, which was not hidden or remote, Deut. XXX. verse 12, but of a defect in the organ or subject, which is called the hardening of the minds. Nor is the veiling of the Mosaic face the cause of not seeing or not acknowledging the glory of Christ, but rather it is because they could not bear the glory and brightness of Moses, which was scarcely a certain shadow of the glory of Christ, that the Mosaic face had to be veiled; but that it is signified by this figure that the Israelites would one day have a veil over their hearts, we easily admit; but by these words is indicated here the veiling of the Mosaic face when he brought the tables of the moral law, not the veiling of the heart of the Israelites, which is only explained by the following words. Moreover, that veiling of the face is said to be 'so that they might not look steadfastly'; which words can be understood as expressing a result, or, if they are understood entirely as expressing a cause, they do not imply that Moses veiled his face to that end, that the view of the glory of the Messiah might be denied, or was to be denied, or was signified as denied to the Israelites of that time; but that it was indicated that the splendor of the glory of the Messiah is incomprehensible to the weakness of the eyes of the heart, and much less could be borne or sustained than the Mosaic splendor could be borne or sustained by the eyes of the body of the Israelites: And therefore that there was need for the imposition of a veil. And although the mysteries concerning Christ were in large part wrapped up in shadows, types, and figures in the Old Testament, which now lie open far more clearly without such a veil in the New Testament, yet that comparison is not intended here: But rather an opposition of the clear and perspicuous proposition of those mysteries made by the Apostles, indicated by the words 'we use much boldness' and the simile of the non-imposed veil, as well as by the mention of the hardening and blinding of the Jews in the time of the New Testament, is instituted, even if this had been foreshadowed by that 'not looking steadfastly' of the Israelites through their own hardening, having contracted an inability to gaze upon the glory of Christ; or if this is deduced from that in this way: Since the glory of the Messiah is so great, which the sharpness of the eyes of the heart can in no way penetrate or bear, even if it is exerted to the utmost in this infirmity: it is no wonder that the Jews, whose minds were hardened, and who by their own fault blinded their eyes, do not bear the same, where to the natural inability and blindness was added a voluntary blinding, and a stubborn exclusion of the illuminating grace. By no means, therefore, says Theophylact, should it seem a wonder to us if the Jews are unable to behold the glory of Christ, or to admit faith in Him: since they could not even gaze upon the glory of the law, which is certainly inferior. For if they had gazed upon this, they would have perceived the glory of Christ. For the glory of the law prefers Christ. Rightly, therefore, the blessed Hunnius here: Now he girds himself to explain the cause why the Jews do not see or acknowledge the supereminence of the Gospel, illustrious with so many miracles and clear with so many arguments. He casts the cause upon their blindness, which had been prefigured by the type and symbol of the Mosaic veil. Moreover, the Jews have developed a callousness of the senses regarding their inveterate opinions, because they are unwilling to know that it is impossible for the law of corrupt nature to be fulfilled, but are most firmly persuaded that the law can be perfectly kept, and therefore they can no longer hear, much less understand, one who teaches the contrary, namely that Christ is the end of the law, that He has made the law void, and has fulfilled it by perfect obedience, so that it can no longer condemn us. Therefore a veil is placed upon their heart, which, covered by the foreskin of the old Adam, always imagines something of its own righteousness, and neglects the Messiah and His merit, or does not leave the glory of righteousness to Him alone, as was fitting, 1 Cor. 1:30-31. Whence it cannot happen that it recognizes the true end of the law, or is led through the law to Christ. They interpret the end in this way, first Augustine in both places cited above, then the commentators, Primasius, Sedulius, Cajetan, and among the Greeks, Theodoret. The Apostle also seems to explain it in this sense a little later, saying: Because in Christ it is made void, as Estius has it here.

verse 14. Ἄχρι γὰρ τῆς σήμερον τὸ αὐτὸ κάλυμμα.

That very mystical veil, which was signified by that visible veil. The law was given on a cloudy day to signify the veil, which takes away from our eyes the prospect of the truth. Thus Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III. 9.

ἐπὶ τῇ διαγνώσει τῆς παλαίας διαθήκης.

Which took place in the temples and synagogues, especially on the Sabbaths. By the old testimony (testament), the books of Moses are understood, the most important part of which is the Sinaitic covenant.

It remains unrevealed, because in Christ it is done away with. Therefore it remains hanging over them, because it cannot be removed except by the knowledge of Christ, according to the mystical sense of Isaiah 25:7. 'Done away with' here is what is soon 'taken away'.

Latin:

Ἀλλ’ ἐπωρώθη τὰ νοήματα ἀυτῶν) Id est, quanquam nunc eum agnoscere debebant, tàm clare revelatum, non agnoscunt tamen. Ita ad internæ justitiæ neglectum com- plurium animi induruere. Volunt vitam æternam per le- gem, quæ nullibi in lege promissa est. ἐπωρώθη כהר.

Misso Vulgatæ versionis vitio, quæ habet in fa- ciem, pro in finem, (quod agnoscit, & justa cen- sura notat Estius) Causa velaminis impositi non erat, quod cognoscere illis temporibus datum non fuerit fulgorem Messiæ, JESUS Christus enim hodiè, heri, idem & in secula, Ebr. XIII. 8. & quomodo sine notitia Messiæ fidem in Mes- siam, aut sine fide in Messiam salutem habere potuissent? Sed quod oculis irretortis apertam faciem Mosis intueri non valerent ob fulgorem & gloriam ejusdem, nedum legi tantum morali intenti penetrare, aut inspectare finem τῶ καταρ- γεμένε, legis, quæ evacuatur, hoc est, Christum, ad cujus gloriam & fulgorem inspectandum opus est Evangelico ministerio & gratia in Evangelio promissa, & per Evangelium conferenda, ac Spiritu vivificante. Dabantur illa etiam istis temporibus, etsi non per legem, sed per ἐπαγγε- λίαν, quemadmodum etiam hoc tempore non contingunt per legem, sed per Evangelium, Gal. III. 2. Non de distantia vel negatione vel occul- tatione objecti vivendi hic agitur, quod non erat absconditum aut remotum, Deut. XXX. vers. 12. sed, de vitio in organo vel subjecto, quod πώρω- σις dicitur τῶν νοημάτων. Nec faciei Mosaicæ ve- latio causa est non visionis, aut non agnitionis gloriæ Christi, sed potius ideò, quia non ferre poterant gloriam & claritatem Mosis, quæ vix umbra quædam gloriæ Christi, velanda erat facies Mosaica, significatum autem per figuram hanc, esse, quod olim velum habituri sint Israëlitæ su- per corda, facilè admittimus; sed his verbis indi- catur hic velatio faciei Mosaicæ, cum tabulas legis moralis afferrer, non obvelatio cordis Israëlitarum, quæ verbis sequentibus demum ex- ponitur. Illa autem faciei velatio facta dicitur πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίσαι; quæ verba ἐκβατικῶς intelli- gi possunt, aut, si omnino αἰτιολογικῶς intelligan- tur, non id inferunt, quod Moses eà fini faciem suam velarit, ut Israëlitis illius temporis denega- retur, vel denegandus, aut denegatus significare- tur intuitus gloriæ Messiæ; sed quod indicare- tur, splendorem gloriæ Messiæ imbecillitati oculorum cordis esse ἀκατάληπτον, & multò minus ferri aut sustineri posse, quàm ferri aut sustineri ab oculis corporis Israëllitarum poterat splendor Mosaicus: Ideoque veli impositione opus esse. Et quanquam umbris, typis & figuris in Veteri Testamento magnam partem involuta fuerint mysteria de Christo, quæ longè cla- rius, quod sine ejusmodi velo in Novo Testa- mento jam patent, non tamen ea hîc compa- ratio intenditur: Sed oppositio potius claræ & perspicuæ propositionis istorum mysteriorum ab Apostolis facta, verbis πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ χρώμεθα & similitudine de non imposito velamine indica- ta, nec non mentione πωρώσεως & excæcatio- nis Judæorum, tempore Novi Testamenti, in- stituitur, utut hæc per indurationem propriam, conciliatâ intuitus gloriæ Christi ἀδυναμίᾳ con- tractâ, per illud μὴ ἀτενίσαι Israëllitarum ad- umbrata fuerit; aut ex illo deducatur hoc pa- cto: Quum tanta sit gloria Messiæ, quam acies oculorum cordis nullatenus penetrare, aut ferre sustineat, etsi vel maximè in hac infirmitate intendatur: non mirum eandem haud ferre Ju- dæos, quibus induruerunt τὰ νοήματα αὐτῶν, qui- que propriâ culpâ sibi oculos excæcarunt, ubi ad naturalem ἀδυναμίαν & cæcitatem volunta- ria accessit excæcatio, & præfracta gratiæ illu- minatricis exclusio. Nequaquam igitur, inquit Theophylactus, mirum nobis videri debet, si ne- queunt vel Christi gloriam spectare Judæi, vel ejus fidem admittere: quippe qui nec legis gloriam, quæ utique inferior est, potuerint intueri. Nam si hanc inspexissent, & Christi gloriam pervidissent. Legis enim gloria Christum præfert. Rectè ita- que hic Beatus Hunnius: Nunc ad exponendam causam se accingit, quare Judæi supereminentiam Evangelii tot miraculis illustrem tot argumentis claram non videant aut agnoscant. Causam reji- cit in illorum cæcitatem, quæ præfigurata fuerit Mosaici velaminis typo atq́; symbolo. Cæterum Ju- dæi callum obduxerunt sensuum quoad opinio- nes inveteratas, quod scire nolint, legem naturæ corruptæ præstitu esse impossibilem, sed legem perfectè servari posse persuasissimi sint, adeoque contraria docentem audire amplius non possint, nedum intelligere, quod nempe Christus legis finis sit, quod legem evacuarit, & perfectâ obe- dientiâ impleverit, ut condemnare nos non va- leat amplius. Ideo velamen cordi eorum impo- situm est, quod præputio veteris Adami tectum, sibi semper aliquid de propria justitia imagina- tur, & Messiam, ejusque meritum negligit, aut gloriam justitiæ soli eidem non relinquit, ut par erat, 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. Unde fieri nequit, ut ve- rum legis finem agnoscat, vel per legem ad Chri- stum adducatur. Finem interpretantur hoc mo- do, primum August. utroque loco super. cit. tum Commentatores, Primasius, Sedulius, Cajetanus, & inter Græcos Theodoretus. Videtur & Apostolus in hunc sensum exponere paulo post semetipsum di- cens: Quoniam in Christo evacuatur, ut hic ha- bet Estius.

vers. 14. Ἄχρι γὰρ τῆς σήμερον τὸ αὐτὸ κάλυμμα.

Illud ipsum velum mysticum, quod per velum illud aspectabile significabatur. Lex data die nubilo ad signi- ficandum velum, quod oculis nostris adimit prospectum veri. Ita Maimonides ductore dubitantium III. 9.

ἐπὶ τῇ διαγνώσει τῆς παλαίας διαθήκης.

Quæ in templis & synagogis fiebat, sabbatis maximè. Per vetus testimonium (testamentum, intelliguntur libri Mosis, cujus pars potissima fœdus Sinaiticum.

Μένει μὴ ἀνακαλυπτόμενον, ὅτι ἐν χρισῷ καταργεῖται) Ideo manet impendens ipsis, quia tolli nisi Christi cogni- to non potest, secundum sensum mysticum, Esaiae XXV. 7. καταργεῖται hic est, quod mox περιαιρεῖται.

## 3:15
But until today, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart. He repeats the sense which he had already set down once, so that he might fix in the mind a matter to be wondered at by all Christians. Moses here stands for the books of Moses, as in Acts 15:21. Some interpret the 'covering of the heart' in Lamentations 3:65 as the blindness of the mind.

The Apostle teaches that the obduracy of the Jews is so great that not even by the reading of the Old Testament is the veil lifted, or can it be removed, which is fixed upon their hearts. For although the Jews, as the Hunnian paraphrase has it here, devote much labor and effort to the reading of the Old Testament, namely the writings of Moses and the Prophets (just as they read them not only publicly every Sabbath, but also privately at home, Acts 15), and although furthermore Christ was promised in the law of Moses and shadowed forth by many figures, and the most evident prophecies concerning him were brought forth in the books of the Prophets: yet that veil remains so firmly placed and fixed upon the hearts of the Hebrews that they can neither find Christ in the Mosaic or Prophetic scripture, nor see him with the eyes of the mind. For that veil cannot be removed from their hearts except through the grace of Christ alone, which they have obstinately rejected, though it was offered to them in so many sermons and commended and established by so many signs of Christ and the Apostles. Estius is correct here: It is not the obscurity of the books of the law and the Prophets, as some would have it, but the dullness of the mind, as we have said, which is produced by earthly and carnal affection, by which the mind is hindered from understanding the scriptures and acquiescing in the truth which they speak—which is to be unwilling to believe—that seems to be signified mystically by the veil. Thus most Commentators, and before them Origen, Homily 12 on Exodus. The commentary of Theophylact also deserves observation: Since he had said above that a certain veil was drawn over their mind in the reading of the Old Testament, lest anyone should happen to think that he calls the obscurity of the law a veil, he says it is not so, but I would call the dullness and crudity of their heart the veil. Which would clearly have been drawn over the face of Moses not for his own sake, but because of their thickness and blindness. Theodoret says: He called the law Moses; but the veil, unbelief.

Latin:

Ἀλλ᾽ ἕως σήμερον, ἡνίκα ἀναγινώσκεται Μωϋσῆς, κάλυμ- μα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν κεῖται) Repetit sensum, quem jam semel posuerat, ut rem omnibus Christianis admiran- dam infigat animo. Moses hic pro libris Mosis, ut Actor. XV. 21. Tegumentum cordis etiam Lam. III. 65. quidam interpretantur animi caecitatem.

Obdurationem Judaeorum tantam esse docet Apostolus, ut ne lectione quidem Veteris Testa- menti velum tollatur, aut removeri possit, quod cordibus ipsorum defixum est. Quamvis enim Judaei, ut paraphrasis Hunniana hic habet, mul- tum laboris & operae ponant in lectione Veteris Te- stamenti, nempe scriptorum Mosis & Prophetarum, (quemadmodum non solum singulis sabbatis pu- blice, sed domi quoque privatim ea lectitabant, Actor. XV.) & quamvis insuper Christus in lege Mosis promissus, multis quoque figuris adumbra- tus sit, & in Prophetarum libris evidentissima de eo prodita vaticinia: Tamen velum illud su- per cordibus Hebraeorum ita manere firmiter im- positum ac defixum, ut nec in Mosaica, nec Pro- phetica scriptura Christum vel invenire, vel oculis mentis videre queant. Neque enim ab illorum cordibus velamen illud tolli posse, nisi per unius Christi gratiam, quam videlicet tot concionibus oblatam, tot signis Christi & Apostolorum com- mendatam, & stabilitam obstinate rejecerint. Recte hic Estius: Non obscuritas librorum legis & Prophetarum, ut quidam volunt, sed mentis, uti diximus, hebetudo, quam parit affectio ter- rena & carnalis, qua nimirum mens impeditur, ne scripturas intelligat, & veritati, quam loquun- tur, acquiescat; quod est nolle credere; mystice per velamen significata videtur. Ita plerique Com- mentatores & ante eos Origenes homil. XII. super Exod. Observationem etiam meretur Commen- tarius Theophylacti: Quoniam dixerat superius, velamentum quoddam in Veteris Testamenti lecti- one esse illorum menti obtentum, ne forte existi- met quispiam, se legis obscuritatem appellare vela- men, haud ita est, inquit, sed illorum cordis obtu- sionem & ruditatem velamen dixerim. Quod plane esset Mosi faciei non ipsius gratia, sed ob istorum crassitudinem & caecitatem obductum. Theodoretius: Legem, inquit, Mosen appellavit; velamen autem incredulitatem.

## 3:16
v. 16. But whenever it shall turn. Namely, 'the heart' from the preceding, and 'shall turn' is a passive used for a reciprocal, where it shall have turned itself, namely to Christ, where it shall have looked back at him.

The veil is taken away. Then they will see how great is the splendor of the Gospel once prefigured. Origen, Against Celsus, book five: 'And we say that when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart, because the will of the law of Moses has been hidden from those who have not embraced the way through Jesus Christ. But we know that if anyone turns to the Lord (and the Lord is the Spirit), the veil having been taken away, he beholds as in a mirror the glory of the Lord with unveiled face in the meanings hidden according to the letters, and partakes of the veiled divine glory into his own glory.' You have things pertaining to the same also in Against Celsus, book 7, and in Rabbi Israel, chapter 3.

Moses was, as Theophylact observes here (as it is brought forth in history), when he repeated his journey to GOD, with face unveiled and open. Which surely presented a figure of things to come, namely when anyone shall have been turned to the Spirit, because the Lord is the Spirit, then he is about to inspect the naked and direct face of the lawgiver, that is, of GOD. These are the words of Theophylact. He draws out further that which he had touched upon concerning the veil being removed through Christ, says the blessed Hunnius, and shows clearly that the veil which hinders the view into the end of the law will not be removed from their minds until the grace of Christ, anticipating the darkness of their heart, dispels it and fills their minds with the new light of recognition, so that they understand that it is utterly impossible for them to fulfill the law: and therefore there was need of another Savior, who would take upon himself the fulfillment and obedience of the law in our place, and liberate us, having been asserted from its servitude, into the freedom of the children of GOD. Estius is not bad here: The sum of the present doctrine is this: Moses turned away from the Lord and veiled in face signified the old people contrary to God and having an obscured heart. But the same Moses turned to the Lord, and having an unveiled face, bore the type of the Christian people turned to God, and contemplating the mysteries of salvation with the face of the heart revealed.

Latin:

v. 16. Ἡνίκα δ᾽ ἂν ἐπισρέψῃ) Nempe ἡ καρδία ex praece- dente, & ἐπισρέψῃ est Passivum pro Reciproco, ubi se con- verterit, nempe ad Christum, ubi eum respexerit.

Περαιρεῖται τὸ κάλυμμα) Tunc videbunt, quantus sit splendor Evangelii olim praefiguratus. Origenes contra Celsum quinto: Καὶ λέγομεν δ᾽ ὅτι, ἡνίκα ἂν ἀναγινώσκη- ται Μωϋσῆς κάλυμμα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν κεῖται, τῷ τοῖς τὴν διὰ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ μὴ ἀσπασαμένοις ὁδὸν ἐπικεκρύφθαι τὸ βό- λημα τῶ Μωϋσέως νόμο. Ἴσμεν δ᾽ ὅτι ἐὰν ἐπισρέψῃ τις πρὸς τὸν κύριον (ὁ δὲ κύριος τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστι) περιαιρεθεὶς τὸ κάλυμμα ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπῳ τῶν ἐν τοῖς κεκρυμ- μένοις νοήμασι κατὰ τὰ γράμματα δόξαν τῶ κυρία ὥσπερεί κατοπτριζόμενος καὶ μεταλαμβάνων τῆς καλυμένης θείας δόξης εἰς τὴν ἑαυτῶ δόξαν. Habes eodem pertinentia etiam contra Cel. sum libro VII. & apud Rabbinum Israelem cap. III.

Erat Moses, quod hic observat Theophylactus, (ut in historia proditum est) cum ad DEUM iter repeteret facie revelata & aperta. Quod sa- ne futurorum praeferebat figuram, videlicet cum ad spiritum quispiam conversus fuerit, quia spiri- tus Dominus est, tunc nudam & rectam latoris legis, hoc est, DEI faciem inspecturus. Haec Theo- phylactus. Diducit id, quod attigerat, de velo, per Christum amovendo amplius, inquit B. Hun- nius, & ostendit liquido, non prius ab illorum mentibus amotum iri velamen, quod impedit in- prospectum in finem legis, quam Christi gratia præ- vertens tenebras cordis illorum discutiat, eorumque mentes nova luce agnitionis compleat, ut intelligant esse sibi legem præstitu prorsus impossibilem: ideo- que alio fuisse opus Servatore, qui legis impletio- nem & obedientiam in se nostro loco susciperet, nos- que ab illius servitute assertos in libertatem filiorum DEI vindicaret. Estius non male hic: Doctrina præsentis hac summa: Moses aversus à Domino & facie velatus significavit populum veterem Deo con- trarium, & cor habentem obscuratum. Idem vero Moses conversus ad Dominum, atque retectam ha- bens faciem typum gessit populi Christiani ad Deum conversi, & revelata cordis facie salutis mysteria contemplantis.

## 3:17
v. 17. But the Lord is the Spirit. Christ was indeed a man, but with divine power, which is called Spirit in Mark 2:8 and Romans 1:4, where see the remarks. Therefore Paul says that when he speaks here of the Lord, he speaks especially of that divine power. Where the Spirit of the Lord is. Just as he has divine power in himself, so he also communicates something of divine power to us, according to our capacity. That is the Spirit of Christ, of whom John 14:26, 15:26. It is called the Spirit of Christ both here and in Galatians 4:6, Philippians 1:19, because it is given through Christ and on account of Christ. There is freedom. And therefore the veil ceases, a sign of subjection, 1 Corinthians 11:10. Understand freedom here from vices. See Romans 6.

The Spirit, not an unsubstantial divine power, but the divine nature of Christ and the very nature of the Holy Spirit, as in 1 Timothy 3:16, 1 Peter 3:18, by reason of which Christ the Lord is the life-giving Spirit, just as the Apostle had said concerning the Holy Spirit in 1 Corinthians 6: 'But the Spirit gives life.' For the Lord, to whom we turn, and GOD the Father, and the Holy Spirit are of one essence, power, and glory, 1 John 5:7. And we have here 'the Lord' Christ the Lord, to whom we turn, and 'the Spirit of the Lord,' the Holy Spirit, and also 'the Lord,' whose Spirit is called the Holy Spirit, that is, God the Father, and thus three divine persons. Theodoret, however, preferred to understand 'the Spirit' in this place as the Holy Spirit. 'But the Lord is the Spirit': He shows that God and the Spirit are equal in honor. For Moses turned his sight to God: but we to the Spirit. Nor indeed, when he wished to show that the new things were superior to the old, would he have made mention of the Spirit, if he had known the Spirit to be a creature. For if he is a creature, as the Arians and Eunomians wish, and we approach him, but Moses approaches God the Father, then ours are far inferior to the old. But if they are not inferior, but even greater, and indeed much greater, then the Holy Spirit is not a creature, but has equal honor and power. But they impudently say that the Lord is called spirit in this place, not the Spirit himself the Lord. But this is full of ignorance and impudence. For the divine Apostle made a comparison altogether between spirit and letter. For he says, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living GOD. And again: Not the letter, but the spirit; and again: For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. And anew: How will the ministration of the spirit not be in glory? It is clear, therefore, that the most holy Apostle called the most holy Spirit Lord. Moreover, what follows also testifies to this. For he says: But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But if he had called the Lord spirit, he would have said, but where the Lord is: But he did not say so; but he called him the Spirit of the Lord, since through him his grace is supplied. And lest anyone should think him to be a minister, he necessarily added that the Spirit is Lord. Thus far Theodoret. Neither explanation is contrary to the analogy of faith.

We have also, according to the latter interpretation, which we have preferred along with Chrysostom and others in System. Theol. Tom. III. p. 766, the mystery of the most holy Trinity: For he also called the Spirit Lord v. 16. When they turned to the Lord, which Lord is that life-giving Spirit in the Gospel and through the Gospel v. 6. whence it is necessary that, having left the law, we turn to the Gospel, that we seek righteousness not in the law, but in the Gospel, and also v. 18. καθάπερ ἀπὸ κυρίε Πνεύματος from the Lord the Spirit. And he called Christ Lord. For we behold the glory of him as in a mirror v. 18. and he called God the Father Lord, when he called the Spirit of the Lord the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, two offices of the Holy Spirit are expressed according to the blessed Balduinus: First, he converts the hearts of men, and in conversion illuminates them, removes perverse opinions about the fulfillment of the law, shows the weakness of human powers, and demonstrates the true sense of the law and its fulfillment: whence all things, which before were difficult and obscure in the law of Moses, become clear and easy. Then also the Spirit of the Lord brings it about that those who are converted do the things that are of the law of their own accord. For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. Liberty here is opposed not to necessity, but to coercion. For it is necessary to do the things that are of the law, for we are debtors, Rom. VIII. But those who are led by the Spirit of GOD do not do what they ought to do by coercion, but willingly and promptly. Therefore, the distinction between the law and the Gospel lies in this verse also. The law always commands, urges, and compels the unregenerate to perform their duty, because they are not yet ruled by the Spirit of God, but are subject to the empire of the flesh. The Gospel, however, advises, exhorts, and beseeches that the regenerate man may do what is pleasing to GOD, because he is ruled by the Spirit of liberty, who has made the nature of the converted man such that he does what is fitting not from fear of punishments, but from love of the good. Thus also Theophylact: In the law there was a yoke and servitude, but in the law of the Spirit and the Gospel there is liberty. Whence it happens that you can easily and freely behold the glory of the Lord. So he. Where the Spirit is, there is liberty, that is, when a man is converted, illuminated, and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, there at last he understands that he is free from the intolerable yoke of the law, by the benefit of Christ alone, who submitted himself in our place both to obedience and to the curse of the law, as here the blessed Hunnius.

Latin:

v. 17. Ὁ δὲ κύριος τὸ Πνεῦμά ἐστι) Christus homo qui- dem fuit, sed cum vi divina, quæ Spiritus dicitur Marci II. 8. & Rom. I. 4. ubi dicta vide. Itaque dicit Paulus, se, cum hic de Domino loquitur, præcipue de vi illa divina loqui. Οὗ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα κυρίου) Sicut ipse vim divinam in se ha- bet, ita & aliquid de vi divina nobis communicat, pro no- stro modulo. Is est Spiritus Christi, de quo Joh. XIV. 26. XV. 26. Dicitur autem Spiritus Christi & hic & Gal. IV. v. 6. Philipp. I. 19. quia per Christum & propter Christum datur. Ἐκεῖ ἐλευθερία) Ac proinde cessat velum, signum subje- ctionis, 1. Cor. XI. 10. Libertatem hic intellige à vitiis. Vide Rom. VI.

Τὸ πνεῦμα non vim divinam ἀνυπόστατον, sed naturam Christi divinam & ipsam Spiritus Sancti naturam, uti 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. 1. Petr. III. v. 18. cujus ratione Christus Dominus Spiritus vivi- ficans est, quemadmodum de Spiritu Sancto I. 6. dixerat Apostolus: Τὸ δὲ Πνεῦμα ζωοποιεῖ. Do- minus enim, ad quem convertimur, & DEUS Pater, ac Spiritus Sanctus unius sunt essentiæ, potentiæ ac gloriæ, 1. Johan. V. vers. 7. Et habe- mus hic τὸν κύριον Christum Dominum, ad quem convertimur, & τὸ Πνεῦμα κυρίου, Spiritum Domi- ni, Spiritum Sanctum, nec non κύριον Dominum, cujus Spiritus dicitur Spiritus Sanctus, hoc est. Deum Patrem, adeoque tres personas divinas. De Spiritu Sancto tamen maluit τὸ πνεῦμα hoc loco intelligere Theodoretus. Dominus autem est Spiritus: Ostendit, Deum & Spiritum esse honore æquales. Moses enim visum ad Deum convertit: nos autem ad Spiritum. Neque vero cùm vellet ostenderet nova esse veteribus præstantiora, Spiritus mentionem fecisset, si spiritum creaturam esse scivisset. Si est n. creatura, ut volunt Ariani & Eunomiani, nos autem ad eum accedimus, Moses autem ad Deum Patrem, nostra ergo longe sunt minora ve- teribus. Sin autem non sunt minora, sed etiam ma- jora, atque adeo multo majora, non est ergo Spiritus Sanctus creatura, sed æqualem habens honorem & potestatem. Sed enim impudenter dicunt Dominum hoc in loco spiritum appellari, non ipsum spiritum Dominum. Hoc autem inscitia & impudentia ple- num est. Divinus enim Apostolus fecit omnino com- parationem spiritus & literæ. Et scripta enim in- quit, non atramento, sed spiritu DEI vivi. Et rursus: Non litera, sed spiritus; & iterum: Litera enim occidit, spiritus autem vivificat. Et denuo: Quomodo non ministratio spiritus erit in gloria? Clarum est ergo, quod sanctissimum Spiritum vocavit Dominum sanctissimus Apostolus. Testantur autem etiam quæ sequuntur. Dicit enim: Ubi autem spi- ritus Domini, ibi libertas. Si autem Dominum spi- ritum appellasset, dixisset ubi autem Dominus: Sed non ita dixit; sed ipsum Domini spiritum appellavit, quoniam per ipsum ejus suppeditata est gratia. Et ne quis ipsum administrum esse putaret, necessario adjecit spiritum esse Dominum. Hactenus Theodore- tus. Neutra explicatio analogiæ fidei est contraria.

Habemus & juxta posteriorem interpretatio- nem, quam cum Chrysostomo aliisque prætulimus System. Theol. Tom. III. p. 766. Sacrosanctæ Tri- nitatis mysterium : Nam & Spiritum ita dixit Do- minum v. 16. Conversi ad Dominum, qui Domi- nus est Spiritus ille vivificans in Evangelio & per Evangelium v. 6. unde opus, ut relicta lege ad Ev- angelium convertamur, non in lege, sed in Evan- gelio justitiam quæramus, nec non v. 18. καθάπερ ἀπὸ κυρίε Πνεύματος à Domino Spiritu. Et Christum dixit Dominum. Hujus n. gloriam velut in speculo intuemur v. 18. & Deum Patrem Dominum dixit, cum Spiritum Domini Spiritum Sanctum vocavit.

Exprimuntur autem duo officia Spiritus Sancti juxta B. Balduinum: Primum corda hominum con- vertit, & in conversione illuminat, opiniones præ- vas de impletione legis aufert, imbecillitatem virium humanarum monstrat, & verum legis sensum, ejus- que impletionem ostendit : unde omnia, quæ antea in lege Mosis erant difficilia & obscura, liquida fiunt & facilia. Deinde & hoc præstat Domini Spiritus, ut conversi ea, quæ legis sunt, sponte faciant. Nam ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Libertas hic op- ponitur non necessitati, sed coactioni. Nam ea, quæ legis sunt, facere necesse est, debitores enim sumus, Rom. VIII. Sed qui Spiritu DEI reguntur, non coacte faciunt, quod facere debent, sed libenter, ac prompte. Latet ergo in hoc quoque versiculo discri- men legis & Evangelii. Lex semper imperat, urget, cogit non renatos ad faciendum officium, quia Spi- ritu Dei nondum reguntur, sed carnis imperio sub- jacent. Evangelium autem monet, hortatur, obse- crat, ut homo renatus DEO rem gratam faciat, quia à Spiritu libertatis regitur, qui ejusmodi fecit naturam hominis conversi, ut non metu pœnarum, sed ex amore boni faciat, quod decet. Ita & Theo- phylactus : In lege jugum & servitus inerant, in spiritus vero lege & Evangelio libertas. Quo fit, ut facile queas & libere Domini gloriam inspectare. Hæc ille. Ubi Spiritus, ibi libertas est, hoc est, quando homo per Spiritum Sanctum conversus, illuminatus & regeneratus est, ibi demum intelligit, se ab intole- rabili jugo legis esse liberum, solius Christi beneficio, qui se nostro loco tum obedientiæ, tum maledictioni legis submiserit, ut hic B. Hunnius.

## 3:18
v. 18. Ἡμεῖς δὲ πάντες) Not Christians made as much from the Jews as from the Gentiles.

Ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπῳ) Directly, not through so many veils of ceremonies.

No veils of ceremonies are mentioned here, and they look not only to believers under the New Testament or Christians; but also to the Messianics of the Old Testament, Acts XV. v. 10. Heb. XI. 6. XIII. 8.

Τὴν δόξαν κυρίε κατοπτριζόμενοι) that is, attentively beholding, just as the Latins also say to speculate: namely because those who consult a mirror behold all things one by one. Thus Christians attentively meditate on how great the glory of Christ reigning in the heavens is. More has fallen to them than once to Moses himself, Exodus XXXIII. and XXXIV.

Τὴν ἀυτὴν εἰκόνα μεταμορφύμεθα.) Not one figure here. For the Present is also put for the Future for the sake of certainty: And we shall be transformed into the image of Christ, that is, having been transformed we shall attain it. We shall be heavenly, just as he himself is heavenly, 1 Cor. XV. 45. Just as he reigns, so also we shall reign, 1 Tim. II. 12. Rev. V. 10.

ὑπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν) It was a great honor to have ministered to Christ, as has already been said: It will be greater to reign with him.

It is not so much a question here of that glory of Christ which shines forth in the exaltation and kingdom of Christ, as that which shines forth in the cross of Christ and his power, which is also called exaltation, John III. 14. chap. XII. 32. 33., who, when he is the brightness of the glory of the Father and the character of his substance, made expiation for our sins by himself, Heb. I. 3. and was made unto us righteousness by God, so that he who glories, may glory in this Lord, 1 Cor. I. 30. 31. which glory radiates especially in the Gospel, so that ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐν δόξῃ may abound, verse 9 above. Yet the glory which he attained after the passion and expiation of sins is not excluded, Luke XXIV. 26. Heb. I. 3. Moreover, the glory of Christ is not only proposed to be viewed attentively in the Gospel under the metaphor of a mirror: but the power of the irradiation of that same brightness is also exhibited in such a way as the blessed Luther emphatically expressed: Nun aber spiegelt sich in uns allen dess Herrn Klarheit mit auffgedecktem Angesicht. This the Hunnian Commentary declares excellently: There is an elegant ἀντίθεσις between the condition of both peoples, the Jews and the Christians. For just as he said that the veil of Moses was placed upon the hearts and eyes of the Jews, so that in the reading of the Old Testament they might not attend to the end of the law: so, conversely, he attributes light to Christians, in the explanation of which he refers us obliquely to the former type. For just as Moses indeed covered his face when he went out into the assembly of the people: But returning to the tabernacle and turning himself to the Lord, with his face now uncovered, he beheld the glory of the Lord: So Paul says that we do not go blind after the manner of the Jews, but with uncovered face behold the glory of the Lord shining in the mirror of the Gospel. And just as Moses obtained this from his secret conversation with God, that his face radiated with a new light: So while we behold the goodness of the heavenly Father and his propitious face in the most limpid mirror of the Gospel: We ourselves also are illuminated by his rays, and are renewed into his image, which from glory to glory, that is, by new increments from time to time, shows itself clearer day by day. And that is done by the Spirit of the Lord, who restores in us the image of God lost through sin by the brightness of his grace. Elegant also here is Theophylact's interpretation, which he received, according to custom, from Chrysostom: To such a degree (he says) do we enjoy a certain nobility and freedom, that we are by no means all in the manner of one Moses, but are with open face. For there is no veil among us believers, so that as if through a mirror looking upon the glory of God we may be transformed into the same image, that is, we may be partakers of his splendor and glory. For we are like a mirror, which, having received the brightness, also sends back the splendor from ourselves. And just as silver placed before the sun reflects gleaming rays back into the sun itself from the encounter with the sun, so also we, having received baptism, purified through the spirit and finally illuminated by his splendor, send back a certain spiritual radiance ourselves from the opposite side and transfer the same image from the glory of the spirit into our own glory and brightness. And such an image, I say, as it is fitting for him to obtain who has received light from the Spirit of the Lord, who is subject to nothing. For since he is Lord, he also possesses royal splendor. But all the faithful are filled with the Holy Spirit by the grace of baptism, and their soul is more radiant. Since even Moses, having looked upon the splendor of God's glory, was transformed into the image of his glory, that is, he himself also partook of divine glory and splendor. His face also shone, when he himself presented the figure of our own.

Finally, by that word κατοπτριζόμενοι is also hinted the imperfection of our knowledge and irradiation which occurs in this life with respect to the other life and intuitive vision. For we see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face, 1 Cor. XIII. 12. But that μεταμόρφωσις is by no means essential, as the fanatics wish, since we cannot be transformed into the substance of Christ; but it is mystical and spiritual, by which we are transformed into the same image which we behold in Christ, when we [partake] of the same righteousness through faith, and of glory through gracious communication, and thus we are rendered partakers of his divine nature, 2 Pet. 1:4, and are renewed into the divine image, which consists in true wisdom and holiness. Therefore, this metamorphosis is not to be expected only in the other life, although then we shall be like him in a more perfect way, when we shall see him as he is, 1 John 3:2. But the same happens to us in this life, lest we be inferior to Moses, who saw the brightness of the Lord here, (which is contrary to his own opinion) whence the Apostle, from whose wording one must not depart, speaks of the present, we are transformed, and adds, from glory to glory. Which phrase is accustomed to designate an increase of a thing, Ps. 84:7, from strength to strength. Finally, there is no need that we should understand the transformation as a figure of a subsequent transformation, or explain it as the kingdom which the elect will have in the heavens with Christ, since the image of Christ, into which we are transformed, is one thing, and the kingdom to which we shall be raised, having been made conformed to his image, is another, Rom. 8:29. We are said to be future heavenly ones, just as he himself is heavenly, 1 Cor. 15:48, by reason of incorruptibility, especially, and immortality, which comparison does not properly apply here. The transformation of which the Apostle speaks at present does not happen at once, but gradually, as the inner man is renewed day by day, 2 Cor. 4:16, from glory to glory, which Theodoret renders: From the glory of the divine Spirit into our glory, as Theophylact did before with Chrysostom.

As from the Lord the Spirit) 'As' here is indeed what signifies the thing itself, as above 1:17, and 'from' here has the force that 'min' sometimes has among the Hebrews. Through the Spirit of Christ we arrive at that glory. For he, imbuing our mind here, endows it with immortality and will one day also make our bodies spiritual, as we said 1 Cor. 15:44 and above 1:22, 5:5, and in this chapter, 6; compare also Rom. 5:4, where 'kata' is what 'apo' is here. There is also a transposition here: 'From the Lord the Spirit' for 'From the Spirit of the Lord'.

If the mind here is imbued with immortality (which I cannot grasp, since the soul is by nature immortal), then certainly this transformation happens in the present: if Grotius wishes the Apostle to be discussing that glory by which both the mind is endowed with immortality here, and the body is one day to be spiritual: which, however, is less consistent with the Apostolic mind. For he explains the communication of the glory of Christ, and the transformation into his same image, which believers have through the Gospel. The transposition of words is also vainly imagined here. For 'from the Lord the Spirit' is 'from the Lord the Spirit', as Theophylact and Theodoret do with Chrysostom, who observe that it is manifest from these words also that he previously called the Spirit the Lord, who restores in us the image of God lost through sin by the brightness of his grace. Add also Basil, book on the Holy Spirit, ch. 21. The Syrian interpreter has it similarly, as 'from the ruling Spirit'. The sum of the whole sentence is thus expressed by Estius: But we all, children of the New Testament, whom Moses, speaking with the Lord with unveiled face, and having it bright and radiant from the association of the Lord's speech, signified, we likewise with the face of the mind unveiled, behold the glory of the Lord through faith, and receiving its splendor in our souls as in certain mirrors, we are in a way transformed into the same image, that is, into the likeness of the glory of God, and that from the brightness of God into our brightness, that is, the brightness of God or the glory of God expressed and represented in us, just as formerly on the face of Moses, we are transformed, I say, as if from the Lord the Spirit, or the Lord the Spirit.

Those who restrict this to ministers alone with Cajetan and Gagney do not grasp the mind of the Apostle. For these things are said about all who have turned to the Lord,

it is about all, not speaking with boldness in ecclesiastical office, but instructed in the spirit of liberty: It is about all beholding the glory of God with unveiled face: such as all believers are.

Latin:

v. 18. Ἡμεῖς δὲ πάντες) Non Christiani tam ex Judæis quam gentibus facti.

Ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπῳ) Recta, non per tot ceremo- piarum umbracula.

Nulla hic ceremoniarum umbracula comme- morata, & spectant illa non ad credentes tantùm sub Novo Testamento seu Christianos; sed etiam ad Messianos Veteris Testamenti, Actor. XV. v. 10. Ebr. XI. 6. XIII. 8.

Τὴν δόξαν κυρίε κατοπτριζόμενοι) id est, attente spectan- tes, quomodo & Latini dicunt speculari : nimirum quia qui speculum consulunt omnia singulatim intuentur. Sic Christiani attente meditantur, quanta sit Christi in cœlis regnantis gloria. Plus illis contigit, quàm olim Mosi ipsi, Exodi XXXIII. & XXXIV.

Τὴν ἀυτὴν εἰκόνα μεταμορφύμεθα.) Non una hic figura. Nam & Præsens ob certitudinem ponitur pro Futuro : Et transfounabimur in speciem Christi, est, transformati eam consequemur. Cœlestes erimus, quomodo ipse cœlestis est, 1. Cor. XVI. 45. Sicut ille regnat, ita & nos regnabi- mus, 1. Tim. II. 12. Apoc. V. 10.

ὑπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν) Magnus honor fuit hic, Christo mi- nistrasse, ut jam dictum est : Major erit, cum ipso regnare.

Non tàm de ea hic agitur Christi gloria, quæ in exaltatione & regno Christi, quàm quæ in cruce Christi, ejusque virtute, quæ etiam exaltatio di- citur, Joh. III. 14. cap. XII. 32. 33. effulget, qui, cum sit effulgescentia gloriæ Patris & character hyposta- seos ejus, per semetipsum peccatorum nostrorum ex- piationem fecit, Ebr. I. 3. nobisque factus est à Deo justitia, ut qui gloriatur, in hoc Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. quæ gloria imprimis in Evangelio radiat, ut abundet ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐν δόξῃ, vers. 9. supr. Non tamen exclusa gloria, quam post passionem & expiationem peccato- rum consequutus est, Luc. XXIV. 26. Ebr. I. 3. Gloria autem Christi, non tantum attente spe- ctanda in Evangelio proponitur sub speculi Meta- phora: Sed vis etiam irradiationis ejusdem ful- goris ita exhibetur, uti emphaticè B. Lutherus expressit: Nun aber spiegelt sich in uns allen dess Herrn Klarheit mit auffgedecktem Angesicht. Quod eximiè declarat Hunnianus Commenta- rius: Elegans est ἀντίθεσις inter utriusque populi conditionem Judæorum & Christianorum. Sicut n. Judæorum cordibus atque oculis velamen Mosis di- xit esse impositum, ut in lectione Veteris Testamenti finem legis non attendant: Ita Christianis lucem è converso attribuit, in qua explicanda nos oblique ad priorem typum remittit. Etenim quemadmodum Moses obtegebat quidem faciem, quando prodibat in concionem populi: Reversus autem ad tabernacu- lum & ad Dominum sese vertens facie jam retecta gloriam Domini contuebatur: Sic ait Paulus, nos non ad modum Judæorum cæcutire, sed retecta facie gloriam Domini in Evangelii speculo relucentem in- tueri. Et quemadmodum Moses ex arcana cum Deo conversatione hoc adeptus est, ut nova luce radiaret ipsius facies: Ita dum nos in speculo Evangelii lim- pidissimo Patris cælestis bonitatem & propitiam ejus faciem intuemur: Illustramur ipsi quoque radiis, & renovamur ad illius imaginem, quæ de gloria in gloriam, hoc est, novis subinde incrementis indies se clariorem profert. Idque fit à Domini Spiritu, qui amissam per peccatum imaginem Dei fulgore gratiæ suæ in nobis instaurat. Elegans etiam hic est Theo- phylacti interpretatio, quam à Chrysostomo, pro more, accepit: Adeo (inquit) ingenuitate quadam nos fruimur & libertate, ut omnes haudquaquam in unius Mosis morem, sed facie simus aperta. Non enim aliquod est apud nos fideles velamen, ut quasi per spe- culum Dei gloriam inspectantes in eandem imaginem transformemur, hoc est, ejus splendoris & gloriæ par- ticipes simus. Nos namque ut speculum sumus, qui claritate excepta & splendorem à nobis remittimus. Et quemadmodum argentum soli objectum, ex solis occursu micantes radios in solem ipsum reflectit, sic & nos baptismo recepto, purgati per spiritum & hu- jus splendore, denique illustrati fulgorem & ipsi spi- ritualem quemdam ex adverso remittimus eandemq; imaginem à spiritus gloria in gloriam nostram & claritatem transferimus. Et talem, inquam, imagi- nem, qualem decens est, ut is sortiatur, qui à Spiritu Domini nulli rei obnoxio lucem acceperit. Dominus enim ille cum sit, & Regium habet splendorem. Fide- les autem omnes baptismi gratia Spiritu Sancto op- plentur, & illorum est fulgentior anima. Quando- quidem & Moses Dei gloriæ fulgore inspecto, in ejus gloriæ imaginem est transformatus, hoc est & ipse divinæ gloriæ & splendoris participavit. Hujus & facies resplendebat, cum ipse nostri præferret figurã.

Denique illa voce κατοπτριζόμενοι innuitur et- iam cognitionis & irradiationis nostræ quæ fit in hac vita imperfectio respectu alterius vitæ & visio- nis intuitivæ. Videmus enim nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem à facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. Illa autem μεταμόρφωσις neutiquam essentialis est, ut fanatici volunt, quum in sub- stantiam Christi transformari nequeamus; sed mystica & spiritualis, qua in eandem imaginem, quam in Christo speculamur, nos transforma- mur, quum ejusdem & justitiæ per fidem, & gloriæ per gratiofam communicationem, adeo- que & divinæ ejus naturæ participes reddimur, 2. Petr. I. 4. & ad imaginem divinam, quæ in fapien- tia & fanctitate vera confiftat, renovamur. Ne- que ergo hæc μεταμόρφωσις demum in altera vita expectanda, etfi tum perfectiori modo fimiles ei erimus, cum videbimus eum, ficuti est, 1. Johan. III. 2. Sed obtingit eadem nobis in hac vita, ne Mofe, qui claritatem Domini hic vidit, inferio- res fimus ea parte, (quod ipfiusmet fententiæ ad- verfum) unde data opera Apoftolus, à cujus λέξει difcedendum non eft, in præfenti loquitur, trans- formamur, additque, ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, de gloria in gloriam. Quæ phrafis incrementum rei defi- gnare folet, Pf. XXIV. 8. de virtute in virtutem. Nec denique opus eft, ut figura alia transforma- tionem intelligamus de confequenti transfurmatio- nis, aut de regno, quod electi habebunt in cœlis cum Chrifto explicemus, quum aliud fit imago Chrifti, in quam transformamur, aliud regnum, ad quod evehemur σύμμορφοι facti imagini ejus, Rom. IIX. 27. 29. cœleftes futuri dicimur, ficut ipfe cœleftis eft, 1. Cor. XV. 48. ratione incorruptibilitatis, im- primis & immortalitatis, quæ comparatio huc proprie non facit. Transformatio, de qua in præ- fenti Apoftolus, non fit ftatim, fed paulatim, cum homo interior renovetur de die in diem, 2. Cor. IV. 16. de gloria in gloriam, quod Theodoretus reddit: A gloria divini Spiritus in gloriam noftram, ut antea cum Chryfoftomo Theophylactus.

Καθάπερ ἀπὸ κυρίυ πνεύματος) καθάπερ hic eft quippe & rem ipfam fignificat, ut fupra I. 17. & ἀπὸ hic valet, ut מן interdum apud Hebræos. Per Spiritum Chrifti perve- nimus ad illam gloriam. Is enim animum hic noftrum im- buens donat eum immortalitate & olim etiam corpora ef- ficiet fpiritualia, ut diximus 1. Cor. XV. 44. & fupra I. 22. V. 5. & hoc capite, 6. confer & Rom. V. 4. ubi κατὰ quod hic ἀπὸ. Eft & hic trajectio Ἀπὸ κυρίυ πνεύματος pro ἀπὸ πνεύματος Κυρίυ.

Si animus hic imbuitur immortalitate, (quod capere non poffum, quum anima naturâ immor- talis fit) utique transformatio hæc in præfenti fit: Siquidem de gloria illa differere Apoftolum velit Grotius, qua & animus donetur hic immortalitate, & corpus olim futurum fit fpirituale: quod verò Apoftolicæ menti minus confentaneum eft. Ex- plicat enim gloriæ Chrifti communicationem, & ad imaginem ejusdem transformationem, quam credentes habent per Evangelium. Trajectio etiam vocum fruftrà hic fingitur. Nam ἀπὸ Κυρίε πνεύ- ματος eft à Domino Spiritu, ut cum Chryfoftomo Theophylactus & Theodoretus, qui ex his etiam ma- nifeftum effe obfervant, quod antea Spiritum Domi- num dixerit, qui amiffam per peccatum Dei imagi- nem fulgore gratiæ fuæ in nobis inftauret. Adde & Bafilium lib. de Spiritu Sancto c. 21. Syrus interpres fimiliter habet, tanquam à dominatore Spiritu. To- tius fententiæ fumma ita exprimitur ab Eftio: Nos autem omnes Novi Teftamenti filii, quos Mofes re- velata facie cum Domino loquens, eamque ex con- fortio fermonis Domini fplendidam ac radiantem habens, fignificavit, itidem facie mentis revelata, gloriam Domini per fidem intuemur, ejusque fplen- dorem in animis noftris velut fpeculis quibusdam recipientes quodammodo transformamur ad eandem imaginem, hoc eft ad fimilitudinem gloriæ Dei, idque à claritate Dei in claritatem noftram, id est, clari- tate Dei feu gloria Dei in nobis expreffa ac repræ- fentata, perinde ut olim in facie Mofis, transforma- mur inquam, velut à Domini Spiritu, vel Domino Spiritu.

Qui ad miniftros folos cum Cajetano & Gagnejo reftringunt, non affequuntur mentem Apoftoli. Nam de omnibus ad Dominum converfis hæc dicta,

| de omnibus non παῤῥησία loquendi in officio Ec- clesiastico, sed spiritu libertatis instructis sermo est: De omnibus gloriam Dei, detecta facie intuen- tibus: Quales verò omnes credentes sunt.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle testifies that he is led by the excellence of his ministry to constancy and the faithful manifestation of the truth, and that it is the fault of the reprobate, whom Satan blinds, that they do not see the clear light of the Gospel. For he preaches Christ faithfully, and is illuminated by God for the illumination of others; and however weak, and subject to various calamities, he nevertheless fearlessly professes the faith, and does not fail, because of the certainty of the eternal glory laid up for him in exchange for temporary affliction.

There are two parts: I. Concerning the Apostle's faith and patience in the ministry, v. 22. II. Concerning the constancy of his profession to verse 18.

PART ONE. Concerning the Apostle's faith in the ministry.

v. 1. Having this ministry) The word diakonia is taken here as above in III. 8. As we have received mercy) Any benefit of God is called eleos by our writers. It is, however, a great benefit to be called to so salutary a ministry. See 1 Cor. II. 25. We do not lose heart) We do not grow weary. See Luke XVIII, 1. .לא ועפנו v. 2. But we have renounced the hidden things of shame) Note the greedy teachers, who wanted their captations to be unknown; apeipametha we repel far from us נטשנו the hidden things of shame are those things which are hidden because of shame. For the genitive here and elsewhere often signifies the impelling cause. the hidden things מסתרים as in Jerem. XLIV. 10.

Since the Apostle, whose minister the Gospel was, has taught in many ways that it excels the law and is greatly distinguished from it against the Pseudo-Apostles, who prefer legal doctrine to the Gospel and mix it with Evangelical doctrine, he now testifies to his faithfulness in such a great office entrusted to him by divine mercy, preserved even in the greatest dangers, exciting the Corinthians by his own example to bear the cross and keep the faith, and tacitly reminding them of the base hiddenness of the false teachers. Most people, with Tertullian, Chrysostom, and Theophylact, render that we do not lose heart as we do not lose courage; or we do not succumb to evils. But more conveniently, with Blessed Luther, Grotius says we do not grow weary. Which is taught both by the perpetual use of the word in the scriptures, which occurs not only in Luke XII. 1. but also in our Apostle, Gal. VI. 9. Eph. III. 13. 2. Thess. III. 13. nay, even below in this chapter v. 16. with that meaning of growing sluggish; as also the Vulgate rendered it here: We do not fail, then the opposite but we have renounced the hidden things of shame, but we drive away, we command to be far off, or we repulse diligently and constantly the hidden things of shame: Which most people refer to base crimes, and understand it concerning the life of the Apostle and his companions being alien to the same, or that they command the same to be far from them. But since the discourse here is about their ministry, in which they assert their faithfulness, or about the renunciation and driving away of the shame of vices, which is done by the power of the corrective office, or about the driving away of doctrine, the shame of which is hidden by the ministers of Satan as much as possible, which is noted here especially in the false Apostles, who transform themselves into ministers of righteousness, 2 Cor. XI. 15.

these things seem to be accepted: whence Paul warns in chapter VI. 14. 17. not to bear the yoke with them, or to foster communion, but to separate themselves from the same. For they were secretly introducing their dogmas, and were afraid to profess them openly: which is usually done by false Doctors: although it is permitted here to understand the secret filthiness of both vices and dogmas: because the eradication of both was incumbent upon the duty of the diligent and faithful servants of Christ. Theophylact understood this concerning the life of the Apostles: We therefore, he says, let us drive away from ourselves and renounce these wicked and painted deeds: and let us not commit such things, which afterwards when they become manifest and have been brought to light, bring ignominy to the perpetrator. But the word is of the Indicative mood: Whence Tertullian and the Vulgate interpret it as we renounce: nor is it said: we renounce from ourselves, but simply ἀπειπάμεθα; and Theophylact acknowledges that false Apostles are indicated in this place, who used to do everything with a certain shadowed and deceitful appearance. But for the rest, he adds less conveniently: that even those who commit wicked things are rightly to be held as false Apostles. B. Hunnius, by the word ἐκκακῆμεν, acknowledges that he is declining the charge of sloth; but the Apostle wishes to remove from himself the rest, because he teaches nothing in secret, just as Pseudo-Doctors do, who are ashamed of their own dogmas. Therefore B. Hülsemann does not refer this to life, but to doctrine, and prefers to understand τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης as the shameful and deliberate corruption of doctrine and the filthiness of morals that for the most part accompanies heterodoxy, just as αἰσχύνη in Phil. III. 19 is taken concerning the shame or blushing of both Pseudo-Apostles and Pseudo-Christians, both on account of hypocrisy in doctrine and in life, as well as concerning the dissimulation or veiling of false doctrine, or concerning the clandestine shameful acts of morals, concerning which Cornelius à Lapide and others accept these things.

Μὴ περιπατῦντες ἐν πανυργίᾳ) בחלקות or חלקלקות not using craftiness, as those who are one thing, but wish to appear another. Μηδὲ δολῦντες τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ) We have had δολῦν in Rom. III. 13. we have δολῦν in Psalm XV. 3. XXXVI. 3. they handle the word of GOD with deceit, who, in order to please men, either keep silent a part of the truth, or mix in false things. Ἀλλὰ τῇ φανερώσει τῆς ἀληθείας) By the free manifestation of the truth, דברים נכחים Prov. XXV. 26. Συνιστῶντες ἑαυτὸς πρὸς πᾶσαν συνείδησιν ἀνθρώπων) Pleasing not all (for that cannot be done), but good consciences ἐνώπιον Θεῦ as if with God looking on.

These things likewise look to the office, they exclude craftiness and deceit in office and doctrine, which the Pseudo-Apostles used, and they testify to a sincere and open manifestation of the truth. As for that ἐν πανυργίᾳ; some note the cunning and craftiness for deceiving others, such as was the devil's πανυργία for seducing the Protoplasts, 2. Cor. XI. verse 3. and that of heretics is πρὸς τὴν μεθοδείαν τῆς πλάνης, Ephes. IV. verse 14. and of those craftily lying in wait for others, 1. Cor. III. 19. and of hypocrites, Luke XX. 23. who tempted Christ, such as were also the Sophistical arts of the Pseudo-Apostles. And therefore rightly B. Hunnius: πανυργία, he says, is when someone strives to propagate his dogmas by wondrous arts, by the illusions and deceits of sophisms, and by other least praiseworthy artifices, by deceiving men and blinding their minds, by casting the color and appearance of truth over false doctrine, and on the contrary by burdening and deforming sound doctrine with calumnies. This is that πανυργία, which we are accustomed to call Sophistical, crafty, gambling, illusory, Sycophantic. Δόλος to the Latins is likewise deceit and fraud or deception, Matth. XXVI. 4. Acts XIII. verse 10. 1. Peter II. verse 1. which is done especially in speech 1. Peter III. v. 10. and δολῦντες τὸν λόγον are those handling the word with deceit, who deprave the text of the word; or corrupt the sense of the same with perverse glosses, or mix doctrines of human intention with the word of GOD, as was done by false Doctors, cf. chapter II. verse 17. Paul teaches that all these things are foreign to him. But on the contrary, he claims for himself a candid zeal for manifesting the truth, which he opposes both to deceitful craftiness and to the perverse handling of the divine word, appealing to the consciences of the Corinthians, and primarily to the testimony of God, concerning which Theophylact says: The Apostles, he says, who have been accustomed to deceive others with painted works, pretend to be others than they are. But I myself would wish the manifestation and nakedness of the truth to be my recommendation, that is, I use the things themselves as witnesses, and you are witnesses to me, just as I have received nothing from any of the faithful, nor have I done those things which these Apostles, whom I have mentioned, are accustomed to do. Whereby it happens that I make myself more commendable before the conscience of all men, namely of the faithful and the unfaithful, and by thus laying my life bare openly, I preach the Gospel, so that everyone has the opportunity of knowing thoroughly how I have lived. Therefore because it might perhaps be permitted to deceive a man, he added before GOD, whom such Apostles would by no means admit as a witness of their conscience.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Apostolus ministerii sui præstantia sese induci testatur ad constantiam & fidelem veritatis manifestationem, & quod reproborum, quos Satanas excæcat, culpa fiat, quod claram Ev- angelii lucem non videant. Se enim Christum fideliter prædicare, & illuminari à Deo, ad aliorum illuminationem; & utut infirmos, variisque calamitatibus subjectos, intrepide tamen fidem profiteri, nec deficere, ob cer- titudinem repositæ sibi pro temporariâ affli- ctione æternæ gloriæ.

PArtes sunt duæ: I. De Apostoli in ministerio fide ac patientia, v. 22. II. De professionis constantiâ ad vers. 18.

PARS PRIOR. De Apostoli in ministerio fide.

v. 1. Ἔχοντες τὴν διακονίαν ταύτην) Vox διακονίας hic su- mitur ut supra III. 8. Καθὼς ἠλεήθημεν) Quodvis beneficium Dei ἔλεος no- stris scriptoribus dicitur. Magnum est autem beneficium vocari ad tam salutare ministerium. Vide 1. Cor. II. 25. Οὐκ ἐκκακῶμεν) Non pigrescimus. Vide Luc. XVIII, 1. .לא ועפנו v. 2. Ἀλλ᾽ ἀπειπάμεθα τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης) Notas doctores lucripetas, qui captationes suas volebant esse ignotas; ἀπειπάμεθα longè à nobis repellimus נטשנו τὰ κρυπτὰ τᾶς αἰσχύνης sunt ea, quæ ob pudorem occultantur. Nam Genitivus hîc & alibi sæpe causam impellentem signi- ficat. τὰ κρυπτὰ מסתרים ut Jerem. XLIV. 10.

Quum Evangelium, cujus minister erat Apo- stolus, multis modis præcellere legem, & ab ea maximopere distingui adversus Pseudo - Aposto- los, doctrinam legalem Evangelio præferentes, & cum Evangelica Doctrina commiscentes docue- rit, jam fidelitatem suam in tanto munere sibi per misericordiam divinam credito, in summis etiam periculis servatam testatur, suo exemplo ad fe- rendam crucem, ac servandam fidem Corinthios excitans, eosque de falsorum Doctorum turpi- tudine occultâ tacite commonefaciens. Illud ἐκ ἐκκακῶμεν cum Tertulliano, Chrysostomo, Theophy- lacto plerique reddunt non despondemus animum; vel non succumbimus malis. Sed convenientius cum B. Luthero Grotius non pigrescimus. Quod docet tùm verbi usus in scripturis perpetuus, quod non modo Luc. XII. 1. sed & penes Apostolum nostrum, Gal. VI. 9. Eph. III. 13. 2. Thess. III. 13. imò etiam infra hoc capite v. 16. illa segnescendi significatione occurrat; uti & hic Vulgata reddi- dit: Non deficimus tùm oppositum ἀλλ᾽ ἀπειπά- μεθα τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης, sed profligamus, procul abesse jubemus, vel repulsamus sedulo, & constanter occulta turpitudinis: Quæ plerique ad turpia crimina referunt, & de vita Apostoli ac sociorum ab iisdem alienâ, vel quod eadem procul à se abesse jubeant, intelligunt. Sed quum de ministerio eorum hic sermo sit, in quo fidem suam adserunt, vel de abdicatione & profligatione tur- pitudinis vitiorum, quæ fit vi muneris Epanortho- tici vel de profligatione doctrinæ, cujus turpitudo à ministris Satanæ, quoad fieri potest, occulta- tur,quod hic notatur imprimis in falsis Apostolis, qui se transfigurant in ministros justitiæ, 2. Cor. XI.15.

hæc accipienda videntur : unde monet Paulus cap. VI. 14. 17. ne cum illis jugum ducant, aut com- munionem alant, sed separent sese ab iisdem. Oc- culte enim ingerebant sua dogmata, ac vereban- tur ipsa palàm profiteri: quod plerumque à falsis Doctoribus fieri solet: quanquam vitiorum & dogmatum occultam turpitudinem simul hic intel- ligere liceat: quia utrorumque profligatio muneri sedulorum ac fidelium servorum Christi incum- bebat. Theophylactus de vita Apostolorum accepit : Nos itaque, inquit, prava hæc & fucata facinora propulsemus à nobis & abdicemus: nec talia commit- tamus, quæ postmodum manifesta cum fiant & in lu- cem edita fuerint, ignominiam afferunt perpetranti. Sed verbum est Indicativi modi : Unde Tertullia- nus & Vulgata interpretantur abdicamus : neque dicitur: abdicamus à nobis, sed simpliciter ἀπειπά- μεθα; & agnoscit Theophylactus, falsos hoc loco Apostolos indicari, qui facie quadam adumbrata & subdola omnia factitarent. De cætero verò mi- nus convenienter subjicit: etiam eos, qui prava committunt, jure pro falsis Apostolis habendos esse. B. Hunnius verbo ἐκκακῆμεν agnoscit desidiæ cri- men declinare; cæteris verò à se amoliri Aposto- lus vult, quod nihil in occulto doceat, quemadmo- dum factitant Pseudo-Doctores, quos suorummet pudet dogmatum. Non ergo ad vitam, sed ad doctrinam refert hæc B. Hülsemannus, & τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης mavult de turpi ac proaretica corrupte- la doctrinæ & concomitante ut plurimum heterodo- xiam turpitudine morum intelligere, uti αἰσχύνη Phil. III. 19. de pudore seu erubescentia tam Pseu- do-Apostolorum, quam Pseudo-Christianorum, tum ob hypocrisin in doctrina, tum in vita sumitur, quàm de dissimulatione seu velamento falsæ do- ctrinæ, sive de clandestinis flagitiis morum, de qui- bus Cornelius à Lapide, & alii hæc accipiunt.

Μὴ περιπατῦντες ἐν πανυργίᾳ) בחלקות vel חלקלקות non vafritie utentes, ut qui aliud sunt, aliud videri volunt. Μηδὲ δολῦντες τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ) Δολιῦν habuimus Rom. III. 13. δολῦν habemus Psalm. XV. 3. XXXVI. 3. dolo tra- ctant verbum DEI, qui ut hominibus placeant aut veri partem tacent, aut falsa admiscet. Ἀλλὰ τῇ φανερώσει τῆς ἀληθείας) Libera veri apparitione, דברים נכחים Prov. XXV. 26. Συνιστῶντες ἑαυτὸς πρὸς πᾶσαν συνείδησιν ἀνθρώπων) Pla- centes non omnibus, (id enim fieri nequit) sed bonis con- scientiis ἐνώπιον Θεῦ velut Deo inspectante.

Hæc itidem ad officium spectant, vafritiem & dolum in officio excludunt & doctrina, quibus Pseudo-Apostoli utebantur, & sinceram atque apertam veritatis manifestationem testantur. Quod ad illud ἐν πανυργίᾳ ; quidam versutiam & calliditatem ad alios decipiendos notant, qualis erat diaboli πανυργία ad seducendos Protopla- stos, 2. Cor. XI. vers. 3. & hæreticorum est πρὸς τὴν μεθοδείαν τῆς πλάνης, Ephes. IV. vers. 14. & astute aliis insidiantium, 1. Cor. III. 19. atque hypocrita- rum, Luc. XX. 23. qui Christum tentarunt, quales erant etiam artes Pseudo-Apostolorum Sophisti- cæ. Ideoque rectè B. Hunnius: πανυργία, inquit, est, cum quis miris artibus sua dogmata propagare nititur sophismatum præstigiis & offuciis, aliisque minime laudatis artificiis decipiendo homines, & illorum mentes præstringendo, doctrinæ falsæ colo- rem & speciem veritatis obducendo, sanam econtra doctrinam calumniis prægravando & deformando. Hæc est πανυργία illa, quam solemus appellare So- phisticam, veteratoriam, aleatoriam, præstigiato- riam, Sycophanticam. Δόλο Latinis itidem dolus & fraus est vel deceptio, Matth. XXVI. 4. Act. XIII. vers. 10. 1. Petr. II. vers. 1. quæ impri- mis sermone fit 1. Petr. III. v. 10. & δολῦντες τὸν λόγον cum dolo tractantes verbum sunt, qui textum verbi depravant; aut sensum ejusdem perversis glossis corrumpunt, aut commiscent cum DEI verbo doctrinas humanae intentionis, ut a falsis Doctoribus fiebat, conf. cap. II. vers. 17. Quae omnia aliena esse docet Paulus. Ex adverso ve- ro sibi vindicat candidum manifestandae veritatis studium, quod tum versutiae deceptrici, tum tra- stationi verbi divini perverse opponit, provocans ad conscientias Corinthiorum, imprimis, ad testi- monium Dei, quo de Theophylactus: Apostoli, in- quit, qui fallere alios consueverunt fucatis operibus, alios se, quam sint, mentiuntur. Ipse vero verita- tis manifestationem & nuditatem commendationi mihi esse velim, hoc est, rebus ipsis pro testibus utor, vosque mihi testimonio estis, quemadmodum nihil a quovis fidelium acceperim, neque ea egerim, quae factitent hi, quos dixi, Apostoli. Quo fit, ut me- ipsum apud omnium hominum conscientiam, fide- lium scilicet & infidelium commendatiorem efficiam, vitamque meam palam sic enudando Evangelium praedico, ut omnibus quemadmodum vixerim, sit pernoscendi facultas. Proinde quia fallere homi- nem forte liceret, coram DEO adjecit, quem haud quaquam istiusmodi Apostoli in testem sua admitte- rent conscientiae.

## 4:3
v. 3. Εἰ δὲ ἐστι κεκαλυμμένον τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον ἡμῶν) He saw that it could be objected to him that there are many who do not acknowledge this truth, καλύπτεσθαι or κρύπτεσθαι, as in Luke XIX. 42. it is also said of that which, although it is conspicuous in itself, yet in reality is not seen, like the sun by the blind.

Ἐν τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις ἐστὶ κεκαλυμμένον) It is a metonymy. For he calls those perishing who have deserved to perish, who favor their own vices, and do not wish the truths to be seen which are opposed to their vices.

The discourse is not about the concealment of moral doctrine concerning vices, but of the Gospel concerning Christ. Therefore the Commentary of the Greeks is more correct here: Of whom Theophylact: Since he said above that a veil was placed upon the Israelites, and that we the faithful look with unveiled face: Now indeed, he says, even if the Gospel is open, yet it is covered to the unfaithful. For what happened then to the Jews in Moses, that very thing was the Gospel to the unfaithful; and just as they could by no means tolerate with their eyes the splendor that was in Moses, so the truth of the Gospel lies hidden from these: Not by the fault of the Gospel, but of themselves, who lack faith. For clearly even to these, if they believed, the glory of Christ and all the Evangelical power would be open.

Latin:

v. 3. Εἰ δὲ ἐστι κεκαλυμμένον τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον ἡμῶν) Vide- bat, objici sibi posse, multos esse, qui veritatem istam non agnoscunt, καλύπτεσθαι aut κρύπτεσθαι, ut Luc. XIX. 42. id etiam dicitur, quod, quamvis per se conspicuum sit, reipsa tamen non conspicitur, ut sol a caecis.

Ἐν τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις ἐστὶ κεκαλυμμένον) Est μετωνυμία. Nam pereuntes vocat eos, qui perire meruerunt, qui vitiis suis favent, & vera videri nolunt, quae vitiis adversantur.

Non de occultatione doctrinae moralis de vitiis, sed Evangelii de Christo sermo est. Rectius itaque se hic habet Commentarius Graecorum: E quibus Theophylactus: Cum superius dixerit, Israëlitis esse velamen impositum, nosque fideles facie revelata prospicere: Nunc vero, etsi apertum est Evange- lium, inquit, infidelibus tamen opertum est. Quod enim tunc temporis Judaeis in Mose contigit, id ipsum & infidelibus Evangelium fuit; Utque illi splendo- rem, qui Mosi inerat, nequaquam tolerare oculis po- terant, sic hos Evangelii veritas latet: Non Evan- gelii culpa, sed ipsorum, qui fide carent. Clare nam- que & his, si crederent Christi gloria, & vis omnis Evangelica pateret.

## 4:4
v. 4. In whom the God of this age has blinded the minds) He understands Satan or the Prince of Demons. Porphyry, dealing with evil Demons, says: the power presiding over them seems to be the greatest God. Thus, as if he were God, he commands men: and the worship of idols returns to his own use. But he called him the God of this age or of this world, just as Christ called him the prince of this world, John 12:31, for the most part, as 1 John 5:19, Eph. 6:12, the majority are evil. Plutarch, concerning Isis, says: every irrational and beastly nature has become the portion of the evil demon. The Devil blinds all things by acting, Eph. 2:2, God by permitting. The Devil is God in the same way as the belly, Phil. 3:19, because he is worshipped in the place of God.

Of the unbelievers) A Hebraizing construction. For the correct construction would have been in whom the unbelievers, then their minds. The Hebrews often put for the Relative that which preceded, or ought to have preceded. See what we have said on Gen. 6, verse 3.

He teaches, therefore, that the fault does not lie in the doctrine, which is simple and clear, but both in the malice of the reprobate who turn away from the truth, and in Satan hardening them in this obstinacy, and effectively blinding their senses. Wherefore, it is not innate blindness that is understood here, which is common to all, but acquired, and voluntarily contracted, and permitted by the judgment of God, when obstinacy is added, strengthened by Satan, 2 Pet. 1:9, 1 John 2:9.
