Therefore, this passage is rashly brought forward for the blinding of the reprobate by the absolute force of divine reprobation from Bucer and Marlurat; nor can it be approved that some Fathers, responding to the Manichaean heretics who from this passage inferred a second principle of things, an evil GOD, understand by the GOD of this age the true God who created the age, which was the explanation of Theodoret, Anselm, and others: Or that Augustine in book XXI against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 2, and Bellarmine in book III on the Word of GOD, chapter 2, transpose the words: referring these to the judicial blinding by GOD, that God blinds the minds of the unbelievers of this age. For here he opposes GOD blessed for ever, intending to illuminate the hearts of men through the Gospel, to the GOD of this age, blinding the hearts of the unbelievers, who despise the Gospel even though it is clearly set forth, whose endeavor is to prevent the light of the Gospel from shining into the minds of the unbelievers, just as Satan is called by Christ the Prince of this world, John XIV, verse 30. and evil demons are called lords of the world and rulers of the darkness of this age, Ephesians VI, verse 12, both by reason of the malignant dominion by which they powerfully rule over the sons of this age, who pursue worldly desires; and by reason of the worship and obedience with which those same people venerate them. Which sense Augustine did not disapprove of in the place cited, and in book II against the adversaries of the law, explaining it as the God of impious men, who wish to flourish only in this age.

That the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ might not shine unto them) That they might not be partakers of that good which Isaiah predicted XLII, v. 6, 16. Ἀυγάσαι הופיע. In the manuscript it is διαυγάσαι, and ἀυτοῖς is absent, not badly, that is, that they may not see that light. For ἀυγάζειν and ἀυγάζεσθαι is often to see. He said Τὸν φωτισμὸν metonymically, placing the name of the effect for the cause. Τὸ φῶς תאור. For אור is for the most part translated φῶς; sometimes φωτισμὸς, as in Job III, v. 9, Psalm XXVII, 1, XLIV, 4, LXXVIII, 14. He calls the Gospel the splendor of Christ, the announcement concerning the miracles of Christ, his resurrection, his ascension into heaven, the heavenly kingdom, and the mission of the Spirit, accomplished through him.

Grotius omits in the splendor of the Gospel the suffering of Christ, in which is our glory, so much so that he who wishes to glory, ought to glory in Christ, and that crucified, with Paul, 1 Cor. I, verse 30, chapter II, v. 3, Gal. VI, verse 16. The splendor consists in this, says Theophylact, that one believes that Christ was both lifted up on the cross, and assumed into heaven, and will bestow future goods. Compare 1 Corinthians XV, verse 3. ἀυγάσαι here is not to see, or to behold: For thus it would have had to be said, ἀυγάσαι ἀυτὲς, not ἀυτοῖς: But to shine, to illuminate, as the Vulgate rightly has it, that it may not shine unto them: Nor is there need to understand Τὸ Φῶς metonymically through τὸν Φωτισμὸν, since the sense is plain, that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine unto them, that is, the Gospel concerning the glory of Christ, illuminating the hearts of men unto eternal life, John I, verse 4, chapter III, verse 12, chapter IX, verse 5, chapter XII, v. 35, 46. Concerning which glory of Christ see John XII, 28, c. XVI, 14, and his exaltation John III, 15, chapter XII, 32, 33.

Who is the image of the invisible God) Namely because just as the species of a man is known from his image; so from those things which Christ did and spoke, the power, wisdom, holiness, and goodness of GOD are known, Hebrews 1, verse 3. Also among the Hebrews the Messiah is called צלם אך, as in the Zohar, and elsewhere. Add Colossians I, v. 15, 1 Timothy III, 16, John I, 18.

Nor do these things pertain to the epithet of Christ, with which he is adorned here, nor to the present description of the Gospel. For the Son of GOD was the image of the invisible God, before anything was, the firstborn of every creature, Col. I, 15, and would have remained so for all eternity, even if he had promulgated no Gospel, nor had done anything or spoken with men, Heb. I, 1, 2, 3. The Son, begotten from eternity by the Father, was the splendor of his glory and the character of the Father's substance from eternity, even if God spoke to us through him only in these last days. He is called the image of the Father because he represents the Father most perfectly, as being of the same power, wisdom, holiness, and goodness as the Father, and most perfectly one with the Father, just as the Holy Spirit is one with the Father in the Trinity, John X, 30, 1 John V, 7. Therefore he did not begin to be the image of the Father only when he referred or represented the power, wisdom, holiness, and goodness of GOD on earth by his words and deeds. He himself, as the substantial image of the Father, consubstantial with God, and the hypostatic substance from eternity, in the fullness of time at last, when the Word was made flesh, and GOD was manifested in the flesh, John I, verse 14, 1 Timothy III, verse 16, said and did such things, from which he himself might be recognized in the assumed flesh and through the same, as Saint John testifies, chapter I, verse 14, and XXI, verse 5, 1 John I, v. 1, 2, 3, whence then he could also testify concerning himself manifested in the flesh: He who sees me, sees also the Father, if indeed I am in the Father, and the Father is in me, John XIV, v. 9, 10. And this is the principal nucleus of the Gospel concerning Christ, whence all its power comes, so that it may serve our illumination, regeneration, and salvation, and thence it is also called the Gospel of the glory of Christ; because, namely, that substantial image of GOD, the consubstantial Son of GOD, willed to be incarnate, and to become a partaker of our flesh and blood, that he might make expiation for our sins by himself, Heb. I, 3, and reconcile us to GOD by his blood, because it pleased him that all fullness should dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things unto himself, that they might be pacified through the blood of his cross, whether they be things in heaven, or things in earth, Col. I, 14, 19, 20, and he himself was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of GOD in him, 2 Corinthians V, 21, and through his death he who had the power of death might be destroyed, and we might be delivered from death, Heb. II, 14. And this He considered His own work, this His own glory, that He should do that will of God, John 4:34, ch. 10:18, Psalm 40:8. And that was what the Apostles preached ἐν πρώτοις, above all, 1 Cor. 15:3, concerning which also all the Prophets had testified, Acts 10:43, and which Christ commanded to be announced throughout the whole world, Luke 24:26, which finally made most against the corruptions of the false Apostles. The blessed Luther also explained this most correctly in a marginal gloss: We ought to shine and preach how one should recognize God's grace, shown to us in Christ. Others may preach works and the law. Therefore, to the words he added in the person of Jesus Christ: Through the knowledge of Christ, not through the face of Moses, which is the knowledge of the law. For through Christ we know God. John 6:68.

Latin:

v. 4. Ἐν οἷς ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου ἐτύφλωσε τὰ νοήματα) Satanam sive Daemonem Principem intelligit. Porphyrius de malis Daemonibus agens, ἡ προεστῶσα αὐτῶν δύναμις δοκεῖ Θεὸς εἶναι μέγιστος. Ita tanquam si Deus esset, hominibus imperat: & idolorum cultus ad ipsius usum redit. Dixit autem eum Deum seculi sive mundi hujus, sicut Christus principem mundi hujus, Joh. XII. 31. ex maxima parte, ut 1. Joh. V. 19. Eph. VI. 12. οἱ πλείους κακοί. Plutarchus de Iside πᾶσα φύσις ἄλογος καὶ θηριώδης τῆς τοῦ κακοῦ δαίμονος γέγονε μοίρας. Excaecat omnia Diabolus agendo, Eph. II. 2. Deus sinendo. Diabolus sic Deus, quomodo venter, Philipp. III. 19. quia Dei vice colitur.

Τῶν ἀπίστων) Constructio Hebraïzans. Nam recta con- structio fuerat ἐν οἷς ἀπίστοις, deinde νοήματα αὐτῶν. He- braei pro Relativo saepe ponunt id, quod antecessit, aut antecedere debuit. Vide, quae diximus ad Genes. VI. vers. 3.

Docet itaque, culpam non haerere in doctrina, quae simplex sit, & perspicua, sed tum in malitia reproborum veritatem aversantium, tum in Sa- tana obfirmante illos in hac pertinacia, & sensus eorum efficaciter excaecante. Quapropter non caecitas connata hic intelligitur, quae omnibus communis est, sed adscititia, & voluntarie contra- cta, ac permissa judicio Dei, cum accedit per- tinacia, a Satana roborata, 2. Pet. I. 9. 1. Joh. II. 9. Ideo temere affertur hic locus ad excaecationem reproborum vi absoluta reprobationis divinae a Bucero & Marlurato; nec probari potest, quod Patres nonnulli Manichæis hæreticis, qui ex hoc loco alterum rerum principium, DEUM ma- lum colligebant, respondentes, per DEUM hujus seculi verum Deum intelligunt, qui secu- lum creavit, quæ explicatio Theodoreti, Anshel- mi & aliorum fuit: Aut quod Augustinus lib. XXI. contra Faust. Manich. cap. 2. & Bellarm. libr. III. de verbo DEI cap. 2. verba trajiciant: Deus excecat mentes infidelium hujus seculi ad judicia- riam DEI excæcationem hæc referentes. Nam hic DEUM benedictum in secula, per Evange- lium illuminare corda hominum intendentem, opponit DEO hujus seculi, corda infidelium ex- cæcanti, qui Evangelium, etsi luculenter propo- situm, despiciunt, cujus studium est impedire, ne lumen Evangelii mentibus infidelium affulgeat, quemadmodum Satanas à Christo Princeps mun- di, Johan. XIV. vers. 30. & mali dæmones mundi Domini, & rectores tenebrarum hujus seculi, E- phes. VI. vers. 12. vocantur tum ratione maligni dominii, quo filiis hujus seculi potenter impe- rant, qui secularia sectantur desideria; tum ra- tione cultus & obsequii, quo illi eosdem vene- rantur. Quem sensum nec Augustinus impro- bavit l. c. & libr. II. contra leg. Advers. exponentis Deum hominum impiorum, non nisi in hoc seculo florere volentium.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ ἀυγάσαι ἀυτοῖς τὸν φωτισμὸν τῦ Εὐαγγελίκ τῆς δόξης τῦ Χρισῦ) Ne participes essent ejus boni, quod præ- dixit Esaias XLII. v. 6. 16. Ἀυγάσαι הופיע. In Manuscri- pto est διαυγάσαι, & abest ἀυτοῖς, non male, id est, non vi- deant illam lucem. Nam ἀυγάζειν & ἀυγάζεσθαι sæpe est videre. Τὸν φωτισμὸν dixit μετωνυμικῶς, effectus nomen ponens pro causa. Τὸ φῶς תאור. Nam אור plerumque φῶς vertitur; interdum φωτισμὸς, ut Jobi III. v. 9. Psalm. XXVII. 1. XLIV. 4. LXXVIII. 14. Evangelium splendens. Christi vocat annuntiationem de Christi miraculis, resur- rectione, ascensu in cœlos, regno cœlesti, de missione spiri- tus, per eum facta.

Omittit Grotius in splendore Evangelii trīcem Christi, in qua nostra gloria, adeo, ut qui glo- riari vult, in Christo, eoque crucifixo gloriari cum Paulo debeat, 1. Cor. I. vers. 30. cap. II. v. 3. Gal. VI. vers. 16. Splendor in eo constat, ait Theo- phylactus, ut Christum quis credat & in crucem fuisse sublatum, & in cælos assumptum & bona futura largiturum. Confer 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 3. ἀυγάσαι hic non est videre, vel aspicere: Sic enim dicendum fuisset, ἀυγάσαι ἀυτὲς, non ἀυτοῖς: Sed splendere, illucescere, ut rectè Vulgata, ut non fulgeat illis: Neque per τὸν Φωτισμὸν opus est metonymice τὸ Φῶς intelligere, quum sensus pla- nus sit, ut non fulgeat illis illuminatio Evangelii glo- riæ Christi, id est, Evangelium de Christi gloria, illuminans corda hominum ad vitam æternam, Joh. I. vers. 4. cap. III. vers. 12. cap. IX. vers. 5. cap. XII. v. 35. 46. De qua Christi gloria vide Joh. XII. 28. c. XVI. 14. & exaltatione Joh. III. 15. cap. XII. 32. 33.

Ὅς ἐσιν εἰκὼν τῦ Θεῦ ἀοράτε) Nimirum quia sicut ex ima- gine hominis species cognoscitur; ita ex iis, quæ egit & loquutus est Christus, DEI potentia, sapientia, sanctitas, bonitas, Hebr. 1. vers. 3. Etiam Hebræis Messias dicitur צלם אך, ut in Zohar, & alibi. Adde Coloss. I. v. 15. 1. Tim. III. 16. Joh. I. 18.

Neque ad epitheton Christi, quo hic ornatur, neque ad præsentem Evangelii descriptionem hæc faciunt. Nam Filius DEI εἰκὼν fuit Dei invisibi- lis, antequam quicquam esset, ὁ πρωτότοκος πά- σης τῆς κτίσεως, Col. I. 15. mansissetque in omnem æternitatem, etiamsi nullum promulgasset Ev- angelium, nec vel egisset quicquam vel loquu- tus esset cum hominibus, Ebr. I. 1. 2. 3. Filius ab æterno à Patre genitus splendor gloriæ, & chara- kter hypostaseos Patris ab aeterno fuit, etsi novis- simis demum diebus nobis per eum loquutus sit Deus. Imago Patris dicitur, quod Patrem per- fectissime referat, ut ejusdem cum Patre potentiae, sapientiae, sanctitatis, bonitatis, & perfectissime unum cum Patre, uti cum Patre unum est τη ἀγίᾳ Spiritus Sanctus, Joh. X. 30. 1. Joh. V. 7. Non ergo demum esse coepit imago Patris, cum in ter- ris DEI potentiam, sapientiam, sanctitatem, bonitatem dictis & factis suis referret aut reprae- sentaret. Ipse ceu imago substantialis Patris Deo ὁμοούσιος, & substantia hypostatica ab aeterno, in temporis demum plenitudine, cum Verbum caro factum, & DEUS in carne manifestatus est, Johan. I. vers. 14. 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. talia dixit & egit, ex quibus ipse in assumpta carne ac per ean- dem agnosceretur, teste Sancto Johanne, cap. I. vers. 14. & XXI. vers. 5. 1. Joh. I. v. 1. 2. 3. unde tum etiam de sese in carne manifestato testari po- tuit: Qui videt me, videt & Patrem, siquidem ego in Patre, & Pater in me est, Joh. XIV. v. 9. 10. Et hic est Evangelii de Christo praecipuus nucleus, unde omnis ejus vis, ut illuminationi, regenera- tioni ac saluti nostrae serviat, atque inde etiam vo- catur Evangelium τῆς δόξης τοῦ χριστοῦ; quod nempe imago illa DEI substantialis, Filius DEI ὁμοούσιος incarnari voluerit, & carnis ac sangui- nis nostri particeps fieri, ut expiationem peccato- rum nostrorum per semetipsum faceret, Ebr. I. 3. nosque sanguine suo DEO reconciliaret, quia in ipso complacuit omnem plenitudinem inhabitare, & per eum reconciliare omnia in ipsum, ut pacificaren- tur per sanguinem crucis ejus, sive quae in caelis, sive quae in terris sunt, Col. I. 14. 19. 20. & peccatum ipse fieret pro nobis, ut nos justitia DEI redderemur in ipso, 2. Corinth. V. 21. ac per mortem ejus de- strueretur ille, qui habebat mortis imperium, nosque a morte liberaremur, Ebr. II. 14. Atque hoc suum opus, hanc suam gloriam duxit Chri- stus, ut istam Dei voluntatem faceret, Joh. IV. 34. cap. X. 18. Psalm. XL. 8. Idque erat, quod prae- dicabant ἐν πρώτοις imprimis Apostoli, 1. Corinth. XV. 3. de quo etiam omnes Prophetae testati erant, Act. X. 43. quodque annunciari per totum orbem jussit Christus, Luc. XXIV. 26. quod denique ad- versus corruptelas Pseudo-Apostolorum maxime faciebat. Id etiam B. Lutherus in glossa Margin. exposuit rectissime: Wir sollen leuchten und pre- digen, wie man GOttes Gnade erkennen soll, in Christo uns erzeiget. Andere mögen Werck und Gesetz leuchten. Ideo ad verba in persona Jesu Christi addidit: Durch das Erkäntniss Christi, nicht durch das Angesicht Mosis, welches ist Er- känntniss des Gesetzes. Dann durch Christum er- kennen wir GOtt. Joh. VI. 68.

## 4:5
v. 5. For we do not preach ourselves) We do not say that we are the leaders of this business, we do not conduct our own affair.

But Christ Jesus the Lord) We say that He is the Lord, whom we must obey in all things.

And ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake) See how modestly he speaks, who calls himself not only the servant of Jesus, but also of all those who believe in Jesus.

Here again the false Apostles are noted, who preached themselves and their own works; but the Apostle wished to know nothing except Jesus, and Him crucified, 1 Cor. 2:3, the power of God and the wisdom of God, 1 Cor. 1:24. How Paul and his colleagues are servants of Christ and the Church is taught in 1 Cor. 3:23, ch. 4:1, 2 Cor. 5:20. The blessed Balduinus explains it thus: as if he were to say: If we perform our ministry rightly (as I proved a little while ago that I have done), no blame can rest with us if any are not enlightened or converted. For we do not refer men to ourselves, to our works or sufferings, as if in them any can place their trust, nor do we command them to have faith in those things which we propose from human instinct, for if we were to do so, we certainly could not be immune from the destruction of many souls. But we propose Jesus Christ, with all his merit, which tends to no one's destruction, provided he has faith in this doctrine: we propose also that doctrine which we have received from the Lord, etc.

Latin:

v. 5. Οὐ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς κηρύσσομεν) Non dicimus, nos esse hujus negotii principes, non nostram rem agimus.

Ἀλλὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν κύριον) Eum dicimus esse Dominum, cui per omnia parendum sit.

Ἑαυτοὺς δὲ δούλους ὑμῶν διὰ Ἰησοῦν) Vide, quam modeste loquitur, qui se non Jesu tantum servum dicit, sed & omnium eorum, qui in Jesum credunt.

Hic iterum falsi Apostoli notantur, qui seipsos & opera sua praedicabant; at Apostolus nil scire vo- luit, nisi Jesum, eumque crucifixum, 1. Cor. II. 3. Dei virtutem & Dei sapientiam, 1. Cor. I. 24. Quo- modo Christi & Ecclesiae sint servi Paulus cum col- legis, 1. Cor. III. 23. cap. IV. 1. 2. Cor. V. 20. docetur. B. Balduinus ita explicat: quasi dicat: Si nos no- stro ministerio recte fungimur, (sicut me fecisse paulo ante probavi) nulla penes nos culpa esse potest, si qui non illuminantur aut convertun- tur. Non enim homines ad nos remittimus, ad opera aut passiones nostras quasi in iis aliquam collocare possint fiduciam, neque etiam iis, quæ ex hu- mano instinctu proponimus, fidem habere jubemus, quod si faceremus, utique à perditione multarum animarum immunes esse non possemus. Sed proponi- mus Jesum Christum, cum universo suo merito, quod nemini vergit ad exitium, modo huic doctrinæ fidem habeat: proponimus & eam doctrinam, quam à Do- mino accepimus, &c.

## 4:6
v. 6. For God) He acknowledges this very thing, that he is a servant of Christians, to be the greatest benefit of God toward him. He who said light to shine out of darkness) Gen. 1:3. He who said, that is, who commanded; the benefits of creation, both old and new, are often compared to the Hebrew word אמר. See what was said at the beginning of the Gospel of John. From the darkness of the law, the light of the Gospel. Who has shone in our hearts) The little word 'is' is missing, in the Hebrew manner. God is the same one who kindles light in our souls. 'Shone' here is for the Hiphil, as above 'triumph'. Thus 'ha'ir', which is in the Hiphil, is translated 'to shine' in Ps. 119:29. For the illumination of the knowledge) That we might illuminate others with the same knowledge. For he is speaking about the ministers of the Gospel, as was evident above in 1.

The work of conversion is indeed compared here with the work of creation; the illumination of the human heart with the creation of the primordial light, but that is not the case in John 1:1-3, where the discourse is absolutely about the beginning of all things and of the primordial creation; nor is the law compared to darkness and the Gospel to light, or the light of the Gospel [derived] from the darkness of the law; but it is taught that the light of knowledge and faith is excited out of the darkness of ignorance and sin through the word of grace, by the power of Him who in the first creation caused light to shine out of darkness by the word of power, Gen. 1:3. By that 'out of darkness,' however, is denoted not the material from which, but the terminus from which, Eph. 5:8. But here it concerns the Apostles and the illumination of their colleagues, that they themselves were brought to the light of true knowledge to that end, that through them the illumination of true knowledge might reach others. Which 'illumination' some understand concerning the Apostles being illuminated; but it is more correctly explained concerning the Apostles illuminating others, Eph. 3:9, as was done by Ambrose, Primasius, Haymo, and Thomas. Cf. Matt. 5:14. Theophylact connects these with the preceding and illustrates them in his own way: Why, he says, do we not preach anything about ourselves? Because God has shone in our hearts, and just as he had once directed his splendor onto the face of Moses, so he has imparted the same to us in the present. Nor did he say, as he had proclaimed at the beginning of the creation of things, 'let light be made out of darkness,' so now he said, and such a splendor was injected into us: But rather he himself became light for us. Inasmuch as he himself shone upon us in the face of Christ, that is, through Christ. Through whose grace the Father injected his brightness into us, and bestowed also the light of knowledge, not of his own substance, but with the clarity of glory. Nor, however, is it to be concluded from this comparison, by virtue of which the regeneration of a man dead in sin is no less an effect of divine omnipotence than the work of creation, as the Reformed do in the Hapie Conference and Molina in Anatom. chap. 46, that the mode of influence is the same, namely an absolute information of the passive subject, so that a man to be converted cannot resist God intending his conversion, just as Chaos could not resist God intending creation. The power is the same, but the mode of influencing is not. The subject to be converted is called fleshly and dead because of the lack of a positive faculty influencing toward conversion, not because of the impotence of the faculty to resist God intending conversion.

Of the glory of God) He calls that the majesty of God which has been given by God. In the face of Jesus Christ) 'Face' (Hebrew 'panim') signifies to the Hebrews everything that is perceived by the exterior senses, such as the words and deeds of Christ, and that splendor on the mountain, and the resurrection, and what followed it. In this, the Majesty of God appeared without a veil.

or shines forth in Christ, through the Gospel, of which it was spoken before. That splendor on the mountain was temporary, and appeared to a few: Here it concerns the Glory of God in the person of Christ, offering itself to be seen by all and perpetually, which we behold not only in the resurrection and ascension into heaven; but in the incarnation and passion and death: because then appeared the glory of divine mercy and the saving grace of God, Tit. 1:7, 8; 2:14, the glory of divine justice, Jer. 23:6, 1 Cor. 1:29, 2 Cor. 5:21, the glory of divine wisdom, Col. 2:3. Some understand 'in the person of Christ,' 2 Cor. 5:19, such as Pelagius, Primasius, and Sedulius. But the former sense is more convenient. Which the blessed Hunnius also followed: The Apostle calls the glory of God in this place the opulence of divine goodness and mercy, and the mystery of admirable wisdom, which he initiated in the counsel of the salvific reparation of men. He writes that this glory shines in the face of Jesus Christ. Since in Christ this immense mercy of God toward us has been declared, and through Christ that adorable counsel of divine wisdom concerning the repairing of man has been most happily perfected and led into the work itself.

Latin:

v. 6. Ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς) Hoc ipsum, quod servus sit Christia- norum, agnoscit, maximum esse Dei in se beneficium. Ὁ εἰπὼν ἐκ σκότους φῶς λάμψαι) Gen. I. 3. ὁ εἰπὼν, id est, qui jussit, אמר sæpe comparantur beneficia creationis, ve- teris & novæ. Vide, quæ ad initium Evangelii Johannis di- cta. Ex tenebris legis lux Evangelii. Ὃς ἔλαμψεν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν) Deest vocula est, more Hebræo. Deus idem is est, qui lucem accendit in ani- mis nostris. ἔλαμψεν hic est pro Hiphil, ut supra ϑριαμβεύειν. Sic האיר quod est in Hiphil, vertitur φαίνειν Ps. CXIX. 29. Πρὸς φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως) Ut alios eadem cognitione illustraremus. Agit enim de ministris Evangelii, ut patuit supra 1.

Confertur sane hic opus conversionis cum opere creationis; illuminatio cordis humani cum creatione lucis primigeniæ, sed id Joh. I. 1. 2. 3. non sit, ubi de principio rerum omnium, & primævæ creationis absolute sermo est; neque lex tenebris, Evangelium luci comparatur, aut è tenebris legis lucem Evangelii; sed è tenebris ignorantiæ & peccati lucem cognitionis & fidei per verbum gratiæ, ejus virtute excitatam esse docetur, qui in creatione prima verbo potentiæ è tenebris lucem splendescere fecit, Gen. I. 3. Per illud autem è tene- bris non materia ex qua, sed terminus à quo deno- tatur, Eph. V. 8. de Apostolis autem & collegarum illuminatione hic agitur, quod ipsi ea fini ad lucem veræ agnitionis perducti sint, ut per eosdem aliis illuminatio veræ agnitionis obtingeret. Quam Φωτισμὸν alii de Apostolis illuminatis intelligunt; sed rectius de Apostolis alios illuminantibus ex- plicatur, Eph. III. 9. ut ab Ambrosio, Primasio, Hay- mo & Thoma factum. Conf. Matth. V. 14. Con- nectit hæc cum præcedentibus, & illustrat suo mo- do Theophylactus: Cur, inquit, nihil de nobis prædi- camus? Quia Deus illuxit in cordibus nostris, & quemadmodum olim in Mosis faciem suum splendo- rem intenderat, sic nobis eundem in præsentia est impertitus. Neque ut initio creandarum rerum edixerat, lux est è tenebris facta, sic nunc dixit, & splendor est ejusmodi nobis injectus: Sed ipsemet potius in lucem nobis effectus est. Siquidem in Christi facie nobis ipse illuxit, hoc est, per Christum. Cujus per gratiam suum in nobis fulgorem injecit Pater, largitusque est & scientiæ lumen, non suæ substantiæ, sed gloriæ claritate. Nec tamen ex hac comparatione, vi cujus regeneratio hominis in peccato mortui non minus effectus est omnipoten- tiæ divinæ, quam opus creationis, id colligendum cum Reformatis in collatione Hapiensi & Molinao in Anatom. cap. 46. eundem esse influentiæ modum, quod absolutam informationem subjecti passi, ut ho- mo convertendus resistere nequeat Deo conversionem intendenti, quomodo Chaos resistere non potuit Deo creationem intendenti. Potentia eadem est, sed non idem influendi modus. Carneum, & mortuum vocatur subjectum convertendum ob defectum facultatis positivæ influentis in conversionem, non ob impotentiam facultatis resistendi Deo conversio- nem intendenti.

Τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ) Majestatem Dei vocat eam, quæ à Deo data est. Ἐν προσώπῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) πρόσωπον פנים Hebræis id omne significat, quod sensibus exterioribus percipitur, ut Christi dicta & facta, & splendor ille in monte, & resurre- ctio, & quæ eam sunt sequuta. In hoc Dei Majestas sine velo apparuit.

vel Christo effulget, per Evangelium, de qua anteà dictum. Ille in monte splendor temporarius erat, & paucis apparebat: Hic de Gloria Dei in persona Christi omnibus & perpetuo se conspiciendum præbente agitur, quam non in resurrectione solum & ascensione in cœlum conspicamur; sed in incar- natione & passione ac morte: quia tum apparuit gloria divinæ misericordiæ & gratia Dei σωτήριος, Tit. I. 7. 8. II. 14. gloria divinæ justitiæ, Jer. XXIII. 6. 1. Cor. I. 29. 2. Cor. V. 21. gloria divinæ sapientiæ, Col. II. 3. Nonnulli intelligunt in persona Christi, 2. Cor. V. 19. ut Pelagius, Primasius, & Sedulius. Sed sensus prior convenientior est. Quem sequutus etiam B. Hunnius: Gloriam Dei hoc loco nominat Apostolus opulentiam bonitatis & misericordiæ di- vinæ, & admirandæ sapientiæ mysterium, quod in consilio salvificæ reparationis hominum inituit. Hanc gloriam fulgere scribit in facie Jesu Christi. Quandoquidem in Christo hæc immensa misericor- dia Dei erga nos declarata est, & per Christum ado- rabile illud sapientiæ divinæ consilium de reparando homine felicissime perfectum, & in opus ipsum ductum est.

## 4:7
V. 7. But we have this treasure) Thus he calls the knowledge of the Gospel. See Matt. 13:44.

In earthen vessels) In a body subject to many evils just like earthenware, which is easily broken, Jer. 22:28. The Platonists oppose the palpable body of man, which they call an 'organ,' to the most subtle body, which they call the 'vehicle of the soul'.

That the excellence of the power may be of God) Here 'may be' signifies 'may appear.' The adversities which we suffer show that the miracles which we perform we do not perform by our own power. For if that power were in our own dominion, we would lack adversities.

And not from us) See above 3:5. There is a certain divine force in us, not from us. Therefore he acts when he wills.

This treasure does not denote a repository for things to be stored, as in Matt. 2, but the material to be stored. The discourse is not only about a treasure of knowledge, but also of the Evangelical ministry, cf. Eph. 3:8, which was entrusted to them like a treasure with the necessary gifts: they had it in earthen vessels, which are so called both because of their fragility and their worthlessness, for what are men themselves but fragile and worthless vessels with respect to such a great treasure of divine grace? Since it pleased God to accomplish the greatest things not through angels, but through men, who are subject to θνηταῖς δυσχερείαις and injuries and many persecutions, for the illumination, conversion, and salvation of those who were stuck in darkness, the power of Satan, and eternal condemnation. But it is not only the human body that is understood, much less that which Plato invented as distinct from it, which might be the ὄχημα ψυχῆς: But the whole person: because the primary recipient of this treasure is not the body, but the soul: And man is like an earthen vessel, who is like clay in the hand of the potter, Is. 45:8, Jer. 18:6, Rom. 9:20. Blessed Balduinus says: The teachers of the Gospel are earthen vessels, not only because of the fragility of their bodies, but also because of the corruption of their whole nature, on account of which man is subject to many infirmities. Therefore, just as an earthen vessel is easily broken, and yet the lamp enclosed within it retains its splendor: So the teachers of the Church easily suffer infirmities, while the doctrine, of which they are divinely appointed heralds, remains unimpaired. Now the objection here is: Since he had said that the ministry of the Gospel was of far more eminent glory than the Mosaic, and the Apostles were very contemptible, subject to many pressures: that it pleased God in this way not only to accomplish such great things through fragile and mortal men, which is common to all men; but through abject and despised ones, so that, namely, these things might be attributed not to men, but to the power of God. Compare 1 Cor. 1:26, 27, 28, ch. 2:4, 5. So that it may be evident (these are the words of Theophylact) that the magnitude of the apparent power by no means proceeds from us, but from God, so that we do not—lest we ourselves think we can accomplish anything by ourselves that is worthy of praise—ascribe to God; and let us repeat that whatever is done well and laudably is His gift. Furthermore, in this place he refutes the false Apostles, Hunnius says: Just as, he says, no one despises the treasure itself because of the fragility of the vessel by which it is offered, but everyone considers the treasure to be valued for its own excellence, so he shows that the Gospel also ought not to be despised, since it is in itself the most excellent treasure under the sun, even though God takes care to offer it to the human race through weak instruments. For the reason is clear to God, by which He was led to will that His Gospel be preached not through the Princes and Monarchs of this world, but through men who are vile and abject before the world: namely, so that the eminence of the power may be of God, and not from men. For if the doctrine of the Gospel were spread through human power, the power and might of God would not stand out and appear in the same way; rather, that work would be indicated as being accomplished by human strength. But now, while the doctrine of the Gospel is propagated against every assault of human power and wisdom through Apostles who are commendable by no authority that could please the world, and who are equipped with no weapons, but only by the foolish preaching of the cross, from this it is most clearly seen that this is not the work of men, but of God alone.

Latin:

V. 7. ἔχομεν δὲ τὸν θησαυρὸν τῦτον) Sic vocat cognitio- nem Evangelii. Vide Matth. XIII. 44.

Ἐν ὀστρακίνοις σκένεσιν) In corpore multis malis obnoxio sicut fictile, quod facile frangitur, Jer. XXII. 28. Platonici corpus hominis palpabile, quod vocant ὄργανον, oppo- nunt τῷ λεπτοτάτῳ σώματι, quod vocant ὄχημα ψυχῆς.

Ἵνα ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τῦ Θεῦ) Hic ᾖ significat, appareat. Adversa quæ patimur ostendunt illa, quæ faci- mus mira non nostra virtute nos facere. Nam si ea virtus in nostro esset dominio, careremus adversis.

Καὶ μὴ ἐξ ἡμῶν) Vide supra III. 5. Est vis quædam di- vina in nobis, non ex nobis. Ideò agit cum vult.

Thesaurus hic non notat thecam rerum repo- nendarum, ut Matth. II. sed materiam reponen- dam. De thesauro non tantum cognitionis, sed etiam ministerii Evangelici sermo est, conf. Eph. III. 8. quod ipsis thesauri instar cum donis neces- sariis concreditum: habebant in vasibus testaceis, quæ tum ob fragilitatem, tum ob vilitatem ita vo- cantur, quia homines ipsi quid nisi fragilia & vilia vasa sunt respectu tanti thesauri gratiæ divinæ? quum placuerit Deo non per Angelos, sed homi- nes & θνηταῖς δυσχερείαις & injuriis, ac persequutio- nibus plurimis obnoxios res maximas efficere ad illuminationem, conversionem & salutem eorum, qui in tenebris, potestate Satanæ, & æterna con- demnatione hærebant. Non verò tantum corpus humanum intelligitur, nedum illud, quod Plato commentus est diversum ab eo, quod ὄχημα ψυ- χῆς sit: Sed suppositum totum: quia πρῶτον δεκτι- κὸν hujus thesauri non est corpus, sed anima: Et vasi testaceo similis homo est, qui instar luti est in manu figuli, Es. XLV. 8. Jer. XIIX. 6. Rom. IX. 20. B. Balduinus: Vasa fictilia, inquit, sunt Evangelii Doctores, non tantum propter corporum fragilita- tem, sed & propter totius naturæ corruptionem, pro- pter quam homo multis obnoxius est infirmitatibus. Quemadmodum ergo vas fictile facile frangitur, & lampas in eo inclusa suum tamen retinet splendorem: Sic Ecclesiæ Doctores facile infirmitates patiuntur, illibata tamen manente ea doctrina, cujus præcones divinitus sunt constituti. Occupatio autem hic est: Siquidem dixerat ministerium Evangelii lon- gè eminentioris esse gloriæ, quam Mosaicum, & Apostoli valde contemptibiles erant, multis ob- noxii pressuris: quod ita Deo placuerit non modo per fragiles & mortales, quod hominibus omni- bus commune est; sed per abjectos & contemptos tanta exequi, ut scilicet non hominibus, sed vir- tuti Dei ea tribuerentur. Confer 1. Cor. I. 26. 27. 28. cap. II. 4. 5. Ut constet (verba sunt Theophylacti) apparentis virtutis magnitudinem nequaquam à nobis, sed à Deo proficisci, ne ut ipsi existimemus ali- quid posse, quod laude dignum sit per nosmetipsos effi- cere, Deo adscribamus: Et illius esse donum, quod- cunque bene & laudabiliter geritur, dictitemus. Falsos præterea hoc loco arguit Apostolos, qui gra- tiam Dei sibi ipsis accensent. Hæc ille B. Hunnius: Sicut, inquit, thesawrum ipsum nemo contemnit ob vasculi tenuitatem, quo mediante offertur: Sed quisque thesaurum ex propria sua præstantia æsti- mandum ducit: Sic ostendit, Evangelium quo- que non debere contemni, cum per se sit thesaurus omnium sub sole præstantissimus: Quamvis per in- firma organa Deus illum generi humano offeren- dum curet. Constare namque Deo rationem, qua ductus non per Principes hujus mundi, & Monar- chas; sed per homines coram mundo viles & abjectos Evangelium suum prædicari velit: Nimirum ut virtutis eminentia sit Dei, & non ex hominibus. Si enim per humanam potentiam spargeretur Evan- gelii doctrina, baud perinde emineret & appareret Dei virtus & potentia; sed indicaretur opus illud perfici humanis viribus. Jam vero dum per Apo- stolos nulla autoritate, quæ mundo placere queat, commendabiles, nullis armis instructos, sola stulta prædicatione crucis, doctrina Evangelii contra omnem impetum humanæ potentiæ & sapientiæ pro- pagatur: exinde liquidissime cernitur, non hominum hoc esse opus, sed solius Dei.

## 4:8
v. 8. In all things pressed, but not crushed) Here to be crushed (στενοχωρεῖν) is something more than affliction (θλίψις). We are pressed, not oppressed. These words are accustomed to be used interchangeably elsewhere, as we said at Rom. II. 9. The Hebrews would say: נלחצים ולא נחלשים.

So much, he says, with Theophylact as interpreter, are all things to be attributed to divine power, that even if we ourselves are earthen vessels, and are urged on all sides by such great straits, we are nevertheless neither broken, nor is the treasure which is hidden within us destroyed. But in all things we are in straits, that is, in any place and in any matters, we suffer pressures both among friends and among enemies, yet we are neither anxious nor confined, since Christ dilates our hearts. Therefore he took it as being about the anguish of the mind: Which is also to be observed in the version of Erasmus: While in all things we are pressed, but are not rendered anxious. But as Estius rightly notes: "Paul's purpose in this place is not to declare the power of God in the fact that the Apostles did not fail in spirit in the midst of the evils which they suffered for the sake of the Gospel, which was a matter of fortitude and constancy: But that they were preserved in life among so many dangers of dying; just as if earthen and fragile vessels, when vehemently shaken, are not broken." That this is what Paul means will be more fully evident from verses 10 and 11.

Perplexed, but not utterly perplexed) To be perplexed (ἀπορεῖσθαι) here is to be at a loss, just as this word is taken in Gal. IV. 20, and the noun perplexity (ἀπορία) in Eph. VIII. 22, Luke XXI. 25. To be utterly perplexed (ἐξαπορεῖσθαι) is to be so perplexed that you despair, as above in I. 8.

And yet the Apostle would be contradicting himself if he were to imply there that he had despaired of life. For here, according to that interpretation, he denies that he despaired in dangers: That word therefore, perplexed (ἀπορούμενοι), which the Latin barbarously rendered: 'We are in perplexity' (Aporiamur), signifies that in a difficult matter they were destitute of counsel, as Theodoret and Oecumenius explained, and Grotius himself does not deny; but by being utterly perplexed (ἐξαπορεῖσθαι) in 2. Cor. I. 8, it is noted that he was not only destitute of counsel, but thought entirely that he would not escape, as if having the sentence of death in himself. But here, 'not utterly perplexed' (ἐκ ἐξαπορούμενοι), says the Apostle, because in such great desperation of life, when they were sometimes placed, they were nevertheless not destitute of divine help, see Acts V, XII, XIV, XVI, XIX, XXVII, 2. Cor. XI. For that word signifies one who, destitute of counsel and hope of escaping, is overwhelmed by danger and does not escape, which the Apostle denies of himself. So also the blessed Hunnius: We are sometimes tossed by events in such a way that, if we wish to follow the judgment of reason, it seems that it is all over for us, because humanly speaking no hope of escaping shines anywhere. Meanwhile, however, we are not destitute, since, when human help fails, the help of God shows itself as if from a machine (ὡς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς), which settles those doubtful and uncertain events with a certain liberation, and leads us, tossed by the waves of adversities, to the harbor of certainty. Less suitable is the interpretation of Ambrosiaster: 'Having suffered want, but not destitute': And that of Tertullian in Scorpiaco chapter 13: 'We are in need, but not in total need.' To which, however, Faber and Erasmus have acceded.

Latin:

v. 8. Ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι ἀλλ' ὀ στενοχωρούμενοι) Hic στενο- χωρεῖν plus aliquid est, quam θλίψις. Premimur, non oppri- mimur. Solent alibi istæ voces promiscue usurpari, ut di- ximus ad Rom. II. 9. Hebræi dicerent: נלחצים ולא נחלשים.

Adeo inquit, Theophylacto interprete, omnia sunt divina potentiæ tribuenda, ut etsi fictilia vasa ipsi præferimus, tantisque undiq; urgemur angustiis; non tamen vel frangimur, vel qui in nobis reconditus est thesaurus, aboletur. In omnibus autem angu- stiamur, hoc est, quovis loco, & quibusvis in rebus, tam apud amicos, quam apud infensos pressuras nos patimur, non tamen vel angimur, vel coarctamur, quandoquidem corda nostra Christus dilatet. De angustia ergo animi accepit: Quod etiam obser- vare est in versione Erasmi: Dum in omnibus pre- mimur, sed non anxii reddimur. Sed quod recte notat Estius: „ Pauli institutum hoc loco non est declarare virtutem Dei in eo, quod Apostoli in me- diis malis, quæ propter Evangelium patiebantur, animo non deficerent, quod erat fortitudinis, & con- stantiæ: Sed quod inter tot moriendi pericula ser- parentur in vita; velut si vasa fictilia atque fragilia vehementer agitata non frangantur. Id Paulum vel- le, patebit amplius ex vers. 10. & 11.

᾿Απορούμενοι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἐξαπορούμενοι) Ἀπορεῖσθαι hic est per- plexum esse, quomodo hoc verbum sumitur Gal. IV. 20. & nomen ἀπορία Ef. VIII. 22. Luc. XXI. 25. ἐξαπορεῖσθαι ita perplexum esse, ut desperes, ut supra I. 8.

Atqui ita secum pugnaret Apostolus, si illic sese de vita desperasse innueret. Hic enim in pe- riculis se desperare juxta istam interpretationem negat: Illud ergo ἀπορούμενοι, quod barbare Lati- nus reddidit: Aporiamur, significat in re difficili inopes consilii fuisse, ut Theodoretius & Oecumenius exposuere, & Grotius ipse non abnuit, per ἐξα- πορεῖσθαι vero 2. Cor. I. 8. notatur, quod non modò consilii inops fuerit; sed omninò putarit, se non esse evasurum, veluti mortis responsum in se habens. Hic autem ἐκ ἐξαπορούμενοι inquit Apo- stolus, quod in tanta desperatione vitæ quando- que positi divina tamen ope non destituti fuerint, vid. Act. V, XII, XIV, XVI, XIX, XXVII. 2. Cor. XI. Verbum enim illud significat eum, qui evadendi consilio ac spe destitutus obruitur periculo nec eva- dit, quod de se negat Apostolus. Ita & B. Hun- nius: Nos interdum ita jactamur casibus, ut si ra- tionis velimus sequi judicium, actum de nobis esse videatur, eo quod humanitus nulla uspiam spes eva- dendi affulgeat. Interim tamen non destituimur, siquidem deficiente auxilio humano, Dei se auxi- lium ὡς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς ostendit, quod casus illos du- bios & ancipites certa liberatione definit, nosque fluctibus adversitatum agitatos ad portum certitu- dinis deducit. Minus conveniens est Ambrosia- stri interpretatio: Inopiam passi, sed non destituti: Et Tertulliani in Scorpiaco cap. 13. Indigemus, sed non perindigemus. Quibus tamen accessere Faber, & Erasmus.

## 4:9
v. 9. Persecuted, but not forsaken) נרדפים ולא נעזבים. We are indeed treated badly by men, but God does not desert us. He comforts us with His Spirit. It is not only about comfort, but about preservation in dangers, as is clear from the whole context. In persecutions, he says, which we suffer for the sake of our ministry, and by which we are agitated, we are not deserted by God; God does not permit us to be killed by persecutors, although He permits us to be seized and treated badly: For He wishes to preserve us for the greater fruitfulness of the Gospel, as Estius rightly says here. Nor does our blessed Hunnius say otherwise: Wherever we finally come to preach the Gospel, some enemies of this doctrine are always found, who on account of it persecute us in a hostile manner, and wish us to be exterminated from human affairs. But the Lord is immediately at hand for us with His help, so that it sufficiently appears that we are deserted by men, but never deserted by God.

Cast down, but not destroyed) נרוחים ולא נבלעים. A simile taken from soldiers, who, having been cast down, rise again. Thus here the Israelites. Jer. XXXIV. הסמני נבוכרונצר Nebuchadnezzar cast me down. All these things were prefigured in the burning bush, and through the journey in the desert, and through the times of Antiochus.

Theophylact refers this to constancy of mind. But here it is not taught how the Apostles were affected in afflictions, but that they were divinely preserved in dangers. Dejection therefore denotes the magnitude of the danger, as when someone in a fight is thrown to the ground by an adversary, about to be killed unless someone brings help. Cf. Ps. 119:3. The world does this (as B. Hunnio interprets), that it may cast us down together with the Gospel, depress us, and finally overwhelm us entirely. But it is well: it is God who in turn raises us up, and establishes His Gospel (though Satan and the world may rage) as if in a high place. Cf. with this whole passage the similar 1 Cor. 4:9 seqq.

Latin:

v. 9. Διωκόμενοι ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἐγκαταλειπόμενοι) נרדפים ולא נעזבים Ab hominibus quidem male tractamur, sed Deus nos non deserit. Solatur nos Spiritu suo. Non de solatio tantum, sed de conservatione in periculis agitur, ut e toto contextu liquet. In persecutionibus, inquit, quas causa ministerii nostri patimur, & quibus agitamur, non deserimur à Deo, non permittit nos Deus à persecutoribus occi- di, quamvis permittat comprehendi & male mul- ctari: Vult enim nos servare ad Evangelii majorem fructificationem, ut recte hic Estius. Nec aliter B. Hunnius noster: Quocunque tandem veniamus prædicaturi Evangelium, semper aliqui reperiun- tur hujus doctrinæ hostes, qui propter illam hostiliter nos persequuntur, & è rebus humanis exterminatos cupiunt. Verum subinde nobis Dominus sua ope præsto est, ut satis appareat, nos ab hominibus deser- tos, à Deo tamen nunquam deseri.

Καταβαλλόμενοι ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἀπολλύμενοι) נרוחים ולא נבלעים similitudo sumpta à militibus, qui dejecti resur- gunt. Sic hic Israelitæ. Jer. XXXIV. הסמני נבוכרונצר Dejecit me Nabachodonosor. Omnia hæc præsignificata in rubo ardenti, & per iter in deserto, & per tempora Antiochi.

Ad constantiam animi hoc refert Theophylactus. At hic non docetur, quomodo fuerint affecti in afflictionibus Apostoli, sed quod divinitus in pe- riculis conservati. Dejectio ergò periculi magni- tudinem denotat, ut cum quis in pugna ab adversa- rio in terram prosternitur, jamjam nisi quis opem ferat, occidendus. Conf. Ps. CXIIX. 3. Mundus hoc agit (B. Hunnio interprete,) ut nos una cum Evangelio dejiciat, deprimat, & omnino tandem opprimat. Sed bene habet: Deus est, qui nos vicis- sim erigit, & Evangelium suum, (fremente licet Satana & mundo) velut in excelso loco constituit. Conf. cum toto hoc loco similis 1. Cor. IV. 9. seqq.

## 4:10
v. 10. Always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord) Νέκρωσις תמותה are miseries and dangers of death, Ps. 79:11. So also with the Rabbis ממית עצם; νέκρωσις of strength, just as νέκρωσις of the womb, Rom. 4:19. Of the Lord, that is, after the example of the Lord. For similar things are accustomed to be called by the names of similar things, as also in the following opposites.

That the life of Jesus might be manifested in our body) that is, a life such as Christ's is, immortal, blessed, heavenly.

Latin:

v. 10. Πάντοτε τὴν νέκρωσιν τῦ κυρίε ἐν τῷ σώματι περι- φέροντες) Νέκρωσις תמותה sunt miseriæ, & mortis peri- cula, Pf. LXXIX: 11. Sic & Rabbinis ממית עצם· νέκρω- σις τῆς ἰσχύος, quomodo νέκρωσις τῆς μήτρας, Rom. IV. 19. Domini, id est, ad exemplum Domini. Solent enim similia similium nominibus nuncupari, ut & in sequenti opposita.

Ἵνα δὲ ἡ ζωὴ τῦ Ἰησῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι ἡμῶν φανερωθῇ) id est, vita talis, qualis est Christi, immortalis, beata, cœlestis.

## 4:11
v. 11. For always) daily, that is, very often.

We who live) We, who still live, who have not yet departed from this life, as many Christians have already.

We are delivered unto death) Here again he calls the dangers of death 'death' metonymically.

For Jesus' sake) for the sake of the Gospel, which has been entrusted to us by Christ.

That the life of Jesus might also be manifested in our mortal flesh) Here ζωὴ signifies the power and efficacy of Christ. For life consists in action. Christ, though immortal, still acts and speaks through mortal Apostles.

Why should the word ζωῆς be taken here in a new sense, different from that which occurs in v. 10? The subject matter is certainly the same, the opposition is the same, the predicates are the same or synonymous. For the Apostle is accustomed, as Theophylact observes here, to explain things that were less clear. Others explain the life of Christ being manifested as the manifestation of the risen Christ through the Apostles and other ministers, which takes place in the ministry of them through power and works, testifying to his glorious life; others [refer it] to the life of Christ in the manifestation of the ministers to be in the other age. But that explanation is to be preferred. For it treats of that which was proper to the Apostles, who were suffering persecution for the sake of the Gospel, and were carrying about the mortification of Jesus in their body, since the Apostle is executing what he had said, that they had the treasure in earthen vessels. But the manifestation of life in the other life will be common to all the faithful. And therefore the blessed Hunnius rightly explained this passage thus: The life of the Lord Jesus, by which He entered through death, is manifested in us, while the world is compelled to feel, whether it will or no, that Christ did not remain in death, but lives in us, and is effective by words and deeds for the propagation of His name through us. Moreover, he calls mortification, on the authority of Flacius, the cross, because the cross contributes to the mortification of the old Adam, or because in it we seem to perish and die: and [he calls it] of Christ, because we sustain it for Christ's sake, through it we serve Christ and are confirmed, and because Christ suffers in His members, and is glorified also. He says that he carries it about everywhere in his body, because it was ready for him everywhere, so that it did not seem to have arisen there, but rather to have been brought in with him. Moreover, he says the life of Jesus is made manifest in his body, because, as the same [author] warns, it can be understood then passively, concerning the life itself by which Jesus lives, and by which it is openly recognized from this, that He always rules, vivifies, and delivers His own from the greatest difficulties: then also actively, those perpetual deliverances or preservations of Paul can be called the life of JESUS or a certain efficacy of His, because He Himself effected them, and finally He Himself lives and flourishes in them. Which latter explanation agrees more with the preceding [remarks] concerning the power of GOD, verse 7. For just as he declared at length the fragility and vileness of the vessels in which the most precious treasure is carried about, which he has now comprehended in the one word of the mortification of JESUS: so he has now embraced the power, or ὑπερβολὴν τῆς δυνάμεως, and the help and assistance of the Lord, which is afforded to the Apostles, in that νεκρώσει through the ζωὴν or life of Jesus, which he further teaches to redound to the faithful themselves, even if they themselves are not equally exposed to dangers, as the Apostles are.

Latin:

v. 11. Ἀεὶ γὰρ) quotidie, id est, sæpissime.

Ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες) Nos, qui adhuc vivimus, qui nondum ex vita hac excessimus, ut multi jam Christianorum.

Εἰς θάνατον παραδιδόμεθα) Iterum hic mortem vocat mortis pericula μετωνυμικῶς.

Διὰ Ἰησῦν) Evangelii causa, quod à Christo nobis com- mendatum est.

Ἵνα καὶ ἡ ζωὴ τῦ Ἰησῦ φανερωθῇ ἐν τῇ θνητῇ σαρκὶ ἡμῶν) Hic ζωὴsignificat vim & efficaciam Christi. Vita enim in actione consistit. Christus immortalis per Apostolos mor- tales adhuc agit & loquitur.

Cur hic novâ, & ab ea, quæ v. 10. occurrit, di- versa significatione vox ζωῆς accipiatur? Eadem certè est materia, eadem oppositio, eadem, vel synonyma prædicata. Consuevit enim Apostolus, quod Theophylactus hic observat, enodare, quæ mi- nus paterent. Vitam autem Christi manifestari ex- plicant alii de Christi redivivi manifestatione per Apostolos aliosque ministros, quæ fit in ministerio eorum per virtutem & opera, de vita ejus glorio- sa testantia; Alii de vita Christi in ministris ma- nifestatione futurâ in altero seculo. Sed illa expli- catio præferenda. Nam de eo, quod proprium erat Apostolis, agitur, qui persequutionem patie- bantur propter Evangelium, & mortificationem Jesu circumferebant in corpore suo, cum exequatur Apostolus, quod dixerat, ipsos the- saurum in vasibus fictilibus habere. Vitæ vero manifestatio in altera vita communis erit omni- bus fidelibus. Ideoque recte B. Hunnius expo- suit hunc locum ita: Vita Domini Jesu, qua per mortem ingressus est, manifestatur in nobis, dum nolit velit sentire cogitur mundus, Christum non mansisse in morte, sed vivere in nobis, & ad nominis sui gloriam per nos propagandam esse dictis factis- que efficacem. Mortificationem autem vocat, au- tore Flacio, crucem, quia crux facit ad mortifi- cationem veteris Adami, vel quia in ea interire morique videmur: & Christi, quia eam ob Chri- stum sustinemus, per eam Christo servimus & confirmamur, & quia Christus in suis membris patitur, & glorificatur etiam. Dicit se eam ubi- que circumferre in corpore, quia illi aedè ubi- que erat parata, ut non ibi ea exorta esse, sed potius cum illo ea illata videretur: Vitam autem Jesu dicit in corpore suo manifestam fieri, quod, eodem monente, tum passive intelligi potest, de ipsâ vitâ, quâ Jesus vivit, quaque propalam ex eo agnoscitur, quod suos semper regit, vivificat, & ex summis difficultatibus liberat: tum etiam activè, illæ perpetuæ liberationes Pauli, aut con- servationes possunt dici vita JESU seu quædam ejus efficacia, quia ipse eas effecit, & denique ipse in eis vivit ac viget. Quæ posterior expli- catio magis convenit superioribus de virtute DEI, vers. 7. Nam uti fragilitatem & vilitatem vasorum, in quibus thesaurus pretiosissimus cir- cumfertur, prolixè declaravit, quam uno verbo mortificationis JESU jam comprehendit: Sic virtutem, vel ὑπερβολὴν τῆς δυνάμεως & auxi- lium atque assistentiam Domini, quæ Apostolis præstetur, in illa νεκρώσει per ζωὴν seu vitam Je- su nunc complexus est, quam porrò docet ad ipsos fideles redundare, etsi ipsi non pariter periculis obnoxii sint, uti Apostoli.

## 4:12
v. 12. ὥστε ὁ μὲν θάνατος ἐν ἡμῖν ἐνεργεῖται, ἡ δὲ ζωὴ ἐν ὑμῖν) It is taken here that ἐνεργεῖται is passive, so that the sense may be: The preaching of the Gospel effects death in us, that is, the dangers of death, but the same preaching of the Gospel will effect eternal life in you, who feel no inconveniences on that account. But lest the Apostles themselves should be held of less account for that reason, because they were subject to so many inconveniences, he prudently adds.

The preaching of the Gospel effects life not only in the other age, or the kingdom of glory, but [also] that which is here of the faithful in the kingdom of grace, not only heavenly, but also spiritual, concerning which [see] Gal. II. verse 20. And thus the life of Jesus Christ exerted itself through the Apostles and their ministry in their mortal flesh, so that the Corinthians felt the efficacy of the same for spiritual life, and will feel it also for that heavenly and eternal one. Blessed Hunnius: While we Apostles profess the doctrine of the Gospel through a thousand dangers of death, there emerges from it and reaches you this salutary fruit, that, through the mediation of our ministry, so laborious and exposed to so many deaths as it were, Christ may be effective in you, and may live and act and reign in you through power. He concludes, says Flacius, from the preceding, that he and other ministers are exposed to a perpetual death as it were: but that it yields to the good of the hearers, while they, taught and confirmed by him, obtain righteousness and life, and become constantly more steadfast in true piety, and are more and more strengthened; to which also pertains that manifestation of the life of Christ, of which he had just spoken. The interpretation of Chrysostom is foreign, as if this were an ironical reproach: Meanwhile, while we are exposed to daily dangers, you live securely and relax your minds, free from dangers. Whom the epitomizer of the same, Theophylact himself, has here deserted.

PARS POSTERIOR. Concerning the constancy of the profession of the Apostle and his associates.

Latin:

v. 12. ὥστε ὁ μὲν θάνατος ἐν ἡμῖν ἐνεργεῖται, ἡ δὲ ζωὴ ἐν ὑμῖν) Sumitur hîc ἐνεργεῖται Passive, ut sensus sit: Evan- gelii prædicatio in nobis efficit mortem, id est, mortis pe- ricula, eadem autem Evangelii prædicatio vobis, qui nulla ob id incommoda sentitis, vitam efficiet æternam. Sed ne ipsi Apostoli ideò minoris haberentur, quod tot subjace- rent incommodis, prudenter subjicit.

Vitam non modo in altero seculo, seu regno gloriæ, sed, quæ hic etiam fidelium est in regno gratiæ, non tantum cælestem, sed etiam spiritua- lem efficit Evangelii prædicatio, de qua Gal. II. vers. 20. Atque ita sese exeruit vita Jesu Christi per Apostolos, eorumque ministerium in mor- tali ipsorum carne, ut efficaciam ejusdem ad vi- tam spiritualem senserint Corinthii, sensuri etiam ad illam cælestem & æternam. B. Hunnius: Dum nos Apostoli doctrinam Evangelii per mille pericu- la mortis profitemur, emergit inde ac pervenit ad vos salutaris hic fructus, ut, mediante nostro mini- sterio, tàm laborioso, totque velut mortibus exposi- to, Christus in vobis sit efficax, & in vobis vivat, & agat & regnet per virtutem. Concludit, inquit Flacius, ex superioribus, se aliosque ministros per- petuæ quasi morti expositos: sed illam cedere in bo- num auditoribus, dum illi à se edocti & confirmati justitiam ac vitam consequuntur, & in vera pietate constantiores subinde fiunt, ac magis magisque cor- roborantur; quo etiam pertinet illa manifestatio vitæ Christi, de qua modo dixerat. Aliena est Chrysostomi interpretatio, quasi hic sit ironica ex- probratio: Interim dum nos quotidianis objicimur periculis, vos securi vitam agitis, & animos relaxa- tis periculorum expertes. Quem hic epitomator ejusdem Theophylactus ipse deseruit.

PARS POSTERIOR. De constantia professionis Apostoli, & sociorum.

## 4:13
v. 13. Ἔχοντες δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως) Having in common with us the Spirit of GOD, which is not given except to those who believe. Here again the Genitive signifies the cause, that is, the required condition. Κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, ἐπίστευσα καὶ ἐλάλησα, καὶ ἡμεῖς πιστεύομεν, διὸ καὶ λαλοῦμεν) These cohere with one another, and he said, ἡμεῖς πιστεύομεν διὸ καὶ λαλοῦμεν, for ἡμεῖς πιστεύσαντες διὰ τοῦτο καὶ λαλοῦμεν. In the Psalm, from which this is taken, (the passage is in the Hebrew codex CXVI. 10.) the Greek [words] have it thus: Ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα, because I believed, therefore I speak.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἔχοντες δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως) Haben- tes communem nobiscum DEI Spiritum, qui non datur nisi credentibus. Iterum hic Genitivus causam significat, id est, conditionem requisitam. Κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, ἐπίστευσα καὶ ἐλάλησα, καὶ ἡμεῖς πι- στεύομεν, διὸ καὶ λαλοῦμεν) Hæc inter se cohærent, & dixit, ἡμεῖς πιστεύομεν διὸ καὶ λαλοῦμεν, pro ἡμεῖς πιστεύσαντες διὰ τοῦτο καὶ λαλοῦμεν. In Psalmo, unde hoc desumptum est, (est autem locus in Hebræo codice CXVI. 10.) Græca sic habent: Ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα, quia credidi, ideò loquor.

## 4:14
v. 14. Εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ ἐγείρας τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ ἡμᾶς διὰ Ἰησοῦ ἐξεγερεῖ, καὶ παραστήσει σὺν ὑμῖν) Of that good, which we acquire for you through so many evils, we shall not be deprived. The raising of Christ from the dead is attributed to GOD the Father, Acts III. v. 15. XIII. v. 30. Rom. IV. 24. X. 9. 1 Cor. VI. 14. but our [raising] is attributed to both GOD and Christ, Rom. VIII. 11. John V. 21. Παραστήσει will present, will set before the tribunal of Christ. Thus below XI. v. 2. Eph. V. 27. Thus he is said to stand, who makes himself available to his Judge. Acts XXVII. 24.

Faith is not the cause of the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit is the cause of faith: who both works faith in us through the word, and for that reason is conferred upon those who believe further, so that they may be confirmed in faith, and the heavenly inheritance may be sealed in them. This Spirit of faith, as in Zech. XII. v. 10. is called the Spirit of supplications, as the cause of faith and prayers. Some understand the Spirit of faith metonymically, that is, faith given by the Spirit: And the same Spirit of faith concerning the same things to be believed as those which David, or the holy Fathers and Prophets of the Old Testament believed, or which the Corinthians believe. But more rightly the same Spirit is understood, which David had, from whom he testifies that he has in common both faith and the profession of faith, and tribulation; for this is added in the cited Psalm: I believed, therefore I have spoken, but I was greatly humbled: and we believe, therefore we also speak. He had already spoken before of the affliction connected with the profession of faith: Therefore, having spurned it, he teaches that he constantly professes the faith, and that by the confidence of a future glorious resurrection, in which he will be set together with them before the Lord; the word παραστήσει does not look to the judgment, but to that presentation which will be obtained by the elect after the final judgment, of which he had treated in 1 Cor. XV. 24, and which he expressed in Eph. V. 27 with the same word παραστήσει. Therefore, he attributes it solely to the Holy Spirit, that He works that faith which, having despised whatever dangers, fears nothing, to openly profess with the mouth that which is believed with a faithful heart, even if the world threatens death, and this life must be left behind on account of the profession of faith. Since indeed the Holy Spirit raises up believers with the confidence of a blessed resurrection, and of a glorious presentation before GOD for the enjoyment of eternal blessedness. He adds, however, 'he will set with you,' lest the Apostles seem to claim this excellent hope for themselves alone, and so that the Corinthians, relying on the same confidence, and other believers, may not hesitate to confess the name of Christ, even if they are compelled to undergo death, Acts XII. 11.

Latin:

v. 14. Εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ ἐγείρας τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ ἡμᾶς διὰ Ἰησοῦ ἐξεγερεῖ, καὶ παραστήσει σὺν ὑμῖν) Ejus boni, quod vo- bis per tot mala acquirimus, nos non erimus expertes. DEO Patri tribuitur excitatio Christi è mortuis, Act. III. v. 15. XIII. v. 30. Rom. IV. 24. X. 9. 1. Cor. VI. 14. nostra autem & DEO & Christo, Rom. VIII. 11. Joh. V. 21. Πα- ραστήσει exhibebit, sistet ante tribunal Christi. Sic infra XI. v. 2. Eph. V. 27. Sic stare dicitur, qui Judici suo co- piam facit. Act. XXVII. 24.

Fides non est causa Spiritus Sancti, sed Spiri- tus Sanctus causa est fidei: qui & fidem operatur in nobis per verbum, & ob eam credentibus por- rò, ut confirmentur in fide, atque obsignetur in ipsis hæreditas cœlestis, confertur. Hic Spiritus fidei, uti Zach. XII. v. 10. Spiritus precum dicitur, ceu causa fidei & precum. Nonnulli metonymi- cè intelligunt Spiritum fidei, id est, fidem à Spiritu donatam: Et eundem Spiritum fidei de iisdem cre- dendis cum iis, quæ David, vel sancti Patres & Pro- phetæ Veteris Testamenti credidere, vel quæ cre- dunt Corinthii. Sed rectius idem Spiritus intel- ligitur, quem David habuit, à quo pariter & fidem & professionem fidei, & tribulationem; hæc enim additur in Psalmo adducto: Credidi, propter quod loquutus sum, ego autem humiliatus sum nimis, se communem habere testatur: & nos credimus, propter quod & loquimur. De afflictione cum professione fidei connexa jam ante dixerat: Ideo, eâ spretâ, sese constanter fidem profiteri docet, idque fiducia futuræ gloriosæ resurrectionis, in qua una cum ipsis sistetur Domino; verbum παρα- στήσει non judicium respicit, sed eam, quæ post judicium novissimum obtinget electis, præsenta- tionem, de qua 1. Cor. XV. 24. egerat, quamque Ephes. V. 27. eadem voce παραστήσει expressit. Spiritui Sancto ergò unice tribuit, quod eam ope- retur fidem, quæ contemtis periculis quibuscun- que nihil extimescat, palam profiteri id ore, quod corde fideli creditur, etiamsi mortem minetur mundus, & vita hæc relinquenda sit propter fi- dei professionem. Siquidem Spiritus Sanctus credentes erigat fiducia beatæ resurrectionis, & præsentationis gloriosæ coram DEO ad fruitionem æternæ beatitudinis. Addit autem, constituet vo- biscum, ne hanc præclaram spem sibi solis vendi- care videantur Apostoli, & ut eadem fiducia freti Corinthii, aliique fideles non dubitent confiteri nomen Christi, etiamsi mortem subire cogantur, Act. XII. 11.

## 4:15
v. 15. Τὰ γὰρ πάντα δι' ὑμᾶς) This whole thing, that Christ died, that He was resurrected, happened not more for my sake than for yours. Ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσασα διὰ τῶν πλειόνων τὴν εὐχαριστίαν περισσεύσῃ εἰς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ) a comma must be placed after πλεονάσασα. For the sense is, that the greater the benefit is, the more abundant the glory of GOD it may elicit, as very many give thanks to Him.

Διὸ ὐκ ἐκκακῦμεν) He repeats that which he had said above in I.

These things pertain rather to the parts of the Apostolic office undertaken for the sake of the salvation of the Corinthians, not without various afflictions. All those things are both performed and endured by us for your sake and for the sake of your salvation. And rightly B. Hunnius: To the Corinthians, he says, also pertains the communion of future blessedness, he proves this from the fact that they are the ones for whom the Apostles willingly expose themselves to so many evils and adversities, so that, indeed, the benefit which overflows through the preaching of the Gospel to others also, may at the same time abound to the glory of God, when, namely, through many converted and brought to the communion of the saving knowledge of GOD, thanks are solemnly given to God as if with one mouth, and His name is glorified thereby. Therefore he testifies that he is not wearied, whether by the gravity of his labors or by the magnitude of his miseries and tribulations.

Latin:

v. 15. Τὰ γὰρ πάντα δι' ὑμᾶς) Hoc omne, quod Christus mortuus est, quod resuscitatus, non mea magis, quam vestra causa accidit. Ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσασα διὰ τῶν πλειόνων τὴν εὐχαριστίαν περισσεύσῃ εἰς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ) ὑποδιαστολὴ ponenda est- post πλεονάσασα. Sensus enim est, ut quo amplius est be- neficium, eo abundantiorem elliciat DEI gloriam, multis admodum gratias ei agentibus.

Διὸ ὐκ ἐκκακῦμεν) Id repetit, quod dixerat supra I.

Hæc potiús ad partes officii Apostolici salutis Co- rinthiorum causà non absque afflictione varia exantlatas spectant. Omnia illa & peraguntur & tolerantur à nobis vestri vestraque salutis gratia. Et rectè B. Hunnius: Ad Corinthios, inquit, etiam pertinere venturæ beatitudinis communionem, inde probat, quia ipsi sint, propter quos Apostoli tot malis & adversitatibus se libenter objiciant, ut nimirum beneficium, quod per Evangelii prædicationem in alios etiam exundat, simal exuberet in gloriam Dei, quando videlicet per multos ad communionem sal- vificæ agnitionis DEI conversos & adductos, uno velut ore solenniter gratiæ aguntur Deo, & nomen illius hinc glorificatur. Ideo sese non defatigari sive laborum gravitate, sive miseriarum & tribula- tionum magnitudine testatur.

## 4:16
v. 16. Ἀλλ’ εἰ κὰι ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος διαφθείρεται, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἔσω ἀνακαινῦται ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ) We have sufficiently explained what is meant by ὁ ἔσωθεν & ἔξω ἄνθρωπος at Rom. VII. 22. The body is attenuated through so many adversities. For that is what διαφθείρεται means here. For even in law, those things are said to perish which become worse. But the mind becomes more vigorous day by day. For this is what ἀνακενῦται means, as if he were to say, it grows young. Which is ἀνανεῦųαι in Ephes. IV. 23. תהדוש in Ps. CII. 5. That also ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ יום יום is a Hebraism, which is translated καθ’ ἑκάσην ἡμέραν in 1. Sam. XVIII. 10. Esth. III. 4. Job. I. 4. That in Latin is indies (daily).

In the Apostolic phrase, the exterior and interior man do not denote the soul and the body; but the spirit and the flesh, or the spiritual and the animal man. For the corruption of the flesh denotes the attenuation and mortification of the whole man; insofar as he is ψυχικὸς. Although, therefore, by the exterior man here, the flesh is not understood abstractly, or as carnal depravity, yet concretely it designates the man who still has remnants of the flesh. That Διαφθορὰ does not indeed signify the destruction of carnal corruption—for we ourselves ought to procure this through the crucifixion of the flesh, Rom. VI. 13. Gal. V. 24—but rather of the man who, because of the sin inhabiting him, is still σαρκικὸς, not fully πνευματικὸς, and sees, albeit with pain, the law in his members warring against the law of his mind, Rom. VII. 14. 17. 23. νέκρωσιν or mortification, which he suffers from others for the name of the Lord, he signifies, and therefore the ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος must be attenuated and corrupted, so that whatever remnants of the flesh and the old Adam still remain may be destroyed in us through the cross and calamity, and so the ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος, the interior man, may be renewed from day to day, and that which is spiritual in us, or the Spirit, may more and more obtain and prevail, so that we may be aroused in the Spirit to act bravely for the name of JESUS, and we may become more exercised in faith, hope, and patience. The external man is corrupted, says our B. Balduinus, and is mortified by calamities, which withdraw the delights of this world, and apply a bridle, as it were, so that he may not be allowed to exercise his powers as before, when he was his own master. And with respect to these carnal desires, the external man is called the old man, and is opposed to the new. He calls the new man the reborn man, who is otherwise called the spirit, and savors those things which are above, not those which are on the earth, Col. III. 2. He is renewed from day to day, because he always resists the flesh that remains even in the reborn, and overcomes it, and is daily strengthened by perpetual exercises of piety (which burn more fervently under the cross). Therefore, the external, as our B. Antecessor has it again, and the internal man, are the same as to substance, or as to the sin inhabiting him before and after regeneration he is called external and is called carnal, 1. Cor. III. 3. but as to the gift of renewal and the holiness arising from it, he is called internal. Which he deduces more fully against the Schwenckfeldians, Calvinists, and Arminius. He brings forward these reasons primarily: 1. The Apostle says of the interior man that he is renewed from day to day: which is only in the reborn, in whom also only the interior man is found: But even the non-reborn have a mind and heart, therefore those things do not signify the interior man to Paul. 2. The works of the flesh are the works of the exterior man, for that reason they are said to be manifest, Gal. V. 19. but the works of the flesh are also in the heart, mind, and will of man, Mark VII. 21. Rom. I. v. 21. Eph. IV. 18. Therefore the heart, mind, and will of man pertain also to the exterior man. 3. The interior man is said to be renewed: But not only the soul, but also the body of man is renewed; therefore the bodies of the saints are said to be temples of the Holy Spirit, 1. Cor. III. & VI. Therefore not the soul only, but the body pertains to the interior man: And it is most false that Arminius names only the soul as the subject of renewal. 4. The internal man is opposed to the external, so that one destroys the other: But the soul is not opposed to the body, nor does one destroy the other, but rather preserves it. Therefore these two, the internal man and the soul, the external man and the body, are not synonyms. THESE ARE B. BALDUINUS'S. With Estius as interpreter, the Apostle wished to signify the daily increase and progress of renewal in the interior man, just as there is a daily approach to corruption in the exterior. Cajetan, however, confesses that the exterior and interior man are one and the same man according to different conditions. For every man, he says, is called the interior man according to the conditions of the mind, and the exterior according to the conditions of the body.

Latin:

v. 16. Ἀλλ’ εἰ κὰι ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος διαφθείρεται, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἔσω ἀνακαινῦται ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ) Quid dicantur ὁ ἔσωθεν & ἔξω ἄνθρωπος, satis exposuimus ad Rom. VII. 22. Cor- pus per tot adversa attenuatur. Id enim hîc est διαφθείρε- ται. Nam & in jure perire dicuntur, quæ deteriora fiunt. At animus indies fit vegetior. Hoc enim est ἀνακενῦται, quasi dicat, juvenescit. Quod ἀνανεῦųαι Ephes. IV. 23. תהדוש Ps. CII. 5. Illud quoque ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ יום יום est Hebraismus, qui vertitur καθ’ ἑκάσην ἡμέραν 1. Sam. XVIII. 10. Esth. III. 4. Job. I. 4. Id Latinis est indies.

Apostolica phrasi homo exterior & interior non animam notant, & corpus; sed spiritum, & car- nem, vel hominem spiritualem, & animalem. Car- nis enim corruptio hominis totius; qua nempe ψυχικὸς est, attenuationem & mortificationem notat. Etsi ergo hîc per hominem exteriorem non caro abstractivè, vel carnalis pravitas intel- ligatur, concretivè tamen homo, qui carnis adhuc reliquias habet, designatur. Διαφθορὰ illa non qui- dem corruptionis carnalis destructionem, hanc enim ipsimet per carnis crucifixionem procurare debe- mus, Rom. VI. 13. Gal. V. 24. hominis tamen, qui adhuc propter peccatum inhabitans σαρκικὸς est, non plene πνευματικὸς, & videt, etsi cum dolore, legem in membris suis repugnantem legi mentis suæ, Rom. VII. 14. 17. 23. νέκρωσιν vel mortificationem, quam ab aliis patitur propter nomen Domini, signi- ficat, atque ideo attenuandus & corrumpendus est ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος, ut quicquid adhuc superest reliquiarum carnis & veteris Adami per crucem & calamitatem in nobis destruatur, adeoque ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος interior homo renovetur de die in diem, ac quod in nobis spirituale vel Spiritus magis ma- gisque obtineat & prævaleat, ut exsuscitemur in Spiritu ad agendum fortiter pro nomine JESU, nosque in fide, spe, ac patientià exercitatiores evadamus. Corrumpitur externus homo, inquit B. Balduinus noster, & mortificatur calamitatibus, quæ delicias hujus mundi subtrahunt, & quasi fre- num injiciunt, ne vires suas, ut ante, cum sui juris erat, exercere patiantur. Et respectu carnalium ho- rum desideriorum externus homo, vetus homo voca- tur, & novo opponitur. Novum hominem vocat hominem renatum, qui alias spiritus appellatur, & sapit ea, quæ sursum, non quæ super terram sunt, Col. III. 2. is de die in diem renovatur, quia semper carni etiam in renatis residuæ resistit, eamque vincit, per- petuisque exercitiis pietatis (quæ sub cruce magis fervent) quotidie corroboratur. Est igitur externus, ut iterum habet B. Antecessor, & internus homo, quoad substantiam idem, seu quoad peccatum inha- bitans ante & post regenerationem externus dicitur & carnalis dicitur, 1. Cor. III. 3. sed quoad donum renovationis & ex illo sanctitatem oriundam; in- in- ternus appellatur. Quod contra Schwenckfeldia- nos, Calvinianos & Arminium uberius deducit. Rationes has imprimis affert 1. de interiore homine dicit Apostolus, quod renovetur de die in diem: quod tantum sit in renatis, in quibus etiam tantum inte- rior homo reperitur: Habent autem etiam non re- nati mentem & cor, ergo ista Paulo non significant hominem interiorem. 2. Opera carnis sunt opera hominis exterioris, ideo enim dicuntur manifesta esse, Gal. V. 19. sed opera carnis sunt etiam in corde, mente & voluntate hominis, Marci VII. 21. Rom. I. v. 21. Eph. IV. 18. Ergo cor, mens, voluntas hominis pertinent etiam ad exteriorem hominem. 3. Inter- nus homo renovari dicitur: Sed non tantum anima, verum etiam corpus hominis renovatur; ideo cor- pora sanctorum dicuntur templa Spiritus S. 1. Cor. III. & VI. Ergo non anima saltem, sed corpus ad interiorem hominem pertinet: Et falsissimum est, quod Arminius animam tantum renovationis subje- ctum nominat. 4. Internus homo opponitur externo, ita ut unus alterum destruat: Anima vero non oppo- nitur corpori, nec unum destruit alterum, sed conser- vat potius. Ergo ista duo homo internus & anima, homo externus & corpus non sunt Synonyma. HÆC B. Balduinus. Estio interprete, voluit Apostolus si- gnificare quotidianum incrementum & profectum renovationis in interiore homine, sicut est in exteriore ad corruptionem quotidianus accessus. Cajetanus au- tem fatetur, exteriorem & interiorem hominem, unum eundemque hominem esse secundum di- versas conditiones. Quilibet enim homo, inquit, secundum conditiones animi vocatur internus homo, secundum conditiones corporis externus.

## 4:17
v. 17. Τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν) τὸ ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως is a Greek idiom for ἡ θλίψις ἐλαφρά. And before παραυτίκα the article ἡ is understood, that is, the affliction of this time, as the Latin also took it. The Greek interpreters take it thus, and Xenophon and Demosthenes use παραυτίκα in this way. But it is called light compared to the glory which is opposed to it in the other member of the antithesis.

Καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατερ γάζεται ἡμῖν) He also said βάρος δόξης here for δόξαν βα- ρεῖαν, and, as if he had said so, he added καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν, εἰς ὑπερ- βολὴν, that is, a most excellently weighty glory: we had καθ᾽ ὑπερ- βολὴν also in Rom. 8, 13. But here the Apostle indicated a certain highest excellence by doubling the word in the Hebrew manner. He called that glory weighty which is solid. For things that are solid, made of gold, weigh more than those that are mixed. Glory itself כבוד among the Hebrews has its name from weight, the adjective of which כבד the Chaldean often translates by יקר, that is, τίμιον.

Μὴ σκοπόντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπό- μενα, Heb. XI. 1.

Latin:

v. 17. Τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν) τὸ ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως Græca loquutio pro ἡ θλίψις ἐλα- φρά. Et ante παραυτίκα subauditur Articulus ἡ, id est, hu- jus temporis afflictio, quomodo sumpsere & Latinus. Ita sumunt & Græci Interpretes, & sic παραυτίκα usurpant Xenophon & Demosthenes. Levis autem dicitur compa- rata ad gloriam, quæ ei opponitur membro altero anti- theti.

Καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατερ γάζεται ἡμῖν) Hic quoque βάρος δόξης dixit pro δόξαν βα- ρεῖαν, &, quasi ita dixisset, adjecit καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν, εἰς ὑπερ- βολὴν, id est, excellentissime gravem gloriam: καθ᾽ ὑπερ- βολὴν habuimus & Rom. 8, 13. Sed hic Hebræo more per verbum geminans Apostolus summam quandam excellen- tiam indicavit. Gravem autem dixit gloriam eam, quæ soli- da est. Nam quæ solida sunt ex auro, plus pendent, quam mixta. Ipsa gloria כבוד apud Hebræos à gravitate no- men habet, cujus Adjectivum כבד Chaldæus sæpe vertit per יקר, id est, τίμιον.

Μὴ σκοπόντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπό- μενα, Heb. XI. 1.

## 4:18
Τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα) πρόσκαιρα are called those things which do not last long, as in Matt. XIII. 21. Mark IV. 17. Heb. XI. 25.

Τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα αἰώνια) that is, without any end. For this word is taken in the books of the New Testament from the very nature of the covenant.

Illud prius τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλί- ψεως ἡμῶν Tertullian in Scorp. and in his book on the resurrection of the flesh reads it thus: For that which is for the present is temporal and light of our pressure. Augustine in Ps. XCIII. in this way: For that which is for the present is temporal and light of our tribulation. The latter καθ᾽ ὑπερβο- λὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν Augustine l. c. reads thus, according to an incredible measure and into an incredible measure. Erasmus renders it, wonderfully beyond measure.
