It is certain that something incomparably greater and more excellent is signified, both extensively, where the momentary and the eternal are opposed to each other; and intensively, as the lightness of afflictions and the inestimable weight are antitheses.

Papistæ è voce κατεργάζεται attempt to carve out some merit: But since the Apostle leaves no proportion between the momentary

and light affliction, compared with eternal and exceeding great glory, the rationale of merit expires entirely, and that word, which is also general in itself, is rendered manifest as not being able to be drawn to meritorious causality, but as having to be accepted as a consequence from the institution or promise of God, not from an intrinsic rationale, just as it is used regarding the mode of occasional efficiency in Rom. V. 3, chap. VII. v. 8, 2 Cor. VII. 11. Concerning which Salmeron on Rom. IV. 15. Nor should you wonder about that word of working. For many things are said to effect something, not of themselves, but by occasion. Andreas Fricius, book IV on the Church, chap. 12, advises regarding the present passage that that word is not to be referred to the dignity of merits and works, which are done by the regenerate with respect to heavenly glory, but to the generous will of God and the merit of Christ, who imputes it to those who do not do it just as if they had done it, and rewards our light and brief labors with great and everlasting glory. For Paul himself detracts from the condignity of our works in comparison to that glory which will be eternal after this life. The blessed Dn. D. Hülsemann in his Vindications of Holy Scripture §. LXXIV has this to say about this passage: The statement 2 Cor. IV. 17, 'The light affliction works a great weight of glory,' is ineptly produced both to prove the merit of good works and for the necessity of a cause without which not (causa sine qua non) for salvation. For first, the subject of the proposition is not a voluntary action of man, but an involuntary passion; θλίψις (tribulation) is said to work a weight of glory. But good works are motions and actions produced by the Holy Spirit through a regenerate man; tribulations are produced by the Devil through tyrants: therefore the subject of the proposition speaks not of a work that is formally good, but evil. 2. Tribulation is said to generate a weight of glory, with the Papists themselves admitting it is not of itself, according to that common saying: 'It is not the punishment, but the cause that makes the martyr.' Therefore the working of a weight of glory is predicated of tribulation accidentally, just as 'working patience' is predicated of the same tribulation, 'working a way' of the law, 'working concupiscence and sin,' and infinite other things are predicated of their subjects accidentally, Rom. V. 3, c. IV. v. 15, c. VII. 8, 17, where the mode of working accidentally is expressly added, because ἁμαρτία ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα (sin, taking occasion) from the law in the Apostle effected all concupiscence, so 2 Cor. IX. 11, c. VII. 10, 11, and elsewhere. 3. The predicate of the proposition does not speak of essential glory, but of the accident of its weight, that is, of degrees and intensity, which is evident from the opposition of τὸ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως (the momentary lightness of the affliction) to the magnitude of the weight in glory. The accident of tribulation is opposed to the accident of glory, not subject to subject, in which sense, namely of an accident, that Greek word βάρος is accustomed to be used. Thus Matt. XX. 12, 'weight' is said for the heat of the day; c. XXVI. 7, 'weight of ointment' for the price of the ointment: see the LXX and Sixtinus Amama, book III of the Antibarbarus, p. 770, on the statement Ps. XXXV. 18, 'I will praise thee in the heavy people.' Where the LXX have βαρεῖ, Symmachus has παμπληθεῖ. 4. The mode of working is not described by the necessity of a cause without which not; but of a cause accidentally. But a cause without which not is reduced to a cause of itself, because the Principal cause can neither work nor produce an effect without this cause, which is called 'without which not.' But that God as the Principal cause cannot save anyone without affliction is manifestly false. Therefore afflictions are not a cause without which not of salvation.

Latin:

Τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα) πρόσκαιρα dicuntur, quæ non diu durant, ut Matth. XIII. 21. Marci IV. 17. Ebr. XI. 25.

Τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα αἰώνια) id est, sine ullo fine. Nam ita vox hæc in libris Novi fœderis ex ipsa fœderis natura sumitur.

Illud prius τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλί- ψεως ἡμῶν Tertullianus in Scorp. & libro de resurr. carnis ita legit: Nam quod ad præsens est temporale & leve pressuræ nostræ. Augustinus in Psal. XCIII. hoc modo: Etenim quod est ad præsens temporale & leve tribulationis nostræ. Posterius καθ᾽ ὑπερβο- λὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν Augustinus l. c. sic legit, juxta incredibilem modum & in incredibilem modum. Erasmus reddit, mirè super modum. Certum est, significari aliquid incomparabiliter majus & ex- cellentius tum extensive, ubi opponuntur sibi momentaneum & æternum; tum intensive, uti levitas afflictionum & pondus inæstimabile sunt antitheta.

Papistæ è voce κατεργάζεται meritum aliquod exsculpere conantur: Sed quum Apostolus nul- lam proportionem relinquat inter momentaneam

& levem afflictionem, comparatam cum æterna & supra modum excellenti gloria, expirat pror- sus meriti ratio, & manifestum redditur verbum illud, quod etiam per se generale est, non posse ad causalitatem meritoriam trahi, sed de consequente ex institutione vel promissione Dei, non ex intrin- seca ratione accipienda esse, quemadmodum id de modo efficientiæ occasionali Rom. V. 3. cap. VII. v. 8. 2. Cor. VII. 11. usurpatur. Quo de Salmero Rom. IV. 15. Neque mireris de verbo illo operan- di. Multa enim dicuntur aliqua efficere, non per se, sed per occasionem. Andreas Fricius libr. IV. de Ecclesia cap. 12. ad præsentem locum monet, ver- bum illud non ad dignitatem meritorum & operum, quæ fiunt à regeneratis cælestis gloriæ respectu refe- rendum esse, sed ad largam Dei voluntatem Christi- que meritum, qui & non facientibus imputat perin- de atque si fecissent, & leves atque breves labores no- stros magnâ & sempiternâ gloriâ recompensat. Ipse enim Paulus condignitatem nostris operibus de- trahit præ ea gloria, quæ post hanc vitam æterna erit. B. Dn. D. Hülsemann. in vindicat. S. Scri- pturæ §. LXXIV. de hoc loco ita habet: Dictum 2. Cor. IV 17. Modicum afflictionis operatur magnum pondus gloriæ, inepte producitur tùm ad proban- dum bonorum operum meritum, tùm ad necessitatem causæ, sine qua non B. O. ad salutem. Primò enim subjectum propositionis non est actio hominis volun- taria, sed passio involuntaria; θλίψις tribulatio dicitur operari pondus gloriæ. Bona opera autem sunt motus & actiones à Spiritu Sancto per hominem regenitum productæ, tribulationes producuntur à Diabolo per Tyrannos: igitur subjectum Proposi- tionis de opere non formaliter bono, sed malo loqui- tur. 2. Dicitur tribulatio generare pondus gloriæ, Papistis ipsis fatentibus non per se juxta vulgatum illud: Non pœna, sed causa facit martyrem. Itaque operatio ponderis gloriæ per accidens prædicatur de tribulatione, quemadmodum operari patientiam de eadem tribulatione operari viam de lege operari con- cupiscentiam & peccatum, atque infinita alia de sub- jectis suis per accidens prædicantur, Rom. V. 3. c. IV. v. 15. c. VII. 8. 17. ubi modus operandi per accidens expreffè additur, quod ἁμαρτία ἀφορμὴν λαβῦσα peccatum occasionem rapiens ex lege in Apostolo effe- cerit omnem concupiscentiam, sic 2. Cor. IX. 11. c. VII. 10. 11. atq; alibi. 3. Prædicatum propositionis non lo- quitur de essentiali gloria, sed de accidente ejus pon- dere, id est, de gradibus & intensione, quod patet ex oppositione τὸ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρᾶ τῆς θλίψεως seu momentaneæ levitatis in afflictione ad magnitudinem ponderis in gloria. Accidens tribulationis opponitur accidenti gloriæ, non subjectum subjecto, quo sensu, de accidente nempe, solet Græcum illud βάρος nuncu- pari. Sic Matth. XX. 12. pondus dici pro calore meri- diei c. XXVI. 7. pondus unguenti pro pretio unguen- ti: vide LXX. & Sixtinum Amama lib. III. Anti- barbari p. 770. ad dictum Pf. XXXV. 18. Laudabo te in populo gravi. Ubi LXX. βαρεῖ Symmachus παμ- πλεθεῖ. 4. Modus operandi non describitur à necessi- tate causæ, sine quâ non; sed causæ per accidens. Cau- sa autem, sine quâ non reducitur ad causam per se, quia causa Principalis nec operari, nec effectum pro- ducere potest sine hac causa, quæ dicitur sine qua non. At sine afflictione Deum tanquã causam Principalem neminem salvare posse, manifesto falsum est. Ergò afflictiones non sunt causa, sine quâ non salutis.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Confidence of a house from God: the Apostle consoles himself regarding the destruction of the earthly tabernacle, and desires it, primarily so that he may not be unclothed, but clothed upon. Otherwise, sealed with the earnest of the Spirit, as one absent from the Lord while traveling, he wishes to travel away from the body and go to dwell with the Lord, and he strives to please the Lord continually, and that because of the future appearance before the tribunal of the Lord: appealing to the consciences of the Corinthians, without vain boasting, and compelled by the love of Christ, who died for all so that we might live for Him, and be a new creature in Christ, he exhorts all, as those reconciled to God by the satisfaction of Christ, as an ambassador of Christ, to be reconciled to God, if indeed Christ was made sin for us, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him.

There are two parts: I. He declares the certainty of his confidence and desire regarding the building from God up to v. 10. II. He explains the satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ, which is the foundation of that confidence and the chief head of the Christian religion, up to v. 21.

PART ONE. He declares the certainty of his confidence and desire regarding the building from God.

v. 1. For we know) These things cohere with the preceding. The Apostle had consoled himself in afflictions and the mortification of the body with the blessed resurrection and the immense glory of the future life: Now he also consoles himself against the destruction of the earthly tabernacle of the body with the perpetuity of the heavenly building, certain of the same through the Spirit, and striving in the fear of God so that he may please God, in which part he appeals to the testimony of God and their own consciences. For the certainty of future glory, even if it be undoubted to the faithful and sealed by the earnest of the Spirit, is nevertheless hypothetical, if indeed we strive to please God, and do not cast it away by having cast off the fear of the Lord through voluntary sins; therefore we are commanded to work out our salvation with fear and trembling, Phil. II. 12. For the Apostle testifies concerning this certainty of his, οἴδαμεν WE KNOW, by which word he declares that not only was he himself taught not from an immediate revelation of the Holy Spirit, as the Papists claim, but that his companion Timothy also, to whom no one would say that an immediate revelation had occurred, was certain, not merely by some conjectural presumption, but by that which is the energy of the word οἴδαμεν, by undoubted knowledge and certainty, which is held from the universal promises of divine grace through subsumption and the application of faith as certainly as the word of the divine promise is certain, and as certainly as he who believes the same knows that he believes, and is confirmed by the internal testimony of the Spirit, which He renders to our spirit, that we are children of God and co-heirs of Christ, Rom. VIII. 16. which Spirit of God is given to us as a pledge and earnest of the heavenly inheritance, and seals it in our hearts, 2. Cor. I. 22. Eph. I. 14. chap. IV. 30. 1. John V. 10. 11. In which manner Paul had also testified with Timothy concerning the certainty of the resurrection to the blessed life in the preceding chapter, verses 13, 14. Having the same spirit, we also believe, and therefore speak, KNOWING εἰδότες, that He who raised up Jesus, will also raise us up with JESUS, or to eternal glory with JESUS, 2. Timothy I. verse 12. πέπεισμαι, I am persuaded, that is, I believe firmly, and with undoubted faith, that God is able to keep my deposit against that day. From that certainty comes that σενάζειν, to groan, verses 2 and 4. Of the same, the Apostle also testifies in verse 5, that for this

He says that God has prepared him, and he uses that θαῤ- ῥῶμεν of his, which is a word full of certainty and sure confidence, more than once in verses 6 and 7. St. Cyprian says excellently in Sermon IV on mortality: God promises you immortality and eternity as you depart from this world, and you doubt. This is not to know God at all; this is to offend Christ, the Master of believers, with the sin of unbelief; this is to have been established in the Church and yet not have faith in the house of faith.

For if our earthly house of the tabernacle) Ἐὰν here is 'even if'. Even if, he says, this body is not only afflicted, but also dissolved before the day of the Lord. Σκῆνος is body both to the Hebrews and the Pythagoreans. Thus γεῶδες κλῆνος is the same as φθαρτὸν σῶμα, Wisdom 9:15. Euryfus in his book on fortune, Theagis in his book on virtues, both Pythagoreans, and Plato in the Axiochus, and the Hebrew book Zohar call it this. Οἰκία τῦ σκήνυς is used exegetically, like 'the fountain of Timavus', 'the town of Antioch', 'the river Eridanus', 'the fig tree'. Σκήνωμα is used in the same sense in 1 Peter 1:13 and in Philo's book 'That the good man is free': 'The mind is truly man, carrying about the sensible form as a house.' Our soul dwells in the body, not as in a house that will stand for a long time, which will soon be called οἰκοδομὴ, but as in a tent which is easily taken down. Chrysostom also noted this, and Jerome interprets it no differently in his commentary on Isaiah 39.

There is no doubt that this mortal body is understood by 'earthly house of the tabernacle', which is called an 'earthly house' not so much because it is dissolved into the earth, as because it is inhabited upon the earth. Furthermore, by the word 'of the tabernacle' reference is made not so much to the habitation itself as to the manner of inhabiting. For the soul does not dwell in the body as in a quiet and durable house, much less in a well-fortified citadel, but as in a tent, which is built at least for a time, exposed to the injuries of various winds and storms, and which is eventually transported from place to place. Therefore, in the last place, it is added that that body is dissolved, namely by diseases and death: for these are those ministers by whom the cords of this earthly dwelling are cut, and it collapses, as the blessed Balduinus says here. Thus our body is called a tabernacle in 2 Peter 1:13, 14 and a 'clay house' in Job 4:19; compare 1 Corinthians 4:7.

We have a building from God) Present for future. We shall have a building made by God, that is, a heavenly, spiritual body, of which 1 Corinthians 15:48, 43, 49 speaks. Nothing of ours will perish.

A house not made with hands) He persists in the similitude of a building, although he is speaking of the body. Thus we have 'a temple not made with hands' in Mark 14:58, 'a circumcision not made with hands' in Colossians 2:11. He wishes to say a body made divinely. Thus 'holy places not made with hands', Hebrews 9:24.

Eternal in the heavens) A body not only immortal, but also suitable to that place, that is, the highest heaven.

There is no need for us to admit here an enallage of the present for the future: since the Apostle rather connects immediately the dissolution of the earthly tabernacle and the inhabitation of the building which is from GOD. This makes for comfort regarding afflictions and death, namely that once the tabernacle of the body is dissolved, the soul is immediately to be received into the heavenly building, and when our 'outer man' and animal man is corrupted, we are to attain for the 'inner man' not only a perfect renewal, but 'an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure', we who look not at these visible things, but at the invisible things in the heavens. For although some, with Theophylact, understand by 'building from God' the spiritual body—an interpretation which especially pleases the Socinians—others, with Photius, more correctly explain it as the heavenly glory of the Elect in the other life. Which opinion the blessed Gerhard approves in his section on death. 299. And we, in our 'Socinismo profligato', have demonstrated this with more arguments on page 1000 and following. Thus, in the description of heavenly blessedness, a house is mentioned in which there are many mansions (John 14:2), and mention is made of heavenly tabernacles (Luke 16:9), and of the heavenly city (Hebrews 11:21, chapter 13:14, Revelation 21:3). But nowhere is the glorious body called a 'building from God', and not even 'heavenly', although we are said to be future 'heavenly ones' and to bear the image of the 'heavenly one' (1 Corinthians 15:48, 49). Nor indeed is the glorious body a 'building from God' in opposition to this earthly body, since this body of ours is the same in substance as the glorious body, not different, and is also from GOD (Job 10 and Psalm 139), and therefore the glorified body is not properly 'not made with hands', because it is not prepared without the work of men, but produced by human generation, being the same in number and in substance with this earthly body. But heaven and heavenly glory and the eternal [glory] prepared by GOD for the elect are without the work of men; and thus heaven is designated by 'holy places not made with hands' (Hebrews 9:24) and is truly eternal, because it was prepared from eternity and remains for eternity. Add that the glorified body can be called 'the habitation from heaven' neither by reason of its matter nor by reason of its origin. We shall indeed be heavenly, but as we bear the image of the heavenly Adam, not by reason of the body in heaven, but by reason of the heavenly life, because, not being addicted to earthly things, we shall live a spiritual and heavenly life. The blessed Gerhard urges the scope of the Apostle, that he wishes to say this: if we are forced to sustain persecutions and exiles, and even death itself, in this life, there is nevertheless no reason for us to be anxious in our soul and fear that a house will be lacking to us, for we have a heavenly house into which we shall be received when driven and chased from the world. But if he understood by the heavenly house an immortal and glorified body, he could not have said that a house would not be lacking to us, because from the day of death until the time of judgment an immortal body will be lacking to us. If you say that 'house' is said here to be 'in the heavens', and is therefore distinguished from the heavens, I reply that it is not distinguished by any other reason than that mansions are distinguished from the Father's house (John 14:2). Heaven is the common [home] of the Elect, but the house of each one is their own τὸ ἐν cœlis: which is also called οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐν ὐρανῷ, because it is of heavenly matter, so to speak, or condition, as if God had built or prepared for each one there their own proper οἰκητήριον, just as the Angels are said to have had their own proper dwelling, which they abandoned, Jude v. 6.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Fiducia domus ex Deo de tabernaculi terreni de- structione solatur sese Apostolus, illamque desiderat, imprimis ut non exuatur, sed super- induatur. Cæteroquin obsignatus arrhabone Spiritus, ceu peregrè absens à Domino, pere- grinari à corpore, & habitatu ad Dominum ire vult, atque ut Domino subinde placeat, contendit, idque propter futuram coram tri- bunali Domini comparitionem: provocans ad conscientias Corinthiorum, citra inanem jactantiam, & charitate Christi compulsus, qui vice omnium mortuus est, ut eidem viva- mus, & nova creatura in Christo simus, hor- tatur omnes, utpote satisfactione Christi Deo placatos ceu legatus Christi, ut Deo re- concilientur, si quidem Christus factus pro nobis peccatum sit, ut nos efficeremur justi- tia Dei in ipso.

PArtes sunt duæ: I. Fiducia & desiderii de ædifi- cio ex Deo certitudinem declarat ad v. 10. II. Sa- tisfactionem & reconciliationem Christi, quæ fidu- ciæ illius fundamentum ac præcipuum caput reli- gionis Christianæ est, explicat ad v. 21.

PARS PRIOR. Fiducia & desiderii de ædificio ex Deo certi- tudinem declarat.

vers. 1. Οἴδαμεν γὰρ) Cohærent hæc cum superioribus. Solatus sese erat Apostolus in afflictionibus & mortificatione corporis, beatâ resurrectione, & im- mensâ gloria futuræ vitæ: Jam etiam solatur sese adversus tabernaculi terreni corporis destructionem cœlestis ædificii perennitate, certus de eodem per Spiritum, atque in timore DEI contendens, ut DEO placeat, qua in parte ad testimonium DEI & conscientias ipsorum provocat. Certitudo enim* futuræ gloriæ, etsi fidelibus indubitata sit & arrha- bone Spiritu obsignetur, hypothetica tamen est, si nempe DEO placere studeamus, nec excusso timore Domini per peccata voluntaria eandem excutiamus; ideò cum timore & tremore salutem operari jubemur, Phil. II. 12. Testatur enim de hac certitudine sua Apostolus οἴδαμεν SCIMUS, quo verbo non se tantum ex immediata Spiri- tus Sancti revelatione, ut Papistæ volunt, edo- ctum; sed socium etiam suum Timotheum, cui immediatam revelationem obtigisse, nemo dixe- rit, certum esse perhibet, non conjecturali tantum quadam præsumtione, sed quæ verbi οἴδαμεν ἐνέρ- γεια est, indubitata scientiâ ac certitudine, quæ è promissionibus divinæ gratiæ universalibus per subsumptionem & applicationem fidei tàm certo habetur, quàm certum est verbum divinæ pro- missionis, & quàm certò, qui credit iisdem, se novit credere, & confirmatur per internum Spi- ritus testimonium, quod spiritui nostro reddit, quod filii Dei & cohæredes Christi simus, Rom. IIX. 16. qui Dei Spiritus nobis ceu pignus & arrha hereditatis cœlestis donatur, eamque in cordibus nostris obsignat, 2. Cor. I. 22. Eph. I. 14. cap. IV. 30. 1. Joh. V. 10. 11. Quo pacto etiam testatus erat Pau- lus cum Timotheo de certitudine resuscitationis ad beatam vitam cap. præced. vers. 13. 14. Habentes eundem spiritum & nos credimus, ideo & loquimur, SCIENTES εἰδότες, quod qui suscitavit Je- sum, & nos cum JESU, seu ad æternam cum JESU gloriam suscitabit, 2. Timoth. I. vers. 12. πέπεισμαι, persuasus sum, hoc est, credo firmiter, & indubitatâ fide, quia potens est Deus, servare depositum meum in diem illum. Ex illa certitudine est illud σενάζειν, gemere, vers. 2. & 4. De eadem testatur quoque Apostolus vers. 5. quia ad id

Deum sefe præparasse dicit, ac suum illud θαῤ- ῥῶμεν, quod verbum est plenum certitudinis & certæ confidentiæ, plus vice simplici adhibet v. 6. & 7. Præclare S. Cyprianus Serm. IV. de mortalitate: Deus tibi de hoc mundo recedenti immortalitatem pollicetur, atque æternitatem, & tu dubitas. Hoc est Deum omnino non nosse; hoc est Christum cre- dentium Magistrum peccato incredulitatis offen- dere; hoc est in Ecclesia constitutum fidem in domo fidei non habere.

Ὅτι ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος ἡμῶν οἰκία τῦ σκήνυς) Ἐὰν hic est etsi. Etsiamsi, inquit, corpus hoc non tantum affligatur, sed etiam dissolvatur ante diem Domini. Σκῆνος & He- bræis & Pythagoricis est corpus. Sic γεῶδες κλῆνος idem quod φθαρτὸν σῶμα, Sap. IX. 15. Appellat sic & Euryfus libro de fortuna, Theagis libro de virtutibus, Pythagorici ambo, & Plato Axiocho, & Hebræus liber Zoar. Οἰκία τῦ σκήνυς quomodo fons Timavi, oppidum Antiochiæ, amnis Eridani, arbor fici ἐξηγητικῶς. Σκήνωμα eodem sensu apud Petrum I. II. 13. apud Philonem libro virum bonum esse liberum: Ὁ νῦς ἀψευδῶς ἄνθρωπος, οἶκον ἐπιφερόμενος τὸ αἰσθητὸν εἶδος. Animus noster in corpore habitat, non tan- quam in domo diu statura; quæ jam dicetur οἰκοδομὴ, sed tanquam in tentorio quod facile tollitur. Annotavit hoc & Chrysostomus, nec aliter interpretatur Hieronymus ad XXXIX. Esaiæ.

Corpus hoc mortale per ἐπίγειον οἰκείαν τῦ σκή- νυς intelligi dubium non est, quod ἐπίγειος οἰκεία dicitur, non tam quod in terram dissolvatur, quam quod super terram inhabitetur. Cæterum voce τῦ σκήνυς respicitur non tam ad ipsam habitationem, quam ad modum habitandi. Non enim habitat ani- ma in corpore, tanquam in quieta & durabili qua- dam domo, multo minus in bene munita quadam arce, sed ut in tabernaculo, quod ad tempus saltem extructum est, ventorum & tempestatum varia- rum injuriis expositum, quodque tandem de loco in locum transportatur. Ideo postremo loco additur, quod corpus illud dissolvatur, nimirum per morbos & mortem: Hi enim sunt ministri illi, per quos funi- culi terreni hujus habitaculi præscinduntur, ipsumque concidit, ut hic B. Balduinus. Ita corpus nostrum tabernaculum dicitur 2. Petr. I. 13. 14. & Job. IV. 19. domus lutea; confer 1. Cor. IV. 7.

Οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ Θεῦ ἔχομεν) Præsens pro Futuro. Habe- bimus ædificium à Deo factum, id est, corpus ἐπυράνιον, πνευματικὸν, de quo 1. Cor. XV. 48. 43. 49. Nihil nobis peribit.

Οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον) Perstat quanquam de corpore lo- quens in similitudine ædificii. Sic ναὸν ἀχειροποίητον ha- bemus Marci XIV. 58. περιτομὴν ἀχειροποίητον Col. II. 11. Vult dicere corpus factum divinitus. Sic ἅγια ἐ χειρο- ποίητα, Hebr. IX. 24.

Αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς) Corpus non immortale tantum, sed & loco isti, id est, summo cœlo conveniens.

Non opus est, ut hic Enallagen admittamus præsentis pro futuro: Quum Apostolus potius immediate connectat dissolutionem terreni taber- naculi, & inhabitationem ædificii quod ex DEO est. Quod facit ad solatium de afflictionibus & mor- te, quod nempe dissoluto tabernaculo corporis anima statim recipienda sit in cœleste ædificium, & cum ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος exterior, & animalis homo noster corrumpetur, ὁ ἔσωθεν interior non modo renovationem perfectam, sed καθ' ὑπερ- βολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος τῆς δόξης con- sequuturi sumus, qui non visibilia hæc spectamus; sed invisibilia in cœlis. Quanquam enim non- nulli cum Theophylacto per οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ Θεῦ cor- pus spirituale intelligant, quæ interpretatio Soci- nianis imprimis placet; rectius tamen alii cum Pho- tio de τῇ cœlesti & gloria Electorum in altera vita explicant. Quam sententiam B. Gerhardus pro- bat de morte §. 299. nosque in Socinismo profli- gato pluribus argumentis demonstravimus pag. 1000. seqq. Ita in cœlestis beatitudinis descriptio- ne domus commemoratur, in qua multæ mansio- nes sunt Joh. XIV. 2. & tabernaculorum cœlestium mentio fit Luc. XVI. 9. Apoc. XXI. 3. ac civitatis cœ- leftis Ebr. XI. 21. c. XIII. 14. Apoc. XXI. 3. Nuspiam autem corpus gloriosum dicitur οἰκοδομὴ ἐκ Θεᾶ, ac ne quidem ἐπεράνιος, etsi nos futuri dicimur ἐπγ- ράνιοι, & portaturi imaginem τῆ ἐπερανία 1. Cor. XV. 48. 49. Neque sane corpus gloriosum οἰκοδομὴ ἐκ Θεᾶ est in oppositione ad terrenum hocce cor- pus, cum hoc corpus nostrum substantia idem sit cum corpore glorioso, non diversum, & à DEO quoque sit Job. X. & Ps. CXXXIX. adeoque corpus glorificatum proprie ἀχειροποίητον non est, quia non sine hominum opera paratum est, sed gene- ratione humana productum, utpote idem numero, & quoad substantiam cum terreno hocce corpore. Cœlum vero & cœlestis gloria, & æterna à DEO electis parata sine hominum opera; & ita cœlum per ἅγια 8 χειροποίητα designatur Ebr. IX. 24. ac vere αἰώνιον est, quia ab æterno paratum & in æter- num manet. Adde, quod corpus glorificatum neq; ratione materiæ, neque ratione originis dici queat τὸ οἰκητήριον τὸ ἐκ᾿ ὐρανᾶ. Erimus quidem cœlestes, sed qua imaginem cœlestis Adami geremus, non ra- tione corporis in cælo, sed ratione vitæ cœlestis, quia terrenis non addicti spiritualem & cœlestem vitam vivemus. B. Gerhardus urget scopum Apo- stoli, quod hoc dicere velit, si vel maxime in hac vita persecutiones & exilia, ipsamque tandem mor- tem sustinere cogimur, non est tamen, quod animo propterea angamur, ac domum nobis defuturam metuamus, habemus enim domum cœlestem, in quam e mundo pulsi ac fugati recipiemur. At si per do- mum cœlestem intelligeret corpus immortale & glo- rificatum, non potuisset dicere, nobis non defuturam domum, quia à die mortis usque ad tempus judicii deerit nobis corpus immortale. Si dicas, οἰκίαν hic dici ἐν ὐρανοῖς, adeoque à cælis distingui, resp. alia ratione non distingui, quam mansiones à domo Patris distinguuntur Joh. XIV. 2. Cælum est τὸ com- mune Electorum, οἰκία vero cujusvis proprium το ἐν cœlis: quod etiam οἰκητήριον vocatur ἡμῶν τὸ ἐν ὐρανῷ, quod cœlestis sit materia, ut ita loqua- mur, vel conditionis, quasi unicuique ibidem suum proprium οἰκητήριον exstruxerit, aut pararit Deus, quemadmodum proprium domicilium habuisse di- cuntur Angeli, quod dereliquerunt Jud. v. 6.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τέτῳ ςενάζομεν) In this body we groan, Rom. VIII. 23. Namely, on account of daily troubles.

Τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν, τὸ ἐξ ὐρανῶ, ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθῶντες) The word ἐπενδύσασθαι or ἐνδύσασθαι, which Paul uses in 1 Cor. XV. 53, corresponds to the Hebrew התלבש which the book of Zohar and others use in this matter. They set forth the example of Enoch and Elijah.

With groanings the Apostle and his colleagues sighed and desired to superindue that heavenly house, which is called ἐξ ἐρανᾶ, just as the heavenly Jerusalem is said to have descended ἐκ τᾶ ἐρανᾶ, Apoc. XXI. 2. Glory, says the blessed Hunnius, is said to be from heaven for a double reason: First, because it is not earthly, but merely heavenly: Secondly, it is said to be from heaven by reason of the Efficient cause, because God will be its author, not man, in which sense the baptism of John is said to be from heaven and not from men, Matt. XXI. We are superinduced with that, however, when the soul, stripped of the tabernacle of the body, which was like a garment to it, shall be received into the heavenly tabernacle, which takes the place of a far more excellent garment. The example of Enoch and Elijah is extraordinary for all who look not to visible and temporal things, but to invisible and eternal things, and is not suitable for those to whom these things have been handed down for consolation. Augustine is cited in book 1 on the baptism of infants. cap. 2. teaching that that desire in Adam, if he had not sinned, would have been fulfilled, so that the animal body, which he would have carried, and in which he was created had been changed into a spiritual and incorruptible body without an intervening death. But others more correctly understand this concerning the common super-clothing of glory, as if that eternal glory were compared by the word ἐπενδύσασθαι to a precious garment, since from elsewhere, namely from GOD, our souls, having put on faith as an ornament and a more precious garment, shall be super-clothed with heavenly glory. If an immortal body is to be super-clothed, it is necessary that a mortal body remain, upon which that may be super-clothed.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τέτῳ ςενάζομεν) In hoc corpore gemi- mus, Rom. VIII. 23. Nempe ob quotidianas molestias.

Τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν, τὸ ἐξ ὐρανῶ, ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθῶντες) Vox ἐπενδύσασθαι aut ἐνδύσασθαι, qua utitur Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 53. respondet Hebreæ התלבש qua in hac re utitur liber Zoar & alij. Exemplum ponunt in Enocho & Elia.

Cum gemitibus suspirabat & desiderabat Apo- stolus cum collegis, ut superindueret domum il- lam cœlestem, quæ ἐξ ἐρανᾶ dicitur, ut Hierusa- lem cœlestis ἐκ τᾶ ἐρανᾶ descendisse dicitur Apoc. XXI. 2. Gloria, inquit B. Hunnius, dicitur ex cælo esse, duplici de causa: Primo quia non est terrena; sed mere cœlestis: Deinde è cælo esse dicitur ratio- ne causæ Efficientis, quia Deus illius erit autor, non homo, quo sensu Johannis baptisma è cælo esse dici- tur & non ex hominibus Matth. XXI. Ea autem superinduimur, cum anima denudata à taberna- culo corporis, quod ei instar indumenti erat, cœ- lesti tabernaculo recipietur, quod longe præstan- tioris indumenti vice est. Enochi & Eliæ exem- plum extraordinarium est omnibus, qui non vi- sibilia & temporalia, sed invisibilia & æterna re- spiciunt, haud conveniens, quorum solatio hæc tradita sunt. Adducitur Augustinus libr. 1. de ba- ptismo parvul. cap. 2. docens, desiderium illud in Adamo, si non peccasset, complendum fuisse, sic ut corpus animale, quod gestasset, & in quo creatus fuerat absque morte media commutaretur in corpus spirituale & incorruptibile. At rectius alii de com- muni superinduitione gloriæ intelligunt, quasi ver- bo ἐπενδύσασθαι conferatur sempiterna illa gloria vesti pretiosæ, siquidem aliunde, nempe à DEO, animæ nostræ fidem indutæ velut ornatus vestisq; pretiosior superinduetur cœlestis gloria. Si super- induendum corpus immortale, oportet manere mortale corpus, cui illud superinduatur.

## 5:3
Verse 3. If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked) That is, if that day should overtake us with the body, not stripped of the body, if we shall be among those who are changed, not among the dead. For that Paul thought it possible that he himself and those who were of the same time might be overtaken by that day while alive, that place makes manifest which I mentioned to the Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians IV. 15, 17; therefore he speaks ambiguously: ἐὰν καταλυθῇ, and ἔιγε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι. Whichever shall happen, he says, we shall not be defrauded of our reward.

Cajetan, Estius, and others, along with Tertullian in his book on the Resurrection of the Flesh, report this sense: that the Apostle speaks conditionally—if indeed we are found clothed, not naked—because in truth some will be found clothed, but others naked. For the elect who will be survivors at the coming of the Lord will be found clothed with a body; but those who have departed from this life before that time will be found stripped of the body. Whereby it will come to pass that these indeed are clothed with a body through resurrection, with the garment of glory simultaneously approaching; but those are only super-clothed with glory, inasmuch as they were not found naked, but still clothed with the body, and not to be despoiled of it. Cf. 1 Cor. XV and 1 Thess. IV. To others, however, it is agreeable that the nakedness of faith and works is included; Paulinus, Ep. V to Severus: If indeed, being despoiled of the body, we are not found naked of work. Thus also Ambrosiaster and Erasmus, concerning what kind of garments in Gal. III. 27, Col. III, and Apoc. XVI. 15. Blessed Hunnius also approves this sense: that the incredulous are excluded from the κοινωνίᾳ of this heavenly glory, who are naked, that is, void of true faith, neither commended by a wedding garment, nor having put on Jesus Christ and His innocence and justice, by which their sins might be covered before GOD. Therefore, this benefit is declared to be prepared only for those who are found clothed, not naked. And Blessed Balduinus: Those are clothed, however, who have put on Christ by faith in baptism, Gal. III. 27; this is that white garment which Christ commands those who are naked by nature to seek from Him, so that the confusion of their nakedness may not appear, Apoc. III; finally, this is that wedding garment by which we may appear with honor at the Royal wedding, Matt. XXII. The Apostle therefore compares the external garment with the internal, that is, the glorious body with which we shall be clothed in the resurrection, with faith in Christ, which we received in baptism; without the latter, no one can become a participant in the former: for the unfaithful will not rise to glory, but to ignominy. The explanation of Blessed Anselm is brought forward at the same time: If indeed in that resurrection we are not found naked of Christ, but clothed with Christ: for immortality will profit only those who, when they have been clothed with a body, shall be found clothed with Christ, that is, surrounded by the garment of justice. Paul could not have thought that he would be among those whom the day of the Lord would overtake alive, because he knew that the Anti-Christ would come first, before the day of the Lord drew near, 2 Thessal. II. 13. Nor does the Apostle speak ambiguously about that nakedness, as if he doubted his own perseverance in faith; but the statement is conditional, not so much for the sake of the Apostle as for our own, so that we may strive, namely, that we not be found naked. Apoc. III. 17, 18; chapter XVI. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἔιγε κὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι ὐ γυμνὶ ἐυρεθησόμεθα) Id est, si nos iste dies deprehendat cum corpore, non exutos à corpore, si erimus inter mutandos, non inter mortuos. Nam ita existimasse Paulum, fieri posse ut ipse & qui ejus- dem erant temporis vivi ab illo die deprehenderentur, ma- nifestum facit locus ille, quem dixi ad Corinthios & primo Thessal. IV. 15. 17. ideo ambigue loquitur: ἐὰν καταλυθῇ, & ἔιγε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι. Utrumvis futurum est, inquit, non fraudabimur nostro præmio.

Tradunt hunc sensum Cajetanus, Estius & alii cum Tertulliano libr. de resurr. Carn. Apostolum idcirco loqui conditionate, si tamen vestiti, non nu- di inveniamur, quia revera quidam vestiti inve- nientur, alii vero nudi. Nam electi qui superstites erunt in adventu Domini, reperientur vestiti cor- pore: Qui vero ante illud tempus ex hac vita mi- graverint, invenientur corpore nudati. Quo fiet, ut hi quidem induantur corpore per resurrectionem, simul accedente indumento gloriæ: Illi vero tantum superinduantur gloria, utpote non nudi inventi; sed corpore adhuc vestiti, nec eo spoliandi. Conf. 1. Cor. XV. & 1. Thess. IV. Aliis tamen includi nuditatem fidei & operum, consentaneum est: Paulinus ep. V. ad Sever. Si tamen exspoliati corpore non nudi inveniamur ab opere. Ita & Ambrosiaster Erasmus, de qualibus vestimentis Gal. III. 27. Col. III. & Apoc. XVI. 15. Quem sensum etiam probat B. Hun- nius: Secludi à κοινωνίᾳ gloriæ hujus cœlestis incre- dulos, qui nudi sunt, id est veræ fide vacui, neque commendati veste nuptiali, nec induti Jesum Chri- stum ejusque innocentiam & justitiam, qua tege- rentur illorum peccata coram DEO. Solis ergo his qui induti non nudi reperiuntur, hoc tantum para- tum beneficium fore perhiberi. Et B. Balduinus: Vestiti autem sunt, qui fide Christum in baptismo induerunt Gal. III. 27. hoc est vestimentum illud album, quod Christus eos, qui natura nudi sunt, à se petere jubet, ut non appareat confusio nuditatis suæ Apoc. III. hæc denique est vestis illa nuptialis, qua in nuptiis Regiis cum honore comparemus Matth. XXII. Confert ergo Apostolus vestimentum externum cum interno, hoc est corpus gloriosum, cum quo in- duemur in resurrectione, cum fide in Christum, quam accepimus in baptismo, illius sine hoc nemo parti- ceps fieri potest: Nam infideles non ad gloriam re- surgent, sed ad ignominiam. Adducta simul B. Ans- helmi explicatio ne: Si tamen in illa resurrectione vestiti corpore non inveniamur nudi Christo, sed Christum induti: Illis enim solis proderit immorta- litas, qui cum fuerint induti corpore, vestiti Christo invenientur, hoc est indumento justitiæ circumdati. Non potuit Paulus existimare, se fore inter eos, quos vivos deprehensurus esset dies Domini, quia noverat, venturũ prius Anti-Christum, antequam dies Domini immineret 2. Thessal. II. 13. Nec am- bigue de illa nuditate loquitur Apostolus, ac si dubitaret de sua in fide perseverantia; sed con- ditionata est sententia non tam Apostoli, quam no- stri causa, ut nempe annitamur, ne nudi invenia- mur. Apoc. III. 17. 18. cap. XVI. 18.

## 5:4
Verse 4. For we who are in the tabernacle do groan, being burdened) He repeats what he had said, and adds the reason why they groan, οἱ ὄντες, while we tarry. Thus Ruth I. 4, וישבו שם. In the Greek, καὶ ἦσαν ἐκεῖ.

Ἐφ᾽ ὧ ὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπενδύσασθαι) This saying is comparative. We prefer not to be stripped of this body, but by a change to be super-clothed with an immortal body. You prefer to gain death.

Ἵνα καταποθῇ τὸ θνητὸν ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς) That the mortal may be consumed by the immortal. The Hebrew book speaks thus, which is called the juice of pomegranates. Namely, without pain.

It is not a repetition, but an Antanaclasis. Concerning natural desire, because we all abhor death as a dissolution of nature, and would prefer not to be stripped but to be immediately super-clothed with glory, through the commutation of mortality into immortality, most explain it; some think these are to be distinguished from those things which precede in verse 2. It seems, says Blessed Balduinus, that he here uses the word 'groaning' a little differently than above. There it was of one rejoicing, here of one grieving. For there he was dealing with the desire for future glory, which they desire with sighs: here with the grief which is from the separation of the soul from the body, which occurs in death. For the desire of the soul for the body is natural: therefore the grief in the dissolution of the soul from the body is also natural. Therefore a man would prefer not to be despoiled, but to be super-clothed; that is, he would prefer that without any death the body be immediately changed and glorified, as was done to Elijah and Enoch, and will happen to those who are found alive on the last day, in whom the immortality of eternal life will absorb the mortality of their bodies in one breath, as it were, without any sense of pain. We who still dwell, thus holds Blessed Hunnius, in this earthly tabernacle of our body, groan for a twofold reason. First, because as long as we carry it about, we feel ourselves burdened, and affected by the troubles that follow as effects. Then, we also groan because we cannot reach that immortal glory unless this mortal body is stripped off through the intervention of death. We, however, abhorring death by a certain sense of nature, prefer to be clothed upon rather than unclothed, that is, we prefer mortality to be swallowed up by life without the intervention of death, just as happened to Enoch and Elijah, and will happen on the last day to those who will be survivors at the coming of the Lord, whose bodies will be transformed without death in a moment, mortality, of course, being swallowed up into life and corruption into incorruptibility. Those things seem opposed to one another, that we groan for the heavenly habitation v. 2 and that we groan and do not wish to be stripped of the body v. 4, which nevertheless must be laid aside so that we may possess the heavenly habitation v. 4. But those groanings are different. There are the groanings of grace on account of the desire for eternal life, which is from the Holy Spirit; here are the groanings of nature on account of the fear of death. The holy man, says Gregory the Great in Cornelius à Lapide, when he sees that he is approaching his passion, is both shaken by the infirmity of his nature and strengthened by the solidity of his hope, and he trembles at near death, and yet he exults because by dying he lives more truly. For one cannot pass to the kingdom unless death is interposed: And therefore by confessing he as it were doubts, and by doubting he as it were trusts, and rejoicing he fears, and fearing he rejoices. And although ordinarily we cannot aspire to eternal life and glory without the intervention of death: The examples of Enoch and Elijah, to whom the faithful who will be caught up alive on the day of the Lord were twins, teach that this can be done by the extraordinary grace of God. Thus, therefore, Paul and Timothy, abhorring death by nature, would also prefer not to be unclothed through death, but to be clothed upon through change and the consumption of the mortal by life, not wishing to experience death, but to be anticipated by life, explains Tertullian, book V against Marcion, chapter 12.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ γὰρ οἱ ὄντες ἐν τῷ σκήνει στενάζομεν βαρύμενοι) Repetit quod dixerat, & addit causam cur gemant οἱ ὄντες dum moramur. Sic Ruth, I. 4. וישבו שם In Græco, καὶ ἦσαν ἐκεῖ.

Ἐφ᾽ ὧ ὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπενδύσασθαι) Dictum hoc comparate. Malumus non exui corpore hoc, sed per- mutationem superindui corpore immortali. Maluntis mortem lucrifacere.

Ἵνα καταποθῇ τὸ θνητὸν ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς) Ut consumatur mortale ab immortali. Ita loquitur & liber Hebræus, qui dicitur succus malorum granatorum. Nempe sine dolore.

Non repetitio est, sed Antanaclasis. De desi- derio naturali, quod abhorremus omnes mortem ceu dissolutionem naturæ, & mallemus non exui sed gloria statim superindui, per commutationem mortalitatis in immortalitatem plerique expli- cant, ab iis, quæ v.2. præcedunt, hæc distinguenda censent nonnulli. Videtur, inquit B. Balduinus, hic paulo aliter usurpare vocem ingemiscendi, quam supra. Ibi lætantis erat, hic dolentis. Ibi enim de desiderio futuræ gloriæ agebat, quam cum suspiriis desiderant: Hic de dolore, qui est ex separatione animæ à corpore, quæ sit in morte. Nam desiderium animæ ad corpus naturale est: naturalis ergo quoque est dolor in dissolutione animæ à corpore. Ideo mal- let homo non expoliari, sed supervestiri; hoc est mallet, ut absque ulla morte corpus statim immute- tur, & glorificetur, quemadmodum Eliæ & Enocho factum, & iis eveniet, qui in die novissimo reperi- entur vivi, in quibus æternæ vitæ immortalitas, corporum mortalitatem uno quasi haustu absque ullo sensu doloris absorbebit. Nos qui adhuc degimus, ita habet B. Hunnius, in terreno hoc tabernaculo corporis nostri, gemina de causa ingemiscimus. Pri- mo quia quamdiu illud circumferimus, sentimus nos gravatos, & eorum, quæ ut effecta consequun- tur molestia affectos. Deinde, ingemiscimus etiam, quod ad immortalem illam gloriam pertingere non valemus nisi mortis interventu exuatur hoc mor- tale corpus. Nos vero quodam naturæ sensu à mor- te abhorrentes præoptamus superindui quam exui, hoc est malumus absorberi mortalitatem à vita sine mortis interventu, quemadmodum contigit Heno- cho & Eliæ, & in novissimo die continget his, qui superstites erunt in adventu Domini, quorum cor- pora citra mortem transmutabuntur in momento, mortalitate nimirum in vitam & corruptione in incorruptibilitatem absorpta. Videntur illa sibi op- posita, quod ingemiscamus habitationem cælestem v.2. & quod ingemiscamus & nolimus expoliari corpore v. 4. quod tamen deponendum est, ut cæ- lestem habitationem possideamus v. 4. Sed gemi- tus illi diversi sunt. Illic gemitus gratiæ sunt ob de- siderium vitæ æternæ, quod à Spiritu S. est; hic gemitus naturæ ob formidinem mortis. Vir san- ctus, inquit Gregorius Magnus apud Cornelium à Lapide, cum passioni se appropinquare conspicit, & naturæ suæ infirmitate concutitur, & spei suæ soli- ditate roboratur, & de vicina morte trepidat, & tamen, quod moriendo verius vivat, exultat. Ad regnum quippe non potest, nisi interposita morte transire: Et idcirco confitendo quasi ambigit, & quasi ambigendo confidit, & gaudens metuit, & me- tuens gaudet. Et licet ordinarie sine interventu mortis non possimus adspirare ad æternam vitam, & gloriam: Fieri tamen id posse extraordinaria. Dei gratia, exempla Enochi & Eliæ docent, quibus gemini erant fideles, quos vivos apprehendet dies Domini. Sic ergo naturæ abhorrentes mortem Paulus & Timotheus, mallent quoque non exui per mortem, sed superindui per commutationem, & absumptionem mortalis à vita, nolentes mortem experiri, sed vita præveniri, exponit Tertullianus libr. V. contra Marc. cap. 12.

## 5:5
Vers. 5. Ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς ἀυτὸ τοῦτο Θεὸς) He who prepared us for this very thing, namely through the knowledge of his Gospel. Thus the Hebrew עשׂה often signifies ἑτοιμάζειν, and is sometimes translated thus. See also Deut. XXXII. 6, where עשׂה is explained by כּוּן.

He prepared us both in the primeval creation unto immortality, namely in our first parents; then in the reparation made through Christ, to which both the merit of redemption, because the whole man was freed by the death of Christ from the power of the Devil, death, and hell 1 Cor. XV, and the benefit of conversion, by which we are regenerated to eternal life, and restored through the indwelling Holy Spirit to blessed resuscitation Rom. VIII. 11, pertains.

Who also gave us the earnest of the Spirit.) That Spirit, who is given by God to believers, is as it were a down payment of that fully spiritual life. See above I. 22. This Genitive is also placed exegetically. For the Spirit himself is the earnest. And here the particle 'is' is again understood, as above I. 21. IV. 6.

The Holy Spirit not only prepares us by his gracious indwelling for the resurrection of our bodies; but also seals this hope in us, nay, is an earnest of heavenly life, promised not to the soul only, but to the whole man, for which not the soul only, but the whole man is prepared by GOD. Estius, however, wrongly restricts this to the ministers of the Word alone.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς ἀυτὸ τοῦτο Θεὸς) Qui nos ad hoc præparavit, per Evangelii nempe sui co- gnitionem. Sic עשׂה Hebræum sæpe significat ἑτοι- μάζειν, & sic vertitur interdum. Vide & Deut. XXXII. 6. ubi עשׂה exponitur per כּוּן.

Præparavit nos tum in primæva ad immorta- litatem creatione, in primis nempe parentibus; tum in reparatione per Christum facta, ad quam & meritum redemptionis, quia totus homo per mortem Christi è potestate Diaboli, mortis, & in- ferni liberatus est 1. Cor. XV. & beneficium conver- sionis, qua regeneramur ad vitam æternam, & re- stauramur per Spiritum Sanctum inhabitantem ad beatam resuscitationem Rom. IIX. 11. pertinet.

Ὁ καὶ δὺς ἡμῖν τὸν ἀῥῥαβῶνα τῦ πνεύματος.) Spiritus ille, qui à Deo credentibus datur, est velut promutuum vitæ illius plene spiritualis. Vide supra I. 22. Est & hic Geni- tivus positus ἐξηγητικῶς. Nam ipse Spiritus est arrhabo. Et subauditur hic rursus particula est, ut supra I. 21. IV. 6.

Spiritus Sanctus non solum gratiosa inhabita- tione nos præparat ad corporum nostrorum re- surrectionem; sed etiam obsignat hanc spem in no- bis, imo arrha est vitæ cœlestis, non animæ tan- tum; sed toti homini promissæ, ad quam non ani- ma tantum; sed totus homo præparatur à DEO. Perperam autem id Estius ad solos ministros Verbi restringit.

## 5:6
Verse 6. Being confident therefore always) We must again understand 'we are'. For thus the Hebrews are accustomed to place participles without a verb for a verb of the present tense, which the Hebrews do not have in verbs. We are of good courage.

And knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord) That is, we are away from his sight: like pilgrims who are absent from their brothers.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Θαῥῥῦντες ὖν πάντοτε) Subaudiendum rursum, sumus. Sic enim solent Hebræi Participia sine verbo po- nere pro verbo præsentis temporis, quod Hebræi in verbis non habent. Sumus bono animo.

Καὶ εἰδότες, ὅτι ἐνδημῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἐκδημῦμεν ἀπὸ Κυρίε) Id est, à conspectu ipsius absumus: ut peregrini, qui à fratribus suis absunt.

## 5:7
Verse 7. For we walk by faith, and not by sight) This is to be read as a parenthesis. The sense is: we order our life (for that is what the Hebrew 'halakh' means) by faith. We have not yet attained the thing seen. 'Eidos' is the thing itself. Num. XI. 8. Similar sense Rom. VIII. 24. 1 Cor. XIII. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατῦμεν, κὰι ὐ διὰ εἴδες) Hoc per parenthesin legendum est. Sensus est vitam nostram componimus (id enim הלך Hebræis) per fidem. Rem vero visam consequuti nondum sumus. Εἶδος תמונה est res ipsa. Num XI. 8. Par sensus Rom. VIII. 24. 1. Cor. XIII. 12.

## 5:8
V. 8. But we are confident) He repeats what he had begun to say, as is sometimes done, the parenthesis being finished.

And we are well pleased rather to be absent from the body, and to be at home with the Lord) We prefer it, namely if we look only at our own condition, as is explained Phil. I. 3.

The Vulgate rendered 'tharruntes' as 'audentes' (daring). But 'tharsos' is rather confidence and boldness. Erasmus explains it: 'Of good courage.' Pilgrimage, however, is designated in a twofold way: First, from the Lord, while we are here in a mortal body: not that the Lord is absent from us, who dwells in the faithful John XIV. 23, 2 Cor. VI. 16, and is with us until the end of the age Matt. XXVIII. 20, nor that we are absent from the Lord: who in the Lord live, and move, and have our being Acts XVII. 28, naturally: and even in him we live and are spiritually Gal. II. 20, John XIV. 20, but that we are still strangers to the visible presence of the Lord and to the intuitive vision of GOD; nor are we so with the Lord that we see his glory John XVII. 24, in which respect the Apostle desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ Phil. I. 2, and it was promised to the thief on the cross, 'Today you will be with me in Paradise' Luke XXIII. 43. The second pilgrimage is from the body, when the soul shall be released from the body, about to journey from this world, of which we are inhabitants, to the Lord, so that it may be present with him forever, from whom, however, it sojourns in such a way that it will inhabit its own glorious body again on the last day, and will never leave it. Those words, 'we walk by faith and not by sight,' some supplement thus: 'and we do not stand by sight': because to walk is only for travelers; but to stand is for the blessed: But there is no need for that ellipsis. For Apoc. III. 4, the blessed are also said to walk in white, and Apoc. XIV. 4, to follow the Lamb wherever they go. It is said, therefore, of the blessed both to walk and to stand before the throne of God Apoc. VII. 9, and to sit on the throne of Christ Apoc. III. 21. All those things befit him in the phrasing of Scripture, without any diminution of blessedness. To walk by faith is to lead a spiritual life in such a way, above all, that faith is the moderator of all spiritual actions and motions, and thus, in those things which must be done in common life, we are also governed by the eye of faith. Because whatever is not of faith is sin Rom. XIV. 23. Here, however, special regard is had to that in which faith and sight are opposed to each other, as far as concerns presence with the Lord: that here in the kingdom of grace, faith indeed has the Lord present, who dwells in our hearts through faith Eph. III. 17, which is of 'things not seen.' But there in the kingdom of glory, we shall have him present according to sight, or visible presence, about to see him face to face 1 Cor. XIII. 12. From which it is manifest that, since we are pilgrims from the body, we walk by sight, and are present with the Lord, we shall not finally see the Lord by sight after the resurrection of the bodies, for then the soul will not be a pilgrim from the body, but will inhabit its own returned glorious body. Purgatorial fire is also extinguished in this way, since the faithful, journeying from the body, are not finally relegated to the punishments of purgatory, and to the satisfaction for sins to be endured there; but are with the Lord, and enjoy his blessed vision. But lest the Calvinists conclude from this pilgrimage the absence of Christ according to his human nature, the blessed Hunnius rightly warned that the word 'to journey' denotes only that absence which is opposed to the visible and manifest conversation of the blessed with Christ, by which they will always be with the Lord 1 Thess. IV. 17, about to see him face to face, just as he is 1 Cor. XIII. 12, 1 John III. 2. And he openly hints at this with the following words: For we walk by faith; that 'to be away' is to be understood in this way, that in this age we do not yet behold or look upon God and Christ; but he has Christ as an object invisible to us in this age, and in this way absent, that is, not yet appearing. Whence it is clear that this pilgrimage is to be referred more to the diversity of condition than to an interval of place. In which sense we are said to be pilgrims not only from the humanity of Christ but also from his very Deity, and thus from the whole Trinity. Conf. Eccl. XII.7.

Latin:

V. 8. Θαῥῥῦμεν δὲ) Repetit, quod dicere cœperat, ut fieri interdum solet, absoluta parenthesi.

Καὶ ἐυδοκῦμεν μᾶλλον ἐκδημῆσαι ἐκ τῦ σώματος, κὰι ἐνδη- μῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον) Malumus, nempe si nostram tan- tum conditionem respicimus, ut explicatur Phil. I. 3.

Θαῥῥῦντες Vulgata audentes reddidit. Sed θάρσος fiducia potius est, & confidentia. Erasmus expo- nit: Bono animo. Peregrinatio autem gemina de- signatur: Prima à Domino, dum hic sumus in mor- tali corpore: non quod Dominus à nobis absit, qui habitat in fidelibus Joh. XIV. 23. 2. Cor. VI. 16. & nobiscum est usque ad consummationem seculi Matth. XXIX. 20. nec quod nos à Domino ab- simus: qui in Domino sumus, movemur, & vivi- mus Act. XVII. 28. naturaliter: etiam in eodem vivi- mus & sumus spiritualiter Gal. II. 20. Joh. XIV. 20. sed quod à visibili Domini præsentia adhuc alieni si- mus & ab intuitiva DEI visione; nec ita sumus apud Dominum, ut ejus gloriâ videamus Joh. XVII. 24. quo respectu dissolvi optat Apostolus & esse cum Domino Phil. I. 2. & latroni in cruce promitte- batur, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso Luc. XXIII. 43. Altera peregrinatio est à corpore, cum solvetur ani- ma à corpore, peregrinatura ex hoc mundo, cu- jus incolæ sumus, ad Dominum, ut præsens ei sit in æternum, à quo tamen ita peregrinatur, ut id in novissimo die gloriosius denuo inhabitatura, & nunquam relictura sit. Verba illa, per fidem am- bulamus & non per speciem, ita supplent nonnulli; & non per speciem stamus: quia ambulare via- torum tantum; stare autem beatorum: Sed non opus est illa ellipsi. Nam Apoc. III. 4. & beati am- bulare dicuntur in albis, & Apocal. XIV. 4. sequi agnum, quocunque iverint. Dicitur ergo de beatis & ambulare & coram throno Dei stare Apoc. VII. 9. & in throno Christi sedere Apoc. III. 21. Omnia illa ei conveniunt phrasi Scripturæ, citra diminutio- nem beatitudinis. Per fidem ambulare est ita vi- tam spiritualem imprimis ducere, ut fides sit o- mnium actionum & motuum spiritualium mode- ratrix, adeoque in iis, quæ in communi vita agen- da sunt, fidei oculo etiam gubernemur. Quia quic- quid non est ex fide, peccatum est Rom. XIV. 23. Hic vero specialiter respicitur illud, in quo fides, & species sibi opponuntur, quantum ad præsentiam apud Dominum: quod hic in regno gratiæ fides quidem Dominum præsentem habeat, qui per fidem in cordibus nostris habitat Eph. III. 17. quæ est τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων. Sed illic in regno gloriæ præsentem habituri simus secundum speciem, seu visibilem præsentiam de facie ad faciem ipsum vi- suri 1. Cor. XIII.12. è quo manifestum est, quia cum peregrinamur à corpore, per speciem ambulamus, & præsentes sumus apud Dominum, nos non demum per speciem visuros Dominum post resurrectio- nem corporum, tum enim non peregrinabitur anima à corpore, sed corpus suum gloriosum red- ditum inhabitabit. Extinguitur etiam ita ignis pur- gatorius, quum fideles à corpore peregrinantes non demum ad pœnas purgatorii relegentur, & ad satisfactionem pro peccatis ibi exantlandam; sed apud Dominum sint, ejusque beata visione fru- antur. Ne autem Calviniani ex hac peregrinatio- ne à Domino absentiam Christi secundum huma- nam naturam concludant, recte monuit B. Hun- nius vocabulum peregrinandi tantum eam nota- re absentiam, quæ opponitur visibili & manifestæ beatorum conversationi cum Christo, qua semper erunt apud Dominum 1. Thess. IV. 17. visuri illum à facie ad faciem, sicuti est 1. Cor. XIII. 12. 1. Joh. III. 2. Idque palam innuit verbis sequentibus: Per fidem enim ambulamus; illud peregrinari sic acci- piendum esse, quod in hoc seculo Deum & Christum nondum intuemur aut suspicimus; sed objecti vice habet Christum nobis in hoc seculo invisibilem, & hoc modo absentem, id est, nondum apparentem. Unde liquet, peregrinationem hanc magis ad diver- sitatem conditionis quam ad loci intervallum esse re- ferendam. Quo sensu non modo à Christi humanitate sed ab ejusdem quoque Deitate, adeoque à tota Trini- tate peregrinari dicimur. Conf. Eccl. XII.7.

## 5:9
Vers. 9. Διὸ καὶ φιλοτιμούμεθα, εἴτε ἐνδημοῦντες, εἴτε ἐκδημοῦντες, εὐάρεστοι αὐτῷ εἶναι) Wherefore, that is, because we do not doubt concerning the resurrection, we strive with all zeal (for that is what φιλοτιμεῖν means, as in Rom. XV. 20. 1. Thess. IV. 1.) that we may please Christ both now and then, now by proving our life to him, then by receiving the reward from him.

The discourse is about absence and presence not with respect to the Lord; but by reason of the body, which is manifest from the Greek text, where it treats of indwelling and pilgrimage: Whether ἐνδημοῦντες, that is, inhabiting the body, or ἐκδημοῦντες, or being pilgrims, namely, v. 8. ἐκ τοῦ σώματος, out of the body or away from the body, so that whether living (as Estius rightly says) in this domicile of the body, or being pilgrims away from it, through death, that is, truly dead, we may please Christ the Lord and be accepted. Therefore, some Latins less correctly refer absence and presence to Christ, in this sense: Whether absent from Christ, or present to him. Nor must it be said here with Estius that we please Christ in this life, whereby we may merit the heavenly reward; nor can we dispose ourselves for that reward after death: But eternal life is a χάρισμα, a purely gratuitous gift of GOD in Christ Jesus Rom. VI. v. ult. After death we obtain the reward immediately, no place then remains for disposition, because through death we pass into life. He who believes, says Christ in John V. 24. μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν: He has passed over (in the Perfect, on account of the certainty of the thing) from death into life. Furthermore, the Apostle, while he says that he strives with all zeal that he may please the Lord, which is not to be restricted only to faith and diligence in executing the ministry, as Estius wishes, nor is it something proper to ministers of the word, but common to all the faithful, whose it is to fight the good fight, to finish the course, to keep the faith 2 Tim. IV. 7. whether he inhabits the body, or is a stranger from the body, he wills this, he devotes effort to this, that whether he lives, or dies, he may please the Lord; That he may live to the Lord & die to the Lord, and living & dying may be the Lord's Rom. XIV. 8. He who in death or dying pleases the Lord, that is, departs in faith, without which it is impossible to please GOD Heb. XI. 6. he after death cannot but please the Lord: Because he who finally believes in Him, does not perish, but is saved, John III. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Διὸ καὶ φιλοτιμούμεθα, εἴτε ἐνδημοῦντες, εἴτε ἐκδη- μοῦντες, εὐάρεστοι αὐτῷ εἶναι) Quapropter, id est, quia de re- surrectione non dubitamus, omni studio contendimus (id enim est φιλοτιμεῖν, ut Rom. XV. 20. 1. Thess. IV. 1.) ut & nunc & tunc Christo placeamus, nunc vitam nostram ipsi probando, tunc ab ipso præmium accipiendo.

De absentia, & præsentia sermo est non respe- ctu Domini; sed ratione corporis, quod è Græco textu, ubi de inhabitatione & de peregrinatione agitur manifestum est: Sive ἐνδημοῦντες inhabitan- tes scilicet corpus, sive ἐκδημοῦντες seu peregrinan- tes nempe, v. 8. ἐκ τοῦ σώματος, extra corpus vel à corpore, ut sive degentes (ut recte Estius) in hoc domicilio corporis, sive ab eo, per mortem, pere- grinantes, id est, vere mortui, Christo Domino placeamus acceptique simus. Minus recte ergo Latini quidam absentiam, & præsentiam ad Chri- stum referunt, hoc sensu: Sive absentes à Christo, sive illi præsentes. Neque dicendum hic cum Eslio, Christo placere nos in hac vita, quo mereamur cæleste præmium; neque post mortem nos dispo- nere possumus ad illud præmium: Sed vita æterna χάρισμα mere gratuitum DEI donum est in Christo Jesu Rom. VI. v. ult. Post mortem consequimur actutum præmium, nullus tum superest locus dis- positioni, quia per mortem transimus in vitam. Qui credit, inquit Christus Joh. V. 24. μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν: Pertransiit (in Perfe- cto, ob rei certitudinem) ex morte in vitam. Por- ro Apostolus dum contendere omni studio sese dicit, ut Domino placeat, quod non tantum restrin- gendum ad fidem & sedulitatem in exequendo mi- nisterio, ut Estius vult, nec aliquod proprium est verbi ministris, sed commune omnibus fidelibus, quorum est bonum certamen certare, cursum con- summare, fidem servare 2. Tim. IV. 7. sive corpus inhabitet, sive peregrinetur à corpore, id vult, id operam se dare, ut sive vivat, sive moriatur, Do- mino placeat; Ut vivat Domino & moriatur Do- mino, ac vivus & moriens Domini sit Rom. XIV. 8. Qui in morte vel moriens Domino placet, hoc est, in fide decedit, sine qua impossibile est DEO placere Ebr. XI. 6. is post mortem Domino non potest non placere: Quia qui finaliter in ipsum credit, non perit, sed salvatur, Joh. III. 16.

## 5:10
V. 10. For we must all be made manifest) That is, to stand παραστῆναι Rom. XIV. 10. נלה to be seen. Before the judgment seat of Christ) As those are accustomed to do, who plead a case, to stand in a conspicuous place before a judge.

These things do not allow us to doubt that in the preceding verses the Apostle sets himself as an example not only to the ministers of the Word, and in the roles of ministers, but to all Christians, and in those things which are common to the faithful. The reason, however, why we ought to be εὐάρεστοι to the Lord, is sought from the future manifestation before the tribunal of the Lord, which is similarly rendered Rom. XIV. 10. For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Moreover, it is more to be Φανερωθῆναι manifested, than to be παραστῆναι presented. For many are presented to judges, who are not manifested, and therefore Theodoret notes that the Apostle did not say to be presented; but to be manifested. Here the Apostle uses the word Φανερωθῆναι, not because we are to be manifested to Christ, who knows all things John XXI. 17. to whose eyes all things are open Heb. IV. 13. But because that manifestation of ours must take place in the public view of all Angels and men: because, as Lyranus holds: That judgment will appear just to all, with each seeing all the good and evil of others. Whence 1 Cor. IV. 5. He is said to be about to bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and to manifest the counsels of the hearts, not to Himself certainly, but to others. Nor indeed can we be said to be manifested then properly to the Judge, to whom we are always manifest; But before the judge. By the tribunal of Christ, however, no material or visible throne is denoted; but because it is a judicial act, it is depicted with similar words; nor is it anything other than the judicial power of Christ, so that before the tribunal of Christ is nothing other than before the judgment of Christ.

That each one may receive the things of the body) Thus the best copies have it, and thus the Latin reads, not through the body. The things of the body are those which are owed to the body. Just as justice is said to render to each his own, which is often that which is fitting. Each one will bring back a reward or punishment, which will be owed to his body, that is, to himself.

According to what he has done, whether good or evil) Suitably to the life which he has led.

The original Greek text is rashly corrected from the Latin. It is evident that the Greek reading was already accepted in the time of Tertullian from his book on the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 43. That each one may report through the body what he has done: and book V against Marcion, ch. 12. what he has committed through the body: And also in the time of Augustine, book XVII of the City of God, ch. 4, and elsewhere, having it thus, according to those things which he has done through the body. Nor does the Syriac read otherwise, rendering: That it may be repaid to each one in his body, and what has been done in it. The word to receive does not imply any compensation, but a simple reception, just as the word to take, for which it is used Gen. XXXVIII. 20. Nor will men receive those things which are owed. For to the wicked, punishment and condemnation are indeed owed; but to the pious, eternal life is not owed; because the wages of sin is death, but eternal life is a gift of God in Christ Jesus Rom. VI. 23. That therefore, that each one may receive the things of the body (namely, the things done) according to what he has done, whether good or evil, so that each one may receive what pertains to those things which have been done through the body, or what he has done, according to what he has acted, whether good or evil, does not import a compensation of both good and evil, or a retribution of good and evil according to merits, as the Papists contend that man is justified by works. For merit, it is required that that by which one ought to merit be an undue work, and perfect, and proportioned to the reward, and so this is owed to the work out of justice, as Angelus de Clavasio says, Merit is an action by which it comes about that it is just for something to be given to him who acts. Whence Bellarmine, book V on Justification, ch. 1, establishes that retribution which, according to commutative justice, regards an absolute equality between works and the reward. But good works are neither undue, Luke XVII. 10, nor perfect or proportioned to the reward of eternal life Rom. VIII. 2 Cor. IV. 17, nor is there any retribution from commutative justice, but a remuneration from mere grace Rom. IV. 8, ch. XI. 6, 35.

Moreover, from this passage it is rightly gathered against the Socinians that the same body, in which and through which those things were done, is to be resurrected, so that in it they may bring back those things which they have done through it, whether good or evil. But the Pelagians wrongly concluded from the same that infants have no sin, because they exercise or do nothing through the body. For infants are not only infected with original sin in soul and body: But also as soon as they live, they are subject to actual sins in their own body. For original sin is never idle; but always pushes forth evil fruits like an evil tree, and every thought, every imagination of the human heart is only evil all the days of the life of man. Gen. VI and VIII.

THE LATTER PART. Explaining the satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ.

Latin:

V. 10. Τὺς γὰρ πάντας ἡμᾶς φανερωθῆναι δεῖ) Id est, stare παραστῆναι Rom. XIV. 10. נלה conspici. Ἔμπροσθεν τῦ βήματος τῦ χριστῦ) Ut solent, qui causam dicunt, stare in loco conspicuo coram judice.

Hæc non sinunt nos dubitare in antecedentibus exemplam se sistere Apostolum non tantum mini- stris Verbi, & in partibus ministrorum, sed omni- bus Christianis, inque iis, quæ fidelibus in com- muni conveniunt. Causa autem, cur Domino εὐάρεστοι esse debemus, petita est à futura manife- statione coram tribunali Domini, quæ similiter red- ditur Rom. XIV. 10. Πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι τῦ χρισῦ. Cæterum plus est Φανερωθῆναι manifestari, quam παραστῆναι. Multi enim judici- bus sistuntur, qui non manifestantur, ideoque Theo- doretus annotat, Apostolum non dixisse sisti; sed manifestari. Hic voce Φανερωθῆναι utitur Aposto- lus, non quod Christo manifestandi simus, qui novit omnia Joh. XXI. 17. cujus oculis omnia sunt aperta Ebr. IV. 13. Sed quod in Panegyrico con- spectu omnium Angelorum, & hominum fieri de- beat illa nostri Φανέρωσις: quia, ut Lyranus ha- bet: Judicium illud apparebit omnibus justum, singulis videntibus omnia bona & mala aliorum. Unde 1. Corinth. IV. 5. illuminaturus dicitur abs- condita tenebrarum, & manifestaturus consilia cordium, non sibi utique, sed aliis. Neque vero tunc proprie Judici manifestandi dici possumus, cui semper manifesti sumus; Sed coram judice. Per tribunal autem Christi non thronus aliquis materialis, aut visibilis denotatur; sed quia actus judicialis est, similibus verbis depingitur; nec aliud est, quam potestas Christi judiciaria, ut ante tri- bunal Christi nihil aliud sit, quàm coram Christi judicio.

Ἱνα κομίσηται ἕκαστος τὰ ἴδια τῦ σώματος) Sic habent optima exemplaria, & sic legit Latinus, non διὰ τῦ σώμα- τος. Ἰδια sunt ea, quæ corpori debentur. Sicut justitia di- citur suum cuique reddere, quod sæpe est τὸ ἁρμόζον. Re- feret quisque præmium vel pœnam, quod corpori ipsius, id est, ipsi debebitur.

Πρὸς ἣ ἔπραξεν, εἴτε ἀγαθὸν, εἴτε κακόν) Convenienter vitæ, quam duxerit.

Temere textus Originalis corrigitur Græcus è Latina. Græcam lectionem jam tempore Tertul- liani receptam fuisse è libr. de resurr. Carn. c. 43. constat. Ut unusquisque reportet per corpus, quæ gessit: & libr. V. contra Marc. cap. 12. quæ per cor- pus admisit: Nec non Augustini tempore libr. XVII. de Civitate Dei cap. 4. & alibi ita habentis, secundum ea, quæ per corpus gessit. Neque aliter legit Syrus reddens: Ut rependetur unicuique in corpore suo, & quod factum est in ipso. Verbum κομίζειν non infert aliquam compensationem, sed simplicem acceptionem, uti verbum לקח, pro quo adhibetur Gen. XXXIIX. 20. Nec ea recipient ho- mines, quæ debentur. Impiis quidem debetur pœ- na, condemnatio; non autem piis debetur æterna vita; quia peccati quidem stipendium mors est, vi- ta autem æterna est χάρισμα Θεῦ, Donum Dei in Christo Jesu Rom. VI. 23. Illud ergo ἵνα κομίσηται ἕκαστος τὰ διὰ τῦ σώματος (scilicet πραχθέντα) πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν εἴτε ἀγαθὸν, εἴτε κακὸν, ut accipiat unusquisque quod ad ea, quæ per corpus scilicet gesta sunt, aut gessit, secundum quæ egit, sive bonum sive malum, non importat & bonorum & malorum compensationem, vel boni & mali retributionem secundum merita, uti Pontificii, operibus justificari hominem, contendunt. Ad meritum requiritur, ut id, quo mereri quis debet, opus indebitum sit, & perfectum, ac proportionatum mercedi, adeo- que ex justitia hæc debeatur operi, ut Angelus de Clavasio, Meritum dicit actionem, qua fit, ut ei, qui agit, sit justum aliquid dari. Unde Bellarmi- nus libr. V. de justific. cap. 1. retributionem eam statuit, quæ secundum justitiam commutativam absolutam æqualitatem inter opera & mercedem re- spicit. At opera bona nec indebita sunt, Luc. XVII. 10. nec perfecta aut proportionata mercedi æternæ vitæ Rom. IIX. 2. Cor. IV. 17. nec ulla est ex justitia commutativa retributio, sed ex mera gratia re- muneratio Rom. IV. 8. cap. XI. 6. 35.

Cæterum ex hoc loco adversus Socinianos recte colligitur, corpus idem, in quo & per quod illa gesta sunt, resuscitandum esse, ut in illo referant ea, quæ gesserunt per illud sive bona sive mala. Perperam verò ex eodem Pelagiani conclude- bant, infantes nullum habere peccatum, quia nihil exercent, vel faciunt per corpus. Nam infantes non modò peccato originali infecti sunt animâ & corpore: Sed & quamprimum vivunt, actuali- bus peccatis obnoxii sunt in proprio corpore. Nunquam enim otiosum est peccatum originale; sed semper malos fructus protrudit ceu arbor mala, & omnis cogitatio, omne figmentum cordis hu- mani tantum malum est omnibus diebus vitæ homi- nis. Gen. VI. & IIX.

PARS POSTERIOR. Satisfactionem & reconciliationem Christi explicans.

## 5:11
V. 11. Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord) Since therefore it is known to us what the true religion is: Which the Hebrews, circumscribing it, call the fear of the Lord, as in the proverbs often.

Beza therefore rendered poorly (although the Belgians and the Weimar theologians followed him) that terror of the Lord, as if the Apostle were shuddering at the final judgment, and were compelled by the fear of it to perform the parts of his office sincerely. This is also what the Gloss of Flacius intends. Nor indeed, as B. Hülsemann rightly warns, could the horror of the learned regarding the rigor of the future judgment be the cause of gently persuading others to accept faith in Christ, which πείθησις or gentle persuasion is called the effect of this φόβος. For which reason φόβος in this place denotes reverence, born rather from love than from the horror of a tremendous judgment, as is clear from v. 20. Whence Heinsius preferred to render it: Knowing how much the reverence due to GOD requires. To which the marginal gloss of B. Luther also tends.

Moreover, before they present that arduous and primary head of religion and the Christian faith concerning the satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ, of which Paul and Timothy were appointed heralds, in which the sum or certainly the nucleus of the Evangelical proclamation consists, and which is the foundation of the certainty of faith and the hope of eternal salvation, they preface again concerning the sincerity of their doctrine and ministry, and appeal to the testimony of GOD and the consciences of the hearers themselves, not for the sake of boasting, but for the confusion of their adversaries, and thus they protest that they seek solely the glory of GOD and the utility of the hearers.

Ἀνθρώπους πείθομεν) We take pains to persuade others to follow that religion.

Θεῷ δὲ πεφανερώμεθα) That is, we have God as a witness of this sincere purpose of ours. The past tense for any time, according to the Hebrew custom.

The Apostle seems to recount two things, in which he labors with all the contention of his soul. The first is, that by reason of his office he may persuade men to obedience toward God: The second, that by reason of his conscience he may be manifest to GOD, and may approve his whole life, and especially the course of his ministry, to the divine Majesty.

I hope also that I have been made manifest in your consciences) I do not doubt that, as far as I am concerned, your conscience also is a witness to me of such a purpose.

Latin:

V. 11. Εἰδότες οὖν τὸν φόβον τοῦ Κυρίου) Cum igitur notum nobis sit, quæ sit vera religio: Quam Hebræi circumscri- bentes vocant יראת יהוה ut in proverbiis sæpe.

Male ergò Beza reddidit (etsi eum sequuti sint Belgæ & Vinarienses) terrorem illum Domini, quasi horreat Apostolus extremum judicium, metuque illius cogatur partes officii sui sincere exequi. Quod vult & Glossa Flacii. Neque vero, rectè B. Hülsemannus monet, horror doctorum ad rigorem futuri judicii poterat esse causa blande persuadendi alios ad fidem in Christum accipiendam, quæ πεί- θησις seu persuasio blanda dicitur effectus hujus φό- βου. Quam ob rem φόβος hoc loco reverentiam, ex amore potius natam, quam ex horrore tremendi judicii notat, ut patet ex v. 20. Unde Heinsius red- dere maluit: Scientes, quantum requirat reveren- tia DEO debita. Quo etiam abit glossa margi- nalis B. Lutheri.

Cæterum antequam arduum illud & primarium religionis & fidei Christianæ caput de satisfactio- ne, & reconciliatione Christi, cujus præcones con- stituti erant Paulus & Timotheus, in quo summa vel nucleus certè Evangelici præconii consistit, quodq; fundamentum est certitudinis fidei, & spei æternæ salutis, exhibeant, de sinceritate doctrinæ suæ & ministerii iterum præfantur, & ad testimo- nium DEI, propriasque Auditorum conscientias provocant, non gloriationis, sed confusionis adver- sariorum causa, adeoque sese unicè gloriam DEI & utilitatem Auditorum quærere protestantur.

Ἀνθρώπους πείθομεν) Damus operam, ut aliis persuadea- mus eam religionem sequi.

Θεῷ δὲ πεφανερώμεθα) Id est, hujus sinceri nostri pro- positi Deum habemus testem. Præteritum pro quovis tem- pore, more Hebræo.

Duo recensere videtur Apostolus, in quibus totâ animi contentione elaboret. Primum est, ut ratione sui muneris hominibus obedientiam er- ga Deum suadeat: Alterum ut ratione suæ con- scientiæ DEO sit manifestus, omnemque suam vitam, cumprimis autem ministerii cursum di- vinæ Majestati approbet.

Ἐλπίζω δὲ κὰι ἐν ταῖς συνειδήσεσιν ὑμῶν πεφανερῶσθαι) Non dubito, quin me quod attinet etiam vestra conscientia mihi talis propositi testis sit.

## 5:12
V. 12. For we do not again commend ourselves to you) He repeats what he had said above in III. 1. Therefore he says πάλιν in this sense.
