I say again that there is no need for me to commend myself to you, you know me well enough. It is a transposition of words for πάλιν γὰρ ἑσυνισά-νομεν, and ἓ συνισάνομεν for λέγομεν ἡ συνισάνον.

But giving you an occasion of boasting on our behalf) Supply, we say these things, and understand ἀφορμὴν καυχήσεως as an occasion of great joy. Concerning the meaning of the verb καυχᾶσθαι and the nouns καυχήσεως and καυχήματος, we have already said enough.

That you may have [something] toward those who boast in appearance and not in heart) That you may have, namely, wherewith to defend my cause against those who please themselves in external things, such as learning and riches, but not in the purity of the heart, such as my actions testify. πρόσωπον is מראה in 1 Sam. XVI. 7, where the Greeks put ὄψιν, all that which among men who are wise in human things is wont to be made much of.

Most others understand this of the false Apostles, and wish them to be noted as boasting ἐν προσώπῳ in certain external things; not so much regarding riches, as regarding knowledge, eloquence, or other gifts. Theophylact: That you may have, (he says) wherewith you may boast on our behalf against such Apostles, who boast in the face, that is, for the sake of ostentation, and do everything with a certain impudent front. For they were imbued with these manners, that they would prefer piety in their countenance, but in their heart they had nothing that was sound or upright. For he does not enjoin boasting always, unless when they themselves extol themselves.

Latin:

V. 12. Οὐ γὰρ πάλιν ἑαυτὸς συνιστάνομεν ὑμῖν) Repetit quod dixerat supra III. 1. Ideo dicit πάλιν hoc sensu. Ite- rum dico non opus esse, ut me vobis commendem, satis me nostis. Est trajectio verborum pro πάλιν γὰρ ἑσυνισά-νομεν, & ἓ συνισάνομεν pro λέγομεν ἡ συνισάνον.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἀφορμὴν διδόντες ὑμῖν καυχήσεως ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) Sup- ple, hæc dicimus, & ἀφορμὴν καυχήσεως intellige, magni gaudii occasionem. De quo significatu verbi καυχᾶσθαι & nominum καυχήσεως & καυχήματος satis jam diximus.

Ἱνα ἔχητε πρὸς τὺς ἐν προσώπῳ καυχωμένες κὰι ὀυ καρδίᾳ) Ut habeatis, nempe unde causam meam tueamini adver- sus eos, qui sibi placent in rebus externis, ut eruditione & divitiis, non autem in cordis puritate, qualem mei actus testantur. πρόσωπον מראה 1. Sam. XVI. 7. ubi ὄψιν po- suere Græci, omne id, quod inter homines humana sapien- tes magni fieri solet.

De falsis Apostolis alii plerique intelligunt, eos- que ἐν προσώπῳ in externis quibusdam gloriantes notari volunt; non tam quoad divitias, quam quo- ad scientiam, facundiam, aliave dona. Theophyla- ctus: Ut habeatis, (inquit) quod nostri gratia ad- versus ejusmodi Apostolos gloriari possitis, qui in facie gloriantur, hoc est, ad ostentationem, & fronte qua- dam impudenti factitant omnia. Erant namque illi moribus hisce imbuti, ut vultu pietatem præferrent, corde vero nihil haberent, quod sanam rectumve esset. Non enim gloriandum semper injungit, nisi cum ipsos se illi extollunt.

## 5:13
V. 13. For whether we are beside ourselves, [it is] to God) The enemies of Paul slandered his ecstasies, as a sign of a mind not always composed. But Paul does not deny that ecstasies happened to him, (for it had also happened to Peter, Acts XI. 7) but he says that this happens to him for the honor of God, who even in that way illustrated Paul's ministry, below XII. 1. ἐξιστάμεθα is understood from the preceding verb. A similar way of speaking is in Rom. II. 28.

Or whether we are of sound mind, [it is] for you) Repeat again σωφρονῦμεν which is understood. Σωφρονεῖν here is to do those things which are of a man who is outside of an ecstasy. See Mark V. 15. Such I am to you, that is, for your uses, when I teach, when I write.

These things are less conveniently drawn to ecstasies. B. Hunnius more correctly paraphrases it thus: If, omitting such boasting, which the adversaries of the truth criminate as insanity, we simply do our duty: we are sane for you. For the administration of our office redounds to your advantage and salvation. That insanity is said κατὰ δόξαν is certain. Which is not wont to be judged by the adversaries in boasting, but in the sharper refutation and correction of such a one. But τὸ σωφρονεῖν pertains to sound and sober moderation. Osiander: If we deal with you with great zeal, and severely correct your errors, so that to some delicate men we seem to be insane, in that matter we are fervent for that pious zeal for the Lord our God, whose glory is at stake. But if we treat you humanely and modestly after a sharp correction, we do it for your advantage, lest you be alienated from the Gospel of Christ, or be oppressed by excessive sadness. (For it behooves a minister of the Church to be now sharp and severe, now gentle and meek, as the necessity of the hearers requires.) Whether therefore we are severe, says Paul, or meek, all that proceeds from true charity, by which we love Christ our Redeemer. For the charity of Christ urges us, that we may strenuously do our duty toward you. For we strive to win as many men as possible to this Savior, and we do this, that Christians may show themselves grateful to Christ in their manners, and indeed in their whole life. That he wished to make mention of his ecstasies

so abruptly is not likely. Nor did that easily come into the mind of any of the interpreters. Theophylact handed it down, as did Oecumenius, as having various senses; but there is nothing in them about an ecstasy. Most Latins with Augustine interpret the excess of mind as the contemplation of sublime mysteries, which exceed the capacity of the weak; but sobriety as doctrine accommodated to the vulgar understanding. But the former sense is simpler: to which Valla adds: Whether we are foolish, or whether we are wise, we are wise for ourselves. Which the comparison of chapters XI and XII also confirms: Estius expresses the same thus: Whether we are insane speaking gloriously about ourselves, we are insane for God: that is, we do this very thing for the glory of God: lest, if we, his ministers, are held in contempt by you, the doctrine preached by us be at the same time despised. Which thing would certainly redound to the contempt of GOD himself: Or if we speak humbly and modestly about ourselves, which men of sound mind are wont to do: We are such for you, that is, we do all that for your sake, accommodating ourselves to your weakness and providing examples of humility.

Latin:

V. 13. Εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέσημεν Θεῷ) Inimici Pauli ἐκστάσεις ejus calumniabantur, tanquam signum animi non semper sui compositi. At Paulus contingere sibi ἐκστάσεις non ne- gat, (nam & Petro contigerat Act. XI. 7.) sed dicit hoc sibi evenire in Dei honorem, qui etiam eo modo Pauli mini- sterium illustrabat infra XII. 1. Subintelligitur ἐξιστάμεθα ex verbo præcedenti. Simile loquendi genus Rom. II. 28.

Εἴτε σωφρονῦμεν, ὑμῖν) Repete iterum σωφρονῦμεν quod subintelligitur. Σωφρονεῖν hic est ea agere, quæ sunt ho minis, qui est extra ἔκστασιν. Vide Marci V. 15. Talis sum vobis, id est, in vestros usus, cum doceo, cum scribo.

Hæc minus commode ad ἐκστάσεις trahuntur. Rectius B. Hunnius ita παραφράζει: Si omissa tali gloriatione, quam adversarii veritatis ut insaniam criminantur, simpliciter nostrum facimus officium: Vobis sani sumus. Cedit enim in vestrum commo- dum ac salutem administratio nostri muneris. In- saniam κατὰ δόξαν dici, certum. Quæ non in glo- riatione, sed acriori etiam confutatione ac cor- rectione talis ab adversariis censeri solet. Τὸ σω- φρονεῖν autem ad sanam, ac sobriam moderatio- nem pertinet. Osiander: Si magno zelo vobiscum agimus, & errata vestra severe corrigimus, ita ut quibusdam delicatulis hominibus insanire videa- mur, ea in re pio illo zelo Domino Deo nostro infer- vimus, de cujus gloria agitur. Sin vero humaniter & modeste post acrem correptionem vos tractamus, vestri commodi gratia id facimus, ne ab Evangelio Christi abalienemini, aut nimia tristitia opprima- mini. (Ecclesiæ enim ministrum modo acrem & severum, modo lenem & mansuetum esse oportet, prout auditorum necessitas requirit.) Sive igitur se- veri sumus, inquit Paulus, sive mites, id omne à ve- ra charitate, qua Christum Redemptorem nostrum diligimus, proficiscitur. Charitas enim Christi ur- get nos, ut strenue erga vos officium nostrum fa- ciamus. Huic enim Salvatori quam plurimos ho- mines lucrifacere studemus, & hoc agimus, ut Chri- stiani sese in moribus suis, adeoque in tota sua vita Christo gratos exhibeant. Ex abrupto ita ἐκστάσεων

suarum mentionem facere voluisse, haud verisi- mile est. Nec facile id cuiquam interpretum in mentem venit. Tradidit Theophylactus, ut & Oe- cumenius varios sensus; sed nihil in illis de ἐκςάσει. Latini plerique cum Augustino mentis excessum in- terpretantur contemplationem sublimium mysterio- rum, quæ capacitatem infirmorum excedunt; sobrietatem verò doctrinam captui vulgari accom- modatam. Sed prior sensus simplicior est: cui ac- cedit Valla: Sive desipimus; sive sapimus, nobis sa- pimus. Quem etiam collatio cap. XI. & XII. con- firmat: Estius eundem ita effert: Sive insani su- mus gloriosè de nobis ipsis loquentes, Deo insani su- mus: id est, hoc ipsum facimus ad gloriam Dei: ne, si nos ejus ministri vobis habeamur contemptui, si- mul ejus doctrina per nos prædicata contemnartur. Quæ res utique cederet in ipsius DEI contemptum: Sive de nobis humiliter, ac modestè loquamur, quod solent homines sanæ mentis: Vobis tales sumus, hoc est, id totum vestri causa facimus imbecillitati vestræ nos accommodantes & humilitatis exempla præbentes.

## 5:14
V. 14. For the love of Christ constraineth us) The love which we owe to Christ compels us to do all things for the sake of God and Christians. Συνέχει is a metaphor taken from women in labor. See Luke 12:50.

The charity of Christ is to be understood not passively, as that by which he is loved by us, but actively, as that by which he himself loved us. Moreover, this most of all constrains us to pursue those things which make for the glory of God and the salvation of men. Since Christ spent his whole self for the glory of God the Father and the salvation of the human race, and wished this to be announced primarily so that we might not live for ourselves, but for him, and being reconciled to God through the death of Christ, we might be converted to God by obeying the ministry of reconciliation, so that through faith we might be made partakers of the righteousness of Christ. For since the Apostle, as the blessed Hülsemann does here, derives the reason for his office from the benefits received through Christ; namely, that through him we were created for eternal life, and from him we received the earnest of the Spirit, v. 5. It is more fitting that 'love' be understood as the active love of Christ toward us, rather than the resulting love of our own toward Christ, which Estius, Salmero, Justinianus, and Saa concede; and indeed exclusively so, that it should be accepted not as both, but only as the charity of Christ toward us. And Alvarez, 6 de auxil. diss. 44, on the merit of Christ undertaken for us out of charity, of which follows. Oecumenius indeed explains it as the charity of the Apostle toward Christ; Ambrosiaster and the Latins who followed him explain it as the love of both. But Estius confesses that, when the matter is weighed more diligently, the former sense is more required. See a similar inference of the Apostle in Rom. 15:3, seq., 1 John 3:16, John 15:13. Thus Theophylact: For the charity of God, manifest to us, urges us and strongly compels us to undergo dangers for his sake. Cornelius à Lapide presents this sense and connection thus: For the charity of Christ, not so much passive as active, by which, to wit, Christ loved men and spent his whole self for them, urges us that we also, by the example and love of Christ, should do the same and spend our whole selves for men, so that we may make them safe from death; and therefore, according to what is expedient for them, we are now beside ourselves, now we are sober.

Κρίναντας τῦτο) as those who judge this.

Latin:

V. 14. Ἡ γὰρ ἀγάπη τῦ χριστῦ συνέχει ἡμᾶς) Dilectio, quam Christo debemus, nos compellit, ut omnia DEI & Christianorum causa agamus. Συνέχει similitudo sumpta à parturientibus. Vide Luc. XII. 50.

Charitas Christi non passive, quâ à nobis dili- gitur, sed activè intelligenda, qua nos dilexit ipse. Hæc autem maxime συνέχει constringit ad ea, quæ ad Dei gloriam, hominumq; salutem faciunt, pro- sequenda. Siquidem Christus semetipsum totum ob gloriam Dei Patris & salutem generis humani impenderit, idque imprimis etiam annuntiari vo- luerit, ut non nobis, sed ipsi vivamus, ac DEO re- conciliati per mortem Christi ministerio recon- ciliationis obsequentes ad Deum convertamur, quo per fidem justitiæ Christi participes redda- mur. Quum enim rationem officii sui, ut hic B. Hül- semannus, deducat Apostolus ab acceptis per Chri- stum beneficiis; videlicet quod per ipsum conditi su- mus ad vitam æternam, ab ipso accepimus arrha- bonem Spiritus v. 5. Convenientius est ἀγάπην de amore Christi activo erga nos, quam de resultante amore nostro erga Christum intelligi, quod conce- dunt Estius, Salmero, Justinianus, Saa, sic & qui- dem exclusive, non de utroque sed sola charitate Chri- sti erga nos accipiendum esse. Et Alvarez 6. de auxil. diss. 44. de merito Christi ex charitate pro nobis suscepto, de quo sequitur. Oecumenius quidem de charitate Apostoli erga Christum, Ambrosiastev eumque sequuti Latini de utriusque amore exponunt. Sed fatetur Estius, re diligentius expensa priorem sensum magis postulari. Vide similem illationem Apostoli Rom. XV. 3. seq. 1. Joh. III. 16. Joh. XV. 13. Sic Theophylactus: Urget enim nos charitas DEI nobis perspicua, & valde compellit, ut ejus gratia pericula adeamus. Sensum hunc & nexum ita ex- hibet Cornelius à Lapide: Charitas enim Christi non tam passiva, quam activa, qua scil. Christus homines dilexit, seque totum iis impendit, urget nos, ut & nos Christi exemplo & amore idem faciamus, nosque totos hominibus impendamus, ut eos faciamus salvos à morte; ideoque, prout eis expedit, nunc mente excedamus, nunc sobrii simus.

Κρίναντας τῦτο) ut qui hoc statuamus.

## 5:15
Ὅτι εἰ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν) If, that is, since.

Ἄρα ὁι πάντες ἀπέθανον) Here also he spoke of the act as an office or that which is owed. All must also die, namely to sin. For the sense is the same, but stated more briefly, as in Romans 6 at the beginning, 1 Peter 4:1, 2.

This gloss is violent, accepted by Socinians, Arminians, and certain Reformed—Calvin, Beza, Marloratus, Piscator, the Dutch in their notes to this passage in the Hague Conference on Article II, p. 117—and even by our own Sarcetius. First, because the clear condition is converted into a causal [particle]. Next, what is explicitly said about the act, οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον, is dragged into the realm of owed duty. Thirdly, since in the consequent ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον the verb ἀπέθανεν must also be accepted in the same sense as it is accepted regarding the act in the antecedent—namely, that Christ died for all—is it not perverse to explain this otherwise than as an act? Since that is accepted in the past tense, should this not likewise be accepted in the same way? Fourthly, the Apostle is occupied with explaining the most intense love of Christ toward us, not indeed with our duty. A new reason for his distortion thus reveals itself here. Fifthly, the Apostle still pursues the love of Christ in v. 15, καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανε: nor has he handed down anything thus far concerning our duty. Sixthly, in order to adorn his misinterpretation, Grotius converts the copulative particle καὶ (AND) into the causal NAM (FOR) by his own private resolution. Seventhly, the Apostle treats of the different ends or fruits of the death of Christ, or to speak more correctly, of the different causes: namely (1) the formal, that his death was vicarious, or undergone in the place of all men. For he says, εἰ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, if one died for all or in the place of all, which he later affirms categorically concerning Christ in v. 15, and he judges—not by human judgment, but moved by the Spirit of GOD—that it is the same as if all had died. For a vicarious death performed in the place of all men is not otherwise estimated or accepted in the judgment of GOD than if all had died, i.e., had satisfied divine justice, because, to wit, one performed it in the place of all: Whence Bernard, Epistle 190 to Innocent: For if one, he says, died for all, all have died, so that, clearly, the satisfaction of one is imputed to all, just as that one bore the sins of all. (2) Concerning the final [cause], ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυτοῖς ζῶσιν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν ἀποθανόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι, so that those who live (restored to spiritual life through him) may not live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them. But Socinus confuses these different causes; indeed, he plainly eliminates the former from this oracle. Eighthly, since the impulsive cause of the death of Christ is established here as the supreme love of Christ toward us, it certainly does not denote the mortification of our flesh, through which we are said to die to sins in Rom. 6:2, because one died for all; but it necessarily designates an expiatory death, which is imputable to all those for whom Christ died. From the Apostle's inference it is clear that this is the chief argument (as the blessed Hülsemann holds here) for the benevolence of Christ toward us, that with one having died, all are considered to have died; but that with Christ having died, all men must die to sins is not an argument, much less a most evident one, and one that constrains us by the extreme benevolence of Christ, but rather by legal justice: For by this he wishes us to die to sins and live to virtues. Which is further declared ninthly in v. 19 and 20. For we are rendered righteous through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, since that one fulfilled the law for us; thus the satisfaction of Christ is hinted to be imputable to us, when it is said in the judgment of GOD to be the same thing that one Christ satisfied, or underwent death, as if we had all satisfied. Tenthly, that [statement] that one died for all is further explained by this reasoning, that God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, to whom these things are also to be understood conveniently, as if all had died; because he sustained the person of all, and was made sin for all by the imputation of guilt and the payment of the penalty. Eleventhly, the benefit received must be entirely distinguished by the Apostle from the duty owed. But that [former point] still pertains to the benefit received from Christ, and the mode and quality of the same, how one died for all, to wit, by satisfying in the place of all; so that his satisfaction is held to be in the place of all, and is imputable to all in the divine judgment; since the particle ἵνα finally refers to the final cause, and by that reasoning our duty is accustomed to be deduced from the benefit. See Rom. 14:7, 1 Cor. 6:last & 7:13, 20, 2 Thess. 5:10, 1 Pet. 4:2. Faulty here is Beza's distinction in verses 14 and 15, which gave occasion to a false interpretation, as if the latter part of v. 14 (all have died) speaks of the same kind of death as v. 16 (that they should not live for themselves), as if bound by such a great benefit, they should henceforth also conform themselves to the will of the Redeemer for the sake of gratitude. The blessed Hülsemann argues thus: Where the duty of our mortification is distinguished by the particle ἵνα from the death of Christ, there the species of Christ's death and our own is not the same, but distinct. Which argument he considers to be evident from a universal induction of all the places of the New Testament. Finally, there are added to this opinion from the Reformed, Perkins in Cathol. Reform. p. 105, Moulin in Anatom. Armin. cap. IX. §. 2, and from the Papists, Bellarmine himself.

Nor indeed should room be left for the interpretation of those who accept the words ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον as referring to the death of misery in original and actual sin: as if the argument were made a posteriori, in this way: Those who had to be redeemed by the death of Christ, those had to have previously died the death of misery, as Augustine argues from this place against the Pelagians and Manichaeans in Book II de Civit. Dei, Book II de Baptismo parvul. c. 27, Book VI contra Julian. c. 4. Which interpretation was also used by the Remonstrants in the Hague Conference p. 179, and assumed by Bellarmine in Book IV de amiss. grat. c. 4, because in this way a plainly different meaning is assumed in the Apostle's inference, nor does this interpretation contribute anything to the Apostolic demonstration. For what kind of demonstration of the benevolence of Christ toward us is: Christ died for all by an expiatory death; therefore all have died the death of misery? This is the argument of our misery, not of the benefit of Christ. Moreover, the force of the argument against the Pelagians still remains intact, even if these things are not understood concerning the death of misery, but concerning the imputation of the death of Christ. For if Christ so died for all, that it is just as if all had died in the judgment of God, it is necessary that we were all liable to the death of misery, so that we might be redeemed from it through satisfaction. Whence Augustine rightly in book XX of the City of God, ch. 6: Therefore all, infected, are dead in sins, with absolutely no one excepted, whether by original sins, or also those added by will. Which same words, as Estius does here, the Venerable Bede reported in his collectanea, and then Hervæus also wove into his Commentary. For the exception, which is read as added in this author, usually cited under the name of Anselm, with the mother of God removed, is inserted against the mind of the author and with the context resisting, by someone having zeal (as I judge) for the mother of God, not according to knowledge. It pleased me to adduce these things from Estius, although incidentally, so that it might be evident by this argument also with what good faith Papists conduct themselves in the writings of the ancients. But Estius rejects that explanation of Cajetan concerning the death of misery, as also that of Bellarmine, because it supposes a general sense of the antecedent, namely, that Christ died for all men in general, not only for the predestined in this way: If Christ died for all, all are dead with the death of sin. Therefore, the Papists are to be set against one another here: Estius prefers the Ordinary Gloss for that reason. the opinion of Thomas and Lyranus: If Christ died for all, therefore all, as far as their depraved actions are concerned, are dead to themselves and ought to live to the Lord. But Estius is rightly corrected by the blessed Hülsemann: Whoever ought to live the life of virtue, for them Christ died. But all mortals ought to live the life of virtue. Therefore. Estius denies this minor premise, by pretending: That all mortals indeed ought to presume that they are of the number of the Elect and that Christ died for them; yet in reality he died for the actually Elect alone. Which makes nothing for the question, it is just as if he had answered: That all ought to presume as if it were incumbent upon them to live according to the Decalogue, but yet in reality only the Elect are held to this obligation. Therefore, if the moral exposition of these words (all have died) is admitted to the greatest extent as meaning all are bound to die to vices and live to virtues; our argument still stands and remains: As many as are obligated to a virtuous life, so many have been redeemed by Christ. All are obligated &c. Therefore. Our blessed Hunnius most correctly expressed the sense and connection of this passage thus: What he began to say about the love of Christ, he now pursues more fully, and declares that it was so ardent that he did not hesitate in the least to expose himself to the most ignominious death of the cross for our salvation. And at the same time, by this occasion, the Apostle prepares for himself a transition to explain the sum of the entire Evangelical preaching, which he demonstrates to turn upon this death of the Savior Christ, as upon a hinge. The sense of the Pauline text is therefore this: With what love Christ burned toward us miserable men, he made testified by that very irrefragable work, while he himself alone deigned to die for all. Which death of the Son the heavenly Father holds in such account, as if we all had died, and by dying had ourselves expiated our sins: Since the death of Christ is entirely ours through faith, when he did not die for himself, but for us, nay, for all men without exception.

V. 15. Καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανε) Καὶ here signifies for. He shows what kind of death Christ endured. Not only what kind of death, to wit, vicarious; but also for whom Christ endured it, to wit, for all men. Which universality, repeated for the third time, immovably confirms our doctrine concerning Christ having died not for the Elect alone, but for all men, with the addition also of the comprehension of all made by the word world, concerning which later, and the continuity of the Apostolic argument, which also Bened. Justinianus urges against certain Scholastics, Lyranus, Estius, and others who restrict the death of Christ here to the Elect alone. Truly, since from this effect the benevolence of Christ toward the whole world and severity rather toward the most powerful part of the world, to wit, the reprobate, does not appear, this argument is not the strongest and binding or holding together the whole world concerning the benevolence of Christ toward itself. But that this treats of benevolence toward the whole world, toward all sinners, is clear from v. 19 and 20, where the subject having suffered or receiving the benevolence of Christ is said to be all sinners needing the righteousness of Christ.

Ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυτοῖς ζῶσιν) Not by their own judgment. Ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν ἀποθανόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι) According to the prescription of Christ. In his honor. A similar manner of speaking Rom. VI. 2. XIV. 7.

He demonstrates the end of the work, says blessed Hunnius, namely of the passion and death of Christ. That end is, that those who have been made alive by his death may henceforth not live for themselves, or obey their own affections; but live and serve him who died and rose again for them. For by the right of redemption they are now bound in turn to their benefactor to perform obsequies and services. This the remembrance of the death of Christ demands of them: His resurrection from the dead persuades, nay, requires the same, that just as he himself was raised through the glory of the Father; so we also should walk in newness of life. Some understand the subject οἱ ζῶντες as concerning natural life with Estius: but Theophylactus with Chrysostom and Theodoret preceded blessed Hunnius; blessed Balduinus, the Vinarions, and others followed, with whom also Flacius and Beza agree, who urge the article οἱ ζῶντες.

The article restricts the universal to those alone who live in Christ. For although we owe even our natural life to Christ; yet here the discourse is concerning spiritual benefits, without which Christ would not have acquired them for us. And not only when we live; but also when we die we must live and die to the Lord Rom. XIV. For the mention of the resurrection of Christ is added, partly so that we may have this duty more joyfully, with hope given to us concerning our resurrection and a type exhibited of our walking in newness of life in the resurrection of Christ Rom. VI. 4, partly and especially, so that through the death of Christ we may acknowledge that satisfaction has been truly paid for us, and that death itself has been overcome. For unless we believed that Christ was raised for believers, we could not be certain of the truth of the satisfaction, which was performed for us, and it would have to be believed that Christ was overcome by death, and not in truth that he had overcome death.

Latin:

Ὅτι εἰ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν) Si, id est, quandoquidem.

Ἄρα ὁι πάντες ἀπέθανον) Hic quoque actum dixit pro officio aut eo, quod debetur. Debent & omnes mori nem- pe peccato. Sensus enim est idem, sed brevius enuntiatum qui Rom. VI. in principio 1. Petr. IV. 1. 2.

Glossa hæc violenta est à Socinianis, Arminia- nis & Reformatis quibusdam Calvino, Beza, Mar- lorato, Piscatore, Belgis in notis ad hunc loc. in collat. Hagiansi ad artic. II. p. 117. etiam Sarcetio nostro accepta. Primum quod conditio luculenta ei in causalem convertitur. Deinde quod diserte de actu dicitur οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον ad officium debi- tum trahitur. Tertio, quum eodem sensu, quo in antecedente verbum ἀπέθανεν accipitur de actu, quod nempe Christus pro omnibus mortuus sit, in consequente ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον accipi etiam debeat, annon perverse hoc aliter, quam de actu explicatur? Quum illud in Praterito accipiatur, annon & hoc pariter ita accipiendum? Quarto oc- cupatur Apostolus in amore Christi explicando er ga nos intensissimo, non vero in officio nostro. Nova ergo στρεβλότητος ratio hic sese prodit. Quinto persequitur adhuc amorem Christi v. 15. Apostolus καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανε: nec quic- quam eousque de officio nostro tradidit: Sexto ut suam ψευδερμηνείαν ornet Grotius, particulam co- pulativam καὶ ET in causalem NAM convertit ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει. Septimo Apostolus de diversis finibus vel fructibus mortis Christi, vel ut rectius loquar de diversis causis agit: nimirum (1) formali, quod mors ejus fuerit vicaria seu vice omnium hominum exantlata. Nam εἰ εἷς inquit ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν si unus mortuus est pro omnibus vel vice omnium, quod Categorice postea de Christo affirmat v. 15. & id judicat non humano judicio, sed divino a DEI Spiritu agitatus, perinde esse, ac si omnes mortui essent. Nam mors vicaria loco omnium hominum praestita, in judicio DEI non aliter aestimatur, vel acceptatur, quam si omnes mortui essent, h. e. justi- tie divinae satisfecissent, quia scil. unus vice omni- um eam praestitit: Ex quo Bernhardus epist. CXC. ad Innocentium: Nam si unus, inquit, pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes mortui sunt, ut videlicet sa- tisfactio unius omnibus imputetur sicut omnium pec- cata unus ille portavit. (2) De finali ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυτοῖς ζῶσιν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν ἀποθα- νόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι, ut qui vivunt, (per ipsum spiri- tuali vitae restituti) non sibi ipsis vivant, sed illi, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resuscitatus. Quas vero diver- sas causas confundit Socinus, imo priorem ex hoc oraculo plane eliminat. Octavo, quum causa im- pulsiva mortis Christi hic constituatur summa Christi erga nos charitas, non sane quod unus pro omnibus mortuus est, mortificationem carnis no- strae, per quam dicimur demori peccatis Rom. VI. 2. denotat; sed necessario mortem expiatoriam de- signat, quae imputabilis est iis omnibus, pro quibus Christus mortuus est. Ex illatione Apostoli patet hoc potissimum esse argumentum (ut hic habet B. Hülsemannus) benevolentia Christi erga nos, quod mortuo uno omnes censentur mortui; sed quod mor- tuo Christo omnes homines oportet demori peccatis, non est argumentum nedum evidentissimum, & συν- έχον ἡμᾶς extreme benevolentia Christi sed justitiae legalis: Hac enim vult nos demori peccatis & vivere virtutibus. Quod porro nono declaratur v. 19. & 20. Nos enim justi reddimur per imputationem justitiae Christi, cum unus ille pro nobis legem im- pleverit; ita satisfactio Christi nobis imputanda innuitur, cum in judicio DEI perinde id esse dici- tur, quod unus Christus satisfecerit, vel mortem sustinuerit, ac si omnes satisfecissemus. Decimo explicatur ulterius illud, quod unus pro omnibus mortuus sit deinceps hac ratione, quod illum, qui non novit peccatum, Deus fecerit pro nobis pecca- tum, cui convenienter intelligenda ista etiam sunt, ac si omnes mortui essent; quia omnium personam sustinuit, & pro omnibus factus est peccatum im- putatione culpa, & luitione poenae. Undecimo bene- ficium acceptum omnino discriminandum est cum Apostolo ab officio debito. At illud adhuc per- tinet ad beneficium a Christo acceptum, & modum ac qualitatem ejusdem, quomodo mortuus sit unus sit pro omnibus, scil. satisfaciendo loco omni- um; ita ut ejusdem satisfactio omnium vice ha- beatur, & omnibus imputabilis sit in divino judi- cio; quum particula ἵνα demum causam finalem re- ferat, & eâ ratione è beneficio officium nostrum de- duci soleat. Vide Rom. XIV. 7. 1. Cor. VI. ult.& VII. 13. 20. 2. Thess. V. 10. 1. Petr. IV. 2. Vitiosa hic est Beza distinctio in commate 14. & 15. quæ occa- sionem dedit falsæ interpretationi, quasi posterior pars v. 14. (omnes mortui sunt) de eodem genere mortis loquatur, de quo v. 16. (non sibi vivant) ut devincti tanto beneficio posthac gratitudinis causa, etiam sese attemperent voluntati redimen- tis. B. Hülsemannus ita argumentatur: Ubi officium mortificationis nostræ per particulam ἵνα distingui- tur à morte Christi, ibi non eadem species mortis Christi & nostræ, sed distincta. Quod argumentum patere censet ex universali inductione omnium lo- corum Novi Testamenti. Denique accedunt etiam huic sententiæ è Reformatis Perkinsius in Cathol. Reform. p. 105. Molineus in Anatom. Armin. cap. IX. §. 2. è Pontificiis Bellarminus ipse.

Nec verò locus relinquendus eorum interpre- tationi, qui verba ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον de morte miseriæ in peccato Originali & actuali accipiunt: quasi argumentum fiat à posteriori, hoc modo: Quos oportuit morte Christi redimi, hos oportuit, morte miseriæ antea defunctos fuisse, uti argumen- tatur ex hoc loco adversus Pelagianos & Mani- chæos Augustinus libr. II. de Civit. Dei. lib. II. de Baptismo parvul. c. 27. lib. VI. contra Julian. c. 4. Quæ interpretatio à Remonstrantibus etiam adhi- bita in collat. Hagiensi pag. 179. & à Bellarmino as- sumpta libr. IV. de amiss. grat. c. 4. quia ita plane diversa significatio assumitur in illatione Apostoli, nec ad demonstrationem Apostolicam quicquam facit hæc interpretatio. Qualis enim demonstratio benevolentiæ Christi erga nos: Christus mortuus est pro omnibus morte expiatoria; Ergo omnes mor- tui sunt morte miseriæ? Argumentum nostræ mise- riæ hoc est, non beneficii Christi. Cæterum vis ar- gumenti adversus Pelagianos adhuc manet integra, etiamsi non de morte miseriæ hæc accipiantur, sed de mortis Christi imputatione. Nam si ita Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, ut id perinde in judicio Dei sit, ac si omnes mortui essent, oportet nos o- mnes morti miseriæ obnoxios fuisse, ut ab illa per satisfactionem redimeremur. Unde recte Augu- stinus libr. XX. de Civitate Dei c. 6. Infecti itaque omnes mortui sunt in peccatis, nemine prorsus exce- pto, sive originalibus, sive etiam voluntate additis. Quæ eadem verba, ut hic Estius, V. Beda retulit in sua collectanea, deinde & Hervæus intexuit suo Com- mentario. Nam exceptio, qua apud hunc autorem, sub Anshelmi nomine citari solitum, apposita legitur dempta matre Dei, contra mentem autoris & repu- gnante contextu, inserta est ab aliquo zelum (ut ar- bitror) habente matris Dei, non secundum scientiam. Hæc ex Estio, obiter licet, adducere placuit, ut qua fide Papistæ in veterum scriptis versentur, isto etiam argumento constet. Reprobat autem Estius illam Cajetani de morte miseriæ, ut & Bellarmini explicationem, quod supponat sensum anteceden- tis generalem, scil. pro omnibus in universum ho- minibus mortuum esse Christum, non solum pro prædestinatis hoc modo: Si pro omnibus mortuus est Christus, omnes mortuos esse morte peccati. Commit- tendi hic ergo inter sese Papistæ: Præfert eo nomi- ne Estius Glossæ Ordin. Thomæ & Lyrani sententiam: Si pro omnibus mortuus est Christus, omnes ergo, quod ad pravas ipsorum actiones attinet, sibi mortui sunt & Domino vivere debent. Sed recte cor- rigitur Estius à B. Hülsemanno: Quicunque debent vivere vita virtutis, pro iis Christus est mortuus. Sed omnes mortales debent vivere vita virtutis. Ergo. Hanc minorem negat Estius, fingendo: Omnes quidem mortales debere præsumere, se esse ex nume- ro Electorum Christumque pro se esse mortuum; reve- ra tamen pro solis actu Electis mortuum esse. Quod nihil ad quæstionem facit, perinde est, ac si respon- disset: Omnes oportere præsumere quasi incumbat sibi vivere juxta Decalogum, sed revera tamen solos Ele- ctos teneri ad hanc obligationem. Itaq;, si maxime ad- mittatur moralis expositio horum verborum (omnes mortui sunt) pro omnes tenentur mori vitiis, & vivere virtutibus; stat tamen & manet no- strum argumentum: Quotquot obligantur ad vitam virtuosam, tot redempti sunt à Christo. Omnes ob- ligantur &c. Ergo. Sensum itaque & connexionem hujus loci B. Hunnius noster rectissime ita expres- sit: Quod de Christi charitate cœpit dicere, nunc fu- sius persequitur, eamq; tam ardentem fuisse prædicat, ut pro salute nostra se morti ignominiosissimæ crucis objicere minime dubitarit. Atque hac simul occasio- ne transitum sibi parat Apostolus ad explicandam totius Evangelicæ prædicationis summam, quam in ista morte Servatoris Christi, ceu cardine, verti demon- strat. Est ergo textus Paulini sensus hic: Quanto amore flagrarit erga nos miseros homines Christus, id ipso irrefragabili opere testatum fecit, dum unus ipse pro omnibus mori dignatus est. Quam Filii mor- tem cælestis Pater eo loco habet, ac si nos omnes esse- mus mortui, & moriendo peccata nostra expiassemus ipsi: Quandoquidem Christi mors tota est nostra per fidem, cum non pro se mortuus sit, sed pro nobis, imo pro omnibus ad unum hominibus.

V. 15. Καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανε) Καὶ hic valet nam. Ostendit qualem Christus mortem pertulerit. Non tantum qualem mortem scil. vicariam; sed etiam pro quibus pertulerit Christus, scil. pro omni- bus hominibus. Quæ tertia vice repetita universa- litas immote firmat nostram doctrinam de Chri- sto non pro solis Electis, sed pro omnibus homini- bus mortuo, accedente etiam omnium compre- hensione voce mundi facta, de quo postea & Argu- menti Apostolici συνεχεία, quam etiam Bened. Ju- stinianus contra Scholasticos quosdam Lyranum, Estium aliosque mortem Christi hic ad solos Ele- ctos restringentes, urget. Nimirum ex quo effectu non patet benevolentia Christi erga universum mundum & severitas potius erga potissimam mun- di partem scil. reprobos, hoc argumentum non est fortissimum & constringens seu συνέχον totum mundum de benevolentia Christi erga se. Sed hic agi de benevolentia erga totum mundum, erga o- mnes peccatores, patet ex v. 19. & 20. ubi subjectum passum seu recipiens benevolentiam Christi dicun- tur omnes peccatores indigentes justitiâ Christi.

Ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυτοῖς ζῶσιν) Non ex suo arbitratu. Ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν ἀποθανόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι) Ex Christi præscripto. In ejus honorem. Simile loquendi genus Rom. VI. 2. XIV. 7.

Finem demonstrat operis, inquit B. Hunnius, nempe passionis & mortis Christi. Is finis est, ut qui morte ipsius vivificati sunt, porro non sibi vivant, aut suis obsequantur affectibus; sed ei vivant & serviant, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Nam jure redemptionis sunt jam benefactori suo ad obse- quia servitiaq́; præstanda vicissim obstricti. Hoc ab eis flagitat recordatio mortis Christi: Idem suadet, imo postulat illius ex morte resurrectio, ut quemad- modum ipse resuscitatus est per gloriam Patris; ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Nonnulli sub- jectum οἱ ζῶντες de vita naturali intelligunt cum Estio: sed B. Hunnio præivit Theophylactus cum Chrysostomo & Theodoreto; sequuti sunt B. Baldui- nus, Vinarienses, & alii, quum quibus etiam faciunt Flacius & Beza, qui urgent articulum οἱ ζῶντες.

Articulus restringit τὸ καθόλε ad solos eos, qui in Christo vivunt. Quanquam enim & vitam natu- ralem Christo debeamus; hic tamen de beneficiis spi- ritualibus sermo est, quo sine morte Christus ea nobis acquisiuerit. Nec tantum cum vivimus; sed etiam cum morimur Domino & vivendum nobis est & moriendum Rom. XIV. Adjungitur enim resurci- tationis Christi mentio, partim ut hilarius habea- mus hoc officium spe nobis facta de resurrectione nostra & typo exhibito nostræ in novitate vitæ ambulationis in Christi resuscitatione Rom. VI. 4. partim & cumprimis, ut per mortem Christi pro nobis verè persolutam esse satisfactionem, mor- temque ipsam devictam agnoscamus. Nam nisi re- suscitatum credentibus Christum, nec de satisfa- ctionis veritate certi esse possemus, quæ pro no- bis præstita, & devictum à morte Christum, non vero vicisse mortem, credendum foret.

## 5:16
V. 16. Ὢστε ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ τῦ νῦν ἰδένα ὄιδαμεν κατὰ σάρκα) We do not estimate anyone from riches, or erudition, which are carnal things, that is, of this age.

Ἐι δὲ καὶ ἐγνώκαμεν κατὰ σάρκα χρισὸν, ἀλλὰ νῦν ὐκ ἔτι γινώσκομεν) Ἐγνώκαμεν here is the Indicative for the subjunctive, in the Hebrew manner. Even if, he says, we had known Christ familiarly in the flesh, that is, while he was still leading a mortal life; yet now we do not consider and honor him as such; but as a heavenly King and judge of the human race. There is an antanaklasis in the verb γνώσκειν which signifies both knowledge and estimation. But this was said against those who, when they had come from Judea to Corinth, preferred themselves to others, for the reason that they had heard Christ himself speaking, had seen him, and perhaps were related to him by some kinship, like those who for that reason were called desposynoi. See what was said at 1. Corinth. I. 12.

Various interpretations of this very difficult verse occur, concerning which Thomas and Estius may be consulted. I. Faustus the Manichaean, as witnessed by Augustine in book XI against Faustus, ch. 1, distorted these words to support his heresy that Christ did not have true flesh, as if Paul, when he had previously felt that Christ was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, Rom. 1, had here corrected himself: even if we have known Christ according to the flesh; now, however, we do not know him. Augustine rightly opposes him: If Christ therefore did not have flesh, then neither did others have flesh, of whom he says: We know no one of these according to the flesh. II. Eutyches, supporting his heresy, perverted the passage in this way, as Cornelius à Lapide notes here: We do not know, he says, Christ according to the flesh: because by the incarnation the flesh and human nature of Christ were absorbed by the divinity: But the same would have to be said of others, whom the Apostle says he did not know according to the flesh. III. The Schwenckfeldians distort the words of the Apostle to mean that Christ after his resurrection no longer has true flesh. But that is refuted by the same reasoning by which the Eutychian heresy is refuted. IV. Regarding the distortion of this passage by the Iconomachs and also the Calvinists, that whatever was carnal in Christ should be consigned to oblivion, and therefore his form should not be painted, Cornelius à Lapide warns that in that case the flesh, death, and passion of Christ should also be forgotten. V. Regarding another Calvinist error, by which they are carried away to deny the substantial presence of the body of Christ in the Holy Supper, the blessed Hülfemann warned: For just as formerly the Iconomachs inferred from the denied knowledge of Christ according to the flesh that his image could not be expressed or ever had been; but that the lineaments of his body immediately fell from the memory of the living, as is reported in the Seventh Synod in Binius, Vol. IV, Action 6. Thus with equal ineptitude Musculus, Pelicanus, and Beza, and others infer from this: That the substantial presence of the body of Christ is thereby refuted, because it does not befit Christians to know Christ according to the flesh. But the Belgian in his Annotations and Marloratus himself admit that 'to know according to the flesh' here signifies that of which the Pseudo-Apostles from the Jews boasted, namely, carnal kinship and conversation with the person of Jesus of Nazareth. VI. Theophylact and Oecumenius, with Chrysostom, interpret that no one is known by Paul henceforth according to the flesh, that is, living according to a carnal life. But had Paul ever known Christ according to the flesh with Timothy in such a way? Therefore, they understand that κατὰ σάρκα differently regarding others, and differently regarding Christ. Christ, however, is then said, according to Theophylact's interpretation, to have lived according to the flesh, when he lived according to nature, yet subject to no passions of guilt, namely when he endured hunger and thirst and labors. But those diverse meanings of the same word do not fit this passage, nor does the latter contribute anything to the matter, if, as the former demands, συνέχεια with them is attended to, so that they might not live for themselves.

VII. Theodoret understands both regarding immortality, and refers it to that which preceded concerning the resurrection; since we have learned that death was dissolved through the death of the Lord, we know that no man is mortal henceforth (he perhaps wishes to say, we know that no one will be mortal after the resurrection). For the Lord himself had a passible body; yet after the passion he made it alien to corruption, destruction, and death. To this also goes the explanation of Augustine, book XI against Faustus, ch. 7 and 8, Vol. VI of his Works, p. 253. Certainly, it is now apparent to anyone that the Apostle said this on account of the resurrection of Christ, since that which preceded these words was that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for all and rose again. For what else is it, to live not for themselves but for him, unless that they should not live according to the flesh in the hope of earthly and corruptible goods, but according to the spirit in the hope of the resurrection, which has already been accomplished in Christ from among them? Therefore, of those for whom Christ died and rose again, and who now live not for themselves but for him, the Apostle knew no one according to the flesh, on account of the hope of the future resurrection, in the expectation of which they lived, which in Christ was no longer a hope, but a reality: whom, even if he had known according to the flesh, when he was still about to die, he now no longer knew, because he knew that he had risen, and that death would no longer have dominion over him. And because we are all in him, even if not yet in reality, yet already in hope, it follows that he says: If therefore any one is in Christ, a new creature. Leo the Great followed Augustine, sermon 1 on the resurrection of the Lord, p. 68, on this passage. Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him no longer, writing thus: For the resurrection of the Lord was not an end of the flesh, but a transformation, nor was the substance consumed by an increase of power. The quality passed away, the nature did not fail, and the body became impassible, which could be killed; it became incorruptible, which could be wounded. And rightly is the flesh of Christ said to be unknown in that state in which it was known, because nothing passible remained in it, nothing infirm remained in it, so that it is the same by essence, and is not the same by glory. But what is the wonder, if he professes this concerning the body of Christ, who says concerning all spiritual Christians: Therefore we from this time know no one according to the flesh? From this, he says, the beginning of the resurrection was made for us in Christ, from which the form of our whole hope preceded in him who died for all. We do not hesitate with distrust, nor are we suspended by uncertain expectation, but having received the beginning of the promise, with the eyes of faith we already discern what is to come: And rejoicing in the advancement of nature, we already hold what we believe. Lombard and Hervaeus report the sense of Augustine almost word for word in their Commentaries, whom Thomas also seems to prefer to the others. Estius finds nothing to oppose to this, except that Paul never saw Christ in mortal flesh: but that the sense remains consistent for him nonetheless, even if he did not see Christ in the flesh with bodily eyes, is not at all obscure. For to have known does not immediately imply seeing with the eyes of the body. VIII. Estius, however, prefers the explanation of Gagnaeus and Erasmus, who do not refer these things to the resurrection, but to those things which precede concerning the life to be led not for ourselves, but for Christ: as if the Apostle, when the Pseudo-Apostles were boasting of the nobility of their lineage, here hints that he is so dead to himself and to his old life, and transformed into another man, that he now values none of those things, and boasts in no one for the sake of carnal kinship, and even if he once thought it great and glorious to be a Gentile and a kinsman of Christ according to the flesh, yet now he is so thoroughly dead to the affections of the old life that he considers it no longer a matter to be boasted of in such things. But when did the Apostle boast in that? Certainly not before his conversion, for then he was harassing Christ with calumnies and persecutions; nor after his conversion: for then he was dead to the affections of the old life. Wherefore that opinion, as it is expressed by Estius, cannot be approved: just as one should not simply accede to the interpretation of those who understand that the Apostle no longer wishes to foster carnal thoughts concerning a worldly kingdom of Christ. For he did not foster them before his conversion, when he held Christ rather to be a false Prophet, nor after his conversion. Nor can it be said that these things are written in the person of other Apostles, since in this whole discussion the Apostle speaks of his ministry or most especially of himself in his own person: the person of the Apostle certainly cannot be excluded in this discourse.

And therefore the explanation of X. Cajetan concerning a carnal Messiah has much less place, which Estius presents thus: Therefore we, from that time in which Christ rose again, have learned and know that no renewer of the age according to the flesh, that is, living according to the duties of the flesh, is to be expected by us. And although the Apostles received Christ living according to the duties of the flesh, when they conversed with him on earth, that was only for a time, until Christ should complete the mystery of our redemption. For henceforth unto eternity neither they, nor we, know Christ as such; but we know him only as living according to the spirit in immortal flesh. XI. B. Hülsemann, having approved that opinion concerning the persuasion of an earthly kingdom, accedes to the explanation of those who wish the carnal relationship and bodily union of Christ to be regarded, whose notes, because they are ἀνέκδοτα, I am pleased to bring here: The connective particle ὥςε, he says, infers something from the Antecedents, there is no doubt; but what that thing is which is immediately intended by the Apostle, authors vary. For most, because Paul in v. 15 warned about the duty of renewal or of renouncing all carnal desires, think: that also in this verse the knowledge of Christ according to the flesh, which Paul denies of himself, signifies the false opinion of the disciples and others concerning a voluptuous and earthly kingdom of Christ. But that ὥςε placed at the beginning of the clause infers something greater, and as it were disparate from the Antecedents, is evident from the usage of the particle in v. 17, ὡς ὅτι in v. 19, and ὥςε in c. IV. 12, c. I. 8, c. II. 7, c. III. 7. and below c. VII. 7, in which places it always [serves as] an illative of the Major from the minor in this way; so that, etc., as much more or as much less, and infers a similar sense. Compare Phil. I. 13, 1 Thess. I. 17. Therefore, not to know Christ according to the flesh indeed denotes something analogous to the preceding phrase (not to live for oneself) but something greater, namely, not to glory in that in which the Pseudo-Apostles gloried, to whom Paul opposes this inference, which is manifestly evident from v. 14 with 13, to wit, that Paul and other Christians were so dead to themselves, that neither the carnal conjunction of blood with Christ, which the Pseudo-Apostles boasted of, nor the association with Christ living on earth, which they boasted of repeatedly, as is evident from 1 Cor. XV. 8.

Rom. IX. 3. Eph. III. 7. seq. Phil. III. 4. seq. as a certain preeminence, on account of which Paul might desire to be preferred to any Doctor, he wishes to allege. But if he should even reach Christ by kinship of the flesh, and have known that Christ of the days of the flesh by sight (which Estius imprudently denies) see 1 Cor. IX. 1. he is so transformed into a new creature that he desires to allege nothing of this as worthy of preference. This seems to be the most congruent opinion for Paul's scope, so that the 'according to the flesh' in this place is understood not as carnal vices or impurity of the flesh, but as preference on account of external things that strike the eyes. Just as Luther also explained in the marginal gloss. From this the Vinarions depart thus far, who explain the words uttered in the person of Paul 'Christ according to the flesh' etc., concerning Paul's false and common opinion regarding Christ's temporal kingdom along with the other disciples. For because Paul thought nothing but the worst of this individual Jesus before his conversion, nor did he presume such a kingdom as the disciples presumed, and therefore the 'to know according to the flesh' said in the person of Paul signifies this: knowledge by sight as above 1 Cor. IX. 1. & chap. XV. 8. For metaphorical words in such allegories are accustomed to have something in common and something singular, as 1 Tim. VI. 5. 6. the word 'gain' in both verses has something in common and something singular. The blessed Lord Socer had noted a similar opinion in Flacius in this way: Those who think the Apostle is lashing out at those empty boastings of certain people who boasted that they and their teachers Peter or James or others had seen Christ in the flesh and had associated with him familiarly; but Paul not at all, and therefore they should be believed more than him. Which opinion, in Flacius's judgment, is probable, provided that the Apostle refutes those same boastings of theirs also in the epistle to the Galatians. Flacius, however, brought forth another XII. sense in this way: He concludes from the preceding that since he has died with Christ and been raised to a new life, therefore he now admires no carnal endowments of anyone, about which the Pseudo-Apostles boasted so insolently, nor does he seek any carnal advantages as they do. Furthermore, he does not so much regard how this Christ lived on earth, as how he now reigns and triumphs in that spiritual kingdom of his in heaven: that there he is joined and addicted to him. To whose explanation that which is read in Beza's Annotations is almost twin. But the Apostle never admired carnal endowments in Christ, nor did he neglect to regard that Christ lived on earth; but he professed to know this one thing only, Jesus crucified 1 Cor. II. 3. How he conducted himself, and what Christ suffered on earth. XIII. Jonas Schlichtingius in his Commentary on this place wishes to refer to the carnal worship of God and circumcision, because they now have no regard or estimation for carnal things and legal rites in anyone; even if they previously looked at Christ according to circumcision and other carnal worships of the law, when he was living in the flesh. But how could Paul know or look at Christ in the days of his flesh? And what does circumcision or the observation of legal rites have to do with this place or the present matter? XIV. Finally, some refer the 'according to' not to the known, but to the knower. Thus Aretius: he infers the conclusion: Therefore I no longer admire carnal endowments, because the love of Christ teaches me otherwise, namely to deny myself, so that I do not live for myself, but for Christ, who died for me. To know someone according to the flesh is to acknowledge someone carnally, i.e., in the way in which the world acknowledges someone, to approve and praise the highest things, or to condemn what the world condemns. Thus the world acknowledges wisdom and eloquence, that is carnal. And 'from now on' becomes the present state of Paul after his conversion; not a moment. Then for the sake of example he adds concerning Christ, that if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so, this is, I once knew Christ according to the flesh before my conversion. He had known Christ carnally, that is, as a man worthy of extreme death, an impious man, and an impostor, therefore he was persecuting him. But now, he says, no longer so: Now I acknowledge him as the Son of God, my savior and deliverer. Piscator easily agrees with Aretius, even though he deduces this conclusion from the preceding things about the sincerity of the Apostle, that from the time of his conversion he judges no one from external things, and thereby implies that he also does not wish to be estimated by the Corinthians in that way, placing a prolepsis here which might meet the thought of those Apostles who could object to the time before his conversion, when Paul had known, that is, had estimated according to the flesh, that is, from poverty and ignominy and the hatred of the Pharisees. Therefore the Apostle confesses that he once judged in that way, but now not so. The blessed Weinrichius followed the interpretation of Aretius step by step. From which the Commentary of the blessed Balduinus does not depart much, nor does the blessed Waltherus in his Harmony on this place. Which Cornelius a Lapide also judges not improbable. Nor is that indeed inconvenient, whether we look at the phrase or the context. For it is the way of the world, not of the faithful, to judge carnally about someone, and Paul joins himself to others, who even if they did not hold Christ for a seducer as Paul did before his conversion: yet they judged similarly about him. It is agreed, however, not to judge about Christ, nor about any man according to the flesh or carnally; but according to the spirit; so that they not only do not live for themselves according to the flesh; but also do not judge about others according to the flesh. By which likewise the carnal judgment of the Pseudo-Apostles about the Apostles is noted. Thus for the blessed Hunnius, to know according to the flesh is to have regard for the external person of men: and he wishes to regard the remaining Apostles as once feeling carnally about Christ, and Paul, even as he was persecuting him: But now, he understands, he no longer estimates his person, and office, and kingdom from the sense of the flesh, or from some carnal judgment. And thus those things cohere more correctly with the immediately preceding ones, that we should not live for ourselves, but for Christ, of which the former is of carnal men; the latter, however, is of spiritual men, and with the following things concerning the new creature in Christ. And the Osiandrian paraphrase also tends toward this: When we understand that we have been redeemed by Christ for this reason, that we might faithfully serve Him, now in loving our neighbor and doing our duty we do not act carnally, nor do we have respect of persons, nor do we seek our own carnal advantages, but we strive to promote the glory of God and the salvation of men. And although many (even of the Apostles themselves) sought carnal advantages in Christ, (inasmuch as they believed for some time that He would be a worldly King, who would bestow upon His own earthly riches and faculties) yet now, having laid aside that false and carnal opinion, we seek not carnal but spiritual and eternal benefits in Christ. This, finally, seems to have been the mind of our blessed Luther in his marginal gloss: To know Christ no longer according to the flesh is to seek or expect nothing carnal in Him, as the disciples did before the Passion, but to be content with His Word, in which they have pure spiritual and eternal good. In which way there is no need either to substitute the subjunctive for the indicative, or to posit an Antanaclasis with Grotius, whom, however, the Belgians preceded here in their notes, just as the authors of the German notes, which were added to the glosses of Toffanus in the recent Frankfurt-on-Main edition, subsequently followed them.

Latin:

V. 16. Ὢστε ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ τῦ νῦν ἰδένα ὄιδαμεν κατὰ σάρκα) Non æstimamus quemquam è divitiis, aut eruditione, quæ sunt res carnales, id est, hujus seculi.

Ἐι δὲ καὶ ἐγνώκαμεν κατὰ σάρκα χρισὸν, ἀλλὰ νῦν ὐκ ἔτι γινώσκομεν) Ἐγνώκαμεν hic est Indicativus pro subjuncti- vo, more Hebræo. Etiamsi inquit, Christum in carne, id est, cum vitam adhuc mortalem ageret, familiariter cognitum habuissemus; nunc tamen eum non ut talem consideramus & colimus; sed ut Regem cœlestem & judicem humani generis. Est ἀντανάκλασις in verbo γνώσκειν quod & no- titiam significat & æstimationem. Dictum autem hoc est adversus illos, qui cum ex Judæa Corinthum venissent, se præferebant cæteris, eo quod Christum ipsum dicentem audissent, vidissent, forte & cognatione aliqua continge- rent, ut illi, qui ob id dicti fuere διοπόσυνοι. Vide quæ dicta ad 1. Corinth. I. 12.

Variæ occurrunt hujus perdifficilis versus in- terpretationes, de quibus Thomas & Estius videri poterunt I. Faustus Manichæus, teste Augustino l. XI. contra Faustum c. 1. hæc ad suam hæresin, Christum non habuisse veram carnem, distorquebat, quasi Paulus, quum ante senserit, Christum factum ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, Rom. I. hic se- metipsum correxerit: etsi agnovimus Christum se- cundum carnem; nunc tamen non novimus. Cui re- cte opponit Augustin. Si Christus ideo non habuit carnem; igitur nec alii habuerunt carnem, de quibus ait: Ex his neminem novimus secundum carnem. II. Eutyches suæ hæresi δικλεύων, ita pervertebat lo- cum, notante hic Cornelio à Lapide: Non novimus, inquit, Christum secundum carnem: quia incarna- tione caro & humana natura Christi absorpta fuit à divinitate: Sed ita idem dicendum foret de aliis, quos se non novisse ait secundum carnem Apo- stolus. III. Schwenckfeldiani verba Apostoli eo detorquent, quod Christus post resurrectionem suam non amplius habeat veram carnem. Sed id eadem ratione, qua hæresis Eutychiana profliga- tur. IV. Iconomachorum ut & Calvinianorum de- torsione hujusce loci, quod quicquid in Christo carnale fuit, oblivioni tradendum, ideoq; nec forma ejus pingenda sit, Cornelius à Lapide monet, sic et- iam obliviscendum fore carnis, mortis & passionis Christi V. De alia Calviniana ςφοδῇ, qua ad negan- dam substantialem corporis Christi præsentiam in S. cœna hæc abripiunt, B. Hülfemannus monuit: Quemadmodum enim olim Iconomachi ex negata no- titia Christi secundum carnem inferebant, neque effi- giem ejus exprimi posse aut potuisse unquam; sed li- neamenta corporis protinus excidisse memoria vi- ventium, ut refertur in VII. Synodo apud Binium T. IV. Actione 6. Ita pari ineptitudine Musculus, Pe- licanus & Beza, aliique ex hoc inferunt: Substantia- lem corporis Christi præsentiam exinde refelli, quia non deceat Christianos nosse Christũ secundũ carnem. Sed Belga in Annot. & Marloratus ipse fatentur, τὸ nosse secundũ carnẽ hic significare id, de quo gloriban- tur Pseudo-Apostoli ex Judæis, sc. carnalẽ cognationẽ & conversationẽ cũ Jesu Nazareni personâ, VI. Theo- phylactus & Oecumenius cum Chrysostomo neminem secundum carnem, id est, secundum carnalem vitam viventem deinceps a Paulo cognosci interpretantur. Sed num ita unquam Christum secundum carnem Paulus cum Timotheo cognoverat? Aliter ergo de aliis, aliter de Christo illud κατὰ σάρκα intelligunt. Christus autem tunc dicitur, interprete Theophylacto, secundum carnem vixisse, quando pro natura passionibus nulli tamen obnoxius culpa vixit, videlicet cum famem & sitim ac labores perpessus est. Sed illae diversae vocis ejusdem significationes huic loco non conveniunt, nec posterior quicquam ad rem facit, si, ut prior postulat συνέχεια cum illis, ut non sibi vivant, attendatur.

VII. Theodoretius utrumque de immortalitate intelligit, & ad id refert, quod de resurrectione praecessit; cum per mortem Domini mortem dissolutam esse didicerimus, nullum deinceps hominem mortalem esse scimus (vult fortasse dicere, nullum mortalem post resurrectionem futurum scimus.) Etenim ipse Dominus habuit corpus patibile; tamen post passionem id a corruptione, interitu, & morte alienum effecit. Quo abit etiam Augustini explicatio libr. XI. contra Faustum cap. 7. & 8. Tom. VI. Operum p. 253. Certe jam nunc cuivis apparet propter resurrectionem Christi hoc dixisse Apostolum, quandoquidem ista verba illud praecessit, ut, qui vivunt, jam non sibi vivant, sed ei, qui pro omnibus mortuus est, & resurrexit. Quid est enim aliud, non sibi, sed illi vivant, nisi ut secundum carnem non vivant in spe terrenorum & corruptibilium bonorum: sed secundum spiritum in spe resurrectionis, qua jam ex ipsis in Christo facta est? Itaque eorum, pro quibus mortuus est Christus & resurrexit, & qui jam non sibi, sed illi vivunt, neminem secundum carnem noverat Apostolus, propter spem futurae resurrectionis, in cujus expectatione vivebant, quae in Christo jam non spes, sed res erat: quem etsi noverat secundum carnem, cum adhuc moriturus esset, jam tamen non noverat, quia resurrexisse eum noverat, & ultra ei mortem non dominaturam. Et quia omnes in illo, etsi nondum in re, jam tamen spe hoc sumus, sequitur ut dicat: Si qua igitur in Christo nova creatura. Augustinum sequutus est Leo M. serm. 1. de resurr. Dn. p. 68. ad h. l. Etsi cognovimus secundum carnem Christum, sed nunc jam non novimus, ita scribens: Resurrectio enim Domini non finis carnis, sed commutatio fuit, nec virtutis augmento consumpta substantia est. Qualitas transiit, non natura defecit, & factum est corpus impassibile, quod potuit occidi, factum est incorruptibile, quod potuit vulnerari. Et merito dicitur caro Christi in eo statu, quo fuerit nota, nesciri, quia nihil in ea passibile, nihil in ea remansit infirmum, ut & ipsa sit per essentiam, & non sit ipsa per gloriam. Quid autem mirum, si hoc de corpore Christi profitetur, qui de omnibus Christianis spiritualibus dicit: Itaque nos ex hoc neminem novimus secundum carnem? Ex hoc, inquit, initium nobis factum resurrectionis in Christo, ex quo in eo, qui pro omnibus mortuus est totius spei nostrae forma praecessit. Non haesitamus diffidentia, nec incerta expectatione suspendimur, sed accepto promissionis exordio, fidei oculis, quae sunt futura, jam cernimus: Et natura provectione gaudentes, quod credimus, jam tenemus. Sensum Augustini pene verbotenus referunt in suis Commentariis Lombardus & Hervaeus, quem etiam caeteris anteferre videtur Thomas. Cui quid opponeret, non invenit Estius, nisi quod Paulus Christum in carne mortali nunquam viderit: sed constare nihilosecius sibi illum sensum, etsi non viderit oculis corporeis Christum in carne, minime obscurum est. Non enim novisse statim q infert videre oculis corporis. VIII. Præfert autem Estius Gagnæi & Erafmi explicationem, qui hæc non ad resurrectionem referunt, sed ad ea, quæ de vitâ non nobis ipsis, sed Christo ducenda præcedunt: quasi Apostolus quum gloriarentur Pseudo-Apo- stoli de nobilitate generis hic innuat, se usque adeò sibi ipsi ac veteri vitæ mortuum esse, & in alium hominem transformatum, ut jam nihil illorum ma- gnifaciat, & in nemine glorietur carnalis propin- quitatis causa, quin etsi aliquando magnum & glo- riosum putaverit, gentilem & consanguineum esse Christi secundum carnem, at nunc ita penitus mor- tuus sit affectibus vitæ veteris, ut non amplius in hujusmodi re gloriatum censeat. Sed quando Apo- stolus in eo gloriatus est? Non certè ante conver- sionem, tum enim Christum calumniis & perse- quutionibus insectabatur; nec post conversionem: tum enim affectibus vitæ veteris mortuus fuit. Quapropter illa sententia ita simpliciter, ut ab Estio exprimitur, probari nequit: Quemadmodum ne- que IX. eorum interpretationi ἁπλῶς acceden- dum, qui carnales cogitationes de regno Christi mun- dano Apostolum non fovere amplius velle intelli- gunt. Eas enim nec ante conversionem fovit, cum Christum pro falso potius Propheta habuerit, nec post conversionem. Nec dici potest, hæc in persona aliorum Apostolorum scribi, quum in tota hac tra- ctatione de ministerio suo vel maxime de sese in persona propria loquatur Apostolus: Excludi cer- te in hac oratione persona Apostoli non potest.

Ideoque multo minus X. Cajetani explicatio de Messia carnali locum habet, quam ita exhibet Estius: Itaque nos ex eo tempore, quo Christus resurrexit, di- dicimus & novimus neminem renovatorem seculi se- cundum carnem, h. e. secundum carnis officia viven- tem, nobis expectandum esse. Et quamvis Apostoli Christum susceperunt secundum carnis officia vi- ventem, quando cum eo conversati sunt in terra, id tantum ad tempus fuit, donec compleret Christus my- sterium nostræ redemptionis. Nam de cætero usque in æternum nec illi, nec nos Christum ut talem novimus; sed solummodo eum novimus viventem secundum spiritum in carne immortali. XI. B. Hülsemannus eâ probata sententia de persuasione regni terreni, illo- rum accedit explicationi, qui carnalē cognationem & corporalem unionem Christi respici volunt, cujus annotata, quia ἀνέκδοτα, huc afferre libet: Parti- culam, inquit, connexivam ὥςε aliquid inferre ex Antecedentibus, dubium non est; sed quale sit illud proxime intentum ab Apostolo variant authores. Plerique enim quia Paulus v. 15. de officio renovatio- nis seu renuntiandi omnibus carnalibus desideriis mo- nuit, sentiunt: etiam hoc versu cognitionem Christi secundum carnem, quam de sese negat Paulus, signi- ficare falsam discipulorum, aliorumque de voluptua- rio & terreno regno Christi opinionem. Verum illud ὥςε initio commatis positum aliquid majus, & quasi disparatum ex Antecedentibus inferre patet ex usur- patione particulæ v. 17. ὡς ὅτι v. 19. & ὥςε c. IV. 12. c. I. 8. c. II. 7. c. III. 7. & infra c. VII. 7. quibus locis semper illativa Majoris ex minore hoc modo; adeo, ut &c. ut multo magis vel ut multo minus, & similem sensum inferat. Confer Phil. I. 13. 1. Thess. I. 17. Itaque non nosse Christum secundum carnem notat quidem analogum quid antecedenti phrasi (non vivere sibi ipsi) sed aliquid majus, videlicet non gloriari in eo, in quo gloriabantur Pseudo-Apostoli, quibus opponit Paulus hanc illationem, quod manifeste patet ex v. 14. cum 13. scil. Paulum aliosque Christianos adeo sibi de- mortuos esse, ut neque carnalē sanguinis conjunctio- nem cum Christo, quam jactabant Pseudo-Apostoli, neque consuetudinem cum Christo in terris vivente, quam identidem jactabant, ut patet ex 1. Cor. XV. 8.

Rom. IX. 3. Eph. III. 7. seq. Phil. III. 4. seq. tanquam ἐξοχὴν quandam, ob quam Paulus cupiat preferri cuipiam Doctori, velit allegare. Verum si maxime cognatione carnis attingat Christum, eumque in die- bus carnis Christum de facie noverit (quod impru- denter negat Estius) vide 1. Cor. IX. 1. adeo in novam creaturam esse transformatum, ut nihil hujus, tan- quam prælatione dignum cupiat allegare. Hæc vi- detur scopo Pauli congruentissima sententia esse, ut τὸ secundum carnem hic loci non vitia carnalia, seu impuritas carnis; sed prælatio ob res extrinse- cas in oculos incurrentes intelligantur. Quomodo Lutherus in glossa Marginali quoque exposuit. Aqua abeunt hactenus Vinarienses, qui verba in persona Pauli prolata κατὰ σάρκα χριστὸν &c. exponunt de falsa communique Pauli opinione circa temporale Christi regnum cum cæteris discipulis. Quia enim Paulus de individuo hoc Jesu ante conversionem suam non nisi pessime sensit, neq; etiam tale regnum præsum- sit, quale præsumebant discipuli, ac proinde τὸ nosse secundum carnem in persona Pauli dictum, hoc signi- ficat notitiam de facie ut supra 1. Cor. IX. 1. & cap. XV. 8. Solent enim ejusmodi Allegoriis verba Me- taphorica aliquid commune habere & aliquid sin- gulare, ut 1. Tim. VI. 5. 6. vocabulum πορισμῦ utro- que versu aliquid commune habet, & aliquid sin- gulare. Hæc B. Dominus Socer. Notarat similem sententiam Flacius in glossa hoc modo: Qui pu- tant Apostolum perstringere illas inanes quorundam gloriationes, qui jactabant, se suosque Præceptores Pe- trum aut Jacobum, aliosve in carne vidisse Chri- stum, cum eoque familiariter versatos; Paulum vero minime, ideoque magis sibi aut illis, quam ipsi cre- dendum esse. Quæ sententia, Flacii judicio, proba- bilis est, siquidem easdem illorum gloriationes etiam in epistola ad Galatas refutet Apostolus. Alium ta- men XII. sensum protulit Flacius hoc modo: Con- cludit ex præcedentibus, quod quoniam cum Chri- sto est mortuus, & ad novam vitam resuscitatus, ideo jam nullius carnales dotes admiretur, de quibus Pseudo-Apostoli tam insolenter gloriabantur, nec ulla carnalia commoda quærat, ut illi. Quin etiam se non tam respicere, quomodo hic Christus in terris versatus sit, quam quomodo jam in cælis in illo suo spirituali regno regnet & triumphet: ibi sese illi ad- junctum addictumque esse. Cujus explicationi ge- mina fere est, quæ in Annotatis Bezæ legitur. Sed nec carnales dotes in Christo admiratus est un- quam Apostolus, nec neglexit respicere, quod Christus in terris versatus sit; sed vel hoc unicum se scire professus est, Jesum crucifixum 1. Cor. II. 3. Qualem se gesserit, & quid passus sit in terris Chri- stus. XIII. Jonas Schlichtingius in Comm. ad h. l. respici vult carnalem Dei cultum & circumcisio- nem, quod nullam in quoquam rerum carnalium & rituum legalium rationem & æstimationem jam habeant; etsi antea Christum secundum circumci- sionem & alios carnales legis cultus spectarint, cum scilicet in carne viveret. Sed quomodo nosse aut spectare Christum poterat Paulus, in diebus car- nis ejus? & quid ad hunc locum aut rem præsen- tem facit circumcisio, aut rituum legalium obser- vatio? XIV. Nonnulli denique τὸ κατὰ non ad co- gnitum, sed ad cognoscentem referunt. Ita Aretius: infert conclusionem: Ergo carnales dotes non amplius admiror, quia dilectio Christi me aliud docet, abnegare sc. me, ne mihi vivam, sed Christo, qui pro me est mor- tuus. Secundum carnem aliquem cognoscere, est ali- quem carnaliter agnoscere, h. e. eo modo, quo mundus aliquem agnoscit, summa probare & laudare, vel da- mnare, quæ mundus damnat. Sic sapientiam & elo- quentiam agnoscit mundus, id carnale est. Et ἀπὸ τ̃ε νῦν fit præsens status Pauli post conversionem; non momentum. Deinde exempli gratia subjicit de Chri- sto, quod si Christum agnovimus secundum carnem, at jam non amplius sic agnoscimus, hoc est, aliquan- do Christum secundum carnem agnovi ante conver- sionem. Christum carnaliter noverat, hoc est homi- nem extrema morte dignum, impium, & imposto- rem, ideo persequebatur illum. At jam, inquit, non amplius ita: Jam Dei filium agnosco, servatorem & liberatorem meum. Accedit facile Aretio Pisca- tor, etsi deducat hanc conclusionem e superiori- bus de sinceritate Apostoli, quod a tempore con- versionis suae neminem censeat e rebus externis, eoque innuat, se quoque a Corinthiis ita aestimari nolle, prolepsin hic ponens, quae occurrat Apo- stolorum eorum cogitationi, qui poterant obji- cere tempus ante conversionem, quo Paulus nove- rat, id est, aestimaverat secundum carnem, hoc est, ex paupertate, & ignominia & odio Pharisaeorum. Fateri itaque Apostolum, se aliquando ita judi- casse, sed nunc non item. Aretii interpretationem κατὰ πόδα sequutus est B. Weinrichius. A qua et- iam non multum abit B. Balduini Commentarius, nec B. Waltherus in Harmonia ad h. l. Quam et- iam non improbabilem censet Cornelius a Lapide. Neque sane inconveniens illa est, sive phrasin, sive contextum spectemus. Nam carnaliter de quodam judicare mundi est, non fidelium, & Paulus se jun- git aliis, qui etsi non perinde ut Paulus ante con- versionem Christum pro seductore habuere: ta- men similiter de illo judicarunt. Convenit tamen nec de Christo, nec de quoquam hominum secun- dum carnem vel carnaliter judicare; sed secun- dum spiritum; ita ut non modo non vivant sibi- metipsis secundum carnem; sed etiam de aliis non judicent secundum carnem. Quo itidem carnale Pseudo-Apostolorum judicium de Apostolis nota- tur. Ita B. Hunnio secundum carnem nosse est respe- ctum habere ad externam hominum personam: & reliquos Apostolos quondam carnaliter de Christo sentientes, & Paulum, ipsum etiam persequentem respici vult: Jam autem non amplius ex sensu car- nis, aut carnali quodam judicio personam ipsius, & officium, & regnum aestimare intelligit. Et ita cum immediate praecedentibus rectius illa cohaerent, ut non nobis ipsis vivamus, sed Christo, quorum illud carnalium; hoc vero spiritualium est, & conse- quentibus de nova in Christo creatura. Atque eo abit etiam paraphrasis Osiandrina: Cum intellige- mus nos a Christo ideo redemptos esse, ut ipsi fideli- ter serviamus, jam in diligendo proximo & faci- endo officio nostro non carnaliter agimus, nec respe- ctum personarum habemus, nec nostra carnalia commoda quaerimus, sed Dei gloriam & hominum salutem promovere studemus. Et quamvis multi (etiam ex ipsis Apostolis) in Christo carnalia com- moda quaesiverint, (quippe quem Regem mundanum fore aliquandiu credebant, qui in suos collaturus esset terrenas opes & facultates) tamen jam depo- sita illa falsa & carnali opinione non carnalia sed spiritualia & aeterna beneficia in Christo quaerimus. Haec denique B. Lutheri nostri etiam mens vide- tur fuisse in glossa marginali: Christum nicht mehr erkennen nach dem Fleisch, ist, nichts fleisch- liches an Ihm suchen noch gewarten, wie die Jün- ger thaten für dem Leyden, sondern an seinem Worte begnügen, darinnen sie eitel geistlich und ewiges Gut haben. Quo pacto non opus est vel subjun- ctivum loco indicativi substituere, vel Antana- clasin statuere cum Grotio, cui tamen hic praeive- re Belgae in notis suis, uti hos deinde sequuti sunt autores notarum Germanicarum, quae ad glossas Toffani accessere in editione nupera Moeno- Francofurtana.

## 5:17
Verse 17. That if any one is in Christ a new creation) He who professes Christ is as it were a new man, and is to be estimated from the progress which he has made in the way of Christ. New creation is spoken of now concerning the Christian life, as in Galatians 6:15, now concerning the Christian man himself. Both are correct. For God produces that life and refashions the man. Compare Romans 6:6. Not far from this is that which Plato says, cited by Eusebius in Preparation 11: "And earth-born men, being produced in this way by necessity, have a stamp and a reason, so that God did not carry them off into another portion." Add what is at John 3:3.

The inference from the preceding is by no means obscure: If any one is in Christ, that is, is engrafted into Christ through faith, he is a new creature, or is truly renewed, so looking in all his actions to the glory of God and the salvation of his neighbor. As Plato knows nothing of Christ and faith in Christ, so he knows just as much of a new creature, and this could have been established even from this passage: Where the powers of nature are thoroughly prostrated. For the Apostle concludes from what has just been said, as the blessed Hunnius rightly [does], that those who are imbued with the knowledge of Christ, not carnally, but truly and spiritually, have all that not from the powers of nature, but from the new creation of God, that is, from the regeneration and illumination of the divine Spirit, and thus through the reparation made in us by Christ.
