Therefore, such persons, as a new creature, ought not to live for themselves, but for Him by whose benefit they have been brought to this newness, namely Christ. But just as a man cannot create himself, or contribute anything to his own creation, so we cannot from the powers of nature contribute anything to our regeneration or new creation, which is the work of God alone, just as much as the primal creation itself. Concerning which he also testifies in verse 19: But all things are from God.

The old things have passed away) Nobility, wealth, philosophy, are nothing.

Behold all things have become new) All things are new which lead us to eternal salvation, from which we are now to be estimated. See Ephesians 3:8. It is, however, a mystical application of the passage in Isaiah 43:18, 19.

The old things are not philosophy, wealth, or nobility. For these are gifts of God to be acknowledged with a grateful mind: nor do they pass away in the new creation, but can well consist with our regeneration and renewal. Some refer them to circumcision and other things of the Old Testament. Which was also done by Schlichting. But here the old things are noted as such things which are repugnant to the new creation of the old internal man, and the new birth is designated. The old things have passed away and all things have become new in the reparation, both as to redemption and as to the new face brought upon the world through Christ. Everything was indeed corrupted through Adam, justice was in exile, sin flourished, death reigned, the Devil held the empire of death and the principality of the world; and these were the old things, which ceased in Christ, with eternal justice brought in, sin abolished, death destroyed, the Devil conquered; and thus all things have become new; both as to justification: The old things pass away, because we obtain the remission of sins; and they become new, because we are made the justice of God in Christ: and as to sanctification; because the old ignorance of the mind, the perversity of the heart, and the disorder of the affections and of all the members pass away: But they become new in our renewal, when the mind is renewed and the heart with the affections, and the members of the old man are mortified, and the new man comes forth. As we are the old man in the first and carnal Adam, or through carnal propagation: But we are a new creature in the second Adam, or through spiritual regeneration. For whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, whatever is born of the Spirit is spirit, John 3:5, 6. Some think that this passage looks to that of Isaiah 43:18, 19: Remember not the former things, and do not consider the ancient things: Behold I make new things and now they shall spring forth, you shall surely acknowledge them. To others, the Apostle seems here to hint at the same time at the prophecy

Isaiah 65:17. Behold I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be in memory, (which also 1 Peter 3:13, Revelation 21:1, where there is discourse about the other life, seems to be looked to) because renewal is begun in this life, and will be consummated in the other. It is certainly treated there of the Church, or the new people, and of the joy of the Elect in the Church, or the kingdom of grace, which is a certain foretaste of heavenly joy in the kingdom of glory, Romans 14:7, Hebrews 6:5. But the renewal of man, by which he becomes a new creature from an old one, looks to that. It is treated there of the fruit of the Gospel, in the time of the New Testament, and of the joy of the people of God, about to arise in the Church, but because that is consummated in the heavens, through the creation of a new heaven and a new earth, we have taught that the state of eternal life is designated at that passage of the Prophet, and that not according to the mystical sense only, but according to the literal sense. But all things are here said by our Apostle to have become new, as regards the faithful and the Church, not that renewal is perfect here, and the Church entirely pure, but in respect to oldness, and in a comparative sense, that just as outside of Christ on account of the first Adam nothing but the oldness of the flesh has a place; so now the turns have been changed in Christ, so that one may exclaim: the old things have passed away, behold all things have become new: both because in Christ there is nothing but a new creature: and because Christ has acquired newness for all, and as far as in Him lies, wishes to impart it to all, and because in the Church all things are new, new grace, a new heart, a new spirit, a new life, as regards those who are properly of the Church, and insofar as they are spiritual and in Christ: in whom, however, the relics of oldness, insofar as they are still in part carnal, remain, nor are they denied by the Apostle here to remain. Compare Romans 7:14 seqq., Galatians 5:17.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὅτι εἴ τις ἐν χριστῷ καινὴ κτίσις) Qui Christum profitetur est velut homo novus, & æstimandus ex pro- fectu quem fecit in via Christi. Nova creatio modo de vita Christiana, ut Gal. VI. 15. modo de ipso Christiano homine dicitur. Recte utrumque. Nam vitam illam pro- ducit Deus & hominem refingit. Conf. Rom. VI. 6. Non multum abit hinc id quod Plato dicit citatus Eusebio præ- parationis XI. Καὶ γηγενεῖς δὲ κατὰ τᾶτον τὸν τρόπον ἐξ ἀνάγ- κης φυόμενοι, ἕτως ἔχειν τύπωμα καὶ τὸν λόγον, ὅπως μὴ Θεὸς αὐτῶν εἰς ἄλλην μοῖραν ἐκόμισεν. Adde quæ ad Joh. III. 3.

Illatio è præcedentibus minime obscura est: Si quis in Christo est, hoc est, per fidem Christo insitus est, nova Creatura, vel verè renovatus est, adeò in omnibus actionibus suis DEI gloriam & pro- ximi salutem spectans. Plato ut de Christo & fide in Christum nihil; ita tantundem etiam de nova creatura novit, idque vel ex hoc loco constare poterat: Ubi vires naturæ penitus prosternuntur. Concludit enim Apostolus ex jam dictis, ut B. Hun- nius rectè, eos qui Christi notitia non carnali, sed verâ & spirituali sunt imbuti, habere id totum non ex naturæ viribus, sed ex nova creatione Dei, hoc est, ex regeneratione & illuminatione divini Spiritus, adeoque per reparationem à Christo in no- bis factam. Proinde tales veluti novam creaturam non sibi vivere debere, sed ei, cujus beneficio ad hanc novitatem traducti sunt, nempe Christo. Quam vero non potest homo seipsum creare, aut quic- quam ad sui creationem conferre, tam non pos- sumus ex naturæ viribus aliquid conferre ad no- stri regenerationem vel novam creationem, quæ Dei solius opus est æque ut ipsa primæva creatio. Quo de etiam v. 19. testatur: Omnia autem ex Deo.

Τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν) Nobilitas, opes, philosophia, ni- hili sunt.

Ἰδὲ γέγονε τὰ πάντα καινά) Nova sunt omnia, quæ ad salutem æternam nos ducunt, ex quibus nunc æstimandi sumus. Vide Eph. III. 8. Est autem mystica applicatio loci Esaiæ XLIII. 18. 19.

Τὰ ἀρχαῖα non sunt Philosophia, opes, aut nobi- litas. Hæc enim dona Dei sunt grato animo agno- scenda: nec transeunt in nova creatione, sed cum nostri regeneratione ac renovatione consistere probè possunt. Nonnulli ea ad circumcisionem & alia Veteris Testamenti referunt. Quod etiam fa- ctum à Schlichtingio. Sed hic τὰ ἀρχαῖα notan- tur ejusmodi, quæ repugnant novæ creationi ve- teris hominis interni, & novi ortus designatur. Transierunt vetera & nova facta sunt omnia in reparatione, tum qua redemptionem, qua nova fa- cies orbi invecta per Christum. Erant utique omnia corrupta per Adamum, justitia exulabat, peccatum vigebat, mors regnabat, Diabolus ha- bebat mortis imperium, & mundi Principatum; atque hæc erant vetera, quæ in Christo desierunt, justitiâ æternâ adductâ, peccato abolito, morte interemptâ, Diabolo devicto; & ita omnia nova facta sunt; tum qua justificationem: Transeunt vetera, quia peccatorum remissionem consequi- mur; & fiunt nova, quia justitia DEI efficimur in Christo: tum qua sanctificationem; quia transit vetus ignorantia mentis, perversitas cordis, & ἀτα- ξία affectuum & membrorum omnium: Nova au- tem fiunt in nostra renovatione, cum mens reno- vatur & cor cum affectibus, & mortificantur mem- bra veteris hominis, novusque homo prodit. Uti ve- tus homo sumus in Adamo primo & carnali, vel per carnalem propagationem: Nova autem crea- tura sumus in Adamo secundo, vel per spiritualem regenerationem. Quicquid enim ex carne natum est, caro est, quicquid ex Spiritu natum est, spiri- tus est Joh. III. 5. 6. Respici censent nonnulli lo- cum istum Esa. XLIII. 18. 19. Ne memineritis pri- orum, & antiqua ne intueamini: Ecce ego facio nova & nunc orientur, utique agnoscetis ea. Aliis videtur Apostolus hic innuere simul vaticinium

Esa. LXV. 17. Ecce ego creo cælos novos & terram novam, & non erunt in memoriam priora, (quod etiam 1. Petr. III. 13. Apoc. XXI. 1. ubi de vita altera sermo est, respici videtur) quia renovatio in hac vita inchoatur, in altera consummabitur. Agitur sanè illic de Ecclesia, vel populo novo, & de Electorum gaudio in Ecclesia, vel regno gratiæ, quod πρόγευσμα quoddam est gaudii cœlestis in regno gloriæ Rom. XIV. 7. Ebr. VI. 5. Eo autem spectat renovatio hominis, qua ex veteri nova creatura fit. Agitur illic de fructu Evangelii, tempore Novi Testamenti, ac de gaudio populi DEI, in Ecclesia orituro, sed quia id consummatur in cœlis, per novi cæli & novæ terræ creationem, vitæ æternæ statum designari ad istum Prophetæ locum docuimus, idque non secundum mysticum tantùm, sed secundum literalem sensum. Omnia autem hic ab Apostolo nostro jam dicuntur nova facta, quod ad fideles & Ecclesiam, non quod perfecta hic sit renovatio, & Ecclesia prorsus pura, sed respectu vetustatis, & in sensu comparato, quod quemadmodum extra Christum ob primum Adamum nil nisi vetustas carnis locum habeat; ita nunc vices commutatæ sint in Christo, ut exclamare liceat: vetera transierunt, ecce omnia nova facta sunt: tum quod in Christo nil nisi nova creatura sit: tum quod Christus omnibus novitatem acquifiverit, & quantum in se est, impartiri omnibus velit, tum quod in Ecclesia omnia nova sint, nova gratia, novum cor, novus spiritus, nova vita, quoad eos, qui proprie de Ecclesia sunt, & quatenus illi spirituales & in Christo sunt: in quibus tamen reliquiæ vetustatis, quatenus adhuc ex parte carnales sunt, restant, neque hic ab Apostolo restare negantur. Conf. Rom. VII. 14. seqq. Gal. V. 17.

## 5:18
Verse 18. But all things) These, namely, from which we are to be estimated. And having given to us the ministry of reconciliation) He made us ministers of His own purpose.

The source and origin of all these things, that Christ died for us all, that being made alive in Christ we do not live for ourselves, that we judge no one according to the flesh, but spiritually, that we have a true and spiritual knowledge of Christ himself, that we are in Christ through faith, that we are a new creature, and that the Church is spoken of as being of the faithful and the assembly of the saints, old things have passed away, all things have become new, is the grace of GOD, both by which he reconciled us to himself through Christ; and by which he gave the ministry of reconciliation, so that we might return to favor with him, and might enjoy in the very act the reconciliation which Christ earned for us. Flacius explains the continuation thus: Since he had thus manifoldly compared the law with the Gospel, and had preferred the glory and efficacy of the Gospel to the law; now at last he concludes, explaining in a summary the true method of salvation and the sum of the Gospel. For although he seemed in this part especially to wish to defend his own person and ministry; yet because he can in no way adorn himself more than by celebrating his doctrine, and because he is otherwise accustomed to pass eagerly from baser matters to nobler ones, especially to celebrating Christ and his benefits: Therefore in this whole part he has discoursed much on the article of justification, and now, as we have said, he constructs here a brief summary of it. He says that the author and architect of salvation is God the Father himself. The cause for which, or the meritorious cause, is his Son, who suffered for us; finally, the applicatory or instrumental cause of such a great benefit is the ministry or heavenly doctrine, of which he himself is an administrator. He sets forth this three-membered sentence first very briefly, then he explains it more fully. Therefore he commemorates here two most excellent works of GOD, which are in the Church especially clear: that the world after the fall was reconciled to God, and that this reconciliation is announced through the ministry of the word, both were highly necessary: First, for the reparation of man, it was required that the justice of God offended by the sins of men be appeased. For unless reconciliation had been made, man would have had to perish in sin and damnation. Then it was necessary that a ministry be made known or ordained for us, which would announce such a benefit to us, so that we might apprehend it by faith. Both of which must be attributed solely to divine grace. Therefore, he first names God as the author of reconciliation. These things indeed, as Theophylact holds here, have been conferred upon us by God, who, through the intervention of his Son, brought it about that we should return into favor with him. For we did not first flee to him of our own accord; but he called us forth through the death of his Son. Then he expresses the benefit itself by καταλλαγὴν, a word taken from human affairs, where enmities that have arisen through the offense of men are quieted by the intervention of a mediator, in which manner the Apostle declares this reconciliation in Rom. V. 10. When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God: just as the word itself καταλλάττειν, by the force of its origin, implies a certain change, as it were, or alteration, by which the offended party is, as it were, made different, and is changed (from ἄλλῳ) not indeed in respect to itself, but in respect to the offender; and just as it was previously angry, offended, and alienated; so, through reconciliation, it is morally changed, and becomes appeased and propitious. Thus 1 Cor. VII. 11, the woman is commanded, τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγήτω, that she be reconciled to her husband, whom she has irritated, striving to repair the broken grace and restore it to its entirety. Furthermore, he who has been reconciled is designated by the word ἡμᾶς, which is not about the Apostles as such, but according to the common lot of men, as they themselves were, and we all, under the wrath of God outside of this καταλλαγὴν. However, God is not said to have reconciled us to himself as if no reconciliation had been made on the part of God; because the wrath of God had to be entirely appeased, to which we were liable on account of sin, since we have all been concluded under sin Rom. XI. 32. Gal. III. 22. but because the denomination of the transaction itself is from the offending party and the one in need of reconciliation. Which the common use of speech teaches. For a Prince is not said to be reconciled to a subject so much, because he himself did not offend, even though reconciliation must be made entirely on his part, so that the pardon of the fault may be obtained; as the subject is said to be reconciled to the Prince, because he himself is the offending party: Therefore Christ also commands the offending brother to be reconciled to the offended brother Matth. V. 24. God does not offend man; but man offends God. And therefore we are not said to be reconciled to God, but we to God. Therefore, as regards Him to whom the human race has been reconciled, so that He might be rendered appeased and propitious to it, the Apostle expresses it with the word ἑαυτῷ; since God reconciled the world to himself out of immense grace, having pity on our inescapable misery, having procured such a καταλλαγῇ, by which, without prejudice to His justice, wrath could be laid aside, and propitiation could be obtained. Accordingly, the Apostle also names the Mediator, through whom it was done, Jesus Christ. For there is one Mediator of God and men, the Man Jesus Christ, who gave himself a ransom for all 1 Tim. II. 5. This, therefore, is the third party intervening, who reconciled the dissenting parties, satisfied divine justice, appeased the wrath of God, and rendered God propitious to us. Thus, in summary, he has the first benefit recounted by Paul.

As to the second, namely the ministry of the Word, by which the redemption made through Christ is announced to the world, it takes its denomination from there, and is called ἡ διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς: By which word both its primary object is explained, and the doctrine of the Gospel is emphatically distinguished from the doctrine of the law. Since the latter indicates only the offense of God and wrath against men, so that the mouth of the whole world may be stopped Rom. IV. 11. chap. III. 19. But the former announces the appeasement of God performed through the blood and death of Christ, and thus offers the divine grace obtained by Christ for the whole human race to all men. The Apostle likewise refers that benefit to God as the Author: Without whose revelation nothing of this divine counsel concerning our salvation would have been known to any mortal, without whose authority no one could have undertaken such an embassy, no one could have deserved or found faith. He gave us the ministry of reconciliation. He does not understand only himself with the other Apostles who were called immediately by God, but also Timothy with any similar ones, or those called mediately. For even those who are called to this ministry by men, while they are called legitimately, are called by God, just as the Holy Spirit is said to have placed the Ephesian presbyters as Bishops to feed the Church of God acquired by his blood, Act. XX. 28. And Timothy, although not called immediately by Christ, is said to have received from God τὴν διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς.

Latin:

V. 18. Τὰ δὲ πάντα) Hæc scilicet, ex quibus censendi sumus. Καὶ δόντος ἡμῖν τὴν διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς) Ministros nos fecit ipsius sui propositi.

Fons & origo istorum omnium, quod Christus pro nobis omnibus mortuus, quod vivificati in Christo ipsi non nobis vivimus, quod non judicamus quenquam carnaliter, sed spiritualiter, quod veram & spiritualem notitiam de Christo ipso habeamus, quod in Christo sumus per fidem, quod nova sumus creatura, quodque de fidelibus & sanctorum cœtu Ecclesia dicatur, vetera transierunt, omnia nova facta sunt, DEI gratia est, tum qua reconciliavit nos sibimetipsi per Christum; tum qua dedit ministerium reconciliationis, ut cum ipso in gratiam redeamus, & reconciliatio- ne, quam Christus promeruit nobis, actu ipso fruamur. Συνέχειαν ita edisserit Flacius: Cum ita multipliciter contulisset legem cum Evangelio, & gloriam efficaciamque Evangelii prætulisset legi; nunc tandem concludit, compendio exponens veram salutis rationem & summam Evangelii. Etsi enim visus est in hac parte potissimum suam personam & ministerium tueri velle; tamen quia nulla ratione seipsum magis ornare potest, quam celebrando suam doctrinam & quia alioqui solet cupide à vilioribus materiis ad nobiliores, præsertim ad celebrandum Christum, ejusque beneficia transire: Ideo in tota hac parte multa de articulo justificationis disseruit, & nunc ficuti diximus, summam ejus brevem hic conficit. Autorem & architectum salutis dicit esse ipsum Deum Patrem. Causam propter quid, aut meritoriam esse Filium ejus, qui pro nobis sit passus; postremo causam applicatoriam aut instrumentalem tanti beneficii esse ministerium aut doctrinam cœlestem, cujus ipse sit administrator. Primum autem brevissime ponit hanc trimembrem sententiam, deinde eam plenius explicat. Duo ergo hic commemorat opera DEI præstantissima, quæ in Ecclesia maxime sunt perspicua: quod mundus post lapsum Deo fuit reconciliatus, & quod reconciliatio ista per mini- sterium verbi annuntiatur, utrumque summe ne- cessarium fuit: Primum ad reparationem homi- nis requirebatur, ut justitia DEI peccatis homi- num offensa placaretur. Nisi enim facta fuisset reconciliatio, homini fuisset in peccato & damna- tione pereundum. Deinde necessum erat, ut nobis innotesceret vel ordinaretur ministerium, quod tantum beneficium nobis annuntiaret, ut fide id apprehendamus. Quod utrumque unice gratiæ divinæ acceptum ferendum est. Ideo autorem reconciliationis primo Deum nominat. Hæc sa- ne universa, ut Theophylactus hic habet, nobis a DEO collata sunt, qui Filii sui interventu, secum ut in gratiam rediremus effecit. Neque enim priores ipsi ad eum ultro confugimus; sed per Filii mortem nos ille excivit. Deinde beneficium ipsum expri- mit per καταλλαγὴν, voce sumpta ab humanis, ubi per offensam hominum inimicitiæ ortæ inter- ventu mediatoris sopiuntur, quo pacto hanc re- conciliationem declarat Apostolus Rom. V. 10. Cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus DEO: quemadmodum ipsum verbum καταλλάττειν, vi originis, infert aliquam velut mutationem, seu alterationem, qua pars offensa velut alia sit, & mu- tatur (ab ἄλλῳ) non quidem sui, sed offendentis respectu; & sicut ante irata erat, offensa & alie- nata; ita, per reconciliationem scilicet, moraliter mutatur, & placata fit atque propitia. Sic 1. Cor. VII. 11. mulieri imperatur, τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγή- τω, ut marito, quem irritarit, concilietur, direm- ptam gratiam resarcire, & in integrum restituere allaboret. Porro is qui reconciliatus est, designa- tur voce ἡμᾶς, quod non de Apostolis qua talibus, sed juxta communem hominum sortem, ut erant & ipsi, & nos omnes sub ira DEI extra hanc κα- ταλλαγήν. Non autem nos ita sibi reconciliasse dicitur Deus, ac si nulla facta sit ex parte DEI reconciliatio; quia ira DEI omnino placanda erat, cui ob peccatum obnoxii eramus, quum omnes sub peccato conclusi fuerimus Rom. XI. 32. Gal. III. 22. sed quia ex parte offendente & re- conciliationis indigente ipsius transactionis sit denominatio. Quod communis loquendi usus docet. Non enim tam Princeps subdito recon- ciliari dicitur, quia ipse non læsit, utut ex parte ejus omnino fieri debeat reconciliatio, ut culpæ obtineatur condonatio; quam subditus Principi, quia ipse pars lædens est: Ideo etiam jubet Chri- stus fratrem lædentem reconciliari fratri læso Matth. V. 24. Deus non offendit hominem; sed homo Deum. Ideoque non Deus nobis recon- ciliari, sed nos DEO dicimur. Quod ergo Eum, cui reconciliatum sit genus humanum, ut illi pla- catus & propitius redderetur, attinet, exprimit Apostolus voce ἑαυτῷ; siquidem DEUS sibiipsi mundum reconciliavit ex immensa gratia, nostræ ineluctabilis miseriæ misertus, procurata ejus- modi καταλλαγῇ, qua, salva justitia sua, ira depo- ni, & propitiatio conciliari posset. Proinde Me- diatorem etiam nominat Apostolus, per quem ea facta sit, Jesum Christum. Unus enim Mediator est DEI & hominum, Homo Jesus Christus, qui se- ipsum dedit redemptionis pretium pro omnibus 1. Tim. II. 5. Hic ergo tertius interveniens est, qui partes dissidentes conciliavit, justitiæ divinæ satisfecit, DEI iram placavit, nobisque DEUM propitium reddidit. Ita summatim habet primum benefi- cium a Paulo recensitum.

Quod ad alterum, ministerium nempe Verbi, quo redemptio per Christum facta, mundo de- nuntiatur, denominationem inde sortitur, & vo- catur Ῥ διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς: Qua voce & ob- jectum præcipuum ejus exponitur, & emphatice discriminatur doctrina Evangelii à legis doctrina. Siquidem hæc offensam tantum DEI & iram indi- cet adversus homines, ut toti mundo os obstrua- tur Rom. IV. 11. cap. III. 19. Illa vero placationem DEI per sanguinem & mortem Christi præsti- tam annuntiat, adeoque gratiam divinam à Chri- sto toti humano generi conciliatam, omnibus hominibus offerat. Refert autem beneficium il- lud Apostolus pariter ad Deum Autorem: Sine cujus revelatione nihil de hoc divino consilio de salute nostra, ulli mortalium constitisset, sine cujus autoritate nullus tantam legationem susci- pere, nullus fidem mereri aut invenire potuisset. Is dedit nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Non se tantum intelligit cum aliis Apostolis ἀμεσοθεο- κλήτοις, sed Timotheum etiam cum similibus qui- busvis, seu mediate vocatis. Nam & qui vocan- tur ad hoc ministerium ab hominibus, dum vo- cantur legitime, à DEO vocantur, uti Spiritus S. dicitur posuisse presbyteros Ephesinos Episcopos ad pascendam Ecclesiam DEI sanguine acquisitam, Act. XX. 28. Et Timotheus etsi non immediate vocatus à Christo, dicitur à DEO accepisse τὴν διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. Ὡς ὅτι Θεὸς ἦν ἐν χρισῷ κόσμον καταλλάσσων ἑαυτῷ) Here ὡς is explanatory, that is, by which we announce in the name of God.

The Apostle now explains in order both benefits; and first indeed that of the reconciliation made by God through Christ. He had attributed that to God as the Efficient cause. But lest Christ seem to be excluded, he now clearly teaches that God, who reconciled the world to himself, was in Christ not by way of a gracious indwelling, as he dwells in the saints through faith: But by way of the personal indwelling of the Word in the flesh with all his fullness Coloff. II. 9. namely, the divinity united with the flesh by a personal union; or to constitute one subsistent being. Therefore, not only God the Father reconciled the world to himself; but also the Son of God, who was made flesh. For God was in Christ, because the Son of GOD, God himself blessed above all things forever, of the same essence with God the Father, in whom the Father is, and the Father in him, through essential περιχώρησιν, and was in the flesh assumed through union, and personal περιχώρησιν, reconciling the world to himself. Since the Son is of the same essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for these three are one 1 John V. 7, he was offended and angry on account of the apostasy of man, whom he had created with the Father and the Holy Spirit in his own image Gen. I. 26, and therefore manifested in the flesh he reconciled to himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit the world, just as the Son of a King, satisfying the Father for a subject guilty of the crime of high treason, committed against the Father and himself, who is σύνθρονον to the Father, is said to reconcile the same both to the Father and to himself. Which, however, is a simile to be taken with a grain of salt.

The object of reconciliation, which the Apostle had designated by the word ἡμᾶς, he now explains more clearly: that not only the Apostles with their companions, nor only the faithful or the elect are noted, but κόσμος the world, that is, the whole human race. For the name of the world nowhere in Scripture denotes only the elect or the faithful, but when it occurs regarding men, it designates either the reprobate or the whole human race, which as a whole had also offended God by sins, and on account of sin was liable to the wrath of God and eternal damnation. Οὐ γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ, πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον, ἐ ὑσερῦνται τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ Rom. III. 22. 23. Πᾶς ὁ κόσμος ὑπόδικος τῷ Θεῷ, The whole world had been made liable to GOD v. 19. And therefore the whole world was to be reconciled, and consequently GOD sent his Son ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν a propitiation for our sins 1 John IV. 10. which, so that it may not be understood of the Elect only, St. John added v. 14. that the Father sent the Son σωτῆρα τοῦ κόσμου the Saviour of the world, which he embraced most expressly above in chap. II. 2: καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, ὀὐ περὶ ἡμετέρων δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου; and he himself was made a propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours; but also for (the sins) of the whole world. Let it be noted here (1.) the absolute position of the word world, which designates all men, not elect or reprobate. Being reprobate or elect does not make a man, and therefore it does not constitute the human race, and thus neither does it mean the world, says Wolffg. Musculus in Comm. on Col. I. 10. Let it be noted (2.) the designation of all men: For those for whom Christ died, they have been reconciled to God through Christ, by virtue of the comparison of v. 14 & 15 with this v. 17. But he is said to have died for all men not once, but three times, without any restriction. Let it be noted (3.) the act of reconciliation. Because reconciliation is of dissenting parties. These, however, were God and men: certainly not just some, but all, who, namely, had incurred the offense of GOD. Not as elect; for these do not need reconciliation; but as concluded under sin, and liable to the wrath of GOD. In which part there is no difference among men. All, therefore, must be reconciled through Christ the Mediator of GOD and men. Who is not the Mediator of the Elect, but of men, not for the Elect, but for all men he gave himself ἀντίλυτρον 1 Tim. II. 6. Let it be noted (4) the community of the Ministry. For to those to whom the διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς (ministry of reconciliation) extends, they must be reconciled to GOD through Christ. For reconciliation could not be announced to them if it did not pertain to them. But the διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς pertains to and extends to all men according to the divine intention and the tenor of the Apostolic mission. Thus concludes Gerhardus de Neufville from the Reformed side, Disp. I. de Prædestin. th. 26. That reconciliation which is announced to all by Christ and offered to be accepted through faith, that is obtained for all. But reconciliation with GOD made through Christ is announced by Christ himself to all and offered to be accepted through faith. Therefore it is obtained for all. Let it be noted (5.) the universality of the exhortations. Whomever God exhorts to be reconciled to GOD through true repentance and conversion, them Christ has reconciled to GOD, that is, for them he has acquired and merited reconciliation before God. But not only the Elect; but GOD exhorts all men through his word to be reconciled to GOD through true repentance and conversion. Therefore. The major premise is clear from the context v. 20. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, beseeching in Christ's stead, be reconciled to God. The illative particle ὖν (therefore) is used, which teaches that the reconciliation made in Christ, which is the reconciliation of propitiation and the appeasing of divine wrath, is the cause and foundation of the exhortation to the reconciliation of our repentance and conversion to God. Let it be noted (6.) the expiation of the sins of the human race. Christ reconciled those to GOD, and those here reconciled are designated by the word world, whose sins he bore and expiated, and for whom he was made sin. But he did not only bear and expiate the sins of the Elect, nor was he made sin only for the Elect; but for all men. Therefore. The major premise is clear both from the comparison of v. 19 & 20, and is sufficiently manifest in itself. The minor premise, however, is confirmed by parallel passages of scripture and especially by that which is most akin to this 2 Cor. V. 21 of ours, namely Isa. LIII. 6. Let it be noted (7) the consensus of certain Reformers. Wolfgangus Musculus on this passage: He reconciled to himself the world, that is, the whole human race, which was, is, and will be from the beginning to the end of the world, while he gave his Son to death for all. Bartholom. Copenius Disp. de satisf. Christi Anno 1616. th. 26. The universal and indeterminate object of the merit are all men in general without exception. For he died for all, and was made reconciliation for the sins of the whole world 2 Cor. V. 19. 1 Tim. II. 6. 1 John II. 2. The Nassau Theologians Joh. Henricus Alstedius and Georgius Fabricius in Judic. de secund. artic. Remonstrant: who allege the passage 2. Cor. V. 19. to prove: that Christ is the expiation for the sins of the whole world, as far as the dignity and sufficiency of the λύτρου (ransom) is concerned. The suffrage of Gerhardus de Neufville has already been cited before.

These things concerning the object of reconciliation. As for the act of reconciliation itself, the word καταλλάσσειν is understood by some Reformers not as the mere acquisition of the remission of sins; but also as the actual forgiveness of sins, as in the Hague Conference p. 136, 203, they explained the benefit of reconciliation v. 18, 19 as the actual justification of the elect, so that they might restrict the interpretation of reconciliation to the Elect alone. But that these things which are now said about reconciliation are to be taken as concerning only the interpretation of reconciliation on the part of Christ, contrasted with the actual restoration to favor, is taught both by the Pauline inference from the universal benefit to the universal duty, which inference would be inept, and could not compel all to die to themselves and live to Christ, if the inviting benefit were particular, destined for very few by divine intention: and by the Apostolic distinction between the impetration of reconciliation, of which v. 18, 19 says he reconciled us to himself; and its application, of which he says later v. 20 Christ beseeches through us, be reconciled to God: Therefore the mode of reconciliation, to the acceptance of which Christians are invited, after the reconciliation of the world already made by Christ, must necessarily be different from that mode of reconciliation which has already preceded, and has been obtained for us on the part of GOD. And therefore Wolf acknowledges concerning the former. Musculus, that the object of that reconciliation is not the assembly of the Elect; but the world, or the human race. For reconciliation, as Musculus again says on Col. I. 20, properly concerns sinners, and thus pertains to the whole human race. The reason for reconciliation is catholic on account of the catholic sin, which separated the human race from GOD, likewise: Where God is said to have reconciled the world, one must not dispute about the reprobate, nor about the Elect. In sum, this reconciliation is to be referred to that catholic enmity of the human race, which we all contracted from Adam, on account of the corruption of our nature, and in respect of this the whole world is said to have been reconciled through Christ. Thus Musculus.

Perversely, therefore, the Socinians deny that the word reconciliation is to be taken here for the reconciliation of the offending party through the intercession and satisfaction of a third party intervening, contending that reconciliation is the same as free and gratuitous remission of an offense, on the part of the offended, without any satisfaction. For a promise of impunity, or a spontaneous forgetting of guilt, is not properly reconciliation: whence we are said to be reconciled to GOD by the blood of Christ Rom. V. 10. 11. and here we are said to be reconciled to GOD through Christ, and the death of Christ is joined to the reconciliation performed for all, by which

God, who was in Christ, reconciled the world to himself: cf. the passage 1 Cor. VII. 11. Concerning a woman leaving her husband and being reconciled to her husband.

Not reckoning their trespasses) Not imputing them in such a way that he would not wish to free them from sins and the punishments of sins through that way which Christ had both shown and entered upon, see Luke XXIII. 34. For there are degrees of the remission of sins, as also of other benefits of God, see John III. 16.

That way is none other than that of faith: for through it alone is the actual remission of sins obtained. But Christ had indeed shown this by his teaching and the proclamation of the word: yet he had not entered upon it himself: for he who had not known sin had no need to be freed from sins and the punishments of sins through the remission of sins. Nor did he believe in himself, nor had he been his own Redeemer. Furthermore, those words, 'not reckoning,' are to be taken in such a way that they explain the reconciliation of the world, effected by Christ, formally, so that they exhibit the mode of the same, because the acquisition of the remission of sins is one thing, the actual remission or non-imputation of the same is another: the former is universal, concerning all men, the latter becomes particular by the fault of men, because not all comprehend it by faith, and thus it is proper to the faithful: but teleologically or finally, it presents the end, since God therefore reconciled the world to himself, that to those who are in Christ, sins might not be imputed, i.e., not intending to impute their sins to them, if, that is, they have believed and received the word of reconciliation, as is right; and therefore those things which are added here are not to be torn away, 'and has placed in us the word of reconciliation.' Or it must be said that that 'not reckoning,' not imputing their sins to them, is one thing: that they actually obtain the remission of sins is another. The former implies both the power of the merit of Christ and the intention of God, by which he would no longer wish to impute sins to anyone reconciled through Christ: the latter implies the actual non-imputation or remission of sins: the former implies the reconciliation effected on the part of God, but the latter at the same time implies the assurance of reconciliation on our part. It is therefore vain what Altingius, from the Calvinists, in the Heidelberg Commonplaces, Part II, Loc. IV, and Marcus Fridericus Wendelinus in his Scholastic Theology on Predestination, ch. XI. p. 43, object, that the reprobate are not reconciled to God, nor have they obtained the remission of sins, so that God does not impute sins to them, and that they cannot even be said to have obtained the remission of sins as reconciled on the part of God through the death of the Mediator (which concerns the merit), because through infidelity they repudiate Christ, reconciliation, and the remission of sins: for they confound things which are most diverse: they deny what is openly asserted here by the Apostle, namely, that the world, that is, the whole human race, has been reconciled to God, and they destroy themselves by contradiction. For if the reprobate through infidelity repudiate the reconciliation of Christ and the remission of sins, it is certain that the remission of sins, reconciliation, and the grace of God have been acquired for them through Christ: since they could not reject them through infidelity unless they were to be believed by them and accepted by faith as true: for how could they be believed by them unless they concerned them? Who will be held to believe that Christ has reconciled himself to God and acquired the remission of sins for himself, for whom he has not reconciled, for whom he has not acquired the remission of sins? No one is damned except on account of the neglect of that thing which in some way pertains to him, says Johannes Crocius, Convers. Pruten. Part II, ch. 16, p. 472. Therefore Paulus Steinius in his Evangelical Ecclesiastical Fraternity, ch. 11, p. 348, admits that it can be said even of the damned that Christ has acquired for them the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life.

But the Photinian sect utterly perverts the most sweet sentiment of the Apostle. For what is said, that God has reconciled us to himself, Schlichtingius so depraves: GOD made friends of enemies to himself by his immense grace, not imputing our transgressions, that is, not only declaring that he wishes to do this, but also, to those converted to him, actually exhibiting it through Christ. But it is not said here that God made friends of enemies to himself, but that God is reconciled to us through Christ, namely, through the death and blood of Christ, when that one died in the place of us all, that we might be reconciled to God. Nor does the Apostle assert that God merely declares that he does not impute sins to us, much less that he wishes to do so out of mere liberality and grace, without any reconciliation of the human race; but that he does not impute sin to us for this reason, because we ourselves have been reconciled through the death of the Son. There is no discussion in these words about the declaration of the remission of sins, but about the non-imputation acquired through the reconciliation of Christ: the announcement, declaration, and publication through the word of reconciliation follows afterwards. Wherefore, there is no question here of that declaration, nor of the exhibition of grace to be performed to the converted, ipso facto; but of the grace of redemption and reconciliation exhibited to the world, by which God is so appeased toward all men that non-imputation or remission of sins has been given to all. Therefore, it is not taught here how God made us friends from enemies, holy and just from sinners, spiritual from carnal, most obedient from refractory, but how, when he was reconciled to us through Christ, he was made appeased from angry, and a friend from an enemy, so that to us sinners condemned to death, on account of the reconciliation of Christ and the satisfaction of his death, he might, without prejudice to justice, not impute, but forgive sins, and receive us into favor.

And having placed in us the word of reconciliation) To place words in someone, or in the mouth of someone, is to give commands to someone, Exod. IV. 15. Thus God had given commands to the Apostles to recall the human race to his friendship.

It is now also explained what had been said in v. 18. Concerning the ministry of reconciliation committed to him: where the Apostle explains the word for giving more emphatically with the verb θέμενος, which, as the blessed Baldwin notes, refers partly to the order established in the eternal counsel of God, where it pleased God to deal with sinners in the ordinary way through the ministry of the Word, and to restore lost grace; partly to the certainty of this doctrine; for those things which God has placed, decreed, and established, cannot fail: partly also to the firmness and stability of this doctrine: for against those things which God has placed, the gates of hell with all heretics and tyrants shall not prevail. For which reason Paul, speaking of his own ministry, gladly uses this phrase: God has placed me into the ministry, see 1 Tim. I. 12. c. II. v. 7. etc. Furthermore, the power of the ministry is also clarified: For all power depends not on the dignity of the ministers, but on the efficacy of the word which they preach. And therefore, in place of ministry, he now puts the word of reconciliation. By that word, however, he understands the word of the Gospel, distinguishing it in that respect from the word of the law. For this announces wrath: but that, the appeasement of wrath and grace. And therefore this passage is to be understood not of a command, by which men are ordered to return into favor with God, but of the word of Evangelical announcement, by which reconciliation procured through Christ is offered to men: even though that announcement is made to the end that the reconciliation of Christ may be received by faith, and thus we may actually enjoy divine grace. Concerning which, in the following verse 20, follows the hortatory office of the Apostle.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ὡς ὅτι Θεὸς ἦν ἐν χρισῷ κόσμον καταλλάσσων ἑαυτῷ) Hic ὡς est ἐξηγητικὸν, hoc est, quo DEI nomine annuntiamus.

Explicat Apostolus jam ordine utrumque be- neficium; & primo quidem reconciliationis à DEO per Christum factæ. DEO id tribuerat ceu causæ Efficienti. Ne autem Christus excludi videatur, dilucide jam docet, Deum, qui sibi mundum re- conciliavit in Christo fuisse non per modum inha- bitationis gratiosæ, uti in sanctis per fidem ha- bitat: Sed per modum personalis τῦ Λόγε inha- bitationis in carne cum omni sua plenitudine Coloff. II. 9. divinitate scilicet unita cum carne unione personali; seu ad constituendum unum ὑφισάμε- νον. Reconciliavit ergo sibiipsi mundum non Deus Pater tantum; sed etiam Filius Dei, qui caro factus est. Nam Deus in Christo erat, quia Filius DEI, Deus ipse benedictus super omnia in secu- la, ejusdem cum Deo Patre essentiæ, in quo Pater est, & Pater in ipso, per essentialem περιχώρησιν, et in carne assumpta erat per unionem, & περιχώρη- σιν personalem, mundum sibiipsi reconcilians. Quum Filius ejusdem sit cum Patre, & Spiritu S. essentiæ, hi enim tres unum sunt 1. Joh. V. 7. offen- sus fuit & iratus propter apostasiam hominis, quem cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto ad imaginem suam condiderat Gen. I. 26. ideoque in carne ma- nifestatus reconciliavit sibi ipsi cum Patre & Spi- ritu Sancto mundum, quemadmodum Filius Re- gis satisfaciens Patri pro subdito criminis læsæ Majestatis reo, adversus Patrem & sese Patri σύν- θρονον commiffi, & Patri & sibimetipsi eundem re- conciliare dicitur. Quod tamen simile cum gra- no salis accipiendum.

Objectum reconciliationis, quod voce ἡμᾶς de- signarat Apostolus, jam dilucidius exponit: quod non Apostolos tantum cum sociis, nec fideles solum aut electi notentur, sed κόσμος mundus, id est to- tum genus humanum. Nomen enim mundi nu- spiam in scriptura, solos electos, aut fideles notat, sed cum de hominibus occurrit, vel reprobos, vel totum genus humanum designat, quod universum etiam peccatis Deum offenderat, & ob peccatum iræ Dei & æternæ damnationi obnoxium erat. Οὐ γάρ ἐσι διασολὴ, πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον, ἐ ὑσερῦν- ται τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ Rom. II. 22. 23. Πᾶς ὁ κόσμος ὑπόδικος τῷ Θεῷ, Totus mundus obnoxius DEO factus erat v. 19. Ideoque reconciliandus erat totus mundus, ac proinde DEUS Filium suum misit ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν propitiationem pro peccatis nostris 1. Joh. IV. 10. quod ne de Electis solum intelligatur, adjecit S. Johannes v. 14. Patrem misisse Filium σωτῆρα τοῦ κόσμου Salvatorem mundi, quod supra cap. II. 2. ita expressissime complexus est: καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, ὀὐ περὶ ἡμετέρων δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου; & ipse propitiatio factus est pro peccatis nostris, non autem tantum pro nostris; sed etiam pro totius mundi (peccatis.) Notetur hic (1.) absolutus vocis mundi positus, quæ omnes homines, non electos vel reprobos designat. Reprobum & electum esse non facit hominem, ideoque nec genus humanum constituit, atque ita nec mundum ait Wolffg. Musculus in Comm. ad Col. I. 10. Notetur (2.) hominum omnium designatio: Nam pro quibus Christus mortuus est, illi per Christum Deo reconciliati sunt, vi collationis v. 14. & 15. cum hoc v. 17. At pro omnibus hominibus non semel, sed ternis vicibus, sine ulla restrictione, mortuus esse dicitur. Notetur (3.) reconciliationis actus. Quia reconciliatio est partium dissidentium. Hæ autem erant Deus & homines: non sane aliqui tantum, sed omnes, qui scil. & offensam DEI incurrerant. Non qua electi; nam hi non indigent reconciliatione; sed qua sub peccato conclusi, & iræ DEI obnoxii. Qua in parte nulla inter homines est differentia. Omnes ergo reconciliatos esse oportet per Christum Mediatorem DEI & hominum. Qui non Electorum Mediator, sed hominum, non pro Electis, sed pro omnibus hominibus semetipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον 1. Tim. II. 6. Notetur (4) Ministerii communitas. Nam ad quos sese porrigit διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς, illos per Christum DEO reconciliatos esse oportet. Non enim annunciari ipsis posset reconciliatio, si eosdem non attineret. At ad omnes homines secundum intentionem divinam & missionis Apostolicæ tenorem pertinet ac sese porrigit διακονία τῆς καταλλαγῆς. Ita è Reformatis concludit Gerhardus de Neufville Disp. I. de Prædestin. th. 26. Quæ reconciliatio à Christo omnibus annuntiatur & offertur per fidem acceptanda, ea omnibus est impetrata. At reconciliatio cum DEO per Christum facta ab ipso Christo omnibus annuntiatur & offertur per fidem acceptanda. Ergo ea omnibus est impetrata. Notetur (5.) adhortationum universalitas. Quoscunque Deus hortatur, ut reconcilientur DEO per veram pœnitentiam & conversionem, illos reconciliavit Christus DEO, hoc est, illis reconciliationem acquisivit & promeruit apud Deum. At non solum Electos; sed omnes homines hortatur DEUS per verbum suum, ut reconcilientur DEO per veram pœnitentiam & conversionem. Ergo. Major liquet è contextu v. 20. Igitur pro Christo legatione fungimur rogantes vice Christi, reconciliemini DEO. Adhibetur vocula illativa ὖν igitur, quæ docet, reconciliationem in Christo factam, quæ est reconciliatio propitiationis & placationis iræ divinæ, causam esse & fundamentum adhortationis ad reconciliationem pœnitentiæ & conversionis nostræ ad Deum. Notetur (6.) Peccatorum generis humani luitio. Illos reconciliavit Christus DEO, illique hic reconciliati, voce mundi, designantur, quorum peccata tulit & luit, ac pro quibus factus est peccatum. At non tulit tantum, luitque peccata Electorum, nec pro Electis solum factus est peccatum; sed pro omnibus hominibus. Ergo. Major cum è collatione v. 19. & 20. liquet, tum per se manifesta satis est. Minor autem confirmatur parallelis scripturæ locis ac præcipue illo, qui huic nostro 2. Cor. V. 21. maxime affinis est, ut- pote Esa. LIII. 6. Notetur (7) consensus Refor- matorum quorundam. Wolfgangus Musculus in hunc locum: Mundum, id est omne genus huma- num, quod inde ab initio ad finem usque mundi fuit, est, ac erit, sibi reconciliavit, dum Filium pro omni- bus in mortem dedit. Bartholom. Copenius Disp. de satisf. Christi Anno 1616. th. 26. Objectum me- riti universale & indeterminatum sunt omnes in universum homines sine exceptione. Pro omnibus enim mortuus est, & factus reconciliatio pro pec- catis totius mundi 2. Cor. V. 19. 1. Tim. II. 6. 1. Joh. II. 2. Thelogi Nassovici Joh. Henricus Alstedius & Georgius Fabricius in Judic. de secund. artic. Re- monstrant: qui allegant locum 2. Cor. V. 19. ut pro- bent: Christum esse expiationem pro peccatis totius mundi, quantum ad dignitatem & sufficientiam λύτρου attinet. Gerhardi de Neufuille suffragium jam ante adductum est.

Hæc de objecto reconciliationis. Quod ad actum ipsum reconciliationis intelligitur verbum καταλ- λάσσειν à Reformatis nonnullis non de sola acqui- sitione remissionis peccatorum; sed etiam de ipsa peccatorum condonatione, ut in collatione Hagi- ensi p. 136. 203. reconciliationis beneficium v. 18. 19. de actuali electorum justificatione exposuere, ut reconciliationis interpretationem ad solos Ele- ctos restringerent. Sed hæc quæ nunc de recon- ciliatione dicuntur de sola interpretatione reconci- liationis ex parte Christi, contradistincta actuali restitutioni in gratiam, accipienda esse docet, tum Paulina illatio ab universali beneficio ad uni- versale officium, quæ illatio inepta esset, neque universos adigere posset, ad moriendum sibiipsis, & vivendum Christo, si beneficium invitans parti- culare esset, paucissimis ex divina intentione de- stinatum: tum distinctio Apostolica inter recon- ciliationis impetrationem, de qua v. 18. 19. recon- ciliavit nos sibi; ejusque applicationem, de qua postea v. 20. Christus obsecrat per nos, reconcilia- mini Deo: Ideoque modus reconciliationis, ad quem admittendum invitantur Christiani, post reconciliationem mundi, à Christo jam factam, diversus sit, necesse est, ab illo modo reconcilia- tionis, quæ jam præcessit, & ex parte DEI nobis obtenta est. Ideoque de priori agnoscit Wolf. Musculus, objectum reconciliationis illius non esse Electorum cœtum; sed mundum, vel genus humanum. Reconciliatio enim, ut iterum Muscu- lus in Col. I. 20. proprie concernit peccatores, atque ita pertinet ad totum genus humanum. Catholica est ratio reconciliationis propter Catholicum peccatum, quod genus humanum à DEO divisit, item: Ubi Deus mundum reconciliasse dicitur, neque de repro- bis est, neque de Electis disputandum. In summa ad inimicitiam illam catholicam generis humani, quam ex Adamo contraximus omnes, propter naturæ no- stræ corruptionem, referenda est hæc reconciliatio, & hujus respectu totus mundus per Christum reconcilia- tus dicitur. Hæc Musculus.

Perverse itaque negant Sociniani, reconciliatio- nis vocem hic sumendam esse pro reconciliatione partis nocentis per intercessionem, ac satisfactio- nem tertii intervenientis, contendentes, reconci- liationem idem esse, quod liberam & gratuitam remissionem offensæ, quoad partem læsam, sine ulla satisfactione. Impunitatis enim promissio, aut spontanea reatus oblivio proprie non est recon- liatio: unde reconciliati dicimur DEO sangui- ne Christi Rom. V. 10. 11. & hic per Christum DEO reconciliati dicimur, & conjungitur mors Christi reconciliationi pro omnibus præstitæ, qua

Deus, qui in Christo erat, mundum sibimetipsi re- conciliavit: conf. locus 1. Cor. VII. 11. De fœmi- na maritum deserente reconciliandà marito.

Μὴ λογιζόμενος τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν) Non ita impu- tans, ut non eos à peccatis & pœnis peccatorum vellet libe- rare per eam viam, quam Christus & monstraverat, & ini- verat, vid. Luc. XXIII. 34. sunt enim peccatorum remissio- nis, ut & aliorum Dei beneficiorum sui gradus, v. Joh. III. 16.

Via illa nulla alia est, quam fidei: per eam enim solum obtinetur actualis remissio peccatorum. Hanc autem monstraverat quidem Christus doctrinâ & præconio verbi: Non autem iniverat ipse: Nam à peccatis & pœnis peccatorum liberari per remissio- nem peccatorum opus non habebat, qui peccatum non noverat. Neque in semetipsum credebat, aut sui ipsius fuerat Redemptor. Porro verba illa, μὴ λογιζόμενος ita accipienda, ut explicent reconci- liationem mundi, à Christo factam, formaliter, ut modum ejusdem exhibeant, quia aliud est acqui- sitio remissionis peccatorum, aliud actualis eorundem remissio, vel non-imputatio: illa universalis est, omnes homines attinens, hæc particularis fit ho- minum culpa, quod non omnes fide eam compre- hendant, adeoque fidelium est propria: sed τελι- xῶς vel finaliter, & finem sistit, quum ideo reconci- liârit sibiipsi mundum Deus, ut illis, qui in Christo sunt, non imputentur peccata, q.d. non imputatu- rus iis peccata ipsorum, si sc. crediderint & verbum reconciliationis, ut par est, susceperint; ideoque non divellenda, quæ adduntur hic, & posuit in no- bis verbum reconciliationis. Aut dicendũ aliud esse illud μὴ λογιζόμενος, non imputans ipsis peccata eo- rum: aliud actu eos consequi remissionem peccatorũ. Illud cùm meriti Christi vim, tum Dei intentio- nem, qua vellet nemini jam peccata imputare re- conciliato per Christum: hoc actualem non-impu- tationem seu remissionem peccatorum: Illud re- conciliationem ex parte Dei factam, hoc verò si- mul reconciliationis fiduciam ex parte nostri importat. Vanum ergò est, quod è Calvinianis Al- tingius LL. CC. Heidelberg. P. II. Loc. IV. Marc. Frider. Wendelinus tr. Theol. Schol. de prædestin. c. XI. p. 43. obvertunt, reprobos non esse reconcilia- tos Deo, nec remissionem peccatorum consequutos, ita ut Deus ipsis peccata non imputet, ac ne quidem ex parte Dei per mortem Mediatoris reconciliatos remissionem peccatorum consequutos dici posse, (quod ad meritum) eò quod per infidelitatem Christum, reconciliationem & remissionem pec- catorum repudient: Confundunt enim, quæ ma- xime diversa sunt: Negant, quod aperte ab Apo- stolo hic assertum est, nempe mundum, id est, to- tum genus humanum Deo reconciliatum esse, seq; ipsos ἀντιλογίᾳ conficiunt. Si enim reprobi per infidelitatem reconciliationem Christi & peccato- rum remissionem repudiant, certum est, quod per Christum ipsis acquisita sit remissio peccatorum, reconciliatio & gratia Dei: quandoquidem per infidelitatem reprobare ea non possent, nisi ea ab illis credenda essent, ac fide acceptanda ceu vera: quomodo enim credenda ab illis, nisi eos attine- rent? Qui credere tenebuntur, Christum sese Deo reconciliasse, & peccatorum remissionem sibi ac- quisivisse, quos non reconciliavit, quibus non ac- quisivit remissionem peccatorum? Nemo damna- tur, nisi propter ejus rei neglectum, quæ aliqua ratio- ne ad ipsum pertinet, ait Joh. Crocius convers. Pru- ten. P. II. c. 16. p. 472. ided Paulus Steinius in Ev- angel. Eccl. fratern. c. 11. p. 348. dici posse admittit etiam de damnatis, quod Christus illis remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, & vitam æternã acquisiverit.

Pervertit autem penitus Apostoli sententiam dulcissimam gens Photiniana. Nam quod Deus nos sibi ipsi reconciliasse dicitur, Schlichtingius ita depra- vat: DEUS ex inimicis sibi amicos fecit ingenti sua gratia transgressiones nostras non imputans, id est, non solum se hoc facere velle declarans, sed etiam ad se conversis ipso facto per Christum exhibens. At non Deus ex inimicis sibi amicos fecisse hic, sed Deus nobis per Christum reconciliatus dicitur, per mortem scil. & sanguinem Christi, quando unus ille omnium nostrum vice mortuus est, ut Deo reconciliare- mur. Nec verò tantum Deum declarare, se non im- putare nobis peccata, Apostolus asserit, nedum id velle ex mera liberalitate & gratia, sine ulla generis humani reconciliatione; sed ideò non imputare nobis peccatum, quia nos ipsi reconciliati sumus per mortem Filii. Non de declaratione remissio- nis peccatorum in his verbis sermo est, sed de non- imputatione acquisita per reconciliationem Chri- sti: Annunciatio, declaratio, & publicatio per λό- γον καταλλαγῆς deinde sequitur. Quapropter nec de ea declaratione, nec de exhibitione gratiæ con- versis, ipso facto, præstandæ hic agitur; sed de mundo exhibita redemptionis & reconciliationis gra- tia, qua ita placatus omnibus hominibus est Deus, ut data sit omnibus non-imputatio vel remissio peccatorum. Non ergò hic docetur, quomodo nos Deus ex inimicis amicos sibi fecerit, ex peccatoribus sanctos & justos, ex carnalibus spirituales, ex refra- ctariis obsequentissimos, sed quomodo cum nobis per Christum reconciliatus ex irato placatus, ex ini- mico amicus factus sit, ut peccatoribus nobis ad mortem condemnatis propter Christi reconcilia- tionem & mortis ejus satisfactionem, salvâ justitiâ, peccata non imputare, sed condonare possit, nos- que in gratiam recipere.

Καὶ θέμενος ἐν ἡμῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς καταλλαγῆς) Ponere verba in aliquo, aut in ore alicujus, est mandata alicui da- re, Exod. IV. 15. Sic Deus Apostolis mandata dederat hu- manum genus ad suam amicitiam revocandi.

Explicatur jam etiam, quod dictum erat v. 18. De mini- sterio reconciliationis sibi commisso: ubi vo- cem dandi magis emphatice exponit Apostolus verbo θέμενος, quod, notante B. Balduino, respicit partim ad ordinem in æterno Dei consilio constitutum, ubi placuit Deo, per ministerium Verbi ordinario modo agere cum peccatoribus, & ad deperditam gratiam reducere; partim ad certitudinem hujus doctrinæ; nam quæ Deus posuit, decrevit & constituit, ea fal- lere non possunt: partim etiam ad firmitudinem & stabilitatem hujus doctrinæ: nam quæ Deus posuit, iis portæ inferorum cum omnibus hæreticis ac tyran- nis non prævalebunt. Quam ob causam Paulus de suo ministerio loquens, libenter utitur hac phrasi: Deus me posuit in ministerium, vide 1. Tim. I. 12. c. II. v. 7. &c. Ulterius etiam dilucidatur διακονίας vir- tus: Nam omnis virtus dependet non à ministro- rum dignitate, sed à verbi, quod prædicant, effica- cia. Ideoque loco διακονίας ponit jam τὸν λόγον τῆς καταλλαγῆς. Per verbum autem illud verbum Evangelii intelligit, id discriminans ea ratione à verbo legis. Hoc enim iram annunciat: Illud vero placationem iræ & gratiam. Ideoque non de man- dato, quo jubentur homines redire in gratiam cum Deo, sed de verbo annuntiationis Evangelicæ hic locus accipiendus est, quo offertur hominibus re- conciliatio per Christum parta: etsi eo fine fiat il- la annunciatio, ut fide suscipiatur Christi reconci- liatio, atque ita actu nos fruamur divina gratia. Quo de vers. seq. 20. sequitur officium Apostoli exhortatorium.

## 5:20
V. 20. Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ) Christ announced this in the name of God, but we in the name of Christ, inasmuch as we have been substituted by him into this office, John VI. 57.

As though God were beseeching through us) What the ambassadors say, the King seems to say. GOD had made Christ an ambassador, and Christ, out of the power given to him by the Father, made the Apostles.

We beseech in Christ's stead) In the name of Christ. Καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ) Return to favor with God. He who offends another is also said to be καταλλάσσεσθαι. As can be seen in Matt. V. 23, 24; 1 Cor. VII. 11; Rom. XI. 15.

We add nothing, because we believe everything is clear from what precedes, except for the commentary of the blessed Balduinus on these words: Both offices were entrusted to Christ by God the Father, both that He should be our Priest, who by His death would acquire for us reconciliation with God the Father; and our Teacher, who by His institution would apply such a treasure to us. But because He departed from the world to the Father into His glory, He delegated this office to the Apostles and other Teachers of the Church, whom our Paul therefore names ambassadors of Christ, in whose name they are to be received and heard, as those who propose not their own dreams, but the mandates of God, whether they console or exhort. For the Greek word παρακαλεῖν signifies both. When, therefore, preachers pray, exhort, and beseech men that they be reconciled to God, having renounced impiety and by a faithful apprehension of Christ, or, to say it in one word, by serious repentance, then they do this in the name of Christ, who not only has merited this grace for us, but also stirs up our minds, which are too negligent of such a matter, and beseeches us to apprehend the salvation offered by God. Musculus agrees with us here. 'I have reconciled,' he says, 'in this place is not to be reconciled to the implacable, but to embrace with a grateful heart, through repentance and faith in the blood of reconciliation, the reconciliation already made in Christ, His Son, who is appeased.' Moreover, since God—that the blessed Hunnius may grant this to us again—prepared everything for entering into a covenant of grace with men, by sending His Son into the world and instituting the ministry of the word: since He Himself is the offended or injured party: and since it is not otherwise customary among humans for the offended party to offer reconciliation to the offender: since, furthermore, nothing of blessedness or perfection accrues to God from this work of reconciliation brought into effect, and nothing is lost to Him from the same being left undone. Since, conversely, the entire salvation of men is situated in this business, and unless they are brought back into favor with God, nothing other than eternal damnation is prepared for them, it is a matter akin to a miracle that God, out of mere gratuitous favor and clearly immense mercy, prays to us humans through His ministers, and beseeches us that we accept this reconciliation so mercifully offered to us, and, having performed repentance, admit and apprehend that saving medium by which we are reconciled to God through Christ, namely, the merit of the sacrifice performed for us by Christ for the expiation of sins.

The sophism of Schlichting is therefore manifest, when from this passage he argues that God was neither angry with the human race, nor appeased and reconciled to men by Christ, but rather that the matter stands against itself, namely, that God strove in every way to appease and reconcile men, who were angry with Him, through Christ and the Apostles, not only by the publication of the remission of all past transgressions and of His paternal grace with the inheritance of eternal life; but also by the published work of an absolutely admirable and ineffable charity toward the human race, which he says is placed immediately by the Apostle as well. For how can it be denied that God was offended and angry with men through sin? Since He cannot but be angry on account of sins by the force of His justice. How can the reconciliation of GOD made through Christ be called into doubt, which is proposed so often in the scriptures and inscribed as if by the rays of the sun, as we have clearly shown in the 'Socinismus Profligatus'? This beseeching, however: 'Be reconciled to GOD,' made in the name of Christ, is posterior in the order of nature to the reconciliation made through the blood of Christ. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, which was done when Christ reconciled us to God by His blood and underwent death in our stead. But then, by the force of this reconciliation made through Christ, He finally placed in His ministry the lógon katalōges, and caused this reconciliation to be announced in the word of the Gospel through the ministers of the word, His ambassadors, and that to this end, that we might be reconciled to God, which does not signify, as Schlichting wants, that we lay aside enmities toward God, but that by the most humble deprecation of the most just wrath of God we seek the grace of God by true faith, (just as an unfaithful spouse is to be reconciled to an offended husband, 1. Cor. VII. 11.) and that by and through Christ our Mediator, and His death, by which He acquired this reconciliation for us; indeed, that we do not reject, but receive, what is offered in the word of the Gospel. For Him προέθετο ὁ Θεὸς ἱλαστήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι, God set forth as a propitiation through faith in His blood, Rom. III. 25. Without this propitiation, no publication of the remission of sins could be made, because without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins, Heb. IX. 22. Nor does the laying aside of a mind averted from God and devoted to works adverse to God happen by the bare publication of the liberal remission of sins, but through the λόγον τῆς καταλλαγῆς, the word of this reconciliation of the world through Christ, the faithful apprehension of it, and the justification that follows therefrom, which is prior to that laying aside; since faith, through which we are justified, is the mother of every good action, and without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI. 6. Indeed, whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. XIV. 23. It is indeed true what Schlichting says, that God does not remit the punishment before men are converted to Him. But conversion is completed by contrition and faith. The amendment of life, however, is a consequence, not an antecedent, of the remission of sins. That, however, is perversely denied by Schlichting, that God is angry with men and has need of reconciliation, from the fact that He Himself seeks their conversion and reconciliation in every way, to such an extent that He even expends His only Son for their conversion and salvation. For different moments in the counsel of God and distinct degrees of divine love are confused. For He seeks our conversion after we ourselves have been reconciled through the death of His Son, and thus He Himself has been appeased toward us. For He expended His Son for us, that He might appease His wrath and acquire reconciliation for us by His death and blood, and thus become a propitiation for the sins of the world, 1 John II. 2. Therefore, one love of God is general, by which He had mercy on the whole world and sent His Son as ἱλασμὸν for the sins of the world, John III. 16. John IV. 10. Another is special, by which He forgives sins to those who believe in the Son, who therefore, for the sake of gratitude, turn their mind away from works adverse to God, and serve God in righteousness and holiness, Luke I. 74.

Latin:

V. 20. Ὑπὲρ Χριστῦ ὖν πρεσβεύομεν) Christus Dei nomine hoc annuntiavit, nos vero Christi nomine, quippe ab ipso in hoc munus substituti, Joh. VI. 57.

Ὡς τῦ Θεῦ παρακαλῦντος δι᾽ ἡμῶν) Legati quod dicunt, id Rex dicere videtur. DEUS Christum legatum fecerat, Christus ex potestate sibi à Patre data Apostolos.

Δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ Χριστῦ) Christi nomine. Καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ) Redite cum Deo in gratiam. Dicitur καταλλάσσεσθαι etiam is, qui alium offendit. Ut videre est Matth. V. 23. 24. 1. Cor. VII. 11. Rom. XI. 15.

Nihil addimus, quia è superioribus omnia constare arbitramur, nisi B. Balduini ad hæc verba commentarium: Christo utrumque officium à Deo Patre erat demandatum, & ut Sacerdos noster esset, qui morte sua nobis reconciliationem cum Deo Patre acquireret; & Doctor noster, qui institutione sua tantum thesaurum nobis applicaret. Sed quia ex mundo abiit ad Patrem in gloriam suam, officium hoc delegavit Apostolis & aliis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus, quos Paulus noster ideo legatos Christi nominat, in cujus nomine recipiendi & audiendi sunt, ut qui non sua somnia, sed Dei mandata proponant, sive consolentur, sive exhortentur. Utrumque enim significat Græca vox παρακαλεῖν. Quando ergo Concionatores orant, hortantur, obtestantur homines, ut reconcilientur Deo, abnegata impietate & fideli apprehensione Christi, seu, ut uno verbo dicam, seria pœnitentia, tunc faciunt id Christi nomine, qui non tantum gratiam istam nobis est promeritus, verum etiam animos nostros tantæ rei negligentiores excitat, & nos ad apprehendendam salutem à Deo oblatam obsecrat. Annuit autem hic nobis Musculus. Reconciliavi, inquit, hoc loco non est reconciliari implacatis, sed reconciliationem jam placati in Christo filio ipsius factam grato animo per resipiscentiam & fidem in sanguinem reconciliationis amplecti. Cæterum quum Deus, ut hoc denuo nobis largiatur B. Hunnius, omnia comparavit ad ineundum gratiæ fœdus cum hominibus, misso Filio in mundum, & instituto verbi ministerio: cum ipse sit pars offensa seu læsa: neque in humanis alias usitatum sit, ut offensa pars reconciliationem deferat offendenti: Cum insuper Deo nihil accedat beatitudinis aut perfectionis ex hoc reconciliationis opere in effectum deducto, nihil eidem decedat ex eodem intermisso. Cum è converso tota hominum salus in hoc negotio sita sit, & nisi cum Deo redigantur in gratiam, aliud nil quam sempiterna damnatio parata eis sit, omen miraculi simile est, quod Deus ex mero favore gratuito & immensa plane misericordia nos homines orat per ministros suos, & obsecrat, ut hanc reconciliationem misericorditer adeo nobis oblatam acceptemus, actaque pœnitentia salutare illud medium admittamus & apprehendamus, quo sumus Deo per Christum reconciliati, nempe meritum sacrificii in expiationem peccatorum pro nobis à Christo præstiti.

Manifestum ergo est sophisma Schlichtingii, quando ex hoc loco Deum nec humano generi iratum, nec à Christo placatum & hominibus reconciliatum esse, imo contra se rem habere, nempe Deum homines, sibi iratos, placasse, & reconciliare per Christum & Apostolos omnibus modis conatum fuisse, non tantum publicatione remissionis omnium præteritarum transgressionum, & paternæ suæ gratiæ cum vitæ æternæ hæreditate; sed etiam admirandæ prorsus & ineffabilis erga genus humanum charitatis edito opere, quod statim etiam ab Apostolo poni, ait. Quomodo enim negari potest, Deum per peccatum hominibus offensum, & iratum fuisse? Quum non possit non irasci ob peccata vi justitiæ suæ. Quomodo in dubium vocari potest reconciliatio DEI per Christum facta, toties in scripturis proposita, & ipsis velut radiis solis exarata, quemadmodum in Socinismo profligato luculenter ostendimus. Hæc autem obsecratio: Reconciliamini DEO, nomine Christi facta, posterior ordine naturæ est reconciliatione per sanguinem Christi facta. Nam Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, quod factum, quum Christus sanguine suo nos Deo reconciliavit ac nostri vice mortem subiit. Dehinc verò vi hujus per Christum factæ reconciliationis demum posuit in ministerio suo lógon katalōges, annunciari curavit hanc reconciliationem in verbo Evangelii per verbi ministros legatos suos, idque eo fine, ut nos Deo reconciliemur, quod non hoc significat, quemadmodum Schlichtingius vult, ut deponamus erga Deum inimicitias, sed ut deprecatione iræ Dei justissimæ humillima gratiam Dei verà fide quæramus, (uti conjux infida reconcilianda est marito offenso, 1. Cor. VII. 11.) idque per, & propter Christum Mediatorem nostrum, ejusq; mortem, quà nobis hanc reconciliationem acquisivit; imò oblatam in verbo Evangelii ne respuamus, sed suscipiamus. Nam eum προέθετο ὁ Θεὸς ἱλα- στήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι proposuit Deus in placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. III. 25. Sine hac propitiatione nulla potuit fieri publicatio remissionis peccatorum, quia sine sanguinis effusione nulla sit remissio pec- catorum, Ebr. IX. 22. Nec depositio animi aversi à Deo & operibus Deo adversis dediti fit nudâ publicatione liberalis remissionis peccatorum, sed per λόγον τῆς καταλλαγῆς verbi reconcilia- tionis hujus mundi per Christum fiducialem appre- hensionem & inde consequutam justificationem, quæ illa depositione prior est; quum fides, per quam justificamur, omnis bonæ actionis genetrix sit, & sine fide impossibile sit Deo placere, Ebr. XI. 6. Imò quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum sit, Rom. XIV. 23. Verum quidem est, quod Schlichtin- gius ait, Deum non remittere pœnam, antequam homines ad ipsum convertantur. Sed conversio absolvitur contritione & fide. Vitæ autem emen- datio consequens est, non antecedens remissionis peccatorum. Illud verò perversè à Schlichtin- gio negatur, Deum hominibus irasci, & reconcilia- tione opus habere, ex eo, quod ipsemet conversio- nem illorum & reconciliationem omnibus modis quærat, adeo, ut etiam unicum Filium suum eorum conversioni ac saluti impendat. Confunduntur enim diversa momenta in consilio Dei, & gradus distincti dilectionis divinæ. Nam conversionem nostram quærit, postquam nos ipsi reconciliati su- mus per mortem Filii ipsius, adeoque ipse nobis placatus est. Filium enim suum nobis impendit, ut iram suam placaret, & reconciliationem nobis acquireret morte & sanguine suo, adeoque propi- tiatio fieret pro peccatis mundi, 1. Joh. II. 2. Dile- ctio itaque Dei alia generalis est, qua totius mundi misertus Filium misit ἱλασμὸν pro peccatis mun- di, Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. IV. 10. alia specialis, qua iis, qui in Filium credunt, peccata remittit, qui pro- inde gratitudinis ergo animum ab operibus Deo adversis avertunt, Deoque in justitia & sanctitate serviunt, Luc. I. 74.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. Τὸν γὰρ μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν) Christ innocent, John VIII. 46. 1 Pet. II. 22. To know sin is to be conscious to oneself of sin.

Ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) For our sake.

Ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησε) A double figure. For it is both an abstract for a concrete, as in the opposite member 'righteousness', i.e., 'righteous', and furthermore 'as' is to be understood. He made him a sinner, that is, as a sinner. He allows him to be treated as a criminal. Thus Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact explain it not badly.

Ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη Θεῦ ἐν αὐτῷ) That we might become through Him righteous with that righteousness which God approves, the most important part of which is in the heart, that is, through Christ, with Christ as leader.

The reason is given why one must return to favor with GOD, and it is explained how and why GOD does not impute, nor wishes to impute, sin to believers, because He made Christ sin for us and in our place, by imputing to Him our sin, who was devoid of all sin. For this is not to know sin, namely, not only not to be conscious to oneself of sin, but not to have known any sin by the knowledge of approval or practical operation. Estius explains: He was so alien from sin as if he were entirely ignorant of sin. But Ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν is not only for our sake, but in our stead and place, as Ὑπὲρ πάντων in the place of all, v. 19, and ἀντὶ πολλῶν, Matt. XX. 28, in the stead of many. He was made sin by God, i.e., a sinner κατ' ἀντονομασίαν, and for the sake of emphasis the abstract is placed for the concrete, sin for the greatest sinner, the extremely wicked; as is customary for the wicked man to be called sin in the abstract. The reason is: because whatever sin there is, it has been imputed to him, in the divine judgment, by reason of guilt just as much as of punishment. All sin has been cast upon him, Is. LIII. 6. Concerning which Theophylact in this place: He made his Son, who knew no sin, that is, who was righteousness itself, to undergo death for us, just as if he were a sinner and a malefactor. For he says: Accursed is he who is hanged on a tree, and he was reckoned with the unjust. For he did not make him a sinner, he brought this in, but sin, which is certainly far greater, so that we might be made the righteousness of God, not from works or the law, but by the grace of God. Since therefore Christ is most innocent, in himself immune from any sin, Heb. VII. 26. and the sins of the whole world have been imposed and imputed to him, God did not impute to the world those things which he imputed to the Mediator substituted in place of the human race, which therefore Christ bore in our stead, both taking upon himself our guilt, and paying the penalty for us, so that he might make expiation for our sins, whence those who believe that Christ bore their sins, and that for his sake he does not wish to impute sins to them, they enjoy the satisfaction and reconciliation of Christ, and obtain the remission of their sins, nay, they become the righteousness of GOD in Christ, that is, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to them by GOD, or they are rendered just by a righteousness which is valid before God, which indeed is had only in Christ, who is Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 6. and has been made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. I. 29. Therefore there is no need for a double figure; nor that a particle of likeness be thrust in, nor is it right or pious to distort or pervert scripture in such a way, by thrusting in, or adding anything to it, and introducing diverse figures to the same word. Nor finally does it befit divine justice to treat anyone as a sinner who is both free from his own guilt, and does not take another's guilt upon himself. Add that God made Christ sin, just as he himself was made a curse, namely ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν for us, that is, in our place, Gal. III. 13. In our place therefore he substituted him, both by imputing our sin to him, and by subjecting him to the curse. He was made the most wicked of all sinners, because he was held in the judgment of God as guilty of the sin of the whole world; he was not therefore treated only as a sinner; but he paid the penalty for the sins of the world. For this is αἴρειν to bear the sin of the world, John I. 29. He bore our sins in his body upon the tree, 1 Pet. II. 24. Having been offered to bear the sins of many, Heb. IX. 28. But he could not have paid our penalty, while preserving justice, unless he had taken our guilt upon himself. Wherefore God placed upon him the iniquity of us all, so that the discipline or chastisement of our peace might be upon him, that is, so that the penalty might be exacted from him himself, but impunity might be obtained by us, Is. LIII. 5. 6. Thus he was made sin, so that he suffered for our sins and bore death, and was delivered up for our sins, Rom. IV. 25. δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων, the just for the unjust, 1 Pet. III. 18. Wherefore just as to the world, that is, to the human race, sins were not imputed by God: So the Apostle implies that the sins of the world, or of the human race, were imputed to Christ, when he was made sin for us. And just as God not only does not impute sins to believers, but also imputes to them the righteousness of Christ, so that all are constituted just by the obedience and righteousness of that one just man, Rom. V. 19. so vice versa, sins were all imputed to Christ by God when he was made sin for us, and indeed the obedience of Christ was also performed in our stead, as if we ourselves had performed the most perfect obedience to God. And the Papist Interpreters, Justinianus, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, acknowledge that Christ is said to have been made sin in the sense of imputation. Nay, Bellarmine admits in book II. on justification, ch. 10, and Becanus in book 1. Man. ch. 16, that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, as if we ourselves had made satisfaction, although they deny that we are just through the imputed righteousness of Christ, which fact we have observed that the Walenburg brothers, Papists, do not deny in Exegem. August. Conf. Art. IV. Nor indeed does the evidence of the present text permit anything else.
