For Paul not only inculcated here the final cause, for which Christ was made sin for us, and that an indefinite one, so that in whatever way we might be made just; but he also added the manner by which we are reconciled, and are rendered righteousness in Christ, namely through the non-imputation of sins, as those which were imputed to Christ, v. 19, and through the imputation of the righteousness and obedience of Christ, as that which Christ performed in our stead, by force of comparison, Rom. V. 19. And just as Christ was made sin and a sinner for us; so we are rendered righteousness and just in Christ before God. But he was made sin and a sinner by the imputation of another's, i.e., of our sin, as the Papists admit: Wherefore we also are rendered righteousness by the imputation of another's righteousness, namely, of Christ, our Redeemer and Mediator. The Apostle had said that our reconciliation happens when God does not impute offenses to us, and this was a work of divine mercy, by which sins are remitted. But because God is also just, it was necessary that the sins of men be punished in another; that was Christ, through whom reconciliation was made. To him therefore God imputes our offenses, and his righteousness to us; and thus while he punishes the sins of the servant in the Son, and bestows the righteousness of the Son upon the servant, we appear before God just, holy and immaculate, having become from children of wrath children of grace, or according to Paul's phrase, reconciled to God; as the blessed Balduinus holds. God therefore willed to pour out upon this most innocent man all the cataracts of His wrath due to our sins, for otherwise His justice could not be satisfied, nor could we be reconciled to Him: So that, namely, we might become the righteousness of God in Him, i.e., that the innocence of Christ might become ours, and we, being in reality sinners, might be reckoned righteous before God, just as Christ, being in reality righteous, was reckoned a sinner. Some indeed, with Ambrose, Pelagius, Primasius, Sedulius, Haymo, Lombard, and Thomas, explain ἁμαρτίαν (sin) as a sacrifice for sin, which sense also pleased Augustine in some places in Enchir. c. 41, and book 2 against Max. c. 2, as also in book III against the two epistles of the Pelagians c. 6, the book on the origin of sin c. 32, and epistle CXX to Honoratus chapter 30. Serm. XLVIII on the word of the Lord chapter 4, serm. VI on the words of the Apostle c. 8, but the matter comes to the same thing, because the foundation of the denomination, why the victim is here called sin, is that sin was imputed to Him, which is clear in the scapegoat, Lev. XVI, nor for any other reason was the piacular victim killed and offered, than because the sin of the transgressors offering the same was imputed to Him, and He was offered in their place: For the soul is in the blood of the beast, therefore it was given in place of the soul of men, Lev. XVII. 11, and therefore Christ was made a sacrifice for the sin of men, because the sin of the world was imputed to Him, and for the same He offered Himself in sacrifice, and laid down His soul for sin, bearing our iniquities, Is. LIII. 10, 11, whence the blessed Hülsemann rightly advises that the foundation of reckoning this victim as satisfactory and adequate to the offending party must necessarily be taken from imputation, and therefore the sense comes to the same thing, whether we say Christ was made sin through the expiation of it, when He was offered as a piacular victim in His passion and death for sin, or through the imputation of sin. For the imputation of the expiation is the foundation; concerning which

Cornelius: The reason for this phrase and metonymy (by which sin is taken for a sacrifice) is that the entire punishment, harm, and vengeance of sin is transferred onto the expiatory victim, and thus sin itself seems to be transferred and transposed into the same. For the harm follows the guilty head. As a symbol of this matter, the priest was accustomed to lay his hands upon the victim and to pray for the sins of the people upon it. For by hands are signified actions and sins, as they are things mostly performed by the hands, says Theodoret on Leviticus ch. 1. Therefore, the laying of hands upon the victim was both a symbol of the offering and a testimony of the guilt transferred onto the victim, so that the victim might become an expiation, and thus might take upon itself sin itself, that is, the entire weight, punishment, and vengeance of sin. In this way, on the solemn day of atonement, the High Priest prayed for the sins of the whole people upon the scapegoat, and then, as if laden with sins, he had it led outside the camp by a certain man and released into the desert to be devoured by wild beasts.

However, because in the apodosis or antithesis of sin—namely, righteousness—by the admission of the Papists themselves, that mode cannot be attributed to believers, so that they are said to be a sacrifice for the sake of acquiring righteousness, in the way that some wish to say Christ is sin, i.e., a sacrifice for the sake of abolishing sin; therefore, in the judgment of the blessed Hülsemann, this interpretation is to be preferred, by which Christ is called sin on account of the imputation of an alien righteousness. The opposition of the sinner through the imputation of alien sins, and of the righteous through the imputation of alien righteousness, is certainly more appropriate than that of a sacrifice for sin and the righteous. Whence the blessed Luther, Commentary on Galatians III. 13, Vol. IV, Jena, Latin, fol. 78: Although these sentences can be correctly explained in this way: Christ was made a curse, that is, a sacrifice for the curse; sin, that is, for sin, etc. Yet it is more pleasing if the proper meaning of the words is preserved, on account of the greater emphasis. Because when a sinner truly comes to the knowledge of himself, he not only feels himself to be a sinner concretely or adjectivally, but also abstractly or substantively; that is, he does not only seem to himself to be calamitous, but the very calamity itself; not only a sinner and cursed, but sin and the curse itself. Just as in the Latin language, when we wish to signify someone as exceptionally wicked, we call him wickedness. For it is a very great thing to bear sin, the wrath of God, the curse, and death; wherefore a man feeling these things seriously, as Christ truly feels for the whole human race, becomes clearly sin itself, death, the curse, etc. But it is ridiculous what Estius objects (not denying, finally, that reputation is signified in both members, that in the former member the reputation of men is understood, and in the latter the reputation of God): that Christ is a sinner before men, who are deceived, but we are righteous before God, who is not deceived, and thus truly and not only imputatively. For our sins were not imputed to Christ so much before men as before God, and in the divine judgment; and that not fallaciously, but truly. For he himself was wounded for our iniquities, and was bruised for our crimes: the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all, and he was reckoned with the wicked, and he bore the sins of many, Isaiah 53:5, 6, 12. Again, we are righteous before God, although imputatively, yet truly, not fallaciously, because God himself imputes to us the righteousness of Christ, who certainly is not deceived. Concerning which, Cardinal Caspar Contarini, in his book on justification, published in the year 1541 (in the blessed Gerhard’s Confessio Catholica, Vol. IV): I entirely think it is said piously and Christianly that we ought to rely—to rely, I say, as upon a stable thing that certainly sustains us—upon the righteousness of Christ given to us, and not upon holiness and grace inherent in us. For this righteousness of ours is begun and imperfect, by which we cannot be protected, so that we do not offend in many things, so that we do not sin assiduously, and therefore have need of prayer, by which we daily ask that our debts be forgiven us. Therefore, in the sight of God, we cannot be held righteous and good on account of this righteousness of ours, in the way that the children of God ought to be righteous and holy; but the righteousness of Christ given to us is a true and perfect righteousness, which entirely pleases the eyes of God, in which there is nothing that offends God, which does not please God in the highest degree. Therefore, we must rely upon this alone as certain and stable, and on account of it alone believe that we are justified before God, that is, held to be and are righteous. The Walenburg brothers, book XIV, on the unity of the Church, ch. VI, § 9: A sinner in the judgment of God is a debtor of eternal punishment. Christ Jesus the Mediator intervenes as one rich in merits, and who satisfies God for the eternal punishment which the sinful man owes, which satisfaction, when it is imputed to the sinner himself, the eternal punishment is remitted to him, and he is freed from its bond before the judge (who is at once also the creditor). Who (the brothers) also vindicate our opinion, that we do not posit a fictitious imputation. § 16: They do not wish, they say, for Protestants to be a fiction of law, but an actual absolution and donation of the righteousness of Christ. And ch. VIII, § 11. they likewise teach the imputation of the righteousness of Christ: From what has been said, it is understood that the non-imputation of sin is an effect of the righteousness of Christ given or imputed to us. For by the very fact that, on account of the satisfaction of Christ imputed to us, the offense and punishment are forgiven us, the guilt itself is held as not committed, and thence man is not ordained to punishment, and thus sin is not imputed, and thus he is deemed not unrighteous. Likewise, thesis 12: It must be said: through the righteousness of Christ given or imputed to us, man is pleasing to God (for it is the merit of Christ given to us) because he is a participant in the righteousness of Christ; and accordingly, speaking abstractly, he is deemed righteous before God, just as if he had in himself that from which he would be deemed righteous. And ch. XI, thesis 15: If it be asked, whether in the judgment of God we are constituted perfectly righteous by the righteousness given and imputed to us by Christ? We shall answer that we are constituted, or rather accounted and held to be perfectly righteous, by that righteousness which is extrinsic to us and most perfect. These things those Brethren [published] publicly and with the consent of their superiors at Cologne in the year 1656, which were brought forward at greater length in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, Article IV, and were deservedly opposed to the calumnies and errors of other Papists.

Furthermore, when the Apostle says that we are made the righteousness of God, or righteous before God, he understands that righteousness which is valid before the tribunal of God, which certainly is not our inherent righteousness, inasmuch as it is in many ways imperfect and unclean, by which no one can stand before GOD, Ps. 143:2, and it is opposed to the righteousness of God, otherwise [known as] habitual righteousness, which is from works, Rom. 4:5, 10:3, Phil. 3:9. Theophylact has it thus: That we might be made the righteousness of God, not from works or the law, but by the grace of God. For that is what the righteousness of God designates, when anyone is made righteous freely, and when no stain is detected in him. And therefore he by no means said, that we might be made righteous, but the righteousness of God, arguing for the immensity of grace. Finally, the description is added here with the phrase ἐν αὐτῷ, so that it may be understood that this righteousness of God is to be sought not in ourselves, but in Christ, who was made sin for us. Cf. Rom. 8:3, Phil. 3:9. Concerning which Anselm [says] in this place: He himself was made sin, just as we are made the righteousness not of ourselves, but of God, and not in us, but in him, just as he himself was made sin not his own, but ours, constituted not in himself, but in us. Ruardus Tapperus, vol. 2, art. 8, Louvain, p. 36: Just as our crimes are imputed to Christ on account of his spontaneous assumption of them and the intimate union of the mystical body; so his righteousness, as that of the head, is imputed to us, his members, for righteousness and eternal life. For the Father placed upon him, willing and spontaneous, all of our iniquities. And he was offered, because he willed it, and he was made a curse and sin for us. Bellarmine himself, book 2 on justification, chapter 10, section 4, admits that the righteousness and merits of Christ are imputed to us, because they are given and applied to us, as if we ourselves had satisfied God: and in response to the 3rd argument: Our sins are imputed to Christ as regards the debt of satisfying, which he voluntarily undertook: Therefore, his righteousness is also imputed to us here as regards the satisfaction which he performed for us.

The Socinians today seem to approach this Apostolic doctrine more than their former ill-fated Master Faustus Socinus, as is evident from Crellius's treatise on the causes of the death of Christ, whose heresy, however, we have detected in the examination of that treatise, as well as in the work 'Socinianism Overthrown'. Jonas Schlichtingius of Buckowiez, in his Commentary on this passage, explains 'he made him sin' in this way: that is, he made him a sinner: he uses a noun for an adjective in the Hebrew phrase, not only for the sake of a more elegant opposition, but also to signify the greatest sinner, who is as it were sin itself. Whom God made Christ, insofar as he permitted him, most innocent and most holy, to be treated as the greatest sinner, that is, to be afflicted with the most grievous and ignominious death of all, I mean the death of the cross. A victim for sin is accustomed to be called sin in the sacred scriptures, and Christ was made a victim for the sin of the world, and if you look at the thing itself, this is what is said here: But he who did not know sin is not so fittingly opposed to a victim, which itself ought to be pure and innocent, as to him who is treated as the greatest sinner. We admit this explanation so far, if the imputation of our guilt is not denied. For Christ, being most innocent, could not have been treated as a sinner while preserving the justice of God, unless he had borne our sins, and the same had been cast upon him; nor was he made a victim for the sin of the world and for us in any other way than that he exhausted the guilt and punishment in our place, or took our guilt upon himself and paid the punishment due to us. But let Schlichtingius continue: 'That we may be or become the righteousness of God'; he explains how Christ was made sin for us, namely, so that we, who are sin itself, that is, become or are guilty of innumerable sins before God, may become the righteousness of God, that is, so that righteousness may be imputed to us by God, and consequently that we may be treated as most righteous and pure from all sin. Schlichtingius further explains it thus: 'Insofar, therefore, as righteousness is imputed to us by God, to that extent we are said to be or become the righteousness of God through an elegant catachresis arising from comparison and opposition.' For to be made righteousness, and that of God, and to be made sin, are elegantly opposed to one another. For righteousness is imputed to us by God, or as the Apostle speaks elsewhere about this very matter and the love of God, we are justified through the death and blood of Christ, Rom. 5:8, 9, 10, insofar as Christ died for our sins according to the will of God, and shed his blood. For by this reason a right has been acquired for us to the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness and justification. Who would not believe that these things are correct and sufficiently orthodox? But a detestable heresy lies hidden in these things, and a heretical depravation of the golden Apostolic Aphorism. For he understands righteousness to be imputed to us by God, not that of Christ, who did not know sin, and was made sin in our place, according to the Apostle; but our own righteousness, so that this, even though it be imperfect, is imputed to us by God as perfect, or is accounted as perfect, which is diametrically contrary to the righteousness of God. For the judgment of God is according to truth, nor can God, in his judgment, esteem or accept as perfect an imperfect righteousness, or one subject to defects and impurities, such as our righteousness is, since by the force of his justice he pronounces a curse on everyone who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. 27:26, that is, who does not fulfill the law completely or most perfectly. Then, if it is explained here how Christ was made sin for us, it must be that Christ was made a sinner because our sin was imputed to Christ, because we are made righteousness when the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us. We are not rendered the righteousness of God in ourselves; but in him, in Christ, who was made sin for us. If for righteousness to be imputed to us by God is the same as for us to be justified through the death and blood of Christ, insofar as Christ died for us, it is necessary that not our own proper righteousness or obedience be imputed to us; but the righteousness and obedience of Christ, as it is clearly taught in Rom. 5:19. For we are not justified through the death of Christ, performed for us, which according to the Apostle's sentiment is in our place, in any other way than that the obedience of Christ even unto death, and thus also the very passion and death of Christ itself, is imputed to us as satisfactory, since without it we would certainly not be justified or absolved, but would have to be condemned, namely, without the reconciliation made through the blood of Christ. If a right has been acquired for us to the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness through the death and blood of Christ, as Schlichtingius says, it must be that justification has been obtained for us by the death and blood of Christ, which consists in the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. But here the heretic speaks similar things, but thinks dissimilar ones. For he understands a right acquired to the remission of sins and the acceptance of our imperfect righteousness as perfect, and that in no other way, as the added words teach, than that GOD binds himself to confer it upon us, and has rendered us entirely certain of it. But He did not therefore deliver His Son to death, or make Him sin for us, because He wished to bind Himself to us for the remission of sins (much less for the imputation of imperfect righteousness) and to render us certain of it; but that a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) might be paid for us, and that He might reconcile us to Himself, and that by the punishment endured by the Son, impunity might be obtained for us, the Son of God being delivered to death in our place, and made a curse for us, that we might be freed from the curse of the law, the Son of God being made sin for us, that we might obtain the remission of sins. And how could the death of Christ render us certain of the remission of sins, if the wrath of God against sins was not appeased by the same? Schlichtingius brings forward two other ways, but they are entirely foreign, that God not only rendered us certain by such a pledge of His love; but also that there is no place for condemnation, after Christ died for our sins by the will of God, and expiated them with His blood. But God delivered His only-begotten Son to death for us, not that we might be rendered certain of the remission of sins by that pledge of love; but that God might be rendered propitious to us by the blood of His Son, and the remission of sins might be acquired through Christ, whom He set forth to us as a propitiation through faith in His blood, Rom. III. 23. The death of the Son of God is not a testimony of the remission of sins, which we could have had in the proclamation of Christ, it is not a martyrdom of the doctrine which He preached, for that could have been confirmed by the blood of other martyrs, and was sufficiently confirmed by divine testimonies. But it is a ransom (λύτρον) and a price of redemption (ἀντίλυτρον), because He laid down His soul in our place, and willed to undergo death, Matt. XX. 28, and expiated our sins with His blood. Which according to Scripture cannot be understood otherwise than that He appeased the wrath of God, and in turn procured for us the grace of God by His death and blood, as has been shown in the refuted Socinianism. Furthermore, what kind of consequence is that, with the satisfaction of Christ performed for us being denied, when Schlichtingius infers it thus: If He who was innocent of sin underwent death due only to sinners, and that for sinners, much more do sinners obtain the imputation of righteousness and eternal life from the grace of God, which was destined only for the just and innocent. For if He did not undergo death in our place, we who were under sin, the curse, and the wrath of God, and subject to the fear of death, were subject to slavery throughout our whole life, Heb. II. 14, how can we hope for the grace of God, the remission of sins, and salvation? The grace of God and eternal life were destined only for the just and innocent; but who of us is just and innocent by his own righteousness? For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, Rom. III. 22, 23. And how could Christ, most innocent, undergo death due only to sinners, for us sinners, if He did not take upon Himself our sins, and was delivered in our place and because of our sins, that is, by the merit of our sins?

As for those words ἐν αὐτῷ, in Him, namely in Christ, Schlichtingius explains them thus: that is, on the condition that we are in Christ, that we believe in Christ, that in Him, who died for our salvation and for our sins, we seek salvation and the remission of sins and justification, not in the law and the works of the law, and consequently obtain it through Him as our Lord and Savior. But those words do not present a condition, but rather express the form and manner, that indeed we are most just before God not by that righteousness which is found in us, but which is in Christ, that is, the righteousness of Christ Himself, Phil. III. 9, Rom. V. 18, 1 Cor. I. 29, Jer. XXIII. 6. Is. XLV. 23, et seqq., although for that righteousness there is need of the apprehension or application of faith, so that everyone through faith in Christ, as one who was delivered for our sins, bore our sins, and expiated them, may seek and obtain salvation and justification, not in his own works, but in the righteousness or obedience of Christ, and the satisfaction of His passion and death performed for our sins, Rom. VIII. 4. But here the heretic comes forth, what he hides under the wrapping of the words of Scripture: For since, he says, the effect of the death of Christ, that is, the imputation of righteousness, depends on the condition of faith in Christ, which embraces both reconciliation with God and all righteousness and holiness, much greater and more perfect than that which the law could effect in anyone, hence it necessarily follows that Christ did not die for the payment of our debts, which once done leaves no place for a condition, but as Scripture everywhere testifies, for the remission of them, which can be suspended, and is suspended, on the condition of faith in Christ and repentance and amendment of life. How the effect of the death of Christ is the imputation or reputation of our imperfect righteousness in place of the perfect one, let the heretics see to that themselves; Scripture certainly is completely ignorant of this effect of the death of Christ, and indeed even of such a reputation; and therefore it cannot be said that it depends on the condition of faith in Christ. For there are no properties of a non-entity. Similarly, that faith in Christ which embraces all righteousness and holiness, much greater and more perfect than that which the law could effect in anyone, is also a non-entity in the Holy Scriptures. For where is faith in Christ described in this way? What law is said to effect holiness in us? It indeed prescribes holiness to us; but it is not able to effect it; indeed, the Apostle teaches that this is impossible for the law, Rom. VIII. 3, where we are taught in the Holy Scriptures that a much greater and more perfect holiness is required of us than that which the law prescribes and requires. The law indeed demands that we be holy, just as God Himself is holy, Lev. XI. 44, ch. XIX. 2, ch. XX. 7, than which neither a more perfect one can exist, nor is a greater one required in the New Testament, 1 Pet. I. 16; it demands that we love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves, Deut. VI. 5, Lev. XIX. 18, than which Christ testifies that nothing more perfect is required and that it cannot be required, Luke X. 27, Matt. XXII. 34. If therefore the imputation of righteousness and justification depends on such a condition, which is indeed among the impossibilities, then justification and salvation and eternal life are not to be hoped for or believed in, but are to be utterly despaired of. But if, according to the Scriptures, the satisfaction of the death of Christ is believed, or that He Himself died for the payment of our debts, that is, in our place, and that He might pay for our sins, or pay those things which He did not steal, which things are perfectly consistent with the gratuitous remission of sins, and indeed are the cause of it, because sins are remitted to us from grace for this reason, that Christ bore our sins in our place and sustained their punishment: then certainly no place is left for such a Socinian condition or faith; but that which remains is our only remedy and comfort, that everyone should apply to himself by true faith the payment made for us, and appropriate to himself the righteousness of Christ, which is imputed to us for our justification. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. X. 4. Let it be known therefore, that through Him the remission of sins is announced, and from all things from which you could not be justified in the law of Moses. In Him everyone who believes is justified, Acts XIII. 38, 39. This concerning the Socinian corruption; from which it will not be obscure to anyone weighing his entire opinion on the article of justification that the Grotian one does not depart much. For Grotius degenerated too much from himself in his later writings.

SECTION II. ADHORTATORY, That they may not receive the grace of God in vain.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Τὸν γὰρ μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν) Christum inson- tem, Joh. VIII. 46. 1. Petr. II. 22. Nosse peccatum est con- scium sibi esse peccati.

Ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) Nostri causa.

Ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησε) Duplex Figura. Nam & abstractum est pro concreto, ut in membro opposito justitiam, i. e. ju- stos, & præterea subaudiendum ὡς. Fecit peccatorem, id est, tanquam peccatorem. Sinit eum tractari tanquam scele- rosum. Ita explicant Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theo- phylactus non male.

Ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη Θεῦ ἐν αὐτῷ) Ut nos per eum fieremus justi ea justitia, quam Deus approbat, cujus pars potissima est in corde, id est, per Christum, Christo duce.

Redditur ratio, cur redeundum sit cum DEO in gratiam, & exponitur, quomodo, & quare DEUS mundo non imputet, nec imputare velit credentibus peccatum, quia Christum pro nobis & nostri loco fecit peccatum, imputando ei peccatum nostrum, qui omnis peccati expers erat. Hoc enim est, non nosse peccatum, scilicet, non modo sibi eon- scium non esse peccati; sed nec ullum peccatum, notitiâ approbationis, vel operationis practica no- visse. Estius exponit: Adeo à peccato fuit alienus, ac si prorsus peccatum ignoraret. Ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν vero non est nostri tantum causa, sed nostri vice ac loco, ut ὑ- πὲρ πάντων loco omnium, v. 19. & ἀντὶ πολλῶν Matth. XX. 28. vice multorum. Factus autem à Deo peccatũ, i. e. peccator κατ' ἀντονομασίαν, & ἐμφάσεως cau- sà posito abstracto pro concreto, peccato pro sum- mo peccatore, extremè scelerato; uti solet extremè sceleratus in abstracto scelus dici. Ratio est: quia quicquid peccati est, ipsi imputatum est, in judicio divino, ratione culpæ pariter ac pœnæ. Omne pecca- tum in ipsum conjectum est, Es. LIII. 6. Quo de Theophylactus in h. l. Filium suum, qui nullum no- verat peccatum, hoc est, qui ipsamet justitia erat, pro nobis fecit mortem obire, perinde ac si peccator esset is, & maleficus. Inquit enim: Execrabilis est is, qui suspensus est ligno, & cum injustis reputatus est. Non enim peccatorem fecit, hic intulit, sed peccatum, quod utique majus est longe, ut nos Dei justitia efficeremur, non ex operibus vel lege, sed Dei gratia. Quum ergo Christus innocentissimus sit, per se immunis à quo- vis peccato, Ebr. VII. 26. & totius mundi peccata ipsi imposita atque imputata sint, mundo ea non imputavit Deus, quæ Mediatori in vicem generis humani surrogato imputavit, quæ proinde porta- vit Christus nostri loco, & culpam nostram suscipi- ens, & pœnam luens pro nobis, ut expiationem fa- ceret peccatorum nostrorum, unde qui Christum peccata sua portasse, ejusque causa sibi non velle peccata imputare credunt, illi fruuntur satisfactio- ne, & reconciliatione Christi, ac peccatorum suo- rum remissionem consequuntur, imo justitia DEI fiunt in Christo, hoc est, imputatur illis à DEO ju- stitia Christi, vel justi redduntur justitia, quæ coram Deo valet, quæ vero nonnisi in Christo habetur, qui est Jehova justitia nostra, Jer. XXIII. 6. & factus nobis à Deo est justitia, 1. Cor. I. 29. Non ergò opus est duplici figura; nec ut ingeratur particula similitu- dinis, neque fas aut pium est, scripturam ita detor- quere, aut pervertere, ingerendo, vel addendo ei quicquam, & diversas figuras eidem voci inferen- do. Nec deniq; justitiæ divinæ congruit, quenquam ut peccatorem tractare, qui & propriâ vacat culpâ, nec alienam culpam in se suscipit. Adde, quod pec- catum Deus fecerit Christum, uti maledictum ipse factus est, nimirum ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis, id est, no- stri loco, Gal. III. 13. In nostri ergò locum illum sur- rogavit, tum peccatum nostrum ipsi imputando, tum maledictioni eundem subjiciendo. Factus est peccator omnium sceleratissimus, quia peccati to- tius mundi reus in judicio Dei habitus; non ergò tantum ut peccator tractatus est; sed pœnam pec- catorum mundi luit. Hoc enim est αἴρειν portare peccatum mundi, Joh. I. 29. Ἀνήνεγκεν ἁμαρτίας ἡ- μῶν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὑτõ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον, 1. Pet. II. 24. Προσενεχθεὶς εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἐνεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, Ebr. IX. 28. Pœnam autem nostram luere, salvâ justitiâ non potuisset, nisi culpam nostram in se suscepisset. Quapropter posuit Deus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum, ut disciplina vel castigatio pacis nostræ esset super eum, id est, ut pœna eo ipso exigeretur, nobis verò impunitas obtingeret, Es. LIII. 5. 6. Factus ita est peccatum, ut pro peccatis nostris passus sit & mortem tulerit, & traditus sit propter peccata no- stra, Rom. IV. 25. δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων, justus loco in- justorum, 1. Pet. III. 18. Quapropter quemadmo- dum mundo, hoc est, generi humano non imputata sunt peccata à Deo: Ita Christo imputata esse pec- cata mundi, seu generis humani, quando pro nobis factus est peccatum, innuit Apostolus. Et uti cre- dentibus non modò non imputat Deus peccata, sed imputat etiam illis justitiam Christi, ut justi consti- tuantur omnes unius illius justi obedientiâ & ju- stitiâ, Rom. V. 19. ita vice versa tum imputata sunt Christo peccata omnia à Deo, cum factus est pro nobis peccatũ, tùm verò obedientia etiam Christi præstita est nostri loco, ac si ipsimet Deo perfectis- simam obedientiam præstitissemus. Et agnoscunt Interpretes Pontificii, Justinianus, Cornelius à La- pide, Estius, Christum factum dici peccatum sensu imputationis. Imo fatetur Bellarminus libr. II. de justif. cap. 10. Becanus libr. 1. Man. cap.16. Christi justitiam nobis imputari, ac si ipsi satisfecissemus, tametsi negent, per imputatam Christi justitiam nos justos esse, quod verò fratres Walenburgicos, Pontificios non inficiari in Exegem. August. Conf. Art. IV. observavimus. Nec verò aliud permittit textus præsentis evidentia. Paulus enim non solum causam finalem, ob quam Christus pro nobis factus est peccatum, eamque indefinitam, ut quocunque modo justi efficeremur, hic inculcavit; sed etiam modum adjecit, quo reconciliamur, & reddimur justitia in Christo, scilicet per non-imputationem peccatorum, útpote quæ Christo imputata sunt, v. 19. & per imputationem justitiæ & obedientiæ Christi, utpote quam Christus nostri loco præstitit, vi col- lationis, Rom. V. 19. Et quomodo Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum & peccator; ita nos reddi- mur in Christo justitia & justi coram Deo. At ille peccatum & peccator factus est imputatione alie- ni, h. e. nostri peccati, fatentibus Pontificiis: Qua- propter etiam nos justitia reddimur imputatione justitiæ alienæ, Christi nempe, Redemptoris & Me- diatoris nostri. Dixerat Apostolus, reconciliationem nostri fieri, quando Deus non imputat nobis delicta, & hoc fuit opus misericordiæ divinæ, quâ remittun- tur peccata. Sed quia Deus etiam justus est, oportuit peccata hominum puniri in alio; is erat Christus, per quem facta est reconciliatio. Huic ergo imputat Deus delicta nostra, ejusque justitiam nobis; & sic dum peccata servi punit in Filio, & justitiam Filii donat servo, nos coram Deo justi, sancti ac immacu- lati comparemus, ex filiis iræ filii gratiæ facti, seu jux- ta Pauli phrasin Deo reconciliati; ut habet B. Bal- duinus. Voluit ergo Deus in innocentissimum hunc hominem, omnes iræ suæ peccatis nostris debita cata- ractas effundere, aliter enim justitiæ suæ satisfieri, & nos ei reconciliari non poteramus: Ut nimirum nos fieremus justitia Dei in ipso, h. e. ut innocentia Chri- sti nostra fieret, & nos revera peccatores existentes justi coram Deo reputaremur, quemadmodum Chri- stus revera justus existens peccator reputatus est. Ex- ponunt quidem cum Ambrosio, Pelagio, Primafio, Sedulio, Haymone, Lombardo & Thoma nonnulli ἁμαρτίαν peccatum per sacrificium pro peccato, qui sensus etiam alicubi Augustino placuit in Enchir. c. 41. & libr. 2. contra Max. c. 2. ut & libr. III. con- tra duas epist. Pelag. c. 6. libr. de peccato Orig. c. 32. epist. CXX. ad Honoratum cap. 30. Serm. XLIIX. de verbo Domini cap. 4. serm. VI. de verbis Apostoli c. 8. sed res eodem recidit, quia fundamentum deno- minationis, cur hostia peccatum dicta hic est, quod ipsi peccatum imputatum est, quod clarum est in hirco ἀποπυμπαίῳ, Lev. XVI. nec alia de causa occidebatur & offerebatur victima piacularis, quâ quia peccatum prævaricatorum eandem offeren- tium ipsi imputabatur, eorumque loco offereba- tur: Anima enim est in sanguine pecudis, ideo daba- tur vice animæ hominum, Lev. XVII. 11. ideoque Christus sacrificium pro peccato hominum factus est, quia peccatum mundi eidem imputatum, pro- que eodem semetipsum obtulit in sacrificium, & posuit animam suam pro peccato, iniquitates no- stras portans, Es. LIII. 10. 11. unde rectè monet B. Hülsemannus, fundamentum reputandi hancce ho- stiam pro satisfactoria & adæquata parti offenden- ti, necessariò ab imputatione accipiendum esse, adeo- que sensum eodè recidere, sive dicamus Christum factum esse peccatum per lutionem ejus, cum ob- latus est ceu victima piacularis in passione & mor- te pro peccato, seu per imputationem peccati. Im- putatio enim lutionis fundamentum est; de quo

Cornelius: Phraseos & Metonymiæ istius (qua pec-| catum pro sacrificio accipitur) ratio hæc est, quod in hostiam piacularem tota peccati pœna, noxa & ultio transcribatur, itaque in eandem peccatum ipsum transcribi & transponi videatur. Noxa enim ca- put nocens sequitur. Hujus rei symbolo solebat sacer- dos hostiæ manus imponere, illíq; peccata populi im- precari. Per manus enim significantur actiones & peccata, utpote quæ manibus plerumq; peraguntur, inquit Theodor. in Levitici c. 1. Manuum ergo im- positio super victimam & symbolum erat oblationis, & testimonium reatus in hostiam translati, ut hostia fieret piaculum, itaque peccatum ipsum, id est, omne pondus pœnam & vindictam peccati in se suscipe- ret. Hoc modo in die solemni expiationis Pontifex hirco emissario peccata totius populi imprecabatur, eumŅ;, deinde, quasi peccatis onustum, per certum ho- minem extra castra deducebat, & dimittebat in deser- tum à feris devorandum.

Cæterum quia in ἀποδόσει vel ἀντιθέσει pecca- ti, justitiâ nempe, Pontificiis ipsis fatentibus, ille modus credentibus attribui non potest, ut dican- tur hostia pro acquirenda justitia, quomodo qui- dam Christum dictu volunt peccatum, i. e. hostiam pro abolendo peccato; ideo B. Hülfemanni judicio, præferenda est hæc interpretatio, qua Christus pec- catum dicitur propter imputationem justitiæ alienæ. Convenientior certe est oppositio peccatoris per imputationem alienorum peccatorum; & justi per imputationem alienæ justitiæ, quàm hostiæ pro pecca- to, & justi. Unde B. Lutherus Commentar. in Gal. III. 13. T. IV. Jen. Lat. f. 78. Quanquam hæ senten- tiæ rectè exponi possint hoc modo: Christus factus est maledictum, id est, hostia pro maledicto; pecca- tum, id est, pro peccato &c. Tamen magis placet, si servetur propria significatio vocum, propter majorem emphasin. Quia cum peccator venit revera in noti- tiam sui, non solum sentit se peccatorem concretivè seu adjectivè, sed etiam abstractivè seu substantivè, hoc est, non solum videtur sibi calamitosus, sed ipsa calamitas, non solū peccator & maledictus, sed ipsum peccatum & maledictum. Ut & in latina lingua, cum excellenter volumus aliquem significare scelestū, vocamus eum scelus. Est enim maxima res portare peccatum, iram DEI, maledictionem & mortem; Quare homo ista seriò sentiens, ut Christus verè sen- tit pro toto genere humano, fit plane ipsum pecca- tum, mors, maledictum &c. Ludicrum autem est, quod obvertit Estius, (non abnuens denique, utro- que membro reputationem significari, in priori mem- bro reputationem hominum intelligi, in posteriori re- putationem Dei) Christum peccatorem esse coram hominibus, qui falluntur: nos autem justos coram Deo, qui non fallitur, & ita vere & non tantum im- putativè. Nam Christo non tam coram homini- bus imputata sunt nostra peccata, quàm coram Deo, & in judicio divino; idque non fallaciter, sed verè. Ipse enim vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, & attritus est propter scelera nostra: Posuit Domi- nus in eo omnium nostrum iniquitatem, & cum sce- leratis reputatus est, & peccata multorum tulit, Es. LIII. 5. 6. 12. Rursus nos justi coram Deo, etsi im- putativè, verè tamen, non fallaciter, quia Deus ipse imputat nobis justitiam Christi, qui profecto non fallitur. Quo de Casp. Contarenus Cardina- lis libr. de justific. anno 1541. edito (apud B. Ger- hardum Conf. Cathol. Tom. IV.) Ego prorsus exi- stimo, pie & Christiane dici, quod debeamus niti, niti inquam tanquam re stabili, quæ certo nos susten- tat, justitiâ Christi nobis donatâ, non autem sanctita- te & gratiâ nobis inhærente. Hæc etenim nostra justi- tia inchoata est & imperfecta, qua tueri nos non pot- est, quin in multis offendamus, quin assidue pecce- mus, ac proinde opus habeamus oratione, qua quoti- die petamus dimitti nobis debita nostra. Idcirco in conspectu Dei non possumus ob hanc justitiam nostra haberi justi & boni, quemadmodum oporteret filios Dei esse justos & sanctos, sed justitia Christi nobis donata est vera & perfecta justitia, quæ omnino pla- cet oculis Dei, in qua nihil est, quod offendat Deum, quod non summopere Deo placeat. Hac ergo sola cer- ta, stabili nobis innitendum est, & ob eam solam cre- dere, nos justificari coram Deo, id est, justos haberi & esse. Fratres Walenburg. lib. XIV. de unitate Eccle- siæ cap. VI. §. 9. Peccator in judicio Dei est debitor pœnæ æternæ. Christus Jesus Mediator intervenit tanquam dives meritis, quique Deo satisfacit pro pœna æterna, quam debet homo peccator, quæ satis- factio cum ipsi peccatori imputetur, remittitur ei pœna æterna & ab ejus nexu coram judice (qui simul est & creditor) liberatur. Qui (Fratres) etiam vindicant nostram sententiam, quod non fictitiam imputationem statuamus. §. 16. Non volunt, in- quiunt, Protestantes esse fictionem juris, sed actua- lem absolutionem & donationem justitiæ Christi. Et cap. IIX. §. 11. docent itidem imputationem justi- tiæ Christi: Ex dictis intelligitur, quod non-imputa- tio peccati sit effectus justitiæ Christi nobis donatæ seu imputatæ. Nam eo ipso, quod propter satisfactionem Christi nobis imputatam donatur nobis offensa & pœ- na, ipsa culpa habetur pro non commissa, indeque homo non ordinatur ad pœnam, & sic non imputa- tur peccatum, sic censetur non injustus. Item th. 12. Dicendum: per justitiam Christi nobis donatam seu imputatam homo sit Deo gratus (est enim meritum Christi nobis donatum) quia est particeps justitiæ Christi; & perinde abstractivè loquendo justus cen- setur coram Deo, ac si in seipso haberet, unde justus censeretur. Et cap. XI. th. 15. Si petatur, an in judicio Dei constituamur perfectè justi, justitiâ à Christo no- bis donatâ & imputatâ? Respondebimus, nos justi- tiâ illâ nobis extrinsecâ & perfectissimâ constitui, vel potius censeri, haberique perfectè justos. Hæc Fratres illi publice & cum superiorum consensu Colon. Agripp. An. 1656. quæ prolixius adducta in Exeg. Aug. Conf. Art. IV. & calumniis atq; erro- ribus aliorum Pontificiorum merito opposita sunt.

Porrò cum nos reddi justitiam Dei, ait Aposto- lus vel justos coram Deo, eam justitiam, quæ co- ram tribunali Dei valet, intelligit, quæ certè non est nostra inhærens justitia, utpote multis modis imperfecta & immunda, quâ nemo coram DEO consistere potest, Ps. CXLIII. 2. & opponitur justitiæ Dei alias justitiæ habituali, quæ est ex operibus, Rom. IV. 5. X. 3. Phil. III. 9. Theophylactus ita ha- bet: Ut nos justitia Dei efficeremur, non ex operibus, vel lege, sed Dei gratia. Id enim designat Dei justitia, cum gratis quispiam justus efficitur, cumque nulla in eo deprehenditur labes. Et ideo nequaquam dixit, ut justi efficiamur, sed Dei justitia, gratiæ arguens im- mensitatem. Deniq; additur hic descriptio voce ἐν αὐτῷ, ut intelligatur, non in nobismetipsis, sed in Christo, qui pro nobis peccatum factus, hanc justi- tiam Dei quærendam esse. Conf. Rom. IIX. 3. Phil. III. 9. De quo Anselm. in h. l. Ipse factus est pecca- tum, sicut nos justitia non nostra, sed Dei, nec in nobis, sed in ipso, sicut ipse factus est peccatũ non suum, sed nostrum, non in se, sed in nobis constitutum. Ruardus Tapperus tom. 2. art. 8. Lovan. p. 36. Sicut Christo nostra scelera ob spontaneam eorum assumptionem, & corporis mystici intimam unionẽ imputantur; ita ejus justitia quasi capitis nobis ejus membris ad justitiam & vitam æternam imputatur. Posuit enim Pater su- per eum volentem & sponsaneum omnium nostrum iniquitates. Et oblatus est, quia voluit, & maledi- ctum & peccatum factus est pro nobis. Bellarminus ipse libr. 2. de justif. cap. 10. §. 4. admittit imputari nobis justitiam Christi & merita, quia nobis donan- tur & applicantur, ac si nos ipsi Deo satisfecissemus: & resp. ad 3. argum. Imputantur Christo peccata nostra quoad debitum satisfaciendi, quod ille sponte suscepit: Hic igitur & nobis imputatur justitia ejus quoad satisfactionem, quam pro nobis præstitit.

Accedere etiam Sociniani magis ad hanc Apo- stolicam doctrinam hodie videntur, quàm olim infaustus ipsorum Magister Faustus Socinus, ut è Crellii tractatu de causis mortis Christi constat, cu- jus tamen hæresin examine tractatus illius, nec non in Socinismo profligato deteximus. Jonas Schlich- tingius à Buckowiez in Comment. ad h. l. illud peccatum fecit ita explicat: id est, peccatorem fecit: ponit Substantivum pro Adjectivo phrasi Hebræa, non tantum ob concinniorem oppositionem, sed etiam ut maximum peccatorem significet, qui ipsum veluti peccatum sit. Quem Deus Christum fecit, quatenus eum innocentissimum & sanctissimum, ut maximum peccatorem tractari, id est, morte omnium dirissima & ignominiosissima, morte crucis inquam affici per- misit. Solet victima pro peccato peccatum appellari in sacris literis, & Christus victima pro mundi pec- cato factus est, idque si rem ipsam spectes, hic dicitur: Sed is, qui peccatum non cognovit, non tam commode victimæ opponitur, quæ & ipsa pura & infons esse debet, quam ei, qui ut peccator maximus tractatur. Quam explicationem hactenus admittimus, si non negetur culpæ nostræ imputatio. Nam nec ut pecca- tor tractari salvâ justitiâ Dei potuisset Christus in- nocentissimus, nisi peccata nostra portasset, ea- demque in ipsum conjecta fuissent; nec alia ratio- ne victima pro mundi peccato factus est, & pro no- bis, quàm quod nostri loco culpam & pœnam ex- antlavit, vel culpam nostram susceperit, pœnam- que nobis debitam luerit. Sed pergat Schlichtin- gius: Ut nos simus vel fiamus justitia Dei; exponit quo pacto pro nobis Christus peccatum sit factus, nempe ut nos, qui ipsum peccatum sumus, id est, innu- merabilium peccatorum coram Deo rei fiamus vel si- mus justitia Dei, id est, ut nobis justitia à Deo impu- tetur, & consequenter ut nos justissimi & omnis pec- cati puri tractemur. Explicat id porrò ita Schlich- tingius: Quatenus igitur justitia nobis à Deo impu- tatur, hactenus justitia Dei esse vel fieri dicimur per κατάχρησιν elegantem ex comparatione & oppositio- ne ortam. Justitiam enim, idque Dei, fieri, & pecca- tum fieri eleganter inter se opponuntur. Imputatur enim nobis justitia à Deo, seu ut alibi hac ipsa de re & charitate Dei loquitur Apostolus, justificamur per mortem & sanguinem Christi, Rom. V. 8. 9. 10. quate- nus Christus pro peccatis nostris ex Dei voluntate mortuus est, & sanguinem suum fudit. Hac enim ra- tione nobis jus quæsitum est ad peccatorum remissio- nem & justitiæ imputationem ac justificationem. Quis hæc non crederet rectè se habere, satisq; or- thodoxa esse? sed latet in hisce detestanda hære- sis, & hæretica depravatio aurei Aphorifmi Apo- stolici. Nam justitiam nobis imputari à Deo in- telligit, non Christi, qui peccatum non novit, & factus est nostri loco peccatum, juxta Aposto- lum; sed propriam nostram justitiam, ita ut hæc, tametsi imperfecta sit, à Deo nobis imputetur ceu perfecta, vel pro perfecta censeatur, quod justitiæ Dei καταδιάμετρον contrarium. Judicium enim Dei est secundum veritatem, nec potest Deus justitiam imperfectam, vel defectibus & immunditiis obno- xiam, qualis nostra justitia est, in judicio suo æsti- mare, aut acceptare pro perfecta, quum vi justitiæ suæ maledictum pronunciet omnem, qui non permanet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, Deut. XXVII. 26. hoc est, qui non ex asse vel perfectissimè legem implet. Tum si hic exponitur, quo pacto pro nobis peccatum factus sit Christus, oportet Christum peccatorem factum, quia Christo imputatum est peccatum nostrum, quia nos efficimur justitia, cum imputatur nobis justitia Christi. Non reddimur justitia Dei in nobis; sed ἐν αὐτῷ, in Christo, qui pro nobis factus est peccatum. Si imputari nobis justitiam à Deo, idem est, quod justificari nos per mortem & sanguinem Christi, quatenus Christus pro nobis mortuus est, necessum est, non nostram propriam justitiam vel obedientiam nobis imputari; sed justitiam & obedientiam Christi, uti clare id docetur Rom. V. v. 19. Nam non aliter justificamur per mortem Christi, pro nobis præstitam, quod juxta Apostoli sententiam est nostri loco, quàm quod obedientia Christi usque ad mortem, adeoque ipsa etiam passio & mors Christi satisfactoria nobis imputatur, quum sine eâ sanè non justificari vel absolvi, sed condemnari nos oporteat, sine reconciliatione scil. per Christi sanguinem factâ. Si nobis jus quæsitum est ad remissionem peccatorum & justitiæ imputationem per Christi mortem & sanguinem, quod ait Schlichtingius, oportet nobis partam esse morte & sanguine Christi justificationem, quæ in remissione peccatorum, & justitiæ imputatione consistit. Sed hic ὅμοια quidem loquitur; ἀνόμοια vero sentit hæreticus. Nam jus quæsitum ad remissionem peccatorum, & justitiæ nostræ imperfectæ pro perfectâ acceptionem intelligit, idque non aliter, quàm uti verba addita docent, quod nempe DEUS semetipsum ad eam nobis conferendam obstringat, nosque de ea plane certos reddiderit. At non ideo in mortem tradidit Filium suum, vel pro nobis peccatum fecit, quod se nobis obstringere ad remissionem peccatorum, (nedum ad justitiæ imperfectæ imputationem) nosque certos de ea reddere voluerit;, sed ut ἀντίλυτρον solveretur pro nobis, utque nos reconciliaret sibi, & pœnâ à Filio exantlatâ nobis impunitas obtingeret, Filio Dei nostro loco tradito in mortem, & maledicto facto pro nobis, ut nos à maledicto legis liberaremur, Filio Dei pro nobis peccato facto, ut nos remissionem peccatorum consequeremur. Et quomodo certos nos reddere potuit mors Christi de peccatorum remissione, si ira Dei adversus peccata non est per eundem placata? Duos affert modos alios, sed alienos prorsus, Schlichtingius, quod non solum tanto pignore charitatis suæ nos certos reddiderit Deus; sed etiam quod damnationi nullus sit locus, postquam Christus pro peccatis nostris ex voluntate Dei mortuus est, eaq; sanguine suo expiavit. Sed in mortem tradidit Deus Filium suum unigenitum pro nobis, non ut pignore isto charitatis nos de remissione peccatorum certi redderemur; sed Deus nobis sanguine Filii sui propitius redderetur, & remissio peccatorum acquireretur per Christum, quem nobis propitiationem proposuit per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. III. 23. Mors Filii Dei non testimonium est remissionis peccatorum, quod habere potuimus in præconio Christi, non martyrium est doctrinæ, quam prædicavit, ea enim per aliorum martyrum sanguinem confirmari poterat, & confirmata satis erat testimoniis divinis. Sed est λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον, redemptionis pretium, quia nostro loco animam suam posuit, mortemque subire voluit, Matth. XX. 28. & sanguine suo peccata nostra expiavit. Quod secundum scripturam aliter intelligi nequit, quàm quod iram Dei placarit, nobisque gratiam Dei vi- cissim conciliarit morte & sanguine, quemadmo- dum in Socinismo profligato ostensum. Porrò, quæ- nam illa est consequentia negatâ Christi satisfactio- ne pro nobis præstita, cum ita infert Schlichtin- gius: Si peccati insons mortem subiit solis peccatori- bus debitam, idq́; pro peccatoribus, multo magis pec- catores justitiæ imputationem & vitam æternam ex Dei gratia adipiscuntur, solis justis & insontibus de- stinatam. Nam si non nostri loco subiit mortem, qui sub peccato, maledictione, & ira Dei & metus morti obnoxii per totam vitam servituti obno- xii eramus, Ebr. II. 14. quomodo gratiam Dei, re- missionem peccatorum & salutem sperare possu- mus? Gratia Dei, & æterna vita non nisi justis & insontibus destinata est; ecquis vero nostrum ju- stus & insons est justitiâ propriâ: Omnes enim pec- cavimus & egemus gloria Dei, nec nisi gratis per gratiam ipsius, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Jesu, justificamur, Rom. III. 22. 23. Et quomodo po- terat Christus innocentissimus mortem solis pec- catoribus debitam, pro nobis peccatoribus sub- ire, si non peccata nostra suscepit, nostrique loco & propter peccata nostra, id est, merito peccato- rum nostrorum traditus est?

Quod ad verba illa ἐν αὐτῷ, in ipso, nempe in Christo, ita ea explicat Schlichtingius, id est, ea conditione, ut in Christo simus, in Christum creda- mus, in ipso, qui pro salute nostra, & pro peccatis no- stris mortuus est, salutem & peccatorum remissionem & justificationem, non in lege & operibus legis quæ- ramus, & consequenter per ipsum tanquam Domi- num & Servatorem nostrum eam obtineamus. At verba illa non conditionem exhibent, sed formam potius & modum exprimunt, quod nempe justis- simus coram Deo non ea justitia, quæ in nobis invenitur, sed quæ in Christo est, hoc est, ipsius Christi justitia, Phil. III. 9. Rom. V. 18. 1. Cor. I. 29. Jer. XXIII. 6. Es. XLV. 23. seqq. licet ad illam justi- tiam opus sit fidei apprehensione, seu applicatio- ne, ut quisque per fidem in Christum, utpote qui propter peccata nostra traditus est, peccata nostra portavit, & expiavit, salutem & justificationem quærat, & consequatur, non in operibus suis, sed in justitia vel obedientia Christi, & satisfactione passionis & mortis ejus pro peccatis nostris præ- stita, Rom. IIX. 4. Sed hic prodit hæreticus, quid sub involucro verborum scripturæ occultet: Quia verò, inquit, mortis Christi effectus, id est, justitiæ imputatio ex conditione fidei in Christum pendet, quæ & reconciliationem cum Deo, & omnem justi- tiam & sanctitatem eâ, quam lex in quoquam effice- re possit, multo majorem & perfectiorem complecti- tur, hinc necessario consequitur, Christum haud esse mortuum in debitorum nostrorum persolutionem, qua facta nullus conditioni relinquitur locus, sed ut scriptura ubiq́; testatur, in eorum remissionem, quæ ex conditione fidei in Christum & pænitentiæ ac emendationis vitæ merito suspendi potest, & suspensa est. Quomodo mortis Christi effectus sit imputa- tio vel reputatio justitiæ nostræ imperfectæ loco perfe- ctæ ipsi viderint hæretici; scriptura certè hunc effe- ctum mortis Christi, imò etiam talem reputatio- nem penitus ignorat; ideoque non dici potest, eam ex conditione fidei in Christum pendere. Non- entis enim nullæ sunt affectiones. Similiter etiam non-Ens in sacris literis est fides illa in Christum, quæ omnem justitiam & sanctitatem eâ, quam lex in quoquam efficere possit multo majorem & perfe- ctiorem complectatur. Nam ubi ita fides in Christum describitur? Quæ lex dicitur efficere sanctitatem in nobis? Præscribit quidem nobis sanctitatem; sed efficere eam non valet, imò impossibile esse hoc legi, docet Apostolus Rom. IIX. 3. ubi multò majo- rem & perfectiorem sanctitatem à nobis requiri, quam eam, quam lex præscribit & requirit, doce- mur in sacris literis. Postulat utique lex, ut sancti simus, quemadmodum Deus ipse sanctus est, Lev. XI. 44. cap. XIX. 2. c. XX. 7. quâ nec perfectior esse potest, nec major requiritur in Novo Testamen- to, 1. Petr. I. 16. postulat, ut Deum diligamus ex toto corde, ex tota anima & tota mente, & proximum, sic- ut nosmetipsos, Deut. VI. 5. Lev. XIX. 18. qua perfe- ctius quid nec requirit Christus & requiri non pos- se testatur Luc. X. 27. Matth. XXII. 34. Si ergo justitiæ imputatio & justificatio à tali conditione pendet, quæ verò ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων est, non speran- da vel credenda, sed desperanda penitus erit justi- ficatio & salus ac vita æterna. Credita verò, juxta scripturas, mortis Christi satisfactione, vel quod mortuus ipse sit in debitorum nostrorum persolu- tionem, hoc est, nostri loco, & ut peccata nostra lueret, vel solveret ea, quæ non rapuerat, quæ cum gratuita peccatorum remissione probe consti- tunt, imò ejusdem causa est, quia ideò nobis ex gratia remittuntur peccata, quia Christus nostri loco peccata tulit, & pœnam eorum sustinuit: Nullus utique tali Socinianæ conditioni vel fidei locus relinquitur; sed id restat, quod unicum re- medium, & solatium nostrum est, ut solutionem pro nobis factam quisque sibi verâ fide applicet, & justitiam Christi sibi appropriet, quæ nobis im- putatur ad nostri justificationem. Nam Christus est complementum legis ad justitiam omni credenti, Rom. X. 4. Notum igitur sit, quia per hunc remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, & ab omnibus, quibus non potuistis in lege Mosis justificari. In hoc omnis, qui credit, justificatur, Act. XIII. 38. 39. Hæc de Sociniana corruptela; à qua non multum abire Grotianam, integram ejus sententiam de articu- lo justificationis perpendenti haud obscurum erit. Nimis enim à seipso degeneravit Grotius in scri- ptis posterioribus.

SECTIO II. ADHORTATORIA, Vt ne gratiam Dei frustra accipiant.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle exhorts the Corinthians not to neglect the grace of God in Christ, exhibited according to the prophecy (Is. XLIX. 8.), and commends his own ministry, that together with Timothy they may avoid all scandals, that in all things they may present themselves as ministers of God in patience and holiness, by the word of truth and the power of God, by the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, and he admonishes them as children that they should have no commerce with infidels, but that as the temple of God, who dwells in them by the promise of His (Lev. XXVI. 12), they should separate themselves from them according to the command of the Lord (Is. LII. 11.), with the added promise (Jerem. XXXI. 1.) of paternal reception.

There are two parts: I. An exhortation concerning the reverent holding of the grace of God, with a commendation of the Apostolic ministry to verse 10. II. An admonition to the Corinthian Church concerning avoiding the company of the wicked to verse 18.

PART I. An exhortation concerning not neglecting divine grace.

Ver. 1. Συνεργοῦντες δὲ καὶ) The discourse coheres with the preceding, and understand 'working together with God', as 1 Cor. III. 9. After καὶ, 'you' is understood.

After the Apostle has set forth the love of Christ, out of which He deigned to die for the human race, so that we ourselves might live, and in Him be a new creature, by whose grace the old things have passed away and all things have become new, and has excellently taught how all those things are to be attributed to the grace of GOD, who willed to reconcile us to Himself through Jesus Christ and to give to us the ministry of reconciliation, and what the reason for that reconciliation and the same ministry is; now he exhorts the Corinthians to hold that grace of GOD reverently: Which some explain specifically concerning the Ministers of the word, that the Apostle wished to admonish them to have regard for divine grace; no less in the proclamation of the Gospel entrusted to them, or the ministry of reconciliation, than in caring for their own salvation, lest they receive the same in vain, and deprive themselves and others of its fruit. For they gather that these things pertain to the ministers of the Church: first from the word συνεργοῦντες, because it seems to have respect to others working together in the ministry of God, especially because they are warned about avoiding scandal, lest the ministry be blamed, v. 3; then from the title of ministers of God, that they ought to show themselves in all things as ministers of God, v. 4, also in the word of truth, inasmuch as the word of truth was peculiarly entrusted to them, verse 7. Likewise from the commemoration of stripes, labors, and watchings, which befit ministers of the word more than others, v. 5. Add that the ministers of the word were accused as deceivers, and that they were enriching many, v. 10. Wherefore, the blessed Hunnius understands χάριν, grace, both as the communication which is offered to all through the word of reconciliation and is apprehended through faith, and also in a peculiar sense, insofar as the preaching of the Gospel is committed to them, so that they might not only confidently apprehend the favor and clemency of the eternal GOD, but moreover announce the same to others. And thus the ancient Latins refer the word συνεργοῦντες to fellow-ministers in the Corinthian Church, and Chrysostom inclines to that. It seems, however, more correct to refer it to God, whose fellow-workers Paul and Timothy make themselves, inasmuch as they had previously professed themselves to be His ambassadors, just as Oecumenius, Lyranus, Cajetan, and subsequently B. Hunnius and others interpret from 1 Cor. III. For the things which follow in verse 3 do not pertain to those whom they are exhorting, but to the exhorters themselves, who commend their own ministry, and that both from the tolerance of evils, and from the integrity of life, and finally from the sincerity of their office, faith, and doctrine. To which is subjoined a dehortation from company with the impious, whether they are prevaricating in doctrine or in life.

Παρακαλῦμεν, μὴ εἰς κενὸν τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ δέξασθαι ὑμᾶς) There is a metonymy here also. For the sense is, we warn you, do not so conduct yourselves that it appears this benefit of God was bestowed upon you in vain. Every benefit of God is accustomed to be called grace. But here, the calling through the Gospel is understood. Just as it is said to be given, so it is sometimes said to be received, even without affection, John VI. 33, Acts II. 32, Rev. III. 8.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Apostolus hortatur Corinthios, ne gratiam Dei negligant in Christo, secundum Prophetiam (Es. XLIX. 8.) exhibitam, suumque com- mendat ministerium, quod cum Timotheo scandala quæque caveant, quod in omni- bus, ut ministros Dei in patientia & san- ctitate Verbo veritatis, & virtute Dei, ar- mis justitiæ, ad dextram & sinistram sese præbeant, eosque ceu filios monet, ut nullum commercium cum infidelibus habeant, sed ut templum Dei, qui in ipsis vi promissionis suæ (Lev. XXVI. 12) habitat, ab iis sese juxta mandatum Domini (Es. LIII. 11.) separent: additâ promissione (Jerem. XXXI. 1.) susceptionis paternæ.

PArtes duæ sunt: I. Exhortatio de gratia Dei reverenter habenda, cum commendatione ministerii Apostolici ad vers. 10. II. Commonefactio Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ de vitando pravorum commercio ad vers. 18.

PARS I. Exhortatio de non negligendâ gratiâ divinâ.

Vers. 1. Συνεργοῦντες δὲ καὶ) Cohæret sermo cum superioribus, & intellige συνεργοῦντες τῷ Θεῷ, ut 1. Cor. III. 9. Post καὶ subintelligitur ὑμεῖς.

Postquam amorem Christi, ex quo pro genere humano mori dignatus est, ut nos ipsi vivamus, & in ipso nova creatura simus, cujus gratiâ vetera transierunt, & omnia nova facta sunt, exposuit Apostolus, & quomodo omnia illa DEI gratiæ, qui nos sibi ipsi reconciliare per Jesum Christum, & ministerium reconciliationis nobis dare voluit, tribuenda sint, quæque reconciliationis istius & διακονίας ejusdem sit ratio, præclarè docuit; Jam exhortatur Corinthios, ut gratiam illam DEI reverenter habeant: Quod nonnulli de verbi Ministris speciatim explicant, quod commonefacere voluerit eos Apostolus, ut gratiæ divinæ rationem habeant; non minus in præconio Evangelii sibi credito, seu διακονίᾳ τῆς καταλλαγῆς, quàm in curanda propria salute, ne in vanum eandem accipiant, seque ipsos, & alios ejusdem fructu privent. Ad ministros enim Ecclesiæ pertinere hæc colligunt: primum è voce συνεργοῦντες, quod illa ad alios cooperantes in ministerio Dei respectum habere videatur, imprimis, quia monentur de cavendo scandalo, ne ministerium reprehendatur, v. 3. deinde è nuncupatione ministrorum Dei, quod se in omnibus exhibere debeant ὡς Θεῦ διάκονοι, v. 4. etiam ἐν λόγῳ ἀληθείας, utpote quibus peculiariter verbum veritatis creditum est, vers. 7. Item è commemoratione plagarum, laborum & vigiliarum, quæ magis ministris verbi conveniunt, quàm cæteris, v. 5. Adde, quod ministri verbi ὡς πλάνοι accusati sint, quodque illi fuerint πολλοὺς πλουτίζοντες, v. 10. Quapropter χάριν, gratiam cùm pro communicatione, quæ omnibus offertur per verbum reconciliationis, & per fidem apprehenditur, tùm ratione etiam peculiari, quatenus Evangelii prædicatio ipsis commissa est, ut non tantum ipsi fiducialiter apprehenderent æterni DEI favorem & clementiam; sed eandem insuper annunciarent aliis, intelligit B. Hunnius. Atque ita vocem συνεργοῦντες ad symmystas in Ecclesia Corinthiaca referunt Latini veteres, eoque propendet Chrysostomus. Videtur tamen rectius ad Deum referri, cujus cooperarios se faciunt Paulus & Timotheus, utpote cujus legatos se antea professi erant, quemadmodum Oecumenius, Lyranus, Cajetanus & deinceps B. Hunnius & alii interpretantur è 1. Cor. III. Quæ enim vers. 3. sequuntur, non pertinent ad eos, quos exhortantur, sed ad ipsos exhortantes, qui suum ministerium commendant, idque tum à malorum tolerantia, tum à vitæ integritate, tum denique ab officii, fidei ac doctrinæ sinceritate. Quibus subjungitur dehortatio à commercio cum impiis sive in doctrinâ, sive in vitâ prævaricantibus.

Παρακαλῦμεν, μὴ εἰς κενὸν τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ δέξασθαι ὑμᾶς) Est & hic μετωνυμία. Sensus enim est, monemus vos, ne ita vos geratis, ut appareat frustra in vos collatum hoc Dei beneficium. Omne beneficium Dei solet appellari χάρις. hic vero intelligitur vocatio per Evangelium. Sicut dari ita accipi dicitur interdum etiam sine affectu, Joh. VI. 33. Actor. II. 32. Apoc. III. 8.

## 6:2
Ver. 2. Λέγει γὰρ, καιρῷ δεκτῷ ἐπήκουσά σου, καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σωτηρίας ἐβοήθησά σοι) These are the very words of the LXX Interpreters, Is. XLIX. 8. 'An acceptable time' in the Hebrew is בְּעֵת רָצוֹן, that time which God chose for procuring the salvation of the people. What was said by Isaiah concerning temporal salvation, the Apostle refers mystically to eternal salvation. ἰδὺ νῦν καιρὸς εὐπρόσδ. κτλ., ἰδὲ νῦν ἡμέρα σωτηρίας) In this time, in which we Apostles live, instructed by such knowledge of things and such great miracles, this is truly the time in which God offers salvation to you in extraordinary ways. The sense is the same as Heb. III. 7, 13, 15, IV. 7.

The grace both of reconciliation obtained through Christ and of calling through the ministry of reconciliation is indicated, which two benefits of divine grace the Apostle had proclaimed in the preceding chapter. We do not receive this grace in vain, however, when we embrace the reconciliation made through Christ with true faith, and reverently receive the ministry of reconciliation by which the same is announced to us, and thus not only acknowledge how greatly our prevarications have offended the justice of God and merited the wrath of God; but also confidently apprehend the divine kindness, by which reconciliation was procured for the world, and we are graciously invited to the fruition of the same by the announcement of so great a benefit, and by the exhortation that we should return to favor with God, who offers us reconciliation and testifies to His ready mind. This, therefore, is what the Apostle warns, that they should not receive that grace in vain, that is, that neither the favor of God toward them, nor the labor of the ministers of the Church should become void in them, which happens to those who have no care, in whose conversion both God and His ministers labor in vain, although the grace of God was also offered to them. Therefore Paul, when he had remembered the grace bestowed upon him and his most holy labors in 1 Cor. XV. 9, writes from the contrary sense that the grace of God was not empty in him, as the blessed Balduinus holds. They receive grace in vain who either do not admit the same when offered, or admit it when bestowed and lose it: The former happens by resisting the Holy Spirit, who intends conversion, Acts VII. 51, and by rejecting Christ, who wills to gather them, Matt. XXIII. 37. By shaking off this grace of God, the faith of Christ, and the Spirit of grace, through aversion from the truth of heavenly doctrine and deliberate sins, Eph. IV. 30. 2. Tim. II. 18. 2. Petr. II. 1. But in vain do Salmero, Cornelius, Justinianus, and others infer from this exhortation, that we should not receive grace in vain, that we can worthily receive grace offered by God through a natural faculty, merely moved and excited by a supernatural principle: because it is one thing not to reject it unworthily, another to receive it worthily; the latter is performed in us by the Holy Spirit, provided we do not place an obstacle in His way. Nor indeed, as the Calvinists in the Hague Conference infer, must it be concluded that, just as we can contribute nothing positively by nature toward receiving or retaining the grace of God, so also by nature we can do nothing privatively to reject grace offered or once received. For that which cannot be hindered by nature, we are admonished in vain not to hinder. And the reason is entirely different between the privation of natural impotence to resist good, and a natural faculty or habit of receiving or admitting good, concerning which the Remonstrants seem to be seen in the said conference, page 397. Therefore, lest we rashly neglect or hold in contempt this grace and the accepted time of salvation, he calls to mind the prophecy of Isaiah, chapter XLIX. 8, which we have shown, regarding the literal sense and that which is properly intended by the Holy Spirit, does not treat so much of temporal as of eternal salvation; and this Apostolic declaration sufficiently teaches: Behold now the accepted time; behold now is the day of salvation. For this discourse is about eternal salvation, for the sake of which GOD was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, and Christ was made sin for us; for the sake of which GOD also placed among us the ministry of reconciliation, and exhorts us to reconciliation, so that we might indeed become the righteousness of God in Christ, and obtain eternal salvation. For GOD speaks through the Prophet to Christ, whom He heard for our sake in the days of His flesh, that He might become for us the cause of salvation, Heb. V. v. 7. to whom therefore it was said, in an acceptable time I have heard thee, and in the day of salvation have I helped thee. For this was the acceptable time, which was sought by the vows and desires of all ages, the year of the Lord's favor or of our reconciliation with God, and the day of the vengeance of our God against our spiritual enemies, the Devil and death, Is. LXI. 2. This day was the day of salvation, in which salvation was procured for the whole world, John VI. v. 51. and the iniquity of the whole earth was taken away, Zech. III. v. 9. in which, immersed in the deep mire in our place, Christ cried out to the Father: Save me, O God, I direct my prayer to thee, O Lord; in the time of thy good pleasure, O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me in the truth of thy salvation, deliver me out of the mire, that I may not sink, lest the deep swallow me up, Ps. LXIX. v. 1. 2. 14. 15. 16. and He was heard, and saved for us, Zech. IX. 9. that by the blood of the covenant He might deliver the prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water, v. 11. therefore Isaiah further treated of this time of grace and salvation, which began to flow from that time of the New Testament, and of the cause of Christ being heard: And I have preserved thee, and given thee for a covenant of the people, to raise up the earth, to restore the desolate heritages, that thou mayest say to the prisoners, go forth; and to them that are in darkness, be revealed. This announcement is made through διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς [the ministry of reconciliation], just as Christ Himself deigned to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, and the acceptable year of the Lord, Is. LXI. v. 1. 2. Most aptly, therefore, is the Prophetic prediction brought forward, by which the state of the New Testament under the kingdom of the Messiah is depicted: Behold now is the acceptable time, which has been so greatly desired and sought until now: Behold now is the day of salvation, in which through Christ manifested in the flesh salvation was to be acquired for mortals, and promulgated in the Gospel throughout the whole world, even to the Gentiles, who in previous ages were alien to God and Christ. The Apostle therefore makes, as the blessed Baldwin warns, a distinction between the time εὐπρόσδεκτον [acceptable] and ἀπρόσδεκτον [unacceptable]. The times of the Old Testament were less acceptable, because then salvation was only promised, not yet manifested. But the New Testament has an acceptable covenant, after the desire of all nations came, and He completed the work of our reconciliation through His blood. This time, therefore, demands other morals, another life. The Apostle uses the same argument in Rom. XIII. 11. seq., where he compared the Old Testament to night, but the new to day.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Λέγει γὰρ, καιρῷ δεκτῷ ἐπήκουσά σου, καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σωτηρίας ἐβοήθησά σοι) Ipsa verba LXX. Interpretum Es. XLIX. 8. καιρὸς δεκτὸς in Hebræo בעת רצון est tempus illud, quod Deus elegit ad salutem populi procurandam. Quod ab Esaia dictum de salute temporali, mystice ad sa- lutem æternam refert Apostolus. ἰδὺ νῦν καιρὸς εὐπρόσδ. κτλ., ἰδὲ νῦν ἡμέρα σωτηρίας) Hoc tempore, quo nos Apostoli vivimus, tanta rerum no- titia, tantis miraculis instructi, hoc verè est tempus, quo Deus eximiis modis vobis offert salutem. Sensus idem, qui Hebr. III. 7. 13. 15. IV. 7.

Gratia tum reconciliationis per Christum partæ, tum vocationis per ministerium reconciliationis indicatur, quæ duo beneficia divinæ gratiæ in præcedenti capite prædicarat Apostolus. Non in vanum autem accipimus hanc gratiam, cum re- conciliationem per Christum factam verâ fide am- plectimur, & διακονίαν reconciliationis, quâ no- bis eadem annunciatur, reverenter suscipimus, adeoque non tantum agnoscimus, quantopere ju- stitiam Dei prævaricationes nostræ ossenderint iramque Dei meruerint; sed & divinam benigni- tatem, qua mundo reconciliatio procurata, nosq; ad ejusdem fruitionem annuntiatione tanti bene- ficii, & exhortatione, ut cum Deo reconciliatio- nem nobis offerente, animumque propensum te- stante, in gratiam redeamus, gratiosè invitamur, fiducialiter apprehendimus. Hoc itaque est, quod monet Apostolus, ne gratiam istam in vanum ac- cipiant, hoc est, ne vel Dei erga ipsos favor, vel mi- nistrorum Ecclesiæ labor fiat in ipsis irritus, quod iis contingit, qui nullam curam habent, in quibus con- vertendis & Deus & ministri ejus frustra laborant, licet ipsis gratia Dei quoque fuerit oblata. Ideo Pau- lus, cum 1. Cor. XV. 9. gratiæ sibi collatæ & sanctissi- morum suorum laborum meminisset, ex contrario sensu scribit, Dei gratiam in se non fuisse vacuam, ut B. Balduinus habet. In vanum accipiunt gratiam, qui vel eandem non admittunt oblatam, vel colla- tam admittunt, & deperdunt: Illud fit resistendo Spi- ritui Sancto, conversionem intendenti, Act. VII. 51. Christum, congregare illos volentem, respuendo, Matth. XXIII. 37. Hoc gratiam Dei, fidem Christi, & Spiritum gratiæ excutiendo, per aversionem à veritate doctrinæ cælestis & peccata proæretica, Eph. IV. 30. 2. Tim. II. 18. 2. Petr. II. 1. Nequicquam autem Salmero, Cornelius, Justinianus aliique ex hac parænesi, ne gratiam in vanum accipiamus, colligunt, nos per naturalem facultatem, motam tantum & excitatam per principium supernatura- le dignè recipere posse gratiam divinitus oblatam: quia aliud est non respuere indigne, aliud digne re- cipere; hoc per Spiritum Sanctum in nobis præ- statur, modo nos ei obicem non ponamus. Nec verò cum Calvinianis in collatione Hagiensi infe- rendum; uti per naturam nihil positivè possumus conferre ad recipiendam vel retinendam Dei gra- tiam; ita per naturam etiam nihil privatīvè agere possumus ad rejiciendam gratiam oblatam, vel se- mel receptam. Quod enim impediri non potest per naturam, ad id non impediendum frustra mo- nemur. Et diversa omninò ratio est inter priva- tionem naturalis impotentiæ ad resistendum bono: & facultatem seu habitum naturalem recipiendi vel admittendi bonum, quo de videantur Remonstran- tes in dicta collatione pag. 397. Ne ergo temere negligamus aut insuper habeamus hanc gratiam & tempus acceptum salutis, in mentem revocat Esaiæ vaticinium cap. XLIX. 8. quod non tàm age- re de temporali, quàm de æterna salute, quoad sen- sum literalem, proprieque intentum à Spiritu San- cto, ad locum illum Propheticum ostendimus; sa- tisque docet hæc Apostolica declaratio: Ecce nunc tempus acceptum; ecce nunc dies salutis. Sermo enim hic de salute æterna est, cujus causa DEUS erat in Christo, reconcilians mundum sibiipsi, & Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum; cujus causa DEUS etiam inter nos posuit ministerium reconciliationis, nosq; hortatur ad reconciliatio- nem, ut scilicet fiamus in Christo justitia Dei, & salute æternâ potiamur. Loquitur enim penes Prophetam DEUS ad Christum, quem nostri causa in diebus carnis exaudivit, ut fieret nobis cau- sa salutis, Ebr.V. v.7. cui proinde dictum, in tem- pore accepto exaudivi te, in die salutis succurri tibi. Hoc enim tempus acceptum erat, quod seculorum omnium votis & desideriis expetitum, annus pla- cationis Domini vel reconciliationis nostræ cum Deo, & dies ultionis Dei nostri adversus hostes no- stros spirituales, Diabolum & mortem, Es. LXI. 2. Hic dies erat salutis, quo toti mundo salus parta, Joh. VI. v. 51. & totius terræ iniquitas ablata est, Zach. III. v. 9. quo nostri loco in limum profundi immersus clamavit Christus ad Patrem: Salvum me fac Deus, dirigo orationem meam ad te, Domine; tempore beneplaciti Deus in multitudine misericor- diæ tuæ exaudi in veritate salutis tuæ, eripe me de lu- to, ut non infigar, ne absorbeat me profundum, Ps. LXIX. v. 1.2.14.15.16. & exauditus, ac salvatus est pro nobis, Zach. IX.9. ut sanguine testamenti eripe- ret vinctos de lacu, in quo non est aqua, v. 11. ideò de hoc tempore gratiæ & salutis, quod ex eo fluere cœpit de tempore Novi Testamenti, deque causa exauditionis Christi, Esaias porro ita egit: Et servavi te, & dedi te in fœdus populi, ut suscitares terram, ut possessiones hæreditarias vastatas restitue- res, ut diceres vinctis, exite; & his, qui sunt in te- nebris, revelamini. Hæc annunciatio fit per διακο- νίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς, quemadmodum etiam Chri- stus ipse prædicare dignatus est captivis indulgen- tiam, & clausis apertionem annumque gratiæ, Es. LXI. v. 1. 2. Aptissime ergo adducitur vaticinium Propheticum, quo status Novi Testamenti sub re- gno Messiæ depingitur: Ecce nunc tempus est acce- ptum, quod tantopere desideratum & expetitum hactenus fuit: Ecce nunc dies salutis, quo per Chri- stum carne manifestatum salus acquirenda erat mortalibus, & in Evangelio promulganda per to- tum terrarum orbem, etiam gentibus, quæ supe- rioribus seculis à Deo & Christo alienæ erant. Facit ergo Apostolus, monente B. Balduino, discri- men inter tempus εὐπρόσδεκτον & ἀπρόσδεκτον. Ve- teris Testamenti tempora erant minus accepta, quia tunc salus tantum promissa, nondum manifestata erat. Novum vero Testamentum habet fœdus acce- ptabile, postquam venit desideratus gentium, & opus reconciliationis nostræ per sanguinem suum consum- mavit. Hoc ergo tempus alios mores, aliam vitam postulat. Eodem argumento utitur Apostolus Rom. XIII. 11. seq. ubi Vetus Testamentum nocti, novum vero dici comparavit.

## 6:3
Vers. 3. Μηδεμίαν ἐν μηδενὶ δόντες προσκοπὴν [Giving no offence in any thing]) This coheres with παρακαλῦμεν [we beseech]. For he shows how seriously he warns, who, in order to achieve something, is terrified by no inconveniences, and neglects no conveniences. Προσκοπὴ [offence] here is what is elsewhere πρόσκομμα [stumbling-block], as in Rom. XIV. 13. that is, everything by which anyone could be turned away from the Gospel מוקש [snare].

Ἵνα μὴ μωμηθῇ ἡ διακονία [That the ministry be not blamed]) that is, our preaching of the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μηδεμίαν ἐν μηδενὶ δόντες προσκοπὴν) Cohæret hoc cum παρακαλῦμεν. Ostendit enim, quàm serio mo- neat, qui ut aliquid proficiat, nullis terreatur incommodis, nulla non commoda negligat. Προσκοπὴ hic quod alibi πρόσκομμα, ut Rom. XIV. 13. id est, omne id, per quod ali- quis averti posset ab Evangelio מוקש.

Ἵνα μὴ μωμηθῇ ἡ διακονία) id est, nostra Evangelii præ- dicatio.

## 6:4
Vers. 4. Ἀλλ' ἐν παντι συνιστῶντες ἑαυτὸς, ὡς Θεῦ διάκονοι [But in all things approving ourselves, as the ministers of God]) that is, proving our faith in this ministry to all. See above IV. 2. Ἐν παντὶ [in all things], that is, in any matter just as now, ἐν μηδενὶ [in nothing], in no matter. Moreover, these also cohere with that παρακαλῦμεν [we beseech].
