Ἐν ὑπομονῇ πολλῇ, ἐν θλίψεσιν, ἐν ἀνάγκαις, ἐν στενοχω- ρίαις [In much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses]) These are to be connected in this way, until it follows, ἐν ἁγνότητι [in pureness]. For he explains in what things that tolerance, or as Tertullian speaks, sufferance, consists. He joined θλίψιν [affliction] and στενοχωρίας [distresses] here, as in Rom. II, 9. Concerning the word ἀνάγκας [necessities], see Luke XXI, 23. 1 Cor. VII, 26. Above he denied that he was στε- νοχωρεῖσθαι [distressed], looking to the consolations of God. But here he sets forth things as they were in themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἀλλ' ἐν παντι συνιστῶντες ἑαυτὸς, ὡς Θεῦ διάκονοι) id est, probantes omnibus nostram in hoc ministerio fidem. Vide supra IV. 2. Ἐν παντὶ, id est, in quavis re sicut modo, ἐν μηδενὶ, in nulla re. Cohærent autem & hæc cum illo πα- ρακαλῦμεν.

Ἐν ὑπομονῇ πολλῇ, ἐν θλίψεσιν, ἐν ἀνάγκαις, ἐν στενοχω- ρίαις) Hæc ita connectenda sunt, usque dum sequitur, ἐν ἁγνότητι. Explicat enim, quibus in rebus ista tolerantia, aut ut Tertullianus loquitur, sufferentia versetur. Θλίψιν & στενοχωρίας hîc conjunxit, ut Rom. II, 9. De voce ἀνάγκας vide Lucæ XXI, 23. 1. Cor. VII, 26. supra negavit se στε- νοχωρεῖσθαι respiciens Dei solatia. Sed hîc res quales in se erant exponit.

## 6:5
Vers. 5. Ἐν πληγαῖς [In stripes]) Acts XVI, 23. below XI, 23, 24.

Ἐν φυλακαῖς [In imprisonments]) In the mentioned place of Acts.

Ἐν ἀκαταστασίαις) Some of the ancients understand this same thing; which he called ἀταξίαν in 1 Cor. IV, 11. But the Syrian interprets it more correctly as seditions. For that Greek word is taken in this way in Prov. XXVI, 28; Luke XXI, 9; 1 Cor. XIV, 33; below XII, 20; James III, 16. Polybius also uses it in this sense in the fragments edited by Valesius. See examples in Acts XVI, 12; XVII, 23, and following.

Ἐν κόποις) κόποι are labors to the point of weariness: See 1 Cor. XV, 58, and below XI, 23, 27; 1 Thess. III, 5. Add Acts XX, 35; 1 Cor. XV, 10; Gal. IV, 11; Col. I, 29; 2 Tim. IV, v. 10.

Ἐν ἀγρυπνίαις) Thus also below XI, 27.

Ἐν νηστείαις) 1 Cor. IV, 1; Philipp. IV, 12.

Some attribute these things to the Corinthians, as if the Apostle were exhorting them that they should offer no offense to anyone: But this is more correctly referred to the exhorting Apostles, who in v. 1 say, 'working together, we beseech.' Thus also Camerarius: we, joining our effort, exhort you, etc. We, I say, giving no offense to anyone. Beza notes that the Greek scholia observed this, and that Erasmus himself, who had previously thought otherwise, later noticed that the word διδόντες should be connected with the verb παρακαλῶμεν. Flacius likewise agrees, as does Erasmus, and also Schmidius in this place. The Apostle therefore speaks of himself and Timothy, proposing his own zeal for holiness, as well as his constancy and sincerity, as an example. I would wish, he says, interpreting with Theophylact as a guide, that you use me. For I have instituted my life in such a way that I have given no occasion to anyone even to accuse me, let alone to be even slightly blamed or harmed. I did this for this reason, so that our administration might not be noted and suffer ignominy. For he did not say, 'so that the things done by me or my institution might not be blamed,' but rather, 'I strive so that they might not admit even the slightest stain or vituperation.' Theophylact adds that the Corinthians are also tacitly rebuked in this way, as those whose evil deeds are already blamed by many, and all the execration of those who blame them redounds upon Christ and his faith. Wherefore Paul and Timothy teach here how greatly they have taken care that no stumbling block should be placed before anyone in any matter, so that no stain might be sprinkled upon the ministry, or their ministry be justly reprehended, but rather that they have openly approved themselves in all things, as becomes ministers of God, namely in much patience, or endurance of passions and labors, exhausted with vigils and fasts in the pursuit of virtues v. 6, and in faithfully executing the parts of their office v. 7. By ϑλίψεις, afflictions, according to the interpretation of B. Hunnius, all those things which happen adversely are touched upon: Necessities are called the objects of misfortune from which no exit is apparent. Στενοχωρία, by the force of the word, signifies a narrow place, when someone is squeezed into a narrow space. Paul therefore understands that kind of affliction by which the heart of a man is so constricted into a narrow space that he finds nowhere to turn. And anxieties differ from necessities in that the latter block off escapes from the outside, but the former drive the heart itself inward into a narrow space, as if they wish to choke the spirit of a man. Stripes are those which the world is accustomed to inflict upon the confessors of the Gospel out of hatred for the doctrine, just as the Savior himself sustained stripes and buffeting on the day of his passion, and the Apostle Paul received from the Jews five times forty stripes save one, 2 Cor. XI. Prisons were so frequent for the Apostle that he wrote almost most of his epistles from chains. Our Schmidius, along with Beza, also understood Ἀκαταστασίας as exiles. But we prefer the sense of Grotius, approved by the blessed Hunnius, the blessed Balduin, and most others along with the Vulgate and Erasmus. For blows and prisons are frequently joined with the seditions or tumults stirred up against Paul, which the Apostle could not pass over here. See also Acts XIX. XXI. XXII. Theophylact restricts the labors to manual works, by which the Apostle supported himself and others; but the labors of his office brought no less weariness, for the sake of which he also macerated himself with vigils and fasting, compare chap. XI. 27.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἐν πληγαῖς) Act. XVI, 23. infra XI, 23, 24.

Ἐν φυλακαῖς) Dicto loco Actorum.

Ἐν ἀκαταστασίαις) Intelligunt quidam veterum idissum; quod ἀταξίαν dixit 1. Cor. IV, 11. Sed rectius Syrus inter- pretatur seditiones. Ita enim vox illa Græca sumitur Prov. XXVI, 28. Luc. XXI, 9. 1. Cor. XIV, 33. infra XII, 20. Jac. III, 16. Utitur hoc sensu & Polybius in fragmen- tis, à Valesio editis. Exempla vide Act. XVI, 12. XVII, 23. & sequentibus.

Ἐν κόποις) κόποι sunt labores ad lassitudinem: Vide 1. Cor. XV, 58. & infra XI, 23, 27. 1. Thessal. III, 5. Adde Act. XX, 35. 1. Cor. XV, 10. Gal. IV, 11. Col. I, 29. 2. Tim. IV, v. 10.

Ἐν ἀγρυπνίαις) Sic & infra XI, 27.

Ἐν νηστείαις) 1. Cor. IV, 1. Philipp. IV, 12.

Nonnulli hæc tribuunt Corinthiis, quasi hor- tetur eos Apostolus, ut nulli offensionem præ- beant: Sed rectius hoc refertur ad exhortantes A- postolos, qui v. 1. συνεργοῦντες inquiunt παρακα- λοῦμεν. Ita etiam Camerarius: nos conjungentes operam nostram cohortamur vos &c. Nos, inquam, nemini præbentes offensionem ullam. Beza notat, id Græca scholia observasse, & Erasmum ipsum, qui prius secus senserat, postea animadvertisse verbum διδόντες coñectendum esse cum verbo παρακαλῶ- μεν. Pariter annuit quoque Flacius, Erasmus, ut & Schmidius in h. l. Apostolus ergò de sese & Ti- motheo loquitur, sanctitatis studium, nec non constantiam & sinceritatem suam in exemplum proponens. Me velim, inquit, interprete Theo- phylacto, duce utamini. Nam sic mihi vivendum institui, ut nulli ne criminandi quidem me dixerim, sed ne vel leviter incusandi lædendive occasionem præbuerim. Quod eo feci, ne nostra notetur admini- stratio, & ignominiam subeat. Non enim, ne cul- pentur res per me gestæ, vel mea institutio dixit, sed ne quam vel tenuem labem aut vituperationem admit- tant, enitor. Addit Theophylactus, tacitè etiam Co- rinthios ita carpi, ut quorum male acta jam vita à multis culpetur, culpantiumque execratio omnis in Christum, ejusque fidem redundet. Quapropter do- cent hic Paulus & Timotheus, quantopere cave- rint, ne scilicet ulla in re ulli poneretur offendi- lum, ut nec macula aliqua ministerio aspergere- tur, aut jure reprehendi possit ipsorum ministe- rium, ex adverso in omnibus sese palam proba- rint, ceu decet ministros Dei, utpote in multa pa- tientia, vel sufferentia passionum & laborum, cum vigiliis & jejuniis exantlatorum in studio virtutum v. 6. & in partibus officii fideliter exequendis v. 7. Per ϑλίψεις afflictiones, interprete B. Hunnio, per- stringuntur omnia illa, quæ adversa eveniunt: Ne- cessitates dicuntur objecta infortunia, è quibus nul- lus patet exitus. Στενοχωρία, vi vocabuli, angustum locum significat, quando quis arctatur in angustum. Intelligit ergo Paulus id genus afflictionis, quo cor ho- minis sic in arctum constringitur, ut quo se vertat, non inveniat. Et differunt anxietates à necessitati- bus, quod hæ forinsecus effugia præcludunt, illa ve- rò cor ipsum intus in angustum cogunt, ut videantur spiritum hominis intercluderè velle. Plagæ sunt, quas mundus odio doctrinæ infligere solet confessori- bus Evangelii, quemadmodum Salvator ipse plagas & colaphos sustinuit in die passionis suæ, & Paulus Apostolus à Judæis quinquies plagas accepit quadra- genas una minus, 2. Cor. XI. Carceres adeo fre- quentes erant Apostolo, ut plerasque ferme epi- stolas ex vinculis scripserit. Ἀκαταστασίας etiam Schmidius noster eum Beza de exiliis intellexit. Sed præferimus sensum Grotii B. Hunnio, B. Bal- duino, & aliis plerisque cum Vulgata & Erasmo probatum. Nam plagis & carceribus optimè seditiones vel tumultus adversus Paulum frequenter excitati conjunguntur, quos hic praeterire non poterat Apostolus. Vide & Act. XIX. XXI. XXII. Labores ad manuum operas restringit Theophylactus, quibus seipsum & alios aluerit Apostolus; sed non minorem lassitudinem labores officii adferebant, cujus causa & vigiliis se, & inedia macerabat, confer. cap. XI. 27.

## 6:6
V. 6. Ἐν ἁγνότητι) In abstinence from Venus, and also from things which could give rise to the suspicion of such a fault. See below XI. 2. 1. Tim. V. 22.

Ἐν γνώσει) In the knowledge of the law according to the letter and according to the more mystical sense.

Ἐν μακροθυμίᾳ) In gentleness toward those who have offended against him.

Ἐν χρηστότητι) In beneficence toward all כחסר.

Ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ) With prophecies, tongues, healings.

Ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἀνυποκρίτῳ) Rom. XII. 9. 1. Petr. I. 22.

These pertain to Christianity and the pursuit of holiness, and are referred to by most people in that way: and therefore they can be explained thus, that they strive toward God in ἁγνότητι, that is, in purity or chastity; toward themselves in γνώσει, in the knowledge (not theoretical, but practical) of the divine will, so that it might be proved what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God, Rom. XII. 2. and that they might follow it as wise men, and understanding what the will of the Lord is, Eph. V. 15. 17. finally toward their neighbor they were devoted to long-suffering and kindness, and devoted diligent effort, and that in the Holy Spirit, that is, with Him granting and governing, inasmuch as He is the efficient cause of these virtues; and in love devoid of hypocrisy toward God and neighbor, which is the ultimate end or scope to which all things ought to be directed, or the highest perfection and complement of all things, Rom. XIII. 9. Theophylact, however, interprets ἁγνότητα as continence or purity preserved in all things; indeed, even that he preached freely and enticed by no gifts. But he interprets γνῶσιν as the wisdom of God, which truly ought to be called knowledge in contrast to exterior and worldly knowledge, upon which the deceitful Apostles relied: but he seems to restrict Μακροθυμίαν and χρηστότητα to the parts of his office: It is, he says, truly the mark of an adamantine soul, when agitated and beset on all sides, not only to preserve the loftiness of the mind, but also to show oneself good and equitable. There follow, however, things that pertain to the office; and among these first the cause, namely the means, the Word of truth and the supreme one, inasmuch as it is the power of God; then the aids, namely weapons divinely supplied; furthermore the doubtful cases, from which they were to be overcome, finally the successes and events, the judgments of both the world and the Spirit up to verse 11. The Apostles were not accustomed to urge the mystical sense of the law, nor does it seem to look here to any catalog of virtues, to which it is also evident that the gifts of prophecies, tongues, or healings do not pertain.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἐν ἁγνότητι) In abstinentia à Venere, atque etiam à rebus, quae talis culpae suspicionem parere poterant. Vide infra XI. 2. 1. Tim. V. 22.

Ἐν γνώσει) In cognitione legis κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν & κατὰ τὴν μυστικωτέραν διάνοιαν.

Ἐν μακροθυμίᾳ) In lenitate adversum eos, qui in ipsum deliquerunt.

Ἐν χρηστότητι) In beneficentia adversus omnes כחסר.

Ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ) Cum prophetiis, linguis, sanationibus.

Ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἀνυποκρίτῳ) Rom. XII. 9. 1. Petr. I. 22.

Haec ad Christianismum & studium sanctitatis pertinent, eoque à plerisque referuntur: ac proinde ita explicari possunt, quod studeant quoad Deum τῇ ἁγνότητι, id est, puritati, vel castitati; quoad semetipsos τῇ γνώσει cognitioni (non Theoreticae, sed practicae) divinae voluntatis, ut probaretur, quae sit bona & placens & perfecta Dei voluntas, Rom. XII. 2. eamque ὡς σοφοὶ, καὶ συνιέντες, τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ κυρίου, sequerentur, Eph. V. 15. 17. denique quoad proximum τῇ μακροθυμίᾳ, καὶ τῇ χρηστότητι longanimitati & benignitati dediti fuerint, operamque sedulam navarint, idque in Spiritu Sancto, id est, eo largiente & gubernante, utpote qui causa est Efficiens harum virtutum; & in charitate hypocrisis experte erga Deum & proximum, quae ultimus finis aut scopus est, quo omnia dirigi debeant, vel perfectio summa & complementum omnium, Rom. XIII. 9. Theophylactus tamen τὴν ἁγνότητα de continentia vel puritate omnibus in rebus servatâ; imò etiam, quod gratis & nullis illectus muneribus praedicavit, interpretatus est. Γνῶσιν verò de Dei sapientia, quae verè scientia dici debet in ἀντιθέσει ad exteriorem & mundanam cognitionem, quâ fallaces Apostoli niterentur: Μακροθυμίαν verò & χρηστότητα ad partes officii restringere videtur: Animi, inquiens, profectò adamantini est agitatum undique & circumpunctum non solum mentis servare celsitudinem, sed & bonum se, & aequum praestare. Sequuntur autem, quae ad officium pertinent; & in his primum causa, media nempè, Verbum veritatis & suprema, utpote, virtus Dei; tùm adminicula, videlicet arma divinitus subministrata; porrò casus dubii, è quibus illi superandi erant, denique successus & eventus, judicia tum mundi, tum Spiritus ad versum usque 11. Sensum legis mysticum neque urgere consueverunt Apostoli, neque huc ulli ad catalogum virtutum spectare videtur, ad quem etiam non pertinere dona prophetiarum, linguarum aut sanationum in aprico est.

## 6:7
Vers. 7. Ἐν λόγῳ ἀληθείας) By preaching the Gospel adulterated in no part, above IV. 2.

Ἐν δυνάμει Θεοῦ, διὰ τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης, τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν) With the power of God supplying us with weapons, as much on the right as on the left, for fulfilling justice. Soldiers carry a spear in the right hand, a shield in the left. In favorable circumstances they use the spear, in hard circumstances the shield. Thus God gave the Apostle and his helpers exceptional strength, through which they might rightly use both favorable and adverse circumstances. The following words demand this sense. A similar proverb is found in Homer: Οἷ δ᾽ ἐπὶ δεξία, οἶδ᾽ ἐπὶ ἀριστερὰ νωμῆσαι βῶν.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἐν λόγῳ ἀληθείας) Praedicando Evangelium nulla ex parte adulteratum supra IV. 2.

Ἐν δυνάμει Θεοῦ, διὰ τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης, τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν) Dei virtute nobis arma subministrante, tam dextra quam sinistra, ad justitiam implendam. Milites dextra hastam gerunt, scutum sinistra. In rebus secundis hasta utuntur, in rebus duris scuto. Sic Deus Apostolo & adjutoribus ejus vires dabat eximias, per quas & secundis & adversis rebus recte uterentur. Hunc sensum exigunt sequentia. Simile proverbium apud Homerum: Οἷ δ᾽ ἐπὶ δεξία, οἶδ᾽ ἐπὶ ἀριστερὰ νωμῆσαι βῶν.

## 6:8
Διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀτιμίας) Whether honor is held for us, or we are despised.

Διὰ δυσφημίας καὶ εὐφημίας) Whether men speak ill or well of us.

Ὡς πλάνοι καὶ ἀληθεῖς) Two words are missing. We are held as impostors, and we are truth-tellers. Calumnies, through which we are traduced as impostors, do not deter us from continuing to speak that doctrine which is true, and for which we are traduced. Concerning the name πλάνων and impostors, which was given to Christ, the Apostles, and Christians, we have spoken at Matt. XXVII. 63. πλάνοι to the Hebrews מסית.

Ὡς ἀγνούμενοι καὶ ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι) Many do not care to know us; but to others we are well known and dear. See what has been said by us at Matt. XIX. 29. Ἀγνούμενοι מרוחים Ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι נכרים.

Latin:

Διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀτιμίας) Sive honor nobis habetur, sive contemnimur.

Διὰ δυσφημίας καὶ εὐφημίας) Sive male, sive bene de nobis homines loquuntur.

Ὡς πλάνοι καὶ ἀληθεῖς) Desunt verba duo. Tanquam impostores habemur, & veridici sumus. Non deterrent nos calumniae, per quas ut impostores traducimur, quo minus pergamus doctrinam illam, quae vera est, & ob quam traducimur eloqui. De nomine πλάνων & impostorum, quod datum Christo, Apostolis ac Christianis, diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 63. πλάνοι Hebraeis מסית.

Ὡς ἀγνούμενοι καὶ ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι) Multi nos nosse non curant; sed aliis bene noti & chari sumus. Vide, quae dicta à nobis ad Matth. XIX. 29. Ἀγνούμενοι מרוחים Ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι נכרים.

## 6:9
V. 9. Ὡς ἀποθνήσκοντες) we are believed to be dying daily. Always like those about to fall, and yet never falling.

Καὶ ἰδὺ ζῶμεν) And behold we live) We still live by the help of God, and we live until God himself shall wish to honor us with a glorious death.

Ὡς παιδευόμενοι καὶ μὴ θανατόμενοι) He explains that very thing which he had just said by adducing the passage from Psalm CXVIII. 18. where in the Greek παιδεύων ἐπαίδευσέ με ὁ κύριος, καὶ τῷ θανάτῳ ὐ παραδέδωκέ με. Boys are properly said to be παιδεύεσθαι, who are corrected by stripes: improperly, men who are most pious, who always become better through these trials.

Latin:

V. 9. Ὡς ἀποθνήσκοντες) credimur quotidie morituri. Semper casuris similes, nunquamque cadentes.

Καὶ ἰδὺ ζῶμεν) Adhuc vivimus Dei ope, & vivimus donec Deus ipse morte gloriosa nos honestare voluerit.

Ὡς παιδευόμενοι καὶ μὴ θανατόμενοι) Id ipsum, quod jam dixerat, explicat adducto Psalmi loco CXVIII. 18. ubi in Graeco παιδεύων ἐπαίδευσέ με ὁ κύριος, καὶ τῷ θανάτῳ ὐ παραδέδωκέ με. Dicuntur παιδεύεσθαι proprie pueri, qui verberibus emendantur: improprie viri summe pii, qui per ista tentamenta semper meliores fiunt.

## 6:10
Vers. 10. Ὡς λυπέμενοι, ἀεὶ δὲ χαίροντες) We seem to be always in sorrow on account of so many adverse things, meanwhile we rejoice on account of the testimony of a good conscience, and the consolations of God.

Ὡς πτωχοὶ, πολλοὺς δὲ πλουτίζοντες) We are held to be most needy, meanwhile we bestow upon others the greatest riches, namely the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Ὡς μηδὲν ἔχοντες, καὶ πάντα κατέχοντες) Having nothing as property, but everything by use. For those who were about to give their own eyes for him, would they have denied him anything of their own goods? Gal. IV. 15. He himself indeed took nothing for himself from these, but gave to the poor Jews as much as he wished, as if from his own. Thus the prophecy of Is. LXI. 4 was eminently fulfilled.

Paul and Timothy had approved themselves as ministers of God, not only by the endurance of evils and the holiness of their lives, but also by the faithfulness and diligence of their office; to which pertains, first, the sincere preaching of the word of truth, through which, as a medium, God works unto salvation, Rom. I. 16. But since that is not situated in human powers, but is of divine power, they refer to it whatever they accomplished in their office; and they profess that they showed themselves faithful to God and troublesome to no one, by nothing other than divine grace and power.

Furthermore, the supports which were needed—namely, the weapons of righteousness both for the right hand and for the left, in prosperity and in adversity—could be drawn from nowhere else than from the divine armory, the Word of GOD: nor could they be put on, or employed with fruit, except by the power of God, Eph. VI. 10. Now they are called weapons of righteousness, not for fulfilling the righteousness which is of the faithful, or which is required of all. For no one is able to fulfill righteousness, to his own δικαιοσύνην. But the weapons of righteousness are righteous weapons, in a manner of speaking customary to the Scriptures, such as are required for fulfilling the righteousness of duty. The Apostle, however, divides them into right and left. For because Satan does not attack the heralds of the Gospel in one way only, but one from the right, setting before them either the allurements of the flesh, or the favor of the powerful, if they accommodate themselves to their wishes in the business of religion: or by the hope of earthly gain, or by some outward show of honor or dignity, striving to snatch them away and lead them astray. Now furthermore, striking them from the left either with internal temptations or attacking them from without with the hatreds and persecutions of the world, it is necessary that they be equipped with suitable weapons to receive blows of both kinds, as the blessed Hunnius rightly says here.

Now as regards the various circumstances in which the weapons of the Spirit are needed, various engines are as it were applied to the ministers of the Word, inasmuch as they are at one time tempted διὰ δόξης καὶ εὐφημίας, through honor and praise, at another διὰ ἀτιμίας καὶ δυσφημίας, through contempt and infamy.

Finally, as regards successes and outcomes, they are presented both according to the judgment of the world and according to the judgment of the Spirit, or κατ' ἀλήθειαν. The world held the Apostles for impostors and did not desire to know them. They were commonly believed to be dying daily and to be subjected to perpetual punishments; they seemed always to be in to be outside, they were held to be most needy, and having nothing: nor did they experience or estimate it otherwise by the sense and judgment of the flesh: But by the judgment of God, and the Spirit, they were truthful, approved by goods, and although they seemed like the dead; yet they lived by the help of God, and boasted that they were not delivered to death: Although they seemed to mourn; yet they always rejoiced in the Lord; even if they were held to be most needy; in reality, however, they were those through whom very many were enriched, even if they were considered to possess nothing of their own, in reality, however, they had enough possessions, as those who possessed God, heaven, and all things with which to satisfy their soul, The whole world of riches belongs to the believer, says Jerome from Prov. XVII. in the version of the LXX. Interpp. Epist. CIII. to Paulinus. We are commonly held to be beggars, who, wandering in uncertain dwellings, possess nothing of our own anywhere. But we are not moved even by this inconvenience: For we are so destitute of all things, that in the meantime we possess all things: In this age indeed only having from time to time as much as the use of this temporary life requires: But at the same time possessing by faith the grace of God, and the righteousness that is valid before Him, and in hope expecting the unfading inheritance stored up in the heavens, as the Hunnian paraphrase has it.

PART II. Dehortation from commerce with infidels.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὡς λυπέμενοι, ἀεὶ δὲ χαίροντες) Videmur semper in moerore esse ob tot res adversas, interim gaudemus ob testimonium bonae conscientiae, & Dei solatia.

Ὡς πτωχοὶ, πολλοὺς δὲ πλουτίζοντες) Habemur egenissimi, interim in alios conferimus summas divitias, dona scilicet Spiritus Sancti.

Ὡς μηδὲν ἔχοντες, καὶ πάντα κατέχοντες) Nihil mancipio habentes, usu omnia. Nam qui oculos suos pro ipso daturi erant, ecquid ipsi de bonis suis negassent? Gal. IV. 15. Ipse quidem de his nihil sibi sumebat, sed dabat pauperibus Judaeis quantum volebat, tanquam de suo. Sic impletum eminenter vaticinium Es. LXI. 4.

Probarant sese Paulus & Timotheus, ut DEI ministri, non tantum malorum tolerantiâ, vitaeque sanctimoniâ, sed etiam officii fide ac diligentiâ; Ad quod primo sincerae verbi veritatis praedicatio pertinet, per quod tanquam medium operatur Deus ad salutem, Rom. I. 16. Quum verò id non in humanis viribus situm, sed virtutis divinae sit, ad eam referunt, quicquid in officio suo effecerunt; seque fidos Deo, nemini importunos praebuisse, non nisi divina gratiâ ac virtute, profitentur.

Adminicula porrò, quibus opus erat, arma nempe justitiae tum ad dextram, tum ad sinistram, in secundis & adversis aliunde depromi non poterant, quàm ex armamentario divino, Verbo DEI: Nec vel indui, vel cum fructu adhiberi, nisi virtute Dei, Eph. VI. 10. Arma autem justitiae dicuntur non ad justitiam implendam, quae fidelium sit, vel ab omnibus requiratur. Justitiam enim implere nemo valet, ad sui δικαιοσύνην. Sed arma justitiae sunt arma justa, modo loquendi scripturis usitato, qualia ad implendam officii justitiam requiruntur. Dividit autem ea Apostolus in dextra & sinistra. Nam quia non uno modo Satanas Evangelii praecones aggreditur, sed unùs à dextris objiciens seu carnis illecebras, seu praepotentum favorem, si in negotio religionis illorum placitis sese accommodent: seu spe terreni emolumenti, aut honoris dignitatisve specie quadam effusa transversos illos abripere contendens. Nunc porrò à sinistris eos vel internis tentationibus percellens, vel forinsecus oppugnans odiis & persecutionibus mundi, necesse est, ut ad accipiendos utriusque generis ictus idoneis armis instructi sint, ut rectè hic B. Hunnius.

Jam quod ad diversos casus, in quibus armis Spiritus opus est, attinet, variae veluti machinae adhibentur Verbi ministris, utpote qui modo tentantur διὰ δόξης ὲ ἐυφημίας, per honorem & laudem, modò δι ἀτιμίας καὶ δυσφημίας, per contemptum & infamiam.

Denique quod ad successus & eventus exhibentur illi & secundum mundi, & secundum Spiritus judicium, vel κατ' ἀλήθειαν. Mundus Apostolos habuit pro impostoribus, nec nosse eos cupiebat. Credebantur vulgò morituri quotidie, & perpetuis castigationibus subjici, videbantur semper in mo- xore esse, habebantur egenissimi, & nihil habentes: nec aliter id sensu & judicio carnis experiebantur vel æstimabant: Sed judicio Dei, & Spiritus veraces erans, bonis probati, atque etsi mortuis similes videbantur; ope tamen Dei vivebant, & gloriabantur, se morti non tradi: Etsi lugere viderentur; tamen semper in Domino gaudebant; etiamsi haberentur egenissimi; revera tamen illi erant, per quos plurimi ditabantur, etiamsi nihil proprii possidere censerentur, revera tamen satis possessionum habebant, utpote Deum, cœlum & omnia, quibus animum explerent, possidentes, Credenti totus mundus divitiarum est, ait Hieronymus è Prov. XVII. versione LXX. Interpp. Epist. CIII. ad Paulin. Habemur vulgo mendici, qui divagantes incertis sedibus nihil uspiam proprii possideamus. Verum, ne hoc quidem movemur incommodo: Ita namque sumus rerum omnium inopes, ut interim possideamus universa: In hoc quidem seculo tantum subinde habentes, quantum hujus temporariæ vitæ usus exigit: Simul autem fide possidentes gratiam Dei, & valentem coram illo justitiam, spe vero exspectantes immarcescibilem hæreditatem in cœlis reconditam, ut paraphrasis Hunniana habet.

PARS II. Dehortatio à commercio cum infidelibus.

## 6:11
V. 11. Our mouth is opened to you, Corinthians) This ἀνέωγε here is for the Hitpael, as is the following passive, התפתח To open the mouth, a frequent expression among the Hebrews, as Job III. 1. Macc. V. 2. XIII. 26. It signifies here not to speak in any way whatsoever, but to speak liberally and openly. For there shines forth in the preceding words a certain wonderful δεινότης, which Augustine observed.

Our heart is enlarged) I am not only liberal toward you in words, but also in the affection of the mind, רחב לב thus התרחב 1 Kings IV. 29. In a similar way, love is said to be poured out in hearts, Rom. V. 5. He also mentions this affection below in VII. 3.

These look not so much to the preceding as to the following. For he conciliates benevolence to himself so that exhortations, which have proceeded from the affection of charity, may be admitted, as if he were saying, with Theophylact as interpreter: I not only prefer my charity toward you in words but in heart, since I have that diffused and enlarged among you. For that ardor of love not only opens my mouth but dilates my mind, and in such a way that it may take you all in. According to the Blessed Hunnius, the opening of the mouth refers to love, the dilation of the heart to candor, and παῥῥησίαν to writing and speaking.

Latin:

V. 11. Τὸ σόμα ἡμῶν ἀνέωγε πρὸς ὑμᾶς Κορίνθιοι) Hoc ἀνέωγε hic est pro Hitpael, ut & passivum sequens, התפתח Aperire os, frequens Hebræis loquutio, ut Job. III. 1. Macch. V. 2. XIII. 26. Significat autem hic non quovis modo loqui, sed liberaliter & apertè loqui. Elucet enim in verbis præcedentibus mira quædam δεινότης, quam observavit Augustinus.

Ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν πεπλάτυνται) Non verbis tantum liberalis sum in vos, sed & affectu animi, רחב לב sic התרחב 1. Reg. IV. 29. Pari modo dicitur dilectio effusa in cordibus, Rom. V. 5. Hunc affectum etiam infra commemorat VII. 3.

Non tàm ad præcedentia, quàm sequentia hæc spectant. Nam benevolentiam sibi conciliat ad adhortationes, ex affectu charitatis profectas, admittendas, quasi dicat, Theophylacto interprete: Non solum meam erga vos charitatem verbis præfero sed corde, cum illud apud vos diffusum habeam & ampliatum. Ardor namq; amoris ille non modo mihi os patefacit, sed mentem dilatat, & ita, ut vos capiat universos. Secundum B. Hunnium apertio oris ad amorem, dilatatio cordis ad candorem, & παῥῥησίαν in scribendo loquendoque refertur.

## 6:12
Vers. 12. You are not straitened in us) That is, you do not possess a small place in our soul קצרתם.

But you are straitened in your own bowels) On your part, the heart is narrow, the affection thin, in me, that is to say. Σπλάγχνα are said not only of pity but also of any other affection below in VII. 15. Philem. v. 20. He says this, however, not to all the Corinthians, but to some.

The Greeks also render this sense. Theophylact: You indeed, he says, although you are as many as possible in my heart, which is certainly most patient, are by no means wandering in a narrow space. But in your own hearts and bowels you are in a narrow place and so restricted that you cannot receive me even one bit liberally, just as if he were saying: I indeed pursue you with great benevolence; you, however, although you are affected with some love toward me, and hold me in an embrace in your hearts; yet this charity of yours is tighter and narrower with which you embrace me. Nor does the Blessed Hunnius interpret it otherwise: As if he were saying, our heart is not at all narrow for receiving you and embracing you with a sincere affection of charity: But it opens itself so entirely that I carry you all and each one enclosed within the recesses of my breast, and love you intimately. And indeed it was fitting that I should be loved by you in turn with an equal love: But it cannot be denied that you are colder and narrower in embracing us in turn, and so your bowels are almost closed to the mutual love of us, so that you are not equally capable of us. Nor do Beza or Flacius deny this, although the latter also praises another interpretation, which B. Balduinus and Estius made their own, as if he were saying: That he is freed from his troubles, and is no longer angry with them; but with an opened mouth, or a broad breast, he deals with them, as a Father with his children, who has been vehemently exhilarated by their conversion. For the rest, however, he praises them as most dear children, because they are straitened in their bowels, that is, because they partly grieve over the former faults, which he had chastised in the previous epistle, and partly condole in their own afflictions. For from thence one can gather their filial affection toward their Apostle, as B. Balduinus has it. The former explanation, however, is more convenient to the text. For he exhorts, as Flacius admits, in the following verse, the Corinthians, that they also, with an equally open and candid breast and most ardent benevolence, may be joined to him, trust him, and promise themselves all the best things from him: Just as he himself dares to pour himself out freely toward them. He wants to be acknowledged and embraced as a Father, just as he himself embraces them as his children, and receives them into his own bosom.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Οὐ στενοχωρεῖσθε ἐν ἡμῖν) Id est, non exiguum locum in nostro animo possidetis קצרתם.

Στενοχωρεῖσθε δὲ ἐν τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ὑμῶν) Vestra ex parte est cor angustum, affectus tenuis, in me scilicet. Σπλάγχνα non tantum de miseratione, sed & de alio quovis affectu dicuntur infra VII. 15. Philem. v. 20. Dicit autem hoc Corinthiis non omnibus, sed quibusdam.

Hunc sensum etiam reddunt Græci. Theophylactus: Vos quidem, inquit, etsi quam plurimi sitis meo in corde, quod sane patientissimũ est, baudquaquam in arcto vagamini. Vestris vero in præcordiis & visceribus in angusto estis & ita adstricti, ut ne vel unum quidem me largiter possitis excipere, perinde ac si inquiæt: Ipse equidem ingenti vos prosequor benevolentia; vos vero etsi aliquo erga me amore estis affecti, & complexum vestris in præcordiis detinetis; arctior tamen vestra hæc charitas est & angustior, qua me complectimini. Nec aliter interpretatur B. Hunnius: Quasi dicat, cor nostrum ad vos recipiendos, & sincera charitatis affectu complectendos, angustum minime est: Sed ita totum se aperit, ut vos omnes atq; singulos intra pectoris mei latebras inclusos geram, intimeque diligam. Et quidem par erat, æquali amore me vicissim à vobis diligi: Sed negari non potest, esse vos frigidiores & angustiores ad nos vicissim com- plectendos, adeoque viscera ad mutuam nostri dilectionem propemodum esse clausa, ut nostri baud perinde sitis capaces. Neque abnuit Beza aut Flacius, etsi hic etiam alteram interpretationem laudet, quam B. Balduinus & Estius suam fecere, quasi dicat: Se aerumnis suis liberatum, & ipsis non amplius iratum esse; sed dilatato ore, seu lato pectore cum ipsis agere, tanquam Patrem cum filiis, qui conversione ipsorum vehementer fuerit exhilaratus. De caetero verò laudet eos, ut charissimos filios, quod angustiantur in visceribus suis, hoc est, quod partim de prioribus delictis, qua castigaverat superiori epistola, doleant, partim in afflictionibus suis condoleant. Exinde enim filialem eorum erga Apostolum suum affectum colligere posse, ut B. Balduinus habet. Convenientior autem est textui prior explicatio. Hortatur enim, fatente Flacio, vers. seq. Corinthios, ut & illi perinde aperto & candido pectore ardentissimaque benevolentia sint ipsi conjuncti, ipsi fidant, & optima quaeque sibi de ipso polliceantur: Sicut ipse audet libere erga eos se effundere. Vult se agnosci & complecti pro Patre, sicut ipse eos tanquam suos filios complectatur, inque suum sinum recipiat.

## 6:13
V. 13. The same recompense (I speak as to children), be you also enlarged) These are to be distinguished in this manner: The same recompense (I speak as to children), be you also enlarged; In turn, you also (for I speak as to children) enlarge yourselves. The recompense is for the sake of a recompense to be repaid in turn. The same, that is, equal to my affection. Thus both the Syrian and the Arab have accepted this passage. Rightly. We have had the word recompense also in Rom. I. 27. The Apostle demands the same below in VII. 2.

He demands, therefore, the same remuneration, as from children, that by rendering like for like they might love the loving Apostle in return. Be enlarged also yourselves: act, he says, and you also, not with so narrow a heart toward me, but in the same manner opened, and thus rightly composed for receiving my paternal corrections with filial reverence. And Blessed Balduinus acknowledges this sense: By ἀντιμισθίαν or remuneration he understands an equal affection of the Corinthians toward him. For he wishes that they too should enlarge their heart and mouth, and promise themselves all the best things concerning their Apostle, as children do concerning a Father, fearing nothing for themselves, and taking in good part that admonition which he was now about to institute. For he was not rebuking them as an enemy; but warning them, and consulting for what things are theirs, as a father. Some, however, whom Cornelius notes, have wrongly understood these things concerning the remuneration of the heavenly reward; as if he were saying, since you are to have the same reward and recompense with me in the heavens, enlarge also your charity toward me. For Cornelius himself admits that another sense underlies this, explaining it thus: Render to me the same measure and breadth of charity: Extend and enlarge your heart and charity toward me with an equal measure. From which, however, no one except Salmero attempts to extract a sense of merit de condigno, as if such a thing lay hidden in the word ἀντιμισθίας. For there is no proportion between the love of children and the love of a Father, and an inequality of the love of the Corinthians and Paul is rather noted here from 2 Cor. 12:15. I, loving you more abundantly, am yet less loved, observes Chrysostom. Nor does the Apostle demand this ἀντιμισθίαν under the aspect of merit, but as a debt of gratitude, as Erasmus and Valla have noted. Nor is there anything here about merit in Theophylact, explaining these things thus: Show the same reciprocation of love, and equal benevolence toward me, and be you also, just as I myself, poured out in charity. And he demands this as a certain debt, when he says, I speak as to children. For I do not seem to be demanding anything more, if, being a father, I have deemed it not unworthy to be honored by my children. For children also ought to perform this duty toward a father.

Latin:

V. 13. Τὴν δὲ ἀυτὴν ἀντιμισθίαν (ὡς τέκνοις λέγω), πλατύνθητε καὶ ὑμεῖς) Distinguenda haec in hunc modum: Τὴν δὲ ἀυτὴν ἀντιμισθίαν (ὡς τέκνοις λέγω) πλατύνθητε καὶ ὑμεῖς· Vicissim & vos (nam ut filiis loquor) dilatate vos. Τὴν ἀντιμισθίαν est pro κατ᾽ ἀντιμισθίαν ad vicem rependendam. Τὴν ἀυτὴν eandem, id est, parem affectui meo. Ita hunc locum accepere & Syrus & Arabs. Recte. Vocem ἀντιμισθίας habuimus & Rom. I. 27. Idem postulat Apostolus infra VII. 2.

Eandem ergo remunerationem, ut à filiis, exigit, ut par pari referentes Apostolum amantem vicissim redament. Dilatamini & vos: agite, inquit, & vos non ita angusto pectore in me, sed eundem in modum aperto, adeoque ad paternas correptiones meas filiali reverentiâ suscipiendas rectè composito. Et agnoscit hunc sensum B. Balduinus: Per ἀντιμισθίαν seu remunerationem intelligit parem affectum Corinthiorum erga se. Vult enim, ut & ipsi cor & os suum dilatent, & sibi optima quaeque de Apostolo suo, tanquam filii de Patre polliceantur, nihil sibi metuentes, & boni consulentes admonitionem illam, quam nunc instituturus erat. Non enim se increpare ut hostem; sed monere, & quaè re ipsorum sunt, consulere, ut patrem. Perperam autem nonnulli, quos notat Cornelius: haec de remuneratione praemii caelestis accepere; quasi dicat, cum idem praemium & mercedem mecum in coelis sitis habituri, dilatate & vos charitatem vestram in me. Alium enim sensum hic subesse fatetur ipse Cornelius, sic exponens: Eandem charitatis mensuram & latitudinem mihi reddite: Pari mensura cor & charitatem vestram in me extendite & dilatate. Ex quo tamen sensum meriti de condigno neque quisquam extrahere conatur Salmero, quasi in voce ἀντιμισθίας tale lateat. Nam proportio nulla est inter amorem filiorum & amorem Patris, & inaequalitatem potius hic notari amoris Corinthiorum & Pauli è 2. Cor. XII. 15. Ego abundantius vos amans, minus tamen diligor, observat Chrysostomus. Neque sub ratione meriti hanc ἀντιμισθίαν postulat Apostolus, sed ut debitum gratitudinis, ut Erasmus & Valla annotarunt. Nec quicquam hic de merito Theophylactus, haec ita explicans: Eandem ipsi amoris vicissitudinem, & parem in me praestate benevolentiam, estoteq́, & vos, quemadmodum ipse, in charitate effusi. Idque pro debito quodam deposcit, cum inquit, tanquam filiis dico. Neque enim videor magis aliquid effagitare, si pater cum sim à liberis coli duxerim non indignum. Debent namque & filii hoc in patrem praestare officium.

## 6:14
V. 14. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers) He admonishes them, as in the previous epistle, not to feast in idol temples. Ἑτεροζυγεῖν means to pull the other part of the yoke, that is, to undergo the same yoke. Wherefore the Syrian here said: Do not be children of one yoke with those who do not believe. And here is a mystical application of the law, Deut. XXII. v. 10, where we have cited passages from Plautus and Calphurnius. See the prohibitive precept CCLXXXI. Ovid: Unequal bullocks do not come well to the plow. Papinius, Thebaid 1, concerning bullocks that are indeed equal, but still untrained: Thus when the farmer seeks to join chosen bullocks with the heavy plow placed upon them, they, indignant, whose neck has not yet descended with much plowing into the high, knotty shoulders, pull in different directions, and loosen the bonds with equal strength and confuse the furrows with a varied path.

For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness) Friendship either finds or makes equals. This must be understood according to the subject matter being discussed. For there is a certain society among all men, but not such as this. These are כלאים (mixed kinds) Levit. XIX. 19, where some interpreters use ἑτεροζύγῳ. Δικαιοσύνη here is the worship of God according to His own prescription. Ἀνομία is religion without divine law, and against it. The same sentiment is in Sirach XII. verse 20, and in Psalm I.

And what communion has light with darkness) Light is the Gospel; darkness, the fables of the Gentiles.

Latin:

V. 14. Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ἀπίστοις) Monet eos, ut & in priori epistola, ne in idoleis convivarentur. Ἑτεροζυγεῖν est alteram partem jugi trahere, id est, idem jugum subire. Quare Syrus hic dixit: Ne sitis filii unius jugi cum iis, qui non credunt. Et est hic applicatio mystica legis, Deut. XXII. v. 10. ubi loca adduximus Plauti & Calphurnii. Vide præ- ceptum vetans CCLXXXI. Ovidius: Non bene inæquales veniunt ad aratra juvenci. Papinius 1. Thebaidos, de æqualibus quidem tauris; sed rudibus adhuc: Sic ubi delectos per torva armenta juvencos Agricola imposito sociare affectat aratro, Illi indignantes, queis nondum vomere multo Ardua nodosos cervix descendit in armos, In diversa trahunt, atque æquis vincula laxant Viribus & vario confundunt limite sulcos.

Τίς γὰρ μετοχὴ δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ἀνομίᾳ) Amicitia pares aut recipit, aut facit. Intelligendum hoc pro materia, de qua agitur. Est enim inter homines omnes quædam societas, sed non talis. Sunt hæc כלאים Levit. XIX. 19. ubi ἑτε- ροζύγῳ quidam Interpretes. Δικαιοσύνη hic est cultus Dei ex ipsius præscripto. Ἀνομία religio sine lege divina, & contra eam. Eadem sententia Sirach. XII. vers. 20. & in Psalmo I.

Τίς δὲ κοινωνία φωτὶ πρὸς σκότος) Lux est Evangelium; tenebræ, gentium fabulæ.

## 6:15
V. 15. And what accord has Christ with Belial) i.e., with any man according to the law. For the LXX translate בליעל as παράνομος (lawless) in Deut. XIII. 13, Jud. XIX. 22, 2 Sam. XVI. 7, XX. 1, XXIII. 5, 1 Kings XXI. 10, VI. 13, Prov. I. 3. It is surely from בלי, which is σφραγὶς (seal), and עול, which signifies yoke, which is Jerome's etymology. Others bring forward others. But the Greeks have followed this one. Christ taught us to obey God; they obey only their own desires. Some books have Βελίαρ with the last letter changed. Thus Βεελζεβὺλ for Βεελζεβοὺβ, Ἀβακὺμ for Ἀβακοὺκ, Ἰωσὴφ for Ἰωσὴβ, Συχὰρ for Συχήμ. See what is said at Matth. X. 25 and at Joh. IV. 5.

Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever) What do they have in common? For so the Hebrews speak, 2 Sam. XXI, Acts VIII. 21.

And what agreement has the temple of God with idols) Συγκατάθεσις is society. For in Exodus XXIII, where in the Hebrew it is תשת ידך עם־רשע, do not put your hand with the wicked, the Greek version has, and you shall not agree (συγκαταθήσῃ) with the unjust. Philosophers call συγκατάθεσις the assent of the mind.

Cornelius wishes the Apostle here to pass, according to epistolary custom and license, to another point, and that it is in vain to ask how these things are connected with the preceding. But the connection is by no means obscure. For since the Apostle has exhorted them not to receive the grace of God in vain, and has taught by his own example how scandals are to be avoided in all things, both in life and in doctrine, he now deservedly dissuades them—having made a certain preparation through the manifestation of his love—from dealings with infidels, so that they may both uniquely adhere to their faithful teachers and escape stumbling blocks and seduction. Furthermore, these things do not pertain to abstinence from things sacrificed to idols and the feasts of infidels, of which no mention is made here, nor to marriage with infidels, as Estius explains from Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian, chapter 5, and in his epistle to Ageruchia on monogamy, chapter 2. Which senses are too restricted, since the Apostle prohibits all dealings with infidels in general, by which, of course, it comes about that one declines into their party by reason of unbelief. The word ἑτεροζυγοῦντες implies inequality of the yoke and an inclination to the other side, as Theophylact notes, who renders the reason for the connection thus: That will indeed manifest your charity toward me, if you have no dealings with infidels, nor have declined to their side. Those who have submitted themselves to the yoke of Christ, if they are coupled with infidels in the same yoke of impiety, are said to be ἑτεροζυγεῖν or to draw a yoke alien to the faith of Christ. Therefore Cornelius explains: Do not draw a yoke, have participation and dealings with infidels in those things which pertain to religion, or so closely and familiarly that you gradually incline into their unbelief, as if he were saying: Separate yourselves from the assemblies, temples, sacrifices, feasts, marriages of infidels, and all their dealings that are either in themselves impious or unjust, or dangerous or scandalous, which sense Chrysostom and Ambrose also note to be the case. By ἀπίστους, Anselm understands the Judaizing pseudo-apostles, whom we have no doubt are included by this word; but the Apostle [speaks of] any infidels whatsoever, whether they be Gentiles and outside the Church, or heretics within the Church, devoid of true faith, whose dealings, especially if the danger of seduction is to be feared from them, are to be avoided, or at least declined in such a way that we in no way incline toward or become entangled in an alien yoke. For ἄπιστοι and Gentiles are called those alien to the Church and the knowledge of the true God, 1 Cor. VI. 6, ch. VII. 12, 13, 14, 15, ch. X. 17, XIV. 22, 23, 24, just as also infidels in the assembly of the Church, even if not destitute of the word of God and the knowledge of the true God, Matth. XVII. 17, Mark IX. 19, Luke IX. 41, John XX. 27, just as the abstract noun ἀπιστία concerning the unbelief of those who are in the Church, even if they are not of the Church, occurs in Matth. XIII. 38, ch. XVII. 20, Mark VI. 6, Rom. III. 3. If you listen to B. Hunnius, there are two things which the Apostle commands to be avoided under the name of an alien yoke: first, the idolomania, superstitions, errors, and darkness of infidels; second, the works which emerge from this, the impious and unfruitful works of darkness. For he wishes not only the ἀπισίαν (unbelief) of the infidels to be avoided, but also their ἀνομίαν (lawlessness), and all that by which they are joined to Belial or the Devil, and which entails a commerce of darkness: as is clear from the subjoined declaration or rather confirmation. From this Apostolic exhortation, moreover, a judgment can be made as to what should be thought of the zeal of those who strive to mix diverse religions, or to reconcile syncretism among men of diverse religion. For what else do they do than ensure that a yoke is drawn with infidels? Indeed, among the peoples hateful to God and the Church, the Samaritans are listed in the first place, Sir. L. Inasmuch as they cherished the true worship of God and ethnic superstitions at the same time, 2 Kings XVII. See what we have expressly written in many works against the Syncretists, from which it is manifest that Grotius easily obtains the first place, both from those things which he disputed against Cassander, and from these his Biblical annotations. The Apostle certainly accumulates so many ἰσοδυναμῦντα (equivalent terms) for this reason, that he may exclude every commerce in ecclesiastical matters and in the cause of faith with men of diverse religion who are alien to the faith of Christ, every ἑτεροζυγίαν (unequal yoking), every μετοχὴν (participation), every κοινωνίαν (communion), every συμφώνησιν (concord), every μερίδα (portion), and finally every συγκατάθεσιν (agreement). First, ἑτεροζυγίαν, that is, an inclination toward another religion, a coupling with the foreign yoke of another religion. Then also every μετοχὴν, participation or commixture. Furthermore, every κοινωνίαν or communion whatsoever, not indeed in external temporal and civil matters, but in causes of religion. Furthermore, also συμφώνησιν, namely, consonance, so that we may abstain from conformity of voices as far as possible. Besides this, every μερίδα, so that we may not enter into even a partial conjunction. Finally, every συγκατάθεσιν, whatever seems to imply a certain consensus, so that we may in no way assent to their opinions, whether formally or interpretatively; whether directly or indirectly, since truth ought to have no commerce at all with falsehood. Nor does the Apostle persist only in the abstract, that lawlessness is to be avoided, that one must not communicate with darkness or idols, but in the concrete he forbids being coupled with ἀπίστοις (infidels). Finally, he teaches that that conjunction of the faithful with infidels is as morally impossible as the participation of righteousness with iniquity or injustice, of light and darkness, of Christ and Belial, or of the Devil. The sense of the argument, according to B. Hunnius, is this: It is not only shameful if anyone should attempt at least to join justice with injustice, etc., but also entirely ἀδύνατον [impossible]. For there is so much between justice and injustice, such a repugnance of light and darkness, such a dissension between Christ and Belial or the Devil, such a great and far-removed separation of the faithful from the unfaithful, and finally such an irreconcilable divorce between the temple of God and idols, that they can by no means be composed or associated: But the one immediately tears down and removes the other: Theophylact therefore implies that the unfaithful not only dwell in darkness, but also adhere to Belial or the Devil, and are not the temple of God, but have enslaved themselves to idols: Since the Apostle wished entirely, he says, that the Corinthians should depart from the company of the unfaithful, he certainly did not say, what conformity can there be of those who are in the light with those who dwell in darkness, or of the followers of Christ with those who follow the parties of demons, but he introduced the things themselves instead of the persons, namely light and darkness, and what was more, Christ to Belial: but he calls Belial an apostate and a deserter. Furthermore, from the appellation of Christ and Belial he renders the speech more atrocious. And furthermore: The unfaithful are indeed a temple of idols, or rather idols, but you are the house of God. And not such a one as they fashion in those fables of theirs, but of the living one. What agreement, therefore, will you have with them? That is, likeness and convention. The antithesis is sufficiently clear, as if he were to say, to express it in the words of B. Hunnius: You Corinthians have been justified through faith, and at the same time made servants of justice begun: The Gentiles, conversely, are entirely devoid of both justice imputed through faith and justice begun through new obedience: You are children of light, illuminated by the saving knowledge of God and Christ: they are children of darkness. You acknowledge Christ as your head and prince; for them Belial, that is, Satan, is prince and head: You are faithful, being endowed with saving faith in Christ: They are ἄπιστοι [unbelievers], entirely alien to the Christian faith; You, finally, are the temple of God, because of the Spirit of Him dwelling in you: they in turn serve idols and images.

Δικαιοσύνη [justice/righteousness] here is not the worship of God according to the prescription of GOD himself; but what Paul is accustomed to call δικαιοσύνην [justice/righteousness], especially as he indicated it in the preceding chapter, last verse, and as he said in ch. III. 9, διακονίαν τῆς δικαιοσύνης [ministry of justice/righteousness]: Nor does ἀνομία [lawlessness] denote religion so universally without divine law, and against it, as specifically, by the force of opposition and the proper signification of the word, transgression, or sin, 1 John III. 4. For those who are devoid of true justice are under sin, just as it is said in Rom. III. 23 concerning all outside of grace and before justification, that they are sinners and are destitute of the glory of God. By darkness, opposed to the light of the divine word, to which belongs not only the doctrine of the Gospel but also of the law, are denoted not only the fables of the Gentiles; but also any inventions adverse to the word of God, and alien to it, because in the cause of religion one must not only not admit what is established against the word of God; but not even what is outside the word of God, Deut. IV. 2, XII. 32, Gal. I. 8, 9. By τὸν βελιὰλ [Belial], because he is opposed τῷ Χριστῷ [to Christ], the Devil is more correctly understood, especially the lawless or παράνομος [transgressor of the law], than a man who follows only his own desires, not God. Thus Jerome, 1 Kings XXII, interprets sons of Belial as sons of the Devil. An idol is opposed to the temple of God. Some read idoliis [idols] instead of idolis, with the approval of the Syriac version, which has in the singular temple of Demons, whence it is suspected that in some Greek Codices it was once written εἰδωλείων [temple of idols] instead of εἰδώλων [idols]. But the Greek reading elio [sic] stands very well on its own. Namely, that idols or the worship of false gods do not agree with the temple of God, which the faithful are, since it thus ceases to be the temple of God and turns into a temple of idols; the temple of God and the temple of idols are opposites, and there is no harmony of the worship of idols with the worship of the true God, no commerce.

Latin:

V. 15. Τίς δὲ συμφώνησις Χριστῷ πρὸς Βελίαλ) i. e. cum quo- vis homine ex lege. Nam בליעל παράνομος vertunt LXX Deut. XIII. 13. Jud. XIX. 22. 2. Sam. XVI. 7. XX. 1. XXIII. 5. 1. Reg. XXI. 10. VI. 13. Prov. I. 3. Nimirum à בלי, quod est σφραγὶς, & עול, quod jugum significat, quæ est Hiero- nymi Etymologia. Alii alias afferunt. Sed Græci hanc sunt sequuti. Christus obedire Deo nos docuit, illi cupi- ditatibus tantum suis obsequuntur. Quidam libri habent Βελίαρ mutata ultima. Sic Βεελζεβὺλ pro Βεελζεβοὺβ, Ἀβα- κὺμ pro Ἀβακοὺκ, Ἰωσὴφ pro Ἰωσὴβ, Συχὰρ pro Συχήμ. Vi- de, quæ ad Matth. X. 25. & ad Joh. IV. 5.

Εἰ τις μερὶς πιστῷ μετ' ἀπίστου) Quid commune? Ita enim loquuntur Hebræi 2. Sam. XXI. Act. VIII. 21.

Τίς δὲ συγκατάθεσις ναῷ Θεῦ μετ' εἰδώλων) Συγκατάθεσις societas. Nam Exodi XXIII. ubi est in Hebræo תשת ne ponas manum tuam cum im- תשת ידך עם־רשע pio, Græca Versio habet, κ' συγκαταθήσῃ μετὰ τοῦ ἀδίκου. Phi- losophi συγκατάθεσιν vocant animi assensionem.

Transire hic Apostolum vult Cornelius, more & licentia epistolari, ad aliud punctum, & frustra quæri, quomodo ita cum præcedentibus conne- xa sint. Sed connexio minimè obscura est. Nam quum exhortatus fuerit Apostolus, ne frustra gra- tiam Dei accipiant, suoque exemplo docuerit, quomodo omnia cum in vita, tum in doctrina cavenda sint scandala, meritò dehortatur nunc, facta quadam præparatione per amoris sui mani- festationem, à commerciis cum infidelibus, ut tum Doctoribus suis fidelibus unice adhæreant, tum offendiculum & seductionem effugiant. Cæ- terum non pertinent hæc ad abstinentiam ab ido- lothytis & conviviis infidelium, quorum nulla hic facta mentio, nec à conjugio cum infidelibus, uti ex Hieronymo libr. 1. contra Jovin. cap. 5. & in epi- stola ad Ageruchiam de monogamia, cap. 2. E- stius explicat. Qui sensus restricti nimium sunt, quum generaliter omnia commercia cum infi- delibus, quibus scilicet fiat, ut in partem illo- rum ratione ἀπιστίας declinent, prohibeat Apo- stolus. Verbum ἑτεροζυγοῦντες, jugi imparita- tem & inclinationem in alteram partem infert, notante Theophylacto, qui ita reddit συνεχείας rationem: Illud sanc vestram erga me patefaciet charitatem, si nullum vobis cum infidelibus erit commercium, nec ad illorum partes declinaveri- tis. Qui Christi jugo sese subdidere, fi cum in- fidelibus eodem impietatis jugo copulentur ἑτε- ροζυγεῖν vel jugum à Christi fide alienum ducere dicuntur. Ideo Cornelius exponit: Nolite ju- gum ducere, participationem & commercium habe- re cum infidelibus in iis, quæ ad religionem pertinent, aut ita arctè & familiariter, ut vos sensim inclinemi- ni in eorum infidelitatem, quasi dicat: Separate vos ab infidelium cætibus, templis, sacrificiis, conviviis, conjugiis, omniq; eorum commercio vel per se impio aut injusto, vel periculoso aut scandaloso, quem sen- sum etiam Chrysostomus, & Ambrosius esse notat. Per ἀπίςες Anshelmus Pseudo-Apostolos Judai- zantes intelligit, quos comprehendi hac voce nul- lum nobis est dubium; sed Apostolus, quorumvis infidelium, sive gentiles sint & extra Ecclesiam, sive hæretici in Ecclesia, veræ fidei expertes, quorum commercia, imprimis si ab iis seductionis pericu- lum metuendum sit, vitanda sint, aut certe ea ra- tione declinanda, ut nullatenus in jugum alienum inclinemus vel involvamur. Nam ἄπιστοι & genti- les dicuntur alieni ab Ecclesia, & veri Dei notitia, 1. Cor. VI. 6. c. VII. 12. 13. 14. 15. c. X. 17. XIV. 22. 23. 24. ut & infideles in cætu Ecclesiæ, etsi non desti- tuti verbo Dei, & notitia veri Dei, Matth. XVII. 17. Marci IX. 19. Luc. IX. 41. Joh. XX. 27. quemadmo- dum & Abstractum ἀπισία de eorum increduli- tate, qui sunt in Ecclesia, etsi non sint de Ecclesia, occurrit Matth. XIII. 38. cap. XVII. 20. Marci VI. 6. Rom. III. 3. B. Hunnium si audias, duo sunt, quæ sub alieni jugi nomine caveri jubet Apostolus : Primo idolomania, superstitiones, errores, ac tenebræ infidelium, secundo opera, quæ hinc emergunt, te- nebrarum impia & infrugifera. Non enim tantum infidelium ἀπισίαν, sed etiam ἀνομίαν, & omne illud, quo Beliali seu Diabolo junguntur, quæque tenebrarum commercium important, vitari vult: ut è subjuncta declaratione vel potius confirma- tione luculentum est. Ex hac autem Apostolica dehortatione judicium fieri potest, quid de eorum studio habendum sit, qui diversas religiones com- miscere, vel syncretismum inter diversæ religionis homines conciliare annituntur. Quid enim aliud illi agunt, quàm ut jugum ducatur cum infidelibus. Sane inter populos Deo & Ecclesiæ exosòs refe- runtur Samaritani primo loco Sir. L. Siquidem cultum Dei verum & superstitiones simul Ethni- cas fovebant, 2. Reg. XVII. Vide, quæ pluribus scri- ptis contra Syncretistas ex professo tractavimus, è quibus facile primas obtinere Grotium, tum ex iis, quæ contra Cassandrum disputavit, tum ex his- ce ejus annotatis Biblicis manifestum est. Apo- stolus certè ideo tam multa ἰσοδυναμῦντα accu- mulat, ut omne in Ecclesiasticis & causâ fidei com- mercium cum diversis religionis hominibus à fide Christi alienis excludat, omnem ἑτεροζυγίαν, o- mnem μετοχὴν, omnem κοινωνίαν, omnem συμφώ- νησιν, omnem μερίδα, omnem denique συγκατάθε- σιν. Primò ἑτεροζυγίαν, h. e. inclinationem ad aliam religionem, copulationem cum alieno jugo alte- rius religionis. Deinde etiam omnem μετοχὴν par- ticipationem vel commixtionem. Insuper omnem quoque κοινωνίαν vel communionem quamcunque non quidem in externis temporalibus & civilibus, sed in causis religionis. Porrò & συμφώνησιν, conso- nantiam videlicet. ut à vocum conformitate, quo- ad fieri potest, abstineamus. Adhæc omnem με- ρίδα, ut nec partialem quidem conjunctionem inea- mus. Deniq; omnem συγκατάθεσιν, quicquid con- sensum quendam inferre videtur, ne ullatenus eo- rum sententiis annuamus, sive formaliter, sive in- terpretativè; sive directè, sive indirectè, quum veri- tati nihil omnino debeat commercii esse cum fal- sitate. Nec tantum in abstracto persistit Apostolus, declinandam esse ἀνομίαν, non communicandum esse tenebris aut idolis, sed in concreto vetat copu- lari cum ἀπίστοις. Denique tam impossibilem esse moraliter illam conjunctionem fidelium cum infi- delibus docet, quàm impossibilis est participatio justitiæ cum iniquitate vel injustitia, lucis & tene- brarum, Christi & Belial, vel Diaboli. Sensus ar- gumenti, interprete B. Hunnio, hic est: Est non modo turpe, si quis conetur saltem justitiam copulare cum injustitia &c. sed etiam prorsus ἀδύνατον. Tan- tum enim est inter justitiam & injustitiam, tanta lucis & tenebrarum repugnantia, tanta dissensio in- ter Christum & Belial seu Diabolum, tanta, tamque longe remota fidelium ab infidelibus disjunctio, tan- demq́; irreconciliabile divortium inter Dei templum & idola, ut nullis unquam modis componi aut conso- ciari queant: Sed alterum subinde convellat ac tollat alterum: Infideles ergo non modo in tenebris ver- sari, sed etiam Beliali vel Diabolo adhærere, nec templum Dei esse, sed idolis sese mancipasse innuit Theophylactus: Cum vellet omnino Apostolus, in- quit, ut Corinthii ab infidelium desciscerent contu- bernio, haud sane dixit, quæ potest esse conformitas eorum, qui in luce sint, cum his, qui in tenebris de- gant, vel Christi sectatoribus, cum his, qui dæmonum partes sectantur, sed res ipsas pro personis induxit, lucem scilicet & tenebras, & quod amplius erat, Christum ad Belial: Belial vero apostatam dicit & desertorem. Porro ex Christi & Belial appellatione atrociorem reddit orationem. Et porrò: Sunt qui- dem infideles idolorum templum, vel idola potius, vos autem ædes Dei. Nec qualem illis fabulis suis confin- gunt, sed viventis. Qui igitur vobis erit cum istis consensus? Hoc est, similitudo & conventio. Anti- thesis satis luculenta est, quasi dicat, ut verbis B. Hunnii eam exprimamus: Vos Corinthii justificati estis per fidem, simulq́; servi facti justitiæ inchoatæ: Ethnici è converso sunt, & imputatæ per fidem, & per novam obedientiam inchoatæ justitiæ penitus ex- pertes: Vos filii lucis estis, salvifica nimirum Dei & Christi notitia illuminati: illi sunt tenebrarum filii. Vos pro capite ac principe agnoscitis Christum; illis Belial, id est, Satanas princeps & caput est: Vos fide- les estis, quippe salvifica in Christum fide præditi: Illi sunt ἄπιστοι, à fide Christiana prorsus alieni; Vos de- nique templum Dei estis, ob inhabitantem in vobis Spiritum ipsius: illi vicissim idolis & simulacris serviunt.

Δικαιοσύνη hic non est cultus Dei ex ipsius DEI præscripto; sed quod Paulus δικαιοσύνην vocare consuevit, imprimis uti cap. præcedente v. ult. eam indigitavit, & prout c. III. 9. διακονίαν τῆς δικαιοσύ- νης dixit: Nec ἀνομία tàm universim religionem notat sine lege divina, & contra eam, quàm specia- tim, vi oppositionis & propriæ vocis significatio- nis transgressionem, seu peccatum, 1. Joh. III. 4. Qui enim expertes sunt veræ justitiæ, sub peccato sunt, quemadmodum Rom. III. 23. de omnibus extrà gratiam & ante justificationem dicitur, quod pec- catores sint, & destituantur gloria Dei. Per tenebras luci verbi divini, ad quod non pertinet sola Evan- gelii; sed etiam legis doctrina, oppositas, non tan- tum gentium fabulæ denotantur; sed etiam quævis commenta verbo Dei adversa, & ab eo aliena, quia in religionis causa non tantum non admittenda, quæ contra Dei verbum statuuntur; sed nec quæ extra Dei verbum Deut. IV. 2. XII. 32. Gal. I. 8. 9. Per τὸν βελιὰλ, quia opponitur τῷ Χριστῷ rectius Diabolus, maximè exlex vel παράνομος, intel- ligitur, quàm homo, qui suis tantum cupiditatibus obsequitur, non Deo. Ita Hieronymus 1. Reg. XXII. filios Belial interpretatur filios Diaboli. Tem- plo Dei opponitur idolum. Quidam pro idolis le- gunt idoliis, annuente versione Syriacâ, quæ ha- bet in singulari templo Dæmoniorum, unde suspi- catur in Græcis quibusdam Codicibus olim pro εἰδώλων scriptum fuisse εἰδωλείων. Sed Græca le- ctio elio optimè sibi constat. Non convenire nempe templo Dei, quod sunt fideles, idola seu falsorum Deorum cultum, quum ita desinat esse templum Dei, & evadat idolorum templum; Opposita sunt templum Dei & templum idolorum, nullusque concentus est cultus idolorum cum cultu veri Dei, nullum commercium.

## 6:16
Verse 16. ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς Θεῦ ἐστε ζῶντος [For you are the temple of the living God].) A temple is where God dwells. God dwells in the pious through the Holy Spirit. Therefore they are the temple of God. The same sense is in 1 Cor. III. 17 and VI. 19. Nor did he add ζῶντος [living] in vain, because the gods of the Gentiles were dead men. See Matt. XXVI. 63, Luke VI. 69, Acts XIV. 15, 1 Thess. I. 9, 1 Tim. III. 15, VI. 17.

Καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ὅτι ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς, καὶ περιπατήσω [As God said, that I will dwell in them, and walk]) This is a mystical application of the passage in Leviticus XXVI, 11 and 12. Where in the Greek: Θήσω τὴν σκηνήν με ἐν ὑμῖν [I will set my tabernacle among you]. Then with certain words interposed καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω ἐν ὑμῖν [and I will walk among you]. Paul cited this passage, as also others, with some liberty: and so he omits things placed in the middle, and changes the person, while preserving the sense. And משכני [my tabernacle], which the LXX correctly translates θήσω σκηνὴν [I will set a tabernacle], he translates ἐνοικήσω [I will dwell], just as the Greeks in Is. XXXIII. 18 and elsewhere do by οἰκεῖν [to dwell] or κατοικεῖν [to inhabit]. Compare Ezek. XXXVII, verse 27, Rom. VIII, verse 11, 2 Tim. I, verse 14.

Not only is there a mystical application here, but the sense of the words of Moses is literal. God dwells in us as in His temple, but He walks in the midst of us as His Church and His people.

Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῶν Θεὸς καὶ ἔσονταί μοι λαὸς [And I will be their God and they shall be my people]) These words are also from the following in Leviticus, where the Greeks have: καὶ ἔσομαι ὑμῶν Θεὸς, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔσεσθέ μοι λαὸς [and I will be your God, and you shall be my people], which words apply much more to Christians than to the ancient Israelites.

Why do these things apply more to Christians than to the ancient Israelites, which were first said to the ancient Israelites? ὑμῖν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία καὶ τοῖς τέκνοις ὑμῶν [For the promise is to you and to your children], says St. Peter to the same, Acts II. 39, then finally adding, καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς εἰς μακράν [and to all who are afar off]. The promises were of the Israelites, Rom. IX. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς Θεῦ ἐστε ζῶντος.) Templum est, ubi Deus habitat. In piis habitat Deus per Spiritum Sanctum. Sunt igitur templum Dei. Idem sensus 1. Cor. III. 17. & VI. 19. Nec frustra addidit ζῶντος, quia Dii gentium erant homines mortui. Vide Matth. XXVI. 63. Luc. VI. 69. Act. XIV. 15. 1. Thessal. I. 9. 1. Tim. III. 15. VI. 17.

Καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ὅτι ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς, καὶ περιπατήσω) Est applicatio mystica loci Levit. XXVI, 11. & 12. Ubi in Graeco: Θήσω τὴν σκηνήν με ἐν ὑμῖν. Deinde verbis quibusdam interpositis καὶ ἐμπεριπατήσω ἐν ὑμῖν. Citavit hunc locum, ut & alios, cum libertate aliqua Paulus: itaque & in medio posita omittit, & personam mutat, salvo sensu. Et משכני quod LXX. θήσω σκηνὴν, recte vertit ἐνοικήσω, quomodo & Graeci Es. XXXIII. 18. alibi per οἰκεῖν aut κατοικεῖν. Conf. Ezech. XXXVII. vers. 27. Rom. VIII, vers. 11. 2. Tim. I. vers. 14.

Non hic mystica tantum applicatio, sed sensus verborum Mosis literalis est. Inhabitat in nobis Deus tanquam in templo suo, ambulat autem in medio nostri ceu Ecclesiae, & populi sui.

Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῶν Θεὸς καὶ ἔσονταί μοι λαὸς) Sunt haec quoque verba ex sequentibus in Levitico, ubi Graeci: καὶ ἔσομαι ὑμῶν Θεὸς, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔσεσθέ μοι λαὸς, quae verba Christianis multo magis, quam veteribus Israëlitis competunt.

Cur magis Christianis, quam Veteribus Israëlitis haec conveniant, quae primo Veteribus Israëlitis dicta sunt? ὑμῖν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία καὶ τοῖς τέκνοις ὑμῶν, ait S. Petrus iisdem, Act. II. 39. tum demum subjiciens, καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς εἰς μακράν. Israëlitarum erant αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι, Rom. IX. 4.

## 6:17
Verse 17. Διὸ ἐξέλθετε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀφορίσθητε λέγει κύριος [Wherefore come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord]) What Isaiah had said about the Babylonians being deserted, LII. v. 11, he adapts with equal right to other idolaters. In the Greek of Isaiah it is: ἐξέλθετε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῆς, ἀφορίσθητε [come out from among her, be separate].

And touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you) In the aforementioned place of Isaiah, before those things which we have had, it preceded: touch not the unclean thing. Furthermore, with some things interposed, it follows: the God of Israel gathering you together. In the Hebrew, מאספכם. The verb אסף is for the most part translated as to gather together and to gather. But also to receive, as in Psalm 27:10, which is the same as to receive into favor. See Romans 14:3, 15:7, Philemon 12, 17. The Hebrews also feel that idolaters are signified by unclean animals and unclean things. See what we have said at Acts 10.

We have refuted the gloss concerning the abandoning of the Babylonians at the passage of Isaiah. Nor are we commanded to withdraw our bodies from external association; but it is taught that there ought to be no communion of Christians with unbelievers in religion and worship, and in pursuits and works that conflict with the profession of the Gospel. And that is hinted at when, in the cited Prophetic saying, it is added: Touch not the unclean thing, by which the Lord defines that withdrawal, and restricts it to those things which are unclean and contrary to His word, easily permitting external association in the remaining things which are not unclean in themselves, nor opposed to the discourse of piety, as the blessed Hunnius rightly says. We now add the commentary of Theophylact: For He did not say, do not do things that are absurd, but do not touch them. Moreover, there is a twofold kind of uncleanness, namely, bodily and spiritual. Spiritual indeed, such as impure and sordid thoughts, and to gaze with lascivious eyes, or to exercise hatreds and weave deceits, and things of that sort. But bodily, such as incest and adultery, and whatever else remains of wicked crime. He wishes, therefore, that the Corinthians preserve purity of both mind and body. Wherefore He says, come out from the midst of the unbelievers, and be separate, that is, now turn away from them and become purer. For I am going to receive with a willing mind you who have been made such. For when anyone is freed from evil actions, he is joined to GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Διὸ ἐξέλθετε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀφορίσθητε λέγει κύριος) Quod de Babyloniis deserendis dixerat Esaias, LII. v. 11. id pari jure aptat ad idololatras alios. In Graeco Esaiae est: ἐξέλθετε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῆς, ἀφορίσθητε.

Καὶ ἀκαθάρτου μὴ ἅπτεσθε, κἀγὼ, εἰσδέξομαι ὑμᾶς) In Esaiae dicto loco ante ea, quae habuimus, praeceffit: ἀκαθάρτου μὴ ἅψησθε. Sequitur porrò quibusdam interjectis: ὁ ἐπισυνάγων ὑμᾶς Θεὸς ἰσραήλ. In Hebraeo מאספכם. Verbum אסף plerumque vertitur ἐπισυνάγειν & συνάγειν. Sed & προσλαμβάνειν, ut Psalm. XXVI. 9. quod idem est cum εἰσδέχεσθαι. Vide Rom. XIV. 3. XV. 7. Philem. 12. 17. Per animalia immunda & res immundas significari idololatras sentiunt & Hebraei. Vide, quae diximus ad Act. X.

Glossam de Babyloniis deserendis ad locum Esaie profligavimus. Nec jubemur corporibus ab externa conversatione secedere; sed docetur religionis & cultus, & studiorum atque operum cum Evangelii professione pugnantium, nullam esse debere Christianorum communionem cum incredulis. Idque subindicatur, cum in allegato dicto Prophetico subditur: Immundum ne tetigeritis, quo seceffionem illam determinat Dominus, ac restringit ad ea, quae immunda sunt & verbo ejus contraria, in reliquis, quae per se immunda non sunt, nec sermoni pietatis adversantur, externam conversationem facilè permittens, ut rectè B. Hunnius. Theophylacti jam addimus commentarium: Neque enim dixit haudquaquam quae absurda sunt, facite, sed ne attigeritis. Est autem duplex immunditiae genus, corporeum scilicet & spiritale. Spiritale quidem, ut impuri & sordidi cogitatus, & oculis lascivientibus intueri, vel odia exercere & dolos nectere, & ejusmodi. Corporeum vero ut incestus & adulterium, & quicquid reliquum est pravi facinoris. Vult itaque Corinthios cum animi tum corporis puritatem servare. Quocirca inquit, exite de medio infidelium, & separamini, hoc est, illos jam declinate & puriores efficiamini. Sum namque vos tales effectos libenti animo suscepturus. Cum enim quis malis actionibus liberatur, DEO conjungitur.

## 6:18
Vers. 18. And I will be to you a Father, and you shall be to me sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty. People commonly think this is taken from the passage in Jer. XXXI. 1. The passage in Jeremiah in the same chapter, verse 9, comes closer. But I think it is taken from some famous hymn among the Hebrews. Παντοκράτωρ corresponds to the Hebrew שרי, or צבאות. For both these words are translated into Greek in this way.

You would more correctly say that verse 1 and verse 9 are referred to together; the former reads thus: 'I will be a God to the race of Israel, and they shall be to me a people.' Verse 33 agrees with this: 'And I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people.' Here, however, he explains what it is to be 'a God' and what it is 'a people,' namely, that it implies the relationship of Father and children: 'For I have become a Father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.' The comparison of other prophetic passages confirms this same sense, Hos. I. 11, Isa. XLVI. 3, so that there is no need to have recourse, with Cajetan, to lost books, or to some hymn famous among the churches, I know not which (Grotius himself undoubtedly did not know it either).

Latin:

Vers. 18. Καὶ ἔσομαι ὑμῖν εἰς πατέρα κὴ ὑμεῖς ἔσεσθέ μοι εἰς ὑιὲς, κὴ θυγατέρας, λέγει κύριος παντοκράτωρ) Vulgo putant defumptum ex loco Jerem. XXXI. 1. Propius accedit lo- cus Jeremiæ eodem capite 9. Sed puto defumptum ex hy- mno aliquo celebri apud Hebræos. Παντοκράτωρ respondet Hebræo שרי, aut צבאות. Nam utraque hæc vox Græce fic vertitur.

Rectius dixeris conjunctim refpici versum 1. & v. 9. ille ita habet ἔσομαι εἰς θεὸν τῷ γένει Ἰσραὴλ, κὴ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μοι εἰς λαόν. Cui confonat v. 33. κὴ ἔσο- μαι αὐτοῖς εἰς Θεὸν, κὴ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μοι εἰς λαόν. Hic vero explicat, quid sit esse εἰς Θεὸν, quid εἰς λαὸν, quod nempe id inferat respectum Patris & filiorũ: Ὅτι ἐγενόμην Ἰσραὴλ εἰς πατέρα, κὴ Ἐφραῒμ πρωτό- τοκός με ἐςίν. Quem sensum pariter aliorum Pro- pheticorum collatio firmat Os. I. 11. Ef. XLVI. 3. ut opus non sit ad libros deperditos cum Cajetano, aut ad hymnum aliquem apud Ecclesias celebrem, nescio quem, (nescivit etiam sine dubio Grotius ipse) recurrere.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle admonishes them to strive for purification and sanctification in view of the divine promises: and declaring his affection toward the Corinthians, he praises their reciprocal love, by which he was uplifted in his calamities, especially since he understood the same abundantly through the arrival of Titus; and he manifests that he is so far from repenting of his former letters, which saddened them, that he was rather gladdened on account of the repentance which the sadness produced, and the zeal that arose from it, and that Titus has actually experienced the truth of the Apostolic boasting concerning them.

There are three parts: I. Exhortatory, presenting an exhortation to the pursuit of holiness, up to verse 1. II. Encomiastic, manifesting mutual charity, up to verse 8. III. Apologetic, excusing the harshness of the former epistle, which turned to their salvation, up to verse 16.

PART I. Exhortatory, regarding the pursuit of holiness.

Vers. 1. Having therefore these promises) That God will always dwell in us. That God will be a Father to us.

Let us cleanse ourselves) וטהרו.

From all defilement of the flesh) Which is opposed to holiness, concerning which see above VI. 6. An evangelical explanation of the laws concerning uncleanness (טמאות).

And of the spirit) The spirit is defiled through evil dogmas and evil acts.

Just as the Apostle had exhorted them to avoid the company of infidels, so now he exhorts them to the pursuit of purification from all defilement and to progress in holiness, so that we may not only withdraw from the impious, but also ourselves strive to cast off whatever impurity remains in us, and to perfect our sanctification more and more. The evangelical explanation of the laws of uncleanness (טמאות) does not concern the purification which is from us by the power of the Holy Spirit, but the purification which was made by Christ through His own blood, Rev. I. 5, chap. V. 9, which was prefigured by the Levitical sacrifices and expiations, Heb. IX. 14, and their chief end was Rom. X. 4, Heb. X. 1, 7. Nevertheless, that the secondary end of the Levitical purifications was the spiritual purification of the faithful, to which the regenerate devote effort in sanctification, having been sprinkled with the blood of Christ 1 Pet. I. 2, and being cleansed through faith in the blood of the Son of God 1 John I. 7, which happens in justification regarding its application

Rom. III. 24. Eph. I. 7. Col. I. 4. just as it was done in the passion of Christ regarding merit and acquisition, Matt. XXVI. 28. By the defilement of the flesh is understood every sin which is completed by carnal pleasure, such as are not only unchastities, carousings, drunkenness; but also injuries, robberies, thefts and the like: but the defilement of the Spirit [is] idolatry, emulations, sects, dissensions, and others, the completion of which consists without the pleasure of the senses; whence the Scholastics made some sins carnal, others spiritual. The former, Cornelius a Lapide says, revolve around a carnal object, and make a man as it were a beast, such as gluttony, lust, drunkenness: the latter revolve around a spiritual object, and make a man as it were a demon, such as anger, pride, envy. But concerning this distinction, Estius rightly warns that it is common to all sins that they defile the Spirit or the mind of man, but that those are called carnal by a peculiar reason which do so through the delight of the flesh and the senses. Theophylact understands by the defilement of the flesh evil actions; but by the defilements of the Spirit or of the mind, impure thoughts.
