It is evident, however, from this exhortation, that the just are not perfectly pure, or immune from every defilement of flesh and blood. For otherwise this exhortation would not be needed. If they were perfectly freed from sins, they would have no need of further purification: Indeed, not even those whom the Papists call perfect, such as they say the Apostles were, are so entirely clean that they no longer need cleansing, as this Estius acknowledges from this passage and Prov. X. 9. For there remain in the regenerate some stains of sins, and of defilements of either flesh or spirit, which original sin, as the fountain of all impurity, pours forth from time to time, so that thoughts, inclinations, and motions are infected, Gen. VI. 5. ch. VIII. 21. Is. VI. 5. ch. LXIV. 6. Job IX. 3. ch. XIV. 1. ch. XVI. 16. Ps. XIX. 13. CXXX. 3. CXLIII. 2. Dan. IX. 18. Rom. VII. 14. seqq. From the Apostolic inference also from the promises of grace to the pursuit of new obedience, it is manifest that the Apostolic doctrine concerning our gratuitous justification and adoption as sons does not undermine the pursuit of piety and holiness; but excites to it, and adds a spur to rendering obedience to God. See Mal. I. 6. Tit. II. 11. 12. 1 Pet. I. 17. seqq. 1 John III. 3.

Ἐπιτελοῦντες ἁγιωσύνην ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ) Fulfilling the holiness of the mind in deed, and that with respect to God.

The word ἐπιτελοῦντες indeed implies perfection, but one which the regenerate pursue here, but do not attain in this life, since this is not the way; but the goal or the fatherland, not of travelers, but of those whom the Scholastics call the comprehenders. Nor do these designate an effect, but a pursuit, that we may strive and contend to perfect holiness: from time to time progressing more and more in holiness 2 Cor. III. 18. Phil. III. 14. Finally, we know that the consequence from a command to the ability does not hold. Many things are commanded, which, however, it is not in our power to do. What? That ἐπιτελοῦντες should perhaps not be rendered as 'perfecting' with the Vulgate, but as 'bringing to an end' with Beza. Furthermore, holiness is joined with purification. For it is not enough to abstain from stains and vices, as Theophylact [says] here, but it is also necessary that some good be performed. By sanctification he understands the same thing, both cleanliness and continence, and finally every integrity of life. But in the fear of GOD he adds that, either because some other [continence] may be done out of industry, to obtain the favor and praise of men, not kept for the fear of God. Or to show us that, fearing GOD, we may show ourselves purer and continent. For even if the concupiscence of the flesh should offer violence, all the fury of lust will soon be dissolved if we fear GOD. But beware, lest with Estius and other Papists you infer from this that the fear of punishment among the faithful contributes to holiness; because the discourse here is not about servile fear, which arises from the fear of punishment, but about filial fear, which redounds from trust toward GOD and the love of God, 1 John IV. 18. That which is rendered ἐν φόβῳ Θεοῦ by Grotius as 'respect for God' can be admitted thus far, if it is understood that we ought to strive for holiness as if in the sight of God, Gen. XVII. 1. But if perfection is considered before God, there is none, even in the most holy, Job XV. 16, Prov. XX. 9. That study of purification and holiness, however, which is attributed to the reborn, by no means implies a natural faculty of preserving oneself in faith and sanctification, as the Papists, Socinians, and Remonstrants falsely opine. For although to remain or progress in sanctification may be in the power of the reborn man, it is not innate, but acquired through regeneration. And therefore the irresistibility of persevering grace is rightly refuted from this statement, as the blessed Hülsemann notes, but the natural faculty of the unregenerate will is ineptly transcribed here, because the discourse here is not about unregenerate subjects, but about the reborn and the faithful.

PART II. Encomiastic of mutual love.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Admonet Apostolus, ut intuitu promissionum di- vinarum purificationi & sanctificationi stu- deant: Suamque erga Corinthios affectio- nem declarans, laudat eorum dilectionem reciprocam, qua se erexit in calamitatibus, maxime cum per Titi adventum eandem af- fatim intellexerit; ac manifestat, quod adeo nec pœniteat literarum priorum, qua ipsos contristarent, ut potius ob pœnitentiã, quam operata est contristatio, & zelum inde or- tum exhilaratus, & quod Titus veritatem gloriationis Apostolicæ de ipsis reapse exper- tus sit.

Partes sunt tres I. παραινετικὴ adhortationem ad sanctitatis studium exhibens ad v. 1. II. Ἐγκωμια- σικὴ mutuam charitatem manifestans ad vers. 8. III. Ἀπολογητικὴ, prioris epistolæ acerbitatem, quæ in salutem ipsorum vertit, excusans ad vers. 16.

PARS I. Paranetica ad studium sanctitatis.

Vers. 1. Ταύτας ὖν ἔχοντες τὰς ἐπαγγελίας) Deum in no- bis semper habitaturum. Deum nobis fore Patrem.

Καθαρίσωμεν ἑαυτὸς) וטהרו.

Ἀπὸ παντὸς μολυσμῦ σαρκὸς) Qui opponitur τῇ ἁγιότη- τι, de qua supra VI. 6. Evangelica explicatio legum de טמאות.

Καὶ πνέυματος) inquinatur Spiritus per mala dogmata & actus malos.

Quemadmodum ad vitandum infidelium com- mercium exhortatus erat Apostolus. Ita nunc ad studium purificationis ab omni inquinamento & profectum sanctitatis hortatur, ut non secedamus modo ab impiis, sed & ipsi studeamus, quicquid in nobis superest impuritatis abdicare, & sanctifica- tionem nostram subinde magis magisque perfice- re. Evangelica explicatio legum טמאות, non con- cernit purificationem, quæ a nobis sit virtute Spiri- tus Sancti, sed purificationem, quæ a Christo facta est per sanguinem ipsius Apoc. I. 5. cap. V. 9. quæ præ- figurata est per Levitica sacrificia & expiationes Ebr. IX. 14. & finis earum fuit præcipuus Rom. X. 4. Ebr. X. 1. 7. Secundarium tamen finem purifi- cationum Leviticarum fuisse spiritualem fidelium purificationem, cui operam navant in sanctifica- tione renati, aspersi sanguine Christi 1. Petr. I. 2. & mundari per fidem Filii DEI sanguine 1. Johan. I. 7. quod in justificatione fit quoad applicationem

Rom. III. 24. Eph. I. 7. Coloff. I. 4. quemadmo- dum in passione Christi factum est quoad meritum & acquisitionem, Matth. XXVI. 28. Per carnis inquinamentum omne peccatum intelligitur, quod carnali voluptate consummatur, uti non tan- tum sunt impudicitiæ, commessationes, ebrieta- tes; sed etiam injuriæ, rapinæ, furta & similia: Spiritus vero inquinamentum idololatriae, æmula- tiones, sectæ, dissensiones, & alia, quorum con- summatio sine sensuum voluptate consistit; unde Scholastici peccata alia carnalia, alia spiritualia fe- cerunt. Illa Cornelius a Lapide dicit versari circa objectum carnale, ac hominem facere quasi be- stiam, uti est gula, libido, ebrietas: hæc versari cir- ca objectum spirituale, & hominem facere quasi dæmonem, ut est ira, superbia, invidia. De qua distinctione verò recte monet Estius, omnibus peccatis id commune esse, quod Spiritum seu mentem hominis coinquinent, sed peculiari ratio- ne carnalia vocari ea, quæ per carnis ac sensuum delectationem id faciunt. Theophylactus per inqui- namentum carnis actiones malas; per inquinamen- ta vero Spiritus vel animi cogitationes impuras intelligit. Patet autem ex hac parænesi, justos non esse perfecte puros, vel ab omni inquinamento car- nis & sanguinis immunes. Alioquin enim ista ex- hortatione opus non foret. Si perfecte forent a peccatis liberati, non opus eis esset ulteriori pu- rificatione: Imo ne tales quidem, quos perfectos vocant Papistæ, quales fuisse Apostolos ajunt, ita prorsus mundos esse, ut amplius mundatione non egeant, ut ex hoc loco & Prov. X. 9. agnoscit hic Estius. Manent enim in renatis sordes peccato- rum aliquæ, & inquinamentorum sive carnis sive spiritus, quas peccatum originis, ceu fons omnis impuritatis subinde effundit, ut inficiantur cogi- tationes, inclinationes, & motus, Gen. VI. 5. cap. VIII. 21. Es. VI. 5. cap. LXIV. 6. Job. IX. 3. cap. XIV. 1. cap. XVI. 16. Psal. XIX. 13. CXXX. 3. CXLIII. 2. Dan. IX. 18. Rom. VII. 14. seqq. Ex illatione etiam Apo- stolica a promissionibus gratiæ ad studium novæ obe- dientiæ, manifestum est doctrinam Apostolicam de gratuita nostri justificatione & in filios ado- ptione non labefactare pietatis & sanctitatis stu- dium; sed ad illud excitare, atque ad obedientiam Deo præstandam calcar addere. Vid. Mal. I. 6. Tit. II. 11. 12. 1. Petr. I. 17. seqq. 1. Joh. III. 3.

Ἐπιτελοῦντες ἁγιωσύνην ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ) Sanctitatem animi implentes opere, idque respectu Dei.

Verbum ἐπιτελοῦντες perfectionem quidem in- fert, sed quam consectantur hic renati, non au- tem in hac vita consequuntur, utpote quæ non via est; sed meta vel patria, non viatorum, sed comprehensorum, quos Scholastici vocant. Neque effectum, sed studium hæc designant, ut annita- mur & contendamus perficere sanctimoniam: subinde magis magisque in sanctitate proficientes 2. Corinth. III. 18. Phil. III. 14. Denique a man- dato ad posse novimus non valere consequentiam. Multa præcipiuntur, quæ tamen ut fiant in no- stra potestate, non est. Quid? quod ἐπιτελοῦντες non tam perficientes reddi debeat cum Vulgata, quam cum Beza ad finem perducentes. Cæterum sanctimonia conjungitur cum purificatione. Nam non sat est, a sordibus abstinere & vitiis, ut hic Theophylactus, quin & boni aliquid peragatur ne- cesse est. Per sanctificationem idem tum mundi- tiem & continentiam, tum omnem denique vitæ in- tegritatem intelligit. In timore vero DEI eò adje- cit, vel quia ex industria sit alia quædam, ad homi- num gratiam & laudem consequendam, non pro ti- more Dei servata continentia. Vel ut nobis ostendat, ut DEUM veriti puriores nos ipsos exhibeamus & continentes. Nam vel si vim inferat carnis con- cupiscentia, dissolvetur mox omnis libidinis furor, si DEUM verebimur. Cave vero, ne cum Estio, aliisque Papistis inde inferas timorem pœnæ apud fideles conducere ad sanctitatem; quia hic non de timore servili, qui ex metu pœnæ oritur; sed filiali, qui ex fiducia erga DEUM & amore Dei redundat, sermo est 1. Johan. IV. 18. Quod ἐν φό- βῳ Θε῵ redditur a Grotio respectu Dei, hactenus admitti potest, si intelligatur, nos sanctitati stu- dere debere, velut in conspectu Dei Genes. XVII. 1. Si autem perfectio respicitur coram Deo, ea nul- la est, etiam in sanctissimis Job. XV. 16. Proverb. XX. 9. Illud vero purificationis, & sanctitatis stu- dium, quod renatis tribuitur, neutiquam infert naturalem conservandi seipsum in fide & sancti- ficatione facultatem, ut Pontificii, Sociniani & Re- monstrantes falso opinantur. Nam, quamvis per- manere vel progredi in sanctificatione, in potesta- te hominis regeniti sit; ea tamen non connata, sed per regenerationem acquisita est. Ideoque irresi- stibilitas perseverantis quidem gratiæ ex hoc dicto recte refutatur, notante B. Hülsemanno, natura- lis autem facultas arbitrii irregeniti inepte huc transcribitur, quia non sermo hic est de subjectis irregenitis, sed de renatis & fidelibus.

PARS II. Encomiastica mutuæ dilectionis.

## 7:2
Ver. 2. χωρήσατε ἡμᾶς) Receive us: namely, into your heart. For the sense is repeated from the previous VI. 3.

Οὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν) We have been a bad example to no one. See 1 Cor. VI. 16. The Syrian here placed the word עלץ, which is to mock someone. Conversely, he signifies that he has dealt with them openly and ingenuously.

Regarding that χωρήσατε, Camerarius: It is either δέξασθε τὰ ῥήματα ἡμῶν. Or εἰς δέξασθε ἡμᾶς εἰς τὰς ψυχάς. A little preface to his small commendation. I beseech you, accept what I shall say. Or embrace us. The Apostle protests his love, lest, being occupied by the Pseudo-Apostles, they might doubt it in any way, or lest from the bitterness of the punishment against the incestuous man, any doubt should arise or remain for anyone concerning the Apostle's fatherly love. And therefore that ἠδικήσαμεν pertains not to a bad example or scandal, but to iniquity or a more iniquitous process. For he testifies that he has been injurious to no one against right and equity: But whatever he did, he did out of sincere love. And therefore οὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν, he says, we have done injury to no one, which the Vulgate rendered: We have harmed no one, οὐδένα ἐφθείραμεν, we have corrupted no one, which can be referred to an example, with the blessed Hunnius: We have made no one among you worse by perverse doctrine or unpraiseworthy examples; rather, by sound doctrine and holy conversion, as much as was in us, we have strenuously striven to make everyone better. Οὐδένα ἐπλεονεκτήσαμεν, we have defrauded no one. Beza: we have made no one a source of gain. Πλεονεξία signifies avarice. Paul therefore demonstrates that he has not gaped after anyone's money or goods through avarice, much less transferred them to himself under any pretext whatsoever, as is indeed customary for the Pseudo-Apostles, but rather that he sought his living by working with his hands, so that he would not be troublesome or burdensome to any of the Corinthians, as the blessed Hunnius says. So also Theophylact: Furthermore, to expose the fraudulent manners of certain Apostles, he thus infers: We have harmed no one, that is, we have offended no one by words or deeds: We have corrupted no one, that is, we have seduced no one, or infected anyone's mind with impious dogmas: We have circumvented no one, that is, we have extorted nothing from anyone by the desire of avarice, or subtracted money under the pretext of preaching. In which last point, not the first, the Syrian employed the word עלב, which Tremellius rendered 'we have occupied,' and Junius notes it properly signifies, by the impulse of avarice, to draw to oneself what belongs to another.

Latin:

Vers. 2. χωρήσατε ἡμᾶς) Recipite nos: scilicet in cor ve- strum. Est enim sensus repetitus ex superiore VI. 3.

Οὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν) Nemini fuimus malo exemplo. Vide 1. Cor. VI. 16. Syrus hic posuit verbum עלץ quod est illudere alicui. Ex contrario significat se aperte & ingenue cum eis egisse.

Ad illud χωρήσατε Camerarius: Vel est, δέ- ξασθε τὰ ῥήματα ἡμῶν. Vel εἰς δέξασθε ἡμᾶς εἰς τὰς ψυχάς. Proœmiolum commendatiunculæ sui. Quæ- so accipite, quod dicam. Vel complectimini nos. De amore suo autem protestatur Apostolus, ne a Pseudo-Apostolis occupati de eodem ullatenus ambigant, neve ex acerbitate pœnæ adversus in- cestuosum dubium ulli de dilectione Apostoli paterna suboriatur vel relinquatur. Ideoque illud ἠδικήσαμεν non ad exemplum malum, vel scanda- lum, sed ad iniquitatem vel processum iniquiorem pertinet. Testatur enim sese nulli injurium fuisse contra fas & æquum: Sed quicquid egit, ex a- more sincero egisse. Ideoque ὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν, inquit, nemini fecimus injuriam, quod Vulgata reddidit: Neminem læsimus, ἐδένα ἐφθείραμεν, ne- minem corrupimus, quod ad exemplum referri potest, cum B. Hunneo: Neminem inter vos vel doctrina perversa vel illaudatis exemplis fecimus deteriorem quin potius doctrina sana, & sancta con- versione, quantum in nobis erat, enixe studui- mus cunctos reddere meliores. Οὐδένα ἐπλεονε- κτήσαμεν, neminem defraudavimus. Beza: nemi- nem quæstui habuimus. Πλεονεξία avaritiam signi- ficat. Demonstrat ergo Paulus, se nullius vel pecu- niis vel bonis inhiaffe per avaritiam, multo minus illa, quocunque tandem prætextu ad se traduxisse, sicut quidem solenne sit Pseudo-Apostolis, quin po- tius laborando manibus quæsivisse victum, ne cui- quam Corinthiorum esset molestus aut onerosus, ut B. Hunnius. Ita & Theophylactus: Porro, ut frau- dulentos patefaciat Apostolorum quorundam mo- res, sic infert: Neminem læsimus, hoc est, nemi- nem vel verbis vel factis offendimus: Neminem corrupimus, hoc est seduximus, vel impiis dogma- tibus nulli mentem infecimus : Neminem circum- venimus, id est, nihil a quoquam avaritiæ cupidi- tate extorsimus, vel pecunias sub prædicationis ob- tentu subtraximus. In quo postremo, non pri- mo adhibuit Syrus verbum עלב, quod Tremellius reddidit occupavimus, & Junius notat proprie si- gnificare, avaritiæ impulsu, quæ sunt alterius ad se pertrahere.

## 7:3
Ver. 3. Οὐ πρὸς κατάκρισιν λέγω) He wishes to correct them, not to traduce them, which is what κατακρίνειν means here. The antecedent for the consequent.

Προείρηκα γὰρ, ὅτι ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν ἐστὲ) Namely, above VI. 12. You have a great place there.

Εἰς τὸ συναποθανεῖν καὶ συζῆν) Thus Horace: I would love to live with you, I would gladly die with you. And elsewhere: We shall go, we shall go, however you lead the way, prepared to tread the final journey.

An excellent χαρακτὴρ of the good shepherd, John X. 11.

This connection is more appropriate than the one B. Hunnius provides here: The Apostle anticipates a silent objection of the Corinthians, who might have thought that such a diligent clearing of the Apostle pertained conversely to an oblique reproach and accusation of them, as if they themselves were either accusing Paul and his associates of those vices, or as if they themselves had performed their duty toward their own preachers less than they should have. Paul therefore responds by denial, that his speech does not look to this end, of which thing he gives them full assurance by the testimony of his own most inclined spirit toward them, adding: Since I have already said to you before (namely, in the preceding sixth chapter) that you are in our hearts to die together and to live together, that is, we love you so intimately that we both gladly live with you, and if the matter should so require, we would not hesitate even to die with you, so far is it from us that we write or say anything to burden you with false suspicions. Theophylact therefore rightly says here: I have by no means said these things for the sake of condemning you. Whence is that clear, someone will say? Namely, from charity itself, because you are in our hearts. And since we can pursue someone with benevolence, yet without the will to undergo dangers, he said 'to die together.' And since many, because of envy, do not rejoice at the prosperity of their friends, he added 'to live together,' just as if he were saying in summary: I will neither desert you in dangers, nor will I envy your favorable and prosperous affairs, but rather I am to lead my life together with you.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Οὐ πρὸς κατάκρισιν λέγω) Corrigere eos vult, non traducere, quod hic est κατακρίνειν. Antecedens pro Consequente.

Προείρηκα γὰρ, ὅτι ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν ἐστὲ) Nempe su- pra VI. 12. magnum ibi habetis locum.

Εἰς τὸ συναποθανεῖν καὶ συζῆν) Sic Horatius : Tecum vivere amem, tecum obeam libens Et alibi: - - - Ibimus, ibimus Utcunque præcedes, supremum Carpere iter parati.

Egregius χαρακτὴρ boni pastoris Joh. X. 11.

Convenientior hic est συνέχεια, quam hic tradit B. Hunnius: Prævertit Apostolus tacitam objectionem Corinthiorum, qui cogitare poterant, tam diligentem Apostoli purgationem pertinere e converso ad obliquam illorum reprehensionem & accusationem, quasi vel ipsi Paulum & socios insi- mulent illorum vitiorum, vel officium suum erga Concionatores suos minus ipsi fecerint. Respon- det ergo Paulus per inficiationem, non huc spectare sermonem suum, cujus rei plenam illis fidem facit testificatione sui in ipsos animi propensissimi, ad- dens : Siquidem jam ante dixi vobis (nimirum præcedente sexto capite) quod in cordibus nostris estis ad commoriendum & convivendum, hoc est,ita vos intime diligimus, ut & libenter vivamus vobis- cum, & si res ita ferat, etiam commori vobis non dubitemus, tantum abest, ut quicquam scribamus aut dicamus ad prægravandos vos falsis suspicion- bus. Recte ergo hic Theophylactus: Nequaquam hæc condemnandi vos gratia dixerim. Unde id liquet, dicet aliquis? Nimirum ex charitate ipsa, quia in cordibus nostris estis. Et quoniam possumus quem- piam prosequi benevolentia, nulla tamen subeun- di discrimina voluntate, ad commoriendum dixit. Cumque plerique ob invidiam nil amicorum pro- speritati congaudent, ad convivendum adjunxit, perinde ac si summatim inquiat: Neque in pericu- lis deserturus vos sum, nec secundis vestris & prospe- ris rebus invidebo, sed vobiscum potius una sum vi- tam ducturus.

## 7:4
Vers. 4. Πολλή μοι παῤῥησία πρὸς ὑμᾶς) I have great right to speak freely among you. There is also a metonymy here.

Πολλή μοι καύχησις ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) I rejoice greatly on your account, when I understand that you persevere and progress in piety.

There is no need for a metonymy, because he is not speaking of a right, but of a work, as is evident from a comparison with the preceding chapter, verse 11: Namely, that he uses this freedom of speech (παῤῥησίᾳ) on purpose, but with a sincere mind; since he cherishes and embraces the same in the bowels of his heart: Therefore he also boasts vehemently about them, when they conduct themselves as it befits them, which is entirely the scope of his free exhortation and freedom of speech (παῤῥησίας). These things also refer back to the preceding, as was rightly observed by Theophylact: I have by no means said these things because I have passed judgment and condemned you; but because I have great confidence among you, and I trust you very much, being desirous to lead you to duty and virtue. But that my mind is far from your condemnation, it is certainly permitted to discern from these things, which I am accustomed to boast of before others on your behalf, that is, for your progress, and to count as glory. Here καύχησις is not joy; but boasting. For the Apostle uses here a rhetorical increment, by which he sets forth his affections toward them, and as it were pours them out. For first he explains παρ́ρησίαν as confidence. For the παρ́ρησία of speech arose from a singular confidence toward them, by which he certainly promises himself every best thing from the Corinthians. Then καύχησιν or boasting, because nothing is earlier, nothing more ancient to him than to boast of them from the truth: Thirdly παράκλησιν or consolation, because he receives great solace in his tribulations from their progress in true piety, and is as it were filled by it. Fourthly χαρὰν or joy, and that he receives it superabundant from thence in all his θλίψει or affliction.

I am filled with consolation, I superabound with joy in all our affliction.) Ἐπὶ here signifies after. Thus ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβεβηκόσι after the event. Among Demosthenes: Ἐπὶ τούτοις πολλὰ ἕτερα διεξῆει. After these he was recounting many other things. He says here generally, what he will now explain more specifically: First saying what the adversities were: then, what that joy and solace was.

But why should the more common meaning of the word ἐπὶ not be retained? For the Apostle obtained joy from the progress of the Corinthians in holiness not only after afflictions, which always remained with the Apostle and never had an end; but in afflictions, and over afflictions. Although we do not deny that that joy is primarily regarded which arose for him through the arrival and report of Titus.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Πολλή μοι παῤῥησία πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Magnum mihi jus libere apud vos loquendi. Est & hic μετωνυμία.

Πολλή μοι καύχησις ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) Multum gaudeo vestri causa, ubi vos in pietate perseverare ac proficere intelligo.

Non opus est Metonymia, quia non de jure loquitur, sed de opere, ut e collatione cap. præced. vers. 11. constat: Nimirum se uti de industria hac loquendi παῤῥησίᾳ, sed animo sincero; quum eosdem in visceribus cordis sui foveat, atque complectatur: Ideo de ipsis etiam vehementer glorietur, cum tales se gerunt, quales ipsos de- cet, qui omnino scopus sit liberæ suæ exhorta- tionis & dicendi παῤῥησίας. Referunt etiam hæc sefe ad superiora, ut recte Theophylacto observa- tum: Haudquaquam hæc dixi, quia in vos sen- tentiam tulerim & condemnarim; sed quia mihi multa fiducia apud vos est, & vobis confido pluri- mum cupidus ad officium & virtutem traducere. Quod autem mihi alienus sit a vestri condemnatio- ne jam animus, licet sane ex his conspicari, quæ pro vobis, hoc est, pro vestro profectu jactare apud alios soleo & gloriæ ducere. Non hic καύχησις est gau- dium; sed gloriatio. Utitur enim Apostolus hic kincremento Rhetorico, quo suos in illos expo- nit, ac velut effundit affectus. Primo enim expo- nit παρ́ρησίαν fiduciam. Nam dicendi παρ́ρησία orta est ex singulari erga illos fiducia, qua optima quæque sibi de Corinthiis sibi certo polliceatur. Deinde καύχησιν vel gloriationem, quod nihil prius, nihil antiquius sit ipsi, quam de ipsis ex ve- ro gloriari: Tertio παράκλησιν consolationem, quod ab ipsorum profectibus in vera pietate ma- gnum accipiat in tribulationibus suis solatium, eo- que veluti impleatur. Quarto χαρὰν quod gaudi- um, idque superabundans inde percipiat in omni sua θλίψει vel afflictione.

Πεπλήρωμαι τῇ παρακλήσει, ὑπερπερισσεύομαι τῇ χαρᾷ ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει ἡμῶν.) Ἐπὶ hic significat post. Sic ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβεβηκόσι post eventum. Apud Demosthenem: Ἐπὶ τούτοις πολλὰ ἕτερα διεξῆει. Post hæc multa commemorabat alia. Dicit hic generaliter, quod jam explicabit specialius: Pri- mum dicens, quæ fuerint adversa: deinde, quod illud gau- dium & solatium.

Cur vero non retineatur usitatior vocis ἐπὶ si- gnificatio? Non enim tantum post afflictiones, quæ semper penes Apostolum durabant, nunquam finem habebant; sed in afflictionibus, & super affli- ctionibus gaudium nanciscebatur Apostolus ex Corinthiorum in sanctitate profectu. Etsi non diffiteamur, illud imprimis respici gaudium, quod ipsi per adventum, & nuncium Titi subortum.

## 7:5
Ver. 5. For indeed when we had come into Macedonia) Acts XX. 3. above I. 16.

Our flesh had no rest) You have the same kind of speaking above III. 13. See also Acts XXIV. 24. and below VIII, 13. We could scarcely breathe from evils, so many were the enemies, so many the plotters.

But in everything being afflicted) Again we are to understand 'we were', in the Hebrew manner, as above V. 6. and often elsewhere. Ἐν παντὶ, as above VI. 4.

Fightings without) From the Gentiles and Jews. For these are the 'without', I Cor. V. 12.

Fears within) From false brothers, XI. 26. There is an allusion to the place in Deuteronomy XXXII. 25. The sword shall destroy them from without, and terror from the chambers.

Thus Theophylact. To others, however, it is more correct that 'without' is externally from any enemies whatsoever, even false brothers. 'Within' is internally from the temptations of the heart. It was not enough to be afflicted externally, unless at the same time the Devil attacked us within with his fiery darts, driving us with various temptations, and among these with that anxious and sad solicitude, whether you were still stable in the faith, or whether the fruit of our labor had been intercepted by the craft of Satan and his instruments, as B. Hunnius not unaptly says here. Thus the place in Deut. XXXII. fits better.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ γὰρ ἐλθόντων ἡμῶν εἰς Μακεδονίαν) Actor. XX. 3. supra I. 16.

Οὐδεμίαν ἔσχηκεν ἄνεσιν ἡ σὰρξ ἡμῶν) Idem loquendi genus habes supra III. 13. Vide & Actor. XXIV. 24. & infra VIII, 13. Vix respirare nobis a malis licuit, tot erant hostes, tot insidiatores.

Ἀλλ̓ ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι) Rursum subauditur fuimus, more Hebræo, ut supra V. 6. & alibi sæpe. Ἐν παντὶ, ut su- pra VI. 4.

Ἔξωθεν μάχαι) A gentibus & Judæis. Hi enim sunt οἱ ἔξω, I. Cor. V. 12.

Ἔσωθεν φόβοι) A falsis fratribus, XI. 26. Est allusio ad locum Deuteron. XXXII. 25. Ἔσωθεν ἀτεκνώσει αὐτὺς μά- χαιρα κὲ ἐκ τῶν ταμείων φόβος.

Ita Theophylactus. Aliis tamen rectius τὸ ἔξω- θεν est forinsecus a quibusvis hostibus, etiam falsis fratribus. Τὸ ἔσωθεν intrinsecus a tentationibus cor- dis. Non satis erat forinsecus affligi, ni simul intus suis nos impeteret ignitis telis Diabolus, tentationi- bus variis nos agens, atque inter has anxia illa & tristi solicitudine, num adhuc essetis in fide stabiles, an vero laboris nostri fructus astu Satanæ & orga- norum ejus esset interversus, ut hic non inconcinne B. Hunnius. Ita locus Deut. XXXII. magis congruit.

## 7:6
Ver. 6. But he who comforts the lowly) He who comforts the afflicted. The place of Isaiah LXI. 1. 3 is regarded. See also Luke I. 52.

God comforted us in the arrival of Titus) See above I. 13. He shows how much he values Titus, so that he may the more extol the services which the Corinthians had rendered to Titus.

And not only in his arrival, but also in the consolation with which he was comforted concerning you) He rejoices not so much for the sake of Titus, as for theirs, because in Titus they had shown how much they valued Paul and the Gospel preached by Paul. He says, however, 'in the consolation', understanding the very narration of the consolation by metaleipsis, such as we have observed elsewhere.

Nor is there need here for such a Metalepsis. For a twofold means of consolation in afflictions is brought forward, namely the arrival of Titus, by whose presence as a colleague he was not a little refreshed: And the report brought by the same, concerning the safe and flourishing state of the Corinthian Church; inasmuch as he was made a partaker also by Titus of that consolation received from them. He then explains the manner, that this was done through the commemoration of Titus.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ἀλλ̓ ὁ παρακαλῶν τὺς ταπεινὺς) Is qui con- solatur afflictos. Respicitur locus Esaiæ LXI. 1. 3. Vide & Luc. I. 52.

Παρεκάλεσεν ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τῦ Τίτυ) Vide supra I. 13. Ostendit quanti Titum faciat, ut eo magis at- tollat officia quæ Corinthii Tito præstiterant.

Οὐ μόνον δ᾽ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτῦ, ἀλλὰ κὲ ἐν τῇ παρα- κλήσει, ᾗ παρεκλήθη ἐφ᾽ ὑμῖν) Gaudet non tam Titi causa, quam ipsorum, quod in Tito ostendissent, quanti Paulum & Evangelium a Paulo prædicatum facerent. Dicit autem ἐν τῇ παρακλήσει, intelligens ipsam narrationem τῆς παρα- κλήσεως per μετάληψιν, qualem & alibi observavimus.

Neque hic tali Metalepsi opus est. Geminum enim affertur consolationis in afflictionibus me- dium, adventus nempe Titi, per cujus sui collegæ adspectum haud mediocriter recreatus sit: Et la- tum ejusdem nuncium, de salvo & florenti Eccle- siæ Corinthiacæ statu; siquidem ejus consolatio- nis ab ipsis acceptæ a Tito quoque particeps red- ditus fuerit. Modum deinde exponit, quod id fa- ctum per commemorationem Titi.

## 7:7
V. 7. Reporting to us your longing) Your desire to see me. Thus also we have had the noun ἐπιπόθησιν in Rom. xv. 23. Ἐπιποθέω corresponds to the words תאב, ערג, אוה. Your mourning) Namely, the grief of the pious at Corinth because of those evils which Paul had endured in Asia and Macedonia. We have also had Ὀδυρμὸν in Matt. II. 8, where it corresponds to the word תמרורים in Jer. XXXI. 18. ניך is translated ὀδύρομαι.

Theophylact and others understand the grief, not only because of the evils which he had suffered; but also because of the Apostle's long absence. But concerning the desire for the same, it had already been spoken of.

Your zeal for me) He understands the ardent study of those pious ones at Corinth in defending Paul's good name against slanders. See John II. 17, 1 Cor. XII. 3, below XI. 2.

So that I rejoiced the more) That I might rejoice the more, seeing the honor of Titus joined with my own.

He teaches that he rejoiced more, according to B. Hunnius, than he was previously saddened, because he perceived such joy from Titus's report that his former anxiety was, as it were, absorbed by it. But Theophylact's paraphrase is most pleasing: Although I was affected by the arrival of Titus, the bearer, I was nevertheless affected by a greater joy from these things which he himself reported to me about you. Nor should the observation of the same Theophylact be passed over: He says these things, not only to heal the former wounds with which he had afflicted the Corinthians themselves, but truly so that he may appear to have received them as amended. For there were many imbued with these lost morals, and not worthy of these praises: Otherwise the Apostle separates nothing from them, but rather makes the praises common to them, and distributes the crimes into the midst, permitting each to recognize their own good or evil deeds according to their conscience.

PART III. Apologetic against the charge of severity.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἀναγγέλλων ἡμῖν τὴν ὑμῶν ἐπιπόθησιν) Desiderium vestrum mei videndi. Sic & ἐπιπόθησιν nomen habuimus Rom. xv. 23. Ἐπιποθέω respondet vocibus תאב, ערג, אוה. Τὸν ὑμῶν ὀδυρμὸν) Mærorem nempe piorum Corinthi ob ea mala, quæ in Asia & Macedonia Paulus pertulerat. Ὀδυρμὸν & habuimus Matth. II. 8. ubi respondet voci תמרורים Jer. XXXI. 18. ניך vertitur ὀδύρομαι.

Theophylactus & alii moerorem intelligunt, non tantum ob mala, quae perpessus erat; sed etiam ob diuturnam Apostoli absentiam. Sed de desiderio ejusdem jam dictum erat.

Τὸν ὑμῶν ζῆλον ὑπὲρ ἐμῦ) Intelligit ardens studium illorum piorum Corinthi in defendenda bona Pauli tama contra calumnias. Vide Joh. II. 17. 1. Cor. XII. 3. infra XI. 2.

"Ωστε με μᾶλλον χαρῆναι) Ut eo magis gauderem videns honorem Titi cum meo conjunctum.

Magis se gavisum docet, secundum B. Hunnium, quam ante contristatum, quod ex Titi relatione tantum perceperit gaudium, ut prior anxietas eodem veluti absorpta fuerit. Placet autem maxime Theophylacti paraphrasis: Etsi ob Titi lator adventum, majori tamen ex his sum jucunditate affectus, quæ ipse mihi de vobis renuntiavit. Nec prætereunda ejusdem Theophylacti observatio: Hæc autem dicit, non solum, ut prioribus ulceribus, quibus Corinthios ipsos affecerat, medeatur, sed vere ut videatur, emendatos hos suscepisse. Erant namque ex his perditis moribus imbuti complures, & laudibus hisce non digni: Alioqui nil eos secernit Apostolus, quin potius & laudes communes his facit, & crimina in medium impartitur, permittens singulis pro eorum conscientia, ut sua vel bona vel prava facinora recognoscant.

PARS III. Apologetica adversus severitatis ἔγκλημα.

## 7:8
Vers. 8. For if I even saddened you in the letter) In that former one in which there are many harsher things, because there were many evils and they had crept far.

I do not repent) Intending to say the same sentiment if he were placed in the same matters, thus Phocion once said of himself.

If I even repented) That is, although it grieved me, namely that because of that generality of words many pious ones had thought themselves also to be noted.

For I see that that letter, if it even saddened you for an hour) For an hour, that is, for a short time. Thus this expression is taken also in Gal. II. 5, Philem. 15. Thus for a season of an hour 1 Thess. II. 17. But the Apostle took the word hour in a more Latin than Greek sense. For ancient Greece expressed the seasons of the year and the occasions of things with this word. But the Latins and later Greeks call a suitable part of time thus: and properly indeed the twelfth part of a day, but by abuse any time not of long duration.

The Apostle excuses or defends himself in this part, because he saddened the Corinthians, inasmuch as the sadness was done for a small time, with notable fruit of repentance, without any detriment; and it generated much solicitude, and zeal and praise, and he would not have written so sharply except for this cause, and so now he has received consolation from their consolation, and joy from the joy of Titus, and can now trust them in all things. But he could not grieve over the fact that he wrote with severity because of the schisms; the tolerated incest, the litigations before the infidels, the abuse of Christian liberty, the disorder in the celebration of the Holy Supper and sacred assemblies, the conversation with the Gentiles, and the atheism of some in denying the resurrection of bodies: For all this was done by divine instinct through inspiration; but that they were saddened by his letter, and those whom that rebuke did not touch at all. These things can also be understood in this way: Even if I have repented, that is, although I myself descended to that severity unwillingly, preferring to spare you if it had been at all possible: yet because the duty had to be performed, and so broad a fruit has sprung from it, namely the rebuilding of your Church, and its purification from the noted offenses: from this it follows that I can in no way repent of that severity; nay, I rejoice, and I interpret the occasion of joy to be provided to me from this, not indeed from the sadness itself, by which you were affected; but from the subsequent, most salutary effect, that you were saddened unto repentance, which is the interpretation of B. Hunnius. Regarding the word βλέπω, Camerarius has it thus: If it is not a κατάχρησις (misuse) of the word βλέπω, then the construction of the words in this place certainly falters. But if we accept that βλέπω signifies ἀναθεωρῶ (I look back/consider) or ἐννοῶ (I understand), everything will be plain with such a sense: For I consider this, that is, I reflect, that although that letter saddened you for a moment, now I am nevertheless affected with joy by the success of your sadness. Those to whom this either did not come to mind or was displeasing, they preferred that νῦν χαίρω be an ἐπανάληψιν (repetition) of what he had said a little before, ὥστε με μᾶλλον χα- ρῆναι, κατὰ μεσοποιΐαν, that is, an accumulation of full sense, which is frequent in the Pauline writings. Thus, that which is said, ἐὶ ἠ πρὸς ὥραν ἐλύπησεν ὑμᾶς, will be left imperfect κατ’ ἀποσιώπησιν (by suppression), with the thought recoiling from there and hastening to pursue the intended signification of joy. This in a certain way: For I see, although that letter offended you a little. But let this be omitted. I now rejoice, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὅτι εἰ καὶ ἐλύπησα ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ) In illa priore in qua multa sunt asperiora, quia multa erant mala & late serpserant.

Οὐ μεταμέλομαι) Dicturus eandem sententiam si in iisdem rebus poneretur, ita olim de se dixit Phocion.

Εἰ καὶ μετεμελόμην) Id est, quanquam doluit mihi, nempe quod illa generalitate verborum multi pii se quoque notari putaverant.

Βλέπω γὰρ, ὅτι ἡ ἐπιστολὴ ἐκείνη, εἰ καὶ πρὸς ὥραν ἐλύπησεν ὑμᾶς) Πρὸς ὥραν, id est, modico tempore. Sic sumitur hæc loquutio etiam Gal. II. 5. Philem. 15. Sic πρὸς καιρὸν ὥρας 1. Thess. II. 17. Sumpsit autem Apostolus vocem ὥρας magis Latino quam Græco significatu. Nam Græcia vetus anni tempestates & rerum occasiones hoc vocabulo expressit. Latini vero & Græci posteriores, congruam temporis partem sic vocant: & proprie quidem diei partem duodecimam, per abusionem vero quodvis tempus non diuturnum.

Excusat vel defendit se Apostolus in hac parte, quod contristarit Corinthios, siquidem ad exiguum tempus, cum insigni fructu poenitentiæ, sine ullo detrimento facta sit contristatio; multamque genuerit solicitudinem, & zelum ac laudem, nec nisi hujus causa tam acriter scripserit, adeoque jam ex eorum consolatione consolationem, ex gaudio vero Titi gaudium acceperit, & in omnibus jam ipsis confidere possit. Non autem dolere potuit de eo, quod scripserit cum severitate propter schismata; incestum toleratum, litigia coram infidelibus, abusum libertatis Christianæ, ἀταξίαν in celebratione S. cœnæ & conventibus sacris, conversationem cum gentibus, & atheismum quorundam in neganda corporum resurrectione: Hoc enim omne factum instinctu divino per θεοπνευσίαν; sed quod contristati fuerint epistola sua & illi, quos illa increpatio adeo non tetigit. Accipi etiam hæc ita possunt: Etiamsi pœnituerit, hoc est, licet ipse invitus ad istam severitatem descenderim, malens vobis parcere, si ullo modo licuisset: tamen quia officium faciundum fuit, & tam latus inde fructus enatus est, nimirum Ecclesiæ vestræ ræædificatio, & a notatis offendiculis repurgatio: hinc adeo fit, ut me severitatis illius nullo modo pœnitere queat, imo gaudeo, & lætitiæ materiam hinc mihi subministrari interpretor, ne equidem ex ipsa per se tristitia, qua fuisstis affecti; sed ex subsequuto tam salutari affectu, quod ad pœnitentiam contristati estis, quæ est B. Hunnii interpretatio. Ad vocem βλέπω ita habet Camerār: Si non est κατάχρησις verbi βλέπω, sane constructio verborum hoc loco labascit. Sed si ac- cipiamus βλέπω significare ἀναθεωρῶ vel ἐννοῶ, omnia erunt plana tali sensu: Hoc enim intueor, id est con- sidero, quod quamvis illa epistola momento vos con- tristarit, nunc ego tamen lætitia afficiar successu ve- stræ tristitiæ. Quibus hoc vel non venit in mentem vel displicuit, ii maluerunt νῦν χαίρω esse ἐπανάλη- ψιν ejus quod paulo ante dixiffet ὥστε με μᾶλλον χα- ρῆναι, κατὰ μεσοποιΐαν, id est pleni sensus accumula- tionem, quæ est frequens in scriptis Paulinis. Ita, id quod dicitur, ἐὶ ἠ πρὸς ὥραν ἐλύπησεν ὑμᾶς, relin- quetur κατ’ ἀποσιώπησιν imperfectū, resiliente inde cogitatione & properante ad prosequendam institutā gaudii significationem. Hoc quodammodo: Video enim, quamvis illa epistola aliquantulum vos offen- derit. Sed hoc omittatur. Ego nunc gaudeo, &c.

## 7:9
Verse 9. Now I rejoice, not that you were saddened, but that you were saddened unto repentance) I rejoice not simply because you were saddened, but for a good reason, because that sadness brought amendment to the whole Church. Sadness according to God is that which is undertaken for the reason that one knows God is offended by sins.

For you were saddened according to God) that is, in accordance with the divine will. Thus, actions according to virtue are actions which are in accordance with virtue.

So that in nothing you might suffer loss from us) So that you received no damage through us. For what damage does he receive who becomes better?

He rejoices, not that they were saddened, but that they were saddened unto repentance. For it was not a human sadness, a certain affection of the flesh murmuring against correction, nor with despair or distrust toward God; but with serious repentance according to God, or the divine will, arising from the fact that they recognized God was vehemently offended, and thus true repentance, and that amendment of those things which had offended God.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Νῦν χαίρω ἐχ’ ὅτι ἐλυπήθητε, ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἐλυπήθητε εἰς μετάνοιαν) Gaudeo non ἁπλῶς, quod doluistis, sed καλέ τι, quia dolor ille emendationem toti Ecclesiæ attulit. Do- lor secundum Deum est is, qui ob id suscipitut, quod scia- tur Deus offendi peccatis.

Ἐλυπήθητε γὰρ κατὰ Θεὸν) id est, convenienter divinæ voluntati. Sic κατ’ ἀρετὴν πράξεις, actiones, quæ virtuti con- veniunt.

Ἵνα ἐν μηδενὶ ζημιωθῆτε ἐξ ἡμῶν) Ita ut nullum per nos damnū acceperitis. Quid enim damni accipit, qui melior fit?

Gaudet, non quod doluerint, sed quod ad pœ- nitentiam doluerint. Non enim dolor humanus quidam affectus carnis fuit correptioni obmur- murantis, neque cum desperatione aut diffidentia erga Deum; sed cum seria pœnitentia secundum Deum, vel voluntatem divinam, inde ortus, quod Deum agnoverint vehementer offensum, adeoq; vera resipiscentia, & emendatione illa tollenda, quæ Deum offenderant.

## 7:10
Verse 10. For sadness according to God works repentance unto salvation not to be repented of) By repentance he understands the very amendment which is accustomed to follow such sadness. And here there is as it were an ἀντανάκλασις (reflection). For if he had said repentance not to be repented of, it would have been a perfect reflection, as when Pliny says: It remains that I perform the repentance of my repentance.

But the sadness of the world works death) Sorrow on account of ignominy received, on account of lost things, on account of snatched-away friends, often either produces deadly diseases, or even drives men to seek death of their own accord. To the pious, neither will happen, as they have learned to bear human things humanly.

The Apostle now distinguishes sadness according to God and the sadness of the world by reason of the effect, because the former works salutary repentance not to be repented of, but the latter works death. The former arises from the sense of sin and divine wrath: But it is joined not only with serious contrition, but also with true confidence, on account of which the same is not harmful, but salutary: and it is said to work repentance not to be repented of unto salvation, because when we are affected by sadness according to God from God on account of sins, from legal threats, and that not to be repented of, because it is life-bringing: the latter is born from impatience of correction, or affliction, and punishment, from sins accusing man, and by the bite of conscience it is called the sadness of the world, because the world is sad when it is afflicted, devoid of consolation from the word of God, and destitute of faith, and therefore such sadness of the world, or of infidels, is joined with despair and works death. Although indeed sadness according to God can be said to be so even by reason of the efficient principle, it is not therefore to be judged as being excited by God from an absolute good pleasure. For even in that, sadness is excited by God through the terrors of the law, which does not attain a salutary end, Rom. IV. 15, ch. VIII. 15. Nor is it probable that all in whom sadness according to God was excited by the Pauline letter were of the number of the elect, since some among them were undoubtedly temporary believers. Blessed Hülsemann in his unpublished Vindications of Scripture has it thus: Regarding the saying in 2 Corinthians VII. 10, sadness according to God works repentance unto stable salvation, etc. it is commonly answered (1) That repentance is called salutary not with respect to the first part or sadness, but with respect to the latter part, that is, faith (2) That it is not said that sadness works repentance, and repentance in turn works salvation, such a dependency of this saying as Bellarmine makes in book IV on justification, chapter 8, but it is said that sadness according to God works salutary repentance, so called in the concrete, or repentance which brings eternal salvation, Acts XI. 8. But the former exposition seems to be repugnant to the scope of the Apostle, if repentance is taken for faith, for what the Apostle understands, he declares in verse 7 when he says: Titus affected me with joy, when he announced your vehement desire, your lamentation, your zeal: and verse 11, Behold sadness according to God, how much zeal, apology, indignation, fear, etc., it worked in you, which it is harsh to take by metonymy for faith. But the latter response seems to grant more than is asked. He grants more who concedes that sadness according to God works salutary repentance than he who says it works repentance, and repentance further works salvation. For between these two there intervenes an accidental connection, between salutary repentance and salvation there intervenes an essential connection, and therefore the eye must be reflected to the quality of sadness according to God when it is asked: Whether the voluntary good works of the reborn are necessary for salvation? For I deny that sadness according to God signifies in this place an act elicited by man from himself; I say it signifies a passion of man, which God excited in him through Paul, which I demonstrate by the active words of the Apostle, verse 8, I saddened you, my letter saddened you, verse 9, I rejoice not that you were saddened, but that you were saddened unto repentance. You were made sorrowful κατὰ θεὸν, according to God; he does not say that you elicited sorrow out of love for God; but you were made sorrowful by me κατὰ θεὸν, according to the will of God, or according to the command of God. For the preposition κατὰ denotes both the norm and the efficient cause, as is evident from the parallels in Matt. 1:1, Mark 1:27, Tit. 3:5, Phil. 3:last, Heb. 11:13, 1 Tim. 5:15, and elsewhere. Therefore, sorrow according to God is explained by Paul as being such that he, by the power and command of God, excited it in the Corinthians, just as, on the contrary, sorrow according to the world signifies sorrow excited by worldly causes, that is, by fear of punishment, infamy, the baseness of a crime, an evil conscience, and other causes which excite sorrow for a committed crime even in Gentiles and the unregenerate. See regarding these and other sayings the solutions of Melanchthon and Chemnitz, Vol. III of the Loci of Chemnitz in his response to the arguments of the adversaries. Gerhard, on Good Works, § 48 and following.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἡ γὰρ κατὰ Θεὸν λύπη μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν ἀμε- ταμέλητον κατεργάζεται) Per μετάνοιαν intelligit ipsam emendationem, quæ talem dolorem subsequi solet. Et est hic quasi ἀντανάκλασις. Nam μετάνοιαν ἀμετανόητον si dixis- set, perfecta fuisset ἀντανάκλασις, ut cum Plinius dicit: Su- pereft ut meæ pœnitentiæ pœnitentiam agam.

Ἡ δὲ τῦ κόσμου λύπη θάνατον κατεργάζεται) Mœror ob i- gnominam acceptam, ob res amissas, ob ereptos amicos, sæ- pe aut morbos mortiferos parit, aut etiam homines ad ul- tro quærendam mortem adigit. Piis neutrum eveniet, ut qui didicerint, ἀνθρώπινα φέρειν ἀνθρωπίνως.

Distinguit jam Apostolus tristitiam secundum Deum, & tristitiam mundi ratione effectus, quod illa pœnitentiam salutarem minime pœnitendam, hæc vero mortem operetur. Illa ex sensu peccati & iræ divinæ oritur: Ast conjuncta est non modo cum contritione seria, sed etiam cum vera fiducia, ob quam eadem non damnosa, sed salutaris est: atque operari dicitur μετάνοιαν ἀμεταμέλητον εἰς σωτηρίαν, quia cum a Deo secundum Deum tristi- tia afficimur ob peccata, ex comminationibus le- galibus, eaque non pœnitenda, quia salutifera: hæc ex correptionis, vel afflictionis, & pœnæ impa- tientia nascitur, e peccatis hominem accusanti- bus, & conscientiæ morsu tristitia mundi dicitur, quia mundus dolet cum affligitur solatii ex verbo Dei expers, ac fide destitutus, ideoque talis mundi, vel infidelium mœror cum desperatione conjun- gitur ac mortem operatur. Quanquam vero do- lor secundum Deum, etiam ratione principii effici- entis ita dici possit, non tamen ideo ex absoluto beneplacito a Deo excitari censendus est. Nam & in illo a Deo per terrores legis excitatur dolor, qui non assequitur salutarem finem Rom. IV. 15. c. VIII. 15. Neque probabile est, omnes in quibus tristitia secundum Deum excitata fuit per episto- lam Paulinam ex electorum numero fuisse, quum nonnulli inter eodem procul dubio πρόσκαιροι fu- erint B. Hülsemannus in Vindic. Script. ἀνεκδότοις ita habet: Ad dictum 2. Corinth. VII. 10. tristitia secundum Deum pœnitentiam ad salutem stabi- lem operatur, &c. communiter responderi solet (1) Pœnitentiam dici salutarem non respectu primæ partis seu doloris, sed respectu partis posterioris, id est, fidei (2) Non dici, quod tristitia operetur pœ- nitentiam, & pœnitentia operetur rursus salutem, qualem dependentiam hujus dicti Bellarm. facit lib. IV. de justificat. cap. 8. sed dici, quod tristitia secun- dum Deum operetur salutarem pœnitentiam in Con- creto sic dictam, seu pœnitentiam, quæ salutem æter- nam affert Act. XI. 8. Verum prior expositio videtur repugnare scopo Apostoli, si pœnitentia sumatur pro fide, qualem enim intelligat Apostolus, declarat v. 7. cum ait: Titus gaudio me affecit, cum nunciaret vehemens desiderium vestrum, ejulatum vestrum, zelum vestrum: & v. 11. Ecce tristitia secundum Deum, quantum in vobis effecit studium, apolo- giam, indignationem, timorem &c. quæ durum est per Metonymiam accipere pro fide. Posterior autem responsio videtur plus largiri quam quæritur. Plus largitur, qui concedit, tristitiam secundum Deum operari salutarem pœnitentiam, quam is, qui dicit, operari pœnitentiam, pœnitentiam autem porro ope- rari salutem. Nam inter hæc duo intercedit nexus accidentalis, inter salutarem pœnitentiam & salu- tem intercedit nexus essentialis, ideoque ad qualita- tem tristitiæ secundum Deum reflectendus est oculus, quando quæritur: An voluntaria renatorum bona opera necessaria sint ad salutem? Nego enim tristi- tiam secundum Deum significare hoc loco actum eli- citum ab homine ex semetipso; dico significare pas- sionem hominis, quam Deus per Paulum in eo exci- tavit, quod demonstro verbis Activis Apostoli v. 8. Ego contristavi vos, epistola mea contristavit vos, v. 9. Gaudeo non quod contristati estis, sed quod con- tristati estis ad pœnitentiam. Contristati estis κατὰ θεὸν, secundum Deum; non dicit, amore Dei vos elicuisse dolorem; sed contristati estis a me κατὰ θεὸν, secundum voluntatem Dei, seu secundum præce- ptum Dei. Utrumque enim notat Præpositio κατὰ normam & causam Efficientem, ut patet ex parallelis Matth. I. 1. Marci I. 27. Tit. III. 5. Philipp. III. ult. Ebr. XI. 13. 1. Tim. V. 15. & alibi. Itaque tristitia se- cundum Deum explicatur a Paulo, quod sit talis quam ille virtute & mandato Dei excitavit in Co- rinthiis, quemadmodum ex opposito, tristitia secun- dum mundum significat dolorem ex causis munda- nis excitatum, id est, formidine pœnæ, infamiæ, turpitudine flagitii, mala conscientia, aliisque de cau- sis, quæ in gentilibus quoque & irregenitis tristitiam ob flagitium commissum excitant. Vid. de his & aliis dictis Melanchth. & Chemnitii solutiones T. III. LL. Chemnitii in responsione ad argumenta Adversa- riorum. Gerhard. de Bonis operib. §. 48. & seqq.

## 7:11
Verse 11. For behold) This 'behold' is a recent example of him bringing forward what he had said.

Diligence, but apology) 'But' here means 'nay' or 'even' (אַף), apology, that is, an excuse for their negligence, first before Timothy, then before Titus. In the glossary, apology is excuse, purgation, satisfaction. And elsewhere: Excused, having made an apology.

But fear) Because of those things which he had written in the former epistle 4:2, 19, 20, 21.

But longing) Namely because Paul had given hope of his return, 1 Cor. 4:16, 16:5 and following.

But zeal) for Paul's good reputation, above 7.

But vengeance) He calls this vengeance, because the Corinthians had deserted such teachers.

Seven fruits of Paul's sharper rebuke and the Corinthians' sorrow are numbered here: (1) diligence, or the solicitous study of amending those things which the Apostle had rebuked, and of governing discipline otherwise, so that in the future such things should not creep into the Church; (2) defense [Apologia], which the Papists, as noted by B. Hunnius, ridiculously place in the context of penitential satisfaction in certain works introduced and imposed by human authority: which insipid gloss the Greek word strangles. For Ἀπολογία denotes a defense that is made with words, not one that consists of the petty works of the Pontificians. By which they cleared themselves of the stumbling blocks, and especially of the incest of their fellow citizen, and testified that they seriously detested it and did not approve of it (3) Ἀγανάκτησιν, indignation against the authors of the scandals (4) Φόβον, fear arising from the Apostle’s threatening, and the reverence due to God (5) Ἐπιπόθησιν, a desire not so much to hear the Apostle’s voice as to follow it, and to live more rightly thereafter (6) Ζῆλον, emulation, or fervor for the divine glory (7) Ἐκδίκησιν, or vengeance for the misdeeds or crimes rebuked by the Apostle, and especially for the incest. Which word Bellarmine rashly [discusses] in lib. IV. de Pœnit. cap. 8. Cotonus, Instit. lib. III, together with the Rheims translators on this passage, snatches away the satisfaction which he makes a part of penance: since it is not a question of vengeance voluntarily undertaken, as Estius falsely asserts, or imposed by a priest; but of excommunication prescribed by the Apostle, which, although it is a punishment, is nevertheless not that punishment which the Papists impose after absolution, as Cornelius à Lapide and Estius here admit. And therefore Emanuel Saa and Justinianus, along with Salmerone, understand it as vindication through separation and flight from the incestuous person, as Grotius does regarding the false teachers. What of the fact that it does not follow, if for certain external offenses satisfaction must be made to offended brethren through a bodily afflictive punishment or external ignominy to avert scandal, which our people do not deny was once in use: therefore such satisfaction is an essential part of penance for any sin whatsoever.

Ἐν παντὶ ἑαυτὸς ἁγνὸς συνεστήσατε εἶναι ἐν τῷ πράγματι) Συνεστήσατε here is rebus probastis (you have proved by your actions). Thus Demosthenes against Callippus explains συνέστησε by δεῖξον (show). You have made it manifest that you are innocent in this matter, namely in those things which were said and done in contempt of me.

Præcisio is that by which he breaks off the list of fruits and shows in summary that nothing has been omitted from them for the declaration of true repentance, but that he has abundantly testified to them that they are pure in this matter of prohibited marriages, inasmuch as they had neither approved of them before, and now, having been admonished, had most severely punished the author of so great an offense, as rightly B. Hunnius, Theophylactus wishes to be considered, which he had said in the previous epistle, "and you are puffed up," which statement made them participants in the crime: As if he were to say: Now, however, you have even worn away such suspicion, and have made it manifest that you were immune from that business, that is, from the sin and the stain.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἰδὺ γὰρ) Hoc ecce est exemplum recens affe rentis ejus quod dixerat.

Σπυδὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀπολογίαν) Ἀλλὰ hic valet imo & אַף ἀπο- λογίαν, id est, excusationem suæ negligentiæ, primum apud Timotheum, deinde apud Titum. In Glossario ἀπολογία excusatio, purgatio, satisfactio. Et alibi: Excusatus ἀπολο- γησάμενος.

Ἀλλὰ φόβον) Propter illa, quæ scripserat in priore epi- stola IV. 2. 19. 20. 21.

Ἀλλὰ ἐπιπόθησιν) Nempe quia spem reditus sui fecerat Paulus, 1. Cor. IV. 16. XVI. 5. & sequentibus.

Ἀλλὰ ζῦλον) pro Pauli bona existimatione, supra 7.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἐκδίκησιν) Vindictam appellat hoc, quod tales do- ctores Corinthii deseruerant.

Septem hic fructus acrioris correptionis Pauli- næ & mœstitiæ Corinthiorum numerantur (1) σπυδὴ diligentia, seu studium solicitum emendan- di ea, quæ reprehenderat Apostolus, & aliter re- gendæ disciplinæ, ne imposterum talia in Eccle- siam irrepant (2) Ἀπολογία, quam Papistæ notante B. Hunnio ridicule de satisfactione pœnitentiali in operibus quibusdam humanitus introductis & impositis collocant : quam glossam insulsam vox Græca jugulat. Ἀπολογία enim defensionem, quæ verbis fit, non quæ opellis Pontificiorum notat. Qua se purgarint de offendiculis, imprimis verò de incestu concivis ac se illa serio detestari, non approbare, testati sunt (3) Ἀγανάκτησιν indignatio- nem adversus scandalorum autores (4) Φόβον timo- rem ex comminatione Apostoli ortum, & reve- rentiam Deo debitam (5) Ἐπιπόθησιν desiderium non tam Apostoli vocem audiendi, quàm sequen- di, rectiusque deinde vivendi. (6) Ζῆλον æmu- lationem, seu fervorem pro divina gloria. (7) Ἐκδί- κησιν vel vindictam de facinoribus vel sceleribus ab Apostolo reprehensis, imprimis verò de ince- stu. Quam vocem temerè Bellarm. lib. IV. de Pœ- nit. cap. 8. Cotonus Instit. lib. III. cum Remensibus ad h. l. ad satisfactionem, quam partem facit pœni- tentiæ, abripit : quum non de vindicta sponte sus- cepta, ut Estius incrustat, aut à sacerdote imposita; sed de excommunicatione ab Apostolo præscripta, quæ etsi pœna sit, non tamen illa pœna est, quam Papistæ post absolutionem imponunt, hic Cornelio à Lapide & Estio fatente, agatur. Ideoque Ema- nuel Saa, & Justinianus cum Salmerone de vindi- catione per separationem & fugam ab incestuoso, ut Grotius à falsis Doctoribus, intelligunt. Quid? quod non sequatur, si pro delictis quibusdam ex- ternis satisfaciendum est offensis fratribus per pœ- nam corporis afflictivam, aut externam ignomi- niam ad scandalum avertendum, quod olim in usu fuisse non negant nostrates: Ergo talis satisfactio est essentialis pars pœnitentiæ de quocunque de- licto.

Ἐν παντὶ ἑαυτὸς ἁγνὸς συνεστήσατε εἶναι ἐν τῷ πράγματι) Συνεστήσατε hic est rebus probastis. Sic συνέστησε per δεῖξον exponit Demosthenes contra Calippum. Manifestum feci- stis, vos insontes esse in hoc negotio, nempe in iis, quæ ad mei contemptum dictaque factaque erant.

Præcisio est, qua catalogum fructuum abrumpit, & summatim ostendit ad declarationem veræ resipi- scentiæ nihil ab illis prætermissum esse, sed abunde satis illis testatum fecisse, quod in isto negotio nuptia- rum prohibitarum puri sint, utpote quas nec antea probarint, & nunc admoniti in autore tanti offendi- culi acerrime vindicarint, ut recte B. Hunnius, Theophylactus respici vult, quod in superiori epi- stola dixerat, & vos inflati estis, quod dictum cri- minis eos faciebat participes: Quasi dicat: Nunc vero vel ejusmodi detrivistis suspicionem, & palam fecistis ejus negotii, hoc est peccati & labis vos fuisse immunes.

## 7:12
Vers. 12. Ἄρα εἰ καὶ ἔγραψα ὑμῖν) If I wrote anything, namely concerning that matter, and that I wrote it is to be understood, as above II. 10. V. 13. and often elsewhere.

Οὐχ ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἀδικήσαντος) Not that I wished him ill, Οὐδὲ ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἀδικηθέντος) Nor that I sought consolation for myself from his suffering. For there is inherent τῇ τιμωρίᾳ τὸ παρηγορεῖν τοὺς πεπονθότας, as we have said in De Jure Belli ac Pacis, book II, XX. 6.

Ἀλλ' ἕνεκεν τοῦ φανερωθῆναι τὴν σπουδὴν ἡμῶν, τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Thus the Greeks. But the Syriac, and perhaps better, has τὴν σπουδὴν ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν without that πρὸς ὑμᾶς, which is also missing in other codices, so that the sense may be: In this matter I had written to God, that is, sincerely, with God as my witness.

The received reading of the Authentic text is not to be called into question. For that πρὸς ὑμᾶς coheres with the verb Φανερωθῆναι, as Beza observes, rendering it in this way: that among you might be made manifest that zeal of ours for you in the sight of God, or at least unfeigned, so that they might be able to approve it to God, Luke I. 6. Camerarius: There is, he says, a convenient sense to those things which are read as published in the Greek books: I wrote those things, he says, so that your zeal toward us might be made manifest, for your sake in the sight of God.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἄρα εἰ καὶ ἔγραψα ὑμῖν) Si quid scripsi, nempe ea de re, & subaudiendum id scripsi, ut supra II. 10. V. 13. & alibi sæpè.

Οὐχ ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἀδικήσαντος) Non quod ei male vellem, Οὐδὲ ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἀδικηθέντος) Nec quod mihi ex ipsius do- lore solatium quærerem. Inest enim τῇ τιμωρίᾳ τὸ παρη- γορεῖν τοὺς πεπονθότας, ut diximus lib. II. de Jure Belli ac pa- cis XX. 6.

Ἀλλ' ἕνεκεν τοῦ φανερωθῆναι τὴν σπουδὴν ἡμῶν, τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Sic Græci. At Syrus & for- te melius τὴν σπουδὴν ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν sine illo πρὸς ὑμᾶς, quod & in aliis codicibus deest, ut sensus sit: In hoc ea de re scripseram Deo, id est, sincere, Deo conscio.

Non est solicitanda recepta textus Authentici lectio. Illud enim πρὸς ὑμᾶς cohæret cum verbo Φανερωθῆναι, ut observat Beza, reddens hoc modo, ut apud vos manifestum fieret, studium illud no- strum pro vobis in conspectu Dei sive minime fu- catum, ut Deo illud possint approbare Luc. I. 6. Ca- merarius: Est autem, inquit, eorum, qua in Græcis libris edita leguntur, commodus sensus: Eo scripsi ea, inquit, ut palam fieret studium erga nos vestrum, vestra causa in conspectu Dei.

## 7:13
V. 13. Διὰ τοῦτο παρακεκλήμεθα ἐπὶ τῇ παρακλήσει ὑμῶν) That is, because of your letter, which you had sent to me by Timothy.

Περισσοτέρως δὲ μᾶλλον) A double comparative, as in Mark 1:26 and 7:36. Such are μᾶλλον εἰδικώτερος in Aeschylus, μᾶλλον ἐντυχέστερον in Euripides, μᾶλλον ὀλβιώτερον in Aristophanes, αἱρετώτερον μᾶλλον in Aristotle. Thus also in Plautus, magis certius, magis majores, magis dulcius, in Virgil magis beatior, in Valerius Maximus, magis locupletior, which are noted in the most learned books on grammar by Vossius.

Ἐχάρημεν ἐπὶ τῇ χαρᾷ Τίτου) We rejoiced in the joy of Titus, which Titus brought back with him from you.

(Ὅτι ἀναπέπαυται τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ πάντων ὑμῶν) That his spirit had been refreshed by you all. Concerning this meaning of the word ἀναπαύειν we have spoken at 1 Cor. XVI. 18.

Others more correctly understand the consolation of Paul not from the letters of the Corinthians brought by Timothy, about which nothing is commemorated anywhere, namely that the Corinthians had written to the Apostle; but from the consolation of the Corinthians, which they themselves felt from the fruits of sorrow according to God, which yielded great consolation to Paul in his own manifold affliction and sadness. To which, just as a certain huge heap, the joy of Titus was added, because having known the state of affairs in the Corinthian Church, now safe, his spirit also was refreshed; so that just as he was previously a participant in Paul's pain from so many stumbling blocks which had been added to his various hardships: so now he may be a sharer and companion of the pleasure resulting from the amendment. Whoever desires the varied reading of the Latin Codices, let him approach Estius; it is not of such importance that it should delay us.

Latin:

V. 13. Διὰ τοῦτο παρακεκλήμεθα ἐπὶ τῇ παρακλήσει ὑμῶν) Id est, ex litteris vestris, quas ad me miseratis per Timotheum.

Περισσοτέρως δὲ μᾶλλον) Duplex Comparativus, ut Marci I. 26. & VII, 36. Talia sunt μᾶλλον εἰδικώτερος apud Æ- schylum, μᾶλλον ἐντυχέστερον apud Euripidem, μᾶλλον ὀλ- βιώτερον, apud Aristophanem, αἱρετώτερον μᾶλλον apud Aristotelem. Sic & apud Plautum, magis certius, magis majores, magis dulcius, apud Virgilium magis beatior, apud Valerium Maximum, magis locupletior, quæ notata in doctissimis de Grammatica Vossii libris.

Ἐχάρημεν ἐπὶ τῇ χαρᾷ Τίτου) Gaudio fuit nobis id gau- dium, quod Titus à vobis secum attulit.

Ὅτι ἀναπέπαυται τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ πάντων ὑμῶν) Quod per vos omnes recreatus fuerat ejus animus. De hoc significatu vocis ἀναπαύειν diximus 1. Cor. XVI. 18.

Rectius alii de consolatione Pauli accipiunt non ex literis Corinthiorum per Timotheum allatis, de quibus nuspiam quicquam commemoratur, quod nempe Corinthii ad Apostolum scripserint; sed ex consolatione Corinthiorum, quam ipsimet senserint è fructibus tristitiæ secundum Deum, quæ Paulo magnæ consolationi cedebat, in ejusdem multivaria afflictione, ac mœstitia. Ad quam vel- ut ingens quidam cumulus accessit gaudium Titi, quod cognito rerum in Ecclesia Corinthiaca sta- tu jam incolumi Spiritus illius quoque refocilla- tus est; ita ut quemadmodum doloris Paulini ex tot offendiculis, quæ variis ipsius ærumnis acces- serant, particeps ante fuit: ita nunc voluptatis ex emendatione profectæ consors sit atque socius. Variam Latinorum Codd. lectionem qui desiderat, Estium adeat; non ea tanti est, ut nos moretur.

## 7:14
Vers. 14. For if I have boasted anything to him concerning you, I was not put to shame) So that if I have proclaimed anything magnificently about your affection for me to Titus, I have not appeared vain in that. Moreover, in the word κατῃσχύνθην the effect is put for the cause. For those who are convicted of a lie, shame is accustomed to follow them.

But as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting which was before Titus was found to be truth) Ἐπὶ Τίτου here is before Titus. Thus ἐπὶ τοσούτων μαρτύρων before so many witnesses, in Lucian. Just as you found all things that I said to you to be true, so also Titus found the things that I had said to him about you to be true.

This therefore is what he says, with Blessed Hunnius as interpreter, bringing another thing as it were an addition to his joy: My joy was also wonderfully increased by this, because by the promptness of your obedience you proved the truth of my judgment, by which I also boasted before Titus, that I did not doubt your obedience even in the slightest. Therefore my hope did not deceive me; but just as we have always endeavored to speak the truth to you; so also my testimony given to you was found before Titus to be consonant with the truth.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ὅτι εἴτι αὐτῷ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κεκαύχημαι, οὐ κατῃ- σχύνθην) Ita ut si quid magnifice de vestro affectu in me apud Titum prædicaverim, in eo non vanus apparuerim. Est autem in voce κατῃσχύνθην effectum positum pro causa. Nam qui mendacii convincuntur, eos pudor sequi solet.

Ἀλλ' ὡς πάντα ἐν ἀληθείᾳ ἐλαλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, οὕτω καὶ ἡ καύχησις ἡ ἐπὶ Τίτου ἀλήθεια ἐγενήθη) Ἐπὶ Τίτου hic est apud Titum. Sic ἐπὶ τοσούτων μαρτύρων apud tot Testes, apud Lucianum. Sicut vos, quæcunque vobis dixi, vera compe- ristis, sic & Titus vera comperit, quæ ipsi de vobis dixeram.

Hoc ergò est, quod dicit, interprete B. Hun- nio, aliud velut auctarium lætitiæ suæ afferens: Gaudium meum bis quoque mirifice fuit auctum, quod obsequii promptitudine comprobastis verita- tem mei judicii, quo etiam apud Titum gloriatus sum, me de obedientia vestra ne tantillum quidem dubitare. Non ergo me mea fefellit spes; sed quem- admodum semper apud vos studuimus loqui vera; sic & testimonium meum vobis datum coram Tito deprehensum est veritati consonum.

## 7:15
Vers. 15. And his affections are more abundantly toward you.) His love toward you is much greater, that is, it is carried. A similar expression in Psalm 145:9.

Remembering the obedience of you all) Namely that which the Corinthians had exhibited to Titus, as to Paul's vicar. See below VIII. 23. how you received him with fear and trembling. See above 11. & Psalm 2:11.

I rejoice, that in everything I have confidence in you) Because you are such that I can promise myself all the best things about you. There is also here a metonymy of the effect for the cause. Thus below X. 1. Add Proverbs 31:11.

Theophylact in you we have confidence, namely because you accepted all my words and deeds toward you with a calmer and willing mind for your edification; as if he were saying, as the commentary of Blessed Balduinus has: I now experience in reality, and on this account I rejoice, that henceforth I can safely think, write, and speak all the best things about you, safely also remind you of necessary matters, and more freely, where there is need, argue, because I have experienced you to be easy and obedient in all things. And he writes all these things not for the sake of flattery, but that he may mitigate his former severity somewhat, and most holily attest his love for them as clearly unblemished. It is a small conclusion, says the Blessed

Hunnius, in which he declares that he rejoices most profusely that, having overcome all the reefs and billows of previous anxiety and dissension, he has arrived as it were at a certain harbor, so that he dares to promise himself with certainty all the best things concerning them.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ τὰ σπλάγχνα αὐτοῦ περισσοτέρως εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐστιν.) Amor ejus erga vos multo magis est, id est, fertur. Locutio similis Psalm. CXLV. 9.

Ἀναμιμνησκομένου τὴν πάντων ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴν) Eam scili- cet, quam Corinthii Tito, tanquam Pauli vicario, exhibue- rant. Vide infra VIII. 23. ὡς μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου ἐδέξασθε αὐτόν. Vide supra 11. & Psal. II. 11.

Χαίρω, ὅτι ἐν παντὶ θαῤῥῶ ἐν ὑμῖν) Quod tales sitis, ut de vobis mihi omnia optima possim polliceri. Est & hic μετω- νυμία effectus pro causa. Sic infra X. 1. Adde Prov. XXXI. 11.

Theophylactus in vobis confidimus, videlicet quia dicta mea erga vos omnia & facta animo æquio- ri & libenti ad vestram ædificationem accepistis; quasi dicat, ut B. Balduini habet commentarius: Reipsa jam experior, & hoc nomine lætor, quod im- posterum tutò optima quæque de vobis cogitare, scribe- re & loqui possum, tuto etiam vos de rebus necessa- riis commonefacere, & liberius, ubi opus fuerit, ar- guere, quia expertus sum vos in omnibus faciles & obsequentes. Et hæc omnia non adulandi gratia scri- bit, sed ut severitatem priorem nonnihil mitiget, & suum in ipsos amorem plane intemeratum quam san- ctissime contestetur. Conclusiuncula est, inquit B.

Hunnius, qua declarat effusissime lætari se, in quod cunctis antegresse solicitudinis ac dissidentiæ scopulis atque fluctibus superatis velut ad portum certum ap- pulerit, ut optima quæque sibi polliceri de illis certo audeat.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having proclaimed the remarkable liberality and singular piety of the Churches in Macedonia, by which the Apostle had been moved to send Titus to the Corinthians, he exhorts the same, that as they are rich in other parts of piety, they may also be rich in munificence, and that for the sake of Christ, who for their sake became poor, that he might enrich them, and that they may now fulfill their former willing mind in reality according to each one's means, so that they themselves may be reciprocally helped in need, and no one may have need to be in want. He praises the zeal of Titus, to whom he had joined one and another faithful colleague for this work for the sake of avoiding suspicion, relying on a great confidence of the liberality of the alms toward them.

I. Exhortation to almsgiving to be bestowed by the example of the Macedonians to v. 16.

II. Commendation of the zeal of Titus and the faithfulness of the companions joined to him in this work of piety to v. 24.

There are two parts

PART I. Exhortation to liberal almsgiving.

Vers. 1. Γνωρίζομεν δὲ ὑμῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ, τὴν δεδομένην ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Μακεδονίας) Truly, what the Macedonians had done was great, by whose example Paul wishes to stir up the Corinthians. But Paul, as Apostles are wont to do, names the cause for the effect, teaching that all things which are done by Christians are owed not to just anyone, but to the excellent goodness of God, as one who has forgiven so many and such grave sins, has revealed his will so openly, has voluntarily called those alienated from himself, and that through so many miracles. These are the causes for which, in the New Testament, there is, and ought to be, a more abundant commemoration of grace than in the Old.

After he had won the minds of the Corinthians to himself with a mutual eulogy of love, he now exhorts them to show beneficence to the needy in Judea, and that both because of the imitation of the Macedonians, and for the demonstration of charity, and for the acknowledgment of the grace of Christ, and because of their own utility, and the relief of indigence, if it should press upon any, so that there may be ἰσότης. He attributes it to the grace of God, and no less to the proven faith of the Macedonians, that they not only abounded with singular joy in great affliction; but also that their extreme poverty overflowed into excellent liberality. For the grace of God is the cause of faith. But faith is not only the cause of joy, even that which persists in tribulations; but it is also the mother, as of every virtue and good action; so also of liberality and beneficence: Which overflows from the joy of the spirit, and this brings it about entirely that the giver is cheerful. Observe, however, as Theophylact advises, how he calls the grace of God a certain more merciful and pious mind, and likewise makes that statement less invidious, and strives at the same time to provoke the Corinthians to seize this grace of God. Nor did he pick out this or that city, but extolled all of Macedonia with praises, so that the Corinthians also might all be intent upon similar duties. He therefore celebrates the faithful in Macedonia, among whom were especially the Philippians and Thessalonians, which Churches the Apostle had founded in Acts

XVI. and XVII. both their constancy in enduring persecutions for the sake of the Gospel 1 Thess. 1 and 2, and their beneficence, which they showed not only according to the measure of their means; but even beyond what the ratio of their means seemed able to bear. The Apostle executes these things in most elegant words, the sense and emphasis of which Chrysostom expressed at greater length, and Theophylact more succinctly according to his custom, in this way: Just as the magnitude of the pressure poured itself out into joy, so their huge and profound poverty was not only no impediment to bestowing alms; but rather made them abound in riches. And he did not say of the thing contributed, but the riches of simplicity, that is, of a mind free from envy, and ready to impart. For we do not measure liberality by the abundance of benefits; but by the promptness of the mind. The true cause, why the Apostle labored so much for alms, was the famine in Judea, which, predicted by Agabus around the first year of Caligula, had begun to rage in the fourth year of Claudius, and was still lasting in the thirteenth, in which this epistle seems to have been written: and it was pressing more heavily upon the converted Jews, inasmuch as they had suffered the plundering of their goods on account of the profession of the Gospel Heb. 10:34. Cf. Gal. 2:10, 1 Cor. 16:1, 2, Rom. 15:25, 26. Schmidius attributes the profound poverty partly to the persecutions of that time in general, and partly in particular to the tributary exactions of Macedonia, which Tiberius Caesar had instituted. Those things which Grotius injects concerning the grace of God forgiving sins being more abundantly to be commemorated by us in the New Testament than in the Old, smell of the lamp of Socinus, as if formerly the remission of sins had not been proposed, concerning which, however, Peter teaches that all the Prophets bear witness Acts 10:43, and the Prophetic writings testify abundantly. Some explain χάριν as referring to alms, as it is taken in v. 4. But the grace of God is mentioned here, not indeed the grace of the Macedonians, the grace bestowed upon the converted, not that which they themselves bestowed upon others.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Deprædicata Ecclesiarum in Macedonia, etsi pauperum, liberalitate insigni, & pietate singulari, qua motus fuerat Apostolus, ut propter Titum Corinthios destinaret, horta- tur eosdem, ut divites in aliis pietatis parti- bus, divites etiam munificentia sint, idque propter Christum, qui ipsorum causa pau- per factus est, ut ipsos ditaret, ac voluntatem pristinam benevolam reipsa pro cujusque fa- cultate jam impleant, ut & ipsis in inopia re- ciproce succurratur, nec quisquam opus ha- beat egere. Laudat studium Titi, cui unum atq; alterum fidum collegam ad hoc opus su- spicionis declinandæ causa adjunxerit, ma- gna liberalitatis eleemosynæ erga ipsos fidu- cia fretus.

I. Adhortatio ad Eleemosynam exemplo Macedonum erogandam ad v. 16.

II. Commendatio studii Titi & fidei sociorum in hoc pietatis opere ipsi adjunctorum ad v. 24.

Partes sunt duæ

PARS I. Adhortatio ad liberalem eleemosynam.

Vers. 1. Γνωρίζομεν δὲ ὑμῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ, τὴν δεδομένην ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Μακεδονίας) Multum sane erat, quod fecerant Macedones, quorum exemplo Paulus Corinthios vult excitare. Sed Paulus, ut solent Apostoli, pro effectu causam nominat, docens omnia quæ a Christia- nis fiunt, deberi non cuivis, sed eximiæ Dei bonitati, ut qui tot & tam gravia peccata remiserit, voluntatem suam tam aperte revelaverit, ultro vocaverit a se abalienatos, & id per tot miracula. Hæ sunt causæ, propter quas in Novo Testa- mento, quam in Vetere, uberior est, & esse debet, gratiæ commemoratio.

Postquam animos Corinthiorum mutuo dile- ctionis elogio sibi conciliarat, jam ad beneficen- tiam egenis in Judæa exhibendam hortatur, idque tum ob Macedonum imitationem, tum ad chari- tatis demonstrationem, tum ad gratiæ Christi agni- tionem, tum ob propriam utilitatem, & indigentia, si quos presserit, sublevationem, ut ἰσότης sit. Gra- tiæ autem Dei, nec minus fidei Macedonum pro- batæ tribuit, quod non tantum gaudio singulari in magna afflictione abundarint; sed & summa ipsorum paupertas in eximiam liberalitatem ex- undarit. Nam gratia Dei causa fidei. Fides au- tem non tantum est causa gaudii, etiam in tribula- tionibus permanentis; sed etiam genitrix est, ut omnis virtutis & bonæ actionis; ita & liberalitatis & beneficentiæ: Quæ e lætitia spiritus redundat, & hæc omnino efficit, ut dator hilaris sit.
