Adverte autem, monente Theophylacto, quemadmodum Dei gratiam dicat mentem aliquam clementiorem & piam, faciatque item id dictum minus invidiosum, nitaturque simul, ut Corinthios provocet ad Dei hanc gratiam rapiendam. Neque hanc illamve urbem de- prompsit, sed universam extulit laudibus Macedo- niam, ut & Corinthii sint universi similibus intenti officiis. Celebrat itaque fidelium in Macedonia, e quibus præcipue erant Philippenses, & Thessaloni- censes, quas Ecclesias fundarat Apostolus Actor.

XVI. & XVII. tum constantiam in persecutionibus Evangelii causa sustinendis 1. Thessal. I. & II. tum beneficentiam, quam non tantum pro modulo facultatum suarum; sed ultra etiam, quam ratio facultatum ferre posse videbatur, exhibuerint. Elegantiissimis autem verbis haec exequitur Apostolus, quorum sensum & emphasin Chrysostomus prolixius, Theophylactus pro more succinctius expressit, hoc modo: Quemadmodum pressura magnitudo in gaudium se effudit, sic ingens illorum & profunda inopia, non solum nulli fuit ad eleemosynam erogandam impedimento; sed potius affluere opibus fecit. Nec rei collata dixit, sed simplicitatis divitias, hoc est, animi vacantis invidia, & ad impertiendum facilis. Non enim beneficiorum copia; sed animi promptitudine liberalitatem metimur. Causa vero, cur tantopere pro Eleemosynis laborarit Apostolus, erat fames in Judaea, quae ab Agabo circa annum I. Caligulae praedicta Act. XI. grassari coeperat IV. Claudii, atque etiamnum XIII. quo haec epistola videtur exarata, durabat: & gravius Judaeos conversos, utpote direptionem facultatum ob Evangelii professionem perpessos Ebr. X. 34. premebat. Conf. Gal. II. 10. 1. Cor. XVI. 1. 2. Rom. XV. 25. 26. Inopiam profundam Schmidius tribuit partim persecutionibus istius temporis in genere, partim in specie exactionibus tributariis Macedoniae, quas Tiberius Caesar instituerat. Quae Grotius de gratia Dei peccata remittentis uberius a nobis commemoranda in Nov. Test. quam in Vetere, ingerit, Socini olent lucernam, ac si quondam remissio peccatorum non fuerit proposita, de qua vero omnes Prophetae testimonium reddere docet Petrus Act. X. 43. & testantur affatim scripta Prophetica. Nonnulli χάριν explicant de eleemosyna, ut v. 4. accipitur. Sed χάρις Θεoῦ hic commemoratur, non vero gratia Macedonum, gratia conversis praestita, non quam ipsi aliis praestitere.

## 8:2
Vers. 2. That in much proof of affliction the abundance of their joy, and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality) In the former clause, 'was' is to be understood. Their joy was great (namely, from the peace of conscience, as above VI. 10.) even then when they were being tested by the greatest adversities. See above II. 9. For the Christian Macedonians had been vehemently vexed both by the Gentiles, Acts XVI. 20. & seqq. & by the Jews, Acts XVII. 5. 13. πτωχεία εἰς τὸ βάθος is extreme poverty, partly from the confiscation of goods, partly because the rich had deserted the Church. The word πτωχὸς in these books often does not signify one reduced to beggary, but one who is of small means, as in Mark XII. 42. κατὰ βάθος, that is, the lowest poverty. Thus an abject condition is called מעמק in Psalm CXXX. 1. βάθος in Rom. VIII. 39. Ἁπλότης is indeed in this place liberality, as below IX. 11. 13. & Roman. XII. 8. just as ἁπλῶς is also taken, James I. 5. It is otherwise a general word, which signifies integrity of mind, as appears in I Chron. XXIX. 17. 2 Sam. XV. 11. Prov. XI. 1. above I. 12. below XI. 3. Ephes. VI. 5. Coloss. III. 22. But πλοῦτος to Paul is everything that is ample and excellent, as we have seen in Roman. II. 4. IX. 23. XI. 12. 33. Ἐπερίσσευσε [Note. There is an excellent antithesis in the words βάθος & ἐπερίσσευσεν. Their extreme poverty, that is, the Macedonians themselves, being very poor, abounded in excellent liberality. Great wisdom of Paul appears here. He praises the poor Macedonians, so that he may obtain so much the more from the rich Corinthians for the relief of the poor in Judea.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὅτι ἐν πολλῇ δοκιμῇ θλίψεως ἡ περισσεία τῆς χαρᾶς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡ κατὰ βάθος πτωχεία αὐτῶν ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς ἁπλότητος αὐτῶν) In priore membro subaudiendum est, fuit. Magnum fuit eorum gaudium (nempe ex pace conscientiae, ut supra VI. 10.) etiam tunc cum per adversa maxima explorarentur. Vide supra II. 9. Macedones enim Christiani vehementer vexati fuerant & a gentibus, Act. XVI. 20. & seqq. & a Judaeis, Act. XVII. 5. 13. πτωχεία εἰς τὸ βάθος est summa paupertas, partim ex confiscatione bonorum, partim quia divites Ecclesiam deseruerant. πτωχὸς vox saepe in his libris non ad mendicitatem redactum; sed re tenuem significat, ut Marci XII. 42. κατὰ βάθος, id est, infima paupertas. Sic conditio abjecta vocatur מעמק Psal. CXXX. 1. βάθος Rom. VIII. 39. Ἁπλότης est hoc quidem loco liberalitas, ut infra IX. 11. 13. & Roman. XII 8. quomodo & ἁπλῶς sumitur, Jac. I. 5. Est alioqui vox generalis, quae quamvis animi integritatem significat, ut apparet I. Paralip. IX. 17. 2. Sam. XV. 11. Prov. IX. 1. supra I. 12. infra XI. 3. Ephes. VI. 5. Coloss. II. 22. Πλοῦτος vero Paulo est omne id, quod amplum eximiumque est, ut vidimus Roman. II. 4. IX. 23. XL. 12. 33. Ἐπερίσσευσε [NW. Egregium est ἀντίθετον in vocibus βάθος & ὑπερίσσευσεν. Ipsorum summa paupertas, id est, ipsi Macedones valde pauperes exundarunt in egregiam liberalitatem. Magna hic apparet Pauli sapientia. Pauperes Macedones laudat, ut tanto plus a Corinthiis locupletibus obtineat ad sublevandos in Judaea pauperes.

## 8:3
Vers. 3. That according to their power I bear witness, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves, with much entreaty beseeching us that we would receive the grace and the fellowship of the ministry which is to the saints) Here also 'they were' is understood before 'beseeching', as the word 'was' just now. So below IX. 13. Then there is a transposition of words. For 'I bear witness' is a parenthesis. But those words 'according to their power' and 'beyond their power' cohere with what follows. Αὐθαίρετοι corresponds to the Hebrew מתנדבים, Nehem. XI. 2. which the Greeks there translate as 'those who offer willingly'. Thus they are called, who do not give something by the prescription of the law, but of their own accord, such as are not to be demanded from the poor, but if they give of their own accord, they can be received, Maimonides says, Tom. III. fol. 85. to give, he says, according to their strength, nay even beyond their strength, that is, in such a way that they inconvenienced themselves: then much they asked me and my associates not to refuse this. Τὴν χάριν, this benefit, as in I Corinthians 16:3. They also asked that we take upon ourselves a part of the labor of carrying those funds to the saints in Judea. For that is called διακονία, just as is everything in which we render ourselves useful to others, below 9:1, 12; I Corinthians 16:15.

According to their strength, nay, beyond their strength. For this, as Theophylact says, is the excellence of abundance of simplicity, that one strives to do greater things than one's means allow. Nor indeed was there need for the spurs of exhortation; but they themselves of their own accord gave willingly and liberally: nay, they besought us with many prayers that we would be willing to accept the alms collected by them and consecrated to the saints in Judea, to be carried to them. It is fitting here to add the annotation of the blessed Hülsemann, vindicating against the abuse of the Papists: the Macedonians, αὐθαίρετοι, according to the subject matter of voluntary liberality, do nothing for the natural freedom of the will in spiritual matters, which Salmeron and Estius contend for here, for the despoiling of children and relatives and the addition of all goods to the foundations of monasteries or other pious causes, as Salmero, Dub. 3; Gretser, de Germ. Princip. liberality toward the Roman See, chapter 3, or for the debt inherent in the good works of the reborn for just perfection, which Salmero repeatedly gathers here from the attribute ὑπὲρ δύναμιν. For that ὑπὲρ δύναμιν is understood comparatively and civilly regarding the liberality of the Macedonians, if you compare it with the liberality of others, as excessive and transcending the means of present wealth, but not regarding a proportion or measure transcending the norm of divine law, about which there is no question here, nor regarding works of what they call supererogation. In chapter 1:8, he says he endured evils ὑπὲρ δύναμιν, not speaking absolutely or humanly in that way. Moreover, Paul so far from praising an excess of liberality beyond one's means that he expressly excludes it in verses 13 and 14. Even Christ's judgment concerning liberality in sacrifices or corbans with the deprivation of sufficient sustenance is sufficiently manifest in Mark 7:11-12; Matthew 15:4-5. and following, where see the commentary of Johannes Ferus, who expressly inveighs against the prodigal benefactors of monasteries and similar institutions. Read also Augustine, Tom. III, chapters 4, 5, and following, on the blessed life, where by the same examples of prodigality in sacred matters he demonstrates that not only can one exceed in these, but that excess is as much a vice as defect. Compare also the prefaces of Bellarmine to the books on the invocation of saints.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ὅτι κατὰ δύναμιν μαρτυρῶ, καὶ ὑπὲρ δύναμιν αὐθαίρετοι μετὰ πολλῆς παρακλήσεως δεόμενοι ἡμῶν τὴν χάριν καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν ῆς διακονίας ῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους δέξασθαι ἡμᾶς) Hic quoque ad δεόμενοι subauditur ἦσαν, ut modo vox fuit. Sic infra IX. 13. Deinde est vocum trajectio. Nam μαρτυρῶ est παρένθεσις. Illa autem κατὰ δύναμιν & ὑπὲρ δύναμιν cum sequentibus cohaerent. Αὐθαίρετοι respondet Hebraeo מתנדבים, Nehem. XI. 2. quod ἑκουσιαζομένους ibi vertunt Graeci. Sic dicuntur, qui non ex legis praescripto, sed sua sponte aliquid donant, qualia a pauperibus non postulanda, sed si ultro dent, recipi posse, Maimonides dicit Tom. III. fol. 85. dedere, inquit, pro viribus, imo supra vires, id est, ita, ut sibimetipsis incommodarent: deinde multum me & socios meos rogarunt, ne hoc recusaremus. Τὴν χάριν beneficium hoc, ut I. Corinth. XVI. 3. Rogarunt etiam, ut in nosmetipsos reciperemus partem laboris, istas pecunias deferendi ad sanctos in Judæa. Id enim διακονία dicitur, sicut & omne id, in quo aliis utiles nos reddimus, infra IX. 1. 12. I. Cor. XVI. 15.

Pro viribus, imo supra vires. Hoc enim, Theo- phylacto dicente, præfert simplicitatis abundantia, ut majora quis facere connitatur, quam ejus patia- tur facultas. Nec vero opus fuit exhortationum stimulis; sed ipsimet suapte sponte dederunt li- benter & liberaliter: Imo multis precibus nos obtestati sunt, ut Eleemosynam a se collectam, & sanctis in Judæa consecratam suscipere vellemus ad illos perferendam. Adjicere hic lubet B. Hülse- manni annotationem, vindicantem abusum Papi- starum: Macedones αὐθαίρετοι secundum subjectam materiam liberalitatis voluntariæ nihil faciunt pro naturali libertate arbitrii in spiritualibus, quod Sal- meron & Estius hic contendunt, pro exspoliatione liberorum & cognatorum bonorumque omnium ad- ditione ad fundationes monasteriorum, aut alias pias causas, ut Salmero Dub. 3. Gretserus de Germ. Princip. liberalitate in sedem Romanam cap. 3. sive pro justa perfectione bonis renatorum operibus inesse de- bita, quam ex attributo ὑπὲρ δύναμιν identidem col- ligit Salmero hic. Illud enim ὑπὲρ δύναμιν compara- tive & civiliter de liberalitate Macedonum, si cum aliorum liberalitate eam conferas, nimia, & præ- sentium opum facultates transcendente intelligitur, non autem de proportione seu mensura transcenden- te normam legis divinæ, de qua hic quæstio non est, neque de supererogationis, quæ vocant, operibus. Ca- pite I. 8. sese mala tolerasse ὑπὲρ δύναμιν non absolute seu humanitus sic loquendo. Excessum autem libera- litatis supra facultates adeo non laudat Paulus, ut eum expresse excludat v. 13. 14. Christi etiam sen- tentia de liberalitate in sacrificia seu corbana cum privatione sufficientium alimentorum satis manife- sta est Marci VII. 11. 12. Matth. XV. 4. 5. & sqq. ubi vide Johannis Feri Commentarium ex professo in- vehentem in prodigos Monasteriorum & similium Evergetas. Lege etiam Augustini Tom. III. cap. 4. 5. seq. de vita beata, ubi iisdem exemplis prodigalita- tis in res sacras demonstrat, non solum in his excedi posse, sed excessum tam esse in vitio, quam defectum. Confer etiam præfationes Bellarm. ad libr. de invo- cat. sanctorum.

## 8:5
Verse 5. And not as we hoped. They did not only that which we were hoping. For 'only' is understood.

But they gave themselves first to the Lord, and to us through the will of God. Not only their goods; but they also promised from their own number that they would give those who would go to Corinth. Here 'and' is put for 'then,' so that it may respond to the word 'first.' In that matter, he says, they devoted themselves both to Christ and to me. Through the will of God, God moving their minds. This expression is taken in various ways: for elsewhere it signifies divine governance, as in Romans 15:32, elsewhere a duty imposed by God.

The Apostle seems to hint at something more, namely that they not only spent themselves so much for Christ and the Apostles that they would accept from them as much as pleased the Apostle for the relief of the poor, but also that they emancipated themselves entirely to Christ and the Apostles according to the divine will, or rather God working such a pious affection in them. Which the Greeks noted. Theophylact: as if he were saying: For they did not, while intending most of all to distribute alms, neglect other duties as if blinded, but rather offered themselves to the Lord, being more inclined with an unhesitating mind to every work acceptable to God. Furthermore, they also delivered themselves to us, that is, being subject to us in all things by a certain divine nod, they preferred charity. Whence it happens that they do this by the will of God, not by any instinct of men. Photius, from Oecumenius, observes six things celebrated in this act of the Macedonians: First, that they contributed according to their strength. Second, that they did so beyond their strength. Third, that they were voluntary. Fourth, that it was with much beseeching. Fifth, that it was more than was hoped from them. Sixth, and the same greater than the rest, that they gave themselves to the Lord and his ministers, as Estius notes here.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ ὐ καθὼς ἠλπίσαμεν) Non hoc tantum fe- cere, quod sperabamus. Subauditur enim μόνον.

᾿Αλλ' ἑαυτὸς ἔδωκαν πρῶτον τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ ἡμῖν διὰ θελή- ματος Θε̊) Non bona tantum sua; sed & de suo numero polliciti sunt, se daturos, qui Corinthum irent. Hic καὶ po- nitur pro ἔπειτα, ut respondeat voci πρῶτον In ea re; in- quit, ipsi semet devoverunt & Christo & mihi. Διὰ θελή- ματος Θε̊, Deo ipsorum animos movente. Varie sumitur hæc loquutio: Alibi enim divinam gubernationem, ut Rom. XV. 32. alibi munus a Deo impositum significat.

Amplius quid videtur Apostolus innuere, quod nempe non tantum semetipsos ita Christo & Apostolis impenderint, ut quantum Apostolo placeret, in pauperum subsidium acciperet ab ipsis, sed etiam se totos Christo & Apostolis man- ciparint secundum divinam voluntatem, vel po- tius Deo tam pium affectum in ipsis operante. Quod Græci notarunt. Theophylactus: quasi dicat: Neque enim cum erogandis eleemosynis intenderent pluri- mum, veluti cæcati officia reliqua negligebant, sed Domino potius sese obtulere, in omne opus Deo acce- ptum animo non hæsitabundo propensiores. Quin etiam & nobis tradidere seipsos, hoc est cunctis in rebus nobis subjecti nutu quodam divino charitatem prætulere. Quo fit ut Dei voluntate, non ullo ho- minum instinctu id agant. Photius ex Oecume- nio sex observat Macedonum in hoc facto celebrata: Primum quod secundum vires contulerunt. Secundum quod supra vires. Tertium quod voluntarii. Quartum quod multa cum obtestatione. Quintum, quod supra, quam ab iis sperabatur. Sextum, idemque cæteris majus, quod seipsos dederunt Domino & ministris ejus, ut hic annotat Estius.

## 8:6
Verse 6. So that we urged Titus, that as he had begun, so he might also complete this benefit among you. They did this so that they might the more effectively ask me to send Titus to you, to fulfill that benefit which he began, namely, of exciting you to relieve the poverty of the brothers in Judea. He began, namely, when he was passing through you.

Not on account of the efficacy of the Macedonians' petition before the Apostle, who was easily moved, was that declaration of mind and piety made from their intention; but Paul testifies that he was moved by the same to solicit Titus's effort in this business, as Theophylact rightly says: So much, he says, did the Macedonians apply themselves earnestly to clemency and to that duty of contributing alms, that I, having perceived the thing itself, added my mind so that you might do likewise, lest you be inferior to them: And I urged Titus to undertake the journey to you, just as he himself began, that is, who before he was impelled by me, had intended to come to you.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Εἰς τὸ παρακαλέσαι ἡμᾶς Τίτον, ἵνα καθὼς προενήρξατο, ὕτω καὶ ἐπιτελέσῃ εἰς ὑμᾶς καὶ τὴν χάριν ταύτην) Fecerunt hoc, ut eo efficacius me rogarent, ut Titum ad vos mitterem, impleturum id beneficium quod cœpit, excitandi scilicet vos ad sublevandum fratrum in Judæa inopiam. Cœpit, nempe cum per vos transiret.

Non ob efficaciam petitionis Macedonum penes Apostolum, qui facile erat exorabilis, declaratio illa animi & pietatis ex intentione ipsorum fiebat; sed Paulus se eadem excitatum testatur ad solicitandam Titi in hoc negotio operam, ut recte Theophylactus: Adeo, inquit, Macedones enixe ad clementiam, & ad id conferendæ eleemosynæ munus se contulerunt, ut ego re ipsa perspecta adjecerim animum, ut itidem & vos faciatis, ne illis sitis inferiores: Et Titum hortatus sum ad vos iter arripere, quemadmodum & ipse cœpit, hoc est, qui priusquam esset per me impulsus, venire ad vos destinaverit.

## 8:7
Verse 7. But just as you abound in everything in faith. Paul was not ignorant of the art of rhetoricians, to move by praising. But it will be best to place a comma after 'in everything'; so that what he said to them in general, he may then explain by species. You excel in all things, first in faith, by believing those things which ought to be believed.

in speech) In instructing others.

καὶ γνώσει) By the knowledge of histories, poets, and other things, which can also have their use in teaching, as Paul shows in these epistles to the Corinthians.

καὶ πάσῃ σπουδῇ) Zeal for doing good things.

Καὶ τῇ ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγάπῃ) Ἐν ἡμῖν instead of εἰς ἡμᾶς. In that love which, from you—that is, from your mind—is borne, supply, toward us.

Ἵνα καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ χάριτι περισσεύητε, ὐ κατ' ἐπιταγὴν λέγω) I think these are best joined in this way: that in this beneficence also you may surpass others; I say this indeed, exhorting of course, yet I do not command.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ἐν παντὶ περισσεύετε πίστει) Non ignoravit Paulus artem Rhetorum, movere laudando. Optimum vero erit, post ἐν παντὶ ponere ὑποδιαστολὴν; ut, quod ei in genere dixit, deinde per species explicet. In omnibus excellitis, primum in fide, credendo ea quæ credi debent.

λόγῳ) In instituendis aliis.

καὶ γνώσει) Cognitione historiarum, Poëtarum, rerumque aliarum, quæ etiam in docendo suum habere usum possunt, ut Paulus in his ad Corinthios epistolis ostendit.

καὶ πάσῃ σπουδῇ) Studium ad agendas res bonas.

Καὶ τῇ ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγάπῃ) Ἐν ἡμῖν pro εἰς ἡμᾶς. In dilectione illa, quæ ex vobis, ex animo scilicet vestro, ad nos, supple, fertur.

Ἵνα καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ χάριτι περισσεύητε, ὐ κατ' ἐπιταγὴν λέγω) Ita hæc puto optime conjungi, ut in hac etiam beneficentia vincatis alios, id dico quidem, adhortans scilicet, non tamen impero.

## 8:8
Vers. 8. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἑτέρων σπουδῆς καὶ τὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀγάπης γνήσιον δοκιμάζων) I say this, of course, so that by the comparison of what the Macedonians have done, I may learn how sincere your love is, namely toward those brothers who are in Judea. As he used δοκιμάζειν here, so he said δοκιμὴν below regarding the same matter in IX. 13.

As he previously stirred the Corinthians to liberality indirectly by the example of the Macedonians, having recounted their praises; so now, openly exhorting them, he does not neglect their own praises. He does not, however, proclaim their temporal riches, which some think are connoted; but spiritual riches: (1) of faith, which apprehends Jesus Christ with all his benefits and treasures; (2) of the Word, which abounded among them by the voice and writings of the Apostles and other faithful fellow-ministers, and enriched them with gifts, 1 Cor. I. 6, 7; Col. III. 16; (3) of knowledge, not of philosophical things, which knowledge they had not received from the Apostles or through the preaching of the Gospel, but of divine things, which is had from Holy Scripture and is better than any treasure, Ps. CXIX. 77, 98; Prov. III. 14, 15; (4) of the study of piety, and also (5) of charity toward the Apostle and his colleagues. To the accumulation of which he wishes χάριν, grace or beneficence, to be added, so that, abounding in that also, they may become richer. The Vulgate has 'good nature' for τὸ γνήσιον, which error, as Cornelius a Lapide himself notes, signifies either 'ingenuous'—as Primasius, Sedulius, and Gagneus read—or the Greek word signifies 'ingenuity'.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἑτέρων σπουδῆς καὶ τὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀγάπης γνήσιον δοκιμάζων) Dico scilicet hoc, ut comparatione ejus, quod fecere Macedones, discam, quam sic sincera vestra dilectio, nempe in illos fratres, qui in Judæa sunt. Ut hic δοκιμάζειν, ita infra δοκιμὴν dixit in re eadem IX. 13.

Ut antea oblique exemplo Macedonum Corinthios, laudibus illorum recensitis, excitaret ad liberalitatem; ita jam aperte eosdem exhortans laudes ipsorum non negligit. Non autem opes ipsorum temporales prædicat, quas connotari nonnulli censent; sed divitias spirituales (1) fidei, quæ Jesum Christum cum omnibus ejus beneficiis ac thesauris apprehendit (2) Verbi, quod voce & scriptis Apostolorum, aliorum symmystarum fidelium penes istos exuberabat, eosque donis ditabat, 1. Corinth. I. 6. 7. Coloff. III. 16. (3) Cognitionis non rerum Philosophicarum, quam notitiam non acceperant ab Apostolis, vel per Evangelii præconium; sed rerum divinarum, quæ e scriptura sacra habetur, omnique thesauro potior est Psal. CXIX. 77. 98. Proverb. III. v. 14. 15. (4) studii pietatis, nec non (5) charitatis erga Apostolum & collegas ejus. Cujus in cumulum accedere vult χάριν gratiam vel beneficentiam, ut ea etiam abundantes ditiores evadant. Vulgata pro τὸ γνήσιον habet ingenium bonum, quod sphalma cum ingenuum, ut Primasius, Sedulius & Gagneus legunt, vel ingenuitatem significet vox Græca, notat ipse Cornel. a Lapide.

## 8:9
Verf. 9. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ] The beneficence of Christ in us, by whose example we also ought to be beneficent toward others.

That for our sake he became poor, being rich) That is, when he possessed that power of performing miracles of every kind, even of raising the dead, he nevertheless bore a person so humble that he did not even have a home of his own, Matt. VIII. 20. and that for the reason that it was conducive to our salvation: עני & דל are epithets of the Messiah.

That you by his poverty might become rich) That humility of Christ, having most perfect obedience as its companion, was the cause through which you have been led to true righteousness. You have received the gifts of the Spirit, you will receive eternal life.

The grace of the Lord, although it embraces his beneficence, yet imports something more: namely, the immense charity from which, for the sake of our salvation, he humbled himself and became poor, and that saving grace by which he spent his whole self for us, Tit. II. 11, 14. Nor does he excite us to beneficence by the example of Christ alone; but he alleges his merit, by which we are more effectively moved: Who being rich became poor for our sake, by which very thing his riches are first designated, that he was rich, not only because of his miraculous power; but because he existed in the form of God, full of all divine majesty and glory, obtaining all riches, as one to whom all things had been given into his hands, John III. 35, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden, Col. II. 3, who had all power, and to whom all things had been delivered by the Father, Matt. XI. 27. John XIII. 3, in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, Col. II. 9. (2) Voluntary poverty, which does not consist in the assumption of our flesh, which Theophylact also seems to refer to here, as Beza, Marloratus, and Pareus wish. For this in itself does not bring poverty, but rather the fullness of all divine riches, since it is established from the Scriptures that the hypostatic union brings the communication of the divine nature, of the hypostasis, and of divine dignities to the Word; but it consists in the emptying or kenosis of divine majesty and the humiliation of Christ made for a time for the sake of our redemption: and therefore it brings not only destitution, but also all things that pertain to the emptying of divine riches, not indeed as regards possession, but as regards use, concerning which Phil. II. The Apostle is not dealing here with the incarnation of the Son of God, but with the humiliation of Jesus Christ, that is, of the Son of God already incarnate. (3) The merit of the emptying and poverty of Christ: because he emptied himself not for his own sake, but for our sake, undergoing poverty and all other things in our place and for our good, which we were to undergo because of our apostasy from God, the supreme good; and therefore he suffered and even died for us, 2 Cor. V. 19, that he might free us from death and all other things which we had deserved by our sins; even from poverty, since we are to be rescued from it at last by the very act, and are to obtain heavenly wealth and riches and an abundance of all things by the merit of that very poverty, Rev. VII. 16, 17, XXI. 4, 7, Job X. 10, Psalm XXXVI. 9. (4) The fruit of the poverty of Christ, that believers in him are enriched in him with all spiritual riches, so that they lack nothing, 1 Cor. I. 5, 7, and are rich in God, 1 Tim. VI. 17, 18, Luke XII. 21, being future heirs of heavenly riches and treasures, Matt. VII. 20, Rom. VIII. 17, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Therefore Zechariah, ch. IX, commands the people of God to rejoice and exult, because the King Messiah comes to him poor: Whereas otherwise subjects can neither rejoice nor glory in the poverty of any earthly King. But the poverty of Christ was, as has been said, meritorious of eternal and heavenly riches, as B. Hunnius says. Estius, from Thomas, notes that this is said for two reasons, namely, for the sake of example and for the sake of a sacrament.

For the sake of example, indeed, because if Christ embraced poverty, we also ought to love and embrace it by his example. But for the sake of a sacrament, because whatever Christ did or endured, he did for our salvation. Whence, just as through the fact that he endured death we have been freed from eternal death and restored to life, so through the fact that he endured want in temporal things, we have been freed from the want of spiritual things and made rich in them. But the liberation from the indigence of temporal things was not to be passed over, just as from temporal death: because liberation from every curse which we have deserved through sin and the acquisition of every blessing must be attributed to Christ; and although believers often labor here in want, God nevertheless provides for them, as much as is fitting for their eternal salvation, because of our unique mediator and intercessor; to whose merit it must also be attributed that we are not to be left in eternal death and corruption, nor in perpetual destitution, but are to be raised to heavenly riches and life. Gregory Nazianzen speaks excellently in Oration I on Easter: Christ became poor, that we might be enriched by his poverty; he took the form of a servant, that we might receive freedom; he descended, that we might be raised up; he was tempted, that we might conquer; he was humbled, that he might affect us with glory; he died, that he might save; he ascended, that he might draw to himself those who were cast down in the fall of sin. The same Estius denies that temporal kingdom and dominion over the whole world befit Christ as a man, since temporal administration is attributed with little convenience to him who chose the lack of temporal goods. But just as that choice was free, and was made when Christ was rich voluntarily; so it did not import an absolute abdication of power and riches: but a kenosis or emptying, and that not of possession, because even in the highest degree of emptying all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in him; but of the use or plenary usurpation: which, however, was followed by exaltation, by which he sat down at the right hand of the throne of God, Phil. II. 8, Heb. XII. 2.

Latin:

Verf. 9. Γινώσκετε γὰρ τὴν χάριν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ] Beneficentiam Christi in nobis, cujus exemplo & nos bene- fici in alios esse debemus.

Ὅτι δι' ἡμᾶς ἐπτώχευσε πλούσιος ὢν) Id est, cùm vi il- la polleret, omnis generis miracula patrandi, etiam mor- tuos resuscitandi, personam tamen gessit tàm humilem, ut ne domum quidem haberet propriam, Matth. VIII. 20. id- que propterea, quod id ad salutem nostram conduceret: עני & דל epitheta Messiae.

Ἵνα ὑμεῖς τῇ ἐκείνου πτωχείᾳ πλουτήσητε) Illa Christi humilitas, perfectissimam obedientiam habens comitem, causa fuit, per quam vos ad veram justitiam perducti estis. Dona spiritus accepistis, vitam accipietis aeternam.

Χάρις τοῦ κυρίου etsi beneficentiam ejus comple- ctatur: amplius quid tamen importat, charita- tem nempe immensam, ex qua nostrae salutis causa se humiliavit, & pauper factus est, & gratiam illam σωτήριον, qua se totum impendit nobis Tit. II. 11. 14. Neque exemplo tantum Christi ad beneficen- tiam excitat; sed meritum ejus, quo efficacius mo- vemur, allegat: Qui πλούσιος ὢν ἐπτώχευσε δι' ἡ- μᾶς, cum dives esset, pauper factus est propter nos, quo ipso primum ejus divitiae designantur, quod πλούσιος fuerit, non ob vim tantum θαυματουργι- κὴν; sed quod ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ in forma Dei extiterit, omni Majestate & gloria divina plenus, omnes di- vitias obtinens, utpote cui data erant omnia in ma- nus Johann. III. 35. in quo omnes thesauri sapientiae & cognitionis absconditi erant Coloss. II. 3. qui omnem potestatem habebat, & cui omnia tradita erant à Patre Matth. XI. 27. Joh. XIII. 3. in quo ha- bitabat πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματι- κῶς Col. II. 9. (2) Voluntaria paupertas, quae non in carnis nostrae assumptione, quam & Theophylactus huc referre videtur, consistit, ut vult Beza, Marlo- ratus, Pareus. Haec enim per se non affert pauper- tatem, sed potius divitiarum omnium divinarum plenitudinem, siquidem unionem hypostaticam communicationem divinae naturae, hypostaseos, & ἀξιωμάτων divinorum τῷ λόγῳ inferre è scri- pturis constat; sed in exinanitione vel κενώσει Maje- statis divinae & ταπεινώσει Christi ad tempus re- demptionis nostrae causa facta: ideoque non solum egestatem infert, sed & omnia, quae ad exinanitio- nem divitiarum divinarum, non quidem quoad κτῆσιν, sed quoad χρῆσιν pertinent, de quibus Phil. II. Non de Filii Dei incarnatione; sed de Jesu Christi, hoc est, Filii Dei jam incarnati humilia- tione hic agit Apostolus. (3) Exinanitionis & pau- pertatis Christi meritum: quia non sui causa; sed propter nos sese ἐκένωσε, nostri loco & nostro bono paupertatem & alia omnia subeundo, quae nobis propter apostasiam à Deo summo bono subeun- da erant; ideoque passus, & mortuus etiam pro no- bis est 2. Cor. V. 19. ut nos à morte, omnibusque a- liis, quae nos peccatis meriti eramus, liberaret; etiam à paupertate, siquidem ex ea actu ipso tan- dem eripiendi coelestes opes ac divitias, omnium- que rerum abundantiam paupertatis ipsius merito consequuturi simus Ap. VII. 16. 17. XXI. 4. 7. Job. X. 10. Psalm. XXXVI. 9. (4) Paupertatis Christi fru- ctum, quod nempe credentes in ipsum ditentur in ipso omnibus divitiis spiritualibus, adeò ut nulla in re egeant 1. Corinth. I. 5. 7. & divites sint in Deo 1. Tim. VI. 17. 18. Luc. XII. 21. futuri haeredes divitia- rum & thesaurorum coelestium Matth. VII, 20. Rom. VIII. 17. 1. Cor. XV. 28. Ideo jubet Zacharias, c. IX. laetari & exultare populum Dei, quod ad illum Rex Messias veniat pauper: Cum quidem alias de Re- gis alicujus terreni paupertate nec laetari nec gloria- ri possint subditi. At Christi paupertas fuit, ut dictum est, aeternarum & coelestium divitiarum meritoria, ut B. Hunnius. Estius è Thoma notat; dici hac pro- pter duo, nempe propter exemplum, & sacramentum.

Propter exemplum quidem, quia si Christus amplexus est paupertatem, & nos illius exemplo eam dilige- re & amplecti debemus. Propter sacramentum au- tem, quia quaecunque Christus egit aut sustinuit pro nostra salute fecit. Vnde quemadmodum per hoc, quod mortem sustinuit, liberati sumus à morte ater- na ac vite restituti, sic per hoc, quod sustinuit in- opiam in temporalibus, liberati sumus ab inopia rerum spiritualium & facti earum divites. Sed praetermittenda non erat liberatio ab indigentia re- rum temporalium, uti & à morte temporali: quia & ab omni maledicto, quod per peccatum me- ruimus, liberatio & omnis benedictionis acquisi- tio Christo accepta referenda; & tametsi hic in- opia saepe laborent fideles, Deus tamen ipsis, quantum saluti ipsorum convenit sempiternae, prospicit propter μεσίτην καὶ ἱκέτην nostrum uni- cum; cujus merito etiam tribuendum, quod nec in morte aeterna & corruptione, nec in perpetua egestate relinquendi, sed ad divitias coelestes & vitam resuscitandi simus. Praeclare Gregorius Na- zianzenus orat. I. in Pascha: Pauper factus est Christus, ut nos illius paupertate ditescamus; servi formam accepit, ut nos libertatem recipiamus; de- scendit, ut evehamur; tentatus est, ut vincamus; humilitatus est, ut nos gloria afficiat; mortuus est, ut servet; ascendit, ut ad seipsum trahat bumi pro- volutos in peccati lapsu. Negat idem Estius Chri- sto ut homini regnum & dominationem tempo- ralem totius mundi convenire, siquidem tempo- ralis administratio parum convenienter attribua- tur ei, qui honorum temporalium inopiam ele- gerit. Sed uti electio illa libera erat, & facta est, cum dives esset Christus voluntariè; ita ea non abdicationem omnimodam potestatis & divitia- rum: sed κένωσιν vel evacuationem, eamque non τῆς κτήσεως vel possessionis, quia in ipso etiam in summo exinanitionis gradu habitabat omnis ple- nitudo Deitatis; sed τῆς χρήσεως vel usurpationis plenariae importabat: quam verò sequebatur ὑ- περύψωσις, quâ consedit in dextrâ throni Dei Phil. II. 8. Ebr. XII. 2.

## 8:10
Vers. 10. κὶι γνώμην ἐν τούτῳ δίδωμι). It is indeed a command of Christ to help the poor, but some measure of liberty is left, which the Macedonians had done; it was such that it could be urged rather than commanded. Thus we had γνώμην δίδωμι concerning celibacy in 1 Cor. VII. 25.

Τῦτο γὰρ ὑμῖν συμφέρει) It is expedient for you to maintain the good reputation which you have begun to attain. I shall now set your own example before you. It is not beautiful to hear. You began better than you end: The last things differ from the first.

It was not so much expedient for a good reputation as for a gratuitous divine retribution. For Paul teaches that this munificence of the Corinthians brings no detriment to their possessions; but rather increases and establishes them in the same, so that they may be constant and stable through the blessing of God. For alms that proceed from faith have ample promises of divine retribution not only in this life, but also in the future, Matt. XXV, Luke XIV.

Οἵτινες ὐ μόνον τὸ ποιῆσαι, ἀλλὰ κὶ τὸ θέλειν προενήρξασθε ἀπὸ πέρυσι) This statement can be defended in some sense: but if anyone compares the following, he will see that it is an inverted manner of speaking; such as many have been noted by learned men in Roman Civil Law and in other writers, where in the comparison of disparate things, that which ought to have followed in natural order proceeds: and thus both the Syrian and the Arab have correctly interpreted this passage. Πέρυσι is translated in the glossary as 'in the past year': although it is also accustomed to be used of a more ancient time. The reason, however, why the Corinthians had previously contributed something, but very little, to help the brothers in Judea, seems to have been that many were exhausted by confiscations or fines, to which that which we had in 1 Cor. X. 13 refers.

Latin:

Vers. 10. κὶι γνώμην ἐν τούτῳ δίδωμι). Est quidem prae- ceptum Christi, juvare pauperes, sed modus aliquis li- bertati relinquitur, quod Macedones fecerant; tale erat, ut suaderi magis, quam juberi posset. Sic γνώμην δίδωμι de coelibatu habuimus 1. Cor. VII. 25.

Τῦτο γὰρ ὑμῖν συμφέρει) Expedit vobis tueri bonam famam, quam coepistis consequi. Vestrum jam vobis ex- emplum proponam. Non est pulchrum audire. Coepisti melius quam definis: Vltima primis — Diftant.

Non tàm expediebat ad bonam famam, quàm ad retributionem divinam gratuitam. Docet enim Paulus, hanc munificentiam Corinthiorum nul- lum afferre detrimentum possessionibus illorum; sed in eodem potius adaugere & stabilire, ut sint ex benedictione Dei constantes & stabiles. Ha- bent enim eleemosynae ex fide profectae amplas divinae retributionis promissiones non solum in hac vitâ; sed etiam in futura Matth. XXV. Luc. XIV.

Οἵτινες ὐ μόνον τὸ ποιῆσαι, ἀλλὰ κὶ τὸ θέλειν προενήρξασθε ἀπὸ πέρυσι) Potest aliquo sensu defendi hoc dictum: sed si quis sequentia comparet, videbit esse loquendi genus inver- sum; qualia multa in Jure civili Romano, in aliisque scri- ptoribus, à Viris eruditis notata sunt, ubi in disparium com- paratione procedit, quod naturali ordine subsequi debuit: & ita hunc locum rectè interpretati sunt & Syrus & Arabs. Πέρυσι in glossario vertitur, anno praeterito: Quanquam so- let & usurpari de vetustiori tempore. Causa autem cur Co- rinthii antehac aliquid quidem, sed pauxillum contulif- sent ad juvandos in Judaea fratres, videtur fuisse, quod confiscationibus aut mulctis plurimi essent exhausti, quo spectat id, quod habuimus 1. Cor. X. 13.

## 8:11
Vers. 11. Now therefore also complete the doing) Now finish what has been well begun. Paul likes, as do the Greeks, to place infinitives in place of nouns, and that with the neuter Article.

That just as the readiness of the willing) That was to be praised, when the strength was not sufficient. πρόθυμος נדיב לב 2 Paralip. XXIX. 31.

So also the completing) Let it be present, of course, concerning which ellipsis we have already treated several times.

Out of that which you have) Out of the abundance, which is now greater for you than it was then לאל יד.

There is no reason for us to admit an inverted manner of speaking. Our people interpret it very well, and among them the blessed Hunnius. For because he first says the Corinthians began not only to do, but also to will, he refers to the voluntary and prompt execution of it, which he had commanded in 1 Cor. XVI. 2, concerning setting aside alms every Sabbath; nor does he understand the willing simply; but with a promptness of mind and alacrity, which in this kind of liberality is more acceptable to God than if one gives by the very act, but unwillingly. The latter willing, however, designates the will to continue also henceforth what was well begun, as if he were saying: You made a praiseworthy beginning last year; but at the same time you declared your most ready will for the future, that you also have the spirit to progress constantly in this kind of duty. But now also complete it by the deed: Thus Theophylact, you did not only give a beginning to the matter to be carried out, but also to the willing, that is, you are executing the matter spontaneously and easily and with no one urging you. But now I advise you this, that you finish the work already begun, so that just as the mind of the will is prompt, so also may it be of the completing from that which you have: Namely, that some good deed may not consist only of promptness and will, but that it may be brought to an end. For just as the will itself renders the mind more inclined to carry out a matter, and thus deeds are completed out of the abundance of things. Whoever therefore possesses goods by fortune, let him both complete the matter itself and impart the alms, but he who has nothing, carries out the benefit by his will. Just as elsewhere, as the blessed Hunnius says again, in any praiseworthy deed these four things generally concur: 1. will, 2. then the beginning of the deed itself, 3. Continuation or progression 4. perfection or bringing to an end. Thus after he had spoken about the will of the Corinthians, and had borne witness to them that they had already begun to do, and had now exhorted them to progress, it remained that he should warn them not to desist from what was begun before they had brought it to the desired end and completed it. For this is what he understands when he commands to complete what they have begun. He adds, however, out of that which you have, by which he again indicates that he does not desire them to be burdened beyond what their means allow. Nor is it said inconveniently with Cajetan and Estius that the Apostle signifies that the Corinthians began not moved by the example of the Macedonians, and that for this reason, lest the Macedonians should take it ill that they were set before them as an example, as if he were saying, in another part you are superior to them, because you began both to do and to will before them, although they have already anticipated you in completing. This sense is confirmed by that which he writes in the following chapter: I boast of you to the Macedonians, that Achaia has been ready since last year, and your emulation has provoked many. For the sense of Cajetan, it makes that the Apostle in 1 Cor. XVI did not say, as I have ordained to the Churches of Macedonia; but only, as I have ordained to the Churches of Galatia, because at that time he had not yet ordained to the Churches of Macedonia that of which he speaks there, as Estius holds here. Concerning the word ἀπὸ πέρυσι, Camerarius holds this: A preposition with an Adverb, just as ἀπ’ ἄρτι, or it will be written as one word, just as πρόπαλαι. However, a certain time is not signified. You who long ago, before others, began not only to do, but also to will. ὅπως καθάπερ lacks γένοιτο, so that the elaboration of the work may correspond to the prompt will according to the means of each one. But the slowness of the Corinthians compared to the Macedonians in collecting the Alms is tacitly criticized, if you listen to Estius, as those who had not yet finished a matter begun a year ago.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Νυνὶ δὲ καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐπιτελέσατε) Nunc per- ficite, quod bene inchoatum est. Amat Paulus, ut & Græ- ci infinitivos ponere vice nominum idque cum Articulo neutro.

Ὅπως καθάπερ ἡ προθυμία τοῦ θέλειν) Ea laudanda fuit, cum vires non suppeterent. πρόθυμος נדיב לב 2. Paralip. XXIX. 31.

Οὕτω καὶ τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι) Adsit scilicet, de quali ellipsi e- gimus jam aliquoties.

Ἐκ τοῦ ἔχειν) Ex copia, quæ nunc vobis major est, quam tunc erat לאל יד.

Non est, quod admittamus inversum loquendi genus. Optime interpretantur nostri, & ex his B. Hunnius. Nam quod primo dicit Corinthios cœpisse non modo facere; sed etiam velle, respicit executionem ejus voluntariam & promptam, quod mandarat 1. Corinth. XVI. 2. de seponendis per singula sabbata eleemosynis; nec τὸ velle simplici- ter intelligit; sed cum promptitudine animorum & alacritate, quæ in hoc genere liberalitatis ac- ceptior est Deo, quam si quis ipso facto det; sed invitus. Posterius autem velle designat voluntatem porro etiam continuandi quod bene cœptum erat, quasi dicat: Vos anno superiore proximo fecistis ini- tium laudabile; sed simul declarastis propensissimam vestram voluntatem in futurum, quod etiam ani- mus vobis sit in hoc officii genere constanter progre- di. Nunc autem & facto perficite: Ita Theophy- lactus, non modo solum ad rem peragendam dedistis initium, quin etiam ad velle, hoc est, sponte & facilis & nemine impellente rem exequimini. Nunc autem vobis id consulo, ut opus jam cœptum termi- netis, ut quemadmodum promptus est animus vo- luntatis, ita sit & perficiendi ex eo, quod habetis: Vi- delicet ut non promptitudine tenus & voluntate con- stet facinus aliquod bonum, sed ad finem ut traduca- tur. Nam quemadmodum ipsa voluntas animum reddit ad rem gerendam propensiorem, & sic facta ex rerum copia perficiuntur. Quicunque ergo for- tuna bonis potitur, & rem ipsam perficiat & eleemo- synam impartiatur, qui vero nil habet, voluntate exequitur beneficium. Quemadmodum alias, di- cente iterum B. Hunnio, in quovis laudabili facto hæc fere quatuor concurrunt 1. voluntas 2. tum ipsius facti initium 3. Continuatio sive progressio 4. perfe- ctio seu ad finem perductio. Sic postquam de volun- tate dixerat Corinthiorum, & testimonium illis per- hibuerat, quod jam cœpissent facere, & nunc ad pro- grediendum exhortatus fuerat, reliquum erat, ut moneret eos, ne desisterent prius cœpto quam ad opta- tum finem id perduxissent ac perfecissent. Hoc enim intelligit, cum jubet ἐπιτελέσαι quod inchoarint. Ad- dit autem ἐκ τοῦ ἔχειν, quo rursum indicat, non se cupere illos, supra quam facultates ferant, gravatos. Nec incommode cum Cajetano & Estio dicitur, Apostolum significare, quod Corinthii inceperint non exemplo Macedonum moti, idque propterea, ne moleste ferrent Macedones sibi in exemplum pro- poni, quasi dicat, alia parte vos estis illis potiores, quia prius quam illi & facere & velle cœpistis, quam- vis illi jam vos prævenerint perficiendo. Sensum hunc confirmat illud, quod scribit capite sequenti: De vobis glorior apud Macedones, quoniam & Achaia parata est ab anno præterito, & vestra æmulatio provocavit plurimos. Pro sensu Cajetani facit, quod Apostolus 1. Cor. XVI. non dixit, sicut ordinavi Ec- clesiis Macedoniæ; sed duntaxat, sicut ordinavi Ec- clesiis Galatiæ, quia tunc Ecclesiis Macedoniæ non dum ordinaverat id, de quo ibi loquitur, ut hic ha- bet Estius. De voce ἀπὸ πέρυσι Camerarius ita ha- bet: Præpositio cum Adverbio, sicut ἀπ’ ἄρτι, vel ὑφὲν scribetur, sicut πρόπαλαι. Non significatur au- tem certum tempus. Qui jamdudum præ cæteris non modo facere, sed velle etiam cœpistis. ὅπως κα- θάπερ deest γένοιτο, ut promptæ voluntati respondeat elaboratio operis pro facultatibus uniuscujusque. Ta- citè vero taxatur, Eftium si audias, Corinthiorum tarditas præ Macedonibus in colligenda Eleemosy- na, ut qui rem ante annum inceptam nondum absol- vissent.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. For if the readiness is present according to what one has, it is acceptable, not according to what one does not have) Here also some word is to be understood, as in 1 Cor. XIV, 34; 1 Tim. IV, 3. The will is pleasing to God according to one's means: Beyond one's means it is not required. God does not demand that which is impossible.

What he just called voluntary, he now calls readiness, and makes it as it were the soul of alms, as Schmidius does here.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Εἰ γὰρ ἡ προθυμία πρόκειται καθὸ ἂν ἔχῃ τις ἐυ- πρόσδεκτος, ὐ καθὸ ὀυκ ἔχει) Etiam hic verbum aliquod sub- audiendum est, ut 1. Cor. XIV, 34. 1. Tim. IV. 3. Grata est Deo voluntas pro facultatibus: Supra facultates non exigitur. Non postulat Deus id quod impossibile est.

Quod modo dixit ἀυθαίρετον, jam vocat προθυ- μίαν, eamque quasi animam eleemosynarum fa- cit, ut hic Schmidius.

## 8:13
Vers. 13. For not that there should be relief for others, but for you affliction) That is to be understood as required. He says more than he had said; not only have I not demanded impossibilities, but not even things that would be burdensome beyond measure. Seneca: I will give to the needy, but so that I myself do not become needy.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οὐ γὰρ ἵνα ἄλλοις ἄνεσις, ὑμῖν δὲ θλίψις) Sub- audiendum illud exigitur. Plus dicit, quam dixerat, non modo impossibilia non exegi, sed nec quæ supra modum molesta essent. Seneca: Dabo egenti, sed ut ipse non egeam.

## 8:13
At the time) Now when that vexation among you ceases. It is a locution not infrequent among the LXX interpreters, as Gen. XXIX. 34. הפעם.

Your abundance for their lack) Supply 'may become', by zeugma. For that word follows: 'abundance' is יתרון, 'lack' is חסרון. The sense is that which is in Xenophon's Cyrus: 'Whatever I see as an abundance of my wealth, with that I shall satisfy the needs of my friends.' Livy: 'so that from that which flows into your resources, you may sustain the necessities of others.'

Theophylact has it thus: For it is not necessary that, so that others may be in luxury through your rest and leisure, you should impart something beyond your strength, whence you might suffer indigence and your own family affairs be rendered more straitened, although the Lord praised the widow for this, because she had contributed her whole substance, which, however, the Apostle by no means contends for from these people at present, both because the Corinthians were still weaker, and because they were both abounding in wealth, and so, if each were to contribute according to their strength, the collection would be very copious and remarkable. But this restriction concerning the bestowing of alms is to be properly observed: That there may not be ἄνεσις (relaxation) for others, but θλίψις (affliction) for you: Which, although it is applied in the hypothesis to alms, nevertheless contains a general rule, that one must do good to others in such a way that no clear loss is brought upon us and our own, because everyone is bound to look after his own, 1 Tim. V. 8. R. Hunnius demonstrated its use here in a disputation on usury, which may be compared by anyone who wishes.

That their abundance may become for your lack) So that if at any time that famine, which now lies upon Judea, shall have ceased, and by chance something adverse happens to you, that which is said may come to pass for you:

He has safeguards in adversity, who lends in prosperity.

Latin:

Ἐν τῷ καιρῷ) Jam cum cesset illa in vos vexatio. Est loquutio non infrequens LXX. interpretibus, ut Gen. XXIX. 34. הפעם.

Τὸ ὑμῶν περίσσευμα εἰς τὸ ἐκείνων ὑσέρημα) Supple γένηται, per πρόζευγμα. Sequitur enim ea vox: περίσσευμα est יתרון, ὑσέρημα חסרון. Sensus is qui in Cyro Xeno- phontis: Ἃ ἂν ἴδω περίσσε ὄντα τῶν ἐμῶν χρημάτων, τέτοις τὰς ἐνδείας τῶν φίλων ἐξαρκέσωμαι. Livius: ut ex eo, quod af- fluit opibus vestris, sustineatis necessitates aliorum.

Theophylactus ita habet: Neque enim ut alii per quietem & otium in deliciis sint, necessarium est præter vires aliquid ipsi impertiatis, unde & indigen- tiam patiamini, & angustior res vestra familiaris reddatur, tametsi Dominus eo viduam laudavit, quia omnem substantiam contulisset, quod tamen impræsentiarum Apostolus ab his haudquaquam contendit, tum quia adhuc infirmiores erant Corin- thii, tum quia & opibus affluebant, & ita, ut si pro viribus singuli collaturi essent, copiosa admo- dum & insignis futura esset collatio. Probe autem observanda est hæc de elargitione eleemosynæ restrictio: Ne aliis sit ἄνεσις relaxatio, vobis vero θλίψις afflictio: Quæ etsi in hypothesi ad eleemosy- nas adhibeatur, generalem tamen regulam conti- net, sic aliis benefaciendum esse, ut nobis non luculentum aliquod damnum nostrisque affera- tur, quia tenetur quisque sua respicere 1. Tim. V. 8. Cujus usum in disputatione de usuris hic monstra- vit R. Hunnius, qui conferatur sicui lubet.

Ἵνα κὴ τὸ ἐκείνων περίσσευμα γένηται εἰς τὸ ὑμῶν ὑσέρημα) Ut si quando fames illa, quæ nunc Judææ incumbit, cessa- verit, & vobis forte aliquid acciderit adversi, eveniat vobis id quod dicitur:

Habet in adversis præsidia, qui in secundis commodat.

## 8:14
Vers. 14. But by equality) The same right for Actius, as for Titius.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἰσότητος) Idem jus Actio, quod Ti- tio.

## 8:14
That there may be equality) That is, that duties may be mutual, just as they ought to be among friends.

Equality is urged here, as B. Hunnius notes, understood not according to arithmetic proportion, but geometric, that is, the Apostle does not wish for contributions to be made from that abundance so that the poor in Judea may be equal in wealth to the Corinthians (for this would be arithmetic proportion) but, as Paul himself explains, so that the abundance of the Corinthian Christians in Achaia and Macedonia may supply the lack of the needy brethren. For this equality consists not in the quality of goods, but in the use of the same, which is the sustenance of this life. Camerarius has it thus: Therefore, either a regard will be had geometrically of time, so that, just as this time is theirs, so another may be yours; or of the thing, so that as you spend your resources on them, so they may spend their effort in doctrine on you. Or even of communication according to harmonic mean. So that he who abounds may bestow upon the needy, which can be rightly established concerning the reason of excess and deficiency. As if something should be taken from the abundant, to be distributed, for thus there will be equality.

The gloss of the Papists on the words of the Apostle, that 'your abundance may be a supply for their want,' is by no means appropriate, in that they maintain these things are to be understood of spiritual matters, for the sake of their heresy concerning the merits of the saints, that the less holy may be helped by them in the future life, as can be seen in Estius: as if it were said, in this life your temporal abundance may supply their temporal want, so that in turn at some time, namely in the future life, their spiritual abundance may become a supply for your spiritual want, Luke 16. For here both 'relief' and 'affliction' pertain to this life: Likewise also that equality which the Apostle inculcates, and also the application of the collection of Manna, Exod. 16, which in no way agree with the state of the future life.

Latin:

Ὅπως γένηται ἰσότης) Id est, ut mutua sint officia, quemadmodum inter amicos esse debent.

Æqualitas hic urgetur, notante B. Hunnio, non juxta proportionem Arithmeticam, sed geometri- cam intellecta, id est, non vult Apostolus in ea co- pia contribui, ut pauperes in Judæa sint opibus æ- quales Corinthiis (hæc enim esset Arithmetica pro- portio) sed quemadmodum Paulus exponit ipse, ut ab- undantia Corinthiorum Christianorum in Achaia & Macedonia suppleat egenorum fratrum inopiam. Æqualitas enim hæc consistit non in qualitate bono- rum, sed eorundem usu, qui est hujus vitæ sustentatio. Camerarius ita habet: Vel respectus igitur γεωμετρι- κῶς habebitur temporis, ut, quemadmodum hoc tem- pus illorum est, ita alterum sit vestrum; Vel rei, ut impenditis vos illis facultates, sic impendant ipsi vo- bis operam doctrinæ. Vel etiam communicationis se- cundum ἁρμονικὴν μεσότητα. Ut qui abundat lar- giatur egenti, id quod de ratione ὑπεροχῆς & ἐλλεί- ψεως recte constitui poterit. Ut si dematur de abun- dante, quod distribuatur, ita enim erit æqualitas.

Nullatenus autem convenit Pontificiorum glos- sa verborum Apostoli, ut & illorum abundan- tia vestra inopia sit supplementum, quod haec de spiritualibus accipienda sint, quam haeresi suae de meritis sanctorum quod illis in futuro seculo mi- nus sancti juventur, obtendunt, ut apud Estium videre est: quasi dicatur, in hoc seculo vestra tem- poralis abundantia suppleat illorum temporalem inopiam, ut vicissim aliquando, nimirum in futu- ro seculo spiritualis illorum abundantia, vestra spi- ritualis inopiae supplementum fiat Luc. XVI. Nam hic & ἄνεσις & θλίψις pertinent ad hoc seculum: Similiter etiam aequalitas illa, quam inculcat A- postolus, nec non applicatio collectionis Manna Ex. XVI. quae statui de futuro seculo nullo pacto congruunt.

## 8:15
Verse 15. 'As it is written, he that had much had nothing over, and he that had little had no lack.' The interpreters of the LXX, Exod. 16:18, use almost the same words: 'He that had much had nothing over, and he that had less had no lack.' It is understood after 'much' and after 'less' that 'having' is implied. An excellent allegory of the history of the Manna. Philo also saw it in his allegories: 'And concerning the Manna it is, and concerning every gift which God bestows upon our race, it is good to take what is numbered and measured, and not to take what is beyond us, which is greed. This the soul gathers from day to day, so that it may not show itself to be the guardian of goods, but the bountiful God.' And in the book, 'Who is the heir of divine things,' when he had already brought forth the said words from the LXX interpreters, he adds: 'When they used the proportion in a wonderful and much-contested manner.' The communion of saints, which we profess in the creed, also looks to this.

He introduces, says Theophylact, what had been done among the Jews when they gathered Manna, so that he may argue how this equalization is made. For he who abounds in many things, a wealthy man, when he has given what is left over to one who has little, neither do his own things increase, nor do they decrease for him who possesses few, inasmuch as he has received them from the rich man, which same thing can be said of the confidence which is accustomed to be had in God from the best actions of life. He accomplishes something else besides, which is greater. For he reveals to the rich, just as with the Manna, whether one had gathered more or less, they were found to have had the same measure, with God punishing immoderate greed. Do not, therefore, you also desire greater and more things.

PART II.

Commendation of Titus and his companions appointed for the alms.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καθὼς γέγραπται, ὁ τὸ πολὺ ἐκ ἐπλεόνα- σε, καὶ ὁ τὸ ὀλίγον ὐκ ἐλαττόνησε) Interpretes LXX. Exod. XVI. 10. iisdem prope verbis: ἐκ ἐπλεόνασεν ὁ τὸ πολὺ, καὶ ὁ τὸ ἔλαττον ὐκ ἐλαττόνησε. Subauditur post τὸ πολὺ & post τὸ ἔλαττον ἔχων. Egregia ἀλληγορία historiae de Manna. Vidit eam & Philo in allegoriis: κὴ ἐπὶ τῆ Μάννα ἐςὶ, κὴ ἐπὶ πάσης δωρεᾶς, ἣν ὁ Θεὸς δωρεῖται τῷ γένει ἡμῶν, καλὸν τὸ ἐνάριθμον κὴ μεμετρημένον, κὴ μὴ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς λαμβάνειν πλεονεξία. Τῦτό γε τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας εἰς εἰς ἡμέραν συναγαγότα ἡ ψυχὴ, ἵνα μὴ ἑαυτὴν φύλακα τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀλλὰ τὸν φιλό- δωρον Θεὸν ἀποφήνῃ. Et in libro, quis sit haeres rerum divi- narum, cum dicta jam verba ex LXX. Interpp. protulisset, addit: Ἡνίκα τὸ τῆς ἀναλογίας ἐχρήσαντο θαυμαςῷ κὴ περι- μαχήτῳ μόρῳ. Spectat & huc ea, quam in symbolo profite- mur, sanctorum communio.

Inducit, inquit Theophylactus, quod gestum apud Judaeos fuerat, cum Manna legerent, ut ar- guat, quo pacto fiat aequatio haec. Nam qui multis abundat vir opulentus, cum pauca habenti, quod superest, dederit, nec sua accrescunt, nec illi decre- scunt, qui paucis potiatur, utpote qui a divite ea acceperit, quod idem dici de fiducia potest, quae in Deo ex optimis vitae actionibus haberi solet. Aliud praeterea quiddam peragit majus. Aperit namque divitibus, quemadmodum Manna, sive qui plus collegisset, sive qui minus eandem habuisse mensu- ram inventi sint, Deo immoderatam cupiditatem castigante. Nolite ergo & vos majora & plura con- cupiscere.

PARS II.

Commendatio Titi & sociorum ad Eleemosy- nas ordinatorum.

## 8:16
Verse 16. 'But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus.' See how he refers everything to God, the author of good things, as also above in 8:1.

When he had discoursed concerning the alms, what things were necessarily to be said, he finally praises those who had been sent to receive it, so that, with every suspicion of avarice removed from them, he might lead them to a greater readiness for contributing: but Paul praises Titus, because he had obtained the primacy among those who were destined for this matter, and asserts that the same man had been stirred up by the work of God to administer a matter of this kind; inasmuch as He had injected into him the same solicitude that He had into himself. Wherefore he exhorts them to be more liberal in contributing, just as if he were saying: If it is certain that God stirred up Titus for the duty of this ministry (under his person God Himself demands it), you ought therefore to contribute gifts that are worthy of God, and to share alms with those laboring in want, as Theophylact says here.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ τῷ διδόντι τὴν ἀυτὴν σπεδὴν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ Τίτυ) Vide ut omnia ad bonorum auctorem Deum referat, ut & supra VIII. 1.

Cum de eleemosyna; quae essent necessario dicen- da, disseruisset, laudat demum, qui eam erant ad recipiendum transmissi, ut omni ab his avaritiae suspicione submota, ad majorem illos induceret con- ferendi promptitudinem: Titum vero, quia pri- matum hos inter, qui essent ad eam rem destinati, obtinuisset, collaudat Paulus, asseritque eundem ad hujusmodi rem administrandam Dei fuisse opera excitatum; quippe qui eandem illi, quam sibi, inje- cerit solicitudinem. Quocirca illos hortatur, ut li- beraliores sint in conferendo, perinde ac si dicat: Si constat, Deum ad id ministerii munus Titum exci- tavisse, (sub hujus persona Deus ipse deposcit) de- betis ergo, quae Deo sunt digna, conferre munera, & eleemosynam partiri inopia laborantibus, ut hic Theophylactus.

## 8:17
Verse 17. 'For he accepted the exhortation.' That one, concerning which above in verse 6. 'But being more forward, he went of his own accord unto you.' The sense is: Titus, when I exhorted him to undertake this journey, showed that he had anticipated my desires, and of his own accord had already desired it. 'Of his own accord,' that is, 'willingly,' as we said above in verse 3.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὅτι τὴν μὲν παράκλησιν ἐδέξατο) Illam, de qua supra 6. Σπεδαιότερος δὲ ὑπάρχων ἀυθαίρετος ἐξῆλθε πρὸς ἡμᾶς) Sensus est: Titus, cum eum hortarer, ut hoc iter susciperet, ostendit se praevenisse mea desideria, & sua sponte jam id cupiisse. Ἀυθαίρετος, id est, ἑκυσιαζόμενος, ut diximus su- pra v. 3.

## 8:18
Verse 18. 'And we have sent with him the brother, whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches.' It was the custom of the Hebrews to set three over the dispensing of alms, as Maimonides notes, Vol. III, fol. 85. Paul follows him here. The opinion of those who think Luke is designated here does not displease me: yet so that by 'the Gospel' is understood not the book which was not yet published at that time, but the very office of the Evangelist, which Luke had faithfully performed in many places in Paul's stead; or the preaching of the Gospel itself, as below in 10:14, 'in' for 'through'.

Others more correctly deny that Luke is understood, by the judgment of B. Hülsemann, who thinks these things agree more with Barnabas: It matters little, he says, to know the individual of this brother, whom others think to be designated as Luke, as Salmero from the supposititious epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians and Jerome on Ecclesiastical writers: Thus Saa, Tirinus, Menochius (Add also Cajetan, Faber, and from the ancients Primasius) and our Luther in the Confession of the Great Supper, Vol. III, Jena, Lat. Weimar, v. 18. Barnabas, because in v. 19 it follows that he was ordained by the Church as a companion of Paul, but in v. 22 they understand Luke as the second companion. And it seems there should be no doubt that it is understood of Barnabas in v. 18, both because of the attributes in v. 18, 19, and because of those things which were said in the previous epistle, ch. 9:8, concerning Paul and Barnabas as companions of the journey. And it is evident from the epoch of the writing of this epistle, after so many notable revelations made to the Apostle, concerning which in chapters 11 and 12, that Luke cannot be understood in either place, neither in v. 18 nor 22, because in Acts 15:44 [sic] he is said to be separated from the company of Paul, at the beginning of the journey undertaken into Macedonia. But the things which the Apostle commemorates here concerning the persecutions endured in Macedonia, and which he had reported above in chapter 1:7, 8, etc., which he commemorates in chapter 2:24, 25, etc., it is plain that they happened after the separation of Luke, cf. Acts 2:29, chapter 12:25, Gal. 2:9, 10. Therefore, by the 'brother' in v. 18 we understand Barnabas. But who is understood in v. 22, we define nothing. Theophylact also seems to favor Barnabas: Some, he says, say that this is Luke, whom Paul calls a brother for the sake of the Gospel, which he had written. Some, however, bring forward Barnabas, who, although he did not write a Gospel, nevertheless calls the preaching which he exercised a Gospel. Yet nothing is poured forth in his praise, as was poured forth in the praise of Titus, and perhaps for this reason, because the name of Barnabas was more obscure to the Corinthians; but that of Titus was known and celebrated. Otherwise, he also attributes enough praise to him. For he says not simply that he preaches the Gospel, but that he has obtained praise in the Gospel. Nor did he attain such glory among two or three, but among all the churches. So also do most other Greek interpreters. That opinion does not please Estius, both because the ministry, of which mention is made in Acts 11, was divided from that which is now being treated; and because that was completed long before Paul came to Corinth, as is held in Acts 12:25; and because in Acts 15 Paul and Barnabas departed from one another, and there is no mention of Barnabas at all thereafter: but those things which are written here concerning the ministry of the saints are far later, as they correspond to the history of Acts 20. Furthermore, he brings forward a third opinion concerning Apollos, who is celebrated in Acts 18. But since he is nowhere read to have been appointed by the churches as a companion of Paul's journey: he adds his vote to the fourth opinion, which is concerning Silas, whose praise for the Gospel preached was great through all the churches, and who, having been chosen in Acts 15 for the Apostolic mission to the Gentiles, and having become much more famous afterwards, when he departed together with Paul from Antioch through the regions of Syria, Cilicia, and the province of Asia, then of Macedonia and Achaia; he preached the Gospel with the greatest fruit, partly confirming the churches long since instituted, partly instituting new ones, as can be seen in Acts ch. 15 & the three following, so that for this reason Silas also deserved the name of Apostle. Compare Acts 15:40.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Συνεπέμψαμεν δὲ μετ' αὐτῶ ἀδελφὸν, ὗ ὁ ἔπαινος ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ διὰ πασῶν τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν) Mos erat Hebræorum eleemosynis dispensandis tres præficere, ut monet Maimonides Tom. III. fol. 85. Eum hic sequitur Paulus. Mihi non displicet illorum sententia, qui hic Lucam designari putant: ita tamen, ut per Evangelium intelligatur liber qui tunc editus nondum erat, sed munus ipsum Evangelistæ, quod Lucas Pauli vice multis in locis fideliter obierat; sive ipsa Evangelii prædicatio, ut infra X. 14. ἐν pro διά.

Rectius alii negant, Lucam intelligi judicio B. Hülsemanni, qui Barnabæ magis hæc convenire putat: Parum quidem interest, inquit, nosse individuum hujus fratris, quem alii putant designari Lucam, ut Salmero ex Ignatii suppositiitia epistola ad Ephesios & Hieronymo de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis: Ita Saa, Tirinus, Menochius (Adde & Cajetanum, Fabrum, & e veteribus Primafium) & noster Lutherus im Bekändtniß vom grossen Abendmal Tom. III. Jenens. Lat. Vinarienses v. 18. Barnabam, quia v. 19. sequitur, quod ab Ecclesia ordinatus sit Pauli comes, v. autem 22. per secundum comitem intelligunt Lucam. Et de Barnaba quidem v. 18. intellectum non dubitandum videtur, cum propter attributa v. 18. 19. tum propter ea, quæ superioris epistolæ cap. IX. 8. de Paulo & Barnaba tanquam sociis peregrinationis dicta sunt. Et patet ex epocha scriptæ hujus epistolæ, post tot insignes revelationes Apostolo factas, de quibus cap. XI. & XII. Lucam neutro loco nec v. 18. nec 22. posse intelligi, quia Act. XV. 44. Sic separatus dicitur a comitatu Pauli, initio suscepti in Macedoniam itineris. Quæ autem Apostolus hic commemorat de persecutionibus in Macedonia toleratis, & quæ supra cap. I. 7. 8. seqq. retulerat, quæ cap. II. v. 24. 25. seqq. commemorat, ea palam est, post separationem Lucæ contigisse, conf. Act. II, 29. cap. XII. 25. Gal. II. 9. 10. Itaque per Fratrem v. 18. Barnabam intelligimus. Quis autem v. 22. intelligatur, nihil definimus. Barnabæ etiam favere Theophylactus videtur: Nonnulli, inquit, Lucam hunc esse dicunt, quem Paulus Evangelii gratia, quod ille conscripserat, fratrem appellat. Nonnulli vero Barnabam afferunt, qui etsi Evangelium minus conscripsit, prædicationem tamen, quam exercebat, Evangelium nuncupat. Cujus tamen in laudes nihil effunditur, quemadmodum in Titi effusus est laudem, & forsan idcirco, quia Barnabæ nomen Corinthiis erat obscurius; Titi vero notum & celebre. Alioqui & illi satis laudum tribuit. Non enim simpliciter (inquit) Evangelium prædicat, sed in Evangelio laudem est adeptus. Neque apud duas trinæsve sed apud omnes Ecclesias hujusmodi est gloriam assequutus. Ita etiam plerique alii Græci Interpretes. Non placet ea opinio Estio, tum quia ministerium, cujusque mentio fit Act. XI. divisum fuit ab eo, de quo nunc agitur; tum quia illud expletum fuit multo ante, quam Paulus Corinthum veniret, ut habetur Actor. XII. 25. tum quia Act. XV. discesserunt ab invicem Paulus & Barnabas, nec omnino deinceps ulla Barnabæ mentio: Ea autem quæ hic de ministerio sanctorum scribuntur longe posteriora sunt, utpote respondentia historiæ Actor. XX. Tertiam porro adducit sententiam de Apollo, qui Actor. XVIII. celebratur. Sed quum is nuspiam legatur ab Ecclesiis comes Paulinæ peregrinationis ordinatus: Quartæ sententiæ, quæ est de Sila, calculum adjicit, cujus laus ob Evangelium prædicatum magna fuit per omnes Ecclesias, quique Act. XV. in legationem Apostollicam ad gentes delectus, & multo clarior postea factus, quando una cum Paulo digressus Antiochia per loca Syriæ, Ciliciæ Asiæque provinciæ, tum Macedoniæ & Achaiæ; maximo cum fructu Evangelium prædicavit, partim confirmans Ecclesias pridem institutas, partim novas instituens, uti videre est Actor. XV. cap. & tribus seqq. ut propter hoc etiam Apostoli nomen Silas meruerit. Confer. Actor. XV. 40.

## 8:19
Verse 19. Not only) He is not only worthy to be highly esteemed: because of this, which I have said.

But also having been appointed by the churches) It was Paul's custom not to take upon himself the election of those who were to administer the funds, but to permit it to the synod, 1 Corinthians 16:3. So far was it from being enough for him to be free from blame, unless he also excluded suspicions. Here also ἐγένετο is understood. Concerning the verb χειροτονεῖν, see what was said in Acts 14:23.

Our fellow traveler) This is inserted by way of parenthesis, and it fits Luke very well, as appears from the acts written by him.

With this grace) By metonymy he calls that which was given out of liberality grace, as also in 1 Corinthians 16:3.

Which is administered by us) Which we have procured, in Macedonia, that is. The verb διακονεῖσθαι is taken here, just as the word διακονίας above in verse 4.

On the other hand, Theophylact teaches that these things fit Barnabas better: He praises the man, even from the judgment of those who had chosen him, saying, not only when he preaches the Gospel does he deserve praise here as an upright man; but he was also appointed by the churches to accompany our journey, for which reason he is also a participant with me in temptations and dangers. But these things fit Barnabas better. For he had been destined for that task and grace, that he might administer the funds together with Paul.

To the glory of the Lord himself) For it is the honor of the Lord when servants perform their duty well.

And your readiness) Namely, to be stirred up by the example of the Macedonians, as above in 1.

This is, with Theophylact interpreting again, so that for this reason both God may attain glory and you may attain readiness in contributing. Since those who receive the money collected by you are also upright, and there is nothing in them that could give rise to suspicion.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Οὐ μόνον δὲ) Non tantum dignus est, qui magni fiat: ob hoc, quod dixi.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν) Mos erat Pauli, electionem eorum, qui pecunias administrarent, non sibi sumere, sed synodo permittere, 1. Corinth. XVI. 3. Adeo non satis illi erat, a culpa abesse, nisi & suspiciones excluderet. Subauditur & hic ἐγένετο. De verbo χειροτονεῖν vide, quæ dicta Act. XIV. 23.

Συνέκδημος ἡμῶν) Hoc per Parenthesin interjectum est, & Lucæ optime convenit, ut ex actis, ab ipso scriptis, apparet.

Σὺν τῇ χάριτι ταύτῃ) Μετωνυμικῶς χάριν vocat, id quod ex liberalitate datum est, ut & 1. Corinth. XVI. vers. 3.

Τῇ διακονουμένῃ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν) Quam nos procuravimus, in Macedonia scilicet. Sumitur hic verbum διακονεῖσθαι, sicut διακονίας vox supra v. 4.

Ex adverso vero Theophylactus Barnabæ hæc magis convenire docet: Laudat hominem, vel ex eorum, qui hunc delegissent, judicio, non modo (inquiens) cum Evangelium prædicat, laudem hic promeretur ut probus; sed ab Ecclesiis etiam est institutus, ut nostrum iter comitaretur, quocirca & tentationum est mihi & discriminum particeps. Hæc autem Barnabæ congruunt magis. Is namque fuerat ad id muneris & gratiæ destinatus, ut cum Paulo una pecunias administraret.

Πρὸς τὴν ἀυτοῦ τοῦ κυρίου δόξαν) Domini enim honor est, cum servi bene officium faciunt.

Καὶ προθυμίαν ὑμῶν) Nempe excitandam, exemplo Macedonum, ut supra 1.

Hoc est, interprete iterum Theophylacto, ut ob id & gloriam affequatur DEUS & vos conferendi promptitudinem. Quandoquidem & probi sunt, qui collatam per vos pecuniam capiunt, & nihil his inest, quod parere queat suspicionem.

## 8:20
Verse 20. Avoiding this) This is to be referred to we sent along, so that those words, not only, and the following, are said parenthetically. Avoiding, fearing, as in Matthew 2:5; but it is placed here for taking care, the cause for the effect. So also 2 Thessalonians 3:6. That is a metaphor, taken from sailors furling their sails.

Regarding it, Schmidius says on this passage: Avoiding this, declining this. A metaphor from sailors lowering their sails, so that the ship may go more slowly, if by chance they see rocks in the way or suspect hidden reefs, lest by a faster movement they be carried into them with damage. The Apostle takes care for himself, lest he fall into calumnies; as if he were going to convert the large collection, which he hopes for from the Corinthians, to his own proper and private advantage: and therefore he wishes more persons worthy of trust to be added to this matter, a thing truly worthy, in the judgment of Theophylact, of Paul's holiness and the care which he had undertaken for them, of his greatness and indulgence. For on that account, he says, we will appoint these. And not one only, but several: because, avoiding the suspicion of grace, we feared lest suspicion might perhaps attack someone, just as if we ourselves were claiming some part of these funds for us. Yet he did not say, lest you, but lest anyone, lest the Corinthians might take it more annoyingly, if perhaps some had been persuaded to suspect something of this kind about Paul, that is, this abundance of money entrusted to us, it would be sufficient to bring suspicion upon the wicked and slanderous unless we had provided for his own security.

Μήτις ἡμᾶς μωμήσηται ἐν τῇ ἁδρότητι ταύτῃ, τῇ διακονουμένῃ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν) He calls Ἁδρότητα a sum of money sufficiently large. שׁלום is translated ἁδροὶ, Job XXIX. 9. XXXIV. 19. In the Glossary: ἁδρὸς grandis. Donatus in the life of Virgil interprets ἁδρὸν as validum. The Greek Scholiasts explain ἁδρότητα as δύναμιν, μέγεθος.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Στελλόμενοι τοῦτο) Hoc referendum est ad συνεπέμψαμεν, ut illa, ὀυ μόνον δὲ, & sequentia sint παρενθετικῶς dicta. Στελλόμενοι metuens, ut Matth. II. 5. id vero hic ponitur pro cavens, causa pro effectu. Sic & 2. Thess. III. 6. Illa est μεταφορὰ, ducta a nautis, vela contrahentibus.

De ea Schmidius ad hunc locum: Evitantes hoc, declinantes hoc. Metaphora a nautis vela dimittentibus, ut remissius eat navis, si forte scopulos vident obvios, aut cæcas cautes suspicantur, ne citiatore motu in eos vel eas ferantur cum damno. Cavet sibi Apostolus, ne in calumnias incidat; quasi in proprium & privatum suum commodum, largam, quam a Corinthiis sperat, λογίαν sit conversurus: ideoque plures fide dignas personas huic rei vult adjungi, dignum id sane, judice Theophylacto, Pauli sanctimonia & cura, quam pro his susceperat, magnitudine & indulgentia. Propterea enim, inquit, hos destinabimus. Neque unum duntaxat, sed plures: quia devitantes gratiæ suspicionem, veriti sumus, ne quem forte incessat suspicio, perinde ac si harum ipsi pecuniarum partem nobis aliquam vendicemus. Nec tamen dixit, ne vos, sed ne quis, ne molestius ferrent Corinthii, si quibus esset forsitan persuasum, sese ejusmodi aliquid de Paulo suspicari, hoc est, pecuniarum hac nobis copia credita, satis valeret ad inferendam improbis & maledicis suspicionem nisi futuram ipsi securitatem prætulissimus.

Μήτις ἡμᾶς μωμήσηται ἐν τῇ ἁδρότητι ταύτῃ, τῇ διακονουμένῃ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν) Ἁδρότητα vocat summam pecuniæ satis magnam. שׁלום vertitur ἁδροὶ, Jobi XXIX. 9. XXXIV. 19. In Glossario: ἁδρὸς grandis. Donatus in Virgilii vita ἁδρὸν validum interpretatur. Scholiastæ Græci ἁδρότητα exponunt δύναμιν, μέγεθος.

## 8:21
Vers. 21. Προνοούμενοι καλὰ ὀυ μόνον ἐνώπιον κυρίου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων) Providing for those things which are honest. This is taken from the Greek, Prov. III. 4. προνοῦ καλὰ ἐνώπιον κυρίου καὶ ἀνθρώπων, where in the Hebrew they read LXX שכל with those points, so that it was not a noun, but merely a verb of commanding: quite rightly indeed. Ἐνώπιον κυρίου καὶ ἀνθρώπων. Those things which both God approves, and good men. A similar expression Rom. XII, 17.

Ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ by a good conscience: ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων by a good reputation. For as Augustine says in the former sermon on the common life of his clerics, with Bede and Primasius citing it in this place: There are two things, conscience and reputation. For our own sake our conscience suffices for us; for the sake of others, reputation is necessary. Conscience, for you; reputation, for your neighbor. He who, trusting in his own conscience, neglects his reputation, is cruel to his neighbor. There are two sermons on the common life of the Clerics of St. Augustine, Vol. 10, on various subjects, numbers 49 and 50, among those added by the Louvain editors, as Estius observes here.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Προνοούμενοι καλὰ ὀυ μόνον ἐνώπιον κυρίου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων) Curantes ea, quæ sunt honesta. Sumptum est hoc ex Græco, Proverb. III. 4. προνοῦ καλὰ ἐνώπιον κυρίου καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ubi in Hebræo LXX. legerunt שכל cum punctis iis, ut non nomen esset, sed verbum modo imperantis : recte sane. Ἐνώπιον κυρίου καὶ ἀνθρώπων. Ea, quæ & Deus probat, & viri boni. Similis loquutio Rom. XII, 17.

Ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ per bonam conscientiam : ἐνώπιον ἀνθρώπων per bonam famam. Nam ut ait Augustinus serm. priore de vita communi suorum clericorum Beda & Primasio in hunc locum citantibus: Duæ res sunt, conscientia & fama. Propter nos conscientia nostra sufficit nobis; Propter alios fama necessaria est. Conscientia, tibi; fama, proximo tuo. Qui fidens conscientiæ suæ negligit famam suam, crudelis est in proximum.
