Sunt duo sermones de vita communi Clericorum S. Augustini T. 10. de diversis numer. 49. & 50. inter additos a Lovaniensibus, ut Estius hic observat.

## 8:22
Vers. 22. Συνεπέμψαμεν δὲ αὐτοῖς τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν) A third person, who would go with Titus and Luke. This perhaps was Epaenetus, mentioned in Rom. XVI. 5.

ὃν ἐδοκιμάσαμεν, ἐν πολλοῖς πολλάκις σπουδαῖον ὄντα) We have found him diligent. In the Glossary σπουδαῖος is sedulus, studiosus, efficax.

Νυνὶ δὲ πολλῷ σπουδαιότερον) If it can be done, he added something to the previous diligence.

Πεποιθήσει πολλῇ τῇ εἰς ὑμᾶς) That is, because, as I am the author, he hopes for all the best things concerning you. See above I. 15.

Others wish Silas to be indicated, most wish Apollos. But that it was not Apollos, in the judgment of B. Hülfemann, is clear, because his authority was already so great among the Corinthians, as is clear from the first epistle ch. I. 12, ch. III. 4, 5, etc., that that little recommendation, which appears in verse 22 of this chapter, would seem clearly frivolous and incompetent for such a famous and well-known Doctor. Which must also be held concerning Silas; Theophylact defines nothing here. Estius thinks it is Zenas the lawyer, of whom in Tit. III; or Sosthenes.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Συνεπέμψαμεν δὲ αὐτοῖς τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν) Tertium aliquem, qui cum Tito & Luca iret. Hic forte fuerit Epænetus, memoratus Rom. XVI. 5.

ὃν ἐδοκιμάσαμεν, ἐν πολλοῖς πολλάκις σπουδαῖον ὄντα) Experti sumus sedulum. In Glossario σπουδαῖος sedulus, studiosus, efficax.

Νυνὶ δὲ πολλῷ σπουδαιότερον) Si fieri potest, adjecit, aliquid ad sedulitatem priorem.

Πεποιθήσει πολλῇ τῇ εἰς ὑμᾶς) Id est, ideo, quod de vobis omnia sperat optima, me autore. Vide supra I. 15.

Alii Silam indigitari volunt, plerique Apollo. Sed non fuisse Apollo, B. Hülfemanno judice, patet, quia ejus tanta jam erat autoritas apud Corinthios, ut patet ex prioris epistolæ cap. I. 12. cap. III. 4. 5. seqq. ut illa commendatiuncula, quæ extat vers. 22. hujus capitis plane frivola & incompetens tam celebri & notissimo Doctori videatur. Quod etiam de Sila habendum, Theophylactus hic nihil definit. Estius Zenam legisperitum, de quo Tit. III. esse putat; aut Sosthenem.

## 8:23
Vers. 23. Εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου) Supply the question. If it is a matter concerning Titus.

Κοινωνὸς ἐμὸς) A partner of my labor in preaching the Gospel.

Καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός) Because it concerns you more closely, he was also a helper to me in part in strengthening you, in part in correcting you.

Εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν) Namely, they come into the discussion. Paul loves hyperbaton, hastening to express the matter. He speaks here of Luke and another.

Ἀπόςολοι ἐκκλησιῶν) Apostles of Christ, sent by Christ their Prince, are one thing; legates of the Churches are another. In the Talmudic writings they are shelihim, who used to carry tithes and other things owed to the Levites to them themselves; they are apostoli in the Theodosian Code concerning the Jews, as we said at Matthew X. 1. Their office is apostolē in Julian and Epiphanius. From there this name was taken.

Δόξα χριστοῦ) Metonymically, that is, they are instruments of the glory of Christ.

The Greeks also render the same sense. Theophylact: Apostles of the Churches, that is, destined and appointed for this by the Church; who also restricts this title δόξα χριστοῦ to this mission: He placed last what was most excellent of all, as if he were saying, the sum of all things which are managed by them turns upon Christ. The Churches, however, by which they were sent, are understood to be in Judea.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου) Supple quæstio est. Si de Tito agitur.

Κοινωνὸς ἐμὸς) Socius laboris in Evangelio prædicando.

Καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός) Quod propius vos spectat, etiam in vobis partim corroborandis, partim corrigendis mihi adjutor fuit.

Εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν) Nempe in disquisitionem veniunt. Amat ὑπερβατὸν Paulus, rem eloqui properans. De Luca & altero hic loquitur.

Ἀπόςολοι ἐκκλησιῶν) Aliud sunt ἀπόςολοι χριστοῦ, a Christo eorum Principe legati, aliud legati Ecclesiarum. In Thalmudicis שלוחין sunt, qui decimas & alia Levitis debita ipsos deferebant, ἀπόςολοι in Codice Theodosiano de Judæis, ut diximus ad Matth. X. 1. ἀποστολὴ eorum munus Juliano & Epiphanio. Inde sumptum hoc nomen.

Δόξα χριστοῦ) Metonymικῶς, id est, instrumenta sunt gloriæ Christi.

Eundem sensum reddunt & Græci. Theophylactus: Apostoli Ecclesiarum, hoc est ab Ecclesiæ ad id destinati & constituti; Qui hoc elogium δόξα χριστοῦ etiam ad hanc missionem restringit: Quod omnium erat præstantius, postremo posuit, ac si inquiat, in Christo rerum omnium vertitur summa, quæ ab illis geruntur. Ecclesiæ autem, a quibus missi sunt, in Judæa intelliguntur.

## 8:24
V. 24. Τὴν οὖν ἔνδειξιν τῆς ἀγάπης ὑμῶν καὶ ἡμῶν καυχήσεως ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν εἰς αὐτοὺς ἐνδείξασθε) It is a Hebraism, ἐνδείξασθε ἔνδειξιν ἀγάπης, and καυχήσεως for ἀγάπην and καύχησιν. Show that they are loved by you. Show that those things which I proclaim concerning your affection toward me and mine are true.

Εἰς πρόσωπον τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν) So that that love of yours may appear to all the surrounding Churches, and especially to those whose decrees have come to you.

Thus εἰς πρόσωπον for ἐν προσώπῳ. Another sense, however, pleased Theophylact and other Greeks: In the person of the Churches, as if he were to say: You are also going to do all that in the person of the Church, which you toward us yourselves have carried, that is, in honor of the Churches. For these people, who are sent by the Churches, represent the person of the Churches.

Latin:

V. 24. Τὴν οὖν ἔνδειξιν τῆς ἀγάπης ὑμῶν καὶ ἡμῶν καυχήσεως ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν εἰς αὐτοὺς ἐνδείξασθε) Est Hebraismus ἐνδείξασθε ἔνδειξιν ἀγάπης, & καυχήσεως pro ἀγάπην & καύχησιν. Ostendite eos a vobis diligi. Ostendite vera esse, quæ de vestro in me & meos affectu prædico.

Εἰς πρόσωπον τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν) Ita, ut illa vestra dilectio appareat omnibus circum Ecclesiis, & iis maxime, quarum decreta ad vos venerunt.

Ita εἰς πρόσωπον pro ἐν προσώπῳ. Alius tamen sensus Theophylacto aliisque Græcis placuit: In personam Ecclesiarum, quasi dicat: Id etiam omne estis in personam Ecclesiæ facturi, quod in nos ipsi gefferitis, hoc est in Ecclesiarum honorem. Praeferunt enim hi Ecclesiarum personam, qui ab Ecclesiis transmittuntur.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle commends the προθυμίαν (readiness) of the Corinthians, which he also proclaimed in Macedonia, for which reason he sent the brothers to them, so that they might not be confounded, and he exhorts them to a more generous and cheerful almsgiving; since GOD loves a cheerful giver, and has promised the grace of a generous reward (Psal. CXII. 9.), and such a contribution not only relieves the indigence of the saints, but also contributes to the celebration of God, both because of the confession of the Gospel, and because of the simplicity of the communication, and because of the prayer for the Corinthians, with which the Apostle concludes with thanksgiving. There are two parts. I. The commendation of the προθυμίας (readiness) of the Corinthians for alms to verse 6. II. The exhortation to a prompt and generous communication to verse 9.

PART I. The commendation of the προθυμίας (readiness) of the Corinthians for Alms.

Vers. 1. For concerning the ministry, which is for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you) These things should have been connected with the preceding. For he shows that he does not wish to use any further exhortations regarding this business of the poor, since he expects all the greatest things from them for many reasons; concerning the word διακονίας (ministry) see above chapter VIII. 4. We believe it is established from the summary and partition already provided that the new chapter is not inappropriately begun. Nor should the ancient distribution be rashly abandoned or criticized. The sense and connection are presented by Estius as if he were saying: I have warned you to show your charity toward the legates of the Churches; and I say nothing about the alms to be collected and administered for the relief of the poor saints who are in Jerusalem: For I consider it superfluous to write to you about it and to exhort you. It was, of course, superfluous for the Apostle to exhort the Corinthians to the alms which they had already decided to give from the previous year; nor did he doubt that they would do it; but the wealthy Corinthians had to be stimulated to make some more generous collection, in proportion to their wealth and abundance. Estius thinks that the Apostle is therefore doing this next. It seemed to our blessed Hülsemann that the discourse in these two chapters, VIII and IX, is about different subjects, whose opinion I am pleased to submit in his own words and commit to the judgment of the readers: Because in the preceding chapter VIII the Apostle had already dealt at length with the beneficence of the Corinthians toward himself and his fellow preachers, as is evident from v. 4. But in this chapter, as if by the removal of the thing granted and clearly undoubtedly, he speaks of another διακονίᾳ εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους (ministry to the saints), it is likely that other subjects, for which this alms was to be destined, are understood in this place. However, we do not dare to restrict these things to only the Christians oppressed in Judea, as Balduinus and the Vinarienses do. For it is evident from 1 Pet. I. 1. 2. seqq. and chapter IV. 12. 13. seqq. and from James I. 2. seqq. Heb. X. 33. seqq. chapter II. 36. seqq. that Christians were despoiled of their goods here and there throughout the whole world, and were thus in need of alms, and that the Apostle does not understand the alms to be destined for one place or nation, nor even about the promise made the previous year, now to be fulfilled from chapter VIII. 11, which the Vinarienses think; but it seems to be most clear from verses 12, 13, 14, where πολλοὶ (many) and πάντες (all) are opposed to those about whom it had been spoken in chapter VIII, that it is about a universal collection for all the brothers dispersed throughout the whole world, just as Chrysostom deduces here at length in his Morals concerning alms even toward the Gentiles. What Salmero elicits from this concerning the obligation of any of the faithful to sustain the pomp and retinue of the Apostolic legates through the courts of Princes and the inns of cities, are trifles, and do not deserve refutation. For the discourse here is not about beneficence toward the Apostles or their legates, but about the brothers dispersed throughout the whole world. The interpretation of Beza does not agree with the following verses: For he understands διακονίαν (ministry) not as alms, nor as the collection of them, but as the ministry of carrying them; whereas the following treatment concerns only the alms themselves, and their collection, cf. v. 12.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Commendat Apostolus προθυμίαν Corinthio- rum, quam etiam in Macedonia praedicavit, cujus causa miserit ad ipsos fratres, ut ne confundantur & ad largiorem hilarioremq; eleemosynam hortatur; siquidem DEUS hi- larem datorem amet, & promiserit gratiam larga retributionis (Psal. CXII. 9.) ac contributio talis non tantum sublevet indi- gentiam sanctorum, sed etiam faciat ad ce- lebrationem Dei, tum ob confessionem Evan- gelii, tum ob simplicitatem communicatio- nis, tum ob precationem pro Corinthiis, quae gratiarum actione concludit Apostolus. Partes sunt duae. I. προθυμίας Corinthiorum ad eleemosynas commendatio ad vers. 6. II. Ad prom- ptam & largam communicationem exhortatio ad vers. 9.

PARS I. προθυμίας Corinthiorum ad Eleemosynas commendatio.

Vers. 1. Περὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας, τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους περισ- σόν μοί ἐστι τὸ γράφειν ὑμῖν) Haec connectenda fuerant cum superioribus. Ostendit enim se nullis ultra hortatibus uti velle super isto negotio pauperum, cum de ipsis omnia ma- xima multis de causis expectet, de voce διακονίας vide supra cap. VIII. 4. Non incommode novum inchoari caput e summario & partitione jam tradita constare arbi- tramur. Neque enim temere antiqua distributio deserenda aut vellicanda. Sensus & connexio ita ab Estio exhibetur, quasi dicat: Monui vos, ut o- stendatis charitatem vestram erga legatos Ecclesia- rum; neque quicquam dico de eleemosyna conferenda ac ministranda in subsidium sanctorum pauperum, qui sunt Jerosolymis: Nam de ea vobis scribere, vosque hortari, supervacaneum censeo. Nimirum supervacaneum erat Apostolo, Corinthios hortari ad eleemosynam, quam ab anno jam superiori face- re constituerant; neque dubitabat, quin essent fa- cturi; Sed exstimulandi erant divites Corinthii ad faciendam largiorem aliquam collectam, pro ra- tione sua opulentiae & abundantiae. Id ergo agere deinceps Apostolum censet Estius. B. Hülseman- no nostro visum fuit, de diversis subjectis sermo- nem esse in his duobus capp. VIII. & IX. cujus sen- tentiam propriis ejus verbis subjicere, & lectorum judicio committere placet: Quia capite VIII. prae- cedente Apostolus de beneficentia Corinthiorum er- ga se suosque socios praedicatores jam prolixe egerat, ut patet ex v. 4. Hoc autem capite quasi per remo- tionem rei concessae & plane indubie de alia διακονίᾳ εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους loquitur, verisimile est, alia subjecta, quibus haec eleemosyna destinanda fuerit, hoc loco in- telligi. Non audemus autem ista restringere ad so- los Christianos in Judea oppressos, ut Balduinus & Vinarienses. Patet enim ex 1. Petr. I. 1. 2. seqq. & cap. IV. 12. 13. seqq. & ex Jac. I. 2. seqq. Hebr. X. 33. seqq. cap. II. 36. seqq. hac illac per universum orbem spoliatos fuisse bonis Christianos, adeoque eleemosy- narum indigos, & intelligere Apostolum eleemo- synam non uni loco aut genti destinandam, neque etiam de promissione superiori anno facta, nunc ad- implenda ex cap. VIII. 11. quod Vinarienses putant; sed de universali collecta pro omnibus fratribus per universum orbem dispersis, videtur esse clarissi- mum ex vers. 12. 13. 14. ubi πολλοὶ & πάντες iis, de quibus cap. VIII. dictum erat, opponuntur, quem- admodum Chrysostomus hic prolixe in Moralibus de eleemosyna etiam erga gentiles deducit. Quæ Sal- mero hinc elicit de obligatione quorumvis fidelium sustentandi pompam & comitatum legatorum A- postolicorum per aulas Principum & diversoria ci- vitatum, nugatoria sunt, & refutationem non merentur. Neque enim hic de beneficentia erga Apostolos aut eorum legatos, sed fratres toto orbe dispersos sermo est. Interpretatio Bezæ non con- venit versibus sequentibus: Intelligit enim διακο- νίαν non de eleemosynis, nec de collectione ipsarum, sed de ministerio earundem deferendarum; cum so- lum sequens tractatio concernat ipsas eleemosy- nas, earumque collectionem, conf. v. 12.

## 9:2
Vers. 2. For I know your readiness) See above VIII. 12, 19.

Which I magnificently proclaim among the Macedonians, about which I triumph.

He says the same thing as above VIII. 10, so that he might not seem to attribute more to the Macedonians because they had given more, he consoles the Achaeans, of whom the Corinthians are the chief, with this honor, that they had begun earlier.

Paul, as the blessed Hunnius notes, with singular artifice both removes the suspicion of distrust and nevertheless, out of pious solicitude, sprinkles reasons by which he may excite them to his purpose. Thus now he again mentions the boasting, with which Paul publicly boasts among the Macedonians, how ready the Corinthians are in this business of the administration to the saints, so that by this means he may obliquely and tacitly remind them to take diligent care, lest he be thought to have boasted of them in vain. And the emphasis of the Pauline locution is to be observed, for he does not use a word of praising, but of boasting, which signifies to boast with a certain πληροφορίᾳ (full assurance) of certainty. I have, he says, interpreting Theophylact, your readiness of mind in contributing money, which I have also been accustomed to boast of, and to say that you Corinthians are not only prepared for it, but the whole of Achaia: that nothing is lacking, except the arrival of those who are to receive the money. Wherefore I shall consider it a matter of shame if I am caught having boasted of these things vainly and falsely.

Ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν ζῆλος) Emulation of your example. Ἡσίδος (הֵעִיר or הֵמִית. He understands the example of readiness, by which they declared themselves prepared a year ago, and made the beginning of a private collection according to the prescription of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 16. You see, Theophylact warns here, how he both excites the Macedonians themselves to beneficence by praising the Corinthians, and provokes the Corinthians by the readiness of the Macedonians approved for that purpose. For you have become, he says, the instructors of those. Do not therefore, since you are the masters, appear more deficient than the disciples.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Οἶδα γὰρ τὴν προθυμίαν ὑμῶν) Vide supra VIII. 12, 19.

Ἣν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν καυχῶμαι Μακεδόσι) Quam apud Mace- donas magnifice prædico, de qua triumpho.

Ὅτι Ἀχαΐα παρεσκεύασται ἀπὸ πέρυσι) Idem dicit, quod supra VIII. 10. ne Macedonibus plus tribuere videretur, quod plus dedissent, Achæos, quorum præcipui Corinthii, hoc honore solatur, quod priores incepissent.

Paulus, notante B. Hunno, singulari artifi- cio & suspicionem diffidentiæ removet & nihilo mi- nus ex pia solicitudine subinde rationes aspergit, qui- bus eos ad institutum suum excitet. Ita nunc iterum meminit gloriationis, qua Paulus apud Macedones publice glorietur, quam sint prompti Corinthii in hoc negotio administrationis in sanctos, ut hoc pa- cto oblique & tacite submoneat, sedulo curent, ne frustra de iis gloriatus esse putetur. Estque obser- vanda Paulinæ loquutionis emphasis, non enim uti- tur laudandi verbo, sed jactandi, quod significat cum quadam certitudinis πληροφορίᾳ gloriari. Com- pertam inquit, interprete Theophylacto, ipse ha- beo vestram animi in conferendis pecuniis prompti- tudinem, quam & jactare consuevi, dicereque non solum ad id paratos vos Corinthios esse, sed univer- sam Achaiam: nihil ultra deesse, nisi eorum adven- tum, qui pecunias sint accepturi. Quocirca verê- cundiæ ducam, si deprehendar inaniter & falso hæc jactitasse.

Ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν ζῆλος) Æmulatio vestri exempli. Ἡσίδος (הֵעִיר vel הֵמִית. Exemplum intelligit promptitudinis, qua jam ante annum se paratos declararunt, & initium privatæ collectionis ad præscriptum Apostoli 1. Cor. XVI. fecerunt. Vides, monet hic Theophyla- ctus, quemadmodum & Macedones ipsos Corinthiis collaudatis ad beneficentiam excitet, & Corinthios provocet, Macedonum probata ad eam rem prom- ptitudine. Estis enim, inquit, illorum Præceptores effecti. Nolite ergo discipulis, cum sitis magistri, vi- deri defectiores.

## 9:3
Verse 3. ἔπεμψα δὲ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς) He sent Titus and two others ahead, intending to follow himself if he could. He sent them ahead, however, so that he might find everything ready upon his arrival.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ἔπεμψα δὲ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς) Titum, & duos alios præmisit, ipse, si posset, secuturus. Præmisit autem, ut cuncta parata inveniret in suo adventu.

## 9:4
Verse 4. ἐν τῇ ὑποστάσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως) In this foundation of my boasting, as in Ezekiel 26:11 in the Greek. Thus also below in 11:17. The Hebrews would say מַצָּב.

Others render it matter, or argument, to which Estius agrees. Theophylact says, he called the substance the thing itself and the collection of alms, or the force and boasting of the glorying. The explanation of Schmid pleases me: In such firm confidence of this boasting: See Polybius on Cocles, where he uses this word similarly, for a certain undaunted consistency of mind. which knows how to yield to no dangers. The sense is similar in 2 Cor. XI. 17. ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως, and Hebr. XI. 1. ἔστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, that is, a firm confidence in things which are hoped for. The paraphrase of Theophylact has it thus: You act, he says, perhaps more confidently with me, as those whom I indulge. Yet there are Macedonians not unknown to you, whose modesty ought to restrain you: Since together with me these also are about to come to you, who if they find you unprepared, that is, refusing alms, will convict me of a lie, who reported that you were prepared, and will accuse you of avarice. For it will be a thing to be ashamed of, if at our arrival this collection of yours is neither ready nor quick: Or if you have nowhere contributed what is fitting for alms. Theophylact also rightly observes the restriction in this substance of boasting, to which the antecedent ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ v. 3. is similar, in this part, q. d. that in other matters, concerning which he had boasted, he does not fear for them, lest they be ashamed; by which tacit commendation he wishes to render them more prompt for alms, lest when they have progressed very much in the rest, they be found not upright in this, and inferior to themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἐν τῇ ὑποστάσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως) In hoc fundamento meæ jactationis, ut Ezech. XXVI. 11. in Græ- co. Sic & infra XI. 17. Hebræi dicerent מַצָּב.

Alii reddunt materiam, vel argumentum, qui- bus accedit Estius. Theophylactus inquit, substan- tiam rem ipsam dixit & eleemosynæ collationem, vel gloriationis vim & jactantiam. Placet Schmidii ex- plicatio: In tam firma fiducia hac gloriationis: Vide Polybium de Coclite, ubi hac voce similiter utitur, pro animi quadam imperterrita consistentia, quæ nullis periculis cedere novit. Similis est sensus 2. Cor. XI. 17. ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως, & Hebr. XI. 1. ἔστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, id est, firma fiducia rerum, quæ sperantur. Paraphrasis Theophylacti sic habet: Agitis, inquit, mecum forte fidentius, utpote qui vobis indulgeam. Sunt tamen Macedones vobis non incogniti, quorum verecun- dia tenere vos debet: Siquidem mecum una ad vos sunt & hi concessuri, qui si vos imparatos invene- rint, hoc est, eleemosynam detrectantes & me menda- cii arguent, qui vos paratos esse retulerim, & vos avaritiæ incusabunt. Erubescendum quippe erit, si in nostro adventu vestra hæc nec prompta sit, nec cita collatio: Aut si nusquam, quod deceat, in eleemosynam contuleritis. Recte etiam observat Theophylactus restrictionem in hac substantia gloriationis, cui si- milis est Antecedens ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ v. 3. in hac parte, q. d. se aliis in rebus, de quibus gloriatus e- rat, de ipsis non vereri, ne pudeat; qua tacita commendatione reddere ipsos vult ad eleemosy- nam promptiores, ne cum in reliquis profecerint plurimum, in hac deprehendantur non probi, & seipsis inferiores.

## 9:5
Your previously announced blessing) εὐλογία ברכה a gift, as 1 Sam. XXV. 27. προκατηγγελμένην, that is, προειρημένην previously spoken of, about which I have already said much. Thus we have προσδοδολωμένους in the third book of Maccabees.

Thus as a blessing, and not as covetousness) Willingly given. We ask, we do not snatch away.

The name of blessing occurs in a similar sense in Gen. XXXII. last verse, 1 Sam. XXV. 27, 2 Kings V. 15. Furthermore, Theophylact refers avarice not to the givers, but to the receivers, in a sense more subtle than appropriate: q. d. For do not think that we will accept what you have contributed for the sake of greed and avarice, but because we are more desirous of bestowing a blessing upon you. Whence it happens that he who extorts alms from an unwilling person seems to demand this very thing as if for avarice. But the sense is in the open: For he hints what alms ought to be by merit, and thus tacitly requires of the Corinthians, since not all were equally prepared and αὐθαίρετοι: That the mind be liberal and kind, and the gift proceeding from the mind be liberal, not too sparing, not sordid, which would betray a mind tenacious, illiberal, and entangled in the snares of avarice.

PART II. Exhortation to prompt and liberal communication.

Latin:

Τὴν προκατηγγελμένην εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν) Εὐλογία ברכה largitio, ut 1. Sam. XXV. 27. προκατηγγελμένην, id est, προ- ειρημένην prædictam, de qua jam multum dixi. Sic προσδοδο- λωμένους habemus in tertio Maccabaico.

Οὕτως ὡς εὐλογίαν, καὶ μὴ ὡς πλεονεξίαν) Volenter data. Rogamus, non eripimus.

Benedictionis nomen simili sensu occurrit Gen. XXXII. ult. 1. Sam. XXV. 27. 2. Reg. V. 15. Cæterum avaritiam Theophylactus refert non ad dantes, sed ad accipientes, sensu subtiliori magis, quam con- gruo: q. d. Neque enim existimetis cupiditatis & a- varitiæ gratia, quæ vos contuleritis, nos accepturos, sed quia sumus benedictione vos condonandi cupidiores. Quo fit, ut qui eleemosynam ab invito extorserit, quasi ad avaritiam videatur hanc ipsam exigere. Sed in aprico est sensus: Innuit enim, qualis me- rito esse debeat eleemosyna, adeoque tacite re- quirit a Corinthiis, quum non omnes ex æquo pa- rati fuerint & αὐθαίρετοι: Ut animus sit liberalis & benignus, & munus ab animo proficiscens liberale sit, non parcum nimis, non sordidum, quod ani- mum prodat tenacem, illiberalem & avaritiæ la- queis illigatum.

PARS II. Ad promptam & liberalem communicationem exhortatio.

## 9:6
Vers. 6. But this) Furthermore indeed: Supply I judged that you ought to be warned, from the preceding. Ἐπ' εὐλογίαις) That is, liberally. Thus also Ezekiel XXXIV. v. 26. Ἐπ' εὐλογίαις καὶ θερίσει) That is, he will receive from God. A frequent translation for the Hebrews, Job IV. 8, Matth. XXV. 24, 26, Luc. IX. 21, 22, Joh. IV. 34, 1 Cor. IX. 11, Gal. VI. 7, 8, 9. Now what he had warned obscurely, he proposes more openly, as if he were saying, according to the paraphrase of the blessed Hunnius, there are perhaps in your Church some not best affected toward this kind of beneficence, who if they could, with witnesses removed, would give either nothing or little. There are others, who weighing the matter more accurately, determine it to be just that the saints be assisted by an honest and liberal gift. Let both diligently consider with themselves what I am about to say: For he who sows sparingly, will also reap sparingly. Others here render Τοῦτο δὲ κατὰ πόδα: This indeed, namely I say; the Apostle seems to allude to Prov. XXII. 8, cf. Eccles. XI. 1. Papists draw these to merits. Estius says it is openly signified here that a man merits the retribution of the future age through works of mercy, but how is that openly hinted, when no apex of merit is held here, and it is not even implicitly inferred? The consequence, at any rate, which Estius regards, does not import merit. Just as seed naturally produces fruit from itself, which is therefore naturally expected from it: so good works by divine ordination avail for obtaining the rewards of eternal life, similarly to be expected from them. Who will say that the seed or the sowing merits the fruit? The fruit indeed follows the sowing by divine blessing, and thus we do not deny that good works also obtain rewards; but the consequence is only regarded in that comparison, not merit. For no reason of merit intervenes here, since both the promise of retribution and the retribution itself are mere grace of God. Which furthermore are to be referred not to eternal life itself, but to rewards in eternal life, not to essential blessing and glory, but to degrees of glory, as Bellarmine acknowledges concerning the parallel passage Gal. VI. 8, in his book on justification, ch. 3, not to mention that firm arguments are not sought from comparisons if they are extended beyond the third point of comparison.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Τοῦτο δὲ) Præterea vero: Supple censui vos mo- nendos, e superioribus. Ἐπ' εὐλογίαις) Id est liberaliter. Sic & Ezechielis XXXIV. v. 26. Ἐπ' εὐλογίαις καὶ θερίσει) Id est, a Deo recipiet. Frequens Hebræis translatio, Job. IV. 8. Matth. XXV. 24. 26. Luc. IX. 21. 22. Joh. IV. 34. 1. Cor. IX. 11. Gal. VI. 7. 8. 9. Jam quod obscure monuerat, apertius propo- nit, quasi dicat, juxta B. Hunnii paraphrasin, sunt forsan in Ecclesia vestra quidam non optime erga hoc beneficentiæ genus affecti, qui si remotis arbitris que- ant, aut nihil aut parum daturi sint. Sunt alii, qui rem accuratius pensitantes, æquum esse statuant, ut honesto ac liberali munere subveniatur sanctis. U- trique diligenter secum reputent, qua dicturus sum: Etenim qui parce seminat, parce & metet. Τοῦτο δὲ alii hic κατὰ πόδα reddunt: Hoc vero, scilicet di- co; alludere videtur Apostolus ad Prov. XXII. 8. conf. Eccles. XI. 1. Papistæ trahunt hæc ad merita. Estius aperte hic significari ait, hominem per opera mi- sericordiæ mereri retributionem futuri seculi, sed quo- modo aperte illud innuitur, quum de merito nul- lus apex hic habeatur, ac ne quidem implicite id inferatur? Consequentia utique, quam respicit Estius, non importat meritum. Sicut semen na- turaliter ex sese profert fructum, qui proinde natu- raliter ex eo expectatur: ita bona opera divina ordi- natione valent ad consequenda præmia vitæ æternæ, similiter ex illis expectanda. Ecquis dicet, semen aut sationem mereri fructum. Consequitur qui- dem fructus divina benedictione sationem, atque ita etiam præmia consequi bona opera non diffi- temur; sequela autem solum respicitur in illa com- paratione, non meritum. Nulla enim hic meriti intervenit ratio, quum mera sit Dei gratia tum re- tributionis promissio, tum ipsa retributio. Quæ præterea non ad ipsam vitam æternam, sed ad præ- mia in vita æterna, non ad essentialem benedi- ctionem & gloriam, sed ad gloriæ gradus referen- da, ut de loco parallelo Gal. VI. 8. agnoscit Bellar- minus l. de justif. cap. 3. ut taceam, quod ex com- parationibus firma argumenta non petantur, si ul- tra tertium comparationis extendantur.

## 9:7
Vers. 7. each as he purposes in his heart) as he wills in his heart, נדיב לבו, Exod. XXX. 5. For προαιρεῖσθαι here is to will, as Prov. XXI. 25. In Greek προαίρεσις is for Aristotle a deliberate will. It is understood here, let him give. Not from grief, or from necessity) For τὸ ἀκούσιον takes away praise from the action. For God loves a cheerful giver) It is a trite sentiment among the Hebrews. Hence the son of Sirach XXXII. in the Greek, in the Latin XXXV. 11. ἐν πάσῃ δόσει ἱλάρωσον τὸ πρόσωπόν σου. That this sentiment was not unusual among the Hebrews, or from Sirach ch. XXXV. 11, is evident. Cf. Prov. XXII. 8, ch. XIX. 17. If good seeds are good works, why are they sown with tears, says Augustine in Sermon XLV. See also the homilies of Chrysostom, that alms is the most profitable of all things.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἕκαστος καθὼς προαιρεῖται τῇ καρδίᾳ) ut vult in corde suo, נדיב לבו, Exod. XXX. 5. Nam προαιρεῖσθαι hic est velle, ut Prov. XXI. 25. In Græco προαίρεσις Ari- stoteli deliberata voluntas. Subauditur hic, det. Μὴ ἐκ λύπης, ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης) Nam τὸ ἀκούσιον laudem de- trahit actioni. Ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ Θεός) Est sententia trita apud Hebræos. Hinc Sirachides XXXII. in Græcis, in Latinis XXXV. 11. ἐν πάσῃ δόσει ἱλάρωσον τὸ πρόσωπόν σου. Apud Hebræos non fuisse sententiam illam in- usitatam vel è Siracide cap. XXXV. 11. constat. Conf. Prov. XXII. 8. cap. XIX. 17. Si bona semina sunt bona opera, quare seminantur cum lacrymis, ait Augustinus Serm. XLV. Vid. & Chrysostomi ho- miliæ, quod eleemosyna sit omnium quæstuosis- sima.

## 9:8
Vers. 8. All grace) Thus he calls the gifts of God, as 1 Cor. III. 10, and elsewhere. περισσεῦσαι εἰς ὑμᾶς) To cause to abound הותיר. For the Greeks take active verbs for doubly active, which the Hebrews call Hiphil. Thus βασιλεύειν, to cause one to reign. Πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν ἔχοντες) that is, content with those things which nature desires. Thus αὐτάρκεια is taken, 1 Tim. VI. 6, and ἀυταρκὴς Phil. IV. 11. Polybius also uses αὐτάρκειαν in this sense. He who uses his own sparingly will be able to give much to others. He meets a tacit objection of those fearing want for themselves if they give more copiously, and it is taught that whatever they have given will return to them with interest. Therefore, just as he had testified concerning the grace of God in v. 7 that He loves a cheerful giver, so concerning the power of God in v. 8. he affirms that He is δυνατὸς [powerful], and can easily provide that all grace may abound in them, both corporal and spiritual, so that not only ἐν παντὶ πάντοτε πᾶσαν ἀυτάρκειαν [in everything always all sufficiency] they may have all temporal sufficiency in all things at all times; but also that they may abound unto every good work, so that through the grace of the Holy Spirit they may take increases in faith, piety, love, and the exercise and study of good works, by which they may be prompt to perform greater works from time to time, and to bring forth fruits of righteousness for the glory of God and the utility of the neighbor, as the blessed Hunnius explains, and from the Papists, Estius: In which manner, as Theophylact warns, he simultaneously instructs in what things the gifts of the Lord are to be used, namely, that they may abound unto every good work; just as if he were saying, in these things indeed, which are of the flesh, I would have wished sufficiency for you. But in spiritual things, (for that is what he intends by 'unto every good work') namely abundance and fruitfulness, so that not only may one be more merciful in a great measure, but may liberally perform every work that pleases God. With which explanation, also approved by Anselm, the proof brought from Psalm 112:9 agrees excellently, and which follow the former in v. 10, in which he has embraced both bodily and spiritual goods.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Πᾶσαν χάριν) Sic appellat Dei dona, ut 1. Cor. III. 10. & alibi. περισσεῦσαι εἰς ὑμᾶς) Facere ut abundent הותיר. Nam, Græci activa sumunt pro dupliciter activis, quæ Hiphil vo- cant Hebræi. Sic βασιλεύειν, facere, ut quis regnet. Πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν ἔχοντες) id est, contenti iis, quæ na- tura desiderat. Sic αὐτάρκεια sumitur, 1. Tim. VI. 6. & ἀυ- ταρκὴς Phil. IV. 11. Usurpat & Polybius ἀυτάρκειαν hoc sen- su. Qui suis parce utitur, multum aliis poterit dare. Occurrit tacitæ objectioni metuentium sibi inopiam, si copiosius tribuant, ac docetur, quicquid dederint, ad ipsos cum fœnore rediturum. Ut ergo de gratia Dei testatus erat v. 7. quod diligat hila- rem datorem, ita de potentia Dei v. 8. affirmat, quod δυνατὸς sit, ac præstare facile possit, ut omnis gratia abundet in ipsis cùm corporalis, tùm spiri- tualis, ut non modo ἐν παντὶ πάντοτε πᾶσαν ἀυ- τάρκειαν in omnibus omni tempore omnem suffici- entiam temporalem habeant; sed & abundent ad omne opus bonum, ut per Spiritus Sancti gratiam incrementa sumant in fide, pietate, dilectione, & exercitio, studioque bonorum operum, quo promti sint ad majora subinde præstanda opera, & ad fructus justitiæ proferendos in gloriam Dei, & utilitatem proximi, ut B. Hunnius explicat, & è Pontificiis Estius: Quo pacto, monente Theophy- lacto, simul instruit, quibus in rebus utendum sit do- nis Domini, ut scilicet abundent in omne opus bo- num; perinde ac si dicat, in his equidem, quæ carnis sunt, sufficientiam vobis optaverim. In spiritualibus vero, (id enim prætendit in omne opus bonum) abundantiam scilicet & ubertatem, ut non solum magnum in modum quis clementior sit, sed omne opus, quod Deum oblectet, liberaliter obeat. Cui ex- plicationi, Anshelmo etiam probatæ, congruit eximiè probatio è Psal. CXII. 9. adducta & quæ priorem sequuntur v. 10. quibus & corporalia & spiritualia bona complexus est.

## 9:9
Vers. 9. Καθὼς γέγραπται, ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν· ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς αἰῶνα) These are the words of the LXX in the Psalm, which is CXII. 8 for the Hebrews. Ἐσκόρπισεν means he scattered; that is, he distributed liberally, as in Prov. XI. 24. δικαιοσύνη here is mercy, as in Matt. VI. 1. Therefore, in the said Psalm, some have placed ἐλεημοσύνη, others φιλανθρωπία. Manet in perpetuum, in the Psalm, signifies that he leaves a long reputation behind him. But according to the sense of Paul, it produces eternal rewards. Namely, if other virtues are also present, which ought to be present, but yet in such a way that mercy may have the greatest value among them.

If the Psalmist speaks of the fame and memory of those who are liberal and exercise mercy remaining, why must it be said that the Apostle draws these to eternal rewards? Does the Apostle deviate from the sense of the Psalmist, or has he not attained the same? For these are very different: a good reputation on earth, and eternal rewards in heaven. However, justice is said to remain forever, not because we attain eternal life through mercy and other virtues, as the Papist Grotius wishes. For this is the gratuitous gift of God in Christ Jesus, Rom. VI. last verse, but with respect to imputed justice, which we attain through faith, the fruit of which is beneficence and mercy, because there is no forgetfulness of it before God, which is also to be proclaimed before that council of the whole world on the last day, and to be crowned forever. But with respect to inchoate justice, to which beneficence also pertains, that its memory remains, both among men and before God, who rewards the same, out of grace, not only in this, but also in the future age.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Καθὼς γέγραπται, ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν· ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς αἰῶνα) Sunt verba LXX. in Psal- mo, qui Hebræis CXII. 8. Ἐσκόρπισεν sparsit; id est, libera- liter erogavit, ut Prov. XI. 24. δικαιοσύνη hic est misericor- dia, ut Matth. VI. 1. Itaque in dicto Psalmo alii posuere ἐλεημοσύνη, alii φιλανθρωπία. Manet in perpetuum, in Psal- mo significat, famam post se longam relinquit. At ex sen- su Pauli præmia parit æterna. Nempe si & aliæ virtutes adfint, quæ adesse debent, sed ita tamen, ut inter eas miseri- cordia plurimum valeat.

Si Psaltes de fama & memoria liberalium & mi- sericordiam exercentium manente loquitur, cur di- cendum Apostolum hæc ad præmia æterna trahe- re? Num deflectit Apostolus à sensu Psaltis, aut assæquutus eundem non est? Maxime enim di- versa hæc sunt, fama bona in terris, & præmia æterna in cælis. Manere autem in æternum di- citur justitia, non quod per misericordiam alias- que virtutes æternam vitam consequamur, uti Papizans Grotius vult. Hæc enim donum Dei gratuitum est in Christo Jesu Rom. VI. ult. sed re- spectu justitiæ imputatæ, quam per fidem conse- quimur, cujus fructus est beneficentia, & mise- ricordia, quod nulla apud Deum ejusdem obli- vio sit, quæ etiam in novissimo die coram illo totius orbis concilio deprædicanda, & in æter- num coronanda est. Respectu autem justitiæ in choatæ, ad quam etiam pertinet beneficentia, quod ejus memoria maneat, tum apud homines, tum apud Deum, qui remuneratur eandem, ex gratia, non in hoc tantum, sed etiam in futuro seculo.

## 9:10
Vers. 10. Ὁ δὲ ἐπιχορηγῶν σπέρμα τῷ σπείροντι) He who gave to you what might be given to the poor. For that is to sow here, as above in 6. Moreover, these words and the following are from Is. LV. 10.

Καὶ ἄρτον εἰς βρῶσιν χορηγήσαι) May he not only give you what is necessary for life. See Matt. VI. 11.

Καὶ πληθῦναι τὸν σπόρον ὑμῶν) But may he also grant that you may be able to give more in the future. Reference is made to the passage in Deut. XXVIII. v. 12.

Καὶ αὐξῆσαι τὰ γενήματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὑμῶν) The same sense as in the previous member. For δικαιοσύνη here also wishes to be understood as τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. Reference is made, however, to the passage in Hosea X. 13, where the Greeks, who omitted the ו, read וידה and took it as a noun, not as a verb.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὁ δὲ ἐπιχορηγῶν σπέρμα τῷ σπείροντι) Qui vo- bis dedit, quod daretur pauperibus. Nam id hic seminare, ut supra 6. Sunt autem verba hæc & sequentia ex Es. LV. 10.

Καὶ ἄρτον εἰς βρῶσιν χορηγήσαι) Non tantum vobis det ad vitam necessaria. Vide Matth. VI. 11.

Καὶ πληθῦναι τὸν σπόρον ὑμῶν) Verum etiam det, ut in posterum plura dare possitis. Respicitur locus Deuteron. XXVIII. v. 12.

Καὶ αὐξῆσαι τὰ γενήματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὑμῶν) Idem sen- sus, qui in superiori membro. Nam δικαιοσύνη hic etiam vult intelligi τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. Respicitur autem locus O- see X. 13. ubi γενήματα δικαιοσύνης Græci, qui omisso ו le- gerunt וידה & sumpserunt ut nomen, non ut ver- bum.

## 9:11
Ἐν παντὶ πλουτιζόμενοι) Here again ἐστέ is understood. See also Rom. IX. 28.

Εἰς πᾶσαν ἁπλότητα) ἁπλότης here is liberality, as in Rom. XII. 8, above VIII. 2.

The word χορηγεῖν, as Camerarius notes, transferred from the expenses formerly for theatrical games, signifies to supply liberally and munificently. These have the force of a wish and a promise, that God, who bestows seed to the sower, and wealth to the one scattering among the poor, will supply the same, bread not only for the sustenance of those who disseminate cheerfully and liberally, but also as seed, which the more it is scattered, the more it is multiplied for them, and that the fruits of his justice may be increased, namely spiritual gifts, or virtues, which are the fruits of justice, Phil. I. 11. At the same time, he prays for these things which confer upon both body and soul, says Theophylact, and makes his words give assurance from this sensible cultivation of the earth. For if God supplies seed to those sowing the earth, and provides food to those nourishing the body, he is going to give seed far more to those who cultivate heaven and nourish the soul. But when he shall provide and multiply your seed, he says, he is discoursing about these temporal riches. Which seed he clearly prefers to be distributed to the needy so that it may be rendered spiritual, and transferred into the soul. For from this any good work grows, and the fruits of righteousness increase besides, and for that reason he also adds that, and will increase the fruits of your righteousness. Chrysostom had preceded: one might admire Paul's prudence here especially, because, just as he drew exhortation from both spiritual and carnal things: so also in the reward he does the same thing again, establishing both turns, to be sure. That indeed, he dispersed, he gave to the poor, his righteousness remains forever, looks to the spiritual reward: But this, may he multiply your seed, to the carnal remuneration. Nor yet does he stop here: but again he passes over to spiritual things, perpetually composing them, to be sure, among themselves. For that, may he increase the fruits of your righteousness, is spiritual. But he does this for the sake of varying the discourse, both to root out their sluggish and inert agitations of mind, and to remove the fear of poverty by many reasons. Which explanation is most excellent and to be preferred to the sense of Grotius and others, who by fruits of righteousness understand alms. Just as our blessed Hunnius himself, even though he wishes to designate by that eulogy the alms, which are as it were the produce and fruit of preceding righteousness, acknowledges in the following words, that you may be enriched in everything, that it pertains both to the temporal riches of this life and the eternal riches of the other age: and that those words IN ALL SIMPLICITY are added, because he prays besides, that that pious simplicity of helping the poor without murmuring may take increase in them. Which promise, however, as regards the increase or multiplication of seed, or the distribution of alms, as far as earthly riches are concerned, is to be understood according to the ordinary manner of divine providence, not absolutely and simply; since for reasons unknown to us it sometimes happens otherwise; God directing all things, especially as He knows them to conduce to our eternal salvation. In the words, he who provides seed for the sower and bread for eating, Estius thinks the place in Isaiah 55:10 is referred to, but although the words among the Septuagint interpreters are analogous, yet here the sower is not understood economically, or concerning the farmer's seed; but ethically, concerning him who liberally scatters riches like seed, and distributes bread among the poor, whom he designates by this periphrasis of God as receiving these gifts from the kindness of God to the end that he may not keep them for himself alone, but also distribute them to the needy neighbor, although we do not deny that there is an allusion to natural seed and its manner. Which comparison is made (1) by reason of origin, because as God bestows seed, so also we have from God the goods which we scatter to others (2) by reason of sowing, because as we scatter seed with no sparing hand; so also alms must be scattered liberally (3) by reason of apparent loss, because seeds in the field are lost for a time, and goods given to the poor seem to be lost (4) by reason of the harvest: We sow in hope, which a more abundant harvest follows, both in natural seed and in the scattering of alms.

Verse 11. Ἥτις κατεργάζεται δι᾽ ἡμῶν εὐχαριστίαν τῷ Θεῷ.) Which is the reason why we give thanks to God; the Syrian reads Δὶ ὑμῶν, not δι᾽ ἡμῶν.

This inference is entirely correct. Through us, however, he says, that is, by the intervention of our ministry, so that the thanks which are given to God by the poor may be understood, to whom the Apostle grants this intercession himself, while exhorting to the celebration of GOD, as the principal author of these gifts: just as the following explain this more openly concerning the ministry of this service.

Latin:

Ἐν παντὶ πλουτιζόμενοι) Hic rursus subauditur ἐστέ. Vide & Rom. IX. 28.

Εἰς πᾶσαν ἁπλότητα) ἁπλότης hic est liberalitas, ut Rom. XII. 8. supra VIII. 2.

Verbum χορηγεῖν, notante Camerario, transla- tum ab impendiis olim in ludos scenicos significat li- beraliter & munifice suppeditare. Voti hæc, & promissionis vim habent, Deum, qui largitur se- men seminanti, opes spargenti inter pauperes, easdem, panem non ad victum tantum istis, qui hilariter & largiter disseminant, subministra- turum, sed etiam ut semen, quo magis spargi- tur, eo magis ipsis multiplicetur, utque augeantur fructus justitiæ ipsius, spiritualia nempe dona, vel virtutes, quæ fructus sunt justitiæ Phil. I. 11. Simul his, quæ cum corpori tum animæ conferunt, com- precatur, inquit, Theophylactus facitque ex sen- sibili hac terræ cultura verbis suis fidem. Nam si terram serentibus semen subministrat Deus, & cibum nutrientibus corpus suppeditat, longe magis & his, qui cælum colunt, & animam alunt, da- turus est semen. Cum autem præstabit & multi- plicabit semen vestrum, inquit, de temporariis hisce opibus disserit. Quod plane semen mavult ut egentibus distributum spirituale reddatur, & transferatur in animam. Ex hoc enim quidvis boni operis succrescit, & justitia insuper mani- puli augescunt, ob idque & illud subjungit, & augebit incrementa justitiæ vestræ. Præiverat Chrysostomus: Pauli prudentiam hinc vel ma- xime quispiam mirari possit, quod, quemadmo- dum & à spiritualibus & à carnalibus cohorta- tionem duxit: ita etiam in mercede rursus idem facit, utrasque nimirum vices constituens. Illud quidem dispersit, dedit pauperibus, justitia ejus manet in seculum, ad spiritualem mercedem spe- ctat: Hoc autem multiplicet semen vestrum, car- nalem remunerationem. Nec tamen hic consi- stit: verum rursum adhuc ad spiritualia transit, perpetuo nempe ea inter se componens. Illud enim, augeat fœtus justitiæ vestræ, spirituale est. Hoc autem varianda orationis causa facit, tum ut ignavas eorum & inertes animi agitationes radi- citus evellat, tum ut paupertatis metum plurimis rationibus eximat. Quæ explicatio pereximia præferenda Grotii & aliorum sensui, qui per fru- ctus justitiæ intelligunt eleemosynas. Quemadmo- dum etiam ipse B. Hunnius noster, etsi illo elogio designari velit eleemosynas, quæ sint velut pro- ventus & fructus justitiæ antegressæ, agnoscit ver- bis sequentibus, ut in omnibus locupletemini pertinere & ad temporale hujus, & ad æternas alterius seculi divitias: addi autem illa IN O- MNEM SIMPLICITATEM, quod pre- cetur insuper, & pia illa simplicitas subveni- endi pauperibus absque murmuratione sumat in illis augmentum. Quæ tamen promissio, quod ad augmentum vel multiplicationem seminis, aut distributionis eleemosynæ, quantum ad opes ter- renas, de ordinaria providentiæ divinæ ratione intelligenda, non absolutè, & simpliciter; siqui- dem ob rationes nobis incognitas nonnunquam aliter eveniat; Deo dirigente omnia, imprimis prout ad æternam nostram salutem ea conducere novit. Verbis, qui subministrat semen ferenti & panem ad manducandum respici locum Es. LV. 10. Estius putat, sed quanquam analoga sint verba apud LXX. Interpp. hic tamen seminans non intel- ligitur œconomicè, vel de agricola semente semen; sed Ethicè, de eo, qui largiter spargit opes instar seminis, & panem distribuit inter pauperes, quem dona hæc à Dei benignitate accipere eo fine, ut non sibi soli retineat, sed proximo etiam egenti distribuat, hac Dei περιφράσει designat, etsi ad semen naturale alludi, ejusque rationem non diffi- teamur. Quæ comparatio fit (1) ratione originis, quia ut sementem Deus largitur, ita & bona, quæ aliis spargimus, à Deo habemus (2) ratione satio- nis, quia uti non parca manu spargimus semen; ita & eleemosyna spargenda est largiter (3) ratione apparentis perditionis, quia semina in agro ad tem- pus perduntur, & bona pauperibus data perdi vi- dentur (4) ratione messis: Seminamus in spe, quam sequitur largior messis, & in semine naturali, & in sparsione eleemosynæ.

Vers. 11. Ἥτις κατεργάζεται δι᾽ ἡμῶν εὐχαριστίαν τῷ Θεῷ.) Quæ causa est, cur nos gratias Deo agamus; Δὶ ὑμῶν, non δι᾽ ἡμῶν legit Syrus.

Illatio hæc omnino se rectè habet. Per nos autem, inquit, id est, interveniente nostro ministerio, ut intelligantur gratiæ, quæ Deo agun- tur à pauperibus, quibus hanc intercessionem gra- tificatur Apostolus ipso ad celebrationem DEI, ceu autoris præcipui istorum dono- rum cohortante: quemadmodum sequentia apertius id explicant de ministerio τῆς λειτυργίας ταύτης.

## 9:12
Ver. 12. For the administration of this service) Take it as at the beginning of this chapter.

Not only is it supplying the wants of the saints) See above VIII. 14.

But also abounding through many thanksgivings to God) Liberality itself is pleasing to God in itself, and then it also brings another fruit to God, in that those who are relieved by that liberality give thanks to God.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὄτι ἡ διακονία τῆς λειτυργίας ταύτης) Sume ut initio hujus capitis.

Οὐ μόνον ἐσὶ προσαναπληρῦσα τὰ ὑσερήματα τῶν ἁγίων) Vide supra VIII. 14.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ περισσεύουσα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαρισιῶν τῷ Θεῷ) Ipsa liberalitas per se Deo grata est, deinde etiam alium Deo fructum fert, eo, quod qui ea liberalitate sublevantur, gratias Deo agunt.

## 9:13
By the proof of this ministry) Experiments of this matter above II. 9. VIII. 2.

V. 13. Glorifying God) The natural discourse would have been glorifying: But we have shown at Mark VI. 40 that the nominative is often put for the oblique, not only among our own, but also among the more elegant Greeks, such as that in Homer Il. 2. Adresase daughter of great-hearted Eetion, Eetion, who dwelt under woody Placus. Likewise: And both sitting, Odysseus was more venerable. It may, however, be doubted whether it is not an error of the scribe, because soon after follows longing.

The suspicion of an error by the scribe is vain, since there is no reason for it, and that mode of speaking, as Grotius himself admits, is not infrequent, concerning which Erasmus Schmid brings forward more at Matt. X. 24, and the Greek Codices entirely agree. Not to mention that Camerarius includes v. 12, for the ministry &c., in a parenthesis, up to those words glorifying God, so that it may be being enriched & glorifying. The name of service, if an offering is brought in, does not ill befit spiritual sacrifices: to which is deservedly reckoned beneficence toward the poor, and almsgiving Heb. XIII. 16.

Latin:

Διὰ τῆς δοκιμῆς τῆς διακονίας ταύτης) Experimenta hujus rei supra II. 9. VIII. 2.

V. 13. Δοξάζοντες τὸν θεὸν) Sermo naturalis fuerat δοξάζοντων: Sed ostendimus ad Marc. VI. 40. rectum pro obliquo sæpe poni, non apud nostros tantum, sed & apud elegantiores Græcos, quale illud in Homero Il. 2. Ἀδρησάση θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἠετίωνος, Ἠετίων, ὃς ἔναιεν ὑποπλάκῳ ὑληίσσῃ. Item: Ἄμφω δ' ἑζομένω γεραρώτερος ἦεν Ὀδυσσεύς. Potest tamen dubitari, an non sit error exscriptoris, quia mox sequitur ἐπιποθόντων.

Vana est suspicio de errore exscriptoris, quum nulla ejus sit ratio, & modus ille loquendi, fatente ipso Grotio, non sit infrequens, de quo plura Erasmus Schmidius affert ad Matth. X. 24. ac Codices Græci prorsus consentiant. Ut taceam, quod Camerarius v. 12. ὅτι ἡ διακονία &c. parenthesi includat, usque ad illa δοξάζοντες τὸν Θεὸν, ut sit πλυτιζόμενοι & δοξάζοντες. Λειτυργίας nomen si oblatio inferatur, spiritualibus sacrificiis non male convenit: quibus accensetur merito beneficentia in pauperes, & eleemosyna Ebr. XIII. 16.

## 9:13
And in the simplicity of the communication to them) Then they rejoice in your liberal communication of goods. See Rom. XV. 26. above VIII. 4. Heb. XIII. 16.

And to all) They also rejoice in your beneficence toward others and give thanks to God, lest they be thought to be conducting only their own business.

And by their prayer for you longing for you because of the exceeding grace of God upon you) And here is a Metonymy. For of those longing is for those loving, meaning those showing their love. When they see you so liberal because of the fellowship of the Gospel, they pray to God for you: and thus, in whatever way they can, they show that you are vehemently loved by them. To long for in this sense you have Ps. CXIX. 131.

Three fruits of liberal almsgiving are brought forward, which redound from this ministry of the Apostles: 1. The relief of the poor, whose lack is supplied by this liberality. 2. Thanksgiving, by which they give thanks to God, as the supreme benefactor directing hearts to munificence. 3. The glorification of God, which is done then both by them and also by others on account of this proven work of the ministry, not only because of obedience toward the Gospel of CHRIST, because they received the Gospel with due subjection of heart and external confession of the mouth: or by hypallage in the confession of obedience; but also because of the simplicity of the communication, redounding not only to some, but to all the faithful oppressed by poverty: which is altogether to be attributed to God: nay, even because of the efficacy of the prayer for the Corinthians. Undoubtedly they glorify God for this reason also, because they are already certainly persuaded, and believe, that their prayer and intercession for their benefactors will not be in vain, rejoicing that they can at least in that way repay thanks. Δέησις therefore is not to be taken simply, as if the saints are said to be about to glorify God for their prayers, or because they were praying for the Corinthians; but with effect, because they are certain that the same will be heard, and with that confidence they glorify God. Some refer the words καὶ αὐτῶν δεήσει to the preceding verb περισσεύουσα; but the structure and connection seem rather to warn that these should not be separated from those immediately preceding; but together with the same, they should be referred equally to that which the Apostle had said in v. 13, δοξάζοντες τὸν θεὸν. In this way Cornelius à Lapide; as if he were saying: The poor of Jerusalem, who receive your alms, while they pray and beseech for you, also glorify God, and thus while thanksgiving (says Cyprian in his sermon on work and alms) is directed to God for the alms, the wealth of the worker is increased by the retribution of God. If, however, notwithstanding the convenience of the structure, you prefer to explain it with Theophylact, as the fruit of the alms, which abounds not only to many thanksgivings, but also to supplications for the benefactors, four fruits of beneficence will be numbered here: the refreshing of the poor, the thanksgiving made to God, the glorification of the same for the good work, and the prayer to God for the salvation of the giver. Most, however, explain that desire not as love for the Corinthians, but as a desire to see them. There is also added (so Theophylact) that they pray to God for your sake, that you might have the opportunity to visit them someday, not out of regard for money, but for the excellence of the divine grace granted to you. We do not deny, however, that the sense here is sufficiently harmonious regarding love toward the Corinthians, which can be admitted without metonymy: They pray to God for us, as those who love you not in an ordinary way, because of the eminent grace shown to you.

Latin:

Καὶ ἁπλότητι τῆς κοινωνίας εἰς ἀυτύς) Deinde gaudent de liberali vestra bonorum communicatione. Vide Rom. XV. 26. supra VIII. 4. Hebr. XIII. 16.

Καὶ εἰς πάντας) Etiam de vestra in alios beneficentia gaudent & Deo gratias agunt, ne credantur suum tantum negotium gerere.

Καὶ αὐτῶν δεήσει ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐπιποθόντων ὑμᾶς διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλεσαν χάριν τῦ Θεῦ ἐφ' ὑμῖν) Et hic est Metonymia. Nam ἐπιποθόντων amantium est pro amorem suum ostendentium. Cum vos viderint tam liberales propter Evangelii consortium, Deum pro vobis precantur: & sic quomodo possunt, ostendunt vos à se vehementer diligi. Ἐπιποθεῖν in hoc sensu habes Ps. CXIX. 131.

Tres fructus liberalis eleemosynæ afferuntur, qui ex hac διακονία Apostolorum redundânt 1. Pauperum sublevatio, quorum defectus hac liberalitate suppletur. 2. Gratiarum actio, qua Deo, ceu supremo benefectori corda ad munificentiam dirigenti gratias illi agunt. 3. Glorificatio Dei, quæ tum ab illis, tum ab aliis etiam fit ob probatam hanc ministerii operam, non modò propter obedientiam erga Evangelium CHRISTI, quòd cum debita subjectione cordis, & externâ confessione oris Evangelium susceperint: vel per hypallagen in confessione obedientia; sed etiam propter simplicitatem communicationis, redundantem non in nonnullos tantum, sed in omnes fideles paupertate oppressos: quæ omninò Deo accepta ferenda: imò etiam ob orationis pro Corinthiis efficaciam. Nimirum glorificant Deum ideò quoque, quod certo jam persuasi sint, & credant, orationem & intercessionem suam pro benefactoribus non fore irritam, gaudentes, quod ea saltem ratione rependere gratiam possint. Δέησις ergò non simpliciter accipienda, quasi glorificaturi Deum dicantur sancti de suis orationibus, vel quòd pro Corinthiis orarent; sed cum effectu, quod certi sint, easdem ex- auditum iri, eaque fiducia Deum glorificent. Nonnulli referunt voces καὶ αὐτῶν δεήσει ad supe- rius verbum περισσεύουσα; sed structura, & con- nexio videtur potius monere, ut hæc ab imme- diatè præcedentibus non sequestrentur; sed cum iisdem pariter ad id, quod dixerat v. 13. Aposto- lus δοξάζοντες τὸν θεὸν referantur. Quo pacto Cornelius à Lapide; quasi dicat: Pauperes Jeroso- lymitani, qui vestram eleemosynam recipiunt, dum pro vobis orant & obsecrant, glorificant etiam Deum, sicque dum gratiarum actio (ait Cyprianus sermone de opere & Eleemos.) ad Deum pro eleemosynis, pau- perum oratione dirigitur, census operantis Dei re- tributione cumulatur. Si tamen, non obstante structuræ convenientia cum Theophylacto expli- care malis, ut fructum eleemosynæ, quæ abundet non modo ad multas gratiarum actiones, sed etiam ad obsecrationes pro benefactoribus, qua- tuor hic beneficentiæ fructus numerabuntur, re- focillatio pauperum, gratiarum actio Deo facta, ejusdem glorificatio de bono opere, & oratio ad Deum pro salute largientis. Desiderium autem illud ple- rique explicant non de amore Corinthiorum; sed de desiderio eosdem videndi. Accedit etiam, (ita Theo- phylactus) quod vestri gratia Deum precantur, ut vos sit eis aliquando visendi facultas, non pecunia- rum respectu, sed divina gratia vobis concessa præ- stantiâ. Non diffitemur autem hic satis concin- num esse sensum de amore adversus Corinthios, qui citra Metonymiam admitti potest: Deum pro nobis precantur, utpote vos non vulgariter aman- tes, ob eminentem gratiam vobis exhibitam.

## 9:14
Ver. 14. By the subjection of your confession to the Gospel of Christ) That is, through confession the Jewish brethren rejoice that you also, through the profession made in baptism, have subjected yourselves to the Gospel of Christ. Thus confession is spoken of also in Heb. III. 1. IV. 14. X. 23. Thus also the verb to confess is taken 1 John IV. 3, 15. 2 John v. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐπὶ τῇ ὑποταγῇ τῆς ὁμολογίας ὑμῶν εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῦ χρισῦ) Id est, δι' ὁμολογίας gaudent fratres Judæi, quod vos quoque per professionem factam in baptismo subjeceritis vosmet Evangelio Christi. Sic ὁμολογία dicitur & Hebr. III. 1. IV. 14. X. 23. Sic & verbum ὁμολογεῖν sumitur 1. Joh IV. 3. 15. 2. Joh. v. 7.

## 9:15
Vers. 15. Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ ἐπὶ τῇ ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ αὐτὸ δωρεᾷ) Paul joins himself to those brothers in Judea in thanksgiving, and as it were sings Amen to them, ἀνεκδιήγητον being that which is so great that it cannot be explained. The same elsewhere is ἀνεκλάλητον, as 1 Pet. 1:8, ineffable, and elsewhere Pliny the Elder called it inenarrabile.

This thanksgiving can be taken generally, so that it does not so much look to that gift, τῆς ὑποταγῆς, τῆς ὁμολογίας & τῆς ἁπλότητος, τῆς κοινωνίας, as it is the conclusion of the present Eucharistic treatment, by which the divine gifts, which he had hitherto commemorated, and especially those which καταλλαγὴν or the reconciliation of the world with God and διακονίαν τῆς καταλλαγῆς the ministry of that reconciliation to be announced, as also παράκλησιν καὶ δέησιν the exhortation and supplication of God to men, through the Ministers of the word warning, nay, asking, that we receive the peace acquired for us and do not neglect the reconciliation on our part: But since God is reconciled to us, that we receive that reconciliation with God by true faith, and enjoy the same. Which benefits are truly ἀνεκδιήγητα. Theophylact brings forward this sense; even though he does not pass over the former common interpretation. He calls the goods which come through alms a gift, both to the givers themselves and to those who have received them. Or he commemorates the goods themselves, with which God has deemed us worthy because of the incarnation of Christ, just as if he were saying, do not by any means think it is something great (for the things we have received from God cannot be explained) that if we ourselves impart some very small and corruptible thing to the needy, what great thing have we done? Which latter sense Chrysostom, whose epitomizer Theophylact acted, deemed altogether preferable. By gift in this place, he says, he understands those so many and so great goods, which are acquired through alms, as much by those who receive as by those who give: or those secret goods surpassing all speech, which through his presence have been most amply and abundantly bestowed upon the whole world. This is something that may be conjectured even more. For on account of this, he brings back to their memory the benefits received from God, and both to restrain their minds from all pride, and to make them more generous. This indeed has the greatest power as an incitement to all virtues, and therefore it has been employed for the conclusion of the discourse. But if the benefit of God is such that it cannot be explained by any words, what then could be equal to the fury and madness of those who curiously busy themselves in investigating his essence? Nor indeed does his benefit alone exceed every faculty of speech: But also that peace, through which he reconciled things above with things below, surpasses every agitation of the mind.

PART III. MINISTERIAL APOLOGY, or OF THE APOSTOLIC OFFICE AGAINST THE ACCUSATIONS OF THE PSEUDO-APOSTLES.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ ἐπὶ τῇ ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ αὐτὸ δωρεᾷ) Paulus in gratiarum actionem se illis in Judæa fratribus ad- jungit, & quasi Amen illis accinit, ἀνεκδιήγητον id quod tan- tum est, ut explicari nequeat. Idem alibi ἀνεκλάλητον, ut 1. Petr. I. 8. ineffabile, & alibi inenarrabile dixit Plinius Major.

Gratiarum actio hæc generaliter accipi potest, ut non tam respiciat donum illud, τῆς ὑποταγῆς, τῆς ὁμολογίας & τῆς ἁπλότητος, τῆς κοινωνίας, quam conclusio sit præsentis tractationis Eucharistica, qua dona divina, quæ hactenus commemora- rat, & imprimis illa, quæ καταλλαγὴν vel recon- ciliationem mundi cum Deo & διακονίαν τῆς καταλ- λαγῆς ministerii reconciliationem illam annunoi- andi ordinationem, ut & παράκλησιν καὶ δέησιν exhortationem, & obsecrationem Dei ad homines, per Ministros verbi monentis, imò rogantis, ut pacem nobis acquisitam suscipiamus & recon- ciliationem ex parte nostri non negligamus: Sed cum Deus reconciliatus nobis sit, reconciliatio- nem illam cum Deo verâ fide suscipiamus, ea- demque fruamur. Quæ beneficia verè sunt ἀνεκδιήγητα. Affert hunc sensum Theophylas tus; etiamsi & priorem communem interpre- tationem non prætereat. Donum dicit, quæ per eleemosynam proveniunt bona, tum largitori- bus ipsis, tum his, qui ea acceperint. Vel bona ipsa commemorat, quibus ob Christi incarnationem nos Deus dignatus est, perinde ac si dicat, nequa- quam existimate magnum aliquid (nequeunt enim quæ à Deo accepimus, explicari) quod si quid & ipsi perexiguum & corruptibile egentibus im- partimur quid magni egimus? Quem poste- riorem sensum Chrysostomus, cujus epitoma- torem egit Theophylactus, omnino præfe- rendum duxit. Per donum hoc loco, inquit, tot ac tanta illa bona intelligit, quæ tam iis, qui accipiunt, quam qui dant, per eleemosy- nam comparantur: vel arcana illa & omni ser- mone præstantiora bona, quæ per ipsius præsentiam orbi terrarum universo amplissime copiosissiméque tributa sunt. Id quod etiam magis conjicere licet. Ob id enim divinitus accepta beneficia ipsis in memoriam redigit, & ut animos eorum ab omni fastu coërceat, & munificentiores eos efficiat. Hoc quippe ad virtutum omnium incitamentum maximam vim habet, ac proinde ad concludendam orationem adhibitum est. Quod si Dei beneficium tale est, ut nullis verbis explicari possit, ecquid tandem eorum furori & amentiæ par esse queat, qui in pervestiganda ipsius essentia curiosè versantur? Nec vero ipsius duntaxat beneficium facultatem omnem sermonis excedit: Sed etiam pax ea, per quam supera cum inferis reconciliavit, omnem mentis agitationem superat.

PARS III. APOLOGIA MINISTERIALIS, vel OFFICII APOSTOLICI CONTRA PSEUDO-APOSTOLORUM ἘΓΚΛΗΜΑΤΑ.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

Through the meekness of Christ he exhorts against partiality, those who despise him as if he were weak in presence, bold in absence, and carnally abusing the power of his office, protesting that he fights with spiritual weapons, and will punish nothing but disobedience; but also that he has his power from Christ, and can exercise such power present as he can absent; however, that he does not wish to boast beyond the measure which God has assigned, but rather to establish this, that he who wishes to boast, ought to boast in the Lord.

There are two parts. For first, an apology is instituted against the rash judgment concerning the abuse of Ecclesiastical power up to verse 6. Then, however, the Apostle vindicates the contempt of his authority up to verse 18.

PART I. Apology concerning the abuse of Apostolic power.

Vers. 1. (But I myself Paul) Because there were still a few, yet there were some at Corinth, who were slandering Paul, Paul defends the dignity of his ministry against them.

(By the meekness and gentleness of Christ) Gentleness here signifies goodness, as in Baruch II. 21, Song of the Three Children 13, Wisdom XII. 18, 2 Maccabees II. 23, X. 4, just as also the gentle are good and easy-going men, Philippians IV. 5, 1 Timothy III. 3, Titus III. 2. He deservedly commemorates these virtues of Christ especially, because he was most despised on account of the imitation of them.

(Who in presence indeed am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you) These things are said mimetically, as certain Greek Interpreters have rightly warned. For it is the same as what is below in chapter 10. His detractors were saying that he acted much more mildly when present, because he feared offenses, or was courting favor. We have also had similar mimeses in the epistle to the Romans.

After the Apostle had sufficiently instituted the apology for his doctrine, in which he had joined himself with Timothy, because the doctrine of both was one, he now undertakes the apology of his Apostolic office against the accusations of his detractors, and especially of the Pseudo-Apostles, which concerned the Apostle himself alone; among which the first is the abuse of Apostolic power. He refutes the criminations of his detractors in such a way that he exhorts his own as gently as possible, nay, he prays and adjures them by the meekness and equity of Christ, that they should beware of rash judgments of his office. But I myself Paul: I that very Paul, whom you know as an Apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God I exhort you (v. 2 follows I beseech, I entreat) by the meekness and gentleness, which he demonstrated in the work of reconciliation and in the humiliation or emptying made for our sake 2. Corinthians V. 19, chapter VIII. 9, and even now demonstrates in the ministry of reconciliation with great meekness, and gentleness or lenity, beseeching even the impious themselves, be reconciled to God 2 Corinthians V. 20, just as the Apostle with Timothy had exhorted the Corinthians, and Christ through them: That you receive not the grace of God in vain 2 Corinthians VI. 1. By which manner he both testifies and hints at the cause, although openly, that he has treated them with nothing but meekness and gentleness after the example of Christ, as an ambassador in the place of Christ. Nor indeed, says Theophylact (following Chrysostom), are the prayers of Paul to be made little of, since he also interposes the meekness of Christ, just as if he were saying: Fear the meekness of Christ, by which I beseech you. At the same time he also reveals why he spares them, namely, because he imitates the meekness of Christ the Savior. Not because he is too powerless to rebuke. Do not therefore give an occasion to me, who am unwilling, to desist from this kindness, which I so greatly desire, that I now judge that even this should be interposed to reconcile my mind toward you. He thus also silently warns that they themselves should also employ candor, equity, and lenity in judging, as if he were saying: No new man, unknown to you, and who has deserved nothing from your Church, contends for this from you: But I myself, Paul, beseech you, whom you do not ignore to have well deserved from your Church, founded and planted and hitherto governed by my labors, and therefore, by a certain right of mine, I ought to obtain what I ask from you. Just as therefore, having imitated the example of the Savior and Master our Lord Jesus, I do not command you with authority; but gently and meekly I ask, and candidly I advise: So I would very much like my petition to be attended to by you with the same gentleness, and in judging my labors, words, and deeds, candor joined with meekness to be applied. Moreover, when he says κατὰ πρόσωπον, in face indeed or presence ταπεινὸς humble among them, and as is evident from the opposite, of little confidence, but absent too confident against the same: he speaks κατὰ μίμησιν and from the sense of the Pseudo-Apostles and others rashly judging and despising. Theophylact indeed brings forward another sense after Chrysostom; but this is sufficiently clear from the Pauline apology. Or that, he says, he speaks ironically, just as if he were using the words of his detractors. For they had this in their mouths, that when Paul is present, that man of no consequence will be found to be. For he is more abject and easily to be despised. But when he is absent, he swells and boasts, and is bolder against us, and threatens. Or certainly he relates these things about himself, namely, when I am present among you, I show myself humble and kind. But now if, being absent, I do something of great importance, I shall not have done it out of desperation, but because I trust in you very much.

Latin:

CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Per mansuetudinem Christi à προσωποληψίᾳ dehortatur contemnentes se quasi infirmum in præsentia, audacem in absentia, & carnaliter abutentem potestate officii, protestatus se spiritualibus armis pugnare, nec nisi inobedientiam vindicare; sed etiam potestatem suam habere à Christo, ac talem præsentem, qualem absentem gerere posse; nolle se autem supra mensuram, quam Deus assignavit, gloriari, imo ita statuere, eum, qui gloriari vult, in Domino gloriari debere.

PArtes duæ sunt. Primum enim instituitur apologia adversus temerarium judicium de potestatis Ecclesiasticæ abusu ad v. 6. Deinde verò autoritatis suæ contemptum vindicat Apostolus ad vers. 18.

PARS I. Apologia de abusu potestatis Apostolicæ.

Vers. 1. Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος) Quia erant adhuc pauci quidem, sed erant tamen Corinthi, qui Paulo obtrectabant, adversus eos Paulus dignitatem ministerii sui tuetur.

Διὰ τῆς πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας τοῦ χριστοῦ) Ἐπιείκεια hic bonitatem significat, ut Baruch. II. 21. Cant. puer. 13. Sap. XII. 18. 2. Macc. II. 23. X. 4. quomodo & ἐπιεικεῖς sunt viri boni ac faciles, Phil. IV. 5. 1. Tim. III. 3. Tit. III. 2. Merito autem has præcipue Christi virtutes commemorat, quia propter earum imitationem maxime spernebatur.

Ὃς κατὰ πρόσωπον μὲν ταπεινὸς ἐν ὑμῖν, ἀπὼν δὲ θαῤῥῶ εἰς ὑμᾶς) Sunt hæc dicta μιμητικῶς, ut Græci quidam Interpretes recte monuerunt. Idem enim est, quod infra 10. Dicebant obtrectatores eum præsentem multo lenius agere, quod offensas metueret, aut gratias captaret. Similes μιμήσεις etiam in epistola ad Romanos habuimus.

Postquam doctrinæ suæ apologiam sufficienter instituerat Apostolus, in qua sese cum Timotheo conjunxerat, quia una erat utriusque doctrina, jam Apostolici sui muneris apologiam aggreditur adversus ἐγκλήματα obtrectatorum, imprimis verò Pseudo-Apostolorum, quæ ipsummet Apostolum solum concernebant; inter quæ primum est abusus potestatis Apostolicæ. Ita vero refellit obtre- ctatorum criminationes, ut suos quam blandissime hortetur, imo oret, atque obtestetur per mansue- tudinem & æquitatem Christi, ut caveant à temera- riis muneris sui judiciis. Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος: E- go ipse ille Paulus, quem nostis Apostolum Jesu Christi, per voluntatem Dei παρακαλῶ hortor vos (v. 2. sequitur δέομαι rogo, obsecro) διὰ τῆς πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας, quam demonstravit in opere reconciliationis & in humiliatione vel exinani- tione nostri causa facta 2. Cor. V. 19. c. IIX. 9. atque etiamnum demonstrat ἐν διακονίᾳ τῆς καταλλαγῆς magna cum mansuetudine, & ἐπιεικείᾳ æquitate vel lenitate, obsecrans ipsos etiam impios καταλ- λάγητε τῷ Θεῷ 2. Cor. V. 20. uti Apostolus cum Ti- motheo hortatus erat Corinthios, & Christus per ipsos: Μὴ εἰς κενὸν τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ δέξασθαι 2. Cor. VI. 1. Quo pacto & testatur simul, & causam innuit, licet opertè, quod ipsos non nisi μετὰ πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας exemplo Christi, ceu legatus vice Christi tractarit. Nec sane, inquit Theophylactus, (Chrysostomum sequutus) parvi sunt facienda Pau- li preces, cum & Christi interponit mansuetudinem, perinde ac si inquiat: Vereamini Christi, per quam vos oro, mansuetudinem. Simul etiam patefacit, cur illis parcat, id scilicet, quia Salvatoris Christi imite- tur mansuetudinem. Non quia ad objurgandum sit impotentior. Nolite ergo nolenti mihi occasionem præ- bere, ut ab hac absistam benignitate, quam tantopere concupisco, ut vel hanc ad meum erga vos animum conciliandum interponendam jam censeam. Monet ita etiam tacite, ut & ipsi in judicando candorem, æquitatem, ac lenitatem adhibeant, quasi dicat: Non hoc contendit à vobis aliquis homo novus, vobis ignotus, & de Ecclesia vestra nihil emeritus: Sed ipse ego Paulus vos oro, quem non ignoratis de vestra Eccle- sia meis laboribus fundata & plantata & hucusque gubernata bene esse meritum, & proinde meo quodam jure, quod peto à vobis, impetrare debere. Quemad- modum igitur imitatus exemplum Salvatoris ac Ma- gistri Domini nostri Jesu, non cum imperio vobis man- do; sed leniter ac mansuete rogo, candideque moneo: Sic pervelim eadem lenitate meam à vobis petitionem attendi, & in censendis meis laboribus dictis factis- que candorem cum mansuetudine conjunctum adhi- beri. Cum autem κατὰ πρόσωπον ait, in facie quidem vel præsentia ταπεινὸς humilis inter ipsos, & ut ex opposito constat, exiguæ confidentiæ, ab- sens verò confidens nimis adversus eosdem: κατὰ μίμησιν & ex sensu Pseudo-Apostolorum & aliorum temere judicantium & contemnentium loquitur. Affert quidem & alium sensum post Chrysostomum, Theophylactus; Sed hic ex apologia Paulina satis liquet. Vel id, inquit, ironice dicit, perinde ac si obtrectantium verbis utatur. Hoc enim illi in ore habebant, cum primum aderit Paulus ille nullius mo- menti esse deprehendetur. Est enim ille abjectior & facile contemnendus. Cum vero abest, intume- scit & gloriatur, audentiorque in nos est, & commi- natur. Vel certe hæc de seipso differit, videlicet apud vos ipse cum præsto sum, humilem me præbeo & benignum. Nunc vero si absens magni aliquid, haudquaquam desperatione id egerim, sed quia plu- rimum vobis confido.

## 10:2
Vers. 2. Δέομαι μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι τῇ πεποιθήσει) I ask that I may not be compelled when I am present to use boldly that confidence which I have in God: namely, that God will fulfill my just desires. Πεποίθησις here is what πίστις is in 1 Corinthians 12:9. Thus you have πεποίθησιν for faith also in Ephesians 3:12. It corresponds to the Hebrew בטח, that is, what he said about coming with a rod in 1 Cor. 4:21.

ᾗ λογίζομαι τολμῆσαι ἐπί τινας, τοὺς λογιζομένους ἡμᾶς, ὡς κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦντας) The former λογίζομαι is I think, as in Rom. 1:3 and elsewhere: that other word λογιζομένυς is 'estimating,' as in Mark 15:28, Rom. 11:26. They walk in the flesh who seek thanks in the ministry of the Gospel, or fear the offenses of the wicked.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Δέομαι μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι τῇ πεποιθήσει) Rogo ne cogar ubi adero audacter uti ea fiducia, quam in Deum habeo: nempe impleturum Deum mea justa desideria. Πεποίθησις hic quod πίστις primo Cor. XII. 9. Sic πεποί- θησιν pro fide habes & Ephes. III. 12. Respondet He- bræ בטח hoc est, quod dixit venire cum virga 1. Cor. IV. v. 12.

ᾗ λογίζομαι τολμῆσαι ἐπί τινας, τοὺς λογιζομένους ἡμᾶς, ὡς κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦντας) Prius illud λογίζομαι est cogito, ut Rom. I. 3. & alibi: Alterum illud λογιζομένυς est æstimantes, ut Marci XV. v. 28. Rom. XI. v. 26. In carne ambulant, qui in ministerio Evangelii gratias ca- ptant, aut offensas improborum metuunt.

## 10:3
Verse 3. 'For walking in the flesh') It is one thing to 'walk according to the flesh,' which we have already had, and another to 'walk in the flesh'; for this signifies being in a condition that is weak and subject to no evils. See Heb. 5:7 and ch. 11:14, Gal. 4:13, 1 John 4:2.

'We do not war according to the flesh') We do not wage weak wars.

Derrerere, according to B. Hunnius, is urging the Corinthians not to rashly support the unjust judgments of the false Apostles: for otherwise it would happen, as he does not wish, that he would be compelled to usurp the same παῥῥησίαν [boldness] against them, which he had previously been forced to use by letter against certain ones who had offended the Church of the Corinthians either by ἑτεροδιδασκαλίᾳ [strange teaching] or by a flagitious life. He says, however: 'because I am estimated to have been bold': by which words he does not deny that he had rebuked the authors of scandals with a free spirit, and he clears away the accusation of his enemies, who kept saying that this was done by him too sharply, and even too licentiously and audaciously, and that proper moderation was not observed. Λογίζομαι, therefore, is rightly rendered passively in the Vulgate, 'I am estimated,' which sense the text demands.
