Concerning which Beza also gave warning: Most wish to take τὸ λογίζεσθαι in a neutral sense for 'I think,' as it is also taken by the Syrian interpreter. But the sentence seems to me to demand entirely that it be taken passively, as the old Latin interpreter also understood it, with the addition of a distinction after τολμῆσαι, and with the meaning of the Aorist preserved, so that ἐπί τινας refers to θαῥῥῆσαι and not to τολμῆσαι. Nor did he say, as Chrysostom warns, 'as I am prepared,' but 'as I am estimated.' For this is not yet determined for me, but they themselves indeed provide the cause and occasion; yet I, even so, do not bring my mind to do this. And yet he was not doing this to avenge his own injuries; but to defend the Gospel. But if, when the cause of the Gospel preaching had to be defended, he does not show himself bitter at all, but rather tergiversates and weaves delays, and asks that such a necessity not be brought upon him: Much less, then, would he have done anything of this kind in repelling his own injuries. This, therefore, he says, grant me, that I may not have the necessity to show that I can use confidence of spirit even in person against those against whom it is fitting, that is, to punish them and subject them to penalty. Do you see how alien he was from all desire for glory, and that he did not do anything for the sake of ostentation, as one who, even when it was necessary, still called it 'audacity.' For I ask, he says, that I may not be bold when present with that confidence with which I am estimated to be bold against certain ones. For this is primarily the duty of a Master, not to exact punishments immediately, but to correct, and to be hesitant and slow in inflicting penalties. But not only hypocrisy or a desire to please, as Grotius wishes; but as Chrysostom and Theophylact warn, he removes insolence primarily with the phrase 'according to the flesh': because he was being argued against most of all concerning the abuse of his power: Although he wishes everything that is appropriate for those walking in the flesh in their duty to be excluded. Yet he purges himself most of all concerning those things which were imputed to him. For when they, as Chrysostom observes, were accusing him as a hypocrite, as wicked, as arrogant ὡς ἀλάζονα, 'we carry the flesh,' he says, 'I do not deny that, but we do not live according to the flesh.' Indeed, he did not even say this, but reserved for a little while what pertained to the praise and commendation of his life: And he discourses first about the preaching, showing that it is by no means human, nor does it stand in need of inferior help. Wherefore he did not say 'we': 'We do not live according to the flesh,' but 'we do not war according to the flesh'; that is, we have indeed undertaken war and conflict: but we do not fight with carnal weapons, nor do we defend ourselves with human aids. I pray, he says, interpreting Theophylact, that you do not compel me to use my power more confidently. For he calls his confidence 'power,' by which 'I am estimated to be bold,' that is, I come into suspicion, because the false Apostles urge me on, inveighing against me, who by slandering me object both hypocrisy and simulation and insolence. For he means this when he says: 'As if we walked according to the flesh.' He adds, however, inconveniently: But note how he calls 'confidence' the avenging of an injury brought on by some, even though he was going to do nothing of his own for the sake of thanks, but for the sake of vindicating the very proclamation of the Gospel. It is, however, more consistent with a Teacher to show himself slower to inflict punishments, and not to leap forth immediately to castigation. The Apostle removes not only the weakness of wars, but any carnal manner of warring; he who was despised in his presence not only as weak, but was also argued against because of excessive audacity and violence used in his absence and through letters. For his Adversaries were accusing him because he had been carried away into that vehemence by some affection of the flesh, and that he was governed by carnal affections in his duty, so that they might derogate from the authority of those things which the Apostle, moved by just zeal, had commanded to be established or corrected, and at the same time might elevate and tear down the dignity of the Pauline ministry. It can be referred at the same time to carnal prudence, as Cornelius a Lapide wishes this to be the genuine mind of the Apostle's words: 'Who think that we walk as if according to the flesh,' as if I use carnal means, namely, carnal, human, and political prudence, industry, and cunning, so that when I do not dare to appear in person, or to command, I do it while absent through bold and threatening letters. 'But we war,' when he says, he shows clearly that he has entered upon a different war and contest by preaching. Not without reason, says B. Hunnius, does he use the metaphor of warring, to indicate that in his duty he must fight against Satan, the world, and the flesh, for which struggle more than human prudence is required: Therefore, what he did out of the reason of his office, namely by excommunicating the incestuous person and rebuking other disorderly ones, that is not to be referred to any human affection of the flesh, but to the power of the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐν σαρκὶ γὰρ περιπατῦντες) Aliud est κατὰ σάρ- κα περιπατεῖν, quod jam habuimus, aliud ἐν σαρκὶ; Hoc e- nim significat in conditione esse infirma & nullis malis ob- noxia. Vide Hebr. V. v. 7. & cap. XI. 14. Gal. IV. vers. 13. 1. Joh. IV. 2.

Οὐ κατὰ σάρκα στρατευόμεθα) Bella gerimus non in- firma.

Derrerere, juxta B. Hunnium, nititur Corin- thios, ne temere suffragentur iniquis judiciis Pseudo-Apostolorum: alias enim fore, ut no- lit, velit eandem παῥῥησίαν in illos comm usur- pare cogatur, qua prius absenti fuerit utendum per epistolam in quosdam, qui vel ἑτεροδιδασκα- λίᾳ vel vita flagitiosa Ecclesiam offenderant Co- rinthiorum. Dicit autem: quia existimor au- dax fuisse: quibus verbis non diffitetur, se libero spiritu scandalorum authores reprehendisse, & cri minationem diluit hostium, qui nimis acriter, nimis etiam licenter & audacter hoc ab illo factum, nec con- venientem moderationem servatam esse dictitabant. Λογίζομαι ergo recte effertur passive in Vulgata, existimor, quem sensum textus postulat. Quo de monuit etiam Beza: Plerique volunt τὸ λογίζεσθαι accipere neutra significatione pro cogito, ut accipi- tur quoque à Syro interprete. Sed sententia mihi videtur omnino postulare, ut passive accipiatur, ut etiam vetus Latinus interpres intellexit, adjecta distinctione post τολμῆσαι, & servata Aoristi signi- ficatione, ita, ut ἐπί τινας referatur ad θαῥῥῆσαι non ad τολμῆσαι. Nec dixit, Chrysostomo monente, qua paratus sum, sed qua existimor. Nec dum enim mihi hoc constitutum est, verum ipsi quidem causam & occasionem præbent; at ego tamen ne sic quidem hoc facere in animum induco. Atqui non ut ipse suas injurias ulcisceretur, hoc faciebat; sed ut Evangelium tueretur. Quod si, ubi prædicationis Evangelicæ causa tuenda erat, minime acerbum se præbet, verum tergiversatur ac moras nectit, rogat- que, ne tanta sibi necessitas inferatur: Multo utique minus in suis injuriis propulsandis quicquam hujus- modi fecisset. Hoc igitur, inquit, mihi indulgete, ut ne necesse habeam ostendere, quod coram etiam, ad- versus quos par sit, animi fiducia uti queam, hoc est eos punire, & supplicio afficere. Videsne, quam ab omni gloria studio alienus esset, nec ostentationis causa quicquam efficeret, ut qui, tum etiam cum ne- cesse esset, audaciam tamen id appellaret. Rogo enim, inquit, ne præsens audeam ea confidentia, qua exi- stimor audere in quosdam. Hoc enim cumprimis ex Magistri officio est, non confestim pœnas sumere, sed corrigere, atque in inferendis suppliciis cun- ctantem ac tardum esse. Non autem tantum hy- pocrisin aut studium placendi, ut vult Grotius; sed ut Chrysostomus & Theophylactus monent, insolentiam imprimis voce κατὰ σάρκα removet: quia de abusu maximè potestatis suæ arguebatur: Quanquam omnia, quæ carnaliter ambulanti- bus in officio conveniunt, exclusa velit. De iis tamen se potissimum purgat, quæ ipsi impu- tabantur. Nam eum illi, observante Chryso- stomo, ut hypocritam, ut improbum, ut arrogan- tem ὡς ἀλάζονα infimulabant, carnem gerimus, inquit, id non inficior, verum carni minime vi- vimus. Imo vero ne hoc quidem dixit, sed ali- quantisper reservavit, quod ad vitæ laudem com- mendationemque pertineret: Ac prius de prædi- catione disserit, ostendens eam minime humanam esse, nec inferiore ope indigere. Quocirca non nos dixit : Non juxta carnem vivimus, sed non se- cundum carnem militamus; hoc est, bellum quidem ac dimicationem suscepimus : at carni- libus armis minime decertamus, nec humanis au- xiliis nos tuemur. Oro inquit, Theophylacto in- terprete, ne me cogatis, ut mea fidentius utar po- testate. Confidentiam enim suam appellat po- tentiam, qua existimor audere, hoc est, in suspi- cionem venio, quia falsi me urgent Apostoli ad- versum me invehentes, qui mihi obtrectando & hypocrisin & simulationem objectant & insolen- tiam. Id enim sentit, cum inquit : Tanquam secundum carnem ambulemus. Addit tamen in- commode : Adverte autem, quemadmodum con- fidentiam vocet, a nonnullis illatam ulcisci inju- riam, tametsi nihil sui ob gratiam, sed pro ipso Evangelii præconio vindicando id esset facturus. Magis tamen est Præceptori consentaneum, tar- diorem se ad pœnas inferendas præstare, nec ad castigationem mox prosilire. Non infirmitatem tantum bellorum, sed quamvis carnalem mili- tandi rationem removet Apostolus; qui non solùm ut infirmus, in præsentia contemnebatur, sed etiam ob nimiam audaciam & violentiam in absentia, & per literas adhibitam argueba- tur. Accusabant enim eum Adversarii, quod ex quodam affectu carnis in eam vehementiam abreptus fuerit, & in officio suo carnalibus af- fectibus regatur, ut autoritatem derogarent iis, quæ Apostolus, justo zelo motus, fancienda aut corrigenda præceperat, simulque ministerii Paulini dignitatem elevarent & convellerent. Referri simul id poterit ad carnalem pruden- tiam, uti Cornelius a Lapide genuinam hanc mentem esse vult verborum Apostoli: Qui ar- bitrantur nos, tanquam secundum carnem ambu- lemus, tanquam carnalibus mediis, carnali scili- cet, humanaque ac politica prudentia, industria, astutia utar, ut cum non ausim præsens compare- re, vel imperare, absens id faciam per audaces & minaces literas. Militamus autem, cum in- quit, ostendit plane, se prædicando bellum & certamen aliud iniisse. Haud abs re, inquit B. Hunnius, militandi utitur metaphora, ut indicet in suo officio depugnandum sibi cum Satana, mun- do, & carne, quam ad luctam plus quam humana prudentia requiratur: Idcirco quod fecerit ex ra- tione sui muneris, excommunicando nimirum ince- stuosum, & objurgando alios inordinatos, id non ad humanum aliquem affectum carnis, sed ad po- testatem Spiritus esse referendum.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. For the weapons of our warfare) With almost the same translation, the Chaldean in Genesis 48:22 understands the prayers of Jacob through the bow and sword. See also Eph. 6:13, 21, 1 Thess. 5:8, and above 6:7.

Not fleshly) Not invalid.

That passage in Genesis 48:22 is irrelevant, as is the sense of the Chaldean interpreter. See our commentary on Genesis at that place. Fleshly, not fleshly, are invalid. For although they may also be invalid, the Apostle nevertheless properly removes and excludes by this word those things which pertain to the flesh: Theophylact explains it thus: that is, they do not prefer wealth, not glory, not the allurements of speech; not certain smoother and feigned words, for such are the weapons of the flesh; which, and other things of this kind, Chrysostom says are excluded.

But mighty through God) That is, through God. From this, take the explanation of the prophecies concerning the victory of the Messiah.

Although valid and invalid are opposed, as carnal and spiritual, the Apostle nevertheless opposes (as far as immediate opposition is concerned) not spiritual things here to carnal things, but rather δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ, valid to God, which are in truth nothing other than spiritual things. Chrysostom notes this: He did not say: We are not carnal; but our weapons. For he speaks first of preaching, and ascribes all power to God. Nor did he say spiritual (although this word ought to be used, so that it might be opposed to carnal), but powerful, by this indeed also signifying and showing that their weapons are weak and feeble. And observe how he himself is devoid of all pride. For he did not say, we are powerful, but our weapons are powerful to God. We did not create them as such, but God himself. For since they themselves were being beaten with scourges, and were being harassed, and were being pressed by countless and most atrocious hardships, which were indeed a proof of weakness, therefore, showing the power of God, he says, but are powerful to God. For this indicates his strength and power above all, that he obtains victory through such weapons. And so, even though we carry these: yet it is he who fights and works through them. Moreover, weapons are called valid to God both because they are employed for God by the Author of the ministry, and because they are directed to the praise of the power of God as to their proper end. They are indeed powerful to God, says Theophylact, the weapons, for by these the power of God is especially made known, and he is the one who does these things and fights, even though we appear to be covered by such weapons.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Τὰ γὰρ ὅπλα τῆς στρατείας ἡμῶν) Pari ferme translatione Chaldæus Genes. XLVIII 22. per arcum & gladium preces Jacobi intelligit. Vide & Eph. VI. v. 13. 21. 1. Thess. V. 8. & supra VI. 7.

Οὐ σαρκικὰ) Non invalida.

Locus ille Genes. XLVIII. 22. alienus est, uti & sensus Chaldaici interpretis. Vid. Comment. noster in Genesin ad illum locum. Σαρκικὰ, non Σαρκικά sunt invalida. Licet enim & invalida sint, re- movet tamen & excludit Apostolus hac voce proprie ea, quæ ad carnem spectant: Theophy- lactus ita explicat: hoc est, non opes præferunt, non gloriam, non sermonis lenocinia; non dicta quædam blandiora & simulata, istiusmodi nam- que sunt carnis arma; quæ, & alia hujusmodi excludi ait Chrysostomus.

Ἀλλὰ δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ) Id est, per Deum. Hinc sume ex- plicationem vaticiniorum de victoria Messiæ.

Etsi valida & invalida opponantur, ut carnalia & spiritualia, opponit tamen (quod ad immedia- tam oppositionem) Apostolus carnalibus hic non spiritualia, verum δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ, valida Deo, quæ vero nulla alia sunt, quam spiritualia. Notat hoc Chrysostomus: Non dixit: Nos haud carnales sumus; sed arma nostra. Nam de prædicatione verba prius facit, potentiamque universam Deo adscribit. Nec dixit spiritualia, (quanquam hoc vocabulum adhi- bendum esset, ut carnalibus opponatur) sed potentia, per hoc nimirum quoque illud significans, atque osten- dens, quod illorum arma infirma & imbecilla sint. Atque animadverte, quam ipse fastus omnis sit ex- pers. Non enim dixit, nos potentes sumus, sed arma nostra Deo potentia sunt. Non nos ea talia condidi- mus, sed Deus ipse. Quoniam enim ipsi flagris cæde- bantur, & exagitabantur, atque innumeris & atro- cissimis incommodis premebantur, quæ quidem im- becillitatis argumentum erant, idcirco Dei poten- tiam ostendens, ait, sed Deo potentia sunt. Nam hoc imprimis ipsius vim ac potentiam indicat, quod per hujusmodi arma victoriam adipiscatur. Itaque tam- etsi hæc gestemus: at ipse tamen est, qui per ea dimi- cat & operatur. Dicuntur autem arma valida Deo cùm quod ab Autore ministerii Deo adhibeantur, tùm quod in laudem potentiæ Dei ceu ad finem proprium dirigantur. Potentia quidem ea Deo sunt, ait Theophylactus, arma, his quippe vel maxime Dei potentia innotescit, & ille est, qui hæc factitat & præliatur, tametsi nos videamur, istiusmodi esse ar- mis operti.

## 10:5
Vers. 5. πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων) He refers to the history of Jesus, who at the sound of the trumpet, with God acting, threw down the fortifications of Jericho; What is τῆχος there in Greek, is ὀχύρωμα here. Men are accustomed to trust in their hands, Jerem. XLVIII. 7. Therefore, whatever it is in which anyone trusts is called ὀχύρωμα by analogy, Prov. XXI. 22. Such was human learning, eloquence, and riches among the Corinthians.

Λογισμοὺς καθαιροῦντες, καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον κατὰ τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ) These cohere with we war, with the rest inserted by parenthesis. Moreover, there is here first a transposition for destroying reasonings and every height; then a hendiadys. For reasonings and every height is put for a height of words. He explains the reduction. For height is the same as a fortification, a tower, and battlements of walls. To these he compares the reasonings of the philosophers, which were opposed to the Gospel. The Gospel is here called by way of excellence the knowledge of God, as above IV. 6. See also Luke I. 77.

Καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ χρι- στοῦ) This is to be understood not of the effect, for the matter does not succeed in all, but of arguments sufficient to produce the whole effect. Thus, that which is not received is also said to be given. Thus Acts V. 31. John VI. 33.

Latin:

Vers. 5. πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων) Respicit histo- riam Jesu, qui ad buccinæ sonum, Deo agente, dejecit munimenta Jerichuntis; Quod ibi in Græco est τῆχος, id hic est ὀχύρωμα. Solent homines manibus fidere, Jerem. XLVIII. 7. Ideo quicquid est, cui quis confidit per similitudinem dicitur ὀχύρωμα, Prov. XXI. 22. Qualis erat apud Corinthios humana eruditio, eloquentia, divitiæ.

Λογισμοὺς καθαιροῦντες, καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον κατὰ τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ) Cohærent hæc cum στρατευόμεθα cæte- ris per parenthesin interjectis. Est autem hic primum tra- jeclio pro καθαιροῦντες λογισμοὺς καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα; Deinde ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Nam λογισμοὺς καὶ πᾶν ὕψωμα positum est pro ὕψωμα λόγων. Explicat ἀπαγωγήν. Nam ὕψωμα idem quod ὀχύρωμα turris & pinnæ murorum. Iis comparat ra- tiocinationes Philosophorum, quæ Evangelio opponeban- tur. Evangelium hic κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur γνῶσις τοῦ Θεοῦ, ut supra IV. 6. Vide & Luc. I. 77.

Καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ χρι- στοῦ) Intelligendum hoc non de effectu, neque enim in o- mnibus res succedit, sed de argumentis sufficientibus ad effectum totum producendum. Sic dari dicitur etiam quod non accipitur. Sic Act. V. 31. Joh. VI. 33.

## 10:6
Καὶ ἐν ἑτοίμῳ ἔχοντες ἐκδικῆσαι πᾶσαν παρακοήν) This is that rod of which we were just speaking, such as Paul used against Elymas, against the guilty party of incest, against Hymenaeus, against Philetus.

Ὅταν πληρωθῇ ὑμῶν ὑπακοή) If you do what is your duty. For there is no place for harsh remedies where the whole Church lies in sickness. Pardon is necessary where the whole army has deserted, says Seneca. It seems that the history of Num. XVI. 26 is being referred to.

The power of the Word is described from its effects, as it is valid both for the destruction of the fortifications of Satan and his organs, such as are partly heretics, partly also tyrants, but here those are especially understood, as they oppose their reasonings like fortifications to the Gospel, and by the loftiness of their speculations, or of their mind, exalt themselves against the knowledge of God; and for the taking captive of every thought or concept under the obedience of Christ; and for the avenging of all disobedience, whether of unbelief or of malicious resistance against those things which are prescribed and commanded by the Word of God. But those who do this, fighting with such weapons, powerful to God, they do not abuse, but use in the best way the apostolic power, or that granted to the sacred ministry; they do not war carnally, but spiritually. Our human intellect always resists the revealed knowledge of God, nay, it considers the word of God as foolishness. And its mind is enmity against God. But the ministry of the Word has such power that it can subject the rebelling reason to Christ through the word: It is not therefore said to act by destroying the intellect, as it destroys opposing reasonings, but by taking it captive: because the use of reason is not taken away in divine matters, but is brought into the obedience of faith. Moreover, the Apostle explains fortifications by reasonings, that is, according to Chrysostom and Theophylact, the syllogisms and captious arguments of enemies or inventions and thoughts. He does not say, however, that he brings forward engines for the sake of destroying; but he immediately adds we have destroyed, so that he may reveal both the ease of the victory and the force of the darts with which he was striking the minds of men. Theophylact judges that the height exalting itself against the knowledge of God can be understood either of the height of the mind or of places, by which the wisdom of God is opposed. B. Hunnius understands not only the sublimity and prudence of monarchs resisting the course of the preaching of the Gospel, but especially that proud wisdom of the philosophers, both despising the word of the Gospel from on high, and rejecting that knowledge of God which is proposed in the Gospel. Moreover, reasonings, which are opposed like fortifications to the word of God, and every thought, which exalts itself like a high tower against the knowledge of God, seem to explain each other, all of which are utterly destroyed and overcome, so that they can no longer oppose themselves to the Word of God, but are brought under the yoke of the obedience of Christ, and are taken captive through the power of the word: Which, according to Theophylact, signifies a more perfect victory, as if he were to say, we not only remove and overcome whatever human counsels and thoughts there are, but we even bring them into servitude. But to that grave name of servitude is joined the sweet obedience in Christ, that is, that servitude which is also more honorable and more wholesome than any other. For they subject themselves to Christ from perdition to salvation, from death to life. If Apostolic power is burdensome to the reprobate, if its weapons are valid and hostile, because they are applied as valid by God and for the praise of divine power, justice, and grace, no abuse of the power, office, or weapons with which the Apostle serves can be argued here, even if he destroys strongholds and casts down enemies exalting themselves and brings them into captivity, just as in war not only are strongholds destroyed, but enemies are also accustomed to being captured. But as it goes well with those who, having subdued human reason, yield their conquered hands to Evangelical doctrine: so those who contumaciously resist the Leader of spiritual warfare experience the punishments of disobedience, not only temporal but also eternal, if repentance is not performed. And thus the blessed Hunnius observes that this member aims directly at the Apostle's prefixed goal; since he declares not obscurely that that thunderbolt of excommunication against the incestuous Corinthian, but also the remaining severity used in the former epistle against the authors of scandals, is to be referred to this part of the ministry, namely the binding key: Therefore, that which has proceeded from duty is not to be blamed. Cornelius a Lapide says almost the same: as if he were to say: It is also prompt and easy for me to avenge the disobedience of the rebels and false Apostles who disparage me, namely by excommunicating them, when your disobedience has been fulfilled. For I do not wish to involve you in the same punishment; I prefer that you yourselves correct what needs to be corrected, I wait for you to fully fulfill what I have commanded; and I defer that vengeance until you are fully corrected and obedient, then finally I will show and draw forth the sword of excommunication against those stubborn detractors.

One must note, against the other sword of the Roman Pontiff Boniface VIII in the Extravagant Unam Sanctam, what Estius has here: Paul, and any successor of the Apostles, avenges all disobedience not with a bodily sword, which was given to a Prince or political magistrate for the punishment of evildoers (Rom. 13) and whose use is in bodily warfare, but with a spiritual sword, that is, with ecclesiastical censures, the chief of which is the power of excommunicating.

But as to what is added: ὅταν πληρωθῇ ὑμῶν ἡ ὑπακοὴ, although others take it to mean that he wishes to wait for the Corinthians, who have already begun to obey, to have complete obedience, so that the Apostle's warnings may be satisfied in the Church before he exercises a more severe punishment against the refractory, the stubborn, and his detractors, and indeed the very Pseudo-Apostles themselves, nevertheless the blessed Hunnius not inappropriately refers this to the end of a more severe punishment, and to those same persons against whom it is exercised, namely that he is prepared to punish all disobedience, even by a more severe method, such as excommunication was; not, however, for perpetual exclusion, but until the disobedience is fulfilled by amendment, so that the wicked themselves may also be turned to obedience to Christ. For this end is the key that binds, not destruction and ruin (unless accidentally, when men, even when warned and chastised, persist in impenitence) but the rescue and salvation of those whose sins are bound. Which is therefore not an abuse, but the most just and equitable use of the power of the ecclesiastical office: Cf. 1 Cor. 5, 2 Thess. 3, 1 Tim. 1. Estius observes here five parts of the Apostolic warfare, taken from a comparison with bodily warfare. The first is to destroy strong and valid fortifications, which Paul says is done through weapons powerful to God. The second is to destroy counsels or thoughts, that is, whatever is ingeniously devised against the Christian faith. The third is to destroy machines which seem impregnable by their height. The fourth is to lead enemies captive and subjugate them to their Prince. The fifth and final one is to punish the disobedient and rebellious through just censure.

PART II. In which the weakness of Apostolic authority is refuted.

Latin:

Καὶ ἐν ἑτοίμῳ ἔχοντες ἐκδικῆσαι πᾶσαν παρακοήν) Hæc est illa virga, de qua modo dicebamus, quali usus Pau- lus in Elymam, in reum incesti, in Hymenæum, in Phi- letam.

Ὅταν πληρωθῇ ὑμῶν ὑπακοή) Si vos, quod vestri est officii, feceritis. Neque enim duris remediis locus est, ubi tota Ecclesia in morbo cubat. Necessaria est venia, ubi totus deseruit exercitus, ait Seneca. Videtur respici historia Num. XVI. 26.

Ab effectibus describitur potentia Verbi, utpote quod validum sit tum ad destructionem munitionum Satanæ & organorum ejus, qualia sunt partim hæretici, partim etiam tyranni, sed hîc illi potissimum intelliguntur, utpote qui λογισμοὺς suos instar munitionum opponunt Evangelio, & celsitudine speculationum, vel mentis sese extol- lunt adversus cognitionem Dei; tum ad captiva- tionem omnis cogitationis vel conceptus sub ob- sequium Christi; tum ad vindicationem omnis in- obedientiæ, sive infidelitatis, sive malitiosæ repu- gnantiæ adversus ea, quæ Verbo Dei præscribun- tur, ac demandantur. Qui vero id agunt, ejus- modi armis, Deo potentibus, vel validis pugnan- tes, illi non abutuntur, sed optimè utuntur potesta- te Apostolica, vel sacro ministerio concessa; non carnaliter militant, sed spiritualiter. Intellectus humanus noster semper reluctatur cognitioni Dei revelatae, imo verbum Dei pro stultitia habet. Estque φρόνημα ejus inimicitia adversus Deum Sed ministerium Verbi eam habet virtutem, ut rebellantem rationem Christo subjicere per verbum possit: Non ergo id jam destruendo intellectum, uti λογισμὸς adversos destruit, agere dicitur, sed captivando: quia non tollitur usus rationis in rebus divinis, sed in obse- quium fidei redigitur. Munitiones autem Aposto- lus per λογισμὸς explicat, id est, secundum Chry- sostomum, & Theophylactum syllogismos & captiun- culas hostium vel commenta & cogitationes. Non autem debellandi gratia tormenta se adferre ait; sed mox destruximus infert, ut & victoria facilita- tem, & spiculorum, quibus animos hominum percel- lebat, vim patefaciat. Altitudinem tollentem se ad- versus cognitionem Dei Theophylactus vel de animi vel de locorum altitudine, qua Dei sapientia adver- setur, intelligi posse censet. B. Hunnius non modo sublimitatem & prudentiam Monarchorum obni- tentium cursui praedicationis Evangelicae, sed cum- primis superbam illam sapientiam Philosophorum, & sublimi despicientium verbum Evangelii, & re- spuentium eam cognitionem Dei, quae in Evangelio proponitur, intelligit. Videntur autem sese mu- tuo explicare λογισμοὶ, qui veluti munitiones op- ponuntur verbo Dei & πᾶν νόημα, quod se ex- tollit instar turris excelsae adversus cognitionem Dei, quae omnia destruuntur prorsus & superan- tur, ut non amplius Verbo Dei sese opponere pos- sint, sed sub jugum obedientiae Christi redigantur, & per verbi virtutem captivantur: Quod secun- dum Theophylactum perfectiorem significat victo- riam, quasi dicat, non modo humana quaecunque con- silia & cogitationes tollimus & superamus, quin & in servitutem redigimus. Ad grave autem illud servitutis nomen subjungitur suave in Christo obsequium, hoc est, ea servitus, quae etiam quavis est honoratior, ac salubrior. Nam a per- ditione in salutem, a morte in vitam Christo sese subjiciunt. Si gravis est reprobis Apostolica potestas, si arma valida & infesta, quia Deo valida adhibentur a Deo, & ad laudem divinae potentiae, justitiae & gratiae, nullus hic argui potest potestatis, officij, aut armorum, quibus militat Apostolus, abusus, etsi destruat munitiones, hostesque se ex- tollentes prosternat & in captivitatem redigat, ut in bello non tantum munitiones destrui, sed ho- stes etiam captivari solent. Ut autem bene agitur cum illis, qui subacta ratione humana, victas ma- nus dant Evangelicae doctrinae: ita spiritualis mili- tiae Duci contumaciter resistentes poenas experi- untur inobedientiae non temporales tantum, sed etiam aeternas, si non agatur poenitentia. Atque ita membrum hoc ad praefixum scopum Apostoli recta collineare, observat B. Hunnius; Siquidem non obscure declaret, fulmen illud excommunicatio- nis adversus incestuosum Corinthium, sed & reli- quam severitatem epistola priore in autores scanda- lorum usurpatam ad hanc partem ministerii, cla- vem nimirum ligantem, referendum esse: Proinde non vitio dandum id, quod ab officio profectum sit. Similiter fere Cornelius a Lapide: quasi dicat: Prom- ptum quoque mihi est & facile ulcisci rebellium & Pseudo-Apostolorum, qui mihi detrahunt, inobedien- tiam, eos scilicet excommunicando, cum impleta fuerit vestra inobedientia. Nolo enim vos eadem poena in- volvere; malo ut vos ipsi, quae corrigenda sunt, corri- gatis, expecto, ut plene impleatis, quod jussi; eumque vindictam differo, donec vos plane correcti & obedi- entes sitis, tum denique in contumaces illos obtrecta- tores ostendam & exeram gladium excommunica- tionis.

Notanda sunt contra gladium alterum Pontificis Romani Bonifacii VIII. in Extravaganti unam san- ctam, quæ hic habet Estius: Ulciscitur autem Pau- lus, & quilibet Apostolorum successor omnem inobe- dientiam non gladio corporeo, qui Principi aut magi- stratui Politico datus est ad vindictam malefacto- rum Rom. XIII. & cujus usus est in militia corpora- li, sed gladio spirituali, id est censuris Ecclesiasti- cis, quarum præcipua est excommunicandi pote- stas.

Quod autem subjicitur: ὅταν πληρωθῇ ὑμῶν ἡ ὑπακοὴ, etsi alii eo etiam accipiant, quod prius ex- pectare velit Corinthiorum, qui jam obsequi cœ- perunt completam obedientiam, ut in omnibus monitis Apostoli satisfiat in Ecclesia, antequam vindictam severiorem adversus refractarios per- vicaces, & obtrectatores suos ipsosque adeo Pseu- do-Apostolos exerceat, non inconcinne tamen B. Hunnius id ad finem severioris vindictæ, & eosdem, adversus quos illa exercetur, refert, quod paratus sit vindicare quidem omnem inobedientiam, et- iam severiori ratione, qualis erat excommunicatio; non tamen ad perpetuam exclusionem, sed donec im- pleatur inobedientia, per emendationem, ut ipsi quo- que improbi flectantur ad obsequendum Christo. Hic enim finis est clavis ligantis non interitus & per- ditio (nisi per accidens, cum homines etiam moniti & castigati in impœnitentia persistunt) sed ere- ptio, salusque illorum, quibus ligantur peccata. Qui non abusus proinde, sed justissimus & æquissimus usus est potestatis officii Ecclesiastici: Conf. 1. Cor. V. 2. Thess. III. 1. Tim. I. Observat hic Estius quinque partes Apostolicæ militiæ, sumptas ex comparatione militiæ corporalis. Prima est destruere munitiones fortes & validas, quod fieri dicit Paulus per arma Deo potentia. Secunda est destruere consilia seu co- gitationes, id est, quicquid ingeniose contra fidem Christianam excogitatur. Tertia destruere machi- nas, quæ sublimitate videntur inexpugnabiles. Quarta hostes captivos ducere & suo Principi sub- jugare. Quinta eaque postrema, inobedientes ac rebelles per justam animadversionem ulcisci.

PARS II. Qua diluitur tenuitas autoritatis Apostolicæ.

## 10:7
Ver. 7. τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον βλέπετε) Do you look only at those things which have value among men? For that is πρόσωπον, as we saw above at V. 12, Gal. 2:6.

We do not disapprove. This is explained in two ways: 1. By way of an admonition in the imperative, as the Vulgate rendered it: Look at the things that are according to the face, or those things which are plain to anyone, exposed to the eyes of all, as if he were teaching that it can be seen even from the very appearance that he is not unlike the detractors of the Apostles, nor can they themselves deny it, as the blessed Cluverus explains in Orthod. Apost. 2. By way of an interrogation: Do you judge according to the external face? As Cajetan and the blessed Luther do with the Greeks: Richtet ihr nach dem Ansehen? Which sense is more suitable. For the sense is reproachful. Nor does it matter, says Estius, whether it is read as an interrogation, as the same Cajetan wishes after Theodoret, or as a statement, except that the interrogation makes the reproach sharper, as if he were saying: Do you Corinthians really see only those things which are in sight, and judge only from those things which appear on the outside? namely, against that saying of the Savior in John 7: Do not judge according to the face, but judge a just judgment. He is evidently correcting his Corinthians because they were judging concerning the ministry and the ministers spiritually, from the quality of their calling, the excellence of their gifts, the kind of doctrine, and the estimation of their labors; but according to the external face, to a deceptive appearance through partiality (προσωποληψία) altogether unworthy of them, as the blessed Hunnius explained. As if he were saying: I have just explained with what weapons we fight in our ministry, and what admirable works God accomplishes through us, not by carnal aids, but by spiritual defenses, for which reason I would not hesitate to appeal to your experience, because you have felt in reality the heavenly power of my Apostleship among you: And yet you are so easily moved, with a mask running into your eyes, that you value the empty boasting of the Pseudo-Apostles more than the labors of your Apostle and his merits toward your Church. Thus also the blessed Balduinus: He argues, he says, the vanity of judgment in these men. You see the things which are according to the face, v. 7, as if he were saying: do you judge my office only according to my external condition? And because you find nothing pompous, nothing austere, nothing that could fill the eyes or ears of the delicate in me, but Apostolic gentleness and simplicity, do you therefore despise me? Schlichting, having retained the interrogation, explained it thus: You see, that is, you note, observe, and notice the things that look to my face and the external habit of my body or flesh: as if he were saying, and do you not also see that I do not walk according to the flesh? Do you not see that I do not wage war according to the flesh? Do you not see that my weapons are not carnal, but powerful to God, and that I am the performer of the divine works which I mentioned? And these things are no less in the open than those which are according to the face.

εἴτις πέποιθεν ἑαυτῷ) A Hebraism for לוֹ, in himself.

χριστῷ εἶναι) Understood from the preceding ἑαυτόν. That he is loved by Christ.

Let him consider this again from himself) Even without my warning, let him think this.

that just as he is Christ’s, so also we are Christ’s) It is apparent to all, he says, from my life and from such excellent and frequent miracles.

But especially also from the doctrine: Because God exhorts through us, and thus testifies in 2 Cor. V. He does not speak only of himself; but these things also apply to Timothy, whence it appears that they refer not so much to miracles as to doctrine and life. For it is not established that Timothy was distinguished by miracles. According to others, to be Christ’s here is the same as to be a Christian, or a chief member of Christ, which they have therefore used to diminish Paul’s authority: since he had only recently come to the knowledge of Christ, and had not seen him in the flesh, nor had he had great familiarity with the Apostles of Christ, to which interpretation Chrysostom and Theophylact also incline.

Latin:

Vers. 7. τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον βλέπετε) Adeone illa tan- tum, quæ apud homines valent, respicitis? Id enim πρόσω- πον, ut vidimus supra V. 12. Gal. II. 6.

Non improbamus. Duobus modis hoc ex- plicatur 1. per modum admonitionis in Imperati- vo, ut Vulgata reddidit: Quæ secundum faciem sunt, videte, seu quæ cuilibet plana sunt, omnium oculis exposita, quasi doceat, ex ipso etiam aspe- ctu videri posse, non disparem esse obtrectatori- bus Apostolorum, nec ipsos id negare posse, ut B. Cluverus in Orthod. Apost. explicat. 2. Per mo- dum Interrogationis: Judicatisne secundum exter- nam faciem? Ut cum Græcis Cajetanus & B. Lu- therus: Richtet ihr nach dem Ansehen? Qui sen- sus convenientior est. Sensus enim est objurga- torius. Neque refert, inquit, Estius, utrum per interrogationem legatur, ut post Theodoretum vult idem Cajetanus, an enuntiative, nisi quod interro- gatio acriorem reddit objurgationem, quasi dicat: Itane vos Corinthii ea, quæ in conspectu sunt, tantum videtis, atque ex iis tantum, quæ foris apparent, ju- dicatis? videlicet contra illud Salvatoris Joh. VII. Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judi- cium judicate. Nimirum corrigit suos Corinthios, quod de ministerio & ministris spiritualiter, ex qualitate vocationis, donorum ἐξοχῇ, doctrinæ gene- re, laborum æstimatione judicabant; sed juxta fa- ciem externam ad speciem fallacem per προσωπολη- ψίαν ipsis prorsus indignam, ut exposuit B. Hun- nius. Quasi dicat: Exposui modo, quibus armis in ministerio nostro depugnemus, & quam admiranda opera Deus per nos efficiat, non carnalibus admini- culis; sed spiritualibus præsidiis, quo nomine haud quaquam dubitem, ad vestram experientiam pro- vocare, quod cælestem virtutem mei inter vos Apo- stolatus reipsa senseritis: Et tamen adeo facile com- movemini, larva in oculos incurrente, ut pluris fa- ciatis Pseudo-Apostolorum inanem jactantiam, quam Apostoli vestri labores, & in Ecclesiam ve- stram merita. Ita & B. Balduinus: Vanitatem, inquit, judicii in istis hominibus arguit. Quæ se- cundum faciem sunt, videtis v. 7. quasi dicat: itane juxta externam meam conditionem tantum judica- tis de officio meo? Et quia nihil pomposi, nihil austr- ri, nihil, quod oculos aut aures delicatorum implere posset, apud me reperitis, sed Apost. mansuetudinem atque simplicitatem, propterea me contemnitis? Schlichtingius retenta interrogatione sic expo- suit: Quæ ad faciem meam & externam corporis seu carnis meæ habitum spectant, videtis, id est, no- tatis, observatis, animadvertitis: quasi dicat, & me secundum carnem non ambulare non simul videtis? Non videtis me secundum carnem non militare? Non videtis arma mea non esse carnalia, sed Deo po- tentia, & me divinorum operum, quæ dixi, patra- torem esse? Atque hæc non minus sunt in propatulo, quam quæ secundum faciem sunt.

εἴτις πέποιθεν ἑαυτῷ) Hebraïsmus לוֹ apud se.

χριστῷ εἶναι) Subauditur ex superiore ἑαυτόν. Se à Chri- sto diligi.

τῦτο λογιζέσθω πάλιν ἀφ’ ἑαυτῦ) Vel me non monente hoc cogitet.

ὄτι καθὼς αὐτὸς χριστῦ, ὕτω καὶ ἡμεῖς χριστῦ) Apparet id omnibus, inquit, ex vita mea & ex miraculis adeò eximiis & frequentibus.

Sed imprimis etiam ex doctrina: Quia Deus per nos hortatur, & ita testatur 2. Cor. V. non de se so- lo loquitur; sed Timotheo hæc etiam conveniunt, unde non tam miracula, quam doctrinam & vi- tam ea respicere apparet. Nam claruisse Timo- theum miraculis, non constat. Secundum alios Christi esse hic idem est, ac Christianum esse, vel præcipuum Christi membrum, quod ideo Pauli autoritatem extenuarint: siquidem ad agnitio- nem Christi nuper accesserit, nec in carne eum viderit, nec cum Apostolis Christi magnam ha- buerit familiaritatem, quò etiam abit Chrysostomi & Theophylacti interpretatio.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. If I should boast somewhat more) If I should say something more about myself than others could say. In self-boasting, Paul’s gravity is always wonderfully joined with modesty.

concerning our authority) Fathers have some right over their children. But Paul is under God and Christ the Father of the Corinthian Church, IV. 15. Those others could not say this of themselves.

which the Lord gave us for building up, and not for your destruction) The right of parents was introduced for the good of their children, not for their harm. Jeremiah had mandates of building and destroying, I. 10. Paul, of building up.

I shall not be put to shame) I shall not be caught being vain, as above VII. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἐάν τε περισσότερόν τι καυχήσωμαι) Si quid plus de me dixero: quam alii possent dicere. In περιαυτολο- γίαις mira semper Pauli gravitas cum modestia conjuncta.

περὶ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἡμῶν) Patres jus aliquod habent in libe- ros. Paulus autem sub Deo & Christo Pater Ecclesiæ Co- rinthiorum IV. 15. hoc illi alii de se dicere non poterant.

ἧς ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ κύριος εἰς οἰκοδομὴν, καὶ ὐκ εἰς καθαί- ρεσιν ὑμῶν) Jus parentum bono liberum, non malo intro- ductum est. Jeremias mandata habebat struendi & de- struendi I. 10. Paulus ædificandi.

ἐκ αἰσχυνθήσομαι) Non deprehendar vanus, ut supra VII. 14.

## 10:9
But that I may not seem as if I would terrify you by my letters) To terrify הִחְרִיד. I will not add more on that matter, lest anyone think these are empty scare-tactics. The event will teach.

As if he were to say: If I should even boast more abundantly, I would not, however, have erred in this part, nor would I be put to shame: for I would be speaking the truth. But it is not my intention to boast much about this matter, lest I seem to want to terrify you by letter, that is, lest the suspicion conceived by some about me I even more confirm, as if I were eager to terrify you by letters while absent, I who, when present, dare not say or decree anything too severe against you. This interpretation is preferred by B. Hunnius, because it coheres beautifully with the following verses, in which the voices of the Pseudo-Apostles are recited and refuted mimetically. The Greeks had preceded him, and among them Theophylact: If I should wish to boast, because God has granted me something more than others, so that I am also able to do good, even if I am compelled by necessity, I am not ashamed to inflict anything for demolition and torture, that is, I myself shall not be found either a liar, or insolent and puffed up, so as to claim for myself those things which have by no means been granted to me by God. And the following verse. Which, he says, is such as this: I could indeed boast, but lest I seem to make little of you through letters, just as the detractors keep saying, who assert that I boast of many things through letters, and write more for the sake of terror, but when present am easily despised, and that I am easily convinced that I am by no means such as my letters represent me to be, I would like whoever it is that has raised these objections to understand that we not only threaten grave things while absent; but that we are also able to carry out the threats when present.

For this reason, the Jesuit Santarelli was condemned by the Sorbonne in the year 1624 for having falsified this text by erasing a negative particle: concerning the power which the Lord gave me for building up and tearing down. See Marcus Antonius Marcellus of Venice, On the Power of the Pope in Temporal Matters, page 209. The Unextinguished Star of Brother Hay for the ancient orders, chapter 43, alleging similar examples of Jesuit corruptions in the Scriptures.

Latin:

ἵνα δὲ μὴ δόξω, ὡς ἂν ἐκφοβεῖν ὑμᾶς διὰ τῶν ἐπιστολῶν) Ter- ritare הִחְרִיד. Non addam plura ea de re, ne quis inania esse putet terriculamenta. Res docebit.

Quasi dicat: Si quid etiam glorier abundan- tius, non tamen vel erravero hac in parte, vel etiam pudefiam: veritatem enim dicerem. Sed institu- tum mihi non est, hac de re multum gloriari, ne vi- dear vos terrere velle per epistolam, id est, ne suspi- cionem à nonnullis de me conceptam etiam magis confirmem, quasi absens per epistolas vos terrere ge- stiam, qui præsens nihil in vos ausim gravius dicere aut statuere. Quam interpretationem præfert B. Hunnius, quod pulchre cohæreat cum seqq. quibus voces Pseudo-Apostolorum μιμητικῶς re- citantur & confutantur. Præiverant Græci, & in iis Theophylactus: Si gloriari voluerim, quia plus quippiam Deus sit mihi quam cæteris elargitus, ita ut & benefacere possim, etsi necessitate cogar, nil me pudet ad demolitionem & cruciatus ingerere, hoc est, nihil ipse vel mendax deprehendar, vel inso- lens & elatus, ut ea mihi asciscam, quæ mihi nequa- quam fuerint per Deum concessa. Et vers. seq. Quod, inquit, tale est: Poteram equidem gloriari, verum ne videar vos per literas parvi facere, quem- admodum dictitant detractores, qui asserunt, me per epistolas jactitare multa, & ad terrorem plura con- scribere, præsentem vero facile contemni, convinci- que, haudquaquam talem me esse, qualem me literæ præferunt, intelligat velim quicunque sit ille, qui ista objecerit, non solum nos gravia comminari absen- tes; quin etiam præsentes posse ad facta comminatio- nes deducere.

Falsavit hunc textum ideo à Sor- bona Anno 1624. condemnatus Jesuita Sancta- rellus eradendo particulam negativam: de pote- state, quam dedit mihi Dominus ad ædificandum & destruendum. Vid. Marcus Antonius Marcel- lus de Venetis de potestate Papæ in temporalibus pag. 209. Astrum inextinctum Fratris Hay pro anti- quis ordinibus cap. 43. similia in Scripturis cor- ruptelarum Jesuiticarum allegans exempla.

## 10:10
Verse 10. For the letters, he says) He says, whom I denote and wish to name: Whoever he is, (for I shall keep his name silent for now.) Weighty) They have the weight of arguments. And strong) Pressed with arguments. But the presence of the body is weak) His countenance and gesture have nothing magnificent. For, as we said above III, 12, presence is also referred to actions by the Syrians. And the speech is despised) His words were not inflated with Achaean dew, as it is in the Catalecta.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὅτι αἱ ἐπιστολαὶ φησὶ) Ait ille, quem denoto, & nominare volo: Quisquis is est, (nam nomen adhuc utcunque tacebo.) Βαρεῖαι) Pondus habent sententiarum. Καὶ ἰσχυραὶ) Pressæ argumentis. ἡ δὲ παῥῥησία τῦ σώματος ἀσθενὴς) Vultus & gestus nihil habet magnificum. Nam, ut diximus supra III, 12. παῥῥη- σία Syris etiam ad actiones refertur. Καὶ ὁ λόγος ἐξυθενημένος) Non erant verba ejus inflata rore Achaico, ut est in Catalectis.

## 10:11
Verse 11. Let such a one consider this) He, whom the mind understands: as Ovid speaks in the Ibis. That such as we are in word by letters when absent, such we are also when present in deed) He does not care to claim eloquence for himself, but says that he will fulfill in deeds when present what he threatens against those who do not correct themselves by letters.

Why the Apostle used singular kindness and gentleness among the Corinthians, he taught in 1 Cor. II. 4, namely, so that their faith might not rest on the external gifts of men, but simply on the power of the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 11. τῦτο λογιζέσθω ὁ τοιῦτος) Ille, quem mens in- telligit: ut Ovidius in Ibin loquitur. ὅτι οἷοί ἐσμεν τῷ λόγῳ δι᾿ ἐπιστολῶν ἀπόντες, τοιῦτοι καὶ πα- ρόντες τῷ ἔργῳ) Non curat sibi eloquentiam vindicare, sed dicit se præsentem rebus impleturum, quæ per epistolas mi- natur in eos, qui se non corrigunt.

Cur singulari humanitate atque mansuetudine usus fuerit apud Corinthios Apostolus 1. Cor. II. 4. docuit, ne scilicet fides ipsorum donis externis ho- minum, sed simpliciter virtuti spiritus inniteretur.

## 10:12
Verse 12. For we do not dare to rank or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves) I do not wish, he says, to either add myself to or compare myself with those learned and eloquent men. I do not seek a laurel wreath from that cake. Let them boast in that hall. Be it so, he says, with B. Hunnius as interpreter, let them traduce me as vile in appearance and abject, when, of course, being present, I do not puff myself up in their Thrasonic manner, nor do I seek empty glories, in which kind of foolish boasting I would not unwillingly concede the palm to them, nor would I wish to be composed or numbered with such men who, after they have no other heralds of their own praises, themselves rattle and trumpet their own praises and virtues. Thus, therefore, he argues the false Apostles of insolence and empty glory, just as if they were accustomed to boast of great things about themselves.

But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves among themselves, do not understand) Photius took these things far differently than others. For he thinks that Paul is speaking here about himself, so that he interprets 'they do not understand' as a participle referring to the hearers. But the interpretation of others is truer. They do not see that they measure themselves not by public standards, but by those which they themselves have made, that is, they are self-sufficient, and then how they give mutual praises among themselves, that is, they scratch each other's backs. That 'themselves' is sometimes said of individuals, as Rom. XI. 33, XII. 16, below XIII. 5, and sometimes of many among themselves, as 2 Cor. VI. 7.

The Vulgate version, therefore, is to be amended here, which likewise has it thus: as if Paul and Timothy were speaking about themselves; but they measure themselves in us. But Theophylact reads it correctly, explaining it thus: They (he says) by no means think it worthy that they should be able to be compared with any mortal, but rather they compare themselves to themselves in a certain mutual competition, and they do not understand what a mockery they are most worthy of, who are proud in this way. For when each one boasts that he is better, they disparage others. Whence it happens that all are convicted of wickedness by one another. How ridiculous that is, they do not perceive. The source of this ambition, says B. Hunnius, and of this salty persuasion is self-love, by which, blinded, they look at themselves, and measure only themselves and their own things among themselves, without meanwhile weighing the gifts and labors of others. Therefore it is not a wonder that they vanish into such stupidity through admiration of themselves, that, having most deeply despised others, they exalt and magnify themselves alone. For certainly, he who, with no canon applied, estimates himself by his own judgment, and compares himself to himself, not to others, is a fool and understands nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὀὐ γάρ τολμῶμεν ἐγκρῖναι, ἢ̓ συγκρῖναι ἑαυτός τισι τῶν ἑαυτὸς συνισανόντων) Nolo enim, inquit, me illis erudi- tis & disertis aut addere aut comparare. Non quæro ex isto mustaceo laureolam. Illi se jactent in ista aula. Esto sanè, inquit, B. Hunno interprete, tradu- cant illi me tanquam vilem aspectu & abjectum, quando nimirum præsens non illorum more Thraso- nico memetipsum effero, nec inanes peto glorias, quo quidem in genere stultæ jactantiæ palmam eis haud invitus concessero, neque me componi aut connumera- ri velim cum talibus, qui postquam alios suarum lau- dum præcones non habent, ipsi suas laudes & virtu- tes crepant & ebuccinant. Ita ergo falsos Aposto- los insolentiæ & inanis gloriæ arguit, perinde ac magna de se jactare consuetos.

Ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτὸς μετρῦντες καὶ συγκρίνοντες ἑαυτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς, ὐ συνιῦσιν) Longe aliter quam cæteri hæc ac- cepit Photius. Putat enim Paulum hic de semet dicere, ut συνιῦσιν interpretetur tanquam Participium de auditoribus. Sed verior est aliorum interpretatio. Non vident illi quam ipsi non publicis, sed quas ipsi fecere, mensuris se metiantur, id est, sibi sint suffeni, deinde quomodo ipsi inter se laudes dent mutuas, id est, mutuum muli scabant. Illud ἑαυτὸς modò de singulis dicitur, ut Rom. XI. 33. XII. 16. infra XIII. 5. modò de pluribus inter se, ut 2. Cor. VI. 7.

Vulgata itaque versio hic emendanda, quæ iti- dem ita habet: ac si de seipsis Paulus & Timotheus loquantur; sed ipsi in nobis nosmetipsos metientes. Recte autem Theophylactus legit, ita exponens: Il- li, (inquit) nequaquam dignum existimant, sese cum ullo conferri posse mortalium, quin potius sibiipsis se comparant mutua quadam concertatione, neque in- telligunt, qua sint irrisione dignissimi, qui hunc in mo- dum superbiant. Nam cum singuli potiores se esse glo- riantur, aliis detrahunt. Quo fit, ut omnes ab invi- cem arguantur improbitatis. Quod quam ridiculum sit, nil sentiunt. Fontem hujus ambitionis, inquit B. Hunnius, & salsa persuasionis Φιλαυτίαν, qua ca- cati seipsos intueantur, solos & sua inter sese metian- tur, non perpensis interim aliorum donis & labori- bus. Itaque mirum non est, ipsos admiratione sui in tantam stoliditatem evanescere, ut cæteris altissime præ se despectis se solos efferant & magnificiant. Nam certe, qui, nullo adhibito canone, suopte judicio se æstimat, seque ipsum sibi, non aliis comparat, stultus est, nihilque intelligit.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. But we will not boast beyond measure) We will not please ourselves beyond measure: לבלי הק on the contrary notes them.

But according to the measure of the rule) A rule is a cord, by which land surveyors assign portions of land to each owner. Thus Aquila translates קו, Job XXXVIII. 5. which others translate as a measuring line and a cord. Thus the Apostles established some churches, others others: Paul established very many: Paul's detractors established none.

which God has apportioned to us as a measure) It seems Paul wrote measure, and the Syriac and Arabic read it so. In that manuscript, which I follow much, this chapter and some parts of the preceding and following are missing. Of that, I say, cord, the measure of which God has attributed to us. Among the Apostolic Canons, so-called, is also this one: that a bishop should not dare to perform ordinations outside his own boundaries. Now the first boundaries were made by occupation: From this equity, no one should have been received into the ecclesiastical ministry at Corinth, unless Paul approved, or the one to whom Paul had mandated it.

to reach even unto you) So that that measure of my Apostleship might reach even unto you.

The Apostle uses a beautiful allusion. For he opposes the unmeasured to the measure, the immense to the measured. The pseudo-Apostles boasted immeasurably, not only because they sang their own praises too much, but also because they were in no legitimate office that could have given a measure to their glory. Our Apostle does not wish to act so foolishly: But if he is compelled to boast of something at all because of the impudence of his adversaries, he sets as the measure of his boasting his Apostleship, which extends itself to Jews and Gentiles alike, Acts XI. 15, XXII. 21. Indeed from Jerusalem even to Illyricum, Rom. XV. 19, therefore he says his measure reaches even to the Corinthians, to whom he affirms by this very fact that he was given by God as a teacher. He calls the gifts and expeditions granted by God the rule or standard of this measure. Within these bounds, therefore, he constrains his glory as it were, and what he says about these labors of his cannot be accused of any vanity, because the thing itself proves the truth. Therefore he repeats that his measure reaches even to the Corinthians, who themselves could testify of his labors, as the blessed Bald. has in his commentary here. For that success of the Apostolic ministry was notorious, of which he could boast truthfully, so that it might be manifest how vain the disparagement of his authority was. Since the presence of the same was not weak to all those to whom he had penetrated, nor was his speech despised, but he was present to them with great authority and efficacy of speech, to which he could also appeal to the Corinthians themselves. Nor is Grotius's gloss sufficiently appropriate: We will not please ourselves beyond measure. For it is not a matter of internal complacency, but of external boasting, such as that of the pseudo-Apostles was: nor is it a solid foundation: for his suspicion concerning a different reading of Paul is destitute of the authority of the original codices. Beza warns that he found that reading in almost all printed and manuscript codices, which should be compared here.

ANNOTATIONS ON II.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἡμεῖς δὲ ὐχὶ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχησόμεθα) Non placebimus nobis supra modum: לבלי הק ex contrario illos notat.

Ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῦ κανόνος) κανών est funis, per quem agrimensores cuique possessori partes terrarum assignant. Ita Aquila vertit קו, Job. XXXVIII. 5. quod alii σχοινίον & σπαρτίον. Sic Apostoli alii alias instituerunt Ecclesias: Plurimas Paulus: Pauli obtrectatores nullas.

ἧ ἐμέρισεν ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς μέτρε) Videtur scripsisse Paulus μέτρον, & ita legisse Syrus & Arabs. In Manuscripto illo, quem multum sequor, hoc caput & sequentis & præceden- tis quædam desunt. Ejus, inquam, funiculi, cujus mensu- ram nobis Deus attribuit. Inter Apostolicos, qui dicuntur Canones, est & ille: ἐπίσκοπον μὴ τολμᾷν ἔξω τῶν ἑαυτῦ ὅ- ρων χειροτονίας ποιεῖσθαι. Termini autem primi facti sunt occupando: Ex hac æquitate nemo debuerat Corinthi re- cipi in ministerium Ecclesiasticum, nisi Paulo approbante, aut eo, cui Paulus id mandasset.

ἐφικέσθαι ἄχρι καὶ ὑμῶν) Ita ut illa mensura mei Aposto- latus ad vos usque pertingeret.

Pulchra allusione utitur Apostolus. Nam τὸ ἄμε- τρον opponit τῷ μέτρῳ, immensum mensuræ. Pseudo- Apostoli gloriabantur in immensum, non tantum, quia laudes suas ipsi decantabant nimium, verum etiam, quia nullo erant in officio legitimo, quod ipsis mensu- ram sua gloriæ dare potuisset. Tam stolide agere non vult Apostolus noster: Sed si omnino propter adversa- riorum impudentiam gloriari aliquid cogatur, men- suram sua gloriationis ponit Apostolatum suum, qui extendit se ad Judæos pariter & gentes Actor. XI. 15. XXII. 21. Imo ab Hierosolymis usque ad Illyricum, Rom. XV. 19. ideo dicit mensuram suam pertingere et- iam usque ad Corinthios, quibus doctorem se a Deo da- tum hoc ipso affirmat. Hujus mensuræ κανόνα seu regu- lam vocat dona & expeditiones a Deo concessas. Intra hos ergo cancellos constringit quasi suam gloriam, & quod de his suis laboribus dicit, nullius vanitatis accu- sari potest, quia res ipsa veritatem comprobat. Ideo re- petit, mensuram suam etiam usque ad Corinthios per- tingere, qui de laboribus suis ipsi testari possent, ut hic B. Bald. Commentar. habet. Ille enim successus A- postolici ministerii notorius erat, de quo ex vero gloriari poterat, ut quam vana sit autoritatis ipsius extenuatio palam constaret. Siquidem præsentia ejusdem illis omnibus, ad quos penetrarat, non fuerit ἀσθενὴς, nec sermo ejus ἐξεθενημένος, sed ma- gna cum autoritate & sermonis efficacia iisdem af- fuerit, de quo etiam ad ipsos Corinthios provoca- re poterat. Nec congrua satis est Grotii glossa: Non placebimus nobis supra modum. Non enim de interna complacentia, sed de externa gloriatione, qualis Pseu- do-Apostolorũ erat, agitur: nec fundamentũ soli- dũ: quippe Codd. Originalium autoritate destitu- ta habet suspicio ejusdem, de diversa Pauli scriptio- ne. Beza monet illam lectionem se in omnibus fere excusis & MSS. Codd. invenisse, qui hic conferatur.

ANNOTATA AD II.

## 10:14
Vers. 14. For we do not stretch ourselves beyond our measure, that is, by a metaphorical possession: But this is our inspection into those places, into which we have not arrived, that is, into which we have no right. We do nothing against the law. Deut. XIX. 14.

For we have reached even unto you in the Gospel of Christ) ἐφθάσαμεν is the same as ἐφικόμεθα. Thus Matt. XII. 28. Luke XI. 20. Rom. IX. 31. Phil. III. 16. 1 Thess. II. 16. Thus Dan. III. 8. IV. 18. it reached even unto heaven, and it reached unto the heaven כננ. In the Gospel, by a Hebrew idiom, for through the Gospel.

These things teach that he was personally present in those places and Churches which God assigned to him, nor did his presence diminish his reputation, nor would he have claimed inspection over them for himself, had he not reached the same according to the rule destined for him by God, since he founded, planted, and built up the Church among the Corinthians by his ministry. Conf. Acts XVIII. 19: Theophylact conjectures that the false Apostles had no thanks for preaching, but rashly went wherever they pleased and boasted from mere arrival, and so as to ascribe the sum of all things to themselves. Therefore, the Apostle says, we do not stretch ourselves beyond our measure, reaching unto you: For we have arrived not in vain, but in the Gospel of Christ, that is, not simply as they have gone to you; but for the sake of preaching the Gospel. But we readily agree here with Grotius. Moreover, what the blessed Hülsemann notes, the opposition between those measuring themselves by themselves and those measuring themselves according to the evidence of effects striking the eyes shows that measuring oneself by oneself is the same as what the mother of the Lord in Luke I. 51 calls the imagination of their heart, that is, one's own imagination, to which, as an insufficient and inept testimony, he opposes the evidence of his effects, what he has accomplished among the Corinthians and other Churches, and this he calls reaching unto them in the Gospel of Christ, namely that he himself not only laid the foundation of that Church as an architect, 1 Cor. III. 10, but also by an extensive mission of quantity disseminated the Gospel more widely than his rivals v. 15, 16. to Rom. XV. 19, 20. Since these things are better known, and not being such by Paul's mere imagination, he concludes from thence that he is superior to his rival Pseudo-Apostles, and that he measures himself not by an imaginary measuring rod, which he calls measuring in himself, but by an evident measuring rod, consisting in ocular demonstration, and this he calls the measure of the rule which God has distributed to us v. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὀυ γὰρ ὡς μὴ ἐφικνούμενοι εἰς ὑμᾶς ὑπερεκτείνομεν ἑαυτούς) Non extendimus nos ipsos, id est, κατὰ μετατυμίαν possessionem: Hoc vero est inspectionem nostram in ea lo- ca, in quæ non pervenimus, id est, in quæ juris nihil habe- mus. Nihil facimus contra legem. Deut. XIX. 14.

ἄχρι γὰρ ὑμῶν ἐφθάσαμεν ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ τῷ χριστῶ) ἐφ- θάσαμεν idem quod ἐφικόμεθα. Sic Matth. XII. 28. Luc. XI. 20. Rom. IX. 31. Phil. III.16. 1.Thess.II.16. Sic Dan.III.8. IV.18. ἔφθασεν ἕως τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ, & ἔφθασεν εἰς τὸν ὀυρανὸν כננ. ἐν τῷ ἐυαγγελίῳ Hebraico more pro per Evangelium.

Hæc docent personaliter præsentem fuisse illis locis & Ecclesiis, quas ipsi assignavit Deus, nec minuit tamen præsentia famam, nec in ipsos sibi inspectionem vindicaturum fuisse, nî attigisset easdem juxta canonem sibi à Deo destinatum, siqui- dem suo ministerio inter Gorinthios fundarit, plantarit, & ædificarit Ecclesiam. Conf. Act.XVIII. 19: Conjicit Theophylact. Falsos Apostolos nulla gra- tia prædicandi, sed temere quocunque profectos ex solo accessu fuisse gloriatos, & ita ut omnium summam si- bi adscriberent. Dicere itaque Apostolum, nequa- quam ad vos pertingentes superextendimus nos ipsos: Pervenimus namque non frustra, sed in Evangelio Christi, hoc est, non simpliciter uti illi ad vos profecti sumus; sed Evangelii gratia prædicandi. Sed annui- mus hîc facile Grotio. Cæterùm, quod B. Hülse- mannus notat, Oppositio inter mensurantes se ἐν ἑαυ- τοῖς & inter mensurantes se juxta evidentiam effe- ctuum in oculos incurrentium ostendit mensuram sui ipsius, penes seipsum idem esse, quod mater Domini Luc. I. 51. διάνοιαν καρδίας ἀυτῶν vocat, id est, pro- priam imaginationem, cui tanquam insufficienti & in- epto testimonio opponit effectuum suorum evidentiam, quid in Corinthiis, aliisque Ecclesiis profecerit, & hoc vocat φθανεῖν ἄχρι ἀυτῶν ἐν ἐυαγγελίῳ χριστῦ pertingere seu pervenire ad ipsos prædicatione Evan- gelii Christi, quod ipse scilicet non solum tanquam architectus fundamentum illius Ecclesiæ posuerit 1. Cor. III. 10. sed etiam misione extensiva quantita- tis latius disseminaverit Evangelium quam æmuli v. 15. 16. ad Rom. XV. 19. 20. Quæ cum notiora sint, non sola imaginatione Pauli sese sic habentia inde concludit, se potiorem esse æmulis Pseudo-Apostolis, metirique sese non imaginaria decempeda, quam vocat mensuram in seipso, sed decempeda evidenti, consistenti in oculari demonstratione, & hanc vo- cat μέτρον κανόνος ᾧ ἐμέρισεν ᾧ θεὸς v. 13.

## 10:15
Vers. 15. Not boasting in things without measure in other men's labors) As those detractors of Paul were doing:

--- To others' pastures.

Having hope, when your faith is increased, that we shall be magnified in you according to our rule abundantly) Having hope, that as your faith increases, we may increase much more through you, in our line, that is, in our possession. Because the Corinthians were great sailors and merchants, he hoped that through them some fame of the Gospel would reach foreign shores, which would give Paul himself access to preach, as had once happened at Antioch, and as was later done among the Indians through a grain merchant. Therefore it follows:

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐκ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχώμενοι ἐν ἀλλοτρίοις κόποις) Ut illi faciebant obtrectatores Pauli:

--- Aliena ad pabula suci.

ἐλπίδα δὲ ἔχοντες ἀυξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν ἐν ὑμῖν μεγα- λυνθῆναι κατὰ τὸν κανόνα ἡμῶν εἰς περίσσειαν) Spem habentes, ut augescente fide vestra, per vos multo magis increscamus, in funiculo, id est, in possessione nostra. Quia Corinthii magni erant navigatores & mercatores, sperabat per eos ali- quam famam Evangelii ad oras exteras perventuram, quæ ipsi Paulo aditum ad prædicandum daret, ut olim factum erat Antiochiæ, ut per mercatorem frumentum postea fa- ctum apud Indos. Ideò sequitur:

## 10:16
To preach the Gospel in the regions beyond you) The Syriac seems to have read to preach the Gospel in the regions beyond you, so that I may be able to announce the Gospel in places situated beyond you, namely with access prepared through you. He seems to hint at the Greek cities situated by the Euxine Sea.

The Apostle therefore shows in this place, as Theophylact warns, that they (the Pseudo-Apostles) sought glory for themselves in the labors of the Apostles and boasted infinitely, that is, they prepared glory for themselves in the highest degree in the labors of others. But, he says, we have hope in God, that we shall preach the Gospel also among those who are beyond you, and that it will come to pass that we may perhaps have to boast even of these, if we have also accomplished something. Some refer that phrase when your faith is increased to having hope, with the Vulgate version, but it is more correctly explained separately, as the Greek punctuation has it, and to refer the hope to the word to be magnified.

the construction teaches that it is referred, since this verb depends on it, having hope, that as your faith grows we may be magnified in you or through you according to our rule, (defined for us by God) into abundance. Whence Estius here amends the Vulgate; the genitives are placed absolutely in the Greek, which it was fitting to render by ablatives, as your faith grows.

By the rule some understand the word of God; but it is taken, without doubt, in the same sense in which it occurs in the preceding v. 12 and the following v. 16. There, however, the measure of the rule, which God has distributed to each herald of the Gospel in the provinces, is understood: concerning which Chrysostom warns: that the Apostle used the word rule and measure conveniently, as one who had set out for the possession of the whole world and a most excellent inheritance. Κανόνα, says Cornelius, the Greeks call a measuring rule, by which geometers and land-surveyors measure out fields: Thus here the Apostle calls his rule all his regions, or whatever lands God had measured out to him as if by a rule, so that he might cultivate that whole space, sow it with the word of God and his own preaching, and add it to Christ. Beza says that although μέτρον and κανών are often taken for the same thing, namely for the measuring instrument itself, here one is necessarily distinguished from the other. Μέτρον therefore in this former place is called the mode, or quantity of the thing measured. Κανὼν however is that very thing which has been measured out to someone: In which sense he mentions his own, that is, to the rule of the territory as if measured out to himself, to which he opposes another's, that is, that which is attributed to others. Therefore κατὰ τὸ μέτρον. 13. τῦ κανόνος Beza rendered according to the measure measured out to us by rule. The Vulgate and Erasmus [rendered it] according to the measure of the rule, which, in Beza's judgment, no one could easily understand. The same [author] says at v. 15: Κανὼν in this place does not signify a rule, but that very space which has been measured out by rule: as if God had divided the orb of the earth among the Apostles to be cultivated. And so in the following verse he calls it ἀλλότριον κανόνα, a measure attributed to another, that is, which God had called another to cultivate. Thus among the Hebrews by the same trope, although with a different translation, an inheritance is called גּוֹרָל (ghoral) that is, a lot; just as the Latins also speak, and with six points חֶבֶל (chebel) that is, a cord, because they measured fields with cords. Thus finally among Pollux, κανὼν is called the space of the pasture itself: nor is there anything more customary than this metalepsis; Camerarius [says] regarding that εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα, [it means] prepared and easy and ready; such as would be, of course, the course of following another's doctrine, and a path already worn by one going before.

ἐν τῶ ἀμέτρῳ καυχᾶσθαι εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα σκοπῶν) But not to please himself, boasting in another's boundaries, which is easy. Εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα, that is, ἑτοίμως. Just as just now εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα was for ἀμέτρως.

It is better to take that τὰ ἕτοιμα with any other interpreters, as the Vulgate rendered it, in those things which are prepared, so that we may not boast in another's rule, namely in those things which have already been occupied by others, and prepared through the cultivation of the Gospel, just as the Pseudo-Apostles were doing, boasting of others' things; for example, of the progress of the Corinthians, who nevertheless were not prepared by them, but by Paul. Conf. Rom. XV. 20. 21. Nor does Beza inappropriately explain that εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα as concerning those things which are not of (our) measure, with this scholium added; Thus the Greeks elegantly say ἐπαινεῖν εἰς δικαιοσύνην, λοιδορεῖν εἰς κακίαν and many similar things. But he calls them ἄμετρα, not those which are excessive in themselves, and which no one could measure, but those which God had not measured out to him. Namely with respect to the adversaries, who attributed to themselves the things of others, as appears from verses 15 and 16, rather than those that simply were not immoderate, which either Paul deservedly credited to God, or his adversaries wrongfully claimed for themselves. Therefore I did not wish to translate [it] into the immense [length] with the Old Interpreter, and Erasmus.

Latin:

εἰς τὰ ὑπερέκεινα ὑμῶν ἐυαγγελίσασθαι) Videtur Syrus legisse εἰς τὸ ὑπερέκεινα ὑμῶν ἐυαγγελίσασθαι, ut in locis ultra vos positis Evangelium annunciare possim, nimirum aditu per vos præparato. Videtur innuere Græcas civitates, ad Pontum Euxinum positas.

Ostendit itaque hoc loco Apostolus, monente Theophylacto, illos (Pseudo-Apostolos) gloriam sibi in Apostolorum laboribus quæsivisse & in infini- tum gloriari, hoc est, maximum in modum in alienis laboribus gloriam parare. Spem autem, inquit, habemus in Deo, quod apud eos etiam, qui ultra vos sunt, Evangelium prædicabimus, futurumque, ut vel de his forsitan sit nobis gloriandum, si et- iam aliquid profuerimus. Illud ἀυξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν nonnulli referunt ad ἐλπίδα spem ha- bentes crescentis fidei vestræ, cum Vulgata versione, sed rectius explicari seorsim, ut distinctio Græ- ca habet, & τὴν ἐλπίδα ad verbum μεγαλυνθῆναι

referri constructio docet, quum hoc verbum in- dependeat, spem habentes, fore, ut crescente fide vestra in vobis vel per vos magnificemur secun- dum regulam nostram, (à Deo nobis definitam) in abundantiam. Unde Vulgatam hic emendat Estius; Genitivi sunt in Græco absolute positi, quos reddere conveniebat per Ablativos, crescente fide ve- stra.

Per regulam nonnulli intelligunt verbum Dei; sed eodem, sine dubio, sensu accipitur, quo oc- currit v. 12. præcedente & v. 16. sequenti. Ibi au- tem mensura regulæ, quam Deus partitus est uni- cuique præconi Evangelii in provinciis, intelligi- tur: de quo Chrysostomus monet: Regula & men- sura vocabulum commode usum esse Apostolum, velut ad orbis terrarum possessionem præstantissi- mamque hæreditatem profectum. Κανόνα, inquit Cornelius, Græci vocant regulam mensoriam, quâ geometræ & agrimensores agros dimetiuntur: Ita hic Apostolus regulam suam vocat omnes suas regio- nes, seu quicquid terrarum Deus velut ad regulam illi admensus erat, ut totum illud spatium excoleret, sereret verbo Dei, suaque prædicationi, & Christo adjiceret. Beza inquit μέτρον & κανόν quum sæ- pe pro eodem accipiantur, nempe pro ipso mensorio instrumento, hic unum ab altero distinguitur neces- sario. Μέτρον igitur hoc priore loco dicitur modus, sive quantitas rei admensæ. Κανὼν autem illud ipsum, quod alicui admensum est: Quo sensu me- minit sui, id est, ad regulam velut sibi admensi ter- ritorii, cui alienum, id est, aliis attributum apponit. Ideò κατὰ τὸ μέτρον. 13. τῦ κανόνος reddidit Be- za secundum modum nobis ad regulam admen- sum. Vulgata & Erasmus ad mensuram regulæ, quod Beza judice, nemo facile intelligat. Idem ad v. 15. inquit: Κανὼν hoc in loco non significat regu- lam, sed illud ipsum spatium, quod ad regulam ad- mensum est: quasi Deus terrarum orbem inter A- postolos diviserit excolendum. Itaque sequentiver- siculo appellat ἀλλότριον κανόνα, mensuram alteri attributam, id est, ad quam excolendam Deus alium vocâsset. Sic apud Hebræos eodem tropo, quamvis diversa translatione hæreditas dicitur גּוֹרָל (ghoral) id est, sors; ut etiam Latini loquun- tur, & cum sex punctis חֶבֶל (chebel) id est, funis, quod funibus agros metirentur. Sic denique apud Pollucem dicitur κανὼν ipsum saltus spatium: ne- que quicquam est hac metalepsi magis usitatum; Camerarius ad illud εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα, paratis & faci- libus atque expeditis; quale nimirum esset cursus sequens alienam doctrinam, & tritum jam iter præ- eunti.

ἐν τῶ ἀμέτρῳ καυχᾶσθαι εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα σκοπῶν σκοπῶν) Non au- tem sibi placere, jactantem se in alienis terminis, quod faci- le est. Εἰς τὰ ἕτοιμα, id est, ἑτοίμως. Sicut modò εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα, fuit pro ἀμέτρως.

Præstat illud τὰ ἕτοιμα cum aliis quibusvis In- terpretibus accipere, ut Vulgata reddidit, in iis, quæ præparata sunt, ut non in aliena regula, vide- licet in iis, quæ jam ab aliis occupata sunt, & per Evangelii culturam præparata, gloriemur, quem- admodum Pseudo-Apostoli faciebant, gloriantes de alienis; exempli gratia, de profectu Corinthio- rum, qui tamen non ab ipsis, sed à Paulo parati erant. Conf. Rom. XV. 20. 21. Nec incommode Beza illud εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα exponit de iis, quæ men- suræ (nostræ) non sunt, hoc addito scholio; Sic dicunt Græci eleganter ἐπαινεῖν εἰς δικαιοσύνην, λοι- δορεῖν εἰς κακίαν & similia multa. Ἄμετρα autem vocat, non quæ per se nimia sint, & quæ nemo possit metiri, sed quæ Deus ipsi non esset admensus. Ad- versariorum videlicet respectu, qui sibi tribuebant aliena, ut apparet ex versibus 15. & 16. quam alio- qui simpliciter non essent immodica, quo vel Paulus merito ferebat Deo accepta, vel ejus adversarii sibi injuriâ vendicabant. Ideo nolui convertere, in immensum cum Vetere Interprete, & Erasmo.

## 10:17
Verse 17. He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord) He who wishes to please himself in something, let him please himself in this, that he knows Christ, and serves God. So also 1 Cor. 1:31. Similar to Jer. 9:24.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ὁ δὲ καυχώμενος, ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ καυχάσθω) Qui sibi in aliquo placere vult, in eo placeat sibi, quod Christum novit, & Deo servit. Sic & 1. Cor. I. 31. Simile Jerem. IX. v. 24.

## 10:18
For not he who commends himself, that one is approved, but whom the Lord commends) To commend, here is to praise, as the Syrian interprets, because those who wish to commend someone are accustomed to praise him. Approved, that is, fit for eternal life. A similitude taken from genuine coins.

It was previously noted that the word boast is accustomed to be taken regarding boasting, not regarding self-complacency, and that is manifest from Lev. 9:24 and 1 Cor. 1:31. The Apostle concludes, however, with a double aphorism: First, regarding boasting, not only that no one should attribute anything to himself, but should attribute all things to the divine canon, measuring himself not by himself, but by the heavenly rule, and not only that all glory should be attributed to the Lord in the success of the ministry; but he shows generally, since he has said many things about boasting, what is truly the glory of all believers, namely the Lord, who has been made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that he who boasts, may boast uniquely in Him by the force of the collation of parallel passages. For these demand that sense. Wittily thus at the same time noting the Pseudo-Apostles, who added the works of the law, and at the same time boasted in them: when righteousness is not except in the Lord, and all the seed of Israel is not justified except in the Lord, and one ought to boast uniquely of Him, Isa. 45:24, 25, and outside this name there is no other in which it is necessary to be saved, Acts 4:12. For all things which he handed down against the Pseudo-Apostles, who were mixing or confusing the righteousness of faith and works, aim at this target. Who, while they sought to set up their own righteousness, were not subject to the righteousness of God, Rom. 10:3. Therefore Paul protests, Gal. 6:14, But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which he established the confidence of the Evangelical proclamation, 1 Cor. 1:21, ch. 2:2. The same also seems to be inferred by the other aphorism.
