For not he who commends himself or his works, and boasts in them, is approved; but whom the Lord commends, which Estius renders: To whom Christ through his merits communicates those things through which he may be commended. Which sense will have to be admitted entirely if approved is explained as fit for eternal life. For we are not fit except through faith in Christ. To which the interpretation of Flacius can also contribute, that he who displays and extols himself is brought low by God, but he who acknowledges his own weakness and ascribes all glory to God alone is glorified, because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, 1 Pet. 5:5, and he who extols himself is humbled, but he who humbles himself by the example of the publican is extolled by God, Luke 18:14.

Schlichting himself takes the former aphorism thus: he teaches about what each one ought to boast, namely about the Lord, about the fact that he knows the Lord, that is Christ, that he believes in Him, that he is His, provided that this boasting is true and corresponds to the things themselves, see 1 Cor. 1:31. And regarding the latter he has it thus: Let us therefore devote effort that we may be commended by the Lord, which will happen if we will boast of no other thing than the Lord, and that truly.

He admits, however, that the other aphorism is more conveniently explained not of those who are approved for eternal life, but who are approved in parts of duty, or in general in those things which make for commendation. So that therefore the causal for in verse 18 is not referred to the immediately preceding verse, which we do not doubt deals with the boasting of true believers in Christ, who is our only righteousness, Jer. 23:6, by the force of the parallelism of the passages: But to the citedly rebuked boasting of the false Apostles: In which we have the blessed Osiander agreeing. For he himself acknowledges in verse 17 that Paul, on the occasion of boasting, proposes a general doctrine: But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord, that is: Not only let us not ascribe the labors of others to ourselves: but let us also attribute our own to divine goodness (and not to ourselves). And let us boast in this, that on account of Christ we have a merciful God, who through faith receives us into grace and liberally pours out the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon us, and gives happy success to our efforts, and then indeed furthermore crowns his gifts in us. But regarding the last verse he observes: Again Paul pricks the false teachers, boasting of their labors in a Thraso-like and false manner. For (he says) not he who commends himself is therefore approved by God, that he is a faithful and useful servant of Christ: but whom the Lord commends: But the Lord commends him in reality, whose work God leads many to the true knowledge of himself. Therefore this is ineptly urged against the certainty of righteousness by Bellarmine, book 3 on justification, chapter 6, and Vega, book 9 on justification, chapter 12. For as Benedict Justinian in this place he has: He is said to commend himself, who celebrates his own praises as if they were his own, and thinks nothing should be attributed to the author of good things. But he who is certain that he is righteous only through the grace or mercy of God, attributes nothing to himself; but everything to the grace of God. That one must glory in Christ alone and his merit is also taught by the spiritual betrothal, of which in the following chapter, v. 2, I have betrothed you to one husband. For the false Apostles were leading the faithful away from this one husband, to whom we are pleasing and to whom we cling only through faith, so that they would not trust solely in his righteousness and merits, nor glory solely in him, while they were striving to erect their own righteousness of works.

Latin:

ὁ γὰρ ἑαυτὸν συνιστῶν, ἐκεῖνός ἐστι δόκιμος, ἀλλ' ὃν ὁ κύριος συνίστησιν) Commendare, hic est laudare, ut interpretatur Syrus, quia, qui commendare aliquem volunt, solent eum laudare. Δόκιμος, id est, idoneus ad vitam æternam. Similitudo à nummis probis sumpta.

De gloriatione, non de sui complacentia verbum καυχάομαι accipi solitum antea monitum, idque è Levit. IX. 24. 1. Cor. I. 31. manifestum est. Concludit autem Apostolus gemino aphorismo: Primum de gloriatione, non tantum ut nemo sibi quicquam, omnia divino canoni tribuat, non seipsum seipso, sed cælesti regula metiens, nec modo, ut Domino omnis gloria tribuatur in successu ministerii; sed generatim monstrat, quum multa de gloriatione dixerit, quænam sit vere omnium credentium gloria, nimirum Dominus, qui factus nobis à Deo est sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio & redemptio, ut, qui gloriatur, unice in ipso glorietur vi collationis locorum parallelorum. Hæc enim illum sensum postulant. Facete ita simul notans Pseudo-Apostolos, qui legis opera adjungebant, inque iis gloriabantur simul: quum non nisi in Domino sit justitia, non nisi in Domino justificetur omne semen Israel, deque eo unice gloriari debeat Esa. XLV. 24. 25. & extra hoc nomen nullum aliud sit, in quo oporteat salvari Actor. IV. 12. Nam ad hunc scopum collineant omnia, quæ adversus Pseudo-Apostolos tradidit, justitiam fidei & operum commiscentes, vel confundentes. Qui dum justitiam propriam erigere quærebant, justitiæ Dei non subjiciebantur Rom. X. 3. Idcirco Paulus protestatur Gal. VI. 14. Mihi vero absit gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi, in qua fiduciam præconii Evangelici constituit 1. Cor. I. 21. cap. II. 2. Idem etiam altero aphorismo inferri videtur. Non enim qui seipsum commendat vel opera sua, inque iisdem gloriatur, probatus est; sed quem Dominus commendat, quod Estius reddit: Cui Christus per sua merita communicat ea, per quæ commendetur. Qui sensus omnino admittendus erit, si δόκιμος exponatur de idoneo ad vitam æternam. Non enim nisi per fidem in Christum idonei sumus. Quo etiam facere potest interpretatio Flacii, quod is, qui semetipsum ostentat, ac extollit, à Deo deprimatur, is vero, qui imbecillitatem suam agnoscit, omnemque gloriam Deo soli adscribit, glorificetur, quia Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam 1. Petr. V. 5. & qui sese extollit, humiliatur, qui vero humiliat sese publicani exemplo, à Deo extollitur Luc. XVIII. 14.

Schlichtingius ipse priorem aphorismum ita accipit: docet, qua de re quisque gloriari debeat, nempe de Domino, de eo, quod Dominum, id est Christum cognoscat, quod in eum credat, quod illius sit, dummodo hæc gloriatio sit vera, & rebus ipsis respondeat, vide 1. Cor. I. 31. Et ad posteriorem ita habet: Demus ergo operam, ut à Domino commēdemur, quod fiet, si nulla alia de re, quam de Domino, idque vere, gloriabimur.

Fatetur tamen alterum aphorismum commodius exponi de iis, non qui δόκιμοι sunt ad vitam æternam, sed qui δόκιμοι sunt in partibus officii, vel in genere in iis, quæ ad commendationem faciunt. Ut proinde causalis γὰρ v. 18. non referen- tur da sit ad immediate præcedentem versum, quem de gloriatione verorum fidelium in Christo, qui unicus justitia nostra est Jerem. XXIII. 6. vi parallelismi locorum, agere non dubitamus: Sed ad cite reprehensam gloriationem falsorum Apostolorum: In quo habemus suffragantem B. Osiandrum. Agnoscit enim ipse v. 17. Paulum occasione gloriationis generalem doctrinam proponere: Qui autem gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, id est: Non modo alienos labores nobis non adscribamus: verum etiam proprios divinæ bonitati, (non autem nobis) acceptos feramus. Et in eo gloriemur, quod propter Christum habeamus Deum clementem, qui per fidem nos recipit in gratiam & liberaliter in nos dona Spiritus sancti effundit, atque conatibus nostris felices dat successus, deinde vero insuper dona sua in nobis coronat. Ad versum verò ultimum observat: Rursus Paulum pungere falsos doctores, Thrafonice & falso suos labores jactitantes. Non enim (inquit) qui seipsum commendat, ille propterea approbatus est à Deo, quod sit fidelis & utilis servus Christi: sed quem Dominus commendat: Eum autem Dominus reipsa commendat, cujus operæ Deus multos ad veram sui agnitionem adducit. Inepte igitur hoc adversus justitiæ certitudinem urgetur à Bellarm. libr. III. de justif. cap. 6. & Vega libr. IX. de justif. cap. 12. Nam ut Benedict. Justinian. in h. l. habet: Seipsum commendare is dicitur, qui suas laudes quasi suas celebrat, nec quicquam bonorum auctori tribuendum putat. At qui certus est, se per solam Dei gratiam vel misericordiam justum esse, nihil sibi tribuit; sed omnia gratiæ Dei. Gloriandum esse in solo Christo ejusque merito etiam desponsatio spiritualis, de qua cap. seq. v. 2. despondi vos uni viro, docet. Nam ab hoc unico sponso, cui non nisi per fidem placemus, & adhæremus, abducebant fideles Pseudo-Apostoli, ne illius justitiæ ac meritis unice confiderent, nec in illo unice gloriarentur, dum justitiam operum propriam erigere satagebant.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

ARGUMENT & DIVISION.

Having premised a small excuse for his self-praise, because of his zeal for their chastity, or that of the virgin betrothed to Christ, lest any be corrupted: he vindicates his own proclamation concerning Christ and the dignity of his Apostolic office, and argues that it should not be despised because of any lack of skill in speech or his gratuitous ministry, and he accuses the false Apostles or disciples, because they transform themselves like Satan into heralds of righteousness. He protests again about the boasting extorted from him, stinging the Corinthians because they tolerate fools, nay, those who subject them to slavery and inflict injuries upon them, and he compares himself with them, his boldness, lineage, office, labors, sufferings, and cares, in all of which, however, he glories in his own infirmity, with an invocation of the divine name, adding specifically the danger of his captivity in Damascus and his liberation.

There are three parts: I. The Apostle's excuse for his self-praise, to v. 3. II. The vindication of the dignity of his office from the contempt of the false Apostles, to v. 16. III. The comparison of the Apostle and the false Apostles' that comparison, which relates to the flesh, is such that Paul is not to be considered inferior even in those respects, but rather in many ways superior:

PART I. An apology for Pauline self-praise.

Vers. 1. ὄφελον ἀνέσχεσθέ με μικρόν τῇ ἀφροσύνῃ) Other codices are better: ἀνείχεσθέ με μικρόν τι τῆς ἀφροσύνης. It is, however, a transposition for μικρόν τι τῆς ἀφροσύνης με. Would that you could bear with me a little in my foolishness. He calls his forced self-praise this way, because it has a certain appearance of foolishness to those who do not examine the matter thoroughly with its circumstances. ὄφελον אַחֲלַי 2 Sam. V. 3. Psal. CXIX. 4. Elsewhere it is used for the Hebrew מִי יִתֵּן, which is itself also an expression of wishing, just as unde is for the Latins.

After he had treated of the Apostolic power and had vindicated the same against the accusation of abuse, he now asserts the dignity of his office against the rash boastings of the Pseudo-Apostles. There he treated of his ministry absolutely, without instituting an express comparison: here, however, he openly institutes a contention between his own administration and that of the Pseudo-Apostles, and confounds their vain boastings by the true performance of his dignities and the celebration of the duties of his office. But, as Theophylact notes, when about to explain his own praises, he chastens them in many ways, lest by praising himself he should offend others: which praises he was induced to proclaim about himself by a certain necessity. For he feared lest his own contempt and the excessive authority of the false Apostles should result in the loss of his disciples.

There is, however, no reason for us to disturb the Greek text, the sense of which is in the open. And Beza admits that most codices have it so, even though he preferred to follow the Vulgate and the authority of other codices, which Grotius supports here. Erasmus rendered the received text: "Would that you had tolerated me!" (I would prefer "tolerated") "in my foolishness." Ἀφροσύνη is not delirium, as Beza says, but foolishness; from which, of course, I shall appear to my rivals to be suffering, because I am singing my own praises.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνέχεσθέ με) Precative modes: Nevertheless I pray you bear with me.

B. Luther rendered it in the indicative: Doch ihr haltet mirs wohl zu gute. This Cluverus prefers, nor can Estius disapprove of it: It can, he says, be translated in the indicative as "you bear with me," and the Greek scholia explain it in that sense, as if the Apostle were saying: Nay, rather you do bear with me; you do what I desire; I am convinced that you love me in such a way that you easily tolerate me speaking foolishly. Chrysostom: While he says "would that," he establishes that this depends on their will; but while he affirms it, he makes it plain that he trusts in their benevolence in the highest degree, and that he both loves them and is loved by them in turn. B. Hunnius: By a correction he softens the rebuke to this effect: What need is there to wish that you had borne with me? Nay, I trust that you will kindly bear with me, and will offer benevolent ears and minds to my defense. Thus also Cornelius à Lapide: Ἀνέχεσθε here seems to be of the indicative mood rather than the imperative. For he corrects what he had said: I would that you could bear with me; nay, he says, you do bear with me, and what I wish were done, that you are doing.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Præmissa excusatiunculâ περιαυτολογίας, quod ob zelum castitatis ipsorum, seu virginis Christo desponsatæ, ne qui corrumpantur: Præconium suum de Christo, & dignitatem muneris Apostolici vindicat, nec quicquam ob sermonis imperitiam, vel ministerium gratuitum id contemni, arguitque falsos Apostolos seu discipulos, quod adinstar Satanæ transforment se in præcones justitiæ. Protestatur denuo de gloriatione sibi extorta, pungens Corinthios, quod stultos, imo servituti se subjicientes, & injuriis afficientes tolerent, ac componit sese cum illis, audaciam, prosapiam, munus, labores, passiones, & curas, in quibus tamen omnibus de infirmitate sua gloriatur, cum obtestatione nominis divini, addens speciatim periculum captivitatis Damascenæ & liberationis.

Partes sunt tres: I. περιαυτολογίας Apostoli exusatio, ad v. 3. II. Dignitatis sui muneris à Pseudo-Apostolorum contemptu vindicatio, ad v. 16. III. Apostoli & Pseudo-Apostolorum quæst ea, quæ ad carnem spectant, comparatio, ut nec quantum ad illa, inferior, quin potius multis modis superior habendus sit Paulus:

PARS I. Περιαυτολογίας Paulinæ excusatio.

Vers. 1. ὄφελον ἀνέσχεσθέ με μικρόν τῇ ἀφροσύνῃ) Melius Codices alii: ἀνείχεσθέ με μικρόν τι τῆς ἀφροσύνης. Est autem trajectio pro μικρόν τι τῆς ἀφροσύνης με. Utinam ferre possitis paululum insipientiam. Ita autem vocat extortam περιαυτολογίαν, ideo quod speciem quandam insipientiæ habeat, apud eos, qui rem non penitus inspiciunt cum suis circumstantiis. ὄφελον אַחֲלַי 2. Sam. V. 3. Psal. CXIX. 4. Alibi ponitur pro Hebræo מִי יִתֵּן, quod & ipsum est optantis, ut unde Latinis.

Postquam de potestate Apostolica egerat, eandemque adversus accusationem abusus vindicarat, jam dignitatem muneris sui adserit adversus temerarias Pseudo-Apostolorum gloriationes. Illic absolute de ministerio suo non instituta expressa comparatione egit: Hic autem apertè contentionem suæ & Pseudo-Apostolorum administrationis instituit, & vanas eorum gloriationes, vera ἀξιωμάτων functione & curarum muneris sui celebratione confundit. Proprias vero laudes, notante Theophylacto, explicaturus pluribus modis illas castigat, ne alios, se laudando, offendat: Quas ad laudes de se prædicandas necessitas quædam induxit. Verebatur enim, ne in discipulorum jacturam cederet sui contemptus & falsorum Apostolorum nimia autoritas.

Non autem est, quod Græcum textum solicitemus, cujus sensus in aprico est. Et habere ita plerosque Codices fatetur Beza, tametsi ille Vulgatam & aliorum Codd. autoritatem sequi maluerit, cui suffragatur hic Grotius. Textum receptum Erasmus reddidit: Utinam me tolerassetis! (malim toleraretis) in insipientia mea. Ἀφροσύνη non est delirium, ut Beza, sed insipientia; qua laborare scil. videbor æmulis, quod proprias laudes decanto.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνέχεσθέ με) Modi precativi: Attamen quæso ferte me.

B. Lutherus in Indicativo reddidit: Doch ihr haltet mirs wohl zu gute. Quod præfert Cluverus, nec improbare potest Estius: Potest, inquit, indicative verti sustinetis, atque in eum sensum exponunt Græcorum scholia, quasi dicat Apostolus: Imò vero sustinetis me, facitis, quod opto, persuasum habeo, vos ita me diligere, ut facile me toleretis insipienter loquentem. Chrysostomus: Dum utinam dicit, hoc eorum arbitrii esse statuit: Dum autem affirmat, planum reddit, se eorum benevolentiæ majorem in modum confidere, atque & eos amare, & ab iis vicissim amari. B. Hunnius: Correctione mitigat reprehensionem in hanc sententiam: Quid attinet optare, ut me tolerassetis, imò confido, vos me benigne toleraturos, & aures animosque benevolos meæ defensioni præbituros esse. Ita & Cornelius à Lapide: Ἀνέχεσθε hic potius videtur esse Indicativi modi, quam Imperativi. Corrigit enim id, quod dixerat: Utinam sustineretis vel sustinuissetis me; imò, inquit, sustinetis me, & quod opto factum, id facitis.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς ζήλῳ Θεῦ) I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy, just as husbands who love their wives ardently, and I do this for the sake of God.

Not only solicitous care, nor love alone burning for the sake of God, but zeal, and that divine, is signified, which Chrysostom explains excellently: He did not say: For I love you, but he sets down what was much more vehement. For the minds of those who are more ardently affected toward those whom they love suffer from jealousy. Nor could jealousy arise from any other source than from sharp and vehement friendship. Then, lest they think that they are sought by him for the sake of either honor or money or any other thing, he added with the jealousy of God. For God is said to be affected with zeal, not that you should suspect any perturbation (for God is removed from all perturbation), but that all may understand that he does everything for no other reason than for the sake of those very persons whom he pursues with jealousy, not that he himself might make any gain from this, but that he might bring salvation to them. For in men, zeal is not brought about in this way, but rather on account of private tranquility: not because those who are loved are treated with insult, but because those who love are not loved in return, but are surpassed, and bear a lesser part among those whom they love. Here, however, the matter does not stand so. For he says, it is not my concern that I should be in an inferior condition among you, but that I should not see you depraved and corrupted. For such is the zeal of God, and such also is mine, at once vehement and pure. Although zeal properly belongs to the bridegroom, it is here transferred to the groomsman, who on account of the bridegroom also burns with zeal, as much, that is, as befits groomsmen, for whom the honor and safety of the newly wedded are a care and a concern of the heart. Yet Christ alone is the bridegroom of the Church, Johan. III. 29, which honor Boniface VIII rashly, nay sacrilegiously, snatched for himself, C. Quoniam tit. 7. de immunitate Ecclesiæ in VI. decretal. The ministers of the Church, however, are the friends of the bridegroom and the groomsmen.

For I have betrothed you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ). He pursues the simile he has begun, and explains the mystical sense of the Song of Solomon, and of that law in Leviticus XXI. 14. Virgins are those who are uncorrupted. Such ought the Church to be, and those who belong to it, Revelation XIV. 4. See what we have said at Luke I. 27. ἡρμοσάμην, I have prepared. Thus Proverbs XIX. 14, 'but from the Lord a wife is prepared for a husband,' where the Greeks read in the Hebrew מַשְׂכֶּלֶת instead of מַשְׂכֶּלֶת; the Chaldean, however, seems to have read מִשְׁכֶּרֶת, for he translates it מִתְמַרְּרָה. παραστῆσαι here is to deliver into the hands, in the way a bride is delivered to a husband. See Genesis XXV. 41, XXIX. 21. This is what the Latins call to give in marriage. I have prepared, he says, that I might deliver: I have adorned you in every way. Thus also Esther V. 27, כַלָּה among the Hebrews is a bride, from adornment. There is also a transposition here: for ἑνὶ ἀνδρὶ and τῷ χριστῷ are separated in place, but cohere in meaning.

The Vulgate renders it: I have betrothed. In which sense the Greek word is used by Herodotus in Terpsichore for μνηστεύεσθαι, where, speaking of a certain Philip, he says, 'who, having betrothed the daughter of Telys the Sybarite, fled from Croton.' For it follows, 'but being disappointed of the marriage, he kept sailing to Cyrene.' This betrothal also includes the conciliation which is employed in Proverbs XIX among the LXX interpreters, because the Apostle had both conciliated and betrothed the Corinthians to Christ. This present time, as Chrysostom and Theophylact say, is suitable for betrothal. But the future is for the nuptials, when that voice shall be made (Matthew XXV), 'Behold, the bridegroom comes.' The Apostle does not here attribute anything peculiar to nuns; but he makes all the faithful virgins without distinction, concerning which likewise Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, say: In the world, virgins remain so before marriage; after marriage, not so. But here, it is not thus. But even if they are not virgins before this marriage, after the marriage is entered into, they are made virgins. In this way, the whole Church is a virgin. For Paul speaks to all, both married men and married women. And Theodoret: He named the whole Church a virgin, calling it so on account of the sincerity of its faith. For not all who believe profess virginity, but it is necessary that all be adorned with a sincere and true faith. Παρθένον ἁγνὴν the Vulgate and

Erasmus explain a chaste virgin. Beza preferred to interpret it as pure, because chastity is also attributed to a wife, whereas here a certain supreme integrity is signified.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς ζήλῳ Θεῦ) Solicite vos custodio, sicut mariti, qui uxores suas ardenter amant, idque facio propter Deum.

Non tantum solicita cura, nec amor solum ardens propter Deum, sed zelus, isque divinus innuitur, quem præclare explicat Chrysostomus: Non dixit: Amo enim vos, sed quod multo vehemen- tius erat, ponit. Zelotypia enim laborant eorum animi, qui erga eos, quos amant, ardentius sunt affecti. Neque enim aliunde oriri queat zelotypia, quam ab acri & vehementi amicitia. Deinde ne putent se ab eo, vel honoris vel pecuniarum vel alius cujusquam rei causa expeti, adjecit Dei æmulatione. Deus enim zelo affici dicitur, non ut perturbationem aliquam suspiceris (Deus enim ab omni perturbatione remotus est) verum ut omnes intelligant, eum non aliam ob causam, quam ob eos ipsos, quos zelotypia prosequitur, omnia facere, non ut ipse quæstum aliquem hinc faciat, sed eis salutem afferat. Nam in hominibus non ita zelus efficitur, verum ob privatam quietem: non propterea, quod contumelia afficiantur, qui amantur, verum quod non amentur ii, qui amant, sed superentur, minoresque partes ferant apud eos, quos amant. Hic autem non ita se res habet. Non enim, inquit, id mihi curæ est, ne inferiore apud vos conditione sim, sed ne vos depravatos & corruptos videam. Hujusmodi enim Dei zelus est, hujusmodi quoque meus, vehemens simul & purus. Quanquam autem zelus proprie sponsi sit, hic tamen transfertur ad paranymphum, qui propter sponsum zelo etiam flagrat, quantum scilicet paranymphis competit, quibus honor & salus novorum nuptorum curæ cordique est. Sponsus Ecclesiæ tamen solus Christus est Johan. III. 29. quem honorem temere, imo sacrilege Bonifacius VIII. sibi rapuit C. Quoniam tit. 7. de immunitate Ecclesiæ in VI. decretal. Ministri autem Ecclesiæ amici sponsi & pronubi sunt.

ἡρμοσάμην γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἑνὶ ἀνδρὶ παρθένον ἁγνὴν παραστῆσαι τῷ χριστῷ). Persequitur cœptam similitudinem, & explicat mysticum sensum Cantici Salomonis, & legis illius in Levit. XXI. 14. Virgines sunt incorruptæ. Talis debet esse Ecclesia, & qui ad eam pertinent, Apoc. XIV. 4. Vide quæ diximus ad Luc. I. 27. ἡρμοσάμην, paravi. Sic Prov. XIX. 14. παρὰ δὲ κυρίου ἁρμόζεται γυνὴ ἀνδρὶ, ubi Græci in Hebræo legere מַשְׂכֶּלֶת pro מַשְׂכֶּלֶת Chaldæus autem videtur legisse מִשְׁכֶּרֶת, vertit eim מִתְמַרְּרָה παραστῆσαι est hic in manus tradere, quomodo pacta viro traditur. Vide Gen. XXV. 41. XXIX. 21. Hoc est, quod collocare in matrimonium dicunt Latini. Paravi, inquit, ut traderem: ornavi vos omnibus modis. Sic & Esth. V. 27. כַלָּה Hebræis sponsa ab ornatu. Est & hic trajectio: Nam ἑνὶ ἀνδρὶ, & τῷ χριστῷ loco dissita sunt, re cohærent.

Vulgata reddit: despondi. Quo sensu Græcum verbum apud Herodotum in Terpsichore pro μνηστεύεσθαι, ubi de quodam Philippo loquens, ὃς, inquit, ἁρμοσάμενος τήλεως τῶν Σιβαριτέων τὴν θυγατέρα ἔφυγε ἐκ κρότωνος. Sequitur enim ψευσθεὶς δὲ τοῦ γάμου εἴχετο πλέων εἰς κυρήνην. Comprehendit etiam hæc desponsatio conciliationem, qua Prov. XIX. adhibetur apud LXX. interpretes, quia Apostolus & conciliarat & desponsarat Corinthios Christo. Præsens hoc tempus, dicente Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, desponsationi accommodum est. Futurum vero nuptiis, cum fiet vox illa (Matth. XXV.) Ecce sponsus venit. Non hic peculiare quid tribuit monialibus Apostolus; sed omnes fideles virgines facit sine discrimine, de quo itidem Chrysostomus, eumque sequutus Theophylactus: In mundo virgines ante matrimonium manent; post matrimonium non item. Hic autem non sic. Verum etiamsi virgines ante hoc matrimonium non sint, post initum matrimonium virgines efficiuntur. Ad hunc modum tota Ecclesia virgo est. Etenim ad omnes & conjugatos & conjugatas Paulus loquitur. Et Theodoreus: Totam Ecclesiam nominavit virginem, ob sinceritatem fidei ita vocans. Neque enim omnes, qui credunt, profitentur virginitatem, sed oportet omnes ornari sincera & vera fide. Παρθένον ἁγνὴν vulgata &

Erasmus exponunt virginem castam. Beza ma- luit puram interpretari, quod castitas uxori etiam tribuatur, hic autem summa quædam integritas si- gnificetur.

## 11:3
Vers. 3. ὡς ὁ ὄφις) That serpent or dragon, through whom Satan is understood, called by the Hebrews נחש הקדמני. See Apoc. XII. 3. 9. and in many other places. Εὔαν ἐξηπάτησεν) 1 Tim. II. 14. Ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ ἀυτοῦ) By his craftiness. Thus Aquila had translated ὄφις ἦν πανουργῶ, Gen. III. 1. οὕτω φθαρῇ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος, τῆς εἰς τὸν χριστὸν) There is a compressed expression here also: That your thoughts may not be corrupted from the simplicity which is toward Christ, instead of that your corrupted thoughts may not be turned away from that simplicity which is directed toward Christ; which regards Christ. This happens when the discourse of the Gospel is adulterated by philosophical doctrines. See above IV. 2. Ἁπλότης here is sincerity, or purity, having nothing foreign mixed in, which corresponds to the virginity of which it began to be spoken.

He makes mention of the virgin Eve, whom the serpent seduced: since he is solicitous about the Corinthian Church as a pure virgin to be brought to Christ; as if he were saying: Beware of the Pseudo-Apostles as if they were pimps of Satan, and as if they were adulterers of the genuine doctrine of Christ, and consequently of the Church and of your souls. For it is manifest that a pure virgin is understood, uncorrupted in the doctrine of Christ in opposition to fornication, vers. 3. 13. But discussing virgins, as Beza notes, he deservedly used the word for corruption and for fraud and for simplicity. For those things suit a ravisher, but this latter suits a pure and integral virgin. But this vice is offered to the mind. And so he preferred to interpret τὰ νοήματα (for he speaks of many) as minds rather than senses. Τῆς εἰς τὸν χριστὸν Erasmus κατὰ πόδα, which was toward Christ: Namely because you were obeying him purely and simply. Theophylact's commentary properly weighs the rest after Chrysostom: Destruction hangs over you, but fear urges me. For he does not say, as if deciding, you are already corrupted, even though they were defiled, but he put that in ambiguity, saying, lest perhaps as the serpent seduced Eve, for he had deceived Eve by promising huge things: So also those lying and boastful Apostles discourse to you of certain very great things, so that they may circumvent your simplicity by their craftiness. But just as neither the serpent's cunning, nor Eve's simplicity was enough for her for pardon, so indeed neither will their words be preferred to ours. Nor did he further introduce that Adam had been seduced by the serpent, so that he might argue that women are easily exposed to deceptions. He did not say do not be deceived, but that your senses may not be corrupted (for virgins themselves are also said to be corrupted) namely that your sloth, which you use toward Christ, may not be corrupted, that is, you ought by no means to be deceived because of your inertia. Wherefore Origen rightly infers in homil. XII. in Levit. cap. 2. If therefore you have received into the bed, O man, the Devil as the adulterer of your soul, your soul has played the harlot with the Devil. If the spirit of anger, if of envy, if of pride, if of unchastity has entered into your soul, and you have received him, and have consented to him speaking, and in your heart have delighted in these things which he suggests to you according to his mind, you have played the harlot with him.

PART II. The vindication of the dignity of the Pauline office from the contempt of the Pseudo-Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ὡς ὁ ὄφις) Serpens ille sive draco, per quem Sa- tanas intelligitur, dictus Hebræis נחש הקדמני. Vide Apoc. XII. 3. 9. & pluribus locis aliis. Εὔαν ἐξηπάτησεν) 1. Tim. II. 14. Ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ ἀυτοῦ) Vafsritie sua. Sic ὄφις ἦν πανουργῶ- verterat Aquila, Gen. III. 1. οὕτω φθαρῇ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος, τῆς εἰς τὸν χριστὸν) Est & hic contracta locutio: Ne corrumpantur co- gitata vestra à simplicitate, quæ in Christum, pro ne cor- rupta cogitata vestra avertantur ab ea simplicitate, quæ in Christum fertur; quæ Christum respicit. Hoc fit ubi Phi- losophicis doctrinis adulteratur sermo Evangelii. Vide supra IV. 2. Ἁπλότης hic est sinceritas, sive puritas, nihil alieni admixtum habens, quæ virginitati, de qua cœptum dici, respondet.

Evæ virginis mentionem facit, quam serpens seduxit: cum de Corinthiaca Ecclesia ceu pura virgine Christo adducenda solicitus est; quasi di- cat: Cavete Pseudo-Apostolos quasi lenones Satanæ, & quasi adulteros genuina Christi doctrina, con- sequenter & Ecclesiæ & animarum vestrarum. Manifestum enim est, virginem puram intelligi, incorruptam in doctrina Christi ex opposito scortationis vers. 3. 13. De virginibus autem diffe- rens, notante Beza, merito usurpavit corruptionis vocabulum & fraudis & simplicitatis. Conveniunt enim ista stupratori, istud vero puræ & integræ vir- gini. Sed hoc vitium menti offertur. Itaque τὰ νοήματα (de pluribus enim loquitur) mentes inter- pretari maluit quam sensus. Τῆς εἰς τὸν χριστὸν Em- smus κατὰ πόδα, quæ erat erga Christum: Nempe quia pure & simpliciter ei obtemperabatis. Cæ- tera post Chrysostomum probe expendit Theophyla- cti commentarius: Vobis quidem impendet interi- tus, me vero urget formido. Neque enim tanquam decernens, corrupti jam estis, inquit, tametsi essent illi coinquinati, sed id in ambiguo posuit, dicens, ne forte ut serpens Evam seduxit, is namque ingentia pollicendo Evam deceperat: Ita & Apostoli illi mendaces & jactabundi permagna quædam vobis edisserunt, ut sua versutia vestram circumveniant simplicitatem. Sed quemadmodum neque serpen- tis astutia, neque Evæ simplicitas satis illi ad ve- niam fuit, sic quidem neque illorum dicta nobis anteponentur. Nec præterea Adam intulit fuisse à serpente seductum, ut arguat facile deceptionibus mulieres patere. Neque nolite decipi dixit, sed ne corrumpantur sensus vestri (corrumpi namque & virgines ipsæ dicuntur) videlicet ne corrumpantur vestra ignavia, qua erga Christum utimini, hoc est, nequaquam debetis præ vestra inertia decipi. Quapropter recte infert Origenes homil. XII. in Levit. cap. 2. Si ergo susceperis in cubili, ô homo, animæ tuæ adulterum Diabolum, meretricata est anima tua cum Diabolo. Si spiritus iræ, si invi- diæ, si superbiæ, si impudicitiæ ingressus fuerit ad animam tuam, & receperis eum, & consenseris ei loquenti, & in corde tuo delectatus fueris his, quæ tibi secundum suam mentem suggerit, meretricatus es cum eo.

PARS II. Dignitatis muneris Paulini à contemptu Pseu- do-Apostolorum vindicatio.

## 11:4
Vers. 4. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἐρχόμενος) He who comes to you from Judea, and says that he was instituted by Christ, 1 Corinth. I. v. 12. Ἄλλον Ἰησοῦν κηρύσσει, ὃν οὐκ ἐκηρύξαμεν) Understand Ἰησοῦς here appellatively as Savior. If he could announce a more certain savior to you than we have announced.

could confer better gifts of the Spirit than we have conferred upon you through the laying on of hands.

or another Gospel, which you have not received) If he could bring a doctrine more heavenly than ours.

Καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε) You would deservedly bear with him, namely in that, that he places me far below himself.

When the Pseudo-Apostles were exalting themselves in the Corinthian Church, the Apostle confounds their vain boasting in more than one way, and vindicates his own ministry from their contempt. First, as regards the proclamation itself, namely the object, Christ, whom he was preaching, if they were announcing another more certain Christ to him, they would deservedly have to be borne or admitted. But not even these false Apostles themselves professed this, namely that there was another Christ than the one whom Paul was announcing. Then, as regards the effect, the communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, if they were imparting more excellent gifts, which not even those who perhaps were adhering to them in the Corinthian Church were going to say. Furthermore, as regards the whole doctrine, if they were bringing another Gospel, namely one more joyful or more desirable, which it was manifest was not being brought by them. Finally, however much they themselves might despise Paul, and set themselves in opposition to contend with the highest Apostles. Paul testifies that he is in no respect inferior to the chief Apostles; and since they did not hesitate to allege his lack of eloquence, the humility of his manner of life, and his free-of-charge Gospel to bring him into contempt, he explains what is to be thought of those accusations. Concerning the false Apostles themselves, he openly declares that they are deceitful workers and merely wear the mask of Apostles of Christ, when in reality they are ministers of Satan. Therefore, regarding what is held in this verse 4, lest it appear contrary to the opinion of the Apostle in Galatians 1, 'If anyone has preached another Gospel, let him be anathema,' by the almost common consent of all interpreters, it is treated here of another, higher, and more excellent Gospel, and it is argued κατ’ ἄνθρωπον (after the manner of men): since not even Paul's rivals themselves dared to say that they were bringing a more certain and excellent Gospel, or even at least another and different one. On the contrary, the Apostle was so certain that another Gospel could not be brought, that he declares anyone who brings another, even if it were an Angel from heaven, to be anathema. If, therefore, he says, those innovators had proposed to you a more certain Christ, if they had come with more notable gifts of the Holy Spirit than you have hitherto seen and experienced, if they were offering an easier way of applying to you the grace of God and of mitigating the heat of conscience, there would certainly be a reason why, neglecting me, you should not only tolerate them but even embrace them with both hands. If they were preaching the true Jesus and not a false one: if through their ministry the Holy Spirit were truly given, but through ours not: if they were announcing the true Gospel and we an adulterated one, then it would certainly be right for you to receive and tolerate them. But now, they can never in eternity demonstrate their doctrine and efficacy in conferring the Holy Spirit. We, in turn, have demonstrated by fact and deed the certainty and at the same time the efficacy of our doctrine. Therefore, it has by no means been done rightly by you that, having put me and the other Apostles aside, you adhere to the false Apostles, as the blessed Hunnius says here. They are therefore led to an absurdity, which is such by their own judgment: but because you cannot in any way be brought to believe that there is another Jesus Christ to be known, another Spirit, another Gospel, than that which was preached by us, just as in reality there is no other (Galatians 1), therefore you cannot allege any such thing for your excuse, as Estius acknowledges in this place with Thomas. And so, with Chrysostom, Theophylact says: Those deceitful Apostles boasted that they themselves had brought something more than the true [ones] of propagating the faith: And because they were raving greatly about empty things and boasting, relying on external wisdom, thus Paul adds: If they were preaching another Christ, whom it was necessary to preach, and I myself had passed over the proclamation of him, or I seemed inferior to these in this preaching, you would rightly endure it: that is, you would rightly bear their ineptitudes: since I had not made any mention of him who was deservedly to be preached. But, if we have laid the foundations by preaching the faith itself, and we have indeed revealed those things which are principal, what then have they brought anything more than we ourselves have brought? Or do you receive another Spirit, that is, have you become richer in spiritual gifts, to obtain which there is no need for the allurements of polished speech? Or another Gospel, when there are no words necessary to explain it that are elegant and ornate? Everywhere, therefore, he reveals that nothing at all is to be heeded if they have brought forward anything beyond what is necessary: But if they bring anything that ought to be said, let them understand that they received it from him. Camerarius on this passage regarding the words καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε has this: an ellipsis of the potential ἄν. You could indeed have endured. The Greek Interpreters [say] otherwise, with the same sense. You rightly endured. If this, which cannot happen, has happened, that a proclamation of another Jesus was made, etc. Οὕτως, he says, διὰ τῆς εἰς ἄτοπον ἀπαγωγῆς ἀυτὸς ἀποτρέπει τοῦ τοῖς ψευδαποστόλοις προσέχειν. For writing to the Galatians, he simply pronounces him accursed who dares to teach a doctrine other than what he himself has taught.

Latin:

Vers. 4. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἐρχόμενος) Ille, qui ex Judæa ad vos venit, & à Christo se institutum dicit, 1. Corinth. I. v. 12. Ἄλλον Ἰησοῦν κηρύσσει, ὃν οὐκ ἐκηρύξαμεν) Ἰησοῦς hic intel- lige appellative Servatorem. Si servatorem vobis certiorem annuntiare potuit, quam nos annuntiavimus.

potiora dona Spiritus conferre potuit, quam nos per ma- nuum impositionem vobis contulimus.

ἡ ἐυαγγέλιον ἕτερον, ὃ οὐκ ἐδέξασθε) Si doctrinam afferre potuit nostra cœlestiorem.

Καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε) Merito eum ferretis, nempe in eo, quod me longé infra se ponit.

Quum Pseudo-Apostoli efferrent se in Ecclesia Corinthiaca, non uno modo vanam eorum ja- stantiam confundit, suumque ministerium ab eo- rum contemptu vindicat Apostolus. Primum, quod ad præconium ipsum, objectum nempe, Chri- stum, quem prædicabat, si alium certiorem illi ar- nuntiarent Christum, merito ferendos vel admit- tendos fore. At hoc ne ipsi quidem falsi Apostoli profitebantur, alium scilicet Christum esse, quam eum, quem annuntiabat Paulus. Deinde, quod ad ef- fectum, communicationem donorum Spiritus sancti, si præstantiora impertirent dona, quod nec illi, qui in Corinthiaca Ecclesia, ipsis forte adhære- bant, dicturi erant. Porro, quod ad universam doctrinam, si aliud Evangelium, nimirum lætius aut exoptatius afferrent, quale ab ipsis haud affer- ri in propatulo erat. Denique, quantumcunque despicerent ipsi Paulum, seque ex adverso cum summis Apostolis contenderent. Paulus nulla in re summis Apostolis se inferiorem esse testatur; Et quum prætendere non dubitarint sermonis impe- ritiam, & humilitatem conversationis ipsius, ac gratuitum Evangelium in contemptum ejus ad- duxerint, quid de illis ἐγκλήμασι habendum sit, explicat. De ipsis vero Pseudo-Apostolis palam profitetur, quod dolosi operarii sint, ac larvam tantum Apostolorum Christi gerant, quum reve- ra sint Satanæ ministri. Quod ergo hoc versu 4. habetur, ne videatur contrarium sententiæ Apo- stoli Gal. I. Si quis aliud Evangelium prædicavit, anathema sit, communi fere omnium Interpp. con- sensu de alio altiori & præstantiori Evangelio hic agitur, & κατ’ ἄνθρωπον disputatur: Siquidem nec ipsimet æmuli Pauli sese certius & præstantius Ev- angelium; vel etiam saltem aliud & diversum affer- re, audebant dicere. Contra vero Apostolus adeo certus erat, aliud Evangelium afferri non posse, ut aliud afferentem, etiamsi Angelus de cœlo fo- ret, anathema dicat. Quod si ergo, inquit, No- vatores illi certiorem Christum vobis proposuis- sent, si insignioribus Spiritus sancti donis, quam hactenus vidistis, & experti estis, venissent, si faci- liorem modum applicandi vobis gratiam Dei, & mitigandi æstum conscientiæ tenderent, esset uti- que, cur me neglecto illos non tantum tolerare- tis, sed etiam ambabus manibus apprehenderetis. Si illi verum prædicarent Jesum, nec falsum: si per ipsum ministerium Spiritus S. vere daretur, per no- strum vero non: Si ipsi annuntiarent Evangelium verum, nos adulterinum, utique recte à vobis fieret suscipiendo & tolerando illos. Jam vero doctrinam suam & efficaciam in conferendo Spiritu S. demon- strare illi nunquam in æternum possunt. Nos vicis- sim re & facto demonstravimus nostræ doctrinæ cer- titudinem simul & efficacitatem. Proinde nequa- quam à vobis recte factum est, quod, me cæterisque Apostolis posthabitis, adhæretis Pseudo-Apostolis, ut hic B. Hunnius. Deducuntur ergo ad ab- surdum, quod tale est proprio ipsorummet ju- dicio: Sed quia nullo modo in animum adducitis, alium cognoscere JESUM Christum, alium Spiri- tum, aliud Evangelium, quam à nobis prædica- tum, sicut revera non est aliud Gal. I. Idcirco non potestis ad excusationem vestri quicquam tale præ- tendere, ut agnoscit h. l. Estius cum Thoma. At- que ita cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: Gloria- bantur fallaces illi Apostoli, quod plus aliquid ipsi, quam veri propagandae fidei attulissent: Et quia plurimum delirabant rerum inanium & ex- terna sapientia nixi jactantia, sic Paulus subdit: Si Christum alium praedicarent, quem praedica- ri oporteiet, & ejusdem ipse praeconium praeteriis- sem, vel his in hoc praedicando viderer inferior, recte pateremini: hoc est, jure illorum ferretis ineptias: quippe qui haud quaquam de eo mentio- nem fecissem, qui erat merito praedicandus. Ve- rum, si fidei ipsius praedicando jecimus fundamen- ta, & ea profecto, quae principalia sunt, patefe- cimus, quid ergo illi amplius quippiam attulerunt, quam ipsimet attulerimus? Vel Spiritum alium accipitis, hoc est, num vos ditiores spiritualibus donis effecti estis, ad quae consequenda nihil opus est expoliti sermonis lenocinio? Num Evange- lium aliud, quando neque id quidem ad explican- dum ulla sint verba necessaria, quae compta sint at- que ornata? Ubique igitur patefacit, nihil esse penitus advertendum, si quid ultra illi protule- rint, quam sit necesse: Sed si quid afferunt, quod dici oporteat, ab se intelligant accepisse. Came- rarius ad h. l. de verbis καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε ita habet: ἔλλειψις τοῦ δυνητικοῦ ἂν. Poteratis sane sustinere. Graeci Interpretes aliter, sensu eodem. Recte sus- tinuistis. Si hoc, quod fieri nequit, factum est, ut de alio Jesu praeconium fieret &c. Οὕτως, inquit, διὰ τῆς εἰς ἄτοπον ἀπαγωγῆς ἀυτὸς ἀπο- τρέπει τοῦ τοῖς ψευδαποστόλοις προσέχειν. Nam Ga- latis scribens simpliciter pronuntiat execrabilem esse eum, qui aliam doctrinam, quam ipse docuerit, do- cere ausit.

## 11:5
V. 5. For I consider that I have fallen short in nothing of the super-apostles) But now the matter stands otherwise: Nor do I have anyone in preaching to whom I yield, I will not say to them, but not even to the Apostles themselves, nay, to the chief of the Apostles, that is, Peter, James, John, Gal. II. 9. Nearly the same words below XII. 11. There is here, however, a double mark of magnitude, ὑπὲρ and λίαν, just as λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ in Mark VI. 51. and an Adverb with a prefixed Article, together for an Adjective. The Hebrews would say המהגרלים מאר מאר. He says this especially against those who professed themselves to be followers of Peter.

Although those impostors might clamor regarding the true Christ preached by him and the power of his Gospel, that Paul was not to be compared with the rest of the Apostles, yet he dares to affirm fearlessly that he was μηδὲν, that is, in no thing inferior even to the highest, whether one considers the breadth of his calling, or the variety of his gifts, or the excellence of his heavenly revelations, or the nations subdued and converted to the kingdom of Christ, or the labors and courses exhausted for the propagation of the Gospel, or the contests with the enemies of the truth, or finally the mass and magnitude of persecutions and dangers, as here again most rightly the blessed Hunnius [notes]. He uses the past tense ὑστερηκέναι rather (which Beza notes) than the present ὑστερεῖν, because he does not look so much at his still-vigorous apostleship in general as at those things which he had performed in the function of his office, using them as judges and witnesses at the same time in this matter. Vulgate: I have done nothing less than the great Apostles. Erasmus much more rightly: That I was in no way inferior to the eminent Apostles. But Beza rightly interprets them as the highest, because τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν Ἀποστόλων literally sounds like those who are Apostles above what is very much. For λίαν is placed in the manner of the Hebrews for σφόδρα καὶ ἐξαιρέτως. The Syrian rendered it: Those who greatly exceed. In the parallel passage chapter XII. 11, the Latin translates, those who are Apostles above measure.

Thus is overthrown the primacy of Peter, which the Pope has invented, while several highest Apostles are asserted. For by the highest Apostles are not understood the Pseudo-Apostles, who boasted of themselves as if they were great, through irony, as seems to some more recent [writers]; But Peter, James, and John, because the proper sense is not to be rashly neglected; and thus the Greek Interpreters Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, as also from the Latins Anselm, Lyranus, Thomas, etc., have expounded, and Grotius admits this, and in the judgment of Cornelius it seems simpler and truer. They are called the same in Gal. II. 9. οἱ δοκοῦντες στύλοι εἶναι, who were held in esteem among the Apostles. Oecumenius rendered it: τοὺς ὄντας τι καὶ κορυφαίους: Chrysostom μεγάλους καὶ ἐξάρχους, great and Princes. But that Paul says he has done nothing less than the highest Apostles, Cornelius rashly restricts to the preaching of Christ, the giving of the Spirit, and the sincerity of the Gospel, because he yielded to none in labors and evangelical graces, and thus denies that it pertains to power and primacy; For he who is inferior to the highest Apostles in NO thing, he does not acknowledge anyone among the Apostles as superior in power and primacy, or who is the head of the Church, and holds primacy and rule over it. Where Scripture speaks absolutely and universally, and excepts nothing, it is not for us to restrict or except anything.

In the parallel passage chapter XII. 11, the Vulgate simply: I was nothing less than those who are Apostles above measure. Oecumenius οὐδὲν ὑστέρησα, οὐδὲν ἀνέλιπον ἢ κατόπιν ἦλθον περὶ Πέτρον: I was nothing less, nor inferior or behind Peter. Whom Chrysostom preceded: We shall not now make a comparison of this kind with them, but with Peter. Justinian in his paraphrase: and no one can prove that I was in any respect inferior to them. The Grotian notes here also are deservedly observed against the primacy of the Pope.

Latin:

V. 5. Λογίζομαι γὰρ μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν ἀποστό- λων) At nunc aliter se res habet: Neque ego in praedicatione habeo, cui cedam, non dicam illis, sed nec ipsis Aposto- lis, imo Apostolorum praecipuis, id est Petro, Jacobo, Johanni, Gal. II. 9. Eadem prope verba infra XII. 11. Est autem hic duplex nota magnitudinis, ὑπὲρ & λίαν, sicut λίαν ἐκ περισσοῦ Marc. VI. 51. & Adverbium praeposito Ar- ticulo, simul pro Adjectivo.Hebraei dicerent המהגרלים מאר מאר. Dicit hoc imprimis adversus eos, qui Petri sectatores se profitebantur.

Quamvis de vero Christo a se praedicato, & Evangelii sui virtute impostores illi clamitarent, Paulum cum reliquis Apostolis non esse conferen- dum, tamen intrepide affirmare audet, se μη- δὲν, id est nulla re fuisse etiam summis inferio- rem, sive quis amplitudinem vocationis; sive do- norum varietatem, sive caelestium patefactionum excellentiam, sive subactas & ad Christi regnum conversas gentes, sive exantlatos pro Evangelii propagatione labores ac cursus, sive concertationes cum veritatis hostibus, sive denique persecutionum periculorumque molem ac magnitudinem intuea- tur, ut hic iterum rectissime B. Hunnius. Uti- tur Praeterito ὑστερηκέναι potius (quod Beza notat) quam Praesenti ὑστερεῖν, quia non tam in genere suum adhuc vigentem Apostolatum respicit quam ea quae in ipsius muneris functione gesserat, eosdem hac in re judices simul & testes adhibens. Vul- gata: Nihil me minus fecisse a magnis Apostolis. Erasmus multo rectius: Nihilo inferiorem fuisse eximiis Apostolis. Recte autem summos inter- pretatur Beza, quia τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν Ἀποστόλων ad verbum sonat iis qui supra quam valde sunt Apo- stoli. Positum enim est λίαν Hebraeorum mo- re pro σφόδρα καὶ ἐξαιρέτως. Syrus reddidit: Eos qui valde excedunt. In loco parallelo cap. XII. 11. Latinus vertit, eos qui supra modum sunt Apo- stoli.

Ita prosternitur primatus Petri, quem Papa commentus est, dum plures summi Apostoli af- seruntur. Per summos enim Apostolos non Pseudo- Apostoli, qui se quasi magnos jactitabant per iro- niam intelliguntur, quod nonnullis recentiori- bus videtur; Sed Petrus, Jacobus, & Johannes, quia proprius sensus temere non negligendus; atque ita Graeci Interpp. Chrysostomus, Theophyla- ctus, Oecumenius, ut & e Latinis Anshelmus, Ly- ranus, Thomas &c. exposuere, idque admittit Grotius, ac judice Cornelio simplicius videtur & verius. Vocantur iidem Gal. II. 9. οἱ δοκοῦντες στύ- λοι εἶναι, qui inter Apostolos in pretio erant. Oecumenius reddidit : τοὺς ὄντας τι καὶ κορυφαίους: Chrysostomus μεγάλους καὶ ἐξάρχους magnos & Prin- cipes. Quod autem nihil minus se fecisse, quam summos Apostolos Paulus dicit, temere restrin- git Cornelius ad praedicationem Christi, donationem Spiritus & sinceritatem Evangelii, quod in labori- bus & gratiis Evangelicis nulli cesserit, adeoque ad potestatem & primatum negat pertinere; Nam qui in NULLA re inferior summis Apostolis est, ille non agnoscit aliquem inter Apostolos superiorem potestate & primatu, aut, qui caput Ecclesiae sit, & principatum ac regimen super ipsam obtineat. Ubi scriptura absolute & uni- versaliter loquitur, nec quicquam excipit, no- strum non est restringere, aut quicquam excipere.

In loco parallelo cap. XII. 11. simpliciter Vulgata : Nihil minus fui ab iis, qui sunt supra modum Apo- stoli. Oecumenius οὐδὲν ὑστέρησα, οὐδὲν ἀνέλιπον ἢ κατόπιν ἦλθον περὶ Πέτρον: Nihilo minor fui, neque inferior aut posterior Petro. Cui Chrysostomus praevivit: Non jam cum illis, sed cum Petro hujus- modi comparationem faciemus. Justinianus in paraphrasi: neque ulla prorsus re me illis inferio- rem fuisse probare quisquam potest. Grotiana et- iam notae hic adversus Papae primatum merito observantur.

## 11:6
Vers. 6. But if also I am an idiot in speech) He returns to that which he says above was objected to him. ἰδιώτης, that is, similar to an unlearned person. See Acts IV. 13. But in knowledge) In the knowledge of the law and the mysteries lying hidden in the law.

That he lacked none of the gifts, even if a contention were made with the greatest Apostles, he had said not for his own sake, but for the sake of his rivals. How then would he immediately and simply concede that he was unskilled in speech? Wherefore Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Theophylact in this place, and Augustine in book IV of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 7, hold that this was said not categorically, but hypothetically, and according to the opinion of the Corinthians: 'even if I were unskilled in speech.' So also Blessed Hunnius: 'If that simplicity of words were to be considered a fault in the highest degree, yet that defect is compensated in turn by a nobler gift, namely knowledge, by the name of which he designates an exact cognition, worthy even of the greatest Prophets and Apostles, of the most abstruse mysteries of God and of all things pertaining to eternal salvation, with which theological knowledge those word-smiths are destitute, and place their wisdom solely in the volubility of their tongue.' But if it be even admitted that the Apostle called himself unskilled in speech categorically, it would nevertheless have to be explained skillfully, and not compared, as the Papists do, with that which the author of the 2nd book of Maccabees, ch. XV. 30, asks for pardon from the reader, where Bellarmine in book I of On the Word of God, ch. 15, says that he is asking for pardon not for errors, but for less polished speech, just as Paul confesses himself to be unskilled in speech. For besides the fact that Paul uses no excuse here, much less asks for pardon, and that, as Cajetan warns, this is said of Paul's ordinary speech and should not be referred to his writings, inasmuch as they were divinely inspired, so that Gregory of Valencia in [the following passage] acknowledges that not only the things themselves, but also the speech and elocution were from the Holy Spirit himself

Analysis, Book VIII, Chapter 5. Ambrosius Catharinus admits at this place that Paul adapts his words to the opinion of the Corinthians; because his speech possessed a spiritual simplicity, and not that secular and affected eloquence: And Salmero in this place, disp. XII, notes that Paul does not admit that he is unskilled in speech simply, but because he did not excel in the splendor of diction and the rhetorical lights of eloquence: not denying, however, that he was most abundantly endowed with divine eloquence through the Holy Spirit, and that these two Epistles to the Corinthians testify to this abundantly, and especially this latter one, which is effective to a miracle, and transforms the Corinthians into whatever affection it might be. Concerning which matter we have spoken more fully in the oration of the Academic lectures at Regiomontanus in the Vestibule of the Epistle to the Hebrews, repeated. The Apostle does not deny that he is an ἰδιώτην (idiot) in speech, says Hunnius, for it was never his concern to have that pompous grandiloquence which false teachers affect and boast of, but he used simple speech, which is customary for truth, and took pains to accommodate himself to the capacity of his hearers for edification by a popular method of teaching, rather than to procure for himself the praise of eloquence by an apparatus of words. Since the false Apostles considered this skill in speaking (these are Theophylact's words) to be their chief glory, Paul shows here that he does not shun rudeness at all, but rather glories in it most of all. Nor does he say that he himself is devoid of letters for this reason, because the rest of the true Apostles also do not know letters, lest he might seem to disparage them as well: But he overturns the entire force of exterior wisdom, just as in the former Epistle, he demonstrated this to be not only useless, but even to devastate the glory of the cross. I am therefore unskilled in speech, not in knowledge, by which words he also argues that those who boast the more in eloquence are the most devoid of divine understanding. And as far as that concerns it, they are found to be completely ignorant. Moreover, Paul's eloquence, as Estius admits, was not sought from the schools of rhetoricians, but was such as would spontaneously follow the tongue of a man full of the divine Spirit and speaking with great affection about great matters. Whence Augustine, Book IV of Christian Doctrine, Chapter 6, says: Just as we do not say that the Apostle followed the precepts of eloquence, so we do not deny that eloquence followed his wisdom. Nor did Jerome hesitate, in Epistle LXI to Pammachius, to call Paul most eloquent, indeed a river of Christian eloquence. Blessed Balduinus here distinguishes between true and painted eloquence; see him on page 715. Blessed Hülsemannus also observes this here against a certain author of Hellenistic innocence against the propositions. the third of the Groffian Triad, from the scope and connection of the discourse, is evident that ἰδιώτην τῷ λόγῳ (unskilled in speech) cannot denote a barbarian or a solecism, as far as the grammatical type of speech is concerned; but simple in the habit of body and gesture or the action of speech. In this third, says he, the Apostle testifies that he was in no way inferior to the highest Apostles, verse 5. Which equality consisted not only in the excellence of miracles and gifts, Galatians II. 9, 1 Corinthians XV. 20, but specifically also in the excellence of congruent and evident speech, apt for understanding. For which reason, since he excelled Barnabas, he was called Mercury by the Gentile hearers, Acts XIV. 11, and 1 Corinthians XIV. 18, he gives thanks to God that he speaks with tongues more than the others. Then the idiotism of Paul consisted ἐν ταπεινώσει ἑαυτῦ (in the humbling of himself), as immediately follows in verse 7, where the Apostle gives the reason why he is considered an idiot. Thirdly, from the opposition of γνώσεως (knowledge),

and indeed passively, or relatively with regard to the Corinthians, who evidently knew the knowledge and excellence of Paul in divine matters, as is said in the consequent part of verse 6, it is evident that the opposite of γνώσεως (knowledge) is not a solecism or a barbarism, but a voluntary simplicity, both of simple words not curled like hair, as 1 Corinthians II. 13, and of the manner of pronouncing and inculcating to the hearers, not in a haughty way, as Herod was orating, Acts XII. 21, but in a gentle and humble way, as 1 Corinthians XII. 8, which simplicity is opposed to τῷ βάσει (to the base), and is called λόγῳ ἐξεθενημένῳ (speech of no account), above in chapter X. 10, by no means a barbarian or a solecism. For the word idiot never signifies one sinning against grammatical rules, or a vulgar mode of speaking, but one lacking the artifice of speech and the excellence of knowledge: Just as the Apostles were called ἀγράμματοι (unlettered) and idiots in Acts IV. 13. and they spoke in their own native language, not only, that is, Galilean, but also in other exotic languages, in such a way that every nation said that they were speaking ἡμετέραις γλώσσαις (in our own tongues), Acts II. 7, 11, without any accusation or exception of a solecism, etc.

᾿Αλλ' ἐν παντὶ φανερωθέντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς (But in everything manifesting ourselves in all things to you): We have used no deceit in any matter. In all things and altogether we act openly with you. Ἐν παντὶ (in everything) is equivalent to בכל (altogether). He obliquely notes his adversaries.

These are more correctly referred to the preceding, because he appeals, regarding those things, to the testimonies of the Corinthians, and to a public notoriety as it were, especially what he is worth in delivering the articles of heavenly doctrine, in which the adversaries were strangers, however much they did not lack talent or artifice for confounding the Law and the Gospel and forging new dogmas.

Latin:

Vers. 6. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ) Redit ad id, quod si- bi objectum supra dicit. ἰδιώτης, id est, similis ἰδιώτῃ. Vid. Act. IV. 13. Ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ γνώσει) Cognitione legis & mysteriorum in le- ge latentium.

Non deesse sibi quicquam donorum, etiamsi contentio fiat cum summis Apostolis, non sui, sed aemulorum causa dixerat. Quomodo ergo idiotam se sermone esse actutum simpliciter conce- deret? Quapropter id non Categorice, sed hypo- thetice dictum, & ex opinione Corinthiorum volunt Chrysostomus, Theodoreto, Theophylactus in h. l. Augustinus lib. IV. de doctrina Christ. c. 7. tametsi idiota sermone essem : Sic etiam B. Hun- nius: Si maxime pro vitio habenda foret illa ver- borum simplicitas, eum tamen defectum nobiliori vicissim dono compensari, nimirum scientia, cu- jus nomine designat exactam, & summis etiam Pro- phetis & Apostolis dignam cognitionem abstrusissi- morum mysteriorum Dei, omniumque rerum ad aeternam salutem pertinentium, qua Theologica scientia λογιδαίδαλοι illi destituantur, & suam sa- pientiam in sola lingua volubilitate collocent. Quod si etiam admittatur se sermone Categorice idiotam dixisse Apostolum, dextre tamen id explicandum foret, nec conferendum cum Pomificiis cum eo, quod autor libr. 2. Maccab. cap. XV. 30. veniam sibi a lectore dari petit, ubi Bellarminus libr. I. de Verbo Dei cap. 15. ipsum non erratorum, sed minus poli- tae orationis veniam petere, uti Paulus se imperi- tum sermone confiteatur, ait. Nam praeterquam, quod nulla Paulus utatur hic excusatione, nedum veniam petat, quodque Cajetano monente, de ordinario sermone Pauli id dictum, non vero ad ejusdem scripta referendum sit, utpote quae divini- tus inspirata erant, ita ut non tantum res ipsas, sed etiam sermonem & elocutionem ab ipso Spiritu sancto fuisse agnoscat Gregorius de Valentia in

Anal. libr. VIII. cap. 5. fatetur Ambrosius Catha- rinus ad h. l. Paulum verba sua ad opinionem Co- rinthiorum accommodare; quia sermo ejus habe- bat simplicitatem spiritualem, & non secularem illam & affectatam eloquentiam: Et Salmero in h. l. disp. XII. notat, Paulum non fateri se sermone im- peritum simpliciter, sed quia splendore dictionis & eloquentiae luminibus Rhetoricis adornate non polle- ret: non negans tamen illum eloquentia divina per Spiritum sanctum cumulatissimum extitisse, idque abunde testari duas hasce ad Corinthios Epistolas, & praesertim hanc posteriorem ad miraculum effi- cacem, & Corinthios ad quemcunque velut affe- ctum transformantem. Qua de re uberius dixi- mus in orat. praelectionum Academicarum in mon- te Regio Auspicali in Vestibulo epistola ad Hebraeos repetita. Non negat Apostolus, se sermone esse ἰδιώτην, inquit Hunnius, neque enim unquam cu- ra sibi fuisse grandiloquentiam illam pomposam, quam affectent, & jactent falsi doctores, sed u- sum oratione simplici, qua veritatis esse soleat, & dedisse operam, ut populari ratione docendi po- tius accommodaret se captui auditorum ad aedifi- cationem, quam ut apparatu verborum sibi elo- quentiae laudem conciliaret. Cum hanc sibi dicen- di peritiam (Theophylacti haec sunt) praecipue gloriae ducerent falsi Apostoli, ostendit hic Paulus, se nihil ruditatem defugere, quin vel maxime de hac gloriari. Neque id dicit, ideo ipse expers sum literarum, quia & reliqui veri Apostoli li- teras nesciunt, ne & illis simul detrahere videre- tur: Sed exterioris sapientiae vim omnem subver- tit, quemadmodum in priori Epistola, hanc de- monstravit non modo inutilem esse, quin etiam & crucis gloriam devastare. Sum itaque sermo- ne non scientia imperitus, quibus dictis & illos ar- guit, quo magis eloquentiam jactent, eo etiam maxime divinae esse notionis expertes. Et quan- tum ad eam spectat, deprehendi prorsus ignaros. Erat autem Pauli facundia, ut Estius fatetur, non ex scholis Rhetorum petita, sed qua linguam viri divino Spiritu pleni magnoque affectu de ma- gnis rebus loquentis sponte sequeretur. Unde Au- gustinus lib. IV. de doctrina Christiana cap. 6. Sicut, inquit, Apostolum praecepta eloquentiae sequutum fuisse non dicimus: Ita quod sapientiam ejus se- quuta sit eloquentia non negamus. Nec dubitavit Hieronymus epist. LXI. ad Pammachium Paulum disertissimum, imo flumen eloquentia Christiana dicere. B. Balduinus hic distinguit inter elo- quentiam veram & fucatam, qui videatur pag. 715. Observat etiam hic B. Hülsemannus con- tra autorem quendam Hellenisticae innocentiae adversus proposit. tertiam Triados Groffianae ex scopo & connexione dicendi patere ἰδιώτην τῷ λόγῳ non posse notare barbarum & soloecum, quantum ad Grammaticum dicendi genus; sed simplicem habitu corporis & gestu seu actione ser- monis. In hoc tertio, inquit, testatur Aposto- lus, se nihilo inferiorem fuisse summis Apostolis vers. 5. Quae aequalitas non tantum in excellen- tia miraculorum & donorum Galat. II. 9. 1. Co- rinth. XV. 20. sed specifice etiam in excellentia congrui, & evidentis sermonis ad intelligendum apti consistebat. Qua de causa cum antecelleret Barnabam, ab auditoribus Gentilibus Mercu- rius vocabatur Actor. XIV. 11. & 1. Corinth. XIV. 18. Deo gratias agit, quod plus caeteris linguis loquatur. Deinde idiotismus Pauli consistebat ἐν ταπεινώσει ἑαυτῦ, ut immediate sequitur vers. 7. ubi rationem reddit Apostolus, quam ob rem ha- beatur pro idiota. Tertio ex oppositione γνώσεως,

& quidem passive, seu relative quoad Corinthios, qui notitiam & excellentiam Pauli in rebus divi- nis evidenter cognoverunt, ut dicitur in conseq. parte vers. 6. patet oppositum γνώσεως non esse so- lœcismum aut barbarismum sed voluntariam sim- plicitatem tum verborum simplicium non calami- stratorum ut 1. Corinth. II. 13. tum modo pronun- ciandi & inculcandi auditoribus non fastuoso, veluti Herodes perorabat Actor. XII. 21. sed man- sueto & humili, ut 1. Corinth. XII. 8. quæ sim- plicitas opponitur τῷ βάσει, & dicitur λόγῳ ἐξε- θενημένῳ, supra cap. X. 10. nequaquam barba- rus aut solœcus. Nec enim vocabulum idiotæ un- quam significat peccantem in Grammaticas regu- las, aut vulgarem dicendi modum, sed caren- tem artificio sermonis & excellentia cognitionis: Quomodo Apostoli dicebantur ἀγράμματοι, & idiotæ Actorum IV. 13. & sermone suo patrio non tantum, id est Galilæo, sed etiam aliis exoticis linguis ita loquebantur, ut quæque natio diceret, ipsos loqui ἡμετέραις γλώσσαις Actorum II. 7. 11. citra ullam accusationem vel exceptionem Solœcismi &c.

᾿Αλλ' ἐν παντὶ φανερωθέντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς) Fucum nulla in re fecimus. In omnibus & omnino aperte vo- biscum agimus. Ἐν παντὶ בכל valet omnino. Oblique notat adversarios.

Rectius hæc ad præcedentia referuntur, quod provocet, quoad ea, ad Corinthiorum testi- monia, & publicam velut notorietatem, im- primis quid valeat in tradendis cœlestis doctri- næ articulis, in quibus adversarii erant hospi- tes, quantumvis ad confundendam legem & Evangelium & nova procudenda dogmata non defuerit illis ingenium aut artificium.

## 11:7
Verse 7. Ἢ ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησα (Or did I commit a sin): He vehemently strikes the heart, asking whether he sinned in that which was of extraordinary virtue, and from which those adversaries were far removed.

Ἐμαυτὸν ταπεινῶν (Humbling myself): Living so vilely, as if I were a slave.

Ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑψωθῆτε (That you might be exalted): That you might obtain the gifts of the Spirit through faith.

Ὅτι δωρεὰν τὸ Θεῦ ἐυαγγέλιον ἐυηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν (Because I preached the Gospel of God to you freely): Without expense to you, Acts XVIII. 3, 1 Corinthians IX. 4, and following.

That ταπείνωσις pertains not only to a lowly diet, but also to any submission whatsoever: because he wished to become all things to all men, and with the greatest humiliation of himself, so that he might save some everywhere 1 Cor. IX. 22. Phil. IV. 12. he treats of the manner of his own sustenance in the following verses. Rightly, therefore, are two things numbered here by others, on account of which Paul was despised by some: First, his own humble conversation among the Corinthians: then, the gratuitous preaching of the Gospel: the former of which they interpreted as sycophancy, the latter, however, as a certain acknowledgment of unworthiness. Estius therefore renders the sense well: Have I sinned in that I humbled myself among you, conducting myself as if I were of no authority, so that you might be exalted before God? And further: So far have I not sinned against you, that I have even bestowed a singular benefit upon you, preaching the Gospel gratuitously, which I did not do among others. If you say: And yet it is commanded to all ministers Matt. X. 8.

freely you have received, freely give. Resp. This is to be understood in such a way that no price ought to be accepted for spiritual gifts, although sustenance of life may be required for the labor expended, because the laborer is worthy of his hire, not that labors should be exposed for gain: Here, however, the Apostle boasts particularly of this, that he preached so gratuitously to the Corinthians that he did not even receive the necessities of life.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἢ ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησα) Vehementer cor ferit quæ- rens an peccaverit in eo, quod eximiæ erat virtutis, & unde illi Adversarii longe aberant.

Ἐμαυτὸν ταπεινῶν) Ita vili vivens, quasi servus es- sem.

Ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑψωθῆτε) Ut vos per fidem dona Spiritus con- sequeremini.

Ὅτι δωρεὰν τὸ Θεῦ ἐυαγγέλιον ἐυηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν) Sine vestro sumptu, Actor. XVIII. 3. 1. Cor. IX. 4. sequenti- bus.

Illa ταπείνωσις non tantum ad vilem victum, sed etiam ad quamcunque submissionem pertinet: quia omnibus omnia fieri voluit, & cum maxi- ma sui humiliatione, ut ubique aliquos serva- ret 1. Corinth. IX. 22. Phil. IV. 12. de sustentatio- nis suæ modo versibus sequentibus agit. Recte ergo duo hic ab aliis numerantur, ob quæ Pau- lus a nonnullis contemptus fuerit: Primum hu- milis ipsius inter Corinthios conversatio: de- inde gratuita Evangelii prædicatio: Quorum illud ceu assentationem, hoc vero, ceu indi- gnitatis quandam agnitionem interpretabantur. Sensum ergo probe reddit Estius: An peccavi in eo, quod meipsum apud vos humiliavi, ge- rens me, tanquam nullius essem autoritatis, ut vos ea exaltaremini apud Deum? Et porro: Usque adeo non peccavi in vos, ut & singulari beneficio vos affecerim, gratis Evangelium præ- dicans, quod apud alios non feci. Si dicas: At- qui omnibus ministris præcipitur Matth. X. 8.

gratis accepistis, gratis date. Resp. Id ita intel- ligendum, quod nullum pretium accipi debeat pro donis spiritualibus, licet ex labore impenso sustentatio vitæ requiri possit, quia dignus est operarius mercede sua, non ut labores ad quæ- stum exponantur: Hic vero peculiariter de eo gloriatur Apostolus, quod ita gratis prædica- rit Corinthiis, ut ne quidem vita necessaria re- ceperit.

## 11:8
Ver. 8.

Verf. 8. I robbed other churches, having received wages for your ministry) I robbed, that is, as I robbed, I received from them. He calls wages something small, such as that which is given to a soldier. For your ministry, to sustain your poor, for that is ministry above VI. 3. VIII. 4. IX. 1. 12. 13. At Corinth, either there were few rich people in the Church at the beginning, or they were very stingy.

By ministry do not understand the service of sustaining the poor, which was carried out by others in Paul's absence, but Paul's office; the word wages, which properly denotes a stipend, not alms, implies this. And the Greek Fathers have interpreted it thus. Theophylact says: He could, he says, indeed say this: With these hands I provided my own living, but in order to urge them with sharper words, he says, I received wages from others, so that I might serve you. Inasmuch as I despoiled others for the sake of providing the Gospel to you, and rendered them diminished in their resources. He argues that these were the Macedonians, who, although they were bound by the utmost poverty of their family circumstances, and, he says, they had me wearing them down, even though I was in need of expenses not for luxuries, but for necessity. For I was receiving wages from them, which, however, you by no means provided to me.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Verf. 8. Ἄλλας ἐκκλησίας ἐσύλησα, λαβὼν ὀψώνιον πρὸς τὴν ὑμῶν διακονίαν) ἐσύλησα, id est, ὡς ἐσύλησα, accepi ab illis. ὀψώνιον vocat modicum aliquid, quale est quod militi datur. Πρὸς τὴν ὑμῶν διακονίαν, ad sustentandos pauperes vestros, id enim διακονία supra VI. 3. VIII. 4. IX. 1. 12. 13. Corinthi aut initio pauci erant divites in Ecclesia, aut præparci.

Per διακονίαν non sustentationis pauperum ministerium, quod ab aliis Paulo absente expeditum, sed officium Paulinum intellige, ὀψωνὶς vox stipendium, quod proprie denotat non eleemosynam, innuit. Atque ita interpretati sunt Græci Patres. Theophylactus: Poterat, inquit, sane id dicere: Hisce quidem manibus victum mihi subministravi, sed ut acrioribus verbis hos urgeat, ab aliis, inquit, accepi stipendia, vobis ut inservirem. Quippe qui alios, vobis Evangelium subministrandi gratia exspoliaverim, & imminutos reddiderim facultatibus. Hos autem Macedonas fuisse arguit, qui cum essent summa rei familiaris adstricti inopia, & me, inquit, habebant se atterentem, tametsi minus ad delicias, sed ad necessitatem sumptibus indigerem. Accipiebam namque ab his stipendia, quæ tamen ipsi mihi haudquaquam suppeditastis.

## 11:8
and I was burdensome to no one) We have this word, and indeed with the Genitive of the person added, twice below XII. 13. 14. Jerome says that this word is taken from the idiom of the Cilicians. It seems, however, to be said of those who, being lazy and sluggish, are for that reason a burden to others. In the Greek Job XXXIII. 19. the multitude of his bones became numb, became torpid. In the Glossary: I become numb, I become torpid.

Latin:

καὶ κατενάρκησα οὐδενὸς) Habemus hoc verbum & quidem addito personæ Genitivo, bis infra XII. 13. 14. Dicit autem Hieronymus vocem hanc desumptam ex Cilicum idiomate. Videtur autem de iis dici, qui cum sint ignavi ac torpidi aliis ob id sunt oneri. In Jobi Græco XXXIII. 19. πλῆθος ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ ἐνάρκησε, obtorpuit. In Glossario: καταναρκῶ obtorpeo.

## 11:9
V. 9. And when I was present with you and was in want) that is, not finding enough from your collections from which your poor might be fed.

Latin:

V. 9. Καὶ παρὼν πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ ὑστερηθεὶς) id est, ex vestris collationibus non satis reperiens unde pauperes vestri alerentur.

## 11:9
For the brethren, coming from Macedonia, supplied my lack) Namely the Philippians, Phil. IV. 15. 16. When I was preparing a meager living for myself with my hands, I received from them that with which I might help the poor.

and in everything I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and will keep myself) In the Glossary: not burdensome.

Paul speaks about himself, not about the poor, nor about the fact that he was not ignorant and sluggish in defending himself, but that he was not a burden by receiving a stipend, as the whole context teaches. Theophylact indeed notes some who interpreted it thus; that I did not show myself in any way negligent or inert and sluggish for preaching: But he prefers the other explanation: You committed, he says, a threefold crime in that matter. For both when I was staying among you, and was serving you, and was needy, no consideration was had for me. Inasmuch as you not only did not transmit anything to me while I was absent, which the Macedonians certainly used to do, but you did not even feed me when I was present. He argues furthermore that the Corinthians had become slower in bestowing alms. Regarding Jerome's judgment on the word I was burdensome, Beza says thus: As for what Jerome notes, that this word is peculiar to the Cilicians, I do not know how true that is, since it is used by Theocritus, Synesius, and Plato.

Latin:

Τὸ γὰρ ὑστέρημά μου προσανεπλήρωσαν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ, ἐλθόντες ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας) Nempe Philippenses, Phil. IV. 15. 16. Cum manibus mihi victum tenuem pararem, ab illis accepi unde pauperes juvarem.

καὶ ἐν παντὶ ἀβαρῆ ὑμῖν ἐμαυτὸν ἐτήρησα, καὶ τηρήσω) In Glossario: ἀβαρὴς non gravis.

De se loquitur Paulus, non de pauperibus, nec de eo, quod haud ignarus fuerit & torpidus sese defendit, sed quod oneri non fuerit accipiendo stipendium, uti totus contextus docet. Notat sane quosdam Theophylactus, qui sic interpretati fuerint; quod me ad prædicandum haudquaquam negligentem præstiti aut inertem & torpidum: Sed alteram explicationem præfert: Triplex, inquit, ea in re facinus admisistis. Nam & apud vos cum manerem, & vobis subministrarem, & essem egenus, nulla mei sit habita ratio. Quippe qui non solum nihil absenti mihi aliquo transmisistis, quod utique Macedones factitarunt, sed ne præsentem quidem vos aluistis. Arguit præterea Corinthios ad eleemosynam erogandam tardiores effectos. De crisi Hieronymi de voce κατενάρκησα ita Beza: Quod autem annotat Hieronymus hanc vocem Cilicibus esse peculiarem, quam verum sit, nescio, quum a Theocrito, Synesio, Platone usurpetur.

## 11:10
Vers. 10. the truth of Christ is in me) I speak the truth with Christ as my witness IX. 1.

That this boasting) This joy of mine, that I was never a burden to you.

shall not be stopped in me in the regions of Achaia) Other codices are better, shall not be stopped, it will not be closed, it will not be silenced. For to stop the mouth is to close the mouth, Rom. III. 19. Heb. XI. 33. and it is a litotes for it will flow far and wide, through all of Achaia.

Chrysostom notes on the word Shall be stopped, (which is altogether to be preferred) a metaphor drawn from rivers, in the manner of which his fame was flowing everywhere, because he received nothing (in stipend): You will not (he says) obstruct my liberty by your generosity. But he did not say you will obstruct (which would have been more bitter) but it will be obstructed in the regions of Achaia: Camerarius: Shall be stopped by the removal of the prefix, shall not be stopped, that is, it will not be excluded, or fail.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἔστιν ἀληθεία χριστοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ) Verum loquor Christo teste IX. 1.

Ὅτι ἡ καύχησις αὕτη) Hoc gaudium meum, quod vobis oneri nunquam fuerim.

οὐ σφραγίσεται εἰς ἐμὲ ἐν τοῖς κλίμασι τῆς Ἀχαΐας) Melius alii Codices, οὐ φραγήσεται לא יסתם non continebitur intra me, non tacebitur. Nam στόμα φράσσειν est os occludere, Rom. III. 19. Hebr. XI. 33. & est λιτότης pro longe ac late manabit, per omnem Achaiam.

Notat Chrysostomus in verbo Φραγήσεται, (quod omnino præferendum) metaphoram ductam a fluminibus, quorum in morem fama ipsius ubique fluebat, quod nihil acciperet (stipendii:) Non (inquit) largitione vestra libertatem meam obstruetis. Sed non dixit obstruetis (quo amarulentius erat) verum obstruetur in rea gionibus Achaiæ: Camerarius: ἡ Φραγήσεται κατ' ἀφαίρεσιν ἐκ ἐμφραγήσεται non obturabitur, id est, non excludetur, vel deficiet.

## 11:11
Vers. 11. Why) What is the cause, he says, why I should wish that to be known?

Because I do not love you?) Is it because I do not love you? For those who do not love someone are accustomed to reproach him with their good deeds.

God knows) He who knows hearts knows that you are held dear by me. There is in these words, as elsewhere, the force of an oath.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Διά τι) Quæ causa est, inquit, cur id sciri ve- lim?

Ὅτι ἐκ ἀγαπῶ ὑμᾶς;) An quod vos non amem? Nam qui aliquem non amant, solent ei benefacta sua expro- brare.

ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν) Qui corda novit, scit vos a me tenere ama- ri. Est in his verbis, ut alibi, vis jurisjurandi.

## 11:12
