Vers. 12. But what I do and will do) I will proceed to make this very thing public.

that I may cut off the pretext, from those who seek a pretext so that they may set themselves before us. Concerning the word ἀφορμῆς see Rom. VII. 8. 11. Those teachers boasted that they took nothing for themselves from the treasury of the Church.

that in what they boast, they may be found just as we are) That at least by my example they may in reality perform what they say they are doing.

He could have inverted the argument, as noted by Chrysostom and Theophylact. Why rather, because I am held by your benevolence, I would not want you to suffer any injury, seeing as you are easily offended. Yet he does not speak these things openly, lest he make their weakness manifest, but turns the discourse to another cause. For since the adversaries were taking pains, as Chrysostom says, to find some handle, it was necessary to amputate this one also. For this was the only thing in which they boasted. So that they might be superior in nothing, this also had to be corrected. Since in other things they were inferior. For nothing, as has been said by me, edifies worldly people as much as taking nothing. Wherefore the devil, for his own perversity, had thrown in this bait above all, striving to affect them with inconvenience in other matters. To me, however, this also seems to have flowed from hypocrisy. Wherefore he did not say: In what they conducted themselves rightly and with virtue: but what? In what they boast. With which words he attacked their arrogance with taunts. For they boasted even of that which they were not. And yet it is not fitting for an excellent man to boast not only of those things which he lacks, but not even of those things which he has. He protests, therefore, that he does not seek the stipends of the Corinthians out of hatred or a desire to defame: But he wishes to amputate the occasion for the adversaries to accuse his avarice, and to hold up a torch to these men by a good example, if by any means they might yet wish to become like him, but because there was almost despair concerning them, he therefore seeks from this an occasion to depict those new troublemakers with his own vivid colors, out of a righteous zeal, so that their flatteries may be the more studiously avoided, as here Blessed Balduinus.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὃ δὲ ποιῶ κὶ ποιήσω) Pergam hoc ipsum publi- care.

ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν, τῶν θελόντων ἀφορμὴν) Ut abscindam prætextum quærentibus eum ut se nobis ante- ponant. De voce ἀφορμῆς vide Rom. VII. 8. 11. Jacta- bant illi Doctores divites se nihil de arca Ecclesiæ sibi su- mere.

ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καυχῶνται, ἐυρεθῶσι καθὼς κὶ ἡμεῖς) Ut sal- tem meo exemplo reipsa præstent quod se dicunt face- re.

Invertere poterat, notante cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, argumentum. Quin potius, quia vestri detineor benevolentia, nolim ullam vos pati injuriam, utpote qui facile offendamini. Haud tamen aperte hæc loquitur, ne illorum perspicuam faciat imbecillitatem, sed ad aliam causam divertit sermonem. Quandoquidem e- nim adversarii operam dabant, Chrysostomo di- cente, ut ansam aliquam invenirent, hanc quoque amputare oportebat. Hoc enim solum e- rat, in quo gloriabantur. Ut itaque nulla re su- periores essent, hoc quoque correctum oportuit. Siquidem in aliis inferiores erant. Nihil enim, ut a me dictum est, mundanos perinde ædificat, ut nihil accipere. Quocirca diabolus pro sua per- versitate hanc potissimum illecebram injecerat, studens eos in aliis rebus incommodo afficere. Mi- bi autem hoc quoque ab hypocrisi manasse videtur. Quamobrem nec dixit: In quo recte & cum vir- tute se gesserunt: sed quid? In quo gloriantur. Quibus verbis eorum arrogantiam cavillis inces- sebat. Jactabant enim id quoque quod non erant. Atqui præstantem virum non modo de iis, quæ ipsi desunt gloriari non convenit, sed ne de iis quidem quæ habet. Protestatur ergo se non ex odio aut cupiditate diffamandi Corinthiorum sti- pendia non expetere: Sed occasionem accusandi suam avaritiam amputare vult Adversariis, bonoque exemplo hominibus istis facem præluce- re, si qua ratione adhuc sibi fieri velint similes, sed quia de istis propemodum jam desperatum erat, ideo hinc occasionem petit ex justo zelo novos illos turbatores vivis suis depingendi coloribus, ut blanditiis ipsorum eo studiosius caveatur, ut hic B. Balduinus.

## 11:13
Vers. 13. For such are false apostles) He notes those especially who, when they had seen Christ, said that they had received from him the commands to preach. Thus false prophets who call themselves prophets, when they have not been called by God.

deceitful workers) They work in the Gospel but not in good faith. Concerning the word ἐργατῶν see Matt. IX. 37. 38. X. 10. XXI. 2. 8. Why of bad faith? They took nothing from the treasury of the Church, but secretly took many things from those who, burdened with sins and not freeing themselves from them, hoped that they could be saved by their prayers: than which kind of men nothing is more pernicious, 2 Tim. III. 6. See also Matt. XXIII. 14.

Transforming themselves into apostles of Christ) מתחפשים. See 1 Sam. XXVIII. 8. Whence you will understand this is said here, that those men put on the persona of the apostles of Christ, when they are far from their virtues. It is understood here again 'are', as above in 6 it was understood. The Hebrews, who do not have verbs of the present tense, are accustomed to use participles in that manner.

He ought to have applied this to the Papists, who, under the pretext of prayers, even the most vain, for deliverance from purgatory, have scraped together vast wealth. But they were not called deceitful workers only because they secretly received a great deal of money: but especially because they were indeed working, as Chrysostom has it, but were tearing up what had been planted. For since, he says, they have it ascertained that they will not otherwise be welcome and accepted, having assumed the mask of truth, they thus finally act out the fable of imposture. And indeed, he says, they do not accept money, so that they may accept more, so that they may destroy souls. Nay rather, that too is false. For they were indeed accepting, but secretly. And he shows this in what follows. And he had already tacitly indicated this when he said, that in that in which they boast, they may be found just as we are: But he signified the same thing more clearly afterwards with these words, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes, if anyone exalts himself, you endure him. Now, however, he attacks them from another side, saying, transforming themselves. Yet the mask and the sheep's skin is theirs. Add that they were deceitful workers, while they were not seeking the glory of the Lord or the salvation of the Church, but private glory and utility, serving their belly, not the Lord, Phil. III.

But why does he call them Pseudo-Apostles, whom he previously denied had introduced another Christ and another Gospel? Theophylact, following Chrysostom, provides the reason: For such workers, while dissembling everything, secretly introduce certain impious decrees. Why not? Since under the guise of a good and right work, they tear up what has been planted, and while they merely put on the figure of Apostles, and covered in a sheep's back, they are altogether more ferocious and rabid wolves. He calls them Pseudo-Apostles, therefore, says the blessed Hunnius, who usurp the Apostolic office for themselves by a false title, when they have not been called to it, nor do they know those things which befit true Apostles. Then he names them workers, but deceitful ones, who indeed preach, but not at all sincerely, nor do they do it with the zeal of propagating the glory of God and the salvation of men, but they deceitfully use this as a pretext for their own design, which is to capture private advantage and to win over to themselves as many applauders of their own opinions as possible. Thirdly, he says that they take on the person of the Apostles of Christ. Which transformation is various in the similarity of doctrine regarding words and phrases, in the simulation of holiness, in the appearance of zeal for the glory of God, in the external contempt of earthly things, etc.

But let him also call them ministers of Satan, whom they truly serve and whom they imitate, by leading away from the simplicity of Scripture to ambiguous, improper, and uncertain senses, nay, from the Word of God to the inventions of reason, or human traditions, etc. Beza is singular here: He calls them Pseudo-Apostles, not, as I indeed opine, because they had scattered some false doctrine (which, however, without doubt they were eventually going to do) but because they did not perform their ministry sincerely, and especially in this deed they acted in no other way than simulatedly, since they were stung by another's glory, which, however, the Apostle did not seek at all.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οἱ γὰρ τοιῦτοι ψευδαπόστολοι) Illos præcipue no- tat, qui cum Christum vidissent, dicebant se ab ipso manda- ta prædicandi accepisse. Sic ψευδοπροφῆται qui se Prophe- tas dicunt, cum a Deo non sint vocati.

ἐργάται δόλιοι) Operantur Evangelio sed non bona fi- de. De voce ἐργατῶν vide Matth. IX. 37. 38. X. 10. XXI. 2. 8. Cur malæ fidei? Nihil sumebant de arca Ecclesiæ, sed clam sumebant plurima ab iis, qui peccatis onerati, neque ab iis se liberantes, sperabant ipsorum precibus se posse servari: quo genere hominum nihil pernitiosius, 2. Tim. III. 6. Vi- de & Matth. XXIII. 14.

Μετασχηματιζόμενοι εἰς ἀποστόλυς χριστῦ) מתחפשים. Vide 1. Sam. XXVIII. 8. Unde intelliges hoc hic dici, illos homines personam induere Apostolorum Christi, cum ab eorum virtutibus longe absint. Subintelligitur hic rursum sunt, ut supra 6. subintellectum sui. Solent Hebræi, qui præsentis temporis verba non habent, participiis ad eum modum uti.

Applicare id debuisset Pontificiis, qui pre- cum, etiam vanissimarum, pro liberatione e purgatorio prætextu ingentes corraserunt opes. Non autem tantum ideo dolosi operarii diceban- tur, quod clam acciperent plurimum pecuniæ: sed maxime quod operarentur quidem, ut ha- bet Chrysostomus, sed quæ plantata sunt, evelle- rent. Quoniam enim, inquit, exploratum ha- bent, se non aliter gratos acceptosque fore veritatis larva assumpta, ita demum impostura fabulam agunt. Et vero, inquit, pecunias non accipiunt, ut plures accipiant, ut animas perdant. Quin po- tius id quoque falsum. Nam & accipiebant, sed furtim. Idque in iis, quæ sequuntur, ostendit. Atque id quidem jam tacite indicavit, quum dixit, ut in quo gloriantur, inveniantur sicut & nos: Cæterum idem dilucidius postea his verbis signifi- cavit, si quis vos devorat, si quis accipit, si quis extollitur, hunc sustinetis. Nunc autem aliunde hos insectatur, dicens, transfigurantes. Larva tamen ipsis ac pellis ovis est. Adde quod dolosi operarii fuerint, dum non quærebant gloriam Domini vel salutem Ecclesiæ, sed privatam glori- am, atque utilitatem, ventri non Domino servientes, Phil. III.

Cur vero Pseudo-Apostolos vocat, quos antea negavit, alium Christum, aliudque Evangelium induxisse? Causam reddit post Chrysostomum, Theophylactus: Nam ejusmodi omnia dissimulan- tes clam tamen vel impia quædam decreta subinfe- runt operarii subdoli. Quidni? Quandoquidem sub boni & recti operis specie, plantata revellunt, & figuram duntaxat Apostolorum dum præferunt, & tergore ovillo obducti, lupi sunt prorsus ferocio- res & rabidi. Vocat ergo Pseudo - Apostolos, in- quit B. Hunnius, qui munus Apostolicum falso ti- tulo sibi usurpant, cum ad id vocati non sint, nec ea sciant, quæ veros decet Apostolos. Deinde operarios nominat, sed dolosos, qui concionentur quidem, sed minime sincere, nec id faciant studio propagandæ gloriæ Dei & salutis hominum, sed hac dolose prætexant suo instituto, quod est pri- vatum captare commodum, & opinionum sua- rum applausores sibi quam plurimos conciliare. Tertio dicit illos sumere personam Apostolorum Christi. Qui μετασχηματισμὸς varius est in do- ctrinæ similitudine quoad verba & phrases, in sanctitatis simulatione, in zeli pro Dei gloria specie, in rerum terrenarum externo contemptu &c.

Dicat autem simul eos Satanæ ministros, cui revera serviunt, quemque imitantur, a simpli- citate scripturæ abducendo ad sensus ambiguos, improprios, incertos, imo a Verbo Dei ad com- menta rationis, vel traditiones humanas &c. Bezæ hic singularis est: Pseudo-Apostolos illos vo- cat, non, ut ego quidem opinor, quod falsam ali- quam doctrinam sparsissent (quod tamen procul du- bio tandem erant facturi) sed quod ministerium suum sincere non obirent, ac præsertim in hoc facto nihil aliud quam simulate se gererent, quum eos ure- ret aliena gloria, quam tamen minime captabat A- postolus.

## 11:14
Vers. 14. κὶ ὀ θαυμασὸν [And it is no wonder]) Nothing new in this matter. ᾿Αυτὸς γὰρ ὁ Σατανᾶς μετασχηματίζεται εἰς ῎Αγγελον φωτὸς [For Satan himself is transformed into an Angel of light]) that is, a light-bringer, as Barnabas speaks in his Epistle. What he says was admitted among the learned, such as those who wanted to appear to be opposing Paul. Porphyry in Eusebius, Preparation IV, concerning demons: Ἐνίοτε δὲ κὶ μεταβάλλου- σι τὰς μορφὰς οἵγε χείρες [And sometimes the worse ones change their forms] and a little later: σφοδρῶς κὶ ἀιφνι- δίως οἷον ὁιόδρας, ὡς τὸ πολὺ ποιεῖται τὰς ἐμπτώσεις, πῆ μὲν λανθάνειν πειρώμενοι [vehemently and suddenly, as if they were ghosts, as for the most part they make their incursions, in one way trying to remain hidden, etc.]. The same Porphyry, II, On Abstinence from Animal Food, concerning the same: ἔτοι γάρ ἱκανοὶ διὰ τῆς τερατεργίας ἀπατῆσαι [for they are capable of deceiving through wonder-working]. He calls that same kind of demons, of a deceitful nature, all-formed, and many-turned. Arnobius says, according to the opinion of the Magi, that anti-gods often creep in instead of the true ones. We have also cited the passages of Iamblichus pertaining to the same matter in the annotations to book IV of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

Latin:

Vers. 14. κὶ ὀ θαυμασὸν) Nihil in hac re novi. ᾿Αυτὸς γὰρ ὁ Σατανᾶς μετασχηματίζεται εἰς ῎Αγγελον φωτὸς) id est, φωταγωγὸν ut loquitur in Epistola Barnabas. Quod dicit confessum erat apud eruditos, quales illi Paulo ad- versantes videri volebant. Porphyrius apud Eusebium præparationis IV. de dæmonibus: Ἐνίοτε δὲ κὶ μεταβάλλου- σι τὰς μορφὰς οἵγε χείρες ac paulo post: σφοδρῶς κὶ ἀιφνι- δίως οἷον ὁιόδρας, ὡς τὸ πολὺ ποιεῖται τὰς ἐμπτώσεις, πῆ μὲν λανθάνειν πειρώμενοι &c. Idem Porphyrius II. de abs- tinentia ab animalibus de iisdem: ἔτοι γάρ ἱκανοὶ διὰ τῆς τερατεργίας ἀπατῆσαι. Id ipsum dæmonum genus vocat, ἀπατηλῶς φύσεως, παντόμορφον, κὶ πολύτροπον. Arnobius ait ex Magorum sententia, antitheos sæpe obrepere pro veris. Citavimus & Jamblichi loca ad eandem rem fa- cientia in annotatis ad libr. IV. de veritate religionis Chri- stianæ.

## 11:15
Vers. 15. ὀὐ μέγα ὧν [It is no great thing]) that is, it is no wonder, as he had just said; see 2 Cor. IX. 11.

Eἰ καὶ οἱ διάκονοι αὐτοῦ [If also his ministers]) For they are certainly ministers of Satan who, for the sake of their own advantage, foster sins.

Μετασχηματίζονται ὡς διάκονοι δικαιοσύνης [They are transformed as ministers of righteousness]) That is, of the Gospel, which is the cause of true righteousness before God. See Rom. I. 17, III. 22.

Theodoret paraphrases thus: It is the custom of the Devil to imitate divine things and to produce pseudo-prophets against the prophets. And to imitate the figure of angels and to deceive men. It is not, therefore, a wonder if these also have put on the persons of the Apostolic appellation and have used the aid of deceit to deceive men. But they will soon have the fruits of their studies. Angels of light are called good angels, because they shine with wisdom, righteousness, and enjoy the light of heavenly blessedness: but not from external light, with which they shine; since, on the contrary, the Devils are smoky, pitchy, and squalid: since the transformation of Satan is such that he himself also appears luminous, just as he appeared to Saul in a form that was certainly not pitchy or squalid when he feigned to be Samuel, 1 Sam. XXVIII, nor does the nature of the Devils, which is spiritual in itself, bring it about that they are black and smoky. But according to some, the history of Eve seems to be looked back upon, as above, verse 3, because he truly transformed himself then into an angel of light when, with the blandishments of words, he moved the mind of Eve away from the simplicity of the divine word, under the scheme of holiness and truth, falsely promising greater progress in wisdom and divine holiness. To his example, therefore, his ministers also put on the appearance of truth and holiness, but it is a mere mask and only a transformation. He is transformed, says Theophylact, into such an angel, the Devil himself, yet he is not made such: Thus, therefore, these also merely put on the figure of the Apostles, not the same power and action, which we can learn thoroughly from the thing itself, that whatever is done for ostentation and boasting, that is especially demonic. Moreover, as B. Hülsemann warns, it is evident not only from the preceding periphrasis of the Pseudo-Apostles, consisting primarily in gestures and words, verse 3, 4, 20, 21, et seqq., and above chapter II. 17, chapter IV. 2, 3, but from the very word μετασχηματίζει and its regular meaning above in chapter IV. 6 of the former epistle, that the transfiguration speaks not of a substantial change or even of accidents or visible qualities, such as the habit of the body, the assumption of an angelic form, and the like, which are called Metamorphosis in Matthew XVII. 2, Mark IX. 2. Although this word is also used for the alteration of internal qualities alone in Romans XII. 2, 2 Corinthians III. 18, concerning the change in the state of grace. And again, μετασχηματίζει [is used] concerning the change of even the external qualities of a mortal body into an immortal one in Philippians III. 21, so that the opinion of Salmeron, Cornelius, and other Latins is clearly inept: [the idea that] just as the demon himself sometimes assumes angelic, human, or beastly forms, so the Pseudo-Apostles and heretics in the time of Paul and our own are transformed regarding the external habit of the body into such forms, which the impure Cacodemon Gretser accuses Luther of in his Academicus: Justinian, Estius, and the Englishman Rob. Gagnaus admit that this is a discourse about an invisible μετασχηματισμῷ of the affections, and it does not follow that in as many ways as Satan himself can and is accustomed to transform himself, so also all heretics whatsoever can and have been accustomed to do.

But they are called ministers of righteousness, not as Beza wishes, as if they were upright and honest ministers, so that the epithet of righteousness is added from a Hebrew idiom, but because they wish to appear to preach true righteousness, just as the ministry of the Apostles is ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης is said from the truth, 2 Cor. III. 9. Thus Chrysostom: What is the ministry of righteousness? That, namely, which we are, preaching to you the Gospel, which possesses righteousness. And Theophylact: That is, as ministers of the Gospel containing righteousness. But there is no reason why, having abandoned the propriety of the word righteousness, we should take it metonymically for the Gospel.

ὧν τὸ τέλος ἔσται κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) That is, the things which they now do secretly will become manifest, and will bring upon them the greatest infamy. See 2 Tim. II. 16, where the same men are discussed.

Not only infamy in the world, but eternal perdition is the end of such men, which they entirely deserve by their detestable hypocrisy and impious pursuits and deeds. Matt. VII. Apoc. XXI. 8.

PART III.

Comparison of the Apostle and the false apostles regarding the external aspects of the ministry.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὀὐ μέγα ὧν) id est, ὀὐ θαυμαστὸν ut modo dixerat vide 2. Cor. IX. 11.

Eἰ καὶ οἱ διάκονοι αὐτοῦ) Nam certe Satanæ ministri sunt, qui sui commodi causa fovent peccata.

Μετασχηματίζονται ὡς διάκονοι δικαιοσύνης) Id est, Evan- gelii, quæ causa veræ apud Deum justitiæ. Vide Rom. I. 17. III. 22.

Theodoretus ita παραφράζει: Mos est Diabolo, divina imitari, & adversus Prophetas Pseudo- prophetas producere. Angelorum autem figuram imitari, & homines decipere. Non est ergo mi- rum, si isti etiam Apostolicæ appellationis personas induerint, & doli auxilio ad homines decipiendos usi sint. Habebunt autem propediem studiorum suorum fructus. Angeli lucis dicuntur Angeli boni, quod luceant sapientia, justitia, atque luce cœlestis beatitudinis fruantur: non vero a luce externa, qua fulgent; quum ex adverso Diaboli fumei, picei & squalidi sint: Siquidem μετασχηματισμὸς Satanæ talis sit, ut lucidus & ipse appareat, quemadmodum Saulo in forma uti- que non picea, vel squalida apparuit, cum Samue- lem mentiretur 1. Sam. XXVIII. neque natura Dia- bolorum, quæ spiritualis per se id inferat, ut atri & fumidi sint. Respici autem juxta nonnullos videtur Evæ historia ut supra vers. 3. quia vere tunc se transfiguravit in Angelum lucis, quan- do blanditiis verborum animum Evæ dimovebat a simplicitate verbi divini, sub schemate sancti- tatis & veritatis, majorem in sapientia & sancti- tate divina profectum mendaciter pollicitus. Ad ejus exemplum ergo ministri ejus speciem veritatis & sanctitatis etiam præ se ferunt, sed mera larva & μετασχηματισμός tantum est. Trans- figuratur, inquit Theophylactus, in hujusmodi Angelum Diabolus ipse, non tamen talis efficitur: Sic igitur & hi figuram duntaxat præ se ferunt Apostolorum, non vim eandem & actionem, quæ ex re perdiscere possumus, quodcunque ad ostenta- tionem & jactantiam geritur, id præcipue dæmo- niacum esse. Cæterum, monente B. Hülsemanno non solum antecedens periphrasis Pseudo-Aposto- lorum potissimum consistens in gestibus & verbis, vers. 3. 4. 20. 21. seqq. & supra cap. II. 17. cap. IV. 2. 3. sed ex ipso verbo μετασχηματίζει ejusque regulari significatione supra prioris epistolæ cap. IV. 6. patet transfigurationem loqui non de substantiali immu- tatione vel etiam Accidentium seu qualitatum visi- bilium, qualis est habitus corporis forma Angelicæ assumptio & similibus loqui, quæ dicuntur Meta- morphosis Matth. XVII. 2. Marc. IX. 2. Quanquam & hoc verbum de solorum qualitatum internarum alteratione usurpetur Rom. XII. 2. 2. Cor. III. 18. de mutatione in statu gratiæ. Et rursus μετασχημα- τίζει de mutatione etiam externarum qualitatum corporis mortalis in immortale ad Phil. III. 21. ut plane inepta sit Salmeronis, Cornelii, aliorumque Latinorum sententia: quomodo dæmon ipse nonnun- quam formas Angelicas, humanas, beluinas assumit; ita Pseudo-Apostolos & hæreticos tempore Pauli & nostri transmutari quoad externum corporis habitum in ejusmodi formas, quod impurus Cacodæmon Gret- serus in Luthero Academico criminatur: Justinia- nus, Estius, Rob. Gagnaus Anglus fatentur, hic de invisibili μετασχηματισμῷ affectuum sermonem esse, nec sequi: quot modis se potest & solet Satan ipse transformare, tot etiam posse & solitos fuisse quoscunque hæreticos.

Ministri autem justitiæ dicuntur, non ut Beza vult, quasi ministri probi & integri, ut epitheton justitiæ ex Ebræorum idiotismo addatur, sed quod videri velint veram justitiam prædicare, quem- admodum Apostolorum ministerium ἡ διακονία τῆς δικαιοσύνης ex vero dicitur 2, Cor. III. 9. Ita Chrysostomus: Quod est ministerium justitiæ? Id videlicet, quod sumus Evangelium, quod habet justitiam, vobis prædicantes. Et Theophylactus: Hoc est, tanquam ministri Evangelii justitiam continentis. Cur autem relicta vocis justitiæ pro- prietate Metonymice eam pro Evangelio accipia- mus, causa nulla est.

ὧν τὸ τέλος ἔσται κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) Id est, quæ nunc clam faciunt aperta fient, & summam illis infamiam patient. Vide 2. Tim. II. 16. ubi de iisdem agitur homini- bus.

Non infamia tantum in mundo, sed perditio æ- terna talium finis est, quem detestanda hypocrisi, & impiis studiis atque factis suis omnino meren- tur Matth. VII. Apoc. XXI. 8.

PARS III.

Comparatio Apostoli & Pseudo-Apostolorum quoad externa ministerii.

## 11:16
Vers. 16. πάλιν λέγω) I repeat several times how I lived among you.

μή τίς με δόξῃ ἄφρονα εἶναι) Lest anyone think that what I have said has escaped from me imprudently.

εἰ δὲ μήγε) If you do not wish to believe that all these things are said by me prudently.

κἂν ὡς ἄφρονα δέξασθέ με, ἵνα κἀγὼ μικρόν τι καυχήσωμαι) δέξασθε means bear, tolerate. קַבֵּל is both δέχεσθαι and ἀνέχειν. Bear with me speaking a little more joyfully about my own affairs, even if you might think this to be impudence. For all self-praise has the appearance of folly, yet it is not always folly, as can be learned from the book which Plutarch wrote on that subject and with that title.

Latin:

Vers. 16. πάλιν λέγω) Aliquoties repeto quomodo inter vos vixerim.

μή τίς με δόξῃ ἄφρονα εἶναι) Ne quis putet mihi impru- denti excidisse quæ dixi.

εἰ δὲ μήγε) Si non vultis credere hæc omnia prudenter a me dici.

κἂν ὡς ἄφρονα δέξασθέ με, ἵνα κἀγὼ μικρόν τι καυχήσωμαι) δέξασθε ferte, tolerate. קַבֵּל est & δέχεσθαι & ἀνέχειν. Fer- te me paulo lætius loqui de rebus meis, etiamsi vos hoc pu- taretis esse impudentiæ. Nam περιαυτολογία omnis spe- ciem habet ἀφροσύνης, non tamen semper est ἀφροσύνη, ut disci potest ex libro quem de ea re eoque titulo fecit Plu- tarchus.

## 11:17
Vers. 17. ὃ λαλῶ, ὐ λαλῶ κατὰ κύριον) I am not here speaking by the command of God or Christ, but according to my own inclination. See 1 Cor. VII. 25.

᾿Αλλ᾿ ὡς ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ) Note the ὡς, for this boasting of his is not in itself folly, but to those not well weighing the circumstances, it can present the appearance of that thing.

ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως) In this firmament of my boasting. See above IX. 5, as things said there.

After he stripped the mask from the false apostles, who rashly exalted themselves above Paul in many ways, he taught that they were not apostles of Christ but ministers of Satan, as far as the internal aspects of their ministry were concerned, whatever they might pretend, having assumed through μετασχηματισμὸν the appearance of ministers of righteousness and apostles of Christ. Now, however, he compares himself with them regarding the external aspects of ministry and those things that pertained to the flesh, since they boasted of these things most of all in the Corinthian Church. He anticipates the matter regarding himself, lest they think that he is a fool when he praises himself, or if they wish to ascribe entirely to foolishness that which he is compelled to praise, lest they think that he speaks these things according to the Lord, but as if in foolishness; not that he denies these things were divinely inspired, but that ὑποθετικῶς Paul does not speak these things according to God, but as if through foolishness in this argument of boasting; although in reality it was nothing but from the Lord and tended toward His glory, which he was speaking, as R. Glassius explains: or because it is not commanded by the Lord by some common law, but he is compelled to that quasi-foolishness by necessity, even though he brings forth nothing at all from the internal prompting of the Spirit even in this argument of boasting. It is the law of the Lord, says Theodoret, which teaches: when you have done all these things, say, we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done. For that reason the divine Apostle said that what I speak, I do not speak according to the Lord, for that which is: I speak these things beyond His law. Chrysostom speaks of this at greater length: For it is a foolish thing, he says, to boast: but I do not do this as a fool, but as one compelled. But if you do not allow yourselves to be persuaded of this; even though you see that I do this of necessity, nonetheless you condemn me, not even then will I refuse to do this. Do you see how he shows what a great necessity of speaking was imposed upon him? For you should consider with yourself how great a force he was enduring to speak, and how he was as it were laboring to bring forth and pour out such speech, even though he did not shrink from even this suspicion. But even so, he used moderation in this matter. For he did not say, 'that I may boast'. And when he was about to boast a little, he used another softening beforehand, saying: That which I speak, I speak according to man, but as in foolishness in this substance of glory. Do you see how it is not boasting according to God? For when you have done all things, he says, say that we are unprofitable servants. Chrysostom adds another explanation of his κατὰ κύριον λαλῶ, but perhaps a more subtle than convenient one: Truly this is not in itself according to God, but it is made such by the mind and will. And for that reason he said, 'that which I speak': criticizing not the cause, but the words. For the scope was so excellent that it brought ornament even to the words. For just as a murderer, even though a crime of this kind is strictly forbidden, has often attained praise from his mind and will: and even if to be circumcised is not according to the Lord, yet it is made such by the intention of the mind: so also is boasting. He also provides a third explanation later, what it is not to be according to the Lord, which does not seem inappropriate here. What is it, he says, according to the flesh? This is from external things, from nobility, from wealth, from learning, from circumcision, from Hebrew ancestors, from that reputation in which they flourish among most people. And observe the sagacity. He sets forth those things which he shows to be nothing: and then finally foolishness. For if it is folly to boast because of things that are truly good, it is certainly much more so because of things that are of no value. And that is what he calls 'not according to the Lord.' For it is of no profit to be a Hebrew and other things of that kind. Therefore, do not think that I put this in the place of virtue. But since they boast, I am compelled to draw a comparison from this. Which he also does elsewhere, saying: If anyone seems to trust in the flesh, I more, Phil. III. Cf. here Keller, lib. II. Miscell. chap. 9, p. 98 et seq., whom Gisbertus Voëtius praises in T. I. disput. select. p. 45 against the statement of some Reformed Theologian concerning the supreme prudence used by the Apostles somewhere.

However, this boasting did not proceed from carnal ambition, as worldly people are accustomed to boast of wisdom, power, and wealth, Jerem. IX. 23, since on the contrary the Apostle voluntarily professes himself to be foolish, weak, and poor below in chap. XII. 6, but from spiritual zeal for the glory of Christ to glorify the Gospel concerning Christ, and his own office which he had from Christ and performed in the place of Christ directly, and it ends in the praise of Christ, chap. XII. 10, chap. X. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ὃ λαλῶ, ὐ λαλῶ κατὰ κύριον) Non hic jam lo- quor ex Dei aut Christi mandato, sed pro affectu meo. Vide 1. Cor. VII. 25.

᾿Αλλ᾿ ὡς ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ) Nota ὡς, non enim hæc de se præ- dicatio in se est, ἀφροσύνη, sed circumstantias non bene ex- pendentibus speciem ejus rei potest præbere.

ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως) In hoc firmamento gaudii mei. Vide supra IX. 5. ut ibi dicta.

Postquam larvam detraxit Pseudo-Apostolis, temere sese præ Paulo efferentibus, multis mo- dis, eosque non Christi Apostolos, sed Satanæ ministros esse docuit, quantum ad interna mini- sterii ipsorum quicquid præ se ferant, assumpta per μετασχηματισμὸν ministrorum justitiæ & A- postolorum Christi specie. Jam autem se cum iis- dem, quantum ad externa ministerii, & quæ ad carnem pertinebant, confert, cum maxime de illis gloriarentur in Ecclesia Corinthiaca. Præoccupat autem de eo, ne censeant, ipsum insipientem esse, cum se laudat, aut si id, quod laudare se cogitur, omnino velint insipientiæ adscribere, ne hæc secundum Dominum se loqui existiment, sed velut in insipientia; non quod neget hæc divinitus inspirata; sed quod ὑποθε- τικῶς hæc dicta Paulum non loqui secundum Deum, sed velut per insipientiam in hoc argu- mento gloriationis; cum tamen reipsa non nisi a Domino erat, & in ejus gloriam tendebat, quod loquebatur, ut explicat R. Glassius: vel quod communi quadam lege a Domino id præ- ceptum non sit, sed ad eam quasi insipientiam necessitate compellatur, etsi nihil quicquam ab interno Spiritus dictamine etiam in hoc gloria- tionis argumento proferat. Lex est Domini, in- quit Theodoretus, quæ docet, quando hæc omnia fe- ceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus, quod debuimus facere fecimus. Ea de causa dixit divinus Apo- stolus, quod loquor non loquor secundum Domi- num pro eo quod est; præter ejus legem hæc loquor. Prolixius hæc loquitur Chrysostomus: Stulta enim res est, inquit, gloriari: Ego vero hoc non ut sto- lidus facio, sed ut coactus. Quod si vobis id non persuaderi sinitis; verum quamvis id me necessa- rio facere videatis, nihilo minus tamen me conde- mnetis, ne sic quidem tamen hoc facere detrectabo. Videsne quo pacto magnam sibi loquendi necessita- tem impositam esse ostendit? Nam qui ne hanc qui- dem suspicionem reformidabat, quantam vim ad loquendum sustineret: quamque hujusmodi sermo- nem veluti parturiret, ac profundere cogeretur, te- cum velim consideres. At sic quoque tamen mode- rationem hac in re adhibuit. Non enim dixit ut glorier. Quumque paulum gloriaturus esset rur- sus etiam altera pramollitione usus est dicens: Quod loquor secundum hominem loquor, sed ut in insi- pientia in hac substantia gloriæ. Vides quemad- modum gloriari secundum Deum non sit? Quum enim omnia feceritis, inquit, dicite, quia servi in- utiles sumus. Addit Chrysostomus aliam illius & κατὰ κύριον λαλῶ explicationem, sed subtiliorem forte quam commodiorem: Verum hoc per se qui- dem secundum Deum non est, sed ab animo ac vo- luntate tale efficitur. Ob eamque causam dixit, quod loquor: non causam, sed verba reprehendens.. Etenim scopus adeo eximius erat, ut & verbis or- namentum afferret. Quemadmodum enim homi- cida, tametsi facinus hujusmodi valde interdictum sit, tamen ab animo & voluntate sæpe laudem est assecuutus: Et circumcidi licet secundum Dominum non sit, tamen ab animi instituto tale efficitur: sic etiam gloriari. Tertiam etiam explicationem postea tradit, quid sit non secundum Dominum, quæ videtur hic non inconveniens. Quid est au- tem, inquit, secundum carnem? hoc est ab exter- nis rebus, a nobilitate, ab opibus, ab eruditione, a circumcisione, ab Hebræis avis, ab ea, qua apud plerosque florent, existimatione. Ac vide sagaci- tatem. Illa ponit, qua nihil esse ostendit: ac tum denique insipientiam. Etenim si ob ea, qua vere bona sunt, gloriari stultitia est, multo certe magis ob ea, quæ nullius pretii sunt. Atque id est, quod non secundum Dominum vocat. Neque enim quid- quam prodest, Hebræum esse aliaque id genus. Non ergo existimetis me hoc virtutis loco ponere. Sed quoniam illi gloriantur, hinc ego comparationem ducere cogor. Quod etiam alibi facit, dicens: Si quis in carne confidere videtur, ego amplius, Phil. III. Conf. hic Kellerus lib. II. Miscell. cap. 9. p. 98. seqq. quem laudat adversus dictum Theologi ali- cujus Reformati de prudentia summa ab Aposto- lis alicubi adhibita Gisbertus Voëtius T. I. disput. se- lect. p. 45.

Gloriatio autem hæc non ex Φιλοτιμίᾳ carna- li profecta, uti solent mundani de sapientia, po- tentia & opulentia gloriari Jerem. IX. 23. quum contra Apostolus stultum se & infirmum atque pauperem ultro profiteatur infra cap. XII. 6. sed ex zelo spirituali pro gloria Christi ad glorifi- candum Evangelium de Christo, suumque offi- cium quod habebat a Christo, & gerebat vice Christi directa, inque laudem Christi desinit cap. XII. 10. cap. X. 17.

## 11:18
Verse 18. (Since many boast according to the flesh) Because many please themselves more in external than in internal things. See above V. 16.

- and I will boast) I also have that in which I may rejoice in those things that fall under sight, if they are held of such value.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἐπεὶ πολλοὶ καυχῶνται κατὰ τὴν σάρκα) Quia multi sibi placent magis in externis, quam in internis rebus. Vide supra V. 16.

- κἀγὼ καυχήσομαι) Habeo & ego de quo gaudeam in rebus illis in aspectum cadentibus, si ea tanti haben- tur.

## 11:19
Verse 19. (For you gladly bear with fools) You are accustomed to tolerate boasters.

being wise) As indeed you seem to yourselves. For it is a concession.

The paraphrase of Theophylact is this: This glory of mine shall be from external things, namely from nobility of birth, from circumcision, and because I have obtained Hebrews as my progenitors. For that was what by no means he had said that he was speaking according to God, namely, to boast of such things. For what does it profit for someone to be descended from the Hebrews? Therefore, I would not consider that a place of virtue, but since they, he says, consider that a glory, I am compelled myself to make myself not unequal to them in these very things. For you gladly suffer fools, since you are wise. You, he says, compel me to say such things. For if you had not excepted them, and I had not foreseen that this would also be to your detriment, I would by no means have descended to these things myself. But he calls those fools who boast in carnal things. For if it is the mark of a madman to attribute spiritual things to himself for glory, how much more will it seem senseless to boast of things which are of no moment at all? That phrase, however, "since you are wise," although it seems said in thanks, nevertheless urges them more sharply and accuses them, as those who were sinning knowingly. For if they had been seized by the disease of madness, they might perhaps have deserved pardon.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἡδέως γὰρ ἀνέχεσθε τῶν ἀφρόνων) Ferre soletis ja- ctabundos.

φρόνιμοι ὄντες) Ut quidem vobis videmini. Est enim συγχώρησις.

Paraphrasis Theophylacti hæc est: Abonis ex- ternis erit mea hæc gloria, videlicet a generis nobi- litate, a circumcisione, & quia Hebræos sim pro- genitores sortitus. Id namque erat quod nequaquam secundum Deum loqui se dixerat, de istiusmodi vide- licet gloriari. Quid enim prodest, ab Hebraeis ali- quem esse oriundum? Non ergo virtutis loco id du- xerim, sed cum illi, inquit, id gloria ducant, cogor & ipse me eis vel hisce ex rebus non imparem facere. Li- benter enim suffertis insipientes, cum sitis sapientes. Vos, inquit, me cogitis hujusmodi dicere. Nam si non illos excepissetis, idque & vobis obfuturum non antea praevidiffem, nequaquam & ipse ad haec de- scendissem. Insipientes autem dicit, qui rebus car- nalibus gloriantur. Nam si dementis est, spiritualia sibi in gloriam accensere, quanto magis, qua nullius sunt prorsus momenti, jactare insulsum videbitur? Illud autem, cum sitis sapientes, etsi ad gratiam di- ctum videtur, urget tamen hos acrius & criminatur, ut qui scientes delinquerent. Nam si fuissent demen- tia morbo correpti, veniam forsitan promeruissent.

## 11:20
Ver. 20. For you suffer, if anyone enslaves you) As there were those who wished to subject the Corinthians to food and legal days.

You perversely tolerate those impostors who, by their perverse doctrine, mix the law with the Gospel and drive you under the servitude of the law, nay, under the halter of their own traditions. But you barely tolerate me for a moment, by whose ministry, through the sincere preaching of the Gospel, you were delivered from the yoke of servitude into liberty, as the blessed Hunnius conveniently puts it.

if anyone devours) Interpret from Matt. XIII. 14. if anyone takes) secretly, namely, as we just said.

Here again the blessed Hunnius rightly observes a silent antithesis: You very easily suffer that they devour you, and under the pretext of ministry strip you of your resources, and take them away from you. But me, who evangelized you without the intervention of any stipend, you can barely suffer.

If anyone exalts himself. This is the third antithesis, passed over by Grotius, by which he reproves the pride of the Pseudo-Apostles and the excessive leniency of the Corinthians in bearing it, as if he were saying: Those are approved by you who exalt themselves in their most honest boastings: it was therefore fair to approve my conversation conducted among you, which was devoid of all arrogance.

if anyone strikes you on the face) That is, holds you in mockery. A species for the genus. For to strike the face is among the greatest mockeries, Luke XXII. 64. Matt. V. 34. 1 Kings XXII. 24.

The fourth antithesis attacks the tyranny of the false teachers, because, affecting dominion over the Church of the Corinthians, they command arrogantly. Therefore Paul wishes to say, you sustain this insolence of theirs and manifest insults of words, I would almost say of blows, with equanimity, no differently than if you were their slaves.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ἀνέχεσθε γὰρ, εἴ τις ὑμᾶς καταδουλοῖ) Ut erant qui Corinthios volebant victui & diebus legalibus subjice- re.

Vos praepostere toleratis impostores illos, qui sua perversa doctrina legem cum Evangelio miscent, & sub servitutem legis, imo sub capistrum suarum tra- ditionum vos adigunt. At me vix parumper tole- ratis, cujus ministerio per sinceram Evangelii predi- cationem a jugo servitutis in libertatem estis vindi- cati, ut commode B. Hunnius.

εἴ τις κατεσθίει) Interpretare ex Matth. XIII. 14. εἴ τις λαμβάνει) clam scilicet, ut modo diximus.

Hic iterum tacitam antithesin recte observat B. Hunnius: Vos perfacile suffertis, quod illi vos exe- dunt, & sub praetextu ministerii vos facultatibus vestris exuunt, easque a vobis auferunt. Me autem, qui nullius stipendii interventu vobis Evangelizavi gratis, aegre sufferre potestis.

Εἴ τις ἐπαίρεται. Tertia haec antithesis est, praetermissa Grotio, qua fastum Pseudo-Apostolorum & in eo ferendo ni- miam lenitatem Corinthiorum reprehendit, quasi dicat: Illi vobis probantur, qui sese efferunt in ho- nestissimis suis gloriationibus: aequum igitur erat ap- probare meam inter vos actam conversationem omnis arrogantiae expertem.

εἰ τις ὑμᾶς εἰς πρόσωπον δέιρει) Id est, ludibrio habet. Species pro genere. Nam faciem verberare inter maxima lu- dibria est, Luc. XXII. 64. Matt. V. 34. 1. Reg. XXII. 24.

Quarta ἀντιθέσεις tyrannidem falsorum docto- rum carpit, quod dominatum affectantes in Ec- clesiam Corinthiorum arroganter imperant. Idcir- co vult dicere Paulus, hanc illorum insolentiam & manifestas contumelias verborum, pene dicam ver- berum, aequanimiter sustinetis, haud aliter, ac illo- rum sitis mancipia.

## 11:21
V. 21. I speak according to dishonor, as that we were weak) The sense is, if it is a matter of ignominies, we have endured the greatest of them. "According to" here means "concerning" or "as regards": "to be weak" is to be afflicted, as "the weak" are the afflicted, 1 Cor. IV. 10. "weakness" is misery, distress, 1 Cor. II. 3. Rom. VIII. 26. below 30. "as" here is redundant, as it often is.

The sense of Grotius does not deserve approval, and Grotius rashly neglects the distinction in the original text. For there the sentence is completed: I speak according to dishonor. Which the Greek interpreters rightly observed; Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Theodoret: I said these things because of the ignominy which is brought upon you by them. The blessed Hunnius: It is certainly not very honorable for you, both because they treat you so unworthily, and because you suffer that tyrannical dominion from them, and meanwhile, while you are powerful to the point of prodigy in that, you can barely and with difficulty suffer me, who am accustomed to embrace and treat you so fatherly. But the rest, "as that we were weak," which Chrysostom says is obscure, he himself and Theophylact with Theodoret explain in this sense: You think that we

do nothing of the sort because of weakness. Can we not also do these things? And yet we do not. For what reason do you suffer them? As if we were unable to do these things? And that also deserves reproof, that you suffer them even while they behave foolishly. But that you even suffer those who so greatly despise you, plunder you, exalt themselves, and strike you, that indeed can have no excuse, no reason. For this is a new kind of imposture. For whereas others who practice imposture are accustomed to give and to flatter, these on the contrary deceive and take, and inflict insult. Therefore, there can be not even a shadow of any excuse for you, seeing that you despise and count as nothing those who, for your sake, humble themselves so that you may be lifted up, and on the contrary, you look up to those who exalt themselves so that you may be brought low. For what? Could we not also do the same? Or did we not wish to? As those who have your utility proposed to us. For they indeed seek your fortunes: but we seek your advantages. The blessed Hunnius provides another sense, by which an approach is prepared for what follows: You so magnify the Pseudo-Apostles, as if they alone were powerful and strong in propagating the Gospel, and we, in turn, compared to them, were weak, who have accomplished nothing or little. So that you may see how they are preferred to me and my associates beyond their merit, I openly confirm to you that in whatever they dare to boast, I also dare to boast no less in that. And although someone might think this is perhaps said by me out of foolishness, nevertheless it is not feigned but true, which I assert in this part. Which is also the explanation of Estius. Most simply, with B. Luther as a guide, you should explain the meaning: I say that this yields to the ignominy of the Church, as if we believers were so weak, destitute of the virtue of the Spirit and of faith, that we are compelled to endure all such things, and there is not in us that strength and ability, because we are able to confound and prostrate those who inflict them with prayers and whatever spiritual weapons.

(In whatever any one dares, I speak in foolishness, I also dare) here to dare signifies to speak more boldly, as in Phil. 1:14, Jude 4. In foolishness here again signifies as in foolishness. That is easily understood from the preceding.

Latin:

V. 21. Κατὰ ἀτιμίαν λέγω, ὡς ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἠσθενήσαμεν) Sensus est, si de ignominiis agitur, nos eas pertulimus maximas. Κατὰ hic valet de: aut quod attinet: ἀσθενεῖν est adfligi ut ἀσθενεῖς afflicti, 1. Cor. IV. 10. ἀσθένεια miseria, aerumna, 1. Cor.II. 3. Rom. VIII. 26. infra 30. ὡς hic abundat ut saepe.

Sensus Grotii non meretur calculum, & teme- re negligit Grotius distinctionem in textu origi- nali. Ibi enim absolvitur sententia: Κατὰ ἀτι- μίαν λέγω. Quod probe Graeci Interpp. observa- runt; Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Theodoretus: Propter eam, quae vobis ab illis infertur, ignomi- niam haec dixi. B. Hunnius: Est certe parum vo- bis honorificum, tum quod vos illi tam indigne tra- ctant, tum quod ab eis tyrannicum illum dominatum suffertis atque interim dum in illo estis ad prodigium usque potentes, vix aegre me potestis sustinere, qui vos adeo paterne complecti & tractare soleo. Caete- ra vero ὡς ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἠσθενήσαμεν, quae obscura esse dicit Chrysostomus in hanc sententiam ipse & Theo- phylactus cum Theodoreto: Vos nos existimatis

| nihil tale facere propter infirmitatem. Annon ipfi quoque hec facere possumus? Et tamen non fa- cimus. Quam ob causam eos suffertis. Antanquam nos hac efficere nequeamus? Atque illud quoque re- prehensionem meretur, quod & stulte se gerentes suffertis. Quod autem etiam usque adeo vos asper- nantes, diripientes, sese extollentes, vos cedentes, id vero nullam excusationem, nullam rationem habere queat. Novum enim est hoc imposturæ genus. Nam quum alii, qui imposturam faciunt largiri atque as- sentari soleant, isti contra fallunt & accipiunt, con- tumeliamque inferunt. Itaq; ne umbra quidem ullæ veniæ vobis esse possit, quippe qui eos, qui vestri causâ, ut vos subvebamini, sese deprimunt, contemnitis & pro nihilo putatis, ac contra eos, qui ut vos deprima- mini, sese efferunt, suspicitis, Quid enim? Num nos quoque idem facere non poteramus? An nolu- mus: Ut qui utilitatem vestram nobis propositam habeamus. Nam illi quidem fortunas vestras quæ- runt: nos vero commoda vestra quærimus. Alium sensum, quo paretur ad sequentia aditus, reddit B. Hunnius: Vos ita magnificitis Pseudo-Aposto- los, ac si ipsi soli fuerint in Evangelio propagando po- tentes & validi, nos vicissim ad illos comparati infir- mi fuerimus, qui nihil aut parum præstiterimus. Ut ergo videatis, quam illi præter meritum mihi & sociis anteponantur, palam vobis confirmo, in quocunque audent isti gloriari, audere & me posse non minus in illo gloriari. Et licet hoc forte per insipientiam dici a me quis existimet, tamen non fictum sed verum est, quod hac in parte assevero. Quæ etiam Estii est explicatio. Simplicissime, prælucente B. Lu- thero, sensum exponas: Ignominiæ hæc cedere Ecclesiæ dico, quasi nos fideles adeo infirmi si- mus, virtutis Spiritus & fidei inopes, ut talia o- mnia sustinere cogamur, nec sit in nobis ea vis & facultas, quia inferentes confundere & pro- sternere valemus precibus armisque quibusvis spiritualibus.

ἐν ᾧ δ' ἂν τις τολμᾷ, ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ λέγω, τολμῶ κἀγὼ) τολ- μᾷν hic valet παῤῥησιάζεσθαι, loqui audentius, ut Phil. I.14. Judæ 4. ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ hic rursum valet ὡς ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ. Facile id intelligitur ex superioribus.

## 11:22
Verse 22. Are they Hebrews? So am I. That is, sprung from Abraham. For Abraham was called עִבְרִי, because he had come from places across the Euphrates, as we said at Gen. 11. These former members are to be read with an interrogation.

The Apostle boasts, however, of his lineage, of his office, of his labors and sorrows in his office, both of mind and of body. That was no small prerogative both in the Old Testament and at the beginning of the New, Rom. 9:4-5. But because they arrogantly exalted themselves by that name, while slothfully despising the doctrine and righteousness of Christ, this vanity was indeed an abomination before God, Rom. 2:25 ff. If, however, one must boast in these things, that origin was not lacking to Paul either. Cf. Phil. 3:4; yet he himself held those things as loss and dung for the sake of Christ, v. 7-8.

Latin:

Vers. 22. 'Εβραῖοί εἰσι; κἀγὼ) Id est, ab Abrahamo orti. Nam Abraham dictus עִבְרִי, quod venisset ex locis trans Euphratem, ut diximus ad Gen. XI. Legenda hæc priora membra cum interrogatione.

Gloriatur autem Apostolus de prosapia, de offi- cio, de laboribus & doloribus in officio tum animi, tum corporis. Non exigua illa erat prærogativa & in Vet. Testam. & sub initium Novi Rom. IX. 4. 5. Sed quia se isto nomine arroganter effere- bant, supine vero doctrinam & justitiam Christi spernebant, vanitas hæc imo βδέλυγμα erat co- ram Deo Rom. II. 25. seqq. Si tamen in his glorian- dum sit, nec Paulo deerat illa origo. Conf. Phil. III. 4. ipse tamen illa pro damno & stercore habebat propter Christum v. 7. 8.

## 11:23
Verse 23. Are they Israelites? So am I. If they please themselves more on account of Jacob, the author of their blood: I also am from him. These things were said against those teachers who had come from Judea.

Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as a madman, I more. For the word 'himself' is missing. And 'as a madman' for 'as one who is a madman'.

From Musculus, B. Glassius has it thus here: The Apostle claims for himself an excellence not of dignity and prelacy, but of ministry, and proposes the argument for it in the multitude of labors and dangers. For this is the lot of the Gospel preached seriously and faithfully in this world, that it renders the minister of Christ liable to every kind of labor, affliction, and danger, so that the more zealously one preaches Christ everywhere, the more and more grievous is involved in dangers, and by this argument is proven excellent in the ministry of Christ. Blessed Hunnius rightly warns that these things are said about the ministers by way of concession from an abundance, if one should grant them even this, that they are true servants of the Lord Jesus (which, however, one could by no means grant), there is and remains nonetheless a clear distinction between himself and them by reason of the labors performed, by reason of the afflictions which had to be devoured for the sake of the Gospel, and indeed even with respect to heavenly revelations.

In labors more abundantly) He now resumes and explains point by point that which he had said. We were weakened. Concerning the word κόπων see above VI. 5.

What was said above is not resumed here: But the labors of the office, about which verse 21, are designated, which were indeed most grievous, both by reason of the end, which is the snatching of men from perdition; and by reason of the opposite, spiritual enemies 2. Corinth. VII. 5. 2. Tim. II. 5. and by reason of the manner Coloss. cap. I. v. 28.

In stripes more exceedingly) See above VI. 5.

In prisons more abundantly) See in the same place.

In deaths often) That is, in dangers of death, above I. 9. 10. IV. 11. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 30.

After labors he passes to pains and calamities, such as stripes, prisons, and dangers of death. Concerning stripes he records how he received from the Jews forty stripes save one, and was beaten with rods three times: But he reports the dangers of death brought upon him by the Gentiles (including the commemoration of the prisons in which he was enclosed when he was struck or beaten with rods) which he sustained when he was stoned, when he suffered shipwreck, when he spent time in the deep, and otherwise on his journeys.

Latin:

Vers. 23. 'Ισραηλῖταί εἰσι; κἀγὼ) Si ob Jacobum sangui- nis autorem magis sibi placent: & ego ex eo sum. Hæc dicta adversus illos magistros, qui ex Judæa venerant.

διάκονοι χριστῦ εἰσι; παραφρονῶν λαλῶ, ὑπὲρ ἐγώ) Plus- quam illi: Deest enim ἀυτὸς. Et παραφρονῶν pro ὡς παρα- φρονῶν.

E Musculo B. Glassius hic ita habet: Excellen- tiam non dignitatis ac prælaturæ sed ministerii vin- dicat sibi Apostolus, illiusque argumentum pro- ponit in multitudine laborum ac periculorum. Est enim hæc sors Evangelii serio & fideliter prædica- ti in hoc mundo, ut obnoxium reddat Christi ministrum omnis generis laboribus, afflictionibus & periculis, ut quo quis majore zelo Christum ubique prædicat, hoc pluribus & gravioribus periculis involvatur, & hoc argumento excellens in Christi ministerio comprobetur. Recte autem B. Hunnius monet, ex abundanti hæc de ministris per concessionem dici, si maxime hoc eis largiatur, quod veri sint servi Domini Jesu (quod tamen haud quaquam largiri queat) nihilo minus esse & manere luculentum discrimen inter se & illos ratione præstitorum laborum, ratione afflictionum, quæ causa Evangelii devoranda erant, quin & cœlestium revelationum respectu.

Ἐν κόποις περισσοτέρως) Resumit jam & membratim explicat id quod dixerat. Ἠσθενήσαμεν. De voce κόπων vide supra VI. 5.

Non hic resumuntur, quæ supra dicta: Sed labores officii de quibus vers. 21. nihil, designantur, qui utique gravissimi erant tum ratione finis, qui est hominum e perditione ereptio; tum ratione oppositi, hostium spiritualium 2. Corinth. VII. 5. 2. Tim. II. 5. tum ratione modi Coloss. cap. I. v. 28.

Ἐν πληγαῖς ὑπερβαλλόντως) Vide supra VI. 5.

Ἐν φυλακαῖς περισσοτέρως) Vide ibidem.

Ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις) Id est, in mortis periculis, supra I. 9. 10. IV. 11. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 30.

Post labores ad dolores, & calamitates transit, ut sunt plagæ, carceres, & mortis pericula. De plagis commemorat, quomodo a Judæis, quinquies quadragenas una minus acceperit, & ter virgis cæsus fuerit: A gentilibus vero illata pericula mortis refert (inclusa carcerum commemoratione quibus inclusus fuit, cum percussus aut virgis cæsus) quæ cum lapidaretur, cum naufragium faceret, cum in profundo ageret, atque alias in itineribus sustinuerit.

## 11:24
Verse 24. by the Jews five times forty save one I received) Stripes is understood. A similar brevity of speech in Luke XII. v. 47. The law permitted forty stripes to be inflicted, it did not command it, Deut. XXV. v. 3. See the precept commanding CV. and forbidding CXCIX. The wise men established it short of that number. Thus before and after the Sabbath they added an hour; these are what are called fences, the safeguards of the law, to do a little less in odious matters, and a little more in favorable ones, than the law commands. Nor does this conflict with the interdict which is in Deut. cap. IV. vers. 2. For to add to the law is to do what the law forbids. To diminish is to omit what the law commands. Neither of these is done in this and similar traditions. The Jews, by the permission of the Romans in Judea and certain neighboring places, had the right to punish their own people even to the point of stripes.

That false interpretation of the Mosaic passage Deut. IV. v. 2, by which Grotius gratified the Papists in his Annotations on Deuteronomy, has now been refuted. It was not, however, out of mercy that the Jews ordained 40 stripes save one, so that they might stop short of the number designated in Deut. XXV. v. 3, even though that seemed to be the case to Lyranus also, the author of the ordinary gloss, and to Erasmus in his annotations; but Schickard notes in his Royal Law that this was done because of the triplicity of the number, so that he would receive two on the back while receiving one on the chest. And Buxtorf in his Hebrew Abbreviations observes in the preface from the Mishnah that the thong with which he was beaten was of ox-hide and oblong, so that it would almost encircle the belly. And on both sides of the ox-hide thong was added a smaller ass-hide thong, but both were bifid, so that the individual strokes were triple, and therefore only 13 stripes were inflicted, which three times thirteen are thirty-nine.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων πεντάκις τεσσαράκοντα παρὰ μίαν ἔλαβον) Subauditur πληγάς. Similis breviloquentia Luc. XII. v. 47. quadraginta verbera infligi ferebat lex, non jubebat, Deut. XXV. v. 3. Vide præceptum jubens CV. & vetans CXCIX. sapientes citra eum numerum constitutuere. Sic ante & post Sabbatum addidere horam, hæc sunt quæ vocant sepimenta, προβυλακὰς legis, in odiosis minus, in favorabilibus paulo plus facere quam lex imperat. Neque hoc pugnat cum interdicto quod est Deut. cap. IV. vers. 2. Nam addere ad legem est facere quod lex vetat. Diminuere est omittere quod lex jubet. Horum neutrum fit in ista & similibus traditionibus. Judæi Romanorum permissu in Judæa & quibusdam locis vicinis jus in suos animadvertendi ad verbera usque habebant.

Ψευδερμηνεία illa loci Mosaici Deut. IV. v. 2. qua Papistis gratificatus est Grotius in Annot. ad Deuter. jam profligata est. Non autem ex misericordia Judæos 40. plagas minus una ordinasse, ut nempe citra numerum Deut. XXV. v. 3. designatum subsisteret, etsi id Lyrano etiam, autori glossæ ordinariæ, & Erasmo in annotatis visum fuerit; sed ob triplicitatem numeri hoc factum esse notat Schickardus in jure Regio, ut scilicet in tergo binos acciperet, dum in pectore singulos. Et Buxtorfius in abbreviatur. Hebr. in præfatione observat ex Mischnah, lorum quo cædebatur, fuisse bubulum & oblongum, ut ventrem pene circumiret. Utrinque autem loro bubulo additum fuisse lorum minus asininum, sed bifidum utrumque, ita, ut singuli ictus triplices essent, & proinde inflictas tantum esse XIII. plagas, qui ter tredecim sunt triginta novem.

## 11:25
Once I was stoned) Acts cap. XIV. vers. 18. Namely through the sedition of the multitude, as can be seen in John X. 31. Acts V. 26. cap. XIV. v. 5. Virgil in his description of sedition: And now torches and stones fly. The same λιθάζειν here, and in the cited place of John, and Acts cap. V. vers. 26. cap. XXIV. vers. 14. Heb. cap. XI. vers. 37. which is λιθοβολεῖν in Matthew c. XXI. v. 35. 37. Mark c. XII. 4.

Luc. XIII. 34. Actor. VII. 58. 59. XIV. 5. Hebr. XII. 20. .סקל

Tρὶς ἐναυάγησα) Of these three shipwrecks of Paul, we have one narrated in the Acts. Others happened before Luke had joined himself to Paul.

And yet that shipwreck of his near Melita happened long after this epistle was written.

Νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα) Ποιῶν signifies duration joined to time, as in James 4:13, Rev. 13:5. The word Νυχθήμερον is frequent among the Greeks, corresponding to the two Hebrew words, ערב ובקר, βυθὸς מצולה, as in Exod. 15:5, Ps. 68:23, Ps. 107:24, is the deep sea.

Erasmus thinks the depth of a prison or some other thing can be understood: But it is more correctly explained as the deep of the sea. Lyranus understands 'night and day' as a long time, during which he penetrated different parts of the earth and islands by sailing. But because he sees that one must not depart from the letter, he resorts to tradition, that Paul, having suffered shipwreck, stood under the waters for a day and a night, with divine power protecting him. The Syrian connects it with the preceding: I was three times in shipwreck, night and day, without a ship, I say, I was in the sea. But since all other things are to be taken separately, these also seem to be distinct, nor does he teach in which shipwreck he was in the deep of the sea, or how many times he was in it, and therefore without doubt he hints at a peculiar and different danger of death: That the preservation in the deep of the sea was miraculous, that oath also, by which he confirms his narration, which might seem incredible, in verse 31, seems to hint. Estius: The Greek word, although nothing else is added, is often accepted among writers for the depth of the sea. Nor do most commentators accept this passage otherwise; and that is convenient to the text. For when he had said: That he had suffered shipwreck three times, certainly in the sea: He subjoined another maritime danger far more grave, namely that he had been submerged from a shipwreck into the deep of the sea, where nevertheless by divine aid he was kept unharmed for a night and a day, and was afterwards liberated from there.

Latin:

Ἅπαξ ἐλιθάσθην) Actor. cap. XIV. vers. 18. Nempe per seditionem multitudinis, ut videre est Johan. X. 31. Actor. V. 26. cap. XIV. v. 5. Virgilius in seditionis descriptione: Iamque faces & saxa volant. Idem λιθάζειν hic, & dicto Johannis loco, & Actor. cap. V. vers. 26. cap. XXIV. vers. 14. Hebr. cap. XI. vers. 37. quod λιθοβολεῖν Matth. c. XXI. v. 35. 37. Marci c. XII. 4.

Luc. XIII. 34. Actor. VII. 58. 59. XIV. 5. Hebr. XII. 20. .סקל

Tρὶς ἐναυάγησα) De tribus his Pauli naufragiis unum in Actis narratum habemus. Alia evenere priusquam Lu- cas Paulo se conjunxisset.

Atqui naufragium illi apud Meletam multo post scriptam hanc epistolam contigit.

Νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα) Ποιῶν tempori ad- junctam durationem significat, ut Jac. IV. 13. Apoc. XIII. v. 5. Νυχθήμερον vox Græcis frequens, respondens He- bræis duobus,ערב ובקר, βυθὸς מצולה, ut Exod.c. XV. v. 5. Psal. LXVIII. 23. Psal. CVII. verf. 24. est altum mare.

Erasmus profunditatem carceris vel alterius rei intelligi posse putat: Sed rectius de profundo ma- ris explicatur. Noctem & diem Lyranus de ma- gno tempore intelligit, quo diversas terræ partes & insulas navigando penetravit. Sed quia a lite- ra discedendum non esse videt, ad traditionem se recipit, Paulum naufragium passum sub aquis ste- tisse per diem & noctem divina virtute eum protegente. Syrus connectit cum præcedenti: Ter fui in naufragio die ac nocte, sine navi, inquam, in mari fui. Sed quum cætera omnia seorsim accipienda sint, videntur & hæc distincta esse, nec vero quo- libet naufragio in maris profundo se fuisse, aut quoto in eo fuerit, docet, ideoque sine dubio, peculiare & diversum periculum mortis innuit: Mi- raculosam fuisse conservationem in profundo ma- ris, etiam illud juramentum, quo narrationem su- am, quæ videri possit incredibilis confirmat verf. 31. innuere videtur. Estius: Vox Græca, licet nihil aliud addatur, sæpe apud Scriptores accipitur pro maris profunditate. Nec aliter Commentatores plerique locum hunc accipiunt; idque convenien- ter textui. Cum enim dixisset: Se ter naufra- gium fecisse, utique in mari: Subjunxit aliud periculum marinum longe gravius, nempe quod demersus fuerit ex naufragio in profundum ma- ris, ubi tamen divina ope fuerit servatus inco- lumis noctem, & diem, atque inde postea libe- ratus.

## 11:26
Vers. 26. Ὁδοιπορίαις πολλάκις) The 'in', here and in the following, is understood ἀπὸ κοινῦ, from that which had preceded: in labors, in prisons, in deaths.

B. Hunnius notes that not even the twentieth part of the journeys of the Apostle has been recorded in writing, in which such frequent journeys it can easily be thought how great and how frequent were the dangers he had to undergo. He made special mention of rivers, however, because he was not only in danger of his life in the vast sea, but also sometimes in rivers, which are sometimes no less dangerous to those sailing than the sea.

Κινδύνοις ἐκ γένες) Namely, from my own, from my own people, from the Jews. Thus Acts 7:9, Gal. 1:14.

Ἐξ ἐθνῶν) They are accustomed to call all those who are not Jews, nor added to the Jews, גוים, by this name.

Κινδύνοις ἐν πόλει, κινδύνοις ἐν ἐρημίᾳ) These singulars are used for plurals.

It is likely that he sustained those dangers among the Gentiles; since he commemorates in order first the labors of the Jews, then of the Gentiles, and finally the dangers of false brothers, and in this distinction, when he deals with the Gentiles, he designates the city and the wilderness, as also the sea: because he does not mean what he suffered from heaven in the sea through a storm, but what he sustained when led by the Gentiles on a voyage.

Ἐν ψευδαδέλφοις) See Gal. II. 4. These are they who pretended to be Christians, that they might learn the affairs of the Christians, then they might betray them. A similar composition is in ψευδομάρτυς, ψευδαπόστολος, ψευδοπροφήτης.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ὁδοιπορίαις πολλάκις) Ἐ, hic, & in sequenti- bus, subauditur ἀπὸ κοινῦ, ex eo, quod præcesserat: ἐν κόποις, ἐν φυλακαῖς, ἐν θανάτοις.

Notat B. Hunnius, ne vigesimam quidem partem itinerum Apostoli in literas relatam esse, in quibus tam frequentibus itineribus facile cogitari potest, quanta sæpicule pericula subire necessum habue- rit. Fluminum autem peculiarem mentionem fecit, quia non tantum in vasto mari periclitatus de vita fuit, sed etiam quandoque in fluminibus, quæ interdum non minus periculosa navigantibus sunt, quam mare.

Κινδύνοις ἐκ γένες) Nempe ἐμᾶ, a mea gente, a Judæis. Sic Actor. VII. 9. Gal. I. 14.

Ἐξ ἐθνῶν) Ita vocare solent omnes, qui non Judæi sunt, neque Judæis additi גוים.

Κινδύνοις ἐν πόλει, κινδύνοις ἐν ἐρημίᾳ) Hæc singularia po- nuntur pro pluralibus.

Penes Ethnicos pericula illa sustinuisse veri- simile est; quum prius labores Judæorum, porro Ethnicorum, denique falsorum fra- trum pericula ordine commemoret, & in hac distinctione, cum de Ethnicis agit, civi- tatem & eremum designat, ut & mare: quia non quæ in mari cælitus passus per tempesta- tem, sed quæ a gentibus navigio deductus susti- nuerit.

Ἐν ψευδαδέλφοις) Vide Gal. II. 4. Hi sunt, qui Chri- stianos se simulabant, ut res Christianorum perdiscerent, deinde eos proderent. Similis compositio in ψευδομάρτυς, ψευδαπόστολος, ψευδοπροφήτης.

## 11:27
Vers. 27. In labor and toil) Μόχθος here is misery עמל.

In watchings often) In vigils, see above IV. 5. See an example in Acts XXVII. & following.

In hunger and thirst) In places, namely, where there was nothing of food or drink.

In fastings often) Understand fasts, voluntarily undertaken to kindle prayers, as Acts XIII. 2. XIV. 23. 1 Cor. VII. 5.

In cold and nakedness) Acts XXVIII. 2. & Rom. VIII. v. 35. But understand nakedness comparatively, that is, clothing so light that it would not sufficiently defend the body, see Mark XIV. 52. John XXI. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Ἐν κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ) Μόχθος hic est miseria עמל.

Ἐν ἀγρυπνίαις πολλάκις) In pervigiliis, supra IV. 5. Ex- emplum vide Act. XXVII. & sequentibus.

Ἐν λιμῷ καὶ δίψει) In locis scilicet, ubi nihil erat esculenti aut potulenti.

Ἐν νηστείαις πολλάκις) Intellige jejunia, sponte susce- pta ad accendendas preces, ut Actor. XIII. 2. XIV. 23. 1. Cor. VII. 5.

Ἐν ψύχει καὶ γυμνότητι) Actor. XXVIII. 2. & Rom. VIII. v. 35. γυμνότητα autem intellige comparate, id est, vesti- tum tam levem, qui corpus non satis defenderet, vide Marci XIV. 52. Joh. XXI. 7.

## 11:28
Vers. 28. Besides those things that are without) Besides these bodily inconveniences.

The pressure upon me, the daily care of all the Churches) I am assaulted daily by that anxiety in which I see the Churches are involved. Ἐπισύστασις is an assault, Numbers XXVI. 9. הצות from נצה, which is to rush in, as if a crowd were formed. See also Acts XXIV. 12.

He now further subjoins the misery of the labors which he had only touched upon, both in general and in particular, by the mention of vigils, hunger and thirst and fastings, cold and nakedness; partly [he subjoins] solicitude and care. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret those words 'besides those things that are without' as if he were saying: I pass over, I omit, so that the sense may be: that Paul did not recount everything in this catalog of his evils. But the explanation of B. Luther seems most convenient, which Musculus also supports along with Calvin. He is speaking not of a hostile incursion, but of the incursion and multitude of business, by which he was harassed every single day, either by the arrival of brethren or by the greetings or consultations of the faithful who were present, or by the letters of those who were absent, the ceaseless multitude and pressing heap of whom is rightly called ἐπισύστασις. The Greek interpreters take this word ἐπισύστασις to mean the tumults stirred up against Paul. But those were more serious, yet not daily. Therefore B. Hunnius more correctly: He reports that the care of all the Churches lies upon him. For he was not bound to any one [church], but as an Apostle, all the Churches were commended to him. Whence it is easy to estimate what the mass and multitude of his occupations was, while he not only had to set out hither and thither, but also sent out disciples to inform or even to visit the Churches and to amend their state: while likewise he had to respond to various questions, while he was occupied in dispatching letters, while he was forced to see with groaning the Churches, which he himself had planted with great sweat, gradually being undermined by false Doctors. B. Hülsemann: Gerson in his treatise on the removability of the Pope from the Church, in Goldast, Monarch. Rom. Tom. I. fol. 588. seqq. & Tom. II. fol. 1411. and others following him in Alphonsus de Castro, book 4, against heresies, under the word Pope, rightly concluded: If a universal episcopacy of all the Churches is established as commended to any of the Apostles exclusively and above the rest, it would be Paul, not Peter, because the particle 'universal' regarding the care of 'all the Churches' is nowhere predicated of anyone. Wherefore the Papists twist themselves in trying to destroy the force of this statement. Bellarmine, book 1, on the Roman Pontiff, chap. 9, restricts it to all the Churches which Paul himself had planted. But the Apostle distinguishes this care from the origin of the planting, of which he speaks in chap. X. vers. 16, by the particles 'besides' and 'without', which were added, beyond those things already commemorated. Saa and Justinianus take 'care' passively, not of the care by which the Apostle provided for the salvation of the Churches; but of the afflictions and adversities which happen to the Apostle as he travels through almost every Church: But not only the word 'pressure' (ἐπισύστασις), which precedes, but also the following exegesis concerning the zeal and compassion of the Apostle toward the evils of fault and punishment befalling others, verse 9, show that the discourse here is about voluntary and elicited solicitude, not afflictions of the body brought on by external force. Concerning the 'pressure' or the concurrence and incursion of many men soliciting us, whom the Romans called clients, see Acts chap. XXIV. vers. 12. and the example of CHRIST, Mark chap. I. last verse, chap. III. v. 21. Which Justinianus is forced to admit, when he explained τὴν ἐπισύ- σασιν & μέριμναν in his paraphrase as a daily rushing troop of cares, and the anxiety which I procure for the salvation of all the Churches with incredible zeal. See Augustinus book IV de doctr. Christian. cap. 7. and Chrysostomus Orat. II de laudibus Pauli interpreting these. Estius and Salmero trifle that all the Churches should be taken by synecdoche for most of them.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς) Praeter haec corporis incom- moda.

Ἡ ἐπισύστασίς μου ἡ καθ' ἡμέραν μέριμνα πασῶν τῶν Ἐκ- κλησιῶν) Oppugnor quotidie ab ea anxietate, in qua versa- ri Ecclesias video. Ἐπισύστασις oppugnatio, Numer. XXVI. 9. הצות a נצה, quod est irruere, velut globo facto. Vi- de & Act. XXIV. 12.

Subjungit jam porro laborum, quos attige- rat tantum, partim miseriam, tum in genere, tum in specie, mentione vigiliarum, famis & sitis & jejuniorum, frigoris & nuditatis; partim solicitudinem & curam. Illa χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς Chrysostomus & Theophylactus interpretantur, quasi dicat: Praetereo, praetermitto ut sit sensus: Paulum nec in hoc suorum malorum catalogo omnia recensuisse. Sed commodissima videtur B. Lutheri explicatio, cui suffragatur etiam cum Calvino Musculus. Loquitur non de hostili, sed de negotiorum incursu ac multitudine, qui- bus singulis diebus vel adventu fratrum vel sa- lutationibus aut consultationibus praesentium fidelium vel literis absentium molestabatur, quorum indefinens multitudo, & cumulus ur- gens recte ἐπισύστασις vocatur. Vocem hanc ἐπισύστασις Graeci Interpretes de tumultibus acci- piunt adversus Paulum excitatis. Sed illi gra- viores erant, non vero quotidiani. Rectius ergo B. Hunnius: Refert sibi incumbere curam omnium Ecclesiarum. Neque enim erat alligatus ad unam aliquam, sed tanquam Apostolo commendatae erant omnes Ecclesiae. Unde aestimare promptum est, quae fuerit occupationum moles & multitudo, dum huc illuc proficisci non modo necessum ha- buit, sed etiam discipulos emisit, ad informan- das vel etiam visitandas Ecclesias, & emendan- dum earum statum: dum item de variis quaestio- nibus respondendum fuit, dum epistolis expedien- dis fuit occupatus, dum videre cum gemitu coa- ctus est, Ecclesias, quas ipse magno sudore plan- taverat, paulatim labefactari a falsis Doctoribus. B. Hülsemannus: Gerson in tractatu de aufferibi- litate Papae ab Ecclesia, apud Goldastum Monarch. Rom. Tom. I. fol. 588. seqq. & Tom. II. fol. 1411. eumque sequuti alii apud Alphonsum de Castro l. 4. contra haereses voce Papa recte concluserunt: Si cuiquam Apostolorum universalis episcopa omnium Ecclesiarum exclusive & prae reliquis statuatur commendata, Paulum non Petrum illum fore, quia particula universalis de cura πασῶν ἐκκλη- σιῶν nusquam de ullo praedicetur. Quamobrem torquent sese Papistae in elidenda vi hujus dicti. Bellarminus libr. I. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 9. restrin- git ad omnes Ecclesias, quas ipse Paulus plantave- rat. Sed Apostolus hanc curam contradistinguit origini plantationis, de qua cap. X. vers. 16. per par- ticulas ὁρὶς & παρεκτὸς, quae accedebant, praeter ea jam commemorata. Saa & Justinianus μέ- ρι- έριμναν passive sumunt, non de cura qua Apostolus pro- curavit salutem Ecclesiarum; sed de afflictionibus & adversitatibus, quæ Apostolo peregrinanti per singulas fere Ecclesias eveniant: Sed non solum vox ἐπισυ- σάσεως, quæ præcedit, verum etiam exegesis sequens de zelo & compassione Apostoli erga mala culpæ & pœ- næ aliis obvenientia vers. 9. ostendunt hic sermonem esse de solicitudine voluntaria & elicita, non afflictio- nibus corporis per vim extrinsecam illatis. De ἐπι- συσάσει seu concursu & ingruentia multorum homi- num nos solicitantium, quos Romani clientes voca- bant, vide Actor. cap. XXIV. vers. 12. & exemplum CHRISTI Marci cap. I. vers. ult. cap. III. v. 21. Quod cogitur fateri Justinianus, quando τὴν ἐπισύ- σασιν & μέριμναν in paraphrasi exposuit, agmen cu- rarum quotidie irruens, & solicitudinem, quæ omni- um Ecclesiarum salutem incredibili studio procuro. Vid. Augustinus libr. IV. de doctr. Christian. cap. 7. & Chrysostomus Orat. II. de laudibus Pauli hæc in- terpretantes. Estius & Salmero omnes Ecclesias per Synecdochen pro plerisque sumendas nugan- tur.

## 11:29
Vers. 29. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Which Church is afflicted, so that I am not afflicted? For that is to be weak, as we said above 21. כשל; a similar sense in Job VI. 9.

Who is offended, and I do not burn? Who is it to whom an offense is cast in the way of piety, so that I do not burn? πυροῦσθαι is Greek, as also the Latin uri, is sometimes said of desire, as 1 Cor. VII. 9, sometimes of the torment of the mind. Thus in Terence: I burn the man. The Hebrews use ענס in the same way.

It is not about the affliction of the Church, but about the weakness in faith of any believer whatsoever, and a fall arising from infirmity, whose lot he testifies he grieves as if he himself were weak, and thus is made weak, who testifies to the affection of commiseration. If anyone is offended by the perverse doctrine or unpraiseworthy life of others, immediately zeal against the authors of the scandals blazes up in me, nor is rest given to me until the stumbling block is removed. Estius interprets it in this way: No one falls into any sin, whose remnants I do not experience and feel in myself. I also experience great weakness of my flesh, I am kindled and carried away to concupiscence, lust, and other sins. But these do not fit the present catalogue of the Apostle's cares, which it is manifest speaks rather of his own burning zeal against sins and scandals, as was rightly observed by B. Luther in the marginal gloss.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Τίς ἀσθενεῖ καὶ οὐκ ἀσθενῶ;) Quæ Ecclesia affligi- tur, ut ego non adfligar? Id enim ἀσθενεῖν, ut diximus supra 21. כשל; similis sensus Job. VI. 9.

Τίς σκανδαλίζεται, κὶ οὐκ ἐγὼ πυρῦμαι;) Quis est, cui offensa objicitur in via pietatis, ut non ego urar? πυροῦσθαι Græcum, ut & Latinum uri, modo de cupidine dicitur, ut 1. Cor. VII. 9. modo de animi cruciatu. Sic apud Te- rentium: Vro hominem. Hebræi ענס eodem modo usur- pant.

Non de afflictione Ecclesiæ, sed de fidelis cujus- vis ἀσθενείᾳ in fide, ac lapsu ex infirmitate ori- undo, agitur, cujus vicem ita se dolere, ac si ipse infirmus sit, adeoque infirmari, qui affe- ctum commiserationis testatur. Si quis offendi- tur aliorum vel perversa doctrina, vel illaudata vita, protinus exardescit in me zelus adversus scandalorum authores, nec datur mihi requies, donec offendiculum submoveatur. Estius inter- pretatur hoc modo: Nemo in peccatum ullum labitur, cujus ego reliquias in me non experior & sentio. Experior & ego magnam imbecillitatem meæ carnis, ad concupiscentiam, libidinem, & alia peccata accendor & rapior. Sed hæc non con- veniunt præsenti catalogo curarum Apostoli, quem de zelo potius suo ardenti, contra peccata & scandala loqui manifestum est, ut recte B. Lu- thero observatum in gloss. marg.

## 11:30
Vers. 30. If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities. In that joy and triumph, that I have endured so many evils for the sake of Christ. See Acts V. 41.

He shows, as interpreted by B.
