Hunnius, if he wishes at all to contend by glorying with the Pseudo-Apostles, that he does not seek the material for this glorying in the riches of this world, in external prosperity, in honors, as indeed they do, but in his infirmity, that is, in the labors which he sustained, in the troubles which he devoured, in the dangers which he approached, in the tribulations which he felt, in the inconveniences of this life which he experienced on account of the Gospel of Christ.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not. There is a transposition here also. For knoweth ought to have been placed in natural order before those words, that I lie not. And here Paul sometimes swears, but in a most serious matter, and one pertaining to God. Who is blessed for evermore, הברוך לעולמים, a title of God, Rom. I. 25, IX. 5.

Some refer this oath to the following account concerning the Damascene captivity and the deliverance from the same, because it happened soon from the beginning of the Apostleship, and was not so well known; or even to the connected revelations, which the Apostle related in the following verse: But it is more correctly referred to those things which hitherto have been mentioned, among which are many things that can exceed belief, some known to GOD alone, to whose testimony he appeals, especially regarding those things which lay hidden in the heart of the Apostle: since he alone tests hearts and kidneys, that he has lied in none of them. The words, who is blessed forever, have emphasis as if he were saying: Far be it that I should abuse his testimony, to whom all praise and honor is due for all eternity.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Εἰ καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ, τὰ τέ ἀσθενείας με καυχήσομαι) In eo gaudio ac triumpho, quod tot mala Christi causa per- tulerim. Vide Act. V. 41.

Ostendit, interprete B. Hunnio, si omnino velit gloriando certare cum Pseudo-Apostolis, non se ma- teriam bujus gloriationis quærere in opibus hujus mundi, in prosperitate externa, in honoribus, ut quidem illi facitent, sed in infirmitate sua, id est in laboribus, quos sustinuit, in molestiis, quas devora- vit, in periculis, quæ adiit, in tribulationibus, quas sensit, in bujus vitæ incommoditatibus, quas propter Evangelium Christi expertus est.

Ὁ Θεὸς κὶ Πατὴρ κυρίε Ἰησῦ χρισῦ οἶδεν, ὁ ὢν εὐλογητὸς εἰς αἰῶνας, ὅτι ὐ ψεύδομαι) Est & hic trajectio. Nam οἶδεν naturali ordine poni debuit ante illa, ὅτι ὐ ψεύδομαι. Et hic interdum jurat Paulus, sed in gravissima, & ad Deum pertinente. Ὁ εὐλογητὸς εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας, הברוך לעולמים, titulus Dei, Rom. I. 25. IX. 5.

Hoc juramentum referunt nonnulli ad sequen- tem relationem de captivitate Damascena, & libe- ratione ex eadem, quia mox ab initio Apostola- tus facta, nec adeo nota fuit; vel etiam ad connexas revelationes, quas versu sequenti retulit Apostolus: Sed rectius id refertur ad ea, quæ hactenus com- memoravit, inter quæ multa sunt, quæ fidem excedere possunt, nonnulla soli DEO cognita, ad cujus testimonium provocat, imprimis quoad ea, quæ in corde Apostoli latebant: Siquidem is solus corda & renes probat, quod in nullo eorum mentitus sit. Verba, qui est benedictus in secula, emphasin habent quasi dicat: Absit, ut abutar ejus testimonio, cui omnis laus & honor debetur in omnem æternitatem.

## 11:32
In Damascus the Ethnarch of King Aretas) This is the same history which is in Acts chap. IX. verses 23, 24, 25. This Aretas was King of the Arabs, whom Josephus mentions in XVIII. 7. and elsewhere. He held Damascus at this time, and had placed a prefect over it, who is here called ethnarch, for the reason that he presided over all of Damascene Syria. We have the same word in the Maccabees and often in Josephus, and in Strabo. Also, he who was the prince of the Jews at Alexandria is so called in the edict of Claudius, which is in the same Josephus. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho, 'that Damascus was and is of the Arabian land, even if it has now been assigned to what is called Syrophoenicia, not even some of you can deny.' Tertullian against Marcion III. 'And Damascus was formerly reckoned to Arabia, before it was transferred to Syrophoenicia, by the distinction of the Syrias.'

King Aretas was the father-in-law of Herod Antipas, Tetrarch of Petraean Arabia, and Lord of the Damascene city, which was near to him. He boasts, however, not of the flight, which even if it was lawful according to Matt. chap. X. verse 23, was nevertheless not a matter of boasting against the Pseudo-Apostles, but of the danger, and such a great one that he would have perished, just as in the deaths or dangers of death reviewed above, had not flight provided for him, and also of a singular divine deliverance.

Latin:

Ἐν Δαμασκῷ ὁ Ἐθνάρχης Ἀρέτα τῶ Βασιλέως) Est eadem historia, quæ Actor. cap. IX. vers. 23. 24. 25. Aretas hic fuit Arabum Rex, cujus meminit Josephus XVIII. 7. & alibi. Is hoc tempore Damascum tenebat, eique præfectum imposuerat, qui hic dicitur ἐθνάρχης, ideo quod tot Syriæ Damascenæ præesset. Habemus eandem vocem in Macchabaicis & Josepho sæpe, & in Strabone. Etiam qui princeps erat Judæorum Alexandriæ, sic vocatur in edicto Claudii, quod est apud eundem Josephum. Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone, ὅτι δὲ Δαμασκὸς τῆ Ἀῥῥαβικῆς γῆς ἦν καὶ ἔστιν, εἰ καὶ νῦν προσνενέμηται τῇ Συροφοινίκῃ λεγομένη, οὐδ' ὑμῶν τινὲς ἀρνήσασθαι δύνανται. Tertullianus adversus Marcion. III. Et Damascus Arabiæ retro deputabatur, antequam transcripta esset in Syrophœnicen, ex distinctione Syriarum.

Aretas Rex socer erat Herodis Antipæ, Tetrarchæ Arabiæ Petrææ, & Damascenæ civitatis, quæ illi vicina erat, Dominus. Gloriatur autem non de fuga, quæ etsi licita fuerit Matth. cap. X. vers. 23. non tamen materia gloriationis contra Pseudo-Apostolos erat, sed de periculo, eoque tanto, ut periturus fuisset, quemadmodum in superius recensitis mortibus vel periculis mortis, nisi fuga consultum ipsi fuisset, necnon de singulari liberatione divina.

## 11:33
Verse 33. Wishing to seize me) Thus we have πιάσαι in John VII. 30, 32, 44, VIII. 20, X. 39, XI. 57, Acts XII. The Hebrews would say תפש.

Through a window) Through a window, joined to the wall.

In a basket) Acts IX. 25, in a hamper. But σαργάνη is a rope, according to Aeschylus. Understand here the rope by which the basket was held. Or, let the ' here be a mark of the instrument in the Hebrew manner. To the Rabbis, סרגנס is a haircloth.

I was let down) הורדתי See Josephus II. 15. and the cited passage of Acts.

This flight on account of personal persecution, undertaken not to the detriment of the Church, but so that the Church might be further propagated through the ministry of the Apostle, was by no means unlawful, as it was consistent with the command of CHRIST in Matt. chap. X. verse 23, and with the examples of the saints, indeed of CHRIST himself, 1 Kings XVIII. 4, chap. XIX. 4, Luke IV. 3, John VIII. 59, chap. XI. 54.

Latin:

Vers. 33. Πιάσαι με θέλων) Sic πιάσαι habemus Joh. VII. 30. 32. 44. VIII. 20. X. 39. XI. 57. Act. XII. Hebræi dicerent תפש.

Διὰ θυρίδος) Per fenestram, muro injunctam.

Ἐν σαργάνῃ) Actor. IX. 25. ἐν σπυρίδι. At σαργάνη est funis, apud Æschylum. Intellige hic funem, quo sporta attenebatur. Aut ،; hic sit more Hebræo nota instrumenti. Rabbinis סרגנס est cilicium.

Ἐχαλάσθην) הורדתי Vide Josephum II. 15. & dictum Actorum locum.

Fuga hæc ob persequutionem personalem non in Ecclesiæ damnum, sed ut Ecclesia amplius per ministerium Apostoli propagaretur, suscepta minime illicita fuit, utpote CHRISTI mandato Matth. cap. X. vers. 23. & sanctorum, imo ipsius CHRISTI exemplis 1. Reg. XIIX. 4. cap. XIX. 4. Luc. IV. 3. Joh. IIX. 59. cap. XI. 54. congrua.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle now boasts of the divine revelations made to him, that he was caught up into the third heaven. For the rest, he boasts of nothing but his own infirmity, since his pride was repressed by a singular thorn, and he was warned that the power of God is made perfect in infirmity, which he experienced in the thing itself. He excuses himself again, however, that he boasted of himself under urgent necessity, when he ought rather to have been praised by the Corinthians as not inferior to the highest Apostles because of the signs done among them, and he testifies to the readiness of his arrival, and his love toward them, for which he is prepared to undergo death for their souls, and that he has been a burden or loss to them neither himself, nor through others, such as Titus and his colleague; finally, he warns them to repent of their contentions, fornications, and similar sins, lest he be affected with sadness upon his arrival.

There are three parts: I. Boasting about revelations to v. 10. II. Excuse for boasting to v. 19. III. Admonition to repentance to v. 21.

PART I. Boasting about revelations.

Vers. 1. Καυχᾶσθαι δὲ ὀυ συμφέρει μοι) To exult with joy is not expedient. The most wholesome thing for the mind is ἡ τ’ οἰήσεως συνολή.

It is sufficiently clear, both from previous warning and from this chapter, especially v. 7, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι, that the word καυχᾶσθαι is to be understood not of joy, but of boasting in these things and those which follow. For those who have cause for boasting are easily puffed up. Moreover, the Apostle adds, it is not expedient for me, because if it had not been expedient at all, nor had this boasting been useful or necessary for the Church, he would undoubtedly have abstained from it. Some refer these things to the preceding. But the particle γὰρ teaches that this little proem pertains to the following, namely to the visions and revelations of the Lord, about which it was certainly not expedient for him to boast, since he had been restrained by the thorn in the flesh, and would not boast of them, nor puff himself up with them. He wishes, therefore, to come to those revelations, only for the sake of the Corinthians. The Vulgate here departs from the Greek in more than one way: If it is necessary to boast (it is not indeed expedient) I will come to visions, etc.

᾿Ελεύσομαι γὰρ εἰς ὀπτασίας κ’ ἀποκαλύψεις Κυρίυ) I must come, he says, to this, if I were seeking material for rejoicing and exulting. ᾿Οπτασία, as it is often translated in Daniel as מַרְאֶה, or ὅρασις, is a visible appearance, presented to one waking or dreaming. ᾿Αποκάλυψις is indeed general, but here it is put for the inspiration or light with which the mind is suffused.

It is not the potential mood. For he is preparing an approach to visions and indeed to the chief of them. He implies, therefore, that he is not saying what he could, but what he would. Lyra, Thomas, and Cajetan distinguish vision and revelation in such a way that revelation intends or presupposes vision, not the contrary. When, therefore, something is seen, the understanding or meaning of which escapes the seer, it is said by them to be only a vision, such as were the visions of Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. But the explanation of Grotius on both sides is to be preferred. The Apostle does not, however, list the visions or revelations which he could proclaim. He brings forward at least one as being very remarkable. Concerning others, see Acts XVI. v. 9, ch. XVIII. 9, ch. XXII. v. 17, ch. XXVII. v. 23. But the fact that he names visions and revelations here in the plural is taken to mean that many things were seen and revealed to the Apostle at the same time, so that, coming to that one vision, he rightly says that he is coming to visions and revelations.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Gloriatur jam Apostolus de revelationibus divinis sibi factis, quod raptus fuerit in tertium cœlum. De cætero non nisi de sua infirmitate glorians, siquidem singulari stimulo repressa elatio, monitusque fuerit, virtutem Dei in infirmitate perfici, quod re ipsa expertus sit. Excusat autem denuo, quod de se gloriatus urgente necessitate fuerit, cum potius a Corinthiis ceu non minor summis Apostolis ob signa inter ipsos facta laudari debuerit, testaturque de promptitudine adventus, atque amore adversus ipsos, ex quo pro ipsorum animabus mortem subire paratus sit, & quod neque ipse, neque per alios, utpote Titum & collegam, ipsis oneri aut damno fuerit, monet denique, ut poenitentiam de contentionibus, scortationibus & similibus peccatis agant, ne sub adventum tristitia afficiatur.

Partes sunt tres I. Gloriatio de revelationibus ad v. 10. II. Excusatio gloriationis ad v. 19. III. Commonefactio ad poenitentiam ad v. 21.

PARS I. Gloriatio de revelationibus.

Vers. 1. Καυχᾶσθαι δὲ ὀυ συμφέρει μοι) Lætitia gestire non expedit. Saluberrimum animo ἡ τ’ οἰήσεως συνολή.

Non de lætitia, sed gloriatione in his & quæ sequuntur verbum καυχᾶσθαι accipiendum esse, & antea monitum, & ex hoc capite, satis liquet, imprimis v. 7. ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι. Efferuntur enim facile, qui gloriandi causam habent. Addit autem Apostolus, non expedit mihi, quia si nullatenus expediisset, neque Ecclesiæ utilis vel necessaria fuisset hæc gloriatio, abstinuisset sine dubio ab eadem. Referunt hæc nonnulli ad præcedentia. Sed particula γὰρ docet, proœmiolum hoc ad sequentia pertinere, ad visiones nempe & revelationes Domini, de quibus gloriari ipsi sane non expediebat, quum coërcitus per stimulum carnis fuerit, nec de illis gloriaretur, iisque sese efferret. Venire ergo ad revelationes illas vult, non nisi Corinthiorum causa. Vulgata hic non uno modo abit a Græco: Si gloriari oportet (non expedit quidem) veniam autem ad visiones &c.

᾿Ελεύσομαι γὰρ εἰς ὀπτασίας κ’ ἀποκαλύψεις Κυρίυ) Eo, inquit, veniendum esset, si gestiendi & exultandi quærerem materiam. ᾿Οπτασία, quomodo apud Danielem sæpe vertitur מַרְאֶה, sive ὅρασις, est species visibilis, objecta vigilanti aut somnianti. ᾿Αποκάλυψις est quidem generale, sed hic ponitur pro afflatu seu luce, qua mens perfunditur.

Non potentialis modus est. Accessum enim parat ad visiones & quidem ad præcipuam earum. Non ergo quid posset, sed quid vellet, jam dicere innuit. Visionem & revelationem Lyra & Thomas & Cajetanus ita distinguunt quod revelatio visionem intendat aut supponat, non contra. Cum ergo aliquid videtur, cujus intelligentia sive significatio videntem latet, visio solum secundum ipsos fuisse dicitur, quales visiones fuere Pharaonis & Nebucadnezaris. Sed præferenda Grotiana utrinque explicatio. Non recenset autem Apostolus sive visiones, sive revelationes, quas poterat deprædicare. Unicam saltem ceu admodum insignem adducit visionem. De aliis vide Actor. XVI. v. 9. cap. XIIX. 9. cap. XXII. v. 17. cap. XXVII. v. 23. Quod vero hic pluraliter visiones nominet, & revelationes, id ita accipiunt, quod multa eodem tempore visa & revelata sint Apostolo, ut merito ad unam illam veniens visionem dicat se ad visiones & revelationes venire.

## 12:2
Vers. 2. Οἶδα ἄνθρωπον ἐν χρισῷ) A Christian. Paul proclaims these things as if they were not his own, as if he were saying: - - - What we have not done ourselves, I hardly think those things are ours. Therefore he speaks this in the third person, like that man in the Controversies of Seneca: Just as, on the other hand, when something must be said which is odious, he assumes the first person for the second.

Πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων) I shall refer this to that, ἐν χρισῷ. Such a man, who had already served Christ for fourteen years.

He speaks of himself, according to the blessed Balduinus, as if of a stranger, partly so that he might not seem ambitious, partly because in truth he was then unknown to himself: For he did not know whether he was in the body or out of the body. πρὸ ἐτῶν properly is before years. He does not therefore report how many years he has already served CHRIST, but how many years ago these things happened. And this is the common exposition of the Interpreters. Nor indeed does Grotius wish it to be at the time of his conversion, as with Lyranus, Damasus in his poem, and Ludov. Capellus in Hist. Eccles. chap. XXXIIX, but that this rapture happened eight years after the same, as Salmeron, Pererius, Cornelius a Lapide, Estius, Baronius at the year XLIV, and others who institute the computation of time more accurately, teach: Since a little before he had been let down by the disciples through the walls of Damascus, namely in the year of the Lord XLIV, the second of the Emperor Claudius. Since his conversion fell in the year of the Lord XXXVI; but this epistle was written in the year of the Lord LVI, the second of Nero, from which they gather that this vision was given in the year in which he received the office of preaching with Barnabas, Acts chap. XII.

Whether in the body I do not know; or out of the body I do not know, God knows, such a one caught up to the third heaven) There is also a transposition here. For that whether in the body, and what follows, ought naturally to have been placed at the end of this verse. The Hebrews do not recognize different spheres in heaven, but they divide heaven into three regions, of which the first is cloud-bearing, the second star-bearing, the third Angel-bearing. The first is called by the Hebrews עולם שפל, the second עולם התיכון. The third עולם העליון. Others call the first רקיע, the second שמים, the third שמי שמים. Therefore the third heaven is called here what is elsewhere the heaven of heavens, the highest heaven, the Angelic. However, it can happen to someone that he sees things far removed in a double way, either if he is carried somewhere by an Angel, which is related in the Additions to Daniel concerning Habakkuk, and how CHRIST is believed to have been carried by Satan, or that without change of place those things which are absent are exhibited to him as if present, by a divinely excited appearance, just as CHRIST saw all the kingdoms of the world, and Ezekiel, when he was at the Chaboras, saw those things which were being done in the Jerusalem temple. But Paul says that he does not know in which way it happened to him, of whom he treats. Ἐν σώματι is in the body translated. Ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος is in the soul, without any motion of the body.

Concerning this rapture, Augustine has it thus in book XII of De Genesi ad literam, chap. 5. That which he saw, caught up to the third heaven, which he also confirms that he knows, he saw properly, not imaginarily. But because that very alienation from the body, whether he left the body altogether dead, or whether his soul was there according to a certain mode of a living body, but his mind was snatched away to see or hear the ineffable things of that vision, this was uncertain. Similarly, the blessed Hunnius discusses this Pauline doubt concerning this rapture, that it was not certain to Paul whether the vision was offered to him while existing in the body, or indeed with the soul separated for some time from the body. The blessed Balduinus says: He did not know, he says, whether he was in the body or out of the body, that is, whether he was carried from place to place in his body, or whether he suffered an ecstasy through the separation of the soul from the body. The blessed Weinrichius says that he did not know whether he was caught up and translated into the seat of the blessed in body and soul together, or in soul alone; where indeed Thomas warns in II. 2. q. 175. arts. 5 & 6, and in his commentary on this place, that in this rapture of Paul the soul was not separated from the body, but remained joined to it, so that only his mind, to see or hear those things which he saw or heard in the rapture, was alienated from the bodily senses. Estius does not dissent from this opinion; for the reason especially that otherwise it would have to be admitted that Paul was dead at the time of the rapture, since the death of a man is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body; and thus that the Apostle was resuscitated from death after the rapture when returning to the body. Although indeed this seems entirely probable, that the soul was not separated from the body, or that a dissolution was made which brings about death, so that there is no need to posit a miraculous resuscitation from death, nor do we have to assert with Thomas Massutius, a theologian of Rain, that Paul speaks of a local rapture, and not merely a mental one: Concerning the soul, caught up into heaven not without the body, but with the body: Since neither is the heaven into which Paul was caught a place, nor if he was caught with the body does it follow that he was caught locally; since rapture can be explained as the elevation of the whole person to the divine presence and to apprehend, know, and contemplate supernatural objects. For it could be said that he was caught without the body without the intervention of death, if indeed it is understood that the soul was not caught without the body in the sense of a constituent part or informed by the soul, but without the body cooperating and admitted to the ἄῤῥητα: since that rapture was a cessation of animal functions in the body, and this rapture does not bring about dissolution but a concentration of the soul upon a supernatural object. For GOD, about to bring Paul to the ineffable happiness of the blessed, did not need for that to happen for the soul to be translated into heaven, but could also exhibit His essence to a mind enclosed in a body, so that the whole weight of that admirable glory could be viewed, while the senses meanwhile were dormant, as the blessed D. Henr. Philipp. Hervvartus, formerly our singular friend, discusses learnedly concerning these things in his work on Paul's rapture exhibited in the year 1671, p. 47. And he praises the supporting opinion of Antonius Gavissolius, a theologian of Montauban. Therefore, necessity does not compel us to posit that Paul doubted whether his soul was separated from his body, or whether he himself was dead or not? Likewise, whether he was translated from place to place in body and soul together? Or whether he had used his bodily senses (so asks the blessed Dn. D. Hervvartus, page 34) to know what was offered to him, and could he not have been ignorant that he had used his bodily senses if the external senses had exercised their act at that time; but alienated from the senses, he did not sufficiently understand, nor did he attend to what was being done around him, being wholly intent on those things which were offered (to the soul) to be viewed? Nor yet must we say with Cameron in his Myrothecium, page 234, that the rational and intelligent faculty is caught up, while the sensitive and vegetative remain. For thus the rational soul is established not only as distinct from the sensitive, but even as divided; (from which, however, Camero shrinks,) and the dogma of the Eutychian Jacobus Syrus concerning two souls in man, condemned in the IV Council of Constantinople, Can. X, and reprobated by Augustine in his book *de duabus animabus* against the Manichaeans, ch. XLI, will have to be admitted. Did the holy Apostle, therefore, doubt in this way: not whether he was alive or dead? not whether the soul then informed the body or not? Not whether his body was translated, or whether he perceived these things in his soul without any change of body? But whether he was admitted to the heavenly vision of GOD, and elevated to the perception of τῶν ἀῤῥήτων, with his body or without his body: since, as Thomas says, II. 5, while this state (of life) remains, the actual conversion to sensible things can be taken away from the soul, so that its elevation into that which exceeds all sensible things may not be hindered.

The same Thomas teaches in II. 2. q. 1. art. 5. that ecstasy occurs perfectly when, the natural and animal powers being bound, the intellect remains released, and the whole vigor of the soul is collected for intellection alone. In which manner he is otherwise said to be ἐν Πνεύματι γενέσθαι (to be in the Spirit), Apoc. ch. 1. v. 8. And with Augustine as author, Quæst. ad Simplic., ecstasy is an alienation from the senses of the body, so that the spirit of man, assumed by the divine Spirit, may be free for receiving and infusing images. Rapture, however, and ecstasy, as Thomas notes, II. 2. q. 178. art. 2., are distinguished only in that ecstasy simply imports an excess from oneself, according to which, namely, someone is placed outside his own ordering: But rapture superadds a certain violence, when indeed one is snatched into that which is different from that toward which his inclination tends, and thus it produces violence, not indeed from the reason of the term, but of the mode. And Estius confesses: It is enough for this passage that Paul is said to have been caught up to the third heaven for the reason that, with his mind alienated from the senses, he was elevated to know certain sublime and supernatural things in a perfect manner, just as the Angels who are in the heavens know them, so that by reason of this kind of cognition he is said to have been in the third heaven according to his soul or mind.

Moreover, with that doubt of the Apostle, whether he was in the body or out of the body, the blessed Hunnius presses the Reformed, who conceive of a corporeal and material heaven: If the heaven into which the Apostle was caught up were such a place, above all visible spheres: the cause for doubting would have been removed, and he would have established with certainty that this vision was shown to him outside the body: Since his body, still ψυχικὸν (natural) and infirm, could in no way have borne such a sudden rapture, which would happen in an instant, through innumerable miles and through so many obstructing bodies: But if that rapture had not happened in an instant, but by a certain succession of time, he could scarcely have arrived there in the space of some years. Let these things then be absurd; we, having rejected them, assert that by the appellation of heaven and Paradise, the state of the other life is designated in this Pauline vision rather than a place. Claudius Mammertus writes beautifully about this in book II of 'On the State of the Soul': Now therefore, if the Apostle was caught up through the stars and came as far as the third heaven, what did he find there above all? But if it had to be sought locally, and could not be found in the first heaven; yet he himself says he was caught up as far as the third heaven, and I know not what divine thing he heard, which it is not permitted for a man to speak. Is it so then, Apostle, that God is sought through places, or is truth not found except in a place? If that is so, then God will also be local, and you will lose locally the God whom you find locally: who, if He is not except in the third heaven, is therefore left to you there, where He was found. But since you are blessed not because of a corporeal heaven, but because of the Lord of heaven, and the Lord of heaven is wholly everywhere, who is neither sought locally nor found locally, etc.

The term is 'third heaven': by which designation it cannot be taught that Paul had regard for the partition of heaven used among the more recent Hebrews. It is not necessary that the third heaven be understood by reason of the number, since it can be called third by reason of excellence, because three is the number of perfection. Musculus departed here from other Reformed thinkers τοῖς ἀεροβατοῦσιν (who walk on air). For me, there is no doubt that the Apostle wished to signify that he had been caught up to the inner and more secret and more sublime secrets of heaven. Wherefore there is no need for us to dispute anxiously about the number of the heavens. But Calvin also confesses that the heavens are not distinguished here in the philosophical manner, but that the ternary number is placed κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence) for the highest and most perfect, indeed that heaven by itself here signifies the blessed and glorious kingdom of GOD. The blessed Glassius, whom the blessed Hervvartus also followed, judged in his mention of it that it refers to the temple of Solomon, which was a type of the eternal temple, Apoc. ch. XXI. v. 22: Let this name also be written among the secrets of sacred Grammar. It can be said with pious simplicity that Paul alludes to the constitution of the Jerusalem temple, which was tripartite, consisting of a vestibule or atrium, the holy place, and the holy of holies, in the third and innermost part of which the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat (that notable type of CHRIST, Rom. ch. III. v. 25) were placed, and in which, above the mercy seat between the Cherubim, GOD gave responses to His people and manifested Himself by that singular illumination, Exod. XXV. v. 22. The Apostle seems to make this third and innermost part of the temple a type of the blessed seats of heaven, where JESUS, the true mercy seat, shows Himself most clearly to be enjoyed by blessed souls. Cf. Heb. ch. VI. v. 19, 20. Estius himself rejects here Thomas, who makes three heavens below the soul, and three in the soul, and as many above the soul, and who posits a peculiar rapture to one of these, philosophizing with wondrous subtlety about a triple intellect of the three heavens.

Furthermore, Grotius rashly distinguishes the third heaven from Paradise (a thing which was also done by Drusius), understanding by the former the place of glory which the pious are to occupy after the resurrection; but by the latter, the place of solace after death and before the resurrection. That the third heaven and Paradise are not distinguished is manifest from the rapture of Paul. For if those seats are distinct, different raptures of Paul must be asserted: the former indeed into the third heaven, or the highest world, but the latter into Paradise. But if the letter of the ternary number be urged, in which, therefore, did he hear ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα, whether in the third heaven, or indeed in Paradise, to the mention of which that hearing is immediately subjected? Although Musculus does not deny that two raptures must be granted to Paul, one into the third heaven, that he might see the glory of God and of Christ reigning in heaven; the other into Paradise, that is, into the seat of the blessed spirits, of the Patriarchs and Prophets; and Salmero contends that there was not one rapture of Paul, but a double one, nevertheless the opinion of Augustine, book XII of 'On Genesis according to the letter', chapter 34, is to be preferred, that the Paradise of which the Apostle speaks is to be understood only in the third heaven. Hence it is called the paradise of paradises; nor ought the visions to be distinguished: for he makes mention of only the time when the rapture into heaven and paradise was made, nor does he report that he saw or heard at distinct times, but speaks as if of one rapture, in which he heard ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα. And who is unaware that Scripture is often accustomed to repeat the same thing in other words? Then indeed Musculus himself confesses that these things ought not to be distinguished. I would not, he says, distinguish here between the third heaven and the heavenly Paradise, the mansion of the blessed spirits, so that I might separate those who are in Paradise from Christ, since He said to the thief: Today you will be with me in Paradise, and this same Paul had it in his prayers to be dissolved and to be with Christ: And Thomas, that Angelic Doctor, himself refutes those who explain the words of Paul concerning a double rapture, whom Lyranus, Cajetanus, Catharinus, and other more recent ones support, however

Ambrosiaster, Primasius, and Anselm propose different raptures. Estius also confirms that there are not two distinct visions, but only one, and therefore a single rapture: First, because the Apostle did not ascribe any other time in the second place, besides that which he had placed at the beginning: 14 years. Then, because in the former part he does not say what he saw, heard, or did: but leaves each narrative to be supplemented by the other, as if nothing different happened in one than in the other. If, therefore, both visions are of the same time, and if he did not see or hear anything else in one than in the other, consequently the place was the same, and the vision was the same. He also adds the common sense of the Church, which, after Christ's ascension into heaven, recognizes no other paradise to which the prayers of the faithful aspire than the heavenly fatherland.

Indeed, he also admits in Luke 23, verse 43, that paradise is posited as a place of beatitude. Cornelius also acknowledges that Paradise and the third heaven are the same, even though he trifles that Paradise is separated in the vast Empyrean heaven (thus he calls the third heaven with other Papists); establishing that as the place of the blessed, and this as a more noble and EMINENT part of heaven. Furthermore, just as in the earthly paradise it was not so much a place of solace as of joy and pleasure, which the first-formed could perceive from their dealings with God, from eating of the tree of life, and from other innumerable delights: so it must be held far more eminently concerning the heavenly Paradise, that it is a place of both solace and immense joy, and where we shall enjoy the vision of God, eat of the tree of life, drink from the river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and the Lamb, Apoc. 2:7, chapter 22:1, etc., and shall be inebriated with other innumerable goods now incomprehensible and ineffable to us. That earthly Paradise was a storehouse of all happiness and joy, exceeding the entire understanding of sensible happiness, as Damascenus speaks in book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 11. Such, therefore, will also be the heavenly paradise, infinitely more excellent in the dignities of happiness, beauty, and joy.

Furthermore, Thomas, Cajetan, and Estius distinguish these names of the third heaven and Paradise more cleverly than solidly, not by reason of the place, but in this way: That the Apostle was caught up not only according to the intellective power for knowing certain sublime mysteries, which are insinuated by the third heaven, but also according to the will, for perceiving from such knowledge a certain special and ineffable sweetness, which is understood by the name of paradise. For paradise signifies a garden of pleasantness and pleasure. Meanwhile, we do not deny that by the name of the third heaven majesty and sublimity are implied, and by the name of Paradise happiness and pleasure.

Episcopius's exception in Institutiones Theologicae, chapter 11, p. 291. That Paul is not said to have been caught up precisely into the third heaven, but ἕως τρίτου ὀυρανῦ, as far as the third heaven, that is, to the vestibule of heaven; his explanation of which is such that not even he himself persists in it. For he says that if anyone wishes to interpret those words as into the third heaven itself, he does not wish to contend much against it. Nor does the opinion of Epiphanius in the Epistle to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, which exists among Jerome's epistles, deserve to be refuted, that the earthly Paradise, from which Adam was driven, is understood here.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Οἶδα ἄνθρωπον ἐν χρισῷ) Christianum. Hæc Paulus prædicat, quasi non sua, quasi diceret: - - - Quæ non fecimus ipsi Vix ea nostra puto. Ideo in tertia persona hoc eloquitur, ut ille in Controversiis Senecæ: Sicut contra ubi aliquid dicendum est, quod odiosum est, pro secunda persona primam assumit.

Πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων) Referam hoc ad illud, ἐν χρισῷ. Hominem talem, qui per annos jam quatuordecim Christo servierat.

Loquitur de se, juxta B. Balduinum, tan- quam de peregrino homine, partim ne ambitio- sus videatur, partim quia revera sibi ipsi tum ignotus fuit: Ignoravit enim an in corpore, an extra corpus fuerit. πρὸ ἐτῶν proprie est ante annos. Non ergo quot annis CHRI- STO jam servierit, sed ante quot annos hæc acciderint, refert. Atque hæc communis est Interpretum expositio. Nec vero tempore conversionis, ut cum Lyrano, Damaso in car- mine, & Ludov. Capello Histor. Eccles. cap. XXXIIX. Grotius vult, sed octennio post ean- dem raptum hunc contigisse, cum Salmerone, Pererio, Cornelio a Lapide, Estio, Baronius ad Ann. XLIV. aliique, qui temporis computum accuratius instituunt, docent: Cum paulo ante a discipulis Damasci per muros demissus esset, anno nempe Domini XLIV. Claudii Imperat. II. Quum conversio inciderit in annum Domini XXXVI; hæc epistola autem anno Domini LVI. scripta sit, Neronis II. unde colligunt, anno eo, quo prædicandi munus cum Barnaba accepit Actor. cap. XII. hanc visionem factam esse.

Εἴτε ἐν σώματι οὐκ οἶδα· εἴτε ἐκτὸς δὲ τοῦ σώματος οὐκ οἶδα, ὁ Θεὸς οἶδεν, ἁρπαγέντα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ) Est & hic trajectio. Nam illam εἴτε ἐν σώματι, & quæ se- quuntur in fine hujus versus poni naturaliter debuerant. Hebræi orbes, in cælo diversos, non agnoscunt, sed cœlum partiuntur in tres regiones, quarum prima est nu- bifera, altera astrifera, tertia Angelifera. Prima dicitur He- bræis עולם שפל, secunda עולם התיכון. Ter- tia עולם העליון. Alii primam vocant רקיע, secundam שמים, tertiam שמי שמים. Ergo tertium cœlum hic dicitur, quod alibi cælum cœlorum, cælum sum- mum, Angelicum. Potest autem evenire alicui, ut longe remota videat duplici modo, aut, si per Ange- lum aliquo avehatur, quod in Additamentis ad Danielem de Habacuco refertur, & quomodo a Satana avectus credi- tur CHRISTUS, aut ut sine loci mutatione ea, quæ sunt ab- sentia, tanquam præsentia ei exhibeantur, divinitus exci- tata specie, quomodo CHRISTUS vidit omnia regna mun- di, Ezechiel cum ad Chaboram esset, ea quæ gerebantur in templo Hierosolymitano. Dicit autem Paulus, nescire se, utro modo ei, de quo agit, id evenerit. Ἐν σώματι est cor- pore translato. Ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος est in anime, sine ulla corporis motione.

De hoc raptu ita habet Augustinus libr. XII. de Genes. ad literam cap. 5. Quod vidit raptus usque in tertium cælum, quod etiam se scire con- firmat, proprie vidit non imaginaliter. Sed quia ipsa a corpore alienatio, utrum omnino mortuum corpus reliquerit, an secundum modum quemdam viventis corporis ibi anima fuerit, sed mens ejus ad videnda vel audienda ineffabilia illius visionis arrepta sit, hoc incertum erat. Similiter de hac Paulina dubitatione de hoc raptu differit B. Hunnius, quod Paulo non constiterit, num visio sibi oblata sit in corpore existenti, an vero anima aliquandiu a corpore separata. B. Bal- duinus: Ignoravit, inquit, an in corpore fu- erit, an extra corpus, hoc est an corpore suo de loco in locum portatus, an vero per separationem anima a corpore ecstasin passus sit. B. Wein- richius ignorasse, ait, An corpore & anima simul fuerit raptus & translatus in sedem beato- rum an vero anima sola; ubi vero Thomas mo- net II. 2. q. 175. artic. 5. & 6. & Comm. in h. l. in hoc raptu Pauli animam non fuisse separatam a corpore, sed conjunctam mansisse, ita, ut mens tantum ejus, ad ea videnda vel audienda, quæ in raptu vidit vel audivit, esset a sensibus cor- poreis alienata. Cui sententiæ non abnuit E- stius; ex ea imprimis ratione, quod alias faten- dum esset, Paulum tempore raptus mortuum fuisse, siquidem mors hominis nihil aliud sit, quam animæ separatio a corpore; adeoque post raptum ad corpus revertente resuscitatum a morte fuisse Apostolum. Quanquam vero hoc omnino probabile videatur, animam non fuisse separa- tam a corpore, vel dissolutionem eam factam esse, quæ mortem infert, ne miraculosam e morte resuscitationem statuere opus sit, nec cum Thoma Massutio Theologo Rainetensi as- serere necessum habeamus, Paulum de raptu lo- cali, non vero mentali solum loqui: De anima, rapta in cælum non sine corpore, sed cum cor- pore: Quum neque cœlum, in quod Paulus raptus est, locus sit, nec si raptus cum corpore fuit, localiter ipsum raptum esse sequatur; quum explicari raptus possit de elevatione totius suppo- siti ad divinam præsentiam & objecta superna- turalia apprehendenda, cognoscenda, contem- planda. Rapta enim sine corpore dici possit citra interventum mortis, si scilicet intelligatur rapta non sine corpore anima in ratione partis consistentis vel ab anima informati, sed sine corpore cooperante & coadmisso ad ἄῤῥητα: si- quidem raptus ille cessatio fuerit animalium fun- ctionum in corpore, neque hic raptus inferat dissolutionem sed concentrationem animæ ad objectum supernaturale. Admoturus namque DEUS Paulum ad ineffabilem beatorum feli- citatem non opus habuit, ut id fieret, anima in cœlum translata, quin potuit etiam menti cor- pori inclusæ essentiam suam, ut totum admirandæ illius gloriæ pondus, sensibus interea feriantibus, spectandum exhibere, ut docte de hisce disserit B. D. Henr. Philipp. Hervvartus, amicus quon- dam noster singularis, in Pauli raptu Anno 1671. exhibito p. 47. Et suffragantem laudat Antonium Gavissolium Montalbanensem Theologum. Non ergo necessitas cogit, ut statuamus, Paulum de eo dubitasse, an anima separata fuerit a cor- pore, seu an mortuus ipse fuerit, necne? Item an corpore simul & anima de loco in locum trans- latus fuerit? Annon vero ita sensibus corporeis fuisset usus (sic quærit B. Dn. D. Hervvartus pag. 34.) ad cognoscenda, quæ sibi offereban- tur, neque potuisset ignorare, sensibus se cor- poreis fuisse usum, si actum suum exercuissent eo tempore sensus externi; abalienatus autem a sensibus non satis intellexit, neque attendit, quæ circa se gererentur, totus iis intentus, quæ spectanda (animæ) offerebantur? Neque ta- men cum Camerone in myrothecio pag. 234. di- cendum; facultatem rationalem & intelligentem rapi, manente sensitiva & vegetativa. Sic enim non tantum distincta statuitur anima rationalis a sensitiva, sed etiam divisa; (a quo vero ab- horret Camero,) & Jacobi Syri Eutychiani dogma de duabus animabus in homine in Con- cil. Constantinop. IV. Can. X. damnatum, & ab Augustino libr. de duabus animabus contra Manich. cap. XLI. reprobatum, admittendum erit. Dubitavit ergo ita S. Apostolus, non vivusne an mortuus fuerit? non an anima tum corpus informaverit, necne? Non an trans- lato corpore an vero sine ulla corporis mutatione in anima hæc senserit? Sed an anima cum cor- pore, an sine corpore admissa fuerit ad cælestem DEI visionem, & elevata ad perceptionem τῶν ἀῤῥήτων: Quum dicente Thoma II. 5. manente hoc (vitæ) statu auferri ab anima possit actualis conversio ad sensibilia, ne impediatur ejus ele- vatio in id, quod omnia sensibilia excedit.

Quod idem Thomas II. 2. quæst. 1. art. 5. docet, ecstasin perfecte fieri, quando naturalibus & animalibus viribus ligatis, solutus manet intellectus, & totus vigor animæ collectus est ad solam intellectionem. Quo pacto alias dicitur ἐν Πνεύματι γενέσθαι Apoc. cap. 1. v. 8. & Augustino autore Quæst. ad Simplic. Ecstasis alienatio est a sensibus corporis, ut spiritus hominis divino Spiritu assumptus capiendis atque infundendis imaginibus vacet. Raptus autem, & ecstasis, notante Thoma, II. 2. quæst. 178. art. 2. ita solum distinguuntur, quod ecstasis simpliciter importet excessum a seipso, secundum quem scilicet aliquis extra suam ordinationem ponitur: Sed raptus superaddat violentiam quandam, quando nimirum rapitur in id, quod est diversum ab eo, in quod ejus inclinatio tendit, & ita parit violentiam, non quidem ex ratione termini, sed modi. Fateturque Estius: Satis esse huic loco, Paulum idcirco dici raptum ad tertium cœlum, quod animo a sensibus alienato fuerit elevatus ad sublimia quædam & supernaturalia perfecto quodam modo cognoscenda, quomodo ea cognoscunt Angeli, qui in cœlis sunt, ut ratione hujusmodi cognitionis in tertio cœlo secundum animam aut mentem fuisse dicatur.

Cæterum dubitatione illa Apostoli, num in corpore an extra corpus fuerit, premit B. Hunnius Reformatos, cœlum corporeum & materiale concipientes: Si cœlum in quod raptus est Apostolus, talis esset locus, supra sphæras omnes aspectabiles: sublata fuisset dubitandi causa, & statuisset certo extra corpus eam visionem sibi commonstratam: Quandoquidem corpus ejus adhuc ψυχικὸν animale & infirmum hujusmodi raptum subitaneum, qui in instanti fieret, per innumerabilia milliaria, perque tot obstantia corpora ferre nullo modo potuisset: Sin vero raptus ille non in instanti, sed quadam temporis succesfione factus esset, vix aliquot annorum spatio potuisset eo pervenire. Hæc tum sint absurda, nos iis rejectis afferimus cœli & Paradisi appellatione statum potius alterius seculi, quam locum in hac quidem Paulina visione designari. Pulchre de hoc Claudius Mammertus libr. II. de statu animæ: Nunc igitur, si per sidera raptus Apostolus usque in tertium cœlum venit, quid istinc potissimum reperit? Quod si localiter quærendum fuit, & in primo cœlo inveniri non potuit; sed ipse dicit raptum sese usque in tertium cœlum, nescio quid audivisse divinum, quod homini loqui non liceat. Itane tandem Apostole, per loca Deus quæritur, aut non nisi loco veritas invenitur? Si istud ita est, & Deus igitur localis erit, & tu Deum, quem localiter invenis, localiter amittis: qui si non, nisi in tertio cœlo est, ibi ergo tibi relictus, ubi repertus est. At cum non de cœlo corporeo, sed de cæli Domino sis beatus, & totus ubique sit Dominus cæli, qui nec localiter quæritur, nec localiter invenitur, &c.

Terminus est tertium cælum: qua denotatione Paulum cœli partitionem apud recentiores Ebræos usitatam respexisse, doceri nequit. Non necessum est, ut ratione numeri tertium intelligatur cœlum, quum tertium dici possit ratione excellentiæ, quia ternarius perfectionis est numerus. Musculus discessit hic ab aliis Reformatis τοῖς ἀεροβατοῦσιν. Mihi non est dubium, voluisse Apostolum ad interiora se & secretiora, sublimioraque cæli secreta fuisse raptum, significare. Quare non est, ut anxie de numero cælorum disputemus. Sed & Calvinus fatetur, cœlos hîc non distingui Philosophico more, sed numerum ternarium κατ’ ἐξοχὴν poni pro summo & perfectissimo, imo cælum per se hîc significare beatum & gloriosum DEI regnum. B. Glassius, quem & B. Hervvartus sequutus est, ejus men- tione, respici ad templum Salomonis, quod typus erat templi æterni Apoc. cap. XXI. v. 22. censuit: Scribatur & hoc nomen inter occulta Grammatices sacræ. Simplicitate pia dici pot- est, alludere Paulum ad constitutionem templi Hierosolymitani, quod tripartitum erat vestibulo seu atrio, sancto, & sancto sanctorum constans, in quorum tertia & intima parte arca fœderis & pro- pitiatorium (typus ille CHRISTI insignis Rom. cap. III. vers. 25.) collocata erant, & in quo su- per propitiatorio inter Cherubim, DEUS re- sponsa populo suo dabat, seseque singulari illa- stratione manifestabat Exod. XXV. v. 22. Hanc tertiam & intimam templi partem facere videtur Apostolus typum beatarum cæli sedium, ubi JE- SUS, verum propitiatorium se clarissime fruen- dum beatis animabus exhibet. Conf. Ebr. cap. VI. vers. 19. 20. Thomam, qui tres facit cœlos infra animam, & tres in anima & totidem su- pra animam, atque ad unum quod istorum po- nit raptum peculiarem, ac mira subtilitate phi- losophantem de triplici intellectu trium cœlo- rum, rejicit hic ipse Estius.

Porro temere cœlum tertium distinguit a Pa- radiso Grotius (id quod etiam a Drusio factum) per illud locum gloriæ, quem post resurrectio- nem pii occupaturi sint; per hunc vero locum solatii post mortem & ante resurrectionem, intel- ligens. Non distingui cœlum tertium & Pa- radisum, e raptu Pauli manifestum est. Nam si distinctæ illæ sedes sint, diversi raptus Pauli asserendi erunt: Et prior quidem in tertium cœlum, vel mundum supremum, posterior vero in Paradisum. Si vero urgeatur numeri ternarii litera, in quo ergo ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα au- divit, num in cælo tertio, an vero in Paradiso, cujus mentioni subjicitur immediate ἀκοὴ illa? Quanquam vero non abnuat Musculus duos ra- ptus Paulo concedendos esse, unum in tertium cœlum, ut videret gloriam DEI & regnantis in cœlo CHRISTI; alterum in Paradisum, hoc est in sedem beatorum Spirituum, Patriarcha- rum ac Prophetarum; & Salmero non unum Pauli raptum, sed duplicem fuisse contendat, præferenda tamen Augustini, libr. XII. de Ge- nes. ad literam cap. 34. sententia, Paradisum de quo Apostolus non nisi in tertio cælo intelligi. Hinc vocari paradisum paradisorum; neque vi- siones distingui debere: Nam non nisi tem- poris mentionem facit, quo raptus in cœlum & paradisum factus, nec quod distinctis vici- bus viderit vel audiverit, refert, sed tanquam de uno raptu, in quo ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα audiverit, loquitur. Et quem latet, quod sæpe Scriptura rem eandem aliis verbis repetere soleat. Tum vero fatetur ipse Musculus hæc distinguenda non esse. Nolim, inquit, hic inter tertium cœ- lum, & Paradisum cælestem beatorum Spiri- tuum mansionem distinguere, ut eos, qui in Pa- radiso sunt, a CHRISTO separem, cum ad latronem ille dixerit: Hodie mecum eris in Pa- radiso, & hic ipse Paulus dissolvi & cum Chri- sto esse in votis habuerit: Ac Thomas, Doctor ille Angelicus refellat ipse eos, qui de duplici raptu verba Pauli explicant, cui suffragantur Lyra- nus, Cajetanus, Catharinus, aliique recentiores, utut

Ambrosiaster, Primasius & Anselmus diver- sos raptus faciant. Estius etiam confirmat, non duas esse distinctas visiones, sed unam tantum, adeoque unicum raptum: Primo, quod secundo loco non aliud tempus adscripserit Apostolus, præter illud, quod initio posuerat 14. annos: Deinde quod in priori parte non dicat, quod viderit, audiverit vel egerit: sed utramque narrationem ex altera supplendam relinquat, quasi nihil diversum in una, quam in altera con- tigerit. Si ergo ejusdem temporis utraque vi- sio est, & si non alia vidit, vel audivit in una, quam in altera, consequenter & locus idem fuit, & eadem visio. Addit & communem Ec- clesiæ sensum, quæ post Christi in cælos ascensio- nem non alium agnoscat paradisum, ad quem fidelium vota suspirent, quam patriam cælestem.

Imo fatetur & Luc. XXIII. vers. 43. paradisum pro loco beatitudinis poni. Cornelius etiam Pa- radisum & tertium cœlum idem esse agnoscit, etsi nugetur in cælo Empyreo vastissimo (ita tertium cœlum vocat cum aliis Papisequis) separatum esse Paradisum; Illud locum beatorum, hunc quasi partem cæli nobiliorem & EMINENTIO- REM constituens. Cæterum ut in paradiso ter- reno non tam locus solatii erat, quam gaudii & vo- luptatis, quam ex commerciis cum Deo, ex esu arboris vitæ, & ex aliis deliciis innumeris perci- pere poterant Protoplasti: Sic de Paradiso cœlesti longe eminentius habendum, quod locus sit & solatii & gaudii immensi, & ubi Dei visione frue- mur, de ligno vitæ edemus, de fluvio aquæ vivæ bibemus, splendido tanquam crystallo, procedente de sede Dei & agni Apoc. II. v. 7. cap. XXII. 1. seqq. aliisque innumeris jam nobis incomprehensibi- libus & ineffabilibus bonis, inebriabimur. Ter- restris ille Paradisus fuit omnis felicitatis & læti- tiæ ταμεῖον, universam sensibilis felicitatis intelli- gentiam excedens, ut loquitur Damascenus l. II. Orthod. fid. c. II. Talis ergo etiam erit paradisus cælestis, felicitatis, venustatis & gaudii ἀξιώμασι in- finities excellentior.

Porro distinguunt hæc nomina cæli tertii & Pa- radisi Thomas, Cajetanus & Estius magis argute, quam solide, non ratione loci, sed hoc modo: Quod Apostolus raptus fuerit non solum secundum vim intellectivam ad cognoscendum sublimia myste- ria quædam, quæ insinuantur per tertium cælum, verum etiam secundum voluntatem, ad percipien- dum ex hujusmodi cognitione specialem quan- dam & ineffabilem suavitatem, quod intelligitur nomine paradisi. Nam paradisus hortum signifi- cat amœnitatis ac voluptatis. Interim nomine tertii cæli majestatem & sublimitatem, nomine Paradisi felicitatem & voluptatem innui non ab- nuimus.

Episcopii exceptio Institut. Theol. cap. XI. p. 291. Paulum non dici præcise raptum in tertium cœ- lum, sed ἕως τρίτου ὀυρανῦ usque ad tertium cælum, id est ad cæli vestibulum; quæ ejus explicatio talis est, ut nec ipse in eodem subsistat. Ait enim, si quis verba illa interpretari velit in ipsum usque ter- tium cœlum, se nolle admodum contra contendere. Nec confutari meretur Epiphanii in Epist. ad Joh. Episc. Jerosol. quæ inter Hieronymi epistolas ex- tat, sententia, Paradisum terrestrem, e quo Adam fuit pulsus, hic intelligi.

## 12:4
Verse 4. (Ὅτι ἡρπάγη εἰς τὸν παράδεισον) According to the custom of the Hebrews, heaven, or the supreme world, is distinguished from Paradise. That supreme heaven is promised to the pious after the resurrection; Paradise after death and before the resurrection: the former is the place of glory, the latter of solace. We have spoken about that matter on Luke chapter 23, verse 43. You will find the same distinction in Rabbi Israel on the soul. And Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact understand Paradise here as something distinct from the third heaven. Hesychius פסק.

Καὶ ἤκουσεν ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λα- λῆσαι) Just as Moses had understood all that dispensation by which GOD protected and ruled the Israelite people, so Paul understood that by which CHRIST governs His Church, whence it happened that he was more apt at giving counsel than Peter himself, who held the primacy in the Church. But these things, which he had understood, he was forbidden to utter.

Concerning those things which he heard in the third heaven and paradise, the Apostle has nothing more than that they were ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα. Whence, therefore, does Grotius have it that he himself received all that dispensation by which CHRIST governs His Church? That conjecture, which he seeks from the conversation of Moses with GOD, does not apply here. For it is nowhere said that the things which Moses had received from GOD were ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα; and they can be gathered from that record: but it is evident by no indication that the Apostle received in the third heaven things that would serve to govern the Church. He undoubtedly received the things which he committed to writing from CHRIST, but through the divine inspiration of the writings which he penned, and not indeed through a rapture into the third heaven or Paradise. For the rest, Grotius should have settled with the Papists concerning that eulogy of Paul, that he was more apt than Peter himself in giving counsel necessary for governing the Church, which one would not easily reconcile with the axiom attributed to Peter by the Papists, that he was constituted by CHRIST as the ecumenical vicar and head of the Church. Furthermore, ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα are not things which he was forbidden to utter, but ineffable things, or things which he could not bring forth. Clement of Alexandria refers it to the ineffable nature of GOD in book 5 of the Stromata. Τὸ ἄῥῥητον τῶ θεῶ ἕτως ἀινισσόμενον ἐν νόμῳ καὶ Φόβῳ παραγγε- λίας τινὸς, τὸ οὐκ ἐξὸν προσίσεις, δυνάμει δὲ ἀγίᾳ ἄφθεγκτον εἶναι τὸ θεῖον μυών: thus signifying the ineffable knowledge of GOD, and not adding that τὸ μὴ ἐξὸν, as if from the fear of some law or mandate; but rather to indicate that the divine name is of such a kind that it cannot be explained by any power, not even by that of the saints. Therefore, those things which Camero discusses at length here do not deserve assent, that they are called ἄῥῥητα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν λαλῆσαι ἀνθρώπῳ, which it is not permitted for any man to utter, so that τὸ licet denotes not power, but authority and right. For as Beza rightly says: It is certain that ἄῥῥητα are properly called, not those things which should not be spoken of generally; but those which cannot be spoken of, from which proper meaning one should not rashly depart. Thus Aphrodisæus called ἀῥῥήτυς ἰδιότητας inexplicable properties. To Hermes, GOD is called ἄῥῥητος, ἀνεκλάλητος. To the Hebrews, the τετραγράμματον is called ἄῥῥητον ἀνέκ- φρασον, ineffable. And those ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν, not inconveniently Beza: Ἀδύνατον or οὐχ οἷον δέ ἐςι, because clearly he could not even grasp them sufficiently in his mind, let alone be able to explain them in words. That passage, therefore, does nothing for those who dream of a certain secret Theology, and transform the Christian religion into Eleusinian mysteries, which it is impossible for a man to utter. For those things are least of all permitted which exceed the capacity of our nature, whence ἐξυσία is called not only συγχώρησις, that is, concession and permission; but the very power and force to effect something.

Which he confirms by the words of Clement recently cited. B. Glassius: More correctly, he says, ἐκ ἐξὸν, not permitted, is asserted to be equivalent to the impossible. For those things are least of all permitted which exceed the grasp and capacity of our nature. Whence ἐξουsία is said to be not only συγχώρησις, concession, permission, but the very power and force of effecting something. Estius notes that this sense pleases not a few, and he approves it. For that is accustomed to be called ineffable which it is not possible for man to utter or explain in words. Thus the same Apostle above in chapter IX calls the gift of GOD ineffable, and in Romans VIII he called groanings ineffable, and Peter in the first epistle chapter I, ineffable joy. And this sense is also more approved by B. Thomas. Therefore the Apostle feels that those things which he heard are such and so great that they cannot be explained in human words, since the magnitude of the matter exceeds the capacity of human speech. Chrysostom refers the τὰ ἄῥάητα to the most eminent glory of the humanity of Christ among the blessed, which is truly incomprehensible and ineffable. Theodoret refers them to the beauty of Paradise, the joys of the blessed, and the numerous and modulated voice of celestial hymns. Saint Peter calls celestial joy ἀνεκλάλητον, 1 Epist. I. 8. Episcopius, book IV, Institut. Sect. IV, cap. XII, p. 253, explains ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα thus, that is: Words containing mysteries and secrets so grand and so sublime pertaining to the celestial Paradise and the glory of Paradise, that to accommodate them to the state of mortal words would be as much as to wish to depreciate them and render them vile, as appears from that which he immediately adds, ἃ ἐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι, which it is not permitted for man to utter, because clearly it would be beneath their dignity, whatever might be brought forth about them in human words by men living in this flesh. By the words, however, I understand metonymically the thing, or the joy which Paul had perceived from those words, but not the sense itself comprehended by the words. By τὸ ἐξὸν, however, both power and authority: Power, because that joy could not be explained by speaking; authority, because it was not right that it should be announced otherwise than worthily and according to the majesty due to it. And while Camero concedes that Paul had a certain secret knowledge of divine things (which he received here), which he did not communicate to the Church, heretics can easily seize an opportunity from that, that not all things which were revealed to him were comprehended in his writings, that some of them were handed down to the Church, to the extent that he would not keep them for himself alone through faith, just as Beza notes that Castellio and other fanatics persuade the unlearned: that Paul wrote only certain rudiments in his epistles; but that he had certain more perfect things which he would teach to the perfect, and from these words they have invented a peculiar book of Cajanus, the ἀποκά- λυψιν or Ascension of Paul, about which Epiphanius speaks in Haeres. XXXIIX. Papists, however, as is evident from Cornelius à Lapide on this passage, conclude that Dionysius in book 5 of the Celestial Hierarchy describes the orders of Angels from the doctrine of St. Paul, when Gregory the Great, Homily IV on Ezekiel, asserts that he heard wonderful things about the nature, gifts, grace, glory, and orders of the Angels. How Camero can sufficiently ἐπιsομίζειν this does not appear. Nor does the argument of Camero hold: Paul undoubtedly perceived these things which he saw with his mind. Therefore he could also express them. Let it be, therefore, that he could not utter them according to the dignity of the things: Yet he could describe them to a certain extent. For we concede that he perceived those things in the third heaven with his mind, which he either saw or heard. But whether those things remained in his mind after that vision ceased, we shall certainly affirm; so that they could only be expressed to a certain extent, since Paul himself did not even know for certain whether he perceived those things in the body or out of the body. Finally, Camero himself concedes that the common explanation can be admitted, by which Paul's words are taken not of authority, but of power. And he says we will not morosely disagree that this could have been the mind of Paul.

But if it be asked: For what purpose did he hear what he could neither utter nor ought to have uttered? B. Glassius answers: Nay, this hearing of the ἀῥῥήτων was most profitable both to Paul and to us men. To him, so that in the most grievous temptations, dangers, and adversities to be endured in the Apostolic office, he might remain unconquered, confirmed by that wonderful and divine reason against so many cohorts of devils and other enemies. To us, so that, being taught about the admirable glory and majesty of the heavens, we might abstain from excessive searching, and yet with pious simplicity might sigh for it and strive for it continually.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὅτι ἡρπάγη εἰς τὸν παράδεισον) More He- bræorum distinguitur cœlum, sive mundus supremus, a Paradiso. Cœlum illud supremum promittitur piis post resurrectionem; post mortem & ante resurrectio- nem Paradisus : ille locus gloriæ, hic solatii. Diximus ea de re ad Lucam cap. XXIII. vers. 43. Reperies idem discrimen apud Rabbinum Israëlem de anima. Et di- stinctum quid, a cœlo tertio, Paradisum intelligunt hic Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus. Hesychius פסק•

Καὶ ἤκουσεν ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λα- λῆσαι) Sicut Moses intellexerat omnem illam dispensa- tionem, qua DEUS populum Israëliticum tuebatur & regebat, sic Paulus illam, per quam CHRISTUS Eccle- siam suam gubernat, unde factum est, ut ad danda con- silia aptior fuerit ipso Petro, qui primas in Ecclesia tene- bat. Sed hæc, quæ intellexerat, vetitus fuit enuntia- re.

De illis quæ audivit in tertio cœlo & para- diso, nihil amplius habet Apostolus, quam quod fuerint ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα. Unde ergo id habet Grotius, quod omnem illam dispensatio- nem, quæ CHRISTUS Ecclesiam suam gu- bernat, ipse acceperit? Conjectura illa, quam petit ex conversatione Mosis cum DEO, huc non facit. Nam quæ Moses a DEO accepe- rat, ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα fuisse nuspiam dicitur; & ex consignatione illa colligi possunt: Aposto- lum vero in tertio cœlo accepisse, quæ ad gu- bernandam Ecclesiam facerent, nullo indicio constat. Accepit sine dubio ea, quæ in literas redegit, a CHRISTO, sed per θεόπνευ- σίαν literarum, quas exaravit, non vero per raptum in tertium cœlum vel Paradisum. De cætero transigendum fuerat Grotio cum Papi- stis de illo elogio Pauli, quod aptior fuerit ipso Petro in dandis consiliis ad Ecclesiam gubernan- dam necessariis, quæ cum axiomate Petro a Pa- pisæquis tributo, quod vicarius œcumenicus, & caput Ecclesiæ constitutus fuerit a CHRI- STO non facile quis conciliaverit. Porro ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα non sunt, quæ vetitus fuit enun- tiare, sed ineffabilia, vel quæ non potuit pro- ferre. Clemens Alexandrinus refert ad ineffa- bilem DEI naturam libr. V. Strom. Τὸ ἄῥῥητον τῶ θεῶ ἕτως ἀινισσόμενον ἐν νόμῳ καὶ Φόβῳ παραγγε- λίας τινὸς, τὸ οὐκ ἐξὸν προσίσεις, δυνάμει δὲ ἀγίᾳ ἄφθεγκτον εἶναι τὸ θεῖον μυών : ita significans DEI ineffabilem notitiam, neque illud τὸ μὴ ἐξὸν adjiciens, quasi ex legis aut mandati alicu- jus metu; sed ut indicet potius divinum nomen ejusmodi esse, ut nulla vi, ne sanctorum quidem explicari possit. Non ergo assensum merentur, quæ prolixe hic disputat Camero, ἄῥῥητα dici, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν λαλῆσαι ἀνθρώπῳ, quæ non licet eloqui ulli homini, ut τὸ licet non potentiam, sed po- testatem & jus denotet. Nam ut recte Beza: Certum est ἄῥῥητα proprie dici, non quæ pas- sim dici non debeant; sed quæ non possint di- ci, a qua significatione propria non est te- mere discedendum. Ita Aphrodisæus ἀῥῥήτυς ἰδιότητας dixit proprietates inexplicabiles. Her- meti DEUS dicitur ἄῥῥητος, ἀνεκλάλητος. Hebræis τετραγράμματον dicitur ἄῥῥητον ἀνέκ- φρασον ineffabile. Et illa ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν non inconve- nienter Beza: Ἀδύνατον vel οὐχ οἷον δέ ἐςι, quo- niam videlicet ne animo quidem satis complecti illa poterat, nedum ut verbis posset ea explica- re. Iste locus igitur nil pro iis facit, qui arca- nam quandam Theologiam somniant, & Christia- nam religionem in Eleusinia mysteria transfor- mant, quæ impossibile sit homini eloqui. Nam ea minime omnium licent, quæ naturæ nostræ ca- ptum excedunt, unde ἐξυσία dicitur non tan- tum, συγχώρησις, id est concessio ac permissio; sed ipsa potestas & vis ad aliquid efficiendum.

Quae verbis Clementis proxime adductis confir- mat. B. Glassius: Rectius, inquit, ἐκ ἐξὸν non li- citum, τῷ impossibili æquipollere asseritur. Nam ea minimè omnium licent, quæ naturæ nostræ captum & facultatem superant. Unde ἐξουsía non tantum dicitur συγχώρησις concessio, permissio, sed ipsa po- testas & vis aliquid efficiendi. Estius notat, non paucis placere hunc sensum, eumque probat. Học enim dici solet ineffabile, quod homini non est possibi- le eloqui seu verbis explicare. Sic idem Apostolus supra cap. IX. donum DEI inenarrabile vocat & Roman. VIII. gemitus inenarrabiles dixit & Pe- trus 1. epistolæ cap. I. lætitiam inenarrabilem. At- que hic sensus etiam B. Thomæ magis probatur. Itá- que sentit Apostolus, illa, quæ audivit, talia & tan- ta esse, ut ea verbis humanis explicari nequeant, quippe cum rei magnitudo facultatem humani ser- monis excedat. Chrysostomus ad τὰ ἄῥάητα refert humanitatis Christi inter beatos gloriam eminentis- simam, quæ vere incomprehensibilis est, & inef- fabilis. Theodoretus pulchritudinem Paradisi, gau- dia beatorum, numerosam & modulatam hymno- rum cœlestium vocem. Sanctus Petrus cœleste gaudium dicit ἀνεκλάλητον, 1. Epist. I. 8. Episcopius libr. IV. Institut. Sect. IV. cap. XII. p: 253. ἄῥῥητα ῥήματα ita explicat, id est: Verba continentia tam grandia tam sublimia mysteria atque arcana ad cœ- lestem Paradisum & Paradisi gloriam pertinentia, ut ea verbis mortalium statui accommodare tantun- dem esset, atque ea depreciare velle, & vilia reddere, uti apparet ex eo, quod statim addit, ἃ ἐκ ἐξὸν ἀν- θρώπῳ λαλῆσαι, quæ non licet homini eloqui, quia videlicet infra dignitatem eorum esset, quicquid de iis, verbis humanis, ab hominibus in carne hac ver- santibus proferretur. Per verba autem intelligo Metonymicè rem, sive gaudium, quod ex verbis istis perceperat Paulus, non autem sensum ipsum verbis comprehensum. Per τὸ ἐξὸν vero tum poten- tiam tum potestatem: Potentiam, quia gaudium istud fando explicari non poterat: Potestatem quia fas non erat, ut istud aliter, quam condigne & pro majestate ei debita enuntiaretur. Et dum Camero concedit, Paulum habuisse cognitionem quandam rerum divinarum arcanam, (quam hic acceperit) quam cum Ecclesia non communicavit, facile inde ansam arripere possunt Hæretici, non omnia, quæ ipsi revelata sunt, scriptis ejus comprehensa, quæ- dam eorum tradita esse Ecclesiæ, eatenus, ne ea- dem per fidem sibi soli retineret, quemadmodum Beza notat, Castellionem & fanaticos alios impe- ritis persuadere: Paulum in epistolis suis rudimen- ta quædam duntaxat scripsisse; cæterum perfectio- ra quædam habuisse, quæ perfectos doceret, & Cajani ex his verbis peculiarem librum ἀποκά- λυψιν seu Ascensum Pauli commenti sunt, de quo Epiphanius Hæres. XXXIIX. Papista vero, ut ex Cornelio à Lapide in hunc loc. constat, colligunt, Dionysium libr. 5. de cælesti hierarchia ex S. Pauli doctrina ordines Angelorum describere, quum Gregorius M. Homil. IV. in Ezechiel. mira de Angelorum natura, dotibus, gratia, gloria & or- dinibus audivisse asserat. Quod quomodo suffi- cienter ἐπιsομίζειν possit Camero, non apparet. Neque vero stringit argumentum Cameronis: Pau- lus hac, quæ vidit, percepit animo baud dubie. Ergo etiam exprimere potuit. Esto igitur, quod ea effari non potuerit pro dignitate rerum: At quadantenus potuit describere. Nam concedimus ea animo per- cepisse in cœlo tertio, quæ vel vidit vel audivit. An vero postquam desuit illa visio, animo ea hæsisse, certo affirmabimus; ita ut quadantenus solum exprimi potuerint, quum ne id quidem certò sciverit Paulus ipse, an in corpore, an vero extra corpus illa perceperit. Denique concit Camero ipse, communem explicationem posse ad- mitti; quà Pauli verba non de potestate, sed de potentia accipiuntur. Potuisse autem, inquit, eam esse mentem Pauli non morose refragabimur.

Quod si quæratur: Quo fine audierit, quod eloqui nec potuerit, nec debuerit? Respondet B. Glassius: Imo & Paulo maxime profuit hac ἀῥῥήτων auditio, & nobis hominibus. Illi, ut in gravissimis tentationibus, periculis & adversitatibus in Aposto- lico munere perferendis, contra tot Diabolorum ali- orumque hostium cohortes mira isthac & divina ra- tione confirmatus perstaret invictus. Nobis, ut de sublimi cælorum gloria & majestate admiranda edocti à nimia scrutatione abstineremus, & pia tamen simplicitate ad eam suspiraremus jugiter ac contenderemus.

## 12:5
v. 5. ὑπὲρ τῦ τοιύτυ καυχήσομαι) the future for the potential, in the Hebrew manner. Of such a man I could rejoice and exult.

ὑπὲρ δὲ ἐμαυτῦ ὐ καυχήσομαι, εἰ μὴ ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις με) I will not say what I have done, but what I have endured, for that is less invidious: And there are few who would seek the fellowship of such joy.

Latin:

v. 5. ὑπὲρ τῦ τοιύτυ καυχήσομαι) futurum pro poten- tiali, more Hebræo. De tali homine gaudere & exultare possem.

ὑπὲρ δὲ ἐμαυτῦ ὐ καυχήσομαι, εἰ μὴ ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις με) Non dicam quæ feci, sed quæ pertuli, id enim minus invidiosum est: Et pauci sunt, qui talis gaudii societatem appetant.

## 12:6
v. 6. Ἐὰν γὰρ θελήσω καυχήσασθαι, ὐκ ἔσομαι ἄφρων) If I wished to say something about my deeds, I would have no need of vain talk. Enough truth would be available to me. We had ἄφρων before for ὡς ἄφρων. Here, however, he is more properly called ἄφρων who, because of his vanity, ascribes to himself what is not his: Fools do this, whom empty glory vexes.

Ἀλήθειαν γὰρ ἐρῶ) For I would speak the truth.

Φείδομαι δὲ) I purposely abstain from the mention of those things.

Μή τις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται, ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με, ἢ ἀκούει τι ἐξ ἐμῦ) I do not want anyone to estimate me from anything other than the very things which he himself has seen me doing, or hears me teaching. The present things suffice for me; I prefer to hide the past in silence.

Commodè Musculus, whom B. Glassius praises here as a most skillful interpreter of Scripture (in most places): He does not say, above that which I am, but above that which he sees me to be, or which he hears from me. The Apostle was a minister of Christ and a steward of the mysteries of GOD. That was manifest. Certain proofs of this were seen and heard from him. He does not want anything to be attributed to him beyond that; in 1 Cor. IV he says: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of GOD. He took diligent care that he should not be valued more highly. It is known what happened to him and Barnabas, Acts XIV, when he had raised the lame man to his feet, etc. B. Hunnius: He hints, he says, that not all things about which he could boast have been mentioned by him, for he is studious to shorten his sails and to cut short this discussion, not because he could not extend it further with truth, but because he spares the Corinthians, lest he stir up suspicion among them as if he were overstepping the mark of Christian modesty, or even lest he seem to affect among them a greater authority than is fitting, by which he might exceed the mode and measure of Apostolic dignity.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἐὰν γὰρ θελήσω καυχήσασθαι, ὐκ ἔσομαι ἄφρων) Si de factis meis dicere aliquid vellem, nihil mihi opus esset vaniloquentia. Satis verum mihi suppeteret. Ἄφρων an- tea habuimus pro ὡς ἄφρων. Hic vero magis proprie ἄφρων dicitur, qui διὰ τὴν χαυνότητα sibi non sua adscribit: Hoc faciunt stulti, quos gloria vexat inanis.

Ἀλήθειαν γὰρ ἐρῶ) Dicerem enim vera.

Φείδομαι δὲ) Consulto ab illarum rerum commemora- tione abstineo.

Μή τις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται, ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με, ἢ ἀκούει τι ἐξ ἐμῦ) Nolo quisquam me aliunde æstimet, quam ex ipsis, quæ ipse vidit me facientem, aut docentem audit. Præsen- tia mihi sufficiunt; Præterita malo occultare silentio.

Commodè Musculus, quem hic laudat B. Glas- sius, ceu scripturæ (in plerisque) dexterrimum interpretem: Non dicit, supra id, quod sum, sed supra id, quod videt esse me, aut quod audit ex me. Erat Apostolus Christi, minister ac dispensator my- steriorum DEI. Id erat manifestum. Videbantur & audiebantur ex eo certa hujus experimenta. Su- pra id non vult tribui sibi quicquam, 1. Cor. IV. dicit: Sic nos æstimet homo, ut ministros Christi & dispen- satores mysteriorum DEI. Ne pluris fieret, sedulo cavebat. Notum est, quid acciderit ipsi & Barna- bæ, Act. XIV. cum claudum hominem in pedes ere- xiffet &c. B. Hunnius: Subinnuit, inquit, non omnia, de quibus gloriari posset, à se esse comme- morata, studio enim se vela contrahere, & præscin- dere hanc tractationem, non quod non cum veritate possit eam amplius deducere, sed quod parcat Co- rinthiis, ne suspicionem apud illos concitet, quasi metam transiliat Christiana modestia, vel etiam ne videatur affectare apud illos majorem, quam par sit, autoritatem, qua modum & mensuram exce- dat Apostolica dignitatis.

## 12:7
Καὶ τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι) Also because of those revelations which I mentioned, lest I be exalted, a heavy bridle was given to me.

From that ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων some infer that in this rapture the Apostle saw the divine essence, which Augustine did not hesitate to affirm in De Genesi ad litteram, ch. 27, and Epist. CXII to Paulinus; Bede, Anselm on this passage, Hugo of St. Victor on this passage, Thomas II. 2. q. 175. art. 3. For if he had not reached that degree of blessedness, the excellence of the revelations would not have occurred at all. Nor does a contradiction seem to be involved if it is said that he saw the essence by a temporary divine intuition, whether through the illumination of the light of glory, or without the light of glory by a mind elevated through the absolute power of God to such a blessed intuition by way of a transient act. Nor from that does the deterioration of the competent state follow after the Apostle's rapture. For it is not an incompetent degradation, but the cessation of grace extraordinarily conferred for a short time, and of a glorious ecstasy.

v. 7. A thorn was given to me in the flesh) Ezek. XXVIII. 24. In the Greek it is a thorn of bitterness, as in the Hebrew סלון ממיר. Now סלון is a thorn, and in Hosea II. 6, where in the Greek it is I will hedge up her way with thorns, in the Hebrew it is בסירים, which likewise signifies thorns. Also Num. XXXIII. v. 55, thorns in your eyes, שכים some interpret as briars. By a thorn, however, placed in the flesh, is signified by similitude a very stinging pain. Tertullian in his work on modesty says that a pain of the ear or head is signified, Chrysostom and Jerome say a headache: Cyprian in his work on mortality says many and grievous torments of the flesh and body.

Angel of Satan) That is, sent to me by Satan. For the word Angel is attributed even to inanimate things, such as wind and fire, Ps. CIV. 4. See what we have said on Gen. III. 23. Moreover, we learn from the history of Job that diseases are also sent upon the pious by Satan, God permitting it. See also Luke XIII. 16.

That he may buffet me) that is, vex me. For it is a species for a genus, as above XI. 20. Thus to be buffeted is also taken in 1 Cor. IV. verse 11.

A thorn to some is a goad, to others a stake; to Aretius a prickle sticking in the body, or a thorn pricking the foot, a shoot, a weapon, a splinter, and according to Dioscorides a sting. To Beza a shoot, because shoots are dangerous to the soles of the feet if one must walk through coppice woods. By B. Glassius it is rendered a fudes, namely a piece of wood sharpened and pointed in battle. Musculus notes that the word is taken for a goad for driving oxen, for a point in military conflict, or for making a hedge and rampart, or for crucifying criminals. This is certain, that metaphorically or by similitude it signifies something very troublesome and painful. However, the Angel of Satan is not called a thorn for that reason, because the Apostle makes mention of both; for Scripture of the New Testament does not use the word Angel otherwise than of a person, nor in construction, but it is said by Apposition, namely an Angel of Satan, and not indeed of Satan, as 2 Cor. II. 11, Acts XXVI. 18. Musculus, with the word as if understood, explains these things thus: There is given to me AS IF a stimulus pricking the flesh, an Angel of Satan, buffeting me. Flacius in the Key to Scripture part I. chap. 817, judges that Paul referred to that atrocious kind of punishment by which criminals were fixed to a stake, inserted through the posterior part of the body and emerging through the shoulders or shoulder blades, which the Turks still use today, just as B. Luther also in his marginal gloss, 'A stake is where one has impaled, crucified, and hanged people,' and in his enarrations on this passage fol. 202, compares the German proverb, 'The cudgel is always tied to the dog's neck,' that is, a stake is tied to the dog's neck, by which we signify that something is attached which afflicts or restrains a man.

But what is understood by the thorn, from which that affliction and greatest annoyance was brought upon Paul by the Angel of Satan, is not agreed upon among Doctors and Interpreters. Some assume the holding back here, and define nothing, to whom B. Luther is added. Since Paul himself does not express what it was, there will be no reason for us to investigate or know it, but it must be confessed that it was hidden and known only to the Apostle. And it is enough for us to know that, just as God made him distinguished and preeminent above all the Apostles by such great revelations that it is not lawful for them to be known by man: so at the same time He added such a stimulus to his flesh, such a troublesome evil to ward off arrogance, namely, so that he would not please himself on account of those revelations, that also no one besides himself could know how direly it pricked and tortured him, or what kind of affliction it finally was. But because others define this evil, I am pleased to bring forward most of the opinions. Most Papists think that Paul was tempted by venereal stimuli, Bellarmine book II. on Monks chap. 30, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, and others, and they introduce Augustine in Psalm LVIII, Theophylact, Anselm, and Thomas into that opinion: which opinion is approved by the Papists especially because they think it agrees with Monastic vows, provided that Paul did not take a wife in those stimuli of the flesh. But Franc. Junius in his animadversions on the cited book of Bellarmine has already warned that Augustine and Theophylact are not brought forward in good faith: nor did Thomas explain it specifically about the stimuli and burnings of lust as Bellarmine did, but in general about concupiscence, and that opinion has already been disapproved by Erasmus and Benedict Justin. from whom he on this passage has it thus: Some interpret this stimulus as the motions and affections of lust, which I am amazed that any learned Theologian would like. Here indeed he pits Irenaeus, Gregory, Jerome with Theophylact, Chrysostom, Augustine, Gregory Nazianzen, Ambrose, Primasius, and even Jerome with Jerome in the exposition of this book, and he rebukes those who think Paul speaks about the stimuli of lust, because they have spoken rashly, and have written that with little wisdom, which can hardly be approved by any learned Theologian. B.
