Hülsemann opposes these arguments to that opinion: (1.) that by the thorn in this place one must understand such a thing as could hinder the excessive estimation of the hearers concerning Paul, is clear from the final cause brought forward, on account of which that stimulus is said to have been sent, verse 6. And thus it is an external end, as far as others are concerned. (2.) The internal end of this stimulus, as far as Paul himself was concerned, was the prevention of Φιλαυτία or arrogance, lest he be exalted beyond measure: But the lust or stimulus of venereal desire could not by itself achieve either of these ends, but would rather have made the Apostle fierce and arrogant, as 1 Tim. V. ver. 11. sqq. Tit. III. v. 3. sqq. chap. I. 16. (3.) The mode of pricking or the formal action of this stimulus is called κολαφίζειν, which is indeed always used of a certain afflictive punishment of the body or soul, or of pain inflicted from without, Matt. XXVI. v. 67. 2 Cor. IV. ver. 11. chap. XI. ver. 20. 1 Peter II. ver. 20. but never of the titillation of venereal lust, even if involuntary. (4.) This Κόλαφος is a species of infirmity, for which Paul prayed a third time, ver. 9. But this very species of infirmity is declared afterwards by such synonyms as denote painful affections having both body and soul as their subject, v. 10. Therefore, by no color is this species of colaphus or infirmity to be extended, much less restricted, to venereal concupiscence. And Bellarmine himself, in his book on Monks, chap. 32, admits that this passage does not entirely prove that species of temptation which is called venereal lust, and he judges that those species of temptation are rather to be understood here, of which 1 Corinth. IX. ver. 27. Romans VII. ver. 21. 23. & 25. But neither do these fit. For in that to the Corinthians, the species of temptation or stimulus is not determined; but the zeal of resisting every temptation: at Rom. VII. it is not a question of a certain Angel of Satan sent by God for this end, that he might buffet Paul, but of the natural stain adhering from the first fall of Adam. The late lamented one adds afterwards: Indeed, if nothing else stood in the way, at least the impiety would hinder it, by which he ascribes the sending of this stimulus to GOD, and indeed for this end, ἵνα με κόλαφίζῃ (there is an error in most copies of Luther's version, 'der mich mit Fäusten schlägt', whereas the final cause of the divine intention is in the source, 'der mich mit Fäusten schlage'), which end directly intended by God, concerning the sending of the evil of fault, such as is venereal ardor, cannot be affirmed without impiety. Read at length Espencæus, book 1 on Continence, ch. 8, who wonders with Erasmus at the insanity of the Papists, who interpret this thorn and πειρασμὸς ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ, Gal. IV. 14, as the disparagement of Paul on account of notorious excess in the foolish fiction of the Monks: If Paul had been afflicted by this kind of temptation, he would have used the very remedy which he had prescribed to others in 1 Cor. VII, namely, marriage. For he testifies openly in 1 Cor. IX that this was not forbidden to him, but lawful, when he writes: Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife? And he prescribes the same to the Bishops and pastors of the Churches, that each one be the husband of one wife, 1 Tim. III, Tit. I. Indeed, he testifies most explicitly, in the same chapter VII, that he is immune from the temptation of lust. For, treating expressly of marriage, and in it of afflictions on account of imminent persecutions, he adds clearly: I would that all men were even as I myself am. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that. Furthermore, it is little fitting to assert that God allowed the Apostle to be tempted by the vice of lust in order to tame the vice of pride in him, i.e., to overcome sin with sin. Moreover, who would think the Apostle to be so improvident that he would insinuate such a thing to the Corinthians, among whom his authority had already been called into doubt by the persuasion of the Pseudo-Apostles, whereby his authority could be even more undermined. Certainly, if any preacher today were to profess such a thing publicly about himself, and explain to his hearers how greatly he is vexed by lusts, he would be judged shameless, and he would diminish his own reputation greatly, etc.

From these, therefore, the second opinion of those who wish for evil concupiscence to be understood in general can easily be judged, which is brought forward by Thomas, and was not disapproved by Flacius in the aforementioned place. It is likely that there were some wicked motions of the old Adam, by which God wished to argue Paul of innate malice, lest, thinking himself so holy and just, he should become insolent. But it is approved especially by Calvin: Under this word (thorn of the flesh) I think is comprehended every kind of temptation by which Paul was exercised. For flesh here signifies not the body, but the part of the soul not yet regenerated: So that the sense is: A thorn is given to me, by which my flesh might be pricked; for I am not yet so spiritual that I am not subject to temptations according to the flesh. But the Apostle did not pray against that adhering evil, so that he might not be subject to any temptation according to the flesh, because he knew that the ὄγκον εὐπερίστατον ἁμαρτίας is not laid aside in this life, nor does that grace fall to anyone, that he is entirely free from all temptation, since the flesh always lusts against the Spirit, Gal. V. 17, nor is the flesh, or that carnal concupiscence, put off except with life.

III. The opinion also brought forward by Osiander is not difficult to evaluate from these things which have already been brought forward. Some, he says, not absurdly opine that Satan from time to time refreshed in Paul the memory of the shedding of the most innocent blood of the Christian Martyrs, and by that grief sharply pricked his conscience. For even when sin is forgiven, new stings of conscience are wont to arise, which are wondrously sharpened by the arts and malice of Satan, as can be seen from Psalm LI of David. While we readily grant this; yet we do not see how it can be gathered from there that such stings are to be understood in this place, since the discourse is about a thorn in the flesh given by GOD, which the Apostle prayed against three times, that is, repeatedly.

Concerning, therefore, a certain evil of punishment, others prefer to understand it here, and from these, the fourth, some concerning a disease of the body.

Augustine in Ps. CXXX. What is this? (to be buffeted by Satan) it is handed down as a certain pain of the body, by which he was vehemently agitated. But pains of the body are for the most part sent by the Angels of Satan; but they cannot do this, unless permitted. Some have expressed even the kind of disease. Thus Jerome reports in his epistle to the Galatians that some understood it as κεφαλαλγίἀ or headache, with which Paul labored vehemently. Thomas explained it as iliac pain: A thorn is given to me, torturing my body through infirmity of the body, so that the soul might be preserved: Because it is said literally that he was vehemently afflicted with iliac pain. So also Lyranus. Salmero, disp. XIII on 2 Corinthians, praises Vincent, a preacher of the Dominican family, who thought it was a pain of the stomach. He also brings forward Nicetas on Gregory Nazianzen, oration 30, who understood it as an infirmity of the kidneys and weakness of the joints or gout. But these descriptions do not sufficiently agree with the description of the most grievous evil inflicted by Satan, the end of which, on the part of God, was that he should not exalt himself by the most eminent revelations.

Wherefore, to others it seems that the persecutions of evil men are being referred to by the Apostle, such as to Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Erasmus, who says, 'To me, indeed, it seems closest what Ambrose says, that the persecution of evil men, who were constantly causing him trouble, is called a thorn'; and to Musculus, who says, 'Chrysostom, in my judgment, approaching more closely to the Apostle's goal, explains it as concerning adversaries who afflicted him with frequent injuries, insults, and persecutions, among whom he specifically recounts Alexander, Hymenaeus, and Philetus.' Which opinion also commended itself to our blessed Franzius in his interpretation of the oracles of Scripture, 78. Just as God granted Satan power over Job: So also, lest the Apostle be puffed up by secret revelations, God sent a singular great Angel of Satan against him, yet with certain limits set for him, so that he could not harm Paul's life. This Angel of Satan stirred up enemies here and there against Paul, far more numerous and fiercer than against the other Apostles, to weaken him (but not to kill him), to weaken him, I say, with insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses, among which, however, the power and help of Christ sustained him. But because the persecution of these does not equal the magnitude of the evil of which the Apostle complains and which he prayed against more often; therefore, VI. Chrysostom does not acquiesce to that in the ten homilies edited by Cardinal Sirlet, but adds another: namely, that the buffeting is a humiliation which is done by enemies, either through prisons, or through abduction to punishment, or through judgment, or through hunger, or through any other thing. Which sense, in the judgment of Salmeron himself, seems to excel the others, because the Apostle used the word σκόλοπος, just as the LXX Interpreters in Numbers 23. Since, however, most of those things in the preceding chapter XI. have already been mentioned, but here the Apostle brings forward something peculiar: Aretius brings forward yet another evil, VII: 'It appears,' he says, 'that Paul was sometimes vexed by Satan with a visible appearance, or at least by a more vehement temptation, to such an extent that he seemed to receive blows, as if he were saying: That Angel of Satan treats me in unworthy ways.' But the Apostle speaks not of blows, but of continuous and most vehement buffetings, and under the metaphor of bruising and blackening of the face, he hints at most troublesome torments and agonies, on account of which he had more often prayed to the Lord with most ardent prayers.

Wherefore, having dismissed these and other opinions, VIII. that of blessed Hülsemann seems to us to be preferred, if one should not rather choose τὸ ἐπέχειν with blessed Luther, as spiritual temptations are indicated among so many external persecutions and afflictions, which the Apostle calls ἀνάγκας in verse 10, not only of the body, but of the mind, and the intervals of hope, concerning which above in chapter IV, verse 8, and 1 Cor. IV, verse 9, sqq. Such temptations from the excessive intensity and duration of external afflictions. In which manner also the Blessed Hunnius testified that he himself embraced that exposition, others being set aside, which is concerning spiritual temptations; yet so that it is understood specifically of a certain one, and one that is very notable and vehement above others. Nor indeed does it stand in the way that it is called a thorn in the flesh, since that very corrupt flesh, prone to pride, was subdued by that spiritual affliction as by a certain thorn, not without exquisite sense of trouble, lest it should be able to exalt itself immeasurably. And in the word σκόλοψ there is a likeness to a spike, a stake, or a pale fixed into the body, and stirring up most bitter pains until it is removed. And he demonstrates that this temptation was not something natural, but the work of Satan, who with that very sharp stake, as if with a poisoned spike and a fiery dart, was most vehemently striking the holy breast of the Apostle, and was striving to cast him altogether into destruction, had he not been sustained by the help of God and immediately delivered. Not unlike is the explanation of the Blessed Luther, Comment. on the Epistle to the Galatians, later, Tom. IV, Jena, Lat. fol. 113. But Paul had not only external temptations, of which we have already spoken, but also internal and spiritual ones, as Christ had in the garden. Such was that of which he complains in 2 Cor. XII, a σκόλοψ in the flesh and an Angel of Satan, who was buffeting him. Whoever is exercised by these spiritual temptations, it is impossible for him to be vexed by lust. I give this warning in passing for this reason, because the Papists, when they saw that the Latin version has 'stimulus carnis' (thorn of the flesh), interpreted that thorn as motions of lust. But in the Greek it is σκόλοψ, which signifies a stake or a very sharp pale. Therefore that was a spiritual temptation. Nor does it stand in the way that he adds the word 'of the flesh,' when he says: 'A stake was given to me in the flesh.' Nay, he deliberately calls it a stake in the flesh, because the Galatians and others, with whom Paul had associated, often saw him affected by great sorrow, trembling, fearing, and being vexed by ineffable pain and sadness. We add here the interpretation which is read in the Table Talk, chapter IX, f. 94. b. The Devil shoots terrible thoughts, which are his fiery darts, also into the hearts of the godly, such as are resentment, anger, hatred against God, despair, blasphemy, etc. Paul understood them in part, and also complains vehemently about it, when he says 2 Cor. 12: 'There is given to me a stake in the flesh, namely the angel of Satan, who strikes me with fists,' etc.

v. 7. Ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι) That every ἔπαρσις (exaltation) of the mind might be repressed by so grave and assiduous a pain. But these words are not found here in the Manuscript, and it would be enough that they were placed above.

Since all other Codices consistently repeat these words, they are not to be considered as interpolated: Nor is it new in the scriptures for the same things to be said twice, so that they may be the more inculcated, and this end is hinted at here, that he might not be exalted, both by the giving of the thorn and by the buffeting itself, on account of which the thorn was given to the flesh, the Angel of Satan. Those things are also repeated in the Syriac and Arabic interpretation.

Latin:

Καὶ τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι) Etiam ob illas, quas dixi, revelationes ne exultem, grave mihi frenum datum est.

Ex illa ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων colligunt nonnulli, in hoc raptu Apostolum vidisse divinam essentiam, quod affirmare non dubitarunt Augusti- nus de Genes. ad lit. cap. 27. & epist. CXII. ad Paulin. Beda, Anselmus in h. l. Hugo de S. Victore in h. l. Thomas II. 2. q. 175. art. 3. Si enim eo bea- titudinis non venisset, revelationum excellentia minime contigisset. Neque contradictio involvi videtur, si dicatur vidisse essentiam divina intuitu temporario, sive per collustrationem luminis gloriæ, sive sine lumine gloriæ elevata mente per absolu- tam Dei potentiam ad beatum ejusmodi intuitum per modum actus transeuntis. Neque ex eo deterioratiq status competentis sequitur post raptum Apostoli. Est enim non degradatio incompetens, sed gratiæ extraordinariè ad breve tempus collatæ, & gloriosæ ecstaseos cessatio.

v. 7. Ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκὶ) Ezech. XXVIII. 24. In Græco est σκόλοψ πικρίας, uti in Hebræo סלון ממיר. Est autem סלון spina, & in Oseæ II. 6. ubi in Græco est Φράσσω τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτῆς ἐν σκόλοψι, in Hebræo est בסירים, quod itidem spinas significat. Etiam Num. XXXIII. v. 55. σκόλοπες ἐν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ὑμῶν, שכים quidam sentes interpretantur. Per spinam autem, carni inditam, significatur per similitudinem dolor admodum pungens. Dolorem auriculæ vel capitis significari, ait Tertullianus de pudicitia, κεφαλαλγίαν Chrysostomus, & Hieronymus: Carnis & corporis multa ac gravia tormenta Cyprianus de mortalitate.

Ἄγγελος Σατᾶν) Id est, immissus mihi à Satana. Nam Ἀγγέλου vox tribuitur etiam rebus non animatis, ut vento, & igni, Ps. CIV. 4. Vide, quæ dicta nobis ad Gen. III. 23. A Satana autem morbos etiam piis immitti, Deo id sinente, ex Jobi historia discimus. Vide & Luc. XIII. 16.

Ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ) id est, vexet. Est enim species pro genere, ut supra XI. 20. Sic κολαφίζεσθαι sumitur & 1. Cor. IV. vers. 11.

Σκόλοψ aliis stimulus, quibussdam palus; Aretio aculeus corpori inhærens, vel spina pedem pungens, surculus, telum, assula, & ex Dioscoride spiculum. Bezæ surculus, quia surculi pedum vestigiis infesti sunt, si per cæduas sylvas est ambulandum. B. Glassio fudes lignum videlicet in acie præustum & aculeatum, redditur. Musculus notat, accipi vocem pro stimulo ad impellendos boves, pro cuspide in conflictu militari, vel ad conficiendum sepem ac vallum, vel ad crucifigendum sceleratos. Id certum est, Metaphoricè vel per similitudinem significare aliquid valde molestum ac dolorificum. Non autem ideo Angelus Satan dicitur σκόλοψ, quod utriusque mentionem faciat Apostolus; Nam neque voce Angeli aliter, quam de persona utitur scriptura Novi Testamenti, nec in constructione, sed per Appositionem dicitur, Ἄγγελος Σατᾶν nempe, non vero τοῦ Σατανᾶ, ut 2. Cor. II. 11. Act. XXVI. 18. Musculus voce ὥσπερ subintellectâ hæc ita explicat: Datus est mihi VELUTI stimulus carnem pungens Angelus Satanæ, colaphis cædens. Flacius in clave scripturæ part. I. cap. 817. respexisse Paulum censet ad atrox illud supplicii genus, quo rei palo affigebantur, inserto per posteriorem corporis partem, & emergente per humeros aut scapulas, quo etiamnum Turcæ utuntur, quomodo etiam B. Lutherus in glossa margin. Pfahl ist, da man die Leute angespiesset, gecreußiget und gehencket hat, & in enarr. h. l. fol. 202. confert Germanicum proverbium, der Knittel ist allezeit dem Hunde an den Hals gebunden, id est, palus est ligatus à collo canis, quo significamus, adjunctum esse, quod hominem affligat vel contineat.

Quid autẽ intelligatur per σκόλοπα, ex quo per Angelum Satanæ afflictio illa & molestia maxima conciliata sit Paulo, non convenit inter Doctores & Interpp. Nonnulli τὸ ἐπέχειν hîc assumunt, nihilque definiunt, quibus accedit B. Lutherus. Cum ipse Paulus non exprimat, quidnam fuerit, non erit, quod nos illud investigemus, aut sciamus, sed occultum, & soli Apostolo cognitum fuisse fatendum erit. Satisque nobis est, scire, quemadmodum illum Deus tantis revelationibus, ut fas non sit, eas ab homine cognosci, insignem & omnibus præstantem Apostolis fecit: Ita simul tantum stimulum carni ejus addidisse, tam molestum malum ad arcendam scil. arrogantiam, ne sibi ipsi ob revelationes illas placeret, ut etiam nemo præter ipsum potuerit cognoscere, quam dire ipsum pupugerit & cruciarit, aut quod tandem genus affli- tionis fuerit. Quia vero alii definiunt hoc malum, sententias plerasque adducere lubet. Pontificii plerique Paulum fuisse tentatum stimulis Venereis putant, Bellarminus libr. II. de Monach. cap. 30. Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, & alii, inque eam sententiam inducunt Augustinum in Psalm. LVIII. Theophylactum, Anshelmum & Thomam: quæ sententia ideo à Pontificiis imprimis probatur, quod votis Monasticis eam congruere putent, siquidem Paulus in istis carnis stimulis non tamen uxorem duxerit. Sed Augustinum & Theophylactum non bona fide adduci Franc. Junius in animadvers. ad l. cit. Bellarm. jam monuit: neque Thomas in specie de libidinum stimulis & ustionibus ut Bellarminus, sed in genere de concupiscentia exposuit, & improbata jam illa sententia ab Erasmo & Benedicto Justin. è quibus ille ad h. l. ita habet: Nonnulli stimulum hunc interpretantur motus & affectus libidinis, quod demiror, ulli docto Theologo placere. Hic verò Irenæum, Gregorium, Hieronymum cum Theophylacto, Chrysostomo, Augustino, Gregorio Naz. Ambrosio, Primafio, quin & Hieronymum cum Hieronymo in expositione hujus libri committit, eosque, qui Paulum de stimulis libidinum loqui putant, reprehendit, quod temere loquuti sint, idque parum cordate scripserint, quod vix ulli docto Theologo probari possit. B. Hülsemannus hæc illi opinioni opponit argumenta: (1.) per σκόλοπα intelligendum esse hoc loco tale quid, quod impedire poterat nimiam æstimationem auditorum de Paulo, patet ex adducta causa finali, propter quam immissus dicitur ille stimulus vers. 6. Et sic est finis externus, quantum ad alios. (2.) finis internus hujus stimuli, quantum ad Paulum ipsum, erat impeditio Φιλαυτίας seu arrogantiæ, ne supra modum efferretur: Sed libido seu stimulus cupiditatis Venereæ, neutrum horum finium per se poterat assequi, sed Apostolum potius ferocem & arrogantem effecisset, ut 1. Tim. V. vers. 11. sqq. Tit. III. v. 3. sqq. cap. I. 16. (3.) Modus pungendi seu actio formalis hujus stimuli dicitur κολαφίζειν, quod semper quidem de pœna quadam afflictiva corporis vel animi usurpatur, seu dolore forinsecus illato, Matth. XXVI. v. 67. 2. Cor. IV. vers. 11. cap. XI. vers. 20. 1. Petri II. vers. 20. nunquam verò de titillatione libidinis Venereæ etiam invitæ. (4.) Κόλαφος isthæc est species infirmitatis, pro qua tertium deprecatus est Paulus vers. 9. Sed hæc ipsa species infirmitatis declaratur postea per ejusmodi synonyma, quæ affectus dolorosos tum corpus tum animum pro subjecto habentes notant, v. 10. Itaque nullo colore hæc species colaphi seu infirmitatis est extendenda, nedum restringenda ad concupiscentiam Veneream. Et Bellarminus ipse libr. de Monach. cap. 32. fatetur, hunc locum non omnino convincere istam tentationis speciem, quæ dicitur libido veneris, & illas potius tentationis species hic intelligi censet, de quibus 1. Corinth. IX. vers. 27. Roman. VII. vers. 21. 23. & 25. Sed nec hæc congruunt. Nam illo ad Corinthios non determinatur species tentationis seu stimuli; sed studium resistendi cuique tentationi: ad Rom. VII. non de quodam Angelo Satanæ divinitus hoc fine immisso, ut Paulum colaphizet, agitur, sed de labe naturali hærente ex primo Adami lapsu. Addit postmodum ὁ Μακαρίτης: Imo vero si nihil aliud obstaret, saltem obesset impietas, qua immissionem hujus stimuli DEO adscribit, & quidem hoc fine, ἵνα με κόλαφίζῃ (sphalma est in plerisque exemplaribus versionis Lutheri, der mich mit Fäusten schlägt, cum causa finalis divinæ intentionis sit in fonte, der mich mit Fäusten schlage,) qui finis directè intentus à Deo, de immissione mali culpæ, quale est ardor Venereus, citra impietatem affirmari nequit. Lege prolixe Espensæum libr. 1. de Continentia c. 8. demirantem cum Erasmo Papistarum insaniam, sti- mulum hunc & πειρασμὸς ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ, Gal. IV. 14. de vilipendentia Pauli ob notorium excessum in libi- dine Venerea passim exponentium. Profligavit etiam insulsum Monachorum commentum B. Hunnius: Si Paulus hoc genere tentationis fuisset afflictatus, eo ipso usurus fuisset remedio, quod aliis 1. Cor. VII. præscripserat, nempe conjugio. Id enim sibi non pro- hibitum, sed licitum fuisse testatur palam 1. Cor. IX. cum scribit : Annon habemus potestatem sororem mulierem circumducendi? Idemque præscribit Eccle- siarum Episcopis & pastoribus, ut quisque sit unius uxoris maritus, 1. Tim. III. Tit. I. Imo disertissime testatur, eodem capite VII. se ab tentatione libidinis immunem esse. Nam ex professo tractans de conju- gio, & in eo afflictionibus propter imminentes perse- cutiones addit perspicuè : Velim omnes homines esse, ut & ego ipse sum. Sed unusquisque habet proprium donum à Deo, alius quidem sic, alius autem sic. Præ- terea parum conveniens est, asserere, quod Deus vi- tio libidinis ideo tentari siverit Apostolum, ut super- biæ vitium in eo domaret, h. e. ut peccatum peccato profligaret. Adhæc quis Apostolum tam improvidum esse sentiat, ut Corinthiis, apud quos ex persuasione Pseudo-Apostolorum jam ante autoritas ipsius in dubium vocata est, tale quippiam insinuet, quo ma- gis etiam illius autoritas labefactari poterat. Certe si quis hodie concionator tale quid de se publice profi- teatur, & suis auditoribus exponat, quantopere di- vexetur libidinibus, impudens judicabitur, & ipse plurimum de sua sibi existimatione diminuet &c.

Ex his ergo II. sententia eorum, qui in genere pravam concupiscentiam intelligi volunt, dijudi- cari facile potest, quæ à Thoma adducitur, nec im- probata fuit Flacio l. c. Verisimile est, fuisse aliquos veteris Adami improbos motus, quibus Deus Pau- lum arguere voluit innatæ malitiæ, ne putans, se adeo sanctum justumque esse, insolesceret. Probata autem imprimis Calvino: Sub hoc vocabulo (stimuli car- nis) comprehendi arbitror omne genus tentationis, quo Paulus exercebatur. Nam caro hic non corpus, sed partem animæ nondum regeneratam significat: Ut sit sensus: Mihi datus est stimulus, quo caro mea pungeretur; neque enim adhuc adeo sum spi- ritualis, quin obnoxius sim tentationibus secun- dum carnem. Atqui non deprecatus Apostolus est malum illud adhærens, ne ulli tentationi obno- xius sit secundum carnem, quia sciebat non depo- ni ὄγκον εὐπερίστατον ἁμαρτίας in hac vita, nec cui- quam eam obtingere gratiam, ut plane liber sit ab omni tentatione, quum caro semper concupiscat adversus Spiritum, Gal. V. 17. nec nisi cum vita caro, vel carnalis illa concupiscentia exuatur.

III. Opinio etiam ab Osiandro adducta, haud difficulter quoque ex his, quæ jam adducta, æsti- matur. Nonnulli, inquit, haud absurde opinantur, Satanam subinde refricasse Paulo memoriam effusi innocentissimi sanguinis Christianorum Martyrum, eoque dolore conscientiam ipsius acriter pupugisse. Solent enim remisso etiam peccato novi stimuli con- scientiæ, qui artibus & livore Satanæ mire acuun- tur, ut ex Psal. LI. Davidis videre est. Quod uti facile largimur; Ita non videmus, quomodo inde colligi queat, quod hoc loco tales stimuli intelli- gendi sint, quum de stimulo in carnem dato à DEO sermo sit, quem ter, id est, sæpius deprecatus fue- rit Apostolus.

De malo ergo quodam pœnæ alii malunt hic in- telligere, & ex his IV. quidam de morbo corporis.

Augustinus in Ps. CXXX. Quid est hoc? (colaphi- zari a Satana) dolore quodam corporis traditur, exagitatus vehementer. Dolores autem corporum plerumque immittuntur ab Angelis Satanæ; sed hoc non possunt, nisi permissi. Nonnulli expressēre etiam genus morbi. Sic refert Hieronymus in epist. ad Gal. quosdam id intellexisse de κεφαλαλγίἀ seu capitis dolore, quo vehementer laborarit Paulus. Thomas de dolore iliaco exposuit: Datus est mihi stimulus crucians corpus meum per infirmitatem corporis, ut anima servetur: Quia ad literam di- citur, quod fuit vehementer afflictus dolore iliaco. Ita & Lyranus. Salmero disp. XIII. in 2. Corinth. Vincentium Dominicanæ familiæ prædicatorem laudat, qui arbitratus sit, fuisse dolorem stomachi. Adducit etiam Nicetam in Gregor. Nazianz. orat. 30. quod renum infirmitatem, atque articulorum debilitatem vel podagram intellexerit. Sed hæ de- scriptiones non satis congruunt descriptioni mali gravissimi à Satanâ inflicti, cujus finis ex parte Dei fuerit, ne se extolleret revelationibus eminentissimis.

Quapropter V. aliis videntur potius malorum hominum insectationes respici ab Apostolo, ut pote Ambrosio, Chrysostomo & Erasmo, qui mihi vero, inquit, proximum videtur, quod ait Ambro- sius, insectationem malorum hominum, quæ illi ne- gotium facessebant assidue, vocari stimulum; & Musculo, qui, Chrysostomus, inquit, propius ad scopum Apostoli meo judicio accedens, exponit de adversariis, qui illam crebris injuriis, contumeliis & persecutionibus afflixerint, inter quos nomina- tim recenset Alexandrum, Hymenæum & Phile- tem. Quæ sententia se etiam probavit B. Franzio nostro de interpret. scripturæ orac. 78. Sicut Deus Satanæ indulsit potestatem super Jobum: Ita quoque, ne nimium arcanis efferretur revelationibus Apo- stolus, Deus singularem magnum Angelum Satan in ipsum immisit, certis tamen ipsi præfixis metis, ne vitæ Pauli nocere possit. Qui Angelus Satan hinc inde adversus Paulum inimicos excitavit longe plu- res & acriores, quàm adversus alios Apostolos, ut infirmarent ipsum, (non vero necarent,) ut infir- marent, inquam, contumeliis, necessitatibus, perse- cutionibus, angustiis, inter quas tamen potentia & auxilium Christi ipsum sustentabat. Sed quia nec horum insectatio magnitudinem mali, de quo queritur, & quod sæpius deprecatus est Apo- stolus, adæquat; ideo VI. Chrysostomus illi non acquiescit in Homiliis decem à Cardinali Sir- leto editis, sed aliam adjicit: quod nempe cola- phizatio sit humiliatio, quæ fit ab inimicis, vel per carceres, vel per abductionem ad supplicium, vel per judicium, vel per famem, vel per quamcunque aliam rem. Qui sensus Salmeronis ipsius judicio præstare videtur cæteris, quia Apostolus usus est voce σκόλοπος, quomodo LXX. Interpp. Num. XXIII. Quum vero pleraque illa cap. anteced. XI. jam commemorata sint, hic autem aliquid peculiare afferat Apostolus: Aretius ad huc aliud VII. affert malum: Apparet, inquit, Paulum visi- bili specie interdum vexatum esse à Satana, aut sal- tem vehementiore tentatione, adeo, ut colaphos sit visus accipere, quasi dicat: Indignis modis me tra- ctat ille Angelus Satan. Sed Apostolus loquitur non de colaphis, sed de colaphizationibus conti- nuis ac vehementissimis & sub metaphora contusio- nis & sugillationis faciei molestissimos cruciatus & angores innuit, ob quos ardentissimis precibus Dominum sæpius deprecatus fuerit.

Quocirca missis hisce aliisque sententiis IIX. B. Hülsemanni nobis præferenda videtur, si non cum Beat. Luthero potius τὸ ἐπέχειν eligendum, tentationes spirituales indigitari inter tot perse- cutiones & afflictiones externas, quas Apostolus ἀνάγκας vocat vers. 10. non corporis solum, sed animi, & intervalla spei, de quibus supra cap. IV. vers. 8. & 1. Cor. IV. vers. 9. sqq. Quales tenta- tiones ex nimia intensione & duratione externa- rum afflictionum Eliæ, 1. Regum XIX. Davidi, Psal. XXX. 8. aliisque perfectissimis hominibus contigit. Quo pacto etiam B. Hunnius eam am- plecti sese, cæteris missis, expositionem testatus est, quæ de spiritualibus tentationibus est; sic tamen, ut in specie de certa quadam, & præ cæteris insigni ac vehementi admodum intelligatur. Nec verò obstat, quod dicitur stimulus in carne, siquidem ea ipsa spirituali afflictione ceu stimulo quodam ca- ro corrupta & ad superbiam prona, non sine exqui- sito sensu molestia subigebatur, ne sese in immen- sum efferre posset. Estque in vocabulo σκόλοψ simi- litudo à spiculo, palo, aut sude infixa corpori, & acerbissimos dolores concitante, donec eximatur. Neque hanc tentationem naturale quippiam fuisse demonstrat, sed Satanæ opus, qui præacuto illo pa- lo tanquam venenato spiculo & ignito jaculo san- ctum pectus Apostoli vehementissime percellebat, & omninò in exitium conjicere moliebatur, in Dei ope sustentatus, & subinde liberatus fuisset. Non absimilis est explicatio Beat. Lutheri Comment. in epistol. ad Galat. poster. Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. fol. 113. Habuit autem Paulus non tantum exter- nas, de quibus jam diximus, sed etiam internas & spirituales, ut Christus in horto, tentationes. Qualis fuit, de qua conqueritur 2. Cor. XII. σκόλοψ in carne & Angelus Satanæ, qui eum colaphis cade- bat. Qui istis spiritualibus tentationibus exerce- tur, illum impossibile est vexari libidine. Hoc ideo obiter admoneo, quia Papistæ, cum viderent La- tinam versionem habere, stimulum carnis, inter- pretati sunt istum stimulum motus libidinis. Sed in Græco est σκόλοψ, quod palum seu sudem præ- acutam significat. Fuit ergo ista spiritualis tentatio. Neque obstat, quod addit vocabulum carnis, cum ait: Datus est mihi palus in carnem. Imo con- sulto vocat palum in carne, quia Galatæ & alii, quibuscum conversatus fuit Paulus, sæpe viderunt eum magno mærore affici, trepidare, pavescere & ineffabili dolore & mæstitia vexari. Addimus hic interpretationem, quæ legitur in Colloquiis mensalibus cap. IX. f. 94. b. Der Teuffel schiesst schreckliche Gedancken, welche seine feurige Pfeile sind, auch in die Hertzen der Gottseligen, als da sind Unwill, Zorn, Hass wider GOtt, Verzweiffelung, Gottslästerung, 2c. St. Paulus hat sie zum theil wohl verstanden, klaget auch hefftig darüber, wann er spricht 2. Cor. 12. Mir ist gegeben ein Pfahl ins Fleisch, nemblich des Satans Engel, der mich mit Fäusten schlage, 2c.

v. 7. Ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι) Ut omnis animi ἔπαρσις, tam gravi & assiduo dolore, reprimeretur. Sed hæc ver- ba in Manuscripto hîc non reperiuntur, & satis esset supra esse posita.

Quum Codices omnes alii constanter hæc ver- ba repetant, non habenda sunt pro irreptitiis: Nec novum est in scripturis, eadem bis dici, ut eo magis inculcentur, & innuitur hic finis, ut non extollatur, tum qua dationem stimuli, tum qua ipsam colaphizationem, ob quam stimulus carni datus, Angelus Satanæ. Repetuntur etiam illa in Syriacâ, & Arabicâ interpretatione.

## 12:8
v. 8. ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα, ἵν᾽ ἀποστῇ ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ) That that pain might depart from me. Concerning the ternary number in prayers, see what was said at Matthew XXVI. 24.

Latin:

v. 8. ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα, ἵν᾽ ἀποστῇ ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ) Ut abiret à me dolor ille. De ternario numero in precibus vide, quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 24.

## 12:9
Καὶ εἴρηκέ μοι) Namely Christ through the בת קול (daughter of a voice).

Musculus also acquiesces in the ternary number; when he had asked once and had not obtained, he asked a second time: when not even then had he obtained what he was seeking, he prayed a third time: and there, being warned by the oracle of God, he ceased. This sense agrees with the threefold prayer of Christ in the garden, that the cup might pass, Matthew XXVI. Others, however, explain the ternary number as a manifold prayer. Aretius, after Chrysostom and Theophylact, 'I prayed three times,' that is, frequently. For I do not believe he prayed three times, but incessantly, or at least he had set prayers against this Angel three times: The Blessed Hunnius: 'Three times,' he says, that is, anxiously and frequently he asked the Lord that He might kindly relieve him of such a burden; but always the answer was given to him by the Lord: 'My grace is sufficient for you.'

v. 9. Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου) It shall be sufficient for you that I wish you well. Ἀρκεῖ, that is, it ought to be sufficient. The pious, when they pray for the alleviation of evils, are not always heard: because they do not pray except under the condition, if it be more conducive to their own good and the honor of God.

Some explain this metonymically regarding the past effect of divine grace, as for instance regarding granted revelations; but it is more correctly understood regarding the present effect: Namely, the Lord refused what he was asking, yet in such a way that He might comfort him with His grace, and promise victory against Satan. My grace is sufficient for you to preserve you, and to work through you, for the things to which you have been sent by Me. Beautifully Jerome in Thomas: The Lord is good, who often does not grant what we want, so that He may grant what we would prefer.

For My power is made perfect in weakness) He gives the reason here why He does not take this evil away from him; because His power, namely Christ's, is the more perfected, that is, illustrated, the more those through whom He acts are subject to adversities. Whoever sees diseases being healed by Paul, let him know that this is not from him (for he himself is also sick) but from Christ. τελειοῦται here means, is more perfectly recognized, just as often Hebrew Hiphil verbs are referred to the effect of knowledge. Otherwise, this is also true, which Pliny says in Epist. 26, book VII: that we are best while we are weak. To which agrees that saying of Seneca: Calamity is the occasion of virtue. And of Quintilian: All rashness of the mind is broken by the calamity of the body. And of Minucius Felix: Calamity is more often the discipline of virtue. And of Salvian: When limbs are afflicted, the strengths of the body are transferred into the virtues of the soul. And this from the same: Holy men make themselves weaker, because if they were strong, they could hardly be holy.

Others understand the acknowledgment of infirmity as leading to a more perfect exhibition of grace, just as Jerome in his Epistle to Ctesiphon says that this is the one perfection of the present life, that you recognize yourself to be imperfect. And the Blessed Chemnitz in Part I of the Loci Communes beautifully says: Those who after renovation do not acknowledge such infirmity, on account of which they continually have need of the grace and power of GOD; in them indeed power is begun, but it is not τελειοῦται, because power is perfected in infirmity. But infirmity here is understood regarding those things which the Apostle was suffering, and power is placed in patience and the victory over infirmities, not in the struggle. Aretius: The power, he says, of Christ is illustrated in great infirmity, because Paul, an infirm man, stood firm against such a great tempting Angel.

Most gladly therefore will I rather boast in my weaknesses) ἥδιστα μᾶλλον is said here for ἥδιον, as καλὸν μᾶλλον for κάλλιον, Mark IX. 42. Elsewhere μᾶλλον κρεῖσσον, μᾶλλον περισσότερον, μᾶλλον περισσοτέρως; so that μᾶλλον is joined with the Positive, Comparative, and Superlative.

That the power of Christ may rest upon me) That is, that the power of Christ may appear the more through me. For σκηνῶ; ἐπισκηνῶ from the Syriac שׁכן is to dwell. To dwell, however, in this place is to show oneself frequently. Just as men are more often at home than outside the house.

In the word ἐπισκηνώσῃ another emphasis is noted by others, as that it may rest upon me, or as if by a certain overshadow with the tabernacle. After, he says, according to the interpreter Theophylact, I myself have perceived that the power of God is made perfect in weakness, I will therefore boast in my weaknesses. For these, the more they abound, the more abundantly they are to bring me the power of God. Beza does not so conveniently refer this to the tabernacle of our dwelling, and its weakness, that the weaker our tabernacles are, the more the power of Christ shines forth in them, since they are not broken by any dangers or labors. The discourse is not about the habitation of our weakness, but about the power of Christ dwelling above us or overshadowing us.

Latin:

Καὶ εἴρηκέ μοι) Nempe Christus per בת קול.

Ternario numero acquiescit & Musculus, cum semel rogasset, nec impetrasset, rogavit se- cundo: Cum ne sic quidem quod petebat, conse- quutus esset, oravit tertio: atque ibi per oracu- lum Dei admonitus cessavit. Hic sensus congruit trinae orationi Christi in horto, ut calix transeat, Matth. XXVI. Alii tamen explicant ternarium numerum de multiplici oratione. Aretius post Chrysostomum & Theophylactum ter oravi, id est, frequenter. Non enim ter orasse credo, sed inde- finenter, vel certe statas preces contra hunc An- gelum ter habuit: B. Hunnius: Ter, inquit, id est, anxie & frequenter rogavit Dominum, ut se tanto onere benigne sublevaret; semper autem sibi respon- sum a Domino: Sufficiat tibi gratia mea.

v. 9. Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου) Sufficiet tibi, quod tibi bene volo. Ἀρκεῖ, id est, sufficere debet. Pii cum malorum levamenta orant, non semper exaudiuntur: quia nec pre- cantur, nisi sub conditione, si ipsorum bono & Dei honori sit conducibilius.

Explicant hoc nonnulli de praeterito gratia di- vina effectu metonymice, utpote de concessis re- velationibus; at rectius accipitur de effectu praesen- ti: Nimirum Dominus, quod petebat, abnuit, ita tamen, ut de sua illum gratia soletur, & vi- ctoriam contra Satanam promittat. Sufficit tibi gratia mea ad conservandum te, & operandum per te, ad quae missus es per me. Pulchre Hieronymus apud Thomam: Bonus Dominus, qui saepe non tribuit, quod volumus, ut tribuat, quod malle- mus.

Ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ τελειοῦται) Causam hic reddit, cur hoc malum ei non auferat; quia potentia ipsius, nempe Christi, hoc magis perficitur, id est, illustratur, quo ii, per quos agit, magis sunt adversis obnoxii. Qui a Paulo videt morbos sanari, sciat, hoc non ab ipso esse; (aegrotat enim & ipse) sed a Christo. τελειοῦται hic est, perfectius agnoscitur, sicut saepe verba Hebraea Hiphil ad notitiae effe- ctum referuntur. Alioqui verum etiam hoc est, quod Pli- nius dicit VII. epist. 26. optimos nos esse, dum infirmi sumus. Cui congruit Senecae illud: Calamitas virtutis occasio est. Et Quintiliani: Temeritas omnis animorum, calamitate cor- porum frangitur. Et Minutii Felicis: Calamitas saepius disci- plina virtutis est. Et Salviani: Affectis artubus vires corpo- rum in virtutes transferuntur animorum. Et hoc ejusdem: Sancti viri infirmiores se faciunt, quia si fortes fuerint, sancti esse vix possint.

Alii agnitionem infirmitatis facere ad perfectio- rem gratiae exhibitionem intelligunt, uti Hierony- mus in Epist. ad Ctesiphontem hanc unam praesen- tis vitae perfectionem esse dicit, ut te imperfectum cognoscas. Et Beat. Chemnitius parte I. LL. CC. pulchre ait: Qui post renovationem non agnoscunt talem infirmitatem, propter quam continue ipsis opus sit gratia & virtute DEI; in illis quidem in- cipitur virtus, sed non τελειοῦται, quia virtus in in- firmitate perficitur. Sed infirmitas hic de iis, quae patiebatur Apostolus, accipitur, & virtus ponitur in patientia, & victoria infirmitatum, non in agone. Aretius: Potentia, inquit, Christi illustratur in magna infirmitate, quia Paulus ho- mo infirmus perstitit contra tantum Angelum ten- tatorem.

Ἥδιστα οὖν μᾶλλον καυχήσομαι ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις μου) ἥδιστα μᾶλλον hic dictum est pro ἥδιον, ut καλὸν μᾶλλον, pro κάλ- λιον, Marc. IX. 42. Alibi μᾶλλον κρεῖσσον, μᾶλλον περισσότε- ρον, μᾶλλον περισσοτέρως; ita ut μᾶλλον conjugatur cum Positivo, Comparativo, & Superlativo.

Ἵνα ἐπισκηνώσῃ ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Χριστοῦ) Id est, ut eo magis vis illa Christi per me appareat. Nam σκηνῶ; ἐπισκην- νῶ ex Syriaco שׁכן est habitare. Habitare autem hoc loco est frequenter se ostendere. Sicut homines saepius domi sunt, quam extra domum.

In voce ἐπισκηνώσῃ alia emphasis ab aliis no- tatur, ut incumbat supra me, seu ut quasi quodam tabernaculo obumbret. Postquam, inquit, inter- prete Theophylacto, ipse animadverti Dei virtutem iri in infirmitate perfectum, gloriabor ergo in in- firmitatibus meis. Hæ namque, quo affluent ma- gis, eo mihi Dei virtutem allaturæ uberius sunt. Beza non ita commode refert ad tabernaculum nostri hospitii, ejusque infirmitatem, quo sunt no- stra tabernacula infirmiora, eo magis elucet in illis Christi virtus, quum nullis periculis aut labo- ribus frangantur. De virtute Christi supra nos ha- bitante vel nos obumbrante, non infirmitatis no- stræ habitaculo sermo est.

## 12:10
v. 10. Διὸ εὐδοκῶ ἐν ἀσθενείαις) I love or I am well pleased with those very adversities.

I did indeed desire, as the paraphrase of Theophylact has it again, to escape from these heavier and less pleasant things, but after I received and understood those things which I drank in with these ears of mine, I boast plainly and am pleased with myself, that is, I am affected with incredible joy, and I take delight in the weaknesses themselves and in evils.

Ἐν ὕβρεσιν) Nay, to be treated contumeliously for the sake of Christ. Ἐν ἀνάγκαις) See above VI. 4. & 1 Cor. VII. 26. Ἐν διωγμοῖς) See Matt. XIII. 21. Mark IV. 17. Acts VIII. 1. Rom. VIII. 35.

Ὅταν γὰρ ἀσθενῶ, τότε δυνατός εἰμι) The more I am pressed by adversities, the greater things God works through me.

Theophylact explains these things more fully: For I myself am then stronger, when I am more harassed: And for the sake of this grace I have obtained strength from God, which is always at hand for me when I labor, and helps me in the greatest degree.

PART II. The excuse for boasting.

Latin:

v. 10. Διὸ εὐδοκῶ ἐν ἀσθενείαις) חפצתי aut רציתי amo ipsa illa adversa.

Cupiebam equidem, ut iterum habet paraphra- sis Theophylacti, à gravioribus hisce & minus gratis liber evadere, sed postquam ea accepi & intellexi, quæ meis his auribus hausi, glorior plane & mihi pla- ceo, hoc est, incredibili jucunditate afficior, & in in- firmitatibus ipsis oblector & malis.

Ἐν ὕβρεσιν) Imo contumeliose tractari Christi causa. Ἐν ἀνάγκαις) Vide supra VI. 4. & 1. Cor. VII. 26. Ἐν διωγμοῖς) Vide Matth. XIII. 21. Marc. IV. 17. Act. VIII. 1. Rom. VIII. 35.

Ὅταν γὰρ ἀσθενῶ, τότε δυνατός εἰμι) Quo magis adversis premor, eo majora Deus per me operatur.

Plenius hæc explicat Theophylactus: Nam & ipse tunc fortior sum, cum magis divexor: Et Dei ob gratiam hanc adeptus sum fortitudinem, quæ laboranti mihi præsto est semper, & maximum in mo- dum opitulatur.

PARS II. Excusatio gloriationis.

## 12:11
v. 11. Γέγονα ἄφρων καυχώμενος) In the Manuscript there is no καυχώμενος. For ἄφρων, that is, ὡς ἄφρων, as often in the preceding chapter, here has the same value as καυχώμενος.

Ὑμεῖς με ἠναγκάσατε) There are certain self-commendations that are extorted, and therefore beyond blame.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ὤφειλον ὑφ’ ὑμῶν συνίστασθαι) You ought not to have expected that I should say anything to commend myself. No one knew me better than you: no one could have provided a better testimony about me.

Οὐδὲν γὰρ ὑστέρηκα τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν ἀποστόλων) Above XI. 5. Εἰ καὶ οὐδέν εἰμι) If I am looked at in myself, outside of Christ, I am nothing, of no value before God. Here οὐδὲν is taken as the opposite of τί, Gal. VI. 3.

The reason is, as B. Hunnius explains, why the Corinthians ought to have labored so that the authority of the Apostle might remain unshaken, because indeed he was in no respect inferior even to the greatest Apostles, whether one looks at the amplitude of his calling, or the excellence of his gifts, or the preeminence of his heavenly revelations, or the clarity of his miracles, or his supreme faithfulness in performing his office, or his indefatigable zeal in enduring labors, and his alacrity and readiness in undergoing dangers for the name of Christ. He adds, moreover: Although I am nothing: By this very thing ascribing all praise and glory not to himself, but to the goodness of God, and at the same time distinguishing and intimating between the humility of his own person and the eminence of the office entrusted to him, that he was indeed in the eyes of the world, by reason of his person, a vile and abject man, but before God a miserable sinner also, and formerly a most bitter enemy and persecutor of the Church of God, and therefore in more than one way altogether unworthy of the majesty of so great and so sublime an office: Nevertheless, that by the singular and immense clemency of GOD he had been raised to the pinnacle of Apostolic dignity.

Latin:

v. 11. Γέγονα ἄφρων καυχώμενος) In Manuscripto non est καυχώμενος. Nam ἄφρων, id est, ὡς ἄφρων, ut sæpe in capite præcedente, hic idem valet, quod καυχώμενος.

Ὑμεῖς με ἠναγκάσατε) Sunt quædam περιαυτολογίαι ex- tortæ, ac propterea extra culpam.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ὤφειλον ὑφ’ ὑμῶν συνίστασθαι) Non debueratis expectare, ut quicquam ad me commendandum dicerem. Nemo me melius noverat, quam vos: nemo melius de me testimonium præbere poterat.

Οὐδὲν γὰρ ὑστέρηκα τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν ἀποστόλων) Supra XI. 5. Εἰ καὶ οὐδέν εἰμι) Si in me specter, extra Christum, nihil sum, nullius pretii apud Deum. Hic οὐδὲν sumitur, sicut oppositum τί Gal. VI. 3.

Ratio est, B. Hunnio explicante, cur elaborare debuerint Corinthii, ut autoritas Apostoli maneret inconvulsa, quia nimirum non fuerit re ulla, sum- mis etiam Apostolis inferior, sive quis spectet ampli- tudinem vocationis, sive donorum excellentiam, sive cœlestium revelationum ἐξοχὴν, sive claritudinem prodigiorum, sive in officio faciendo fidem summam, sive in laboribus exantlandis studium indefessum, & in periculis pro nomine Christi subeundis alacrita- tem ac promptitudinem. Addit autem: Tametsi nihil sum: Hoc ipso laudem gloriamque omnem non sibi, sed Dei bonitati adscribens, simulque inter per- sonæ suæ humilitatem, & concrediti muneris emi- nentiam distinguens & innuens, esse quidem se coram mundi oculis ratione personæ suæ hominem vilem & abjectum, coram Deo autem miserum etiam pecca- torem & olim Ecclesiæ Dei fuisse hostem & perse- quutorem acerbissimum, ideoque non uno modo tanti tamque sublimis officii majestate prorsus indignum: Attamen ex singulari & immensa clementia DEI ad fastigium Apostolicæ dignitatis evectum esse.

## 12:12
v. 12. The signs of the Apostle) By which I am recognized as being an Apostle, no less than those twelve.

In all patience) He placed patience before the gifts. It is truly Apostolic to endure adversities more bravely than others.

In signs, and wonders, and mighty works) במופתים,בגבורות באותות.

Latin:

v. 12. Τὰ μὲν σημεῖα τοῦ Ἀποστόλου) Per quæ cognoscor ego esse Apostolus, non minus, quam illi duodecim.

Ἐν πάσῃ ὑπομονῇ) ὑπομονὴ posuit ante charismata. Vere Apostolicum est, plura, quam cæteri, adversa fortiter tolerare.

Ἐν σημείοις, καὶ τέρασι, καὶ δυνάμεσι) במופתים,בגבורות באותות.

## 12:13
v. 13. For what is it, in which you were inferior to the rest of the churches?) Did you receive lesser gifts through the laying on of my hands than those churches which Peter and the other Apostles founded?

What more these things import, the blessed Hunnius explains them in such a way, as if he were saying: If you Corinthians do not acknowledge my Apostleship, bewitched no doubt by the most empty persuasion of the Pseudo-Apostles. Come, let one of you explain to me, and what that is, in which the other churches, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, excel your church: as if this church of yours, founded and planted by my ministry, had been ennobled by me with fewer and more obscure signs of Apostolic dignity, but the remaining churches by other Apostles, with more and more august ones. This, I say, I ask to be clearly demonstrated to me?

If not) By the appearance of an exception he strengthens more what he says. For it is irony.

That I myself was not a burden to you. I was not lazy to your detriment. I did not take from you what would free me from the labor of my hands. See above XI. 9.

Forgive me this wrong?) And this is a very effective irony. They are unjust who take more than is fitting. Paul here made a figure from the contrary. If it is injustice among you to take less than is owed, I ask that you forgive me this fault. Forgive is what the Rabbis would say מחלו.

Theophylact paraphrases it thus: If you accuse me of that matter, because I have been a burden to none of you, but preached the Gospel for free, I ask for pardon. If that is any crime, grant it as a gift. If this is that sin of mine, that, sparing you, I refused to accept stipends, I truly think it is of such a kind that it ought to obtain pardon among you by its own merit.

Latin:

v. 13. Τί γάρ ἐστιν, ὃ ἡττήθητε ὑπὲρ τὰς λοιπὰς ἐκκλησίας;) An minora dona per impositionem manuum mearum vos recepistis, quam illæ Ecclesiæ, quas Petrus & alii Apostoli fundarunt?

Amplius quid hæc important, ideo ea ita edisserit Beat. Hunnius, quasi dicat: Si vos Corinthii non agnoscitis meum Apostolatum, fascinati nimirum inanissima persuasione Pseudo-Apostolorum. Age edisserat mihi vestrum aliquis, & quid illud sit, in quo cæteræ Ecclesiæ vel Judæorum vel gentium antecellant Ecclesiæ vestræ: quasi hæc vestra meo fundata & plantata ministerio paucioribus & obscurioribus signis Apostolicæ dignitatis fuerit per me nobilitata, reliquæ autem Ecclesiæ per alios Apostolos, pluribus & augustioribus. Hoc inquam peto mihi dilucide commonstrari?

Εἰ μὴ) Specie exceptionis magis firmat, quod dicit. Est enim εἰρωνεία.

Ὅτι αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ὐ κατενάρκησα ὑμῶν. Non fui piger vestro damno. Non sumpsi à vobis, quæ me à manuum labore liberarent. Vide supra XI. 9.

χαρίσασθέ μοι τὴν ἀδικίαν ταύτην;) Et hæc valde efficax est εἰρωνεία. Ἀδικοι sunt, qui plus sumunt, quam oportet. Paulus hîc ex contrario fecit figuram. Si apud vos injustitia est, minus quam debetur sumere, rogo, hanc culpam mihi condonetis. χαρίσασθε est, quod Rabbini dicerent מחלו.

Theophylactus ita παραφράζει: Si me ejus rei insimulatis, quia nulli ex vobis oneri fuerim, sed gratis Evangelium prædicarim, veniam postulo. Id si quid est criminis, dono date. Si hoc est peccatum illud meum, quod, parcens vobis, stipendia recusarim accipere, puto sane id esse ejus generis, ut veniam apud vos suo quodam merito obtinere debeat.

## 12:14
v. 14. Behold, this third time I am ready to come to you) He does not say this, that he will come for the third time, but that it is now the third time that he prepares himself for a journey to them and is hindered. I am ready, namely in spirit, as in Acts XXI. 13. see also Dan. III. 15.

And I will not be a burden to you) I have determined to persist in my resolve, of not burdening you, see above XI. 9.

Οὐ γὰρ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν ἀλλ’ ὑμᾶς) I seek nothing of yours, but I desire to render you safe for eternity. A truly Apostolic saying.

Οὐ γὰρ ὀφείλει τὰ τέκνα τοῖς γονεῦσι θησαυρίζειν, ἀλλ’ οἱ γονεῖς τοῖς τέκνοις) Supply ὀφείλεσι θησαυρίζειν. Natural reason, as a kind of tacit law, assigns the inheritance of parents to children, says the Jurisconsult Paulus. See what we have said concerning the Law of War and Peace, book II, chapter VII, 5.

He shows that he is so far from being led by repentance for that deed, that in his third coming, which he is preparing, he will observe the same thing to the letter: so that they may not think that he will accept anything from them upon his arrival. And he gives this reason: because he does not seek their wealth, but them, and the Corinthians, and their salvation. By which he tacitly notes the Pseudo-Apostles who are gaping after their goods. Concerning that: τρίτον ἑτοίμως ἔχω Beza: Some explain this as if τρίτον pertained to the verb ἐλθεῖν, which does not please me. For I think the Apostle had come to Corinth only twice at most, as I shall say below in chapter XIII, 1. Furthermore, τρίτον is placed in such a way that it is sufficiently clear it refers to ἑτοίμως ἔχω: and it is easy to explain this: For first of all he had been prepared to go from Ephesus to Macedonia, and from there to Corinth Acts XIX, 21, and 1. Cor. XVI. 5. 8. then when the Lord had hindered this plan, he had decided to go straight from Ephesus to Corinth, as he shows above I, 15, which plan having been changed again, he had come into Macedonia: from where now at last he had decided to visit them for the third time.

Latin:

v. 14. Ἰδὺ τρίτον τῦτο ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Non hoc dicit, tertio se venturum, sed jam tertium esse, quod se parat itineri ad ipsos & impeditur. Ἑτοίμως ἔχω, animo nempe, ut Act. XXI. 13. vide & Dan. III. 15.

Καὶ ὐ καταναρκήσω ὑμῶν) Constitui perstare in meo instituto, nihil vos gravandi, supra XI. 9.

Οὐ γὰρ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν ἀλλ’ ὑμᾶς) Nihil vestrum expeto, sed vos in æternum salvos præstare cupio. Dictum vere Apostolicum.

Οὐ γὰρ ὀφείλει τὰ τέκνα τοῖς γονεῦσι θησαυρίζειν, ἀλλ’ οἱ γονεῖς τοῖς τέκνοις) Supple ὀφείλεσι θησαυρίζειν. Ratio naturalis, quasi lex quædam tacita, liberis parentum hæreditatem addicit, ait Jurisconsultus Paulus. Vide, quæ diximus de Jure belli & pacis libr. II. cap. VII. 5.

Ostendit adeo se non duci pœnitudine istius facti, ut in tertio, quem paret, adventu idem ad amussim observaturus sit: ne putent, eundem deinceps quid sub adventum suum ab ipsis accepturum. Et rationem hanc reddit: quia non quærat ipsorum opes, sed ipsos, & Corinthios, eorumque salutem. Qua tacite notat Pseudo-Apostolos bonis ipsorum inhiantes. De illo: τρίτον ἑτοίμως ἔχω Beza: Hoc nonnulli ita explicant, quasi τρίτον pertineat ad verbum ἐλθεῖν, quod mihi non placet. Puto enim Apostolum bis duntaxat venisse Corinthum ad summum, ut dicam infra cap. XIII. 1. Deinde ita collocatum est τρίτον, ut satis liqueat referri ad ἑτοίμως ἔχω: & facile est hoc explicare: Nam primum omnium paratus fuerat Epheso Macedoniam ire, & inde Corinthum Act. XIX. 21. & 1. Cor. XVI. 5. 8. deinde cum Dominus hoc consilium impedivisset, constituerat Epheso rectà ire Corinthum, ut ostendit supra I. 15. quo consilio rursus mutato in Macedoniam venerat: unde nunc tandem tertio decreverat eos invisere.

## 12:15
v. 15. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἥδιστα δαπανήσω) I will spend my own things, although they are meager.

Καὶ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν) I will spend myself. For the passive here, as often, is for the reciprocal, which the Hebrews call Niphal for Hithpahel, ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, that is, for you. על נפשותי כם.

Although I love you more abundantly)

Ἧττον ἀγαπῶμαι) I am less loved by you than other teachers.

Theophylact says these things are of one both reproving and loving. For he says: I have done these things for the sake of those whom I myself pursue with benevolence, not those who respond equally to my love. See in how many ways he urges them: First, because he accepted nothing, which he could have taken by right, and because he lacked necessary things, and preached the Gospel to them freely, and bestowed rather than accepted. And not simply and sparingly, but abundantly and liberally. And what is greatest, that he gives and devotes himself to those who love him less. Beza renders that περισσοτέρως without comparison as abundantly. It is likely that the Apostle did not love other Churches less than the Corinthian.

Latin:

v. 15. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἥδιστα δαπανήσω) Res meas, quanquam tenues sunt, impendam.

Καὶ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν) Memetipsum impendam. Nam Passivum hîc ut sæpe est pro reciproco, quod Hebræi dicunt Niphal pro Hithpahel, ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, id est, pro vobis. על נפשותי כם.

Εἰ καὶ περισσοτέρως ὑμᾶς ἀγαπῶν) Cum diligam vos plus, quam alias Ecclesias.

Ἧττον ἀγαπῶμαι) Minus à vobis diligor, quam doctores alii.

Theophylactus hæc & arguentis & amantis esse ait. Dicit enim: Hæc quidem eorum gratia fecerim, quos ipse prosequor benevolentia, non qui æquæ amori respondeant meo. Vide quot modis hos urgeat: Primum quia nihil acciperet, quod jure capere poterat, & quia necessariis rebus careret, gratisque & his Evangelium prædicaret, largiretur potius quam acciperet. Nec simpliciter quidem & parce, sed abunde & liberaliter. Quodque permaximum est seipsum & dedat colatque, qui se minus ament. Illud περισσοτέρως sine comparatione Beza reddit abunde. Non minus dilexisse Apostolum alias Ecclesias, quam Corinthiacam, verosimile est.

## 12:16
v. 16. But be it so, I did not burden you

But being crafty, I took you with guile) Perhaps they will say that I, as a crafty man, did through interposed persons what I did not want to do through myself. He objects this to himself, as if from the words of his Adversaries, so that he may immediately solve it.

The Greeks explain it in the same sense. Theophylact: I indeed demanded nothing from you by asking for the sake of avarice, although perhaps someone might suspect that I, by a certain craftiness and cunning, had determined to accept nothing from you, but had sent my own to you, who would demand something from you. By that art, so that even while accepting, I might seem to have accepted nothing, which is certainly entirely alien to the truth. I would therefore like you to consider whether the matter is so, or not? Others, and also the Blessed Hunnius, explain the craftiness a little differently, that by a singular plan, both to blunt the calumny, as if he were evangelizing for the sake of private gain, and to condemn the avarice of the Pseudo-Apostles, and to detract authority from them, and to attach the minds of the Corinthians to himself. This plan of his he calls craftiness or guile, says the Blessed Hunnius, by which he caught them, because he had concealed the goal which he had set for himself in the abstinence of a lawful thing, so that he might arrive at where he wanted. But this craftiness is not turned to vice for the Apostle, but to praise, since both the means which he used was lawful, namely abstinence from a stipend, and the end was most excellent and most wholesome, namely the perpetual salvation of the Corinthians. But the opinion of the Greeks seems simpler here, that the rivals argued the craftiness itself, whose accusation he refutes, but he himself did not profess the craftiness. To whom the Blessed Balduinus adds: It is mimesis; for the adversaries could object such things, namely that Paul used a certain crafty plan: that he himself present taught for free, and yet through others, whom he sent to Corinth subsequently, was troublesome to them. The Apostle answers, appealing to the testimony of the Corinthians themselves: Did I circumvent you through any of those whom I sent to you? v. 17. In Greek it is ἐπλεονέκτησα, did I plunder you through a desire of having? or did I send my friends to you for that reason, so that I might milk you of money and enrich myself?

Latin:

v. 16. Ἔστω δὲ, ἐγὼ ὀὐ κατεβάρησα ὑμᾶς) Forte mihi hoc concedent illi, me vobis palam gravem non fuisse.

Ἀλλ’ ὑπάρχων πανοῦργος, δόλῳ ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον) Forte dicent, me ut hominem versutum fecisse per interpositas personas, quod per memetipsum facere nolueram. Objicit hoc sibi, tanquam ex Adversariorum verbis, ut statim solvat.

Eodem sensu exponunt Græci. Theophylactus: A vobis equidem nihil ad avaritiam flagitando exegi, tametsi forsitan aliquis suspicetur, calliditate me quadam & astutia potius, nihil à vobis accipere destinasse, sed meos ad vos transmisisse, qui aliquid à vobis efflagitarent. Ea arte ut vel accipiens nihil videar accepisse, quod sane est à vero penitus alienum. Velim itaque consideretis, utrum ita sese habeat res, necne? Paulo aliter alii, etiam Beat. Hunnius explicant astum, quod singulari consilio, tum ob retundendam calumniam, quasi privati commodi causa evangelizaret, tum ut Pseudo-Apostolorum avaritiam damnaret, & autoritatem eis detraheret, sibi vero Corinthiorum animos adjungeret. Hoc suum consilium nominat astum sive dolum, inquit Beat. Hunnius, quo illos ceperit, quia scopum, quem in abstinentia rei licitæ præfixum habebat, dissimulaverat, ut perveniret eo, quo vellet. Astus autem hic non vitio vertitur Apostolo, sed laudi, quandoquidem & medium, quo utebatur, erat licitum, videlicet abstinentia à stipendio, & finis erat longe præstantissimus & saluberrimus, nimirum perpetua Corinthiorum salus. Sed simplicior hic videtur Græcorum sententia, quod astu usum ipsum arguerint æmuli, quorum ἔγκλημα refellit, non vero ipse astum professus sit. Quibus accedit Beat. Balduinus: Mimesis est; Talia enim objicere potuerunt adversarii, Paulum videlicet astuto quodam consilio usum: se præsentem gratis docuisse, & vero per alios, quos subinde Corinthum misit, eis molestum fuisse. Respondet Apostolus provocans ad ipsorum Corinthiorum testimonium: Numquid per aliquem eorum, quos ad vos misi, circumveni vos? v. 17. In Græco est ἐπλεονέκτησα nunquid cupiditate habendi expilavi vos? vel num ideo amicos meos ad vos misi, ut pecuniis vos emungerem & me locupletarem?

## 12:17
V. 17. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I have sent to you) Think through Timothy, 1 Cor. XVI. 10. ἐπλεονέκτησα, בצעתי. See above VII. 2. there is here an antiprosis, as - - - The city which I establish, is yours.

Most others say these things were said generally, and then applied specifically to Titus, but not to Timothy. Yet the Grotian interpretation can easily be admitted, having nothing discordant.

Latin:

V. 17. Μή τινα ὧν ἀπέσταλκα πρὸς ὑμᾶς, δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐπλεονέκτησα ὑμᾶς) Puta per Timotheum, 1. Cor. XVI. 10. ἐπλεονέκτησα, בצעתי. Vide supra VII. 2. est hic ἀντίπτωσις, ut - - - Urbem quam statuo, vestra est.

Alii plerique generaliter hæc dicta, specialiter deinde applicari ad Titum, non verò ad Timotheum spectare ajunt. Facile tamen etiam Grotiana interpretatio admitti potest, nihil absoni habens.

## 12:18
v. 18. I exhorted Titus) I urged him to go to you, above VIII. 6.

And I sent with him the brother) Who is thought to be Luke. See above VIII. 18.

Did Titus take advantage of you?) Did he make gain of you?

Did we not walk in the same spirit?) Here, spirit signifies the disposition of the mind.

Did they not follow in the same steps?) Did they not tread in my footsteps? that is, they imitated me in all things.

Nor even a little (so the paraphrase of Theophylact has it) he says, have I departed from this purpose of mine. And not only did I myself do this, but my followers, moreover, most keenly followed my footsteps. And yet Paul not only chastened himself by these laws, but he also instructed those who were with him, that they might not be defiled by any gain, even if it were more just. Others more correctly understand that τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι as referring to the Holy Spirit. And here Beza has already corrected Castellio: Do we not see in reality that we are ruled by one and the same Spirit of GOD? It is therefore a very pregnant Hebraism, which we have therefore gladly kept intact. For if you were to say in Latin with Castellio: Have we not entered with the same mind? you would have lost half the energy.

Latin:

v. 18. Παρεκάλεσα Τίτον) Hortatus sum, ut ad vos iret, supra VIII. 6.

Καὶ συναπέστειλα τὸν ἀδελφὸν) Qui putatur Lucas. Vide supra VIII. 18.

Μή τι ἐπλεονέκτησεν ὑμᾶς Τίτος;) An ex vobis lucrum fecit?

Οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι περιεπατήσαμεν) Πνεῦμα hic affe- ctum animi significat.

Οὐ τοῖς ἴχνεσι) Nonne illi meis institerunt vestigiis? id est, me per omnia imitati sunt.

Neque vel paululum (ita habet Theophylacti pa- raphrasis) inquit à meo hoc instituto decessi. Et non solum ipse id egi, sed mei insuper sectatores acer- rime mea sunt sectati vestigia. Atqui non modo se- ipsum his legibus Paulus castigabat, quin &, qui secum essent, instituebat, ne quo vel justiori lucro inquinarentur. Illud τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι rectius alii de Spiritu Sancto accipiunt. Et castigavit hic Be- za jam Castellionem: Nonne reipsa videmus, nos uno eodemque Spiritu DEI regi? Est igitur valde prægnans Hebraismus, quem idcirco libenter serva- vimus integrum. Nam si Latine cum Castellione dixeris: Nonne eodem animo ingressi sumus? di- midium energia amiseris.

## 12:19
v. 19. Do you think again that we are making our defense to you?) You think perhaps that I repeat this so often only for the sake of clearing myself. There is something else that I am chiefly looking at here.

In the sight of God we speak in Christ. But all things, beloved, are for your edification) I think the punctuation mark after λαλοῦμεν should be removed and τάδε πάντα should be read. We say all these things, with God as witness, and with that truthfulness which Christ taught us, for the sake of your progress, namely, that if I should become vile to you, the Gospel also might become vile to you, such as I preached it to you. Compare Gal. I. 20. Col. I. 22.

The Vulgate formerly wrongly had 'again' for πάλιν, as if it were πάλαι, which fits not at all. By no means, as the interpretation of Theophylact has it, do we speak these things to you for favor, as if using an excuse, but just as if God were watching, and we speak in Christ, that is, through Christ we thus declare it. The Greeks admit the punctuation, and they do not read τάδε, but τὰ δὲ, as the codices commonly have it: in which there should be a religious scruple to change anything at will. But τὰ δὲ πάντα are best referred to all the things which the Apostle says, who testifies thus, that he has referred all his counsels and actions to this end, that they might contribute to the utility and edification of the Corinthian Church. For which reason they can also be referred at the same time to the immediately preceding things, and the sense of Grotius can be admitted, without changing the text. Theophylact wishes these to refer to Paul's gratuitous ministry: For neither (he says) did I do it for this reason, nor did I receive anything at all from you on that account, because you were weaker and more feeble (for that would have offended their minds) but for the sake of edifying you, and I received nothing, so that I might not disturb you, but rather help and benefit you. By which means a transition seems to be made to the following admonition, and to indicate, according to the Blessed Hunnius, that Paul is not for his own sake, but for the sake of the Corinthians, so diligently removing the sinister opinion regarding the stipend not accepted, that it was not done with an unfriendly mind, nor are these things said to sting them, but in the sight of God, before whom he speaks these things, his speech is directed solely to that goal, that from the comparison they may understand how far the Pseudo-Apostles are from the faithfulness of their Apostle Paul, and that, having bid farewell to the judgments which they had perhaps formed less favorably about him, they may persevere in the doctrine preached by him, and compose their own life to the prescription of that doctrine.

PART III. Admonition to repentance.

Latin:

v. 19. Πάλιν δοκεῖτε, ὅτι ὑμῖν ἀπολογούμεθα) Putatis for- te, me hoc toties repetere, mei tantum purgandi causa. Aliud est, quod præcipue hîc specto.

Κατενώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ λαλοῦμεν. Τὰ δὲ πάντα, ἀγαπητοὶ, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν οἰκοδομῆς) Puto auferendam διαστολὴν post λαλοῦμεν & legendum τάδε πάντα. Dicimus hæc omnia, conscio DEO, & ea veracitate, quam Christus nos docuit, vestri profectus causa, nempe ne si ego vobis vilescam, vilescat vobis & Evangelium, quale id vobis prædicavi. Confer. Gal. I. 20. Col. I. 22.

Vulgata pro πάλιν iterum male habet olim, quasi esset πάλαι, quod minimè convenit. Nequaquam, ut iterum Theophylacti habet interpretatio, ad gratiam vobis hæc loquimur, tanquam excusatione utentes, sed perinde, ac Deo spectante & in Christo loquimur, hoc est, per Christum ita enunciamus. Admittunt Græci διαστολὴν, nec τάδε legunt, sed τὰ δὲ, ut communiter habent codices: In quibus religio sit, pro arbitrio quiequam mutare. Τὰ δὲ πάντα autem referuntur optime ad omnia, quæ ait Apostolus, qui testatur ita, quod ad hunc finem universa sua consilia & actiones retulerit, ut ad Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ utilitatem & ædificationem cederent. Qua ratione etiam ad immediate præce- dentia referri simul possunt, & admitti sensus Gro- tii, citra textus immutationem. Theophylactus ea spectare vult gratuitum Pauli ministerium: Neque enim (inquit) eam hac ob causam egerim, vel à vo- bis nil prorsus ea ratione accepi, quia infirmiores vos sitis & imbecilles (horum namque animos offendisset) sed ædificandi vos gratia & nihil accepi, ne vos ob- turbarem, sed juvarem potius & prodessem. Quo pacto transitio fieri videtur ad sequentem com- monefactionem, atque indicare, secundum Beat. Hunnium, Paulum non sui, sed Corinthiorum cau- sa tam diligenter amoliri sinistram opinionem ob non acceptum stipendium non alieno animo id factum, neque hæc eò dici, ut illos pungat, sed in Dei conspe- ctu, coram quo loquatur ista, sermonem hunc suum unicè tendere ad istum scopum, ut ex collatione in- telligant, quantum à fidelitate Pauli Apostoli sui ab- sint Pseudo-Apostoli, & ut judiciis, quæ de ipso mi- nus commoda forte conceperant, valere jussis in do- ctrina per ipsum prædicata perseverent, suamque vitam ad præscriptum ejus doctrinæ componant.

PARS III. Commonefactio ad pœnitentiam.

## 12:20
v. 20. For I fear that when I come, I may not find you such as I wish) I fear that I may find you corrupted by those teachers who flatter vices.

Having mentioned his arrival, he warns them to prepare themselves, lest he should perhaps find them other than he would wish. He fears, moreover, that he may find them either insufficiently constant and corrupted in doctrine, or less than approved in the conduct of their lives.

Κἀγὼ εὑρεθῶ ὑμῖν, οἷον ὐ θέλετε) that is, lest I be forced to use severity against you, as 1 Cor. IV. 21. above X. 6.

You see, says Theophylact, Paul's most diligent care and spiritual providence. While others were sinning, he himself was tormented by fear. Nor does he condemn the sinners, but as if doubtful and uncertain he says, lest when I come I perhaps find you such as I would not, that is, corrupt and depraved, and I myself also be found such as you would not, that is, a chastiser and inflicter of punishments.

Μήπως ἔρεις) Supply, even now after so many remedies applied, they might be found among you, 1 Cor. I. 11. III. 3.

Ζῆλοι) In the cited passage 1 Cor. III. 3.

Θυμοὶ) wraths, as Acts XIX. 28. Gal. V. 20. Eph. IV. 31. Col. III. 8.

Ἐριθεῖαι) Of which mention is made in the cited passage to the Galatians. See also Rom. II. 8. Phil. I. 16. Jas. III. 14. 16.

Καταλαλιαὶ) You have this noun also at 1 Pet. II. 1. and καταλάλους at Rom. I. 30. where we have spoken of its meaning.

Ψιθυρισμοὶ) You have Ψιθυριστὰς in the same passage to the Romans, where see what was said.

Φυσιώσεις) Puffs of glory on account of riches, learning, eloquence. He notes those whom he mentions at 1 Cor. IV. 18. 19. V. 2. where you have the verb φυσιῦσθαι, as also at 1 Cor. VIII. 1. XIII. 4.

Ἀκαταστασίαι) Seditions, which are accustomed to be born from schism, as the epistle of Clement to the Corinthians teaches us. Concerning this word see Luke XXI. 9. 1 Cor. IV. 33. above VI. 5.

He explains by enumeration what he wishes to be corrected, recounting eight enormous vices which he had already censured in the former epistle, which could easily sprout again if they allowed the teaching of Paul to be despised among them: such as are (1.) contentions in the Church and (2.) emulations, by which some envied the gifts of others. And further in common life (3.) wraths, by which the union of minds or the bond of charity is disturbed; and (4.) ἐριθεῖαι, contentions, such as they had carried on before gentile courts, 1 Cor. VI. as also (5.) backbitings, by which some detract from the honor of others: likewise (6.) ψιθυρισμοὶ, whisperings, secret slanders by which a neighbor was harmed. Then (7.) Φυσιώσεις, swellings, by which they were puffed up and bloated in admiration of themselves, and exalted themselves above others. (8.) finally ἀκαταστασίαι, seditions, disturbing the public state whether in the Church or in the polity. He advises that all these things be removed from the midst, with the reason subjoined, lest he should have to mourn instead of rejoice upon his arrival.

Latin:

v. 20. Φοβοῦμαι γὰρ μὴ πῶς ἐλθὼν, οὐχ οἵους θέλω, εὕρω ὑμᾶς) Metuo, ne vos inveniam corruptos à Doctoribus illis, qui vitiis blandiuntur.

Injecta mentione sui adventus submonet, ita se comparent, ne forsan deprehendat alios quàm velit. Metuit autem, ne inveniat eos vel in do- ctrina parum constantes & corruptos, vel in vitæ conversatione minus probatos.

Κἀγὼ εὑρεθῶ ὑμῖν, οἷον ὐ θέλετε) id est, ne severitate uti in vos cogar, ut 1. Cor. IV. 21. supra X. 6.

Vides Pauli, inquit Theophylactus, diligentissimam curam & providentiam spiritualem. Delinquentibus aliis ipse formidine angebatur. Nec peccantes condemnat, sed quasi dubius & anceps inquit, ne veniens vos forte deprehendam, quales non velim, hoc est corruptos & depravatos, deprehendarque item & ipse, qualem non vultis, id est, castigator & pœnarum ingestor.

Μήπως ἔρεις) Supple, etiamnum post tot remedia adhibita inter vos reperiantur, 1. Cor. I. 11. III. 3.

Ζῆλοι) Dicto loco 1. Cor. III. 3.

Θυμοὶ) iræ, ut Actor. XIX. 28. Gal. V. 20. Ephes. IV. 31. Coloss. III. 8.

Ἐριθεῖαι) Quarum mentio dicto ad Gal. loco. Vide & Rom. II. 8. Philipp. I. 16. Jac. III. 14. 16.

Καταλαλιαὶ) Habes hoc nomen & 1. Petr. II. 1. & καταλάλους Rom. I. 30. ubi de significatu diximus.

Ψιθυρισμοὶ) Ψιθυριστὰς habes in eodem ad Romanos loco, ubi dicta vide.

Φυσιώσεις) Gloriarum flatus ob divitias, eruditionem, eloquentiam. Notat illos, quos 1. Cor. IV. 18. 19. V. 2. ubi habes verbum φυσιῦσθαι, ut & 1. Cor. VIII. 1. XIII. 4.

Ἀκαταστασίαι) Seditiones, quæ ex schismate nasci solent, ut nos docet epistola Clementis ad Corinthios. De hoc vocabulo vide Luc. XXI. 9. 1. Cor. IV. 33. supra VI. 5.

Exponit per enumerationem, quæ velit corrigi, octo recensens enormia vitia, quæ taxaverat jam priori epistola, quæ facile repullulascere poterant, si doctrinam Pauli inter se contemni paterentur: ceu sunt (1.) in Ecclesia contentiones & (2.) æmulationes, quibus alii aliis sua invidebant dona. Et porro in communi vita (3.) iræ, quibus conjunctio turbatur animorum, vel charitatis vinculum; ac (4.) ἐριθεῖαι concertationes, quales coram judiciis gentilibus agitarant, 1. Cor. VI. ut & (5.) obtrectationes, quibus alii aliis honorem detrahunt: item (6.) ψιθυρισμοὶ susurri occultæ delationes, quibus proximus lædebatur. Tum (7.) Φυσιώσεις tumores, quibus sua ipsius admiratione inflati turgebant, & supra alios sese efferebant. (8.) denique ἀκαταστασίαι seditiones publicum statum sive in Ecclesia, sive in politia turbantes. Quæ omnia, ut è medio tollantur, monet, subjuncta ratione, ne pro lætitia sub adventum lugere necesseum habeat.

## 12:21
v. 21. Lest when I come again my God will humble me among you) There is a transposition here also. For πάλιν ἐλθόντα με coheres with πρὸς ὑμᾶς, when I shall have returned to you. Ταπεινῦν here is to affect with sorrow, whence ταπείνωσις, Luke I. 48. Acts VIII. 33. Ps. XC. verse 3, in the Greek. May God affect me with sorrow, that is, may I mourn because of God.

Ταπείνωσις does not indeed formally signify sadness in the cited passages, but humiliation; yet here it is joined with sadness, by the force of the following word, ϰ͵ πενθήσω; As the Apostle judged his own exultation, or that of his ministry, when the Churches were profiting through it: So he estimated his humiliation when they were failing, whether in doctrine or in life. For the glory of Teachers are pious and obedient hearers. See 1 Thess. II. 19, 20.

And I shall mourn for many of those who have sinned before) There is a metonymy here. For he says I shall mourn, for I shall be compelled to punish, which the Apostles did not do without signs. Just as the Romans, when about to condemn a citizen, would put on a dark toga. Concerning this sense of the word πενθεῖν, see what was said at 1 Cor. I. 2.

And have not repented) I mean those who shall not have corrected themselves before my arrival.

For the uncleanness) He understands those lusts which he signifies by the same word at Rom. I. 24.

And fornication) By this word we have said that both whoredom and illicit marriages are included. See Acts XV. verse 20, 1 Cor. V. 1.

And lasciviousness, which they have practiced) Every kind of wantonness. See

There is no metonymy here. The Apostle truly mourned for those who had sinned before and had not repented, over the impurity and whoredom and wantonness which they committed: Not about the punishment of the impenitent Corinthians here, but about his own sorrow over their impenitence. For just as the repentance of hearers brings joy to the Ministers of the word; so does their impenitence bring mourning, by which the Holy Spirit is grieved in the hearts of Teachers, Is. LXIV. 10, Eph. IV. 30, and they themselves are compelled to perform their duty groaning, Heb. XIII. v. 17, whose only prayer is, with Nazianzen: Would that none of my hearers might perish! He fears for both, both that new crimes may have emerged, and that many may not have performed serious repentance for their former sins.

Latin:

v. 21. Μὴ πάλιν ἐλθόντα με ταπεινώσῃ ὁ Θεός με πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Est & hic trajectio. Nam πάλιν ἐλθόντα με cohæret cum πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ubi ad vos rediero. Ταπεινῦν hîc est mœrore afficere, unde ταπείνωσις, Luc. I. 48. Act. VIII. 33. Ps. XC. vers. 3. in Græco. Deus me mœrore afficiat, id est, Dei causa mœream.

Ταπείνωσις non quidem tristitiam formaliter significat in locis allegatis, sed humiliationem, ea vero conjuncta hic est cum tristitia, vi vocis sequentis ϰ͵ πενθήσω; Ut exultationem suam judicabat Apostolus vel ministerii sui, cum proficiebant per id Ecclesiæ: Ita humiliationem suam æstimabat, cum deficiebant, sive qua doctrinam, sive qua vitam. Gloria enim Doctorum sunt pii & morigeri auditores. Vide 1. Thess. II. 19. 20.
