Καὶ πενθήσω πολλοὺς τῶν προημαρτηκότων) Est hîc μειωνυμία. Nam lugeam dicit, pro punire cogar, quod Apostoli non faciebant sine signis. Sicut Romani civem damnaturi sumebant pullam togam. De hoc sensu vocis πενθεῖν vide, quæ dicta 1. Cor. I. 2.

Καὶ μὴ μετανοησάντων) Eos dico, 'qui ante adventum meum se non correxerint.

Ἐπὶ τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ) Illas libidines intelligit, quas eadem voce ad Rom. I. 24.

Καὶ πορνείᾳ) Hoc vocabulo diximus & scortationem comprehendi & nuptias illicitas. Vide Act. XV. vers. 20. 1. Cor. V. 1.

Καὶ ἀσελγείᾳ, ᾗ ἔπραξαν) Omni genere lasciviæ. Vide

Nulla hic Metonymia. Lugebat vere Apostolus eos, qui antea peccarant, nec resipuerant, super impuritate & scortatione & protervia, quam patrarunt: Non de pœna hic Corinthiorum impœnitentium, sed de mœrore suo super impœnitentia. Ut enim gaudium conciliat verbi Ministris auditorum pœnitentia; ita luctum impœnitentia, qua Spiritus Sanctus in cordibus Doctorum contristatur, Ef. LXIV. 10. Eph. IV. 30. ipsique facere coguntur officium suum gementes, Ebr. XIII. v. 17. quorum votum unicum est, cum Nazianzeno: Utinam nemo meorum auditorum pereat! De utroque metuit, tùm ne nova crimina emerserint, tùm ne multi de prioribus peccatis seriam haud egerint pœnitentiam.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. AND THE LAST. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He threatens that he is unwilling to spare sinners upon his arrival after the investigation of the case, so that they may experience the mighty works of Christ, who lives by the power of God. He wishes that they test themselves and acknowledge his Apostolic office, testifying that he rejoices in their strength, and therefore, while absent, he exhorts them so that there may be no need for severity when he is present, and he stirs them up to joy, the pursuit of perfection, mutual comfort, unanimity, and concord, promising the assistance of God, and with greetings added, he ends the epistle with an Apostolic vow.

There are three parts: I. A threatening against the impenitent up to verse 4. II. An exhortation to self-examination and true amendment up to verse 11. III. A final admonition to joy, the pursuit of perfection, and peace, with greetings and a final vow up to verse 13.

PART I. A threatening against the impenitent.

v. 1. Ἰδὺ τρίτον τῦτο ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς) That is, I am now preparing for the third time for the journey. For it is the same as what he had said above in XII. 14. And it is customary for the name of the effect to be given to attempts. In the Manuscript, however, it is clearer, just as above: ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς. And thus the Syriac reads.

Thus there is no need for us to conclude with Beza that the Apostle is recounting his two epistles as so many journeys to them, because he is acting no differently by writing to them than if he were present with them in body. Furthermore, Beza does not calculate badly in order to show that the historical narrative does not allow for Paul's arrival after this epistle was written to have been the third, not only because Luke makes no mention of any second arrival (for he did not write down every single thing), but because it is certain that his first arrival in this city was when he came there from Athens, as Luke narrates in Acts chapter 18, at which time he laid the first foundations of the Corinthian Church. From there he crossed to Ephesus and went straight to Jerusalem. From there he came to Caesarea and afterwards to Antioch. Having stayed at Antioch for a little while, he traveled in order through Galatia and Phrygia, until he arrived at Ephesus, having traveled through upper Asia. From where he wrote the former epistle to the Corinthians, where, after 27 months had been spent, he was expelled by the faction of Demetrius and came into Macedonia, from where he wrote this second epistle a little before he himself crossed from Macedonia into Greece, where he spent three months.

Ἐπὶ σόματος δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν σαθήσεται πᾶν ῥῆμα) That is, when I have already said this twice or thrice, at length it will be ratified. Which the Hebrews call יקום; For it is an application as it were by parody of the law, Deut. XIX. 15. A nearly similar application of the same law is in Matth. XVIII. 16.

This gloss is vain and forced, nor is there anything analogous to it in Matth. XIIX. 16, even though it is approved by Estius and others. The discourse is not about that which he has said twice or thrice, but about the testimony of two or three witnesses, both in the Mosaic law and here. Nor were those who were to be condemned or punished to be convinced by the Apostle's repeated words or epistles, but by the mouth of two or three: and thus rightly the Greeks, Ambrosiaster, Cajetan, Baldwin, and others say that the Apostle teaches that he will proceed in judging and punishing sinners according to the form of the divine law, namely, having heard two or three witnesses, so that they might not think that he is going to judge precipitately and rashly, or that he is going to employ a great multitude of witnesses.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ET ULTIMUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Minatur se peccatoribus sub adventum post cognitionem causæ minime parcere velle, ut experiantur virtutem Christi, qui vivit in potentia Dei. Vult ut se probent, munusque suum Apostolicum agnoscant, testatus se latari de ipsorum robore, atque ideo absentem hortari, ne præsenti opus sit severitate, excitatque ad gaudium, perfectionis studium, mutua solatia, unanimitatem & concordiã, promittens Dei assistentiam, & additis salutationibus voto Apostolico finit epistolam.

PArtes tres sunt: I. Comminatio adversus impœnitentes ad v. 4. II. Adhortatio ad sui probationem & veram emendationem ad v. 11. III. Novissima commonefactio ad gaudium, perfectionis studium & pacem, cum salutationibus & voto finali ad v. 13.

PARS I. Comminatio adversus impœnitentes.

v. 1. Ἰδὺ τρίτον τῦτο ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Id est, tertium me jam itineri paro. Est enim idem, quod dixerat supra XII. 14. Et solet conatibus dari nomen effectus. In Manuscripto autem est planius, ita ut supra: ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Et sic legit Syrus.

Ita non opus est, ut cum Beza Apostolum binas suas epistolas pro totidem ad eos profectionibus recensere statuamus, quia sese scribendo haud aliter cum ipsis agere, quàm si corpore præsens apud illos esset. De cætero non male calculum init Beza, ut doceat, non pati historicam narrationem, ut Pauli post hanc epistolam scriptam adventus fuerit tertius, non modo quia secundi alicujus adventus non facit mentionem Lucas, (neque enim is singula perscripsit) sed quia constat, cum fuisse primum ejus in hanc urbem adventum, quum Athenis illuc venit, ut narrat Lucas Act. cap. XIIX. quo tempore prima jecit Corinthiaca Ecclesiæ fundamenta. Inde trajecit Ephesum, & recta contendit Hierosolymam. Inde Cæsaream, & postea Antiochiam venit. Antiochiæ aliquantulum commoratus, ordine peragravit Galatiam & Phrygiam; donec Ephesum, peragrata superiore Asia, deveniret. Unde priorem ad Corinthios epistolam scripsit, ubi consumptis 27. mensibus à Demetrii factione expulsus in Macedoniam venit, unde hanc alteram scripsit epistolam paulo antequam ipse ex Macedonia in Græciam transiret, ubi tres menses consumsit.

Ἐπὶ σόματος δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν σαθήσεται πᾶν ῥῆμα) Id est, cum jam bis terve id dixerim, tandem ratum erit. Quod Hebræi dicunt יקום; Est enim applicatio quasi per παρῳδίαν legis, Deut. XIX. 15. Similis ferme applicatio le- gis ejusdem Matth. XVIII. 16.

Vana & coacta est hæc glossa, nec quicquam illi analogum Matth. XIIX. 16. etsi Estio, aliisque probata. Non de eo, quod bis aut ter idem dixe- rit, sed duorum vel trium testium testimonio & in lege Mosaica & hic sermo est. Nec ex iteratis Apostoli dictis vel epistolis convincendi erant, qui damnandi, vel pœna afficiendi, sed ex ore duorum vel trium: adeoque recte Græci, Am- brosraster, Cajetanus, Balduinus aliique docere ajunt Apostolum, se in judicandis & puniendis peccatoribus processurum secundum formam di- vinæ legis, scilicet auditis duobus vel tribus testi- bus, ne putent, quod vel præcipitanter ac temere judicaturus sit, vel magnam testium multitudi- nem adhibiturus.

## 13:2
v. 2. ὧς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον) Present for future, as if I were to be with you again.

This is more suitable than what Beza has, as if he were saying: I formerly warned you of this and I warn you a second time, as if present by this epistle, which I write while absent.

Τοῖς προημαρτηκόσι) Those who have already sinned more gravely, see above XII. 21.

Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς πᾶσιν) If there are any who are yet to sin.

Ὄτι ἐὰν ἔλθω εἰς τὸ πάλιν) ἐὰν here signifies 'when'. When I shall have returned to you.

Οὐ φείσομαι) I will act severely according to the merits of the crimes.

Latin:

v. 2. ὧς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον) Præsens pro futuro, velut iterum apud vos futurus.

Convenientius hoc, quam quod Beza habet, quasi dicat: Olim id vobis denunciavi & secundo denuncio, ut præsens hac scilicet epistola, quam ab- sens scribo.

Τοῖς προημαρτηκόσι) Iis, qui jam peccarunt gravius, su- pra XII. 21.

Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς πᾶσιν) Si qui adhuc peccaturi sunt.

Ὄτι ἐὰν ἔλθω εἰς τὸ πάλιν) ἐὰν hîc valet & quando. Ubi ad vos rediero.

Οὐ φείσομαι) Agam severe pro criminum meritis.

## 13:3
V. 3. Ἐπεὶ δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε τῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλῦντος Χρισῦ.) Since you act in such a way that you seem to wish to make a trial of what Christ, in whose name I preach the Gospel, can accomplish through me. See above V. 20.

ὃς εἰς ὑμᾶς εἰκ ἀσθενεῖ, ἀλλὰ δυνατεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν) It is the present for the past. You have no need to make a trial of that matter, since Christ has long since given among you through me mighty works of His power. See above XII. 12.

Not only through miracles and the manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit, but also in the punishment of delinquents, such as the incestuous person, 1 Cor. V, as also those who, by receiving the body and blood of the Lord unworthily, had fallen into various sicknesses or had even been snatched away by death, 1 Cor. XI. B. Hunnius. It will therefore be necessary, unless you take great heed, to demonstrate in reality at last that my threats are not empty, but valid through the power of the reigning Christ. And certainly Christ has hitherto been among you through my ministry not weak, but efficacious: see to it, therefore, that He who has hitherto been powerful among you for your salvation, does not now begin to be efficacious for the judgment of those who persevere in their sins without repentance.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἐπεὶ δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε τῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλῦντος Χρισῦ.) Quan- doquidem ita agitis, ut periculum facere velle videamini quid Christus, cujus nomine Evangelium prædico, per me efficere possit. Vide supra V. 20.

ὃς εἰς ὑμᾶς εἰκ ἀσθενεῖ, ἀλλὰ δυνατεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν) Est Præsens pro Præterito. Non opus habetis ejus rei periculum facere, cum jampridem Christus per me apud vos ingentia dederit potentiæ suæ signa. Vid. supra XII. 12.

Non tantum per miracula, & Spiritus Sancti multiplicia dona, sed & in punitione delinquentium, utpote incestuosi, 1. Cor. V. ut & eorum, qui indi- gne sumendo corpus & sanguinem Domini in varias ægritudines inciderant, vel etiam morte abrepti erant, 1. Cor. XI. B. Hunnius. Necessarium erit ergo, nisi oppido caveatis, reipsa tandem demon- strare, minas meas non esse inanes, sed regnantis Christi potentia validas. Et certe fuit hucusque Christus inter vos per meum ministerium non in- firmus, sed efficax: videte ergo, ne qui fuit in vobis hucusque validus ad salutem vestram, nunc incipiat efficax esse ad judicium eorum, qui in peccatis absque pœnitentia perseverant.

## 13:4
v. 4. For even if he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. Weakness here is the frail and infirm condition which Christ had taken upon himself for our sake. Understand the power of God as the same which had worked in him, and compare Rom. 1, verses 3, 4; 1 Pet. 3:18. Paul indicates tacitly, however, that he ought not to be despised because of the many adversities he was bearing, since Christ had entered upon the same path.

Beza rightly [interprets] ἐξ ἀσθενείας, that is, as regards that infirm form of a servant which he accepted, emptying himself. For this declares the same thing as κατὰ σάρκα, Rom. 1:3, except that σὰρξ declares the substance, but ἀσθένεια truly the quality of his substance, to which is opposed the power of God, that is, that most powerful divinity which exerted itself most especially in the resurrection of the flesh. And concerning the latter, 'he lives by the power of God,' Theophylact has not inappropriately advised: that the power of the Father and of Christ himself is to be understood. For there are, he says, things common to the Son and to the Father, and things of the Father which are the Son's. Whence it happens that one and the same power resides in both (who are one). Or rather, the Son is the power of the Father; therefore the Son also raised himself, as he had said: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.'

For we also are weak in him) That is, we suffer many things for his sake. For we have often seen already that this is what it means to be weak. The particle ἐν often has the force of 'for' among the Hebrews. But in the Manuscript it is σὺν αὐτῷ, not badly, following his example.

But we shall live with him, by the power of God toward you) That is, we shall obtain immortal life through the same power of God which has worked such great things among you through us; see what we have said at 1 Cor. 15:44.

These things are foreign to the present [discussion] concerning immortal life. For it is not about the power which not only the Apostle, but all the faithful are to obtain after death, but about the power which the Apostle can exert against the Corinthians, that is being treated here. And the particle 'toward you' confirms this sufficiently. Therefore, the Greek interpreters and Beza and others have handed down the connection and sense much more conveniently: especially the blessed Hunnius: You Corinthians look perhaps more at the outwardly apparent infirmity in the ministers of the Church than at the power involved in the ministry which they perform, and hence that contempt for pious admonitions is born. But it was fitting to know that, just as Christ was once weak in the state of emptying himself for our sake, so that he sought the ignominious death of the cross, now, however, he lives by the power of GOD, and reigns most powerfully at the right hand of Majesty forever. Thus in a certain way and degree the same must be felt concerning his ministers, that although they appear outwardly infirm and contemptible, yet their office through the divine power of Christ is powerful and effective in the penitent indeed for salvation, but in the impenitent for judgment and condemnation, of which thing you will take no obscure experiment in my approach to you, where those stubborn despisers of pious admonitions will feel in reality that we are not invalid like the dead by the power of GOD working with us, but that we live, and our threats are held valid before God, and are joined with solid effect.

PART II.

An exhortation to self-examination, the recognition of the Apostolic office, and the amendment of life.

Latin:

v. 4. Καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἐσαυρώθη ἐξ ἀσθενείας, ἀλλὰ ζῇ ἐκ δυνάμεως Θεῦ) Ἀσθένεια hîc est conditio caduca & infirma, quam Chri- stus nostri causa susceperat. Virtutem Dei intellige ean- dem, quæ in ipso operata fuerat, & confer Rom. I. vers. 3. 4. 1. Pet. III. 18. Tacite autem indicat Paulus, non debere se propter multa, quæ ferebat adversa contemni, cum eadem via Christus ingressus fuerit.

Recte Beza ἐξ ἀσθενείας, id est, quod attinet ad infirmam illam formam servi, quam accepit, se- ipsum exinaniens. Idem enim hoc declarat, atque κατὰ σάρκα, Rom. I. 3. nisi quod σὰρξ declaret ὁσί- αν, ἀσθένεια vero ejus ὁσίας qualitatem, cui opponi- tur potentia Dei, id est, divinitas illa potentissima, quæ sese in resurrectione carnis potissimum exeruit. Et de posteriori vivit ex virtute Dei non incomo- de monuit Theophylactus: Patris & Christi ipsius virtutem intelligi. Sunt enim, inquit, Filio, quæ & Patris communia, & Patri, quæ Filii. Quo fit, ut una insit utrisque (qui unum sunt) & eadem virtus. Quin potius Filius Patris est virtus, ergo & Filius semet suscitavit, ut dixerat: Solvite tem- plum hoc, & in triduo suscitabo illud.

Καὶ γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἀσθενῦμεν ἐν αὐτῷ) Id est, propter ipsum multa patimur. Id enim esse ἀσθενεῖν, sæpe jam vidimus. Particula ἐν sæpe apud Hebræos valet propter. At in Ma- nuscripto est σὺν αὐτῷ non male, ad illius exemplum.

Ἀλλὰ ζησόμεθα σὺν αὐτῷ, ἐκ δυνάμεως τῶ Θεῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς) Id est, vitam consequemur immortalem per eandem Dei virtutem, quæ per nos inter vos tam magna operata est, vi- de, quæ diximus ad 1. Cor. XV. 44.

Aliena hæc in præsenti sunt de vita immortali. Non enim de virtute, quam post mortem non A- postolus solum, sed omnes fideles consecuturi sunt, sed quam Apostolus adversus Corinthios exerere queat, hic agitur. Idque particula εἰς ὑμᾶς satis firmat. Nexum ergo & sensum longe con- venientius Græci Interpp. & Beza aliique tradide- re: Imprimis B. Hunnius: Vos Corinthii fere ma- gis respicitis in Doctoribus Ecclesiæ ad illorum in- firmitatem forinsecus apparentem, quam ad poten- tiam ministerio, quo funguntur, involutam, & hinc ille nascitur piarum commonefactionum con- temptus. Sed scire conveniebat, quod quemadmo- dum Christus fuit olim in statu exanitionis infir- mus propter nos, adeo ut ignominiosam mortem crucis oppeteret, nunc autem ex virtute DEI vivit, & ad dextram Majestatis in sempiternum regnat potentissime. Sic certo modo & gradu idem de mini- stris ejus sentiendum sit, quod licet extrinsecus ap- pareant infirmi & contemptibiles, tamen illorum munus per divinam virtutem Christi sit potens & efficax in pœnitentibus quidem ad salutem, in im- pœnitentibus autem ad judicium & condemnatio- nem, cujus rei experimentum non obscurum capie- tis in meo ad vos accessu, ubi refracti illi piarum admonitionum contemptores reipsa sentient, quod ex virtute DEI cooperantis non invalidi simus tanquam mortui, sed vivamus, & nostræ comminationes ra- tæ apud Deum habeantur, cumque solido effectu conjunctæ sint.

PARS II.

Adhortatio ad sui probationem, Apostolici muneris agnitionem, & vitæ emen- dationem.

## 13:5
v. 5. Examine yourselves whether you are in the faith) Look around again and again, whether you well retain all those doctrines which I have handed down to you.

Test yourselves) 1 Cor. 11:28. The sense is the same as Zeph. 2:1 according to certain interpreters. This is missing in the Manuscript.

Or do you not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you) Do you not feel that Christ is present in you through his Spirit? If you feel that, treat such a guest well, Eph. 4:30.

Unless you are disqualified) Unless you are counterfeit, that is, Christians in name but not in reality, 1 Cor. 9:27; 2 Tim. 3:8; Tit. 1:16; Heb. 6:8. Opposed to these are the approved, who are what they seem, Rom. 14:18; 16:10; 1 Cor. 11:19; above 10:18; 2 Tim. 3:11; Jas. 1:12; and here shortly in verse 7.

They are warned not only about examining dogmatic faith, but primarily about saving faith: as if to say, you can experience in yourselves the power of Christ, who dwells in the hearts of the faithful. For He works faith in you, which you can notice and prove from the motions of the Holy Spirit, from prayers, from efficacious consolation, from living hope, unless you have become completely reprobate, that is, unless through your impenitence you have lost faith and the Holy Spirit, for in these the power of Christ also has ceased to work, as blessed Balduinus holds. Search the hidden recesses of your hearts, and diligently examine yourselves, whether you have true faith in Christ Jesus. When one has discovered that in you, consider from where it comes to you; certainly from God, who nevertheless does not give it immediately, but through my ministry and that of the remaining colleagues he has worked in you mediately. From this draw your judgment, whether that office of mine was empty, so that it ought to be despised by those impenitent ones, as B. Hunnius [says]. Which even the Papist interpreters acknowledge. Estius proves that it cannot be understood of the faith which is common to all Christians, both because the Corinthians could know without new proof that they possessed such a faith. For St. Augustine testifies in book XIII de Trin. cap. 1 that we have most certain knowledge of the faith which is in us, and Dr. Thomas, writing on this passage, affirms that we know that we hold the faith which the Catholic Church teaches and holds, and the same in 1,2. q. 112. art. 5. ad 2. Whoever, he says, has faith, is certain that he has it. Also because through such faith Christ is not immediately said to be in us according to the custom of Scripture. Therefore he prefers the sense concerning the faith which works through love: And he says that it sufficiently agrees with the scope of the Apostle, inasmuch as he reproves the Corinthians not for infidelity, but for evil works. Salmero, disp. XIV on this passage, confesses that both faith, or a true and sound sense concerning things to be believed consisting in knowledge and assent, and the sense of the indwelling divine grace, which we call assurance, can be known, and is known by the faithful by the very act: and he alleges Bernard, serm. I in septuag., explaining this knowledge, or this sense, concerning the sense of election and predestination. Which explanation the Greek interpreters Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others have also embraced. B. Hülsemann on this passage has it thus: That the Apostle here appeals to such an effect of his ministry, so that from the evidence and sense of that effect the Corinthians might be convinced that Paul had fulfilled all the requirements of an Apostolic man, and was not a hypocrite, nor a Pseudo-Apostle, we willingly confess. For just as he perpetually used this mode of arguing against the Pseudo-Apostles, to teach the faith performed in office a posteriori or from the effect, as in chapter X, verses 13, 14 of this epistle and chapter XII, verses 11, 12, 13. The same we also urge is inferred here by the Apostle, and the Corinthians are warned to take the argument or demonstration of Apostolic efficacy from the effect produced in themselves. For that this is the scope of the Apostle is clear from verses 6, 7, where from the sense of internal affections in the Corinthians he infers that he is not rejected, or has not taught ἀδόκιμα and things displeasing to God, and indeed not theoretical ἀδόκιμα, or those which are against the truth, as is clear from v. 8, but that that object or effect to be detected and detectable by the sense of the Corinthians is finished and terminated in the sole sense of theoretical truth or knowledge concerning the truth of the credible object, but that that sense or scrutiny of sense is not to be extended to assurance toward God and God's benevolence; that indeed we deny. For a fortiori he proved the sense of a tranquilized conscience toward God, or the internal certification of the Corinthians that they have a propitious God, [by] the divinity of the Apostolic office in this way: Whatever doctrine as a cause not only informs us about the truth of credible things, but also tranquilizes our consciences toward God, that is most divine: But such is the doctrine of Paul. Therefore the doctrine of Paul is not Pseudo-Apostolic, or is not ἀδόκιμος, but most δόκιμος. For that the Apostle intended this conclusion when he appeals to the internal sense of the Corinthians, so that from this document he might demonstrate the quality of the sense of his doctrine, is clear, as we have said, from the preceding verse 3, δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε, and the following ones, 6, 7, 8. And Justinian and others are entirely false, contending here that the Apostle wished to demonstrate the faith and efficacy of his office only from such an effect which also strikes the eyes of others. For the Apostle speaks not of a sense evident and notorious to others, but internal and immanent in the Corinthians, ἑαυτὸς πειράζετε. From this internal and immanent sense of every believer the Apostle wishes it to be established what kind of effect it is, namely holy and clearly divine, salutary, etc., [and] that such also is the cause which produced such an effect. Just as the Apostle also elsewhere infers internal effects remaining indeed in the believing subject alone, but nevertheless evident and detectable by the sense of the believer, so that from such a sense he might demonstrate the efficacy of the Evangelical doctrine, as most clearly Gal. III. 2, Rom. VII. 16, 2 Cor. X. 7, Eph. III. 12, just as a physician rightly appeals to the sense of the patient detecting the efficacy of a medicine, although that sense is terminated in the individual patient alone, and from the indications of that sense he rightly pronounces on the nature, power, and efficacy of the medicine. These are the words of B. Dn. Socer against Bellarmine, book III de justific. cap. 9. Therefore a firm argument from here concerning the certainty of grace. For he who ought to test himself, whether he is in the faith, and to know whether Christ is in him, he certainly can be more certain concerning the grace of God, which is apprehended through faith. Cf. 2 Tim. I. 12.

Latin:

v. 5. Ἑαυτὸς πειράζετε εἰ ἐςὲ ἐν τῇ πίςει) Etiam atque etiam circumspicite, an omnia ea dogmata bene retineatis, quæ vobis tradidi.

Ἑαυτὸς δοκιμάζετε) 1. Cor. XI. 28. Sensus idem Soph. II. vers. 1. secundum quosdam Interpretes. Deest hoc in Ma- nuscripto.

Ἤ ὐκ ἐπιγινώσκετε ἑαυτὸς, ὅτι Ἰησῦς Χριςὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐςιν) Nonne sentitis Christum per Spiritum suum in vobis præ- sentem esse? Si id sentitis, bene tractate tantum hospitem, Eph. IV. 30.

Εἰ μή τι ἄρα ἀδόκιμοί ἐσε) Nisi adulterini estis, id est, nomine non re Christiani, 1. Cor. IX. v. 27. 2. Tim. III. 8. Tit. I. 16. Hebr. VI. 8. His oppositi δόκιμοι probi qui sunt, quod videntur, Rom. XIV. 18. XVI. 10. 1. Cor. XI. 19. supra X. 18. 2. Tim. III. 11. Jac. I. 12. & hic mox 7.

Non de fide dogmatica solum exploranda mo- nentur, sed imprimis de fide salvifica: q. d. vir- tutem Christi, qui in cordibus fidelium habitat, in vobis ipsis experiri potestis. Is enim fidem in vobis operatur, quam ex motibus Spiritus Sancti, ex pre- cibus, ex consolatione efficaci, ex spe viva animad- vertere & probare potestis, nisi prorsus reprobi fa- cti estis, id est, nisi per impœnitentiam vestram fidem & Spiritum Sanctum amisistis, in his enim virtus quoque Christi operari desiit, ut habet B. Balduinus. Excutite abditos recessus cordium vestrorum, & diligenter examinate vos, an fidem habeatis in Chri- stum Jesum veram. Quam ubi deprehenderit is in vobis, cogitate, undenam illa vobis proveniats utique ex Deo, qui tamen illam non immediate, sed meo & reliquorum collegarum ministerio media- te est in vobis operatus. Hinc judicium facite, fue- ritne munus meum illud inane, ut ab impœnitenti- bus illis contemni debeat, ut B. Hunnius. Quod agnoscunt etiam Pontificii Interpretes. Estius pro- bat, non posse intelligi de fide, quæ omnibus Christianis communis est, tum quia scire poterant Corinthii sine nova probatione, se talem fidem habere. Testatur enim S. Augustinus libr. XIII. de Trin. cap. 1. nos habere certissimam scientiam fidei, quæ in nobis est, & D. Thomas in hunc locum scribens, affirmat nos scire, quod teneamus fidem, quam Ecclesia Catholica docet ac tenet, idemque in 1,2. q. 112. art. 5. ad 2. Quis- quis, inquit, fidem habet, certus est, se eam habere. Tum quia per hujusmodi fidem non continuo Chri- stus in nobis esse dicitur juxta morem scripturæ. Ideo sensum præfert de fide, quæ per dilectionem opera- tur: Eumque satis congruere scopo Apostoli ait, ut- pote qui reprehendat Corinthios non de infidelitate, sed malis operibus. Salmero disp. XIV. in h. l. fatetur & fidem, seu verum sanumque sensum de rebus cre- dendis consistentem in notitia & assensu, & sensum inhabitantis divinæ gratiæ, quem nos fiduciam vo- camus, cognosci posse, & actu ipso cognosci à fide- libus: allegatque Bernhardum serm. I. in septuag. exponentem hanc cognitionem, seu hunc sensum de sensu electionis & prædestinationis. Quam expli- cationem etiam Græci Interpp. Chrysost. Theophy- lactus & alii amplexi sunt. B. Hülsemannus in h. l. ita habet: Apostolum hic provocare ad ejusmodi effectum ministerii sui, ut ex ejus effectus evidentia & sensu convincerentur Corinthii, Paulum exegisse omnes numeros Viri Apostolici, non esse hypocritam, neque Pseudo - Apostolum, libenter confitemur. Quemadmodum enim perpetuo usus est hoc argu- mentandi modo contra Pseudo-Apostolos, ut fidem in officio præstitam doceat à posteriori seu ab effectu, ut cap. X. vers. 13. 14. hujus epist. & cap. XII. vers. 11. 12. 13. Idem etiam urgemus hic inferri ab Apo- stolo, & moneri Corinthios, ut argumentum seu de- monstrationem efficaciæ Apostolicæ ab effectu in se- ipfis producto sumant. Nam hunc scopum esse A- postoli, patet ex vers. 6. 7. ubi ex sensu intrinseco- rum affectuum in Corinthiis infert, se non esse reje- ctaneum, seu non docuisse ἀδόκιμα & Deo displicen- tia, & quidem non ἀδόκιμα theoretica, seu quæ con- tra veritatem sint, ut patet ex v. 8. sed quod objectum seu effectus ille sensu Corinthiorum deprehendendus & deprehensibilis, finiatur & terminetur in solo sensu veritatis theoreticæ seu notitiæ circa verita- tem objecti credibilis, non autem extendendus sit ille sensus seu scrutinium sensus ad fiduciam erga Deum, Deique benevolentiam; id vero negamus. Nam à fortiori probabat ille tranquillatæ conscientiæ er- ga Deum sensus, seu intrinseca certificatio Corin- thiorum se habere Deum propitium divinitatem of- ficii Apostolici hoc modo: Quæ doctrina tanquam causa nos non solum informat de veritate rerum credibilium, sed tranquillat etiam conscientias no- stras erga Deum, ea maxime divina est: Sed talis est doctrina Pauli. Ergo doctrina Pauli non est Pseudo-Apostolica, seu non est ἀδόκιμος, sed ma- xime δόκιμος. Hanc enim conclusionem intendisse Apostolum, quando ad sensum intrinsecum Corin- thiorum provocat, ut ex hoc documento sensus quali tatem doctrinæ suæ demonstret, patet, ut diximus, ex v. antecedente 3. δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε & sequentibus, 6. 7. 8. Suntque omnino falsi Justinianus & alii, hic contendentes, Apostolum fidem & efficaciam offi- cii sui demonstrare voluisse tantum ex tali effectu, qui etiam in aliorum oculos incurrat. Apostolus n. de sensu non aliis evidenti & notorio, sed intrinse- co & immanente in Corinthiis loquitur, ἑαυτὸς πει- ράζετε. Ex hoc sensu intrinseco & immanente cu- juscunque fidelis constare vult Apostolus, qualis est effectus sanctus videlicet, & plane divinus, saluta- ris &c. talem etiam esse causam, quæ produxit talem effectum. Quomodo Apostolus etiam alibi infert effectus intrinsecos manentes quidem in solo subjecto credente, sed evidentes tamen, & sensu credentis de- prehensibiles, ut ex tali sensu efficaciam doctrinæ Ev- angelicæ demonstret, ut clarissime Gal. III. 2. Rom. VII. 16. 2. Cor. X. 7. Ephes. III. 12. quomodo me- dicus recte provocat ad sensum patientis deprehen- dentem efficaciam pharmaci, quanquam ille sensus terminetur in solo individuo patiente, & ex indiciis illius sensus recte pronuntiat de natura, vi & effica- cia pharmaci. Hæc B. Dn. Socer adversus Bellar- minum libr. III. de justific. cap. 9. Firmum ita- que hinc argumentum de certitudine gratiæ. Nam qui seipsum tentare debet, an sit in fide, & cogno- scere, an Christus in se sit, is utique de gratia Dei, quæ per fidem apprehenditur, certior esse potest. Conf. 2. Tim. I. 12.

## 13:6
v. 6. I hope however that you will know that we are not ἀδόκιμοι) We will show this by the deeds themselves, by not winking at crimes, as others do.

The paraphrase of B. Balduinus is more correct here: I do not doubt that you will have faith in my warnings, from which it will be established to you all that Christ has been most powerful through my ministry, in both instructing and correcting you. For I am not a reprobate, or a useless man, whose ministry is inefficacious, and through whom Christ is unwilling to work anything further: and he hopes that the Corinthians themselves will finally acknowledge this. And thus he mitigates the former harshness somewhat, and converts the severity of the reproofs into prayers.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἐλπίζω δὲ ὅτι γνώσεσθε, ὅτι ἡμεῖς οὐκ ἐσμὲν ἀδόκι- μοι) Ostendemus hoc factis ipsis, non connivendo ad cri- mina, ut alii faciunt.

Rectius hic sese habet paraphrasis B. Balduini: Non dubito, quin monitis meis sitis fidem habituri, unde vobis omnibus constabit, Christum per meum ministerium maxime potentem fuisse, in vobis & erudiendis & corrigendis. Non enim sum reprobus, vel homo inutilis, cujus ministerium sit inefficax, & per quem Christus nihil amplius operari velit: idque Corinthios ipsos tandem agnituros sperat. Et sic aspe- ritatem priorem nonnihil mitigat, severitatemque reprehensionum in preces convertit.

## 13:7
But I pray to God) that is, I pour out prayers to God for that reason.

That I may not be forced to inflict punishment on anyone, which is called evil, because it is hard to endure. Ποιῆσαι with the Accusative, for which the Latins would put the Dative, Matt. XXVII. 22, Luke XV. 19.

There is no need for a new construction. The Apostolic vow does not sound concerning the punishment not being inflicted upon them, but concerning no sin being committed. Attend, says Theophylactus, to Paul's charity toward them. He was held in contempt among them, and was assailed with insults, as if he were a man of no consequence, and relied on nothing by virtue, but was boastful and insolent in his letters. But now he not only defers the punishments due to their crimes, but even asks with prayers that they may never commit any offense, lest he himself be forced to inflict punishments from his merits. The following words further confirm this sense, ἵνα ὑμεῖς τὸ καλὸν ποιῆτε.

v. 7. Οὐχ ἵνα ἡμεῖς δόκιμοι φανῶμεν, ἀλλ’ ἵν’ ὑμεῖς τὸ κα- λὸν ποιῆτε, ἡμεῖς δὲ ὡς ἀδόκιμοι ὦμεν) There is here a transposition of ὅχ’ ἵνα for ἵν’ ὅχ. Such a trajection in the same word ἵνα is in Eph. 3:18. The sense is: I make those prayers, because I prefer you to be good, rather than my sincerity to be attested by your punishments. I would rather remain without such proof, than that you should fall into such sins.

There is no trajection here. Everything flows in order. Not that we may appear approved, that is, that we may have need, by applying sharper remedies, to render the power of our ministry approved in a more severe censure against you, but that you may do what is good, that is, but that you, by the amendment of your life, anticipating our censure, may do what is honest, and we may be as reprobates, that is, unarmed and invalid in that more severe part, after, of course, the cause for sharper animadversion has been removed. For he prefers to seem powerless in correcting, rather than that they themselves, by contumacious impenitence, should extort his Apostolic virtue. Therefore, to be a reprobate here is the same as to seem powerless and destitute of the virtue of Christ, which he had previously threatened them with. He says, therefore, that his vow is that in good they may grow in the meantime, and his power in punishing may be considered to decrease. The sense is, says Estius, I will easily suffer myself to be held as a reprobate, that is, vile, destitute of glory and power, nor do I wish any regard to be had for my dignity, provided that you persevere constantly in good, and admit nothing

Latin:

Εὔχομαι δὲ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν) id est, ad Deum preces ea de causa fundo.

Μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακὸν μηδὲν) Ne cogar cuiquam pœ- nam infligere, quæ malum dicitur, quia dura est toleratu. Ποιῆσαι cum Accusativo, pro quo Latini Dativum ponerent, Matth. XXVII. 22. Luc. XV. 19.

Non opus est nova constructione. Non de pœna ipsis haud infligenda, sed de peccato nullo committendo votum sonat Apostolicum. Atten- de, inquit Theophylactus, Pauli in eos charitatem. Contemptui apud eos erat, & contumeliis incesseba- tur, tanquam nullius esset momenti vir, & nihil vir- tute, sed epistolis niteretur jactabundus & insolens. Nunc vero non solum differt illorum debitas sceleri- bus pœnas, quin & precibus postulat, ut nihil un- guam delinquant, ne ipse è meritis inferre pœnas co- gatur. Quem sensum verba sequentia ulterius firmant, ἵνα ὑμεῖς τὸ καλὸν ποιῆτε.

v. 7. Οὐχ ἵνα ἡμεῖς δόκιμοι φανῶμεν, ἀλλ’ ἵν’ ὑμεῖς τὸ κα- λὸν ποιῆτε, ἡμεῖς δὲ ὡς ἀδόκιμοι ὦμεν) Est hic transpositio ὅχ’ ἵνα pro ἵν’ ὅχ. Qualis trajectio in eadem voce ἵνα est Ephes. III. 18. Sensus est: Preces illas facio, quod malo vos bonos esse, quam meam sinceritatem vestris pœnis testatam fieri. Maneam ego potius sine tali documento, quam vos in peccata talia incidatis.

Nulla hic trajectio. Fluunt omnia ordine. Non ut nos probati appareamus, hoc est, ut necesse habea- mus acrioribus remediis adhibitis vim nostri mini- sterii probatam reddere in graviore adversus vos cen- sura, sed ut vos, quod bonum est, faciatis, hoc est, sed ut vos emendatione vitæ censuram nostram præ- venientes, quod honestum est, faciatis, nos vero vel- uti reprobi simus, id est, in istam severiorem partem inermes & invalidi, postquam scilicet causa acrio- ris animadversionis sublata est. Mavult enim impo- tens videri in corripiendo, quam ut ipsi contumaci impœnitentia virtutem suam Apost. extorqueant. Est ergo hic reprobum esse idem ac impotentem & destitutum virtute Christi videri, quam illis antea minatus erat. Votum ergo suum esse ait, ut in bono subinde crescant, & sua in puniendo potentia de- crescere censeatur. Sensus est, inquit Estius, fa- cile patiar, me haberi ut reprobum, id est, vilem, glo- riae ac potestatis expertem, nec volo, ullam meae digni- tatis haberi rationem, dummodo vos constanter in bo- no perseveretis, & nihil admittatis, quod me cogat ostendere virtutem, quam a Christo accepi.

## 13:8
v. 8. For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth) That power was given to us, that we might use it rightly, not wrongly. Far be it from us that we should afflict the innocent for the sake of increasing our own authority. ἀλήθεια to our writers, as to the Hebrews אמת or אמונה, often signifies that which is right and just, John III.22, where see the remarks, and III John 3.

ἀλήθεια can also be understood in a more famous sense, so that a reason may be given why he is forced to exercise severity, namely, on account of the truth of the doctrine above all, lest it be ill-spoken of and come into danger, as if he were saying, my profession requires that I be powerful against the stubborn, unarmed against the obedient, lest the truth of the doctrine suffer any detriment, which I cannot desert, and therefore cannot allow it to be ill-spoken of on account of the malice of a few, as B. Hunnius, Balduinus, and others.

Latin:

v. 8. Οὐ γὰρ δυνάμεθά τι κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας) Potestas illa nobis data est, ut recte ea utamur, non ut male. Absit a nobis, ut nostrae autoritatis augendae cau- sa affligamus innocentes. Ἀλήθεια nostris scriptoribus, ut Hebraeis אמת vel אמונה, saepe significat id, quod re- ctum justumque est, Joh. III.22. ubi dicta vide, & III. Joh. 3.

Potest etiam ἀλήθεια sensu famosiori retineri, ut ratio reddatur, cur saevitiam exercere cogatur, nimirum propter veritatem imprimis doctrinae, ne ea male audiat, & in discrimen veniat, quasi dicat, ita requirit professio mea, ut potens sim in contu- maces, inermis in obsequentes, ne veritas doctri- nae aliquid detrimenti patiatur, quam ego deserere non possum, ac proinde non admittere, ut ea pro- pter paucorum malitiam male audiat, ut B. Hun- nius, Balduinus, aliique.

## 13:9
v. 9. For we rejoice, when we are weak) that is, appear as if infirm, not producing those proofs of divine power in us which we have spoken of. but you are strong) that you may be valiant and vigorous.

The first part could be explained by hypothesis according to the Hebrew manner of speaking, as Rom. VI. v. 17. thanks be to God, because you were servants of sin, etc. that is, I rejoice that you are powerful, even if I am held to be infirm and a reprobate, not able to use power. Furthermore, even according to the common interpretation, the sense is clear: And in this part we rejoice greatly, when we are weak, and as it were stripped of our power, while meanwhile you are firm in faith, stable, and blameless in conduct.

And this also we pray for, your restoration) That you may do your duty, lest you fall into evils. Κατάρτισις is תכונה, which is wont to be translated ἑτοιμασία, a right constitution, just as κατηρτισμέν is נכון, as we said at Luke VI. 40. add what we said at Gen. XXXIV. 21.

The Vulgate rendered it consummation. Wrongly. Beza more correctly, restoration: The meaning of the word καταρτίζειν, he says, is various and manifold: But to me, comparing the next verse with this one, the Apostle seems to signify nothing else by this term than that this is his purpose, that in the Corinthian Church, with the members that had been dislocated now as it were put back into their place, all things there might be restored: or that with all dissensions removed they might be joined together again. And so it was also permissible to interpret it as reconciliation.

Latin:

v. 9. Χαίρομεν γὰρ, ὅταν ἡμεῖς ἀσθενῶμεν) id est, apparea- mus velut infirmi, non edentes illa, quae diximus potentiae in nobis divinae documenta. ὑμεῖς δὲ δυνατοὶ ἦτε) ut vos sitis valentes & vegeti.

Posset prior pars juxta modum loquendi E- braeum exponi per hypothesin, ut Rom. VI. v. 17. gratiae sint Deo, quia fuistis servi peccati &c. hoc est, gaudeo vos esse potentes, etsi ego infirmus ac reprobus habear, non valens uti potestate. De caetero etiam secundum communem interpretatio- nem, sensus est in aprico: Et hac in parte gaude- mus magnopere, cum nos infirmi sumus, & nostra velut potestate exuti, dum interim vos estis firmi in fide stabiles, & in conversione inculpati.

Τῦτο δὲ καὶ εὐχόμεθα τὴν ὑμῶν κατάρτισιν) Ut officium fa- ciatis, ne in mala incidatis. Κατάρτισις est תכונה, quod ἑτοιμασία solet verti, recta constitutio, sicut κατηρτισμέν- נכון, ut diximus ad Luc. VI. 40. adde, quod diximus ad Gen. XXXIV. 21.

Vulgata reddidit consummationem. Male. Re- ctius Beza instaurationem: Varia, inquit, est, & multiplex verbi καταρτίζειν significatio: Mihi vero proximum versiculum cum isto comparanti videtur Apostolus nihil aliud hoc nomine significare, quam suum esse hoc consilium, ut Corinthiaca Ecclesia membris, quae luxata fuerant, rursus in locum suum veluti repositis, omnia illic instaurentur: vel ut omnibus sublatis dissidiis rursus inter se conjungan- tur. Itaque licebat etiam reconcinnationem inter- pretari.

## 13:10
v. 10. For this reason I write these things while absent, that being present I may not use sharpness, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for edification, and not for destruction) Therefore, he says, I use threats, nor am I forced to execute them. To use sharpness, that is, to act severely. For to use is sometimes placed absolutely with no noun following. Thus they used more harshly, 2 Maccab. XII. verse 14. Sharpness, severely. Thus also Tit. I. 13. sharpness, severity, Rom. XI. 22. sharp wrath, sharp judgment, Wisd. V. 20. VI. 5. In the glossary, sharp, rigid. By authority here he understands that power divinely given for inflicting diseases, blindness, even death, which was given to the Apostles, not for harm, but for the utility and progress of the Church. See above X. 8.

After he has now struck them greatly by threatening, he says in excuse, I write such things to you while absent, because I would prefer that this severity of mine be ended by letters alone, not be brought forward in deed. For if I find that you have not yet been tamed and amended, it will be necessary that I afflict you with sharper punishments, since the Lord has conferred this power upon me, as Theophylactus has it; Then proceeding thus in the paraphrase. The Lord indeed primarily does not at all wish to destroy, or to torment anyone, but to edify, that is, to bestow benefits. Otherwise, if destruction is brought upon those who cannot be corrected, it must be held in place of edification. These are the words of Theophylactus. Therefore Paul ought not to destroy, but to edify. Therefore he wished to show his severity rather by threatening in letters than to exercise it by punishing in his presence: And by that reason he freed himself from all suspicion of moroseness, even when he was most free in rebuking, as B. Balduinus has it.

PART III. The Apostle's final admonition or Epilogue.

Latin:

v. 10. Διὰ τῦτο ταῦτα ἀπὼν γράφω, ἵνα παρὼν μὴ ἀπο- τόμως χρήσωμαι, κατὰ τὴν ἐξουσίαν, ἣν ἔδωκέ μοι ὁ κύριος εἰς οἰκοδομὴν, καὶ ὀυκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν) Ideo, inquit, minas adhi- beo, nec eas exequi cogar. Χρῆσθαι ἀποτόμως, id est, severe agere. Nam χρῆσθαι interdum absolute ponitur nullo no- mine sequente. Sic ἀναγωγότερον ἐχρῶντο, 2. Maccab. XII. vers. 14. Ἀποτόμως severe. Sic & Tit. I. 13. ἀποτομία se- veritas, Rom. XI. 22. ἀπότομος ὀργὴ, κρίσις ἀπότομος, Sap. V. 20. VI. 5. In glossario ἀπότομον, rigidum. Ἐξουσίαν hic intelligit potestatem illam divinitus datam ad immitten- dos morbos, caecitatem, mortem etiam, quae data Apo- stolis, non ad damnum, sed ad utilitatem & profectum Ecclesiae. Vide supra X. 8.

Postquam hos plurimum comminando jam per- culit, excusans inquit, ideo ad vos istiusmodi vel absens scribo, quia mallem solis literis hanc meam terminatum iri duritiem non re praeferri. Nam si nondum edomitos vos ipse & emendatos comperero, acrioribus necesse erit, vos paenis afficiam, quando- quidem potestatem hanc mihi contulit Dominus, ut habet Theophylactus; Deinceps in paraphrasi ita pergens. Dominus quidem imprimis haudquaquam vult vel destruere, vel tormentis quempiam divexa- re, sed ædificare, hoc est, afficere beneficiis. Alioqui his, qui corrigi nequeunt, si exitium inferatur, ædificatio- nis loco habendum est. Hæc Theophylactus. Non ergo destruere debuit Paulus, sed ædificare. Ideo se- veritatem potius suam literis minando ostendere, quam præsentia sua puniendo exercere voluit: Ea- que ratione se ab omni suspicione morositatis libera- vit, etiam cum fuit in objurgando liberrimus, ut B. Balduinus habet.

PARS III. Novissima Apostoli commonefactio vel Epilogus.

## 13:11
v. 11. Λοιπὸν ἀδελφοὶ) as for what remains. It is a word used by one hastening to finish a discourse.

Χαίρετε) Fare well. For thus the Greeks use this.

This admonition is like an epilogue, embracing most things said in the Epistle. Erasmus and Beza rendered χαίρετε as 'fare well'. But the Greeks and the Vulgate interpret it more correctly here as joy: 'Rejoice', as also B. Luther: 'Freuet euch'. For he wishes that the Corinthians may rejoice in the Lord, and not rashly admit anything by which that joy might be contaminated. Theophylact says: I myself, he says, have performed what was my part, it remains that you also contribute what is yours, namely, that being corrected and amended, you may procure joy for yourselves from a clear conscience, which will undoubtedly not be lacking, even though I have discussed unpleasant and sad things with you.

Καταρτίζεσθε) Be made perfect, which becomes you. See above 9. It is here Niphal for Hithpahel.

Nay, the Apostle admonishes that they should be restored in turn, and be compacted and joined together by the bond of faith and charity into one body; which is not loosened or gaping in any part of itself, but is solid and whole on all sides, so that in this way both individuals gradually and all together collectively may strive toward that perfection which can be obtained here. 'Seek perfection', that is, as interpreted by Theophylact, both by thinking what is right and embracing truer dogmas, and by cultivating yourselves in life and morals. Supply what is lacking to you.

Παρακαλεῖσθε) And this is of the same form. Comfort yourselves, namely, if any adversity should occur.

The Vulgate rendered it: 'Exhort one another'. Theophylact also interpreted it in this sense, though not neglecting the sense of consolation: Since there were many temptations and dangers, 'exhort', he says, that is, strive for better things by a proper and mutual exhortation. For a clear conscience is accustomed to comfort us especially. Estius, however, acknowledges that it is more appropriate if it is rendered, 'receive consolation'. For they had been saddened. Whence Beza explained it as 'have consolation'. Be of good courage, and be fortified and strengthened against afflictions of every kind, and mutually strengthening one another with the comfort of the divine Spirit.

Τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε) Be of one mind. For φρονεῖν in Paul refers to the affection, not to the intellect. In a similar way we had τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν in Rom. XII. verse 16. XV. verse 59. Phil. II. 2. III. 16. IV. 2.

The Syriac: 'Let there be concord among you'. And why should not τὸ φρονεῖν be referred to the intellect? The word itself implies it. He therefore commands a consensus of minds, so that they may indeed think the same thing in the doctrine of faith, and that thus all schisms and dissensions, about which he had also warned in the former epistle, may be banished.

Εἰρηνεύετε) Mark IX. 50. Rom. XII. verse 18. 1 Thess. V. verse 13.

Along with unity of minds in the faith, peace and concord of will is also required, so that tranquility may flourish. And therefore Theophylact rightly says: To be of the same mind is to think the same thing concerning the faith and the dogmas themselves. But to have peace is to embrace one another with mutual charity.

And the God of love and peace shall be with you) He will favor you, and will be your help. See Luke 1:28 and what is said there. The God of peace and love, that is, the author of peace and love. See Rom. 15:33, 16:20, 1 Cor. 14:33. Thus the Hebrews say, אל שלום, אל אהבה.

We add the explanation of Theophylact: He performs not only the office of one admonishing, but of one praying, although in this place he seems to pray for nothing, but to predict what things are to happen hereafter, namely, if you will use peace, God will be present with you. He is called the God of love here, either because He is the fountain and origin of charity, or because He shows forth a certain immense benevolence toward us, or because wherever there is a conjunction of love, there also God must necessarily be present, and the primacy of this charity appears to be held. He is called the God of peace, both because peace has its origin from Him, and because He has pacified heavenly and earthly things, and because He possesses it by right of dominion. All of which Beatus has vigorously embraced. Our Hunnius: He adds a promise, that if they study charity, if concord, if peace in this manner, God will be with them with His gracious presence, who is the God of charity, indeed within His own essence is charity itself, and outside of it the fountain and principle of charity among creatures: And the God of peace, inasmuch as He most kindly restored it, having been disturbed by the craft of the Devil, through His only-begotten Son.

Latin:

v. 11. Λοιπὸν ἀδελφοὶ) quod restat. Verbum est pro- perantis sermonem absolvere.

Χαίρετε) Bene valete. Ita enim Græci hoc usurpant.

Hæc commonefactio epilogi instar est, pleraque complectens in Epistola dicta. χαίρετε valete red- didit Erasmus & Beza. Sed rectius hic de gaudio interpretantur Græci & Vulgata: Gaudete, ut & B. Lutherus: Freuet euch. Vult enim, ut Corinthii lætentur in Domino, nec quicquam temere admit- tant, quo gaudium illud contaminetur. Theophy- lactus: Ipse, inquit, peregi, quod mea interfuit, reli- quum est; ut & vos conferatis, quæ vestra sunt, vide- licet ut correcti & emendati ex recti conscientia vo- bis lætitiam comparetis, nequaquam procul dubio de- situram, tametsi injucunda & tristia vobis disserui.

Καταρτίζεσθε) Satite, quod vos decet. Vide supra 9. Est hîc Niphal pro Hithpahel.

Imò monet Apostolus, ut vicissim redintegren- tur, fideique & charitatis vinculo compacti & co- agmentati sint in unum corpus; quod nulla sui par- te laxatum aut hiulcum sit, sed undiquaque soli- dum & integrum, ut hoc pacto & singuli sensim & universi conjunctim ad eam perfectionem conten- dant, quæ hic obtineri potest. Perfectionem secta- mini, hoc est, interprete Theophylacto, cùm ea, quæ recta sunt sentiendo, & dogmata veriora amplecten- do, tùm vita & moribus vos excolendo. Quæ vobis defunt, supplete.

Παρακαλεῖσθε) Et hoc ejusdem formæ. Solemini vos- met, nempe si quid adversi inciderit.

Vulgata reddidit: Exhortamini. Quo sensu etiam interpretatus est Theophylactus, non negle- cto tamen consolationis sensu: Cum plurimæ essent tentationes & pericula, exhortamini, inquit, hoc est, propria & mutua quadam exhortatione ad meliora nitamini. Apprime enim recti conscientia conso- lari nos solet. Agnoscit autem Estius magis con- gruere, si reddatur, consolationem accipite. Con- tristati enim fuerant. Unde Beza, consolationem habete, exposuit. Estote bono animo, & adversus omnis generis afflictiones muniti ac roborati, vosque mutuo roborantes solatio divini Spiritus.

Τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε) Concordes este. Nam φρονεῖν Paulo ad affectum, non ad intellectum, refertur. Simili modo τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν habuimus Rom. XII. vers. 16. XV. vers. 59. Phil. II. 2. III. 16. IV. 2.

Syrus: Sit inter vos concordia. Quidni enim referatur τὸ φρονεῖν ad intellectum? Vox ipsa id infert. Præcipit ergo consensum animorum, ut nempe idem sapiant in doctrina fidei, utque ita exulent omnia schismata & dissensiones, de qui- bus in priori quoque epistola monuerat.

Εἰρηνεύετε) Marci IX. 50. Rom. XII. vers. 18. 1. Thess. V. vers. 13.

Cum unitate animorum in fide pax etiam & concordia voluntatem requiritur, ut tranquilli- tas floreat. Ideoque recte Theophylactus : Est autem idipsum sapere idem de fide & dogmatibus ipsis sentire. Habere autem pacem mutua se chari- tate complecti.

Καὶ ὁ Θεὸς τῆς ἀγάπης καὶ τῆς εἰρήνης ἔσται μεθ' ὑμῶν) Vobis favebit, & auxilio erit. Vide Luc. I. 28. & ibi dicta. Deus pacis & dilectionis, id est, autor pacis & dilectionis. Vide Rom. XV. 33. XVI. 20. 1. Cor. XIV. 33. Sic Hebræi dicunt, אל שלום, אל אהבה.

Addimus Theophylacti explicationem : Non so- lum commonefacientis officio fungitur, sed compre- cantis, tametsi nihil hoc loco his videatur precari, sed prædicere, quæ deinceps futura sint, videlicet, si vos pace utemini, vobis affuturus est Deus. Dilectionis autem hic dicitur, vel quia charitatis fons sit & origo, vel quia immensam quandam erga nos præ se ferat benevolentiam, vel quia ubicunque fuerit amoris conjunctio, ibidem & Deus adsit, necesse est, & charitatis hujusce tenere appareat principatum. Pacis autem dicitur Deus, & quia ex eo ortum pax habeat, & quia cælestia & terrena pacaverit tum quia eam dominationis jure possideat. Quæ omnia nervose complexus est Beat. Hunnius noster: Ad- jicit promissionem, si charitati, si concordiæ, si paci hunc in modum studeant, fore cum illis gratiosa sua præsentia Deum, qui est Deus charitatis, quippe intra suam ὀυσίαν ipsa charitas, & extra illam cha- ritatis fons atque principium apud creaturas : Et Deus pacis, utpote quam astu Diaboli turbatam per unigenitum filium suum benignissime redintegra- vit.

## 13:12
ver. 12. Greet one another with a holy kiss) Rom. 16:16.

Beza notes from Xenophon's book of the Cyropaedia, and Herodotus in Clio, that this was the custom of the Jews, as well as of other nations of the East, that they would greet one another with many kisses, joined together by the highest friendship and intimacy. And that the Jews indeed had approached the custom and manners of the Persians is easy to recognize from sacred history, so much so that the kiss was a symbol not only of some friendship, but also of a certain equality of honor. Which Justin in his Apology testifies was also observed in the ecclesiastical assembly. It is pleasing to add what Theophylact has: Greet one another with a holy kiss, not feigned and deceitful, as Judas kissed Christ. For we show a kiss for this reason, that we may kindle benevolence to a greater degree, since, beyond the other members, the mouth itself binds souls. Moreover, when returning home from abroad, we kiss with the mouth so that we may show the conjunction of our souls. Or otherwise: Since we present ourselves as the temple of GOD, we kiss the mouth, which is the vestibule of this temple. Furthermore, through it Christ also enters, when we receive His most holy body.

All the saints greet you) Namely, those who are in Macedonia.

Who were with the Apostle, namely at Philippi, from where this epistle was sent: Whence it appears that those saints were privy to Paul's writing, and without doubt that that epistle dictated by the Holy Spirit was read to them, and therefore they asked the Apostle to greet the Corinthians in their name, and to wish them all good things. He calls them saints, as being washed by the blood of Christ, and regenerated and sanctified by the Spirit of GOD.

Latin:

vers. 12. Ἀσπάζεσθε ἀλλήλους ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ) Rom. XVI. v. 16.

Notat Beza ex Xenophonte libro Cyripediæ, & Herodoto in Clio, hanc fuisse uti Judæorum, ita etiam aliarum gentium Orientis consuetudinem, ut multis osculis sese salutarent summa amicitia ac necessitudine conjuncti. Et Judæos quidem ad Persarum consuetudinem & mores accessisse ex sacra historia facile esse cognoscere, adeo ut oscu- lum esset non modo amicitiæ alicujus, sed cujus- dam etiam ὁμοτιμίας symbolum. Quam etiam in Ecclesiastico cœtu observatam Justinus in Apol. testatur. Placet addere, quæ Theophylactus ha- bet: Salutate invicem in osculo sancto, non ficto & subdolo, ut Judas est Christum deosculatus. Idcir- co enim osculum exhibemus, ut majorem in modum accendamus benevolentiam, quandoquidem præ cæ- teris membris, os ipsum devinciat animos. Quin etiam domum redeuntes peregre, ut animorum præ- feramus conjunctionem, ore exosculamur. Vel ali- ter: Cum enim DEI nos templum præferimus, os quidem, quod hujus est templi vestibulum, deoscu- lamur. Per idipsum præterea & Christus ingre- ditur, cum sacrosanctum sumimus corpus.

Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ ἅγιοι πάντες) Nempe, qui in Ma- cedonia sunt.

Qui erant cum Apostolo, Philippis nempe, unde missa est hæc epistola: Unde apparet, san- ctos illos scriptionis Paulinæ fuisse conscios, sine dubio etiam epistolam illam à Spiritu Sancto di- ctatam illis prælectam esse, ideoque ab Apostolo petiisse, ut Corinthios suo nomine salutare, iisque omnia fausta precari velit. Sanctos autem vocat, utpote sanguine Christi lotos, & DEI Spiritu re- genitos & sanctificatos.

## 13:13
v. 13. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all) Supply 'be', as in Rom. 16:24, 1 Cor. 16:23. But here, as also in baptism, are openly the names of the Trinity which Christians worship.

A most notable final prayer: in which he vows and prays for them whatever the Saints could vow and wish for themselves from the holy Trinity: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who liberated us by his blood from the power of Satan, and acquired us for himself, and by his obedience merited eternal life for us, so that through faith in him we might have the remission of sins and true righteousness, and attain eternal salvation. Concerning which grace of Christ he had warned in chapter V. 19, 21, as also in c. IIX. 9. The love of God, namely the Father, which has been reconciled to us by the death of Christ, and by which he embraces us intimately in Christ, having been justified through faith in him, John III. 16, Rom. V. 18, Eph. I. 6, and the κοινωνίαν, the active communication of the Holy Spirit, who makes us partakers of the glory of Christ and the love of God, and who seals in us the love of the Father and the grace of Christ the Redeemer, and thus bestows whatever contributes to our sanctification and salvation. After he has joined everyone, says Theophylact, with love, a kiss, and the duty of greeting, he prays also for them, according to his custom, for the grace of the Son, by which, through no works but by his own kindness alone, having undergone death, he made us safe, and furthermore bestowed the love of the Father, by which he embraced us so intensely that for our sake he handed over his only-begotten Son. Nor, if the Apostle were asked by anyone in this manner, whence then does the grace of the Son proceed? He says thus: Namely, from the love of the Father. But what did he accomplish? Certainly the communication of the Holy Spirit, that is, the participation and draught of the Spirit himself, by whom we have attained holiness. Because of the coming of the Paraclete into us, we have become partakers of him, which Spirit we ourselves also bring forth by participating. Where in the world are those who deny that he is the Spirit, because Paul nowhere expressed this in the beginnings of his epistles? But behold, now he has most openly named the Spirit, and the Trinity is returned and explained to you from that complete number. So he. Concerning the order of the Most Holy Trinity, the blessed Balduinus advises this: that the Apostle does not invert the order of origin among the persons of the Most Holy Trinity, but (1.) wishes to show the equality of essence among the persons of the Trinity, whose order he could not have otherwise inverted if he were granting to the eternal Father a certain priority of dignity or essence. (2.) Then, that he wished to inculcate Christ primarily to his hearers, in whom the love of God and the communication of the Holy Spirit is founded. Therefore he writes in 1 Cor. II. 2: I judged that I knew nothing among you, except Jesus Christ and him crucified: and he wished to show the meritorious cause of heavenly benefits, which cannot be found outside of Christ. Therefore he places Christ in the first place, as the author and finisher of our faith and salvation, Hebr. XII. 2. But we have treated these and other things pertaining to this in more detail in Tom. III. Syst. Theol. Let it be with you all, namely, through the manifold effects of the grace of Christ, and the love of the Father, and the communication of the Holy Spirit. But that Grotius says the word Amen was added not by the Apostle, but by the Corinthian Church, is purely precarious. In the Pauline Epistles and other canonical writings there is nothing which is not θεόπνευστον. Therefore the Apostle himself added the word Amen, both praying to the Holy Spirit that this prayer be ratified, and teaching us that we ought to seal the same similarly with true confidence of heart and certainty of the hearing of our prayers: Which may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the communication of the Holy Spirit work in us, to which Most Holy Trinity be praise, honor, and glory, as it was in the beginning, and now and always, for ever and ever,

AMEN.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν) Sup- ple sit, ut Rom. XVI. 24. 1. Cor. XVI. 23. Sunt autem hic ut & in baptismo aperte nomina τῆς Τριάδος ejus quam Christiani colunt.

Votum finale maxime insigne: quo vovet & precatur ipsis, quicquid à sancta Trinitate vovere, sibique optare poterant Sancti: Gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, qui nos sanguine suo à potestate Satanæ liberavit, sibique acquisivit & obedientiâ suâ nobis vitam æternam promeruit, ut per fidem in ipsum remissionem peccatorum & justitiam veram habeamus, & salutem æternam consequamur. De qua gratia Christi cap. V. 19. 21. ut & c. IIX. 9. monuerat. Charitatem Dei, Patris nempe, quæ nobis morte Christi conciliata est, quaque nos in Christo, per fidem in ipsum justificatos, intime complectitur, Joh. III. 16. Rom. V. 18. Eph. I. 6. & κοινωνίαν communicationem activam Spiritus Sancti, qui nos participes facit gloriæ Christi & dilectionis Dei, quique charitatem Patris, & gratiam Christi Redemtoris in nobis obsignat, adeoque quicquid ad sanctificationem & salutem nostram facit, largitur. Postquam universos, inquit Theophylactus, charitate, osculo, & salutandi officio copulavit, comprecatur & his pro sua consuetudine Filii gratiam, qua nullis operibus, sed sua sola benignitate, morte adita, nos salvos effecerit, & Patris præterea charitate donarit, qua nos ille enixè adeo complexus est, ut nostri gratia traderet unigenitum. Nec secus quàm à quopiam hujusmodi rogaretur Apostolus, unde ergo Filii gratia procedit? Sic ait: Nempe ex Patris charitate. At quid ille peregit? Certe Spiritus Sancti communicationem, hoc est, ipsius Spiritus, quo sumus sanctitatem adepti, participationem & haustum. Ob Paracleti in nos adventum illius effecti participes, quem Spiritum & nos ipsi participando proferimus. Ubinam gentium sunt, qui eo Spiritum esse negant, quia hunc in epistolarum suarum primordiis nusquam expresserit Paulus? Sed ecce jam nunc apertissime Spiritum nominavit, & Trinitas tibi ex eo integro numero redditur & explicatur. Hæc ille. De ordine SS. Trin. hæc monet B. Balduinus: Apostolum non invertere ordinem originis, inter personas SS. Trin. sed (1.) ostendere velle æqualitatem essentiæ inter personas Trinitatis, quarum ordinem alias invertere non potuisset, si is æterno Patri quandam dignitatis aut essentiæ prioritatem largiretur. (2.) Deinde Christum imprimis Auditoribus suis inculcare voluisse, in quo charitas Dei & communicatio Spiritus S. fundata est. Idcirco scribit 1. Cor. II. 2. Non judicavi me scire aliquid inter vos, nisi Jesum crucifixum: Causamque meritoriam monstrare voluit beneficiorum cælestium, quæ extra Christum inveniri non potest. Ideo Christum primo loco ponit, tanquam autorem & consummatorem fidei & salutis nostræ, Hebr. XII. 2. Sed hæc & alia huc facientia pluribus exequuti sumus Tom. III. Syst. Theol. Sit cum omnibus vobis, scil. per multiplices effectus gratiæ Christi, & charitatis Patris, & communicationis Spir. Sancti. Quod verò vocem Amen non ab Apostolo, sed ab Ecclesia Corinthiaca additam ait Grotius, mere precarium est. In Epistolis Paulinis, aliisque scriptis Canonicis nihil est, quod non sit θεόπνευστον. Addidit ergo ipse Apostolus vocem Amen, & precans Spir. Sanctum, ut ratum sit hoc votum, & docens nos verâ cordis fiduciâ & certitudine de exauditione precum easdẽ similiter obsignare debere: Quam in nobis operetur gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi, charitas Dei Patris, & communicatio Spiritus S. cui SS. Trinitati sit laus, honor & gloria, sicut erat in principio, & nunc & semper in secula seculorum,

AMEN.

# Galatians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO THE GALATIANS.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA IN EPISTOLAM S. PAULI AD GALATAS.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius's Preface
GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

TERTULLIAN, in his first book against Marcion, thinks this epistle was among the first of Paul's. His words are: From that Paul, certainly, who was still raw in grace, and finally trembling lest he had run or was running in vain, when he first conferred with the preceding Apostles. Therefore, if fervently, as a Neophyte still, he thought something in the conduct against Judaism was to be reprehended, namely the passive association, later being himself to become all things to all men, that he might win all, to the Jews as a Jew, and to those who were under the law, as under the law: you wish the reprehension of the conduct alone, which would later please his accuser, to be held suspect, etc. It appears sufficiently that he is more vehement in this epistle than in others. However, I think there were other causes than those Tertullian suspects, namely that those who wished to snatch the liberty of Jewish rites from those called from the nations were not Jews, to whom something in that matter was to be pardoned, but foreigners who had lived in Judea, the leader of whom was Cerinthus, such as were also those who taught the same things at Philippi, as Paul himself is an index, Phil. III, 3. because the same men taught the necessity of Judaizing, moved by no piety, but that by that means they might obtain honors and commodities from the Jews: and at the same time escape the inconveniences which pressed upon the Christians. For in those times, by Roman laws and edicts, the exercise of religion was free for the Jews, but not so for the Christians, who it appears from the Acts and other epistles of Paul had already begun to be vexed even then. But Paul, upon whom the conversion of the nations rested more specially than upon the others, saw what a great impediment this injunction of a new burden would bring. But when those detractors of Paul, who was strenuously defending liberty, said that Paul had not received the right of teaching except from Peter, John, and James, and therefore that their institutes were to be held before Paul's institutes, and furthermore that Paul himself had been inconsistent in this matter, Paul on the contrary with a great spirit shows that he received his Apostleship from Christ no less than the other Apostles, and that Peter, John, and James do not teach anything other than what he himself teaches, and that he also, although he was accustomed in the use or omission of rites to accommodate himself to the utility of those with whom he lived, nevertheless always taught the same thing concerning that liberty: And he confirms this dogma of his, with the types of the old testament explained mystically. The time when this epistle to the Gallo-Greeks was written, just as I cannot designate it, so I seem to see that it was not far from the time when the epistle to the Romans was written.

OBSERVATIONS On Grotius's Preface with other prolegomena.

AS TERTULLIAN'S judgment concerning the cause of the Apostolic vehemence in this epistle could not approve itself to GROTIUS: So Tertullian's censure concerning Paul's reprehension of Peter is to be utterly disapproved, that he was still raw in grace and trembling lest he had run or was running in vain when he conferred with the Apostles, and that he, still fervently as a Neophyte, thought something in the conduct against Judaism was to be reprehended, which would later please his accuser. For it will be manifest from chapter II that the Pauline reprehension was just, and that the Apostle never repented of it. And what a Neophyte still, or raw in grace, would have been such a great Doctor of the nations, who was not less than the highest Apostles, 2 Cor.

XI. 5. and he had already spent seventeen years in this arduous and divine office of Apostleship, Gal. I. 18. chap. II. 1, 11. and thus he had already filled everything from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ, Rom. XVI. 3. 4. From which it easily appears that this epistle was by no means among the first of Paul's, which we have established as ninth in the order of time, having considered the matter in the preface to the epistle to the Romans, Sect. I. And Grotius asserts here that it was not far from the time when the epistle to the Romans was written, which was indeed written at last in the 22nd year of Paul's conversion. And Chrysostom, as also Theophylact, makes the present one prior to the epistle to the Romans, which seems to be the seventh in order of time, but conjecturally. The subscription testifies that it was written at Rome, when the Apostle was already bearing the marks of the Lord in his body, Gal. IV. 17. Theodoret observed that this epistle was written therefore in the 25th year approximately of Paul's conversion, and at the minimum six years after the conversion of the Galatians. He sent this from Rome, when he had seen the Galatians and had taught them, says Athanasius in the Synopsis. That it is later than the Roman one is to be gathered from the fact that in Rom. XV. he signifies that he is already occupied in collecting alms for the saints who were at Jerusalem, which he testifies had already been done by him in this epistle, chap. II. verse 10. And from that it also appears that this epistle was not sent from Ephesus, which the argument prefixed to the Latin copies wishes, but rather from Rome. For when he was staying in Asia, in which Ephesus is situated, that was still being done, that Achaia and Macedonia should make a collection for the poor Jews. Schlichting, with his Crellius, does not deny at verse 2 of chapter I. It appears, they say, that this epistle was written after all the times during which he had freely traveled among the nations for the sake of preaching the Gospel. Wherefore, unless one wishes to say that it was written from a journey to Jerusalem or from Caesarea, where he was held captive for some time, Acts XXIII, it seems to be concluded that it was written at Rome, just as the ancient subscriptions also hold. For from chapter II it can be established that this epistle was written after the alms had been collected among the brethren of foreign nations for the poor of the Jerusalem Church. For he says there in verse 10 that he had been eager to do that which the Apostles had advised him at Jerusalem, namely that he should be mindful of the poor, and he speaks of this eagerness as of a past matter. But as long as the Apostle traveled freely among the nations, and was without chains, he never laid aside this eagerness.

The adversaries with whom the Apostle has business are the Pseudo-Apostles, of whom Tertullian says in the cited passage: But even if he described certain false brethren as having crept in, who wished to transfer the Galatians to another Gospel, he himself demonstrates that that adultery

of the Gospel, not to transfer it to the faith of another God and Christ, but to have had the intention of preserving the discipline of the law. Perceiving, namely, that they were asserting circumcision, and observing the times and days and months and years of the Jewish ceremonies, which they ought to have acknowledged as already excluded according to the renewed disposition of the Creator. Noting the false Apostles and Brethren in this cause, by which they were transferring the Gospel of Christ the Creator from the novelty announced by the Creator to the antiquity rejected by the Creator. Grotius thinks that they were not Jews but foreigners who had lived in Judea, of whom Cerinthus was the leader, such as also taught the same things to the Philippians, Phil. III. 3. But it is established by no evidence that the Apostle noted Cerinthus and his followers here, or in the epistle to the Philippians, or foreigners, not Jews. For although something had to be conceded to the Jews in ceremonies, yet not when they urged the necessity of them for obtaining salvation: since by that error both Christian liberty would be torn away, and indeed the doctrine of Apostolic justification would be overturned. And Epiphanius testifies that Cerinthus himself was a Jew by nation and circumcised, and therefore contended that all Christians must be circumcised. Furthermore, Cerinthus impiously divided Jesus from Christ as if they were two persons, feigning that Christ descended into Jesus in the form of a dove when he was being baptized by John, and that Jesus suffered and rose again, but not Christ, who then flew away from Jesus. Of which monstrous error there appears absolutely no evidence in those whom Paul noted in this epistle. Most say the Nazarenes, with whom the Apostle has business here, who were also called Jesseans, according to Epiphanius, from Jesse, the father of David, because of the persecutions then hanging over Christians everywhere from the Jews, mixed the Gospel of Christ with the use and observation of the ceremonies of the law: but acknowledged Jesus the son of Mary for the Son of God and Christ or Messiah promised to the Fathers. Concerning whom Jerome in his epistle to Augustine, and Augustine himself in chapter IX of his book on heresies, and book XIX against Faustus, c. 18, and book 1 against Cresconius.

But whoever those false Apostles may have been, against whom he acted here; the occasion and cause of the Apostle's writing was not only that, that they taught the necessity of Judaizing, so that they might obtain honors and advantages from the Jews, and escape the disadvantages which were pressing upon the Christians, but primarily also that, that the same persons taught that moral works were equally necessary with faith for salvation, which Blessed Luther observed from the Jerusalem Council, Acts XV, in the Apostolic treatment in this epistle and other similar ones, and Flacius confirmed with many arguments in the general preface to the epistles of St. Paul: In which we also have the ancient interpreters agreeing. For the false Apostles were mixing the law and the Gospel, and not only urged circumcision and the observation of legal ceremonies with faith in Christ, but also required the fulfillment of the law, as altogether necessary for salvation, Acts XV. 1, 5, whence the Apostles refuted them, because they were attempting to impose a yoke upon the disciples, which neither they themselves could bear, nor their fathers had been able to. Whereas, on the contrary, it must be believed that we obtain salvation through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, v. 11. After, therefore, the Galatians had been converted from Heathenism to the Christian faith (to whom the Apostle was indeed prohibited from preaching the Gospel, Acts XVI, but only until it had been preached to the Macedonians, to whom he was warned by a vision to bring aid) and was held in the greatest honor by the Galatians,

the Apostle, whom they received as an Angel of God, nay, as Jesus Christ, the Galatian Churches were vehemently disturbed by the envy and craft of Satan through the false Apostles. Who both disseminated their heterodoxy everywhere through them concerning the undertaking of circumcision, and the seeking of justification in Levitical ceremonies, as also in the works of the moral law, and indeed detracted from the authority of the Apostle, which they well understood was hindering their design, as much as was in them, caviling that Paul did not deliver the same doctrine as the other Apostles, and that these latter, as those who had seen Christ in the flesh and had been informed in his school, were rather to be followed.

Wherefore, that we may come to the argument of the treatment, the Apostle before all things asserted his authority, and taught that he had received his office not from men, but from Christ, and that there was no other Gospel than that which he himself delivered, nor could any other be received, even if an Angel from heaven should announce it, since he had learned his Gospel not from any man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. For which end he commemorates the history of his conversion and preaching, primarily, that he met no one of the Apostles except Peter, and that only three years after his conversion, and James, and fourteen years after his conversion, having gone up to Jerusalem by revelation, he conferred with James, Cephas, and John, who acknowledged the grace granted to the Apostle, and it was agreed among them that he should preach among the Gentiles, just as they among the Jews. Finally, he relates how at Antioch he openly withstood Peter himself, who was not walking correctly, but was Judaizing in his conduct.
