By which manner, with the authority of his Apostolic office and the truth of his Gospel established, he proposes the principal theme, that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but solely through faith in Christ, etc., confirms it with immovable arguments, delivers the use of the law, and accurately distinguishes it from the Gospel, then discourses concerning external ceremonies, from which we are emancipated under the New Testament through the advent of the Son of God, and refutes those who still desired to be under the law by the allegory of the two sons of Abraham, namely those born of the bondwoman and of the free, and warns them to persist in the liberty which Christ has produced, teaching gravely concerning the danger of the error of the Pseudo-Apostles. Finally, lest adversaries accuse the doctrine of faith itself of hindering piety, he diligently inculcates love of neighbor and abstinence from the works of the flesh, and urges the fruits of the Spirit, that they may crucify the flesh, walk in the Spirit, and strive for humility, meekness, and beneficence, and he repeats the sum of his doctrine in place of a conclusion: and he commands that rule to be observed, sealing the epistle with a very brief prayer.

The principal parts of the epistle, therefore, after the inscription and the prayer consistent with the principal theme, are three. The first is the vindication of his Apostolic proclamation, or his just ἐκδίκησις, from chapter I and II up to verse 15. The second is the informative, or necessary διδασκαλία, concerning the faith in which the Galatians were troubled, both as to what is true and false in the article of justification, which he proposes in the thesis in the remainder of chapter II, and in the antithesis, regarding the exclusion of moral works from justification, which the Pseudo-Apostles especially required as necessary for the same in chapter III, and regarding the overthrow of the necessity of ceremonial works in chapter IV, and also as to the moment of the controversy, that through the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles they are captured under a servile yoke, are emptied of Christ, fall from grace, and the whole mass of the Christian religion is corrupted, from chapter V to verse 12. The third is an admonition concerning charity and the fruits of the Spirit, a weighty παιδεία [instruction/discipline] indeed for confounding the calumny of false teachers and the vain persuasion of those negligent in the pursuit of piety, in the remaining part of chapter V, as also in the whole of chapter VI. Therefore, regarding the chief head of doctrine, our blessed Luther, as he rightly noted the occasion in his former Commentary in the Jena Tom. III: The Galatians, having been taught by the Apostle the sound faith first—that is, to trust in Jesus Christ alone, not in their own or the law's righteousness—were afterwards disturbed again by Pseudo-Apostles into a trust in the works of legal righteousness, deceived, namely, most easily by the falsely commended name and example of the great and true Apostles: Thus he wrote excellently concerning the primary matter of the Apostolic treatment in his later Commentary in the Latin Jena Tom. IV, in the argument of the epistle: Paul wishes to establish the doctrine of faith, grace, the remission of sins, or Christian righteousness, so that we may have a perfect knowledge and distinction between Christian righteousness and all other righteousnesses. For that most excellent righteousness, namely of faith, which GOD imputes to us through Christ without works, is neither political, nor ceremonial, nor the righteousness of divine law, nor does it consist in our works; but it is entirely different, that is, a merely passive righteousness (just as those former ones are active). For there we do nothing or render anything to GOD, but we only receive and suffer another working in us, namely God. Therefore, it is pleasing to call that righteousness of faith or Christian righteousness 'passive righteousness.' And this is the righteousness hidden in a mystery, which the world does not understand; nay, even Christians do not hold it sufficiently, and they apprehend it with difficulty in temptations. Therefore, it must always be inculcated and assiduously cultivated by use. And he who does not hold or apprehend it in afflictions and terrors of conscience cannot stand. For no other consolation of consciences is so firm and certain as that passive righteousness. And a little later: The highest art and wisdom of Christians, therefore, is to be ignorant of the law, to be unaware of works, and of all active righteousness, especially when the conscience struggles with the judgment of GOD, just as outside the people of GOD the highest wisdom is to know, inspect, and urge the law, works, and active righteousness. Which things, and others, must be properly observed not only against the modern Pseudo-Apostles who utterly pervert the article of justification—the Papists, Arminians, Socinians—but also against the Innovators, the Majorists, Calixtines, and other Syncretists who disturb our Churches under the mask of Lutherans, whom we have demonstrated with ocular evidence to depart too much from the Evangelical doctrine of the Great Man, and to incur entirely the Apostolic anathema of Galatians 1:8, 9, in our Calixtine-Heretical Harmony. To whom the twin annotations of Grotius will be revealed in the progress. entirely incur, we have demonstrated with ocular evidence in our Calixtine-Heretical Harmony. To whom the twin annotations of Grotius will be revealed in the progress.

It is therefore now in the open that it is not inappropriately said that the present epistle is a certain compendium of the epistle to the Romans, both regarding the dogmatic part, especially as to the article of justification by faith without the works of the law; and also regarding the moral part concerning the love of one's neighbor and the pursuit of holiness.

Commentaries on this epistle, if you set aside those who have expounded all the Pauline ones, or even all the shorter ones only, to the Galatians, Ephesians, and those following—which was recently done copiously by Johannes Crocius—have been illustrated by Alexander, Bishop of Cappadocia, in the year 255; Severianus, Bishop of Gabala, in the year 400; Jerome, Augustine, Claudius of Turin, the blessed Luther, who published a double commentary on the same, the former exhibited in the year 1519 in the Latin Jena Tom. I; the latter, however, in the year 1535, which is contained in the Latin Jena Tom. IV: B. Bugenhagen, B. Joh. Brentius, B. Wigandus, B. Hesbusius, B. Winkelmannus, B. D. Hoë, B. D. Georgius Weinrichius, B. D. Bartholomaeus Battus, B. D. Henr. Höpfnerus, B. D. Andreas Kunadus, B. Kromajerus, and from the Reformed, Hyperius, Olevianus, Copius, Pareus, etc.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

TERTULLIANUS, in primo adversus Marcio- nem, hanc epistolam inter primas Pauli fuisse existimat. Verba ejus sunt: Ab illo certè Paulo, qui adhuc in gratia rudis, trepidans denique, ne in vacuum cucurrisset, aut curreret, tum primum cum antecessoribus Apostolis conferebat. Igitur si ferventer, ut adhuc Neophytus, adversus Judaismum, aliquid reprehenden- dum in conversatione existimavit, passivum scilicet convictum, postmodum & ipse usu omnia omnibus futurus, ut omnes lu- cretur, Judæis quasi Judæus, & eis, qui sub lege, tanquam sub lege: tu illam solius conversationis placituræ postea accusa- tori suo reprehensionem suspectam vis haberi &c. Vehemen- tiorem in hac, quam aliis epistolis, esse satis apparet. Cau- sas tamen alias, quam suspicatur Tertullianus, existimo, nempe quod illi, qui rituum Judaicorum libertatem vocatis è gentibus volebant eripere, non Judæi essent, quibus ali- quid ea in re erat condonandum, sed alienigenæ, qui in Ju- dæa vixerant, quorum princeps erat Cerinthus, quales fue- re & illi, qui docuere eadem Philippis, ut index est ipse Pau- lus, Philipp. III, 3. quod iidem Judaizandi necessitatem do- cerent, nulla pietate moti, sed ut ea ratione honores & com- moda à Judæis adipiscerentur: simulque effugerent incom- moda, quæ Christianos premebant. Nam eis temporibus Judæis per leges Romanas & edicta, libera erat religionis functio non item Christianis, quos vexari jam tunc cœpisse ex actis, & aliis Pauli epistolis, apparet. Videbat autem Paulus, cui specialius, quam cæteris incumbebat gentium conversio, quantum impedimentum allatura esset hæc novi oneris injunctio. Cum autem isti Pauli, libertatem stre- nue defendentis, obtrectatores, dicerent Paulum jus docen- di non nisi à Petro, Johanne, & Jacobo accepisse, ac proinde illorum instituta Pauli institutis ante habenda, præterea Paulum ipsum in hac re fuisse varium, Paulus contra magno animo ostendit, se non minus quam alios Apostolos Apo- stolatum suum à Christo accepisse, neque Petrum, Johan- nem, & Jacobum aliud docere, quam ipse doceat, se quoque, etsi in usu aut omissione rituum solitus esset, se accommo- dare utilitati eorum, quibuscum viveret, idem tamen de ista libertate docuisse semper: Et hoc suum dogma, typis veteris testamenti μυστικῶς explicatis, confirmat. Tempus, quo scripta est hæc ad Gallogræcos epistola, sicut designate indicare non possum: ita videre mihi videor, non longe ab- fuisse ab eo tempore, quo ad Romanos scripta est epistola.

OBSERVATIONES Ad Grotii Præloquium cum aliis prolego- menis.

UT TERTULLIANI judicium de causa vehe- mentiæ Apostolicæ in hac epistola GROTIO sese probare non potuit: Ita improbanda penitus censura Tertulliani de reprehensione Petri Pauli- na, quod adhuc in gratia rudis fuerit ac trepidans, ne in vacuum cucurrisset aut curreret, cum conferret, cum Apostolis, quodque ferventer adhuc ut Neo- phytus adversus Judaismum aliquid in conversatio- ne reprehendendum existimarit, postea accusatori suo placiturâ. Nam justam fuisse Paulinam repre- hensionem, nec unquam ejus pœnituisse Aposto- lum, à cap. II. manifestum erit. Et qui Neophytus adhuc, vel rudis in gratia fuisset tantus gentium Doctor, qui non minor summis Apostolis fuit, 2. Cor.

XI. 5. & septendecim annos jam exegerat in hoc arduo & divino Apostolatus munere, Gal. I. 18. cap. II. 1, 11. adeoque ab Hierusalem ad Illyricum usque omnia Evangelio Christi jam repleverat, Rom. XVI. 3. 4. Ex quo facile apparet, hanc epistolam nequaquam fuisse è primis Pauli, quam nonam in ordine temporis habita ratione constituimus in præloquio ad epist. ad Rom. Sect. I. Et Grotius hic non longe abfuisse ab eo tempore, quo ad Romanos scripta est epistola, asserit, quæ vero anno demum XXII. conversionis Paulinæ scripta est. Et priorem quidem epistolâ ad Romanos, quæ septima ordine temporis videtur, facit præsentem Chrysostomus, ut & Theophylactus, sed ςοχασι- κῶς. Romæ autem hanc scriptam esse, subscriptio testatur, quum ferret jam Apostolus stigmata Do- mini in corpore suo, Gal. IV. 17. Anno itaque con- versionis Paulinæ XXV. circiter hanc epistolam scriptam esse, & ad minimum sex annis post con- versionem Galatarum, Theodoretius observavit. Hanc misit è Roma, cum vidisset Galatas & docuis- set, ait Athanasius in Synopsi. Quam posterio- rem esse Romana ex eo colligere est, quia Rom. XV. significat se jam occupari in eleemosyna pro sanctis, qui Hierosolymis erant, colligenda, quod verò jam à se factum fuisse testatur in hac episto- la cap. II. vers. 10. Atque inde etiam apparet, non Epheso, quod argumentum Latinis exemplaribus præmissum vult, sed Româ potius missam esse hanc epistolam. Nam quum in Asia versaretur, in quâ Ephesus sita est, id adhuc agebatur, ut Achaia & Macedonia collationem in pauperes Judæos face- rent. Non abnuit Schlichtingius cum Crellio suo ad v. 2. cap. I. Apparet, inquiunt, hanc epistolam post omnia tempora, quibus inter gentes prædicandi Evangelii causa fuerat libere versatus, scriptam fuisse. Quare nisi quis dicere velit, eam fuisse scri- ptam ex itinere Hierosolymitano aut Cæsarea, ubi captivus per tempus aliquod fuit detentus, Actor. XXIII. concludendum videtur, eam fuisse Romæ scriptam, quemadmodum etiam habent veteres sub- scriptiones. Nam ex capite II. constare potest, hanc epistolam esse scriptam post eleemosynam inter fra- tres gentium exterarum, pro pauperibus Hierosoly- mitanæ Ecclesiæ collectam. Dicit enim ibi v. 10. se stu- duisse id facere, quod Apostoli eum Hierosolymis mo- nuerant, nempe ut pauperum esset memor, loquitur- que de hoc studio tanquam de re præterita. At quam- diu Apostolus libere inter gentes, & sine vinculis fuit versatus, nunquam hoc studium deposuit.

Adversarii, cum quibus negotium est Apostolo, sunt Pseudo-Apostoli, de quibus Tertullianus loco citato: Sed et si quosdam falsos fratres irrepsif- se descripsit, qui vellent Galatas ad aliud Evange- lium transferre, ipse demonstrat, adulterium illud

Evangelii non ad alterius DEI & Christi fidem transferendam, sed ad disciplinam legis conservan- dam habuisse intentionem. Deprehendens scilicet il- los circumcisionem vindicantes, & observantes tem- pora & dies & menses & annos Judaicarum ceremo- niarum, quas jam exclusas agnovisse debuerant se- cundum innovatam dispositionem Creatoris. Falsos & Apostolos & Fratres notans in hac causa, qua Evangelium Christi Creatoris transferrent a novi- tate prænuntiata a Creatore ad vetustatem recusa- tam a Creatore. Grotius non Judæos sed alieni- genas, qui in Judæa vixerant, quorum princeps Cerinthus fuerit, illos fuisse putat, quales etiam Philippis eadem docuerint Phil. III. 3. Sed nullo indicio constat, Cerinthum & asseclas hic, aut in epistola ad Philippenses, aut alienigenas, non Ju- dæos notasse Apostolum. Etsi enim Judæis ali- quid in ceremoniis condonandum fuerit, non tamen cum necessitatem earum urgebant ad con- sequendam salutem: Siquidem eo errore tùm li- bertas Christiana convelleretur, tùm vero doctri- na de justificatione Apostolica everteretur. Et testatur Epiphanius, Cerinthum ipsum natione Ju- dæum ac circumcisum fuisse, ideoque omnes Chri- stianos circumcidendos contendisse. De cætero Cerinthus Jesum a Christo tanquam duas personas divisit impie fingens Christum in specie columbæ in Jesum, quum a Johanne baptizaretur, descen- disse, Jesum passum esse ac resurrexisse non verò Christum, qui a Jesu tùm evolarit. Cujus mon- strosi erroris in iis, quos hac epistola notavit Pau- lus, nullum prorsus apparet indicium. Nazaræos plerique dicunt, cum quibus hic res est Aposto- lo, qui & Jessei, teste Epiphanio, a Jesse, Davidis Patre dicti, propter persecutiones undiquaque tunc Christianis a Judæis impendentes Christi Ev- angelium cum usu & observatione ceremonia- rum legis miscuerint: Jesum autem Mariæ Filium pro DEI Filio & Christo sive Messia Patribus pro- misso agnoverint. De quibus Hieronymus in epi- stola ad Augustinum, & Augustinus ipse cap. IX. de hæresib. & libr. XIX. contra Faust, c. 18. libr. 1. contra Crescon.

Sed quicunque tandem illi fuerint Pseudo-A- postoli, contra quos hic egit; occasio, & causa scri- ptionis Apostoli non fuit illa tantum, quod isti Judaizandi necessitatem docerent, ut honores & commoda a Judæis adipiscerentur, incommoda vero, quæ Christianos premebant, effugerent, sed imprimis etiam illa, quod iidem opera momlia juxta cum fide necessaria esse ad salutem docerent, quod è Concilio Hierosolymitano Act. XV. tracta- tione Apostolica in hac epistola aliisque simili- bus B. Lutherus observavit, & Flacius in præfa- tione generali epistolarum S. Pauli multis argu- mentis confirmavit : In quo etiam veteres Inter- pretes consentientes habemus. Miscebant enim falsi Apostoli legem & Evangelium, nec solum circumcisionem & observantiam ceremoniarum legalium cum fide in Christum urgebant, sed et- iam legis impletionem requirebant, ceu ad salu- tem omnino necessariam Act. XV. 1. 5. unde Apo- stoli redarguebant eosdem, quod jugum disci- pulis imponere tentarent, quod neque ipsi por- tare possint, neque Patres ipsorum potuerint. Quum ex adverso credendum sit per gratiam Do- mini nostri Jesu Christi salutem nos consequi v. 11. Postquam ergo Galatæ ex Ethnicismo ad fidem Christianam conversi essent (quibus Act. XVI. prohibebatur quidem Apostolus Evangelium præ- dicare, sed tantum donec Macedonibus, quibus subvenire per visionem monitus est, prædicatum erat) & à Galatis in maximo honore haberetur,

Apostolus, quem ut Angelum DEI, imo ut Jesum Christum excipiebant, invidiâ & astu Satanæ per Pseudo-Apostolos vehementer turbatæ sunt Ec- clesiæ Galaticæ. Qui tum heterodoxiam suam de suscipienda circumcisione, & in ceremoniis Le- viticis, ut & legis moralis operibus quærenda justi- ficatione passim disseminarunt per easdem, tum vero autoritate Apostoli autoritati Apostoli, quam suo instituto officere probe intelligebant, quan- tum in ipsis erat, detrahebant, Paulum non ean- dem cum cæteris Apostolis doctrinam tradere, hos vero, utpote qui Christum in carne viderant, inque ejusdem schola informati fuerant, potius sequendos esse, cavillati.

Quapropter ut ad argumentum tractationis ac- cedamus, Apostolus ante omnia autoritatem su- am asserebat, seque munus suum non ab homini- bus, sed à Christo accepisse, nullumque aliud Ev- angelium esse, quam quod ipse traderet, nec aliud suscipi posse, si vel Angelus de cœlo id annuntia- ret, docebat, siquidem Evangelium suum non ab ullo homine, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi didicerit. Qua fini conversionis & prædicationis suæ historiam commemorat, imprimis, quod ne- minem Apostolorum convenerit nisi Petrum, idque triennio demum post conversionem, atque Jacobum, & quatuordecim post conversionem an- nis ex revelatione Hierosolymam profectus cum Ja- cobo, Cepha & Johanne, gratiam Apostolo conces- sam agnoscentibus contulerit, interque ipsos con- ventum sit, ut prædicaret inter gentes, quemad- modum ipsi inter Judæos. Refert denique quo- modo Antiochiæ ipsimet Petro non recte inceden- ti, sed in conversatione Judaizanti palam restititerit. Quo pacto stabilita Apostolici muneris au- toritate atque Evangelii sui veritate thema præci- puum, quod homo non per legis opera justifice- tur, sed unice per fidem in Christum, proponit, &c. argumentis immotis confirmat, legis usum tradit, eamque ab Evangelio accurate discriminat, tum de ceremoniis externis, è quibus emancipati sub Novo Testamento sumus per adventum Filii Dei, disserit, eosque qui sub lege adhuc esse cupiebant, allegoria duorum filiorum Abrahæ ex ancilla nem- pe, & è libera prognatorum redarguit, & ut in libertate, quam Christus peperit, persistant, mo- net, de periculo erroris Pseudo-Apostolorum gra- viter docens. Denique ne officere ipsum fidei doctrina pietati criminentur adversarii, dilectio- nem proximi, & abstinentiam ab operibus carnis sedulo inculcat, fructusque Spiritus urget, ut car- nem crucifigant, Spiritu incedant, & humilitati, mansuetudini, beneficentiæ studeant, ac summam doctrinæ suæ conclusionis loco repetit: eamque re- gulam observari jubet perbrevi voto epistolam obsignans.

Partes itaque epistolæ principales post inscri- ptionem, & themati præcipuo consentaneum vo- tum, sunt tres. Prima est Apostolici præconii vindi- catrix, vel justa ejus ἐκδίκησις c. I. & II. usque ad v. 15. Altera de fide, in qua turbati erant Galatæ, infor- matrix, vel necessaria διδασκαλία tum quà verum & falsum in articulo de justificatione, quem pro- ponit in thesi cap. II. reliquo, & antithesi, quoad exclusionem operum moralium à justificatione, quæ imprimis ceu necessaria ad eandem require- bant Pseudo-Apostoli cap. III. & quoad profliga- tionem necessitatis operum ceremonialium cap. IV, tum qua momentum controversiæ, quod per Pseu- do-Apostolorum doctrinam sub servile jugum captiventur, à Christo evacuentur, gratia exci- dant, ac tota religionis Christianæ massa inficia- tur. cap. V. ad v. 12. Tertia est de charitate & fru- stibus Spiritus commonitrix, gravis nempe παιδεία ad confundendam falsorum doctorum calumni- am, vanamque pietatis studium negligentium per- suasionem capite V. reliquo, ut & cap. VI. inte- gro. Quod ergo præcipuum doctrinæ caput, B. Lutherus noster, uti occasionem in Comm. priori Tom. III. Jenensi rectè notavit: Galatæ primum ab Apostolo sanam fidem, id est, in solum Jesum Christum non in suas aut legis justitias, fidere do- cti, post per Pseudo-Apostolos rursum deturbati sunt in fiduciam operum legalis justitiæ, decepti vi- delicet quam facillime magnorum & verorum Apo- stolorum falsò commendato & nomine & exemplo: Ita eximie de primaria tractationis Apostolicæ materia in posteriori Comment. Tom. IV. Je- nensi Latino in argumento epistolæ scripsit: Pau- lus vult stabilire doctrinam fidei, gratiæ, remissio- nis peccatorum, seu justitiæ Christianæ, ut habea- mus perfectam cognitionem & differentiam inter justitiam Christianam, & omnes alias justitias. Ista enim excellentissima justitia, nempe fidei, quam DEUS per Christum nobis absque operibus impu- tat, nec est politica, nec ceremonialis, nec legis di- vinæ justitia, nec versatur in nostris operibus; sed est planè diversa, hoc est mere passiva justitia, (sicut illæ superiores activæ.) Ibi enim nihil opera- mur aut reddimus DEO, sed tantum recipimus & patimur alium operantem in nobis scilicet Deum. Ideo libet illam fidei seu Christianam justitiam ap- pellare passivam justitiam. Hæcque est justitia in mysterio abscondita, quam mundus non intelligit, imo Christiani non satis eam tenent, & difficulter in tentationibus apprehendunt. Ideo semper est in- culcanda & usu excolenda assidue. Et qui eam in afflictionibus & terroribus conscientiæ non tenet aut apprehendit, non potest consistere. Nulla enim alia tam est firma & certa consolatio conscientiarum, quam illa passiva justitia. Et paulo post: Sum- ma igitur ars & sapientia Christianorum est, ne- scire legem, ignorare opera, & totam justitiam acti- vam, præsertim cum conscientia luctatur cum ju- dicio DEI, sicut extra populum DEI summa sapi- entia est nosse, inspicere & urgere legem, opera, & activam justitiam. Quæ & alia non tantùm ad- versus modernos Pseudo-Apostolos articulum de justificatione penitus pervertentes Pontificios, Arminianos, Socinianos, sed etiam adversus No- vatores, Ecclesias nostras sub larva Lutherano- rum turbantes Majoristas, Calixtinos, & alios Syn- cretistas probe observanda sunt, quos nimium quantum à Megalandri doctrina Evangelica re- cedere, & anathema Apostolicum Galat. I. 8. 9. omnino incurrere Harmoniâ Calixtino-Hæreti- câ ὀφθαλμοφανερῶς demonstravimus. Quibus gemella tradere annotata Grotiana in progressu patebit.

Id itaque in aprico jam est, nontx incommode epistolam præsentem epistolæ ad Romanos com- pendium quoddam dici, tùm quoad partem dogma- ticam, quantum imprimis ad articulum de justi- ficatione per fidem sine operibus legis; tùm etiam quoad partem moralem de dilectione proximi & studio sanctitatis.

Commentariis hanc epistolam, si ab illis dis- cesseris, qui omnes Paulinas, vel etiam brevio- res solum omnes, ad Galatas, Ephesios & sequen- tes enarrarunt, quod nuper à Johanne Crocio co- piose factum, illustrarunt Alexander Episcopus Cappadociæ Ann. CCLV. Severianus Gabalens. Episcopus Ann. CCCC. Hieronymus, Augusti- nus, Claudius Antissiodorensis, B. Lutherus, qui ge- minum in eandem edidit commentarium, priorem Anno 1519. T. I. Tomo Jenensi Latino continetur: B. Bugenhagius, B. Joh. Bren- tius, B. Wigandus, B. Hesbusius, B. Winkelman- nus, B. D. Hoë, B. D. Georgius Weinrichius, B. D. Bartholomaeus Battus, B. D. Henr. Höpfnerus, B. D. Andreas Kunadus, B. Kromajerus, atque è Re- formatis, Hyperius, Olevianus, Copius, Pareus, &c.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. Containing the Ἐκδίκησιν [vindication] or defense of the Apostolic proclamation. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul, having premised the authority of his calling and a votive salutation, marvels at the aversion to another Gospel, denying that another Gospel is given, and striking the bringer of one with an anathema; protesting that he does not preach to please men and that he did not receive his Gospel from men, but from Christ; after he explained his persecution of Christians in Judaism and his zeal for the law of his fathers, as well as the gracious calling of GOD to the proclamation of the Gospel, he relates that he did not confer about it with the Apostles at Jerusalem beforehand, but having departed into Arabia and returned again to Damascus, he preached the Gospel, and afterwards, finally, after three years, having gone to Jerusalem to see Peter, and having seen no other Apostles except James, he came into Syria and Cilicia, unknown by face to the Churches in Judea; for the rest, they were celebrating God on account of that persecutor, who was now preaching the Word.

There are three parts: I. Preliminaries of the epistle to verse 5. II. Reprehension concerning the aversion of the Galatians to another Gospel than that which had been preached to them by the Apostle from the revelation of Christ, to verse 12. III. Relation concerning his former zeal under Judaism, and concerning his calling to the proclamation of the Gospel undertaken without prior communication with the Apostles and carried out for some years with the doxology of the converted Jews, to verse 24.

PART I. Preliminary epistle.

Vers. 1. Οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, ἐδὲ δι ἀνθρώπε [Not from men, nor through man]: This office was not imposed upon me by men, by their own will, nor even by the command of GOD through mere men, in the way that many were ordained in the Churches by the Apostles, at the dictation of the Spirit, as Matthias, who was nominated by the Apostles, but by Christ himself, who was already constituted outside of men, in divine power. Christ, through his ascension into heaven, is not a man—namely, such as he was, and such as we are, that is, mortal.

Immediately at the threshold, the Apostle asserts his divine calling, recounting a threefold kind of calling. The first is when a calling is made by men, or by mere human authority; such callings to the Holy ministry are altogether illegitimate. The second is when a calling is indeed made by GOD, but through the intervention of men; such callings are not only those which are made immediately by GOD, whether by lot or by the express announcement of some person, although they are deferred δι ἀνθρώπε [through man], just as Aaron was called by Moses at the immediate command of GOD; but also those which are made by the Church, by divine direction, even if not through a certain command of a man θεοπνέυσε [divinely inspired] and divinely called, whom specifically

Titus appointed according to his own judgment Tit. I. 5. just as the Ephesian presbyters are said to have been appointed by the Holy Spirit Acts XX. 28. The third, when the calling is made immediately by GOD, calling the person called and committing the office to him, such as this divine Pauline calling was, made by Christ Acts IX. & XXII. & that of the other Apostles. Jerome similarly assigns four kinds of those sent from this passage: The first which is neither from men, nor through men, but from GOD: The second from GOD through a man: The third from a man, not from GOD: The fourth neither from a man, nor from GOD. Blessed Luther elegantly warns here about the calling to be awaited, Comment. on the former, f. 2. Await the caller, meanwhile be secure. Indeed, if you were wiser than Solomon and Daniel himself, yet unless you are called, flee more than hell, lest you pour forth a word. If He needs you, He will call you; if He does not call, your knowledge will not burst you. Finally, it is not true, but it seems like knowledge to you, and you most foolishly imagine for yourself a fruit which you might be able to produce. No one produces fruit with the word, unless he who is called to teach without his own desire. For there is one Master of ours, Jesus Christ; He alone teaches and produces fruit through His called servants. But he who teaches without being called, does not teach without harm both to himself and to his hearers, because Christ is not with him.

Moreover, Christ is here opposed to men, not because by his ascension into heaven he is no longer a man, such as we are (as regards the substance of the body), which gloss is pleasing to the Socinians, but because He is God blessed forever over all things Rom. IX. 5. For the callings of the remaining Apostles also, although made by Christ while He was still mortal as regards His human nature, were made ουκ απ' ανθρωπων, ουδε δι' ανθρωπου, but δια ιησου χριστου, who is God manifested in the flesh 1 Tim. III. 16, are truly and immediately divine. The argument therefore is invincible against the Socinians: He who, as far as nature is concerned, is distinguished from mere men, is not by nature ψιλος ανθρωπος, but it is necessary that another nature be present in Him besides; and since by reason of this He is joined in the calling to the Apostleship, it is necessary that He be of the same divine nature and ομοουσιος with GOD the Father. And to be from man is opposed to that which is from heaven or from GOD Matt. XXI. 25. Acts V. 39.

Αλλα δια Ιησου χριστου) From Him, who immediately after the resurrection began to be called God by Thomas. See John XX. 28.

Although before the resurrection Christ was not called GOD by the Apostles; yet He professed Himself to be God and equal to the Father, and defended this against the Jews John V. & X. and attributed divine axioms to Himself, and taught that He was GOD through miracles and the oracles of the Old Testament explained by Himself, and thus was treated by the Apostles and others in the days of His flesh with the divine honor of adoration and invocation.

Και Θεου Πατρος εγειραντος αυτον εκ νεκρων) In order to commend His office the more, He ascends through the intermediate cause to the primary one. For that power by which Christ rules the Church and called Paul to the Apostleship comes to Him from GOD the Father, above whom there is nothing.

Christ is not joined here as an intermediate cause, but as one of the same divine virtue and power with GOD the Father, such as is that of appointing Apostles and committing to them the proclamation of the Gospel through the whole world with a gracious promise of operation and assistance through it Matt. XXVIII. 19, 20. John XX. 21, 22, 23. And therefore by the single preposition δια, both divine persons, Jesus Christ and God the Father, are joined and established in the same kind of causality. For although Christ received divine power from the Father as man, He is nevertheless of the same power and essence with the Father as God John V. 17, seqq. ch. X. 30. 1 John V. 7. And it is clear from this passage that the preposition δια is not a mark of an intermediate or less principal cause, because here, as also 1 Cor. I. 1, 2 Cor. I. 9, it is referred to the Father. For Schlichtingius is inept, along with his Crellius, when they say that the particle διὰ is taken here in one way concerning God the Father, and in another concerning Christ: Concerning God the Father, to denote the principal cause: Concerning Christ, to denote the intermediate cause: Surely the same word placed only once in the same passage will obtain a different meaning at the same time?

Moreover, mention of Christ's resurrection from the dead is added, partly because he could be considered of no less esteem, having been called by Christ who had entered into glory and was already exalted at the right hand of the Father, than those who, having been called before Christ's passion, were confirmed anew after his resurrection, but did not receive the Apostleship from him once he had been taken up to heaven; partly because in this way he tacitly refuted the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles, who established man's righteousness in the observance of the law. For if righteousness is through the law, Christ died and was raised in vain Gal. II. 21. who was delivered for our sins and raised for our righteousness Rom. IV. 24. partly so that he might repeat for us that supreme consolation at the very threshold, that God the Father raised Christ from the dead, who was delivered for our sins: Therefore he will also raise us, who believe in Christ Jesus, to eternal life. Concerning these things, Blessed Luther in his former Commentary. But that he should insert the resurrection of Christ seems superfluous. Truly, the Apostle is accustomed to commemorate the resurrection of Christ willingly, especially against those who trust in their own righteousness. Thus he also mentions it in the salutation of the same in Romans, and more copiously, because he argues there strongly against the righteousness of works. For those who are such, it is necessary that they deny, nay, mock the resurrection of Christ. For in Rom. IV, Christ (he says) died for our sins, and rose again for our justification. Therefore, whoever presumes to be righteous by any other way than by believing in Christ, this person rejects Christ from himself, and considers his passion and resurrection superfluous. But he who believes in Christ dying, at the same time he himself also dies to sin with Christ. And he who believes in the rising and living one, by the same faith he himself also rises and lives in Christ, and Christ in him. Therefore the resurrection of Christ is our righteousness and life, not only by example, but also by power. Without the resurrection of Christ, no one rises, however much he may do good works. Again, through the resurrection, everyone rises, however much he may have done evil, as these things [are discussed] more broadly in [the commentary] on the Romans. Perhaps he is also accustomed to mention the resurrection in the salutation for this reason, that the Holy Spirit was given through the resurrection of Christ, by which Spirit the gifts of the Apostleship and others were distributed, so that he might thus assert himself as an Apostle by divine authority, through the Spirit of the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

But there is no argument of the Socinians: He whom God the Father raised, he is not God. For that must be corrected: He is not God according to that nature according to which he was raised by the Father. Rather, both natures are established from this, the Human, for according to the human nature he was raised, and the divine: For according to the same power he has the same [power] as the Father, John V. 17. seq.

Latin:

PARS I. Ἐκδίκησιν vel vindicias Apostolici praeconii continens. CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Paulus praemissa vocationis suae autoritate, & salutatione votiva miratur aversionem ad aliud Evangelium, negans aliud dari Evangelium, & afferentem anathemate feriens, se non ad placitum bominum praedicare & Evangelium suum accepisse non ab bominibus, sed à Christo protesta- tus, postquam suam Christianorum per- sequutionem in Judaismo, & zelum pro lege patria, nec non gratiosam DEI ad Evangelii praeconium vocationem expli- cuit, sese de ea Hierosolymis prius cum Apostolis baud contulisse tradit, sed in Arabiam profectum, ac denuo Damascum reversum Evangelium praedicasse ac post- modum demum post triennium ad Petrum videndum Hierosolymam nullisque aliis Apostolis praeter Jacobum visis, in Syriam & Ciliciam venisse, ignotum Ecclesiis in Judaea quoad faciem; de caetero Deum ob persecutorem istum, Verbum jam praedi- cantem, celebrantibus.

PArtes tres sunt I. Praeliminaria epistolae ad v. 5. II. Reprehensio de aversione Galatarum ad aliud Evangelium, quam quod ab Apostolo ex revelatione Christi praedicatum ipsis fuerat ad v. 12. III. Relatio de zelo pristino sub Judaismo, & de vocatione ad Evangelii praeconium sine praevia communicatione cum Apostolis suscepta & aliquot annis cum Judaeorum conversorum δοξολογίᾳ expedita ad v. 24.

PARS I. Epistola praeliminaria.

Vers. 1. Οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, ἐδὲ δι ἀνθρώπε) Munus hoc mihi, neque ab hominibus, suopte arbitratu, impositum est, neque etiam DEI jussu, per meros homines, quomodo multi in Ecclesiis ordinati fuere per Apostolos, dictante Spi- ritu, ut Matthias, ab Apostolis nominatus, sed ab ipso Chri- sto, jam extra homines, in divina potestate, constituto. Chri- stus per evectionem suam in coelum non est homo, nempe qualis fuit, & quales nos sumus, id est, mortales.

Mox in limine asserit Apostolus divinam suam vocationem, triplex genus vocationis recensens. Prius cum vocatio fit ab hominibus, seu auto- ritate mere humana; quales vocationes ad S. ministerium prorsus illegitimae sunt. Alterum cum à DEO quidem fit vocatio, sed interventu hominum, quales vocationes non tantum sunt, quae immediatè à DEO, sive per sortem, sive per expressam denuntiationem alicujus per- sonae, licet δι ἀνθρώπε deferuntur, uti Aaron per Mosen ad immediatum DEI mandatum vo- catus est; sed etiam quae ab Ecclesia, directione divina fiunt, etsi non per mandatum quoddam viri θεοπνέυσε & divinitus vocati, quos oppidatim

Titus constituit pro arbitrio Tit. I. 5. quomodo a Spiritu S. Presbyteri Ephesini constituti dicun- tur Act. XX. 28. Tertium, cum immediate a DEO vocatio fit, personam vocatam compellante, eique officium committente, qualis vocatio divina haec fuit Paulina Act. IX. & XXII. & caeterorum Apo- stolorum a Christo facta. Hieronymus quatuor missorum genera similiter ex hoc loco assignat: Primum quod neque ab hominibus, neque per ho- mines, sed a DEO: Secundum a DEO per homi- nem: Tertium ab homine, non a DEO: Quartum nec ab homine, nec a DEO. Eleganter hic monet B. Lutherus de vocatione expectanda Comment. priori f. 2. Expecta vocantem, interim esto securus. Imo si esses sapientior ipso Salomone & Daniele, ta- men nisi voceris, plus quam infernum fuge, ne ver- bum effundas. Si tui eguerit, vocabit te, si non vo- cabit, non te rumpet scientia tua. Denique neque est vera, sed videtur tibi scientia, & stultissime tibi fingis fructum, quem possis facere. Nemo fructificat verbo, nisi qui sine suo voto vocatur ad docendum. Unus est enim Magister noster Jesus Christus, hic solus docet & fructum facit per vocatos servos suos. Qui autem non vocatus docet, non sine damno & suo & auditorum docet, quod Christus non sit cum eo.

Caeterum Christus hic opponitur hominibus, non quod per evectionem in caelum non sit amplius homo, quales nos sumus, (quantum ad substantiam corporis) quae glossa Socinianis grata est, sed quod Deus sit benedictus in secula super omnia Rom. IX. 5. Nam & reliquorum Apostolorum, etsi a Christo, dum adhuc mortalis erat, quoad humanam natu- ram, factae vocationes, ουκ απ' ανθρωπων, ουδε δι' αν- θρωπου factae sunt, αλλα δια ιησου χριστου, qui est Deus manifestatus in carne 1. Tim. III. 16. vere & imme- diate divinae sunt. Argumentum itaque invictum est contra Socinianos: Qui, quod ad naturam at- tinet, hominibus meris contradistinguitur, is non est natura ψιλος ανθρωπος, sed aliam in eo opor- tet insuper naturam inesse; Et quum ejus ratio- ne in vocatione ad Apostolatum conjungatur, di- vinae simul naturae sit, & ομοουσιος DEO Patri ne- cessum est. Et esse ab homine, opponitur ei, quod est e coelo vel a DEO Matth. XXI. 25. Act. V. 39.

Αλλα δια Ιησου χριστου) Ab eo, qui statim a resurrectione Deus a Thoma dici coepit. Vide Joh. XX. 28.

Etsi ante resurrectionem ab Apostolis DEUS dictus non sit Christus; se tamen Deum esse & Patri aequalem professus est, idque contra Judaeos defendit Joh. V. & X. & axiomata divina sibi tri- buit, seque DEUM esse per miracula, & oracula Veteris Testamenti a se explicata, docuit, adeoque ab Apostolis, aliisque in diebus carnis divino ado- rationis & invocationis honore affectus fuit.

Και Θεου Πατρος εγειραντος αυτον εκ νεκρων) Quo magis suum munus commendet, per causam mediam ascendit ad primam. Nam potestas illa, qua Christus Ecclesiam re- git, & Paulum ad Apostolatum vocavit, venit ei a DEO Patre, supra quem nihil est.

Non hic Christus ut causa media, sed ut ejusdem cum DEO Patre divinae virtutis, & potestatis, qua- lis est illa constituendi Apostolos, iisque praeco- nium Evangelii committendi per totum terrarum orbem cum promissione gratiosa per illud ope- rationis, & assistentiae Matth. XXVIII. 19. 20. Joh. XX. 21. 22. 23. conjungitur. Ideoque unica praeposi- tione δια utraque persona divina Jesus Christus & Deus Pater conjungitur, & in eodem causalitatis genere constituitur. Quamvis enim potestatem di- vinam Christus a Patre acceperit, ut homo, ejus- dem tamen est cum Patre & potestatis & essentiae, ut Deus Joh. V. 17. seqq. cap. X. 30. 1. Joh. V. 7. Et patet ex hoc loco, praepositionem δια non effe- notam causæ mediæ: aut minus principalis, quia hic, ut & 1. Cor. I. 1. 2. Cor. I. 9. ad Patrem refertur. Ineptus enim est Schlichtingius cum Crellio suo, cum particulam διὰ hic aliter de Deo Patre, aliter de Christo accipi ajunt: De Deo Patre, ut causam prin- cipalem denotet: De Christo, ut causam mediam: Scilicet eadem vox in eodem loco semel tantum posita diversam simul obtinebit significationem?

Additur autem mentio resuscitationis Christi à mortuis, tùm quia à Christo ad gloriam ingresso, & ad dextram Patris jam exaltato vocatus non minoris æstimii haberi poterat, quàm illi, qui ante passionem Christi vocati, post resurrectio- nem ejus denuo confirmati sunt, non autem ab eo, jam ad cœlum evecto, Apostolatum accepe- runt: tùm quia ita Pseudo-Apostolorum doctri- nam tacite refellebat, qui justitiam hominis in le- gis observatione constituebant. Nam si per legem justitia, Christus frustra mortuus & resuscitatus est Gal. II. 21. qui propter peccata nostra mortuus & propter justitiam nostram resuscitatus Rom. IV. 24. tùm ut supremam illam consolationem in ipso li- mine nobis repeteret, quod Deus Pater Christum propter peccata nostra traditum ex mortuis sus- citavit: Ergo & nos, qui in Christum Jesum cre- dimus, ad vitam æternam suscitabit. De hisce B. Lutherus in priori Comm. Quod autem resurre- ctionem Christi insererit, videtur otiosum. Verum, solet Apostolus libenter resurrectionem Christi com- memorare, potissimum contra eos, qui in justitiam propriam confidunt. Sic & in Rom. salutatione ejus- dem & copiosius meminit, quod & ibidem fortiter contra justitiam operum disputat. Qui enim tales sunt, necesse est, ut resurrectionem Christi negent, imo irrideant. Nam Rom. IV. Christus (inquit) mor- tuus est propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit pro- pter justificationem nostram. Idco qui alia via præ- sumit justus esse, quàm credendo in Christum, hic Christum à se rejicit, & otiosam ejus passionem & resurrectionem ducit. Qui autem in Christum mo- rientem credit, simul & ipse moritur peccato cum Christo. Et qui credit in resurgentem & viventem, eadem fide & ipse resurgit & vivit in Christo, & Christus in eo. Ideo resurrectio Christi est justitia vitaque nostra, non tantum exemplo, sed & virtute. Sine resurrectione Christi nemo resurgit, quantum- libet operetur bona. Rursum per resurrectionem qui- libet resurgit, quantumlibet operatus sit mala, ut hæc latius ad Romanos. Forte etiam ideo meminisse solet in salutatione resurrectionis, quod S. S. datus est per re- surrectionem Christi, quo Spiritu distributa sunt dona Apostolatus & alia, ut sic se Apostolum asserat autori- tate divina, per Spiritum resurrectionis Jesu Christi.

Nullum autem est Socinianorum argumentum: Quem resuscitavit Deus Pater, ille non est Deus. Nam corrigendum id: Non est Deus secundum eam naturam, secundum quam resuscitatus est à Patre. Utraque potius natura hinc adstruitur, Hu- mana, nam secundum humanam naturam resusci- tatus est, & divina: Nam secundum eandem po- testatem eandem habet, quam Pater Joh. V. 17. seq.

## 1:2
V. 2. And all the brethren who are with me). Paul, as I judge, was among the Galatians some time before he came to Corinth, Acts XVI. 6. and XVIII. 1. But it seems that he instituted the second journey to the Galatians, of which [he speaks] in Acts XVIII. 23, after this writing.

Because the epistle was written from Rome, the Roman brethren rather seem to be indicated. He implies, therefore, the consent of the brethren or of the entire Church, to whom without doubt the epistle was read, as it was to be inscribed in the name of the same [Church] to the Galatian Churches at the same time. The Pseudo-Apostles were accusing Paul of departing from everyone else. This subscription refutes them. They could understand

The Galatians' consensus of the faithful, among whom there were undoubtedly many from the circumcision, and not held in contempt by the Galatians, which is of great value for correcting the unrefined common people, as Jerome notes, as well as the common grief which the troubled state of the Galatian churches brought upon them.

Ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Γαλατίας) To the Ancyrans, the Tavianis, the Pessinuntians: he does not add the title 'saints' here, because they had begun to decline from the Gospel.

Galatia is a region of Asia, looking toward Cappadocia and the river Halys on the East, Bithynia on the West, Pamphylia on the South, and the Euxine Sea on the North, which the Gauls, having set out from Europe into Asia, once inhabited, whence it was called Gallo-Graecia and Graeco-Gallia, and later Galatia. The name Paphlagonia remained in some part of Galatia, because the Phrygians and Paphlagonians first held the Galatians. The more important cities are named Synope, Pompejopolis, Claudiopolis, Laodicea, Antiochia, Nicopolis, and Ancyra, which is the metropolis. See Pliny the Younger, book V, ch. 32, and Cluverius in his introduction to Geography. That the Apostle called them simply the Churches of Galatia, Chrysostom and Theophylact take as an indication of indignation and grief. Yet he does not deny the title of Church. For they had received Christ, and had not entirely cast Him off: they were Churches, even if many in them had been seduced by the Pseudo-Apostles. Therefore, the Calixtine innovators gather in vain from the fact that the name of Church was given to them, even though they erred greatly in doctrine, that the name of Church must not be denied to Papists and Calvinists either. For there is no doubt that in Papistic and Calvinistic assemblies God still gathers some Church for Himself. For in them also is given that which is Christian: the word of God, which is read, and baptism, which is dispensed to infants; there is also given that which is Anti-Christian: such as idolomania, heretical opinions, superstitions, etc. Through the former, God is effective for conversion, so that some are nevertheless regenerated and adhere to the Word with simple faith; even if they are deservedly condemned and rejected for the latter.

Bellarmino denies, from the title of Church attributed to the Galatians, that the sincere preaching of the word is a mark of the Church. But one must distinguish both the degrees of sincerity of doctrine, and the men in the Church, the seducers and the seduced, and those who were still free from seduction, the infants, the simple, and the ears of some learners were purer than the lips of the teachers. Nor were there lacking some at least sincere teachers among the Galatians; because the Apostle admonishes that he who is instructed in the doctrine should share with him who instructs in all good things (Gal. VI. 6), and he prays for peace and mercy for those who walk according to the rule of the word (v. 16).

Latin:

V. 2. Καὶ ὁι σὺν ἐμοὶ πάντες ἀδελφοὶ). Corinthii, ut ego arbitror, fuit apud Galatas Paulus aliquanto ante, quam Co- rinthum veniret, Act. XVI. 6. & XVIII. 1. Videtur autem secundum ad Galatas iter, de quo Act. XVIII. 23. instituis- se post hanc scriptionem.

Quia Romæ scripta epistola, fratres potius Ro- mani indigitari videntur. Consensum ergo fratrum vel Ecclesiæ integræ innuit, cui sine dubio præle- cta epistola fuit, utpote ejusdem nomine simul Ga- latia Ecclesiis inscribenda. Criminabantur Pseu- do-Apostoli, Paulum ab omnibus in diversum abire. Hos refellit hæc subscriptio. Intelligere poterant

Galatæ consensum fidelium, inter quos sine dubio multi è circumcisione fuere, & non contemptui habiti à Galatis, qui multum valet ad rudem ple- bem corrigendam, notante Hieronymo, ut & com- munem dolorem, quem illis afferret turbatus Ga- laticarum Ecclesiarum status.

Ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Γαλατίας) Ancyranis, Tavianis, Pessinuntiis: non addit hic titulum sanctis, quia cœperant ab Evangelio declinare.

Galatia regio est Asiæ, ab Oriente Cappadociam & Halym fluvium, ab Occidente Bithyniam, à Me- ridie Pamphyliam, ab Aquilone Pontum Euxinum respiciens, quam olim Galli ex Europa in Asiam profecti inhabitarunt, unde Gallo-Græcia & Græ- co-Gallia, post Galatia nuncupata est. Paphla- goniæ nomen mansit in aliqua parte Galatiæ, quia primum Galatiani tenuere Phryges & Paphlagones. Urbes potiores nominantur Synope, Pompejopo- lis, Claudiopolis, Laodicea, Antiochia, Nicopolis, Ancyra, quæ metropolis. Vid. Plinius secundus libr. V. c. 32. & Cluverus in introduct. ad Geogr. Quod nudè nominarit Ecclesias Galatiæ Aposto- lus, Chrysostomus & Theophylactus accipiunt ceu indignationis, & doloris indicium. Ecclesiæ tamen titulum non negat. Receperant enim Christum, nec prorsus abjecerant: Ecclesiæ erant, etsi multi in iisdem seducti fuerint à Pseudo-Apostolis. Ideo frustra Novatores Calixtini ex eo, quod Ecclesiæ nomen datum illis sit, quum maximopere in do- ctrina errarint, colligunt, etiam Papistis & Calvi- nianis Ecclesiæ nomen denegandum non esse. Nam in cœtibus Papisticis & Calvinianis Ecclesiam ta- men aliquam Deum adhuc sibi colligere nullum est dubium. Nam & in illis datur, quod Christia- num est, verbum Dei, quod prælegitur, baptismus, qui parvulis dispensatur; datur & quod Anti-Chri- stianum: ceu sunt idolomania, hæreticæ opiniones, superstitiones &c. Per illa est Deus ad conversio- nem efficax, ut nonnulli tamen regenerentur, simplicique fide Verbo adhæreant; etsi hac me- rito damnentur & rejiciantur.

Bellarminus negat, è titulo Ecclesiæ Galatis tri- buto, notam Ecclesiæ esse sinceram verbi prædica- tionem. Sed distinguendi sunt tum gradus sin- ceritatis doctrinæ, tum homines in Ecclesiæ, se- ductores, & seducti, & illi, qui adhuc à seductione liberi erant, infantes, simplices, erantque quorun- dam discentium aures puriores, quam labia do- centium. Neque defuere aliqui saltem sinceri Do- ctores Galatis; quia monet Apostolus, ut qui in- formatur in doctrina, communicet τῷ κατηχῦντι de bonis omnibus Gal. VI. 6. precatur pacē & mise- ricordiam iis, qui incedunt juxta verbi regulam v. 16.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χριστῦ) In the Manuscript καὶ Κυρίυ Ἰησῦ χριστῦ, as in Rom. I. and 1 Cor. I. 3, 2 cap. I. 2.

This prayer was most necessary for them. For they had sinned by receding from the truth of the Gospel, and therefore they were in need of the remission of sins, and also the correction of errors, for which grace was needed, from which not a few had fallen. By the name of peace, not only internal peace of conscience, peace and external concord, but also happiness of every kind is usually denoted. But he prayed especially for peace with God, of which in Rom. V. 1, from whom they had in large part alienated themselves. These two words, says Blessed Luther in his later Commentary, fol. 9, Grace and peace, comprehend the whole of Christianity; grace remits sin, peace renders the conscience tranquil. Our two devils, who torment us, are sin and conscience. But Christ has conquered and trampled these two monsters in this age and the future.

These two words, Grace and Peace, embrace the whole of Christianity; Grace, the remission of sins; peace, a tranquil and joyful conscience. Furthermore, the peace of conscience can never be had unless sin is remitted. It is not, however, remitted on account of the fulfillment of the law, because no one satisfies the law; but the law rather shows sin, accuses and terrifies the conscience, announces the wrath of GOD, and drives one to despair. Much less is sin taken away by works and efforts devised by men, such as impious cults, religions, vows, and pilgrimages. In sum, it is taken away by no works, but is rather increased by them. For the more that those who seek righteousness labor and sweat to take away sin, the worse they fare. It is taken away, however, by grace alone, and simply in no other way. Therefore, Paul in all the salutations of his epistles opposes grace and peace to sin and an evil conscience, etc. This must be considered most diligently. The words are easy, but in temptation it is most difficult to establish firmly in the heart that we have the remission of sins and peace with GOD through grace alone, with all other means that are in heaven and on earth excluded. Jerome also, in his prayer for grace, notes that the Apostle prudently pleads his case against those who were preoccupied with the law, so that they might know that they were saved by grace, and that they ought to persevere in that which they had begun. Theophylact warns that the Apostle calls Christ Lord here, so that they might think that the law is not our Lord, but Jesus Christ, and that therefore one must adhere uniquely to Him. For He is the one Lord not only by right of creation, but primarily also of redemption, by which He acquired us for Himself as a peculiar possession. This is the one Jesus, through whom they can be saved, Acts IV. 12, chapter XV. 10. Christ was anointed by the Father with the immense gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that He might be Prophet, Priest, and King, from whom it is not permitted to depart outside the danger of salvation. When you are occupied, says the blessed Luther in his later Commentary, fol. 10, in the place of justification, and you are disputing about finding GOD, who justifies or accepts sinners, where and how He is to be sought, then know absolutely no God outside of this man Jesus Christ; embrace Him, and cling to Him with your whole heart, omitting speculation about the Majesty. For the searcher of Majesty is overwhelmed by the glory; I know from experience what I say. But fanatical men, who deal with God having excluded the Mediator Christ, do not believe me. Christ Himself says in John XIV, I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. Therefore, besides this way, Christ, you will simply find no other way to the Father, but error; not truth, but hypocrisy and falsehood; not life, but eternal death.

Latin:

Vers. 3. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χριστῦ) In Manuscripto καὶ Κυρίυ Ἰησῦ χριστῦ, ut Rom. I. & 1. Cor. I. 3. 2. cap. I. 2.

Precatio hæc maximè neceffaria ipsis erat. Pec- caverant enim ab Evangelii veritate recedendo, ideoque remissione peccatorum indigebant, nec non errorum emendatione, ad quam opus erat gratiâ, à qua non pauci exciderant. Pacis nomine non tan- tum pax conscientiæ interna, pax & concordia ex- terna, sed etiam omnis generis felicitas denotari so- let. Sed pacem maxime cum Deo precabatur, de qua Rom. V. 1. qui à DEO se magnam partem alie- naverant. Hæc duo vocabula, inquit B. Lutherus Comment. poster. f. 9. Gratia & pax comprehen- dunt universum Christianismum, gratia remittit peccatum, pax tranquillam reddit conscientiam. Duo Diaboli nostri, qui nos excruciant, sunt pec- catum, & conscientia. Sed hæc duo monstra Chri- stus vicit & conculcavit in hoc seculo & futuro.

Complectuntur autem hæ duæ voces Gratia & Pax totum Christianismum; Gratia remissionem pecca- torum, pax tranquillam & lætam conscientiam. Porro pax conscientiæ nunquam haberi potest, nisi peccatum remissum sit. Non remittitur autem pro- pter impletionem legis, quia nemo legi satisfacit; sed lex potius ostendit peccatum, accusat & perter- refacit conscientiam, iram DEI annunciat, & in desperationem adigit. Multo minus tollitur pecca- tum operibus & studiis ab hominibus excogitatis, ut sunt impii cultus, religiones, vota, peregrinatio- nes. Summa, nullis operibus tollitur, sed iis potius augetur. Quo magis enim justitiarii laborant & sudant ad tollendum peccatum, hoc pejus habent. Tollitur autem sola gratia, & simpliciter nullo alio modo. Ideo Paulus in omnibus salutationibus epi- stolarum suarum opponit peccato & malæ conscien- tiæ gratiam & pacem &c. Hoc diligentissime consi- derandum est. Verba facilia sunt, sed in tentatio- ne difficillimum est, in corde certo statuere, quod per solam gratiam exclusis omnibus mediis aliis, quæ sunt in cœlo & in terra, habeamus remissio- nem peccatorum & pacem cum DEO. Hierony- mus etiam precatione gratiæ notat, prudenter cau- sam agere Apostolum adversum eos, qui erant lege præventi, ut scirent, se salvos esse gratia, in eo per- severare debere, quod cœperant. Theophylactus mo- net Apostolum Christum hic Dominum vocare, ut cogitent, non legem esse Dominum nostrum, sed Jesum Christum, adeoque huic unicè adhæren- dum esse. Hic enim unus Dominus est non tan- tum jure creationis, sed imprimis etiam redem- ptionis, qua nos sibi acquisivit in peculium. Hic unus est Jesus, per quem possint salvari Act. IV. 12. cap. XV. 10. Christus unctus est à Patre donis Spiritus Sancti immensis, ut sit Propheta, Sacer- dos & Rex, à quo extra salutis periculum recede- re non liceat. Cum versaris, inquit B. Lutherus Comm. poster. f. 10. in loco justificationis, & dis- putas de DEO inveniendo, qui justificat seu acce- ptat peccatores, ubi & quomodo is quærendus sit, tum prorsus nullum Deum scito, extra istum homi- nem Jesum Christum, hunc complectere, & toto corde in eo hære, omissa speculatione Majestatis. Scrutator enim Majestatis opprimitur à gloria; Ego expertus scio quid dico. Sed phanatici homi- nes, qui excluso Mediatore Christo cum Deo agunt, mihi non credunt. Christus ipse dicit Joh. XIV. Ego sum via, veritas & vita, nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Præter hanc igitur viam Christum simpli- citer nullam invenies aliam viam ad Patrem, sed errorem; non veritatem, sed hypocrisin & menda- cium; non vitam, sed æternam mortem.

## 1:4
Verse 4. Tῦ δόντος ἑαυτὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, ὅπως ἐξέληται ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῦ ἐνεστῶτος αἰῶνος πονηρῦ) He gave, understand, unto death, as in Rom. IV. 25, VIII. 32, Ephes. V. 2, Tit. II. 14. The death of Christ has many effects: this among others, that by the example of admirable obedience, He might draw us away from sins, 1 Pet. I. 18. Αἰὼν here, as γενεὰ in Acts II. 40, xόσμος in 1 John I. 11, 17, V. 19. It seems, however, to touch most upon the Jews, who were expecting the kingdom of this world. Ἐξίληται יצילנו Isaiah XLII. 22. Other books have here, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, just as Justin says baptism is given ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀνομίας τῶν λαῶν, in his dialogue with Trypho.

There is nothing here about an example of obedience by which we are to be drawn away from sins, nor did Christ by His death rescue us by drawing us away by His example from sins, which is the Socinian gloss, but He gave Himself for our sins, and was delivered for our sins, Romans IV. last, He delivered Himself in our place, 1 Tim. II. 6, Tit. II. 14, Ephes. V. 16, and by that reason He freed us from the punishment of sins, because He Himself sustained the punishment of sins in our place, 2 Cor. 5:21. Isa. 53:4 ff. that he might deliver us from the present evil age, or from the world, which is wholly placed in wickedness, and is concluded under sin, and is subject to God 1 John 5:19. Rom. 3. that we might not perish with the world. Which is done through justification and sanctification. For the end of Christ's satisfaction for our sins is our justification and sanctification, that we, who together with the world were lying in evil, might be delivered from the malice of the world, and the power of the Prince of the world, from whom all that malice is, delivered from that most desperate life of men and most miserable condition. For these are the things of the present evil age. The matter comes to the same thing, whether we are said to be delivered from the age or evil world, or from the malice of the age or world. The world or the age has nothing evil in itself and by itself, as the Manichaeans raved, but evil was introduced by the Devil and through his seduction by man; and therefore the age is evil accidentally on account of the evil actions of the Devil and of men living in the age: For there is nothing, says Theophylact, in these days by their own nature of malignity. For what wickedness can be present in that solar course or in these intervals of days? Furthermore, neither does this life of ours, and the air which we breathe, contain in itself any depravity, in which we both have knowledge of God and philosophize about future things. But the evil age calls those actions depraved, and the corrupted appetites of the mind, just as we are accustomed to use a saying of this kind: I have had an evil day, blaming not the time itself, but the crisis, and the things that have happened, the adversities. Blessed Luther has it thus in his former Commentary: Blessed Jerome explains the trope of this locution beautifully and at length, saying: Just as forests are defamed when they are full of robberies. We detest also the sword, by which human blood has been shed, and the cup, by which poison has been mixed, not for the sin of the sword and the cup, but because those who have used them badly deserve hatred. Thus the age, which is a space of times, is not good or evil by itself, but is called either good or evil by those who are in it. The same St. Augustine understands the evil age as evil men in the age. Yet receive all these things in such a way that you also acknowledge yourself to be a part of this evil. For every man is a liar and there is no one righteous on the earth Ps. 13. lest you be too much exalted in pride above others. Therefore when Christ delivers you from the age, he certainly delivers you from yourself, as the worst enemy of all to you. As Paul says in Rom. 7, there does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh, any good. Therefore you will not overcome the evil age and your vices by your own strengths; efforts are in vain unless Christ alone delivers you. Wherefore beware, lest fasts, vigils, studies, temperance, sobriety, and other virtues make you an irredeemable hypocrite.

Thus therefore in the very vow, while he says that Christ gave himself for our sins, he teaches where we ought to seek our salvation, not in our works or legal ceremonies, but in the passion and death of Christ, who gave himself for our sins. Which Theophylact likewise observed with Chrysostom: He gave himself, that he might free us from sins, from which the law could not free us. How therefore, having dismissed your deliverer, do you attend to your law, which will profit you nothing?

The word ἐξαίρειν is to pluck out, just as an eye is plucked out on account of a stumbling block Matt. 5:29, ch. 18:9. To deliver, just as Joseph was delivered from calamity, the Israelites from tribulation in Egypt Acts 7:10, 34. Peter from the hand of Herod Acts 12:11. Paul from the snares of the Jews ch. 23:27 and ch. 26:12. Hence it is applied to deliverance from the wickedness of the age or world. Cf. 1 Pet. 1:18.

The end or effect of Christ's death is not exemplary, but rather it would have to be ascribed to the life and obedience of Christ. For we neither can nor ought to imitate the death of Christ, which was a ransom and a counter-ransom for men Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45, 1 Tim. 2:6, and not indeed a testimony only: But we ought to imitate the life of Christ Matt. 11. Nor does the Jewish opinion about the worldly kingdom of the Messiah contribute anything to this. For Christ did not deliver us from this world, as far as its wealth, honors, and power are concerned, such as the Jews dreamed of in the worldly kingdom of Christ, but as far as the malice and wickedness of the same. Not even the Socinians themselves, Crellius and Schlichtingius, interpret this periphrasis of Christ so coldly, although they cannot conceal their heresy. For our sins, they say, it is said that Christ died, because he died for this reason, that he might take away the guilt and punishments of our sins, or procure for us their remission out of divine kindness. And furthermore: He notes the final cause of this benefit of Christ, which is, not that it may be permitted for us to sin with impunity, which perhaps the false teachers, who urged the power of the law, were accustomed to object to the doctrine of Paul: but that, having obtained the right of remission of all sins, we may live holily and blamelessly hereafter. Which would be correct, if they understood the remission obtained through the death of Christ in the sense of the Catholic Church, and analogous to scripture itself. But they do not understand it so: For thus they explain: He died, so that he might establish and sanction his doctrine, and what is contained in it, the new covenant, which promises to us the remission of sins, and thus might procure for us a certain right to obtain the remission of sins. But what is this other than that the death of Christ was merely a confirmation of doctrine, as the death of martyrs is, or a μαρτύριον; but not indeed an ἀντίλυτρον. They do indeed add: Add also, that he might obtain the power of pardoning all our sins, and of actually averting their punishments from us. But in this way he would have acquired something by his death not so much for us, as for himself. And yet Christ always had the power of pardoning sins as God, he had also received it as man, and had exercised it before his death, nor was it necessary for him to die for us in order to acquire it for himself, except insofar as it was necessary to satisfy divine justice for our sins, so that, with that preserved, God could pardon our sins for us. Since it required that men should be subjected to death on account of sin. But God, having had mercy on us, delivered his Son to death for us to expiate our sins, so that he might pardon us their punishment, which the Son deigned to undergo for us as the Mediator of God and men, who gave himself as an ἀντίλυτρον for all 1 Tim. II. 6.

Furthermore, blessed Luther warned particularly about the pronoun ἡμῶν in his first commentary: Do not pass over the pronoun 'our' with contempt. For it will profit you nothing to believe that Christ was delivered for the sins of other saints, but to doubt for your own. For both the wicked and the demons believe this. But you must presume with constant confidence that he was delivered for yours also, so that you may be one of those for whose sins he himself was delivered. This faith justifies you, and will make Christ dwell, live, and reign in you. This is the testimony of the Spirit, which he renders to our spirit, by which we are children of God. Wherefore you may easily perceive, if you pay attention, that this affection is not in you from your own powers. It must therefore be obtained through a humble spirit, and one that is desperate in itself. Therefore, the tales of the scholastic speculators, that a man is uncertain whether he is in a state of salvation or not, are fables. Beware, you, that you are never uncertain, but certain, because you are lost in yourself, but you must labor so that you may be certain and solid in the faith of Christ delivered for your sins. How can it be that you do not feel this faith, if it is in you, when the Blessed Augustine asserts that it is seen most certainly by him who has it? Now see, Paul does not say, for your sins, but he does not say you. By which thunderbolt of the Word he again crushes the presumption of free will, of the law, and of our works of righteousness. Not (he says) do these things deliver us, but Christ delivered, if only you believe that you are delivered.

According to the will of God and our Father) He shows incidentally that Christ did not only die willingly, but by the decree of the Father, namely to sanction a new covenant, different from the legal one. Exordia are praised which prepare the hearer for that which is to be performed: And here he joins different attributes, as in Eph. 1:3, 1 Thess. 1:3, 1 Pet. 1:3.

Not incidentally, but by design does the Apostle add this, which the Greek Interpreters have rightly observed. Theophylact: When they, he says, thought that by omitting the law they would by no means obey GOD, he soon corrects their presumed opinion, demonstrating that it pleased GOD that we should be liberated through the Son. But when he also calls God our Father, he again remembers Christ, who confers benefits upon us, who made Him his Father and ours. Why therefore do you fall away from Him, who shows himself so very liberal toward us? Cf. Job 10:14, Ps. 40:3-4, Heb. 10:7, Luke 22:42. Blessed Luther in his former Commentary: According to his will, this is, that we are delivered, is not of the power of our running, but of the merciful will of GOD. Just as he does in Ps. 51: Do good, O Lord, in your good will to Zion. And Luke 2: And on earth peace to men of good will, not their own, but GOD'S. As in the Greek εὐδοκία. For just as men of mercy are so called, because they are taken up not by their own merit, but by the mercy of GOD: So men of good will, because they are saved not by their own strengths, but by the good pleasure of the divine will, so that glory may stand to GOD alone for ever and ever Amen, as the Apostle said here. Where you have recognized this to be, he says in the later Commentary, the will of GOD through Christ, the whole face of wrath ceases, fear, trembling, etc., cease. Nor does any other God appear, except the merciful one, who by a definite counsel willed his Son to die for us, that we might live through him. That knowledge exhilarates the heart, so that it may certainly conclude that God is not angry, but so loves us miserable sinners that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. Not in vain, therefore, does Paul inculcate that Christ was delivered for our sins, by the will of the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Tῦ δόντος ἑαυτὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, ὅπως ἐξέληται ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῦ ἐνεστῶτος αἰῶνος πονηρῦ) Dedit, sub- audi, in mortem, ut Rom. IV. 25. VIII. 32. Ephes. V. 2. Tit. II. 14. Mors Christi multos habet effectus: hunc inter alios, ut admirabilis obedientiæ exemplo, à pecca- tis abstrahat, 1. Petr. I. 18. Αἰὼν hic, quod γενεὰ Act. II. 40. xόσμος 1. Joh. I. 11. 17. V. 19. Videtur autem maxime Ju- dæos tangere, qui regnum hujus mundi expectabant. Ἐξί- ληται יצילנו Efa. XLII. 22. alii libri hic habent, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, quomodo baptismum dari ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀνομίας τῶν λαῶν, dicit Justinus, colloquio cum Tryphone.

Nihil hic de exemplo obedientiæ, quo abstrahen- di simus à peccatis, nec Christus per mortem eri- puit nos exemplo suo abstrahendo à peccatis, quæ glossa Sociniana est, sed semetipsum dedit pro pec- catis nostris, & propter peccata nostra traditus Romanor. IV. ult. tradidit seipsum nostri loco 1. Timoth. II. 6. Tit. II. 14. Ephes. V. 16. nos- que eâ ratione à peccatorum pœna liberavit, quia ipse nostri loco peccatorum pœnam sustinuit, 2. Cor. V. 21. Esa. LIII. 4. seqq. ut eriperet nos de præsenti seculo malo, vel è mundo, qui totus in maligno positus, & sub peccato conclusus, Deo que obnoxius est 1. Joh. V. 19. Rom. III. ne cum mundo periremus. Quod fit per justificationem, & sanctificationem. Finis enim satisfactionis Chri- sti pro peccatis nostris est justificatio & sanctifi- catio nostra, ut nos, qui una cum mundo in malo jacebamus, è malitia mundi, & potestate Princi- pis mundi, à quo omnis illa malitia est, eriperemur è desperatissima illa hominum vita & miserrima conditione. Hæc enim sunt τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος αἰῶνος πονηροῦ. Res eodem recidit, sive à seculo vel mun- do malo, sive à malitia seculi vel mundi erepti di- camur. Mundus vel seculum per & in se nihil mali habet, ut Manichæi delirabant, sed à Dia- bolo & per ejus seductionem ab homine inve- ctum est malum; ideoque malum est seculum per accidens ob Diaboli, & hominum in seculo viventium actiones malas: Non enim aliquid in- est, inquit Theophylactus, diebus hisce suapte natu- ra malignitatis. Nam quid potest solari illi decur- sui vel dierum his intervallis interesse nequitiæ? Quin etiam neque vita hæc nostra, & aura, quam spiramus, aliquid in se continet pravitatis, in qua & DEI habemus cognitionem, & de futuris philo- sophamur. Sed nequam seculum pravas illas actio- nes appellat, & corruptos animi appetitus, quemad- modum usurpare istiusmodi dictum solemus: Ma- lum nactus sum diem, non tempus ipsum, sed discri- men, &, quæ obtigere, adversa culpantes. B. Luthe- rus ita habet priori Commentario: Tropum bu- jus loquutionis B. Hieronymus pulchre & late ex- plicat, dicens: Sicut infamantur saltus, cum latro- ciniis pleni sunt. Detestamur & gladium, quo hu- manus effusus est cruor, & calicem, quo venenum temperatum est, non gladii calicisque peccato, sed quod odium mereantur illi, qui iis male usi sunt. Ita seculum, quod est spatium temporum, non per semetipsum bonum aut malum est, sed per eos, qui in ipso sunt, aut bonum aut malum appellatur. Idem S. Augustinus malum seculum intelligit ma- los homines in seculo. Hæc tamen omnia sic accipe, ut & te partem hujus mali agnoscas. Nam omnis homo mendax & non est justus in terra Psal. XIII. ne superbia super cæteros nimium eleveris. Ideo quando Christus te eripit à seculo, certe à teipso, ut omnium tibi pessimo hoste te eripit. Sicut Paulus Rom. VII. non habitat in me, hoc est, in carne mea bonum. Igitur non tuis viribus seculum nequam & vitia tua vinces, frustra sunt opera, nisi Christus te eripiat solus. Quare cave, ne jejunia, vigiliæ, studia, temperantia, sobrietas, aliaque virtutes te hy- pocritam irreparabilem faciant.

Ita ergo in ipso voto dum dicit Christum se- ipsum tradidisse pro peccatis nostris, docet, ubi quærere debeamus salutem nostram non in ope- ribus nostris vel ceremoniis legalibus, sed in pas- sione & morte Christi, qui sese pro peccatis no- stris tradidit. Quod observavit itidem cum Chry- sostomo Theophylactus: Dedit seipsum, ut liberet nos à peccatis, à quibus lex liberare non potuit. Quo- modo ergo, liberatore vestro dimisso legi vestræ at- tenditis, quæ nihil vobis profuerit?

Verbum ἐξαίρειν est eruere, uti oculus eruitur ob scandalum Matth. V. 29. cap. XIIX. 9. Eripere, uti Josephus è calamitate, Israelitæ è tribulatione in Ægypto erepti sunt Act. VII. 10. 34. Petrus è ma- nu Herodis Act. XII. 11. Paulus è Judæorum insi- diis cap. XXIII. 27. & cap. XXVI. 12. Hinc ereptio- ni è seculi vel mundi nequitia accommodatur. Conf. 1. Petr. I. 18.

Non mortis Christi finis aut effectus exempla- ris est, sed potius vitæ & obedientiæ Christi oc adscribendum foret. Non enim mortem Chri- sti imitari vel possumus vel debemus, quæ fuit λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον pro hominibus Matth. XX. 28. Marci X. 45. 1. Tim. II. 6. non verò μαρτύ- ριον tantum: Sed imitari debemus vitam Christi Matth. XI. Neque huc facit quicquam opinio Judaica de regno Messiæ mundano. Non enim eripuit nos Christus de hoc mundo, quantum ad ejus opulentiam, honores & potestatem, qua- lia somniabant Judæi in mundano Christi regno, sed quantum ad malitiam & nequitiam ejusdem. Ne Sociniani quidem ipsi, Crellius & Schlichtin- gius adeo frigide hanc Christi περίφρασιν inter- pretantur, tametsi hæresin suam dissimulare ne- queant. Pro peccatis nostris, inquiunt, dicitur Christus mortuus, quia ideo mortuus est, ut pecca- torum nostrorum reatum & pœnas tolleret, seu eo- rum remissionem nobis ex divina benignitate pa- raret. Et porro: Finalem causam istius beneficii Christi notat, quæ est, non ut nobis impune peccare liceat, quod fortassis falsi Doctores, qui opem legis urgebant, objicere doctrinæ Pauli folebant: sed ut jus remissionis omnium peccatorum adepti, sanctè & inculpatè imposterum vivamus. Quæ recte se haberent, si partam remissionem per mortem Christi sensu Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, & ipsi scripturæ analogo intelligerent. At non intelligunt ita: Sic enim explicant: Mortuus est, ut doctrinam suam, & quod in ea continetur, fœdus novum, quod re- missionem peccatorum nobis pollicetur, stabiliret ac sanciret, & sic jus quoddam ad remissionem peccatorum obtinendam nobis compararet. Quid vero hoc aliud est, quam quod mors Christi con- firmatio modò fuerit doctrinæ, uti martyrum mors est seu μαρτύριον; non verò ἀντίλυτρον. Addunt quidem: Adde etiam, ut potestatem omnia nobis peccata condonandi, eorumque pœnas reipsa à no- bis avertendi, adipisceretur. Sed ita non tàm no- bis, quàm sibi aliquid morte sua acquisivisset. At- qui potestatem peccata condonandi semper ha- buit Christus ut Deus, acceperat etiam ut homo, & usurparat ante mortem, nec ut eam sibi acqui- reret, pro nobis mori necessum habuit, nisi qua- tenus justitiæ divinæ satisfaciendum erat pro pec- catis nostris, ut eâdem salvâ Deus nobis pecca- ta condonare posset. Quum ea requireret, ut ho- mines ob peccatum morti subjicerentur. Deus vero nostri misertus Filium suum pro nobis in mortem tradiderit pro peccatis nostris expiandis, ut eorum pœnam nobis condonaret, quam Filius pro nobis subire dignatus est ceu Mediator DEI & hominum, qui semetipsum tradidit ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus 1. Tim. II. 6.

Porro de Pronomine ἡμῶν peculiariter monuit B. Lutherus Comm. priori: Verum pronomen no- stris ne contemptum prætereas. Nihil enim tibi pro- fuerit credere, Christum esse pro peccatis Sancto- rum aliorum traditum, pro tuis autem dubitare. Nam hoc & impii & Dæmones credunt. Verum constanti fiducia præsumendum est tibi, quod & pro tuis, ut unus sis illorum, pro quorum pecca- tis ipse traditus est. Hæc fides te justificat, Chri- stum in te habitare, vivere & regnare faciet. Hæc est testimonium Spiritus, quod reddit spiritui no- stro, quo simus filii DEI. Quare facile sentias, si advertas, hunc affectum ex tuis viribus in te non esse. Impetrandus ergo per humilem, & in seipso desperatum spiritum. Fabulæ ergo sunt opinatorum scholasticorum, hominem esse incertum in statu sa- lutis nec ne. Cave tu, ne aliquando sis incertus, sed certus, quod in teipso perditus, laborandum autem, ut certus & solidus sis in fide Christi pro peccatis tuis traditi. Quomodo potest fieri, ut hanc fidem, si sit in te, non sentias, cum B. Augustinus asserat, eam videri certissime ab eo qui habet? Nunc vide, Paulus non ait, pro peccatis vestris, sed nostris, certus enim erat. Ita & illud: Eriperet nos, non ait vos. Quo iterum fulmine Verbi contundit præ- sumptionem arbitrii, legis, & operum justitiæ no- stræ. Non (inquit) ista eripiunt nos, sed Christus traditus, si modo credas te eripi.

Κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν) Ostendit obiter, Christum non tantum volentem esse mortuum, sed ex decreto Patris, nempe ad sanciendum fœdus no- vum, diversum à legali. Laudantur exordia, quæ audito- rem ad id, quod præstandum est, præparant: Καὶ hic di- versa attributa conjungit, ut Ephes. I. 3. 1. Thessal. I. 3. 1. Petr. I. 3.

Non hoc obiter, sed ex instituto addit Aposto- lus, quod probe observarunt Græci Interpretes. Theophylactus: Cum illi, inquit, existimarent lege omissa, se nequaquam DEO obtemperaturos, eo- rum mox corrigit præsumptam opinionem, demon- strans DEO libitum esse, ut per Filium liberemur. Cum autem & Patrem nostrum Deum appellat, rursum beneficia in nos conferentis commeminit Christi, qui Patrem suum & nostrum effecerit. Cur ergo ab eo deficitis, qui sese erga nos tantopere liberalem exhibeat? Conf. Job. X. 14. Ps. XL. 3. 4. Ebr. X. 7. Luc. XXII. 42. B. Lutherus in priori Comment. Secundum suam voluntatem, hoc est, quod nos eripimur, non currentis est virtutis no- stræ, sed miserentis voluntatis DEI. Sicut facit Pfal. LI. Benigne fac Domine in bona voluntate tua Sion. Et Lucæ II. Et in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis, non suæ, sed DEI. Ut in Græco εὐδοκία. Sicut enim viri misericordiæ dicuntur, quod non suo merito, sed DEI misericordia susci- piuntur: Ita homines bonæ voluntatis, quod non suis viribus, sed divinæ voluntatis beneplacito salventur, ut stet gloria soli DEO in secula seculorum Amen, ut hic Apostolus dixit. Ubi hanc esse, inquit poster. Comm. voluntatem DEI agnoveris per Christum, cessat universa facies iræ, cessat pavor, tremor &c. Nec apparet alius Deus, nisi misericors, qui definito consilio voluit mori Filium suum pro nobis, ut per ipsum viveremus.
