Ea cognitio exhilarat cor, ut certo statuat, Deum non irasci, sed ita diligere nos miseros peccatores, ut daret unigenitum Filium pro nobis. Non frustra igitur inculcat Paulus, Chri- stum traditum esse pro peccatis nostris, voluntate Patris.

## 1:5
V. 5. To whom be glory for ever and ever) See Rom. 16:25, Deut. 32:5.

The Galatians did not seem to glorify God: to celebrate the glory of divine grace, righteousness, and truth, because they were seeking salvation not in the redemption of Christ, in which it shone forth (Tit. 2:11), but in their own works and the ceremonies of the law. Which John opposes: The law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Christ (John 1:17). Therefore, by his own doxology, the Apostle recalls them to duly glorifying God with the Angels (Luke 2:14), Zechariah (Luke 1:68), and the whole choir of the church militant and triumphant (Rev. 5:9, 12). To this pertain those words of Blessed Luther's later Commentary: I remember, he says, at the beginning of my cause, D. Staupitz, then a supreme man and Vicar of the Augustinian order, saying to me: This pleases me, he says, that this doctrine which you preach attributes glory and all things to GOD alone, and nothing to men. But to GOD (which is clearer than light) too much glory, goodness, etc., cannot be attributed. That voice vehemently consoled and confirmed me then.

And it is true that the doctrine of the Gospel takes away from men all glory, wisdom, righteousness, etc., and attributes these to the Creator alone, who makes all things out of nothing. But it is much safer to attribute too much to GOD than to men.

PART II. Reprehension on account of the turning away from the Gospel.

Latin:

V. 5. ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) Vide Roman. XVI. 25. Deut. XXXII. 5.

Galatæ non videbantur glorificare Deum: ce- lebrare gloriam divinæ gratiæ, justitiæ, & verita- tis, quia non in redemptione Christi, in qua ea il- luxit Tit. II. 11. sed in operibus propriis, & ceremo- niis legis quærebant salutem. Quæ opponit Johan- nes: Lex per Mosen data, gratia & veritas per Christum facta Joh. I. 17. Sua ergo δοξολογία re- vocat eosdem Apostolus ad Deum rite glorifi- candum cum Angelis Luc. II. 14. Zacharia, Luc. I. 68. toto Ecclesiæ militantis & triumphantis choro Apoc. V. 9. 12. Huc pertinent illa B. Lutheri Com- ment. poster. Memini, inquit, initio meæ causæ D. Staupitium, tunc summum Virum, & Vicarium ordinis Augustiniani, ad me dicere: Hoc mihi, in- quit, placet, quod hæc doctrina, quam predicas, glo- riam, & omnia soli DEO tribuit, hominibus nihil. DEO autem (id quod luce clarius est) nimium gloriæ, bonitatis &c. attribui non potest. Ea vox vehementer me tunc consolabatur, & confirmabat.

Et verum est, doctrinam Evangelii adimere homi- nibus omnem gloriam, sapientiam, justitiam &c. & ista tribuere soli Creatori, qui ex nihilo omnia facit. Multo autem tutius est, tribuere nimium DEO, quam hominibus.

PARS II. Reprehensio ob aversationem ab Evangelio.

## 1:6
V. 6. I marvel that you are so soon removed from him that called you in the grace of Christ unto another Gospel) Removed, that is, you allow yourselves to be transferred by those new Doctors. In Hebrew גֹלִים, which Jerome says alludes to the name of the Galatians. Caesar says that the Gauls, from whom the Galatians originated, were mobile in making decisions and generally studied new things. Called is rightly joined with the word Christ. To call us, that is, to invite those thinking nothing of salvation, God the Father is very often said to do. But because he does this through Christ, Christ is also rightly said to do this. In grace, that is, kindly, very lovingly. For the Hebrews say this as בְּחֵן, but when he says Christ, he understands his doctrine. And he calls it another Gospel by a figure of similarity, that is, a new doctrine, as if it were a Gospel. Thus Satan is the god of this world, because he is worshipped as if he were God.

Vehement, according to Blessed Luther in his former Commentary, is the sentiment of Paul, and yet most modest. He says he is amazed, while he shows himself to be indignant and burning within, namely, invading sweetly, not according to the impulse conceived. Certainly a good example for all Ecclesiastical rulers, especially those prompt to hurl thunderbolts, even for a thing of nothing. He says they do not err, they do not sin, but [are] worse in evil, having been entirely transferred outside the Gospel, alienated from GOD. For it is milder if a tree remains, with some branches broken or harmed by some other inconvenience, than if it is entirely transferred, uprooted from its place to a place where it must necessarily wither and become sterile. So terrible is it to seek one's own righteousness and to trust in the law and the judgment of works. For this is to deny Christ, to cast away grace and faith, and, as he will teach below, to set oneself up as an idol. Concerning which Job XXXI. If I have kissed my hand with my mouth, which is the greatest iniquity and a denial against the most high God. For to kiss the hand with one's own mouth (as the Holy Fathers understand) is to praise one's own works, to trust in one's own righteousness. And yet by this iniquity it happens that we do not glory in GOD, but in ourselves, and we withdraw glory from GOD. And Isaiah II: They worshipped the work of their own hands, which their fingers made. Against this, in Psalm II it is said, kiss the Son, as it is in Hebrew, for 'lay hold of instruction,' that is, believe in Christ with pure faith and worship Him. For faith is owed to truth, which is nothing unless it is God alone. Therefore faith is the truest and most interior worship. Hence we understand that which is asserted from Blessed Augustine: a twofold evil, against faith and against good morals. The evil of faith in the best of morals makes heretics, proud men, schismatics, whom Scripture properly calls impious. Bad morals make sinners while faith is saved, at least that of others, that is, they do not attack the faith, even if they know they do not have it and ought to, therefore they are easily curable. But the evil of faith immediately also accuses and persecutes the faith of others so that it may establish its own. Saint Jerome notes this word 'to convert' [transferre], because from the Greek μεταστρέψαι it signifies that which is in front to be put behind the back, and that which is behind the back to be put in front. For it is a future infinitive. Therefore Paul means that the Gospel, which is the doctrine of Spirit and grace, they are attempting to have recalled backwards into the letter long since left behind the back, when through the Gospel it had been brought about that one should progress more and more into the Spirit of liberty. Therefore, in these words the proposition of the epistle is contained, insinuated under the figure of amazement. Because he wishes to rebuke and convince the Galatians that they have been transferred from Him who had called them into the grace of Christ, to another Gospel, about to assert then his authority

his own, by whose ministry they were called, then the truth of the Evangelical doctrine, from which they had suffered themselves to be transferred. Is the doctrine of Christ denoted here by Christ?

That the doctrine of Christ himself is understood by Christ, is unusual, nor does it suit this place. For if Christ is said to have called here, which Grotius wishes, Christ is not the doctrine here. They were called by Christ to the Gospel or the doctrine of Christ. But what would this be, to be called from the doctrine of Christ to the doctrine or Gospel of Christ? Crellius and Schlichtingius interpret the word χάριτι by the Ablative, which was also done by the Syrian and Erasmus, and by Christ here they likewise understand the doctrine or Gospel of Christ: Jerome assigns a hyperbaton, ordering the words thus: I marvel that you are so soon transferred from Christ Jesus, who called you into grace. But what need is there for this? Why should not the words be retained as they lie? From him who called you ἐν χάριτι χριστοῦ; or if ἐν be rendered by 'as' 1 Cor. 12:3, 9, 13, since they were called altogether by the grace of Christ, or also by 'for them' as 1 Cor. 7:15, 1 Thess. 1:18, Heb. 4:11, just as Tertullian in his prescription against heretics reads, and the Vulgate has: to the grace of Christ.

For thus it is taught that they are drawn away from GOD the Father, whose glory they believed themselves to be defending by a conference to the law, having abandoned or joined the Gospel, being taught. And when GOD called them into the grace of Christ, that is, into the justification and salvation partly by his merit: The translation is opposed to the permanence in the same station, or place: That is, that they may remain in the faith and grace of GOD. (B. Luther noting, the word 'transferred' is aptly adapted to the Galatians, because 'Galata' signifies 'transfer' in the Hebrew translation, as if the Apostle had taken the occasion of this opening from their own name, as if he were saying: You are true Galatians and ready to be transferred, the matter agrees with your name; by a Hebrew allusion of language.

Most others refer it to the Gospel. The Apostles boasted more perfectly. But another Gospel (Marcion and angelium from hence is it proved?) from which the Apostle denies that a different one is given. Marcion concluded from thence that there was only one Gospel, namely Luke's, which alone he received; but it is one thing that many have consigned the Gospel of Luke, another that there are many, as to the matter, Gospels. That you may be one: says Chrysostom, the Gospel is one, it is not affirmed by the number of those writing, but from hence, whether they are the same, or different in what they write? (Εἰ μή τινές εἰσιν οἱ ταράσσοντες ὑμας) Unless that there are some who have disturbed your minds, (βασι, who cast scruples upon you. Καὶ θέλοντες μεταστρέψαι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ χριστοῦ) He changes the reward, who admits something foreign, the Doctors of the doctrine of Christ were mixing the necessity of the Jewish law, which Christ had not willed to be imposed upon them, especially those who were called from the Gentiles, and he had hinted at this while living a mortal life, rather than said it: But the Apostle had explained it more openly, after the resurrection, both by himself, and by the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

V. 6. Θαυμάζω, ὅτι ὅτω ταχέως μετατίθεσθε ἀπὸ τῶ κα- λέσαντ@ ὑμᾶς, ἐν χάριτι χρισῦ, εἰς ἕτερον Εὐαγγέλιον) Με- τατίθεσθε, id est, sinitis vos transferri, per novos illos Doctores. Hebraice גֹלִים quod ad nomen Galatarum alludere ait Hieronymus. Cæsar Gallos, unde orti Galatæ, ait in consiliis capiendis fuisse mobiles, & novis plerumque rebus studuisse. Καλίσαντ@ recte conjungitur cum voce χρισῦ. Vocare nos, id est, nihil cogitantes ad salutem in- vitare, Deus Pater sæpissime dicitur. Sed quia id facit per Christum, recte & Christus hoc facere dicitur. Ἐν χάριτι, id est, benigne, amanter admodum. Id enim Hebræi di- cunt בְּחֵן, Christum autem cum dicit, ipsius doctrinam intelligit. Et alterum Evangelium dicit figura à simili, id est, novam doctrinam, quasi esset Evangelium. Sic Sata- nas Deus hujus seculi, quia quasi Deus colitur.

Vehemens, secundum B. Lutherum in priori Comm. est sententia Pauli & tamen modestissima. Mirari se dicit, cum indignari, & ardere penitus sese infra ostendat, scilicet suaviter non pro impetu concepto invadens. Utique bono exemplo omnibus rectoribus Ecclesiasticis præsertim in fulmina prom- ptis, etiam pro re nihili. Non errare, non peccare eos dicit, sed pejore malo, prorsus translatos extra Evangelium, alienatos à DEO esse. Nam mitius est, si arbor maneat, fractis aliquot ramis aut alio incommodo læsa, quam si penitus transferatur evul- sa de loco suo in locum, ubi necesse sit eam arescere, & sterilescere. Adeo terribile est, justitiam suam quærere, & in legis ac arbitrii operis fidere. Nam hoc est Christum abnegare, gratiam & fidem abji- cere, & ut infra docebit, seipsum in idolum statuere. De quo Job. XXXI. si osculatus sum manum meam ore meo, quæ iniquitas maxima & negatio con- tra Deum altissimum. Osculari enim manum ore proprio (ut S. Patres sapiunt) est sua opera laudare, in sua justitia fidere. Atqui hac iniquitate fit, ut non in DEO gloriemur, sed in nobis ipsis, & glo- riam DEO subtrahamus. Et Es. II. Opus manuum suarum adoraverunt, quod fecerunt digiti eorum. Contra Ps. II. dicitur, osculamini Filium, ut est Ebrai- ce, pro apprehendite disciplinam, id est, in Christum pura fide credite & hunc colite. Fides enim debetur veritati, quæ nulla est, nisi solus Deus. Ideo fides est verissima & interior latria. Hinc illud intelligimus, quod ex B. Augustino duplex malum asseritur con- tra fidem & contra bonos mores. Malum fidei in optimis moribus facit hæreticos, superbos, schisma- ticos, quos scriptura proprie impios vocat. Mali mo- res peccatores faciunt salva fide, saltem aliorum, hoc est, non impugnant fidem, etsi eam sciunt, se non habere & debere, ideo sunt facile curabiles. Malum autem fidei mox etiam criminatur & persequitur fidem aliorum ut suam statuat. Hoc verbum con- vertere D. Hieronymus notat, quia ex Græco μετα- στρέψαι significat id, quod in facie est, post tergum facere, & quod post tergum est, post faciem ponere. Est enim infinitivus futurus. Vult itaque Paulus Ev- angelium, quod est Spiritus & gratiæ doctrina, co- nantur illi retrorsus in literam jamdiu post tergum relictam, revocatum iri, cum per Evangelium effe- ctum sit, ut in Spiritum libertatis magis ac magis pro- ficeretur. Itaque in his verbis propositio epistolæ con- tinetur, sub admirationis schemate insinuata. Quia redarguere & convincere vult Galatas, quod trans- lati sint ab eo, qui vocarat eos in gratiam Christi, ad aliud Evangelium, asserturus tum autoritatem

cujus ministerio vocati erant, tum veritatem doctrinae Evangelicae, a qua se transferri patierant. An per Christum doctrina hic notetur Christi?

Per Christum doctrina ipsius intelligi, & insolitum est, nec huic loco convenit. Nam si Christus hic vocasse dicitur, quod vult Grotius, Christus hic doctrina non est. Vocati erant Christo ad Evangelium vel doctrinam Christi. Quid vero hoc esset, vocatos à doctrina Christi ad doctrinam vel Evangelium Christi? Crellius & Schlichtingius vocem χάριτι per Ablativum interpretantur, quod etiam à Syro & Erasmo factum, & per Christum hic itidem doctrinam seu Evangelium Christi intelligunt: Hieronymus hyperbaton affignat, ita verba ordinans: Miror, quod ita cito transferimini à Christo Jesu, qui vos vocavit in gratiam. Quid vero hoc opus est? Cur non verba, ut jacent, retineantur? Ab eo, qui vos vocavit ἐν χάριτι χριστοῦ; sive ἐν reddatur per ut 1. Corinth. XII. verf. 3. 9. 13. quum omnino per Christi gratiam vocati sint, sive etiam per eis ut 1. Corinth. VII. verf. 15. 1. Thessal. I. verf. 18. Ebr. IV. verf. 11. quemadmodum Tertullianus de praescript. aduersus haeret. legit, & Vulgata habet: ad gratiam Christi.

Sic enim docetur eos abstrahi à DEO Patre, cujus gloriam se tueri confertione ad legem, relicto vel conjuncto Evangelio, edocti credebant. Et quum vocarit eos DEUS in gratiam Christi, hoc est, merito ejus partim justificationem & salutem: Translatio opponitur permanentiae in eadem statione, vel loco: Ut scilicet permaneant in fide & gratia DEI. (notante B. Lutheri, verbum transferimini congrue ad Galatas aptatum, quod Galata Ebrais translationem significat, quasi Apostolus ex eorum proprio nomine, occasionem hujus exordii sumpserit, ac si diceret: Vera Galata estis & transferri prompti, res congruit cum nomine vestro; allusione scilicet Hebraica lingua.

Alii plerique ad Evangelium referunt. Perfectius jactitabant Apostoli. Sed aliud Evangelium(Marcionis & angelium ab hinc probetur?) à quo diversum dari negat Apostolus. Marcion inde nonnisi unum Evangelium esse, nempe Lucae, quod solum recipiebat, conclusit; sed aliud est, plures, quam unam Lucae Evangelium consignasse, aliud plura, quod ad materiam, Evangelia. Ut unicum sis: inquit Chrysostomus, Evangelium mel unum, non affirmatur numero scribentium, sed hinc, eadem sint, an diversa qua scribuntur? (Εἰ μή τινές εἰσιν οἱ ταράσσοντες ὑμας) Nisi quod sunt quidam, qui animos vestros commoverint, (βασι, qui scrupulos vobis injiciunt. Καὶ θέλοντες μεταστρέψαι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ χριστοῦ) Mutat mercem, qui aliquid admittet extraneum, ushi Doctores doctrinae Christi miscebant legis Judaicae necessitatem, quam Christus noluerat imponi iis, praesertim qui ex gentibus erant vocati, idque vitam quidem mortalem agens innuerat magis, quam dixerat: Aperius autem ex-plicaverat Apostolus, post resurrectionem, tum per se, tum per Spiritum sanctum.

## 1:8
V. 8. Ἀλλὰ κὰν ἦν ἡμεῖς ἢ ἄγγελος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐυαγγελίζηται ὑμῖν, παρ' ὃ ἐυηγγελισάμεθα ὑμῖν, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω) παρ' ὃν. 4:18, 11:34, and 'preach' here is taken for 'to teach' by that figure which we have already observed. What he says about an Angel is indeed spoken hyperbolically, yet not altogether absurdly. For there were once deserters among the Angels in heaven; and not once, but it happened more often that Angels turned from good to evil, the Hebrews think. In the old covenant there is mention of a certain new covenant. But in the covenant of Christ not only is no later one promised, but it is also asserted that no later one will exist, as may be seen Matt. 28:20. 'let him be anathema', that is, let there be no commerce between you and him, no more than with those whom the Synagogue or the Church has utterly cut off. See Rom. 9:3, 1 Cor. 12:3, 16:22. Propositio παρὰ is not only 'against' but also παρὰ (beyond.

Grotius with the Papists assumes the former meaning, lest traditions invented beyond scripture be struck by anathema, provided it contains nothing against scripture. But the latter is the more common signification Rom. 11:15, 1 Cor. 3:11, which the Vulgate also retained. Nor otherwise Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, who say, if he says that if they preach contrary things, but even if they preach a little something beyond what we have preached. What is said about an Angel (and it is a hyperbole) is undoubtedly to be understood hyperbolically. For although Angels could have failed before, and did fail, yet good Angels, who are called Angels from heaven, because they are confirmed in good, cannot fail, nor could the Apostle err in doctrine, as one teaching θεοπνεύσως.

It is therefore a hyperbole; as 1 Cor. 13:1 and Obadiah v. 14. He adds, however, that he is doing this to beat back the calumny of the Pseudo-Apostles, which was that Paul preached one thing among the Gentiles, another among the Jews. For he could not beat it back more strongly than by devoting himself to anathema, if he preached another Gospel. Those things which Grotius inserts here about the old and new covenant are foreign. In general, the Apostle reprobates foreign doctrine, which is sold for the Gospel.

In V. 7. however, the doctrine of the gratuitous remission of sins through

Again he hurls an anathema, to show how utterly detestable is anything taught as an article of faith beyond Scripture. Theophyla&us gives this reason for the repetition: lest they perhaps think that Paul said this either out of anger or to vindicate his own glory. He therefore sets out the same things again, indicating that he had firmly resolved upon them, not rashly or with uncertain judgment, but from his true inward conviction. He had spoken of himself and of an angel from heaven. He now extends the matter and pronounces universally, so that nothing can be excepted. B. Lutherus in priori Comment. Whether the Greek word “anathema,” which signifies things hung up and set apart in temples, conveys the full force of the Hebrew word, let the grammarians decide. For us it is enough that the Apostle, burning with zeal for the Gospel, would rather have himself, angels, and heavenly beings—to say nothing of the Apostles—estranged, devoted to destruction, accursed, cut off, and condemned, than allow the truth of the Gospel to be endangered. And the repetition redoubles this force. Not that he believed heavenly angels, or he himself, or the Apostles would preach anything different, but because those who taught the law under the name and example of the Apostles had to be overwhelmed, as it were, by a sudden assault, and—as he writes to Titus—have their mouths stopped and be utterly cut off at the root. It is as though he were saying: “You vaunt the name and authority of the Apostles against me. Suppose something greater: that even I and angels from heaven teach, or could teach, something different. I wish even these to be anathema. How much less, then, ought you to be intimidated by the title of Apostles!” Therefore, let us confidently say with Paul: “Let every doctrine perish and be accursed, whether brought from heaven, from earth, or from wherever you please, that teaches us to trust in works, in righteousness, or in merits other than those of Jesus Christ.” Nor are we thereby defiant toward the Pontiffs and successors of the Apostles; rather, we are faithful and true to Christ. For he must be preferred to them; and if they will not tolerate this, we must shun them altogether as accursed.

Christ is contained, not truly at last in the New Testament, so that we might win over the minds and favor and applause of the listeners for ourselves, and approve ourselves to them. He says, therefore, that in teaching he seeks not the favor and approval of men but of GOD, which he explains more clearly presently, when he says: Or do I seek to please men?

Thus also Theophylactus understands it. The Greek word itself also not rarely signifies this, as in Euripides' Medea it says: πείθειν δῶρα καὶ θεούς, which our Poet interprets, saying: Gifts, believe me, appease both men and Gods; Even Jupiter himself is appeased by gifts.

And especially B. Luther in his former Commentary. In the Greek accusative case, do they persuade men, or God? That is, the doctrine which I teach is not from men, but from God, as he himself will explain more broadly presently, when he will say that the Gospel was neither according to man, nor to be from man. Moreover, this trope is not rare even in the Latin language. I read Virgil; I expound Jerome, and 1 Cor. 1: we preach Christ the power of God, etc. The preceding things fit this sense aptly, as if he were to say, why should I not wish that those who teach otherwise be anathema? Do I not teach divine things, and not rather human things, to which all heavenly and earthly things deservedly should be silent and yield? And that which is opposed to divine things is worthy of a curse.

Latin:

V. 8. Ἀλλὰ κὰν ἦν ἡμεῖς ἢ ἄγγελος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐυαγγελίζηται ὑμῖν, παρ' ὃ ἐυηγγελισάμεθα ὑμῖν, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω) παρ' ὃν. IV. 18. XI. 34. & ἐυαγγελίζηται hic fume, pro doceta ea figura, quam jam observavimus. Quod de Angelo dicit, est quidem exaggeranter dictum, non tamen plane absurdum. Nam Angeli defetores olim in caelo fuere; neque semel, sed saepius accidite, ut Angeli ex bonis maleterent, putant Hebraei. In veteri foedere mentio est foederis cujusdam novi. At in Christi foedere non modo nullum posterius promittitur, sed etiam asseritur nullum exstiturum posterius, ut videat est Matth. XXVIII. 20. ἀνάθεμα ἔστω, id est, cum eo nihil vobis fit commercii, non magis, quam cum iis, quos Synagoga aut Ecclesia penitus abscidit. Vide Rom. IX. 3. 1. Corinth. XII. 3. XVI. verf. 22. Propositio παρὰ non tantum est contra sed etiamπαρὰ (praeter.

Grotius cum Papistis priorem assumit ligni-praeter. ficationem, ne traditiones prater scripturam inventae anathemate feriantur, dummodo nihil continet contra scripturam. At usitator est significatio posterior Rom. XI. 15. 1. Cor. III. 11. quam etiam Vulgata retinuit. Nec aliter Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, qui ἐὰν εἴπῃ, ὅτι ἐὰν ἐναντία κἀὶ ἀγγέλωσιν, ἀλλὰ κὰν μικρόν τι ἐυαγγελίζωνται παρ' ὃ ἐυηγγελισάμεθα. De Angelo quod dicitur De Angelo(et fit hyperbole) hyperbolice procul dubio intelligendum. Nam etsi antea potuerint deficere Angeli, & defecerint, tamen Angeli boni, qui dicuntur Angeli de caelo, quia confirmati sunt in bono, deficere nequeunt, neque in doctrina errare poterat Apostolus, utpote θεοπνεύσως docens.

Hyperbole ergo est; ut 1. Cor. XIII. 1. & Obadia v. 14. Addit autem sefe ad retundendam calumniam Pseudo-Apostolorum, quae erat, aliud praedicare Paulum inter gentes, aliud inter Judaeos. Non enim retundere poterat fortius, quam se anathemati, si aliud praedicaret Evangelium, d...evovendo. Aliena sunt, quae de foedere veteri & novo hic ingerit Grotius. In genere Apostolus reprobat alienam doctrinam, quae pro Evangelio venditatur.

In V. 7. scriptis autem doctrina de gratuita remissione peccatorum per

Iterum anathema vibrat, ut quantopere, quod præter scripturam credendum docetur, detestandum sit, ostendat. Theophyla&us cur hoc repetatur, causam hanc reddit: Ne forsan existiment illi, vel præ me hac Paulum, vel gloriæ gratiæ vindicanda dixisse, itemq; eadem illa exponit, indicans non temere & incerto judicio, sed vera animi sententiá firmiter hæc apud se decrevisse. Dixerat de se & de Angelo de cælo. Rem extendit & universaliter pronunciat, ne quicquam excipi possit. B. Lutherus in priori Comment. An autem anathema Græcum, quod ea significat, quæ in templis suspenduntur & seponuntur, vim Ebrai verbi impleat, viderint Grammatici. Nobis satis est, quod Apostolus zelo Evangelii fervens potius seipsum, Angelos & cælestes, nedum Apostolos, vellet alienos, devotos, execratos, separatos & maledictos, quam ut veritas Evangelica periclitaretur. Atque id repetitio ingeminat. Non quod Angelos cælestes, aut seipsum aut Apostolos aliud prædicaturos crederet, sed quod velut impetu opprimi, & (ut ad Titum scribit) os illis obstrui & penitus ac radicitus præcidi oportebat, qui nomine & exemplo Apostolorum legem docebant, ac si diceret, Apostolorum jactatis mihi nomen & autoritatem, fingite amplius, quod & ego, & Angeli de cælo aliud doceant aut docere possint, hos etiam anathema esse volo, quanto minus Apostolorum titulo terreri vos oportet. Igitur cum Paulo fidentes dicamus, pereat, maledictaq; sit omnis doctrina de cælo, de terra, unde libet allata, quæ docet in operibus, in justitiam, in merita alia confidere, quam ea, quæ sunt Jesu Christi. Nec in hoc contumaces sumus in Pontifices, Apostolorumque successores, sed pii atque veraces in Christum. Hunc enim eis præferri oportet, & si id pati nolint, ipsos penitus, ut anathemata fugere.

Christum contineri, non verd demum in N. T. ut auditorum animos favoremque & applausum nobis conciliemus, illiusque nos approbemus. Ait igitur se docendo non hominum sed DEI favorem approbationemque venari, quod mox clarius exponit, cum inquit: Aut quaero hominibus placere.

Sic & Theophylactus intelligit. Id etiam ipsa Graeca vox non raro significat, ut apud Euripidem Medea inquit: πείθειν δῶρα καὶ θεούς, quod Poeta noster interpretatur, dicens: Munera, crede mihi, placant hominesque Deosq; Placatur donie Iupiter ipse datis.

Et imprimis B. Lutherus in priori Comment. In Graeco accusandi casu, homines suadeant, an Deum? Boe est, doctrina, quam ego doceo, non ex hominibus, sed ex Deo est, ut latius flatim ipse explicabit, quando Evangelium fuere, neque secundum hominem, nec ex homine esse dicet. Est autem tropus iste non rarus etiam in Latina lingua. Virgilium lego; Hieronymum enarro & 1. Cor. I. nos predicamus Christum Dei virtutem &c. Ad hunc sensum apte quadrant precedentia, ac si dicat, cur non optem, anathema esse eos, qui alia docent? Nunquid humana, ac non potius divina doceo, quibus omnia caelestia & terrestria merito fileant & cedant? Ac maledictione dignum est, quod divinis adversatur.

## 1:10
a servant of Christ; if I were still pleasing people) I would not be a true servant of Christ. For he requires the whole person, Matth. VI. 24. By speaking of himself, he censures those others by contrast.

But as for what he says in 1 Cor. 10:19, that he strives in all things to please all men, this is to be understood according to God and for the edification of men, not according to the mere breeze and will of men, with the word of God set aside. That kind of eagerness to please men, which by reason of its principle springs from love of the glory of God and of the salvation of men, and observes means consistent with the word of God, is not to be disapproved but praised. But what is done solely to win men's favor and grace, with no regard for the divine will, cannot please God, nor is it consistent with sincere service of Christ. It has also been rightly observed by B. Luther: "Do I now seek to please men?" He says this because the Pseudo-Apostles also taught legal righteousness for this reason, lest they suffer persecution from the Jews on account of the Gospel, who raged against all men for the law of Moses against the word of the cross, as he writes in 1 Thess. 2, and as he also says below in chapter 6: "As many as desire to make a fair show in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ." Therefore Paul, his spirit roused against this faint-heartedness, teaches that for love of Christ men are to be despised, and the word is not to be omitted in order to please them.

V. 10. Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω, ἢ τὸν Θεόν) Now, that is, from the time I became an Apostle. Here he signifies I make it my own, as we said at Matt. XXVIII 14. Thus in the Greek. 1 Sam. XXIV. 8. καὶ ἵππος Δαβὶδ τὰς ἄσέβας αὐτὺ ἀνέλογεν. He strikes his adversaries from an oblique angle, who, while they fled the wrath of men, did not care for the wrath of God.

Others refer that ἄρτι to the preceding sentence, so that the sense may be, that he has sufficiently shown by those things proposed, whether he rightly πείθειν τὸν θεὸν or truly τὸν ἄνθρωπον. But the sense of Grotius, especially as regards the word πείθω, is not to be disapproved, because it is confirmed by the preceding words, εἰ γὰρ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον.

It certainly deserves to be preferred to the interpretation of Oecumenius, because the Apostle is pleading his cause not before men, but before God, and to that of Jerome and Augustine, to whom it is to render approved; and to that of Cornelius, to whom it is to endeavor to persuade God. For what need was there to render himself approved to God, or to plead his cause before God? For the Apostle was most certain that his cause was approved by God. Erasmus, Vatablus, and Beza refer it to doctrine, in this way: do I try to teach or persuade human or divine things? Pareus explains that Paul does not lead to men by his Gospel but to God. But the interpretation of Grotius is more convenient here, which Flacius also handed down: it signifies to persuade men or God, by persuading and teaching I am compelled to bind to myself. For by metalepsis here it does not signify properly the instruction itself, but that which follows, namely to please himself, to bind, to reconcile. For in persuading, that is especially sought, that we might win over the minds and favor and applause of the listeners for ourselves, and approve ourselves to them. He says, therefore, that in teaching he seeks not the favor and approval of men but of GOD, which he explains more clearly presently, when he says: Or do I seek to please men? Thus also Theophylactus understands it. The Greek word itself also not rarely signifies this, as in Euripides' Medea it says: πείθειν δῶρα καὶ θεούς, which our Poet interprets, saying:

Latin:

χριστοῦ δοῦλος· εἰ ἔτι ἤρεσκον) Non essem genuinus Christi servus. Is enim solidum hominem postulat Matth. VI. 24. de se loquendo, illos alios ex contrario notat.

Quod vero 1. Cor. X. vers. 19. ait, se studere per omnia omnibus placere, intelligendum secundum Deum, & ad hominum ædificationem, non verò secundum auram & voluntatem nudam hominum, posthabito verbo divino. Studium ejusmodi placendi hominibus, quod principii ratione ex amore gloriæ Dei, & salutis hominum sit, & media observat verbo Dei consentanea, non improbandum, sed laudandum. At quod solum in gratiam hominum, & ut ipsorum favorem & gratiam aucupemur, non attentâ voluntate divina sit, Deo placere non potest, nec consistit cum sincera Christi servitute. Rectè etiam observatum B. Luithero: Hoc an quaero hominibus placere, ideo dicit: Quia Pseudo-Apostoli etiam hac ratione docebant legales justitias, ne propter Evangelium paterentur persecutiones à Judæis, qui pro lege Mosis adversus verbum crucis insaniebant in omnes homines, ut 1. Thessal. II. scribit, quod & infra VI. cap. dicit. Quicunque volunt placere in carne, hi cogunt vos circumcidi, tantum, ut crucis Christi persecutionem non patiantur. Ideo Paulus contra hanc pusillanimitatem spiritus erectus docet, amore Christi contemnendos esse homines, & non omittendum verbum, quò illis placeatur.

V. 10. Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω, ἢ τὸν Θεόν) Nunc, id est, ex quo Apostolus factus sum. Hic significat proprium mihi facio, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVIII 14. Sic in Graeco. 1. Sam. XXIV. 8. καὶ ἵππος Δαβὶδ τὰς ἄσέβας αὐτὺ ἀνέλογεν. Ex obliquo adversarios ferit, qui, dum hominum iras effugerent, Dei iram non curabant.

Illud ἄρτι alii referunt ad precedentem sententiam, ut sensus sit, se ea proposita satis ostendisse, anne recte πείθειν τὸν θεὸν an verdτὸν ἄνθρωπον. Sensus autem Grotii, imprimis quod ad verbum πείθω, non improbandus, quia confirmatur verbis precedentibus, εἰ γὰρ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον.

Praferri utique meretur Oecumenii interpretationi, quod Apostolus causam non apud homines, sed apud Deum agat, & Hieronymi & Augustini, quibus est probatum reddere; & Cornelii, cui id est Deo persuadere conari. Quid enim opus erat Deo probatum se reddere, vel apud Deum causam agere? Deo enim causam suam probari certissimus erat Apostolus. Erasmus, Vatablus, & Beza ad doctrinam referunt, hoc modo, num humana an divina doceo vel persuadere conor? Pareus exponit Paulum suo Evangelio non ducere ad homines sed ad Deum. Sed convenientior hic est Grotii interpretatio, quam etiam Flacius tradidit: Homines aut Deum suadere significat, suadendo & docendo mihi devincire cogor. Per Metalepsin enim hic non proprie ipsam institutionem, sed id, quod consequitur, sibi nempe placare, devincire, conciliare significat. Nam in fuadenda id potissimum captatur, auditorum animos favoremque & applausum nobis conciliemus, illiusque nos approbemus. Ait igitur se docendo non hominum sed DEI favorem approbationemque venari, quod mox clarius exponit, cum inquit: Aut quaero hominibus placere. Sic & Theophylactus intelligit. Id etiam ipsa Graeca vox non raro significat, ut apud Euripidem Medea inquit: πείθειν δῶρα καὶ θεούς, quod Poeta noster interpretatur, dicens:

## 1:11
V. 11. Γνωρίζω δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοί.

Not that they had not known it before. For they had received the Apostle as an Angel of God. But because that knowledge seemed to have been obliterated in their minds. Here B. Luther excellently inculcates the distinction between law and Gospel: Gospel and law properly differ in this, that the law preaches things to be done and to be omitted, indeed things already committed and omitted, and impossible to be done and omitted, and therefore it provides only the knowledge of sin: but the Gospel [preaches] sins forgiven, and fulfills all things, and makes [them fulfilled].

For the law says: Pay what you owe. But the Gospel, your sins are forgiven you. Thus Rom. III. by the law is the knowledge of sin, and Rom. IV. the law works wrath. For where there is no law, there is no transgression. But concerning the Gospel he says in the last chapter of Luke: Thus it behooved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and to be preached. dear in his name (note remarkably, in his name, not ours) repentance and remission of sins among all nations.

Behold the preaching of the remission of sins through the name of Christ, that is, the Gospel. And Romans X. How beautiful are the feet of those evangelizing peace, announcing peace, that is, the remission of sins and grace, the fullness of the law through Christ.

Thence, justified by grace, fleeing from the law to the Gospel, he says: Forgive us our debts. And shortly after in Paul: Therefore the voice of the Gospel is sweet, as in the Canticles: Let thy voice sound in my ears, for thy voice is sweet. And again: Thy words are better than wine, fragrant with the best ointments, that is, the words of Christ, with which he feeds his faithful, are better than the words of the law, because they breathe the word of grace, by which, sins being remitted, the wounds of nature are healed.

Thus Psalm XLV. grace is poured out on thy lips, not science, not knowledge, which was poured out on the lips of Moses, but grace, that is, thy words are gracious and pleasant to lost sinners, because they announce remission and grace.

This is what he also prays in Psalm LI: I will teach (he says) the wicked thy ways, and the impious shall be converted to thee, as if he were saying, I beseech thee, let me not teach the ways of men, and the doctrine of our own justice, since thus they will not be converted to thee, but will be turned away further; I pray that thou open my lips, so that my mouth may rather announce thy praise, that is, the grace by which thou remittest sins.

For from this it will come to pass that man may praise, glorify, and love thee, when he has felt the benefit of thy mercy, and has not praised himself in his own justice. For those who are just are not taught, are not converted to thee, do not praise thee, but themselves; they are healthy, they do not need a physician.

Therefore, the praise of thy grace cannot be announced to them, of whom he says shortly after in the same place: Deliver me from blood, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue shall exalt thy justice. Not our human justice, but thy grace, by which thou bestowest justice upon us, through which thou art also the God of our salvation. Οὐκ ἔστι κατὰ ἄνθρωπον) It has nothing of human affection mixed in.

Præpositio κατά They note that this Preposition, when constructed with the Accusative, sometimes signifies agreement, as in Romans

III. v. 5, Galatians III. v. 15, 1 Corinthians III. verf. 3; sometimes the Efficient cause, as dià with the Genitive in Mark I. v. 27, Galatians II. v. 2. The former seems to fit here, because the Apostle was not preaching according to the grasp of human reason or the pleasure of men: yet the latter fits better, because the Apostle is not speaking so much of the proclamation as of the Gospel itself: that it was not devised by men, but originated and was revealed by God; or as Peter speaks, ὁ θελήματι ἀνθρώπω ἠνέχθη 2.

Epist. I. v. 21. Which sense is that of Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others, and is confirmed in verse 1 and following, where the Apostle proves that the Gospel which he preached was not κατὰ ἄνθρωπον. For he neither received it first from man, nor was he more fully taught about it by him, but all that he preached was held from the immediate revelation of Christ himself. Which he thought necessary to inculcate particularly to the Galatians, against the Pseudo-Apostles, who objected that Paul had not heard Christ like the other Apostles.

Latin:

V. 11. Γνωρίζω δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοί.

Non quod antea id haud noverint. Susceperant enim Apostolum ut Angelum Dei. Sed quod obliterata in animis ipsorum videbatur illa notitia. Inculcat hic egregie B. Lutherus legis & Evangelii discrimen: Evangelium & lex proprie in hoc differunt, quod lex predicat facienda & omittenda, imo jam commissa & omissa, ac impossibilia fieri & omitti, ideo solam peccati ministrat cognitionem: Evangelium autem remissa peccata, & omnia implere, facitque.

Lex enim dicit: Redde, quod debes. Evangelium autem, dimittuntur tibi peccata tua. Sic Roman. III. per legem cognitio peccati, & Rom. IV. Lex iram operatur. Ubi enim non est lex, nec prevaricatio. At de Evangelio dicit Luce ultimo: Sis oportuit Christum pati & a mortuis resurgere, & praedicari. in nomine ejus (nota insigniter, in nomine ejus, non nostro) pænitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes.

Ecce prædicatio remissionis peccatorum per nomen Christi, hoc est, Evangelium. Et Roman. X. Quam speciosi pedes evangelizantium pacem, annuntiantium pacem, id est, remissionem peccatorum & gratiam, legis plenitudinem per Christum.

Inde justificatus per gratiam à lege ad Evangelium fugiens dicit: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Et Paulo post: Igitur vox Evangelis dulcis est, ut in Canticis: Sonet vox tua in auribus meis, vox enim tua dulcis. Et iterum: Meliora sunt verba tua vino, fragrantia unguentis optimis, id est, verba Christi, quibus pascit fideles suos, sunt meliora verbis legis, quia spirant verbum gratiæ, quo remissis peccatis, sanantur naturæ vulnera.

Ita Ps. XLV. diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis, non scientia, non cognitio, qua in Mosis labiis diffusa est, sed gratia, id est, gratiosa & jucunda sunt verba tua peccatoribus perditis, quia remissionem & gratiam nuntiant.

Hoc est, quod Psal. LI. quoque orat: docebo (inquit) iniquos vias tuas, & impii ad te convertentur, ac si diceret, obsecro, non doceam vias hominum, & doctrinam justitiæ nostræ, quoniam sic non ad te convertentur, sed longius avertentur, labia mea quæso aperias tu, ut os meum tuam potius annuntiet laudem, id est, gratiam, qua peccata remittis.

Ex hoc enim fiet, ut homo te laudet, glorificet, diligat, dum senserit beneficium misericordiæ tuæ, & non seipsum laudavit in justitia sua. Qui enim justi sunt, non docentur, non ad te convertuntur, non te laudant, sed seipsos, sani sunt, medico non egent.

Ideo nec annuntiari eis potest laus gratiæ tuæ, de quibus mox ibidem: Libera me de sanguinibus Deus, Deus salutis meæ, & exaltabit lingua mea justitiam tuam. Non nostram hominum justitiam, sed gratiam tuam, qua justitiam nobis tribuis, per quam & Deus salutis nostræ es. Οὐκ ἔστι κατὰ ἄνθρωπον) Nihil humani affectus admixtum habet.

Præpositio κατά Hanc Præpositionem cum Accusativo constructam notant aliquando significare convenientiam ut Roman.

III. v. 5. Gal. III. v. 15. 1. Cor. III. vers. 3. aliquando causam Efficientem, ut dià cum Genitivo Marci I. v. 27. Gal. II. v. 2. Prior hic videtur convenire, quia non juxta rationis humanæ captum vel hominum placitum prædicabat Apostolus: Posterior tamen magis quadrat, quia non tàm de præconio ja[1] loquitur Apostolus, quàm de Evangelio ipso: quod id non ab hominibus excogitatum, sed à Deo ortum & revelatum sit; vel ut Petrus loquitur, ὁ θελήματι ἀνθρώπω ἠνέχθη 2.

Epist. I. v. 21. Qui senius Chrysostomi, Theophylacti, & aliorum est & vers. 1. seqq. confirmatur, quo probat Apostolus Evangelium, quod prædarit, non fuisse κατὰ ἄνθρωπον. Neque enim se ab homine id vel accepisse primum, vel de illo uberius edoctum esse, sed totum quod prædicavit, ab ipsius Christi revelatione immediata haberi. Quod contra Pseudo-Apostolos, qui Paulum non audivisse Christum ut cæteros Apostolos objiciebant, peculiariter Galatis inculcandum duxit.

## 1:12
Verf. 12. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐγὼ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου παρέλαβον) It did not come to me from the tradition of Hillel. Οὔτε ἐδιδάχθην) Gamaliel did not teach me this. Ἀλλὰ δι ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) I learned it through heavenly revelation. Again he opposes Jesus Christ to men, that is, to mortals.

Thus Moses is called by the Angel in the bush. He does not here oppose the revelation made by Christ to the prior information accepted in Judaism, but he denies that he learned the Gospel concerning Christ Jesus from anywhere else than immediately from Christ himself, as Peter and the other Apostles had received it.

And he is not dealing with his vocation, but with the immediate revelation of the Gospel. Because in that respect he was considered inferior to the other Apostles. Therefore he teaches that he received the Gospel from no man, not even from the Apostles, nor was he taught in any part, namely, that Jesus is that promised Messiah, who delivered himself to death for us, that he might snatch us from the malice of the world (for he had exhibited this as the sum of the Gospel), but that he received it ἀμέσως through the revelation of Christ, who is not a mere man but God-man; as if he were saying, in the interpretation of Theophylact, that same one also revealed the Gospel to me, who instructed the companions and associates of Peter, as he did Peter himself.

Moreover, the revelation was made through the Holy Spirit, who also led the other Apostles into all truth.

He was indeed sent to Ananias in Acts IX, but not so that he might teach him the Gospel, but that by the laying on of hands his sight might be restored to him, and that, baptized, he might be filled by the Holy Spirit himself, verse 17. For then εὐθέως he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God, v. 20.

PART III. An account of his former zeal under Judaism, and his devotion to the preaching of the Gospel, undertaken without prior communication with the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐγὼ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου παρέλαβον) Non ex Hillelis traditione hoc ad me venit. Οὔτε ἐδιδάχθην) Non hoc Gamaliel me docuit. Ἀλλὰ δι ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Per revelationem cœlestem addidici. Iterum Jesum Christum hominibus, id est, mortalibus opponit.

Sic Moses vocatur per Angelum in rubo. Non hic revelationem à Christo factam opponit informationi priori in Judaismo acceptæ, sed de Evangelio de Christo Jesu, quod non didicerat negat se aliunde quam immediate ab ipso Christo id accepisse, ut Petrus, & alii Apostoli acceperant.

Neque de vocatione, sed Evangelii revelatione immediata agit. Quia ea parte cæteris Apostolis inferior censebatur. Quapropter docet, se Evangelium ab homine nullo, ac ne Apostolis quidem accepisse, aut ulla parte edoctum esse, quod nempe Jesus sit promissus ille Messias, qui se pro nobis in mortem tradidit, ut nos è mundi malitia eriperet (hanc enim Evangelii summam exhibuerat) sed ἀμέσως per ἀποκάλυψιν χριστοῦ, qui non ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος sed Θεάνθρωπος est, accepisse; quasi dicat, interprete Theophylacto, ille idem & mihi Evangelium revelavit, qui Petri contubernales instruxit & socios, ut & ipsum Petrum.

Revelatio autem facta est per Spiritum sanctum, qui etiam Apostolos cæteros in omnem veritatem duxit. Missus quidem est ad Ananiam Actor.

IX. sed non ut Evangelium ipser edoceret, sed ut manus impositione ipsi visus restitueretur, & baptizatus ab ipso Spiritu sancto impleretur vers. 17. Tum enim εὐθέως in synagogis prædicavit Christum, quod ille fit Filius Dei v. 20. PARS III.

Relatio de zelo pristino sub Judaismo, & devotione ad Evangelii prædicationem, fine pravia communicatione cum Apostolis suscepta.

## 1:14
14. Καὶ προέκοπτον ἐν τῷ ἰουδαϊσμῷ) In the knowledge of the Jewish religion, or in the study of the law. Ὑπὲρ πολλοὺς συνηλικιώτας ἐν τῷ γένει μου) מן חילרים, עַל כָּל בְּנֵי גִילִי, as is Dan. I.

10. אשר כנרילי Maimonides speaks somewhere. But he here said genus for nation, as in 2.

Cor. XI. 26. Περισσοτέρως ζηλωτὴς ὑπάρχων τῶν πατρικῶν παραδόσεων) By the word παραδόσεων he understands both the law itself and the interpretation of the law.

See Matth. XV. 2. And ζηλωτὴς is a more ardent zealous one. See Acts

XXI. 20, Rom.

X. 2, Phil.

III. v. 6. πατρικαὶ παραδόσεις here, as ἰη πατρικά, AΘ.

XXVIII. v. 7. are laws and institutions received from the ancestors. See

AΘ. XXIII. vers. 6. All these things Theophylact expressed in a clear paraphrase, which we subjoin: For you have heard of my conversation once in Judaism; whence it is clear, if you ask, that I received the Gospel through revelation.

Namely, from my former life and custom. For how could I, who had been so fierce a persecutor of the Church, have so suddenly changed my mind, unless something had drawn me to itself? But that I so bitterly persecuted the Church of God, is evident even from this, that the report about me has reached you, who are so far distant from Judea, that I persecuted the Church of God beyond measure, and was destroying it.

Observe how he amplifies each detail. For he did not say only that he persecuted, but that he persecuted the whole Church beyond measure. Nor content with that, but he was destroying it, that is, he desired to overthrow and abolish it. For that was the business of a persecutor, and I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my nation. (V. 7. Ὁ ἦν ἴση ἄμο) Which thing has nothing absurd in it: for it refers to the whole matter.

(Romano-Evangelium ober-opens cum fide ad salutem requiritur?) They wanted to seem to deliver the Gospel more fully, while they required works with faith for salvation. But the Apostle teaches that in this way the Gospel of Christ is in reality overthrown. For if salvation is obtained through our works, or they are necessary for salvation, the obedience of Christ, both active and passive, will not suffice, by which alone we are constituted just according to the Gospel, Romans

V. v. 19. In his one name Christ commanded the remission of sins to be preached, Luke

XXIV. And Peter testified that there is no other name in which we must be saved, Acts

IV. 12. Moreover, Christ abolished the ceremonial law both by word (Matth.

IX. 13. and by deed Matth. XII. 8. and elsewhere not once, and by his coming brought an end to it; just as when the body comes, shadows and figures cease, Col.

II, Ebr. X. And that the sacrifices, which were types of him, were to have an end at his death, was predicted in Dan. IX. Observe here, B.

Luther warns diligently in his later Commentary, that every teacher of works and of the righteousness of the law is a disturber of churches and consciences. But who would ever have believed that the Pope, Cardinals, Bishops, Monks, and that whole synagogue of Satan, especially those authors of holy orders (some of whom, however, God could save by miracle), would be disturbers of consciences?

Indeed, they are even worse than the Pseudo-Apostles. For these taught that, besides faith in Christ, the works of the divine law were necessary for salvation. But those, having omitted faith, taught human traditions and works not divinely commanded, but devised by themselves against and contrary to the Word of God. And they not only equated them with the Word of God, but exalted them far above it.

And afterwards: I would gladly keep that justifying righteousness of grace, and that other righteousness of the law, on account of which God would regard me. But to admit the latter to the former is, as Paul says here, to overthrow the Gospel of Christ.

It appears a light matter to mix the Gospel and the law, faith and works, but it brings more harm than human understanding can grasp. For not only is the knowledge of grace obscured, but Christ is taken away with all his benefits, and the whole Gospel, as Paul says here, is overthrown.

my own, being more abundantly a zealot for my paternal traditions. Above others, he says, who were of my age, I showed much more ardor, and I made progress in the war which I had undertaken against the Church of God, and the greatest honors were conferred upon me by the Jews. Nor is it a wonder, as one whom they had seen to be the most ardent zealot of paternal traditions and of the law. For do not think that Paul had persecuted the Church out of anger or hatred, or for the sake of vain glory, but out of zeal for God and the law. Ignorant, however, of how ungrateful a crime he had committed against God himself. He says, therefore, for how can it be that I, who showed myself such in Judaism, should now, having known the truth, preach one thing after another for the sake of the desire for human glory, not those things which truth itself demands, and Christ himself taught me. Conf. Phil. III. 5.

He had approved the persecution VII. but now, which was more, he declares that he himself had persecuted the Church or the faithful of Christ, and had shone among the persecutors, whom he then indeed held as apostates, and excommunicated heretics IX. 2. who were not the Church of the malignant, but the true Church and disciples of the Lord Act. IX. 1. ch. XXII. 4. The Vulgate rendered ἐπόρθουν, I was storming.

Which Valla criticizes, because the Church cannot be stormed. Nor does the word πορθέω denote that, notes Beza against Erasmus. Nor could the Vulgate bring forward any example of its meaning from any suitable author, ὑπερασπίσσης h. in l. Benedicti. Justin. It is therefore more correctly translated I was laying waste.

For it is noted that the persecution was not light, but more severe, by which the assemblies of the faithful were dispersed, which also became known to the Galatians as far more difficult, he says he was a zealot, not so much of the law or of Moses and the Prophets, to which the Gospel delivers nothing alien, as of paternal traditions, namely, the unwritten ones, which the Pharisees insisted upon, against which Christ spoke openly Matth. V. XV. XXIII. In that zeal he persecuted and laid waste, and by that he had become known to all by himself. Not out of any private hatred of certain persons, just as Haman, incited by hatred of Mordecai, was trying to cast out the whole Jewish nation, not out of private offense, not for private gain, but out of love for the Jewish religion. B.

Luther, however, understands paternal traditions concerning the law, when they are viewed with the end of the Gospel, and he explains this excellently in his former Comment.

The law is not only ceremonial, but also moral, and finally the most sacred decalogue itself is the letter of the eternal precepts of God and by the tradition of the letter is life-giving and not justifying, as B. Augustine abundantly proves de Spir. & lit. but killing and making sin abound. For however much it may be taught or observed, the heart itself is not purified by this.

But with the heart not purified, what are good works, whether ceremonial or moral, if not the very species of piety and hypocrisy? Just as Christ calls the Pharisees outwardly beautiful, but inwardly full of filth. Whence it happens that, although he does not commit theft, does not commit adultery outwardly in deed, yet he is entirely the same inwardly, or he abstains out of love for his own convenience, or out of fear of punishment, and as if he overcomes one sin with another, as Augustine says de nuptiis & concupisc.

For love of convenience and fear of punishment are vices, a certain kind of idolatry, since love and fear are owed to God alone. Therefore, from this impurity of the heart nothing but faith liberates Act.

XV. Purifying their hearts by faith, so that the word of Paul may be fulfilled Tit. I. All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean.

He says the same rule Rom. II. You who teach not to steal, do you steal? etc., with B. Augustine as interpreter, you steal, namely, not in deed, which you teach should not be done, but in guilty will.

Wherefore, unless the doctrine of faith, by which the heart is purified and justified, is revealed, the learning of all precepts, literal and paternal tradition, is [nothing]. For the precept teaches what things are to be done. Which when they have been impossible, the doctrine of faith (that is the Gospel) teaches how they may be made possible.

For this teaches to flee to the grace of God, and to implore God himself, the Master and Teacher, who with the finger of his Spirit writes his letters in our hearts, living and shining and burning, by which, illuminated and kindled, we may cry Abba Father! And this is not paternal, but divine learning.

And in Comm. poster. He calls paternal traditions in this place not Pharisaical or human, as Jerome rightly admonishes.

For he does not treat here of Pharisaical traditions, but of a matter of far greater difficulty. And so he calls the holy law of Moses itself paternal traditions, that is, accepted and inherited from the Fathers. For these, he says, I was most zealous in Judaism. He speaks in the same manner also to the Philippians

III. According to the law, he says, I was a Pharisee, according to zeal persecuting the Church of God, according to the justice which is in the law, having lived without blame, as if he were saying, how I could boast, and insult here the whole Jewish nation, and the best and most holy of the circumcision, so that they might produce from all of them one for me, a more ardent or more vehement defender of the law of Moses than I once was. I was clearly a zealot of paternal traditions above the rest, that is, most studious of legal justice. This ought to have moved you Galatians, not to believe these impostors, who magnify the justice of the law, and as a matter of the greatest moment, when in this very legal justice, if one were to boast, I could more truly and excellently boast.

Vide Matth. XV. 2. & ζηλωτὴς est ardentior studiosus. Vide Act.

XXVIII. v. 7. sunt leges & instituta, a majoribus accepta. Vid.

AΘ. XXIII. vers. 6. Hæc omnia dilucida periphrasi expressit Theophylactus, quam subjicimus: Audivistis enim conversationem meam aliquando in Judaismo; unde liquet, si quæras, Evangelium per revelationem me accepisse.

Nimirum ex pristina mea vita consuetudine. Nam quo pacto, qui tam acerrimus fueram Ecclesiæ persecutor, repente adeo animum immutassem, rentem ad se traxisset? Quod autem tam acriter fini Ecclesiam Dei feciatus, vel ex eo perspicuum est, quid & ad vos de me fama pervenit, qui tanto intervallo à Judæa distatis, quam supra modum persequeutus sum Ecclesiam Dei, & expugnabam illam.

Advertite ut singula magis amplificet. Neque enim solum persequebar dixit, sed super modum universam Ecclesiam sum persecutus. Neque eo contentus, sed expugnabam, hoc est, eversiere cupiebam & tollere. Id enim erat persequentis negotium, & proficiebam in Judaismo super multos coætaneos meos in genere (V. 7. Ὁ ἦν ἴση ἄμο) Quae res nihil in se habet absurdi: enim ad totam rem refertur. (Romano-Evangelium ober-opens cum fide ad salutem requiritur?) Videri volebant Evangelium plenius tradere, dum opera cum fide requirebant ad salutem.

Sed ita Evangelium Christi reapse everti docet Apostolus. Si enim per opera nostra obtinetur salus, vel ea ad salutem necessaria sunt, non sufficiet obedientia Christi eum activa tum passiva, qua sola nos justi constituimur secundum Evangelium Roman.

V. v. 19. In suo unius nomine juffit Christus praedicari remissionem peccatorum Luc.

XXIV. Nec aliud esse nomen, in quo nos oporteat salvari, testatus est Petrus Act.

IV. 12. Porro legis ceremonialis abdicationem Christus & Verbo do- (Matth.

IX. 13. & facto Matth. XII. 8. & alias non semel, eique adventu suo finem attulit; quemadmodum corpore adventante umbrae & figurae cessant Col.

II. Ebr. X. & in morte ejus finem habere habitura sacrificia, quae ejusdem typi fuerunt, praedictum est Dan. IX. Observa hic, monet B.

Lutherus Comm. poster. diligenter, quod omnis Doctor operum & justitiae legis fit perturbator Ecclesiarum & conscientiarum. Quis autem unquam credidisset, quod Papa, Cardinales, Episcopi, Monachi, & tota illa Satana synagoga, praecipue illi sanctorum ordinum autores (quorum tamen aliquos Deus per miraculum salvare potuit) essent perturbatores conscientiarum? Imo etiam deteriores sunt Pseudo-Apostoli.

Nam hi docuerunt, prater fidem in Christum opera legis divina necessaria esse ad salutem. Illi vero omissa fide tradidiones humanas & opera non divinitus praecepta, sed à seipsis fine & contra Verbum Dei excogitata, docuerunt. Eaque non solum aquaverunt Verbo Dei, sed longe supra illud extulerunt. Et postea: Ego libenter servare velim justitiam illam gratia justificantem, & alteram illam legis, propter quam Deus me respiceres.

Sed illam alteri admittere, est ut Paulus hic dicit, Evangelium Christi evertere. Apparet autem res levis esse commiscere Evangelium & legem, fidem & opera, sed plus damni affert, quam humanus captus assequi potest.

Nam non solum obscuratur cognitionem gratiae, sed Christum cum omnibus suis beneficiis tollit, & totum Evangelium, ut Paulus hic ait, evertit.

meo, abundantius aemulator existens paternarum mearum traditionum. Praecateru inquit, quimes erant aetate, ardoris plurimum prae me ferebam, proficiebamque bello, quod adversus Ecclesiam Dei susceperam, & a Judaeis mihi maximi honores deferebantur. Nec mirum, ut quem viderant ardentissimum paternarum traditionum & legis aemulatorem. Neque enim existimes, Paulum ira vel odii, vel inanis gloria gratia fuisse Ecclesiam persequutum, sed Dei zelo & legi. Ignarus tamen, quam Deo ipsi ingratum facinus esset aggressus. Ait igitur, quin enim fieri potest, ut qui talem me in Judaismo praestiterim, nunc cognita veritate ob humanae gloriae cupiditatem alia atque alia predicem, non ea, quae veritas ipsa deposcit, & Christus ipse me docuit. Conf. Phil. III. 5.

Approbaverat persequutionem VII. sed jam, quod amplius erat, perhibet, se nempe ipsum persequutum esse Ecclesiam vel fideles Christi, & inter persequutores emnuisse, quos tunc quidem pro apostatis, & excommunicatis habebat haereticis IX. 2. qui non Ecclesia malignantium, sed vera erant Ecclesia & discipuli Domini Act. IX. 1. cap. XXII. 4. ἐπόρθουν Vulgata reddidit, expugnabam.

Quod reprehendit Valla, quia Ecclesia expugnari nequit. Nec id significare verbum πορθέω notat Beza contra Erasmum. Neque ullum significationis ejus exemplum ab ausore quodam idoneo adducere potuit Vulgata ὑπερασπίσσης h. in l. Benedicti. Justin. Rectius ergo vertitur vastabam.

Notatur enim non levem fuisse persequutionem, sed graviorem, qua dispersi fuerint coetus fidelium, quae etiam longe difficilis Galatis innotuerit, zelotem ie fuisse dicit, non tam legis seu Mosis & Prophetarum, a quibus nihil aliene tradit Evangelium, quam traditionum paternarum, videlicet non-scriptarum, quas Pharisaei inculcabant, contra quas Christus ex professo egit Matth. V. XV. XXIII. In illo zelo persequebatur ac vastabat, & eo per se innotuerat omnibus. Non ex aliquo privato certarum personarum odio, sicut Haman odio Mardochai acensus totam Judaeorum gentem eiicere tentabat, non ex offensa privata, non ob privatum commodum, sed amore Judaicae religionis. B.

Lutherus tamen traditiones paternas de lege, cum fine Evangelio spectantur, intellegit, idque praeclare exponit in priori Comment.

Lex non modo ceremonialis, verum etiam moralis, denique ipse sacratissimus decalogus aeternarum praeceptorum Dei litera est & litemis traditioneque vivificans neque justificans, ut abunde probat B. August. de Spir. & lit. sed occidens & peccatum faciens abundare. Quantumcunque enim doceatur aut observetur, non per hoc cor ipsum purificatur.

Corde autem non purificato, quid sunt opera bona, sive ceremonialia sive moralia, nisi species ipsa pietatis & hypocrisis? Sicut Christus Pharisaeos foris speciosos, intus plenos spurcitia dicit. Quo fit, ut licet non faciat furtum, non adulteretur extra in opere, tamen vel intus in eadem prorsus est, vel amore commodi fui, vel timore poenae abstinet, ac si alio peccato vincit aliud, ut Augustine dicit de nuptiis & concupisc.

Nam amor commodi & timor poenae vitia sunt, quoddam genus idololatriae, cum soli Deo amor & timor debeatur. Ab hac igitur impuritate cordis nihil nisi fides liberat Act.

XV. Fide purificans corda eorum, ut sic fiet verbum Pauli Tit. I. Omnia munda mundis, mundis vero & incredulis nihil mundum.

Eadem regula Rom. II. dicit. Qui doces non furandum, furaris &c. interprete B. Augustino, furaris scil. non opere, quod doces non faciendum, sed rea voluntate.

Quare nisi doctrina fidei, qua cor purificatur & justificatur, revelatur, omne omnium praeceptorum eruditio, literalis & paterna traditio est. Praeceptum enim docet, quae sint facienda. Quae cum fuerint impossibilia doctrina fidei (id est Evangelium) docet, quomodo fiant possibilia.

Hec enim docet ad gratiam Dei confugere, & implorare ipsum met Deum, Magistrum & Doctorem, qui digito sui Spiritus scribat in corda nostra suas literas, vivas & lucentes & ardentes, quibus illuminati & accensi clamemus Abba Pater! Et haec non est paterna, sed divina eruditio.

Et in Comm. poster. Paternas traditiones hoc loco vocat non Pharisaicas aut humanas, ut Hieronymus recte admonet.

Nam hic non agit de Pharisaicis traditionibus, sed de re longe majoris ardua. Itaque ipsam sanctam legem Mosis vocat traditiones paternas, hoc est, a Patribus acceptas & hereditatas. Pro his, inquit, maxime in Judaismo zelavi. Ad eundem modum loquitur & ad Philipp.

III. Secundum legem, inquit, fui Pharisaeus, secundum aemulationem persequens Ecclesiam Dei, secundum justitiam, quae in lege est, conversatus sine querela, quasi dicat, quam gloriari possem, & insultare hic universa genti Judaicae, & optimis & sanctissimis ex circumcisione, ut ex omnibus unum mihi producerent, ardentiorem aut vehementiorem propugnatorem legis Mosis, quam ego olim fuerim. Insignis plane prae ceteris eram zelotes paternarum traditionum, hoc est studiosissimus legalis justitiae. Hoc vos Galata movere debebat, ne crederetis istis impostoribus, qui legis justitiam magnificiunt, ac rem maximi momenti, cum in hac ipsa justitia legali, si gloriandum esset, ego verius excellenter gloriari possem.

## 1:15
Verf. 15. ὅτε δὲ εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς) This ἰοδόκησεν coheres with that which follows, ἀποκαλύψῃ.

When it seemed good to God, to make his Son known through me. ἰοδόκησεν , is said of those, whose reasons God is not accustomed to render. ὁ ἀφορίσας με ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός μου) This locution is accustomed to be used proverbially, and often ὑπερβολικῶς; as Psalm

XXII. 10. LVIII. 4. LXXI. 6. Esa. XLVIII. 8. But here, however, the propriety of the meaning must be retained.

For the place Jerem. I. verf. 4 is looked to, which Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed II. v. 31 explains well. A good temperament of the brain is required for prophecy: not, however, that those who have it become Prophets, but those to whom GOD wills to grant this.

Not dissimilar is the locution in Philo: ὅτι κατὰ γαστρὸς ἐκ τῆς τῆς φύσεως ἐργαστήριον διαπλάττεται αὐτοκράτορα. Alien are those things which are brought forward from Jewish trifles concerning a good temperament of the brain.

For they do not depend on the temperament of the brain of the Holy Spirit, but on the singular grace of GOD. Paul claims nothing for himself, but for the good pleasure and benevolence of GOD: not for his own disposition or preparation, but for the love or grace of GOD.

But he separated him, as Theophylact says, not by chance GOD, but by foreknowledge, as one whom he had seen long before to be a worthy herald of the Gospel. But GOD is said to separate from the mother's womb, not because he had not so decreed from eternity, but because then at birth he begins to execute that eternal decree, which was done here in the circumcision of Paul, through which he was received into the covenant of grace, even if he violated it in part, and GOD permitted for a time, for reasons most just, but hidden to us, that he should rage against the Church, until he would solemnly call and filter him as a herald of the Gospel. Concerning which Theophylact: One might ask, if Paul was separated from his mother's womb to preach the Gospel, and chosen by GOD, why was he left so long in Judaism by the dispensation of the ministry? Namely, so that such a sudden change of his and the multitude might create faith, and draw many to Christ.

B. Luther applies this to the present matter in his cited Commentary, f. 8. It is one thing to know the law, and to have excelled in its righteousness, and another to have known the Son of GOD. For the former works salvation, the latter perdition. And see what a grateful and sincere confessor he is of divine grace. He says, the Son of GOD was not revealed to me, because I had thus progressed in the righteousness of the paternal law by my own merit, but because it so pleased GOD to happen, when I had long deserved the contrary. But that it pleased Him without my merits, that is proven by the fact that He set me apart before I was born, and prepared me as such in my mother's womb.

Then also He called me by grace, so that from all this you may understand that faith and the knowledge of Christ did not come to me from the law, but from the predestinating and calling grace of GOD. Wherefore salvation cannot be yours from the law either. And again (v. 16) by grace. He understands that calling of which Acts IX. 5 and following speak. But that proceeded from a certain singular benevolence of GOD toward him, who at that time was acting as the greatest enemy of Christianity.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅτε δὲ εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς) Hoc ἰοδόκησεν cohaeret cum illo, quod sequitur, ἀποκαλύψῃ.

Cum Deo visum est, per me cognitum facere Filium suum. ἰοδόκησεν , dicitur de iis, quorum Deus rationes reddere non solet. ὁ ἀφορίσας με ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός μου) Solet quidem haec loquutio proverbialiter, & saepe ὑπερβολικῶς, usurpari; ut Psalm

XXII. 10. LVIII. 4. LXXI. 6. Esa. XLVIII. 8. Sed hic tamen proprietas significationis retinenda est.

Respicitur enim locus Jerem. I. vers. 4. quem bene explicat Maimonides ductoris dubitantium II. v. 31. Requiritur ad prophetiam bonum cerebri temperamentum: non tamen, qui id habent, Prophetae fiunt, sed ii, quibus hoc DEUS vult concedere.

Non dissimilis loquutio est apud Philonem: ὅτι κατὰ γαστρὸς ἐκ τῆς τῆς φύσεως ἐργαστήριον διαπλάττεται αὐτοκράτορα. Aliena sunt, quae a Judaicis nugis de bono cerebri temperamento afferuntur.

Non enim de Spiritus Sancti a temperamento cerebri dependent, sed a gratia DEI singulari. Non sibi quicquam vendicat Paulus, sed DEI beneplacito & benevolentiae: non suae dispositioni vel praeparationi, sed amori vel gratiae DEI.

Segregavit autem bunc, Theophylacto dicente, non forte DEUS, sed praescientia, ut quem dignum Evangelii praeconem longe ante vidisset. Ab utero autem matris segregare DEUS dicitur, non, quod ab aeterno haud ita decreverit, sed quod tum in nativitate aeternum illud decretum jam exequi incipiat, quod hic factum in circumcisione Pauli, per quam in foedus gratiae receptus est, etsi ex parte fui id violarit, ac DEUS ad tempus permiserit, ex causis justissimis, nobis autem occultis, ipsum furere contra Ecclesiam, donec follenniter vocaret & filteretur preco Evangelii. Quo de Theophylactus: Quaret aliquis, si ex utero matris in Evangelium segregatus est Paulus praedicandum, & a DEO electus, cur ministerii dispensatione est tamdiu in Judaismo relictus? Id scilicet, ut tam repentina illius immutatio & multie faceret fidem, & ad Christum traheret multos.

Applicat hoc ad rem praesentem B. Lutherus Comm. laudato f. 8. Aliud est legem nosse, & in justitia ejus excelluisse, & aliud Filium DEI cognovisse. Hoc enim salutem, illud perditionem operatur. Et vide, quam gratus & sincerus confessor sit gratiae divinae. Non, inquit, revelatus est mihi Filius DEI, quia sic profectum in justitia paternae legis non meo merito, sed quia DEO ita placuit fieri, cum ego longe meruissem contraria. Quod autem placuerit ei fine meritis meis, id convincit, quod me in hanc fortem, antequam natus essem, segregarit, & in utero matris meae talem praeparavit.

Deinde & per gratiam vocarit, at his omnibus intelligatis, quod fides & cognitio Christi mihi non ex lege venerit, sed ex praedestinante & vocante gratia DEI. Quare nec vobis ex lege salus esse poterit. Καὶ πάλιν ας διὰ τῆς χάριτος (v. 16) Vocationem illam intelligit, de qua Act. IX. 5. & seqq. Illa autem proveniebat ex singulari quadam DEI benevolentia in eum, qui tunc cum maxime hostem agebat Christianismi. Verf.

## 1:16
Verf. 16. To reveal His Son in me. And, this is the 'per'. He wished His Son to be made known through me to many. And the Syrian thus accepted it. Why is the ordinary sense of the particle 'in' not retained? Certainly, Christ had first to be revealed to Paul himself, whom he was thereafter to preach to others. And he celebrates both of these accordingly. And here Theophylactus rightly notes the emphasis: He did not say 'to me', but 'in me', arguing that he had not learned this by words alone, but with the fixity of the inner man suffused, and that he had been imbued with much Spirit, with Christ speaking in him.

Add that it is tacitly hinted that He revealed it inwardly, without an external teacher, so that he might not hear from without, but that the revelation might be made to the internal heart. The following words deal with the other matter, to which Theophylactus says: He revealed the Son to me also, so that I might not only see Him with these eyes, but also carry His name to others. Therefore he departs here from Vatablus, Piscator, and Pareus, who similarly render it 'through me', so that the instrument might be noted, and from Calvin, who explains it as 'in me'; Job.

Crocius agrees. For he says, he speaks of the revelation which was made to that end, that the Gospel might be revealed through him. Therefore, the revelation is not understood as being through him, but as being made to him. Here you hear, says B. Luther in his later Commentary, what kind of doctrine the Gospel is, which is the revelation of the Son of GOD. It is a doctrine diverse from the law; which does not reveal the Son of GOD, but shows sin, terrifies the conscience, reveals death, the wrath and judgment of GOD, and hell, all of which are not the Son of GOD.

The Gospel is therefore a doctrine of salt, which admits no law. O that you had known how to distinguish well here, so as not to seek the law in the Gospel, but to discern it from the law as far as heaven is distant from the earth. That difference is easy, certain, and full in itself, but to us it is difficult, nay, almost incomprehensible. You might easily say that the Gospel is nothing other than the revelation of the Son of GOD, which is the knowledge of JESUS Christ, that it is not the revelation or knowledge of the law, but in the agony of conscience, and in practice itself, to establish this certainly is difficult even for the most exercised.

But if the Gospel is the revelation of the Son of GOD, as Paul defines it here, then certainly it does not accuse and terrify consciences, it does not threaten death, and lead into despair, as the law does, but it is a doctrine concerning Christ, who certainly is neither law nor work, but our righteousness, wisdom, sanctification, and redemption 1. Cor. I. Although this was clearer than the midday light: yet such was the dementia and blindness of the Papists, that they made a law of charity out of the Gospel, and a legislator out of Christ, who bore heavier precepts than Moses himself.

But the Gospel teaches that Christ did not come to bring a new law, and to deliver precepts concerning morals, but says that He came for this reason, that He might become a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, and that sins might be remitted to us, and eternal life be given, on account of Him, not on account of the works of the law or our own righteousness. The Gospel properly preaches of this inestimable treasure, freely given to us. That I might preach Him among the Gentiles. 'That' here stands for 'so that', in which sense it is placed in 1.

Cor. IX. 14 and Apoc. XIII. For he explains the manner in which God wished His Son to be known through Paul, namely, by Paul preaching to the Gentiles, Acts IX. 15. Immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood. He signifies that he immediately, that is, with no delay interposed, began to perform his duty, as can be seen in the cited place of Acts, verse 20. But he preferred to express it by negation. 'I conferred' is the same as 'to approach someone' for the sake of taking counsel. Diodorus Siculus and Lucian use it thus. Flesh and blood here signify man, and indeed a mortal one, as Eph.

VI. 12, Matth. XVI, 17. I did not seek from any man whether I ought to obey: For I knew that the most grievous punishments awaited me if I did not obey, 1. Cor. IX. 16. These things pertain entirely to this, that he might show that he gives nothing, either to love for the Gentiles, or to hatred for the Jews, but that he does what he does for the sake of GOD and Christ. The Gentiles are named not exclusively, but primarily: because he had to preach the Gospel especially to them, Acts IX. 15. And he made mention of them here, so that he might also beat back his adversaries.

For if his name was to be carried to the Gentiles through me, how could I have preached circumcision to the Gentiles? as Theophylactus says here. By 'flesh and blood', Chrysostom and Theophylactus understand the Apostles, or in general mortal men: Jerome understands men subject to sins or carnal men. That does not please Crocius, because Paul wishes to show that he was not taught by men, which he would not obtain by saying that he did not confer with carnal men. And therefore those who understand it of the Jews and kinsmen, or those who interpret it of Paul's carnal reason, do not explain it adequately either.

Wherefore the sense of Theophylactus is to be preferred, which Flacius and others follow, as does Grotius here, that he consulted no mortal at all. This is also a manifest indication, or Flacius, of divine institution and vocation, that he was immediately made solidly learned in such great mysteries: whereas, on the contrary, all human instruction requires a long time, much labor, and even habituation, and that he immediately began the ministry of the Gospel, as one divinely commanded: whereas otherwise the matter, if done humanly, would have demanded diligent consultation and collation in such an arduous and dangerous endeavor with friends and skilled supporters as to whether, what, and how it seemed that it should be done?

That 'immediately' pertains to the fact that he preached immediately in Arabia, and thus the text coheres: When it pleased GOD to reveal His Son to me &c. IMMEDIATELY, (I did not confer with flesh and blood, nor did I return to Jerusalem to the Apostles, but) I went away into Arabia, or I returned again into Ambia. Therefore, that it is said in Acts IX. 20 (Conciliation with Acts IX.

20) that he preached in the Synagogues at Damascus immediately after his conversion is not excluded here, but it is said that he went immediately into Arabia. For this 'immediately' is not to be understood absolutely, but relatively to the journey to the Apostles, with whom he denies having communicated beforehand. Therefore it does not conflict with the fact that he is said to have stayed with the disciples at Damascus for a few days, and to have taught there immediately after his conversion. For a few days having passed, immediately, and that before

Jerusalem he is said to have gone to Arabia before he betook himself to the Apostles. Therefore, he first preached for some days at Damascus, then departed into Arabia, although Luke passed over that journey in the Acts, and spent three ...years there. Then he returned again to Damascus, and there fell into danger of his life. And all these things happened before he had conferred with the Apostles at Jerusalem.

Latin:

16. Ἀποκαλύψῃ τὸν ὑιὸν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ) Et, hic est per. Voluit Filium suum per me cognitum facere plurimis. Et sic accepit Syrus. Cur non retineatur ordinarius particulae ἐν sensus? Sane primum ipsi Paulo revelandus erat Christus, quem deinceps aliis praedicare debebat. Quod utrumque proinde celebrat. Notatque hic recte Theophylactus emphafin: Non dixit mihi, sed in me arguens, non verbis solum se hunc didicisse, fid corde interioris hominis fixentia circumfuso, & Christo in eo loquente multo Spiritu fuisse imbutum.

Adde, quod tacite innuitur interius, sine externo magistro revelasse, ut non foris audiret, sed interno cordi revelatio fieret. De altero verba sequentia agunt, ad quae Theophylactus: Revelavit mihi & Filium, ut non modo eum bis oculis cernerem, sed ad alios etiam illius nomen perferrem.
