Ideo recedit hic a Vatablo, Piscatore, Pareo, similiter, ut Grotius reddentibus, per me, ut instrumentum notetur, & Calvino, qui exponit, in me, accedit Job. Crocius. Loquitur enim, inquit, de revelatione, quae eo fine facta est, ut per ipsum Evangelium revelaretur.

Non igitur revelatio per illum, sed illi facta intelligitur. Hic audis, inquit B. Lutherus, poster. Comment. cujusmodi doctrina Evangelii, que est revelatio Filii DEI. Es diversa doctrina est a lege; qua non revelat Filium DEI, sed ostendit peccatum, perterrefacit conscientiam, revelat mortem, iram & judicium DEI, ac infernum, que omnia non sunt Filius DEI. Est ergo Evangelium doctrina salis, que nullam legem admittit.

O qui hic bene distinguere nasses, ne in Evangelio legem quaereret, sed id ab illa tam longe dicerneret, quam distas caelum a terra. Differentia illa in se facilis certa & plena est, sed nobis difficilis, imo fere incomprehensibilis est. Facile quidem dixeris, Evangelium nihil aliud esse, quam revelationem Filii DEI, quam cognitionem JESU Christi, non esse revelationem aut cognitionem legis, sed in agone conscientia, & in ipsa praxi hoc certo statuere est difficile etiam exercitissima. Si autem Evangelium revelatio Filii DEI est, ut Paulus hic definit, tunc certe non accusat & perterrefacit conscientias, non minatur mortem, & in desperationem adducit, ut lex facit, sed est doctrina de Christo, qui certe neque lex neque opus est, sed nostra justitia, sapientia, sanctificatio & redemptio 1.

Cor. I. Quanquam hoc meridiana luce clarius fu: tamen tanta Papistarum fuit dementia & caecitas, ut ex Evangelio legem charitatis, ex Christo legislatorem fecerint, qui graviora praecepta tulerit, quam Moses ipse.

Sed Evangelium docet, Christum non venisse, ut ferret novam legem, & traderet praecepta de moribus, sed ideo venisse dicit, ut hostia fieret pro peccatis totius mundi, quodque remittantur nobis peccata, & donetur vita aeterna, propter ipsum, non propter opera legis aut nostram justitiam. De hoc inestimabili thesauro, nobis gratis donato, proprie Evangelium concionatur. ἵνα ἰυαγγελίσωμαι αὐτὸν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν) ἵνα hic fumo pro ita, ut, quo sensu ponitur in 1. Cor. IX. 14. & Apoc.

XIII. Explicat enim modum, quo Deus voluerit per Paulum Filium suum cognosci, nempe Paulo gentibus praedicante, Act. IX. 15. Εὐθέως προσανεθέμην σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι) Significat statim fe, id est, nulla mora interposita, coepisse fungi suo munere, ut dicto Actorum loco, commate 20. videre est. Sed maluit id efferre per negationem. Προσανεθέμην idem, quod ἀνατίθεσθαι, aliquem adire, consilii capiendi causa. Usurpant fic Diodorus Siculus, & Lucianus. Caro & sanguis significant hic hominem, & quidem mortalem, ut Eph.

VI. 12. Matth. XVI, 17. Non quaesivi ex homine ullo, an parendum mihi esset: Sciebam enim, mihi gravissimas poenas imminere, nisi paruiffem, 1. Cor. IX. 16. Haec omnino eo pertinent, ut oftendat, se nihil dare, aut amori in gentes, aut odio in Judaeos, sed se, qua facit, facere DEI & Christi causa. Gentes nominantur non exclusive, sed primario: quia praecipue illis Evangelium praedicare debuit Actor. IX. 15. Et earum mentionem hic fecit, ut ita quoque retunderet adversarios. Si enim ad gentes erat illius nomen deferendum per me, quo pacto & gentibus circumcisionem praedicaverim? ut hic Theophylactus.

Per carnem Caro & sanguinem Chrysostomus & Theophylactus Apostolos, vel in genere homines mortales intelligunt: Hieronymus homines peccatis obnoxios seu carnales. Non placet id Crocio, quod Paulus ostendere velit, se non esse ab hominibus edoctum, quod non obtineret dicendo, se non cum carnalibus contulisse. Ideoque nec adaequate exponunt, qui de judais, & consanguineis intelligunt, nec qui de carnali Pauli ratione interpretantur.

Quapropter praeferendus videtur Theophylacti sensus, quem Flacius & alii sequuntur, ut & hic Grotius, quod nullum omnino mortalium consuluerit. Hoc quoque est manifestum indicium, aut Flacius, divina institutionis & vocationis, quod statim factus sit folide in tantis mysteriis doctus: cum contra omnis humana institutio, longo tempore, multoque labore, & etiam assuefactione, usque indigeat, quodque statim inchoaverit Evangelii ministerium, utpote divinitus jussus: cum alioqui res humanitus acta, in tam arduo periculosoque conatu flagitasset diligentem consultationem & collationem cum amicis & peritis fautoribus an, quid, & quomodo agendum esse videretur?

Illud εὐθέως eo pertinet, quod statim praedicarit in Arabis, atque ita cohaeret textus: Quando placuit DEO retexere Filium suum me &c. STATIM, (non contuli cum carne & sanguine, neque Hierosolymam ad Apostolos reversus, fed) abii in Arabiam, vel denuo reversus sum in Ambiam.

Quod ergo Actor. IX. 20. εὐθέως statim post conversionem dicitur praedicaffe in Synagogis (Conciliatio cum Act. IX. 20.) Damasci hic non excluditur, sed εὐθέως in Arabiam abiisse dicitur. Nam hoc εὐθέως non intelligendum absolute, sed relate ad profectionem ad Apostolos, cum quibus se negat prius communicasse. Non ergo cum eo pugnat, quod aliquot diebus Damasci penes discipulos substitisse, ac statim post conversionem fuam ibi docuiffe dicitur. Nam paucis diebus exactis, statim, idque antequam

Hierosolymam ad Apostolos se conferret, in Arabiam abiisse dicitur. Primum itaque Damasci aliquot diebus praedicavit, mox in Arabiam discessit, etsi iter illud Lucas in Actis praeterierit, ibique triennium consumpsit. Dehinc denuo Damascum ...rediit, ibique in periculum vitae incidit. Atque haec omnia acciderunt, antequam cum Apostolis Hierosolymis contulisset.

## 1:17
Ver. 17. Οὐδὲ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἀποστόλους [I did not go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who were before me] Peter, John, James, who were acting mostly at Jerusalem around those times. Ἀπὸ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἀραβίαν [I went away into Arabia]) Into places near Damascus.

For Damascus itself was then under the kingdom of the Arabs. This is the first of the nations to whom Paul announced the Gospel: In this also he is similar to Moses, for whom, after leaving Egypt, the first station was in Arabia. Thus the prophecy of Isaiah XLII, 11 was mystically fulfilled. Luke did not narrate this journey because he was not present for it. It is not established that he went to places near Damascus. Indeed, we have already pointed out that he came to Jerusalem in transit, which is distant from Damascus by an interval of forty miles. But he went to Arabia Petraea, of which Chrysostom says: Consider his fervent mind; he was eager to occupy regions hitherto cultivated by no one, but which even now lay vast and uncultivated. How many and how great were those he converted to Christ in Arabia, he passes over for the sake of modesty, as Theophylact warns with the same Chrysostom. He would not have stayed there for three years if he had borne no fruit, or, as Jerome thinks, had accomplished nothing there worthy of the Apostleship, which cannot be gathered from Luke's silence.

Latin:

Ver. 17. Οὐδὲ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἀποστόλους Petrum, Johannem, Jacobum, qui plurimum circa illa tempora Hierosolymis agebant. Ἀπὸ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἀραβίαν) In loca Damasco proxima.

Ipsa enim Damascus tunc sub Arabum erat regno. Haec prima est gentium, cui Paulus Evangelium annunciaverit: In hoc quoque Mosi similis, cui, post relictam Aegyptum, prima statio in Arabia fuit. Sic impletum mystice vaticinium Esa. XLII, 11. Hoc iter Lucas non enarravit, quia ei non adfuit. Loca Damasco vicina ipsum adiisse non constat. Imo in transitu Hierosolymam, quae Damasco quadraginta milliarium intervallo distat, ipsum venisse jam monuimus. Adiit autem Arabiam Petram, de quo Chrysostomus: Considera ferventem animum, studebat occupare regiones antehac a nemine cultas, sed quae etiamnum vasta incultaeque jacebant. Quot autem quantosque in Arabia ad Christum converterit, modestie causa praeterit, ut cum eodem Chrysostomo Theophylactus monet. Non haesisset ibi per triennium, si nullos tulisset fructus, aut, quod Hieronymus putat, nihil dignum Apostolatu illic perpetrasset, quod ex Lucae silentio colligi non potest.

## 1:19
19. Εἰ μὴ Ἰάκωβον, τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ Κυρίου [except James, the brother of the Lord]) Εἰ μὴ here means "but," as in Matt. XII, 4; Gal. I, 7; II, 16; Apoc. II, 4, and elsewhere often. I found none of the Apostles, since they were going elsewhere for the sake of spreading the Gospel, but I found him who was performing their duties, James the brother of the Lord.

The suspicion about the changed name of Cephas is vain. No argument for it can be brought forward. All the codices agree. But he was not visiting Peter so that he might be confirmed by him in his office, which Papists babble about. For scripture knows nothing of that, nor does it suit this place, where he confirms the authority of his own office, and that also for the reason that he received his office not from any of the Apostles, but immediately from Christ, and had already exercised it for three years, and had never seen Peter. Thomas, on this passage, says (Paul) "although I did not go to my predecessors of my conversion, because I was already instructed by Christ, yet compelled by the affection of charity, after three years, namely, of my conversion, I came to Jerusalem, since I had so long desired to see Peter, not to learn from him, but to visit him." Lombard on this passage: "To see Peter, not to learn anything from him, but to see him on account of the affection of the Apostleship, and so that Peter might know that I would be a Co-Apostle to him." Since he had no need of Peter, says Chrysostom, nor did he need his voice, but was ἰσότιμον [equal in honor] to him, yet he went up to him, namely for the sake of honor and love, so that he might become familiarly known to such a great Apostle. Theophylact: "Even this, he says, shows humility, since he betook himself to Peter regarding the things he had done. Not for the sake of any utility, but of visiting, so that he might venerate and magnify him who was equally more advanced. And just as we ourselves, when we see men adorned with holiness, proceed, even though we do it so that we might profit somewhat in virtue, so also Paul approached Peter merely for the sake of honor." That he acknowledged him as the head of the Apostles is supported by no evidence. Indeed, when Chrysostom says he met Peter as an equal (ἰσότιμον), he says he entered to James with much modesty, ὡς πρὸς μείζονα καὶ τιμιώτερον [as if to a greater and more honorable one]. Most understand him to be the brother of Alphaeus, who in the Jerusalem Synod dictated the decree AB. XV, and left the canonical epistle. Herod had removed the brother of John AB. XII. Grotius wishes to designate some other James, who was not from the College of Apostles, but who performed their duties. And therefore he changes the usual meaning of the particle εἰ μὴ, which is exceptive. Whom he also makes the author of the Epistle of James. But because he dealt at length with him in the preface of that Epistle, we think the discussion of this opinion should be reserved for there. Ἐπίμονα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡμέρας διατρίβης [to stay with him fifteen days]) A great guest of a great host. Visitation undertaken for the sake of honor: Staying pertains to friendship, as Chrysostom and Theophylact have it. But Jerome rashly seeks a mystery in the 15 days: Nor does he attribute so many days to learning doctrine from Peter, because he teaches here that he had it from no mortal. Justinian observes that the number of those days is expressed so that the Galatians might understand that Paul's doctrine contains nothing from Apostolic doctrine.

Latin:

19. Εἰ μὴ Ἰάκωβον, τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ Κυρίου) Εἰ μὴ hic valet sed, ut Matth. XII, 4. Gal. I, 7. II, 16. Apoc. II, 4. & alibi. Nullum reperi Apostolorum, quippe qui alio irent, Evangelii spargendi causa, sed reperi eum, qui eorum vices obibat, Jacobum fratrem Domini.

Vana est suspicio de commutato Cepha nomine. Nullum ejus argumentum afferri potest. Consentiunt Codd. omnes. Non autem visebat Petrum, ut ab ipso in officio suo confirmaretur, quod Papistae nugantur. Nihil enim de eo novit scriptura, nec id huic loco convenit, ubi auctoritatem sui muneris confirmat, idque ea etiam ratione, quod non ab Apostolorum ullo, sed immediate a Christo officium suum acceperit, eoque jam triennium functus sit, nec unquam Petrum viderit. Thomas in hunc locum, dicit (Paulus) licet nonadierim mea conversionis, quia jam eram instructus a Christo, tamen ex affectu charitatis compulsus, post annos tres scilicet conversionis mea, veni Hierosolymam, quoniam tamdiu desideravi videre Petrum, non ut disceram ab eo, sed ut visitem eum. Lombardus in h. l. Videre Petrum, non discere aliquid ab eo, sed videre eum propter affectum Apostolatus, & ut Petrus sciret, me fore sibi Co-Apostolum. Cum nihil opus haberet Petro, inquit Chrysostomus, nec illius egeret voce, sed ἰσότιμον ὧν honore par illi esset, tamen ad illum ascendit, scilicet honoris & amoris causa, ut familiariter tanto Apostolo innotesceret. Theophylactus: Vel hoc quidem, inquit, praefert humilitatem, siquidem quas res gesserat, ad Petrum se contulit. Non utilitatis cujuspiam gratia, sed visendi, ut eum, qui esset aeque provectior, veneraretur & magnificaret. Es quemadmodum ipsi viros sanctitate ornatos vidimus procedimus, tametsi ipsi id agimus, ut aliquid virtute proficiamus, ita & Paulus honoris duntaxat gratia ut Petrum spectaret, accessit. Caput Apostolorum agnovisse ipsum nullo indicio constat. Imo cum Petrum ut ἰσότιμον convenisse ait Chrysostomus, ad Jacobum dicit cum plurima modestia ingressum, ὡς πρὸς μείζονα καὶ τιμιώτερον velut ad majorem & honoratiorem. Alphai fratrem plerique intelligunt, qui in Hierosolymitana Synodo dictavit decretum AB. XV, & canonicam reliquit epistolam. Johannis fratrem AB. XII, sustulerat Herodes. Grotius alium quempiam Jacobum, qui non fuerit e Collegio Apostolorum, sed eorum vices obierit, designari vult. Atque ideo particulae εἰ μὴ usitatam significationem immutat, quae exceptiva est. Quem etiam autorem facit Epistolae Jacobi. Sed quia de eo in procemio istius Epistolae prolixe egit, illuc etiam discussionem hujus opinionis reservandam ducimus. Ἐπίμονα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡμέρας διατρίβης) Magnus hospes magni hospitis. Visitatio honoris causa suscepta: Mansio ad amicitiam pertinet, ut Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus habent. Temere autem in diebus 15. quaerit mysterium Hieronymus: Neque tot dies tribuit discendae a Petro doctrinae, quia à nemine mortalium eam se habuisse hic docet. Justinianus ided numerum illorum dierum exprimi observat, ut intelligant Galatae, Pauli doctrinam nihil ab Apostolica doctrina continere.

## 1:20
20. Ἃ δὲ γράφω ὑμῖν, ἰδὲ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι οὐ ψεύδομαι [Now the things which I write to you, behold before God, that I do not lie]) He uses an oath, as in Rom. I, 17; 2 Cor. I, 23, and often elsewhere. But the cause was grave, so that he might be believed to be an Apostle, made by Christ, not substituted by other Apostles. He taught in Antioch in Syria. He went into Cilicia, in which Tarsus is his fatherland; cf. Acts IX. 30, ch. XI. v. 25.

Why is it necessary, asks B. Luther, for us to hear that he came into Syria and Cilicia? Namely, that he proves he had teachers as Apostles almost nowhere, but that he was a teacher everywhere, always looking toward this and aiming the bow of his narrative in such a way that he might finally strike most robustly all those who taught and thought things contrary to him. Because he himself taught divine things, not human, while they taught human things, not divine.

Latin:

20. Ἃ δὲ γράφω ὑμῖν, ἰδὲ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι οὐ ψεύδομαι) Juramentum adhibet, ut Rom. I, 17. 2. Cor. I, 23. & alibi saepe. Causa autem gravis erat, ut crederetur Apostolus, à Christo factus, non ab aliis Apostolis subfittutus. In Syria docuit Antiochiæ. Ivit in Ciliciam, in qua Tarsus patria conf. Act. IX. 30. cap. XI. V. 25.

Quid necesse, quærit B. Lutherus, nos audire, quod in Syriâm & Ciliciam venerit? Nempe nusquam fefè Doctores Apostolos habuisse, sed Doctorem ubique se fuisse probat, semper huc spectans & arcum narrationis eo tendens, ut tandem robustissime feriat omnes, qui ei contraria docebant & sapiebant. Quia divina non humana ipse docuerit, illi vero humana, non divina.

## 1:22
Verf. 22. Ἦμεν δὲ ἀγνοούμενοι τῷ προσώπῳ ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Ἰουδαίας, ταῖς ἐν Χριστῷ) Tῷ προσώπῳ here is what the Latins call "by face" (de facie). Thus Cicero to Piso, and others; this is inserted so that it might appear that what was being spread about him—that he himself taught the necessity of Jewish rites in Judea—is false.

Latin:

Verf. 22. Ἦμεν δὲ ἀγνοούμενοι τῷ προσώπῳ ταῖς ἐκκλη-σίαις τῆς Ἰουδαίας, ταῖς ἐν Χριστῷ) Tè προσώπῳ hic est, quod Latini dicunt, de facie. Ita Cicero ad Pisonem, & alii, hoc intersertur, ut appareat, falsum esse, quod de illo spargebatur, ipsum in Judæa docuisse necessitatem rituum Judaicorum.

## 1:23
Verf. 23. Μόνον δὲ ἀκούοντες ἦσαν) He commanded ἐκκλησίας, and the masculine follows, for those who were in the churches are understood. Ὄτι ὁ διώκων ἡμᾶς ποτε) that is, διώξας. For thus the participle is often placed among the Hebrews.

See Sirach XLVIII. 7. Νῦν εὐαγγελίζεται τὴν πίσιν, ἥν ποτε ἐπόρθει) He calls the word, which is believed, πίσιν by metonymy.

Thus also below III. 2. 5. 23. 25.

On the word ἐπόρθει see above 13; on the matter, Acts IX. 21.

Thus Theophylact: "I was indeed unknown by face to the Christians who were then living in Judea; how then could it happen that I would preach circumcision to those to whom I was not known by face?" For these people were disparaging Paul's false claims because he had already preached about circumcision in Judea. Whence he infers this: they had only heard by report that I had been converted to Christ, and that I was now preaching this very person. The Apostle wishes to intimate here most justly that he was so far from having received doctrine and learning from the Apostles as teachers, that he was hardly known by face to the Jews converted to the faith, who were disciples of the Apostles.

Latin:

Verf. 23. Μόνον δὲ ἀκούοντες ἦσαν) Præcepit ἐκκλησίας, & sequitur Masculinum, intelliguntur enim illi, qui in Ecclesiis erant. Ὄτι ὁ διώκων ἡμᾶς ποτε) id est διώξας. Nam fic Benoît sæpe ponitur apud Hebræos.

Vide Sirach. XLVIII. 7. Νῦν εὐαγγελίζεται τὴν πίσιν, ἥν ποτε ἐπόρθει) Πίσιν vocat μετωνυμικῶς τὸν λόγον, cui creditur.

Sic & infra III. 2. 5. 23. 25.

De voce ἐπόρθει vide supra 13. de re Act. IX. 21.

Ita Theophylactus: Eram quidem Christianis, qui tunc in Judæa versarentur, incognitus facie, qui ergo fieri poterat, ut circumcisionem his prædicarem, quibus non essem ex facie notus? Ob id namque Pauli falsa hi detrectabant, quia in Judæa de circumcisione jam prædicasset. Unde hoc infert, duntaxat auditu perceperant, quia ad Christum effem conversus, & hunc ipsum mox prædicarem. Justissimâ hic vult id innuere Apostolum, tantum abesse, ut Apostolis Magistris doctrinam atq; eruditionem perceperit, ut vix facie notus esset Judæis ad fidem conversus, qui Apostolorum erant discipuli.

## 1:24
V. 24. Καὶ ἐδόξαζον ἐν ἐμοὶ τὸν Θεὸν) Ἐν ἐμοὶ, on my account. A Hebraism. He does not say, "they admired me, they praised me, and they were astonished," but they glorified God, i.e., they gave thanks to God concerning me.

Or more humbly, with Theophylact saying here, he preferred "through him," because he said nothing about himself for the sake of boasting, but they were wondering, he says, at my conversion, and were astonished. Whence it happens that he ascribes the whole matter to God. For he says they glorified God and extolled with praises Him who had worked such a thing in me.

Therefore, as B. Luther says here, he now demonstrates that he taught with the authority of all the churches as his witness, when, preaching the faith, he was praised by those churches and God was glorified, by whose example, however, the Pseudo-Apostles were compelling the Galatians to the law, manifestly proving that it was not truly the churches of Judea that agreed among themselves that the Gospel was entrusted to him among the Gentiles, as it was to Peter among the Jews, and that they acknowledged the grace given to him, and that Paul should preach to the Gentiles with Barnabas, nor did they mention the needy. Furthermore, the Apostle commemorates how he himself resisted Peter at Antioch when he withdrew himself from the Gentiles on account of the Jews, and publicly contradicted him regarding the compulsion of the Gentiles to the observance of Jewish ceremonies, establishing on that basis the main head of the epistolary treatment: that, namely, a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Christ, and by his own example, that he is dead to the law, and lives solely in the faith of the Son of God, who gave himself for him, he confirms this.

There are two parts I.

Historical, reviewing both Paul's profession at Jerusalem and the agreement among the Apostles concerning the preaching of the Gospel by Paul among the Gentiles up to v. 10, and the rebuke of Peter at Antioch on account of the compulsion of the Gentiles in matters of indifference up to v. 15. II. Dogmatic, concerning the justification of man before God not by works of the law, but by faith in Christ up to v. 21, which is the beginning of the second part of the whole epistle.

PART I.

Historical, concerning the profession of Paul and the Petrine rebuke.

Verf.

Latin:

V. 24. Καὶ ἐδόξαζον ἐν ἐμοὶ τὸν Θεὸν) Ἐν ἐμοὶ, mei causa. Hebræismus. Non dicit, admirabantur me, laudabant me stu-pebantq;, sed glorificabant Deum, i. e. Deo gratias agebant de me.

Vel humilius hic dicente Theophylacto, per hùc prætulit, quia nihil de se ad jactantiam dixerit, sed mirabantur, inquit, meam conversionem, & obstupebant Quo fit ut eam rem omnem Deo adscribat. Inquit enim Deum glorificabant & efferebant laudibus, qui rem tantam in me esset operatus.

Igitur, ut hic B. Lutherus, jam autoritate omnium Ecclesiarum sese teste docuisse demonstrat, quando fidem prædicans ab illis Ecclesiis laudatus est & Deus glorificatus, quarum tamen exemplo Pseudo-Apostoli Galatas ad legem cogebant, manifeste probans, quod non vere Ecclesiæ Judææ exem-ipfi Evangelium inter gentes, ut Petro inter Judæos creditum, & gratiam ipsi datam agnoscerent, convenerit inter eosdem, ut Paulus cum Barnaba gentibus prædicaret, nec egenorum demum minissent. Porro commemorat Apostolus, quomodo Petro ipsimet Antiochiæ restiterit, cum se ob Judæos gentibus subduceret, publiceque ipsi circa coactionem gentium ad observantiam Judaicarum ceremoniarum contradixerit, statuens ea ratione præcipuum caput epistolicæ tractationis: quod nempe homo non justificetur per opera legis, sed per fidem in Christum, suóque exemplo, quod legi mortuus, unice in fide Filii Dei, qui se tradidit pro ipso, vivat, id confirmat.

Partes sunt duæ I.

Historica, recensens tum pro-Partitio. fessionem Pauli Hierosolymitanam & conventionem inter Apostolos de prædicando a Paulo Evangelio inter gentes ad v. 10. tum reprehensionem Petri Antiochenam ob coactionem gentium in adiaphoris ad v. 15. II. Dogmatica de justificatione hominis coram Deo non per opera legis, sed per fidem in Christum ad v. 21. quæ initium est partis totius epistolæ alterius.

PARS I.

Historica de professione Pauli & reprehensione Petrina.

Verf.

## 2:1 Argument
1. Ἔπειτα διὰ δεκατεσσάρων ἐτῶν) I am more attentive to the codices which have τεσσάρων instead of δεκατεσσάρων. For since numbers were written by marks, it could easily happen that an I was added before Δ by error, and we have shown at Luke IV. 26 and elsewhere that errors of writing often flowed from one exemplar into many others. Moreover, we have made it clear at many Old Testament locations that very many errors were admitted by copyists in numbers.

Testament locations. But I find nothing more credible than that this very journey of Paul is noted by these, the mention of which is in Acts XV. 2, which could not have been fourteen years later than the conversion of Paul, or even, if one prefers it, the end of the Arabian pilgrimage; διὰ is taken here as in Matthew

XXVI. 61 and Mark II.

1. Ἀνέβην ἐν ἀποκαλύψει κατὰ Βαρνάβα) This same Barnabas is joined to Paul as a companion, as stated in the Acts passage. Always, as often as the Hebrews speak of Jerusalem, they say "to ascend," even when they are in external places, because they were accustomed to speak that way at home, Acts

XV. 2. XXI. 4. 12. 15. XXV. 1. Βαρνάβα is a genitive, like Ἀβραάμ.

The Grotian itch to correct the original text by private judgment for reasons that are not at all compelling is to be detested. For what sufficient reasons for such audacity can be found, by which the divine scripture is called into suspicion of falsehood? But no reason is asserted, not even a plausible one.

For why could the Jerusalem synod not be later than the Pauline conversion? There are not lacking those who relegate this journey, which most admire as having been made to the Jerusalem synod, to the seventeenth or eighteenth year of the Pauline conversion, with the beginning of the counting of these 14 years made from the return from Arabia, to which Flacius adds in his Gloss.

But if that opinion cannot perhaps be reconciled with the Chronology, I do not see, however, why the common opinion of the Interpreters, that this journey should be placed in the fourteenth year of the Pauline conversion—which is proven by Bede in Acts XV, the author of the Ordinary Gloss on this place, Aquinas, Cajetan, Pererius in the Preface to Romans, Estius on this place and on the year of the Lord LI, Baronius, and most of our people—should be rejected.

Paul had indeed gone to Jerusalem with Barnabas in Acts XI, but only to carry there the alms collected by the churches.

But as with unless when that dispute had been stirred up by the Pseudo-Apostles, which he also treats in this epistle, he betook himself to that place in Acts XV, and that again with Barnabas, as one who had said to them in Acts IX. 27 that Paul was unknown, from whom the believers at first shrank, and who was joined to him as a herald among the Gentiles of the Gospel, which the Pseudo-Apostles were corrupting: for whose sake he wove this history into the present account, both to bring forward his own authority, and indeed to confirm the truth of his doctrine, for the sake of which he especially brings up this journey to Jerusalem.

For this was undertaken so that the controversy concerning the necessity of circumcision and good works for salvation might be decided by the common judgment of the Apostles.

Whence from this council and its Acts the state of the present discussion is best understood.

Concerning which Luther, Comm. poster.

Paul taught that the Gentiles are justified by faith alone without the works of the law.

When he had scattered this here and there among the Gentiles, he came to Antioch and announced it to the disciples. There, those who were imbued with the custom of the law rose up against Paul, indignant that he was preaching freedom from the law to the Gentiles, and a very sharp contention arose, which subsequently stirred up new disturbances.

Paul and Barnabas stood firmly and testified, saying: Wherever we have preached among the Gentiles, the Holy Spirit came and fell upon those who heard the word of God, and this happened throughout all the Churches of the Gentiles.

We preached, however, not circumcision, nor did we demand the observation of the law, but we only preached faith in Christ. And to this preaching of faith in Christ, God gave the Holy Spirit to the hearers. Therefore, the Holy Spirit approves the faith of the Gentiles without the law and circumcision.

For unless that preaching of the Gospel and the faith of the Gentiles in Christ had pleased Him, He would not have descended with a visible sign upon the uncircumcised who heard the word. Since, therefore, He fell upon them through the hearing of faith alone, it is most certain that by this sign the Holy Spirit approved the faith of the Gentiles.

For that was never before known to have happened at the preaching of the law. This was the argument of Paul and Barnabas.

There the Jews and many of the Pharisees, who had believed, and yet for the sake of defending the glory of the law still zealously contended and fought, opposed themselves with great force to Paul, who affirmed: That the Gentiles were justified by faith alone without the works of the law; and they contended: It is necessary for the law to be kept and for the Gentiles to be circumcised, otherwise the Gentiles cannot be saved.

These are the words of B. Luther.

But if, therefore, after these fourteen years Peter was still in Jerusalem and soon after in Antioch v. 11, how could he have been Pope in Rome for XXV years? Let those who affirm this see what they are to answer Paul here, unless perhaps they wish to feign for us a two-bodied Peter, one of whom would sit in Rome and the other in Jerusalem, and acted as an Apostle elsewhere, as Schmidius rightly says here.

Latin:

1. Ἔπειτα διὰ δεκατεσσάρων ἐτῶν) Attentior codicibus, qui pro δεκατεσσάρων habent τεσσάρων. Cum enim numeri per notas scriberentur, facile fieri potuit, ut ante Δ per errorem I adderetur & ex uno sæpe exemplari scripturæ vitia in multa fluxisse alia, ostendimus ad Luc. IV. 26. & alibi. In numeris autem plurimos admiffos errores ab exscribentibus, apertum fecimus ad multa Vet.

Test. loca. Nihil autè credibilius reperio, quam notari his illud ipsum Pauli iter, cujus mentio Act. XV. 2. quod non potuit toti quatuordecim annis posterius fuisse, aut conversione Pauli, aut etiam, si quis id malit, fine Arabicæ peregrinationis διὰ hic sumitur, ut Matth.

XXVI. 61. & Marci II.

1. Ἀνέβην ἐν ἀποκαλύψει κατὰ Βαρνάβα) Hic idem Barnabas Paulo comes adjungitur, dicto Actorum loco. Semper, quoties Hebræi de Hierosolymis loquuntur, dicunt ascendere, etiam ubi in externis sunt locis, quia domi ita loqui erant soliti, Actor.

XV. 2. XXI. 4. 12. 15. XXV. 1. Βαρνάβα Genitivus, quales Ἀβραάμ.

Detestandum est Grotianum Cacoëthes corri-Correctio gendi textum Originarium privato arbitrio ob Grotiana causas minime prægnantes. Quænam enim causæ textus dele-tantæ audaciæ possunt inveniri sufficientes, qua in suspicionem falsitatis divina scriptura vocatur? At nulla, ne verisimilis quidem, asseritur ratio.

Cur enim non possit synodus Hierosolymitana posterior esse conversione Paulina? Non desunt, qui hanc profectionem, quam ad synodum Hierosolymitanam factam pleriq; admirant, in decimum & septimum vel octavum annum conversionis Paulinæ rejiciunt, initio numerationis horum 14. annorum facto a reditu ex Arabia, quibus accedit Flacius in Glossa.

Sed si ea forte sententia cum Chronologia conciliari nequeat, non video tamen, quare communis Interpp. sententia, quod hæc profectio in decimum quartum conversionis Paulinæ conjicienda sit: Quam probant Beda in Act. XV. Auctor glossæ ordinariæ in hunc locum, Aquinas, Cajetanus, Pererius in Præloq. ad Rom. Eftius h. l. & ad ann. Dom. LI. Baronius & plerique nostrati.

Profectus quidem Hierosolymam cum Barnaba Paulus fuerat Act. XVI. sed solum, ut eo deferrent eleemolynam ab Ecclesiis collectam.

Sed ut cum nisi cum mota esset a Pseudo-Apostolis ea disputatio, quam etiam in hac epistola tractat, eo se contulit Act. XV. idque denuo cum Barnaba, utpote qui Paulum ignotum, a quo abhorrebant primum fideles, ad illos dixit Act. IX. 27. quique ei iunctus erat inter gentes Evangelii, quod corrumpebant Pseudo-Apostoli, praeco: quorum causa tum auctoritatem suam afferendam hanc historiam in praesenti texit, tum vero ob doctrinae suae veritatem comprobandam, ob quam imprimis hanc profectionem Hierosolymitanam adducit.

Haec enim suscepta est, ut controversia de necessitate circumcisionis & operum bonorum ad salutem communi Apostolorum calculo decideretur.

Un de ex hoc concilio & Actis ejusdem optime intelligitur status praesentis tractationis.

Quo de Lutherus Comm. poster.

Paulus docebat, gentes sola fide justificari sine operibus legis.

Hoc ubi sparserat passim inter gentes, venit Antiochiam, & nuntiavit discipulis. Ibi resurgebant contra Paulum, qui consuetudine legis imbuti erant, indignantes quod gentibus libertatem a lege praedicaret, ortaque est acerrima contentio, quae subinde novos motus excitavit.

Paulus & Barnabas stabant fortiter & testificabantur, dicentes: Ubicunque nos inter gentes praedicavimus, venit Spiritus sanctus & cecidit super eos, qui verbum Dei audiebant, bocque contigit per omnes Ecclesias gentium.

Praedicavimus autem non circumcisionem, nec exegimus observationem legis, sed tantum fidem in Christum praedicavimus. Et ad hanc fidei in Christum praedicationem dedit Deus Spiritum sanctum auditoribus. Ergo Spiritus sanctus approbat fidem gentium sine lege & circumcisione.

Nisi enim placuisset ei illa Evangelii praedicatio & fides gentium in Christum, non descendisset visibili signo super incircumcisos, qui verbum audierunt. Cum itaque per solum auditum fidei ceciderit super ipsos, certissimum est, quod hoc signo approbarit Spiritus sanctus fidem gentium.

Id enim nunquam antea compertum est accidisse ad praedicationem legis. Hoc erat Pauli & Barnaba argumentum.

Ibi Judaei & multi ex Pharisaeis, qui crediderant, & tamen pro gloria legis defendenda adhuc vehementer zelabant & dimicabant, magno impetu opposuerunt sese Paulo, affirmanti: Quod gentes sola fide sine operibus legis justificarentur; & contendebant: Oportet legem servari & gentes circumcidi, alias non posse salvari gentes.

Haec B. Lutherus.

Quod si ergo post hos quatuordecim annos Petrus adhuc fuit Hierosolymis & mox Antiochia v. 11. quomodo XXV. annis Pontifex Roma esse potuit? Viderint, qui hoc affirmant, quid Paulo hic sint responsuri, Nisi forte bicorporem nobis Petrum volent fingere, quorum unus Roma sederet alter Hierosolymis, & alibi Apostolum egerit, ut hic recte Schmidius.

## 2:1
Συμπαραλαβὼν καὶ Τίτον Titus at that time was not an Evangelist, but a companion of Paul, such as Timothy was for a long time.

But the fact that Titus is not mentioned in Acts XV comes from the fact that it contributed nothing to the history of that place. Here, however, he mentions that he also took him along, even though he was uncircumcised, to testify to the boldness (παρρησίαν) of his cause, since he did not set out to the Apostles out of any hesitation, but to confound the Pseudo-Apostles, who boasted that they disagreed with Paul and acted with them, propagating the necessity of circumcision and other ceremonies and good works for obtaining salvation.

He refers everything to the revelation (ἀποκάλυψιν), which especially concerned his doctrine for the sake of repelling his adversaries.

But he is not warned here of the first revelation, as some wish, which was only general, nor did it define journeys to be instituted long after, such as this one undertaken fourteen years after the first revelation (ἀποκάλυψιν). Wherefore the Apostle was taught, or at least confirmed, by a special revelation (ἀποκάλυψιν) about undertaking this journey.

I went up, he says, not summoned by Peter and the Apostles, not ordered by men, nor by private counsel and devotion, but called to Macedonia by an immediate divine revelation,

Act. IX. 9. Καὶ ἀνέβην αὐτοῖς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, ὃ κηρύσσω ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν) Here ἀνέβην means I narrated, as in Acts.

XXV. vers. 14. in which sense Plutarch also uses that word.

That αὐτοῖς here, if we catch at the little words, has nothing to which it may refer.

If we look at the sense, it is easy to understand that they signify those who were in Jerusalem, because the name of that city preceded it. The Vulgate renders: He conferred with them.

Augustine How, however, it has: And I explained to them, which Jerome hints was done in the manner of one conferring.

Not , however, as an inferior confers with superiors, as Peter with the others, which the Papists would prefer, but as Jerome, with Estius himself approving, has it, as an equal with equals.

For among those conferring, he says, there is equality; between one teaching and one learning, he who learns is the lesser. He conferred, therefore, as Estius has it, not as an inferior, but as an equal in the office of preaching.

Cornelius a Lapide in

Gal. I. vers. 16 says he conferred, not as if doubtful or not sufficiently instructed, so that he might be instructed more fully and certainly, but so that the believers whom he was teaching might perceive that he communicated and agreed in faith and doctrine with Peter and the other Apostles, and thus might attribute more faith to his Gospel. And on this passage: He conferred, he says, with the Apostles about the Gospel, not for his own sake, but for the sake of others converted to the faith of Christ, among whom Paul had been defamed by the Judaizing Pseudo-Apostles, because he disparaged the law of Moses among the Gentiles, when James, Peter, and John taught and did the contrary, and indeed Paul himself judaized among the Jews.

Certainly he did not go up to Jerusalem for the purpose that his doctrine might be confirmed by Peter, as the head of the Apostles, as is sufficiently taught here: Because he conferred not only with Peter, but also with other colleagues, and names James in the first place, and testifies that those who seemed to be something, and thus not even Peter, conferred nothing upon him, v. 6, and equates himself to Peter, saying that he who worked with Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision, also worked with me among the Gentiles v. 8. he says that the right hands of fellowship were given to him by James, Cephas, and John v. 9. What? That you resisted Peter to his face, not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, v. 11, which he would not have dared at all if he had acknowledged him as the head. Καὶ ἴδιον δὲ τοῖς δοκοῦσι) Δοκοῦντες are those who are of illustrious fame beyond the others, Euripides: --- Λίγω γὰρ ἐν τ' ἀδοξοῦσιν ἰὼν Κἀν τῶν δοκοῦντων, αὐτὸς ὦ Παῦλον δίνα.

Plato also uses the word here several times. The Rabbis would say חֲשׁוּבִים, but it appears from those things which follow that it is not the other Apostles who are understood, but the overly fervent followers of those Apostles.

The Vulgate renders: Who seemed to be something: which two little words "to be something," however, are not read in many MSS. Codices, nor in Jerome, nor in Augustine book

II. quaest. Evangel. cap. 40. & elsewhere, nor in the Greek Codices in this place, and Estius acknowledges that this crept in here from v. 6, even though the Vulgate is fortified by Papal authority, and he proves by the Greek phrase δοκοῦντες that those who are held in value and are of great estimation are spoken of. Concerning which Beza: Τοῖς δοκοῦσι is, τοῖς εὐδοκιμοῦσι, to whom they are opposed. tur οἱ ἀδοξοῦντες, he explains, who are in esteem.

Schmidius renders it, who were held in authority, which may be compared to Mark 10:42. But that it is not the followers of the Apostles, but the Apostles themselves, James, Peter, and John, who are signified, is clear from verse 6, where they are called those who seemed to be somewhat, and verse 9, those who seemed to be pillars, and by most interpreters the Apostle called them great and super-eminent Apostles. He conferred, however, not concerning circumcision only, as Estius wishes, but concerning the Gospel and those things which the false Apostles, the adversaries, had moved against the doctrine of the Gospel.

Some think that this conference was held privately. Publicly indeed, says Estius, he conferred in such a way as to show that the Gentiles ought not to be circumcised, and to keep the law of Moses, whence the question had arisen, as can be seen in Acts 15. But in a private and secret colloquy held with the Apostles, it pleased them also that the Jews should be freed from the observance of the Mosaic law, as being already extinct and dead through Christ.

But whence is it certain that that private conference was different from the public one? Cajetanus indeed wishes the latter to be an explanation of the former: I conferred with the Apostles my Gospel: with them, I say, who were of chief name among the faithful, and I did it privately.

Although indeed most others take the pronoun αὐτοῖς generally, not of the Apostles alone, by which words following τοῖς δοκοῦσι it is clear that those with whom he conferred ναὶ idian are signified, yet by reason of the argument it is not clear that the conference was different.

But, says B. Luther in his later commentary, that question was agitated in this conference of the Gospel: Whether men can be justified without the law? Or: Whether the observance of the law is necessary for justification? There Paul said: I, to the Gentiles, according to my Gospel, which I received divinely, preached faith in CHRIST, not the law, and to this preaching of faith they received the Holy Spirit.

And of this matter I have Barnabas as a witness. Wherefore I conclude that the Gentiles are not to be burdened with the law, nor to be circumcised. Yet I do not forbid this to the Jews, who, if they wish to keep the law and be circumcised, I permit it, provided they do so with a free conscience.

And thus I taught and lived among the Jews, so also as a Jew to the Jews, etc. Yet always saving my Gospel. Nor indeed was it acted upon in the synod itself only concerning the Gentiles, but generally concerning any, that the yoke of the law, as being unbearable to all, ought not to be imposed on anyone, and that all, whoever are to be saved, ought to be saved only by the grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, Acts 15:10. And that ναὶ idian can be explained peculiarly, so that there is no need to understand it of a secret conference, or if the Apostle explained the course of his doctrine separately and secretly, ἰδιᾳηματικῶς it will be permitted to explain these things, the Apostle commemorated privately the course of my doctrine, would that seem vain?

B. Luther wisely advises concerning the circumstances in his former commentary: First, he says, after fourteen years, to which, if you add the three years which he mentioned above, you will find he had already preached for seventeen or eighteen years before he wished to confer, so that it seems impossible that what he had preached in so many places, to so many peoples, could have been revoked. And therefore he did not go up for his own sake, as if he feared (as Jerome thinks) that he had preached falsely for seventeen years, but that he might show to others that he had not run in vain, with the Apostles approving and testifying to his course. For if he had doubted whether he was teaching true or false, it would have been a sign of remarkable and unheard-of rashness and impiety, having delayed the necessary conference, to trifle with so many peoples with uncertain doctrine. Secondly, he would never have ascended, unless warned by the revelation of God, not moved by the importunity of others, so far is it from being the case that he conferred because he was diffident of the certainty of his doctrine, having no necessity at all to ascend for this cause. Thirdly, to Jerusalem itself, where the Princes were already of the synagogue as well as the Church, prepared to confer with all, fearing neither the multitude of the Jews nor the most bitter emulators of the law. Fourthly, not alone but with Barnabas and Titus of a different kind, most apt witnesses, lest he be thought to have done one thing present and another absent, as if he were doing too much for the Jews. Titus the Gentile would betray it, and again Barnabas the Jew would oppose it too much for the Gentiles. Wherefore see his confidence, he took these two with him, and had each as a witness. Finally, offering himself with both, he was about to make it manifest that it was lawful to be a Gentile with Titus, and a Jew with Barnabas, and thus he proved the liberty of the Gospel in both, that it is lawful to be circumcised, and yet it is not made necessary to be circumcised, so one must think of the whole law. Μήπως εἰς κενὸντρέχω, ἢ ἔδραμον) Lest my labor should fall into nothing, both of that time and of what was done before; namely, if that rumor were spread, that I teach one thing, and they, who were called Apostles before me, another.

As regards the kind of speaking, you have a similar one in Philippians 2:16. Tertullian against Marcion IV: he ascended to know the Apostles, and to be refuted, lest by chance he had run in vain, that is, lest he had believed according to them, and was not evangelizing according to them.

Therefore these things are not to be snatched at with certain Papists, as if Paul had run in vain without the authority of Peter, or of the supreme Pontiff. For the cause was not I, but because of the weak and malevolent, that conference was needed, not to be instituted with Peter either solely or chiefly, but with those who seemed to be pillars, James, Peter, and John, and in the whole synod. Therefore that μήπως lest as the Vulgate interprets, lest by chance, does not teach that Paul was in doubt, whether he was running in vain, but looks to others, who were being rendered doubtful by the Pseudo-Apostles.

Facius rightly: But what he says, lest by any means, in vain, etc., he did not say of his own doubt, but of the thoughts and speeches of many others, whether of the weak or even of the evil, and indeed looking to that very strife which had then been intended against him at Antioch. For the same reason also the Baptist sends his disciples to Christ for the sake of their confirmation, not because he himself doubted concerning the person of the Messiah, whom he had adorned with such illustrious testimonies and baptized.

For because the Pauline method of teaching, on account of the diversity of hearers, since he became all things to all men, was somewhat different from others, while the Jerusalemites still indulged the Jews somewhat more in ceremonies; therefore deservedly some could doubt that perhaps the Pauline doctrine differed from that of Peter, John, and James, especially with such various calumniators approaching. Therefore that conference of doctrine and mutual testimony was then so much the more necessary, because by that very strife of the Pseudo-Apostles concerning the necessity of works for salvation, the whole doctrine or Gospel of Paul, excluding works entirely from justice and salvation, was being called into doubt.

The very words of the Apostle explain themselves abundantly: for he speaks not of his own mind or doubt, but of the success, lest I should run in vain, that is, lest I should profit little by preaching because of the calumniators and the doubts of men concerning me and my doctrine. So also Lyranus: By the word 'perhaps' it is not understood that the Apostle doubted, ret, that he had preached some things less true, or doubtful, because by the revelation of GOD he was certain of the truth of his preaching, he refers this entirely to the estimation of the simple, who might doubt this, had he not conferred it with the principal Apostles.

Concerning which Theophylact says thus: It would indeed be an act of folly, that he who was running with such haste, and had already traversed so many regions, should have to learn long after whether he had run in vain or not: But if for this reason he returned to Jerusalem, that he might be made more certain of his own course, it would have seemed clearly absurd.

But when he saw that many would be offended, observing that Peter admitted circumcision, and that he himself forbade it, and thinking him therefore to have prevaricated the law, he sought Jerusalem again by the revelation of the Spirit. The same Spirit suggesting that he should go there, so that those who had been offended by this dissension might be persuaded that there was nothing different from Peter's preaching in what he himself had already preached, and might believe that those who had also permitted circumcision, permitted it by a certain dispensation: since they also preached the Gospel to the circumcised.

The most learned Camerarius brings forward two expositions of others, to which he adds a third, which is not inappropriate: Μήπως εἰς κενὸν, this others read as a figure of speech in the form of a question, so that by this form the certain and fruitful course of the Apostle might be more vehemently affirmed.

Have I commemorated the course of my doctrine privately or secretly, lest it should seem vain? Others, reading it simply, referred these things causally to that which he had said, privately. But they say, he says that he conferred privately with those who were of some reputation concerning his doctrine, lest if this were done before the multitude, the course of the newly-planted might be scandalized in vain.

To them, privately will mean separately and in secret. But I do not know whether there is any need for such expositions. For how can Ἔπειτα πῶς be accepted in the usual form of common speech, in this way: I conferred with them so as to put an end to the disputes once and for all, lest I should run in vain.

So that they might cease to inquire and doubt themselves concerning the course of my preaching, not so that any doubt might be removed from me. Theophylact thus brings forward a middle view: Since, as we have said, many were offended separately, when they were with Peter, Paul speaks, lest any faction should arise, and a discord far sharper than was accepted should be excited.

For there were almost countless numbers who took it ill that the Apostle had now rendered circumcision vain and superfluous. Wherefore if they had heard him preaching this publicly, and abolishing it, it would perhaps have resulted in a tumult among the hearers and everything would have been thrown into confusion. Therefore, he preaches separately, having Titus and Barnabas as witnesses, who could confirm to all with good leave that it seemed to the other Apostles that nothing else was to be preached than what he himself had already preached.

Why the course of the work of preaching? The Apostle calls his work of Evangelical preaching a course, because he was engaged in fulfilling it with the greatest alacrity.

Conf. 1 Cor. IX. v. 26. 2 Tim. IV. v. 6, 7. Concerning which B.

Luther, Tom. III. Jenenf. Latin. comment. on the former in this place. Note the Hebrew trope or one proper to sacred scripture, that to run signifies the office of teaching or announcing the word of God, taken from messengers, who are sent and run.

Thus above from Jerem. 23 he said: They ran and I did not send them, and Psalm CXLVI. His word runs swiftly, and many such things in the sacred scriptures. By which it is signified that the heralds of the word of GOD ought to be prompt and faithful messengers, so that they may run more than they sing.

So also Isa. LII. how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings, etc., and Ezech. I. describes his living creatures with feet and a course. And Ephes. VI. he commands them to have their feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel, and the office of all feet, the course, the mission, and the ministry of the Word of God signify this in the sacred scriptures. Verf.

3. Ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ Τίτος ὁ σὺν ἐμοὶ, ἴσαων ὢν ἀναγκάσθη περιτμηθῆναι) that is, those Apostles at Jerusalem did not demand this of me, that I should have Titus circumcised, intending to do so perhaps, if he had been a Jew in any part, like Timothy from his mother, Acts XVI. 2, 3. but since he was of another nation, no one demanded it of him. That he was perhaps going to do it, which Grotius adds of his own, is dissolved by the perhaps not going to do it.

For whence is it certain that if Titus had had a Jewish mother, the Apostles would have compelled the same to circumcision? The Apostles were rather acting in this synod so that they might teach that neither circumcision nor other ceremonies were necessary for anyone to observe, just as it is evident from Luke, Acts XV.

Timothy was circumcised, lest the weak and unlearned Jews should be offended, but Titus was not circumcised, lest he should seem to yield to false brethren. Moreover, as B.

Luther warns, the whole force of this controversy consists not in the works of the law, whatever they may be, but in the necessity and liberty of the works of the law. For the works of the law and the law itself are not so mortified and finished by Christ, that it is in no way permitted to perform them (as D. Jerome, led by his Origen, contends in more than one place) but only that salvation should not be believed to be through them, but through Christ alone, who is the end of the law, for whom the precepts were to be. For after CHRIST came, he so abrogated the works of the law that they can be held indifferently, but they no longer compel, just as below in c.

IV he will give a beautiful paradigm of the infant heir. Therefore the other Apostles did these things with the faithful Jews.

But Paul and Barnabas sometimes did them, sometimes did not, to show that they were entirely indifferent, and such as he who would do them should be, as 1 Cor. IX. I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might gain the Jews, to those who are under the law, as if I were under the law, when I myself was not under the law, to those who are without the law, as if I were without the law. How could he have explained Evangelical liberty more clearly?

I came, he says, to the Jews, about to preach CHRIST. But that they might hear me, it was necessary for me on their account not yet to use this liberty, and to despise them with their works. I did, therefore, what they themselves were doing, until I could teach that they were not necessary, but that the faith of Christ alone sufficed. Thus I came to the Gentiles, I did nothing certain, which I had done among the Jews, but I ate and drank entirely what they also did, until I could teach them Christ, how would they have admitted me, if I had immediately loathed them in those neutral matters? And further: Therefore the Apostle vigilantly does not say, he did not want, it was not permitted, but he was not compelled to be circumcised.

To be circumcised was not an evil, but now that Christ alone justifies us by grace, to be compelled to circumcision as necessary, so that you may be justified, this was impious, and injurious to the justifying grace of Christ. Wherefore the works of the law are after CHRIST, just as wealth, honor, power, civil justice, and whatever other temporal thing, which if you have, you are not therefore better before God, if you lack them, you are not therefore worse. But you would be the worst, if you were to bring them forward as necessary, by which you might please God. Therefore see the words of the Apostle, in which the force of the understanding is situated.

Compelled, (he says) likewise liberty, servitude, subjection. By which he sufficiently explains that it was among those who observed him, that he sometimes kept the law for his liberty and license, and sometimes did otherwise, according as he saw it for gaining souls and preaching the Gospel.

Latin:

Συμπαραλαβὼν καὶ Τίτον Titus eo tempore non erat Evangelista, sed comes Pauli qualis diu Timotheus.

Quod vero Titus non commemoretur Act. XV. factum inde, quod ad ejus loci historiam id nihil fecerit. Hic autem eum etiam se assumpsisse, etsi incircumcisum commemorat, ut παρρησίαν suae causae testetur, quum non ex aliqua haesitatione ad Apostolos profectus sit, sed ut confunderet Pseudo-Apostolos, qui eosdem a Paulo dissentire, ac secum facere jactabant, necessitatem circumcisionis, aliarumque ceremoniarum & operum bonorum ad consequendam salutem propagantes.

Omnia ad ἀποκάλυψιν refert, quae imprimis doctrinam ejus concernebant ad retundendos adversarios.

Non autem hac de prima revelatione, ut nonnulli volunt, monitus est, quae tantum generalis fuit, nec profectiones longe post instituendas, qualis haec decem & quatuor annis a prima ἀποκάλυψιν suscepta, definivit. Quapropter peculiari ἀποκάλυψιν de hac profectione suscipienda edoctus, aut certe confirmatus est Apostolus.

Ascendi, inquit, non citatus a Petro & Apostolis, non jussus ab hominibus, nec privato consilio, & devotione, sed ex immediata divina revelatione in Macedoniam vocatus,

Act. IX. 9. Καὶ ἀνέβην αὐτοῖς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, ὃ κηρύσσω ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν) Hic ἀνέβην significat narravi, ut Actor.

XXV. vers. 14. quo sensu ea voce & Plutarchus utitur.

Illud αὐτοῖς hic, si voculas captamus, non habet, quo referatur.

Si sensum, facile est intelligi, eos significare, qui Hierosolymis erant, quia nomen id urbis praecessit. Vulgata reddit: Contulit cum ipsis.

Augustinus Quomodo tamen habet: Et exposui illis, quod more conferentis factum, innuit Hieronymus.

Non autem ut cum Petro inferior cum superioribus confert, quod Papistae mallent, sed ut Hieronymus; approbante ipsomet Estio, habet, ut aequalis cum aequalibus.

Nam inter conferentes, inquit, aequalitas est, inter docentem & discentem minor est ille, qui discit. Contulit ergo, ut Estius habet, non ut inferior, sed ut in munere praedicandi aequalis.

Cornelius a Lapide in

Gal. I. vers. 16. contulisse ait, non quasi dubium aut non satis instructum, ut plenius & certius instrueretur, sed ut fideles, quos docebat, cernerent, cum in fide & doctrina communicare & consentire cum Petro, aliisque Apostolis, sicque plus fidei ejus Evangelio tribuerent. Et in hunc locum: Contulit, inquit, cum Apostolis Evangelium, non propter se, sed propter alios ad fidem Christi conversos, apud quos a Pseudo-Apostolis Judaizantibus diffamatus erat Paulus, quod apud gentes legi Mosis detraheret, cum contrarium docerent & facerent Jacobus, Petrus, & Johannes, imo ipse Paulus apud Judaeos judaizaret.

Certe eo fine non ascendit Hierosolymam, ut a Petro doctrina sua confirmaretur, ceu Apostolorum capite, hic satis docetur: Quia non cum Petro solum, sed etiam cum aliis collegis contulit, ac Jacobum primo loco nominat, & nihil sibi illos, qui videbantur aliquid esse, adeoque nec Petrum contulisse, perf. 6. testatur, ac se aequat Petro, qui operatus est, inquiens cum Petro in Apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est & mibi inter gentes vers. 8. a Jacobo, Cepha & Johanne dextras fraternitatis sibi datas ait vers. 9. Quid? quod Petro etiam, non ambulanti recto pede ad veritatem Evangelii, in faciem restiteris vers. 11. quod ausus minime fuisset, si eum pro capite agnovisset. Καὶ ἴδιον δὲ τοῖς δοκοῦσι) Δοκοῦντες sunt qui praeter caeteros illustri sunt fama, Euripides: --- Λίγω γὰρ ἐν τ' ἀδοξοῦσιν ἰὼν Κἀν τῶν δοκοῦντων, αὐτὸς ὦ Παῦλον δίνα.

Utitur hic voce & Plato aliquoties. Rabbini dicerent חֲשׁוּבִים, apparet autem ex iis, quae sequuntur, non intelligi Apostolos alios, sed illorum Apostolorum nimis fervidos sectatores.

Vulgata reddit: Qui videbantur aliquid esse: quas tamen duas voculas aliquid esse in multis Codicibus MSS. non legi, nec apud Hieronymum, nec apud Augustinum libr.

II. quaest. Evangel. cap. 40. & alibi, nec in Graecis Codicibus hoc loco, atque huc e vers. 6. irrepsisse agnoscit Estius, ut ut Vulgata munita sit autoritate Papali, probatque phrasi Graeca δοκοῦντες dici qui in pretio habentur, magnaque sunt existimatione. Qua de Beza: Τοῖς δοκοῦσι est, τοῖς εὐδοκιμοῦσι, quibus opponuntur. οἱ ἀδοξοῦντες, exponit, qui sunt in pretio.

Schmidius reddit, qui habebantur in autoritate, qui conferatur ad Marci X. vers. 42. Non autem sectatores Apostolorum, sed Apostolos ipsos significari Jacobum, Petrum & Johannem e vers. 6. ubi dicuntur, qui videbantur aliquid esse, & vers. 9. qui videbantur columna esse, liquet, & a plerisque interpretibus Apostolus magnos & supra modum Apostolos dixit. Contulit autem non de circumcisione tantum, ut Estius vult, sed de Evangelio & iis, quae contra Evangelii doctrinam moverant adversarii falsi Apostoli.

Collationem eam privatim factam nonnulli putant. Publice quidem, inquit Estius, ita contulit, ut ostenderet gentes non circumcidi debere, & servare legem Mosis, unde nata erat quaestio, quemadmodum videre est Actor. XV. Privato autem & secreto colloquio cum Apostolis habito placuit ipsis quoque Judais ab observantia legis Mosaica, utpote jam extincta & mortua per Christum, esse liberandos.

Sed unde illa privata collatio, a publica diversa constat? Cajetanus sane posteriora vult priorum esse ἐξήγησιν: Contuli cum Apostolis Evangelium meum: cum iis, inquam, qui praecipui nominis erant apud fideles, idque privatim feci.

Quanquam vero alii plerique pronomen αὐτοῖς generatim accipiunt non de solis Apostolis, quibus verbis sequentibus τοῖς δοκοῦσι ἐsignificari constat, cum quibus ναὶ idian contulerit, argumenti tamen ratione diversam fuisse collationem, non liquet.

Fuit autem, inquit B. Lutherus, comment. poster. agitata in hac Evangelii collatione illa quaestio: Utrum homines possint sine lege justificari? Aut: Utrum ad justificationem necessaria sit observatio legis? Ibi Paulus dixit: Ego gentibus, secundum Evangelium meum, quod divinitus accepi, praedicavi fidem in CHRISTUM, non legem, & ad hanc fidei praedicationem acceperunt Spiritum sanctum.

Atque hujus rei testem habeo Barnabam. Quare concludo, gentes non esse onerandas lege, nec circumcidendas. Judais tamen hoc non prohibeo, qui si volunt legem servare & circumcidi, permitto, modo hoc libera conscientia faciant.

Sicque docui & vixi inter Judaeos, ita & Judais Judaeus &c. Salvo tamen semper Evangelio meo. Nec vero in ipsa synodo tantum de gentibus actum, sed generaliter de quibusvis, quod nemini jugum legis, utpote omnibus ἀβάστακτον imponi debeat, quodque omnes, quicunque salvandi sint, non nisi gratia Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI salvari oporteat Actor. XV. vers. 10. Et potest illud ναὶ idian exponi peculiariter, ut non opus fit, de secreta collatione intelligere, aut si seorsim & secreto exposuit Apostolus cursum doctrinae, ἰδιᾳηματικῶς licebit haec exponere, commemoravit privatim Apostolus cursum doctrinae meae, nunquid inanis ille videretur?

De circumstantiis erudite monet B. Lutherus Comment. priori: Primum, inquit, post annos quatuordecim, quibus, si annos tres, quos supra memoravit, adjunxeris, jam decem & septem & decem aut octo annos eum praedicasse invenies, antequam conferre voluerit, ita, ut impossibile videatur, quod tot locis, tot populis praedicarat, potuisse revocari. Ideoque non sua causa ascenderit, quasi timuerit, (ut Hieronymus sentit) ne falsum per decem & septem annos praedicasset, sed ut offenderet aliis, sese non in vacuum cucurrisse approbantibus & castris Apostolis suum cursum. Si enim dubitasset, verumne, an falsum doceret, insignis & inaudita temeritatis ac impietatis fuerat, dilata necessaria collatione, tot populos ludere incerta doctrina. Secundo non ascendisset unquam, nisi revelatione Dei monitus, non aliorum importunitate commotus, tantum abest, ut de doctrina certitudine diffisus, contulerit, nullam habens prorsus necessitatem ascendendi in hanc causam. Tertio ad ipsam Hierosolymam, ubi erant Principes jam synagoga quam Ecclesia, paratus cum omnibus conferre, nec multitudinem Judaeorum, nec legis acerrimos emulatores formidans. Quarto non solus sed cum Barnaba & Tito diverso genere, aptissimos testes, nec aliud egisse praesens, aliud absens crederetur, ut si quid pro Judeis nimium faceret. Titus gentilis proderet, & rursus nimis pro gentibus Barnabas Judaus obsisteret. Quare fiduciam ejus vide, hos duos secum duxit, & utrumque testem habuit. Denique cum utroque sese offerens, manifestum facturus, quod cum Tito gentilem, cum Barnaba Judaeum esse licuerit, & sic Evangelii libertatem in utroque probaret, quod circumcidi licet, & tamen circumcidi non fit necessarium, ita de tota lege sentiendam. Μήπως εἰς κενὸντρέχω, ἢ ἔδραμον) Ne in irritum caderet meus labor, tum ejus temporis, tum anteactus; nempe si fama ea spargeretur, aliud me docere, aliud eos, qui ante me vocati erant Apostoli.

Loquendi genus quod attinet, habes simile Philipp. II. vers. 16. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem IV. ascendit ad cognoscendos Apostolos, & confutandos, ne forte in vacuum cucurrisset, id est, ne secundum illos credidisset, & non secundum illos evangelizaret.

Non ergo haec eo abripienda sunt cum Papificis quibusdam, ac si in vacuum cucurrisset Paulus sine autoritate Petri, seu Pontificia summi. Non enim fui causa sed propter infirmos & malevolos collatione illa opus erat non cum Petro sive unice sive praecipue instituenda, sed cum iis, qui columnae videbantur, Jacobo, Petro & Johanne, & in tota synodo. Illud ergo μήπως ne quomodo Vulgata interpretatur, ne forte non docet dubium fuisse Paulum, anne in vacuum curreret, sed alios respicit, qui dubii reddebantur a Pseudo-Apostolis.

Recte Facius: Quod vero dicit, ne quo modo, frustra &c. non dixit de sua dubitatione, sed de aliorum multorum, vel imbecillium, vel etiam malorum cogitationibus & sermonibus, & quidem respiciens in eam ipsam litem, quae tunc ipsi Antiochia intenta fuerat. Eadem ratione prorsus etiam Baptista mittit suos discipulos ad Christum confirmationis ipsorum gratia, non quia ipsemet de persona Messiae, quem tam illustribus testimoniis ornarat & baptizarat, dubitaret.

Quia enim Paulina ratio docendi ob diversitatem auditorum, cum omnia omnibus factus est, fuit nonnibil diversa ab aliis, dum Hierosolymita adhuc aliquanto plus indulgerent Judais in ceremonie; ideo merito aliqui addubitare potuerunt, forte Paulinam doctrinam discrepare a Petri, Johanne & Jacobi, praesertim accedentibus tam variis calumniatoribus. Ideo vero erat tunc tanto magis necessaria illa collatio doctrina mutuumque testimonium, quia illa ipsa Pseudo-Apostolorum lite de operum necessitate ad salutem tota doctrina aut Evangelium Pauli opera prorsus a justitia & salute excludentis in dubium revocabatur.

Verba ipsa Apostoli sese abunde explicant: loquitur enim non de suo animo aut dubitatione, sed de successu, ne frustra currerem, id est, ne parum ob calumniatores & dubitationes hominum de me meaque doctrina praedicando proficerem. Ita & Lyranus: Per τὸ forte non intelligitur, quod Apostolus dubitaret, se aliqua minus vera, vel dubia praedicasse, quia per revelationem DEI erat certus de veritate praedicationis suae, id totorefertud ad aestimationem simplicium, qui possent de hoc dubitare, nisi cum principalibus Apostolis hoc contulisset.

Quo de ita Theophylactus: Esset utique insipientia accendendum, ut ei qui festinus adeo curreret, & regiones tam multas jam peragrasset, si longe post perdiscendum fuisset, utrum cucurrisset in vanum nec ne: At si ob id Hierosolymam repeteret, ut certior de proprio cursu efficeretur, visum esset id plane absurdum.

Sed cum videret multos iri offensum, animadvertentes Petrum circumcisionem admittere, & se prohibere, eoque legem praevaricatum existimantes ex Spiritus revelatione iterato Hierosolymam petiit. Spiritu eodem, ut eo pergeret, suggerente, ut hi qui fuerant hac dissensione offensi, persuasum haberent, nihil a Petri praedicatione differre, quod ipse jam praedicasset, crederentque, qui circumcisionem etiam permississent, dispensatione quadam permittere: quandoquidem & circumcisis Evangelium praedicarent.

Doctissimus Camerarius affert duas aliorum expositiones, quibus addit & tertiam, quae non inconcinna: Μήπως εἰς κενὸν, hoc alii ἐσχηματισμένως κατ’ ἐρώτησιν legerunt, ut hoc forma vehementius affirmaret certus & fructuosus cursus Apostoli.

Peculiariter seu privatim commemoravi cursum doctrinae meae, nunquid inanis ille videretur? Alii simpliciter legentes retulerunt haec αἰτιολογικῶς ad id quod dixerat, κατ’ ἰδίαν. Ideo autem, inquiunt, ait se privatim cum iis, qui in existimatione aliqua essent, contulisse de doctrina sua, ne si coram multitudine hoc fieret, ἐκενώθη πῶς ὁ δρόμος σκανδαλιζομένων τῶν νεοπαγῶν.

His κατ’ ἰδίαν erit seorsim & secreto. Sed baud scio, an talibus expositionibus opus non sit. Ἔπειτα πῶς enim usitata forma sermonis communis hoc dictum accipi potest, hoc quodammodo: Ἀνεθέμην ἐκείνοις ὡς τε παῦσαι ἄπαξ τὰς ἀμφισβητήσεις, μήπως εἰς κενὸν τρέχω.

Ut desinerent querere & dubitare ipsi de cursu praeconii mei, non ut mihi dubitatio aliqua eximeretur. Mediam ita affert Theophylactus: Quoniam erant eare, ut diximus, multi offensi seorsim, cum Petro essent, alioquitur Paulus, ne factio aliqua oriretur, & acrior longe, quam erat accepta, excitaretur discordia.

Erant namque fere innumeri qui aegre ferrent, circumcisionem Apostolum inanem jam & supervacaneam reddidisse. Quocirca si publice hunc praedicantem audissent, & eam tollentem, nimirum tumultuatum forsitan per auditores denique foret & omnia obturbata. Propterea igitur seorsim concionatur, Titum habens in testem & Barnabam, qui apud omnes possent bona venia confirmare, caeteris Apostolis visum, baudquaquam aliud praedicandum, quam ipse jam praedicasset.

Opus praedicationis cursus cur? Opus Evangelicae praedicationis cursum suum vocat Apostolus, quod in eo obeundo summa cum alacritate versaretur.

Conf. 1. Corinth. IX. vers. 26. 2. Tim. IV. vers. 6. 7. Quo de B.

Lutherus Tom. III. Jenenf. Latin. comment. priori in h. l. Tropum Ebraeum vel scripturae sacrae proprium nota, quod currere significet officium docendi seu verbum Dei nuntiandi, sumptum a nuntiis, qui mittuntur & currunt.

Sic supra ex Jerem. 23. dixit: Currebant & non mittebam eos & Pfalm. CXLVI. Velociter currit sermo ejus, & multa in sacris literis ejusmodi. Quo significatur, oportere verbi DEI praecones esse promptos & fideles nuntios, ut magis currant, quam cant.

Ita & Esa. LII. quam speciosi pedes evangelizantium &c. & Ezech. I. animalia sua cum pedibus & cursu describit. Et Ephes.

VI. calceatos jubet habere pedes Evangelico apparatu, & omnium pedum officium, cursus, missio, at familiaministerium Verbi Dei significant in sacris literis. Vers. 3. Ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ Τίτος ὁ σὺν ἐμοὶ, ἴσαων ὢν ἀναγκάσθη περιτμηθῆναι) id est, non exegerunt hoc a me illi Hierosolymis Apostoli, ut Titum facerem circumcidi, facturi id forte, si Judaeus fuisset aliqua ex parte, ut Timotheus ex matre, Actor. XVI. 2. 3. at cum esset gentis alterius, nemo id ab eo exegit. Illud forte facturus, quod de suo addit Grotius, per forte non facturus dissolvitur.

Nam unde constat, quod si matrem Judaeam habuisset Titum, eundem Apostoli ad circumcisionem adacturi fuissent? Id potius agebant Apostoli hac synodo, ut neque circumcisionem, neque alias ceremonias ulli observatu necessarias esse docerent, quemadmodum ex Luca constat Actor.

XV. circumcisus est Timotheus, ne infirmi atque rudes Judaei offenderentur, Titus vero non circumcisus est, ne falsis fratribus cedere videretur. Caterum, quod B.

Lutherus monet, tota vis bujus controversiae consistit non in operibus legis, quecunque illa sint, sed in necessitate & libertate operum legis. Non enim opera legis & lex ipsa ita sunt mortificata, & finita per Christum, ut ea nullo modo liceat operari (ut D. Hieronymus ex Origene suo ductus, non uno loco contendit) sed tantum, ue absque eis salus credatur, per solum Christum qui finis legis est, in quem futurum erant praecepta. Postquam enim CHRISTUS advenit, legis opera sic abrogavit, ut indifferenter ea haberi possint, non autem amplius cogant, sicut infra c.

IV. pulchrum dabit paradigma de harede parvulo. Ideo caeteri Apostoli ea fecerunt cum Judaeis fidelibus.

Paulus autem & Barnabas aliquando fecerunt, aliquando non fecerunt, ut ostenderent ea prorsus esse indifferentia, & talia, qualia esse ille, qui faceret, ut 1. Cor. XII. factus sum Judais, tanquam Judaeus, ut Judaeos lucrifacerem, iis qui sub lege sunt, quasi sub lege essem, cum ipse non essem sub lege, is, qui sine lege sunt, quasi sine lege essem.

Quomodo potuit libertatem Evangelicam clarius explicare? Veni, inquit, ad Judaeos, praeditaturus CHRISTUM. At ut me audirent, necesse mihi fuit propter eos nondum hac uti libertate, & eos contemnere cum suis operibus. Feci ergo, quae ipsi faciebant, donec docerem non esse necessaria, sed solam Christi fidem sufficere. Ita veni ad gentes, jam nihil certum egi, quae apud Judaeos egeram, sed omnino edebam, bibebam, quae & illi, donec docerem eos Christum, quomodo me admisissent, si eos flatim fastidiissem in rebus illis neutralibus? Et porro: Proinde Apostolus vigilanter non ait, non voluit, non licuit, sed non est compulsus circumcidi.

Circumcidi malum non erat, sed jam Christo solo per gratiam nos justificante cogi ad circumcisionem tanquam necessaria, ut justificeris, hoc impium erat, & in Christi justificatricem gratiam contumeliosum. Quare legis opera sunt post CHRISTUM, sicut divitia, honor, potestas, justitia civilis, ac quaecunque alia res temporalis, quas si habeas, non ideo melior es coram Deo, si careas, non ideo pejor. Esses autem pessimus, si eas necessarias afferreres, quo Deo placeres. Igitur verba Apostoli vide, in quibus vis intelligentia sita est.

Compulsus, (inquit) item libertatem, servitutem, subjectionem. Quibus id satis exponit fuisse scilicet inter eos, qui observarunt eum, quod legem pro libertate & licentia sua quandoque servarit, quandoque contra fecerit, prout lucrandis animabus & praedicando Evangelio videbat.

## 2:4
ANNOTATIONS ON GALATIANS CH. II. v. 4. 6.

ought to agree. And those prudent men, accusing him because he did not keep the law, did not circumcise the Gentiles, etc., wished to compel him, which he here calls subjection, so as to extort from us the liberty brought forth through Christ, and [bring us into] servitude. For that liberty, which he boasts we have in Christ, is that we are bound to no single external work whatsoever, but are free for anything, to anyone, at any time and in any manner, unless where fraternal peace and charity is shown, just as in Romans XIII: "Owe no man anything, but to love one another."

Ver. 4. (But because of the false brethren brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage; to whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.) In the Sinaitic Manuscript, this word pareisaktous (brought in privily) appears here either as a redundancy of speech, not infrequent in Hebraisms, or as an error of the scribe. The sense is: But for the sake of those Jews who pretended to be Christians, in order to extort from us the liberty brought forth through Christ, we yielded nothing of the purpose of that liberty, both to be defended and to be transmitted to you all; pareisaktous are those who pareiselthon (came in privily) in Jude 4; they are so called who insinuate themselves by art, introduce themselves secretly, and creep in. Similar pareisaktous in both the Sinaitic and the Lambertian [manuscripts]. See what was said on Acts XV. 34. We have the word pseudadelphous (false brethren) also in 2 Corinthians XI. verse 26. The word for "to spy out" appears to be a military term. By katadoulōsōntai (bring into bondage), he signifies here the plotting of evil against another under the guise of friendship, as spies are wont to do; but it is also an evil opinion that brings useless servitude. En Christō Iēsou (in Christ Jesus), that is, through Christ Jesus, who gave us full knowledge of this liberty, when before the effect of the matter [was]... oude pros hōran (not even for an hour), not even for the shortest time, as in 2 Corinthians VII. verse 8, 1 Thessalonians II. verse 17, Philemon v. 15, 17. Hypotagē (subjection), that is, in such a way that we would not acknowledge that the pious from among the Gentiles were subject to that yoke.

By no means to be admitted, the pronoun hois [is] an error of the scribe [for] parelthein. Verse 4 can be referred to 3, that nothing was brought in by the Apostles, to whom they would not yield even for an hour. Camerarius: "But because of the false brethren and those who came among them, and let the elders read among them." And soon "to whom not even for an hour," instead of "to whom not even for an hour." I wonder that many labor here over Erasmus, because Paul's speech is imperfect, whereas all the parts consist very well, and se is taken for dē. Justinian, Cornelius, and Glassius in Grammat. 5, page 573, agree with this interpretation.

That Tertullian, in book V against Marcion, chapter 3, renders pareisaktous as "superinductitios" (those brought in over and above). Chrysostom correctly explains it regarding those who had been furtively introduced or had entered in the manner of spies into the Church. Spies, says his epitomizer, Theophylact, sent forth, undergo a clandestine entry into the camp for no other reason than that, having perceived the conditions of the enemies, they may be able to destroy and subdue them more easily. Which, indeed, these men were also doing. For what kind of men were the circumcised through servitude, who had liberty in Christ—that is, who were by no means subject to the law—so that they might detect them, and once known, be circumcised, and bind us with the consecrated servitude of the law, from which Christ exempted us. From this, therefore, it is clear that the Apostles permitted those things which were of the law, so that they might gradually be withdrawn from the servitude of the law: these men, however, on the contrary, were plotting to stabilize such servitude. Which Irenaeus in book III, chapter 3, Tertullian in book V against Marcion, chapter 3, and Ambrose in Tom. II affirmatively read, "to whom we yielded for an hour," [but this is] supported by neither the Greek Codices, nor most Latin ones later than Jerome, nor the Syriac versions, and [it is] contrary to the purpose, and he is entirely concerned with teaching that one must not yield to false brethren who strive to spy out the liberty brought forth by Christ. And therefore the Greeks, Chrysostom, Theodorus, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, and among the Latins, Jerome and Augustine, read the negative. He calls it the TRUTH OF THE GOSPEL, that is, the doctrine concerning CHRIST, the only Mediator, and gratuitous justification through Him. So that it may remain with you, for among them it was in peril. En Christō is not "who gave us full knowledge of this liberty," but "who brought it to us": For by His advent and passion the ceremonies were abolished, which He prefigured.

ANNOTATA AD GALATAS CAP. II. v. 4. 6.

debat convenire. Et illi prudentes accufantesque, quod legem non servaret, non circumcideret gentes &c. volebant cum cogere, quam vocat hic subjectionem, ut libertatem per Christum partam, nobis extorquere & servitutem. Est enim libertas illa, quam in Christo nos habere gloriatur, quod nulli prorsus uni externo operi sumus alligati, sed liberi in quodlibet, ad quemlibet, quocunque tempore & modo, nisi ubi fraterna pax & charitas ostenditur, sicut Roman. XIII. nulli quisquam debeatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis.

Vers. 4. Διὰ δὲ τὰς παρεισάκτους ψευδαδέλφους οἵτινες παρεισῆλθον κατασκοπῆσαι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν ἡμῶν, ἣν ἔχομεν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἵνα ἡμᾶς καταδουλώσωνται· οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν εἴξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ εὐαγγελίου διαμείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς.) In Manuscripto Σιναϊτικῷ, Apparet autem illis illud hic παρεισάκτους, aut abundantia sermonis, non infrequentia Hebraizis, aut exscribentis errore. Senfus est: At illorum Judæorum causa, qui se Christianos simulabant, ut libertatem, per Christum partam, nobis extorquerent, nihil cessimus de proposito ejus libertatis, & tuendæ, & ad vos omnes transmittendæ; παρεισάκτους sunt, qui παρεισῆλθον Judæ 4. ita dicuntur, qui se arte insinuant, subintroducunt, subinferunt. Simile παρεισάκτους & Σιναϊτικῷ & Λαμβέρτεια. Vide quæ dicta Actor. XV. 34. 2. Petr. II. vers. 1. ψευδαδέλφους vocem habemus & 2. Corinth. XI. vers. 26. explorandi verbum apparet esse castrense. Significat autem hic per καταδουλώσωνται, specie amicitiæ malum alii struere, ut solent exploratores, est autem malum etiam opinio servitutem afferens inutilem.
