Ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, id est, per Christum Jesum, qui nobis hujus libertatis plenam notitiam fecit, cum ante rei effectum troverfæ, οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν, ne ad minimum quidem tempus, ut 2. Corinth. VII. vers. 8. 1. Thessal. II. vers. 17. Philemon. v. 15. 17. ὑποταγῇ, id est, ita, ut non agnosceremus, pios ex gentibus isti jugo esse obnoxios.

Nullatenus admittendum, Pronomen οἷς exscribentis errore παρελθειν. Potest versus 4. referri ad 3. quod Tim. neque ab Apostolis quidquam subintroductum, quibus ne ad horam quidem cederent. Camerarius: Διὰ δὲ τὰς παρεισάκτους ψευδαδέλφους καὶ ἐλθόντας ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀναγνωσθῆναι δὲ πρεσβυτέρους ἀναγινώσκειν ἐν αὐτοῖς. Et mox οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν, ἀντὶ οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν. Erasmum plures miror hic laborare, quod Pauli fermo sit imperfectus, & quum omnes partes optime constent, & se pro δὴ accipiatur. Cui interpretationi annuunt Justinianus, Cornelius, Glaffius in Grammat. 5. pag. 573.

Quod παρεισάκτους Tertullianus libr. V. contra Marcionem cap. 3. superinductitios reddit. Chryfostomus recte exponit de iis, qui furtim introducti aut ingressi erant exploratorum more, in Ecclesiam. Exploratores, inquit epitomator ejus, Theophylactus, dimissi, nihil ob aliud clandestino ingressu fubeunt castra, nisi ut hostium perspectis condicionibus delere illos & subigere queant facilius. Quod sane & hi faciebant. Nam quales essent circumcisi per servitutem, qui in Christo haberent libertatem, hoc est, qui nequaquam legi subjecti essent, ut eos deprehendant, cognitaque circumcidi, & nos sacrato legis servitute obstringant, qua Christus exemit. Inde igitur liquet, Apostolos ea permisisse, quæ legis essent, ut se pedetentim a legis subtraberentur servitute: Hi vero contra, ut servitutem hujusmodi stabilirent, machinabantur. Quod Irenæus libr. III. cap. 3. Tertullianus libr. V. contra Marcionem cap. 3. & Ambrosius. affirmative Tom. II. legunt, quibus ad horam cessimus, nec Codicibus Græcis, nec Latinis plerisque Hieronymo posterioribus, nec Syriace versiones competi & proposito candidiffe, & in eo totus est, ut doceat non cedendum esse falsis fratribus, libertatem a Christo partam, explorare contendentibus. Ideoque negativam legunt & Græci, Chrysostomus, Theodorus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius, & inter Latinos Hieronymus & Augustinus. VERITATEM autem EVANGELII dicit, id est doctrinæ de CHRISTO, unico Mediatore, & gratuita per illum justificatione. Ut apud vos permaneat, apud ipsos enim periclitabatur. Ἐν χριστῷ non est, qui libertatis hujus plenam notitiam nobis fecit, sed qui eam nobis attulit: Nam adventu & passione ejus ceremoniæ sublata sunt, quam ille figurabant.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. (But of those who seemed to be somewhat, whatsoever they were, it makes no difference to me; God accepts no man's person; for they who seemed to be, added nothing to me.) In the Manuscript: "God accepts no man's person." See what was said on Acts X. v. 34. But these things must be written from "the apostles" up to "accept" through pareisaktous. The Apostle began the speech in such a way as if he were about to say "from those who seemed to be somewhat, they added nothing to me," but having interjected pareisaktous, he repeats the word "from those who seemed to be somewhat," that is, "from those who seemed to be somewhat," and added "they added nothing to me," that is, they added nothing of authority or of knowledge, of course; you have a similar transition in Ephesians I. v. 13 and often elsewhere. Dokountōn is those who seemed to be something great, thus 1 Corinthians III. v. 7, 2 Corinthians III. verse 5; thus on the contrary [it means] nothing great, 1 Corinthians VIII. verse 4, just as James and John, 1 Corinthians I. verse 28. He is dealing with those who were thought to be the most learned among the Christians in Judea; but what kind of men they are (for "themselves" here is for an indefinite time, and it is possible that some of them were dead when Paul wrote these things) he denies that he is anxious about that, since God does not attend to such things in the matter of salvation; for the word "person" is taken here as in 2 Corinthians V. verse 12, X. v. 7, see the things said there, "my brothers, friends, I do not care," [says] the Syrian.

There is no need for a change of the received reading, which is entirely correct. Regarding the brothers, the speech, however, as Grotius advised, others have similarly advised: Erasmus, Beza, Camerarius, Schmid. Camerarius has it thus: Hopoioi pote ēsan (whatsoever they were). Doubled pareisaktous and Sinaitic 18, diplologia, gar, in this way, (whatsoever they were indeed), for this is nothing to me, for GOD does not respect the person of those masters, nor does it make more, it does not make more. Those therefore who seemed to be something, changed nothing in my doctrine by their disputations. But it is an allologikē epanalēpsis (an alternative repetition) of what he had said. Whatsoever they were indeed, and this is enallagmenē, that is, the form of speech is now different, passing from the Genitive to the Nominative. For it was a simple apologia, "from those who seemed to be somewhat, they added nothing to me." Simply, however, the sense seems to be here, according to which there is no need for parenthesis, nor ellipsis, nor epanalepsis, nor enallage, or any other form of speech, and the preposition apo may be rendered "OF," and be understood of the object, as is noted by the blessed Glassius, Gram. 5, p. 358. But of those (or as regards those) who are considered to be of great authority, whatsoever they were formerly, it is no concern of mine: God does not look upon the person of men: For those men, conspicuous in authority, communicated nothing to me. Which sense the German version of the blessed Luther expressed. That no others than the Apostles are understood here is the common opinion of all, from which Grotius departs without cause. Some, however, with Augustine, wish to refer to their previous life, which was an object for Paul, which was not done by others, because he says: Their life... To scrutinize the past is not my business, nor does it pertain to the matter; others [refer it to] the former condition, that they were once cast down, who are not held in esteem, such as the unlearned, fishermen; which is the opinion of Ambrosiaster, Thomas, Cajetan, and most of the Latins. Others [refer it to] the doctrine which they once held, whether they had observed the law, and taught by their examples that it should be observed, or not, with Chrysostom: Which, however, does not please Augustine when disputing with Jerome. For it is not to be thought that Paul found fault with anything in the doctrine of Peter and the other Apostles.

B.

Luther, whom we do not contradict, prefers to refer it to dignity in this way: What kind of men they were ought to be referred to dignity, and it was said against the Pseudo-Apostles, who boasted of the glory of the Apostles, that they had conversed with CHRIST, had seen, heard, and received everything while Christ was present, and therefore were to be preferred to Paul, and that the law was to be kept with them. Paul, however, blaming the Apostles for nothing, and admitting that the things which are objected are true, meets them with an excellent and most wholesome response, namely, that all this, by which they themselves are puffed up, pertains nothing to the matter. For a thing is not true or good because it is done or brought forth by a great or holy person, or by anyone at all, but because it proceeds from GOD alone. For what did it profit Judas the traitor to have conversed with Christ, and to have had everything in common with the Apostles? In vain, therefore, do they boast of the mask and external glory of the Apostles against the Word of GOD, which God reveals and teaches without that person.

If God despised the person of the Apostleship in Judas, certainly He did not accept it in others either. But that [phrase], "for those who seemed to be something, contributed nothing to me," Estius rightly explained with most Interpreters thus: In that communication which I had concerning my Gospel with the chief Apostles, they contributed nothing to me, that is, I received nothing from them, I learned nothing, nothing accrued to me through that collation. For the preposition πρὸς, added to the front of the Greek verb which he said above, "I communicated" (contuli), seems to signify some accession resulting from the collation. Whence also Augustine reads this passage thus: "For those who seem to be something, added nothing to me"; and Chrysostom and Theophylact explain it in this sense, as do almost all the Latins.

He adds that Valla also approves of that sense, and follows Erasmus in the paraphrase, although in his annotations he had previously taught differently, not without Valla’s criticism. Beza rendered it, "they communicated nothing further with me." But he explained the same thing in the same way in his notes. Namely, he says, I do not say this rashly or arrogantly, but because in truth they did not presume to add anything to those things which I had previously received from Christ and taught among the Gentiles. For this is the notation of the verb προσανέθετο, which Budaeus wrongly interprets in his Commentaries as "they communicated nothing, but on the contrary abhorred me." For he neglected the preposition πρὸς, and wrongly believed that Paul is here dealing with that which is narrated in Acts.

IX. 26. Flacius also aptly [notes] here: The Holy Spirit surely foresaw that there would come those who, under the pretext of the praises of Peter and his fictitious primacy, would pervert the truth of the Gospel, oppress the liberty of the Church, and preach a plainly different Gospel. Wherefore he here timely broke and rejected such boasting of persons or prerogatives. But what would Paul say if he now saw these wolves, tyrannizing over the whole Church of God for the sake of I know not what empty name of the chair of the see of Peter, and overturning the whole of Christianity from the foundations? Observe, indeed, that Paul also sought or received nothing at all from Peter: therefore there was plainly no primacy of his over the other Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 6. (Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, ὁποῖοί ποτε ἦσαν οὐδέν μοι διαφέρει, πρόσωπον Θεὸς οὐ λαμβάνει· οἱ γὰρ δοκοῦντες οὐδέν μοι προσανέθεντο.) In Manuscripto: Πρόσωπον Θεὸς οὐ λαμβάνει. Vide quæ dicta Actor. X. v. 34. Scribenda autem sunt ista ab ἀποστόλοις, usque ad λαμβάνειν per παρεισάκτους. Cæterat ita instituere sermonem Apostolus, quasi dicturus esset ἀπὸ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι οὐδέν μοι προσανέθεντο, sed interjecta παρεισάκτους repetit vocem ἀπὸ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, id est, ἀπὸ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, & subintulit οὐδέν μοι προσανέθεντο, id est, addiderunt aut autoritatis, aut cognitionis scilicet; similem transitum habes Ephes. I. v. 13. & alibi sæpe. Δοκοῦντων & id est, qui magni aliquid esse videbantur, sic 1. Corinth. III. v. 7. 2. Corinth. III. vers. 5. sic contra id est, nihil magni, 1. Corinth. VIII. vers. 4. quomodo & Ἰακώβ & Ἰωάννης, 1. Corinth. I. vers. 28. agit de illis, qui in Judæa inter Christianos doctissimi putabantur; quales autem sunt (nam ipsos hic est pro indefinito tempore, & fieri potest, ut qui dam eorum, cum scriberet hæc Paulus, mortui fuerint) de eo negat se esse sollicitum, cum Deus in salutis negotio talia non attendat; πρόσωπον enim vox hic sumitur, ut 2. Corinth. V. vers. 12. X. v. 7. ibi dicta vide ἀδελφοί μου, φίλοι, non curo, Syrus.

Non opus mutatione receptæ lectionis, quæ omnino recte se habet. De fratribus sermonem vero quod monuit Grotius, similiter & monuerunt alii, Erasmus, Beza, Camerarius, Sibmidius. Camerarius ita habet: Ὁποῖοί ποτε ἦσαν) Duplicata παρεισάκτους & Σιναϊτικῷ 18. διπλολογία, γαρ, hoc quodam modo, (qualescunque sane illi fuerint) nihil enim hoc mea refert, nam personam DEUS non moram illis dominis, nec magis efficit non magis efficit. Qui effe igitur aliquid videbantur, & nihil in mea doctrina mutarunt disputationibus suis. Est autem ἀλλολογικὴ ἐπανάληψις ejus quod dixerat. Qualescunque sane illi fuerint, & est ἐνναλλαγμένη hac, id est, alia jam sit forma sermonis, transeuntis a Genitivo ad Nominativum. Erat enim simplex ἀπολογία, ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, οὐδέν μοι προσανέθεντο. Simpliciter tamen videtur hic sensus, juxta quem nec parenthesi, nec ellipsi, nec epanalepsi, nec enallage, vel alia sermonis forma opus est, & Præpositio ἀπὸ reddatur DE, & de objecto intelligatur, uti a B. Glaffio accipi notatur Gram. 5. p. 358. De iis vero (vel quod ad eos) qui autoritatis magnæ esse censentur, quales quondam illi fuerint, mea non interest: Personam Deus hominum non suspicit: Mihi enim illi autoritate conspicui nihil communicarunt. Quem sensum expressit B. Lutheri versio Germanica. Intelligi autem hic non alios, quam Apostolos, communis fore omnium est sententia, a qua citra causam discedit Grotius. Respicci vero nonnulli cum Augustino vitam eorum antecedaneam volunt, quod objectum Paulo fuerit, quod ab aliis non factum, quod dicat: Vitam eorum (22) 3 prateritam scrutari non est meum, neque ad rem facit; alii conditionem pristinam, quod fuerint aliquando abjecti, qui non sunt in pretio, utpote idiotae, piscatores; quae Ambrosiiastri, Thomae, Cajetani, & Latinorum plerorumque est sententia. Alii doctrinam, quam illi olim tenuerunt, an legem observarant, & exemplis observandam docuerint, nec ne, cum Chrysostomo: Quod vero Augustino cum Hieronymo disputanti non placet. Neque enim existimandum est, Paulum in Petri & aliorum Apostolorum doctrina quicquam reprehendisse.

B.

Lutheri, cui non abnuimus, placet id ad dignitatem referre hoc modo: Quales fuerint, ad dignitatem referri debet, & dictum est in Pseudo-Apostolos, qui Apostolorum gloriam jactabant, quod cum CHRISTO conversati essent, omnia vidissent, audissent, accepissent, Christo praesente, ideoque Paulo preferendos legemque, cum illis servandam. Paulus autem Apostolos nihil vituperans, & vera esse, qua objiciuntur, admittens, optima & saluberrima eis obviat responsione, scilicet totum hoc nihil ad rem pertinere, quo ipsi inflantur. Non enim ideo verum aut bonum aliquid est, quia a magno, sancto, aut cujusque tandem personae fit, profertur, sed quia a solo DEO proficiscitur. Quid enim Jude traditori profuit, cum Christo fuisse conversatum, & omnia cum Apostolis communia habuisse? Frustra ergo larvam, & externam Apostolorum gloriam illi jactant adversus Verbum DEI, quod Deus fine ista persona revelat & docet.

Si personam Apostolatus in Juda despexit Deus, certe nec in aliis eam accepit. Illa autem, mihi enim qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil contulerunt, recte cum plerisque Interpretibus ita exposuit Estius: Mihi in illa communicatione, quam de Evangelio meo cum praecipuis Apostolis habui, nihil illi contulerunt, id est, nihil ab eis accepi, nihil didici, nihil per eam collationem mihi accessit. Nam accessionem aliquam collatione provenientem significare videtur praepositio πρὸς a fronte addita Graeco verbo, quod superius dixit, contuli. Unde & Augustinus hunc locum ita legit: Mihi enim qui videntur aliquid, nihil apposuerunt; & in hunc sensum Chrysostomus & Theophylactus exponunt, ac Latini fere omnes.

Addit & Vallam illum sensum probare, & Erasmum sequi in paraphrasi, cum in annotationibus suis antea diversum docuisset non absque Valla reprehensione. Beza reddidit, nihil mecum praeterea contulerunt. Sed eodem modo eadem exposuit in notis. Nempe, inquit, hoc non temere, nec arroganter dico, sed quoniam revera illi nihil presumpserunt iis adjicere, quae prius a Christo acceperam & docueram inter gentes. Hac enim notatio est verbi προσανέθε-το, quod perperam Budaeus in Commentariis interpretatur nihil communicarunt, sed contra a me abhorruerunt. Neglexit enim praepositionem πρὸς, & male credidit Paulum hic agere de eo, quod narratur Act.

IX. 26. Opportune etiam hic Flacius: Pravidit nimirum Spiritus sanctus, venturos olim, qui sub praetextu encomiorum Petri & commentitiis ejus primatus, veritatem Evangelii pervertant, & libertatem Ecclesiae opprimant, & plane aliud Evangelium praedicent. Quare hic mature talem personarum jactationem aut praerogativas fregit rejecitque. Quid autem diceret Paulus, si jam videret istos lupos, ob nescio quod inane nomen cathedrae sedis Petri, super totam Ecclesiam Dei tyrannizantes, & totum Christianismum funditus evertentes? Observa vero, quod etiam Paulus nihil prorsus a Petro petiit aut accepit: igitur nullus plane ejus primatus fuit super alios Apostolos.

## 2:7-8
Vers. 7. 8. 9. "But on the contrary, seeing that I have been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcision, just as Peter with that of the circumcision. (For He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision, worked also in me for the Gentiles.) And knowing the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship." First, in that most ancient Manuscript, the name of Cephas is not interposed between James and John, which I think is more correct. For it is sufficiently clear that the name of Peter, or Cephas, had preceded, and it is not the custom for him who is made the head of the college to be named in the middle place, but either first, as Matt. X. v. 2, or last, as Mark XVI. v. 7. Furthermore, ancient writers dealing with this passage name Peter in the first place.

There is also here a parenthesis, beginning from "For He who" and ending at "seeing," and a certain transposition. For according to the natural order of speaking, James and John ought to have been named with the participle "seeing." For the sense is: So far are those Jews from having contributed anything to me, either of authority or of knowledge, that they themselves, the chief in the Church, James and John, acknowledged me as not inferior, but a colleague, and as such gave me the right hand. For to give the right hand among the Hebrews is a sign of society, as it seems, Levit. VI. v. 2, Jerem. I. v. 5. But when they did this, he brings forward the cause, because both James and John saw that things no less were accomplished through Paul among the Gentiles than through Peter himself among the Jews, so that Paul had nothing for which he should yield anything to others, or to Peter himself, in the Apostolic office.

But that "energy" and "grace given" pertain both to miracles and to the conversion of a huge number of men. But what Paul says here, that the apostleship of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter, and to himself that of the uncircumcised, is to be understood as "for the most part," or "as prevailing." For Peter also converted Cornelius, an uncircumcised man, and Paul [converted] some Jews, as we learn from the Acts. See Acts IX. v. 15, but the chief effort for Peter was around the Jews, for Paul around the other Gentiles. But Peter’s helpers and as it were endorsers were, for the most part, James and John: but for Paul, Barnabas, and he himself was divinely called to this, whom therefore the Greeks not badly name the fourteenth Apostle. That dative "to Peter," as also "to me," is governed by the preposition "in," which is in the verb "worked in."

He says, however, of James and John, "who seemed to be pillars," because the Church was believed to be supported by those two as if by columns: such columns as the Greeks call "parastatas." Paul seems to allude to those columns which were in the temple of Solomon, 2 Chron. III, 17. We have taken "uncircumcision" for uncircumcised men, Romans II. 25.

"That we to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision." In the Manuscript [it is] "we indeed." There is also here an ellipsis, which will be best supplied: "might perform the apostleship," namely from that "apostleship" which had already preceded. Flacius notes an emphasis in the verb "I have been entrusted." Observe that in the phrase "the Gospel" there exists a singular emphasis. For there is indicated here both the excellence and the difficulty of the Evangelical ministry, and finally, with what faith it must be handled. Grotius again relies most poorly on the faith of one MS against all other Greek, Latin, Syriac, etc., codices. His reason, that Peter was the head of the Apostolic college, which he borrowed from the Papists, as he did many other things, is a begging of the question.

Nor did Estius here observe the diversity among the Ancients in the order, who diligently compared the various readings of the ancients. He rather gives the reason why James was named first, and he equates Paul and even Barnabas to Peter as Co-Apostles: "They gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas my colleague," i.e., as partners in the apostleship, and well agreeing with them in the doctrine of the Gospel, and they received them as such. For to join right hands was a symbol of society and concord. Paul therefore signifies that he and Barnabas were received by those highest Apostles, not as disciples, such as Titus and the others who had stood with them were acknowledged, but as Co-Apostles and equals in the ministry of the Gospel. Furthermore, he names James in the first place for the honor of the Lord, whose brother he was, and because he was the Bishop of Jerusalem, where these things were being done, and he was of the greatest name among the Jews for his holiness. opinion of the state, as is clear from Josephus and Hegesippus. For what Augustine writes, that those three named by Paul were present at the Lord's transfiguration, understanding namely James the brother of John, which is also read in a certain homily of the Sabbath after the first Sunday of Lent, among those which are falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa; it is a manifest lapse of memory. For it is certain that James, the brother of John, had been killed by the sword of Herod long before the Council of Jerusalem. Nor does Paul speak of any other James than the one he mentioned in the chapter above, and who spoke his opinion in the council held at Jerusalem.

This is Estius. Whence Blessed Luther in his first Commentary, f. 12: There were not yet in the Church these contentions about the preeminence of Churches and Pontiffs. Peter, John, James do not disdain Paul and Barnabas as their associates and equals, but with the passage of time and of vices (as Jerome says) the society declines into power and preeminence. It is very memorable, says Flacius, that the fact of the society entered into between Paul, James, Peter, and John is explained in the following 4 verses, which clearly shows that the other Apostles not only approved of the doctrine and vocation of Paul, but also acknowledged him as their equal, because they enter into society with him as with a colleague, but as a superior, because they concede to him a more arduous function and a wider province as to one more suitable and divinely called and ordained for greater works.

Moreover, in this verse he narrates that they acknowledged and confessed that he was divinely called and ordained for this, that he should preach the Gospel of Christ among the Gentiles, and indeed that he was armed and instructed for this function both by gifts and by the presence of Christ, and that he had already most excellently administered this great province by his work.

Bellarmino, however, brings forward Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, who place Peter first. But the Commentary ascribed to Ambrose is not his, as the Papists themselves admit. Augustine, however, does not read "Peter and James" in the text. And who will assure us that that order is from Jerome? Chrysostom, at any rate, Theophylact, and Oecumenius retain one order in the text, as do Justinian and Estius from among the Papists.

Furthermore, although there have not been wanting those who made Cephas here someone other than Peter, Estius refutes them in this place: But whom he calls Cephas here, some call into doubt, because of that which he immediately adds about Cephas being rebuked by him, which they thought unworthy to be understood of Peter, the Prince of the Apostles. Therefore, they say that this Cephas rebuked by Paul was not the Apostle, but one of the LXX disciples of Christ, of the same name as Peter the Apostle. Eusebius reports this, book 1, book of Eccl. hist. ch. 12, from Clement of Alexandria, book 5 of the Hypotyposes, and again Oecumenius reports it from Eusebius in his Commentary, and Helor Pintus in Daniel 1 contends that this opinion is true by certain arguments. And indeed, those who have cataloged the LXX disciples have numbered a certain Cephas among them. But Jerome rightly rejects this opinion, without naming the authors, as a fabrication, denying that the name of any other Cephas was known to him, except for him who in the Gospel and in the epistles of Paul is written now as Cephas, now as Peter, with one and the same signification.

For what we call a rock in Latin and Greek, he says, the Hebrews and Syrians, because of the proximity of their languages to one another, call Cephas; concerning which whole argument the epistle, as the same Jerome says, is repugnant to this opinion. Nor could so obscure a disciple be compared with James and John, the chief Apostles, as a pillar of the Church. Nor does Paul act in such a way that he might appear to have been received into the society of the Apostolate by any of the disciples who were not Apostles, but by the Apostles themselves, and those primary ones.

St. Gregory refutes the same opinion from the context of scripture, homily 18 on Ezekiel. As for the word oi δοκῶντες, they seemed, Beza notes the emphasis here: oi δοκῶντες, i.e., those whom these men alone hold as pillars, as if I were of no account: in that indeed they themselves differ from them, whose authority they abuse to deceive you. See above v. 6. So also Flacius: Observe, however, at the same time, that he not obscurely taxes the opinion of men, who then held those three as pillars of the Church, and preferred them by far, wishing to sub-indicate that Christ alone is the base and the pillar and the cornerstone and the unique foundation of the Church, and that He preserves it in His own hand by divine power.

We acquiesce here, however, rather in Blessed Luther, whose opinion Chrysostom also handed down, when he says that he joins the common sense and judgment of all with the truth of the matter. By them also were thought to be pillars those who pressed Paul with their authority. Therefore he preferred to use the word δοκῶντες, so that he might the more strongly constrain their adversaries with their praised suffrage, whom they held as pillars.

Moreover, it is one thing to be the foundation upon which the Church is built, which is Christ, and another to be a pillar of the Church, serving for the sustaining or adorning of the structure of God. But it is manifest here, as Flacius also warns, that Peter was, both in fact and by divine right, and by the human law of the Jews, not the Apostle of the Gentiles throughout his whole life. What then does the Apostolate matter to us, who have been converted from the Gentiles? With this also agrees the memory of the time of the Acts of the Apostles and the epistle of Paul, which clearly and openly show that Peter never spent 25 years in Rome in the Episcopate or Papacy, as the Papists pretend.

For as often as Paul seeks Peter, he seeks him at Jerusalem, not at Rome: As often as he writes from there, or to there, and names so many Romans, he says nothing of Peter sitting there, or reigning in a triple crown. But Theophylact rightly expressed the argument and the connection: And so much so, he says, that my words were far from rebuking, that they even proved and agreed that he himself and Barnabas should preach the Gospel to the uncircumcision among the Gentiles, while they themselves should preach to the circumcision, to the Jews.

In the duty of preaching, (thus Chrysostom renders Paul's mind) we have divided the world among ourselves. If there had been war and contention among us, they would by no means have received them. Ver. 10. Μόνον τῶν πτωχῶν ἵνα μνημονεύωμεν) Of the poor, namely, who were in Judea. To remember is to take care of, Psalm 8:5, 106:4, Luke 23:42, and elsewhere. Peter, John, and James asked Paul and Barnabas that what they had already begun to do (see Acts 11:29), they should continue to do, collecting money from the Gentiles, by which the poverty of the Jews might be relieved. ὁ γὰρ ἰσχάδετα αὐτὸ τοῦτο ποίησαν) It is a Hebraism.

For the Hebrews after the relative שֶׁ add a demonstrative pronoun of the thing or person. Concerning the matter itself, see 1 Cor. 15:1, 2 Cor. 8. Observe, Flacius again warns, in such a sacred passion, that among the greatest matters, the care of the poor of Christ, who were at Jerusalem, was not the last, and that Paul was by no means unmindful of them. But God also willed this to be done for this reason, that by that means also the Gentiles might be admonished, whence they had received the Christian doctrine, so that the consensus of the Churches might be seen from it, and that he might satisfy the gifts from the Gentiles as the prophets promised. After the preaching of the Gospel, says B. Luther in his later Commentary, the remaining care of a good pastor is that he be mindful of the poor. For where the Church is, there it is necessary that there be poor, who also for the most part are the only true disciples of the Gospel.

That, in which I was also diligent, Schmidius rightly explains thus: But I have always done this studiously before now, so that there would have been no need for that admonition. Thus, clearly, they contributed nothing to my doctrine. There is also emphasis in the particle μόνον, lest anyone say that this was done after they had corrected the kind of Pauline doctrine, and he himself bound the faith, by proposing the Gospel in no other way than as they themselves prescribed; the Apostle anticipates, with a prudently expressed condition, which alone the Apostles agreed upon: Which, however, as we have said, there was no need for at all.

Latin:

Vers. 7. 8. 9. Ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον ἰδόντες, ὅτι πεπίστευμαι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς ἀκροβυστίας, καθὼς Πέτρος τῆς περιτομῆς. (Ὁ γὰρ ἐνεργήσας Πέτρῳ εἰς ἀποστολὴν τῆς περιτομῆς, ἐνήργησε καὶ ἐμοὶ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη.) Καὶ γνόντες τὴν χάριν, τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι, Ἰάκωβος καὶ Κηφᾶς, καὶ Ἰωάννης, οἱ δοκοῦντες στῦλοι εἶναι, δεξιὰς ἔδωκαν ἐμοὶ καὶ Βαρνάβᾳ κοινωνίας Primum in Manuscrito illo antiquissimo, non est interpositum, inter Jacobo & Johannis, nomen Cephae, quod rectius arbitror. Satis enim ruit praecessisse Petri, sive Cephae nomen, neque moris est, eum, qui princeps fit collegii, medio loco nominari, sed aut primo, ut Matth. X. v. 2. aut postremo, ut Marci XVI. vers. 7. Praeterea scriptores veteres, de hoc loco agentes, Petrum primo loco nominant.

Est autem & hic παρεμβολῆς, incipiens ab ὁ γὰρ, & desinens in ἴδην, & trajectio quaedam. Nam secundum naturalem loquendi ordinem Jacobus & Johannes nominari debuerant cum Participio ἰδόντες. Sensus enim est: Tantum abest, ut illi Judzi mihi quicquam contulerint, aut auctoritatis, aut notitiae, ipsi illi, in Ecclesia praecipui, Jacobus & Johannes, me non imparem, sed collegam agnovere, & ut tali dedere dextram. Nam dextram dare apud Hebraeos signum societatis, ut videtur est Levit. VI. vers. 2. Jerem. I. vers. 5. Hoc autem cum fecerint, causam adfert, quod viderent & Jacobus, & Johannes, res non minores effectas per Paulum apud gentes, quam per ipsum Petrum apud Judzos, ita ut nihil haberet Paulus, cur in Apostolico munere aut aliis, aut ipsi Petro cederet quicquam.

Illa autem ἐνέργεια, & χάριν δοθεῖσαν, tum ad miracula pertinent, tum ad ingentis hominum numeri conversionem. Quod autem dicit hic Paulus, creditum fuisse Petro Apostolatum circumcisionis, sibi autem incircumcisorum, id intelligendum est τὸ πολὺ, sive καὶ ἐπικράτου. Nam & Petrus Cornelium convertit, incircumcisum, & Paulus Judaeos nonnullos, ut ex Actis discimus. Vide A&or. IX. vers. 15. sed praecipuum studium erat Petro circa Judaeos, Paulo circa gentes alias. Petro autem adjutores & velut adstipulatores, plerumque, Jacobus, & Johannes: Paulo autem Barnabas, & ipse divinitus ad hoc vocatus, quem proinde Graeci non male Apostolum decimum quartum nominant. Dativus ille Petro ut & ἐμοὶ regitur a Praepositione ἐν, quae est in verbo ἐνήργησε.

Dicit autem de Jacobo & Johanne, οἱ δοκοῦντες στῦλοι εἶναι, quia Ecclesia superfedificata duobus illis, quasi columnis, sustentari credebatur: quales scilicet columnas Graeci παραστάτας vocant. Videtur autem Paulus alludere ad columnas illas, quae erant in templo Salomonis, 2. Paral. III, 17. ἀκροβυστία pro hominibus incircumcisis habuimus, Roman. II. 25.

"Ἵνα ἡμεῖς εἰς τὰ ἔθνη, αὐτοὶ δὲ εἰς τὴν περιτομὴν" In Manuscripto ἡμεῖς μὲν. Elt autem hic ἐκμονῆς, quae optime supplebitur: Apostolatu fungerentur, nempe ex illo ἀποστολὴν, quod jam praecesserat. In verbo προσέψευμαι emphasin notat Flacius. Observa in loquutione Evangelium concretum esse singularem emphasin existere. Subindicatur enim hic tum praestantia, tum & difficultas Evangelici ministerii, tum denique, quanta fide id tractandum sit. Pessime iterum unius fui MS. fide nititur Grotius contra omnes alios codices Graecos, Lati- nos, Syriacos & c. Ratio ejus quod Petrus princeps fit collegii Apostolici fuerit, quam a Papistis mutuo, ut git Codices. alias plurima, sumpsit, ἀἴησις est τῆ ἐν ἀρχῇ.

Neque hic diversitatem apud Veteres in ordine observavit Estius, qui diligenter varias veterum lectiones contulit. Causam potius reddit, cur Jacobus prius nominatus fit, & Paulum imo & Barnabam Petro aequat ut Co-Apostolos: Mihi & Barnaba collega meo dextras societatis dederunt, i.e. in Apostolatu socios, atque in Evangelii doctrina bene secum consentientes, & ut tales receperunt. Nam jungere dextras societatis & concordie symbolum erat. Significat ergo Paulus, se & Barnabam susceptos ab illis summis Apostolu, non ut discipulos, quales agnoscebant Titus & ceteri, qui cum ipsis astenderant, sed ut Co-Apostolos & in ministerio Evangelii pares. Porro Jacobum primo loco nominat ad honorem Domini, cujus erat frater, & quia Hierosolymorum Episcopus erat, ubi hac gerebantur, idemque maximi nominis apud Judaeos ob sanctitatem. tatis opinionem, ut liquet ex Iosepho & Egesippo. Nam quod Augustinus scribit, tres istos a Paulo nominatos Dominicae transfigurationi interfuisse, videlicet Iacobum intelligens fratrem Iohannis, quod & legitur in homil. quadam sabbati post Dom. I. quadrag. inter eas, quae Eusebii Emisseni falso feruntur; lapsus memoriae est manifestus. Constat enim Iacobum Iohannis fratrem multo ante concilium Hierosolymitanum gladio Herodis occubuisse. Nec utique de alio Iacobo Paulus loquitur, quam cuius superiori capite meminit, & qui in concilio Hierosolymis habito fensentiam dixit.

Haec Estius. Unde B. Lutherus in Comm. priori f. 12. Nondum erant in Ecclesia contentiones iste de praecellentia Ecclesiarum & Pontificum. Petrus, Iohannes, Iacobus non, dedignantur Paulum & Barnabam socios & aequales suos, sed successu temporis & vitiorum (ut ait Hieronymus) societas deficit in potestatem & praecellentiam. Valde memorabile, inquit Flacius, factum inita societatis inter Paulum, Iacobum, Petrum, & Iohannem sequentibus 4. versibus exponitur, quod liquido ostendit, alios Apostolos non solum comprobasse doctrinam & vocationem Pauli, sed etiam agnovisse, cum sibi parem, quia ineunt cum eo societatem, tanquam cum collega, superiorem vero, quia etiam magis arduam functionem, latioremque provinciam tanquam magis idoneo, & ad ampliora opera divinitus vocato ac ordinato concedunt.

Caeterum in hoc versu narrat, eos agnovisse & confessos esse, ipsum ad hoc divinitus vocatum & ordinatum esse, ut inter gentes Evangelion Christi praedicet, quin etiam ad hanc functionem tum donis, tum & praesentia Christi armatum instructumque esse, atque adeo jam opere suo praeclarissime hanc tantam provinciam administrasse.

Bellarminus tamen adducit Ambrosium, Augustinum & Hieronymum, qui Petrum praemittant. Sed Commentarius Ambrosio adscriptus eius non est, fatentibus Papistis. Augustinus vero in textu non legit Petrus & Iacobus. Et quis certos nos reddet ordinem illum esse ab Hieronymo? Chrysostomus utique Theophylactus, & Oecumenius retinent in textu unum ordinem, ut e Pontificiis Iustinianus, & Estius.

Porro etsi non defuerint, qui Cepham hic aliquem alium, quam Petrum fecerint, eos tamen Estius refellit hoc loco: Quem vero Cepham hic nominet, nonnulli vocant in dubium, propter illud maxime, quod statim subiungit de Cepba, a se reprehenso, quod de Petro, Apostolorum Principe intelligi, putaverunt indignum. Itaque Cepham hunc a Paulo reprehensum dicunt non Apostolum, sed ex LXX. Christi discipulis unum fuisse, eiusdem nominis cum Petro Apostolo. Refert hoc Eusebius, libr. 1. biss. Eccl. cap. 12. ex Clementis Alexandr. libr. 5. hypotyp. ac rursum ex Eusebio refert Oecumenius in Commentario, eamque sententiam Helor Pintus in Dan. I. quibusdam argumentis veram esse contendit. Ac sane qui LXX. discipulorum catalogum sexuerunt, Cepham quendam inter eos numerarunt. Sed opinionem hanc, tacito autorum nomine, velut commentitiam merito reijcit Hieronymus, negans cuiusquam alterius Cepha nomen sibi cognitum esse, praeterquam eius, qui in Evangelio & in epistolis Pauli modo Cephas modo Petrus scribitur, una prorsus eademque significatione.

Quam enim, inquit, nos Latine & Graece petram nominamus, hanc Hebraei & Syri, propter linguae inter se viciniam, Cepham nuncupant; de quod totum argumentum epistola, ut idem, ait Hieronymus, huic opinioni repugnat. Neque enim tam obscurus discipulus cum Iacobo & Iohanne praecipuis Apostolis, tanquam Ecclesia columna comparari potuit. Neque Paulus hoc agit, ut in societatem Apostolatus ab aliquo discipulorum, qui non erant Apostoli, receptus videatur, sed ab ipsis Apostolis, iisque primariis.

Eandem opinionem ex contextu scripturae refellit S. Gregorius hom. 18. in Ezech. Quod ad verbum oi δοκῶντες videbantur, Beza hic emphasin notat: oi δοκῶντες sc. id est quos solos isti pro columnis habent, quasi ego fine nihili: in eo quidem ab illis ipsi diffidentes, quorum autoritate ad vos decipiendos abutuntur. Vide fupra v. 6. Ita & Flacius: Observa vero simul, quod non obscure taxet opinionem hominum, qui tunc illos tres pro columnis Ecclesiae habuerunt, ac ipsi longissime praetulerunt, volens subindicare, solum Christum esse basin, & columnam, angularemque lapidem ac fundamentum unicum Ecclesiae, eumque illam in sua manu divina potentia conservare.

Acquiescimus autem hic potius B. Lutheri, cuius sententiam & Chrysostomus tradidit, cum rei veritate, inquiens, communem omnium sensum atque iudicium coniungit. Ab is etiam putabantur esse columnae, qui Paulum illorum premebant autoritate. Ideo maluit verbo δοκῶντες uti, ut eo fortius stringeret adversarios eorum laudato suffragio, quos illi pro columnis habebant.

Caeterum aliud est fundamentum, super quod extruitur Ecclesia, quod est Christus, aliud columna Ecclesiae, inserviens Dei tuftendandae vel ornandae structurae. Manifestum autem hic est, eodem Flacio monente, Petrum tum de facto, tum de iure divino, ac humano iudeorum, non gentium Apostolum per totam vitam fuisse. Quid ergo ad nos Apostolatus, quâ ex gentibus sumus conversi? Cum hoc quoque convenit memoria temporis Actorum Apostolicorum & epistolae Pauli, quae dilucide & aperte ostendunt, Petrum nunquam 25. annos Romae Epifopatu vel Papatu perfunctum esse, ut Papistae fingunt.

Quoties enim Paulus Petrum quaerit, Hierosolymis cum quaerit, non Romae: Toties & tam multa Romana aut inde scribit, & tam multos Romanos nominat, nec tamen quicquam de Petro ibi sedente, aut in triplici corona regnante dicit. Argumentum autem & συνέχειαν recte Theophylactus expressit: Et adeo, inquit, ut dicta mea reprehenderent, longe ab abfuere, ut etiam probarent & convenirent ut ipse quidem & Barnabas in praeputium inter gentes Evangelium vulgarem, ipsi vero in circumcisionem obesset, Iudaeis evangelizarent.

In praedicandimunere, (ita Chrysostomus reddit Pauli mentem) partiti sumus internos orbem terrarum. Si bellum fuisset internos & contentio, nequaquam illi recepissent. Vers. 10. Μόνον τῶν πτωχῶν ἵνα μνημονεύωμεν) Pauperum scilicet, qui in Iudaea. Meminisse est curam gerere, Psalm. VIII. 5. CVI. 4. Luc. XXIII. 42. & alibi. Rogarunt Petrus, Iohannes, Iacobus, Paulum & Barnabam, ut quod facere jam coeperant, (vide Actor. XI. 29.) id porro facerent, ex gentibus pecuniam colligentes, quibus Iudaeorum egestas sublevaretur. ὁ γὰρ ἰσχάδετα αὐτὸ τοῦτο ποίησαν) Hebraismus est.

Nam Hebrai post relativum שֶׁ addunt pronomen demonstrativum rei aut personae. De re ipsa vide 1. Cor. XV. 1. 2. Cor. VIII. Observa, monente iterum Flacio, in tam sacra passione, de rebus longe maximis non postremam curam habitam pauperum Christi, qui erant Hierosolymis, eorumque Paulum nequaquam immemorem fuisse. Hoc vero etiam ideo voluit Deus fieri, ut ea quoque ratione gentiles admonerentur, unde doctrinam Christianam accepissent, ut item consensus Ecclesiarum inde conspiceretur, atque prophetis pollicentibus munera a gentilibus satisfaceret. Post predicationem Evangelii, inquit B. Lutherus Comment. poster. reliqua cura boni pastoris est, ut fit memor pauperum. Nam ubi Ecclesia est, ibi necesse est, pauperes esse, qui & plerumque soli veri sunt discipuli Evangelii. Illud, in quo & diligens fui, recte Schmidius ita exponit: Sed hoc jam antea semper studiose feci, ut illa admonitione opus non fuisset.

Ita plane nihil doctrina mea contulerunt. Emphasis etiam est in particula μόνον, ne dicat quis, id factum postquam correxerunt doctrinae Paulinae genus, ac fidem ipse obstrinxit, de non aliter proponendo Evangelio, quam ut ipsi praescripsere; praeoccupat Apostolus, prudenter expressa conditione, quam solam Apostoli pacti: Qua vero, uti diximus, minime opus fuerat.

## 2:11
Verse 11. "Οτε δὲ ἦλθε Πέτρος εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν) In the Manuscript here again πᾶς. It seems to signify that time, of which in Acts XIII. L The time is uncertain to others: whether this Antiochene action was prior to the Jerusalem journey, or whether it was later? Augustine, epistle XIX, which is to Jerome, makes it prior.

Others judge it later, because of the order of the Pauline narrative present here, and because from Acts XV it appears that after the Jerusalem council was finished, Paul immediately returned to Antioch, and so it is likely that Peter also arrived there, and that these things happened there then. Which, however, could also have happened when Paul left Antioch again, Acts XVIII.

On the other hand, it is hardly likely that after the council the Jews and Gentiles did not acquiesce, or that Peter himself had wavered so. But that Antioch of Syria, and not Pisidia, is understood, there is no doubt. Κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστη) I disapproved of his counsel to his face. For κατὰ πρόσωπον is 'to the face', which is also accustomed to be translated as ἐνώπιον, and ἔναντι, and is often accustomed to be placed with ἀπέναντι, as Deut.

VIII. 24, IX. 2, John I. 5. But ἀντίον here is to be understood in friendly words. For בְּפָנִים, which is not even to answer, is translated by ἀντιστάν. "Οτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν) κατεγνωσμένος often is nothing other than 'to disapprove less', among Demosthenes, Aeschines, and others, and κατεγνωσμένος here is, in the Hebrew manner, a participle for the verbal noun καταγνωσίς.

Not only to his face, which the emphasis of this word imports, is he said to have resisted him, and not only does the response made in bland words rely on this, but resistance, and contradiction, of which Theophylact says: That he resisted him to the face, and as if by agreement, as the Jews, then contention. But one must not assent to Jerome, who held that this contention and rebuke of Peter was only feigned, and dispensatory, and as if done by agreement, so that the Jews, whose authority moved Peter most, seeing Peter himself yielding to the rebuking Paul, might be healed from the error concerning the necessity of the observation of the law for salvation.

Therefore Augustine contradicted Jerome, showing that this was a true rebuke, and that Peter was entirely blameworthy, because he was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, while by his simulation, by which he withdrew himself from the company of the Gentiles and kept the legal observances, he even compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, see Jerome, epistle 86 and following up to 97.

Augustine, epistle 8 and following up to 19. Jerome indeed appeals to Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris, Eusebius of Emesa, and Theodore of Heraclea, but almost all of them, as Thomas notes, are marked by the Fathers for the heresy of perverse doctrine.

But Augustine brings forward for himself Cyprian, epistle LXXI to Quirinus, to whose opinion also were added Tertullian, book V against Marcion, ch. 3, Ambrosiaster on this place, Gregory the Great, book XXVIII of Morals, ch. 12 and homily XII on Ezekiel, and almost all the Latins. And Estius observes that Jerome himself conceded to Augustine's opinion, and obliquely retracted his own opinion, that Peter did not sin in that for which he was rebuked by Paul, in his Dialogue against the Pelagians, book 1, ch.

8. Which retraction of his, Augustine himself observed in epistle CCLX to Oceanus, as also in book III of Jerome's Apology against Rufinus, ch. 1, and concerning these see Thomas in this place, and in the Summa I-II, q. 103, art. 4, ad 2, and II-II, q. 33, art. 4, ad 2, and q. 43, art. 6, ad 2, where he teaches that Peter sinned entirely, and in what he sinned.

Whence Estius confesses that he cannot accede to the opinion of certain others, who, while recognizing a serious rebuke here with Augustine and the other Latins, nevertheless strongly deny that anything was sinned by Peter, such as Erasmus and some other later writers. Therefore, we can here compare Estius with these more recent ones, especially Baronius, who at length in the year LI contends that Peter sinned entirely. To whom Grotius wished to lend support here, that Paul responded to Peter's counsel only with friendly words, or warned him of something, or disapproved of it less.

Which, however, could not please even the Papists themselves. Since Paul explicitly argues that Peter did not walk with a straight foot, according to the truth of the Gospel, and resisted him to his face. ἀνθιστάν - ἀντίστασιν. For 'vay' is to resist, to oppose, to set oneself against, by the force of the word and the usage of the same received.

The word κατεγνωσμένος is καταγνώσεως ἄξιος, as Camerarius has it, in which Adam Sasbouth notes the Hebrew phrase, which becomes frequent, indeed perpetual, for the Hebrews, so that what we express by a verbal noun of the passive voice, they signify by a passive participle, e.g., 'loved' for 'lovable', etc. 2 Sam. I. 23, Psalm LXXXIII. 1, etc., so that he said 'rebuked' for 'reprehensible', just as Jerome rendered this perpetually, which word therefore presupposes a state worthy of rebuke and condemnation.

Chrysostom called it ἐπιταλῆν ἐπιτιμησιν Φοδεστέραν. Oecumenius σφοδρὰν τῆς ἐπιτιμήσεως. Therefore Bellarmine, book I on the Roman Pontiff, ch. 27, §. The Apostle Peter, he says, because he was the Apostle of the Jews especially, wished to offend the Gentiles rather than the Jews. But Paul disapproved of that choice, and rebuked Peter QUITE SHARPLY.

Salmero, Disp. XXII on Gal. II. The fault, he says, of Peter was public, and demanded a public correction. Cornelius a Lapide in the preface on the Pauline Epistles. Doctor of Peter, nay Doctor of the Apostles, nay Doctor of the Angels. Paul with remarkable wisdom and constancy rebuked, recalled, and corrected Peter, who was deviating from the straight path of Christian liberty and declining somewhat toward Judaism.

Benedictus Justinianus in this place signifies (by the word κατεγνωσμένῳ) that the Apostle Peter was worthy to be rebuked and condemned. Thomas Aquinas in the Catena on this place. The cause of the rebuke was not light. For there was danger that the truth of the Gospel would have perished, if men were compelled to keep the legal observances, which Peter was inducing, not indeed by command, but by his example. Examples are stronger than words, as Pope Leo teaches. The Papists clearly see that these things do not agree with the Oecumenical primacy or the Papacy of Peter. Therefore they twist themselves greatly, and turn in various directions. Baronius calls this history difficult to grasp. Alexander Carerius turns himself to that comment of Clement of Alexandria, that it was not Peter the Apostle, but another who was rebuked by Paul.

But Spondanus, the abbreviator of Baronius, ingenuously says: these things pleased neither Jerome of old, nor us now; nor did they please Bellarmine in Book I of the Roman Pontiff, ch. 16, in response to the 5th objection, or Estius, as noted before. Piggius, in Book III of the Hierarchia, ch. 11, says it is not an improbable opinion that that rebuke by Paul was feigned, to which Carerius also agrees. But that is already disapproved by Augustine, because it approves of a lie and brings in scriptures, as Estius acknowledges; if the words of Paul are to be explained in such a way to excuse Peter, so that Peter was not truly rebukable, nor was it truthfully said of him that he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, but rather that he was rebuked by Paul only in outward appearance as if he were not walking uprightly, it is to be feared that a place is given to lies in scripture.

Such simulation and lying, however, befits neither the Apostle nor the holiness of scripture. Therefore, this exception is also rejected by Bellarmine (l. c.) and by Thomas, and has been refuted by Estius.

Others, therefore, except that Paul's rebuke was not indeed feigned; but that there was no sin here on Peter's part, judging with Erasmus: That Peter cannot be blamed here in that he acted with good intention, and that which in itself was not evil, but only such that by its occasion some evil might arise, that is, the scandal of the Gentiles.

But Estius refutes them: With what face, he says, would Paul write these things about Peter, that he was rebukable and did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, if he had not sinned in it even venially?

For to those things which they object on the contrary, there is a ready response from St. Augustine, Thomas, and others; who well teach that these deeds of Paul were not such as would of themselves provide any occasion of scandal to the Gentiles. For Timothy was a Jew by his mother, and therefore, while the law was dead, but not yet buried, he could be circumcised, and this reason Luke himself, who narrates the deed, sufficiently insinuated in Acts 16. Paul, moreover, shaving his head according to the custom of the Nazarenes, lived as a Jew among Jews.

But that he purified himself with the Jews, and that at James's suggestion, when he was in Jerusalem, he had a manifest and necessary reason, which is clearly described in Acts 21. Finally, none of these things drew Paul back from association, not with the Jews, first conversing with the Gentiles, but afterwards, on account of the observance of the law, withdrawing himself from their table, although he did it with a good intention, lest the Jews who had arrived should be offended: yet he provided an occasion for the Gentiles to suspect that it was necessary to abstain from foods forbidden by the law, because they saw Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, correcting his own deed in that matter.

Certainly that inconstancy of Peter in the same matter could not but offend the Gentiles, and this Paul urges when he says that he did not walk with a straight foot, because he was indeed limping in both directions.

Wherefore Stapleton objects that Paul rebuked Peter insofar as he was Cephas, that is, the Apostle of the Jews, not insofar as he was Peter, that is, the universal Bishop, superior to all.

But this is inept; for Peter and Cephas are the same and signify the same. And Peter is named here, not Cephas, v. 11: when Peter had come to Antioch, I withstood him to his face. Nor does it fit the primacy-argument of the Papists for the Oecumenical primacy of Peter, from Matth. XVI. 16. You are Cephas, upon this rock &c. Whence others object in turn that Peter sinned, but venially, and in conduct, not mortally and in faith.

But by that reasoning they cannot untie the knot of the Oecumenical primacy: which we impugn not so much from Peter's fault—from which, however, Thomas, Estius, and others acknowledge Peter could not be absolved—as from Paul's rebuke: because the Roman Pontiff, as Oecumenical, does not wish to be rebuked by others.

C. si Papas dist. 40. Therefore, if Peter, sinning only in conduct, was rebuked by Paul, that decree will surely have to be amended: "If the Pope, negligent of his own and his brother's salvation, is found useless, even if no mortal presumes to rebuke his faults."

For our argument strikes more strongly if the sin was only in conduct.

For they do not want the Pope to be rebuked in such a way that they except if he is deviant from the faith. Furthermore, if Peter was rebuked by Paul, and that publicly, how did Paul hold Peter as Oecumenical and head?

For although a greater can be rebuked by a lesser, which Bellarmine excepts, yet the Papists deny that the Oecumenical Pontiff can be rebuked by any mortal: the Pontiffs in no way permit themselves to be publicly and to their face resisted and contradicted.

The Oecumenical Pontiff, according to the Papists, is ἀνευθύνου, that is, beyond all risk of rebuke.

But Peter was not ἀνευθύνου. Estius acknowledges that the words of the Apostle are to be explained thus with Augustine: when Peter had come to Antioch, there, for this very cause of which we are now treating, I withstood him before many present, with rebuke, because he had committed a matter worthy of public rebuke, by which it could not be corrected without it.

The plain text of the Apostle and the subjoined proof demand this sense. But let someone reconcile these things with the Oecumenical primacy of Peter.

For no Pope erring only in deed ought to be rebuked according to the Papists, much less with public rebuke. Therefore M. Anton. de Dominis rightly says: If there were not parity between Peter and Paul, if Peter had been the monarch of the whole Church, if not, I do not see how Paul could be excused from great imprudence, excessive audacity, and forwardness. The Ordinary Gloss and Lyranus here: Which he would never dare, unless he felt himself not unequal.

Add here what was said before about the partition of works between Peter and Paul.

For it is absurd that he who has empire over all provinces should divide provinces with another. Where Chrysostom urges the particle καθὼς in this way: Thus he shows himself equal in honor to the rest, and compares himself not to those others, but to the highest himself, declaring that each of these is equal in dignity.

Cajetan, however, to this place: It does not suffice, he says, for Paul to show himself equal to the other chief Apostles: But he shows that he had also exhibited himself greater in action than the summit of the Apostles, Peter. Ver.

Latin:

Vers. 11. "Οτε δὲ ἦλθε Πέτρος εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν) In Manuscripto hic rursum πᾶς. Videtur significare id tempus, de quo in Actis XIII. L Tempus incertum aliis est: anne actio haec Antiochena profectione Hierosolymitana prior, num vero posterior fuerit? Augustinus epist. XIX. quae est ad Hieronymum, ea priorem facit.

Alii posteriorem censent, ob ordinem narrationis Paulinae praesentis, & quia ex Actor. XV. apparet absoluto concilio Hierosolymitano, Paulum statim reversum esse Antiochiam, adeoque verisimile est, eo etiam Petrum advenisse, atque tum ista illic contigisse. Quae tamen etiam contingere potuere, cum iterum Paulus Antiochia exiit Actor. XIIX.

Contra vix verisimile, post concilium non acquiesse Iudaeos & gentes, aut Petrum ipsum ita titubasse. Antiocham vero Syria, non vero Pisidia intelligi, nullum dubium est. Κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστη) Coram ipso improbavi ejus consilium. Nam κατὰ πρόσωπον est coram, quod & ἐνώπιον, & ἔναντι verti solet, & saepe solet poni cum ἀπέναντι, ut Deut. VIII. 24. IX. 2. Joh. I. 5. ἀντίον autem hic intelligendum verbis amicis.

Nam בְּפָנִים, quod nec respondere, per ἀντιστάν vertitur. "Οτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν) κατεγνωσμένος saepe nihil aliud est, quam minus probare, apud Demosthenem, Aeschinem & alios, & κατεγνωσμένος hic est, more Hebraeo, participium pro verbali καταγνωσίς.

Non tantum coram ipso, quod emphasis vocis haec importat in faciem, ipsi restitisse dicitur, nec solum responsio blandis verbis facta in-nititur, sed resistentia, & contradictio, de qua Theophylactus: Quod autem ille in faciem restiterit, ac veluti ex composito factam, ut Iudae, tum contentionem. Non est autem assentierdum Hieronymo, qui hanc contentionem & reprehensionem Petri simulatam tantum fuisse, & dispensatoriam, ac veluti ex composito factam, ut Iudai, quos Petri maxime movebat auctoritas, videntes, Petrum ipsum reprehendenti Paulo cedere, sanarentur ab errore de necessitate observationis legis ad salutem.

Ideo contradixit Hieronymo Augustinus, ostendens veram hanc fuisse reprehensionem, ac Petrum omnino reprehensibilem fuisse, propterea, quod ad veritatem Evangelii non recte ambularet, dum simulatione sua, qua se a gentili convictu subtrahens legalia servabat, etiam gentes judaizare cogeret, vid.

Hieronymus epist. 86. & seqq. usque ad 97. Augustinus epist. 8. seqq. usque ad 19. Provocat quidem Hieronymus ad Origenem, Didymum, Apollinarem, Eusebium Emissenum, & Theodorum Heracleotem, sed illi fere omnes, ut notat Thomas de haeresi pravae doctrinae a Patribus notati sunt. Augustinus vero pro se adducit Cyprianum epist. LXXI. ad Quirinum, cujus etiam sententiae addiati fuerunt Tertullianus libr.

V. contra Marcion. cap. 3. Ambrosiaster in hunc loc. Gregor. M. 1. XXIIX. Moral. cap. 12. & homil. XII. super Ezech. & Latini fere omnes. Et observat Estius, Hieronymum ipsum in Augustini sententiam concessisse, & suam opinionem, quod Petrus in eo, de quo a Paulo reprehensus erat, non peccavit, oblique retractasse Dial. contr.

Pelag. 1. 1. c. 8. Quam ejus retractationem observavit ipse Augustinus epist. CCLX. ad Oceanum, uti & libr. III. Apol. Hieronymi adversus Ruffinum cap. 1. & de hisce vid. Thomam in h. l. & in summa I. secundae q. 103. art. 4. ad 2. & II. secundae quaest. 33. art. 4. ad 2. & quaest. 43. art. 6. ad 2. ubi docet, Petrum omnino peccasse, & in quo peccarit. Unde Estius fatetur se non posse accedere quorundam opinioni, cum Augustino caeterisque Latinis seriam hic agnoscentes reprehensionem, fortiter tamen negant, a Petro quicquam peccatum fuisse utpote Erasmo, & aliis nonnullis posterioribus.

Committere itaque hic possumus Estium cum recentioribus istis, imprimis Baronio prolixe ad ann. LI. contendente, Petrum omnino peccasse. Quibus hic velificari voluit Grotius, quod ad consilium tantum Petri verbis amicis responderit, vel aliquid monuerit Paulus, vel id minus probarit.

Quae tamen nec ipsis Papistis placere potuere. Siquidem Paulus diserte arguit Petrum, quod non incesserit recto pede, secundum veritatem Evangelii, eidemque in faciem restiterit. ἀνθιστάν - ἀντίστασιν. vay enim est resistere, obsistere, sese opponere, vi vocis & usus ejusdem recepti.

Verbum κατεγνωσμένος est καταγνώσεως ἄξιος, ut ut Camerarius habet, in quo Ebraeam phrasin notat Adamus Sasbouth, quod Ebraeis frequens imo perpetuum fit, ut quod nos per nomen verbale passivae vocis enunciamus, illi participio Passivo significant, e. g. amatum pro amabili &c. 2. Sam. I. 23. Psalm. LXXXIII. 1. &c. ut reprehensum ita dixerit pro reprehensibili, quemadmodum Hieronymus perpetuo hoc reddidit, Quod verbum proinde fatum reprehensione & condemnatione dignum, supponit.

Chrysostomus & ἐπιταλῆν ἐπιτιμησιν Φοδεστέραν dixit. Oecumenius σφοδρὰν τῆς ἐπιτιμήσεως. Ideo Bellarminus libr. I. de Rom. Pont. cap. 27. §. Apostolus Petrus, inquit, quia Iudaeorum praecipue Apostolus erat, gentiles potius, quam Iudeos offendere voluit. Paulus autem electionem illam improbavit, & Petrum SATIS ACRITER reprehendit.

Salmero Disp. XXII. in Gal. II. Delictum, inquit, Petri erat publicum, & publicam correptionem exigebat. Cornelius a Lapide in procem. super Epist. Paulin. Doctor Petri, imo Doctor Apostolorum, imo Doctor Angelorum. Paulus insigni sapientia, & constantia Petrum a recto tramite Christianae libertatis deviantem & nonnihil ad judaismum declinantem redarguit, revocavit, & correxit.

Benedictus Justinianus in h. l. significat (verbo κατεγνωσμένῳ) Apostolum Petrum fuisse dignum, qui reprehenderetur, & damnaretur. Thomas Aquinas in catena ad h. l. Non levis causa reprehensionis erat. Periculum enim erat, ne periisset veritas Evangelii, si cogerent homines servare legalia, quod inducebat Petrus non quidem imperio, sed exemplo suo. Exempla autem sunt validiora, quam verba, ut Papa Leo docet. Probe vident Papistae, haec non convenire Oecumenico primatui vel Papatui Petri. Ideo valde se torquent, & in varias partes convertunt. Baronius historiam hanc dicit capsu difficilem. Alexander Carerius convertit se ad illud Clementis Alexandr. cemmentum, non Petrum Apostolum, sed alium a Paulo reprehensum.

Sed Spondanus Baronii breviator ingenue, hac, inquit, nec olim placuere Hieronymo, nec nunc nobis; nec ea placuere Bellarmino libr. I. de Rom. Pontifice cap. 16. resp. ad 5. obiect. aut Estio, ut antea notatum. Piggius libr. III. Hierarch. cap. II. haud improbabilem esse sententiam aut fimulatam fuisse illam reprehensionem Pauli, cui etiam annuit Carerius. Sed ea jam improbata Augustino, quod mendacium approbet & inferipturas invehat, ut Estius agnoscit; si verba Pauli ad excusandum Petrum sic exponantur, ut nec vere reprehensibilis fuerit Petrus, nec veraciter de eo dictum fit, quod non recte ambulaverit ad veritatem Evangelii, sed ideo, quia tanquam non recte ambularet, fuerit externa duntaxat specie reprehensus a Paulo, metuendum esse, ne mendaciis in scriptura detur locus.

Simulatio utique talis & mendacium, nec Apostoli nec scripturae sanctitatem decet. Idcirco etiam haec exceptio rejicitur a Bellarmino l. c. & a Thoma, & Estio profligata est.

Alii proinde excipiunt, non simulatam quidem fuisse Pauli reprehensionem; sed a Petro tamen hic non fuisse peccatum, censentes, cum Erasmo: Quod Petrus non possit hic culpari in eo, quod bona intentione fecerit, quodque secundum se malum non erat, sed tale duntaxat, cujus occasione malum aliquod proveniret, id est, scandalum gentilium.

Sed hos refellit Estius: Qua fronte, inquit, Paulus haec scriberet de Petro & reprehensibilem fuisse & non recte ad veritatem Evangelii ambulasse, si ne venialiter quidem in eo peccasset?

Nam ad ea, quae e diverso objiciunt, in promptu responsio est ex S. Augustino, Thoma & aliis; qui bene docent hac Pauli facta non fuisse talia, qua ex se praeberent aliquam scandali occasionem gentilibus. Timotheus enim ex matre Judaeus erat, ideoque lege mortua quidem, sed nondum sepulta circumcidi poterat, & hanc rationem ipse Lucas, qui factum narrat satis insinuavit Act. XVI. Paulus autem more Nazaraeorum caput sibi tondens Judaeus inter Judaeos versabatur.

Quod vero purificaret se cum Judaeis, idque Jacobo suggerente, cum Hierosolymis esset, manifestam ac necessariam habuit rationem, que luculente describitur Actor. XXI. Postremo nihil horum retraxit Paulum a conversatione, non Judaeorum, prius cum gentilibus conversens, postea vero propter legis observationem ab eorum mensa se subducens, quamvis bona intentione, ne Judae, qui supervenerant, offenderentur, id faceret: Occasione tamen gentilibus praebuit suspicandi, quod oporteret a cibis lege vetitis abstinere, quia Petrum Apostolorum Principem in ea re factum suum corrigere prius viderent.

Certe illa Petri inconstantia in eadem re non poterat non gentiles offendere, & hoc Paulus urget, quando dicit, eum non recto pede ambulasse, quia nimirum claudicabat in utramque partem.

Quapropter excipit Stapletonus, Paulum reprehendisse Petrum, quatenus Cephas hoc est Judaeorum Apostolus, non quatenus Petrus erat, hoc est, universalis Episcopus, omnibus superior.

Sed hoc ineptum est; Nam Petrus & Cephas idem sunt & significant. Et Petrus hic nominatur, non Cephas v. 11. cum venisset Petrus Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti. Nec congruit Papistarum primato argumento, pro Oecumenico Petri primatu, e Matth. XVI. 16. Tu es Cephas super hanc petram &c. Unde alii obvertunt, peccasse Petrum sed venialiter, & in conversatione, non mortaliter & in fide.

Verum ea ratione salvare primatum Oecumenicum nodum possunt: Quem non tam e Petri culpa, a qua tamen non absolvi posse Petrum, Thomas, Estius, aliique agnoscunt, quam e Pauli reprehensione impugnamus: quia Romanus Pontifex, ceu Oecumenicus ab aliis reprehendi non vult.

C. si Papas dist. 40. Proinde si Petrus in conversatione tantum peccans reprehensus fuit a Paulo, utiq; emendandum erit decretum illud: Si Papa suae & fraternae salutis negligens deprehendatur inutilis, etsi huius culpas istas redarguere presumat mortalium nullus.

Argumentum enim nostrum magis stringit, si in conversatione tantum peccatum.

Nam ita nolunt Papam reprehendi, ut excipiant, si a fide fit devius. Porro si reprehensus fuit Petrus a Paulo, idque publice, quomodo habuit Paulus pro Oecumenico & capite Petrum?

Quamvis enim major a minori reprehendi possit, quod Bellarminus excipit, Oecumenicum tamen Pontificem ab ullo mortalium reprehendi posse negant Papistae: publice & in faciem resisti ac contradici sibi nullatenus permittunt Pontifices.

Oecumenicus Pontifex juxta Pontificios est ἀνευθύνου, id est extra omnem reprehensionis aleam.

At Petrus non fuit ἀνευθύνου. Agnoscit Estius, verba Apostoli sic exponenda esse cum Augustino: cum Petrus Antiochiam venisset, ibi propter hanc ipsam causam, de qua nunc agitur, coram & multis praesentibus ei restiti, cum objurgatione, quia rem commiserat publica reprehensione dignam, qua nec fine ea corrigi possit.

Sensum hunc exigit planus Apostoli textus & subjuncta probatio. Conciliet autem haec quis cum Oecumenico Petri primatu.

Nullus enim Papa errans tantum in opere reprehendi debet secundum Papistas, nedum cum publica objurgatione. Ideo recte M. Anton. de Dominis: Si non esset inter Petrum & Paulum paritas, si Petrus totius Ecclesiae monarcha fuisset, si non videre, quomodo Paulus a magna imprudentia, nimia audatia & procacitate possit excusari. Glossae ordinaria & Lyranus hic: Quod nunquam auderet, nisi se non imparem sentiret.

Adde hic quae de operarum partitione inter Petrum & Paulum antea dicta.

Absurdum enim, eum, qui in omnes provincias habet imperium, cum alio dividere provincias. Ubi Chrysostomus particulam καθὼς hoc modo urget: Itaque se cateris honore parem ostendit, nec se reliquis illis, sed summo ipsi comparat, declarans, quod horum unusquisque parem fit tertius dignitatem.

Cajetanus vero ad hunc locum: Non sufficit, inquit, Paulo, monstrare se se equalem aliis Apostolis primis: Sed monstrat se exhibuisse quoque majorem in actione summe Apostolorum vertice Petro.

## 2:12
12. Πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τινὰς ἀπὸ Ἰακώβου) that is, from Jerusalem, over which Church James then presided: from James, that is, from that place where James was, as the Syrian rightly takes it here. Thus we say: Let us go to me.

They are said to have come more rightly from James. That they came sent from James, without doubt, was so that they might know the state of the Church and report back to him. Μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιεν) It was not a question of that which was permitted (for Peter did not doubt concerning it) but of that which was more useful.

Status quaestionis.

The status of the question Flacius has best explained at v. 11. There was then for the Apostle, just as there had been before for Christ, and indeed even for the Prophets, a very great contention with the Jews and the Judaizers, whether men were justified and saved by faith alone through the sacrifice and merit of the Messiah, or indeed also through the works of the law? But by how much the more clearly Jesus and his disciples testified that men are justified and saved by the sole expiation of the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, by so much did he neglect the observation of the law, especially the ceremonial and judicial, which otherwise was then to be abrogated; on the contrary, those who were judging for this very reason urged the Mosaic ceremonies all the more, so that they might testify and teach that the observation of the whole law was necessary for justification and salvation. Therefore, it was not primarily a matter of food, ceremonies, or circumcision; but it was established and pronounced by the other side as a certain sign or symbol of the justice of the works of the whole law, as he himself just said, that he therefore did not wish to circumcise Titus, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain safe among them, namely that we are made saved by faith, freely, without works, through Christ alone. For if he had permitted that to be done, he would have seemed to confess by that very fact that the works of the whole law were necessary for salvation, and that therefore men could by no means be saved by the merit of Christ alone. Concerning this very controversy, it had already been wisely determined by public consent. For the judgment concerning Peter is known, that he entered unto Cornelius, and baptized him, and received him into the Church without circumcision and the observation of the law, as having been abundantly purified and justified by the grace of Christ alone, Acts 11. Then also Acts 15. Again in the full synod. Peter, therefore, in this place eating any foods with the Gentiles, was testifying according to the truth of the matter and the prior decrees, that men are justified and saved by faith, freely, without the works of the law: But soon, from fear of those Judaizing Jacobites, withdrawing himself from the banquets of the Gentiles, he seemed to testify the contrary, to confirm the opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles against Paul and the truth, and all sincere Doctors: which was in reality not to walk with a straight foot toward the purity of the Gospel, but even to overturn it from the foundations, so that it might not be preserved any longer in the Church, especially among the Gentiles, just as above vers. 5. Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθον) Those from Jerusalem. (ὑπόκρισις καὶ ἀφώριζεν ἑαυτὸν) ἰνορίμεν to withdraw, Job 13:8, Hab.

2:4. φοβούμενος τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς) Fearing lest he should offend them, and thus give an occasion to defend the most Christian, rùs ἐκ περιτομῆς, as in Acts 10:45.

Peter therefore sinned most gravely, as Flacius holds here, because he was moved too much by a certain carnal fear, fearing lest through those Jacobites all the Jews might be alienated from him, with whom, however, by reason of his function, he had especially to deal and converse, and therefore he feigned that he felt that they were not yet sufficiently cleansed by the grace of Christ alone, since they did not observe the law, wherefore they had to be compelled to it. Finally, he sinned most gravely because by that simulation he confirmed the opinion of those Judaizing deceivers, concerning the necessity of the works of the law for salvation, among the spectators, the hearers, and all others.

But Peter fell here, as Flacius again says after many things, as far as his own person and mind are concerned, not in doctrine, but in life; but in such a way that his fall tended at the same time toward the most grave ruin of doctrine and faith. His fall was therefore clearly in doctrine, if you look at the outcome which followed from it, however much he himself might have felt otherwise in his heart: for by his external deeds and conduct he was not walking with a straight foot toward the preservation of the Gospel, but rather was confirming the error of the Pseudo-Apostles concerning the necessity of the works of the law for salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τινὰς ἀπὸ Ἰακώβου) id est ab Hierosolymis, cui Ecclesiae tum praesidebat Jacobus: Jacobo, id est, ab eo loco, ubi erat Jacobus, quomodo recte hic sumit Syrus, Sic dicimus: Eamus ad me.

Rectius a Jacobo venisse dicuntur. Quod a Jacobo missi venerint, sine dubio, ut statum Ecclesiae cognoscerent eique referrent. Μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιεν) Non erat quaestio de eo, quod liceret (neque enim Petrus de eo dubitabat) sed de eo, quod esset utilius.

Status quaestionis.

Statu quaestionis optime exposuit Flacius ad v. 11. Erat tunc Apostolu, sicut et antea Christo, atque adeo etiam Prophetis fuerat, maxima contentio cum Judais et Judaizantibus, an solum Messiae sacrificium meritumque homines fide justificarent et servarent, aut vero etiam per opera legis? Quo autem tanto luculentius testatur faceret Jesus ejusque discipuli, sola expiatione agni Dei mundi peccata tollentis, homines justificari ac salvari, neglegebat legis observationem praesertim ceremonialis ac judicialis, quae alioqui tunc abroganda erat; contra judizantes ob hoc ipsum tanto magis urgebant ceremonias Mosaicas, ut testarentur ac docerent, totius legis observationem esse necessariam ad justificationem et salutem. Non igitur praecipue agebatur de foliciis, ceremoniis, aut circumcisione; sed eo, tanquam signo quodam aut symbolo ab altera parte statuebatur ac pronuntiabatur de justitia operum totius legis, ut modo ipsemet dixit, se ideo noluisse Titum circumcidere, ut veritas Evangelii apud ipsos incolumis permaneret, quod scilicet fide, gratis, sine operibus, per solum Christi salvi fiamus. Si enim id fieri permisisset, visus fuisset confiteri eo ipso facto, opera totius legis esse necessaria ad salutem, eoque homines nequaquam per solum Christi meritum salvari posse. De hac ipsa controversia jam antea sapieus publico consensu constitutum fuerat. Notum enim est judicium de Petro, quod intraverit ad Cornelium, eumque baptizaverit, et in Ecclesiam receperit sine circumcisione et legis observatione tanquam sola Christi gratia abunde purificatos et justificatos, Actorum undecimo. Deinde etiam Actorum XV. Denuo in plena synodo. Petrus igitur hoc loco comedens quosvis cibos cum gentilibus, testabatur secundum rei veritatem et decreta priora, homines fide, gratis justificari et servari sine operibus legis: Mox vero metu illorum Judaizantium Jacobitarum, sese subducens a Gentilium conviviis, videbatur contrarium testari, Pseudo-Apostolorum sententiam contra Paulum ac veritatem, omnesque sinceros Doctores, confirmare: quod erat revera non recto pede incedere ad puritatem Evangelii, sed etiam funditus evertere, ut ea non conservaretur diutius in Ecclesia, praesertim gentilibus, sicut supra vers. 5. dixerat. Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθον) Illi Hierosolymitani. (ὑπόκρισις καὶ ἀφώριζεν ἑαυτὸν) ἰνορίμεν se subducere, Job. XIII, 8. Abac.

II. 4. φοβούμενος τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς) Metuens, ne eos offenderet, et sic occasionem daret, Christianissimum defendendi, rùs ἐκ περιτομῆς, ut Act.

X. 45. Peccavit igitur gravissime, ut hic habet Flacius, Petrus, quod carnali quodam metu nimium motus est, timens, ne per illos Jacobitas omnes Judaei a se alienarentur, cum quibus tamen ei, ratione functionis, potissimum agendum versandumque erat, eoque simulavit se sentire, illos sola Christi gratia nondum sufficienter mundatos esse, cum legem non observarent, quare ad eam illos adigendos esse. Peccavit denique gravissime, quod ea simulatione Judaizantium illorum seductorum opinionem, de necessitate operum legis ad salutem, apud spectatores, auditoresque et alios omnes confirmavit.

Lapsus est autem hic Petrus, ut post aliquam multa iterum Flacius, quod ad suam personam animumque attinet, non in doctrina, sed in vita; verum ita, ut ejus lapsus simul in gravissimam perniciem doctrinae fideque tenderet. Fuit igitur ejus lapsus plane in doctrina, si spectes eventum, qui inde consequebatur, quantumvis ipse reae in corde suo fenseret: externis enim factu ge-suque non recto intedebat pede ad conservationem Evangelii, sed potius errorem Pseudo-Apostolorum de necessitate operum legis ad salutem confirmabat.

## 2:13
Verf. 13. Καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι) Namely, those who were at Antioch, if the ancient Codices were to assent, I would think it should be read here, συνεκλίθησαν, and soon τῇ ὑποκλίσει. For ὑποκλίσει is the same as that which was just said, ὑποκρίσει. They withdrew themselves from the familiar custom of the circumcised Christians, and certainly the Syriac reads thus, for אָחַר is ὑποκλίσει. (Ὧτε καὶ Βαρνάβας συναπήχθη αὐτῶν τῇ ὑποκρίσει) ὥτε with the indicative, in place of the infinitive, we have among the best Greek writers, Isocrates, Aristophanes, Plato, Xenophon, Plutarch. But he speaks of a great matter, that the force of such an example given by Peter was so great that even Barnabas, the companion of Paul's journeys, and with him the Teacher of the Gentiles, did the same.

Grotius favors the Oecumenical primacy of Peter for the sake of the Papists to such an extent that he would even wish the scripture to be otherwise here, so that it would not be necessary to acknowledge Peter as having been accused of hypocrisy by Paul. Which, lest he admit it, Cornelius a Lapide, an impudent Jesuit, dared to deny that which Paul openly affirms: When in fact, he says, there is some cause for hiding the truth, there is no hypocrisy or lie in it. But here the cause is not at all just. Nor did he only hide the truth, he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, he confirmed by his example those led into error. And so, by avoiding the scandal accepted, he became guilty of the scandal given. Yet Peter is not to be called a hypocrite with Porphyry and Julian. For this was one action of Peter, not a habit. And he admitted the correction, and changed his conversation. The action was not deliberated with mature counsel, but undertaken out of vain fear. Jerome, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius acknowledge ὑπόκρισιν and simulation, but they excuse it, and call it a dispensation and prudence. But Augustine more rightly teaches that it was the vice of hypocrisy, because it is repugnant to truth and simplicity. Nor was the damage arising from it small, given not to a few, but to many. For the remaining Jews, namely the Antiochenes, withdrew themselves from the Gentiles, they did not eat food with them. He says he feigned with Peter. Therefore, the contagion arose from Peter, whose example others followed, so that even Barnabas was carried away into that hypocrisy; ὥστε which Beza had rendered 'therefore' in the first edition, he more rightly translated in the latter as 'so that': which meaning is more apt here according to Gomarus and Grotius. He had mentioned the grave evil that arose from Peter's deed. Now he adds a graver one: namely that Barnabas, who had hitherto strenuously defended Christian liberty with Paul, disturbed by the deed of the primary Apostle, was drawn away from the straight path into a path not good.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι) Nempe, qui Antiochiae erant, si Codices vetusti assentirentur, legendum hic putarem, συνεκλίθησαν, et mox τῇ ὑποκλίσει. Nam ὑποκλίσει idem est cum eo, quod modo dictum est ὑποκρίσει. Subduxerunt se a familiari consuetudine circumcisorum Christianorum, et certe fie legit Syrus, nam אָחַר est ὑποκλίσει. (Ὧτε καὶ Βαρνάβας συναπήχθη αὐτῶν τῇ ὑποκρίσει) ὥτε cum indicativo, vice infinitivi, habemus apud optimos scriptores Graecos, Isocratem, Aristophanem, Platonem, Xenophontem, Plutarchum. Rem autem magnam dicit, tantam ejus exempli a Petro editi fuisse vim, ut etiam Barnabas, itinerum Pauli comes, et cum eo gentium Magister, idem fecerit.
