Adeo Petri primatui Oecumenico in Papistarum gratiam favet Grotius, ut optaret etiam, aliter hic se habere scripturam, ne scilicet Petrum hypocriseos postulatum a Paulo agnoscere opus esset. Quod ne admitteret Cornelius a Lapide, Jesuita impudens, negare ausus est id, quod Paulus aperte affirmat: Cum in facto, inquit, jussa est aliqua causa tegendi veritatem, nullam in eo esse hypocrisin vel mendacium. At hic causa minime justa. Nec texit tantum veritatem, coëgit gentes judaizare, exemplo suo confirmavit seductos in errore. Itaque vitando scandalum acceptum, reus factus est scandali dati. Nec tamen Petrus cum Porphyrio, et Juliano hypocrita dicendus. Nam una haec fuit Petri actio, non habitus. Et admisit correptionem, et mutavit conversationem. Erat actio non deliberata maturo consilio, ex inani metu suscepta. Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus et Oecumenius agnoscunt ὑπόκρισιν et simulationem, sed excusant, vocantque dispensationem, et prudentiam. At rectius Augustinus vitium fuisse docet hypocrisin, quod veritati, et simplicitati repugnat. Nec parvum inde damnum ortum non paucis, sed multis datum. Judaei enim reliqui, scilicet Antiocheni, subducebant se gentibus, non cum illis vescebantur cibis. Simulasse cum Petro ait. A Petro ergo contagium ortum, cujus exemplum alii sequuti, adeo, ut etiam Barnabas in eam abreptus hypocrisin fuerit; ὥστε quod Beza in priori editione reddiderat itaque, rectius in posteriori transtulit adeo, ut: quae significatio juxta Gomarum et Grotium hic aptior. Grave malum ex Petri facto ortum memoraverat. Jam addit gravius: nempe quod Barnabas, qui libertatem Christianam adhuc cum Paulo strenue defenderat, primarii Apostoli facto perturbatus a recta via abstraheretur in viam non bonam.

## 2:14
V. 14. Ἀλλ' ὅτε εἶδον, ὅτι οὐ ὀρθοποδοῦσι, πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου) That is, when I saw that they were not walking straight in that path which was most conducive for propagating the Gospel truth everywhere, so here this word must be taken for that which the Hebrews call ישר דרך. Tertullian against Marcion pf. It was not marked by Paul concerning preaching but concerning conversation. That τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιεῖν, is opposed to τῇ σκολίᾳ and ἐκτρεπόμενα. But this matter does not admit such a harsh interpretation.

This interpretation is not harsh nor adverse to the present matter. For the scandal was most grave. Therefore, as soon as he knew it, not by hearsay, but through ἀυτοψίαν (direct observation), he interposed the remedy without delay. We spoke of this at v. 12. Peter could, Barnabas could, while living among the weak Jews, use ceremonies, although they were dead, so that they might be buried honorably; he could not use them as necessary, he could not force the Gentiles to use them, yet he forced them by his own example. This was not walking with a straight foot, as was consistent with the truth of the Gospel. For the Gentiles could think that the observance of ceremonies was necessary both for the Jews and for themselves, because Peter was withdrawing himself from them, as Crocius rightly notes here. The truth of the Gospel, which is well observed by Flacius, does not here signify the true Gospel, as some wrongly explain, nor does it signify according to the prescription or norm of the Gospel, but rather the sincerity and purity of the Gospel to be retained. If the leaven of the necessity of legal works for salvation were added, that sincerity of the Gospel would have perished. That ὀρθῶς (rightly), therefore, must be admonished by the same Flacius, is to be received in its true sense concerning the final cause, which he had clearly explained above in verse 5, and not indeed by PER, JUXTA, or SECUNDUM. For he says that that simulation, and Peter's crooked walk, were directed not to the conservation, but to the destruction of the Gospel. But this is also the very question or proposition itself, namely, that he affirms that Peter, by that act and simulation of his, overturns the sincerity of the Gospel and the efficacy of grace, and the merit of Christ, as if that alone were not sufficient for justice and salvation, without the works of the law. Εἶναι τῇ Πίστει ἄμπωδον πάντων

In a great assembly. If you listen to Justinianus, he noted not so much Peter as the others, because Peter held the true opinion in his mind, and at least in external action was simulating. But Paul does not separate Peter from the others, and he is said to have spoken this to Peter, as the author of the scandal. And not privately, but before all, both Jews and Gentiles. Augustine explains the reason for this: Because he said it to him before all, necessity compelled it, so that all might be healed by his rebuke. For it was not useful to amend in secret an error that was harmful in public. Εἰ οὐ Ἰουδαῖος ὑπάρχων

You use your liberty, namely where it seems so to you. See above 12. Acts X. In the Manuscript: Ἐθνικῶς ἐν Ἰουδαίοις ζῆς (You live as a Gentile among the Jews). Τί τὰ ἔθνη ἀναγκάζεις Ἰουδαίζειν; (Why do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?) In the Manuscript, πῶς τὰ ἔθνη &c. in the same sense, why do you live by your example.

Thus we have the same word in Matt. XIV. 22, Mark VI. 45, Luke XIV. 23, Acts XXVI. 1. There is a similar word ἀναγκάζειν (to compel) in Luke XXIV. 29, Acts XVI. 15, 2 Cor. XII.

11. B. Luther rightly warns in his former Commentary, f. 13, that Paul does not rebuke Peter for having lived as a Gentile (as B. Jerome wishes), for then he would have rebuked himself as well, but because he simulated.

The simulation, he says, of Peter, Paul did not tolerate. For he approves of this, that you lived as a Gentile, and again as a Jew, but he reproves, that when the Jews came, you withdrew and separated yourself from the food of the Gentiles, by which withdrawal you became an author to the Gentiles and Jews that Gentile things were illicit, and Jewish things necessary, when the text indicates that Peter did not ignore that these were free, because previously (he says) he ate with the Gentiles, and also fearing those who had come from James. Therefore, he did this out of fear, not out of ignorance. For Paul does not say, why do you live as a Gentile? nor does he say: Why do you return to Judaism? Both were permitted to be done, but why do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize? That coalition was reprehensible through simulation and withdrawal, whereby the Gentiles and Jews believed Jewish things to be necessary and Gentile things illicit. Thus he does not find fault with the other Jews having agreed in food either Gentile or Jewish (for they held these to be permitted), but in conformity to Peter and the compulsion of Gentiles and Jews to Judaism as necessary. Likewise he does not find fault with Barnabas having eaten with them in a Jewish and Gentile manner, but with him, led away into the same simulation, having agreed in that coalition of Gentiles and Jews toward Judaism. Therefore Paul fights for liberty against necessity. For faith alone in Christ is necessary, that we may be just; all other things are most free, neither commanded any longer nor prohibited. If therefore Peter had done both with an upright face, he would not have been to be reproved. As Paul did both with confidence. Peter therefore sinned, acting hypocritically in those things from which the Pseudo-Apostles and those seduced by them could be confirmed in their opinion, and presume that Peter judged with them, that Gentiles are not justified by the grace of Christ alone and without the law, but moreover that the works of the law are themselves necessary for salvation and justice, and that they are by no means free from the servitude of the law. Therefore Peter is reproved for hypocrisy, because he believes one thing in reality, while by that hypocritical act and example he now testifies and professes another. He uses, however, the form of interrogation, that he may strike the heart more forcefully: You who are a Jew, and before the coming of the faithful Jerusalemite Jews used the common table with converted Gentiles, observing no choice of foods at all, nor holding the ceremonial laws of any account, why do you now drive the Gentiles by your example to the observance of Mosaic laws, as necessary for salvation? Why by the very deed do you stir up this opinion in them, as if they were still unclean and alien from the grace of GOD, with whom it is not permitted to associate on account of circumcision not received, and so by this institution of yours you lead them also into this pestiferous opinion, as if salvation and justification depended upon ceremonies and works of the law. Therefore B. Luther explains this in his Commentary, that is: You are a Jew, who is bound to live according to the Jewish law, that is, to abstain from foods prohibited in the law. And yet you live as a Jew in a Gentile manner, that is, freely you act against the law, you transgress and trample upon it. For you eat (& in this you do rightly) common or unclean foods, like another Gentile who is free from the law. But by this very thing, that, frightened by the presence of the brothers from among the converted Jews, you now abstain from things prohibited in the law and keep the law, you compel the Gentiles to Judaize, that is, to keep the law necessarily. For by this your example, that you abstain from profane foods, you give the Gentiles occasion for thinking: Peter now avoids the Gentile foods which he previously ate, therefore we also ought to avoid them, and live in the Jewish manner, otherwise we shall not be just, nor shall we be saved. You see therefore, that Paul does not reprove in Peter ignorance, for it was held to be free to eat with any Gentiles whatsoever; but simulation, by which he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. Certainly it is altogether certain that Peter had not erred in doctrine, nor in dogma, whether in Evangelical liberty or in justification before GOD gratuitous. The error was therefore, as B. Hunnius rightly holds, only in the application of doctrine or in practice, in the legitimate use of Christian liberty, and thus in conduct, in that he applied himself to the brothers sent from James in such a way that meanwhile he neglected and offended the others, who were from the Gentiles.

Nevertheless, it seemed by the act itself that the article concerning Christian liberty was being overturned (from the opinion of the Gentile Christians), as if the Gentiles were not free from the law of circumcision and the Mosaic statutes, and as long as they remain uncircumcised; it is not permitted to [live] with them in the same way to converse and to take food. Which error immediately drew with it another error, as if the taking up of circumcision and the Mosaic law were necessary for them for justification and salvation, and as if neither justification nor salvation could stand unless they were circumcised and observed the law. Which two false dogmas were indeed not Peter's, but the Pseudo-Apostles'. But Peter's action could be so taken, nay, it was so taken by the Gentile Corinthians, as if he were in some measure applauding the dogma of the Pseudo-Apostles in both articles. For healing this scandal, therefore, and for removing this perverse opinion from their minds, the correction which Paul used against the Apostle Peter was necessary. And thus the Apostle prepared for himself an approach to the main theme and to the overthrowing of the necessity of the observation of the law for salvation.

Concerning which the second part of chapter II now begins to treat. PART II. OF CHAPTER II. DOGMATIC, ON JUSTIFICATION, THAT IT IS DONE NOT BY THE WORKS OF THE LAW, BUT BY FAITH IN CHRIST; Wherein begins at the same time THE SECOND PART OF THE PRINCIPAL EPISTLE ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΙΚΗ, Whose

SECTION I. Concerns the purity of the doctrine of justification. V. 15. '

Humeis physei Ioudaioi' Here, the narrative being finished, Paul pursues the discourse begun to the Galatians. We are Jews by nature, not like those Doctors of yours, who, being from the Gentiles, Judaize. He here subjoins a notable argument to refute Peter's conversation, and by it so constrains him that he simultaneously enters into the stronghold of the cause and the main theme, which is drawn from Peter's and his own common knowledge.

We are Jews by nature, Israelites descending from Abraham, Israel, or Jacob. For Jews were commonly called Israelites, not only those originating from the tribe of Judah, from which Paul did not descend, but from the tribe of Benjamin Philip. III. 5. If by the name 'Ioudaioi' it be said that that external holiness is also regarded, concerning which Rom. XI. 6, 1 Cor. VII. 14, when they are opposed to those from the Gentiles as 'hamartoloi', we do not deny it; provided it be held that the Jews are opposed to the Gentiles not in respect of the covenant, in which they were through the sacrament of circumcision, not te physei; but by reason of lineage.

Hence Crocius does not rightly conclude from this that we are Christians by nature. We are indeed Christians from parents who are Christians, but not as they are Christians. For they did not beget them as they were grafted into Christ through baptism, but by the power of divine blessing granted to marriage. The reason for the name of Jewish or Israelite is not the same. But Christians, as Tertullian's well-worn rule has it, are not born, but made. The Calvinists overturn this when they say that holy sons and daughters are begotten by parents, and that they are born in the covenant of GOD. We are federated, says Crocius in his Commentary on this place, disputing against our B. Balduinus. We are not born outside the Church, we are born in the Church. But by birth we have the right to the sacraments. But if we are in the covenant before baptism, then we are not finally received into the covenant through baptism. But the Sacramentarians wish this, that through baptism the right of the covenant is not conferred, but only sealed. Therefore this interpretation of the opinion of the Reformers is not malicious, as he argues against B. Balduinus, but it is their genuine opinion. To be born in the Church is spoken of ambiguously, either in the assembly in which the Church is, or in the assembly which is the Church. Likewise, that by birth we are members of the Church, or that we have access to the benefits of the Church; but it is entirely true that no one is received into the covenant by natural generation, but by his own faith. Which Crocius says concerning adults and the interior society of the covenant, not concerning infants.

But infants are not received into the covenant on any other ground than adults. They are received, he says, by way of promise: I will be your God and the God of your seed after you, Gen. XVII. But for the application of the promise, another and individual one, faith is required. Let us consider the arguments of B. Balduinus, and, because Crocius attacks them, let us defend them. The first is: Those with whom God covenants as God, those are sons of God. But sons are those who believe, Joh. I. 13, and through faith Gal. III. 26. Crocius rashly limits or enlarges the major premise: they are, or shall be, sons of God. For if actually in the covenant; they must actually have faith. He says that Joh. I. and Gal. III. treat of adults. But just as adults, so also infants become sons of GOD only through faith. Thus far their case is the same.

Nor do infants become heirs of eternal life or are saved otherwise than adults. Namely, no one attains salvation except through faith, through the imputed righteousness of Christ, which is imputed only through faith. In Christ Jesus, as there is neither male nor female, Gal. III. 28, so neither adult nor infant. All are one in Christ, all one through faith. He says: Faithful infants, since it is not established that they have faith in their mother's womb: Yet they are not sons of the Devil. But by nature they are sons of wrath, Ephes. II. 3, and hitherto under the kingdom of Satan. For no one enters the kingdom of GOD unless he be regenerated.

If by nature sons of wrath, then certainly by nature they are not sons of GOD. This is the second argument: Baptism is the laver of regeneration, not because the covenant is sealed by it, but because it is conferred through it. Tit. III. 5. Eph. V. 26. 1. Joh. III. 5. He replies, it does not follow, baptism is the laver of regeneration. Therefore Christians are not born from Christians. But Christians are made through regeneration, and are truly not born through carnal propagation. He denies that the right of the covenant is first conferred through baptism, because otherwise the children of Christians would have no more access to baptism than the Turks.

But it is one thing to have access to baptism, and thus to reception into the covenant; another to be in the covenant. Entrance into the kingdom of GOD is indeed made through baptism. But that entrance is reception into the covenant, by which the possession of the kingdom of GOD is promised to the children of GOD. Crocius denies this, because reception, he says, precedes, entrance into the covenant of GOD follows. If you understand the kingdom of grace, when one is received into the covenant, he enters into it. If the kingdom of glory, it is promised through the covenant. Abraham indeed was in the covenant of GOD through faith, which he had conceived from the Word, but at that time the sacrament of circumcision had not yet been instituted. Which was then the ordinary medium of regeneration, initiation, and reception into the covenant of GOD. Nor do infants today have any other medium than baptism: which succeeded into the place of circumcision: And thus all dying before baptism would be outside the covenant, and would have no hope of salvation. Resp. baptism is the ordinary medium: But God can outside the ordinary way receive the infants of Christians, commended to Him by the prayers of the Church, into the covenant without the sacrament, since he has not bound himself, but us, to this medium, and neither the deprivation, but the contempt of the Sacrament condemns.

The third reason is: In the kingdom of GOD no one is born, but through baptism is received into it, Joh. III. v. 5. Therefore no one can be called a Christian by nature. For to be born of GOD, to put on Christ, to be reborn, is to become a Christian. Therefore, only through baptism do they become Christians. He answers: It is so: In the kingdom of GOD, that is, in the kingdom of glory, no one is born. But neither are we born in the kingdom of grace, because by nature we are children of wrath. Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. That there were those in the Old Testament who were federated with GOD by birth is a begging of the question. They were so through circumcision, not through carnal birth. That the former was only a sign of the covenant, and not the first door of the covenant and salvation, is just as false as if that were said of baptism. For each sacrament is a medium of the initiation of grace and salvation. Crocius admits that we are not born of God by the first birth, but by the second. Not to be reborn from parents, nor to put on Christ through generation, but through sacrament and faith. He denies, however, that we are therefore not Christians by nature. But this is to answer the conclusion. But what do you say, Crocius, to the argument: to be born of God, to put on Christ, to be reborn, is to become a Christian? Here the water sticks for you. You are more mute than a fish.

Fourthly, the Fathers were brought forward: Tertullian, Apol. cap. 17. Christians are not born, but made. And Augustine, lib. 1. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9. A Christian is not born of Christians, because generation does not make a Christian, but regeneration. He answers: That Tertullian speaks of adult Gentiles. But the case of infants is not different, as far as Christianity is concerned. For in Christ Jesus we are all one. But regarding Augustine, he denies in lib. I. cap. 9. that those things which were brought forward exist there. The same things are held in the same words in lib. III. cap. 9. What will you answer, why a Christian is not born of Christians, unless it is because generation does not make Christians, but regeneration. Where it is manifest that not even the Pelagians admitted that which the Pelagianizing Calvinists say, namely, that Christians are born of Christians. And Augustine is dealing there not with adults, but with infants.

Fifthly, the blessed Balduinus had employed this argument: That parents do not generate from that part by which they are Spirit and reborn, but by which they are flesh and polluted, just as a circumcised Jew without a foreskin generates a son with a foreskin. Crocius answers: From this it is correctly gathered that children are not born spiritual, but carnal: that they are not born without sin: that they are not born holy, that is, endowed with the virtue of holiness: Correct. Therefore they are not born federated. For in the covenant no one is without faith. But where there is faith, there is holiness. In vain, therefore, he says: You do not correctly gather that they are not born citizens of the Church and federated. For the blessed Balduinus had correctly pointed out that for the federated and citizens of the Church, faith, the grace of GOD, adoption, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and similar spiritual goods are required, which are joined by an individual bond and cannot have a place in those not yet baptized. Crocius insists with his Pareus: Mohammedans and pagans do not generate, in that they are Mohammedans and pagans, but in that they are humans. Yet from them are born Mohammedans and pagans. Citizens do not generate children in civil society, in that they are citizens, but in that they are humans, and yet their children are born citizens. Thus Paul says he is a Roman citizen by nature, Acts XXII. v. 28. He is not speaking of the nation, but of the right of citizenship, as appears from v. 27. He answers: From

Mohammedans and pagans, those addicted to the Mohammedan and pagan faith or religion, or rather incredulity and superstition, are not born. They imbibe it afterwards through education. Just as neither are Papists born from Papists, or Calvinists from Calvinists, nor are citizens born from citizens, so that they are citizens by birth alone: Because this arises from a peculiar right, not from birth itself. In certain places, the right of citizenship must even be redeemed from adults by certain teachers. But such a right, that they are in the covenant and are holy, who are procreated by the federated of God and the holy, the Calvinists cannot bring forward. For without distinction it is true: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. Crocius admits that for citizens of the Church, who are in interior holiness, the grace of God, faith, and adoption are required. But he says that the children of Christians are born Christians and in the Church as far as the exterior society is concerned. But the Calvinists do not attribute only this to the children of Christians: But an interior communion, and holiness, and other spiritual gifts. Let the places alleged by the blessed Balduinus be seen, from which Calvin had proven the inveterate error concerning hereditary Christianity, or concerning the natural holiness of children born of pious parents, lib. IV. institut. cap. 16. Beza, respons. II. ad Colloq. Mompelg. p. 102. Pareus in Comm. ad Rom. pag. 1177. and in Comment. 1. ad Corinth. pag. 414. Let those things also be seen which were brought forward in the preface dedicated to the Critici sacri directed against Crocius. To which Crocius has replied nothing, either here or elsewhere. He only rashly accuses us of malignant interpretation. He says that he asserts only the external right of the covenant, with which the infection of original stain does not conflict any more than disease conflicts with the right of earthly citizenship. But that the Calvinists understand interior holiness, the inspected places teach: Which they deny is conferred through baptism. They wish it only to be sealed through the same. Crocius himself here: But why, he says, can spiritual gifts not have a place in the unbaptized? But holiness, not external but internal, pertains to spiritual gifts: With which the infection of original stain certainly conflicts. For if they are holy by nature, by nature they are not infected with original sin, by nature they are not children of wrath. Therefore Augustine already refuted this in the Pelagians: Using among others the same argument as we do, when opposing those who say that a just man ought to beget a just man, he replies in l. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9: As if anyone generates carnally because he is just. From this, he says, he generates, because he still drags the old, among the children of this age, not from this, that he promotes into newness among the children of God. For the children of this age generate and are generated. Thence also, that which is born is such, because that which is born of the flesh is flesh. But they are not righteous, unless they are sons of God. Insofar, however, as they are sons of God, they do not beget from the flesh, because they themselves were born of the Spirit, not of the flesh.

Sixthly, for this reason, says Blessed Baldwin, at Antioch they were first called Christians, who had previously been instructed by the Apostles and had been made disciples of Christ, Acts 11:26. For the Apostles knew that 'Christian' was not the name of a nation, but of a religion, of a faith, in which no one is born, but is regenerated through baptism or the word. Crocius responds: They were Christians before they were so called. Correct. But they were so not by birth, but through instruction and regeneration by the word and baptism. Nor indeed were only adults called Christians, but also infants initiated through baptism. Crocius retorts: What is this to the point? Therefore, are the children of Christians not to be called Christians before they are baptized? I respond: It is so. Augustine had proven this, nor could the Pelagians themselves deny it. He retorts in turn: If they are not Christians before, they are not to be baptized. I answer with Augustine: Nay, rather, because they are not Christians by generation, but by regeneration, they are to be baptized, that they may be regenerated and become Christians. Baptism is indeed the treasure of Christians, because it is proper to the Christian Church, but not therefore because it is imparted to Christians, but because it is imparted in the Christian Church, whether to those born of Christians, or to those needing it from Christians, so that they may become Christians.

Seventhly, B. Balduinus urged: The reason is this, why Peter commands the Jews, with whom he had said God had made a covenant, to repent and be baptized, certainly not that they might receive the sealing of the covenant, in which they had been born, but that by this medium they might be adopted into the covenant, Acts

III. Crocius replies that those who believe and repent are in the covenant even before baptism.

But whence are such believers, unless because they are born of faithful parents? Thus faith itself will be natural and hereditary. Or is it because they receive faith through the word? In which cases we do not deny that faith is sealed and confirmed by baptism, as circumcision was to Abraham, who had already believed and had been justified before, the seal of righteousness, Rom. IV. 11.

Therefore, the examples of the thief on the cross not baptized, and of catechumens dying without baptism, are foreign. They are not outside the covenant, since they have obtained faith through the word. Yet, they are not in the covenant by birth.

Peter extends the promise to the children of those who repent, not yet baptized. It is true that he does not exclude them from the promise; yet for its actual participation and fruition, faith is needed, which is hereditary to none, but arises through regeneration, through the word and baptism.

Nothing against this opinion of Paul: We are Jews by nature: that they are said to be born Gentiles or not Christians from Christian parents?

Which B. Balduinus had rightly shown against the peer in quest. II. For Paul did not say that he and Peter were Jews by nature, because the Jewish faith and religion had been hereditary to them, or because they had been in the covenant as Jews by birth before circumcision: but because they were sprung from Israelitish lineage, to which circumcision and the ceremonial laws once belonged.

Foreign and beyond controversy are the things he brings from Krakevitius, that infants born in the Church, because of the external society and being nearer to those who are outside, are part of the Church regarding access to Christ, and what is from B. Balduinus himself, that they have access to the benefits of the Church, which the children of Gentiles do not have. It is permitted that they have access to the Church as a benefit. Gentiles are finally bound to seek that.

Those who are born of Christian parents are in the possessory, as the jurists like to speak: those from the Gentiles, in the petitory.

It is a horrible saying, says Crocius, that the children of Christians before baptism are outside the hope of eternal life. Is the sentence of Christ so horrible, John III. verse 5. Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.

But that it seems so to Crocius is from absolute predestination, which Calvin called horrible. For they suspend faith from this, not from baptism.

That to those whom the Lord has not chosen, even if they be baptized a thousand times, faith or the Holy Spirit is never given, but that they are left to perish by their own fault by the just judgment of God, was a horrible voice of Beza and his associates in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 469. But these are to those things which Crocius croaked here against the blessed Balduinus. We must now return to the Apostolic text. And from the Gentiles sinners

That is, idolaters, and ignorant of the divine law. For those new Doctors were indeed that.

He does not deny that he is by nature a sinner ; for we are all sinners and children of wrath by nature. There is no distinction in him , Rom. III. 22. 23. chap. V. 12. Ephes. II. verse 3. John III. 5. He opposes the Jew and the sinner from the Gentiles: the Jew by lineage, and the Gentile by lineage. But he calls this one a sinner , yet not exclusively. A Gentile was indeed considered a notable sinner, Matt. XVIII. 17. But not because of lineage, which exempts no one from the stain of sin, nor makes one a more notable sinner than others. For by reason of carnal birth we are all equal. Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. Who can give the clean, begotten from an unclean seed? Whence therefore? Because they were born from the Gentiles and remaining among the Gentiles were without Christ alienated from the commonwealth and strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope, and without God in the world, Ephes. II. 12. Those born of Israel were received into the covenant of God by circumcision on the eighth day. Not so the sinners from the Gentiles. They were bound to the ceremonies of the law, which did not obligate the Gentiles. Both were sinners: neither could be justified by the works of the law, whether they were born Jews or sinners from the Gentiles. Therefore the word sinners can be taken here generally: it can also be taken specially of those who are so called by way of excellence , saving the connection.

How Crocius renders this: Since we, who are born posterity of Abraham, circumcised and sprung from strangers, do not seek righteousness in the law, why do you compel the Gentiles to judaize? But if sinners repent from among the Gentiles, not only, as destitute of that external sanctity, because they were not born into the people of God as Jews, but plainly outside the Church, even with respect to external society, but also because in Gentilism they were wholly given over to sins and have lived shamefully, such as the Gentiles were before conversion, the inference will be this: Although we Jews are by nature, born of Israelitish lineage, and in the midst of the people of God and by circumcision brought into the covenant of GOD soon in earliest infancy, nor originating from a Gentile people alien to the promise of the testament, nor inserted into the covenant of GOD, nay rather given over to idolatry and other gross crimes: Yet we know certainly that we are by no means justified by works of the law, but by faith alone in Christ Jesus. Therefore we also, having omitted confidence in works, have believed in Christ Jesus, we are justified by faith in Christ, and not by works of the law. For it is a universal axiom, comprehending both Jews and Gentiles alike, that all flesh is not justified by works of the law, that is, no man at all.

Concerning which B. Luther in his former Commentary: He compares, he says, Jews and Gentiles. We, he says, Jews by nature, exceed the Gentiles in the righteousness of the law, who are sinners, if they are compared to us, as those who have neither the law nor its works. But not even in this are we justified before God. That righteousness of ours is external. And he treats this opinion most copiously in Rom. I. and II. where he first declares the Gentiles to have been the greatest sinners, but in chapter II. turning to the Jews, even if they are not such as he had described the Gentiles, he nevertheless asserts them to be sinners, because they do not keep the law outwardly, not inwardly. observed, and glorying in the law, have dishonored GOD by the transgression of the law. We are just, he says, as Jews by nature, not sinners as the Gentiles, but by the justice of the work of the law, by which no one is justified before God. Therefore, we also, like the Gentiles, our own justice having been counted as dung, seek to be justified through the faith of Christ, now being at once sinners with the Gentiles, and at once justified with the Gentiles, since God has made no distinction (as Peter says in Acts XV) between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.

It must be understood, however, as Flacius warns: With what conscience or hope, therefore, could we invite the unclean and polluted Gentiles to hope for salvation from the works of the law? Certainly, if anyone could be saved by the works of the law, we would have been saved by it. Because we cannot be justified by it, as we have been taught by the word of the Gospel, and we are saved solely through Christ, much less will they be justified by the law.

Thus, from his own example, he also argues for gratuitous justification in Phil. III: And up to this point, the words of Paul spoken to Peter at Antioch seem to be recited, which he repeats, because he publicly challenged Peter the Apostle to consent before the Church in this way, and not only was the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles defeated, and the true Evangelical faith defended: But he also diligently took care, lest even indirectly it be brought into danger through the scandal of conversation and the undermining of Christian liberty in life, with Peter himself approving, and not taking Paul's contradiction and rebuke with difficulty. Therefore, on the occasion of this Antiochene paroxysm, he not only remotely and indirectly insinuated and proved his main theme, but also by the revelation of those things which he had said at Antioch, he proposed that theme directly, not without artifice, which he now begins to treat by design against the Pseudo-Apostles, both with the direct assertion of Evangelical doctrine, and with the weight and momentum of the asserted Evangelical doctrine, to avoid any corruption and the shaking of the purer doctrine.

Latin:

V. 14. Ἀλλ' ὅτε εἶδον, ὅτι οὐ ὀρθοποδοῦσι, πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου) Id est, ubi vidi, non insistere eos eam viam, quae ad propagandam ubique veritatem Evangelicam erat maxime conducibilis, ita hic sumendum hoc verbum pro eo, quod Hebraei dicunt ישר דרך. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem ps. Non de praedicatione sed de conversatione a Paulo denotabatur. Illud τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιεῖν, opponitur τῇ σκολίᾳ et ἐκτρεπόμενα. Sed materia haec non admittit tam duram interpretationem.

Non est dura vel materiae praesenti adversa haec interpretatio. Scandalum enim erat gravissimum. Ideoq; quam primum id cognovit non ex auditu, sed per ἀυτοψίαν, fine mora interposuit remedium. Diximus de eo ad v. 12. Poterat Petrus, poterat Barnabas inter infirmos versans Judaeos, uti ceremoniis, licet essent mortuae, ut boneste sepelirentur, non poterat iis uti tanquam necessariis, non poterat earum usum adigere gentes, adigebat exemplo suo. Hoc non erat pede recto incedere, ut Evangelii congruebat veritati. Gentes enim putare poterant, observantiam ceremoniarum & Judaeis & sibi esse necessariam, quia Petrus se ab ipsis subduceret, ut recte hic Crocius. Veritas Evangelii, quod probe observatum Flacio, hic non significat verum Evangelium, ut aliqui male exponunt, non autem significat juxta praescriptum aut normam Evangelii, sed ad sinceritatem ac puritatem Evangelii retinendam. Non admixto fermento necessitatis operum legalium ad salutem, jam illa sinceritas Evangelii periisset. Illud ergo ὀρθῶς, admonendum eodem Flacio, vero suo sensu recipiendum de finali causa, quam supra vers. 5. clare exposuerat, non vero PER, JUXTA, aut SECUNDUM. Dicit enim illam simulationem, pravumque incessum Petri non ad conservationem, sed ad exitium Evangelii fuisse directum. Hac vero etiam ipsa est quaestio aut propositio, nempe quod affirmat. Petrum suo illo facto & simulatione evertere sinceritatem Evangelii & efficaciam gratiae, meritque Christi, ut quod solum non sufficeret ad justitiam & salutem, sine operibus legis. Εἶναι τῇ Πίστει ἄμπωδον πάντων

In magno consessu. Justinianum si audias, non tam Petrum, quam caeteros notavit, quia Petrus veram in animo tenebat sententiam, & externa saltem actione simulabat. At Paulus non separat Petrum a caeteris, & Petro id dixisse dicitur, utpote auctori scandali. Nec seorsim, sed coram omnibus tam Judaeis, quam gentibus. Cujus causam hisce exponit Augustinus: Quod ei coram omnibus dixit, necessitas coëgit, ut omnes illius objurgatione sanarentur. Non enim utile erat, errorem, qui palam noceret, secreto emendare. Εἰ οὐ Ἰουδαῖος ὑπάρχων Judaeus ex Judaeis, quem probabilius est, lege Mosis teneri, quam illos, qui ad Abrahami stirpem nihil pertinent. Ἐθνικῶς ζῆς

Uteris libertate, nempe ubi tibi ita visum est. Vide supra 12. Act. X. In Manuscripto: Ἐθνικῶς ἐν Ἰουδαίοις ζῆς. Τί τὰ ἔθνη ἀναγκάζεις Ἰουδαίζειν; In Manuscripto, πῶς τὰ ἔθνη &c. sensu eodem, cur vitas exemplo tuo.

Sic idem verbum habuimus Matth. XIV. 22. Marci VI. 45. Luc. XIV. 23. Act. XXVI. 1. Est simile verbum ἀναγκάζειν Luc. XXIV. 29. Act. XVI. 15. 2. Cor. XII.

11. Recte monet B. Lutherus in Comment. priori f. 13. Paulum Petrum non reprehendere, qui gentiliter vixisset, (ut vult B. Hieronymus) tunc & idem in seipso reprehendisset, sed quia simulavit.

Simulationem, inquit, Petri Paulus non tulit. Nam hoc approbat, quod gentiliter vixeras, & iterum Judaice, sed reprobat, quod venientibus Judaeis subtrahebat ac segregabas se a cibis gentilium, qua subtractione gentibus & Judaeis autor fiebat, gentilia esse illicita, & Judaica necessaria, cum textus indicat, Petrum non ignorasse hac esse libera, quia prius (inquit) cum gentibus edebat, item timens eos, qui a Jacobo venerant. Timore ergo, non ignorantia hec fecit. Non enim dicit Paulus, quare tu gentiliter vivis? nec dicit: Quare ad Judaismum reverteris? Utraque licuit facere, sed quare cogis gentes judaizare? Coalitio ista per simulationem & subtractionem reprehensibilis erat, qua gentes & Judaei credebant esse Judaica necessaria & gentilia illicita. Sic non queritur, caeteros Judaeos consensisse in cibum vel gentilem vel Judaeum (fiebant enim esse licitum) sed in formulationem Petri & coactionem gentium & Judaeorum, ad Judaismum, ut necessarium. Item non queritur Barnabam edisse cum eis Judaice & gentiliter, sed abductum in eandem simulationem, & coalitionem gentium & Judaeorum ad Judaismum consensisse. Igitur contra necessitatem pro libertate pugnat Paulus. Sola enim fides Christi necessaria est, ut justi fimus, caetera omnia liberrima neque praecepta amplius, neque prohibita. Si ergo Petrus recta fronte utraque fecisset, non fuisset reprehendendus. Sicut Paulus utraque cum fiducia fecit. Peccavit ergo Petrus, hypocritice ea agens, ex quibus Pseudo-Apostoli & ab iis seducti confirmari poterant in sua opinione, ac praesumere, Petrum secum statuere, gentiles sola Christi gratia ac sine lege non justificari, sed insuper opera legis ad salutem & justitiam ipsas necessaria esse, eosque nequaquam liberos esse a legis servitute. Ideoque arguitur Petrus hypocritice, quod aliud revera credat, quam nunc hypocritico illo facto & exemplo testetur, ac prae se ferat. Utitur autem interrogandi forma; ut fortius cor pulset: Tu qui Judaeus es, & ante adventum Judaeorum Hierosolymitanorum fidelium cum gentibus conversis communi mensa usus es, delectu ciborum minime observato, nec ceremoniales leges pensi habuisti, quid nunc gentes ad legum Mosaicarum observantiam, tanquam ad salutem necessariam adigis exemplo tuo? Cur facto ipso hanc in eis opinionem concitas, ac si sint adhuc immundi, & a DEI gratia alieni, quibuscum non liceat conversari propter non susceptam circumcisionem, adeoque inducis eos etiam per hoc tuum institutum in hanc pestiferam opinionem, ac si salus & justificatio a ceremoniis & operibus legis dependeat. Ideoque haec explicat B. Lutherus Comment. id est: Tu Judaeus es, qui tenetur lege Judaice vivere, hoc est abstinere a cibis in lege prohibitis. Et tamen Judaeus vivis gentiliter, hoc est, libere contra legem facis, transgrederis & conculcas eam. Comedia enim (& in hoc recte facis) communem seu immundos cibos, ut alius gentilis, qui a lege liber est. Hoc ipso autem, quod absberritus praesentia fratrum ex Judaeis conversorum, abfines nunc a prohibitie in lege & servas legem, cogis gentes judaizare, id est legem necessario servare. Nam hoc tuo exemplo, quod abstines a prophanis cibis, prabes gentibus occasionem fit cogitandi, Petrus jam vitas cibos gentiles, quos antea comedit, ergo & nos debemus vitare eos, & Judaice more vivere, alioquin non erimus justi, neque salvabimur. Vides ergo, quod Paulus in Petro non reprehendat ignorantiam, fiebat enim liberum esse, vesci cum gentibus quibuslibet; sed simulationem, qua coëgit gentes judaizare. Certe omnino est, Petrum in doctrina non errasse, neque in dogmate sive libertate Evangelica, sive justificationis coram DEO gratuita. Fuit ergo error, uti recte B. Hunnius, tantum in applicatione doctrinae sive praxi, libertatis Christianae legitima usu, atque sic in conversatione, quod ita se applicabat fratribus a Jacobo missis, ut interim alteros, qui ex gentibus erant, negligeret & offenderet.

Nihilominus autem videbatur ipso facto convelli (ex opinione gentilium Christianorum) articulus de libertate Christiana, quasi gentes non sint a lege circumcisionis & statutorum Mosaicarum libera, & quamdiu manent incircumcisae; non liceat perinde cum eis conversari et cibum capere. Qui error immediate secum trahebat alterum errorem, ac si susceptio circumcisionis et legis Mosaicae necessaria eis sit ad justificationem et salutem, et quasi nec justificatio nec salus constet, nisi circumcidantur et legem observent. Quae quidem duo falsa dogmata non erant Petri, sed Pseudo-Apostolorum. At factum Petri ita poterat accipi, imo a Gentilibus Corinthianis sic accipiebatur, ac si dogmati Pseudo-Apostolorum in utroque articulo quadantenus applauderet. Ad hoc ergo sanandum offendiculum et perversam opinionem mentibus eximendam necessaria fuit correctio, qua in Petrum Apostolum usus est Paulus. Atque ita aditum sibi paravit Apostolus ad thema principale et profligandum necessitatem observationis legis ad salutem.

Quo de jam parte cap. II. altera agere incipit. PARS II. CAPITIS II. DOGMATICA, DE JUSTIFICATIONE, QVOD EA NON PER OPERA LEGIS, SED PER FIDEM IN CHRISTVM FIAT; Qua inchoatur simul PARS ALTERA EPISTOLAE PRINCIPALIS ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΙΚΗ, Cujus

SECTIO I. Concernit doctrinae de justificatione puritatem. V. 15. '

Humeis physei Ioudaioi' Hic, absoluta narratione, Paulus inchoatum ad Galatas sermonem persequitur. Nos natura Judaei, non ut illi vestri Doctores, qui cum sint ex gentibus, judaizant. Argumentum hic insigne, ad arguendam Petri conversationem, subjicit, eoque ipsum ita constringit, ut simul arcem causae et thema principale jam ingrediatur, quod a Petri et sua communi scientia depromptum est.

Nos natura Judaei Israelita ex Abrahamo, Israele vel Jacobo descendentes. Dicebantur enim Judaei communiter Israelita, non solum ex tribu Judae oriundi, ex qua non descendebat Paulus, sed ex tribu Benjamin Philip. III. 5. Si respici dicatur nomine 'Ioudaioi' etiam externa illa sanctitas, de qua Rom. XI. 6. 1. Cor. VII. 14. cum opponuntur illis ex Ethnicis 'hamartoloi', non abnuimus; modo id teneatur, opponi Judaeos gentibus non respectu foederis, in quo erant illi per sacramentum circumcisionis, non te physei; sed ratione prosapias.

Proinde non recte colligit hinc Crocius, nos natura Christianos esse. Sumus quidem Christiani ex parentibus, qui Christiani sunt, sed non qua Christiani sunt. Non enim, qua per baptismum Christo inferti sunt, procrearunt, sed vi benedictionis divinae conjugio concessae. Non par est ratio nominis Judaicae vel Israeliticae sint. Christiani autem, ut habet Tertulliani trita regula, non nascuntur, sed fiunt. Evertunt hanc Calviniani, cum sanctos et sanctas parentibus procreari, riosque in foedere DEI nasci ajunt. Foederati sumus, inquit Crocius Comment. in h. 1. adversus B. Balduinum nostrum disputans. Non nascimur extra Ecclesiam, in Ecclesia nascimur. At nativitate jus habemus sacramentorum. At si in foedere sumus ante baptismum, non ergo per baptismum in foedus demum recipimur. Id vero volunt Sacramenta rii, per baptismum non jus foederis conferri, sed solum obsignari. Non ergo haec interpretatio sententiae Reformatorum est maligna, ut B. Balduinum arguit, sed germana ipsorum est sententia. In Ecclesia nasci ambigue dicitur, vel in caetu, in quo est Ecclesia, vel in coetu, qui est Ecclesia. Item ut per nativitatem simus membra Ecclesiae, vel ut aditum habeamus ad beneficia Ecclesiae; verum omnino est, in foedus neminem recipi per naturalem generationem, sed per fidem propriam. Quod de adultis dat et interiori foederis societate Crocius, non de infantibus.

At non alia ratione infantes in foedus recipiuntur, quam adulti. Recipiuntur, inquit, via promissionis: Ero Deus tuus et feminis tui post te Gen. XVII. Sed ad applicationem aliam et individualem promissionis opus est fide. Videamus rationes B. Balduini, et, quia eas impugnat Crocius, vindicemus. Prima est: Quibuscum Deus Deus foedus paciscitur, illi sunt filii Dei. Filii autem sunt, qui credunt Joh. I. 13. et per fidem Gal. III. 26. Temere limitat vel ampliat majorem Crocius: illi sunt, vel erunt filii Dei. Nam si actu in foedere; actu fidem habeant, oportet. Dicit de adultis agi Joh. I. et Gal. III. Sed ut adulti; ita et infantes filii DEI fiunt non nisi per fidem. Eorum hactenus eadem est ratio.

Nec aliter haeredes vitae aeternae fiunt aut salvantur infantes quam adulti. Scilicet nulli consequuntur salutem nisi per fidem, per justitiam imputatam Christi, quae non nisi fide imputatur. In Christo Jesu, uti non est mas vel famina Gal. III. 28. ita nec adultus vel infans. Omnes unus sunt in Christo, omnes unum per fidem. Dicit: Infantes fideles, cum in utero matris habere fidem non constat: Nec tamen sunt filii Diaboli. At natura sunt filii irae Ephes. II. 3. atque hactenus sub regno Satanae. Nemo enim regnum DEI ingreditur, nisi regeneretur.

Si natura filii irae, natura certe non sunt filii DEI. Altera ratio haec est: Baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis, non quod eo foedus hoc obsignetur, sed quod per eum conferatur. Tit. III. 5. Eph. V. 26. 1. Joh. III. 5. Respondet, non sequi, baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis. Ergo ex Christianis non nascuntur Christiani. At Christiani fiunt per regenerationem, non vero nascuntur per carnalem propagationem. Negat jus foederis primum conferri per baptismum, quia Christianorum liberi ita non magis aditum ad baptismum haberent quam Turcarum.

At aliud est aditum habere ad baptismum, et ita ad receptionem in foedus; aliud esse in foedere. Ingressus in regnum DEI utique per baptismum fit. At ille ingressus est receptio in foedus, quo regni DEI possessio filiis DEI spondetur. Negat hoc Crocius, quia receptio, inquit, praecedit, ingressus in foedus DEI sequitur. Si regnum gratia intelligas, cum quis in foedus recipitur, in illud ingreditur. Si regnum gloriae, spondetur id per foedus. Abrahamus quidem erat in foedere DEI per fidem, quam e Verbo conceperat, sed tum nondum institutum erat sacramentum circumcisionis. Quod medium deinde ordinarium erat regenerationis, initiationis, et receptionis in foedus DEI. Nec aliud medium habent infantes hodie, quam baptismum: qui in locum circumcisionis successit: Atque ita omnes ante baptismum decedentes extra foedus essent, ac spem salutis non haberent. Resp. baptismus est medium ordinarium: Potest autem Deus extra ordinem infantes Christianorum, precibus Ecclesiae ipsi commendatos in foedus recipere sine sacramento, quum non sefe, sed nos ad hoc medium adstrinxe- rit, nec privatio, sed comtemtus Sacramenti da- mnet.

Tertia ratio est: In regno DEI nemo nascitur, sed per baptismum in illud recipitur, Joh. III. v. 5. Ergo nemo dici potest natura Christianus. Nam ex DEO nasci, Christum induere, renasci, est Christianum fieri. Ergo per baptismum demum fiunt Christiani. Respondet: Ita est: In regno DEI, id est, in regno gloriæ nemo nascitur. At nec in regno gratiæ nascimur, quia natura sumus fi- lii iræ. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est. A nativitate in Vet. Test. fuisse fœderatos DEI, petitio principii est. Erant per circumcisionem, non per nativitatem carnalem. Illam tantum fœderis signum, non primam fœderis & salutis ja- nuam fuisse, æque falsum, ac si de baptismo id dicatur. Medium enim utrumque sacramentum est initiationis gratiæ & salutis. Fatetur Crocius, non nasci nos ex Deo nativitate prima, sed secun- da. Non renasci ex parentibus, nec Christum in- duere per generationem, sed per sacramentum & fidem. Negat autem, nos ideo non esse natura Chri- stianos. At hoc est, respondere ad conclusionem. Quid vero Croci ad argumentum dicis, ex Deo nasci, Christum induere, renasci, est Christianum fieri? Hic hæret tibi aqua. Magis mutus es, quàm piscis.

Quarto adducti erant Patres Tertullianus Apo- log. cap. 17. Non nascuntur, sed fiunt Christiani. Et Augustin. lib. 1. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9. Christianus de Christianis non nascitur, quia non facit generatio, sed regeneratio Christia- num. Respondet. Tertullianum loqui de genti- libus adultis. At non est dispar infantum ratio, quantum ad Christianismum. In Christo Jesu enim omnes unus sumus. Apud Augustinum vero ne- gat libr. I. cap. 9. extare ea, quæ adducta sunt. Habentur eadem totidem verbis lib. III. cap. 9. Quid respondebitis, quare de Christianis non Chri- stianus nascatur, nisi quia non facit generatio, sed regeneratio Christianos. Ubi ne quidem Pelagia- nos id admisisse, quod Calviniani Pelagianizantes ajunt, Christianos nempe nasci de Christianis, ma- nifestum est. Et agit ibi Augustinus non de ad- ultis, sed de infantibus.

Adhibuerat Quintò B. Balduinus hoc argu- mentum: Quod parentes non generent ex ea parte, qua sunt Spiritus & renati, sed qua caro sunt & polluti, sicut Judæus circumcisus absque præputio generat filium cum præputio. Respondet Crocius: Ex eo colligi recte, liberos non nasci spirituales, sed carnales: non sine peccato nasci: non nasci san- ctos, id est, virtute sanctitatis præditos: Recte. Ergo non nascuntur fœderati. In fœdere enim nemo est sine fide. Ubi autem fides, ibi sancti- tas est. Frustra ergo dicit: Non recte colligas, non nasci cives Ecclesiæ, & fœderatos. Nam ad fœ- deratos & cives Ecclesiæ requiri fidem, gratiam DEI, adoptionem, Spiritus Sancti inhabitatio- nem, & similia spiritualia bona, quæ individuo nexu juncta sunt, & in nondum baptizatis locum habere non possunt, recte monuerat B. Baldui- nus. Instat cum Paræo suo Crocius: Mahume- dani & pagani non generant, qua sunt Mahume- dani & pagani, sed qua homines. Ex iis tamen nascuntur Mahumedani & pagani. Cives non generant in civili societate liberos, qua sunt cives, sed qua homines, & tamen eorum liberi nascuntur cives. Sic Paulus dicit se natura esse Romanum civem Actor. XXII. vers. 28. Non loquitur de gen- te, sed civitatis jure, ut ex v. 27. apparet. Resp. Ex

Mahumedanis, & paganis non nasci Mahume- dana & pagana fidei seu religioni vel potius incre- dulitati & superstitioni addictos. Eam postmo- dum per educationem imbibunt. Quemadmo- dum nec Papistae e Papistis, aut Calviniani e Cal- vinianis nascuntur, e civibus non nascuntur cives, ut propter nativitatem solam cives sint: Quia hoc ex peculiari jure oritur, non ex nativitate ipsa. In quibusdam locis etiam certis didactris ab adultis demum redimendum est jus civitatis. Tale autem jus, quod in foedere & sancti sint, qui a foederatis Dei & sanctis procreantur, ad- ferre nequeunt Calviniani. Sine discrimine enim verum est: Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est. Fatetur Crocius, ad cives Ecclesiae, qui sunt in in- teriori sanctitate, gratiam Dei, fidem, adoptionem requiri. Christianorum autem liberos Christianos nasci & in Ecclesia quoad exteriorem societatem. Hoc sufficere ait. At non hoc tantum tribuunt Christianorum liberis Calviniani: Sed commu- nionem interiorem, & sanctitatem ac alia dona spi- ritualia. Videantur loca a B. Balduino allegata, e quibus inveteratum errorem de haereditario Christianismo, seu de naturali sanctitate libero- rum ex piis parentibus progenitorum probarat Calvinus libr. IV. institut. cap. 16. Beza respons. II. ad Colloq. Mompelg. p. 102. Pareus in Comm. ad Rom. pag. 1177. & in Comment. 1. ad Corinth. pag. 414. Videantur & ea, quae in praefat. dedic. Critici sacri contra Crocium directa sunt adducta. Ad quae nihil sive hic, sive alibi reposuit Crocius. Temere solum nos arguit malignae interpretatio- nis. Jus foederis externum suos tantum asserere ait, cum quo non magis pugnet infectio originalis labis, quam morbus cum jure civitatis terrena. Sed in- teriorem sanctitatem intelligere Calvinianos, loca inspecta docent: Quam negant per baptismum conferri. Obsignari tantum per eundem volunt. Crocius ipse hic: Cur vero spiritualia, inquit, dona in non baptizatis locum habere non possunt? sanctitas autem non externa, sed interna pertinet ad spiritualia dona: Cum qua certe infectio labis originalis pugnat. Si enim natura sancti sunt, natura non sunt peccato originali infecti, natura non sunt filii irae. Ideo in Pelagianis id jam pro- fligavit Augustinus: Inter alia eodem, quo nos, argumento usus, cum opponentibus, quod justus justum gignere debeat, haec reponit l. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9. Quasi ex hoc quisque carna- liter gignat, quod justus est. Ex hoc, inquit, gignit, quod adhuc vetustum trahit, inter filios hujus seculi, non ex hoc, quod in novitatem promovet inter filios Dei. Filii enim seculi hujus generant & generantur. Inde &, quod nascitur, tale est, quia & quod nasci- tur de carne, caro est. Justi autem non sunt, nisi filii Dei. In quantum autem sunt filii Dei, carne non gignunt, quia ex Spiritu ipsi, non carne nati sunt.

Sexto hac de causa, inquit B. Balduinus, An- tiochiae primum Christiani appellabantur, qui ab Apostolis prius instituti, & discipuli Christi facti fuerant, Act. XI. 26. Apostoli enim noverant, Chri- stianum non esse nomen gentis, sed religionis, fidei, in qua nemo nascitur, sed per baptismum vel verbum regeneratur. Respondet Crocius: Christianos fuis- se, priusquam appellarentur. Recte. Sed erant non nativitate, sed per institutionem & regenera- tionem per verbum & baptismum. Nec vero tan- tum adulti Christiani nuncupati sunt, sed etiam infantes per baptismum initiati. Regerit Crocius: Hoc quid ad rem? Ergone liberi Christianorum non sunt Christiani appellandi priusquam baptizen- tur? Respond. Ita est. Probarat hoc Augustinus, nec inficiari poterant ipsimet Pelagiani. Regerit vicissim: Si non ante Christiani, non sunt baptizandi. Resp. cum Augustino: Imo vero ideo, quia non sunt Christiani per generationem, sed per regenerationem, baptizandi sunt, ut regenerentur..., & Christiani fiant. Baptismus quidem Christianorum thesaurus est, quod Christianae Ecclesiae proprius, non autem ideo, quod impertiatur Christianis, sed quod in Ecclesia Christiana impertiatur sive ex Christianis prognatis, sive à Christianis id egentibus, ut Christiani fiant.

Septimò urgebat B. Balduinus: Hac ratio est, cur Petrus Judaeos, cum quibus Deum foedus pepigisse dixerat, resipiscere & baptizare jubet, certe, non ut obsignationem foederis acciperent, in quo nati essent, sed ut per hoc medium in foedus adoptarentur, Act.

III. Reponit Crocius, credentes & resipiscentes etiam ante baptismum esse in foedere.

Sed unde sunt credentes tales, anne quod è fidelibus prognati parentibus? Ita fides ipsa naturalis erit & hereditaria. An vero quod per verbum fidem accipiant? In qualibus non negamus fidem obsignari & confirmari per baptismum, ut circumcisio Abrahamo, qui jam crediderat & justificatus erat antea σφραγὶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης fuit, Rom. IV. 11.

Alie-na ergo exempla latronis in cruce non baptizati, & catechumenorum sine baptismo decedentium. Illi non extra foedus sunt, cum fidem consequuti sunt per verbum. Non tamen, per nativitatem in foedere sunt.

Petrus promissionem extendere ad resipiscentium liberos nondum baptizatos. Verum est, quod à promissione eos non excludat; ad cujus tamen actualem participationem, & fruitionem fide opus est, quae nullis hereditaria est, sed per regenerationem, per verbum & baptismum oritur.

Nihil contra hanc Pauli sententiam: Nos natura Judaei: quod ex parentibus Christianis dicantur nasci gentiles vel non Christiani? Quod recte dici B. Balduinus contra parem quaest. II. ostenderat.

Non enim natura Judaeos se, & Petrum dixit Paulus, quod haereditaria sibi fuerit fides & religio Judaica, vel quod in foedere Judaeis fidelibus proprio fuerint per nativitatem ante circumcisionem: sed quod ex Israelitica prosapia oriundi, ad quam pertinebant quondam circumcisio, & leges ceremoniales.

Aliena sunt, & extra controversiam aleam posita, quae affert è Krakevizio, quod infantes in Ecclesia geniti quod externam societatem & proximiorem praeis, qui extra sunt, ad Christum aditum pars sunt Ecclesiae, & quae ex ipso B. Balduino, quod aditum habeant ad Ecclesia beneficia, quem non habeant gentilium liberi. Habere illos licet aditum ad Ecclesia esse beneficium. Illud gentiles demum petere tenentur.

Qui à Christianis prognati sunt parentibus, in possessorio versantur, ut JCtis loqui amant: Qui ex gentilibus, in petitorio.

Horrida vox est, inquit Crocius, quod Christianorum liberi ante baptismum sint extra spem vitae aeternae. Itane horrida vox est sententia Christi Joh. III. vers. 5. Amen amen dico tibi, nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi regnum caelorum.

Sed quod ita videatur Crocio, ex absoluta praedestinatione, quam horrendam dixit Calvinus, est. Nam ab hac suspendunt fidem, non à baptismo.

Quos Dominus non elegit, etiamsi millies baptizentur, illis tamen nunquam fidem aut Spiritum Sanctum donari, sed justo DEI judicio relictos sua culpa perire, vox horribilis erat Beza & sociorum in Colloq. Mompelg. pag. 469. Sed haec ad ea, quae hic crocitavit adversus Beat. Balduinum Crocius. Redeundum nunc est ad textum Apostolicum. Καὶ ἐκ ἐθνῶν ἁμαρτωλοὶ

Id est, idololatrae, & legis divinae ignari. Nam id quidem fuere illi novi Doctores.

Non negat, seφύσει ἁμαρτωλῶν ; nam omnes peccatores sumus & filii ire natura. Nulla in eo estδιαστολὴ , Rom. III. 22. 23. cap. V. 12. Ephes. II. vers. 3. Johan. III. 5. opponit Judaeum, & ex Ethnicis peccatorem: prosapia Judaeum, & prosapia Ethnicum. Hunc autemἁμαρτωλῶν dicit, at non exclusive. Ethnicus sane pro insigni peccatore habebatur Matth. XVIII. 17. At non ob prosapiam, quae neminem à peccati labe eximit, aut insigniorem pre aliis peccatorem facit. Ratione enim carnalis nativitatis omnes pares sumus. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est. Quis potest mundum dare, ex immundo procreatum semine? Unde ergo? Quia ex Ethnicis orti & inter Ethnicos manentes erantχωρὶς Χριστοῦ ἀπαλλοτριούμενοι τῆς πολιτείας καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντες, καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, Ephes. II. 12. Ex Israelis prognati per circumcisionem octavo die recipiebantur in foedus DEI. Non item peccatores ex Ethnicis. Illi adstringebantur ad ceremonias legis, quae Ethnicos non obligabant. Utrique peccatores erant: neutri justificari poterant per opera legis, sive nati essent Judaei, sive è gentilibus peccatores. Potest ergo voxἁμαρτωλῶν hic accipi generaliter: potest etiam specialiter de iis, quiκατ' ἐξοχὴν ita dicti, salva connexia.

Quam hanc reddit Crocius: Cum nos, qui sumus nati Abrahami posteri circumcisi & ab extraneis orti, in lege non quaramus justitiam, cur cogis gentes judaizare? Sed si resipiscant è gentilibus peccatores, non tantum, ut destituti illa exteriori sanctitate, quod non ut Judaei in populo Dei nati, sed plane extra Ecclesiam sint, etiam quoad externam societatem, sed etiam, quod in gentilismo peccatis prorsus dediti, turpiterque vixerint, quales ante conversionem fuere gentiles, ita habebit illatio: Quamvis nos Judaei simusnatura, nati prosapia Israelitica, & in medio populi Dei & per circumcisionem in DEI foedus mox in prima infantia relati, nec oriundi ex populo gentili à testamenti promissionis alieno, nec foederi DEI inferto, imo idololatriae, aliisque crassis flagitiis dedito: Tamen certo scimus, nequaquam per opera legis nos justificari, sed sola in Christum Jesum fide. Propterea & nos omissa fiducia operum, in Christum Jesum eredidimus, justificamur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Universale enim axioma est, Judaeos pariter & gentes comprehendens, quod non justificetur ex operibus legis omnis caro, hoc est, nullus omnino hominum.

Quo de B. Lutherus Comment. priori: Comparat, inquit, Judaeos & gentes. Nos, inquit, natura Judaei in lege justitia excedimus quidem gentes, qui peccatores sunt, si nobis conferantur, ut qui nec legem, nec opera ejus habeant. Verum nec in hoc justifumus comm DEO. Externa est ista justitia nostra. Et hanc sententiam copiosissime tractat Rom. I. & II. ubi primum gentes declarat maximos peccatores fuisse, sed in capite II. ad Judaeos vertens, etiamsi tales non sint, quales gentiles descripserat, nihilominus peccatores asserit, quod legem foris non intus servaverint, & in lege gloriantes per legis transgressionem DEUM inhonorauerint. Iusti, inquit, sumus, sicut natura Iudaei, non peccatores, sicut gentes, sed iustitia operis legis, qua nullus iustificatur coram Deo. Ideo & nos, sicut gentes, ...iustitia nostra pro stercore ducta, per fidem Christi iustificari quærimus, iam simul peccatores cum gentibus, simul iustificati cum gentibus, quando Deus nihil discreuit (ut Petrus Act. XV. dicit) inter nos & illos, fide purificans corda illorum.

Subintelligendum autem est, monente Flacio: Quæ igitur conscientia aut spe immundos & pollutos gentiles invitaremus ad sperandam ex operibus legis salutem. Certe si quis ex operibus legis servari posset, nos per eam servati fuissemus. Quod finos per eam iustificari nequimus, uti verbo Evangelii docti sumus, nos unicè per Christum salvari, multo minus isti per legem iustificabuntur.

Sic à suo exemplo pro gratuita iustificatione etiam Phil. III. argumentatur: Atque huc usque videntur recitari verba Pauli ad Petrum Antiochiæ dicta, quæ repetit, quod publice ita coram Ecclesia ad Petri Apostoli consensum provocarit, nec tantum Pseudo-Apostolorum doctrina profligata, veram fidem Evangelicam adfuerit: Sed etiam, ne vel indirectè ea, per conversationis scandalum, & libertatis Christianæ in vita labefactationem in discrimen adducatur, sedulo cauerit, approbante ipso Petro, contradictionem & reprehensionem Pauli haud ægrè ferente. Quapropter occasione huius paroxysmi Antiocheni non modo remotius & indirectè suum thema principale & insinuavit & comprobavit, sed etiam revelatione eorum, quæ Antiochiæ dixerat, thema illud directe, non fine artificio, proposuit, quod ex instituto tractare jam contra Pseudo-Apostolos aggreditur, cum qua doctrina Evangelicæ directam assertionem, tum qua assertæ doctrinæ Evangelicæ pondus & momentum, ad evitandam quamcunque corruptelam & purioris doctrinæ concussionem.

## 2:16
v. 16. Εἰδότες, ὅτι οὐ δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἔργων νόμου That is, one is not led to that true and spiritual justice which prepares eternal life through the works of the law.

See what we have said regarding the epistle to the Romans, in the Prolegomena, and in Acts III and IV, where by acting according to the law, man became accustomed to a certain justice, and one having a temporal reward. In the Manuscript it is added, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, in a locution not unlike that which is in 2 Cor. III. 5, except that there it is ἄς, here ὅτι, so that the sense is that the works of the law can serve to prepare true justice, but that this does not properly proceed from them, nor is this absolutely required for that.

But in this way, the Apostolic doctrine is significantly corrupted, and the state of the controversy is perverted. For first, Grotius assumes that our own justice produces eternal life, which is a mere gratuitous gift of GOD in Christ Jesus, Rom. VI. last, which we do not obtain by our own justice, but Christ has obtained for us an obedience, both active and passive, by which alone we are constituted just before GOD, Rom. V. v. 19. Then, wrongly correcting all the Codices from one Manuscript, and forming it from ὅτι ὡς, as if it ought to be read εἰδότες ὅτι ἐκ δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, he attempts to elicit a sense that is clearly alien and contrary, by a comparison of a place that is entirely different, 2 Cor. III. 5, namely that a man is indeed justified to some extent by the works of the law, but not as if by the works of the law; the former of which is opposed both to the present sentiment of the Apostle, and to the perpetual analogy of faith, since both here the Apostle and elsewhere the sacred scripture simply denies that a man is in any way justified before GOD through the works of the law, nay rather he will deny that the law can be fulfilled by us, Rom. VIII. 3. Acts XV. 10. just as afterwards he professes concerning himself, and concerning Peter, and other Jews, that they are not justified through the works of the law, but solely through the faith of Christ: And furthermore he asserts universally, that no flesh, none of mortals, is justified through the works of the law. See, says Theophylactus, how freely, and with nothing hesitating, he speaks all things. For we did not, he says, leave the law because it was more unjust, but because it would be weaker, and impotent to bestow justification. For no one could carry out its works, because they were heavy, and not easy to be done.

And where, I ask, is it taught in the scriptures that the works of the law can serve to prepare true justice, that is, for justification, for thus Grotius interprets it. Before justification, certainly, there is no place for anything but sin and impiety, since GOD justifies the impious, Rom. IV. 5, and justification consists in the remission of sins, and the non-imputation of iniquities, as the Apostle teaches; where justification is described by that reason, that true and spiritual justice, that is, holiness inherent in us, is generated or arises in us? Or as the Papists love to express the same thing, that a habit of justice or charity is infused into us? This is a Papistic fiction, which Grotius encrusts with other words, but not an Apostolic dogma.

As for the latter, it is to be assumed as if that were not from the works of the law, unless the words are encrusted and perverted, nor is it contained here κατὰ διάνοιαν, nay, it is repugnant to the sense. For the works of the law are simply excluded from justification, but not with that inept restriction, as if by the work of the law. They are simply opposed to the faith of Christ or in Christ, so that the justification of Christ is denied to them, and is ascribed solely to his obedience, just as they are opposed, that we are constituted just by our own obedience, and that we are constituted just not by our own obedience, but only by the obedience of Christ, imputed to us through faith.

The third question with the Pseudo-Apostles was not, whether by performing the works which the law requires we attain holiness and spiritual justice? But whether by the same we are justified before the tribunal of God and saved eternally? Which the Apostle denies: and it had already been denied in the Synod of Jerusalem: then because no one can perfectly perform the law, its yoke is ἀβάστακτον: then because solely through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, apprehended by true faith, we attain eternal salvation, as all the Prophets bear witness to Christ, S. Peter teaching that in his name, not through the works of the law, they obtain remission of sins, that is, all who believe in him are justified, Act. XLIII. And Paul at Antioch of Pisidia openly testified Act. XIII. 24. Be it known unto you, men and brethren, that through this (Jesus) remission of sins (or justification) is announced to you, and from all things by which you could not be justified in the law of Moses: In this (Jesus) everyone who believes is justified.

Fourthly, it is false that man, by acting according to the law, becomes accustomed to a certain justice, but a carnal one, and one having a temporal reward. For the law is spiritual, and if it were perfectly fulfilled, it would bring not a carnal, but a spiritual justice. But it can be fulfilled by no one even after regeneration, because man is still carnal in part, and not spiritual by affection, as is taught in Roman. VII. 14. The law does not promise only temporal goods to those who fulfill it, as Grotius errs with the Pelagians and Socinians, but eternal life itself, Lev. XIX. 5, with Christ as the interpreter above every greater exception, Luc. X. 28, as also our Apostle in this very demonstration of his theme, Gal. III. verf. 12. Fifthly, if the justice by which we stand before GOD does not proceed from the works of the law, nor are these absolutely required for it, through that justice, by which by which we are justified, or constituted just before God, cannot be understood as one's own inherent justice. For this is done through the works of the law and their observance, nor does it have any place without the observance or works of the law. For how is anyone holy or inherently just without the works or observance of the law? Since the law is the norm of holiness and inherent justice, and holiness or inherent justice is nothing other than the observance of and conformity with the law, just as the opposite of this, sin (ἁμαρτία), is lawlessness (ἀνομία), or illegality, deformity, and aberration from the law or transgression of the law, 1 John 3:4.

Sixth: Although we do not deny that the law is in some measure fulfilled, and that the external observation of the law can in some way be called justice, yet it is not justice in the divine forum, nor is the law content with such external obedience, but it requires a most perfect justice, absolute in all respects, which no one after the fall can provide, which is found only in Christ. But it is imputed to us through faith, since Christ has been made justice for us by God, 1 Cor. 1:29.

Therefore, the blessed Luther diligently inculcates this distinction in his prior Commentary. First, therefore, it must be known that man is justified in two ways, and in entirely opposite ways. First, from without, by works, from one's own powers, such as those human justices acquired by use (as it is said) and custom. Such as Aristotle and other philosophers describe; such as civil and ecclesiastical laws [require] by ceremonies; such as the dictate of reason and prudence produces. For thus they think that by doing just things one becomes just, by tempering one becomes temperate, and the like. The law of Moses makes this. The Decalogue itself also, namely where God is served by fear of punishment or promise of reward, one does not swear by the name of God, parents are honored, one does not kill, one does not commit theft, one does not commit adultery, etc. This is servile, mercenary, feigned, specious, external, temporal, worldly, human justice, which profits nothing for future glory, but in this life receives reward, glory, riches, honor, power, friendship, health, or at least peace and tranquility, and fewer evils than those who act otherwise, just as Christ describes the Pharisees. Second, from within, by faith and grace, where man, utterly despairing of the former justice as if from menstrual filth, rushes before God, groaning humbly as a sinner, and having confessed himself, says with the publican: God be merciful to me a sinner. This man, says Christ, went down justified to his house. For this is nothing other than the invocation of the divine name. But to one thus justified in heart through faith, which is in his name, God gives them the power to become children of GOD, the Holy Spirit being soon diffused in their hearts, which dilates them with charity, and makes them peaceful and joyful, workers of all good things, victors over all evils, even contemners of death and hell. Here soon all laws cease, the works of all laws, all things are now free, licit, and the law is fulfilled through faith and charity. Behold, this is what Christ merited for us, namely that the name of the Lord be preached (that is, the mercy, the truth of God), in which whoever believes shall be saved. This is Megalander. law and adequately opposes faith to itself, furthermore excludes all doubt, brings forward Abraham, instructed in moral works, as an example, who is not justified by them but by faith, and expressly treats of those works concerning which Moses says in Leviticus 18:5:

He who shall do them shall live in them, where it is most clear that it is a matter of the works of the moral law; of that law through which all things are concluded under sin, Gal. 3:22, from whose curse Christ has freed us, verse 23, to which he subjected himself, chapter 4:4, whose work is charity, chapter 5:6, which is indeed the moral law: Therefore there is no place for that exception of the Papists. Which therefore many of them today abandon and refute. William Estius on this passage. From which passage (Rom. 3) it must also be sought what the Apostle understands by the works of the law, from which he denies that man is justified, namely not only the ceremonial works of the Mosaic law, such as circumcision, the Sabbath, the new moon, etc. Concerning which many explain this passage. But in general, works of whatever kind from the law, that is, done from the knowledge of the law, even if they are only moral. For in the doctrine of the Apostle, by which he removes justice from the works of the law, we have shown by clear arguments in the exposition of the epistle to the Romans that the law is understood in its whole genus, as it comprehends moral and ceremonial [works] together. Benedictus Justinianus on this passage. Although Paul, he says, especially acts against the ceremonies of the law; yet here he excludes all works of the law in general, which are of the law.

Others therefore (2.) distinguish between the works of the law and the works of faith and the Spirit. That only the works of the law are excluded, and merits, not the works of faith and the Spirit, as Salmero [does] here. But if merits are excluded, why then do the Papists establish merits, and assert that man can merit justification by congruity, or dispose himself by the powers of free will to the infusion of justice? As Salmero himself [says] here: Faith alone, he says, does not in this passage exclude good morals of free will disposing to justice. 2. The Apostle does not say, not by the merits of works, but not by the works of the law. 3. The error of the Pseudo-Apostles did not consist in this, that they established that our works were meritorious of justification, but when they admitted faith in Christ, they wanted the works of the law to be joined to it. If they had believed that the works of the law merited justification, they would have admitted that there was no need for faith in Christ. The Papists themselves explain the sentiment of the Pseudo-Apostles at great length: That doctrine of the Judaizers, says Estius, against whom the Apostle acts, is to mix the law with the faith of Christ, and to expect salvation equally from both. The error of the Judaizers, says Adam Sasbouth, was not that they rejected faith, but that, not content with faith, they joined to it the works of the law, fearing that faith would not suffice. 4. The works of faith and the Spirit are rashly opposed to the works of the law. For those are called works of the law which have the law as their norm and are done according to the law. But those works which proceed from faith and are fruits of the Spirit must likewise have the law as their norm and be done according to the law. 5. The Apostle therefore simply excludes works which have the law as their norm, and thus no work can be excepted here. For either the work is good, and thus it is lawful (ἔννομον) and has the law as its norm and conforms to it, or it is evil and lawlessness (ἀνομία), or it is sin. 6. Truly good works done are not truly good works. 7. The Apostle excludes his works: Which were indeed done from faith. He denies justification to those works, for which we were created, Eph. 2:8 ff. But this

Moreover, by this

are they works of the Spirit? 8. The Galatians, to whom he writes, were reborn; when, therefore, he teaches them the mode of justification, denying that they are justified by the works of the law, he certainly excludes the works of the reborn from justification. 9. Papists oppose works done without grace to the works of grace and the Spirit. But besides the fact that this is a contradiction in terms, to feign good works without grace, such things cannot be understood here, because Abraham, at the time when faith was imputed to him, had long since been in the grace of God. Since, therefore, Abraham is denied to have been justified by the works of the law, who certainly was not destitute of the works of faith and the Spirit, it is manifest that the works of faith and the Spirit are removed from justification. Whence Bellarmine, lib. IV. de justif. c. 18, betakes himself to another exception, that Abraham had already been just before, since he could do just works, and thus by faith he was not made just from being ungodly, but more just from being just.

Some Papists therefore distinguish between primary and secondary justification; the former is done without works of the law, the latter not so. But this distinction is clearly unknown to Scripture: nor is the question here how one can be made more just or more holy from being just or holy: but how God justifies the ungodly? And the Jesuit Hager acknowledges in Coll. A.
