C. with the Council of Trent, p. 250, that by the justice which Abraham is said to have acquired here, primary as well as secondary justification is to be understood: and therefore it is necessary that by the opposition of faith and works, works are clearly excluded in both, since it becomes manifest that they are entirely excluded here from justification. Estius agrees here: What it is to be justified, he says, can be understood equally from those things which we have commented upon in the epistle to the Romans. For it extends to every acquisition of truly saving and beatific justice, whether primary, by which a just man is made from an ungodly one; or secondary, by which a just man is justified further. The same Estius acknowledges that a man is justified by faith alone, when he proceeds thus: But a man is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, insofar as, acknowledging Christ the Redeemer through it, he expects and receives from his merit the remission of sins and justice from GOD. But what he adds, that this is done through those means which Christ himself instituted for providing justification to men, such as invocation, works of penance, sacraments, and the observance of the divine law, according to that: The doers of the law shall be justified, Rom. II., that is opposed by the Apostle κατὰ μέλλον, who admits no other medium on our part than faith, but entirely excludes works. How then does Estius dare to insert here the observance of the law, and works of penance, and invocation, which is a work of the second commandment of the decalogue? We ourselves do not exclude the sacraments: But they are means on the part of God, of which there is no question here. A similar εὐλόγησις is that of Cornelius à Lapide: That the little word 'only' excludes the works of the law, not the law itself, fear, charity, penance, which faith begets and produces: For these are understood under faith, as daughters under a mother. For are not the works of hope, fear, charity, penance, works of the law? Do they not have the law as their norm? Are they not done according to the law? But all works of the law are excluded by that exclusive 'only by faith'. And how can works be comprehended under faith as under a mother and cause, and as daughters and effects, when justification is so attributed to faith alone, that works are universally excluded? And they follow faith indeed, but after we have been justified by it alone. For good works, as the rule of Augustine has it, follow the justified, but do not precede the one to be justified. Good works are the fruits and effects of justice. But the effect and fruit is not prior to its cause, and the tree, whose fruit it is. And so much for the Papists.

The Socinians, interpreted by Crellius in Comment. ad h. l. in operib. Exeg. p. 396, have devised this gloss: That faith, to which justification is simply ascribed, is opposed not to any works whatsoever, but only to works taken κατ' ἐξοχὴν, that is, perfect, and embracing the perpetual execution of the divine will, and that not as contrary to contrary, but as broader to narrower, and as that which admits imperfection, even the obedience of God's commandments, to that which demands what is perfect and entirely exact. But that gloss is adverse to the Apostle, who excludes any works whatsoever: nor did the contrary opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles demand anything else. For they did not teach that a man is justified by works taken κατ' ἐξοχὴν, i.e., perfect; because they also required faith alongside works, nor did they deny the remission of sins. But what need is there of this, where there is the perpetual and perfect execution of the divine will? Nor is the Apostolic antithesis such: that we are justified not by perfect works, but by faith admitting a more imperfect obedience to God's commandments. Perfect works after the Adamic fall are truly a non-entity. What was the point of inquiring whether we are justified by a non-entity, or by that which is in truth ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων? Again, how can faith admit an imperfect obedience to the commandments of GOD and acquiesce in it: whether we act κατ' ἀλήθειαν or κατ' ἄνθρωπον. For in truth, a curse remains upon imperfect obedience by the power of divine justice, because cursed is everyone by the voice of God who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. XXVII. verf. 26, which the Apostle repeats here Galat. III. verf. 10. But that he is justified as such, who is condemned by the power of divine justice, is contrary to divine justice. But in arguing κατ' ἄνθρωπον, it is so far from the case that the Gospel of Christ acquiesces in a more imperfect obedience, that it rather, according to the Socinians, prescribes much more perfect commandments. What Crellius brings forward here concerning the sense of the law, partly literal, partly mystical, are mere ineptitudes, since there is but one sense of the law. But whatever may be the case, if the law promised eternal life in any sense whatsoever, it must have required perfect obedience, have delivered perfect commandments, and it cannot be feigned that they could be more perfect in the Gospel. But if these are prescribed in the Gospel for obtaining justification and eternal life, how then does the Gospel or the faith of Christ acquiesce in a more imperfect obedience for obtaining justification? What, finally, is that gloss? Are we justified by faith without works, that is, by imperfect obedience without perfect obedience, by possible obedience without impossible? In no one besides Christ can perfect obedience be found, since all have sinned. To say nothing of the fact that faith is thus converted into a moral work, which is not of such value as is required to satisfy the divine law, which nevertheless God, out of mere liberality, might be willing to accept for a certain justice, just as a creditor, who could demand a hundred florins, accepts ten for the full payment, as the blessed Hülfemann in Manuali A. C. p. 813, from Socinus lib. IV. de Servat. cap. 4. p. 463, apud Sibrandum & Smalcium disp. IV. contra Francium th. 23. deduces, and teaches that Hager the Jesuit in collat. Aug. Conf. cum Concil. Trid. p. 250, and also Bellarmine lib. I. de justif. cap. 17. lib. II. cap. 9. & Cornel. à Lapide in cap. III. Rom. 28. conspire in this with the Photinians: All of which are repugnant to divine justice, namely, that God should accept an imperfect obedience for perfect.

But concerning these in the Exegesis of Augustine.

Conf. & what is in the Epistle to the Romans. Unless through the faith of Jesus Christ.

Here "unless" (ἐὰν μὴ) signifies "but."

See what we have said on John.

19. add Revelation.

27. faith of Jesus Christ, that is, in Jesus Christ.

We have noted a similar manner of speaking in Mark XI.

22. where see the things said.

In vain, therefore, do the Papists catch at this little word "unless" (ἐὰν μὴ), as if the Apostle were distinguishing between works of the law done without faith and those done through faith, abrogating justification for the former only, not for the latter.

For that "if not" (εἰ μὴ) can be taken adversatively is also clear from Galatians.

I. verse.

7.

Corinthians.

VII. verse.

17. is evident, nor is it explained otherwise by Augustine; indeed, if he were expressing a condition here, without which a man is not justified by the works of the law, the Apostle would be contradicting himself, both in this discourse and in Romans.

III. verse.

For this is what his antagonists were doing, to claim justification for works done from faith equally with faith.

Meanwhile, the little word "unless" (ἐὰν μὴ) is not only taken adversatively, but also exclusively, as it happens, meaning "but only," or "not except through faith in Christ."

Estius notes that it can be taken in a twofold way, or exceptively in this manner: not from the works of the law, unless through the faith of Christ, or when the faith of Christ is added.

The same Estius acknowledges this sense to be foreign, as does Crellius.

If indeed the Pseudo-Apostles meant this, requiring works conjunctively with faith for justification: Or exclusively, that justification is obtained for us not from works, or through works of the law, but only through the faith of Christ, or from faith in Christ.

Which sense must be entirely admitted.

And that it ought to be understood in this way, not only do all the most learned Greek and Latin interpreters agree, but it is also gathered from those things which follow shortly after, and from the words of the Apostle in Romans.

VII. that we are justified by the faith of Christ, not by the works of the law, Estius admits.

Cornelius à Lapide alleges the Syriac, Oecumenius, and Beza, and says that this sense is evident from the antithesis, that the Apostle wishes justification not to be attributed to the works of the law, but to the faith of Christ: which he also illustrates with this example, e.g.

When I say: a man does not live, except through the soul; "except" here means the same as "only."

For this exceptive proposition means the same as these two, by which it ought to be explained, namely: a man lives through the soul, and, a man lives through no other thing than the soul.

How clear these are for our opinion, yet Cornelius refutes us, and certainly without judgment: Therefore, the Novators wrongly explain it here as "unless through the faith of Christ," that is, they say, "but only through the faith of Christ."

But what else had Cornelius taught by the example he brought?

Nor could he deny that Thomas and Adam Sasbout teach our opinion expressly: Add, he says, even if the Apostle meant and said this, he would still say nothing for their "faith alone justifying," for here D. admits this proposition.

Thomas and Adam Sasbout: A man is not justified from the works of the law, but only from the faith of Christ.

Adam has it thus: This exposition, "a man is not justified from the works of the law, unless faith is added," since it attributes justification partly to the works of the law, partly to faith, it is established that it is impious.

For it is certain that Paul is speaking of the justification of the ungodly, which is entirely gratuitous.

He adds: If you ask: From that proposition: "A man is justified not except by faith," is it rightly inferred, therefore he is justified by faith alone, it must be said that it is.

And afterwards: Although in this our time Catholic writers in no way bear that proposition, thinking that there is poison in that particle (alone), yet even Thomas does not seem to abhor it.

If any (he says) were just in the old law, they were not just from the works of the law, but only by the faith of Christ.

The true sense is, not except by faith, by no merits; since he distinguishes faith against works.

The faith of Jesus Christ, although by reason of its principle it can be so called, because it is stirred up in us by Christ through the Holy Spirit, yet here it should rather be taken by reason of its object, for faith in Christ Jesus, just as "faith of God" is said in Mark.

XI. verse 22. because it is soon declared thus: "And we have believed in Christ Jesus": nor was it to be said here concerning the author of faith, but rather concerning the object, just as "works of the law" are spoken of, not because the law is the principle and cause of the works, but because our works look to the law, and ought to be done according to the law.

The precepts of the law exhibit the object of working and of works, which are occupied with the love of GOD and neighbor.

But the object of faith is exhibited in the Gospel, which is occupied solely with Christ Jesus, or with the salvation provided through Christ: There, things to be done are proposed; here, things to be believed; there, love of GOD and neighbor to be executed by work; here, the redemption and salvation of Christ, through which Jesus is to be embraced and received by faith.

There, our work, our works, and our own obedience, by which we are liberated from the curse of the law, is required: Here, however, the work of Christ, his redemption, and his obedience, which was performed for us to the law, is to be apprehended by faith alone, and applied to us for the obtaining of the remission of sins and eternal life. "And we have believed in Jesus Christ" (Καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Ἰησῦν Χρισὸν ἐπισεύσαμεν) "And" here signifies "also."

We also had embraced Christianity, certainly persuaded that Judaism was not sufficient, for otherwise Christ would have had to be preached to the Gentiles alone.

To believe in Christ is not only to embrace Christianity, which is also done by hypocrites, but to place trust in Christ, to embrace the same as our JESUS through faith, to so appropriate and claim for ourselves by true faith his satisfaction performed for our sins, and his obedience exhibited in our place to the divine law, to which Christ himself was not subject, as if we ourselves had satisfied GOD for our sins, and had fulfilled the law of GOD: because those things were performed for us by Christ.

But what is this, that Judaism is not sufficient, and what is contained in these, otherwise Christ would have had to be preached to the Gentiles alone? If Judaism is taken concerning the observation of the law, whether moral, ceremonial, or even forensic, it contributes nothing at all to justification and salvation, because justification is not obtained through the law, and therefore it does not come into account here, neither alone nor with the admixture of Christianity: But it is excluded by that "without works," Romans IV. It cannot be held as an adequate and sufficient, nor an inadequate or insufficient principle or medium of justification or salvation, and this was what the Apostle was urging against the Judaizing Pseudo-Apostles, desiring to know nothing here except Christ crucified, 1 Cor. II. 3. Just as neither does Peter know any other name in which we may obtain salvation, Acts IV. v. 12. But if Judaism is the religion proper to the faithful Israelites, who with Simeon and Hannah awaited the consolation of Israel, Christ, after the manner of the believing father Abraham, who desired to see the day of the Lord, John VIII. 56, whose faith had for its object the Messiah, to be delivered for our sins, and to be raised for our justification, as the Apostle demonstrates in Romans IV. 25, that faith was indeed sufficient for the Patriarchs and the faithful of the Old Testament, who obtained salvation through the same, Acts XV. 11 and Heb. XI. 5. But after the Son of GOD

GOD came in the flesh, born of a woman in the fullness of time, Gal. IV. verf. 4. It was not enough for the promulgated Gospel to have known and believed the Messiah, but there was also a need to believe in and know this Jesus of Nazareth, that he is the Messiah, and that anointed Christ of the Lord, our Redeemer and Savior, which therefore had to be preached to both Jews and Gentiles. If Judaism, that is, the observance of the law, had sufficed for salvation, it would also have had to be proposed to the Gentiles, if they were to be saved, unless perhaps another method of justification had to be established for the Jews, and another for the Gentiles. So much for the ὀυγιες (soundness) in these Grotian writings. Righteousness, through which we obtain eternal life, is not our own, but Christ's righteousness: who is Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 6. which we apprehend solely not by works, but by faith, and make our own, so that we may be constituted righteous before God by this one's obedience and righteousness, Rom. V. verf. 19. And this is the first argument of the contention of the Apostolic thesis, artfully interwoven into the proposition itself, drawn from the common faith of Peter and Paul: which these Apostles had also handed down in their doctrine, and cherished in their heart, and professed with their mouth for salvation: in which at the same time the application of faith is taught.

For to that, not only general knowledge is required, that we know how a man is justified before God, namely not from the works of the law, but through faith in Christ Jesus: But also individual application, that each one may believe in Christ Jesus, that is, acknowledge the same as his own Jesus, and apply his merit to himself by faith, so that each one may thus be justified not from the works of the law, but solely through the faith of Jesus Christ. This common knowledge, says Crocius not badly, is a firm argument both against Peter's lapse and against the error of the Pseudo-Apostles. Since the Apostles certainly know this, that a man is not justified from the works of the law, but through the faith of Christ Jesus, why does Peter compel the Gentiles to live Judaically, why do the Pseudo-Apostles boast that the observance of ceremonies and the whole law is necessary for justification? And further: He subjects common faith to common knowledge. When he says: We, he notes again himself, Peter, and the faithful well-instructed from among the Jews. He does not say: We have professed, we have taught, for by teaching and professing Jesus they were not yet justified. For even hypocrites taught and professed, who were never justified; but we believe in Christ, that is, having abandoned the errors of the Pharisees, having shaken off the confidence in the law and our own righteousness, we have embraced one Jesus Christ, as our only savior, and in him alone have we placed our trust. We have placed it there, so that we may be absolved from all sins, from which we could not be absolved through the law of Moses, and that from a simple, true, living faith, not from any works, whether external or internal, whether ceremonial or of the moral law.

There follows a second argument from the nature and condition of the law, fortified by the Davidic testimony, as far as the removal of one's own righteousness is concerned: It holds thus in Ps. CXLIII. 2. ὅτι ἐ δικαιωθήσεται ἐνώπιόν σου πᾶς ὁ ζῶν (that no one living shall be justified in thy sight), as it is read in the edition of the LXX interpreters. Because the saying was trite and most well-known, therefore he does not expressly name the scripture, much less express the place.

But he declares the mind of David both by reason of the subject, because πᾶς ζῶν (every living one) is πᾶσα σὰρξ (all flesh), every living being, namely all human flesh: since the name σαρκός (flesh) is taken synecdochically for the whole living being, namely man: not undeservedly denominated from flesh, because naturally he is only flesh, outside the grace of regeneration subject to sin and death.

Rightly B. Luther here in his later Comment. Therefore, he signifies by flesh the whole nature of man with his reason and all his powers. That, he says, is justified not from works, not even of the law. He does not say: Flesh is not justified from works against the law, such as murders, adultery, gluttony, etc., but from works done according to the law, which are good. Therefore, for Paul, flesh signifies the sum of righteousness, wisdom, worship, religion, intellect, as much as can exist in an animal man.

Then by reason of the predicate, by which he had designated justification in the sight of GOD, or before the divine judgment: Enter not into judgment with thy servant; For no one living would be righteous before thee: and here the Apostle properly discusses justification before the divine tribunal. He adds, however, for the sake of explanation, ἐξ ἔργων νόμου (from the works of the law), because David understands this entirely, when he prays that he may not enter into judgment with his servant, that is, that he may not wish to judge according to righteousness and the tenor of his law from the works owed by the servant and performed by himself.

Since in this way no one could stand before the divine judgment, and he himself would have to perish entirely; graphically describing, both the hostility the soul exerts against us through the law as the power of sin, and sin as the sting of death against all who are under the law, 1. Cor. XV. 56. and the affliction and anguish of his spirit and heart, which he must needs experience on account of sin, if God should wish to enter into judgment with his servant, and to demand a strict account of the service performed according to the law. Conf. Job. IX. 2. Ps. 38, 2. ff. Matth. XXII. 24. Whence David had to flee solely to divine grace with that debtor servant, Matth. XIIX. as in v. 6. 7. of Psalm CXLIII it is to be seen how anxiously he longs for the same, and awaits it, and desires to be refreshed, for the sake of the name of the Lord, and to be delivered from his anxiety on account of the righteousness of the Lord, v. 11. which righteousness has been manifested in the Gospel χωρὶς νόμου (without the law), or works of the law, and is the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ unto all, and upon all them that believe (coming) Rom. III. 21. 22. where the Apostle had likewise adduced the Davidic place, v. 20. Διότι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου ἐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ (For by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified in his sight).

The force of the argument is: If no flesh can stand before the divine judgment, or be justified, when God enters into judgment with man according to the law, neither are the Gentiles to be compelled to the observance of the law, as necessary for justification and salvation, nor can it be admitted that a man can in any way be justified and saved by the works of the law, as was boasted by the false Apostles. For implicitly there is contained here an antithesis, that we are justified in the divine judgment solely by the grace of God on account of the righteousness of Christ, as that which is exhibited in the adduced Psalm.

That saying of Gratius, the law conferred righteousness on no one, faith in greater things is needed, which the law promises, they are σκύβαλα. The law would altogether confer righteousness, if the whole could be kept; but since it cannot be kept, it confers none at all: For whoever is a transgressor of the law in one point is guilty of the whole law, James II. vers. 10. By faith in greater things he understands that by which the reward of eternal life promised is received; but this was likewise promised in the law, truly to those who should do all things which were written in the law of Moses, which however no one could do; therefore not knowledge, or Iva δικαιωθῶμεν ἐν πίστει Χριστοῦ, καὶ οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων νόμου in this place does not avail did, as Rom. III. 20. δικαιωθῶμεν understands we might obtain righteousness, that which draws eternal life with it. Διότι ἐ δικαιωθήσεται ἐξ ἔργων νόμου πᾶσα σὰρξ A locution, which among the Hebrews denies universally, namely, where a negative is added to a verb, as rightly noted here by others. The law conferred that righteousness on no one, faith in greater things is needed, which the law promises.

the recognition of such a reward is sufficient, but faith is required in him, who earned eternal life for us.

For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. 10. He who believes in him will not be judged, John 3:28. He does not perish, but has eternal life, v. 6. Verf. 17. Ei δὲ ζητοῦντες δικαιωθῆναι ἐν Χριστῷ) that is, through Christ, or through faith, had in his Gospel. Συρίθωνες καὶ αὐτοὶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ) 'sinners' here is to be understood not in that looser sense, but in the stricter one, that is, men of a wicked life. He clearly touches those Doctors of circumcision, whose lives were not at all amended: But he speaks odiously, as he is wont, in the first person. Ἄρα Χριστὸς ἁμαρτίας διάκονος) This is to be read with a final interrogation. The sense is: Now the unbelievers will say that Christ has increased nothing but the license to sin. They will gather this from our life, unless it surpasses both the uncircumcision of the Gentiles and the life of those who Judaize. Μὴ γένοιτο.) This is to be read as a παρὰθεσις (parenthesis), and it is that of one who abhors, Rom.

3:4, 31; ch. 6:13, 15; ch. 7:7, 13, 14; 11:1, 11.

4. 31. chap. VI. ver. 13. 15. chap. VII. ver. 7. 13. 14. XI. v. 1. 11.

The third argument The third argument concerns the thesis, or the assertion of justification by faith alone in Christ, from the justice and the nature of Christ's office.

If those who seek to be justified in Christ, that is, through Christ's righteousness apprehended by faith, are still found to be sinners themselves, so that they have need of justification by the observation of the law, and by their own righteousness, then Christ will be a minister of sin.

Far be it. q.d. But this consequence is absurd. Therefore, the antecedent is also. The force of the major premise lies in this, that Christ has been made a propitiation for our sins, and thus a satisfaction for our sins, and yields the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to believers, who seek to be justified solely in Christ; but if that is not enough, but they are still such in sin, and cannot be justified before the tribunal of GOD, unless they perform the works of the law, Christ will not be a propitiator for sin, or made righteousness for us by GOD, but a minister of sin, not taking away or washing away sin with his blood, much less restoring true righteousness, but leaving sin still, and condemnation, and making us sinners, needing the righteousness of the law: Which is supremely injurious to the office of Christ.

This nerve of the argument was well observed by the Blessed Luther in both Commentaries in this former rendered paraphrase: 'But if we who seek to be justified, etc.' that is, we have already said that we believe in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ. But if we are thus justified, and yet are still found to be sinners, and in need of justification, (because you force us to be justified by the works of the law) then justification by faith is nothing, and Christ by his faith has made us sinners, and in need of the righteousness of the law, which is most absurd, and Christ is utterly abolished. Because thus he is a minister of sin to us, which would be washed away by the law, and now the Apostle of the law has become [one who argues] from the impossible and the absurd; as if he were to say: If the law is necessary for us, who seek to be justified in Christ: Therefore, we who are justified through Christ are still found to be sinners, and debtors to the law. Which is to say, Christ has not now justified us, but has only made us sinners, so that we might be justified only by the law, which is impossible. Wherefore this also is impossible, that the law (I say) is necessary, and that we are justified by the works of the law. For we who are justified in Christ are not found to be sinners, but righteous, because Christ is not a minister of sin, but of righteousness.

And in the latter, f. 40: 'If this is true,' he says, 'that we are justified in Christ, it is impossible that we are sinners, or justified by the law. Conversely, if it is not true, but it behooves us to be justified by the law, and its works, then it is impossible that we are justified through Christ. One or the other must be false: Either we are not justified in Christ, or not in the law. But we are justified in Christ, therefore not in the law.' He argues, therefore, in this way: 'If those who seek, etc.' That is, if we strive to be justified by faith in Christ, and thus justified are found to be still sinners, needing the law, by which it might justify us as sinners: If there is need, I say, of the observation of the law for justification; so that those who are righteous in Christ are not finally righteous, but still have need of a justifying law.

Or: If one justified through Christ must still be justified by the law, then Christ is nothing other than a legislator and minister of sin. Therefore, one justified in Christ is not justified and holy, but still has need of the righteousness and holiness of the law. But certainly we are justified and righteous in Christ, because the truth of the Gospel teaches that a man is not justified in the law, but in Christ.

But if those who are justified in Christ are found to be still sinners, that is, they still pertain to the law, and are under the law, as the Pseudo-Apostles teach, then they are not yet justified. Because the law accuses and argues that they are still sinners, and demands that they do the works of the law, so that they may be justified. Therefore, those justified in Christ are not justified. And thus it necessarily follows that Christ is not a justifier, but a minister of sin. With these words he most gravely accuses the Pseudo-Apostles, and all justiciaries, because they pervert everything, because they make grace out of the law, the law out of grace, Christ out of Moses, and Moses out of Christ.

For they teach that after Christ and all the righteousness of Christ, there is need of the observation of the law, to be justified. Thus the law becomes Christ by an intolerable perversity, because that which properly belongs to Christ is attributed to the law. 'If you do,' they say, 'the works of the law, you will be justified; if you do not do them, you will not be justified, even if you believe in Christ.' But if it is true that Christ does not justify, but is a minister of sin, as necessarily follows from their doctrine. Therefore Christ is the law, because we have nothing else from it, when it teaches us that we are sinners, than what we have from the law: And thus the Doctor of sin, Christ, sends us to the law and Moses as a justifier. And so the Papists, and as many as are ignorant of the righteousness of Christ, or do not rightly hold it, cannot but make Moses and the law out of Christ, and Christ out of the law. For thus they teach: 'Faith in Christ does indeed justify, but at the same time the commandments of GOD must also be kept: For it is written, if you wish to enter into Christ, keep the commandments of GOD.' There Christ is immediately denied, and faith is abolished.

Because that which is of Christ alone is attributed to the commandments of GOD or the law. For Christ is definitively the justifier and Redeemer from sins. If I attribute this to the law, now the law is my justifier, freeing me from sins, because I do its works. And thus the law is Christ, and Christ totally loses his name, office, and glory, and is nothing other than a minister of the law, arguing, terrifying, offering, and sending the sinner to another, which is to justify him, which is truly the office of the law. But the proper office of Christ is to embrace and absolve from sins the sinner who has been made and constituted guilty by the law, if he believes the Gospel. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes; for he himself is the lamb of GOD, who bears the sins of the world.

But because the Papists and fanatical Spirits do not hold the doctrine of justification, they invert everything, making Moses out of Christ, and Christ out of Moses. And this is their true (although they say otherwise in words) principal proposition

Christ is Moses, etc. These things are solidly and clearly [stated] according to his custom by Megalander. Which are to be noted especially not only against the Papists, but also the Calixtines..., whom he refutes there at length and gravely: Scripture, especially of the New Testament, everywhere inculcates faith in Christ, and magnificently proclaims it. He who, he says, believes in him, is saved, is not perished, is not judged, is not confounded, has eternal life. They on the contrary: He who believes in him, is damned, etc., because he has faith without works, which damns. Thus they pervert everything, making Christ simply a destroyer, and Moses the Savior. But is it not an inestimable blasphemy to teach thus: By doing the law and works you will be made worthy of eternal life, but by believing in Christ you will be guilty of eternal death? Does the law kept save, and faith in Christ damn? The adversaries do not indeed use such words, but in reality they teach thus. Because faith, they say, infused (which they properly call faith in Christ) does not liberate from sins, but faith formed by charity. From this it follows that faith alone in Christ without law and works does not save. This is certainly to affirm that Christ leaves us in sins and the wrath of God, and makes us guilty of eternal death. On the contrary, faith [has] law and works, since faith justifies, because it has works, without which otherwise faith is of no use. Therefore works justify, not faith: because for whatever reason each thing is such; that is more such; if faith justifies on account of works, therefore works justify more than faith. Profound are the blasphemous abominations of this doctrine.

Paul therefore argues from the impossible, and by sufficient division: If we, justified in Christ, are still sinners, to be justified by something else than Christ, namely by the law: therefore Christ cannot justify us, but only accuses and condemns us: therefore he died in vain, and he who believes in the Son has eternal life; indeed the whole scripture, which testifies that Christ is the justifier and Savior of the world, is false. For if we are found sinners after we have been justified in Christ, it must follow that those doing the law without Christ are justified. If this is true, then we are Turks, Jews, Tartars, retaining only in appearance the word and the name of Christ, but in use and reality altogether denying Christ and his word.

But Paul wants faith to be αὐτόπρξιον. Therefore it is an error and impiety to assert that infused faith does not justify unless it is adorned with works of charity.

But if the adversaries wish to defend this entirely, why do they not altogether reject the faith of Christ? Especially since they make nothing of it, than an empty quality in the soul, which without charity profits nothing, why do they not rather call a spade a spade? That is, why do they not rather say in clear words that works justify, not faith? Also why do they not manifestly deny the whole Gospel and Paul in general (as they truly do), who attribute righteousness to faith alone, not to works? For if faith with works justifies, the whole argument of Paul is false, who expressly says that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ.

Blessed Luther also notes very well that it is a Hebrew phrase to be a minister of sin, which Paul also uses in 2 Corinthians III. There, he says, he treats magnificently and most clearly of these two ministries, namely the letter and the Spirit, the law and grace, or death and life. And he says that Moses is a minister of the law, which he calls the ministry of sin, wrath, death, and damnation.

But far be it that we should make Christ such a one. With one voice he rejects it: Far be it. Since, with Chrysostom as author, against vehemently absurd things there is no need of an orator's reasons, but it suffices only to deny.

Thus also Flacius explains this argument, as if he were saying: We, not previously understanding the true face of Moses' heart or mind, fled to him, hoping for righteousness and life from him: but we found him to be manifoldly a minister of sin, as one who both reveals sins to us, and irritates the malice of our old Adam, and finally aids sin in destroying us, or executes the punishments merited and demanded by sin by his own sentence, by imposing on us curse and death. Wherefore, despairing, we flee from this minister of sin to the Messiah, the remover of sin, as the only port and asylum of our salvation, hoping that he himself will perfectly wash us from our sins with his blood. But if here also our new Lord does not fully cleanse and liberate us, but rather leaves us in sins and uncleanness, as you Pseudo-Apostles wish: then indeed we fall beyond all hope again into a new minister of sin. And this is most absurd and fights with the whole scripture, which asserts that he fully expiates and takes away the sins of the world: Therefore your antecedent is also false, that namely we are not fully justified through Christ without works, and that they are necessary for salvation.

The explanation of B. Hunnius is the same.

There are not wanting those who wish to meet Paul here against the objection of the Pseudo-Apostles: If they justify sinners without the works of the law, the zeal for doing good will be taken away, because it suffices to believe in Christ, even if one maliciously persists in sins, by a denial of the consequence, μὴ γένοιτο far be it, and they think that the reason for the denied consequence is brought by the Apostle in the following. Thus Crocius on this passage.

Nor is the commentary of B. Balduinus alien.

But the explanation of B. Luther fits the text and scope better, also agreeing best with the Apostolic phrase. Which even the Papists acknowledge to be of the ancient Doctors, and prefer to the explanations of others.

Cornelius a Lapide: But if seeking, etc., as if he were saying: If we are still in sin, because we sought the remission of sin and righteousness in the Christi faith, when it is not to be sought there, but in the law, as the Judaizers wish, therefore Christ fosters sin. For he took away the law, by which alone sin is removed. Is Christ therefore a minister of sin, as if he were saying: Does Christ serve sin by fostering and preserving it, by this very fact that he takes away the law for justification, and for the deletion of sin, which they say is necessary, and establishes his own law of grace, which alone justifies, when, as they say, it cannot justify without the law? and he says: By no means. Thus Jerome, Chrysostom, Primasius, Anselm, Theophylact. Concerning which sense he adds later: The first sense, which is of the Fathers, is more pressing and better, because it supplies nothing from elsewhere, as the second of Vatablus, that they are called sinners because they teach that the law must be kept with the Gospel. The third because they indulge in desires. Then because it is more from the mind and scope of the Apostle, for he wants to prove that we are justified by the faith of Christ, not by the law of Moses: otherwise if, following the faith of Christ, we are still found sinners, it follows that Christ deceives us, promising righteousness from faith, which he could not provide, and he will be not a victor of sin, not a destroyer, but a fosterer, abettor, and minister.

These things he [says]. Nor do the things which further follow in the Apostle serve to refute the objection of the Pseudo-Apostles, but to affirm the Apostolic faith. That the vices of the doctors of circumcision are touched upon here does not appear: nor does anything occur concerning the life of the Apostles, that it ought to surpass both the life of the Gentiles and of the Judaizers, as Grotius wants. v. 18. Εἰ γὰρ ἃ κατέλυσα) By teaching. Ταῦτα πάλιν οἰκοδομῶ) By living badly.

Παραβάτην ἐμαυτὸν συνίστημι. In the manuscript, συνίστημι, in a similar sense, that is, I show, παραβάτην, that is, an impious person, and one who says things far different than what I do. פריע which is translated παραβάτης, ἀσεβής [impious].

The fourth argument concerning destruction. This is the fourth argument of the Apostle, from the destruction of the law, as far as justification and condemnation are concerned.

If our doctrine of the law is destroyed in such a way that it is not useful for justification to those who seek justification in Christ, nor can it condemn them; then the observance of the law cannot, in any case, be urged as necessary for justification and salvation.

But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is as well. The Apostle expresses this in this way: "For if I build again those things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor": implying that he had destroyed the law through his doctrine of justification in Christ: and therefore he could not build up the law again without constituting himself a παραβάτην [transgressor], which would certainly happen if he made the observance of the law in any way necessary for salvation. He destroyed it thus far in the article of justification; who, therefore, would build it up again in the article of justification without a doctrine of his own that is a transgression? For he speaks of the destruction of the law in the words immediately following: "For I through the law am dead to the law, that I might live unto GOD": He who is dead to the law, that he might live unto GOD both in doctrine and in practice, cannot teach the law as necessary for that purpose, so that one might live unto GOD, without transgression. The blessed Luther sometimes understands by those things which are destroyed by the doctrine of the Gospel, sin and death; sometimes he also includes the law, which amounts to the same thing, if the law is viewed in terms of its use, whether justificatory, as if it could save, or condemnatory, regarding those who cannot keep the law, even if they believe in Christ. If its fulfillment is urged as necessary for justification and salvation, the law is built up again in the sphere of the article of justification, where it had been destroyed: indeed, sin and death are built up, because the law, for those who cannot fulfill it, if they are urged to fulfill it, works nothing but wrath and death, and only increases sin, but does not take it away. Regarding which the blessed Luther says in his former Commentary: "If I destroyed those things, etc." that is: "When I, through the preaching of faith, taught justification in Christ, and that the law was fulfilled, and thereby destroyed sins, if I were to teach again that the law must be kept, and was not fulfilled, what else would I be doing than establishing sins again, and that they still must be overcome by our works?" In which matter I would do nothing but show that I had acted wrongly either then or now, that is, I would establish myself as a prevaricator, indeed, I would make myself an alien to Christ, in whom I was justified, and would again deliver myself under the law and sins, just as much a prevaricator as I was before Christ.

And thus the blessed Luther teaches that it is not the law, but sin, that is destroyed by the doctrine of the Gospel; indeed, that the law is established by it, namely, insofar as it has been fully fulfilled for us by Christ, and thus we have satisfied the law in Him: and the same satisfaction is imputed to us in justification according to the doctrine of the Gospel, so that the law, and τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου [the righteousness of the law], is fulfilled in us, Rom. VIII. verses 4, 5. On the other hand, it is also rightly said that the law is destroyed by the doctrine of the Gospel, as far as the necessity of observing the law for salvation is concerned, and the power of condemning precisely those who do not observe the law, nor can fully observe it, even if they embrace Christ by faith, or insofar as it is thrust into the article of justification, which was done by the Pseudo-Apostles, and was therefore destroyed by the Apostolic doctrine.

Concerning which the blessed Luther further states in his former Commentary: The Apostle uses his tropes again, therefore the Interpreters vary. St. Jerome wishes "destroyed" and "built up" to be understood as the ceremonial law. Which opinion, although true, is nevertheless too narrow to be considered in agreement with other places in Scripture. The blessed Augustine calls the works of the law "destroyed," indeed, the pride that boasts and presumes upon the works of the law. Nor do I condemn this. But by comparing the Apostle with the preceding and other places, he seems to destroy sins (as I said), not the law, especially since in Romans III he denies that he destroys the law through faith, but rather establishes it. But he destroys sins in Romans VI, so that the body of sin might be destroyed. For through faith, sins are destroyed, which were present and abounded through the law. For sin is not destroyed unless the law is fulfilled. But the law is not fulfilled except through the righteousness of faith. Thus it happens that through faith the law is at once established, and sins are destroyed. For while satisfaction is made to the law through faith, sins cease, and the law remains in force. But to rebuild sins is to preach the law again, and to think it must be kept and fulfilled. But where the law must be fulfilled, righteousness has not yet been done; indeed, sin remains. For it is sin not to have yet fulfilled the law; thus the sins return which were previously taught to be destroyed through faith. Therefore, to build up sin is the same as to weaken, destroy, and make the law void. But to destroy sin is the same as to establish, build up, and fulfill the law. Whoever, therefore, has taught that the law is fulfilled, and that righteousness is done, thus certainly destroys sins. But he does this who teaches that through faith in JESUS Christ we are made righteous, that is, fulfillers of the law. But he who says that the law must be fulfilled, and that righteousness has not been done, he therefore again establishes and resurrects sins, and constitutes them debtors to the law, and makes them guilty of keeping the law. And in the later Commentary: "For if I destroyed those things, etc." as if to say: I did not preach in such a way that what I once destroyed, I would build up again. For if I did this, I would not only labor in vain, but I would constitute myself a prevaricator, and in the manner of the Pseudo-Apostles, I would pervert everything, that is, I would again make the law and Moses out of grace and Christ, and conversely, grace and Christ out of the law and Moses. But I destroyed through the ministry of the Gospel sin, sadness, wrath, and death. For I taught thus: your conscience, O man, is subject to the law, to sin, and to death, from which you cannot be freed by any human or angelic help; but now the Gospel comes and announces to you the remission of sins through Christ, who abrogated the law, and destroyed sin and death. Believe in Him, then you will be freed from the curse of the law, from the tyranny of sin and death, you will be righteous and will have eternal life. Thus, through the preaching of the Gospel, I destroyed the law, so that it might no longer rule in the conscience. For when the new guest, Christ, comes into a new house, so that He alone may dwell in it, the old tenant, Moses, must yield and move elsewhere. But where Christ is the new guest, there the law, sin, wrath, and death have no place, but mere grace, righteousness, joy, life, and mere filial trust toward a placated, favorable, and propitious Father on account of Christ are present. Therefore, having expelled Christ and destroyed the very kingdom which I planted through the Gospel, should I build up the law again and erect the kingdom of Moses? Which would happen if, as the Pseudo-Apostles are accustomed to do, I were to teach that circumcision and the observance of the law are necessary for salvation. And in this way, I would restore sin and death in the place of righteousness and life.

For the law only shows sin, effects wrath, and kills. Nor could the Jesuit Cornelius entirely deny this sense: For if what I destroyed, if the power of justifying, which I withdrew from the observance of the law, I rebuild, that is, I bring it back to the law, as the Jews slander me of secretly Judaizing, then I am a prevaricator, because like a Proteus I change my faith with every wind.

There is another argument, proving that Christians must persist in the abolition of the law. But the gloss of Grotius is entirely alien: because the Apostle is not teaching therein that he has not given himself to a flagitious life, as if he were establishing the law by teaching, and destroying it by living wickedly. This has nothing to do with the present state of the controversy. He does not bring forward his own piety, but impugns the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles, and thoroughly destroys that same doctrine of the Gospel, and does not teach that he can persist with it.

Latin:

v. 16. Εἰδότες, ὅτι οὐ δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἔργων νόμου Id est, non perducitur ad veram ac spiritualem illam iustitiam, quæ vitam æternam parat per opera legis.

Vide, quæ ad epistolam ad Romanos diximus, in Prolegomenis, & Act. III. & IV. agendo secundum legem, homo assuevit ad iustitiam quandam, & præmium habentem temporale. In Manuscripto additur, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, locutione non dissimili ea, quæ est 2. Cor. III. 5. nisi quod ibi est ἄς, hic ὅτι, ut sensus sit, legis opera posse inservire ad parandam veram iustitiam, sed hanc ex illis proprie non procedere, neque hoc ad illam absolute requiri.

Ita verò corrumpitur insigniter doctrina Apostolica, & pervertitur iustitia controversiæ. Nam primo assumit Grotius, iustitiam nostram propriam vitam æternam parere, quæ donum DEI mere gratuitum est in Christo Jesu, Rom. VI. ult. quod non nostra iustitia consequimur, sed Christus nobis peperit obedientiam suâ tum activâ, tum passivâ, quæ sola justi coram DEO constituimur, Rom. V. v. 19. deinde è Manuscripto uno Codices omnes perperam corrigens, & ex ὅτι ὡς efformans, quasi legi debeat εἰδότες ὅτι ἐκ δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, sensum plane alienum & contrarium elicere, collatione loci prorsus disparis, 2. Cor. III. 5. conatur, quod nempe iustificetur quidem homo quadrantenus ex operibus legis, sed non quasi ex operibus legis; quorum prius adversatur & præsenti Apostoli sententiæ, & perpetuæ analogiæ fidei, quum simpliciter & hic Apostolus & alibi scriptura sacra neget, hominem ullatenus coram DEO per opera legis iustificari, imò legem impleri à nobis posse inficietur, Rom. VIII. 3. Actor. XV. 10. quemadmodum postea de se profitetur, & de Petro, aliisque Judæis, quod non iustificentur per opera legis, sed unice per fidem Christi: Et præterea universaliter asserit, nullam carnem, nullum mortalium per opera legis iustificari. Vide, inquit Theophylactus, quàm libere, & nihil hesitans omnia proloquatur. Non enim, inquit, legem reliquimus, quia iniquior, sed quia infirmior esset, & impotens iustificationem largiri. Nam exequi illius opera poterat nemo, quia gravia erant, nec factu facilia.

Et ubi obsecro, in scripturis docetur, legis opera inservire posse ad parandam veram iustitiam, hoc est, ad iustificationem, sic enim illa interpretatur Grotius. Ante iustificationem certe non nisi peccatum & impietas locum habet, quum DEUS impium iustificet, Rom. IV. 5. & iustificatio constat in remissione peccatorum, & non-imputatione iniquitatum, docente Apostolo; ubi iustificatio ea ratione describitur, quod iustitia vera, & spiritualis, id est, sanctitas in nobis inhærens generetur vel oriatur in nobis? Vel ut Papistæ eandem rem efferre amant, quod nobis habitus iustitiæ vel charitatis infundatur? Commentum hoc est Papisticum, quod aliis verbis incrustat Grotius, non vero dogma Apostolicum.

Quod ad posterius, assumendum quasi illud ex operibus legis neque αὐτολεξεὶ nisi verba incruftentur & pervertantur, neque κατὰ διάνοιαν hic continetur, imò sensui repugnat. Nam simpliciter opera legis à iustificatione excluduntur, non verò cum restrictione illa ineptâ, tanquam legis operâ. Simpliciter ea opponuntur fidei Christi vel in Christum, ut illis denegetur iustificatio Christi, ejusque obedientiæ unicè adscribatur, quemadmodum opposita sunt, justos nos constitui obedientia propria, & justos nos constitui non propria obedientia, sed solum obedientia Christi, nobis per fidem imputata.

Tertia quæstio cum Pseudo-Apostolis non erat, anne opera, quæ lex requirit, præstando nos sanctitatem & iustitiam spiritualem consequamur? Sed anne per eadem coram tribunali Dei iustificemur & æternum salvemur? Quod negat Apostolus: & negatum jam erat in synodo Hierosolymitana: tùm quia legem nemo perfecte præstare potest, jugum ejus est ἀβάστακτον: tùm quia unice per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi vera fide apprehensam salutem æternam consequimur, quemadmodum omnes Prophetæ Christo testimonium perhibent, docente S. Petro, quod in nomine ejus, non per opera legis, remissionem peccatorum consequantur, hoc est, iustificentur omnes, qui in ipsum credunt, Act. XLIII. Et Paulus Antiochia Pisidia palam testatus est Act. XIII. 24. Notum sit vobis, viri fratres, quia per hunc (Jesum) vobis remissio peccatorum (seu iustificatio) annunciatur, & ab omnibus, quibus non potuistis in lege Mosis iustificari: In hoc (Jesu) omnis, qui credit, iustificatur.

Quartò fallum est, hominem agendo secundum legem affuefieri ad iustitiam quandam sed carnalem, & præmium habentem temporale. Lex enim spiritualis est, & perfecte si impleretur, iustitiam afferret non carnalem, sed spiritualem. Sed à nemine impleri potest etiam post regenerationem, quia homo carnalis est adhuc ex parte carnalis, non ex affe spiritualis est, ut Roman. VII. 14. docetur. Lex adimplentibus eam non promittit tantum temporalia bona, ut cum Pelagianis & Socinianis Grotius errat, sed vitam ipsam æternam, Lev. XIX. 5. interprete omni exceptione maiori Christo, Luc. X. 28. ut & Apostolo nostro in hæc ipsa thematis sui demonstratione, Gal. III. vers. 12. Quintò si iustitia, qua coram DEO consistimus, non procedit ex operibus legis, neque hæc ad illam requiruntur absolute, per iustitiam illam, qua justificamur, vel justi constituimur coram Deo, non potest propria, & inhaerens justitia intelligi. Haec enim per legis opera, & observantiam fit, nec fine observantia vel operibus legis ullatenus locus habet. Quomodo enim sanctus vel inhaesive justus quis est sine operibus vel observantia legis? Quum lex sit norma sanctitatis & justitiae inhaerentis, nec aliud fit sanctitas vel justitia inhaerens, quam legis observantia & conformitas cum lege, quemadmodum oppositum ejusdem ἁμαρτία est ἀνομία, seu illegalitas, difformitas, & aberratio a lege vel transgressio legis, 1. Johan. III. vers. 4.

Sexto: Quamvis non negemus, legem quadantenus praestari, atque justitiam aliquo modo dici posse externam legis observationem, non tamen ea in foro divino justitia est, neque lex contenta est ejusmodi externa obedientia, sed perfectissimam, omnubusque numeris absolutam requirit justitiam, quam nemo post lapsum praestare potest, quae non nisi in Christo reperitur. Sed per fidem nobis imputatur, quum Christus nobis a Deo factus sit justitia, 1. Cor. I. vers. 29.

Quapropter sedulo discrimen hoc inculcat B. Lutherus in Comment. prior. Imprimis itaque sciendum, quod homo dupliciter justificatur, & omnino contrariis modis. Primo ab extra ab operibus, ex propriis viribus, quales sunt humanae justitiae, usu, (ut dicitur) & consuetudine comparata. Qualem describit Aristoteles aliique Philosophi; Qualem leges civiles & Ecclesiasticae ceremoniis; Qualem dictamen rationis & prudentia parit. Sic enim putant operando justa justum fieri, temperando temperatum & similia. Hanc facit ex lex Mosis. Ipse quoque decalogus, scilicet ubi timore pana aut promissione mercedis servitur Deo, non juratur per nomen Dei, honorantur parentes, non occiditur, non mpitur, non adulteratur &c. Hec est justitia servilis, mercenaria, ficta, speciosa, externa, temporalis, mundana, humana, quae ad futuram gloriam nihil prodest, sed in hac vita recipit mercedem, gloriam, divitias, honorem, potentiam, amicitiam, sanitatem, aut certe pacem ac tranquillitatem, minusque malorum, quam ii, qui secus agunt, sicut Christus Pharisaeos describit. Secundo ab intra ex fide & gratia, ubi homo de priore justitia prorsus desperans tanquam ab immunditia menstruata proruit ante Deum, gemens humiliter peccatorem, sese confessus cum publicano dicit: Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori. Hic, inquit Christus, descendit justificatus in domum suam. Haec enim est aliud nihil, quam invocatio nominis divini. Justificato autem sic corde per fidem, qua est in nomine ejus, dat eis Deus potestatem filios DEI fieri, diffuso mox Spiritu Sancto in cordibus eorum, qui charitate dilatet eos, ac pacatos hilaresque faciat, omnium bonorum operatores, omnium malorum victores, etiam mortis contemptores & inferni. Hic mox cessant omnes leges, omnium legum opera, omnia sunt jam libera, licita, & lex per fidem & charitatem est impleta. Ecce hoc est, quod Christus nobis meruit, scilicet predicari nomen Domini, (id est, misericordiam, veritatem Dei) in quod qui crediderit, salvus erit. Haec Megalander. legis & fidem sibi adaequate opponat, praeterea dubium omne excludat, Abrahamum operibus moralibus instructum in exemplum adducat, quod per ea justificatus non fit, sed per fidem, & de illis operibus expresse agat, de quibus Moses Levit. XVIII. vers. 5.

Qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis, ubi luculentissimum est, de operibus legis moralis agi; de illa lege, per quam omnia sub peccatum conclusa sint, Gal. III. vers. 22. a cujus maledicto Christus nos liberavit, vers. 23. cui se subjecit, cap. IV. vers. 4. cujus opus est charitas, cap. V. vers. 6. quae profecto est lex moralis: Proinde nullus locus est illi Papistarum exceptioni. Quam ideo plerique ex ipsis hodie deferunt & refellunt. Guilielmus Estius in hunc locum. Ex quo etiam loco (Rom. III.) petendum, quanam Apostolus intelligat opera legis, ex quibus negat hominem justificari, videlicet non sola ceremonialia legis Mosaicae, velut circumcisionem, sabbatum, neomeniam &c. De quibus plerique locum hunc exponunt. Sed in universum opera qualiacunque ex lege, id est, ex fata legis cognitione, facta, etiam si moralia tantum sint. Nam in doctrina Apostoli, qua justitiam ab operibus legis removet, legem intelligi toto genere, prout moralia simul & ceremonialia comprehendit, perspicuis argumentis ostendimus in exposit. epist. ad Rom. Benedict. Justinian. in h. l. Tametsi Paulus, inquit, praecipue agit contra legis ceremonias; hic tamen in universum omnia excludit opera legis, qua legis sunt.

Alii proinde (2.) distinguunt inter opera legis, & opera fidei & Spiritus. Opera tantum legis excludi, & merita, non opera fidei & Spiritus, ut hic Salmero. Sed si merita excluduntur, cur ergo Papistae merita statuunt, & hominem de congruo mereri justificationem, vel per vires liberi arbitrii se disponere posse ad infusionem justitiae, afferunt? uti hic ipse Salmero: Sola fides, inquit, hoc loco non excludit bonos mores liberi arbitrii ad justitiam disponentes. 2. Non ait Apostolus, non per operum merita, sed non per opera legis. 3. Error Pseudo-Apostolorum non in eo consistebat, quod statuerent, opera nostra meritoria esse justificationis, sed quum fidem in Christum admitterent, eidem opera legis jungi volebant. Si opera legis mereri justificationem credidissent, fide in Christum opus non esse, admisissent. Longeliter Papistae ipsi Pseudo-Apostolorum sententiam exponunt: Ea judaizantium, inquit Estius, adversus quos agit Apostolus, est doctrina, legem cum fide Christi miscere, & ex utraque pariter salutem expectare. Error judaizantium, ait Adamus Sasbouth, non in eo erat, quod rejiciebant fidem, sed quod fide non contenti jungebant ipsi opera legis, timentes, quod fides non sufficeret. 4. Opera fidei, & Spiritus temere opponuntur operibus legis. Nam opera legis dicuntur, quae legem normam habent, & fiunt secundum legem. At quae ex fide proficiscuntur opera, & fructus Spiritus sunt, pariter legem pro norma habere debent, & fieri secundum legem. 5. Apostolus itaque simpliciter item opera excludit, quae legem pro norma habent, adeoque excipi hic nullum opus potest. Nam aut bonum est opus, & ita ἐννομον, ac legem pro norma habet, eique congruit, aut malum est, & ἀνομία, aut peccatum est. 6. Vere bona opera facta, non sunt vere bona opera. 7. Apostolus excludit opera sua: Quae utique ex fide facta. Illis operibus negat justificationem, ad qua conditi sumus, Ephes. II. vers. 8. seqq.

Hac autem

annon Spiritus funt opera. 8. Galatæ, ad quos scribit, renati erant, cum ergo ipsos modum justificationis docens, negat per opera legis eos justificari, opera renatorum utique excludit à justificatione. 9. Opera fine gratia facta opponunt Papistæ operibus gratiæ & spiritus. Sed præterquam quod fit hæc contradictio in adjecto, fingere opera bona fine gratia, non possunt talia hic intelligi, quia Abraham, tum, quando ei fides imputata, jampridem fuerat in Dei gratia. Quum ergo Abraham negetur justificatus ex operibus legis, qui sane non destitutus erat operibus fidei, & Spiritus, manifestum est, opera fidei & Spiritus removeri à justificatione. Unde Bellarm. lib. IV. de justif. c. 18. ad aliam exceptionem sese recipit, Abrahamum jam ante fuisse justum, cum opera justa facere potuerit, eoque fide non factum esse justum ex impio, sed justiorem ex justo.

Distinguunt ergò nonnulli Papistæ 3. inter justificationem primam, & fecundam; illam fine operibus legis fieri, hanc non item. Sed hæc distinctio scripturæ plane ignota est: neque de eo hic agitur, quomodo quis ex justo vel sancto justior vel sanctior fieri possit: sed quomodo impium justificet Deus? Et agnoscit Jesuita Hagerus in Coll. A. C. cum Concilio Trident. p. 250. per justitiam, quam Abraham hic acquivisse dicitur, primam pariter cum secunda justificatione intelligendam esse: Ideoque oportet per oppositionem fidei & operum, in utraque opera planè excludi, quum ea omninò hic à justificatione excludi manifestum fit. Annuit hic Estius: Justificari, inquit, quid fit, æque ex iis, quæ in epistolam ad Romanos commentati sumus, intelligi potest. Extenditur enim ad omnem vere salutaris, ac beatificæ justitiæ acquisitionem seu primam, quà quis ex impio justus fit; seu fecundam, quà justus justificatur adhuc. Agnoscit idem Estius per fidem solum hominem justificari, cum ita pergit: Justificatur autem homo per fidem Jesu Christi, quatenus per eam Christum Redemptorem agnoscens ex ejus merito remissionem peccatorum atque justitiam à DEO expectat & percipit. Quod verè addit, id fieri per ea media, quæ Christus ipse ad justificationem præstandam hominibus instituit, uti funt invocatio, pœnitentiæ opera, sacramenta, legisque divinæ observatio, juxta illud: Factores legis justificabuntur, Rom. II. id Apostolo xaddiάμελξον adversatur, qui medium ex parte nostri nullum aliud, quàm fidem admittit, opera vero prorsus excludit. Quomodo ergo audet legis observationem, & pœnitentiæ opera, atque invocationem, quæ opus est secundi præcepti decalogi, hic ingerere Estius? Sacramenta nos ipsi non excludimus: Sed ea funt media ex parte Dei, de quibus hic non agitur. Similis ſεελότης est Cornelii à Lapide: Voculam tantum solum excludere opera legis, non spem, timorem, charitatem, pœnitentiam, quæ fides gignit & producit: Hac enim sub fide, quasi filias sub matre intelligi. Num enim spei, timoris, charitatis, pœnitentiæ opera non funt opera legis? Annon legem pro norma habent? Añon secundum legem fiunt? At omnia legis opera excluduntur per illam exclusivam tantum per fidem. Et quomodo sub fide tanquam sub matre, & causâ opera, tanquam filiæ, & effectus comprehendi possunt, quum ita soli fidei justificatio tribuatur, ut opera universim excludantur? Et fidem sequuntur illa quidem, sed post quam justificati sumus per eandem solam. Nam opera bona, ut trita habet Augustini regula, sequuntur justificatum, non vero antecedunt justificandum. Opera bona funt fructus & effectus justitiæ. Non vero effectus & fructus prior est causa sua, & arbore, cujus fructus est.

Atque hæc de Papistis. Sociniani, interprete Crellio in Comment. ad h. l. in operib. Exeg. pag. 396. hanc glossam excogitarunt: Fidem, cui justificatio simpliciter adscribitur, non quibusvis operibus, sed tantum operibus κατ' ἐξοχὴν sumptis, hoc est, perfectis, & perpetuam voluntatis divinæ exequutionem complectentibus opponi, idque non ut contrarium contrario, sed ut latius angustiori, & ut id, quod imperfectionem, etiam Dei mandatorum obedientiam admittit, ei, quod perfectam & exactam omninò postulat. Sed ea glossa Apostolo adversa, qui opera quævis excludit: neque aliud sententia contraria Pseudo-Apostolorum postulabat. Non enim illi docebant operibus κατ' ἐξοχὴν sumptis, h. e. perfectis hominem justificari; quia fidem etiam requirebant juxta cum operibus, neque negabant remissionem peccatorum. Quid autem hac opus, ubi perpetua, & perfecta voluntatis divinæ exequutio? Nec antithesis Apostolica talis est: non perfectis operibus, sed fide admittente imperfectionem mandatorum Dei obedientiam nos justificari. Opera perfecta post lapsum Adamicum vere funt non-Ens. Quid attinebat disquirere, an per non-Ens, vel id, quod revera ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων est, justificetur? Rursus quomodo fides admittere potest imperfectam obedientiam præceptorum DEI eaque àquiefcere: sive κατ' ἀλήθειαν seu κατ' ἄνθρωπον agamus. Nam ex rei veritate imperfectam obedientiam maledictio manet vi justitiæ divinæ, quia maledictus voce Dei omnis est, qui non manet in omnibus, quæ scripta funt in libro legis, Deut. XXVII. verf. 26. quod hic repetit Apostolus Galat. III. verf. 10. Illum autem justificari qua talem, qui vi justitiæ divinæ condemnatur, justitiæ divinæ contrarium est. Κατ' ἄνθρωπον vero disputando tantum abest, ut Evangelium Christi imperfectioni obedientia acquiescat, ut potius secundum Socinianos præcepta multo perfectiora præscribat. Quæ hic affert Crellius de legis sensu partim literali, partim mystico, meræ ineptiæ funt, cum non nisi unicus legis sensus fit. Quicquid autem de eo fit, ſi lex quocunque tandem sensu vitam æternam promisit, oportet ipsam perfectam requivisse obedientiam, perfecta tradidisse præcepta, nec in Evangelio fingi posse perfectiora. Si autem hæc in Evangelio ad justificationem & vitam æternam consequendam præscripta, quomodo ergo Evangelium vel fides Christi acquiescit imperfectioni obedientia ad consequendam justificationem? Quæ denique illa glossa? Justificamur fide absque operibus, id est, obedientia imperfecta absque perfecta obedientia, obedientia possibili absque impossibili? In nullo præter Christum obedientiam perfectam reperiri, quum omnes peccaverint. Ut taceam, quod ita fides in opus morale convertatur, quod tanti quidem valoris non fit, quantus ad fatisfaciendum divinæ legi requiritur, quod tamen Deus ex mera liberalitate acceptare velit pro quadam justitia, quomodo creditor, qui poterat centum florenos exigere, recipit ſe pro integra solutione decem accepturum, ut B. Hülfemannus in Manuali A. C. p. 813. ex Socino libr. IV. de Servat. cap. 4. p. 463. apud Sibrandum & Smalcio disp. IV. contra Francium th. 23. deducit, & Hagerum Jesuitam in collat. Aug. Conf. cum Concil. Trid. p. 250. nec non Bellarm. lib. I. de justif. cap. 17. lib. II. cap. 9. & Cornel. à Lapide in cap. III. Rom. 28. in eo cum Photinianis conspirare docet: Quæ omnia justitia divina repugnant, Deum nempe acceptare imperfectam obedientiam pro perfecta.

Sed de his in Exegem. August.

Conf. & quæ in Epist. ad Romanos. Ἐὰν μὴ διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

Hic ἐὰν μὴ valet ἀλλὰ.

Vide, quæ diximus Joh.

19. adde Apoc.

27. fide Jesu Christi, id est, in Jesum Christum.

Simile loquendi genus notavimus Marci XI.

22. ubi dicta vide.

Frustra itaque Papistæ hac vocula ἐὰν μὴ captant, quasi Apostolus discernat inter opera legis fine fide, & per fidem facta, illis solum, non istis abroget justificationem.

Nam εἰ μὴ accipi posse adversative etiam è Gal.

I. vers.

7.

Corinth.

VII. vers.

17. patet, nec aliter ab Augustino exponitur, imo si conditionem hic exprimeret, citra quam homo ex operibus legis non justificetur, Apostolus sibi ipsi adversus esset, tùm in hoc discursu, tum Roman.

III. vers.

Hoc enim agebant ejus antagonistæ, ut operibus ex fide factis juxta cum fide justificationem vindicarent.

Interim vocula ἐὰν μὴ non tantum adversative accipitur, sed etiam exclusive, ut fit, sed tantum, vel non nisi per fidem in Christum.

Duplici modo notat Estius, accipi posse vel exceptive hoc modo: non ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Christi, seu cum accedit fides Christi.

Quem sensum alienum esse agnoscit idem Estius, ut & Crellius.

Siquidem hoc voluerint Pseudo-Apostoli, conjunctim opera cum fide ad justificationem requirentes: Vel exclusive, quod non ex operibus, seu per opera legis, sed tantum per fidem Christi, seu ex fide in Christum obtingat nobis justificatio.

Qui sensus omnino admittendus.

Atque ita intelligi debere hoc loco, non modo doctissimos quosque interpretes Græcos & Latinos consentire, sed etiam colligi ex his, quæ paulo post sequuntur, & ex verbis Apostoli Rom.

VII. quod justificemur ex fide Christi, non ex operibus legis, fatetur Estius.

Cornelius à Lapide allegat Syrum, Oecumenium, & Bezam, & patere illum sensum ex antithesi ait, quod Apostolus velit justificationem non tribui operibus legis, sed fidei Christi: quem etiam illustrat hoc exemplo: v.g.

Cum dico: homo non vivit, nisi per animam; nisi hic idem valet, quod tantum.

Hæc enim propositio exceptiva idem valet, quod hæ duæ, per quas exponi debet, scilicet homo vivit per animam, &, per nullam aliam rem vivit homo, quam per animam.

Hæc quam luculenta sint pro nostra sententia, redarguit tamen nos Cornelius, & certe sine judicio: Malè ergò Novantes hic exponunt, nisi per fidem Christi, id est, inquiunt, sed tantum per fidem Christi.

Quid vero aliud Cornelius allato exemplo docuerat?

Neque diffiteri potuit, Thomam, & Adamum Sasbout, nostram sententiam ῥητῶς tradere: Adde, inquit, licet id vellet, ac diceret Apostolus, nihil tamen diceret pro eorum fide sola justificante, hanc enim propositionem hic admittit D.

Thomas & Adamus Sasbouth: Homo non justificatur ex operibus legis, sed tantum ex fide Christi.

Adamus ita habet: Hac expositio, non justificatur homo ex operibus legis, nisi adjuncta fide, cum justificationem tribuat partim operibus legis, partim fidei, constat eam impiam esse.

Nam certum est, Paulum loqui de justificatione impii, quæ prorsus gratuita est.

Addit: Si quæras: Anne ex propositione ista: Homo justificatur non nisi ex fide, recte inferatur, ergo sola fide justificatur, dicendum, quod sic.

Et postmodum: Quanquam hac nostra tempestate Catholici scriptores nullo modo illam propositionem ferant, putantes, venenum esse in illa particula (sola) sed nec Thomas abhorrere videtur.

Si qui (inquit) in veteri lege justi erant, non ex operibus Sed de legis iustierant, sed solum fide Christi.

Verus sensus est, non nisi ex fide, nullis meritis; Siquidem distinguit fidem contra opera.

Fides Jesu Christi etsi ratione principii dici possit, quia à Christo per Spiritum Sanctum in nobis excitatur, hic tamen ratione objecti potius accipienda, pro fide in Christum Jesum, ut πίστις Θεῦ dicitur Marc.

XI. vers. 22. quia mox ita declaratur. Καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Χρισὸν Ἰησῦν ἐπισεύσαμεν: nec de autore fidei, sed de objecto potius dicendum hic erat, quemadmodum & ἔργα νόμυς dicuntur, non quod lex sit principium & causa operum, sed quod opera nostra respiciant legem, & secundum legem fieri debeant.

Legis præcepta objectum exhibent operandi & operum, quæ circa dilectionem DEI & proximi occupantur.

Objectum autem fidei in Evangelio exhibetur, quæ circa Christum Jesum occupatur unice, vel circa salutem per Christum præstitam: Ibi agenda, hic credenda proponuntur, ibi dilectio DEI proximique opere exequenda, hic redemptio & salus Christi, per quam eis Jesus fiducia amplectendus & suscipiendus est.

Ibi opus nostrum, opera nostra, & obedientia propria, quà nos à legis execratione liberati, requiritur: Hic vero opus Christi redemptio, & obedientia ejus, quæ pro nobis legi præstita est, fide tantum apprehendenda, nobisque applicanda est ad consequendam remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam. Καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Ἰησῦν Χρισὸν ἐπισεύσαμεν) Καὶ hic valet etiam.

Etiam nos Christianismum susceperamus, certò persuasi, Judaismum non sufficere, alioqui enim gentibus solis prædicandus fuerat Christus.

In Christum credere non est tantum Christianismum suscipere, quod etiam ab hypocritis fit, sed fiduciam in Christum collocare, eundem ut JESUM nostrum per fidem amplecti, ejusdem satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris præstitam, & obedientiam nostri loco legi divinæ, cui se Christus obnoxius non erat, exhibitam, vera fide ita nobis appropriare ac vendicare, ac si ipsimet DEO satisfecissemus pro peccatis nostris, & legem DEI implevissemus: quia illa pro nobis præstita sunt à Christo.

Quid vero hoc est, Judaismum non sufficere, & quæ in his συνέχεσα, alioqui gentibus solis prædicandum fuisse Christum? Judaismus si de observatione legis tùm moralis, tùm ceremonialis aut etiam forensis accipiatur, ad justificationem & salutem nihil quicquam confert, quia per legem non obtingit justificatio, ideoque nec solus, nec cum admixtione Christianismi hic in censum venit: Sed excluditur per illud χωεὶς ἔργων, Rom. IV. nec adequatum & sufficiens, nec inadequatum vel insufficiens principium, aut medium justificationis vel salutis haberi potest, & hoc erat, quod adversus Judaizantes Pseudo-Apostolos urgebat Apostolus, nihil hic scire cupiens, nisi Christum crucifixum, 1. Cor. II. 3. Quemadmodum nec Petrus aliud nomen novit, in quo salutem nos consequamur, Act. IV. v. 12. Si vero Judaismus sit religio fidelium Israelitarum propria, qui cum Simeone & Hanna expectarunt solatium Israelis Christum, ad Abrahami Patris credentium instar, qui desiderabat videre diem Domini, Joh. IIX. 56. quorum fides pro objecto habuit Messiam, tradendum propter peccata nostra, & resuscitandum propter justitiam nostram, demonstrante Apostolo Rom. IV. 25. sufficiebat quidem illa fides Patriarchis, & fidelibus Veteris Testamenti, qui per eandem salutem adepti sunt, Act. XV. 11. & Ebr. XI. 5. Sed postquam Filius

DEI in carne in venit, natus e muliere in temporis plenitudine, Gal. IV. vers. 4. non sufficiebat promulgato Evangelio, novisse & credere Messiam, sed etiam opus fuit, in hunc Iesum Nazarenum credere ac novisse, quod ille Messias fit, & Christus ille unctus Domini, Redemptor & Salvator noster, quod proinde & Iudaeis & gentibus praedicandum erat. Si Iudaismus, id est, observatio legis suffecisset ad salutem, ea etiam gentibus proponenda fuisset, si salvari debuissent, nisi forte alia statuenda iustificationis ratio quoad Iudaeos, alia quoad gentes. Adeo ὀυγιες in hisce Grotianis. Iustitia, per quam vitam aeternam consequimur, non nostra est, sed Christi iustitia: qui est Jehovah iustitia nostra, Ier. XXIII. 6. quam non per opera, sed per fidem unice apprehendimus, nostramque facimus, ita justi coram Deo constituamur hujus unius obedientia & iustitia, Rom. V. vers. 19. Atque hoc est primum argumentum contentionis theseos Apostolicae, artificiose intertextum ipsimet propositioni, à communi fide Petri & Pauli depromptum: quam & Apostoli hi tradiderant doctrina sua, & fovebant corde, ac profitebantur ore ad salutem: in quo simul docetur fidei applicatio.

Nam ad illam requiritur non tantum notitia generalis, quod sciamus, quomodo homo iustificetur coram Deo, scilicet non ex operibus legis, sed per fidem in Christum Iesum: Sed etiam applicatio individualis, ut quisque in Christum Iesum credat, hoc est, eumdem suum Iesum agnoscat, ejusque meritum fide sibi applicet, ut ita iustificetur quisque non ex operibus legis, sed unice per fidem Iesu Christi. Haec communis scientia, inquit Crocius non male, est firmum argumentum tum erga Petri lapsum, tum adversus Pseudo-Apostolorum errorem. Cum hoc certo sciant Apostoli, hominem non iustificari ex operibus legis, sed per fidem Christi Iesu, cur Petrus gentes cogat vivere Iudaice, cur Pseudo-Apostoli jactent obfervantiam ceremoniarum & totius legis ad iustificationem esse necessariam? Et porro: Scientia communi communem facit fidem. Cum ait: Nos, iterum se, Petrum, & fideles e Iudaeis bene institutos notat. Non dicit: Nos professi sumus, nos docuimus, docendo enim & profitendo Iesum non errant iustificati. Nam etiam hypocritae docebant & profitebantur, qui nunquam fuere iustificati; sed credimus in Christum, id est, defertis Pharisaeorum erroribus, excussa fiducia legis & propriae iustitiae, unum Iesum Christum, tanquam unicum nostrum servatorem sumus amplexi, in eoque fiduciam collocavimus unice. Eo collocavimus, ut absolvamur ab omnibus peccatis, a quibus per legem Mosis absolvi non poteramus, idque ex simplici, vera, viva fide, non ex ullis sive externis, sive internis, sive ceremonialibus, sive moralis legis operibus.

Succedit alterum argumentum à legis natura & conditione, Davidico testimonio, quantum ad remotionem propriae iustitiae, munitum: Illud ita habet Ps. CXLIII. 2. ὅτι ἐ δικαιωθήσεται ἐνώπιόν σου πᾶς ὁ ζῶν, ut legitur in editione LXX. interpretum. Quia dictum erat tritum & notissimum, ideo non diserte nominat scripturam, nedum locum exprimit.

Declarat autem mentem Davidis tum ratione fubjetti, quia πᾶς ζῶν est πᾶσα σὰρξ, omnis vivens, omnis caro scilicet humana: quum nomen σαρκός synecdochice de toto vivente, homine scilicet accipiatur: non inmerito à carne denominato, quia naturaliter caro tantum est, extra regenerationis gratiam peccato & morti obnoxius.

Recte B. Lutherus hic in Comment. poster. Significat ergo caro totam naturam hominis cum ratione & omnibus viribus suis. Illa, inquit, iustificatur non ex operibus, ne legis quidem. Non dicit: Caro non iustificatur ex operibus contra legem, ut sunt caedes, stuprum, crapula &c. sed ex operibus factis secundum legem, qua bona sunt. Significat igitur Paulo caro summam iustitiam, sapientiam, cultum, religionem, intellectum, quanta potest esse in homine animali.

Tum ratione praedicati, qua iustificationem in conspectu DEI, vel coram judicio divino designarat: Ne ingrediaris in judicium cum servo tuo; Nam non esset justus coram te ullus vivens: & de iustificatione coram tribunali divino hic proprie disserit Apostolus. Addit autem ἐξηγήσεως causa ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, quia hoc intelligit omnino David, cum precatur, ne in judicium ingrediatur cum servo suo, id est, secundum iustitiam & legis suae tenorem ex operibus servo debitis & abs se praestitis judicare velit.

Siquidem ita nec quisquam coram judicio divino consistere possit, ipfique omnino pereundum fit; graphice describens, tum hostis animae in nos exerit per legem lentiam, quam hostis animae in nos exerit per legem ceu virtutem peccati, & peccatum ceu mortis stimulum adversus omnes, qui sub lege sunt, 1. Cor. XV. 56. tum spiritus & cordis sui afflictionem & angustiam, quam ob peccatum experiri necesseum habeat, si Deus ingredi in judicium velit cum servo suo, & de servitio praestito rationem districtam secundum legem exigere.
