Tertium argumentum Tertium argumentum concernit thesin, vel assertionem justificationis per solam fidem in Christum à justitia & officii Christi ratione.

Si illi, qui quaerunt justificari in Christo, id est, per Christi justitiam fide apprehensam, adhuc & ipsi inveniuntur peccatores, ut opus ipsis sit justificationem observatione legis, & justitia propria, Christus utique peccati minister erit.

Absit. q. d. At consequens hoc est absurdum. Ergo & Antecedens. Majoris consequentia in eo sita est, quod Christus propitiatio factus sit pro peccatis nostris, adeoque satisfactio pro peccatis nostris, & legis complementum ad justitiam cedat credentibus, qui quaerunt in Christo unice justificari; quod si non sufficit, sed adhuc tales in peccato sunt, nec justificari possunt coram tribunali DEI, nisi opera legis praestent, Christus non erit propitiator pro peccato, aut justitia nobis à DEO factus, sed minister peccati, non tollens aut abluens sanguine suo peccatum, nedum reducens veram justitiam, sed relinquens adhuc peccatum, & condemnationem faciensque nos peccatores, legis justitia egentes: Quod summe injuriosum est in Christi officium.

Quem argumenti nervum probe observavit Beat. Lutherus in utroque Comment. in priori hac reddita paraphrasi: Quod si quaerentes justificari &c. id est, diximus jam nos in Christum credere, ut justificaremur ex fide Christi. At fine sic justificamur, imo adhuc invenimur peccatores, & justificationis indigentes, (quia ex operibus legis tu cogis nos justificari) ergo justificatio ex fide nihil est, & Christus sua fide nos peccatores fecit, & legis justitia egentes, quod est absurdissimum, & Christus prorsus abolet. Quia sic peccatum nobis minister, quod per legem dilueretur, & jam effet legis Apostolus ab impossibili & absurdo; quasi dicat: Si lex necessaria est nobis, qui in Christo quarimus justificari: Ergo justificati per Christum adhuc peccatores invenimur, & legis debitores. Quod hoc est, jam Christus non justificavit nos, sed peccatores tantum fecit, ut per legem tantum justificemur, quod est impossibile. Quare & hoc est impossibile, legem (inquam) esse necessariam, & operibus legis nos justificari. Justificati enim in Christo non invenimur peccatores, sed justi, quia Christus non peccati, sed justitiae minister est.

Et in posteriori f. 40. Si hoc verum est, inquit, quod in Christo justificamur, impossibile est, nos esse peccatores, aut per legem justificari. Contra si verum non est, sed oportet nos justificari per legem, & opera ejus, tum impossibile est, nos per Christum justificari. Alterutrum falsum esse oportet: Aut non justificamur in Christo, aut non in lege. Sed in Christo justificamur, Ergo non in lege.

Argumentatur igitur hoc modo: Si quaerentes &c. Hoc est, si conamur per fidem in Christum justificari, & sic justificati invenimur adhuc peccatores, indigentes lege, qua nos peccatores justificet: Si opus est, inquam, legis observatione ad justificationem; ut qui justi sunt in Christo, non fine justi, sed opus habeant adhuc lege justificante. Vel: Si justificatus per Christum debet adhuc per legem justificari, tunc Christus nihil aliud est, quam legislator & minister peccati. Ergo justificatus in Christo non est justificatus & sanctus, sed opus adhuc habet justitia & sanctitate legis. Sed certe sumus justificati & justi in Christo, quia veritas Evangelii docet, quod homo non in lege, sed in Christo justificetur.

Si autem illi, qui in Christo justificantur, inveniuntur adhuc peccatores, id est, pertinent adhuc ad legem, & sunt sub lege, ut Pseudo-Apostoli docent, ergo nondum justificati sunt. Quia lex accusat & arguit eos adhuc esse peccatores, & exigit, ut opera legis faciant, ut justificentur. Ergo justificati in Christo non sunt justificati. Et sic necessario sequitur, Christum non esse justificatorem, sed peccati ministrum. His verbis gravissime accusat Pseudo-Apostolos, & omnes justitiarios, quod omnia pervertant, quia ex lege gratiam, ex gratia legem, ex Mose Christum, ex Christo Mosen faciant.

Docent enim, quod post Christum & omnem justitiam Christi opus sit observatione legis, se justificari velu. Sic lex fit Christus pervertitate intolerabili, quia legi tribuitur, quod proprie Christo competit. Si feceris, ajunt, opera legis, justificaberis, si non feceris, non justificaberis, ut maxime in Christum credas. Si autem verum est, quod Christus non justificat, sed est peccati minister, ut necessario sequitur ex eorum doctrina. Ergo Christus est lex, quia nihil ex ea aliud habemus, cum doceat nos peccatores esse, quam quod ex lege habemus: Et sic Doctor peccati, Christus, mittit nos ad legem & Mosen justificatore. Itaque Papistae, & quotquot justitiam Christi ignorant, aut non recte tenent, non possunt non facere ex Christo Mosen & legem, & ex lege Christum. Sic enim docent: Fides in Christum justificat quidem, sed simul fervari oportet etiam praecepta Dei: Quia scriptum est, si vis in Christum ingredi, serva mandata DEI. Ibi flatim Christus negatus, & fides abolita est.

Quia mandata DEI five legi tribuitur, quod est folius Christi. Est enim Christus definitive justificator & Redemptor a peccatis. Si hoc legi tribuo, jam lex meus est justificator, liberans me a peccatis, quia opera ejus facio. Sicque lex est Christus, & Christus in totum amittit suum nomen, officium & gloriam, nihilque aliud est, quam legis minister, arguens, terrens, offerens & mittens peccatorem ad alium, quod fit eum justificare, quod vere est legis officium. Sed proprium Christi officium est, peccatorem per legem reum factum & constitutum, amplecti & absolvere a peccatis, si Evangelio credit. Christus enim est finis legis ad justitiam omni credenti; ipse enim est agnus DEI, qui portat peccata... mundi.

Quia vero Papistae & fanatici Spiritus non tenent doctrinam de justificatione, invertune omnia, ex Christo Mosen, & ex Mose Christum facientes. Efique hac re vera (etsi verbis aliud dicant) principalis eorum propositio

Christus est Moses &c. Hæc solide & præclare pro more suo Megalander. Quæ non modo contra Papistas, sed etiam Calixtinos apprime notanda sunt, quos illic prolixe & graviter refellit: Scriptura præfertim Novi Testam. ubique inculcat fidem in Christum, & magnifice prædicat eam. Qui, inquit, credit in eum, salvatur, non pernitur, non judicatur, non confunditur, habet vitam æternam. Illi contra: Qui credit in eum, damnatur &c. quia habet fidem sine operibus, quæ damnat. Sic pervertunt omnia, ex Christo simpliciter perditorem, ex Mose Salvatorem facientes. Nonne autem inæstimabilis blasphemia est, sic docere: Faciendo legem & opera efficieris dignus vita æterna, credendo autem in Christum reus eris mortis æternæ? Lex servata salvat, fides in Christum damnat? Istiusmodi verbis quidem adversarii non utuntur, revera tamen ita docent. Quia fides, inquiunt, infusa (quam proprie vocant fidem in Christum) non liberat a peccatis, sed fides formata charitate. Ex hoc sequitur, quod sola fides in Christum sine lege & operibus non salvat. Hoc certe est affirmare, quod Christus relinquat in peccatis & ira Dei, & reos nos faciat æternæ mortis. Econtra fides legem & opera, cum fides justificat, quia habet opera, sine quibus alioqui fides nihil prodest. Ergo opera justificant, non fides: quia propter quod unumquodque est tale; illud magis est tale; si fides propter opera justificat, ergo opera magis justificant, quàm fides. Profunda sunt abominationes blasphemæ hujus doctrinæ.

Argumentatur ergo Paulus ab impossibili, & sufficienti divisione: Si nos justificati in Christo adhuc sumus peccatores, justificandi per aliud, quam per Christum, scilicet per legem: ergo Christus non potest nos jusitificare, sed tantum accusat & condemnat nos: ergo gratis mortuus est, & qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam; imo tota scriptura, quæ testatur, Christum esse justificatorem & Salvatorem mundi, falsa est. Nam si invenimur peccatores, postquam in Christo justificati sumus, necesse est sequi, facientes legem fine Christo esse justificatos. Hoc siverum est, tum sumus Turca, Judai, Tartari, retinentes tantum in speciem verbum, & nomen Christi, usu autem & revara prorsus negantes Christum & verbum ipsius.

At Paulus vult fidem esse αὐτόπρξιον. Ideo error & impietas est, asserere, fidem infusam non jusitificare, nisi ornata sit operibus charitatis.

Quod si autem hoc adversarii omnino defendere volunt, cur in totum fidem Christi non abjiciunt? præfertim cum ex ea nihil faciant, quàm inanem qualitatem in anima, quæ fine charitate nihil prosit, cur non potius appellant scapham scapham? hoc est, cur non potius claris verbis dicunt, opera jusitificare, non fidem. Item cur in universum manifeste non negant totum Evangelium & Paulum, (ut revera negant) quæ soli fidei non operibus tribuunt justitiam? Nam si fides cum operibus justificat, falsa est tota disputatio Pauli, qui diserte dicit, hominem non justificari operibus legis, sed fide Jesu Christi.

Optime etiam notat B. Lutherus, phrasin Ebraicam esse, peccati ministrum esse, qua utitur etiam Paulus 2. Corinth. III. Illic, inquit, magnifice & clarissime tractat de duobus his ministeriis, scilicet litera Spiritus, legis gratia, feu mortis & vita. Et ait Mosen ministrum legis, quod vocat peccati, iræ, mortis, & damnationis ministerium.

Absit autem, ut talem faciamus Christum. Una voce id reprobat: Absit. Siquidem, Chrysostomo autore, adversus vehementer absurda nihil opus est oratoris rationibus, sed sufficit solum negare.

Sic etiam explicat hoc argumentum Flacius, quasi dicat: Nos antea non intelligentes Mosis veram cordis aut mentis faciem, confugimus ad eum, sperantes ab eo justitiam & vitam: verum reperimus, cum esse multipliciter ministrum peccati, ut qui & revelet nobis peccata, & irritet malitiam nostri veteris Adami, & denique adjuvet peccatum in nobis perdendis, seu pænas a peccato promeritas & flagitatas sua sententia exequatur, nobis maledictionem mortemque imponendo. Quare desperantes confugimus ab isto ministro peccati ad Messiam ablatorem peccati, tanquam unicum salutis nostræ portum & asylum, sperantes, ipsum nos suo sanguine perfecte a peccatis nostris abluturum. Quod si hic quoque novus noster Dominus nos non plene mundat ac liberat, sed potius in peccatis immunditiaque relinquit, ut vos Pseudo-Apostoli vultis: tum sane nos præter omnem spem denuo incidimus in novum ministrum peccati. Atque hoc est absurdissimum & cum tota scriptura pugnat, quæ asserit, cum plane expiare & auferre peccata mundi: Igitur etiam vestrum Antecedens est falsum, quod videlicet per Christum non plene justificemur sine operibus, quodque ea sint necessaria ad salutem.

Eadem est B. Hunnii explicatio.

Non desunt sane, qui Paulum hic objectioni Pseudo-Apostolorum: Si absque operibus legis justificent peccatores, tolletur bene operandi studium, quod sufficiat in Christum credere, licet in peccatis malitiose perseveretur, occurri velent, per negationem consequentiæ, μὴ γένοιτο absit, ac sequentibus rationem negatæ consequentiæ afferra ab Apostolo censeant. Ita Crocius in hunc locum.

Neque alienus est B. Balduini commentarius.

Sed textui & scopo magis convenit B. Lutheri explicatio, phrasi etiam Apostolicæ optime congruens. Quam etiam Papistæ veterum Doctorum esse agnoscunt, & aliorum explanationibus præferunt.

Cornelius a Lapide: Sed si quarentes &c. quasi dicat: Si adhuc sumus in peccato, quia peccati remissionem & justitiam quæfivimus in Christi fide, cum ibi non fit quærenda, sed in lege, ut volunt Judaizantes, ergo Christus peccatum fovet. Sustulit enim legem, qua sola peccatum tollit. Numquid ergo Christus peccati minister est, quasi dicat: An Christus peccato in servit vid fovendo & conservando, hoc ipso quo legem tollit ad justificationem, & peccati deletionem, ut ipsi ajunt, necessariam, & suam statuit legem gratiæ, quas sola justificat, cum, ut ipsi ajunt, sine lege jusitificare non possit? ac fidicat: Minime. Ita Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Primasius, Anshelmus, Theophylactus. De quo sensu addit postea: Primus sensus, qui est Patrum, pressior est & melior, quia nihil aliunde supplet, ut secundus Vatabli, peccatores dici, quod doceant, legem cum Evangelio servandam esse. Tertius quia cupiditatibus indulgent. Deinde quia magis est ex mente & scopo Apostoli, vult enim probare ex fide Christi, non ex lege Mosis nos justificari: alioqui si fide Christi sectantes adhuc invenimur peccatores, sequitur, quod Christus nos decipit, promittens justitiam ex fide, quam præstare non potuit, eritque peccati non victor, non destructor, sed fotor, fautor & minister.

Hæc ille. Nec quæ porro sequuntur penes Apostolum, ad diluendam Pseudo-Apostolorum objectionem faciunt, sed ad afferendam Apostolicam fidem. Tangi hic vitia doctorum circumcisionis non apparet: neque de vita Apostolorum, quod ea & gentium & Judaizantium vitam superare debeat, quod vult Grotius, quicquam occurrit. v. 18. Quartum argumentum de destructione Quartum hoc est Apostoli argumentum, à legis, quantum ad justificationem, & condemnationem, destructione.

Si lex doctrina nostra ita destructa est, ut eadem illis, qui in Christo justificationem quaerunt, utilis non sit ad justificationem, neque illos condemnare possit; non potest utique legis observatio urgeri, ceu necessaria ad justificationem & salutem.

At verum est prius. Ergo & posterius. Effert vero id hoc modo Apostolus: Si enim qua destruxi, ea iterum aedifico, transgressorem meipsum constituo: innuens, legem se destruxisse per doctrinam suam de justificatione in Christo: ideoque se non posse iterum legem aedificare, quin semetipsum παραβάτην constitueret, quod omnino futurum, si legis observationem ullo modo necessariam faceret ad salutem. Destruxit eam hactenus in articulo de justificatione, qui ergo iterum eandem in articulo de justificatione extrueret citra παραβάτην doctrinam propria. De legis enim destructione loqui verbis immediate subjunetis: Ego enim per legem legi mortuus sum, ut DEO vivam: Qui legi mortuus est, ut DEO vivat & doctrina & praxi, ille legem docere non potest citra transgressionem, tanquam ad id necessariam, ut quis DEO vivat. Beat. Lutherus modo per ea, quae destructa sunt per doctrinam Evangelii, peccatum & mortem intelligit, modo legem etiam complectitur, quae eodem redeunt, si lex ratione usus sive justificatorii, quasi ea servare possit, sive condemnatorii, quoad eos, qui non possunt legem servare, etiamsi credant in Christum, spectetur. Num urgetur ejus impletio, ceu necessaria ad justificationem & salutem, aedificatur iterum lex in articulo sphaera justificationis, ubi destructa erat: imo aedificatur peccatum & mors, quia lex penes illos, qui implere eandem nequeunt, si urgeantur, ut impleant, nil nisi iram & mortem operatur, ac peccatum tantum auget, non vero tollit. Quo de ita Beat. Lutherus in priori Comment. Si qua destruxi &c. hoc est: Quando ego per fidei praedicationem docui justificationem in Christo, & legem impletam, ac per hoc peccata destruxi, si iterum legem docerem servandam, & non impletam, quid aliud facerem, quam quod peccata rursus statuerem, & adhuc esse superanda operibus nostris? In qua re nihil facerem, nisi quod me vel tunc, vel modo male egisse ostenderem, hoc est praevaricatorem statuerem, imo facerem me alienum à Christo, in quo justificatus fui, & denuo sub legem & peccata me traderem, aeque praevaricatorem, sicut ante Christum fui.

Atque sic Beat. Lutherus non legem, sed peccatum per doctrinam Evangelii destrui, imo legem per eandem statui docet, scilicet quatenus plene impleta est pro nobis à Christo, & ita legi satisfecimus in ipso: eademque satisfactio in justificatione secundum doctrinam Evangelii nobis imputatur, ut lex, & τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου impleatur in nobis, Rom. IIX. vers. 4.5. Rursus autem recte etiam dicitur legem destrui per doctrinam Evangelii, quantum ad legis observandae necessitatem ad salutem, & vim condemnandi praecise eos, qui non observant legem, nec plene observare possunt, etiamsi Christum fide amplectantur, vel quatenus eadem in articulum justificationis ingeritur, quod per Pseudo-Apostolos fiebat, adeoque per doctrinam Apostolican destruebatur.

De quo sic porro habet Beat. Lutherus in priori Comment. Iterum suis tropis utitur Apostolus, ideo variant Interpretes. D. Hieronymus destructa & adificata vult intelligi legem scilicet ceremonialem. Qua sententia, etsi vera, angustior tamen est, quàm ut satis fit caeteris scripturae locis convenire. Beat. Augustinus destructa vocat opera legis, imo suberbiam gloriantem & praesumentem de operibus legis. Nec hunc damno. Verum Apostolum cum praecedentibus & aliis locis compannendo peccata, (ut dixi) videtur destruere, non legem, praesertim cum Roman. III. neget se destruere legem per fidem, sed potius statuere. Peccata autem destruit Romanorum VI. ut destruatur corpus peccati. Nam per fidem destruuntur peccata, quae per legem erant & abundabant. Peccatum enim non destruitur, nisi lex impleatur. At non, nisi per fidei justitiam, lex impletur. Ita fit, ut per fidem simul lex statuatur, & peccata destruantur. Dum enim per fidem satisfit legi, desinunt peccata, & lex permanet in robore. Reedificare vero peccata, est rursum legem praedicare, & putare servandam, & implendam. Ubi vero implenda lex est, nec dum justitia facta est, imo peccatum superest. Peccatum enim est legem nondum implevisse, ita redeunt peccata, quae prius destructa per fidem docebantur. Quare aedificare peccatum idem est, quod infirmare, destruere, irritumque facere legem. Destruere autem peccatum idem est, quod legem statuere, aedificare & implere. Quicunque ergo docuerit legem impletam, fallamque justitiam, sic utique destruit peccata. Hoc autem facit, qui docet, per fidem JESU Christi justos fieri, id est, legis impletores. Qui vero dixerit legem implendam, neque factam justitiam, hic itaque rursum statuit & resuscitat peccata, & debitores legis constituit, ac reos facit servanda legis. Et in Comment. poster. Si enim qua destruxi &c. quasi dicat: Non sic prae-dieavi, ut quod semel destruxi, denuo aedificem. Nam si hoc facerem, non solum frustra laborarem, sed meipsum praevaricatorem constituerem, & more Pseudo-Apostolorum omnia perverterem, hoc est, ex gratia & Christo iterum legem & Mosen, & vicissim ex lege & Mose gratiam & Christum facerem. Destruxi autem per ministerium Evangelii peccatum, tristitiam, iram & mortem. Sic enim docui, conscientia tua, o homo, es obnoxia legi, peccato & morti, à quibus nulla ope humana aut Angelica liberari potes, jam vero Evangelium venit & annuntiat tibi remissionem peccatorum per Christum, qui legem abrogavit, peccatum & mortem destruxit. In hunc crede, tum libereris à maledicto legis, à tyrannide peccati & mortis, eris justus & habebis vitam aeternam. Sic per praedicationem Evangelii destruxi legem, ne amplius dominetur in conscientia. Nam cum novus hospes Christus in novam domum venit, ut solus in ea habitet, oportet veterem colonum Mosen cedere, & alio migrare. Ubi autem Christus novus hospes est, ibi lex, peccatum, ira, mors non habent locum, sed adest mera gratia, justitia, laetitia, vita, mera filialis fiducia erga placatum, faventem & propitium Patrem propter Christum. Non ergo expulso Christo & destructo ipso regno, quod per Evangelium plantavi, iterum edificarem legem, & erigerem regnum Mosis? Quod fieret, si, ut Pseudo-Apostoli solent, docerem circumcisionem & observationem legis necessariam ad salutem. Atque hoc modo restituerem in locum justitiae & vitae peccatum & mortem.

Lex enim tantum ostendit peccatum, efficit iram & occidit. Nec diffiteri hunc sensum omnino potuit Jesuitz Cornelius: Si enim quod destruxi, si vim justificandi, quam detraxi legis observantia, readifico, id est, rursum legi eam affero, ut calumniantur Judaei me occulte judaizare, ergo pravaricator sum, quia quasi Proteus ad omnem ventum fidem muto.

Est aliud argumentum, probans, perstandum esse Christianis in abolitione legis. Alienautem prorsus Grotii glossa: quia non in eo Apostolus ut doceat, se vite flagitiosae minime deditum esse, quasi legem adstrueret docendo, destrueret male vivendo. Haec nihil ad praesentem controversiae statum. Non suam pietatem adferet, sed Pseudo-Apostolorum doctrinam impugnat, eandemque doctrinam Evangelii penitus destruit, non vero cum eadem persistere posse docet.

## 2:19
Verf. 19.

For I through the law am dead to the law. Rightly, he says, do I abhor these things. For I live far otherwise. By the law here he understands both the law of Moses and the Prophetic writings. And that he was led by them themselves, so as not to hold the law in esteem any longer: namely, because a certain greater righteousness is promised therein. The circumcision of the heart, the inscription upon the heart. I am dead to the law, that is, I no longer conform my life to it. A locution similar to Rom. VII. 1. but the sense is the same as at the beginning of Rom. VII. (that I might live to God) namely, according to the prescription of Christ.

Nor do these things agree with the words or the intention of the Apostle, and they proceed from a false hypothesis. It is one thing to die to the law, another for the law not to be held in esteem, nor to conform one's life to it any longer, but that the divine law should not be held in such esteem that we no longer conform our life to it. Which was the madness of the Antinomians. Nor is the law therefore not to be held in esteem, because a certain greater righteousness is promised in Moses and the Prophets: namely, the circumcision of the heart, the inscription upon the heart. Surely there is no greater righteousness, nor can there be, than that which the law itself urges. Moses and the Prophets show the righteousness of Christ, Acts X. 43. Rom. III. 22. who perfectly fulfilled the law for us: but he did not demand from us a righteousness greater than the law. Nor is the righteousness of Christ to be confounded with the circumcision of the heart. For this pertains to renewal. But Christ is our righteousness in justification, Rom. V. 19. Those things of Grotius are akin to the Pelagian and Socinian heresy, not conformable to the Apostolic doctrine. But by the law, to which we are dead, although the doctrine itself of Moses and the Prophets, who bear witness to the righteousness of faith, Rom. III. 22. can be understood, and some also understand the moral law, insofar as it is a schoolmaster to Christ, and others understand it insofar as Christ was killed by it, lest the Apostle should say that he was killed in Christ by application: yet more rightly by the law, through which we die to the law, with Blessed Luther, is understood the doctrine of faith, which the Apostle had delivered: since this also is frequently designated by the name of law in the Hebrew phrase, with the agreement of Blessed Hunnius, who makes this the force of the Apostolic argument: as if, having been made free by Him, he certainly cannot expect life and righteousness from it.

I, Paul, am dead to the law, and have bid it farewell, as having been liberated from it through Christ. Therefore I can neither expect, nor ought I to expect, life and righteousness from it. But that he is liberated from the law, he teaches from the comparison in Rom. VII. 1. Similarly Flacius: He declares, he says, how he is said to have destroyed something before, which he now does not wish to rebuild. The law, he says, previously taught me, its own servant, by uncovering, accusing, irritating, and damning my most wicked nature, that I could not rightly serve it, nor could it repay me any other reward than injustice and eternal damnation for this my unfaithful servitude. And so it drove me from itself to seek another master, with whom I might fare better: Thus therefore was that law to me a schoolmaster to Christ; I am dead to the law, and have devoted myself to Christ justifying and regenerating me, that hereafter I might serve God, not the law, seeking righteousness and life from it, and yet receiving nothing but malediction. But if now I were to return to the law on account of righteousness, then surely by this very act of mine I would condemn that former defection of mine from it to Christ, and would again affirm that it can justify and save, which before I utterly denied, and would again live to him to whom once before I died.

But if I were now to return to the law, and for the sake of righteousness, then indeed I would condemn this very act of mine, that former desertion from it to Christ, and would again affirm that it can justify and save, which I previously denied, and would again live to it, to which I had once already died. He treats this matter more copiously in the sixth and seventh chapters of Romans, you will say: The law rules over man as long as he lives. But first of all, Blessed Luther explains this excellently in his commentary.

This doctrine human reason and wisdom do not grasp, therefore it perpetually teaches the contrary, namely, if you wish to live to God, you must keep the law: because it is written: Do this, and you shall live, etc. And this is the principle and one greatest of all Theologians: Living according to the law lives TO GOD. Paul says something plainly different, namely that we cannot live to God unless we are dead to the law. Therefore we must rise up into that heavenly height, so as to determine with certainty that we are far above the law, indeed altogether dead to the law. But if we are dead to the law, then the law has no right over us, just as it has no right over Christ, who redeemed us from it, that through Him we might live to God. All these things look to this, that we are not justified by the law, but by faith alone in Christ. Grotius concurs: He could say, the law is dead to me: he preferred, as Chrysostom well observes, to say: I am dead to the law, that is, I am not under the law, I am liberated from it. I do not seek salvation in it, I do not place confidence of salvation in it. He declares this Rom. VII. 2. 3. by the similitude of the married woman: she, her husband being dead, is free from the law of her husband: Thus he shows himself dead to the law. This is not understood in the same sense concerning the whole law. He was dead to the Ceremonial law because it demanded necessary observance, justification & condemnation: to the Moral law not with respect to observance, but with respect to justification & condemnation. Therefore he did not seek his righteousness in the law, nor did he place in it the confidence of justification & salvation. Nor could Cornelius entirely deny this sense: For I, through the law pointing out Christ, and ceasing and dying in Him, am dead to the law, that is, I have ceased to be subject to the law, certainly absolutely & entirely to the ceremonial law, but to the moral law & decalogue not absolutely, but insofar as that law was only a schoolmaster accusing and was an avenger of crimes. So Augustine. See Chrysostom. This is the 2nd argument (the 1st was at v. 17.) proving that we are justified not from the law, but by faith in Christ, as if he said: The law itself pointed out & showed Christ to me, it itself referred & led me to Christ, it itself testified & professed that I cease, die & come to an end in Christ. Why then, O Jews, do you wish to raise up & restore to life the law, dead of its own accord, and yielding to Christ?

Thus Cornelius, who truly with a horrible slander perverts the sentiment of Blessed Luther, as if he had asserted that the law of the decalogue, as to obligation, had ceased through Christ: Which no one has impugned more sharply and with greater zeal than Blessed Luther in the Antinomians, here.

here also in this place sufficiently indicating, that he indeed does not care for the law in justification: Which he thus explains on fol. 44 of the later Commentary. He who lives to the law, that is, seeks to be justified by the works of the law, is and remains a sinner: Therefore he is dead and damned. For the law cannot justify and save, but it accuses, terrifies, and kills him. Therefore to live to the law is to die to GOD. And conversely, to die to the law is to live to GOD. Therefore if you wish to live to GOD, it is necessary that you die to the law, but if you live to the law, you will be dead to GOD. Now to live to GOD is to be justified by grace or faith on account of Christ without the law and works. Wherefore a Christian, if he is properly and distinctly defined, is a son of grace and of the remission of sins, who has no law at all, but is above the law, sin, death, and hell.

But that Luther did not abrogate the moral law, as far as obligation is concerned, the things which he adds in the same place sufficiently testify: Blind sophists dream that faith does not justify unless it performs works of charity. In this way faith, which believes in Christ, becomes idle and void, because the power of justifying is taken away from it, unless it is formed by charity. But you, set aside the law and charity to another place and time, and direct your mind to the state of the present cause. Now that state is, that JESUS Christ the Son of GOD dies on the cross, and bears my sin, the law, death, and the Devil in his own body: These enemies and tyrants, though conquered, press upon me and now make business for me; Therefore I am anxious as to how I may be freed from them, justified, and saved. Here I do not find the law, any work or charity, which can free me from these. But Christ alone takes away the law, kills my sin, destroys my death in his own body, and in this way evacuates hell, judges the Devil, crucifies and thrusts him down to hell. In sum, all things that previously tortured and oppressed me, Christ has taken away from the midst, exposed, shown openly, and triumphed over them by himself, so that now they can no longer dominate, but are forced to serve me.

From these things it can be sufficiently understood that nothing needs to be done here, other than to hear that these things have been so accomplished and to apprehend them with undoubted faith, and that is truly formed faith. Afterwards, Christ being thus apprehended by faith, with me dead to the law, justified from sin, and freed from death, the devil, and hell through Christ, I do good works, I love God, I give thanks, I exercise charity toward my neighbor. But that charity or the following works do not inform my faith, nor adorn it: But my faith adorns and informs charity. What that Cornelius a Lapide alleged from the Commentary on chapter IV of Galatians, from Vol. I of the Wittenberg edition, is not found there. But the Blessed Luther taught the contrary to these things everywhere. Let the Jesuit therefore take back that harsh Jesuit calumny! Let them retract the most impudent accusation! Here Crocius himself vindicates Luther, certainly not a disciple of Luther, in the place cited.

Cornelius a Lapide says: that for Luther to die to the law is nothing other than not to be obligated to the law, and to be free from it: For it is certain that the decalogue was given to the Jews alone, not to us: To them indeed it was given long ago: yet we are held by the same. Luther in the Commentary in the place cited does not say that to die to the law is nothing other than not to be obligated to the law, but to be free from it, namely as regards justification and condemnation. The commentary inscribed to Ambrose says: He dies to the law: who is freed from it. Is it heretical? Surely, or Luther does not expound it heretically. The mind of both is the same. What? The Apostle himself says that the Romans were mortified to the law in the body of Christ, and that we are now free from the law, Rom. VII. ver. 4, 7. That, that I might live to GOD, Crocius explains thus:

He expresses the end, for whose sake he died to the law: Not that he might live to himself, not that he might live to the world; for he who lives to himself and the world, he is a sinner, he is already perishing. Much less, he says: that we might live to sin; for he who lives to it, he is a living man dead in sin. What is it to live to GOD? It is to live a holy, just, and to GOD pleasing life by faith embracing Christ and working through charity: It is to present these weapons of justice to GOD, Roman. VI. v. 13. But the Blessed Luther understands this more correctly in this way, that he stands within the sphere of justification. For although a holy life conformable to the law follows, yet the Apostle does not treat of it here. That I might live to GOD, that is, he says in the later Commentary, that I might be alive to God. You see therefore that it is not life, unless you have been without the law, nay, unless you have been utterly dead to the law, namely in conscience. Meanwhile, however, as long as the body lives, as I have often already admonished, the flesh must be exercised by laws, and vexed by the exactions and punishments of laws. But the internal man, owing nothing to the law, nay, being free from it, is a living, just, and holy person, not through himself, or in his own substance, but in Christ, because he believes in him, as follows: I am crucified with Christ.

The end, says the Blessed Hunnius, is assigned for this liberation from the law. It is, that being freed from the condemnation of the law he might live before GOD, and be a partaker of justice and an heir of eternal life through grace. That this is the opinion of Flacius is evident from the preceding. The Blessed Hülfemann in the funeral oration for Lyfer held in this place notes that the particle 'that' is opposed to the previous Pharisaic life, which sought justice from the law, Rom. IX. 30, 31, by which the Apostle says he does not now live, but that he is therefore dead to the law, that he might live to Christ through faith.

Although this can be referred to explaining or confirming that which he had said, that he died to the law, yet it would not be beside the point if a peculiar argument were begun here, which will be the fifth in order, from the nature and causes or the definition of the causes of justification: Which is so constituted that it in no way admits the concurrence of works or the observation of the law, but consists without it.

For the formal cause is situated in the appropriation of the cross and satisfaction, and also in the vivification and justification of Christ, and that he was delivered for our sins, and raised again for our justification, Rom. IV. last. For we have been crucified with Christ crucified for our sins, whoever of us seeks justification in Christ with Paul, who sets himself here as an example of the justified. For because one died for all, it is the same as if we all had died, 2. Cor. V. v. 14. And therefore each one appropriates this to himself through faith.

Just as Christ himself, says the Blessed Luther in the paraphrase of this place in the later commentary, was crucified to the law, to sin, to death, to the Devil, so that they might have no right over him any longer, so also I through faith crucified to Christ in the Spirit am crucified and die to the law, to sin, etc., so that they themselves might have no right over me any longer, but might be crucified and dead to me. But Paul speaks here not of the imitation of crucifixion or of an example: Because to imitate the example of Christ is also to be crucified with him, which crucifixion pertains to the flesh, 1. Petr. II. Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you might follow his footsteps: But he speaks here of that sublime co-crucifixion, by which sin, the Devil, and death are crucified in Christ, not in me. Here Christ alone does all things, but believing I am crucified to Christ through faith, so that those things might be dead and crucified to me also.

Just as he is crucified, so also I have crucified, that is, with torment I have killed, all vices, Rom. VI. ver. 6.

But just as he says he is crucified and died with Christ through the appropriation of the satisfaction of Christ’s cross and death; so too he implies that he lives, having been resurrected with Christ, when he adds: I live; yet not I now, but Christ lives in me: And that I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God.

Although Christ was crucified and died for our sins, he nevertheless satisfied for sins and the law by his own death, crucified to the sins of the world, because he himself was innocent and just; just as he ought to be justified and absolved from sin, and its guilt imputed to him, after he paid what he had not stolen in the judgment of God, and thus be liberated from death and restored to life, so that we might also be absolved and vivified in him: whence he is said to be resurrected for our justification. Rom. IV. 23. Not, says the interpreter B.

Luther, (the Apostle) I speak thus of my death and crucifixion, as if I were no longer living, nay rather I live, because by that very death and crucifixion, by which I die, I am vivified. This is, while I am liberated by grace and faith from the law, sin, and death, I truly live. Therefore that crucifixion and death, by which I am crucified and die to the law, to sin, to death, and to all evils, is to me resurrection and life.

For Christ crucifies the Devil, kills death, condemns sin, and binds the law: Believing this, I am liberated from the law, etc.

Not I now, that is, not in my person or substance. There he shows clearly how he lives, and teaches what Christian justice is, namely that by which Christ lives in us, not that which is in our person.

But Christ living in me abolishes the law, condemns sin, mortifies death, because at his presence those things cannot but vanish. For Christ is eternal peace, consolation, justice, and life. But to these the terror of the law, the sadness of the mind, sin, hell, and death must yield.

By which method the opinion of the Pseudo-Apostles is again firmly defeated, and it is taught: That we are not justified by the observation of the law, but solely by the satisfaction and justice of Christ apprehended by true faith.

Thus Paul strives to withdraw us entirely, as again B.

Luther warned, from the inspection of ourselves, of the law, and of works, and to transplant [us] into Christ himself and the faith of Christ, so that we look at nothing at all in the method of justification, than grace, and that we separate it most distantly from the law and works, which ought to be far from here.

Grotius with some others here mixes in sanctification; but that is foreign, both to the Apostolic thesis, which treats of justification, and to the argument which the Apostle now uses, which tends to this, that the justice of works is excluded here.

Nor could he prove that in Jerome, which he nevertheless followed himself.

If anyone, says Jerome in Grotius, with members mortified upon the earth and dead to the world, has been configured to the death of Jesus Christ, he is crucified with Jesus, and fixes the trophy of his mortification on the wood of the Lord’s passion.

Grotius notes that in this way: I do not deny that he was thus crucified together, but here he notes the communion of the cross which I have with the crucified Christ, rather, but so that he may express the efficacy of Christ’s crucifixion all the more strongly, and render the cause why he died to the law, that he might live to God, he says: I am crucified together with Christ, that is, I am so closely united to the crucified Christ, I perceive the full fruit of his crucifixion so certainly, as if I had hung on the cross with him in my own person.

For being grafted into the wood of the cross, I draw from there the juice of grace, from which the fruit is born in me.

In explaining this fruit he was far from the scope.

That fruit, he says, is justification and sanctification.

True indeed this: But sanctification does not make for this.

The explanation of Cornelius a Lapide is related: as if he were to say: I have been crucified with Christ through baptism and have died to sin and the old life, to ceremonies and the law, as I have already said, and from there I have been as it were refitted from the old tree, but that I might be grafted as a new branch onto the new tree of Christ, and live from it, and draw the juice of grace; so that not I now, but Christ lives in me: because not the law, not nature, not concupiscence, not my own will, but Christ himself by his grace as if by the soul, and by the motions of virtues as if by powers, drives me to every good, and to the vital actions of virtues, so that Christ’s humility, fortitude, wisdom, joy, peace, and other virtues live and flourish in me: But here it is a matter of participating in the life and victory of the resurrected Christ unto justice, which is viewed in the act of justification, from which the Apostle removes the works of the law.

Much more rightly therefore to the scope of the Apostle B.

Luther: But because he lives in me, therefore whatever in me is grace, justice, life, peace, salvation, is of Christ himself, and yet that very thing is mine through the conglutination and infusion, which is through faith, through which we are made Christ and I as it were one body in the Spirit: Because therefore Christ lives in me, it is necessary that grace, justice, life, and eternal salvation be present with him, and the law, sin, and death be absent.

Wherefore faith is to be taught purely, that namely through it you are so conglutinated to Christ, that from you and him is made one as it were person, which cannot be separated, but perpetually adheres to him: So that you can say with confidence: I am Christ, that is, Christ’s justice, victory, power, etc. is mine: And conversely Christ says: I am that sinner, that is, his sins, death, etc. are mine, because he adheres to me, and I to him.

For we are joined through faith into one flesh and bone Ephes. V. We are members of the body of Christ of his flesh and of his bones.

So that this faith couples Christ and me more tightly than a husband is coupled to a wife. Therefore faith is not an idle quality, but its magnitude is so great, that it obscures and removes those most foolish dreams of Sophistic doctrine, concerning the fiction of formed faith and charity, concerning merits, concerning our dignity or quality, etc.

Therefore the Grotian interpretation concerning the living of the crucifixion can in no way merit calculation: which pertains to the consequences of justification, not to justification itself, concerning which the treatment is instituted here.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἐγὼ γὰρ διὰ νόμου νόμῳ ἀπέθανον.

Merito, inquit, ego haec abominor. Longe enim ego vivo aliter. Per legem hic intelligit & legem Mosis, & scripta Prophetica. Atque se per ea ipsa adductum, ne legem ultra in pretio habeat: nimirum, quia justitia quaedam major ibi promittitur. Circumcisio cordis, inscriptio in cor. Mortuus sum legi, id est, non ultra ad cam vitam meam compono. Locutio similis Rom. VII. 1. sensus autem idem, qui Rom. VII. in principio. (ἴνα θεῷ ζήσω) nempe secundum Christi praescriptum. Vide Rom. VI. 10. 2. Cor. V. 15.

Nec verbis, aut intentioni Apostoli haec conveniunt, & ex falsa hypothesi procedunt. Aliud est legi mori, aliud, legem non habere in pretio, nec ultra ad vitam componere, at ut lex divina ita non habeatur in pretio, ut non amplius ad eandem vitam componamus. Qui furor erat Antinomorum. Nec ideo lex non habenda in pretio, quod justitia quaedam major in Mose & Prophetis fit promissa: Circumcisio nempe cordis, inscriptio in cor. Nulla utique major justitia est, nulla esse potest, quam ea, quam lex ipsa urget. Justitiam Christi monstrant Moses & Propheta, Act. X. 43. Rom. III. 22. qui legem perfecte pro nobis praestitit: non autem majorem lege justitiam à nobis exegit. Neque justitia Christi confundenda est cum cordis circumcisione. Haec enim ad renovationem pertinet. Christus vero nostra est justitia in justificatione, Rom. V. 19. Pelagiane & Socinianae haeresi affinia sunt illa Grotiana, non doctrinae Apostolicae conformia. Per legem autem, qui mortui sumus legi, etsi intelligi possit doctrina ipsa Mosis, & Prophetarum, qui testimonium perhibent justitiae fidei, Rom. III. 22. nonnulli etiam legem moralem, quatenus est paedagogus ad Christum, intelligant, alii eandem quatenus per ipsam occisus est Christus, ne se in Christo per applicationem occisum dicat Apostolus: Rectius tamen per legem, per quam morimur legi, cum B. Lutheri intelligitur doctrina fidei, quam tradiderat Apostolus: Siquidem & haec saepiuscule designetur legis nomine phrasi Hebraea, annuente B. Hunnio, qui hanc vim argumenti Apostolici facit: tanquam ab eo liber factus, ab eo certe vitam & justitiam expectare non potest.

Ego Paulus legi sum mortuus, eique valedixi, tanquam ab ea liberatus per Christum. Ergo vitam & justitiam ab ea nec possum expectare, nec debeo. Legi autem, ei e ab lege liberari, docet à collatione Rom. VII. 1. Similiter Flacius: Declarat, inquit, quomodo antea destruxisse aliquid dicatur, quod nunc readificare non velit. Lex, inquit, antea me suum famulum, pessimam meam naturam detegendo, accusando, irritando, & damnando edocuit, nec me sibi recte servire posse, nec se mihi aliud praemium, quam injustitiam & aeternam damnationem, pro hac mea infideli servitute, rependere posse. Atque ita abegit me à se ad quaerendum alium herum, apud quem melius haberem: Sic igitur illa mihi fuit paedagogus ad Christum, egone legi sum mortuus, & Christo me justificanti & regeneranti addixi, ut posthac Deo, non legi, ab ea justitiam vitamque quaerendo, & tamen nil nisi maledictionem reportando servirem. Quod si nunc ad legem rediren, justitiaeque causa, tum sane ego hoc ipso factum meum illud prius transfugium ab ea ad Christum damnarem, denuoque affirmarem, eam posse justificare ac servare, quod antea pernegavi, denuoque ei viverem, cui antea semel sum mortuus.

Hanc materiam Romanorum sexto & septimo copiosius tractat, inquies: Lex dominatur homini, quamdiu vivit. Sed imprimis id praeclare explicat B. Lutherus comment. post. Pseudo-Apostoli docebant, nisi vixcris legi, mortuus es Deo; hoc est, nisi vixeris secundum legem, coram Deo es mortuus. Paulus plane contrarium dicit: Nisi fueris mortuus legi, non poteris vivere Deo. Eadem hodie est doctrina adversariorum, quae tum Pseudo-Apostolorum fuit. Si vis, inquiens, Deo vivere, vive legi, vel secundum legem. Nos contra: Si vis vivere Deo, oportet te prorsus mortuum esse legi.

Hanc doctrinam ratio & sapientia humana non capit, ideo perpetuo contrarium docet, scilicet, si vis vivere Deo, oportet te legem servare: quia scriptum est: Fac hoc, & vives &c. Estque hoc principium, & una maxima Theologorum omnium: Vivens secundum legem vivit DEO. Paulus plane diversum dicit, scilicet nos non vivere posse Deo, nisi legi simus mortui. Itaque oportet nos assurgere in istam caelestem altitudinem, ut certo statuamus, nos longe supra legem, imo prorsus legi mortuos esse. Si autem legi mortui sumus, tum lex nihil juris habet in nos, ut neque in Christum aliquid juris habet, qui nos ab ea redemit, ut per ipsum Deo vivamus. Hec omnia eo spectant, per legem nos non justificari, sed sola fide in Christum. Consonat Grotius: Dicere poterat, lex mihi mortua: maluit, ut bene observat Chrysostomus, dicere: Legi sum mortuus, id est, non sum sub lege, sum ab ea liberatus. Non quaero in ea salutem, non fiduciam salutis in ea pono. Id declarat Rom. VII. 2. 3. similitudine mulieris conjugatae: illa, viro mortuo, libera est à viri lege: Sic ostendit, se legi mortuum. Hoc non eodem fenju capitur de lege tota. Ceremoniali mortuus erat quod observantiam necessariam, justificationem & condemnationem: Morali non quoad observantiam, sed quoad justificationem & condemnationem. Ideo non quaerebat in lege justitiam suam, non in ea collocabat justificationis & salutis fiduciam. Nec diffiteri hunc sensum prorsus potuit Cornelius: Ego enim per legem ostendentem Christum, in coque desinentem & mortuum, legi mortuus sum, id est, desi legi obnoxius esse, ceremoniali quidem absolute & omnino, morali vero & decalogo non absolute, sed quatenus lex illa paedagogus tantum accusabatur ad vindex erat scelerum. Ita Augustinus. Vide Chrysostomum. Est haec 2. (1. enim fuit v. 17.) ratio probans, nos justificari non ex lege, sed fide Christi, quasi dicat: Lex ipsi mihi Christum indicavit & ostendit, ipsa me ad Christum remisit, & deduxit, ipsa me in Christo desinere mori & finiri testata & professa est. Cur ergo, o Judaei, legem sua sponte mortuam, Christoque cedentem, resuscitate & restituere vultis in vitam.

Hac Cornelius, qui vero horrenda calumnia sententiam Beat. Lutheri pervertit, quasi legem decalogi quoad obligationem, per Christum, defisse adfuerit: Quod nemo acrius & majori zelo, quam Beat. Lutherus in Antinomis impugnarit, hic.

hic etiam loci satis indicans, quod nempe legem plane non curet in justificatione: Quod ita explicat fol. 44. Comment. poster. Qui vivit legi, hoc est, quaerit per opera legis justificari, peccator est & manet: Ergo mortuus & damnatus est. Lex enim non potest justificare & salvare, sed accusat, perterrefacit & occidit eum. Ergo vivere legi est mori DEO. Et contra legi mori, est vivere DEO. Itaque si vis vivere DEO, legi oportet moriaris, si autem vives legi, mortuus eris DEO. Est autem vivere DEO justificari per gratiam seu fidem propter Christum sine lege & operibus. Quare Christianus, si proprie & differte definiatur, est filius gratiae & remissionis peccatorum, qui nullam prorsus legem habet, sed est supra legem, peccatum, mortem, infernum.

Non autem abrogasse Lutherum moralem legem, quantum ad obligationem, ea quae subjungit ibidem satis testantur: Sophistae caeci somniant, fidem non justificare, nisi faciat opera charitatis. Hoc modo fides, quae credit in Christum, fit otiosa & irrita, quia ei detrahitur vis justificandi, nisi formata sit charitate. Tu vero sepone legem & charitatem in alium locum & tempus, & intende animum ad statum praesentis causae. Is autem status est, quod JESUS Christus DEI Filius moritur in cruce, & portat meum peccatum, legem, mortem, Diabolum, in fernum in corpore suo: Hi hostes & tyranni in victi me premunt & mihi jam negotium faciunt; Ideo solicitus sum, quomodo ab eis liberer, justificer, & salver. Hic non invenio legem, opus aut charitatem aliquam, quae me possit ab his liberare. Sed solus Christus tollit legem, occidit peccatum meum, destruit mortem meam in corpore suo, atque hoc modo evacuat infernum, Diabolum judicat, crucifigit & detrudit ad infernum. Summa, omnia, quae me antea cruciaverunt & oppresserunt, illa Christus a medio sustulit, exposuit, ostentavit palam, & de illis per seipsum triumphavit, at jam amplius non possunt dominari, sed cogantur servire mihi.

Ex his satis intelligi potest, hic nihil oportere agi, quam audire ista sic gesta esse & indubitata fide apprehendere, eaque est vere formata fides. Postea, Christo sic fide apprehenso, me mortuo legi, justificato a peccato, & liberato a morte, diabolo & inferno per Christum, facio bona opera, diligo Deum, ago gratias, exerceo charitatem erga proximum. Sed illa charitas vel sequentia opera non informant meam fidem, nec ornant: Sed fides mea ornat & informat charitatem. Quae allegavit Cornelius ille Lapideus è Comment. in cap. IV. Gal. è T. I. Witteb. f. 189. 190. illic non inveniuntur. Contraria autem istis passim docuit B. Lutherus. Resorbeant ergo jesuita duram illam Jesuita calumniam! Retradent accusationem impudentissimam! Vindicat hic Lutherum Crocius ipse, non sane Lutheri discipulus l. c.

Cornelius à Lapide dicit: Lutherum mori legi nihil aliud esse, quàm ad legem non esse obligatum, ab eaque liberum: Certum enim, decalogum solis Judaeis, non nobis esse datum: Illis quidem datus olim: nos tamen eodem tenemur. Lutherus in Comment. b. l. non dicit mori legi esse nihil aliud, quam ad legem non esse obligatum, sed esse ab ea liberum, nempe quoad justificationem & condemnationem. Commentarius Ambrosio inscriptus ait: Moritur legi: qui liberatur ab ea. Num haereticè? Sane, aut Lutherus non haereticè exponit. Eadem utriusque mens. Quid? Apostolus ipse dicit, Romanos esse mortificatos legi in corpore Christi, nos esse nunc liberos a lege, Rom. VII. vers. 4. 7. Illa, ut DEO viverem, Crocius ita explicat: Finem exprimit, cujus causa mortuus sit legi: Non ut sibi, non ut mundo viveret; sibi enim & mundo qui vivit, is peccator, is jam perit.

Multo minus ait: ut peccato vivamus; Cui qui vivit, is vivens mortuus est in peccato. Quid est vivere DEO? Fide Christum amplectente & per charitatem operante vivere vitam sanctam, justam, DEO gratam: Est sistere hec arma justitiae DEO, Roman. VI. v. 13. Sed rectius hac ita Beat. Lutherus intelligit, ut sistat intra sphaeram justificationis. Etsi enim vita sancta legi conformis sequatur, non tamen de ea hic agit Apostolus. Ut viverem DEO, hoc est, inquit in Comment. posteriori, ut comm Deo sim vivus. Vides ergo non esse vitam, nisi fueris sine lege, imo nisi prorsus legi mortuus fueris, scilicet in conscientia. Interim tamen donec corpus vivit, ut saepe jam admonui, debet caro exerceri legibus, & vexari exactionibus ac paenis legum. Internus autem homo nihil debens legi, imo liber ab ea, est vita, justa & sancta persona, non per se, aut in sua substantia, sed in Christo, quia in illum credit, ut sequitur: Ego sum Christo crucifixus.

Finis, inquit B. Hunnius, assignatur hujus a lege liberationis. Is est, ut a damnatione legis liberatus vivat coram DEO, sit justitiae particeps & vita aeterna bares per gratiam. Eandem elle Flacii sententiam, is superioribus constat. B. Hülsemannus in concione funebri Lyferiana hoc loco habita notat, particulam eti opponi vita priori Pharisaica, quae ex lege justitiam sectabatur, Rom. IX. 30. 31. qua se nunc non vivere ait Apostolus, sed ideo legi mortuum esse, ut Christo viveret per fidem.

Quanquam hoc ad explicandum, aut confirmandum id, quod dixerat, se legi mortuum esse referri possit, non tamen abs re fuerit, si hic inchoetur peculiare argumentum, quod Quintum in ordine erit, a natura & causis vel causis definitione justificationis: Quae ita comparata est, ut nullatenus admittat concursum operum vel observationis legis, sed sine ea consistat.

Nam causa formalis in appropriatione crucis & satisfactionis, nec non vivificatione & justificatione Christi sita est, utque sit traditus est propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram, Rom. IV. ult. Christo enim crucifixo pro peccatis nostris nos cum ipso crucifixi sumus, quicunque in Christo justificationem quaerimus cum Paulo, qui sese hic ceu exemplum justificati sistit. Quod enim unus pro omnibus est mortuus, perinde est, ac si omnes mortui essemus, 2. Cor. V. v. 14. Ideoque id sibi quisque appropriat per fidem. Sicut Christus ipse, inquit in paraphrasi hujus loci comment. poster.

B. Lutherus, legi, peccato, morti, Diabolo, crucifixus est, ut nullum jus amplius in eum habeant, ita & ego per fidem crucifixus Christo in Spiritu crucifigor & morior legi, peccato &c. ut & ipsa nullum jus amplius in me habeant, sed mihi crucifix a & mortua sint. Loquitur autem Paulus hic non de crucifixionis imitatione seu exempli: Quia imitari exemplum Christi est etiam cum eo crucifigi, quae crucifixio pertinet ad carnem, 1. Petr. II. Christus passus est pro vobis, relinquens vobis exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus: Sed loquitur hic de illa sublimi concrucifixione, qua peccatum, Diabolus, mors, crucifigitur in Christo, non in me. Hic Christus solus omnia facit, sed credens crucifigor Christo per fidem, ut & mihi illa sint mortua & crucifixa.

Sicut ille crucifixus est, ita & ego crucifixi, id est, cum cruciatu interemi, vitia omnia, Rom. VI. vers. 6.

Ut autem se crucifixum & commortuum dicit per appropriationem crucis & mortis Christi satisfactione; ita etiam cum Christo resuscitatum vivere innuit, cum addit: Vivo; tamen non iam ego, sed vivit in me Christus: Quod autem nunc vivo in carne, per fidem vivo Filii Dei.

Christus etsi propter peccata nostra crucifixus & mortuus, morte tamen sua satisfecit pro peccatis & lege, peccatis mundi crucifixus, quia innocens & justus ipse fuit; veluti justificari & absolvi a peccato, ejusque reatu sibi imputato, postquam solvit, quod non rapuerat in judicio Dei, adeoque a morte liberari, & in vitam restitui debuit, ut nos in ipso etiam absolveremur & vivificaremur: unde resuscitatus dicitur propter justitiam nostram Rom. IV. 23. Non inquit, interprete B.

Luthera, (Apostolus) de morte & crucifixione mea sic loquor, quasi jam non vivam, imo vive, quia ipsa morte & crucifixione, qua morior, vivificor. Hoc est, dum gratia & fide liberor a lege, peccato & morte, vere vivo. Itaque illa crucifixio & mors, qua crucifigor & morior legi, peccato, morti & omnibus malis, est mihi resurrectio & vita.

Christus enim crucifigit Diabolum, occidit mortem, peccatum damnat, & ligat legem: Hoc credens liberor a lege &c.

Non jam ego, hoc est, non in persona vel substantia mea. Ibi ostendit clare, quomodo vivat, & doceat, que sit justitia Christiana, ea scilicet, qua Christus in nobis vivit, non qua est in persona nostra.

Vivens autem in me Christus abolet legem, peccatum damnat, mortem mortificat, quia ad presentiam ipsius illa non possunt non evanescere. Est enim Christus aeterna pax, consolatio, justitia & vita. His autem cedere oportet terrorem legis, merorem animi, peccatum, infernum, mortem.

Quo pacto iterum firmiter profligatur Pseudo-Apostolorum sententia, doceturque: Non justificari nos per legis observationem, sed unice per Christi satisfactionem & justitiam vera fide apprehensam.

Sic Paulus conatur nos prorsus abstrahere, ut iterum B.

Lutherus monuit, ab inspectione nostri, legis, & operum, & in ipsum Christum & fidem Christi transplantare, ut nihil plane spectemus in ratione justificandi, quam gratiam, & eam longissime separemus a lege & operibus, que procul hinc abesse debent.

Grotius cum aliis nonnullis hic immiscet sanctificationem; sed ea aliena est, cum a thesi Apostolica, que tractat de justificatione, tum ab argumento, quo nunc utitur Apostolus, quod eo tendit, ut hic excludatur justitia operum.

Nec probare id potuit in Hieronymo, quod tamen ipse sequutus est.

Si quis, inquit Hieronymus apud Grotium, mortificatis membris super terram & mundo mortuus configuratus fuerit morti Jesu Christi, crucifigitur cum Jesu, & tropaum mortificationis sue in ligno dominice passionis affigit.

Notat id Grotius hoc modo: Sic fuisse una crucifixum non negem, sed hic communionem potius crucis notat, quam habeo cum Christo crucifixo, sed ut efficaciam crucifixionis Christi tanto fortius exprimat, & causam reddat, cur legi sit mortuus, ut Deo viveret, ait: Una cum Christo crucifixus sum, id est tam arcte unior Christo crucifixo, tam certum plene fructum crucifixionis ejus percipio, ac si cum ipso in propria persona in cruce pependissem.

Infertus enim ligno crucia inde succum gratia fugo, unde in me fructus nascitur.

In explicando hoc fructu a scopo aberat.

Fructus ille, inquit, est justificatio & sanctificatio.

Verum quidem hoc: Sed sanctificatio huc non facit.

Affinis est explicatio Cornelii a Lapide: quasi dicat: Ego per baptismum cum Christo crucifixus atque peccato & veteri vita, ceremoniis & legi, uti jam dixi, mortuus sum, indeque quasi ab arbore veteri refectus sum, at arbori nove Christi Christo novue quasi ramue inserar, ab eaque vivam, & succum gratia fugam; ita ut non iam ego, quam vivat in me Christus: quianon lex, non natura, non concupiscentia, non voluntas propria, sed Christus ipse fue gratia quasi anime, & virtutum quasi potentiarum motibus me agit ad omne bonum, & ad vitales virtutum actiones, ut Christi humilitas, fortitudo, sapientia, gaudium, pax, alieque virtutes in me vivant & vigeant: Sed hic de vita ac victoria Christi redivivi ad justitiam participante agitur, qua vice in actu justificationis spectatur, a quo removet Apostolus opera legis.

Longe ergo rectius ad scopum Apostoli B.

Lutherus: Quia vero in me vivit, ideo quicquid in me est gratia, justitia, vite, pacis, salutis, est ipsius Christi, & tamen illud ipsum meum est per conglutinationem & inbafionem, que est per fidem, per quam efficimur Christus & ego quasi unum corpus in Spiritu: Quia ergo vivit in me Christus, necesse est, simul cum eo adesse gratiam, justitiam, vitam & salutem eternam, & abesse legem, peccatum, mortem.

Quare fides pure est docenda, quod scilicet per eam sic conglutineris Christo, ut ex te & ipso fiat una quasi persona, qua non possit segregari, sed perpetuo adhereat ei: Ut cum fiducia dicere possis: Ego sum Christus, hoc est, Christi justitia, victoria, vim &c. est mea: Et vicissim Christus dicat: Ego sum ille peccator, hoc est, ejus peccata, mors &c. sunt mea, quia adheret mibi, & ego illi.

Conjuncti enim sumus per fidem in unam carnem & os Ephes. V. Membra sumus corporis Christi de carne ejus & de ossibus ejus.

Ita ut hec fides Christum & me arctius copulet, quam maritus uxori est copulatus. Ergo fides non est otiosa qualitas, sed tanta est ejus magnitudo, ut obscuret & tollat ista stultissima somnia doctrine Sophistice, de fictione fidei formate & charitatis, de meritis, de dignitate aut qualitate nostra &c.

Calculum itaque mereri nullatenus potest Grotiana interpretatio de crucifixionis viviorum: que ad consequentia justificationis pertinet, non ad ipsam justificationem, de qua hic tractatio instituitur.

## 2:20
Verse 20. (I live however in faith) that is, I am not he who I had been.

I am changed much more; than that other Saul, 1 Sam. X. 6.

(Christ lives however in me) who namely governs me by his Spirit.

(which I live now in the flesh) that I still perform those functions, which mortal life demands.

As Philipp. I. 22. &amp; it is placed here thus, as Rom. VI. 10. (in faith, that of the Son of God) I sustain this under the hope of a better life, of whose promises, made to me by the Son of God himself, I have the fullest faith.

These are wrongly drawn to sustenance or patience under the hope of a better life, when they treat of the life, by which the reborn person lives in faith in Christ the Son of God, through the apprehension of the satisfaction of Christ, as is added, who loved me, and delivered himself for me.

For these infer the satisfaction and because of the pronoun me and ἐμοῦ the application or apprehension of the same.

He does not name himself, so that he may exempt or prefer himself from the number of others: But so that he may apply to himself through faith, ἰδιοποιῶν by appropriating, as Chrysostom speaks, and show the cause, why he does not place the confidence of salvation in the law, [and] does not seek justification.

These words, says B.

Luther, loved ME, of the fullest faith, and who could say this short pronoun ME with that faith, and apply it to himself, as Paul, would also be the best disputant together with Paul against the law.

Not inelegantly according to Chrysostom does Paul declare a double benefit here: one that Christ restores the dead to life, the other, that by his death he has bestowed life. Furthermore, Theophylact also thinks that Christ’s merit here attributes both sensible or natural life and spiritual life, whom others follow, interpreting those words in this way: "And that I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God": What I have related, he says, is spoken of spiritual life, and you will find no less that even sensible life is present in me from Christ.

For the Law itself, if it is not kept at all, renders all subject to sin and subjects them to torments: nor does it prevent all from perishing as transgressors, just as happened in the flood.

But Christ, arriving, exempted those justified by his death from condemnation.

Whence it happens that we possess this sensible life, which we lead in the flesh, by our faith in Christ, which both made us righteous and snatched us from the condemnation of the Law.

But if that "I live in the flesh" is taken more for natural life than for spiritual, which could be explained as being lived in Christ while the Apostle was still acting in the flesh: yet it is not indicated, although that is otherwise most true, that the preservation of sensible life, like other benefits, should be attributed to the merit of Christ; but the time is expressed, how long "I live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God."

But you would interpret it most correctly regarding spiritual life; so that the very act of divine, mystical, and spiritual life is attributed uniquely to Christ, and meritoriously to faith in Christ, and organically to the latter: Whatever spiritual life is in me, even if I still act in the flesh, it is not from me, or my carnal birth, but from Christ, and his merit, and efficacy, through spiritual regeneration, not by my works, but solely by faith, apprehending the grace and satisfaction of Christ, it consists.

As Christ lives in us, by freeing us from the death of the soul, and conferring upon us the life by which we enjoy God.

Col. II. 13. Rom. VIII. 6. Thus we live in Christ, being participants of him through the same, who live in the faith of the Son of God, into whom we are inserted through faith.

Concerning which, regarding the Papists, Jansenius, Comment. on the Evang. Concord. chap. 20. on John III. But what is said, "he who believes in him," shows with what ease we obtain life, not temporal, but eternal, while by faith alone, a thing indeed most easy, it is required that we be incorporated into Christ, and rendered participants of his merits.

For this is the sum of God’s kindness, that he deigns to make us participants of his grace by such a means.

Christ lives in us, both as to substance and as to grace and energy, because he is in us, he dwells, and remains not absent by reason of substance, but present.

Eph.

III. 16. 2. Pet. I. 3. and thus he also works in us the life which we draw uniquely from him, who are all dead in ourselves. For in him is the life of men.

I am the way, the truth, and the life.

And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son: he who has the Son (through faith) has life.

This faith is to be taught purely, says B.

Luther on this passage, so that you may be glued to Christ through it, so that from you and him there is made as it were one person, which cannot be separated, but perpetually adheres to him, so that you can say with confidence: I am Christ, that is, Christ’s righteousness, victory, and life is mine.

And conversely Christ may say: I am the sinner: That is, his sins, death, etc., are mine, because he adheres to me, and I to him, for we are joined through faith, etc.

He handed down the connection with the preceding and the scope thus in the former Comment. B.

Luther: I said that I no longer live, but Christ in me.

But lest you think, or occasion seems to be given to future heretics, that the Christian life is outside the flesh in the religion of Angels, in walking in wonders above oneself, thus Christ lives in me: So that I nevertheless lead life in the flesh, but not so live in the flesh, that my life is from the flesh in the flesh, or according to the flesh, but in the faith of the Son of God.

But they themselves also live in the flesh, that is, they act in the present life, but they do not lead this life in the faith of Christ, but in the works of the law, therefore they lead a life dead in sins. Τὰ ἀγαπήσαντός με Namely as a part of the human race.

For the following words demand this meaning here, given as a common benefit, it also pertains to individuals. Καὶ παραδόντος ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ Rom.

25. Here you have described, by the interpreter B.

Luther, in the later Comment., the true reason for justification, and an example of the certainty of faith.

He who could say these words, "I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me," with certain and constant faith with Paul, he would be truly blessed.

And with those very words Paul entirely abrogates and removes the righteousness of the law and of works.

And further: For me, I say, who was a most miserable and most lost sinner.

Therefore through that handing over of the Son of God into death I breathe, and I apply it to myself, and so application is the true power of faith.

Thus the worker does not say: Christ loved me, etc.

Paul opposes these words, which are the purest preaching of grace and Christian righteousness, to the righteousness of the law, as if he were saying, if the law is indeed divine, it has its glory, but it did not love me, nor did it give itself for me, nay, it accuses, terrifies, and drives me into desperation.

But now I have another, who freed me from the terrors of the law, from sin and death, and transferred me into the liberty, righteousness of God, and eternal life, who is called the Son of God, loving me, and giving himself for me, to whom be glory for ever and ever, Amen!

Faith therefore, as I said, apprehends and involves Christ the Son of God, given for us, as Paul teaches here, which being apprehended through faith, we have righteousness and life.

For Christ is the Son of God, who out of pure love gave himself for us to be redeemed.

Latin:

Vers. 20. (ζῶ δὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει) id est, is qui fueram, non sum.

Mutatus sum multo magis; quam alter ille Saul, 1 Sam. X. 6.

(ζῶ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ χριστὸς) qui scilicet me Spiritu suo gubernat.

(ὃ διῶ νῦν ἐν σαρκὶ) quod adhuc fungor eis functionibus, quas mortalis vita exigit.

Sicut Philipp. I. 22. & hia ita positum, ut Rom. VI. 10. (ἐν πίστει, τῇ τοῦ υἱῦ τοῦ θεοῦ) Sustineo hoc sub spe vite melioris, cujus promillis, a Filio ipso Dei mihi factis, fidem plenissime habeo.

Perperam hec trahiuntur ad sustinentiam vel patientiam sub spe vite melioris, quum de vita agant, qua vivit renatus in fide in Christum Dei Filium, per apprehensionem satisfactionis Christi, ut additur, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me.

Hec enim satisfactionem & propter Pronomen me & ἐμοῦ applicationem vel apprehensionem ejusdem inferunt.

Non se nominat, ut se aliorum numero eximat vel præferat: Sed ut sibi per fidem, ἰδιοποιῶν appropriando, ut loquitur Chrysostomus, applicet, & causam ostendat, cur non in lege ponat fiduciam salutis, non querat justificationem.

He voces, inquit B.

Lutherus, dilexit ME, plenissime fidei, & qui hoc breve pronomen ME illa fide dicere, & sibi applicare posset, qua Paulus, etiam futurus esset optimus disputator una cum Paulo contra legem.

Non inconcinne secundum Chrysostomum Paulus duplex hic declarat beneficium: unum quod Christus mortuum recreat ad vitam, alterum, quod per mortem suam largitus sit vitam. Porro utrumque & sensibilem, vel naturalem vitam & spiritualem Christi merito hic tribuit Theophylactus etiam existimat, quem sequuntur alii, hoc modo interpretans illa: Quod autem nunc vivo in carne, in fide vivo Filii Dei: Quae retuli, inquit, de spirituali dicta sunt vita, nec minus vel sensibilem mihi comperies à Christo inesse.

Lex enim ipsa, si nequaquam fervetur, omnes reddit peccato obnoxios, & tormentis supponit: nec prohibet, quo minus omnes, ut pravaricatores perdantur, quemadmodum in diluvio contigit.

Christus vero adveniens, sua morte justificatos à damnatione exemit.

Quo fit, ut sensibili hac, quam in carne ducimus, vita, ab nostram in Christo fidem, nos potiamur, quae & nos justos effecit, & à legis damnatione eripuit.

Sed si maxime illud vivo in carne de naturali vita accipiatur, quam de spirituali, quae in carne adhuc agente Apostolo in Christo agebatur, explicari possit: non tamen id indicatur, ut verissimum id ceteroquin sit, vita sensibilis conservationem, ut alia beneficia, Christi merito acceptum ferri debere; sed tempus exprimitur, quousque in carne vivo, in fide Filii Dei vivo.

Rectissime autem de vit spirituali interpreteris; ut actus ipse vit divin mystic & spiritualis unice Christo, ac fidei in Christum illi meritorie, huic organicè tribuatur: Quicquid vita in me est spiritualis, etsi in carne adhuc agam, non à me, aut carnali nativitate mea, est, sed à Christo, ejusque merito, & efficacia, per spiritualem regenerationem, non operibus meis, sed unice fide, apprehen-dente gratiam, & satisfactionem Christi, constat.

Ut Christus vivit in nobis, à morte animæ nos liberando, & vitam, qua Deo fruimur, nobis conferendo .

Coloss. II. 13. Rom. VIII. 6. Ita nos vivimus in Christo vir ejus participes per eamdem, qui vivimus in fide Filii Dei, cui inserimur per fidem .

Quo de Pontificiis Jansenius Comment. in Concord. Evang. cap. 20. in Joh. III. Quod vero dicitur, qui credit in eum, ostendit, quanta facilitate vitam non temporalem, sed æternam consequamur, dum sola fide, res scilicet facillima exigitur, ut in Christo incorporemur, & meritorum ejus reddamus participes.

Hæc est enim summa Dei benignitatis, ut tali medio dignetur nos suæ gratiæ facere participes.

Christus vivit in nobis, tum quod substantiæ, tum quod gratiam & ἐνέργειαν, quia in nobis est, habitat, & manet non absens substantiæ ratione, sed præsens .

Eph.

III. 16. 2. Petr. I. 3. atque ita in nobis etiam operatur vitam, quam ex ipso unicè trahimus, qui toti mortui sumus ipse ipso. In ipso enim est vita hominum .

Ego sum via, veritas, & vita .

Et hoc est testimonium, quod vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus, & hæc vita in Filio ejus est: qui Filius habet (per fidem) vitam habet .

Hæc fides pure est docenda, inquit B.

Lutherus ad hunc locum, ut scilicet sic per eam conglutineris Christo, ut ex te & ipso fiat quasi una persona, qua non possit segregari, sed perpetuo adhæreat ei, ut cum fiducia dicere possis: Ego sum Christus, hoc est, Christi justitia, victoria, vita est mea.

Et vicissim Christus dicat: Ego sum peccator: Hoc est, ejus peccata, mors, & c. sunt mea, quia adhæret mihi, & ego illi, conjuncti enim sumus per fidem &c.

Connexionem cum præcedentibus & scopum ita tradidit in Comment. priori B.

Lutherus: Dixi me jam non vivere, sed Christum in me.

Verum ne existimetis, aut hæreticis futuris occasio data videatur, quod vita Christiana fit extra carnem in religione Angelorum, in mirabilibus supra se ambulando, sic vivit in me Christus: Ut tamen in carne vitam agam, non autem sic in carne vivam, quod ex carne in carne, aut secundum carnem fit vita mea, sed in fide Filii Dei.

Justificari vero & ipsi carne quidem vivunt, id est in præsenti vita agunt, verum hanc vitam non agunt in fide Christi, sed in operibus legis, ideo mortuam in peccatis vitam agunt. Τὰ ἀγαπήσαντός με Nemp ut partem humani generis.

Eum enim hic sensum exigunt sequentia, datum in commune beneficium etiam ad singulos pertinet. Καὶ παραδόντος ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ Rom.

25. Hic descriptam habes, interprete B.

Luthero, Comment. poster. veram rationem justificationis, & exemplum certitudinis fidei.

Qui hæc verba, vivo in fide Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me, certa & constanti fide cum Paulo dicere posset, is vere beatus esset.

Et illi ipsis verbis Paulus in totum abrogat, & tollit justitiam legis & operum.

Et porro: Pro me, inquam, qui eram miserrimus & perditissimus peccator.

Per illam igitur traditionem Filii Dei in mortem respiro, & eam applico mihi, itaque applicatio est vera vis fidei.

Sic non dicit operarius: Christus dilexit me &c.

Ista verba, que sunt purissima prædicatio gratiæ & justitiæ Christianæ, opponit Paulus justitia legis, quasidicat, si lex sane divina, habeat suam gloriam, sed ea non dilexit me, nec tradidit seipsum pro me, imo accusat, perterrefacit, & in desperationem adigit me.

Nunc autem alium habeo, qui liberavit me à terroribus legis, à peccato & morte, ac transtulit me in libertatem, justitiam Dei & vitam æternam, qui vocatur Filius Dei, diligens me, & tradens seipsum pro me, cui sit gloria in secula seculorum, Amen!

Fides ergo, ut dixi, apprehendit & involvit Christum Filium Dei, pro nobis traditum, ut Paulus hic docet, quo apprehenso per fidem, habemus justitiam & vitam.

Christus enim est Filius Dei, qui ex charitate mera tradidit seipsum pro nobis redimendum.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. οὐκ ἀθετῶ τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ I do not spurn this gift of God, that is, the Gospel, לֹא מָאֹס not only do I not live dissolutely, but I follow a more exact norm than that which is in the law. Ἀθετεῖν is to reject, to despise, to render void. He says, therefore, that he, having been affected by such a benefit from Christ, neither wants nor is able to despise and render void such great grace, that is, the gratuitous love not of a mere man but of God.

It would be a horrible sin for a little man, who had perished by his own fault, to despise and reject the most admirable benevolence and love of that highest God.

Therefore, it was most alien to the present state in which he was.

He was not alone.

There were also other true believers.

Therefore, while he speaks of himself, he shows the Galatians what the sense of all ought to be; nay, he also indicates not obscurely what a horrible guilt they contract, as many of them as seek to be justified from the works of the law, because they despise and reject the true grace of God, than which nothing can be committed more alien to the Christian mind, nothing more foul, nothing more abominable; those who were Judaizing denied that they were rejecting the grace of God, they were joining themselves to those in the observance of the law: but the Apostle in his own person shows the Galatians that it is rejected where it is not entirely attributed to faith, as Crocius here has with Pareus.

Let us hear Megalandrus: He who has made the law for this reason, that you wish to be justified through it, rejects grace, denies Christ and his sacrifice, does not want to be saved through this inestimable price, but wants to satisfy through the righteousness of the law.

for sins, or to merit grace through his own righteousness. He certainly blasphemes and rejects the grace of God. But it is horrible to say that a man can be so perversely evil that he even rejects the mercy and grace of God. And a little before: But consider here diligently that to wish to be justified by the works of the law is to reject the grace of God. What, I ask, can be more impious, or what more horrible sin can there be, than to reject the grace of God? And not to wish to be justified by faith in Christ? It is certainly enough and more than enough that we are impious and transgressors of all the commandments of God. Now, moreover, we add this sin of sins, that we so securely reject the grace and remission of sins offered to us through Christ, etc. Grotius's gloss: I do not reject this gift of God, that is, the Gospel with that paraphrase, I do not live dissolutely, but I follow a more exact norm than that which is in the law, is diluted, alien, and contrary to the analogy of faith. It is diluted to understand the gift of the Gospel through τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ, when properly the grace of God itself, exhibited in Christ, is understood, not the gift of grace metonymically, much less the Gospel as the medium of grace. It is diluted to interpret 'to reject' as 'to despise', 'to cast away', 'to render void' regarding observance, as if he were hinting that he renders grace void who does not follow the norm of life in the Gospel. It is alien, because here the Apostle differs concerning justification, not concerning the observance of a stricter norm than the moral law is. How the grace of God is rejected by those who seek to be justified by the law is taught, since God exhibited grace to us most of all in this, that He willed Christ to die for us: But not how a more exact norm is either prescribed by God or not neglected by Paul. Finally, it is a false Gospel to prescribe a more exact norm of living, than which nothing can be more exact than the law, which is the διατύπωσις of the righteousness of God, which is to be done and which is to be fled, and brings in and requires absolute obedience, perfect in all numbers and degrees, and therefore most exact.
