Εἰ γὰρ διὰ νόμου δικαιοσύνη, id est, if that righteousness which pleases God and produces eternal life could be had through the law, or if that legal righteousness suffices. Ἄρα χεῖρας δωρεὰν ἀπέθανε, There was no need for Christ. Δωρεὰν here is worth μάτην, as it is translated in Proverbs.

30. Ezech. XIV. 23. For what need was there for the Gospel, if the law sufficed: and if there was no need for the Gospel, there was no need for the death of Christ: because it was destined by God for this, that the Gospel should be sanctioned by His own blood.

The Sixth Argument

The sixth argument is contained here from the absurd; or the end of the death of Christ by deduction from the absurd: From which it follows that Christ died in vain, by that the grace of God is rejected. But from justification by the works of the law it follows that Christ died in vain. Therefore the assertors of justification by the works of the law reject the grace of God. Concerning which Theophylact: For if the law, he says, can both prepare salvation and justification, Christ died freely and in vain, who for this reason died, that by His death He might render us saved, whom the law itself could not save.

But if it had been permitted for the law to do this, truly the death of Christ would have been superfluous. But if you yourself were to assert this, I shall see to what point of impiety the blasphemy would progress. Crocius notes here that the Apostle does not say, if righteousness is by the law alone, but if by the law the Judaizers did not attribute it to the law alone. They attributed it to the law and to Christ, saying that a man is justified by faith in JESUS Christ and the law. Paul on the contrary shows that from a mixture even of law and faith it follows that Christ would have died in vain.

But we, with Paul, says B. Luther, constantly affirm (for we do not wish to reject the grace of God) that either Christ died in vain or the law does not justify. But Christ did not die in vain. Therefore the law does not justify. Christ the Son of God justified us out of mere grace and mercy, therefore the law could not perform this. For if it could have, He would have acted foolishly, in that He delivered Himself for our sins, so that through this we might be justified. We conclude therefore, that we are justified neither by merit of congruity or condignity, nor by the cross or afflictions, nor by the law itself, but by faith in Christ alone.

Who further notes and wishes it to be diligently observed, that Paul, when he here makes mention of righteousness, is engaged in a spiritual, not a political or economic matter; that is, he does not treat of civil righteousness, which God approves and requires to be set forth beforehand, but which also sets forth its own rewards, and which reason can in some measure supply; but here he treats of righteousness before God, by which we are delivered from the law, sin, death, and all evils, and are made partakers of grace, righteousness, and life, and finally are constituted lords of heaven, earth, and of all creatures. That righteousness neither divine nor human law can supply. Those heavenly thunders and lightnings in Paul against the righteousness of the law and one's own ought deservedly to terrify us away from it. There was once struck down by lightning and condemned whatever there is of monasteries, orders, and righteousnesses in observances, whether legal or self-chosen. But who would not reject his own vows, tonsure, cowl, human traditions, likewise the law of Moses, if he hears that on account of these very things he casts away the grace of God and makes void the death of Christ? When the world hears these things, it does not believe them to be true, because it does not think so great a malice can fall into the human heart, that it should cast away the grace of God and account the death of Christ as nothing, and yet this horrible sin is most common. For whoever seeks righteousness outside faith in Christ, whether through works, satisfactions, or afflictions, or through the law of God, casts away the grace of God and despises the death of Christ, however much with his mouth he may say the opposite.

These things B. Luther.

Nor is there anything for the modern Papists to except, that righteousness is indeed not had from works without Christ's death. But that Christ by His death merited for us the first grace, that is, the faculty of meriting by our works. For the Apostle disputes against the Pseudo-Apostles, who taught that righteousness is had partly from faith, partly from works, and against these he concludes, if righteousness, whether whole or half, is from the law, Christ died in vain. For Christ had to die, not that He might merit the first grace, or the first justification through the habit of charity, as the Papists wish, but that He might merit for us entire righteousness.

For the whole demonstration of the Apostle turns between two immediate contraries, faith and the law or works: From the position of one to the negation of the other or conversely; if we are justified by faith, therefore not by works: or we are not justified by works, therefore by faith: since we must be justified either by faith or by works, either by one's own righteousness or by another's, that is, Christ's righteousness. But a mixture of both, of faith and works, of Christ's righteousness and one's own, cannot have a place. Grotius's gloss corrupts both the scope and the Apostolic text.

The scope is also to destroy by the merit of Christ's death the heresy of the Pseudo-Apostles concerning justification by the law. The sense is clear: If righteousness is by the law, that is, if by the observance of the law we are justified before God (not truly if that legal righteousness suffices: For what would suffice,) if the law could be fulfilled by us?

When the sentence of the law becomes, "he who shall do these things shall live in them," Christ died in vain or without cause, namely for us, as is clear from verse 20. For what need was there for Christ to be delivered into death in our place, if we could obtain eternal life by our own justice through the observation of the law?

That the death of Christ was needed for this purpose, that it was destined for this, that the Gospel, that is, a more exact norm of life than the law, should be sanctioned by the blood of Christ, is as contrary to the whole of Scripture as it is to the Apostolic treatment: since the death of Christ was not a martyrdom for the doctrine of a more exact way of living, but a λύτρον (ransom) & ἀντίλυτρον (counter-ransom) paid in our stead for liberation from the curse of the law, and the merit of eternal life.

Those Grotian ideas smack of the heresy of Pelagius & Socinus, not the Apostolic faith.

If you say these do not consist: that the death of Christ is both a λύτρον (ransom), or a satisfaction performed in our place, and a merit of life: since in a λύτρον there is a payment for another, and thus there is a payment of a debt; whereas in merit, the performance of what is not owed is required.

I respond: the death of Christ is to be considered both as a passion and a satisfaction: thus it was performed in our stead, and as the payment of the debt due to us: and as the highest degree of Christ's obedience, who was obedient even unto the death of the cross, by subjecting himself to the law in our place, and fulfilling all the justice of the law: which was entirely the performance of what was not owed; because he himself was not a debtor but the Lord of the law; but he willed to be subjected to the law for us, so that by his passion he might liberate us from sin and death: and that the obedience, which shines forth most in his passion, might merit and acquire for us justice and life, and that our salvation is to be attributed to the sum of his obedience, both active and passive, which, if it depended in any way on our own obedience, the virtue of the death of Christ would be evacuated, nay, Christ would have died in vain for us, nor would he have either satisfied for sin by his death, or merited for us justice and life.

For whoever can in any way at least satisfy God himself, and at least merit for himself, for him Christ has died in vain thus far; to whom alone and only the glory of meritorious satisfaction is to be attributed.

24. 25. XLV. 21. 24. 25. Jer. IX, 24. 1 Cor. I. 31. CHAPTER III.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having taxed the Galatians' departure from faith in the crucified Christ, he confirms justification by faith alone through the gift of the Holy Spirit, whom they received not through the law, but the word of faith, from the example of Abraham, to whom faith was imputed for justice, and the prediction of the like justification of the Gentiles through faith, from the curse of workers, by the power of the curse of the law, from the testimony of the Prophet (Hab. II. 4.) that the just shall live by faith, from the liberation of Christ from the curse, when he was made a curse for us; he urges the letter of the Testament concerning the seed that is blessed, and the cause of the law, not for obtaining the inheritance, but for manifesting sin, nor given except through the hand of a Mediator, by which it does not vivify, but concludes us under sin, so that through faith in Christ we may uniquely possess the promise. Finally, he teaches how they were concluded under the law to Christ, to whom the law led like a pedagogue, so that they might be justified through faith, and that they are children of God through faith in Christ, and have put on the same in baptism, without discrimination, so that they are the seed of Abraham, and heirs of the promise.

There are two parts.

The former is ἀποδεικτικὴ (demonstrative) in the further confirmation of justification by faith in Christ, up to verse 14. The other is διδακτικὴ (didactic) concerning the testament, concerning the seed Christ, and the inheritance to be obtained in the same, and concerning the law, which was added only for the sake of sin, and so that it might be a pedagogue to Christ, and so that through faith in Christ we might be heirs of the promise. PART I.

Ἀποδεικτικὴ, they further confirm justification by faith in Christ.

Verse.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐκ ἀθετῶ τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ Non sperno hoc Dei donum, id est, Evangelium, לֹא מָאֹס non modo non vivo dissolute, sed exactiorem sequor normam, quam eam, quæ est in lege. Ἀθετεῖν est rejicere . contemne-re . irritum reddere . dicit igitur, se tanto beneficio affectum à Christo, nec velle, nec posse contemnere, ac irritum reddere tantam gratiam, id est, gratuitam dilectionem non hominis nudi sed Dei.

Horrendum foret peccatum, homuncionem, qui sua culpa perierat, contemnere & abjicere summi illius Dei tam admirandam benevolentiam & dilectionem.

Alienissimum igitur à statu præsenti, in quo erat.

Non ille solus erat.

Erant & cæteri vere fideles.

Dum igitur de se loquitur, ostendit Galatis, quis sensus omnium esse debeat; quin & haud obscure indicat, quam horribilem contrahant culpam, quotquot ipsorum justificari quærant ex operibus legis, quod scilices vera gratiam Dei contemnant, abjiciantque, quæ nihil à mente Christiana alienius, nihil foedius, nihil magis abominandum possit committi judaicantes negabant, se gratiam Dei abjicere, se conjungere illis legis observantiam: verum Apostolus in sua persona Galatis ostendit, abjici, ubinon totum ei tribuitur in fidem, ut hic Crocius cum Pareo habet.

Audiamus Megalandrum: Qui legem fecerit hoc nomine, quod per eam justificari velis, abjicit gratiam, negat Christum & sacrificium ejus, non vult per hoc inestimabile pretium salvari, sed vult per justitiam legis satisfacere.

pro peccatis, aut per suam iustitiam mereri gratiam. Is certe blasphemat et abjicit gratiam Dei. Horrendum autem dictu est, quod homo tam perverse malus esse possit, ut etiam misericordiam, et gratiam Dei abjiciat. Et paulo ante: Considerabie autem hic diligenter, quod velle justificari ex operibus legis sit abjicere gratiam Dei. Quid quaeso magis impium, aut quod horribilius peccatum esse potest, quam abjicere gratiam Dei? Et non velle justificari fide in Christum? Satis certe superque satis est, nos esse impios et transgressores omnium mandatorum Dei. Nunc insuper etiam hoc peccatum peccatorum addimus, quod gratiam et remissionem peccatorum per Christum nobis oblatam, tam secure respuimus etc. Grotius glossa: Non sperno hoc Dei donum, id est, Evangelium cum illa paraphrasi, non vivo dissolute, sed exactiorem sequor normam, quam eam, quae est in lege, diluta, aliena, adversa analogiae fidei est. Dilutum, per τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ Evangelii donum intelligi, quum proprie ipsa Dei gratia, in Christo exhibita intelligitur, non donum gratiae metonymice, nedum medium gratiae Evangelium. Dilutum est, spernere, hoc est, contemnere, abjicere, irritum reddere interpretari de observatione, quasi is irritam reddere gratiam innueat, qui normam vitae in, Evangelio non sectatur. Alienum, quia hic de justificatione disserit Apostolus, non de observatione normae strictioris, quam est lex moralis. Quomodo gratia Dei spernatur per eos, qui per legem justificari quaerunt, docetur, quum maxime in eo gratiam nobis exhibuerit Deus, quod Christum voluerit pro nobis mori: Non autem quomodo exactior norma, vel a Deo praescripta, vel a Paulo non neglecta fit. Falsum denique Evangelium exactiorem praescribere vivendi normam, quam lege nihil exactius esse possit, quae διατύπωσις est iustitiae Dei, qua facienda et qua fugienda, et absolutam infert ac requiret obedientiam, omnibus numeris et gradibus perfectam, adeoque exactissimam. Εἰ γὰρ διὰ νόμου δικαιοσύνη, id est, si per legem haberi potuit illa iustitia, quae Deo placet, et vitam aeternam parit, aut si illa iustitia legalis sufficit. Ἄρα χεῖρας δωρεὰν ἀπέθανε, Nihil opus fuit Christi. Δωρεὰν hic valet μάτην, quomodo transfertur Proverb.

30. Ezech. XIV. 23. Quid enim opus Evangelio, si lex sufficiebat: et si Evangelio non erat opus, nec morte Christi erat opus: quia in hoc a Deo destinata est, ut Evangelium ipsius sanguine sanciretur.

Sextum argumentum

Sextum hic argumentum continetur ab absurdo; vel fine mortis Christi per deductionem ab absurdo: Ex quo sequitur, Christum frustra esse mortuum, illo abjicitur Dei gratia. At ex justificatione ex operibus legis sequitur Christum frustra esse mortuum. Ergo assertores justificationis ex operibus legis abjiciunt Dei gratiam. Quo de Theophylactus: Si enim lex, inquit, et salutem parare, et justificationem poterit, gratis et frustra mortem obiit Christus, qui ideo mortuus est, ut morte sua salvos nos redderet, quos salvare lex ipsa nequibat.

Quod si facere legi id licuisset, profecto supervacanea mors Christi extitisset. Quod si ipse asseveraveris, videro, quo impietatis progressura esset blasphemia. Notat Crocius hic, quod non dicat Apostolus, si per solam legem est iustitia, sed si per legem Judaizantes non soli tribuebant legi. Tribuebant legi et Christo dicentes, hominem justificari per fidem JESU Christi et legem. Paulus contra ostendit, ex mixtura etiam legis ac fidei sequi, quod Christus frustra esset mortuus.

Nos vero cum Paulo, inquit B. Lutherus, constanter affirmamus, (nolumus enim abjicere gratiam Dei) aut Christum gratis mortuum esse, aut legem non justificare. Sed Christus non est gratis mortuus. Ergo lex non justificat. Christus Dei Filius ex mera gratia et misericordia nos justificavit, ergo lex hoc non potuit praestare. Si enim potuissit, stulte egisset, quod seipsum tradidisset pro peccatis nostris, ut per hoc justificaremur. Concludimus igitur, neque merito congrui aut condigni, neque cruce aut afflictionibus, neque ipsa lege, sed sola fide in Christum nos justificari.

Qui porro notat et diligenter observari vult, quod Paulus, cum hic mentionem facit de iustitia, versetur in loco spirituali non politico aut economico, hoc est, non agit de iustitia civili, quam Deus approbat et requirit praefari, butque proponat sua premia, quam et ratio aliquo modo praestare potest; sed de iustitia coram Deo hic agit, qua a lege, peccato, morte et omnibus malu liberamur, et participes gratiae, iustitiae et vitae efficimur, ac denique Domini caeli, terrae, et creaturarum omnium constituimur. Illam iustitiam, neque lex divina, neque humana praestare potest. Ista tonitrua et fulmina caelestia in Paulo contra iustitiam legis et propriam deberent nos merito abterrere ab ea. Ibi semel fulmine prostratum ac damnatum est, quicquid est monasteriorum, religionum et iustitiarum in cultibus, aut legalibus aut electitiis. Quis autem sua vota, rasuram, cucullum, traditiones humanas item legem Mosi non confuat, si audiat propter ipsa se abjicere gratiam Dei, et inanem facere mortem Christi? Ista cum audit mundus, non credit esse vera, quia non putat tantam malitiam cadere posse in cor humanum, quod gratiam Dei abjicere, et mortem Christi pro renibili ducere debeat, et tamen hoc peccatum horribile communissimum est. Nam quicunque extra fidem in Christum, sive per opera, satisfactiones aut afflictiones sive per legem Dei quaerit iustitiam, is gratiam Dei abjicit et mortem Christi contemnit, ut maxime ore diversum dicat.

Haec B. Lutherus.

Nec est, quod excipiant Papistae moderni, non haberi quidem iustitiam ex operibus sine Christo Christi morte. Christum vero sua morte nobis meritum esse primam gratiam, hoc est, facultatem merendi operibus nostris. Nam disputat Apostolus contra Pseudo-Apostolos, qui iustitiam haberi docebant partim ex fide, partim ex operibus, et contra hos concludit, si iustitia sive tota sive dimidia fit ex lege, Christum frustra esse mortuum. Mori enim debuit Christus, non ut primam gratiam, vel primam justificationem per habitum charitatis, ut Papistae volunt, sed ut integram nobis iustitiam promereretur.

Tota enim Apostoli demonstratio versatur inter duo contraria immediata, fidem et legem seu opera: A positione unius ad negationem alterius vel contra; si justificamur fide, ergo non operibus: vel non justificamur operibus, ergo fide: quoniam vel fide, vel operibus justificari nos oportet, vel iustitia propria vel aliena, hoc est Christi iustitia. Mixtura vero ex utroque ex fide et operibus, iustitia Christi et propria locum habere non potest. Glossa Grotii corrumpit et scopum et textum Apostolicum.

Scopum est et mortis Christi merito profligare Pseudo-Apostolorum haeresin de justificatione per legem. Sensus in aprico est: Si per legem iustitia est, hoc est, si per observationem legis justificemur coram Deo (non vero si illa legalis iustitia sufficit: Quid enim sufficeret,) si lex à nobis impleri posset?

Quum legis sententia fit, qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis) Christus frustra vel sine causa mortuus est, scilicet pro nobis, ut è vers. 20. liquet. Quid opus enim erat, Christum nostri loco tradi in mortem, si nos propria nostra justitia per legis observationem vitam æternam consequi potuimus?

Morte Christi ad id opus fuisse, quod in hoc destinata, ut Evangelium, id est, exactior vitæ norma, quam lex, sanciretur Christi sanguine, ut toti scripturæ, ita & tractationi Apostolicæ ἀδιάμετρον adversum est: Quum mors Christi non martyrium fuerit doctrina de exactiori vivendi ratione, sed λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον nostri vice persolutum per liberatione ab execratione legis, & meritum vitæ æternæ.

Pelagii & Socini hæresin sapiunt illa Grotiana, non fidem Apostolicam.

Si dicas hæc non consistere: mortem Christi & λύτρον esse, vel satisfactionem nostri loco præstitam, & meritum vitæ: quum in λύτρω sit persolutio pro alio, adeoque ibi debiti fiat solutio: In merito autem requiratur præstatio indebiti.

Respond. mortem Christi & ut passionem considerari ac satisfactionem: ita esse vice nostri præstitam, debitaque pane nostræ luitionem: et ut obedientie Christi supremum gradum, qui obediens fuit usque ad mortem crucis, nostri loco sese legi subjiciendo, & omnem justitiam legis implendo: quæ omnino fuit præstatio indebiti; quia ipse non erat debitor sed Dominus legis; pro nobis autem legi subjici voluit, ut passione ita sua nos à peccato & morte liberaret: obedientia autem, quæ maxime in passione relucet, nobis justitiam & vitam promereretur & acquireret, et ut solidum obedientiæ ejus tam activæ, tam passivæ salus nostra tribuenda sit, quæ si ullatenus à propria nostra obedientia dependeret, evacuaretur virtus mortis Christi, imo frustra Christus Christus mortuus esset pro nobis, nec morte sua vel satisfecisset pro peccato, vel meruisset nobis justitiam & vitam.

Qui enim ullatenus saltem Deo ipse satisfacere, & saltem mereri potest, pro eo Christus hactenus frustra mortuus est; Cui vero soli & uni satisfactionis meritoriæ gloria tribuenda Es.

24. 25. XLV. 21. 24. 25. Ier. IX, 24. 1. Cor. I. 31. CAPUT III.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Taxata Galatarum à fide in Christum crucifixum discessione confirmat justificationem per solam fidem à dono Spiritus Sancti, quem non per legem, sed verbum fidei accepere, ab exemplo Abrahæ, cui fides ad justitiam imputata, & prædictione justificationis parilis gentium per fidem, ab operariorum maledictione, vi maledicti legis, à testimonio Prophetæ (Hab. II. 4.) quod justus fide victurus sit, à liberatione Christi à maledictione, cum factus est nobis maledictum; urget literam Testamenti de semine benedicto, & causam legis, non ob consequendam hereditatem, sed ad manifestandum peccatum, nec nisi per manum Mediatoris date, qua non vivificat, sed sub peccato concludit nos, ut per fidem in Christum unice promissione potiamur. Docet denique, quomodo conclusi fuerint sub lege ad Christum, ad quem pædagogi instar duxit lex, ut per fidem justificarentur, & quod filii Dei per fidem in Christum sint, eundemque in baptismo induerint, sine discrimine, ut Abrahæ semen, & hæredes sint promissionis.

Partes sunt duæ.

Prior est ἀποδεικτικὴ in ulteriori confirmatione justificationis per fidem in Christum occupata, usque ad vers. 14. Altera est διδακτικὴ de testamento, de semine Christo, & consequenda in eodem hæreditate, & de lege, quæ accesserit peccati tantum causa, & ut pædagogus esset ad Christum, ac per fidem in Christum promissionis hæredes essemus. PARS I.

Ἀποδεικτικὴ, ulterius confirmant justificationem per fidem in Christum.

Vers.

## 3:1 Argument
1. Ω ἀνόητοι Γαλάται) That this paternal rebuke does not conflict with the precept of Christ, appears from those things which were said at Matt. V. 22. Ἀνόητοι.

He calls them foolish, not in the way in which Christ forbids anyone to be called a fool or stupid in Matt. V. For he does not offer them an insult out of private anger, or a desire for vengeance, but wishing the best for the persons of the Galatians, he taxes their stupidity, with this sole end, that he may recall those who are wandering, and raving about the dogmas of the Pseudo-Apostles, to the pristine wisdom of the Gospel.

In the same way the Savior himself calls the disciples going to Emmaus foolish and slow of heart to believe those things which were said by the Prophets, as here B. Hunnius. Τίς ὑμᾶς ἐβάσκανε) Βασκαίνειν properly is to corrupt the eyes.

But it is transferred from the eyes to the mind, just as the Latin fascinare (to bewitch) is derived from it. Τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι) That is, so that you did not obey the truth once delivered: so that you did not retain it. Οἷς κατ' ὀφθαλμοὺς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς προεγράφη ἐν ὑμῖν ἐσταυρωμένος) It ought to be construed ἐν οἷς ὑμῖν, in whom, namely, you.

It is a Hebrew way of speaking.

Thus Joshua XIII.

21. οἱ ἐπάταξε Μωϋσῆς αὐτούς. Thus Peter II. 24. ὃ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθητε. But it is better that that ἐν ὑμῖν be omitted in the Manuscript, as superfluous.

The sense is: Christ was so described before you, with his cross, that he was as if set before your eyes.

There is need indeed of the word προεγράφη here, as also in Romans XV.

4. & προέγραψα in Ephesians

III. 3. signifies past time, as in προορισάμενος, Romans III. 9. thus προεῖπον below V. 21. I Thessal. IV. 6. & προελήγομεν I Thess. III. 4. and no differently soon in προεὐηγγελίσατο. Historical discourse is wont to be compared to a painting, and hence the name διατυπώσεις, which one might call a bringing under the gaze. Quintilian calls it a form of things expressed in words.

The Apostle understands here, however, the death of Christ with its effects.

We admit that the death of Christ with its effects is understood, by which the same satisfaction was performed for us, and eternal life acquired for us, which effects are looked upon here in justification, namely the remission of sins, and the donation of the justice of Christ.

For he depicted Jesus Christ, just as he was crucified for us, as is evident from the 19th verse of the preceding chapter, so sedulously and accurately before the Galatians, so that they might imprint that efficacy upon their heart, and by faith receive the crucifixion of Christ, and the death endured for us, and in it alone seek justice.

That πρὸ can be referred both to time, and to the subject, which namely was depicted before his eyes, so that it might always be before them.

Christ crucified, as πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν (before the eyes). This pertains to aggravating their guilt. But if those who were lightly imbued with faith fall away from it, it is ascribed to infirmity. But those in whom faith was deeply impressed, without doubt sin more grievously when they depart from it: and therefore this is said to them for a reproach: that they, having deserted Him whom they had seen stripped for their sake, nailed to the cross, wounded by a lance, etc., recur to the law, and are persuaded that such great tortures endured for us were in no way sufficient for satisfaction for sins, with the charm (fascination) having blinded the eyes of their minds, so that they would not obey the truth so clearly placed πρὸ ὄμματα (before their eyes).

The truth was further, that by faith alone in the Gospel is the righteousness in Christ, delivered and crucified for us, held, Fascinum Galatae (The fascination of the Galatians). by faith indeed is salvation held, but not by faith alone, and therefore not by the passion of Christ alone, but also by circumcision, and the observation of the works of the law, as if we were not already crucified together with Christ and dead to the law, but were still under the law, and are freed from the guilt of sin by the crucifixion of our lusts, and can, nay must, satisfy for sins and merit grace in another way, so that we may be justified and obtain salvation.

Therefore, that ἐν ὑμῖν ἐσταυρωμένον (crucified among you) is not to be taken in a bad sense, nor to be explained concerning the Galatians, as if they by their apostasy had crucified Christ again for themselves, which is said of those who commit the sin against the Holy Spirit (Heb. 6, 7; ch. 10, 29), but concerning the ministry of the Apostles, by which Christ was so depicted to them, as if they had seen Him hanging on the cross before their eyes.

Theophylact beautifully summarized these things after Chrysostom: It is certain, he says, that Jesus was affixed to the cross in Jerusalem, why then does he say before their eyes, and that He was lifted up on the gibbet among you? Because they beheld Him with the eyes of faith much more keenly than those who were present and saw Him. For most of them derived no utility from that bodily sight. But these, who by no means saw the cross with their eyes, contemplated it much better through faith. Christ was therefore proscribed by preaching, He was depicted and designated, so that you, truly giving faith to the preaching, saw Him just as if He were present. Indeed, these things are granted to the Galatians for praise and for reproach. For praise, because they received with such certainty what was said concerning Christ. For reproach, because, failing from Him whom they saw stripped, affixed to the wood, and dead, they fled to the law. See how Paul, leaving others aside, brings the cross into the middle, so that the faithful may attend to this and be charmed, not the law. In a bad sense, however, B.

Luther takes it in this way: To whom Jesus is prescribed before their eyes as crucified among you, that is: Behold, you yourselves see, as it was effected by me by the aforementioned arguments, that it is clear and depicted before your eyes and written beforehand, that Jesus Christ is crucified among you. That this is the meaning, if you attend to the preceding, nay, to the argument of the whole epistle, I believe, will not be denied. For he had premised, I do not reject the grace of God, I do not live. Also, if righteousness is from the law, then Christ died in vain. All of which tend to this, that Christ is crucified in them (as in the Jews) whoever do not trust in Him, but in themselves and the law. For when the grace of God is rejected, Christ does not live in them. What then remains, but that He is dead and crucified in them? as is held in the former Comment. But the interpretation of Chrysostom and Theophylact (which is also that of most others) seems preferable; because if he had said ἀνόητος (foolish), that they had crucified Christ, he would not have added anything further, I would wish to learn in words, since nothing more or graver could be said with that, than that they had crucified Christ.

Therefore, he properly brings an argument here, why he calls them ἀνόητας (foolish), because, forsooth, they had received the Spirit not by the works of the law, but by the hearing of the word, and had begun in the Spirit, but now wish to finish in the flesh, having been fascinated by false teachers, of which later.

Calvinists, constrained by these things, because the faithful, such as they were among the Galatians, whom he now calls ἀνόητας (foolish), who no longer follow the truth, can fall away from faith, rashly seek an escape in this, that it is one thing to speak of the faith of the whole assembly, another of the faith of individuals. That the assembly is said to have fallen away, because the greater part in it had fallen away. But that the faith of the truly faithful had not therefore fallen away. This, I say, is a κενόφύγετον (empty evasion). For in that assembly, even those to whom Christ crucified had been depicted before their eyes, whose faith, by the admission of Chrysostom and Theophylact, the Apostle praises, are now called ἀνόητοι (foolish) and apostates, not because all in that church had fallen away, but because some, who, forsooth, had been fascinated and seduced by the Pseudo-Apostles and translated to another Gospel (Gal. 1, 7). Rightly therefore Jerome, while he asks: if they received the Spirit, how are they foolish? he answers that they received the Spirit from the beginning, but that it was afterwards taken away from them. On the contrary, contradictorily, Crocius to this place, page 75: The Spirit of regeneration is not entirely taken away from those to whom it has once been bestowed? But even those who have received the Spirit can act foolishly. It is evident by the example of Peter, denying Christ three times. So he. But ἀτιφατικῶς (negatively). For to act so foolishly, as these Galatian ἀνόητοι (foolish), no longer to obey the truth, that is, in the interpretation of Crocius, not to believe: whom Grotius, in the words of Chrysostom and Theophylact, says made Him altogether useless, how can they be judged or called [faithful], who are still endowed with the Spirit of regeneration? How do they have faith, and the Spirit of regeneration, which is the Spirit of faith (2 Cor. 4, 13), who deny Christ not once, but again and again with execration or an execratory oath?

Latin:

1. Ω ἀνόητοι Γαλάται) Hanc paternam increpationem non pugnare cum præcepto Christi, apparet ex iis, quæ dicta ad Matth. V. 22. Ἀνόητοι .

Stultos dicit, non eo modo, quo Christus quem quam fatuum aut stultum dici vetat Matth. V. Non enim convitium eis facit ex iracundia privata, vel cupiditate vindictæ, sed perfonis Galatarum optime cupiens, floliditatem illorum taxat, hoc unico fine, ut exorbitantes, & circa dogmata Pseudo-Apostolorum insanientes, ad pristinam Evangelii sapientiam revocet.

Quem in modum Salvator ipse discipulos euntes Emauntem appellat stultos & tardos corde ad credendum iis, quæ dicta sunt per Prophetas, ut hic B. Hunnius. Τίς ὑμᾶς ἐβάσκανε) Βασκαίνειν proprie est oculos corrumpere.

Sed ab oculis ad animum transfertur, ut & Latinum inde deductum fascinare. Τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι) Id est, ita ut non pareretis veritati semel traditæ: ut eam non retineretis. Οἷς κατ' ὀφθαλμοὺς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς προεγράφη ἐν ὑμῖν ἐσταυρωμένος) Construi debet ἐν οἷς ὑμῖν, in quibus, nempe vobis.

Est loquendi genus Hebraicum.

Sic Josua XIII.

21. οἱ ἐπάταξε Μωϋσῆς αὐτούς. Sic Petrus II. 24. ὃ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθητε. Sed melius in Manuscripto omittitur illud ἐν ὑμῖν, ut fupetvacuum.

Sensus est: Ita antehac descriptus est vobis Christus, cum sua cruce, ut quasi ob oculos vobis versaretur.

Need enim in voce προεγράφη hic, ut & Roman. XV.

4. & προέγραψα Ephes.

III. 3. tempus anteactum significat, ut in προορισάμενος, Roman. III. 9. sic προεῖπον infra V. 21. I. Thessal. IV. 6. & προελήγομεν I. Thess. III. 4. nec aliter mox in προεὐηγγελίσατο. Solet sermo historicus conferri picturæ, & hinc διατυπώσεις nomen, quod subjectionem sub aspectum vocare liceat. Quintilianus formam rerum expressam verbis.

Intelligit autem hic Apostolus mortem Christi cum suis effectibus.

Mortem Christi cum effectibus suis scilicet intelligi admittimus, qua eadem satisfactio pro nobis præstita, nobisque vita æterna acquisita est, quæ effecta hic in justificatione, peccatorum nempe remissione, & justitia Christi donatione respiciuntur.

Ideo enim Jesum Christum, prout crucifixus pro nobis erat, ut è 19. vers. capit. præcedent. constat, tam sedulo, & accurate coram Galatis depinxit, ut efficaciam illam cordi suo imprimerent, fideque Christi crucifixionem, & mortem pro nobis exantlatam susciperent, & in ea unice justitiam quærerent.

Illud πρὸ & ad tempus referri potest, & ad subjectum, quod nempe pro oculis ipsi depictus fit, ut ante ipsos versaretur semper.

Christus crucifixus, ut πρὸ ὀφθαλμῶν. Pertinet hoc ad culpam eorum aggravandam. Si vero qui leviter tincti fuerunt fide, ab ea deficiant, infirmitati id adscribitur. Quibus vero penitus fides impressa sine dubio gravius peccant, cum ab ea recedunt: ideoque ad vituperium illis hoc dicitur: quod quem viderant pro ipsis nudari, clavis affigi, lance vulnerari &c. eo deserto ad legem recurrant, ac tantos cruciatus pro nobis exantlatos minime suffecisse satisfactioni pro peccatis persuasi sint, fascino oculis mentis obduto, ne obsequerentur veritati tam luculenter πρὸ ὄμματα positae.

Veritas amplius erat, sola fide Evangelii justitiam in Christo pro nobis tradito & crucifixo haberi, Fascinum Galatae. fide quidem salutem haberi, sed non sola, adeoque nec passione Christi sola, sed etiam circumcisione, & operum legis observatione, quasi nos non jam crucifixi una cum Christo legi mortui simus, sed nos sub lege adhuc simus, & crucifixione nostrarum cupiditatum a reatu peccati liberemur, ac satisfacere pro peccatis, gratiamque mereri alia ratione possimus, ima debeamus, ut justificemur, ac salutem consequamur.

Non ergo illud ἐν ὑμῖν ἐσταυρωμένον in malam partem accipiendum, nec de Galatis explicandum, quasi isti apostasia sua Christum denuo sibi crucifixerint, quod de iis dicitur, qui peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum committunt Ebr. VI. 7. cap. X. 29. sed de ministerio Apostolorum, quo Christus ipsis ita depictus erat, ac si coram oculis ipsum in cruce pendentem etuissent.

Pulchre haec post Chrysostomum complexus est Theophylactus: Constat sane, inquit, Hierosolymis fuisse Jesum cruci affixum, cur ergo ante horum oculos ait, & in vobis in patibulum hunc fuisse sublatum? Quia fidei oculis longe acrius bi conspexere, quam qui praesentes fuere & conspicati sunt. Illorum namque plerique ex eo corporali aspectu nihil retulere utilitatis. Hi vero, qui nequaquam oculis crucem proptexerunt, per fidem longe melius sunt contemplati. Proscriptus itaque est Christus praedicatione, depictus est & designatus, ut vero praedicationi fidem praebentes, perinde ac praesentem vidistis. Enimvero Galatis hac in laudem, & in vituperationem concedunt. In laudem quidem, quia tanta cum certitudine, quae de Christo sunt dicta, exceperint. In vituperationem, quia ab eo, quem nudum praesidem viderunt ligno suffixum & mortuum deficientes ad legem profagerint. Vide ut Paulus caeteris omissis crucem in medium deferat, ut hanc attendant & fellentur fideles, non legem.

In malam tamen partem accipit B. Lutherus hoc modo: Quibus in oculis seu ante oculos Jesus praescriptus est in vobis crucifixus, hoc est: Ecce vos ipsi cernitis, ut argumentis praedictis essectum est à me, ut clarum & in oculis vobis depictum & ante scriptum sit, Jesum Christum esse in vobis crucifixum. Hunc esse sensum, si praecedentia, imo totius epistolae argumentum attendas, credo, non negabitur. Pramiferat enim, non abjicio Dei gratiam, vivo non ego. Item si ex lege justitia, jam Christus gratis mortuus est. Quae omnia eo tendunt, quod Christus sit in iis crucifixus (sicut in Judaeis) quicunque non in eum, non in seipsos ac legem confidunt. Nam cum est abjecta gratia Dei, non vivit in eis Christus. Quid ergo restat, nisi quod fit mortuus & crucifixus in eis? ut habetur in Comment. priori. Praeferenda autem videtur Chrysostomi & Theophylacti (quae & aliorum plerorumque est,) interpretatio; quia si ἀνόητος dixillet, quod Christum crucifixerint, non quafl amplius quid adderet, hoc unum discere verbis velim, quum illo nihil amplius aut gravius dici potuerit, quod Christum crucifixerint.

Itaque hic argumentum proprie affert, cur eos ἀνόητας dicat, quia nimirum Spiritum acceperant non per legis opera, sed ex auditu verbi, & inceperant in Spiritu, nunc autem in carne consummare velint, fascinati a falsis doctoribus, de quo postea.

Calviniani his praestricti, quod fideles, quales fuerunt inter Galatas, quos nunc ἀνόητας vocat, qui non amplius sequantur veritatem, deficere possint a fide, temere effugium in eo quaerunt, quod aliud sit loqui de fide totius caetus, aliud de fide singulorum. Coetum quidem defecisse dici, quod major pars in illo defecerit. Sed non ideo defecisse fidem vere fidelium. Vanum hoc, inquam, κενόφύγετον est. Nam in illo coetu illi etiam, quibus ante oculos depietus erat Christus crucifixus, quorum fidem, fatente Chrysostomo, & Theophylacto, laudat Apostolus, ἀνόητοι jam dicuntur & apostatae, non quod omnes in Ecclesia illa defecerint, sed quod aliqui, qui scil. à Pseudo-Apostolis fascinati & seducti erant & in aliud Evangelium translati. Galat. I. 7. Recte ergo Hieronymus dum quaerit; si spiritum accepere, quomodo stulti? respondet ab initio accepisse Spiritum, sed post ab eis sublatum esse. Ex adverso contradictorie Crocius ad hunc locum pag. 75. Spiritus regenerationis non penitus aufertur ab iis, quibus semel est collatus? Sed possunt etiam illi stulte agere, qui Spiritum acceperint. Patet exemplo Petri, Christum ter abnegantis. Hac ille. Sed ἀτιφατικῶς. Nam ita stulte agere, ut hic Galatae ἀνόητοι, non obsequi amplius veritati, id est, interprete Crocio, non credere: quos Grotius verbis Chrysostomi & Theophylacti dicit omnino inutilem faciebant, quomodo censeri aut dici possunt, qui adhuc Spiritu regenerationis praediti sunt? Quomodo fidem habent, & Spiritum regenerationis, qui Spiritus fidei est 2. Cor. IV. 13. qui Christum non semel, sed iterum iterumque cum execratione vel juramento execratorio abnegant? vers.

## 3:2
verf. 2. Τότε μόνον θέλω μαθεῖν ἀφ' ὑμῶν (I only wish to learn from you)

a figurative question, under the guise of wishing to learn something, urging the adversary. ἐξ ἔργων νόμου τὸ πνεῦμα ἐλάβετε (Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law?) The Holy Spirit is not given, unless to those already righteous; or cleansed in mind. Therefore you were righteous when you received Him. But not by the works of the law. For you were not following the law at that time. Η ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως; (Or by the hearing of faith?) That is, by the Gospel preached to you. For ἀκοή, as also the Hebrew שמועה, signifies a report, as John 12, 38; Rom. 10, 16. But faith for that which is believed, we have had also above 1, 23. So also 1 Tim. 4, 1. This Apostolic argument holds thus: If they received the Holy Spirit by faith in the Gospel, that faith must suffice for justification. But they received the Spirit by faith in the Gospel, and not indeed by the law; Therefore faith in Christ must suffice for justification, and there is no need for the works of the law. The reason for the conclusion is manifest, because He does not give the Holy Spirit, except to the friends of the Son alone, reconciled and justified by faith through Christ. Whence the scholia of Jerome hold thus: You received the Holy Spirit by faith alone, who is not received except by the righteous. But it is certain that you are righteous without the works of the law. For it is a discourse concerning the Spirit of adoption, not concerning the gifts of miracles of the Spirit: as these did not happen to all, but to a few, and sometimes even to those who did not follow Christ (Mark 9, 39), nor were they righteous (Matt. 7, 22, 23; conf. Eph. 1, 13; 1 Cor. 1, 22). Crocius joins the miraculous gifts of the Spirit and the Spirit. rite of adoption .

But those could be given even to the unjustified, so they contributed nothing to confirming the Apostolic argument, nor were they ordinarily obtained by the hearing of faith, that is, by the word of faith heard.

Is. 53:1. Whence it is more correctly explained by B. Hanius and B. Balduinus concerning the Holy Spirit, who has sealed righteousness in their hearts: From which doctrine they have the earnest of righteousness, and from the same also righteousness itself. But they do not have the earnest of righteousness from the law, but from the Gospel. Therefore. By the Spirit he understands the gift of the Holy Spirit, testifying in their hearts concerning the eternal inheritance. That gift is not conferred through the works of the law, for they are the effects of the Holy Spirit, whom it is necessary to be already present in those who desire to perform works of the law pleasing to God: But through the hearing of faith, that is, through the doctrine of faith or through the Gospel; therefore, when the Apostles preached the doctrine concerning Christ, the Holy Spirit fell upon those who heard them Acts 8:17 and chapter 10:44.

Verf. 3. Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit) Having already attained those heavenly gifts. Having begun in the Spirit is a Greek mode of speaking for having begun in the Spirit. Are you now made perfect by the flesh?) You return to carnal precepts, such as those of the law, Heb. 7:16, below 6:12, 13, Phil. 3:3, 4. Made perfect here, as elsewhere, to be made perfect is passive in voice, active in sense, in the Attic manner. Some understand this beginning and completion in terms of the reason for justification, because the emissaries had persuaded the Galatians that the beginning of justification is had from faith, and the completion from works, as Pareus explains, who says: Will you be so foolish as to believe?

But this would be the same as wishing to seek a perfect light from the sun, and a particle of light from darkness, than which nothing is more insane.

But here it is not the beginning and completion of justification that is compared, but of doctrine and faith, which had been the case for the Galatians before, when they obeyed the truth, and as it is now, when, having been bewitched by the Pseudo-Apostles, they forgot the merits of the crucifixion of Christ, because they had indeed begun well according to the instruction of the Holy Spirit, and had placed their trust in the merit of Christ, which had been depicted before their eyes as the only one, but now, having lost that doctrine of the Holy Spirit, they follow the mind of corrupt flesh, and prefer the animal judgment of man in so great a mystery, who does not understand the things which are of the Spirit of God Rom.

8:6, 1 Cor. 2:14. By this are noted both the false Doctors, who, puffed up with worldly wisdom, did not acquiesce in the Evangelical truth concerning the righteousness of faith through the seduction of the flesh, but strove to set up their own righteousness Rom. 10:3, and the bewitched Galatians, who had lent their ears to the Spirit of truth, the teacher in the Apostles, and had already been sealed by the earnest of the Spirit concerning the righteousness of faith, having received through the hearing of faith the doctrine of the Gospel, the Spirit of adoption, but now they follow the judgment of corrupt flesh, which certainly is not of a mind that is spiritually wise and sound, but truly foolish.

Thus B. Hunnius wishes the doctrine concerning the righteousness of faith to be called of the Spirit and spiritual: Again, he says, the Apostle applies the rod of correction, rebuking them because, regarding an argument so clear, the strength and efficacy of which they themselves had felt, they are so stupid, or even foolish, who at the beginning of their conversion had obtained the Holy Spirit through the preaching of the Gospel concerning the grace of God, now, loathing it, they fall back to the dogmas of the Pseudo-Apostles, not dictated by the Spirit of God, but proceeding from the sense of the flesh: So that they close an excellent beginning with an evil end, and do not progress in the school of the Holy Spirit, but unlearn former things, and in this way deprive themselves of the fruits of piety and of the labor undertaken for the Gospel.

Where B. Luther's observation, which is had in his later Commentary, fol. 59, is not to be noted perfunctorily. The pious, he says, experience how willingly they would hold the heard word with full faith, and root out the opinion of the law and of their own righteousness: But they feel the struggle in the flesh resisting the Spirit with all its might.

For reason and flesh simply wish to cooperate. This IT IS NECESSARY to be circumcised and to keep the law, cannot be entirely removed from us, but remains in the hearts of all the pious. Therefore, there is a perpetual struggle for the pious with the hearing of faith and the works of the law, because the conscience always murmurs and thinks that this way is too easy, because righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and eternal salvation are promised from the hearing of the word alone. But test it seriously and try how easy it becomes to hear the word of faith. Great indeed is He who gives, and then He gives great things willingly and simply, and upbraids no one: But your capacity is difficult and your faith is weak, causing you a struggle, so that you cannot receive the offered gift. But the conscience certainly murmurs and recurs immediately (this is necessary) yet you endure and stand for a while, until you overcome that IT IS NECESSARY. Thus, as faith grows, that opinion of the righteousness of the law gradually decreases. But this cannot be done without a great struggle.

And concerning the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles, fol. 60. The Pseudo-Apostles, he says, contended and vehemently urged the Galatians, already justified by faith in Christ, that they ought to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, if they wished to be freed from sins and the wrath of God and to obtain the Spirit.

And yet by this very thing they burdened them more with sins, because sins are not taken away through the law, nor is the Spirit given through it, but rather it only accomplishes this, and strikes terror.

Others, however, understand the spiritual doctrine in terms of the author, in which way B.

Balduinus interprets it in terms of the object: Again he upbraids them for their madness, because they had begun to think well, but ended badly.

He opposes the Spirit to the flesh, that is, the gratuitous justification to the works of the law.

For gratuitous justification is applied and sealed by the Holy Spirit through faith.

But the works of the law are 1. ceremonial and carnal, which are concerned only with external senses and are otherwise called the elements of the world Col. 2:8. Thus below they are said to wish to please in the flesh, who urged circumcision Gal. 6:12, and the ceremonial works of the law are expressly called the righteousness of the flesh Heb. 9:10. 2. There are moral works of the law, even those done by the regenerate, which are called flesh, because they are weak and imperfect, and yet the workers place their trust in them.

But both, that which is weak and that in which trust is placed, is called flesh in Scripture Gen. 6:3, Jer. 17:5. Thus when it is written that Abraham was not justified by works, it is said he did not find righteousness according to the flesh Rom. 4:1, 2. And Paul, when he denies that he himself was justified by the works of the flesh, writes that he has no confidence in the flesh Phil. 3:4. Therefore, the Galatians are rebuked here because they had previously embraced a better doctrine, and had believed that they would be justified by faith, the testimony of which they had received from the Holy Spirit, but now they progress for the worse, while they seek righteousness from the works of the law, which is the way of fools.

That this latter interpretation cannot be joined to the former, I do not see.

For why should it not be called carnal and spiritual both in terms of the principle and in terms of the object?

The Galatians had begun in the Spirit, when under the teaching of the Spirit they had received a truly spiritual righteousness; they end in the flesh when, following the dictates of the flesh, they mix in a carnal righteousness and do not rest content with that spiritual and most perfect righteousness which is imputed to faith.

Since even the righteousness of the reborn, by comparison with that more abundant righteousness, becomes imperfect and impure on account of the flesh lusting against the Spirit, so that Paul himself complains that the law is spiritual, but he is carnal, sold under sin, Rom. VII. 14. But what would such righteousness contribute to our justification before God? The flesh, says B. Luther, is righteousness itself, the wisdom of the flesh, and the thought of reason, which strives to be justified through the law. Whatever, therefore, is best and most excellent in man, Paul calls flesh, that is, the highest wisdom of reason, and the righteousness of the law itself. B. Luther also observes, not rashly, that change of the verb, that the Passive is used instead of the Active: This also must be considered, that Paul says, you began in the Spirit, there he ought to have added Passive he says: You are perfected by the flesh. Thus the righteousness of the law, which Paul here calls flesh, does not justify, so that those who, after having received the Spirit through the hearing of faith, fall away to it, are perfected by it, that is, are finished and utterly destroyed. Therefore, those who teach that the law must be done to this end, that men may be justified through it, while they wish to confound consciences, they harm them most, while they wish to justify them, they condemn them. But Paul always obliquely attacks the Pseudo-Apostles. For they urged the law, saying: Faith in Christ alone does not take away sin, does not appease the wrath of God, does not justify. Therefore, if you wish to obtain those benefits, you ought not only to believe in Christ, but at the same time also to keep the law, to be circumcised, to observe feast days, to sacrifice, etc. By doing this you will be free from sin, from the wrath of God, etc. Nay, by this very thing, says Paul, you establish unrighteousness, you provoke the wrath of God, you add sin to sin, you fall from grace, and you cast it away, you extinguish the Spirit, and together with your disciples you are perfected by the flesh.

Latin:

2. Τότε μόνον θέλω μαθεῖν ἀφ' ὑμῶν) ἰρώτησις

figurata, specie volentis aliquid discere, urgens adversarium. ἐξ ἔργων νόμου τὸ πνεῦμα ἐλάβετε) Spiritus Sanctus non datur, nisi jam justis; sive mundatis animo. Justi ergo eratis, cum eum accepistis. At non per opera legis. Neque enim eo tempore legem sequebamini. Η ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως;) Id est, per praedicatum vobis Evangelium. Nam ἀκοή, ut & Hebraeum שמועה, sermonem significat, ut Joh. XII. 38. Rom. X. 16. Fidem autem pro eo, quod creditur, habuimus & supra I. 23. Sic & 1. Tim. IV. 1. Argumentum hoc Apostolicum ita habet: Si per fidem in Evangelium Spiritum Sanctum acceperunt, fidem illam oportet sufficere ad justificationem. At per fidem in Evangelium, non vero per legem acceperunt Spiritum; Itaque fidem in Christum oportet sufficere ad justificationem, nec opus est legis operibus, Ratio confectionis in propatulo est, quia Spiritum Sanctum non dat, nisi amicis Filii solis, fide reconciliatis & justificatis per Christum. Unde scholia Hieronymi ita habent: Spiritum Sanctum sola fide accepistis, qui non nisi à justis accipitur. Justos autem fine legis operibus vos constat. De Spiritu enim ὑποθεσίας, non de donis miraculorum Spiritus sermo est: utpote quae non omnibus contingebant, sed paucis, & quandoque etiam illis, qui Christum non sequebantur Marci IX. 39. nec justi erant Matth. VII. 22. 23. conf. Epb. I. 13. 1. Cor. I. 22. Crocius conjungit Spiritus dona miraculosa & Spiritum. υἱοθεσίας.

Sed illa dari poterant etiam non justificatis, ita nihil ad argumentum Apostolicum firmandum faciebant, nec etiam ordinarie ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως obtinebantur, id est, per verbum fidei auditum.

Es. LIII. 1. unde rectius de Spiritu Sancto, qui justitiam obsignarit in cordibus ipsorum, explicatur à B. Hannio & B. Balduino: Ex quo doctrina habent arrham justitiae, ex eadem etiam ipsam justitiam. Non autem ex lege, sed ex Evangelio habent arrham justitiae. Ergo. Per Spiritum intelligit donum Spiritus Sancti, testificantis in cordibus ipsorum de hereditate eterna. Illud donum non confertur per opera legis, ea enim sunt effectus Spiritus Sancti, quem jam adesse oportet in iis, qui opera legis Deo grata praestare cupiunt: Sed per auditum fidei, id est per doctrinam fidei seu per Evangelium; idcirco predicantibus Apostolis doctrinam de Christo, cadebat Spiritus Sanctus super eos, qui audiebant eos AEI.

VIII. 17. & capite X. 44. Vers. 3. Οὕτως ἀνόητοί ἐστε; ἐναρξάμενοι πνεύματι) Consequuti jam illa coelestia dona. ἐναρξάμενοι πνεύματι Graecus loquendi modus pro ἀρξάμενοι ἐν πνεύματι. Νῦν σαρκὶ ἐπιτελεῖσθε;) Reditis ad carnalia praecepta, qualia sunt illa legis, Hebr. VII. 16. infra VI. 12. 13. Philip. III. 3. 4. ἐπιτελεῖσθε hic, ut alibi, ἐπιτελεῖσθαι est passivum voce, sensu activum, more Attico. Initium & complementum hoc nonnulli intelligunt ratione justificationis, quod Galatis emissarii persuaserint, justificationis initium ex fide, complementum ex operibus haberi, ut Pareus explicat, qua-sidicat: Itane stulti eritis, ut credatis?

Hoc vero perinde fuerit, atque ex sole particulam lucis, ex tenebris perfectam lucem velle petere, quo nihil insanius.

Sed hic confertur non initium & complementum justificationis, sed doctrinae & fidei, quod Galatis antea fuerit, cum veritati obsequerentur, & qualis jam fit, cum fascinati à Pseudo-Apostolis meritorum crucifixionis Christi obliviscerentur, quod in-ceperint quidem bene juxta Spiritus S. informationem credere, & in Christi merito, qui ipsis ante oculos depictus erat unicae fiduciam collocare, jam amissa illa Spir.

S. doctrina carnis corruptae φρόνημα sequantur, hominisque ψυχικὸν judicium in tanto mysterio praeferant, qui non intelligit ea, quae Spiritus Dei sunt Rom. VIII. 6. 1. Cor. II. 14. quo notantur tum Doctores falsi, qui sapientia mundana turgidi carnis seductione veritati Evangelicae de justitia fidei non acquiescebant, sed suam justitiam erigere fatagebant Rom. X. 3. tum fascinati Galatae, qui Spiritui veritatis doctori in Apostolis aures praebuerant & per arrham Spiritus de justitia fidei jam obsignati erant, accepto per auditum fidei doctrina Evangelii Spiritu τῆς υἱοθεσίας, jam autem carnis corruptae judicium sequuntur, quod sane non est mentis spiritualiter sapientis & sanae, sed vere ἀνοήτης.

Ita doctrinam de justitia fidei τῦ πνεύματος & spiritualem dici vult B.

Hunnius: Iterum castigaticem, inquit, ferulam admovet Apostolus, objurgans eos, quod ad argumentum tam perspicuum, cujus ipsi robur & efficacitatem senserant, tam sint stupidi, quin etiam stulti, qui sub initium fue conversionis adepti Spiritum Sanctum per concionem Evangelii de gratia Dei, nunc eam fastidientes recidunt ad dogmata Pseudo-Apostolorum, non à Dei Spiritu dictata, sed à carnis sensu profecta: Ita ut optimum principium malo fine claudant, & in fibola Spiritus Sancti non proficiant, sed priora dediscant, atque hoc modo antegressa pietatis & suscepti pro Evangelio laboris fructu sese privent. Ubi B. Lutheri observatio non perfunctorie notanda, quae habetur in Comment. poster. fol. 59. Pii, inquit, experiuntur, quam libenter vellent plena fide verbum auditum tenere, & evellere opinionem legis & justitiae propriae: Sed sentiunt luctam in carne resistentem omni vi Spiritui.

Nam ratio & caro simpliciter volunt cooperari. Hoc OPORTET circumcidi & servare legem, non potest nobis penitus eximi, sed manet in cordibus omnium piorum. Ideo perpetua est piis lucta cum auditu fidei & operibus legis, quia conscientia semper remurmurat & cogitat, nimis facilem hanc viam esse, quod ex solo auditu verbi promittitur justitia, Spiritus Sanctus, & salus aeterna. Sed tenta serio & experire, quam facile fit auditu verbum fidei. Magnus quidem est, qui dat, deinde magna dat volens & simpliciter, ac nemini exprobrat: Sed tua capacitas difficilis & fides infirma est, faciens tibi luctam, ut oblatum donum non possis accipere. Sed remurmurat sane conscientia & recurrat subinde (hoc oportet) tamen tu tantisper perdura & consiste, donec illud OPORTET vincas. Sic crescente fide paulatim decrescit illa opinio justitiae legis. Sed hoc fine magno certamine fieri non potest.

Et de Pseudo-Apostolorum doctrina fol. 60. Pseudo-Apostoli, inquit, contenderunt & vehementer urserunt Galatas, jam fide in Christum justificatos, debere circumcidi & legem Mosis servare, si à peccatis & ira Dei liberari & Spiritum consequi vellent.

Et tamen hac ipsa re eos plus onerabant peccatis, quia per legem non auferuntur peccata, neque Spiritus per eam datur, sed immo tantum efficit, & terrores incutit.

Alii tamen spiritualem doctrinam intelligunt ratione autoris, quo pacto ratione objecti B.

Balduinus interpretatur: Iterum dementiam ipsis exprobrat, quod bene sentire ceperint, male autem desinant.

Spiritum opponit carni, id est, justificationis gratuitam operibus legis.

Nam justificatio gratuita à Spiritu Sancto per fidem applicatur & obsignatur.

Opera vero legis sunt 1. ceremonialia & carnalia, qua circa externos tantum sensus versantur & alii elementa mundi appellantur Coloss. II. 8. Sic infra dicuntur in carne placere velle, qui circumcisione urgebant Gal. VI. 12. & opera legis ceremonialia vocantur expresse justitia carnis Hebraer. IX. vers. 10. 2. sunt opera legis moralia etiam à renatis facta, quae caro vocantur, quia infirma & imperfecta sunt, & tamen fiduciam in iis collocant operarii.

Utrumque autem & quod infirmum est, & in quod fiducia perpenditur, caro in scriptura dicitur Genes. VI. vers. 3. Jerem. XVII. vers. 5. Sic cum Abraham non ex operibus justificatus esse scribitur, justitiam non secundum carnem invenit dicitur Romanor. IV. vers. 1. 2. & Paulus, cum seipsum ex operibus carnis justificatum negat, nullam se habere confidentiam in carne scribit Philipp. III. vers. 4. Reprehenditur ergo hic in Galatis, quod prius meliorem doctrinam amplexi fuerint, & ex fide se justificaturos crediderint, cujus testimonium acceperint à Spiritu Sancto, jam in deterius proficiant, dum ex operibus legis justitiam quaerant, quod stultorum est.

Quae posterior interpretatio ut priori conjungi nequeat, non video.

Quidni enim & ratione principii & ratione objecti, quid carnale & spirituale dicatur?

In Spiritu coeperant Galata, cum doctore Spiritu vere spiritualem justitiam susceperant: In carne desinunt, cum carnis dictaturam sequenti carnalem justitiam immiscent, nec illa spirituali & perfectissima justitia, quae fidei imputatur, acquiescunt.

Siquidem etiam renatorum justitia comparatione cum illa abundantiori justitia, ob carnem concupiscentem adversus Spiritum, imperfecta & impura fit, adeò, ut Paulus ipse queratur, legem spiritualem esse, fe autem carnalem venundatum sub peccatum, Rom. VII. 14. Quid autem talis justitia conferret ad nostram justificationem coram Deo? Caro, inquit B. Lutherus, est ipsa justitia, sapientia carnis, ac cogitatio rationis, quae per legem conatur justificari. Quicquid ergo optimum ac praestantissimum est in homine, Paulus vocat carnem, hoc est summam sapientiam rationis, & ipsam justitiam legis. Obfervat etiam B. Lutherus, non temere lane, illam permutationem verbi, quod loco Activi Passivum adhibeatur: Considerandum est & hoc, quod Paulus dicit, Galatas coepisse Spiritu, ibi addere debebat Passive dicit: Carne consummamini. Adeo justitia legis, quam Paulus hic carnem vocat, non justificat, ut bi, qui post acceptum Spiritum per fidei auditu ad eam deficiunt, ea consummentur, hoc est, finiantur & prorsus perdantur. Itaque qui docent, legem faciendam esse hoc fine, ut homines per eam justificentur, bi dum volunt confudere conscientias, maxime eis nocent, dum eas justificare volunt, damnant. Semper autem oblique petit Paulus Pseudo Apostolos. Hi enim urgebant legem dicentes: Fides in Christum sola non tollit peccatum, non placat iram Dei, non justificat. Itaque si illa beneficia consequi vultis, non debetis tantum credere in Christum, sed simul etiam legem fervare, circumcidi, ferias agere, sacrificare &c. Hoc facientes liberietis à peccato, ira Dei &c. Imo hoc ipso ait Paulus statuitis injustitiam, provocatis iram Dei, peccatum peccato additis, à gratia exciditis, & eam abjicitis, Spiritum extinguitis, & una cum discipulis vestris carne consummamini.

## 3:4
Verf. 4. Ταῦτα ἐπάθετε εἰκῆ You have suffered so many things in vain, on account of the profession of Christianity, when you could have avoided them by professing Judaism, which they persuade you to do.

They were not so much persuading them to Judaism, as they were mixing it with Christianity. Nor is that argument taken precisely from the sufferings of Christians, inflicted by the Jews themselves: but from their former constancy in the Evangelical doctrine, because they did not hesitate to endure such great tribulations and persecutions for that truly saving doctrine of the Spirit, while they were still running well, because they had begun in the Spirit; who is the Spirit of faith and confession, 2. Cor. IV. 13. For which doctrine, therefore, they, strengthened by the Spirit, did not hesitate to endure so many things, they ought by no means to have abandoned it.

Those passions, says B. Balduinus, of the Galatians were not only the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit when they were converted, where they did not without labor purge the flesh, so that they might assent to the doctrine of the Gospel: But also the dangers, afflictions, contempt, and other things, which followed their conversion in the world. He says they have suffered all these things in vain, if they were now falling away from their former doctrine.

B. Luther also beautifully says: You have suffered so many things in vain, as if he were to say: Do not only consider that you have lost the good beginnings and the course so well begun, likewise that you have not only fallen away from the first fruits and fruits of the Spirit, having relapsed into the ministry of sin and death and into the sad and miserable slavery of the law: but also consider this, that you have suffered many things on account of the Gospel and Christ, namely, the loss of goods, blasphemies, and insults, dangers of body and life, etc. Everything among you was in the most beautiful course and success, you were teaching rightly, you were living holily, and you were constantly suffering evils for the name of Christ; but now that doctrine, as well as faith, as well as action, as well as passion, as well as the Spirit, as well as the fruits themselves, have perished in you. Εἰκῆ γὰρ εἰκῆ that is, if yet only in vain, that is, without benefit, he tacitly hints that this change is not only to render the former patience void, but also to be joined with the greatest damage, namely, the loss of that Spirit, unless they return to a good mind. These things are not added for the sake of amplification, but are a certain correction, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others note, because he still fosters a better hope, that their passions were not in vain, but that they would be led back to a good mind in turn. It is a correction, says B. Luther, by which he mitigates the previous, somewhat harsher rebuke, and he does this so that the Apostle might not too much terrify the Galatians. He rebukes indeed, but in such a way that he always pours in oil alongside, so as not to drive them to despair. He says therefore: If yet in vain: as if he were to say: I have not altogether cast away hope for you. But if you truly wished thus, having abandoned the Spirit, to be perfected by the flesh, that is, to follow the righteousness of the law, as you are doing, then know that all your glory and confidence in God is empty, and all your passions are in vain.

Latin:

Verf. 4. Ταῦτα ἐπάθετε εἰκῆ Mala tot tolerastis, ob professionem Christianismi frustra, cum ea evitare potueritis, Judaismum, quod illi fuadent, profitendo.

Non tam illi Judaismum fuadebant, quam cum Christianismo eumdem commiscebant. Nec argumentum illud à Christianorum passionibus, à Judaeis ipsis illatis, praecise petitum: sed à pristina in doctrina Evangelica constantia, quod pro ea tantam doctrina Spiritus vere salutifera non dubitarint tribulationes & persecutiones sustinere, cum adhuc bene currebant, quia in Spiritu coeperant; qui est Spiritus fidei & confessionis, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Ob quam ergo doctrinam ipsi à Spiritu confortati tam multa sustinere non dubitarunt, eam deferere minime debuere.

Passiones ille, inquit B. Balduinus, Galatarum erant non tantum lucta carnis & Spiritus cum converterentur, ubi non fine labore expungarunt carnem, ut assentirentur doctrina Evangelii: Verum etiam pericula, afflictiones, contempus, & alia, quae conversionem ipsorum in mundo sunt sequuta. Haec omnia ipsos frustra toleraffe ait, si jam à pristina doctrina deficerent.

Pulchre etiam B. Lutherus: Tanta passi estis frustra, quasi dicat: Non solum considerate bona initia, & cursum optime inceptum amisertis, item quod non solum defeceritis à primitiis & fructibus Spiritus, relapsi in ministerium peccati & mortis & in tristem ac miseram servitutem legis: sed etiam hoc considerate, quod multa passi estis propter Evangelium & Christum, scilicet, minam bonorum, blasphemias, & contumelias, pericula corporis & vitae &c. Omnia apud vos erant in pulcherrimo cursu & successu, recte docebatis, sancte vivebatis, & constanter pro nomine Christi mala patiebamini; jam vero periistam doctrina quam fides, tam actio, quam passio, tam Spiritus quam fructus ipsus in vobis. Εἰκῆ γὰρ εἰκῆ id est, si tamen frustra tantum, id est, fine commodo, tacite innuit hanc mutationem non modo priorem patientiam reddere irritam, sed & cum maximo damno, amplione nempe illius Spiritus, fore conjunetam, nisi ad bonam mentem redeant. Non haec amplificationis causa adduntur, sed correctio quaedam sunt, ut Chrysostomus, Theophylactum, & alii notant, quod spem adhuc foveat meliorem, non frustra fuisse passiones ipsorum, sed ad bonam mentem ipsos vicissim reductum iri, Correctio est, inquit B. Lutherus, qua mitigat superiorem objurgationem paulo duriorem, hocque facit, ut Apostolus, ne nimium perterrefaciat Galatas. Objurgat quidem, sed ita, ut semper oleum juxta infundat, ne eos ad desperationem adigat. Dicit ergo: Si tamen frustra: quasi dicat: Non omnino abjecti spem de vobis. Si vero sic velletis, deferto Spiritu, carne consummari, hoc est, justitiam legis sequui, ut capitis, tum scitose omnem vestram gloriam & fiduciam in Deo inanem, & omnes passiones vestras frustraneas esse.

## 3:5
Verf. 5. Ὁ ἐπιχορηγῶν ὑμῖν τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ ἐνεργῶν δυνάμεις ἐν ὑμῖν, ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, ἢ ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως The manuscript is ἐργαζόμενος τὸ Πνεῦμα ἐλάθετε, nor do I think Paul wrote otherwise.

For the construction is similar to that which we had above II. 16. both are not according to the letter, but according to the clarification.

Where, beginning the discourse about the receiver, he defines it in the giver, here, having begun the discourse about the giver, he passes to the receiver. Similar to John XVII. 2. it was a customary locution for him above II. 16. the gifts of the Spirit, how frequent they were in those times, can be known from I. Cor.

XII. This is a rash emendation of the codices from one manuscript: for the construction of which one must sweat so much, which is however plain in the received codices; for the Galatians are further urged, whether he, who supplied the Spirit to them, and worked powers in them, did it from the works of the law, or from the hearing of the word of God, or the preaching of the Evangelical word, which is to be received by faith, and had been received by them. Certainly not through the works of the law: because he had granted the Spirit to them, before they had labored at the works of the law, through whom he also worked powers in them: but when they were already justified, not indeed so that they might obtain righteousness through the same. Some explain powers as miracles, which is also done here by Grotius. But those were not of all the faithful, nor did they contribute to the justification of faith, nor did they arise from the hearing of faith, or were they ordinarily conferred through the same, although they contributed to the confirmation of the universal Apostolic doctrine, not precisely this one, which is about the justification of faith, the article about which is treated here. Wherefore others more rightly [explain it] of the virtues, which follow faith and justification as effects, and are proper to the justified, and have the Spirit as their author, which God works through the faithful, instructed by his Spirit, which, like the gift of the Holy Spirit itself, not through the law or the works of the law, but through the word of the Gospel, which is the power of God Rom. I. 10. living and effective Heb. IV. 12. and bears many fruits in the hearts of believers as spiritual seed Luke IX. 16. such as are filial trust, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Spirit, patience in adversities, etc. When the preacher, says B.

Luther, is a proclaimer, so that the word is not frustrated of its fruits, but is effective in the hearers, that is, when faith, hope, charity, patience, etc. follow. There God ...supplies the Spirit, and works virtues in the hearers.

In a similar way Paul says here, that God supplied the Spirit to the Galatians, and had worked virtues in them, as if he were to say: God not only effects through the preaching not that you should believe my [word], but that you should also live holily, produce many fruits of faith, and suffer evils. Likewise, by the same power of the Spirit, you have been made from greedy, adulterous, unclean, impatient, enemies, etc., into generous, chaste, meek, patient, lovers of your neighbors. Hence, in chapter IV, he bears witness to them that they received him as an angel of God, nay, as Jesus Christ, and that they loved him so vehemently that they were prepared to pluck out their eyes, etc. But to love one's neighbor so ardently that you are prepared to spend money, property, eyes, life, and everything for his salvation, and then to patiently tolerate all adversities, etc., are certainly virtues of the Spirit.

Latin:

Verf. 5. Ὁ ἐπιχορηγῶν ὑμῖν τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ ἐνεργῶν δυνάμεις ἐν ὑμῖν, ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, ἢ ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως Manuscriptus is ἐργαζόμενος τὸ Πνεῦμα ἐλάθετε, nec aliter putem scripsisse Paulum.

Est enim constructio similis ei, quam habuimus supra II. 16. utraque est non κατὰ λέξιν, sed κατὰ σαφηνισμὸν.

Ubi de accipiente inchoans sermonem definit in dantem, hic de dante cum sermonem coepisset, transit ad accipientem. Simile Joh. XVII. 2. usitata loquutio fuerat ei supra II. 16. dona Spiritus, quam illis temporibus fuerint frequentia, cognosci potest ex I. Cor.

XII. Temeraria haec est codicum ex uno manuscripto emendatio: ob cujus constructionem tantopere sudandum, quae vero plana est in receptis codicibus; urgentur enim porro Galatae, an, qui subministravit ipsis Spiritum, & operatus est virtutes in ipsis, ex operibus legis id fecerit, an vero per auditum verbi Dei, seu praeconium verbi Evangelici, quod fide suscipiendum est, & ab ipsis fuisceptum erat. Non fane per opera legis: quia Spiritum ipsis concesserat, antequam legis operibus operam dederant, per quem etiam virtutes in ipsis operatus est: sed jam justificatis, non vero, ut per easdem justitiam consequerentur. Explicant nonnulli δυνάμεις de miraculis, quod etiam à Grotio hic factum. Sed illa nec omnium fidelium erant, nec ad justificationem fidei faciebant, neque ἐξ ἀκοῆς τῆς πίστεως oriebantur, aut per eandem ordinarie conferebantur, etsi ad confirmationem doctrinae Apostolicae universae, non praecise hujus, quae est de justificatione fidei, articuli de quo hic agitur, conducebant. Quapropter rectius alii de virtutibus, quae sequuntur fidem & justificationem effecta, ac justificatorum propria sunt, ac Spiritum autorem habent, quas operatur Deus per fideles, Spiritu suo instructos, quae uti & donum ipsum Spiritus S. non per legem aut opera legis, sed per verbum Evangelii, quod δύναμις τῷ θεῷ est Rom. I. 10. vivum & efficax Ebr. IV. 12. & fructus multos fert in cordibus credentium ut semen spirituale Luc. IX. 16. quales sunt fidialis fiducia, pax conscientiae, gaudium in Spiritu S. patientia in adversis &c.

Cum concionator, inquit B. Lutherus, sit predicator, ut verbum non frustretur suis fructibus, sed efficax sit in auditoribus, hoc est, cum sequitur fides, spes, charitas, patientia &c. Ibi Deus subministrat Spiritum, & operatur virtutes in auditoribus.

Simili modo Paulus hic dicit, Deum subministrasse Spiritum Galatis, & operatum fuisse virtutes in eis, quasi dicat: Deus non solum efficit per praedicatione nem meam ut crederetis, sed ut etiam sancte vivere- tis, multos fructus fidei faceretis, & mala pateremi- ni. Item eadem virtute Spiritus facti estis ex ava- ris, adulteris, immundis, impatientibus, hostibus &c. largi, casti, mites, patientes, amantes proximorum. Hinc cap. IV. testimonium ipsis præbet, quod excepe- rint se tanquam angelum Dei, imo tanquam Jesum Christum, quodque tam vehementer dilexerint, ut parati fuerint oculos eruere &c. Amare autem pro- ximum tam ardenter, ut paratus sis impendere pe- cuniam, rem, oculos, vitam, & omnia pro ipsius sa- lute, deinde patienter tolerare omnia adversa &c. certe virtutes sunt Spiritus.

## 3:5
5:5, where the Greeks say: Κἀγὼ ἑστήκειν ἀνὰ μέσον κυρίου καὶ ὑμῶν, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ, the Latin: I was a sequester and mediator between the Lord and you, at that time, namely as a negotiator between litigating parties, which the Rabbis call מְצִיעָא: and that indeed for the reason that grave vices still clung to the people: whence also the sound of the law was terrible, which sound indeed the most learned of the Hebrew people believe was perceived by the people, but the voice was not distinctly perceived except by Moses.

Others feel the same, except that they except the first two commandments, concerning which matter see Moses Maimonides. Ἐν χειρὶ is a Hebrew idiom for "by". Verse 20. Ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστι) ἑὸς h

ic (here) from the neuter, a mediator is not accustomed to interpose himself between those who are one, that is, who agree well. Thus ἑνὸς is taken in John 10:30, 17:11, 21, 22, 1 Cor. 3:8. Ὁ δὲ θεὸς εἷς ἐστι)

That is: God is consistent with himself, he is like himself, Mal. 3:6. Thus the Latins say: King Jupiter is the same to all. Thus Cicero: You have been found to be the same as you have always been. The sense is equal in Eph. 4:6. God is not changed, Mal.

3:6, namely unless the man is changed: wherefore unless many and grave offenses had intervened, God would have shown himself as calm and friendly to the Israelites as he had shown himself formerly to their ancestors, nor would there have been more need now than then for another mediator who would interpose himself.

Many of the more recent writers, after Epiphanius against the Manichaeans and Gennadius , understand Moses as the mediator, which the Socinians readily seize upon, as we have noted in Socinismo profligato, page 525.

But the ancients more correctly understood it of Christ. Origen in his Apology (as cited by Pamphilus the Martyr), Athanasius, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylact among the Greeks; Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Bede, Primasius, Bruno, Thomas Lyranus among the Latins; to whom are added from the more recent ones Calvin, Aretius, Hyperius, Bullinger, Polanus, Pareus, Sasbout, Job. Crocius, etc. Blessed Luther also agrees in his Commentary published in the year 1520, fol. 48. Therefore, first, we have no reason to depart from the opinion handed down by the ancients and by Blessed Luther in the cited passage.

Socinus indeed appeals to the arguments of Beza, but we have refuted them in the cited passage. Furthermore, the word μεσίτης, when it concerns a Mediator between God and men, is nowhere, so far as I know, used in the Holy Scriptures for anyone other than Christ. Thirdly, here one is called μεσίτης, the Mediator of God and men (1 Tim. 2:5).

Therefore, another is not to be admitted rashly: what is proper to Christ alone is not to be transferred to others. Fourthly, for a Mediator between God and men, a reconciliation of the dissenting parties is required, made through the intervention of a ransom (λύτρον), as the Apostle describes him: Who gave himself the price of redemption for all: which words are not restrictive, as if besides such a one another Mediator were given, who does not become a propitiator (ἱλασικὸς) or a redeemer (λυτρωτὴς), but becomes a Mediator of intercession only, as the Papists claim, but they are descriptive, expressing the nature and property of a mediator between God and men, and therefore are to be taken not specifically, but reduplicatively. Fifthly, there was need for such a Mediator in the promulgation of the law; who would interpose himself between God, who is a consuming fire through his law (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29), and men, not only the Jewish people with Moses abstracted, but the whole human race, and therefore Moses himself, who, equally terrified with the rest of the Israelites by the voice of the law, says, I am afraid and trembling (Heb. 12:21), needed a mediator, lest he be consumed by that fire.

Sixthly, it was appropriate to speak here of that Mediator, where the end and rigor of the law in accusing and condemning transgressions, and the liberation of us from the condemnation of the law, were being discussed, which is obtained only through that one Mediator, not through our works or the merits of others. And therefore that introduction of the Mediator in the present passage is most convenient to the Apostolic scope.

Seventh, the mention of Moses would have contributed nothing here, because the law was disposed through his hand, or as a Mediator: rather, one might easily conclude that holy Moses, and indeed other saints also, contribute to reconciling God to others, whose sins God is angry at, and indeed to their justification, which is the subject here, if Moses were introduced here as Mediator.
