Eighth, the emphasis is on the phrase ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτης, in the hand: by which, if you explain it by the Hebrew phrase as a mediator of the distinction between the Angels, among whose ranks the law was disposed, it is indicated that they indeed were the attendants and ministers: But properly that διαταγὴ of the law belongs to the mediator, who had absolutely to intervene in the disposing of it, unless those to whom the law was promulgated were to perish: and therefore some explain it thus, that it was ordained in the hand of the mediator, that is, through the intervention of his work, who, disposing the law with his hand, interposed himself as a medium or surety: who was also to be the one to perform perfect obedience to the law, at some time in the flesh assumed (the prelude of which was this form, in which he seems to have promulgated the law), and to draw upon himself the execration of the law, and to liberate us all from the execration of the law. Whence also Ambrose says that the law was given in the hand of Christ, because it is in the power of Christ to save those to whom the law was given. But above all Blessed Luther explains it in the cited place: That he says in the hand of a mediator, this in my judgment he said, because the law is not placed in our hand, that we should fulfill it, but in the hand of the coming Christ, who would fulfill it. Wherefore it was not placed so that it might justify, but that it might rather accuse sinners, and require the hand of the Mediator. To us through the law is knowledge, but to Christ alone fulfillment and operation. Until the seed should come, to which the promise was made, that is, in which blessing, righteousness and the fullness of the law were to be given, and transgressions, which were by the law, no longer to be restrained, but extinguished. Most excellently it falls out, says Crocius, that the law was ordained in the hand of the Mediator, who was to receive into himself the malediction denounced by the law on account of transgressions, and to bring blessing, so that justification and salvation might be not from the law, but from the Gospel. And thus also ninthly and by the συνεχείᾳ of the Apostle that explanation is confirmed, which further Blessed Luther explains so splendidly that it could not be more splendidly: It appears that the Apostle wants the law to be the letter, and therefore to exist only as the power of sin. Great indeed it is that it was ordained through Angels, but this contributes nothing to righteousness; since the Angels can neither fulfill it for us, nor give that by which it may be fulfilled. But therefore ordained through Angels, yet not in the hand of the Angels, nay rather of some Mediator, who might absolve those guilty under the law and justify them. For I understand this by in the hand of the Mediator, that he alone should have in his power the law ordained through the Angels, not subject to the law, as one who owes nothing to it himself, and whom he wills, the same might liberate. But the very law holds us in its hand, and subject through sin. By all which he means that it is impossible for us to be saved by ourselves; but easy, through the hand of another, namely the Mediator.

Tenthly, thus those things which the Apostle says, in whose context (συνεχείᾳ) interpreters otherwise struggle greatly, as we have shown in the cited passage, fit together excellently. For what was the point of urging now that the Mediator is not of one, if Moses were understood, who in any case was known to have been the medium between God and the people, because the law was given in his hand as Mediator: What need was there to add: But God is one? For what is said by Grotius, that Moses then had to interpose himself between the people and God, who was alien to them, for which Mediator the Fathers had no need, corresponds neither to the truth nor to the text, so that rather, because the law was given because of transgressions (παραβάσεων χάριν), and concluded both Moses and the Fathers, and all men whatsoever under sin, to the seed of the blessing: and therefore Moses and the Patriarchs, however holy, had need of that mediator just as the rest of men, as all were alien to God through sin, and not to be reconciled to God except through Christ the only mediator.

This, therefore, is what is taught: because where there is a Mediator, he is a Mediator not of one party only but of dissenting parties, therefore since the law was disposed in the hand of the Mediator the Son of God, which can be gathered from the history itself, two dissenting parties existed here which were to be reconciled.

it is necessary, nor of God only, who is not but one, but also of men, in respect of the mediator, it is clear that there was need here. By which manner it is again confirmed, the Apostolic thesis against the Antagonists: If because of the law the transgressions of men were argued, there was need of the intervention of a mediator, it behooves him to perform the office of mediation between God on one side and the human race on the other, since a mediator is not of one only, but God is one, and so to reconcile the human race to God, that therefore man may not obtain justification and the grace of God by his own works or through the law, but solely through faith in this Mediator.

Now that saying, says B. Luther, "But a mediator is not of one," from the name of Mediator I conclude that we are sinners, so that we cannot be satisfied by the work of the law. If (he says) you were just, you would no longer need a mediator. But neither is God, since he himself is one, agreeing perfectly with himself. Therefore, a mediator is sought between two, between God and men: as if he were saying: It is most impious ingratitude if you reject the Mediator, and remit it to God, who is one. But if it is rejected that you can be justified by the law, it will happen that he can neither be a Mediator for you, as one who is unwilling; nor for God, as one who does not need it. Therefore also the law will now be in your hand, and thus not ordained by Angels, so that it might be fulfilled through a Mediator, but entirely obtained by yourselves.

Aretius: Where there is a μεσίτης [mediator], he says, there it is necessary to take two parts, as if two extremes on either side, between which the μεσίτης becomes the middle. But the law was given through a μεσίτην: Therefore there were two extremes here conflicting, because of which a Mediator would be necessary. Now God, who is one, did not need a Mediator. And so on the other side are to be taken men, never fully performing the law, for whose sake the μεσίτης was employed.

Thus the Apostle speaks of Christ 1. Tim. VI. 5. For there is one God, who gave himself ἀντίλυτρον [a ransom] for all.

In that, however, Aretius does not deserve assent, because he understands here by the Mediator Moses, and wishes that God looked only to Christ the true μεσίτην in him, when Christ alone is to be understood.

Bullinger more correctly on this passage: Now lest anyone interpret this concerning Moses, but all may be able to understand that Christ is that Mediator, by whose benefit we are freed from the execration of the law, he argues from the interpretation of the name to this passage: The law was ordained in the hand of a mediator.

But we must understand the hand of the mediator as his power and virtue, which also D. Jerome handed down. But an intercessor and mediator is ordained between two or more who are dissenting. Now in this business of the law, God, who is by nature one, cannot be at variance with himself. But because God is sound, and we are profane, and the law of God is holy and good, but we are corrupt, and sold under sin, thence is the dissension between God and men, which dissension is revealed by the law.

As also Johannes Grotius: He spoke, he says, the Apostle concerning the Mediator by comparison of God. He has already said: That a mediator is not of one, therefore of many; the false one of two dissenters. God is one, in essence, and so in will, immutable, never dissenting from himself, always consistent with himself in his justice and holiness. As therefore he is not at variance in this cause; so he did not change his opinion, when because of transgressions he promulgated the law, he did not recede from the promise and blessing made to Abraham and his seed Christ. Nay rather, he showed that he is consistent with himself by a most clear example, while by the authority of the Mediator he willed the law to be ordained by Angels, who was to satisfy the same, while he was to receive the curse upon himself, so that the blessing might exist among the gentiles in him.

Although indeed B. Luther, in his later Commentaries, constitutes Moses as the mediator; yet his arguments move me to think that his former explanation is to be adhered to, which he could not entirely abandon in the last, without also establishing that it signifies both Moses and Christ, which indeed cannot be admitted because of the unity of the scripture.

The name of Mediator, he says fol. 88, properly signifies him, who acts as Mediator between the offender and the offended. We are the offenders, GOD is offended with his law. And such is the offense, that God cannot remit it, nor can we satisfy for it. Therefore between God, who is one by himself, and us, there is the greatest dissension. Furthermore, God cannot revoke his law, but wills it to be kept. Nor can we, who have transgressed the law of God, flee from the sight of God. There therefore Christ interposed himself as Mediator between two most diverse, and by an infinite and eternal separation most disjointed, and reconciled them etc.

In what way? He blotted out, as Paul says elsewhere, the handwriting that was against us, which was opposed by decrees, that is, the law, and took it away: out of the midst, having been affixed to the cross, and having despoiled principalities and powers he showed them openly, triumphing over them by himself. Therefore there is not one Mediator, but of two most greatly dissenting among themselves.

This passage is also powerful and effective for refuting the justice of the law, and for rescuing us, because in the cause of justification the law is to be removed as far as possible. Also, the very word Mediator itself provides a sufficiently firm argument, that the law does not justify, otherwise what need would there be for a Mediator? Since therefore human nature cannot hear the law, it is manifest that it is much less able to do it, and to agree with the law. Therefore the law does not justify.

To which, however, can be added those things which are gathered from the history of the promulgated law, where God promises another Prophet like Moses, who indeed is also to be the future Mediator.

Latin:

V. 5. ubi Graeci: Κἀγὼ ἑστήκειν ἀνὰ μέσον κυρίου καὶ ὑμῶν, ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ, Latinus: Ego sequester & medius fui, inter Dominum & vos, tempore illo, nempe tanquam inter partes litigantes pararius, qui Rabbinis מְצִיעָא: id vero idea, quia populo gravia vitia adhuc adhaerebant: unde & terribilis fuit sonus legis, quem sonum quidem perceptum volunt populo Hebraeorum doctissimi, sed vocem distincte non perceptam nisi a Mose.

Alii idem sentiunt, nisi quod excipiunt duo prima praecepta, qua de re vide Mosen Maimonidem. Ἐν χειρὶ Hebraea loquutio pro per. Vers. 20. Ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστι) ἑὸς h

ic fumo à Neutro, non solet fequeter se interponere inter eos, qui unum sunt, id est, bene conveniunt. Sic ἑνὸς is sumitur Joh. X. 30. XVII. 11. 21. 22. 1. Cor. III. 8. Ὁ δὲ θεὸς εἷς ἐστι)

Id est: Deus sibi constat, sibi est similis Malach. III. 6. Sic dicunt Latini: Rex Jupiter omnibus idem. Sic Cicero: Idem qui semper fueris, inventus es. Par sensus Ephes. IV. 6. Non mutatur Deus, Malach.

III. 6. nempe nisi homine mutato: quare nisi muite ac gravia interveniffent delicta, Deus tam placidum se atque amicum exhibuturus fuerat Israelitis, quam se exhibuerat olim eorum majoribus, neque nunc magis, quam tunc opus fuisset medio alio, qui se interponeret.

Mosen per mediatorem intelligunt sane post Epiphanium contra Manichaeos & Gennadium recentiorum non pauci, quod prompte arripiunt Sociniani, ut in Socinismo profligato pag. 525. notavimus.

Sed rectius veteres de Christo accepere. Origenes apud Pamph. Martyrem in Apolog. Athanasius, Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus e Graecis: Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Beda, Primasius, Bruno, Thomas Lyranus e Latinis; quibus accedunt e recentioribus Calvinus, Aretius, Hyperius, Bullingerus, Polanus, Pareus, Sasbout, Job. Crocius &c. Annuit & B. Lutherus in Comment. anno 1520. edito fol. 48. Primum ergo nullam causam habemus discedendi a veterum & B. Lutheri loco citato tradita sententia.

Provocat quidem Socinus ad rationes Bezae, sed eas loco citato diluimus. Deinde vox μεσίτης, cum de Mediatore inter Deum & homines agitur, nuspiam, quod sciam, in sacris literis de alio quam de Christo adhibita est. Tertio hic unus dicitur μεσίτης Mediator Dei & hominum 1. Tim. II. 5.

Non ergo temere alius admittendus: quod uni Christo proprium est, aliis transferendum non est: Quarto ad Mediatorem inter Deum & homines requiritur partium dissidentium conciliatio per interventum λύτρον facta, ut describit eum Apostolus: Qui dedit semetipsum pretium redemptionis pro omnibus: quae verba non sunt restrictiva, quasi praeter talem alius detur Mediator, qui non ἱλασικὸς fit, aut λυτρωτὴς sed intercessionis tantum Mediator fit, ut Pontificii ajunt, sed descriptiva, naturam & proprietatem mediatoris inter Deum & homines exprimentia, adeoque non specifice, sed reduplicative accipienda sunt. Quinto tali opus erat Mediatore, in promulgatione legis; qui se inter Deum, qui ignis est consumens per legem suam Deut. IV. 24. Ebr. XII. 29. & inter homines interponeret, non tantum populum Judaicum abstracto Mose, sed universum genus humanum, adeoque Mosen ipsum, qui pariter cum caeteris Israelitis voce legis territus, φοβός εἰμι, inquit, καὶ ἔντρομος Ebr. XII. 21. mediatore indigebat, ne ab igne illo consumeretur.

Sexto de illo Mediatore hic attinebat dicere, ubi de fine ac rigore legis in accusandis & condemnandis transgressionibus, deque liberatione nostri a condemnatione legis agebatur, quae non nisi per unicum illum Mediatorem, non per nostra opera, aut aliorum merita obtineatur. Ideoque scopo Apostolico maxime conveniens est illa Mediatoris introductio in praesenti loco.

Septimo, nihil huc fecisset Mosis commemoratio, quod per ejus manum lex disposita sit, seu Mediatoris: quin potius aliqui ita sanctum Mosen, adeoque alios etiam sanctos ad conciliandum Deum aliis, quorum peccatis iratus est Deus, & quidem ad justificationem ipsorum, de qua hic agitur, conferre facile quis colligeret, si Moses Mediator hic introduceretur. Octavo emphasis est in voce ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτης in manu: qua si explices phrasi Hebraea per mediatorem discrimen inter Angelos, inter quorum agmina disposita est lex, indicatur, quod illi quidem essent stipatores interfuerint & ministri: Sed proprie διαταγὴ illa legis conveniat mediatori, quem eidem disponendae intervenire omnino oportuit, nisi pereundum fuisset illis, quibus lex promulgata: ideoque ita explicant nonnulli, quod in manu mediatoris, id est opera ejus interveniente ordinata fit, qui manu sua legem disponens medium seu vadem se interposuit: qui & legi aliquando in carne assumpta, cujus praeludium hic forma, in qua legem promulgasse videtur, fuit, obedientiam perfectam praestiturus, & legis execrationem in se derivaturus, nosque omnes ab execratione legis liberaturus erat. Quo ab etiam Ambrosius in manu Christi datam esse legem, quod in potestate Christi sit, salvare eos, quibus lex data erat. Sed imprimis id explicat B. Lutherus loco citato: Quod dicit in manu mediatoris, id meo judicio dixit, quia lex non sit posita in manu nostra, ut nos eam impleamus, sed in futuri Christi eam impleturi. Quare non ut justificaret, posita est, sed ut magis peccatores argueres, & manum Mediatoris requireret. Nobis per legem cognitio, soli autem Christo impletio & operatio. Donec veniret semen, cui promissum erat, id est, in quo benedictio, justitia & plenitudo legis danda erat, & transgressiones, quae per legem erant, non jam cobibende, sed extinguendae. Optime cesidit, inquit Crocius, quod lex ordinata est in manu Mediatoris, qui maledictionem a lege, propter transgressiones denunciatam in se erat recepturus, & allaturus benedictionem, ut non ex lege, sed ex Evangelio esset justificatio & salus. Atque ita nono etiam & συνεχείᾳ Apostolica explicatio illa roboratur, quam porro sic praeclare explicat B. Lutherus, ut non possit praeclarius: Apparet Apostolum velle legem esse literam, ideoque non nisi virtutem peccati existere. Magnum quidem est per Angelos ordinatum esse, sed hoc nihil ad justitiam; cum Angeli non possint, nec pro nobis eam implere, nec dare id, quo impleatur. Sed ergo ordinata per Angelos, sed non in manu Angelorum, imo Mediatoris alicujus, qui reas per legem absolvat & justificet. Nam hoc intelligo in manu Mediatoris, ut ipse legem per Angelos ordinatam in potestate habeat solus, non subjectus legi, ut cui ipse nihil debeat, & quem volet, eadem liberet. Nos vero ipsa lex in manu habet, & subjectos per peccatum. Quibus omnibus id vult, impossibile esse, nos per nos salvos fieri; facile autem esse, per manum alterius, scilicet Mediatoris.

Decimo sic optime quadrant, quae Apostolus, in quorum συνεχείᾳ alias se valde torquent Interpretes, ut loco citato ostendimus. Quid enim attinebat jam urgere, Mediatorem non esse unius, si Moses intelligeretur, quem utique eo ipso constaret inter Deum & populum medium fuisse, quod in manu ejus ceu Mediatoris lex lata: Quid opus erat addere: Deus autem unus est? Nam quod dicitur a Grotio, Mosen tunc inter populum a Deo alienum sese interponere debuisse, quali Mediatore opus non habuerint Patres, adeo nec veritati, nec textui congruit, ut potius, quia παραβάσεων χάριν lex data, & Mosen & Patres, omnesque omnino homines sub peccato concluderit ad semen benedictum: adeoque mediatore isto opus habuerit juxta cum reliquis hominibus Moses & Patriarchae, utut sanctissimi, utpote omnes alieni per peccatum a Deo, nec nisi per Christum unicum mediatorem Deo conciliandi.

Hoc ergo est, quod docetur: quia ubi Mediator est, non unius tantum partis sed partium discrepantium est Mediator, ided cum in manu Mediatoris Filii Dei lex disposita sit, quod ex ipsa historia colligi potest, duas hic diffidentes partes, quae conciliandae fuerint extitisse.

oportet, nec Dei tantum, qui non nisi unus est, sed hominum etiam respectu mediatore hic opus fuisse luculentum est. Quo pacto iterum firmatur Apostolica thesis contra Antagonistas: Si ob legem transgressiones hominum argumentem mediatoris interventu opus erat, illum inter Deum ab una & humanum genus ab altera parte mediationis munus expedire oportet, quum mediator non unius tantum fit, Deus autem unus fit, adeoque genus humanum Deo reconciliare, ut proinde homo non suis operibus vel per legem, sed unice per fidem Mediatoris istius justificationem & gratiam Dei consequatur.

Jam illud, inquit B. Lutherus, Mediator autem unius non est, ex nomine Mediatoris concludo nos esse peccatores, ut legis opere satis esse nequeant. Si (inquit) justi essis, jam mediatore non egetis. Sed neque Deus, cum ipse fit unus secum optime conveniens. Inter duos ergo quaritur mediator, inter Deum & homines: ac si dicat: Impissima fit ingratitudo, si Mediatorem rejicitis, & Deo, qui unus est, remittitis. Rejicitur autem hi justificari potestis ex lege, ita fiet, ut nec vobis Mediator esse possit, ut qui nolit; nec Deo, ut qui non egeat. Proinde quoque lex jam in manu vestra erit, & sic non ordinata per Angelos, ut per Mediatorem impleatur, sed prorsus impetrata per vos ipsos.

Aretius: Ubi μεσίτης est, inquit, illic duas oportet accipere partes, quasi duo extrema utrinque, inter qua μεσίτης fit medius. Sed lex data est per μεσίτην: Ergo erant dua extrema hic pugnantia, ob quae necessarius esset Mediator. Nunc Deus, qui unus est, non indigebat Mediatore. Itaque ab altera parte sunt accipiendi homines, legem nunquam plene praestantes, propter quos adhibitus est μεσίτης.

Sic de Christo loquitur Apostolus 1. Tim. VI. 5. Unus enim Deus, qui dedit semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus.

In eo tamen assensum non meretur Aretius, quod hic per Mediatorem Mosen intelligat, inque eo solum respexisse Deum Christum verum μεσίτην velit, quum unice Christus intelligendus sit.

Rectius Bullingerus ad hunc locum: Jam nequis de Mose hac interpretaretur, sed omnes possint intelligere Christum illum esse Mediatorem, cujus beneficio a legis exsecratione liberemur, ex interpretatione nominis ad hunc locum argumentatur: Lex ordinata est in manu mediatoris.

Manum autem mediatoris potentiam ejus & virtutem, quod & D. Hieronymus tradidit, intelligere debemus. Atqui intercessor & mediator inter duos aut plures ordinatur dissidentes. Jam in hoc legis negotio Deus, qui natura unus est, non potest disfidere a seipso. Quia vero Deus fanus est, nos prophani sumus, & lex Dei sancta & bona est, nos vero corrupti, & sub peccatum venditi sumus, inde disidium est inter Deum & homines, quod disidium per legem proditur.

Ut & Johannes Grotius: Loquutus, inquit, Apostolus de Mediatore comparatione Dei. Jam dixit: Mediatorem non esse unius, plurium igitur; falsem duorum dissidensium. Deus unus est, essentia, sic & voluntate, immutabilis, a seipso dissentiens nunquam, semper sibi constat in sua justitia & sanctitate. Ut igitur non est disfidit hujus causa; sic non mutavit sententiam, quando propter transgressiones non mulgavit legem, non recessit a promissione benedictione Abrahamo & femini ejus Christo facta. Quin imo sibi se constare, clarissimo ostendit exemplo, dum auctoritate Mediatoris legem voluit ordinari per Angelos, qui eidem erat facturus satis, dum maledictionem in se recepturus erat, ut benedictio extaret in gentibus in ipso.

Quamquam vero B. Lutherus, in posterioribus Commentariis Mediatorem constituat Mosen; argumenta tamen ejus me movent, ut priori ejus inhaerendum explicationi censeam, quam nec in ultima deferere omnino potuit, quin & Mosen & Christum significare statueret, quod vero ob unitatem fenus scripturae admitti nequit.

Mediatoris nomen, inquit fol. 88. proprie significat eum, qui Mediatorem agie inter offenjum & offendentem. Nos sumus offendentes, DEUM cum lege sua est offensus. Et offensio talis est, ut Deus eam non possit remittere, nec nos possimus pro ea satisfacere. Ideo inter Deum, qui per se unus est, & nos, maximum est disfidium. Praeterea non potest Deus revocare legem suam, sed vult servari eam. Neque nos, qui transgressi sumus legem Dei a conspectu Dei fugere possumus. Ibi ergo interposuit sese Christus Mediatorem inter duos diversissimos, & infinita ac aeterna separatione disjunctissimos, & illas conciliavit &c.

Quo modo? Delevit, ut Paulus alibi inquit, quod adversus nos erat chirographum, quod per decreta, id est, legem advertebatur novae, & sustulit illud: e medium, affixum cruci, expoliatosque principatus ac potestates ostentavit palam, triumphans de illis per semetipsum. Ideo non est unius Mediator, sed duorum inter se maxime disfidientium.

Est & hic locus potens & efficax ad confutandam justitiam legis, & ad eruendos nos, quod in causa justificationis longissime removenda sit lex. Item, ipsa vox Mediator satis firmum etiam praebet argumentum, quod lex non justificet, alioquin quid opus esset Mediatore? Cum igitur natura humana non possit audire legem, manifestum est, quod multo minus possit eam facere, atque cum lege convenire. Ergo lex non justificat.

Quibus tamen addi possunt, quae ex historia promulgatae legis, ubi Deus alium promittit similem Mosi Prophetam, qui vero etiam Mediator futurus fit, colliguntur.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. καθὼς Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσε τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) It is no wonder that faith is now held in high regard by God, since God has always held it as an excellent thing. For this is what λογίζεσθαι εἰς δικαιοσύνην means, as we have shown in the prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans, and IV. 3.

From the experience and personal sense of the Galatians, which even those who had already fallen away from the truth had experienced, the Apostle proceeds to Scripture, and brings forward the example of Abraham, the Father of believers, to whom God had also supplied the Spirit, and in whom He had worked virtues, not from the works of the law, but from the hearing of faith, and who therefore was justified solely through faith, as it was said: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. The Grotian commentaries brought forward in the Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans have been sufficiently discussed by us there. Moreover, the example of Abraham provides a clear argument for justification; because just as he was justified, so also are we justified: both because there is only one and the same method of justification and salvation for all, Acts XV. 11, and because Abraham is the Father of believers, which the Lord wished to be indicated by his very name. Now, indeed, Abraham was not justified by the works of the law, but only by faith; because he believed God, or the word of the divine promise, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, concerning which Gen. XV. 6, in the Commentary on Genesis and in the Biblia Illustrata, as also around the parallel passage Rom. IV. 3, it has been treated. Faith was not imputed because it was an exceptional and most excellent thing. It was not imputed as a virtue or an act. For there is no mention of work here: and the Apostle's disputation excludes works, as was also explicitly done from this example of Abraham in Rom. IV. 6, when it is said that God imputed righteousness without works. Abraham, although adorned with virtues and in the middle of his course of good works, is not introduced as working, but as believing, and it is imputed to him for righteousness not as some virtue or pursuit of works, but because he believed God, and he is said to be justified solely through faith. But faith was not materially imputed to him for righteousness, but objectively and relatively, because it had Christ as its object, the unique shield against the curse of the law, and the reward or the cause of the gracious reward, the meritorious cause of eternal blessedness, because in Christ we have both liberation from the wrath of God, the guilt of sin, and the curse of the law, and the acquisition of grace, righteousness, and eternal salvation, whom Abraham therefore apprehended by faith in that word of promise: I am your shield and your reward very great: And by apprehending Him through faith, he apprehended the righteousness of Christ, which was imputed to him without works for righteousness, who by the obedience of that one was constituted righteous before God, Rom. V. 19. Therefore, this is to be observed first of all, that there is no mention in any word of the merits of Abraham, nor is justification ascribed to works, but to the word of faith apprehending the promise; and that the Apostle's argument speaks of Abraham, already constituted in the very state of new obedience, when in Gen. XV he is said to have believed, and by believing to have been justified. For long before, in chapters XI and XII, he is introduced as a believer, and distinguished by many good works, and nevertheless Paul denies that he was justified even by these works, and ascribes his justification solely to faith in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 6. καθὼς Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσε τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐ- τῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) Non mirum est, fidem nunc magni à Deo fieri, cum semper eam Deus pro re egregia habuerit. Hoc enim est λογίζεσθαι εἰς δικαιοσύνην, ut ostendimus in prolegomenis in Epistolam ad Romanos, & IV. 3.

Ab experientia & sensu proprio Galatarum, quem etiam illi experti erant, qui jam à veritate defecerant, ad scripturam progreditur Apostolus, & exemplum Abraham, Patris credentium adducit, cui Deus etiam Spiritum subministrarat, & in quo virtutes operatus erat, non ex operibus legis, sed ex auditu fidei, quique proinde per fidem uni- ce justificatus est, sicut dictum est: Abraham cre- didit Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam. Com- menta Grotiana in Prolegomenis epist. ad Rom. adducta illic satis à nobis discussa sunt. Exem- plum autem Abraham luculentum præbet argu- mentum justificationis; quia sicut ille justificatus est, ita & nos justificamur: tum quod non nisi una eademq; ratio sit justificationis & salutis omnium Act. XV. 11. tum quod Abraham Pater credentium sit, quod nomine ipso ejus indicatum voluit Do- minus. Jam vero Abraham non per opera legis ju- stificatus est, sed tantum per fidem; quia credidit Deo, vel verbo promissionis divinæ & imputatum id ei est ad justitiam, de quo Gen. XV. 6. in Comment. ad Gen. & in Bibliis Illustr. ut & circa locum paral- lelum Rom. IV. 3. actum. Non imputata fides, quod res esset eximia & præstantissima. Non imputata ut virtus, vel actus. Nulla enim hic operis mentio: & disputatio Apostoli excludit opera, uti diferte etiam factum ex hoc Abrahami exemplo Rom. IV. 6. cum dicitur, Deum imputasse justitiam absque operibus. Abraham quanquam ornatus virtutibus & in medio cursu bonorum operum non introdu- citur ut operans, sed ut credens, & imputatur ei ad justitiam non ut virtus aliqua, aut studium ope- rum, sed quod credidit Deo, ac per fidem unice justificatus dicitur. Non autem fides materialiter imputata est ei ad justitiam, sed objective & relati- ve, quia pro objecto habuit Christum scutum uni- cum adversus maledictionem legis, & mercedem vel causam mercedis gratiosæ, æternæ beatitudinis meritoriam, quia in Christo & liberationem habe- mus ab ira Dei, peccati reatu, & maledictione le- gis, & acquisitionem gratiæ, justitiæ, & salutis æter- næ, quem proinde fide apprehendit Abraham in il- lo promissionis verbo: Ego sum scutum tuum & merces tua valde magna: Eoque per fidem appre- henso apprehendit justitiam Christi, quæ imputata est ipsi sine operibus ad justitiam, qui obedientia ipsius unius justus constitutus est coram Deo Ro- man. V. 19. Id ergo imprimis observandum, quod nec ullo verbo mentio fiat meritorum Abrahami, nec operibus adscribatur justificatio, sed fidei ver- bum promissionis apprehendentis;quodque argu- mentum Apostoli sonet de Abrahamo, in ipso no- væ obedientiæ statu jam constituto, quando Gen. XV. credidisse, & credendo justificatus dicitur. Nam multo ante c. XI. & XII. introducitur ut fide- lis, multisque bonis operibus insignis, & nihilominus his etiam operibus illum Paulus justificatum ne- gat, & soli in Christum fidei justificationem ejus unice transcribit.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. Γινώσκετε ἄρα, ὅτι οἱ ἐκ πίστεως, ὗτοί εἰσιν υἱοὶ Ἀβραάμ) His mystical offspring, as in Rom. IV. 12. γινώσκετε, know, as the Syriac has it here.

From what has preceded, he concludes, and leaves it to the Galatians to gather, that not those who wish to be justified by works in any way, but those who are solely by faith, are the sons of Abraham: because Abraham, the Father of believers, was in no way justified by works before God, but solely through faith. If, therefore, they wish to be his genuine sons, let them not contend that works are required together with faith for justification, as the Pseudo-Apostles do, but let them seek righteousness only in Christ through faith, let them not set up their own righteousness before God, but let them rely only on the righteousness of Him who has been made for us righteousness by God, 1 Cor. I. 29. The word ἄρα teaches that this is not a new argument, or a confirmation of the former, as it has seemed to some, but that it is an inference, which nevertheless contributes to a richer illustration of the theme, and to the confirmation of the Galatians in the truth, if they wish to be genuine sons of Abraham. Thus also the Apostle fights, as B. notes. Luther, against the confidence of the Jews, proudly boasting: We are the seed of Abraham. Very well, Abraham was circumcised and kept the law, we do the same. I concede. What then? Do you therefore wish to be righteous and saved? By no means. Rather, let us approach the Patriarch Abraham himself, and see by what method he was justified and saved. Certainly not because of his exceptional virtues and holy works, not because he left his country, kindred, and his father's house: Not because he received circumcision and kept the law, not because, at God's command, he was about to sacrifice his son Isaac, in whom he had the promise of posterity, but because he believed God. Therefore, he was justified by absolutely nothing else but faith. Thus, if you wish to be justified by the law, it was much more necessary for Abraham your father to be justified by the law. But he could not be justified, nor receive the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit, except by faith. Since this is true by the testimony of Scripture, why do you fight for the law and circumcision, and contend that righteousness and salvation come to you through them, when Abraham himself, your father, source, and head, of whom you boast, was justified and saved without them, by faith alone? From these things it is manifest, as Blessed Luther says again, that the children of Abraham are not children of the flesh, since he is not the father of the nations according to the flesh, but children of faith, as Paul declares in Rom. IV, 'I have made you a father of many nations before God, in whom you believed.' Therefore, Paul makes two Abrahams: the begetter and the believer. Abraham has children, and is the father of many nations. Where? Before God, where he believes, not before the world, where he begets. For there he is a son of Adam, a sinner, or at the same time, a worker of the righteousness of the law, living according to reason, that is, in the human manner, but this is nothing to the believer. This example of Abraham therefore involves at the same time holy Scripture itself, which says that we are reckoned righteous by faith. Therefore, this argument is most firm on a double account, both because of the example of Abraham and also because of the authority of Scripture.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Γινώσκετε ἄρα, ὅτι οἱ ἐκ πίστεως, ὗτοί εἰσιν υἱοὶ Ἀ- βραάμ) Proles ejus μυστικὴ, ut Rom. IV. 12. γινώσκετε scitote, quomodo hic Syrus.

Ex antegressis concludit, & colligendum Gala- tis relinquit, quod non qui ex operibus justificari quacunque ratione volunt, sed qui ex fide unice, il- li sint filii Abraham: quia Abraham, Pater creden- tium, nullo modo ex operibus justificatus est co- ram Deo, sed unice per fidem. Si ergo filii ejus γνήσιοι esse velint, ne contendant opera ad justifi- cationem cum Pseudo-Apostolis simul requirere, sed justitiam solum quærant in Christo per fidem, ne erigant justitiam propriam coram Deo, sed ni- tantur solum justitia ejus, qui nobis à Deo factus est justitia 1. Cor. I. 29. Vox ἄρα docet, non hic vel no- vum argumentum, vel prioris confirmationem, quod nonnullis visum, sed illationem haberi, quæ tamen facit ad uberiorem thematis illustrationem, & Galatarum, si filii genuini Abraham esse velint, in veritate confirmationem. Sic etiam pugnat Aposto- lus, notante B. Luthero, contra fiduciam Judæorum, superbe gloriantium: Nos sumus semen Abrahæ. Be- ne, Abraham est circumcisus & servavit legem, nos idem facimus. Concedo. Quid tum? Num ideo vultis esse justi & salvi? Minime. Quin accedamus ad ipsum Patriarcham Abraham, & videamus, qua ratione justificatus & salvatus sit. Non certe propter egregias virtutes & sancta opera sua, non quia dese- ruit patriam, cognationem, & domum patris sui: Non quia circumcisionem accepit & legem serva- vit, non quod jubente Deo, immolaturus erat filium Isaac, in quo habebat promissionem posteritatis, sed quia credidit Deo. Ergo nulla prorsus alia re justifi- catus est, nisi fide. Itaque si vos lege justificari vultis, multo magis oportuit Abraham patrem vestrum lege justificari. Sed non potuit neque justificari, neque acci- pere remissionem peccatorum, & Spiritum S. nisi fide. Cum hoc verum sit testimonio scripturæ, quid pugna- tis pro lege & circumcisione, & contenditis per ea contingere vobis justitiam & salutem, cum ipse Ab- raham Pater, fons, & caput vestrum, de quo gloria- mini, sine illis, sola fide justificatus ac salvatus sit. Ex his manifestum est, ut iterum B. Lutherus, Abra- ha filios non esse carnis filios, cum non sit Pater gen- tium secundum carnem, sed filios fidei, ut Paulus Rom. IV. declarat, Patrem multarum gentium con- stitui te coram Deo, cui credidisti. Itaque Paulus fa- cit duos Abraham, generantem & credentem. Abra- ham habet filios, & est Pater multarum gentium. Ubi? Coram Deo, ubi credit, non coram mundo, ubi generat. Ibi enim est filius Adæ, peccator, vel simul- tum, operator justitiæ legis, vivens secundum ratio- nem, id est, humano more, sed hoc nihil ad creden- tem. Involvit igitur hoc exemplum Abrahæ simul ipsam scripturam sanctam, quæ dicit nos fide repu- tari justos. Ideo hoc argumentum duplici nomine fir- missimum est, cum propter exemplum Abrahæ, tum etiam propter autoritatem scripturæ.

## 3:8
Vers. 8.) προἰδοῦσα δὲ ἡ γραφὴ) He speaks of Scripture as of a person, and says that it foresees, because it pre-signifies. You have a similar instance below III. 22. see also Joh. VII. 38. 42. Rom. IV. 3. IX. 17. X. 11. XI. 2.

Ὄτι ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοῖ τὰ ἔθνη ὁ Θεὸς) The present for the future, for it looks to the time of the Gospel, when not only Jews, but also the nations were led to true righteousness through faith.

Προευηγγελίσατο τῷ Ἀβραάμ) He foretold to Abraham long before; but Paul preferred to use that word, which would signify that the matter of the Gospel was contained latently in these words.

Ὄτι ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) You have ἐνευλογιθήσονται in the Greek, Gen. XII. 3. and so also Gen. XXII. 18. in certain copies. For in others it is ἐνλογηθήσονται. Thus & Ps. LXXII. 17.

So also Acts III. 25.

The sense is, through you all nations shall obtain the highest goods, or even acknowledge themselves to have obtained them, which הִתְבָּרְכוּ means, Gen. XXII. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 8.) προἰδοῦσα δὲ ἡ γραφὴ) De scriptura, ut de ho- mine loquitur, & prævidere eam dicit, quod præsignificat. Simile habes infra III. 22. vide & Joh. VII. 38. 42. Rom. IV. 3. IX. 17. X. 11. XI. 2.

Ὄτι ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοῖ τὰ ἔθνη ὁ Θεὸς) Præsens pro futuro, respicit enim tempus Evangelii, cum non Judæi tantum, sed & gentes ad justitiam veram perducti sunt per fidem.

Προευηγγελίσατο τῷ Ἀβραάμ) multo ante prædixit Ab- rahamo; sed maluit Paulus illo uti verbo, quod significa- ret, latenter in his vocibus contineri rem Evangelii.

Ὄτι ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) ἐνευλογιθήσον- ται habes in Græco, Gen. XII. 3. sic & Gen. XXII. 18. in qui- busdam exemplaribus. Nam in aliis est ἐνλογηθήσονται. Sic & Psal. LXXII. 17.

Sic & Actor. III. 25.

Sensu est, per te summa bona adipscentur gentes omnes, aut etiam adeptas se agnoscent, quod vult הִתְבָּרְכוּ, Gen. XXII. 18.

## 3:9
Ver. 9. ὅτι οἱ ἐκ πίστεως] i.e. The believers.

See the same kind of speaking in Rom. IV. 12. and below 10. Εὐλογοῦνται σὺν τῷ πιστῷ Ἀβραάμ] They shall obtain the greatest goods after the example of Abraham.

Thus οὐ is taken in Rom. VIII. 32.

So ץ of Ecclesiastes II. 16. It is translated into Latin similarly.

Nor are the words συμπάσχομεν, συνδοξάζομεν, and others of that kind to be taken otherwise.

Now, that it may be certain that the example of Abraham also pertains to the Gentiles, and that they are likewise justified by faith, Paul proves that the Scripture foresaw that God would also justify the Gentiles through faith, from the prediction and promise made to Abraham, and thus the Apostle brings a new argument from the blessing, which happens only through faith in Christ, which is as follows: By the same reason that all nations are rendered partakers of the saving blessing, by that same reason they are also justified.

But through faith alone in Christ, they are rendered partakers of the saving blessing, not through works. Therefore they are also justified through faith alone.

The major premise shines with its own light, because the saving blessing is either justification itself, or at least consists of the same causes: And it is confirmed by ver. 10 from the removal of the curse, to which we are liable through the law, from which, however, we are not freed, except through Christ, the seed of Abraham, which liberation happens in our justification, when we obtain the remission of sins, and are adopted to the inheritance of salvation.

To be blessed in this promise, as the blessed Hunnius says, is to be freed from the curse of the eternal law, and conversely to have righteousness and heavenly goods. And since the Apostle himself concludes from the blessing of the Gentiles in the seed of Abraham to the justification of the same through faith, by that promise of blessing apprehended by faith, and that Abraham was justified, and all, whoever from any nations are justified, it ought to be undoubted to us.

For the minor premise is expressly exhibited by these things: they who are of faith are blessed, or are rendered partakers of the spiritual saving blessing, just as Abraham the believer σὺν τῷ πιστῷ Ἀβραάμ. He who apprehends this promise by faith, and has been made a partaker of that blessing through faith.

Which promise was made many times to Abraham in Gen. XII. 3. and XXII., to Isaac in ch.

XXVIII., to Jacob in ch. XXVIII. And in the first place it is repeated, but in that sense in which it has been explained, when it was repeated to Abraham in Gen.

XXII., where the exposition of the former promise is held, that in you, it is in your seed: nor does the promise look to the person of Abraham, but to Christ, then existing in the loins of Abraham, the seed of Abraham. For not in Abraham, but in his seed are all the nations of the earth blessed, under whom Abraham is indeed also contained, who however is not blessed in himself, but in his seed, Christ, whence the word ἐξηγητικὸν is held in Gen. XXVIII. 14.

They shall be blessed in you, and (that is) in the seed, as Paul himself subjoined this explanation in v. 16. That PRESAW B.

Luther wishes to refer to the time before the law with Chrysostom and Theophylact: The Scripture foresaw long before the law, that the Gentiles are not to be justified by the law, but by the blessing of the seed of Abraham, which was promised to him four hundred and thirty years before the law was given. But it says more simply the foreknown calling and justification of the Gentiles through faith. The pseudo-Apostles taught, as Chrysostom here, that he who relies on faith alone is execrable; against these the Apostle taught that he who relies on faith alone is blessed.

In political righteousness, says B. Luther, laws and works are to be regarded, but in spiritual, divine, and heavenly [matters], all laws and works are to be removed from the eyes, and only the promise and blessing of Abraham is to be looked upon, which proposes Christ the blesser, the giver, and the savior. So that spiritual righteousness without law and works looks, purely looks, at the grace and blessing exhibited through Christ, as it was promised to Abraham and believed by him.

From this it easily appears that this argument is most strong. For if the blessing is to be hoped for and received through Christ alone, it follows necessarily by the contrary, that it is not received through the law. Because the blessing was delivered before and without the law to the believing Abraham.

But by that faith, by which he himself believed in the future Christ the blesser, by the same we believe in the present one. And thus we are justified by faith, as Abraham was justified by faith.

Therefore they who are under the law are not blessed, but remain liable to the curse. And a little before: Therefore the believing Abraham is to be separated from the working one, as much as heaven is distant from the earth.

The believer is clearly a divine man, a son of God, heir of the world, and victor of the world, of sin, of death, of the Devil, etc. Therefore he cannot be praised enough. Let us not allow that faithful Abraham to be hidden in the sepulcher, as he is to the Jews, but let us extol him with the highest praises and preach him, and in his name let us fill heaven and earth, so that before this faithful Abraham we may see nothing at all of Abraham the worker.

For speaking of the faithful Abraham, we are in heaven, but afterwards doing those things which Abraham the worker did, which were human and earthly, not divine and heavenly (unless insofar as they were given divinely), we converse among men on earth. Therefore the believing Abraham fills heaven and earth. Thus every Christian fills heaven and earth with his faith, so that besides it he should see nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ὅτι οἱ ἐκ πίστεως] i. e. Credentes.

Vide idem loquendi genus Rom. IV. 12. & infra 10. Εὐλογοῦνται σὺν τῷ πιστῷ Ἀβραάμ] Maxima bona con-sequentur ad exemplum Abrahami.

Ita οὐ sumitur Rom. VIII. 32.

Sic ץ Ecclesiastæ II. 16. Latine vertitur similiter.

Nec aliter sumenda verba συμπάσχομεν, συνδοξάζο-μεν, & alia ejusmodi.

Jam ut gentes etiam attinere exemplum Abraham, easque pariter ex fide justificari constet, Paulus id prævidisse scripturam, quod Deus etiam gentes justificaturus sit per fidem, probat è prædictione & promissione Abrahamo facta, adeoque novum argumentum adducit Apostolus à benedictione, quæ non nisi per fidem in Christum contingit, quod tale est: Qua ratione participes redduntur omnes gentes benedictionis salutiferæ, ea ratione etiam justificantur.

At per fidem solam in Christum, benedictionis salutiferæ participes redduntur, non per opera. Ergo etiam per fidem solam justificantur.

Major sua luce radiat, quia benedictio σωτήριος vel ipsa justificatio est, vel certe iisdem causis constat: Et confirmatur per vers. 10. è sublatione maledictionis, cui obnoxii sumus per legem, à qua vero non liberamur, non nisi per Christum, semen Abrahæ, quæ liberatio fit in nostri justificatione, cum remissionem peccatorum consequimur, & ad hereditatem salutis adoptamur.

Benedicti in hac promissione, B. Hunno dicente, est liberari à maledictione legis æternæ, & vicissim habere justitia & bonorum cœlestium. Et quum Apostolus ipse à benedictione gentium in semine Abraham concludat ad justificationem earundem per fidem, promissione illa benedictionis fide apprehensa, & Abrahamum justificatum esse, & omnes, quicunque ex ullis gentibus justificantur, indubitatum nobis esse debet.

Nam Minor propositio expresse hisce exhibetur, qui ex fide sunt, benedicuntur, vel benedictionis spiritualis salutiferæ participes redduntur, perinde, ut Abraham fidelis σὺν τῷ πιστῷ Ἀβραάμ. Qui hanc promissionem fide apprehendit, & benedictionis istius per fidem particeps factus est.

Quæ promissio multoties facta ad Abrahamum Genes. XII. 3. & XXII. ad Isaacum cap.

XXVIII. ad Jacobum cap. XXVIII. Et primo quidem loco repetitur, sed eo sensu, quo ea explicata est, cum ad Abraham repetita fit Gen.

XXII. ubi ἔκθεσις habetur prioris promissionis, quod in te, sit in semine tuo: nec promissio ad personam Abrahæ spectat, sed ad Christum, tum in lumbis Abrahæ existentem, semen Abrahæ. Neque enim in Abrahamo, sed in semine ejus benedictæ sunt omnes gentes terræ, sub quibus Abraham utique etiam continetur, qui vero non in seipso benedictus est, sed in semine suo, Christo, unde verbum ἐξηγητικὸν habetur Gen. XXVIII. 14.

Benedicentur in te, & (id est) in semine, ut Paulus ipse hanc explicationem subjunxit v. 16. Illud PRÆVIDIT B.

Lutherus tempore ante legem respicere vult cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto: Scriptura prævidit longo tempore ante legem, quod gentes non sint justificandæ lege, sed benedictione feminis Abrahæ, quæ ei promissa est quadringentis & triginta annis antequam lex dabatur. Sed simplicius dicit prævisa gentium vocatio & justificatio per fidem. Pseudo-Apostoli docebant, ut hic Chrysostomus, qui sola fide nititur, execrabilis est, his contra docebat Apostolus, qui sola fide nititur, cum benedictum esse.

In justitia politica, inquit B. Lutherus, spectanda leges & opera, sed in spirituali divina & cœlesti prorsus ex oculis removende sunt omnes leges & opera & sola promissio & benedictio Abrahæ inspisienda est, quæ proponit Christum benedictorem, largitorem & salvatorem. Ita ut spiritualis justitia sine lege & operibus intuetur, pure intuetur gratiam & benedictionem per Christum exhibitam, ut erat Abrahæ promissa & ab eo credita.

Ex hoc facile apparet hoc argumentum est fortissimum. Nam si per solum Christum speranda & accipienda est benedictio, necessario sequitur à contrario, quod per legem non accipiatur. Quia benedictio tradita est ante & fine lege credenti Abrahæ.

Ea autem fide, qua ipse credidit in futurum Christum benedictorem, eadem nos credimus in præsentem. Sicque fide justificamur, ut Abraham fide justificatus est.

Ergo qui sub lege sunt, non benedicuntur, sed manent, obnoxii maledictioni. Et paulo ante: Tantum separandus est igitur Abraham fidelis ab operante, quantum distat cœlum à terra.

Fidelis plane est divinus homo, filius Dei, heres orbis terrarum & victor mundi, peccati, mortis, Diaboli &c. Ideo satis laudari non potest. Illum fidelem Abraham non sinamus abstrusum in sepulchro, ut Judæis est, sed summis laudibus extollamus & prædicemus eum, & nomine ipsius cœlum & terram repleamus, ut præ hoc fideli Abrahæ nihil prorsus videamus de Abraham operante.

Loquentes enim de Abraham fideli, sumus in cœlo, postea vero facientes ea, quæ Abraham operans fecit, quæ fuerunt humana & terrena, non divina & cœlestia (nisi quatenus ea donata erant divinitus), conversamur inter homines in terra. Credens igitur Abraham implet cœlum & terram. Sic unusquisque Christianus implet cœlum & terram fide sua, ut præter eam nihil videre debeat.

## 3:10
Ver. 10. ὅσοι γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων νόμου εἰσὶν, ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσίν.] That is, they have no promises of eternal and heavenly life.

They are accustomed to take the name of private persons by a figure of speech, because such things seem so comparatively. Here the matter is not about the promises of the law, but about the guilt of those who wish to be justified by the works of the law. So far is it from being the case that they obtain life by the law in any way, that they are even concluded under the curse by the force of the law, unless they perform it most exactly, which can be done by no one.

From the law, says B. Luther, or the works of the law, they wish to be justified: From faith, sin, life, and death are contrary things. They are of the law who wish to be justified by the law: They are of faith who trust that they are justified by mercy alone for the sake of Christ. He who says that righteousness is of faith, curses and condemns the righteousness of works.

On the contrary, he who says that righteousness is of the law, curses and condemns the righteousness of faith. They are therefore precisely contrary.

Γέγραπται γὰρ, ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς, ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τοῦ νόμου, τοῦ ποιῆσαι αὐτά] From the Greek of Deut. XXVII. 26. where we read: ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς λόγοις τοῦ νόμου τούτου, ποιῆσαι αὐτούς; where the Greeks added ἐν πᾶσι to the sense, and from the Greeks the Samaritans, already in the time of Jerome.

For all the other precepts are understood, which had not yet been named in that chapter. It can be objected here, that there were certain expiations handed down for some committed sins, and much more for omissions. That is true, but those expiations freed from death, either violent or untimely, but they brought no remedy against death: they did not promise resurrection and eternal life, as that remission of sins which is in the Gospel, and if in the Prophets something of the sort is hinted at rather than said, it is borrowed, taken from the grace of the Gospel.

In the manuscript it is, ὅτι ἐὰν κατάρατ. That particle is often prefixed to quotations.

See John XV. 25.

It is false that the expiations in the Old Testament brought neither remission of sins nor eternal life.

For we have fully taught, in its proper place, in Lev. XI., that they did bring them, and that Socinianism has been routed, etc., even though they did not bring them here.

they did so αὐτοενεργητικῶς [by their own operation] and by their own virtue, but by the power of the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, which they received by faith, who, offering Levitical sacrifices, obtained remission of sins and salvation. But to return to the Apostle, the argument is strengthened, because the law only announces a curse to transgressors who do not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law, but does not bring a blessing. For by that through which only a curse is denounced to all, by that no one obtains a blessing. But by the law a curse is denounced to all: Because all transgress the law: there is no one who keeps it perfectly, and remains in all things which are written in the book of the law. Whence even the saints are compelled to seek the remission of sins. Therefore, no one obtains a saving blessing, righteousness, and eternal life through the observance of the law, but it is necessary to obtain the same solely through faith. To be 'of faith' is to seek blessing or justification through faith, and therefore to be 'of works' is to seek it through works. Therefore, to be 'of the works of the law' is not to perform the works of the law, but to wish to be saved through the works of the law. That they do not even concur with faith for obtaining blessing and justification, their imperfection teaches, by the power of which they obtain a curse through the sentence of the law in Deut. XXVII. 26, not a blessing. For not only those who violate all or many of the precepts of the law are under a curse: but also those who do not perfectly observe even one, James II. 10. Theophylact says, the Apostle shows now not only that faith justifies and blesses, but also that the law is a cause of sin and a curse. For no one can do the things which are written in the law, and he who does not do them is cursed. The Hebrew יקים properly means to stand erect, namely in the observance of the law; so that you do not cross the line. The opposite is to fall or to sin, to slip from the line, to fail in rectitude. Blessed Luther discourses here at length and excellently on the reconciliation of Moses and Paul, concluding finally thus: Therefore the sentence of Moses: 'Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things, which etc.' does not conflict with Paul, who pronounces those cursed who are of the works of the law. For Moses requires a doer who perfectly performs the law. But where shall we find him? Nowhere. Moses himself confesses that he is not such a one, because in Exod. XXXIV. he says that no one is innocent before God. And David: 'Enter not into judgment with thy servant etc.' And Paul in Rom. VII: 'I do not do what I want etc.' Wherefore Moses, together with Paul, necessarily compels us to Christ, through whom we may be doers of the law, and guilty of no transgression. In what way? First, through the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness on account of faith in Christ. Then through the gift and the Holy Spirit, who produces a new life, new motions, etc., in us, so that we may also formally perform the law. But what is not done is forgiven on account of Christ. Then whatever sin remains is not imputed.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ὅσοι γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων νόμου εἰσὶν, ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσίν.] Id est, nulla illi habent promissa vitæ æternæ, atque cœlestis.

Solent σερήσεις sumere nomen τῶν ἰδιωτῶν, quia comparate talia videntur. Non hic de promissis legis, sed de eorum, qui ex operibus legis justificari volunt, reatu agitur. Quod tantum abest, ut per legem vitam consequantur ulla ratione, ut etiam vi legis maledictione concludantur, nisi eam exactissime præstent, quod à nemine fieri potest.

Ex lege, inquit B. Lutherus, seu operibus legis justificari volunt: Ex fide peccatum, vita & mors contraria sunt. Ex lege exim sunt, qui per legem justificari volunt: Ex fide sunt, qui sola misericordia propter Christum se justificari confidunt. Qui ex fide dicit esse justitiam, maledicis & damnat justitiam operum.

Contra quæ ex lege dicit justitiam esse, maledicit & damnat justitiam fidei. Sunt igitur præcise contraria.

Γέγραπται γὰρ, ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς, ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τοῦ νόμου, τοῦ ποιῆσαι αὐτά] Ex Græco Deut. XXVII. 26. ubi legimus: ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς λόγοις τοῦ νόμου τούτου, ποιῆσαι αὐτούς; ubi ἐν πᾶσι Græci addidere ad sensum, & ex Græcis Samaritani, jam Hieronymi tempore.

Intelliguntur enim omnia præcepta cetera, quæ nondum eo capite nominata fuerant. Objici hic potest, esse quorundam commissorum, multoque magis omifforum, expiationes quasdam proditas. Verum id est, sed illæ expiationes libebant à morte, aut violenta, aut immatura, nullum autem contra mortem remedium afferebant: non pollicebantur resurrectionem & vitam æternam, ut remissio illa peccatorum, quæ est in Evangelio, quod si in Prophetis tale aliquid innuitur magis, quam dicitur, id promutuum est, sumptum de gratia Evangelica.

In manuscripto est, ὅτι ἐὰν κατάρατ. Particula illa sæpe præponitur allegationibus.

Vide Joh. XV. 25.

Falsum est, quod expiationes in Vet. Test. nec remissionem peccatorum, nec vitam æternam attulerint.

Attulisse enim omnino suo loco docuimus in Lev. XI. & Socinismo profligata &c. etsi non attu-lerint

lerint αὐτοενεργητικῶς & propria virtute, sed vi sa- crificii Christi propitiatorii, quod fide suscipie- bant, qui sacrificia offerentes Levitica remissio- nem peccatorum & salutem consequebantur. Sed ut ad Apostolum revertamur, fortius adstringitur argumentum, quod lex tantum maledictionem an- nuntiet transgressoribus, qui non permanent in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, non vero benedictionem afferat. Per quod enim tantum ma- ledictio omnibus denunciatur, per illud nemo bene- dictionem consequitur. At per legem omnibus de- nunciatur maledictio: Quia omnes legem trans- grediuntur: nemo est, qui eam perfecte servet, & in omnibus maneat, quæ in libro legis scripta sunt. Unde etiam sancti coguntur petere remissionem peccatorum. Non ergo per legis observantiam benedictionem salutiferam justitiam ac vitam æternam quisquam consequitur, sed unice per fi- dem eandem obtinere necessum est. Ex fide esse est benedictionem vel justificationem per fidem quærere, ideoque ex operibus esse est eam per opera quærere. Non ergo ex operibus legis esse est ope- ra legis præstare, sed per opera legis servari velle. Quæ vero quod ne concurrant quidem cum fide ad benedictionem & justificationem consequen- dam, imperfectio eorum docet, vi cujus male- dictionem per sententiam legis Deut. XXVII. 26. consequuntur, non benedictionem. Non enim tantum, qui omnia vel multa legis præcepta vio- lant, sub execratione sunt: sed etiam, qui unam tantum non perfecte observant Jac. II. 10. Theo- phylactus, ostendit, inquit, Apostolus nunc non so- lum, quod & justificet fides & benedicat, sed etiam quod lex peccati & maledictionis causa sit. Nemo enim potest facere, quæ scripta sunt in lege, qui vero non facit, maledictus est. Ebr. יקים proprie est erectum stare, nimirum in observantia legis; ita ut lineam non transgrediaris. Contrarium est ca- dere seu peccare, a linea excidere, a rectitudine deficere. Prolixe hic & præclare de conciliatione Mosis & Pauli disserit B. Lutherus, ita tandem con- cludens: Quare Mosis sententia: Maledictus omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ &c. non pu- gnat cum Paulo, qui maledictos pronunciat eos, qui ex operibus legis sunt. Moses enim requirit facto- rem, qui perfecte legem faciat. Sed ubi accipiemus illum? Nusquam. Moses ipse fatetur, se non esse talem, quia Exod. XXXIV. ait, nullum esse innocen- tem apud Deum. Et David: Ne intres in judicium cum servo tuo &c. Et Paulus Rom. VII. Non facio, quod volo &c. Quare Moses una cum Paulo neces- sario nos cogit ad Christum, per quem simus factores legis, & nullius transgressionis rei. Quo modo? Primum per remissionem peccatorum, & imputa- tionem justitiæ propter fidem in Christum. Deinde per donum & Spiritum sanctum, qui parit novam vitam, novos motus &c. in nobis, ut etiam legem formaliter faciamus. Quod autem non fit, ignosci- tur propter Christum. Deinde quicquid peccati reliquum est, non imputatur.

## 3:11
Verse 11. 'But that no one is justified by the law before God, it is evident' [Gal. 3:11]. That there is no one who through the law of Moses attains that righteousness which pleases God; that righteousness is valid among men, not before God, namely as the giver of eternal life.

'That the just shall live by faith' [Gal. 3:11]. See Rom. I. 17 and what is said there. There are many things that move me to believe that this epistle, and that to the Romans, were dictated at nearly the same time. But this one is harsher, because the evil among the Galatians was more serious.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὅτι δὲ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, δῆλον) Neminem esse, qui per legem Mosis eam justitiam assequatur, quæ Deo placet, valet illa justitia apud homi- nes, non apud Deum, nempe ut datorem vitæ æternæ.

Ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται) Vide Rom. I. 17. & ibi dicta. Multa sunt, quæ me movent, ut hanc epistolam, & illam ad Romanos, prope eodem tempore dictatas cre- dam. Sed hæc est asperior, quia malum apud Galatas erat gravius.

## 3:12
Verse 12. 'And the law is not of faith' [Gal. 3:12]. He understands here by the law the precepts given at Sinai, in which there is no mention of faith, and he looks especially to those, because those with whom he was dealing thought little of the rest.

'But the man who does them shall live in them' [Gal. 3:12]. That is, he shall have a happy life here, Lev. XVIII. 5. For to live for the Hebrews is often to live happily: to die, miserably.

By the law we would indeed obtain righteousness, not that which avails only among men, but that which avails before God himself, if the law could be fulfilled by us. Now, for anyone to perform external obedience in such a way that he is justified before men, or held to be righteous, contributes nothing to justification before God, concerning which it is discussed here, for which perfect internal and external obedience is necessary. Since, however, the same is found in no one, it is plain that no one is justified by the law before God. But the Apostle uses another argument here, from the means of justification defined by God, in this way: If a man lives only by faith, the works of the law contribute nothing to salvation, or he does not attain salvation and life, or is justified before God, by both faith and the works of the law. But the former is true from the testimony of the Prophet Hab. II. 4. Therefore, the latter is also true. That no one is justified by the law before God, δῆλον is manifest. He implies that this consequence is clear: Whoever lives by faith, that is, through faith, he is not justified in the law, or by the works of the law, which consists in the immediate opposition of the observance or works of the law and faith, or the fiducial apprehension of the righteousness of Christ. For if we live by the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith, certainly we do not attain life by our own righteousness in any way, and much less will the same contribute anything to our justification. Ó δίκαιος is righteous in this phrase of Scripture, either he to whom the righteousness of Christ is imputed, or he who is endowed with inherent righteousness, although neither can the former be without the latter, nor the latter without the former. The righteous man, however, lives not by his own proper righteousness, but by faith, or the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith, which is imputed to him by God. Nor, however, is it required, indeed it is not even possible, that anyone should first be righteous and then ascend to faith by the purity of life, because before faith there is no righteousness; but we are both righteous through faith and live eternal life, or attain eternal salvation, only through faith.

Pareus, as also Crocius, wishes it to be read: the righteous shall live by faith, that is, everyone who is justified by faith before God attains eternal life. But the question was already about this, whether a man is justified by faith alone before God, and the Apostle urges this conclusion, that no one is justified by any reason through the works of the law, because the righteous man lives only by faith. Since, therefore, we have righteousness and eternal life not through the works of the law, but through faith alone, the Apostle concludes that we are certainly justified not through the works of the law, but through faith alone, because there are no other causes of justification than of salvation: And since we attain eternal life, which is consummated salvation, by faith alone, much more do we attain justification, which is salvation begun in respect to eternal life itself, by faith alone. Therefore, the Apostle employs his δῆλον here. That the consequence is in open light, and manifest, and greater than any exception. Furthermore, since there is a perpetual antithesis of the righteousness of works and of faith in the words of the Apostle, and indeed it is pronounced even concerning the righteous that they live by faith, it is legitimately inferred: therefore not by works. And consequently, not even the regenerate, or what is the same thing, the righteous, live by works, but solely by faith. Which argument is the more valid in that it embraces not only justification, but salvation itself, or the attainment of salvation designated by the word life, as G. Hunnius holds.

Although these things are clear, the Apostle still further illustrates them in such a way that he establishes his thesis with a new argument at the same time, v. 12, when he says: The law, however, is not of faith or through faith, or in faith. For we see these particles ἐξ, διὰ, and ἐν being interchanged here, so that, namely, by faith- teaches the immediate opposition of law and faith, that there is no commerce between law and faith, nor between faith and law, the law demands works, and promises life through works; but faith obtains life without works: That the law promises, but to those who work; as faith on the contrary does not require works or the observance of the law for salvation, but seeks and obtains life without works in Christ. His opinion is: He who shall have done these things, not he who shall have believed, shall live in them: The latter's [opinion is]: He who shall have believed, not he who shall have done these things, which the law commands, shall live by his faith.

This, therefore, is what the Apostle teaches, that the justification of the law and of faith are opposite; and that they cannot stand together in the same subject, but that one removes the other: and therefore that we are justified before God either by the law, or by Evangelical justification, either by works or by faith, that both justifications cannot be mixed, just as faith is not from the law, nor is the law from faith: But these are distinct as heaven and earth.

Whence we must be justified by faith alone.

And this is the reason why the exclusive particle 'alone' must be retained at all costs, so that in the cause of our justification every mixture of law and Gospel, of works and faith, may be avoided.

What need is there of a long disputation, says the Apostle, as interpreted by B.

Luther, thus I produce the most clear testimony of the Prophet, which no one can cavil at; the just lives by faith.

If by faith, then not by the law, because the law is not from faith.

And Paul takes the word 'faith' exclusively and by way of contrast.

As the Sophists are prepared to evade the scriptures, [they evade] this passage, by [saying it is] working, or formed by charity.

But if faith is unformed, it does not justify.

This gloss they themselves have invented, and by it they do violence to the words of the Prophet.

If they call formed faith true and theological, or, as Paul [calls it], ἀνυπόκριτον, which God calls [it], you would not offend me with this gloss of theirs.

For then faith would not be distinguished against charity, but against a vain opinion of faith, just as we also distinguish between a child-faith and a true one.

But they themselves speak of faith formed by charity, and they indeed make faith unformed and formed.

This most pestilential and Satanic gloss I cannot but vehemently detest.

Although, they say, infused faith is present, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit, and acquired, which we ourselves produce for ourselves by many actions of believing, yet both are unformed, and are formed by charity.

But faith without charity, as they dream, is like a painting and a beautiful thing in the dark, which is then first seen when light, that is, charity, has arrived.

And in this way charity is the form of faith and faith is the pure matter of charity.

To prefer this is to prefer charity to faith, and to attribute justification not to faith but to charity.

Because that which is the cause of each thing is such, and it itself is more so.

Therefore, since they do not attribute righteousness to faith, except because of charity, they attribute nothing at all to faith.

Then they say, as destroyers of the Gospel of Christ, that even infused faith, which is not received by hearing, or by any other means acquired, but which the Holy Spirit creates in man, stands in mortal sin, and that the worst men can have it.

Therefore if it is alone, it is idle and useless, even if it does miracles.

Thus they take away its own office from faith entirely, and attribute it to charity, so that faith is worth absolutely nothing, unless the form, that is charity, has arrived.

Therefore according to this pestilent figment of the Sophists, that miserable virtue of faith will be a certain unformed chaos, of no work, efficacy, and life; but only passive matter.

All these things are blasphemous against God and Satanic, which entirely overturn the doctrine of faith and obscure it, and draw [men] away from Christ the Mediator, and from faith, which apprehends Him.

For if charity is the form of faith, as they trifle, I am immediately forced to feel that charity itself is the principal and greatest part of the Christian religion.

And thus I lose Christ, His blood, wounds, and all His benefits, and I cling to charity, and I love and come into moral doing, like the Pope, a pagan Philosopher, or a Turk.

All these things [are from] B.

Luther, which are apt and to be noted first, not because of the corruptions of the Papists, but also because of the new Majorist Calixtines.

The Sophists say (B.

Luther continues, which we add, so that the Novators may be more confounded) the just lives, if faith is formed.

Paul on the contrary: The law is not from faith.

But what is the law?

Is it not also a commandment of charity?

Nay, the law commands nothing else than charity, as the text itself has: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart: Item, on these two commandments the whole law and the Prophet depend.

If therefore the law commanding charity fights with faith, then neither is charity from faith.

Thus Paul clearly refutes the gloss invented by the Sophists concerning formed faith, and speaks of faith alone, setting aside the law.

But with the law set aside, charity is set aside and all things which are of the law, and faith alone is left, which justifies and gives life.

From the most clear testimony of the Prophet, therefore, Paul argues that justification and life before God happen simply to no one, except to the believer, who obtains righteousness and life, without law and love, from faith.

The reason is because the law is not from faith, that is, the law is not faith, or anything of faith, because it does not believe, nor are the works of the law faith.

Therefore faith is a different thing from the law, as a promise is a different thing from the law.

For a promise is apprehended not by working, but by believing.

Just as therefore in first philosophy, by the division of substance and accident they are distinct: So in Theology the promise and the law, and consequently faith and works, are so far distant from each other.

It is impossible, therefore, for faith to be from the law.

Since faith only clings to the promise, only receives and knows God, and is engaged in receiving and giving to God.

On the contrary, the law and works are engaged in doing and giving to God.

As Abel offering gives to God, but believing receives from God.

Paul therefore concludes most strongly from the passage of Habakkuk, that the just lives by faith, namely, alone.

Because the law pertains nothing to faith.

For the law is not a promise; but faith adheres to and leans on the promise.

Therefore as the law and the promise are distinguished, so also are works and faith.

Hence the gloss of the Sophists is impious and false, by which it joins the law with faith, indeed extinguishes faith and puts the law in the place of faith.

This is our way again, B.

Here again B. Luther.

Theophylactus explains these things thus: You show, therefore, that by the law men are made execrable and subject to the curse, but by faith blessings are accumulated.

For he plainly demonstrates that faith itself has in itself the power of justifying, even alone, and he brings in Habakkuk saying: Because by faith, not by the law, the just lives.

For the law not only demands faith, but works.

But you have spoken rightly before God.

For among men perhaps those are believed just who have clung to the law, such as the Pharisees were, who displayed themselves as righteous in the sight of men.

The law, therefore, since on account of its difficulty it did not justify at all, and bound us with a curse, grace received, showing an easy path to righteousness, by which being justified we obtain the blessing.

Moreover the words of Moses

Lev. XVIII.5. do not treat of the happiness of this life, but of eternal life, as is clear from Luke

Rom.

X.; indeed from the comparison of Hab.

4. and the opposition of the curse, which the law denounces, and by which Christ redeemed us, it is also made manifest in the present passage.

Rightly therefore B. Hunnius: By these words is not designated temporal life, which happens no less to the impious even without faith: But spiritual life before God is noted, by the grace of which a faithful man is freed from eternal death, and is constituted heir of perpetual life: which is the same as justification.

ANNOTATA AD GALAT. CAP. III. v.

13. participating in sins, and the justice of Christ, and consequently the salvation dependent upon it.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὁ δὲ νόμος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ πίστεως) Legem hic in- telligit præcepta, in Sinai data, in quibus nulla fidei men- tio, ea autem præcipue respicit, quia ii, quibuscum res ipsi erat, cætera parvi ducebant.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ, ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς) Id est vitam hic habebit felicem, Lev. XVIII. 5. Nam vivere Hebraeis, saepe est feliciter vivere : mors misere.

Per legem sane justitiam obtineremus, non quae apud homines tantum; sed quae apud Deum ipsum valeat, si lex impleri a nobis posset. Jam ita externam obedientiam quemquam praestare, ut coram hominibus justificetur, vel justus habeatur, nihil ad justificationem facit apud Deum, de qua hic disseritur, ad quam perfecta obedientia interna & externa opus est. Quum autem eadem in nullo reperiatur, neminem justificari per legem coram Deo planum est. Sed Apostolus alio hic utitur argumento, a medio justificationis a Deo definito, hoc modo: Si homo non nisi fide vivit, opera legis nihil ad salutem conferunt, vel non & fide, & operibus legis salutem & vitam consequitur, aut coram Deo justificatur. At verum prius ex testimonio Prophetae Hab. II. 4. Ergo & posterius. Nullum autem ex lege apud Deum justificari, δῆλον manifestum est. Consequentiam hanc luculentam esse innuit: Quicunque ex fide, id est, per fidem vivit, ille non justificatur in lege, vel per opera legis, quae immediata oppositione observantiae vel operum legis & fidei, vel fiducialis apprehensionis justitiae Christi constat. Si enim justitia Christi per fidem apprehensa vivimus, utique justitia nostra propria vitam nullatenus consequimur, ac multo minus eadem ad justificationem nostram quicquam conferet. Ó δίκαιος justus est in hac phrasi scripturae vel cui justitia Christi imputatur, vel qui inhaerente justitia praeditus est, quanquam nec illa sine hac, neque haec sine illa esse possit. Vivit autem justus non sua propria justitia, sed ex fide, vel justitia Christi per fidem apprehensa, quae ipsi a Deo imputatur. Nec tamen requiritur, imo nec fieri potest, ut quis prius sit justus & tum puritate vitae ad fidem ascendat, quia ante fidem nulla est justitia, sed & justi per fidem sumus & vivimus aeterna vita, vel salutem aeternam consequimur, non nisi per fidem.

Pareus ut & Crocius vult, legendum esse justus ex fide vivet, hoc est, omnis qui fide justificatur coram Deo, vitam aeternam consequitur. Sed de hoc quaestio jam erat, an fide sola justificetur homo coram Deo, & hanc conclusionem urget Apostolus, quod nemo ulla ratione per opera legis justificetur, quia justus non nisi per fidem vivit. Quum ergo non per opera legis, sed per solam fidem justitiam, & vitam aeternam habeamus, utique non per opera legis, sed per fidem solam etiam nos justificari concludit Apostolus, quia non aliae causae justificationis sunt, quam salutis: Et quum vitam aeternam, quae est salus consummata, sola fide consequamur, multo magis justificationem, quae salus inchoata vitae ipsius aeternae ratione est, consequimur sola fide. Ideo suum δῆλον hic adhibet Apostolus. Quod in aperta luce, & manifesta, omnique exceptione major sit consequentia. Porro cum verbis Apostoli perpetua insit antithesis justitia operum & fidei, & vero de justis etiam pronuntietur, quod ex fide vivant, legitime infertur, ergo non ex operibus. Et proinde ne renati quidem, seu quod idem est, justi vivunt per opera, sed unice per fidem. Quod argumentum eo validius est, quod non modo justificationem, sed ipsam salvationem, sive salutis consecutionem vitae vocabulo designatam complectitur, ut habet G. Hunnius.

Quae etsi luculenta sint, ita tamen adhuc illustrat Apostolus porro, ut novo simul argumento thesin suam stabiliat v. 12. cum ait: Lex vero non est ex fide vel per fidem, vel in fide. Nam videmus has particulas ἐξ, διὰ, & ἐν hic permutari, ut scilicet fide- doceat immediatam oppositionem legis et fidei, quod nihil fit commercii legi cum fide, nec fidei cum lege, lex opera exigat, et per opera vitam promittat; fides vero sine operibus vitam consequatur: Quod lex promittat, sed operantibus; uti fides contra non requirit ad salutem opera vel legis observantiam, sed fine operibus vitam quaerit et consequitur in Christo. Illius sententia est: Qui fecerit ea, non qui crediderit, vivet in eis: Hujus, qui crediderit, non qui fecerit ea, quae lex praecipit, fide sua vivet.

Id ergo est, quod docet Apostolus, justificationem legis et fidei esse oppositam; nec simul stare in eodem subjecto, sed unam tollere alteram: ideoque aut legi, aut Evangelica justificatione nos coram Deo justificari aut operibus aut fide, non posse commisceri utramque justificationem, perinde uti ex fide non est lex, neque ex lege est fides: Sed haec toto coelo distincta sunt.

Unde sola fide nos justificari oportet.

Atque haec causa est, cur omnino retinenda sit particula exclusiva sola, ut in causa justificationis nostrae omnis mixtura legis et Evangelii operum et fidei caveatur.
