Quid opus est longa disputatione, inquit Apostolus, interprete B.

Lutheri, sic produco clarissimum testimonium Prophetae, quod nemo potest cavillari; justus ex fide vivit.

Si ex fide, ergo non ex lege, quia lex non est ex fide.

Et Paulus fidei vocabulum exclusive et per contrarium accipit.

Sophistae ut parati sunt ad eludendum scripturas, hunc locum, operante, vel formata charitate.

Si vero est fides informis, non justificat.

Hanc glossam ipsi finxerunt, eaque vim faciunt Propheta verbis.

Si fidem formatam vocant veram et theologicam, vel, ut Paulus, ἀνυπόκριτον, quam Deus vocat, nihil me offenderes hac ipsorum glossa.

Tunc enim fides non distingueretur contra charitatem, sed contra vanam opinionem fidei, quomodo et nos distinguimus inter fidem filiam et veram.

Sed ipsi loquuntur de fide formata charitate, faciuntque quidem fidem informem et formatam.

Hanc pestilentissimam et Satanicam glossam non possum non vehementer detestari.

Quamvis, inquiunt, adsit fides infusa, quae donum Spiritus S. est, et acquisita, quam nos ipsi parimus nobis multis actionibus credendi, tamen utraque est informis, et formatur charitate.

Sed fides sine charitate, ut ipsi somniant, est quasi pictura et res spectosa in tenebris, quae tum primum cernitur, cum lux, id est, charitas accesserit.

Atque hoc modo charitas est forma fidei et fides pura materia charitatis.

Hoc praeferre est charitatem fidei, et tribuere justificationem non fidei sed charitati.

Quia propter unumquodque est tale, et ipsum magis.

Itaque cum non tribuunt justitiam fidei, nisi propter charitatem, fidei nihil omnino tribuunt.

Deinde dicunt Evangelii Christi eversores, fidem etiam infusam, que non accipitur audiendo, aut ulla alia ratione acquirititur, sed quam Spiritus S. creat in homine, stare in peccato mortali, eaque pessimos homines posse habere.

Ideo si sola fit, otiosam et inutilem esse, etiam si mirabilia faciat.

Ita fidei suum officium prorsus auferunt, et tribuunt charitati, ut fides prorsus nihil valeat, nisi accesserit forma, id est charitas.

Ergo juxta hoc pestilens figmentum Sophistarum fides illa misera virtus, erit quoddam informe chaos, nullius operis, efficaciae et vitae; sed tantum passiva materia.

Ista omnia blasphema in Deum et Satanica sunt, quae prorsus evertunt fidei doctrinam et obscurant, a Christo Mediatore, et a fide, apprehendente ipsum, retrahunt.

Nam si charitas est forma fidei, ut ipsi nugantur, statim cogor sentire, ipsam charitatem esse principalem et maximam partem Christiana religionis.

Et sic amitto Christum, sanguinem, vulnera et omnia beneficia ejus, et inhaereo charitati, et diligo ac venio in facere morale, ut Papa, gentilis Philosophus, aut Turca.

Haec omnia B.

Lutherus, quae non propter Papistarum corruptelas, sed etiam propter novellas Majoristas Calixtinos apta et primae notandae.

Sophistae dicunt (pergit B.

Lutherus, quae addimus, ut magis confundantur Novatores) justus vivit, si fides sit formata.

Paulus contra: Lex non est ex fide.

Quid autem est lex?

An non etiam est charitatis praeceptum?

Imo lex nihil aliud praecipit, quam charitatem, ut textus ipse habet: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo: Item in his duobus mandatis lex tota et Propheta pendent.

Si ergo lex praecipiens charitatem pugnat cum fide, ergo nec charitas est ex fide.

Sic Paulus clare confutat confictam a Sophistis glossam de fide formata, loquiturque de fide sola, seponens legem.

Seposita autem lege, seponitur charitas et omnia, qua legi sunt, et sola fides relinquitur, quae justificat et vivificat.

Ex clarissimo igitur testimonio Prophetae argumentatur Paulus, quod simpliciter nemini contingat justificatio et vita coram Deo, nisi credenti, qui justitiam et vitam consequitur, sine lege et dilectione ex fide.

Ratio quia lex non est ex fide, hoc est, lex non est fides, vel aliquid fidei, quia non credit, nec opera legis sunt fides.

Ergo fides est diversum quiddam a lege, ut promissio est diversum quiddam a lege.

Nam promissio non operando, sed credendo apprehenditur.

Sicut erga in Philosophia prima, divisione substantia et Accidentis distincta sunt: Ita in Theologia promissio et lex, et per consequens fides et opera tam longe inter se distant.

Impossibile est ergo, fidem esse ex lege.

Si quidem fides solum haeret in promissione, solum accipit et cognoscit Deum, et versatur in recipiendo et dando Deo.

Contra lex et opera versantur in faciendo et dando Deo.

Ut Abel offerens dat Deo, sed idone credens recipit a Deo.

Concludit ergo Paulus fortissime ex loco Habacuc, justum ex fide, scilicet sola, vivere.

Quia lex nihil pertinet ad fidem.

Nam lex non est promissio; fides autem adhaeret et nititur promissione.

Erga ut lex et promissio distinguuntur, ita et opera et fides.

Hint glossa Sophistarum impia et falsa est, qua legem conjungit cum fide, imo exstinguit fidem et legem ponit in locum fidei.

Haec nus iterum B.

Lutherus.

Theophylactus haec ita explicat: Ostenditis igitur, lege execrabiles reddi homines et maledictioni subesse, fide vero benedictiones accumulari.

Nane plane demonstrat, fidem ipsane vel solam justificandi in se habere virtutem, et Abacuc dicentem inducit: Quia ex fide, non a lege, vivit et justus.

Lex namque non solum exigit fidem, sed opera.

Recte autem apud Deum dixistis.

Nam apud homines justi forte creduntur, qui legi inhaeserint, quales Pharisaei fuere, qui se in hominum conspectu justitiae praestenderent.

Lex itaque cum ob ejus difficultatem haudquaquam justificaret, et nos execratione obstringeret, accepit gratia, facile ad justitiam iter ostendens, qua et justificati benedictionem assequimur.

Caterum verba Mosis

Lev. XVIII.5. non de felicitate hujus vitae, sed de vita aeterna agere e Luc. X.

Rom.

X. liquet; imo ex collatione Hab. II.

4. et oppositione maledictionis, quam denunciat lex, et qua Christus nos redemit, loco praesenti etiam manifestatum est.

Recte itaque B. Hunnius: Non designatur bisce verbis vita temporalis, quae non minus impiis contigit etiam sine fide: Sed vita notatur spiritualis coram Deo, gratia cujus homo fidelis a morte sempiterna redditur liber, perpetuae vita haeres constituitur: quod idem est, quod justifis.

ANNOTATA AD GALAT. CAP. III. v.

13. ficari à peccatis, & justitia Christi & consequenter salutem ab ea dependentem reddi participem.

## 3:13
Verf. 13.) Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law) Namely, the author and revealer of eternal and heavenly life, ἐξαγοράζων, as also ἀγοράζων, often signifies liberation, though it may: here, as also below in IV. 5, it signifies that which was done at a great price; κατάρα νόμου is death, under which the law leaves men, and that lot was even common to those who did not have the law given by God: wherefore the liberation pertains to all, which is what ἡμᾶς signifies here.

Having become a curse for us) There is a double figure here. For κατάρα stands for κατάρατος, just as circumcision stands for the circumcised: and ὡς is understood: for Christ was treated in such a way as if he were a κατάρατος to God. Nothing worse could happen to the most wretched man in this life. See 2 Cor. V. 21 and what is said there. From this it appears how much he valued our salvation, and this truly points to the fact that his benefits should not be held in low esteem. For it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree) In the manuscript there is again ὅτι here, a note, namely, of the place to be cited.

Among the Hebrews there was no punishment of either the cross or the gallows: for those who were to be strangled were strangled standing, but the bodies of those who had been stoned for grave crimes, such as idolatry, were hung on a gallows for some hours as a spectacle to the people, so that those who had not been present at the execution itself might be deterred from crimes by that contempt: but if it was so shameful to be hung after death, the punishment of the cross was certainly much more shameful, which itself also has suspension joined with affliction, and according to Roman customs was most infamous, whence the name 'cruciarius'.

The Apostle confirms what he had taught from the collation of Moses and the prophet Habakkuk, that those who wish to be justified by the law are under a curse, and that no one is justified and attains life except through faith in Christ: and thus they establish their thesis concerning the justice of faith by a new argument from the Redemption of Christ, that we have been freed from the curse of the law and eternal death by the satisfaction of Christ alone.

For it is concluded thus: Those who have been redeemed from eternal death by the satisfaction of Christ alone, they are justified by faith in Christ alone, when they are justified or obtain the remission of sins, and are constituted heirs of eternal life.

But we have all been redeemed by the satisfaction of Christ alone: Therefore: The consequence is obvious: because that satisfaction and redemption is apprehended through faith alone: not through work or the observance of the law, and that redemption, which was made through the satisfaction of Christ, we are made participants of it as to merit through faith as to efficacy or act.

For those who approve of the same, which is done through faith, which is that very approbation, they enjoy that redemption. For when the price has been paid for some, and the redemption acquired by the paid price, and life, those who do not spurn the same, but appropriate it to themselves, enjoy the same entirely. Add that we have been freed from execration on account of Christ, so that through faith in him we may obtain the blessing: in which blessing justification is included. Wherefore it is concluded again from this that justification is through faith in Christ, who also acquired for us liberation from execration, and blessing and justification.

But Christ was not only treated as if he were a κατάρατος to God, but was entirely made one; one must have recourse to metonymy from the letter, where necessity does not compel; then because ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, this is, Christ was made an execration in our stead.

But we were not only to be treated as κατάρατοι, but we were entirely subject to τῇ κατάρᾳ and were κατάρατοι: then because our liberation or redemption demands this.

For in order that we might be truly redeemed from execration, it was necessary that Christ should truly undergo the execration.

The Apostle does not nakedly name execration, but of the law.

The execration under which men were was not unjust, but just, not a decree of human will, nor proceeding from an enemy, but from the Lord, who has the power of blessing and cursing; not silent, but promulgated through the law, which is the voice of God, the supreme Lord and Ruler.

The execration of the law is a sentence of temporal and eternal condemnation, as Grotius rightly says here.

The emphasis is on the abstract word κατάρα: The Apostle could have said: He is cursed for us; but he preferred to say: He was made an execration, that is, supremely cursed.

Now is adduced the law of Moses, Deut. XXI, as the cause of that thing, that he who has been hung is cursed . 29. because of the cause of that thing, that he who has been hung is cursed 29.

If anyone should say: Is it very absurd and shameful to call the Son of God a sinner and cursed?

I answer in the words of B. Luther: If you deny that he is a sinner and cursed, you also deny that he suffered, was crucified, and died.

For it is no less absurd to say that the Son of God (as our faith confesses and prays) endured the pains of sin and death on the cross, than to call him a sinner or cursed.

But if it is not absurd to confess and believe that Christ was crucified among thieves, neither is it absurd to call him cursed and a sinner of sinners.

Certainly these are not empty words in Paul, Christ was made a curse for us.

God made Christ, who had not known sin, sin for us, that we might be made the justice of God in him, 2 Cor.

V. In the same manner John the Baptist calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

He himself is indeed innocent, because he is the immaculate and uncontaminated Lamb of God: But because he bears the sins of the world, his innocence is pressed by the sins and guilt of the whole world.

Whatever sins I, you, and we all have committed, and will commit in the future, are as much Christ's own as if he himself had committed them.

In sum, our sin must become Christ's own sin, or we shall perish eternally.

This is B.

Luther, who further concludes thus: From these things it is evident that the doctrine of the Gospel, most sweet and full of the richest consolations, does not preach about our works or the works of the law, but about the incomprehensible and ineffable mercy and charity of God toward us unworthy and lost men, namely, that when the merciful Father saw us oppressed by the curse of the law, and so held under it that we could never be freed from it by our own powers: he sent his only-begotten Son into the world, and cast upon him all the sins of all, saying: You be that Peter the denier, that blasphemous and violent Paul the persecutor, that David the adulterer, that sinner who ate the apple in Paradise, that thief on the cross. In sum, you be the person who has committed the sins of all men, think therefore, so that you may pay and make satisfaction for them. There the law comes, and says: I find the sins of men in him, and no other sin besides, except in him: Therefore let him die on the cross; and thus it invades him and kills him. With this done, the whole world is purged and expiated from all sins: Therefore also freed from death and all evils. But with sin and death removed through that one man, God would see nothing else in the whole world, especially if one believed, than mere purgation and justice, even if any remnants of sin remained, yet before that Christ alone God would not see them. Thus it behooves us to magnify the article of Christian justice against the justice of the law and works, although there is no word or eloquence by which one can worthily conceive, much less express, its magnitude.

Thus happily (adds Megalander, f. 77) He took upon Himself our sinner-state and our house, together with our innocent and avenging person. Clothed and dressed in this, we are freed from the curse of the law, because Christ Himself willingly became a curse for us. I, He says, for the sake of my person of humanity and divinity, am blessed, and clearly lack nothing. But I will empty myself, I will assume your mask and garment, that is, human nature, and in it I will walk about, and I will suffer death, so that I may free you from death. And when He thus carried the sin of the whole world in our mask, He was seized, suffered, was crucified, died, and was made a curse for us. But because He was a divine and eternal person, it was impossible for Him to be held by death. Therefore, He rose from the dead on the third day, and now lives forever, and sin, death, and our mask are no longer found in Him, but mere righteousness, life, and eternal blessing. We must gaze upon this image and apprehend it with firm faith. Whoever does this has this innocence and victory of Christ, however great a sinner he may be. But this cannot be apprehended by will or love, but by reason illuminated by faith. Therefore, we are justified by faith alone, because faith alone apprehends this victory of Christ. Insofar as you believe this, you have it. If you believe that sin, death, and the curse have been abolished, they are abolished. Because Christ conquered and removed them in Himself, and He wants it to be believed that, just as in His person there is no longer any mask of a sinner, no trace of death: so neither is there in ours, since He did everything for us, etc.

Theophylact summarizes the sum of the matter and the συνέχειαν (continuity) of the text as follows: Lest anyone perhaps object in this manner: I agree indeed that it is true that he who does not execute the law is to be cursed, and has the power of justifying faith. But I fear, for when we have once submitted to the yoke of the law, we ourselves become subject to the curse. Therefore, Paul shows that this curse was dissolved through Christ, with the price having been paid. And that in Himself He tore up such a condemnation, and redeemed us from the curse of the law, which He Himself had avoided, inasmuch as He fulfilled the law. And we underwent the same, because we were unable to execute the law. Nor did Christ act otherwise with us than someone who, when another is condemned to death, takes the place of the one who is to be punished, and, being innocent himself, removes him so that he may not be put to death, himself suffering death for him. Therefore, Christ affixed the curse to Himself, by which He hung on the tree, and solved the same, which undoubtedly hung over us for not fulfilling the law, although He Himself was subject to nothing, as one who fulfilled the law and was devoid of sin.

Explanation of others. Others explain the words of the Apostle "He became a curse" as a sacrifice for a curse by Metonymy: But it is better to understand it simply with Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others. Concerning which Blessed Luther (f. 78) says: Although these sentences can be correctly explained in this way: Christ was made a curse, that is, a victim for sin, etc. Yet it is more pleasing if the proper meaning of the words is kept for the sake of greater emphasis: Because when a sinner truly comes to the knowledge of himself, he should not only feel himself a sinner concretely or adjectivally, but also abstractly or substantively, that is, he should not only seem to himself calamitous, but the very calamity itself, not only a sinner and cursed, but sin and the curse itself. Just as in the Latin language we excellently wish to signify someone is wicked if we call him "wickedness" (scelus).

For it is a very great thing to carry sin, the wrath of God, the curse, and death. Wherefore, a man seriously feeling these things, as Christ truly feels them for the human race, becomes clearly sin, death, and the curse itself, etc. Truly, therefore, Paul treats this passage with an Apostolic Spirit. Because no Sophist, Legist, Jew, fanatic, or anyone else speaks in this way. For who would dare to allege this passage from Moses and interpret it concerning Christ? By what reason, therefore, Paul adapted this sentence, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," etc., to Christ, by the same reason we can also collect not only that whole chapter of Deuteronomy XXVII, but also all the curses of the Mosaic law, and interpret them concerning Christ. For just as Christ Himself is innocent in this general law for His own person: so He is also in all others. And just as He is the thing in this general law when He was made a curse for us and was ordered to be on the cross, as a wicked man, a blasphemer, a parricide, a traitor, etc., so He is guilty in all other laws as well. For all the curses were heaped upon Him and placed upon Him; and therefore He carried and sustained them in His body for us. Therefore, He was not only cursed, but was made a curse for us. This is truly to interpret the scriptures in the Apostolic manner.

For a man without the Holy Spirit cannot speak in this way, namely, that he should comprehend the whole law in one statement (to wit: Christ was made a curse for us) and heap it all at once upon Christ. And conversely, that he should comprehend all the promises of scripture and say they are fulfilled at once in Christ. Therefore, this argument is Apostolic and most firm, taken not from one place of the law, but from the whole of the law, upon which Paul also vehemently relies.

Regarding ἐξαγορασμῷ (redemption), that it implies satisfaction and redemption made by a price against the Socinians, we have spoken in Socin. Profl. p. 499, cf. also p. 479, as well as p. 443 et seqq.

Paul understands the curse of the law when he adds "the" as passive. In this way, he says, it signifies the curse as the punishment established by the law for transgressors, namely, eternal death. From this, therefore, Christ first redeemed us, since He made us immune from this punishment. Otherwise, the curse of the law is the cursing sentence of the law, or the law itself cursing, which is nothing else than God Himself, being angry at sins, cutting off sinners, or the wrath of God. From this, secondly, Christ also redeemed us, because He satisfied the wrath and vindicating justice of God for us. Although these things are true, nevertheless, no other meaning can directly have a place here except the active one, of which, however, a necessary consequence is liberation from the curse understood passively: which, therefore, we do not deny is inferred in a mediated sense.

Latin:

Vers. 13.) Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου) Nempe autor & revelator vitæ æternæ ac cœlestis, ἐξαγοράζων ut & ἀγοράζων sæpe quamvis liberationem significat: hic, ut & infra IV. 5. eam significat, quæ facta est magno pretio, κατάρα νόμου est mors, sub qua lex homines relinquit, ea vero fors etiam iis communis erat, qui legem à Deo datam non habebant: quare & liberatio ad omnes pertinet, id hic valet ἡμᾶς. Γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα) Duplex hic figura.

Nam & κατάρα pro κατάρατος, quomodo circumcisio pro circumcisis: & subauditur ὡς: nam Christus ita tractatus est, quasi esset Deo κατάρατος. Nihil homini pessimo in hac vita pejus evenire poterat. Vide 2. Cor. V. 21. & ibi dicta. Inde apparet, quanti nostram salutem fecerit, id vero eò spectat, ne parvi ducantur ejus beneficia. Γέγραπται γὰρ ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς, ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου) In manuscripto hic rursum est ὅτι, nota scilicet loci citandi.

Apud Hebræos non erat pœna aut crucis, aut patibuli: nam strangulandi stantes strangulabantur, sed eorum, qui ob gravia crimina, puta ob idololatriam, erant lapidati, corpora patibulo suspensa per aliquot horas erant ostentui populo, ut, qui supplicio ipsi non interfuissent, eo contemptu à criminibus absterrerentur: at si tam contumeliosum erat, post mortem suspendi, multò certè contumeliosius erat crucis supplicium, quod & ipsum cum afflictione suspensionem conjunctam habet, & Romanis moribus erat maxime infame, unde nomen cruciarii.

Confirmat Apostolus, quod è Mosis & Prophetæ Habacuc collatione docuerat, eos qui per legem justificari volunt, sub maledictione esse, non autem justificari ac vitam consequi quenquam nisi per fidem in Christum: adeoque novo etiam argumento thesin suam de justitia fidei stabiliunt a Christi Redemptione, quod solius Christi satisfactione liberati fimus à maledictione legis & morte æterna.

Ita enim concluditur: Qui solius Christi satisfactione redempti sunt ab æterna morte, illi justificantur sola in Christum fide, cum justificantur vel remissionem peccatorum consequuntur, & hæredes vitæ æternæ constituuntur.

At nos omnes solius Christi redempti sumus satisfactione: Ergo: Consequentia in aprico est: quia per solam fidem apprehenditur illa satisfactio & redemptio: non per opus vel observantiam legis & redemptionis istius, quæ per satisfactionem Christi facta est, quantum ad meritum participes reddimur per fidem quoad efficaciam vel actum.

Nam qui eandem fit approbriant, quod per fidem fit, quæ est ipsa illa approbriatio, fruuntur ea redemptione. Cum enim pretium persolutum est pro aliquibus, & soluto pretio acquisita redemptio, & vita illi, qui eandem non spernunt, sed appropriant sibi, eadem omnino fruuntur. Adde quod ab execratione liberati fimus propter Christum, ut per fidem in ipsum benedictionem consequamur: in qua benedictione includitur justificatio. Quapropter iterum hinc concluditur justificatio per fidem in Christum, qui & ab execratione nobis acquisivit liberationem, ac benedictionem & justificationem.

Non autem tantum tractatus est Christus quasi esset Deo κατάρατος, sed omnino factus Metonymiam à litera confugiendum, ubi non cogit necessitas; tum quia ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν hoc est vice nostris factus est Christus execratio.

Nos autem non tantum tractandi eramus, ut κατάρατοι, sed omnino obnoxii eramus τῇ κατάρᾳ & κατάρατοι: tum quia liberatio vel redemptio nostri hoc postulat.

Ut enim verè nos redimeremur ab execratione, necessum erat, ut Christus verè subiret execrationem.

Non nude nominat Apostolus execrationem, sed legis.

Execratio, sub qua homines erant, non erat injusta, sed justa, non humanæ voluntate decretum, bon ab hoste profecta, sed à Domino, qui habet potestatem benedicendi ac execrandi; non tacita, sed promulgata per legem, qua est Dei supremi Domini ac Rectoris vox.

Execratio legis est sententia condemnationis temporalis ac æternæ, ut hic recte Grotius.

Emphasi est in voce abstræcta κατάρα: Poterat Apostolus dicere: Maledictus est pro nobis; sed maluit dicere: Factus est execratio, id est, summe maledictus.

Adducitur autem lex Mosis Deut. XXI, qua causa ejus rei, quod suspensus maledictus . 29. quia causa ejus rei, quod suspensus maledictus 29.

Si dicat aliquis: Valde absurdum & contumeliosum est, Filium Dei appellare peccatorem & maledictum?

Respondeo verbis B. Lutheri: Si negare eum esse peccatorem & maledictum, negato etiam passum, crucifixum & mortuum.

Non enim minus absurdum est dicere, Filium Dei, (ut fides nostra confitetur & orat) crucifixum panas peccati & mortis sustinuisse, quam peccatorem aut maledictum dicere.

Si vero non est absurdum confiteri credere Christum crucifixum inter latrones, neque absurdum fit, eum dicere maledictum & peccatorem peccatorum.

Certe non sunt inanes voces in Paulo, Christus factus est pro nobis maledictum.

Deus fecit Christum, qui peccatum non noverat, pro nobis peccatum, ut efficeremur justitia Dei in ipso 2. Cor.

V. Ad eundem modum vocat eum Johannes Baptista agnum Dei tollentem peccata mundi.

Ipse quidem innocens est, quia est immaculatus & incontaminatus Dei agnus: Sed quia portat peccata mundi, premitur ejus innocentia peccatis & reatu totius mundi.

Quæcunque peccata ego, tu & nos omnes fecimus, & in fuurum faciemus, tam propria sunt Christi, quam fia ipse fecisset.

In summa oportet peccatum nostrum fieri Christi proprium peccatum, aut in æternum peribimus.

Hæc B.

Lutherus, qui porro ita concludit: Ex his constat doctrinam Evangelii omnium jucundiffimam & uberrimis consolationibus plenam, non concionari de nostris aut legis operibus, sed de incomprehensibili & ineffabili misericordia & charitate Dei erga nos indignos & perditos homines, quod scilicet cum videret misericors Pater, nos maledictione legis opprimi, & ita sub ea teneri, ut nunquam nostris viribus potuerimus ex ea liberari: miserit unigenitum Filium suum in mundum, ac conjecerit in eum omnia omnium peccata dicens: Tu fis Petrus ille negator, Paulus ille persequutor blasphemus & violentus, David ille adulter, peccator ille, qui comedit pomum in Paradiso, latro ille in cruce. In summa tu fis persona, quæ fecerit omnium hominum peccata, cogita ergo, ut solvas, & pro eis satisfacias. Ibi lex venit, & dicit: Invenio illum hominum peccata in se, & nullum præterea peccatum, nisi in illo: Ergo moriatur in cruce; atque ita invadit eum & occidit. Hoc facto totus mundus purgatus & expiatus est ab omnibus peccatis: Ergo etiam liberatus à morte & omnibus malis. Sublatis vero peccato & morte per unium illum hominem, Deus nihil aliud videret in toto mundo, præfertim si crederet, quam meram purgationem & justitiam, eisi qua peccati reliquia manerent, tamen præ illo solo Christo Deus eas non cerneret. Ita oportet nos magnificare articulum justitiæ Christianæ contra justitiam legis & operum, quam quam nulla vox aut eloquentia fit, qua digne possit concipere, multo minus eloqui ejus magnitudinem.

Sic feliciter (addit Megalander f. 77.) communis nobiscum suscepit peccatricem nostram & domum nobiscum suam innocentem & vltricem personam. Hac induti & vestiti liberamur a maledictione legis, quia Christus ipse volens factus est pro nobis maledictum. Ego inquiens pro mea persona humanitatis & divinitatis benedictus sum, & plane nullius rei egeo. Sed exinanibo me, assumam larvam & vestem vestram, hoc est, humanam naturam, atque in ea obambulabo, & mortem patiar, ut vos a morte liberem. Atque cum ita gestaret in nostra larva peccatum totius mundi, comprehensus, passus, crucifixus, mortuus, & pro nobis maledictum factus est. Quia vero divina & aeterna persona erat, impossibile fuit morte teneri eam. Ideo resurrexit die tertia a morte, & nunc in aeternum vivit, nec amplius invenitur in ea peccatum, mors & larva nostra, sed mera justitia, vita, & benedictio aeterna. Hanc imaginem oportet nos intueri, & firma fide apprehendere. Qui hoc facit, habet hanc innocentiam & victoriam Christi, quamlibet magnus sit peccator. Sed ea non potest apprehendi voluntate dilectione, sed ratione illuminata fide. Ergo sola fide justificamur, quia sola fides apprehendit hanc victoriam Christi. Quatenus igitur hoc credis, eatenus habes. Si credis peccatum, mortem, & maledictionem abolita esse, abolita sunt. Quia Christus ea in semetipso vicit & sustulit, & vult credi, quod sicut in sua persona nulla est amplius larva peccatoris, nullum vestigium mortis: Ita neque in nostra, cum pro nobis omnia fecerit & c.

Summam rei & συνέχειαν textus ita complectitur Theophylactus: Ne quis forte hunc in modum occurrat: Assentior equidem, id verum esse, ut execrandus sit, qui legem non exequatur, & fidem justificandi habere facultatem. Verumreor namque, ne cum semel legis subierimus jugum, & ipsi fimus maledictioni obnoxii. Ostendit itaque Paulus, maledictionem hanc per Christum, pretio depenso fuisse solutam. Et ut in se ejusmodi obsecrationem conscinderet, a legis maledictione nos redemisse, quod ipse quidem defugerat, utpote qui legem adimplevit. Et nos idipsum subivimus, quia legem exequi nequierimus. Nec secus Christus nobiscum egit, quam aliis quipiam, qui morti damnaturum in se ipse & innoxius eximat, ne capite ille plectatur, males ipse pro eo mortem subire. In se itaque Christus maledictionem afixit, qua in ligno pependit, & solvit eandem, que haud dubie nobis impendebat pro lege non adimplenda, cum ipse nil esset subjectus, ut qui legem impleverit, & peccati expers.

Alior. explicatio. Alii explicant verba Apostoli factus est execratio de sacrificio pro execratione per Metonymiam: Sed praestat simpliciter intelligere cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto & aliis. Quo de B. Lutherus f. 78. Quanquam he sententia recte exponi possunt hoc modo: Christus factus est maledictum, id est, hostia pro peccato & c. Tamen magis placet, si fervetur propria significatio vocum propter majorem emphasin: Quia cum peccator venit revera in notitiam sui, non solum fensisse peccatorem concretive seu adjective, sed etiam abstractive seu substantive, hoc est, non solum videretur sibi calamitosus, sed ipsa calamitas, non solum peccator & maledictus, sed ipsum peccatum & maledictum. Vt & in Latina lingua excellenter volumus aliquem significare scelestum, si vocamus eum scelus.

Est enim maxima res, portare peccatum, iram Dei, maledictionem & mortem. Quare ista homo serio sentiens, ut Christus vere sentit, pro genere humano, fit plane ipsum peccatum, mors, maledictum & c. Vere ergo Apostolico Spiritu Paulus hunc locum tractat. Quia nullus Sophista, Legista, Judaeus, fanaticus, aut quisquam alius ita loquitur. Quis enim auderet allegare hunc locum ex Mose: interpretari de Christo? Qua ergo ratione Paulus hanc sententiam, maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno & c. ad Christum accommodavit, eadem & nos non solum totum illud caput Deuter. XXVII. sed etiam omnes maledictiones Mosaica legis colligere, & de Christo interpretari possumus. Nam sicut Christus ipse innocens est in hac generali lege pro sua persona: Ita etiam in omnibus aliis. Et sicut ipse res est in hac generali lege cum maledictum pro nobis factus est jussus est in cruce, ut homo scelestus, blasphemus, parricida, proditor & c. ita & in omnibus aliis legibus reus est. Omnes enim maledictiones in eum congestae positae sunt; ideoque eas portavit & sustinuit in corpore suo pro nobis. Non solum igitur fuit maledictus sed factus est maledictum pro nobis. Hoc vere est interpretari Apostolico more scripturas.

Nam homo fine Spiritu Sancto non potest ita loqui, nempe quod totam legem comprehendat uno dicto (scil. Christus maledictum factus pro nobis) ac eam totam semel congemat in Christum. Et contra, quod omnes promissiones scriptura comprehendat, & semel in Christo impletas dicat. Ideo Apostolicum & firmissimum est hoc argumentum, non ex uno loco legis, sed ex universo legis sumptum, quo etiam vehementer nititur Paulus.

De ἐξαγορασμῷ quod inferat satisfactionem & redemptionem pretio factam contra Socinianos diximus in Socin. Profl. p. 499. conf. & p. 479. ut & p. 443. seqq.

Execrationem legis intelligit Paulus cum ad. ve tum passive. Hoc modo, inquit, significat execrationem panam transgressoribus lege statutam, mortem videlicet aeternam. Ab hac ergo primum nos redemit Christus, quoniam ab hac pana nos immunes fecit. Alive execratio legis, est sententia execratria legis, seu ipsa lex execrans, qua nihil est aliud, quam ipse Deus, irascens peccatis, exscindens peccatores, vel im Dei. Ab hac fecundo etiam nos redemit Christus, quia ira & justitia Dei vindicatrici satisfecit pro nobis. Quae etsi vera fint, non tamen hic nisi unica significatio directe locum habere potest, acti-scilicet, cujus tamen consequens necessarium est liberatio ab execratione passive intellecta: Quam proinde fenfu mediato inferri non negamus.

## 3:14
Verse. 14. ἵνα εἰς τὰ ἔθνη ἡ εὐλογία τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ γένηται, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ: "pro" (for) stands for "per" (through), and the noun is repeated for the pronoun. For the sense is, through Him: and εὐλογία τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ (the blessing of Abraham) are those great goods which it had been predicted would come to the nations through Abraham, that is, through someone from his lineage. ἵνα τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος λάβωμεν διὰ τῆς πίστεως: "nempe" (namely) is understood here. For this is the "ira" (wrath/consequence) of the preceding "ἐπαγγελίαν" (promise). For what greater good could be separated in this life than the gifts of the Holy Spirit, especially since those very things make men certain of heavenly life?

But those gifts are manifest, for [it is] that to those believing in Christ, not walking through the works of the law; ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος, that is, the promised Spirit, in the Hebrew manner: See Acts II. 33, add Acts I. 4, Hebrews ch. VI. 11, 15, ch. X. v. 36. By τὰ ἔθνη (the nations), some understand the Gentiles as contrasted with the Jews, which is also done by Theophylact. But because the blessing in Christ, the seed of Abraham, made in the promise of Abraham (v. 8), extends to πάντα τὰ ἔθνη (all the nations), here, where the cause of the promise and the fulfillment of that promise is explained, it is by no means to be restricted: But it must necessarily have equal breadth. For all nations, peoples, and populations of the whole earth, that is, for all men, Christ had to become a curse. all Therefore, blessing was also acquired through him, with the curse removed, as far as merit is concerned; thus, the bestowal of the actual blessing, which is the end of this exagorasmou (redemption), is also intended by God. For those for whom Christ was made a curse, the blessing of Abraham extends itself in Christ to them by the power of the divine intention, and it ought to reach them.

H hē eulogia Abraam (the blessing of Abraham) is understood either as that which was promised to Abraham, or that which occurs in the seed of Abraham, as Theophylact explains. But the former is more convenient: because in whom it occurs is added afterwards, namely, in Christ Jesus. Thus, therefore, it is taught again that the same occurs through faith alone: because we obtain the same in Christ Jesus. Therefore, not through our works or the observance of the law; but we obtain the same solely through faith in Christ Jesus: Which is again asserted when it is added by the Apostle, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith, as Calvin and Pareus intend. The promise made, however, is explained either formally as a spiritual promise; or objectively, as a promise concerning the Spirit. In neither way does anything depart from the Apostolic scope: The latter explanation, however, is to be preferred, both because mention has already been made tēs eulogias tou Abraam (of the blessing of Abraham) promised, and because the argument of the Apostle is more strongly tightened here. For if we obtain even the sealing of the Holy Spirit itself, which is promised in the Gospel, only through faith, if we are sealed or confirmed by the Holy Spirit for eternal salvation not through works of the law, but through faith in Christ, then certainly justification will be attributed much more solely to faith, and in no way to our works.

We see here, as blessed Luther says, what merits of congruity and condignity we bring, and by what reason we acquire that blessing: That is preparation, that is, the merit of congruity and condignity, those are the works by which this righteousness is prepared, that Christ Jesus was made a curse for us. For we are ignorant and enemies of God, we are dead in sins and cursed. Therefore, our merit is clearly nothing. For what would a cursed sinner deserve, ignorant of God, dead in sins, subject to the wrath and judgment of God? When the Pope excommunicated someone, whatever he did was cursed. How much more is he who is cursed before God, as we all are, before Christ is known, doing nothing but cursed things. Wherefore, that is the only way of escaping the curse, to believe and to say with certain confidence: You, Christ, are my sin and my curse, or rather: I am your sin, your curse, your death, your wrath of God, your hell, you on the contrary are my righteousness, blessing, life, grace of God, my heaven. Because the text clearly says: CHRIST was made a curse for us. Therefore, we are the cause that he was made a curse, nay, we are his very curse.

PART II.

DIDACTIC.

Concerning the testament concerning the seed Christ, and the inheritance to be obtained in the same, and the law, which was added only for the sake of sin, and that it might be a pedagogue unto Christ, and that through faith in Christ we might be heirs of the promise.

Vers.

Latin:

Verf. 14. ἵνα εἰς τὰ ἔθνη ἡ εὐλογία τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ γένηται, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ: pro per, & nomen repetitur pro pronomine. Sensus enim est, per ipsum: & εὐλογία τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ funt bona illa magna, quae gentibus per Abrahamum, id est, per aliquem ex ipsius stirpe, eventura praedictum fuerat. ἵνα τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος λάβωμεν διὰ τῆς πίστεως: Subauditur hic nempe. Est enim hoc ira praecedentis ἐπαγγελίαν. Nam quod majus bonum in hac vita poterat feparari Spiritus Sancti donis, praesertim cum illa ipsa certos faciant homines de vita coelesti?

Illa autem dona manifestum, nam quod credentibus in Christum, non per legis opera incedentibus; ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος, id est Spiritus promissus, more Hebraeo: Vide Act. II. 33. adde Aet. I. 4. Hebraeor. c. VI. 11, 15. cap. X. v. 36. Per τὰ ἔθνη nonnulli intelligunt gentes Judaeis contradistinctas, quod etiam fit a Theophylacto. Sed quia benedictio in Christo Abrahae femine in promissione Abrahae facta v. 8. extenditur ad πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, hic ubi causa promissionis, & complementum promissionis... istius explicatur, restringenda ea minime est: Sed aequalem latitudinem habeat necesse est. Pro omnibus gentibus, nationibus, & populis universae terrae, hoc est, pro omnibus hominibus Christus fieri debuit execratio. omnibus ergo etiam per ipsum acquisita est benedictio, sublata execratione, quod ad meritum; ita etiam intenditur à Deo actualis benedictionis collatio, quæ finis est istius ἐξαγορασμοῦ. Pro quibus enim Christus factus est execratio, in illos benedictio Abrahæ in Christo sese porrigit vi intentionis divinæ, & ad illos ea pertingere debet.

H ἡ εὐλογία Ἀβραὰμ intelligitur vel quæ Abrahæ promissa est, vel quæ in semine Abrahæ, ut Theophylactus explicat, contingit. Sed prius est convenientius: Quia in quo ea contingat, post additur, nempe in Christo Jesu. Ita ergo iterum per solam fidem contingere eandem, docetur: quia in Christo Jesu eandem consequimur. Non igitur per opera nostra, vel observantiam legis; sed unice per fidem in Christum Jesum eandem obtinemus: Quod rursus adstruitur, cum additur ab Apostolo, ut promissionem Spiritus accipiamus per fidem, ut vult Calvinus & Pareus. Promissio facta tamen explicatur vel formaliter spiritualis promissio; vel objective, promissio de Spiritu. Neutro modo decedit quicquam Apostolico scopo: Posterior tamen explicatio præferenda, tùm quia mentio jam facta τῆς εὐλογίας τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ benedictionis Abrahæ promissæ, tùm quia fortius adstringitur hic argumentum Apostoli. Si enim etiam ipsam Spiritus Sancti obsignationem, quæ promissa est in Evangelio, non nisi per fidem consequimur, si ad salutem æternam non per opera legis; sed per fidem in Christum obsignamur vel confirmamur à Spiritu Sancto, utique multo magis justificatio tribuenda unice erit fidei, nullo vero modo operibus nostris.

Videmus hic, b. Lutherum dicente, qua merita congrui, ac condigni afferamus, ac qua ratione acquiramus istam benedictionem: Ista est præparatio, hoc est, meritum congrui & condigni, illa sunt opera, quibus paratur hæc justitia, quod Christus Jesus factus sit pro nobis maledictum. Nos enim sumus ignorantes & inimici Dei, sumus mortui in peccatis & maledicti. Ergo meritum nostrum plane nullum est. Quid enim mereretur maledictus peccator, ignorans Dei, mortuus in peccatis, obnoxius iræ & judicio Dei? Cum Papa aliquem excommunicavit, quicquid is faciebat, maledictum erat. Quanto magis maledictus coram Deo, ut omnes sumus, ante Christum cognitum, nihil facit, præter maledicta. Quare illa unica via est evadendi maledictionem, credere & certa fiducia dicere: Tu Christe es peccatum & maledictum meum, seu potius: Ego sum peccatum tuum, maledictum tuum, mors tua, ira Dei tua, infernus tuus, tu contra es justitia, benedictio, vita, gratia Dei, cœlum meum. Quia textus clare dicit: CHRISTUS factus est pro nobis maledictum. Itaque nos sumus causa, quod factus sit maledictum, imo nos ipsius maledictum sumus.

PARS II.

DIDACTICA.

De testamento de semine Christo. & consequenda in eodem hæreditate, & lege, quæ accesserit tantum peccati gratia, & ut pædagogus esset ad Christum, ac per fidem in Christum promissionis hæredes essemus.

Vers.

## 3:15
15. Adelphoi (Brethren).

Whom he had called senseless above, he now calls brethren. For the former is of one more austere and harsh, the latter of one mitigating and placid: I speak, he says, a human example I am about to bring to you, as here Theophylact.

But not only in the MS. of Grotius but in most others the name adelphoi is read, and it is expressed in the received codices. kat' anthrōpon legō (I speak after the manner of men) That is, a human example, from a merely human matter.

The Talmudists are accustomed to use that softening, as often as they attribute something human to God. See what we said on Rom. ch. III. 6. In the Manuscript adelphoi is added here, which both the Latin and the Syriac have read. homōs anthrōpou kekyrōmenēn diathēkēn oudeis athetei ē epidiatassetai diathēkē here signifies a promise, concerning which word we spoke in the prolegomena to the New Testament, and homōs anthrōpou here is, or of a man: For thus we speak, when we bring forward something less than that which is, which we wish to indicate.

If anyone has promised something to another, in such a way that those things which are required for a legitimate promise are present, (for that is kekyrōmenēn Gen. XXII. 19.) no one who is of good faith will either act against it, or change that instrument. The particle homōs here signifies something later, as epiginōskein, Acts XXVII. 13. It is therefore epidiatassetai to constitute something later, namely such that that which had been done before is changed, diathēkē is put for the Hebrew shud (covenant).

The Apostle confirms the certainty of the promise made to Abraham not only because it was firmly sanctioned by a testament, and therefore immutable, since no one even in a human testament epidiatassetai (adds a codicil to) anything regarding the law when it is confirmed, since the divine testament sanctions the blessing in no one but the seed, Christ. But also because by the law, as being much later, it could in no way be rendered void, and consequently he teaches that the letter of the testament and the circumstances of time show the inheritance was given freely not through the law, but through the promise, which we apprehend by faith: Declaring further, for whose sake therefore the law supervened, not to invalidate the testament, most firmly strengthened: But rather to lead us to the promised seed, and the only mediator Christ, so that sin being acknowledged, and its power through the law in us concluded under sin applying itself, if we betake ourselves solely to Christ, and through faith alone in him we may possess the promise of the inheritance.

Faith, he says, in his paraphrase Theophylact, he strives to show, as it were a testament, to be even older than the law. Nor is the law rightly preferred to this, whence he also introduces an example. If a man, he says, has made a Testament, certainly no man will dare either to overturn it: or to dispose anything beyond it, that is, to add anything. Far therefore from God will it be more to be observed.

For he instituted the testament of Abraham, that from his seed might come forth a blessing to the nations, but the seed of Abraham is Christ. Nor did he say seeds, as the posterity of Abraham is understood of the future offspring, such as the Israelites were the Jews, but he preferred seed in the singular number, which is Christ. By what pact therefore could that testament, I say agreement, and promises, the law make void? Lest in Christ the nations be blessed, but rather in the mandates of the law. For what else would that be, than to render the promise of God superfluous? which is clearly absurd.

Blessed Hunnius wishes these things to be said kat' anthypophoran (by way of objection): The objection, he says, comes to this: If righteousness happened from the promise, certainly the law would not have been promulgated only after the promise made to Abraham.

But it is certain that the law was given much later. Therefore, righteousness does not happen from faith through the promise, but through obedience to the law; since later things are accustomed to derogate from earlier ones.

Paul, on the contrary, by an argument deduced from the nature of testaments, makes it plain that the promise, and the righteousness of faith depending on this, was not made void by the subsequent promulgation of the law. By diathēkēn Grotius wishes only a promise, not a testament, to be understood. But why must we depart from the proper sense of the word?

The Apostle certainly confirms that by a rule received in a testament, as if he were to say: The custom known to you, built upon law and right, that a testament legitimately established by some man, and already confirmed by the death of the testator, is accustomed to be held so sacrosanct, that it is a sin to add anything over and above it, or, as Grotius rightly says, to constitute something later, namely such that that which was done before is changed, which is done by adding, subtracting, or disposing quite otherwise. And that is also proven by the word kekyrōmenēn (ratified).

For these testaments. a testament not only lawfully established, but also confirmed by death, which brings with it its full strength already attained. Add to this that not only were promises made to Abraham, but that they obtain the force of a testament, as Zechariah testifies in Luke 1:72. Whence also Paul used the word "testament" in Hebrews 9:16, where it is acknowledged by most that diathēkēn implies not merely a covenant, much less only a promise, but a testament. B.

Hoë, in his Commentary on this passage, p. 151, brings forward ten points of comparison for a testament here: 1. In testaments, the serious and constant will of the testators is posited: So in Holy Scripture, etc. 2. In a testament, certain heirs are named; so here, believers, etc. 3. In testaments, certain legacies are defined: So here, the remission of sins, the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, the possession of grace, and the glory of eternal life, etc. 4. Legacies are assigned to heirs not by merit, but by the grace and benevolence of the Testator: So here, Ephesians 2, Romans 4, etc. 5. Legacies are free and so arranged that the Testator has had plenary power to assign them to the heirs: So here, spiritual goods are most free, and in the plenary power of Christ; neither Moses, nor Satan, nor death, nor hell, nor anyone else has the power to weaken or impede the inheritance on this account. 6. Last wills are committed to writing for the sake of greater certainty: In the same way, the Lord willed His testament to be comprised in the Holy Scriptures. 7. Moreover, proper, perspicuous, and intelligible words are used in testaments: By a like reason, the Holy Spirit has revealed His mind in sufficiently perspicuous and most clear words. 8. In a solemn testament, most trustworthy witnesses are required: Thus in the divine testament, etc. See 1 John 5:7, 8; Acts 10:43. 9. A testament is ratified in the dead, etc. Hebrews 9. 10. Testamentary tablets are read publicly and the will of the testator is manifested: So also the Most High willed His testament to be announced to all nations, etc.

If you say, "But before the law was given, the testament was not yet ratified by the death of Christ": I answer: To God all things are present, and nothing is future to Him. Because, therefore, that kyrōsis (ratification) had been divinely decreed through the death of Christ, it was far most certain; indeed, it was promulgated already in Paradise, long before that solemn nekrothesian (death-appointment), Genesis 3:15. The testament here, to be strengthened one day by the death of Christ, was as firm as if the death of Christ had already intervened; therefore, the Lamb is also said to be slain from the foundation of the world, Revelation 13:8. If anyone, however, refuses to admit that sense of a testament here, he certainly would not easily call it a "mere promise" with Grotius, but a "covenant of confirmation," since diathēkēn undoubtedly carries something more than a promise. Now, conventions, treaties, and pacts, confirmed or ratified by mutual stipulations, signs, and seals, are held among men as asyla (inviolable). Those who deny that these must be kept—arguing with the Jesuits that faith need not be kept with heretics—dissolve the supreme bond of human society; which being broken and dissolved, it is necessary that all things be disturbed by dissensions, seditions, and wars, and that tranquility never be ratified or secure. Finally, that humanity itself is destroyed. Concerning which, elsewhere. But if human pacts are inviolable, how much more so are divine ones; since all the gifts, promises, and covenants of God are utterly ametamelēta (irrevocable), Romans 11:29, and it is impossible for God to lie, Hebrews 6:19, or to deny Himself, 2 Timothy 2:13.

As for the application to the present matter against the Pseudo-Apostles and Papists (which also holds against the Novator Calixtines), Blessed B. Luther has it thus, fol. 8, Tom. II: "They say, unless you are circumcised, unless you keep the law, unless you do many things and suffer them, you cannot be saved. This is not the last will or testament of God.

For He did not say to Abraham: 'If you do this or that, you will obtain the blessing,' or 'those who are circumcised and do the law will obtain it.' But 'In your seed,' etc., as if to say: 'I, out of mere mercy, promise you Christ, who will come from your seed, who will bring the blessing to all nations oppressed by sin and death; that is, who will deliver the nations from eternal curse, that is, from sin and death, by receiving this promise in your seed by faith,' etc.

" Wherefore, as the Pseudo-Apostles of old, so today all Papists and justiciaries are subverters and destroyers, not of a human testament (because they are prohibited by law), but of God's, whom, although He is a consuming fire, they nevertheless do not fear. For such is the nature of hypocrites, that they religiously observe human things, but most securely despise and violate divine things.

But they will bear a horrendous judgment in their own time, those rash despisers and destroyers of the word of God. Verse 16. Τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐῤῥήθησαν αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι) Namely by God, who is of the best faith: promises, repeated several times. Καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ) Rightly: For what was said in one place, Genesis 12:3, concerning Abraham, that same is said of his seed in Genesis 22:18, so that we may clearly understand that that great good would come to the human race through Abraham, namely because from the blood of Abraham there would arise one who would bring it to effect. It was therefore said to Abraham in one way, and to his seed, Christ, in another.

To the former, as to him whom the pact or testament concerned: To the latter, as to him in whom it was struck and established, and who was its object not so much as its basis and foundation. To Abraham, the promise was spoken so that he might embrace for himself by faith the righteousness of the promised seed.

To Christ, however, the seed, it was spoken in no other sense than that the promised blessing was to be obtained through Him, so that it might overflow to the nations. Yet it seems simpler to say: By "seed" here are meant the descendants of Abraham: the promise was spoken to Abraham and to his descendants or children.

Provided that the following words—"He does not say 'in seeds,' etc."—are not torn away to a collective seed, against the express letter of Paul and the collection, which was done by Beza, who here treats things entirely foreign, as if regard were had not to the promise of Genesis 22, but to chapter 18, and as if the speech were not concerning the monadic seed, which is Christ, as Paul explains, but concerning the collective seed, the posterity of Abraham: nor concerning the blessing through Christ, but concerning the coalition of the nations into one body of the promised offspring of Abraham. These things contribute nothing to justification by faith, which the Apostle treats. Beza's argument is weak, that the Apostle says not en spermati (in seed), but, with the preposition omitted, with the copulative particle kai tō spermati sou (and to your seed), which is to be taken in the dative.

For the ellipsis of the preposition en, to which en in Greek corresponds, is not unusual. Compare also Acts 3:25.

Aretius refutes Beza, albeit anonymously. I am not ignorant of what others here bring forward concerning the seed collected from Jews and Gentiles, whose head is Christ and which is called the Church. But let them sweat and labor in the explanation and application of the argument to the purpose. Add that they thrust figures upon the Apostle unwilling.

The Apostle himself interprets it concerning that one seed, that it is Christ. What, therefore, does it avail to explain it concerning the Church and the members of Christ? Certainly, that specious argument is perverted by that interpretation. But that I take "seed" in the former member collectively, not monadically, as in the latter member, where the words of Scripture are placed, this very diversity makes it so, that here no place of Scripture is cited, but simply to Abraham and to his seed. Let the promises mentioned be spoken of: But afterwards, by the words λέγεις [thou sayest], a certain promise regarding the Messiah is looked to, namely that which the Apostle had previously brought forward from Moses in verse 9. So that it is not necessary to take the word σπέρματι [seed], occurring twice in verse 16, in the same sense.

It is certain that the promises concern not only Abraham, but all his seed: Among which stands out that promise concerning all the kindreds of the earth being blessed in that monadic seed, in which seed alone the Apostle teaches that the blessing is founded, and in no other than Christ alone.

Rightly does the Blessed Luther press the word "testament" here, fol. 81.

Here he calls the promises of God spoken to Abraham concerning Christ, the future blesser of all nations, by the new term "testament."

Nor is a promise anything other than a testament not yet revealed, but still sealed. A testament, however, is not a law but a donation. For heirs expect not laws, exactions, or any burden, but an inheritance from a testament. Οὐ λέγει τοῖς σπέρμασιν, ὡς ἐπὶ πολλῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐφ᾽ ἑνός, καὶ τῷ σπέρματι, ὅς ἐστι χριστός [He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ]. For although the Hebrew זֶרַע [seed] is not accustomed to be said in the plural number, Moses could nevertheless have used the word זֶרַע or זְרָעִים [seeds] which would correspond to that Greek σπέρμασι [seeds]: but he did not do so, because he was indicating that there would be one eminent person among the descendants of Abraham who would bring that good to the nations, and that he would not arise from Ishmael, but from Isaac, who in that sacrifice, which is treated there, had borne the figure of Christ.

In a similar way, Christ would be that singular one who was to arise from David, Acts II. 30. Grotius rashly denies that the Hebrew זֶרַע is said in the plural; for it occurs in 1 Sam. VIII. 15. Not without cause, however, does the Apostle urge the singular name of SEED, which, although it may seem collective, the Apostle teaches must here be taken μοναδικῶς [monadically]: Not in seeds, as if many, but as in ONE, and in thy seed, which is OF THY FLESH.

For it is evident that the firmness of the Apostolic thesis, alerted against antagonists, stands in such a peculiar way. For if our works did anything toward obtaining justification, the blessing would not be obtained in that ONE seed: If we were justified before God by our own justice, the blessing and salvation, or beatitude, would not be situated in one Christ, but would be instructed in MANY SEEDS, that is, in all good works of all people. But these things are to be vindicated for the one CHRIST according to the Apostle; for we are all justified through the obedience of that one alone, but no one is justified by his own obedience at the same time. I pass over Calvin, since Grotius refutes his absurdity—that a collective word is taken for one only—in this place.

Jerome notes that "seed" is collective. It is in the promise in Gen. XVII. 7 and elsewhere; yet not always. For does he not leave "seed" behind him who leaves one son?

That it is said of one son is clear from Gen. IV. 25, where Eve says concerning the person of Seth: God has appointed me another seed; and concerning Ishmael in chapter XXI. 13, God says to Abraham: because he is thy seed.

Thus also the LXX Interpreters referred that in Gen. III. v. 15, τὸ σπέρμα τῆς γυναικὸς [the seed of the woman], to the one person of the Messiah, translating with a change of gender: Αὐτός τηρήσει σοὶ κεφαλήν [He shall watch thy head]. Verse

Latin:

15. Ἀδελφοί.

Qvos superius dixerat insensatos, nunc fratres appellat. Illud enim austerioris & duri, hoc mitigantis & placidi: Humanum inquit sum vobis exemplar aliquod allaturus, ut hic Theophylactus.

Non autem in MS. tantum Grotii sed in plerisque; aliis nomen ἀδελφοί legitur, & in receptis codicibus exprimitur. κατ' ἄνθρωπον λέγω) Id est exemplum humanum, à re mere humana.

Solent Talmudici ea emollitione uti, quoties Deo humani aliquid tribuunt. Vide quæ diximus Rom. cap. III. 6. In Manuscripto hic additur ἀδελφοί, quod & Latinus & Syriæ legerunt. ὅμως ἀνθρώπου κεκυρωμένην διαθήκην οὐδεὶς ἀθετεῖ ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεται δαβίης hic significat promissum, de qua voce diximus in prolegomenis ad novum testamentum, & ὅμως ἀνθρώπου hic est, vel hominis: Ita enim loquimur, ubi minus aliquid afferimus, quam id est, quod indicare volumus.

Si quis alteri quid promiserit, ita, ut, quæ ad legitimam promissionem requiruntur, adfuerint, (id enim est κεκυρωμένην Gen. XXII. 19.) nemo qui fit bonæ fidei aut contra faciet, aut instrumentum illud mutabit. Particula ὅμως hic aliquid posterius significat, ut ἐπιγινώσκειν, Aθ. XXVII. 13. est ergo ἐπιδιατάσσεται posterius aliquid constituere, nempe tale, quod id, quod prius factum fuerat, immutetur, διαθήκη ponitur pro Hebræo שׁוּד.

Confirmat Apostolus Abrahæ factæ promissionis certitudinem non modo, quod per testamentum firmiter sancitum, adeoque immutabile, cum nemo etiam in hominum testamento aliquid de jure ἐπιδιατάσσεται cum firmatum est, quandoquidem testamentum divinum non nisi in uno semine Christo benedictionem sanciat. Sed etiam quod per legem ceu multo posteriorem id nullatenus potuerit irritum reddi, & per consequens literæ testamenti & circumstantiæ temporis hæreditatem docet gratis donatam non per legem, sed per promissionem, quam fide apprehendimus: Declarans porro, cujus ergo gratia lex supervenerit, non ad irritandum testamentum, multo firmissime roboratum: Sed potius ad deducendum nos ad promissum semen, unicumque mediatorem Christum, ut peccato agnito, ejusque vi per legem in nobis sub peccato conclusis sese applicante, si ad Christum unice nos recipiamus, & per fidem solam in ipsum promissione hæreditatis potiamur.

Fidem, inquit, in paraphrasi sua Theophylactus, nititur patefacere, veluti testamentum aliquod, esse & lege vetustiorem. Nec jure huic legem præponi, unde & exemplum inducit. Si homo, inquit, fecerit Testamentum, nullus certe hominum vel evertere id audebit: vel ultra aliquid disponit, hoc est, aliquid addit. Longe ergo a Deo id magis erit servandum.

Is namque Abrahæ testamentum instituit, ut ejus ex semine prodiret gentibus benedictio, Abrahæ autem semen est Christus. Nec seminibus dixit, ut Abrahæ futura prolis intelligitur posteritas, quales Judæi fuere Israelitæ, sed semine singulari numero prætulit, quod est Christus. Quo ergo pacto id testamentum, conventionem dico, & promissa poterat lex irrita facere? Ne in Christo gentes benedicantur, sed potius in legis mandatis. Id namque quid aliud esset, quam supervacaneam Dei reddere promissionem? quod plane absurdum est.

B. Hunnius hæc κατ' ἀνθυποφορὰν dici vult: Objectio, inquit, huc redit: Si ex promissione contingeret justitia, utique non demum post promissionem Abrahæ factam, promulgata fuisset lex.

At constat, legem multo post fuisse latam. Ergo non ex fide per promissionem, sed per obedientiam legis contingit justitia; siquidem posteriora derogare solent prioribus.

Paulus contra argumento ex natura testamentorum deducto, planum facit, promissionem, & ab hac dependentem fidei justitiam non esse factam irritam per infectum legis promulgationem. Per διαθήκην Grotius promissum tantum, non testamentum intelligi vult. Sed cur à proprio vocis sensu discedendum?

Firmat utique illum Apostolus regula in testamenti recepta, quasi dicat: Nota vobis consuetudo legi atq; juri superstructa, quod testamentum ab homine aliquo legitime conditum, & jam per mortem testatoris confirmatum, ita soleat haberi sacrosanctum, ut nefas sit, quicquam insuper ei addere, vel, ut recte Grotius, posterius aliquid constituere, nempe tale, id, quod prius factum, immutetur, quod fit addendo, demendo, vel plane aliter disponendo. Idque etiam voce κεκυρωμένην ratificata comprobatur.

Hæc enim testamenta. testamentum non modo legitime sancitum, sed etiam morte confirmatum, quod plenum suum robur jam consequutum infert. Adde quod non tantum promissiones Abrahæ factæ sint, sed quod vim testamenti eædem obtineant, teste Zacharia Luc. I. 72. Unde & Paulus voce testamenti usus est Ebr. IX. 16. ubi διαθήκην non pactum solum, nedum promissum tantum sed testamentum inferre penes plerosque in confesso est. B.

Hoë in Comment. ad h. l. p. 151. membra decem comparationis testamento huc affert 1. in testamentis feria & constans testatorum voluntas ponitur: Ita in scriptura sacra &c. 2. in testamento certi hæredes nominantur; ita hic credentes &c. 3. in testamentis certa legata definiuntur: Ita hic remissio peccatorum, imputatio justitiæ Christi, possessio gratiæ, & gloria vitæ æternæ &c. 4. Hæredibus non ex merito, sed ex gratia & benevolentia Testatoris assignantur legata: Ita hic Ephes. II. Rom. IV. &c. 5. Legata sunt libera & ita comparata, ut Testator plenariam potestatem habuerit, ea hæredibus assignandi: Ita spiritualia bona liberrima sunt, & in plenaria potestate Christi non habet vel Moses, vel Satanas, vel mors, vel infernus, vel quisquam alius, qui hoc nomine hæreditatem enervare vel impedire queat. 6. Ultima voluntates majoris certitudinis causa in literas scriptas referuntur: Eodem modo & Dominus testamentum suum scripturis sanctis comprehendi voluit. 7. Adhibentur autem in testamentis verba propria, perspicua & intelligibilia: Pari ratione Spiritus Sanctus mentem suam satis perspicuis & clarissimis verbis patefecit. 8. In folemni testamento testes fide digniffimi requiruntur: Sic in divino testamento &c. Vide 1. Job. V. 7. 8. Act. X. 43. 9. Testamentum in mortuis ratum est &c. Hebr. IX. 10. Tabula testamentaria publice præleguntur & voluntas testatoris manifestatur: Ita & Altiffimus testamentum suum annuntiari voluit omnibus gentibus &c.

Si dicas, atqui ante legem latam nondum fuit ratificatum per mortem Christi testamentum: Respondeo: Deo omnia præfentia esse, nec quicquam ipsi futurum. Quia igitur decreta divinitus erat illa κύρωσις per mortem Christi longe certissima erat, imo jam in Paradiso, longe ante folemnem illam νεκροθεσίαν promulgata Gen. III. 15. Tam firmum fuit hic testamentum morte Christi olim roborandum, ac si jam mors Christi intervenisset; ideo etiam agnus dicitur ab origine mundi occisus Apoc. XIII. 8. Si quis tamen hic illum testamenti sensum admittere renuat, nudam promissionem certe cum Grotio non facile dixerit, sed pactum confirmationem, quum διαθήκην fine dubio amplius quid portet, quam promissum. Jam conventiones etiam fœdera ac pacta, mutuis stipulationibus, signis & figillis confirmata vel ratificata apud homines habentur ἄσυλα inviolabilia: Quæ qui servanda esse negant cum Jefuitis, hæreticis fidem servandam non esse disputantibus, supremum vinculum societatis humanæ solvunt: quo rupto & soluto necessum est omnia turbari dissidiis, seditio-nibus, bellis, nec unquam ratam aut tutam esse tranquillitatem. Denique humanitatem ipsam tolli. Quo de aliàs. Si autem inviolabilia sunt humanæ pacta, quanto magis divina; quum omnia Dei dona, promissa, fœdera prorsus sint ἀμεταμέλητα Rom. XI. 29. & impossibile fit, Deum mentiri Ebr. VI. 19. ac se ipsum abnegare 2. Tim. II. 13.

Quod ad applicationem ad rem præfentem adversus Pseudo-Apostolos & Papistas, (quæ etiam adversus Novatores Calixtinos valet) ita habet B. Lutherus fol. 8. Dicunt nisi circumcidaris, legem servaveris, multa Tom. II. sed opereris, & patiaris, non potes salvus fieri. Hac non est ultima voluntas aut testamentum Dei.

Non enim dixit ad Abraham: Si hoc aut illud feceris, benedictionem consequeris, aut circumcisis & facientes legem consequentur eam. Sed in semine tuo &c. quasi dicat: Ego ex mera misericordia promitto tibi Christum, ex semine tuo venturum, qui benedictionem afferet omnibus gentibus, peccato & morte oppressis, hoc est, qui ab æterna maledictione, id est peccato & morte liberabit gentes, fide accipientes hanc promissionem in semine tuo &c.

Quare ut olim Pseudo-Apostoli, ita hodie omnes Papistæ & justitiarii sunt eversores & destructores non hominis testamenti, quia jure prohibentur; sed Dei, quem, etsi ignus consumens est, tamen non timent. Ea enim est natura hypocritarum, ut humana religiose obfervent, divinæ securissime contemnant & violent.

Sed portabunt horrendum judicium suo tempore illi temerarii contemtores & destructores verbi Dei. Vers. 16. Τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐῤῥήθησαν αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι) Nempe a Deo, qui optimæ est fidei: promissa, aliquoties repetita. Καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ) Recte: Nam quod uno loco Gen. XII. 3. dictum erat de Abrahamo, id Gen. XXII. 18. de semine ejus dicitur, ut nimirum intelligamus, illud magnum bonum eventurum humano generi per Abrahamum, quia scilicet ex sanguine Abrahami fit exstiturus, qui id effecturus fit. Aliter ergo Abrahamo dictum id fuit, aliter semini ejus Christo.

Illi, ut quem attineret pactum vel testamentum: Huic ut in quo feriebatur id & sanciebatur, quique erat ejusdem non tàm objectum, quam basis & fundamentum. Abrahæ dicta est promissio, ut illam fide amplexaret sibi justitiam promissi feminis.

Christo autem semini sensu non alio dicta, quam quod per ipsum benedictio promissa concilianda, ut redundaret in gentes. Simplicius tamen videtur dici: Per semen hic intelligi posteros Abrahæ: promissionem dictam esse Abrahamo & posteris ejus vel filiis.

Dummodo non sequentia: Non dicit in seminibus &c. ad semen collective contra disertam Pauli literam & collectionem abripiantur, quod à Beza fatum, qui hic prorsus aliena tractat, quasi non ad promissionem Gen. XXII. sed cap. XVIII. respectus habeatur, non de semine monadico, quod est Christus; uti Paulus explicat, sed de semine collectivo, posteritate Abrahami sermo fit: Nec de benedictione per Christum agatur, sed de gentium coalitione in unum corpus sobolis Abrahæ promissæ: Quæ ad justificationem per fidem, de qua tractat Apostolus, nihil faciunt. Argumentum Bezæ leve est, quod Apostolus dicat non ἐν σπέρματι, sed omissa Præpositione cum particula copulativa καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σου, quod in dativo accipiendum fit.

Ellipsis enim Præpofitionis ἒ, cui in Græco ἐν respondet, non insolens est. Conf. & Act. III. 25.

Bezam refellit Aretius etsi ἀνωνύμως. Non ignoro, quid alii hic afferant de semine collecto ex Judais & gentibus, cui caput est Christus & Ecclesia dicitur. Sed sudent & laborent in argumenti explicatione & applicatione ad propositum. Adde quod figuras obtrudunt Apostolo invito.

Apostolus ipsum interpretatur de semine illo unico, quod is fit Christus. Quid igitur attinet id, de Ecclesia & membris Christi explicare? Certe pervertitur speciosum argumentum illa interpretatione. Ad ut autem semen in priori membro collective accipiam non monadice, ut in posteriori membro, ubi ponuntur verba scripturæ, facit hæc ipsa diversitas, quod hic nullus locus scripturæ afferatur, sed simpliciter Abrahamo & semini ejus promissiones dictæ dicantur: Postea verò verbis λέγεις certa promissio respiciatur de Messia, illa nempe, quam antea Apostolus è Mose adduxerat vers. 9. ut proinde non necessum sit, vocem σπέρματι in v. 16. bis occurrentem eodem sensu accipere.

Certum est non tantum Abrahamum, sed omne ejus semen concernere promissiones: Inter quas eminet illa de omnibus cognationibus terræ, in semine illo monadico benedicendis, quam non in alio, præterquam in solo Christo fundari docet Apostolus benedictionem.

Recte hic B. Lutherus vocem testamenti premit fol. 81.

Hic novo vocabulo promissiones Dei Abrahæ dictas de Christo benedicsore futuro omnium gentium, appellat testamentum.

Neque aliud quiddam est promissio, quam testamentum nondum revelatum, sed adhuc obsignatum. Testamentum autem non est lex sed donatio. Heredes enim non leges, exactiones aut gravamen aliquod, sed hereditatem ex testamento expectant. Οὐ λέγει τοῖς σπέρμασιν, ὡς ἐπὶ πολλῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐφ᾽ ἑνός, καὶ τῷ σπέρματι, ὅς ἐσι χρισός) Nam quanquam Hebræum זֶרַע plurali numero dici non folet, poterat tamen Moses usurpasse vocem זֶרַע aut זְרָעִים quæ isti Græco σπέρμασι responderet: at id non fecit, quia indicabat, unum aliquem fore inter posteros Abrahami eximium, qui illud bonum gentibus effet allaturus, & eum quidem non ex Ismaele oriturum, sed ex Isaaco, qui in eo sacrificio, de quo ibi agitur, Christi gesserat figuram.

Simili modo Christus fingulariter ille esset, qui ex Davide oriri debebat, Act. II. 30. Ebræum זֶרַע temere negat in Plurali dici Grotius; Occurrit enim 1. Sam. IIX. 15. Non absque causa autem urget Apostolus nomen fingulare SEMINIS, quod etsi collectivum videatur; hic tamen μοναδικῶς accipiendum docet Apostolus: Non in seminibus, quasi multis, sed ut in UNO & in semine tuo, quod est CARNIS TUÆ.

Constat enim ita peculiari ratione theseos Apostolicæ adversus Antagonistas alertæ, sua firmitas. Nam si nostra opera quicquam ad justificationem consequendam facerent, non in UNO illo semine obtingeret benedictio: Si nostra justitia coram Deo justificaremur, in MULTIS SEMINIBUS, omnium puta bonis operibus, instruatur pietate, non in uno Christo sita esset benedictio ac salus, vel beatitudo. At hæc uni CHRISTO vindicanda fecundum Apostolum funt etiam per unius ipsius obedientiam o- mnes justificamur, non vero quisquam justificatur sua simul obedientia. Calvinum taceo, cum illius absurdum, verbum collectivum de uno tantum accipi, Grotius refellat h. l.

Hieronymus notat, semen esse collectivum. Est in promissione Gen. XVII. 7. & alibi; non tamen semper. Annon enim relinquit semen post se, qui unum relinquit filium?

De uno filio dici, patet è Genef. IV. 25. ubi de Sethi persona dicit Eva: Posuit mihi Deus semen aliud; & de Ismaele cap.

13. Abrahamo Deus dicit: quia semen tuum est. Sic etiam LXX. Interpretes illud Gen. III. v. 15. τὸ σπέρμα τῆς γυναικὸς ad unam Messiæ personam retulerunt, mutato genere vertentes: Αὐτός τηρήσει σοὶ κεφαλήν. Vers.

## 3:17
17. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω [And this I say]) After he explained the sense of the promise, he returns to the discourse which he had interrupted, and shows to what that which he had said pertains, namely that promises having their perfection are not rescinded. Διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ εἰς χρισόν [A covenant confirmed before of God in Christ]) That is, that promise already perfected by God, pertaining to Christ.

In the Manuscript, that εἰς χρισόν [in Christ] is missing. It is read commonly in other Codices, nor was it rashly added by the Apostle; the testament is said to be confirmed in Christ, both so that it might be ratified by the death of Christ the testator, Heb. IX. v. 15, and because the benefits promised by the same—justification, adoption, the inheritance of eternal life—do not come except by faith in Christ, indeed once to be exhibited, but now exhibited. Ὁ μετὰ ἔτη τετρακόσια κὴ τριάκοντα γεγονὼς νόμος· ὐκ ἀκυροῖ [The law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul]) This number is taken from the passage in Exod.

XII. v. 40, where we said that the beginning seems to be taken from that revelation made to Abraham, which is described in Gen. XII. 11, 12, but a little before that, that promise mentioned in Gen. XII. 3 had preceded; wherefore Paul preferred to keep this number, which was most well-known to the Hebrews, rather than to add even a little, nor did it matter, since the lesser is comprehended in the greater number.

Not for this reason was the law given at such a later time, so that what Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the Patriarchs had believed would be, might be made void; one must therefore look to what Christ brings, not what the law brought. Εἰς τὸ καταργήσῃ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν [that it should make the promise of none effect]) He explains what he had said. You have the same words in Rom. ch. IV. verse 14, where see what is said.

The calculation of the 430 years is not so much to be reckoned from Gen. XII. 11, 12—which is the opinion of Grotius, following the Hebrews and Mercator, namely from the departure of Abraham into Egypt—as from the time of the first promise, in the 75th year of Abraham's age, which we taught in the Sacred Chronicle; nor does Pareus profit anything, however much Grotius follows him, here recounting three confirmations: one through the federal sacrifice in Gen.

XV, another through the general sacrament in Gen. XVII, the third through the solemn oath in Gen. XXII. v. 16.

The first was made in the 85th year of Abraham's age. The second after 14 years, in the 99th year of his age. The third again after 26 years, in the 125th year of his age: and he refers the beginning of this epoch to the first. But the time of that first confirmation is nowhere found defined in the sacred history, as we noted in the Chronicle, as neither is that of the third, concerning which see our commentary on Gen.

XXII. Nor does the Apostle begin from the confirmation but from the promise in v. 16, and he primarily regards that: he brings in the confirmation properly only for the sake of certainty, lest anyone dare to superadd anything, although this is not permitted even to the divine promise; for the sake of greater strength, namely. Moreover, you would more rightly refer the covenant and the testament to Gen.

XV, where the sacrament of circumcision was instituted, which pertained to the old covenant or testament: from which, however, the beginning of the epoch is not to be drawn, as Pareus himself acknowledges. The Blessed Luther collects this epoch thus in Tom. I. Jen.

Latino fol. 352, commentary on this passage. Now this is to be seen, that the law was given after 430 years.

For those years are counted from Abraham's departure out of his land, when he first received the promise Gen. XII, up to the departure of the children of Israel in this way: Abraham went out of his land in his 75th year Gen. XII; being a hundred years old, however, he begat Isaac (so you have 25 years); Isaac, being sixty years old, begat Esau and Jacob Gen. XXI.

(mark 60 years); Jacob, being ninety years old, begat Joseph (mark 90 years), as is gathered from Genesis through many chapters. Joseph lived 110 years, Gen. last. After him the servitude of Egypt lasted 65, as Job. Annius says from Philo; then Moses was born, in whose 80th year the children of Israel went out. Therefore from the 75th year of Abraham to the 80th year of Moses there are 430 years. Thus also Aretius on this passage. The Blessed Luther beautifully illustrates the matter itself: Paul says (fol. 81 b.) that the law cannot abrogate the promise. Therefore that promise made to Abraham 430 years before the law remains firm. And that the thing may be understood more, I will illustrate it with some similitude. If some rich man, not compelled, but of his own good will, should adopt a certain unknown person, to whom he plainly owed nothing, and should appoint him heir of all his goods. Then, after some years having passed after this benefit shown to him, he should impose upon him a law, of doing this or that. He could not then say that he had merited by his own works this benefit, since so many years before, with him asking for nothing, he had received this freely out of mere grace. Thus, neither could God look to works and merits preceding justice. Because the promise and the gift of the Holy Spirit was four hundred and thirty years before the law.

Latin:

17. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω) Postquam promissi sensum explicavit, redit ad sermonem, quem interruperat, & oftendit, quo pertineat illud, quod dixerat, promissa perfectionem suam habentia non rescindi. Διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ εἰς χρισόν) Id est, promissum illud jam perfectum à Deo, pertinens ad Christum.

In Manuscripto deeft illud εἰς χρισόν. Legitur id in aliis Codicibus communiter, nec temere additum ab Apostoło, confirmatum dicitur testamentum in Christum, tùm ut Christi testatoris morte ratificaretur Ebr. IX. v. 15. tùm quia beneficia eodem promissa, justificatio, adoptio, hereditas vitæ æternæ, non nisi fide in Christum olim quidem exhibendum, nunc vero exhibitum contingunt. Ὁ μετὰ ἔτη τετρακόσια κὴ τριάκοντα γεγονὼς νόμος· ὐκ ἀ- κυροῖ) Numerus hic desumitur ex loco Exod.
