XII. v. 40. ubi diximus, initium videri sumendum ab ea revelatione, Abrahamo facta, quæ describitur Gen. XII. 11. 12. paulo vero ante id præcesserat promissio illa memorata Genes. XII. 3. quare hunc numerum Hæbræis notissimum servare, quam aliquantillum adjicere maluit Paulus, nec quicquam intererat, quando in numero majore comprehenditur minor.

Non ob id tanto post tempore data est lex, ut quod Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus & Patriarchæ crediderant futurum, id irritum fieret, respiciendum ergo, quid Christus afferat, non quid lex attulerit. Εἰς τὸ καταργήσῃ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν) Explicat quod dixerat. Eadem verba habes Rom. cap. IV. vers. 14. ubi dicta vide.

Calculus annorum CCCCXXX. non tam ineundus à Gen. XII. 11. 12. quæ Grotii est opinio ab Ebræis & Mercatore, à profectione nempe Abrahami in Ægyptum, quam à tempore primæ promissionis, anno ætatis Abrahæ 75. quod in Chronico facro docuimus, nec quicquam proficit Pareus, utut eum sequatur Crotius tres hic recensens κυρώσεις, unam per sacrificium fœderale Gen.

XV. alteram per sacramentum generale Gen. XVII. tertiam per jusjurandum solenne Gen. XXII. v. 16.

Primam, ætatis Abrahæ anno 85. Alteram post annos 14. ætatis anno 99. Tertiam rursus post annos 26. ætatis anno 125. factam: & ad primam hujus epochæ initium refert. Sed primæ istius κυρώσεως tempus nuspiam definitum legitur in S. historia, quod in Chronico monuimus, ut neque tertiæ, de qua ad Gen.

XXII. commentarius noster videndus. Nec Apostolus à κυρώσει sed ab ἐπαγ-γελία initium facit v. 16. eamque primario respicit: κυρώσει proprie tantum certitudinis causa, ne quis audeat aliquid superordinare, quanquam nec promissioni divinæ hoc liceat, adducit; majoris scilicet roboris gratia. Cæterum fœdus, & testamentum rectius referas ad Gen.

XV. ubi circumcisionis institutum est sacramentum, quæ ad fœdus vel testamentum vetus pertinebat: ex quo vero initium epochæ ducendum non esse, Pareus ipse agnoscit, B. Lutherus epocham hanc ita colligit Tom. I. Jen.

Latino fol. 352. comment. in h. l. Nunc id videndum, quod lex post 430. annos data est.

Supputantur enim anni isti ab exitu Abrahæ de terra sua, quando primo accepit promissionem Gen. XII. usque ad exitum filiorum Isräel boc modo: Abraham 75. anno egressus est de terra sua Gen. XII. centenarius autem genuit Isaac, (sic habes 25. annos) Isaac sexagenarius genuit Esau & Jacob Gen. XXI.

(signa 60. annos) Jacob nonagenarius genuit Joseph (90. annos signa) ut ex Genesi per multa capita colligitur. Joseph vixit 110. annos Gen. ult. Post hunc duravit servitus Ægypti 65. ut Job. Annius ex Philone dicit, tunc Moses natus, cujus anno 80. exierunt filii Ismel. Igitur à 75. anno A- brahæ ad 80. annum Mosis sunt 430. anni. Sic etiam Aretius in hunc locum, Rem ipsam pulchre illustrat B. Lutherus: Paulus dicit (fol. 81 b.) legem non posse abrogare promissionem. Ideo promissio illa Abrahæ facta 430. annis ante legem manet rata. Et ut res intelligi possit magis, illustrabo aliqua similitudine. Si aliquis dives non coactus, sed ex bona voluntate ignotum quendam, cui plane nihil deberet, adoptaret sibi & institueret heredem omnium bonorum suorum. Deinde trunsaslis aliquot annis post exhibitum hoc illi beneficium imponeret ei legem, hoc vel aliud faciendi. Is jam non posset dicere, se meritum suis operibus hoc beneficium, cum tot annis ante, ipso nihil petente, ex mera gratia hoc gratis accepisset. Ita nec Deus respicere potuit opera & merita praecedentia justitiam. Quia promissio & donum Spiritus Sancti fuit quadringentis & ...triginta annis ante legem.

## 3:18
Verse 18. Ἐν γὰρ ἐκ νόμῳ ἡ κληρονομία) The possession of eternal life and happiness. See the place already mentioned in Romans. Οὐκ ἔτι ἐξ ἐπαγγελίας) Namely, concerning Christ: For this promise is spoken of by way of eminence, Acts II. 39. VII. 17. XIII. 32. Τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐκ χαρίσαι ὁ Θεός) Namely, God gave Christ as a descendant to Abraham after many generations, and that according to the ancient promise. Thus God is said to have given a lamp to David, long after the time of his death, 2 Kings VIII. 19. That κεχάρισαι ὁ Θεός does not have Christ the descendant as its object, but the inheritance of eternal life.

For it is concerning this that it is discussed here. The Apostle therefore now urges the argument here from opposites: If the inheritance is from the law, it is not from the promise. But it is from the promise. For God gave the inheritance to Abraham through a promise. Therefore, it is not from the law. The major premise is clear, because the law and the promise are immediate opposites, which mutually posit and remove each other, and can by no means be joined or mixed, as is most certain from the entire Apostolic treatment in this epistle and the one to the Romans: not as if the doctrine of the law and the Gospel are repugnant to each other, but because the legal and Evangelical modes of justification cannot stand together or be mixed into one. Concerning which the Blessed Luther speaks excellently again in this place. Thus Rom. IV., if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is abolished and the promise is void. Nor can it be otherwise, because this distinction is most clear, that the law is a thing most different from the promise. Indeed, natural reason, however blind, is nevertheless forced to confess that it is one thing to promise, another to demand; one thing to give, another to receive. The law demands our works from us; the promise offers to the faithful the spiritual and eternal offices of God, and indeed freely on account of Christ. Therefore, we obtain the promise or inheritance from the promise, not the law: Because the promise says: In your seed shall be blessed, etc. Therefore, having the law is not enough: Because one does not yet have the blessing, without which one is forced to remain under a curse. Therefore, the law cannot justify, because the blessing was not added to it. Furthermore, if the law were the inheritance, God would be found a liar and the promise would be made void. Likewise, if the law could obtain the blessing, why would God promise it in your seed? etc. Why would He not rather say, do this and you will receive the blessing? Or: You can merit eternal life by doing. This argument is from opposites: the inheritance is given from the promise. Therefore, not from the law. The emphasis of the words must also be observed: For the inheritance is not obtained by merits, but is obtained freely: The promise is not apprehended by works but by faith. And that κεχάρισαι, God has gratified, that is, has given out of grace, to that works contributed nothing. For if it is by grace, it is not by works, otherwise grace would not be grace, Rom. XI. 6. The Blessed Luther also notes in his earlier Commentary, Vol. III. fol. 28, that the Apostle calls the testament of God promises, and implies that it would come to pass that God would die: so that in this way the incarnation and passion of God might be understood at the same time.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἐν γὰρ ἐκ νόμῳ ἡ κληρονομία) Possessio aeternae vitae & felicitatis. Vide jam dictum ad Romanos locum. Οὐκ ἔτι ἐξ ἐπαγγελίας) Nempe de Christo: Nam haec ἐπαγγελία dicitur per eminentiam, Actor. II. 39. VIL 17. XIII. 32. Τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐκ χαρίσαι ὁ Θεός) Nempe Christum nepotem post multos gradus Abrahamo dedit, idque secundum vetus promissum. Sic Deus dicitur lucernam dedisse Davidi, multo post mortem ejus tempore, 2. Reg. VIII. 19. Illud κεχάρισαι ὁ Θεός pro objecto non habet Christum nepotem, sed hereditatem vitae aeternae.

De ea enim hic disseritur. Argumentum itaque hic jam urget Apostolus à contrariis: Si haereditas est ex lege, non est ex promissione. At est ex promissione. Haereditatem enim Abrahae Deus per promissionem donavit. Non ergo est ex lege. Major liquet, quia legem & promissionem esse contraria ἄμεσα, quae se mutuo ponant & tollant, ac conjungi vel misceri nulla ratione queant, ex tota Apostolica tractatione in hac & ad Romanos epistola, quam certissimum est: non quasi doctrina legis & Evangelii sibi repugnet, sed quod justificationis modus legalis & Evangelicus simul stare, aut in unum misceri non possint. Quo de praeclare iterum B. Lutherus in h. l. Sic Rom. IV. si qui ex lege sunt, haeredes sunt, abolita est fides & promissio irrita. Neque aliter fieri potest, quia ista distinctio clarissima est, quod lex diversissimum quiddam est à promissione. Imo ratio naturalis, quamlibet caeca tamen fateri cogitur, quod aliud sit promittere, aliud exigere, aliud donare, aliud accipere. Lex exigit à nobis opera nostra, promissio feminis offert officia Dei spiritualia & aeterna, & quidem gratis propter Christum. Ergo ex promissione non lege consequimur promissionem seu hereditatem: Quia promissio dicit: In semine tuo benedicentur &c. Ergo habens legem non habet satis: Quia nondum habet benedictionem, sine qua cogitur manere sub maledicto. Igitur lex non potest justificari, quia non addita est ei benedictio. Deinde si lex esse esset hereditas, Deus inveniretur mendax & promissio fieret irrita. Item si lex posset impetrare benedictionem, cur Deus eam promitteret in semine tuo? &c. Cur non potius diceret, fac hoc & accipies benedictionem? Vel: Tu potes faciendo mereri vitam aeternam. Hoc argumentum ex contrariis est: ex promissione datur hereditas. Ergo non ex lege. Observanda etiam vocum emphatis: Nam hereditas non obtinetur meritis, sed gratis obtinetur: Promissio non apprehenditur operibus sed fide. Et quod κεχάρισαι gratificatus est Deus, id est ex gratia donavit, ad id nihil contulere opera. Si enim ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia Rom. XI. 6. B. Lutherus notat etiam in priori Comment. Tom. III. fol. 28. quod apostolus testamentum Dei promissiones vocet, atque innuat fore, ut Deus moreretur: ut ita simul incarnatio & passio Dei intelligatur.

## 3:19
Verse 19. Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος· τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη) Other codices are better: Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος· τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη. Why then the law, someone might say? Paul answers that the law was added, namely after the promises, because the vices of the Israelite people in Egypt had increased, and they had to be restrained by the evils of punishments, lest they gradually slide into impiety through that depraved custom.

See below, V. 23. and 1 Timothy I. 9. The reading of Irenaeus ὁ νόμος τῶν πράξεων προσετέθη, which he follows and

III. 7. as Beza warned, and V. 21. is less suitable for this place.

He raises a doubt, but in such a way that he establishes his thesis. He asks: For what good then is the law? He answers: That it was only added, or a certain accessory, not for this, that the blessing should be from it, but for the sake of another use, namely παραβάσεων χάριν, not that it might provoke and argue transgressions, which Pareus wants. For he himself admits that this is by accident, because of the depravity of nature, by which we all strive for what is forbidden; nor does that pertain to the present discussion: But that it might manifest and argue the same, just as he had hinted before, when he commemorated the execration of the law: and further that it might compel us to flee to Christ. Although indeed the law also serves to restrain transgressions, that does not properly pertain here. Which the Blessed Luther taught excellently in his Commentary on this place, Anno 1524. But what D. Jerome denies, he understands as if transgressions were restrained through the law; to this he resists first, because then it should rather have been said to be placed for the sake of justification; for the law is placed for the sake of observance. Secondly, because this trope becomes familiar to the Apostle: The law is the power of sin, the occasion of sin, the law of death, the law of wrath. Thus Rom. IV., the law works wrath. For where there is no law, there is neither transgression nor remission. Where there is no remission, there is no salvation. Therefore, as remission is for the sake of salvation, so is transgression for the sake of remission, so is the law for the sake of transgression. The law posits sin, sin posits remission, remission posits salvation. All this, because without the law, sin is dead and is not known, Rom. V. and VII. Sin was in the world, but it was not imputed until Moses. The sense is therefore: The law was placed for the sake of transgression, so that transgression might be and abound, and thus through the law man, brought to the knowledge of himself, might seek the hand of the merciful God, who without the law, ignorant of sin, seems healthy to himself. Thirdly, nor do the following parts agree, until the seed should come. For it is absurd that transgression should be restrained until Christ comes: since it is situated that it should not be restrained, when the Apostle meant the opposite, that sin through the law was not only not restrained, but also increased, until Christ coming might end sin, by fulfilling the law and giving grace, as Gabriel says in Dan. IX., that sin might receive an end, and everlasting righteousness be brought in. As if he were saying: Sin took its beginning in Adam, through the law also its increase, through Christ alone it will receive its end, who brings in everlasting righteousness with sin dead, as in Ps. CX. and CXI. His righteousness remains for age after age. Fourthly, nor does it agree with that: Therefore is the law against the promises of God? Nor would this be inferred if the Apostle wanted the law to be understood as placed for restraining transgression, because then it would not be against the promises, but for the promises. But now, because it increases sin, and likewise provokes it, it appears not to provoke God to fulfill the promises, but rather to irritate and hinder. By understanding it thus, the context coheres beautifully, otherwise you would have to invent so many things, which are necessary constructions. Fifthly, what he says, in the hand of a Mediator, which in my judgment he says because the law was not placed in our hand, so that we might fulfill it, but in the hand of the future Christ, to be fulfilled by him. Wherefore it was not placed to justify, but rather to argue sinners, and to require the hand of a Mediator. For human pride had to be resisted, lest it believe the Son of God was incarnated by its own merits, and become ungrateful for such great mercy. Now, having fallen into demerits, we love a God who is the more faithful and merciful, the more unworthy we were to whom He showed such great mercy. For to us, through the law, comes knowledge: but to Christ alone, fulfillment and operation. reason, until the seed should come, to whom it was promised, that is, in whom the blessing, justice, and fullness of the law was to be given: And the transgressions, which were by the law, were not now to be restrained, but to be extinguished, which is effected through faith in Christ. The law therefore manifests and condemns transgressions, but not so that we should perish by its curse, but that you might look to the divine intention, but that through the same as a pedagogue we might be led to Christ: therefore it was given into the hand of the Mediator Christ, because otherwise by the thunderbolt of the same, men would have perished: which Mediator between two parties, God and men, intervened even in the very promulgation of the law, lest the law should exercise the power of cursing, as one who was about to derive the deprecation of the law into himself, and was about to deliver us from it.

Argument a new one is born hence; If the law so manifests and condemns transgressions, that with respect to the divine intention in the very promulgation of the law, we are convinced that we have need of a Mediator, unless we are to perish eternally, therefore liberation or the remission of sins and justification cannot in any way be derived through the law itself. (For these are entirely opposite, the condemnation of transgressions, and the forgiveness of transgressions) but it must be obtained solely through the Mediator. But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. Here B. Luther is to be heard again, who in his Comment. post. fol. 84. says: The law also, he says, is a light, which shines and shows not the grace of God, not justice and life, but sin, death, wrath, and the judgment of God.

For just as on Mount Sinai thunder, lightning, a dark cloud, a smoking and burning mountain, and all that terrifying appearance did not gladden, nor did it give life to the children of Israel, but terrified them, rendered them almost lifeless, and showed how they could not bear, and showed how they could not [bear] the presence of God speaking from the cloud. So the law when it is in its true use, does nothing else than reveal sin, causes wrath, accuses and terrifies men, so that they are not far from despair. This is the proper use of the law, thus it has an end, and it ought not to proceed further. On the contrary, the Gospel is a light, which illuminates, gives life, consoles, and raises up fearful minds. For it shows that God is propitious to sinners and the unworthy on account of Christ, if they believe that they are liberated through his death from the curse, that is, from sin and eternal death, and through his victory [that he gives] to them the blessing, that is, grace, the remission of sins, and eternal life. A little later: The law shows men to themselves, that he is a sinner, guilty of death, and worthy of eternal wrath.

To what purpose does that humiliation, bruising, and contrition by that very hammer, namely the law, serve? It serves for this, that the way to grace might be opened to us. Thus therefore the law is a minister and preparer for grace.

For God is the God of the humble, the miserable, the afflicted, the oppressed, the desperate, and of those who have been reduced to nothing; and his nature is to exalt the humble, to feed the hungry, to illuminate the blind, to console the miserable and afflicted, to justify sinners, to give life to the dead, to save the desperate and the damned, etc. For he is the almighty creator, making all things out of nothing. But to this his natural and proper work, that most harmful plague, the opinion of justice, does not allow him to arrive, which does not want to be sinful, unclean, miserable, and damned, but just, holy, etc. Therefore it is necessary for God to employ the hammer itself, namely the law, which might break, crush, grind, and utterly reduce to nothing this beast with its vain confidence, wisdom, justice, power, etc., so that at length by its own evil it might learn that it is lost and damned. And there then, the conscience being thus terrified by the law, the doctrine of the Gospel and grace has a place, which again raises up and consoles, saying: That Christ came into the world, not to despise the bruised reed, not to extinguish the smoking flax, but to announce the Gospel to the poor, to heal the contrite in heart, to preach remission to the captives, etc.

Thus by Accident (continues the Man of God, with a few things interposed) with its own office it also profits for justification, not indeed justifying, but urging toward the promise of grace, and making it sweet and desirable.

Wherefore we do not abrogate the law, but we indicate the true use and office of it: which is, namely, that it becomes a most useful minister, urging toward Christ. Therefore after the law has humbled you, terrified you, and utterly crushed you, so that you are now near to despair, see that you know how to use the law rightly. Because its office and use is, not only to show sin and the wrath of God, but also to compel toward Christ. The Holy Spirit alone shows this use of the law in the Gospel, where he testifies that God is present to the contrite in heart, etc. Wherefore if you are crushed by this hammer, do not perversely use this contrition, so that you burden yourself with more laws, but hear Christ saying: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. When the law thus urges you, with all your affairs desperate, to seek help and consolation from Christ, then it is in its true use, and serves through the Gospel for justification, until it is the best and most perfect use of the law. B.

Brentius on this passage fol. 836. And then when Paul says (on account of transgressions) it is to be understood, to be shown, illustrated, amplified, exaggerated, and recognized in the conscience. For in the testament, which God established with Abraham and his seed, which is Christ, God promised the blessing, or justice and salvation to all peoples on account of Christ.

Human nature is so blinded by original sin that it does not recognize its own injustice, but thinks that by its own powers it can attain justice and salvation, and does not need Christ. For what Satan said to Eve: You shall be as Gods, this still clings in the flesh and blood of man, so that he attributes to his depraved nature some divinity, and does not acknowledge himself to be a slave of Satan, but rather imagines himself to be a certain god, who can help by his own powers. Therefore the law was given, the decalogue was given, that it might show us our sin, that it might illuminate sin in our conscience, that it might magnify sin, and in short, that it might declare that we are not Gods, but rather devils or slaves of the devil and liable to Gehenna; on which matter see in epist. ad Rom. cap. IV. & VI. But to what end does the law show us sins, and declare us slaves of the devil? Nothing less: For he says: I live, I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live. The law therefore shows us both the magnitude and the gravity of sin and binds us over to Satan, that it may compel us to seek Christ. Rightly therefore B. Hunnius: The sense is: The law was given, not that it might confer justice upon men of sinful nature, but that it might rather arraign them for injustice, and, with transgressions demonstrated to the Israelite people, remove their perverse opinion concerning the justice of works and of salvation to be expected from the law. Ἄχρις οὗ ἔλθῃ τὸ σπέρμα, ᾧ ἐπήγγελται) that is, it would have its force (for this is here understood) until that descendant of Abraham should come, through whom the nations were to receive the highest goods, and toward whom that promise made to Abraham looked, plainly, as if it had been made to them; the same thing is said here as at the beginning of cap. VII. ad Romanos. Plainly genuine are these epistles, and strong is the argument, if the law now binds not even the Jews, much less the nations. Other Codices read ᾐ ἐπήγγελται semen promissum. promiſſum.

Hunnius: The sense is: The law was given, not to confer justice upon men who are sinners by nature, but rather to hold them guilty of injustice and, with the transgressions demonstrated to the Israelite people, to remove the perverse opinion concerning the justice of works and salvation to be expected from the law. Ἄχρις οὗ ἔλθῃ τὸ σπέρμα, ᾧ ἐπήγγελται) that is, about to have its power, (for that is understood here) until that descendant of Abraham should come, through whom the nations were to receive the highest goods, and to whom that promise, made to Abraham, looked, plainly, as if it had been made to him, he says the same thing here, which he says at the beginning of chapter VII to the Romans. These epistles are plainly related, and the argument is valid, if the law does not now bind even the Jews, much less the nations. Other Codices ᾐ ἐπήγγελται the promised seed. until the seed should come, to whom the promise was made, namely of the blessing to be procured, and as far as the benevolent intention of God is concerned, also to be conferred upon all the nations of the earth, in the way that Christ is said to have received the promise of the Holy Spirit in Acts 2:33, and therefore that also holds very well.

But the whole economy of the law had to last only until the blessed seed, so that it might be the more evident that the end and completion of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. 10:4, and so that for that reason also the pedagogical use of the law might be established. With respect to which divine intention, the blessed Luther rightly teaches that it is spiritually hinted here that the law ought not to dominate consciences any longer than until the seed comes. When, therefore, he says, the law shows me sin, terrifies me, and has revealed the wrath and judgment of God, so that I begin to grow pale, to despair, etc. There the law especially has its mode, time, and end, so that it may cease to exercise its tyranny. Because then it does its duty, it sufficiently shows the wrath of God and has terrified. Here it must be said: cease, law, you have sufficiently terrified and crushed me. All your waves have passed over me, your terrors have troubled me. Likewise: Do not turn your face away from your servant in anger, O Lord; do not, I pray, rebuke me in your fury, etc. When these fears and complaints come, it is the time and hour of the blessed seed. Let the law therefore yield, which was indeed added for the sake of revealing and increasing transgressions, but only for so long, until the seed comes, in whose presence the law ceases to reveal transgressions and to terrify, and hands over the kingdom to another, namely to the blessed seed, that is, to Christ, who has gracious lips, with which he does not accuse, terrify, etc., but speaks of things far better than the law, namely of grace, peace, remission of sins, victory over sin, death, etc., by his own death and resurrection shared and given to believers. Although the blessed Luther takes it thus spiritually, as he says, he does not, however, deny that the economy of the law and the Mosaic cult are said here literally to have had to last until the time of grace, see Matt. 11:13, 9:27, Heb. 10:1; but if we inquire into the cause of that matter, he wishes to hint at that which he has already explained: which is explained in v. 22. Which in the earlier edition of the Commentary of the blessed Luther published in the year 1520 is in our judgment most conveniently explained: We have cited his words above. Thus, therefore, perhaps it will not be inappropriately said that the particle ἄχρι does not denote the time of the duration of the Mosaic law, but notes the order or the end, that it surely explains its power in us up to that point and to that end, which transgressions the law is to argue and condemn, until the seed arrives to whom the promise was made, so that it may effectively penetrate to us with the blessing, which ἄχρι introduces not an order of time, but rather a reason of divine dispensation, Rev. 7:3, concerning not harming the earth until ἄχρις the servants of God are sealed. For the servants of God are not sealed first in time, before the evil angels can ἀδικεῖν, and until that point they rest or are restrained. But the reason of the divine economy is designated, that God restrains the evil angels to that end, so that the servants of God, as if peculiarly sealed by God, may not be harmed. Not only until Christ (by reason of time) does the law have the power to argue and condemn transgressions, but at all times it has its power until Christ is recognized in the word of promise and apprehended by faith. Until, says the blessed

Brentius, the seed should come, to whom it was promised, that is, the law therefore reveals transgressions, so that it may drive us to Christ, and does not cease to condemn us, except while Christ is coming, except while we receive Christ through faith. For then the law no longer condemns us, but lets us go free.

Whence he also says later: The scripture has concluded all under sin, so that the promise of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Here is the same end of punishments and afflictions, by which GOD does not wish to destroy us, but to invite us to seek salvation in Christ his Son, something most despised and utterly rejected. Brentius is therefore here entirely of one mind with us: Similarly also Bullinger: To this pertains what is immediately added for the explanation of the sentence: Until the seed should come, to whom it had been promised. For this he says: The law was promulgated for the sake of the very seed promised to Abraham, namely so that no one in the meantime, trusting in his own strength, might seek righteousness and life in anything other than the promised seed. For hence the law was added as a pedagogue, which would lead straight to Christ, and lead away from others, from idols, from creatures, from merits, from our own righteousnesses. For the law attaches us to the one God, and concludes all under sin, so that we may understand that the promise, that is, the inheritance, righteousness, and life, is given from the faith of Jesus Christ to those who believe. Theophylact explained this sentence of Paul thus: Nor yet was the law given forever, but until the coming of Christ, to whom it was promised that in him the nations would be blessed: If therefore the law was given because Christ was to come, why do you pursue it further? Which exposition, as it has nothing false, so the former has more support from the consequences, but it is also simpler. Διαταγεὶς δι' ἀγγέλων)

He says the law was ordained through Angels, that is, one Angel, pronouncing it in the name of God, Acts 7:38, with the others attending him, Deut. 33:2, Heb. 2:2. See what has been said by us in the Commentary on the Decalogue.

He opposes the Angels to the Son, through whom the Gospel was given. The law was not promulgated by a created Angel, but by the Son of God, the Angel of the new covenant, as we have shown regarding the difficult Grotian trifles on Exodus.

But δι' ἀγγέλων, this is, among the Angels, as the word διὰ is taken in 2 Tim. 2:2, διὰ πολλῶν μαρτύρων among many witnesses, and elsewhere. For the Angels were present attending the Son of God, to whom the blast of the trumpet, lightnings, etc., are attributed.

And that Angel of the new covenant designated in Acts 7:38 is expressed here by μεσίτην, as we are about to say. Ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου)

With Moses interposing himself as a mediator between God and the people, Deut.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος· τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσε-τέθη) Melius alii Codices: Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος· τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη. Quorsum ergo lex, dicat aliquis? Respondet Paulus, appositum fuisse legem, nempe post promissia, quia vitia populi Israelitici in Aegypto increverant, & poenarum malis debebant coërceri, ne prava illa consuetudine paulatim ad impietatem prolaberentur.

Vide infra, V. 23. & 1. Timoth. I. 9. Lectio Irenaei ὁ νόμος τῶν πράξεων προσετέθη, quem ille sequitur &

III. 7. ut monuit Beza, & V. 21. minus huic loco convenit.

Dubium movet, sed ita, ut thesin suam statuminet. Quaerit: Cui ergo bono lex fit? Respondet: Appositam tantum fuisse, seu accessorium quoddam, non ad hoc, ut ex ea esset benedictio, sed alterius usus causa, nimirum παραβάσεων χάριν, non ut transgressiones irritaret & argueret, quod Pareus vult. Hoc enim ex accidente esse, ob naturae pravitatem, qua omnes nitimur in vetitum, fatetur ipse; nec id ad praesentem tractationem facit: Sed ut easdem manifestaret & argueret, quemadmodum antea innuerat, cum execrationem legis commemoravit: ac porro ut confugere ad Christum nos compelleret. Quanquam vero lex etiam faciat ad transgressiones coercendas, id tamen huc proprie non facit. Quod praeclare docuit B. Lutherus Comment. in h. l. Ann. 1524. Verum quod D. Hieronymus negat intelligit, ut per legem transgressiones cohiberentur, huic resistit primum, quod tum potius propter justificationem posita dici debuis; lex enim propter observationem ponitur. Secundo quod iste tropus fit Apostolo familiaris: Lex est virtus peccati, occasio peccati, lex mortis, lex irae. Sic Rom. IV. lex iram operatur. Ubi enim non est lex, nec praevaricatio, nec remissio. Ubi non est remissio, ibi nec est salus. Proinde ut remissio propter salutem, ita praevaricatio propter remissionem, ita lex propter transgressionem. Lex ponit peccatum, peccatum remissionem, remissio salutem. Hoc totum, quia fine lege, peccatum mortuum est & non cognoscitur Rom. V. & VII. Peccatum erat in mundo, sed non imputabatur usque ad Mosem. Est ergo sensus: Lex propter transgressionem posita est, ut transgressio sit & abundet, atque sic per legem homo in fui cognitionem adductus, quaerat manum miserentis Dei, qui fine lege peccatum ignorans sibi sanus videtur. Tertio nec sequentia consonant, donec veniret semen. Absurdum est enim transgressionem cohiberi, donec Christus veniat: qua situm sit non cohibenda, cum Apostolus contrarium voluerit, quod peccatum per legem non solum non sit cohibitum, sed auctum quoque, donec Christus veniens peccatum finiret, legem implendo & gratiam dando, ut Dan. IX. Gabriel dicit, ut finem accipiat peccatum, & adducatur justitia sempiterna. Ac si dicat: Peccatum sumpsit initium in Adam, per legem etiam incrementum, per solum Christum finem accipiet, qui justitiam adducit peccato mortuo sempiternam ut Psal. CX. & CXI. Justitia ejus manet in seculum seculi. Quarto nec cum illo convenit: Ergo lex adversus promissa Dei? Nec hoc inferretur, si Apostolus vellet intelligi legem pro cohibenda transgressione positam, quia tum non esset adversus promissa, sed pro promissis. Nunc vero quia peccatum auget, itemque provocat, appareat non provocare Deum ad solvenda promissa, sed potius irritare & impedire. Sic intelligendo contextus sibi pulchre cohaeret, alioqui tot fingas, quod sunt constructiones necesse est. Quinto quod dicit, in manu Mediatoris, quod meo judicio dicit, quia lex non sit posita in manu nostra, ut nos eam impleamus, sed in futuri Christi, eam impleuri. Quare non ut justificaret posita est, sed magis peccatores argueret, & manum Mediatoris requireret. Resistendum enim fuit humane superbiae, ne Filium Dei suis meritis incarnatum crederet, & tanta misericordia ingrata fieret. Nunc in demerita lapsi tanto fideliorem & misericordiorem Deum amamus, quanto indignioribus tantam misericordiam exhibuit. Nobis enim per legem cognitio: Soli autem Christo impletio & operatio, donec veniret semen, cui promissum erat, id est, in quo benedictio, justitia & plenitudo legis danda erat: Et transgressiones, que per legem erant, non jam cobibende, sed extinguende, quod per fidem Christi efficitur. Manifestat ergo & condemnat lex transgressiones, sed non ut pereamus ejus execratione, sed divinam respicias intentionem, sed ut per eandem ceu pædagogum ad Christum ducamur: ideo data fuit in manu Mediatoris Christi, quod alias per ejusdem fulmen pereundum fuisset hominibus: qui Mediator inter duas partes, Deum & homines, jam in ipsa legis promulgatione intervenit, ne lex vim maledicendi exerceret, utpote qui exorationem legis in se derivaturus, nosque ab ea liberaturus erat.

Argumentum hinc novum nascitur; Si lex ita transgressiones manifestat & condemnat, ut intentionis divinæ in ipsa promulgatione legis respectu nos opus habere Mediatore, nisi pereundum æternum nobis sit, convincamur, non ergo per legem ipsam à transgressione ullatenus liberatio vel peccatorum remissio & justificatio derivari potest. (Hæc enim prorsus opposita sunt transgressionum condemnatio, & transgressionum condonatio) sed eam unice per Mediatorem obtingere oportet. At verum prius. Ergo & posterius. Audiendus hic iterum B. Lutherus, qui in Comment. post. fol. 84. Lex etiam, inquit, lux est, que lucet & ostendit non gratiam Dei, non justitiam & vitam, sed peccatum, mortem, iram & judicium Dei.

Nam sicut in monte Sinai tonitru, fulmen, nubes caliginosa, mons fumigans & ardens & tota illa terrifica facies non exhilambat, nec vivificabat filios Israël, sed perterrefaciebat, reddebat fere exanimes, & ostendebat, quam non ferre possent, & ostendebat, quam non ditie præsentiam Dei loquentis è nube. Sic lex quando in suo vero usu est, nihil aliud facit, quam quod revelat peccatum, efficit iram, accusat & perterrefacit homines, ut non procul absint à desperatione. Is proprius est usus legis, sic finem habet, nec amplius progredi debet. Contra Evangelium lux est, que illuminat, vivificat, consolatur & erigit pavidas mentes. Ostendit enim Deum propitium esse peccatoribus & indignis propter Christum, si credant per mortem ipsius liberatos à maledictione, id est à peccato & morte æterna, & per suam victoriam illis benedictionem, id est gratiam, remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam. paulo post: Lex ostendit hominibus sibiipsi, quod sit peccator, ergoreus mortis, & dignus æterna ira.

Ad quid prodest illa humiliatio, contusio & contritio per ipsum malleum, legem scilicet? Ad hoc prodest, ut gratiæ ad nos pateat aditus. Sic ergo lex ministra & præparatrix est ad gratiam.

Nam Deus est Deus bumilium, miserorum, afflictorum, oppressorum, desperatorum, & eorum, qui in nihilum redacti sunt; ejusque natura est, exaltare bumiles, cibare esurientes, illuminare eccos, miseros & afflictos consolari, peccatores justificare, mortuos vivificare, desperatos & damnatos salvare & c. Est enim creator omnipotens, ex nihilo faciens omnia. Ad hoc autem suum naturale & proprium opus non finit eum pervenire nocentissima pestis illa, opinio justitiæ, qua non vult esse peccatrix, immunda, misera, & damnata, sed justa, sancta & c. Ideo oportet Deum adhibere malleum ipsum, legem scilicet, que frangat, contundat, conterat, & prorsus ad nihilum redigat hanc beluam cum sua vana fiducia, sapientia, justitia, poten. & c. ut tandem suo malo discat, se perditam & damnatam. Atque ibi tum, conscientia sic lege conterrita, locum habet doctrina Evangelii & gratiæ, que rursum erigit & consolatur dicens: Christum venisse in mundum, non ut quassatum calamum contemnt, non ut linum fumigans extinguat, sed ut pauperibus Evangelium annuntiet, contritis corde medeatur, captivis predicet remissionem & c.

Sic per Accidens (pergit Vir Dei, paucis interjetis) cum suo officio etiam prodest ad justificationem, non quidem justificans, sed urgens ad promissionem gratiæ, & faciens eam suavem ac desiderabilem.

Quare legem non abrogamus, sed indicamus verum usum & officium ipsius: quod scilicet fit utilissima ministra, urgens ad Christum. Ideo postquam te lex humiliavit, perterrefecit & prorsus contrivit, ut jam sis desperationi proximus, vide ut lege recte noris uti. Quia officium & usus ejus est, non solum ostendere peccatum ac iram Dei, sed etiam compellere ad Christum. Hunc usum legis solus Spiritus Sanctus ostendit in Evangelio, ubi testatur Deum adesse contritis corde & c. Quare si contritus es malleo isto, ne perverse utaris contritione ista, ut oneres te pluribus legibus, sed audi Christum dicentem: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, ego reficiam vos. Quando lex te sic urget, desperatis rebus omnibus tuis, ad quærendum auxilium & solatium apud Christum, tum est in vero usu, & servit per Evangelium ad justificationem, usque est optimus ac perfectissimus legis usus.

B. Brentius in hunc locum fol. 836. Et tunc cum dicit Paulus (propter transgressiones) subintelligendum est, ostendendas, illustrandas, amplificandas, exaggerandas, & agnoscendas in conscientia. Nam in testamento, quod Deus instituit cum Abrahamo & semine ejus, qui est Christus, promisit Deus benedictionem, seu justitiam & salutem omnibus populis propter Christum.

Naturæ humanæ in tantum est excæcata peccato originali, quod non agnoscit injustitiam suam, sed putat, se suis viribus posse consequi justitiam & salutem nec indigere Christo. Quod enim Satan dixit ad Evam: Eritis sicut Dii, hoc adhuc hæret in carne & sanguine hominis, ut naturæ suæ depravatæ tribuat sibi aliquam divinitatem, nec agnoscat, se Satanæ esse mancipium, sed potius existimet, se Deum quendam esse, qui suæ viribus juvare queat. Data igitur est lex, datus est decalogus, ut ostendat nobis peccatum nostrum, ut illustret peccatum in conscientia nostra, ut amplificet peccatum, ac breviter, ut declaret, nos non esse Deos, sed potius diabolos aut diaboli mancipia & Gehennæ obnoxios, De qua re vide in epist. ad Rom. cap. IV. & VI. In quem autem finem lex ostendit nobis peccata, & declarat nos diaboli mancipia? Nihil minus: Dicit enim: Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed magis, ut convertatur & vivat. Lex igitur ostendit nobis & magnitudinem & gravitatem peccati & addicit nos Satana, ut cogat nos Christum inquirere. Recte ergo B. Hunnius: Sensus est: Lex lata est, non ut conferat hominibus naturæ peccatoribus justitiam, sed ut illos potius reos agat injustitiæ & populo Israelitico transgressionibus commonstratis eximat perversam opinionem de justitia operum & salute ex lege expectanda. Ἄχρις οὗ ἔλθῃ τὸ σπέρμα, ᾧ ἐπήγγελται) id est, vim suam habitura, (id enim hic subintelligitur) donec veniret ille nepos Abrahami, per quem gentes bona summa debebant accipere, & ad quem promissio illa, Abrahamo facta, spectabat, plane, quasi ipsi facta esset, idem hic dicit, quod initio capitis VII. ad Romanos. Plane germanæ sunt istæ epistolæ, & validum est argumentum, si ne Judæos quidem lex nunc obligat, multo minus gentes. Alii Codices ᾐ ἐπήγγελται semen promissum. promiſſum.

Recte quidem dicitur lex vim ſuam habitura, donec veniret semen, cui promissio facta scilicet benedictionis conciliandae, & quantum ad intentionem Dei benevolam, etiam conferenda omnibus cognitionibus terrae, quomodo Spiritus sancti promissum Christus accipisse dicitur Actorum II. v. 33. ideoque illud & optime se habet.

Sed tota oeconomia legis ideo usque ad semen benedictum durare tantum debuit, ut eo luculentius esset, finem & complementum legis esse Christum ad justitiam omni credenti Rom. X. 4. utque ea quoque ratione legis usus paedagogicus constaret. Respectu cujus intentionis divinae recte B. Lutherus docet, spiritualiter hic subinnui, legem non debere diutius dominari in conscientias, quam donec veniat semen. Quando ergo, inquit, lex ostendit mihi peccatum, perterrefacit me, & revelavit iram & judicium Dei, ut incipiam pallescere, desperare &c. Ibi praecipue modum, tempus & finem habet lex, ut desinat suam tyrannidem exercere. Quia tunc facit officio suo, satis ostendit iram Dei & perterrefecit. Hic dicendum est, desine lex, satis exterruisti & contrivisti. Omnes tui fluctus super me transierunt, terrores tui conturbaverunt me. Item: Ne avertas, Domine, in ira faciem tuam a servo tuo, ne, quaeso, in furore tuo arguas me &c. Quando isti pavores & querele veniunt, tempus & hora est feminis benedicti. Cedat igitur lex, quae quidem addita est, propter transgressiones revelandas & augendas, sed tantisper tantum, donec semen veniat, quo praesente, desinat lex revelare transgressiones & perterrefacere, tradatque regnum alteri, semini scilicet benedicto, hoc est, Christo, qui habet gratiosa labia, quibus non accusat, terret &c. sed de rebus longe melioribus loquitur, quam lex, nempe de gratia, pace, remissione peccatorum, victoria peccati, mortis & c. sua morte & resurrectione partis & donatis credentibus. Quae quanquam ita spiritualiter, ut ait, accipiat B. Lutherus, non negat tamen legis oeconomiam & cultum Mosaicum hic ad literam dici durare debuisse usque ad tempus gratiae, vide Matth. XI. 13. IX. 27. Ebr. X. 1. sed si causam ejus rei sciscitemur, eam, quam jam exposuit, subinnui vult: quae explicatur v. 22. Quod in priori editione Commentarii B. Lutheri Anno 1520. divulgati nostro judicio convenientissime expositum est: Verba ejusdem supra adduximus. Ita ergo forte non incommode dicetur, particulam ἄχρι non tempus denotare durationis legis Mosaicae, sed ordinem vel finem notare, quod nimirum eo usque & ad eum finem in nobis explicet vim suam, quas transgressiones arguendas & condemnandas transgressiones lex, donec adveniat semen, cui promissio facta, ut scilicet illud cum effectu ad nos penetret cum benedictione, quae ἄχρι non temporis ordinem, sed potius dispensationis divinae rationem infert Apoc. VII. 3. de non laedenda terra, donec ἄχρις & obsignentur servi Dei. Non enim tempore prius obsignantur servi Dei, antequam Angeli mali queant ἀδικεῖν, & eo usque illi quiescant aut cohibeantur. Sed designatur oeconomia divinae ratio, quod scilicet Deus eo fine cohibeat malos Angelos, ut servi Dei, quasi peculiariter a Deo obsignati non laedantur. Non tantum usque ad Christum (temporis ratione) lex vim habet transgressiones arguendas & condemnandas, sed omni tempore vim suam habet usque ad Christum in verbo promissionis agnitum & fide apprehensum. Donec, inquit B.

Brentius, veniret semen, cui promissum est, hoc est, lex ideo revelat transgressiones, ut nos ad Christum adigat, nec cesset nos damnare, nisi dum veniat Christus, nisi dum accipiamus Christum per fidem. Tunc enim non amplius damnat nos lex, sed dimittit nos liberos.

Unde & postea ait: Conclusit scriptura omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio Jesu Christi daretur credentibus. Hic idem est finis suppliciorum & afflictionum, quibus non vult DEUS nos perdere, sed invitare ad quaerendam salutem in Christo Filio suo, aliquio contemptissimo & prorsus abjecto. Ett ergo Brentius hic nobis prorsus ὁμόψυφος: Similiter & Bullinger: Huc pertinet quod ad explicationem sententiae statim subjungitur: Donec veniret semen, cui promissum fuerat. Hoc enim dicit: Lex propter ipsum Abrahae promissum semen promulgata est, nempe ne quis interim fretus suis viribus justitiam & vitam in alia alia re, quam promisso semine quaereret. Hinc enim addita est lex ceu paedagogus, qui recta ad Christum duceret, ab aliis abduceret, ab idolis, a creaturis, a meritis, a justitiis nostris. Uni enim Deo affigit lex, & omnes sub peccatum concludit, ut intelligamus promissionem, idest hereditatem, justitiam & vitam dari ex fide Jesu Christi credentibus. Theophylactus hanc Pauli sententiam sic enarravit: Nec tamen data est lex in perpetuum, sed ad Christi usque adventum, cui promissum est, fore, ut in se gentibus benediceretur: Si igitur quod Christus advenerit, lex tradita est, quid ultra illam sectaris? Quae expositio ut nil falsi, ita prior plus firmamenti habet ex consequentibus, sed & simplicior est. Διαταγεὶς δι' ἀγγέλων)

Legem ait praeceptam per Angelos, id est, Angelo uno, nomine Dei eam pronuntiante, Actor. VII. 38. ceteris eum stipantibus, Deut. XXXIII. 2. Hebr. II. 2. Vide quae a nobis dicta in Commentario ad Decalogum.

Opponit Angelos Filio, per quem datum est Evangelium. Non ab Angelo creato, sed a Filio Dei, Angelo novi foederis lex promulgata est, ut ad Exodum difficullis Φλυαρίας Grotianis ostendimus.

Sed δι' ἀγγέλων hoc est, inter Angelos, uti vox διὰ 2. Tim. II. 2. accipitur, διὰ πολλῶν μαρτύρων inter multos testes, & alibi. Aderant enim Angeli Filium Dei stipantes, quibus tubae clangor, fulgura, &c. tribuuntur.

Atque ille Angelus novi foederis Act. VII. 28. designatus, hic per μεσίτην exprimitur, ut mox dicturi sumus. Ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου)

Mose medium se interponente inter Deum & populum Deut.

## 3:21
Verf. 21. ὁ οὖν νόμος κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ; μὴ γένοιτο. [Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid.] If the law had promised life, namely eternal: For the law is said to do what it promises, in the Hebrew manner. The locution is not unlike, 2. Corinth. III. 6. it touches the chief error of the Jews of that time, as also in the epistle to the Romans. ὅτως δὲ νόμος ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνην) [But if the law were for righteousness] In the Manuscript ἄν ἦν [it would have been], then also righteousness would have been revealed through the law, agreeing with eternal life, that is, internal and spiritual, such as the Evangelical [righteousness] is.

Latin:

Verf. 21. ὁ οὖν νόμος κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ; μὴ γένοιτο. Si lex promissa habuisset vitae, nempe aeternae: Nam dicitur lex facere, quod promittit, more Hebraeo. Loquutio non dissimilis, 2. Corinth. III. 6. tangit praecipuum errorem Judaeorum illius temporis, ut & in epistola ad Romanos. ὅτως δὲ νόμος ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνην) In Manuscripto ἄν ἦν, tunc etiam justitia per legem fuisset revelata, vitae aeterne conveniens, id est, interna ac spiritualis, qualis est Evangelica.

## 3:22
Verf. 22. Ἀλλὰ συνέκλεισεν ἡ γραφὴ πάντα ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν) [But the scripture hath concluded all under sin] all namely τὰ ὅλα [all things]. The Scripture involved all peoples in sins, that is, declared them involved, not those only, who were at the time of the flood, and the Sodomites, and the Amorites and the Egyptians, but also the Israelites. There is here a locution similar to that which we have already had. For the scripture is said to do that which it shows. ἵνα ἡ ἐπαγγελία ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δοθῇ τοῖς πιστεύουσι) [that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe] That the benefit might be so much the more distinguished, when formerly that true and spiritual righteousness was given through faith to those, who were about to believe in Christ Jesus. Ἐπαγγελία [The promise] here is the thing promised, as above 14.

Grotius entirely perverts the opinion of the Apostle. For first, it is not asked here concerning the offering or the ablation of the promise: But since the promise of God is ἀμεταμέλητον [irrevocable] of the Apostle, does the law, which προσετέθη [was added], pervert the contrary to the Evangelical promise, when the law condemns transgressions? But does the promise made to Abraham bring the forgiveness of them?

For thus interpreted by B.

Luther in the cited place, one solved question raised another for itself. For if the law increases transgressions, it now seems to irritate the goodness of the one promising. This would be true if the promise of blessing rested upon the law, or justice upon our works in the law. But now it rests upon the truth of the one promising, therefore the law is not against the promises of God, but rather for the promises of God. How? Because while it shows sins, and convinces that no one can be justified through it, and that sin is even increased through it, it compels one to seek, invoke, and expect the fulfillment of the promise all the more, as being much more necessary than when the law did not exist. So far, therefore, is it from being against the promises, that it vehemently commends them, and renders them most desired to those whom it humbles by the knowledge of their own sins. Next, it is not denied here that the law has promises of eternal life, which would be to contradict the law, Christ, and the Apostle himself . . . .

It is a question of what the law can do after the fall of man, not what it promises. Nor was this the error of the Jews, that the law has promises of eternal life, but that they thought they could fulfill the law . . Thirdly, the discussion here is not whether justice suitable for eternal life is revealed through the law, which Grotius interprets as internal and spiritual, such as he imagines it to be in the Gospel (since the Gospel is a proclamation of grace, and not a precept of internal and spiritual holiness, or of inherent justice, which should be considered more perfect than legal justice)? But whether we now obtain justice and eternal salvation through the law, which is the theme the Apostle denied against the Pseudo-Apostles and overturned with the most solid arguments.

Fourthly, it is not said of the Gentiles only, or of the Gentiles of individuals, but of any men whatsoever, or of individuals of the kinds, that they are concluded under sin, because Christ was made a curse for all men, all men gather the Evangelical promises, and that all men are concluded under sin, as the scope and nerve of the Apostolic disputation, and the comparison of parallel passages Rom. III. 19. 20. cap. XI. 32. clearly shows.

Fifthly, ἡ ἐπαγγελία and justice, which is obtained through faith by those who believe in Christ, is rashly restricted to the times of the New Testament, since it pertains to all times, and concerns all who have ever been justified . . . . . . Nor does the whole present treatment of the holy Apostle demand this at all.

Its sense is in the open: If the law were able to vivify, justice standing before God would truly be obtained through the law. But it is not obtained. For what need would there be for Christ or the redemption of Christ, what need for the Gospel if the law itself could justify us, that is, if through works and the observance of the law we could obtain true justice valid before the divine tribunal and eternal life and salvation. The consequence is clear, because vivification or the bestowal of eternal life includes or presupposes justification in the divine court.

Paul signifies by these words, says B. Luther, Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. fol. 89, that no law simply can vivify, but only kill.

Therefore my works, which I do not only according to the laws of the Pope or human traditions, but even the law of God, do not justify me before God, but constitute me a sinner, do not appease the wrath of God, but irritate it: They do not obtain justice, but take it away; they do not vivify, but mortify me. which when he says, if the law had been given etc., he teaches in most clear words that not even the divine law vivifies, but has the plain contrary effect. And further: Paul does not suffer that addition, that faith justifies with works, but proceeds simply by the negative Rom. III. and above cap. II. By the works of the law, he says, no flesh is justified. And in this place: The law was not given to vivify. But the Apostle solves the objection and establishes his thesis, when he casts the blame and the cause of that misery not upon the law itself, but upon the sin by which the nature of men is corrupted; for which cause the scripture of the law concluded all men (τὰ ἔθνη) under sin, so that the promise might be given from the faith of Jesus Christ to those who believe, whence it is absurd to expect either justice or life from the law: and thus it remains that the promise of justice and life is given from faith excited through the Gospel, not to those working, but to those believing in Christ Jesus.

The law, he says, interpreted by Theophylact, cannot free man from sins, but rather cooperated to decline, so that men might be concluded under sin, that is, that it might argue that they had sinned, and compel them to seek the forgiveness of sin and to flee to Christ, who can provide this. The promise is the inheritance itself, says B. Luther, in the cited place, or the blessing of Abraham, that is, liberation from the law, sin, death, and the Devil. And the donation of grace, justice, salvation, and eternal life. That promise, he says, is not obtained by any merit, by any law, by any works, but is donated.

To whom? To those who believe. In whom? In Jesus Christ, who is the blessed seed, which redeemed believers from the curse, that they might receive the blessing. Therefore he inverts the first objection.

For he shows that if the law had been given, which could vivify, it would truly be contrary to the promise. Before the fall it could vivify. If it had the same power today, it would fight with the promise. For then there would be justice through it, if there were justice through it, it would justify: If it justified, then the contrariety of the law and the promise would be manifest. For the promise brings the justice of faith, the law the justice of works, if it is fulfilled. The Apostle opposes the word ὄντως to the Pseudo-Apostles, and to the opinion of those seduced Galatians.

These thought that justice was from the law, the Apostle proved it was not: he says it is truly so, if the law could vivify, as Grotius here. Then he presses the scope. That which serves the promise is in no way opposed to it, the Law serves the promise: because it concludes all under sin, not that they should perish eternally, but that they should be saved, which however is an accidental end of the law. It does not tend to it by itself, but God, by convincing all of sin through the law, intends this end. Since the Jews did not even feel their own sins (the same must be held concerning others), for not feeling them they did not desire remission, he gave the law, which would reveal the wounds, so that they might seek a physician, says Chrysostom.

Latin:

Verf. 22. Ἀλλὰ συνέκλεισεν ἡ γραφὴ πάντα ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν) πάντα nempe τὰ ὅλα. Scriptura omnes populos peccatis involvit, id est, involutos declaravit, non illos tantum, qui diluvii tempore fuerant, & Sodomitas, & Amorrhaeos & Aegyptios, fed & Israelitas. Est hic loquutio similis ei, quum jam habuimus. Nam facere scriptura dicitur, id quod ostendit. ἵνα ἡ ἐπαγγελία ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δοθῇ τοῖς πιστεύουσι) Ut tanto insignius esset beneficium, cum olim justitia illa vera ac spiritualis daretur per fidem iis, qui in Christum Jesum erant credituri. Ἐπαγγελία hic est res promissa, ut supra 14.

Prorsus pervertit Apostoli sententiam Grotius. Primo enim hic non quaeritur de oblatione aut sententiam ablatione promissi: Sed... quum promissum Dei sit Apostoli ἀμεταμέλητον, anne lex, quae προσετέθη, contraria pervertit sit promissioni Evangelicae, quum lex condemnet transgressiones. Promissio autem Abrahae facta condonationem earum afferat?

Sic enim interprete B.

Luthero loco citato, soluta una quaestio aliam sibi suscitavit. Si enim lex transgressiones auget, jam irritare promittentis bonitatem videtur. Hoc verum esset, si promissio benedictionis inniteretur legi, aut justitia nostris... in lege. Nunc vero fols veritati promittentis innititur, ideo lex non adversus promissa Dei, imo pro promissis Dei. Quomodo? quia dum peccata ostendit, et convincit, non posse per eam quemquam justificari, quin et augeri peccatum per eam contingit, jam eam ergo magis promissionis impletionem quari, invocari, expectari cogit, ut multo magis necessariam, quam dum lex non esset. Tantum ergo abest, ut contra promissa sit, ut eadem vehementer commendet, et optatissima reddat iis, quos suorum peccatorum cognitione humiliat. Deinde non hic negatur legem promissiones habere vitae aeternae, quod esset legi, Christo et Apostolo ipsi contrariari. . . . eo quid possit lex post lapsum hominis, non vero, quid promittat, agitur.

Nec is Judaeorum error erat, quod lex promissa habeat vitae aeternae, sed quod censuerint, se legem implere posse. . Tertio non de eo hic sermo est, an per legem justitia vita aeterna conveniens, quod interpretatur Grotius de interna ac spirituali, qualem in Evangelio esse fingit (quum Evangelium concio gratiae sit, non vero praeceptum internae et spiritualis sanctitatis, aut inhaerentis justitiae, quae legali perfectior censenda sit) revelata sit? Sed an per legem nunc consequamur justitiam et salutem aeternam, quod thema contra Pseudo-Apostolos negavit et solidissimis argumentis evertit Apostolus.

Quarto non de gentibus tantum, aut gentibus fingulorum, sed de hominibus quibusvis, sive singulis generum dicitur, quod sub peccato conclusi sint, quia pro omnibus hominibus Christus maledictum factus est, omnes homines promissiones Evangelicae conserunt, et omnes homines concluso esse sub peccatum, tum scopus et nervus Apostolicae disputationis, tum collatio locorum parallelorum Rom. III. 19. 20. cap. XI. 32. luculenter ostendit.

Quinto ἡ ἐπαγγελία et justitia, quae per fidem obtingit illis, qui in Christum credunt, temere refringitur ad tempora Novi Testamenti, quum ad omnia tempora pertineat, omnesque qui unquam justificati sunt, concernat. . . . . . Nec postulat omnino tota praesens tractatio S. Apostoli.

Sensus ejus in aprico est: Si lex vivificare valeret, revera per legem justitia coram Deo consistens obtineretur. At non obtinetur. Ecquid enim opus foret Christo vel redemptione Christi, ecquid Evangelio si lex ipsa nos justificare posset, hoc est, si per opera et observantiam legis veram justitiam coram tribunali divino valentem ac vitam et salutem consequeremur aeternam. Consequentia patet, quia vivificatio seu vitae aeternae collatio justificationem in foro divino aut includit aut praesupponit.

Paulus significat his verbis, inquit B. Lutherus Tom. IV. Jen. Lat. fol. 89. nullam simpliciter legem posse vivificare, sed tantum occidere.

Ergo mea opera, que non solum juxta leges Papa seu traditiones humanas, sed etiam legem Dei facio, non justificant me coram Deo, sed peccatorem constituunt, non placant iram Dei, sed irritant: Non consequuntur justitiam, sed tollunt eam; non vivificant, sed mortificant me. que cum dicit, si lex data esset et c. clarissimis verbis docet, ne legem quidem divinam vivificare, sed plane contrarium effectum habere. Et porro: Non patitur Paulus istam additionem, fides cum operibus justificat, sed simpliciter per negativam procedit Rom. III. et supra cap. II. Ex operibus legis inquit non justificatur omnis caro. Et hoc loco: Non est data lex ad vivificandum. Solvit autem objectionem et statuminat thesin suam Apostolus, cum culpam et causam adunae mias illius non in ipsam per se legem, sed in peccatum quo corrupta est hominum natura rejicit; cujus causa scriptura legis πάντα (τὰ ἔθνη) omnes homines sub peccatum conclusit, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus, unde absonum est a lege vel justitiam expectare vel vitam: adeoque relinquitur, promissionem justitiae et vitae dari ex fide per Evangelium excitata, non operantibus, sed credentibus in Christum Jesum.

Nequit lex, inquit, interprete Theophylacto, a delictis hominem liberare, quin potius ad declinandum cooperabatur, ut homines sub peccato concluderentur, hoc est, ut eos deliquisse argueret, compelleretque ad peccati veniam deposcendam et ad Christum confugere, qui hanc possis praestare. Promissio est haereditas ipsa, dicente B. Lutherum, loco citato, seu benedictio Abrahae, hoc est liberatio a lege, peccato, morte et Diabolo. Et donatio gratiae, justitiae, salutis et vitae aeternae. Ille promissio, inquit, nullo merito, nulla lege, nullis operibus impetratur, sed donatur.

Quibus? credentibus. In quem? In Jesum Christum, qui est semen benedictum, quod credentes a maledicto redemit, ut acciperent benedictionem. Invertit ergo primum objectionem. Ostendit enim si data lex esset, quae posset vivificare, vere contrariam fore promissioni.

Ante lapsum poterat vivificare. Si vim eandem haberet hodie, pugnaret cum promissione. Tum enim per eam esset justitia, si per eam esset justitia, justificaret: Si justificaret, utique contrarietas legis et promissionis manifesta esset. Promissio enim affert justitiam fidei, lex justitiam operum, si impleatur. Apostolus opponit vocabulum ὄντως Pseudo-Apostolis, et ab iis seductorum Galatarum opinioni. Hi opinabantur ex lege esse justitiam, non esse probavit Apostolus: vere esse dicit, si lex vivificare posset, ut hic Grotius.

Deinde scopum premit. Quod inservit promissioni, adversatur eidem nequaquam, Lex inservit promissioni: quia concludit omnes sub peccatum, non ut aeternum pereant, sed serventur, qui tamen finis legis est Accidentarius. Non per se eam tendit, sed Deus per legem omnes peccati convincens hunc intendit finem. Quoniam ne sentiebant quidem sua peccata Judaei (idem et de aliis habendum) non sentientes enim nec desiderabant remissionem, dedit legem, quae proderet vulnera, quo medicum requirerent, inquit Chrysostomus.

## 3:23
Verf. 23. πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τὴν πίστιν) That is, before the Gospel came, which is called faith metonymically. Thus we have had the word πίστεως also above 1, 23. and here above, 2. ὑπὸ νόμῳ ἐφρουρούμεθα συγκεκλεισμένοι) In the manuscript συγκεκλεισμένοι. We Israelites, wrapped in sins, as the others, were guarded by the law, that is, we were coerced by the fear of legal punishments, lest the nature of the mind should escape --- with the nature of the mind removed. See on this matter the epistle of Eleazar, which is in the preparation of Eusebius, he treats of the people, such as it was ἐπὶ πᾶσαν. For ὡς μοι ἐμφράγματα τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, says Isocrates in the Areopagiticus. σὶν τῇ μέδουσαι πίστει ἀποκαλυφθῆναι) That is, until the time, until the Gospel should be revealed.

By faith some understand Christ, by Metonymy, such as Hyperius, Aretius, Pareus & Gomarus, with Bullinger, who also commends Ambrose and Theophylact for this matter, and they compare verse 19, until the seed should come. We have previously warned that this word ἄχρι is to be understood not so much temporally as finally. And although the matter comes to almost the same thing, as Glarus judges, whether Christ or the preaching of Christ is understood, since in the operation and preaching of faith Christ is always joined with his word, so that Christ is even called our hope, Col. 1:28, yet it is certain that faith itself is nowhere called Christ, nor does that conjunction of Christ with his word properly make this: And the error of Weigelius is to be avoided, that faith is Christ himself dwelling within.

To others, therefore, by faith, with Grotius, is understood in this place the faith by which one believes, which they call, or the doctrine of the Gospel, which is the cause of the faith by which one believes, and not simply the doctrine of the Gospel, but more clearly revealed. For even in the Old Testament they had the same doctrine of faith; but there it was still properly ἐπαγγελία, that is, the promise concerning Christ to be exhibited, which here is εὐαγγέλιον or that broad message concerning Christ already exhibited. Before, therefore, faith, that is, this doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ exhibited, came or was announced, the Israelites were kept under the law. Which meaning they gather from those things which are presently subjoined: εἰς τὴν πίστιν (in the New Testament) was to be revealed, namely, more clearly and openly. Whence Calvin: Faith in this place signifies the full revelation of those things which then lay hidden under the obscurity of the shadows of the law, for he does not take away faith from the Fathers who lived under the law.

But some understand faith here as that by which one believes, as the Socinians, Calixus, and other Innovators, as if that faith had not existed in the Old Testament, but only had a place in the New Testament, which is false. Since we are saved by the same faith by which the ancients were saved, Acts 15:11, and Paul here attributes the same faith to Abraham, verse 9, and to other Fathers, Heb. 11, nay, even makes Abraham, in respect of the same, the Father of all believers, Rom. 4, nor is there any faith of all except one, Eph. 4:5, just as there is no salvation except in one Christ, Acts 4:12, ch. 10:43.

Furthermore, that heretical gloss being excluded, it is permitted to understand faith entirely in the proper sense of that faith by which we believe; by which we are children of God, and put on Christ, by which we are justified and constituted heirs. For all things contribute to this notion of faith, which comes to those who are shut up under the law; since they are therefore shut up under the law, that faith might be manifested or revealed, or rendered more manifest. For they were kept in that dark prison, so that the faith to come might be revealed in them, and might exert its efficacy the more clearly. Which B. Luther rightly explains in his Commentary, ed. 1520. To all (he says) who are under the law, before they are justified by faith, the law itself is as a certain prison, in which they are shut up and kept. And that, before faith came, is understood not only of the faith which was revealed after Christ, but of all the faith of all the just. For the same faith came to the fathers of old, and indeed the law of God first revealed to them compelled them to seek the grace of God. Although it was not then preached so much through the world, it was nevertheless preached privately through the families of the fathers.

Which are added, ὑπὸ νόμον ἐφρερούμεθα, we were kept under the law, συγκλεισμένοι, shut up unto the faith which was to be revealed, are inconveniently taken by Calvin in a good sense concerning a pleasant and grateful custody: He says they were shut up under the faith, by which it was to be revealed, these words testify that those who were under the custody of the law were partakers of the same faith.

Just as, being besieged on every side, they were held by the curse: so against this siege they had a custody set opposite, which would protect them from the curse. Nor indeed are they said to be shut up unto faith, but kept under law, and shut up εἰς τὴν πίστιν in faith, or unto faith, which was to be revealed, so that by the word the final cause may be noted. See Ephes. IV. 17. 1. Timoth. IV. 3. which is explained verse 24. the law was a paedagogue εἰς χρισὸν in or unto Christ, just as by the law, as a hard paedagogue, we are compelled to long for and desire Christ: so by the shutting up and custody under law we are said to be compelled unto faith, which was to be revealed. But that those who were under the custody of the law were partakers with us of faith, this is not from the legal custody and shutting up of which the Apostle is at present treating, but from the force of the Evangelical promises concerning the Messiah, which they had under the Old Testament. Of which B. Luther has already admonished in his Commentary published in the Year 1520, fol. 51.

See that you do not arrange the context thus: Shut up in faith, as if you would understand them shut up in faith as in a prison, when he affirms this of the law: But we were shut up in the prison of the law, and this unto the faith to come, or so that we might be freed by the faith to come, indeed the law did this in its prison, that through faith we might desire to be freed.

Just as above the testament of God was confirmed in Christ, that is, so that it might be confirmed in the future Christ, and soon the law was our schoolmaster in Christ, that is, unto Christ. Therefore, a custody opposed to the curse of the law is not expressed here, because Paul distinguishes between the pedagogy of the law and the doctrine of faith, and ascribes to the law nothing but the curse of transgressors. Aretius therefore more rightly explains this custody: We lived under the law as under a prison and a rigid exactor.

Others with Theophylact interpret ῥρουρὰν as a custody, by which they were preserved from idolatry and other horrible crimes, kept as if by a certain wall.

Which Grotius does not disapprove: This is, he says, something, and that not small. For the Jews, then, by a corrupt nature and bad education, and by the wicked examples of the nations among whom they lived, easily fell away from the true worship of God. Therefore the law was imposed upon them as a safeguard, by which they might be contained in the acknowledgment of their own misery and the desire for the promised Messiah. Yet the Apostle seems to indicate more. Protected by a safeguard, they are separated from the foreign enemy by walls, ditches, and ramparts: Thus the Jewish people, protected by the safeguard of the law, were separated from all foreigners. There was a middle wall of partition between him and other nations, Eph. 2:14. He was kept impregnable and unmixed until the advent of Christ, separated from all other peoples, by which he was most distinctly separated from others. Although all these things may be true, yet they do not properly belong here, where the Apostle does not entirely abandon his main theme concerning justification by faith, but rather explains the economy of the law for its sake, that it was instituted not that we might be called away from Christ, but that we might be led to the same: and that we are kept under the law, not so much on account of the coercive use of the law, as on account... of the coaditive and pedagogical use. Therefore the relation here is not from a safeguard and rampart, as Grotius wishes, but rather from a prison, in which we were kept as if shut up before faith, just as the other also A comparison drawn from a harsh schoolmaster can teach us that Crocius did not ramble on about the word συγκεκλεισμένοι. "Without doubt," he says, "he understands the conclusion, of which verse 21 speaks: 'Concluded under sin.'" On this point Pareus also says: "Now he says that there was also, in place of a prison, a custody by which they were held confined, namely under sin, as was said in verse 21. For from that he here repeats the participle συγκεκλεισμένοι, 'confined,' namely under sin by God." The coercive use of the law also has a place even after the coming of faith: but here the discussion is properly about that use of the law which presses most severely, until faith comes. And although through the curse and the terror of punishment we too are consequently restrained from sins, and in that way the Jews were restrained by many laws, nevertheless this is not, as we have said, what is properly treated here. And therefore Luther's paraphrase in the last Commentary, fol. 91, is more correct here: "The law concludes men not civilly, but also theologically, that is, the law is also a spiritual prison and truly a hell. For when it reveals sin and threatens death and the eternal wrath of God, man cannot escape nor find consolation. It is not in man's power to shake off these terrible terrors which the law produces, or any other sorrow of heart." Hence those miserable cries of the saints, etc. For man is then confined in a prison, from which he cannot go out, nor does he see how he can be loosed from these chains, that is, be freed from these terrors. Nor should we pass over the observation which Luther adds: "But these terms, 'to be kept' and 'to be concluded' under the law, are not idle, speculative, or sophistical, but true and serious. That custody or prison signifies true and spiritual terrors, by which the conscience is so confined that in the broadest circle of the earth it finds no place where it can be. Indeed, while those fears endure, the conscience feels such great anxiety that it thinks heaven and earth, even if they were ten times greater and more spacious, are narrower than its own grave. Then man is plainly abandoned, with all wisdom, strength, righteousness, counsel, and help gone. For the conscience is a most delicate thing; therefore when it is thus confined in the prison of the law, no way out lies open to it anywhere, but that distress appears to it to increase continually unto infinity. For it then feels the wrath of God, who is infinite, whose hand it cannot escape, as Psalm 139 says: 'Where shall I go from your Spirit?' Therefore, just as a conclusion or prison in the civil sense is bodily affliction itself, by which the confined person is deprived of the use of his body, so theologically the prison is the disturbance and anxiety of the mind, by which the confined person is deprived of peace of conscience and quiet of heart; yet not forever, as reason judges when it feels that prison, but unto future faith. Therefore the mind confined under the law must be raised up and consoled in this way: 'Brother, you are indeed confined, but know that this is not done so that you should be held confined in that prison forever, because it is written that we are concluded unto future faith. You are therefore shut up in that prison not for your destruction, but so that through the seed of blessing you may be revived; you are put to death by the law, so that through Christ you may be made alive.' These two contraries, therefore, must be joined together, things which in reality are most diverse. For what is more contrary than to fear and dread the wrath of God, and likewise to hope in his mercy? The one is hell, the other is heaven, and yet they must be most closely joined in the heart. Speculatively, they are joined most easily, but to join them in practice is the most difficult of all things: something I have very often learned by my own experience. The Papists and the authors of the sects know nothing to any purpose about this matter. Therefore, when they read or hear these words of Paul, they are plainly obscure and unknown to them

similitude can be learnedly [applied], and sought from a harsh schoolmaster: and when the law shows them sin, accuses and terrifies them, they find neither counsel nor help, but simply despair, like Cain and Saul.

Since therefore the law, as has been said, is our torturer and prison, it is certain that one does not love it, but vehemently hates it.

Therefore, he who says he loves the law lies, and knows not what he says.

A thief or robber would be insane and out of his mind who would love a prison and shackles.

But since the law, as I have said, shuts us up, it is certain that we are its most bitter enemies.

In sum, we love the law and its justice as much as a murderer loves a prison.

How then could we be justified by the law?

Therefore the blessed Luther understands these things not as an opposition of uses between the time of the Old and New Testament; but as the opposite state of any man whatsoever under law and under grace.

The time of the law, he says, is when the law exercises me, harasses me, saddens me, and reduces me to the knowledge of sin, and increases it.

There then the law is in its true use, which the Christian feels, as long as he lives and is true.

And this is the time of the law, under which the Christian is always according to the flesh.

For the flesh perpetually lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, in one more, in another less.

The time of grace is when the heart is again raised up by the promise of the gratuitous mercy of God, and says, why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?

Do you see nothing besides the law, sin, terror, sadness, despair, death, hell, and the Devil?

Is there not also grace, remission of sins, justice, consolation, joy, peace, life, heaven, Christ, God? - Cease, my soul, to trouble me.

What are the law, sin, and all evils compared to these?

Hope in God, who did not spare his own Son, but for your sins delivered him to the death of the cross.

This then is to be shut up under the law according to the flesh, not for eternity, but for the future Christ.

And hence the conclusion on fol. 93.

From these it is easily evident that all the sentences in which Paul treats of the spiritual use of the law are to be understood as concerning those to be justified, not those already justified.

For these, insofar as they remain in Christ, are far outside and above all law.

Therefore, the law must be imposed on those to be justified, so that they may be kept under it for a time, until the justice of faith comes.

Not that they obtain that justice through the law, for this would be to abuse, not rightly use, the law, but so that, terrified and humbled by the law, they may flee to Christ, who is the end of the law for justice to every believer.

Therefore, first of all, all self-justifiers and hypocrites abuse the law, who dream that men are justified by the law.

For that use does not exercise and urge toward future faith, but makes them future, secure, and proud hypocrites, swelling and presuming of justice and works of the law, and it hinders the justice of faith, etc.

For it must be observed that the holy Apostle writes to the Galatians, who were not under the pedagogy of the law, whom he joins to himself, and to whom that use applies, just as it is confessed concerning the pedagogical use, about which we are now inquiring.

For this belongs to all times and all men.

And since the discourse is still about the moral law, and not about ceremonial and forensic laws, under the reason of προσετέθη [it was added], it is again evident that by that it is not understood such a thing by which the Jews were once distinguished from the remaining Gentiles.

For the moral law belongs to all, not only to the Jews, just as also that whole disputation about the use of the law, wherefore προσετέθη [it was added] to the promise, pertains to all men:
