and concerning justification by faith without distinction of times, it is treated in verse 24. And concerning adoption, which through faith in Christ Jesus has come to us no less than to the Fathers in the Old Testament, than to us in the New Testament.

And, lest any distinction be imagined here, it is expressly added, that in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, etc., that all believers in Christ are one, and are Christ's and Abraham's seed (spiritually) and heirs according to the promise. Which explanation concerning the use of the law, not only regarding the Jews, but regarding all men, not only in the Commentary adorned in the year 1519 and published the following year, Megalander delivered, but he also repeats it in the recognition made in the year 1524; nor is it understood only of the faith which was revealed after Christ, but of all the faith of all the just. For which most excellently agrees with the connection and intention and scope of the Apostolic disputation in our judgment. His entire paraphrase in Tom. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 29 has it thus: But before faith came, it is understood not only of the faith which was revealed after Christ, but of all the faith of all the just. For the same faith came also to the Fathers of old, because the law of God, first revealed to them, compels them to seek grace: Although then it was not so preached throughout the world, yet it is preached privately through the families of the patriarchs. Verf. 24. Ὡς ὁ νόμος παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν γέγονεν εἰς χριστόν.

There are ages of men, as also of peoples, as Florus shows. The age of the Israelite people under the law was as it were childhood, below IV. 9. Namely that to which a pedagogue is wont to be added, or a guardian, as Horace speaks Gen. IV. 9. Who might draw them back from graver offenses. This office the law performed for that people, which, had it not been, they would have fallen into such great impiety, through which they would have become deaf to the voice of the Gospel. But a pedagogue is nothing but a temporary authority. Simplicius uses the similitude of a pedagogue toward Epictetus a little differently, but which does not depart far from this: [Greek text]. Afterwards: [Greek text]. Let him see who has leisure for the whole passage to that of Epictetus: 'The work of the uneducated, etc.' "that we might be justified by faith"

That in his own time we might obtain true justification through the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 23. πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τὴν πίστιν) Id est priusquam veniret Evangelium, quod μετωνυμικῶς fides dicitur. Sic vocem πίστεως habuimus et supra 1, 23. et hic supra, 2. ὑπὸ νόμῳ ἐφρουρούμεθα συγκεκλεισμένοι) In manuscripto συγκεκλεισμένοι. Nos Israelita involuti peccatis, ut caeteri, per legem custodiebamur, id est, poenarum legalium formidine coercebamur, ne imum exfiliret --- frenie natura remota. Vide hac de re Eleazari epistolam, quae est in praeparatione Eusebii, agit de populo, qualis erat ἐπὶ πᾶσαν. Nam ὡς μοι ἐμφράγματα τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, ait Isocrates Areopagitico. σὶν τῇ μέδουσαι πίστει ἀποκαλυφθῆναι) Id est, ad tempus usque, dum revelaretur Evangelium.

Per fidem nonnulli intelligunt Christum, per Metonymiam, utpote Hyperius, Aretius, Pareus & Gomarus, cum Bullingero laudante eam in rem etiam Ambrosium & Theophylactum, & conferunt vers. 19. donec veniret semen. Quam illam vocem ἄχρι non tam χρονικῶς, quam τελικῶς intelligendam esse, antea monuimus. Et quanquam res eodem fere recidat, ut Glarus judicat, sive Christus, sive praedicatio Christi intelligatur, quum in operatione & praedicatione fidei conjunctus cum verbo suo Christus semper fit, ut Christus spes nostra etiam dicatur Col. I. 28. nuspiam tamen ipsum fidem dici certum est, nec illa Christi cum verbo suo conjunctio hoc proprie facit: Et cavendus Weigelii error, quod fides fit ipse Christus in habitans.

Aliis ergo per fidem cum Grotio intelligitur hoc loco fides qua creditur, quam vocant, seu doctrina Evangelii, quae causa fidei est, qua creditur, nec simpliciter doctrina Evangelii, sed luculentius revelata. Nam & in Veteri Testam. habuere eandem doctrinam fidei; sed ibi ἐπαγγελία adhuc proprie fuit, id est, promissio de Christo exhibendo, quod hic est εὐαγγέλιον seu latum illud nunnium de Christo jam exhibito. Antequam ergo fides, id est, doctrina haec Evangelii de Christo exhibito veniret vel annuntiaretur, sub lege custoditi fuere Israelitae. Quam significationem ex iis, quae mox subjiciuntur, colligunt: εἰς τὴν πίστιν (in N. Testam.) revelanda erat, scilicet luculentius & apertius. Unde Calvinus: Fides hoc loco significat revelationem plenam eorum, quae tunc latebant sub obscuritate umbrarum legis, neque enim fidem adimit Patribus, qui sub lege vixerunt.

Nonnulli autem fidem hic intelligunt qua creditur, ut Sociniani, Calixus, & alii Novatores, quasi ea fides in Veteri Testamento non fuerit, sed demum in novo Testamento locum habeat, quod falsum. Siquidem eadem fide nos salvemur, qua veteres salvati sunt Actor. XV. 11. & Paulus hic eandem fidem Abrahamo tribuat vers. 9. aliisque Patribus Ebr. XI. imò Abrahamum ejusdem respectu Patrem omnium credentium faciat Rom. IV. nec fit, nisi una omnium fides Ephes. IV. 5. sicut non est nisi in uno Christo salus Actorum IV. 12. cap. X. 43.

Ceterum exclusa illa glossa haeretica intelligere omnino fidem licet sensu proprio de fide illa, qua credimus; per quam filii Dei sumus, & Christum induimus, per quam justificamur & haeredes constituimur. Omnia enim in hanc fidei notionem inferunt, quae advenit illis, qui conclusi sunt sub lege; cum ideo concludantur sub lege, ut manifester vel reveletur, sive manifestior reddatur fides. Ideo enim in obscuro illo carcere custoditi sunt, ut fides futura in ipsis reveletur, suamque exerat eo luculentius efficaciam. Quod recte explicat B. Lutherus Comment. An. 1520. edit. Omnibus (inquit) qui sub lege sunt, antequam fide justificentur, lex ipsa velut quidam carcer est, in qua concludantur & serventur. Et illud, priusquam veniret fides, non tantum de fide, qua post Christum revelata est, sed de omni fide omnium justorum intelligitur. Nam & patribus olim eadem fides venit, quin & lex Dei eis primo revelata coegit eos gratiam Dei quaerere. Licet tum non ita per orbem praedicaretur, predicabatur tamen privatim per familias patrum.

Quae adduntur ὑπὸ νόμον ἐφρερούμεθα sub lege custodiebamur συγκλεισμένοι conclusi in fidem revelandam, incommode à Calpino in bonam partem de jucunda & grata custodia accipiuntur: Dicit conclusos fuisse sub fidem, qua erat revelanda, testantur his verbis participes fuisse ejusdem fidei, qui sub legis custodia erant.

Quemadmodum undique obsessi tenebantur a maledictione: ita huic obsidioni habebant oppositam custodiam, quae eos a maledictione protegeret. Nec vero concludi custodiuntur sub fidem, sed custodi sub lege, & conclusi εἰς τὴν πίστιν in fidem, vel ad fidem, quae revelanda erat, ut voce causa finalis notetur. Vide Ephes. IV. 17. 1. Timoth. IV. 3. quod explicatur vers. 24. lex paedagogus erat εἰς χρισὸν in vel ad Christum, sicut a lege, ut paedagogo duro, compellimur ad exoptandum & desiderandum Christum: Ita conclusione & custodia sub lege ad fidem, quae revelanda, compelli dicimur. Quod vero participes nobiscum fuerunt fidei, qui sub legis custodia erant, non est ex legalis custodiae & conclusionis, de qua impraesentiarum Apostolus agit, sed ex vi promissionum Evangelicarum de Messia, quas sub Veteri Testamento habuerunt. Quo de jam monuit B. Lutherus in Commentar. Anno 1520. edito fol. 51.

Vide, ne sic contextum ordines: Conclusi eam in fidem, quasi in fide, velut in carcere conclusos intelligi velis, cum hoc de lege affirmet: Sed sumus conclusi carcere legis, & hoc in fidem futuram, seu in hoc, ut fide futura liberemur, quin lex carcere suo id fecit, ut per fidem optaremus liberari.

Sicut supra testamentum Dei confirmatum in Christum, id est, ut in futuro Christo confirmaretur, & mox lex paedagogus noster in Christum, id est, ad Christum fuit. Non ergo opposita maledictioni legis custodia hic exprimitur, quia Paulus inter legis paedagogiam & doctrinam fidei distinguit, legique non nisi maledictionem transgressorum adscribit. Rectius ergo hanc custodiam exponit Aretius: Sub lege tanquam carcere & rigido exactore vivebamus.

Alii cum Theophylacto ῥρουρὰν interpretantur de custodia, qua praeservati fuerint ab idololatria, aliisque sceleribus horrendis veluti muro quodam custoditi.

Quod non improbat Grotius: Est hoc, inquit, aliquid, idque non exiguum. Judaei enim tum natura corrupta ac educatione mala impetu, tum pravis gentium, quas inter vivebant, exemplis infecti, facile deficiebant a vera Dei cultu. Ideo lex instar praesidii eis imponebatur, quo in agnitione sua miseria, & desiderio Messiae promissi continerentur. Plus tamen videtur Apostolus indicare. Praesidio muniti separantur ab hoste extraneo muris, fossis, vallis: Sic populus Judaicus legis praesidio munitus ab omnibus extraneis separabatur. Erat paries inter eum & alias gentes intergerinus Ephes. II. 14. servabatur inexpugnabilis & impermixtus usque ad Christi adventum, separatus ab omnibus aliis populis, quo ab aliis entissime secernebatur. Quae etsi vera sint omnia, huc tamen proprie non faciunt, ubi thema suum principale de justificatione per fidem non deserit prorsus Apostolus, sed ejus causa potius oeconomiam legis explicat, quod non, ut avocemur a Christo, sed ut ad eundem deducamur, instituta fuerit: quodque sub lege custodiamur, non tam ob... legis usum coërcitivum, quam ob usum coaditivum & paedagogicum. Non ergo hic habitudo a praesidio & vallo est, ut Grotius vult, sed potius a carcere, quo veluti conclusi custoditi fuimus ante fidem, quemadmodum altera etiam ſimilitudo docere poteſt, à duro pædagogo petita, quod circa vocem συγκεκλεισμένοι non diſſiretur Crocius. Haud dubie, inquit, concluſionem intelligit, de qua verſ. 21. Concluſi ſub peccatum. Quo de etiam Pareus: Nunc dicit etiam pro carcere fuiſſe cuſtodiam, qua concluſi tenerentur, nempe ſub peccato ut ſuit verſ. 21. Exinde enim repetit hic participium συγκεκλεισμένοι concluſi nempe ſub peccatum à Deo. Uſus legis coërcitivus etiam poſt adventum fidei locum habet: Hic verò de illo legis uſu proprie agitur, qui maxime urget, uſque dum venerit fides: Et licet per execrationem & terrorem pœnæ conſequenter etiam nos coërceamur à peccatis, eaque ratione Judæi multis legibus coërciti fuerint, id tamen hic, ut diximus, proprie non agitur. Ideoque rectius hic habet B. Lutheri paraphraſis in Commentar. ult. fol. 91. Lex concludit homines non civiliter, ſed & theologice, hoc eſt, lex eſt etiam carcer ſpiritualis & vere infernus. Quia cum revelat peccatum, minatur mortem & iram æternam Dei, homo non poteſt effugere, nec conſolationem invenire. Non eſt in poteſtate hominis, hos terribiles terrores, quos lex efficit, aut aliam cordis triſtitiam excutere. Hinc illa miſerabiles ſanctorum voces &c. Homo enim tunc in carcere eſt concluſus, ex quo non poteſt egredi, nec videt, quomodo ex his vinculis ſolvi, hoc eſt, ex his terroribus liberari poffit. Nec prætereunda eſt obſervatio, quæ ſubjungitur à B. Luthero: Sunt autem iſta vocabula, cuſtodiri & concludi ſub lege, non otioſa, ſpeculabilia ſeu ſophiſtica, ſed vera & ſeria. Cuſtodia ſeu carcer ille ſignificat veros & ſpirituales terrores, quibus conſcientia ſic concluditur, ut in latiſſimo orbe terrarum non inveniat locum, ubi ſua eſſe poſſit. Immo durantibus illis pavoribus conſcientia tantam anxietatem ſentit, ut cælum & terram, ſi etiam decies majores & ampliores eſſent, putet eſſe anguſtiora, quam ſepulchrum suum. Ibi tum plane deſtituitur homo, omni ſapientia, viribus, juſtitia, conſilio & auxilio. Conſcientia enim res eſt tenerrima, ideo cum ſic carcere legis concluditur, nuſquam patet ei exitus, ſed apparet ei iſtam anguſtiam ſubinde augeri uſque in infinitum. Sentit enim tunc iram Dei, qui infinitus eſt, cujus manum effugere non poteſt ut Pſalm. CXXXIX. ait: Quo ibo à Spiritu tuo? Sicut ergo concluſio vel carter civiliter eſt ipſa afflictio corporalis, quâ concluſus uſu corporis ſui privatur: Ita Theologice carcer eſt perturbatio & anxietas animi, quâ concluſus privatur pace conſcientiæ & quiete cordis; non tamen in æternum, ut ratio judicat, cum iſtum carcerem ſentit, ſed in futuram fidem. Erigendus eſt igitur & conſolandus animus ſub lege concluſus hoc modo: Frater concluſus quidem es, ſed ſcias hoc non agi, ut perpetuo in iſto carcere concluſus tenearis, quia ſcriptum eſt, concludi nos in futuram fidem. Affigeris ergo carcere iſto non in perniciem tuam, ſed ut per ſemen benedictionis recreeris; lege occideris, ut per Chriſtum vivificeris. Iſta ergo duo contraria ſunt conjungenda, quæ reipſa diverſiſſima ſunt. Quid enim magis contrarium, quam metucere & perhorreſcere iram Dei, & ſimiliter ſperare in miſericordia ejus? Alterum infernus, alterum cælum eſt, & tamen oportet ea in corde eſſe conjunctiſſima. Speculative, conjunguntur facillime, ſed practice ea conjungere eſt omnium difficillimum: Id quod propriâ experientiâ ſapiſſime didici. Papiſtæ & ſectarum auctores de hac re proſruſ nihil noverunt. Ideo legentes ſeu audientes iſta verba Pauli ſunt illis plane obſcura & igno

similitudo docte potest, & duro pædagogo petita: et cum lex ostendit eis peccatum, accusat & perterrefacit eos, nullum inveniunt neque consilium neque auxilium, sed simpliciter desperant, sicut Cain & Saul.

Cum igitur lex, ut dictum est, tortor & carcer noster sit, certum est eam non diligere, sed vehementer odisse.

Ideo qui dicit se legem diligere, mentitur, & nescit, quid dicat.

Insanus & mente captus esset fur aut latro, qui amaret carcerem & compedes.

Cum autem lex, ut dixi, nos concludat, certum est, nos esse hostes ejus infensissimos.

Summa, tam amamus legem, & justitiam ipsius, quam homicida carcerem.

Quomodo igitur lege justificaremur?

Intelligit ergo hæc B. Lutherus non de oppositione usuum inter tempus Veteris & Novi Testamenti; sed de opposito statu hominis cujuscunque sub lege & sub gratia.

Legis tempus, inquit, est, quando lex me exercet, divexat, contristat & redigit in cognitionem peccati, ac illud auget.

Ibi tum lex est in vero suo usu, quem Christianus sentit, donec vivit & vero.

Hocque tempus legis est, sub quo Christianus secundum carnem semper est.

Caro enim perpetuo concupiscit adversus Spiritum, & Spiritus adversus carnem, in alio tamen plus, in alio minus.

Tempus gratiæ est, cum cor iterum erigitur promissione gratuitæ misericordiæ Dei, & dicit, quare tristis es anima mea, & quare conturbas me?

Nihil præterea vides quam legem, peccatum, terrorem, tristitiam, desperationem, mortem, infernum & Diabolum?

An non est etiam gratia, remissio peccatorum, justitia, consolatio, gaudium, pax, vita, cælum, Christus, Deus? - Desine anima mea perturbare me.

Quid lex, peccatum, & omnia mala ad ista?

Spera in Deo, qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro peccatis tuis eum tradidit in mortem crucis.

Hoc tunc concludi est sub lege secundum carnem non in eternum, sed in futurum Christum.

Et inde conclusio fol. 93.

Ex his facile constat, omnes sententias, in quibus tractat Paulus spiritualem usum legis, intelligendas esse de justificanda non de justificatis.

Hi enim, quatenus in Christo manent, longe extra & supra omnem legem sunt.

Imponenda est igitur lex justificandis, ut sub ea tantisper custodiantur, donec justitia fidei veniat.

Non quod per legem justitiam illam consequantur, hoc enim esset abuti, non recte uti, lege, sed ut pavefacti & humiliati lege confugiant ad Christum, qui finis est legis ad justitiam omni credenti.

Abutuntur ergo lege primum omnes justitiarii & hypocritæ, qui somniant homines lege justificari.

Is enim usus non exercet & urget in futuram fidem, sed efficit faturos, securos & superbos hypocritæ, tumentes & præsumentes de justitia & operibus legis, & impedit justitiam fidei &c.

Observandum enim, quod S. Apostolus ad Galatas scribat, qui non fuere sub legis pædagogia, quos sibi conjungat, quibusque usus ille conveniat, quemadmodum id in confesso est de usu pædagogico, de quo jam quæritur.

Hic enim omnium est temporum, omniumque hominum.

Et quum adhuc sermo fit de lege morali, non vero de ceremonialibus & forensibus legibus, sub ratione προσετέθη, iterum patet, per illud non intelligi tale quid, quo Judæi olim a gentibus reliquis discernebantur.

Nam lex moralis est omnium non tantum Judæorum, quemadmodum etiam tota illa disputatio de usu legis, quare προσετέθη adjecta fit promissioni ad omnes homines spectat:

et de justificatione per fidem citra discrimen temporum agitur vers. 24. deque υἱοθεσία, quæ per fidem in Christum Jesum obtigit non minus Patribus in veteri Testamento, quam nobis in novo Testamento.

Et, ne ullum hic fingatur discrimen, diserte additur, in Christo Jesu non esse Judæum aut Græcum &c, Omnes fideles in Christo unum esse, & Christi esse & Abrahæ semen (spirituale) & secundum promissionem hæredes. Quam explicationem de usu legis non quoad Judæos tantum, sed quoad omnes homines non tantum in Comment. Anno 1519. adornato & sequenti anno edito tradidit Megalander, sed etiam in recognitione Anno 1524. facta repetit; nec fidem tantum, quæ post Christum revelata est, sed de omni fide omnium justorum intelligitur. nam quæ optime τῇ συνεχείᾳ & intentioni ac scopo Apostolicæ disceptationis nostro judicio congruit. Integra ejus paraphrasis Tom. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 29. sic habet: Prius autem quam veniret fides, non tantum de fide, quæ post Christum revelata est, sed de omni fide omnium justorum intelligitur. Nam & Patribus olim eadem fides venit, quia & lex Dei eis primo revelata cogit eos gratiam quærere: Licet tum non ita per orbem prædicaretur, prædicatur tamen privatim per familias patrum. Vers. 24. Ὡς ὁ νόμος παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν γέγονεν εἰς χριστόν.

Sunt ut hominum, ita & populorum ætates, ut Florus ostendit. Ætas Israëliti-ci populi sub lege erat quasi pueritia, infra IV. 9. Nempe illa, cui solet addi παιδαγωγός, sive custos, ut Horatius loquitur שמר Gen. IV. 9. Qui eos a gravioribus delictis retrahat. Hoc officium lex illa populo præstitit, quod ni fuisset, prolapsi essent ad tantam impietatem, per quam obfurduissent ad vocem Evangelii. Et autem παιδαγωγὸς non nisi temporaria autoritas. Simplicius ad Epictetum pædagogi similitudine paulo aliter utitur, sed quæ ab hac non longe abit: οὐ ἀπαιδεύτου τῶι τοῦ τῆς μὲν παιδαγωγὸς, ὡς κακαὶ αὐτοῖς αἰτίες μῦθοι. Postea: Παιδεία μὲν γάρ ἐστι κυρίως, ἃ τῆι ἐν ὑμῖν παιδαγωγῶι ἐπανορθώσει· καὶ πῶς μὲν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀλογία τὸ μὲν ὠφέλιμον μὴ ὁρῶσα, πρὸς δὲ τὸ ἡδὺ τεταγμένη μόνον, ὥσπερ οἱ παῖδες· Παιδαγωγὸς δὲ ὁ λόγῳ ῥυθμιζων τὰ μετῶν τὰς ἀλόγους ἐν ἡμῖν ὀρέξεις, κὴ πρὸς τὰ ὠφέλιμον ἀπευθύνων αὐτάς. Videat si cui vacat locum totum ad illud Epicteti: 'Απαιδεύτου ἔργον &c. "ἵνα ἐκ πίστεως δικαιωθῶμεν"

Ut suo tempore veram justitiam consequeremur per Evangelium.

## 3:25
Verf. 25. Ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς πίστεως) as above 23. Οὐκ ἔτι ὑπὸ παιδαγωγόν ἐσμεν) Another age demands other customs. Horace says. Grotius rashly distinguishes ages as far as faith is concerned, which as to substance was always the same in every age.

Nor indeed did the Israelite people have the law, but also the Gospel, which was already promulgated in Paradise itself and repeated to the Patriarchs; nor was true justification to be revealed only at the time of the New Testament, but through the same also the ancient believers were justified, there is no other single reason for justification, nor is it to be believed that the ancient just were destitute of true justice, and that they were saved by another than true justice. But here the blessed Luther is again excellently affected and has expounded the mind of the holy Apostle, in the interpretation of the pedagogical office of the law, Tom. III. Jen. fol. 29. There he simultaneously warned about rightly constituting the text: Again beware, lest you read the context thus: The law was our pedagogue in Christ, as if to those already living in Christ, the law might be our pedagogue in Christ, as our translation has it, and seems to savor. For this utterly perverts the sense of the Apostle. But just as boys are under a pedagogue for the sake of the inheritance; that is, that they may be educated, so that they may arrive at the inheritance: So the law is our pedagogue unto Christ, that is, that being led and exercised through the law, we may be prepared to seek and sigh for Christ, for faith, for the inheritance. For the law (as I said) prepares for grace, while it reveals and increases sin, humbling the proud to desire the help of Christ. And the Apostle supports this sense with the following particle; unto Christ I say, that we might be justified by faith, who were becoming sinners through the law. Thus Ps. LXVIII. "Because thy mercy is sweet, O Lord". Why? because thy law is beloved, O Lord. Therefore the boy will not remain under a pedagogue, but will be educated toward receiving the inheritance more sweetly: So also the law renders and commends the grace of God more sweetly. Excellently therefore he declares the faith of the law, namely not to be our justice and fulfillment; but a sighing after Christ, that it may be sought to be fulfilled through his faith. But our justificarians have their own laws as their end, the very laws and their works, nor do they order them unto Christ, but into works only, so that they may perish forever with the Jews, whom they imitate, understanding neither the law nor its works.

For ἔκθεσιν the man of God repeats in his later Commentary, Tom. IV. Jenenf. Latin fol. 93. Therefore the law was our pedagogue unto Christ. Again he joins law and Gospel by affection, which in reality are most widely separated from each other, when he says, the law our pedagogue unto Christ. But this similitude concerning the pedagogue is also very notable, and therefore must be diligently considered. Although a pedagogue is most useful and greatly necessary for boys to be educated and instructed, yet give but one disciple or boy who loves his own pedagogue &c. A pedagogue is therefore applied to a boy, that he may instruct and guard him, and as it were hold him captive in prison. To what end, and for how long? Is it that this harsh and odious dominion of the pedagogue and servitude of the boy may endure forever? By no means, but unto a predetermined time, so that obedience itself, prison, and discipline may work out good for the boy, so that in due time he may become heir and king. For it is not the Father's will that the son be perpetually subject to the pedagogue, and that the rod fall upon him from him, but that by his instruction and discipline he may be rendered fit for the succession of the inheritance. Thus the law is nothing else, says Paul, than a Pedagogue, not perpetually, but unto Christ, as above he also said in other words: The law was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come &c. Likewise Scripture concluded all things under sin, that the promise &c. Likewise we were kept under the law, shut up unto that faith which was to be revealed. Wherefore the law is not simply a pedagogue, but unto Christ. With this beautiful similitude therefore Paul shows the true use of the law, namely that it does not justify hypocrites, because they remain outside Christ in presumption and security. And on the contrary, that it does not leave the contrite, if they use the law in this manner as Paul teaches, in damnation and death, but urges them toward Christ. But those who persist in those terrors in their own pusillanimity and do not apprehend Christ by faith, at last despair. Most clearly therefore does Paul paint the true use of the law with this allegory of the pedagogue. For as he rebukes, presses, and saddens boys, not with this counsel, that this pedagogy may endure perpetually, but that it may cease when the boys have been properly educated and instructed, so that afterwards without compulsion of the pedagogue they may be eager and free to enjoy liberty and their father's goods. So let those who are terrified and crushed by the law know that these terrors and contritions will not be perpetual, but that by them Christ is being prepared for them in the future, and the liberty of the Spirit &c. We rather lean upon this explanation as being most solid than upon the interpretation of those who speak of the moral and ceremonial law under the Old Testament before the advent

...and interpreted the text of the fullness of time. Such is the interpretation of Calvin, Pareus, and Crocius, that the law was a schoolmaster, by whose work the Jews were led as if by the hand, and that the office of the law was temporal, which ought to have expired once Christ was exhibited, as Pareus says in this place: who summarized the matter thus: I shall speak more briefly: since there was a threefold law, there was a threefold pedagogical discipline.

The moral law led to Christ by accidental direction, as has been explained. The ceremonial law by direct signification and duration: for ceremonies shadowed forth Christ, being destined to cease at his arrival. Finally, the forensic law or polity, by the distinction of the nation from the rest of the peoples and by its duration until Christ. These are the words of Pareus, which Crocius also repeats in almost the same words in his own customary manner.

But however true all these things may be, they nevertheless seem foreign here.

For (1) the subject here is not what was peculiar and proper to the Jews, but the use of the law in general, which the entire context of the Apostolic treatment teaches.

(2) The subject of the heir as an infant placed under a tutor and curator is treated only in the following chapter.

Which we do not deny pertains properly to the state of the Jews. Here the Apostle is still occupied with a general treatment.

(3) Nor does he speak of the ceremonial, but of the moral law, which he teaches was promulgated because of transgressions: and he proved that its exaction only brings [wrath], because it is observed by no one, so that justification is obtained only through faith.

(4) That sacrifices, ceremonies, and washings served to fix the eyes of the people upon this sin, that is from the moral law, from which alone the recognition of sin was had; nor were those ceremonies, namely sacrifices and washings, instituted primarily for the cleansing of spiritual filth, but rather for the sake of the expiation and ablution to be sought through faith in Christ’s sacrifice and blood: in which part they did not look to the law, of which the Apostle discourses here, but were appendices and symbols of the Gospel, and a sermon, as it were, real, concerning Christ’s passion and blood.

By this direct signification, even if the ceremonial law led to Christ, it was not, however, in that respect properly a schoolmaster (παιδαγωγός).

For Pareus had described him thus: A schoolmaster is given to boys so that their wanton age may be restrained, that they may be imbued with good morals, and that they may be informed and prepared by childish rudiments for greater studies: when they have arrived at these, the schoolmaster lays down his rod and his office. Regarding this stated signification, and the typical reason of the ceremonial law, these things cannot be conveniently applied.

(5) The duration of the law is not the subject here, and therefore neither is the duration of the ceremonial law.

For if the time of duration were being considered, the moral law itself ought also to have had an end, since they wish the discourse to be about the law in general.

(6) There is nothing here about the distinction of the forensic law, much less about its duration until Christ.

Nor do those things contribute anything to the present scope, which is added explicitly by the Apostle, that we might be justified by faith.

(7) Wherefore these things must be accepted in such a way that one does not depart from that scope which the Apostle presses and urges most strongly.

Namely, he deals with the pedagogical use of the law toward Christ, not that the law had to last until Christ, but that it perpetually becomes a schoolmaster to us toward Christ, so that we may be justified through faith in Christ.

For what then?

Did not the law lead to CHRIST as a schoolmaster before the advent of CHRIST under the Old Testament, so that the ancients also might be justified through faith in CHRIST; did this method of justification only have a place after the advent of CHRIST?

And is the law not still a schoolmaster to us εἰς χριστὸν (unto Christ), so that we may be justified through faith, but that was proper and peculiar to the Jews under the Old Testament.

Therefore, from those words, "that we might be justified by faith," it is not established here that the term of the pedagogy of the law is the time of Christ’s advent in the flesh, but that the use and end of the pedagogy of the law is defined, that it indirectly drives us to Christ, so that we may seek and obtain righteousness through faith in him, so that he, as Theophylact says, who imparts the condemnation of guilt, and justifies by faith, which was the end of the law, as Pareus rightly says, was accidental.

For it accidentally compelled those captive under sin to seek Christ.

B. explains this.

Glassius in this way: It is rightly said that the law is our schoolmaster unto Christ, while 1. the law urges its own ἀκριβοδίκαιον (exact justice), and requires the fullest obedience, which when it does not find in us, therefore 2. it demonstrates and argues the emptiness of our mind and the depravity of our will, Romans III. 20. afterwards 3. it accuses and condemns, and thus shakes out the innate deed and strikes terror, Rom. IV. 15. 1 Cor. XV. 56. 4. Having accomplished these things, it leads obliquely to Christ.

For if we wish to escape the threats and punishments, it suggests by a certain silent instinct that another physician must be sought, through whom we may be freed from that curse.

Compare Romans V. 20. chapter VII. 7. &c.

These things are correct, but it is less correctly posited that the present verse is referred to the distinction between the state of law and grace only by accommodation, and not according to the literal meaning.

For that the Apostle intends this directly is shown even by what he adds, ἵνα ἐκ πίστεως δικαιωθῶμεν (that we might be justified by faith), which does not look to the distinction of time before and after Christ, but pertains to all times.

Concerning which B. Luther, Comment. poster. fol. 94. "that we might be justified from this": The law is not a schoolmaster unto another legislator, who demands good works, but unto Christ the justifier and Savior, so that we may be justified through faith in him, not by works.

The true use of the law is that I know that I am led by the law into the knowledge of sin and humbled, so that I may come to Christ and be justified by faith.

Faith, however, is not a law nor a work, but a certain trust, which apprehends Christ, who is the end of the law, Roman.

X. How?

Not that it abrogates the old law, and they taught a new one, so that the Judge is to be appeased by works, as the Papists taught, but it is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, that is, everyone who believes in him is righteous. The law cannot accuse him, &c.

This force and use of the law is true.

It is therefore holy, good, useful, and necessary, provided one uses it lawfully.

But hypocrites abuse the law first, who attribute to it the power of justifying.

Then the despairing, who are ignorant that the law is a schoolmaster unto Christ, that is, the law strikes God, so that he may heal; it kills, so that it may make alive, &c.

(8) The same is proven by equivalent sentences, which B. Luther compares here, namely that the scripture (of the law) has concluded all under sin, that the promise might be given by faith of Christ to them that believe; that before faith came, we were kept, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed; it is undoubted that the former of these pertains to all times.

And B. Luther no less truly posits the same regarding the latter by the force of ἰσοδυναμία (equivalence).

For up to that point, and for that very end, we are kept under the law, and we are shut up, until faith comes, and so that the future faith might then be revealed more illustriously.

For where sin abounds, there grace abounds more.

He repeats that conclusion from v. 21.

Pareus also concluded, συνέκλεισεν, that we are indeed concluded under sin by the law, but that the end of the prison is salutary, εἰς τὴν πίστιν μέλλουσαν &c., unto the faith which was to be revealed. (9) Furthermore, the Apostle says that after faith has come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. But this cannot be understood as referring to the time of Christ’s advent. For in that way, the law would in no wise be a schoolmaster to us unto Christ any longer: not even by way of accommodation. For there is no accommodation that is contrary to the literal sense. If, therefore, the letter of the text means that after Christ came in the flesh we are no longer under a schoolmaster, how will an accommodation have a place here, [suggesting] that we are still under that schoolmaster in the time of the New Testament? The state of the New Testament, says Pareus, is marked by being under grace, with Christ exhibited. He expressly affirms that the office of the schoolmaster has now expired and no longer has a place. We are no longer, he says, under a schoolmaster, that is, under the law. For when boys have become mature enough to perceive the precepts of a superior master, the schoolmaster lays down his rod and resigns his office. Thus, when the people were mature in faith regarding Christ exhibited, the law laid down its pedagogy. Thus, in one word, he clearly teaches that the law is abrogated in the New Testament. Bullinger is more correct here: after faith has come, that is, after we have arrived at Christ and faith has shone in the hearts of men, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. For we are moved by the free and spontaneous Spirit of Christ and are led directly, so that there is no need for an exactor or schoolmaster. What of the fact that the blessed Luther also excellently teaches that the regenerate are in a certain sense under a schoolmaster? If we could, he says (fol. 94), perfectly apprehend Christ, who abrogated the law and reconciled us sinners to the Father by His death, that schoolmaster would have no right over us at all. But the law of the members rebelling against the law of the mind prevents us from being able to perfectly apprehend Christ. The defect, therefore, is not in Christ, but in us, who have not yet put off the flesh, in which sin clings as long as we live. Therefore, as far as we are concerned, we are partly free from the law and partly under the law. With Paul, we serve the law of God with the mind, but the law of sin with the flesh (Rom. VII). From this it follows that, according to conscience, we are plainly free from the law. Therefore, that schoolmaster ought not to dominate it; that is, he ought not to be troublesome to it with his terrors, threats, and captivity. And even if he attempts this to the utmost, the conscience is not moved by that thing at all. For it has in its sight Christ crucified, who took away all the offices of the law and blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us (Col. II). And a little later: Insofar, therefore, as the flesh remains, so far also remains the law as a schoolmaster, which is wont to terrify and sadden the conscience from time to time by the showing of sin and the commination of death. Yet the conscience itself is always raised up again by the daily coming of Christ, who, just as He once came into the world at a certain time to redeem us from the harshest empire of our schoolmaster, so He comes to us daily in a spiritual manner, bringing it about that we grow in faith and the knowledge of Him, that the conscience may day by day more perfectly apprehend Christ, and that the law of the flesh and of sin, the dread of death, and whatever evils the law brings with it, may be diminished more and more. As long, therefore, as we live—which is not without sin—the law returns from time to time and performs its office, in one more, in another less, according as faith is weak or strong, yet not unto destruction, but unto salvation. For this exercise of the law in the saints is the daily mortification of our flesh, reason, and powers, and the renewal of our mind (2 Cor.

IV. (10) Pareus cannot extricate himself, how the law is abrogated, since it is eternal. He says it is abrogated as to justification, damnation, coercion, signification, not as to doctrine, obedience. But the law could never justify after the fall, nor was it given that it might justify. For if the law were given, which could (at any time, whether of the Old or New Testament) make alive, truly righteousness would be from the law, v. 21. Therefore what the law did not have, or what in no way belongs to the law at the time of the Old Testament, or before Christ, on account of this the law cannot be said to be abrogated at the time of the New Testament, or after the advent of Christ. Nor indeed can it rightly be said to be abrogated at this time as to damnation. It inflicted a curse, he says, upon transgressors, remitting nothing, forgiving nothing, only condemning. But the moral law does this equally after the advent of Christ, just as before His advent. For it concludes all under sin, and through sin under a curse. Nor is there any forgiveness in the law or through the law. Furthermore, as to the coercion of the law, it obtains equally after Christ, as to those who are outside the state of grace, with respect to the moral law, just as before Christ. And therefore not even here can the moral law be said to be abrogated at the time of the New Testament. Finally, as to signification, Pareus explains it thus: that the law (ceremonial) signified that Christ and His grace would come by obscure shadows. The people of GOD (the forensic law) it separated from all others, and thereby expiated. But since the ceremonial law has ceased, nor does the forensic law further bind us, how can those ceremonies or forensic laws still signify anything to us, or discern for us things which no longer remain, or are no longer in use? Although formerly the Jewish people were distinguished not only by the forensic, but also by the ceremonial law; but what has this to do with the Apostolic treatment of justification? Now as to doctrine and obedience, the law had the same character formerly, as it still has, if the moral law be in question: But as to the ceremonial and forensic, because that bound the Jews alone, while the Levitical worship and their polity flourished, now it expires of itself, after the worship, temple, and polity of the Jews have ceased: as to binding us, however, it could not bind us, because it never bound us, nor was it enacted, that it might bind Christians or any other people than the Jewish, and that also only unto a certain time.

(11) Pareus understood well that the reason does not seem sufficiently strong, you are not under a schoolmaster, because you are sons of God. For were not the Fathers also heirs and sons, but little ones, under a schoolmaster and servitude; yet they were not yet adult sons, emancipated, admitted to the inheritance, as we are. But the treatment of the following chapter is rashly confused with the present one. In how many ways, however, the Fathers were little ones under tutors, in nothing differing from slaves, will be said there. That indeed has no bearing on the present matter, where it is said of the justified at whatever time, that all are sons of God through faith in Christ. Nor are only adult and emancipated sons understood here, but the discourse is generally about the sons of God, whether they are under tutelage or not, namely whoever are justified through faith in Christ, which cannot be denied of the Fathers of the Old Testament. All, he says, you are sons of God through faith in Christ. But were not the Fathers also sons of God through faith in Christ? You say, they were not such; but where is this restriction in the text? and how with faith in Christ? For through it all are of equal condition. For there is neither Jew nor Greek in Christ.

B.

Glassius acknowledges that adult sons are not meant here: The similitude of the pedagogue seems to imply by the word ἤπιοι [infants] that adult sons are already understood, to whom the νήπιοι [infants] are opposed in ch. IV. v. 1, 3. But because the Apostle mixes two similitudes, the first of which is taken from infants, the other from the condition of servants, as is evident from v. 23, 24 of ch. IV. 1-7, therefore it is better that by ἤπιοι sons are understood, insofar as they are opposed to servants.

Compare ch. IV. v. 5, 6 with Rom. VIII. 15, 16. But here no mixture appears in the Apostle.

He teaches that those who are justified through Christ are not under a pedagogue, and calls them sons of GOD. Which has place no less in the Old Testament than in the New, and therefore B. Glassius praises the explanation of Hyperius: The sentiment is: Sons are not bound to heavier burdens in the same way that servants are bound, but are recognized by all right as free from them. But believers in Christ are sons, therefore those who believe in Christ are not bound to the burdens of the law, but are freed from the law. But if they are freed from the heavy law, why would they be ordered to seek righteousness from it?

These things, however, pertain equally to believers in the Old as in the New Testament. Crocius says that they are called sons, not in any way, but by excellence and comparatively. For he says, he does not precisely deny the right of sonship to the ancient fathers, but attributes a more excellent mode to the New Testament. But in ἤπιοι through faith in Christ there is no preeminence [ἐξοχή], all are equally sons, as Crocius expressly confesses a little later: He does not hand down one and another reason for sonship in Jews and Gentiles, he hands down one and the same [reason] equally granted to all, one medium, one principal cause. He names faith as the medium.

Above he had named the sons of Abraham, now he speaks more deeply, to God himself, namely, who is the Father of all those who are called sons: of whom Abraham himself is also a son. Through faith, he says, Chrysostom notes, not through the law. Whence it appears, he is not dealing with sonship, which depends on creation. Nor through just any faith, but that which is in Christ Jesus, meriting and applying, which embraces Jesus Christ as the sole Mediator with his merit and efficacy by faith, and seeks salvation in him alone. And thus he names the gratuitous cause of sonship as the principal one, lest any of them arrogate anything to themselves from works, from their own dignity and merit.

But Crocius does not deny that all these things must also be said of the Fathers of the Old Testament time. Therefore there is no diversity in these, the medium of sonship was the same, the same principal and meritorious cause, the same sonship. And since Abraham himself lived as the Father of believers before Christ, are we to be considered sons of GOD by a more excellent reason than he was the Father of believers?

He deals with sons who have put on Christ, that is, his righteousness. But that truly applies no less to the fathers of the Old Testament time than to us under the New Testament. For they were not justified and saved by any other reason than we were, Aflor.

XV. And as to these; so also the law is a pedagogue to us ἤπιοι, so that Christ with his righteousness and merit may be put on as a tunic of righteousness and a garment of salvation, Isa. LXI. He deals with such sons of God, who are the seed of Abraham, through faith. But were not believers also before Christ was exhibited the seed of Abraham through faith in the Messiah? He deals with their justification through faith and sonship of GOD, who according to the promise are heirs of eternal life. But this no less agrees with the Fathers before Christ than with believers after Christ. In sum, no distinction of the sons of GOD is yet established here, or of the Fathers in the Old Testament, and believers in the time of the New Testament, whether regarding the sonship of GOD, or the inheritance of salvation, or faith in the Messiah, or justification through faith.

But the same reason for faith, justification through faith, sonship of GOD, and inheritance of eternal life is urged and pressed, namely, that the former (faith) always and solely looks to Christ, but the latter, justification, sonship of GOD, and inheritance, is obtained only through faith in Christ, without distinction of times, and for the same [purpose] the law is a pedagogue, until faith comes or is revealed. Verf. 26. All you who are sons of GOD through faith, in Christ Jesus) You, who have believed in Christ, so as it behooves, and as you persevere in believing, are adult sons (of GOD, namely), such as those who are, begin to enjoy paternal goods. So also you have received the Spirit of the Father.

Indeed, the Israelites under the law of GOD are also called sons, Deut. XVI. 1, but as children, whose dignity did not yet appear: for they were ruled in a servile manner, below IV. 1. We have already warned that there is no place here for this determination, that they are sons of GOD, namely, adults. Such as those who are, Grotius teaches, that they begin to enjoy paternal goods, and receive the Spirit of the Father.

But who doubts that the Fathers also in the time of the Old Testament were made partakers of the goods of the heavenly Father, when GOD promised to Abraham: I will be Thy God and of Thy seed. Nor can it be denied by any right that the same Fathers received the Spirit, which we have shown elsewhere against the Socinians. Does not the Apostle equate us in this, that we have the same Spirit of faith, which David had, 2 Cor.

IV. 13. Therefore B. Luther is excellent on this passage: Paul as an excellent Doctor of faith always has in his mouth those words through faith, in faith, from faith which is in Christ Jesus etc.

He does not say, you are sons of GOD, because you were circumcised, heard the law and did its works, as the Jews dreamed, and the Pseudo-Apostles taught, but through faith in Christ Jesus. The law therefore does not make (much less human traditions) sons of GOD, it cannot generate into a new nature or birth, but sets before the eyes that old birth, by which we were born into the kingdom of the Devil. And thus it prepares for the new birth, which is made through faith in Christ Jesus, not through the law, as Paul most clearly testifies, you are all sons of God through faith etc. i.e. even if you were vexed, humbled and killed by the law, nevertheless it did not make you righteous, it did not make you sons of GOD, but faith.

Which? in Christ. Faith therefore in Christ makes sons of GOD, not the law. John I testifies the same, he gave them power to become sons of GOD, to those who believe etc.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς πίστεως) ut supra 23. Οὐκ ἔτι ὑπὸ παιδαγωγόν ἐσμεν) Alia ætas alios mores postulat. Ait Horatius. Grotius temere ætates quantum ad fidem distinguit, quæ quoad substantiam omni ætate semper eadem fuit.

Nec vero legem habuit populus Israëliticus, sed etiam Evangelium, quod in ipso Paradiso jam promulgatum & ad Patriarchas repetitum fuit; nec justitia vera demum tempore Novi Testamenti revelanda erat, sed per eandem etiam veteres fideles justificati sunt, non nisi unica fit justificationis ratio, negue credendum fit veteres justos vera destitutos fuisse justitia, & aliâ, quam vera justitia salvatos esse. Optime autem hic iterum B. Lutherus affectus est & exposuit sancti Apostoli mentem, in interpretatione pædagogici officii legis Tom. III. Jen. fol. 29. Ibi simul monuit de textu recte constituendo: Iterum cave, ne sic contextum legas: Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christo, quasi in Christo jam viventibus, lex pædagogus noster sit in Christo, ut nostra translatio habet, & sapere videtur. Hoc enim Apostoli sensum penitus pervertit. Sed sicut pueri sunt sub pædagogo ad hæreditatem; id est, quo erudiantur, ut ad hæreditatem pertingant: Ita lex est noster pædagogus ad Christum, id est, ut per legem acti & exerciti, ad Christum, ad fidem, ad hæreditatem quærendam & suspirandam paremur. Lex enim (ut dixi) ad gratiam præparat, dum peccatum revelat & auget, humilians superbos ad auxilium Christi desiderandum. Et hunc sensum Apostolus juvat particula sequente; ad Christum inquam, ut fide scilicet justificemur, qui peccatores fiebamus lege. Sic Ps. LXVIII. "Quoniam suavis est misericordia tua Domine". Quare? quia amata est lex tua Domine. Non ergo puer sub pædagogo manebit, sed ad hæreditatem dulcius accipiendam erudietur: Ita & lex gratiam Dei dulciorem reddit & commendat. Egregie itaque fidem legis declarat, non esse scilicet nostram justitiam & impletionem; sed suspirium ad Christum, ut per fidem ejus quæratur impleri. At nostri justificarii legum suarum finem habent, ipsas leges & opera earum, nec eas ad Christum ordinant, sed in opera solum, ut in æternum pereant cum Judæis, quos imitantur, nec legem nec opera ejus intelligentes.

Nam ἔκθεσιν repetit Vir DEI in poster. Comment. Tom. IV. Jenenf. Latin fol. 93. Itaque lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christum. Iterum affeclu conjungit legem & Evangelium, quæ reipsa longissime inter se separata sunt, cum inquit, lex pædagogus noster in Christum. Est autem & ista similitudo de pædagogo valde insignis, ideo diligenter consideranda est. Quanquam pædagogus est utilissimus & valde necessarius pueris educandis & instituendis, tamen da vel unum discipulum aut puerum, qui suum amet pædagogum &c. Adhibetur ergo pædagogus puero, ut eum erudiat & custodiat, ac velut in carcere captivum teneat. Ad quid & quamdiu? Num ut perpetuo duret istud durum & odiosum Dominium pædagogi & servitus pueri? Minime, sed ad præfinitum tempus, ut ipsa obedientia, carcer & disciplina sedat puero in bonum, ut suo tempore fiat hæres & Rex. Non enim est Patris voluntas, ut filius perpetuo subditus sit pædagogo, & cadatur virga ab ipso, sed ut ipsius institutione & disciplina idoneus reddatur ad successionem hæreditatis. Sic lex nihil aliud est, inquit Paulus, quam Pædagogus, non perpetuo, sed in Christum, ut supra aliis verbis quoque dixit: Lex propter transgressiones addita est, donec veniret semen &c. Item scriptura conclusit omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio &c. Item custodiebamur sub lege, conclusi in eam fidem, quæ erat revelanda. Quare lex non est simpliciter pædagogus, sed in Christum. Hac pulchra ergo similitudine ostendit Paulus verum legis usum, quod videlicet hypocritas non justificet, quia manent extra Christum in præsumtione & securitate. Et contra, quod contritos, si hoc modo lege utantur, ut Paulus docet, non relinquat in damnatione & morte, sed ad Christum urgeat. Qui vero in illis pavoribus perdurant in ista sua pusillanimitate & Christum fide non apprehendunt, ad extremum desperant. Clarissime ergo pingit Paulus verum usum legis hac allegoria de pædagogo. Nam ut is objurgat, urget, & contristat pueros non hoc consilio, ut perpetuo duret ista pædagogia, sed ut desinat, ubi pueri probe educati & instituti sunt, ut postea sine coactione pædagogi alacres & liberi fruantur libertate & bonis paternis. Ita qui perterrefiunt & conteruntur lege, sciant istos terrores & contrisiones non fore perpetuas, sed illis sese parari in futurum Christum & libertatem Spiritus &c. Huic explicationi utpote solidissimæ potius innitimur, quam eorum interpretationi, qui de lege morali & ceremoniali sub V. Test. ante adventum

Christi & plenitudinem temporum textum interpretati sunt. Qualis est Calvini interpretatio, Parei, atque Crocii, legem fuisse paedagogum, cujus opera ceu manu deducerentur Judaei, ac temporale fuisse munus legis, quod exhibito Christo expirare debuit, ut hoc loco Pareus: qui summam rei sic complexus est: Dicam brevius: cum triplex lex fuerit, triplex paedagogica disciplina.

Lex moralis ad Christum ducebat accidentali directione, ut explicatum est. Lex ceremonialis directa significatione & duratione: Ceremonia enim Christum adumbrabant ejus adventu cessature. Denique forensis lex seu politia, distinctione gentis a reliquis populis & duratione ad Christum usque. Haec Pareus, quae & alia iisdem fere verbis more sibi solemni repetit Crocius.

Sed utut haec vera sint omnia, tamen hic aliena videntur.

Nam (1) non agitur hic de eo, quod Judaeis peculiare fuerit ac proprium, sed de usu legis in communi, quod tota συνέχειᾳ tractationis Apostolicae docet.

(2) De herede infantili sub tutore & curatore constituto sequenti demum capite tractatur.

Quod ad Judaeorum statum proprie pertinere non diffitemur. Hic in communi tractatione adhuc occupatur Apostolus.

(3) Nec de ceremoniali, sed morali lege ait, quam docet transgressionum gratia promulgatam: quamque exactionem tantum afferre, quia a nemine observatur, evicit, ut justificationem tantum per fidem esse obtineat.

(4) Quod sacrificia, ceremoniae, lotiones eo fecerint, ut ad hoc peccati populo oculos ponerent, id a lege morali est, ex qua habebatur unice agnitio peccati; nec πρώτως ad sordium spiritualium mundationem ceremoniae illae, sacrificia nempe ac lotiones instituta erant, sed potius ob expiationem & ablutionem in Christi sacrificio & sanguine per fidem quaerendam: qua parte non ad legem spectabant, de qua hic disserit Apostolus, sed appendices erant & symbola Evangelii, & concio de Christi passione & sanguine quasi realis.

Directa hac significatione lex ceremonialis etsi ad Christum duceret, non tamen ea proprie parte erat παιδαγωγός.

Hunc enim ita descripserat Pareus: Paedagogus datur pueris, ut aetas lasciviens refrenetur, bonis moribus imbuatur, rudimentis puerilibus informetur & praeparetur ad majora studia: ad quae quando provenerunt, ferulam & munus suum paedagogus deponit. Quoad hanc dictam significationem, & rationem typicam legis ceremonialis applicari commode non possunt.

(5) De duratione legis hic non agitur, ideoque nec de duratione legis ceremonialis.

Nam si durationis tempus respiceretur, ipsa etiam lex moralis finem habuisse debuit, quum in genere de lege sermonem esse velint.

(6) Nihil hic de distinctione forensis, nedum de duratione ejus usque ad Christum.

Nec ea ad scopum praesentem quicquam faciunt, qui additur differte ab Apostolo, ut ex fide justificaremur.

(7) Quapropter ita haec accipienda, ut a scopo illo non discedatur, quem premit, urgetque cum maxime Apostolus.

Nimirum de legis usu paedagogico ad Christum agit, non quod usque ad Christum durare debuerit lex, sed quod perpetuo nobis paedagogi instar fit ad Christum, ut per fidem in Christum justificemur.

Quid enim?

Annon ante adventum CHRISTI sub Vet. Test. ad CHRISTUM lex ceu paedagogus adducebat, ut veteres quoque per fidem in CHRISTUM justificarentur, num haec justificationis ratio demum post adventum CHRISTI locum habuit?

Et annon etiamnum paedagogi instar nobis est lex εἰς χριστὸν, ut justificemur per fidem, sed proprium ac peculiare id erat Judaeis sub Veteri Testamento.

Pater ergo ex illis, ut per fidem justificemur, non constitui hic terminum paedagogiae legis tempus adventus Christi in carnem, sed definiri usum & finem paedagogiae legis, quod indirecte nos ad Christum agat, ut per fidem in ipso justitiam quaeramus & consequamur, ut eum, dicente Theophylacto, qui noxae condemnationem impertiatur, & ex fide justificet, qui finis legis, ut recte Pareus, accidentarius fuit.

Per accidens enim cogebat captivos sub peccato quaerere Christum.

Explicat id B.

Glassius hoc modo: Recte dicitur legem paedagogum nostrum ad Christum esse, dum 1. lex suum ἀκριβοδίκαιον urget, & plenissimam obedientiam requirit, quam in nobis cum non invenit, igitur 2. mentis nostrae vacuitatem & voluntatis pravitatem demonstrat & arguit Roman. III. 20. postmodum 3. accusat & damnat, atque sic factum insitum excutis terroremque incutit Rom. IV. 15. 1. Cor. XV. 56. 4. Quibus peractis ad Christum oblique ducit.

Si enim minas panasque effugere velimus, alium quaerendum esse medicum, per quem a maledictione ista liberemur, tacito quodam instinctu suggerit.

Confer. Roman. V. 20. cap. VII. 7. &c.

Haec recte se habent, sed per accommodationem tantum ita ad discrimen status legis & gratiae versum praesentem referri, non vero quoad literalem sententiam, minus recte statuitur.

Nam directe hoc intendere Apostolum vel id docet, quod addit ἵνα ἐκ πίστεως δικαιωθῶμεν, quod non respicit discrimen temporis ante & post Christum, sed ad omnia tempora pertinet.

Quo de B. Lutherus Comment. poster. fol. 94. ut ex hoc justificemur: Lex non est paedagogus in alium legislatorem, qui bona opera exigit, sed in Christum justificatorem & Salvatorem, ut per fidem in ipsum, non per opera justificemur.

Verus usus legis est, quod sciam me lege adduci in cognitionem peccati & humiliari, ut ad Christum veniam & fide justificer.

Fides autem non est lex neque opus, sed certa fiducia, quae apprehendit Christum, qui est finis legis, Roman.

X. Quomodo?

Non quod abroget veterem legem, & novam docuerunt, ut Judex fit operibus placandus, ut Papistae docuerunt, sed finis est legis ad justitiam omni credenti, hoc est, omnis, qui credit in eum, est justus. Lex eum non potest accusare &c.

Hac vis & usus legis verus est.

Est igitur sancta, bona, utilis & necessaria, modo quis ea legitime utatur.

Abutuntur autem lege primum hypocrita, qui vim justificandi ei tribuunt.

Deinde desperantes, qui ignorant legem esse paedagogum in Christum, hoc est, legem Deum enim percutit, ut sanet; occidit, ut vivificet &c.

(8) Idem comprobant aequipollentes sententiae, quas hic confert B. Lutherus, nempe quod concluserit scriptura (legis) omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio ex fide Christi daretur credentibus; quod antequam veniret fides, custoditi fuerimus conclusi in fidem futuram; quarum priorem ad omnia tempora pertinere indubium est.

Nec minus vero de posteriori id statuit B. Lutherus vi ἰσοδυναμίας.

Eo usque enim, & eo etiam fine custodimur sub lege, & conclusi sumus, donec veniat fides, & ut fides futura illustrius tum reveletur.

Ubi enim peccatum abundat, ibi magis abundat gratia.

Conclusionem illam e v. 21. repetit

etiam Pareus συνέκλεισεν, concludi nempe per legem sub peccatum, sed finem carceris esse salutarem εἰς τὴν πίστιν μέλλουσαν &c. in fidem revelandam. (9) Accedit quod Apostolus dicat, postquam advenit fides, non amplius nos sub pædagogo esse. Quod vero intelligi non potest de tempore adventus Christi. Sic enim nobis lex nullatenus esset pædagogus amplius ad Christum: ne quidem per accommodationem. Nulla enim accommodatio, quæ literali sententiæ contraria est. Si ergo litera textus id vult, postquam Christus in carnem venit, non amplius sub pædagogo nos esse, quomodo hic accommodatio locum habebit, nos adhuc Novi Testamenti tempore esse sub pædagogo illo. Status Novi Testamenti, inquit Pareus, sub gratia Christo exhibito notatur. Jam pædagogii munus expirasse, nec locum amplius habere diserte affirmat. Non, inquit, amplius sumus sub pædagogo, id est, sub lege. Quando enim pueri percipiendis magistri superioris præceptis maturi sunt facti; pædagogus ferulam suam deponit, munus resignat. Ita lex cum populus maturus fidei esset de Christo exhibito, pædagogiam suam deposuit. Sic uno verbo perspicue docet, legem in Novo Testamento esse abrogatam. Rectius hic Bullingerus, postquam venit fides, id est postquam nos pervenimus ad Christum, & fides illuxit in cordibus hominum, non amplius sub pædagogo sumus. Libero enim & spontaneo Christi Spiritu agimur, & recta ducimur, ut non opus sit exactore aut pædagogo. Quid? quod etiam renatos certa ratione esse sub pædagogo egregie doccat B. Lutherus: Si possemus, inquit fol. 94. Christum, qui legem abrogavit, & nos peccatores Patri morte sua reconciliavit, perfecte apprehendere, nihil prorsus juris haberet in nos pædagogus ille. Sed lex membrorum rebellans legi mentis obstat, ut Christum perfecte apprehendere non possimus. Defectus igitur non est in Christo, sed in nobis, qui nondum exuimus carnem, in qua donec vivimus, haret peccatum. Ideo quod ad nos attinet, partim liberi a lege, partim sub lege sumus. Servimus cum Paulo mente legi DEI, carne legi peccati Rom. VII. Ex hoc sequitur, quod secundum conscientiam plane liberi sumus a lege. Ideo pædagogus ille non debet dominari in ea, hoc est, non debet ei esse molestus suis terroribus, minis & captivitate; Et ut maxime hoc tentet, tamen conscientia nihil movetur illa re. Habet enim in conspectu Christum crucifixum, qui abstulit omnia officia legis et conscientia Coloss. II. delens, quod adversabatur nobis per decretachirographum &c. Et paulo post: Quatenus igitur manet caro, eatenus etiam manet lex pædagogus, qui subinde perterrefacere & contristare solet conscientiam ostensione peccati & comminatione mortis: Ipsa tamen semper iterum erigitur quotidiano adventu Christi, qui, ut semel certo tempore venit in mundum, redempturus nos a durissimo imperio pædagogi nostri: Ita quotidie spiritualiter ad nos venit, hoc agens, ut in fide & cognitione ipsius crescamus, ut conscientia de die in diem perfectius se Christum apprehendat, & indies magis magisque minuatur lex carnis & peccati, pavor mortis, & quicquid malorum lex secum affert. Quamdiu igitur, quæ fine peccato non est, vivimus, subinde redit lex, & facit suum officium in alio plus, in alio minus, ut est infirma aut forti fide, non tamen ad perniciem, sed salutem. Hoc enim exercitium legis est in sanctis quotidiana mortificatio carnis, rationis & virium nostrarum, & innovatio mentis nostræ 2. Cor.

IV. (10) Non expedire poteſt ſeſe Pareus, quomodo lex abrogata, cum fit æterna. Abrogatam dicit quoad juſtificationem, damnationem, coactionem, ſignificationem, non quoad doctrinam, obedientiam. At nunquam juſtificare potuit lex poſt lapſum, nec data ut juſtificaret. Nam ſi data lex, quæ poſſit (ullo tempore ſeu Veteris ſeu Novi Teſtamenti) vivificare, revera ex lege eſſet juſtitia v. 21. Quod ergo lex non habuit, vel quod legi nullatenus convenit Veteris Teſtamenti tempore, vel ante Chriſtum, ejus ratione lex abrogata dici nequit tempore Novi Teſtamenti, vel poſt adventum Chriſti. Neque etiam abrogata ea hoc tempore recte dici poteſt quoad damnationem. Maledictionem, inquit, irrogabat tranſgreſſoribus, nihil remittens, condonans, tantum damnans. At id æque lex moralis præſtat poſt adventum Chriſti, uti ante ejus adventum. Nam omnes concludit ſub peccatum, & per peccatum ſub maledictionem. Nec in lege aut per legem condonatio ulla eſt. Porro quod ad coactionem legis, ea pariter poſt Chriſtum obtinet, quoad eos, qui ſunt extra ſtatum gratiæ, quantum ad legem moralem, quemadmodum ante Chriſtum. Ideoque ne hic quidem lex moralis abrogata dici poteſt tempore Novi Teſtamenti. Quod denique ad ſignificationem eam ita explicat Pareus, quod lex (ceremonialis) Chriſtum ejusque gratiam obſcuris umbris venturum ſignificarit. Populum DEI (lex forenſis) ab aliis omnibus ſepararit, atque eatenus expiarit. Sed quum lex ceremonialis ceſſavit, neque lex forenſis porro nos obligat, quomodo ſignificare amplius ceremoniæ illæ aut leges forenſes nobis quid poſſunt, vel nos diſcernere quæ non ſuperſunt, vel non in uſu ſunt amplius? Quanquam non modo per forenſem, ſed etiam per ceremonialem legem populus Judaicus diſcretus olim fuerit; quid vero hoc ad tractationem Apoſtolicam de juſtificatione? Jam quoad doctrinam & obedientiam lex eadem ratione ſeſe habuit olim, uti etiamnum, ſi de lege morali quæratur: Quod vero ad ceremonialem & forenſem, quia illa Judæos ſolum, dum vigebat cultus Leviticus & politia ipſorum, obligabat, nunc ultro expirat, poſtquam cultus, templum, & politia Judæorum ceſſavit: quoad vero nos obligare non potuit, quia nunquam nos obligavit, nec lata eſt, ut Chriſtianos vel populum alium obligaret quam Judaicum, idque etiam ſolum ad certum tempus.

(11) Intellexit probe Pareus, non ſatis validam videri rationem, non eſtis ſub pedagogo, quia eſtis filii DEI. An-non enim Patres etiam hæredes & filii, sed parvuli, sub pedagogo & servitude; nondum vero erant filii adulti, emancipati, in hæreditatem immisi, sicut nos. Sed temere confunditur tractatio capitis sequentis cum praesenti. Quot modis autem Patres parvuli ſub tutoribus nihil differentes a ſervis fuerint, illic dicetur. Id vero nihil ſpectat ad rem præſentem, ubi de juſtificatis quocunque tempore dicitur, omnes filios DEI eſſe per fidem in Chriſtum. Nee vero hic tantum filii adulti, & emancipati intelliguntur, ſed generatim de filiis DEI ſermo eſt, sive ſub tutela ſint, sive non, quicunque ſcilicet juſtificati ſunt per fidem in Chriſtum, quod de Patribus Veteris Teſtamenti negari non poteſt. Omnes, inquit, filii DEI eſtis per fidem in Chriſto. Anne vero Patres non erant filii DEI per fidem in Chriſto? Dicis, non fueretales; ſed ubi hæc reſtrictio in textu? & quomodo convenit fidei in Christum? Per illam enim omnes sunt parilis conditionis. Non est enim nec Iudaeus nec Graecus in Christo.

B.

Glassius agnoscit, hic non intelligi adultos filios: Similitudo paedagogi videtur innuere voce ἤπιοι adultos iam factos filios intelligi, quibus νήπιοι parvuli cap. IV. v. 1. 3. opponuntur. Sed quia duas similitudines Apostolus commiscet, quarum prima a parvulis, altera a servorum conditione desumpta est, ut ex v. 23. 24. cap. IV. 1-7. patet, igitur praestat, per ἤπιοι filios intelligi, quatenus servis opponuntur.

Confer cap. IV. v. 5. 6. cum Rom. VIII. 15. 16. At hic nulla apparet in Apostolo commixtio.

Qui justificati sunt per Christum, non esse sub paedagogo docet, eosque filios DEI dicit. Quod non minus in Veteri Testamento, quam Novo locum habet, ideoque laudat B. Glassius Hyperii explicationem: Sententia est: Filii non obstringuntur ad graviora onera, eodem modo, quo obstringuntur servi, sed omni jure agnoscuntur ab illis liberi. Atqui credentes in Christum sunt filii, igitur qui in Christum credunt, non sunt ad onera legis obstricti, sed sunt a lege liberati. Si autem sunt a gravi lege liberati, cur juberentur ab ille justitiam petere?

Haec vero aeque pertinent ad fideles in Veteri ut in Novo Testamento. Crocius filios nominari ait, non utcunque, sed per excellentiam & comparate dictos. Neque enim, inquit, veteribus patribus jus filiationis negat praecise, sed excellentiorem modum novo Testamento tribuit. At in ἤπιοι per fidem in Christum nulla est ἐξοχή, omnes aequaliter filii sunt, ut paulo post expresse fatetur Crocius: Non aliam atque aliam filiationis rationem in Judaeis & gentibus tradit, tradit unam eandemque aequaliter omnibus concessam, unum medium, unam causam principem. Medium nominat fidem.

Supra filios Abrahami nominaverat, jam altius dicit, ad ipsum scilicet Deum, qui Pater est omnium eorum, qui filii appellantur: Cujus & ipse Abraham filius est. Per fidem, inquit, Chrysostomus notat, non per legem. Unde apparet, non agere de filiatione, quae ex creatione pendet. Nec per fidem quamlibet, sed quae est in Christo Jesu promerente & applicante, quae Jesum Christum, tanquam unicum Mediatorem cum ejus merito & efficacia fiducialiter amplectitur, & in eo solo querit salutem. Atque sic nominat causam filiationis gratuita principem, ne quicquam eorum sibi arroget ex operibus, ex sua dignitate atque merito.

At haec omnia dicenda etiam de Patribus Veteris Testamenti tempore, non diffitetur Crocius. Nulla ergo in his diversitas, idem erat medium filiationis, eadem causa princeps, & meritoria, eadem filiatio. Et quum Abraham ipse Pater credentium ante Christum vixerit, num filii ejus nos excellentiori ratione filii DEI censendi, quam fuerit ille credentium Pater.

(12) De filiis agit, qui Christum, hoc est, justitiam ejus induerunt. Id vero non minus patribus Veteris Testamenti tempore competit, quam nobis sub Novo Testamento. Non enim alia ratione ipsi justificati sunt & salvati quam nos Aflor.

XV. (13) Et ut his; ita etiam nobis lex paedagogus es ἤπιοι, ut scilicet Christus cum sua justitia & merito induatur ceu tunica justitiae & vestis salutis Esa. LXI. (14) De talibus filiis dei, qui sunt semen Abraham, per fidem, agit. At annon etiam ante Christum ex-hibitum erant fideles semen, Abrahae per fidem in Messiam. (14) De eorum justificatione per fidem & filiatione DEI agit, qui secundum promissionem haeredes sunt aeternae vitae. At hoc non minus convenit Patribus ante Christum, quam fidelibus post Christum. Summa, nullum hic adhuc discrimen filiorum DEI constituitur, aut Patrum in Veteri Testamento, & credentium, tempore Novi Testamenti, sive qua filiationem DEI, sive qua haereditatem salutis, sive qua fidem in Messiam, sive qua justificationem per fidem.

Sed urgetur premiturque eadem fidei, justificationis per fidem, filiationis DEI, & haereditatis vitae aeternae ratio, nimirum, quod illa (fides) Christum semper & unice respiciat, haec vero justificationis, filiatio DEI, & haereditas non nisi per fidem in Christum obtingat, citra discrimen temporum, & ad eandem lex paedagogus sit, donec, veniat aut reveletur fides. Vers. 26. Πάντες υἱοὶ θεοῦ ἐστε διὰ τῆς πίστεως, ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Vos, qui in Christum crediditis, ita, ut oportet, ac si credere perseveratis, estis filii (DEI nempe) adulti, quales qui sunt, incipiunt bonis paternis frui. Sic & vos accepistis Patris Spiritum.

Dicuntur quidem & Israelitae sub lege DEI filii, Deut. XVI. 1. sed tanquam pueri, quorum dignitas nondum apparebat: regebantur enim servilem modum, infra IV. 1. Jamjam monuimus nullum huic determinationi, filii DEI esis nempe adulti, locum hic esse. Quales qui sunt, ita docet Grotius, quod nempe incipiunt bonis paternis frui, & accipiant Patris Spiritum.

At Patres etiam Veteris Testamenti tempore bonis Patris coelestis participes factos esse, ecquis dubitat, quum DEUS promiserit Abrahamo: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui. Nec ullo jure negari potest, eosdem Patres Spiritum accepisse, quod contra Socinianos alias ostendimus. Annon aequat nos in eo Apostolus, quod eundem Spiritum fidei habeamus, quem David 2.

Cor. IV. 13. Optime ergo ad hunc locum B. Lutherus: Paulus ut optimus fidei Doctor semper in ore habet illas voces per fidem, in fide, ex fide que est in Christo Jesu Sc.

Non dicit, estis filii DEI, quia circumcisi estis, audistis legem & fecistis opera ejus, ut Judaei somniabant, & Pseudo-Apostoli docebant, sed per fidem in Christum Jesum. Lex ergo non facit, (multo minus traditiones humanae) filios DEI, non potest generare in novam naturam aut nativitatem, sed illam veterem nativitatem, qua in regnum Diaboli nati sumus, ob oculos ponit. Atque ita preparat ad novam nativitatem, que fit per fidem in Christum Jesum, non per legem, ut Paulus clarissime testatur, omnes filii Dei estis per fidem &c. q. d. etiam si per legem estis vexati, bu-militati & occisi, tamen ea non fecit vos justos, non fecit vos filios DEI, sed fides.

Quae? in Christum. Fides ergo in Christum efficit filios DEI non lex. Idem Joh. I. testatur, dedit eis potestatem filios DEI fieri, bis qui credunt &c.

## 3:27
Verf. 27. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ) Baptized into Christ, is by baptism to profess oneself a disciple of Christ.

See what is said at Matth. XXVIII. 19. You have put on Christ) Just as garments are taken from baptism, so you promised that you would put on Christ, that is, that you would live according to the rule of Christ.

Rom. XIII. 14. A similar allusion to the rite of baptism Rom.

VI. 2 & 5. The Apostle proves that we are sons of GOD through faith in Christ, because we were baptized into Christ.

This argument is: Whoever have put on Christ, are sons of GOD. But those who are baptized into Christ, have put on Christ. Therefore those who are baptized, are sons of GOD.

The effect of baptism is the putting on of Christ, and the sonship of GOD is the effect of the putting on of Christ, which is made through faith. For otherwise we do not put on Christ and apprehend his obedience and righteousness, and apply them to ourselves, so that we may be clothed with the same as with a certain garment, and the foulness of our spiritual nakedness may be covered, Apoc. 3:18, which is through faith. Crocius takes exception, along with his Pareus, that not all who are baptized put on Christ, except sacramentally. But it is one thing, according to Lombard, to put on sacramentally, and another to put on also in reality. But the Apostle's statement sounds universally: As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ — namely, as regards God's saving intention, who willed this sacrament to be a means unto the putting on of Christ, and as regards the efficacy of baptism conferred by God Himself, not merely as regards the earthly matter, because it is not bare water, but water comprehended with the Word of God, and the washing of water in the Word, Eph. 5 — but as regards the whole sacrament, inasmuch as it is the means of regeneration, Tit. 3:5, Joh. 3:6, and has efficacy for all from God's gracious intention, for those who use it, provided they do not resist grace and hinder the operation of the Holy Spirit. Since this does not happen in infants, we do not doubt that they are all regenerated through baptism and put on Christ. There is therefore no valid objection from Simon Magus, inasmuch as he resisted saving grace, and to that extent did not put on Christ, which is what that saying of Jerome means: If anyone receives only the washing of this bodily water, which is seen by the eyes of the flesh, he is not clothed with the Lord Jesus Christ. For that Simon Magus too had received the washing of water, but because he did not have the Holy Spirit, he was not clothed with Christ.

and the shame of our spiritual nakedness is covered.

Pareus asks here, as many of you as have been baptized into Christ. For he says it is to be noted that not all who are baptized with water are also baptized into Christ; but only those who receive baptism with true faith. But the Apostle says to be baptized into Christ is not to be baptized by Christ. Nor is this a limitation, but a description of baptism, which is not completed by water alone, but is done into Christ and his merit, in the name of Christ, and of the whole most holy Trinity. Therefore, its efficacy is not to be estimated by reason of the earthly thing alone, but insofar as it consists of water and the Holy Spirit. And the Trinity is united to the most holy water, in whose name we are sprinkled, and thus we have Christ also with his righteousness, whence it has its efficacy, which is the first addition, by which it exerts itself in a fruitful act, where it is not hindered. For it is not merely a sign or symbol, which the Calvinists often say is empty with regard to the elect; but an efficacious medium of regeneration: And therefore the blessed Luther notes this again against the Zwinglians in this place. Luther

laws, justices, worships and religions (for we must not imagine that the Gentiles were entirely contemptuous of honesty and religion, but all nations of all ages, dispersed throughout the whole world, had their own laws, worships and religions, without which it is impossible for the human race to be governed.) These, I say, are nothing at all before God in all these ornaments. Whatever, therefore, is of economic, political, and divine justice (such as was the justice of the law) with the highest obedience, execution of law, and holiness, is worth absolutely nothing before God. What then? The garment of Christ, whom we put on in baptism. Thus, let a servant serve his master faithfully, let a free man preside over and govern the republic or his private affairs with praise; likewise, whatever a man does as a man, by taking a wife, by well administering his domestic affairs, by obeying the magistrate, by conducting himself honestly and decently toward everyone, if a matron has lived chastely, has obeyed her husband, has diligently cared for her home, has well educated her children (which are certainly magnificent and excellent works), yet all these things are nothing toward justice before God. In sum: Whatever there is in the whole world of laws, ceremonies, worships, justices, and works, even of the Jews themselves, who first had a kingdom and priesthood divinely instituted and ordained with their own laws, religion, and worship, yet all these things do not take away sins, do not deliver from death, do not save.

Therefore your Pseudo-Apostles, O Galatians, seduce you while they teach the law as necessary for salvation, and in this way snatch you from the greatest glory of your birth and sonship, and recall you to your old birth and the most miserable slavery of the law, making you from most free sons of GOD into slaves of the law, while they wish to distinguish persons according to laws. There is certainly a distinction of persons in law and before the world, and there it ought to be, but not so before God, where all men are equal, all have sinned and are void of the glory of God, etc. All you, who are one in Christ Jesus. The manuscript has it more briefly and simply: All you who are one in Christ, which also coheres well with what follows.

They are said to be in Christ who put on Christ, who obey Christ, John XVII. 21. Rom. XVI. 7. who are Christ's, as now follows. Paul says that such are the Christian Galatians, from the better part, and because he wished that all might be such, and hoped well of many.

But are all other codices to be corrected from one MS.? And would it not be more convenient if it were inserted here that all are one in Christ, rather than that all are in Christ, after he says that through faith there is neither Jew nor Greek, etc. Although it may be added: If you are Christ's, yet that [reading] is not therefore to be preferred to that of being in Christ. For they are equally Christ's who are one in Christ, as those who are in Christ.

But that reason is more to the point, that the distinction of nations, statuses, and sexes has been abolished as far as the enjoyment of the benefits of Christ is concerned, because we are all one in Christ through faith, which is to be understood both of the unity with Christ and of the unity of believers among themselves in the mystical body of Christ, inasmuch as we all, who adhere to Christ through faith, become one spirit with him 1 Cor. VI, and as it were constitute one person with him, having thus put on Christ. B. Glassius p. 827. And these arcana, he says, are that ineffable union of believers among themselves and with Christ, of which he himself speaks, sighing most ardently in his προαγωγίον prayer to the Father: I pray for those who are to believe in me, that they all may be one, as you Father are in me, and I in you, that they may be one in us John XVII. 20. 21. and which he compares to the grafting of branches into the true vine John XV. 5. I am the vine, you are the branches; he who remains in me and I in him, this one bears much fruit. 7. If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, whatever you will, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you &c., through which believers are made partakers of the divine nature in Christ their head 2 Petr. I. 4. and are filled with all the fullness of God Eph. III. 17. 19., through which God holds believers in his hand and cherishes them with a most pleasing affection of love and keeping Deut. XXXIII. 3. Joh. X. 28. 29., from which flows such a donation of all goods to sons through faith Joh. XV. 22. and communion made with him their head in the cross and afflictions Matth. XXV. 35. 40. Act. IX. 5. Col. I. 24.
