Through which finally the whole body of the Church, joined together and compacted in Christ the head, through every joint of supply according to the effectiveness, in the measure of each part, makes increase of the body, unto the edifying of itself in charity, as Paul speaks Eph. IV. 16. B. Luther in the later Commentary.

Fanatical spirits today speak in the manner of the Sophists about faith in Christ, forming it to be a quality existing in the heart, with Christ excluded.

This is a pernicious error. But Christ must be set forth in such a way that you see nothing at all besides him, and believe that nothing is nearer and more intimate to you than he himself. For he does not sit idle in heaven, but is most present to us, working and living in us, above chapter 2: I live now not I, but Christ lives in me, etc. And here: You have put on Christ. Therefore faith is the most tenacious gaze, which looks upon nothing besides Christ the conqueror of sin and death, and the bestower of justice, of salvation and of eternal life. Hence Paul, in nearly every verse of his epistles, sets forth and inculcates Jesus Christ. He sets him forth, moreover, through the word, nor can he be apprehended otherwise than by faith in the word. Add what he has in the former Commentary: For all you are one in Christ Jesus, that is, in the faith of Christ you are one, although on account of the necessity of the body and of this life it must needs be that you be divided into diverse persons, like many members, yet one body under one head. Where B. Luther does not deny that union in Christ and unity with Christ which we said before belongs to each believer. For, he says, Christ cannot be separated from us, nor we from him, since we become one with him and in him, as the members are one in the head and with the one head. Therefore, as the promise of God cannot be understood of anything other than Christ, so, since we are nothing other than Christ, it must be understood also of us. Theophylactus also joins both together: Of these, he says, either individually, who, sprinkled with the water of baptism, cast off their private nature and all receive a new figure and form. Nor bearing in themselves Christ as the angel of someone, but as Lord. It comes about therefore that we all become one in Christ Jesus, that is, insofar as we have been strengthened into one figure of Christ imposed upon us. Or because we have all been made one body, we have Christ alone as head and Leader.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Ὅσοι γὰρ εἰς χριστὸν ἐβαπτίσθητε) In Christum baptizati, est per baptismum se profiteri Christi discipulum. Vide quae dicta ad Matth.

XXVIII. 19. Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε) Sicut a baptismo vestes sumuntur, ita vos promifistis, vos induturos Christum, id est, victuros secundum Christi regulam. Rom.

XIII. 14. Similis allusio ad ritum baptismi Rom.

VI. 2. & 5. Probat Apostolus nos esse filios DEI per fidem in Christo, quia baptiati fuimus in Christum.

Argumentum hoc est: Quicunque induerunt Christum, filii DEI sunt. At qui baptizati sunt in Christum, induerunt Christum. Ergo qui baptizati sunt, filii DEI sunt.

Effectus baptismi est induitio Christi, & filiatio DEI est effectus induitionis Christi, quae fit per fidem. Aliter enim non induimus Christum ejusque obedientiam & justitiam apprehendimus, nobisque applicamus, ut eodem velute veste quadam amiciamur, ac turpitude nuditatis nostræ spiritualis obtegatur Apoc. III. 18. quam per fidem. Crocius excipit cum Pareo suo, non omnes, qui baptizantur, induere Christum, nisi sacramentotenus. Aliud autem esse juxta Lombardum, sacramentotenus induere, alind induere etiam reipsa. Sed universa- liter sonat Apostoli sententia: Quotquot bapti- zati estis in Christum, induistis Christum, scilicet quod ad intentionem DEI salutiferam, qui sacra- mentum hoc voluit esse medium ad inductionem Christi & quod ad efficaciam baptismi a DEO ipsi collatam, non quantum ad materiam tantum terrenam, quia non est nuda aqua, sed aqua Ver- bo DEI comprehensa, & lavacrum aquæ in Verbo Eph. V. sed qua totum sacramentum, utpote quod medium est regenerationis Tit. III. 5. Joh. III. 6. & penes omnes efficaciam habet ex gratiosa DEI intentione, eodem utentes, modo non resistant gratiæ, & operationem Spiritus Sancti impediant. Quod quum in infantibus non fiat, eos omnes per baptismum regenerari, ac Christum induere non dubitamus. Nulla ergo est instantia de Si- mone mago, utpote qui gratiæ salutari restitit, adeoque Christum non induit, quod facit illud Hie- ronymi: Si quis hoc corporeum, quod oculis carnis aspicitur, aqua tantum accipit lavacrum, non est indutus Dominum Jesum Christum. Nam & Si- mon ille magus acceperat lavacrum aquæ, verum, quia Spiritum Sanctum non habebat, non erat in- dutus Christum.

ac turpitudo nuditatis nostrae spiritualis obtegitur .

Pareus hic quaerit, quotquot baptizati estis in Christo. Notari enim ait, non omnes, qui baptizantur aqua, baptizari etiam in Christo; sed tantum qui vera fide baptismum suscipiunt. Sed in Christum baptizari ait Apostolus non baptizari Christo. Nec limitatio haec est, sed descriptio baptismi, qui non absolvitur aqua sola, sed fit in Christum ejusque meritum, in nomine Christi, & totius sacrosanctae Trinitatis. Ideo non ratione solius terrenae rei est ejus aestimanda efficacia, sed quatenus aqua & Spiritu S. constat . & unita est aquae sacrosanctae Trinitas, in cujus nomine adfpergimur, adeoque Christum etiam cum sua justitia, unde efficaciam suam habet, quod adjectum primum, qua se actu secundo exerit, ubi non impeditur. Neque enim solum est signum aut symbolum, quod saepe inane esse ajunt Calviniani quod ad electos; sed medium efficax regenerationis: Ideoque denuo Zvinglianos id notat hoc loco B. Lutherus

legibus, justitiis, cultibus ac religionibus (non enim imaginari debemus gentiles prorsus fuisse contemptores honestatis & religionis, sed omnes gentes omnium ætatum, per totum terrarum orbem disper- sa, habuerunt suas leges, cultus & religiones, fine quibus impossibile est, regi genus humanum.) Hi, inquam, omnibus istis ornamentis nihil sunt coram Deo. Quicquid igitur est justitiæ economicæ, politicæ & divinæ, (qualis erat justitia legis) cum summa obedientia, executione juris & sanctitate nihil prorsus valet coram Deo. Quid tum? Indumentum Christi, quem in baptismo induimus. Sic servus utro, fideliter serviat, liber præsit & gubernet rempublicam aut privatam cum laude; item quicquid fecerit masculus ut masculus, ducendo uxorem, bene administrando rem suam domesticam, obediendo magistratui, gerendo se erga quosque honeste & decenter, si matrona vixerit casta, paruerit marito, diligenter curaverit domum, bene eduxerit liberos (quæ certe magnifica & egregia sunt opera) tamen ipsa omnia nihil ad justitiam coram Deo. Summa: Quicquid est in toto orbe terrarum legum, ceremoniarum, cultuum, justitiarum & operum, etiam ipsorum Judæorum, qui primi habuerunt regnum & sacerdotium divinitus institutum & ordinatum cum suis legibus, religione & cultu, tamen ista omnia non auferunt peccata, non liberant a morte, non salvant.

Ideo Pseudo-Apostoli vestri, Galatæ, seducent vos, dum legem necessariam ad salutem docent, atque hoc modo rapiunt vos a maxima gloria vestræ nativitatis & filiationis, & revocant in veterem nativitatem, & miserrimam legis servitutem, facientes vos ex filiis DEI liberrimis servos legis, dum secundum leges personas distinguere volunt. Est certe distinctio personarum in lege, & coram mundo, & ibi eam oportet esse, non item coram Deo, ubi omnes homines æquales sunt, omnes peccaverunt & vacui sunt gloria Dei &c. Πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς, εἷς ἐστε ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Manuscriptus brevius ac simplicius habet: Ἄπαντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς ἑν ἐστε χριστῷ quod & bene cum sequentibus coharet.

Esse in Christo dicuntur, qui Christum induere, qui Christo obediunt, Joh. XVII. 21. Rom. XVI. 7. qui Christi sunt, ut jam sequitur. Dicit autem tales esse Galatas Christianos Paulus, ex parte potiore, & quia optabat, ut omnes tales essent, & de multis bene sperabat.

Atqui ex uno MS. omnes cæteri Codd. emendandi? Et annon convenientius hic inferebatur, quod omnes unus sint in Christo, quam quod omnes in Christo sint, postquam per ἄγον non est inquit Judæus, neque Græcus &c. Licet vero addatur: Εἰ δὲ τὸ χριστῷ, non tamen ideo præferendum illud ἔσε ἐν χριστῷ. Nam æque Christi sunt, qui unus sunt in Christo, ut qui in Christo.

Magis autem ad rem facit illa ratio, quod sublatum fit discrimen gentium, statuum & sexuum, quantum ad fruitionem beneficiorum Christi, quia nos omnes unus sumus in Christo per fidem, quod tum de unitate cum Christo, tum de unitate fidelium inter se in Christi corpore mystico intelligendum, siquidem nos omnes, qui Christo per fidem adhæremus, unus cum ipso Spiritus fimus 1. Cor. VI. & quasi unam personam constituamus cum ipso sic induti Christum. B. Glassius p. 827. Et hæc arcana, inquit, illa ac ineffabilis credentium inter se & cum Christo unitio est, de qua ipse loquitur, in προαγωγίῳ sua precatione ad Patrem suspirans ardentissime: Oro pro iis, qui credituri sunt in me, ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ut ipsi in nobis unum sint Joh. XVII. 20. 21. & quam insitioni palmitum in severam vitem comparat Joh. XV. 5. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites; qui manet in me & ego in eo, hic fert fructum multum. 7. Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint, quicquid volueritis, petetis, fiet vobis &c. per quam in Christo capite suo credentes efficiuntur divinæ consortes naturæ 2. Petr. I. 4. & implentur in omnem plenitudinem Dei Epb. III. 17. 19. per quam frugulari dilectionis affectu & custodia gratissima Deus credentes in manu sua habet foveque Deut. XXXIII. 3. Joh. X. 28. 29. ex qua fluit omnium bonorum talis filium donatio per fidem Joh. XV. 22. & cruce afflictionumque, ipsi capitis facta communio Matth. XXV. 35. 40. Act. IX. 5. Col. I. 24. Per quam demum totum Ecclesiæ corpus in capite Christo coagmentatum & compactum, per omnem commissuram subministrationis secundum efficaciam, in mensura uniuscujusque partis incrementum corporis facit, in ædificationem sui ipsius per charitatem, uti Paulus loquitur Epb. IV. 16. B. Lutherus in poster. Comment.

Fanatici Spiritus hodie loquuntur more Sophistarum de fide in Christum formiantes eam esse qualitatem habentem in corde, excluso Christo.

Is perniciosus error est. Verum ita proponendus est Christus, ut præter eum plane nihil videas, nihil esse tibi propius & intimius ipso credas. Non enim sedet otiosus in cælo, sed præsentissima est nobis operans & vivens in nobis, supra cap. 2. Vivo jam non ego, sed vivit in me Christus &c. Et hic, Christum induistis. Quare fides est pertinacissimus intuitus, qui nihil aspicit præter Christum victorem peccati & mortis, & largitorem justitiæ salutis & vitæ æternæ. Hinc Paulus in epistolis suis fere in singulis versibus proponit & inculcat Jesum Christum. Proponit autem per verbum, neque aliter potest apprehendi quam fide in verbum. Adde quæ habet in priori Commentario: Omnes enim vos unum estis in Christo Jesu, id est in fide Christi unum estis, etsi pro corporis & vitæ hujus necessitate necesse fit, in personas diversas dividi, sicut multa membra, tamen unum corpus sub uno capite. Ubi non negat B. Lutherus illam unionem in Christo & unitatem cum Christo, quam unicuiq; fideli convenire antea diximus. Non enim, inquit, potest Christus separari a nobis, nec nos ab illo, cum unum fimus cum illo & in illo, sicut membra unum in capite & cum capite uno. Ut ergo de alio quam Christo promissio Dei intelligi non potest, ita cum aliud quam Christus non simus, de nobis quoque intelligatur, oportet. Conjungit etiam utrumque Theophylactus: Eorum, inquit, vel singuli, qui baptismi aqua perfusi, privatam abjecere naturam & novam omnes accipere & figuram & formam. Nec Angeli cujuspiam sed domini Christum in se præferentes. Fit itaque, ut unum fimus omnes in Christo Jesu, hoc est, in quantum unam fortiti sumus Christi nobis injectam figuram. Vel quia omnes fimus unum corpus effecti, Christum unicum in caput habemus ac Ducem.

## 3:29
V. 29. If you are Christ's, if not by name only, but also belong to Christ. Then you are Abraham's seed, mystically the sons of Abraham, as above 7. Christ communicates his name and dignity to you: even through you other nations are converted. And heirs according to the promise, namely of eternal life.

See above 18. Those who are through the faith of Christ have put on the same, and adhere to him, inasmuch as being united, and one with him, they are the seed or sons of Abraham, the Father of believers, who is also one with Christ and was CHRIST'S through faith. The seed not according to the flesh, but according to the promise: because Abraham believed, and it was imputed to him for justice Gen. XV. 6. Rom. IV. Wherefore they also are heirs of the promise through faith, as Abraham Rom. IV. Thus all things are attributed to faith in Christ, but the works of the law are excluded, because the promise is received only by faith. Concerning which B. Luth. speaks beautifully here in his later commentary, fol. 96.

Thus Paul briefly transfers all the glory of Lebanon, that is, of the Jewish people, to the desert, that is, to the Gentiles, and this passage contains most abundant consolation, namely that the Gentiles are the children of Abraham, and consequently the people of God. But they are children of Abraham not by carnal generation, but by promise. Therefore the kingdom of heaven, life, and eternal inheritance belongs to the Gentiles. And the scripture signified this long before, when it says, I have made you a father of many nations: Item, in your seed shall all nations be blessed.

Since therefore we Gentiles believe and by faith receive the blessing of Abraham promised through Christ exhibited, therefore the scripture calls us heirs and children of Abraham not according to the flesh but the promise. Thus the promise also, in your seed, pertains to all nations, and Christ is ours according to it.

Indeed, the promise was made to the Jews, not to us Gentiles, Ps. CXLVII. He declares his word to Jacob, etc. He has not done so for any nation, etc.

Yet this which was promised comes to us through faith, by which alone the promise of God is apprehended. Although therefore it was not promised to us, yet it was promised concerning us.

For we are named in the promise, in your seed. For the promise clearly shows that Abraham was not only to be the Father of the Jewish people, but of many nations; and that he was to be the heir not of one kingdom, but of the whole world, Rom. IV.

Thus the glory of the whole kingdom of Christ has been transferred to us. Wherefore all laws have been abrogated in the heart and conscience of the Christian, though they remain outwardly in the flesh.

And so much for the Apostle's principal treatment concerning the justification of the sinful man before God, that it is not done by the works of the law, but by faith alone in Christ.

SECTION II.

THE OVERTHROW OF THE NECESSITY OF CEREMONIAL WORKS UNDER THE NEW TESTAMENT.

Latin:

V. 29. Εἰ δὲ τὸ χριστῷ (sic) Si Christi estis, si non nomine tantum, sed & read Christum pertinetis. “Ἀρα τῦ Ἀβραὰμ σπέρμα ἐσὲ) filii mystice Abrahami, ut supra 7. Christus nomen suum & dignitatem vobis communicat: etiam per vos convertuntur aliæ gentes. Καὶ κατ’ ἐπαγγελίαν κληρονόμοι) Nempe vitæ cœlestis.

Vide supra 18. Qui per fidem Christi sunt, eundem induerunt, eique adhærent, utpote cum uniti, & unum sunt cum ipso, illi semen vel filii Abrahæ sunt Patris credentium, qui unum etiam cum Christo & CHRISTI fuit per fidem. Semen non secundum carnem, sed secundum promissionem: quia credidit Abraham, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam Gen. XV. 6. Rom. IV. Quapropter illi etiam hæredes promissionis sunt per fidem, ut Abraham Rom. IV. Ita omnia fidei tribuuntur in Christum, excluduntur autem opera legis, quia promillio non nisi fide accipitur. Quo de pulchre hic B. Luth. in poster. com. f. 96.

Sic Paulus brevi transfert totam gloriam Libani, hoc est, Iudaici populi ad desertum hoc est ad gentes, & continet hic locus uberrimam consolationem, nempe quod gentes Abrahe filii, & per consequens Dei populus sint. Sunt autem filii Abrahe non ex carnali generatione, sed ex promissione. Ergo regnum caelorum, vita & hereditas aeterna pertinet ad gentes. Hocque longe ante significavit scriptura, cum inquit, Patrem multarum gentium constitui te: Item in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes.

Quia ergo nos gentes credimus & fide accipimus benedictionem Abrahe promissam per Christum exhibitam, ideo scriptura nos vocat heredes & filios Abrahe non secundum carnem sed promissionem. Sic promissio etiam, in semine tuo, ad omnes gentes pertinet, & Christus fatundum eam est noster.

Est quidem folie Iudaeis non nobis gentibus facta promissio Psal. CXLVII. Annuntiat verbum suum Iacob &c. Non fecit taliter omni nationi &c.

Hoc tamen quod promissum est, ad nos venit per fidem, qua sola apprehenditur promissio Dei. Litet igitur non nobis, tamen de nobis promissum est.

Sumus enim in promissione, in semine tuo nominati. Nam promissio clare ostendit; Abraham non tantum fore Patrem Iudaici populi, sed multarum gentium; & heredem fore non unius regni, sed totius mundi Rom. IV.

Sic gloria totius regni Christi ad nos translata est. Quare omnes leges in universum abrogata sunt in corde & conscientia Christiani, foris tamen in carne manent.

Atque haec de principali tractatione Apostoli de iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo, quod ea non fiat per opera legis, sed per solam fidem in Christum.

SECTIO II.

PROFLIGATIO NECESSITATIS OPERUM CEREMONIALIUM SUB NOVO TESTAMENTO.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

By the similitude of a child under a tutor differing nothing from a servant, the state of the Ancients under external elements is illustrated until the fullness of time, by which, having been liberated by Christ, we receive the Spirit, and are no longer servants; and by a comparison of the former state of the Galatians, in which they served those who by nature are not gods, they are warned not to return to the servitude of weak elements, lest the Apostolic labor be frustrated, and their former zeal for the Apostle, from whom the Pseudo-Apostles were striving to lead them away, is praised.

Furthermore, the allegory concerning the two sons of Abraham is set forth, figuring the two testaments, the one generating to servitude, the other to liberty, whose fruitfulness, predicted (Es. LV. v. 1.), teaches that the faithful are free according to the promise of Isaac, even if they suffer persecution from the sons of the handmaid, just as he once did from Ishmael, by being cast out with his mother (Gen. XXI. verf. 10.), and thus are children not of the handmaid but of the free woman.

There are three parts: I. A demonstration of the difference between the state of the old servitude and the new liberty from the similitude of wards, up to verse 7. II.

A reproof of the conversion to the servitude of weak elements, and of the detestation of the truth, up to verse 20. III. A confirmation of the distinction between the Testament of servitude and the mother who is a bondwoman, and the testament of liberty and the mother who is free, through an allegorical interpretation of the history of Hagar and Sarah, up to verse 31.

PART I.

An explanation of the difference between the old and new state through the similitude of wards. Verf. 1. Λόγω δὲ ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον ὁ κληρονόμος νήπιος ἐστιν i. e. a son.

He takes the similitude from a boy whose father is traveling abroad; God is compared to such a Father, dissimulating many human deeds. A similar comparison in Matt. XXI. 33. XXX. v. 1. Οὐδὲ διαφέρει δοῦλε For he is also beaten, like a servant, Sirach XXX. v. 1. Κύριε πάντων A figurative locution, because the word signifies in a way, with the title of lordship added, when he is attributed as a son, as he institutes, concerning the quality and difference of heirs, in his own D. concerning children and posthumous ones, he is indeed called master by expectation: servants in comedies call the younger one master.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Similitudine a parvulo sub tutore nihil a servo distante illustratur status Veterum sub externis elementis usque ad plenitudinem temporum, qua a Christo liberati Spiritum accipimus, nec amplius servi sumus, & comparatione status pristini Galatarum, quo illis, qui natura Dii non sunt, servierunt, monentur, ne redeant ad servitutem egenorum elementorum, ne frustretur labor Apostolicus, ac laudatur prior eorum zelus pro Apostolo, a quo ipsos Pseudo-Apostoli abducere nitebantur.

Porro exposita allegoria de duobus filiis Abraham, figurantibus duo testamenta, altero ad servitutem generante, altero ad libertatem, cuius fecunditas predicta (Es. LV. v. 1.) docet fideles esse Isaaci secundum promissionem liberos, etsi persecutionem a filiis ancillae, uti olim ille ab Ismaele, ideo cum matre ejiciendo (Gen. XXI. vers. 10.) patiantur, adeoque non ancillae sed liberae filios.

Partes sunt tres: I. Discriminis status veteris servitutis & novae libertatis a similitudine pupillorum demonstratio ad vers. 7.

II. Conversionis ad egenorum elementorum servitutem, & detestionis a veritate exprobratio ad vers. 20. III. Distinctionis Testamenti servitutis & matris servae ac testamenti libertatis matrisque liberae per allegoriam historiae Hagaris & Sarae interpretationem confirmatio ad vers. 31.

PARS I.

Discriminis status veteris & novi per similitudinem pupillorum explicatio. Vers. 1. Λόγω δὲ ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον ὁ κληρονόμος νήπιος ἐστιν i. e. filius.

Similitudinem sumit a puero, cuius pater peregrinatur, tali Patri comparatur Deus, multa humana facta dissimulans. Similis comparatio Matth. XXI. 33. XXX. v. 1. Οὐδὲ διαφέρει δοῦλε Nam & caeditur, ut servus, Sirach. XXX. v. 1. Κύριε πάντων Loquutio figurata, quod significat vox quodammodo, addito dominii titulo, cum is filius tribuitur, ut Instituit, de heredum qualitate, & differentia, in suis D. de liberis & posthumis, nimirum dicitur herus expectatione: herum minorem dicunt servi in comoediis.

## 4:2
Verf. 2. Ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐστὶ καὶ οἰκονόμους He calls them ἐπιτρόπους as tutors, who, in the father's absence, perform his role.

For this Greek word, also brought over to the Jews and Syrians, אפיטרופוס, does not always signify a tutor, but any person set over a person or thing, as can be seen among the Chaldean Paraphrasts, Gen. XXXIX. 4. XLI.

34. XLIII. 15. Eph. I. 8. II. 3. Ὁ κόσμος are the actors, who under the inspection of tutors administer the ward's property, and do not allow him to use them, except by the tutors' judgment. Ἄχρι τῆς προθεσμίας τοῦ Πατρός Until that time which the father has predetermined, until the father judges him fit, so that he may be of his own guardianship. The word προθεσμία is Greek, used by Aristotle and others; for it the Rabbis say, זמן קבוע or זמן קבע .

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐστὶ καὶ οἰκονόμους Επιτρόπους vocat quasi tutores, qui, patre absente, ipsius vice fungantur.

Etenim vox haec Graeca etiam ad Iudaeos & Syros deducta, אפיטרופוס, hec semper tutorem, sed quemvis alium personae aut rei praepositum significat, ut videre est apud Chaldaeos Paraphrastas, Genes. XXXIX. 4. XLI. 34. XLIII. 15. Eph.

I. 8. II. 3. Ὁ κόσμος sunt actores, qui sub tutorum inspectione res pupilli administrant, nec eum patiuntur eis uti, nisi tutorum arbitratu, Ἄχρι τῆς προθεσμίας τοῦ Πατρός Ad tempus illud, quod pater praefinierit, donec pater eum iudicarit idoneum, ut fiet suae tutelae. Προθεσμία vox Graeca apud Aristotelem & alios, pro eo Rabbini dicunt, זמן קבוע vel זמן קבע .

## 4:3
Verf. 3. Οὕτω καὶ ἡμεῖς He speaks of the Jews, as the following shows. Ὅτε ἦμεν νήπιοι The whole age of the Israelite people, after the exodus from Egypt, until Christ, corresponds to the adolescent age. Ὑπὸ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου ἦμεν δεδουλωμένοι Erasmus: subject to those rites which were common to us with the world: such as temples, altars, victims, libations, and the like imposed upon the Israelites for this reason, lest they slip away to idols through love of such things; στοιχεῖα are called the rudiments of any art, because what elements are in the nature of things, those are in the arts, so in the matter of piety there are certain στοιχεῖα, Heb. V. 12. which, because they are common to the Jews with the world, are called στοιχεῖα by the greater part of those who use them, as also Col. II. v. 8. 20. A similar translation in the Rabbinic word, יסודות .

Having finished the treatment concerning the moral law, the observance of which the Pseudo-Apostles required with faith as necessary for obtaining justification and eternal salvation; he now treats of the ceremonial law, which they likewise made necessary for salvation to be observed. The diversity of the argument is evident. For before, he had dealt with only that law which supervened by grace because of transgression, which concludes all under sin, and is like a prison and a schoolmaster, not only to the Jews but to all, unto Christ: But now, concerning the law proper to the Jews, which held the people of God like a ward, constituted under a tutor and curator, within the bounds of its own discipline, and did not admit them to full liberty, until the time of the προθεσμία, which obtained only until the πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου: concerning the clemency of the world, it differs sufficiently from the servitude of the Old Testament, to which the infirm and needy had to serve by observing days, months, feasts, and years.

But that he may beat back the Pseudo-Apostles, who were striving to reduce the faithful under that servitude: and that he may solidly inform the Galatians concerning liberty under Christ, he proposes and explains the difference of the state before Christ, and after Christ was exhibited, by an illustrious similitude, which could be perceived by all: then indeed he does not hesitate to compare the servitude, to which the Pseudo-Apostles wished to enslave them to observe ceremonial things superstitiously to bear with the worship of idols, with which they served formerly those who by nature are not Gods, before the knowledge of the true God, to which they were led by the labor of the faithful Apostles, having once received him as an Angel of God, nay, as Christ himself. Finally, having elegantly exhibited the distinction between both Testaments and the old synagogue or mother of servitude and the Church of Christ, which brings forth free children, he recalls them to acknowledge the dignity of their liberty, lest they be cast out from the family of the Church like Hagar the handmaid.

Where, by the force of the continuity of the Apostolic treatment, it is again manifest that these things properly concern the servitude of the elements of the world of the needy, by which, on account of the Levitical constitutions, they were subject to a much harsher and more servile condition, who were bound to them, than those who enjoyed Christian liberty. This is taught for example's sake by the laws concerning the religious observation of feasts, and the worship to be performed only in the temple at Jerusalem, to which all had to come not without great trouble, concerning abstinence from certain foods, and the distinction between clean and unclean, concerning the Levitical uncleanness to be contracted in many ways, and the various sacrifices for taking away the uncleanness of the flesh, concerning ablutions of more than one kind, concerning circumcision, by which the flesh of males had to be wounded in tender infancy, etc.

I say, however, says the Apostle, I do not [speak] from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ.

For there was need here of Apostolic authority to define the controversy which the adversaries had moved. The Vulgate inserts this pronoun, v. 1. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω, which Crocius with his Pareus refers to the preceding, so that the sense is: What I have said concerning the use and duration of the law, that I declare here, and I wish it to be understood, whatever the rivals might murmur, and attempt to persuade you. But here the Apostle addresses other things, namely, concerning the ceremonial law, which the Pseudo-Apostles urged to be observed, the necessity of which he overthrows.

He brings forward a first simile, and a very well-known civil constitution.

Because, as blessed Luther says, the common people grasp things more easily by similes and examples than by arduous and subtle Disputations. They more willingly see a well-painted image than a well-written book. Hence, after the simile concerning the testament of a man, concerning the prison and the pedagogue, he assumes this very well-known one concerning the heir.

That it refers to a father who is traveling, there is no indication here. Nor is the place in Matt. XXI parallel to this: it deals with the leasing of a vineyard, not with tutors or curators of wards. The simile is rather sought here from a deceased father, who by testament has constituted tutors or curators, according to Chrysostom and others, because mention is made of an heir in a testament, for the father commanded this (heir), as Theophylact has, that he should abstain from the administration of goods until the legitimate age; this will must be obeyed entirely, and the testament.

But whether it has been constituted by testament or not; it is certain that tutors and stewards are ordained for wards by force of laws and custom. But for the explanation of the Mosaic servitude or of the ancient people under the law, he brings forward three things in the simile of παιδείας [training]:

1. The condition of the ward is almost servile. For when the heir is an infant, he differs nothing from a servant.

He is an heir, to whom the father's property adheres, to whom the inheritance belongs by right: Or so called, because he becomes as it were the master, that is, the Lord, as Cujacius wishes. Which indeed Schardius in his Lexicon of Law refutes, and prefers to derive heir from Eva, that is, earth. Κληρονόμον, who has a κλήρον νέμες, a lot or inheritance divided by lot. Another is born, he is his son, to whom the inheritance belongs by right of birth. Of this the Apostle treats. And this is an infant or an adult according to the Acts, major or minor. By infant νήπιον, as if νήπιον, who cannot speak, he understands any minor, who cannot yet speak for himself in judgment at all, or not yet. Therefore he defines the infancy of the heir not by age, but by right. And those words imply this, ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον, namely, as long as the infancy defined by right lasts.

In it he says the heir differs nothing from a servant, which however must be understood as to how. For a servant is not an heir or does not differ from the Lord; but concerning the infant it is soon said, that he becomes Lord of all. But subjection is referred to then, because as a servant is not of his own right, but subject to the power of his master: So the heir, because he is still a minor and νήπιον, is not of his own right, but is under the authority of tutors: then provision: Because as it is provided for a servant concerning food by his master: So it is provided for a ward concerning curators, and he ought to acquiesce in their provision; then discipline and chastisement, which is due to a servant when he does not do his duty. Sir. XXXIII. 25. Since indeed even a ward is subject to discipline and chastisement, that he may be well educated.

Therefore he is said to differ nothing from a servant, not by nature, because he is free, but by the manner of living, or the necessity of obeying, which is explained v. 2. Ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐςι, ὁικονόμους but he is under tutors and curators. Erasmus says the former word is said from the permission of authority or right, the latter from the dispensation of domestic affairs. Interlinear Gloss: Tutors, who defend the ward against enemies, actors, who plead causes for him and inform his morals. But these are according to Latin words.

They are learnedly explained in Greek by Grotius, a Tutor, according to the Acts, as it is in the Lexicon of Schardius, is a defender of the ward, who is attributed to the ward's person before all things, that they may nourish him, then lest the ward's things be neglected, perish, or be corrupted. On the other hand, a curator is primarily constituted, that he may diligently look after the minor's things, then that he may assist the persons with his work. Whence B. Hunnius rightly distinguishes them. He, he says, (tutor) labors especially in educating the orphan, and in forming his childhood; but this one (curator) is occupied about the care of goods, and the dispensation for the use of the ward.

Thus the boy is subject in his ward-state by a double reason, both because it is not permitted to him through a master and former of childhood to do whatever he pleases, and because it is not permitted to him to trade his faculties or goods at will, but others constituted for guardianship dispose of them at their discretion for the utility of the ward.

The dignity of the ward, that although by the said reason he differs nothing from a servant, yet he becomes heir and Lord of all. Heir, because the paternal inheritance belongs to him by right of birth, although he is not admitted to the same as long as he is constituted in minority. Lord of all, namely by hope and expectation, not yet however in reality and possession. III.

The definition of the ward's time: Ἀχρὶ τῆς προθεσμίας τῦ Πατρός.

The office of tutors and curators, and the subjection of wards, does not last perpetually, but has a defined time, which is determined either by the Father's testament, or by law, if the father dies intestate, whence a tutor is either testamentary, or legitimate. But the time of a tutor is until the age of puberty or the fourteenth year of age, of a curator until the twenty-fifth. Whence Jerome, the legitimate time, he says, which is sanctioned by Roman laws, is terminated by the space of 25 years. But here the discourse is concerning testamentary tutors and curators, because their time is extended according to the predefinition of the Father.

That he defines guardianship by the Father's ordination alone according to Paul, when also many modes are enumerated by which guardianship may be finished, is because this mode alone corresponded to the simile, some derive προθεσμίαν from θεσμός, a law. more correctly others [derive it] from τῷ θεοῖς & τῷ θεοδιδάκτῳ, whence τῷ θεοδιδάκτῳ, "predestined," "constituted beforehand," whence τῷ θεοδεσμίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ & simply τῷ θεοδεσμίᾳ in Lucian and Dioscorides, Book VII, chap. 4. 'Ανθρώποις.

The Apostle now adds ἀνθρώποις: "So also we, when we were infants." The subject is comprised in the word ἡμεῖς ("we"), which includes the Apostle and the Galatians. But because the discourse concerns the people of the Old Testament themselves, it is manifest that this is expressed by κωμωδούσιν, which the blessed Hunnius elegantly expresses: "Since in this member of the application he speaks not obscurely of the people of the Old Testament, to whom neither Paul nor the Galatians could, strictly speaking, be reckoned, yet because of that bond of undivided society between the Church of the Old and New Testament, the Apostle speaks through the figure of communication, as if the Galatians themselves had also once lived under the Old Testament."

He shows, therefore, that the ancient people, who lived before Christ was born, were in a state of pupilage, and that the Israelites were νήπιος ("infants"), for which similitude Pareus brings forward various reasons: that the old Church was like a little one lying in a cradle (1) in quantity, because it was enclosed within the straits, now of one family, now of a few, and finally of the one Jewish nation. (2) In intelligence: because the mysteries of heavenly things were obscure to the Fathers. (3) In discipline: because, just as the first elements are handed down to schoolboys, and that under the rod, until they grow up: so God imbued and governed the ancient people with figures and shadows as if with initial rudiments. But just as the time before the Jewish polity does not pertain here, where the matter concerns Mosaic ceremonies; so also the remaining members of the comparison, except for the last, are οἰκονομία ; and thus Crellius’s gloss is alien here, concerning infants by reason of judgment in the matter of religion, which it is certain from the example of David and others that the faithful in the Old Testament did not lack.

And so that the ἀπόδοσις may correspond to the προτάσει, the Apostle teaches that the Israelites, bound as they were to ceremonial laws, were like pupils, first—regarding the state proper to them—they differed nothing from servants: then by reason of subjection, because they were under laws as if under a master, which lorded it over them: which, although some understand it of the moral law, must nevertheless be taken here properly of the ceremonial, partly because the Apostle’s institution demands it, who is now arguing against the necessity of the law, not the moral but the ceremonial, and partly because the νήπιος, of whom we are treating here, are spiritually sons and heirs and Lords, and thus the discourse is about the faithful, who are not under the law as if under a master. For the νόμος is not laid down for the righteous, 1 Tim. I. 9. Then by reason of the promise: because the ancients were not in full possession of goods, speaking comparatively— their taskmasters were the ceremonial laws, by which both persons were governed and affairs were administered. For all things were accurately defined by the Levitical laws, which they were bound to serve. In the Old Testament there were very many grave, laborious, troublesome, and expensive ceremonies, which the fathers were compelled to obey by the edict of the laws: therefore their state differed little from the condition of servants.

They are also called στοιχεῖα ("elements"), so that the childish state and the imperfection of the ceremonial laws might be more expressed, because those laws were only elements by reason of the information of the faithful under the New Testament, inasmuch as they were not only much clearer, but also more perfect: as στοιχεῖον, noting Erasmus, sometimes designates the beginning and origin of a thing being born, sometimes the very letters, just as Aristotle subjects στοιχεῖα as elements to principles and causes, and Justinian called the books of the Institutes elements of law, as it were rudiments; therefore Lyranus on this passage [says] under elements, i.e. under legal observances. Which are called elements, i.e. letters, because just as in learning a boy begins from those elements, so that he may know how to name and distinguish them, but as time proceeds, having abandoned this occupation he is engaged with the sciences: So the legal observances were certain figures disposing toward Christ, for which reason at His advent they were set aside. Beautifully Brentius on Num. XIX. fol. 968. Just as in the study of letters the elements, which are the letters themselves or the Alphabet or Abecedarium, seem childish and of no moment whatsoever: & yet knowledge of them is most necessary for erudition. For no one has ever been created Doctor of the good arts who has not first learned the Alphabet: Therefore, because without these small elements great things cannot stand: So in the knowledge and attainment of true justice there are its own elements or beginnings, which are the Mosaic rites, & they indeed seem childish, but by these beginnings God educated His children, until the Son of GOD came, & taught true & perfect justice, & created His Apostles (as we may say) as Doctors on the day of Pentecost. Conf. Ebr. IX. 14. Moreover they are called στοιχεῖα τῷ κόσμῳ, elements of the WORLD, not because the earthly law promised only transitory things, like the world, not heavenly things, as the glossa ordinaria has it. For also the remission of sins through sacrifices, offered in true faith, was promised, nor that they were prepared especially for men given over to the world & the flesh, as Hyperius judges, or that they were common to the Jews with the world, as Grotius, because the Apostle looks to the whole people of the Old Testament at once as heirs & Lords, not to the impious alone & those given over to the world, but because they were only external & worldly things, whence blessed Luther rendered them äußere Gabungen [external dispensations]. For the ceremonial laws deal with external & sensible things, namely sacrifices, washings, tithes, festivals & similar things.

But that those things were imposed on the Jews, so that they might relapse more readily through love into idols, is a Grotian fiction. God did not accommodate himself to their propensity for idolatry, but consulting their childhood, he instructed them with figures and elements, and in his incomprehensible wisdom he wished first to sharpen their desires with the shadows of ceremonies, rather than to exhibit the substance itself. Not that wisdom was more lacking: for we are just as unfit as they were for perceiving mysteries, but because it so pleased divine wisdom. But just as they are infants who have Moses, and the Prophet [has] very many most illuminated divinely, whom it is certain were not infants or children, but notable heroes. It is answered that the discussion now is not about the privileges of a few persons, who in the infancy of the Church [they] excelled: But concerning the entire state of the Church: which it is agreed was truly infantile in comparison to the new state. Indeed, even regarding those most enlightened ones, their faith and knowledge were more obscure than that of the infirm citizens of the new Church. For he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is pronounced by Christ himself to be greater than John the Baptist. And Prophets and Kings are said to have desired to see what we see, and did not see it. Therefore, the distinction between the old and the new Church remains evident. It also seems to stand in the way that the Apostle reproves the Corinthians and Hebrews as children who have need of milk. Childhood, therefore, did not cease after Christ. I answer: Again, what is said here is to be understood not of a few persons, but of the state of the whole Church. There were once, in the infantile Church, also some adults, heroes of faith: but few, by singular privilege: Thus, in the adult Church, most always remain children by their own fault, as here Pareus.

Next, the dignity of the ancient people in the *apodosis* [the application of the comparison] is to be observed: which the Apostle leaves to be gathered only from the *prothesis* [the premise of the comparison]. For although the condition of the ancient people was almost servile, yet he was heir and Lord of all. He served, indeed, under guardianship, nor had he been manumitted into possession of the inheritance and full lordship: yet the inheritance and lordship truly looked toward him. Whence it is manifest that the ancient faithful were also sons of God, and had the promised inheritance of heavenly life, and its hope and confidence just as we do (cf. Acts XIII), and were saved by faith in the Lord of the inheritance no less than we. This is rashly denied by the Socinians, Anabaptists, and Grotius, who followed them, already noted by us more than once. Nor does it stand in the way that they were little children. For the Apostle also called the little child the heir of all. He is indeed Lord only by hope and expectation, but he also has the right of lordship and the usufruct, that is, he receives food and sustenance in reality. Thus the people of the Old Testament were Lords by hope and expectation regarding the full fruition of liberty, which belongs to Lords, yet they enjoyed the goods of the inheritance, because provision was made for them regarding spiritual sustenance, as much as was necessary. Nor should the simile be extended beyond the third point of comparison, which the Apostle designates by name and expressly, namely, that they were reduced to servitude under the elements of the world, so that in the matter of liberty they might be distinguished from the faithful in the New Testament, who are not held to serve the same. Those were Lords of all, but reduced to servitude.

Thirdly, the time of duration is to be noted: How long that guardianship and servitude extended: Until the time which the Father had predetermined, or until the *plērōma chronou*, the fullness of time, should come. Then, therefore, it ought to have ceased. This presses against the Pseudo-Apostles, convicting them most solidly: Since God himself did not wish that guardianship or curatorship to be perpetual, but only until the *prothesmia*, until the time predetermined by himself, which he had reserved in his own power. It is wrong for the Pseudo-Apostles to reduce Christians under servitude again: since to feign a perpetual servitude of the law, and to wish to foist it upon the Christian Church, is no less absurd than to make a tutelary power perpetual, and to wish to keep adult heirs who have come of age under the same. Whence it is further easy to conclude that there is no need for ceremonies in the New Testament, much less can they be judged necessary for justification and salvation: Which were not even necessary in the Old Testament as pertaining to the inheritance of salvation, because the faithful of the Old Testament were heirs through faith, but were ordained only so that the heirs might still be kept under guardianship, because they were still *nēpioi* [infants], until the adults were emancipated from that guardianship and admitted to Evangelical liberty. Although, therefore, the heavenly goods belonged entirely to them as legitimate heirs, which they also attained through faith in the future Messiah, yet they still acted under a tutor and curator, namely, reduced to servitude under those elements of the world. Here Crocius notes his Calvin, because he defers the time of those elements to the end of the age. In this, he seems (a great interpreter: so he calls him) to be carried too far, because he thinks they are under these elements until the second coming of Christ. The Apostle places the end at the first coming. In that, therefore, they are called not only elements of the world, but also weak and beggarly elements (v. 9), and Christians are warned away from their servitude as from idolatry. But Crocius himself errs with Pareus: The Apostle, he says, understands not only the ceremonies of the law, but the whole legal pedagogy, and thus also the moral law, which terrified the Fathers and as it were compelled them by the commination of punishments and the fear of a curse. For this office of the moral law has no end, nor did it pertain only to the Fathers, nor was it the Apostle's purpose to treat of it here. But of the tutors, whose duty was until the *prothesmia tou patros* [the time appointed by the Father], so that he might establish the difference of time and the state of Christians under the New Testament from the time and state of the Israelite people under the Old Testament against the Pseudo-Apostles who were abolishing it, and might overthrow that Judaic error.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Οὕτω καὶ ἡμεῖς De Iudaeis loquitur, ut ostendunt sequentia. Ὅτε ἦμεν νήπιοι Aetati ephebicae respondet omnis aetas Israelitici populi, post exitum ex Aegypto, ad Christum. Ὑπὸ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου ἦμεν δεδουλωμένοι Erasmus subiecti ritibus illis, qui nobis cum mundo erant communes: qualia sunt templa, arae, victimae, libamina & finilia imposita Israelitis in hoc, ne talium amore ad idola dilaberentur, στοιχεῖα dicuntur in quaque arte ejus rudimenta, quia quod in rerum natura sunt elementa, id illa in artibus, ita in re pietatis sunt quaedam στοιχεῖα, Hebr. V. 12. quae quia Iudaeis cum mundo sunt communia, vocantur στοιχεῖα a majore ea usurpantium parte, ut & Coloss. II. v. 8. 20. Similis translatio in voce Rabbinica, יסודות .

Expedita tractatione de lege morali, cujus observationem cum fide requirebant Pseudo-Apostoli ceu necessariam ad consequendam justificationem & salutem aeternam; jam de lege ceremoniali tractat, quam itidem observatu necessariam ad salutem faciebant. Patet diversitas argumenti. Nam antea de lege tantum illa, quae transgressionem gratia supervenit, quae omnes sub peccato concludit, & veluti carcer, & paedagogus est non Iudaeis tantum, sed omnibus ad Christum, egerat: Jam vero de lege Iudaeorum propria, quae populum Dei instar pupilli, sub tutore & curatore constituti, intra metas disciplinae suae continebat, nec ad plenam libertatem admittebat, usque ad tempus προθεσμίας, quae obtinuit tantum usque ad πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου: de clementia mundi, infirmis & egenis, quibus servire debuerunt observando dies, menfes, festa & annos de servitute Veteris Testamenti satis onerosa differt.

Ut autem Pleudo-Apostolos, sub servitutem illam fideles redigere fatagentes retundat: Galatas vero de libertate sub Christo solide informet, discrimen status ante Christum, & post exhibitum Christum illuftri similitudine, quae ab omnibus percipi poterat, proponit & explicat: tum vero servitutem, cui mancipare ipsos volebant Pseudo-Apostoli ad colenda superstitiose ceremonialia, non dubitat conferre cum cultu idolorum, quo servierunt olim iis, quae natura Dii non sunt ante veri Dei cognitionem, ad quam fideli Apostoli opera perducti, ipsum quondam ceu Angelum Dei, imo ceu ipsum Christi ipsum susceperint. Denique Testamenti utriusque ac synagogae veteris seu matris servitutis & Ecclesiae Christi, quae liberos parit, discrimine eleganter exhibito ad libertatis suae dignitatem agnoscendam revocat, ne instar Hagaris ancillae e familia Ecclesiae ejiciantur.

Ubi vi συνεχειας tractationis Apostolicae iterum manifestum est, haec proprie spectare servitutem egenorum mundi elementorum, qua ob Leviticas constitutiones multo duriori, magisque servili conditioni obnoxii erant, qui ad illas adstricti fuere, quam qui libertate Christiana gaudebant. Quod exempli causa docent leges de religiosa festorum observatione, & cultu in solo templo Hierosolymitano peragendo, quo non sine magna molestia omnibus veniendum erat, de abstinentia a certis cibis, & discrimine mundorum ac immundorum, de immunditia Levitica multiplici ratione contrahenda, variisque ad immunditiam carnis tollendam sacrificiis, de ablutionibus non unius generis, de circumcisione, qua masculorum caro in tenerrima infantia vulneranda erat &c.

Dico autem, inquit, ego Apostolus non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum.

Nam autoritate Apostolica hic opus erat ad definiendam controversiam, quam moverant adversarii. Vulgata ingerit pronomen hoc, v. 1. Τῦτο δὲ λέγω, quod ad praecedentia refert Crocius cum Pareo suo, ut sensus sit: Quod de legis usu ac duratione dixi, id ego hic declaro, atque intelligi volo, quicquid obmurmerent aemuli, ac vobis persuaderi tentent. Sed hic alia aggreditur Apostolus, nimirum de lege ceremoniali, quam urgebant Pseudo-Apostoli agere, cujus observandae necessitate profligat.

Adducit primum simile, & constitutionem civilem notissimam. Quia, ut B.

Lutherus, vulgus similitudinibus & exemplis facilius capit, quam arduis & subtilibus Disputationibus. Libentius videt bene pictam imaginem, quam librum bene scriptum. Hinc post similitudinem de Testamento hominis, de carcere & pedagogo assumit & hanc notissimam de haerede.

Patrem, qui peregrinetur, respici, nullum hic est indicium. Nec locus Matth. XXI. huic parallelus est: De elocatione vineae agit, non de tutoribus, aut curatoribus pupillorum. A patre potius defuncto, qui Testamento constituerit tutores aut curatores petita hic similitudo, secundum Chrysostomum aliosque, quia haeredis mentio fit Testamento, namque; mandavit huic (haeredi) pater, ut Theophylactus habet, ut bonorum administratione ad aetatem usque legitimam abstineret, huic voluntati parendam omnino est, & testamento.

Sive autem testamento id constitutum fuerit, sive non; pupillis tamen vi legum & consuetudinis ordinari tutores & oeconomi certum. Ad explicationem vero servitutis Mosaicae vel populi veteris sub lege in παιδείας similitudinis adducit tria 1.

Pupilli conditione fere servilem. Quando enim haeres infans est, nihil differat a servo.

Haeres est, cui res Patris haeret, ad quem haereditas jure pertinet: Vel ita dictus, quod quasi herus fit, id est Dominus, ut Cujacius vult. Quod vero Schardius in Lex. jur. refellit & haeredem ab Eva id est terra, dictú mavult. Κληρονόμον, qui κλήρον νέμες sortem, vel haereditatem forte divifam habet. Alius est natus, eius est filius, ad quem jure nativitatis haereditas spectat. De hoc agit Apostolus. Et hic est infans vel adultus secundum Actos major vel minor. Infantem νήπιον quasi νήπιον, qui farinon potest, νήπιον intelligit quemvis minorem, qui vel nondum omnino, vel nondum pro se in judicio loqui potest. Infantiam itaque haeredis non aetate, sed jure definit. Idque verba illa innuunt, ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον, nempe quamdiu durat infantia jure definita. In ea haeredem nihil differre a servo dicit, quod tamen κατά quemodo intelligendum. Servus enim non est haeres aut non differat Dominus; De infante autem mox dicitur, quod fit Dominus omnium.

Respicitur autem tum subjectio, quia ut servus non est sui juris, sed potestati heri subditus: Ita haeres, quia adhuc minor est & νήπιον, non est sui juris, sed subest tutorum imperio: tum provisio: Quia ut servo prospicitur de alimentis ab hero: Ita pupillo prospicitur de ali-curatoribus, eurumque; provisione eum acquiescere oportet; tum disciplina & castigatio, quae servo, cum officium suum non facit, debetur. Sir. XXXIII. 25. Siquidem etiam pupillus sub disciplina fit & castigationi subjectus, ut probe educetur.

Nihil ergo a servo differre dicitur, non natura, quia liber est, sed vivendi ratione, seu obsequendi necessitate, quod explicatur v. 2. Ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐςι, ὁικονόμους sed sub tutoribus est & curatoribus. E-rafmu prior vox, inquit, dicta est a permissio arbitrio seu jure-posterior a dispensatione rerum domesticarum. Glossa interlinearis: Tutores, qui pupillum contra hostes defendant, actores, qui pro eu causas agant & mores ejus informent. Sed haec juxta Latinas voces.

Graece docte a Grotio explicantur, Tutor, secundum Actos, ut est in Lexico Schardii defensor est pupilli, qui ante omnia personae attribuitur pupillari, ut eum alant, deinde ne res pupillares neglectae pessumeant aut vitientur. E diverso curator imprimis constituitur, ut rebus minoris sedulo prospiciat, deinde ut personis sua opera adsit. Unde recte B. Hunnius hos distinguit. Ille, inquit, (tutor) in educando potissimum orphano, formandaque illius pueritia laborat; bic vero (curator) circa bonorum curam, & in usum pupilli dispensationem occupatus est.

Ita duplici ratione subjectus est puer in pupillari suo statu, tum quod non licei ei per magistrum & formatorem pueritiae facere quicquid lubet, tum quod non permittitur ei pro libitu traflare facultates sive bona, sed alii ad tutelam constituti, de iis pro arbitrio ad utilitatem pupilli disponunt.

Pupilli dignitatem, quod etsi dicta ratione nihil differat a fer-guim. vo, haeres tamen & Dominus fit omnium. Haeres, quod ad ipsum jure nativitatis spectet paterna haereditas, etsi ad eandem non admittatur, quamdiu est in minorennitate constitutus. Dominus omnium scilicet spe & expectatione, nondum vero re & possessione III.

Temporis pupillaris definitio-nem: Ἀχρὶ τῆς προθεσμίας τῦ Πατρός.

Tutorum & curatorum officium, & pupillorum subjectio, non perpetuo durat, sed definitum habet tempus, quod vel Patris testamento determinatum est, vel lege, si pater intestatus decedat, unde tutor est vel testamentarius, vel legitimus. Tempus autem tutoris est usque ad ephebum seu annum aetatis decimum quartum, curatoris usque ad vigesimum quintum. Unde Hieronymus, legitimum, inquit, tempus, quod Romanis legibus sancitum est 25. annorum spatio terminatur. Hic autem de testamentariis tutoribus & curatoribus sermo est, quia tempus eorum extenditur juxta praefinitionem Patris.

Quod aute Paulum tutelam definit sola Patris ordinatione, cum etiam plures modi enumerentur, quibus finiatur tutela, ideo est, quod hic solus modus congruebat similitudini, προθεσμίαν nonnulli a θεσμός lex deducunt, rectius alii α τῷ θεοῖς & τῷ θεοδιδάκτῳ, unde τῷ θεοδιδάκτῳ, præstitutus, ante constitutus, unde τῷ θεοδεσμίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ & simpliciter τῷ θεοδεσμίᾳ apud Lucianum & Dioscoridem libr. VII. cap. 4. 'Ανθρώποις.

Subjicit jam Apostolus ἀνθρώποις: Ita & nos cum effemus infantes. Subje&um voce ἡμεῖς comprehenditur, complectente Apostolum & Galatas. Quia vero de populo Veteris Testamenti sermo est ipsi, manifestum est per κωμωδούσιν hoc efferri, quam eleganter exprimit B. Hunnius: Cum in hoc membro applicationis haud obscure loquatur de populo Veteris Testamenti, cui nec Paulus, nec Galatæ proprie loquendo accenseri poterant, tamen propter illum nexum indivisæ societatis inter Ecclesiam Veteris & Novi Testamenti, per communicationis figuram fic loquitur Apostolus, ac situm ipse tum quoque Galatæ olim quoque sub Veteri Testamento vixerint.

Ostendit ergo populum veterem, qui vixit ante natum Christum pupillarem, & Israelitas νήπιος fuisse, cujus similitudinis Parens varias affert rationes, quod vetus Ecclesia quasi jacens in cunabulis parvula fuerit (1) quantitate, quia inclusa angustiis modo unius familiæ, modo paucarum, tandem unius gentis Judaicæ. (2) Intelligentia: Quia mysteria rerum cœlestium obscura fuere Patribus (3) Disciplina: quia ut scholasticis pueris traduntur prima elementa, idque sub ferula, donec adolescant: Ita Deus veterem populum figuris & umbris ceu initialibus rudimentis imbuit, gubernavit. Sed ut tempus ante politiam Judaicam huc non spectat, ubi de ceremoniis Mosaicis res est; ita & οἰκονομία funt reliqua comparationis membra præter ultimum: adeoque & aliena hic Crellii glossa est de infantibus ratione judicii in religionis negotio, quo non caruisse fideles in Veteri Testamento, exemplo Davidis & aliorum fatis constat.

Et ut ἀπόδοσις respondeat προτάσει, parvulos fuisse Israelitas adstrictos legibus ceremonialibus docet Apostolus, quod instar pupillorum primo quidem quod ad statum eorundem propriam attinet, nihil a servis differrent: tum ratione subjectionis, quia legibus ceu hero suberant, quæ ipsis dominabatur: quod etsi de lege morali nonnulli intelligant, proprie tamen hic de ceremonialis accipiendum, partim quia id institutum Apostoli poscit, qui adversus necessitatem legis non moralis sed ceremonialis jam differit, partim quia νήπιος, de quibus hic agitur, filii & hæredes ac Domini funt spiritualiter, adeoq; de fidelibus fermo est, qui sub lege ceu hero non funt. Nam justo νόμος & κείτᾳ 1. Tim. I. 9. tum ratione promissionis: quia non in plena bonorum possessione erant veteres, comparate loquen-APP: ratores eorum fuere leges ceremoniales, a quibus & personæ gubernabantur, & res administrabantur. Omnia enim Leviticis legibus definita funt accurate, quibus servire tenebantur. Erant in Veteri Testamento plurimæ ceremoniæ graves, laboriosæ, molestæ, sumptuofæ: quibus obtemperare patres cogebantur edicto legum: ideo a servorum conditione parum aberat status eorum.

Dicuntur & στοιχεῖα, ut status puerilis, ut legum ceremonialium imperfectio magis exprimatur, quia leges illæ elementa tantum erant ratione informationis fidelium sub Nov. Test. utpote quæ non modo luculentiùs multo, sed etiam perfecti-ùs: uti στοιχεῖον, notante Erasmo, interdum initium ac primordium rei nascentis designat, interdum i- psas literas, quemadmodum Aristoteles στοιχεῖα elementa principia & causis subjicit, & Justinianus liabros Institutionum elementa juris vocavit, velut rudimenta, ideo Lyranus in hunc locum sub elementis, i.e. sub legalibus observantiis. Quæ dicuntur e- lementa, i. e. literæ, quia sicut in addiscendo puer incipit ab iis elementis, ut sciat ea nominare & distinguere, procedente vero tempore, dimissa hac occupatione circa scientias occupatur: Ita legales observantiæ fuerunt quædam figuræ disponentes ad Christum, propter quod in ejus adventu funt dimissæ. Pulchre Brentius in Num. XIX. fol. 968. Quemadmodum in studio literarum elementa quæ sunt literæ ipsæ seu Alphabetum aut Abecedarium videntur puerilia, ac nullius planè momenti: & tamen cognitio eorum ad eruditionem pernecessaria. Neque enim ullus unquam Doctor bonarum artium creatus est, qui non antea didicerit Alphabetum: Propterea, quod sine his parvis elementis constare magna non possunt: Ita in cognitione & assecutione veræ justitiæ sua sunt elementa seu initia, quæ sunt ritus Mosaici, & videntur quidem puerilia, sed his initiis educavit Deus pueros suos, donec Filius DEI venit, & docuit veram & perfectam justitiam, ac creavit Apostolos suos (ut ita dicamus) in Doctores in die Pentecoftes. Conf. Ebr. IX. 14. Vocantur autem στοιχεῖα τῷ κόσμῳ MUNDI elementa, non quod lex terrena tantum promiserit vel transitoria, ut mundus, non cœlestia, ut glossa ordinaria habet. Nam & remissio peccatorum per sacrificia, vera fide oblata, promissa, nec quod hominibus mundus & carni deditis potissimum parata sint, ut Hyperius censet, aut quod Judæis cum mundo communia, ut Grotius, quia ad totum Vet. Test. populum simul ad hæredes & Dominos respicit Apostolus, non ad impios tantum & mundo deditos, sed quia externa tantum erant & mundana, unde B. Lutherus außerliche Gabungen reddidit. Nam de externis & sensibilibus agunt leges ceremoniales, utpote sacrificiis, lotionibus, decimis, feriis & similibus.

Quod autem illa Judæis imposita fuerint, ut meliùs amore ad idola relaberentur, Grotianu sigmentum est. Non propensioni ad idololatriam sese accommodabat iisdem Deus, sed pueritiæ eorum consulens figuris & elementis instruebat, & sapientia sua incomprehensibili prius umbris ceremoniarum desideria acuere, quam substantiam ipsam exhibere voluit. Non quod magis sapientia rejudicaret: Æque enim ac illi inepti sumus in percipiendis mysteriis, sed quod ita placeret divinæ sapientiæ. Sed quemadmodum insantes sunt qui Mosen habent, & Propheta plurimos illuminatissimos diviniùs, quos minimè insantes aut pueros, sed heroes insignes fuisse constat. Respondetur non agi nunc de privilegiis paucarum personarum, quæ in infantismi Ecclesiæ excelluerunt: Sed de toto statu Ecclesiae: quem constat respectu status novi vere infantilem fuisse. Quin etiam, quod ad illuminatissimos illos attinet, obscurior eorum fuit fides & cognitio, quam sit civium infirmorum novae Ecclesiae. Qui enim minimus est in regno caelorum, a Christo ipso Joh. Baptista major pronunciatur. Et Prophetae ac Reges dicuntur cupivisse videre, quae nos videmus, nec vidisse. Manet igitur discrimen veteris & novae Ecclesiae evidens. Etiam obstare videtur, quod Apostolus Corinthios & Hebraeos reprehendit ceu pueros, qui lacte indigeant. Pueritia igitur nondum desiit post Christum. Respondeo: Rursus non de paucis personis sed de statu totius Ecclesiae intelligendum est, quod hic dicitur. Fuerunt olim in infantili Ecclesia etiam quidam adulti fide heroes: sed pauci, singulari privilegio: Sic in adulta Ecclesia plurimi semper manent pueri suo vitio, ut hic Pareus.

Deinde observanda in ἀποδόσει veteris populi dignitas: quam e προθέσει tantum colligendam relinquit Apostolus. Nam etsi fere servilis erat conditio veteris populi, erat tamen haeres & Dominus omnium. Sub tutela quidem serviebat, nec in possessionem haereditatis & Dominium plenum manumissus erat: Vere tamen ad eundem spectabat haereditas & dominium. Unde veteres etiam fideles Dei filios fuisse, ac promissam habuisse haereditatem vitae caelestis, ejusque spem & fiduciam aeque ut nos manifestum est (conf. Act XIII.) & Dominus haereditatis, adeoque per fidem non minus atque nos servatos fuisse. Quod temere negant Sociniani, Anabaptistae, & qui eos sequutus est Grotius non semel a nobis jam notatus. Nec vero obstat, quod parvuli fuerunt. Nam & parvulum haeredem omnium dixit Dominum Apostolus. Est quidem Dominus spe tantum & expectatione, sed & jus dominii habet & usumfructum, hoc est alimenta & sustentationem reipsa percipit. Sic populus Veteris Testamenti spe & expectatione Dominus erat, quoad plenam fruitionem libertatis, quae Dominorum est, bonis tamen fruebatur haereditatis, quia ipsi prospiciebatur de spirituali sustentatione, quantum opus erat. Neque extendendum simile extra tertium comparationis, quod nominatim & expresse designat Apostolus, quod nempe fuerint in servitutem redacti sub elementis mundi, ut ratione libertatis ab iisdem distinguantur fideles in Novo Testamento, qui servire iisdem non tenentur. Domini illi erant omnium sed in servitutem redacti.

Tertio notandum est durationis tempus: Quousque se extenderit illa tutela & servitus: Usque ad tempus quod Pater praefinierat, vel donec veniret πλήρωμα χρόνε plenitudo temporis. Tum ergo cessare debuit. Id urget contra Pseudo-Apostolos, convincens eosdem ita solidissime: Quum Deus ipse noluerit tutelam aut curatelam illam perpetuam esse, sed usque ad προθεσμίαν, ad tempus a se praedefinitum, quod in sua potestate reservarat. Perperam sub servitutem iterum Pseudo-Apostolos redigere Christianos: quum servitutem legis perpetuam fingere, & Ecclesiae Christianae obtrudere velle, non minus absurdum sit, quam tutelarem potestatem perpetuam facere, & sub eadem haeredes adultos & majores factos continere velle. Unde porro in proclivi est concludere, ceremonias in Nov. Test. nihil opus esse, nedum easdem ad justificationem & salutem necessarias censeri posse: Quae ne quidem in Vet. Test. ceu ad salutis haereditatem, quia fideles Veteris Testamenti haeredes erant per fidem, necessariae erant, sed tantum, ut sub tutela adhuc continerentur haeredes, ordinatae erant, quia adhuc νήπιοι erant, donec adulti emanciparentur illa tutela & ad libertatem Evangelicam admitterentur. Licet ergo ad illos tanquam legitimos haeredes pertinerent omnino bona caelestia, quae etiam consequuti sunt per fidem in futurum Messiam, tamen adhuc sub tutore & curatore agebant nimirum in servitutem redacti sub illa mundi elementa. Notat hic Calvinum suum Crocius, quod elementorum illorum tempus in finem seculi differat. In eo videtur (magnus interpres: sic eum vocat) longius provehi, quod sub his elementis non esse putat usq; ad secundum Christi adventum. Finem ponit Apostolus in primo adventu. In illo ergo non elementa solum mundi, sed & infirma & egena elementa v. 9. vocantur, & ab illorum servitute ceu idololatria absterrentur Christiani. Perperam autem Crocius ipse cum Pareo: Apostolus, inquit, intelligit ceremonias legis non solum, sed totam legalem paedagogiam, adeoque & legem moralem, quae Patres terrebat & velut cogebat poenarum comminatione & metu maledictionis. Nam hoc legis moralis officium nullum finem habet, nec ad Patres tantum spectavit, neque de eo hic agere propositum erat Apostolo. Sed de tutoribus, quorum munus erat usque ad προθεσμίαν τῦ πατρὸς, ut differentiam temporis & status Christianorum sub Novo Testamento, a tempore & statu Israëlitici populi sub Veteri Testamento contra Pseudo-Apostolos illam tollentes stabiliret, eumque errorem Judaicum profligaret.

## 4:4
Ver. 4. *Hote de ēlthe to plērōma tou chronou* [But when the fullness of the time came]) that is, the end of that *prothesmia*. For thus *plērousthai* or *symplērousthai* is taken for the end of time, Acts II. 1, Gen. XXV. 24, XXIX. 21, L. 3, Lev. VIII. 23, and often elsewhere. Thus *plērōma kairōn*, Eph. I. ver. 10.

*Exapesteilen ho Theos ton huion autou* [God sent forth his Son]) The firstborn, to whom, in the absence of the Father, the care pertained; he sent, that is, he gave him extraordinary power.

*Genomenon ek gynaikos* [Born of a woman]) Not created in the way that Adam had been created, but born of a woman's birth, by which he might be more similar to us.

*Genomenon hypo nomon* [Born under the law]) Most Codices more correctly *genomenon hypo nomō*, that is, subject to the law, because he was a Jew.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθε τὸ πλήρωμα τῦ χρόνε) id est, finis illius προθεσμίας. Sic enim πληρῦσθαι aut συμπληρῦσθαι sumitur de fine temporis, Act. II. 1. Gen. XXV. 24. XXIX. 21. L. 3. Lev. VIII. 23. & alibi saepe. Sic πλήρωμα καιρῶν, Eph. I. vers. 10.

Ἐξαπέσειλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ὑὸν αὑτῦ) Primogenitum, ad quem, absente Patre, cura pertinebat; misit, id est, potestatem ei dedit eximiam.

Γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς) Non creatum eo modo, quo Adamus creatus fuerat, sed natum partu muliebri, quo nobis esset similior.

Γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον) Plerique Codices rectius γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμω, id est, subditum legi, quia erat Judaeus.

## 4:5
Ver. 5. *Hina tous hypo nomon exagorasē* [That he might redeem those under the law]) That he might free those subject to the law first from vices, then also from the obligation of the law, *hoi hypo nomon*, Jews and Proselytes, 1 Cor. IX. 21.

*Hina tēn huiothesian apolabōmen* [That we might receive the adoption of sons]) Equally, of course, Jews and Gentiles, with the wall removed by which they were separated. Just as he had compared child-sons to servants, so, pursuing this similitude, he calls *huiothesian* that permission of the father by which sons are permitted to have certain things of their own, and to do certain things at their own discretion, namely, while obedience to the Father remains, but without special prescriptions. See what was said at Luke XVII. 10.

The Apostle now explains the *prothesmia tou patros* with clear words, *hote de ēlthe to plērōma tou chronou*. It is called the fullness of time, because the time (the *prothesmia*) predetermined in the secret counsel of the Father was then filled, namely, when the Son was sent by God, born of a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that by that redemption, which had been figured to the ancients as pupils under the elements of the world, being actually performed, that servitude might cease, and we might fully attain the *huiothesian*. The right and *axiōma* [dignity] of sons, who are no longer under their guardianship, now emancipated, and we might enjoy the full liberty of the sons of GOD, with liberty from those external elements and the servitude under tutors. The fullness of time, by a customary Hebraism, is the full or complete time. Which comes under the name of the latter days, Mich. IV. 1, and is called the accepted time, and the day of salvation, 2 Cor. VI. 1, the year of good pleasure, Isa. LXI. 1, concerning which see Dan. IX, Hagg. II.

God the Father is said to have sent the Son, because he himself is the principle and origin of the Son, who begat him from eternity. night, but in the fullness of time He sent the same. The Son is not only the firstborn, but the μονογενής (only-begotten) and unigenite sent into the world, made the son of man, that we might be made sons of GOD. For this mission took place in the incarnation, John 14, ch. 1, v. 14 , John 3, v. 16, but not in a legation, which was undertaken after baptism, as the Socinians wish, concerning which see what has been treated against them regarding the Preexistence of the Son of God.

Therefore, the emission is not local or separative, because the Son is always in the Father, and in the Spirit of the Father, John 1, v. 18, ch. 8, v. 16, 29, ch. 14, v. 10, ch. 16, v. 32, and is one with the Father, John 10, v. 30, 1 John 5, v. 7. It is not a servile mission, because it is the mission of the Son of God, the only-begotten and proper. But as Augustine says to CHRIST, tract. 36 on John: Thy mission is Thy incarnation. And as Lyranus says: We must understand Him to be sent, because from that incomprehensible and ineffable secret of the profound majesty of God, the Word was not only where He might empty Himself, but also when He might dwell in us.

Augustine, book 4 of the Trinity, ch. 20, says of this: According to this it can now be understood, not only that the Son is said to be sent because the Word was made flesh, but He is sent so that the Word might become flesh, and through His bodily presence might perform those things which are written: that is, that not only the man is understood to be sent, because the Word was made flesh, but also the Word is sent, that He might become man: because He is not sent according to an unequal power, or substance, or anything that is not equal to GOD the Father, but according to that which the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son.

Therefore it is added, that He was sent γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς (made of a woman), which was done in the incarnation: when He was conceived in the womb of His mother, and born of her, according to the flesh.

Whence He is said to be sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, John 8, v. 3. The Word ἐξαπέστειλε (He sent forth) does not lack emphasis. For it is implied that He was sent both from heaven and into these lands in inestimable light, which is otherwise expressed by the word πέμπειν (to send), Job 4, 34, ch. 5, 23, 24, 37, ch.

6, 37, 38, 40, 44, ch. 6, 16, 18, 28, 33. In some Codices it is read γεννώμενον (born). But most favor our reading, and thus He is born of the virgin Mary, so that He was made of her, that is, truly formed from her substance according to the flesh, and therefore He is truly ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) to us, except that He was not generated from male seed, but created and formed by the Holy Spirit from the substance of the virgin mother.

For because the flesh of the Lord was not concreted in the womb of the virgin from human seed and made a body, but by the effect and virtue of the Holy Spirit, therefore the Apostle says 'made' not 'born', as interpreted by Lyranus.

For it is one thing to generate with seed mixed and blood coagulated: it is another to be procreated not by mixture but by virtue. For men can generate children, but not make them. Thomas, in Blessed Glassius, says that two errors are destroyed: 1. That of Valentinus, saying that CHRIST did not take a body from the virgin, but brought it from heaven, and passed through the blessed virgin as through a pipe or canal.

But the Apostle says here to the contrary: Made of a woman. But this preposition 'Ex' (of/from) designates the material cause. 2. That of Nestorius, saying that the blessed Virgin is not the mother of the Son of GOD, but of the son of man.

But the Apostle says to the contrary, that GOD sent His Son, made of a woman. For he who is made of a woman is her son. If therefore the Son of God is made of a woman, namely of the blessed Virgin, it is manifest that the blessed virgin is the mother of the Son of God, etc. Theophylactus notes that it is said 'made of a woman', not 'through a woman', lest they find an occasion, who falsely imagine that the Lord proceeded into the world as through a canal, but 'of a woman', that is, that He produced the fruit of the virginal womb, receiving a body from the substance of the woman herself.

But he said 'woman' instead of 'virgin'. For by the Hebrew idiom אשה (woman) it also denotes a pure virgin, Gen.

2, v. 22. By which name, says Augustine, Tom. 3, book 2 of the Trinity, ch. 5, who among Catholics would not know that he wished to signify not the loss of virginity, but the difference of sex in the Hebrew manner of speaking. When he names only the female sex, it is the same as when he says 'made of a woman', as if he were saying, 'made of a virgin', says B.

Luther in this place. Conf. Gen. 3, 15, Isa. 7, 14. Furthermore, he says γεννώμενον ὑπὸ νόμον (made under the law), because He was not by birth subject to the law by Himself, because the Lord is the author of the law, as Calvin acknowledges here, which is to be noted against Piscator and others: But He voluntarily subjected Himself to the law for our sake; but He is not said to be made ὑπὸ νόμον (under the law) because He wished to submit Himself only under the ceremonial law, concerning which we have warned that the Apostle is here specifically arguing, or because He wished to submit Himself only under the moral law, as it seemed to Piscator; but it is to be understood of the whole law of Moses, which He wished to fulfill in all things, because He had to fulfill all the righteousness of the law, Matt.

3, and by His obedience He was about to liberate us from the rigor of the whole law, as Pareus also acknowledges, because the Father made the incarnate Son under the law 1.

Forensically and Politically, insofar as He wished Him to be born of a people subject to the law, or while the polity of the Mosaic law still stood; 2.

Ceremonially, insofar as He wished Him to be circumcised in subjection to the whole law; 3. Morally, insofar as He wished Him to be in all things conformable to moral precepts, and in His innocence to become subject to the execration of the law and to death.

Where, however, Pareus, akin to the errors of Piscator, involves himself in contradictions, when he says that Christ is by Himself subject to the ceremonial and political law, as the seed of Abraham.

And He also had to render obedience to the moral law, since He is a man and our brother. But Christ is the Lord of the law, even the ceremonial, Mark 2, 28. Therefore He is not by Himself subject to it, nor a servant of it. Nor does it appear how He could have redeemed the Jews from the ceremonial and forensic law, if He did not voluntarily subject Himself to it, to whom, therefore, it would have been necessary to remain under the execration for the violation of those laws, if they had not been liberated from the execration of the same.

Wherefore Pareus is here deservedly noted by B. Balduinus, p. 817, that CHRIST as a man was subject to the law of nature.

That is, he says, to make the Lord of the law a debtor of the law. But the obedience of Christ, which He rendered to the law, must be undue, otherwise it could not be meritorious for us: For no one can merit anything for others by his own debts: therefore the Lord Himself says that He paid what He did not take, Ps.

69, v. 5. But Pareus followed his Piscator entirely, who denied that the active obedience of Christ was necessary for the work of redemption, concerning which error we have spoken in 'Gründlichen Beweiss', p. 248, et seqq. The Apostle assigns a twofold end of the Son's subjection under the law: The former ἵνα τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον ἐξαγοράση (that He might redeem those who were under the law).

By those who were under the law, he does not understand only those who were under the law as a tutor, but in general all men, because the law was incumbent upon all to be kept, the execration of the law pressed upon all, and the whole world was subject to the law, Rom.

Then therefore it ought to cease. This he urges against the Pseudo-Apostles, convicting them most solidly: Since God Himself did not will that guardianship or curatorship to be perpetual, but only until the προθεσμία, until a time predetermined, which He had reserved in His own power. The Pseudo-Apostles act wrongly in reducing Christians again under servitude: since to feign the servitude of the law perpetual, and to wish to impose it upon the Christian Church, becomes no less absurd than to make the guardianship perpetual, and to wish to keep heirs who have become adult and of age under it.

Whence, further, it is easy to conclude that ceremonies are not needed in the New Testament, much less that the same can be judged necessary for justification and salvation: which were not even necessary in the Old Testament for those who were heirs of salvation through faith, but were only ordained so that the heirs might still be kept under guardianship, because they were still νήπιοι (children), until, grown to maturity, they should be emancipated from that guardianship and admitted to Evangelical liberty.

The Apostle places the end in the first advent.
