Paulus in concreto dicit: Non jam erit servus. Sententia autem planior erit, si eam in abstracto efferamus modo: Non erit servitus in Christo, sed mera filiatio. Nam veniente fide servitus illa cessat, ut supra capite 3. quos. ait. Quem sensum in aphorismis B. Balduinus etiam sequutus est pag. 819.

Renati non sunt servi, sed filii, v. 7. quorum corda sunt templa Spiritus Sancti, 1. Cor. VI. 19. ideo non servili metu, sed filiali cum reverentia ad Deum accedunt, & res suas ei ut Patri dilectissimo commendant.

Quemadmodum autem non amplius ut servi patris æterni & omnipotentis Dei extimescere, nec ex formidine pæna opera Deo grata præstare tenentur: Ita vicissim ut filii Deum Clementissimum Patrem timere, & prompto animo, quæ divinitus præcepta sunt, facere debent. Nam si ego Pater sum, ubi est honor meus, & si Dominus ego sum, ubi est timor meus, inquit Dominus Malach. I. vers. 6. Hinc Christus ad discipulos suos: Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis, quæ præcipio vobis: Jam non dico vos servos meos, quia servus nescit, quid faciat Dominus &c. Joh. XV. 14.

## 4:7
(εἰ δὲ υἱὸς καὶ κληρονόμος Θεοῦ διὰ χριστὸν) An heir to be, not only by expectation, but also by possession of the thing, which Christ will give. See Rom. VIII. 17. By Hebrew law only sons are heirs, but under that name all the faithful are indicated, of whatever sex they may be.

Although this sonship and inheritance, which Christ acquired for us by His active and passive obedience even to the death of the cross, is common to the faithful of the Old and New Testament, yet the distinction that they were under curators, but we in the New Testament are not under such guardianship, is clear both from the very fullness of time, as far as the πρεθεσμία τῦ παλρὸς extends, and from the actual completion of the work of redemption, of which the Apostle here treats; as whose shadow the old ceremonies were, which, once the substance itself was exhibited, ceased, which are here set forth as elements (στοιχεῖα) and the same earthly things suitable for little children, for which therefore there is no place in adult age, just as the Apostle 1 Cor. XIII. 11: when I became a man, I put away childish things (τὰ τῦ νηπίς); and according to Heb.

V. 12, the elements (στοιχεῖα) are suitable for those who have need of milk, not solid food, but for adults, as being more perfect, the elements (στοιχεῖα) and milk or thinner food are not for use, but there is need of solid food (τερεᾷ τροφῇ καὶ βρώματι), 1 Cor. III. 2.

A double demonstration of the Apostolic truth is therefore had here, and a refutation of the heterodoxy of the Pseudo-Apostles. The former is from the definition of time. Because they had to be under the guardianship of ceremonial laws only until a certain time according to the πρεθεσμία τῦ πατρὸς, they are free from that guardianship once that time defined by the Father has passed, and the observation of ceremonial laws is not necessary for them, not even by reason of a command, much less by reason of a means, as if they could be considered to contribute to eternal salvation and the obtaining of the heavenly inheritance.

Not that, because of a command Here therefore it is manifest that the Apostle is urging the principal theme, that we obtain the inheritance of life only through Christ apprehended by true faith. Which B. Luther again excellently handed down: For he who is a son, you will say fol. 106, must also be an heir. For by this very fact, that he is born, he deserves to be an heir. No work, no merit brings him the inheritance, but birth alone. And thus the inheritance comes to him merely passively, not actively, that is, to be born himself, not to beget, not to labor, not to take care, etc., makes him an heir.

He does nothing for this, that he may be born, but only suffers. And so we arrive at those eternal goods, the remission of sins, righteousness, the glory of the resurrection, and to eternal life, passively, not actively. Nothing at all intervenes here; faith alone apprehends the offered promise. As therefore a son in politics and economy becomes an heir only by being born: So here faith alone makes sons of God, born of the word, which is the divine womb, in which we are conceived, carried, born, educated, etc.

By this birth, therefore, by this passion, by which we suffer ourselves to be made and formed into a new creature through faith in the Word, let us be Christians, sons and heirs of God through Christ. Being heirs, however, we are free from Death, the Devil, etc., and we have righteousness and eternal life. And to the words: Through Christ: Paul always has Christ in his mouth, he cannot forget Him. For he foresaw that nothing would be less known in the world, even among those who were to profess themselves Christians, than Christ and His Gospel. Therefore he perpetually inculcates it, and places Him before our eyes.

And as far as he speaks of grace, righteousness, promise, sonship, and inheritance, he is always accustomed to add, in or through Christ; obliquely through this also attacking the law, as if he were saying, these things do not come to us through the law or its works (much less through our own powers, or the works of human traditions) but through Christ alone. the rigor of the mandate lasts until the προθεσμίαν (appointed time) of the Father, from which it must be estimated: Not this, because the observation of the Levitical laws was by no means a means of obtaining the inheritance, just as subjection under the tutelage of guardians is not a means of obtaining an inheritance: inasmuch as it is owed to the son by nature or generation, and to the ancients the heavenly inheritance by regeneration, but not through obedience performed to ceremonial laws, it was fitting by grace, not by works, or by the merit of compliance, so that by the certain and most wise counsel of GOD the Father, they had to be held and served under the tutelage of ceremonial laws, which was not a light, but a most strenuous servitude.

Later, concerning the nature of the ceremonial laws, which were only στοιχεῖα (elements) fitting for the world as children. Whatever observations were like rudiments and external elements for children, those can no longer be urged, as if necessary for those who, having emerged from youth, are no longer children. But the Apostle taught that such were the observations of the Levitical ceremonial laws, fitting for nothing but στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου (elements of the world) and not for adults, but for νηπίοις (infants) or children, such as the Ancients commonly were before Christ was exhibited, and ordered so that by them as by an abecedary they might be led through external figures and pictures or an image to the truth, which we have in the New Testament without shadows.

Whence what he here calls στοιχεῖα τῷ κόσμῳ (elements of the world) Coloff. II, where also in verse 20 he uses that name, in verse 11 he called σκιὰν τῶν μελλόντων (a shadow of things to come), and Heb. X. verse 1, σκιὰν τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν (a shadow of good things to come) opposing to it τὸ σῶμα τὸ ἐν Χριστῷ (the body in Christ), and the very image of the things. This is the force of the Apostolic refutation, to which however strength is added from the confirmation conjoined or inserted into the principal theme.

For if Christ, sent for our sake, and subject to the law, redeemed us from the exasperation and rigorous observation of the law in general, so that through his redemption, apprehended by faith, we might receive τὴν υἱοθεσίαν (the adoption of sons), surely not by the observation of the law, whatever it may be, or by our compliance and work, or by his obedience alone through faith, do we obtain the right of sonship, and thus also the inheritance of eternal life, and so through his obedience alone apprehended by faith we shall also be constituted just.

But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. Indeed, Christ was made under the law, when he took upon himself in our place the curse of the law due to us, sent into the world, that he might redeem us, who were under the curse of the law, or he was made under the law, when he fulfilled not only the moral law with perfect obedience, but rendered obedience to the entire law, and truly fulfilled all the justice of the law, not even refusing the yoke of the Levitical laws, to which he immediately submitted himself in early infancy, when he was circumcised and offered in the temple, Luke II. verses 21, 22, so that he might liberate those who were under the law, subject to the same, from rigorous observation, true justice having been acquired for them.

As therefore by that taking upon himself of the curse he redeemed us from the curse of the law, and by the obedience and perfect justice rendered to the law acquired for us true justice, so by the voluntary bearing of the yoke of ceremonial laws he rendered Jews and proselytes, such as all nations truly are, inasmuch as they were gathered to the Israelitic people, whose was the υἱοθεσία (adoption), Rom. IX. verse 5,

according to the prophecies of the Prophets, Isa. II. verse 2, Mic. IV. verse 2, and John X, free from that yoke of ceremonies. Furthermore, to add this to the present text, Emimus notes the diversity of the reading.

Vulgate, as also

PART II. Sharp reproach of the conversion of the Galatians to the servitude of external elements, and of their defection from the truth.

Latin:

(εἰ δὲ υἱὸς καὶ κληρονόμος Θεοῦ διὰ χριστὸν) Hæres futurus non expectatione tantum, sed & rei possessione, quam Christus dabit. Vide Rom. VIII. 17. Jure Hebræo filii tantum hæredes, sed sub illo nomine indicantur omnes fideles, cujuscunque sint fexus.

Quanquam vero hæc filiatio & hæreditas, quam Christus obedientia sua usque ad mortem crucis activa & passiva nobis acquisivit, communis fit fidelibus Veteri & Novo Testamento, discrimen tamen illud, quod isti fuerunt sub curatoribus, nos vero in Novo Testamento sub tali tutela non fimus, tum ex ipsa temporis plenitudine, quoad usque πρεθεσμία τῦ παλρὸς, se porrigat, tum ex actuali complemento operis redemptionis, de quo hic agit Apostolus, liquet; utpote cujus umbra fuere veteres ceremoniæ, quæ exhibita ipsa substantia cessarunt, quæ hic ceu στοιχεῖα elementa eademque terrena parvulis convenientia sistuntur, quibus proinde locus non est in adulta ætate, quemadmodum Apostolus 1. Cor. XIII. 11. ὅτε δὲ γέγονα ἀνὴρ, κατήργηκα τὰ τῦ νηπίς; & secundum Ebr. I. 12. τὰ στοιχεῖα illis conveniunt, qui lacte opus habent, non solido cibo, adultis vero utpote perfectioribus τὰ στοιχεῖα & lac vel cibus tenuior non usui sunt, sed opus est τερεᾷ τροφῇ καὶ βρώματι, 1. Cor. III. 2.

Duplex ergo demonstratio hic habetur veritatis Apostolicæ, & confutatio heterodoxias Pscu-do-Apostolorum. Prior à temporis definitione. Quod ad certum tempus secundum πρεθεσμίαν τῦ πατρὸς tantum sub tutela legum ceremonialium esse debuerunt, illi exacto illo à Patre definito tempore liberi sunt ab illa tutela, illisque observatio legum ceremonialium necessaria, ne quidem ratione mandati, nedum ratione medii, quasi ad salutem æternam & hæreditatem cœlestem consequendam faciant, censeri non potest. Non illud, quia Hic ergo manifestum, urgere Apostolum principale thema, hæreditatem vitæ, non nisi per Christum vera fide apprehensum, nos consequi.

Quod egregie iterum B. Luther. tradidit: Nam qui filius est, inquies fol. 106. & hæredem esse oportet. Hoc enim ipso, quod nascitur, meretur esse hæres. Nullum opus, nullum meritum affert ei hereditatem, sed sola nativitas. Atque ita mere passive, non active contingit ei hereditas, hoc est, ipsum nasci, non gignere, non laborare, non curare &c. facit eum hæredem.

Nihil facit ad hoc, ut nascatur, sed tantum patitur. Itaque passive, non active pervenimus ad ista æterna bona, remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, gloriam resurrectionis, & advitam æternam. Nihil prorsus bic intercedit, sola fides apprehendit oblatam promissionem. Sicut ergo filius in politia & œconomia tantum nascendo fit hæres: Sic hic sola fides efficit filios Dei, natos ex verbo, quod est uterus divinus, in quo concipimur, gestamur, nascimur, educamur &c. Hac ergo nativitate, hac passione, qua patimur nos fieri & formari novam creaturam per fidem in Verbum, fimus Christiani, filii & heredes Dei per Christum.

Existentes autem hæredes liberi sumus à Morte, Diabolo &c. & habemus justitiam & vitam æternam. Et ad verba: Per Christum: Paulus semper in ore habet Christum, non potest eum oblivisci. Prævidit enim nihil minus notum fore in mundo, etiam apud eos, qui professuri essent, se esse Christianos, quam Christum & ejus Evangelium. Ideo perpetuo inculcat, & eum ob oculos nobis ponit. Et quoad loquitur de gratia, justitia, promissione, filiatione & hæreditate, semper addere solet, in vel per Christum; oblique per hoc etiam petens legem, quasi dicat, ista nec, per legem aut opera ipsius (multo minus per vires nostras, aut opera traditionum humanarum) sed per solum Christum contingunt nobis.

Quanquam vero hæc filiatio & hæreditas, quam Christus obedientia sua usque ad mortem crucis activa & passiva nobis acquifivit, communis fit fidelibus fub Veteri & Novo Testamento, differi-men tamen illud, quod isti fuerint fub curatoribus, nos vero in Novo Testamento fub tali rute non fimus, tum ex ipsa temporis plenitudine, quod usque πρoθεσμία τὰ πλῶς, τε πορρίgat, tum ex actuali complemento operis redemptions, de quo hic agit Apostolus, liquet; utpote cujus umbræ fuere veteres ceremoniæ, quæ exhibita ηλὰ fubstantia cessarunt, quæ hic ει ευ τοιχα ελemen-ta eademque terrena parvulis convenientia fitiun-tur, quibus proinde locus non est in adulta ætate, quemadmodum Apostolus 1. Cor. XIII. 11. ὅτε δὲ γέγονα ἀνὴρ, κατέλιπα τὰ τῶ νηπία; & fecundum Ebr. I. 12. τὰ τοιχα ἰλὶς conveniunt, qui lade opus habent, non iolido cibo, adultis vero utpote perfectionibus τὰ τοιχα & lac vel cibus tenuior non ufui sunt, sed opus est σεεεα τροφῆ καὶ βρώματι, 1. Cor. III. 2. Duplex ergo demonstratio hic habetur veri-Duplex de-tatis Apostolica, & constatatio heterodoxias Pſeu-monstratio do-Apostolorum. Prior is temporis definitione. Qui tentatu & ad certum tempus fecundum πρεσβεσίαν τὰ πλῶ-confutatio τῆς ταντμ fub tutela legum ceremonialium esse heterodo-deberuerunt, illi ex eo illo à Patre definito tempo-xias. re liberi sunt ab illa tutela, illisque obfervatio legum ceremonialium necessaria, ne quidem ratione mandati, nedum ratione medii, quasi ad salutem æternam & hæreditatem cælestem consequendam faciant, cenferi non potest.

Non illud, quia mandati rigor durat usque ad προθεσμίαν Patris, ex qua æstimandum est: Non hoc, quia legum Leviticarum observatio medium haudquaquam fuit obtinendæ hereditatis, quemadmodum nec subjectio sub curatela tutorum medium est hereditatis consequendæ: utpote quæ filio debetur natura vel generatione, ac veteribus hereditas cœlestis regeneratione, non autem per obedientiam legibus ceremonialibus præstitam, ex gratia, non ex operibus, vel obsequii merito conveniebat, ut certo DEI Patris, eoque sapientissimo consilio ipsis sub tutela legum ceremonialium haerendum ac serviendum fuerit, quæ non levis, sed maxime nervosa servitus fuit.

Posterior à legum ceremonialium indole, quæ στοιχεῖα tantum fuere τῷ κόσμῳ νηπίοις convenientia. Quæcunque observationes instar rudimentorum & elementorum externorum fuerunt pro parvulis, illæ non amplius urgeri possunt, ceu necessariae illis, qui ex ephebis egressi, nec amplius parvuli sunt. At tales fuisse observationes legum ceremonialium Leviticarum Apostolus docuit, nil nisi στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου nec adultis, sed νηπίοις vel parvulis, quales communiter fuerant Veteres ante Christum exhibitum convenientia & ordinata, ut iisdem tanquam abecedarii deducerentur per externas figuras & picturas vel imaginem ad veritatem, quam in novo Testamento fine umbris habemus.

Unde quod hic στοιχεῖα τῷ κόσμῳ vocat Coloss. II. ubi etiam vers. 20. utitur eo nomine, vers. 11. vocavit σκιὰν τῶν μελλόντων, & Ebr. X. vers. 1. σκιὰν τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν opponens illi τὸ σῶμα τὸ ἐν Χριστῷ, & αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα τῶν πραγμάτων. Hæc vis est Apostolicæ confutationis, cui tamen accedit robor è principalis thematis subjuncta vel interjecta confirmatione.

Nam si Christus, nostri causa missus, legique subjectus, nos ab exaceratione ac rigorosa observatione legis in genere redemit, ut per redemptionem ejus, fide apprehensam, τὴν υἱοθεσίαν acciperemus, non sane legis, quæcunque illa fit, observatione, aut obsequio & opere nostro, aut sola ipsius obedientia per fidem, ut jus filiationis, ita & hereditatis vitæ æternæ consequimur, adeoque per obedientiam solam ejus fide apprehensam justi etiam constituemur.

At verum est prius. Ergo & posterius. Nimirum sub lege factus est Christus, cum maledictionem legis nobis debitam in se suscepit nostri loco, missus in mundum, ut nos, qui sub execratione legis eramus, redimeret, seu legi factus est, cum legem non moralem tantum perfecta obedientia implevit, sed universæ legi obedientiam præstitit, omnemque justitiam legis verè implevit, ne detrectato etiam jugo legum Leviticarum, cui statim in prima infantia se submisit, cum circumcisus & in templo oblatus est, Luc. II. vers. 21. 22. ut eos, qui sub lege erant, eidem subjecti à rigorosa observantia liberaret, vera ipsis justitia acquisita.

Quemadmodum ergo per illam maledictionis susceptionem nos à maledictione legis redemit, ac per obedientiam & justitiam perfectam legi præstitam nobis justitiam veram acquisivit, ita per jugi legum ceremonialium ultroneam portationem Judæos ac proselytos, quales revera omnes gentes sunt, utpote ad populum Israeliticum, cujus erat υἱοθεσία, Rom.

IX. vers. 5. secundum vaticinia Prophetarum, Es. II. vers. 2. Mich. IV. vers. 2. & Joh. X. aggregatæ à jugo illo ceremoniarum liberos reddidit. Cæterum, ut ad textum præsentem hoc adhuc adjiciamus, Emimus diversitatem lectionis notat.

Vulgata, ut&

PARS II. Conversionis Galatarum ad externorum elementorum servitutem, & defectionis à veritate acris exprobratio.

## 4:8
Verse 8. Ἀλλὰ τότε μὲν οὐκ εἰδότες τὸν θεὸν (But then indeed not knowing God) τότε (then), as if with a finger pointed, designates all the time that had passed before the calling of the Galatians, when he says, οὐκ εἰδότες θεὸν (not knowing God), not knowing God, namely that eternal maker of the universe, he understands the greatest part, to which compared the Philosophers, not all (for neither Aristotelians ought to be excepted, nor Epicureans, and many like them) were very few, and not even they correctly expressed that which they believed in their mind. Ἐδουλεύσατε τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς (You served those who by nature are not gods) In the Manuscript: Τοῖς φύσει μὴ θεοῖς (To those by nature not gods), that is, who in reality were not Gods: Τοῖς λογομένοις θεοῖς (To those called gods), 1 Cor. VIII. 5. not a dissimilar manner of speaking among Aristotle on the parts of animals II, 2. ὅτε τὸ ψυχρὸν φύσει τις (when something is cold by nature), Ἀλλ' οὐ σίγησις δεῖ (But not silence is needed) Deut. XXXII. 21. אֱלֹהֵי לֹא אֵל (gods that are not God) there the Greeks: ὃν οὐκ ἦσαν (which they were not), that is, τῇ φύσει μὴ ὄντες θεοὶ (by nature not being gods) thus φύσει is taken and Eph. II. 3. Verse 9. Νῦν δὲ γνόντες θεὸν (But now knowing God) by the benefit of Christ, John XVIII. 3. Μᾶλλον δὲ γνωθέντες ὑπὸ θεοῦ (But rather being known by God) Which is more, approved by GOD himself. For also that in the Hebrews, See Ps. I. 6. 1 Cor. VIII. 3. and Paul loves to join the same words with the meaning somewhat changed. But God had approved , spiritual gifts having been given. Πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα (How do you turn back again to the weak and poor elements) He says they return to those elements of piety, not because they had Judaized before, but because they had usurped many things common with the Jews, such as the choice of foods, the distinctions of days, and the Gauls the God of the Mother, which being worshipped by the Galatians, were not indeed circumcised, but castrated.

Such elements he calls , because they did not have the power to command the mind: and πτωχὰ (poor), because they did not carry with them those riches of spiritual gifts: confer Heb. VII. 18, 19. Οἷς πάλιν ἄνωθεν δουλεύειν θέλετε (To which again from above you wish to serve) πάλιν (again) and ἄνωθεν (from above) have the same value, as ἄνωθεν and αὖθις often among Homer, πάλιν ἄξαρχῆς (again from the beginning) among Aristophanes, πάλιν ἐκ δούλων (again from slaves), Matt. XXVI. 42. which repetition denotes the novelty or indignity of the thing. The Apostle had compared the state of the Old and New Testament.

Now he brings into contention the death of Gentilism and Christianity. That under the former indeed the Galatians both were ignorant of the true God, and served those who by nature are not Gods, under the latter however they know the true God, nay, through the same conversion they are also known by God by a knowledge of affection and love, but now they wish to be converted again to weak, namely, and poor elements, to which they wish to serve anew, superstitiously observing days, and months, and times and years, as if salvation consisted in that external worship.

Which he implies to be idolatry, because they thus serve again τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς (those who by nature are not gods), expecting salvation from such. Which Theophylact observed also with Chrysostom: He intends this against those who had believed from the Gentiles, arguing that the observation of days is idolatry, and these indeed far more than formerly to be bound by sin, Not formerly (he says) did you not know God, as those who were being led into error by the darkened eyes of your minds, by which you were led, you served those who were not gods, who are far removed from the divinity of nature.

But now, after the truth has been known, by observing days and times, nothing else is done by you, except that worship is offered to the elements, than which a certain impiety will surely be worse.

Therefore, he attributes to the Galatians in their former state (1) ignorance of God, who, even though they could have known God from the light of nature, and from the contemplation of creatures could have inferred the Creator, Rom.

1, v. 20. Yet they are called not knowing God, because they did not acknowledge that one true GOD, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to the knowledge of whom they have now been brought, having been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ch. 3, v. 27. Matt. 28, v. 19. Whence is refuted the error of Calixtus regarding the Mahometans, Jews, and Pagans, that they acknowledge God the Creator of heaven and earth, attributing to them the knowledge of the true God; of which it is spoken in the Appendix to the Syncretism of Calixtus.

(2) slavery or their worship, who are not gods by nature, because they offered religious worship to creatures and idols.

From which it is manifest that slavery and worship are held as synonymous, which is to be noted against the empty distinction of the Papists, that they cannot be absolved from idolatry, who deny that Christ is God by nature, yet offer him religious worship, which we observe against the anthropolatry, or the religion, adoration, and invocation of Christ, whom they hold to be a mere man, which the Socinians vend as the chief part of the Christian religion; whom we convict of idolatry professedly on this head in natural and revealed Theology, which may be seen here.

This Paul signifies, says B.

Luther, fol. 108, when he says: When you did not know God, that is, when you did not know what the will of God was, you served those who by nature were not gods, that is, the dreams and thoughts of your heart, by which without the word you imagined that God was to be worshipped in this or that rite.

For from this, that men naturally hold this proposition, God is, all idolatry was born, which would not have come into the world without the knowledge of divinity.

But because men had this natural knowledge of God, they conceived outside of and against the word vain and impious thoughts about God, which they embraced as the truth itself, and thus imagined God otherwise than he is in nature.

But in the modern state of the Galatians, there is attributed to them (1) knowledge of God, and that reciprocal, namely, that they both acknowledge the true GOD, and have devoted themselves to his worship, and so have been known by God himself.

But when the Galatians in the sacrament of baptism devoted themselves to the faith and worship of the name of the Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and having been brought to the faith and worship of CHRIST, have religiously served him, here is an invincible argument that CHRIST is true GOD by nature.

For he whom the Galatians acknowledged and celebrated after their conversion is without doubt GOD by nature, because in him the modern state is distinguished from the former, in that before they served those who are not gods by nature.

But now they are converted and serve none but the true GOD by nature, insofar as they are converted.

But CHRIST is he whom the faithful Galatians acknowledged and worshipped after their conversion.

Therefore CHRIST is true GOD by nature.

He who would not be GOD by nature should not be worshipped religiously, lest by worshipping him who is not God by nature, they become guilty of idolatry.

But the Apostle adds: but rather having been known by God, which can be taken even as a consequence, so as to hint at the true faith and happiness of the Galatians, because if the faith had not been true, they would not have been known by God, by which is understood not a simple knowledge of GOD, by which he knows all things, but one joined with affection, just as the words of knowledge bring in affection in the Hebrew phrase, Ps.

1, last verse. John 10, v. 14. 2 Tim. 2, v. 19. Nor is there any greater happiness than to be loved by God, and to enjoy his grace and benevolence: Or it is understood of the preceding visitation of our knowledge teaching through the word; As B.

Luther: In truth our knowledge is more passive than active, that is, it is rather to be known than to know.

Our acting is to suffer GOD working in us.

He gives the word, by which, through faith divinely given, we are born sons of GOD.

The meaning therefore is: You have been known by GOD, that is, you have been visited by the Word, you have been gifted with faith and the Holy Spirit, by which you have been renewed.

Wherefore also by these words, you have been known by God, he derogates justice from the law, and denies that the justice of God comes to us on account of the dignity of our works.

For no one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.

Likewise, the knowledge of himself will justify many, because he himself will bear their iniquities.

Therefore our knowledge of GOD is merely passive.

So also B.

Hunnius: That the benefit of the saving knowledge of GOD may derogate from all human powers, and ascribe it entirely to the gracious operation of GOD: As if he said, when GOD knew you, and mercifully looked upon you with the eye of divine grace, there at last you emerged from the deadly darkness of ignorance into this light and clear light, so that you now acknowledge the true and living GOD, Father and Son with the Holy Spirit, and serve him with true worship.

Theophylact wishes 'known' to be taken for 'assumed' by GOD.

Chrysostom and Oecumenius use the word 'attracted'.

For unless GOD had assumed or attracted them, they would not have found GOD by their own labor.

Beza in the first edition rendered it: Taught, made to know, which Cornelius a Lapide proves.

The verses at least differ, but they easily agree in sense.

The turning to superstitious and idolatrous slavery, to be offered to weak and beggarly elements under the opinion of necessity for salvation: As if he said, in the interpretation of B.

Luther, fol.

106. You have teachers, by whom they wish to reduce you into the slavery of the law.

Which I did not do, but by my doctrine I called you from the darkness and ignorance of God into the admirable light and knowledge of GOD, I brought you out of slavery, and established you in the liberty of the sons of God, not by this, that I preached to you the works of the law, and the merits of men, but the grace and justice of GOD, and the donation of heavenly and eternal goods through Christ.

Since the matter is so, why do you so easily leave the light and return to darkness?

Why do you so easily allow yourselves to be reduced from grace to the law, from liberty into slavery?

And afterwards: The Jew serving the law with this opinion, that by the very observance of the law he wishes to please God, (to be justified) does not worship the God of his fathers, but is an idolater, and an idol of his own heart, which is nowhere.

For the God of his fathers, whom he boasts he worships, promised the seed of Abraham, through which all nations would be blessed.

Therefore, not through the law, but through the Gospel concerning Christ is God known and blessing is given.

Such a God, who on account of the observations of worship etc. forgives sins, and justifies, is nowhere found.

Therefore it is a vain thought and a dream, and a fabrication of an idol in the heart.

For nowhere does God promise that he wishes to justify and save a man. men because of religions, observances, cults, etc.

Because in order that He might bless, that is, deliver us from the law, sin, death, and all evils, and might give His own Son, but for us all He delivered Him up, etc.

This is the certain and true knowledge of GOD, and divine persuasion, which does not deceive, it depicts the very GOD in a certain form, outside of which there is no GOD.

But the Apostle calls them weak and beggarly elements; because they have no power and efficacy for justification.

Beggarly, because now they are destitute even of the representation of the thing which they once shadowed forth, after the body having arrived, the shadows and figures were plainly evacuated.

Not otherwise than a shadowy line drawn by the hand of a painter as the *skia* (shadow) of a future image immediately vanishes, when the image itself expressed in living colors succeeds, Heb.

X. 1. Col. II. Which, although they once had their use under the Old Testament by the ordination of GOD, yet after the coming of Christ they have finished their duty, and therefore are utterly antiquated, weak, and beggarly.

Ambrosiaster and Augustine understand the sun and moon as alien; Cyril, among the Greek scholiasts, understands the particles of the universe by the elements of the world, but because they were declining toward Judaism and did not wish to return to Gentilism, Jerome and Theodoret, more correctly in the fifth book against Marcion, ch. 4, explain them as the sacraments and Jewish observances, which were given to them as first rudiments.

But Cornelius says wrongly that they are called weak and beggarly because they did not justify *ex opere operato* (by the work performed), as the sacraments of the new law, but *ex opere operantis* (by the work of the one performing), that is, from the faith and devotion of the one receiving.

Because neither the N.

Test. sacraments profit without faith, nor did the sacraments of the O.T. before they were still in use, otherwise than received through faith, bring salvation, not as *ex opere operantis*: for no merit is attributed to any work of ours; but they were received by the faithful in the Old Testament with trust placed in the Messiah.

The little word *palin* (again), as Adam Sasbouth notes, refers not to the whole discourse, but to a part, so that a repeated servitude is signified, although not the old one, but a new one, which is no better than the other.

Therefore, there is no reason for us to think here of those things which the Gentile Galatians had in common with the Jews, as Grotius wishes; those things certainly which follow concerning new moons and *kairois* (seasons) and Sabbatic years, as Grotius explains them, cannot be taught to have been once received among the Gentile Galatians.

XXVI. 42. quæ repetitio rei novitatem aut indignitatem notat. Compararat Apostolus statum Veteris & Novi Testamenti.

Jam in contentionem adducit obitum gentilismi & Christianismi. Quod sub illo quidem Galatæ tum ignorarint verum Deum, tum servierint iis, qui natura non sunt Dii, sub hoc verò verum Deum cognoscant, imo per conversionem eandem etiam à Deo cogniti sint cognitione affectus & amoris, jam autem converti velint iterum ad infirma nempe & egena elementa, quibus denuo servire velint, superstitiose observando dies, & menses, & tempora & annos, quasi in externo illo cultu salus consistat.

Quam idololatriam esse innuit, quod iterum ita serviant τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς, à talibus salutem expectantes. Quod Theophylactus observavit etiam cum Chrysostomo: Hæc in eos intendit, quæ ex gentibus credidissent, arguens dierum observationem idololatriam esse, & hos quidem longe magis, quam olim peccato obstringi, Non quondam (inquit) Deum ignobatis, utpote qui mentis caligantibus oculis in errorem deducebamini, quo ducti, soli infervistis ac lane, qui procul absunt a divinitate natura.

Nunc vero post cognitam veritatem, dies & tempora observando, nihil per vos aliud agitur, nisi quod elementis cultus praestatur, quo sane deterior erit quaedam impietas.

Tribuit ergo Galatis in priori statu (1) ἄγνοιαν τῷ θεῷ, qui etsi e lumine naturae agnoscere potuerunt Deum, & ex intuitu creaturarum opificem colligere, Roman.

I. vers. 20. Ideo tamen ἐκ εἰδότες τὸν θεὸν dicuntur, quod unum illum verum DEUM Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum non agnoverint, ad cujus cognitionem jam perducti in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti baptizati, cap. III. vers. 27. Matth. XXIIX. vers. 19. Unde refellitur Calixti error Mahumedanis, Judaeis & Paganis, quod Deum Conditorem agnoscant coeli & terrae, veri Dei notitiam adscribentis; Quo de in Appendice Syncretismi Calixt. dictum.

(2) δουλεία vel cultus eorum, qui non sunt natura Dii, quod creaturis & idolis cultum religiosum exhibuerint.

E quo manifestum est, δουλείαν & λατρείαν haberi ceu ἰσοδυναμοῦντα, quod contra inanem Pontificiorum distinctionculam notandum, etiam ab idololatria non absolvi posse, qui Christum natura Deum esse negant, eidem tamen cultum religiosum exhibent, quod adversus ἀνθρωπολατρείας, vel Christi, quem ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον habent, religionem adorationem & invocationem, quam Sociniani ceu praecipuam partem religionis Christianae venditant, observamus; quos ex professo ex hoc capite idololatriae convincimus in Theologia naturali & revelata, quae hic videatur.

Hoc Paulus significat, inquit B.

Lutherus fol. 108. cum ait: Cum ignorabatis Deum, id est, cum nesciebatis, qua esset Dei voluntas, serviebatis iis, qui natura Deinon erant, id est, somniis & cogitationibus cordis vestri, quibus fine verbo fingebatis, Deum hoc vel illere colendum esse seu ritu.

Nam hinc quod homines naturaliter hanc propositionem tenent, Deus est, nata est omnis idololatria, quae sine cognitione divinitatis non venisset in mundum.

Quia vero homines hanc naturalem cognitionem de Deo habebant, conceperunt extra & contra verbum vanas & impias de Deo cogitationes, quas amplexi sunt pro ipsa veritate, atque ita Deum finxerunt aliter, quàm in natura est.

In statu autem moderno Galatarum tribuitur ipsis (1) γνῶσις τῷ θεῷ, eademque reciproca, quod scilicet & verum DEUM agnoscant, ejusque cultui sese addixerint, adeoque ab ipso Deo cogniti sint.

Quum autem Galatae in sacramento baptizatis sese addixerint fidei & cultui nominis Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti, & ad fidem & cultum CHRISTI perducti, eidem religiose servierint, invictum hic est argumentum, CHRISTUM esse verum natura DEUM.

Is enim, quem agnoscebant & celebrabant post conversionem Galatae, verus est fine dubio τῇ φύσει DEUS, quia in eo distinguitur status modernus a pristino, quod ante quidem servierint iis, qui natura Dii non sunt.

Jam vero converti non serviunt, nisi vero natura DEO, quatenus scilicet converti.

Atqui CHRISTUS est, quem agnoscebant & colebant post conversionem suam Galatae fideles.

Ergo CHRISTUS est verus natura DEUS.

Qui τῇ φύσει non esset DEUS, colendus minime esset religiose, ne colendo ipsum τὸν μὴ ὄντα φύσει θεὸν, idololatriae rei fiunt.

Addit autem Apostolus: μᾶλλον δὲ γνωσθέντες ὑπὸ θεῦ, quod vel de consequenti accipi potest, ut Galatarum veram fidem & felicitatem innuat, quia nisi vera fuisset fides, non fuissent ipsi γνωσθέντες ὑπὸ θεῦ, quod non simplex DEI notitia, qua res omnes cognoscit, intelligitur, sed cum affectu conjuncta, quemadmodum verba notitiae affectum inferunt phrasi Hebraea Psal.

I. vers. ult. Johan. X. vers. 14. 2. Timoth. II. vers. 19. Neque vero major est felicitas, quàm à Deo amari, ejusque gratia & benevolentia frui: Vel intelligitur de antecedenti nostrae cognitionis visitatione docente per verbum; Uti B.

Lutherus: Revera nostra notitia est magis passiva, quàm activa, hoc est, est potius cognosci, quam cognoscere.

Nostrum agere est pati operantem in nobis DEUM.

Is dat verbum, quo per fidem divinitus datam apprehenso nascimur filii DEI.

Est ergo sententia: Cogniti estis à DEO, id est, visitati estis per Verbum, donati estis fide & Spiritu Sancto, quo renovati estis.

Quare & his verbis, cogniti estis à Deo, derogat legi justitiam, ac negat propter dignitatem operum nostrorum contingere nobis justitiam Dei.

Item notitia sui justificabit multos, quia iniquitates eorum ipse portabit.

Theophylactus cognitos esse vult pro assumptos à DEO.

Chrysostomus & Oecumenius utuntur verbo ἐπεστράφελο attraxit.

Versus saltim hi discrepant, sensu facile conveniunt.

H ἐπιστροφὴ ad servitutem superstitiosam & idololatricam, elementis infirmis & egenis praestandam sub opinione necessitatis ad salutem: Quasi dicat interprete B.

Lutheri fol.

106. Vos habetis Doctores, quo redigere vos volunt in servitutem legis.

Id quod ego non feci, sed mea doctrina vocavi vos è tenebris & ignorantia Dei in admirabilem lucem & cognitionem DEI, afferas vos è servitute, & constitui vos in libertatem filiorum Dei, non per hoc, quod predicavi vobis opera legis, & merita hominum, sed gratiam & justitiam DEI, ac donationem caelestium & aeternorum bonorum per Christum.

Cum res ita se habeat, quare tam facile relicta luce reditis ad tenebras?

Quare tam facile finitis vos à gratia ad legem, à libertate in servitutem reduci?

Et postea: Judaus servans legem hac opinione, quod per ipsam obfervantiam legis velit placere Deo, (justificari) non colit Deum patrium, sed idololatra est, adomnum & idolum cordis sui, quod nusquam est.

Nam Deus Patrum suorum, quem jactat se colere, promisit Abraba semen, per quod benedicentia essent omnes gentes.

Itaq; non per legem, sed per Evangelium de Christo cognoscitur Deus & donatur benedictio.

Ejusmodi Deus, qui propter observationes cultus & c. remittit peccata, & justificat, nusquam invenitur.

Ideo vana cogitatio & somnium est, & confictio idoli in corde.

Nusquam enim Deus promittit, quod velit justificare & salvare homini. homines propter religiones, observationes, cultus &c.

Quia ut benediceret, id est, liberaret nos a lege, peccato, morte & omnibus malis, & donaret proprio suo Filio, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum &c.

Hac certa & vera est cognitio DEI, & divina persuasio, qua non fallit, depingit ipsissimum DEUM certa forma, extra quam non est DEUS.

Vocat autem Apostolus infirma & egena elementa ; quia nullam vim & efficaciam habent ad justificationem.

Egena, quia nunc destituuntur etiam representatione rei, quam olim adumbrabant, postquam adventante corpore umbrae & figurae evacuata plane sunt.

Haud aliter atque linea adumbratilis ducta manu pictoris tanquam futurae imaginis σκιά protinus evanescit, quando succedit ipsa imago vivis coloribus expressa, Ebr.

X. 1. Col. II. Quod licet olim sub Veteri Testamento suum habebant usum ex DEI ordinatione, nubes tamen post adventum Christi suo sunt defunctae munere, ideoque prorsus antiquatae, infirmae & egenae.

Aliene Ambrosiaster & Augustinus solem & lunam: Cyrillus apud scholiastem Graecum particulas universi per elementa mundi intelligunt, sed quia declinabant ad Judaismum, non reverti volebant ad gentilismum, rectius veteris libri V. contra Marcionem cap. 4. Hieronymus & Theodoretus sacramenta & observantias Judaicas exponunt, quae ipsis tanquam prima rudimenta data sunt.

Perperam autem infirma & egena illa dici ait Cornelius, quod non justificarint ex opere operato, ut legis novae sacramenta, sed ex opere operantis, id est, ex fide & devotione suscipientis.

Quia nec N.

Test. sacramenta prosunt sine fide, nec sacramenta V. T. ante adhuc in usu erant aliter, quam per fidem, suscepta salutem adferebant, non ut ex opere operantis: nam nulli operi nostro talus tribuitur; sed fiducia in Messiam collocata a fidelibus suscipiebantur in Veteri Testamento.

Vocula πάλιν iterum, notante Adamo Sasbouth, refertur non ad totam orationem, sed ad partem, ut significetur iterata servitus, quamvis non antiqua, sed nova, quae altera non melior.

Non ergo est, quod hic cogitemus ea, quacum Judaeis communia habuerint Galatae gentiles, ut Grotius vult, ea certe, quae sequuntur de neomeniis & καιροῖς & annis Sabbaticis, ut illa explicat Grotius, quondam recepta fuisse apud Galatas gentiles, doceri non potest.

## 4:10
Ver. 10. *Hēmeras paratēreisthe* (You observe days) Sabbaths. *Kai mēnas neomēnias* (And months new moons). *Kai kairous* (And seasons) As unleavened bread, the law of tabernacles, the day of atonement. *Kai eniautous* (And years) The Sabbatic year.

Certain species are named, but the whole genus of Levitical observances is understood: because the reason for the other species is the same: And indeed those species are named here which seem to have been able to be retained still, or to be useful for propagating the worship of GOD.

But he understands the observance of ceremonies, not simply, but as the Jews and the Pseudo-Apostles demanded it on account of circumcision; namely, under the condition of necessity and merit for salvation.

Johannes Crocius explains the new moon days as the days from the first of the month up to the fourteenth, on which the lamb as a victim was brought back, and from the fourteenth up to the twenty-first of the same month, when unleavened bread was eaten.

Some, with Augustine, take them concerning the astrological days of the Chaldeans, which the Gentiles observed in performing affairs and in expecting the events of life and business.

Most, however, more correctly understand by days the weekly Sabbaths, whose rigorous observation the Jews deemed necessary for salvation.

But they commonly interpret months as new moons, even if some wish the observation of the first and seventh month to be implied. They generally explain *kairois* (seasons) unanimously, as Grotius does, concerning anniversary feasts, Passover, Pentecost, and the feast of tabernacles: but *eniautous* (years) concerning the seventh, which was of remission, and the fiftieth, which was the jubilee.

Although indeed the worship of Sabbaths is here also reckoned among the ceremonies, and the weak and beggarly elements of the world: yet that detracts nothing from the morality of the Sabbath, because the Apostle here does not regard the necessity by reason of the command, but by reason of the means and merit, in order to salvation, which the Pseudo-Apostles were urging: and the Apostle deals with Jewish Sabbaths, concerning which he had the matter with the Pseudo-Apostles: nor does he equate those observances in all things, but only in that respect of necessity by which they were required by the adversaries, who made the observance of both moral and Levitical commandments necessary for salvation, and for that reason were plainly perverting the Evangelical doctrine.

How, however, Sabbaths are necessary from their first consecration from the beginning of creation, how from the Sinaitic sanction to Gen.

II. v. 1. & Exod. XX. we have said. Rightly therefore B.

Luther: Paul instructs the conscience, therefore he does not speak of that Gentile rite of observing days, etc.

What remains pertains to the body, but he speaks of the law of GOD, and of the observation of days, months, etc., according to the law of Moses, that is, of religious days, months, and times, which the Galatians, instructed by the Pseudo-Apostles, were observing for justification.

For in Moses it was commanded to the Jews that they should religiously keep the Sabbath day and new moons, months, the first and seventh, the three stated times or feasts, namely of Passover, of Weeks, of Tabernacles, the year of remission and the Jubilee.

They themselves, compelled by the Pseudo-Apostles, were observing the same rites as necessary for salvation.

Hence he says that, having lost grace and Christian liberty, they are reverting to the servitude of weak and beggarly elements.

For they had been persuaded by the Pseudo-Apostles that those laws must necessarily be kept, and that, kept, they grant righteousness, and neglected, they condemn.

Against this, Paul in no way permits consciences to be bound by the Mosaic law, but frees them from the law.

Behold I Paul, he says below in chapter

5. say to you, that if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. And Coloss II.

Let no man judge you in meat and in drink, or in respect of a holyday or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days, etc.

This B.

Luther: Who also meets the objection of the Anabaptists and some Calvinists: Let someone say: If the Galatians sinned by observing days and times, why do you not sin by doing the same?

I answer: We observe the Lord's day, the birthday of the Lord, Easter, and similar holidays most freely.

We do not burden consciences with those rites, nor do we teach, as the Pseudo-Apostles and Papists, that they are necessary for righteousness, or that through them we can satisfy for sins, but that all things may be done in order and without tumult in the Church, and lest external concord (for in the Spirit we have another concord) be broken; As once happened, when the Roman Pontiff Victor excommunicated all the Churches of Asia, for no other cause than that they celebrated the day of Easter at a different time than the Roman Church.

But we observe such holidays primarily so that the ministry of the Word may be preserved, so that the people may gather on certain days and times to hear the Word, so that they may learn to know God, so that they may use communion, and so that they may pray publicly for all needs. Likewise, so that they may give thanks to GOD for His spiritual and corporal benefits.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε) Sabbata. Καὶ μῆνας νεομηνίας. Καὶ καιροὺς) Ὡς azyma, tabernaculorum legem, diem propitiationum. Καὶ ἐνιαυτοὺς) Annum Sabbaticum.

Nominantur certae species, sed intelligitur totum genus Leviticarum observationum: quia aliarum specierum eadem est ratio: Et quidem eae nominatae hic sunt species, quae magis videntur adhuc retineri potuisse, aut ad cultum DEI propagandum utiles esse.

Ceremoniarum autem observantiam intelligit, non simpliciter, sed pro ut Judaei, & ex circumcisione Pseudo-Apostoli eam exigebant; scilicet sub ratione necessitatis & meriti ad salutem.

Dies neomenias explicat Johannes Crocius dies a decima mensis prima, usque ad decimam quartam, qua agnus victima referebatur, & a quarta decima usque ad vigesimam primam ejusdem mensis, quando azyma comedebantur.

Nonnulli de diebus Astrologicis Chaldaorum, quod gentes observarint in peragendis rebus, & expectandis eventibus vitae, & negotiorum certos quosdam dies cum Augustino accipiunt.

Plerique tamen rectius per dies intelligunt sabbata hebdomadalia, quorum observationem rigorosam ceu necessariam ad salutem censebant Judaei.

Menses autem communiter de neomeniis interpretantur, etsi nonnulli mensis primi & septimi observationem innui velint. Καιροὺς fere ὁμοθυμαδὸν exponunt uti Grotius, de festis anniversariis, pashate, pentecoste, & tabernaculorum festo: Ἐνιαυτοὺς vero vel annos de septimo, qui remissionis, & quinquagesimo, qui jubeleus erat.

Quanquam verò sabbatorum cultus hic etiam ceremoniis accenseatur, & egenis ac infirmis mundi elementis: Id tamen moralitati sabbati nihil derogat, quia hic non necessitatem ratione mandati respicit, Apostolus, sed ratione medii & meriti, in ordine ad salutem, quam urgebant Pseudo-Apostoli: & de Sabbatis Judaicis agit Apostolus, de quibus ipsi res erat cum Pseudo-Apostolis: nec exaequat per omnia illas observationes, sed illo solum necessitatis respectu, quo requirebantur ab adversariis, qui & mandatorum moralium & Leviticorum observantiam necessariam ad salutem faciebant, eaque ratione doctrinam Evangelicam plane pervertebant.

Quomodo autem sabbata necessaria sint à prima inde consecratione ab initio creationis, quomodo à sanctione Sinaitica ad Genes.

II. v. 1. & Exod. XX. diximus. Recte proinde B.

Lutherus: Paulus instituit conscientiam, ideo non de isto gentili ritu observandi dies &c.

Quae restant ad corpus pertinet, sed de lege DEI loquitur, & de observatione dierum, mensium &c. secundum legem Mosis, hoc est, de diebus, mensibus & temporibus religiosis, que Galata instructi à Pseudo-Apostolis observabant ad justificationem.

In Mose enim praeceptum erat Judeis, ut religiose servarent diem sabbati & neomenias, menses, primum & septimum, tria stata tempora seu festa, scilicet Paschae, Hebdomadarum, tabernaculorum, annum remissionis & Jubileum.

Eosdem ritus & ipsi per Pseudo-Apostolos coacti observabant tanquam necessarios ad salutem.

Hinc dicit eos amissa gratia & libertate Christiana reverti ad servitutem infirmorum & egenorum elementorum.

Persuasi enim fuerant à Pseudo-Apostolis, istas leges necessario servandas esse, & servatas donare justitiam, neglectas damnare.

Contra Paulus nullo modo permittit conscientias lege Mosaica obligari, sed eas à lege liberat.

Ecce ego Paulus, inquit infra cap.

5. dico vobis, quod si circumcidamini, Christus vobis nihil proderit. Et Coloss II.

Nemo vos judicet in cibo & potu, aut in parte diei festi aut Neomeniae, aut sabbatorum &c.

Hac B.

Lutherus: Qui occurrit etiam Anabaptistarum & Calvinianorum nonnullorum objectioni: Dicat aliquis: Si Galata peccaverunt observando dies & tempora, cur vos idem facientes nec peccatis?

Respondeo: Nos observamus diem Dominicum, natalem Domini, Pascha & similes ferias liberrime.

Non oneramus illis ritibus conscientias, neque docemus, ut Pseudo-Apostoli & Papistae, eos necessarios esse ad justitiam, aut quod per illos satisfacere possimus pro peccatis, sed ut omnia ordine & sine tumultu in Ecclesia gerantur, neve externa concordia (in Spiritu enim habemus aliam concordiam) scindatur; Ut olim accidit, ubi Romanus Pontifex Victor excommunicavit omnes Ecclesias Asiae, non ob aliam causam, quam quod diem Paschae celebrarent alio tempore, quam Ecclesia Romana.

Potissimum autem observamus hujusmodi ferias, ut conservetur ministerium Verbi, ut populus conveniat certis diebus & temporibus ad audiendum verbum, ut discat cognoscere Deum, ut communione utatur, ut oret publice pro omnibus necessitatibus. Item ut agat gratias DEO pro spiritualibus & corporalibus ejus beneficiis.

## 4:11
Verf. 11. (ἐφοβήθην ὑμᾶς) That is, your affairs strike fear into me. (Μήπως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς) Lest perhaps all the labor spent by me on you should fall into vain. This is because that adulation of Jewish rites could be a step toward stripping away Christianity entirely; with the word μήπως he tempers his speech well, between fear and hope: he predicts nothing certain, but points out the danger.

The Apostle fears that a return to Jewish superstition might undo all the labor which he had spent not without care on the conversion of the Galatians, the Evangelical doctrine having been corrupted, namely, in the highest head of faith concerning justification. For the Apostle had labored not in converting and confirming one or two, but in all, not lightly, but even to exhaustion, which the word κοπίαν implies.

Latin:

Vers. 11. (ἐφοβήθην ὑμᾶς) Id est, res vestra timorem mihi incutiunt. (Μήπως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς) Ne forte totus labor, à me in vos impensus, in irritum cadat. Hoc ideo, quia illa adulatio Judaicorum rituum gradus esse poterat ad exuendum penitus Christianismum, voce μήπως bene temperat sermonem, inter metum ac spem: nihil certi praedicit, sed offendit periculum.

Metuit Apostolus, ne reditus ad superstitionem Judaicam perfundet laborem omnem, quem in Galatarum conversionem non fine cura impenderat, corrupta nimirum doctrina Evangelica in summo fidei capite de justificatione. Laboraverat enim Apostolus non in uno & altero convertendo, confirmandoque, sed in omnibus non leviter, sed usque ad defatigationem, quod verbum κοπίαν infert.

## 4:12
Verf. 12. (Γίνεσθε ὡς ἐγὼ) Be as I am, that is, another self, namely, most friendly to me: This is the greatest love, to love another as oneself. Cicero also in like manner, who called me another self, as the learned have noted.

(ὅτι κἀγὼ ὡς ὑμεῖς ἀδελφοὶ) (כנפשכם) as you yourselves, I am most friendly to you. Some understand this exhortation with Jerome, Theophylact, and Oecumenius as being about Paul in the matter of omitting Jewish ceremonies, and they take it in the past tense. For I also, as you, namely formerly, was, that is, I was led, as you, by a zeal for legal ceremonies: But it is more correctly understood as mutual love.

These words, says B. Luther fol. 112, are to be understood not of doctrine, but of affections. Therefore the meaning is not: Be as I am, that is, think about doctrine as I do; but be affected toward me as I am toward you, as if he were saying: Perhaps I have sharply rebuked you, but forgive me this harshness, judge the heart not from the words, but from the affection of the heart.

The words indeed seem harsh and the rod rough, but the heart is gentle and fatherly. Therefore, my Galatians, receive this rebuke of mine in the same spirit in which I rebuked you. For the matter demands that I show myself so harsh toward you. Let there be, therefore, in you that affection toward me which is in me toward you. I have a friendly heart toward you. I require the same in you. By a wonderful phrase he signifies his benevolence toward them. I embrace you with such sincere, such ardent affection, as if I had been transformed into you yourselves, and I were as you yourselves, and you were another self: I am as studious of your salvation as of my own: And he does this so that they may understand so much more clearly that all that which might seem to have been said more harshly proceeded from the innermost sincere affection of love, and that they should not change their affection toward him who stands so firmly in benevolence toward them, as this is rendered with Beza by Crocius.

(Δέομαι ὑμῶν) The words παρακαλω. (Οὐδέν με ἠδικήσατε) You have not injured me privately, why should you believe that you are being treated by me more harshly than before. What I have said is born of love.

To others it seems that what he asks has already preceded: Be as I am; but you have not injured me in those things. The Apostle does not deny that he was offended by that conversion of the Galatians to the Pseudo-Apostles in his Apostolic office, but that no injury was done to his person, and he does this only so that it might not be judged that he used such vehemence because of the offense and injury brought upon him, as if he were saying: (as here B. Luther fol. 112) Why should I be angry with you or disparage you out of evil pain of mind, when you have not injured me? Why then do you say that we are subverted, deserters of your doctrine, mindless, bewitched .

Do these things not sufficiently testify that we have offended you? Nay, not me, but you have offended yourselves. And therefore I am tormented by anger not for my sake, but for yours. Therefore do not think that my rebuke proceeded from an angry heart, hatred, or any other vice. For I call GOD to witness that you have done me no injury at all, but on the contrary, you have conferred many benefits upon me, as follows.

Thus, flattering the Galatians, he prepares their minds to bear fatherly castigations with filial affection; and this is to temper wormwood and a bitter potion with honey and sugar, so that it may become sweet again.

Latin:

Vers. 12. (Γίνεσθε ὡς ἐγὼ) Estote velut ego, id est, alter ego, nimirum amicissimi mihi: Haec est dilectio maxima, alterum diligere tanquam semetipsum. Cicero quoque pari modo, qui me alterum, dixit, ut docti notarunt.

(ὅτι κἀγὼ ὡς ὑμεῖς ἀδελφοὶ) (כנפשכם) tanquam vos ipsi, amicissimus sum vobis. Adhortationem hanc nonnulli cum Hieronymo, Theophylacto, & Oecumenio de Paulo in omittendis Judaicis ceremoniis intelligunt, & illa in Praeterito accipiunt. Nam & ego, quasi vos, scilicet olim, fui, id est, ductus sum, uti vos, zelo ceremoniarum legalium: Sed rectius accipitur de mutuo amore.

Ista verba, ait B. Lutherus f. 112. non de doctrina, sed de affectibus intelligenda sunt. Non est igitur sententia: Estote, ut ego sum, hoc est, sentite de doctrina sicut ego; Sed sitis affecti erga me, ut ego erga vos, quasi dicat: Fortenimis acriter objurgavi vos, sed condonate mihi hanc asperitatem, aestimate cor non ex verbis, sed ex affectu cordis verbi.

Verba quidem dura & virga aspera videntur, sed cor suave & paternum est. Ideo mei Galatae, objurgationem hanc meam eo accipite animo, quo vos objurgavi. Nam res postulat, ut me tam durum erga vos ostenderem. Sit ergo in vobis es affectus erga me, qui est in me erga vos. Ego amicum cor erga vos habeo. Hoc idem requiro in vobis. Mira phrasi suam erga eos significat benevolentiam. Ego vos tam sincere, tam ardente amplector affectu, ac si in vos ipsos essem transmutatus, & essem quasi vos ipsi, & vos essetis alter ego: Tam vestra sum salutis, quam mea studiosus: Idque facit, ut tanto clarius intelligant, ab intimo sincera amoris affectu profectum esse id omne, quod asperius dixisse videri posset, neque mutent affectum erga eum, qui in benevolentia erga ipsos stat tam firmiter, ut hic redde cum Beza Crocius.

(Δέομαι ὑμῶν) Verba παρακαλω. (Οὐδέν με ἠδικήσατε) Nihil me privatim laesistis, cur credere debeatis, vos à me tractari durius, quam antehac. Quae dixi, ex amore nascuntur.

Aliis videtur id, quod roget, jam praecessisse: Estote sicut ego; vos autem illis nihil me laesistis. Non negat Apostolus, se etiam illa Galatarum ad Pseudo-Apostolos conversione in officio suo Apostolico offensum esse, sed nullam personae suae factam injuriam, idque agit solum, ut ne ob offensionem & injuriam sibi illatam, tanta vehementia uti judicetur, quasi dicat: (ut hic B. Lutherus fol. 112.) Cur deberem vobis irasci aut ex malo animi dolore vobis detrabere, cum me non laeseritis? Cur ergo dicis nos subversos, desertores doctrinae tuae, amentes, fascinatos .

Ista satis testantur, quod te offenderimus? Imo non me, sed vosipsos offendistis. Ideoque non propter me, sed propter vos ira angor. Ne igitur putetis increpationem meam ex irato corde, odio, aut aliquo alio vitio profectam esse. Testor enim DEUM, quod nulla prorsus injuria me affeceritis, sed contra, multa beneficia in me contuleritis, ut sequitur.

Sic blandiens Galatis, praeparat animos eorum, ad ferendas paternas castigationes filiali affectu; hocque est temperare absinthium & amaram potionem melle & saccharo, ut iterum dulcescat.

## 4:13
Verf. 13. (Οἴδατε δὲ, ὅτι δι ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν τὸ πρότερον) As if he were saying: Through various chances, through a thousand dangers of things I have gone, so that I might instruct you, for that is δι ἀσθένειαν.

Rom. VIII. 26. 1. Cor. II. 2. 1. Cor. XI. 30. XII. 19. But here it often signifies all that of man which comes into view; τὸ πρεσβύτερον, namely when I was present. For even absent he now teaches them.

He explains the benefits once shown to him by the Galatians, and proclaims their affection toward him, both to show that he poured out nothing against them out of anger, and so that they might continue to be such as they showed themselves from the beginning: And in the first place he celebrates, what he deems the greatest among all things, that they were not offended by the infirmity of the flesh and the temptations and dangers by which he himself was almost overwhelmed, but that they received him as an Angel of GOD, nay, as Christ Jesus. This is certainly a great commendation, says the Blessed Luther fol. 112, of the Galatians, that they accepted the Gospel from a man so despised and afflicted as Paul was. For he preached the Gospel among them while the Jews and Gentiles were rioting and raging. For whatever was powerful, wise, learned, religious, hated, persecuted, spat upon, trampled, and blasphemed Paul. By all these things the Galatians were not at all offended, but removing from their eyes those specters of infirmity, temptations, and dangers, they not only heard the needy, despised, miserable, afflicted Paul, but they recognized his disciples, but furthermore they even received and heard him as an Angel of GOD, nay, as Christ Jesus. That is the outstanding praise and virtue of the Galatians, and certainly he never attributed such praise to any to whom he wrote as he does here to the Galatians.

Therefore the infirmity of the flesh is not to be referred with Jerome to the hearers, who could not subject the flesh to the Word. For he preaches the contrary in the Galatians: but to the Apostle the Teacher: nor is it to be understood of an infirmity or some sickness of the body, of which nothing is certain, nor would it contribute anything to the matter, nor of speech or doctrine only humble and contemptible before the wise of the world, as he testifies to the Corinthians, that he did not preach ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, 1. Cor. II. 4. For he is not now dealing so much with the kind and manner of teaching, as with the infirmity of his own person, held in contempt, both because he came vile, abject, and despised, and because he was subject to various insults, persecutions, and dangers.

These are called the infirmity of the flesh, because to be subject to them is considered a great weakness in the judgment of men at least, or because they bring pain to the flesh, and weaken the flesh, but not the Spirit, which rather corro-

corroborate, as with Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, B. Luther from the collation of 1 Cor. IV, 2 Cor. IV, VI, XI, XII, it is sufficiently evident. Paul calls the infirmities of the flesh the afflictions which he suffered according to the flesh, and had in common with other Apostles, Prophets, and all the pious: yet in the Spirit he was powerful. For the virtue of Christ dwelt in him, which always reigned and triumphed through him. Compare 2 Cor. XIII. 4. You know, says Theophylact as interpreter, how through the infirmity of the flesh, that is, through dangers and seditions, I preached the Gospel to you, and you did not despise me, being shaken by dangers, nor did the temptation of my flesh, that is, persecution and blows, and many other things of this kind, either offend you or lead you to hold me in contempt. He also silently impels them to shame, when he reveals how many evils he himself suffered for their sake from his adversaries.

Latin:

Vers. 13. (Οἴδατε δὲ, ὅτι δι ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν τὸ πρότερον) Quasi dicat: Per varios casus, per mille pericula rerum perrexi, ut vos instituerem, id enim δι ἀσθένειαν.

Rom. VIII. 26. 1. Cor. II. 2. 1. Cor. XI. 30. XIL 19. Saepe autem hic significat omne id hominis, quod in aspectum venit; τὸ πρεσβύτερον, nempe cum praesens essem. Nam & absens nunc eos docet. Explicat beneficia, sibi quondam à Galatis exhibita, & affectum ipsorum erga se depradicat, tum ut ostendat, se nihil ex ira in eos effudisse, tum ut tales esse pergant, quales ab initio se praebuerunt: Et primo quidem loco celebrat, quod maximum inter omnia reputat, quod non offensi fuerint infirmitate carnis ac tentationibus & periculis, quibus pene obrutus ipse fuit, sed susceperint ipsum ceu Angelum DEI, imo ceu Christum Jesum.

Haec certe magna, inquit Beat. Lutherus fol. 112. commendatio est Galatarum, quod acceperunt Evangelium ab homine tam contempto & afflicto, ut Paulus erat. Praedicavit enim apud illos Evangelium, tumultuantibus & furentibus Judaeis & Gentibus. Nam quicquid emt potens, sapiens, doctum, religiosum, oderat, persequebatur, conspuebat, conculcabat, & blasphemabat Paulum. Istis omnibus Galatae nihil fuerunt offensi, sed removentes ex oculis ista spectra infirmitatis, tentationum & periculorum, non solum audierunt egentem, despectum, miserum, afflictum Paulum, sed, agnoverunt discipulos ipsius, sed insuper etiam eum tanquam Angelum DEI, imo tanquam Christum Jesum susceperunt & audierunt. Ea est egregia laus & virtus Galatarum, & certe nunquam ullis, ad quos scripsit, tantam laudem tribuit, quam hic Galatis.

Infirmitas igitur carnis non cum Hieronymo ad audientes referenda, qua non potuerunt carnem subjicere verbo. Contrarium enim praedicat in Galatis: sed ad Apostolum Doctorem: nec de infirmitate vel aegritudine quadam corporis accipienda, de qua nihil constat, neque ea ad rem quicquam faceret, nec de sermone aut doctrina solum humili, & coram sapientibus mundi contemptibili, uti testatur Corinthiis, se non praedicasse ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, 1. Cor. II. 4. Non enim tam de genere ac modo docendi jam agit, quàm de personae suae infirmitate, despicatui habita, tum quod vilis, abjectus & contemptus venerit, tum quod variis contumeliis, persecutionibus, ac periculis obnoxius fuerit.

Haec carnis infirmitas dicuntur, quia illis subjici magna censetur imbecillitas judicio saltim hominum, vel quia dolorem inferunt carni, & carnem infirmant, non autem Spiritum, quem potius

corroborant, ut cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Oecumenio B. Lutherus è collatione 1. Cor. IV. 2. Cor. IV, VI, XI, XII. satis constat. Paulus vocare infirmitates carnis, afflictiones, quas secundum carnem passus est, & communes habuit cum aliis Apostolis, Prophetis, & omnibus piis: Spiritu tamen potens erat. Habitabat enim in illo Christi virtus, quæ semper regnabat & triumphabat per eum. Confer 2. Cor. XIII. 4. Nostis, inquit, Theophylacto interprete, quemadmodum per carnis infirmitatem, hoc est, per discrimina & seditiones vobis Evangelium predicaverim, nec vos me periculis devixatum contempseritis, nec tentatio meæ carnis, hoc est, persecutionis & plagæ, & alia pleraque istiusmodi vos aut offendit aut induxit, ut me contemptu haberetis. Tacitè etiam ad verecundiam cos impellit, cum aperit, quanta sit ipse illorum gratia ab adversariis mala perpessus.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. And my temptation, which was in my flesh, you did not despise, nor did you reject) He calls the very adversities through which men are wont to be tested temptations, James I. 3. And "you rejected" is more than "you despised": for the latter signifies contempt, the former also abomination, such as many are wont to show toward the unfortunate, and it is a translation drawn from foods and drinks, which, if they greatly displease, we are wont to spit out.

Thus Catullus: And we pray for our prayers... . As an Angel of God you received me) He speaks in the Hebrew manner, signifying the highest honor that was or should be held for him, 2 Sam. XIX. 27. As Christ Jesus) You could hardly have received him with greater honor, had Christ himself come to you in the flesh. effica.

Recalls to their minds the benefits conferred by them upon himself, so that it might be less believed that he was hostile to them, because he would say: I am not so hard as to forget such things. Jerome understands the temptation or exploration of the Galatians, but it is more correctly understood as the exploration or temptation of Paul, which he himself experienced among the Galatians by divine permission, so that his faith, constancy, and patience might be proved. Not indeed, as the Vulgate has it, the pronoun "your" (ὑμῶν), but "my" (μὲ) (temptation) occurs in the Greek Codices. He indicates that they rightly did not reject him, who was enduring many things for their salvation. Nor indeed had they not only not rejected him, but had received him with great honor, not as a messenger of some earthly King, but as an Angel of GOD, which some read and interpret. But since the voice of the Angels of GOD, or of the Lord, is not easily taken in the New Testament otherwise than of celestial Angels, it is most correctly explained thus, that he was received with such reverence as if God had sent an Angel herald to them from the heavens; therefore, for the sake of greater praise, it is added: Nay, as Jesus Christ, not that they exhibited divine honor to him, which he would entirely reject, as in Acts XIV with sacrifices, but that they received him for the sake of the ministry which he performed, as they would the Lord himself from whom he was sent.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Καὶ τὸν πειρασμόν μου, τὸν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, οὐκ ἐξουθενήσατε, οὐδὲ ἐξεπτύσατε) Tentationes vocat ipsa adversa, per quæ explorari solent homines, Jac. I. 3. & plus est ἐξεπτύσατε, quam ἐξουθενήσατε: Hoc enim contemptum, illud & abominationem significat, qualem multi ostendere solent adversum infelices, & est translatio, ducta ab esculentis & poculentis, quæ si vehementer displicent, exspuere solemus.

Sic Catullus: Precesque nostras Oramus cabe delpuas. Ἀλλ' ὡς Ἄγγελον Θεοῦ ἐδέξασθέ με) Loquitur Hebræa, summum honorem ipsi habitum aut habendum significans, 2. Sam. XIX. 27. Ὡς Χρισὸν Ἰησοῦν) Ipsum Christum, si in carne ad vos venisset, vix potuissetis majore honore excipere. effica.

Revocat illis in mentem ab ipsis collata in se beneficia, quo minus crederetur eis infensus esse, quia diceret: Non ita sum durus, ut talium obliviscar. Tentationem vel explorationem Galatarum Hieronymus intelligit, sed rectius de exploratione vel tentatione Pauli, quam ipse apud Galatas divina permissione expertus est, ut fides, constantia & patientia ejus probaretur. Non vero, ut vulgata habet, pronomen ὑμῶν vestrum, sed μὲ (tentationem) mei in Græcis Codicibus occurrit. Indicat jure ipsos non respuisse eum, qui propter ipsorum salutem plurima sustinebat. Nec vero non respuerant tantum, sed magno cum honore susceperant, non ut nuncium quendam Regis terreni, sed ut Angelum DEI, quod nonnulli legant interpretantur. Sed quum Angeli DEI, vel Domini vox non facile aliter in Novo Testamento accipiatur, quam de Angelis cœlestibus, rectissime ita explicatur, quod tanta reverentia susceptus fuerit, ac si Deus è cœlis Angelum præconem ipsis misisset, ideo majoris elogii causa additur: Imò ut Jesum Christum, non quod divinum honorem ipsi exhiberent, quem omnino respueret, ut Actor. XIV. sacrificia, scilicet quod ipsum ministerii causa, quod obibat, ut ipsum Dominum à quo missus erat, acciperent.

## 4:15
Vers. 15. What then was your blessedness)

Manuscript: How was your blessedness, as other very ancient Codices also have, where now is that proclamation of your happiness from my arrival? You have the word "blessedness" (μακαρισμὸν) also in Romans IV. v. 6, as also "to call blessed" (μακαρίζειν) in Luke I. 48, James V. 11, and in the book of Wisdom, and several times in Sirach. There is no need for a change of the received Codices; the sense is in the open.

The Vulgate is also wrong: Where is then your blessedness! In the Greek, "is" (ἐσί) is not held, but "was" (ἦν). Although "blessedness" (μακαρισμὸς) is made from "I call blessed" (μακαρίζω), Luke I. 48, James V. 11, and brings with it an estimation of blessedness, even according to Jerome, Theophylact, Beza, the Dutch, Crocius: How blessed therefore were you then to be estimated: I do not see why it should not be understood with B. Luther as "blessedness" (μακαριότης) itself, as it becomes the voice of one admiring: How blessed you were then! For blessed are they who hear and keep the word of God, Luke XI. 28. Therefore Piscator, Parcus, and others also rendered it thus. For your blessedness) Everywhere I am wont to testify this concerning you: if it were possible) that is, if that could have profited me. You would have plucked out your own eyes and given them to me) Such is that: Unless I loved you more than my eyes. He also said the same of digging out an eye, as Seneca in Oedipus, which others call to excise, to root out. Not only, he says, did you treat me with the highest humanity and reverence, justifying me as an Angel of GOD, etc. But if the matter and necessity had demanded it, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me, nay, you would even have spent your lives for him. And certainly the Galatians spent their lives for him. For by receiving and fostering Paul, whom the world then thought to have nothing more harmful, nothing more cursed and execrable, they were deriving upon themselves, as the receivers and defenders of Paul, the indignation and hatred of all nations and of the Jews.

There is therefore no need to posit a hyperbole here. Which Crocius also posits here, yet he acknowledges the incredible love with which they had embraced Paul from the beginning. They held him, he says, dearer than their own eyes. For there is almost nothing in the human body more excellent than the light of the eyes, and which is more rightly valued. The eyes are the most precious part of the body, which distinguish life from death by the use of light, says Pliny book II. cap. 37. Thence we see, and he placed it as if in a citadel, says Philo in his book on Abraham. Thence God himself, when he wishes to designate those most dear, compares them with the apple of the eye.

Saying, whoever touches you, touches the apple of my eye, Zach. II. 8. V. 16. So have I become your enemy, speaking the truth to you) That is, do you now think, because I tell you the truth, that I am of an enemy's mind toward you? This sense agrees best with the preceding and following. He now takes an argument from his own innocence according to other Interpreters, because he gave them no cause to presume enmity, nor is he held in hatred by them except for the hatred of the truth, because he was upholding the evangelical truth against the Pseudo-Apostles, who had insinuated themselves into them, nay, had demented them: But it is considered more correct to decline the cause of an enemy's affection, which they could suspect from the present rebuke, than the words "speaking the truth to you" imply. It is the duty of a friend to admonish friends more freely if they err, nor does the one admonished, if he is wise, grow angry at the other because of a friendly admonition and the truth offended, but he has and gives him thanks. All these things are said by Paul to confirm that: Be as I am.

You have not harmed me, etc., as here B. Luther fol. 114. Vers. 17. They are zealous for you) One is said to be zealous (ζηλοῦν) for someone who affects to be greatly loved by him: because such desire is wont to have as a companion jealousy (ζηλοτυπίαν).

It is therefore a metonymy. See 2 Cor. XI. 2. But he treats here of those new Teachers, of whom also above. Not well) They do not enter upon the way they ought: They ought to have obtained this from you by deserving well: not by deceit. But they wish to exclude you) So also the Manuscript, not "you" (ὑμᾶς). The sense is: They wish to exclude you from my friendship. The Syrian reads "to enclose" (ἐγκλείειν), as many Greek Codices also have. They want to keep you for themselves. See below VI. 12. 13. That you may be zealous for them) That you may also hold it as a great thing to be loved by them.

B. Hunnius correctly expressed the sense: Just as Paul desires the Galatians' original love toward himself to be restored, so conversely he labors to remove from them their preposterous and destructive love toward the Pseudo-Apostles.

The Apostle’s concept: whom he tries to render hateful and odious to them as most harmful wolves, having exposed their pestilential counsel, which they have set before themselves in perverting the Galatians. In Greek it is ζηλῶσιν. And the sense comes to this: They have zeal toward you, and they eagerly court you, so that they may draw you into their parties, so that they may exclude you from the true Apostles, and consequently from Christ, only so that you may emulate them at the cost of your salvation, and with a certain preposterous zeal adhere to their false doctrines. There is therefore no cause, with Beza, to be solicitous about the Greek reading, as if ὑμᾶς should be read in place of ἡμᾶς. Crocius notes that the matter comes to the same thing: If, he says, the particle ὑμᾶς is retained, the sense will be, they want to exclude you from us, that is, to abstract you, so that you do not remain joined to us in faith and Christian conversation. Which Luther expressed, translating thus: Sie wollen euch von mir abfaͤllig machen. But if, with Beza, Piscator, and the Belgians, 'us' is read, the sense will be: They do this solely so that you may not follow me and my colleagues and co-workers with your former affection, but that you may be separated entirely from us, and remain alien to our doctrine. Both readings come to the same thing. Nor should the word ἐκκλεῖσαι (to exclude) be changed, for the sake of one codex or another, into ἐγκλεῖσαι (to include) with Erasmus, as Ludov. de Dieu gathered from the Syriac; as if he were saying: They want to include you like captives under the yoke of the law. Boderianus also translates the Syriac as 'to exclude.' Theophylact: To exclude is to disturb and eject from the more perfect state and knowledge of Christ, and to cast into the imperfect condition of the law. For jealousy is not to tolerate a rival, whether that rival be good or bad. The Pseudo-Apostles required legal observances, so that as assertors of the Mosaic doctrine they might be loved by the Galatians, neglecting Paul, who denies that the observation of ceremonies is necessary for salvation.
