Manuscriptus: Πῶς ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν, quomodo & alii habent Codices perveteres, ubi nunc illa prædicatio felicitatis vestræ ex adventu meo? Μακαρισμὸν vocem habes & Roman. IV. v. 6. quomodo & μακαρίζειν Luc. I. 48. Jac. V. 11. & in Sapientia libro, & apud Sirachidem aliquoties. Nulla opus est Codicum receptorum immutatione; Sensus in aprico est.

Male etiam Vulgatus: Ubi est ergo beatitudo vestra! In Græco non habetur ἐσί, sed ἦν. Etsi autem μακαρισμὸς à μακαρίζω beatum prædico, Luc. I. 48. Jac. V. 11. fit, & beatitudinis æstimationem inferat, etiam secundum Hieronymum, Theophylactum, Bezam, Belgas, Crocium: Quam beati igitur tum æstimandi eratis: Non video, cur non cum B. Lutherop ipsâ μακαριότης intelligi debeat, ut fit vox admirantis: Quam tunc eratis beati! Nam beati, qui audiunt & custodiunt verbum Dei, Luc. XI. 28. Ideo sic reddidere etiam Piscator, Parcus, alii. Μακαριὰ γὰρ ὑμῶν) Ubiq; hoc ego de vobis testari soleo: ὅτι εἰ δυνατὸν) id est, si id mihi prodesse potuisset. Τὸς ὀφθαλμὸς ὑμῶν ἐξορύξαντες, ἂν ἐδώκατέ μοι) Tale illud: Ni te plus oculis meis amarem. Idem & fodere oculum dixit, ut & Seneca in Oedipode, quod alii exsculpere, eruere. Non solum, inquit, summa humanitate & reverentia tractastis me, justificiendo velut Angelum DEI &c. Sed si res & necessitas postulasset, cruissetis oculos vestros, & dedissetis mihi, imo etiam vitam vestram impendissetis pro eo. Et certe Galatæ impenderunt vitam suam pro eo. Nam suscipientes & foventes Paulum, quo mundus tunc putabat se nihil habere nocentius, nihil magis maledictum & execrabile, derivabant & in se, ut susceptores & defensores Pauli, indignationem & odium omnium gentium & Judæorum.

Non ergo opus est, hyperbolem hic statuere. Quam Crocius etiam hic ponit, agnoscit tamen amorem incredibilem, quo Paulum amplexi erant ab initio. Habuerunt, inquit, suis oculis chariorem. Nihil enim fere est in humano corpore oculorum lumine præstantius, quodque pluris optimo jure fiat. Oculi pars corporis pretiosissima, qui lucis usu vitam distinguunt à morte, inquit Plinius libr. II. cap. 37. Linde vidimus, & tanquam in arce collocavit, inquit Philo libr. de Abraham. Inde ipse Deus, cum charissimos designare vult, confert cum oculi pupilla.

Qui, inquiens, tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei, Zach. II. 8. V. 16. Ὥσε ἐχθρὸς ὑμῶν γέγονα, ἀληθεύων ὑμῖν) Id est, an nunc, quia vera vobis dico, ideo putatis, me inimico in vos esse animo? Hic sensus optime cum præcedentibus & sequentibus convenit. Argumentum jam ab innocentia tua sumit juxta alios Interpretes, quod nullam de inimicitia præsumendi causam ipsis dederit, nec nisi ob veritatis odium ab ipsis odio habeatur, quod scilicet contra Pseudo-Apostolos, qui sese ipsis infinuerant, imo eos dementarant, veritatem Evangelicam sustinebat: At rectius declinare censetur causam inimici affectus, quem è præsenti objurgatione, quam verba illa, veritatem loquendo vobis, inferunt, suspicari poterant. Munus amici est, amicis, si quid erret, admonere liberius, ne que admonitus, si modo sapit, irascitur alteri propter amicam admonitionem, & veritatem offensam, sed habet & agit ei gratias. Ista omnia dicuntur à Paulo ad confirmandum illud: Estote, sicut ego sum.

Nihil me læsistis &c. ut hic B. Lutherus fol. 114. Vers. 17. Ζηλοῦσι ὑμᾶς) ζηλοῦν aliquem dicitur, qui valde ab eo amari affectat: quia talis cupiditas comitem solet habere ζηλοτυπίαν.

Est ergo μεταωνυμία. Vide 2. Cor. XI. 2. agit autem hic de novis illis Doctoribus, de quibus & supra. Οὐ καλῶς) Non eam ineunt, quam oportet viam: Debebant hoc bene merendo à vobis consequi: non doloffari. Ἀλλὰ ἐκκλεῖσαι ὑμᾶς θέλουσι) Sic & Manuscriptus, non ὑμᾶς. Sensus est: Secludere vos volunt à mea amicitia. Syrus legit ἐγκλείειν, quomodo & multi Græci Codices habent. Volunt vos sibi servare. Vide infra VI. 12. 13. Ἵνα αὐτοὺς ζηλῶτε) Ut & vos magni habeatis ab ipsis amari.

Recte sensum expressit B. Hunnius: Sicut amorem Galatarum Paulus erga se pristinum instauratum cupit, sic è converso laborat eis eximere præposterum & exitiosum amorem erga Pseudo-

Apostolos conceptum: quos tanquam nocentissimos lupos eis exosos & invisos reddere conatur, detecto illorum pestilenti consilio, quod in pervertendis Ga- latis sibi præfixum habeant. In Græco est ζηλῶσιν. Et huc redit sensus: Zelum illi habent erga vos, & studiose vos ambiunt, ut in suas partes vos pertra- hant, ut à veris Apostolis vos excludant, & conse- quenter à Christo, tantum ut ipsos cum dispendio salutis amulemini, & præpostero quodam zelo fal- sis illorum doctrinis adhæreatis. Non ergo causa est cum Beza lectionem Græcam solicitandi, quasi loco ὑμᾶς legendum sit ἡμᾶς. Rem eodem reci- dere notat Crocius: Si retineatur, inquit, particu- la ὑμᾶς, sensus erit, volunt vos à nobis excludere, id est, abstrahere, ne nobis maneatis in fide & con- versatione Christiana conjuncti. Quod expressit Lu- therus, sic vertens: Sie wollen euch von mir ab- faͤllig machen. Si autem cum Beza, Piscatore, Bel- gis legatur nos, erit sensus: Hoc unice agunt, ne me, meosque collegas & cooperarios pristino prosequami- ni affectu, sed prorfus à nobis separemini, & à no- stra doctrina maneatis alieni. Eodem recidit utraꝙ lectio. Neq; verbum ἐκκλεῖσαι excludere in unius aut alterius codicis gratiam cum Erasmo in ἐγκλεῖ- σαι includere commutandum, ut è Syro Ludov. de Dieu collegit; quasi dicat: Volunt vos velut captivos includere jugo legis. Syrum etiam ver- tit Boderianus excludere. Theophylactus: Exclu- dere est è perfectiori Christi statu atque scientia de- turbare atque ejicere, & in imperfectam conjicere le- gis conditionem. Zelotypia enim est, non ferre ri- valem, sive bona ea sit, sive mala. Pseudo-Apo- stoli legales observantias requirebant, ut tanquam Mosaicæ doctrinæ assertores diligerentur à Gala- tis, neglecto Paulo, qui ceremoniarum observa- tionem necessariam esse ad salutem inficiatur.

## 4:18
V. 18. Καλὸν δὲ τὸ ζηλῦσθαι ἐν καλῷ πάντοτε) It was right that you should always strive that I should seek to be loved by you, for this being loved is honorable. Theocritus: Τίτυρό μοι τὸ καλὸν πεφιλαμένε.

Καὶ μὴ μόνον ἐν τῷ παρεῖναί με πρὸς ὑμᾶς) When I was present, you valued that highly, which you have now begun to despise: intervals of place do not disjoin well-founded friendships.

Again he recalls to memory and commends the former zeal, which was ἐν καλῷ (in good) for the honor of Christ and the love of truth among the Galatians: but he complains that it was not constant in them, because it did not last always, but only as long as he was present with them, whereas now they are led by zeal for the Pseudo-Apostles, but not a good one. The Vulgate has 'emulamini,' as if it were ζηλῦσθε: which perhaps some Latins follow. In the Greek text it is ζηλῦσθαι and thus Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius have it.

Latin:

V. 18. Καλὸν δὲ τὸ ζηλῦσθαι ἐν καλῷ πάντοτε) Rectum erat, ut semper operam daretis, ut ego à vobis amari expe- terem, est enim hoc amari honestum. Theocritus: Τίτυρό μοι τὸ καλὸν πεφιλαμένε.

Καὶ μὴ μόνον ἐν τῷ παρεῖναί με πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Cum ad- essem, magni id faciebatis, quod nunc cœpistis contemne- re: amicitias bene fundatas intervalla locorum non dis- jungunt.

Iterum pristinum zelum, qui ἐν καλῷ in bono pro Christi honore & veritatis amore fuerit Gala- tis, in memoriam revocat, atque commendat: Sed in eisdem haud constantem fuisse queritur, quod non semper, sed tantum quousque ipsis præsens fuerit, durarit, nunc verò zelo ducantur pro Pseu- do-Apostolis, sed non bono. Vulgatus habet æmu- lâmini, quasi sit ζηλῦσθε: quem forte aliqui Lati- ni sequuntur. In Græco textu est ζηλῦσθαι atq; ita habent Chrysostomus, Theophylact. & Oecumenius.

## 4:18
GALATIANS CHAP. IV. v. 18. 19.

affection. For while he calls them his little children, he claims their generation for himself, indeed he explicitly says that he is giving birth to them again, and not without the heavy pains of childbirth, which the word ὠδίνω implies. For he had generated them before through the Gospel not without labor, modesty, and sickness. Elsewhere he compares himself with a father, here with a mother, so that the Galatians might recognize in themselves the anxiety and piety of both parents, as Jerome says. He also adds that, just as a mother carries a fetus in her womb with great trouble until it perfectly takes on its form and reaches maturity; so he persists in care, labor, and troubles, until the image of Christ is restored in them again, and they receive their former form, through true knowledge of Christ and faith: at the same time hinting at an intimate union and conformity with Christ. Christ is formed, according to Augustine, through faith in the inner man, called into the liberty of grace with a meek and humble heart, not boasting of the merits of works, which are none. Thus, he who through sin and falling away from Christ had ceased to be a spiritual man, is conceived anew through repentance, and the form of CHRIST is introduced into him through faith. For the form of the Christian soul, as blessed Luther says on folio 116, is faith or trust of the heart, which apprehends Christ, adheres to Him alone, and to nothing else besides. A heart endowed with this trust, that we are righteous on account of Christ, has the true form of Christ. Moreover, it is prepared by the ministry of the word, 1 Cor. IV: 'Through the Gospel I have begotten you,' namely in the Spirit, so that you might know and believe in Christ. Likewise 2 Cor. III: 'You are an epistle of Christ, ministered and written by us, not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living GOD.' For the word proceeds from the mouth of the Apostle, or minister, and reaches the heart of the hearer. There the Holy Spirit is present, and imprints the word upon the heart, so that it may assent to it. In this way, every pious Doctor is a father, who through the ministry of the Word generates and forms the true figure of the Christian soul. This, therefore, according to the same interpreter, is what the Apostle says: 'I have rightly begotten you through the Gospel.' But those corrupters and depravers came, and fashioned a new face in your heart, not of Christ, but of Moses: so that your trust now no longer relies on Christ, but on the works of the law. That is not the true form of Christ, but an alien and utterly Diabolical one. Nor does he say: 'I am again in labor with you, until my form is formed in you,' but 'until Christ is formed in you.' That is, I labor so that you may again receive the figure and likeness of Christ.

To the textual doubt, that, since humans are conceived by mothers in order to be formed, and once formed are finally brought forth, the Apostle says he is again in labor with them until Christ is formed in them, St. Augustine replies, and Crocius from him: Let us understand this labor as being placed for the agonies of cares, with which he labored with them so that they might be born in Christ: and he is again in labor because of the dangers of seductions, by which he sees them being disturbed. The solicitude of such cares, by which he says he is in a way in labor, will be able to last as long as until they arrive at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that they are no longer moved by every wind of doctrine. It was not said, therefore, on account of the beginning of faith, by which they had been born, but on account of the strength of perfection. Perhaps the simplest explanation here will be that of Grotius, unless perhaps it must be said that that labor is not completed until Christ receives form in them: So that the time of labor is defined by the form of CHRIST. To be carried as if in the womb of the mother Church, and of the ministers of the Church, throughout the whole life, and until they bring us forth to eternal life. Up to that point, however, the form of Christ is always to be perfected, which then through shines forth the irradiation of the same image in us, 2 Cor. III. & IV. then through the likeness and conformity of the life and holiness of Christ. But that the Apostle brings forth the Galatians again, and forms those who have fallen anew, makes against the Novatians, as Flacius observes, who admit no repentance after a fall following baptism. It also makes against the Calvinists, who deny that the faithful can fall, in such a way that they totally lose grace. Verf. 20. Ἤθελον δὲ παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἄρτι καὶ ἀλλάξαι τὴν φωνήν μου) That is, to speak now more harshly, now more gently, according to how I might find you affected. For that is more evident to those present and speaking face to face. Ὅτι ἀποροῦμαι ἐν ὑμῖν) I am in doubt about you, namely, as to what kind of speech I ought to use. The Apostle desires to be present, so that according to the diversity of persons and other circumstances he might change his voice. But now, because he is detained in bonds at Rome, he shows that he is almost destitute of counsel as to how these evils are to be remedied in his absence, lest by writing more sharply he might perhaps alienate those who otherwise might lean toward the side of the Pseudo-Apostles, or if he treats them more gently, he might perhaps accomplish little in so great a matter among them: He describes this his anxiety so accurately, that he might rouse them, so that they themselves might think about the medicine to be salutarily applied, and in this way diminish, or rather entirely remove, the care of their Apostle, by returning, namely, to the purity of the Evangelical truth, as the blessed Hunnius has it here. Hunnius, with the blessed Luther leading the way. Luther.

PART III. Confirmation of the distinction between the Testament of servitude and of liberty through the allegorical interpretation of the history of Hagar and Sarah.

Latin:

LATAS CAP. IV. v. 18. 19.

affectum. Dum enim filiolos suos vocat, genitu- ram eorum sibi vendicat, imò diferte se ipsos iterum parturire ait, nec absque partus gravibus doloribus, quos verbum ὡδίνω importat. Genue- rat enim eos antea per Evangelium non sine la- bore, modestia, ægritudine. Alibi se cum Patre confert, hic cum matre, ut Galatæ utriusque an- xietatem & pietatem parentis in se agnoscant, di- cente Hieronymo. Addit etiam, ut mater fœtum in utero magna cum molestia gerit, donec for- mam perfecte inducat, & ad maturitatem perve- niat; ita se in cura, labore & molestiis persistere, usque dum in iisdem imago Christi denuo re- stauretur, & pristinam formam recipiat, vera Chri- sti cognitione ac fide: Simul intimam cum Chri- sto unionem, & conformitatem innuens. Forma- tur autem Christus, secundum Augustinum, per fidem in interiori homine, vocato in libertatem gratiæ miti & humili corde, non se jactante de operum meritis, quæ nulla sunt. Ita qui per pec- catum & defectionem à Christo homo spiritua- lis esse desierat, per pœnitentiam denuo conci- pitur, eique CHRISTI forma per fidem in- ducitur. Est enim forma Christiani animi, B. Luthero dicente fol. 116. fides seu fiducia cordis, quæ apprehendit Christum, huic soli adhæret, & nulli præterea rei. Cor hac fiducia præditum, quod pro- pter Christum simus justi, habet veram formam Christi. Ea autem paratur ministerio verbi, 1. Cor. IV. Per Evangelium vos genui, scilicet in Spiritu, ut cognosceretis & crederetis in Christum. Item 2. Cor. III. Estis epistola Christi ministrata & à no- bis scripta, non atramento, sed Spiritu DEI vivi. Verbum enim procedit ex ore Apostoli, seu mini- stri, & pertingit ad cor audientis. Ibi Spiritus San- ctus adest, & imprimit cordi verbum, ut illi assen- tiatur. Hoc modo omnis Doctor pius est pater, qui per ministerium Verbi generat & format veram fi- guram Christiani animi. Hoc ergo, eodem inter- prete, est, quod dicit Apostolus: Ego per Evange- lium vos recte generavi: Sed venerunt corruptores & depravatores illi, & finxerunt novam faciem in corde vestro, non Christi, sed Mosis: Ita ut fidu- cia vestra jam non nitatur Christo, sed operibus le- gis. Ea non est vera aut Christi forma, sed aliena & prorsus Diabolica. Neque dicit: Ego iterum vos parturio, donec mea forma in vobis formetur, sed donec formetur in vobis Christus. Id est, laboro, ut iterum accipiatis figuram & similitudinem Christi.

Ad dubium textuale, quod, cum homines à matribus concipiantur, ut formentur, formati autem demum pariantur, Apostolus dicat, se ite- rum eos parturire, donec Christus in ipsis forme- tur, respondet S. Augustinus, & ex eo Crocius: Parturitionem hanc pro curarum angoribus posi- tam intelligamus, quibus eos parturivit in eo, ut nascerentur in Christo: & iterum parturit propter seductionum pericula, quibus eos conturbari videt. Sollicitudo autem talium curarum, qua se quodam- modo parturire dicit, tamdiu esse poterit, donec per- veniant in mensuram ætatis plenitudinis Christi, ut jam non moveantur omni vento doctrinæ. Non ergo propter initium fidei, qua nati erant, sed propter robur perfectionis dictum est. Simplicissima for- san Grotii hĩc erit explicatio, nisi forte dicendum, non prius parturitionem illam perfici, donec Chri- stus formam in ipsis recipiat: Ut tempus parturi- tionis à forma CHRISTI definiatur. Gestandum veluti in utero matris Ecclesiæ, & ministrorum Ecclesiæ per totam vitam, & donec parturiant illa nos ad vitam æternam. Eo usque autem per- ficienda est semper forma Christi, quæ tum per irradiationem imaginis ejusdem in nobis effulget, 2 Cor. III. & IV. tum per similitudinem & conformitatem vitæ & sanctitatis Christi. Quod autem Galatas Apostolus parturiat rursus, & lapsos de integro formet, contra Novatianos, Flacio observante, facit, qui nullam admittunt ex lapsu post baptismum pœnitentiam. Facit & contra Calvinianos, qui fideles labi posse, ita ut gratia totaliter excidant, inficiantur. Vers. 20. Ἤθελον δὲ παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἄρτι καὶ ἀλλάξαι τὴν φωνήν μου) Id est, modo asperius, modo lenius loqui, prout vos reperirem affectos. Id enim præsentibus, & coram loquentibus magis patet. Ὅτι ἀποροῦμαι ἐν ὑμῖν) Hæsito circa vos, nempe quo genere sermonis uti debeam. Optat Apostolus, se præsentem esse, ut pro diversitate personarum & circumstantiarum aliarum mutet vocem suam. Nunc autem, quia Romæ detineatur in vinculis, ostendit, se consilii prope inopem esse, quomodo in absentia his malis medendum sit, ne scribens acrius forte magis etiam se abalienet eos, qui alioquin ad Pseudo-Apostolorum partes propendeant, aut si mollius eos tractet, parum fortassis in re tanta apud ipsos proficiat: Hanc suam solicitudinem idco tam accurate describit, ut exsuscitet illos, quo ipsimet de medicina salutariter adhibenda cogitent, atque hoc modo curam Apostoli sui minuant, imò planè tollant, redeundo nimirum ad puritatem veritatis Evangelicæ, ut hic habet B. Hunnius, præeunte B. Lutheri.

PARS III. Distinctionis Testamenti servitutis ac libertatis per allegoricam historiæ Hagaris & Saræ interpretationem confirmatio.

## 4:19
V. 19. Τεκνία μꝫ, ὓς πάλιν ὠδίνω) He compares himself to a mother, whose affection for her children is most tender. And here ὠδίνω is הריתי, that is, I carry in the womb. For הרה, which the LXX called ὠδίνειν in Isaiah XXVI. 18, is translated in many places as ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν. A physical fetus can be carried and brought forth only once: a moral fetus more often. Elsewhere Paul compares himself to a father, as in 1 Cor. IV. 15, Phil. IV. But the comparison of a mother is more apt for signifying labors and troubles together. At the same time he shows that he loves the Galatians more than Moses had loved Israel, Num. XI. 12.

Ἄχρις ὗ μορφωθῇ ὁ χρισὸς ἐν ὑμῖν) A fetus gradually receives its form in the womb, which the LXX call ἐξεικονίζεσθαι in Exodus XXI. 22; Macrobius called the womb the mint of the forming human. Understand Christ here as the very dogma of Christ, which, impressed upon souls, makes a man a Christian; compare Apoc. XII. A similar locution is found in Philo in his embassy: Θεόχρησα γὰρ λόγια τὲς νόμυς εἶναι ὑπολαμβάνοντες, καὶ τῦτο ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας τὸ μάθημα παιδευθέντες, ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἀγαλματοφορᾶσι τὰς τῶν διατεταγμένων εἰκόνας. Εἶτα ἐναργεῖς τύπες, καὶ μορφὰς ἀυτῶν καθορῶντες ἀεὶ τοῖς λογισμοῖς ἀυτῶν τεθύπασι.

It was not enough to have named them brothers. He calls them little children with a more flattering address, and testifies to his maternal

Latin:

V. 19. Τεκνία μꝫ, ὓς πάλιν ὠδίνω) Comparat se matri, cujus est tenerrimus in liberos affectus. Est autem hîc ὠδί- νω הריתי, id est, utero gesto. Nam הרה, quod ὠδίνειν dixere LXX. apud Esaiam XXVI. 18. multis in locis vertitur ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχειν. Fœtus physicus non nisi semel gestati & edi potest: fœtus moralis sæpius. Alibi Paulus patri se comparat, ut 1. Cor. IV. 15. Phil. IV. Sed matris compa- ratio aptior est ad labores & molestias una significandas. Simul ostendit, se plus amare Galatas, quam Moses amave- rat Israëlem, Num. XI. 12.

Ἄχρις ὗ μορφωθῇ ὁ χρισὸς ἐν ὑμῖν) Fœtus paulatim in utero formam suam accipit, quod ἐξεικονίζεσθαι dicunt LXX Exodi XXI. 22. uterum formandi hominis monetam dixit Macrobius. Christum hic intellige ipsum dogma Christi, quod impressum animis hominem facit Christianum, con- fer Apoc. XII. Similis locutio apud Philonem in legatio- ne: Θεόχρησα γὰρ λόγια τὲς νόμυς εἶναι ὑπολαμβάνοντες, καὶ τῦτο ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας τὸ μάθημα παιδευθέντες, ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἀγαλματοφορᾶσι τὰς τῶν διατεταγμένων εἰκόνας. Εἶτα ἐναργεῖς τύπες, καὶ μορφὰς ἀυτῶν καθορῶντες ἀεὶ τοῖς λογισμοῖς ἀυτῶν τεθύπασι.

Non satis erat, fratres nominasse. Filiolos blan- diori compellatione vocat, ac maternum testatur

## 4:21
Verf. 21. Λέγετέ μοι, οἱ ὑπὸ νόμον θέλοντες εἶναι, τὸν νόμον οὐκ ἀκούετε) Do you not consider the more mystical sense of the words of Moses? Verf. 22. Γέγραπται γὰρ· ὅτι Ἀβραὰμ δύο υἱοὺς ἔσχε, ἕνα ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης, καὶ ἕνα ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας) He compares the sense of the history with those notes which pertain to the allegory, concerning which we began to treat at Rom. IX. 7. 8. 9. Philo interprets Sarah in the allegory in his book as virtue, which is free-born. But Hagar as the knowledge of the arts, which ought to serve virtue, or otherwise be cast out, both in the book Cherubim, and elsewhere; you have both explained by the same Philo in the book, περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ προπαιδεύματα συνόδου.

Because the manner of the Old Testament involved the observation of ceremonial laws, so that the scruples concerning the necessity of the same, and at the same time the federal and Evangelical distinction, might be more fully resolved, it pleased the Apostle to employ an allegorical tradition of it.

But by the law here, Crocius understands not only the moral, but also the legal ceremonies. To be under the law is to be under the works of the law, Galat. III. that is, to seek righteousness in ceremonies and moral works. They wished to be justified by ceremonies before GOD, and by moral works.

They had indeed been led into this error by the fraud of false Doctors, who were also for circumcision: Yet they had not consented unwillingly: they had consented willingly: Hence he objects the voluntary error to them, so that they might understand that they perish by their own will, if they persist pertinaciously in their purpose. But there is an Antanaclasis in the word law, which is taken first for the voice of the law, then for the books of Moses. To wish to be under the law is to desire to be saved by the works of the law. Conf. the phrase in chap. IV. 4. chap. V. 18. Roman. VI. 14. 1 Cor. IX. 20. Moreover, this is not a double sense, whatever may be the case with the Jewish commentaries, of which we have spoken in the Comment. on Genesis, Prolegom. But the allegorical interpretation of the history, having been neatly made with Apostolic authority, is held even at this time not entirely unknown, and perhaps κατ' ἄνθρωπον is considered introduced.

The blessed Hunnius is right here: As if he were to say: The history indeed is to be understood according to the letter, but the Holy Spirit wished to adumbrate under it typically some certain thing, namely, the two Testaments, the Old and the New. That Old one indeed, given long ago on Mount Sinai, which mountain is also called Agar, the boundary of Abraham, and that mountain reaches in a continuous tract from Arabia even to Judea, where Jerusalem is. This is the old testament, namely, the law, promulgated from Mount Sinai, it generates not into liberty or the inheritance of the sons, but into servitude: Just as Agar the handmaid bore a son, not the heir of paternal goods, but of the same servile condition as she herself was. And so Agar is mystical, that is, the earthly Jerusalem or the legal Jewish people, who through the observation of the law desire to be justified and saved, serves with her sons, subject still to the sad servitude, and to the dire curse of the law, and does not reach the heavenly inheritance of the sons of GOD. V. 23. Καὶ ὁ μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης κατὰ σάρκα γεγένηται) That is, according to the accustomed order of nature, in the just ages of the parents, על דרך בשר (in the way of flesh). Thus the Jews to Abraham, that is, in a natural way. The LXX often use the word παιδίσκης for handmaid. See at Matth. XXVI. 69. Ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας, διὰ τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) A Metonymy, that is, through that extraordinary power which God brings forth. Thus through the word of GOD Christians become believers, the mystical offspring of Abraham. This difference between the birth and conception of Isaac and Ishmael is that the former was according to the promise expressly made by GOD, but the latter was conceived from the sole carnal counsel of Sarah. For because Sarah despaired of her fecundity, therefore by the instinct of the flesh she bids her husband to go in to the handmaid, and says: Perhaps I shall be built up from her, Gen. XVI. She herself therefore confesses that God had not promised Abraham seed from Hagar: But she thinks it is permitted to her, that in order to fulfill that which God had once promised, she might employ whatever means. Because therefore without the word, Ishmael is generated only by the counsel of Sarah, for that reason Paul rightly says that he was born κατὰ σάρκα (according to the flesh). On the contrary, God expressly promised Isaac to Abraham, Gen. XVII. Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac.

Here the word of promise is clearly proclaimed: for nature could not then produce children for Abraham, because his body was dead for generation, Rom. IV. nor did Sarah, naturally barren and worn out, give birth naturally: Therefore whatever happened in the generation of Isaac, it becomes manifest that it was done by divine promise. For this reason the Scripture describes the generation of Isaac, Gen. XXI. with a peculiar phrase, that God visited Sarah: namely, that it might be shown, that not by the usual manner, but by the singular goodness of GOD, Sarah became the mother of Isaac &c. as here the blessed D. Hoë renders it on this passage. See Glaff. pag. 732. Tom. II. Exeg. Evangel. & Epist. text. Confer Rom. IV. 19.

The blessed Luther thus delivered the application: This was the distinction, (fol. 118.) Ishmael was born of the handmaid according to the flesh, that is, not of the promise, and therefore he could not be heir. So Agar is mystical, that is, Mount Sinai, on which the law was given, and the old testament was established, generated a people to God, the great Abraham, but without promise, that is, carnal and servile, not an heir of God. Because to the law are not added the promises, concerning Christ the blesser, concerning liberation from the curse of the law, from sin and death, likewise concerning the free gift of the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life. But the law says, whoever does these things shall live in them. Therefore the promises of the law are conditional, not freely promising life, but to those who do them. But is there a double sense? knowing the law: And therefore they leave consciences in doubt, because no one makes the law.

The promises of the New Testament, however, have no attached condition, nor do they demand anything from us, nor do they depend on the condition of our dignity, but they bring and grant to us freely the remission of sins, grace, justice, and eternal life on account of Christ.

V. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Λέγετέ μοι, οἱ ὑπὸ νόμον θέλοντες εἶναι, τὸν νόμον οὐκ ἀκούετε) Non consideratis sensum μυσιώτερον verborum Mosis? Vers. 22. Γέγραπται γὰρ· ὅτι Ἀβραὰμ δύο υἱοὺς ἔσχε, ἕνα ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης, καὶ ἕνα ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας) Sensum historiæ confert cum illis notis, quæ ad ἀλληγορίαν pertineant, de qua agere cœpimus ad Rom. IX. 7. 8. 9. Saram in ἀλληγορίᾳ libro τὴν ἀρετὴν interpretatur Philo, quæ ingenua est. Agarem vero artium cognitionem, quæ virtuti famulari debet, aut alioquin expelli, tum in libro Cherubim, tum alibi, utrumque habes ab eodem Philone fuisse explicatum in libro, περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ προπαιδεύματα συνόδου.

Quia Veteris Testamenti ratio implicabat ceremonialium legum observationem, ut scrupuli de necessitate ejusdem simul & distinctio fœderalis & Evangelici plenius expediatur, Allegoricam illius traditionem adhibere placuit Apostolo.

Per legem autem hic Crocius intelligit non solam moralem, sed & legales ceremonias. Esse sub lege est esse sub operibus legis, Galat. III. id est, in ceremoniis & moralibus operibus quærere justitiam. Volebant justificari ceremoniis coram DEO, & moralibus operibus.

Inducti quidem erant in hunc errorem fraude falsorum Doctorum, qui erant & circumcisione: Non tamen inviti consenserant: consenserant volentes: Inde voluntarium errorem iis objicit, ut intelligerent propria voluntate perire, si in proposito pertinaciter perseverent. Antanaclasis autem est in voce legis, quæ primo pro voce legis accipitur, deinde pro libris Mosis. Sub lege esse velle, est, per legis opera salvari cupere. Conf. qua phrasin cap. IV. 4. cap. V. 18. Roman. VI. 14. i. Cor. IX. 20. Cæterum non geminus hic sensus, quicquid fit de Judæorum commentis, de quibus diximus in Comment. Genes. Prolegom. Sed historia allegorica interpretatio, auctoritate Apostolica concinne facta, vel isto etiam tempore non omninò ignota, & forte κατ' ἄνθρωπον adducta habetur.

Recte hic B. Hunnius: Quasi dicat: Historia quidem est intelligenda secundum literam, voluit autem Spiritus Sanctus sub ea typicè quampiam bilumbis adumbrare, duo videlicet Testamenta, Vetus & Novum. Vetus quidem illud olim in monte Sinai latum, qui mons etiam Agar dicitur, arche Abrabæ, & pertingit ille mons continuo quodam tractu ex Arabia in Judæam usque, ubi est Jerusalem. Hæc testamentum vetus, nempe lex, è monte Sinai promulgata, generat non in libertatem aut hæreditatem filiorum, sed in servitutem: Plane ut Agar ancilla filium peperit, non paternorum bonorum hæredem, sed ejusdem servilis conditionis, cujus erat ipsa. Itaque Agar mystica, hoc est, Jerusalem terrena sive populus legalis Judaicus, qui per legis observationem justificari cupit & salvari, servit cum filiis suis, subjectus adhuc tristi servituti, ac diræ maledictioni legis, nec pertingit ad cœlestem hæreditatem filiorum DEI. V. 23. Καὶ ὁ μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης κατὰ σάρκα γεγένηται) Id est, secundum consuetum naturæ ordinem, justis parentum ætatibus, על דרך בשר. Sic Judæi Abrahamo, id est, modo naturali. Vocem παιδίσκης pro ancilla sæpe usurpant LXX. Vide ad Matth. XXVI. 69. Ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας, διὰ τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Μιτωνυμία, id est, per eam vim extraordinariam, quam Deus proferat. Sic per DEI verbum Christiani fiunt credentes, mystica Abrahami soboles. Hæc differentia inter nativitatem & conceptionem Isaaci & Ismaëlis est, quod ille juxta promissionem à DEO expresse factam, hic vero ex sola carnali Sara consilio suscipiebatur. Nam quia Sara desperabat de fecunditate sua, ideo instinctu carnis jubet maritum ingredi ad ancillam, & ait: Forte ex illa ædificabor, Gen. XVI. Fatetur ergo ipsamet, quod Deus non promiserit Abrahæ semen ex Hagare: Putat autem sibi licere, ut ad implendum id, quod Deus olim pollicebatur, quavis media adhiberet. Quia ergo fine verbo, tantum consilio Saræ Ismaël generatur, idcirco Paulus ipsum recte κατὰ σάρκα natum ait. Econtra Isaacum expresse promittebat Deus Abrahæ Gen. XVII. Sara uxor tua pariet tibi filium, & vocabis nomen ejus Isaac.

Hic diserte verbum promissionis promulgatur: natura enim nec Abraham liberos procreare tunc poterat, quia corpus emortuum ad generationem erat, Rom. IV. nec Sara, natura sterilis & effæta, naturaliter peperit: Quicquid ergo in generatione Isaaci contigit, id ex promissione divina factum esse, manifestum evadit. Eapropter scriptura generationem Isaaci Gen. XXI. peculiari phrasi describit, quod Deus visitaverit Saram: nimirum ut ostendatur, non consueta ratione, sed ex singulari DEI bonitate Saram Isaaci matrem fieri &c. ut hic redde B. D. Hoë in locum hunc. Vide Glaff. pag. 732. Tom. II. Exeg. Evangel. & Epist. text. Confer Rom. IV. 19.

Applicationem ita tradidit B. Lutherus: Hoc fuit discrimen, (fol. 118.) Ismaël natus erat ex ancilla secundum carnem, id est, non ex promissione, ideoque non potuit esse hæres. Sic Agar mystica, id est, mons Sina, in quo lata lex, & vetus testamentum conditum est, generavit Deo, Abrahæ magno, populum, sed fine promissione, hoc est, carnalem & servilem, non hæredem Dei. Quia legi non sunt additæ promissiones, de Christo benedictore, de liberatione à maledictione legis, à peccato & morte, item de donatione gratuita remissionis peccatorum, justitia, & vita æternæ. Sed qui fecerit ea, inquit lex, vivet in eis. Sunt ergo promissiones legis conditionales, non gratis promittentes vitam, sed facientibus an bis geminus sensus? cientibus legem: Ideoque relinquunt conscientias in dubitatione, quia nemo legem facit.

Promissiones verò Novi Testamenti nullam habent annexam conditionem, neque quicquam exigunt à nobis, neque pendent ex conditione nostrae dignitatis, sed afferunt & donant nobis gratis remissionem peccatorum, gratiam, justitiam, & vitam aeternam propter Christum.

## 4:24
Which things are allegorized) He assumes what was confessed among the Jews, that in those histories, beyond the historical sense, another more eminent one is hidden, which is the מדרש כפולים, the doubled words of Moses Maimonides.

They are allegorized, that is, they contain a figure of a greater thing, as Chrysostom explains here. -

For these are the two covenants) A similar kind of speaking Gen.

XLI.

26. & 1.

Cor.

4. Calvinian abuses 9.

24. The Calvinists prove their sign-meaning from this, which they inject into the words of the Lord's Supper.

But even if an example of the same signification were had here, what is this to the words of Christ's Testament, where there is no allegory?

But it is indicated what is offered to us by the exhibited Eucharistic bread, namely the body of Christ itself, and not indeed a figure of the same.

Nor indeed is it said that the two mothers are the two testaments; but the things allegorized are the two testaments, as Junius admits in lib. II.

Parall.

Tremellius renders: these are the allegories of the two passions. Therefore 'another' is put for 'these things', as B. Glassius noted in Gramm.

S. p.

196. These allegorized things (as Arias Montanus rendered) or these things, which are understood in the spiritual sense required in history, are the two testaments.

And thus B.

Meisnerus warned that the following words also must be explained in part I.

Phil. sobr. p.

122. by sub-understanding the word 'allegorized'.

The testament of servitude is the thing allegorized, or the antitype of the handmaid Hagar, which is the proper predication of an Accident of a subject: because this happens to the Testament, which is made burdened by the handmaid Hagar. - One indeed) Namely, the covenant. - From Mount Sinai) Namely, given.

He writes 'Sina', as Strabo, Justin, & Sulpitius do.

In Hebrew הר סיני: Mount Sinaion to Appion, the 'Jod' is easily lost in pronunciation. - Bearing children into servitude) Generating offspring into a servile condition.

Verf.

25. Which is Hagar) Here, contrary to the thing signified, he gives the name of the thing signifying.

For the sense is that by Hagar is signified the covenant made at Sinai. -

24. Ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα) Sumit, quod confessum erat inter Judaeos, in historiis illis, praeter sensum historicum, alium eminentiorem occultari, qui מדרש כפולים verba duplicata Mosis Maimonidae.

Sunt ἀλληγορούμενα, id est, figuram rei majoris continent, ut hic explicat Chrysostomus. -

Gen. XLI.

26. & 1.

Cor.

24. Calviniani suum σημαινὸν hinc probant, quod in verbis S. coena ingerunt.

Sed etiamsi hic significationis ejusdem haberetur exemplum, quid hoc ad verba Testamenti Christi, ubi nulla allegoria est?

Sed indicatur, quid exhibito pane Eucharistico nobis praebeatur, ipsummet nempe corpus Christi, non vero figura ejusdem.

Nec verò dicitur, duas matres esse duo testamenta; sed τὰ ἀλληγορούμενα sunt duo testamenta, ut fatetur Junius lib. II.

Parall.

Μία μὲν) Nempe διαθήκη. - Ἀπὸ ὄρους Σινᾶ) Nempe data. Σινᾶ scribit, quomodo Strabo, Justinus, & Sulpitius.

25. Ἥτις ἐστὶν Ἄγαρ) Hic contra rei significatae dat nomen rei significantis.

## 4:25
For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia) In the Manuscript: But Hagar, he adds the reason why Hagar signified that covenant, because Mount Sinai also, where that covenant was made, is called Hagar, by synecdoche namely, because there is the town Agra according to Pliny, Agara according to Dio in the affairs of Trajan: the people themselves are the Agareni, according to Strabo and Stephanus: for which later Greeks say Agareni & the Chaldeans אגרי.

Whence is Mount Hagar?

Why that mountain is called Hagar seems to be able to be gathered from Moses.

For Hagar fled into Arabia twice: once when rebuked by her mistress, while she carried a womb, Gen.

XVI. then when she was sent away by Abraham together with Ishmael, whence also the Arabs were called Hagareni, as Crocius says here. - And it is allied to the Jerusalem that now is) It is with equal right with the Jerusalem of the Jews.

For things are called allied to one another, and things similarly lacking in something toward something. For things are called allied, which are so orderly arranged, that they have a mutual respect among themselves:

The Hebrews would say 'it is against'. - And it serves with her children) In the Manuscript: for it serves by right, because Hagar is equally subject, that is, the Agarene people, and individuals pertaining to it, to circumcision, and to sacrifices, and to the distinction of days, although not by the law of Moses, but from their own laws, or the customs of the Ishmaelites, who are also Agareni and Saracens.

Concerning circumcision we have spoken in the annotations to the first book on the truth of the Christian religion, in the condition of free and servile, not only among the Romans and Greeks, but also among the Hebrews and Arabs, the offspring followed the right of the mother. - To others, 'allied' is to have an analogy, which B.

Glassius teaches, primarily from Chrysostom and Theophylact, and Calvin: it is certain, says Calvin, that the Apostle here did not think of proximity, nor of the location of places, but of the similarity, in the figure, which he treats. And 'allied' is composed to a just proportion in trees, as well as in other things.

Therefore in the same sense he said, Mount Sinai is allied to that which is now Jerusalem, just as Aristotle writes 'counter-turning' for Rhetoric and Dialectic, a metaphor taken from the Lyric poets, whose custom it was to set two parts in opposition, of which one would respond to the other in harmony.

In sum, 'allied' is nothing other than to be coordinated.

Aretius: As a 'row', he says, is a series of soldiers, from the front of the battle line to the very end, by which those following always insist upon the backs of those preceding: Thus in the allegorical argument there are words, pertaining to the same series and signification.

You have here two series, one of the old law, the other of grace in Christ.

Crocius: The word 'allied' seems entirely to be referred to the word 'one'.

Thus Paul shows, where that legal pact is now made, where it may flourish, namely in the Jerusalem that now is, that is, in the Jewish synagogue, there still reigning.

He adds, 'which now is', lest he seem to bring injury to the old city, in which pious Kings and fathers dwelt.

Nor does B.

Glassius deny this, rendering the sense: These things allegorized are the two testaments, one indeed from Mount Sinai (deriving its origin and) generating into servitude, which is Hagar, (whose type and figure is Hagar) v. 25. For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, (not only in reality, but also in name they respond to each other, since Mount Sinai is called Hagar by the Arabs) and it is allied to that which is now Jerusalem, (not only is Hagar a type and figure of Mount Sinai, and of the law promulgated in it, and thus of the Old Testament: but also to this earthly Jerusalem, as it consists especially of Jews, repudiating Christ and attempting to establish their own justice from the law) but it serves (Allegorical Hagar, or the legal and Jerusalemite people) with its children etc.

And in Philol.

S. lib.

II. p.

374. things are called allied among others, which are cognate, kin, and consociable: As if you should say, a man is allied with other living creatures insofar as he is mortal, and also that a man using an irrational soul is allied to the rest of the animals, according to Budeus p. 632. The sense therefore of the words of the Apostle is, that Hagar has a correspondence with Jerusalem regarding the mystical sense, that is, that it denotes the Jewish people, whose metropolis is Jerusalem.

For just as Hagar obtained the place of a handmaid in the house of Abraham, and was finally cast out from it: So the Jews in the time of the Apostle were under the servitude of the law, and because they wished to be justified by the works of the law, they were cast out from the house of GOD.

Others say Mount Sinai is joined to Jerusalem by reason of location, or also by the continuation of the journey; but these seem alien.

The former is refuted by the inspection of the Geographical table.

The other, which pleases Thomas Aquinas, is absurd.

For thus Mount Sinai is no more joined to Jerusalem than Egypt, or any other land, as Crocius says here.

Theophylact forcefully: By Hagar the Old Testament is understood.

For the law was delivered from Mount Sinai, which mountain is both in Arabia, and is called Hagar in the language of the Arabs.

But it is joined to Jerusalem, that is, it is neighboring and contiguous.

Or because it is compared to the lower Jerusalem, and is similar, and by a certain proportion equal to it, and is taken for it, and thus one face of both is made.

Just as therefore Hagar was both a handmaid, and generated them into servitude, so also the law itself, which proceeds from Mount Sinai, otherwise called Hagar, and now very similar to Jerusalem itself, generates into servitude those who obey it.

The Grotian opinion, that 'allied' is to be by equal right, is proved neither by the manner of speaking, nor by the thing or matter. fits the present subject matter, for it was not relevant here to say that the Agarene race is subject to circumcision, sacrifices, and the distinction of days by Paul’s right, as is Jerusalem and the Jewish people: But he shows only an analogy, by force of allegorical explanation, between Hagar and Jerusalem, which now is, by reason of servitude.

Therefore it is added: She serves indeed with her children, which most refer to Hagar, but Crocius prefers it to be referred to Jerusalem, which was then fervent with her children, who were devoted to Judaism. Truly, the Greek text does not easily permit this, in which it appears that both are said of Hagar: συστοιχεῖ δὲ τῇ νῦν ἱερουσαλήμ, δουλεύει δὲ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς. It is taught, however, that συστοιχίας here implies the reason that Hagar was a slave, and bore children into servitude, since Jerusalem, which now is, is likewise a slave, and bears children only into servitude.

The words therefore are only to be read in parentheses (τὸ γὰρ Ἁγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ) by which it is illustrated why the testament, which is from Mount Sinai, is compared with Hagar, because, namely, by the name of Hagar also comes Mount Sinai in Arabia. For the same mountain, which the Jews call Sinai: (Which seems to have its appellation from brambles and thorns) the Arabs in their own language call Agar. This is what, besides Paul, Ptolemy and the scholia of the Greeks also testify.

In the same manner, other and different names are attributed to other mountains among different peoples. Thus the mountain which Moses calls Hermon, is called Syrion by the Sidonians, and Senir by the Amorites, as B. has it here.

Luther. The Grotian parity of right is also refuted by Grotius himself: Since Jerusalem indeed once had circumcision, sacrifices, and festivals from the law of God; the Agarenes had them from their own laws, as he himself says.

Jerusalem however, which now is, since those figures and Levitical laws have ceased, has none of these, and therefore cannot be compared with the Agarenes on that account.

Latin:

Τὸ γὰρ Ἀγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν Ἀραβίᾳ) In Manuscripto: Τὸ δὲ Ἀγὰρ, causam addit, cur Agar illud foedus significaverit, quia & mons Sina, ubi illud factum est foedus, vocatur Agar, κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν nempe, quia ibi est oppidum Agra Plinio, Agara Dioni in rebus Trajani: gens ipsa Ἀγαῖοι, Straboni & Stephano: pro quo Graeci posteriores dicunt Ἀγαρηνοὶ & Chaldzi אגרי.

Mons Hagar unde?

Cur mons ille Hagar dictus, ex Mose videtur colligi posse.

Hagar enim bis in Arabiam fugit: semel ab hera objurgata, cum uterum ferret, Gen.

XVI. deinde cum ab Abrahamo una cum Ismaele dimitteretur, unde & Arabes dicti Hagareni, ut hic Crocius. - Συστοιχὲι δὲ τῇ νῦν Ἰερουσαλὴμ) Pari jure est cum Hierosolymis Judae.

Nam σύστοιχα λέγεται ἀλλήλοις, καὶ τὰ ὁμοίως ἄχοιλα πρός τινα.

Hebraei dicerent היא כנגד. - Δουλεύει δὲ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς) In Manuscripto: δουλεύει γὰρ jure est, quia pariter subjecta est Agar, id est, gens Agarena, & singuli ad eam pertinentes, circumcisioni, & sacrificiis, & dierum discrimini, quamquam non lege Mosis, sed ex suis legibus, aut moribus Ismaelitarum, qui & Agareni & Saraceni.

De circumcisione diximus in annotatis ad librum primum de veritate religionis Christianae, in conditione libera & servili, non apud Romanos tantum & Graecos, sed & apud Hebraeos & Arabes, partus jus maternum sequebatur. - Aliis σύστοιχα est analogiam habere, quod è Chrysostomo & Theophylacto imprimis, & Calvinò, docet B.

Glassius: certum est, inquit, Calvinus, non de propinquitate, nec situ locorum hic Apostolum sensisse, sed de similitudine, in figura, quam tractat. Σύστοιχα enim dicuntur, quae ita sunt ordinate collata, ut mutuum inter se respectum habeant: Et σύστοιχα tam in arboribus, quàm aliis est composita ad justam proportionem series.

Eodem ergo sensu dixit, montem Sina σύστοιχα ei, quae nunc est, Jerusalem, qua Aristoteles Rhetoricam et Dialecticam ἀντίστροφον scribit, Metaphora à Lyricis sumpta, quibus moris erat, ex adverso statuere partes duas, quarum una alteri in concentu responderet.

In summa, σύστοιχα nihil aliud est, quam coordinari.

Aretius: Ut σῶιχον, inquit, est series militum, à fronte aciei ad ultimum usque finem, qua sequentes semper antecedentium tergoribus insistunt: Sic in allegorico argumento sunt voces, ad eandem seriem & significationem pertinentes.

Habes hic duas series, unam veteris legis, alteram gratiae in Christo.

Crocius: Omnino videtur verbum σύστοιχα ad vocem μία referendum.

Sic Paulus ostendit, ubi jam fit illa pactio legalis, ubi vigeat, nempe in Jerusalem, quae nunc est, id est, in Judaica synagoga, ibi adhuc regnante.

Addit, quae nunc est, ne videatur injuriam inferre veteri urbi, in qua pii Reges & patres habitabant.

Nec abnuit B.

Glassius, hunc sensum reddens: Haec τὰ ἀλληγορούμενα sunt duo testamenta, unum quidem à monte Sina (originem ducens &) in servitutem generans, quae est Agar, (cujus typus ac figura est Agar) v. 25. Agar enim Sina mons est in Arabia, (non reipsa solum, sed nomine etiam sibi respondent, cum Arabibus mons Sina dicatur Agar) σύστοιχα δὲ respondet vero (etiam) ei, quae nunc est Jerusalem, (non solum Agar typus est & figura montis Sina, & promulgata in illo lege, atque sic Testamenti veteris: sed & terrena huic Jerusalem, prout scilicet ex Judaeis potissimum constat, Christum repudiantibus & ex lege suam propriam justitiam stabilire conantibus) servit autem (Agar Allegorica, seu populus legalis & Jerosolymitanus) cum filiis suis &c.

Et in Philol.

S. lib.

II. p.

374. σύστοιχα dicuntur inter alia, quae sunt cognata, συγγενῆ, & consociabilia: Ut si dicas, hominem cum ceteris animantibus σύστοιχα ἐφ' ὅσον θνητός ἐστιν, atque etiam τὸν ἄνθρωπον τῇ ἀλόγῳ ψυχῇ χρώμενον, τοῖς λοιποῖς τῶν ζώων σύστοιχον εἶναι, juxta Budeum p. 632. sensus igitur verborum Apostoli est, quod Agar quoad mysticum sensum convenientiam habeat cum Jerusalem, hoc est, quod notet populum Judaicum, cujus metropolis est Jerusalem.

Quemadmodum enim Agar ancille locum in domo Abrahae obtinuit, & ex ea tandem ejecta est: Sic Judaei tempore Apostoli erant sub servitute legis, & quia per opera legis justificari voluerunt, ex domo DEI sunt ejecti.

Alii montem Sina conjunctum Hierosolymam dicunt ratione situs, vel etiam itineris continuatione; sed haec aliena videntur.

Prius confutatur tabula Geographica inspectio.

Alterum, quod Thoma Aqu. placet, absurdum.

Sic enim non magis mons Sina conjunctus Hierosolymae, quam Aegyptus, aut quavis alia terra, ut hic Crocius.

Nervose Theophylactus: Per Hagar Vetus Testamentum intelligitur.

Lex namque, è monte Sina tradita est, qui mons & in Arabia est, & Agar Arabum lingua nuncupatur.

Conjunctus autem est Hierusalem, hoc est, vicinus est & contiguus.

Vel quia inferiori Hierusalem compamtur, & similis est, & proportione quadam illi par, & pro ea accipitur, proinde una utriusque fit facies.

Quemadmodum igitur Agar & serva erat, & ad servitutem illos generabat, sic & lex ipsa, quae ex monte Sina, alias Agar vocitato, & nunc Jerusalem ipsi persimili, prodit, in servitutem gignit, qui sibi obtemperant.

Sententia Grotiana, quod σύστοιχα fit pari jure esse, nec è modo loquendi probatur, nec rei vel materiae materia praesenti convenit, non enim attinebat hic dicere gentem Agarenam, Pauli jure subjebdam esse circumcisioni, sacrificiis, & discrimini dierum, uti Hierosolyma & populus Judaicus: Sed analogiam tantum, vi allegoricae explicationis monstrat inter Agarem & Hierosolymam, quae nunc est, ratione servitutis.

Ideo additur: Servit vero cum filiis suis, quod plerique ad Agar referunt, sed ad Jerusalem referri mavult Crocius, quae tunc fervebat cum filiis suis, Judaismo deditis. Verum id non facile permittit textus Graecus, in quo de Agare utrumque dici apparet: συστοιχεῖ δὲ τῇ νῦν ἱερουσαλήμ, δουλεύει δὲ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς. Docetur autem ita, συστοιχίας hic eam innuire rationem, quod Agar ferva fuerit, & in servitutem generarit, quum Jerusalem, quae nunc est, serva sit pariter, nec nisi in servitutem generet.

Verba itaque illa tantum legenda in parenthesi (τὸ γὰρ Ἁγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ) quibus illustratur, cur testamentum, quod est e monte Sinai, cum Agar comparetur, quia scilicet Agaris nomine etiam venit mons Sina in Arabia. Nam eundem montem, quem Judaei appellant Sina: (Quae appellatione habere videtur a rubetis & dumis) Arabes sua lingua vocant Agar. Id quod praeter Paulum testantur etiam Ptolemaeus & Graecorum scholia.

Ad eundem modum & aliis montibus alia atque alia nomina tribuuntur, apud diversas gentes. Sic mons, quem Moses appellat Hermon, Sydonii Syrion, & Amorrhaeis Senir dicitur, ut hic habet B.

Lutherus. Paritas etiam juris Grotiana a Grotio ipso refellitur: Quum Jerusalem quidem olim ex lege Dei habuerit circumcisionem, sacrificia & ferias; Agareni ex legibus, ut ipse ait, propriis.

Jerusalem autem, quae nunc est, nulla lege cessantibus illis figuris & legibus Leviticis ea habeat, ideoque componi cum Agarenis ea ratione non possit.

## 4:26
26. But Jerusalem which is above

The above , as Phil. III. 14.

By the name of Jerusalem here is understood the other covenant, namely the Evangelical, and that because of the etymology.

For Jerusalem signifies the vision of peace, which name befits the Gospel, Luke II. verf. 14. Rom. V. 1. X. 15. I. Cor. VII. 15. Ephes. II.

17. The Hebrews expect a more beautiful Jerusalem. Zohar on Numbers, Jarchi on the Song of Songs: But that truly beautiful Jerusalem has already arrived, Rev. XXI.

2. It is said, however, to have come from above, because God the Father, not descending onto a mountain, but remaining in heaven, revealed it to his Son by mission.

This sense is taught to us by the writer to the Hebrews XII. verf. 25. Ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶ free from vices and rites, similar to Sarah. Ἥτις ἐστὶ μήτηρ πάντων ἡμῶν the name of mother befits the Greek word τῇ διαθήκῃ: That is the covenant, which bore us to God: us, as well those converted from the Jews as from the Gentiles.

The Apostle opposes to Jerusalem ἣν νῦν, the Jerusalem τὴν ἄνω; Therefore, as by the former is understood not the old testament, but the people of the Old Testament, or those serving the Sinaitic law, which by allegory to Paul is Hagar the handmaid, or slave, not free, just as Hagar herself corresponded to that people κατ’ ἀναλογίαν; so by the heavenly Jerusalem is not to be understood the new testament or the Gospel, but the faithful people, or the Christian Church, which is ἄνω by reason of its origin, which it has through regeneration from heaven or divine, Job III. v. 5. by reason of its breath, which acts not so much on earth as in the heavens, and there has its citizenship Phil. III. it is governed not so much by earthly as by heavenly laws, and is free from occupations, not seeking those things which are on earth, but which are above Col. III. 1. elevated from the earth and earthly things, although it must still do battle on earth: by reason of its end, because it tends toward the sublime and toward heaven Heb. XIII. 14. and perfection, and the heavenly goal Phil. III. 14. Add also by reason of its name, because Jerusalem signifies the vision of peace, which God procures for the Christian Church; and by reason of its figure: because the earthly Jerusalem was a type of the Christian Church, or the spiritual Jerusalem; and by reason of its propagation: because it went forth from Mount Zion and the doctrine of the Gospel Eph.

II. 3. Luke

XXIV. v. 47. and the beginning of the collection and propagation of the Church throughout the whole world was made there, and with the aggregation of the Gentiles to the Jewish Church having been made, the Catholic Church arose, disseminated through the whole world by the Christian faith. Indeed, just as Hagar figured the old Testament, which referred its origin to Mount Zion, so also Zion figured the new testament, because τὰ ἀλληγορούμενα were two testaments; but in these present words the discourse is about the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church adhering to Christ through faith, as Irenaeus, Chrysostom, and Theophylact explain: two testaments are named for the New testament, the Apostle now names its seat, namely the Christian Church, the Jerusalem above, which is opposed to the Jerusalem serving Mosaic laws: and therefore it is called ἐλευθέρα free, and thus is simultaneously compared with Sarah, who was free, not a slave, and bore a son, not a slave, but free; the Church is free, not with civil liberty: for the Gospel, as it does not abolish the state: so neither does it abolish civil servitude I.

Cor.

VII. verf. 11. but with spiritual, insofar as it is liberated from the curse and servitude of sin and the yoke of the Mosaic law. It is also the mother of us all.

Concerning which Crocius: Just as Hagar the handmaid is the mother of Ishmael the servant, and the legal covenant corresponding to him, and therefore the earthly Jerusalem is the mother of those who, loving servitude, seek to serve the legal ceremonies and seek righteousness from the works of the law, but Sarah the free woman finds the son Isaac. Thus he calls the Jerusalem descending from above the mother, because of the generation of free children. He does not call her a carnal mother.

For she does not generate from herself according to the flesh: But a spiritual one, which generates from the divine seed, which is the Gospel.

He could say , of all free men. He does not say; He prefers to say of us all, so that he may declare the common mother of all truly believing people converted from Gentilism and Judaism to Christ, who obtain the Spirit of liberty and glory in Christ.

He says therefore, with B. as interpreter.

Luther fol. 18.

That Jerusalem , which now is, that is, the earthly and temporal, is not Sarah, but pertains to Hagar, because in it the kingdom of Hagar is exercised. For it is the law generating into servitude, in it is the cult, the temple, the kingdom, the priesthood, and whatever was ordained at Sinai from the law itself as mother, this is carried out in Jerusalem, and therefore I link it with Sinai, and I embrace both with the same word, namely Sinai or Hagar.

To none of us does it seem very convenient that Sinai be called Hagar, and Jerusalem Sarah.

But Paul indeed makes Jerusalem Sarah, not however this corporal one, but he simply joins it to Hagar herself, but the spiritual and heavenly one, in which the law does not reign, nor a carnal people, as in Jerusalem, which serves with her children, but in which the promise reigns, and the people are spiritual and free.

That earthly Jerusalem , he says, which is below, having a legal polity, is Hagar, and serves with her children, that is, it is not liberated from the law, sin, and death.

But the Jerusalem, which is above, that is, the spiritual one, that is Sarah (Paul however does not add the word Sarah as a proper name, but calls her free appellatively) this is the true Mistress and free woman, and our mother,... generating not into servitude, as Hagar, but into liberty.

That heavenly Jerusalem , which is above, is the Church, that is, believers scattered throughout the whole world, who have the same Gospel, the same faith in Christ, the same Spirit. Spirit, and they have the same sacraments. Therefore, do not understand 'upward' (anagogically), as the Sophists do, concerning the Church triumphant (for so they speak) in the heavens, but concerning the militant [Church] on earth. And it is... no wonder, because the pious are said to dwell in the heavens Phil. III. Our citizenship is in the heavens. Not locally, but insofar as a Christian believes, insofar as he apprehends the ineffable, heavenly, and eternal gifts, to that extent he is in the heavens Eph. I. Who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places through Christ. Thus blessed Luther.

Against various senses of scripture There are also things worthy to be read here, which a Man of GOD opposed to the comment of various senses, which we have already exploded, so that we may teach the consensus of Megalander in this place also: Wherefore Jerusalem, which is above, that is, heavenly, is the Church in this time, not (anagogically) a future heavenly fatherland, or the Church triumphant, as idle and unlearned monks and scholastic doctors have trifled, who handed down that there are four senses of scripture: the literal, the tropological, the Allegorical, and the anagogical, and according to these they interpreted almost every word of scripture ineptly. As Jerusalem literally signified to them the city of that name; tropologically, a pure conscience; allegorically, the militant Church; anagogically, the heavenly fatherland or the Church triumphant. By these insipid and trifling fables, by which they tore the scriptures into so many meanings, they caused it to be that consciences could be certainly instructed in no matters. But Paul says here that that old and earthly Jerusalem pertains to Hagar, and serves with her children, and has been abolished. But the new and heavenly [Jerusalem], by which she becomes Mistress and free, has been established divinely, not in the heavens, but on earth, so that she may be the mother of us all, from whom we have been generated, and are daily generated. Therefore it is necessary that this mother of ours, as well as her generation, be on earth among men. Yet she generates in the Spirit by the ministry of the Word and sacraments, etc., not in the flesh.

Latin:

26. Ἡ δὲ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ

Ἡ ἄνω, ut Phil. III. 14.

Nomine autem Jerusalem hic intelligitur alterum foedus, nempe Evangelicum, idque ob ἐτυμολογίαν.

Nam Jerusalem significat visionem pacis, quod nomen Evangelio competit, Luc. II. verf. 14. Rom. V. 1. X. 15. I. Cor. VII. 15. Ephef. II.

17. Hebraei pulchriorem Jerusalem expectant. Zohar ad numeros, Jarchi ad Canticum: Sed vere illa pulchra Jerusalem jam advenit Apoc. XXI.

2. Dicitur autem superne venisse, quia Deus Pater eam non in montem descendens, sed in caelo manens missio filio suo revelavit.

Hunc sensum docet nos scriptor ad Hebraeos XII. verf. 25. Ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶ libera a vitiis & ritibus, Sarae similis. Ἥτις ἐστὶ μήτηρ πάντων ἡμῶν matris nomen convenit Graece voci τῇ διαθήκῃ: Illa est pactio, quae nos Deo peperit: nos, tam conversos ex Judais, quam ex gentibus.

Hierosolymae ἣν νῦν opponit Apostolus Hierosolymam τὴν ἄνω; Ut ergo per illam intelligitur non testamentum vetus, sed populum Veteris Testamenti, vel legi Sinaiticae servientem, quae per allegoriam Paulo est Agar ancilla, vel serva, non libera, quemadmodum etiam populo illi respondebat κατ’ ἀναλογίαν ipsa Hagar; sic per supernam Hierosolymam non novum testamentum aut Evangelium intelligendum, sed populus fidelis, vel Ecclesia Christiana, quae ἄνω est ratione ortus, quem habet per regenerationem de caelo vel divinam Job. III. v. 5. ratione flatus, quae non tam in terris, quam in coelis agit, ibique suum πολίτευμα habet Phil. III. non tam terrenis, quam caelestibus regitur legibus, & vacat occupationibus, non quaerens ea, quae in terris, sed quae sursum sunt Col. III. 1. a terris & terrenis elevata, quamvis adhuc in terris ei militandum sit: ratione finis, quia tendit ad sublimia & ad coelum Ebr. XIII. 14. & perfectionem, ac metam caelestem Phil. III. 14. Adde & ratione nominis, quia Jerusalem significat visionem pacis, quam Deus Ecclesiae Christianae procurat; & ratione figurae: quia terrena Jerusalem typus erat Ecclesiae Christianae, vel Jerusalem spiritualis; & ratione propagationis: quia e monte Zion & Evangelii doctrina prodiit Ef.

II. 3. Luc.

XXIV. v. 47. & initium illic factum est collectionis & propagationis Ecclesiae per totum orbem, factaque aggregatione gentium ad Ecclesiam Judaicam, orta est Catholica Ecclesia, disseminata per mundum universum fide Christiana. Sane ut Hagar figurabat vetus Testamentum, quod ortum ad montem Sion referebat, ita & Sion figuravit novum testamentum, quia τὰ ἀλληγορούμενα erant duo testamenta; sed his praesentibus verbis de Jerusalem spirituali, id est, Ecclesia per fidem Christo adhaerente fermo est, ut Irenaeus, Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus exponunt: duo testamenta nominantur pro testamento Novo jam sedem ejus nominat Apostolus, nempe Ecclesiam Christianam, Hierusalem supernam, quae opponitur Hierosolymae ferventi legibus Mosaicis: ideoque ἐλευθέρα libera dicitur, & ita simul cum Sara componitur, quae libera non serva erat, & filium pariebat, non servum, sed liberum; Libera est Ecclesia, non civili libertate: Evangelium enim, ut non tollit politiam: Ita nec servitutem civilem I.

Cor.

VII. verf. 11. sed spirituali, quatenus a maledictione & servitute peccati ac jugo legis Mosaicae liberata. Est & mater omnium nostrum.

Quo de Crocius: Sicut Hagar ancilla Ismaelis servi mater, & ei respondens pactio legalis eoque Hierosolyma terrena mater eorum, qui servitutem amantes fervire ceremoniarum legalium ex legis operibus justitiam quaerunt, at Sara libera reperit filium Isaacum. Sic Hierusalem superne descendentem vocat matrem, propter generationem liberorum filiorum. Non vocat carnalem matrem.

Non enim ex se generat secundum carnem: Sed spiritualem, quae generat ex divino semine, quod est Evangelium.

Dicebat poterat, omnium liberorum. Non dicit; Mavult dicere omnium nostrum, ut communem declaret matrem omnium vere credentium a Gentilismo & Judaismo ad Christum conversorum, qui Spiritum libertatis & glorie obtinent in Christo.

Dicit igitur, interprete B.

Luthera fol. 18.

Ista Jerusalem, quae nunc est, id est, terrena & temporalis, non est Sara, sed pertinet ad Hagar, quia in ea exercetur regnum Hagar. Est enim ea lex generans in servitutem, est in ea cultus, templum, regnum, sacerdotium, & quicquid in Sina ordinatum est ex ipsa lege matre, hoc in Jerusalem geritur, ideoque eam annello cum Sina, & utrasque complector eodem vocabulo scilicet Sina seu Hagar.

Nulli nostrum videtur valde commodum fuisse Sina Hagar, & Jerusalem Saram dici.

At Paulus facit quidem Jerusalem Saram, non autem istam corporalem, sed simpliciter adjungit ipsi Hagar, sed spiritualem & caelestem, in qua non lex regnat, nec populus carnalis, ut in Jerusalem, qua servit cum filiis suis, sed in qua promissio regnat, & populus spiritualis & liber est.

Terrena illa Jerusalem, inquit, qua deorsum est, habens politiam legalem est Hagar, & servit cum filiis suis, id est non liberatur a lege, peccato & morte.

At Jerusalem, qua sursum est, id est, spiritualis, illa est Sara (Paulus tamen non addit vocabulum Sara nomine proprio, sed appellative vocat eam liberam) hoc est vera Domina & libera, ac mater nostra,... generans non in servitutem, ut Hagar, sed in libertatem.

Est autem illa Jerusalem caelestis, qua sursum est, Ecclesia, id est credentes sparsi per totum orbem, qui idem Evangelium, eandem fidem in Christum, eundem Spiritum. sanctum, & eadem sacramenta habent. Ideo sursum non intellige ἀναγωγικῶς, ut Sophistae, de Ecclesia triumphante (sic enim loquuntur) in caelis, sed de militante in terris. Nec mirum, quia pii dicuntur versari in caelis Phil. III. Nostrum νο...- λίτευμα in caelis est. Non localiter, sed quatenus Christianus credit, quatenus apprehendit inenarrabilia, caelestia & eterna dona, eatenus est in caelis Eph. I. Qui benedixit nos omni benedictione spirituali in caelestibus per Christum. Haec Beat. Lutherus.

Contra varios sensus scripturae Digna etiam sunt, quae hic legantur, quae opposuit Vir DEI commento variorum sensuum alias a nobis exploso, ut consensum Megalandri hoc etiam loco doceamus: Quare Jerusalem, quae sursum est, id est, caelestis, est Ecclesia in hoc tempore, non ἀναγωγικῶς futura vita patria, vel Ecclesia triumphans, ut otiosi & ineruditi monachi, & scholastici doctores nugati sunt, qui tradiderunt quatuor esse sensus scripturae, literalem, tropologicum, Allegoricum & anagogicum, & secundum hos singula fere verba scripturae interpretati sunt inepte. Ut Jerusalem literaliter significabat illis urbem ejus nominis; tropologice, conscientiam puram; allegorice, Ecclesiam militantem; anagogice, caelestem patriam seu Ecclesiam triumphantem. His insulsis & nugacibus fabulis, quibus discerpserunt scripturas in tot sententias, fecerunt, ut de nullis rebus conscientia certo erudiri potuerint. Sed Paulus hic ait, veterem & terrestrem illam Jerusalem pertinere ad Hagar, & servire cum filiis suis & abolitam esse. Novam autem & caelestem, qua Domina fit & libera, constitutam esse divinitus, non in caelis, sed in terris, ut sit omnium nostrum mater, ex qua nos sumus generati, & quotidie generamur. Ergo necesse est, hanc matrem nostram, ut & ejus generationem esse in terris inter homines. Generat tamen in Spiritu ministerio Verbi & sacramentorum &c. non in carne.

## 4:27
Ver. 27. Rejoice, O barren one, who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor; for many are the children of the desolate one, rather than of her who has a husband.

These are the very words of the LXX Elders, Is. LIV. vers. 1. where it is first to be noted that the present participles are used for the past, which the sense also demands, and is manifest in the Hebrew. But what is said there concerning the city of Jerusalem, long desolate and destitute of a kingdom, that her offspring would be greater than the land of those always inhabited and ruled, Paul most elegantly adapts (mystically) to the Gospel, [namely] that while Christ was preaching, she bore few, but after he was removed from mortal life, very many, so that the Jews were few compared to the Christians. "Eρημος here, which in Hebrew is שׁממה, appears from the opposite member to be understood as a widow, in the way it is taken, and Lam. I. vers. 13. Otherwise, the word, both Hebrew and Greek, can signify one bereft of children, deserted by friends, and [having] a large family. "Ρήγνυθαι can indeed signify the birth itself: But the Hebrew text demands more that the eruption of the voice be understood, as in 'break forth and shout' in Job VI. 5. and the word itself, which is here in Hebrew פצח, is translated by βοᾶν, Is. XIV. vers. 7. XLIV. vers. 23. Philo on Cain: Τὴν δι' αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων ῥήξεως φωνήν.

For Sarah also had been as a widow, when Hagar possessed Abraham.

The Apostle proves that the primitive Church of the New Testament, which he had called the mother of us all, bears children according to the promise: Just as Sarah was once made a barren offspring by promise in a Prophetic place, fittingly applying here Is. LIV. verf. 1. which does not treat of the Gospel, but of the Church. Although the Gospel becomes the medium through which the Church generates children to God, yet she herself is not the mother or begetter.

And the literal sense of the prophecy (which is intended solely by the Holy Spirit) is greatly perverted by Grotius, when it is explained that Jerusalem, long desolate and destitute of a kingdom, would have a greater offspring than the lands always inhabited and ruled, and this is snatched away to the Gospel, which, while Christ was preaching, bore few, but after he was removed from mortal life, was to bear very many. For there is nothing in that [passage] about Jerusalem being long desolate, nothing about her having a very great offspring afterward. Nor is there any mystical sense here different from the literal.

Concerning which we have spoken of the Isaianic place, where we have examined this prophecy at length with the Apostolic explanation and the Grotian misinterpretation.

We now add the explanation of Crocius, which can be compared with ours: He calls her barren, who does not bear, nor is in labor.

Just as Sarah was once barren, she did not bear, nor was she in labor.

The Jews interpret the prophecy concerning the earthly restoration of Jerusalem, once destroyed.

The Chiliasts [interpret it] concerning the Church to reign on earth a thousand years before the second coming of Christ.

Chrysostom and Jerome take it concerning the Church of the Gentiles, which once sat in darkness without the Word and the knowledge of GOD.

It pertains to the Church of the Gentiles, but not insofar as she lacked the Word of God and knowledge in the Old Testament, but [insofar as] she bore the Gentiles to Christ after his ascension into heaven.

Namely, the Church, betrothed to Christ in the fullness of time, after the death of Christ until Pentecost, in which the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the Apostles, sat sad, as if barren, and did not bear, nor was she in labor, but hope shone forth humanly, of a numerous offspring, while in the meantime the synagogue exulted, which, as if married to a husband, the law, boasted proudly of a numerous offspring.

For almost all those Jews adhered to it, with few exceptions, who believed in Jesus Christ.

She is called desolate, who sat as if she did not have a husband, she did not bear.

She, bearing more children, than she who boasted of her own husband and fruitful marriage.

Thus it happened.

At Pentecost she bore three thousand free ones.

In a short space of time the number grew to five thousand .

This is little.

They bore not in Judea alone: She extended her curtains, she lengthened her cords, to the right and to the left they prepared to break forth into the whole habitable earth a countless multitude of children.

Whence Jerome does not judge it necessary to speak of the Christian multitude and the paucity of the Jews, when the banners of the cross shine throughout the whole world, and scarcely a rare and notable [Jew] appears in the cities of Judea.

The synagogue had only one nation.

The Churches fill the whole of Greece, Barbary, the land, the sea, and finally the whole world, says Chrysostom.

B. Luther soars to greater heights, and here seeks the distinction between law and Gospel, that he may sail toward the aim of the Apostle, whose exposition it pleases [him] to set forth for pious learned men to weigh: By this allegory (he says fol. 119.) the Prophet Isaiah shows Paul the distinction between Hagar and Sarah, that is, of the synagogue and the Church, or of the law and the Gospel.

The law is a fruitful husband, that is, the synagogue generates very many children.

For men of all ages, not only the unlearned, but whoever are most wise and best (that is, the whole human race except the children of the free woman) do not see or acknowledge any other righteousness, much less a more excellent one than that of the law (I include, however, under the name of law, all laws, human and divine.) And so if they follow the law, and do its external works, they think themselves to be righteous.

Although these may be fruitful, abound in disciples, and flourish in righteousness and the beautiful works of the law; yet they are not free, but are slaves; because they are the children of Hagar, who generates into slavery.

But if they are slaves, they will not be partakers of the inheritance, but will be cast out from the house.

For slaves do not remain in the house forever; indeed, they have already been cast out from the kingdom of grace and liberty.

For he who does not believe, has already been judged.

They remain, therefore, under the curse of the law, sin, death, and under the power of the Devil, wrath and judgment of God. Against Sarah the free, that is, the true Church seems to be barren: Because the Gospel, which is the word of the cross, which the Church teaches, does not shine so brightly as the Doctrine of the law and works, and therefore has few disciples who adhere to it.

The Prophet concedes that the Church is in mourning, otherwise he would not exhort her to joy. He concedes that she is barren before the world, otherwise he would not call her barren and deserted, who does not bear. But before GOD he says she is fruitful, and therefore commands her to rejoice, as if to say: You who are deserted and barren, do not have the law as a husband, and therefore neither children. But rejoice, because even if you are without the law as a husband, like a nubile virgin deserted (for he does not wish to call her a widow) who indeed would have a spouse, if she were not deserted by him, or if the spouse had not been killed for her, you, I say, solitary and deserted by the law as a husband; and not subjected to the marriage of the law, you shall be the mother of infinite children. Wherefore the people or Church of the New Testament is entirely without law, (as far as conscience is concerned) and therefore appears before the world to be deserted. But although she may appear in appearance to be barren without law and works; yet before GOD she is most fruitful, and generates infinite children, and those free.

By what? Not by the merit of the law, but by the word and Spirit of Christ, which is given through the Gospel, she conceives, generates, and educates children.

By this allegory, therefore, Paul most clearly shows the distinction between the law and the Gospel. First, when he calls Hagar the old Testament, and Sarah the new. Then when he calls the one a handmaid, and the other free; likewise when he says that the married and fruitful one is infirm, and with her other children is cast out of the house, against the barren and deserted one who will be fruitful, and will bear infinite children, and those heirs.

These are the essential differences of the faith and the people of the law. The people of faith do not have the law as a husband, do not serve, are not born of the mother Jerusalem, which now is, but have the promise, are free, and are born of Sarah the free. He separates, therefore, the spiritual people of the new Testament from the people of the law, when he says that they are not the offspring of Hagar the married, but of Sarah the free, who knows not the law. And by this he establishes the people of faith far above and outside the law. But if they are above and outside the law, then they are not justified by the law and works, but by spiritual birth alone, which is nothing else but faith.

But as the people of grace do not have nor can have the law: So the people of the law do not have nor can have grace: Because it is impossible for the law and grace to be able to exist together. Either, therefore, it behooves us to be justified by faith, and to lose the righteousness of the law, or by the law, and to lose the grace and righteousness of faith. But shameful and unhappy is the loss, when having lost grace we retain the law. And on the contrary, happy and salutary is the loss, when having lost the law we retain grace.

He calls the Church barren, because her children are not generated by the law, nor by any human efforts or strengths, but in the Holy Spirit through the Word of faith; there is mere birth, no operation. On the contrary, the fruitful labor and exercise themselves too much in bringing forth, and there is mere operation, no birth.

But because they attempt to obtain the righteousness of the law or their own as the right of children and heirs, even if they are exhausted by excessive labor unto death, because they attempt to obtain the will of God by their own works, which God wishes to give to believers out of mere grace for the sake of Christ. Believers also do good works, but they do not become children and heirs through this. For birth brings this to them. But as children already made through Christ, they glorify God with their good deeds and help their neighbors.

Latin:

Ver. 27. Γήγησαι καὶ ἰφράνθητι στεῖρα, ἡ οὐ τίκτουσα, ῥῆξον βοῆσον ἡ οὐκ ὠδίνουσα, ὅτι πολλὰ τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐρήμου μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς ἐχούσης τὸν ἄνδρα.

Sunt ipsa verba LXX. Senum, Es. LIV. vers. 1. ubi primum notandum, participia praesentia poni pro praeteritis, quod & sensus exigit, & in Hebraeo manifestum est. Quod autem ibi dicitur de urbe Hierosolymorum, diu deserta, & regno destituta, majorem ejus fore sobolem, quam terram semper habitatarum ac regnatarum, id μυσικῶς per quam eleganter ad Evangelium aptat Paulus, quod, Christo praedicante, paucos peperit, eo vitae mortali exempto, plurimos, ita ut Judaei prae Christianis pauci essent. "Eρημος hic, quod in Hebraeo est, שׁממה apparet ex membro opposito intelligendum viduam, quomodo sumitur, & Lam. I. vers. 13. alioquin vox & Hebraea & Graeca, potest significare orbam liberis, desertam ab amicis, & multa familia. "Ρήγνυθαι potest quidem & ipsum partum significare: Sed Hebraeus textus magis exigit, ut eruptio vocis intellegatur, quomodo ῥῆξον βοῆσον Jobi VI. 5. & verbum ipsum, quod hic in Hebraeo est, פצח per βοᾶν vertitur, Es. XIV. vers. 7. XLIV. vers. 23. Philo de Caino: Τὴν δι' αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων ῥήξεως φωνήν.

Non abscedit a coepta similitudine. Nam & Sara, quasi vidua fuerat, cum Hagar Abrahamum possideret.
