Probat Apostolus Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti primitivam, quam matrem omnium nostrum dixerat, secundum promissionem liberos parere: Sicut Sara quondam sterili facta erat promissio soboles loco Prophetico aprime huc faciente Es. LIV. vers. 1. qui non de Evangelio, sed de Ecclesia agit. Evangelium etsi medium fit, per quod Deo liberos generat Ecclesia, non tamen mater vel genitrix ipsa est.

Et pervertitur valde a Grotio sensus literali vaticinii, (qui unice a Spiritu sancto intenditur) cum de Hierusalem diu deserta & regno destituta majorem sobolem habitura, quam terras semper habitatas & regnatas explicatur, idque ad Evangelium abripitur, quod Christo praedicante paucos peperit, eo vitae mortali exempto plurimos parturo. Nihil enim in illo de Hierusalem diu deserta, nihil de ea post sobolem plurimam habitura. Nec ullus hic mysticus a literali diversus sensus.

Quo de locum Esaianum diximus, ubi prolixe hoc vaticinium cum explicatione Apostolica, & ψευδερμηνείᾳ Grotiana expendimus.

Addimus jam Crocii explanationem, quae cum nostra conferri poterit: Vocat sterilem, quae non parit, nec parturit.

Sicut Sara erat aliquando sterilis, non pariebat, nec parturiebat.

Judai prophetiam de instauratione terrena Hierusalem olim destructa interpretantur.

Chiliastae de Ecclesia mille annos ante secundum Christi adventum in terris regnatura.

Chrysostomus & Hieronymus de Ecclesia gentium accipiunt, quae olim sine Verbo & DEI cognitione sedit in tenebris.

Ad Ecclesiam gentium pertinet, non autem quatenus in Veteri Testamento Dei verbo & cognitione caruit, sed que gentes Christo peperit post ejus adscensionem in caelum.

Nempe Ecclesia in temporis plenitudine Christo desponsata post Christi mortem usque ad Pentecosten, in qua Spiritus sanctus super Apostolos effundebatur, sedebat maesta, tanquam sterilis, nec pariebat, nec parturiebat, sed spes humanitis affulgebat, numerosa prolis, interim exultante synagoga, quae legi, velut viro nupta, numerosa prole se superbe jactabat.

Illi enim omnes fere Judaei adhaerebant, vix paucis exceptis, qui in Jesum Christum credebant.

Deserta dicitur, quae sedebat, quasi virum non haberet, non pariebat.

Illa plures parturiens filios, quam quae de suo se jactabat viro & conjugio facundo.

Sic factum.

In Pentecoste peperit ter mille liberas.

Brevi temporis spatio excrescebat numerus ad quinque millia.

Hoc parum.

Pariebant non in una Judaea: Extendebat aulae suas, prolongabat funes suos, dextrorsum & sinistrorsum parabant prorumpiens in tota terra habitabili innumeram filiorum multitudinem.

Unde Hieronymus non necessarium judicat, dicere de multitudine Christiana, & Judaeorum paucitate, cum orbe toto crucis vexilla resplendeant, & vix varus atque notabilis in urbibus Judae appareat.

Synagoga unam duntaxat habebat gentem.

Ecclesiae totam Graciam, Barbariam, terram, mare, denique orbem universum implent, inquit Chrysostomus.

B. Lutherus sublimius vehitur, & quaerit hic discrimen legis & Evangelii, ut scopo Apostoli velificetur, cujus ἐξήγησιν pie eruditis expendendam subjicere placet: Hac allegoria (inquit fol. 119.) Esaia Propheta ostendit Paulus discrimen Hagar & Sara, hoc est, synagoga & Ecclesia, seu legis & Evangelii.

Lex maritus facunda, hoc est synagoga valde multos filios generat.

Nam homines omnium aetatum non solum idiote, sed quique sapientissimi & optimi (hoc est, totum genus humanum prater filios libera) non vident aut agnoscunt aliam justitiam, multo minus excellentiorem quam legis (complector autem nomine legis, omnes leges, humanas & divinas.) Itaque si legem sectantur, & externa opera ejus faciunt, se justes esse putant.

Hi quamquam facundi sint, abundent discipulis & floreant justitia, & speciosis operibus legis; tamen non liberi, sed servi sunt; quia sunt filii Hagar, quae in servitutem generat.

Si autem servi sunt, non erunt participes hereditatis, sed ejicientur a domo.

Servi enim non manent in domo in aeternum; imo jam ejecti sunt e regno gratia & libertatis.

Qui enim non credit, jam judicatus est.

Manent ergo sub legis maledictione, peccato, morte, sub potestate Diaboli, ira et judicio Dei. Contra Sara libera, id est, vera Ecclesia videtur esse sterilis: Quia Evangelium, quod est verbum crucis, quod docet Ecclesia, non ita fulget, ut Doctrina de lege et operibus, ideoque paucos habet discipulos, qui ei adhaerent.

Concedit Propheta, Ecclesiam esse in luctu, alioquin non adhortaretur eam ad laetitiam. Concedit esse sterilem coram mundo, alioquin non appellaret sterilem et desertam, qua non parit. Sed coram DEO dicit eam esse facundam, ideoque jubet eam laetari, quasi dicat; Tu quae deserta et sterilis, non habes maritum legem, ideo neque filios. Sed gaude, quia etsi es sine marito lege, ut virgo nubilis deserta (non enim vult appellare viduam) quae quidem haberes sponsum, si non deserta esset ab eo, aut si sponsus ei non esset occisus, tu inquam solitaria et deserta a marito lege; et non subjeda conjugio legis, mater eris infinitorum filiorum. Quare populus seu Ecclesia Novi Testamenti est prorsus sine lege, (quod ad conscientiam attinet) ideoque apparet coram mundo deserta esse. Sed ut maxime in speciem fit sterilis fine lege et operibus; tamen coram DEO facundissima est, et generat infinitos filios, eosque liberos.

Per quid? Non per meritum legem, sed per verbum et Spiritum Christi, qui datur per Evangelium, concipit, generat, educat filios.

Hac ergo allegoria Paulus clarissime ostendit discrimen legis et Evangelii. Primum cum Hagar vetus Testamentum, Saram novam vocat. Deinde cum alteram ancillam, alteram liberam vocat; item cum maritatam et facundam ait infirmari, et cum aliis suis filiis ejici e domo, contra sterilem et desertam facundam fore, et parituram infinitos filios, et eos heredes.

He differentiae essentiales sunt fidei et legis populi. Populi fidei non habet legem maritum, non servit, non natus est ex matre Jerusalem, quae nunc est, sed promissionem habet, liber est, et nascitur ex Sara libera. Separat ergo populum spiritualem novi Testamenti a legis populo, cum dicit, eum non esse prolem Hagar maritate, sed Sara libera, quae nescit legem. Et per hoc constituit populum fidei longe supra et extra legem. Si autem supra et extra legem est, ergo non legi et operibus, sed sola spirituali nativitate, quam nihil aliud est, nisi fides, justificatur.

Ut autem populus gratiae non habet nec habere potest legem: Ita legis populus non habet nec habere potest gratiam: Quia impossibile est, legem et gratiam posse simul existere. Aut igitur fide nos justificari oportet, et justitiam legis amittere, aut lege, et gratiam et justitiam fidei amittere. Turpis autem et infelix est amissio, quando amissa gratia legem retinemus. Et contra felix et salutifera est amissio, quando lege amissa gratiam retinemus.

Appellat autem Ecclesiam sterilem, quia filii ipsius non lege, non ullis conatibus aut viribus humanis, sed in Spiritu sancto per Verbum fidei generantur, ibi mera nascentia est, nulla operatio. Contra facundi laborant et exercent se nimium parturiendo, ibique mera operatio est, nulla nativitas.

Sed quia justitia legis seu propria conantur consequi jus filiorum et haeredum, etiamsi ad mortem usque nimio labore defatigentur, quia voluntatem Dei suis operibus consequi conantur, quod Deus ex mera gratia propter Christum credentibus donare vult. Credentes etiam bene operantur, non autem per hoc filii et haeredes fiunt. Hoc enim affert eis nativitas. Sed ut jam filii facti per Christum, benefactis suis glorificent Deum et adjuvent proximos.

## 4:28
V. 28.

"We, brothers, are children of promise after the manner of Isaac" that is, after the example of Isaac, the son of promise. We have obtained a new nature, through God's grace, promised of old: So also Rom.

IX. 1. B. Hunnius: We who are justified by faith through Christ, are in the house of God, which is the Church, not servants, but free, liberated, I say, from the rigor and curse of the law, and thus we are children, and heirs according to the promise, and that in the likeness of Isaac, who, born of a free woman, was reckoned as a son and heir of his father's goods.

Latin:

V. 28.

"Hμείς δέ, ἀδελφοί, μετὰ Ἰσαὰκ ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα ἐσμέν" id est ad exemplum Isaaci, filii promissionis. Adepti sumus novam naturam, per Dei gratiam, olim promissam: Sic et Rom.

IX. 1. B. Hunnius: Nos qui per Christum justificamur fide, sumus in domo Dei, que est Ecclesia, non servi, sed liberi, liberati inquam a rigore et maledictione legis, adeoque filii sumus, et secundum promissionem haeredes, idque ad similitudinem Isaaci, qui ex libera prognatus, pro filio et haerede paternorum bonorum reputabatur.

## 4:29
V. 29.

"As then he who was born according to the flesh" Ismael: The sophist to Philo. He shows that the condition of the Church is not better in all things, inasmuch as it was most gravely vexed by the synagogue: But this is light and temporary in comparison to such great goods.

"persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit" Supplegenitum. He calls Spirit that divine power, through which Sarah had received fruitfulness at an alien time. See 2 Cor. X. 3. Ismael is said to be perfect in Isaac, because he irritates him, that is, his piety, as we have said from the Hebrews, at Gen. XXI. 3. By Isaac, Philo understands joy, which is in the minds of the pious. The same in his Allegories. [Greek text]. "For so" so also now those Jews, addicted to rites, whom you wish to imitate, pursue Christians with the greatest hatred.

Latin:

V. 29.

"Ὡς τότε ὁ κατὰ σάρκα γεννηθείς" Ismael: Ὁ σοφιστής Philoni. Ostendit non in omnibus meliorem conditionem esse Ecclesiae, quippe quae a synagoga gravissime vexaretur: Sed hoc esse leve et temporarium pro tantis bonis.

"ἐδίωκε τὸν κατὰ πνεῦμα" Supplegenitum. Πνεῦμα vocat vim illam divinam, per quam Sara foecunditatem alieno tempore acceperat. Vide 2. Cor. X. 3. Dicitur perfectus esse Ismael Isaacum, quia eum irritat, id est, pietatem ejus, ut ex Hebraeis diximus, ad Gen. XXI. 3. Per Isaacum intelligit Philo gaudium, quod est in animis piorum. Idem in ἀλληγορίαις. Φίσι σεμνυομένη, γέλωτα ἰσοῦσι με Κυρίῳ. "ὃς γὰρ ἀνάγκη, συγχρῆται μοι. Λιπαπασάμενος εἰ ἄτα εἰ μῦται παραδιδαξὶ τελετὰς ἱερατείας. Ὁ γέλως ἐστὶ ἡ χαρά. Τὸ δὲ ἐποίησεν ἱεω τῷ ἐγένετο, ὡς ὅταν τὸ λεγόμενοι τούτου. Ἰσαὰκ ἐγέννησεν Κύριῳ. Αὐτὸς γὰρ παῖς ἐστι τῆς τελείας Φύσεως." "Ουτω γὰρ" sic et nunc Judaei illi, ritibus addicti, quos vultis imitari vos, maximo odio prosequuntur Christianos.

## 4:30
V. 30.

"But what says the scripture? Cast out the handmaid, and her son. For the son of the handmaid shall not inherit with the son of the free woman" Manuscript here: her handmaid. In the LXX Gen. XXI. 10. "Cast out this handmaid, and her son. For the son of this handmaid shall not inherit with my son Isaac." But it is Sarah who speaks there, who was free-born and a matron. Among the Hebrews, by a most ancient custom, which seems to have obtained even before Abraham, those of concubines, who were free, and could be called wives, succeeded to the portion intestate before others: But children born of a handmaid did not at all, Maimonides in the title [Hebrew], that ejection signifies those who cling to rites, not about to arrive at true and heavenly righteousness.

Confer. John VIII. 35. V. 31. "Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the handmaid, but of the free woman" In the Manuscript: Therefore we, brothers, we Christians. And 'therefore' here is worth 'ergo' and 'as' signifies, we recognize that we are not children of the handmaid, that is, obligated to Jewish rites.

By an 'anthypophora' Chrysostom notes these things said: One might say, what is this liberty itself? Those who were receiving grace in Christ without the mixture of the law for salvation were being gravely afflicted by the Jews. Therefore he teaches: That even Ismael, who was born by the power of nature from a handmaid, had once persecuted Isaac according to the Spirit, that is, not born by the power of nature, but by the power of divine promise. Concerning which history, see what is said in our Commentary on the place in Genesis.

B. Luther here thus reveals his opinion concerning the mockery of Ismael: Ismael was studious of religion, he sacrificed, and exercised himself by doing good works. And therefore he laughed at his brother Isaac, and wished to appear better than him on a double account: On account of religion and worship: Then also on account of civil dominion and inheritance. And those two he seemed to himself to justly arrogate. For he thought that as the firstborn, the priesthood and the kingdom belonged to him by divine right. And so he persecuted Isaac spiritually on account of religion and corporally on account of inheritance. There is no need for the Apostle to provide a long apodosis, because it was in the eyes of all. For the Israelitic people adhering to the law, with whom the Pseudo-Apostles were siding, like Ismael were persecuting the Christian Church, the Israel of God, adhering to Christ by true faith.

But what says the scripture? Cast out the handmaid and her son: This ejection, Paul teaches, was a type of the exclusion of the Jews from the kingdom of God, on account of the despised benefit of gratuitous justification through Christ and liberation from the servile rigor, and curse of the law. Paul concludes, therefore, that we Christians are not children of the handmaid, but of the free woman, and consequently that we are not saved by services rendered to the law, but by the gift of the liberation of Christ, who [has freed] us from sin, death

redeemed [us] from death and hell; and mercifully asserted [us] into the liberty and inheritance of the children of GOD, as B. Hunnius most correctly [states] here.

Latin:

V. 30.

"Ἀλλὰ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή; ἔκβαλε τὴν παιδίσκην, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς. Οὐ γὰρ μὴ κληρονομήσῃ ὁ υἱὸς τῆς παιδίσκης, μετὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἐλευθέρας" Manuscriptus hic: παιδίσκης αὐτῆς. In LXX. Gen. XXI. 10. "Ἔκβαλε τὴν παιδίσκην ταύτην, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς. Οὐ γὰρ μὴ κληρονομήσῃ ὁ υἱὸς τῆς παιδίσκης ταύτης μετὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ μου Ἰσαάκ." Est autem Sara, quae ibi loquitur, quae erat ingenua et matrona. Apud Hebraeos ex vetustissimo more, qui et ante Abrahamum obtinuisse videtur, illi concubinarum, quae libera essent, et in uxorem dici potuissent, succedebant parti intestato ante caeteros: At filii ex ancilla nati minime, Maimonides in titulo ירושות, illa ejectio significat eos, qui in ritibus haerent, non perventuros ad justitiam veram et coelestem.

Confer. Joh. VIII. 35. V. 31. "Ἄρα, ἀδελφοί, οὐκ ἐσμὲν παιδίσκης τέκνα, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐλευθέρας" In Manuscripto: Ἄρα ἡμεῖς, ἀδελφοί, nos Christiani. Et ἄρα hic valet ergo et ὡς ἐσμὲν significat, merimerimus nos non esse ancilla liberos, id est, obligatos ritibus Judaicis.

Per ἀνθυποφοράν haec dicta Chrysostomus notat: Diceret quis, quaenam est ipsa libertas? Qui credentes in Christum ejus gratiam citra legis mixturam suscipiebant ad salutem, graviter a Judaeis affligebantur. Ideo docet: Quod et Ismael, qui vi naturae ex ancilla procreatus erat, persequeutus quondam fuerit Isaacum secundum Spiritum, hoc est, non natura vi, sed vi divinae promissionis natum. De qua historia vide, quae ad locum Gene-seos in Commentario nostro dicta.

B. Lutherus hic ita suam de Ismaelis illusione prodit sententiam: Ismael fuit studiosus religionis, sacrificavit, et bene operando se exercuit. Ideoque risit fratrem Isaac, et voluit videri melior eo duplici nomine: Propter religionem ac cultum: Deinde etiam propter civilem dominationem et haereditatem. Et illa duo videbatur sibi juste arrogare. Cogitavit enim ad se ut primogenitum jure divino pertinere sacerdotium et regnum. Itaque persecutus est Isaac spiritualiter propter religionem et corporaliter propter haereditatem. Non est, quod prolixe reddat apodosin Apostolus, quia ea erat in omnium oculis. Populus enim Israeliticus adhaerens legi, cum quo Pseudo-Apostoli faciebant, Ismaelis instar persequebant Christianam Ecclesiam Israelem Dei, Christo vera fide adhaerentem.

Sed quid dicit scriptura? Ejice ancillam et filium ejus: Hanc ejectionem, docet Paulus, fuisse typum exclusionis Judaeorum e regno Dei, ob spretum beneficium gratuitae justificationis per Christum et liberationis e servili rigore, et maledictione legis. Concludit ergo Paulus nos Christianos non esse filios ancillae, sed libere, et proinde non per servitia legi praestita nos salvari, sed per donum liberationis Christi, qui nos a peccato, morte

morte, & inferno redemit; & in libertatem haeredi- tatemque filiorum DEI clementer asseruit, ut rectissi- me hic B. Hunnius.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT & PARTITION.

He exhorts them to persist in Christian liberty, and not to receive circumcision, through which Christ is rendered useless, and they themselves are obligated to perform the whole law, so that they might not be emptied and fall from the grace of God, who wish to be justified by the law, whereas on the contrary the truly faithful expect the hope of righteousness through faith, and in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails, but faith, which is operative through love. He reproves the Galatians because, having abandoned their former course, they allowed themselves to be led away from the truth, with a curse against the disturbers regarding judgment and excision. They are also warned not to abuse liberty for the pleasure of the flesh, but to serve one another in mutual love, and to walk in the Spirit; and having reviewed the catalog of the works of the flesh that exclude one from the kingdom of GOD, and the fruits of the Spirit, they are stirred up to crucify the flesh and flee ambition.

There are two parts: I. Concerning the preservation of Christian liberty, up to verse 12. II. Concerning carnal license, which is an abuse of liberty, to be avoided, up to verse 26. That part concludes the second part of the whole epistle. By this, however, the third principal part is begun.

PART I. OF CHAPTER V. Concerning the preservation of Christian liberty, which constitutes section II. of the TREATISE OF THE DOGMATIC EPISTLE ON THE WEIGHT OF THE DOCTRINE OF JUSTIFICATION.

Vers. 1. Τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ᾖ, ᾗ χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσε, στήκετε, καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε) These cohere correctly in this way, though poorly separated in certain Codices, such that a part of these adheres to the preceding chapter: the native phrasing would have been: Ἐν τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ. For with that preposition, verbs of standing are accustomed to be placed, as 1 Cor. 16:13, Phil. 1:27, 4:1, 1 Thess. 3:8, but such particles are often understood: and ᾗ here is πρὸς ἣν, לאשר. He calls ζυγὸς δουλείας not only what the Hebrews call עול תורה, the yoke of the law, but also the opinions and rites by which the Gentiles had bound themselves. Ἐνέχεσθαι here means to be bound, to be constrained, a verb frequent among good writers. In the Glossary, ἐνεχόμενος means obligated. For Christ imposed a yoke upon us, but a sweet one. See Matthew 11, verse 29.

Since he has hitherto excluded from the circle of justification both moral and ceremonial works, and has taught that man is justified and saved by faith alone in Christ: now, lest this dispute against the Pseudo-Apostles, and the information of the Galatians seduced by them, should appear to be of slight moment, the Apostle teaches how much weight the doctrine of justification by faith alone has, so that they may the more flee error in this chief article of faith, and be recalled to the purity of Apostolic faith, and persist in it alone. And since on that occasion he dealt with the liberation from the yoke of the Mosaic law and the liberty obtained through Christ, he hands down how great the value of that liberty is, and how it ought to be used: lest it degenerate into license of the flesh, so that at the same time the mouth of calumny may be obstructed, as if through the doctrine of justification by faith alone the door to the license of the flesh were opened, and the pursuit of piety undermined. Wherefore he warns that Christian liberty is to be preserved in such a way that we do not abuse it for the license of the flesh. Therefore, regarding the weight and moment of the controversy concerning justification, because through the Apostolic doctrine the liberty acquired through Christ is preserved intact: because through the heterodoxy of the Pseudo-Apostles, who required the observation of the law alongside faith in Christ for salvation, a yoke of servitude ἀβάςακτον [unbearable] was imposed upon the necks of Christians, the Apostle, having adduced most weighty reasons, diligently admonished them to persist in that liberty with which Christ made us free, and not to submit themselves again to the yoke of servitude. To explain that, these three things in the first part of the chapter contribute: 1. A serious exhortation to preserve liberty, verse 1. 2. The most weighty reason for the exhortation, verses 2-4. 3. A pathetic comparison of the fruit of the Apostle's and the brethren's faith and the damage of the seduction of the false teachers, verse 5. to 12. It is evident, therefore, that the first verse is more correctly constituted as the beginning of a new chapter than joined to the preceding, which Grotius does not deny here, contrary to the old Vulgate, which is authentic to the Papists: and the particle ὖν indicates this, which Ambrosiaster retained, and which Chrysostom and Theophylact acknowledge. Indeed, by way of inference, the Apostle concludes here from the fact that the faithful are free children, that they must persist in liberty, and he introduces his exhortation, which he carries out in this chapter. That exhortation concerns both the preservation of liberty and the flight from the yoke of servitude. It is no light thing to lose liberty, than which nothing is more precious, such as that is, in particular, into which Christ has vindicated us. And since by a certain impulse of nature we are accustomed to be tenacious even of earthly liberty, how much more does it befit us to be desirous and strenuous assertors of this divine liberty, which cost us so great a price, inasmuch as it was not some earthly King, or indeed even an Angel, but the only-begotten Son of the eternal GOD who acquired it for us, for whose sake He Himself assumed the form of a servant and shed His blood for us, that He might restore it to us. Wherefore we must stand in that spiritual liberty which brings immunity from legal ceremonies and the curse and coercion of the moral law. Chrysostom explains the reason interwoven in the parenthesis thus: Did you free yourselves, since you are returning to your former master? It is He who freed you, it is He who gave the price for you. Nor did He deliver us only from the curse of the moral law by His blood, but by fulfilling in reality the types and shadows of the Levitical ceremonies, He at the same time abolished the Levitical law, so that we might no longer be bound to its observance, as the blessed Hunnius says here. Since the Israelites bound themselves to God by a testamentary covenant to the observance of the entire Mosaic law, Exod. XXIV. verse 17. He does not exhort them to seek liberty, to value and praise it: but to persist in it, and to remain immovable in faith and unshaken with a foot fixed on the one Savior. How great the importance of this liberty is, the blessed Luther explained thus: 'For Christ made us free, not politically, not carnally, but theologically or spiritually, that is, He freed us in such a way that our conscience might be free and joyful, fearing nothing of the wrath to come. That is the truest and inestimable liberty, to the magnitude and majesty of which all others (political and carnal) compared are scarcely one drop or tiny droplet. For who can express how great a thing it is for someone to be able to determine with certainty that God will never be angry, but will be a favorable and merciful Father forever on account of Christ? Great Indeed, it is an incomprehensible liberty to have that supreme Majesty favoring, protecting, and helping us, and finally even liberating us bodily in such a way that our body, which is sown in corruption, in dishonor, and in weakness, may rise again in incorruptibility, in glory, and in power. Wherefore, the liberty is ineffable: that we are free from the wrath of God forever, and greater than that is the other liberty by which we are made secure and free through Christ from the law, sin, death, the power of the Devil, hell, etc. For just as the wrath of God cannot terrify us, for Christ has freed us from it: so the law, sin, etc., cannot accuse and condemn us. And although the law may argue, and sin may terrify us, yet they cannot drive us to despair. Because faith, the victor of the world, immediately says: that is nothing to me, for Christ has freed me from these. Thus death, than which nothing is more powerful and horrible in the world, lies conquered in the conscience through this liberty of the Spirit. Wherefore that majesty of Christian liberty must be diligently estimated and weighed. Those words indeed, "liberty from the wrath of God, the law, sin, death, etc.," are easy to say, but to feel the magnitude of this liberty, and to apply its fruit to oneself in the struggle, in the agony of conscience, in practice, this is more difficult than can be told.

How much the momentum of "again be entangled with the yoke of bondage" is illustrated and by its opposite.

It would be extreme dementia for those who, having been made free from slaves, to wish to become slaves instead of free men. Toward the one who deserved well, they would be declaring themselves ungrateful, despising Him who liberated, and loving him who dragged them into servitude. The law no longer had a master, since Christ had once liberated them from its dominion. Therefore, he diligently dissuades them from a new servitude. Nor does he note the servitude nakedly, but the yoke of servitude, to signify the trouble of the business. Thus, says Jerome, he calls the law hard, difficult, laborious, which consumes its worshipers with heavy work by day and night. He understands here primarily and proximately the observance of legal ceremonies. The Jews had experienced the gravity of the burden. Those who were to be converted from gentilism to Christ had not indeed experienced it; yet they were no less liberated from the curse of the law and that servitude, so that they might not undergo it. Indeed, even in gentilism they served a shameful servitude, worshiping idols which by nature were not Gods. If they wished to embrace the ceremonies with the Jews, they would be entangled in a new yoke, as Grotius says here.

With the emphasis of the word "yoke," he unfolds the emphasis contained in the word "yoke" as the Blessed [Luther] does.

Luther: Paul, he says, so that he may detract from the glory of the law by justice, seems here to compare those seeking justice through it to oxen enclosed in a yoke. For just as oxen pulling a yoke with great labor have nothing from it but fodder, and when they are no longer fit for pulling the yoke, they are slaughtered. So those seeking justice through the law are captives, and are pressed by the yoke of servitude, that is, the law, and when they have long wearied themselves with great labor and pain with the works of the law, this is finally what they bring back as a reward: that they are miserable and eternal slaves.

Of what thing? Of sin, death, the wrath of God, the Devil, etc. Therefore, there is no greater and harder servitude than that of the law. Not in vain, therefore, does Paul call it the yoke of servitude.

It is not a matter here of a trivial or worthless thing, but of either infinite and eternal liberty or servitude. For just as the liberty from the wrath of God and all evils is not political or carnal, but eternal: so the servitude of sin, death, the Devil, etc., by which those who wish to be justified and saved through the law are pressed, is not corporal, which lasts for some time, but perpetual. For such workers, who do everything seriously (for Paul speaks of such), are never quiet and at peace. In this life they always doubt the will of God, they fear death, wrath, and the judgment of God, and after this life they will pay the penalty of their unbelief, eternal destruction. And so the operators of the law are rightly called the Devil’s (to speak in the manner of the common people) Martyrs, because they acquire hell with far greater labor and trouble than the martyrs of Christ acquire heaven.

For they are crushed by a double contrition. First, while they live here doing many and great works, they miserably torture themselves in vain. Afterward, when they die, they acquire the reward, eternal damnation and punishment. Thus they are most miserable martyrs in the present and future life; and their servitude is eternal.

But that Grotius refers the yoke of servitude to the opinions and rites by which the nations had bound themselves is entirely foreign. For the Apostle did not dispute about those against the false Doctors, but about the yoke of the Mosaic law, which it is established by the definition of the Council of Jerusalem (Acts XV) was "unbearable" to Jews and Christians alike. V.

2. It is a word of one exciting attention. "I, Paul," an Apostle, called by Christ, which those doctors of yours cannot say of themselves. "I say to you, that if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing." If you are circumcised, that is, you procure yourselves to be circumcised, namely with the certain persuasion that you, who are of the Gentiles, are obligated to it.

For God has established either Judaism or Christianity as the way of eternal salvation. For it is sufficiently established that Paganism is not from God. If Judaism is that way, Christianity is not that way: if Christianity is that way, Judaism is not that way: otherwise, that circumcision is not condemned in itself, both Paul often shows, and Justin against Trypho.

This assertion is opposed to that false assertion which is treated in Acts XV. 1. He prefaces the reason for the exhortation with the little word of attention "behold," and his own Apostolic authority. For these things which he says, he asserts not so much in the name of other believers as for his own Apostolic office, or as a God-breathed legate of Christ: But he does not insinuate by this form of speaking what seemed to Pareus, who says that they are as certain as that Paul himself is called: If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.

This example teaches that the observance of Levitical ceremonies is also included under Christian liberty. He assumes the principal one, which also obtained a certain place of a sacrament. If it takes away the fruit of Christ's redemption, now that it is observed under the condition of necessity and merit for salvation, after it has indeed been abrogated, how much more must that be established concerning other ceremonies, which never had that condition of necessity and utility? For that was a sacrament of regeneration.

But he urges the greatest damage. For to whom Christ does not profit with His merit, what can profit him? For outside of Christ there is no salvation (Acts IV. 12).

Grotius establishes a twofold way of salvation, Judaism and Christianity. But Scripture knows only one. Namely, Christ (John XIV. 6), or faith in Christ, and His grace (Acts X. 43, Rom. III. 24).

If Judaism is called the religion of the ancients, by which the Fathers in the Old Testament were led to salvation, it does not differ from Christianity regarding substance, but only regarding circumstances. The ancients believed in Christ to be exhibited; we believe in Him exhibited. The ancients had the "promises" and the shadows of ceremonies; we have the "gospel," the complement of the promises, and the body itself, with those figures and shadows abrogated, which vanished at the presence of the body (Col. II, Heb.).

X. That therefore now, with Christ exhibited, the circumcision of the flesh is not only useless but it also becomes harmful, the cause of which seems to be that, since the necessity of it for salvation is posited after Christ has been exhibited, the fulfillment of the figure of circumcision in Christ is denied: it is denied that Christ came as the one figured by it, it is denied that He fulfilled the law, it is denied that He redeemed us with His blood.

For that removal of the foreskin figured this, and in it the shedding of blood, and through it the obligation to fulfill the law that was to come from Christ was signified. For since all Abrahamites were obligated through circumcision to keep the law, which, however, no one could keep, it remained that one should come forth from the loins of Abraham who would undertake the same and fulfill the divine law for us.

Regarding which B. Hunnius has it thus: Circumcision was a sign of the covenant between God and men. But there is no grace of God with men, except under the condition of the law being kept and fulfilled: since the grace of God does not reign unless the justice of God is fully satisfied. Therefore, in order for circumcision to profit Abraham and the other males under the Old Testament, it was necessary that they either keep the whole law themselves, or, because this was impossible for them, that they apprehend through faith another satisfaction and fulfillment of the law, that is, the obedience of the coming Messiah, which He was about to perform for the law in its entirety.

And in this way circumcision was made useful to him, as a seal of the justice of faith embracing Christ.

But because the Lord never instituted circumcision so that it would continue even after the Messiah was exhibited and the work of redemption was fulfilled: But because it was annexed together with the Old Testament, it had to be antiquated and abolished: Therefore, after Christ was manifested in the flesh and fulfilled His work on earth, circumcision has now finished its duty, with baptism substituted in its place Col. II.

Hence it comes about that those who now undertake circumcision as necessary, by the very act demonstrate that they are receiving upon themselves, together with circumcision, the entire and heavy yoke of keeping the whole law.

And this is what the Apostle says, that he testifies to every man who is circumcised under the opinion of necessity, that he becomes a debtor to keep the whole law: and because in this way he captures his own justice in the law, it happens that Christ profits him nothing, and, cast out from the grace into which he had previously been asserted by the benefit of Christ, he is reduced entirely under the miserable servitude and curse of the law.

Chrysostom renders another reason for this consequence of the Apostolic inference, "if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing," and that a twofold one: The first is this: He who is circumcised is circumcised as if fearing the law. He who fears it distrusts the powers of grace. Furthermore, he who distrusts takes no fruit from that which he distrusts. The latter, however, is this: He who is circumcised makes the law divine and powerful in authority. But he who thinks that it is divine, and transgresses it for the greater part, while keeping it for the lesser, subjects himself to execration, rejecting the liberty that is in faith; how can he be saved? For if it is lawful to say something incredible, this man trusts neither in Christ nor in the law, but stands in the middle, wishing to make a profit from here and there, and therefore he will receive profit neither from here nor from there.

But these reasons come down to this, that by the undertaking of circumcision an obligation is made to keep the whole law, which is set before us as impossible: and thus, those who determine to establish their own justice are not subjected to the justice of Christ; for those who wish to be justified by their own fulfillment of the law, Christ is neither necessary nor does He profit them.

And therefore, the undertaking of circumcision does not simply evacuate the merit of Christ, but insofar as it is undertaken under the opinion of necessity or for salvation. For if anything besides the merit of Christ contributes to salvation, Christ is neither our perfect Savior nor the only one: So that He Himself would have most fully satisfied the law, and salvation would be situated in Him alone, but there will also be need of our own shedding of blood, in the amputation of the foreskin, so that what is lacking in the sufficiency of the passion and merit of Christ may be supplemented by our passion: If Christ is neither the only nor the perfect Savior, He is in no way a Savior.

For an imperfect merit is no merit; an imperfect redemption is no redemption; an imperfect satisfaction is truly ἀντικείμενα εἰς προοικείωσιν, that is, it is not a satisfaction.

Therefore God does not wish Christ to profit those who do not seek salvation in Him alone. Those who seek salvation through circumcision besides faith do not seek salvation in Christ alone.

Therefore, Christ neither wishes nor ought to profit such people for salvation, because He wishes to be held as either a perfect Savior or none at all.

To join circumcision with Christ was to deny that Christ suffices for salvation: Which is to deny Christ Himself. But to those who deny Christ, what will Christ profit?

And in this sentiment Liberus speaks excellently.

This is a very harsh sentence, by which Paul says that to be circumcised is the same as to make Christ idle.

Not indeed in itself, but to the Galatians, who, circumvented by the deceits of the Pseudo-Apostles, believed [it necessary] besides faith in Christ, without which salvation could not happen to them.

And this passage is the Lydian stone, by which we can most certainly and freely judge all doctrines, works, worships, and ceremonies of all men. Whoever they may be, whether Papists, or Jews, or Turks, or heretics, etc., they teach something necessary for obtaining salvation besides faith in Christ, or institute some work or worship, and likewise observe any rule, tradition, or ceremony whatsoever with this opinion, that they wish to obtain through such things the remission of sins, justice, and eternal life.

These hear the sentence of the Holy Spirit pronounced against them by the Apostle twice, that Christ simply does not profit them.

And Paul, which is very wonderful, dares to bring this sentence against the law and circumcision divinely handed down; what would he not dare against the chaff of human traditions? Wherefore this is a terrible thunderbolt against the kingdom of the Pope, etc.

And further: It is therefore a most clear sentence, Christ is useless, that is, born, suffered, etc., in vain for this man who is circumcised, that is, who trusts in circumcision.

For Paul is not dealing, as I said above, with the work itself, which without trust and the opinion of justice does no harm, but with the use of the work, that is, with the trust and justice added to the work.

For we must understand Paul according to the subject matter, or according to the argument undertaken, which is that men are not justified by the law, works, circumcision, etc. He does not say that works in themselves are nothing, but the trust and justice of works: For that makes Christ idle.

Therefore, he who accepts circumcision with this opinion, that it is necessary for justification, to him Christ profits nothing.

And to the following words.

You have been evacuated from Christ, you who are justified in the law: Here Paul explains himself, that he is not speaking about the law or the work of circumcision simply, but about the trust and opinion of justification through it, as if he were saying: I do not condemn circumcision or the law simply. For it is lawful for me to eat, drink, and converse with the Jews according to the law, it is lawful for me to circumcise Timothy, etc.

But to wish to be justified by the law, as if Christ had not yet come, or as if He, being present, could not justify alone, this I condemn, this is to be evacuated from Christ.

Likewise: The true knowledge of Christ or of faith does not dispute whether you have done good works for justification; or evil ones for damnation.

But it simply determines thus: whether you have done good works, you are not justified for that reason; or whether you have done evil ones, you are not damned for that reason. I do not detract from good works their glory, nor do I praise evil ones.

But in the cause of justification I say that one must see how I may retain Christ, lest He become idle for me, if I am to be justified I desire to read. For Christ alone justifies me against my evil works, and without my good works. If I feel this way about Christ, I apprehend the true Christ. But if I judge that He demands from me the law and works for justification, He has become idle to me, and I have been emptied of Him.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM & PARTITIO.

Hortatur, ut persistant in libertate Christiana, nec circumcisionem suscipiant, per quam Christus redditur inutilis, ipsique obligantur ad totam legem praestandam, ut ne evacuen- tur & excidant gratia Dei, qui per legem ju- stificari volunt, quum contra vere fideles per fidem spem justitiae expectent, & in Christo neque circumcisio, neque praeputium valeat, sed fides, quae per charitatem operosa est. Redarguit Galatas, quod relicto cursu pri- stino a veritate se abduci passi sint, cum omine adversus turbatores de judicio & ex- cisione. Monentur etiam, ne libertate ab- utantur ad carnis placitum, sed mutua cha- ritate sibi serviant, & in Spiritu ambulent, ac recensito catalogo operum carnis e regno DEI excludentium, & fructuum Spiritus excitantur, ut carnem crucifigant, & am- bitionem fugiant.

PArtes duae sunt I. de libertate Christiana custo- dienda ad vers. 12. II. De licentia carnali, quae abusus libertatis, fugienda, ad v. 26. Illa conclu- ditur pars totius epistolae secunda. Hac vero in- choatur pars tertia principalis.

PARS I. CAPITIS V. De libertate Christiana custodienda, Quae constituit sectionem II. TRACTATIONIS EPISTOLAE DOG- MATICAE DE DOCTRINAE DE JUSTI- FICATIONE PONDERE.

Vers. 1. Τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ᾖ, ᾗ χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσε, στή- κετε, καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε) Haec sic recte co- haerent, male in quibusdam Codicibus divulsa, ita ut pars horum capiti praecedenti adhaereat: nativa loquutio fuerat: Ἐν τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ. Nam cum ea praepositione verba standi po- ni solent, ut 1. Cor. XVI. 13. Phil. I. 27. IV. 1. 1. Thessal. III. 8. sed tales particulae saepe subintelliguntur: & ᾗ hic est πρὸς ἣν, לאשר. ζυγὸς δουλείας non tantum vocat id quod Hebraei dicunt עול תורה legis jugum, sed & opiniones & ritus, quibus gentes semetipsos devinxerant. Ἐνέχεσθαι hic vinci- ri, adstringi, frequens apud bonos scriptores verbum. In Glossario ἐνεχόμενος obligatus. Christus enim jugum nobis imposuit, sed suave. Vide Matth. XI. vers. 29.

Quum hactenus excluserit e circulo justifica- tionis opera tum moralia, tum ceremonialia, & sola fide in Christum hominem justificari & salva- ri docuerit: jam ne levis forte momenti haec ad- versus Pseudo-Apostolos disputatio, ac Galata- rum ab iis seductorum informatio videatur, quantum doctrina de justificatione per solam fidem ponderis habeat, Apostolus docet, ut er- rorem in hoc praecipuo fidei capite eo magis fugiant, & ad puritatem fidei Apostolicae revo- centur, inque eadem unice persistant. Et quum ea occasione de liberatione a jugo legis Mosaicae, ac libertate per Christum parta egerit, quantum pretium sit istius libertatis, ac qualiter ea uten- dum sit, tradit: ne in licentiam carnis ea dege- neret, ut calumniae simul os obstruatur, quasi per doctrinam de justificatione per solam fidem licentiae carnis porta aperiatur, & studium pie- tatis labefactetur. Quapropter ita libertatem Christianam custodiendam esse monet, ut ne abutamur eadem ad carnis licentiam. Quod ita- que ad pondus & momentum controversiæ de ju- stificatione, quia per doctrinam Apostolicam libertas per Christum acquisita farta tecta con- servatur: Per Pseudo-Apostolorum heterodo- xiam legis observationem juxta cum fide in Chri- stum ad salutem requirentium jugum servitutis ἀβάςακτον cervicibus Christianorum imponeba- tur, sedulo ac rationibus gravissimis adductis, commonefecit Apostolus, ut in illa libertate, qua Christus nos liberos fecit, persistant, nec iterum jugo servitutis sese submittant. Ad id ergo explicandum, tria hæc in prima capitis parte faciunt 1. Seria de libertate custodienda adhortatio vers. 1. 2. Gravissima adhortationis ra- tio vers. 2. 3. 4. 3. Pathetica fructus fidei Aposto- li & fratrum ac damni seductionis falsorum Docto- rum comparatio vers. 5. ad 12. Patet ergo, versum primum rectius initium novi capitis constitui, quam præcedenti conjungi, quod hic contra veterem vulgatam, Papistis authenticam, non abnuit Grotius: idque indicat etiam particula ὖν, quam Ambrosiafter retinuit, & agnoscunt Chrysostomus ac Theophylactus. Nimirum per mo- dum illationis hic Apostolus ex eo quod fideles sint liberi filii concludit, persistendum esse in libertate, suamque infert adhortationem, quam hoc capite exequitur. Adhortatio illa concernit tum libertatis custodiam, tum jugi servitutis fu- gam. Non leve est, libertatem perdere, qua ni- hil est pretiosius, qualis imprimis ea est, in quam nos vindicavit Christus. Et quum naturæ quodam ductu terrenæ etiam libertatis tenaces esse solea- mus, quanto magis divinæ hujus libertatis cupi- dos, ac strenuos assertores esse convenit, quæ tanto nobis constitit pretio, utpote quam non Rex aliquis terrenus, imo ne Angelus quidem, sed æterni DEI Filius unigenitus nobis acquisivit, cujus causa ipse servi formam assumsit, & sangui- nem pro nobis effudit, ut eam nobis restitueret. Quapropter nobis standum est in libertate illa spirituali, quæ immunitatem a ceremoniis le- galibus & legis moralis maledictione ac coactio- ne importat. Chrysostomus rationem ipsi paren- thesi intextam ita edisserit: Num vos ipsos libera- stis, quandoquidem missum ad priorem recurritis dominatum? Ipse est qui vos liberavit, ipse est, qui pretium dedit pro vobis. Nec vindicavit nos solum a maledictione legis moralis sanguine suo, sed implendo reipsa Leviticarum ceremoniarum typos & umbras sustulit simul legem Leviticam, ne ad illius observationem porro simus obstricti, ut hic Beat. Hunnius. Quum ad observationem legis Mosaicæ universæ testamentaria pactione se Deo obligarint Israelitæ Exod. XXIV. vers. 17. Non hortatur, ut quærant libertatem, ut æstiment ac laudent: sed ut in ea persistant, & fide immo- biles & inconcussi pede in uno Salvatore fixo per- maneant. Quantum momentum libertatis hujus sit, Beat. Lutherus ita exposuit: 'Nam Christus nos liberos fecit, non politice, non carnaliter, sed theologice seu spiritualiter, hoc est, sic liberavit nos, ut conscientia nostra sit libera & læta, nihil timens venturam iram. Ea est verissima ac inæstimabilis libertas, ad cujus magnitudinem & majestatem cæ- tera (politica & carnalis) collata, vix sunt una stil- la vel guttula. Quis enim potest eloqui, quanta res sit, aliquem posse certo statuere, Deum neque un- quam iratum futurum, sed in æternum fore faven- tem & clementem Patrem propter Christum? Magna profecto et incomprehensibilis libertas est, habere summam illam Majestatem faventem, protegentem et juvantem, et tandem etiam corporaliter nos ita liberantem, ut corpus nostrum, quod seminatur in corruptione, in ignominia, et in infirmitate, resurgat in incorruptibilitate, in gloria et potentia. Quare inenarrabilis est libertas, nos esse liberos ab ira Dei in aeternum, majorque ea alia libertas, qua securi et liberi efficimur per Christum a lege, peccato, morte, potestate Diaboli, inferno etc. Sicut enim ira Dei non potest perterrefacere nos, nam Christus ab ea nos liberavit: Ita lex, peccatum etc. accusare et condemnare nos non possunt. Et quanquam lex arguat, et peccatum perterrefaciat nos, tamen non possunt nos in desperationem adigere. Quia fides victrix mundi mox dicit: illa nihil ad me, Christus enim liberavit me ab his. Sic mors, qua nihil potentius et horribilius est in mundo, victa jacet in conscientia per hanc libertatem Spiritus. Quare illa majestas Christianae libertatis diligenter aestimanda et ponderanda est. Verba quidem illa, libertas ab ira Dei, lege, peccato, morte etc. dictu facilia sunt, sed magnitudinem hujus libertatis sentire, et fructum ejus in certamine, in agone conscientiae, in praxi applicare sibi, hoc plus, quam dici potest, difficile est.

Quantum πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε momentum illustratur et contrario.

Extrema foret dementia, eos, qui e servis facti liberi, pro liberis velle fieri servos. Erga bene meritum essent ingratos se declaraturi, contemnentes eum, qui liberavit, et amantes eum, qui in servitutem pertraxit. Lex non habebat amplius dominum, cum Christus eos semel a dominatu illius liberasset. Ideo a nona servitute eos sedulo dehortatur. Nec tamen servitutem nude, sed jugum servitutis notat, ut negotii molestiam significet. Sic vocat, inquit Hieronymus, legem duram, difficilem, laboriosam, que ac nocte suos cultores gravi opere consumit. Intelligit autem hic imprimis et proxime observantiam ceremoniarum legalium. Judai expersi erant oneris gravitatem. Quie gentilismo ad Christum erant converti, non quidem experti; non minus tamen a legis maledictione et ista servitute, ne illam subirent, liberati erant. Quin et in gentilismo turpem servierunt servitutem, idola colentes, quae natura non erant Dii. Si vellent cum Judaeis amplecti ceremonias novo implicarentur jugo, ut hic Grotius.

Emphasi Vocis ζυγῷ Emphasin in voce ζυγῷ comprehensam ita evolvit Beat.

Lutherus: Paulus, inquit, us deroget legi gloriam justitia, videtur hic quarentes justitiam per eam comparare bobus jugo conclusis. Ut enim boves magno labore trahentes jugum, nihil inde habent quam pabulum, et ubi amplius non sunt idonei ad trabendum jugum, mactantur. Ita quarentes per legem justitiam, captivi sunt, et premuntur jugo servitutis, hoc est, lege, et ubi diu magno labore et dolore defatigarunt sese legis operibus, hoc tandem reportant praemii, quod miseri et eterni servi sunt.

Cujus rei? Peccati, mortis, ire Dei, Diaboli etc. Ideo non est major et durior servitus quam legis. Non frustra ergo Paulus vocat jugum servitutis.

Non agitur hic de re levicula aut nihili, sed vel de infinita et aeterna libertate vel servitute. Ut enim libertas ab ira Dei et omnibus malis non est politica aut carnalis, sed aeterna: Ita servitus peccati, mortis, Diaboli etc. qua premuntur, qui per legem volunt justificari et salvari, non est corporalis, quae ad tempus aliquod duras, sed perpetua. Nam tales operarii, qui serio agunt omnia (de talibus enim loquitur Paulus) nunquam quieti et pacati sunt. In hac vita semper dubitant de voluntate Dei, timent mortem, iram, et judicium Dei, et post hanc vitam luent poenam incredulitatis suae, interitum aeternum. Itaque operatores legis recte vocantur Diaboli (ut more vulgi loquar) Martyres, quia longe majori labore et molestia acquirunt inferos, quam martyres Christi caelum.

Duplici enim contritione conteruntur. Primum dum hic vivunt multa et magna opera facientes, frustra misere se excruciant. Postea cum moriuntur, premium acquirunt, aeternam damnationem et poenam. Sic miserrimi martyres sunt in praesenti et futura vita; esque eorum servitus aeterna.

Quod vero jugum servitutis ad opiniones et ritus, quibus gentes seipsas devinxerant, refert Grotius, alienum prorsus est. Non enim de iis disputavit Apostolus contra falsos Doctores, sed de jugo legis Mosaicae, quod ἀβάστακτον Judaeis pariter et Christianis esse ex definitione Concilii Hierosolymitani Act. XV. constat. V.

2. Vox est attentionem excitantis. Εγὼ Παῦλος Apostolus, a Christo vocatus, quod illi vestri Doctores de se dicere non possunt. Λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε, χεῖρός ὑμᾶς οὐδὲν ὠφελήσει Si circumcidimini, id est, circumcidi vos procuratis, nempe cum certa persuasione, vos, qui gentibus estis, in id obligari.

Nam viam salutis aeternae Deus constituit aut Judaismum, aut Christianismum. Paganismum enim a Deo non esse, satis constat. Si Judaismus ea via est, Christianismus ea via non est: Si Christianismus ea via est, Judaismus ea via non est: alioquin circumcisionem per se non damnari, et Paulus saepe ostendit, et Justinus contra Tryphonem.

Opponitur haec assertio illi falsae assertioni, de qua agitur Act. XV. 1. Rationi adhortationis praemittit attentionis voculam ἰδὲ, et autoritatem suam Apostolicam. Haec enim, quae dicit, non tam fidelium aliorum nomine, quam pro munere suo Apostolico, seu legatus Christi θεόπνευστος asseverat: Non autem bac loquendi forma id insinuat, quod Pareo visum, que dicit, tam esse certa, quam quod ipse Paulus appelletur: Si circumcidamini, Christum nihil vobis profuturum.

Sub libertate Christiana etiam comprehendi ceremoniarum Leviticarum observationem, hoc exemplum docet. Assumit praecipuam, quae etiam sacramenti vicem quandam obtinebat, Ea si tollit redemptionis Christi fructum, jam sub necessitatis et meriti ad salutem ratione observata, postquam scilicet abrogata est, quanto magis id statuendum de aliis ceremoniis, quae eam necessitatis et utilitatis rationem nunquam habuere? Fuit enim illa sacramentum regenerationis.

Damnum autem maximum urget. Cui enim Christus non prodest cum merito suo, quid ei prodesse possit? Nam extra Christum non est salus Act. IV. 12.

Grotius geminam salutis viam constituit Judaismum et Christianismum. Sed scriptura non novit nisi unicum. Christum scilicet Job. XIV. 6. vel fidem in Christum, ejusque gratiam, Act. X. 43. Rom. III. 24.

Si Judaismus veterum religio dicatur, qua Patres in Veteri Testamento ad salutem perducti sunt, a Christianismo non differt quoad substantiam, sed quoad circumstantias solum. Crediderunt veteres in Christum exhibendum, nos credimus in exhibitum. Habuerunt veteres ἐπαγγελίας, promissiones, et umbras ceremoniarum; nos habemus εὐαγγέλιον, promissionum complementum, et corpus ipsum abrogatis illis figuris et umbris, quae evanuere ad praesentiam corporis Col. II. Ebr.

X. Quod ergo nunc exhibito Christo circumcisio carnis non inutilis modo sed noxia etiam fit, ejus causa videtur esse, quod posita ejus ad salutem necessitate post exhibitum Christum negetur impleta figura circumcisionis in Christo: negetur Christus figuratus per eandem venisse, negetur legem implevisse, negetur sanguine suo nos redemisse.

Nam hanc figurabat illa praeputii ablatio, & in ea sanguinis effusio, & per eam futura Christi ad legem implendam significata obligatio. Quum enim omnes Abrahamitae per circumcisionem obligati fuerint ad legem servandam, quam vero nemo servare poterat, id restabat, ut e lumbis Abrahae prodiret, qui eandem susciperet, & legem divinam pro nobis impleret .

Quo de B. Hunnius ita habet: Circumcisio signum erat foederis inter Deum & homines . Fausus autem gratia Deo cum hominibus nullum est, nisi sub conditione servata & impleta legis: Siquidem gratia Dei non regnat, nisi justitia Dei ad plenum satisfiat. Ergo ut Abrahamo, caterisque sub Veteri Testamento masculis prodesset circumcisio, necesse erat, ut aut ipsimet totam servarent legem, aut, quia hoc illis erat impossibile, per fidem apprehenderent aliam satisfactionem, & legis impletionem, hoc est, obedientiam venturi Messiae, quam legi in solidum excoliturus erat.

Atque hac ratione facta ei est utilis circumcisio, tanquam justitia fidei Christum amplexantis finaculum .

Quia vero Dominus circumcisionem eo nunquam instituit, ut exhibito Messia, & opere redemptionis impleto porro etiam duraret: Sed quia una cum Vet. test. annexa erat, antiquari debuit, & aboleri: Ideo postquam Christus carne manifestatus, suum in terris opus implevit, circumcisio suo munere jam defuncta est, surrogato in ipsius locum baptismo Col. II.

Hinc adeo fit, ut, nunc circumcisionem, ut necessariam suscipiunt, vi reipsa demonstrent, se una cum circumcisione recipere in se universam amque jugum servanda totius legis.

Atque hoc est, quod inquit Apostolus, se contestari omnem hominem, qui sub opinione necessitatis circumciditur, quod is fit totius servandae legis: & quia hoc pacto caprat suam in lege justitiam, fit, ut Christus ei nihil prosit, & ex gratia, in quam beneficio Christi prius assertus fuerat, excussus, sub miserabilem servitutem & maledictionem legis ab integro redigatur.

Chrysostomus aliam reddit ἀκολουθίας hujus illationis Apostolicae, si circumcidamini, Christus vobis nihil proderit, rationem, eamque geminam: Primam hanc: Qui circumciditur, tanquam legem metuens circumciditur. Eam qui metuit, diffidit viribus gratiae. Porro qui diffidit, nihil fructus capit ab ea, cui diffidit. Posteriorem vero istam: Qui circumciditur, legem facit divinam & autoritate pollentem. Qui vero putat illa esse divinam, eamque ex majori parte transgreditur, ex minori servans semetipsum subjicit execrationi, libertatem, quae est in fide, repellens, quomodo potest esse salvus? Nam si dicere fas est quoddam incredibile, hic neque Christo, neque legi fidit, sed in medio consistit, & hinc & illinc volens lucrum facere, eoque neque hinc, neque illinc lucrum accipiet.

Sed hae rationes eo recidunt, quod suscepta circumcisione fit obligatio ad servandum legem totam, quae nobis impossibilis praestituit: adeoque propriam justitiam stabilire constituentes, Christi justitiae non subjiciuntur, qui volunt sua ipsorum legis impletione fallari, illis nec opus sit, nec profit Christus.

Ideoque non simpliciter illa circumcisionis susceptio evacuat Christi meritum, sed quatenus eadem sub opinione necessitatis aut salutem suscipitur. Nam si quicquam praeter Christi meritum ad salutem facit, Christus nec perfecte est Salvator noster, nec solus: Ita ut plenissime ipse legi satisfecererit, & in eo solo sita sit salus, sed opus erit etiam nostra sanguinis profusione, in praeputii amputatione, ut, quod sufficientiae passionis & meriti Christi deest, suppleatur nostra passione: Si Christus nec solus nec perfectus est Salvator, nullo modo Salvator est.

Nam meritum imperfectum nullum est meritum; redemptio imperfecta nulla est redemptio; satisfactio imperfecta vere est ἀντικείμενα εἰς προοικείωσιν, hoc est, non est satisfactio.

Ideo non vult Deus Christum prodesse, nisi iis, qui in eo solo salutem quaerunt . Qui praeter fidem circumcisione quaerunt ad salutem, in solo Christo salutem non quaerunt.

Talibus igitur ad salutem prodesse nec vult nec debet Christus, quia vel perfectus vel nullus vult haberi Salvator.

Circumcisionem cum Christo conjungere, erat Christum negare ad salutem sufficere: Quod est, ipsum Christum negare. Negantibus autem Christum, quid proderit Christus?

Atque in hanc sententiam praeclare Liberus .

Hec valde dura est sententia, qua Paulus circumcidi idem esse dicit, quod Christum otiosum fieri.

Non quidem in se, sed Galatis, qui dolis Pseudo-Apostolorum circumventi, credebant praeter fidem in Christum, sine qua non posset illis contingere salus.

Atque hic locus Lydius lapis est, quo certissime & liberrime judicare possumus omnes doctrinas, opera, cultus, ceremonias omnium hominum. Quicunque sine sint Papista, sive Judei, sive Turca, sive haeretici &c. aliquid docent ad salutem consequendam necessarium, praeter fidem in Christum, aut opus, cultumve aliquem instituunt itemque regulam, traditionem aut ceremoniam quamcunque observant hac opinione, quod per talia consequi velint remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & vitam aeternam.

Hi sententiam Spiritus S. contra se latam ab Apostolo bis audiunt, quod Christus illis simpliciter non profit.

Et Paulus, quod est valde mirum, istam sententiam audet ferre contra legem & circumcisionem divinitus traditam, quid non auderet contra paleas traditionem humanarum? Quare is locuste terribile fulmen est contra regnum Papae &c.

Et porro: Clarissima ergo sententia est, Christus inutilis, id est, frustra natus, passus, & c. est huic, qui circumciditur, id est, qui confidit circumcisione.

Non enim agit Paulus, ut supra dixi, de ipso opere per se, quod fine fiducia & opinione justitiae nihil obest, sed de usu operis, hoc est, de fiducia & justitia operi adjecta.

Oportet n. nos Paulum intelligere secundum materiam subjectam, seu secundum argumentum susceptum, quod est, lege, operibus, circumcisione & c. homines non justificari. Non dicit opera per se nihil esse, sed fiduciam & justitiam operum: Ea enim Christum facit otiosum.

Ideo qui accipit circumcisionem hac opinione, quod necessaria sit ad justificationem, huic Christus nihil prodest.

Et ad verba sequentia .

Evacuati estis a Christo, qui in lege justificamini: Hic Paulus seipsum exponit, se non loqui de lege aut opere circumcisionis simpliciter, sed de fiducia & opinione justificationis per eam, quasi dicat: Non damno circumcisionem aut legem simpliciter. Licet enim mihi edere, bibere, conversari cum Judaeis secundum legem, licet mihi circumcidere Timotheum & c.

Sed velle justificari per legem, quasi Christus nondum venerit, aut jam praesens solus justificare non possit, hoc damno, hoc est evacuati a Christo.

Item: Vera cognitio Christi seu fidei non disputat, utrum feceris bona opera ad justificationem; aut mala ad damnationem.

Sed simpliciter ita statuit, sive feceris bona opera, non ideo justificari, sive feceris mala, non ideo damnaris. Non detrabo bonis operibus suam gloriam, nec mala laudo.

Sed in causa justificationis dico videndum esse, quomodo Christum retineam, ne otiosus mihi fiat, si justificari lege cupiam. Christus enim solus me iustificat contra opera mea mala, & sine operibus meis bonis. Si sic de Christo sentio, verum Christum apprehendo. Si autem judico eum exigere a me legem & opera ad justitiam, factum est mihi otiosus, ac ego ab eo evacuatus sum.

## 5:3
3. I testify again to every man who is circumcised, that he is a debtor to do the whole law) Understand again circumcision, from that opinion which we have already stated.

If Judaism is a way to salvation, the whole of Judaism must be observed: one must not choose from it and despise what one wishes. Those new Doctors did not observe many things of the law, below VI. 13, certainly because they looked to that one thing, that the Romans might consider them Jews, and thus allow them to be free from the laws that forbid new religions. But they saw that this could be sufficiently obtained through circumcision. Arrian also says in the Epictetea that Jews are known by circumcision, and Martial says that the part which is circumcised is condemned to taxes.

That πάλιν (again) is not to be referred to the following sentence, as Crocius wishes.

There is no doubt, he says, that he has already handed down the same doctrine: For where did he hand this down, that he who is circumcised is a debtor to the whole law? But to the preceding testimony: I, Paul, say to you. I said, he says, that Christ will not profit you if you are circumcised. I say again and testify not to you alone, but to every man who is circumcised, that he is a debtor to the whole law: What then does it profit Christ himself, if he is bound to perform the whole law himself? But what is the connection between undertaking circumcision and keeping the whole law? A twofold reason for the connection (συνεχείας) can be brought forward.

4. You have been severed from Christ) You show that you do not wish to be bound by the laws of Christ.

A similar expression in Rom. VII. 2. You who are justified by the law) That is, with which justice you are content, which the law can produce, which justice is carnal and has earthly rewards. You have fallen away from grace) He understands grace by way of excellence, the Evangelical grace.

Now the Gospel no longer pertains to you, you have fallen away.

He led the Galatians, who were requiring circumcision for salvation, to an absurdity, that they are debtors to the whole law, which in truth those who are circumcised neither kept (c. 6, 13; Acts 7, 53) nor could keep (Acts 15, 10). If they say, however, that they keep it entirely, and thus wish to be justified by the observation of the law, he declares to them against the Apostles that they are emptied of Christ and fall from grace, who wish to be justified by the law.

For what need is there of Christ's merit, what need of the grace of the remission of sins for those who perfectly keep the law? Since, therefore, the Pseudo-Apostles did not want to appear to empty Christ and the grace of God, or rather to fall away from Christ: For the Greek word implies that, you have fallen away, you have become apostates, aliens from Christ, for alienation is a denial (Rom. 7, 2), and to fall from the grace of God: it is necessary that they abandon that necessity of observing and fulfilling the divine law to obtain eternal salvation.

There is a tacit prolepsis underlying this, according to Pareus, by which he destroys their tergiversation: even if we require the works of the law, we do not send a message of dismissal to Christ, because we join works with faith in justification.

In vain, he says, this is absurd, such a mixture is impossible: You who are justified by the law, that is, who wish to be justified, whether entirely or in part: You are aliens from Christ: You have no commerce with Christ.

Why so?

Because to attribute even the slightest bit to works in the merit of salvation is to derogate entirely from Christ: Because the Savior wishes to be either perfect or nothing. And this is a graver fault, to deny the Christ who has been acknowledged, to fall away from the Christ whom you had embraced by faith, than not to perceive the fruit from Him, which he said before, Christ profits you nothing.

Therefore, when Papists teach that a man is justified by his own charity formally, to be saved meritoriously through the works of faith, what is this other than to make Christ void, and to openly defect from Christ? However they may purge their apostasy, they deny Christ under the name of Christ.

Those who wish to be justified or saved by their own charity or the merits of works, whether in whole or in part, do not wish to be justified and saved solely by the grace of God; they take it away and thus fall from the grace of God.

If by grace, not of works, etc. Rom. XI. 6.

It is impossible, says the Blessed

Luther. 128. to have Christ and the law in the heart at the same time.

For either the law or Christ must yield. But if you are in the persuasion that Christ and trust in the law can dwell together in the heart, then know for certain that not Christ, but the Devil dwells in your heart, under the mask of a Christ who is sharpening and terrifying you, and demanding the law and its works for righteousness.

Let it be noted that such persons not only take away the justifying grace of God, which cannot consist with works and their merits, but also, if they were previously in grace, they fall from divine grace, according to the judgment of the Apostle.

From which it is evident that that opinion concerning the necessity of good works for salvation is a fundamental error, not only overturning the grace of God, depriving salvation of the grace of God, and being a devourer of salvation, as Tertullian speaks.

They are not to be looked at coldly, warns the Blessed

Luther fol. 128. &amp; carelessly: For they are very emphatic: Ye are fallen from grace.

He who falls from grace loses simply the expiation, the remission of sins, righteousness, liberty, life, etc., which Christ earned for us by his resurrection and death, and in their place acquires the wrath and judgment of God, death, sin, slavery to the Devil, and eternal damnation. And this passage strongly fortifies and confirms our Doctrine of faith, or the article of justification, and wonderfully consoles us against the furies of the Papists, who persecute and condemn us as heretics because we teach this article.

This passage ought by right to terrify all enemies of faith and grace, that is, all workers, so that they might cease to persecute and blaspheme the Word of grace, life, and eternal salvation. But they are so hardened and obstinate that seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear.

Let us therefore leave them. For they are blind, and leaders of the blind.

I would like the Calixtines to weigh these things, who absolve the Papists from fundamental error, and render themselves subject to the Apostolic thunderbolt through the necessity of works for salvation.

It is also evident that the faithful can defect from Christ and fall from the grace of God. For the Apostle does not speak hypothetically, as Pareus and Grotius pervert it, "if you wish to be justified by the law," but categorically: "you who are being justified by the law," that is, who wish to be justified, or presume to be.

Nor can it be said that some with the aforementioned Calvinists had fallen, while others had been truly faithful. For he who was not in grace cannot fall from grace. But no one is in grace except he who is truly faithful.

Therefore invert that Parean argument: They were hypocrites, therefore they had fallen: in this way: They fell from the grace of God. Therefore they were truly faithful, not hypocrites.

For without faith it is impossible to please God, or to be in the grace of God. Grotius's gloss: You show that you do not wish to be obligated by the grace of Christ, the Evangelical grace does not pertain to you, you are content with that righteousness which the law can produce, which righteousness is carnal, has earthly rewards, is vain and heretical, and is diametrically opposed to the mind of the Apostle.

It is vain to introduce laws here, where nothing is held concerning the law but concerning Christ and the grace of God. It is heretical to make Christ a new legislator, to constitute Evangelical grace into a law of new observances, and to attribute to the law only carnal righteousness and only earthly promises, when the law is spiritual, and those who keep it have the promise of eternal life, they contradict the Apostle and his present treatment: Since here it is dealt with professedly against the observance of the law, and the redemption of those who were under the law or liberation from the yoke of the law is brought by Christ, and Evangelical grace is opposed to works and their merits in the gratuitous remission of sins.

Latin:

3. Μαρτύρομαι δὲ πάλιν παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτεμνομένῳ, ὅτι ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν, ὅλον τὸν νόμον ποιῆσαι) Intellige rursum circumcisio, ex ea opinione, quam jam diximus.

Si Judaismus via est ad salutem, totus Judaismus est observandus: non ex eo eligendum & spernendum quod velis. Isti novi Doctores multa legis non observabant, infra VI. 13. nimirum quia illud unum spectabant, ut Romani ipsos pro Judæis haberent, ac sic liberos esse sinerent a legibus, novas religiones vetantibus. Id autem videbant satis obtineri posse per circumcisionem. Ex circumcisione nosci Judæos, dicit etiam Arrianus in Epicteteis, & Martialis damnatam tributis dicit eam partem, quæ circumciditur.

Illud πάλιν non ad sententiam sequentem referendum est, ut Crocius vult.

Non dubium est, inquit, quin eandem doctrinam jam tradiderit: Ubi n. hoc tradidit, ei qui circumciditur, debitorem esse totius legis? Sed ad præcedentem testificationem: Ego Paulus dico vobis. Dixi, inquit, Christum vobis non profuturum, si circumcidamini. Iterum dico & testificor non vobis solum, sed omni homini, qui circumciditur, debitor est totius legis: Quid ergo ipsi Christo prodest, si tenetur ipse totam legem præstare? Quis vero nexus est suscipiendæ circumcisionis, & servandæ totius legis? Gemina potest συνεχείας ratio afferri

4. Κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τὲ χρισῦ) Ostenditis vos Christi legibus obligari nolle.

Similis loquutio Rom. VII. 2. ὅτινες ἐν νόμῳ δικαιοῦσθε) Hoc est, qua ea justitia contenti estis, quam lex potest producere, quæ justitia est carnalis, præmia habet terrena. Τῆς χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε) Gratiam intelligit κατ' ἐξοχὴν Evangelicam.

Jam ultra Evangelium ad vos non pertinet, ἐξεπέσατε.

Deduxit Galatas circumcisionem ad salutem requirentes ab absurdum, quod totius legis debitores sint, quam vero nec servabant, qui circumciduntur c. 6, 13. Act. 7, 53. nec servare poterant Act. 15, 10. Si dixerint tamen, se omnino servare eandem, adeoque justificari velle per observationem legis, edicit eis contra Apostolos, evacuati eos a Christo, & gratia excidere, qui justificari per legem volunt.

Quid n. Christi merito opus, quid gratia remissionis peccatorum iis, qui legem perfecte servant? Quum ergo Pseudo-Apostoli videri nollent evacuare Christum & gratiam Dei, vel potius deficere a Christo: Nam id Græca vox importat, defecistis, apostatæ facti estis, alieni a Christo, κατ' ἀρνησις est alienatio Rom. 7, 2. & a gratia Dei excidere: necessitatem illam observandæ & implendæ legis divinæ ad consequendam æternam salutem dimittant, necellum est.

Subest tacita prolepsis, juxta Pareum, qua tergi versationem eorum destruit: etsi legis opera requiramus, Christo nuncium non mittimus, quia cum fide opera in justificatione conjungimus.

Frustra, inquit, hoc est absurda, impossibilis est talis mixtura: Qui lege justificamini, hoc est, justificari vultis, sive in solidum sive ex parte: Alieni estis a Christo: Nihil vobis cum Christo commercii.

Quid ita?

Quia in merito salutis vel tantillum operibus tribuere est Christo totum derogare: Quia servator vult esse vel perfectus vel nullus. Atque hæc gravior culpa est, Christum agnitum abnegare, a Christo, quem fide amplexus fueras, deficere, quam fructum ex eo non percipere, quod antea dixit, Christus vobis nihil prodest.

Papistæ ergo cum docent hominem justificari per suam charitatem formaliter, per opera fidei salvari meritorie, quid aliud quam Christum evacuant, & a Christo palam deficiunt? Quomodocunque apostasiam suam purgant, Christum sub Christi nomine abnegant.

Qui charitate sua vel operum meritis sive in totum, sive ex parte justificari aut salvari volunt, gratia Dei unice justificari ac salvari nolunt, eam tollunt & ita gratia Dei excidunt.

Si per gratiam, non ex operibus &c. Rom. XI. 6.

Impossibile est, inquit B.

Luther. 128. Christum & legem simul habere in corde.

Aut enim legem, aut Christum cedere oportet. Si vero in ea persuasione es, Christum & fiduciam legis cohabitare posse in corde, tum certo scias, non Christum, sed Diabolum in corde tuo habitare, sub larva Christi acutantis & perterrefacientis te, ac exigentis legem & opera ejus ad justitiam.

Notetur tales non solum gratiam Dei justificatricem, quæ cum operibus eorumque meritis consistere non potest, tollere, sed etiam si in gratia prius fuerint, gratia divina excidere, ex sententia Apostoli.

E quo constat sententiam illam de bonorum operum necessitate ad salutem errorem esse fundamentalem ad mentalem, gratiam Dei non tantum evertentem, salutem & gratia Dei privantem, ac salutis devoratorium, ut Tertullianus loquitur.

Non sunt frigide, monet B.

Lutherus fol. 128. & oscitanter inspiciendat verba: A gratia excidistis: Sunt enim valde emphatica.

Qui excidit a gratia, amittit simpliciter expiationem, remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, libertatem, vitam, &c. quam Christus resurrectione sua & morte nobis emeruit, & vicissim acquirit in locum eorum iram & judicium Dei, mortem, peccatum, servitutem Diaboli, ac damnationem aeternam. Et hic locus fortiter munit & confirmat Doctrinam nostram de fide, seu articulum justificationis, & nos mirabiliter consolatur adversus furores Papistarum, persequentium & condemnantium nos tanquam hereticos, quod istum articulum docemus.

Debebat merito iste locus perterrefacere omnes hostes fidei & gratiae, hoc est, omnes operarios, ut desinerent persequi & blasphemare Verbum gratiae, vite & salutis aeternae. Sed adeo indurati & obstinati sunt, ut videntes non videant, & audientes non audiant.

Sinamus igitur illos. Caci enim sunt, & cacorum duces.

Expendant haec velim Calixtini, Papistas ab errore fundamentali absolventes, seque ipsos per necessitatem operum ad salutem fulmini Apostolico obnoxios reddentes.

Patet etiam fideles a Christo deficere, ac gratia Dei excidere posse. Nam non hypothetice, ut Pareus pervertit, & Crotius, si vultis justificari per legem, sed categorice loquitur Apostolus, qui per legem justificamini, hoc est, justificari vultis, aut præsumitis.

Nec alii dici possunt cum prædictis Calvinianis excidisse, alii vere fideles fuisse. Nam excidere gratia non potest, qui in gratia non fuit. Non autem in gratia est, nisi qui vere fidelis.

Invert itaque illud Pareanum: Illi fuerant hypocritae, ideo exciderant: hoc modo: Illi exciderunt gratia Dei. Ergo vere fideles fuerunt, non hypocritae.

Sine fide enim impossibile est Deo placere, vel in gratia Dei esse. Grotii glossa: Ostenditis, vos Christi gratia obligari nolle, gratia Evangelica ad vos non pertinet, ea quæ justitia contenti estis, quam lex potest producere, quæ justitia est carnalis, præmia habet terrena, vana & hæretica est, ac menti Apostoli e diametro contraria.

Vanum est hic ingerere leges, ubi nihil de lege sed de Christo & gratia Dei habetur, Hereticum est, Christum facere novum legislatorem, gratiam Evangelicam, in legem novarum observantia constituere, legique solam carnalem justitiam, sola terrena promissa tribuere, quum lex spiritualis sit, & qui eam servant, vitæ promissum habent eternæ Apostolo contrariantur, ejusque præsenti tractationi: Siquidem hic ex professo contra legem observantiam agitur, & redemptio eorum qui sub lege erant vel liberatio a jugo legis Christo afferatur, atque gratia Evangelica in gratuita peccatorum remissione operibus eorumque meritis opponatur.

## 5:5
Ver. 5. 'Ημεῖς γὰρ πνεύματι ἐκ πίστεως ἐλπίδα δικαιοσύνης ἀπεκδεχόμεθα We within our spirit through faith await that hope which is proposed for righteousness (namely, spiritual). I interpret πνεῦμα here as the spirit/mind, which is opposed to the flesh, in which is circumcision.

He called hope metonymically the reward itself, which is hoped for, and that is eternal life.

Thus the name of hope is placed also in Rom. VIII 24. Coloss. I. 5. 1. Thes. I. 3. 1. Petr. I. 3. &amp; elsewhere.

Hope of righteousness here, which is the crown of righteousness. 2. Tim. IV. 8.

The Apostle now issues a profession of faith, not only his own, but also in the name of those faithful who were with him, that not through ceremonial or moral law observance, but through faith alone do they await the hope of righteousness in the Spirit: because in Christ Jesus, to whom alone they adhere through faith, and whose righteousness they testify they rely upon alone, and hope for eternal salvation, neither circumcision and the observance of the law, to which those things obligated them, nor uncircumcision avails anything, but only faith, which is effective through charity.

Subject of the profession which it concerns: We, says the Apostle, not the Jews, as Pareus wishes, but understanding all the brothers who were with him, whose faith was one, the twin faith of all who had received an equal faith throughout the world 2. Petr. I. 1. For there is no other than one faith Eph. IV. 5.

This therefore is the ecumenical and Catholic profession of faith.

Cause of it is not flesh and blood, but the Spirit of the Lord Mattb. XVI. 17. by which the faithful are ruled, by which they are made certain of the heavenly inheritance, by which they await the same and desire it Rom. VIII. 23.

Some wish the Spirit to be called the grace in Christ, to which the flesh is opposed Gal. III. 3. that is, legal righteousness, which adhered to the flesh, just as circumcision, flattered the flesh and produced carnal trust; to Pareus it seems the Spirit is opposed to the body, as 1. Cor. VII. 34. Eph. IV. 21.

We await the Spirit, that is, with our mind and heart: But the former explanation is more convenient, which is approved by Chrysostom,
