Theophy- lact, and Oecumenius. The means by which it is concluded: not circumcision or other ceremonies, not works of the moral law. Compare a similar decree in Acts

XV. 11. The object is ἐλπὶς δικαιοσύνης hope of righteousness, that is, the hoped-for good or heavenly inheritance by Metonymy, as Col.

I. 5. not of our righteousness: For this is excluded in the present with any moral works whatsoever, but the grace of the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith is awaited.

For we are not saved by our own righteousness, but we have righteousness in the Lord, in the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified Es. XLV. ver.

24. 26. The crown of glory therefore is the hope of the righteousness of faith 2.

Timoth. IV. ver.

6. Others explain, we await the hope of righteousness from faith, we confess that we have righteousness, and are going to have it from faith and not from the law: So that by the word await, not so much the hope of a future thing is noted, as the confidence of present righteousness of faith.

Grotius thinks that by hypallage the righteousness of hope, that is, the hoped-for, can be understood: But there is no need for that. For the Apostle, having professed his faith by antithesis against the heresy of the Pseudo-Apostles, says that he attains not only justification but also eternal salvation through nothing but faith.

Faith and hope by reason

B. Luther neatly distinguishes the object here: Faith has truth as its object, which it teaches must be adhered to certainly and firmly, and it looks into the word of the thing or the promise of things. Hope has goodness as its object, and it looks into the thing of the word, that is, into the promised thing or into the things to be hoped for, which faith has dictated must be received. It also differs in subject; because faith is (also) in the intellect, hope in the will: and in office; because faith dictates, directs, teaches, and is knowledge (yet not alone), hope is an exhortation, because it rouses the soul so that it may be supported and erect, so that it may dare, bear, endure in evils, and in them expect better things: and in order; because faith is before every tribulation, the beginning of life, Heb. 11, hope is later, born from tribulations, Rom. 5, and in contraries; because faith, says the Doctor, is the Judge and is fighting against errors and heresies, judging spirits and doctrines. Hope is the Emperor or Leader of war, fighting against tribulation, the cross, impatience, sadness, pusillanimity, despair, blasphemy, and it expects good things under evils. When, therefore, instructed by faith in the word of GOD, I apprehend Christ, and with the whole trust of my heart (which, however, cannot happen without the will) I believe in him, by this knowledge I am righteous. Thus, with me justified by faith or this righteousness, immediately comes the Devil, the father of lies, and strives to extinguish faith with deceits, that is, with lies, errors, heresies. Then, because he is a murderer, he tries to oppress it also by force. There, hope struggling apprehends the thing dictated by faith, becomes courageous, and conquers the Devil, who is attacking faith; which being conquered, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit follow. In reality, therefore, faith and hope can hardly be distinguished, and yet there is some difference between them. Just as in politics, prudence without fortitude is vain. So faith in Theology without hope is nothing, because hope bears and endures in evils, and conquers them. And conversely: Just as fortitude without prudence is rashness; so hope without faith is presumption in the Spirit and a tempting of GOD. For it lacks the knowledge of truth or of Christ, which faith teaches, therefore it is blind and rash fortitude. Wherefore, first of all, a pious person ought to have a right opinion and an intellect informed by faith, according to which the soul may be governed in afflictions, so that it may hope for the best in evils, which faith has dictated and taught. Faith, therefore, is dialectic, by which it conceives the idea of all things to be believed. Hope is Rhetoric, which amplifies, urges, exhorts, and persuades to constancy, so that faith may not succumb in temptation, but may retain the word and firmly adhere to it. This elegantly, according to his custom, the Blessed Theander.

Latin:

Vers. 5. 'Ημεῖς γὰρ πνεύματι ἐκ πίστεως ἐλπίδα δικαιοσύνης ἀπεκδεχόμεθα Nos intra animum per fidem exspectamus spem illam, quæ justitiæ (nempe spirituali) proposita est. Πνεῦμα hic animum interpretor, qui opponitur cuti, in qua est circumcisio.

Spem vero dixit μετωνυμικῶς ipsum præmium, quod speratur, id vero est vita æterna.

Sic spei nomen ponitur & Rom. VIII 24. Coloss. II. 5. 1. Thes. II. 19. 1. Petr. I. 3. & alibi.

Spes justitiæ hic, quæ corona justitia. 2. Tim. IV. 8.

Professionem jam fidei non fuæ tantum, sed & eorum, qui cum ipso erant, fidelium nomine edit Apostolus, quod non per ceremonialia aut moralis legis observantiam, sed per fidem unice spem justitiæ in Spiritu exspectent: eo quod in Christo Jesu, cui soli per fidem adhærent, & cujus justitia se unice niti testantur, ac sperare salutem æternam non valeat quicquam sive circumcisio, & legis, ad quam ea obligabantur, observatio, sive præputium, sed unice fides, quæ per charitatem efficax est.

Subjetum professionis quod concernit: Nos, inquit Apostolus, non Judæos, ut Pareus vult, sed omnes, qui cum ipso erant, fratres intelligens, quorum fides una erat, gemina omnium, qui ἰσότητον fidem acceperant per orbem 2. Petr. I. 1. Non est enim nisi una fides Eph. IV. 5.

Hæc ergo œcumenica & Catholica est fidei professio.

Causa ejus est non caro & sanguis, sed Spiritus Domini Mattb. XVI. 17. quo reguntur fideles, quo certi redduntur de hæreditate cœlesti, quo exspectant eandem atque desiderant Rom. IIX. 23.

Nonnulli Spiritum dici volunt gratiam in Christo, cui caro opponatur Gal. III. 3. id est legalis justitia, quæ carni inhærebat, veluti circumcisio, carni blandiebatur & carnalem fiduciam pariebat, Pareo videtur Spiritus opponi corpori, ut 1. Cor. VII. 34. Eph. IV. 21.

Exspectamus Spiritum, id est, mente & corde nostro: Sed prior explicatio convenientior est, quæ Chrysost.

Theophy- lacto, & Oecumenio probata. Medium, quo concludive: non circumcisio aut aliæ ceremoniæ, non opera legis moralis. Confer simile decretum AB.

XV. 11. Objectum est ἐλπὶς δικαιοσύνης spes justitiæ, id est speratum bonum vel hæreditas cœlestis per Metonymiam, ut Col.

I. 5. non justitiæ nostræ: Hæc enim in præsenti cum operibus quibusvis moralibus excluditur, sed justitiæ Christi per fidem apprehensæ gratia exspectatur.

Non enim propria nostra justitia salvamur, sed in Domino justitiam habemus, in Domino justificatur omne semen Israel Es. XLV. vers.

24. 26. Corona ergo gloria est spes justitiæ fidei 2.

Timoth. IV. vers.

6. Alii exponunt, nos exspectamus spem justitiæ ex fide, nos confitemur, justitiam nos habere, & habituros esse ex fide & non ex lege: Ut verbo exspectamus, non tam spes rei futuræ, quam fiducia præsentis justitiæ fidei notetur.

Crotius per hypallagen justitiam spei, id est speratam intelligi posse putat: Sed ea opus non est. Nam Apostolus fidem suam per antithesin professus adversus Pseudo-Apostolorum hæresin, non modo justificationem sed & salutem æternam se non nisi fide consequi dicit.

Fidem & spem ratione

objecti concinne B. Lutherus ita hic distinguit: Fi- des habet objectum veritatem, cui docet certo & firmiter adhærendum esse, & intuetur in verbum rei seu promissionis rerum. Spes habet objectum bo- nitatem, & intuetur in rem verbi, hoc est in rem promissam seu in res sperandas, quas fides dictavit suscipiendas. Differenotat & subjecto; quia fides est (etiam) in intellectu, spes in voluntate: & of- ficio; quia fides dictat, dirigit, docet, estque no- titia, (nec tamen sola) spes exhortatio est, quia exsuscitat animum, ut sit fultus & erectus, ut au- deat, ferat, perduret in malis, ac in illis expectet meliora: & ordine; quia fides est ante omnem tribulationem, initium vitæ Ebr. XI. spes posterior ex tribulationibus parta Roman. V. & contrariis; quia fides inquit Doctor & Judex est pugnans con- tra errores & hæreses, judicans spiritus & doctrinas. Spes Imperator seu Dux belli est, pugnans contra tribulationem, crucem, impatientiam, tristitiam, pusillanimitatem, desperationem, blasphemiam, & expectat bona sub malis. Quando igitur fide in ver- bum DEI edoctus apprehendo Christum, & tota fiducia cordis (quod tamen sine voluntate fieri non potest) credo in eum, hac notitia justus sum. Sic fide seu hac justitia me justificato, statim venit Diabo- lus mendacii pater, & nititur extinguere fidem dolis, hoc est mendacio, erroribus, hæresibus. Dein- de quia homicida est, conatur eam etiam vi op- primere. Ibi spes luctans apprehendit rem fide dicta- tam, sit animosa & vincit Diabolum, impugnan- tem fidem, quo victo, sequitur pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Reipsa igitur fides & spes vix dis- cerni possunt, & tamen est aliquod discrimen inter ipsas. Sicut in politia prudentia sine fortitudine vana est. Ita fides in Theologia sine spe nihil est, quia spes fert & perdurat in malis, ac vincit ea. Et vicissim: Sicut fortitudo sine prudentia teme- ritas est; Ita spes sine fide præsumptio in Spiritu & tentatio DEI est. Caret enim notitia veritatis vel Christi, quam fides docet, ideo cæca & temera- ria fortitudo est. Quare primum omnium pius habere debet rectam opinionem, & intellectum fidei informatum, secundum quem in afflictioni- bus regatur animus, ut speret in malis optima, quæ fides dictavit & docuit. Fides igitur est dialectica, qua concipit ideam omnium credendorum. Spes Rhetorica, quæ amplificat, urget, exhortatur & persuadet ad constantiam, ne fides in tentatione succumbat, sed retineat verbum, & firmiter illi adhæreat. Hæc eleganter pro more suo Beat. Theander.

## 5:6
V. 6. (For in Christ Jesus) That is, in the law of Christ. Thus also Moses is often put for the law.

(Neither circumcision avails anything) And consequently neither do other precepts of the law. For the Jews call the precept of circumcision the chief and stable one, because this alone of so many commanding precepts, if it is omitted, has the added penalty of ἐξολοθρεύσεως (excision) of that Angel who had the power of cutting off the uncircumcised, a power which Origen says was destroyed by Christ, Against Celsus IV.

(Nor uncircumcision) He says this for this reason, lest anyone, because he is uncircumcised, think himself more pleasing to God.

(But faith working through love) Faith here also comprehends hope, to which if love that works is added, nothing more is desired for obtaining eternal salvation: and clearly πίσις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργεμένη (faith working through love) is worth the same as a new creation: below VI. 15. and the observation of the precepts of God, namely the Evangelical ones, 1 Cor. VII. 19. 1 John II. 3. that is, in Christianity, the whole thing.

The reason for the profession is rendered: because in Christ Jesus and the grace exhibited in him, external things avail nothing, whatever they may be, neither the work of circumcision nor any other works of ours, however good and excellent, just as neither does uncircumcision harm anything: but faith alone avails, which works through charity. That 'in Christ Jesus' Grotius wrongly explains concerning the law of Christ, calling it another law, the same as the law of Moses, and a more perfect one, which error we noted above: Pareus understands it concerning the kingdom of Christ, but here it is a matter of the cause of justification and salvation, not of the quality of the subjects of the kingdom of Christ. Crocius observes that the Apostle does not say: 'It never availed,' but, 'it avails nothing,' namely, after the death of Christ. But circumcision is not viewed here as a sacrament, but as a work of the law, and in Christ Jesus there were also fathers in the Old Testament, to whom that external work also availed nothing, or any legal observation according to the Apostolic definition, Acts XV. 10. And Crocius himself acknowledges this when he adds what follows: When the Apostle names circumcision, he understands the whole apparatus of legal ceremonies joined with it. Among men it availed something because of the perverse opinion of some who had been converted to Christ from circumcision. Before God it availed nothing at all, no righteousness was to be hoped for from it, not a part of righteousness. Who also praised the ancients for this opinion: Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius interpret: Just as circumcision in the Church of Christ avails nothing for salvation, so neither does uncircumcision harm. Finally, he adds and approves the testimonies of his own: Aretius and Pareus hold this, that uncircumcision avails nothing, that is, does not harm salvation. That it avails nothing, that is, contributes nothing to salvation, is clear by itself. Therefore, the Apostle teaches that faith alone avails for justification and salvation: he does not say it exists alone, because it is not alone or idle, indeed it is efficacious or industrious through charity toward God and neighbor; but that it alone avails in Christ Jesus. For it alone apprehends the righteousness of Christ, it alone embraces the grace exhibited in Christ, or the remission of sins. This is the work of faith, not indeed of any work or act of ours commanded by the law. He does not say, 'faith avails, by which it is industrious through charity,' but 'which is industrious.' He does not say, as the Blessed Luther notes. fol. 131. faith, which justifies through love; nor does he say, faith, by which it makes one pleasing through love: Much less does he say: love makes one pleasing: But he says thus, faith which works through love. He says that works are done from faith through love, not that a man is justified through love. But who is so unrefined a grammarian, who does not understand from the force of the words, that to be justified is one thing, to work is another? For the words of Paul are clear and open, faith works through love. Which he observes against the Papist Sophists, who wish it to be implied here that faith does not justify, unless it is informed by love, as if he were saying, faith does not justify, nay it is nothing, unless operative love approaches to inform the faith. Furthermore, as Luther says again, Paul here does not make faith unformed, and as it were a crude chaos, of which there is nothing, neither to be nor to act, but he attributes the operation itself to faith, and not to love. Not feigning a certain crude and unformed quality, but bringing forward an efficacious and industrious quiddity, and as it were a substance or (as they call it) a substantial form. For he does not say, love is efficacious, but faith is efficacious. Love does not work, but faith works. Concerning this rancid and absurd distinction of the Papists between unformed and formed faith, we have spoken in Article VI. c. I. th. 10. of the Exegesis of the Augustan Confession. The Apostle rejects that which is unformed, which is without love, when he teaches that faith works through love. For whatever works through love, that must be joined with love. But true and living faith works through love, of which faith it is the property to be δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη,

from it, the working through love cannot be separated. But this is proper to the faith which is valid in Christ Jesus. The Apostle also refutes a formed faith, since he teaches that faith does not receive its form or is formed through love, but that it is through love that it is industrious or effective. Therefore, it is certain that love and works do not constitute faith, but follow it, and flow from the same.

The passive interpretation of the word 'works' in the Vulgate, which some Papists hold, renders the Vulgate barbaric. The interpreter is without cause, which Justinianus himself disapproves; the word ἐνεργουμένη occurs actively in the New Testament elsewhere Rom. 7, 5 , 2. Cor. 4, 12 , Eph. 3, 20 , Col. 1, 29 , 1. Thess. 2, 13 , 2. Thess. 2, 7 , Jac. 5, 16 . Yet it is nowhere used passively.

In all these places, says B. Johannes Major in his disputation on this passage, page 7, the word is read as middle, but only in an Active signification, which is so manifest that nothing is more manifest. For God and His power and word act and work, they effect, or have and confer efficacy, they are not acted upon, they are not subject to operation, they are not effected, nor do they receive efficacy from elsewhere, cf. LV. v. 10, 11, 12 . Thus also faith is neither begotten, nor formed, nor fashioned, nor inflamed, nor vivified, nor armed by love, nor in and from love, but it is prior to love (for there is no desire for the unknown), no love begets, kindles, vivifies it, and it is revealed and exerted through it; what is ignored, what is disapproved, that is never loved.

But the more exactly something is known, the more usefully and perfectly it is perceived, the more fervently it is sought when known, and loved when perceived. Whence Salmero writes most ineptly (Tom. XV. disp. 91.) that faith works through love, as if through its form and perfection, from which faith itself also has all its power both in justifying and in performing, and in meriting. These men, by understanding, cause that they understand nothing, as if indeed the τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν [desiring faculty], in which love gives form and power and perfection to the τὸ ἡγεμονικῷ [ruling faculty] in which faith is.

Therefore, it is not as Justinianus says, that faith works through love as through its form. For Scripture never established that as the form of faith.

And the Apostle here excludes love, and whatever things are of the law, from the circle of justification and salvation Gal. 2, 16 , Rom. 3, 28 , and there is a perpetual ἀντίθεσις [opposition] here between faith and works, and thus also love.

But one of opposites is not the form of the other opposite.

Love is from faith 1. Tim. 1, 5 , therefore it cannot be the form of faith. For an effect cannot be the form of a cause, nor does it follow that faith works through love.

Therefore as through a form. The soul also works through the body, yet the body is not the form of the soul.

Fire works through heat, not therefore is heat the form of fire. The sun works through light, but shall we call light the form of the sun?

Bellarminus himself acknowledges that faith without love is not defined as faith.

How therefore is love a form? For a form gives being to a thing.

See book II. on justification, ch. 4. Faith is not from the law.

Therefore the Apostle says that the law is not from faith Gal. 3, 12 . But love is from the law, because it consists entirely in working according to the law. Faith is from the Gospel, but love is not.

For this is the fulfillment of the law. How therefore can love be established as the form of faith? Grotius, acting like a Papist, joins love to faith for obtaining eternal salvation, and says that it comprehends hope.

But it appears that neither is faith comprehended under hope in this Aphorism, and the Apostle openly distinguishes love from faith. We do not obtain eternal salvation through our love or charity, but by faith alone or the grace of GOD apprehended through faith Eph. 2, 8, 9 . Our love, by which we love both God and neighbor, is a fruit of faith 1. Tim. 1, 5 , and a consequence, not an antecedent, of justification. Therefore it is not the cause of our justification, and thus not of salvation.

For the causes of justification and salvation are the same. As to the passage Gal. 6, 15 καινὴ κτίσις [new creature], it can likewise be understood of faith, by metonymy by way of parallel, because regeneration, which is a new creation, is the cause of faith; unless 'new creature' is bound subjectively, that is, the man who is reborn and renewed by the Spirit of GOD to faith in Christ.

The sense therefore is, if the word καινὴ κτίσις is taken in the abstract for regeneration or for faith, circumcision, which the Pseudo-Apostles required for the same, contributes nothing to the state of grace or justification and salvation AB , nor does uncircumcision hinder it, which the same men thought: But that here only regeneration is valid, by which we are converted from infidelity to faith through the Holy Spirit, and are transferred from spiritual death to spiritual life, and become a new creature in Christ 2. Cor. 5, 17 . But if one wishes to understand a reborn man in the concrete, it is indicated that Christ does not regard whether one obtains grace and salvation through Christ, whether he be circumcised or uncircumcised, provided he be reborn and faithful.

Others respond that the reason for that passage is different: because there he had dealt with the mortification of the flesh, and with the debt of daily sanctification, and thus the renewal of morals is the adequate object of the discourse: whence the phrase of the underlying life ought to be restricted in Christ Jesus, whereas here the underlying matter is justification and salvation. Thus B. Hülfemannus in Vindicat, ἀνεκδότοις §. 68. But as to the other passage 1. Cor. 7, 18 , it is in the open, that it does not deal with the business or causes of justification and salvation, but that it is taught that everyone ought to persist in his own state, as he has been called: for those external things are nothing or profit nothing, such as circumcision or uncircumcision, but τήρησιν ἐντολῶν θεοῦ [keeping of the commandments of God], to which keeping, however, S. John requires faith primarily, For this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another 1. Epist. 3, 23 . Here the Novator Calixtines also pour cold water on the Papists, contending that faith justifies, insofar as it exerts itself through love, and works; and requiring love for that, so that faith may become alive, as if faith were not alive in itself and by itself, by which it apprehends the grace of God and the merit of Christ, but only then attains life when it is informed by love.

See Hornejus in his disputation on the justification of faith, not of any kind, but that which works through love, and he repeats and brings forward th. CX. CXXVI. and what we have said about these in Harmon. Calixt. Hæret, sect. II. ch. VI. and VII. Which subversion of the articles on justification the Apostle here expressly refuted in the Pseudo-Apostles, and pronounced an anathema against them for the same.

Since, namely, our justification and salvation are not ascribed to Christ alone or to the obedience of Christ, but also to love or our works, not to faith in Christ alone, but together with faith to the love of God and neighbor, or to the works of the law: and thus to faith, not as it apprehends the obedience of Christ, and relies solely on that in the judgment of GOD, but as it exerts itself through love, and is industrious in the love of GOD and neighbor. To which Hornejan depravity B. D. Johannes Major, Senior Theologian of Jena, and the 86th year being now in his year, he opposed the praised dissertation on this passage, inasmuch as it was especially abused with Calixtus.

Hornejus, to bring forward the Majorism of that ancient Witebergensian Major's heterodoxy concerning the necessity of good works for salvation, along with other writings, asserted that faith is taken here not in the special sense, in which it is justice and saving, but in the general meaning, Rom. 1, v. 8, Gal. 6, v. 20, for the doctrine divinely revealed, which Paul had delivered to the Galatians through the preaching of the Gospel, to whom he had proposed the faith which is believed, from which and through which not only sin, and the death and damnation which lies upon it, but also the remedy, and the justice, life, and salvation which emerges from it, is recognized, and is declared and exhibited by the duties and works of love, neither admitting that this treats of justification or salvation, but of Christianity, namely that Christ, in those who are to be converted and who have been converted to Him, neither has regard for, nor intends, nor esteems circumcision or uncircumcision, but solely attends to and requires faith, that it may be rightly recognized, and love, that it may be obeyed. I. v. 8. Galatians VI. verse 20 [sic]. Regarding the divinely revealed doctrine which Paul delivered to the Galatians through the proclamation of the Gospel, to whom he had proposed the faith which is believed, from which and through which not only sin, and the death and damnation which weigh upon it, but also the remedy, and the righteousness, life, and salvation which emerge from it, are recognized, and are declared and exhibited by the duties and works of love; and not admitting that this concerns justification or salvation, but rather Christianity, namely that Christ, in those being converted and those converted to Him, neither considers, nor intends, nor values circumcision or uncircumcision, but solely attends to and requires faith, so that He may be rightly acknowledged, and love, so that He may be obeyed.

Concerning that faith, he says, page 14, he speaks, not by which one embraces Christ with trust, but by which one embraces one's neighbor with love, which is done by man, not in the judgment set before GOD, laboring under the evil of sin, bearing the wrath of GOD, feeling comfort, desiring pardon and grace, but in the world conversing with others, bound under the law of love, he is held to wish well, and to do well, not to hinder salvation, but to gain them for Christ.

Following him in that part, the blessed one and Megalandrus, who, Paul says, fol. 131, does not treat in this place of what faith is, or what it avails before GOD, I say he does not dispute about justification.

For he had treated this prolixly above, but concludes briefly as if with an epiphonema, what the Christian life itself is, saying: in Christ JESUS neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love, that is, faith not feigned, nor hypocritical, but true and living, it is that which exercises and urges works through love.

Which the blessed Luther observed against the sophisms of the Papists, as the blessed Doctor Major observed against the sophisms of the Innovators.

For what kind of dialectic, he says, would that be: Man is soul and body, and cannot exist without soul and body. Therefore the body understands, the soul alone does not understand.

The same dialectic is: The Christian life is faith and love, or faith effective through love. Therefore love justifies, not faith alone.

Concerning which, let those things be compared which he has in Tom. VII, fol. 445.

In the First Writing on the Sophistry of the Adversaries in the Article on justification, where the blessed Luther teaches how the syncretizing Papists wished to join this passage with the Apostolic sentence of Rom. 3 concerning justification, so that they might obtain that faith, insofar as it is operative through love, justifies, which was also the artifice and design of the modern syncretists Calixtus and Hornejus.

Although indeed this explanation of the Apostolic Aphorism is not inappropriate, because here the Christian life, which consists without circumcision, is described, since it is not reproved by Hornejus himself, th. 1, he says:

The whole Christian doctrine is contained in these two heads: 1. Faith in GOD and Christ His Son; 2. Love of GOD and neighbor, or, in a word, faith working through love, Gal. 5, v. 6.

Nevertheless, the sophism of the adversaries can be resolved by faith, even if it be admitted that this place also treats of justifying faith, and of justification and salvation itself, which seems to us truly consistent.

Because the Apostle discourses not only of excluding the necessity of circumcision, but of excluding any of our works whatsoever from the circle of justification, and explains the momentum of the cause, namely, how much it matters for the merit of Christ not to be evacuated, for the grace of GOD not to be overturned, so that justification and salvation may be vindicated for faith alone, with all works of the law, both moral and especially ceremonial, excluded. To this, by the force of the connection with the preceding verse, he renders the reason in this aphorism, why the hope of justice is sought through faith alone, which indeed pertains to justification and salvation. Finally, with this epiphonema the Apostle concludes the entire dispute against the Pseudo-Apostles, who, along with faith, required for justification and salvation not only circumcision and the observation of other Levitical ceremonies, but also the observation of the moral law as altogether necessary, and prepares for himself an approach to the other part of the epistle, namely the parenetic, which so coheres with the didactic, that love flows with faith, and thus flows and redounds from it; having briefly embraced the sum of the matter, that indeed neither love, in which the moral law consists, nor faith with love in Christ JESUS avails for salvation, nor circumcision itself; or any work whatsoever of the ceremonial law, but faith alone.

But he dilutes that caution, and puts to flight the persuasion of hypocrites, as if true faith could exist without love, and therefore for their sake he adds faith not hypocritical but truly living, which is effective through love; and which is the sign and mark of the life of faith, is required, not because love bestows life upon faith, which life is not lacking when it apprehends Christ, for this is not the work of dead faith, but of living, which draws life and the power of vivifying solely from Christ into whom it is carried, but because love demonstrates the life of faith as a living body is recognized by respiration, Jac.

II, last. Dead faith, says the blessed Major, by which is opposed the living, that is, which has its life, flower, and vigor from Christ, through Christ, and in Christ, and is received either from empty persuasion, or from the external profession of faith alone, is no more faith than a corpse is a man.

Nor is that elucidation of the blessed Major, page 8, foreign to this sense, that in this aphorism, from uncircumcision no less than from circumcision, is taken away before Christ in His kingdom, both of grace and of glory, the ἰσχύς, force, value, worth, weight, utility, esteem, respect, and is assigned to faith.

Nor does the explanation of the blessed Luther disagree, as to the principal cause: This is, he says, only to say, whoever wishes to be truly Christian, or in the kingdom of Christ, must be a believer. But he does not truly believe, if the works of love do not follow faith. And thus on both sides, from the right and from the left, he excludes hypocrites from the kingdom of Christ.

From the left, Jews and workers, saying, in Christ neither circumcision, that is, no works, no worship, no manner of life at all, but faith alone avails without trust in works. From the right, the slothful and inert and idle, because they say: if faith justifies without works, then let us do nothing. But let us only believe and do what we wish.

Not so the impious, says Paul. It is true that faith alone justifies without works. But I speak of true faith, which after it has justified, does not snore idle, but is operative through love.

The blessed Brentius teaches that it is indeed explained here in very few words, in what true Christianity consists (which is not denied by us either), but he observes, (missing) Paul does not add this appendix concerning efficacy through charity because he feels that faith justifies on account of works. For he does not say: faith, which justifies through love, but [he says it] to refute both hypocrites and the impudent or impenitent.

Blessed Chemnitius argues in XIII on justification, exclusive in the article of justification & salvation, thesis 17.

Rightly, he says, did Luther act, in that at the Diet of Ratisbon he refused to admit that cothurnus [buskin/mask]: That faith justifies which becomes efficacious through charity (in the Papistic sense, that is, by which it is efficacious). It is indeed true that justifying faith is efficacious through charity, but it does not justify by that reason, nor by that respect by which it works, but by which it apprehends the merit of Christ alone, and opposes that to the judgment of God. And in the examination of the Council of Trent on justification, p. 344: Nor do we attribute justification to an idle or dead faith, but we say that faith, if it is true and living, is not idle, but efficacious through charity.

But the life which faith imparts to those who apprehend it, it does not borrow or receive from charity, but from Christ, whom it embraces, who is our life and salvation. Wherefore the blessed Luther rightly taught that the Apostle is not here defining what justifying faith is, but is describing faith by its effect, that in believers it does not become idle or dead, but like a good tree brings forth good fruits.

Cf. Jac. Heerbrand, disp. on the justification of the sinful man, p. 304, 311.

Tilemann Heshusius in this place. Balthasar Menzer, disp. V against Pistet, where he notes that this saying is opposed both to laborious justiciaries and to the slothful and inert, as if he were saying: in Christ, works do not avail, nor any cult, such as circumcision and the like, but only faith.

And yet that faith is not idle; truly, after it has justified, by apprehending Christ (which is the life of justifying faith), it is industrious and efficacious and exerts itself through charity or love, which is its effect or fruit and at the same time its witness. Rightly, therefore, also observed by the blessed Hülsemann in his Vindiciae ἀνενδοτοις [unyielding defenses] S.

LXIIX. That epithet, "working through charity," is attributed to faith which has already justified, not attributed to faith which is yet to justify, much less is it the form or essence of justifying faith: 1. Because the Apostle had already expressly described the office and quality of faith justifying before God in chapters 2 and 3, so that it would not be necessary, nor even probable, that the Apostle would act here a second time concerning the office of faith toward God in accepting the benefit of justification. 2. He had described in chapter 3, v. 12 & 13, the nature and quality of faith in the office of justifying privatively, that justifying faith has nothing in common with works in the office of justifying.

The law is not of faith, he says, but whoever shall do these things shall live by them; that it does not signify the same thing in another Greek phrase, that it does not partake of its form and essential qualities. Luther in his Commentary on this place shows this in many ways, and it is evident from parallels: to be of God, to be of the Devil, to be of the world, John VIII, verse 46.

1. John IV, verse 6. John XV, 19. That is, to imitate the nature of God, the nature of the Devil, the nature of the world.

Therefore, the Apostle by that attribute (to work through charity) by no means describes the form in the office of justifying faith by which it justifies, but another office of it, namely gratitude toward God and utility toward men. 3. This end of the added periphrasis or epithet is evident from the following verse 13: you have been called to liberty, only do not take this liberty as an occasion for sinning, namely as the Apostle is accustomed to treat distinct effects of faith distinctly, as is evident from the connection of chapter XI.

XII, XIII to the Romans; he rendered this periphrasis of faith in such a way that he might pave the way for dealing with the other office of faith also, toward men, which he pursues to verse 13 of this chapter until the end of the epistle, namely that it is of the nature of true faith not only to apprehend justice, but also to work through charity; but that working through charity concurs to the apprehension or acquisition of justice and the remission of sins, this can no more be gathered from this periphrasis: "faith which works through charity," than it can be gathered: the periphrasis of Mary Magdalene, whose mention is made in the resurrection of Christ, namely that she was the one of Mark XVI, 9, from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons, concurred to visiting the body of Christ in the sepulcher.

And there are six hundred such epithets of subjects which in no way concur to that effect which is predicated of those subjects whose epithets they are, but are added for other specifying causes, namely, and for distinguishing the subjects from other subjects, see some examples Job I, verse 41, 43, 45, 46. Thus, when it is said that in Christ JESUS nothing avails but faith, which is efficacious through charity, it cannot be proved by any suitable reason that that epithet, "to work through charity," concurs to the value in Christ Jesus, but this follows: that the epithet is specifying that faith which avails in Christ Jesus, and distinguishing it from imaginary or dead faith. This the blessed

Hülsemann, whom we cite for the sake of harmony; as one who acknowledges with us, and it must be acknowledged entirely, that "to avail in Christ Jesus" in this place is the same as to avail for justifying and saving, but he denies that that epithet of faith, "to work through charity," concurs to justification: And the blessed

Luther, when he denies that the Apostle is here teaching what faith avails before GOD, speaks of this epithet, "to work through charity," that it does not concur to the form of faith so that it may avail in Christ Jesus; but it is the epithet of that faith which avails in Christ JESUS. Therefore faith and charity remain distinct, the predicates of both remain distinct: faith in Christ alone avails for justification and salvation, not charity; that is, it alone is justificatory and salvific. Charity is not justificatory and salvific, but follows justifying faith, which through the same exerts itself and is industrious, occupied in the love of GOD and neighbor, in those who have apprehended and obtained grace and the remission of sins through Christ by faith.

Which the blessed Jacob Andreae excellently explained thus in his disp. on the justification of the sinful man before GOD, page 406. They err with their whole heaven who opine that charity is from the number of those things which confer salvation.

When therefore the Apostle (Gal. V) writes, in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love: he did not wish to define what faith is, but teaches that in believers it does not become idle or dead. For the true, sufficient, and perfect definition or description of justifying faith is that by which it is said: Faith is not only historical knowledge about Christ, but also a true and certain trust, which the Holy Spirit works in the Elect; by which man, despairing of all his own and others' holiness, places all his justice, which can stand before GOD, in the merit and obedience of Christ alone, on account of whom GOD the Father by mere grace and mercy receives us into favor, remits sins, and pronounces us just. Charity, however, just as it is a virtue distinct from faith, so also charity and works are distinct from faith. Nor does charity bestow anything upon faith, whose being resides in Christ, but faith [bestows] upon charity. For we cannot love [Him] of whose grace we are not certain, but [instead] feel His most present and horrible wrath.

And faith provides [this], by which it establishes that we are loved by God on account of Christ, before we [love] Him.

we have loved.

As it is written: For when we were yet enemies, we were reconciled to God. Wherefore their discourse is dangerous, who say: To believe in God is to love by believing. Which form of speech Scholastic Theologians have abused, and have transferred the honor, which the Holy Spirit attributes to Christ alone, and to His own obedience and merit, to charity and its works, by whose merit one is justified before God.

And although trust in God is never without the love of God, yet it is one thing and signifies one thing to trust in God, and another to love Him. And therefore faith and charity are two diverse and truly distinct virtues. And although their common object is, namely Christ, yet they affect it in different ways.

For faith trusts in Christ, so that through Him or on account of Him it may obtain the remission of sins, and the sinful man may be reconciled with God the Father. But charity does not love Christ so that it may be reconciled to God, but because man has been reconciled through faith on account of Christ, therefore he also begins to love. But this distinction is the more obscure because, since faith and charity are together in time, and therefore always conjoined, they can only be separated by mind and thought.

This, therefore, is the Prophetic, Apostolic, and Catholic doctrine concerning the justification of man before God, by which we teach: that man is justified, that is, pronounced just, and absolved from sins by the mere mercy of God through faith on account of the obedience and merit of the sons of Christ, without any regard for preceding civilly good works, or present or subsequent truly good works.

Wherefore man is justified through faith, and ought not to look at his own infirmity or disposition, which adheres even to the reborn until the danger of death, and which they cannot lay aside as long as they live in this world, nor should he doubt of the grace of God on account of it. See B. Major, p. 33.

In short: the Apostle does not say that faith in Christ Jesus avails for justice and salvation, but that which works through charity, but that which works: nor is it to be understood reduplicatively, but specifically, which sense B. Major does not disapprove, and so his arguments are only opposed in a reduplicative sense v. 9.

Whoever are saved, whenever they are saved, they are saved by faith alone without works; they are not saved by faith working through charity, because this faith in the act of salvation is not alone and naked, but has works necessarily present, adhering, and associated and coupled with it within the course of justification, that is, faith in the act of salvation does not bring before the sight of God works, which have been performed, so that they may be rewarded by justice, but sins, which have been committed, so that they may be remitted by mercy: and in this passage (if I may so speak) faith is conscious to itself in the heart of the suppliant of evil works, which are many and great and proper to men: but of good works, which are either none, or not his own, it truly knows nothing. Evils weigh down the conscience in those who are tempted and set in judgment, good works do not relieve it. All children of God are saved by faith alone without their works. Therefore they are not saved by faith working through charity, namely reduplicatively, that is, as such.

No faith ought to be called justifying & salvific, which either insofar as it is such, that is, which involves a respect of quality and quantity, from which and through which ἐνέργεια, or by reason of its quality or quantity, by which it is to be measured, but insofar as it is this faith and true faith, that is, insofar as it is fixed and leaning only on the Gospel concerning Christ. Faith working through charity is such, that is, it involves a respect of quality and quantity. Therefore it is not to be called salvific and justifying faith.

That faith is, and can and ought to be called salvific, and necessary for salvation, which is distinguished and occupied only in apprehending Christ, and adheres in seeking and embracing His merit. Faith working through charity is not only distinguished in apprehending Christ, but also in loving the neighbor. Therefore it ought not to be called salvific and necessary for salvation ἀκριβῶς, not παχυλῶς, accurately, properly, and distinctly, not confusedly and generally speaking.

Item: Justifying and salvific faith is solicitous about obtaining the remission of sins. Faith through love is not solicitous about the remission of sins, but about performing the obedience or love to be exhibited. Therefore it is not justifying and salvific.

Justifying and salvific faith seeks, finds, obtains, and appropriates the remission of sins (both original and actual) to the believer. Faith working through charity ἐνεργουμένη does not seek, does not find, does not obtain, does not appropriate the remission of sins. Therefore it is not justifying and salvific, namely as such, as it works through charity.

Where faith behaves itself ἐνεργητικῶς and not ὀργανικῶς, there it is not justifying. In operation through charity it behaves itself ἐνεργητικῶς, not ὀργανικῶς. Therefore also from this, action does not belong to faith as an instrument from itself, but from a higher cause, by which it is moved and drawn: And insofar as faith is ἐνεργουμένη δι ἀγάπης, it pertains to the quality, or if you prefer, to the predicament of action, but not indeed of relation.

Whence it is again clear, that it is a virtue and quality, and not indeed a correlative of the Evangelical promise, and in which it trusts.

Finally, whatever faith conjoins the begun obedience, which is ours, in the article or sphere of justification with the imputed obedience, which is Christ's, that is not justifying and salvific. Faith working and busy through charity conjoins begun obedience with imputed. Therefore it is not salvific.

For we would be justified imputatively and inchoatively, which is Popish. Faith active through charity is of renewal and sanctification, not of regeneration and justification, to which those are prior in order, more powerful in degree, more perfect in act, wider in extent. For they are not only in adults, but also together with faith not yet working in minors.

These things B. Major. Which all are most rightly opposed to Hornejus and the Papists in the praised dissertation, and from the same, as now available to few, and inscribed to me by a presbyter of the theologians of our age, when I was still teaching in Danzig, it pleased me to adduce.

We must still speak concerning the Socinians, among whom Crellius in his lectures on this epistle, taken and edited by Schlichtingius, wishes to show here what sort of spiritual worship is that by which righteousness is sought by Christians, namely such as consists chiefly in charity and its works, which is made in place of legal ceremonies, and what sort of faith he himself understands, when he attributes justification to it simply, or with no other thing added, namely such as is, as it were, animated by charity, not therefore that charity and its effects are to be excluded from obtaining justification for us, which by comparison of 1. Cor. VII. 19. 1. Joh. III. 14. Matth. XXV. 34. seqq. and especially Jac. II. 14. 17. seqq. he proves, that they so concur with faith, that faith holds the place of the body, good works the place of the Spirit, as also by the present text, that Paul distinguishes that faith which has the power of justifying from that which has not such power, which difference since it necessarily coheres with true faith, as effect with its proper cause, and so is also necessary for obtaining salvation, he thinks that part is to be taken from the work in accepting that faith to which alone justification is attributed on our part. But where did the Apostle teach that our righteousness is to be sought in spiritual worship? Where, that spiritual worship is made in place of all ceremonies? Those words, in Christ Jesus nothing avails circumcision etc., are rashly asserted to import this. Nor indeed is faith or even charity in place of legal ceremonies; and since in the Old Testament faith and charity had their place, indeed sacrifices and circumcision were of no avail from the mere work performed, as the scholastics are wont to speak barbarously: nor did faith succeed in the place of ceremonies in the New Testament, but Christ, whose shadow those things were. Furthermore, because justification is attributed simply to faith on our part, not only with no other thing added, but with all others excluded, so that justifying and saving faith is opposed to charity and works, faith, in so far as it justifies, cannot be understood as being animated by charity; just as faith cannot be animated by charity, seeing that it is its effect. For an effect cannot be the soul of its own cause.

Concerning the passage 1 Cor. 7:19, it has already been noted that nothing is treated there concerning justification; nor are we said to be translated from death to life through charity in 1 John 3:14, but to acknowledge that translation, which is attributed solely to faith, not to charity, John 5:24, Hab.

2:4, Rom. 1:17, Gal. 3:11, Heb. 10:38, Eph. 2:8.

But in Matt. 25:34 ff., good works are designated not as the cause of blessedness, but as signs of saving faith, to be produced in the process of the final judgment, James ch. 2. Nor is it a question of the justification of a sinful man before God, but of the demonstration of justification before men, and the power of saving is denied to faith that is not true, but only hypocritical, which, being destitute of works, is dead in itself, not that it receives life from works, because it has true life from Christ alone, but that without them it lives as little as a body lives without respiration and motion: Whence the Holy Spirit does not join faith to the body, and good works to the spirit, but faith to the soul, from which is the life of the natural body, as from faith is the spiritual life to the reborn man, Hab.

2: 4. But he compares good works and charity to respiration, which he understands by the spirit (τὸ πνεῦμα).

Paul, however, as far as this passage is concerned, distinguishes faith which has justifying power from that which does not have it, but [shows it] through an external mark and fruit (γνώρισμα), just as a good tree is known by its fruits, both because the internal and essential difference of faith had already been sufficiently declared in the treatment of the nature and proper object of justifying faith as such, and because he had already decided to deal with it, how faith exercises itself in the second moment, and demonstrates itself outwardly.

For faith has a twofold energy (ἐνέργειαν), the first internal, when it extends itself to Christ, and apprehends his satisfaction and merit, in which it then has life itself, and brings life to the subject man, otherwise dead in sins.

For in Christ, who is true God and eternal life, it apprehends life, and appropriates it to the believer: the other external, when it exerts itself through charity toward God and neighbor, and demonstrates and shows itself to be not dead, but truly alive, both to the believers themselves and to others.

By the former, faith rises to Christ, as its own proper object and correlate, and looks upon him and apprehends him trustfully in the promise of the Gospel, John 6:4, ch.

3:14, 15. By the latter, it lowers itself to the neighbor, and does him good through charity, indeed it is also raised to God, but with the weak wings of love, which it is bound to love with all its heart, with all its soul, and with all its strength, but is by no means able to do as it ought.

Whence, when it is asked by virtue of which energy it justifies, the answer is ready, that faith does not justify by that operation by which it lowers itself through charity to relieve the need of the neighbor, or even attempts to ascend to God, and to embrace him with the love that God requires, but by the other, by which, rising to Jesus Christ, as the throne of grace and Mediator of the human race, it apprehends him without the aid of annexed charity; namely, by the saving look at Christ the Mediator, even if it is not meanwhile separated from charity, but exerts itself through the same for the praise of God and the use of the neighbor, yet so that in that arduous and divine act of justification faith looks not to charity, not to the works of charity, nay, not even to itself, but solely to Jesus Christ, and thus justifies and saves man in God's sight, not by the merit of charity or works, or by its own proper virtue, but solely by the obedience of Christ, which it apprehends, Rom.

Latin:

V. 6. Ἐν γὰρ χρισῷ Ἰησοῦ) Id est, in lege Christi. Sic & Moses pro lege sæpe ponitur.

Οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει) Ac proinde nec alia legis præ- cepta. Nam præceptum circumcisionis Judæi præcipuum ac stabile vocant, quia hoc solum de tot præceptis juben- tibus si omittatur, pœnam habet additam ἐξολοθρεύσεως Angeli illius, qui vim habebat exscindendi non circumci- sos, vim a Christo destructam ait Origenes contra Celsum IV.

Οὔτε ἀκροβυςία) Hoc ideo dicit, ne quis ob id, quod incircumcisus est, Deo se gratiorem putet.

Ἀλλὰ πίσις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργεμένη) Fides hic etiam spem comprehendit, quibus si accedat dilectio operans, nihil desideratur amplius ad obtinendam salutem æternam: pla- neque idem valet πίσις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργεμένη, quod nova creatio: infra VI. 15. & observatio præceptorum Dei, nempe Evangelicorum, 1. Cor. VII. 19. 1. Joh. II. 3. hoc est in Christianismo τὸ πᾶν.

Ratio professionis redditur: quia in Christo Je- su & gratia in ipso exhibita nihil valent externa, quæcunque illa sint, nihil circumcisionis opus aut ulla alia opera nostra quomodocunque bona & præstantia, sicut nec præputium quicquam no- cet: sed unice valet fides, qua per charitatem ope- ratur. Illud in Christo Jesu perperam Grotius de Christi lege explicat, aliam eandem a Mosis lege, eamque perfectiorem vocans, quem errorem su- pra notavimus: Pareus de regno Christi intelligit, sed de justificationis ac salutis causa, non de qualita- te subditorum regni Christi hic agitur. Crocius obser- vat, quod non dicat Apostolus: Nihil unquam valuit, sed, nihil valet scil. post Christi mortem. At circumcisio hic non spectatur ut sacramentum, sed ut opus legis, & in Christo Jesu fuere etiam patres in Veteri Testamento, quibus etiam nihil valuit externum illud opus, vel ulla legalis obser- vatio secundum definitionem Apostolicam, Act. XV. 10. Idque agnoscit Crocius ipse, cum addit quæ sequuntur: Circumcisionem cum Apostolus nomi- nat, intelligit totum ceremoniarum legalium appa- ratum cum ea conjunctum. Apud homines aliquid valebat ex prava aliquorum opinione, qui ex cir- cumcisione ad Christum erant conversi. Apud Deum nil. quicquam valebat, non inde speranda justitia, non pars justitiæ. Qui etiam in eam sententiam laudavit veteres: Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius interpretantur: Sicut circumcisio in Christi Ecclesia non valet quicquam ad salutem, sic neque nocere præputium. Denique addit & appro- bat suffragia suorum: Aretius & Pareus hoc te- nent, quod præputium nil valeat, id est, non noceat saluti. Quod nihil valeat, id est, nihil ad salutem conferat, perse patet. Fidem ergo solam valere ad justificationem & salutem Apostolus docet: non ait solam existere, quia sola vel otiosa non est, imo per charitatem adversus Deum & proximum effi- cax vel operosa est; sed solam valere in Christo Jesu. Ea enim sola apprehendit Christi justitiam, ea sola gratiam in Christo exhibitam, vel remissio- nem peccatorum amplectitur. Hoc fidei est, non vero ullius operis vel actus nostri a lege imperati. Non ait, fides valet, qua operosa est per chari- tatem, sed quæ operosa est. Non dicit, ut Beat. Lutherus notat. fol. 131. fides, quæ per charitatem justificat; nec dicit, fides, qua per charitatem gratum facit: Multo minus dicit: charitas gratum facit: Sed sic dicit, fides quæ per charitatem operatur. Opera fieri dicit ex fide per charitatem, non justifi- ficari hominem per charitatem. At quis est tam ru- dis Grammaticus, qui non ex vocabulorum virtute intelligat, aliud esse justificari, aliud operari? Clara enim & aperta sunt verba Pauli, fides per charita- tem operatur. Quæ observat adversus Sophistas Pontificios, qui fidem non justificare, nisi sit infor- mata per charitatem, hic innui volunt, quasi dicat, fides non justificat, imo nihil est, nisi accedat ope- ratrix charitas quæ fidem informet. Porro ut ite- rum Lutherus, Paulus hic non facit fidem in- formem, & rude velut chaos, cujus nihil sit neque esse neque agere, sed operationem ipsam tribuit fidei, & non charitati. Non fingens rudem quandam & informem qualitatem, sed afferens efficacem & opero- sam quidditatem, ac velut substantiam seu formam (ut vocant) substantialem. Non enim dicit, chari- tas est efficax, sed fides est efficax. Non charitas ope- ratur, sed fides operatur. De hac Pontificiorum rancida & absurda distinctione inter fidem infor- mam & formatam diximus Articulo VI. c. I. th. 10. Exegem. Augustan. Confess. Informem, quæ sine charitate sit, profligat Apostolus, cum fidem docet per charitatem operari. Quicquid enim per charitatem operatur, id cum charitate con- junctum esse oportet. At vera & viva fides operatur per charitatem, cujuscunque fidei proprium est, esse δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη,

ab ea τὸ operari per charitatem separari non potest. At fidei, quæ in Christo Jesu valet, hoc proprium est. Formatam etiam fidem Apostolus refellit, cum non per charitatem formam suam accipere fidem vel formari, sed per charitatem operosam vel efficacem esse docet. Charitatem ergo & opera, non fidem constituere, sed consequi, & ex eadem fluere certum est.

Passiva vocis operatur in Vulgata interpretatio, quam Papistæ nonnulli tenent, barbarum reddit vulgatum. Interpretem citra causam, quam Justinianus ipse improbat, vox ἐνεργουμένη active in Novo Testamento alibi occurrit Rom. VII. 5. 2. Cor. IV. 12. Eph. III. 20. Col. I. 29. 1. Thessal. II. 13. 2. Thess. II. vers. 7. Jac. V. 16. Nusquam tamen passive adhibetur.

In bis locis universis, inquit B. Johannes Major disp. in hoc loco pag. 7. legitur verbum medium, sed non nisi in significatione Activa, quod tam manifestum, ut nihil manifestius. Deus enim ejusque virtus & verbum agunt & operantur, efficiunt, sive efficatiam habent & conferunt, non aguntur, non operationi subjacent, non efficiuntur, neque aliunde efficatiam accipiunt, cf. LV. v. 10. 11. 12. Sic etiam fides nec per charitatem, nec in & a charitate gignitur, vel formatur, vel efformatur, vel inflammatur, vel vivificatur, vel armatur, sed prior charitate (ignoti enim nulla cupido) nullus amor eam gignit, accendit, vivificat, & per eam proditur, & exseritur, quod ignoratur, quod improbatur, id nunquam amatur.

Quo vero exactius aliquid cognoscitur, utilius perfectiusque percipitur eo ferventius expetitur cognitum, & diligitur perceptum. Unde ineptissime scribit Salmero (Tom. XV. disp. 91.) fides per dilectionem operatur, tanquam per formam suam & perfectionem, ex qua etiam ipsa fides vim suam totam habet & in justificando & in perpetrando, & in promerendo. Homines isti intelligendo faciunt, ut nihil intelligant, quasi vero τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν, in quo charitas det formam & vim atque perfectionem τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ in quo fides.

Non ergo est, quod Justinianus dicit, fidem operari per charitatem tanquam per formam suam. Nunquam enim eam formam fidei constituit scriptura.

Et Apostolus hic charitatem, & quæcunque legis sunt, a justificationis & salutis circulo excludit Gal. II. 16. Rom. III. 28. ac perpetua hic inter fidem & opera, adeoque & charitatem est ἀντίθεσις.

Oppositorum autem unum non est forma alterius oppositi.

Charitas est ex fide 1. Tim. I. 5. non ergo fidei forma esse potest. Effectus enim nequit esse forma causæ, neque vero sequitur, fides per charitatem operatur.

Ergo ut per formam. Operatur & anima per corpus, nec tamen corpus est forma animæ.

Ignis per calorem operatur, non ideo calor est forma ignis. Sol operatur per lucem, sed non solis formam dicemus lucem?

Agnoscit Bellarminus ipse fidem sine dilectione non definire esse fidem.

Quomodo ergo dilectio forma est? Forma enim dat esse rei.

Videatur libr. II. de justif. cap. 4. Fides non est ex lege.

Ideo Apostolus dicit, legem non esse ex fide Gal. III. 12. Dilectio autem est ex lege, quia tota in operando consistit secundum legem. Fides ex Evangelio est, non vero charitas.

Hæc enim complementum legis est. Quomodo ergo charitas forma fidei statui potest? Grotius Papizans fidei dilectionem jungit ad consequendam æternam salutem, illamque spem comprehendere ait.

Sed nec fidem sub spe in hoc Aphorismo comprehendi apparet, & dilectionem a fide aperte distinguit Apostolus. Non per charitatem vel dilectionem nostram salutem æternam consequimur, sed sola charitate vel gratia DEI per fidem apprehensa Eph. II. 8. 9. Charitas nostra, qua cum Deum tum proximum diligimus, fructus est fidei 1. Tim. I. 5. & consequens non antecedens justificationis. Non ergo causa nostræ justificationis, adeoque nec salutis.

Eadem enim sunt justificationis & salutis causæ. Quod ad locum Gal. VI. 15. καινὴ κτίσις nova creatura potest itidem de fide intelligi, per metonymiam vi paralleli, quia regeneratio, quæ nova creatio est, fidei causa est; nisi subjective ligatur nova creatura, hoc est, homo, qui DEI Spiritu ad fidem in Christum renatus & renovatus est.

Sensus ergo est, si vox καινὴ κτίσις in abstracto accipiatur pro regeneratione aut pro fide, nihil facere ad statum gratiæ vel justificationem ac salutem circumcisionem, quam Pseudo-Apostoli ad eandem requirebant AB. nec eidem quicquam obesse præputium, quod iidem censebant: Sed unice hic valere regenerationem, qua per Spiritum sanctum ab infidelitate ad fidem convertimur, & e morte spirituali ad vitam spiritualem transferimur, ac nova creatura in Christo evadimus 2. Cor. V. 17. Si autem in concreto quis hominem renatum velit intelligere, id indicatur a Christo non respici, ut quis gratiam & salutem consequatur per Christum, sive circumcisus sit, sive præputiatus, dummodo renatus & fidelis sit. Alii respondent, disparem esse rationem illius loci: quia ibi de mortificatione carnis egerat, & de debito sanctificationis quotidianæ, adeoque renovatio morum objectum adæquatum sit sermonis: unde vitæ substratæ phrasis indefinita valere in Christo Jesu refringi debeat, quum contra hic materia substrata fit justificatio & salus.

Ita B. Hülsemannus in Vindicat, ἀνεκδότοις §. 68. Quod autem ad alterum locum 1. Cor. VII. 18. in aprico est, ibi non agi de negotio, vel causis justificationis, ac salutis, sed doceri, quemvis in suo statu persistere debere, prout vocatus est: nihil enim externa illa esse aut prodesse, puta circumcisionem aut præputium, sed τήρησιν ἐντολῶν θεοῦ, observationem mandatorum Dei, ad quam tamen τήρησιν fidem imprimis requirit S. Johannes, Hoc enim est mandatum ejus, ut credamus in nomen Filii ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus nos invicem 1. Epist. III. 23. Frigidam hic Papistis affundunt etiam Novatores Calixtini, fidem justificare contendentes, quatenus per charitatem sese exerit, atque operatur; ac charitatem ad id requirentes, ut fides viva fit, quasi fides in se ac per se viva non sit, qua apprehendit gratiam Dei ac meritum Christi, sed tum demum vitam consequatur cum charitatem informatur.

Vid. Hornejus in disp. de justif. fidei non cujuslibet, sed quæ operatur per charitatem, & iterat. adfert. th. CX. CXXVI. & quæ Harmon. Calixt. Hæret, sect. II. cap. VI. & VII. de his diximus. Quam articuli de justificatione eversionem in Pseudo-Apostolis ex professo hic profligavit Apostolus, eisque anathema ob eandem dixit.

Cum scilicet non soli Christo aut obedientiæ Christi nostra justificatio & salus adscribitur, sed etiam charitati vel operibus nostris non soli fidei in Christum, sed juxta cum fide dilectioni Dei & proximi, vel operibus legis: adeoque fidei, non qua apprehendit obedientiam Christi, eaque in judicio DEI unice nititur, sed qua exerit-se per charitatem, atque operosa est in dilectione DEI & proximi Cui Hornejana depravationi B. D. Johannes Major, Theologus Senior Jenensis, & LXXXVI. annum jam agens, laudatam dissertationem de hoc loco, utpote, quo præcipue abusus est cum Calixto.

Hornejus ad afferendum Majorismum antiqui illius Witebergensis Majoris heterodoxiam de bonorum operum necessitate ad salutem juxta cum aliis scriptis opposuit, fidem hic sumi asserens non in sensu speciali, quo est justitia & salvifica, sed in significatu generali Roman. I. v. 8. Galat. VI. vers. 20. pro doctrina divinitus revelata, quam Paulus per Evangelii præconium Galatis tradidit, quibus fidem, quæ creditur, proposuerat, ex qua & per quam non tantum peccatum, & quæ illi incumbit, mors & damnatio, sed etiam remedium, & quæ ex illo justitia, vita & salus emergit, agnoscitur, & dilectionis officiis & operibus declaratur & exhibetur, neque admittens, hic agi de justificatione vel salute, sed de Christianismo, quod nempe Christus in convertendis & ad se conversis neque rationem habeat, neque intendat aut æstimet circumcisionem vel præputium, sed unice attendat & requirat fidem, ut recte agnoscatur, & dilectionem, ut sibi obtemperetur.

De fide illa, inquit pag. 14. loquitur, non qua Christum fiducia, sed qua proximum charitate completitur, id quod fit ab homine, non in judicio DEI constituto, sub male peccati laborante, iram DEI perferentis, solatium sentiente, veniam & gratiam desiderante, sed in mundo cum aliis conversante, sub lege charitatis obstrictus tenetur bene velle, & bene facere, salutem non impedire, sed Christo eos lucrari.

Sequutus ea in parte o Μακαρίτης et Megalandrum, qui ad hunc locum Paulus, inquit fol. 131. hoc loco non agit, quid sit fides, aut quid coram DEO valeat, non inquam de justificatione disputat.

Hoc enim superius prolixe egerat, sed brevi velut epiphonemate concludit, quid sit ipsa vita Christiana, dicens: in Christo JESU neque circumcisio, neque præputium quicquam valet, sed fides per charitatem operosa, id est, fides non ficta, nec hypocritica, sed vera & vivax, ea est, que exercet & urget opera per charitatem.

Quæ Bcat. Lutherus ad Papistarum, uti Beat. Doct. Major ad Novatorum sophismata propugnanda observavit.

Qualis enim, inquit, esset ea Dialectica: Homo est anima & corpus, nec fine anima & corpore esse potest. Ergo corpus intelligit, anima sola non intelligit.

Eadem Dialectica est: Vita Christiana est fides & charitas seu fides per charitatem efficax. Ergo charitas justificat, non sola fides.

Quo de conferantur, quæ habet Tom. VII. fol. 445.

In der Ersten Schrifft von der Widersacher Sophisteren in dem Artikel von der justification, ubi docet B. Lutherus, quomodo syncretizantes Pontificii hunc locum cum sententia Apostolica Rom. III. de justificatione conjungere in notula conciliatoria voluerint, ut fidem, quatenus per charitatem operosa est, justificare obtinerent, quod etiam modernorum syncretistarum Calixti & Hornejii artificium; & institutum fuit.

Quanquam vero non inconcinna fit hæc Aphorismi Apostolici explicatio, quod hic vita Christiana, quæ sine circumcisione consistit, describatur, cum nec ab ipso Hornejio ea reprobetur, th.

1. ait. Tota doctrina Christiana duobus bisce capitibus continetur 1. Fide in DEUM & Christum Filium ejus; 2. Charitate DEI & proximi, seu, uno verbo, fide per charitatem operante Galat. V. vers. 6.

Expediri tamen fide potest sophisma adversariorum, etiamsi admittatur, de fide justificante, deque ipsa justificatione ac salute hoc etiam loco agi, quod nobis vere consentaneum videtur.

Quia non de excludenda tantum circumcisione necessitate, sed de excludendis quibusvis operibus nostris a justificationis circulo disserit Apostolus, & momentum causæ exponit, quanti scilicet intersit ad meritum Christi non evacuandum, gratiam DEI non evertendam, ut fidei soli justificatio & salus vindicetur exclusis operibus universis legis tum moralis, tum imprimis ceremonialis. Ad hæc vi συνεχείας cum versu præcedenti rationem reddit hoc aphorismo, cur per solam fidem expetetur spes justitiæ, quod utique ad justificationem & salutem spectat. Denique hoc epiphonemate concludit Apostolus universam disputationem adversus Pseudo-Apostolos, qui juxta cum fide ad justificationem & salutem requirebant non tantum circumcisionem, & aliarum ceremoniarum Leviticarum, sed etiam legis moralis observationem ceu omnino necessariam, aditumque sibi parat ad alteram partem epistolæ paræneticam nempe, quæ cum didactica ita cohæret, ut cum fide charitas, & ita ex eadem fluit, ut charitas ex fide fluit & redundat; breviter complexus summam rei, quod nempe non dilectio in qua consistit lex moralis, non fides cum dilectione in Christo JESU ad salutem valeat, neque circumcisio ipsa; aut opus quodcunque legis ceremonialis, sed fides sola.

Eam vero cautionem lam diluit, atque hypocritarum persuasionem profligat, quasi fides vera esse possit sine dilectione, ideoque eorum causa addit fidem non hypocriticam sed vere vivam, quæ per charitatem efficax est; quæque indicium & nota est vitæ fidei, requiri, non quod charitas vitam largiatur fidei, quæ vita non destituta est, cum apprehendit Christum, hoc enim non mortuæ fidei opus est, sed vivæ, quæ vitam & vim vivificandi unice haurit e Christo in quem fertur, sed quod charitas vitam fidei demonstret ut vivum corpus per respirationem agnoscitur Jac.

II. ult. Fides mortua, inquit Beat. Major, qua opponitur viva, hoc est, quæ vitam, florem & vigorem suum a Christo, per Christum & in Christo habet, & vel de inani persuasione, vel de externa solum fidei professione accipitur, non magis est fides, quam cadaver homo.

Neque ab hoc sensu aliena est illa Beat. Majoris dilucidatio pag. 8. quod hoc aphorismo præputio non minus atque circumcisioni detrahatur coram Christo in regno ejus tam gratiæ quam gloriæ ἰσχύς vis, pretium, valor, pondus, utilitas, æstimium respectus, affignetur.

Nec discrepat, quantum ad causam præcipuam explicatio Beat. Lutheri: Hoc est, inquit, tantum dicere, qui vult esse vere Christianus, seu in Christi regno, hunc oportet esse credentem. Vere autem non credit, si opera charitatis fidem non sequuntur. Et sic utrinque a dextris & sinistris excludit a regno Christi hypocritas.

A sinistris Judæos & operarios, dicens, in Christo neque circumcisio, id est, nulla opera, nullus cultus, nullum prorsus vitæ genus, sed sola fides fine fiducia operum valet. A dextris ignavos & inertes ac desides, quia dicunt: si fide sine opere justificat, ergo nihil operemur. Sed credamus solum & faciamus, que volumus.

Non sic impii, dicit Paulus. Verum est fine operibus solam fidem justificare. Sed defide vera loquor, quæ postquam justificaverit, non stertet otiosa, sed est per charitatem operosa.

B. Brent. exponi quidem hic paucissimis docet, in quo constet verus Christianismus (quod a nobis etiam non negatur) observat autem, Paulum hanc appendicem de efficacia per charitatem non addere, quod sentiat fidem, justificare propter opera. Non enim dicit: fides, quae per dilectionem justificat, sed ad refutandos tum hypocritas, quam impudentes seu impoenitentes.

Beat. Chemnitius disputat. XIII. de justific. exclusiv. in articul. justificat. & faly. thes. 17.

Recte, inquit, Lutherus fecit, quod in colloquio Ratisbonensi noluit admittere cothurnum illum: Eam fidem justificare, quae efficax fit per charitatem (sensu Papistico, hoc est, qua efficax est) verum quidem est, fidem justificantem esse efficacem per charitatem, sed non ea ratione, non eo respectu, quo operatur, justificat, sed quo apprehendit solius Christi meritum, & illud opponit judicio Dei. Et in exam. Concil. Trident. de justif. p. 344. Nec tamen otiosa vel mortua fidei tribuimus justificationem, sed dicimus fidem, si vera est & viva, non esse otiosam, sed efficacem per charitatem.

Vitam autem, quam fides apprehendentibus, non mutuatur aut accipit a charitate, sed a Christo, quem complectitur, qui est vita & salus nostra. Quapropter recte Beat. Lutherus docuit, non hic definire Apostolum, quid fit fides justificans, sed describere fidem ab effectu, quod in credentibus non otiosa fit, aut mortua, sed tanquam arbor bona bonos fructus proferat.

Conf. Jae. Heerbrandus disp. de justif. hom. peccat. p. 304. 311.

Tilem. Hesbusius in h. l. Balthasar Menzerus disp. V. contra Pistet. ubi notat hoc dictum tum operosis justitiariis, tum ignavis & inertibus opponi, quasi dicat, in Christo non valent opera, neque ullus cultus, ut circumcisio & similes, sed tantum fides.

Et tamen illa fides non est otiosa, verum postquam justificavit, apprehendo Christo (quae est vita fidei justificantis) operosa atque efficax est & sese exerit per charitatem sive dilectionem, quae est ejus effectus seu fructus & simul testis. Recte itaque etiam observatum a Beat. Hülsemanno in vindiciis ἀνενδοτοις S.

LXIIX. epitheton illud, operari per charitatem attributum esse fidei, quae jam justificavit, non attributum fidei, quae adhuc justificatura est, multominus formam aut essentiam fidei justificantis: 1. Quia Apostolus officium & qualitatem fidei erga Deum justificantem cap. 2. & 3. ex professo jam descripserat, ut necesse non esset, neque etiam probabile, Apostolum bie acturum secunda vice de officio fidei erga Deum in acceptando justificationis beneficium. 2. Descripserat cap. 3. v. 12. & 13. naturam & qualitatem fidei in officio justificandi privative, quod fides justificans cum operibus nihil commune habeat in justificandi officio.

Lex non est ex fide, inquit, sed quisquis fecerit ea, vivet per ea; non esse alia phrasi Graeca tantundem significare, quod non participare de ejus forma & qualitatibus essentialibus. Lutherus in Comment. hujus loci multis ostendit, & patet ex parallelis ex Deo esse, ex Diabolo esse, ex mundo esse Job. VIII. vers. 46.

1. Joh. IV. vers. 6. Joh. XV. 19. id est, naturam Dei, naturam Diaboli, naturam mundi imitari.

Igitur Apostolus per attributum illud (operari per charitatem) nequaquam formam in officio fidei justificantis, qua justificat, sed aliud ejus officium nempe gratitudinem erga Deum & utilitatem erga homines describere. 3. Patet bic finis addita periphraseos seu epitheti ex sequente vers. 13. vos ad libertatem vocati estis μόνον, sed nolite hanc libertatem rápere ad peccandi occasionem, nempe ut solet Apostolus distinctos effectus fidei distine tractare, ut patet ex connexione cap. XI.

XII. XIII. ad Roman. ita periphrasin hanc fidei reddidit, ut sterneret viam agendi de altero etiam officio fidei erga homines, quod persequitur ad vers. 13. hujus capitis usque ad finem epistolae, nempe vera fidei naturae esse non solum apprehendere justitiam, sed etiam operari per charitatem, quod autem operari per charitatem concurrat ad apprehensionem seu acquisitionem justitiae & remissionis peccatorum, hoc adeo non colligi potest ex hac periphrasi: fides quae per charitatem operatur, quam non colligi potest: Periphrasin Maria Magdalenae, cujus mentio fit in resurrectione Christi fuisse nempe eam Marci XVI. 9. ex qua Jesus ejecerat septem demonia, concurrisse ad visitandum corpus Christi in sepulchro.

Et sexcenta ejusmodi epitheta subjectorum, quae nullo modo concurrunt ad effectum illum, qui praedicatur de illis subjectis, quorum sunt epitheta, sed adduntur propter causas alias specificativas nempe & discretivas subjectorum a subjectis aliis, vid. aliquot exempla Job. I. vers. 41. 43. 45. 46. Ita quando in Christo JESU nihil valere dicitur, quam fides, quae per charitatem efficax est, nulla idonea ratione probari potest, epitheton illud, operari per charitatem, concurrare ad valorem in Christo Jesu, sed hoc sequitur epitheton esse specificans illam fidem, quae valet in Christo Jesu, & discernens eam a fide imaginaria seu mortua. Haec Beat.

Hülsemannus, quem ὁμοφωνίας causa adducimus; utpote qui nobiscum agnoscit, concedi posse, & concedendum omnino esse, τὸ valere in Christo Jesu hoc loco idem esse, quod valere ad justificandum & salvandum, sed epitheton illud fidei, operari per charitatem concurrere ad justificationem negat: Et Beat.

Lutherum cum negat, Apostolum hic docere, quid coram DEO valeat fides, de hoc epitheto, operari per charitatem, loqui, quod id non concurrat ad formam fidei, ut valeat in Christo Jesu; sed epitheton fidei illius fit, quae valet in Christo JESU. Manent ergo distincta fides & charitas, manent distincta utriusque praedicata: fides in Christo sola valet ad justificationem & salutem, non charitas, hoc est sola est justificativa & salvifica. Charitas non est justificativa & salvifica, sed fidem, justificantem consequitur, quae per eandem sese exerit & operosa est, in dilectione DEI & proximi occupata, in illis, qui gratiam & remissionem peccatorum per Christum fide apprehendunt adepti sunt.

Quae eximie Beat. Jacobus Andrea ita exposuit disp. de justif. hom. peccat. coram DEO pag. 406. Toto caelo errant, qui charitatem ex numero eorum opinantur, quae salutem conferunt.

Quando igitur Apostolus (Gal. V.) scribit, in Christo Jesu neque circumcisio, neque preputium quicquam valet, sed fides per dilectionem operans: non quid fides fit, definire voluit, sed quod in credentibus non otiosa aut mortua fit, docet. Vera enim, sufficiens & perfecta fidei justificantis definitio seu descriptio est, qua dicitur: Fides non solum notitia historia est de Christo, sed & fiducia vera & certa, quam Spiritus sanctus in Electis operatur; qua homo de universa sua & aliorum sanctitate desperans, omnem justitiam suam, quae coram DEO consistere valet, in solius Christi merito & obedientia collocat, propter quem DEUS Pater mera gratia & misericordia nos in gratiam recipit, peccata remittit, & justos pronuntiat. Charitas vero, quemadmodum a fide distincta virtus est, sic etiam charitas & opera a fide distincta sunt. Nec charitas fidei aliquid largitur, cujus esse in Christo residet, sed fides charitati. Etenim diligere non possumus, de cujus gratia non sumus certi, sed praesentissimam eamque horribilem iram ejus sentimus.

Et fides praestat, qua flatuit, nos a Deo diligi propter Christum, priusquam eum nos

dilexerimus.

Sicut scriptum est: Nam cum adhuc inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo. Quapropter periculosa est eorum oratio, qui dicunt: Credere in Deum est credendo amare. Quae forma sermonis abusi scholastici Theologi, honorem, quem Spiritus S. soli Christo, & ipsius obedientiae ac merito tribuit, ad charitatem & opera ejus transtulerunt, quorum merito coram Deo justificetur.

Etsi vero fiducia in Deum nunquam est sine amore Dei, aliud tamen est & significat Deo fidere, & aliud, eundem amare. Ideoque duae diversa & revera distinctae virtutes sunt fides & charitas. Et quamvis earum objectum commune sit, videlicet Christus, aliter tamen atque aliter id afficiunt.

Fides enim Christo confidit, ut per ipsum seu propter ipsum remissionem peccatorum consequatur, & cum Deo Patre homo peccator reconcilietur. Charitas autem Christum non diligit, ut Deo reconcilietur, sed quia homo reconciliatus est per fidem propter Christum, ideo diligere quendem quoque incipit. Distinctio autem hec eo obscurior est, quod cum fides & charitas tempore simul, ideoque, semper conjunctae sint, non nisi mente & cogitatione separari queant.

Est ergo hac Prophetica Apostolica & Catholica doctrina de justificatione hominis coram Deo, qua docemus: hominem justifica-ri, hoc est, justum pronunciari, & absolvi a peccatis mera Dei misericordia per fidem propter filios Christi obedientiam & meritum, nullo, neque praecedentiom civiliter bonorum, aut praesentium aut sequentium vere bonorum operum respectu.

Quapropter homo per fidem justificatur, neque infirmitatem, neque dispositionem suam intueri debet, quae etiam renatis usque ad mortis periculum adhaeret, camque, deponere non possunt, quamdiu in hoc seculo vivunt, nec propter illam de gratia Dei dubitet. Vide B. Major. p. 33.
