Breviter: non ait Apostolus, fidem in Christo Jesu valere ad justitiam ac salutem, sed qua operatur per charitatem, sed qua operatur: nec reduplicative intelligendus est, sed specifice, quem sensum B. Major non improbat, adeoque argumenta ejus tantum reduplicativo sensu opposita sunt v. 9.

Quicunque salvantur, quandoque, salvantur sola fide sine operibus, illi non salvantur fide per charitatem operante, quia hac fides in actu salvationis non est sola & nuda, sed habet sibi intra curriculum justificationis necessario praesentia, adhaerescentia & affociata atque copulata opera, hoc est, fides in actu salvationis non affert in conspectum Dei opera, quae praestita, ut remunerentur per justitiam, sed peccata, quae patrata, ut remittantur per misericordiam: & in hoc passu (ut ita loquar) fides est sibi in corde supplicantis malorum operum conscia, quae multa & magna hominibus propria: Bonorum vero, quae vel nulla, vel non sua, vere nescit. Conscientiam in tentatis & in judicio constitutis aggravant mala, non relevant bona opera. Omnes filii Dei salvantur sola fide sine suis operibus. Ergo non salvantur fide operante per charitatem, scilicet reduplicative, hoc est, qua talem.

Nulla fides debet dici justificans & salvifica, qua vel quatenus talis, hoc est, quae involvit respectum qualitatis & quantitatis, a qua & per quam ἐνέργεια, seu ratione sua qualitatis vel quantitatis, qua metienda, sed quatenus est hac fides & vera fides, hoc est, quatenus Evangelio de Christo solum affixa & innixa. Fides per charitatem operosa est istas, id est, involvit respectum qualitatis & quantitatis. Ergo non est dicenda fide salvifica & justificans.

Illa fides est, potest, debetque dici salvifica, & ad salutem necessaria, quae solum in Christo apprehendendo distinetur & occupatur, & in merito ejus ambiendo & complectendo heret. Fides per charitatem operans non solum distinetur in Christo apprehendendo, sed & in proximo diligendo. Ergo non debet dici salvifica & ad salutem necessaria ἀκριβῶς non παχυλῶς, accurate, proprie, & distincte, non confuse & generate loquendo.

Item: Fides justificans & salvifica est solicita de impetranda remissione peccatorum. Fides per dilectionem non est solicita de remissione peccatorum, sed de praestanda obedientia vel dilectione exhibenda. Ergo non est justificans & salvifica.

Fides justificans & salvifica quaerit, invenit, impetrat, appropriat peccatorum (tum originalis tum actualium) remissionem credenti. Fides per charitatem ἐνεργουμένη non quaerit, non invenit, non impetrat, non appropriat remissionem peccatorum. Ergo non est justificans & salvifica, scilicet qua talis, qua operatur per charitatem.

Ubi fides se habet ἐνεργητικῶς & non ὀργανικῶς, ibi non est justificans. In operatione per charitatem habet se ἐνεργητικῶς, non ὀργανικῶς. Ergo & hinc non competit fidei ceu instrumento actio a seipso, sed a causa superiore, a quo movetur, & trahitur: Et quatenus fides est ἐνεργουμένη δι ἀγάπης, ad qualitatem, vel si mavis actionis pertinet predicamentum, non vero relationis.

Unde iterum liquet, quod sit virtus & qualitas, non vero correlativum promissionis Evangelicae, & in qua confidit.

Denique quaecunque fides obedientiam inchoatam, qua nostra, conjungit in articulo seu sphera justificationis cum obedientia imputata, quae Christi, illa non est justificans & salvifica. Fides per charitatem operosa & negotiosa conjungit obedientiam inchoatam cum imputata. Ergo non est salvifica.

Justificaremur enim imputative & inchoative, quod Pontificium. Fides per charitatem actuosa est renovationis & sanctificationis, non regenerationis & justificationis, qua illis ordine priora, gradu potiora, actu perfectiora, ambitu latiora. Sunt enim non solum in adultis, sed etiam una cum fide nondum operosa in minorenribus.

Hec B. Major. Quae omnia rectissime Hornejo & Papistis opponuntur laudata dissertatione, & ex eadem utpote jam paucis obvia, mihique à Theologorum nostri seculi presbytero, quum adhuc Dantisci docerem, inscripta, adducere placuit.

Dicendum adhuc de Socinianis, e quibus Crel- lius in praeled. ad hanc epistol. a Schlichtingio ex- ceptis & editis hic ostendi vult, qualis sit cultus spiritualis, quo justitia a Christianis queratur, talis videlicet, qui in charitate ejusque operibus imprimis consistat, qui ceremoniarum legalium loco fit, & qualem ipse fidem intelligat, cum illi justificationem simpliciter, feu nulla alia re adjecta tribuit talem nimirum, qua charitate sit velut animata, non ergo charitatem & ejus effecta excludenda esse e comparanda nobis justificatione, quod collatione 1. Cor. VII. 19. 1. Joh. III. 14. Matth. XXV. 34. seqq. & imprimis Jac. II. 14. 17. seqq. probat, quod ea ita cum fide concurrant, ut fides locum corporis teneat, bona opera locum Spiritus, ut & textu praesenti, quod Paulus fidem eam, quae vim justificandi habet, ab ea distinguat, quae vim talem non habet, quam differentiam cum fide vera, tantum effectum cum causa propria necessario cohaerere, adeo que ad salutem consequendam etiam necessariam esse, accipienda fide illius, cui soli ex parte nostri justificatio tribuitur, partem ex opere censet. At ubinam docuit Apostolus, quod justitia nostra in cultu spirituali quaerenda sit? Ubi, quod ceremoniarum omnium loco cultus fit spiritualis? Verba illa, in Christo Jesu nihil valet circumcisio &c. hoc importare, temere asseritur. Nec vero fides aut etiam charitas loco ceremoniarum legaliu est; quum & in V. Test. fides, atque charitas locum habuerit, imò sacrificia & circumcisio minimè pro-fuerint ex solo opere operato, uti scholastici barbarè loqui solent: nec in N. Test. in ceremoniarum locum fides successerit, sed Christus, cujus umbra illæ fuere.

Porro quia fidei ex parte nostri simpliciter tribuitur justificatio, non modo re nulla alia adjecta, sed omnibus etiam exclusis, ita ut fides justificans & salvifica opponatur charitati atque operibus, non potest fides, in quantum justificat, intelligi, quæ charitate sit animata; quemadmodum nec fides animari potest charitate, utpote quæ ejus effectus est. Nam effectus nequit anima esse causæ suæ.

De loco 1. Cor. VII. 19. jam monitum, illic nihil de justificatione tractari; neque 1. Joh. III. 14. per charitatem translatio dicimur è morte in vitam, sed agnoscere translationem illam, quæ non charitati, sed fidei unice tribuitur, Joh. V. 24. Hab. II. 4. Rom. I. 17. Gal. III. 11. Ebr. X. 38. Eph. II. 8. At Matth.

XXV. 34. seqq. bona opera non ut causa beatitudinis, sed ut indicia fidei salvificæ designantur, in processu extremi judicii producenda, Jacob. c. II. Nec de justificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo agitur, sed de justificationis demonstratione coram hominibus, & fidei non veræ, sed hypocriticæ solum vis salvandi derogatur, quæ operibus destituta mortua est in semetipsa, non quod vitam ab operibus accipiat, quia à solo Christo veram vitam habet, sed quod fine iis tam non vivat, quam corpus sine respiratione ac motu non vivit: Unde Spiritus Sanctus non fidem corpori, opera bona Spiritui, sed fidem animæ, à qua vita corporis naturalis, ut à fide homini renato est vita spiritualis, Hab. II. 4. componit.

Opera vero bona & charitatem respirationi, quam per τὸ πνεῦμα intelligit, comparat.

Paulus verò, quod hunc locum attinet, distinguit fidem, quæ vim justificatam habet ab ea, quæ non habet, sed per externum γνώρισμα & fructum, quemadmodum arbor bona è fructibus dignoscitur, tum quia interna & essentialis differentia fidei jam satis declarata erat, in tractatione de fidei justificantis qua talis natura & objecto proprio, tum quia jam constituerat de eo agere, quomodo se fides in momento secundo exercat, & ad extra demonstret.

Geminam enim fides habet ἐνέργειαν, primam internam, cum se extendit ad Christum, ejusque satisfactionem & meritum apprehendit, in quo tum vitam ipsa habet, tum subjecto homini, in peccatis cæteroquin mortuo, vitam affert.

Nam in Christo, qui verus Deus & vita æterna est, vitam apprehendit, & credenti appropriat: alteram externam, cum sese per charitatem erga Deum & proximum exerit, & non mortuam, sed vere vivam esse tum credentibus ipsis, tum aliis demonstrat & ostendit.

Priori ad Christum assurgit fides, tanquam proprium suum objectum, & correlatum, eumque in promissione Evangelii fiducialiter aspicit & apprehendit, Joh.

VI. 4. cap. III. 14. 15. Posteriori ad proximum sese demittit, & per charitatem ei benefacit, imò ad Deum quoque evehitur, sed alis dilectionis infirmis, quem toto corde, tota anima, totisq; viribus amare tenetur, sed minime, prout par est, valet.

Unde cum quæritur, cujus ἐνέργειας respectu justificet, in proclivi responsio est, quod fides non justificet ea operatione, qua per charitatem ad proximi indigentiam sublevandam se demittit, aut etiam conatur ad Deum ascendere, eumdemque dilectione, quam Deus requirit, complecti, sed altera, quâ ad Jesum Christum, ut thronum gratiæ, & Mediatorem generis humani affurgens, eundem citra adminiculum adjunctæ charitatis apprehendit; salvifico nimirum Christi Mediatoris aspectu, etsi à charitate interim separatus non fit, sed per eandem sese exerat ad laudem Dei & usus proximi, sic tamen, ut in arduo illo & divino justificationis actu fides non charitatem, non opera charitatis, imo, ne seipsam quidem, sed unice Jesum Christum aspiciat, atque sic hominem in Dei conspectu justificet & salvet, non charitatis aut operum merito, aut propria sua virtute, sed unicè obedientia Christi, quam apprehendit, Rom.

## 5:7
Ver. 7. ἐτρέχετε καλῶς] The Christian life is often compared to a race, because great alacrity and exertion are needed for it, see above II, 2. Phil. II. 16. Hebr. XII. 1. 2. Tim. IV. 7. 1. Cor. IX. 24. tís ὑμᾶς ἐνέκοψε, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι] In the manuscript, τίς ὑμᾶς ἀνέκοψε, μὴ πείθεσθαι, not as some wish ἀνέκοψε. Ἐγκόπτω properly means to build something across, by which a journey might be impeded, whence by a certain metaphor it signifies to hinder, Acts XXIV.

4. Rom. XV. 22. 1. Thess. II. 8. and ἐγκοπή, an impediment 1. Cor. IX. 12. He excellently calls the Gospel itself the truth. See above III, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ἐτρέχετε καλῶς] Saepe vita Christiana currui comparatur, quia magna ad eam alacritate & contentione opus est, supra II, 2. Phil. II. 16. Hebr. XII. 1. 2. Tim. IV. 7. 1. Cor. IX. 24. τίς ὑμᾶς ἐνέκοψε, τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι] In manuscripto, τίς ὑμᾶς ἀνέκοψε, μὴ πείθεσθαι, non ut quidam volunt ἀνέκοψε. Ἐγκόπτω proprie est transversum aliquid struere, quo iter impediatur, unde translatione quadam significat, impedire, Act.

XXIV. 4. Rom. XV. 22. 1. Thess. II. 8. & ἐγκοπή, impedimentum 1. Cor. IX. 12. veritatem eximiè vocat ipsum Evangelium. Vide supra III, 1.

## 5:8
Ver. 8. ἡ πεισμονὴ οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς] here he demonstrates. For it is put for αὕτη ἡ πεισμονὴ, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς, not from God, who called us to eternal life, in such a way that he would have that power be held as unique through Christ, 2. Tim. I. 12. God is not contrary to himself.

Ratio ordinis. Having completed the didactic treatment both of the truth and of the weight of the Evangelical doctrine concerning justification, in which indeed the corroboration of this weight is not neglected, the Apostle intermixes, before he turns himself to instruction and exhortation to the pursuit of good works, which is joined in an inseparable bond with true faith.

For, reproving that declination from the course begun in the way of Evangelical doctrine, he exhibits the gravity of the danger even from a small leaven, and, hoping well of the Galatians, he denounces a grave judgment upon their seducers, and protests that he himself is immune from that guilt, but also wishes excision by Apostolic Spirit upon the seducers, so that by that means he may the more abstract his Galatians from them, and deter them, and excite them to preserve the liberty into which they were called. He tempers this exhortation in such a way that liberty may not be turned into carnal license, and therefore he gravely exhorts them to mutual services of charity and to a spiritual life, which is the other part of the present chapter. He calls it a course, because according to the prescribed rule they had not only walked, but had run strenuously in the way of truth, and indeed of holiness: and by this metaphor taken from runners, he commends to the Galatians the study and ardor, not infrequent in Scripture, of proceeding in the study of truth, faith, piety, and liberty.

For he adds καλῶς, well; because all indeed run in the stadium, but not all obtain the prize, because, namely, they do not run καλῶς, 1. Cor. IX. 24. They had received Paul as an Angel of God, as Jesus Christ, they had greedily embraced the simple truth concerning justification by faith without the works of the law, they had not entangled themselves in the yoke of ceremonies. τίς ὑμᾶς ἐνέκοψε , as if he were cutting in, by which thorns the course is obstructed, and men do not run, but limp.

But this, as Chrysostom warns, is not of one asking, but of one deploring and anxious. How has so great a course been interrupted? Who is it who could do so much? Which things of Chrysostom are to be understood comparatively, that he does not so much ask as deplore: Or cumulatively, that he does not only ask, as he adds: These things are rather of one exclaiming and lamenting. For although he argues their inconstancy not obscurely, he nevertheless attributes the cessation of the course not so much to the Galatians themselves as to others, whose perverse attempt, that they might consider it more deeply, he excites with this form of asking and grieving.

But he uses the singular, even though there were many of them, so that he might [address] each one of them, that they have contributed their impious effort to this matter, THAT YOU SHOULD NOT OBEY THE TRUTH, is to be understood concerning continuation, that you should not continue to obey, or proceed to obey the truth of the Gospel, which he had not received from men, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ, chap. I. 12. He does not obey the truth who does not bring his intellect into the obedience of Christ, 2. Cor. X. 4. Which words, even if they had been missing in some of Jerome's Codices, omitted by the fault of the scribes; Chrysostom nevertheless reads the same, as also the Syrian, and not least Ambrosiaster and Augustine, and likewise Theophylactus, and Oecumenius, nor are they missing in modern Codices.

By those words, persuasion is not from him who calls you, tacitly the doctrine concerning the necessity of good works and circumcision for salvation is condemned as Diabolical, which persuasion in the doctrine of faith, which is not from Christ, must be made by the Devil. The Pseudo-Apostles, says B. Luther fol. 132, were great men, far surpassing Paul in appearance in doctrine and piety. Deceived by this mask, the Galatians, when they heard them, thought they were hearing Christ, and therefore judged their persuasion to be from Christ. On the contrary, Paul sub-obscurely and modestly indicates that this persuasion and doctrine is not from Christ, who had called them in grace, but from the Devil. Ver.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἡ πεισμονὴ οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς] hic demonstrat. Est enim positum pro αὕτη ἡ πεισμονὴ, ἐκ οὐκ ἐκ καλοῦντος ὑμᾶς, non ex Deo, qui nos ad vitam aeternam vocavit, ita ut vellet eam vim haberi unicam per Christum, 2. Tim. I. 12. Non est Deus sibi contrarius.

Ratio ordinis. Absoluta tractatione didactica cum de veritate, tum de pondere doctrinae Evangelicae de justificatione ἐπανόρθωσιν, in qua vero ponderis istius corroboratio non negligitur, immiscet Apostolus, antequam ad παιδείαν & exhortationem ad studium bonorum operum sese convertat, quod invulso nexu cum vera fide conjunctum est.

Reprehendens enim illam à cursu coepto in via doctrinae Evangelicae declinationem, & periculi è modico etiam fermento gravitatem exhibet, & bene sperans de Galatis seductoribus ipsorum judicium grave denunciat, seque ab ista culpa immunem esse protestatur, sed seductoribus etiam excisionem Spiritu Apostolica optat, ut eo magis eisdem Galatas suos abstrahat, & deterreat, & ad libertatem, in quam vocati sunt, custodiendam excitet. Quam paranefin ita temperat, ut ne libertas in licentiam carnalem vertatur, ideoque ad charitatis fervitia mutua, & vitam spiritualem eosdem graviter exhortatur, quae altera est pars praesentis capitis. Cursum vocat, quia secundum regulam praescriptam non ambularant tantum, sed strenue cucurrerant in via veritatis, imo & sanctitatis: atque hac metaphora à cursoribus petita scripturae non infrequenti studium & ardorem pergendi in studio veritatis, fidei, pietatis & libertatis in Galatis commendat.

Addit enim καλῶς bene; quia currunt quidem in stadio omnes, sed non consequuntur omnes brabeum, quia scilicet non currunt καλῶς, 1. Cor. IX. 24. susceperant Paulum, ut Angelum Dei, ut Jesum Christum, cupide amplexi erant simplicem veritatem de justificatione ex fide sine operibus legis, jugo ceremoniarum sese non implicarant. τίς ὑμᾶς ἐνέκοψε , quasi incidit, quibus inficis sufflaminatur cursus, nec currunt homines, sed claudicant.

Id vero monente Chrysostomo, non interrogantis est, sed deplorantis & anxii. Quomodo tantus cursus interruptus est? Quis est, qui tantum potuit? Quae Chrysostomi comparative intelligenda sunt, quod non tam interroget, quam deploret: Vel cumulative, quod non interroget tantum, uti addit: Haec potius sunt exclamantis, & lamentantis. Licet enim inconstantiam eorum non obscure arguat, cursum tamen cessationem non tam Galatis ipsis, quam aliis tribuit, quorum conatum perversum ut altius considerent, hac interrogandi, dolendique forma excitat.

Singulari autem utitur, etsi plures eorum fuerint, ut unumquemque eorum, met eam in rem impiam contulere operam, UT NON OBSEQUEREMINI VERITATI, est de continuatione accipiendum, ut non porro obsequeremini, vel obsequi pergeretis veritati Evangelii, quod non ab hominibus acceperat, sed revelationem Jesu Christi, cap. I. 12. Non obsequitur veritati, qui non redigit intellectum in obsequium Christi, 2. Cor. X. 4. Quae verba etsi desiderata fuerint in quibusdam Hieronymi Codd. vitio librariorum omissa; Chrysostom tamen legit eadem, ut & Syrus, nec non Ambrosiaster & Augustinus, Theophylactus item, & Oecumenius, nec desiderantur in hodiernis Codicibus.

Verbis illis persuasio hac non ex eo est, qui vocat vos, tacite doctrina de bonorum operum & circumcisionis necessitate ad salutem damnatur tanquam Diabolica, qua persuasio in doctrina fidei, quae non à Christo est, à Diabolo fit oportet. Pseudo-Apostoli, inquit B. Lutherus fol. 132. erant magni viri, longe in speciem superantes Paulum doctrina & pietate. Hoc fuco decepti Galatae, cum audirent ipsos, putabant se Christum audire, ideoque judicabant persuasionem ipsorum esse ex Christo. Contra Paulus subobscure & verecunde indicat hanc persuasionem & doctrinam non esse ex Christo, qui vocaverat eos in gratia, sed ex Diabolo. Vers.

## 5:9
9. Μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ] It is a similitude, by which it is signified that, with the beginning made by a few, this deceitful persuasion of theirs was spread far and wide among the Galatians.

See Matt. XIII. 33. and 1. Cor. V. 6. Augustine refers the same to a few masters of error, similarly Jerome: that a perverse doctrine beginning from one, even if from the beginning it finds hardly two or three Authors, yet gradually creeps, like a cancer in the body.

But more convenient is the interpretation of Ambrosiaster concerning erroneous doctrine, just as the leaven of doctrine, which a small seen error can infect the whole substance of religion; which Chrysostom and Theophylactus refer to the handed-down necessity of circumcision, by which they could be easily swept away into total Judaism. Beautifully here B.

Luther: In Philosophy, he says fol. 133, a small error in the beginning is in the end a very great one. Thus in Theology a small error overturns the whole doctrine. Wherefore doctrine and life are to be distinguished most widely. Doctrine is not ours, but God's, of whom we are only called ministers. Therefore we cannot remit or change even an apiculum of it. It is our visa, therefore as far as it pertains to it, the sacramentarians can demand nothing from us, which we do not wish and ought even to accept, condone, and bear, saving however the doctrine of faith, concerning which we always say this of Paul, a little leaven etc.

In this part we cannot yield even by a hair. For doctrine is like a Mathematician's point, it cannot therefore be divided, that is, it can bear neither subtraction nor addition. On the contrary, life, which is like a physical point, can always be divided, can always concede something. A most minute straw in the eye offends the eye. Hence the Germans say concerning remedies for the eyes: Nothing is good in the eyes. And Christ says: The lamp of the body is the eye. When therefore your eye shall be simple, your whole body shall be lucid, etc. And then: If your body shall not have any part of darkness, it shall be all lucid etc. By this allegory Christ signifies that the eye, that is, doctrine, ought to be simply pure, clear, and sincere, so that it has plainly no part of darkness, no little cloud etc. Therefore doctrine ought to be one certain perpetual and round golden circle, in which there is no fissure. With the slightest approach of it, the circle is no longer whole etc. If you deny God in one article, you have denied him in all: because God is not divided into many articles, but is all in each, and one in each article.

Paul therefore warns by this sentiment as much the Doctors as the hearers, that they should not think the doctrine of faith is a small thing or of no account, with which we can play according to our lust. It is a solar ray coming from heaven, which illuminates, kindles, and directs us. But as the world with all its wisdom and power cannot bend the rays of the sun extending from heaven directly to the earth, so neither can anything be taken away from or added to the doctrine of faith, or it is overturned in its entirety, etc.

Latin:

9. Μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ] Similitudo est, per quam significatur, à paucis facto initio, late admodum inter Galatas sparsam fallacem istam persuasionem.

Vide Matth. XIII. 33. & 1. Cor. V. 6. Augustinus idem referat ad paucos erroris magistros, similiter Hieronymus: doctrinam perversam ab uno incipientem, etsi ab initio vix duos aut tres reperiat Autores, paulatim tamen ferpere, ut cancrum in corpore.

Sed convenientior est Ambrosiastri interpretatio de doctrina erronea, quemadmodum fermentum doctrinae, quod parvus visus error totam religionis substantiam inficere possit; quod Chrysostomus & Theophylactus ad traditam circumcisionis necessitatem referunt, qua possint in totum Judaismum facile abripi. Pulchre hic B.

Lutherus: In Philosophia, inquit fol. 133. modicus error in principio, in fine est maximus. Sic in Theologia modicus error totam doctrinam evertit. Quare longissime discernenda sunt doctrina & vita. Doctrina non est nostra, sed Dei, cujus nos tantum vocati sumus ministri. Ideo ne apiculum quidem de ea remittere aut mutare possumus. Visa nostra est, ideo quod ad eam attinet, nihil possunt sacramentarii à nobis exigere, quod non velimus & debeamus etiam suscipere, condonare & ferre, salva tamen doctrina de fide, de qua semper dicimus hoc Pauli, modicum fermenti &c.

Hac in parte ne pilo quidem cedere possumus. Est enim doctrina instar Mathematici puncti, non potest igitur dividi, hoc est, neque ademptionem, neque additionem ferre potest. Contra vita, quae est instar physici puncti, semper dividi, semper aliquid concedere potest. Minutissima festuca in oculo offendit oculum. Hinc Germani dicunt de remediis oculorum: Nichts ist in die Augen gut. Et Christus inquit: Lucerna corporis oculus est. Cum igitur oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit, &c. Et deinde: Si corpus tuum non habuerit aliquam partem tenebrarum, erit lucidum totum &c. Hac allegoria significat Christus, oculum, hoc est, doctrinam debere simpliciter esse puram, claram & sinceram, qua plane nullam partem tenebrarum, nullam nubeculam habeat &c. Debet igitur doctrina esse unus quidam perpetuus & rotundus aureus circulus, in quo nulla fit fissura. Ea accedente vel minima, circulus non est amplius integer &c. Si Deum in uno articulo negas, in omnibus negasti: quia Deus non dividitur in multos articulos, sed est omnia in singulis, & unus in singulis articulis.

Admonet ergo Paulus hac sententia tam Doctores, quam auditores, ne cogitent doctrinam fidei rem exiguam esse aut nihili, cum qua ludere possumus pro libidine nostra. Ipsa est radius solaris è caelo veniens, qui illuminat, accendit, & dirigit nos. Ut autem mundus cum omni sapientia sua & potentia non potest flectere radios solis è caelo tendentes directe in terram, ita neque doctrinae fidei aliquid auferri aut addi potest, vel in totum evertitur &c.

## 5:10
Ver. 10. I trust in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else) That is, I have that hope in the goodness of God toward you, that at length, the matter having been well weighed, you will be affected as I am. He says this because he saw that they had fallen not out of evil malice, but out of a certain thoughtlessness and fear.

You will think nothing else is to be understood concerning doctrine and faith, than what you have heard and learned from me. I trust (he says, according to the interpretation of Theophylact) in you, and it is no wonder, since I am acquainted with the conditions of my disciples, and I am not ignorant that their return to the way will be easy. And since I myself do not despair of you, because I understand that you can be converted to the good, I trust nevertheless, and primarily in God, by whose will not even the least things perish. He exhorts, moreover, that they themselves also should show forth concerning themselves, what they may contribute, and have their hope firmly fixed in the Lord. For in no other way can divine goods be obtained, unless you yourselves also (he says) strive to bring forth what is fitting for you.

But he who disturbs you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be) They will pay the penalty, whoever they are who are the cause of these disturbances: he who disturbs .

See Acts 15:10, where the same dogma is treated. βασάσει means to bear something that is heavy, as 2 Kings 18:14, Matthew 20:12, Acts 15:10. κρῖμα means punishment, Matthew 23:14, Mark 12:40, Luke 20:47, ch. 23: 10. With this sentiment, according to B. Luther, fol. 134, Paul, sitting as a judge before the tribunal, condemns the Pseudo-Apostles, calling the disturbers of the Galatians by a very hateful name, whom they themselves considered most pious and doctors far better than Paul. At the same time, he wishes to move the Galatians with this horrible sentence, by which he condemns the Pseudo-Apostles with such certainty, that they might avoid them as a most harmful plague, as if he were to say, why do you listen to those plagues, who do not teach, but only disturb you?

The doctrine which they deliver to you is nothing other than a disturbance of consciences. Therefore, however great they may be, they will have their condemnation. He says 'disturb', because they were striving to render Paul's doctrine suspect, and to persuade a mixture of the law with the Gospel in the matter of justification. Thus he declares that his own sense concerning the Galatians and their disturbers is very different. He hopes for the best concerning the Galatians. Not therefore will the disturbers go unpunished. For it is not right, says Chrysostom, that the probity of others should support the malice of others.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἐγὼ πέποιθα εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐν κυρίῳ, ὅτι οὐδὲν ἄλλο φρονήσετε) Id est, ego eam spem habeo in Dei erga vos bonitate, ut tandem, re nempe bene expensa, futuri sitis affecti, ita, ut ego sum. Hoc ideo dicit, quia illos videbat non mala malitia, sed incogitantia quadam & metu lapsos. Nihil aliud sentietis intelligi de doctrina & fide, quam quod ex me audistis & didicistis. Confido (inquit interprete Theophylacto) in vobis, nec mirum, qui meorum calleam discipulorum conditiones, & eorum facilem fore in viam reditum non ignorem. Cumque de vobis nihil ipse desperem, quia ad bonum converti posse intelligo, confido tamen & Deo imprimis, cujus arbitrio nec minima pereunt. Hortatur praeterea, ut & ipsi de se praestent, que conferant, & spem in Domino habeant obfirmatam. Neque enim aliter possunt divina bona parari, nisi & ipsi (inquit) pro vestra virili proferre vos que deccant, adnitamini. ὁ δὲ ταράσσων ὑμᾶς βασάσει τὸ κρῖμα, ὅτις ἂν ᾖ) Poenas dabunt, quicunque harum turbarum causa sunt: ὁ ταράσσων .

Vide Actor. 15, 10. ubi de eodem dogmate agitur. βασάσει est ferre aliquid, quod grave est, ut 2.

Reg. 18, 14. Matth. 20, 12. Actor. 15, 10. κρῖμα poena, Matth. 23, 14. Marc. 12, 40. Luc. 20, 47. C. 23, 10. Hac sententia, juxta B.

Lutherum fol. 134. Paulus velut judex pro tribunali sedens, condemnat Pseudo-Apostolos, vocans valde odioso nomine conturbatores Galatarum, quos ipsi ducebant piissimos, & longe meliores Paulo doctores.

Simulque permovere vult Galatas hac horribili sententia, qua tanta certitudine damnat Pseudo-Apostolos, ut illos vitent tanquam nocentissimam pestem, quasi dicat, quod auditis illas pestes, qua non docent, sed tantum perturbant vos? Doctrina, quam tradunt vobis, nihil aliud est, quam perturbatio conscientiarum. Ideo quantumvis magni sint, habebunt suam condemnationem. Turbare dicit, quia Pauli doctrinam suspectam reddere, ac legis cum Evangelio mixturam in justificationis negotio persuadere studebant. Ita de Galatis & eorum turbatoribus longe diversissimum esse suum sensum declarat. De Galatis optime sperat. Non idco impune turbatores ferent, Non enim par est, inquit Chrysostomus, ut aliorum probitas aliorum malitiam sublevet.

## 5:11
Ver. 11. And I, brethren, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted?) If it were true, what they say, that I myself after conversion taught the necessity of circumcision, I would have no care to bear such hard things as I do.

For the Jews, as we have said, for the sake of religion, were suffering no evils. Then the scandal of the cross is abolished) In the Manuscript is added 'of Christ'. The sense is: If that is so, the cross will cease, which offends so many. The scandal of the cross, that is, the cross which is the scandal. For the Genitive is very often used among the Hebrews, and sometimes among other nations, in an appositive sense. The cross is said to be whatever we bear for Christ's sake, Matthew 16:24, Luke 9:23, ch. 14:

27. He does not say, if I were circumcised: for he had circumcised Timothy, not out of an opinion of necessity, but for the sake of avoiding scandal: But if I still preach circumcision. He does not deny that he circumcised, he denies that he preached circumcision.

For he who preaches, establishes a dogma, and enjoins that it must be done perpetually, as here Theophylact. But he who has done anything by dispensation, does it not only that he may act well, but according to the necessity of things and time. He proves, however, that he did not preach it, from the persecution which he was suffering from the Jews, concerning which he speaks at length in 2 Cor. 11:24 ff., as if he were to say, according to Jerome the interpreter, all the hatred of the Jews against me, and the madnesses that were against me, is for no other reason than that I teach the Gentiles that they ought not to be circumcised, and to keep the superfluous burdens of the law now abolished. But since I suffer persecution, it is manifest that I do not preach circumcision, which I destroy. Ver. 12. I wish that they who disturb you would even cut themselves off) Here is an optative. Since they so glory in the cut-off skin, I wish that the whole seminal member were cut off from them, by which they might triumph the more, כרות שפכה.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐγὼ δὲ ἀδελφοὶ, εἰ περιτομὴν ἔτι κηρύσσω, τί ἔτι διώκομαι;) Si verum esset, quod illi dicunt, meipsum post conversionem docuisse necessitatem circumcisionis, nullam haberem curam, tam dura ferendi, quam fero. Nam Judzi, ut diximus, religionis causa, nulla mala patiebantur. ἄρα κατήργηται τὸ σκάνδαλον τοῦ σταυροῦ) In Manuscripto additur τὸ χριστοῦ.

Sensus est: Jam si id est, cessabit crux, quæ tam multos offendit. Σκάνδαλον σταυροῦ, id est, ὁ σταυρὸς, ὃς ἐστι σκάνδαλον. Nam Genitivus fæpiffime apud Hebræos, interdum & apud alias gentes, appofitivo sensu ponitur. Crux dicitur, quicquid Christi causa ferimus, Matth. 16, 24. Luc. 9, 23. C. 14, 27. Non ait, si circumcidi: Nam circumciderat Timotheum, non necessitatis opinione, sed scandali avertendi causa: Sed si circumcisionem adhuc pradico.

Non negat circumcidisse, negat pradicaffe circumcisionem. Qui enim predicat, sancit dogma, ficerique id perpetuo oportere injungit, ut hic Theophylactus. Qui autem per dispensationem egerit quippiam, non solum ut bene agat, sed pro rerum & temporis necessitate id facit. Probat autem, se non pradicaffe ex persecutione, quam patiebatur à Judæis, de qua prolixe 2.

Cor. XI. 24. seqq. quasi dicat, Hieronymo interprete, omne in me odium Judæorum, & qua adversum me fuerunt insania, ob nihil aliud est, nisi quod docco gentes, non debere circumcidi, & legis onera superflua jam abolita custodire. Cum autem persecutionem patiar, manifestum est, me circumcisionem non prædicare, quam destruo.

## 5:12
In Greek, he who is cut off, Deut. 23:1, is he to whom, to speak with Horace, the lustful tail has been cut off. That 'they cut off their genitals' is also in Stephanus, where he speaks of the Gauls, the god of war, such as they were also in Pessinus, a city then of Galatia, when this epistle was being written. Dion concerning Heliogabalus: 'he circumcises the genital, by the cutting of flesh, as if he were becoming purer by these things, he was castrated.

He castrated himself entirely, having bent it down.' This 'cut off' is the same as 'I cut off' in the LXX and Paul. And it appears that Chrysostom accepted this passage thus: 'If I wish, let them not only be circumcised, but let them be cut off. How then do these who dare to cut themselves off, not draw back the foreskin and slander the creation of God.' Nor does Jerome say otherwise: If they think this profits them, let them not only be circumcised, but also be cut off. For if the stripping of a member was profitable, much more is the amputation.

It seems that the Visigothic law ch. 12. III. 4 looks to this place. 'But those who have presumed to exercise circumcisions of the flesh in Judea or in a Christian [land]: whoever shall have permitted these things to be done either uselessly to another, or to be done by another to himself, shall be punished with total amputation.' 'Disturbing' here is the same as 'disturbing'.

See Acts 17, c. 21, 38. With this wish, the Apostle removes from himself very far the impediment to the course of the Galatians in the stadium of truth, faith, and liberty. But the impure gloss of Grotius concerning amputation, although Thomas and Adam Sasbout favor it along with Jerome and the Greeks, and it could not prove itself to other Papists like Salmeron and Cornelius, and was rejected by the Socinians themselves, and judged unworthy of commemoration.

Beza interprets it as separation from God, Calvin as destruction, which the Apostle designates, alluding to the circumcision which the impostors were urging. This does not please Crocius. If he were alluding to circumcision, he says, he would rather say 'I wish they would cut themselves around', so that the paronomasia of 'circumcision' and 'amputation' might be clear. Rather, therefore, he looks to the word 'he cut back', v. 7, so that the sense may be, that they might 'cut you back': I wish they themselves would 'cut back'.

Thus D. Pareus. Beza also thinks it can be taken for excommunication, and with him Piscator, the Belgians in their notes, and likewise Cornelius à Lapide and Salmero. But the Apostle would rather have urged excommunication than wished for it. He wishes for excision, therefore, not out of carnal affection, but by the Spirit of God, by which he was so rapt into love for the Church, that he would rather have a few incorrigible impostors perish than the whole body of the Church. Whence to that question, whether it is lawful for Christians to curse?

B. Luther answers in this place: It is lawful, but not always, and for any cause.

When it has come to that, that the word must be cursed or the doctrine blasphemed, and consequently God himself, then invert the sentence and say, let God and His word be blessed, and let whatever is outside the word and God be cursed, whether it be an Apostle or an Angel from heaven. But if they leave the word whole and uninjured for us, we are prepared not only to keep charity and concord with them, but we offer ourselves to be their servants, and to do nothing that we would not do. If they do not perish and be cast down to hell, not only they, but the whole world also with the pious and the impious, provided that God remains. With Him remaining, life and salvation remain, and the pious will remain. Rightly, therefore, does Paul act, because he curses those disturbers, and pronounces the sentence that they are anathema with all things that they are, teach, and do, and that he prays against them, that they may be cut off from this life, and especially from the Church, that is, that God may not govern and prosper their doctrine and all their actions. And this curse has proceeded from the Holy Spirit.

Thus Peter in Acts 8 curses Simon, your money, he says, perish with you, etc. And there is frequent use of curses in the sacred scriptures against such disturbers of minds, especially in the Psalms, as Psalm LV: let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell. Likewise, let sinners be turned into hell, etc. But we are taught here to observe the distinction between seducers or wolfish dogmatists, and the seduced little sheep, by the example of the Apostle, who desires that false teachers be cut off, but does not anathematize the seduced Galatians, but calls them back most gently into the way of truth and salvation.

PART II. CHAP. V. Concerning carnal license, which is an abuse of liberty, to be shunned, Wherein begins

PART THREE OF THE EPISTLE, PAEDEUTIC CONCERNING MUTUAL CHARITY AND the works of the flesh, and the fruits of the Spirit in general.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται οἱ ἀναστατοῦντες ὑμᾶς) ναι hic est ἐπιλακτικόν. Quandoquidem illi in pellicaba abscissa ita gloriantur, utinam illis abscindatur infuper totum seminale membrum, quo magis triumphent, כרות שפכה Græcè ὁ ἀποκοπτόμενος, Deut. 23, 1. est is, cui, ut cum Horatio loquar, cauda falax demessa est. Id ἀποκόψονται τὰ αἰδοῖα etiam Stephano, ubi de Gallis martis Deum, quales & Pestinunte erant, urbe tunc Galatiæ, cum hæc epistola scribere-tur.

Dion de Heliogabalo τὸ αἰδοῖον περιτέμνω, τῇ χμεινω κρεῶν, ὡς τῇ καθαρώτεροι ἐκ τέτων θεραπεύων, ἀπέκειλο. Εὐνουχίσατο μὲν παντάπασι αὐτὸ καλακλίνας. Hic καλακόψω idem est, quod ἀποκόψω apud LXX. & Paulum. Et sic hunc locum accepisse Chrysostomum apparet, εἰ βούλομαι, μὴ περιτεμνέτωσαν μόνον, ἀλλὰ περικοπτέσθωσαν. Πῶς τοίνυν οὗτοι οἱ τολμῶντες ἀποκόπτειν ἑαυτοὺς, μὴ τὴν ἀκρὸν ἐπισπώμενοι κὶ τὴν τὰ θεῦ δίμικείαν διαβάλλοντες. Nec aliter Hieronymus: Si putant sibi hoc prodesse, non solum circumcidant, sed etiam abscindantur.

Si enim exspoliatio membri profuit, multo magis abscissio. Videtur ad hunc locum respicere ex V. vifigotti ca XII. III. 4. Illi vero, qui carnis circumcisiones in Judæa vel Christiana exercere præsumpserint: quisquis hac aut in-utiliter alteri, aut fieri ab altero permiserit sibi, heretri ex toto amputatione plectetur. Ἀναστατοῦντες hic idem ταράσσοντες.

Vide Actor. 17, c. 21. 38. Hoc voto Apostolus à se longissime alienum esse impedimentum cursus Galatarum in veritatis, fidei & libertatis stadio. Gloffa vero impura Grotii de abscissione, etsi cum Hieronymo & Græcis eidem faveant Thomas & Adamus Sasbout, nec Papistis aliis Salmeroni & Cornelio se probare potuit, & ab ipsis Socinianis reprobata, atque commemoratione indigna judicata est.

Beza de separatione à Deo, Calvinus de exitio interpretatur, quod designet Apostolus, alludens ad circumcisionem, quam impostores urgebant. Non id placet Crocio.

Si ad circumcisionem, inquit, alluderet, diceret potius ὄφελον περὶ ἐμῶνται, ut constaret paronomaia περιτομῆς, ἀποτομῆς. Potius igitur respicit ad verbum ἀνέκοψε, v. 7. ut sensus fit, illi vos ἀνακόψωσιν: Utinam ipsi ἀνακόψωσιν. Sic D. Pareus. Accipit etiam pro excommunicatione posse censet Beza & cum eo Piscator, Belgæ in notis, Cornelius item à Lapide & Salmero.

Sed excommunicationem fuaffet potius, quam optasset Apostolus. Excisionem ergo optat non ex carnali affectu, sed Spiritu Dei, quo in amorem Ecclesiæ ita raptus fuit, ut perire maluerit paucos impostores incorrigibiles, quam totum Ecclesiæ corpus. Unde ad quæstionem illam, utrum liceat Christianis maledicere? respondet B. Lutherus hoc loco: Licet, non tamen semper, & ex qualibet causa. Cum eo ventum est, ut verbum fit maledicendum feu doctrina blasphemanda, & per consequens Deus ipse, tum inverte sententiam & dic, benedicatur Deus & verbum ipsius, & maledicatur quicquid est extra verbum & Deum, sive fit Apostolus, sive Angelus è cælo.

Si autem relinquunt nobis integrum & illæsum verbum, parati sumus non solum charitatem & concordiam servare cum ipsis, sed offerimus nos fore servos eorum, & nihil non facturos. Si non pereant & detrudantur ad infernum, non solum ipsi, sed totus mundus etiam cum piis & impiis, modo ut Deus maneat. Hoc manente, manet vita & salus, manebunt & pii. Recte igitur facit Paulus, quod perturbatoribus illis maledicit, & pronunciat sententiam, eos esse anathema cum omnibus, quæ sunt, docent & faciunt, quodque imprecatur cis, ut exscindantur ex hac vita, & præcipue ex Ecclesia, hoc est, ne Deus gubernet & fortunet doctrinam & omnes actiones eorum.

Et hæc maledictio profecta est à Spiritu Sancto. Sic Petrus Actor. VIII, maledicit Simoni, pecunia tua, inquit, sit tecum in perditionem &c. Et frequens usus est maledictionum in sacris literis contra tales conturbatores mentium, precipue in Psalmis, ut Psalm. LV. veniat mors super illos, & descendant in infernum viventes. Item convertantur peccatores in infernum &c. Docemur autem hic, inter seductores vel lupos dogmatistas, & seductas oviculas discrimen observare exemplo Apostoli, qui doctores falsos exscindi optat, seductos autem Galatas non anathematizat, sed in viam veritatis & salutis blandissime revocat.

PARS II. CAP. V. De licentia carnali, que libertatis abusus, fugienda, Qua inchoatur

PARS TERTIA EPISTOLAE, PAEDEUTICA DE CHARITATE MUTUA ET carnis operibus, fructibusque Spiritus universis.

## 5:13
Ver. 13. For you, brethren, were called unto liberty) You were called, namely, to salvation in a state of liberty. 'Ἐπὶ' among Greek writers often signifies a state or condition. Only do not use liberty for an occasion to the flesh) The Apostle here interjects the moral part, which he begins to treat elsewhere, having finished the dogmatic part, into the dogmatic [sections], the occasion being taken from the word liberty.

Christ gave liberty to his own in things which have nothing of honesty in themselves: but in those things which are commended by nature or by the sense of common utility, he demands more than any law. The word 'ἀφορμὴ' is missing here, it is a pretext, as in Rom. VII. 8. Do not give to the flesh, that is, to the desires of the flesh, this name of liberty, as a covering for vices: as if, forsooth, the mercy of God were so great that he would wish to give eternal life to men, however they live, as the Jewish Doctors used to say, that every Israelite would have a portion in the world to come.

Christian liberty is not to be understood in this way. But by love serve one another) Not only do not harm, but also serve all. This, therefore, is what the Apostle teaches, that Evangelical liberty is to be joined with grateful service, by which God is obeyed, by walking according to the Spirit, and by mortifying the deeds of the flesh, both so that the Pseudo-Apostles may not slander that by the Evangelical doctrine of justification by faith a window is opened to the desires of the flesh, and so that others may not rashly persuade themselves that it is lawful for them, by virtue of Evangelical liberty, to indulge the flesh and its depraved desires.

Wherefore he warns that we are so free from Levitical ceremonies and the coercion and curse of the moral law, that in the meantime we remain bound to perform holy duties to God, and offices of brotherly love to our neighbor, with a free and spontaneous spirit. Our liberty makes us servants to God and to our neighbor. Chrysostom notes that he did not say simply, love, but serve, declaring an intense and vehement friendship. For when he had taken away the yoke of the law, lest they should be idle, he imposes another yoke upon them, namely, that of charity, which is indeed stronger than the former, but much lighter and more pleasant.

To serve is to seek the advantage of others, to do good, to gratify to the best of one's ability. He prescribes mutual servitude, just as they were bound to love one another: Charity does not seek its own, but that of the neighbor, as Crocius here. An ellipsis is thus supplied by Camerarius: Only see that you do not take this liberty as an occasion to the flesh.

But he teaches by this antithesis that the right use of liberty consists in the services of mutual charity.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ὑμεῖς γὰρ ἐπ' ἐλευθερίᾳ ἐκλήθητε, ἀδελφοί) Vocati estis, nempe ad salutem in statu libertatis. Ἐπὶ apud Græcos scriptores sæpe statum aut conditionem significat. Μόνον μὴ τὴν ἐλευθερίαν εἰς ἀφορμὴν τῇ σαρκὶ) Apostolus hic partem moralem, quam alibi tractare incipit, absoluta parte dogmatica, dogmaticis interserit, occasione sumpta ex voce libertatis.

Libertatem Christus suis dedit in rebus, quæ se nihil habent honesti: in illis verò rebus, quæ natura aut sensu communis utilitatis commendantur, plus exigit, quam lex ulla. Deest hic vox ἀφορμὴ est prætextus, uti Rom. VII. 8. Nolite carni, id est, carnis cupiditatibus hoc nomen libertatis largiri, in obtegmentum vitiorum: nimirum quasi tanta sit Dei misericordia, ut hominibus, quomodocunque viventibus, velit dare vitam æternam, quomodo Judaici Doctores dicebant, omnem Israelitam partem habiturum in futuro seculo.

Non sic intelligenda est Christiana libertas. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης δουλεύετε ἀλλήλοις) Non tantum non nocete, sed & servite omnibus. Hoc ergo est, quod docet Apostolus, libertatem Evangelicam cum grata servitute conjungendam esse, qua Deo obeditur, ambulando secundum Spiritum, & facta carnis mortificando, tùm ne Pseudo-Apostoli calumnientur, per doctrinam Evangelicam de justificatione per fidem fenestram aperiri carnis cupiditatibus, tùm ne alii temere sibi persuadeant, integrum sibi esse, vi libertatis Evangelicæ indulgere carni, pravisque ejus desideriis.

Quapropter monet, ita nos liberos esse à Leviticis ceremoniis & coactione ac maledictione legis moralis, ut interim Deo ad sancta obsequia, & proximo ad fraternæ dilectionis officia spiritu libero & spontaneo præstanda maneamus obstricti. Libertas nostra facit nos Deo & proximo servos. Chrysostomus monet, quod non simpliciter dixerit, diligite, sed servite, intensam ac vehementem declarans amicitiam. Etenim cum legis jugum detraxisset, ne subfilirent, aliud ipsis imponit jugum, nimirum charitatis, illo quidem validius, sed multo levius ac jucundius.

Servire est commodum aliorum quærere, benefacere, gratificari pro virili. Servitutem præscribit mutuam, sicut mutuo se debebant diligere: Charitas non quærit, quod suum est, sed quod proximi, ut hic Crocius. Ἔλλειψις ita suppletur à Camerario: Μόνον ὀᾶτε, μὴ παραλάβητε τὴν ἐλευθερίαν ταύτην πρὸς ἀφορμὴν τῇ σαρκί.

Docet autem hac ἀντίθεσις rectum libertatis usum in charitatis mutuæ fervitiis consistere. Confer 1. Petr. II. 16. Rom. XIII. 8.

## 5:14
Compare 1 Pet. II. 16. Rom. XIII. 8. Ver. 14. For all the law is fulfilled in one word) Just as rudiments are fulfilled by a more perfect doctrine. The law joins Israelites only among themselves: the Gospel joins all men, and that not in any way, but for the sake of God: Then that 'ἀγάπιον' in the law is understood according to the precepts of the law, in the Gospel, according to the Evangelical precepts, which are much more sublime.

See Rom. XIII. 9. In the manuscript it is 'πεπλήρωται'. In that, You shall love your neighbor as yourself) These words indeed exist in Lev. XIX. 18, but there 'ὁ πλησίον' is an Israelite, or a proselyte, here it is every man: There love is required in certain deeds: here both in mind and in greater deeds.

He teaches not in what the rudiments of the law are fulfilled, so that they may be perfected, because the law of Moses was not imperfect, but perfect, admitting no addition or diminution, Deut. IV. 2. chap. XII. 32. nor are they merely rudiments, as Grotius calls them, because this very precept is contained in the same words, Lev. XVIII. But it embraces the sum of the law, which is comprehended in that one 'λόγῳ' or precept, so that to love is the same as to fulfill the whole law, contrary to which Christ acted everywhere, Matt. V. 44, 45. Luke VI. 27, etc. The love of God is not excluded, which the law primarily requires, but the love of the neighbor presupposes it, and sprouts from it as from a root, and is its certain document, and norm and rule. For the neighbor is to be loved according to and for the sake of God.

He who says he loves God, and does not love his neighbor, is a liar, 1 John IV. 20. Conf. Rom. XIII. 18. as if he were saying, in the interpretation of B. Luther, fol. 138: There is no need to burden you with circumcision and Mosaic rites; but above all persevere in the doctrine of faith which you have received from me. Afterwards, if you wish to do good works, I will show you in one word the highest and greatest works, and how you may fulfill all laws. Love one another through charity, and there will not be lacking those to whom you can do good. For the world is full of men who are in need of the help of others. This is the perfect doctrine of faith and charity, and the shortest and longest theology.

Brief as to words and sentences, but broader, longer, deeper and more sublime in use and in reality than the whole world. That only an Israelite, or a benefactor, is to be understood by neighbor is a Pharisaical gloss, against which Christ acted everywhere, Matth. V. 44. 46. Luc. VI. 27. seqq. &c. That anyone whatsoever is to be understood as one in need of our help, Christ taught the lawyer, Luc. X. 30. The neighbor in this passage is not to be sought by nearness of blood, but by fellowship of reason, in which all men are fellows, says Augustine epist. LII. ad Marcum, πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστίν, ἡ ὁμοιοπαθὲς καὶ λογικὸν ζῶον ἄνθρωπος, says Justinus in the Dialogue with Trypho. Nor is less required of affection of love and cordial love in the law than in the New Testament.

For the law is spiritual, Rom. VII. 14, and commands to love the neighbor as ourselves. But do we not love ourselves from the heart, or only by external deeds?

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ὁ γὰρ πᾶς νόμος ἐν ἑνὶ λόγῳ πληροῦται) Sicuti rudimenta implentur per doctrinam perfectiorem. Lex Israelitas tantum inter se jungit: Evangelium homines omnes, idque non quovis modo, sed propter Deum: Tum illud ἀγάπιον in lege intelligitur, secundum præcepta legis, in Evangelio, secundum præcepta Evangelica, multo sublimiora.

Vide Rom. XIII. 9. In manuscripto est πεπλήρωται. ἐν τῇ, ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον ὡς ἑαυτόν) Extant quidem hæc verba Levit. XIX. 18. sed ibi ὁ πλησίον est Israeli-ta, aut proselyrus, hic omnis homo: Ibi dilectio exigitur in factis quibusdam: hic & in animo, & in factis majoribus.

Non in quo impleantur rudimenta legis, ut perficiantur docet, quia lex Moysis non imperfecta fuit, sed perfecta, nullam additionem vel diminutionem admittens, Deut. IV. 2. cap. XII. 32. nec sola rudimenta, quæ vocat Grotius, quia hoc ipsum præceptum totidem verbis continetur, Levit. XVIII. Sed summam legis complectitur, quæ in uno illo λόγῳ vel præcepto comprehendatur, ut diligere fit idem, quod totam legem implere, contra quam passim Christus egit Matth. V. 44. 45. Luc. VI. 27. seqq. Non excluditur Dei dilectio, quam lex primario requirit, sed dilectio proximi illam præsupponit, & ex illa tanquam radice pullulat, ejusque certum est documentum, ac norma & regula. Diligendus enim est proximus secundum & propter Deum.

Qui Deum diligere se dicit, & proximum non diligit, mendax est, 1. Johan. IV. 20. Conf. Roman. XIII. 18. quasi dicat, interprete, B. Luthero, fol. 138. Non opus est onerare vos circumcisione & ritibus Mosaicis; sed ante omnia perseverate in fidei doctrina quam à me accepistis. Post si vultis bene operari, ego uno verbo ostendam vobis summa & maxima opera, & quomodo omnes leges impleatis. Diligite vos mutuo per charitatem, non deerunt, quibus benefacere poteritis. Mundus enim plenus est hominibus, qui ope aliorum egent. Hac perfecta est doctrina de fide & charitate, & theologia brevissima & longissima.

Brevissima quod ad verba & sententias attinet, sed usu & reipsa latior, longior, profundior & sublimior toto mundo. In lege tantum Israelitam, aut benefactorem intelligi, glossa Pharisaica est, contra quam passim Christus egit, Matth. V. 44. 46. Luc. VI. 27. seqq. &c. Quemvis intelligendum esse nostræ opis indigum, Christus legisperitum edocuit, Luc. X. 30. Proximus hoc loco non sanguinis propinquitate, sed rationis societate petandus est, in quo socii sunt omnes homines, ait Augustinus epist. LII. ad Marcum, πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστίν, ἡ ὁμοιοπαθὲς καὶ λογικὸν ζῶον ἄνθρωπος, ait Justinus in Dialogo cum Tryph. Nec minus dilectionis affectus & dilectio cordialis in lege, quam in Novo Testamento requiritur.

Nam lex spiritualis est, Rom. VII. 14. & diligere jubet proximum, sicut nosmetipsos. An vero non diligimus nos ipsos ex animo, num factis solum externis?

## 5:15
Ver. 15. But if you bite one another) In words: For there were dissensions among the Galatians. Do not consume) that is, you harm by deeds. Take heed that you be not consumed one by another) Beware, he says, of such things, lest by these mutual hatreds you stir up the wrath of God and most grievous punishments upon yourselves. See Heb. XII. v. 19.

Some gather from these things, and not without reason, that there was contention among the Galatians, with quarrels and accusations concerning the doctrine of faith and works.

B. Luther: Paul, he says, fol. 139, testifies in these words, that peace and concord cannot exist in the Churches, neither in doctrine nor in life, if the foundation is subverted by impious Doctors, which is faith in Christ, but that other and yet other opinions and dissensions concerning doctrine and life arise continuously.

But once the concord of the Church is violated, there is neither measure nor end to the dissensions. For the authors of schisms, disagreeing among themselves, teach this thing here, and another thing there, as a work necessary for righteousness. And whoever approves his own opinion and superstition, condemns that of another. There it is necessary that disagreements and factions arise.

Whence it happens that they bite and devour one another, that is, judge and condemn, until they finally perish. With unity ceasing, according to the Mathematicians, the number progresses to infinity. Thus, with the unity of the Spirit injured and taken away, it is impossible for concord to remain, neither in doctrine nor in morals, but new errors arise continuously to infinity.

Here these mutual bitings and devourings are called by that metaphor not unfamiliar to the Germans. And it is referred not unaptly by Jerome to higher things. But if love ceases, and there is no charity, through which the whole law is fulfilled, it will be a certain public robbery among men, so that devouring and biting one another, they are consumed by one another.

He says not only, you bite, which is indeed of one who is agitated, but he adds also, you devour, which is of one persevering in malice. For he who bites, what he has seized, has satisfied his anger, but he who devours, exhibits a specimen of extreme duration and inhumanity, as Chrysostom says. A sad spectacle, when wild beasts have fallen upon one another with mutual bites, if they do not only wound one another, but also devour, which, however, wild beasts of the same species very rarely do.

The Galatians exhibited a much fouler spectacle, harming themselves with mutual dissensions like biting and carnivorous wild beasts, such as wolves, lions, hyenas. These are heavier wounds. For he who has tasted human flesh has not caused as much evil as he who has fixed it again in his mind.

For by how much the soul is more excellent than the body, by so much more grievous it is to have injured it, as Crocius says here.

Latin:

Vers. 15. εἰ δὲ ἀλλήλους δάκνετε) Verbis: Erant enim dissidia inter Galatas. μὴ κατεσθίετε) id est, læditis factis. Βλέπετε, μὴ ὑπὸ ἀλλήλων ἀναλωθῆτε) Cavete vobis, inquit à talibus, ne mutuis istis odiis Dei iram & pœnas gravissimas in vosmetipsos concitetis. Vide Hebr. XII. v. 19.

Colligerent ex his nonnulli, nec immerito, inter Galatas contentionibus, rixis & criminationibus de doctrina fidei & operum certatum esse.

B. Lutherus: Paulus, inquit fol. 139. his verbis testatur, in Ecclesiis non posse constare pacem & concordiam, neque in doctrina, neque in vita, si per impios Doctores subvertatur fundamentum, hoc est fides in Christum, sed subinde oriri alias atque alias opiniones & dissensiones de doctrina & vita.

Semel autem violata Ecclesiae concordia, non est modus neque finis dissensionum. Autores enim schismatum inter se diffidentes hic illud, alius aliud opus docet ad justitiam necessarium. Quique suam opinionem & superstitionem probat, alterius reprehendit. Ibi necesse est oriri dissidia & factiones.

Unde fit, ut alii alios mordeant & devorent, hoc est, judicent & condemnent, donec tandem pereant. Cessante unitate secundum Mathematicos, progreditur numerus usque in infinitum. Sic lesa & ablata unitate Spiritus neque in doctrina, neque in moribus possibile est manere concordiam, sed subinde novi errores nascuntur usque in infinitum.

Hic vocantur morsus & devorationes mutuae Metaphora illa Germanis non insueta. Et refertur id non inconcinae ab Hieronymo ad superiora. Quod si cesset dilectio, & non sit charitas, per quam lex universa completur, publicum quoddam inter homines latrocinium erit, ut contra se invicem devorantes seque mordentes consumantur ab invicem.

Non solum dicit, mordetis, quod sane est commoti, sed addit etiam devoratis, quod est in malitia perseverantis. Nam qui mordet, quod apprehendit, iram explevit, sed qui devorat, extreme diuturnis & immanitatis specimen edit, dicente Chrysostomo. Triste spectaculum, cum ferae in se mutuo inciderunt mutuis morsibus, si non vulnerant se tantum, sed & devorant, quod tamen ejusdem speciei ferae rarissime faciunt.

Multo foedius spectaculum Galatae exhibebant, sese mutuis dissidiis laedentes instar mordacium & carnivorarum ferarum, quales lupi, leones, hyaenae. Graviora hae vulnera. Nam qui carnem gustavit humanam, non tantum mali dedit, quantum is, qui rursum fixit in animum.

Siquidem quanto corpore praestantior est anima, tanto gravius est hanc laesisse, ut hic Crocius.

## 5:16
Ver. 16. But I say, walk by the Spirit) That is, conduct your life according to the Spirit of Christ, which always harmonizes with the words of Christ, Rom.

Vers. VIII. 1. 10. 13. 14. and here below 18. & 23. Καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς μὴ τελέσητε) So it will happen that you do not do those things which, supply only, please the flesh.

Those who do this are said to have a care for the flesh unto its lusts, Rom. XIII. 14. to walk according to the flesh, Rom. VIII. 1. To be in the flesh, Rom. VIII. 9. The flesh and the affections, which arise from the flesh, seek pleasant things, and do not consider what is right or not right, which distinction reason dictates to some extent, but the precepts of God most fully.

Such affections are called ἐπιθυμία σαρκός, John 2, 16. Eph. 2, 3. 1 Pet. 2, 11. They err who think μὴ τελέσητε is an Imperative, nor does the passage which they cite show that in any way.

On the contrary, μὴ, having a following subjunctive, signifies that which can happen or is wont to happen, Matt. 5, 18. ἃ μὴ παρέλθῃ, as also Luke 21, 32. Matt. 10, 23. ἃ μὴ τελέσητε, and 42. ἃ μὴ ἀπολέσῃ, c. 16, 8. ἃ μὴ γεύσωνται, Heb. 8, 11. ἃ μὴ διδάξωσιν, Apoc. 18, 7. ἃ μὴ ἴδω τε τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν to perform it by deed, thus ἁμαρτία ἀπολελεσμένη, James 1, 15. The general precept concerning avoiding the abuse of liberty is followed by another concerning the remedy of the abuse, namely, the curbing of the license of the flesh by the grace of the Spirit: And the Apostle resumes explaining what at v. 13 seemed said somewhat obscurely: with that formula which he previously used at cap. III. 17. and cap. IV. 1., as if he were saying, I have admonished you not to take liberty as an occasion for the flesh, I shall say it more explicitly. The Papists understand Spirit as reason and intellectual appetite, and flesh as sensuality or sensitive appetite.

But the Apostle does not form an Ethical life with Aristotle, but a Christian one, which is not only praised civilly, but also approved by God, as the life of the children of God. And the Spirit in the Scriptures, when it is opposed to the flesh, where there is a discourse on morals, denotes the part of man reborn in the Spirit of God, or the new man, or the flesh denotes the original depravity of nature, or the part of man not reborn or the old man. Furthermore, both Spirit and flesh occupy the faculties of the whole man, as well the higher as the lower, as well the logical and governing, as the appetitive and irascible. Concerning which B. Luther fol. 140. I do not deny that the concupiscence of the flesh embraces lust, yet not that alone: Because it embraces all vicious affections, with which the pious struggle, some more, some less, such as pride, hatred, avarice, impatience, lust, etc. Nay, among the works of the flesh, Paul recounts not only those gross vices, but also idolatry, heresies, etc., below. It is certain, therefore, that he speaks of the whole concupiscence of the flesh, and the entire polity of sin, which struggles in the pious, who have received the firstfruits of the Spirit against the polity of the Spirit. Therefore, he speaks not only of lust, pride, etc., but also of incredulity, diffidence, desperation, hatred, contempt of God, idolatry, heresies, etc. Therefore, to walk in the Spirit is to walk according to the instinct and impulse of grace infused by the Holy Spirit, who through the word suggests to hearts what is to be done and what is to be omitted, to institute actions and life, and as befits new men, to walk reborn by the Spirit of God.

He uses the word "walking" to designate the whole course proposed to the Christian on the way to the goal, and the progress to be made continuously. But one must walk in the Spirit, so that the vicious concupiscence of the flesh, that is, not only appetitions, but also thoughts, and even the concepts of the mind, and the desires of the will, which are opposed to the Spirit of God, and do not suit a man reborn by the Spirit, are not fulfilled. Those cannot be entirely avoided in this infirmity, but one must beware, when we are tickled by them, through the remnants of the flesh, that we do not carry them out and fulfill them, or complete them by deed. Vers. 17. ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός) That is, by nature they are carried in different directions, the flesh toward pleasant things, the spirit toward those things which are pious and holy. ταῦτα δὲ ἀντίκειται ἀλλήλοις) Namely, in many things many things delight which are not fitting: and on the contrary.

This saying has the force of a comparison. ἵνα μή, ἃ ἂν θέλητε, ταῦτα ποιῆτε) This is to be construed with the nearest member, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ σαρκός, therefore the Spirit opposes itself to the flesh, lest you do those things which otherwise you would wish, namely, if the flesh alone led you. See Rom. 8, 13. Some among Chrysostom interpret the flesh as the body, the spirit as the soul.

But concupiscence is not of the body, it is of the soul. Nor do soul and body oppose one another. Origen takes it away to the spiritual and carnal sense. Not concerning the double sense of Scripture here, which Scripture nowhere delivered, but concerning the struggle of those things which are in man; the Scholastics, as was indicated before, understand by the flesh the sensitive appetite, by the Spirit reason, to which the Socinians do not refuse, as far as the flesh is concerned.

By the flesh, says Schlichtingius from his Crellius, is understood the appetite or that power of our soul which moves the affections: by the Spirit, however, he understands the divine power and efficacy, which is in all Christians, and gives them mind and strength, so that in life they cultivate piety. But he confuses it with the Holy Spirit, from which it must be altogether distinguished, as from the author, whatever Spirit is in us. For that which is from the Spirit born is, it is Spirit, as Christ testifies John 3. 16. Yet Crellius and Schlichtingius depart in this from their Socinus, who explains the Apostle concerning the unregenerate man, in whom certainly there is no efficacy of the Spirit of God: and it has been shown that the Apostle applies these things to himself also at Rom. 7. 14. Although, therefore, that struggle of reason and appetite is not to be denied, it is nevertheless in all men, and it is certain that the Apostle speaks of the regenerate.

Nor does the Apostle restrict the flesh only to appetite, since the struggle of flesh and Spirit is in the very rational faculty of man, which Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide, and Justinianus acknowledge. And most manifestly of all, from v. 19, as B. Luther in his former Commentary, fol. 86, is the author, it is clear that flesh is not taken only for lustful concupiscences, but for everything whatsoever that is contrary to the Spirit of grace.

For heresies and sects or dissensions are the vices of the most subtle minds, and those shining with a most holy appearance: and thus by flesh the whole man is signified, and by Spirit equally the whole, and the inner and outer man or the new and old are not distinguished according to the difference of soul and body, but according to the affections. For since the fruits or works of the Spirit are peace, faith, continence, etc. And these are done in the body, who can deny that the Spirit and its fruit are in the body and carnal members?

As is expressly stated in 1 Corinthians 6. Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit? Behold, not only the soul, but the members also are a spiritual temple. And again, glorify and carry God in your body, he does not say, in your soul. On the other hand, when enmity, (he says) leads only the soul, who will deny that the flesh is in the soul? Therefore, the spiritual man is the whole man, insofar as he savors the things that are of God; the carnal man is the whole man, insofar as he savors the things that are his own.

The flesh lusts by hindering good motions, and by exciting wicked thoughts, desires, and motions against that part of man regenerated by the virtue of the Holy Spirit. But the Spirit lusts against the flesh, both by repressing wicked thoughts, machinations, etc., and by suggesting good thoughts, desires, and motions through the grace of the Holy Spirit. There are not wanting those who admit that the corruption of concupiscence and the renewal of the Spirit are opposed here, but they place in the middle the soul or the will of man, having in its power good and evil, to will and to nill: thus the soul is the subject of that contrariety, but it does not mediate between flesh and Spirit, as if not subject to the flesh, but it is flesh insofar as it is corrupt. Spirit is renewed through grace, as if by the Spirit of God to the image of God.

The Apostle says simply and in the present: The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, to indicate a continuous struggle. One must act in a perpetual struggle against the Spirit. He adds the cause, because these are opposed to one another. Therefore, that struggle can never have an end as long as the remnants of the flesh remain in man.

Even in the very victory of the Spirit, the struggle is detected because of our infirmity and the imperfection of our renewal. Therefore, it hinders us so that we do not do the same things that we would have willed. For although we do some things that we will, yet none as we will and as we ought: Because imperfection adheres to all things.

The flesh does not allow us to do in this way the things that we will according to the Spirit. Grotius has from the Socinians that sometimes, or in many things, those things that are not becoming delight us. For the flesh always opposes the Spirit. This the Spirit does, that you may not accomplish whatever you would have willed according to the flesh; this the flesh does, that you may not do or omit whatever you would have willed according to the Spirit, as is fitting.

These two leaders, says B. Luther, fol. 141, in your body, flesh and Spirit oppose each other, so that you do not do those things that you would have willed.

I take these words potentially, that is, so that you cannot do what you would have willed. With these sentiments he consoles the tempted, as if to say, it is impossible that you should follow the Spirit as leader in all things, without any sense or impediment of the flesh. Indeed, the flesh will oppose, and will so oppose, that you cannot do what you would willingly have done. Here it is enough that you resist the flesh, lest you accomplish its concupiscence, that is, that you follow the Spirit, not the flesh, which is easily broken by impatience, desires vengeance, bites, doubts, murmurs, hates God, is infected by it, despises, etc.

Whoever is ignorant of this doctrine and thinks that the pious ought to be entirely free from every defect, and yet feels the contrary, he is in the end absorbed by the Spirit of sadness and despairs. But he who knows this doctrine, and rightly relies upon it, to him it is necessary that even evils work together for good. For when the flesh is accustomed to incite him to sin, by this occasion he is excited and urged to seek the remission of sins for the sake of CHRIST, to embrace the righteousness of faith, which otherwise he would not value so much, nor would he sigh for it with such desire. Therefore, it is very profitable that we sometimes feel the malice of our nature and flesh, so that even in this way we may be awakened and excited to faith and to the invocation of CHRIST.

And by this occasion the Christian becomes a most powerful craftsman and a wondrous creator, who can make joy out of sadness, consolation out of terrors, righteousness out of sin, life out of death, while in this way, restraining the flesh, he reduces it to servitude and subjects it to the Spirit. Wherefore, those feeling the concupiscence of the flesh should not therefore immediately despair of salvation. Let them feel it indeed, provided they do not assent to it: Let anger, lust, etc., indeed move them, provided it does not move them to action: Let sin solicit them, provided they do not perform it. Indeed, the more pious each one is, the more he feels that struggle.

Hence are those complaints of the Saints in the Psalms and in the Scripture.

Latin:

Vers. 16. λέγετε δέ, πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε) Id est, vitam instituete secundum Spiritum Christi, qui semper Christi verbis consonat, Rom.

VIII. 1. 10. 13. 14. & hic infra 18. & 23. Καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς μὴ τελέσητε) Ita fiet, ut non agatis ea, quae carni, supple tantum, placent.

Quod qui faciunt, dicuntur carnis curam habere ad cupiditates, Rom. XIII. 14. ambulare secundum carnem, Rom. VIII. 1. In carne esse, Rom. VIII. 9. Caro & affectus, qui ex carne oriuntur, quaerunt jucunda, nec considerant, quid rectum aut non rectum fit, quod discrimen aliquatenus dictat ratio, Dei autem praecepta plenissime.

Tales affectus vocantur ἐπιθυμία σαρκός, Joh. 2, 16. Ephes. 2, 3. 1. Petr. 2, 11. errant, qui μὴ τελέσητε putant esse Imperativi, nec locum, quem citant, id ullo modo ostendit.

Contra μὴ, sequentem habens subjunctivum, significat id, quod fieri potest aut solet, Matth. 5, 18. ἃ μὴ παρέλθῃ, ut & Luc. 21, 32. Matth. 10, 23. ἃ μὴ τελέσητε, & 42. ἃ μὴ ἀπολέσῃ, c. 16, 8. ἃ μὴ γεύσωνται, Hebr. 8, 11. ἃ μὴ διδάξωσιν, Apoc. 18, 7. ἃ μὴ ἴδω τε τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν opere eam perficere, sic ἁμαρτία ἀπολελεσμένη, Jac. 1, 15. Praeceptum generale prius de libertatis abusu vitando sequitur alterum de remedio abusus, licentia scil. carnis Spiritus gratia frenanda: Et resumit Apostolus explicare, quod v. 13. videbatur dictum obscurius: formula qua prius cap. III. 17. & cap. IV. 1. usus, quasi dicat, monui, ne libertatem accipatis in occasione carnis dicam explicatius. Papistae Spiritum de ratione, & appetitu intellectuali, carnem de sensualitate seu appetitu sensitivo intelligunt.

Sed Apostolus non Ethicam vitam cum Aristotele, sed Christianam format, quae non modo civiliter laudetur, sed & Deo approbetur, ut vita filiorum Dei. Et Spiritus in Scripturis, cum carni opponitur, ubi de moralibus sermo est, partem hominis in Spiritu Dei renatam, seu novam hominem, aut caro pravitatem originalem naturae, vel partem hominis non renatam seu veterem hominem denotat. Adhac tam Spiritus quam caro totius hominis facultates tam summas, quam inferiores, tam λογικὴν & ἡγεμονικὴν, quam ἐπιθυμητικὴν & θυμικὴν occupat. Quo de B. Lutherus fol. 140. Non nego concupiscentiam carnis complecti libidinem, non tamen solam: Quia omnes vitiosos affectus complectitur, quibus pii laborant, alii magis, alii minus, ut sunt superbia, odium, avaritia, impatientia, libido &c. Imo inter opera carnis non solum crassa illa vitia, sed etiam idololatriam, haereses &c. infra recenset Paulus. Constat igitur eum loqui de tota concupiscentia carnis, & universa politia peccati, quae luctatur in piis, qui primitias Spiritus acceperunt contra politiam Spiritus. Non solum igitur loquitur de libidine, superbia, & c. sed etiam de incredulitate, diffidentia, desperatione, odio, contemptu Dei, idololatria, haeresibus &c. Spiritu ergo incedere est juxta instinctum & impulsum gratiae Spiritu Sancto inditae, qui per verbum suggerit cordibus facienda, & omittenda, actiones vitam, quae instituere, & ceu novos homines decet, per Spiritum Dei renatos ambulare.

Incessus verbo utitur, ut cursum totum Christiano propositum in via ad metam ingredium & progressum subinde instituendum designet. Incedendum autem Spiritu, ut concupiscentia carnis vitiosa, hoc est, non tantum appetitiones, sed etiam cogitationes, adeoque etiam conceptus mentis, & desideria voluntatis, quae Spiritui Dei adversantur, nec conveniunt homini per Spiritum renato, non perficiantur. Non possunt illa omnino in hac infirmitate vitari, sed cavendum, cum iisdem titillamur, per carnis reliquias, ut ne eadem exequamur & perficiamus, vel opere compleamus. Vers. 17. ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός) Id est, natura in diversum feruntur, carnis in fauva, spiritus in ea, quae pia & sancta sunt. ταῦτα δὲ ἀντίκειται ἀλλήλοις) Nempe in multis rebus multa delectant, quae non decent: & contra.

Hoc dictum vim habet παραθέσεως. ἵνα μή, ἃ ἂν θέλητε, ταῦτα ποιῆτε) Hoc construendum est cum proximo membro, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ σαρκός, ideo Spiritus re carni opponit, ne ea faciatis, quae alioqui velletis, nempe si caro sola vos duceret. Vide Rom. 8, 13. Nonnulli apud Chrysostomum carnem corpus, spiritum animam interpretantur.

Sed concupiscentia non est corporis, anima est. Nec anima & corpus sibi invicem adversantur. Origenes ad spiritualem & carnalem sensum abripit. Non de duplici hic scriptura sensu, quem nuspiam scriptura tradidit, sed de pugna earum, quae in homine sunt; Scholastici, quod ante indicatum, per carnem appetitum sensitivum, per Spiritum rationem intelligunt, quibus non abnuunt Sociniani, quod ad carnem attinet.

Per carnem, inquit Schlichtingius e suo Crellio, intelligitur appetitus seu vis illa animae nostrae, quae movet affectus: per Spiritum tamen vim & efficaciam divinam intelligit, quae omnibus Christianis infit, iisque animum & robur indat, ut vita pietatem colant. Sed cum Spiritu Sancto confundat, a quo omnino distinguendum est, tanquam ab autore, quicquid in nobis est Spiritus. Nam quod ex Spiritu natum est, Spiritus est, teste Christo Ioh. III. 16. Abeunt tamen in eo Crellius & Schlichtingius à Socino suo, qui cum Pelagio de homine non regenito Apostolum explicat, in quo certe non est efficacia Spiritus Dei: et Apostolum hæc sibi etiam applicare ad Rom. VII. 14. ostensum est.

Etsi ergo non neganda sit pugna illa rationis & appetitus, ea tamen est in omnibus hominibus, Apostolumque de renatis loqui certum est. Nec carnem tantum ad appetitum restringit Apostolus, quum in ipsa etiam rationali hominis facultate pugna sit carnis & Spiritus, quod agnoscunt Bellarminus, Cornelius à Lapide, Justinianus. Et omnium manifestissime, è v. 19. B. Lutherus in Comment. priori fol. 86. autore, patet, carnem non pro libidinosis tantum accipi concupiscentiis, sed pro omni prorsus eo, quod contrarium est Spiritui gratiæ.

Nam hæreses & sectæ seu dissensiones sunt vitia subtilissimarum mentium, & sanctissima specie fulgentium: adeoque per carnem totum hominem significari, per Spiritum æque totum atque hominem interiorem & exteriorem seu novum & veterem non distingui juxta differentiam animæ & corporis, sed juxta affectus. Nam cum fructus seu opera Spiritus sint pax, fides, continentia &c. Et hæc in corpore fiant, quis potest negare Spiritum & fructum ejus in corpore membrisque carnalibus esse?

Sicut expresse primo Corinthios VI. An nescitis, quod membra vestra templum sunt Spiritus Sancti? Ecce non tantum anima, sed membra quoque sunt spirituale templum. Et iterum glorificate & portate Deum in corpore vestro, non dicit, in anima vestra. Contra quando inimicitia, (inquit) ducit tantum animum, quis negabit, carnem esse in anima? Igitur spiritualis homo totus homo est, quantum sapit, quæ Dei sunt; carnalis totus quantum sapit, quæ sua sunt.

Caro concupiscit tùm impediendo bonos motus, tàm excitando pravas cogitationes, cupiditates, motiones adversus partem hominis Spiritus Sancti virtute regenitam. At Spiritus concupiscit adversus carnem, tum reprimendo pravas cogitationes, molitiones &c. tum suggerendo bonas cogitationes, desideria, motus per Spiritus Sancti gratiam. Non desunt, qui corruptionem quidem concupiscentiæ & renovationem Spiritus sibi hic opponi admittant, sed in medio constituant animam seu voluntatem hominis habentem in potestate sua bonum & malum, velle & nolle: sic anima est subjectum illius contrarietatis, non autem mediat inter carnem & Spiritum, quasi carni non obnoxia, sed est caro natura quatenus corrupta. Spiritus per gratiam quasi Spiritu Dei ad imaginem Dei renovata.

Simpliciter ait Apostolus & in præsenti: Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum, & Spiritus adversus carnem, ut continuam indicet pugnam. In perpetua Spiritui lucta agendum. Causam addit, quia hæc inter se opposita. Non potest ergo unquam finem habere illa lucta, donec supersunt carnis reliquiæ in homine.
