In ipsa etiam victoria Spiritus lucta deprehenditur ob infirmitatem nostram, & renovationis imperfectionem. Ideo impedit, ut non quæ voluerimus, eadem faciamus. Etsi enim quædam faciamus, quæ volumus, nulla tamen ita ut volumus, & ut debemus: Quia omnibus adhæret imperfectio.

Caro non finit nos ita facere, quæ volumus secundum Spiritum. A Socinianis habet Grotius, quod quandoque tantum, vel in multis nos ea delectent, quæ non decent. Caro enim semper adversatur Spiritui. Hoc agit Spiritus, ut non quæcunque facere juxta carnem velletis, perficiatis, hoc agit caro, ut non quæcunque secundum Spiritum facere aut omittere velletis, prout par est, faciatis aut omittatis.

Hi duo duces, inquit B. Lutherus fol. 141. in corpore vestro, caro & Spiritus adversantur sibi, ut non quæcunque volueritis, illa faciatis.

Ista verba potentialiter accipio, id est, ut non possitis facere, quæ velletis. His sententiis consolatur tentatos, quasi dicat, impossibile est, ut per omnia ducem Spiritum sequamini, sine ullo sensu aut impedimento carnis. Imo caro obstabit, & ita obstabit, ut non possitis facere, quæ libenter velletis. Hic satis est, ut carni resistatis, ne concupiscentiam ejus perficiatis, hoc est, ut Spiritum sequamini, non carnem, que facile impatientia frangitur, cupit vindictam, mordet, dubitat, murmurat, odit Deum, inficitur ei, despectat Sc.

Qui ignorat hanc doctrinam & cogitat, pios prorsus carere debere omni defectu, & tamen sentit contrarium, is ad extremum absorbetur Spiritu tristitia & desperat. Qui vero hanc doctrinam novit, & recte ea nititur, huic etiam mala necesse est cooperari in bonum. Nam cum caro foletitat eum ad peccandum, hac occasione excitatur & urgetur ad quærendam remissionem peccatorum propter CHRISTUM, ad justitiam fidei amplectendam, quam alioqui tanti non faceret, neque tanto desiderio suspiraret. Itaque valde prodest, ut nonnunquam sentiamus malitiam naturæ & carnis nostræ, us vel hoc modo expergefiamus & excitemur ad fidem & invocandum CHRISTUM.

Atque ista occasione Christianus fit artifex potentissimus & mirificus creator, qui ex tristitia gaudium, ex terroribus consolationem, ex peccato justitiam, ex morte vitam, dum hac ratione coercens carnem eam in servitutem redigit, & Spiritui subjicit, facere potest. Quare sentientes concupiscentiam carnis, non ideo statim desperent de salute. Sentiant sane eam, modo eidem non assentiantur: Moveat sane eos ira, libido &c. modo non permoveat: Sollicitet eos peccatum, modo non perficiant illud. Imo quo quisque magis pius est, hoc plus sentit illam pugnam.

Hinc sunt illa querela Sanctorum in Psalmis & tom Scriptura.

## 5:18-19
5:18, 19. Therefore, that working through charity coheres with true and justifying faith, as an effect with its proper cause necessarily, is indeed undoubted, but that charity, or the works of charity, flow together with faith unto justification and salvation, that we deny.

But, not even can any faith be feigned, says Schlichtingius from the Crellian lectures, which necessarily produces charity and good works, if good works are established as contributing nothing to justification.

But how so? For thence it happens, he says, that true faith, which is the cause of justification, necessarily brings forth the first works as far as we are concerned, because it is an induction of the mind of such a kind, and a persuasion resting on certain foundations, that one will not otherwise, unless one has lived piously, obtain eternal life, and that therefore the piety of life or good works are the condition and cause of obtaining salvation.

Take away such an opinion and persuasion from faith, and you will have taken away from it the necessity of producing good works.

For if you believe that they contribute nothing to salvation by themselves, as a thing, what will compel you to faith, that you think they must necessarily be performed by you, and therefore be performed in reality?

He who does not live piously for the sake of salvation, he will not live piously necessarily for the sake of anything.

But these are mere petitions of the principle.

For that which is in question (τὸ κεινόμενον) is assumed, that good works are necessary for salvation; that Socinian faith is assumed, by which they induce their mind, and persuade themselves, that eternal life cannot otherwise be obtained, except through good works, which persuasion and faith is indeed said to rest on certain foundations of scripture, but no foundations of scripture are produced nor can they be produced: For it is diametrically contrary to scripture, which teaches that we are justified before God and obtain salvation not through our piety, but through the righteousness of Christ.

If righteousness were by the law, Christ would have died in vain, Gal.

2: 21. But that no one is justified in the law before God is manifest (δῆλον), says the Apostle, because the just shall live by his faith, Gal.

3:11. Although, however, we believe that good works contribute nothing to salvation according to scripture: yet we know from the scriptures that they must necessarily be performed.

They are not indeed necessary by reason of a means, as if they were a cause or a certain means for obtaining salvation on our part: because faith is not only the first, but the sole cause of justification and salvation on our part, which good works follow, as effects of faith, and fruits of righteousness.

For these do not precede justification, but follow justification.

But works are necessary by reason of the command: because they are commanded by God, not that we may obtain salvation through them, but that we may show our gratitude to God, and that we may not, through the intermission of the commandments of God, and the commission of those things which are positively contrary to the commandments of God, shake off faith, and fall from the grace of God and salvation.

Thus far, therefore, one must live piously for the sake of salvation, not that we may merit or acquire salvation by piety, as Schlichtingius with the Papists establishes such a merit, by which, with divine grace added, our works have power to produce justification, namely according to that: if by grace, then not by works, otherwise grace would not be grace, Rom.

11:6, but that by the neglect of piety, salvation through Christ alone uniquely brought forth, and appropriated to us through faith, let us fall away, and perish eternally.

Latin:

V. 18. 19. Cohærere itaque τὸ operari per charitatem cum fide vera & justifica, tanquam effectum cum causa propria necessario, indubitatum quidem est, sed coinfluere charitatem, aut opera charitatis cum fide ad justificationem & salutem, id verò negamus.

Atqui, ne fingi quidem, inquit Schlichtingius è Crellianis prælectionibus, ulla fides potest, quæ necessario charitatem & bona opera producat, si bona opera nihil ad justificationem conferre statuantur.

Qui verò sic? Inde enim fit, inquit, ut fides vera, quæ justificationis causa est, quoad nos prima opera necessario pariat, quia ejusmodi animi est inductio, ac certis fundamentis nixa persuasio, ne aliter, nisi pie vixeris, sempiternam vitam consequuturum, atque adeo pietatem vitæ seu bona opera salutis adipiscendæ conditionem causamque esse.

Tolle hujusmodi ex fide sententiam ac persuasionem, & sustuleris ab ea necessitatem bona opera pariendi.

Si enim ea nihil ad salutem facere per se credis, qua res, quæ fides te adiget, ut ea necessario tibi putes præstanda, atque adeo reipsa præstes?

Qui salutis causa pie non vivit, is nullius rei causa pie necessario vivet.

Sed hæ mere sunt petitiones principii.

Assumitur enim τὸ κεινόμενον, bona opera esse necessaria ad salutem; assumitur fides illa Sociniana, qua animum inducunt suum, fibiq; persuadent, aliter non posse vitam sempiternam impetrari, nisi per bona opera, quæ persuasio & fides niti quidem certis scripturæ fundamentis dicitur, sed nulla scripturæ fundamenta producuntur nec produci possunt: Est enim scripturæ è diametro contraria, quæ non per nostram pietatem, sed per justitiam Christi nos coram Deo justificari & salutem adipisci docet.

Si per legem justitia esset, Christus frustra mortuus esset, Gal.

II. 21. Quod autem in lege nemo justificetur, coram Deo δῆλον manifestum esse, ait Apostolus, quia justus fide sua vivet, Gal.

III. 11. Quanquam verò nihil bona opera ad salutem facere juxta scriptura credamus: Necessariò tamen ea præstanda è scripturis omnino scimus.

Non necessaria quidem sunt ratione medii, quasi ad salutem consequendam ex parte nostri causa, vel medium quoddam sint: quia fides non modo prima, sed unica ex parte nostri causa est justificationis ac salutis, quam bona opera consequuntur, ut effecta fidei, & fructus justitiæ.

Hæc enim non antecedunt justificationem, sed consequuntur justificationem.

Necessaria autem sunt opera ratione mandati: quia à Deo præcepta, non ut per ea salutem impetremus, sed ut gratitudinem nostram Deo exhibeamus, nec per intermissionem præceptorum Dei, & commissionem eorum, quæ positive sunt adversa Dei præceptis, fidem excutiamus, ac gratia Dei & salute excidamus.

Hactenus ergo salutis causa pie vivendum est, non ut pietate salutem mereamur aut acquiramus, quemadmodum Schlichtingius cum Papistis tale meritum statuit, quo divina gratia accedente ad justificationem pariendam vim habeant opera nostra, scilicet juxta illud: si ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia, Rom.

XI. 6. sed ne pietatis neglectu, salute per Christum unice parta, & per fidem nobis appropriata excidamus, ac aeternum pereamus.

## 5:18
Verf. 18. Ei δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε) This coheres again with that member which I mentioned. ἄγεσθε here is to be led, governed, ruled, as

Rom. 8. 14. Οὐκ ἐστὲ ὑπὸ νόμον) It is wrongly ἄγεσθε in some Codices, who are led by the Spirit, so that now, having become of age, they will have no need of the law, the guardian of adolescence, above 3. 25. Although the flesh may perpetually struggle against the Spirit, it must nevertheless be done so that dominion is not permitted to the flesh, nor do we follow its leading, but we offer obedience to the Spirit, and allow ourselves to be led and governed by the Spirit, indeed, to be led by the Spirit, that is, by the faculty and grace granted to us by the Holy Spirit through renewal.

Crocius does not speak badly: To be led by the Spirit is, by the gift of regeneration, which is from the indwelling Holy Spirit, to be driven and impelled in the way of truth, faith, and piety toward the goal, to holy thoughts, appetites, motions, and actions. Thus those who are led by the Spirit are not under the law accusing, condemning, compelling, and terrifying them. For they do spontaneously and willingly and joyfully, aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, what the law commands.

Yet no one is so led by the Spirit that he does not have sin. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, 1 John ch. 1. verf. 8. But in vain from this the error of the Antinomians concerning Antinomians. from the law to be proscribed by the Church, they have confirmed. For the Apostle does not teach that the reborn are free from the obedience due to the law, since he himself calls it the law of love (under the law) (to be led by the Spirit), compelling and condemning, of course, even if he wishes them to live according to the rule of the laws. The reason for the consequence: Let us be led by the Spirit, thus we shall not be under the law, this is: Because the Spirit leading us is the Spirit of adoption, and of liberty, and sealing for us the liberty of the children of God, Gal. 4:6, 2 Cor. 1: 22. B. Luther, under that being led by the Spirit, includes also faith in Christ, fol. 142. When someone feels this struggle of the flesh, he should not therefore cast away his spirit, but resist in the Spirit and say: I am a sinner and I feel sin; because I have not yet been stripped of the flesh, in which sin clings for as long as it lives. But I shall obey the Spirit, not the flesh, that is, I shall apprehend Christ by faith and hope, and raise myself by his word, and being raised in this way, I shall not fulfill the concupiscence of the flesh. And afterwards, fol. 143. Therefore the pious are not under the law, namely, the Spirit. For the law cannot accuse and pass a sentence of death against them, even if they themselves feel sin and confess that they are sinners.

Because the right has been taken away from the law through Christ, who was made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law. Therefore this, which is truly sin against the law, the law cannot accuse as sin in the pious. So great, therefore, is the power of the dominion of the Spirit, that what is truly sin, the law nevertheless cannot accuse. For our righteousness is Christ, whom we apprehend by faith, he is irreprehensible, therefore he cannot be accused by the law. As long as we cling to him, we are led by the Spirit, and we are free from the law. Thus, when the Apostle also teaches good works, he does not forget the disputation concerning justification, but always indicates that it is impossible for us to be able to be justified by works.

If you are led by the Spirit, that is, if you raise yourselves by faith in Christ, etc., you are not under the law. Paul therefore teaches in this summary disputation concerning the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit, that the saints or believers cannot perfect that which the Spirit wills. For the Spirit would willingly be entirely pure, but the flesh joined to it does not permit it. Yet they are saved through the remission of sins, which is in Christ. Furthermore, because they also walk and are led by the Spirit, they are not under the law, that is, the law cannot accuse and terrify them, etc., or even if it attempts this, it cannot drive them to despair.

We are led by the Spirit, therefore, both by that faith by which we raise ourselves to Christ, and by that by which we flee the concupiscences of the flesh, and in the Spirit, we walk in the newness of life. We are not yet the Spirit, but we are led by the Spirit, says B. Luther in his former Commentary on this passage. Ver. 19. (Now the works of the flesh are manifest) That he may show where the flesh leads, with the reins removed, he points with his finger to certain most base things, compare Matt.

15:19. In particular, the Apostle now recounts both the works of the flesh and the fruits of the Spirit: He calls the former (manifest), which are known even by nature, and are held as sins even by those who are strangers to the Word of God and not reborn. The Sophists make their own habits out of the fruits, subjectively clinging in the soul: but the Apostle makes them vital works of the Spirit, and diffused through the whole man: For he opposes them to the works of the flesh: He calls the works of the flesh not fruits, the fruits of the spirit not works. Why this? B. Luther gives the reason, namely that the works of the flesh are not useful, because no one can enjoy thorns and thistles, but they become evil works, only harmful.

But the works of the Spirit are profitable, so that we may enjoy them eternally, they are the figs and grapes of the promised land, and therefore, as the witness says, they are commended by the name of fruit. B. Luther distributes the works of the flesh according to the three faculties of man. From these it is evident that Paul calls the flesh whatever is in man, embracing all three powers of the soul, namely the concupiscible will, the irascible will, and the intellect. The works of the concupiscible will are adultery, fornication: Of the irascible, quarrels, contentions, slaughters: Of the reason or intellect, errors, false religions or cults, superstitions, idolatries, heresies, sects.

Grellius says that three classes are recounted here, or three kinds of sins: one, which concerns ourselves: another, which concerns GOD: a third, which concerns our neighbor: of which the first is again divided into two: for it is referred either to venereal pleasures, or to the pleasure of food and drink. He will place that kind of sin in the front, as being most carnal and that to which the flesh is most strongly carried, and which had already passed into a kind of nature for those Gentile men by perpetual use and custom, and had in some way put off its shame among them: but he placed this at the end.

In the middle, however, he placed those sins which concern God and neighbor. Moreover, B.

Luther observes in his former Commentary the opposition in the catalog of the works of the flesh and the fruits of the Spirit. Even though the Apostle does not oppose individual fruits to individual works, but one to many, and many to many. For seven works of the flesh are recounted in the Greek text, even if the Latin editions vary, both among themselves and from the Greek codex. Only nine fruits of the Spirit are held in the source, even if through the ignorance of some, by diligence, they have been made twelve in the Latin version.

Thus he observes that charity and joy are opposed to fornication, impurity, luxury, which are perverse loves, perverse joys: peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, to enmities, contentions, quarrels, anger, brawls, dissensions: faith to heresies, idolatry, and benefits: continence to drunkenness and carousing: I add meekness to envy and homicides. But that heresies are subordinated not to luxury but to dissensions, its cause can be sought from that ordinary consequence of the works of the flesh, which B. Luther notes can be gathered better by experience and the example of two adversaries than by description: For first they are enemies and discordant, while at any given opportunity they soon litigate, but the litigants are envious, while each strives to be superior to the other, but the envious become angry, and the angry seek, on both sides, what they may say, or do, or omit, which may bite and provoke the other, this is how they quarrel.

But the quarreling dissent, and each is prompt to defend his own, and to weaken another's. From which then sects and heresies are made, while each draws others to his own side, and draws away from the other. Hence envy, a cruel evil, is nourished, and finally they rush into slaughters and homicides. And this is the end of this evil.

Take an example between two forensic adversaries, or two republics mutually opposed, or between two Sophists or Theologians contending for their opinions. Therefore, he distinguished that bitter and choleric concupiscence of the flesh by nine degrees or heads. So much does the Apostle detest the lack of charity. (adultery) Adultery in the law of Moses is the coitus of a celibate man, or a husband with another's wife: In the Gospel also of a husband with her who is not married, because Christ willed the rights of the sexes to be equal, contrary to what was done, where only men were excluded, the women were the masters of the laws, and the Vulgate omitted the capital crime against the sixth commandment. Very badly. That difference of μοιχείας (adultery) between the Law and the Gospel, which Grotius established with Crellius and Schlichtingius, is nothing. For μοιχεία does not mean anything else than what it was formerly under the Law. Adultery was then no less a crime when a husband had relations with an unmarried woman than it is today. For he violated the faith and the law of marriage, by the power of which he ought to have been and remained one flesh with his spouse, according to the matrimonial law. For even there that great maxim of the Apostle was true or held force: The husband (man) has not power over his own body, but the wife, 1. Corinth. VII. v. 4. Nor does the πολυγαμία (polygamy) of the ancients make for this, for that was not according to the law. Πορνεία (Fornication)) Under this name come sexual relations outside of marriage, and illegitimate marriages, as can be seen in 1. Cor. V. 1. See those things which were said in Acts XV. 20. Ἀκαθαρσία (Uncleanness)) This word is quite broad, as we said at Matthew ch. XXIII. verse 27, but it seems here, as also in Romans ch. I. v. 24 and 2. Cor. ch. XII. verse 21, to be contracted to unnatural lust. Thus Barnabas in his epistle calls it ἀκαθαρσίας (uncleanness) of the ἀνοῦσαν (unseemly), which is done by the mouth. Balsamon on the Basilica interprets ἀκαθαρσίας as ἀνομίας (lawlessness), that is, ערוה (nakedness). Ἀσέλγεια (Lasciviousness)) It signifies, as we said in the aforementioned place in 2. Corinthians, every kind of lasciviousness, in which the incentives of lust hold the primary parts. Verse 20. Εἰδωλολατρεία (Idolatry)) The worship of false deities, which was usually accustomed to be celebrated at images. We observe here, on account of Calixtus, those things which B. Luther said concerning Idolatry: Every such religion, he says, by which God is worshipped without His Word and command, is idolatry. And the holier and more spiritual it is in appearance, the more pernicious and pestilential it is. For it turns men away from faith in Christ, and causes them to rely on their own strengths, works, and justices. Therefore, fasting, hair-shirts, the most holy actions, the rule and the whole life of the Carthusians, whose order is nevertheless most rigid, are works of the flesh, indeed Idolatry. Because they imagine themselves to be holy and to be saved not through Christ. Whom they fear as a severe judge, but they have observed their own rule. And a little later: No one will persuade the Papists today that the private Mass is the highest blasphemy of God and idolatry, than which nothing more horrible has ever been constituted in the Church by the Apostles. Let the Helmstadt Syncretists (I mean the Calixtines) go now, and while they desire to appear Lutheran, let them still profess that they see no idolatry in the Papacy. But what is the wonder, that they absolve the Papists from idolatry, when they also absolve the Jews and the Mahometans from idolatry. Idolatry is subjoined to fornication, by which is meant spiritual fornication. He who once permits himself the pleasure of luxury does not look back to the Creator. Φαρμακεία (Sorcery)) Properly it signifies poisoning, but it often corresponds to the Hebrew word כשפים (sorceries) Exod. ch. VII. verse 11, 12, and כשפים (sorceries) Is. ch. XLVII. verse 9, 12, where it treats of magical arts, I believe, because the same people were usually both sorcerers. See the Pharmaceutria of Theocritus and Virgil. It is subjoined next to idolatry, therefore not so much that poisoning, by which poisons are mixed to harm a neighbor, as magical arts and collusions with the Devil are designated. Ἔχθραι (Enmities)) Enmities, that is, lingering hatreds. Not only lingering hatreds, but any enmities whatsoever are designated by this name, Rom. VIII. v. 7, James IV. 9. Ἔρεις (Strifes)) Contention of words arising from anger, Rom. I. 27, XIII. 13, 1. Cor. I. 11, III. 3, 2. Cor. XII. 20. Ζῆλοι (Emulations)) An improper emulation concerning honor. It is accustomed to be joined with the word ἔρις (strife), as Rom. XIII. v. 13, 1. Cor. III. verse 3. a most powerful and nearby deity; to this one, the belly, to that one, the things below the belly, serve. And Comus preserves and invigorates Venus, otherwise Venus freezes without Ceres and Bacchus. Καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τάτεις) [And you arrange the name] Of equals, the judgment is equal. Ἀπαξ λέγων ὑμῖν, καθώς χρὴ ἀκούειν) [Once saying to you, as it is necessary to hear] Briefly above v. 13. Ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες, βασιλείαν Θεοῦ ἐ κληρονο-μήσουσι) [That those who do such things will inherit the kingdom of God] That "such things" is redundant here. For it would have been enough to say "away." But because certain words had intervened, it did no harm to replace the same meaning with other small words. Do not restrict πράσσοντες [doing] to ἔξω [outside], but also take it to mean acts πραττομένοις [being done].

Where these are found, the Spirit does not yet reign.

They say that not the acts of sins, but the habits, condemn society, which we have refuted in their proper place. Schlichtingius, however, here with Crellius, thinks the word πράσσοντες [doing] should be understood differently according to the different nature of the works of the flesh. In those things, however, in which a lapse is easy, not a single act, considering divine benevolence in the New Testament, condemns, but the habit and repeated actions, or of one kind, as if someone frequently gets angry, mocks, gets drunk with wine, etc. But other things are so shameful that they cannot be committed by anyone who is endowed with true fear of GOD and true faith, and a single act of these excludes one from the kingdom of GOD, such as idolatry, sorcery, adultery, homicide, and similar things.

But a double meaning of a single word cannot be imagined in the same place, nor is any sin so light that it does not condemn, if you consider its nature and the force of the law, Deuteron. cap. XXIII. vers. 26. For every act of sin offends the infinite justice of GOD, and incurs divine malediction by itself as ἀνομία [lawlessness].

Behold, says Hieronymus in this place, enmity, contention, anger, strife, dissension, drunkenness also and other things, which we consider small, exclude us from the kingdom of GOD: Nor does it matter whether one is excluded from blessedness by one or by many, since all similarly exclude. But that sins are forgiven to the faithful is accidental, with respect to sins, not from their nature.

However, we have shown in Exeg. August. Conf. art. XII. cap. II. that this forgiveness, through repentance and faith in Christ, pertains to us not only regarding actual but also habitual sins. It is a ψευδός [falsehood] of the Socinians that they deny original sin, which is entirely habitual and is not put off throughout life.

Hence, no one is entirely free from habitual sin in this life: and that hereditary evil ever springs forth anew, pouring itself out into sins of every kind, since every fashioning of the human heart is only evil all the days of its life, Gen. VI. & VIII.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ei δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε) Hoc iterum cum illo, quod dixi, membro cohæret. ἄγεσθε hic est duci, gubernari, regi, ut Rom.

VIII. 14. Οὐκ ἐστὲ ὑπὸ νόμον) Male in quibusdam Codicibus ἄγεσθε, qui Spiritum ducuntur, ut jam majores annis facti non opus habebunt lege, adolescentiæ custode, supra III. 25. Quanquam perpetuo luctetur caro adversus Spiritum, id tamen agendum, ut dominium non permittatur carni, nec ductum ejus sequamur, sed Spiritui obsequium prætermus, & à Spiritu nos duci gubernarique sinamus, imo Spiritu, hoc est, facultate & gratia nobis à Spiritu Sancto per renovationem concessa ducamur.

Non male Crocius: Duci Spiritu, est dono regenerationis, quod est ab inhabitante Spiritu Sancto, in via veritatis, fidei & pietatis ad metam agi, impelli ad sanctas cogitationes, appetitiones, motus, actiones. Ita quæducuntur Spiritu, non sunt sub lege se accusante, damnante, cogente, terrente. Sponte enim & libenter & jucunde faciunt Spiritus Sancti gratia adjuti, quæ lex præcipit.

Nemo tamen ita Spiritu ducitur, ut non habeat peccatum. Nam si dicimus, quod peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis, 1. Johann. cap. I. vers. 8. Frustra autem hinc Antinomi errorem de Antinomi. de lege ex Ecclesia proscribenda firmarunt. Non enim docet Apostolus, renatos ab obedientia legi debita liberos esse, siquidem ipse dilectionis legem (ὑπὸ νόμον) (Spiritu duci) ait, cogente ac damnante scilicet, etsi velit eos vivere secundum legum regulam. Ratio consequentiae: Ducamur Spiritu, ita non erimus sub lege, haec est: Quod Spiritus nos ducens Spiritus adoptionis est, & libertatis, & arrhabo libertatem filiorum Dei nobis obsignans, Gal. IV. 6. 2. Cor. I. v. 22. B. Lutherus sub illo Spiritu duci complectitur etiam fidem in Christum fol. 142. Cum aliquis sentit hanc carnis pugnam, non ideo abjiciat animum, sed resistat Spiritu & dicat: Ego sum peccator & peccatum sentio; quia carne nondum exutus sum, in qua tantisper haeret peccatum, donec vivit.

Sed Spiritui non carni obsequar, hoc est, apprehendam fide & spe Christum, ac ipsius verbo me erigam, atque hoc modo erectus concupiscentiam carnis non perficiam. Et postea fol. 143. Itaque pii non sunt sub lege scilicet Spiritu. Lex enim non potest accusare & ferre sententiam morte contra eos, etiam si ipsi peccatum sentiant & fateantur se peccatores esse. Quia jus ademptum est legi per Christum, qui factus est sub legem, ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret.

Ideo hoc, quod vere peccatum est, contra legem, lex pro peccato non potest accusare in piis. Tanta est igitur potentia dominii Spiritus, ut quod vere peccatum est, tamen lex non possit accusare. Justitia enim nostra Christus, quem fide apprehendimus, irreprehensibilis est, ideo a lege non potest accusari. Donec in illo haeremus, Spiritu ducimur, & a lege liberi sumus. Sic cum Apostolus etiam bona opera docet, non obliviscitur disputationis de justificatione, sed semper indicat impossibile esse nos operibus posse justificari.

Si Spiritu ducimmi, hoc est, si fide in Christum vos erigatis & c. non estis sub lege. Docet ergo Paulus in summa hac disputatione de lucta carnis & Spiritus, quod sancti seu credentes non possint perficere hoc, quod Spiritus vult. Libenter enim Spiritus vellet totus esse purus, sed caro conjuncta illi non permittit. Salvi tamen sunt per remissionem peccatorum, quae est in Christo. Deinde quia etiam ambulant & ducuntur Spiritu, non sunt sub lege, hoc est, lex non potest accusare & perterrefacere eos & c. aut si etiam hoc tentet, tamen non potest adigere eos ad desperationem.

Spiritu ergo ducimur, tum qua fide in Christum nos erigimus, tum qua carnis concupiscentias fugimus, & in Spiritu, in novitate vitae ambulamus. Nondum Spiritus sumus, sed Spiritu ducimur, inquit B. Lutherus in priori Comment. in hunc locum. Vers. 19. (φανερὰ δέ ἐστι τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός) Ut ostendat, quo ducat caro, remotis frenis, turpissima quaedam digito ostendit, confer Matth. XV. 19. In specie jam tum opera carnis, tum fructus Spiritus recenset Apostolus: Illa (φανερὰ) manifesta dicit, quae natura etiam nota sunt, & à Verbi Dei expertibus & non renatis habentur pro peccatis.

Sophistae ex fructibus faciunt suos habitus in anima subjective haerentes: Apostolus autem facit eos opera Spiritus vitalia, & per totum hominem diffusa: Opponit enim eos operibus carnis: Carnis opera non fructus, spiritus fructus non opera vocat. Cur hoc? Causam reddit B. Lutherus, nempe quod opera carnis utilia non sint, quia spinis & tribulis nemo frui potest, sed fiunt opera mala tantum nocentia. Opera autem Spiritus prosint, ut frui illis possimus in aeternum, sint ficus & uva terrae promissionis, ideoque teste fructus nomine commendentur.

Distribuit autem B. Lutherus opera carnis secundum tres hominis facultates. Ex his constat, Paulum vocare carnem, quicquid est in homine, complectendo omnes tres potentias animae, scilicet voluntatem concupiscibilem, voluntatem irascibilem & intellectum. Opera voluntatis concupiscibilis sunt adulterium, scortatio: Irascibilis, rixae, contentiones, caedes: Rationis seu intellectus errores, falsae religiones seu cultus, superstitiones, idololatriae, haereses, sectae. Grellius tres classes hic, ait, recenseri, vel tria peccatorum genera: unum, quod nos ipsos respicit: alterum, quod DEUM: tertium quod proximum: quorum primum iterum in duo dividitur: vel enim refertur ad voluptates venereas, vel ad voluptatem cibi & potus.

Illud peccatorum genus in fronte collocabit, utpote maxime carnale & in quod potissimum caro rapitur, quodque gentilibus illis hominibus perpetuo usu ac consuetudine jam veluti in naturam abierat, & turpitudinem quodammodo apud eos deposuerat: hoc vero posuit in fine. In medio autem ea peccata collocavit, quae Deum & proximum respiciunt.

Caeterum observat B. Lutherus in priori Commentario oppositionem in catalogo operum carnis & fructuum Spiritus. Etsi Apostolus non singulos fructus singulis operibus, sed unum multis, & multa multis opponat. Septem enim opera carnis in textu recensentur Graeco, etsi varient Latinae editiones, tum inter se, tum à Graeco codice. Novem tantum fructus Spiritus habentur in fonte, etsi imperitia aliquorum diligentia duodecim facti sint in versione Latina. Ita charitatem & gaudium observat fornicationi, immunditiei, luxuriae, quae sunt perversae dilectiones, perversae gaudia opponi: pacem, longanimitatem, benignitatem, bonitatem, inimicitiis, contentionibus, litibus, irae, rixis, dissensionibus: fidem haeresibus, idololatriae & beneficiis: continentiam ebrietati & commessationibus: addo mansuetudinem invidiae & homicidiis.

Quod autem haereses subjugantur non luxuriae sed dissensionibus, ejus causa ex ordinaria illa operum carnis consequatur peti potest, quam B. Lutherus experientia & exemplo duorum adversariorum melius, quam descriptione colligi posse notat: Primum enim sunt inimici atque discordes, dum data quacunque occasione mox litigant, litigantes autem aemulantur, dum quisque alteri superior esse nititur, aemulantes autem irascuntur, irati autem quaerunt, utrinque quid dicant, aut faciant, aut omittant, quod alterum mordeat ac provocet, hoc de rixantur.

Rixantes autem dissentiunt, & quisque sua defendere promptus est, alienaque infirmare. Ex quibus tunc sectae & haereses fiunt, dum quisque, alios in suam partem trahit, & alteri abstrahit. Hinc alitur invidia atrox malum, tandem in cades & homicidia ruunt. Et hic finis hujus mali. Exemplum sume inter duo forenses adversarios, aut duas respublicas invicem adversarias, aut inter duos Sophistas aut Theologias pro opinionibus suis certantes.

Novem ergo gradibus seu capitibus distinxit concupiscentiam illam carnis amarulentam atque cholericam. Adeo detestatur charitatis Apostolus. (μοιχεια) Μοιχεία in lege Mosis est concubitus viri caelibis, aut mariti cum nupta aliena: In Evangelio etiam mariti cum ea, quae nupta non est, quia Christus jura sexuum aequalia esse voluit, contra quam factum est, ubi soli viri exclusis, foeminis legum erant Domini, Vulgata omisit scelus capitale contra sextum praeceptum. Pellime. Differentia illa μοιχείας e lege & Evangelio, quam Crellio & Schlichtingio statuit Grotius, nulla est. Non enim aliud μοιχεία habet, atque erat olim sub lege. Adulterium tum non minus fuit, cum maritus rem habuit cum innupta, quam hodie. Violavit enim fidem, legemque conjugii, vi cujus cum conjuge in carnem unam esse & manere debuit, secundum legem matrimonialem. Nam & ibi verum erat illud seu valebat illa maxima Apostoli: Vir (maritus) non habet potestatem corporis sui, sed uxor, 1. Corinth. VII. v. 4. Neque huc facit πολυγαμία veterum, ea enim non erat secundum legem. Πορνεία) Sub hoc nomine veniunt concubitus extra nuptias, & nuptiae illegitimae, ut videre est 1. Cor. V. 1. Vide ea, quae dicta Act. XV. 20. Ἀκαθαρσία) Vox haec satis late patet, ut diximus ad Matth. cap. XXIII. vers. 27. sed videtur hic, ut & Roman. cap. I. v. 24. & 2. Cor. cap. XII. vers. 21. contrahi ad libidinem extra naturam. Sic Barnabas in epistola ἀκαθαρσίας vocat eam ἀνοῦσαν, quae ore fit. Balsamo ad Basilicum ἀκαθαρσίας interpretatur ἀνομίας, id est, ערוה. Ἀσέλγεια) Significat, ut dicto 2. ad Corinthios loco diximus, omne lasciviz genus, in quo primas obtinent partes libidinum incitamenta. Vers. 20. Εἰδωλολατρεία) Cultus falsorum numinum, qui plerumque apud simulachra celebrari solebat. Observamus hic propter Calixtum nos, quae de Idololo. B. Lutherus: Omnis talis religio, inquit, qua Deus colitur fine Verbo & mandato ejus, idololatria est. Et quoca est sanctior, & spiritualior in speciem, hoc perniciosior & pestilentior est. Avertit enim homines à fide in Christum, & facit, ut nitantur propriis viribus, operibus, justitiis. Igitur jejunium, cilicium, sanctissimae actiones, regula & tota vita Carthusianorum, quorum tamen ordo rigidissimus est, sunt opera carnis, imò Idololatria. Quia imaginantur se sanctos esse & salvari non per Christum. Quem ut sevrum judicem formidant, sed regulam suam observaverunt. Et paulo post: Nemo persuadebit hodie Papistis, quod Missa privata sit summa blasphemia Dei & idololatria, qua horribilior nunquam fuerit in Ecclesia ab Apostolis constituta. Eant nunc Syncretistae Helmstadienses, (C. lixtinos intelligo) & quum Lutherani videri cupiant, adhuc profiteantur, in Papatu nullam videre idololatriam. Sed quid mirum, eos Papistas ab idololatria absolvere, quum & Judaeos, & Mahumetanos absolvant ab idololatria. Subjungitur idololatria scortationi, qua spiritualis est scortatio. Qui semel se luxuriae voluptatis permittit, non respicit creatorem. Φαρμακεία) Proprie quidem veneficium significat, sed saepe respondet Hebraeae voci כשפים Exod. cap. VII. vers. 11. 12. & כשפים Es. cap. XLVII. vers. 9. 12. ubi de magicis artibus agitur, credo, quod iidem plerumque essent & venefici. Vide Pharmaceutriam Theocriti & Virgilii. Proxime subjungitur idololatriae, ideo non tam veneficium illud, quod miscentur venena ad nocendum proximo, quam artes maleficae & collusiones Magicae cum Diabolo designantur. Ἔχθραι) Inimicitiae, id est, manentia odia. Non tantum odia manentia, sed quaevis inimicitiae hoc nomine designantur, Rom. VIII. v. 7. Jac. IV. 9. Ἔρεις) Verborum certamina ex ira, Rom. I. 27. XIII. 13. 1. Cor. I. 11. III. 3. 2. Cor. XII. 20. Ζῆλοι) Aemulatio improba de honore. Solet jungi cum voce ἔρις, ut Rom. XIII. v. 13. 1. Cor. III. vers. 3. numen potentissimum & vicinum, huic venter, illi ea, quæ infra ventrem sunt, serviunt. Et Comos venerem fervat ac vegetat, alioqui sine Cerere & Baccho friget Venus. Καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τάτεις) De paribus par judicium. Ἀπαξ λέγων ὑμῖν, καθώς χρὴ ἀκούειν) Breviter supra v. 13. Ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες, βασιλείαν Θεοῦ ἐ κληρονο-μήσουσι) Illud τὸ τοιαῦτα abundat hic. Satis enim fuerat dixisse ἀπῶ. Sed quia voces quædam intercesserant, nihil nocuit, eandem significationem aliis voculis reponere. Πράσσοντες noli restringere ad ἔξω, sed sume etiam de actibus πραττομένοις.

Ubi hæc reperiuntur, ibi nondum regnat Spiritus.

Societatem non actus peccatorum, sed habitus damnare ajunt, quos suo loco confutavimus. Schlichtingius tamen hic cum Crellio vocem πράσσοντες putat pro diversa operum carnis ratione diversimode accipi debere. In iis vero, in quibus facilis est lapsus non actum unicum, habita divina benignitatis in Novo Testamento ratione, damnare, sed habitum & actiones iteratas, five unius generis, ut fi quis crebro irasscatur, irrideat, vino inebrietur &c. alia vero adeo turpia esse, ut à nemine, qui vero DEI timore, & vera fide præditus sit, committi possint, eorumque unum actum à regno DEI excludere, qualia sunt idololatria, incantatio, adulterium, homicidium, & his paria.

Sed vocis unius geminus non potest in eodem loco fingi sensus, neque ullum peccatum tam leve est, ut non damnet, si naturam ejus & vim legis respicias, Deuteron. cap. XXIII. vers. 26. Omnis enim actus peccati offendit infinitam DEI justitiam, & maledictionem divinam per se utpote ἀνομία incurrit.

Ecce, inquit Hieronymus in hunc locum, inimicitia, contentio, ira, rixa, dissensio, ebrietas quoque & cætera, quæ parva arbitramur, excludunt nos à regno DEI: Nec refert, uno quis à beatitudine excludatur; an pluribus, cum omnia similiter excludant. Quod autem condonentur fidelibus peccata, ex Acciden

Quam vero condonationem per pœ-nitentiam & fidem in Christum non tantum quoad actualia, sed etiam habitualia peccata nobis obtingere in Exeg. August. Conf. art. XII. cap. II. ostendimus. Πέπτω γεύδω Socinianorum est, quod peccatum originis, quod omninò habituale est, & per totam vitam non exuitur, insicientur.

Unde nemo est, qui prorsus expers sit peccati habitualis in hac vita: & pullulat semper malum illud hæreditarium, effundens sese in omnis generis peccata, quum omne figmentum cordis humani tantum malum sit omnibus diebus vitæ, Genes. VI. & VIII. capp.

## 5:22
Verf. 22. Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τῦ Πνεύματός ἐσι) [But the fruit of the Spirit is] Fruit, that is, works, as in Matth. III. 8, 10; VII. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20; XII. v. 33; Luc. III. 8; VI. 43; Joh. V. 2; XII. 24; and elsewhere. Understand Πνεῦμα [Spirit] here, as above, as the Holy Spirit.

B. Lutherus more correctly understands by Spirit, as a little above in verses 16 and 17, the interior man, or the regenerate part of man, by force opposed to the flesh or the exterior and carnal man. For although those fruits belong to the Holy Spirit, here it is regarded not as the remote and universal cause, but as the proximate and particular one.

Ἀγάπη) [Love] elsewhere taken more generally. Here it signifies beneficence: it is opposed to ἔχθραις [enmities] & φόνοις [murders].

Χαρὰ) [Joy] Gladness at another's good, which is opposed to envy.

Εἰρήνη) [Peace] Flight from strife, opposed to ἔριδι [contention].

Μακροθυμία) [Longsuffering] Hope for the amendment of the fallen, opposed to ζήλῳ [zeal]. (χρηστότης) [Kindness] Sweetness in intercourse, opposed to ἐρίθειαν [strife]. Vers. 23. (Ἀγαθωσύνη) [Goodness] That goodness which takes doubtful things in the better part, and does not easily condemn or despise anyone, Roman. cap. XV. v. 14. This prevents ἀκαθαρσίαν [impurity]. (πίστις) [Faith] Here understood as an open profession of true faith, opposed to ἀπιστίᾳ [unbelief]. (πραότης) [Gentleness] Flight from anger. Opposed to θυμῷ [wrath]. (ἐγκράτεια) [Self-control] Temperance, which is opposed to both the above-mentioned lusts and drunkenness.

Those Grotian ἀντιθέσεις [antitheses] do not seem inappropriate: But according to them, nothing is opposed to idolatry, sorcery.

Perhaps idolatry and sorcery should also be considered excluded by ἔξω [outside], because idolatry is opposed to faith in GOD, and indeed sorcery, which involves a tacit or express pact with the Devil. B. Lutheri's adversaries, even Thomas, handed down, praised by Glassius: To fornication, which is illicit love, charity responds. To impurity, however, immodesty and luxury, which are carnal allurements and arise from fornication, joy is opposed, which is spiritual delight, consequent from charity.

To that, which is the servitude of idols, peace is opposed. To that, which says sorceries, etc., up to dissensions, patience, longanimity, and goodness. To that, which is called anger, faith is opposed. To that, which is called envy, kindness.

To that, however, which is called homicides, meekness.

To that, which is called drunkenness, carousings and similar things, modesty, continence, and other things are opposed, etc. Concerning charity, B. Lutherus in his earlier Commentary, fol. 89: This is sweet death in GOD, angry and offending the neighbor. For then the charity of GOD is proven, when it strikes and disturbs, as was shown in the martyrs, and in Christ suffering. But then the charity of the neighbor is proven, when the neighbor offends and seems to deserve hatred.

Otherwise, no virtue is more prone to simulation, so much so that Roman. cap. XII. 4. the apostle cared only for this, namely, that charity be without simulation. For GOD has many lovers, who are written in the Psalm: He will confess to you, when you have done him good. And Psalm. LXXVII. And they loved him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue. Let it therefore lie hidden in peace, but in war nothing is felt more vividly than charity, hope, faith, unless they do not feel diffidence, despair, hatred also. Joy, the second fruit (like charity) is in GOD and the neighbor.

In GOD, when we are joyful about divine mercy, even in the midst of the world's storms, praising GOD's gifts in them. But just as followers of the flesh feign charity in calm times, so also joy: They praise GOD and GOD's gifts in men, but until they are offended, while the works of the flesh break forth, they detract from GOD's gifts, which they had praised before, they are saddened if their detraction is not successful, nor does the reputation of the neighbor threaten. For no one believes how deep the malice of the flesh is, so many secure ones it has lost. is peace, which is also twofold.

In God, this is a good conscience, mixed with the mercy of Christ, but it sometimes surpasses all understanding, while it is disturbed, with GOD hiding himself, and turning away his face, conscience left to itself. In the neighbor, however, when one yields to his will. For this peace with men can never stand. If everyone justifies, defends, seeks, demands his own, as today the Roman forum, and laws have filled the Church with lawsuits, quarrels, and causes. Lyra interprets faith as fidelity, which Cicero calls the foundation of justice, since what is said is done by us, or by others, or is the truth in words and deeds. Although faith toward God can also be understood, when we keep fidelity to Him, which also happens in the profession of doctrine, and in the constancy of religion along with faith toward one's neighbor. For nothing prevents both from being comprehended under that name, both being fruits of the Spirit: against both is heresy, as explained before.

B. Luther notes a twofold faith here in his former commentary, fol. 90. One toward God, to whom we are faithful, not so much because we keep our promises, as because we believe His promises. The other toward man, to whom we are faithful, keeping and holding fast to pacts and promises. Trust, which is the cause of justification, has no place here: for this precedes justification, and is the mother of these fruits of justice and the Spirit.

Latin:

Verf. 22. Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τῦ Πνεύματός ἐσι) Fructus, id est, opera, ut Matth. III. 8. 10. VII. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. XII. v. 33. Luc. III. 8. VI. 43. Joh. V. 2. XII. 24. & alibi. Πνεῦμα hic intellige, ut supra, Spiritum Sanctum.

Rectius intelligit B. Lutherus Spiritum, uti paulo ante verf. 16. & 17. hominem interiorem, vel partem hominis regenitam, vi oppositæ carnis vel exterioris hominis & carnalis. Etsi enim fructus illi sint Spiritus Sancti, hic tamen non causa remota & universalis, sed proxima & particularis spectatur.

Ἀγάπη) alibi generalius sumitur. Hic beneficentiam significat: opponitur ἔχθραις & φόνοις.

Χαρὰ) Gaudium ex bonis alterius, quod invidiæ opponitur.

Εἰρήνη) Fuga dissidiorum opponitur ἔριδι.

Μακροθυμία) Spes de lapsorum emendatione opposita ζήλῳ. (χρηστότης) Suavitas in convictu opposita ἐρίθειαν. Vers. 23. (Ἀγαθωσύνη) Bonitas illa, quæ dubia accipit in partem meliorem, nec facile quemquam aut condemnat, aut contemnit, Roman. cap. XV. v. 14. Hæc impedit ἀ- καθαρσίαν. (πίστις) Intelligenda hic aperta professio fidei veræ, opposita ἀπιστίᾳ. (πραότης) Ira fuga. Opponitur θυμῷ. (ἐγκράτεια) Temperantia, quæ & libidinibus suprame-moratis, & ebrietati opponitur.

Non incommode videntur Grotianæ illæ ἀντιθέσεις: Sed juxta illas idololatria, veneficio nihil opponitur.

Nihi forte per ἔξω etiam idololatriam & veneficia excludi censendum fit quia fidei in DEUM idololatria opponitur, imo & veneficium, quod tacitum vel expressum pactum cum Diabolo involvit. B. Lutheri adversaries etiam Thomæ tradidit, laudatus Glas-fio: Fornicationi, quæ est amor illicitus, conine respondet charitas. Immunditiæ vero impudicitia & luxuriæ, quæ sunt carnales illecebræ, & ex fornicatione proveniunt, contraponitur gaudium, quod est spiritualis delectatio, consequens ex charitate.

Ei vero, quod est idolorum servitus, contraponitur pax. Ei vero, quod dicit veneficia &c. usque ad dissensiones, patientia, leni-ganimitas & bonitas. Ei vero, quod dicitur ira, contraponitur fides. Ei vero, quod dicitur invidia, benignitas.

Ei autem, quod dicitur homicidia, manfuetudo.

Ei, quod dicitur ebrietas, comessationes & his similia, contraponitur modestia, continentia & cætera &c. De charitate B. Lutherus priori Commentario fol. 89. Est hæc dulcis mors in DEUM irascentem & proximum offendentem. Tunc enim probatur charitas DEI, quando percutit & perturbat, sicut in martyribus monstratum est, & in Christo passo. Tunc autem probatur charitas proximi, quando proximus offendit & odium mereri videtur.

Alioqui nulla virtus simulatio-tioni magis patet, adeo, ut Roman. cap. XII. 4. posfolus id unum curarit, videlicet ut sit charitas sine fimulatione. Habet enim DEUS multos amatores, qui in Psalm. scribuntur: Confitebitur tibi, cum benefeceris ei. Et Psalm. LXXVII. Et dilexerunt eum in ore suo, & lingua mentiti sunt ei. Lateat ergo in pace, sed in bello nihil vivacius sentitur, quam charitas, spes, fides, nisi diffidentiam, desperationem, odium quoque non sentiant. Gaudium, secundus fructus (aquæ ut charitas) in DEO & proximo est.

In DEO, quando de divina misericordia læti sumus, etiam in mediis mundi procellis, laudantes DEI dona in illis. At sicut carnis sectatores fingunt charitatem tempore sereno, ita & gaudium: Laudant DEUM & DEI dona in hominibus, sed donec offendantur, dum opera carnis proruunt, detrà-hunt donis DEI, quæ prius laudarunt, tristantur si detractioni eorum non fit successus, nec minatur existimatio proximi. Nemo enim credit, quam profunda sit malitia carnis, tam multos securos perdus) est pax, quæ & ipsa duplex est.

In Deo hæc est bona conscientia, in misericordia Christi mixta, sed exuperat quandoque omnem sensum, dum turbatur, abscondente se DEO, & faciem avertente, conscientia sibi relicta. In proximo vero dum ceditur ejus voluntati. Nam pax hæc cum hominibus stare nunquam potest. Si quilibet sua jusfificet, tueatur, quærat, exposfulet, sicut hodie forum Romanum, & jura Ecclesiam repleverunt litibus, jurgiis, causis. Fidem de fidelitate interpretatur Lyra, quam Cicero fundamentum dicit justitiae, cum quod dictum est, fit à nobis, vel ab aliis, seu quae est veritas in dictis & factis. Quanquam & fides erga Deum intelligi possit, cum fidelitatem ipsi servamus, quod etiam fit in doctrina professione, & religionis constantia una cum fide erga proximum. Nam utramque eo nomine comprehendi nihil vetat, utraque fructus est Spiritus: Utrique adversa est αἵρεσις, uti antea explicatum.

Fidem duplicem hic notat B. Lutherus in priori commentario fol. 90. Unam erga Deum, cui fideles sumus, non tam quod servemus promissa nostra, quam quod credimus illius promissis. Alteram erga hominem, cui sumus fideles, servantes & tenaces pactorum ac promissorum. Fiducia, quae justificationis causa est, hic locum non habet: Haec enim antecedit justificationem, & genitrix est horum fructuum justitiae & Spiritus.

## 5:23
Verf. 23. κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστι νόμος.

If men had been such, there would have been no need for the law of Moses, or any other penal law, above III. 19. It is a saying of the Greeks: He is just, who uses the law in the way he should.

Tacitus, Annal. III. The most ancient of mortals lived without any evil lust, without shameful crime, and without punishment or coercion.

It is not taught what the condition was before sin, but what fruits are fitting for men liberated from sin and regenerated: although even before the fall there was law and the threat of punishment. Nor is the discourse about the fruits of the Spirit, as some wish, that there is no law against them, which is clear in itself: but about men, who like fertile trees bear such fruits: that the law does not condemn them.

For although they may labor under manifold and great imperfection, yet it is not imputed to them who are led by the Spirit, of whom the discourse is, whom he had previously said in v. 18, in the same sense, not to be under the law.

Latin:

Vers. 23. κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστι νόμος.

Si homines fuissent tales, nihil opus fuisset lege Mosis, aut alia lege poenali supra III. 19. Graecorum est dictum: Δίκαιος ἐστὶν, ᾧ τῷ τρόπῳ χρῆσῃ νόμῳ.

Tacitus Annal. III. Vetustissimi mortalium nulla adhuc mala libidine, sine probro scelere, que sine poena aut coercitionibus agebant.

Non qualis conditio fuerit ante peccatum, sed quinam fructus conveniant hominibus à peccato liberatis & regenitis docetur: Quanquam etiam ante lapium lex & poena comminatio fuerit. Neque de fructibus Spiritus sermo est, ut nonnulli volunt, quod adversus illos lex non fit, quod per se luculentum est: Sed de hominibus, qui tanquam arbores fertiles ejusmodi fructus ferunt: quod lex eos non damnet.

Etsi enim imperfectione multiplici & magna laborent, ea tamen non imputatur illis, qui Spiritu ducuntur, de quibus sermo est, quos antea v. 18. sensu eodem dixerat, non esse sub lege.

## 5:24
Verf. 24. Οἱ δὲ τῷ Χριστῷ. In the Manuscript: Οἱ δὲ τῷ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ: but those who belong to Jesus Christ: who give themselves to be ruled by Him.

Τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν) They hold the flesh constrained, and break its strength, namely for sinning, just as a man affixed to a cross is constrained, broken, and with his blood his strength departs from him.

See Rom. VI. 6. Σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι) By passions here he understands the affections of the irascible faculty. Καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις) By the affections of the concupiscible faculty, the desires.

Regarding the word παθήματα, Philippus noted, Galen on the causes of Symptoms, that πάθος denotes the disease itself, but παθήματα denote the motions and impulses of diseases, which are called paroxysms.

Which can be applied to evil original concupiscence, and its evil desires and solicitations to evil. But what if by life or passions he understands the perturbations of the irascible faculty, raging in the bitterness of the heart, and by concupiscences the affections of the concupiscible faculty flattering in the titillation of the flesh?

Let everyone abound in his own sense, says B. Luther in his former Commentary. We do not disapprove of that sense, also approved here by Grotius: because affections and concupiscences are distinguished from the flesh or original sin, from which they proceed.

He speaks in the past tense, CRUCIFIED, either referring to baptism, by which we were bound to this crucifixion, nay, by whose virtue the Spirit of God received the grace of crucifixion in us: or so that it may more excite the zeal of mortifying the flesh in us, as if he were saying, that those who have not yet crucified, or have begun to crucify, they lie that they are Christ's, and glory in vain.

But how does this agree with what he had said, the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh? If the faithful have crucified the flesh, therefore the flesh in them can no longer lust against the Spirit?

Resp. Certainly it could not, if they had crucified it perfectly: But this crucifixion is only begun. Therefore the flesh, half-crucified, does not cease to lust against the Spirit even in the most holy.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Οἱ δὲ τῷ Χριστῷ. In Manuscripto: Οἱ δὲ τῷ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ: qui vero ad Jesum Christum pertinent: qui se ei dedere regendos.

Τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν) Ii carnem constrictam tenent, viresque ejus, ad peccandum scilicet, confringunt, fict homo cruci affixus constringitur, frangitur, & cum sanguine vires ei abscedunt.

Vide Rom. VI. 6. Σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι) Παθήματα hic intelligit affectus τῦ θυμοῦδς. Καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις) Affectibus τῦ ἐπιθυμητικῦ, ἀρεστῶν.

De voce παθήματα notavit Philippus, Galenam de causis Symptom. πάθη ipsum morbum, παθήματα vero motus & impetus morborum, qui vocantur paroxysmi, notare.

Quod applicari potest ad pravam concupiscentiam originalem, esque desideria prava & solicitationes ad malum. Quid autem, si per vita seu passiones intelligat perturbationes irascibilis virtutis, in amarulentia cordis furentes, & per concupiscentias affectus concupiscibilis in titillatione carnis blandientes.

Quisque suo sensu abundet, inquit B. Lutherus in priori Commentario. Non improbamus sensum illum, Grotio etiam hic probatum: quia affectus & concupiscentiae distinguuntur à carne vel peccato originali, à quo prodeunt.

Dicit verbo praeterito, CRUCIFIXERUNT, vel reficiens ad baptismum, quo ad hanc crucifixionem obligati fuimus, imo cujus virtute crucifixionis gratiam in nobis cepit Spiritus Dei: vel ut studium mortificandae carnis magis in nobis excitet, quasi dicat, quod nondum crucifixernnt, vel crucifigere caperunt, illi se Christi esse mentiuntur, frustra gloriantur.

Quomodo vero hoc convenit cum eo, quod dixerat, caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum, & qui sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt. Si fideles carnem crucifixerunt, ergo caro in eis non amplius potest concupiscere adversus Spiritum?

Resp. Sane non posset, si perfecte crucifixissent: Sed crucifixio hac tantum est inchoata. Ergo caro femiplene crucifixa non cessat concupiscere adversus Spiritum etiam in sanctissimis.

## 5:25
Verf. 25. Εἰ ζῶμεν Πνεύματι) If our soul is moved by the Spirit of God.

So also below VI. 16. For to be moved is to live. Πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν) Let us express the same thing by acts, which the Hebrews call לְהַלֵּךְ.

See what is said at John XII. 8. 9. 10. 1. Corinth. VII. 17. 2. Cor. V. 7. Ephef. II. 1. 17. V.

15. Here is regarded primarily the crucifixion of Christ, as is evident from chap. VI. 14, the effect of which the Apostle teaches to be the mortification of the flesh. Cf. Rom. VI. v. 5, which also moves the reborn, so that they may crucify their sins, when they think that our sins were expiated by the blood of our crucified Savior. The nails, says B.

Luther in his former Comment. fol. 91, are the Word of God, penetrating through the impulse of God's grace, and forbidding the flesh to fix its desires. Thus Eccles. last. The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fixed deep, which are given by the counsel of masters from one shepherd, that is, through the Apostles and Prophets from Christ.

Yet we do not deny that this is also hinted at by this metaphorical locution, that just as one crucified is no longer his own master, nor can move his feet or hands, or is even mortified by the torments of the cross, so in the spiritual crucifixion of the flesh, evil concupiscence is by no means made free, but is as if bound, nay, even from time to time as if it must be mortified, even if it finally perishes with the death of the body. Which, according to B. Luther fol. 148, happens when they not only repress the petulance of the flesh with fasts or other exercises, but as Paul said above, when they walk in the Spirit, that is, when, admonished by divine threats, by which GOD threatens that He will severely punish sin, and they abstain from sinning, when they are instructed by word, faith, and prayer, not resisting the flesh, they affix it to the cross with nails with its affections and desires, so that, although the flesh is alive, and still moves itself, yet it cannot accomplish what it wills, when it is affixed to the cross with hands and feet bound.

Therefore, the pious, while they live here, crucify the flesh, that is, they indeed feel its concupiscences, but do not obey them.

For clothed in the armor of God, faith, hope, and the sword of the Spirit, they resist the flesh, and with these spiritual weapons, or certain nails, they affix it to the cross, so that even against its will it is forced to be subject to the Spirit. Afterward, dying, they put off the flesh entirely, etc.

The Vulgate here begins the sixth chapter.

Which B. Luther followed in his German version, although he noted that the Greeks and Jerome in the following chapter call the brethren the last: because he believed it did not matter much. By Spirit is not understood the Holy Spirit, although He is the author of both life and spiritual motion in us, but the inner man, or that which is born of the Spirit in us, and is the spirit as of the reborn man as such, by which we live. spiritually; whence also by this Spirit, as an internal principle—namely, the faculty implanted in us by the Holy Spirit—we walk. The proper force of this word, as B. Luther notes from Erasmus, is to proceed in order, to advance by a straight path, which the Apostle is said to use conveniently in this place, so that they may not decline either to the right hand or to the left, but may advance in a straight order.

He intends these things to be said particularly against kenodoxia (vainglory), as if he were to say: If it is true that we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in order and walk in the Spirit. For where the Spirit is, He renews men, He begets in them new motions; that is, from being vainglorious, irascible, envious, etc., He makes them humble, meek, patient, etc. Such men do not seek their own glory, but God’s; they do not provoke or envy one another, but yield to one another and anticipate each other in honor.

Conversely, those who are desirous of glory, who provoke and envy one another, may indeed boast that they have the Spirit and that they live by the Spirit, but they deceive themselves; they follow the flesh and perform its works, and they have their judgment, that they shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Let us therefore walk in the Spirit; that is, let us remain in order, that is, in the doctrine of truth once delivered, in brotherly charity, and in the concord of the Spirit.

Let us preach Christ with a simple heart, and the glory of God, and let us ascribe all things to Him; let us not prefer ourselves one to another, let us not stir up sects. For this is not to walk straight, but to abandon the true order and to institute a new and perverse one.

It is, however, a general exhortation that we should walk, speak, converse, and work not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. A spiritual walk or progress is an indication of spiritual life. Life is recognized by respiration (Jac. II. v. ult.). Thus, it is recognized even more by one’s walk.

The Apostle specifically dissuades from kenodoxia in the following verse. Ver. 26. Μὴ γινώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλες προκαλέμενοι, ἀλλήλοις φθονοῦντες) Paul inculcates these things more specifically because these evils had prevailed most of all in the Galatian churches. Kenodoxoi are those who hunt for honor from those things in which true honor is not situated, such as riches, erudition, or eloquence; the vice of these is kenodoxia (Sap. XIV. 14; Philipp. II. 3). Prokaloumenoi (provoking) is said of those who call others to a contest, whether military or judicial. Thence, by translation, it is said of those who, in any other contest—for instance, of erudition or eloquence—hope that they will be superior to others: this is the mark of those who deem themselves better; the mark of others is envy, but neither becomes a Christian. A triad of vices stifling the spiritual walk is especially noted: Kenodoxia, the ardor of contending when we provoke others, and envy, by which one envies others for their degree of virtue, goods, or honors.

These two latter follow the pursuit of empty glory. The flesh is such a subtle beast, says B. Luther (Comment. post. fol. 150), that it abandons order, depraves and corrupts true doctrine, and dissolves the concord of churches for no other cause than this cursed kenodoxia. Therefore, it is not without cause that Paul attacks it so sharply here and elsewhere.

The ambitious provoke their inferiors with contempt, injuries, and insults, and challenge them to contests, whence arise contentions, schisms, and heresies. Such was Diotrephes (2 Joh. v. 9). But they envy their superiors and equals for their virtue and fortune.

Cyprian (lib. I. epist. 3) teaches that ambition sleeps sweetly in the bosom of priests especially, reposing there under the shade, and hiding itself fraudulently in the secret of the chamber. That inflation, he says, and proud boasting does not come from the teaching of Christ, who teaches humility, but is born of the spirit of Anti-Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Εἰ ζῶμεν Πνεύματι) Si animus noster Dei Spiritu movetur.

Sic & infra VI. 16. Nam moveri est vivere. Πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν) Actibus idipsum exprimamus, quod לְהַלֵּךְ Hebraei dicunt.

Vide, quae dicta ad Joh. XII. 8. 9. 10. 1. Corinth. VII. 17. 2. Cor. V. 7. Ephes. II. 1. 17. V.

15. Respicitur hic imprimis crucifixio Christi, ut è cap. VI. 14. patet, cujus effectum ille mortificationem carnis docet Apostolus. Conf. Rom. VI. v. 5. quae etiam movet renatos, ut pravas concupiscentias Christi crucifixum esse: idque debuisse sanguine crucifixi nostri Salvatoris expiari.

Clavi, inquit B. Lutherus in priori Comment. fol. 91. sunt Verbum Dei, per impulsum gratiae Dei penetrantes, & carnem prohibentes, ne figatur sua desideria. Sic Eccles. ult. Verba sapientum sicut stimuli, & quasi clavi in altum defixi, que per magistrorum consilium data sunt à pastore uno, id est, per Apostolos & Prophetas à Christo.

Id tamen etiam innui hac metaphorica locutione non abnuimus, quod ut crucifixus non amplius fui juris est, nec pedes vel manus movere potest, vel etiam per tormenta crucis mortificatur, sic in spirituali carnis crucifixione concupiscentia prava minimè libera fit, sed veluti ligata, imo etiam subinde quasi mortificanda fit, etsi demum cum morte corporis intereat. Quod, secundum B. Lutherum fol. 148. fit, cum non solum jejuniis aut aliis exercitiis petulantiam carnis reprimunt, sed ut supra Paulus dixit, cum Spiritu ambulant, hoc est, cum admoniti divinis comminationibus, quibus comminatur DEUS, se peccatum fevere puniturum, & peccando abstinent, cum verbo, fide & oratione instruuntur, non resistentes carni, clavis cruci eam affigunt cum affectibus & desideriis, ut, quanquam caro fit viva, & adhuc moveat se, tamen non possit perficere, quod velit, cum manibus & pedibus ligatis cruci affixa est.

Pii ergo dum hic vivunt, crucifigunt carnem, hoc est, sentiunt quidem concupiscentias ipsius, sed non obsequuntur eis. Induti enim armatura Dei, fide, spe & gladio Spiritus, repugnant carni, ac istis armis spiritualibus, seu clavis quibusdam eam affigunt cruci, ut etiam invita Spiritui subjecta esse cogatur.

Postea morientes prorsus carum exuunt &c.

Vulgata hic orditur caput sextum. Quam sequutus est in versione Germanica B. Lutherus, etsi Graecos & Hieronymum notem voce ἀδελφοὶ sequente capite ultimorum odiri: quod id non multum referre crederet.

Per Spiritum non intelligitur Spiritus Sanctus, etsi autor is fit & vitae & motus spiritualis in nobis, sed sed homo interior, vel quod, natum est ex Spiritu in nobis, & spiritus est quasi hominis renati qua talis, per quam vivimus. spiritualiter, unde etiam per hunc Spiritum, ceu principium internum, facultatem scilicet nobis à Spiritu Sancto inditam ambulamus, cujus verbi propria vis, ut ex Erasmo notat B. Lutherus, est ordine incedere, recta via procedere, qua commode uti hoc loco dicit Apostolum, ut scilicet non declinent, neque ad dextram, neque ad sinistram, sed ordine recto incedant.

Quæ adversus κενοδοξίαν peculiariter dicta vult, quasi dicat, si verum est, quod Spiritu vivimus, ordine etiam incedamus, & in Spiritu ambulemus. Nam ubi Spiritus est, renovat homines, parit in eis novos motus, hoc est, ex vane gloriosis, iracundis, invidis &c. facit humiles, mansuetos, patientes &c. Tales non suam gloriam, sed Dei quærunt, non invicem provocant & invident, sed alii aliis cedunt, & honore præveniunt.

Contra qui cupidi sunt gloriæ, qui invicem provocant & invident, illi quidem jactare possunt, se Spiritum habere, se vivere Spiritu, sed seipsos fallunt, carnem sequuntur, & ejus opera perficiunt, habentque judicium suum, quod regnum Dei non consequuntur. Spiritu ergo incedamus, hoc est, maneamus in ordine, hoc est, in doctrina veritatis semel tradita, in charitate fraterna & concordia Spiritus.

Simplici corde prædicemus Christum, & gloriam Dei, & illi omnia accepta feramus, non præferamus nos invicem alii aliis, non suscitemus sectas; Hoc enim non est recta incedere, sed verum ordinem relinquere, & novum ac perversum instituere. Est autem generalis adhortatio, ut ambulemus, loquamur, conversemur, operemur, non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum.

Ambulatio feu incessus spiritualis est indicium vitæ spiritualis. Ex respiratione agnoscitur vita, Jac. II. v. ult. Sic ex incessu magis cognoscitur.

A κενοδοξία versu sequenti specialiter dehortatur Apostolus. Vers. 26. Μὴ γινώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλες προκαλέμενοι, ἀλλήλοις φθονοῦντες) Hæc ideò specialius inculcat Paulus, quod hæc mala maxime in Ecclesiis Galaticis invaluissent. Κενόδοξοι sunt, qui honorem venantur ex iis rebus, in quibus verus honor situs non est, ut ex opibus, eruditione, eloquentia, horum vitium κενοδοξία, Sap. XIV. 14. Philipp. II. 3. Προκαλέμενοι provocare dicitur de iis, qui ad certamen, aut bellicum, aut judiciale alios vocant. Inde per translationem dicitur de iis, qui in quovis alio certamine, puta eruditionis aut eloquentiæ, sperant se aliis fuperiores fore: hoc est eorum, qui potiores se arbitrantur: aliorum est invidia, neutrum vero Christiano convenit. Trias vitiorum spiritualem incessum fufflaminans maxime notatur: Κενοδοξία, ardor concertandi cum provocamus alios, & invidia, qua quis aliis vel virtutis, vel bonorum & honorum gradum invidet.

Quæ duo posteriora inanis gloriæ studium sequuntur. Tam subdola bestia caro est, inquit B. Lutherus Comment. poster. fol. 150. ut propter nullam aliam causam ordinem deferat, doctrinam veram depravet & corrumpat, ac Ecclesiarum concordiam diffuat, quam propter maledictam istam κενοδοξίαν. Ideo non fine causa tam acriter hic & alibi eam insectatur Paulus. Ambitiefi inferiores provocant contemptu, injuriis, contumeliis & ad certamina laceffunt, unde contentiones, schismata, hærefes.

Qualis erat Diotrephes, 2. Job. v. 9. Superioribus vero & æqualibus virtutem & fortunam ipforum invident.

Cyprianus lib. I. epist. 3. docet, ambitionem in sinu præcipue sacerdotum suaviter dormire, ibi sub umbra recumbere, in secreto thalami se fraudulenter occultare. Inflatio illa, inquit, & superba jactatio non est de Christi magisterio, qui humilitatem docet, sed de Anti-Christi spiritu nascitur.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He exhorts to meekness, humility, and beneficence toward teachers and all others, but especially toward those who are of the household of faith. And by way of a colophon, he testifies to his love through his idiographia (autograph) and the circumcision of his antagonists, who, because of their flight from the cross, urge the law but do not observe it, and are full of kenodoxia. Boasting again of the cross of Christ, he tacitly warns them to walk according to the prescribed rule, so that such may enjoy peace and mercy, and he dissuades them from henceforth causing trouble to him who bears the stigmata of Jesus. Finally, he seals the epistle with a vow of the grace of Christ. There are two parts: The former still pertains to moral treatment and is parainetikē (exhortatory), which exhorts to a triad of homiletic virtues up to v. 10. The latter exhibits the conclusion of the epistle up to v. 18, which we therefore call epilogikē.

PART I. Parainetikē, exhorting to a triad of homiletic virtues.

Ver. 1. Ἐὰν καὶ προληφθῇ ἄνθρωπος ἐν τινι παραπτώματι) prolēphthē here is "having been caught," just as prolēphthēis is taken in Sap. XVII. 17. He wishes to say, however, "having been caught before this epistle comes to you, in some fault," namely, of those which I have already mentioned, especially dichostasias (dissension) or heresy. That anthrōpos is put for "someone," as also below in v. 7, because the Hebrews place ish in this way. hymeis hoi pneumatikoi) You, who have crucified the flesh, who are led by the Spirit. Katartizete ton toiouton) Katartizein is to make fit; sometimes also to heal that which is corrupt (Matth. IV. 21; Marci I. 19), which signification agrees well with this place, if a fallen beast of burden ought to be restored (Exod. XXIII. 5), how much more a man. En pneumati praotētos) With a gentle spirit, according to the rules of Ecclesiastical discipline indeed, but with fraternal admonitions also added.

For Ecclesiastical discipline itself, when it is instituted for the good of those who have fallen, does not stand in the way of lenity (2 Thess. III. 15). Skopōn seauton) Looking to yourself; but "to look to" is put for "to beware." For those who beware of themselves are accustomed to look around. There is, however, a transition here from the plural to the singular, because it is the same thing whichever you say first. Thus it is above IV. 6, 7. Mē kai sy peirasthēs) This verb is to be understood here with its full effect, that is, "lest you also at some time succumb to some temptation." Thus also the active peirazein is taken in 1 Cor.

VII. 5; 1 Thess. III. 5; add what was said on Matth. VI. 13. Ver. 2. Allēlōn ta barē basazete) Sins also are burdens: He bears the sins of others who does not proudly despise the fallen, but hopes for better things from him. Kai hōtōs anaplērōsate ton nomon christou) Thus most Codices have it, so that it is of one commanding: "Even in this way show that you are lovers of your neighbor, which the law of Christ commands" (Joh. XIII. v. 34; XV. 12). The Apostle does not speak of one caught before this epistle, but of anyone who, at any time, might be caught in any fault, as if he were to say: If anyone should at any time be prevented by temptation and fall into sin, raise him up and restore him in turn.

The past verb is used on account of the consequent katartismon, which presupposes a paraptōma. Nor is there talk of schism or heresy, but of any paraptōma whatsoever. This parainēsis (exhortation), "bear one another's burdens," does not apply so much to the restoring of heretics or those who have fallen into heresy, as to those who have fallen into mortal sins.

To the presbyters these things seem to some to be said, whose duty it is to restore those who have fallen: but they are common precepts. In particular (the emphasis is: Even if he has fallen. And preoccupation is to be understood with effect. Spiritual persons to the Apostle are not priests, as Salmero wishes, but the perfect and stronger, whom he opposes to the carnal, animal, little ones in Christ, and the infirm 1 Cor. 2 & 3, as Estius admits. He requires a spirit of gentleness, whereas otherwise he himself threatens with a rod 1 Cor. 4:21, because one must proceed differently with others. For obstinate sinners in the works of the flesh, persisting without repentance, are to be severely rebuked and driven out 1 Cor. 5:11, 12; Tit. 1:13. It is one thing to be preoccupied by some fall, another to sin by daily use and depraved custom. Cf. Ps. 141:5; Prov. 9:8, ch. 13:14, ch. 27:5; Matt. 18:16 sqq. Concerning which Gregory, part 3 of Pastoral Care, ch. 33. Those who are overcome by sudden concupiscence are to be admonished in one way, those who are bound in guilt by design in another; πρεληφθῇ he is preoccupied, namely, by the fraud of Satan and the infirmity of the flesh, whence he also later names temptation.

In the word καταρτίζετε, some note a metaphor from ruined buildings, whose parts are to be repaired and restored: but the metaphor is more aptly derived from a dislocated member in the human body, to which other members both condole and are intent on restoring, not with violence, but with due gentleness and prudence. The Apostle hints at this by the word πνευματικοὶ, and that by the word πραότητι.

For prudence is the work of the Spirit, and charity, which was just now called the fruit of the Spirit. Nothing so becomes a spiritual man, says Augustine, as the treatment of another's sin, when it meditates on his liberation rather than his inflation, and on aids rather than reproaches, and as far as ability is granted, that the fallen be kindly received. Correct your brother, he says, interpreting Chrysostom, but with gentleness, and accusing the incursion of the demon rather than the negligence of the mind. Considering yourself, as if he were saying: Let the same be measured in yourself by your own foot. And it can easily happen to you, that you also be preoccupied by some fall, tempted by the flesh and Satan. Therefore, what you wish to be done to you, show also to another. Since there is no man who is without sin, lest he dermit the sins of his neighbor too sharply, he admonishes: but that he should bear it especially so that his own may also be tolerated by others, as Theophylact says. For nothing, says Augustine, inclines one so much to mercy as the thought of one's own danger. What happens to anyone can happen to anyone. To which verse 3 also pertains: For if anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

He uses, however, now the singular number, because it is more apt for addressing the conscience of each one. Therefore, admonishing them of common infirmity, he adds: Bear one another's burdens. The burdens of sins, as those by which the conscience is greatly burdened and depressed, and feels itself weighed down by them Ps. 38:5. βαστάζειν brings in an onerous and difficult portion, such as the yoke of the laws; joined to it is that bearing of a neighbor's burdens, yet it is not to be shunned. A Christian ought to have strong shoulders and robust bones, which can bear the flesh, that is, fraternal infirmity, says B. Luther in this place. B. Gerhard here employs the similitude of Augustine in Enarrat. Psalm 129: Stags are said, when they cross the straits into nearby woods, for the sake of pasture, to place their heads upon one another, and the one who is in front carries the head alone, and does not place it upon another. But when he himself has failed, he lifts himself from the front part, and returns to the back, and he himself rests upon another. And thus all bear their burdens, and arrive at what they desire, they do not suffer shipwreck, because charity is as it were a ship to them. Therefore charity bears burdens. Aretius on this passage: It is an argument taken from the custom of travelers. Those who make a journey together are accustomed to take up one another's burden or at least to set a part of it upon their own shoulders. The life of a Christian man is a pilgrimage; travelers, I say, are the Ministers and Hearers (all Christians); therefore let them use toward one another with equal facility what travelers are accustomed to use. He bears his neighbor so much as he loves him. For if you love, you bear. If you cease to love, you cease to tolerate, Gregory M. saying in homil. 13 on Ezekiel: He wishes to be borne not by connivance, flattery, and hardening in evil, which is not to bear but to aggravate the burden: but by gentle admonition, correction, forgiveness of offenses Coloss. 3:12, 13, 14. We bear the burdens of infirmity for one another, saying that with lightness we sustain the anger of another, and while we indulge him who has injured us, if he asks it, as the ordinary Gloss has here.

Therefore Thomas wrongly snatches these things to the satisfactions of others. One cannot pay the penalty for another, who merits it for himself. And mutual duties are hinted at here. But are satisfactions mutual? The satisfactions of the Papists are arbitrary: But this mutual bearing of burdens is necessary by the law of Christ. It does not explain concerning the burden of penance, to Peltan 1 on satisfaction: but concerning the burden of sins, Justinianus and Estius explain: He calls sins burdens, which depress us by their guilt and render us liable to punishments. But the speech is Metaphorical, taken from those who in carrying burdens mutually relieve one another. He therefore warns the Galatians, that they should in a way count the infirmities and sins of others as their own, by condoling, dissembling, bearing, gently admonishing, fraternally correcting, and finally by doing this, that he may be corrected rather than punished.

2 As to the law of Christ concerning fraternal charity, it is not opposed to the law of Moses, which likewise demands the charity of a neighbor, so that we love our neighbor as ourselves Lev. 19:18; Mark 10:28. But it is called the law of Christ, because he both laboriously inculcated the same, and explained it at length everywhere, and confirmed it by his own new and admirable example John 15:12, 13.
