But concerning the word of fulfillment, Hemmingius rightly says in this place: The word of fulfillment or perfection is accepted in two ways in scripture. For sometimes it is opposed to the imperfection of a work, sometimes to simulation, lying, and hypocrisy. In the former way, no one in this life can fulfill the law of God, except Jesus Christ alone, who for that reason is preached by the Apostle as the consummation of the law unto righteousness for every believer. But in the latter way, all the children of God are said to fulfill the law of Christ, because they sincerely strive to approve their life to God, and without simulation pursue their neighbor with love. Theophylact with emphasis on the word ἀναπληρώσατε. For he did not say you will fulfill, but you will fill up, that is, by common consent you will all perfect the law of Christ, tolerating one another, namely, that the one who is slow to anger may sustain the quick-tempered, and the slower may bear the impetus of the quick, so it will happen that neither will that one sin, if he is tolerated by this one, nor that one, if he is borne by the other: Nor do I say that, that you should execute the law of Christ among yourselves with hands stretched out to one another in turn, but that whatever is lacking to the neighbor, each one should suffice by tolerating.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Hortatur ad mansuetudinem, humilitatem, & beneficentiam erga magistros, & quosvis alios, imprimis autem fidei consortes: Et colophonis loco testatur amorem per ἰδιογραφίαν & Antagonistarum circumcisionem, ob crucis fugam, urgentium, legem autem non observantium, κενοδοξίαν, gloriansque denuo de cruce Christi, tacite monet, ut juxta regulam præscriptam ambulent, quod tales pace & misericordia fruantur, ac dehortatur, ne sibi stigmata Jesu portanti deinceps molestias facessant. Denique voto gratiæ Christi obsignat epistolam. Partes duæ sunt: Prior ad tractationem moralem adhuc pertinet, estque παραινετικὴ, quæ ad virtutum homileticarum trigam adhortatur ad v. 10. Posterior conclusionem epistolæ ad v. 18. exhibet, quam ἐπιλογικὴν ideo dicimus.

PARS I. παραινετικὴ, exhortans ad trigam virtutum homileticarum.

Vers. 1. Ἐὰν καὶ προληφθῇ ἄνθρωπος ἐν τινι παραπτώματι) προληφθῇ hic est, deprehensus fuerit, quomodo προληφθεὶς sumitur Sap. XVII. 17. vult autem dicere deprehensus antequam hæc epistola ad vos veniat, in aliquo delicto, nempe eorum, quæ jam dixi, præfertim διχοστασίας aut hæreseos. Illud ἄνθρωπος ponitur pro aliquis, ut & infra 7. quia Hebræi sic ponunt אִישׁ. ὑμεῖς οἱ πνευματικοὶ) Vos, qui carnem crucifixistis, qui spiritu ducimini. Καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον) Καταρτίζειν est aptum reddere: interdum & sanare, quod corruptum est, Matth. IV, 21. Marci I. 19. quæ significatio bene congruit huic loco, si jumentum prolapsum restitui debet, Exod. XXIII. 5. quanto magis homo. Ἐν πνεύματι πραότητος) Leni animo secundum regulas quidem disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ, sed accedentibus etiam fraternis monitis.

Ipsa enim disciplina Ecclesiastica, cum bono etiam ipsorum, qui lapsi sunt, fit instituta, lenitati non obstat, 2. Thess. III. 15. Σκοπῶν σεαυτὸν) Temet circumspectans, circumspectare autem ponitur pro cavere. Solent enim, qui sibi cavent, circumspicere. Est autem hic transitus à plurali ad singularem, quia, utrum prius dicas, perinde est. Sic est supra IV. 6. 7. Μὴ καὶ σὺ πειρασθῇς) Intelligendum hoc verbum hic cum pleno effectu, id est, ne & tu aliquando tentationi alicui succumbas.

Sic & activum πειράζειν sumitur 1. Cor. VII. 5. 1. Thess. III. 5. adde, quæ dicta ad Matth. VI. 13. Vers. 2. Ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βασάζετε) Etiam peccata sunt onera: Portat aliena peccata, qui non superbe lapsum contemnit, sed sperat de eo meliora. Καὶ ὅτως ἀναπληρώσατε τὸν νόμον χριστοῦ) Sic plerique Codices habant, ut fit imperantis: etiam hoc modo ostendite, vos esse amantes proximi, quod jubet lex Christi, Joh. XIII. v. 34. XV. 12. Non de præoccupato ante hanc epistolam, sed de quocunque, qui tempore quocunque in aliquo delicto præoccupatus fuerit, loquitur Apostolus, quasi dicat: Si quis aliquando tentatione præventus labatur in peccatum, illum erigite ac constituite vicissim.

Verbum præteritum adhibetur, ob consequentem καταρτισμὸν, qui præsupponit παράπτωμα, Nec de schismate aut hæresi sermo est, sed de quovis παραπτώματι. Non tam conveniunt hæreticis, vel in hæresin prolapsis instaurandis, quæ hæc parænesis habet, ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βασάζετε, quam prolapsis in peccata mortalia.

Ad presbyteros videntur haec dicta quibusdam, quorum est lapsos instaurare: sed praecepta sunt communia. In particula (emphasis est: Etsi praelapsus fuerit. Et praeoccupatio cum effectu intelligenda est. Spirituales Apostolo non sunt sacerdotes, ut Salmero vult, sed perfecti & firmiores, quos opponit carnalibus animalibus parvulis in Christo, & infirmis 1. Cor. II. & III. Estio fatente. Spiritum lenitatis requirit, cum alias ipse virga minetur 1. Cor. IV 21. quia cum aliis aliter procedendum. Obstinati enim peccatores in operibus carnis fine poenitentia perseverantes severe arguendi sunt, & profligandi 1. Cor. V. 11. 12. Tit. I. 13. Aliud est lapsu aliquo praeoccupari, aliud usu quotidiano & prava consuetudine peccare. Conf. Psal. CXL I. 5. Prov. IX 8. c. XIII. 14. c. XXVII. 5. Matth. XVIII. 16. sqq. Quo de Gregorius parte III. curae pastoral. cap. 33. Aliter admonendi sunt, qui repentina concupiscentia superantur, aliter qui in culpa ex consilio ligantur, πρεληφθῇ praeoccupatus est scilicet per satanae fraudem & carnis infirmitatem, unde & tentationem postea nominat.

In verbo καταρτίζετε metaphoram ab aedificiis ruinosis, quorum partes reficiendae & instaurandae, alii notant: sed commodius metaphora a membro in corpore humano luxato deducitur, cui membra alia & condolent, & restituendo intenta sunt, non cum violentia, sed debita lenitate & prudentia.

Hanc per vocem πνευματικοὶ, illam voce πραότητις innuit Apostolus. Prudentia enim Spiritus opus est, & charitate, quae Spiritus fructus modo dicebatur. Nihil ita post Spiritualem virum, inquit Augustinus, ut peccati alieni tractatio, cum liberationem ejus potius, quam inflationem, potiusque auxilia, quam convitia meditetur, & quantum facultas tribuitur, lapsum benigne suscipi. Corrige fratrem tuum, inquit, interprete Chrysostomo, sed cum mansuetudine, & daemonis incursionem accusans magis, quam animi negligentiam. Considerans teipsum quasi dicat: Idem in te pede tuo metiaris. Et tibi facile contingere potest, ut & ipse lapsu aliquo praeoccupatus, tentatus à carne & Satana. Quod ergo tibi vis fieri, alteri etiam exhibeas. Quoniam nemo est hominum, qui peccati sit expers, ne acrius proximi peccata dermitet, commonefacit: quin eo maxime ferat, ut & sua ab aliis tolerentur, dicente Theophylacto. Nibil enim, inquit Augustinus, ad misericordiam sic inclinat, quam proprii periculi cogitatio. Quod cuiquam accidit, cuivis accidere potest. Quo etiam versus 3. facit: Nam si quis videtur aliquid esse, cum nihil sit, seipsum fallit.

Utitur autem jam singulari numero, quod is ad compellandum unius cujusq; conscientiam aptior fit. Ideo de communi infirmitate eosdem commonefaciens addit: Alii aliorum onera portate. Onera peccatorum, utpote quibus valde oneratur conscientia & deprimitur, & iisdem se gravatum sentit Psal. XXXVIII 5. βαστάζειν onerosam & difficilem portionem infert, qualis est jugi legum conjuncta fit illa onerum proximi portatio, non tamen eam defugiendam esse. Oportet Christianum habere fortes humeros & robusta ossa, quae possint ferre carnem, hoc est, infirmitatem fraternam, ait B. Lutherus hoc loco. B. Gerhardus hic adhibet Augustini in enarrat. Pfalm. CXXIX. similitudinem: Dicuntur cervi, quando transeunt freta in proximas sylvas, pascua gratia, capita super se invicem ponere, & unus, qui ante est, solus portat caput, & non ponit super alterum. Sed cum & ipse defecerit, tollit se ab anteriore parte, & redit posterius, & ipse requiescat in altero. Et sic omnes portant onera sua, & perveniunt ad id, quod desiderant, non patiuntur naufragium, quia quasi navis est illis charitas. Itaque charitas portat onera. Aretius hunc locum: Est argumentum à more peregrinantium sumptum. Qui simul iter faciunt, solent unius alterius sarcinam subire vel partem saltim suis humeris opponere. Vita Christiani hominis peregrinatio est, viatores, inquam, sunt Ministri, & Auditores (omnes Christiani) igitur pari facilitate in se mutuo utantur, qua viatores uti solent. Tantum portat proximum, quantum amat. Si enim amas, portas. Si desisti amare, desisti tolerare, dicente Gregorio M. homil. XIII. in Ezech. Portari vult non conniventia, adulatione, & in malo obduratione, quod non est portare, sed aggravare onus: sed mansueta admonitione, correptione, offensarum donatione Coloss. III. 12. 13. 14. Onera infirmitatis invicem portamus, dicente levitate iram alterius sustinemus, & dum ei, qui lesit, si petit, indulgemus, ut hic Glossa ordinaria habet.

Perperam ergo Thomas ad alienas satisfactiones haec rapit. Non potest prae alio poenam solvere, qui pro se meretur. Et mutua hic innuuntur officia. Num vero mutuae sunt satisfactiones? Pontificiorum satisfactiones sunt arbitrariae: Haec vero mutua onera portatio ex lege Christi est necessaria. Non de onerante panitentiae, ad Peltan. I. de satisfactione: sed de onere peccatorum explicat Justinianus & Estius: Onera vocat peccata, quae reatu suo nos deprimunt, & poenis obnoxios reddunt. Est autem sermo Metaphoricus ab iis sumptus, qui in portandis oneribus invicem se sublevant. Monet ergo Galatas, ut alii aliorum infirmitates & peccata quodammodo reputent sua, condolendo, diffimulando, ferendo, leniter admonendo, fraterne corripiendo, denique hoc agendo, ut corrigatur potius, quam puniatur.

2 Quod ad legem Christi de fraterna charitate, non Legem ea legi Mosis opponitur, qui itidem charitatem proximi sic postulat, ut proximum ceu nos ipsos diligamus Lev. XIX. 18. Marci X. 28. Sed lex Christi dicitur, quod eandem & operose inculcavit, & prolixe passim explicavit, & novo atq; admirabili exemplo suo confirmavit Job. XV. 12. 13. De impletionis autem voce recte hoc loco Hemmingius: Impletionis seu perfectionis vox duobus modis accipitur in scriptura. Alias enim opponitur imperfectioni operis, alias simulationi, mendacio & hypocrisi. Priori modo nemo legem Dei in hac vita implere potest, nisi unus Jesus Christus, qui eam ob causam legis consummatio in justitiam omni credenti ab Apostolo praedicatur. At posteriori modo omnes filii Dei dicuntur legem Christi implere, quia sincere student vitam suam Deo approbare, & sine simulatione proximum amore prosequuntur. Theophylactu emphasi in voce ἀναπληρώσατε. Non enim implebitis dixit, sed adimplebitis, hoc est, communi consensu omnes Christi legem perficietis, vos ipsos invicem tolerantes, videlicet ut incundus ad iram tardum sustineat, & tardior incundi impetum ferat, sic fiet, ut ne quis ille delinquat, si ab hoc toleretur, neque is, si ab illo feratur: Nec illud dico, ut inter vos porrectis invicem manibus Christi legem alternis mox exequamini, sed quod proximo deerit, unusquisque sufficiat tolerando. Vers.

## 6:3
3. If anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing) Here and in 4. and 5. they are taken comparatively, that is, if anyone esteems himself more highly than he is. See 1. Cor. III. 7. X. 19. XIII. 2. 2. Cor. XII. 12. δοκεῖ thinks. He deceives his own mind, as James I. 26 says; he will sooner deceive himself than others. From this word φρεναπάται, Tit. I. 10., those who seduce minds. Vers. 4.

Latin:

3. Ἐι γάρ δοκεῖ τις, εἶναι τι, μηδὲν ὢν) Hic & 4. & 5. sumuntur comparate, id est, si quis pluris se aestimet, quam fit. Vide 1. Cor. III. 7. X. 19. XIII. 2. 2. Cor. XII. 12. δοκεῖ putat. Ἑαυτὸν φρεναπατᾷ) Decipit cor suum, ut loquitur Jac. I. 26. se citius fallet quam alios. Ab hoc verbo φρεναπάται, Tit. I. 10. qui animos seducunt. Vers.

## 6:4
Let each one test his own work) Singular for the plural, just as we have the same word ἔργον (Hhh) 1 Pet.

1 Pet. 1:17 & Apoc. 22:12. Let each one weigh his own deeds, 1 Cor. 11:27. Many among the Galatians thought themselves great, because they were less evil than others.

But: There is no glory in passing by the donkeys. And then he will have his boasting in himself alone He will rejoice in the examination of himself. And not in another not by comparison with worse men. Verse 5. For each one will bear his own burden Each one will bear his own burden, that is, he will bear the punishment for his sins, he will not be relieved by comparison with worse men; as there are degrees of sins, so there are degrees of punishments.

These things pertain to humility, lest anyone through pride think himself to be something, namely in those things in which he is nothing, or is worth nothing, by which method he will only deceive himself, and will persuade no one else by his imaginary persuasion. In truth, man is also nothing, of no virtue or justice, in the sight of God. For all are by nature children of wrath, whatever they are, or whatever gifts they have, it is from God; he who ascribes them to himself, deceives himself 2 Cor. 4:7. But the remedy for the vice opposed to pride, and the means of humility, is when each one rightly tests his own work, so that he may not rest so much in the praises of others, as in his own conscience.

What does it profit if the whole world praises you, if your own conscience condemns you. When he names his own work, he recalls from the rigid examination of the faults of others, to the discussion of his own, lest anyone should rely on the weakness of one lying down, or of one falling by a slip, but on his own strength, as Jerome says.

To test is to examine and accurately discuss, what it is, with what mind, with what intention, with what end, and how the deed is approved by God. Let him examine, I say, and let each one diligently search out his own deeds, for when he tests them, he says, he designates, lest perhaps he has done these things for the sake of vain glory, or of hypocrisy, or of any other human occasion. Then it will happen, that he may have glory not in another, but in himself, as Theophylact says here, following Chrysostom. A metaphor seems to underlie this, taken from goldsmiths, who test gold with fire, so that they may discern and separate the genuine from the adulterated. But let it suffice to have glory in oneself, nor is it right that we should boast by comparing ourselves to others, or that we should take an occasion for boasting from the infirmity of others.

Little glory certainly arises from that, if a stronger man compares himself with a weak one, or an adult with a child. Finally, he proposes for consideration the final judgment, in which each one will bear his own burden.

But this does not contradict the previous sentence, about bearing the burden of others. That pertains to the present life, in which we ought to support one another in sinning with sympathy, counsel, and prayers. Here it concerns the final judgment: in which he will not be judged by the sin and comparison of a weaker person, but each one will be condemned according to his own work. Which is to bear one's own burden. Therefore live thus, O man, that you may test your conscience and the acts of your life before God, the judge of all, neither caring greatly for the judgments of others about you, nor rashly inquiring into others.

Let the heart and voice of David be yours Ps. 139:23, 24. If you do this, you will have the boasting of a good conscience in yourself: but if less, your own burden will have to be borne by you, 2 Cor. 10, as the Glassian paraphrase has it. On that day, says B. Luther fol. 154, on which the Lord will judge the hidden things of men, the testimony of conscience will stand for you or against you. Against you, if you have had glory in others: For you, if you have had it in yourself, that is, if your conscience has borne witness to you, how uprightly and faithfully you have administered the ministry of the Word, looking only to the glory of God and the salvation of souls, or have done your duty rightly according to your vocation.

He does not treat of the remission of sins, but compares true and hypocritical works. But humility follows by merit of meekness.

For arrogance is an impediment to the mutual exercise of meekness. Verse 6. Let him who is taught the word share with him who teaches in all good things There is no need to place a stop here after 'teaches'.

This is what it means: he who is taught the word, that is, the Gospel, which is called the word by excellence, Acts 16:16. (For the word 'to catechize' is used here a little more loosely, as also Rom. 2:18, not as elsewhere concerning only the first rudiments) Rom. 12:13, Phil. 4:15, and concerning the receiver, as Rom. 15:27. It answers to the Hebrew חָלַק. And here it is worth 'through', for all good things, that is, not only through food, but also other obsequies and duties, see 1 Cor. 9:11, 1 Tim. 5:17. It was necessary for this to be said to the Galatians, because those new Doctors were not receiving from the Christians, but from the Jews. Many Galatians were following these through tenacity, because they had no expenses to make upon them. Of such it is said אָרוּר נִבְלָה Mal. 1:14. There follows now an exhortation to beneficence, especially towards the ministers of the Word. 'He who is taught the word' - being instructed, who is catechized or informed in the Word of God. 'To catechize' properly denotes the information of the ears, which is returned by a reciprocal sound, and resounds in the mouth of both learners and teachers, and returns like an Echo, which is done through mutual questions and answers.

Here it is taken a little more generally concerning the doctrine, which is handed down by living voice. The Gospel is called the word by antonomasia Acts 4:4, ch. 8:4, ch. 14:25, ch. 16:6. It is also called the Word of the Lord Acts 15:35. The Word of God, Acts 12:24, ch. 13:5, 1 Thess. 3:13. By 'him who catechizes' some understand him who teaches the first rudiments, but it is a general exhortation, and every Doctor of the Word is designated 'in all good things', namely in all temporal things, which are communicable, and in duties and obsequies, as Grotius rightly says here: Although at Acts 2:42 he hinted at a new interpretation concerning communication through conversations, which in no way fits this place. For it is treated here of the communication of goods, which are not to be denied to the teacher for his information, unless we wish to be ungrateful.

To whom therefore with a sincere heart and cheerfully and liberally it is to be communicated by those from whom information is received. Conf. 1 Cor. 9:7 ff. 2 Cor. 9:7. Verse 7. Do not be deceived That is, do not deceive yourselves, Niphal for Hithpahel. God is not mocked Job 4. God does not allow himself to be mocked. For this word also is to be understood with effect. Polycarp also has this opinion. Because those who ought to share their goods with their teachers often use frivolous excuses, 'do not err', says the Apostle, that is, interpreting Jerome, let no one think himself excused in vain, by pretending poverty: God is not mocked, that is, he cannot be deceived.

For he knows your hearts, he is not ignorant of your resources. The plausible excuse of a man cannot be hidden or please: God cannot be deceived. Add, that here it is not treated only of the sustenance of a man, but how much Christ is esteemed, and his Gospel, or the legate of the same.

Latin:

4. Τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἑαυτοῦ δοκιμαζέτω ἕκαστος) Singulare pro plurali, quomodo idem vocabulum ἔργον habemus (Hhh) 1. Pet.

1. Pet. I. 17. & Apoc. XXII. 12. sua quisque facta expendat, 1. Cor. XI. 27. Multi apud Galatas magni se faciebant, quod minus mali essent, quam alii.

At: Nulla est gloria praeterire afellos. Καὶ τότε εἰς ἑαυτὸν μόνον τὸ καύχημα ἕξει Gaudebit redo fui examine. Καὶ οὐκ εἰς τὸν ἕτερον non deteriorum comparatione. Vers. 5. ἕκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον φορτίον βασάσει Quisque suum onus feret, id est, pro delictis feret poenam, non sublevabitur pejorum comparatione; ut delictorum, ita poenarum sunt gradus.

Hæc ad humilitatem spectant, ne quis per superbiam putet, se aliquid esse, scilicet in iis, in quibus nihil est, aut valet, quo pacto seipsum tantum decipiet, aliis persuasione sua imaginaria nihil persuadebit. Revera etiam homo nihil est, nullius virtutis aut justitiæ, in conspectu Dei. Omnes enim in se sunt filii iræ, quicquid sunt, vel donorum habent, à Deo est, qui sibi adscribit, fallit se 2. Cor. IV. 7. Remedium autem vitii oppositi superbiæ, & medium humilitatis est, cum quisque suum opus rite probat, ut non tam aliorum elogiis acquiescat, quam conscientiæ propriæ.

Quid id juvat, si totus mundus te collaudet, propria si damnet conscientia. Cum opus suum nominat, revocat ab examine rigido nævorum alienorum, ad discussionem propriorum, ne quisquam infirmitatem jacentis, aut lapsu impingentis, sed fortitudinem suam confideret, ut ait Hieronymus.

Probare est examinare & accurate discutere, quale sit, quo animo, qua intentione, quo fine, & quomodo factum Deo approbetur. Examinet inquam, & diligenter suas quisque res gestas disquirat, id namque cum probet inquit, designat, ne has forsitan, sive inanis gloriæ, sive fimulationis, sive alterius cujusvis humanae occasionis gratia gesserit. Tunc fiet, ut non in altero, sed in seipso gloriam quia assequatur, ut praeeunte Chrysostomo hic Theophylactus. Metaphoram hic videtur subesse ab aurifabris petita, qui aurum igne probant, ut genuinum ab adulterino discernant & seperant, Sufficiat autem in seipso habere gloriam, nec est, ut adferus alios gloriemur, aut ex aliorum infirmitate gloriandi occasionem captemus.

Parum certe gloriæ inde furgit, si cum infirmo firmier se conferat, vel adultus cum puero. Proponit denique cogitandum judicium novissimum, in quo unusquisque proprium bajulabit onus.

Non autem hoc adversatur priori fententiæ, de portando aliorum onere. Illa ad præsentem vitam pertinet, in qua peccantes nos mutuo debemus sustentare sympathia, consilio, precibus. Hic de judicio novissimo agitur: in quo non ex alterius peccato & comparatione debilioris judicabitur, sed juxta proprium opus unusquisque damnabitur. Quod est onus proprium portare. Ita igitur vive, ô homo, ut Deo judici universorum conscientiam tuam & vitæ acta probes, nec aliorum de te judicia magnopere curans, nec in aliorum temere inquireres.

Esto cor & vox Davidis tibi Psal. CXXXIX. 23. 24. Hoc si feceris, bonæ conscientiæ gloriationem in te ipso habebis: fin vero minus, onus proprium tibi bajulandum erit, 2. Cor. 10. ut habet paraphrasis Glassiana. In illo die, inquit B. Lutherus fol. 154. quo judicabit Dominus occulta hominum, stabit testimonium conscientiæ pro te aut contra te. Contra te, si habueris gloriam in aliis: Prote, si eam babueris in seipso, hoc est, si conscientia tua testimonium tibi praebuerit, quam probe & fideliter admini-straveris ministerium Verbi, spectando tantum gloriam Dei & salutem animarum, vel tuum officium secundum vocationem recte feceris.

Non agit de remissione peccatorum, sed confert vera & hypocritica opera. Sequitur autem humilitas merito mansuetudine.

Arrogantia enim impedimentum est mansuetudinis mutuo exercendæ. Vers. 6. Κοινωνείτω δὲ ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον τῷ κατηχοῦντι ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς Non est hic ponenda ὑπεστιγμὴ post κατηχοῦντι.

Hoc vult dicere: is, qui docetur verbum, id est, Evangelium, quod κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur λόγος, Actor. XVI. 16. (Nam vox κατηχεῖν hic paulo laxius sumitur, ut & Rom. II. 18. non ut alibi de primis tantum rudimentis) Rom. XII. 13. Phil. IV. 15. & de accipiente, ut Rom. XV. 27. Respondet Hebræo חָלַק. & hic valet per, pro omnes res bonas, id est, non per alimenta tantum, sed & alia obsequia & officia, vide 1. Cor. IX. 11. 1 Tim. V. 17. necesse erat dici hoc Galatis, quia illi novi Doctores non accipiebant à Christianis, sed a Judais. Hos multi Galatæ sequebantur per tenacitatem, quia nihil in eos sumptus faciendam habebant. De talibus dicitur אָרוּר נִבְלָה Mal. I. 14. Sequitur jam adhortatio ad beneficentiam, imprimis erga Verbi ministros. ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον - μαθη-τευομενος, qui catechizatur vel informatur in Verbo Dei. Κατηχεῖν proprie denotat informationem χωδῶν, quæ reciproco sono redditur, ac in ore tam discentium quam docentium resonat, & velut Echo retro commeat, quod per quæstiones & responsiones mutuas fit.

Hic paulo generalius accipitur de doctrina, qua viva voce traditur. Evangelium κατ' ἀντονομασίαν verbum dicitur AB. IV. 4. c. VIII. 4. c. XIV. 25. cap. XVI. 6. Vocatur & Verbum Domini AB. XV. 35. Verbum Dei, AB. XII. 24. cap. XIII. 5. 1. Thessal. III. 13. Per κατηχεῖντα non nulli eum, qui prima rudimenta tradit, intelligunt, sed parænesis generalis est, & quilibet Verbi Doctor designatur ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς in omnibus bonis scilicet temporalibus, quæ communicabilia sunt & officiis atque obsequiis, ut recte hic Grotius: Tametsi ad Actor. II. 42. novam ἐξήγησιν innuerit de communicatione per colloquia, quæ nullatenus huic loco convenit. Agitur enim hic de communicatione bonorum, quæ doctori pro informatione deneganda non sunt, nisi ingrati esse velimus.

Quibus proinde sincero corde & hilariter atque liberaliter communicandum est illis, a quibus accipitur informatio. Conf. 1. Cor. IX. 7. seqq. 2. Cor. IX. 7. Vers. 7. Μὴ πλανᾶσθε Id est, ne decipite vosmetipsos, Niphal pro Hithpahel. Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται Jobi IV. Deus non finit sibi illudi. Nam verbum hoc quoque cum effectu intelligendum est. Habet hanc sententiam & Polycarpus. Quia excusationibus frivolis sæpe utuntur, qui communicari de bonis suis debent doctoribus, nolite errare, inquit Apostolus, id est interprete Hieronymo, nemo excusatum vane se existimet, paupertatem prætendendo: Deus non irridetur, id est, non potest falli.

Scit enim corda vestra, non ignorat facultates. Excusatio verisimilis hominis, non potest latere vel placere: Deus non potest fallere. Adde, quod hic non agatur tantum de hominis victu, sed quantum æstimetur Christus, ejusque Evangelium, vel legati ejusdem.

## 6:8
Verse 8. He who sows to his own flesh, will reap corruption from it It is a frequent proverb among all nations.

Aeschylus, Euripides, Gorgias, Plautus in Captivi, Cicero, II de Oratore use it: As you have made the sowing, so also you will reap. Job 4:8, Prov. 11:18, and elsewhere have similar sentences. To sow often means to work, to reap means to bear punishment or reward, Matt. 25:24, 26, 2 Cor. 9:6 & seq. He who sows to his own flesh Who makes all expenditures on the pleasures of the body. Will reap corruption from the flesh For the flesh itself is corruption 1 Cor. 15:53, and will deservedly find such an end, as that to which it has applied itself. But he who sows to the Spirit Who makes expenditure on those things which the Spirit of God dictates. Will reap eternal life from the Spirit 'From the Spirit', that is, on account of that Spirit, who is incorruptible. Thus the Hebrews use 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.

There was already 1 Cor. 9:11 & 2 Cor. 9:6, that similitude, and it does not occur otherwise here. Although indeed these things can be taken generally: He who works carnal things, and makes them like seed in his flesh, so that he may satisfy his flesh, and from the flesh he shall reap corruption and temporal and eternal death. It is manifest, however, that the application here is intended for the communication or distribution of resources, so that to sow in one's flesh is to spend one's resources only for usury, for gain, luxury, and pleasures, without regard for religion, the church, or the poor. In general, indeed, says B. Glassius on Sunday XV after Trinity, epistle p.

489, these words can be explained, as in Prov. 11:18, etc., but yet properly in this place, they are accommodated to commend the zeal for Christian beneficence. And the same metaphor of sowing is used in a similar matter by the most wise king in Eccl. 11:6. To sow in the flesh, to the Apostle, is to be given to avarice, and to think of all things in life for the sake of commending wealth and conferring other things: that is, to spend the same for χῆσιν, or use—not for pious uses pleasing to God, but for luxury, pride, worldly splendor, carnal pleasure, etc.

What do those who sow in such a way reap? Φθορὰν, corruption. What this is, is explained in 1 Tim. 6:9. To sow in the Spirit is to look to heaven rather than to earth, and to confer one's resources for spiritual uses and for preserving the worship of God, the sustenance of the ministry, and the use of the poor. To sow in the Spirit, says B. Glassius again, is to spend temporal goods, well collected and acquired by just title, for the glory of God, the preservation of the Church, the sustenance of ministries, and the nourishment of a needy neighbor, etc.

(besides those things which pertain to the διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, the food and clothing, of the house and family, 1 Tim. 6:8) out of the love of God. And what do they reap from it? Eternal life. Which Paul himself explains almost plainly in 1 Tim. 6:17, 18, 19. From the Spirit he shall reap eternal life. Merit is not brought in here, as Salmero contends; for can a farmer, no matter how much labor he expends, merit the harvest?

Eternal life is a χάρισμα, a gift, in Christ Jesus, Rom. 6:last verse. Neither Justinianus, nor Tirinus, nor Cornelius à Lapide seek here an argument for the merit of glory. And Bellarmine himself explains concerning the degrees of glory in lib. 5 de justif. cap. 3. B. Hunnius: Between the communication, he says, of earthly goods from hearers to teachers, and eternal life, there is no symmetry, no proportion, but an infinite difference: since it is most certain that the earthly and the heavenly, the temporal and the eternal, differ in their whole kind.

It is absurd, therefore, to wish to interpret the Apostle's passage concerning merit, and indeed concerning the merit of eternal life, which, in respect of the sole and single passion and death of the Son of God, can be called merit, but in respect of us, it is the gratuitous gift of GOD through our Lord Jesus Christ, Rom. 6. It remains, therefore, that Paul is speaking in this place of gratuitous retribution, excluding all our merit: and that he considers eternal life not simply in itself, as it is described by the vision of God, beatitude, and joy, but as joined under differences to the degrees of glory, so that the sense becomes: Those who, by the leading of the Spirit, contribute liberally to the preservation of the ministry, are to receive from the Lord, out of the immense grace of God, a most bountiful retribution in eternal life.

B. Höpfnerus especially weighs this argument in de justif. p. 126. Those who work in this way, they also shall reap from the Spirit, that is, from spiritual or good works, eternal life; that is, because the kind and quality of the works is good, the outcome of the same kind, that is, good, will also follow, just as after the sowing of grains and legumes, each in its own kind—barley from barley, wheat from sown wheat—is reaped, not barley from wheat.

In this, good and evil works generally agree, that they have such an outcome as they themselves are. But they differ in the manner of the outcome and in specific nature, because this, that the outcomes of evil works precede, so that they are at the same time their cause, is of the nature not of works in general, but in the species of evil works.

For the special mission of evil works is far different from that of good ones; the former are perfectly evil, so that whoever has committed one evil work has violated the whole law at once, as it is said in James 2:10: For whoever has kept the whole law, but has offended in one (one precept excepted), has become guilty of all: not indeed that all special sins concur in one sin, but that in any part of the transgression the whole law is violated, and in every sin the incentive of all sins, namely original concupiscence, is joined.

But he who does one good work has not fulfilled the whole law. 2. One evil work is enough for damnation because of the general guilt which every transgression carries with it. Yet one good work, if the most perfect one could be given, would not suffice to obtain salvation. Nor is ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος here "on account of the spirit," as Grotius rashly says.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ὁ σπείρων εἰς τὴν σάρκα ἑαυτοῦ, τότε τὴν θέρισει Est proverbium frequens apud omnes gentes.

Utuntur eo Æschylus, Euripides, Gorgias, Plautus Captivis, Cicero, II. de Oratore: Ut sementium feceris, ita & metes. Similes sententias habet Job. IV. 8. Prov. XI. 18. & alibi. Setere febrais fæpe operari, metere pœnam aut præmium ferre, Matth. XXV. 24. 26. 2. Cor. IX. 6. & seq. Ὅτι ὁ σπείρων εἰς τὴν σάρκα ἑαυτοῦ Qui omnia impendia facit in corporis voluptates. Ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς θέρισει φθοράν Nam & caro ipsa φθοράν 1. Cor. XV. 53. merito talem exitum reperiet, quale est id, cui studuit. Ὁ δὲ σπείρων εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα Qui impendium facit in eas res, quas dictat Dei Spiritus. Ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος θέρισει ζωὴν αἰώνιον Ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος id est, propter illum Spiritum, qui est ἀφθαρτὸς. Sic Hebraei 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 usurpant.

Fuit jam 1. Cor. IX. 11. & 2. Cor. IX. 6, illa similitudo, nec aliter hic occurrit. Quamvis enim hæc generaliter accipi possunt: Qui operatur carnalia, eaque instar sementis facit in carnem suam, ut pacat suam carnem, et de carne metet corruptionem et mortem temporalem ac aeternam. Manifestum tamen est, hic applicationem intendi ad communicationem vel erogationem facultatum, ut seminare in carnem suam fit facultates suas tantum ad usuras, ad quaestum, luxum, et voluptates impendere, non habita religionis, ecclesiae, pauperum ratione. In genere quidem, inquit B.

Glassius ad Dom. XV. post Trin. epist. p. 489. haec verba exponi possunt, ut Prov. XI. 18. &c. sed tamen proprie hoc loco, ad commendandum beneficentia Christiana studium accommodantur. Et eadem seminationis metaphora utitur in simili negotio rex sapientissimus Eccl. XI. v. 6. In carnem seminare Apostolo est, avaritiae deditum esse, & ad commendandas opes omnia vite cogitare & alia conferre: quod χῆσιν sive usum, non pios Deoque placentes usus, sed ad luxum, superbiam, splendorem mundanum, voluptatem carnalem &c. eadem erogare.

Taliter seminantes quid metunt? Φθορὰν corruptionem. Quae quid sit 1. Tim. VI. exponitur, v. 9. Seminare in Spiritu coelum magis quam terram respicere, facultates suas ad usus spirituales & cultum Dei conservandum, ministerii sustentationem, & pauperum usum conferre. In spiritu seminare, ait iterum B. Glassius, est bona temporalia bene collecta, & acquisita justo titulo, in Dei gloriam, Ecclesiae conservationem, ministeriorum sustentationem, proximi indigentis alimentum &c.

(praeter ea, quae ad domus & familia διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα pertinent 1. Tim. VI. 8.) ex amore Dei erogare. Et quid illi mesunt? Vitam aeternam. Quod & ipsum ferme plano explicat Paulus 1. Tim. VI. 17. 18. 19. De spiritu metet vitam aeternam. Non hic meritum affertur, ut Salmero contendit, num enim agricola, quantoscunque etiam impendat labores, mereri potest messem?

Vita aeterna χάρισμα est in Christo Jesu Rom. VI. v. ult. Nec Justinianus, nec Tirinus, nec Cornelius à Lapide hic quaerunt argumentum meriti gloriae. Et de gradibus gloriae explicat Bellarminus ipse lib. V. de justif. cap. 3. B. Hunnius: Inter communicationem, inquit, terrenorum bonorum ab auditoribus in doctores, inter aeternam vitam nulla symmetria, nulla proportio est, sed infinita prorsus differentia: siquidem terrenum & celeste, temporale & aeternum toto genere differre certissimum est.

Absurdum igitur, velle locum Apostoli de merito interpretari, & quidem de merito vitae aeternae, quae respectu solius & unius passionis & mortis Filii Dei meritum appellari potest, nostri vero respectu est gratuitum donum DEI per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum Rom. VI. Relinquitur ergo, Paulum hoc loco de retributione gratuita, omneque meritum nostrum secludente, verba facere: et vitam aeternam non in semetipsa simpliciter, ut Dei visione, beatitudine gaudioque describitur, sed sub differentiis adjuncta gloriae gradibus considerare, ut sensu fit: Qui ductu Spiritus ad ministerii conservationem liberaliter contribuunt, eos ex immenso Dei gratia in vita aeterna largissimam retributionem accepturos a Domino.

Expendit hoc argumentum imprimis B. Höpfnerus de justif. p. 126. Qui sic opemntur, illi quoque de spiritu, hoc est, spirituallibus seu bonis operibus metent vitam aeternam, hoc est, quia operum genus & qualitas est bona, etiam eventus ejusdem generis, hoc est, bonus consequetur, quemadmodum post frumentorum & leguminum sationem, quodlibet in suo genere, hordeum de hordeo, triticum de tritico seminato metitur, non hordeum de tritico.

In hoc generatim conveniunt bona & mala opera, quod talem habeant eventum, qualia sunt ipsa. Differunt autem modo eventus & natura specifica, quia hoc, quod mala operis antecedant exitum, ut simul ejus sint causa, est de natura non operum in genere, sed in specie operum malorum.

Longe namque alia missio specialis malorum operum, quam bonorum, illa 1. perfecta mala, ut qui unum malum opus patraverit, totam legem simul violarit, sicut Jac. II. 10. dicitur: Quia quis totam legem servaverit, offenderit autem in uno (uno praecepto excepto) factus est reus omnium: Non quidem quod in uno peccato omnia specialia concurrant, sed quod tamen in quavis parte transgressionis tota lex violetur, & in quolibet peccato conjunctus sit fomes omnium peccatorum, nempe originalis concupiscentia.

At qui unum bonum opus facit, non implevit totam legem. 2. Unum malum opus satis est ad damnationem propter reatum generalem, quem qualibet transgressio secum trahit. Non tamen unum bonum opus, si maxime perfectissimum dari posset, ad salutem impetrandam sufficeret. Neque hic ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος est propter spiritum, ut temere Grotius.

## 6:9
Verse 9. Τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιοῦντες μὴ ἐκκακῶμεν) "And let us not grow weary in doing good." Τὸ καλὸν, that is, first those things which are of justice, then those which are of mercy; he who does not do these, like the tenacious Galatians, will do those much less.

Thus the order is established. The Apostle teaches that we must do good even to those who are not bound to us by the bond of religion. The common bond of nature demands this. And therefore they sin who persecute those who are strangers to their religion, but do not do good to them.

But benefits are especially to be shown to the household of faith: those who are in the same house with us, the Church. Just as everyone is especially bound to look after his own household. Concerning the ministers of the Word who are to be supported by liberality, Crocius rightly complains in this place on page 184. It is to be lamented that superstition is the mother of greater liberality than the profession of Evangelical truth. In the Papacy, how many idle bellies were there, who, flying about, drained the people?

Today, scarcely one or two ministers are meagerly supported. In Israel, the voice sounded: What shall we bring to the man of God? In the Papacy, too, it was heard, and is still heard. Today, among the Evangelicals, that voice sounds everywhere: What shall we take away?

Come, let us possess the habitations of God by hereditary right. In the time of Moses, the Israelites contributed so liberally to the construction of the tabernacle that it had to be proclaimed in the camp that no one should offer any more, Exod. XXXV. & XXXVI. There is no need for such a prohibition today. There is no city, says B. Luther, fol. 155, that is known to us, which supports its own Doctors, but all are supported from goods, not as to Christ, to whom no one gives anything (for when born he uses a manger instead of a bed, since there is no room for him in the inn; living on earth, he has nowhere to lay his head: finally, stripped of his clothes, naked on the cross, hanging between two thieves, he dies most miserably) but as to the things given to the Pope for his abominations.

But what calamities will follow this ingratitude, they will soon experience. For they lose both, carnal and spiritual things. For it is necessary that this sin be followed by the most grievous punishments. And indeed I think that for no other reason were the Churches in Galatia, Corinth, etc., so troubled by the Pseudo-Apostles, than that they neglected their own true Doctors.

It is most rightly done, that he who denies a penny to God, who offers all good things and eternal life, gives a golden one to the Devil, the author of all evils and death.

He who does not wish to serve God in a small matter with his own greatest convenience: let him serve the Devil in a great matter, with the greatest detriment.

THE SECOND PART OF CHAPTER VI. EPILOGUE.

Which exhibits the conclusion of the whole epistle.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιοῦντες μὴ ἐκκακῶμεν) Τὸ καλὸν, id est, primum ea, quae sunt justitiae, deinde ea, quae sunt misericordiae, qui illa non facit, ut Galatae tenaces, haec multo minus faciet.

Ita ordo statuitur. Docet Apostolus iis etiam, qui religionis vinculo nobis obstricti non sunt, benefaciendum esse. Postulat id commune naturae vinculum. Ideoque peccant, qui alienos a religione sua persequuntur, non autem benefaciunt iisdem.

Sed domesticis tamen fidei maxime exhibenda sunt beneficia: qui in una nobiscum domo sunt, Ecclesiae. Quemadmodum quisque domestis suis praecipue tenetur prospicere. De liberalitatis ministris Verbi exercendae defede- au moderno non abs re queritur Crocius hoc loco pag. 184. Dolendum est, superstitionem majoris esse liberalitatis matrem, quam veritatis Evangelicae professionem. In Papatu quot abierant otiosi ventres, qui circumvolitantes exhauriebant populum?

Hodie vix unus & alter minister tenuiter alitur. In Israele vox sonabat: quid afferemus viro Dei? In Papatu quoque audiebatur, & adhuc auditur. Hodie passim inter Evangelicos sonat vox illa: Quid auferemus?

Agite, hereditario jure possideamus habitacula Dei . Mosis tempore ad tabernaculi exstructionem tam liberaliter conferebant Israelitae, ut in castris promulgandum esset, ne quis ultra offerret Exod. XXXV. & XXXVI. Non opus hodie prohiberi. Nullam atvitas, inquit B. Lutherus fol. 155. est, quae quidem nobis fit nota, quae suos Doctores alat, sed omnes aluntur de bonis, non qua Christo, cui nemo aliquid dat (natus enim utitur praesepi, loco lectuli, cum ipsi non fit locus in diversorio; conversans in terris, non habet, ubi caput suum reclinet: Postremo spoliatus vestibus, nudus in cruce inter duos latrones pendens miserrime moritur) sed qua Papa donata sunt pro suis abominationibus.

Sed quae calamitas istam ingratitudinem sequuture sint, brevi experientur. Utraque enim amittunt, carnalia & spiritualia. Nam hoc peccatum necesse est, poenas gravissimas consequi. Et profecto puto ob nullam aliam causam Ecclesias in Galatia, Corintho &c. per Pseudo-Apostolos sic turbatas esse, quam quod suos veros Doctores neglexerint.

Rectissime fit, ut qui Deo negat obulum, offerenti omnia bona ac vitam aeternam, is Diabolo ausori omnium malorum & mortis det aureum.

Qui Deo non vult servire in modico cum maximo suo commodo: Is serviat Diabolo in maximo, cum summo detrimento.

PARS ALTERA CAPITIS VI. ΕΠΙΛΟΓΙΚΗ.

Que totius epistolae conclusionem exhibet.

## 6:11
Ver. 11. See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. In the end of other epistles he used to write certain things with his own hand, 1 Cor. XVI. 21. 2 Thess. III. 18. & Col. IV. 18. the rest by another's hand, as can be seen in Rom. XVI. 22. But here Paul wrote with his own hand all that now follows, as Jerome rightly thinks.

But this was a great deal for a man so occupied, and as it seems, not much accustomed to write in Greek, with such large letters, that is, with so many. Adjectives of magnitude are wont to be used for adjectives pertaining to number. Thus the Greek word 'tosos' is used in both senses. Paul was accustomed to write certain more notable sentences with his own hand, and such as were to be kept perpetually. Ver. 12. As many as desire to make a fair show in the flesh, that is, he calls them inconveniences, because they want to appear great among men. And 'flesh', for 'according to the flesh', and 'flesh' for 'man'. 'Euprosopon' properly means beautiful. By translation, whatever pleases others. Thus Demosthenes said 'euprosopous logous' (fair-seeming words). Namely, by example and doctrine.

See above III. 14. Only that they should not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ) He calls the inconveniences to be borne for Christ 'the cross of Christ', alluding at the same time to that peculiar punishment which Christ suffered, among other things, to give us an example of patience, so also Phil. III. 18, which epistle seems to have been written about the same time, and for similar reasons.

See what we have said in the preface to this epistle, and above C. V. 11. The Cross of Christ is spoken of in that way, just as the sufferings of Christ are in 1 Cor. I. 5. Undoubtedly, Gaius Caesar, Octavianus Augustus, and Tiberius, the successor of Augustus, had promulgated laws that the Jews, who were dispersed throughout the whole world of the Roman Empire, should live by their own rite and serve their country's ceremonies.

Whoever, therefore, was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was considered by the Gentiles as a Jew. But he who, without circumcision, showed that he was not a Jew by his foreskin, was exposed to the persecutions of both Gentiles and Jews. To avoid this persecution, the Pseudo-Apostles urged circumcision, as Crocius says in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἴδετε πηλίκοις ὑμῖν γράμμασιν ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ in aliarum epistolarum fine quaedam scribebat sua manu, 1. Cor. XVI. 21. 2. Thess. III. 18. & Col. IV. 18. cetera manu aliena, ut videre est Rom. XVI. 22. Hic vero Paulus sua manu scripsit omnia, quae jam sequuntur, ut recte putat Hieronymus.

Id autem multum erat in homine adeo occupato, & ut videtur, non multum assueto Graece scribere, quantis literis, id est, quam multis. Solent adjectiva magnitudinis pro adjectivis ad numerum pertinentibus. Sic Graecum τόσος utroque sensu usurpatum. Solebat sua manu Paulus scribere fententias quasdam insigniores, ac perpetuo retinendas. Vers. 12. Ὅσοι θέλουσιν εὐπροσωπῆσαι ἐν σαρκὶ id est, vocat incommoda, quod apud homines magni videri volunt. Et σαρκὶ, pro παρὰ σαρκὶ & caro pro homine. Εὐπρόσωπον proprie pulcher. per translationem, quicquid placet aliis. Sic λόγους εὐπροσωπους dixit Demosthenes. Nempe exemplo & doctrina.

Vide supr. III. 14. Μόνον ἵνα μὴ τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ χριστοῦ διώκωνται) σανρὸν χριστοῦ vocat incommoda, ob Christum ferenda, alludens simul ad illud peculiare supplicium, quod passus est Christus, inter alia, ut nobis patientiae exemplum daret, Sic & Philipp. III. 18. quae epistola sub idem tempus scripta videtur, & paribus de causis.

Vide quae diximus in praefatione ad hanc epistolam, & supra C. V. 11. Crux Christi eo modo dicitur, quomodo perpesiones Christi a. Cor. I. 5. Nimirum Cajus Caesar, Octavianus Augustus, & Tiberius successor Augusti leges promulgaverant, ut Judaei, qui erant in toto Romani Imperii orbe dispersi, proprio ritu viverent, & patriae ceremoniis deservirent.

Quicunque igitur circumcisis erat, licet Christum crederet, quasi Judaeus habebatur a gentibus. Qui vero absque circumcisione, se non esse Judaeum, praeputio praeferebat, persecutionibus tam gentium quam Judaeorum erat obnoxius. Hanc persecutionem ut devitarent Pseudo-Apostoli, circumcisionem urgebant, ut Crocius in hunc locum.

## 6:13
Ver. 13. For neither do they themselves who are circumcised keep the law) They are not held to such zeal for the law that they observe all its precepts; they easily find excuses.

See what we have said in Matt. XXIII. 4. and above V. 3. But they desire you to be circumcised) They want, that is, they labor for this. Metonymy. A manuscript has it in the same sense, 'hamartylontai'. That they may glory in your flesh) That they may exult in your carnal fear, so that your inconstancy, in bearing inconveniences, may yield honor to them among the Jews.

The Pseudo-Apostles urged the necessity of keeping circumcision and the whole law: indeed, they used the observation of the law as a pretext for circumcision: yet they themselves neither kept the law, nor could they keep it, which is said of the Jews likewise in Acts VII. 53. But they sought this primarily, when the Gentiles were willing to be circumcised, so that they might glory among the Jews about the extorted circumcision, or that the Gentiles were circumcised by their ministry, namely, that they had corrected the Galatians, who had been badly instructed by Paul, and had led them to circumcision and the observation of the law.

Not therefore by zeal for piety, but by vain desire for glory, they did this, as Chrysostom and Theophylactus rightly understood. Obliquely, says B. Hunnius in this place, he touches upon the other error concerning legal righteousness, and testifies that this one emerges from the former, which undermines the liberty of the Gospel, and at the same time he censures the inconstancy of those legal teachers, as if he were saying: The Pseudo-Apostles are clearly consistent with themselves: They seek righteousness before God from the observation of the law, and meanwhile they themselves do not keep the law at all, not only because they cannot keep that moral law of the Decalogue (which they have in common with other men) but also because, at their pleasure, they either observe or neglect the ceremonial laws, as they wish, and for as long as they wish. Whence it is clear that they do not seriously pursue that cause, but aim at this, that they may approve themselves to men, that they may avoid dangers, that they may have as many followers of their doctrines as possible, that they may establish their own reputation among men, and on the other hand, that they may undermine the authority of the true Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ περιτεμνόμενοι αὐτοὶ νόμον φυλάσσουσιν) Non tanto tenentur studio legis, ut omnia ejus praecepta exaete observent, facile inveniunt excusationes.

Vide, quae diximus Matth. XXIII. 4. & supra V. 3. Ἀλλὰ θέλουσιν ὑμᾶς περιτέμνεσθαι) Volunt, id est, in id laborant. Μετωνυμία. Manuscriptus eodem sensu, ἁμαρτύλονται. Ἵνα ἐν τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ σαρκὶ καυχήσωνται) Ut exultent ex vestro metu carnali, ut veltra inconstantia, in ferendis incommodis, ipsis honori cedat apud Judaeos.

Pseudo-Apostoli urgebant necessitatem servandae circumcisionis & universae legis: imo circumcisioni praetexebant legis observationem: nec tamen ipsi legem aut servabant, aut servare poterant, quod de Judaeis pariter dicitur Aa. VII. 53. Id autem quaerebant imprimis, cum gentiles circumcidi vellent, ut apud Judaeos de extorta circumcisione, vel quod suo ministerio gentes circumcisae sint glorirentur, quod nempe male institutos a Paulo Galatas emendarint, & ad circumcisionem & legis observationem perduxerint.

Non ergo pietatis studio, sed vana gloriae cupiditate agebant id, ut haec recte accepere Chrysostomus & Theophylactus. Oblique, inquit B. Hunnius in hunc locum, alterum errorem de legali justitia perstringit, & hunc ex priore, qui libertatem Evangelii labefactat, emergere testatur, simulque taxat legalium istorum Doctorum inconstantiam, ac si dicat: Egregie scilicet constant sibi Pseudo-Apostoli: Ex observatione legis captant justitiam coram Deo, atque interim ipsimet minime legem servant, non modo, quia moralem illam Decalogi legem servare nequeunt (quod commune habent cum caeteris hominibus) sed etiam, quia pro lubitu ceremoniales leges, quas volunt, & quamdiu volunt, vel observant, vel negligunt. Unde liquet, eos causam istam non agere serio, sed hoc spectare, ut sese hominibus approbent, ut pericula declinent, ut quamplurimos habeant dogmatum suorum asseclas, ut suam apud homines existimationem stabiliant, & econtra vervorum Apostolorum autoritatem labefactent.

## 6:14
Ver. 14. But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ) It is mine to rejoice, not that, by changing something, I may avoid the inconveniences of the doctrine, but that, for the sake of defending the doctrine, I may bravely suffer all things: the same sense is in 2 Cor.

XI. 30. & XII. 5. 9. add those things which are in Phil. I. 29. Therefore the world is crucified to me) Those customs of men, serving the world, I despise, just as those crucified are wont to be despised by those standing by.

See Matt. XXVII. 39. And I to the world) I in turn am despised by them. What is this that Grotius brings in, that Paul was a man not much accustomed to write in Greek?

Did he not write from divine inspiration? Thus indeed his writings would not be 'theopneusta' (God-breathed), and therefore not canonical. Impious. I say nothing of the fact that the Apostle was well instructed in all literature. Therefore he testifies that he was compelled by the affection of love to this autograph of such a long epistle, and he wished that from this the Galatians might understand how much he esteemed them, with what love he embraced them, and that they might not doubt that this was in all things his mind, which, had they not read it in his own hand, the adversaries of the Apostle could easily have cast a scruple upon them, which has also been noted by Chrysostom and Theophylactus.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἐμοὶ δὲ μὴ γένοιτο καυχήσασθαι, εἰ μὴ ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Meum est gaudere, non quod, mutando aliquid, doctrina incommoda defugiam, sed quod, ob doctrinam tuendam, omnia fortiter patiar: idem sensus 2. Cor.

XI. 30. & XII. 5. 9. adde ea, quae Philipp. I. 29. Διὸ ἐμοὶ ὁ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται) Mores illos hominum, mundo servientium, ego defpicio, quomodo cruciarii ab adflantibus despici solent.

Vide Matth. XXVII. 39. Κἀγὼ τῷ κόσμῳ) Ego vicissim ab illis defpicior. Quid hoc est, quod ingerat Grotius, Paulum hominem fuisse non multum assuetum Grace scribere?

Annon scribebat ex inspiratione divina? Sic vero scripta ejus non forent θεόπνευστα, ideoque nec Canonica. Ἀσεβές. Taceo, quod in omni literatura probe institutus fuerit Apostolus. Ad ἰδιογραφίαν itaque talis prolixae epistolae se charitatis affectu compulsum testatur, & voluit, ut ex eo intelligerent Galatae, quam eos aestimet, quo amore eos complecteretur, neque dubitarent, eam per omnia esse mentem suam, quam manu ipsius propria nisi legissent, scrupulum ipsis injicere facile adversarii Apostoli potuissent, quod Chrysostomo & Theophylacto etiam notatum.

## 6:15
Verf. 15. "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation." "Neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation," some of the ancients say was written in a book named *The Apocalypse of Moses*: and in the same words this passage is read in a manuscript: perhaps that book was written by some Christian. For *kainē ktisis* (new creation) is a Christian expression, as can be seen in 2 Cor. 5:17, although the thing itself was predicted in Isa. 42:9, and signifies the state of the new man, of whom Paul speaks in Col. 3:10, Eph. 2:15, Rom. 6:4. The sense of this sentence is the same as that above in verse 6.

The Apostle opposes his own solid boasting to the vain boasting of the Pseudo-Apostles, and explains in what he desires uniquely to boast, in such a way that he repeats the theme of his discourse and all those things which he had treated here through a brief summary and *anakephalaiōsis* (recapitulation), and impresses them anew upon the minds of his readers: which was THE CROSS OF CHRIST. "But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." He asserted this glory among the Corinthians against Jews and Gentiles alike, since to the former the cross of Christ was a stumbling block, and to the latter foolishness, 1 Cor. 1 and 2. He asserts this among the Galatians against the Pseudo-Apostles, who were emptying the cross of Christ while they wished to be justified by the law (Gal. 5:4, ch. 2:21). To boast in the cross of Christ is to acknowledge and celebrate the grace of Christ obtained by the cross, and to seek in Christ’s passion and merit the glory which we can find in ourselves in no way (Rom. 3:23); and to rely upon the same before the very tribunal of God, and indeed uniquely so, in such a way that we trust that we can stand, be justified, and be saved before God only through the meritorious satisfaction or the passive obedience of Christ. This was the argument of the Apostolic discourse. Therefore, he does not understand the cross which he himself was bearing for Christ’s sake, but that which Christ bore for our sake, because he lived solely by faith in the Son of God, whom he believed was delivered up for him (Gal. 2:20). "What is it," says Chrysostom, "that he boasts of the cross of Christ? That Christ for my sake took the form of a servant, and for my sake endured what He suffered; for me, I say, who was a servant, who was an enemy, who was ungrateful, yet He loved me so as to expose Himself. What can be equated to this?" Theophylact says: "To them, circumcision is a matter of glory, a thing truly superfluous, just as it is now obsolete and dead. But far be it from me to boast in worldly things. Let it be permitted, however, to boast in the one cross and death of Christ Jesus, which renders the custom of circumcision empty." When he says "far be it," he tacitly detests circumcision as forbidden, to escape which he invoked the help of God. Someone will ask, in what way does one boast in the Lord’s cross? Namely, because for my sake (who was of no use to You), He was affixed to the cross, and embraced me with such love that He offered Himself to death. Why, therefore, did it redound to the glory of Paul and of every believer? Because the Lord’s love toward us was revealed. For who, being a servant, would not consider the benevolence of his master toward him a glory? Thus also the Blessed Hunnius, as well as Flacius and others of our own. The Apostle adds: "Through whom the world has been crucified to me." By "world" he understands the sins with which the whole world outside of Christ is filled (Gal. 1:4), which are crucified in Christ, inasmuch as He who bore our sins in His own body on the wood of the cross (1 Pet. 2:24), which bearing of our sins, crucifixion, and mortification he receives by true faith as having been done for him; and therefore, he says, the world is crucified TO ME through Christ; because he applied the meritorious satisfaction of Christ to himself through faith, as he had professed above: "Christ loved me and gave Himself for me" (ch. 2:20). To which contributes what the Blessed Luther compares here in his former Commentary to the passage in ch. 2:19. To be crucified to the world is (as he said above in ch. 2) that now it is not he himself, but Christ living in him, and that which in ch. 1:4 Christ is said to have rescued us from the present evil age.

He explains "crucified" with Pareus in this way: He says that all things which are specious and great in the world are made as if dead to him, so that he no longer cares for, loves, or fears and abominates them any more than a criminal’s corpse justly affixed to a cross: or they have no more power to move his soul than if all things were utterly extinguished and hanging from a cross: but you could more rightly refer this to the other member: *kagō tō kosmō* (and I to the world) have been crucified or died: For we die to the world when we crucify and mortify our sins, just as we are said to die to sin and live to God (Rom. 6:11) and "having died to sins" (1 Pet. 2:24), which is the consequence of the crucifixion of the world and sin having been accomplished on the cross of Christ and applied to us through faith. But in order that we may thus die to the world and sin, it is necessary that we abominate what the world loves. Therefore, it can also be noted here what the Blessed Luther noted on Gal. 2:19. The Blessed Augustine, in *De Trinitate*, lib. III, c. IV, teaches that the passion of Christ is both a sacrament and an example: A sacrament, because it signifies and grants to believers the death of sin in us: An example, because it behooves us also to imitate Him by suffering and dying. He says he is crucified to Christ according to the sacrament, because it has mortified sin and consciences, and because, as he elegantly said on Gal. 2:19: "Just as Christ Himself was crucified to the law, to sin, to death, and to the Devil, so that they have no more right over Him: but TO ME THEY ARE CRUCIFIED AND DEAD." Which he observed in the same place is not to be understood of the imitation or example of crucifixion, but of that sublime crucifixion by which sin, the Devil, and death are crucified in Christ, not in me. Concerning which we have spoken more copiously in that same place.

And the following sentence, subjoined here by way of reason, confirms this sense. "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but a new creature," that is, faith, which is effective through love, as he had said in ch. 5:6. For through regeneration, faith is produced in us, which is not idle, but active through love: and thus there is need of faith and love for *kainēn ktisin*, a new creature. Beautifully, the Blessed Luther: "A new creature is the work of the Holy Spirit, who purifies the heart by faith, and effects the fear of God, love, chastity, etc., and grants the power of subduing the flesh and fleeing the justice and wisdom of the world: For where the heart conceives new light, new judgment, and new motions through the Gospel, it happens that the external senses also are renewed. For the ears desire to hear the word of God, no longer human imitations and dreams. The mouth and tongue do not boast of their own works, justices, and rules, but with joy preach only the mercy of God exhibited in Christ, etc." These are changes, if I may say so, not verbal but real, which bring about a new mind, a new will, new senses, and new actions. Paul, the Blessed Luther had said a little before (fol. 159), by these two, circumcision and uncircumcision, excludes simply all things that are in the whole nature of things, and denies that they avail anything in Christ Jesus, that is, in the cause of faith and salvation. For he takes by synecdoche the part for the whole, that is, by uncircumcision he understands all the Gentiles, by circumcision all the Jews, with all their powers and all their glory, as if he were saying: Whatever the Gentiles can perform with all their wisdom, justice, laws, power, kingdoms, and empires, avails nothing in Christ Jesus. Likewise: Whatever all the Jews are and can do, with all their Moses, law, and circumcision, worship, temple, kingdom, and priesthood, avails absolutely nothing. Wherefore, in Christ Jesus, or in the cause of justification, one must not dispute about the laws of the Gentiles or the Jews, whether the ceremonial or moral law. bad justifications: but simply that negative must be posited: In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision. Are the laws therefore evil? No. Indeed they are good and useful, but according to order and place, that is, in bodily and civil matters, which cannot be administered without laws. Next, we observe in the Churches also certain ceremonies and laws, not because that observance avails for justification, but for good order, example, tranquility, and concord, according to that: Let all things be done decently and according to order. But if laws are so proposed and demanded that, being kept, they justify, and being omitted, they condemn, they must be utterly abrogated and removed. Because Christ loses His office and glory, who alone justifies, administers the Spirit, etc. Paul therefore in these words most clearly affirms that neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature, etc. But since neither the laws of the Gentiles nor of the Jews avail anything at all in Christ, the Pope acts most impiously, because he compelled us to keep his laws with the opinion of justification. The passage of Isaiah XLII. 9. is neither proper to the present cause, nor does it teach that a new creation had place before Christ, which Grotius intends. Confer what is said on that passage in the Illustrious Bible of the Old Testament. If anyone, against that which he says, that he glories only in the cross of Christ, objects that the Apostle also glories everywhere in other things: in the gratuitousness of his preaching, concerning which he says: I would rather die, than that anyone should make my glorying void. In the testimony of his conscience, concerning which he says: This is our glorying, the testimony of a good conscience, that with simplicity we have behaved ourselves among you: In his revelations, when he says: of this I will glory, etc. Jerome rightly answers that all that glorying, referred to the cross of Christ, is the glory of the cross. For the whole ministry of the Apostle was concerning the cross of Christ, as Pareus [notes] here.

Latin:

Verf. 15. Ἐν γὰρ χρισῷ Ἰησ. ὅτε περιτομὴ τί ἰσχύει, ὅτε ἀ-κροβυσία, ἀλλὰ καινὴ κτίσις; Oυτε περιτομὴ τί ἐσι, ὅτε ἀ-κροβυσία, ἀλλὰ καινὴ κτίσις, dicunt veterum quidam fcriptum fuiffe in libro, cui nomen ἀποκαλυψις Μωσέας: Et iisdem verbis locus hic legitur in manufcripto: forte is liber ab aliquo Chriftiano fcriptus fuerit. Nam καινὴ κτίσις eft loquutio Chriftiana, ut videre eft 2. Cor. 17. quanquam res ipfa prædicta Efa. XLII. 9. fignificatque ftatum novi hominis, de quo Paulus Col. III. 10. Eph. II. 15. Rom. VI. 4. fenfus hujus fententiæ idem, qui fupra V. 6.

Vana gloriationi Pseudo-Apoftolorum folidam fuam gloriationem opponit Apoftolus, & in quo unice gloriari cupiat, exponit, ita, ut thema tractationis, & ea omnia, quæ hic egerat, per brevem complexionem & ἀνακεφαλαιωσιν repetat, denuoque mentibus legentium imprimat: Quod erat CRUX CHRISTI. Ame vero abfit gloriari, ei μὴ nifi in cruce Domini noftri Jefu Chrifti. Hanc gloriam adferuit apud Corinthios adverfus Judæos pariter & gentiles, quum illis crux Chrifti effet fcandalum, his vero ftultitia, 1. Cor. I. & II. Hanc afferit penes Galatas adverfus Pseudo-Apoftolos, qui crucem Chrifti evacuabant, dum per legem juftificari volebant Gal. V. 4. c. II. 21. Gloriari in cruce Chrifti, eft agnofcere ac celebrare gratiam Chrifti cruce partam, ac gloriam, quam in nobis nullam invenire poffumus, Rom. III. 23. in Chrifti paffione ac merito quærere; eodemque coram ipfius Dei tribunali niti, & quidem unice, ità, ut non nifi Chrifti satisfactione meritoria, vel obedientia & pafliva nos coram Deo confistere, juftificari, & falvari poffe confidamus. Quod argumentum fuit tractationis Apoftolicæ. Non ergo crucem intelligit, quam Chrifti caufa ipfe fuftinebat, fed quam Chriftus noftra caufa fuftinuit, quia vivebat unice fide filii Dei, quem pro fe traditum credebat Gal. II. 20. Quid eft, inquit Chryfoftomus, quod de cruce Chrifti gloriatur? Quod Chriftus mei caufa formam fervi accepit, & mea caufa, quæ paffus eft, pertulit, propter me inquam, qui fervus eram, qui inimicus, qui ingratus, fed me dilexit, ut feipfum exponeret. Quid huic poffit æquiparari? Theophylactus, illi, inquit, circumcifionem hanc gloriæ ducunt rem fane fupervacaneam, perinde ac obfolesam jam & defiram. A me vero procul fit cæterum rerum jactantia. Liceat tamen in una Chrifti Jefu cruce & morte admodum gloriari, qui inanem reddit circumcidendi confuetudinem. Cum autem abfit dicit, tacite circumcifionem ut vetitam detestatur, quam ut effugeret, Dei opem afcivit. Quæret aliquis, quo pacto gloriarius in Domine cruce? Nempe quia mei ob gratiam, (qui nulli tei fum ufus) ille fit cruci affixus, & me tanta fit charitate complexus, ut morti feipfum obtulerit. Cur itaque in Pauli gloriam & fidelis cujusque conceffit? Quia Domini fit charitas erga nos patefacta. Quis enim qui fervus cum fit, non gloriæ duxerit heri in fe benevolentiam? Sic etiam B. Hunnius ut & Flacius, aliique è noftris. Addit Apoftolus: Per quem mundus mihi crucifixus eft. Per mundum intelligit peccata, quibus repletus totus mundas extra Chriftum Gal. I. 4. quæ crucifixa funt in Chrifto, utpote, qui peccata noftra portavit in fuo corpore in lignum crucis 1. Pet. II. 24. quam peccatorum fuorum portationem, crucifixionem & mortificationem ceu fibi factam vera fide fufcipit, ideog; mundus, inquit, per Chriftum MIHI crucifixus eft; quia meritariam Chrifti satisfactionem fibi applicabat per fidem, ut profeffus fupra erat: Chriftus me dilexit, & dedit femetipfum pro me, cap. II. 20. Quo facit, quod B. Luth. hic confert in priori Comm. locum cap. II. 19. Effe crucifixum mundo eft, (ut fupra cap. II. dixit) jam non ipfum, fed Chriftum in ipfo vivere, & quod cap. I. 4. Chriftus nos dicit-

tur eripuiffe à præfenti feculo nequam. Cruciat explicat cum Pareo hoc modo: Dicit omnia, quæ in mundo fpeciofa & magna, fibi facta quafimortua, ut non magis curet, amet, non magis exhorrefcat & abominetur, quam fcelerati cadaver ex justa causa cruci affixum: vel non plus habeant virium ad animum fuum commovendum, quam fi omnia penitus extincta de cruce penderent: fed hoc ad alterum membrum rectius referre poffis: κἀγὼ τῷ κόσμῳ & ego mundo crucifixus vel mortuus fum: Morimur enim mundo, cum crucifigimus & mortificamus peccata, quemadmodum nos peccato mori dicimur, & vivere Deo Rom. VI. 11. & ἀπογενόμενοι ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις 1. Pet. II. 24. quod confequens eft crucifixionis mundi & peccati in cruce Chrifti factæ, nobisque per fidem applicatæ. Ut autem ita moriamur mundo & peccato, opus eft, ut quæ mundus amat, nos abominemur. Notari ergo & hic poteft, quod ad Gal. II. 19. B. Lutherus ex Auguftino notavit. B. Auguftinus lib. III. de Trinit. c. IV. paffionem Chrifti effe & sacramentum & exemplum docet: Sacramentum, quod fignificet & credentibus donet mortem peccati in nobis: Exemplum, quod & nos eum imitari oportet patiendo, moriendoque. Crucifixum fe dicit Chrifto juxta sacramentum, quod peccatum & conscientias mortificaverit, & quod ad Gal. II. 19. eleganter dixit: Sicut Chriftus ipfe legi, peccato, morti, Diabolo crucifixus eft, ut nullum jus in eum amplius habeant: fed MIHI CRUCIFIXA ET MORTUA funt: Quod obfervavit ibidem non de crucifixionis imitationis feu exempli intelligendum effe, fed de illa fublimi crucifixionis, qua peccatum, Diabolus, mors crucifigitur in Chrifto, non in me. Quo de ibidem diximus copiofius.

Atque hunc fenfum firmat fubfequens fententia, per modum rationis hic fubjuncta. In Chrifto Jefu enim neque circumcifio, neque præputium aliquid valet, fed nova creatura, hoc eft, fides, quæ per charitatem efficax eft, ut cap. V. 6. dixerat. Nam per regenerationem fides in nobis producitur, quæ non otiofa eft, fed operofa per charitatem: atque ita fide & charitate opus eft ad καινὴν κτίσιν novam creaturam. Pulchre B. Lutherus: Nova creatura eft opus Spiritus S. qui fide purificat cor, & efficit timorem Dei, charitatem, castitatem &c. ac donat virtutem domande carnu, & fugiende justitiæ ac sapientia mundi: Nam ubi cor novam lucem, novum judicium, & novos motus per Evangelium concipit, fit ut externi quoque fenfus innoventur. Aures enim verbum Dei, non amplius immitationes & fomnia humana geftiunt audire. Os & lingua non fua opera, justitias & regulam jactant, fed folam mifericordiam Dei in Chrifto exhibitam cum gaudio prædicant &c. He funt mutationes, ut fic dicam, non verbales, fed reales, quæ affirunt novam mentem, voluntatem, novos fenfus & actiones. Paulus, dixerat paulo ante B. Lutherus fol. 159. per ifta duo circumcifionem & præputium, excludit fimpliciter omnia, quæ in tota rerum natura funt, negatque ea valere in Chrifto Jefu, hoc eft, in caufa fidei & falutis. Accipit enim per Synecdochen partem pro toto, hoc eft, per præputium intelligit omnes gentes, per circumcifionem omnes Judæos, cum tota viribus & omni gloria fua, quafi dicat: Quicquid gentes præstare poffunt cum omni fua sapientia, justitia, legibus, potentia, regnis, imperiis, nihil valet in Chrifto Jefu. Item: Quicquid funt & poffunt omnes Judæi, cum toto fuo Mofe lege & circumcifione, cultu, templo, regno, facerdotio, nihil prorfus valet. Quare in Chrifto Jefu, feu in caufa justificationis non eft disputandum de legibus gentium vel Judæorum, num lex ceremonialis aut moralis malus justifices: sed simpliciter illa negativa ponenda est: In Christo Jesu neque circumcisio aliquid valet, neque præputium. Ergo leges malæ sunt? Non. Imò bonæ & utiles sunt, sed pro ordine & loco, hoc est, in rebus corporalibus & civilibus, quæ fine legibus non possunt administrari. Deinde observamus in Ecclesiis, etiam quasdam ceremonias & leges, non quod illa observatio valeat ad justitiam, sed ad bonum ordinem, exemplum, tranquillitatem & concordiam, juxta illud: Omnia decenter & secundum ordinem fiant. Si autem leges ita proponuntur & exiguntur, quod servate justificent, & omissæ damnent, prorsus abrogandæ & tollendæ sunt. Quia Christus amittit officium & gloriam suam, qui solus justificat, subministrat Spiritum &c. Paulus igitur his verbis clarissime affirmat, neque circumcisionem aliquid valere, neque præputium, sed novam creaturam &c. Cum autem in Christo nihil prorsus valeant neque leges gentium, neque Judæorum, impiissime agit Papa, quod nos coëgit servare leges suas cum opinione justitiæ. Locus Esaiæ XLII. 9. nec præsenti causæ proprius est, nec docet ante Christum novam creationem, quod intendit Grotius, locum habuisse. Confer quæ ad locum illum in Bibl. Illustr. V. T. dicta. Si quis contra illud, quod dicit, se in sola Christi cruce gloriari, objiciat, Apostolum, etiam in aliis rebus, passim gloriari: in gratuita sui prædicatione, de qua dicit: Moriar potius, quam ut aliquam gloriationem meam quis inanem reddat. In testimonio conscientiæ suæ, de quo dicit: Gloriatio nostra hæc est, testimonium bonæ conscientiæ, quod cum simplicitate conversati sumus inter vos: In revelationibus suis, cum dicit: de hoc gloriabor &c. Recte Hieronymus respondet, quod omnis illa gloriatio ad crucem Christi relata, sit gloria crucis. Totum enim Apostoli ministerium erat de cruce Christi, ut hic Pareus.

## 6:16
Verse 16. And as many as shall walk by this rule, peace be on them and mercy. In the manuscript [we have] στοιχοῦσι, concerning which word see what [is said] above [in] verse 25; we have the locution στοιχοῦσι and Phil. III. 16.

Thus in Micah VII. 4 we read in the Greek: he who walks by a rule. A rule is called here the way, which is made according to a rule, that is, plainly straight, to the rigor, as the lesser ones say. Such is the way of those new creations, peace and mercy, that is, happiness, all things by God favoring.

Thus we have grace and peace conjoined [in] 1 Cor. I. 3, 2 Cor. I. 2, Eph. I. 2, Col. I. 2, 1 Thess. I. 1; grace, mercy, peace, 1 Tim. I. 2, 2 Tim. I. 2. And upon the Israel of God) As if he were to say, I do not so wish these things for the Gentiles, that I exclude the Israelites, provided that the same also be true Israelites before God, that is, spiritual imitators of Jacob, as it were conquering God with prayers, exercised by evils, as Jacob was. See John I. 47, Rom. IX. 6. Note Israel with the article, how [it is] את ישראל, Psalm XXV. 22. A rule is not a way made to a rule, but a divine rule of our walking. To walk by a rule therefore is to walk according to a rule. The metaphor is taken from architects, who use a rule, so that all things may follow in a right order. Such a rule is prescribed here, which he comprehends in the following aphorism: what avails in Christ, and the doctrine which he has embraced in the whole epistle, which is succinctly contained in that aphorism. And so the epistle, and similarly the whole scripture. For the same is the reason of all God-breathed scriptures. The rule for us is both of believing and of living, which he has prescribed both in this epistle, and has here epitomized. Whence Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 69, called scripture the unbending rule of truth. By the name of peace and mercy are comprehended all things that can be wished for. For peace denotes happiness and salvation of every kind, or peace with God, concerning which the Apostle [speaks in] Rom. V. 1, which he who has, is truly blessed: But mercy denotes the grace of God, which is the fountain and origin of salvation. By Ishmael of God [he means] those who are Israelites according to the spirit, so that they do not descend from Israel. The particle and is not conjunctive, but exegetical. For these are not that Israel of God, who show off carnal propagation, and boast in the circumcision of the flesh, but who walk according to the holy rule. To whom he wishes peace and tranquility, and the grace of God exhibited to those believing in Christ. He commits the Jews and the incredulous, who either prescribe or observe an adulterous rule, to the judgment of God. The Israel of God, says Theodoret, he called the faithful, as those who see God through faith. Theophylact observes that that [phrase] peace upon the Israel of God [was] taken from David, Psalm CXXVIII. 6. He concludes, as Flacius says, this exhortation and even the whole epistle and this doctrine concerning gratuitous justification and adoption, and concerning defending Christian liberty, with a most beautiful promise, that those following this doctrine may obtain the peace and mercy of God, and be of the number of that true Israel, which is generated by faith from Abraham the father apprehending the gratuitous promise, either by carnal propagation, or even by their own works and observations of the law: which clause, as it were a seal affixed to this epistle of Paul, and convenient to the whole scripture with that placed at the beginning, if anyone shall have preached another Gospel, etc., should be most diligently observed. Vers.

17. The rest) that is, henceforth.

He uses [it] thus [in] Demosth. Let no one cause me trouble) Let them abstain, I pray, from vexing me, who wish to be called Christians. I have enough from elsewhere, which I may bear. For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body) Those new teachers are circumcised. I also am, but I esteem this as nothing compared to the more certain marks of my faith in Christ, that is, the welts and scars from those blows, stonings, and beatings, of which he makes mention in 2 Cor. XI. 23, 24. 25. Moreover, he took the similitude from soldiers, who were marked with points that would last in the skin, as we said [in] Apoc. XIII. 16, where we also showed that the word στίγματα is taken in that sense from Aelian. Chrysostom says this was said to press their careless spirit, and to cast them into greater terror, and not to allow them always to waver. It is the final admonition, according to Flacius, by which he both warns the Galatians themselves, that being content with this solid instruction, they may return to the truth, nor suffer themselves to be deceived any longer, and also the Pseudo-Apostles themselves, that they may cease to calumniate him. He adds indeed the reason, because he himself bears those marks of Christ in his body, from which it can be clearly recognized that he is a faithful servant of Christ, and that he handles and delivers his sound and salutary doctrine sincerely. Moreover, this metaphor is taken from slaves, whom masters formerly used to mark with certain signs, whence they might be recognized. Theophylact: I have (he says) in place of an excuse among those who accuse me of hypocrisy, and say that elsewhere I preached and established this circumcision, the very marks and distinctions, which I undertook fearlessly for the sake of Christ's grace.
