For these testify more clearly than any voice, how I have exposed myself to dangers not at all for the law, but for the doctrine that is according to Christ. And he did not say, I have, but I carry, just as if I raise aloft some trophy and royal insignia higher and visible to all, and I glory in such things. He calls the bonds, prisons, scars of blows, stigmata, as it were infamous marks, such as were burned onto barbarian, fugitive, and criminal slaves for disgrace. From which it seems to be gathered that this epistle was written from Rome, from bonds. Recalling to memory, says Theodoret, the labors which he undertook, while he preached the divine Gospel to them, he burst into this word as it were a certain testimony. No longer, he says, shall I bring myself to write to you, but instead of letters I will show welts, and the signs of blows, which will bear testimony to the preaching of the truth. For for it I bring myself to endure all things. Concerning the stigmata of Francis and other fables, Crocius can be read here.

ANNOTATIONS ON GALATIANS CH. VI. v. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσιν, εἰρήνη ἐπ' αὐτοὺς καὶ ἔλεος. In manuscripto στοιχοῦσι, de qua voce vide quæ supra V. 25. locutionem σε στοιχοῦσι habemus & Phil. III. 16.

Sic Michæ VII. 4. in Græco legimus: ὁ βαδίζων ἐπὶ κανόνι. Κανὼν hic dicitur via, quæ ad regulam facta, id est, plane recta, ad rigorem, ut dicunt minores. Talis est via illæ novæ creationis, pax & misericordia, id est, felicitas omnia à Deo favente.

Sic χάρις & εἰρήνη conjuncta habemus 1. Cor. I. 3. 2. Cor. I. 2. Eph. I. 2. Col. I. 2. 1. Thess. I. 1. χάρις, ἔλεος, εἰρήνη, 1. Tim. I. 2. Tim. I. 2. Καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰσραὴλ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Quasi dicat, non ita hæc opto gentibus, ut Israelitas excludam, dummodo iidem etiam veri apud Deum sint Israelitæ, id est, spirituales Jacobi imitatores, precibus Deum quasi vincentes, malis, ut Jacobus, exerciti. Vide Joh. I. 47. Rom. IX. 6. Nota τὸν Ἰσραὴλ cum articulo, quomodo את ישראל, Psal. XXV. 22. Κανὼν non est via ad regulam facta, sed regula incessus nostri divina. Τῷ κανόνι στοιχεῖν ergo est secundum regulam incedere. Metaphora ab architectis petita est, quæ regula utuntur, ut omnia recto ordine se consequantur. Talis regula hic est præscripta, quam sequenti aphorismo comprehendit: quod in Christo valeat, & doctrina, quam tota epistola complexus est, quæ isto aphorismo succincte continetur. Itaque epistola, ac similiter scriptura tota. Eadem enim omnium scriptorum θεοπνεύστων est ratio. Regula nobis est cum credendi, tum vivendi, quod utrumque præscriptit in hac epistola, & hic ἐπιτομικῶς complexus est. Unde scripturam τὸν κανόνα τῆς ἀληθείας ἀκλινῆ vocavit Irenæus lib. IV. cap. 69. Pacis & misericordiæ nomine comprehenduntur omnia, quæ voveri possunt. Pax enim felicitatem & salutem omnigenam, aut pacem cum Deo, de qua Apostolus Rom. V. 1. quam qui habet, verè beatus est: Misericordia vero gratiam Dei, quæ fons est, & origo salutis, notat. Per Ismelem Dei eos, qui sunt Israelitæ secundum spiritum, ut ab Israele non descendant. Particula καὶ non conjunctiva est, sed exegetica. Neque enim hi sunt Israel ille Dei, qui carnalem propagiam ostentant, & carnis circumcisione se jactant, sed qui juxta regulam sanctam incedunt. Quibus pacem & tranquillitatem, & gratiam Dei in Christum credentibus exhibitam vovet. Judæos & incredulos adulterinam regulam vel præscribentes vel observantes judicio Dei committit. Israel Dei, inquit Theodoretus, appellavit fideles, ut qui Deum per fidem videant. Theophylactus observat, illud pax super Israel Dei à Davide desumptum Psal. CXXVIII. 6. Claudit, dicente Flacio, hanc adhortationem atque adeo totam epistolam & doctrinam hanc de gratuita justificatione ac adoptione, deque tuenda libertate Christiana, pulcherrima promissione, quod sequentes hanc doctrinam pacem & misericordiam Dei consequantur, sintque futuri de numero illius veri Israelis, qui fide gratuitam promissionem ex apprehendente Abrahamo patre genemtur, vel carnali propagatione, vel etiam suis operibus ac legis observationibus: quæ clausula ac veluti sigillum appensum huic epistolæ Pauli, totique scripturæ conveniens cum illa initio posita, si quis aliud Evangelium prædicaverit &c. diligentissime observetur. Vers.

17. Τὸ λοιπὸν) id est, posthac.

Utitur sic Demosth. Κόπος μοι μηδεὶς παρέχηται) Abstineant quæso me vexare ii, qui Christiani dici volunt. Satis aliunde habeo, quod feram. Ἐγὼ γὰρ τὰ στίγματα τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματί μου βαστάζω) Circumcisi sunt isti novi Doctores. Sum & ego, sed hoc nihili æstimo præ certioribus meæ in Christum fidei notis, id est, vibicibus, ac cicatricibus ex plagis illis, lapidationibus & verberibus, quorum meminit 2. Cor. XI. 23. 24. 25. Similitudinem autem sumpsit à militibus, qui victuris in cute punctis signabantur, ut diximus Apoc. XIII. 16. ubi & vocem στίγματα eo sensu ab Æliano sumi ostendimus. Chrysostomus hoc dictum ait, ut illorum socordem animum premat, & in majorem conjiciat terrorem, nec sinat ipsos semper vacillare. Ultima admonitio est, secundum Flacium, qua tum ipsos Galatas monet, ut hac solida instructione contenti, ad veritatem redeant, nec se amplius decipi patiantur, tum etiam ipsos Pseudo-Apostolos, ut desinant se calumniari. Addit vero rationem, quia ea stigmata Christi ipse circumferat in corpore suo, ex quibus liquido agnosci possit, quod sit fidelis Christi servus, sanamque ejus ac salutarem doctrinam sinere tractet, tradatque. Sumpta autem est hæc metaphora à servis, quos olim heri fui solebant certis quibusdam signis notare, unde agnoscerent. Theophylactus: Excusationis (inquit) habeo loco apud eos, qui me hypocrisis criminantur, & dicunt, alibi me circumcisionem banc prædicaffe & adstruxisse, stigmata ipsa & discrimina, qua Christi ob gratiam obii intrepide. Hæc namque vel voce quavis clarius testificantur, quemadmodum nequaquam pro lege, sed pro eo, quod secundum Christum est dogmate, periculis antebas meipsum objecerim. Neque habeo dixit, sed gesto perinde scilicet ac tropæum aliquod & insigne Regium altius & cunctis videndum attollo, & in istiusmodi glorior. Stigmata autem vocat vincula, carceres, cicatrices plagarum, ceu notas scilicet infames, quales servis barbaris, fugitivis, maleficis inurebantur ad infamiam. Ex quo colligi videtur, Romæ ex vinculis scriptam esse hanc epistolam. In memoriam revocans, inquit Theodoretus, labores, quos suscepit, dum eis divinum prædicant Evangelium, in hanc vocem veluti testimonium quoddam erupit. Non amplius, inquit, ad vos scribere in animum inducam, sed pro literis vibices offendam, & plagarum signa, ea veritatis prædicationi ferent testimonium. Pro illa enim omnia perpeti in animum induco. De Francifci stigmatibus aliisque fabulis legi hic poterit Crocius.

ANNOTATA AD GALAT. 

## 6:18
(v. 18. ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί) In other epistles he says: With you all. With your Spirit, to signify that he prays especially for those things which pertain not to the comforts of the body, but to the perfection of the soul. In the same way the epistle of Barnabas ends, and the same is the locution in the Greek, Latin, and other liturgies. (Final Votum) A final votum, in which he wishes that that grace might as it were cohabit, and fill them, illuminate, comfort, rule, and bless them for all eternity, namely the grace of reconciliation, justification, sanctification, and glorification.

But when he prays for good things for them, he shows, as Theophylact warns, that he did not speak out of anger or hatred, which is lacking, nor does it hold the place of a prayer, but of instruction and doctrine, which concludes and terminates all that has been said. He notes the same, that grace is commemorated, by which they who had believed would obtain, not by the law but by the gift of Christ. He notes, that he said, not with you, but with your spirit, because they had received the Spirit not from the law, but from grace. By Spirit the Apostle understands not the mind, not the Holy Spirit, but that faculty which the Holy Spirit had granted to them: just as Chrysostom warns, that Spirit is named, so that it might call them away from carnal things, and he says that this very prayer together with the doctrine serves them in the place of a double wall. For both the doctrine reminding them how great goods they had received, contains them more in the dogmas of the Church, and the prayer invoking grace, does not let the Spirit depart from them. But we conclude at last this epistle, with the Apostolic votum repeated: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, Amen!

To Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever and ever AMEN!

Latin:

(Vers. 18. ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί) In aliis epistolis dicit: Μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Μετὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ut significet, se ea præcipue precari, quæ ad corporis commoda, sed ad animi perfectionem pertinent. Eodem modo finit epistola Barnabæ, & eadem est loqutio, in liturgia Græca, Latina & aliis. (Votum finale) Votum finale, quo optat, ut gratia illa quasi cohabitet, illosque impleat, illuminet, consoletur, regat, & in omnem æternitatem beet, gratia nempe reconciliationis, iustificationis, sanctificationis & glorificationis.

Cum autem bona illis precetur, optice, Theophylacto monente, ostendit, non ira vel odio dixisse, qui desit, neque comprecationis id obtinet locum, sed instructionis & doctrinæ, quæ dicta omnia concludat ac terminet. Notat idem, commemorari gratiam, qua non lege sed Christi munere sint, qui credidissent, potituri. Notat, quod dixerit, non vobiscum, sed cum Spiritu vestro, quod Spiritum non a lege, sed a gratia acceperint. Per Spiritum Apostolus intelligit non mentem, non Spiritum Sanctum, sed facultatem illam, quam Spiritus Sanctus illis concesserat: quemadmodum Chrysostomus monet, Spiritum nominari, ut avocet eos a carnalibus, & hanc ipsam precationem cum doctrina duplicis muri vicem illis exhibere ait. Nam & doctrina commonefaciens illos, quantum bonorum accepissent, magis continet illorum Ecclesiæ dogmatibus, & precatio gratiam invocans, non finit Spiritum ab illis discedere. Sed concludimus tandem hanc epistolam, repetito voto Apostolico: Gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi cum Spiritu vestro, Amen!

Ipsi cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto fit gloria in secula seculorum AMEN!

# Ephesians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

Latin:

ANNOTATA IN EPISTOLAM AD EPHESIOS.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
GROTIAN PREFACE.

From the first chapter of this epistle, to its second chapter, which is called the second to the Thessalonians, to the second epistle of John 18. and the following III. 9. IV. 1. and the following, and to a certain more furious explanation of the Apocalypse, we have published our annotations on the Gospels.

Those who have the leisure may consult it. We shall take from there, and from elsewhere, as much as is convenient for the manner of this treatise: Paul had sown the Church at Ephesus, as can be seen in Acts XVIII. XIX. Many digressed from there, who, while the Christians were suffering many evils, and fearing greater ones for the sake of the Gospel, persuaded them that men could both live rightly, and obtain eternal life, by following the tenets of the Philosophers, such as Heraclitus, who had been an Ephesian, or Pythagoras, who, as the Greeks note here, had many followers in Ephesus. Furthermore, there were many Jews in Ephesus, as appears from the Acts and Josephus. These also strove to translate the Christians to their rites. Therefore Paul, now old in the Apostolic office, and bound in Rome for the Gospel, shows them how great is the power of the Gospel above all doctrines: How all the counsels of God from all eternity tended to this: how admirable is the efficacy in God: equaling the sublimity of things with more sublime words than any human language ever had.

Nearest to this in both argument and words is that to the Colossians, written, if I am not mistaken, at the same time. But that the epistle to the Laodiceans was written in exactly the same tenor can be gathered from those things which Tertullian has against Marcion. For Marcion calls this epistle to the Laodiceans, from the faith, as is believed, of the Laodicean Church. For why would he lie in that matter, there was no cause. And we believe this to be the one which Paul calls τὴν Λαοδίκειας Col. IV. 16. not written by a Laodicean, but to the Laodiceans: which itself is rightly signified by the possessive case. For the letters are his, to whose messenger they were delivered, and much more so, where they were also returned.

L. if the epistle D. on the acquisition of the ownership of things. This epistle explains briefly the sum of God's benefits and the grace which we owe to Him in words and deeds. Grotius has prefaced these things in his Annotations. But from those things which he commented on at the beginning of the Pauline epistle to the Ephesians, or chapter I, those things touched upon by him here, pertain hither to the prolegomena, which are read added to the title of the Apostle. Which we shall now subjoin.

The rest likewise to each verse from that preceding explanation of the annotation, which we have at hand, for the sake of collation and examination we are about to subjoin immediately. This epistle has always been held among the excellent ones written by the Apostle, now long having fulfilled the Apostolic office, when he was in chains at Rome, to the Ephesians, the chief city of Asia, and from which city many learned men, and wise in the affairs of the age had come forth, and so he shows solicitously, how much all doctrines ought to yield before the Gospel, whose sublimity he expresses in admirable and truly Apostolic thoughts. But he ascribes the Apostolic dignity to himself both in this and in other epistles, the matter compelling it, because there were many who said that he had received the office of teaching from Peter, John, and James, and used their name, although they themselves were unwilling, so that they might impose the servitude of Jewish rites upon those who had been called from the Gentiles. But this epistle pertains especially to the refuting of the authority of those who, selling themselves under the name of foreign erudition, were for that reason called Gnostics, of which argument is also that to the Colossians, clearly akin to this, and that to Titus, both to Timothy, the second of Peter and of Jude. Paul wrote the epistle to the Laodiceans in exactly the same manner, as can be gathered from Tertullian's books against Marcion.

And that perhaps is the epistle Λαοδικείας, that is, written to the Laodiceans, of which mention is made Col. IV. 13. PROLEGOMENA TO THIS EPISTLE. These things give us occasion to preface concerning ten chapters.

First, concerning the author, Why does he call himself an Apostle of Jesus Christ here and in other epistles? That this was done from the necessity imposed by those who said that he had received the office of teaching from Peter, John, and James, and by the pretext of these wished to impose the servitude of Jewish rites upon the converted Gentiles, is not clear. Nor does he have business with them in all the epistles. Nor does the Apostle treat that argument about Jewish rites in this epistle of ours. When he deals with them, he asserts his calling more laboriously, as we saw in the nearest epistle, Gal. I. and II. It was done, however, for the sake of authority, that as a legate and Apostle of Jesus Christ he might be received with his doctrine and admonitions, and that this scripture might be venerated as canonical, as proceeding from divine inspiration, proper to the Apostles.

II. The object, or those to whom this epistle was written, the Ephesians, are converted. Ephesus, situated in Ionia, once called Trichia, and Orygia, and Ptelea, as also Solimona, is called by Pliny, book V., the second light of lesser Asia on account of the wealth of its merchandise and the frequency of its citizens.

But this city was given over especially to idolatry, and above all to the worship of Diana, whose most splendid temple was the most celebrated in the whole world, Acts XIX. 27. Then to magic, concerning which in the same place. likewise to read is verse 13, 19.

But whether Paul first sowed the Gospel there, some, as Theodoret testifies, raise a doubt, who think that the Apostle was the first to establish a church in this city. But Irenaeus attributes this to Paul in book III against heresies, ch. 3, namely that the Ephesian Church was founded by Paul, but cared for by John, who remained there until the times of Trajan.

But he first preached the Gospel there to the Jews, coming to Ephesus from Corinth, by whom he was also equally dismissed at that time. Acts 18:19.

Afterwards he arrived at Ephesus again, and there for three years he remained, first in the public synagogue of the Jews for three months, but for the rest of the time he preached the Gospel concerning the kingdom of God in the school of Tyrannus to the Jews and Gentiles, announcing to them the whole counsel of God. Acts 19:10; 20:27.

31. At which time he gathered a notable Church for Christ there. For a great door was opened to him in that same place 1 Cor. 16:9, and it pleased the divine clemency so, that although such a great Apostle remained in a city so famous and populous, even if given to idolatry and bound to the Devil, not only were many there snatched from the kingdom of Satan, but also the Gospel was disseminated far and wide throughout the world.

Into which there was a very great influx from various places on account of trade and the convenience of navigation. For Ephesus was situated on the extreme shore of Asia Minor towards the west, and almost also the south, so that it had to be passed through by those sailing from Syria or Egypt to Greece, Macedonia, and Pontus and conversely, and likewise from Asia Minor to Rome and vice versa: Just as the Apostle himself, namely setting out for Macedonia or Greece, and returning again, passed through there.

By which conveniences, without doubt, the Apostle John was moved to wish to remain there for a very long time.

To what dangers Paul was exposed there, especially on account of the tumult stirred up by Demetrius, is reported in Acts 19:23 ff., where he also had to fight with beasts 1 Cor. 15. His speech, very valedictory and full of affections, and effective with more vehement stimuli, stands described in Acts.

XX. To that Church, planted with such labor and such dangers, Paul inscribes this epistle, and in it, against the false deities which they had previously worshipped, he opposes that one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; against the riches of Diana, all the unsearchable riches of divine grace; for the magnificent temple of Diana, he adorns the structure of a spiritual temple.

III. Place III.

Place, from where this epistle was written, is commonly believed to be Rome, both from the subscription and from the commemoration of captivity and bonds. ch. 4; cf. ch. 6:20.

But Beza asserts that it seems it could have been sent from elsewhere. He brings forward no reason for his opinion, which is clearly singular. It is therefore merely precarious.

IV. Time IV.

As regards time, S. Athanasius indeed in his synopsis thinks it was written before the Apostle had come to Ephesus. But because it was written from bonds, Theodoret rightly departs from him here. Since the Apostle himself converted the Ephesians.

And the Acts of the Apostles testify that Paul had come to Ephesus in a simple capacity before he was sent to Rome. Cf. Acts 18, 19, & 27, 28.

Occasion V.

Occasion.

Grotius wishes it to have been given partly by Philosophers and partly by Judaizers. And indeed many of the Philosophers, as Chrysostom holds, were in this city. It is said also that Pythagoras came from here, which is both true, yet meanwhile all that Ionian school is from there, and indeed those who were with Parmenides, Zeno, and Democritus.

For which cause, says Chrysostom, there was indeed need of much study to write to them, but that they gave the cause for writing by their opinion concerning the method of attaining eternal life, of that there is nothing held either in Chrysostom or in other ancients, nor does any trace of that matter appear in this epistle. Perhaps Paul feared, in the judgment of Grotius, that they might be seduced by pseudo-Apostles and other impostors, who wandered here and there, even through Asia, especially in the more opulent places, just as they had seduced the Galatians not too far from them, and it appears in 1 Tim. that the Ephesian Bishop, those seducers and troublemakers, had also been there long before. 2 Tim. 1:15.

But especially the Apostle feared that the weak might be deterred on account of his bonds. Nor was he ignorant that after his departure there would arise those who would speak perverse things and seduce others, which he had predicted to them. Acts 20:30.

VI. Scope VI.

The scope therefore was: that as if warned by a brief letter, he might exhort the Ephesians to perseverance in the faith, its sum having been repeated and diligently commended to them, and he might inflame them to the pursuit of piety. Therefore he gives thanks to God for the grace granted to them, and prays for increases for them, and exhibits the chief articles of faith, and recalls them to the foundation of faith, and commends his own Apostolic office to the same end, that they might not become sluggish on account of his afflictions, he asks, and testifies that he prays for their constancy.

VII. Matter VII.

The matter of the writing as well as the sublime character of the discourse, Grotius rightly calls it, which Chrysostom also noted. It is an epistle, he says, full of sublime sentiments and dogmas. And again: For what he has spoken almost nowhere else, he says here. But it proceeds in the form of exposition, not as in the epistle to the Romans and Galatians by way of disputation.

Relationship VIII.

Grotius affirms that the epistle to the Colossians is related, but he did not explain that relationship. That, which he subjoins exhortations to dogmas, is common to it with most other epistles: yet it inculcates those pertaining to the economic state especially with this our epistle, that which was written to the Colossians. The agreement is less with this our epistle, with Titus and both to Timothy, with the second of Peter and the epistle of Jude. Grotius ought to have taught it, not simply asserted it.

But concerning a peculiar epistle written to the Laodiceans, there is no certain testimony from antiquity.

Nor does Col. 4:16 concern an epistle to the Laodiceans, or τῆς Λαοδικείας, but ἐκ τῆς Λαοδικείας, an epistle namely written from Laodicea, as is held in the Greek and Syriac text. Just as also the Latin version, by its first conception of the epistle of the Laodiceans, implies not an epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans, but one written by the Laodiceans.

Who ever called an epistle of Timothy or Titus, which the Apostle wrote to Timothy or Titus? Therefore Chrysostom and Theodoret understand an epistle from the Laodiceans, but truly and many others explain it of the first to Timothy, which is said to have been written ἀπὸ Λαοδικείας.

Bellarmine himself, when he had written in book IV on justification, ch. 4, it is certain that the epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans perished, in the recognition of his books corrected it in this way: I do not approve what I said, that it is certain that the epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans perished. For it is indeed probable that the Apostle in the epistle to the Colossians at the end speaks of his epistle written to the Laodiceans, as Anselm and some others teach in their commentary on that place, yet it is not altogether certain, because S. Chrysostom in his commentary on that place writes that some thought that the Apostle speaks of an epistle written by the Laodiceans. to him, not about the epistle written to the Laodiceans by him, and he weighs the Greek words, where it is read, and that which is from Laodicea, but not, and that which is to the Laodiceans. The commentaries of Anselm on the epistles of Paul, as noted by Bellarmine himself in his book on ecclesiastical writers for the year of Christ 1081, are more truly attributed to Herveus. But the opinion of the Greeks, Chrysostom and Theodoret, is without doubt to be preferred to the Greek, Syriac, and Latin text, which is not in agreement with the Hervean text, with which Oecumenius also agrees. And Baronius followed that, Pamelius in annotation 259 to book V of Tertullian against Marcion. Cornelius à Lapide in this place openly testifies that the epistle to the Laodiceans was exploded in antiquity, Jerome in Volume I of his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers on Paul: Some read also to the Laodiceans, but it is exploded BY ALL. Philastrius on heresies. Although, he says, it is read by some, yet the epistle written to the people at Laodicea is not read in the Church. The reason which Baronius brings against that supposed epistle to the Laodiceans is not futile: Truly, he says, it is sufficiently certain that no epistle was given by Paul to that same messenger for the Laodiceans: While in that which he then wrote to the Colossians, he commands those who were at Laodicea to be greeted, chapter IV, 16. For if he had then written to the Laodiceans, he himself would have performed such a duty by his own epistle, nor would he have had need to delegate that to the Colossians. But if Paul had written to the Laodiceans before, he would certainly have given them orders (as he just did writing to the Colossians) to hand over their letters to be read by the Colossians. The opinion of Theophylact is less probable. For how could the Colossians have gathered from the words of the Apostle that he designates the former epistle to Timothy? Nor was that approved by Baronius for the year of Christ 60, no. 12. Nor indeed did Tertullian teach that an epistle was written by Paul to the Laodiceans: But he has something far different in book V against Marcion, chapter 11. I pass over here also about another epistle, which we have written to the Ephesians, but THE HERETICS to the Laodiceans: and chapter 17, We have indeed committed that epistle to the Ephesians to the truth of the Church, not to the Laodiceans, but Marcion sometimes desired to interpolate a title onto it, as if he were also in that a most diligent explorer. Grotius therefore did not look at Tertullian here. But Epiphanius in book I, Volume III, chapter 42, against Marcion, expressly judged the epistle to the Laodiceans added to the Pauline ones to be both superfluous and outside the Apostle, not in the Apostle. Which Stapleton raises in Volume I of his defense of ecclesiastical authors, book II, chapter 2, p. 941. If the Laodiceans had written any epistle to Paul, that epistle would likely not be at Laodicea now but in the hands of Paul: this can easily be refuted if it is said that it was sent by Paul to the Colossians at the same time as that which he himself was writing to them. By which the words of Paul can also be taken, and this (namely, which I now show you at the same time) written to me from Laodicea, etc. Regarding that which Jacobus Faber Stapulensis edited, and Sixtus Senensis inserted into his Library, Sixtus himself doubts whether it is Paul's. Baronius openly rejects it: That which is circulated under the name of Paul to the Laodiceans as SPURIOUS, was by no means known by the ancients. Cornelius à Lapide on Colossians IV teaches with not bad reasons that it is the same as the supposititious one.

IX. The argument of the epistle is information about the doctrine of faith and the Christian life, a calling worthy of faith, so that they may persist in it; for its sake are explained the dogmas concerning predestination, justification, calling, concerning the exaltation of Christ to the right hand of God, vivification and salvation, the gathering of the Gentiles into the Israelite Church, and the building upon the same foundation in chapter II, and the incorporation and communion of promises, so that they may be filled with all divine fullness in chapter III. But for this cause, admonitions are instituted for concord and holiness in chapter IV, for the imitation of God and Christ, with the fleeing of sins and the proving of the divine will and the celebration of the divine name in chapter V, with a special admonition also added for spouses in the rest of chapter V, for children and parents, servants and masters, and a common exhortation that they arm themselves against diabolical insults and resist them bravely. Which Grotius has embraced succinctly.

X. There are therefore two parts. The former is dogmatic, in the three prior chapters, with the title, inscription, and prayer of Paul having been premised: The latter is parenetic, in the remaining three chapters, with the report concerning the cause of Tychicus being sent having been subjoined in verses 21, 22 of chapter VI, and the final prayer in verses 23, 24.

The Apostle carries out the former dogmatic undertaking indeed partly by a formula of thanksgiving, partly of prayers in chapters I and III, so that the information may penetrate more and be more effective: But from the very material of the Apostolic blessing and prayer, his intention and zeal clearly appear, namely that he wished to influence, confirm, and stabilize them in the faith once delivered, so that they might not allow themselves to be moved from it: concerning which he tacitly admonished the Ephesians in chapter I, 9, 15, 17, chapter II, 20, chapter III, 4, 5, 18, but expressly in chapter IV, 14.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

Ab epistolæ huius caput primum, ad secundum caput eius, quæ secunda dicitur ad Thessalonicenses, ad Johannis epistolam II. 18. & sequentibus III. 9. IV. 1. & sequentibus, & ad quædam Apocalypseos fusiorem explicationem edidimus pone annotata nostra ad Evangelia.

Eam consulere poterunt, quibus id est otii. Nos & inde, & aliunde sumemus, quantum huius tractationis modo convenit: Ephesi Ecclesiam Paulus severat, ut videre est Act. XVIII. XIX. Eo digressi multi exticere, qui Christianis multa mala ferentibus, & maiora metuentibus Evangelii causa, persuaderent, posse homines & recte vivere, & vitam æternam consequi, sequendo Philosophorum scita, puta Heracliti, qui Ephesius fuerat, aut Pythagoræ, qui ut hic Græci notant, multos habebat Epheli sectatores. Præterea multi erant Ephesi Judæi, ut ex actis & Josepho apparet. Hi quoque studebant, Christianos ad suos ritus traducere. Ideo Paulus iam vetus in Apostolico munere, & ob Evangelium Romæ vinctus, ostendit illis, quanta fit vis Evangelii præ doctrinis omnibus: Quomodo omnia Dei consilia ab omni ævo eo tetenderint: quam admiranda fit in Deo efficacia: rerum sublimitatem adæquans verbis sublimioribus, quam ulla habuit unquam lingua humana.

Proxima huic & argumento & verbis etiam est illa ad Colossenses, eodem, ni fallor, scripta tempore. Ad Laodicenses vero plane eodem tenore scriptam fuisse epistolam colligere licet ex iis, quæ Tertullianus habet adversus Marcionem. Nam Marcio vocat hanc epistolam ad Laodicenses, ex fide, ut creditie est, Ecclesiæ Laodicensis. Nam cur in ea re mentiretur, nihil erat causæ. Et hanc esse credimus, quam Paulus dicit τὴν Λαοδίκειας Coloss. IV. 16. non scriptam a Laodicense, sed ad Laodicenses: quod ipsum recte significatur casu possessivo. Nam literæ eius sunt, cuius tabellario sunt traditæ, multoq

L. si epistolam D. de acquir. rerum dominio. Exponit autem breviter hæc epistola summa Dei beneficia & gratiam, quam ei debemus verbis factisque. Hæc præfatus est Grotius in Annotatis suis. Ex iis autem, quæ in principium epistolæ Paulinæ ad Ephesios, vel caput I. commentatus est, hic ab ipso tacta, huc ad τὰ προλεγόμενα pertinent, quæ ad titulum Apostoli adjecta leguntur. Quæ iam subjiciemus.

Cætera pariter ad quemque versiculum ex illa explicatione antecedanea annotationis, quæ præ manibus habemus, collationis & examinis causa immediate subjuncturi. Epistola hæc semper inter eximias est habita scripta ab Apostolo, iam diu functo Apostolicum munus, cum in vinculis esset Romæ, ad Ephesios civitatem Asiæ præcipuam, & qua urbe multi viri docti, & in seculi rebus sapientes prodierant, itaque folicite ostendit, quantum omnes doctrinæ fordere debeant præ Evangelio, cujus sublimitatem admirandis & vere Apostolicis cogitatis exprimit. Apostolicam autem dignitatem sibi adscribit & in hac & in aliis epistolis, cogente re, quod multi essent, qui ipsum docendi munus a Petro, Johanne & Jacobo accepisse dicerent, eorumque nomine, quanquam ipsis illis nolentibus uterentur, ut rituum Judaicorum servitutem iis, qui e gentibus vocati erant, imponerent. Pertinet autem maxime hæc epistola ad demendatam autoritatem iis, qui eruditionis extraneæ nomine se venditantes ob id Gnostici vocabantur, cujus argumenti est & ad Colossenses huic plane germana, & illa ad Titum, utraque ad Timotheum, Petri altera & Judæ. Scripsit Paulus eodem plane exemplo epistolam ad Laodicenses, ut ex Tertulliani libris contra Marcionem colligere est.

Et illa forte est epistola Λαοδικείας id est, Laodicensibus scripta, cujus mentio Coloss. IV. 13. PROLEGOMENA AD HANC EPISTOLAM. Causam ista nobis præbent de X. capitibus præfandi.

Primum circa autorem, Cur se Apostolum Jesu Christi hic & in aliis epistolis nominet? Quod id factum ex necessitate ab illis imposita, qui docendi munus ipsum a Petro, Johanne & Jacobo se accepisse dixere, & horum prætextu gentibus convertis rituum Judaicorum servitutem imponere voluere, non liquet. Neque cum iisdem in omnibus epistolis ipsi negotium est. Nec argumentum illud de ritibus Judaeis in hac nostra tractat Apostolus. Quando cum illis agit, operosius suam vocationem asserit, ut vidimus in proxima epistola Gal. I. & II. Factum autem autoritatis causa, quo tanquam legatus & Apostolus Jesu Christi cum doctrina & monitis suis suscipiatur, & scripturæ hæc ceu canonica, utpote a divina inspiratione, Apostolis propria, profecta colatur.

II. Objectum vel illi, ad quos exarata hæc epistola, Ephesii conversi sunt. Ephesus in Ionia sita, quondam Trichia, & Orygia, & Ptelea, ut & Solimona nuncupata, alterum minoris Asiæ lumen ob mercaturarum opulentiam, & frequentiam civium, Plinio libr. V. dicitur.

Sed dedita fuit hæc civitas maxime tum idololatriæ, & imprimis cultui Dianæ, cujus templum splendidissimum fuit toto orbe celeberrimum Act. XIX. 27. tum magia, de qua ibidem. pariter legere est vers. 13, 19.

An autem Paulus primum Evangelium ibi severit, nonnulli, teste Theodoreto, dubium movent, qui in hac civitate tantum Apostolum primum Ecclesiam constituisse putant. Sed Irenaeus tribuit hoc Paulo libr. III. adv. haer. c. 3. quod nempe a Paulo fundata fuerit Ephesina Ecclesia, a Johanne vero, permanente illic usque ad Trajani tempora, curata.

Primum autem illic Judaeis praedicavit Corintho Ephesum veniens, a quibus aeque tum dimissus est Act. XVIII. 19.

Post denuo Ephesum pervenit, ibique per triennium substitit primum in publica Judaeorum synagoga per tres menses, reliquo autem tempore in Tyranni schola Judaeis & gentibus praedicavit Evangelium de regno Dei, annuncians ipsis omne consilium Dei Act. XIX. 10. c. XX. 27.

31. quo tempore Christo insignem ibi collegit Ecclesiam. Magnum enim ostium apertum ei fuit ibidem 1 Cor. XVI. 9. & placuit ita divinae clementiae, ut in urbe tam celebri & populosa, etsi idolatriae dedita & Diabolo devincta persisteret tantus Apostolus, & non tantum multi ibidem e regno Satanae eriperentur, sed etiam longe lateque Evangelium per orbem disseminaretur.

In quam maximus erat è variis locis confluxus ob mercaturam & navigationis commoditatem. Sita quippe erat Ephesus in extremo Asiae minoris littore versus occasum, & ferme etiam meridiem, ut illac transeundum fuerit navigantibus ex Syria aut Aegypto in Graecam, Macedoniam & Pontum ac contra, itemque ex Asia minore Romam & vicissim: Sicut & ipse Apostolus nempe proficiscens in Macedoniam aut Graeciam, & iterum rediens illac transivit.

Quibus commoditatibus procul ambiguo motus Johannes Apostolus ibi diutissime commorari voluit.

Quantis ibi periculis obnoxius fuerit Paulus, imprimis ob tumultum a Demetrio excitatum, refertur Act. XIX. 23. seqq. ubi & cum bestiis esse pugnandum fuit 1 Cor. XV. Oratio ejus valde valedictoria affectibus plena, stimulisque vehementioribus efficax descripta extat Act.

XX. Illi Ecclesiae tanto labore, tantis periculis plantatae inscribit Paulus hanc epistolam, & in ea falsis numinibus, quae antea coluerant, opponit unum illum verum Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum; Opibus Dianae omnes impervestigabiles divinae gratiae; templo Dianae magnifico structuram spiritualis templi adornandam.

III. Locus III.

Locus, unde scripta haec epistola, Roma communiter creditur, tum e subscriptione, tum e captivitatis & vinculorum commemoratione e. IV. t. c. VI. 20.

Temere autem Beza videri posse aliunde missam affirmat. Nullam sententiae suae plane singularis affert rationem. Mere ergo precaria est.

IV. Tempus IV.

Tempus quod attinet, S. Athanasius quidem in synopsi scriptam putat, antequam Ephesum venisset Apostolus. Sed quia scripta e vinculis, recte hic ab eo discedit Theodoretus. Siquidem Apostolus ipse Ephesios converterit.

Et testantur acta Apostolorum, Paulum prius vice simplici Ephesum venisse, quam Romam mitteretur. Conf. Act. XVIII. XIX. & XXVII. XXVIII.

Occasio V.

Occasio.

Grotius partim a Philosophis partim a Judaizantibus datam vult. Et sane multi Philosophorum, ut habet Chrysostomus, fuerunt in hac urbe. Dicitur & Pythagoras hinc prodiisse, quod utrumque fit, interea tamen hinc est omnis illa Ionica schola, quin & qui cum Parmenide, Zenone, Democritoque fuerunt.

Cujus rei causa multo quidem studio opus fuisse ad illos scribendi, ait Chrysostomus, sed quod illi scribendi causam dederint opinione sua de ratione consequendi vitam aeternam, de eo nec apud Chrysostomum, nec apud alios veteres quicquam habetur, nec ejus rei ullum in hac epistola apparet vestigium. De pseudo-Apostolis forte metuit Paulus, Grotii judicio, ne ab iis, aliisque impostoribus, qui passim oberrarunt etiam per Asiam praesertim in locis etiam opulentioribus, seducerentur, sicut & Galatas non ita nimis procul ab eis disitos seduxerant, & 1 ad Timoth. Ephesinum Episcopum apparet, illos seductores ac turbatores illic quoque dudum antea fuisse 2. Tim. I. 15.

Sed imprimis metuebat Apostolus, ne ob vincula abterrerentur infirmi. Neque ignorabat, post suum discessum illic exorituros, qui perversa loquantur, aliosque seducant, quod praedixerat ipsis Act. XX. 30.

Scopum VI.

Scopus itaque fuit: ut tanquam brevi monitus Ephesios ad perseverantiam in fide hortaretur, summa ejus repetita, sedulo illis commendata, & ad studium pietatis eosdem inflammaret. Ideo gratias agit Deo, pro gratia ipsis concessa, & incrementa eis precatur, ac praecipuos fidei articulos exhibet, & ad fundamentum fidei eos revocat, & Apostolicum suum officium eadem fini commendat, ut ne ob afflictiones suas segnescant, rogat, seque pro eorum constantia precari testatur.

VII. Materiam VII.

Materiam scriptionis ut & characterem dicendi sublimem merito dicit Grotius, quod etiam notavit Chrysostomus. Est epistola, inquit, plena sublimibus sententiis & dogmatibus. Et iterum: Nam quae nusquam fere est loquutus, hic dicit. Procedit autem forma expositionis, non ut in epistola ad Romanos & Galatas per modum disputationis.

Cognatio VIII.

Cognatam epistola ad Colossenses affirmat Grotius, sed eam cognationem non exposuit. Illud, quod dogmatibus subjungit adhortationes, commune ipsi est cum plerisque aliis epistolis: ad statum tamen Oeconomicum spectantes cum hac nostra imprimis illa, quae ad Colossenses exarata est, inculcat. Minor est convenientia huic nostrae, cum Titum & utraque ad Timotheum, cum Petri altera & Jude epistola. Docere eam debuisset Grotius, non simpliciter asserere.

De epistola autem peculiari ad Laodicenses per-scripta, nullum ex antiquitate habet certum testimonium.

Neque Col. IV. 16. de epistola ad Laodicenses agitur, aut τῆς Λαοδικείας, sed ἐκ τῆς Λαοδικείας, Epistola in qua scilicet e Laodicea scripta, ut in textu Graeco & Syriaco habetur. Quemadmodum etiam versio Latina epistolam Laodicensium primo conceptu infert epistolam non Pauli ad Laodicenses, sed a Laodicensibus scriptam.

Quis unquam epistolam Timothei aut Titi dixit, quam ad Timotheum aut Titum scripsit Apostolus. Ideo Chrysostomus & Theodoretus intelligunt epistolam a Laodiceis vero & alii plurimi de priori ad Timotheum explicant, quae ἀπὸ Λαοδικείας scripta dicitur.

Bellarminus ipse cum libr. IV. de justif. c. 4. scripsisset, certum est, periisse epistolam Pauli ad Laodicenses in recognitione librorum suorum id emendavit hoc modo: Non probo, quod dixi certum esse periisse epistolam Pauli ad Laodicenses. Nam probabile quidem est, Apostolum in epistola ad Coloss. extrema loqui de epistola sua scripta ad Laodicenses, ut Anselmus & aliqui alii in Commentario ejus loci docent, tamen non est omnino certum, quia S. Chrysostomus in Commentar. ejus loci scribit, aliquos existimasse, Apostolum loqui de epistola scripta a Laodicensibus ad ipsum, non de epistola scripta ad Laodicenses ab ipso, & ponderat verba Græca, ubi legitur, & eam quæ est ex Laodicea, non autem, & eam quæ est ad Laodicenses. Commentaria Anshelmi in epistolas Pauli, notante ipso Bellarmino libr. de script. Eccl. ad ann. Christi 1081. verius Hervæo tribuuntur. Præferenda autem sine dubio Græco- rum Chrysostomi & Theodoreti sententia, textui Græco, Syro & Latino conformis, Hervæa, textui haud consentaneæ, quibus consonat etiam Oecu- menius. Illamque sequutus est Baronius, Pame- lius annot. 259. ad l. V. Tertull. contra Marc. Cor- nel. à Lapide in h. l. explosam in antiquitate epi- stolam ad Laodicenses palam testatur, Hieronymus Tom. I. catal. script. Eccles. in Paulo: Legunt qui- dam & ad Laodicenses, sed AB OMNIBUS ex- ploditur. Philastrius de hæres. Etsi, inquit, legitur à quibusdam, non tamen in Ecclesia legitur epistola populo ad Laodicenses scripta. Ratio, quam affert contra illam ad Laodicenses putatitiam epistolam Baronius, non est futilis: Sanè, inquit, nullam eidem tabellario ad Laodicenses fuisse à Paulo datam epistolam satis constat: Dum in ea, quam tum scri- psit ad Colossenses, salutari mandat eos, qui Laodiceæ essent, fideles cap. V. 23. Si enim ad Laodicenses tunc scripsisset, ipse sua epistola ejusmodi functus esset of- ficio, nec opus habuisset illud Colossensibus delegare. Si vero antea ad Laodicenses scripsisset Paulus, illis utique (ut modo fecit scribens ad Colossenses) ut suas literas legendas traderent Colossensibus in mandatis dedisset. Theophylacti sententia minus probabilis est. Quomodo enim Colossenses colligere è ver- bis Apostoli potuissent, quod epistolam priorem ad Timotheum designet? Nec ea Baronio probata ad ann. Christi 60. n. 12. Nec vero Tertullianus epistolam ad Laodicenos scriptam à Paulo, docuit: Sed longe aliud libr. V. contra Marcionem cap. 11. habet. Prætereo hic & de alia epistola, quam nos ad Ephesios perscriptam habemus, HÆRETICI vero Laodicenos: & cap. 17. Ecclesia quidem veritati epistolam istam ad Ephesios habemus commissam, non ad Laodicenos, sed Marcion ei titulum aliquan- do interpolare gestiit, quasi & in isto diligentissimus explorator. Non inspexit ergo hic Grotius Tertul- lianum. Epiphanius vero libr. I. Tom. III. cap. 42. contra Marcionem diserte epistolam ad Laodi- censes superadditam Paulinis & superfluam & ex- tra Apostolum, non in Apostolo judicavit. Quod Stapletonus movet Tom. I. autor. Eccles. defens. l. II. cap. 2. p. 941. Si Laodicenses ad Paulum scripsif- sent aliquam epistolam, non jam Laodiceæ sed in ma- nibus Pauli illa epistola verisimiliter foret: dilui facile potest, si dicatur, simul illam à Paulo Co- lossensibus missam cum ea, quam ipse ad eosdem scribebat. Quo accipi etiam queunt verba Pauli κ, τὴν & hanc (scilicet quam simul jam vobis exhi- beo) ex Laodicea ad me scriptam &c. Quam Jaco- bus Faber Stapulensis edidit, & Sixt. Senensis Bi- bliothecæ suæ inseruit, de ea ipse Sixtus dubitat, an Pauli sit. Baronius eam palam rejicit: Quæ ad Laodicenses Pauli nomine SPURIA fertur, nequa- quam ab antiquioribus cognita fuit. Cornelius à Lapide ad Coloss. IV. supposititiam eandem esse ra- tionibus non malis docet.

IX. Argumentum epistolæ est informatio de do- ctrina fidei & vita Christiana vocatione ad fidem digna, ut in illa persistant, illius gratia explican- tur dogmata de prædestinatione, justificatione, vo- catione, de Christi ad dextram Dei exaltatione, vivificatione & salvatione, gentium ad Israëlaiticam Ecclesiam congregatione, & super eodem funda- mento extructione cap. II. & ἐνσωματώσει ac com- munione promissionum, ut repleantur omni di- vina plenitudine cap. III. Hujus verò causâ com- monefactiones instituuntur ad concordiam & f- sanctitatem cap. IV. ad imitationem Dei & Christi, cum fuga peccatorum & probatione voluntatis divinæ & celebratione nominis divini cap. V. ad- dita etiam speciali commonitione pro conjugibus, reliquo cap. V. pro liberis ac parentibus, servis ac Dominis, & exhortatione communi, ut adversus insultus Diabolicos se arment, iisque fortiter re- sistant. Quæ Grotius complexus est succincte.

X. Partes itaque duæ sunt. Prior est dogma- tica, tribus prioribus capitibus, præmisso tamen titulo, inscriptione ac voto Pauli: Posterior est parænetica, reliquis tribus capitibus, subjuncta tamen relatione de causa Tychici missi v. 21. 22. cap. VI. & voto finali v. 23. 24.

Prius sane institutum dogmaticum exequitur Apostolus partim εὐχαριστίας, partim precationum formula cap. I. & III. ut eo magis penetret, atque efficacior sit informatio: Sed ex ipsa εὐλογίας & precationis Apostolicæ materia satis apparet in- tentio ac studium ejusdem, quod nempe influe- re, confirmare, ac stabilire eosdem voluerit in fide semel tradita, ne ab ea dimoveri sese patian- tur: quo de Ephesios tacite cap. I. 9. 15. 17. cap. II. 20. cap. III. 4. 5. 18. expresse vero cap. IV. 14. com- monefecit.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. DOGMATIC PART OF THE EPISTLE. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With the Apostolic salutation premised, Paul gives thanks to God for the spiritual blessing in Christ, in gratuitous election, justification, the revelation of the mystery of His will, the summing up of all things made in Christ, and the admission of believers into Christ, predestined to the heavenly inheritance: and specifically for the calling of the Ephesians to the Gospel, and the sealing of the faithful by the Holy Spirit, and he testifies that he gives thanks to God for them without ceasing, and prays that they may be instructed by the Spirit of wisdom, and illuminated for the recognition of the hope, calling, and divine power in believers, by which He raised Christ Himself, and placed Him at His right hand above all thrones, and subjected all things to His feet, having constituted Him primarily as the Ecclesiastical head of His mystical body.

There are three parts: I. The Pauline greeting, v. 1 & 2. II. The Apostolic blessing to v. 14. III. The testimony concerning the Eucharist and his prayers for the illumination of the churches to v. 23.

PART I OF THE FIRST CHAPTER. The Pauline greeting.

vers. 1. Διὰ θελήματος Θεῦ) Thus also 1 Cor. 1:1, 2 Cor. 1:1, Col. 1:1. The same is said in Gal. 1:4, κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς, and κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεῦ Πατρὸς 1 Tim. 1:1. He shows by his own example how great a benefit the calling is. For he himself and other men were doing something far different.

Τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς ὖσιν ἐν ἐφέσῳ) The same title is given to Christians in 1 Cor. 1:2, 2 Cor. 1:1. Christians first become צדיקים, then חסידים. See the prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans. In the manuscript, τοῖς ἁγίοις πᾶσι τοῖς ὖσιν &c.

And to the faithful in Christ Jesus) That is, those who have hitherto persevered in this pious institution, as the name πιστῶν is very often taken, so that it corresponds to the Hebrew נאמנים.

Here we subjoin, as we received at the beginning, what Grotius has in the explanation previously published with the annotations, namely, to the Gospels at the beginning of the epistle to the Ephesians, even if perhaps the same and similar things are said.

Διὰ θελήματος Θεῦ by the will of God) Made an Apostle not by human choice. So also 1 Corinthians 1:1, and 2 Corinthians 1:1, and Colossians 1:1, 1 Timothy 1:1, and 2 Timothy 1:1; it is worth the same as what is more expressly stated at the beginning of Galatians: οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλὰ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and at the beginning of the first to Timothy: κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεοῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, according to the command of God the Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.

To the saints who are in Ephesus) To all the saints who are at Ephesus. Thus he calls not only the celibate, but also those who use marriage holily. See below v. 22 and following.

And to the faithful in Christ Jesus) πιστὸς in the Greek language is properly one who provides faith and makes his promises valid. By the Greek writers of the New Testament, it is often taken in a less proper sense, so that it signifies a believer, as can be seen in John 20:27, Acts 10:45, 16:1, 1 Timothy 4:3, 12, 5:16, Titus 1:6. But in this place, it is more correctly taken in that more proper meaning, as in Matthew 24:45, 25:21 and 23, Luke 12:42, 16:10, 11, 12, 19:17, 2 Timothy 2:2, and concerning God, 2 Corinthians 1:18, 1 Thessalonians 5:24, 2 Thessalonians 3:3, 2 Timothy 2:13, Hebrews 10:23, 1 Peter 4:14, because after the title of saints, a title that signifies constancy in holiness is better subjoined than one that signifies the assent held to the Gospel. In the same way, those are called faithful who were previously called called and chosen, Revelation 17:14.

I do not see why πιστοὶ should not be called faithful in this place. For that this name is later than the saints, it is by way of explanation, so that we may know that those are truly saints who believe in Christ; without faith, by which hearts are purified, Acts 15:9, there is no holiness. They could not be universally denominated from perseverance or constancy in faith, because without doubt, even among those converted to the faith, many were temporary. What Grotius has concerning the married is from Chrysostom, who says on this place: Behold holy men, who have both children and wives and servants. Therefore, holiness and religion are not to be restricted to monastic cloisters. Chrysostom also notes against the Arians the preposition διὰ attributed to the Father. Behold, he gave διὰ BY to the Father. What then? Shall we say he is lesser? Not at all. The mouths of those who wage war with the divinity of the Only-Begotten are stopped, as Theodoret noted. The will of God, according to Crocius, he opposes both to the lust of one's own flesh, by which false teachers are rashly carried away, and to the will of men, by which ordinary ministers are called. He shows, therefore, that he did not rashly leap into the midst, not by his own choice, not by the decree of men, whom he expressly removes from here in Galatians 1:1, nor was he admitted by his own merit, but called by the mere good pleasure and mercy of God, which he commends with a grateful heart in 1 Timothy 1:12, 13, 14, 15, 16. Elsewhere he calls it the command of God, 1 Timothy 1:1, in the same sense. Crocius takes the name of God personally concerning the first person of the Godhead, but there is no reason why it should not be taken essentially, so that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are included, even if Jesus Christ is mentioned peculiarly. Compare John 17:3, 1 Timothy 2:5.

Latin:

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ DOGMATICA. CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissa salutatione Apostolicâ gratias agit Deo Paulus pro benedictione spirituali in Chri- sto, in gratuita electione, justificatione, my- sterii voluntatis suæ revelatione, ἀνακεφα- λαιώσει omnium in Christo factâ, & admis- sione credentium in Christum, prædestina- torum ad hæreditatem cælestem: & specia- tim Ephesiorum vocatione ad Evangelium, & fidelium obsignatione per Spiritum San- ctum, ac testatur, quod sine intermissione pro iisdem Deo gratias agat, ac precetur, ut Spiritu sapientiæ instruantur, & illu- minentur ad agnitionem spei, vocationis & virtutis divinæ in credentes, qua ipsum- met Christum excitavit, & ad dextram suam super omnes thronos collocavit, ejus- que pedibus omnia subjecit, constituto eo- dem imprimis capite Ecclesiastico corporis sui mystici.

Partes tres sunt I. Salutatio Paulina v. 1. & 2. II. Εὐλογία Apostolica ad v. 14. III. Testificatio de Eucharistia & precibus suis pro illuminatione Ec- clesiarum ad v. 23.

PARS I. CAPITIS PRIMI. Salutatio Paulina.

vers. 1. Διὰ θελήματος Θεῦ) Sic & 1. Cor. I. 1. 2. Cor. I. 1. Coloss. I. 1. Idem dicitur Gal. I. 4. κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς, & κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεῦ Πατρὸς 1. Tim. I. 1. Ostendit suo exemplo, quantum sit beneficium vocationis. Et ipse enim & cæteri homines longe aliud agebant.

Τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς ὖσιν ἐν ἐφέσῳ) Idem titulus Christianis datur 1. Corinth. I. 2. 2. Corinth. I. 1. Christiani primum fiunt צדיקים, deinde חסידים. Vide prolegomena in Epistolam ad Romanos. In Manuscripto τοῖς ἁγίοις πᾶσι τοῖς ὖσιν &c.

Καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Id est, qui hactenus in pio isto instituto perseverarunt, quomodo nomen πιστῶν, sæpissime sumitur, ut respondeat Hebræo נאמנים.

Hic subjungimus, ut initio recepimus, quæ habet Grotius in explicatione prius edita cum annotatis scilicet ad Evangelia in principium epistolæ ad Ephesios, etiamsi forte eadem & similia dicantur.

Διὰ θελήματος Θεῦ per voluntatem Dei) Non humano arbitratu factus Apostolus. Sic & 1. Corinth. I. 1. & 2. Corinth. I. 1. & Col. I. 1. Tim. I. & II. idem valet quod expressius initio ad Gal. ὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπων, ὐδὲ διὰ ἀνθρώπω, ἀλλὰ διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστῦ non ab hominibus neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum, & initio prioris ad Timotheum κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ secundum imperium Dei Patris & Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi.

Τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς ὖσιν ἐν ἐφέσῳ) Omnibus sanctis, qui sunt Ephesi. Sic appellat non cælibes tantum, sed & conjugio sancte utentes. Vide infra v. 22. & seqq.

Καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ, & fidelibus in Christo Jesu) πιστὸς Græco sermone proprie est, qui fidem præstat, ac pollicita sua rata facit. A scriptoribus Græcis novi fœderis sæpe sumitur in sensu minus proprio, ut πιστεύοντα credentem significet, ut videre est Johan. XX. 27. Actor. X. 45. XVI. 1. 1. Timoth. IV. 3. 12. V. 16. Tit. I. 6. Sed hoc loco rectius & significatu illo magis proprio sumi, quomodo Matth. XXIV. 45. XXV. 21. & 23. Luc. XII. 42. XVI. 10. 11. 12. XIX. 17. 2. Timoth. II. 2. & de Deo, 2. Corinth. I. 8. 1. Thessal. V. 24. 2. Thessal. III. 3. 2. Timoth. II. 13. Hebr. X. 23. 1. Petr. IV. 14. quia post titulum sanctorum melius subjungitur titulus, qui constantiam in sanctimonia significet, quam qui assensum Evangelio habitum. Eodem modo πιστοὶ dicuntur, qui ante κλητοὶ & ἐκλεκτοὶ vocati & electi Apocal. XVII. 14.

Non video cur πιστοὶ non dicantur hoc loco fideles. Quod enim posterius sit hoc nomen τοῖς ἁγίοις, sit κατ' ἀπεξήγησιν, ut sciamus, eos demum vere sanctos esse, qui credunt in Christum, sine fide, qua corda purificantur, Actor. XV. 10. nullam esse sanctitatem. A perseverantia vel constantia in fide non adeo denominari universim poterant, quia procul dubio etiam inter conversos ad fidem, multi fuerunt πρόσκαιροι. Quod de conjugatis habet Grotius, à Chrysostomo est, qui ad hunc locum: Ecce sanctos viros, qui habent & filios & uxores & servos. Non ergo sanctitas & religio ad claustra Monastica coarctanda. Notat & Chrysostomus contra Arianos Præpositionem διὰ Patri tributam. Ecce διὰ PER dedit Patri. Quid ergo? Dicemus eum minorem? Minime. Quo etiam eorum, qui cum divinitate Unigeniti bellum gerunt, ora obstrui notavit Theodoreus. Voluntatem Dei, secundum Crocium, opponit tum libidini propriæ carnis, quæ rapiuntur temere falsarii, tum voluntati hominum, qua vocantur ministri ordinarii. Ostendit ergo, se non temere prosiliisse in medium non suopte arbitratu, non hominum decreto, quos diserte hinc submovet Gal. I. 1. neque suo merito adscitum, sed vocatum mero Dei beneplacito & misericordia, quam grato animo commendat 1. Tim. I. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. Alibi appellat ἐπιταγὴν τῦ Θεῦ 1. Tim. I. 1. eodem sensu. Nomen θεῶ personaliter de prima Deitatis persona accipit Crocius, sed nulla est causa, cur non accipiatur essentialiter, ut & Filius & Spiritus Sanctus comprehendantur, etsi Jesu Christi peculiariter mentio fiat. Conf. Job. XVII. 3. 1. Tim. II. 5.

## 1:2
verse 2. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ) Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:3, 2 Corinthians 1:2, Galatians 1:3.

verse 2. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ) Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ) He wishes them the favor of God and Christ, and what is connected to it, true happiness, which our writers, following the example of the Hebrews, call by the name of peace.

Zanchius wrongly distinguishes these, as if spiritual benefits were understood by grace, and temporal benefits by peace. For grace is the fountain of all benefits, just as peace embraces happiness, however much it redounds from grace; but that grace is especially regarded, which is the cause and spring of spiritual blessing, is clear from verse 3, though temporal blessing is not excluded, and for that reason, peace is also peculiarly looked to, which follows the gratuitous remission of sins, namely, the tranquility of conscience; there is no doubt, but that it is by no means excluded, but that any other happiness is simultaneously included. However, these are not to be distributed in such a way that grace is claimed for the Father only, and peace for Christ Jesus, but that both are attributed to both, not excluding the Holy Spirit, 2 Corinthians 13:14. The Father is the fountain, Christ is the Mediator of grace and peace, and through the Holy Spirit, the communication of the same is made. Nor should the word κυρίου be connected by a copula with the word ἡμῶν, because Christ is not joined to us, who receive grace and peace, but to the Father, from whom grace and peace come to us, which the Syrian indicates by the repeated particle Meus, and which is clearly evident from 2 Tim. 1:2 and 2 John v. 3.

PART II. Apostolic Blessing. Ver. 3.

Latin:

vers. 2. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Rom. I. 7. 1. Corinth. I. 3. 2. Corinth. I. 2. Gal. I. 3.

vers. 2. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ Κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Gratia vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro & Domino Jesu Christo) Favorem eis Dei, Christique optat, & quæ ei connexa est veram felicitatem, quam nostri scriptores ad Hebræorum exemplum pacis nomine appellant.

Male Zanchius hæc distinguit, quasi per gra- tiam spiritualia, per pacem temporalia benefi- cia intelligantur. Gratia enim fons est omnium beneficiorum, quemadmodum pax felicitatem quamvis è gratia redundantem complectitur, sed imprimis gratiam respici, quæ est causa & sca- turigo benedictionis spiritualis è vers. 3. liquet, non exclusa tamen temporali benedictione, at- que ea ratione peculiariter etiam spectari pacem, quæ gratuitam remissionem peccatorum consequi- tur, tranquillitatem nempe conscientiæ, dubium nullum est, sed ut minime excludatur, sed simul comprehendatur quævis alia felicitas. Non au- tem distribuenda hæc ita, ut gratia Patri tantum vindicetur, Christo Jesu autem pax, sed utrum- que utrique tribuatur non excluso Spiritu San- cto 2. Corinth. XIII. 13. Pater fons est, Christus est Mediator gratiæ & pacis, per Spiritum San- ctum fit communicatio ejusdem. Neque conne- ctenda est per copulam vox κυρίου cum voce ἡμῶν, quia non nobis Christus jungitur, qui accipimus gratiam & pacem, sed Patri, à quo nobis obtin- git gratia & pax, quod Syrus repetita particula Meus indicat, & è 2. Tim. I. 2. 2. Johan. v. 3. lu- culenter constat.

PARS II. Εὐλογία Ἀποστολικη. Vers. 3.

## 1:3
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ) He begins with the praise of God, as in 1 Cor. 1:3, where the words are the same. Εὐλογητὸς is ברוך in Gen. 9:26 and often elsewhere.

He who has blessed us) It happens here as is frequent with Paul, that the same word is taken in a different sense with hardly any interval. For εὐλογεῖν has already been to praise, now it is to do good, as in Job 42:12, surely because both proceed from a kind spirit. And similar things are accustomed to exchange names with one another.

with every spiritual blessing) Not with those earthly benefits which you have in Lev. 26, Deut. 7:13, and 28.

in the heavenly places) The perfection of this happiness will not be on the land of Canaan, but in the highest heaven. See what will be said below at 20. Tertullian sometimes rendered ἐπουράνια as supercelestial; ἐπὶ, both by itself and in composition, sometimes signifies over, sometimes in. If you take it in the former way, you must understand heaven here as the starry region. If in the latter, the highest or third heaven itself.

in Christ) That is, through Christ as the secondary cause. Thus most codices, not χρηστῷ.

ver. 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ) εὐλογεῖν signifies to bless and to praise, and to do good (as in Job 42:12 and elsewhere) because, indeed, it proceeds from a benevolent spirit, no less than good words; thus often similar things obtain the name of similar things.

in every spiritual blessing) He has not affected us with those benefits which God had promised to the Hebrews pertaining to this life, both elsewhere and in Deuteronomy 7:13, but with eternal and heavenly ones. Therefore he adds

in the supercelestial places in Christ) Those were carried out on earth, Exod. 3:8; these place us in heaven both by hope and by right, Matt. 5:3, 10; Phil. 3:20.

Those things would be correct regarding spiritual benefits, if ὑποὺλον were not cherished regarding the promises of the Old Testament, which it has from Pelagius and Socinus, into which error Aretius also falls here: namely, that they contained only temporal things; which we have frequently noted already. But since the Apostle, having weighed the reason for his design, because he wished to inform them about spiritual benefits, makes no mention of corporal ones, it is not to be presumed from that that only spiritual benefits were procured for us by Christ, and not temporal ones. For as outside of Christ nothing was obtained on account of sin except a curse, both temporal and eternal:

Thus we are neither delivered from the curse itself, nor has the blessing been acquired for us from the opposite, except through Christ, in whom all the families and nations of the earth were to be blessed, Gen. XII. 3. In whom all the promises are yes and amen, 2 Cor. I. in whose name also we must ask whatever we ask, and through whom and on account of whom we are heard in our prayers, and obtain whatever we ask, whether corporal or spiritual goods, John XVI. 23. Coloss. III. 17. There is also held here first a general complex of spiritual benefits, which are all comprehended under the name of spiritual blessing; but afterwards some are recounted in particular, both those which are common to all the faithful, and those which have fallen peculiarly to the Ephesians, v. 5. seqq. It is added in the heavenly places, because all those spiritual things are truly heavenly, both by reason of their origin, inasmuch as they descend from the Father, who is heavenly, Matt. XVIII. 35, and by reason of their quality, because in dignity and eminence they are not earthly, not celestial, as regards the created and material heavens, but super-celestial, into which even the angels in heaven rejoice to look, 1 Pet. I. 12, which are truly above mind, above word, above every comprehension of created nature; and by reason of their end, because we enjoy the blessing obtained in Christ not only in the kingdom of grace in these lands, but also in the kingdom of glory in the heavens, which super-celestial happiness is the ultimate end of the obedience of Christ and of our faith in Christ, 1 Pet. I. 9. But he does not treat of corporal blessing, which, even if it be given from heaven, is nevertheless earthly, leads to earthly life, and ceases with the same on earth, but of heavenly blessing. But what Grotius philosophizes about a third heaven established above the starry heaven in System. Theol. Tom. III., we have refuted among the Calvinian matters. God is not said to be locally above the starry heaven, but tropically by reason of Majesty and eminence, whom the heaven of heavens does not contain, 1 Kings VIII. 27, 1 Tim. VI. 16. And will God cease to be heavenly when not only the earth, but also the heaven shall perish, Luke XIII. 17, ch. XXI. 33? Or will Christ cease to sit in the heavenly places, Eph. I. 20, or the elect to be heavenly in the kingdom, 2 Tim. IV. 18?

Nor does Grotius rightly call Christ the secondary cause of spiritual blessing. For as he is God the same with the Father: so also he is equally the principal cause as the Father, John V. 19. He is indeed in his Mediatorial office a meritorious cause, but because he is Mediator, and as GOD, and as man, and the merit is not purely human, but theanthropic, therefore one must deservedly abstain from the name of secondary or less principal cause.

Moreover, in all the epistles, except the three to the Galatians, to Titus, and to the Hebrews, the Apostle began with a blessing or thanksgiving. Here, however, he spends almost the entire first chapter on the same. The Apostle directs his verbal blessing to GOD the Father, who is the fountain of real blessing, whom he calls Father not only of Christ, or of the Messiah, which the Jews admit literally, but of JESUS Christ, which they deny, who do not hold JESUS for the Messiah, asserting immediately the Christian faith against Jewish perfidy. Therefore he also adds of our Lord, that he may be the common Lord of the faithful, so that he may lay the foundation of perseverance in faith. Nor does he say of my Lord, but of ours, to signify the communion of saints and to plant mutual charity in the hearts of the faithful. He renders the cause of his blessing or thanksgiving the divine blessing, by which he signifies divine benefits. For for God to bless is to do good, just as to say is for him to do, Ps. XXXIII. 9. But when he joins the noun to the verb he blessed with every blessing, interpreters observe that the excellence of the blessing is noted, just as he said to Abraham, Gen. XXII. 17, In blessing I will bless thee, he teaches that every blessing happens in Christ, because outside of Christ there is no salvation, Acts IV. 12, and thus he silently exhorts to perseverance in faith. For who would withdraw from Christ, in whom every blessing is deposited?

Latin:

Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) A laude Dei orditur, ut 1. Cor. I. 3. ubi verba eadem. Εὐ- λογητὸς ברוך Gen. IX. 26. & alibi sæpe.

Ὁ εὐλογήσας ἡμᾶς) Evenit hic quod frequens est Paulo, ut eadem vox vix ullo intervallo in sensu diverso sumatur. εὐλογεῖν enim jam fuit laudare, nunc est benefacere, ut Job. XLII. 12. nimirum quia utrumque ex benigno ani- mo proficiscitur. Et solent similia inter se nomen permu- tare.

ἐν πάσῃ εὐλογίᾳ πνευματικῇ) Non illis beneficiis terre- nis, quæ habes Lev. XXVI. Deut. VII. 13. & XXVIII.

ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις) Perfectio hujus felicitatis non erit in terra Canaan, sed in summo cœlo. Vide quæ dicentur infra 20. ἐπουράνια supercœlestia reddidit aliquoties Ter- tullianus, ἐπὶ tum per se, tum in compositione modo valet super, modo in. Si priori modo sumas, cœlum hic intelli- gere debebis astriferam regionem. Si posterius, ipsum cœlum summum sive tertium.

ἐν χριστῷ) Id est per Christum tanquam causam secunda- riam. Sic plerique codices, non χρηστῷ.

vers. 3. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰη- σοῦ Χριστοῦ, benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi) εὐλογεῖν benedicere & laudare significat, & be- nefacere (ut Jobi XLII. 12. & alibi) quia nimirum id ex benevolo proficiscitur animo, non minus quam bo- na dicta, ita sæpe similia similium obtinent nomen.

ἐν πάσῃ εὐλογίᾳ πνευματικῇ, in omni benedictione spiri- tuali) non illis nos beneficiis affecit, quæ ad hanc vi- tam spectantia Hebræis Deus promiserat, tum alibi, tum Deuteronomii VII. 13. sed æternis ac cœlestibus. Ideo addit

ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις ἐν χριστῷ, in supercœlestibus in Chri- sto) Illa in terris peragebantur Exod. III. 8. hæc nos & spe & jure in cœlo collocant Matth. V. 3. 10. Phil. III. 20.

Recte se illa haberent de beneficiis spiritua- libus, nisi ὑποὺλον foveretur de promissis Vete- ris Testamenti, quod à Pelagio & Socino habet, in quod vero incidit etiam hic Aretius: Ea scili- cet tantum continuisse temporalia; Quod fre- quenter jam notavimus. Cum autem Apostolus instituti ratione pensi habita, quia de spirituali- bus beneficiis informare volebat, nullam men- tionem facit corporalium, ex eo præsumendum non est à Christo nobis solum spiritualia par- ta esse beneficia, non temporalia. Nam ut extra Christum nihil obtinebat propter pecca- tum nisi maledictio tum temporalis tum æterna:

Ita nec ab ipsa maledictione liberati sumus, nec acquisita nobis ex adverso est benedictio, nisi per Christum, in quo benedicendæ erant omnes gentes & nationes terræ Genes. XII. 3. In quo omnes promissiones sunt næ & amen 2. Cor. I. in cujus nomine etiam perendum est, quicquid ex- petimus, & per quem ac propter quem exaudi- mur in precibus, & consequimur, quæcunque petimus sive corporalia, sive spiritualia bona Jo- han. XVI. 23. Coloss. III. 17. Habetur & hic pri- mum generalis complexio beneficiorum spiritualium, quæ universa nomine εὐλογίας πνευματικῆς com- prehenduntur; postmodum vero recensentur in specie nonnulla, tum quæ omnibus fidelibus com- munia sunt, tum quæ peculiariter obtigere Ephe- siis v. 5. seqq. Additur ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις, quia omnia illa spiritualia vere sunt ἐπυράνια, tum ratione originis, utpote quæ à Patre, qui est ἐπυράνιος Matth. XVIII 35. descendunt, tum ratione quali- tatis, quia dignitate & eminentia sunt non ter- rena, non cœlestia, quod ad cœlos creatos & materiales, sed supercœlestia, in quæ etiam Angeli in cœlis gaudent παρακύψαι 1. Petr. I. 12. quæ vere sunt ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτισῆς Φύσεως; tum ratione finis, quia non solum in regno gratiæ in his terris, sed etiam in regno gloriæ in cœlis parta in Christo be- nedictione fruimur, quæ supercœlestis felicitas est finis ultimus obedientiæ Christi & fidei no- stræ in Christum 1. Petr. I. 9. Non agit autem de benedictione corporali, quæ etsi de cœlo detur, terrena tamen est, ad terrenam vitam con- ducit, & cum eadem in terra esse definit, sed de cœlesti. Quod autem Grotius philosopha- tur de tertio cœlo constituto super cœlum stellife- rum in System. Theol. Tom. III. in Calvinianis profligavimus. Deus non τοπικῶς super cœlum stellatum esse dicitur, sed τροπικῶς ratione Ma- jestatis & eminentiæ, quem cœli cœlorum non continent, 1. Reg. VIII. 27. 1. Tim. VI. 16. Et num ἐπυράνιος Deus esse desinet, cum non tan- tum terra, sed etiam cœlum peribit Luc. XIII. 17. cap. XXI. 33. Aut num desinet Christus tum sedere ἐν ἐπυρανίοις Eph. I. 20. aut electi in regno esse ἐπυράνιοι 2. Tim. IV. 18.

Neque recte Christum causam secundariam benedictionis spiritualis dicit Grotius. Nam ut idem est cum Patre Deus: Ita etiam princeps æ- que causa est, ac Pater Joh. V. 19. Est quidem in officio suo Mediatorio causa meritoria, sed quia Mediator est, & ut DEUS, & ut homo, & me- ritum non est ψιλῶς ἀνθρώπιν, sed θεανθρώπιν, id- circo abstinendum meritò à nomine causæ secun- dariæ vel minus principalis.

Cæterum in omnibus epistolis, exceptis tribus ad Galatas, ad Titum, & ad Hebræos in- cepit à benedictione vel gratiarum actione Apo- stolus. Hic autem fere totum caput primum impendit eidem. Ad DEUM Patrem, qui est fons benedictionis realis, dirigit εὐλογίαν suam verbalem Apostolus, quem Patrem non Christi tantum dicit, vel Messiæ, quod admittunt κατὰ λέξιν Judæi, sed JESU Christi, quod negant, qui JESUM pro Messia non habent, adserens sta- tim fidem Christianam adversus perfidiam Judai- cam. Ideo etiam addit Domini nostri, quod communis sit fidelium Dominus, ut fundamen- tum jaciat perseverantiæ in fide. Nec Domini mei dicit, sed nostri, ad significandam commu- nionem sanctorum & plantandam mutuam chari- tatem in cordibus fidelium. Causam benedi- ctionis vel gratiarum actionis suæ reddit benedi- ctionis ctionem divinam, qua beneficia divina significat. Dei enim benedicere est benefacere, uti dicere ejus facere est Psal. XXXIII. 9. Cum vero no- men jungit verbo benedixit omni benedictione, excellentiam benedictionis notari observant in- terpretes, uti Abrahæ dixit Genes. XXII. 17. Be- nedicendo benedicam tibi, omnem in Christo con- tingere docet, quia extra Christum non est salus Actor. IV. 12. & ita tacite ad perseverantiam in fide hortatur. Quis enim à Christo recederet, in quo omnis deposita est benedictio?

## 1:4
Vers. 4.

Just as he chose us in him) Here the decree takes the name of the act, as below II. 6 and 2 Tim. I. 9. Election is sometimes postponed to calling. But even calling itself is a certain election, that is, a certain excellent benefit, leading to eternal life: of which kind the benefits are, all those now rightly come under the name of election, just as formerly those which looked to the comforts and honors of this life. In him, through him. For even what the Apostles did in this matter, they did by the command of Christ, so that Christ himself is said to have done it, Acts XIII. 47, John XII. 32. Through him, not through Moses.

Before the foundation of the world) The Jews begin their election from Abraham, and boast of that antiquity, or sometimes even from the exodus out of Egypt, which time is called Qedem, Psalm LXXIV. 2. But in the divine constitution Christ was much prior to Abraham, as he himself teaches John VIII. 56 and following. Kataballesthai is to lay foundations, Heb. VI. 1, Yasad; hence katabole is said of a house, 2 Macc. II. 30, and by similitude of the world, Matt. XIII. 35, XXV. 34, Luke XI. 50, John XVII. 24, Heb. IV. 3, IX. 26, 1 Pet. I. 20, Rev. XIII. 8, XVII. 8. Scripture is accustomed to speak of God as of man. A man about to build a house first figures its use in his mind. GOD, about to create the world for the sake of man, and man indeed that he might worship GOD, proposed to himself a certain most perfect worship, to which, having pre-structured certain steps, he was to lead man, and that through his son. In a similar way the Hebrews say that before the world there were the law, repentance, and the name of the Messiah. Thus the mystery of the Gospel is said to be hidden from the ages below III. 4, Coloss. I. 28, before the ages, 1 Cor. II. 7, which itself is said to be hidden from the foundation of the world in the cited place Matt. XIII. 35. Grace given, that is, destined to be given before eternal times, 2 Tim. I. 9, which has the same value as the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, Matt. XXV. 34, glory given to Christ before the foundation of the world, John XVII. 24, Christ foreknown, that is, predecreed before the foundation of the world, 1 Pet. I. 20.

That we should be holy and without blame before him in love) The words 'to be' are understood here; he shows the goal toward which that calling tends, first in the decree, then in the act, namely that those thus called might produce works of great piety and be free from every crime. In the old law, the rams and oxen that were offered to God had to be תמימים ἄμωμοι [without blemish], Exod. XXIX. 2. Levit. I. 7. 10. III. 1. 6. and often elsewhere. Christians now offer themselves, Romans XII. 1. It is therefore fair that they too should be ἄμωμοι, below verse 27, Colossians I. 21, Jude 24, Mark XIV. 5, or ἀμώμητοι [without reproach], as in Philippians II. 15, 2 Peter III. 14, or ἄμεμπτοι [blameless] as in Philippians II. 15, 1 Thessalonians III. 13. Exceptional probity and innocence are required so that such an admirable calling may achieve its full effect. These two things are best comprehended in the name of love, in which is the whole of the Gospel. And it is rightly added, before him. For the purity of the mind is also required, which God alone inspects.

So far, what Grotius wrote in his Annotations on this Epistle. We now append those things which he handed down in another place concerning these matters.

Vers. 4.

As he chose us in him) Both Jews and pagans objected that the Gospel was a new thing; therefore, in many places he shows that this flowed from a most ancient decree, which he often proves both from the old types and from the predictions. To choose, as in common speech, so in the Holy Scriptures, has various meanings. It is election to a sweet and long life, to the possession of a very fertile land, to the knowledge of the law, to a kingdom, to the priesthood, to prophecy, to liberty and a return to the fatherland, and to other things. In the new covenant, however, election likewise signifies many things, such as election to the Apostolic office, to some embassy, or to the function of a Deacon. Often election signifies the approval of those who believe the Gospel, as can be seen especially in James 2:5, to which you may rightly refer also 1 Corinthians 1:27, 28, and 2 Thessalonians 2:13, and many passages in Romans. In this place, however, it seems that the calling through Christ or through his Gospel is signified: just as, conversely, the election of believers is sometimes called a calling, as in 1 Corinthians 1:24, 26. Not without reason, however, is that excellent benefit indicated by the word election, reserved for those who were to live in the times of the Messiah, or not long after, and were to be spectators of so many miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus the word ἐκλογῆς is taken in 1 Thessalonians 1:4, but this also is to be noted here, that the calling itself is not marked here, but the decree concerning the calling of the Jews and Gentiles, and among them also the Ephesians, is marked through a metonymy frequent enough, which gives the name of the effect to the counsel. In a similar way, Paul 2. Timothy 1:9 says χάριν, δοθεῖσαν ἡμῖν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, the grace which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the secular times. And soon he is about to say in chapter 2:6 that we have been placed by God in the heavenly places through Christ. In which sense Augustine also explains the passage in John 17:5.

Πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, before the foundation of the world) You will not find this note added rashly to just any decrees of God, but to excellent ones, with a comparison taken from those who, about to build a house, prefigure in their mind its entire use, and direct everything toward that end. See Matthew 25:34, John 17:24, 1 Peter 1:20. Thus ἑξ αἰῶνος from the age, Ecclesiastes 1:40, ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος Acts 15:18, ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων from the ages in this epistle 3:9, and Colossians 1:26, πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, before the ages 1 Corinthians 2:7, πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων before secular times 2 Timothy 1:9, Titus 1:2. In this sense the Hebrews say that the law, the name of the Messiah, and repentance were before the world was founded. See if you like the Talmudic title on Vows, and Rabbi Israel.
