Καταβάλλεσθαι is to lay a foundation. From that similitude, καταβολὴ κόσμου is the beginning of the founded world in the places already mentioned, and Matthew 13:35, Luke 11:50, Hebrews 4:3, 9:26, Revelation 13:8, 17:8.

Εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ, that we should be holy and immaculate in his sight in love) ἔσεσθαι of the little words εἰς τὸ or πρὸς τὸ as often. To this, of course, the decree of calling looks, and the calling itself through the Gospel, so that those who obey the calling may shine with an excellent probity and innocence, which may please God, proceeding indeed from a mind loving God, both because of benefits already bestowed and because of rewards hoped for from him. Chrysostom well says on this place: Ἱνα τοίνυν μὴ ἀκύσας, ὄτι ἐξελέξατο τὴν πίστιν ἀρκεῖν νομίσῃς μόνον, καὶ τὸν βίον προστίθησι, that is, lest therefore when you have heard, he chose, you might think that faith alone suffices, he added also life. Just as some are ἄμεμπτοι without complaint, according to the law of Moses, Luke 1:6, Philippians 3:6, so there are some according to the prescriptions of the Gospel ἄμεμπτοι Philippians 2:15, 1 Thessalonians 2:10, 3:13, ἀμώμητοι or ἄμωμοι immaculate, here below in verse 27. Philippians 2:15, Colossians 1:22, 1 Peter 3:14, Jude 24, Revelation 14:5, abstaining of course from all those faults which exclude a man from the Evangelical covenant, in which sense they are also said not to sin, 1 John 3:6, 9.

He begins in the enumeration of spiritual blessings from the eternal decree of God, election to eternal life, and proceeds thence to those things which befall us in time. Not that election is the cause of them, as the Calvinists wish; but that the former was made from eternity, while the latter happen in time, and that the former is to be declared by the latter in succession, nor does it become known to us except from temporal blessings: by which we are led to that blessedness to which we were predestined from eternity. There follows also with the Apostle after election προορισμὸς εἰς ὑοθεσίαν, not that election is prior in the order of nature to this preordination or predestination, or is the cause of the same: But that it makes for its explanation. For election and predestination mutually explain each other, and are as it were synonyms; therefore what the Apostle said here ἐξελέξατο, he expressed in Romans 8:29, 30 with the word προώρησεν, and he now says that election was made by predestination, ἐξελέξατο προορίσας he chose by predestining, but that that election was not made absolutely, as if he had absolutely predestined and chosen some to adoption or to eternal life out of simple good pleasure, and not because of the works or merits of men, but because of Christ and his merit apprehended by true faith, and so that those are not chosen whom he predestined to eternal life either out of mere good pleasure or because of their foreseen good works, but those whom he foresaw would finally believe in Christ, or would die in the faith of Christ, is clearly evident from the present passage: Not that faith, as it is our act or work, is the impulsive cause of election; but since faith is nothing other than the apprehension of the merit of Christ, which merit of Christ is the sole impulsive cause, by which the faithful appropriate it to themselves, and God from eternity foresaw that these or those would appropriate it to themselves, and would die in that faith: Because 1. ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν χριστῷ he chose us not without Christ or in view of the merit of Christ, which is not ours except through faith or application: But in Christ Jesus, i.e., insofar as he foresaw that they would be his in Christ through faith. He did not choose that we might be in Christ, in the way he is said to have chosen us that we might be holy and immaculate before him in love: But he chose in Christ, or because we are in Christ in the divine foreknowledge. For the particle ἐν introduces the impulsive cause: See Matthew 6:7, Acts 7:29, Ephesians 3:13, just as the Hebrew ב is accustomed to be the same as διὰ because of: See Genesis 29:18, Deuteronomy 14:16. Nor can it be taken here otherwise than as concerning the impulsive cause, in him, that is, because of him.

The Calvinists indeed seek various contrary explanations, but they find none that is consonant and consistent. For the fact that Maccovius first, in Coll. Theol. quæst. de prædest. disp. VI., posits a transposition, as if the words should be arranged thus: He chose us, that we might be holy and blameless IN him, that is too forced, and those words, that we might be holy, pertain to the end of election. The word ἐν ἀυτῷ, however, is used to define the form or quiddity of election, not its end. But the fact that secondly the Contra-Remonstrants in Coll. Hag. page 72, and Gomarus in Tom. III. Op. disp. X. th. LVII. wish to denote by the words ἐν ἀυτῷ the principal efficient cause, so that it is the same as δι᾽ ἀυτõ, through him as being with the Father and the Holy Spirit the cause or Author of predestination; it does not agree, either with the words, because nowhere is ἐν ἀυτῷ the same as by him, or δι᾽ ἀυτõ, or with the text, because the author of election is designated by the words ὁ θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τõ κυρίꙋ ἡμῶν ἰησõ χριστõ, verse 3. And Johannes Crocius refuted that gloss here on page 299. You will say, God chose us in Christ, not as Christ is man, but as he is God. But the Apostle sufficiently shows that he is speaking of Christ the incarnate Mediator, while he not only names Jesus Christ many times, but also makes mention of his blood in verse 7. Add that there is no reason why Christ should be considered otherwise here than in the preceding verse, where God is said to have blessed us in Christ. Is he considered there merely as God? Nay, as Mediator according to the promise: In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, Genesis XXII. 18. Nor does it stand in the way that in Colossians I. 16 all things are said to have been created in Christ as he is God. For the circumstances compel us to embrace that sense; here nothing compels us. Some, even Crocius himself, explain the text thus: Who predestined us, whom he would adopt as sons through JESUS CHRIST. But by the words εἰς ὑοθεσίαν it is indicated, not whom he predestined, but to what, namely to perfect adoption: which Crocius does not deny is hinted at here. There are those who indeed acknowledge that ἐν ἀυτῷ should be rendered as in him, but they explain it in such a to explain that God chose us in Christ, as members in the head, they wish, with Zanchius in his book on the nature of God, book V, chapter 2, and Polanus in his Didactica, page 41, that the order is shown, namely that the head was chosen first, then the members in the head. But the Apostle treats of our election, not indeed of the election of Christ, nor does he hand down here anything about such an order of election. Not to mention that this order does not agree with the hypotheses of the Calvinists, since they maintain that we were first chosen absolutely, and then the plan concerning our redemption through Christ and the ἀνακεφαλαιώσει was entered into, because God first willed the end, then ordained the means leading to the end. For which reason this explanation was rejected by Gomarus himself, Vol. II of his Works, fol. 61. And therefore others acknowledge that we were chosen in Christ as Mediator: But they say that something must be understood, namely, that God chose us in Christ the Mediator TO BE ADOPTED, which Beza adds. But it is not for us to add anything to Scripture: For if it were permissible, what would not be added eventually? What certainty would then be left in Scripture? He did not choose so that He might adopt us in Christ, as Piscator with Beza wishes, but He chose us in Christ to eternal life, as the Apostle has it. Whence Zanchius himself explains the words of the Apostle, God chose us in Christ, thus in the cited place, p. 673: that we were chosen on account of Christ: Or at least he concludes this from those words of the Apostle. But especially here Joh. Crocius in his Commentary, p. 282, adds his vote for us against the associates of the faith. There are those who say, He chose in Christ, that is, so that He might save through Christ, as Mediator, or that He destined to the obtaining of salvation in Christ. It pleases me more that the cause FOR WHICH God chose us be noted, so that the sense may be, He chose us in Christ, that is, through and on account of Christ, as the Helvetic Confession and Hyperius have it in this place. Thus election is founded on the satisfaction and merit of Christ. Great, I confess, he says p. 299, theologians both among the Papists and among us teach that not our election from the foreseen merit of Christ, but only the execution was done. But first the Apostle says expressly, He chose us in him, namely Christ. Therefore not only the execution of election, but also our election was done through Christ. For thus Chrysostom, Photius, and others everywhere accept it. Secondly, he says v. 8, he predestined us, whom he would adopt, through Jesus Christ. Therefore not only adoption, but also the predestination of adoption was done through Christ. Crocius therefore grants us the agreement not only of Chrysostom, Photius, and others, but also of Hyperius and the Helvetic Confession, which in chapter X (in the Syntagma Confessionum it is the prior Helvetic) has it thus: Therefore not without a medium, but not on account of any merit, but in Christ and on account of Christ God chose us. In the same opinion Joh. Crocius, in his defense part II of the Prussian conversion, page 225, also praised the Gallican Confession article XII, the later Anglican chapter XVII, the Scottish Art. VIII, and the Belgic Art. XVI, by which we are said to be chosen through Christ; And that in view of the merit of Christ, as a cause, God chose whomever He chose, Scripture clearly teaches, and reason sought from the word of God confirms it, says Crocius in the cited place. Scripture, he says, teaches, when it says we were chosen in Christ Eph. I. 4. For that is nothing other than that we were chosen through and on account of Christ. Namely, He satisfied for sin, and brought it about that He could choose sinners, whom He wished, without prejudice to His justice. Thus God is said to have blessed us in Christ in the same place: and reason confirms this: God is a consuming fire, Deut. IV. 24. Therefore to the sinner there is no access open to God, unless satisfaction is interposed. Therefore in satisfaction is founded the love of God, because He chooses certain ones to eternal life. In this sense, therefore, Christ is the cause of election. This is Crocius.

2. God is said προορίσας ἡμᾶς εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ εἰς ἀυτὸν: Predestining us into adoption through Jesus Christ into himself, that he chose us, where whether that διὰ Ἰησοῦ is joined with προορισμῷ, which is altogether more convenient if the words cohere in this way: προορίσας ἡμᾶς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς ἀυτὸν, predestining us through Jesus Christ into himself, i.e., to himself, εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, into the adoption of sons. For he predestined us to himself into sons and heirs, but he predestined through Christ: Or whether that διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ is connected with the words εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, it is manifest that the election in Christ, not outside of Christ, or without Christ, was done. For in the former way we are said to be predestined through and on account of Christ to adoption, which is to the plenary fruition of the power of the sons of God, and thus to eternal life. Therefore that predestination was not done from an absolute decree and good pleasure, but on account of the merit of Christ, and that apprehended by faith; because election and predestination is not universal, just as the merit of Christ is universal, but concerns only those who are about to obtain eternal life, who alone are believers. And therefore those who are predestined in view of faith or the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, or κατὰ πρόγνωσιν τῆς πίστεως, according to the foreknowledge of faith, were chosen, and not indeed from simple good pleasure and absolute grace, preceding all causes. In the latter way we are again said to be predestined to the adoption of the sons of God, that is, to eternal life, (for thus ὑιοθεσία is accepted Rom. VIII. 23.) not outside of Christ, but through and on account of Christ. Nor should that εἰς ἀυτὸν (which Castellio wrongly reads as εἰς αὑτὸν, 'into himself') be vexed with Calvin, Beza, and Hyperius; as if it were ἐν ἑαυτῷ, and it were indicated that the Lord looked at nothing outside himself, but predestined us εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, because he willed it. Crocius himself rejects this sense on page 285. The sense, he says, is not bad, which Zanchius would willingly retain if the interpretation of εἰς ἀυτὸν as ἐν ἑαυτῷ could be defended, but he fears that it cannot be defended. Piscator interprets it as 'to the glory of his grace.' But this end is expressed later in verse 6. Zanchius, therefore, following the Syriac interpreter, explains it thus: 'in himself,' that is, he decreed to adopt sons for himself. Since he had only one Son, and him natural, he willed this honor for himself from eternity, that in time he might assume many sons, and become the Father of many. Excellent. Nor do we allow the words 'through Christ' to be snatched away by the Calvinists to the execution, as if the προορισμὸς to adoption or eternal life were indeed made from absolute good pleasure, yet we are led to the same not without Christ, but διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ; because the matter here is about predestination to life, which was done not without Christ, but through and because of Christ, not about salvation; about the decree, I say, not about the execution of the decree: Nor should anything be thrust into the text here, as if we were said to be predestined to life through obtaining Christ, since it is not about the manner of obtaining eternal life, but about the decree of predestination to eternal life that is treated here, and how that formally stands, not how it is to be brought into effect, is taught: Although this too must be believed without doubt, that God leads us to eternal life in no other way than he chose us to eternal life, and that the execution is entirely conformable to the decree. If, however, God had predestined to life from his bare and absolute good pleasure those whom he willed, solely because it so pleased him to choose these or those, and no others, to eternal life, without regard to the merit of Christ or faith in Christ in those being chosen, it would also be necessary that those who are saved be saved without regard to the merit of Christ or faith in Christ. Which the Calvinists themselves acknowledge to be false. Wendelin further objects in his treatise on predestination, chapter XVII: The merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, is indeed a cause of salvation. But it is not therefore a cause of the decree of salvation. We admit that the decree of salvation and of election to life do not differ. But who would grant that the causes of the decree of life and of salvation are the same? But in this way God is necessarily established as mutable; if from eternity He decreed to save Peter, for example, and chose him to life, moved by no cause, and not even by the merit of Christ apprehended by Peter through faith: yet in time He willed to save him, moved by the merit of Christ apprehended through faith. For how could this happen without a change in the Divine will, that from eternity He willed Peter's salvation absolutely, moved by no impulsive cause; but in time He wills his salvation not absolutely, but moved by the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, as an impulsive cause or reason.

3. We seek an argument from the divine blessing, for just as we are blessed ἐν Χριστῷ (in Christ) with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places: so also God chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid; which sentiment shines forth written in the very text with solar rays: Εὐλογήσας ἡμᾶς ἐν Χριστῷ (having blessed us in Christ), καθὼς (just as) ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀυτῷ (He chose us in Him). But we are blessed in Christ for this reason, that our blessing comes to us not from an absolute good pleasure, but through Christ, so that Christ is the meritorious cause of our blessing. And therefore for the same reason we are also chosen in Christ, that is, because our election was made not by the absolute good pleasure of God, but through and because of Christ, so that Christ is the meritorious cause of our election. In Christ, says Crocius on page 281, that is, through and because of Christ, or through His satisfaction and merit, we obtain whatever we obtain. If we, as we are, or considered in ourselves, are worthy of a curse, through and because of ourselves we never obtain anything: for there is no merit of ours in the business of salvation. Christ, the only Redeemer of the human race, carries every point. Because of Him we have whatever we have. In Him we have what we do not yet have in ourselves. He is the seed in whom all nations were to be blessed, Gal. III. 14, 16. And page 297: Every spiritual blessing is to be sought in Christ alone, therefore not in the law, Gal. 3, 10, not in ourselves, Deut. 27, 20, not in other men, Act. 4, 12. It must be added, not in the absolute good pleasure of God, Gal. III, 8, 9.

4. From our love in Christ: Those who are not loved by God, except in Christ, or insofar as they are in Christ through faith, they are not chosen by God to eternal life. But men concluded under sin are not loved by God, except in Christ, or insofar as they are in Christ through faith. Therefore, men concluded under sin are not chosen by God to eternal life, except in Christ, or insofar as they are in Christ through faith. This argument is clear from the συνεχεία (continuity) of the text and the words of the Apostle: V. 6, ἐν ᾗ (χάριτι) ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (in which grace He graced us in the Beloved), He predestined us to adoption through Jesus Christ, etc., to the praise of the glory of His grace, in which He loved us or embraced us with grace in that Beloved (namely, His own Son), in whom we have redemption. As therefore God embraced and loved us with His grace, in Christ, apprehended by faith, not outside of Christ or faith in Christ: Because outside of Christ there is nothing but wrath and condemnation because of sin, Rom. 3, 9, ch. 11, 22, Gal. 3, 22, and without faith it is impossible to please God, or to be loved by God, Heb. 11, 6. So neither did God choose us to eternal life, except in Christ, apprehended by faith, because election was made out of love and grace. Let this alone be noted: that the love of God is one thing, universal and general, from which the mission of the Son of God proceeded, John III. 16, 1 John IV. 16, and another, spiritual and proper, to which election is to be ascribed, by which He

God ἐχαρίτωσε (graced) us, when He chose us to eternal life, which happens to the faithful ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (in that Beloved), that is, through and because of the only-begotten Son of God, as the Apostle testifies. For here the Apostle establishes that Beloved Son of God, and His ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption), as the meritorious cause of this love and grace for that reason. The Apostle uses the emphatic and new verb ἐχαρίτωσε, which is not found elsewhere in the New Testament in the active form, nor in the passive, except once concerning Mary, who in Luke I. 78 is called κεχαριτωμένη (highly favored), that is, freely loved, namely in that ἠγαπημένῳ (Beloved). Therefore, it is that He freely loved us, or God freely makes us pleasing to Himself. Namely, by a new verb, as Crocius says here, a new and indeed remarkable benefit is described here. By our corrupt nature and condition we were not pleasing to God, but children of wrath, Eph. II. 3, indeed enemies, Rom. V. 10, because of sin, which separates us from God, Is. LIX, nor could we be made pleasing by any virtue or merit of our own. For what is born of the flesh is flesh, John III. 6. And the mind of the flesh is enmity against God, Rom. VIII. 7. But neither could any mere creature make us pleasing, because none can blot out sin, from which all enmity arises. And yet we had to perish, unless we were made pleasing to God. Therefore, so that we would not perish, He Himself made us friends from enemies, when we were worthy of hatred in ourselves, and rendered us dear and accepted by His own goodness and glorious benevolence. But that was not done, except ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (in the Beloved), of whom Crocius further says: He names Christ as the cause for which God renders us dear to Himself. Indeed, the elect are also called ἠγαπημένοι (beloved), Col. III. 12. Beloved by the Lord, 2 Thess. II. 13. and beloved according to the election, Rom. XI. 28. But Christ is called that beloved by antonomasia, both because he is supremely beloved by the Father, and because those who are loved by the Father are loved through him, on account of him, and in him; no one is loved apart from or outside of him. Moreover, the Apostle added the word from the Father's sentence already long ago spoken through Isaiah, chap. 42, 2. Matt. 12, 18. and afterwards both at his baptism, Matt. 3, 17. and at his glorification, Matt. 17, 5. Mark 1, 11. 2 Pet. 1, 17. openly proclaimed from heaven. Those who seek the cause of their love either in themselves or in others, however holy and dear to God they may be, do not sufficiently consider this. He is the one Mediator between God and men, 1 Tim. 2, 5. Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven that has been given among men by which we must be saved, Acts 4, 12. This is Crocius: He ought to have added against the associates of his faith: Nor do those who assign that love and grace outside of Christ and faith in Christ, from the absolute good pleasure of God, sufficiently consider that sentence, because those who are loved by the Father are loved uniquely through him, on account of him, and in him; no one is loved apart from him or outside of him.

5. From the redemption made through the blood of Christ. If we are not redeemed except through the merit of Christ, then certainly we are not elected except through the merit of Christ: Because God chose us in Christ, because he loved us in him, and made us acceptable to himself, or reconciled us to himself in Christ. He truly loved us or reconciled us in Christ, because in him we have τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τῶ αἵματος ἀυτῶ: Redemption made through his blood. Election presupposes grace and love. Grace and love presuppose reconciliation with regard to those who, on account of sin, were under wrath. Reconciliation presupposes or brings about ἀπολύτρωσιν, redemption made by the price of the blood of Christ. For we have not been reconciled except through the blood of the Son of God, Rom. 5, 9. Redemption was made from the wrath of God, 1 Thess. 1, 10. Rom. 5, 9. from the power of the Devil, Col. 1, 13. 14. Heb. 2, 14. Luke 1, 71. from sin, Gal. 1, 4. Tit. 2, 14. 1. Pet. 1, 18. under whose power (namely, of the Devil, of sin, of the law, of death, and of hell) we were not, except by the force of the most just wrath of God, which we had deserved through sin. We were therefore to be redeemed and liberated from the wrath of God, and to be brought back into favor with God, and to be reconciled to Him through the intervention of the precious λύτρα (ransom) of the blood of Christ. Therefore, neither grace nor election had a place, or could have had one, without the ἀπολυτρώσει (redemption) of the blood of Christ, and the propitiation made through the blood of Christ our Mediator, 1 Tim. 2:6. Hence Crocius rightly says: The decree concerning the sending of Christ the Redeemer is in order prior to the decree of election; and page 305: Reconciliation was made in Christ alone, the fountain of all grace. The matter is clear. He is that beloved one, h.l. v. 6. Compare Rom. 5:10, Col. 1:20, 21, 22, 2 Cor. 5:19, 20.

6. From the remission of sins: If sins are not remitted to us out of absolute grace, but on account of Christ and His ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption), which is apprehended by faith, then certainly we were not chosen for eternal life through the absolute grace of God, but on account of Christ and His ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption), which is apprehended by faith. But the former is true. In whom, says the Apostle, we have the ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption) through His blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of His grace, that is, of that grace in which He has graced us in the Beloved, v. 5, 6. How we have the remission of sins, says Crocius, through the redemption of Christ, the Apostle does not indeed express here, yet elsewhere we read that we have it through faith. For God set forth Christ to be a propitiation through faith in His blood to declare His righteousness through the remission of sins, Rom. 4:25. and we conclude that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law, Rom. 3:28, with which that of Peter agrees: To this all the prophets give witness, that through His name whoever believes in Him shall receive remission of sins, Acts 10:43. Therefore the latter is also true. The consequence shines with its own light, both from the continuity of the Apostolic treatment and from the nature of the thing; because election to life and salvation presupposes the grace and love of God, who chooses us for eternal salvation. That electing grace of God is nothing, unless, as they say, in the sign of reason, the grace that forgives sins precedes it: because it is a greater thing to choose for life than to be willing to forgive sins: and that Divine grace, by which He wills to forgive us our sins and the punishment of sins, eternal death, on account of Christ, is altogether presupposed before the grace of God by which it pleased Him to predestine us to eternal life.

7. From the foundation of the Divine purpose. For the Apostle testifies in v. 9 that the divine purpose was not absolute, nor does it imply here an absolute εὐδοκίαν (good pleasure), as the Calvinists wish, but that the εὐδοκίαν (good pleasure) is founded on the merit of Christ: κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν ἁυτῦ ἧν προέθετο ἐν ἁυτῷ, according to that good pleasure which He had purposed (for Himself) in Him, namely, in Christ. For so the Codex Claromontanus, Chrysostom, Theophylact, B. Luther, Bullinger, etc., read. That, he says (as Theophylact says), He did according to His own will and pleasure, and as He purposed and predestined in Him, that is, in Christ.

8. From the ἀνακεφαλαιώσει (summing up) of all things in Christ. If in Christ, that is, through and on account of Christ and His merit, all who are in heaven and who are on earth are summed up through restoration, recollection under one head, and reduction to true unity in Him, then certainly election to eternal life was not made outside of Christ, but in Christ and on account of Christ: The reason for this consequence is: Because election, just like the mission of Christ, also presupposes the ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν (summing up) made through Christ; and it is necessary that this be prior in order to that in the divine decrees: For they are not chosen for eternal life unless those who have been restored, recollected under one head, and reduced to true unity, which indeed happens to all men if you look at the merit of Christ

and the intention and counsel of God: but if you look at the effect, to the faithful, or those who are in Christ through faith: who are said to be ἐν αὐτῷ, IN HIM, Rom. 8:1. We who were previously in the power of the Devil, are now joined to God, says Crocius. Concerning this ἀνακεφαλαιώσει (summing up) made through Christ, and His holy Angels: And these, when they were previously our enemies because of God offended by our sins, are henceforth friends. Now, however, not those who are in the society of the devil, but those who are joined to God, and His Angels, i.e., the faithful—for we are not joined to God except through faith—are chosen for eternal life. For no one is excluded from this recollection, except he who excludes himself by his own perfidy and fault, again as Crocius says. For the sentence of God is invariable: Whoever believes shall be saved, Mark 16:16. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also.

9. As we obtain an inheritance in Christ; so also we are predestined in Christ to that inheritance of eternal life. But we obtain the inheritance in Christ, insofar as we are in Christ through faith; since that inheritance does not come to us except through and on account of the merit of Christ, while we appropriate it to ourselves by faith. Which is certain from the article concerning justification by faith, and is placed outside of all controversy between us and the Calvinists. Therefore we are also predestined in Christ to the inheritance of eternal life, insofar as we are in Christ through faith. The major premise is established both from the harmony of the decree and the execution of the decree: and it is clear from the very words of the Apostle and that golden chain of salvation and predestination which is exhibited here: v. 11. in whom also we have obtained an inheritance, (as far as the right and certainty of the inheritance is concerned,) being predestined according to the divine purpose: because the obtaining of the inheritance and the predestination to the inheritance are thus connected, and both, having been made in Christ, are said to be in a like manner, which becomes even clearer from a comparison of v. 4 and 11. But it is most clear of all if that whole continuity is observed.

10. From the express mention of faith: Lest any doubt should remain, although all those things are above all doubt, the Apostle adds v. 12. εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, (predestinated according to his purpose) that we should be to the praise of his glory, τοὺς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ, who first trusted in Christ: What could have been said more clearly than this for faith foreseen, or election made from faith foreseen? For it is most well known from the received phrase of Scripture that by hope in Christ, trust in Christ is understood, and the following verse declares it sufficiently, that those hoping in Christ are called τοὺς πιστεύσαντας. Moreover, that πρὸ, in the word προηλπικότας, clearly indicates that we believed FIRST, as regards the order of foreknowledge and divine decrees; in the divine mind, than we were προορισθέντες predestinated κατὰ πρόθεσιν according to the purpose of God. For προορισμὸς was entirely made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν according to the foreknowledge of faith in Christ: Therefore indeed. we are called elect κατὰ πρόγνωσιν according to the foreknowledge of faith in Christ, 1 Pet. 1, 2. ὓς προέγνω, κὶ προώρισε, Rom. 8, 29. namely, God predestinated those to eternal life whom he foresaw would finally believe in Christ, τοὺς μέλλοντας πιστεύειν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ, εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, 1 Tim. 1, 16.

In the explanation of Grotius we find not a few things lacking, 1. that he explains election as vocation, and furthermore by vocation understands metonymically the decree of vocation. There is no need for these circumlocutions, since election can be understood properly, and indeed concerning the very decree of predestination. For thus election is called 1 Thess. 2, 13, and here it is explained by the same reasoning through predestination, viz. v. 5. προορίσας ἡμᾶς, and again v. 11. προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν. And since this is a common interpretation, it does not appear why from the same one must depart; which is also supported by the Calvinists in the Synod of Dort concerning divine predestination, art. I, can. VII & VIII. Nor indeed could a passage be brought forward in which election is the same thing as the decree of calling. We acknowledge that 'to elect' is used for various things, both in the Old and in the New Testament; but where election is taken for the decree of calling, Grotius has not shown, much less where it occurs for calling, in such a way that calling, signified by the word, denotes the decree of calling: Least of all where election denotes the decree of calling, to look at miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Which is held in 1 Thess. 1:4. 'Knowing, brethren beloved by God, τὴ έκλογὴν η̉μω̃ν our election' refers to the election of Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy to the sacred office, which the Thessalonians knew, or certainly could have known, from the efficacy of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ of them, v. 5. 2. That the word έν αὐτω̃ is to be taken concerning the meritorious cause, which we have hitherto proved, Grotius denies not obscurely; nay, he ineptly drags in here what the Apostles did in their calling, saying that Christ himself did it. For did the Apostles make the decree of calling πρὸ καταβολη̃ς κόσμέ? 3. It is irrelevant that Christ was prior to Abraham regarding his constitution. For it is not a question here of the constitution of Christ, but of our election in Christ: Nor is Christ said to be prior to Abraham in John 8:56 ff. by reason of ordination in the Divine decree, which is the gloss of the Socinians, but by reason of real pre-existence before Abraham, as was shown by us in a special disputation concerning the προυͤπάρξει before Abraham. 4. The discussion here is not about the most perfect Divine worship, to which God had proposed to lead man to Himself, having built up certain stages, but about the election of man to eternal life, made from eternity in Christ, the Son of God. In which way, if the Hebrew saying, which is the name of the Messiah, that is, the merit of the Son of God from eternity, be understood by reason of the divine intuition, it is correct: Because the Lamb of God was slain from the foundation of the world, Rev. 13:8. Nor is it alien to the truth that the law of God is eternal; but how the repentance of men is from eternity cannot be explained. 5. Calling is also wrongly explained by Grotius, concerning an extraordinary benefit, reserved for those who were to live in the times of the Messiah, or not long after: Where Grotius could not teach that calling is taken in that sense: But the calling to the kingdom of God does not only look to the times of the Messiah and those that followed not long after, but is of all times, Matt. 20 and 22. 6. The end of the calling and of the decree of calling is not established, either here or elsewhere, as that the called might be spectators of notable miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it a question here of the end of the calling, but of election and predestination, which is that we should be holy and blameless; to denote by these a greater probity and innocence than had been prescribed by the law is a Pelagian-Socinian error. Certainly, none greater than that can be imagined, since that is most perfect, so much so that it could not be performed by anyone after the fall, but had to be performed and was performed in our place by Christ alone, who was subject to the law. Similar is what Grotius says, that the 'all' of the Gospel is love. For the Gospel does not inform us about our charity, whether towards God or towards our neighbor, but the law does, insofar as it is distinguished from the Gospel in both tables, in the former concerning the love of God, in the latter concerning the love of our neighbor. But the Gospel is a discourse concerning the grace and love of God towards us, from which He gave us His only-begotten Son, who might fulfill the law for us, and redeem us from the curse of the law, and He 'made us accepted' (ἐχαρίτωσεν) in the Beloved, and in Him received us as sons and heirs of eternal life. But that miserable confusion of law and Gospel, the 'all' in these annotations of Grotius, obscuring the whole law, overturning the whole Gospel! 7. When Chrysostom warned that faith alone does not suffice, he did not mean that for obtaining eternal life it makes our life holy and blameless: But just as he explained 'he chose us in him' (ἐξέλεξατο ἐν αὐτῷ), he chose through faith in Christ, which John Crocius, although an enemy of faith foreseen in election, acknowledged and noted in his commentary on this passage. in this very Chrysostom and Theophylact is the same as 'through faith in him,' since because of the consonance of the decree and the execution, it is a consequence that we are not only chosen through faith in Christ, but also saved solely through faith in the merit of Christ, and by no means through our works. But Chrysostom indicates with Paul that faith alone does not suffice for one to be a true Christian, inasmuch as we are chosen through faith in Christ, not so that we may live as we please, but so that we may be holy and blameless. This is the end of election, but not the impulsive cause of election or salvation, which is the execution of the decree of election. For the Apostle places this solely in the merit of Christ, both here and elsewhere. It pleases me to transcribe the entire explanation of Theophylact, who is an epitomizer of Chrysostom, so that the matter may be clear: 'As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world: He blessed us (he says) through Christ, just as he also chose through the same, that is, through faith had in Christ. But he chose before the foundation of the world. Inasmuch as the things which are being done with us at this time were predestined from on high, not recently delivered, but prepared from the beginning.' He rightly introduced 'foundation' (καταβολὴν), which we interpret as foundation in Greek, and the interpreter said 'constitution' in Latin, to show that this world was let down and founded from a certain divine power and sublimity. 'But when he chose,' he says, he designates both the clemency of God and their virtue: inasmuch as God had set them apart, as those who would be upright. That we should be holy and immaculate in his sight: Lest perhaps that thought should enter the mind, that God has already chosen those whom he wills to be saved, and thus the mind should grow sluggish, thinking that there is nothing further to be striven for in virtue, so that one may attain life. Since they are already chosen according to the will of God, and there is no hope left for the others, he says to this: God chose us, that we might be holy, and without blemish, and that we might live in that holiness, which the Lord has bestowed upon those washed by baptism. Let us therefore persist, and let us keep a life endowed with virtue. For everyone who is a partaker of faith is holy: But he is immaculate, who in living is ensnared by no filth. Nor does God demand from us only this holiness and life free from fault, but that we should keep this very thing in his sight. Although holiness is required by these things, yet it is not in any way established by Theophylact as the cause of salvation. For it is so far from the case that Theophylact intended this, that he even explained ἀγάπην here not as our charity, but as God's, and expressly denied that salvation consists in our virtue, and ascribed it solely to Divine kindness. Blessedness, he says, is prepared by no labors, but by grace. Those who were of no value, says Chrysostom here, and deserved nothing, he found, in order to advance them to riches. What can be compared to this skillful ease? He who was an enemy, who was hateful, he suddenly ascends on high. J. Crocius preferred to explain ἀγάπην as the love of God, with which he loved us, along with Budaeus, and others after Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Augustine in his book on perfect justice, chapter 16, rather than with his own Calvin and Beza and Piscator and Ambrosiaster as the love of God and neighbor, so that the sense is, that God did not choose us for any merit of ours or cause that is in us, but because he loved us, nor does Bucer reject that sense, as neither do Haymo and Lombard. If anyone objects to the punctuation of the verses, it is easy for that ἐν ἀγάπῃ to be referred to the word ἐξελέξατο, he chose us in him through love. Nor does it stand in the way, in the judgment of Crocius, what Piscator objects, that the word chose is too remote. For it is not harsh for a word to be joined with a more remote, not with the nearest verb. Whatever, however, of that conjunction and composition may be, the Apostle indicated with a resonant voice that our election proceeded from the grace of God, and is by no means to be attributed to our works, when he asserts that we were chosen in Christ; when he asserts that we were chosen so that we might be holy and blameless; when he asserts that we were chosen for the praise of His grace, which made us pleasing to Him in that Beloved One. For if in Christ and because of Christ, then not because of our works, Gal. 3, 21. If so that we might be holy, then not because of our holiness as an impulsive cause; if for the praise of His grace, then not from works, Rom. 11, 6. Whence not a few even among the Papists themselves, even the Jesuits, acknowledge that our predestination was not made from works. Thomas on this passage: He posits the voluntary predestination of God, of which it is said in Rom. 8. Those whom He predestined, these He also called; the reason for which predestination is indeed not our works, but the mere will of God, for which reason he adds according to His purpose. Salmero T. XVI. disp. I. on 1 Pet. I. p. 53. Election to the end of possessing eternal life is firm and certain in itself, and does not depend on our works. Pererius on chapter VIII of Romans, disp. XXIII. That the foreknowledge of good works and the good use of free will is the cause of predestination seems contrary to divine scripture. Add also Bellarmine, book II, on grace and free will, chapters IX and XV, where he proves that men are chosen freely not only for grace, but also for glory. Which opinion Barradius also asserted, T. IV. Herm. book 4, chapter 18, praising Jerome's explanation of this passage: Paul does not say, He chose us when we were holy and immaculate, but He chose us so that we might be immaculate and holy, i.e., who were not holy and immaculate, so that we might be so afterwards: And St. Augustine on the predestination of the saints, chapter 7. God chose the faithful so that they might be, not because they were already holy. Scotus, Lychetus, Mayrous, Richardus, Aegidius, Capreolus, Bassolus, Cordubensis, Ferrariensis, Arrubel, Consaletus agree with these, according to Franc. Amicus Consentinus, T. I. Curs. Theol. disp. XV. s. 4. Suarezius, Tannerus, Estius and others: Although others among the Scholastics, Jesuits, and Papists go in the opposite direction, namely Alensis, Bonaventura, Albertus, Occam, Ruvio, Lessius, Becanus, Turrianus, Catharinus, Molina, according to the same Consentinus, who agrees with them, as also Piggias, Osorius, Tapperus, Driedo, Eccius, Stapletonus, Gregor. de Valentia according to Becanus in Theol. Schol. part. I. tr. 1. cap. 14. p. 146. 9. This is still to be observed, that that end, so that we might be holy and immaculate in His sight, is explained by some not only regarding holiness begun, but also imputed, which we have in Christ. For therefore, says the blessed Balduinus, God had the purpose of saving men, so that through the merit of Christ we might appear holy in the judgment of God, and might please Him even with the begun integrity of our life. And this is said to happen in the sight of God, because before the world that perfect holiness and integrity of life, which the faithful have from the obedience of Christ, does not appear. But God in His judgment recognizes that perfection which is subjectively in Christ, but becomes ours through the imputation of faith. Some also take this regarding consummated holiness, which likewise was not disapproved by the blessed Balduinus: Some, he says, interpret 'so that we might be holy, etc.' as 'so that we might be saved,' just as they say it is to be taken in Eph. 5, 26. 27, as also in Col. 1, 20. 21. 22. 23, and they understand that which is added about charity as the charity of God, through which we were chosen. Nor is the interpretation entirely inept. For the ultimate end of election is our salvation, where our holiness will be truly perfect and blameless. See Joh. Arnoldus Corvinus in the defense of Arminius against Tilenus, page 214. Conf. also the blessed Hunnius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καθὼς ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀυτῷ) Hic decretum sumit nomen actus, ut infra II. 6. & 2. Timoth. I. 9. Vocatio- ni interdum postponitur electio. Sed & ipsa vocatio est electio quædam, id est, beneficium quoddam eximium, ducens ad vitam æternam: cujus generis quæ sunt be- neficia, illa omnia tam nunc recte sub electionis nomi- ne veniunt, quam olim ea, quæ ad hujus vitæ commoda & honores spectabant. ἐν ἀυτῷ, per ipsum. Nam & quod Apostoli hac in re fecere, Christi fecere mandato, adeo, ut Christus ipse id fecisse dicatur Act. XIII. 47. Joh. XII. 32. Per ipsum, non per Mosen.

Πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) Judæi electionem suam ab Abrahamo auspicantur, eaque se jactant antiquitate, aut & interdum ab exitu ex Aegypto, quod tempus dici- tur קדם Psalm. LXXIV. 2. At in constitutione divina multo prior fuit Abrahamo Christus, ut ipse docet Johan. VIII. 56. & sequentibus. καταβάλλεσθαι est jacere funda- menta Hebræor. VI. 1. יסד hinc καταβολὴ de domo dici- tur 2. Macc. II. 30. & per similitudinem de mundo Matth. XIII. 35. XXV. 34. Luc. XI. 50. Johan. XVII. 24. Hebr. IV. 3. IX. 26. 1. Petr. I. 20. Apoc. XIII. 8. XVII. 8. Solet scri- ptura de Deo, ut de homine loqui. Homo domum stru- cturus prius usum ejus animo figurat. DEUS mundum conditurus hominis causa, hominem vero ut DEUM coleret, cultum quendam perfectissimum sibi proposuit, ad quem, præstructis gradibus quibusdam, hominem esset perducturus, idque per filium suum. Simili modo Hebræi dicunt, ante mundum fuisse legem, pœnitentiam & nomen Messiæ. Sic mysterium Evangelii dicitur abs- conditum ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων infra III. 4. Coloss. I. 28. πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων 1. Corinth. II. 7. quod ipsum dicitur κεκρυμ- μένον ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου dicto loco Matth. XIII. 35. Gratia data, id est dari destinata πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων 2. Tim. I. 9. quod idem valet atque regnum paratum ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου Matth. XXV. 34. gloria Christo data πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου Johan. XVII. 24. Christus προεγνωσμένος, id est, prædecretus πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου 1. Petr. I. 20.

Εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον ἀυτῶ ἐν ἀγά- πῃ) Subauditur hic εἰς τὸ, ostendit, quo tendat vocatio illa prius in decreto, deinde in actu, nempe ut sic voca- ti edant magnæ pietatis opera, & ab omni crimine va- cent. In veteri lege arietes & boves, qui Deo offerebantur, debebant esse תמימים ἄμωμοι Exod. XXIX. 2. Levit. I. 7. 10. III. 1. 6. & alibi sæpe. Christiani nunc semet offerunt Roman. XII. 1. Aequum ergo est, ut & ipsi sint ἄμωμοι, Infra vers. 27. Coloss. I. 21. Judæ 24. Marci XIV. 5. sive ἀμώμητοι, ut Philipp. II. 15. 2. Petr. III. 14. sive ἄμεμ- πτοι ut Philipp. II. 15. 1. Thessal. III. 13. Eximia & probi- tas & innocentia requiritur, ut plenum sortiatur effectum il- la tam admiranda vocatio. Hæc autem duo optime com- prehenduntur in nomine dilectionis, in qua est Evange- lii τὸ πᾶν. Et recte additur κατενώπιον ἀυτῶ. Nam & ani- mi puritas requiritur, quam solus Deus inspicit.

Hactenus, quæ in Annotatis ad hanc Epi- stolam Grotius. Subjungimus nunc ea, quæ in altero loco de hisce tradidit.

Vers. 4.

Καθὼς ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀυτῷ, sicut elegit nos in ipso) Rem novam esse Evangelium objectabant & Judæi & pagani, ideo multis in locis ostendit fluxisse hoc ex vetustissimo decreto, quod sæpe & ex typis veteribus & ex prædictionibus probat. Eligere ut in sermone communi, ita in sacris literis varios habet si- gnificatus. Est electio ad vitam suavem, & diuturnam, ad possessionem terræ uberrimæ, ad legis cognitio- nem, ad regnum, ad sacerdotium, ad prophetiam, ad libertatem reditumque in patriam, ad alia. In no- vo autem fœdere electio multa itidem significat, ut est electio ad Apostolicum munus, ad legationem ali- quam, ad functionem Diaconi. Sæpe electio signifi- cat approbationem eorum, qui Evangelio credunt, ut videre est maxime Jacob. II. 5. quo recte referas & illa 1. Corinth. I. 27. 28. & 2. Thessal. II. 13. & ad Romanos multa. Hoc vero loco videtur significari vo- catio per Christum sive per Evangelium ejus: sicut con- tra illa credentium electio vocatio interdum dicitur, ut 1. Corinth. I. 24. 26. Non immerito autem electionis voce indicatur beneficium illud eximium, reservatum iis, qui Messiae temporibus, aut non multo post erant victuri, & spectatores futuri tot miraculorum ac dono- rum Spiritus Sancti. Sic ἐκλογῆς vox sumitur 1. Thess. I. 4. sed & hoc hic notandum est, hic non ipsam voca- tionem notari, sed de vocandis Judaeis & gentibus, atque inter eas etiam Ephesiis decretum per μετωνυμίαν satis frequentem, quae consilio dat effectus nomen. Simili ferme modo Paulus 2. Tim. I. 9. ait χάριν, δοθεῖ- σαν ἡμῖν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων gratiam, quae data est nobis in Christo Jesu ante tempora secularia. Et mox dicturus est cap. II. 6. nos a Deo collocatos in locis coelestibus per Christum. Quem in sensum & Au- gustinus locum Joh. XVII. 5. exponit.

Πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, ante mundi constitutionem) Non temere quibusvis Dei decretis adjectam hanc no- tam reperias, sed eximiis, comparatione ab iis sumpta, qui domum structuri omnem ejus usum animo sibi prae- figurant, & ad id cuncta dirigunt. Vide Matth. XXV. 34. Johan. XVII. 24. 1. Petr. I. 20. Sic ἑξ αἰῶνος à se- culo Eccles. I. 40. ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος Actor. XV. 18. ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων à seculis hac epistola III. 9. & Coloss. I. 26. πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, ante secula 1. Cor. II. 7. πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων ante tempora secularia 2. Tim. I. 9. Tit. I. 2. Hoc sen- su ajunt Hebraei legem, nomen Messiae & poenitentiam fuisse ante mundum conditum. Vide si libet titulum Thalmudicum de Votis, & Rabbi Israelem. Καταβάλ- λεσθαι est jacere fundamentum. Ab ea similitudine κα- ταβολὴ κόσμου initium mundi conditi locis jam dictis, & Matth. XIII. 35. Luc. XI. 50. Hebr. IV. 3. IX. 26. Apo- cal. XIII. 8. XVII. 8.

Εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀ- γάπῃ, ut essemus sancti & immaculati in conspectu ejus in charitate) ἔσεσθαι vocularum εἰς τὸ vel πρὸς τὸ ut sae- pe. Huc scilicet & spectat decretum vocandi, & ipsa per Evangelium vocatio, ut qui vocationi obtempe- rant, eximia quadam fulgeant probitate atque inno- centia, quae Deo placeat, procedens quippe ex animo Deum diligente, tum ob beneficia jam praestita, tum ob sperata ab ipso praemia. Bene ad hunc locum Chryso- stomus: Ἱνα τοίνυν μὴ ἀκύσας, ὄτι ἐξελέξατο τὴν πίστιν ἀρκεῖν νομίσῃς μόνον, καὶ τὸν βίον προστίθησι, ne igitur cum audiis, elegit, fidem solam sufficere existimes, adjecit & vi- tam. Sicut quidam sunt ἄμεμπτοι sine querela, secun- dum Mosis legem Luc. I. 6. Phil. III. 6. sic sunt quidam secundum Evangelii praescripta ἄμεμπτοι Phil. II. 15. 1. Thess. II. 10. III. 13. ἀμώμητοι sive ἄμωμοι immacu- lati, hic infra V. 27. Phil. II. 15. Coloss. I. 22. 1. Petr. III. 14. Judae 24. Apoc. XIV. 5. abstinentes scilicet ab omni- bus illis culpis, quae hominem ab Evangelico foedere excludunt, quo sensu etiam dicuntur non peccare 1. Jo- han. III. 6. 9.

Orditur in enumeratione benedictionum spi- ritualium ab aeterno Dei decreto, electione ad vi- tam aeternam, & progreditur dehinc ad ea, quae in tempore nobis obtingunt. Non quod electio eorum causa sit, quod Calviniani volunt; sed quod illa ab aeterno facta sit, haec vero in tempo- re fiunt, quodque illa per haec deinceps declaran- da sit, nec nisi e temporalibus benedictionibus nobis innotescat: quibus ad beatitudinem illam, ad quam ab aeterno praedestinati sumus, perdu- cimur. Sequitur etiam apud Apostolum electio- nem προορισμὸς εἰς ὑοθεσίαν, non quod electio prior sit ordine naturae hac praeordinatione vel praedesti- natione, vel causa ejusdem sit: Sed quod ad e- jus explicationem faciat. Nam electio & praede- stinatio mutuo explicant sese, ac veluti Synony- ma sunt; ideo quod hic ἐξελέξατο dixit Apostolus, Rom. VIII. 29. 30. verbo προώρησεν expressit, & ἐκλογὴν jam dicit factam προορισμῶ, electionem praedestinatione, ἐξελέξατο προορίσας elegit prae- destinando, electionem autem illam non factam esse absolute, quasi ex simplici beneplacito aliquos absolute ad ὑοθεσίαν, vel ad vitam aeternam, prae- destinarit atque elegerit, nec ob opera vel meri- ta hominum, sed ob Christum ejusque meritum vera fide apprehensum, adeoque non electos esse, quos sive ex nudo beneplacito, sive ob prævisa opera ipsorum bona prædestinavit ad æternam vitam, sed quos prævidit finaliter in Christum credituros, vel in fide Christi decessuros, è loco præsenti luculenter constat: Non quod fides, qua actus noster vel opus est, sit causa impulsiva electionis; sed quum fides nihil aliud sit, quam meriti Christi apprehensio, quod meritum Christi unice causa impulsiva sit, qua fideles id sibi appropriant, & ab æterno Deus prævidit, hos vel illos sibi id appropriaturos, & in ea fide decessuros: Quia 1. ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν χριστῷ elegit nos non sine Christo aut intuitu meriti Christi, quod nostrum non est, nisi per fidem vel applicationem: Sed in Christo Jesu, scil. quatenus in Christo per fidem suos fore prævidit. Non elegit, ut essemus in Christo, quemadmodum elegisse nos dicitur, ut sancti essemus, & immaculati coram ipso in charitate: Sed elegit in Christo, vel quia in Christo sumus in προγνώσει divina. Particula enim ἐν infert causam impulsivam: Vid. Matth. VI. 7. Actor. VII. 29 Ephes. III. 13. quemadmodum Ebræorum ב in solet idem esse, quod διὰ propter: Vid. Gen. XXIX. 18. Deut. XIV. 16. Neque aliter hic quam de causa impulsiva accipi potest, in ipso, hoc est, propter ipsum.

Varias quidem adversas explicationes quærunt Calviniani, sed nullam consonantem & constantem inveniunt. Nam quod primo Maccovius in coll. Theol. quæst. de prædest. disp. VI. trajectjonem statuit, quasi verba ita sint constituenda: Elegit nos, ut essemus sancti & inculpati IN ipso, id coactum nimis est, & verba illa, ut essemus sancti, ad finem electionis pertinent. Vox autem ἐν ἀυτῷ ad electionis formam vel quidditatem definiendam adhibita est, non ad finem ejusdem. Quod vero secundo Contra-Remonstr. in Coll. Hag. pag. 72. & Gomarus Tom. III. Op. disp. X. th. LVII. verbis ἐν ἀυτῷ notari volunt causam efficientem Principalem, ut sit idem, quod δι᾽ ἀυτõ per ipsum tanquam cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto causam seu Autorem prædestinationis; Non convenit sive verbis, quia nuspiam ἐν ἀυτῷ id est, quod ab ipso, vel δι᾽ ἀυτõ, sive textui, quia autor electionis voce ὁ θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τõ κυρίꙋ ἡμῶν ἰησõ χριστõ designatus est v. 3. Et confutavit illam glossam hic Johan. Crocius pag. 299. Dices, Deum nos elegisse in Christo, non qua Christus homo est, sed qua Deus. Atqui Apostolus satis ostendit, se loqui de Christo Mediatore incarnato, dum non solum multoties Jesum Christum nominat, sed & ejus sanguinis mentionem facit vers. 7. Adde quod nulla causa sit, cur aliter hic consideretur Christus, quam versu præcedente, ubi Deus dicitur nobis benedixisse in Christo. Num ibi consideratur nude, qua Deus? Imò qua Mediator juxta promissionem: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terræ Genes. XXII. 18. Nec obstat, quod Coloss. I. 16. omnia dicuntur in Christo, qua Deus est, condita. Circumstantiæ enim cogunt, nos illum sensum amplecti, hic nulla cogit. Nonnulli, etiam Crocius ipse, textum sic exponunt: Qui prædestinavit nos, quos adoptaret in filios per JESUM CHRISTUM. Sed per verba εἰς ὑοθεσίαν indicatur, non quos prædestinarit, sed ad quid, ad adoptionem puta perfectam: quam hic innui non diffitetur Crocius. Sunt qui agnoscant quidem, ἐν ἀυτῷ reddendum esse in ipso, sed id ita explica- explicare, quod in Christo, ut membra in capite, nos elegerit Deus, velint cum Zanchio de nat. Dei libr. V. cap. 2. & Polano in Didafc. pag. 41. quod scilicet ordo monstretur, primum caput esse electum, de- inde membra in capite. Sed Apostolus de electio- ne nostri, non verò de electione Christi agit, nec de ordine tali electionis hic quidquam tradit. Ut taceam, quod ordo ille non conveniat hypothefi- bus Calvinianorum, cum statuant, primum nos absolutè electos esse, deinde verò confilium de no- stri redemptione per Christum & ἀνακεφαλαιώσει initum, quod primum Deus finem voluerit, deinde media ad finem ducentia ordinarit. Ex qua causa à Gomaro ipso T. II. Oper. fol. 61. hæc explicatio reprobata est. Ideoque alii agnoscunt, in Christo ut Mediatore nos electos esse: Sed subaudiendum esse aliquid ajunt, nimirum, elegisse nos Deum, in Christo Mediatore ADOPTANDOS, quod Beza addit. Sed nostrum non est, Scripturæ aliquid ad- dere: Quod si integrum fit, ecquid non adderetur tandem? Quæ certitudo tùm relinqueretur in scriptura? Non elegit, ut in Christo adoptaret nos, ut Piscator cum Beza vult, sed elegit nos in Christo ad vitam æternam, ut habet Apostolus. Unde Zan- chius ipse verba Apostoli, Deus elegit nos in Christo, sic explicat l. c. p. 673. nos propter Christum electos esse: Vel certe ex illis Apostoli verbis hoc conclu- dit. Sed imprimis hic calculum suum nobis contra fidei socios adjicit Joh. Crocius in Com̃ent. p. 282. Sunt, qui dicunt, elegisse in Christo, id est, ut per Christum, tanquam Mediatorem, servaret, vel de- stinasse ad salutem in Christo adipiscendam. Mi- hi magis placet, notari causam PROPTER QVAM nos Deus elegerit, ut sensus sit, elegit nos in Christo, id est, per & propter Christum, ut habet confessio Helve- tica & Hyperius in h. l. Ita fundatur electio in Chri- sti satisfactione & merito. Magni fateor, inquit p. 299. tum inter Papistas, tum inter nos Theologi non electionem nostram ex merito Christi præviso, sed so- lam executionem factam esse docent. Atqui primo di- cit Apostolus disertè, elegit nos in ipso, scilicet Christo. Ergo non tantùm executio electionis, sed & electio no- stra per Christum facta est. Sic enim Chrysostomus, Photius & alii passim accipiunt. Secundo dicit v. 8. prædestinavit nos, quos adoptaret, per Jesum Chri- stum. Non igitur solùm adoptio, sed & prædestinatio adoptionis facta est per Christum. Largitur ergo Crocius nobis consensum non solum Chrysostomi, Photii, & aliorum, sed etiam Hyperii & confessionis Helveticæ, quæ cap. X. (in Syntagm. Conf. est prior Helvetica) ita habet: Ergo non sine medio, sed non propter ullum meritum, sed in Christo & propter Christum nos elegit Deus. In eandem sententiam laudavit Joh. Crocius defens. part. II. convers. Pru- ten. pag. 225. etiam Confess. Gallicam artic. XII. Anglicanam posteriorem cap. XVII. Scoticam Art. IIX. & Belgicam Art. XVI. qua per Christum electi dicimur; Et intuitu meriti Christi, tanquam causæ, electos esse, quoscunque elegit Deus, Scripturam cla- re docere, & rationem ex verbo Dei petitam id confir- mare, ait Crocius l. c. Scriptura, inquit, docet, cum nos in Christo electos esse dicit Eph. I. 4. Idenim ni- bil aliud est, quam per & propter Christum nos ele- ctos esse. Nempe ille satisfecit pro peccato, & effecit, ut posset peccatores, quos vellet, salva sua justitia eli- gere. Ita dicitur Deus benedixisse nobis in Chri- sto ibidem: idque ratio confirmat: Deus est ignis consumens, Deut. IV. 24. Peccatori igitur non patet ad Deum accessus, nisi interposita satisfactione. Ergo in satisfactione fundatur dilectio Dei, quod quos- dam ad vitam æternam eligit. Hoc ergò sensu Chri- stus est causa electionis. Hæc Crocius.

2. Dicitur Deus προορίσας ἡμᾶς εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ εἰς ἀυτὸν: Prædestinans nos in adoptionem per Jesum Christum in ipsum nos elegisse, ubi sive cum προορισμῷ conjugatur illud διὰ Ἰησοῦ, quod convenientius omnino est, si hoc modo cohærent verba: προορίσας ἡμᾶς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς ἀυτὸν, prædestinans nos per Jesum Christum in sese, i. e. sibi ipsi, εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, in adoptionem filiorum. Nam prædestinavit nos sibiipsi in filios & hæredes, sed prædestinavit per Christum: Sive connectatur illud διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ cum vocibus εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, electionem in Christo, non extra Christum, aut sine Christo factam esse, manifestum est. Nam priori modo prædestinati per & propter Christum dicimur ad adoptionem, quod ad plenariam fruitionem τῆς ἐξουσίας filiorum Dei, adeoque ad vitam æternam. Non ergo facta est illa prædestinatio ex absoluto decreto & beneplacito, sed propter Christi meritum, idque fide apprehensum; quia electio & prædestinatio non est universalis, quemadmodum meritum Christi universale est, sed concernit eos solum, qui vitam æternam consecuturi, qui soli credentes sunt. Ideoque qui prædestinati sunt intuitu fidei seu meriti Christi, fide apprehensi, vel κατὰ πρόγνωσιν τῆς πίστεως, secundum prævisionem fidei electi sunt, non vero ex simplici beneplacito & gratia absoluta, omnes causas antegrediente. Posteriori modo iterum prædestinati dicimur ad adoptionem filiorum Dei, hoc est, ad vitam æternam, (sic enim ὑιοθεσία accipitur Rom. IIX. 23.) non extra Christum, sed per & propter Christum. Nec illud εἰς ἀυτὸν, (quod Castellio male legit εἰς αὑτὸν in eundem) cum Calvino, Beza & Hyperio vexandum; quasi sit ἐν ἑαυτῷ, ac indicetur, Dominum nihil extra seipsum spectasse, sed prædestinasse nos εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν, quia voluerit. Quem sensum reprobat ipse Crocius pag. 285. Sensus, inquit, non malus, quem Zanchius libenter retineret, si defendi posset interpretatio εἰς ἀυτὸν pro ἐν ἑαυτῷ, at veretur, ut possit defendi. Piscator interpretatur ad gloriam gratiæ suæ. Atqui hic finis postea exprimitur vers. 6. Zanchius igitur Syriacum interpretem secutus, sic exponit, in sese, id est, sibi ipsi filios adoptare decrevit. Cum unum tantum haberet Filium, eumque naturalem, ab æterno hunc honorem sibi voluit, ut in tempore assumeret multos filios, multorumq; fieret Pater. Optime. Neque verba per Christum permittimus cum Calvinianis abripi ad executionem, quasi προορισμὸς ad ὑιοθεσίαν vel æternam vitam quidem ex absoluto beneplacito factus sit, ad eandem tamen perducamur non sine Christo, sed διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ; quia agitur hic de prædestinatione ad vitam, quæ facta non sine Christo, sed per & propter Christum, non de salvatione, de decreto inquam, non de executione decreti: Nec ingerendum hic quicquam textui, quasi dicamur prædestinati ad vitam per Christum consequendam, quum non de modo consecutionis vitæ æternæ, sed de decreto prædestinationis ad vitam æternam hic agatur, & quomodo illud sese habeat formaliter, non quomodo in effectum id deducendum sit, doceatur: Quanquam & hoc indubitato credendum sit, non aliter ad vitam æternam nos Deum perducere, quam elegit nos ad æternam vitam, & executionem omnino conformem esse decreto. Si autem ex nudo & absoluto beneplacito prædestinasset Deus ad vitam, quos voluit, solum, quia ita placuit, hos vel illos, non alios, ad vitam æternam eligere, sine intuitu meriti Christi, aut fidei in Christum in eligendis, necessum esset etiam, eos, qui salvantur, sine intuitu meriti Christi, aut fidei in Christum salvari. Quod falsum esse agnoscunt ipsi Calviniani. Obvertit adhuc Wendelinus tr. de prædest. cap. XVII. Meritum Christi fide apprehensum est quidem causa salvationis. At decreti salvationis propterea causa non est. Admittimus decretum salvationis & electionis ad vitam non differre. Easdem vero & vitæ decreti & salvationis esse causas, quis concesserit? Sed ita necessario Deus constituitur mutabilis; Si ab æterno quidem Petrum v.g. decreverit salvare, & ad vitam elegerit, nulla motus causa, ac ne merito quidem Christi à Petro fide apprehenso: In tempore autem voluerit ipsum salvare, motus Christi merito per fidem apprehenso. Quomodo enim hoc absque mutabilitate voluntatis Divinæ fieri potuit, ut ab æterno quidem voluerit Petri salutem absolute nulla motus causa impulsiva; In tempore autem ipsius salutem velit non absolute, sed motus Christi merito, fide apprehenso, ceu causa vel ratione impulsiva.

3. Argumentum petimus à divina benedictione, ut enim benedicimur ἐν Χριστῷ in omni benedictione spirituali in supercœlestibus: Ita etiam elegit nos Deus in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta; quæ sententia solis radiis scripta in ipso textu effulget: Εὐλογήσας ἡμᾶς ἐν Χριστῷ, καθὼς sicut ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀυτῷ. At benedicimur in Christo, hac ratione, quod non ex absoluto beneplacito, sed per Christum nobis obtingat benedictio nostra, ut Christus sit causa meritoria nostræ benedictionis. Ideoque eadem ratione etiam in Christo electi sumus, hoc est, quia non absoluto Dei beneplacito, sed per & propter Christum facta est nostri electio, ita ut Christus electionis nostræ causa meritoria sit. In Christo, inquit Crocius pag. 281. id est, per & propter Christum, seu per ejus satisfactionem & meritum consequimur, quicquid consequimur. Si nos, tanquam nos, seu in nobis ipsis consideremur, digni sumus maledictione, per & propter nos nihil unquam impetramus: Nullum enim est nostrum meritum in negotio salutis. Omne punctum fert Christus, unicus generis humani Redemptor. Propter illum habemus, quicquid habemus. In illo habemus, quod in nobis nondum habemus. Ille est semen, in quo gentes omnes benedicendæ erant, Gal. III. 14. 16. Et pag. 297. Omnis spiritualis benedictio quærenda in solo Christo, non igitur in lege, Gal. 3, 10. non in nobis, Deut. 27, 20. non in aliis hominibus, Act. 4, 12. Addendum, non in absoluto Dei beneplacito, Gal. III, 8. 9.

4. E nostri in Christo dilectione: Qui non diliguntur à Deo, nisi in Christo, vel qua per fidem in Christo sunt, illi non electi sunt à Deo ad vitam æternam. At homines sub peccatum conclusi non diliguntur à Deo, nisi in Christo, vel qua per fidem in Christo sunt. Ergo homines sub peccatū conclusi non electi à Deo sunt nisi in Christo, vel qua per fidem in Christo sunt, ad vitā æternam. Quod argumentum è συνεχεία textus & verbis Apostoli luculentum est: V. 6. ἐν ᾗ (χάριτι) ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, prædestinavit nos ad adoptionem per Jesum Christum &c. ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, in qua nos dilexit vel gratia complexus est in dilecto illo, (Filio scil. suo) in quo habemus redemptionem. Uti ergo gratia sua complexus est & dilexit Deus, in Christo, fide apprehenso, non extra Christum, aut fidem in Christum: Quia extra Christum non est nisi ira & condemnatio ob peccatum, Rom. 3, 9. cap. 11, 22. Gal. 3, 22. & sine fide impossibile est Deo placere, aut à Deo diligi, Ebr. 11, 6. Ita nec elegit nos Deus ad vitam æternam, nisi in Christo, per fidem apprehenso, quia electio facta est ex dilectione & gratia. Id solum notetur: Dilectionem Dei aliam esse universalem & generalem, ex qua missio Filii Dei profecta, Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. IV. 16. aliam spiritualem & propriam, cui adscribenda est electio, qua nos

ἐχαρίτωσε Deus, cum elegit nos ad vitam æter- nam, quæ ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, in dilecto illo, h. e. per & propter Filium Dei Unigenitum fidelibus contin- git, teste Apostolo. Hujus enim dilectionis & gra- tiæ causam meritoriam hic ea ratione constituit A- postolus dilectum illum Dei Filium, ejusque ἀπο- λύτρωσιν. Utitur Apostolus verbo emphatico & novo ἐχαρίτωσε, quod in Activa forma alibi non reperitur in Novo Testamento, nec in Passiva, nisi semel de Maria, quæ Luc. I. 78. κεχαριτωμένη, id est, gratis dilecta dicitur, sc. in illo ἠγαπημένῳ dilecto. Est ergo illud gratis dilexit nos, vel gratis sibi effe- cit Deus gratos. Nempe novo verbo, ut hic Crocius, novum idq́; insigne beneficium hic describitur. Natu- ra nostra corrupta conditione non eramus Deo grati, sed iræ filii, Eph. II. 3. hostes quippe, Rom. V. 10. pro- pter peccatum, quod nos à Deo separat, Es. LIX. nec virtute aut merito ullo nostro poteramus fieri grati. Quod enim ex carne natum est, caro est, Joh. III. 6. Et intelligentia carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum, Rom. VIII. 7. Sed nec ulla nuda creatura poterat nos gratos efficere, quia nulla potest delere peccatum, un- de omnis inimicitia. Et tamen pereundum nobis erat, nisi Deo grati efficeremur. Ne igitur periremus, ipsa nos ex inimicis fecit amicos, cum in nobis essemus odio digni, charos acceptosq́; reddidit sua bonitate & be- nevolentia gloriosa. Id vero non factum est, nisi ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, in dilecto, de quo porro Crocius: Causam propter quam Deus sibi charos reddit, Chri- stum nominat. Dicuntur quidem etiam electi ἠγα- πημένοι, Col. III. 12. ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ Κυρίε, 2. Thess. II. 13. & κατὰ τὴν ἐκλογὴν ἀγαπητοὶ, Rom. XI. 28. at Christus per ἀντονομασίαν ille dilectus dicitur, tum quia summe dilectus Patri, tum quia, qui à Patre di- liguntur, per illum, propter illum, & in illo dilicun- tur, nemo citra, aut extra illum diligitur. Accessit au- tem Apostolus vocem à Patris sententia jam olim di- cta per Esaiam, cap. 42, 2. Matth. 12, 18. & postea tum in baptismo, Matth. 3, 17. tum in glorificatione, Matth. 17, 5. Marc. 1, 11. 2. Pet. 1, 17. è cælo palam pro- nuntiata. Quam non satis illi considerant, qui vel in seipsis, vel in aliis, quamvis sanctis & Deo charis, dile- ctionis suæ causam quærunt. Ille unus est Mediator inter Deum & homines, 1. Tim. 2, 5. Nec in alio quo- quam salus, nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos ser- vari, Act. 4, 12. Hæc Crocius: Addere debuit con- tra fidei suæ socios: Nec satis illam sententiam considerant, qui dilectionem & gratiam illam ex- tra Christum & fidem in Christum, ex absoluto Dei beneplacito assignant, quia qui à Patre dili- guntur unice per illum, propter illum & in illo di- liguntur, nemo citra illum, aut extra illu diligitur.

5. A redemptione per sanguinem Christi facta. Si non sumus redempti nisi per Christi meritum, utique nec electi sumus, nisi per meritum Christi: Quia elegit nos Deus in Christo, quod dilexerit nos in ipso, & gratos sibi nos effecerit, vel recon- ciliarit sibi in Christo. Dilexit vero nos vel recon- ciliavit hos in Christo, quia in ipso habemus τὴν ἀ- πολύτρωσιν διὰ τῶ αἵματος ἀυτῶ: Redemptionem per sanguinem ejus factam. Electio præsupponit gratiam & dilectionem. Gratia & dilectio præsup- ponit reconciliationem quoad eos, qui propter peccatum erant sub ira. Reconciliatio præsuppo- nit vel infert ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem pretio sanguinis Christi factam. Non enim reconciliati su- mus, Nisi per sanguinem filii Dei, Rom. 5, 9. Redem- tio facta est ab ira Dei, 1. Thess. 1, 10. Rom. 5, 9. à po- testate Diaboli, Col. 1, 13. 14. Ebr. 11, 14. Luc. 1, 71. à peccato, Gal. 1, 4. Tit. 2, 14. 1. Petr. 1, 18. sub quo- rum potestate (Diaboli nempe, peccati, legis, mor- tis & inferni) non eramus, nisi vi iræ Dei justissi- mæ, quam per peccatum promeriti eramus. Ab ira ergo Dei redimendi & liberandi eramus, ac cum Deo in gratiam reducendi, eique reconciliandi in- terventu pretiosi λύτρα sanguinis Christi. Quapro- pter nec gratia, nec electio locum habuit, aut ha- bere potuit, sine ἀπολυτρώσει sanguinis Christi, & propitiatione facta per Christi Mediatoris nostri sanguinem, 1. Tim. 2, 6. Ideo recte Crocius: Decre- tum de mittendo Christo Redemptore ordine prius est decreto electionis; & pag. 305. Reconciliatio facta est in solo Christo, fonte omnis gratiæ. Res clara. Is est ille dilectus h. l. v. 6. Conf. Rom. 5, 10. Coloss. 1, 20. 21. 22. 2. Cor. 5, 19. 20.

6. E peccatorum remissione: Si peccata nobis non remittuntur ex absoluta gratia, sed propter Chri- stum, ejusq; ἀπολύτρωσιν, quæ fide apprehenditur, utiq; nec electi sumus ad æternam vitam per abso- lutam Dei gratiam, sed propter Christum ejusque ἀπολύτρωσιν, quæ apprehenditur per fidē. At ve- rum est prius. Ἐν ὧ, inquit Apostol. ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπο- λύτρωσιν διὰ τῶ αἵματος αὐτῦ τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν παρα- πτωμάτων κατὰ τὸν πλῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτῦ, illius sc. χάριτος, ἐν ᾗ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, v. 5. 6. Quomodo habeamus remissionem peccatorum, inquit Crocius, per redemptionem Christi, hic quidem non exprimit Apostolus, alibi tamen expressum legi- mus, habere per fidem. Deus enim proposuit Chri- stum, ut esset placamentū per fidem in sanguine ipsius ad declarandam justitiam suam per remissionem pec- catorum, Rom. 4, 25. & colligimus, hominem justifi- cari fide, absq; operibus legis, Rom. 3, 28. cui consonat illud Petri: Hinc omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accepturum per nomen ejus quemvis, qui crediderit in eum, Act. 10, 43. Ergo verum & posterius. Consequentia luce sua radiat tùm è συνεχείᾳ tractationis Apostolicæ, tùm è na- tura rei; quia electio ad vitam & salutem præsup- ponit gratiam & dilectionem Dei, nos eligentis ad æternam salutem. Gratia vero illa Dei electrix nulla est, nisi in signo rationis, ut loquuntur, ante- eat gratia condonatrix peccatorum: quia plus est ad vitam eligere, quam remittere velle peccata: & præsupponitur omnino gratia illa Divina, qua no- bis vult peccata nostra & pœnam peccatorum mortem æternam propter Christum condonare ante gratiam Dei, qua placuit nos ad vitam æter- nam prædestinare.

7. Ex propositi Divini fundamento. Non enim propositum divinum fuisse absolutum, aut εὐδο- κίαν hic absolutum beneplacitum inferre, quod Calviniani volunt, sed fundari ἐυδοκίαν in Christi merito testatur Apostolus v. 9. κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν ἁυτῦ ἧν προέθετο ἐν ἁυτῷ secundum illud benepla- citum, quod proposuerat (sibi) in ipso, Christo scilicet. Ita enim legit Codex, Claramountanus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, B. Lutherus, Bullin- ger &c. Id inquit, (dicente Theophylacto) pro suo arbitrio & voluntate fecit, & quemadmodum pro- posuit & prædestinavit in eo, hoc est, in Christo.

8. Ex ἀνακεφαλαιώσει omnium in Christo. Si in Christo, id est, per & propter Christum, ejusq; meritū recapitulantur per restaurationem, recollectionem sub unum caput, reductionem ad veram unitatem omnes, qui sunt in cœlo, & qui in terra in ipso, non sane extra Christū, sed in Christo & propter Chri- stum facta est electio ad vitam æternam: Ratio con- sequentia hæc est: Quia electio uti Christi missio- nem: ita etiam ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν per Christum factā præsupponit; & hanc illa ordine priorē esse opor- tet in decretis divinis: Non n. ad æternam vitam eliguntur, nisi qui restaurati, sub unū caput recol- lecti, & ad veram unitatē reducti sunt, quod omni- bus quidem hominibus cōtigit, si meritum Christi

& intentionem ac confilium Dei spectes: fidelibus autem, vel iis, qui per fidem sunt in Christo, si effe- ctum respicias: qui ἐν αὐτῷ, IN IPSO, esse dicuntur Rom. 8, 1. Nos qui antea in Diaboli potestate era- mus, nunc conjuncti sumus Deo, inquit Crocius. De hac ἀνακεφαλαιώσει per Christu facta, ejusq; san- ctis Angelis: Et hi cum essent antea, propter Deum, peccatis a nobis offensum, hostes nostri, deinceps amici sunt. Jam a. non qui in diaboli societate, sed qui Deo conjuncti sunt, & Angeli ejus, h. e. fide- les, non enim, nisi per fidem, Deo conjungimur, e- lecti sunt ad æternam vitā. Nemo a. ab hac recolle- ctione excluditur, nisi qui seipsum excludit sua perfidia & culpa, iterū dicente Crocio. Sententia n. Dei est invariabilis: Quicunq; crediderit, salvabitur Marc. 16, 16. At verum est prius. Ergo & posterius.

9. Uti in Christo nos hæreditatem consequimur; Ita etiam in Christo prædestinati sumus ad hæredi- tatem illam æternæ vitæ. At in Christo hæreditatem consequimur, quatenus in Christo sumus per fidē; siquidem non nisi per & propter Christi meritum, dum id fide nobis appropriamus, obtingat nobis illa hæreditas. Quod ex articulo de justificatione per fidem certum, & inter nos & Calvinianos ἔξω πάσης τῆς συῤῥάξεως κείμενον, extra omnem controversiā positum est. Ergo etiam in Christo ita prædestina- ti sumus ad hæreditatem vitæ æternæ, quatenus in Christo sumus per fidem. Major tum ex harmonia decreti & executionis decreti constat: tum ex ipsis Apostoli verbis & aurea illa salutis & prædestina- tionis catena, quæ hic exhibetur, luculenta est: v. 11. ἐν ᾧ κ, ἐκληρώθημεν προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶ Θεῶ, in quo & hæreditatem consecuti sum9, (quan- tum ad jus & certitudinem hæreditatis,) prædesti- nati secundum propositum divinum: quia conne- ctitur ita hæreditatis consequutio, & ad hæredita- tem prædestinatio, & utraque, in Christo facta, pa- rili ratione dicitur, quod è collatione v. 4. & 11. ad- huc luculentius evadit. Omnium autem luculen- tissimum est, si tota illa συνέχεια spectetur.

10. E fidei expressa mentione: Ne qua dubium ullū restet, quanquam omnia illa omni dubitatione su- periora sint, addit Apostol. v. 12. εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτῶ, (prædestinati secundum propositum ejus) ut simus in laudem gloriæ ejus, τὲς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ, prius speravimus in Christo: Quo quid clarius dici poterat pro fide prævisa, vel electione, ex fide prævisa, factâ? Nam per spem in Christo, fiduciam in Christum intelligi è phrasi scripturæ recepta, notissimum est, & v. seq. satis declarat, sperantes in Christum dici τὲς πιστεύ- σαντας. Illud autem πρὸ, in voce προηλπικότας, clare indicat, PRIUS nos credidisse, quoad prævisio- nis & decretorum divinorum ordinem; in mente di- vina, quam προορισθέντες prædestinati sumus κατὰ πρόθεσιν secundū propositum Dei. Nam προορισμὸς omnino factus est κατὰ πρόγνωσιν secundū prævisio- nem fidei in Christū: Ideo n. ἐκλεκτοὶ dicimur κατὰ πρόγνωσιν secundū prævisionem fidei in Christum, 1. Pet. 1, 2. ὓς προέγνω, κὶ προώρισε, Rom. 8, 29. nimi- rum eos prædestinavit Deus ad vitam æternā, quos prævidit finaliter in Christum credituros, τὲς μέλ- λοντας πισέυειν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ, εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, 1. Tim. 1. 16.

In Grotii explicatione non pauca desideramus, 1. quod electionem explicet de vocatione, ac porro per vocationem metonymice decretum vocationis intelligat. Quibus ambagibus opus non est, quum proprie intelligi possit electio, & quidem de ipso prædestinationis decreto. Nam sic electio dicitur 1. Thess. 2, 13. & hic eadem ratione explicatur per prædestinationem, sc. v. 5. προορίσας ἡμᾶς, & iterum v. 11. προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν. Et quum commu- nis hæc sit interpretatio, non apparet, cur ab eadē discedendum sit; cui suffragantur etiam Calviniani in synodo Dordracena de divina praedest. art. I. can. VII. & VIII. Neq; vero locus adduci potuit, quo e- lectio idem sit, quod decretum vocandi. Agnosci- mus, eligere ad res varias adhiberi, tum in Vet. tum in N. Testamento; sed ubi electio accipiatur pro decreto vocationis, non monstravit Groti9, nedum ubi pro vocatione occurrat, ita ut vocatio ex voce significata notet decretum vocandi: Minime o- mnium, ubi electio decretū notet vocandi, ad spe- ctanda miracula, & dona Spiritus S. Quod 1. Thess. 1. 4. habetur. Nostis fratres dilecti à Deo τὴ έκλογὴν η̉μω̃ν electionem nostram respicit Pauli, & Sylvani, & Timothei electionem ad munus sacrum, quam noverant, novissè certe poterant Thessalonicenses, ex efficacia Spiritus S. donis, & πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ ipsorum v. 5. 2. Vocem έν αὐτω̃ de causa meritoria accipiendam esse, quod hactenus probavim9, haud obscure negat Grotius, imo inepte huc rapit, quod Apostoli in vocatione fecerunt, Christum ipsum fecisse dici. Num n. Apostoli fecerunt decretū vo- cationis πρὸ καταβολη̃ς κόσμέ? 3. Alienū est, quod Christus Abrahamo fuerit prior quoad constitutionẽ. Nam non de Christi constitutione hic agitur, sed de nostri in Christo electione: Neq; Joh. 8, 56. seqq. Christus Abrahamo prior dicitur non ratione or- dinationis in decreto Divino, quae Socinianorum glossa est, sed ratione praeexistentiae realis ante Ab- rahamum, uti peculiari disputatione à nobis fuit ostensum de προυͤπάρξει ante Abrahamum. 4. Non hic de perfectissimo cultu Divino, ad quẽ Deus ho- minem, praestructis gradibus quibusdam, perduce- re sibi proposuerat, sed de electione hominis ad vi- tam aeternam sermo est, facta ab aeterno in Christo, Filio Dei. Quo pacto, si Ebraeorum dictoriū, quod nomen Messiae, hoc est meritum Filii Dei ab aeterno fuerit, intelligatur, ratione intuitus divini, recte se habet: Quia agnus Dei occisus est ab origine mundi, Apoc. 13, 8.
