Neq; legem Dei aeternam esse alienum est à veritate; sed quomodo poenitentia hominum ab aeterno sit, explicari nequit. 5. Vocatio etiā per- peram explicatur à Grotio, de beneficio eximio, re- servato iis, qui Messiae temporibus, aut non multo post erant victuri: Ubi eo sensu vocatio accipiatur, non docere potuit Grotius: Vocatio vero ad regnum Dei non modo ad tempora Messiae & non multo post sequuta spectat, sed omnium est temporum, Matth. 20. & 22. 6. Finis vocationis ac decreti vo- cationis nō constituitur sive hic sive alibi, ut vocati sint spectatores insignium miraculorum ac donorum Spiritus S. Neq; hic de fine vocationis, sed electionis & praedestinationis agitur, qui est, ut simus sancti & immaculati; quibus notari probitatem & innocen- tiam majorem, quàm à lege praescripta fuerit, error Pelagio-Socinianus est. Major certe eà nulla fingi potest, quum illà perfectissima sit, adeo, ut à nemi- ne post lapsum praestari potuerit, à solo Christo, le- gi subjecto, nostri loco praestanda & praestita fue- rit. Simile est, quod ait Groti9, Evangelii τὸ πα̃ν esse dilectionẽ. Nō n. de nostra charitate, sive erga Deū, sive erga proximum, Evangelium nos informat, sed lex, quatenus distinguitur ab Evangelio in utraque tabula, in priori de dilectione Dei, in posteriori de dilectione proximi. Evangelium vero est concio de gratia & dilectione Dei erga nos, ex qua dona- vit nobis Filium suum unigenitum, qui legem pro nobis impleret, & nos ab execratione legis redime- ret, & nos έχαρίτωσεν έν τω̃ ἠγαπημένῳ, atq; in ipso suscepit nos in filios & haeredes vitae aeternae. Sed misera illa confusio legis & Evangelii est, τὸ πα̃ν in annotatis hisce Grotianis totam legem obscurans, totum Evangelium evertens! 7. Cum Chrysostom9 monuit, fidem solam non sufficere, non id voluit ad vitam æternam consequendam vitam nostram san- ctam & inculpatam facere: Sed uti hæc, ἐξέλεξατο ἐν αὐτῷ, elegit in ipso, exposuit, elegit per fidem in Chri- stum, quod agnovit & notavit Joh. Crocius, etsi fi- dei in electione prævisæ hostis, in cōment. ad h.l. in ipso hoc Chrysostomo & Theophylacto idem est, quod per fidem in ipsum, cum ob consonantiam de- creti & executionis non electos tantūm nos per fi- dem inChristum, sed etiam salvari nos unice per fi- dem in Christi meritum, nullatenus vero per ope- ra nostra, consequens est. Id autem indicat cum Paulo Chrysostomus, non sufficere fidem solam, ut quis verus Christianus sit, siquidem electi ideo per fidem in Christum simus, non ut vivamus, prout libet, sed ut simus sancti & inculpati. Finis hic est electionis, non vero causa electionis vel salutis, quæ executio est decreti electionis, impulsiva. Hunc enim unice in Christi merito & hic & alibi Apostolus. Placet integram explicationem Theophylacti, qui epito- mator est Chrysostomi, adscribere, ut res patescat: Sicut elegit nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem: Nobis (inquit) benedixit per Christum, quemadmodū & per eundem elegit, hoc est, per fidem in Christum habitam. Elegit autem ante mundi constitutionem. Siquidem erant, quæ nobiscum aguntur hoc tempore, ex alto prædestinata, non nuper tradita, sed à princi- pio præparata. Recte autem καταβολὴν intulit, quod Græce fundationem interpretamur, & Latine consti- tutionem dixit Interpres, ut ostendat è quadam divi- na potentia sublimitate demissum & fundatum fuisse hunc mundum. Cum vero elegit, inquit, & Dei desi- gnat clementiam, & eorum virtutem: quippe quos Deus secreverit, ut probos futuros. Ut essemus sancti & immaculati in conspectu ejus: Ne forte illud sub- eat mentem, elegisse jam Deum salvos fore quos velit, & sic torpeat animus existimanti, nil ultra esse vir- tuti studendum, ut vitam quis assequatur. Quando- quidem electi jam sint pro Dei arbitrio, & nihil cæte- ris esse spei jam reliquum, ad id inquit: Elegit nos Deus, ut sancti simus, & sine labe, & in ea scilicet san- ctitate vivamus, quam baptismo ablutis largitus est Dominus. Perstemus itaq́, & vitam servemus virtute præditam. Sanctus enim est quisque, qui est fidei particeps: Immaculatus vero, qui nullis vivendo sor- dibus irretitur. Nec hanc sanctimoniam modo & vi- tam culpa vacantem à nobis exigit Deus, sed ut in ej9 conspectu hanc ipsam servemus. Quanquā vero hisce sanctitas requiratur, non tamen ea causa salutis ul- latenus à Theophylacto constituitur. Id enim, tantŧ abest, ut intenderit Theophylactus, ut etiam ἀγάπην hic non de charitate nostra, sed Dei exposuerit, ac diserte negarit, nostra virtute constare salutem, eamq; unice adscripserit Divinæ benignitati. Bea- titudo, inquit, nullis laboribus paratur, sed gratia. Qui nullius erant pretii, inquit Chrysostomus hic, & nihil merebantur, eos invenit, ut proveheret ad di- vitias. Quid potest æquiparari huic solerti facilitati? Qui erat inimic9, qui exosus, is repente sursum ascen- dit. Ἀγάπην etiam de dilectione Dei, qua nos dilexit, cum Budæo, & aliis post Chrysostomum, Theodoretũ & Augustinum libr. de perfecta justitia cap. 16. ma- luit explicare J. Crocius, quam cum suis Calvino & Beza & Piscatore & Ambrosiastro de dilectione Dei & proximi, ut sensus sit, Deum nos non elegisse ul- lo nostri merito vel causa, quæ sit in nobis, sed quia nos dilexerit, neq; reprobat sensum eum Bucerus, uti nec Haymo, & Lombardus. Si quis objiciat ver- suum distinctionē, in proclivi est, ad verbum ἐξε- λέξατο referri illud ἐν ἀγάπῃ, elegit nos in ipso per charitatẽ. Nec obstat, judicio Crocii, quod Piscator objicit, nimis remotum esse verbum elegit. Durum enim non est, vocem cum remotiore, non cum proxi- mo verbo conjungi. Quicquid autem de ista conjun- ctione & compositione sit, ex gratia Dei profectam esse electionem, nec ullatenus operibus nostris tri- buendam, sonora voce Apostolus indicavit, cum in Christo nos electos; cum electos nos, ut simus san- cti & inculpati; cum nos electos in laudem gratiæ suæ, quæ gratos nos effecit sibi in illo dilecto asserit. Nam si in Christo & propter Christum, non ergo ob nostra opera, Gal. 3, 21. Si ut simus sancti, non ergo ob sanctitatem nostram, ceu causam impulsi- vam; Si in laudem gratiæ suæ, non ergo ex operi- bus, Rom. 11, 6. Unde ex ipsismet Pontificiis, etiam Jesuitis, non pauci, ex operibus factam non esse prædestinationem nostram, agnoscunt. Thomas su- per hunc locum: Ponit voluntariam Dei prædesti- nationem, de qua dicitur Rom. 8. Quos prædestina- vit, hos etiam vocavit; cujus quidem prædestinatio- nis ratio non sunt opera nostra, sed mera Dei voluntas, propter quod subdit secundum propositum ejus. Salmero T. XVI. disp. I. in 1. Petr. I. p. 53. Electio ad finem vitæ æternæ possidendum firma est & certa per seipsam, & à nostris operibus non pendet. Pererius in cap. IIX. Rom. disp. XXIII. Præscientiam bono- rum operum, & bonum usum liberi arbitrii, esse cau- sam prædestinationis, contrarium videtur divinæ scri- pturæ. Adde & Bellarminum lib. II. de gratia & li- bero arbitrio cap. IX. & XV. ubi probat, non so- lum ad gratiam, sed etiam ad gloriam homines gratis eligi. Quam sententiam etiam asseruit Barradius T. IV. Herm. l. 4. c. 18. laudans explicationem in hunc locum Hieronymi: Non ait Paulus, elegit nos, cum essemus sancti, & immaculati, sed elegit nos, ut essemus immaculati & sancti, h. e. qui sancti & im- maculati non fuimus, ut postea essemus: Et D. Augu- stini de prædest. sanct. c. 7. Elegit Deus fideles, ut sint, non quia jam erant sancti. Consonant his Sco- tus, Lychetus, Mayrous, Richardus, Ægidius, Capreo- lus, Bassolus, Cordubensis, Ferrariensis, Arrubel, Con- saletus, apud Franc. Amic. Consentin. T. I. Curs. Theol. disp. XV. s. 4. Suarezius, Tannerus, Estius & alii: Etsi alii è Scholasticis, Jesuitis & Pontificiis in contrarium abeant, Alensis nempe, Bonaventu- ra, Albertus, Occam, Ruvio, Lessius, Becanus, Turria- nus, Catharinus, Molina apud eundem Consenti- num, iis accedentem, ut & Piggias, Osorius, Tap- perus, Driedo, Eccius, Stapletonus, Gregor. de Va- lentia apud Becanum in Theol. Schol. part. I. tr. 1. cap. 14. p. 146. 9. Id adhuc observandum, finem illum, ut essemus sancti & immaculati in conspectu ejus, explicari à nonnullis de sanctitate non tantum inchoata, sed etiam imputata, quam habemus in Christo. Idco enim, inquit B. Balduinus, Deus propo- situm habuit de salvandis hominibus, ut per meritum Christi sancti appareremus in judicio Dei, & inchoa- ta etiam integritate vitæ nostræ ei placeremus. Et hoc in conspectu Dei fieri dicitur, quia coram mundo illa perfecta sanctimonia ac vitæ integritas, quam ex obedientia Christi habent fideles, non apparet. Deus autem in judicio suo perfectionem illam agno- scit, quæ in Christo subjective est, nostra autem fit per imputationem fidei. Nonnullos etiam hæc accipe- re de sanctitate consummata, quod itidem non im- probatum B. Balduino: Nonnulli, inquit, ut esse- mus sancti &c. ita interpretantur, ut essemus salvi, quemadmodum Eph. 5, 26. 27. accipi dicunt, ut & Col. 1, 20. 21. 22. 23. illudque, quod de charitate addi- tur, de charitate Dei, per quam electi sumus, intelli- gunt. Nec inepta prorfus est interpretatio. Nam finis electionis ultimus est salus nostra, ubi sanctitas nostra vere perfecta & inculpata erit. Vide Joh. Arnoldum Corvinum in defensione Armin. contra Tilen. pag. 214. Conf. & B. Hunnius in hunc locum.

## 1:5
V. 5. Having predestined us unto adoption through Jesus Christ unto Himself) When He had determined to make us sons for Himself through Christ.

For 'unto Himself' is for the Dative in the manner of the Hebrew 'lo': And the noun 'adoption' thus governs the Dative, just as the verb 'to adopt' itself does, such as is that construction: What is that touching of her to you? Formerly Israel was a firstborn son. The calling tends to this, that being purified we might obtain that spirit which makes us sons of God, that is, imitators of the divine will. Just as there are decrees of God of a different kind, so also the words 'to purpose,' 'to predestine,' 'to foreknow,' and the nouns derived from them 'purpose,' 'predestination,' 'foreknowledge,' are not taken in the same way. For they signify sometimes a decree of permitting conjoined with a certain foreknowledge, as Acts 2, 22. chapter 4, 28. Rom. 3, 25; sometimes a decree of God without condition, Acts 8, 28. chapter 9, 11, here below 3. 1 Pet. 1, 20. Rom. 8, 28. 1 Cor. 2, 7. But here and elsewhere His decree, which God wills to do, if men also do what they ought, although that condition is not always expressed, but is sufficiently understood from other passages, indeed even from those which are coherent in the same place. Thus God had determined to save Paul and his companions in the navigation, namely if they also applied all effort to that end: And to make Paul an Apostle, if he were not disobedient to the heavenly vision. In a similar way 'to purpose' is also accustomed to be taken regarding human purpose, Rom. 1, 13.

According to the good pleasure of His will) So as it pleased His own will. 'To be well-pleased' and 'good pleasure' [Hebrew word], where they do not directly regard a person, to whom then the preposition 'in' is accustomed to be placed, but an action, they denote such an action, the reason for which is not accustomed to be given. God is accustomed to give the reasons for His vindicating judgments liberally: But of benefits He sometimes gives them, sometimes He does not. Concerning this second kind of benefits, which regard nothing that is in man, it is treated in Isa. 40, 13, likewise chapter 11, 34. 35. Thus the Hebrews say the world was created 'out of good pleasure,' because it seemed so to God. Even among the Latins, Servius noted that whenever judgment and reason do not appear, 'it seemed so' is accustomed to be interposed. Thus if anyone should ask why that most excellent calling happened to the men of that age, and among them to the Ephesians, nothing else can be answered than that it seemed so to God. Add, if you please, what was said by us on Exod. 33, 19.

Grotius has these things thus in the annotations on this passage in the notes on chapter I of Ephesians, published separately:

Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself.) Who predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself. The Apostle diligently urges this both here and elsewhere, to show that those things which were then being dispensed had come from a decree made long before. That preceding decree is called προορίζειν, to predetermine. Πρόθεσις is purpose, and sometimes also πρόγνωσις is foreknowledge. The first word is read in Acts 4:28, where it treats of providential permission and direction, Romans 8:28, 30, 1 Corinthians 2:7, and soon in verse 11. The verb of the second word is in Romans 3:25, and here soon in verse 9. The noun made from it is in Romans 8:28 and 9:11, and here soon, chapter 3:11. The verb of the third in this sense (for there is a place where it signifies approval more) is 1 Peter 1:20, but the noun is in Acts 2:23, where likewise the discourse is of providential permission and direction, and 1 Peter 1:2. When mention is made of such preceding decrees, a condition is not always added, since it can often be sufficiently understood from the very nature of the business and from the preceding words and the following serious admonitions. Thus Paul says to the Romans, chapter 1, verse 13, Προεθέμην ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, I purposed to come unto you, namely, if more necessary business would allow it. Thus Romans 8:29, in which chapter it treats of enduring evils, καὶ προώρισε συμμόρφυς τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὑτοῦ εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς, he predestinated them to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren, that is, he decreed that they also should arrive at the highest goods by the same way as Christ, provided, of course, they do not desert the signs of the cross, as he had said before in chapter 8:17. if so be that we suffer with him, Paul set apart by God for the Apostolic office, Galatians 1:15, but certainly so, if he were not disobedient to the heavenly vision, Acts 26:19. To the same man and his companions, safety was promised in the greatest danger of the sea, Acts 27:24, if they themselves, of course, did what was in them: kept the sailors in the ship, chapter 27:31, used food, 34, cast out the cargo, 38, swam, 43, 44. So here he says it was decreed beforehand by God, that he might not only make those who were called friends out of enemies, but also adopt them as sons to himself (for εἰς αὑτὸν, to himself, here and elsewhere is worth αὑτῷ to himself, that is לו), have them for sons, and treat them as such, through and for the sake of Christ, namely, if they obey the calling as they ought; thus everywhere conditions, both from the quality of the matter and from many other most clear passages, ought to be held as tacitly expressed. Jerome on this passage: He predestinated this, that men who had wished to believe might have the power to become the sons of God.

According to the good pleasure of his will) According to the absolute purpose of his will. Εὐδοκία and εὐδοκεῖν, where they are placed absolutely, i.e., without the addition of a preposition governing the name of a person, or something similar, signify a decree, so free that no one is held to render an account of it to another, Luke 12:32, Rom. 15:26, 27, 1 Cor. 1:21, Gal. 1:15, Col. 1:19, 1 Thess. 2:8, Matt. 11:26, Luke 10:21. So also 2 Maccab. 14:35. If anyone should ask, why did God bestow those great goods of those times upon the men of those times? It can be answered for God: Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? Matt. 20:15, and I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, Rom. 9:15. Thus חפץ is placed regarding decrees, the cause of which is unknown, notes Abravanel on Is. 53:10. Servius at the beginning of the third Aeneid: Whenever a reason or judgment does not appear, it is interposed: thus it seemed. Thus the world was founded by God ἐξ εὐδοκίας, from his pleasure, says Rabbi Israel from Rabbi Joseph, son of Carnitol.

In these Grotian writings we find these things lacking: 1. Because he thinks this concerns those things which were being dispensed at that time, concerning that extraordinary calling which happened to the men of that century, and among them the Ephesians. For those things which are handed down here concerning election, predestination, and the purpose and good pleasure of God are so constituted that they suit all times and any elect persons whatsoever, and are by no means to be restricted to those times of the Apostle, which Interpreters commonly acknowledge. Nor indeed were others elected or predestinated from eternity by any other reason than the Ephesians, but one and the same is the decree of election and predestination regarding all. But because Grotius restricts these to a peculiar mode of calling, and explains them not concerning the decree of predestination and election, but concerning the singular calling of the Ephesians, in that he departs from the common opinion of Interpreters, and from the Apostolic text itself, and this is merely an ἰδία ἐπίλυσις (private interpretation). 2. Because he suspends the election and predestination of this place upon a condition: If he understood the condition of faith, i.e., of the apprehension of the merit of Christ, it should not be denied. But it is now established that he, with certain Papists, understands the condition of holiness. Of which there is no trace here or elsewhere in election or predestination. 3. Because he interprets predestination unto adoption in such a way that God determined to make us sons to himself, i.e., imitators of his will. But υἱοθεσία or adoption as sons, which is included in προορισμῷ or predestination, designates the ultimate end, the consummated adoption, as Rom. 8:23. Because the Apostle is not discussing here the calling to the imitation of God, but election to eternal life; nor is υἱοθεσία anywhere the imitation of the Divine will, even if the sons of God, while they are established in the kingdom of grace, strive to conduct themselves conformably to the Divine will. 4. If the good pleasure of his will is to be understood in this place concerning the absolute will of God, which founded the world, because it so seemed good to God; which Grotius seems to assert in his annotations, why does he in other notes suspend the predestination, concerning which the Apostle is discussing, upon a condition, namely that he adopts us as sons, has us for sons, and treats us as such, namely if we obey the calling, as is right? 5. If to adopt as sons is to cause that we be imitators of the Divine will, how can that condition be added, if we obey the calling, that is, to cause that we be of the Divine will, if we be imitators of the Divine will? What tautology is this? Furthermore, if to adopt as sons is to have and treat as sons, therefore it is not to cause that we be imitators of the Divine will. But these are the things that are lacking in the Grotian writings.

Moreover, here is an explanation of the election made in Christ, namely that we have been predestinated to the heavenly inheritance through Christ, i.e., on account of the merit of Christ unto him, which we can easily admit to be explained as unto himself. For God makes us sons to himself, heirs to himself, just as through faith in Christ we are rendered sons of God and heirs of God: Thus we have been predestinated through faith in Christ unto adoption, so that the impulsive cause of both our adoption and our predestination unto adoption is Christ apprehended by faith, and faith receiving and apprehending Christ and his merit, John 1:12, Gal. 3:26, 27, but not that our merits and works, or the absolute grace of God, are held to be the cause of predestination. And our people rightly observe that there is no real difference between election and predestination. For Paul uses these words promiscuously, and explains one by the other. There is only some distinction in this, that election has respect to the reprobate, from whom the election and separation of the faithful is made: For they are elected out of the world, John 15:19, but predestination has respect to the end or term of our election, which is eternal life, to which the elect are ordained and destined; there is separation, but here is ordination; as the blessed Balduinus has it here.

Latin:

V. 5. Προορίσας ἡμᾶς εἰς ὑοθεσίαν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς αὑ- τόν) Cum constituisset nos sibi per Christum filios facere.

Nam εἰς αὐτὸν est pro Dativo ad modum Hebræi לו : Et nomen ὑιοθεσίαν sic Dativum regit, quomodo ipsum ver- bum ὑιοθετῶ, qualis est illa constructio: Quid tibi illam tactio est? Olim Israel בן בכור. Vocatio huc tendit, ut purgati adipiscamur spiritum illum, qui nos faciat Dei fi- lios, id est, divinæ voluntatis imitatores. Sicut diversi ge- neris sunt Dei decreta, sic & verba προτιθέναι, προορίζειν, προγινώσκειν, & deducta inde nomina πρόθεσις, προορισμός, πρόγνωσις, non eodem sumuntur modo. Significant enim interdum decretum permittendi cum præscientia quadam conjunctum, ut Act. 2, 22. cap. 4, 28. Rom. 3, 25. interdum decretum Dei sine conditione, Act. 8, 28. c. 9, 11. hic infra 3. 1. Petr. 1, 20. Rom. 8, 28. 1. Cor. 2, 7. Hic vero & alibi decretum ejus, quod Deus facere vult, si & homines fa- ciant, quod debent, quanquam illa conditio non semper exprimitur, sed ex aliis locis, imo etiam ex iis, quæ eodem loco sunt cohærentia, satis intelligitur. Sic Deus consti- tuerat Paulum, & ei in navigatione comites servare, nem- pe si & ipsi omnem ad id adhiberent operam: Et Paulum Apostolum facere, si non inobediens esset viso cœlesti. Si- mili modo προτίθεσθαι etiam de humano proposito sumi solet, Rom. 1, 13.

Κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ) Ita ut placuit voluntati ipsius. Εὐδοκεῖν & εὐδοκία חפץ, ubi non per- sonam directe respiciunt, cui tunc præpositio ἐν solet præ- poni, sed actionem, talem denotant actionem, cujus ratio non soleat reddi. Deus judiciorum suorum vindicantium rationes liberaliter solet reddere: Beneficiorum autem reddit interdum, interdum non reddit. De secundo hoc beneficiorum, nihil, quod in homine sit, respicientium, ge- nere agitur Es. 40, 13. item cap. 11, 34. 35. Sic mundum conditum ἐξ εὐδοκίας, quia Deo ita visum fuit, dicunt He- bræi. Etiam apud Latinos, quoties judicium & ratio non apparet, solere interponi, sic visum, notavit Servius. Ita si quærat aliquis, cur illa tam eximia vocatio contigerit il- lius seculi hominibus, & inter eos Ephesiis, responderi ni- hil aliud potest, quam ita visum Deo. Adde, si placet, quæ à nobis dicta ad Exod. 33, 19.

Hæc in annotatis ad hunc locum in notis ad cap. I. Eph. peculiariter editis ita habet Grotius:

Προορίσας ἡμᾶς εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς αὑτόν.) Qui prædestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Je- sum Christum in ipsum. Hoc & hic & alibi sedulo agit Apostolus, ut ostendat, ex multo ante constituto venisse, quæ tum dispensabantur. Ea antecedens con- stitutio vocatur προορίζειν prædecernere. Πρόθεσις propositum, interdum & πρόγνωσις præcognitio. Pri- ma vox legitur Act. 4, 28. ubi de provida permissione & directione agitur, Rom. 8, 28. 30. 1. Cor. 2, 7. & mox v. 11. alterius vocis verbum Rom. 3, 25. & hic mox v. 9. Nomen inde factum Rom. 8, 28. & 9, 11. & hic mox, cap. 3, 11. Tertiæ verbum hoc sensu (est enim, ubi approbationem magis significat) 1. Petr. 1, 20. nomen autem Act. 2, 23. ubi itidem de provida permissione & directione sermo, & 1. Petr. 1, 2. Talium anteceden- tium constitutorum cum fit mentio, conditio non sem- per additur, quippe quæ ex ipsa negotii natura, sæpe & ex verbis præcedentibus & ex sequentibus seriis ad- monitionibus satis potest intelligi. Sic Paulus dicit Romanis, cap. 1. vers. 13. Προεθέμην ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, proposui venire ad vos, nempe si negotia magis neces- saria id paterentur. Sic Rom. 8, 29. quo capite de ma- lis sufferendis agitur, καὶ προώρισε συμμόρφυς τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὑτοῦ εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖς ἀδελφοῖς, prædestinavit conformes fieri imaginis filii sui, ut sit ipse primogenitus in multis fratribus, id est, decrevit, ut & ipsi ad summa bona perveniant eadem, qua Chri- stus via, modo scilicet crucis signa hon deserant, ut an- te dixerat cap. 8, 17. εἴπερ συμπάσχομεν, si tamen com- patimur, Paulus ad Apostolicum munus Deo sepositus, Gal. 1, 15. sed nimirum ita, si non inobediens esset cœ- lesti viso, Act. 26, 19. Eidem & comitibus promissa in summo maris periculo salus, Act. 27, 24. si & ipsi sci- licet, quod in ipsis erat, facerent, nautas in navi reti- nerent, cap. 27, 31. alimentis uterentur, 34. jactum fa- cerent, 38. natarent, 43. 44. Ita hic dicit ante consti- tutum à Deo, ut illos vocatos non tantum ex inimi- cis amicos faciat, sed & sibi (nam εἰς αὑτὸν, in ipsum, hic & alibi valet αὑτῷ sibi, id est לו) filios adoptet, pro filiis habeat, tractetque, per & propter Christum, nempe si vocationi, ut debent, obediant, ita passim conditiones tum ex rei qualitate, tum ex locis aliis plurimis & clarissimis, tacitæ pro expressis haberi de- bent. Hieronymus ad hunc locum: Hoc prædestina- vit, ut haberent potestatem filii Dei fieri homines, qui credere voluissent.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὑτοῦ) Secundum absolutum propositum voluntatis suæ. Εὐδοκία & εὐδο- κεῖν ubi absolute ponuntur, i. e. non addita præpositio- ne personæ nomen regente, aut aliqua re simili, decre- tum significant, ita liberum, ut ejus rationem aliquis al- teri reddere non teneatur, Luc. 12, 32. Rom. 15, 26. 27. 1. Cor. 1, 21. Gal. 1, 15. Col. 1, 19. 1. Thess. 2, 8. Matth. 11, 26. Luc. 10, 21. Sic & 2. Maccab. 14, 35. Si quis quæ- rat, cur Deus tanta illa bona illorum temporum homi- nibus impertiverit? pro Deo responderi potest: Non licet mihi de meo facere quod volo? Matth. 20, 15. & miserebor cujus miserebor, Rom. 9, 15. Sic חפץ po- ni de decretis, quorum causa ignoratur, notat Abra- baniel ad Es. 53, 10. Servius ad initium tertiæ Æneidos: Quotiescunque ratio vel judicium non apparet, sic vi- sum, interponitur. Sic mundum a Deo conditum ἐξ εὐδοκίας ex lubitu, ait Rabbi Israel ex Rabbi Josepho filio Carnitolis.

In hisce Grotianis hæc desideramus, 1. quod putet hic agi de his, quæ tum dispensabantur, de vo- catione illa eximia, quæ seculi illius hominibus contigit, & inter eos Ephesiis. Quæ enim de ele- ctione, prædestinatione & proposito ac beneplaci- to Dei hic traduntur, ita comparata sunt, ut omni- bus temporibus, & electis quibusvis conveniant, nequaquam vero ad ista Apostoli tempora restrin- genda sint, quod communiter agnoscunt Interpre- tes. Nec vero alia ratione electi aut prædestinati sunt ab æterno alii, quam Ephesii, sed unum idem- que est electionis ac prædestinationis decretum, quoad omnes. Quod autem hæc ad peculiarem vocationis modum restringat, & non de prædesti- nationis & electionis decreto, sed de vocatione E- phesiorum singulari explicet Grotius, in eo disce- dit a communi Interpretum sententia, & ab ipso textu Apostolico, estque hæc mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις. 2. Quod ἐκλογὴν & προορισμὸν hujus loci a condi- tione suspendat: Quod si conditionem fidei, h. e. apprehensionis meriti Christi intelligeret, non ab- nuendum. Sed ipsum cum Papistis quibusdam conditionem sanctitatis intelligere jam constitit. Cujus hic & alibi nullum est in electione aut præ- destinatione vestigium. 3. Quod προορισμὸν εἰς υἱοθεσίαν ita interpretetur, quod constituerit Deus nos sibi filios facere, i. e. voluntatis suæ imitatores. At υἱοθεσία vel adoptio in filios, quæ includitur προο- ρισμῷ vel prædestinationi, finem ultimum, adopti- onem consummatam designat, ut Rom. 8, 23. Quia non de vocatione ad Dei imitationem, sed de ele- ctione ad vitam æternam hic disserit Apostolus; nec uspiam υἱοθεσία est imitatio voluntatis Divinæ, etsi filii Dei, dum in regno gratiæ constituti sunt, studeant Divinæ voluntati sese conformes gerere. 4. Si εὐδοκία τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ intelligenda hoc loco de voluntate Dei absoluta, quæ mundum con- didit, quia Deo ita visum; quod asserere in annota- tis videtur Grotius, cur προορισμὸν, de quo disserit Apostolus, in alteris notis a conditione suspendit, quod nempe nos filios adoptet, pro filiis habeat tractetque, nempe si vocationi, ut par est, obedia- mus. 5. Si adoptare in filios est efficere, ut simus imi- tatores voluntatis Divinæ, quomodo illa conditio addi potest, si vocationi obediamus, hoc est, efficere, ut simus voluntatis Divinæ, si simus imitatores vo- luntatis Divinæ? Quæ hæc battologia? Porro si adoptare in filios est pro filiis habere & tractare, non ergo est efficere, ut imitatores voluntatis Di- vinæ simus. Sed hæc de iis, quæ in Grotianis desi- deranda.

Est autem hic explicatio τῆς ἐκλογῆς in Christo fa- ctæ, quod nempe prædestinati simus ad hæreditatem cælestem per Christum, i. e. propter meritum Chri- sti εἰς αὐτὸν, in ipsum, quod facile admittere possu- mus explicari SIBI ipsi. Nam Deus nos sibi filios, sibi hæredes facit, sicut per fidem in Christum red- dimur filii Dei & hæredes Dei: Sic prædestinati sumus per fidem in Christum εἰς υἱοθεσίαν, ut causa impulsiva & υἱοθεσίας nostræ & προορισμῦ εἰς υἱοθε- σίαν sit Christus fide apprehensus, & fides Christum ejusque meritum recipiens & apprehendens, Joh. 1, 12. Gal. 3, 26.27. non autem vel merita & opera nostra, vel absoluta Dei gratia causa prædestina- tionis habeantur. Et recte observant nostri, quod nulla sit realis differentia inter electionem & præ- destinationem. Paulus enim promiscue utitur his vocibus, & unam per alteram explicat. In eo tantum aliquod est discrimen, quod electio habet respectum ad reprobos, ex quibus fit fidelium electio & separa- tio: Electi enim sunt ex mundo, Joh. 15, 19. præde- stinatio vero respectum habet ad finem seu terminum electionis nostræ, qui est vita æterna, ad quam electi ordinantur & destinantur, ibi est separatio, hic vero ordinatio; ut hic habet B. Balduinus.

## 1:6
V. 6. To the praise of the glory of his grace) So that glorious praise may be rendered to him for so great a benefit. For praise of glory here is worth glorious praise, in the manner of the Hebrews, who place genitives for Adjectives. And here does not signify the end, at least not the primary one, but something that follows. Nothing is more equitable than that praises should always be rendered to God for so great a benefit. Even Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX, 2, says that honor is to be rendered to Gods and parents, for nothing equal can be rendered: See Deut. 26.

In which he has graced us) In the Manuscript with a similar sense: with which he has graced us, with which he has affected us. But the Hebrews, as also the Latins sometimes, love to add cognate verbs to nouns: חֵן is grace, חָנַן is the verb to grace, which the Septuagint often translate by to have mercy and to pity. See what was said on Luke 1:28. Mary bore the image of the Church.

In the beloved) In the beloved, see Is. 5:1. Since God never loved anyone more than Christ, Matt. 3:17, it is no wonder if he showed himself clement and beneficent to the human race not only through him, but also on account of him. For he also often showed himself such to the Israelites on account of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Similar things are read in the beginning of the epistle to the Ephesians.

V. 6. To the praise of the glory of his grace. The primary end of God is not indicated here, but that which is just, that we render thanks to God for his highest benefits, 1 Pet. 2, 8. 1 Cor. 6, 19. 20. Nor indeed can anything proceed from us that is more suitable to our nature, or more pleasing to God, see Ps. 50, 14. and following. But the subject here is that praise and thanksgiving which follows the state of adoption.

In which he hath made us accepted, χάρις is a benefit, χαριτεῖν is to affect with a benefit, corresponding clearly to the Hebrew חָנַן. Moreover, ἐν χάριτι χαριτεῖν is to make accepted by grace; a Hebrew pleonasm, an abundance of speech, or rather an emphatic expression, as to die the death, to serve a servitude, and a thousand others of that kind.

In the beloved, Ἐν for propter (on account of), as below III. 19. and elsewhere. Just as God in the old covenant often says he does good to the Hebrews on account of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, on account of Moses, on account of David, so in the new covenant he does good to those who believe in Christ on account of Christ, whom he loved more ardently than any other, see Matt. 3, 17.

But why should the praise of the glory of the grace of God not be the end of adoption? For here too we are adopted as sons to that end, that the grace of God may be glorified, and in the other life we may attain the plenary adoption, that we may eternally praise and glorify that immense grace of God. And the glory or eternal glorification of God is altogether the primary and supreme end of election and predestination to eternal life. Regarding that ἐχαρίτωσε, the observation of Chrysostom is to be noted: he does not say, ἣν ἐχαρίσατο, that is, which he freely gave; but ἐχαρίτωσεν, i.e., he made us accepted, that is, he not only freed us from sins, but also made us lovable. He made us most acceptable, and desirable to himself, ἐπιχαρεσάτους καὶ ἐραστῶς ποθεινές. The Apostle adds, in the beloved. For we are not lovable in ourselves, but in Christ, that is, on account of Christ, and through faith in him, without which it is impossible to please God, Heb. 11, 6. The eyes of the Lord look upon faith, Jer. 5, 2. But we are not made accepted on account of Christ in such a way as God showed benefits to his people on account of Abraham, in the sense of Grotius.

For it happened to Abraham himself, who was blessed, that for all the nations of the earth in his seed, which is Christ, as is evident from Gen. XII. XVIII. XXII. & Gal. III., that is, on account of the merit of Christ; but the blessing did not come to the people on account of Abraham's merit, but solely on account of the merits of the Messiah. It is therefore on account of Abraham, on account of the promise made to Abraham, in which promise the all is Christ, and therefore it is the same as on account of Christ.

Latin:

V. 6. Εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτῦ) Ut laus glorio- sa ei reddatur pro beneficio tanto. Nam ἔπαινος δόξης hic valet ἔπαινος ἔνδοξος, Ebræorum more, qui genitivos po- nunt pro Adjectivis. Et εἰς hic non finem saltem prima- rium, sed consequens aliquid significat. Nihil æquius, quam pro tanto beneficio laudes Deo semper reddi. Etiam Aristoteles Nicomachiorum IX, 2. Diis & parentibus reddi ait honorem, æquale enim nihil reddi posse: Vide Deut. XXVI.

Ἐν ᾗ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς) In Manuscripto pari sensu: ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς, quo nos affecit. Sed Hebræi, ut & La- tini interdum amant nominibus addere verba cognata: חֵן est χάρις, חָנַן verbum χαριτῦν, quod per ἐλεεῖν & οἰκτείρειν sæpe vertunt LXX. Vide, quæ dicta ad Luc. I. 28. Maria Ecclesiæ gerebat imaginem.

Ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ) בִּידִיד, vid. Es. V. 1. Cum nullum Deus unquam magis quam Christum dilexerit, Matth. 3, 17. nihil mirum est, si non modo per eum, sed & propter eum clementem & beneficum se ostenderit humano generi. Nam & talem sæpe se Israëlitis ostendit propter Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Jacobum.

Similia leguntur in principium epistolæ ad E- phesios.

V. 6. Εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτῦ) In laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ. Non hîc finis Dei primarius indi- catur, sed id, quod æquum est, nos pro summis benefi- ciis Deo reddere, 1. Petr. 2, 8. 1. Cor. 6, 19. 20. Neque vero quicquam à nobis proficisci potest, quod naturæ nostræ sit convenientius, aut Deo gratius, vid. Ps. 50, 14. & sequentibus. Agitur autem hic de ea laude & gra- tiarum actione, quæ statum adoptionis consequitur.

Ἐν ᾗ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς, in qua gratificavit nos) χάρις est beneficium χαριτεῖν afficere beneficio, respondens plane Ebræo חָנַן. Est autem ἐν χάριτι χαριτεῖν grati- ficari gratia; Hebraicus πλεονασμὸς abundantia ser- monis, aut potius locutio διεγερτική efficax loquutio, ut morte mori, servitutem servire, & mille ejus generis alia.

Ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, in dilecto) Ἐν pro propter, ut in- fra III. 19. & alibi. Sicut Deus in fœdere veteri sæpe se benefacere ait Hebræis propter Abrahamum, Isaa- cum & Jacobum, propter Mosen, propter Davidem, ita in novo fœdere bene facit credentibus in Christum pro- pter Christum, quo nullum amavit ardentius, vide Matth. 3, 17.

Cur vero laus gloriæ gratiæ Dei non sit finis ad- optionis? Nam & hic eo fine adoptamur in filios, ut glorificetur gratia Dei, & in altera vita plenaria adoptionem consequamur, ut æternum laudemus & glorificemus immensam illam Dei gratiam. Est- que gloria vel æterna glorificatio Dei omnino finis primarius & supremus electionis & prædestinatio- nis ad vitam æternam. Circa illud ἐχαρίτωσε no- tanda est observatio Chrysostomi, non dicit, ἣν ἐχα- ρίσατο, id est, quam gratis donavit; ἐχαρίτωσεν, i. e. gratos effecit, hoc est, non solum à peccatis liberavit, sed etiam fecit amabiles. Fecit gratississimos, & sibi desiderabiles ἐπιχαρεσάτους καὶ ἐραστῶς ποθεινές. Addit Apostolus, ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ. Non enim nos amabiles sumus in nobis ipsis, sed in Christo, id est, propter Christum, & per fidem in ipsum, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. 11, 6. Oculi Do- mini respiciunt fidem, Jer. 5, 2. Non a. ita grati effi- cimur propter Christum, uti beneficia Deus populo suo exhibuit propter Abrahamum, sensu Grotiano.

Nam Abrahamo ipsi benedicto obtigit, uti omni- bus nationibus terræ in semine ipsius, quod est Christus, ut e Gen. XII. XVIII. XXII. & Galat. III. constat, hoc est, propter meritum Christi; non au- tem propter Abrahami meritum, sed unice pro- pter Messiæ merita populo contigit benedictio. Propter Abrahamum ergo est, propter promissionem Abrahæ factam, in qua promissione τὸ πᾶν est Chri- stus, ideoque idem est, quod propter Christum.

## 1:7
V. 7. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins) The same words are in Col. 1, 14, except that for sins there is transgressions in the same sense. He seems to go backward here and in that place to the Colossians, because having spoken of adoption and holiness, he comes to the remission of sins. But he does not do this in vain, as Chrysostom and others note here. For in no thing does the goodness of God appear more than in that he gave his most beloved son to death for us, while we were still his enemies. You may here best understand the remission of sins as that indulgence of God by which, when the human race had fallen into the most grievous crimes, he not only did not wish to preclude the ways of repentance, but furthermore opened new and never before heard of reasons, through which it might be invited to repentance. But that very remission is also called redemption, that is, פִּדְיוֹן, as that which is given for redeeming is wont to be called, Exod. 21, 30, namely so that we may know that this remission did not happen without great expense, not indeed made by us, as in that law of Exodus, but in Christ for us. See what we have said on Luke 23, 34. God could have done this by his own right without any victim intervening: But because not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles had been accustomed for nearly four thousand years to use victims to expiate sins, lest the ease of pardon should make sins be considered of less account, therefore God also wished a much more worthy victim to intervene here, but so that his goodness might appear the more, given by himself, not by us. The action is redemption. The life of Christ spent for us is a ransom, Matt. 20, 28, and a substitute ransom, 2. Tim. 2, 6.

According to the riches of his grace) In the Manuscript, of his kindness. Riches for Paul signifies abundance, as we said Rom. 2, 4, ch. 9, 23, 2. Cor. 8, 2, so also below 18, ch. 3, 16, Col. 1, 27, and the same phrase riches of grace, below 2, 7. Again, there is a Hebraism in it, in that the abundance of goodness is said for abundant goodness. Truly abundant goodness, because he who is in need of nothing of ours, of his own accord called us who were turned away from him to himself, and that this might happen, he willed his son to die.

More clear are those things which are read in the other place, as far as the remission of sins, the merit of Christ, by which the remission of sins has been obtained for us, the redemption through the blood of Christ. And so Grotius there verbatim.

V. 7. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins) Just as in the old law pardon was not obtained for those things which could receive pardon in that state, except by the bloody death of a victim; so in the new covenant God remits the sins of those who believe in Christ, for the reason that Christ obtained this for us from him by his own bloody death, as a most perfect sacrifice, and one most pleasing to God, full of obedience, submission, love, and patience. Redemption is a most full liberation, namely from guilt: Although the word redemption is sometimes wont to be referred by a certain metaphor to any liberation whatsoever, yet in this argument it shows that such a liberation is understood as does not happen without great expense, as the passage Matt. 20, 28 shows, where the life of Christ spent for us is called a ransom. Philo: The good man is the redemption of the bad man.

According to the riches of his grace) that is, for his most abundant goodness, as also below c. 2, 17. Thus riches of kindness, Rom. 11, 4. Riches of glory, Rom. 9, 23, and below here v. 18, and c. 3, 16, and Col. 1, 27. So also riches of the fullness of understanding, Coloss. 2, 2.

In this later place (we say later by reason of time, because the annotations in the New Testament are later in time than those which he had written separately at the beginning of the Epistle to the Ephesians) not only is the explanation of the remission of sins less clear, but also less sound, as he has already seemed to lean here toward the Remonstrant-Socinian view. For he understands the remission of sins as new and never before heard of reasons, through which we are invited to repentance. But the remission of sins is one thing, an invitation to repentance is another: Nor are these new reasons here, but by the same reasons the ancients were invited to repentance, and by the same grace of Jesus Christ they obtained salvation, Acts 15, 11. Nor indeed is redemption so much a reason for an invitation to repentance as it is the meritorious cause of the remission of sins, which is so manifest that in his earlier notes he even acknowledged it rather, namely that God remits sins to those who believe in Christ because Christ obtained this for us from him by his own bloody death, as a most perfect sacrifice, and one most pleasing to God, full of obedience, submission, love, and patience. And that we may not touch upon this controversy at present (for we have dealt with the same elsewhere), whether God could have remitted sins to us without any victim intervening, without the propitiation or satisfaction of Christ, the Grotian reason, why it pleased God that the victim of Christ should intervene to expiate sins, is both nothing and detracts from the satisfaction of Christ: Nothing, because what sane person would believe that God wanted a victim after the example of the Jews and Gentiles? The Jews were rather bound by the command of God to offer victims to expiate sins, and that for the purpose of prefiguring the expiatory victim of Christ. The Gentiles, however, through a perverse zeal at the instigation of the Devil, offered sacrifices intending a mockery of the expiatory victim of Christ. But it detracts not a little from the satisfaction of Christ that victims were offered only so that the ease of forgiveness might not make sins seem of less account, when rather Christ ought to have been offered as a victim, because by sins the wrath of God and eternal punishment were deserved, so that God might be appeased, and Christ might satisfy for sins in our place, and for the sake of foreshadowing and applying Him through faith, sacrifices had to be offered in the Old Testament, concerning which [see] in Socinismo profligato, and in the treatise Anti-Crell. on the causes of the death of Christ. Concerning this benefit, Chrysostom [speaks] beautifully: It is not only admirable that He gave His Son, but that He gave Him in such a way as to slaughter His own beloved. There is much hyperbole (exuberance of love) [in that] He gave His beloved for those who were held in hatred. See how highly He esteems [us]. If, when we held Him in hatred and were enemies, He gave His beloved, what will He not do hereafter, when we are reconciled to Him through grace! There is nothing equally great, he says further, as for the blood of God to be shed for us. And this is greater than the adoption of sons and other gifts, that He did not even spare His Son. It is a great thing that sins have been forgiven; but it is greater that it is through the blood of the Lord.

Latin:

V. 7. Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐ- τοῦ τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν παραπτωμάτων) Eadem verba Col. 1, 14. nisi quod pro παραπτωμάτων ibi est ἁμαρτιῶν sensu eodem. Retro videtur gradi & hic & illo ad Colossenses loco, quia loquutus de adoptione & sanctitate venit ad remissionem peccatorum. Sed hoc non frustra facit, ut Chrysostomus & alii hic notant. Nulla enim in re magis apparet Dei boni- tas, quam quod pro nobis, hostibus adhuc suis, filium dile- ctissimum in mortem dederit. Remissionem peccatorum hic optime intelligas illam Dei indulgentiam, qua humano generi in gravissima lapso crimina, non tantum vias pœni- tentiæ præcludere noluit: Sed novas insuper & nunquam antehac auditas rationes aperuit, per quas ad pœnitentiam invitaretur. Ea vero ipsa remissio etiam ἀπολύτρωσις di- citur, id est, פִּדְיוֹן quomodo vocari solet id, quod ad redimendum datur, Exod. 21, 30. nempe ut sciamus, hanc remissionem non contigisse sine gravi impendio, non qui- dem a nobis facto, ut in illa Exodi lege, sed in Christo pro nobis. Vide, quæ diximus ad Luc. 23, 34. Poterat Deus suo jure id facere nulla victima intercedente: Sed quia non Judæi tantum, sed & gentes solitæ erant ab annis fer- me quatuor mille ad expianda peccata uti victimis, ne fa- cilitas veniæ peccata minoris duci faceret, ideo & hic Deus victimam multo digniorem voluit intercedere, sed quo ma- gis ejus bonitas appareret, a se, non a nobis datam. Actio est ἀπολύτρωσις. Vita Christi impensa nobis λύτρον, Matth. 20, 28. & ἀντίλυτρον, 2. Tim. 2, 6.

Κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ) In Manuscripto χρηστότητος αὐτοῦ. Πλοῦτος Paulo abundantiam signifi- cat, ut diximus Rom. 2, 4. cap. 9, 23. 2. Cor. 8, 2. sic & in- fra 18. cap. 3, 16. Col. 1, 27. & eadem locutio πλοῦτος τῆς χά- ριτος, infra 2, 7. Rursum in eo Hebraismus, quod abun- dantia bonitatis dicitur pro bonitate abundante. Vere abundans bonitas, quod qui nostri nulla in re indiget, nos a se aversos ultro ad se vocavit, & ut id fieret, filium mori voluit.

Paulo luculentiora sunt, quæ in altero loco le- guntur, quantum ad remissionem peccatorum, i meritum Christi, quo impetrata nobis est peccato- rum remissio, τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ita autem illic Grotius αὐτολέξει.

V. 7. Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐ- τοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν παραπτωμάτων, in quo habemus red- emptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccato- rum) Sicut in veteri lege non obtinebatur venia eo- rum, quæ in eo statu veniam accipere poterant, nisi cruenta morte victimæ; ita in novo fœdere remittit Deus peccata credentibus in Christum, ideo, quia Chri- stus id sua morte cruenta, quippe sacrificio perfectissi- mo, Deoque gratissimo, pleno obedientiæ, demissionis, dilectionis ac patientiæ ab ipso nobis impetravit. Ἀπολύτρωσις est plenissima liberatio, a reatu scilicet: Quanquam autem vox ἀπολύτρωσις tralatione qua- dam ad liberationem quamvis referri interdum solet, in hoc tamen argumento talem intelligi liberationem, quæ non sine magno impendio fiat, ostendit locus Matth. 20, 28. ubi vita Christi nobis impensa λύτρον redemptio dicitur. Philo: Ὁ σπουδαῖος τοῦ φαύλου λύ- τρον, vir bonus hominis mali redemptio.

Κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ, secundum divitias gratiæ ejus) id est, pro uberrima sua bonitate, ut & in- fra c. 2. 17. Sic πλοῦτος χρηστότητος divitiæ bonitatis, Rom. 11, 4. Πλοῦτος δόξης, divitiæ gloriæ, Rom. 9, 23. & infra hic v. 18. & c. 3, 16. & Col. 1, 27. Sic & πλοῦτος πληροφορίας τῆς συνέσεως, divitiæ plenitudinis intellectus, Coloss. 2. 2.

In hoc posteriori loco (posteriorem dicimus ratione temporis, quia annotata in N. Test. tempo- re posteriora sunt illis, quæ in initium Epistolæ ad Ephesios separatim scripserat) non solum minus lu- culenta est remissionis peccatorum explicatio, sed etiam minus sana, quam visus jam sit ad Remon- strantico-Sociniam hic propendere. Remissionem enim peccatorum de novis & nunquam antehac auditis rationibus, per quas ad pœnitentiam invite- mur, intelligit. At aliud est peccatorum remissio, aliud ad pœnitentiam invitatio: Nec novæ hic jam rationes sunt, sed iisdem rationibus ad pœniten- tiam invitati sunt veteres, eadem gratia Jesu Chri- sti salutem consequuti sunt, Act. 15, 11. Nec vero ἀπολύτρωσις tàm est ratio invitationis ad pœni- tentiam, quam causa meritoria remissionis pecca- torum, quod adeo manifestum, ut in prioribus no- tis etiam agnoverit potius, Deum nempe ideo credentibus in Christum remittere peccata, quia Christus id sua morte cruenta, quippe sacrificio perfectissimo, Deoque gratissimo, pleno obedien- tiæ, demissionis, dilectionis & patientiæ ab ipso no- bis impetravit. Et ne hanc controversiam in præ- senti (alibi enim de eadem egimus) attingamus, an Deus sine ulla victima intercedente, sine propitia- tione vel satisfactione Christi nobis peccata remittere potuerit, ratio Grotiana, cur placuerit Deo, ut victi- ma Christi intercederet ad peccata expianda, & nulla est, & satisfactioni Christi derogat: Nulla, quia ad exemplum Judæorum & gentium Deum voluisse victimam, ecquis sanus credet? Judæi potius ex mandato Dei victimas debuerunt offerre ad expi- anda peccata, idque ad præfigurandam victimam Christi expiatoriam. Gentes vero per κακοζηλίαν instinctu Dæmonis subsannationem victimæ Chri- sti expiatoriæ intendentis obtulere sacrificia. Sa- tisfactioni autem Christi id non parum derogat, quod tantùm, ne facilitas veniæ peccata minoris ducī faceret, victimæ oblatæ sint, quum potius offerrī debuerit Christus in victimam, quia peccatis ira Dei & pœna æterna promerita, ut Deus placare- tur, & pro peccatis nostri loco satisfaceret Chri- stus, ejusque adumbrandi & applicandi gratia per fidem offerenda fuerint in V. Test. sacrificia, quo de in Socinismo profligato, & in tract. Anti-Crell. de causis mortis Christi. De hoc beneficio pulchre Chrysostomus: Non solum est admirabile, quod Fi- lium dederit, sed quod etiam eo modo dederit, ut ipsum mactaret dilectum. Multa est ὑπερβολὴ (amo- ris exuperantia) dilectum dedit pro iis, qui habeban- tur odio. Vide quantinos æstimet. Si quando ipsum habebamus odio & eramus inimici, dedit suum dile- ctum, quod non deinceps faciet, quum simus ei recon- ciliati per gratiam! Nihil est æque magnum, inquit porrò, quàm Dei sanguine esse pro nobis effusum. Et filiorũ adoptione & donis aliis hoc est majus, quod ne Filio quidē pepercerit. Magna res est, peccata remissa esse; sed majus est, quod per sanguinem Dominicum.

## 1:8
V. 8. ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς ἡμᾶς) Περισσεύειν, like the Hebrew רבב, יתר, שאן, is sometimes said of him who receives, sometimes of him who gives, as here and 2 Cor. 9:8, 12; 1 Thess. 3:12. Not content with having placed the noun πλοῦτος, he added the verb πε- ρισσεύειν, so that he might imprint upon [our] minds the incomprehensible magnitude of this goodness.

Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ κὰι φρονήσει) Σοφία is wisdom: Φρόνησις is understanding, Prov. 1:3. It was of wisdom to find the reasons for healing the human race: of prudence to arrange them. In the death of Christ there was both a testimony to the truth of the doctrine promulgated by Him, and at the same time the most perfect example of all Christian virtues. And there followed also in the resurrection a pledge of the reward promised to us.

Saner are those things which the earlier Grotius notes contain, to which, however, Vertumnus has betaken himself in these annotations. We shall append the same. They read thus:

V. 8. ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς ἡμᾶς, which superabounded in us) περισσεύειν is said elsewhere of him who receives or has. But here, as also 2 Cor. 9:8 and 12 and 1 Thess. 3:12, it is said of him who gives liberally.

Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ κὰι φρονήσει) In all wisdom and prudence) Namely, in that He gave us all that wisdom and knowledge which suffices for salvation, which is the prudence of the just, Luke 1:17. What follows shows and explains this meaning: These things are opposed to that erudition of which the Greeks and Asiatics boasted. These, I say, are the sounder [views]. For in those [writings], first, the evacuation of the satisfaction of Christ is not obscure, when he makes the death of Christ only a μαρτύριον & παράδειγμα, and that indeed in those [passages] where he explains the reasons for healing the human race. In the death of Christ, he says, there was both a testimony concerning the truth of the doctrine promulgated by him, and at the same time the most perfect example of all Christian virtues. Grotius says nothing here about satisfaction, nothing about the merit of Christ. But neither does the Apostle treat here of the divine σοφία & Φρόνησις, which is in God, but of that which comes to us from God by grace, namely, that we should know the mystery of his will, which sense Grotius himself acknowledges in his earlier notes that the following [words] demonstrate and explain. And thus Chrysostom and Theophylact also explain it. Concerning this grace, the former exclaims: O the wonder, what friendship! For he tells us his mysteries. He made known to us what is in his heart. Crocius does not poorly explain wisdom and prudence as faith: Here, he says, is described the faith by which we receive the treasure of grace. There is the wisdom of the world, and the prudence of the flesh. The Apostle does not mean that, for God has made that foolish, 1 Cor. 1:20. That [other] is enmity with God, Rom. 8:6. He departs, therefore, from Calvin, who wishes the Gospel to be adorned with these titles, and explains it rather as the gift of faith, which is conferred upon us through the Gospel, so that wisdom may denote the knowledge of God and Christ and heavenly things, so that the particle may signify all perfection, opposed to obscure and mutilated notions, but prudence may be referred to the knowledge of God and Christ, as regards its use, since faith comprehends two things: first, that we should know the will of God concerning Christ and his grace revealed in the Gospel; second, that we should rightly apply it, that is, that with true confidence of heart we should apprehend Christ, who is known, with all his benefits for the glory of God and our salvation, which we should work out with fear and trembling, conforming our manners to Christ; which is the prudence of the just, as Crocius again holds.

Latin:

V. 8. ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς ἡμᾶς) Περισσεύειν ut Hebræa רבב, יתר, שאן, modo de eo, qui accepit, dicuntur, mo- do de eo, qui dat, ut hic & 2. Cor. 9, 8. 12. 1. Thess. 3, 12. Non contentus posuisse nomen πλύτε addidit verbum πε- ρισσεύειν, ut bonitatis hujus ἀκατάληπτον magnitudinem imprimeret animis.

Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ κὰι φρονήσει) Σοφία חכמה: Φρόνησις בינה Prov. 1, 3. Sapientiæ fuit invenire rationes sanandi generis humani: prudentiæ eas disponere. In morte Christi fuit & testimonium de veritate doctrinæ ab ipso promulgatæ, & simul omnium virtutum Christianorum perfectissimum exemplum. Secuta autem & resurrectione pignus promissī nobis præmii.

Saniora sunt, quæ habent priores notæ Grotia- næ, ad quas tamen se in hisce annotatis recepit Vertumnus. Apponemus easdem. Ita habent:

V. 8. ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς ἡμᾶς, quæ superabundavit in nobis) περισσεύειν alibi de eo, qui accipit, aut ha- bet, dicitur. Hic vero, ut & 2. Cor. 9, 8. & 12. & 1. Thess. 3, 12. de liberaliter dante.

Ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ κὰι φρονήσει) In omni sapientia & pru- dentia) Eo scilicet, quod nobis omnem eam sapientiam & cognitionem dedit, quæ ad salutem sufficit, quæ φρόνη- σις δικαίων prudentia justorum, Luc. 1, 17. Hunc sen- sum monstrant & explicant, quæ sequuntur: Opposita hæc sunt ei eruditioni, de qua Græci & Asiatici glo- riabantur. Saniora hæc inquam sunt. Nam in illis primum haud obscura est evacuatio satisfactionis Christi, quando mortem Christi tantum facit μαρτύριον & παράδειγμα, & id quide illis, ubi exponit rationes sanandi generis humani. In morte Christi, inquit, fuit & testimonium de veritate doctrinæ ab ipso pro- mulgatæ, & simul omnium virtutum Christianorum perfectissimum exemplum. Nihil hic Grotius de sa- tisfactione, nihil de merito Christi. Sed nec de σο- φίᾳ & Φρονήσει divina, quæ in Deo est, hic agit A- postolus, sed de ea, quæ nobis à Deo obtingit ex gratia, quod nempe cognoscamus mysterium vo- luntatis ejus, quem sensum monstrare & explicare, quæ sequuntur, agnoscit Grotius ipse in prioribus notis. Atq; ita explicat etiam Chrysostomus & Theo- phylactus. De hac gratia exclamat ille: Papæ, quan- ta amicitia! Nobis n. dicit sua mysteria. Nota no- bis fecit, quæ sunt in suo corde. Crocig non male sa- pientiam & prudentiam de fide explicat: Hic descri- bitur, inquiens, fides, qua thesaurū gratiæ recipimus. Est sapientia mundi, & prudentia carnis. Eam non intelligit Apostolus, illam enim Deg infatuavit, 1. Cor. 1,20. Ista est inimicitia cum Deo, Rom. 8, 6. Discedit itaque à Calvino, qui Evangelium his titulis ornari vult, & explicat potius de dono fidei, quod per Ev- angelium nobis confertur, ut sapientia notet co- gnitionem Dei & Christi rerumque cœlestium, ut particula omnem perfectionem significet, opposi- tam obscuris & mutilis notitiis, Φρόνησις autem re- feratur ad cognitionem Dei & Christi, quoad ejus usum, quum fides duo comprehendat, primo ut volun- tatem Dei de Christo ejusq; gratia in Evangelio reve- latam cognoscamus, deinde, ut recte applicemus, id est, vera cordis fiducia Christum cognitum cum omnibus beneficiis apprehendamus ad Dei gloriam & nostram salutem, quam cum timore & tremore operemur, mo- res nostros Christo conformantes; quæ est prudentia justorum, ut iterum habet Crocius.

## 1:9
V. 9. Γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τῶ θελήματὸς ἀντῶ) The secret, or, as Tertullian speaks, the sacrament of the will, is the will of God long hidden, partly by silence, partly by the wrappings of figures so dark that not even the Angels perceived what was to be, 1 Pet. 1:12. Κατεῖχεν ἐν μυστηρίῳ καὶ διετήρει τὴν σοφὴν ἀυτῶ βυλὴν, says Justin to Diognetus.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν ἣν προέθετο ἐν ἀυτῷ) He shows what that will of God was, namely, most free, most ancient, hidden. For ἐν ἀυτῷ here is within himself. For αὐτῷ in these books often stands for ἑαυτῷ.

In his earlier notes, Grotius had handed down almost the same things:

V. 9. Γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τῶ θελήματὸς ἀυτῶ, that he might make known to us the sacrament of his will) Μυστήριον θελήματὸς, the sacrament of the will, in the Hebrew manner of speaking, is a secret counsel, that is, one which lay hidden for a long time. Thus, Chrysostom noted in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans 11:25 and 1 Cor. 15:51 that by the word mystery/sacrament is understood τὸ ἀγνοώμενον, that which is unknown. Tertullian translates it as the sacrament of the will. This counsel had been for a long time unknown not only to men, but also to Angels, 1 Pet. 1:12. Justin, in his epistle to Diognetus: Ἐννοήσας δὲ μεγάλην καὶ ἄφραστον ἔννοιαν, ἣν ἐκοινώσατο μόνῳ τῷ παιδὶ ἐν ὅσῳ μὲν ἦν κατεῖχεν ἐν μυστηρίῳ καὶ διετήρει τὴν σοφὴν ἀυτῶ βυλὴν, ἀμελεῖν ἡμῶν καὶ ἀφροντιστεῖν ἐδόκει, ἐπεὶ δὲ ἀπεκάλυψε, διὰ τῶ ἀγαπητῶ παιδὸς, καὶ ἐφανέρωσε τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡτοιμασμένα, πάνθ' ἅμα παρέσχεν ἡμῖν: Weigh, however, that great and inexplicable counsel, which he revealed only to the Son. As long as he kept it closed in a secret place and held his wise will within himself, he seemed to neglect us and to place us outside his care. But from the time he revealed it through his beloved Son and made manifest to us what he had prepared from the beginning, he provided all things for us at once, and what follows.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν ἀυτῶ, ἣν προέθετο ἐν ἀυτῷ, according to his good pleasure, which he proposed in himself) He often inculcates this, either in the same or in changed words, that it flows both from this free decree and from the most ancient one: The former, so that we do not call God to account when he uses his own right; the latter, so that novelty may not be suspected, and so that the Jews may not boast of their antiquity. Ἐν ἀυτῷ is here, as often elsewhere, ἐν ἑαυτῷ, within himself.

The mystery of the Lord's will concerns not so much those things which are handed down subsequently, as those which he had already handed down; not so much the divine economy in the calling, as the economy of redemption, and that secret counsel of election and eternal predestination: In which [are] especially the riches of his superabundant grace, in which [is] εὐδοκία, that gracious will of God, ἣν προέθετο ἐν Χριστῷ, or the good pleasure which he proposed in Christ: Which mystery the Angels long to look into, 1 Pet. 1:12, not because it is unknown to them, but because they can never sufficiently delight themselves in a deeper intuition of it. The Apostle therefore points out the manifestation of the Gospel with the words: γνωρίσαι ἡμῖν τὸ μυσήριον τῶ θελήματος αὑτῶ κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτῶ, ἣν προέθετο ἐν αὑτῷ εἰς οἰκονομίαν τῶ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ, τά τε ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς, κὰ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Having made known to us the mystery of His will according to His benevolence, which He purposed in Him (Christ) for the dispensation of the fullness of times, (proper to the fullness of times) to gather together all things in Christ, whether they are in heaven, or whether they are upon earth:

Which is a notable description of the Gospel. For what else is the Gospel than the making known of the mystery of the will of God according to His gratuitous benevolence, not that absolute one, but which He purposed and decreed in Christ, namely for the dispensation in the fullness of times, that by which all things are in turn gathered together, and that in Christ. The internal impulsive cause of the Divine will, manifested in the Gospel, is the εὐδοκία of God: The external is the merit of Christ, because God purposed to exhibit grace not according to mere good pleasure, but in Christ and on account of Christ. But how in Christ? Through that admirable οἰκονομία, which was reserved for the fullness of times, with regard to the execution of that Divine purpose, and which was directed to this, that all things might be gathered together in Christ. The particle therefore ἐν ἀυτῷ retains the customary sense IN HIM (namely Christ) and is not placed for ἐν ἑαυτῷ, as Grotius wishes, who says that this commutation of these pronouns is frequent in these books; he does not prove it, nor should it be rashly admitted.

Crocus therefore assigns another reading with Calvin, Zanchius, and Piscator, as if it were ἐν αὑτῷ: But Chrysostom does not read it so, nor Theophylact, nor the Vulgate Interpreter, nor B. Luther, nor Bullinger, nor Aretius, and the Claromontanus approved by Beza does not have αὑτῷ, as Calvin, Piscator, and others would prefer on account of their absolute decrees, but αὐτῷ. Nor is the discourse here about the εὐδοκία of the calling to the communion of Christ, but that which appears in the mystery of redemption, concerning which Matt. 3:17 and in the parallel passage, Col. 1:19-20, which illustrates this. Namely, the Apostle blesses God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ with a verbal blessing, on account of His real, manifold blessing in spiritual benefits and heavenly gifts in Christ, which blessing he first designated generally in v. 3, then executed specifically by parts, both regarding eternal and temporal benefits. Eternal is our election in Christ, v. 4, and predestination to the adoption of the sons of God through Christ, v. 5; but temporal are firstly the conciliation of graciousness and lovability in that beloved Son, v. 6 (by B. Baldwin it is called justification) made, both through redemption, by which that was acquired for us, and through the remission of sins, without which we can in no way be lovable to God; and therefore is proclaimed secondly the redemption made through the blood of Christ, and also thirdly the remission of sins, v. 7, and furthermore fourthly the donation of gracious faith, v. 8, if indeed we cannot possess the fruit of Christ's redemption, the remission of sins, without faith, and faith does not come to us except through the grace of God, Phil. 1:29, which when He gives God [acts] toward us not immediately but mediately through the Word; hence, fifthly, the gracious manifestation of the Gospel is celebrated, v. 9, and on that occasion the economy of grace is proclaimed, exhibited in Christ, for the summing up of all things, v. 10, because the Gospel is the address or proclamation of that grace: Sixthly, the gracious leading into the eternal inheritance in Christ is celebrated, and thus the Apostle returns to predestination, of which that is the execution, v. 11, and he explains it more fully in that same v. 11 and the following v. 12. He teaches that all these benefits have come to us in Christ, through and because of Christ, by the pronoun 'us,' joining himself with the holy faithful Ephesians, because the benefits of Christ pertain to all, since in him all the nations of the earth are to be blessed, according to the gracious intention of God; yet they are appropriated to the faithful through faith.

Latin:

V. 9. Γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τῶ θελήματὸς ἀντῶ) Ar- canum, sive, ut Tertullianus loquitur, sacramentum volun- tatis est voluntas Dei diu abscondita partim silentio, par- tim involucris figurarum tam tenebrosis, ut ne Angeli quidem id, quod futurum erat, perspicerent, 1. Petr. 1, 12. Κατεῖχεν ἐν μυστηρίῳ καὶ διετήρει τὴν σοφὴν ἀυτῶ βυλὴν, ait Justinus ad Diognetum.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν ἣν προέθετο ἐν ἀυτῷ) Ostendit, qua- lis fuerit ista Dei voluntas, nempe liberrima, antiquissima, recondita. Nam ἐν ἀυτῷ hîc est intra se. Αὐτῷ enim in his libris sæpe valet ἑαυτῷ.

In notis prioribus fere eadem tradiderat Gro- tius:

V. 9. Γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τῶ θελήματὸς ἀυτῶ, ut notum faceret nobis sacramentum voluntatis suæ) Μυστή- ριον θελήματὸς sacramentum voluntatis Ebræo loquen- di genere est consilium arcanum, id est, quod diu latuit. Sic μυστηρίυ sacramenti voce intelligi τὸ ἀγνοώμενον, id quod ignotum est in epistolam ad Romanos 11, 25. & 1. Cor. 15, 51. notavit Chrysostomus. Sacramentum vo- luntatis vertit Tertullianus. Fuerat hoc consilium diu non hominibus tantum, sed & Angelis ignotum, 1. Petr. 1, 12. Justinus epistola ad Diognetum : Ἐννοήσας δὲ με- γάλην καὶ ἄφραστον ἔννοιαν, ἣν ἐκοινώσατο μόνῳ τῷ παιδὶ ἐν ὅσῳ μὲν ἦν κατεῖχεν ἐν μυστηρίῳ καὶ διετήρει τὴν σοφὴν ἀυτῶ βυλὴν, ἀμελεῖν ἡμῶν καὶ ἀφροντιστεῖν ἐδόκει, ἐπεὶ δὲ ἀπεκά- λυψε, διὰ τῶ ἀγαπητῶ παιδὸς, καὶ ἐφανέρωσε τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡτοιμασμένα, πάνθ' ἅμα παρέσχεν ἡμῖν: Expende autem magnum illud & inexplicabile consilium, quod soli aperuit Filio. Quamdiu in arcano clausit, secumque continuit sapientem voluntatem, negligere nos & extra curam suam ponere videbatur. At ex quo per dilectum filium aperuit & manifesta nobis fecit, quæ ab initio præparaverat, una omnia nobis præbuit, & quæ sequun- tur. Quod autem hoc fuerit consilium, explicant se- quentia.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐυδοκίαν ἀυτῶ, ἣν προέθετο ἐν ἀυτῷ, secundum beneplacitum ejus, quod proposuit in semetipso) Sæpe aut iisdem, aut mutatis verbis inculcat, & ex libero hoc de- creto fluere, & ex antiquissimo: Illud, ne Deum jure suo utentem ad rationes vocemus: Hoc, ne suspecta sit no- vitas, ac ne Judæi se antiquitate jactent. Ἐν ἀυτῷ est hic, ut alibi sæpe, ἐν ἑαυτῷ, intra se.

Mysterium voluntatis Domini non tam ea con- cernit, quæ deinceps traduntur, quàm illa, quæ jam tradiderat, non tam œconomiam divinam in vo- catione, quàm οἰκονομίαν redemptionis, & arca- num illud electionis ac prædestinationis æternæ consilium: In quo imprimis divitiæ superabundan- tis gratiæ, in quo εὐδοκία, gratiosa voluntas illa Dei, ἡν προέθετο ἐν Χριστῷ, vel beneplacitum, quod propo- suit in Christo: Quod mysterium Angeli gestiunt παρακύψαι, 1. Pet. 1, 12. non quod ipsis ignotum, sed quia nunquam satis sese oblectare possunt ejus- dem penitiori intuitu. Patefactionem ergo Evan- gelii indigitat Apostolus verbis: γνωρίσαι ἡμῖν τὸ μυσήριον τῶ θελήματος αὑτῶ κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐ- τῶ, ἣν προέθετο ἐν αὑτῷ εἰς οἰκονομίαν τῶ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ Χρι- στῷ, τά τε ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς, κὰ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Patefa- cto nobis mysterio voluntatis suæ secundum benevo- lentiam suam, quam proposuit in ipso (Christo) ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum, (propriam plenitudini temporum) ad recolligendum omnia in Christo, sive quæ in cælis sunt, sive quæ super terra:

Quæ est insignis descriptio Evangelii. Nam quid aliud est Evangelium, quam patefactio mysterii vo- luntatis Dei secundum gratuitam ejus benevolen- tiam, non absolutam illam, sed quam proposuit ac decrevit in Christo, nimirum ad dispensationem in plenitudine temporum, eam, qua omnia vicis- sim recolligantur, idque in Christo. Causa impul- siva interna voluntatis Divinæ, in Evangelio ma- nifestatæ est εὐδοκία Dei: Externa est meritum Christi, quod non secundum merum beneplaci- tum, sed in Christo & propter Christum exhibere gratiam Deus proposuerit. Quomodo vero in Christo? Per οἰκονομίαν illam admirandam, quæ reservata erat plenitudini temporum, quod ad executionem προθέσεως illius Divinæ, quæque eo directa erat, ut omnia in Christo recolligantur. Particula ergo ἐν ἀυτῷ sensum usitatum retinet IN IPSO (Christo scilicet) non vero ponitur pro ἐν ἑαυτῷ, ut vult Grotius, qui hanc commutationem istorum Pronominum in his libris esse dicit frequen- tem; non probat, neque temere ea admittenda.

Crocius itaque aliam lectionem assignat cum Calvi- no, Zanchio, & Piscatore, quasi sit ἐν αὑτῷ: Sed non ita legit Chrysostomus, non Theophylactus, non In- terpres Vulgatus, non B. Lutherus, non Bullingerus, non Aretius, & Bezæ probatus Clarœmontanus non habet αὑτῷ, uti mallent Calvinus, Piscator, & alii propter absoluta sua decreta, sed αὐτῷ. Neque hic de εὐδοκίᾳ vocationis ad communionem Christi, sed quæ in mysterio redemptionis apparet, sermo est, de qua Matth. 3, 17. & in loco parallelo, Col. 1, 19. 20. qui hunc illustrat. Nimirum benedicit Apostolus Deo ut Patri Domini nostri Jesu Christi verbali be- nedictione, ob benedictionem ejus realem, multipli- cem, in spiritualibus beneficiis, & donis supercœle- stibus in Christo, quam benedictionem primum generatim designavit v. 3. dehinc per partes specia- tim executus est, cum quoad æterna, tum quoad temporalia beneficia. Æterna est electio nostra in Christo, v. 4. & prædestinatio ad adoptionem filio- rum Dei per Christum, v. 5. temporalia autem sunt primo gratiositatis & amabilitatis conciliatio in illo dilecto Filio, v. 6. (B. Balduino dicitur justificatio) facta, tum per redemptionem, qua illa nobis ac- quisita, tum per remissionem peccatorum, sine qua amabiles Deo esse minime possumus; Ideoque de- prædicatur secundo redemptio per sanguinem Christi facta, nec nō tertio remissio peccatorum, v. 7. ac por- ro quarto gratiosæ fidei donatio, v. 8. siquidem redem- ptionis Christi fructu, remissione peccatorum potiri non possimus sine fide, fides a. non nisi per gratiam Dei nobis obtingat, Phil. 1, 29. quam quum donet Deus nobis non ἀμέσως sed ἐμμέσως per Verbum; hinc quinto celebratur gratiosa Evangelii patefactio, v. 9. eaque occasione οἰκονομία gratiæ deprædicatur, in Christo exhibitæ, πρὸς τὴν ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν τῶν πάντων, v. 10. quia Evangelium est gratiæ istius concio vel præconium: Sexto celebratur gratiosa in Christo ad æternam hæreditatem perductio, & ita redit ad prædestinationem Apostolus, cujus illa est executio, v. 11. eamque uberius explicat v. illo 11. & seq. 12. Quæ beneficia omnia in Christo, per & propter Christum nobis obtigisse docet Pronomine ἡμᾶς, se cum sanctis fidelibus Ephesiis conjungens, quia beneficia Christi omnes attineant, quum in ipso omnes nationes terræ benedicendæ sint, juxta gratiosam Dei intentionem; fidelibus tamen appropriantur per fidem.

## 1:10
V. 10. For the economy of the fullness of the times) God had retained this with himself for this reason, that he might publish and distribute it only in his own time, among Jews and Gentiles. It is a simile taken from a household, in which the head of the family, or someone in his place, gives out from the storeroom what has been measured. This is attributed here to God, elsewhere to the ministers of God, as below III. 2, 1 Cor. IX. 17, Col. I. 25, 1 Tim. I. 4. The fullness of times is the maturity of time, or more clearly, the mature time. For among the Hebrews, the fullness of the day is called the time which has been brought to its goal, Acts II. 1. Thus the fullness of times, Gal. IV. 4, the fulfillment of days, Ezek. V. 2, Dan. X. 3. It is credible that there is a reference here to the weeks of Daniel.

To sum up all things in Christ) κεφαλαιῶν, Sir. XXXII. 9, ἀνακεφαλαιοῦν, Rom. XIII. 9, is to gather things into a sum. For κεφάλαιον is a sum, in Hebrew תכן or צתכנת, in Chaldean סוכם. Hence, as the simile proceeds, he who gathers the dispersed into one rank is rightly said to sum them up, just as in Latin 'to collect.' In Christ, through Christ as the head.

Things in the heavens and things on earth) This is what the Hebrews call the superior and inferior family of God. Compare Col. I. 20. For all power has been given to Christ both in heaven and on earth, Matt. XXVIII. 18, see below 21, and with that place compare Col. I. 16, where 'was created' seems to be 'were ordered,' concerning which meaning of this word we have said something in the Prolegomena to the Gospels. Formerly, some angels favored the Jews, others the Persians, others the Greeks, as can be seen in Daniel X. 13, 20, XII. 1. Now all, because of Christ, willingly serve Christians, as those called to angelic dignity, Heb. I. 14. For examples see Matt. XVIII. 10, Acts V. 19, XII. 2, XVI. 26, XXVII. 23. The Jews hated foreigners as idolaters; the Jews were hated by the Gentiles because of the diversity of their institutions. Concerning which matter we have spoken in book II of 'On the Law of War and Peace' XV, 9. Now those who come to Christ from both groups are friends, indeed brothers among themselves, one people of God at the same time.

In him) It would have been enough to have said 'in Christ.' But he thought it should be repeated, as if he were saying, 'through him, I say, one, not through any other.' This was not done through Moses, not through the philosophers.

Grotius interprets 'economy' as the distribution of the mystery to the Jews and Gentiles in its publication; 'summing up' as the gathering of the dispersed into one rank; 'things in the heavens and things on earth' as the superior and inferior family of God, about which he had written in almost the same way before, in some points only explaining his mind more clearly, as now follows:

V. 10. For the dispensation of the fullness of the times) To dispense is to distribute the stored provisions, as in Luke 16, 2 and following. In the best Latin this is called 'to dispense,' whence comes the office of dispensers. Thus the distribution of that counsel to the Jews and Gentiles is called a dispensation, 1 Cor. IX. 17. Here below III. 2. And in that [epistle] to the Colossians, as it were a blood-relative of this epistle, II. 2, and 1 Tim. I. 4. Therefore God had retained that with himself, so that he might publish it at a convenient time. The fullness of the times, which is also the fullness of the times, Gal. IV. 4, is that time in which most and the most important prophecies were fulfilled and had their outcome.

can be said to sum up, which meaning is most suitable for this place. All things, understand the intelligible things, in Christ, that is, under Christ as leader,

Things in heaven) Before, there were factions and partisanship among the angels for the peoples, see Daniel X. v. 13, and add Job IV. 18, and those things which Jerome says about the angels against Jovinian II, and Maximus in the Dialogue. Christ removed those things, having been made King even of the angels, gathering for himself one people out of so many peoples, to whom the angels now owe service, Heb. I. v. 14. See the example Acts V. 19, XII. 11, XVI. 26, XXVII. 23, 44. Add Matt. XVIII. 10, and 1 Cor. XI. 10, where it is a matter of the angels of prayer, of whom the Hebrew book Chasidia makes mention, and Tertullian in his book on prayer. Philo, in 'On Philanthropy,' calls them overseers according to the experience of the wise, lest there be anything discordant in the song. Some refer to the kingdom of Christ, which he has obtained over the angels, that which is in Col. I. 16, because 'to create' often signifies a new ordering. Certainly, just as most of the epistle to the Colossians agrees with this epistle, so also this passage seems to bring light to this one, and in turn to borrow light from it. The angels, hostile to the Gentiles because of idolatrous worships, favor the same ones when they are converted to Christ.

And things on earth) The Jews and those born from the Gentiles, as many as obey the calling, the partition having been broken: with the hatred, which had been the greatest, removed in addition. For just as the Jews held those foreigners as abominable men, in whom neither homicide nor adultery could be committed, since they considered them worse than beasts, and their marriages as non-marriages, as we learn from Joseph Albo, Moses Maimonides, Bacchai, and others, in the explanation of Deut. XXI. 11; so these in turn held the Jews as enemies of the immortal gods, as Cicero teaches us in 'Pro Flacco,' and as violators of human society, as appears from Apollinaris, Molo, Diodorus Siculus, and many others. But if we look to God, for many centuries only the Jews were the people of God: now all who believe in Christ are Christ's, and through Christ, the people of God. The Jews themselves also, having despised true piety and placed their empty confidence in rites alone, were for the most part hateful to God. Now all things are changed; men of both kinds, who have obeyed the calling, are reconciled both to God and to one another.

Ἐν αὐτῷ, in him) It had been enough that what preceded was ἐν Χριστῷ, but he wished to repeat it, so that he might the more impress upon the minds of the readers that there is one King of those in heaven and those who inhabit the earth, that is to say, of the pious, Matt. XXVIII. 18.

This is Grotius. As for the οἰκονομία, the Apostle is not dealing here with the publication of the mystery of the Gospel, which we know was published even in the Old Testament, nay, was promulgated immediately in Paradise, Gen. 3, 15, and he had already spoken of the manifestation of the mystery of the gracious divine will, v. 9, but with the object of the gracious will of God, which he proposed (from eternity) in Christ, because that εὐδοκία and πρόθεσις tends εἰς οἰκονομίαν, toward the dispensation to be executed in the fullness of time, situated namely in the ἀνακεφαλαιώσει τῶν πάντων ἐν τῷ χριστῷ.
