For although sometimes οἰκονομία is used for the dispensation of an office, Eph. 3, 2, 1 Cor. 9, 17, whence also the Apostles are called οἰκονόμοι μυσηρίων Θεῦ, 1 Cor. 4, 1, yet this οἰκονομία is situated in the ἀνακεφαλαιώσει τῶν πάντων, as the Apostle interprets, which imports something more than the dispensation of the Gospel among Jews and Gentiles. Nor is it unknown what the Greek Fathers mean by οἰκονομία when the discourse is about the mysteries of Christ: namely, that divine dispensation which He employed in the business of our salvation through Christ the Mediator and Savior of the human race, namely, that He deigned to ordain His only-begotten Son, so that He might put on our flesh, and in it both fulfill the divine law for us and satisfy for our sins, so that through faith in Him we might obtain the remission of sins, righteousness, and salvation. This admirable dispensation of our salvation the Greek Church called οἰκονομία: nor would I doubt that this meaning of the word is founded here: which can also have a place in the similar passage Col. 1, 26, ἧς ἐγενόμην ἐγὼ διάκονος κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῦ θεῦ τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι εἰς ὑμᾶς πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ. For Paul had been made a minister of the Church regarding that divine economy, which he says was given to him, or entrusted to him to be announced among and to the Colossians: because we can neither know it without a divine gift, and that we may be heralds of the same, it is a work of divine concession, Matt. 11, 27. c. 13, 11. Rom. 10, 14. 15.

And the Apostle also deals with this ὀικονομίᾳ Θεῦ τῇ ἐν πίσει in 1 Tim. 1, 4, which is to be delivered in the Church, passing over useless questions and genealogies. By the word οἰκονομία, says the blessed Hunnius on this passage, Paul looks to the order of administration, by the grace of which, through Christ the Mediator, these things are carried out and administered by these means, in this order and process in execution, just as the Lord decreed and established in His counsel that they should be carried out. Similarly, the blessed Balduinus: To this fullness of time is attributed the dispensation, i.e., ὀικονομία, because all things were performed by Christ in that order in which it was established and predetermined in the eternal counsel of God. Nor did Chrysostom explain it otherwise, to whom, even if οἰκονομία is the πλήρωμα τ̄ καιρω̄ν, he nevertheless explains this πλήρωμα concerning the very advent of the Son of God in the fullness of times, and thus he discourses on this οἰκονομία in this place. For after He had done everything both through angels and through prophets, and through the law, and nothing was succeeding, and there was a danger that man had been made in vain, or rather to his own ruin, with all perishing, and more so than in the flood, He found this dispensation, which is done through grace, so that he would not have been made in vain and to no purpose. He calls this the fullness of times and wisdom, because when they were most about to perish, then they were saved. Theodoret says, the Divine nature alone is free from need. But every creature had need of the medicine of the dispensation of the assumed flesh. Nor does Lombard depart entirely from this sense, who, having retained the Vulgate version, gives this interpretation: In this time of grace, in which divine providence rationally dispensed that which was promised and prefigured in other times. Others, however, render it more expressly, understanding the dispensation of salvation, which the Father enjoined upon Christ to be exercised and perfected. Hugo also expressed the matter itself, even if perhaps he draws the word οἰκονομία less conveniently from law, because, namely, a dispensation is a relaxation of law. He says, therefore, that God the Father dispensed with us when He sent His Son to redeem the human race, because if He were to deal with us according to the rigor of justice, He would leave us in perpetual servitude. Hugo calls the fullness of time, by a Hebraism, a full time, and he calls this full, because it was full of graces, fulfilling the old figures, which, even if it is correct again regarding the matter, the word πλήρωμα does not look to a fullness of graces, but the time is called completed with respect to the divine definition: because this time was destined divinely, nor were these things to be perfected before that very time was completed, which was altogether mature and opportune according to the divine counsel, Gal. 4, 4. Which can also be so named, because it is the last according to Theophylact: See Heb. 1, 1. and 1 Pet. 1, 20. 1. John 2, 18. 1 Cor. 10, 10.

Regarding ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, the Vulgate rendered this word ἀνακεφαλαιώσασϑαι as 'to restore.' Erasmus and Bullinger as 'to restore summarily,' Tertullian in his book on monogamy at the beginning as 'to be reciprocated,' Beza and Piscator as 'to gather together,' Jerome translates it as 'to recapitulate,' and that in the sense of the orators. The Syriac translation, interpreted by Tremellius, as 'to renew from the beginning.' But it is best explained as 'to recall again to one head.' Which sense both the word itself introduces, and the subject matter demands, because all things which were in heaven and which were upon the earth, the intellectual things, needed to be recalled under one head, under which they were indeed established by creation, since both men and angels had one head, God, but through sin they were torn away from God, and men became rebels to Him, nor did they remain any longer with the angels, who persisted in the truth, under that one head and Lord, therefore through

Christ it was necessary for them to be further ανακεφαλαιώσασθαι, to be recalled anew to one head. This is the simplest interpretation. Those who extend τὰ πάντα to other creatures, using their intellect, cannot sufficiently explain how all creatures destitute of reason were under the same head, and how they ceased to be under the same, or how they began in turn to be recalled under the same head with the νοεροĩς in Christ, as can be seen in Theodoret and others. But those who take it concerning those who were in heaven when the Apostle was writing these things, namely, the spirits of the perfect just, will neither correctly resolve the opposition, since even at that time when this epistle went to the Ephesians, very many could have migrated to heaven, nor do they satisfy the Apostolic intention, which is by no means this, to teach that both those who died in the Lord and were received into heaven, and the faithful acting on earth, have been recalled under one head in Christ: And the ανακεφαλαίωσις, which was done in Christ, if you look to the intention of God the Father and the merit of Christ, is altogether universal, and thus pertains not only to the elect, but also to the reprobate, even if the fruit of the same does not redound to these, but only to those, and that by the fault of unbelief. Thus Chrysostom: What is ανακεφαλαιώσασθαι? To join together. Who also explains it thus: He placed one head for all: And He subjected all to one head. Thus indeed (he adds) it will come to pass that the union will be so accurate and perfect a conjunction: When all things have been reduced into one head, they have a certain necessary bond from above. Similarly Theophylact: The heavenly things, he says, were torn from these earthly ones, so that they did not have one head. For even if, according to the reason of the creation of this world, there was one God for all, yet He was not yet recognized as the one who would be joined to us by charity. Wherefore God proposed to restore the heavenly things together with the earthly, that is, to impose one head upon all. For the same reason the blessed Hunnius: The Greek word ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι emphatically designates that restoration and reparation of things lost through the fall of the first men, and the recollection of those dispersed from one another, and also the reconciliation of those who had been offended by the sins of men. Furthermore: The Apostle embraces all those things which either stood in need of restoration, or were to be reconciled with the human race, or were to be brought back into their original society and concord. For first, the ruin of the human race had to be entirely restored, which could not be done unless peace and reconciliation were established between the human race on earth and God in heaven. Then, although nothing is obtained for the Angels through the death of Christ, yet something is obtained for all, which has a certain respect to the Angels, namely that the Angels, who were previously alienated from men on account of transgression, now acknowledge them again as their fellow servants, companions, and partners of the same joy and kingdom, and so do not disdain to serve them. Blessed Hunnius indeed adds: But in this respect all things in heaven and on earth have been restored, insofar as the whole universality of the Church of all the elect has been reduced into one body through Christ, so that not only the Church militant on this earth feels the efficacy of his merit, but also the same Church triumphant in heaven perpetually enjoys it, and thus through the saving ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν (recapitulation) by the power and work of Christ all things have been restored, reintegrated, recollected, and reconciled. But these things pertain to the effect of the ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως (recapitulation), of which there is speech here. However, it seems that here it is only a matter of the recapitulation which was made through the blood and on the cross of Christ: which is openly distinguished from the calling and leading to the heavenly inheritance, v. 11, and is restricted to the reconciliation and pacification of all things in heaven and on earth, which was made διὰ τῦ αι̅́ματος τῦ σαυρῦ αὐτῦ (through the blood of his cross), Col. 1. 20. But there is no doubt that this reconciliation of all things, and the pacification of those things which are in heaven and on earth, pertains to the reconciliation of all men εἰς αὐτὸν (unto him), to God, and with God, and to the pacification, whether of those things which are on earth, that is, of men, or of those which are in heaven, i.e., of the Angels, from which is distinguished that ἀποκαταλλαγὴ (reconciliation) of which v. 22 and 23 speak, namely that which is proper to the faithful, which imports the application of the reconciliation made through the death of Christ, just as also 2 Cor. V. 19, 20, καταλλαγὴ τῦ κόσμυ, the reconciliation of the whole world as to the universal merit of Christ, is distinguished from the καταλλαγὴ to which the Apostle exhorts, in regard to the reception of the reconciliation which is made through faith. For that was accomplished through the death of Christ; but this one occurs while the λόγος καταλλαγῆς (word of reconciliation) is announced, and we are warned, 'be reconciled to God.' As for the head, under whom we are again converted through this ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (recapitulation), although some make Christ that head, the Apostle nevertheless does not say that we are recapitulated under Christ, but ἐν τῷ Χρισῷ (in Christ), and he repeats it notably, ἐν ἀυτῷ (in him). Doubtless, the head to which we are brought back, and under which we are again joined, must be that under which we were once joined before the fall, both men and angels, which is not Christ, but the Triune God. Christ, however, is that Θεάνθρωπος (God-man) in whom and through whom we are again joined under one head, or recalled to one head, which is what it means to be recapitulated. But one must not say, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, that Christ was set as head over the angels regarding his divine, incorporeal nature, but over men according to the condition of the flesh: for Christ is established by the Apostle as the head of his Church, which is his mystical body, regarding both natures. For this is a title of office. Now, titles of office apply to Christ not regarding one or the other, but regarding both natures. I do not find in the Scriptures that angels are recalled to Christ's mystical body, and thus that Christ is called the head of the angels, even though he is their Lord and must be worshipped by them even according to his human nature, Phil. 2:9, Heb. 1:10. How much less does Grotius's gloss deserve assent, in which, moreover, we note unwritten and contradictory inventions, such as those concerning the factions and mutual dissensions among the good angels before Christ, which neither befit the holiness of angels nor are consistent with Scripture, for that passage in Job 4:18 is irrelevant here: in Dan. 10:13, the factions of good and evil angels are opposed, not those of the good among themselves: and also concerning the ministry of angels, as if it were only now exhibited to men—after Christ became King of the angels (regarding his human nature, that is, after the exaltation of Christ)—as if they had been called to angelic dignity, when not only Christians, but all the faithful before Christ had angels as ministers, which is evident from the history of the Patriarchs and Evangelists, and from the promises made to all the faithful, Ps. 34. Ps. 91. That angelic ministry Christ indeed acquired for us by the merit of his death, and through that ἀνακεφαλαίωσις τῶν πάντων (recapitulation of all things): But concerning Christ, the Apostle says in Heb. 13:8, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever: His merit was profitable both forward and backward: and concerning the creation of angels, of which Col. 1:16 speaks, that it is a new ordering—from which passage Grotius tries wrongly to explain this ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (recapitulation), when the κτίσις τῶν πάντων (creation of all things), the creation of all things both visible and invisible, and the ἀνακεφαλαίωσις τῶν πάντων (recapitulation and gathering together of all things to one head) are most different: the latter presupposes not creation, but the tearing apart of created things, on account of which there is a need for recollection and recall and reduction to one head. We have spoken expressly about that Socinian misinterpretation of the Apostolic passage in Col. 1:16 in a separate exercise, and therefore we do not wish to repeat the act here. What is said about the broken middle wall of partition between Jews and Gentiles is irrelevant here, where the subject is the recapitulation of all men, insofar as they had been torn away by sin from the one head, God, and separated from the angels, who were never torn away from their head, which was accomplished by the merit of Christ: where no distinction of men, nor distribution of Jews and Gentiles, or the hatred that existed between those peoples, has any place, and therefore neither does their condition. This pertains to the fruits of the recapitulation and reconciliation, as it is universal, by virtue of which all are called through

the Word of the Gospel to the communion of God and Christ. For that is prior to the calling, just as the calling is prior to the partition, even in this Apostolic sequence. Concerning the calling, it follows now.

Latin:

V. 10. Εἰς οἰκονομίαν τῶ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν) Ideo hoc Deus penes se retinuerat, ut suo demum tempore id publicaret, dispartiretque in Judæos & gentes. Est similitudo sumpta à familia, in qua paterfamilias, aut aliquis ejus loco, ex cella deprompta dimensæ dat singulis. Id hic Deo tribuitur, alibi ministris Dei, ut infra III. 2. 1. Cor. IX. 17. Col. I. 25. 1. Tim. I. 4. πλήρωμα καιρῶν est maturitas temporis, aut clarius, maturum tempus. Nam מלאת-היום Ebræis dicitur tempus, quod ad metam suam perductum est, Act. II. 1. Sic πλήρωμα χρόνων, Gal. IV. 4. πλήρωσις ἡμερῶν, Ezech. V. 2. Dan. X. 3. Credibile est, respici hic ad hebdomadas Danielis.

Ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ) κεφαλαιῶν, Sir. XXXII. 9. ἀνακεφαλαιοῦν, Rom. XIII. 9. est æra in summam colligere. Nam κεφάλαιον est summa, Ebræis תכן aut צתכנת, Chaldæis סוכם. Hinc procedente similitudine, qui dispersos in unum agmen cogit, recte dicitur eos ἀνακεφαλαιοῦν, sicut Latine colligere. Ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ per Christum tanquam caput.

Τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ ἐπὶ γῆς) Hoc est, quod Ebræi dicunt familiam Dei superiorem & inferiorem. Conf. Col. I. 20. Christo enim omnis potestas data & in cœlo & in terra, Matth. XXVIII. 18. vide infra 21, & cum eo loco confer Col. I. 16. ubi ἐκτίσθη videtur esse ordinata sunt, de qua hujus vocis significatione diximus aliquid in Prolegomenis ad Evangelia. Angeli olim alii Judæis, alii Persis, alii Græcis favebant, ut videre est apud Danielem X. 13. 20. XII. 1. Nunc omnes propter Christum libenter inserviunt Christianis, ut ad Angelicam dignitatem vocatis, Ebr. I. 14. Exempla vide Matth. XVIII. 10. Act. V. 19. XII. 2. XVI. 26. XXVII. 23. Judæi alienigenas oderant ut idololatras Gentibus invisi Judæi ob institutorum diversitatem. Qua de re diximus libr. II. de jure belli & pacis XV, 9. Nunc qui ex utroque genere ad Christum veniunt, amici, imò fratres inter se, unus simul Dei populus.

Ἐν αὐτῷ) Satis fuerat dixisse ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ. Sed repetendum censuit, quasi diceret, per ipsum inquam unum, non per ullum alium. Non hoc factum per Mosen, non per Philosophos.

Οἰκονομίαν de dispertitione mysterii, in Judæos & gentes, in ejusdem publicatione; ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν de dispersorum in unum agmen coactione; τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς de familia Dei superiori & inferiori Grotius interpretatur, de quibus eodem ferme modo antehac scripserat, in nonnullis tantum disertius mentem suam explicans, uti jam sequitur:

V. 10. Εἰς οἰκονομίαν τῶ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν) ad dispensationem plenitudinis temporum) Οἰκονομεῖν est penum observatam distrifbuere, ut Lucæ 16, 2. & sequentibus. Latinissime id dicitur dispensare, unde munus dispensatorum. Sic consilii illius distributio in Judæos & gentes οἰκονομίας dispensationis dicitur 1. Cor. IX. 17. Hic infra III. 2. Et in illa ad Colossenses hujus epistolæ velut consanguinea II. 2. & 1. Tim. I. 4. Ideo retinuerat apud se illud Deus, ut convenienti tempore publicaret. Πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν, plenitudo temporum, quod & πλήρωμα χρόνων, Gal. IV. 4. est tempus illud, quo vaticinia pleraque ac potissima impleta sunt, eventumque habuerunt.

de dici potest ἀνακεφαλαιῶσαι, quæ significatio huic loco maxime convenit. Τὰ πάντα omnia, intellige τὰ νοη- τὰ, intellectu utentia, ἐν τῷ Χρισῷ, in Christo, id est, sub Christo duce,

Τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς, quæ in cælo) Antea inter Angelos factiones erant & studia pro populis, vide Danielem X. v. 13. & adde Jobum IV. 18. & ea, quæ de Angelis dicit Hieronymus adversus Jovinianum II. & Maximus in Dialogo. Ea sustulit Christus, Rex factus etiam Ange- lorum, unum ex tot populis sibi populum colligens, cui Angeli ministerium nunc debeant, Ebr. I. v. 14. Vide exemplum Act. V. 19. XII. 11. XVI. 26. XXVII. 23. 44. Adde Matth. XVIII. 10. & 1. Cor. XI. 10. ubi de Ange- lis orationis agitur, quorum & liber Ebræus Chasidia meminit, & Tertullianus libro de oratione. Philo: Πε- ρὶ φιλανθρωπίας de humanitate eosdem vocat ἐφόρες κατὰ τὴν τῶν σοφῶν ἐμπορίαν, θεασαμένης, μήτι τ᾽ ὠδῆς ἐμμελές, inspectores, ut docet sapientum experientia, ne quid in cantu sit absonum. Ad Christi regnum, quod in Angelos est adeptus, nonnulli referunt id, quod est Col. I. 16. quia κτίζειν creare sæpe ordinationem novam significat. Certe ut pleraque epistolæ ad Colossenses cum hac epistola congruunt, ita & locus iste huic lu- cem afferre, & vicissim ab eo lucem mutuari videtur. Angeli infensi gentibus ob idololatricos cultus favent iisdem ad Christum conversis.

Καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, & quæ in terra sunt) Judæos & ex gentibus genitos, quotquot vocationi obtemperant, ru- pto intersepso: Sublato insuper odio, quod maximum fuerat. Nam sicut Judæi illos alienigenas habebant pro hominibus abominandis, in quo nec homicidium nec adulterium committi posset, cum ipsos ducerent fe- ris deteriores, & nuptias eorum innuptas, ut ex Josepho Albo, Mose Maimonide, Bacchai & aliis, in explicatio- ne Deut. XXI. 11. discimus; Ita hi vicissim Judæos ha- bebant pro hostibus Deorum immortalium, ut Cicero pro Flacco nos docet, & pro violatoribus humanæ socie- tatis, ut ex Apollinario, Molone, Diodoro Siculo, aliis- que multis apparet. Quod si Deum respicimus, per multa secula soli Judæi Dei populus: nunc omnes in Christum credentes Christi, & per Christum Dei popu- lus. Judæi ipsi quoque contempta vera pietate, & in solis ritibus posita inani fiducia, plerique Deo invisi. Nunc mutata omnia, conciliati & Deo inter se utrius- que generis homines, qui vocationi paruere.

Ἐν αὐτῷ, in ipso) Satis fuerat, quod præcessit, ἐν Χρι- στῷ, sed repetere id voluit, quo magis animis legentium imprimeret, unum esse cœlitum & terras colentium, piorum scilicet, Regem, Matth. XXVIII. 18.

Hæc Grotius. Quod ad οἰκονομίαν, non de publi- catione mysterii Evangelii hic agit Apostolus, quod etiam in V. T. publicatum, imo statim in Paradiso promulgatum novimus, Gen. 3, 15. & de patefactio- ne mysterii voluntatis divinæ gratiosæ jam verba fecerat, v. 9. sed de objecto voluntatis gratiosæ Dei, quam proposuit (ab æterno) in Christo, quod εὐ- δοκία & πρόθεσις illa vergat εἰς οἰκονομίαν in di- spensationem in plenitudine temporum exequen- dam, sitam nempe in ἀνακεφαλαιώσει τῶν πάντων ἐν τῷ χριστῷ. Quanquam enim quandoque οἰκονο- μία pro dispensatione officii adhibeatur, Eph. 3, 2. 1. Cor. 9, 17. unde & οἰκονόμοι μυσηρίων Θεῦ dicun- tur Apostoli, 1. Cor. 4, 1. Hæc tamen οἰκονομία sita est in ἀνακεφαλαιώσει τῶν πάντων, interprete A- postolo, quæ amplius quid importat, quam dispen- sationem Evangelii inter Judæos & gentes. Ne- que ignotum est, quid οἰκονομίαν dicant Græci Pa- tres, cum de Christi mysteriis sermo est: Divinam nempe illam dispensationem, quam adhibuit in negotio salutis nostræ per Christum Mediatorem & Salvatorem generis humani, quod nempe di- gnatus est, Filium suum unigenitum ordinare, ut is carnem nostram indueret, & in ea pro nobis tum divinam legem impleret, tum pro peccatis nostris satisfaceret, ut per fidem in ipsum remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & salutem consequeremur. Quam salutis nostræ admirandam dispensationem οἰκονομίαν vocavit Græca Ecclesia: Neque dubita- rim, eam significationem vocis hic fundatam esse: Quod etiã in loco simili Col. 1, 26. ἧς ἐγενόμην ἐγὼ διάκονος κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῦ θεῦ τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι εἰς ὑμᾶς πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ, locῦ habere potest. Nam minister Ecclesiæ Paulus factus erat quoad œconomiam illam divinam, quâ sibi datam, vel ad anuntiandum creditam penes & inter Colossenses ait: quia neq; novisse eam possumq sine divino dono, & ut præcones ejusdem simus, divina concessionis opus est, Matth. 11, 27. c. 13, 11. Rom. 10, 14. 15.

Et hac ὀικονομίᾳ Θεῦ τῇ ἐν πίσει agit etiam Apostolus 1. Tim. 1. 4. quæ tradenda in Ecclesiâ præteritis inutilibus quæstionibus & genealogiis. Οἰκονομίας voce, inquit B. Hunnius in hunc locum, ad ordinem administrationis respicit Paul9, gratia cujus per Christum Mediatorem his mediis, hoc ordine & processu in executione geritur & administratur, sicuti gerèndum in consilio suo sanxit & constituit Dominus. Similiter B. Balduinus: Huic plenitudini temporis tribuitur dispensatio s. ὀικονομία, quia omnia eo ordine à Christo peracta sunt, quo in consilio Dei æterno constitutum ac prædefinitum fuit. Nec aliter Chrysostomus exposuit, cui etsi οἰκονομία sit πλήρωμα τ̄ καιρω̄ν, hoc tamen πλήρωμα exponit de ipso Filii Dei adventu in plenitudine temporum, atq; ita de hac οἰκονομίᾳ differit in h. l. Nam postquam omnia fecit & per Angelos & per Prophetas, & per legem, & nihil proficiebat, & periculum erat, ne temere factus esset homo, imò vero suo malo, pereuntibus omnib9, & magis, quã in diluvio, hanc dispensationẽ invenit, quæ fit per gratiam, ne temere & frustra esset factus. Hanc temporũ plenitudinem dicit & sapientiam, quod quando maxime erant perituri, tunc salvi fuerunt. Theodoretius, sola, inquit, Divina natura est ab egestate aliena. Omnis vero creatura opus habebat susceptæ carnis dispensationis medicamento. Nec ab hoc sensu omnino abit Lombardus, qui retenta versione Vulgata hanc reddit interpretationem: Hoc tempore gratiæ, quo impleri, quæ cæteris temporibus promissa & figurata sunt, divina providentia rationaliter dispensavit. Alii tamen expressius eum reddunt, dispensationem salutis intelligentes, quam Pater Christo exercendã perficiendamq́, injunxit. Rem ipsam expressit etiam Hugo, & si forte minus convenienter vocem οἰκονομίας è jure arcessat, quod nempe dispensatio sit relaxatio juris. Dispensasse ergo Deum Patrẽ nobiscum ait, quando miserit Filium ad redimendũ genus humanum, quia si secundum rigorem justitiæ nobiscum ageret, dimitteret nos in perpetua servitute. Plenitudinem temporis Hugo dicit per Ebraismum plenum tempus, & hoc plenum dicit, quia fuit plenum gratiarum, implens figuras veteres, quod etsi iterum sese quoad rem recte habeat, non tamẽ vox πλήρωμα plenitudinem gratiarũ respicit, sed tempus completum dicitur respectu definitionis divinæ: quia hoc tempus destinatum erat divinitọ, nec prius, quam ipso illo cōpleto hæc perfici debebant, quod omninò maturũ & opportunũ juxta divinũ consiliũ fuit, Gal. 4, 4. Quod etiã ita nũcupari potest, quia est novissimum juxta Theophylactum: Vid. Ebr. 1, 1. & 1. Pet. 1, 20. 1. Joh. 2, 18. 1. Cor. 10, 10.

Quod ad ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν reddidit hoc verbum ἀνακεφαλαιώσασϑαι vulgatus instaurare. Erasmus & Bullingerus sumatim instaurare, Tertullianus lib. de monogam. ad initium reciprocari, Beza & Piscator recolligere, Hieronymus vertit recapitulare, idq; Oratorum sensu. Translatio Syriaca, interprete Tremellio, de integro renovare. Sed optime exponitur iterum ad unum caput revocare. Quem sensum & ipsum verbũ infert, & materia postulat, quia omnia, quæ in cœlo, & quæ super terrã τὰ νοερὰ indigebãt revocari sub unum caput, sub quo erant quidẽ cōstituta per creationem, quum & homines & Angeli unum caput Deum habuerint, sed per peccatum à Deo divulsi, illiq; rebelles facti sunt homines, nec cum Angelis, qui in veritate perstiterunt, sub uno illo capite ac Domino manserunt amplius, ideo per

Christu oportuit ea amplius ανακεφαλαιώσασθαι, ad unum caput denuo revocari. Hæc simplicissima est interpretatio. Qui ad alias creaturas extendunt τὰ πάντα, quam intellectu utentes, non adeo, quo- modo sub eodẽ capite creaturæ ratione destitutæ universæ fuerint, & quomodo sub eodem esse desi- erint, aut sub idẽ caput cum τοĩς νοεροĩς revocari in Christo vicissim cœperint, satis explicare possunt, ut apud Theodoretum & alios videre est. Qui vero de illis, qui in cœlo tum erant, quum hæc scriberet A- postolus beatis, scil. justorum perfectorum spiriti- bus accipiunt, nec oppositionem recte expedient, quum vel illo tempore, quo hæc epistola transiit ad Ephesios, plurimi in cœlũ migrare potuerint, nec intentioni Apostolicæ satisfaciũt, quæ minime hæc est, docere, quod tàm in Domino defuncti cœlo re- cepti, quam in terris agentes fideles, sub unũ caput in Christo revocati sint: Et ανακεφαλαίωσις, quæ in Christo facta, si intentionem Dei Patris, & meritũ Christi respicias, universalis omnino est, adeoque pertinet non tantum ad electos, sed etiam ad re- probos, etsi fructus ejusdem non ad hos, sed ad illos tantum redundet, idq; culpa infidelitatis. Sic Chry- sostomus: Τί ἐστιν ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι; συνάψαι. Qui etiam ita explicat: Unum omnibus posuit caput: Et omnes uni subjecit capiti. Ita n. (addit) fiet unio ita accurata & perfecta fuerit conjunctio: Quando o- mnia reducta fuerint in unũ caput, superne quod- dam necessarium habeant vinculum. Similiter Theophylactus: Erant, inquit, cælestia à terrenis istis discissa, ita ut non unum caput haberent. Nam etsi pro mundi hujus creationis ratione, unus esset omnibus Deus, nondum tamen qui charitate nobis conjungeretur, dignoscebatur. Quocirca propo- suit Deus instaurare cælestia simul & terrena, hoc est unum ca- put cunctis imponere. Eadem ratione B. Hunnius: Græca vox ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι ἐμφατικω̃ς designat instaurationem illam & reparationem rerum per lapsum primorum hominum amis- sarum, & ab invicem dispersarum recollectionem, nec non recon- ciliationem eorum, qui peccatis hominum offensi fuerant. Et porro: Apostolus universa ea complectitur, quæ vel instaura- tione indigebant, vel cum genere humano reconcilianda erant, aut in pristinam redigenda societatem & concordiam. Nam primo ruina generis humani omnino redintegranda erat, quod fieri non poterat, nisi constituta inter genus humanum in terris, & Deum in cælis pace & reconciliatione. Deinde etsi Angelis nihil impetratur per mortem Christi; tamen omnibus aliquid impetratur, quod quendam ad Angelos respectum habet, vide- licet quod Angeli, qui prius ab hominibus ob transgressionem erant alienati, jam illos pro suis conservis, sociis & consortibus ejusdem gaudii & regni rursum agnoscunt, adeoq; ipsis inservire non dedignantur. Addit quidem B. Hunnius: Sed hoc respe- ctu omnia in cælis & in terris sunt instaurata, quatenus tota u- niversitas Ecclesiæ omnium electorum in unum corpus ita reda- cta est per Christum, ut efficaciam meriti ipsius per fidem sentiat non solum militans in hac terris Ecclesia: verum etiam eadem perpetuo fruatur Ecclesia in cælis triumphans, atq; sic per saluta- rem ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν virtute operaque Christi sunt instaurata, redintegrata, recollecta, & reconciliata omnia. Verum hæc ad effectũ τῆς ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως, de qua hic sermo est, pertinent. Videtur autem hic solum de recapi- tulatione, quæ per sanguinem & in cruce Christi fa- cta est, agi: quæ à vocatione & perductione ad hæ- reditatem cœlestem aperte distinguitur, v. 11. & ad recõciliationem & pacificationem omniũ in cœlo & in terra, quæ facta διὰ τῦ αι̅́ματος τῦ σαυρῦ αὐτῦ per sanguinem crucis restringitur, Col. 1. 20. Hanc autem reconciliationem omnium, & pacificatio- nem eorum, quæ in cœlo & in terra sunt, ad recon- ciliationem omnium hominũ εἰς αὐτὸν, ad Deũ, & cũ Deo, & ad pacificationẽ, sive eorũ, quæ in terris, id est hominum, sive quæ in cœlis, i. e. Angelorum, pertinere non est dubium, à qua distinguitur ἀπο- καταλλαγὴ illa, de qua v. 22. & 23. fidelium nempe propria, quæ applicationem reconciliationis, per mortem Christi factæ, importat, quemadmodum & 2. Cor. V. 19. 20. καταλλαγὴ τῦ κόσμυ reconcilia- tio totius mundi quoad meritum Christi universale à καταλλαγῇ, ad quam hortatur Apostolus, quo- ad susceptionem reconciliationis, quæ per fidem fir, distinguitur. Illa enim facta est per mortem Christi; hæc vero sit, dum λόγος καταλλαγῆς annun- tiatur, & monemur καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ. Quod ad caput, sub quo iterum per hanc ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν convertimur, etsi nonnulli Christum id faciant, A- postolus tamen non sub Christum recapitulari nos dicit, sed ἐν τῷ Χρισῷ, idq; notanter repetit ἐν ἀυτῷ. Nimirum caput, ad quod reducimur, & sub quo iterum conjungimur, illud sit, oportet, sub quo olim conjuncti fuimus ante lapsum homines atque Angeli, quod non est Christus, sed Deus Trinunus. Christus vero Θεάνθρωπος ille est, in quo & per quem nos iterum conjungimur sub uno capite, vel revocamur ad unum caput, quod est recapitulari. Non vero est cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto di- cendum, quod Christus Angelis caput sit impositus quoad Divinam incorpoream naturam; hominibus vero secundum carnis conditionem: Nam Christus caput Ecclesiæ suæ, quæ corpus ejus mysticum est, ab Apostolo constituitur, quoad utramq; naturam. Est enim hoc nomen officii. Nomina autem officii Christo conveniunt non quoad alterutram, sed quoad utramq; naturam. Angelos ad corpus Chri- sti mysticum revocari, & ita Angelorũ caput Chri- stum vocari, etsi Dominus eorum sit ab ipsis etiam secundum Humanam naturam adorandus, Phil. II. 9. Ebr. I. 10. in scripturis non invenio. Quanto minus assensum meretur Grotii glossa, in qua præ- terea commenta ἄγραφα καὶ ἀντίγραφα nota- mus, utpote tum de Angelorum bonorum ante Chri- stum inter sese factionibus & dissidiis mutuis, quæ nec sanctitati Angelorum conveniunt, nec scriptu- ræ consentanea sunt, nam locus ille Job. IV. 18. hic ἀλλότριος est: Dan. X. 13. oppositæ sunt factiones An- gelorum bonorum & malorum, non vero bonorum inter se: tum de ministerio Angelorum, quasi id ho- minibus nunc demum, postquam Christus Angelorum Rex factus est (quoad humanam naturam, hoc est, post exaltationem Christi) ceu ad Angelicam di- gnitatem vocatis exhibeatur, quum non tantum Christiani, sed & fideles omnes ante Christum An- gelos habuerint ministros, quod ex historia Pa- triarcharum, & Evangelistarum constat, & ex pro- missionibus fidelibus omnibus factis, Ps. XXXIV. Ps. XCI. quod ministerium Angelicum Christus quidem nobis acquisivit merito mortis suæ, & per illã ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν τῶν πάντων: Sed de Christo A- postolus Ebr. XIII. 8. Jesus, inquit, Christus heri, ho- die, idem & in secula: Ejusdem meritum profuit & antrorsum & retrorsum: tum de creatione An- gelorum, de qua Col. I. 16. quod sit nova ordinatio, ex quo loco hanc ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν perperam ex- plicare conatur Grotius, quum maxime diversa sint κτίσις τῶν πάντων, creatio omniũ tum visibilium tum invisibilium, & ἀνακεφαλαίωσις τῶν πάντων, recapi- tulatio & recollectio omnium ad unum caput: quæ non creationem, sed creatorum etiã divulsionem supponit, ob quam opus est recollectione & revo- catione ac reductione ad unũ caput. Diximus a. ex professo de loci Apostolici Col. I. 16. ψευδερμηνείᾳ illa Sociniana peculiari exercitatione, ideoq; hic a- ctũ agere nolumus. Quæ de rupto pariete intergeri- no Judæorum & gentium dicuntur, hic aliena sunt, ubi de recapitulatione omnium hominum, quate- nȩ per peccatum avulsi erant ab uno capite Deo, & separati ab Angelis, qui nunquã à capite suo avulsi sunt, merito Christi facta, agitur: Ubi nulla homi- num διασολὴ, nec distributio Judæorum & gentiũ, aut odium, quod inter istos populos fuit, locũ ha- bet, adeoq; nec eorundem cōditio. Hæc ad fructus τῆς ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως κὶ ἀποκαταλλαγῆς, utpote universalis pertinet, vi cujus omnes vocantur per

Verbum Evangelii ad communionem Dei & Chri- sti. Illa enim prior est vocatione, uti vocatio prior partitione, etiam in hac συνεχεία Apostolica. De vocatione jam sequitur.

## 1:11
V. 11. In whom also we have obtained an inheritance) נחל כו, we have received a possession, that is, the right of possession, not a terrestrial one, as our ancestors did through Jesus the son of Nun, but a celestial one. Thus the Father is said to 'leave an inheritance to the sons' in some Greek codices in Isa. 17, that is, to leave a possession to the sons. Often, however, the right to a thing takes the name of the thing, as below in 2:6, Phil. 3:20. What he had previously said generally about Christians, he now distributes more distinctly into two kinds, and first he deals with himself and the Apostles, and others who had been called from among the Jews. In the Manuscript it is ἐκλήθημεν (we were called), not badly.

Latin:

V. 11. Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἐκληρώθημεν) נחל כו, possessionem, id est, jus possessionis accepimus, non terrestris, ut majores nostri per Jesum filium Nuu, sed coelestis. Sic Pater di- citur πληρᾶν τὺς ὑὺς in Graecis codicibus nonnullis Es. XVII. id est, possessionem filiis relinquere. Saepe autem jus ad rem rei nomen accipit, ut infra II. 6. Phil. III. 20. Quae prius generaliter de Christianis dixerat, jam distin- ctius in duo genera dispertit, priusque agit de se & Apo- stolis, & aliis, qui ex Judaeis vocati fuerant. In Manuscri- pto est ἐκλήθημεν, non male.

## 1:11
V. 11. In whom also we have obtained an inheritance) Of whom we have been made the patrimony. Among the Hebrew people, those lands which had fallen to each person in the first division were called kleros: because, of course, the first division there had been made by lot, as also among other nations, whence heirs were called kleronomoi. From this similarity, the Hebrew people were once called the kleros of God, Deut. 4:20, 9:26, 32:9, 1 Kings 8:51. But now those who believe in Christ, 1 Pet. 5:3. This word signifies that God wishes to have such persons, insofar as they are and remain such, perpetually as His own. Just as landed property among the Hebrews remained in the family and could not be alienated like movable goods. He speaks here properly of the Jews, who were called first, Matt. 10:5, 15:24, Acts 13:36, soon to lead the discourse to other believers, as Tertullian rightly observed in book 5 against Marcion.

Predestinated according to the purpose) what he had said generally above, he here applies first to the human race distributed into two parts, the Jews, as those called first; and so this prothesis, purpose, is the same here as eudokia was above.

Of Him who works all things according to the counsel of His will) by a circumlocution very appropriate to the matter, he designates God, so that we may understand that the revelation of the Gospel (for it is about that and the things depending upon it that we are dealing here, as the phrase 'all things' is accustomed to be restricted to the business at hand) flowed from no other source than the most free constitution of God.

Latin:

V. 11. Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἐκληρώθημεν, in quo etiam nos sortem adepti sumus) Cujus patrimonium nos facti sumus. Κλῆρος dicebantur in populo Ebraeo terrae, quae in pri- ma divisione cuique obtigerant: quia scilicet ibi pri- ma divisio forte facta fuerat, ut & in aliis gentibus, un- de haeredes dicti κληρονόμοι. Hinc ducta similitudine populus Ebraeus olim dictus κλῆρος Dei, Deut. IV. 20. IX. 26. XXXII. 9. 1. Reg. VIII. 51. Nunc vero ii, qui in Christum credunt, 1. Pet. V. 3. Significat haec vox Deum tales, qua scilicet tales sunt & manent, perpetuo pro suis habere velle. Sicut res soli apud Ebraeos in familia manebant, nec alienari poterant, ut res mobi- les. Loquitur autem hic proprie de Judaeis, qui prio- res sunt vocati, Matth. X. 5. XV. 24. Act. XIII. 36. mox ad alios credentes deducturus orationem, ut recte ob- servavit Tertullianus adversus Marcionem libro V.

Προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν, praedestinati secundum propositum) quod generaliter supra dixerat, id distri- buto humano genere in duas partes, Judaeis, ut prius vo- catis, prius aptat; itaque idem hic est πρόθεσις propo- situm, quod supra ἐνδοκία.

Τῶ τὰ πάντα ἐνεργῶντος κατὰ τὴν βυλὴν τῶ θελήμα- τος ἀυτῶ, ejus, qui operatur omnia secundum consi- lium voluntatis suae) circumlocutione ad rem valde apposita Deum designat, ut intelligamus revelationem Evangelii, (de eo enim & rebus inde pendentibus hic agitur, ut solet vox τὰ πάντα omnia ad id negotium, de quo agitur, adstringi) fluxisse non ex alio fonte, quam ex liberrima Dei constitutione.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. Being predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, that we should be to the praise of his glory) He shows that that calling of the Jews before others came from God's decree, namely, that they themselves should carry throughout the whole earth to the praise of God those things which Christ had done, and which had happened to Christ. Concerning the word προορίζεσθαι (to be predestined) and the word πρόθεσις (purpose), we have spoken before. But Paul describes God here by this title, that he brings about all things that he willed: from Isa. 46:10. Which is to be understood of those actions which are God's alone, such as sending Christ with commands, and raising him from the dead. See Rom. 9:19.

Those who first trusted in Christ) This is a description of the Jews, who were called first, and first believed in Christ, and placed their hope in him. Thus 2 Thess. 2:13, 'that God chose you from the beginning,' pertains to the Jews, who, because of Christianity, had been driven by the Jews and had gone to Thessalonica.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶ τὰ πάντα ἐνερ- γῶντος κατὰ τὴν βυλὴν τῶ θελήματος ἀυτῶ, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῶ) Ostendit illam Judaeorum ante alios vocationem venisse ex Dei decreto, nempe ut ipsi per omnem terram in Dei laudem perferrent ea, quae Christus egerat, quaeque Christo evenerant. De verbo προορίζεσθαι & de voce προθέσεως diximus ante. Deum autem Pau- lus hic describit hoc titulo, quod omnia effecta det, quae voluit: ex Es. XLVI. 10. Quod intelligendum de iis actio- nibus, quae Dei solius sunt, quale est Christum mittere cum mandatis, & eum mortuum resuscitare. Vid. Rom. 9, 19.

Τὸς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ) Haec est descriptio Ju- daeorum, qui priores vocati, & priores in Christum credi- dere, ac spem suam in eo collocarunt. Sic 2. Thess. II. 13. ὅτι εἵλετο ὑμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς, pertinet ad Judaeos, qui ob Christianismum à Judaeis pulsi Thessalonicam conces- serant.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. That we should be to the praise of His glory) Whence it is that He Himself obtains most deserved praises through our ministry, see what was said above.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῶ, ut simus in laudem gloriae ejus) Unde sit, ut nostro ministerio ipse laudes meritissimas assequatur, vide,quae supra.

## 1:13
V. 13. In whom also you, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, in whom also having believed) The correct order would have been, 'and having believed in him.' But the Greeks also sometimes place the postpositive article for a demonstrative. The Gospel is called here, as also in 2 Cor. 6:7, Truth, because it has nothing of the false mixed in, which the doctrines of the philosophers have: nor does it have shadows, as the law of Moses, but solid things. It is also called the Gospel of our salvation, because it is the way not only most certain, but at this time also the only one, which leads men to eternal salvation.

You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise) You were not sealed on the outside, as the Jews were circumcised, and the Greeks marked with the punctures of idols, but on the inside by the Holy Spirit whom God had promised through Christ, Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4, ch. 2:33. The mark of a ring impressed upon an instrument renders that which has been done indubitable. See what was said at John 3:33 and 6:27. Thus also those gifts of God, such as prophecies, healings, tongues, and the casting out of demons, rendered believers certain of God's fatherly benevolence toward them, Romans 5:5, 8:15, 16.

Similar things to these are read in the earlier notes of Grotius.

Latin:

V. 13. Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκύσαντες τὸν λόγον τ᾽ ἀληθείας τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ὑμῶν, ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες) Rectus ordo fuerat, κ᾿ ἀυτῷ πιστεύσαντες. Sed & Graeci articulum postpositivum nonnunquam ponunt pro demonstrativo. Evangelium vocatur hic, ut & 2. Cor. VI. 7. Ἀλήθεια, quia nihil habet admixtum falsi, quod habent doctrinae Philo- sophorum: neque umbras habet, ut lex Mosis, sed res so- lidas. Vocatur & Evangelium τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν, quia via est non tantum certissima, sed hoc tempore etiam uni- ca, quae ad aeternam salutem homines perducat.

Ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ Πνέυματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ) Non extra signati estis, quomodo Judaei circumcisi, & Graeci, idolorum punctis notati, sed intus Spiritu S. quem Deus per Christum promiserat, Luc. XXIV. 49. Act. I. 4. cap. II. 33. Signum annuli instrumento impressi reddit indu- bitabile, quod actum est. Vide, quae dicta ad Joh. III. 33. & VI. 27. Sic & dona illa Dei, puta Prophetiae, sanatio- nes, linguae, ejectiones Daemonum, certos reddebant cre- dentes de paterna Dei in se benevolentia, Roman, V. 5. VIII. 15. 16.

Gemina his leguntur in prioribus notis Grotianis

## 1:13
Verse 13.

In whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, (in whom also you, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation) You, namely, Ephesians, having now become Christians. The Gospel, the word of truth, is opposed to the shadows of the ancient law, so that truth signifies solidity at the same time, John 1:17, Rom. 15:8, Heb. 9:24. The first thing that is required is that the Gospel be heard.

In whom also having believed, (in whom also believing) The second thing is that faith be had in him. The correct phrasing would have been, and having believed in him. But the Apostles did not care for those minute rules of construction: and so they often changed genders, cases, and pronouns, being careless of words when such great matters occupied their minds.

You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, (you were sealed with the Spirit of promise, the Holy one) What is more astonishing than that those nations, alienated from God, despised by the Hebrews, were not only converted to piety, but also made equal to the Prophets, with gifts of tongues, healings, prophecies, and other similar things? But he increases the magnitude of the matter, because the Prophets had signified that this very thing would happen, as Joel 3:1, and Christ had expressly promised, Mark 16:17, Luke 24:49, John 7:38, 39. But just as the sign of a ring impressed upon the tablets of a contract makes what has been done firm and indubitable, so also those gifts did not allow believers to doubt concerning God's fatherly benevolence toward them, Rom. 5:5, 8:15, 16. In the same sense the word to seal is used, 2 Cor. 1:22. Moreover, it is frequent for the holy writers to employ several similitudes in explaining one thing, and that mixed: Thus eternal life is a price and an inheritance: the gifts of the Spirit are the impression of a seal and an earnest. It is to be noted, however, that this sealing was not given except to those already believing, John 14:17, Gal. 4:6. And this sealing is opposed, as being much more worthy, to that which was given to the Jews, who were marked on the skin, like the Samphorae and Coppatiae.

The word we were made heirs is rendered by others with the Vulgate, we were called by lot. Grotius previously rendered it we have obtained a lot, and explained it as, whose patrimony we have become. But in the Greek it is in whom, and therefore he later explained it more correctly as, we have received a possession (in Christ), that is, the right of possession, or of the heavenly inheritance. For the Apostle does not teach that we have become Christ's patrimony, but that we have obtained an inheritance in Christ, or the right to an inheritance, or that we have been called to that inheritance. But that Grotius restricts this to the Apostles and others who were called from among the Jews, no sufficient reason appears. The Apostle speaks of himself and other saints and believers through communication. It is not necessary to explain the word having hoped before as referring to the Jews, because they were called earlier and believed in Christ earlier, since it can be taken, as we warned before, of all the predestined, in the sense that faith is regarded before (in the Divine foreknowledge) the decree of predestination is made. For God predestined us according to purpose as having hoped before, who first believed in Christ, since we were predestined through faith in Christ, or in Christ, apprehended by faith: And faith was the cause of our election to eternal life. For it is customary for Holy Scripture that hope is taken for faith, Ps. 2:13, Matt. 12:21, John 5:41, Acts 24:26, Rom. 15:15, Col. 1:23, 1 Tim. 6:17. Which sense is not disapproved by Jerome. For he refers this word, as Crocius admits, to the Divine foreknowledge, in which the faithful had hoped from eternity. But that has nothing in common with the error of Origen. For to God even future things are present because of His eternal foreknowledge. In that 2 Thess. 2:13, chosen from the beginning is from the beginning of creation, or from eternity, because eternity is accustomed to be described in that way, because before creation there was nothing but mere eternity: But election was already made when things began to be created. Cf. John 1:1.

4. John I. 1. Therefore those periphrases are interchanged: from the foundation of the world, Matt. XIII. 15. Luke XI. 50. Rev. XIII. 8. chap. XVII. 8. And before the foundation of the world, John XVII. v. 24. Eph. I. v. 4. 1 Pet. I. 20.

But that the Apostle later in verse 13 addresses the Ephesians specifically, does not prove firmly enough that the former concern only the Jews, since those things which he had said generally about the elect having the remission of sins and being called into the heavenly inheritance, he could have applied specifically to the holy and faithful Ephesians, which is exactly what was done here. Nor indeed are only those times looked to in which these things were written. But election, calling, justification, and inheritance concern the faithful of all times, nor is it assumed except falsely, as if at another time there was another way to salvation, whereas at this time there is a single way, the Gospel. For no one ever comes to salvation otherwise than through the Gospel: which was promulgated to all men in the Protoplasts, Gen. III. 15. since no one comes to the Father except through the Son, Heb. XI. 6. The words 'that we should be to the praise of his glory' do not look only to the Apostolic office or the sacred ministry, but to the end of all the predestined and faithful, inasmuch as they were predestined for this, that they might be to the praise of his glory, just as also the sealing, done through the Spirit of promise, does not look to the signs of healings, tongues, and prophecies, through which Divine benevolence was confirmed to the Gentiles, but to a further confirmation of the faithful, which the faithful Ephesians had in common with other saints, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles. For the Spirit of promise is not restricted to Apostolic times, but [is given] to the faithful at all times, not only in the New, but also in the Old Testament, and in all of them he seals eternal life in their hearts, of which the Holy Spirit is also the earnest among all.

He is named, however, the Spirit of promise, both because he is conferred and given according to the Divine promise, Is. XLIV. 2. Ezek. XXXVI. 26. Joel II. 28, 29. John VII. 37, ch. XIV, XV, XVI, Acts I, and because he confirms the Divine promises in our hearts and makes us certain of them. That 'in whom also having believed' can be referred to Christ, because through Christ we both hear the Word of truth and believe the Word. For both benefits are of Christ, and the preaching of the Word and the gift of faith are to be credited to his merit. There is no reason, therefore, why Paul should be argued with, along with other Apostles, because they do not care for the rules of construction, because they often interchange genders, cases, and pronouns, nor is it a worthy eulogy for God-breathed writers that they were careless of words, when such great matters occupied their mind, much less is it fitting for Scripture, which ought to instruct us unto salvation. Crocius agrees. In whom, namely Christ, to whom he referred all the preceding benefits, v. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 13. For so I would prefer to take it with Lombard and Zanchius, rather than interpret it with Piscator as concerning the Gospel: Nor is there any need for an ellipsis, 'in whom also you having heard,' just as Zanchius supplies 'you were allotted,' as does also Cornelius à Lapide: Others, with Calvin, Beza, and Arias Montanus, understand the word 'you hoped.' But the blessed Luther rightly rendered it without a supplement: 'Through whom you also have heard the Word of truth.'

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκύσαντες τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ Εὐαγγέ- λιον τῆς σωτηρίας ὑμῶν, in quo & vos cum audiissetis ver- bum veritatis Evangelium salutis vestræ) Vos nimi- rum Ephesii Christiani jam facti. Evangelium λόγον ἀληθείας verbum veritatis opponitur umbris antiquæ legis, ita ut veritas soliditatem simul significet, Joh. I. 17. Rom. XV. 8. Ebr. IX. 24. primum, quod exigitur, est, ut audiatur Evangelium.

Ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιϛεύσαντες, in quo & credentes) Alterum ut fides ei habeatur. Rectus sermo fuerat, καὶ ἀυ- τῷ πιϛεύσαντες, & ipsi credentes. Sed Apostoli minu- tas illas constructionis regulas non curabant: itaque genera, casus, pronomina sæpe commutabant, verbo- rum incuriosi, cum tantæ res mentem ambirent.

Ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ Πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ, si- gnati estis Spiritu promissionis Sancto) Quod magis stupendum, quam gentes illas, à Deo alienas, ab Ebræis contemptas, non modo ad pietatem conversas, sed & Prophetis æquatas, donis linguarum, sanationum, va- ticiniorum, aliisque similibus? Sed auget rei magni- tudinem, quod hoc ipsum futurum Prophetæ signifi- caverant, ut Joel III. 1. & Christus diserte promiserat Marci XVI. 17. Luc. XXIV. 49. Joh. VII. 38. 39. Sicut autem signum annuli impressum tabulis contractus firmum atque indubitabile reddit, quod actum est, ita & dona illa credentes de Dei in se paterna benevolentia dubitare non sinebant, Rom. V. 5. VIII. 15. 16. Eodem sensu usurpatur vox σφραγίζεσθαι signare, 2. Cor. I, 22. Frequens autem est sanctis scriptoribus, ut in una re explicanda plures adhibeant similitudines, idque per- mixtæ: Sic vita æterna, pretium & hæreditas: Dona Spiritus, sigilli impressio & arrhabo. Notandum au- tem hanc obsignationem non datam nisi jam credenti- bus, Joh. XIV. 17. Gal. IV. 6. Et opponitur hæc ob- signatio ut multo dignior ea, quæ Judæis erat data, qui in cute signabantur, ut Samphoræ & Coppatiæ.

Vox ἐκληρώθημεν ab aliis redditur cum Vul- gata, sorte vocati sumus. Grotius prius reddidit sortem adepti sumus, & exposuit, cujus patrimonium facti sumus. Sed in Græco est ἐν ᾧ, ideoque rectius postea exposuit, possessionem accepimus (in Christo) id est, jus possessionis, vel hæreditatis cælestis. Non enim quod nos Christi patrimonium facti, sed quod in Christo hæreditatem adepti simus, vel jus ad hæreditatem, Apostolus docet, vel quod ad hæ- reditatem illam vocati simus. Quod autem hæc ad Apostolos, & alios, qui ex Judæis vocati fuerint, restringit Grotius, nulla sufficiens causa apparet. Loquitur de se, & aliis sanctis & fidelibus per com- municationem Apostolus. Vocem προηλπικότες non necessum est de Judæis, quod priores vocati & priores in Christum crediderint, explicare, quum accipi possit, ut antea monuimus, de omnibus præ- destinatis, eo sensu, quod prius (in προγνώσει Divi- na) fides respiciatur, quam decretum prædestina- tionis fiat. Prædestinavit enim Deus κατὰ πρόθε- σιν nos ceu προηλπικότας, qui prius credidimus in Christum, quum per fidem in Christum prædesti- nati simus, vel in Christo, fide apprehenso: Et fi- des causa electionis nostræ fuerit ad vitam æter- nam. Spem enim pro fide accipi solenne est scri- pturæ sacræ, Psal. II. 13. Matth. XII. 21. Joh.V. 41. Act. XXIV. 26. Rom. XV. 15. Col. I. 23. 1. Tim. VI. 17. Qui sensus non improbatus Hieronymo. Refert enim hanc vocem, fatente Crocio, ad præscientiam Divinam, in quà fideles sperarint ab æterno. Id autem cum errore Origenis nihil habet commercii. Nam Deo etiam futura sunt præsentia ob æternam ejus πρόγνωσιν. In illo 2. Thess. II. 13. electi ἀπ’ ἀρ- χῆς est ab initio creationis, vel ab æterno, quod ita soleat æternitas describi, quia ante creationem ni- hil nisi mera fuit æternitas: Electio autem facta jam sit, cum inciperent res creari. Conf. Joh. I. 1.

4. Joh. I. 1. Ideo permutantur illæ περιφράσεις ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, Matth. XIII. 15. Luc. XI. 50. Apoc. XIII. 8. cap. XVII. 8. Et πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, Joh. XVII. v. 24. Eph. I. v. 4. 1. Petr. I. 20.

Quod autem postea vers. 13. Ephesios peculiariter compellat Apostolus, non satis firmiter probat, quod priores Judaeos tantum concernant, quum ea, quae generatim dixerat de electis remissionem peccatorum & in haereditatem coelestem vocatis, speciatim ad Ephesios sanctos & fideles applicare potuerit, quod hic omnino factum. Nec vero tantum illa tempora respiciuntur, quibus haec scripta sunt. Sed electio, vocatio, justificatio, haereditas fideles omnium temporum concernit, nec nisi falso assumitur, quasi alio tempore alia ad salutem via fuerit, hoc vero tempore unica fit via, Evangelium. Non enim unquam aliter, quam per Evangelium ad salutem quis venit: quod in Protoplastis omnibus hominibus promulgatum est, Gen. III. 15. quum nemo veniat ad Patrem, nisi per Filium, Ebr. XI. 6. Verba εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτῦ, non respiciunt tantum munus Apostolicum, vel ministerium sacrum, sed finem omnium praedestinatorum & fidelium, utpote qui ad id praedestinati sunt, ut sint in laudem gloriae ejus, quemadmodum & obsignatio, per Spiritum promissionis facta, non respicit signa sanationum, linguarum, & vaticiniorum, per quae Divina benevolentia gentibus confirmata sit, sed ulteriorem confirmationem fidelium, quam Ephesii fideles cum aliis sanctis, sive è Judaeis, sive è gentibus communem habebant. Spiritus enim promissionis non ad Apostolica tempora restrictus, sed fidelibus omnibus temporibus, nec in novo solum, sed etiam in Veteri Testamento, iisque omnibus obsignat in cordibus ipsorum vitam aeternam, cujus etiam arrhabo est Spiritus S. penes omnes.

Nominatur autem Spiritus promissionis, tum quia ex promisso Divino confertur & datur Es. XLIV. 2. Ezech. XXXVI. 26. Joel. II. 28. 29. Joh. VII. 37. c. XIV. XV. XVI. Act. I. tum quia promissiones Divinas in cordibus nostris confirmat, nosque de illis certos reddit. Illud ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες, ad Christum referri potest, quia per Christum & Verbum veritatis audimus, & Verbo credimus. Utrumque enim beneficium Christi est, ejusque merito acceptum ferendum verbi praedicatio & donum fidei. Non ergo est, cur arguatur Paulus cum aliis Apostolis, quod constructionis regulas non curent, quod genera, casus, pronomina saepe commutent, nec dignum hoc est θεοπνεύστοις scriptoribus elogium, quod verborum incuriosi fuerint, cum tantae res mentem ambirent, nedum conveniens scripturae, quae nos instruere debet ad salutem. Annuit Crocius. In quo, scilicet Christo, ad quem superiora omnia beneficia retulit, v. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 10. 13. Sic enim malim cum Lombardo & Zanchio accipere, quam cum Piscatore de Evangelio interpretari: Neque ellipsi aliqua opus est, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκούσαντες, quemadmodum Zanchius subaudit ἐκληρώθητε, ut & Cornelius à Lapide: Alii cum Calvino, Beza & Ariamontano verbum ἠλπικάτε sperastis subintelligunt. Recte autem B. Lutherus sine supplemento reddidit: Durch welchen auch ihr gehöret habt das Wort der Wahrheit.

## 1:14
V. 14. 'Who is the earnest of our inheritance') In the Manuscript 'which is' with the same sense. Concerning the word 'earnest' we spoke at 2 Cor. I. 22 and V. 5. It is a Canaanite or Phoenician word, which came thence into Greece through trade. And it fits this matter very well. For an earnest is a part of the price given in advance, so that there may be less doubt about the full payment. Thus those heavenly gifts of the Spirit were a certain portion of heavenly and eternal happiness, and they gave assurance of it. That heavenly happiness is called an inheritance, because it will never depart from us, no more than hereditary lands among the Hebrews, the ownership of which always returned to the original masters.

Ἐις ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως) That is, to give assurance that it will come to pass that those who have believed and obeyed will also be resurrected to heavenly life. Ἀπολύτρωσις here, as also below IV. 30, is understood not as that which makes a way to repentance, nor that cleansing from vices which occurs in this life, but that full freedom from all infirmities of soul and body, that is, the blessed resurrection, Romans VIII. v. 23, below IV. verse 30. Περιποίησις, however, after the Hebrew manner, is an abstract for a concrete: That people acquired by GOD, as is said 1 Peter II. verse 9 and Acts XX. verse 20. This word, moreover, has emphasis. For we are accustomed to value highly those things which cost us dearly. Another perhaps might prefer to understand ἀπολύτρωσιν περιποιήσεως here as that liberation which brings life with it, for the Hebrew מחיה is ζωοποίησις, Ezra IX. v. 8, 9, περιποίησις 1 Chronicles XIV. v. 13.

Ἐις ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης ἀυτοῦ) The Apostle often repeats the word praise. Those gifts of the Spirit, which once had happened to a few in the Hebrew people, were now happening to most Christians, even those who, not born of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but of idolaters, had themselves been idolaters before.

We now add what Grotius had already commented before on these same words to the same effect:

Verse 14. Ὅς ἐστιν ἀῥῥαβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν) who is the earnest of our inheritance) Thus also elsewhere he calls those gifts by the name of earnest, as in the mentioned place 1 Corinthians I. verse 22 and V. verse 5. The word ἀῥῥαβὼν is not Greek in origin, but Syriac ערבון, as appears in Genesis XXXVIII. verse 17, from the word ערב, which signifies to pledge. Doubtless, the Greeks received this word from the most ancient Phoenician merchants through trade. An earnest, or as the Latins say more briefly, an arrha, is a part of the price, given in advance, so that assurance may be given of the whole price to follow. Thus those gifts, coming from heaven, were a certain part of future happiness, and of the principal thing to follow (which, because it followed Christians by perpetual right, is called an inheritance), and gave them most certain assurance. Thus, so that one does not distrust that peace has been made, hostages are accustomed to be given.

Ἐις ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως in redemption of the acquisition) that is, that earnest makes us certain of the blessed resurrection to follow. Ἀπολύτρωσις, redemption, besides that which is from the habit of vices, is mentioned as twofold in the new covenant: the former from the guilt of sins, which is promised to believers; the other from miseries and death itself, which is nothing other than the blessed resurrection, as I said, which is called by the same name in Romans VIII. v. 23 and below IV. verse 30. Περιποίησις, acquisition, however, will here be best understood as the Church or the university of Christians, which Peter in 1 Epistle II. v. 9 calls λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, a people of acquisition. The Church is called this in respect to GOD, who περιεποιήσατο διὰ τῦ ἰδίυ αἵματος, acquired it through his own blood, that is, through the bloody death of his Son. There is somewhat more in the word περιποιήσεως, acquisition, than in the word κλῆρος, lot, which we had before. Κλῆρος signifies a lot, a proper and perpetual right; περιποίησις signifies acquisition, and this also signifies the manner of acquiring, which is grave and laborious. We are accustomed to value highly those things which cost us much.

Ἐις ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτῦ, in praise of his glory) He repeats that often, so that we may never forget to give thanks to God for so many benefits: first for our calling, then for the right given to eternal life, and furthermore, because he has made us certain of that right.

But in these we especially desire that which he understands as the earnest of the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit. For these were neither granted to all believers, but primarily to the Apostles and other Ministers of the Word for the confirmation of the Evangelical doctrine, nor do they pertain to all times, like the Spirit of promise and the earnest of the inheritance, but they pertained to the primitive Church and to ministering gifts, not to sanctifying ones, nor, finally, were they a part or portion of happiness or of the heavenly inheritance; for what do gifts of healings, or of tongues, or of the expulsion of demons and the like have to do with this? What is said about ἀπολυτρώσει, that one is that which makes a way to repentance, another is the cleansing from vices which occurs in this life, another is the liberation from all infirmities of soul and body, or the blessed resurrection, is not analogous to the scriptures. For in that, ἀπολύτρωσις is said to be about the redemption made by the λύτρῳ or price of the blood of Christ, not as a way to repentance, but as the meritorious cause of our salvation, Romans III. v. 24, Ephesians I. v. 2, Colossians I. v. 14, or about the liberation from the guilt of sins, which is done by the virtue of the λύτρῳ of Christ, and is situated in the remission of sins, Hebrews IX. 15, or the liberation of the body, which is likewise to be attributed to the merit of Christ, and is not only in the blessed resurrection, Luke XXI. v. 28, but also in a blessed death, Romans VIII. v. 28. Therefore Christ is said to be made for us ἀπολύτρωσις, 1 Corinthians I. v. 30, because by his merit we obtain redemption not only from sin, but also from the misery of this life. However, pure and full redemption is understood here, as Chrysostom calls it; for now indeed we are involved in the world, and many human things happen, and we are with the ungodly. But pure redemption is when there will be neither sins, nor human affections, nor will we be with all the rest of the unclean.

Περιποίησις, with the abstract used for the concrete, can be taken as the acquired inheritance, which is indeed a pledge and earnest of the Holy Spirit for the plenary redemption of the acquired inheritance; which, as it was acquired for us by the blood of GOD, Acts XX. 28, that is, of Christ, who is God, blessed over all forever, Rom. IX. 5. (For we showed there that the περιποίησις is not attributed to the Father, but to Christ, against the Socinianizing gloss of Grotius:) Thus the earnest of the Holy Spirit is confirmed to us, until we fully enjoy that redemption. Ἀπολύτρωσις therefore τῆς περιποιήσεως is the full enjoyment of the redemption of the inheritance acquired for us, which is expected in eternal life. For then there will be absolute liberty, when sin will cease entirely, and when the individuals of those who have offended will be freer by the fellowship, and those who are God's portion and have been sought out will be revealed, so that they themselves will be for a people, as Theophylact says here. Yet this sense of Grotius is not inconvenient, who understands the plenary redemption of the people acquired through περιποίησις, or τῆς περιποιήσεως, who is called λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν in 1 Pet. II. v. 9. Theophylact also noted this sense, that some interpret it thus, into the redemption of the acquisition, that is, of us, whom God has acquired, in this place, which is also approved by Bullinger, Calvin, Hyperius, and Piscator. We spoke of the sealing and the earnest of the Holy Spirit at 2 Cor. I. 23. Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Ambrosiaster take the sealing to refer to the gifts of the Holy Spirit indefinitely. Lombard and Hugo explain it as the gift of sanctification, or the image of God reformed in us. Crocius approves this sense, because by sealing the image of the seal is imprinted, and thus the image, wisdom, and holiness of the Holy Spirit are imprinted upon the faithful, the chief part of which is charity, which is imprinted in sanctification. While, therefore, the light of wisdom, the heat of charity, and the brightness of holiness are conferred upon the Ephesians, in whom faith had been kindled by the Gospel, they are sealed by that very seal impressed upon their hearts as if upon wax, and thus they are both more and more conformed to the Spirit, as the archetype of holiness and the imprinting seal, and are distinguished from the flock of the Devil, and are more confirmed regarding the certainty of the promises. Not otherwise than as a letter is confirmed by a seal. For while the Gospel is written by the pen of the Holy Spirit in their hearts, they become the letter of GOD, 2 Corinth. III. 3. But after they have become the letter of God, they are sealed. By the former act, faith is generated in their hearts; by the latter, it is strengthened, so that, fighting bravely against every doubt, it may rest entirely in the truth of God, as Crocius not inaptly says here. The firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, which are conferred upon us here, are also called an earnest, because they are, as it were, a certain small portion of the goods which we expect in the other life in full measure, and of the heavenly inheritance, which certainly is not to be understood as concerning extraordinary gifts proper to a few certain heirs to come, but as concerning ordinary ones, common to all the faithful, though in varying degrees. Yet it is not to be concluded from the name of earnest money that the faithful, who have once received the Spirit of promise, cannot fall away from the same, or that he who has that earnest is absolutely certain of the plenary payment of the sum and of consummated salvation, as Grotius gathers. For a likeness is not to be extended beyond the comparison shown in scripture, much less against scripture, which teaches that the faithful can totally and finally fall away from divine grace, and lose the Holy Spirit, Luke 8:12, Heb. 6:4 seqq. Whence Eph. 4:30 we are warned not to grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom we are sealed unto the day of redemption.

PART III. The Apostolic testimony concerning the Eucharist and his prayers for the illumination of the Ephesians.

Latin:

V. 14. Ὅς ἐστιν ἀῤῥαβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν) In Manuscripto ὅ ἐστι pari sensu. De voce ἀῤῥαβὼν diximus 2. Cor. I. 22. & V. 5. Vox est Cananaea sive Phoenicissa, quae per commercia inde in Graeciam venit. Et valde huic rei convenit. Est enim arrhabo pars pretii in antecessum data, quo minus de plena solutione dubitetur. Sic dona illa Spiritus coelestia portio quaedam erant felicitatis coelestis & aeternae, & de ea fidem faciebant. Dicitur autem felicitas illa coelestis haereditas, quia nunquam à nobis discedet, non magis quam terrae haereditariae apud Ebraeos, quarum proprietas semper redibat ad veteres Dominos.

Ἐις ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως) Id est, ad fidem fa- ciendam, futurum ut qui credidere & obsecuti sunt, etiam resuscitentur ad vitam cœlestem. Ἀπολύτρωσις hic, ut & infra IV. 30. intelligitur non illa, quæ viam facit ad pœni- tentiam, neque ipsa, quæ in hac vita contingit a vitiis emun- datio, sed illa plena libertas ab omnibus animi corporisque infirmitatibus, id est, beata resurrectio, Roman. VIII. v. 23. infra IV. vers. 30. Περιποίησις autem Ebræo more abstra- ctum pro concreto: Populus ille DEO acquisitus, ut dici- tur 1. Petr. II. vers. 9. & Actor. XX. vers. 20. Habet autem hæc vox ἔμφασιν. Solemus enim magni facere ea, quæ no- bis magni constant. Alius forte malit ἀπολύτρωσιν περι- ποιήσεως hic intelligere eam liberationem, quæ vitam se- cum ferat, Nam מחיה Ebræum est ζωοποίησις, Esdr. IX. v. 8. 9. περιποίησις 1. Paral. XIV. v. 13.

Ἐις ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης ἀυτοῦ) Sæpe repetit Apostolus vo- cem ἐπαίνου. Dona illa Spiritus, quæ olim paucis in Ebræo populo contigerant, nunc contingebant plerisque Chri- stianorum, etiam illis, qui non ab Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo, sed ab idololatris orti, ante & ipsi idololatræ fuerant.

Addimus nunc, quæ in eandem sententiam jam ante ad hæc verba commentatus erat Grotius:

Vers. 14. Ὅς ἐστιν ἀῥῥαβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν) qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ) Sic & alibi dona ista arrhæ vocabulo appellat, ut dicto loco 1. Cor. I. vers. 22. & V. vers. 5. Vox ἀῥῥαβὼν non Græca est origine, sed Syriaca ערבון, ut apparet Gen. XXXVIII. vers. 17. a voce ערב, quod spondere significat. Nimirum a Phœnicibus mer- catoribus antiquissimis hanc vocem Græci per com- mercia accepere. Est autem arrhabo, sive ut Latini brevius dicunt, arrha, pars pretii, data in antecessum, ut de toto pretio secuturo fides fiat. Sic illa dona, ex cœlo venientia, pars quædam erant futuræ felicitatis, & rei principalis secuturæ, (quæ, quod perpetuo jure Christianos sequebatur, hæreditas dicitur) fidem ipsis faciebant certissimam. Sic ne factæ paci diffidatur, obsi- des dari solent.

Ἐις ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως in redemptionem ac- quisitionis) id est, arrhabo ille nos certos facit secuturæ beatæ resurrectionis. Ἀπολύτρωσις redemptio, præter eam, quæ est a vitiorum consuetudine, duplex in novo fœdere memoratur, prior a peccatorum reatu, quæ credentibus promittitur, altera a miseriis & morte ipsa, quæ nihil est aliud, quam beata, quam dixi, resurre- ctio, quæ eodem nomine appellatur Roman. VIII. v. 23. & infra IV. vers. 30. Περιποίησις, acquisitio vero hic optime intelligetur Ecclesia sive universitas Christiano- rum, quæ Petro 1. Ep. II. v. 9. λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν popu- lus acquisitionis. Vocatur autem sic Ecclesia DEI re- spectu, qui eam περιεποιήσατο διὰ τῦ ἰδίυ αἵματος ac- quisivit per sanguinem suum, id est, per mortem cruen- tam Filii sui. Plus aliquanto est in voce περιποιήσεως acquisitionis, quam in voce κλήρε fors, quam ante ha- buimus. Κλῆρος fors jus proprium perpetuumque si- gnificat, περιποίησις acquisitio & hoc & modum acqui- rendi gravem ac laboriosum. Solemus autem plurimi ea facere, quæ magno nobis constant.

Ἐις ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτῦ, in laudem gloriæ ipsius) Sæpe id repetit, ne unquam obliviscamur Deo pro tot beneficiis gratias agere, primum pro vocatione, deinde pro jure dato ad vitam æternam, præterea vero, quod ejus juris certos nos fecerit.

In quibus vero id maxime desideramus, quod arrham intelligat de donis extraordinariis Spiri- tus sancti. Nam hæc neque concessa sunt fideli- bus omnibus, sed imprimis Apostolis aliisque Ver- bi Ministris ad confirmationem doctrinæ Evan- gelicæ, neque ad omnia tempora pertinent, ut Spiri- tus promissionis & arrhabo hæreditatis, sed ad primitivam Ecclesiam, & ad dona ministrantia pertinebant, non ad sanctificantia, nec denique pars vel portio quædam erant felicitatis aut hære- ditatis cœlestis, quod enim ad hanc dona fanatio- num, aut linguarum, aut expulsionis Dæmonum & similia? Quod de ἀπολυτρώσει dicitur, quod alia sit, quæ viam facit ad pœnitentiam, alia quæ in hac vita contingit a vitiis emundatio, alia ab omnibus animi corporisque infirmitatibus liberatio, vel beata resurrectio, scripturæ analogum non est. In eo e- nim ἀπολύτρωσις de redemptione λύτρῳ vel pre- tio sanguinis Christi facta dicitur, non ut via ad pœnitentiam, sed ut causa meritoria salutis no- stræ, Rom. III. v. 24. Eph. I. v. 2. Col. I. v. 14. vel de liberatione a peccatorum reatu, quæ fit virtu e λύτρῳ Christi, & in remissione peccatorum sita est Ebr. IX. 15. vel liberatione corporis, quæ itidem merito Christi tribuenda, nec tantum in beata re- surrectione sit, Luc. XXI. v. 28. sed etiam morte beata, Rom. IIX. v. 28. Ideo Christus nobis factus dicitur ἀπολύτρωσις 1. Cor. I. v. 30. quia merito ejus redemptionem non a peccato tantum, sed & a miseria hujus vitæ consequimur. Intelligitur au- tem hic pura & plena redemptio, ut vocat Chry- sostomus; Nam nunc quidem & in mundo versa- mur, & multa humana accidunt, & cum impiis sumus. Pura vero redemptio est, quando neque pec- cata fuerint, neque affectus humani, neq; cum reliquis omnibus immundis fuerimus.

Περιποίησις abstra- cto posito pro concreto, de acquisita hæreditate accipi potest, quod nempe pignus sit & arrhaba Spiritus sancti ad redemtionem plenariam hære- ditatis acquisitæ; quæ uti acquisita nobis est san- guine DEI Actor. XX. 28. hoc est Christi, qui est Deus, super omnia benedictus in secula Rom. IX. 5. (Non n. Patri illic tribui τὴν περιποίησιν, sed Chri- sto, adversus Socinianizantem glossam Grotii illic ostendimus:) Ita arrha Spiritus sancti nobis con- firmatur, donec redemptione illa plenarie frua- mur. Ἀπολύτρωσις ergo τῆς περιποιήσεως est plena fruitio redemptionis hæreditatis nobis acquisitæ, quæ in æterna vita expectatur. Tum enim futura est & absoluta libertas, cum penitus cessabit peccatum, & cum delinquentium erunt sanctiores singuli consor- tio liberi, & patebunt, qui Deo parti sunt & quæsiti ita ut ipsi sint futuri in populum, ut hic Theophyla- ctus. Non tamen incommodus hic sensus Grotii, qui redemptionem plenariam populi per περι- ποίησιν acquisiti, vel τῆς περιποιήσεως, qui λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν 1. Petr. II. v. 9. dicitur, intelligit. Notavit hunc sensum etiam Theophylactus, quod nonnulli ita interpretentur, in redemptionem acquisitionis, hoc est, nostri, quos acquisivit Deus, in h. l. qui etiam probatus Bullingero, Calvino, Hyperio, Pisca- tori. De obsignatione & arrhabone Spiritus sancti diximus ad 2. Cor. I. 23. Chrysostomus, Oecumenius & Ambrosiaster obsignationem de donis Spiritus sancti accipiunt indefinite. De dono sanctificatio- nis explicant Lombardus & Hugo, vel imagine Dei in nobis reformata. Quem sensum probat Crocius, quia obsignando imprimitur imago sigilli, & sic imprimitur fidelibus Spiritus sancti imago, sapien- tia, & sanctitas, cujus præcipua pars est charitas, quæ in sanctificatione imprimitur. Dum igitur Ephesiis, in quibus fides erat per Evangelium accen- sa confertur lux sapientiæ, calor charitatis, & nitor sanctimoniæ eo ipso sigillo cordi ipsorum, tanquam cere, impresso, obsignantur, adeoque tum magis & magis conformantur Spiritui, tanquam sanctitatis archetypo & sigillo imprimenti, tum discernuntur a grege Diaboli, tum magis confirmantur de promissio- num certitudine. Non aliter atque epistola sigillo con- firmatur. Dum enim Evangelium stylo Spiritus san- cti in eorum cordibus scribitur, fiunt epistola DEI 2. Corinth. III. 3. At postquam facti sunt Dei epistola, obsignantur. Priori actu gignitur fides in eorum cor- dibus; posteriori roboratur, ut contra dubitationem omnem fortiter pugnans in Dei veritate penitus ac- quiescat, ut non inconcinne hic Crocius. Arrha etiam vocantur primitiæ Spiritus sancti, quæ hic nobis conferuntur, quia scilicet portiuncula quæ- dam sunt bonorum, quæ πίονι μέτρῳ in altera vita expectamus, & hæreditatis cœlestis, quam certe non de donis extraordinariis paucis quibusdam hæredibus futuris propriis, sed de ordinariis, omnibus fidelibus, gradu tamen dispari, communibus intelligere oportet. Nec tamen ex arrha nomine concludendum, fideles, qui Spiritum promissionis semel acceperunt, excudere eundem non posse, aut qui arrham illam habet, absolute eum certum esse de summae solutione plenaria & de salute consummata, ut Grotius colligit. Non enim simile ultra comparationem in scriptura monstratam, nedum contra scripturam extendendum, quae docet, fideles totaliter & finaliter excidere posse divina gratia, ac Spiritum sanctum amittere, Luc. IIX. 12. Ebr. VI. 4. seqq. Unde Eph. IV. 30. monemur, ne contristemus Spiritum sanctum, quo signati sumus, usque in diem redemptionis.

PARS III. Testificatio Apostolica de Eucharistia & precibus suis pro illuminatione Ephesiorum.

## 1:15
Vers. 15. For this cause) Because we owe thanks to God for such great benefits, which is the one thing we can render to Him.

Having heard of the faith among you) Your faith specifically. For κατὰ is partitive. The Apostle speaks, however, of the progress of the Gospel among the Ephesians, since he himself had departed from them.

In the Lord Jesus) Faith in GOD founded in Christ.

And the love unto all the saints) He rightly joined faith and love, a wonderful pair, as the Greek Fathers say. Faith, unless love be added, will not lead us to eternal life. See what was said at Gal. 5:6.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Διὰ τοῦτο) Quia Deo pro tantis beneficiis gratias debemus, quod unum ei reddere possumus.

᾿Ακούσας τὴν καθ᾽ ὑμᾶς πίστιν) Vestram speciatim fidem. Nam κατὰ est partitivum. Loquitur autem Apostolus de profectu Evangelii apud Ephesios, ex quo ipse ab illis discesserat.

᾿Εν τῷ κυρίῳ ᾿Ιησοῦ) Fidem in DEUM fundatam in Christo.

Καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους) Bene conjunxit fidem & dilectionem θαυμαστὴν ξυνωρίδα, ut loquuntur Graeci Patres. Fides nisi dilectio accedat, nos ad vitam aeternam non perducet. Vide quae dicta Gal. V. 6.

## 1:16
Vers. 16. I cease not to give thanks for you) For we owe thanks to God not only for ourselves, but also for others brought to Christ. This part is of the communion of saints.

Making mention of you in my prayers) It is loved to join thanksgiving and prayers: the former for things obtained, the latter for obtaining other things.

They are entirely similar to those which are read in the previous notes and are as follows: Vers. 15. For this cause) because we are bound to acknowledge God's benefits with a grateful mind.
