Having heard of the faith among you in the Lord Jesus, and I hearing your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus) that is, in the Lord Jesus. For these writers often interchange such particles. And the love unto all the saints) He rightly added this, because that faith alone brings salvation which, when the time is given, shows itself through love. See James. The Greek Doctors call faith and love a wonderful pair. Vers. 16. I cease not to give thanks for you) we owe thanks to God not only for ourselves, but also for our brothers: And this is some part of our incorporation. Making mention of you in my prayers) The Apostle usually joins prayers with thanksgiving: the former are referred to the past, the latter to the future.

Concerning that Popish hypothesis, that faith, unless love be added, does not lead us to eternal life, there is no reason for us to speak. See what we said at Gal. 5:6. The observation of St. Chrysostom is altogether beautiful: Everywhere the Apostle joins and glues together faith and love. But in the article concerning justification he does not join these, but opposes them: We conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law, Rom. 3:28. Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, unless, that is, but only through the faith of Jesus Christ, and we believe in Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law, Gal. 2:16. But here we rightly venerate with Chrysostom τὰ σπλάγχνα of the Apostle: There was nothing that could be compared to the Apostolic bowels: There was nothing like the compassion and benevolence of blessed Paul, who poured out all his prayers for cities, for peoples. And to them all he writes this, I give thanks to God for you, making mention of you in my prayers. Think how many he had in his mind, of whom it was even difficult to remember, how many he remembered in his prayers, giving thanks to God for all, as if he himself were affected by the greatest benefits. I do not cease, he says. That proceeded from a most tender love, that he would never cease both to give thanks to God for the Ephesians, and to pray for the same, and would not allow himself to be hindered by any thing, because he made mention of them before God in his prayers.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ᾿Ου παύομαι ἐυχαριστῶν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) Deo enim gratias non pro nobis tantum, sed & pro aliis, ad Christum perductis, debemus. Haec pars est communionis sanctorum.

Μνείαν ὑμῶν ποιούμενος ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν με) Amant jungi gratiarum actio & preces: Illae pro impetratis, haec ad alia impetranda.

Similia prorsus sunt, quae in prioribus notis leguntur & ita habent: Vers. 15. Διὰ τοῦτο, propterea) quia tenemur Dei benefacta grato animo agnoscere. ᾿Ακούσας τὴν καθ᾽ ὑμᾶς πίστιν ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ ᾿Ιησοῦ, & ego audiens fidem vestram, quae est in Domino Jesu) id est, εἰς τὸν κύριον ᾿Ιησοῦν. Saepe enim tales particulas permutant hi scriptores. Καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους, & dilectionem in omnes sanctos) Recte hanc adjunxit, quia ea demum fides salutem affert, quae per dilectionem, dato tempore, se ostendit. Vide Jacobum. Fidem & dilectionem θαυμαστὴν ξυνωρίδα Graeci vocant Doctores. Vers. 16. ᾿Ου παύομαι ἐυχαριστῶν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, non cesso gratias agens pro vobis) non pro nobis tantum, sed & pro fratribus gratias Deo debemus: Et haec pars est aliqua nostrae concorporationis. Μνείαν ὑμῶν ποιούμενος ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν με, memoriam vestri faciens in orationibus meis) Cum gratiarum actione plerumque Apostolus preces jungit: Illae ad praeteritum, hae ad futurum referuntur.

De illa Papizante hypothesi, fidem nisi dilectio accedat, nos ad vitam aeternam non perducere, non est, quod dicamus. Vide quae diximus ad Gal. V. 6. Pulchra omnino est observatio S. Chrysostomi: Πανταχοῦ συνάπτει κ͵ συγκολλᾷ τὴν πίστιν κ͵ τὴν ἀγάπην: Ubique conjungit & conglutinat fidem & dilectionem Apostolus. Sed in articulo de justificatione haec non conjungit, sed opponit: Arbitramur, fide hominem justificari non operibus, Rom. III. 28. Scientes quod non justificetur homo ex operibus legis, ἐὰν μὴ, nisi, id est, sed solum per fidem Jesu Christi, & nos in Christum credimus, ut justeficemur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis Gal. II. v. 16. Merito autem hic cum Chrysostomo veneramur τὰ σπλάγχνα Apostoli: Nihil fuit, quod posset aequiparari visceribus Apostolicis: Nihil fuit simile commiserationi & benevolentiae beati Pauli, qui omnes suas fundebat preces pro civitatibus, pro populis. Et ad illos omnes hoc scribit, Deo gratias ago pro vobis, memo- riam vestri faciens in orationibus meis. Cogitate, quam multos habuerit in mente, quorum erat etiam difficile meminisse, quam multorum meminisset in orationibus, pro omnibus Deo agens gratias, tan- quam ipse maximis afficeretur beneficiis. Non desi- no, inquit. A tenerrimo id amore proficisceba- tur, quod nunquam cessaret & gratias agere Deo pro Ephesiis, & orare pro iisdem, nullaque re sese impediri pateretur, quia eorum mentionem apud Deum in orationibus suis faceret.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. Ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) See John XX. vers. 17. If God is called the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, much more justly is he called the God of Christ, whom God raised to the heavenly Kingdom, and gave him the highest authority under himself.

Ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης) אל כבוד, as the Hebrews say מלך הכבוד Psalm. XXIV. 7. Similar is ὁ Πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν, 2. Cor. I. v. 3. God not only has glory, but also gave glory to Christ, and will give it to Christians. But he is called Father, who is the cause of some thing.

Δῴη ὑμῖν πνεῦμα σοφίας) The Spirit of God, which is given to believers, among other things also imprints wisdom upon minds, not of the things of this age, in which the Philosophers boasted, but of those which lead to a better life, Act. VI. 3. 1. Cor. II. v. 7. 2. Cor. I. 12. Col. I. 9. 28. Jac. I. 5.

Καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως) The same Spirit also reveals to his own future or hidden things, which cannot be known by human aid. See 1. Cor. XIV. 6. 26. and what is said there: and below III. 3.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ) that is εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ, so that we may know God more and more. Γνῶσις is knowledge: Ἐπίγνωσις is a more exact knowledge of God, Rom. III. 20. below IV. 13. Col. I. v. 9. 10. 11. III. v. 10. 11. 2. Petr. I. v. 2. 1. Tim. II. v. 4. 2. Tim. II. v. 4. 25. cap. III. v. 7. Tit. I. v. 1. Philem. vers. 6. 2. Petr. I. v. 2. 3. 8. II. v. 20. So also Hosea VI. 6. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Vide Johan. XX. vers. 17. Si Deus dicitur Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi, multo justius dicitur Deus Christi, quem in cœ- lestem Regiam Deus evexit, summumque ei secundum se imperium tribuit.

Ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης) אל כבוד, ut ajunt Ebræi מלך הכבוד Psalm. XXIV. 7. Simile ὁ Πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν, 2. Cor. I. v. 3. Deus non tantum claritudinem habet, sed & clari- tudinem dedit Christo, & dabit Christianis. Pater autem dicitur, qui causa est alicujus rei.

Δῴη ὑμῖν πνεῦμα σοφίας) Spiritus Dei, qui credenti- bus datur, inter alias etiam sapientiam imprimit animis, non rerum hujus seculi, qua Philosophi se jactabant, sed earum, quæ ad vitam meliorem ducunt, Act. VI. 3. 1. Cor. II. v. 7. 2. Cor. I. 12. Col. I. 9. 28. Jac. I. 5.

Καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως) Idem Spiritus etiam res futuras aut latentes, quæ humana ope sciri nequeunt, suis revelat. Vide 1. Cor. XIV. 6. 26. & ibi dicta: & infra III. 3.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ) id est εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ, ut magis magisque Deum noscamus. Γνῶσις est cognitio: Ἐπίγνωσις cognitio Dei exactior, Rom. III. 20. infra IV. 13. Col. I. v. 9. 10. 11. III. v. 10. 11. 2. Petr. I. v. 2. 1. Tim. II. v. 4. 2. Tim. II. v. 4. 25. cap. III. v. 7. Tit. I. v. 1. Philem. vers. 6. 2. Petr. I. v. 2. 3. 8. II. v. 20. Sic & Oseæ VI. 6. & alibi.

## 1:17
Vers. 17.

That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ.) God is called the Father of Christ, both His and our God, John XX, verse 17. The word Θεὸς, God, corresponds here, of course, to the Hebrew אלהים, which signifies right and authority.

Father of glory) The primary Author of future brightness.

May give you a Spirit of wisdom) The Holy Spirit, who follows faith, brings other things, and also causes the mind of believers to be more and more illuminated, not with the wisdom of this world, in which the Ephesians had once boasted, but with spiritual wisdom. See Acts VI. 3, 1 Cor. II. v. 6, 2 Cor. I. v. 12, Col. I. 9, 28, James I. 5.

And of revelation) This word signifies a certain singular manifestation of excellent things, not known to all, 1 Cor. XIV, v. 6 and 26. Here below III. 3.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτῶν, in agnitione ejus) Ἐπίγνωσις properly is a greater and more exact knowledge, as Rom. III. v. 20. Col. I. vers. 10. 2. Petr. I. 2. But understand the knowledge of GOD, not of the inscrutable Divine nature, but of his properties and counsels, and actions pertaining to us.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ἵνα ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ut Deus Domi- ni nostri Jesu Christi.) Deus Christi Pater & ipsius & no- ster Deus dicitur Joh. XX. vers. 17. Respondet hic ni- mirum vox Θεὸς Deus Ebrææ אלהים quæ jus atq; im- perium significat.

Ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης Pater gloriæ) Futuræ claritatis Au- tor primarius.

Δῴη ὑμῖν Πνεῦμα σοφίας, det vobis Spiritum sapientiæ) Spiritus sanctus, qui fidem subsequitur, tum alia adfert, tum etiam ut mens credentium magis magisque illu- stretur sapientia non hujus seculi, qua gloriati olim erant Ephesii, sed spirituali. Vid. Act. VI. 3. 1. Cor. II. v. 6. 2. Cor. I. v. 12. Col. I. 9. 28. Jac. I. 5.

Καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως, & revelationis) Hæc vox singu- larem quandam, & eximiarum rerum, non omnibus cognitarum, patefactionem significat, 1. Cor. XIV, v. 6. & 26. Hic infra III. 3.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτῶν, in agnitione ejus) Ἐπίγνωσις pro- prie est major exactiorque cognitio, ut Rom. III. v. 20. Col. I. vers. 10. 2. Petr. I. 2. Cognitionem autem DEI intellige, non naturæ Divinæ imperscrutabilis, sed pro- prietatum ejus & consiliorum, actionumque ad nos pertinentium.

## 1:18
Vers. 18.

Πεφωτισμένους τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν) καρδίας not διανοίας, the Manuscript also has. By πρόθεσιν he shows that that wisdom and revelation is a true and excellent illumination of the interior eyes, which great men were accustomed to desire, Psalm. XIII. vers. 4. And which the law of Moses provided in a small part, Psalm. XIX. v. 9. לב, καρδία, to the Hebrews is the mind. Eyes are attributed to it, as we have shown in many places on Matth. VI. v. 2. Clement in his epistle to the Corinthians: Ἐμβλέψωμεν τοῖς ὄμμασι τῆς ψυχῆς. Ears are also attributed to it, because there is something in the mind analogous to them.

Εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς, τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτοῦ) He shows further what those principal things are, about which that wisdom and revelation are concerned: Namely those good, eternal and heavenly things, which are called the hope of the divine calling, because the calling also tends to this, that they should be hoped for. Therefore in the word hope there is a Metonymy, such as in the same word in Galat. V. 5. Coloss. I. v. 5. Tit. I. 5. Tit. II. 13. Ebr. VI. 18.

Καὶ τίς ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις) πλοῦτος δόξης is abundant glory. See above 8. That will be in the saints. But that glory is said to be τῆς κληρονομίας, that is, κληρονομεῖσθαι, because it will be held not by right of usufruct but of ownership, and that by the gift of God, which is indicated here by the Genitive αὐτοῦ, and as in Roman. VIII. vers. 17. The Israelites had had a κληρονομία from God not to be despised: But which, when compared to that heavenly one, deservedly seems base.

He had handed down almost the same things, although in slightly different words, in the earlier notes, which, so that nothing from the Grotian notes might be missing, we subjoin:

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Πεφωτισμένους τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν) καρδίας non διανοίας, habet etiam Manuscriptus. Per πρόθεσιν ostendit illam sapientiam & revelationem, veram & exi- miam esse illuminationem oculorum interiorum, quam optare solebant Viri magni, Psalm. XIII. vers. 4. Et quam lex Mosis exigua quadam parte præstabat, Psalm. XIX. v. 9. לב, καρδία, Ebræis est animus. Ei tribuuntur oculi, ut mul- tis ostendimus ad Matth. VI. v. 2. Clemens in epist. ad Co- rinthios: Ἐμβλέψωμεν τοῖς ὄμμασι τῆς ψυχῆς. Tribuuntur ei & aures, quia est in animo illis aliquid analogum.

Εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς, τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτοῦ) Ostendit porro, quæ sint præcipua illa, circa quæ illa & sapientia & revelatio versentur: Nempe bona illa, æterna & cœlestia, quæ dicuntur spes vocationis divinæ, quia & vocatio eo tendit, ut ea sperentur. Itaque in voce spei est Μέτωνυμία, qualis in eadem voce Galat. V. 5. Coloss. I. v. 5. Tit. I. 5. Tit. II. 13. Ebr. VI. 18.

Καὶ τίς ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις) πλοῦτος δόξης est abundans claritudo. Vide supra 8. Ea futura erit in sanctis. Illa autem claritudo dicitur esse τῆς κληρονομίας, id est, κληρονομεῖσθαι, quia habebitur non fructuario sed mancupii jure, idque dante Deo, quod hic per Genitivum αὐτοῦ indicatur, & ut Roman. VIII. vers. 17. Israelitæ habuerant a Deo κληρονομίαν non spernendam: Sed quæ ad cœlestem illam comparata merito sordeat.

Eadem fere, etsi paulo aliis verbis tradiderat in prioribus notis, quas, ne quid de Grotianis deside- retur, subjungimus:

## 1:18
Vers. 18.

Πεφωτισμένες τὺς ὀφθαλμὺς τῆς καρδίας ὑμῶν, illuminatos oculos cordis vestri) κατὰ πρόθεσιν ἐξηγητικὴν, by an apposition explaining the matter, he explains what kind of knowledge that is, consisting, as we have said, in the illumination of the mind. Καρδία, heart, is here put for the human soul, to which the mind is as eyes. Philo on the creation of the world: Ὅπερ νῦς ἐν ψυχῇ τῦτ’ ὀφθαλμὸς ἐν σώματι, which the mind is in the soul and the eye in the body. See what has been noted at length on this matter at Matth. VI. vers. 22.

Ἐις τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς, τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτῦ, ut sciatis, quæ sit spes vocationis ejus) When he had designated the manner of obtaining knowledge, he now also explains the principal things to be known. The hope proposed to the calling, ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡ ἀποκειμένη ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς, the hope laid up in the heavens. Col. I. vers. 5. It is that immortal and most blessed life, which the sacred scriptures explain by various figures, of a banquet, of magnificent clothing, of a temple, of a kingdom; furthermore, they show by the most effective words they can that there is in it not only liberation from evil, but also the most full possession of goods, which are accustomed to be understood by the name of riches, honor, and joy, likeness to God, body, intellect, will, all things most perfect, fellowship with God, the Angels, and the saints of all times and places. These things and things similar to these God so imprints upon the minds of the pious through the Spirit, that they behold them as if present, and in comparison with them count all the pomp of this age, the comforts of life, and finally life itself as nothing: See Joh. XII. vers. 25. 26. 1. Corinth. XV. v. 19.

Καὶ τίς ὁ πλῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, & quæ divitiæ gloriæ hæreditatis ejus in sanctis) Why that blessedness is called the inheritance promised to the saints appears from what precedes, namely because it is perpetual, and is not alienated from its possessors. Πλῦτος δόξης, riches of glory, which is joined with that blessedness, and an excellent splendor, a certain taste of which Christ gave to his Apostles on the mountain. See a similar manner of speaking above, 8.

In the prayer of the Apostle it must be seen 1. Whom he prays to, he is described, then, that he is the God of our Lord Jesus CHRIST, where Grotius wrongly institutes a comparison with the names, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as if they differed only in degree, which were exhibited to Christ, to whom he also says that he attributed the highest authority only according to the Father himself: Scripture on the contrary testifies that all power in heaven and on earth was given to him, Matth. XXIX, vers. 19. and that glory and Majesty not finite, but infinite were granted; that he was not raised to an authority next to the Father, but the same, which is the Father's, and into the throne of the Father himself, as it testifies, Joh. V. vers. 19. Apocal. III. cap. VI. etc. concerning which in the examination of the doctrine concerning the person of Christ page 250. seqq. expressly: then that he is the Father of glory, that is, full of glory, and is most glorious; and of infinite glory, as Acts VII. vers. 2. He is called the God of glory, and from him is all glory and brightness, as from a fountain and origin, just as he is also called the Father of lights, Jac. I. vers. 17. Nor indeed is that brightness, which is given to Christians, of the same kind as the brightness given to Christ. For this is eternal, and infinite, the very glory and Majesty of the Father Matth. XVI. vers. 27. Grotius with Zanchius also wishes the Father of glory to be said, because he is the fountain of divine glory in the Son, as also in the Holy Spirit. But the name of God and the name of Father is not taken in this place personally concerning the first person of the Deity, but essentially concerning the Triune God, who is the God of Christ by reason of his human nature, and the Father of glory, in whom and from whom is all glory.

2. What does he pray for? First that he may give to the Ephesians the Spirit of wisdom, which Grotius understands as wisdom of things leading to a better life, and of revelation, which he understands as concerning future or hidden things. But such an ἀποκάλυψιν, revelation, GOD neither wishes to give to all the faithful, nor does the Apostle pray for it from God. And therefore an ordinary revelation is rather understood, which is through the word, than an extraordinary one, such as happened to the Prophets and Apostles, Galat. I. vers. 12. Eph. III. vers. 3. Wisdom and revelation are joined, however, so that it may be noted that the wisdom of the world is not regarded, but that which is had from the revelation of the Word. But he says the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, not wisdom and revelation; because he prays for them, not only the gifts of the Spirit, but the Spirit himself, the Author of the gifts. This does not please Grotius, forsooth, because they had already obtained the gift of wisdom, but now he was asking for increases. In the Holy Spirit no increases and decreases fall. Therefore he censures our blessed Hunnius here. But the Apostles also had received the Holy Spirit John XX. vers 22. and yet they prayed that the Holy Spirit be given to them, whom they also received on the feast of Pentecost, Act. II. Does he who has received the Holy Spirit no longer have to pray that the Holy Spirit be further given to him? And although the person of the Holy Spirit does not suffer increase, yet the Holy Spirit himself is given with an increase of the gifts of wisdom and revelation. For neither are the person of the Holy Spirit and his gifts to be abstracted; nor does he dwell in the faithful only by reason of the operation of gifts, but ὑποστατικῶς, that is, in such a way that the person of the Holy Spirit himself is in us, just as the Father and the Son also come to us, and make their abode in us, Johan. XIV. The Apostle also adds the means through which the Spirit of wisdom and revelation is given, ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ. Grotius explains ἐν as εἰς, so that we may know God more and more. Thus also the Greek scholia wish the use of wisdom and revelation to be noted, so that we may know God and what He has given us. And so also blessed Luther. Nor does Crocius acknowledge it to be a novelty that ἐν is taken for εἰς, citing these passages: Eph. IV. v. 4, 1 Thess. IV. v. 7, 1 Tim. III. v. 16, Heb. IV. v. 11, ch. VIII. v. 1, ch. XI. v. 9. We prefer, however, to persist in the more received and proper meaning of the preposition, and since the Greek codices do not have αὐτοῦ, but αὐτοῦ, even though Erasmus and blessed Luther seem to have read it in the former way, we understand it of Christ, through whose knowledge and faith the Spirit of wisdom and revelation is given to us more and more. For the more one acknowledges Christ, the wiser one becomes, and the more one understands the revelation of the Divine Word.

Secondly, he prays that the eyes of the heart of the Ephesians be enlightened. As the eyes of the body are necessary for seeing corporeal things, so the eyes of the mind are necessary for seeing spiritual things. There is need, however, for the illumination of the mind, or, which is the same thing but used for the sake of elegance, of the eyes of the mind; just as the knees of the heart are spoken of in Eph. III. v. 14. Certainly, there is need not only for the gift of the Spirit, but also for the illumination of our mind, which happens through the Holy Spirit by means of the Word; and Crocius rightly notes that not only the gift, but also the use of the gift, not only the will and the faculty, but also the act itself in spiritual matters, depends on the grace of God. The end is therefore added, that you may know what that hope of His calling is: because in order that we may know that in reality and more fully, there is need of the gift of the Spirit of wisdom and revelation and the illumination of the eyes of the mind through that Spirit, by means of the divine Word, the power of which word is noted in Psalm XIX. v. 9, not so much for the Law as for the Gospel, of which that Psalm is explained, agreeing with Romans X. All of which things, therefore, the Apostle wishes and prays for the Ephesians. There is no reason why the hope of the calling should be explained metonymically, as was done by Grotius, since there is no [reason for us], as he rightly argues against Bullinger and Heming.

Let necessity compel Piscator, whom Crocius follows, to accept it improperly, provided that the proper signification has a place, nay rather, that the thing hoped for be distinguished here from hope, and be joined to it by the particle AND. So that the sense may be, that you may the more recognize how sublime, how great, and how certain, by reason of its foundation, is the hope by which the Lord has commanded us to hope for the promised happiness. Crocius adds that the Spirit shows the immovable foundations of hope both outwardly and inwardly. Outwardly, while He shows in the Word, 1. The promise of eternal salvation made to us who believe by God, who cannot lie. 2. The oath of GOD, by which He confirms the promise, Heb. VI. v. 17. 18. 3. The blood of Christ, by which it is obtained, h. l. v. 7. 4. The calling, which is without repentance, Rom. XI. v. 29. 5. The power of God, by which it is kept for us in heaven, 1. Pet. I. v. 4. 6. The earnest given, by which we are sealed, h. l. v. 14. 7. Election, by which we are predestined to it, h. l. v. 4. 5. 8. Finally Christ, who as head has already entered into it, from whom the members cannot be separated, h. l. v. 20. 22. 23. Inwardly the same Spirit shows it, while He opens the eyes of our mind, that we may see those foundations of hope so solid. Which, even if we approve of them when rightly understood, are nevertheless, according to the mind of the Reformers, neither firm nor rightly held. That is because they can neither have faith, nor apply to themselves the grace of God and the merit of Christ, being destitute of universal propositions concerning the grace of God and the merit of Christ; nor can they appropriate to themselves the blood of Christ or the calling without repentance through the power of God, because those pertain only to a few absolutely elect, of whose number they must doubt whether they are, and perhaps make that Piscatorian [view] their own. Therefore, that they are sealed by the earnest, and are members of Christ, cannot be shown to them from the Word, because these are proper to the elect, whom God has indeed predestined by His absolute good pleasure. This, because the interior demonstration of the Calvinists, which is done through the Spirit, if it be sequestered from the Word, has no foundation in Scripture: but to the Word is granted the power of illuminating, which is intrinsic to it according to Scripture; but illumination is not to be expected immediately from the Holy Spirit.

And this is the first thing which the Apostle desires, that the Ephesians may know what is the hope of the Lord's calling; the second, which he prays may be known with eyes illuminated by the Word, is the glory of eternal salvation: which is described here with emphatic words, which are truly inexplicable: Τίς ὁ πλᾶτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτõ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις. The Apostle, differing from human language, says Theodoret, since he cannot praise the Lord as he wishes, and show the magnitude of the gifts, heaps up many names at once, striving to show them according to his strength.

Riches of glory, says Chrysostom, that is, ineffable glory. For what speech could explain that glory, of which the saints will then be partakers? What speech? None. But in truth there is need of grace, that the mind may learn, and may receive at least a small ray. When he names riches, he indicates an abundance in which nothing can be desired: when he says riches of glory, he means heavenly wealth, compared to which worldly wealth, however glorious it may appear, is to be judged true misery, and devoid of all solid glory. Or he understands the riches of glory as that ineffable Majesty in eternal happiness, where there is an immense abundance of glory, and the weight of the excellently excellent glory of Majesty, 2. Cor. IV. v. 17. the unfading crown of glory, 1. Pet. V. v. 4. the glory of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. V. v. 3. the kingdom of God and glory, 1. Thess. II. v. 11. But it is called the glory of the inheritance, namely the heavenly inheritance, with which no worldly inheritance, however ample, however Royal and Imperial, can in any way be compared: The inheritance of the kingdom of God, Acts XIV. v. 22. The inheritance of God, Rom. VIII. v. 16. The inheritance ἄφθαρτος, ἀμίαντος κ' ἀμάραντος, 1. Pet. I. v. 4. the inheritance prepared from eternity, Matt. XXV. v. 34. where there was nothing created, but mere eternity: Whence in that inheritance God will be ALL in all to the elect, 1. Cor. XV. v. 28. The inheritance of the saints in light, Col. I. v. 12. κληρονομίας αὐτῶ is added: it is Christ's, because it is acquired by Christ, and is conferred by Christ; it is also Christ's, because we are rendered his co-heirs, Rom. VIII. v. 16. O the wonder, exclaims Chrysostom, how great is this dignity! We shall possess Christ's kingdom, Christ's throne, because we shall possess the inheritance of Christ, as co-heirs of Christ, Rev. XXII. v. 5. ch. III. v. 21. By the name of inheritance is also hinted both the gratuitous attainment and the certainty of future salvation. For those things which we obtain by inheritance, as sons, or by the right of υἱοθεσίας, are not owed to us by merit, but are conferred by grace. Those things which we possess by right of inheritance, we possess certainly. Finally, he adds ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, either because these riches of glory are in the holy of holies, into which our High Priest has entered, for this comes under the name of τῶν ἁγίων, Heb. IX. v. 12. or because that glory is to be expected only among believers, who have been sanctified by the blood of Christ and the Spirit of God, and will then be perfectly just in the assembly of the elect, where nothing but justice dwells, Heb. XII. v. 23. 2. Pet. III. v. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Πεφωτισμένες τὺς ὀφθαλμὺς τῆς καρδίας ὑμῶν, illu- minatos oculos cordis vestri) κατὰ πρόθεσιν ἐξηγητικὴν, appositione explicante rem, explicat, qualis sit illa co- gnitio, in mentis, ut diximus, illustratione consistens. Καρδία cor hic pro animo humano ponitur, cui mens pro oculis. Philo de mundi conditura: Ὅπερ νῦς ἐν ψυχῇ τῦτ’ ὀφθαλμὸς ἐν σώματι, quod mens in animo & oculus in corpore. Vide quæ multis ad eam rem notata ad Matth. VI. vers. 22.

Ἐις τὸ εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς, τίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς κλήσεως αὐτῦ, ut sciatis, quæ sit spes vocationis ejus) Cum modum adi- piscendæ cognitionis designasset, jam & cognoscendo- rum explicat præcipua. Spes vocationi proposita, ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡ ἀποκειμένη ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς, spes reposita in cœlis. Col. I. vers. 5. Est vita illa immortalis ac beatiffima, quam variis figuris explicant sacræ literæ, convivii, ve- stitus magnifici, templi, regni, præterea verbis quam possunt efficacissimis ostendunt ei inesse non tantum a malo liberationem, sed & plenissimam honorum, quæ nomine divitiarum, honoris, gaudii intelligi solent, pos- sessionem, cum Deo similitudinem, corpus, intelle- ctum, voluntatem, perfectissima omnia, consuetudinem cum Deo, Angelis, sanctisque omnium temporum & locorum. Hæc atque his similia ita per Spiritum Deus imprimit mentibus piorum, ut ea velut præsentia con- spiciant, præque eis omnem seculi hujus pompam, vi- tæque commoda, vitam denique ipsam pro nihilo du- cant: Vid. Joh. XII. vers. 25. 26. 1. Corinth. XV. v. 19.

Καὶ τίς ὁ πλῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, & quæ divitiæ gloriæ hæreditatis ejus in sanctis) Hæ- reditas sanctis promissa cur dicatur illa beatitudo, ex an- tecedentibus apparet, nempe quod perpetua sit, nec a possessoribus alienetur. Πλῦτος δόξης, divitiæ gloriæ, quæ cum ea beatitudine conjuncta est, & splendor exi- mius, cujus gustum aliquem Apostolis suis Christus de- dit in monte. Vide loquendi genus simile supra, 8.

In oratione Apostoli videndum 1. Quem oret, describitur, tum, quod sit Deus Domini nostri Je- su CHRISTI, ubi perperam collationem instituit Grotius cum nominibus, Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, & Jacobi, ac si gradu tantum differrent, quæ Chri- sto exhibita sunt, cui etiam summum secundùm se Patrem solum tribuisse imperium ait: Scriptura ex adverso ipsi datam esse omnem potestatem in cœ- lo & in terra testatur, Matth. XXIX, vers. 19. ac gloriam & Majestatem non finitam, sed infini- tam concessam; imperium non proximum secun- dum Patrem, sed idem, quod Patris est, inque thronum ipsius Patris evectum esse testetur, Joh. V. vers. 19. Apocal. III. cap. VI. &c. quo de in exam. doctr. de persona Christi pag. 250. seqq. ex pro- fesso: tum quod sit Pater gloriæ, id est plenus glo- ria, & maxime gloriosus est; & infinitæ gloriæ, titi Actor. VII. vers. 2. Deus gloriæ dicitur, & ab ipso omnis est gloria & claritudo, tanquam de fonte & origine, uti & Pater luminum dicitur, Jac. I. vers. 17. Nec vero claritudo illa, quæ Christianis datur ejusdem est generis cum claritudine Christo data. Nam hæc æterna est, & infinita, ipsius Pa- tris gloria & Majestas Matth. XVI. vers. 27. Cro- cius cum Zanchio Patrem gloriæ dici etiam vult, quia fons divinæ gloriæ est in Filio, ut & in Spiritu sancto. Sed nomen Dei & nomen Patris non ac- cipitur hoc in loco personaliter de prima persona Deitatis, sed essentialiter de Deo Triuno, qui Deus Christi est ratione humanæ naturæ, & Pater glo- riæ, in quo & a quo omnis gloria.

2. Quid oret? Primo ut det Ephesiis Spiritum sapientiæ, quam de sapientia rerum, ad meliorem vitam ducentium, & revelationis, quam de rebus futuris aut latentibus intelligit Grotius. Sed ta- lem ἀποκάλυψιν nec dare vult DEUS omnibus fidelibus, nec precatur a Deo Apostolus. Ideo- que potiùs ordinaria revelatio intelligitur, quæ per verbum sit, quam extraordinaria, qualis Pro- phetis & Apostolis obtigit, Galat. I. vers. 12. Eph. III. vers. 3. Conjungitur autem sapientia & reve- latio, ut notetur, non sapientiam mundi respici, sed eam, quæ ex revelatione Verbi habetur. Spi- ritum autem dicit sapientiæ & revelationis, non sapientiam & revelationem; quia precatur ipsis, non dona solum Spiritus, sed ipsum etiam Spiri- tum, Autorem donorum. Non placet id Crocio scilicet, quia jam erant sapientiæ donum consecuti, nunc autem petebat augmenta. In Spiritum san- ctum nulla cadunt incrementa & decrementa. Ideo taxat B. Hunnium nostrum hic. Sed acceperant & Apostoli Spiritum sanctum Johan. XX. vers 22. & tamen petierunt, sibi Spiritum sanctum dari, quem etiam in festo Pentecostes acceperunt, Act. II. Num qui Spiritum sanctum accepit, non am- plius petere habet, ut sibi porro detur Spiritus sanctus? Et licet Spiritus sancti persona non pa- tiatur incrementum, datur tamen ipse Spiritus sanctus cum incremento donorum sapientiæ & revelationis. Nec enim abstrahenda sunt persona Spiritus sancti, & dona ejusdem; neque habitat tantum ratione operationis donorum in fidelibus, sed ὑποστατικῶς, hoc est, ita ut ipsa persona Spiri- tus sancti in nobis sit, quemadmodum & Pater ac Filius ad nos veniunt, & habitationem in nobis faciunt, Johan. XIV. Addit autem Apostolus me- dium, per quod Spiritus sapientiæ & revelationis datur, ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτõ. Grotius exponit ἐν per εἰς, ut magis magisque Deum noscamus. Sic etiam scholia Græca usum sapientiæ & revelationis nota- ri volunt, ut cognoscamus Deum, & quæ nobis donavit. Atque ita etiam B. Lutherus. Neq; novum esse, ἐν accipi pro εἰς agnoscit Crocius, adducens hæc loca Eph. IV. vers. 4. 1. Thess. IV. v. 7. 1. Tim. III. v. 16. Ebr. IV. v. 11. cap. IIX. v. 1. cap. XI. v. 9. Malumus tamen in receptiori & propria significa- tione præpositionis perstitere, & cum Codices Græci non habeant αὐτõ, sed αὐτõ, etsi Erasmus & B. Lutherus priori modo legisse videantur, de Christo intelligimus, per cujus cognitionem & fi- dem nobis magis magisque datur Spiritus sapien- tiæ & revelationis. Quo enim quis magis agno- scit Christum, eo sapientior fit, & revelationem Divini Verbi magis intelligit.

Secundo precatur Ephesiis illuminatos oculos cordis. Ut oculi corporis ad videndum corpora- lia: Sic oculi mentis ad videndum spiritualia ne- cessarii sunt. Opus autem est illuminatione men- tis, vel quod idem est, sed elegantiæ causa adhi- bitum, oculorum mentis; ut genua cordis dicun- tur Eph. III. vers. 14. Nimirum non Spiritus do- natione tantum opus est, sed illuminatione etiam mentis nostræ, quæ fit per Spiritum sanctum me- diante Verbo; & recte notat Crocius, non tantum donum, sed etiam usum doni, non voluntatem & facultatem, sed etiam ipsum actum in rebus spiri- tualibus a Dei pendere gratia. Additur itaque fi- nis, ut sciatis, quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius: quia ut reipsa & plenius illud sciamus, dono Spiritus sapientiæ & revelationis & illuminatione oculo- rum mentis per illum Spiritum, mediante Verbo divino opus est, quæ verbi vis Psalm. XIX. vers. 9. notatur, non tam legi, quam Evangelio, de quo Psalmus ille exponitur, Roman. X. conveniens. Quæ omnia proinde vovet, ac precatur Aposto- lus Ephesiis. Spes vocationis non est cur Metony- mice explicetur, uti a Grotio factum, quum nulla nos, ut recte arguit contra Bullingerum, Heming.

Pifcatorem, quos ille sequitur Crocius, cogat ne- cessitas, improprie accipere, siquidem propria significatio locum habeat, imo res sperata a spe hic distinguatur, & ei per particulam ET conjunga- tur. Ut sensus sit, ut magis agnoscatis, quam sub- limis, quanta & quam certa, ratione fundamenti sui, sit spes, qua nos sperare jussit Dominus felici- tatem promissam. Addit Crocius, Spiritum mon- strare fundamenta immota spei tum exterius, tum interius. Exterius, dum monstrat in Verbo, 1. Sa- lutis æternæ promissionem nobis credentibus factam a Deo, mentiri nescio. 2. Juramentum DEI, quo promissionem confirmat, Ebr. VI. v. 17. 18. 3. Christi sanguinem, quo parta est, h. l. v. 7. 4. Vocationem, quæ est sine pœnitentia, Roman. XI. v. 29. 5. Virtu- tem Dei, qua nobis in cœlo servatur, 1. Petr. I. v. 4. 6. Arrhabonem datum, quo obsignamur, h. l. v. 14. 7. Electionem, qua ad eam prædestinati sumus, h. l. v. 4. 5. 8. Denique Christum, qui ut caput jam eam adiit, a quo membra sejungi non queunt, h. l. v. 20. 22. 23. Interius monstrat idem Spiritus, dum aperit oculos mentis nostræ, ut videamus illa spei funda- menta tam solida. Quæ etsi recte intellecta pro- bemus, non tamen ex mente Reformatorum vel firma sunt, vel recte se habent. Illud quia nec fi- dem habere, vel gratiam Dei & meritum Christi sibi applicare possunt destituti universalibus de gratia Dei & merito Christi propositionibus; nec Christi sanguinem aut vocationem sine pœniten- tia per virtutem Dei sibi appropriare, quia illa at- tinent solum paucos absolute electos, e quorum numero an sint, dubitare ipsos oportet, & forte illud Piscatorinum suum facere. Arrhabone ita- que ipsos obsignari, & membra Christi esse e Ver- bo monstrari ipsis non potest, quia hæc electo- rum propria sunt, quos nempe Deus absoluto be- neplacito suo prædestinavit. Hoc, quia interior Calvinianorum demonstratio, quæ per Spiritum fit, si a Verbo sequestretur, nullum in scriptura fundamentum habet: Verbo autem concessa vir- tus illuminandi intrinseca ipsi est juxta scriptu- ram; non vero immediata expectanda est a Spiri- tu sancto illuminatio.

Atque hoc primum est, quod optat Apostolus, ut cognoscant Ephesii, quænam sit spes vocationis Domini; Alterum, quod cognosci oculis illumi- natis Verbo precatur, est salutis æternæ gloria: Quæ hic emphaticis vocibus describitur, quæ vere inexplicabiles sunt: Τίς ὁ πλᾶτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κλη- ρονομίας αὐτõ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις. Carnea lingua differens Apostolus, inquit Theodoretus, cum non possit, ut vult laudare Dominum, & ostendere donorum ma- gnitudinem, multa nomina simul congerit, ea pro viribus ostendere contendens.

Divitias gloriæ, in- quit Chrysostomus, hoc est, gloriam ineffabilem. Etenim quænam oratio potuit illam explicare gloriam, cujus sancti tunc erunt participes? Quænam oratio? Nulla. Sed revera opus est gratia, ut mens discat, & omnino parvum utique radium excipiat. Cum divitias nominat, indicat copiam, in qua nihil de- siderari possit: Cum divitias gloriæ dicit, opes cœ- lestes, ad quas opes mundanæ, quam gloriosæ etiam appareant, veræ miseriæ, omnisquefolidæ gloriæ expertes judicandæ. Aut divitias gloriæ intelligit de ineffabili illa Majestate in felicitate æterna, ubi copia immensa gloriæ, & Majestatis excellenter excellentis gloriæ pondus, 2. Corinth. IV. v. 17. immarcessibilis gloriæ corona, 1. Petr. V. v. 4. gloria regni cœlorum Matth. V. vers. 3. regnum Dei & gloria, 1. Thessal. II. vers. 11. Glo- ria autem hæreditatis dicitur, hæreditatis scilicet cœlestis, cum qua nulla mundana, quamvis am- plissima, quamvis Regia & Imperatoria hæredi- tas ullatenus conferri potest: Hæreditas regni Dei Actov. XIV. vers. 22. Hæreditas Dei Rom. IIX. vers. 16. Hæreditas ἄφθαρτος, ἀμίαντος κ' ἀμάραντος, 1. Petr. I. vers. 4. hæreditas ab æter- no parata, Matth. XXV. vers. 34. ubi non fuit creati quicquam, sed mera æternitas: Unde in illa hæreditate Deus electis erit OMNIA in omni- bus, 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 28. Hæreditas sancto- rum in luce, Col. I. vers. 12. Additur κληρονομίας αὐτῶ: Christi est, quia a Christo acquisita, & a Christo confertur; Christi etiam, quia cohære- des ipsius reddimur, Roman. IIX. vers. 16. Papæ, exclamat Chysostomus, quanta hæc dignitas! Christi regnum, Christi thronum possidebimus, quia Chri- sti hæreditatem, cohæredes Christi, possidebimus, Apocal. XXII. vers. 5. cap. III. vers. 21. Hæreditatis nomine etiam tum gratuita consecutio, tum cer- titudo salutis futuræ innuitur. Nam quæ hæredi- tario consequimur, ut filii, vel jure υἱοθεσίας, ea non ex merito nobis debentur, sed ex gratia con- feruntur. Quæ hæreditatis jure possidemus, ea certe possidemus. Denique addit ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, sive quod in sancto sanctorum sint divitiæ istæ glo- riæ, in quod ingressus est Pontifex noster, hoc enim τῶν ἁγίων nomine venit, Ebr. IX. vers. 12. sive quod inter solos credentes, qui sanctificati sunt sanguine Christi & Spiritu Dei, ac perfecte justi tum erunt in cœtu electorum, ubi non nisi justitia habitat, Ebr. XII. v. 23. 2. Petr. III. v. 23. ea gloria expectanda sit.

## 1:19
Ver. 19.

And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe) He seems to step back from the heavenly life to the resurrection, but he did that deliberately, so that having shown the goodness of GOD, he might also show His supreme power. See Phil. III. v. 21. It is surely of great power, not only to restore all the bodies of the pious to life, but also to carry them above all the regions of the sky that we know.

According to the working of the strength of his might, which he wrought in Christ, raising him from the dead) these things cohere with those which preceded, the surpassing greatness of his power; and what had been said about us is said about Christ, but in other words, so that the discourse might be more copious. We ought not to wonder that God will exert such force of power in us, since he has already exerted such in Christ, when he raised him from the dead. The word κατὰ signifies the likeness of a thing. What has been done, it is apparent, can be done again. Ἐνεργεῖν here is to show by act, as below III. v. 20.

In the previous notes concerning these matters, Grotius held as follows:

Ver. 19.

And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, and what is the supereminent greatness of his virtue toward us, who believe) That promised blessedness shows not only the supreme goodness of God, but also his admirable power. See Phil. III. v. 21, where this very power is signified by the word ἐνέργειας, efficacy. For what greater argument of power is there than to make all who have ever believed alive from the dead, and to make bodies of earthly structure better than heavenly ones, and to give them a dwelling place that will remain forever above all known regions of the sky? But because he is not speaking of just any resurrection, but of the blessed one, which is תְחִיָּה to the Hebrews, therefore to the word ἡμᾶς, lest it be believed that he was speaking of all men, he added τοὺς πιστεύοντας.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ τὶ τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶ εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας) Videtur retrocedere a vita cœlesti ad resu- scitationem, sed id consulto fecit, ut ostensa DEI boni- tate, etiam potentiam ejus summam ostendat. Vid. Phil. III. vers. 21. Magnæ sane potentiæ est, omnia piorum corpora non tantum in vitam restituere, sed & efferre su- per omnes, quas cognoscimus, cœli regiones.

Κατὰ ἐνέργειαν τῶ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτῶ, ἣν ἐνέργησεν ἐν χριστῷ, ἐγείρας αὐτὸν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν) cohærent hæc cum illis, quæ præcessere, ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως; & quod de nobis dictum erat, de Christo dicitur, sed ver- bis aliis, quo copiosior sit oratio. Mirari non debemus, tantam vim potentiæ, Deum in nobis exerturum, cum talem jam exeruerit in Christo, cum eum e mortuis ex- citavit. Vocabulum κατὰ rei similitudinem significat. Quod factum apparet, id iterum fieri potest. Ἐνεργεῖν hic est actu ostendere, ut infra III. v. 20.

In prioribus notis de hisce ita habebat Grotius:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ τί τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶ εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας, & quæ sit supereminens magnitudo virtutis ejus in nos, qui credimus) Illa beatitudo pro- missa non tantum summam Dei bonitatem, sed & ad- mirabilem ejus ostendit potentiam. Vide Phil. III. v. 21. ubi hæc ipsa potentia ἐνέργειας efficaciæ voce significatur. Quod enim potentiæ majus argumentum, quam omnes, qui unquam credidere, ex mortuis vivos facere, & ter- renæ compagis corpora meliora efficere cœlestibus, & supra omnes cognitas cœli regiones illis domicilium sem- per mansurum dare? Quia autem non de quavis resur- rectione sed de beata agit, quæ תְחִיָּה Ebræis, ideo ad vocem ἡμᾶς, ne de omnibus hominibus loqui credere- tur, adjecit τοὺς πιστεύοντας.

## 1:20
Ver. 20.

According to the working of the strength of his might, which he wrought in Christ, raising him from the dead, according to the operation of the power of his virtue, which he wrought in Christ, raising him from the dead.) These things cohere with those, the surpassing greatness of the power, so that the future things might be more believed, GOD showed to human eyes, as much as he could, in Christ our head and Leader. That future proof of power will correspond to this one already exhibited, which the preposition κατὰ signifies. Nor is κράτος ἰσχύος, the power of virtue, anything other than the surpassing greatness of power, the supereminent greatness of virtue. He was able to raise Christ from the dead: He will therefore be able to raise us also. Since to this is added the most open promise of God and of Christ, there is nothing for us to doubt. To the Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, Christ says most excellently: You err, not knowing the scriptures, which clearly promise this, and the power of God, which surely extends even so far, Matt. XXII. verse 29. Tertullian translates this passage thus: He operated in Christ his power, by raising him from the dead.

This is the third thing which the Apostle prays that the Ephesians may acknowledge, namely, what is the power of God in those who believe, both regarding faith itself, excited and preserved in them, that they may believe; and regarding those things which are given to them through faith. Grotius does not wish for the power of GOD to be considered regarding faith itself, which is no wonder, because he believed, with Pelagius and Socinus, that faith is situated in human powers. But the words of the Apostle are clear, as to what is that surpassing greatness of his power IN US who believe, according to the working of his mighty strength, which he exerted in CHRIST. The Apostle does not say what power he is about to exert in us when he shall raise us to the blessed life; there is no word here about that resurrection of ours: therefore, that is rashly introduced. It is indeed about the power which he exerted in the resurrection of CHRIST, verse 4, that it treats: but that is compared not with the power which is exerted in our resurrection, but with that by which we believe, or by which faith is excited and fostered in us; nay, both are attributed to the same power and divine virtue, both our faith and the resurrection of CHRIST. For it is expressly said that we believe according to the working of his mighty strength, which he exerted in CHRIST, when he raised him from the dead. Grotius indeed strives to separate these words, but against the text. For those words μετὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν cohere with the word πιστεύοντας, and it is celebrated in this, that faith is excited in us, which is the ἔργον τῦ Θεῦ, John VI. verse 29, and is to be given to us by GOD on account of CHRIST, who grants us both to will and to perform, Phil. I. verse 29, chap. II. verse 13, by no less an immense power of GOD than by divine grace and mercy; which argument the Apostle also pursues further after the digression concerning the exertion of divine power in the exaltation of CHRIST, which indeed serves the Apostle's purpose excellently, since in our regeneration and vivification we, who were dead in sins, are not only exerted upon by the same divine power, but we are altogether vivified by the virtue of the vivification and resurrection of CHRIST, and raised with him and placed in the heavenly places, and are his ποίημα κτισθέντες ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησῦ, chap. II. verses 5, 6, 10, to which indeed the infinite virtue, which was exerted in the first creation, is required, since both the ἀνάκτισις and the κτίσις are of the same virtue. And therefore St. Chrysostom here clearly noted the force and power of GOD, which exerts itself in the operation of faith according to the Apostle: and he especially observed the συνέχειαν diligently, namely, how the Apostle here confirms those things which are not yet, from those things which have been done. And he desires indeed, he says, that the Spirit of wisdom and revelation be given to them. But he himself also confirms with reasons whatever he can from those things which have already been. For since he was about to say some things which had already been done, but others which had not yet happened: from those things which have been done, he gives assurance of those things which have not been done. Of which kind is this: That we may know, he says, what is the hope of your calling. It is still, he says, not manifest.

But not to the faithful. And what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. This also is still not manifest. But what is manifest? That we have believed that he raised CHRIST by his power. For it is far more admirable to have persuaded minds than to have raised a dead man. Because that might seem wonderful, St. Chrysostom explains it thus: But I will attempt to persuade you of this. For hear. CHRIST said to the dead man, Lazarus come forth, and he immediately obeyed. Peter said to Tabitha, arise, and she did not contradict. He himself will say on the last day, and all shall rise, and with such speed that those who are still living shall not prevent those who have slept, so that all things happen in a moment, and in the twinkling of an eye. But in believing it is not so. But hear him again saying: How often would I have gathered your children and you would not, Luke XIII. This is more difficult. Wherefore from this he proves the whole. For it is much more difficult to persuade free will by human reasons than to operate upon nature, namely, because of the corruption of sin. For this reason Chrysostom hints that the ἀνάκτισις, or ἀνάπλασις, is more difficult than the κτίσις and πλάσις, because in a non-entity, from which a creature is made, no resistance is given. But in him who is to be regenerated and converted through ἀνάκτισις and ἀνάπλασις, resistance is given. He now adds an explanation of the divine virtue: Thus he rightly said: The surpassing greatness of his power toward us who have believed. For when the Prophets profited nothing, when Angels and Archangels, when every creature visible and invisible—the visible indeed set in the midst and not able to lead, and much that is invisible—then he dispensed his advent, showing that the matter required divine virtue.

Chrysostom also notes the συνέχειαν of the following chapter according to this explanation to verse 1. See therefore how Paul, when he had already shown it to be very great, and that it is greater to heal a soul affected by death than to raise the dead; now also places it thus as something great. So also the Greek scholia explain: And what is the surpassing greatness? He says something future, and speaks of what has happened; so that from this he may give assurance of those things. But what is this? This very thing, that we have believed. For it is truly the greatest proof of the power of GOD, that we, who were so beastly, have believed in God and philosophize about heavenly things. So also Photius in the same: For, he says, the surpassing greatness of his unspeakable power is also demonstrated toward us who believe. How? Because, having all our senses deadened by passions, and the very reason buried and overwhelmed by them, he raised and vivified us to receive the brightness and splendor of his faith. Truly this is the might of his power.

Theophylact interpreted it in the same way: That is of great power and virtue, to change the mind from its former habit, and especially to rescue it from errors, to withdraw a man from which, while he has long been clinging to them, such great force is required that it does not appear to be at all equal to that which is demanded in raising the dead. For the Lord restored the dead to life with even a single word, but He did not convert the Jews to Himself by persuasion, not even with copious speech and miraculous deeds. He says, therefore, that the revelation of the Spirit is necessary for us even for this, that we may learn thoroughly that this very faith which we have received was accepted from the greatest power and work of God. For just as He also raised CHRIST from the dead, when He had departed this life, so also when we were dead, having been rescued from unbelief, He brought us over to the light. And therefore, because of the magnitude of the supereminent power, he said that this was done, and by the power of might. Similarly also τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες B. Hunnius. In us who believe, as if he were saying, God did not so contain the strength of His power within Himself, that He brought forth none of its ἐνεργείας for our salvation. But rather He made us feel that strength of His in a saving way: When He rescued us from the power of the Devil, sin, death, and damnation: And daily protects and defends His Church against the gates of hell.

Among the Reformed, Calvin here refers this τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες not to the word we believe, but to the magnitude of divine power, and he departs from Musculus, who explains it concerning the declaration of future divine power, along with Piscator and Crocius, teaching that this is the sense of the Apostle: that we believe, not by our own faculty, but by the actual efficacy or operation of divine power. The Apostle, he says, does not speak of absolute power, by which GOD can do all things, even those He does not will, but [power] conjoined with His will, and that not insofar as it exerted itself in creating the world, and still exerts itself in commonly ruling the same, but insofar as it is specially occupied about believers, which is the saving power by which GOD grants faith to us the elect, regenerates, sanctifies, preserves in faith, rescues from every evil and protects, and finally will raise us to glory and make us eternally blessed. And to that extent that power reaching itself into the future is regarded, because by that same power of God we are guarded through faith unto salvation, 1 Pet. 1:5, which grace of God in the elect he both preached, and thereafter determined to preach further, intending the leading of the same to a blessed inheritance, and the Apostle has brought forward its cause, the vivification and exaltation of Christ, as the meritorious and procuring cause of our vivification and exaltation. Whence the confidence of the Ephesians could be strengthened. For if He had raised them from sins by His immense power, faith having been granted to them, would He not protect the same against any enemies whatsoever, and glorify those raised from death? For the argument from the present benefits of God to the future is correct. The explanation of Lombard and Thomas Aquinas, as well as the ordinary gloss, concerning an excellent degree of glory which the Apostles were to have above other saints, is foreign, because the Apostle is not dealing here with things that are peculiar to the Apostles, but with those that are common to believers, nor is he dealing with glory here, but with faith. Furthermore, the wonderful ἔμφασις of the words amplifies this power of GOD, which exerts itself in our regeneration: It is not enough to say δύναμιν Θεῦ, which is certainly infinite, nor δυνάμεως Θεῦ μέγεθος, the magnitude of divine power, which cannot but be the highest, since there is nothing in God that is not the highest, but he adds τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος, surpassing, supereminent, and excellent. Nor does he rest in these, because he still adds κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ. Thus also it pleased him to designate the divine strength as τὸ κράτος, and not that alone, but also τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ, the strength of His fortitude, which is truly immense and invincible. To such an extent is the holy heart carried away into admiration of the immense power which God exerts in His own, and he would wish to carry others away with him, and testify openly to all, that there is no power in the world, in sin, or in death, which the magnitude of divine power does not surpass in infinite ways, as Crocius not badly says here: provided that the irresistible force of GOD, asserted by the Calvinists in conversion, does not underlie it. Regarding the latter three terms, otherwise not inappropriately Calvin and Zanchius, with the same Crocius approving: That strength is as it were the root, power or fortitude the tree, efficacy the fruit, that is, so that ἰσχὺς or δύναμις is natural force and power considered in itself, κράτος the power or force exerted by which one does something, ἐνέργεια the effective operation itself. These things the Apostle gathered with a singular ardor of contemplation of divine power, so that he might kindle the Ephesians with a desire to know the same more fully, and might fortify them both against the sense of their own weakness, and against pride and contempt for grace.

Καὶ ἐκάθισεν) In the Manuscript, καὶ καθίσας αὐτὸν, and after he had seated him. For καθίζω here is transitive, as in many places which we have produced in the commentary on the second chapter of the second [epistle] to the Thessalonians.

Ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτõ) In the Manuscript, ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτõ. He attributes to him a dignity next to himself. See what was said in Matt. 20:21. Two thrones are imagined in heaven, one of God, the other of the Lamb, that is, of Christ, Rev. 22:1, 3. But that of God is to be understood where it is simply named θρόνος, Rev. 5:3. To the Hebrews כסא כבוד, θρόνος δόξης.

Ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς κὴ ἐξουσίας, κὴ δυνάμεως κὴ κυριότητος) Some understand this of earthly empires. But the passage in Col. 1:16 and what is here below in 3:10 proves that this is about the excellent classes of Angels. A similar distinction of orders is also in the kingdom of Satan below in 6:12, 1 Cor. 11:24, Rom. 8:38, where we explained whence these names have their origin.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Κατὰ ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, ἣν ἐνέργη- σεν ἐν χριστῷ, ἐγείρας αὐτὸν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, secundum ope- rationem potentiæ virtutis ejus, quam operatus est in Chri- sto, suscitans illum a mortuis.) Cohærent hæc cum illis τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως, supereminens ma- gnitudo virtutis, ut futuræ magis crederentur, DEUS oculis humanis, quantum posset, in Christo capite & Duce nostro, ostendit. Illud futurum potentiæ docu- mentum huic jam exhibito respondebit, quod significat ræpositio κατὰ. Nec aliud est κράτος ἰσχύος poten- tia virtutis, quam ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος δυνάμεως super- eminens magnitudo virtutis. Christum a mortuis ex- citare potuit: Poterit ergo & nos suscitare. Cui cum accedat apertissima promissio Dei & Christi, nihil est quod dubitemus. Sadducæis, resurrectionem ne- gantibus, optime Christus, erratis, inquit, ignoran- tes scripturas, quæ scilicet id pollicentur, & Dei po- tentiam, quæ nimirum etiam eo usque se extendit, Matth. XXII. vers. 29. Tertullianus hunc locum sic vertit: Inoperatus est in Christum valentiam suam, susci- tando eum a mortuis.

Tertium hoc est, quod ut agnoscant Ephesii, precatur Apostolus, quæ scilicet sit potentia Dei in ipsis, qui credunt, tum quoad fidem ipsam, in illis excitatam, & conservatam, quod credant; tum quoad ea, quæ per fidem ipsis donantur. Grotius non vult potentiam DEI quoad fidem ipsam respici, non mirum, quia fidem in viribus humanis sitam cum Pelagio & Socino credidit. At verba Apostoli luculenta sunt, quæ sit excel- lens illa magnitudo potentiæ ipsius IN NOBIS, qui credimus, pro efficacia fortis roboris ipsius, quam exeruit in CHRISTO. Non dicit Apo- stolus, quam potentiam sit in nobis exerturus, quando nos ad beatam vitam resuscitabit, de illa resuscitatione nostra nullum hic verbum ex- tat: Temere ergo illa ingeritur. De potentia quidem, quam exeruit in CHRISTI resusci- tatione, vers. 4. agitur: Sed comparata illa non cum virtute, quæ in nostri resuscitatione exere- tur, sed cum ea, qua credimus, vel qua fides in nobis excitatur & fovetur, imo eidem potentiæ & virtutis divinæ opus utrumque tribuitur, & fidei nostræ, & resuscitationis CHRISTI. Diserte enim dicitur, nos credere pro efficacia fortis roboris ipsius, quam exeruit in CHRISTO, cum excitavit eum a mortuis. Quæ verba sepa- rare quidem satagit Grotius, sed invito textu. Il- la enim μετὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν cohærent cum voce πιστεύοντας, & celebratur in eo, quod fides in no- bis excitetur, quod est ἔργον τῦ Θεῦ, Johan. VI. vers. 29. nobisque a DEO dandum est propter CHRISTUM, qui & velle & perficere in no- bis largitur Phil. I. vers. 29. cap. II. vers. 13. non minus immensa DEI potentia, quam gratia & misericordia divina, quod argumentum etiam porro exequitur Apostolus post digressionem de exertione potentiæ divinæ in CHRISTI exal- tatione, quæ vero Apostoli instituto apprime inservit, siquidem in nostri regeneratione & vi- vificatione nos, qui in peccatis mortui eramus, non tantum eadem potentia divina exseratur, sed nos virtute vivificationis & resuscitationis CHRISTI omnino vivificemur, & cum ipso resuscitati & in cælestibus positi, ipsiusque ποίημα simus κτισθέντες ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησῦ, cap. II. vers. 5. 6. 10. ad quod utique virtus infinita, quæ in prima creatione exerta est, requiritur, quum ejusdem virtutis sit & ἀνάκτισις & κτίσις. Ideoque hic præ- clare notavit S. Chrysostomus vim & potentiam DEI, quæ in fidei operatione sese exerit juxta Apostolum: ac συνέχειαν imprimis observavit se- dulo, quomodo scilicet Apostolus hic confir- met ea, quæ nondum sunt, ex iis, quæ facta sunt. Atque optat quidem, inquit, eis dari Spiri- tum sapientiæ & revelationis. Ceterum ipse quo- que confirmat rationibus quæcunque potest ex iis, quæ jam fuerunt. Nam quoniam erat dicturus alia quidem; quæ jam facta fuerant, alia autem quæ nondum contigerant: Ex iis quæ facta sunt, fidem facit eorum, quæ facta non sunt. Cujusmo- di est hoc: Ut sciamus, inquit, quæ sit spes voca- tionis vestræ. Est adhuc, inquit, non manifesta.

Sed non fidelibus. Et quæ divitiæ gloriæ hæreditatis ejus in sanctis. Hoc quoque est adhuc non manife- stum. Quid est autem manifestum? Quod cre- didimus, eum virtute sua CHRISTUM susci- tasse. Est enim longe admirabilius persuasisse animis, quam suscitasse mortuum. Id quia mirum videri possit, ita explicat sanctus Chrysostomus: Ego autem tentabo hoc vobis persuadere. Audi enim. CHRISTUS dixit mortuo, Lazare veni foras, & statim obedivit. Petrus dixit Tabithæ, surge, & non contradixit. Ipse dicet in die ulti- mo, & omnes resurgent, & cum tanta celeritate, ut qui adhuc vivunt, non sint præventuri eos, qui dormierunt, adeo ut omnia fiant in momento, & in ictu oculi. In credendo autem non ita sit. Sed audi eum rursus dicentem: Quoties volui con- gregare filios vestros & noluistis, Luc. XIII. hoc est difficilius. Quamobrem ex hoc probat uni- versum. Est enim multo difficilius humanis ra- tionibus persuadere libero arbitrio, quam operari naturam, scilicet ob corruptionem peccati. Ideo enim difficiliorem esse ἀνάκτισιν, vel ἀνά- πλασιν, quam κτίσιν & πλάσιν, innuit Chrysosto- mus, quod in non-Ente, ex quo creatura sit, nulla detur resistentia. In eo autem, qui rege- nerandus & convertendus est per ἀνάκτισιν & ἀνάπλασιν resistentia datur. Addit jam explica- tionem virtutis divinæ: Sic merito dixit: Super- eminens magnitudo virtutis in nos, qui credidi- mus. Quando enim Prophetæ nihil profecerunt, quando Angeli & Archangeli, quando omnis creatura aspectabilis & non aspectabilis, aspecta- bilis quidem in medio proposita & non valens de- ducere, multa autem inaspectabilis, tunc suum dispensavit adventum, ostendens rem egere virtute divina.

Notat etiam Chrysostomus συνέχειαν sequen- tis capitis juxta hanc explicationem ad vers. 1. Vide ergo, quomodo Paulus, quum jam valde magnum ostendisset, & quod majus sit morte affectæ mederi animæ, quam suscitare mortuos; nunc quoque sic ponit tanquam magnum. Sic etiam exponunt scholia Græca: καὶ τί τὸ ὑπερ βάλλον μέγεθος; Εἰπέ τινα μέλλοντα, λέγει κὶ γε- γονὸς; ἵνα ἐκ τέτε πισώσηται κἀκεῖνα. Ποῖον δὲ τῦτο; Αὐτὸ τὸ πισεῦσαι ἡμᾶς. Ὄντως γὰρ μέγισον δυνάμεως Θεῦ δεῖγμα, τὸ ἡμᾶς τὸς ἕτω θηριώδες πισεῦσαι Θεῷ καὶ τὰ ὀράνια φιλοσοφῶν. Sic & Photius in iisdem: Τὸ γὰρ, inquit, καθ’ ὑπερ- βολὴν μέγεθος τῆς ἀφάτε δυνάμεως ἀυτῦ, καὶ εἰς ἡμᾶς τὸς πισεύοντας ἐπιδείκνυται. Πῶς, ὅτι τοῖς πάθεσι πάσας τὰς ἀισθήσεις νενεκρωμένας ἔχοντες, κὶ αὐτὸν τὸν λογισμὸν τότοις ἐντεθαμμένον καὶ συγκε­ χωσμένον ἀνέσησε κὶ ἐζώωσεν εἰς τὸ δέξαθαι ἡμᾶς τῆς πίσεως ἀυτῦ τὴν ἀἴγλην κὶ τὴν λαμπρότητα. Ὄντως τῦτο κράτος ἰχύος ἀυτῦ.

Eodem modo interpretatus est Theophylactus: Magnæ illud potentiæ est, & virtutis, animum a pristina consuetudine immutare, & ab erroribus præsertim eruere, a quibus hominem jampridem his inhærentem ut subtrahas, vis tanta require- tur, ut haudquaquam par exigi in mortuis susci- tandis appareat. Mortuos namque vel unico verbo Dominus vitæ restituebat, Judæos vero nec copio- sa quidem oratione & mirabilibus factis ad se con- vertit persuadendo. Inquit itaque, vel ad id nobis Spiritus est revelatio necessaria, ut perdiscamus, hanc ipsam, quam nos excepimus fidem ex maxima Dei virtute & opera fuisse acceptam. Nam quem- admodum & CHRISTUM a mortuis excita- vit, vita defunctum, sic & nos cum mortui esse- mus ab infidelitate subtractos ad lucem traduxit. Et ideo supereminentis virtutis magnitudine dixit id factum & virtutis potentia. Similiter quoque τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες B. Hunnius. In nos qui cre- dimus, quasi dicat, Deus potentiæ suæ robur non in- tra seipsum ita continuit, ut nullas ejus ἐνεργείας ad salutem nostram perferret. Sed potius fecit nos salutariter id suum robur sentire: Cum nos eruit e potestate Diaboli, peccati, mortis & da- mnationis: Atque indies Ecclesiam suam tuetur ac defendit adversus inferorum portas.

E Reformatis a Calvino hic suo τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες non ad verbum credimus, sed ad di- vinæ potentiæ magnitudinem refert, & a Muscu- lo, de declaratione futuræ potentiæ divinæ ex- plicante discedit cum Piscatore, Crocius, docens, quod hic sensus sit Apostoli, nos credere, non nostra facultate, sed actuali efficacitate, seu operatione potentiæ divinæ. Non loquitur, in- quit, Apostolus de absoluta potentia, qua DEUS omnia potest, etiam quæ non vult, sed conjuncta cum voluntate, eaque non quatenus ea se exeruit in creando mundo, & adhuc exerit in eodem com- muniter regendo, sed quatenus specialiter circa credentes occupata est, quæ salvifica est poten- tia, qua DEUS nos electos fide donat, regene- rat, sanctificat, conservat in fide, ab omni malo eripit ac tuetur, tandemque ad gloriam suscitabit & æternum beabit. Atque eatenus ea potentia in futurum sese porrigens respicitur, quod ea- dem virtute Dei custodiamur per fidem ad sa- lutem, 1. Petr. I. vers. 5. quam gratiam Dei in ele- ctis & prædicavit, & deinceps porro prædicare constituerit, intendentem eorundem ad hære- ditatem beatam perductionem, ejusque causam Christi vivificationem & exaltationem, ceu no- stræ vivificationis & exaltationis meritoriam & parariam adduxerit Apostolus. Unde Ephesio- rum fiducia corroborari poterat. Qui enim sua immensa potentia a peccatis ipsos suscitarat, fide iisdem donata, annon eosdem tueretur adver- sus quosvis hostes, & a morte resuscitatos glo- rificaret? A beneficiis enim Dei præsentibus ad futura recta est argumentatio. Lombardi & Tho- mæ Aquinatis, nec non glossæ ordinariæ explica- tio de excellenti gradu gloriæ, quem Apostoli præ aliis sanctis sint habituri, aliena est, quia non de iis, quæ peculiaria sunt Apostolis, sed quæ credentibus communia sunt, nec de gloria hic, sed de fide agit Apostolus. Cæterum mira verborum ἔμφασις amplificat hanc DEI poten- tiam, quæ in nostri regeneratione sese exerit: Non satis est δύναμιν Θεῦ, quæ utique infinita, nec δυνάμεως Θεῦ μέγεθος, magnitudinem di- vinæ potentiæ, quæ non potest non esse summa, quum in Deo nihil sit, quod non sit summum, dicere, sed addit τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος super- grediens, supereminens, & excellens. Nec iis ac- quiescit, quia subjicit adhuc κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῦ κράτες τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ. Sic & τὸ κράτος robur divinum designare placuit, nec id solum, sed etiam τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος ἀυτῦ robur fortitudi- nis ipsius, quæ vere immensa & invicta. Adeo in admirationem immensæ potentiæ, quam Deus in suis exerit, & sanctum pectus rapitur, & vellet alios secum rapere, omnibusque palam testari, nul- lam esse in mundo, peccato, morte, potentiam, quam non infinitis modis exuperet magnitudo potentiæ divina, ut hic non male Crocius: dummodo non subsit irresistibilis DEI vis, in conversione as- serta a Calvinianis. De posterioribus tribus no- minibus cæteroquin non incommode Calvinus & Zanchius, laudante eodem Crocio: Quod ro- bur sit quasi radix, potentia seu fortitudo arbor, efficacia fructus, id est, ut ἰσχὺς seu δύναμις sit na- turalis vis & potentia in se considerata, κράτος potentia seu vis exerta, qua quis aliquid agit, ἐνέργεια ipsa efficax operatio. Quæ singulari ar- dore contemplationis divinæ potentiæ congessit Apo- stolus, ut Ephesios ejusdem plenius cognoscendæ de- siderio accendat, & tum adversus infirmitatis pro- priæ sensum, tum adversus superbiam & gratiæ contemptum præmuniat.

Καὶ ἐκάθισεν) In Manuscripto, καὶ καθίσας αὐτὸν, & post- quam eum collocasset. Nam καθίζω hic transitivum est, ut in multis locis, quos produximus in commentario ad caput secundum secundæ ad Thessalonicenses.

Ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτõ) In Manuscripto, ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτõ. Dignita- tem ei a se proximam tribuit. Vide quæ dicta Matth. XX. v. 21. Finguntur in cœlo duo solia, alterum Dei, alterum Agni, id est, Christi, Apoc. XXII. v. 1. 3. Sed illud Dei intelligendum, ubi simpliciter θρόνος nominatur, Apocal. V. v. 3. Ebræis כסא כבוד θρόνος δόξης.

Ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς κὴ ἐξουσίας, κὴ δυνάμεως κὴ κυριό- τητος) Intelligunt quidam de imperiis terrenis. Sed locus Col. I. v. 16. & quod hic infra est III. v. 10. evincit, agi hic de eximiis Angelorum classibus. Similis ordinum distin- ctio etiam in Satanæ regno infra VI. vers. 12. 1. Cor. XI. v. 24. Rom. IIX. vers. 38. ubi exposuimus, unde ortum habe- ant hæc nomina.

## 1:20
Vers. 20.

And he sat at his right hand in the heavenly places, & constituting at his right hand in the supercelestial places) Just as the power of God is not only going to raise us from the dead, but also to increase us with the greatest honors, and to place us above heaven, so he wished this also, no less than that, to appear in Christ. For the Apostles saw Christ taken up into heaven: Stephen, Paul, John, etc., saw him reigning in supercelestial Majesty. Nor is there less testimony of this matter in the Holy Spirit, whom he himself, as he had promised, had sent into the Apostles and believers from the sublime Palace. Therefore, there is no reason to doubt that he can also raise us to the highest honor, albeit of our own degree. See John XVII. v. 24. Ἐπεράνια supercelestial are called those places of the blessed seat, Matt. XVIII. verse 25. John III. v. 12. 1 Cor. XV. 40. 48. 49. in this epistle several times. Phil. II. v. 10. 2 Tim. IV. v. 18. In the epistle to the Hebrews often, with respect to that region of heaven which contains the stars. Otherwise, the same region is also called heaven by the Hebrews, and indeed the third, above the air and the ether. To sit at the right hand is an idiom of the East, signifying the dignity next to the King, 1 Kings XI. v. 19. Ps. XLV. v. 10. Thus in Daniel thrones are placed for God and the Messiah. And in the Apocalypse τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τõ θρόνε κὴ τῷ ἀρνίῳ εὐλογία κὴ τιμὴ, κὴ ἡ δόξα, κὴ τὸ κράτος εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, blessing, and honor, and glory, and power for ever and ever, v. 13. see what Matt. XX. 21. But just as the throne of God, as the writer to the Hebrews speaks XIII. 3. and Apoc. VII. 10. and XIV. v. 5. which is the throne of glory כסא כבוד to the Hebrew masters, is next to the throne of the Messiah, so the thrones of the Apostles are next to the throne of the Messiah, Luke XXII. 30. Then of other heralds of the Gospel, Apoc. IV. 4. and finally of all believers, who themselves also shall reign 2 Tim. II. verse 12. Apoc. III. verse 21. V. verse 10. XXII. verse 5. in their own order and degree, of course.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Καὶ ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτõ ἐν τοῖς ἐπερανίοις, & con- stituens ad dextram suam in supercælestibus) Sicut poten- tia Dei nos non tantum ex mortuis excitatura est, sed & maximis auctura honoribus, & supra cœlum collocatu- ra, ita hoc quoque non minus quam illud, in Christo ap- parere voluit. Nam Christum in cœlum sublatum vi- dere Apostoli: Regnantem in Majestate supercœlesti vidit Stephanus, Paulus, Johannes &c. Nec minus e- jus rei testimonium est in Spiritu sancto, quem ipse, ut promiserat, in Apostolos & credentes e sublimi Regia miserat. Ergo quin nos quoque in summum honorem, nostri tamen gradus, evehere possit, nulla dubitandi est ratio. Vide Joh. XVII. v. 24. Ἐπεράνια supercœlestia vo- cantur loca illa beatæ sedis, Matth. XVIII. vers. 25. Joh. III. v. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 40. 48. 49. in hac epistola aliquo- ties. Phil. II. v. 10. 2. Tim. IV. v. 18. In epistola ad E- bræos sæpe, respectu ad illam cœli regionem, quæ sidera continet. Alioqui eadem regio etiam cœlum vocatur Ebræis, & quidem tertium, supra aerem, ætheremque. Ad dextram sedere locutio est orientis, proximam a Re- ge dignitatem significans, 1. Reg. XI. v. 19. Ps. XLV. v. 10. Sic apud Danielem solia posita Deo & Messiæ. Et in Apocalypsi τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τõ θρόνε κὴ τῷ ἀρνίῳ εὐλογία κὴ τιμὴ, κὴ ἡ δόξα, κὴ τὸ κράτος εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, se- denti in throno & Agno, benedictio, & honor, & gloria & potestas in secula seculorum, v. 13. vide quæ Matth. XX. 21. Sicut autem solio Dei, ut loquitur scriptor ad Ebr. XIII. 3. & Apoc. VII. 10. & XIV. v. 5. quod solium glo- riæ כסא כבוד magistris Ebræis, proximum est so- lium Messiæ, ita Messiæ solio proxima solia Apostolo- rum, Luc. XX, 30. Deinde aliorum præconum Evange- lii, Apoc. IV. 4. ac postremo credentium omnium, qui & ipsi regnabunt 2. Timoth. II. vers. 12. Apol. III. vers. 21. V. vers. 10. XXII. vers. 5. in suo scilicet ordine & gra- du.

## 1:21
Καὶ παντὸς ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένε ἐ μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ κὴ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι) If there are still any names of Angels more august than those, which we shall know in the other age בעולם הבא, Christ commands even those. The name שם among the Hebrews often signifies dignity. The present participle by σύλληψιν contains also the future.

We add here the earlier notes of Grotius, in which almost the same things are contained:

Latin:

Καὶ παντὸς ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένε ἐ μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ κὴ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι) Si quæ sint adhuc illis nominibus au- gustiora Angelorum vocabula, quæ noscemus in seculo al- tero בעולם הבא,etiam illis Christus imperat. שם nomen apud Ebræos dignitatem sæpe significat. Partici- pium præsens per σύλληψιν continet, & futurum.

Addimus hic notas Grotii priores, in quibus eadem propemodum habentur:

## 1:21
Verse 21. Ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς, κὴ ἐξουσίας, κὴ δυνά- μεως, καὶ κυριότητος, far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion) He depicts the Majesty of CHRIST more and more, so that the greater honor of his satraps, that is, of the Christians, may be understood. Moreover, those ἀρχαὶ, ἐξουσίαι, δυνάμεις, κυριότητες, principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, are names of the most sublime Angelic classes, very frequent among the Hebrews, as appears in Rom. VIII. 38, 1 Cor. XV. 24, Col. I. 16, taken from the names of the dignities of the Persian empire; as if you were to say, to take names from the later Roman empire, prefects of the praetorium, Vicars, Presidents, Counts; θρόνοι, which are added in the epistle to the Colossians, are Kings: such as some were under the great King of the Persians, who for that reason was called King of Kings. Christ, therefore, is said here to rule over all those, even the most exalted Spirits, as King of Kings and Lord of lords.

And every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future) If there shall be any Spirits more worthy than those whom we have designated, such as those who are thought to be obscurely denoted among the Hebrews by the name הורן in Ezekiel (the ancient heretics of the Christians, as also Tatianus, translated that word as αἰῶνας), whose true names and offices shall be known in the future age, Christ obtains authority even over them, with no nature excepted except the Father, 1 Cor. XV. 27.

Concerning the resurrection of Christ, we observe only this, that it was not inappropriately noted by Musculus and Zanchius, that he is not said to be raised from death, but from the dead, so that it may be shown that Christ in death was joined to the other dead, whence he is called the firstborn from the dead, Coloss. I. 18, and the firstfruits of those who rise again, 1 Corinth. XV. 23; the inference is obvious: If he is raised, the brothers and members are also to be raised. Furthermore, when Christ is said to be placed at the right hand of GOD, it is not a dignity next to GOD that is implied, but a truly divine power and Majesty attributed to him. For the right hand of GOD is the virtue and power of GOD himself, truly infinite and immense. But he is said to be at the right hand and in the right hand of GOD, not as if he sits in a place next to God on some throne, which are childish thoughts, but because he has been exalted to the right hand, or to the infinite virtue and power and glory, according to his human nature, and in that virtue and according to the same he sits, that is, he reigns. For thus the Apostle explains this sitting from Psalm CX. 1, 1 Corinth. XV, because for this divine government a divine and truly infinite virtue is required. For the Father gave all judgment, all dominion to the Son, so that the Son may be honored just as the Father, John V. 22. This sitting, therefore, is something other than when Solomon wished his mother Bathsheba to sit at his right hand, 1 Kings II. 19, whom he certainly did not admit to the communion of the kingdom, but treated her with the honor due to a mother, not in a place next to himself, but superior to it, outside the Majesty of government, out of filial reverence. Whence, if Christ's session at the right hand of the Father is to be estimated, the vain talk of the Socinians will prevail, that a superior place was granted to Christ. But while the Queen, the spiritual spouse of Christ, is said to stand at the right hand of the spouse, Psalm XLV. 10, not so much her dignity as her happiness is expressed, just as the Elect also are to be placed at the right hand of CHRIST in the final judgment; which will be a sign not of dignity, but of justice and blessedness. Nor indeed are two thrones to be imagined in heaven, one of GOD, the other of the Lamb, but one and the same throne of GOD and the Lamb is introduced, Apoc. XXII. 3, from which throne of both the Holy Spirit proceeds like a crystalline river, just as

Ebr. XII. 2. Christ is said to have sat on the throne, and the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, is called, Apoc. VII. 17. That the throne of Christ, Apoc. III. 21, is distinguished from the throne of GOD the Father, is done for this reason, not that Christ does not sit on the throne of GOD the Father, for he clearly professes there, just as I overcame and sat down with my Father in his throne; but because it is called the throne of Christ there, which he acquired for us, and which he is about to grant to us, but not that throne on which Christ himself sits. For the dignity which he earned for us by his merit, and which he is about to give to us who overcome through faith, is not that to which he himself was raised according to his human nature, since he himself received a name above every name, Phil. II. 10, exalted above all Principalities, Angels, etc., as the Apostle teaches here v. 21. We do not deny that there will be distinct degrees of glory among the elect themselves, so that in the first order the Apostles are constituted, Luke XX. 21, then other heralds of the Gospel, Apoc. IV. 4, finally other believers, 2 Tim. II. 12. But the dignity conferred upon Christ according to his Human nature, because it is truly immense and infinite, differs not only in degree, but in its whole kind from the dignity of the Elect, therefore the same glory is deferred to the Lamb as to the Father, Apoc.
