V. 13, John V. 23. But the right hand of GOD, at which Christ is constituted, is not some place in heaven, as is held in the Helvetic confession, from which Crocius deservedly departs. God, he says, does not properly have a right and left. For he is a Spirit, not having flesh and bones. Nor is the session here a position of the body, distinct from standing. There is no chair in heaven in which Christ perpetually remains immobile. But neither is the right hand of GOD a place in which Christ might dwell. For it is distinguished from heaven, nor is the right hand included by heaven, as if it were not outside of heaven. It is therefore a metaphorical form of speech, by which the Apostle declares that God, by his immense power, constituted Christ, having been raised to the highest glory, as King and Governor of heaven and earth, so that he gave him all power in heaven and on earth, so that together with the Father, according to both natures, as head of the Church, he might gloriously rule all things, with all things subjected to him, each one doing what is its own.

In this, however, Crocius is mistaken, in that he says Christ sits at the right hand of GOD according to both natures. For He sits at the right hand of GOD according to that nature according to which He was exalted and established at the right hand of the Father. Let someone say this regarding the divine nature, that Christ was exalted to the right hand of GOD according to the same, and Arius will immediately snatch him into his fellowship. Nor is there any reason for Crocius to say that sitting at the right hand of GOD is an axiom of office. For we deny this. The sitting itself is one thing, which is also to reign, and is an axiom of the Kingly office: sitting at the right hand of God is another, which implies at the same time the mode of communion of the kingdom through elevation to the right hand of GOD; which does not apply to the divine nature. For this can receive no dignity in time, this can in no way be exalted, being most high and most eminent. Nor is reigning gloriously in the flesh the same thing, which we do not deny is fitting for the divine nature of Christ, as reigning placed at the right hand of God, which in no way fits Christ as God. Nor is the inference of Crocius firm, that according to the nature by which Christ is the head of the Church, according to that He is placed at the right hand of the Father. For to be the head of the Church is an axiom of office. But to be raised to the right hand of God pertains to the state of Christ and is equally proper to the Human nature of Christ, just as the emptying. For neither falls into the divine nature of the Word.

Furthermore, by τὰ ἐπουράνια, according to Crocius, and likewise Grotius, supercelestial places are understood. But just as the right hand of GOD is not included by heaven, as if it were not outside of heaven, as Crocius admits, so neither is the Human nature of Christ, sitting at the right hand

of GOD must be confined to heaven, so that it is not outside of heaven. Or it will have to be said that he sits at the right hand of GOD in only one place in heaven. And yet, says Crocius, it follows that he is present at the right hand of GOD; it does not follow that he is present according to his essence in all places in which the right hand of GOD is. But he ought to have remembered what Crocius had said before, that sitting at the right hand of GOD is governing heaven and earth. But does he govern while absent, or while present? There is certainly no other than one rule, one government of Christ, of GOD and man: which is not of one who is absent, but of one who is present. Concerning which in the examination of the doctrine of the Reformed concerning the person of Christ, expressly. Let the followers of Calvin solve those arguments which are proposed there, if they can. Crocius criticizes Aegidius Hunnius because he notes that the Apostle does not say in the heavens, but in the heavenly places, so that the supercelestial kingdom may be understood. This annotation is light in his own judgment. But why? We acknowledge, he says, a supercelestial kingdom. But does the Apostle deny a supercelestial place? But it was for him to prove that the Apostle assigns a supercelestial place, not to ask whether he denies it? Although by that very fact it is sufficiently denied, because a supercelestial PLACE is nowhere asserted in the scriptures. For what scripture is silent about in these mysteries, it denies by its silence: Certainly it commands us also to be silent. I pass over the fact that below in 6:12 the spirits of wickedness are said to be in the heavenly places. Will Crocius establish those in supercelestial places? But in Heb. 8:1 he says, in the heavens. Therefore Crocius dismisses this statement, and betakes himself to another: But in that one he finds that heaven is named: But he does not find a SUPERCELESTIAL place, in which Christ according to his Human nature is confined, so that he is not outside of it. But who has ever denied that Christ is in the heavens? The Father also is in the heavens: But is he therefore circumscriptively in the heavens, or is he contained by the heavens: and is he not outside of heaven, as indeed some of the associates of Crocius, or Patriarchs, Piscator, Danaeus, and others have said, (See System. Theol. Vol. II, p. 383.) but Crocius would not have conceded that, if he were alive. Christ is said to be about to come from the heavens; but is it not also said in the Apostolic creed that he sits at the right hand of GOD the Father, about to come from there to judge the living and the dead. Is the right hand of the Father therefore also a place, because he is said to be about to come from there. And how often is God and the Son of GOD said to have descended from heaven? Has God and the Son of GOD therefore deserted heaven, and descended locally, or is he contained by the place of heaven from which he descended? But when the heavens will burn up at the consummation of the world, and thus these created things, except for the intellectual ones, are about to perish, where then will a supercelestial PLACE remain, or that third heaven, which those who measure the heavens above the airy and ethereal heaven establish locally? To say nothing of the fact that Christ is said to have ascended far above the heavens below in chapter 4:10 and therefore is not comprehended by any heaven. These things have been otherwise abundantly settled by us against the followers of Calvin. There is no need for us to be occupied with them now. And Crocius indeed wanted to nibble at Hunnius here, but he left most of the Hunnius material untouched, because he could not satisfy them at all, whence we deservedly repeat them here, and oppose them to the Calvinist flock as indissoluble. But neither (the words are of the blessed Hunnius, page 52) does the Apostle here simply say in the heavens, but in the heavenly places, in the supercelestials, in the heavenly being, so that he may clearly indicate that that kingdom of Christ at the right hand of GOD is distinguished by this added determination from the earthly habit and form of the kingdoms of this world, provided that Christ now is, lives, and rules in a certain heavenly, invisible, and incorruptible kingdom at the very right hand of God the Father.

Just as that passage in Heb. 8 is also to be accepted, where it is said that he sat at the right hand of the majesty in heaven, that is, in the heavenly and invisible kingdom. Just as this most frequent meaning of heavens occurs, so that it must necessarily be accepted not of a place but of a heavenly state, and be opposed to the earthly condition. Just as when we say: Our Father, who art in heaven. Likewise when God is said to look down from heaven upon the sons of men, Psalm 14; that he is said to send help from heaven, Psalm 57; to hear from heaven, 1 Chron. 6; to descend from the heavens, Exod. 19. The Son of GOD himself also in the incarnation to descend from the heavens. Where it would be most absurd to understand those created heavens, as if he looks down upon us from heavens so far distant from here, and from there sends down his help through all the lower celestial spheres, and hears from such a distant place, and the Lord in appearances, or the Son of GOD in the incarnation, descends from those highest heavens, until he comes through the orbs of the Planets and the air down to the earth: All of which things at the same time fight against the infinite nature of GOD. But it must necessarily be conceded that by the word heavens in these just-cited sayings of scripture is denoted the heavenly Majesty, glory, blessedness, and inaccessible light of GOD, and thus that heavenly kingdom, of which GOD is nowhere, not even on earth, deprived. Whence it is understood that there is no need on account of this determination (in the heavenly places) to attach anything local to GOD, or to the right hand of GOD, or to the session of Christ at this right hand. Since, as has been said, nothing else is indicated by Paul, than that that glory of Christ, which he obtains at the right hand of the Father, is completely absolute from all conditions of this earthly life and age, and is plainly heavenly, nay, transcestial and supercelestial. Thus far the blessed Hunnius. Who treated the whole matter concerning the Majesty of the flesh of Christ in his commonplaces on this passage against the Calvinists. But Crocius failed here, because he had nothing to reply.

Furthermore, Christ is here said to be not only established ἐν ἐπουρανίοις in the supercelestial places, but also ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς, καὶ ἐξουσίας, καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ κυριότητος, above all the Angels of the most sublime classes, concerning whom Crocius rashly doubts: PERHAPS, he says, you might gather that there is some order among the Angels, both good and bad. Grotius more correctly affirms and proves this as indubitable. For where the testimonies of Scripture are clear, it is not for us to doubt, but to believe, even if we cannot explain the how. Therefore, Bucer and Zanchius, whom Crocius praises here, did not think piously enough that the Apostle had rather used these terms, by which the Hebrews designated various ranks among the Angels, than that he certainly knew the matter to be so, as if the Apostle had not written by divine inspiration, or the Holy Spirit, by whom he was moved, had not certainly known it.

In this, however, Grotius does not deserve assent, in that those orders were derived by the Hebrews from the custom of the Persian empire, and were likewise designated by the Apostle. For it is not clear by any certain document that the very same classes of dignities were observed among the Persians, and were accustomed to be placed among the Hebrews in the exact same order in which they are placed by the Holy Spirit, much less should it be proved that Paul had regard for the fictitious names of the Heretics, of Valentinus, Nero, and similar monsters, which had not yet arisen at that time, nor would they have been held in such regard that the Angelic dignities should be compared with them, not to mention that the evil spirit rather strove to foist certain similar divinities through his instruments to the insult of those. Nor does the Apostle place Christ only above all the Angels of even the most eminent dignity, but also ὑπεράνω παντὸς ὀνόματος

named, not only in this age, but also in the one to come. Where the words 'not only in this age' &c. are rashly abstracted from the words immediately preceding, and are snatched away to the words far preceding, 'he sat at his right hand,' as if it were noted that Christ was established at the right hand of GOD not only in this age, but also in the future, which distraction of Calvin, Beza, and Zanchius could not even approve itself to Crocius, but rather he would accede to Theodoret, the Greek scholia, Lombard, Thomas, and others, who join this with the verb 'is named,' so that the sense is that Christ has been raised far above all that which excels, whether on earth or in heaven, and is now comprehended or will one day be comprehended by human knowledge. Thus he extends 'powers, principalities, &c.' even to those dignities which excel on earth. But although this holds correctly as a consequence. For if he is raised above the heavenly Principalities, much more so above the earthly ones, yet no mention of earthly dignities is made in these words: Which we wish to be understood only of those words which are adapted to the Angelic classes: not of EVERY name; he who is established above EVERY name, even that which is named in THIS AGE, by that very fact is also raised above all earthly principalities, which look directly to this age.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς, κὴ ἐξουσίας, κὴ δυνά- μεως, καὶ κυριότητος, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem) CHRISTI Majestatem magis magisque depingit, ut eo major etiam satraparum ejus, id est, Christianorum, honor in- telligatur. Sunt autem ista ἀρχαὶ, ἐξουσίαι, δυνάμεις, κυριότητες, principatus, potestates, virtutes, dominatio- nes, nomina sublimissimarum classium Angelicarum frequentissima apud Hebræos, ut apparet Rom. VIII. 38. 1. Cor. XV. 24. Col. I. 16. desumpta ex nomini- bus dignitatum imperii Persici, quasi dicas, ut ex Ro- mano imperio posteriore sumamus nomina, præfectos prætorio, Vicarios, Præsides, Comites, θρόνοι, qui in epistola ad Colossenses adduntur, sunt Reges: quales nonnulli erant sub magno Persarum Rege, qui ob id dictus βασιλεὺς βασιλέων. Christus igitur omnibus illis etiam excelsissimis Spiritibus imperare hic dicitur, ut Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium.

Καὶ παντὸς ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένου ὐ μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ κὰὶ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι, & omne nomen, quod no- minatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed & in futuro) Si qui erunt Spiritus illis, quos designavimus digniores, puta quales apud Ezechielem nomine הורן obscure denotari putantur apud Hebræos (αἰῶνας eam vocem verterunt veteres Christianorum hæretici, ut & Ta- tianus) quorum in futuro seculo cognoscentur vera nomina ac munera, etiam in illos imperium Christus obtinet, nulla natura excepta præter Patrem 1. Cor.XV. 27.

De resuscitatione Christi hoc tantum observa- mus, non inconcinne a Musculo & Zanchio no- tatum esse, non suscitatum dici a morte, sed ex mortuis, ut ostendatur, Christum in morte re- liquis mortuis fuisse conjunctum, unde primoge- nitus ex mortuis dicitur Coloss. I. 18. & primitiæ resurgentium, 1. Corinth. XV. 23. prona sit illa- tio: Si ille resuscitatus est, etiam fratres & mem- bra resuscitaturi iri. Cæterum cum ad dextram DEI collocatus dicitur Christus, non proxima a DEO dignitas, sed prorsus divina potestas, & Majestas ipsi tributa innuitur. Dextra enim DEI est virtus & potestas ipsius DEI vere infi- nita & immensa. A dextra autem & in dextra DEI esse dicitur, non quasi loco proximo sedeat in throno quodam penes Deum, quæ pueriles sunt cogitationes, sed quod ad dextram, seu vir- tutem & potestatem ac gloriam infinitam exalta- tus sit secundum humanam naturam, & in illa virtute ac juxta eandem sedeat, id est, regnet. Sic enim τὸ sedere explicat Apostolus e Psal. CX. 1. 1. Corinth. XV. quia ad hoc divinum regimen re- quiritur virtus divina ac vere infinita. Omne enim judicium, omne dominium Christo Pater dedit, ut honoretur Filius, quemadmodum Pa- ter, Johan. V. 22. Aliud itaque est hoc sedere, quam cum Salomo Bathsebam matrem suam a dextris sedere voluit, 1. Reg. II. 19. quam certe ad communionem regni non admisit, sed hono- re matri debito affecit, non proximo sibi loco, sed superiori eandem, extra regiminis Majesta- tem, dignatus est filialis reverentiæ ergo. Unde si æstimanda sit Christi ad dextram Patris sessio, Socinianorum obtinebit matæologia, quod Chri- sto superior locus concessus sit. Dum autem Regina, sponsa Christi spiritualis, a dextris sponsi stare dicitur, Psalm. XLV. 10. non tam digni- tas, quam felicitas ejusdem exprimitur, quem- admodum Electi etiam ad dextram CHRISTI constituendi sunt in novissimo judicio; quod non dignitatis, sed justitiæ & beatitudinis signum erit. Neque vero duo sunt in cœlo fingenda so- lia, alterum DEI, alterum Agni, sed unus idem- que thronus DEI & Agni, Apoc. XXII. 3. intro- ducitur, a quo utriusque throno Spiritus Sanctus instar fluvii crystallini procedit, quemadmodum

Ebr. XII. 2. Christus in throno sedisse dicitur, & Agnus, qui in medio throno est, vocatur, Apoc. VII. 17. Quod thronus Christi Apoc. III. 21. a thro- no DEI Patris distinguitur, ea ratione fit, non quod Christus non sedeat in throno DEI Patris, hoc enim diferte illic profitetur, quemadmodum ego vici & consedi cum Patre meo in ipsius throno; sed quod Christi thronus illic dicatur, quem acqui- sivit nobis, quemque nobis concessurus est, non autem thronus ille, in quo Christus ipse sedet. Dignitas enim, quam merito suo nobis peperit, quamque nobis, qui per fidem vincimus, daturus est, non est illa, ad quam ipse secundum humanam naturam est evectus, siquidem ipse acceperit no- men supra omne nomen, Phil. II. 10. exaltatus su- pra omnes Principatus, Angelos &c. ut hic v. 21. docet Apostolus. Inter electos ipsos gradus gloriæ distinctos fore, ut primo ordine Apostoli, Luc. XX. 21. tum alii præcones Evangelii, Apoc. IV. 4. denique credentes alii, 2. Tim. II. 12. constituan- tur, non abnuimus. Sed dignitas Christo secundum Humanam naturam collata, quia vere immensa est & infinita, non gradu tantum, sed toto genere differt ab Electorum dignitate, ideo Agno ea- dem defertur gloria, quæ Patri, Apoc. V. 13. Joh. V. 23. Dextra autem DEI, ad quam constitutus est Christus, non est locus aliquis in cœlo, ut in Helvetica confessione habetur, a qua merito disce- dit Crocius. Deus, inquit, dextram & sinistram proprie non habet. Spiritus enim est, carnem & ossa non habens. Nec sessio hic est situs corporis, a statione distinctus. Non in cœlo sella, in qua Chri- stus perpetuo hæreat immobilis. Sed neque dextra DEI est locus, in quo Christus versetur. Distin- guitur enim a cœlo, neque cœlo includitur dextra, quasi non sit extra cœlum. Est igitur forma lo- quendi Metaphorica, qua declarat Apostolus, quod Deus immensa sua potentia Christum in summam gloriam evectum constituerit Regem & Gubernato- rem cœli & terræ, ut dederit illi omnem potestatem in cœlo & terræ, ut una cum Patre secundum u- tramque naturam, tanquam caput Ecclesiæ omnia gloriose regat, subjectis illi rebus omnibus, unaquaque faciente, quod ipsius est.

In eo tamen fallitur Crocius, quod Christum secundum utramque naturam ad dextram DEI se- dere dicit. Nam secundum eam naturam sedet ad dextram DEI, secundum quam naturam ex- altatus est, & constitutus est ad dextram Patris. Dicat hoc quis de divina natura, Christum se- cundum eandem exaltatum esse ad dextram DEI, & actutum eum in societatem suam rapiet Arius. Nec est, quod dicat Crocius, sessionem ad dex- tram DEI esse axioma officii. Hoc enim nega- mus. Aliud est τὸ sedere ipsum, quod & regnare est, & axioma officii Regii: Aliud est sedere ad dextram Dei, quod implicat simul modum commu- nionis regni per evectionem ad DEI dexteram; qui non cadit in divinam naturam. Hæc enim in tempore nihil dignitatis accipere, hæc exaltari nullatenus potest, utpote altissima & eminentissi- ma. Neque idem est gloriose regnare in carne, quod divinæ Christi naturæ convenire non negamus & regnare collocatum ad dextram Dei, quod Christo, qua Deus, minime convenit. Neque firma est collectio Crocii, secundum quam naturam Chri- stus est caput Ecclesiæ, secundum eam ad dextram Patris collocatus est. Nam caput esse Ecclesiæ est axioma officii. Ad dextram autem Dei evehi, ad statum Christi pertinet & æque Humanæ Christi naturæ proprium est, uti τὸ exinaniri. Neutrum enim cadit in divinam τοῦ λόγου naturam.

Porro per τὰ ἐπουράνια secundum Crocium, pariter & Grotium loci supraccœlestes intelligun- tur. Sed ut dextra DEI cœlo non includitur, quasi non sit extra cœlum, fatente Crocio, sic nec Humana Christi natura, sedens ad dextram

DEI cœlo concludenda est, ut extra cœlum non sit. Aut dicendum erit in uno tantum cœli loco ad dextram DEI sedere. Atqui prœsto esse dextrœ DEI, inquit Crocius, sequitur; adesse secundum es- sentiam locis omnibus, in quibus est dextra DEI, non sequitur. At meminisse debebat, quod dixe- rat ante Crocius, sedere ad dextram DEI esse gu- bernare cœlum & terram. Num vero gubernat absens, an vero præsens? Non est utique, nisi unum imperium, unum regimen Christi DEI, & homi- nis: quod non absentis est, sed præsentis. Quo de in exam. doctrinæ Reform. de person. Christi ex pro- fesso. Solvant ea, quæ illic proposita sunt argu- menta, si possunt Calvinisequæ. Sugillat Crocius Ægydium Hunnium, quod notet, Apostolum non dicere in cœlis, sed ἐν ἐπουρανίοις, ut intelliga- tur supracceleste regnum. Levis hæc ipsius judicio annotatio. Cur vero? Supercœleste regnum, in- quit, agnoscimus. An vero negat Apostolus locum supracœlestem? At probandum ipsi erat, quod Apostolus assignet locum supercœlestem, non quærendum, an neget? Quanquam eo ipso satis negetur, quod nuspiam in scripturis asseratur LOCUS supracœlestis. Quod enim scriptura de hisce mysteriis tacet, tacendo negat: Certe nos etiam tacere jubet. Taceo, quod infra VI. 12. τὰ πνεύματα τῆς πονηρίας dicantur ἐν ἐπουρανίοις. Num illa in locis supracœlestibus constituet Cro- cius? At Ebr. IIX. 1. ait, ἐν τοῖς ὀρανοῖς. Dimittit ergo Crocius hoc dictum, & ad aliud se recipit: Sed in eo quidem cœlum nominari invenit: Lo- cum vero SUPERCOELESTEM, in quo Christus secundum Humanam naturam conclu- datur, ut extra illum non sit, non invenit. Ecquis vero negavit unquam Christum in cœlis esse? Etiam Pater in cœlis est: Sed num ideo circum- scripeive est in cœlis, aut cœlis continetur: nec extra cœlum est, ut quidem nonnulli e sociis Cro- cii, vel Patriarchis, Piscier, Danaus, & alii dixere, (Vid. System. Theol. T. II. p. 383.) sed non con- cesserit id Crocius, si viveret. Venturus dicitur Christus e cœlis; sed annon etiam in symbolo A- postolico dicitur sedere ad dextram DEI Patris, venturus inde ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Ergone etiam dextra Patris locus est, quia inde venturus dicitur. Et quoties descendisse de cœlo Deus & Filius DEI dicitur? Num ideo Deus ac Filius DEI cœlum deseruit, ac localiter descen- dit, vel e cœli loco, e quo descendit, continetur? Cum vero cœli conflagrabunt in consummatione mundi, & ita hæc creata præter τὰ νοερὰ interi- tura sunt, ubi tunc LOCUS supererit supercœlestis, aut tertium illud cœlum, quod localiter consti- tuunt, qui cœlos γεωμετροῦσι supra cœlum aere- um & ætherium? Ut taceam, quod Christus ὑπερ- άνω τῶν ὀρανῶν ascendisse dicatur infra c. IV. 10. ideoque cœlo nullo comprehendatur. Sunt hæc alias affatim a nobis contra Calvinisequas expe- dita. Non opus est, ut iis jam occupemur. Et arrodere hic quidem B Hunnium voluit Crocius, Hunniana autem pleraque intacta reliquit, quia iis satisfacere minime potuit, unde merito illa hic repetimus, & Calviniano gregi, ceu ἀδιά- λυτα opponimus. Sed neque (verba sunt B. Hun- nii pag. 52.) Apostolus bic simpliciter dicit in cœ- lis, sed ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, in supercœlestibus, im himmlischen Wesen, ut clare indicet, regnum illud Christi ad dextram DEI hac adjecta determina- tione distingui a terreno habitu, & forma regno- rum bujus mundi, siquidem Christus jam sit, vi- vat, & dominetur in cœlesti quodam invisibili, in- corruptibilique regno ad ipsam Dei Patris dextram.

Quemadmodum etiam illud Ebr. VIII. est accipi- endum, ubi dicitur sedisse ad dextram majestatis in cælo, id est, in cælesti invisibilique regno. Sicut cæli frequentissima hæc significatio occurrit, ut non de loco sed de statu cælesti necessario accipiatur, & terrenæ conditioni opponatur. Veluti cum dicimus: Pater noster, qui es in cælis. Item cum Deus di- citur prospicere de cælo super filios hominum, Psal. XIV. quod auxilium dicitur mittere e cælo, Psalm. LVII. exaudire de cælo, 1. Paral. VI. descendere de cælis Exod. XIX. Ipse quoque filius DEI in in- carnatione descendere de cælis. Ubi absurdissimum foret, creatos illos cælos intelligere, quasi tam pro- cul ex cælis longe hinc dissitis super nos prospiciat, & inde per omnes inferiores sphæras cælestes suum auxilium demittat, & e tam longinquo loco exau- diat, & ex altissimis illis cælis Dominus in appa- ritionibus, vel Filius DEI in incarnatione de- scendat, donec per orbes Planetarum & aerem in terram usque veniat: Quæ simul omnia cum in- finita DEI natura pugnant. Sed necessario conce- dendum est, notari voce cæli in his modo citatis scripturæ dictis cælestem Majestatem, gloriam, bea- titudinem & lucem inaccessam DEI, adeoque cæ- leste illud regnum, quo DEUS nullibi, ne in ter- ris quidem destituitur. Unde intelligitur, opus non esse propter hanc determinationem (in cælestibus) aliquid vel DEO, vel dextræ DEI, vel sessioni Christi ad hanc dextram affingere locale. Siqui- dem, ut dictum est, nihil a Paulo indicatur ali- ud, quam quod illa Christi gloria, quam in dextra Patris obtinet, ab omnibus conditionibus terrenæ hujus vitæ atque seculi penitus absoluta, planeque cælestis, imo transcælestis ac supracælestis est. Ha- ctenus B. Hunnius. Qui universam materiam de Majestate carnis Christi in LL. CC. ad hunc locum adversus Calvinianos tractavit. Crocius ve- ro hic defecit, quia quod reponeret, non habuit.

Porro Christus hic dicitur non solum consti- tutus ἐν ἐπουρανίοις in supercælestibus, sed etiam ὑπεράνω πάσης ἀρχῆς, καὶ ἐξουσίας, καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ κυ- ριότητος, super omnes Angelos sublimissimarum classium, de quibus temere dubitat Crocius: FOR- TASSE colligas inquit, esse aliquem inter Ange- los tum bonos tum malos ordinem. Rectius hoc indubitato affirmat probatque Grotius. Ubi enim clara sunt scripturæ testimonia, non est nostrum dubitare, sed credere, etsi τὸ πῶς explicare non possimus. Ideo Bucerus & Zanchius, quos Cro- cius hic laudat, non satis pie existimarunt, Apo- stolum potius has voces, quibus Ebræi varios gra- dus inter Angelos designarunt, posuisse, quam quod certe novisset, rem ita se habere, ac si non scri- psisset Apostolus ex θεοπνευσίᾳ, aut Spiritus San- ctus, quod ipse agitatus fuit, non certe noverit.

In eo tamen nec Grotius assensum meretur, quod ex consuetudine imperii Persici ordines illi ab Ebræis deducti, & ab Apostolo pariter designati sint. Nam apud Persas easdem omnino classes dignitatum observatas, tum penes Ebræos eodem prorsus ordine collocari solitas, quo a Spiritu Sancto collocantur, nullo certo documento liquet, mul- to minus vero probari debet, Paulum ad Hæreti- corum fictitia nomina, Valentini, Neronis & simi- lia portenta respexisse, quæ tum nondum enata erant, nec eo loco habita fuissent, ut cum iisdem componerentur dignitates Angelicæ, ne dicam, quod Spiritus malignus potius in istarum contume- liam similia quædam Numina per sua instrumenta obtrudere sategerit. Nec super omnes tantum An- gelos etiam eminentissimæ dignitatis Christu col- locat Apostolus, sed etiã ὑπεράνω παντὸς ὀνόματος

ὀνομαζομένε & μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τότῳ, ἀλλὰ κὴ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι. Ubi temere & μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι &c. abstrahuntur ab immediatè præcedentibus ver- bis, & abripiuntur ad longe præcedentia, ἐκάθι- σεν ἐν δεξιᾷ ἀυτῶ, quasi notetur, non tantum in hoc seculo, sed & in futuro ad dextram DEI con- stitutum esse Christum, quæ distractio Calvini, Be- zæ & Zanchii nec ipsi Crocio sese probare po- tuit, quin potius accederet Theodoreto, scholiis Græcis, Lombardo, Thomæ, aliis, cum verbo no- minatur hæc conjungentibus, ut sensus sit, Chri- stụm evectum esse longe supra omne illud, sive in terra, sive in cœlo excellit, & cognitione hu- mana jam comprehenditur aut olim comprehen- detur. Ita potestates, principatus &c. ad dignitates etiam illas, quæ in terris excellunt, extendit. At quamvis hoc consequenter sese recte habeat. Si enim super cœlestes Principatus, multo magis super terrenos evectus est, nulla tamen in his vo- cibus terrenarum dignitatum facta est mentio: Quod de vocibus illis solum intellectum volu- mus, quæ Angelicis classibus aptantur: non de OMNI nomine; qui super OMNE nomen consti- tuitur, etiam quod in HOC SECULO nomina- tur, eo ipso etiam super omnes principatus ter- renos, qui ad hoc seculum directe spectant, eve- hitur.

## 1:22
Verse 22. And he put all things in subjection under his feet.) A mystical application of Psalm 8:7. Where in Greek: 'You have put all things in subjection under his feet.' See how much the second Adam excels the former. To the latter, cattle and herds were subjected; to the former, the armies of Angels.

And he gave him as head over all things to the Church.) There is a transposition; the sense is: he gave him, placed over all things, to the Church, as its head. A great consolation, that he who exercises such authority does so for the good of the Church, just as the head provides for the body. See Heb. 1:14. We have seen the name of head given to Christ with respect to the Church, 1 Cor. 11:3. See also below 4:15, 5:23, Col. 1:18, 2:19.

The fullness of him who fills all in all.) He gives the reason why the Church is called the body of Christ, because it is filled by him just as the human body is from the brain. 'Fullness' has an active meaning in some places, and a passive one in others. Here the passive fits more correctly, because of the passage twin to this, Col. 2:10, and below here in 5:18. Nor should the same word be taken otherwise in Col. 1:19. And 'filling' is said here in the Attic form, with a passive sound but an active sense, in the way that both Plato in the Timaeus and Xenophon in the sixth book of his Greek history use this verb. Christ in all, that is, in believers, fills all things: the mind with light, the will with pious affections, the body itself with the faculty of obedience, to which perpetual gifts were added in the earliest times, even those spiritual gifts, of which there is much mention in the first epistle to the Corinthians, and of which we have also touched upon something here above.

Grotius had noted the same things in his earlier observations, in this way:

Verse 22. And he put all things in subjection under his feet) that is, he gave him the power of subjecting all enemies and finally death itself, 1 Cor. 15:27, Phil. 3:21.

And he gave him as head over all the Church) He holds this authority for the good of the Church. See Heb. 1:14.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Καὶ πάντα ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τὲς πόδας ἀυτῶ.) My- stica applicatio Psal. VIII. 7. Ubi Græce: Πάντα ὑπέταξας ὑπὸ τὲς πόδας ἀυτῶ. Vide quantum secundus Adamus priori præstet. Huic subjecta pecora & armenta, illi An- gelorum exercitus.

Καὶ ἀυτὸν ἔδωκε κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ) Est trajectio, sensus est: ipsum super omnia, supple positum, dedit Ecclesiæ, ut caput ejus. Magna consolatio, quod tantum imperium habeat is, qui id exercet Ecclesiæ bono, sicut caput consulit corpori. Vid. Ebr. I. 14. capitis nomen respectu Ecclesiæ Christo datum vidimus, 1. Cor. XI. 3. Vi- de & infra IV. 15. V. 23. Col. I. 18. II. 19.

Τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρωμένε) Causam reddit, cur Ecclesia dicatur corpus Christi, quia ab illo im- pletur sicut corpus humanum e cerebro. Πλήρωμα alibi activam, alibi passivam habet significationem. Hic pas- siva rectius convenit, ob locum huic geminum Col. II. 10. & infra hic V. 18. Nec aliter sumenda vox eadem Col. I. 19. Et πληρωμένε hic dictum forma Attica, sono passivo, sensu activo, quomodo hoc verbum usurpant & Plato in Timæo, & Xenophon Græcæ historiæ sexto. Christus in omnibus, credentibus scilicet, implet omnia, mentem luce, voluntatem piis affectibus, corpus ipsum obsequendi fa- cultate, ad quæ dona perpetua accedebant primis tempo- ribus etiam χαρίσματα illa πνευματικὰ, quorum mentio multa in priore ad Corinthios, & de quibus etiam hic su- pra aliquid attigimus.

Eadem annotarat in prioribus observationi- bus Grotius, hoc modo:

Vers. 22. Καὶ πάντα ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τὲς πόδας ἀυτῶ, & omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus) id est, potestatem ei dedit omnia inimica ac postremo mortem ipsam subju- gandi, 1. Cor. XV. 27. Phil. III. 21.

Καὶ ἀυτὸν ἔδωκε κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, & ipsum dedit caput super omnem Ecclesiam) In bonum Ecclesiæ obtinet hoc imperium. Vide Ebr. I. 14.

## 1:23
Verse 23. Which is his body) See below 4:12, 15, 16, 5:23, Col. 1:18. Just as in the human body the Spirit flowing down from the head contains, nourishes, and increases all the members, so the Spirit of Christ [contains, nourishes, and increases] all the members of the Church, which Paul teaches us very wisely in Col. 2:19, and Christ himself illustrates with another similitude at the beginning of the fifth chapter of John.

The fullness of him who fills all in all,) as in John 1:16, Col. 2:9, and then that which is filled, Rom. 11:25, 15:29. You may more correctly take it in the latter sense here. Thus below in 5:18, 'be filled with the Spirit,' and Col. 2:10, 'you are filled in him, who is the head of all principality and power,' which passage is of the same value as this one. And for that reason the Church is called 'fullness' in the same epistle to the Colossians 1:19. Thus also what follows, concerning Christ 'who fills all in all,' because he fills all in all, is the same as below in 4:10, 'he who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.' Christ in all, that is, in believers, for it is of them that we are treating here, fills all things: the mind with light, the will with pious affections, the body itself with the faculty of obedience, to which were added in those times, when the Apostle was speaking, those admirable spiritual gifts, of which he made mention above.

Not only is the mystical application of Psalm VIII held here, but the literal sense is adduced. In the Psalm, it is not a matter of Adam or a mere man, but of Christ the Θεάνθρωπος [God-man] and his both humiliation and exaltation, to whom the sacred singer subjects not only the hosts of angels, but also cattle and herds, and whom he establishes over all the works of God's hands, with absolutely nothing excepted, Heb. II. 8. 1 Cor. XV. 27. Therefore, not only are enemies noted, as Musculus and Zanchius think this phrase implies when something is said to be subjected under the feet of one who dominates: But also all other things, because Paul excepts nothing except God, whence EVERY creature attributes honor, glory, and strength to him, Rev. V. 8, 13, as Crocius admits here. See our Annotations on these matters at Psalm VIII. The Apostle also designates Christ here as established over all things as the head of the Church. Moreover, he would not be over all things unless he had all power and reigned in heaven and on earth. Nor could he protect the Church against all its enemies, both corporal and spiritual, unless he had supreme power over all things, which defends the entire Church safe and sound against the very gates of hell, and fills it with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, he defends the Church everywhere in all places against enemies, not absent, but present, and he rules in the midst of his enemies, Psalm CX. 1, 2. Nor indeed would Christ, the head of the Church, fill his body, just as the spirit flowing from the head fills the human body, unless he were mystically present to all the members of the body, and presentially infused his grace and gifts, just as spirits flow into all the members of the human body, and impart efficacy to them by their true and real presence. Whence the power and gifts of Christ, through which Christ flows into all believers, ought not to be abstracted from Christ himself, who by the power of his promise deigns to be with the faithful by his substantial presence and gracious indwelling, Matt. XXIX. 20, John XIV. 26, and ascended above all the heavens, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα [that he might fill all things], Eph. IV. 10, and therefore he is said to be πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρούμενος [filling all in all], not only in believers, to whom Grotius rashly restricts this, but simply IN ALL THINGS, just as he is said to be established OVER ALL THINGS. Furthermore, although the Church may rightly be called τὸ πλήρωμα [the fullness] in a passive sense, the passage, Col. I. 9, πλήρωμα, concerns something far different: namely, πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος [all the fullness of the Godhead], which dwells in Christ according to the divine εὐδοκία [good pleasure], as is evident from a comparison with chapter II. But how the Church dwells in Christ, if Grotius understands that by πλήρωμα, and indeed to that end, that all things might be reconciled through him, I confess that I cannot grasp.

Johannes Crocius, in order to detract from the Majesty of the omnipresence of Christ's flesh, to which all things are subjected, and to decline the force of the argument of our blessed Hunnius, that places and spaces of places cannot be excepted from this subjection of all things, as if these were not subjected to him, nay, that they have this power, that they might obstruct the presence of the reigning Christ on earth and elsewhere: he says that God subjected all things to Christ the Θεάνθρωπος [God-man], and hence the omnipresence of Christ is rightly concluded, but not the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ: Nor from the subjection of all places follows the inexistence in all places, but rather dominion and empire. But no one can turn aside the force of the Hunnian argument. For if God subjected all things to Christ the God-man, we ask, did He subject all things to Him according to the Divine or according to the Human nature? They cannot say the former. For the Divine nature is common to Him with the Father. According to it, He always had, as the Father, all things subject to Himself. The latter must therefore be said. If, therefore, omnipresence is rightly concluded from the subjection of all things, the omnipresence of Christ's flesh is most rightly concluded from it. Then, if Christ according to the flesh has dominion over all places, which Crocius does not deny follows from the subjection of all things, I ask, does dominion belong to one who is absent, or indeed to one who is present? The dominion of one who is absent cannot be spoken of, because dominion is divine, and as Christ is one and the same Lord, God and man, so the dominion of Christ is one and the same, as He is God and as He is man, unless one ought to believe in two Lords. Furthermore, who will admit that divine dominion is exercised in absence, and not in presence? Since, therefore, Christ as man has the same empire with the Father, just as He also sits on the same throne and is honored with the same worship, and this empire of the Father is not administered in absence, but in presence, the same must be believed entirely concerning the present dominion of Christ's Human nature, that it does not administer it as absent, but as present, not as absent but as present it resists enemies, defends the Church, and flows into all the members of the Church with His grace, and dwells in them, and fills all in all. Whence, however, inclusion and local inexistence in all creatures ought not to be inferred, just as no follower of Calvin would say that the Father is included, or that He exists in all apples, cheeses, stones, and creatures by local inexistence. That Christ governs the triumphant Church externally today is obvious to all, says Crocius. From which government it is a sin to exclude the human nature. But He will govern forever. For of His kingdom there shall be no end, Luke 1. If, therefore, it is a sin to exclude the human nature from the government of all things, He will be present to all the elect ἀδιαςάτως. Or must it be believed that Christ according to the human nature will be present in one place of heaven only to those who are nearest to Him, because the Calvinists make heaven local, but will not be present at all in innumerable other places and to innumerable Elect; since, according to them, the flesh of Christ cannot be present except in one place. Most of the Elect will therefore lack the presence of the flesh of Christ, so desired, even in the heavens themselves. Thus, the faithful must also lack the promised presence of the Human nature of Christ on earth in the Church, Matthew 28:20. Of which most desired presence and assistance of their brother, of their own flesh and blood, of their head, the Calvinists deprive the faithful, as much as in them lies. Crocius confesses that, just as Christ is the head of the Church according to both natures, so He also performs the office of head according to both. Yet he does not therefore think that the humanity is necessarily present to all the faithful and creatures by a substantial presence without distance of place, just as it is not necessary that the head be joined to the hands and feet by reason of place, but the conjunction of the Spirit suffices. But it is not necessary that the likeness of the head should extend itself to all things: For the mystical head, as it flows into all members, so it flows not in the manner of one absent, but united and joined to all members, to all the faithful in whom He dwells, whom He moves, acts, sustains, protects, vivifies, not absent, but present, not by the Deity alone, as that is nowhere alone and outside the flesh, after He assumed flesh into His hypostasis and dwelt in the flesh with all His fullness, but with the flesh, because the presence is of the whole suppositum, which is not whole where the other nature is not present. With respect to other creatures, Christ is indeed not the head by the phrase of Scripture, yet He carries all things by the word of His power, Heb. 1:3, and has all things in His hands, John 3:35, ch. 13:3, and that as God and Man, and therefore He preserves and sustains all things not as absent but as present, by substantial presence and ἀδιαςασίᾳ.

That 'above all things to the Church' is not to be rendered with the Vulgate, but 'over the whole Church,' nor is it to be drawn with Thomas, Albert, Gregory of Valencia, and Suarez to the point that He is established as the head of the Angels, for whom they argue besides that Christ merited both grace and glory: when yet the Angels are neither part nor members of the mystical body of Christ, nor was Christ born or did He suffer for the grace of the Angels, but they would have been confirmed in grace and attained glory even if man had not been created, nor the Son of God incarnate. Nor is there need for the transposition of Grotius, since some have interpreted it exegetically by ellipsis, in this way: 'He gave Him as head, who is above all things.' Others by ellipsis of the resultative 'so that' and of the existential 'to be,' in this way: 'so that He is above all things the head to the Church,' that He might be the supreme and omnipotent head of the Church, or even the sole and unique head, as Camerarius notes. He is certainly the unique and solitary head: For He has no divided empire with anyone, nor can anyone be coordinated with Him; which is in the open: But neither can one be subordinated, so that a head is under a head, for thus the Church would be two-headed. Which, since it is diffused through the whole world, cannot be ruled by one man, who is a mere man, nor does it have need of another vicar and supposititious head, since it has Christ as the true head present everywhere: just as subjects, who always and everywhere have their Lord and King present, do not need a Vicar and Pro-Regent.

For Christ fills all in all. Theodoret understands this here indeed of God the Father, as if the Church were called the body of Christ, and he himself its head, were the complement of the Father, who fills all in all. But all things sound of Christ, whose body and πλήρωμα the Church is called, who is also said to fill all things, Eph. IV. 10. Christ holds his Church in such high esteem, loves it so tenderly, that he considers himself in a way imperfect and maimed, unless he is joined to us, and we ourselves, as the body, are united to the head, as his πλήρωμα. Some take the word πληρουμένου passively, as if to say the Church is the body of Christ, he himself the head, and thus it is completed, that is, that structure and joining together is perfected. Just as follows συνθετικῶς. That the Church is that full and absolute work, which is completed or perfected κατὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν, that is, thoroughly in all things, so that no one for his own part may fear and suspect that this construction and arrangement of the Church is less than whole and full, as Camerarius has it here. But certain Greeks more correctly explain that πληρουμένου actively, that is, as filling, of him who fills all things. This active sense of Calvin, Beza, Zanchius, Aretius, and others, Crocius not undeservedly prefers to the passive interpretation of Musculus, namely, lest anyone hearing that the Church is the complement of Christ should impute this to a defect or need of Christ, he adds that it is Christ who fills all in all. But what it is to fill all things, God himself explains to us, Jer. XXIII. 23. Am I a God at hand, saith the Lord, and not a God afar off? Do not I fill heaven and earth? Therefore, to fill all things is to be present at hand, and to work as present all things in all, just as the same phrase applied to the Holy Spirit, Wis. 1:7, implies His presence. Since, therefore, Christ has attained this through His exaltation to the right hand of GOD, there is no doubt that, with respect to His human nature, He has attained this, that He fills all things in all, and nothing is left empty of His presence and operation.

There is no need here to invent anacolutha, which for such a reason neither Jerome nor anyone else detects in the present passage, even though Camerarius posits a hyperbaton, which, however, it will appear later is not the case. Grotius, however, seems to have invented whatever he pleased, both by inventing a parenthesis and by taking those words, placed by the Apostle with singular care, δὲ and καὶ, v. 4 and 5, as redundant, so that he does not need to admit that v. 3 is about original sin, common to all men. But that parenthesis does not fit at all, so far is it from being necessary. Indeed, he applies the benefits, which commonly accrue to the saints and the faithful in Christ, celebrated in chapter 1, specifically to the Ephesians, which are rendered more illustrious when we weigh what kind of people we are outside of Christ under the state of wrath. He describes the state of wrath both with respect to actual sins and also regarding original sin, inasmuch as they were not only dead in sins, insofar as they lived and passed their life in the lusts of the flesh according to the age or the manner of living, not only of most people, but of this whole world which is outside of Christ, according to the Prince of the world, who works in the sons of disobedience, such as all are outside of Christ, but also that they were children of wrath τῇ Φύσει by original stain propagated hereditarily, just as all other mortals are. Therefore, the state of misery, in which they were commonly with the Jews, is compared here first with the state of grace, in which both were then, in the first part; then, however, finally in the other part, the state of misery of the Ephesians is compared, in which they were as Gentiles before the Jews, with the happiness which subsequently befell them in Christ or by virtue of His merit through the calling of the Gospel. Since, therefore, they are said to have been dead in sins, nothing peculiar to the Ephesians is noted, but this is common to all outside of Christ. Just as also mercy has been shown to all in Christ, and Grotius rightly acknowledges here at v. 4 that the grace by which God loved us is common to the whole human race, wrongly separating these from each other by a parenthesis, which the Apostle intended to be joined, as witnessed by the coherence of reason and the adversative particle δὲ, which he himself wishes to be deleted. For God has concluded all under unbelief, that He might have mercy upon all, Rom. 11:32. And lest we believe it was peculiar to the Ephesians that they were dead in trespasses and sins, in which they once walked according to the Prince of the world, the Apostle makes himself a sharer of the same misery with the Jews in v. 3, because they too once walked among the sons of disobedience in the desires of their flesh; what could be said more clearly than that this is the common misery of all, in which we are outside of Christ! And therefore, so that the Vulgate might express the sense more clearly, at the beginning of the chapter it added from v. 5, And He has quickened you together, when you were dead. Which Crocius says almost all the Reformed follow, but there is no need for us to repeat the verb only from verse 5, since everything in this Apostolic treatment coheres perfectly, so that one would sooner snatch the club from Hercules than the coherence from the Apostle. He had said of Christ that He fills all in all: And you, CHRIST, the head of the Church, now fills you, whose faith in the Lord JESUS and love toward all the saints has become clear, ch. 1:15, when you were once dead in trespasses and sins. Unless perhaps with some evil men one should repeat the verb ἐγείρας ἐκ νεκρῶν from v. 20 of the preceding chapter, and He raised you from the dead. Theophylact says, He said that God has brought to bear upon us the same power and operation for His own sake, which Christ also performed.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἥτις ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀυτῶ, quæ est corpus ipsius) Vide infra IV. 12. 15. 16. V. 23. Col. I. 18. Sicut in hu- mano corpore ex capite defluens Spiritus omnia mem- bra continet, nutrit, augetque, ita Christi Spiritus omnia Ecclesiæ membra, quod sapienter admodum nos docet Paulus Col. II. 19. & alia similitudine illustrat Christus ipse Johannis V. initio capitis.

Τὸ πλήρωμα τῶ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρωμένε, & pleni- tudo ejus, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet,) ut Joh. I. 16. Col. II. 9. tum id quod impletur Rom. XI. 25. XV. 29. Posteriore sensu rectius hic accipias. Sic infra V. 18. πληρᾶσθε ἐν πνεύματι, implemini Spiritu Sancto, & Col. II. 10. ἐσὲ ἐν ἀυτῷ πεπληρωμένοι, ὃς ἐςιν ἡ κεφαλὴ πά- σης ἀρχῆς κὴ ἐξεσίας, estis in illo repleti, qui est caput omnis principatus & potestatis, qui locus huic idem valet. Et ob id Ecclesia vocatur πλήρωμα, plenitudo, in eadem ad Col. I. 19. Sic & quod sequitur, de Christo τῶ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρωμένε, quia omnia in omnibus adimplet, idem est, quod infra IV. 10. ὁ ἀναβὰς ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα, qui afcendit super omnes cælos, ut impleret omnia. Christus in omnibus, credentibus scilicet, nam de iis hic agitur, omnia im- plet, mentem luce, voluntatem piis affectibus, corpus ipsum facultate obsequendi, ad quæ accedebant illis temporibus, quibus loquebatur Apostolus admiranda illa χαρίσματα πνευματικά dona spiritualia, quorum supra meminit.

Non mystica tantum Psalmi VIII. applicatio hic habetur, sed literalis sensus adducitur. In Psal- mo non de Adamo aut homine mero, sed de Chri- sto Θεανθρώπῳ ejusque tum exinanitione tum ex- altatione agitur, cui non modo Angelorum exer- citus, sed pecora quoque & armenta subjicit Hie- ropsaltes, quemque super omnia manuum DEI opera constituit, nullo prorsus excepto, Ebr. II. 8. 1. Cor. XV. 27. Non ergo tantum hostes notantur, ut Musculus & Zanchius, hoc inferre phrasin, cum sub pedes dominantis aliquid subjici dicitur, exi- stimant: Sed omnia etiam alia, quia Paulus nihil nisi Deum excipit, unde OMNIS creatura ipsi honorem, gloriam & robur tribuit, Apoc. V. 8. 13. fatente hic Crocio. Vid. de his ad Psalm. VIII. Annot. nostr. Caput etiam Ecclesiæ Christum su- per omnia constitutum Apostolus hic designat. Non esset autem super omnia, nisi omnem po- testatem haberet atque in cœlo, & in terra regna- ret. Nec tueri posset Ecclesiam adversus omnes ejus hostes, tum corporales, tum spirituales, nisi in omnia potestatem haberet supremam, quæ ad- versus ipsas inferorum portas, salvam & incolu- mem universam Ecclesiam defendat, & Spiritus Sancti donis impleat. Defendit autem Ecclesiam ubique locorum adversus hostes non absens, sed præsens, ac dominatur in medio inimicorum, Psalm. CX. 1. 2. Nec vero impleret corpus suum Christus Ecclesiæ caput, sicut corpus humanum ex capite defluens Spiritus implet, nisi omnibus membris corporis mystice præsens esset, & gra- tia & donis suis præsens influeret, quemadmo- dum Spiritus influunt in universa corporis hu- mani membra, iisque præsentia vera & reali, effi- caciam impertiunt. Unde abstrahi non debent virtus & dona Christi, per quæ influit Christus in omnes credentes ab ipsomet Christo, qui vi pro- missionis suæ substantiali præsentia, & gratiosa inhabitatione dignatur fideles, Matth. XXIX. 20. Johan. XIV. 26. & super omnes cælos afcendit, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα, Ephes. IV. 10. atque ideo dicitur πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρέμενος, non tantum in credentibus, ad quos hoc temere restringit Grotius, sed simpliciter IN OMNIBUS, quemadmodum constitutus dicitur SUPER OMNIA. Cæterum ut Ecclesia τὸ πλήρωμα sensu passivo recte dicatur, locus tamen, Col. I. 9. πλήρωμα, longe aliud concernit: πᾶν nempe τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, quod in Christo habitat juxta εὐδοκίαν divinam, ut e collatione cap. II. con- stat. Quomodo vero Ecclesia in Christo, si illam per πλήρωμα intelligat Grotius, habitet, & quidem ea fini, ut omnia per ipsum reconcilientur, fa- teor, me capere non posse.

Johannes Crocius ut Majestatem omnipræsen- tiæ Christi carni, cui subjecta sunt omnia, dero- get, & argumenti B. Hunnii nostri vim declinet, quod ab hac omnium significatione loca & loco- rum spatia eximi non possint, quasi hæc illi sub- jecta non sint, imo hanc vim habeant, ut regnan- tis Christi præsentiam in terris & alibi interver- tant: Christo, ait, Θεανθρώπῳ Deum omnia subjecisse atque hinc recte omnipræsentiam Christi concludi non autem omnipræsentiam carnis Christi: Nec e' subjectione locorum omnium sequi inexistentiam in omnibus locis, sed dominatum & imperium. Sed de- clinare vim argumenti Hunniani nullus potest. Si enim Christo θεανθρώπῳ Deus subjecit omnia, quærimus, num secundum Divinam, an secundum Humanam naturam ei omnia subjecerit? Prius dicere nequeunt. Divina enim natura ipsi cum Patre communis est. Secundum eam semper ha- buit, ut Pater, sibi subjecta omnia. Dicendum ergo posterius. Si itaque omnipræsentia recte concluditur ex subjectione omnium, carnis utique Christi omnipræsentia rectissime inde concludi- tur. Tum si Christus secundum carnem omni- bus locis dominetur, quod non negat sequi ex subjectione omnium Crocius, quæro, anne domi- nium sit absentis, an vero præsentis? Absentis do- minium dici nequit, quia dominium est divinum, & ut unus idemque Dominus est Christus Deus & homo, ita est unum idemque dominium Christi, qua Deus & qua homo est, nisi duos Dominos cre- dere oporteat. Porro dominium divinum quis ab- senter geri, & non præsenter admittet? Quum er- go Christus ut homo idem imperium habeat cum Patre, uti etiam in eodem throno sedet, eodemque cultu honoratur, hoc autem Patris imperium non absenter administratur, sed præsenter, idem omni- no de Humanæ Christi naturæ præsenti dominio credendum erit, quod id non absens administret, sed præsens, non absens sed præsens hostibus re- sistat, Ecclesiam defendat, & in omnia Ecclesiæ membra gratia sua influat, inque iisdem habitet, & omnia in omnibus impleat. Unde tamen inclusio & localis inexistentia in omnibus creaturis inferri non debet, quemadmodum nec Patrem includi, aut locali inexistentia omnibus pomis, caseis, la- pidibus, creaturis inexistere quisquam Calvini- sequarum dixerit. Triumphantem Ecclesiam Chri- stum hodie gubernare externe, omnibus est in pro- clivi, ait Crocius. A qua gubernatione humanam naturam excludere nefas. At in æternum guberna- bit. Regni enim ejus non erit finis, Luc. I. Si er- go nefas est, excludere humanam naturam ab o- mnium gubernatione, omnibus electis præsto erit ἀδιαςάτως. Aut num credendum, in uno cœli loco illis tantum, qui ipsis proximi sunt, quia cœlum locale faciunt Calvinistæ, Christum secundum hu- manam naturam adfuturum, in innumeris vero locis aliis, & innumeris Electis minime præsto futurum; cum non possit juxta ipsos caro Christi, nisi uno in loco, præsens esse. Carebunt ergo ple- rique Electi præsentia carnis Christi tam deside- rata in ipsis etiam cœlis. Sic carere etiam opor- tet fideles promissa Humanæ naturæ Christi præ- sentia in terris in Ecclesia, Matth. XXIX. 20. Qua fratris sui, carnis & sanguinis sui, capitis sui ex- optatissima præsentia & assistentia privant fideles, quantum in ipsis est, Calviniani. Fatetur Crocius, ut Christus secundum utramque naturam est caput Ecclesiæ, ita etiam secundum utramque facere offi- cium capitis. Neque tamen ideo censet, humani- tatem necessario esse omnibus fidelibus & creaturis præsentem substantiali præsentia absque indistantia loci, sicut non necesse est, ut caput manibus & pe- dibus ratione loci sit conjunctum, sed sufficit Spiri- tus conjunctio. At non necesse est, ut capitis simi- litudo ad omnia sese extendat: Caput enim my- sticum ut influit in omnia membra, ita influit non absenti ratione, sed unitum & conjunctum mem- bris omnibus, omnibus fidelibus, in quibus habi- tat, quæ movet, agit, sustentat, tuetur, vivificat, non absens, sed præsens, non sola Deitate, utpote quæ nusquam sola est, & extra carnem, postquam car- nem in suam hypostasin assumsit, & in carne cum omni sua plenitudine habitavit, sed cum carne, quia præsentia est totius suppositi, quod totum ibi non est, ubi altera natura præsto non est. Aliarum creaturarum respectu caput quidem non est Christus phrasi scripturæ, portat tamen omnia verbo virtutis suæ, Ebr. I. 3. & omnia in manibus suis habet, Johan. III. 35. cap. XIII. 3. idque ut Deus & Homo, ideoque conservat & sustentat omnia non absens sed præsens, substantiali præsentia & ἀδιαςασίᾳ.

Illa ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ nec cum Vulgata reddenda, sed per omnem Ecclesiam, nec cum Thoma, Alberto, Gregorio de Valentia, Suarezio eo trahenda, ut caput esse Angelorum statuatur, quibus insuper & gratiam & gloriam meruisse Christum, ipsi arguunt: Quum tamen Angeli nec pars, aut membra mystici corporis Christi sint, nec Angelorum gratia Christus vel natus vel passus sit, sed illi in gratia confirmati, gloriamque consecuti fuissent, etiamsi nec homo fuisset conditus, nec Filius DEI incarnatus. Neque tamen trajectione Grotii opus est, quum ἐξηγητικῶς illa interpretati sint nonnulli καθ᾽ ἔλλειψιν, hoc modo, αὐτὸν ἔδωκε κεφαλὴν, τὸν ὄντα ὑπὲρ πάντα. Alii καθ᾽ ἔλλειψιν τοῦ ἀποβατικοῦ ὥςε & τοῦ ὑπαρκτικοῦ εἶναι hoc modo, ὥςε εἶναι αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ πάντα τὴν κεφαλὴν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, summum ut esset & omnipotens caput Ecclesiæ, vel etiam solum & unicum caput, notante Camerario. Unicum certe caput ac solitarium est: Nec enim cum ullo divisum habet imperium, nec ullus ei coordinari potest; quod in aprico est: Sed nec subordinari, ut caput sit sub capite, nam ita Ecclesia biceps foret. Quæ quum per totum orbem diffusa sit, ab uno homine, qui ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, non potest regi, nec alio vicario ac supposititio capite opus habet, quum Christum caput verum ubique præsentem habeat: quemadmodum subditi, qui semper & ubique Dominum ac Regem suum præsentem habent, non indigent Vicario ac Pro-Rege.

Implet enim Christus omnia in omnibus. Quod quidem de Deo Patre hic intelligit Theodoretus, quasi Christi quidem corpus dicatur Ecclesia, & ipse ejus caput, complementum sit Patris, qui omnia in omnibus impleat. Sed de Christo sonant omnia, cujus & corpus & πλήρωμα vocatur Ecclesia, qui etiam omnia implere dicitur, Eph. IV. 10. Tanto in pretio Christus suam habet Ecclesiam, tam tenere amat, ut se quodammodo imperfectum & mancum reputet, nisi nobis conjungatur, & nos ipsi, tanquam corpus capiti uniamur, ceu πλήρωμα ejus. Nonnulli vocem πληρουμένου passive accipiunt, q. d. Ecclesia est corpus Christi, ipse caput, & ita completur, id est, absolvitur compago & coagmentatio ista. Quemadmodum sequitur συνθετικῶς. Esse Ecclesiam plenum illud & absolutum opus, quod compleatur seu perficiatur κατὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν, id est, penitus in universis, ne quis pro sua parte vereatur, atque suspicetur, minus esse integram & plenam hanc extructionem & collocationem Ecclesiæ, ut hic habet Camerarius. Sed rectius ἐνεργητικῶς explicant Græci quidam illud πληρουμένου, id est πληροῦντος ipsius, qui omnia implet. Quem activum sensum Calvini, Bezæ, Zanchii, Aretii, & aliorum Crocius passivæ Musculi interpretationi non immerito præfert, nempe, ne quis audiens, complementum Christi esse Ecclesiam, id Christi defectui aut indigentiæ imputet, addit Christum esse, qui omnia in omnibus impleat. Quid autem sit implere omnia, Deus ipse nobis enarrat, Jer. XXIII. 23. Deus e propinquo ego sum, dicit Dominus & non e longinquo, num quid non cælum & terram ego impleo. Illud ergo omnia implere, est in propinquo adesse, & præsentem omnia in omnibus operari, sicut eadem phrasis de Spiritu Sancto, Sap. I. 7. adhi- bita præsentiam ejus infert. Quum ergo per ex- altationem ad dextram DEI Christus hoc conse- cutus sit, nullum dubium est, Humanæ naturæ respectu id consecutum esse, ut omnia in omni- bus impleat, & nihil relinquatur ab ipsius præ- sentia & operatione vacuum.

Non opus hic fingere ἀνανπόδοτα, quæ tali ra- tione nec Hieronymus, nec quisquam alius in præ- senti loco deprehendit, etsi hyperbaton Camerarius statuat, quo tamen op9 non esse, deinde apparebit. Grotius autem, quæcunque libuit, commentus vi- detur, tum παρενθήκην fingens, tum vocabula illa, singulari studio ab Apostolo posita, δὲ & καὶ, v. 4. & 5. ut πλεονάζοντα sumens, ut ne opus habeat ad- mittere, v. 3. de labe originali, omnibus homini- bus communi, sermonem esse. Sed παρενθήκην illa nullatenus congruit, tantum abest, ut necessaria sit. Nimirum applicat beneficia, quæ in Christo sanctis & fidelibus communiter obtingunt cap. I. celebrata, peculiariter Ephesiis, quæ illustriora redduntur, cum quales extra Christum sub statu iræ simus, expendimus. Statum autem iræ de- scribit tum respectu peccatorum actualium; tum quoad originale peccatum, siquidem non tantum mortui in peccatis fuerint, quatenus in iis secun- dum seculum vel rationem vivendi, non tantum plerorumque, sed mundi hujus universi, qui extra Christum est, secundum Principem mundi, qui in filiis incredulitatis operatur, quales omnes sunt extra Christum, conversati sint & vitam transge- rint in carnis concupiscentiis, sed etiam filii iræ sint τῇ Φύσει per labem originalem propagatam hæreditario, sicut & reliqui mortales omnes. Confer- tur ergo hic primum status miseriæ, in quo com- muniter cum Judæis fuerunt, cum statu gratiæ, in quo tum erant utrique, in parte priori; tum vero demum in parte altera confertur status miseriæ Ephesiorum, in quo tanquam gentiles præ Judæis fuere cum felicitate, quæ illis in Christo vel vir- tute meriti ejus deinceps obtigit per vocationem Evangelii. Cum itaque mortui dicuntur fuisse in peccatis, non notatur aliquid proprium Ephesiis, sed commune hoc omnibus est extra Christum. Quemadmodum etiam misericordia omnibus ex- hibita est in Christo, & gratiam, qua dilexit nos Deus, universo humano generi communem recte hic agnoscit ad v. 4. Grotius, male hæc a se invi- cem separans per parenthesin, quæ conjuncta voluit Apostolus, teste rationis ἀκολουθίᾳ & par- ticula Adversativa δὲ, quam deletam ipse cupit. Conclusit enim Deus omnes sub incredulitate, ut omnium misereretur, Rom. XI. 33. Et ne peculiare hoc Ephesiis credamus fuisse, quod mortui fue- rint in delictis & peccatis, in quibus versati quondam erant secundum mundi Principem, ejusdem miseriæ consortes se cum Judæis facit Apostolus v. 3. quod & ipsi inter filios incredu- litatis conversati olim sint in cupiditatibus car- nis suæ, quo quid clarius dici poterat, commu- nem hanc omnium esse miseriam, qua extra Chri- stum sumus! Ideoque ut sensum liquidius expri- meret Vulgatus, sub initium capitis, e v. 5. adjecit, Et vos una vivificavit, cum essetis mortui. Quem fere omnes Reformatos sequi, ait Crocius, sed non opus est, ut e vers. 5. demum verbum repeta- mus, cum optime cohæreant omnia in hac tra- ctatione Apostolica, ut citius Herculi clavam, quam Apostolo συνέχειαν quis excutiat. Dixe- rat Christi πάντα πλησέμενον ἐν πάσι: Καὶ ὑμᾶς, & vos implet jam CHRISTUS, Ecclesiæ ca- put, quorum fides in Domino JESU, & charitas in omnes sanctos inclaruit, cap. I. 15. cum esse- tis quondam mortui in delictis & peccatis. Nisi forte cum quibusdam malis e vers. 20. præce- dentis capitis verbum ἐγείρας ἐν νεκρῶν repetere, & vos excitavit a mortuis. Dixit superius, inquit Theophylactus, eandem in nos virtutem & operam pro se Deum tulisse, quam & Christus præstulerit.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle reminds the Ephesians of the state of misery in which, dead in sins, they walked in the lusts of the flesh, still children of wrath by nature, as were the rest: And also of the state of grace in which, through the mercy of GOD, who quickened us together with Christ, raised us up, and established us in heavenly goods, they are saved in Him through faith, not from works, even though they were created in Christ for good works; that formerly, when they were uncircumcision, they were aliens from Christ and without God, but now have been made near through the blood of Christ, who took away the middle wall of partition between the Jews and the Gentiles, and procured grace with God for both in one mystical body, as one who both acquired and announced peace to all. Therefore he teaches that they are no longer guests and strangers, but citizens and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Christ being the cornerstone, into a spiritual building of God.

There are two parts: The first, a proclamation of divine grace in our vivification and salvation, up to verse 10. The second, a comparison of the state of the Ephesians outside of Christ and in Christ, up to verse 22.

PART I.

A proclamation of divine grace in vivification and salvation.

Vers. 1. Καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκρὸς τοῖς παραπτώμασι, καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις) It is not so difficult to resolve the anapodota of Paul, which Jerome and others have noted to be frequent in him. For if you take what follows here up to comma 4 as a parenthesis, and then the δὲ, which follows in comma 4, and the καὶ, which follows in comma 5 (unless you prefer to take δὲ as ὅμως, and καὶ as καίπερ), as pleonastic in the Hebrew manner, which often interpose their ו, which signifies both δὲ and καὶ, you will have a well-coherent discourse. Moreover, there is here an inessis of the little word ἐν, such as in Prov. VI. 12. The full expression is in the passage which is a twin to this, Coloss. II. 13. and here in the Syriac, as also below in 6. Therefore, this is a Dative for the case which is called the sixth, and signifies the cause. Otherwise, if the Dative is taken in its own proper sense, ἀποθνήσκειν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ indicates something far different from what is signified here, as can be seen in Rom. VI. 2. Dead in sins are men immersed in vices, so that there is hardly any hope that they can rise again to a better life, for whom the Pythagoreans used to build a cenotaph, and whose examples the law of the Nazarites teaches us to avoid, in a mystical sense. In Seror Hamor you have רשעים בחייהם קרויים מתים. But such had been most of the Gentiles, even among the philosophers, as we showed at Rom. I. These words, παραπτώματα and ἁμαρτίαι, are sometimes interchanged, as was evident above 1. 7. Sometimes they are distinguished, so that ἁμαρτία is חַטָאת, or אָשָׁם: For both Hebrew words are translated by that term; but παράπτωμα is מַעַל, in which way that Hebrew word is translated, Ezech. XIV. 13. XV. 8. XVIII. 24. XX. 27. Elsewhere it is ἀνομία, ἀπόστασις, ἀποστασία. Thus the Latins distinguish flagitium from scelus. For he said that he also raised him from the dead, and willed that he should preside over all things. But concerning us he speaks thus: Truly, when we were affected by death, not indeed bodily, which took its beginning from Adam, but spiritual, which consists chiefly of ourselves and flowed down from sins, he lifted us up and raised us. Whence it happens that with equal power he both raised the Lord from bodily death, and us from the animal death, which is called the death of wicked deeds. Nay rather, it is to be considered of greater importance to lead back straying souls addicted to sins into the way, than to raise the dead. Here, therefore, he makes the lot of the Ephesians common with his own in misery, so that he may more clearly celebrate the same benefit that happened to them with himself, and he excites them thus to bless God, and to proceed briskly in the course of faith and piety: Inasmuch as they were dead in sins, but made alive in Christ by the rich mercy of GOD, and saved by grace.

He understands death, however, not of the body, as Hyperius wishes, but of the soul, which most other interpreters acknowledge with a unanimous opinion. Since indeed the vivification, which happened in Christ, is also spiritual. Therefore, they are called dead in sins, not those who have died to flesh and sin, Rom. VI. 11, but those who are mortified by the guilt and poison of sin, or are utterly deprived of spiritual life, such as are not only men immersed in vices, so that hardly any hope remains that they can rise again to a better life, nor only most among the Gentiles, but all who are not reborn; For whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, John III. 5, whence there is no hope for any to rise again to a better life, unless he be regenerated by GOD. But there is no need to labor here over the distinction of those words παράπτωμα and ἀνομία. Haymo, Thomas, and Lombard wish to denote by παράπτωμα a sin of omission, and by ἁμαρτίαν a sin of commission, which Augustine also thought, though hesitantly, q. XX in Levit., judging that by that word 'delictum' [offense], what is done imprudently, and by this word 'peccatum' [sin], what is committed by one who knows, could be understood. Some, with Gualther, wish by παράπτωμα a will inclined to sin, and by ἁμαρτίαν a deed perpetrated; others, with Jerome, by the former the beginnings of sins, and by the latter the consummation; others the former as original sin, the latter as actual; others, on the contrary, wish these to be designated in reverse order, with Aretius. None of these can be proven. The Apostle takes these words for the same things in Rom. V. 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 21. From these also it appears by comparison with v. 5 and Col. II. 13 that they are to be taken in this way. And therefore, it seems rather that the huge multitude of sins, and the lethal force of all and each, is noted by the conjunction of both words.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Apostolus commonefacit Ephesios de statu mi- seriæ, quo in peccatis mortui in concupi- scentiis carnis ambularunt, adhuc filii iræ natura, uti & reliqui: Nec non de statu gratiæ, quo per misericordiam DEI, qui nos una cum Christo vivificavit, resusci- tavit, & in cælestibus bonis constituit, in ipso salvati sunt per fidem, non ex ope- ribus, etsi conditi in Christo ad bona ope- rasimus; quod quondam, cum præputium erant, alieni fuerint a Christo, & sine Deo, jam vero propinqui facti sint per sangui- nem Christi, qui parietem intergerinum inter Judæos & gentes sustulit, & utrisque in uno corpore mystico gratiam concilia- vit cum Deo, ut pote qui pacem & acquisi- vit & annunciavit omnibus. Proinde do- cet, eos non amplius esse hospites, & pere- grinos, sed cives & domesticos Dei, extru- ctos super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, lapide angulari existente Christo, in ædificium Dei spirituale.

PArtes duæ sunt: Prima, gratiæ divinæ in vivi- ficatione & salvatione nostri deprædicatio, ad v. 10. Altera status Ephesiorum extra Christum & in Christo comparatio ad v. 22.

PARS I.

Gratiæ divinæ in vivificatione & salva- tione deprædicatio.

Vers. 1. Καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκρὸς τοῖς παραπτώμασι, καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις) Non ita difficile est, solvere Pauli ἀνανόδοτα, quæ in illo frequentia esse notarunt Hieronymus & alii. Nam si quæ hic sequuntur usque ad comma 4. sumas, ut παρενθήκην, & deinde δὲ, quod sequitur commate 4. & καὶ, quod sequitur commate 5. (nisi malis δὲ sumere pro ὅμως, & καὶ pro καίπερ) sumas ut πλεονάζοντα more Ebræo, qui suum ו, quod & δὲ & καὶ valet, sæpe sic interponunt, habebis orationem bene cohærentem. Est autem hic ines- sis voculæ ἐν, qualis Prov. VI. 12. Plena locutio est in loco, qui huic est geminus, Coloss. II. 13. & hic in Syria- co, ut & infra 6. Est ergo hic Dativus pro casu, qui sextus dicitur, & causam significat. Alioqui si Dativus in proprio suo sensu sumatur, ἀποθνήσκειν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ longe aliud in- dicat ab eo, quod hic significatur, ut videre est Rom. VI. 2. Mortui in peccatis sunt homines immersi vitiis, ita ut vix ulla spes sit, eos ad vitam meliorem posse resurgere, qua- libus Pythagorei struebant κενοτάφιον, & qualium exempla vitanda docet lex Nazaræatus, in sensu mystico. In Seror הױרשעים בחייהם קרויים מתים Hamor habes Ies autem fuerant in gentibus plerique, etiam ex Philo- sophis, ut ostendimus ad Rom. I. Voces istæ, παραπτώ ματα & ἁμαρτίαι, interdum permutantur, ut patuit supra 1. 7. Interdum dittinguuntur, ita ut ἁμαρτία sit חַטָאת, vel אָשָׁם: Utrumque enim Ebræum illa voce transfertur παράπτωμα vero מַעַל, quomodo vertitur ista vox Ebræa, Ezech. XIV. 13. XV. 8. XVIII. 24. XX. 27. Alibi ἀνομία, ἀπόστασις, ἀποστασία. Sic Latini distinguunt flagi- tium a scelere. Nam & hunc dixit a mortuis suscitasse, & volu- isse, ut omnibus præsideret. De nobis vero sic loqui- tur: Nos sane cum essemus morte affecti, nec cor- porea quidem, quæ ex Adamo sumpsit initium, sed spirituali, quæ a nobis ipsis præcipue constat, & a peccatis defluxit, extulit ille & suscitavit. Quo fit, ut pari virtute & Dominum a morte corporea ex- citavit, & nos ab animali, quæ pravorum dicitur facinorum mors. Quin potius majoris est facien- dum, devias animas & peccatis addictas in viam reducere, quam mortuos suscitare. Hic ergo Ephe- siorum sortem sibi communem in miseria jam facit, ut idem secum ipsis contigisse beneficium, luculentius celebret, eosque ita ad Deum bene- dicendum, & in cursu fidei & pietatis alacriter pergendum excitat: Utpote in peccatis mortuos, sed divite DEI misericordia in Christo vivifica- tos, & ex gratia servatos.

Mortem autem intelligit non corporis, ut Hy- perius vult, sed animæ, quod plerique alii Inter- pretes unanimi sententia agnoscunt. Siquidem vivificatio, quæ in Christo contigit, etiam spiri- tualis sit. Mortui ergo peccatis dicuntur, non qui carni & peccato demortui, Rom. VI. 11. sed qui peccati reatu & veneno mortificati, vel vita spiri- tuali penitus privati sunt, quales sunt non tan- tum homines vitiis immersi, ut vix ulla spes su- persit, eos ad vitam meliorem posse resurgere, nec plerique tantum in gentibus, sed omnes non re- nati; Quicquid enim ex carne natum est, caro est, Joh. III. 5. unde nulli spes est resurgere ad melio- rem vitam, nisi ex DEO regeneretur. De vocum autem illarum παράπτωμα & ἀνομία distinctio- ne hic laborandum. Haymo, Thomas, & Lombar- dus παράπτωμα peccatum omissionis, ἁμαρτίαν peccatum commissionis notare volunt, quod etiam Augustinus, sed dubitanter, putavit, q. XX. in Levit. per illud delictum, quod imprudenter, per hanc peccatum, quod a sciente patratur, intelligi posse etiam censens. Nonnulli per παράπτωμα voluntatem ad peccatum propensam, per ἁμαρτίαν factum perpetratum cum Gualthero; alii per illud cum Hieronymo peccatorum initia, per hanc ve- ro consummationem; Alii priori peccatum origi- nale, posteriori actuale; alii contra inverso or- dine hæc designari volunt cum Aretio. Nihil ho- rum probari potest. Apostolus pro iisdem sumit has voces Rom. V. 12. 15. 17. 18. 20. 21. Ex his quo- que ita accipere e v. 5. & Col. II. 13. collatione apparet. Ideoque potius ingens peccatorum mul- titudo, ac omnium singulorumque vis lethifera, vocis utriusque conjunctione, notari videtur.

## 2:2
Vers. 2. In which you once walked) You also, Ephesians, were given then to other vices, and to magical arts. See what was said in Acts XX. 19. Περιπατεῖν, הלך, signifies a custom.

According to the age of this world) αἰὼν signifies many things: Sometimes life, and by metonymy the manner of living, which is דרך to the Hebrews: You lived as was the custom for most.

According to the prince of the power of the air) There are many kinds of demons. Ignatius to the Ephesians: 'In which all war of aerial and earthly spirits is brought to nothing.' Those are called earthly κοσμοκράτορες τῦ σκότυς [world-rulers of darkness], because those who lie under the earth are obscure. But those in the air are τὰ πνεύματα τῆς πονηρίας ἐν ἐπυρανίοις [the spirits of wickedness in heavenly places]: Below VI. 12. Plato: 'Demons are an aerial race.' You have the same in the Hebrew book which is called the Cedar of Lebanon: And the book מנחה חדשה says that everything from the earth to the sky is full of spirits. Those earthly ones suggest coarser spirits, such as those which are perceived by the external senses. But those aerial ones suggest pride, revenge, κενοδοξίαν [vainglory], idolatry, vices not less but more subtle. ὁ ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τῦ ἀέρος [the prince of the power of the air] is he who commands all those powers of the air, the singular being put in place of the plural. Concerning that Prince, see Matt. IX. 34, XII. 24, Mark III. 22, Luke XI. 15, John XII. 31.

Of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience) Τῦ πνεύματος, the singular for the plural, which is frequent where the whole genus is treated, just as ἄνθρωπος is the human race. He says of those spirits, who even now dominate not in you, but in all those who have rejected the Gospel offered to them. υἱοὶ ἀπειθείας [sons of disobedience], both here and in Coloss. III. 6, are by Hebrew idiom men who do not wish to subject themselves to divine laws, although they are holy and have clear testimonies of divine power. A similar description is in Deut. XXXII. 9.

The things which Grotius philosophizes too crudely about the different kinds of demons are hardly worthy of being refuted. For they are handed down without Scripture. There are not some demons that are earthly and others that are aerial, so that the former seduce to coarser appetites, but the latter to more subtle vices. And how will it be taught that earthly spirits, that is, according to Grotius's lexicon, by the κοσμοκράτορες τῦ σκότυς [world-rulers of darkness] who lie under the earth, the Grotius-style aerial demons are to be understood by the τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις [spiritual things of wickedness in heavenly places]? Or that by the prince of the power of the air, not he who commands all demons, but he who dominates only the powers of the air, is designated, when the cited passages rather designate the Prince Demon, who is also called the Prince of the world. He who is called the Prince of the air, not because he was created for this, that he might preside over the air, which is the gloss of Theodoret here; he taught us openly that the power of the air was indeed once entrusted to the Devil, but when he had fallen from it on account of his wickedness, he became the Master of impiety and wickedness. Nor because he is the Prince of the aerial powers, as Grotius imagines, whence Cajetan, noted by Estius, attributing to them a subtle body, namely that he mostly exercises command in the air with his own, so that the sense may be, to whom is the power of the air τῦ πνέυματος through an antiprosis, the Genitive placed for the Accusative, as Piscator notes, and blessed Luther rendered it. Theophylact here: He calls the Devil the prince of the power and of the air, not the creator of the world, as the Manichaeans assert.
