And a prince indeed, because men voluntarily submitted themselves to the Devil: For more obey and serve him than GOD: Otherwise this is his Principality in this age. Nor does he insinuate himself into the air, so that he might have any place in heaven, but he holds these lower things, and those subject to heaven. And therefore Paul calls him the Prince of the power of the air, not because he has any dominion in the air, so that he might, for instance, either temper or moderate it, that is indeed far from it, but because he insinuates himself into it. Who indeed works not only in those who reject the Gospel offered to them, but in all Gentiles, nay in all constituted outside of Christ. For they all are shut up εἰς ἀπείθειαν, Rom. XI. 32. and are called ὑοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας, and so also Col. III. 6., whence ὁ ἀπειθῶν τῷ ὑῷ, and ὁ πισέυων εἰς τὸν ὑὸν, Joh. III. 26. exhaust the whole world or the human race. Compare verses 16, 18.

Crocius notes here a twofold kind of Diabolical actions from Musculus and Zanchius: Some are of temptations, by which he tempts the hearts of men with the breath of evil thoughts: Others of energies, by which he drives them, where he wishes, as if they were captives. The former kind obtains as much in the pious as in the impious. The latter mostly in the impious. For although he also acts in the pious, when he attacks them, tempts them, and drives them to sin in various ways, yet not everywhere and always with success and without resistance. For they often resist by faith, struggle, and often struggle out. But he agitates the contumacious, like slaves, according to his own pleasure. He adds, however, that he works NOW in the sons of disobedience, either because his operation still flourishes now in this age, but is finally to be emptied at the end of the world, as Antonius Scaynus notes, or because he then had efficacy in the rebellious and unregenerate, lest he should have ceased now the Ephesians clearly consider the operation of Satan, and that they may the more beware of ἀπειθείᾳ [disobedience] and the snares of Satan, who is striving to lead them into it. The Apostle therefore proves that spiritual death reigned as far as the Ephesians were concerned, because they walked in sins, not only gross ones, but also those to which they were addicted without any scruple of conscience, such as superstitions and idolatrous worship. For to walk is to order one's life, to set one's study and effort upon something, and it is used both of the good, who are said to walk with GOD in the Spirit, in charity, and in the law of GOD, Gen. V. 22, 24, Psal. CXIX. 1, 3, Gal. V. 16, Joh. V. 2, and who order their life in such a way; and of the bad, who walk according to the flesh, Roman. VIII. 1, who are outside of Christ. Here, therefore, to walk in trespasses and sins is not simply to sin, but to pass one's life in them securely without the fear of GOD, and to delight oneself according to the desires of the flesh, in the manner of those who walk about for the sake of their own pleasure. Αἰὼν signifies the time of life, as ἄνερ ἀπ' αἰῶν@ νέ@ ὤλεο, as also in this place, as if a certain age of the world might seem to be understood, and the Greeks interpret τὸν αἰῶνα as τὸν ἐν ἁμαρτίαις διερραμμέ- νον βίον [the life spent in sins]. Thus, therefore, he says, you lived, just as the age of this world, that is, men in this earthly life, are accustomed to do. The explanation which follows is that the Devil is the ruler of that age, to whom he attributes a certain aerial principality, so that his force and power may be understood to be immense, as here Camerarius.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἐν αἷς πότε περιεπατήσατε) Vos etiam Ephesii, dediti tum vitiis aliis, tum magicis artibus. Vide quæ di- cta Actor. XX. 19. Περιπατεῖν הלך consuetudinem signi- ficat.

Κατὰ τὸν αἰῶνα τῦ κόσμυ τύτυ) αἰὼν multa significat: Interdum vitam, & per Μετωνυμίαν rationem vivendi, quæ דרך Ebræis: Vixistis, ut mos erat plerisque.

Κατὰ τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τῦ ἀέρος) Dæmonum multa sunt genera. Ignatius ad Ephesios: Ἐν ᾗ πᾶς πό- λεμος καταργεῖται ἀερίων κὴ ἐπιγείων πνευμάτων. Illi terre- stres vocantur κοσμοκράτορες τῦ σκότυς, quia, qui sub terra latent, obscuri sunt. Illi vero in aere, τὰ πνεύματα τῆς πονηρίας ἐν ἐπυρανίοις: Infra VI. 12. Plato: Δαίμονες ἀέριον γένος. Habes idem in libro Ebræo, qui dicitur Ce- drus Libani: Et liber מנחה חדשה ait a terra ad cœ- lum omnia plena spiritibus. Terrestres illi suggerunt spi- ritus crassiores, quales sunt, qui externis sensibus perci- piuntur. Illi vero aerei superbiam, ultionem, κενοδοξίαν, idololatriam, vitia non minora sed subtiliora, ὁ ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τῦ ἀέρος est is, qui omnibus illis potestatibus aeris imperat, singulari posito vice pluralis. De eo Princi- pe vide Matth. IX. 34. XII. 24. Marc. III. 22. Luc. XI. 15. Joh. XII. 31.

Τῦ πνεύματος τῦ νῦν ἐνεργῦντος ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπει- θείας ) Τῆ πνεύματος , singulare pro plurali, qnod fre- quens, ubi de toto genere agitur, quomodo ἄνθρωπος est humanum genus. Illorum inquit spirituum, qui etiam nunc dominantur non in vobis, sed in omnibus illis, qui Evangelium sibi oblatum repudiarunt, vioὶ ἀπειθείας & hic & Coloss. III. 6. locutione Ebræa sunt homines, qui di- vinis legibus, quanquam & sanctis, & clara divinæ poten- tiæ testimonia habentibus, subjicere se nolunt. Descriptio similis Deut. XXXII. 9.

Quæ de diversis Dæmonum generibus nimis crasse philosophatur Grotius, vix sunt digna, quæ retractentur. Ἄτερ γραφῆς enim traduntur. Non sunt Dæmones alii terrestres alii aerii, ut illi ad appetitus crassiores, hi vero ad vitia subtiliora seducant. Et quomodo Spiritus terrestres, hoc est, juxta Lexicon Grotii per τὺς κοσμοκράτορας τῦ σκότυς, qui sub terra latent, per τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις Dæmones aerios Gro- tianos intelligi docebitur? Aut per τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξυσίας τῦ ἀέρος, non qui imperat omnibus Dæmonibus, sed qui potestatibus aeris solum do- minatur, designari, quum loca allegata potius Principem Dæmonem, qui & Princeps mundi di- citur, designent. Qui Princeps aeris dicitur, non quod ad id creatus sit, ut aeri præsideat, quæ Theo- doreti hic glossa est; aperte nos docuit, Diabolo quidem olim fuisse creditam aeris potestatem, cum ab ea autem excidisset propter improbitatem, im- pietatis & improbitatis Magister effectus est. Nec quod Princeps sit potestatum aerearum, ut Grotius fingit, unde Cajetanus ab Estio notatus illis cor- pus subtile tribuens, scilicet quod plerumque in aere imperium cum suis exerceat, ut sensus sit, cui potestas est aeris τῦ πνέυματος per ἀντίπτω- σιν Genit. pro Accusativo positum, ut Piscator notat, & reddidit B. Lutherus. Theophylactus hic: Principem autem potestatis & aeris Diabolum di- cit, non mundi fabricatorem, ut adstruunt Mani- chæi. Et principem quidem, quia ultro homines Diabolo sese subdiderunt: Plures enim illi quam DEO obsequuntur ac serviunt: Alioqui hoc in se- culo hujus est Principatus. Nec in aerem se ille in- sinuat, ut ullum habeat in cælo locum, sed inferiora hæc tenet, & cælo subjecta. Et ideo Paulus Princi- pem potestatis aeris dicit, non quod ullam habeat in aere ditionem, ut illum scil. vel temperet vel mo- deretur, id quidem sit procul, sed quia se in illo in- sinuet. Qui vero operatur non solum in iis, qui Evangelium sibi oblatum repudiant, sed in omni- bus gentilibus, imo in omnibus extra Christum constitutis. Illi enim omnes εἰς ἀπείθειαν con- clusi sunt, Rom. XI. 32. & ὑοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας, & sic etiam Col. III. 6. dicuntur, unde ὁ ἀπειθῶν τῷ ὑῷ, & ὁ πισέυων εἰς τὸν ὑὸν, Joh. III. 26. totum mun- dum vel genus humanum exhauriunt. Confer. vers. 16. 18.

Duplex hic ex Musculo & Zanchio notat Cro- cius genus actionum Diabolicarum: Quædam sunt tentationum, quibus malarum cogitationum afflatu corda hominum tentat: Alia energiarum, quibus, quo vult, tanquam captivos impellit. Illud genus obtinet tam in piis, quam in impiis. Hoc fere in impiis. Etsi enim in piis quoque agit, quando eos adoritur, tentat, & ad peccatum variis modis im- pellit, non tamen ubique & semper cum successu & absque resistentia. Resistunt enim sæpe fide, luctantur, ac sæpe eluctantur. At contumaces agitat, tanquam mancipia, pro lubitu suo. Addit autem NUNC in filiis incredulitatis illum operari, sive quod nunc adhuc operatio ejus vigeat in hoc seculo, tandem autem in fine mundi evacuanda sit, ut Antonius Scaynus notat, sive quod in rebellibus & non re- natis tunc habebat efficaciam, ne cessasse nunc plane operationem Satanæ Ephesii putent, & ut eo magis ab ἀπειθείᾳ & insidiis Satanæ, ad eam inducere satagentis caveant. Mortem ergo spiri- tualem probat, quoad Ephesios, Apostolus re- gnasse, quod in peccatis ambularint, non crasfio- ribus tantum, sed etiam illis, quibus sine scrupu- lo conscientiæ addicti erant, quales fuerunt su- perstitiones & cultus idololatrici. Ambulare enim est vitam instituere, studium & operam in aliquo ponere, & tum de bonis, qui cum DEO in Spiri- tu, in charitate & in lege DEI ambulare dicuntur, Gen. V. 22. 24. Psal. CXIX. 1. 3. Gal. V. 16. Joh. V. 2. & taliter vitam instituunt; tum de malis, qui se- cundum carnem ambulant Roman. VIII. 1. adhi- betur, qui extra Christum sunt. Hic igitur am- bulare in delictis & peccatis non est simpliciter peccare, sed vitam in iis citra DEI timorem se- cure traducere, atque se oblectare juxta cupidi- tates carnis, more eorum, qui animi causa de- ambulant. Αἰὼν significat vitæ tempus, ut ἄνερ ἀπ' αἰῶν@ νέ@ ὤλεο, ut & hoc loco, quasi ætas quæ- dam mundi intelligi posse videatur, & Græci τὸν αἰῶνα interpretantur τὸν ἐν ἁμαρτίαις διερραμμέ- νον βίον. Sic igitur, inquit, vixistis, quemadmo- dum seculum hujus mundi, id est homines in hac vita terrena consueverunt. Quæ sequitur expli- catio, seculi illius esse gubernatorem Diabolum, cui principatum quendam aëreum tribuit, ut vim & potentiam ejus esse ingentem intelligatur, ut hic Camerarius.

## 2:3
Vers. 3. Ἐν οἷς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνεστράφημέν ποτε) Lest the Gentiles should think that they alone were being burdened, he adds the Jews, who at that time ἐπιτοπολὺ [for the most part] were no better, as appears from the sacred scriptures and from Josephus. He says ἡμεῖς [we], however, although he himself had not been such a one (for he had lived a life, not indeed in any way to be compared with that which he led afterwards as a Christian, but yet more upright than the Jews of his own time, Phil. III. 6), using the figure of κοινώσεως [communion], through which we make those things which are odious common to ourselves. See Dan. IX. 5. Servius on that: And do we still doubt? And do you doubt? He mixed his own person. Such also is that of Homer: Τυδείδη τι παθόντε λελάσμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς [Tydides, what has happened to us that we have forgotten our furious strength?]. See also what we have said in VII. to the Romans. Ἐν οἷς [in which] namely, trespasses. See Coloss. III. 7. Ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν [in the desires of our flesh]) after the example of our ancestors, whose history is Num. XI. 34. Ποιοῦντες τὰ θελήματα τῆς σαρκὸς [doing the desires of the flesh]) indulging in those grosser actions, for instance, fornications, adulteries, and drunkenness. Καὶ τῶν διανοιῶν [and of the minds]) those more subtle vices, which are more ἐν τῷ θυμοειδεῖ [in the irascible part], and seem to approach more closely to virtues.

There is no reason why we should exclude Paul and admit the figure of κοινώσεως [communion], just as it is not to be admitted in Dan. IX. 5; where it must be denied that Daniel was confessing his own sins at the same time, as is proper in true repentance, 1. Reg. XIIX. 46, 1. Job. I. 9. And here the common misery of all before conversion is denoted, not just of the majority, nor only of that time, but of all times. Nor does that eulogy, that he was ἄμεμπτος κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ [blameless according to the righteousness which is in the law], Phil. III. 6, exempt Paul. For this must be accepted at least according to the mind of the Pharisees, who were content with the external obedience of the law, as is evident from Matth. V. 9; but not as regards the perfection in the law required by GOD. For according to that same law, Paul judged far otherwise. The law is spiritual, he says Rom. VII. 14, but I am carnal, sold under sin. And the Apostle notably says: Ἡμεῖς πάντες, WE ALL, so that he may express the common state, comparing all Jews without exception to the infidel Gentiles, because they were equally dead in sins. All, says Chrysostom; for it is not permitted to say that anyone is exempt. Jerome and Haymo understand the word ἐν οἷς [in which] as referring to sins: But it is more correctly taken as referring to infidel men, among whom the Prince of the world is effective, which name is more appropriate and agrees in kind. He says that he and the others once lived among the Gentiles in carnal desires, not so much by conjunction of place, for in this way the Jews were rather separated from the Gentiles, as by similarity of morals and life: By flesh understanding the whole corrupted nature, as Job. III. 7, Gal. V. 17, 19, 20. By ἐπιθυμίας [desires] its depraved longings, to which he also subjects depraved acts of desire, doing what was pleasing to the flesh and to the thoughts: Where we do not disapprove of the distinction of Grotius, that some are grosser, others more subtle, if it is correctly accepted: Just as according to Jerome and others, those are said to do the desires of the flesh who are given to slaughter, lust, avarice, and injustice: But those are said to do the desires of the mind who are subject to perfidy, heresy, and idolatry. For just as he professes himself to be equal to the Gentiles, not only by desiring but by doing depraved things, not only by not resisting desires, but even by perfecting the same willingly, and not without delight: So he does not deny that he committed those things which the corrupted nature, partly the grosser part embracing the animal, irascible, and concupiscible power, and all the affections of the flesh, was craving; and partly the more subtle, namely the mind, was dictating against the law of GOD. For although not all Jews were equally liable to blame, yet all were concluded under ἀπειθείᾳ, all were doing the will of the flesh and of their own thoughts before conversion. By flesh, says Blessed Balduinus, he understands the ἄλογον part of man, or the sensitive appetite; by thoughts, τὸ λογικὸν, or the reason: he teaches that both are corrupted by sin, and thus leaves nothing sound in the whole man. From these very evil effects, therefore, he shows that the Jews also are by nature dead in sins.

[And we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest] In the Manuscript, and we were by nature children. That this is not about original stain, the preceding parts sufficiently show, where the vices are described from which many of the ancients were immune. Thus in these books it is often a penalty; they are children of wrath who have deserved the penalty, just as children of death are those who have deserved death, 2 Sam. XII. 5, John XVII. 12, 2 Thess. II. 3. Φύσει, however, signifies not by opinion, but in reality, as in Gal. IV. 8, ἀληθῶς, genuinely, as Oecumenius has it here. Nor does Theophylact say otherwise. The Syriac has מליאית, fully, entirely. Just as Jerome also says it was accepted by the ancients. Such were most of the Israelites, such as Moses had predicted they would be in Deut. XXXII. 5, 20, and such as Isaiah describes in LVII. 5.

These things pertain entirely to original sin. Nor is Grotius's quibble of any value, that in the preceding verses vices are described from which many of the ancients were immune (which we have already said how it is to be admitted), since to actual sins, even if they are not common, a sin common to all can be added, namely, Original sin.

The word Φύσει is not incorrectly rendered by nature: nor is it taken otherwise in Gal. IV. 8 than as referring to one who is truly God by nature. To which Chrysostom also tends, explaining: Just as, if he is a son of man, he is by nature a man, so we also, just as the rest. Augustine and most Latins who followed him understand nature as birth, or, which amounts to the same thing, nature itself, not as it was created in the first man, but as it is received by individuals through being born, having become such through his transgression. Whence they hold this passage of the Apostle to be one of the principal ones by which it is taught that every man is born in original sin. The passages of Augustine are Sermon XIV on the words of the Apostle, Book I of Retractations, chapters X and XV, and passim against Pelagius. So also Prosper, Book I on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 18. And Fulgentius on faith to Peter, chapter 26, and Bede in his collection on this epistle, where he draws out several testimonies from Augustine. But also Jerome in his Commentary pursues this sense at length, as Estius observed here, who gives this explanation Furthermore he proves: Nor indeed does any other understanding fit better. First because in Greek there is no word that properly signifies sons, as if men who are irritating, that is, provoking the wrath of God, are called sons of wrath; just as a little before they were called sons of disobedience, that is, unbelieving men: But in Greek it is τέκνα, which word expresses birth or offspring more explicitly. Next because the order of the Greek text here is: And we were by nature sons of wrath, as if he were saying, sons, as regards nature, of wrath, that is, natural sons of wrath, so that the Apostle opposes sons by nature to those who are called sons by adoption, such as men become after birth. Add that the Apostle writes these things in the person of the Jews, most of whom boasted that they were a holy seed, as being sons of Abraham, as we have in Matt. III. John VIII. But they despised the Gentiles because they were born of idolatrous parents, as sinners and unclean from birth. Whence they also cursed that blind man as if he were a Gentile, saying, you were born entirely in sins John IX. certainly reckoning that they themselves were not born in sins. Therefore, to repress pride of this kind, the Apostle most aptly says in their person: We were by nature sons of wrath, even as the rest. Where one must supply from the previous part the universal sign all, so that the sense may be: And we Jews, just like the rest of men, whom we are accustomed to despise in comparison to ourselves on account of the holiness of our race, were all at one time subject to divine wrath, and indeed from the very origin of birth, by which we received nature from our parents. B. Balduinus urges the opposition. The word Φύσει is properly taken here, and is opposed to τῇ χάριτι, by nature to by grace: For just as in this verse we are called sons of wrath by nature, so afterwards in v. 8 we are said to be saved by grace. Therefore the same thing here as τῇ Φύσει is from birth, from the womb, we are subject to wrath and divine punishment on account of the sins in which we are born, not finally on account of actual offenses, just as it is written in Gal. II. 15, we are Jews by nature, gebohrne Juden, which word is opposed to proselytes, who were Jews not by nature but by custom. Thus also the Gentiles are said to do by nature the things that are of the law, that is, by natural power, not from habit, Rom. II. v. 14. Certainly the words sufficiently teach that sin is described here as common, not to most Jews, but to all. ἡμᾶς πάντες. And that it is common not only to all Jews, but also to the Gentiles, is hinted at by the following words, ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποί. For by these he wishes to teach that the Jews are no better than the Gentiles by communion of nature: Since all are equally sons of wrath by nature. And indeed not only the communion of punishment, but also of guilt is indicated. For the wrath of GOD, as being most just, does not fall except upon those who deserve it by their own fault. Nor does Hyperius note the emphasis here in vain: That all are bound to damnation by the highest right, just as sons are bound to their parents. Just as in Hebrew a son of death is called one who is guilty of a capital crime, a son of hell, one who has bound himself to the punishments of hell, Matt. XXV. 15, a son of perdition, one who has made himself subject to perdition, John XVII. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐν οἷς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνεστράφημέν ποτε) Ne nimirum onerari se putarent gentes, addit & Judæos, qui illo tem- pore ἐπιτοπολὺ nihilo meliores fuerant, ut ex sacris literis & ex Josepho apparet. Dicit autem ἡμεῖς, quanquam ipse talis non fuerat (vixerat enim vitam, non quidem ullo modo comparandam cum ea, quam duxit postea Christia- nus, sed tamen probiorem, quam sui temporis Judæi, Phil. III. 6.) utens figura κοινώσεως, per quam ea, quæ sunt odio- sa, nobis facimus communia. Vid. Dan. IX. 5. Servius ad illud: Et dubitamus adhuc? Et dubitas. Miscuit per- sonam suam. Tale & illud Homeri: Τυδείδη τι παθόντε λελάσμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς. Vide & quæ diximus in VII. ad Romanos. Ἐν οἷς nem- pe παραπτώμασι. Vide Coloss. III. 7. Ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν) ad exemplum Majo- rum nostrorum, quorum historia est Num. XI. 34. Ποιοῦντες τὰ θελήματα τῆς σαρκὸς) indulgentes actioni- bus illis crasfioribus, puta scortationibus, adulteriis & vinolentiis. Καὶ τῶν διανοιῶν) subtilioribus illis vitiis, quæ sunt ma- gis ἐν τῷ θυμοειδεῖ, & propius ad virtutes videntur ac- cedere.

Non est, quod excludamus Paulum, & figu- ram κοινώσεως admittamus, sicut nec Dan. IX. 5. ea admittenda; ubi sua simul peccata confiteri, ut par est in vera pœnitentia, Danielem negan- dum, 1. Reg. XIIX. 46. 1. Job. I. 9. Et hic commu- nis omnium denotatur miseria ante conversionem, non tantum plerorumque, nec illius tantum tem- poris, sed omnium temporum. Neque illud elo- gium, quod ἄμεμπτος κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ fuerit, Phil. III. 6. Paulum eximit. Nam hoc secundum mentem Pharisæorum saltem accipien- dum, qui externa legis obedientia contenti erant, ut ex Matth. V. 9. constat; non vero quoad per- fectionem in lege à DEO requisitam. Secundum eandem enim Paulus longe aliter judicavit. Lex spiritualis est, inquit Rom. VII. 14. ego vero car- nalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum. Et notanter Apostolus dicit: Ἡμεῖς πάντες, NOS OMNES, ut communem statum exprimat, comparans gen- tilibus infidelibus omnes sine exceptione Judæos, quod pariter in peccatis mortui fuerint. Omnes, inquit Chrysostomus; Non enim licet dicere, quod exemptus sit aliquis. Vocem ἐν οἷς de peccatis in- telligunt Hieronymus & Haymo: Sed rectius de hominibus infidelibus accipitur, inter quos Prin- ceps mundi efficax est, quod nomen propinquius est, & genere convenit. Inter gentiles autem se conversatos olim in carnalibus cupiditatibus di- cit, non tam conjunctione loci, sic enim separati potius erant à gentibus Judæi, quam similitudine morum & vitæ: Per carnem intelligens totam na- turam corruptam, ut Job. III.7. Gal. V. 17. 19. 20. Per ἐπιθυμίας prava ejus desideria, quibus actus ἐπιθυμίας etiam pravos subdit, facientes, quæ carni & co- gitationibus libebant: Ubi distinctionem Grotii non improbamus, quod alia crassiora, alia subti- liora, si recte accipiatur: Quemadmodum Hie- ronymo & aliis carnis θελήματα facere dicuntur, qui cædibus, libidini, avaritiæ, & injustitiæ dediti: Mentis autem θελήματα, qui perfidiæ, hæresi, ido- lolatriæ obnoxii sunt. Ut enim parem se profite- tur gentibus, non concupiscendo tantum, sed ope- rando prava, non modo non resistendo concu- piscentiis, sed easdem etiam perficiendo sponte, nec sine delectatione: Ita ea se patrasse non diffi- tetur, quæ naturæ corruptæ pars tum crassior po- tentiam animalem, irascibilem, concupiscibilem, omnesque carnis affectus complectens appetebat; tum subtilior, mens sc. contra legem DEI dicta- bat. Nam tametsi non omnes Judæi æqualiter cul- pæ obnoxii fuerint, omnes tamen sub ἀπειθείᾳ conclusi erant, omnes voluntatem carnis ac co- gitationum suarum faciebant ante conversionem. Per carnem, inquit B. Balduinus, intelligit partem hominis ἄλογον, seu appetitum sensitivum; per co- gitationes, τὸ λογικὸν, seu rationem: Utrumǫ, docet esse corruptum per peccatum, adeoque nihil sani in toto homine relinquit. Ex his ergo pessimis effectis osten- dit etiam Judæos in peccatis natura esse mortuos.

[Καὶ ἦμεν τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς, ὡς καὶ ὁι λοιποὶ) In Manu- scripto, καὶ ἦμεν φύσει τέκνα. Non agi hic de labe origina- ria, satis ostendunt præcedentia, ubi describuntur vitia, à quibus multi veterum fuere immunes. Ita in his libris sæ- pe est pœna, filii iræ sunt, qui pœnam meruere, sicut filii mortis, qui mortem, 2. Sam. XII. 5. Joh. XVII. 12. 2. Thess. II. 3. Φύσει autem significat non opinione, sed revera, ut Gal. IV. 8. ἀληθῶς, γνησίως, ut hic habet Oecumenius. Nec aliter Theophylactus. Syrus מליאית plene, omnino. Quomodo & Hieronymus ait à veteribus acceptum. Ta- les erant plerique Israëlitæ, quales fore prædixerat Moses Deut. XXXII. 5. 20. & quales describit Esa. LVII. 5.

Hæc omnino ad peccatum originale pertinent. Nec ullius valoris est argutia Grotii, quod in præ- cedentibus vitia describantur, à quibus multi ve- terum immunes fuerint, (quod quomodo admit- tendum sit, jam diximus) quum actualibus pecca- tis, etiamsi communia non sint, subjungi possit commune omnibus peccatum, nimirum Originale.

Vox Φύσει non inrecte naturâ redditur: nec ali- ter Gal. IV. 8. accipitur, quam de vero naturâ Deo. Quo etiam abit Chrysostomus explicans: Quomo- do, si sit filius hominis, natura est homo, ita nos quoque sicut & cæteri. Augustinus & plerique Latini eum se- quuti naturam intelligunt nativitatem, vel quod eo- dem redit, naturam ipsam, non qualis in primo ho- mine condita est, sed qualis, per ejus transgressionem facta, à singulis nascendo accipitur. Unde hunc Apo- stoli locum volunt unum esse ex præcipuis, quibus doceatur, hominem omnem nasci in peccato origi- nali. Augustini loca sunt serm. XIV. de verb. Apost. libr. I. retract. cap. X. & XV. & passim contra Pela- gium. Sic & Prosper libr. I. de vocat. gentium c. 18. Et Fulgentius de fide ad Petrum cap. 26. & Beda in collect. super hanc epistolam, ubi ex Augustino com- plura testimonia depromit. Sed & Hieronymus in Comment. sensum hunc late prosequitur, ut obser- vavit hic Estius, qui hanc explicationem datam porro probat : Nec vero alius intellectus magis congruit. Primum quia in Græco non est vocabu- lum, quod proprie filios significet, tanquam filii iræ dicantur homines irritantes, id est, iram Dei pro- vocantes ; sicut paulo ante dicti sunt filii diffiden- tiæ, id est, homines increduli: Sed Græce est τέκνα, quæ vox nativitatem seu partum expressius impor- tat. Deinde quia Græci textus hic est ordo: Et era- mus filii natura iræ, quasi dicat, filii, quod ad na- turam, iræ, id est, filii naturales iræ, ut filios natu- ra opponat Apostolus iis, qui filii dicuntur adoptio- ne, quales fiunt homines post nativitatem. Adde quod Apostolus hæc scribit in persona Judæorum, quorum plerique jactabant se esse semen sanctum, utpote filios Abrahæ, sicut habemus Matth. III. Joh. VIII. Gentiles vero quod ex parentibus idololatris essent progeniti, tanquam ex nativitate peccatores & immundos aspernabantur. Unde & illi cæco quasi gentili maledicebant, dicentes, in peccatis natus es totus Joh. IX. utique reputantes, sese non esse natos in peccatis. Igitur ad hujusmodi fastum reprimendum aptissime dicit in eorum persona Apostolus: Era- mus natura filii iræ, sicut & cæteri. Ubi supplen- dum ex superiori parte signum universale omnes, ut sensus sit: Et nos Judæi perinde ut cæteri homi- nes, quos præ nobis contemnere solemus ob generis nostri sanctitatem, omnes eramus aliquando iræ di- vinæ obnoxii, & quidem ex ipsa nativitatis origine, qua naturam à parentibus accepimus. B. Baldui- nus urget oppositionem. Vox Φύσει proprie hic ac- cipitur, & opponitur τῇ χάριτι, natura gratiæ: Nam quemadmodum hoc versiculo dicimur natura filii iræ, ita postea v. 8. dicimur gratia salvari. Proin- do idem est hic τῇ Φύσει ac à nativitate, ab utero, sumus iræ pœnæque divinæ obnoxii propter peccata, in quibus nascimur, non demum ob actualia deli- cta, quemadmodum Gal. II. 15. scribitur, nos Φύσει Judæi sumus, gebohrne Juden, quæ vox opponitur proselytis, qui Judæi erant non Φύσει sed τῷ ἔθει. Sic etiam gentes τῇ Φύσει dicuntur facere, quæ legis sunt, hoc est, naturali vi, non ex assuefactione, Rom. II. v. 14. Sane peccatum hic commune, non ple- risque Judæis, sed omnibus, describi, verba satis docent. ἡμᾶς πάντες. Nec Judæis tantum omni- bus, sed etiam gentibus commune esse, verbis se- quentibus innuitur, ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποί. His enim do- cere vult, Judæos naturæ communione nihilo meliores esse gentibus: Quum omnes ex æquo sint filii iræ τῇ Φύσει. Nec vero pœnæ tantum commu- nio, sed etiam culpæ indicata. Non enim cadit ira DEI, utpote justissimi, nisi in eos, qui culpa sua eam merentur. Neque temere emphasin Hyperius hic notat: Summo jure damnationi obstrictos omnes esse, perinde atque filii obstricti sunt pa- rentibus. Sicut Ebræis filius mortis dicitur, qui capitalis criminis reus, filius gehennæ, qui sese pœnis gehennæ obstrinxit, Matth. XXV. 15. filius perditionis, qui perditioni se obnoxium fecit, Job. XVII. 12.

## 2:4
V. 4. But God, being rich in mercy) רב־חסד, Ex. XXXIV. 7.

Because of the great love with which he loved us) us, that is, the whole human race. This is that antecedent love, about which Rom. V. 8. 1 John IV. 10.

And when we were dead in trespasses he made us alive together with Christ) We spoke above about those two particles δὲ and καὶ, which are redundant here. He made us live with Christ, that is, after the example of Christ. To make alive is shadowed forth from the Hebrew החיה, which we have in Deut. XXXII. 39. and elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 4. ὁ δὲ Θεὸς πλύσιος ὣν ἐν ἐλέει) רב־חסד, Ex. XXXIV. 7.

Διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀγάπην ἧν ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς) nos, id est, to- tum humanum genus. Hæc est dilectio illa antecedens, de qua Rom. V. 8. 1. Joh. IV. 10.

Καὶ ὄντας ἡμᾶς νεκρὺς τοῖς παραπτώμασι συνεζωοποίησε τῷ χρισῷ) De istis duabus particulis δὲ & καὶ, quæ hic πλεο- νάζεσι, diximus supra. Fecit nos vivere cum Christo, id est, ad exemplum Christi. Ζωοποιεῖν adumbratum ex E- bræ החיה, quod habemus Deut. XXXII. 39. & alibi.

## 2:5
By grace you have been saved) Many interpreters take it as a parenthesis. But Chrysostom does not seem to have read that in this place, and it can be believed that it was placed there by the haste of the writer, from that which is below in verse 8.

Latin:

Χάριτί ἐστε σεσωσμένοι) Sumunt multi interpretes, ut παρένθεσιν. Sed Chrysostomus istud hoc loco non videtur legisse, & credi potest festinatione scriptoris positum, ex eo, quod est infra 8.

## 2:6
And raised us up together) namely by hope, as is said in Rom. VIII. 24. Therefore he raised Christ, so that we might know that the same thing will happen to us.

And made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus) We also therefore shall reign, Matt. XIX. 21. XX. 21. 2 Tim. II. 11. Into whom therefore? It is difficult to say. It is a mystery, as Chrysostom says here. The thing, however, is true. By the firstfruits the whole collection of crops is sanctified. Thus Christ obtained possession of heaven, not for himself only, but also for us. A right to a thing, as we also said above, often takes the name of the thing.

Those particles are by no means redundant. The Apostle has said thus far what kind of people Paul and all the Jews were before conversion. But now he teaches what kind they are by the grace of Christ: That namely when they were dead equally in sins, like the Gentiles, they were recalled to life through Christ, made alive together with him; which is not after the example of Christ. For in this way no one can be made alive with Christ; who was put to death in the flesh, or human nature, and made alive in the Spirit, or by the power of the divine nature, 1 Pet. III. 18. but by the merit of Christ: who was delivered up for our sins, and raised again for our justification, Rom. IV. 25. Concerning which compare Hos. VI. 2. For we are made partakers of this merit through faith, therefore it is added by grace you have been saved. We have not been saved, he says, but so that he may conclude the Ephesians at the same time, YOU have been saved, just as he had said above concerning himself and all the faithful, he chose us, and predestined us to adoption, chap. I. 4. 5. and v. 11. Estius: This sudden change of person seems to be attributable to the affection of the Apostle himself toward the Ephesians, to whom, as his disciples, he wished the benefit of the grace of God to be singularly commended. Whence there is no reason why we should suspect those words to have been placed here from v. 8 by the haste of the writer. The codices agree, nor is some universal corruption to be admitted. Everything also holds together more correctly when those things are added: For the application of merit was not to be neglected, especially because it is subjoined, and he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. He has not only established us with Christ in heavenly goods, but also in Christ, which the latter brings in faith, so that there may be joined both the merit, by the power of which we have been made alive, resurrected, and established in the heavenly places with Christ, and the application of the same through faith, through which we are in Christ and are saved, and are made partakers of his vivification, resurrection, and exaltation to heavenly glory, not only when we are spiritually made alive here, rise from the death of sin, and enjoy his heavenly benefits, just as GOD has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, Eph. I. 3. But also when by the power of the same merit we shall be made alive and resurrected on the last day to eternal virtue, and shall be established in the heavenly places in the other age through and on account of Christ, just as he himself has been made alive and resurrected in the heavenly places, Eph. I. 20. Thus, therefore, he looks back at the same time to the antecedents, which the blessed Hunnius also observed, so that he may declare that we also become partakers of the same benefit in our own way and measure, saying, he made us alive together with Christ, that is, he brought us back to a new spiritual life, both to be led before him in this age in righteousness and holiness, and also to the other eternal life, to which he will also one day raise our bodies.

It does not please Crocius that these should be taken either with certain ones among Theophylact concerning spiritual resurrection, or with Theodoret and Augustine concerning the hope of resurrection: He gives the reason, because our resurrection was certain before Christ was resurrected. He wishes, therefore, with Chrysostom, Theophylact, Beza, Zanchius, and Musculus, that we have been raised in Christ, as members in the head, and as when the firstfruits were blessed in ancient times, the remaining crops, of which they were the firstfruits, were blessed at the same time, and that not by potentiality, not by hope, but in act and in reality. Because in the firstfruits all the remaining fruits of the same kind were contained. But that is true not actually and in reality, but by divine intention and estimation. Thus in Adam, when he was being blessed for the propagation of his kind, all men were being blessed who were contained in him, not actually and in reality, but by potentiality and divine estimation: That God, by blessing him, blessed at the same time those who would arise from him. Let this be applied to Christ, that he being raised, we also are all raised: Yet the nerve is not yet fully touched. For that which is the chief point is passed over. That indeed is the merit of Christ, which the Apostle indicates, 1 Cor. XV. 22. For as in Adam we all die, as far as his demerit is concerned; because in one we all sinned, Rom. V. 12. So in Christ we are all made alive, as regards the merit of the same, because he merited life for us all, when he gave his flesh for the life of the whole world, John VI. 51. For that one died for all, in divine estimation is the same as if we all had died, 2 Cor. V. 19. And what do those things of Crocius mean for themselves: We still crawl on the ground, we suffer, we groan; but in our head we already reign in heaven, not by hope, but actually. Does not the Apostle himself say, τῇ γὰρ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν, Rom. VIII. 24. & 2 Cor. IV. 8. you already (by your persuasion) reign: And would that you did reign! Nay, our head actually reigns: But we at least reign by hope. However, we are said to be placed in Christ in the heavens because of the truth of the merit and the certainty of the hope. It certainly cannot be explained how we already actually reign, unless we wish to say with the Praetorians and other fanatics that we are already actually in the heavens. Crocius says that here there is not only a reason of communion, because our flesh, which Christ assumed in the unity of his person, reigns, but also because we are intimately joined to him as members, by the bond of election and of the Spirit; of election, because we were chosen in him to glory: of the Spirit, because having received his Spirit we are flesh of his flesh, bone of his bones. But election was made from eternity. Thus, therefore, we are joined to him from eternity by the bond of election as members, placed with him actually and in reality in the heavens! Thus also it must be that Christ was from eternity actually and in reality placed in the heavens, and we with him. However, believers are indeed intimately joined to him by the bond of the Spirit; but faith, and that conjunction through faith, presupposes the merit of Christ. Therefore, that it may be more fully explained how we have been made alive with Christ, raised with Christ, and established in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, it must be said that this was done both by reason of merit, because he being our Mediator and Redeemer made alive, raised, and placed in the heavenly places, we have been made alive with him, and raised with him, and placed with him in the heavenly places. Because he himself as our Mediator and Redeemer merited that for us, when he himself as our vessel and sponsor was delivered into death for us, which is the same as if we had undergone death: And therefore he being raised from death, we have been raised, not otherwise than when satisfaction has been rendered by a sponsor, not only is he free, but also he for whom he had given himself as sponsor: and then by reason of application, because we apprehend by faith and apply to ourselves the merit and satisfaction of Christ, and by that reason we are actually spiritually made alive, and are awakened from the death of sin, so that we may have our πολίτευμα in the heavens, being also to be made alive and raised one day to another heavenly life, so that we may sit with Christ ἐν ἐπουρανίοις, and reign, Matt. XIX. 28. Luke XXIII. 30. Rom. VIII. 17. 2 Tim. II. 12. Apoc. III. 21. c. XXII. 5. Conf. Col. II. 12. cap. III. 1. 2.

If you say that a double sense is thus introduced, when we are said to be made alive, raised, and established in the heavenly places with Christ, whether we explain it concerning the merit, by which life, resurrection, and heaven are procured for us by Christ, when he himself was made alive, raised, and placed in the heavens; for thus those things are said of Christ in one way, and of us in another by the same word: Or concerning the fruit and the explanation of the merit, which two things, being very distinct, if they are expressed at the same time by the same words, an even greater ambiguity seems to arise. I reply: That the preposition σὺν can be referred to the believers from the Gentiles, because these were made alive together with the believing Jews in Christ, or so that they may live to Christ, or that τῷ χριστῷ is the same by the ellipsis of the preposition as v. sq. ἐν χριστῷ, or if because of the regard to verse 20 of the preceding chapter. the preposition σὺν is referred to Christ, and is joined with τῷ χριστῷ, we shall be said to be made alive with him, not because we have been made alive in the same manner as he; for he did not need spiritual vivification, because he was never in spiritual death: But because we have been made alive as equally or as truly as he, even if by a different manner; or it must be said that Christ being made alive to heavenly life, we also have been made alive with him to heavenly life, as far as merit is concerned, and in him as our Redeemer, and also to a certain hope, as in our head. And thus also we have been raised with Christ, not when we were awakened from spiritual death, but because as regards merit and certain hope we have been raised with Christ and in Christ to eternal life, he himself having been raised to life, which is especially clear from the last benefit added. For how are we placed in the heavenly places with Christ in this kingdom of grace, who has been exalted into glory? Certainly not as regards the actual possession of glory. For thus the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of glory would be confused: But as regards the merit and the hope of heavenly blessedness through Christ, and in Christ, which will be completed in us as regards the soul at the end of life, as regards the soul with the body at the end of the age, when we are to reign with Christ for ages. Which sense the blessed Balduinus also prefers, even if he explains vivification concerning regeneration and glorification: He speaks of a future thing as if it were past because of the certainty. For we have not yet been raised with Christ, we have not yet been made participants of his glorious kingdom, but we have the hope of all those things, and a hope that is in every way certain and infallible: Because the regenerated adhere to Christ, as members to their head, from whom they are not even in death severed. When therefore the Father raised up the Son, and set him at the right hand of his Majesty, by that very act he also raised up those who believe in the Son, and exalted them to the glory of his Son according to their measure, because these things happened to the members in their head, which they themselves also in their own time, after the tabernacle of mortality has been laid aside, shall be glorified in eternal life, as it is written: If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; 2 Tim. II. 12. Augustine explains this verse in the same sense in book 11 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 8. He already sits in the heavens, not yet we, but because we hold by certain hope what is to come, he said that we sit together in the heavens, not yet in ourselves, but already in him, etc. Theophylact thinks that those words, he raised us up together, are not to be understood of the resurrection, but of regeneration and vivification through baptism. But the former opinion is better. Grotius asks over whom we are to reign, and says that it is difficult to say, and does not explain it. But Scripture teaches that we shall reign over spiritual enemies, over the world and the devils. For the Elect shall judge these, 1 Cor. VI. 2, 3, and Satan is crushed under the feet of the elect, Rom. XVI. 20.

Moreover, that the application of the fruit of merit may be clearer, he says not only that we have been placed with Christ in the heavenly places in Christ. But he also adds: By grace you have been saved: Which the blessed Hunnius wishes to add, so that the difference may be shown between Christ's resurrection and our own. Which difference consists in this, that Christ indeed merited to be raised from the dead to life, as it is written, for that his soul labored he shall see the fruit, with which he shall be satisfied. For he did not die on account of his own sins, since he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. We, however, do not have it from our own merit, but as the Apostle teaches through that parenthesis, by grace. Which words Beza and Piscator, with Ambrosiaster and the Vulgate interpreter, having added the pronoun by whose grace you have been saved, (after the example of 1 Pet. 1:14, 1 John 3:12) prefer to supply, rather than to admit a parenthesis with the blessed Luther and his Calvin, in which matter we think little is at stake, provided the sense itself is agreed upon.

In that merit, therefore, the riches of divine mercy are judged. He is rich in mercy, first intensively, because its riches are immense: For God's mercy is as great as He Himself is, Sirach 2:23; then extensively, because His mercy extends itself to all, John 3:16, Prov. 11:32; then duratively, because it reaches out to eternity and has no end. He is rich in mercy, because it is purely gratuitous toward the undeserving, wonderfully gracious toward those who deserve to be damned, joined with great μακροθυμίᾳ (long-suffering) toward those subject to many infirmities, and is ἀμεταμέλητος (without repentance), Rom. 2:4, ch. 11:29. He made us alive, not because of any reason of merit, but when we were dead in sins, and had deserved nothing but wrath and eternal condemnation. And therefore the προηγουμένη (primary) cause was solely the love of GOD, and indeed the great love with which He loved us, which the Son of GOD Himself celebrates in John 3:16 and the Apostle in Romans 5:8. Although indeed this rich mercy, both regarding the love of the Father and regarding the merit of vivification in Christ, extends itself to all, John 3:16, 1 John 4:16, ch. 2:2. Regarding the fruit, however, it belongs specially to the faithful, who are saved by the grace of God, which happens through faith. Deprived of that, therefore, they do not enjoy the love of GOD and the vivification of Christ unto salvation.

Latin:

Καὶ συνήγειρε) nempe spe, ut dicitur Rom. VIII. 24. Ideo Christum excitavit, ut sciremus, idem nobis eventurum.

Καὶ συνεκάθισεν ἐν τοῖς ἐρανίοις ἐν χρισῷ ἰησῦ) Etiam nos ergo regnabimus, Matth. XIX. 21. XX. 21. 2. Tim. II. 11. In quos ergo? Difficile dictu. Mysterium est, ut ait hic Chrysostomus. Res tamen vera. Per ἀπαρχὰς sanctificatur tota frugum congeries. Sic Christus cœli possessionem ad- eptus est, non pro se tantum, sed & pro nobis. Jus ad rem, ut & supra diximus, sæpe rei nomen accipit.

Particulæ illæ minime πλεονάζυσι. Quales ante conversionem Paulus & universi Judæi fuerint, dixit hactenus Apostolus. Jam vero quales sint gratia Christi docet: Quod nempe cum mortui essent æque in peccatis, ut gentes, in vitam revo- cati sint per Christum, cum ipso convivificati; quod non est ad exemplum Christi. Sic enim ne- mo vivificari potest cum Christo; qui mortifica- tus carne, vel humana natura, vivificatus est Spi- ritu, vel divina naturæ virtute, 1. Petr. III. 18. sed merito Christi: qui traditus est propter peccata no- stra, resuscitatus autem propter justitiam nostram, Rom. IV. 25. Quo de conf. Os. VI. 2. Meriti enim hujus participes reddimur per fidem, idcirco ad- ditur gratiâ salvi facti estis. Non salvi facti sumus, inquit, sed ut concludat simul Ephesios, salvi facti ESTIS, uti de sese & omnibus fidelibus supra dixe- rat, elegit nos, & prædestinavit nos ad ὑοθεσίαν, cap. I. 4. 5. & v. 11. Estius: Hæc repentina personæ mutatio tribuenda videtur affectui ipsius Apostoli erga Ephesios, quibus, ut discipulis suis, singulariter commendatum esse voluit beneficium gratiæ Dei. Unde causa nulla est, cur illa verba festinatione scriptoris hic è v. 8. posita suspicemur. Conso- nant codices, nec admittenda est universalis quæ- dam corruptela. Rectius etiam omnia se habent, cum illa adduntur: Nam applicatio meriti non erat negligenda, imprimis quia subjungitur, καὶ συνήγειρε καὶ συνεκάθισεν ἐν ἐρανίοις ἐν Χρισῷ Ἰησῦ. Non tantum cum Christo in cœlestibus bonis nos constituit, sed etiam in Christo, quod posterius fidem infert, ut conjungatur tum meritum, vi cu- jus cum Christo vivificati, resuscitati, constituti in cœlestibus sumus, tum applicatio ejusdem per fidem, per quam in Christo sumus & salvamur, & participes reddimur vivificationis, resuscitatio- nis, & exaltationis ejus ad cœlestem gloriam, non tantum cum spiritualiter hic vivificamur, à morte peccati resurgimus, & beneficiis ejus cœlestibus fruimur, sicut in Christo nos DEUS benedixit omni ἐυλογίᾳ πνευματικῇ ἐν τοῖς ἐπερανίοις, Eph. I. 3. Sed etiam cum ejusdem meriti virtute vivi- ficabimur & resuscitabimur in novissimo die ad æternam virtutem, & constituemur ἐν ἐπερανίοις in altero seculo per & propter Christum, quem- admodum ipse vivificatus & resuscitatus est ἐν τοῖς ἐπερανίοις, Eph. I. 20. Ita ergo respicit simul ad antecedentia, quod etiam observavit B. Hunnius, ut declaret nos ejusdem beneficii suo quodam modo & mensura etiam consortes fieri, convivi- ficavit nos, inquiens, cum Christo, hoc est, reduxit ad novam spiritualem vitam, tum in hoc seculo co- ram illo ducendam in justitia & sanctitate, tum et- iam ad vitam æternam alteram, ad quam etiam corpora nostra aliquando suscitabit.

Crocio non placet, ut hæc sive cum quibusdam apud Theophylactum de spirituali excitatione, sive cum Theodoreto & Augustino de spe resurrectio- nis accipiantur: Rationem dat, quia certa fuit no- stri resuscitatio, priusquam Christus resuscitaretur. Vult ergo cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Beza, Zanchio & Musculo nos excitatos esse in Christo, ut in capite membra, & uti in primitiis cum olim benedicerentur, simul benedicebantur reliquæ fru- ges, quarum primitiæ erant, idque non potentia, non spe, sed actu & reipsa. Quia in primitiis continebantur omnes reliquæ ejusdem generis fruges. Id verò etiam non actu & reipsa sed intentione ac æstimatione divina. Ita in Adamo, cum benedicê- retur ad propagationem generis sui, benedice- bantur omnes homines, qui continebantur in ipso non actu & reipsa, sed potentia & æstimatione di- vina: Quod Deus illi benedicendo benedixerit simul ex illo orituris. Applicetur hoc ad Chri- stum, quod excitato ipso etiam nos excitati omnes simus: Nondum tamen nervus plene tangitur. Nam quod præcipuum est, præteritur. Id verò est Christi meritum, quod indicat Apostolus, 1. Cor. XV. 22. Ut enim in Adamo omnes morimur, quan- tùm ad ejus demeritum; quia in uno peccavimus omnes Rom. V. 12. Ita in Christo omnes vivificamur, quoad meritum ejusdem, quia meruit nobis o- mnibus vitam, cum carnem suam dedit pro totius mundi vita, Joh. VI. 51. Quod enim unus pro omni- bus mortuus est, in æstimatione divina perinde est, ac si omnes mortui essemus, 2. Cor. V. 19. Et quid illa Crocii sibi volunt: In nobis adhuc humi repi- mus, patimur, gemimus; at in capite jam regnamus in cælo, non spe, sed actu. Nonne Apostolus ipse, τῇ γὰρ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν, Rom. XII. 24. & 2. Cor. IV. 8. vos jam (persuasione vestra) regnatis: Atque utinam regnaretis! Imo caput nostrum actu regnat: Nos verò saltem spe regnamus. Collocati autem in Christo in cælis dicimur ob meriti veritatem & spei certitudinem. Explicari certe non potest, quomodo jam actu regnemus, nisi cum Prætorio, aliisque fanaticis, nos jam actu in cælis esse dicere velimus. Dicit Crocius, hic non tantum commu- nionis rationem esse, quia caro nostra, quam Chri- stus in persona unitatem assumpsit, regnat, sed etiam, quia nos illi tanquam membra intime juncti sumus, nexu electionis & spiritus; Electionis, quia in ipso electi ad gloriam: Spiritus, quia accepto ejus Spiri- tu sumus caro de carne ejus, os de ossibus ejus. Sed electio ab æterno facta. Ita ergo nos electionis nexu ab æterno ipsi juncti tanquam membra, cum illo collocati actu & reipsa in cælis! Ita & Chri- stum ab æterno in cælis actu & reipsa collo- catum fuisse oportet, & nos cum ipso. Nexu au- tem Spiritus intime quidem ipsi junguntur fide- les; sed fides, & illa per fidem conjunctio præ- supponit meritum Christi. Ut ergo plenius ex- plicetur, quomodo cum Christo vivificati, cum Christo resuscitati, cum Christo in cælestibus constituti simus in Christo Jesu, dicendum, quod id factum sit tum ratione meriti, quod ipso ceu Mediatore & Redemptore nostro vivificato, re- suscitato & in cælestibus collocato nos vivifica- ti cum ipso simus, & resuscitati cum ipso, & in cæ- lestibus cum ipso collocati. Quia ipse nobis ceu Mediator & Redemptor noster id promeruit, cum ipse tanquam vas, & sponsor noster pro nobis in mortem traditus est, quod perinde est, ac si nos mortem subi决策issemus: Ideoque resuscitato ipso è morte nos resuscitati sumus, non secus, atque præ- stita satisfactione à sponsore, non solum hic liber est, sed etiam ille, cujus sponsorem se dederat: tum ratione applicationis, quod fide apprehenda- mus, nobisque applicemus meritum Christi & satisfactionem, atque ea ratione actu spiritualiter vivificamur, & à morte peccati excitamur, ut πο- λίτευμα nostrum in cælis habeamus, vivificandi etiam ac resuscitandi olim ad alteram cælestem vitam, ut cum Christo ἐν ἐπουρανίοις consideamus, & regnemus Matth. XIX. 28. Luc. XXIII. 30. Ro- man. IIX. 17. 2. Tim. II. 12. Apoc. III. 23. c. XXII. 5. Conf. Col. II. 12. cap. III. 1. 2.

Si dicas, ita geminum sensum invehi, cum vivi- ficati, refuscitati, & in cælestibus constituti cum Christo dicimur, sive de merito explicemus, quo nobis vita, resuscitatio, & cœlum parta sunt à Christo, cum ipse vivificatus, resuscitatus & in cœlis collocatus est; Sic enim aliter illa de Chri- sto, aliter de nobis dicuntur eadem voce: Sive de fructu & meriti explicatione, quæ duo mul- tum distincta, si simul iisdem vocibus exprimun- tur, adhuc major oriri videtur ambiguitas. Resp. Posse Præpositionem σὺν referri ad fideles è gen- tibus, quod hi juxta cum Judæis fidelibus vivi- ficati sint Christo, vel ut Christo vivant, aut ut τῷ χριστῷ idem sit per ellipsin Præpositionis, quod v. sq. ἐν χριστῷ, aut si ob respectum ad vers. 20. capitis præced. referatur Præpositio σὺν ad Chri- stum, & conjungatur cum τῷ χριστῷ, nos vivi- ficati cum ipso dicemur, non quod eadem ratio- ne ut ipse vivificati simus; ipse enim spirituali vivificatione non indiguit, quia in morte spiri- tuali nunquam fuit: Sed quod æque vel tam ve- re ut ipse, vivificati simus, etsi dispari ratione; vel dicendum, quod Christo ad vitam cælestem vivificato nos ad vitam cælestem cum ipso etiam vivificati simus, quantum ad meritum, & in ipso ut Redemptore, nec non ad spem certam, ut in ca- pite nostro. Atque ita etiam cum Christo resusci- tati sumus, non cum à morte spirituali excitati, sed quod quoad meritum & spem certam cum Christo & in Christo resuscitati simus ad æter- nam vitam ipso ad vitam resuscitato, quod ex ad- dito postremo beneficio imprimis luculentum est. Nam quomodo collocati in cælestibus su- mus cum Christo in hoc regno gratiæ, qui in gloriam exaltatus est? Certe non quoad gloriæ possessionem actualem. Ita enim confunderetur regnum gratiæ & regnum gloriæ: Sed quoad me- ritum & spem beatitudinis cælestis per Christum, & in Christo, quæ complebitur in nobis quoad animam in fine vitæ, quoad animam cum corpo- re in fine sæculi, cum regnaturi sumus cum Chri- sto in secula. Quem sensum præfert etiam B. Bal- duinus, etsi vivificationem de regeneratione & glorificatione exponat: Loquitur de re futura, tanquam de præterita ob certitudinem. Nondum enim cum Christo resuscitati sumus, nondum glo- riosi sui regni participes facti, sed spem eorum omni- um habemus, spem autem undiquaque certam & infallibilem: Quia regenerati adhærent Christo, ut membra capiti suo, à quo ne quidem in morte sunt divulsa. Cum ergo Pater resuscitavit Filium, & ad dextram Majestatis suæ constituit, eo ipso et- iam credentes in Filium resuscitavit, & ad gloriam Filii sui pro modulo suo evexit, quia in capite suo membris ista contigerunt, quæ & ipsa suo tempore post depositum mortalitatis tabernaculum in vita æterna glorificabuntur, sicut scriptum est: Si com- mortui sumus, & convivemus, si sustinemus, & conregnabimus; 2. Tim. II. 12. In eundem sensum hunc versiculum exponit Augustinus libr. 11. con- tra Faustum Manich. cap. 8. In cælestibus jam se- det, non autem nos, sed quia spe certa quod futurum est, jam tenemus, simul sedere nos dixit in cælesti- bus, nondum in nobis, sed jam in illo &c. Theophy- lactus existimat, illa verba, consuscitavit nos, non de resurrectione accipienda esse, sed de regeneratio- ne & vivificatione per baptisma. Sed prior senten- tia melior est. Quærit Grotius, in quos regnaturi simus, idque difficile dictu ait, neque explicat. Sed scriptura docet, nos in hostes spirituales regnatu- ros, in mundum & Diabolos. Hos enim Electi judicabunt, 1. Cor. VI. 2. 3. & sub pedibus electo- rum conteritur Satanas, Rom. XVI. 20.

Cæterum ut applicatio fructus meriti luculen- tior sit, non tantum ait, nos cum Christo colloca- tos esse in supercœlestibus in Christo. Sed etiam subjungit: Gratia salvati estis: Quod B. Hunnius addi vult, ut differentia ostendatur inter Christi resuscitationem & nostram. Quæ differentia in eo consistit, quod Christus quidem ex mortuis ad vitam resuscitari meruit, sicut scriptum est, pro eo, quod laboravit anima ejus videbit fructum, quo saturabitur. Neque enim ob sua peccata est mortuus, cum iniquitatem non fecerit, nec dolus in ore ejus sit repertus. Nos vero non habemus ex merito nostro, sed ut per istam parenthesin docet Apostolus, per gratiam. Quæ verba Beza & Pi- scator cum Ambrosiaftro, & Vulgato interprete ad- dito Pronomine cujus gratia salvati estis, (ad exemplum 1. Petr. I. 14. 1. Joh. III. 12.) supplere malunt, quam cum B. Luthero, & Calvino suo parenthesin admittere, qua in re parum situm esse arbitramur, dummodo de sensu ipso constet.

In eo ergo merito dijudicantur divitiæ mi- sericordiæ divinæ. Dives est misericordia, tum intensive, quia divitiæ illius immensæ sunt: Tan- ta enim Dei misericordia, quantus ipse, Sirac. II. 23. tum extensive, quia ad omnes sese extendit ejus misericordia, Joh. III. 16. Prov. XI. 32. tum du- rative, quia ad æternitatem se porrigit, nec ul- lum finem habet. Dives est misericordia, quia erga immeritos mere gratuita, erga merito da- mnandos, mirabiliter gratiosa, erga multis infir- mitatibus obnoxios cum magna μακροθυμίᾳ con- juncta, & ἀμεταμέλητος est, Rom. II. 4. cap. XI. 29. Vivificavit nos, non quod id ulla ratione me- riti, sed quum in peccatis essemus mortui, nec nisi iram & condemnationem æternam prome- riti. Ideoque causa προηγουμένη fuit unice chari- tas DEI, & quidem magna charitas, qua dile- xit nos, quam ipse Filius DEI celebrat Joh. III. 16. & Apostolus, Roman. V. 8. Quanquam vero hæc dives misericordia, tum quoad dilectionem Patris, tum quoad vivificationis in Christo meritum ad omnes sese porrigat, Johan. III. 16. 1. Johan. IV. 16. cap. II. 2. Quoad fructum tamen fidelibus specialiter convenit, qui gratia Dei servantur, quod per fidem fit. Ea ergo destituti non fruun- tur charitate DEI, & vivificatione Christi ad salutem.

## 2:7
Verse 7. That He might show in the ages to come the exceeding riches of His grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus) what we now obtain by hope and by right, we shall then obtain in the thing itself. Αἰῶνες οἱ ἐπερχόμενοι (the ages to come), עולם הבא (the world to come), the time after the resurrection. Αἰὼν ὁ μέλλων (the age to come) above 1:21, Heb. 6:5. πλοῦτος χάριτος (riches of grace) as above 1:8. And for the sake of emphasis he added ὑπερβάλλοντα (exceeding), as 2 Cor. 3:10, 9:14, above 1:17, below 3:19. And after χάριτος (grace) he added ἐν χρηστότητι (in kindness), so that by this abundance of words he might signify the magnitude of the benefit. Thus Isaiah 63:7 placed רב טוב (abundant good) and רחמין (mercies) and again רב חסדיו (abundant in His mercies). Again he adds ἐν χριστῷ (in Christ), so that we may know that after GOD we owe all these things to Christ. In the manuscript it is ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος, as if πλοῦτος were a neuter of the third declension. And so it is accustomed to be placed perpetually in that book, πλοῦτος with neuter adjectives.

Not concerning the ages of the other life, or after the resurrection, but concerning the ages of this world following, most Papists with Lombard and Thomas explain these things, with the Calvinists commonly agreeing: But we easily accede here to Grotius, whom Chrysostom, Theodoret, Ambrose, Theophylact, Haymo, and Erasmus also favor, interpreting these things concerning the future age, or the other life. For then that ἔνδειξις (showing) will be most clear: then we shall use the ὑπερβάλλοντα πλοῦτον (exceeding riches) of His grace as if with our very eyes, and we shall touch them with our hands; and this is the ultimate end of our spiritual vivification, concerning which the Apostle spoke just now, and in it consists our salvation, concerning which the following verse speaks. Nor indeed, if that showing is understood which is made in the kingdom of grace, can this be conveniently restricted to the ages succeeding the resurrection of Christ, or the times of the New Testament, since the riches of grace in Christ were also shown to the ancient faithful, who obtained salvation by no other grace, Acts 15:11. In Paul indeed, πρώτῳ ἐνδείξηται ἰησοῦς χριστὸς τὴν πᾶσαν μακροθυμίαν πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν τῶν μελλόντων πιστεύειν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (that in me first Jesus Christ might show all long-suffering for a pattern to them who should believe on Him to life everlasting), 1 Tim. 1:16, which passage Crocius says responds beautifully to this one of ours: But there it is a matter of the singular example of Paul, which is deservedly set before others to excite faith in the long-suffering of GOD; here, however, a common benefit is celebrated, which has come to all, because we have all been made alive in Christ. Therefore, here ἐνδείκνυσθαι (to show) is not to provide a spectacle and propose an example: But to show the riches of grace in the other age to those same ones by whom life was acquired, just as the illustrious ἔνδειξις (showing) or demonstration of justice is that which is exhibited in our justification, through the propitiation of Christ and the ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption) made by His blood, Rom. 3:26. Wherefore this grace ought not to be restricted to the Jews and Gentiles of that time, as if it were exhibited to them so that a specimen might be shown in them to the following ages. For these benefits are common to all, just as the misery was common, as Crocius admits. It concerns all, therefore, as far as the divine intention pertains, since GOD made all alive with Christ, so that He might show the riches of grace in all. Even if, as far as actual fruition is concerned, these things befall only the faithful. What? That here there is no immediate discourse about the Gentiles, so far is it from the case that they are set forth as an example. For the Apostle employs the pronoun 'us', speaking of himself and other faithful ones from the Jews, when he thus distinguishes himself from the Ephesians and Gentiles, whom he expressed with the pronoun 'you', verse 1, even if those benefits concern both jointly, and therefore are also applied to the faithful Ephesians: Which also happens in the following.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἵνα ἐνδείξηται ἐν τοῖς αἰῶσι τοῖς ἐπερχομένοις τὸν ὑπερβάλλοντα πλοῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἐν χρηστότητι ἐφ' ἡμῶν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) quod nunc spe ac jure obtinemus, tunc in re ipsa obtinebimus. Αἰῶνες οἱ ἐπερχόμενοι עולם הבא tempus post resurrectionem. Αἰὼν ὁ μέλλων supra I. 21. Hebr. VI. 5. πλοῦτος χάριτος ut supra I. 8. Et au- gendi causa adjecit ὑπερβάλλοντα ut 2. Cor. III. 10. IX. 14. supra l. 17. infra III. 19. Et post χάριτος adjecit ἐν χρη- στότητι, ut ista verborum abundantia magnitudinem be- neficii significaret. Sic Esaias LXIII. 7. posuit רב טוב & רחמין & rursus רב חסדיו Rursum addit ἐν χει- στῷ, ut sciamus, nos post DEUM Christo omnia ista debere. In Manuscripto est ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος, quasi πλοῦτος esset neutrum declinationis tertiæ. Et ita perpetuo in illo libro poni solet πλοῦτος cum Adjectivis neutris.

Non de seculis alterius vitæ, vel post resurre- ctionem, sed de seculis hujus mundi subsequen- tibus plerique Pontificii cum Lombardo & Tho. ma hæc explicant, annuentibus communiter Cal- vinianis: Sed facile accedimus hic Grotio, cui et- iam favent Chrysostomus, Theodoretes, Ambrosius, Theophylactus, Haymo & Erasmus de futuro secu- lo, vel altera vita hæc interpretantes. Tum enim illa ἔνδειξις maxime luculenta erit: tum ὑπερβάλ- λοντα πλοῦτον, summas divitias gratiæ ejus veluti oculis ipsis usurpabimus, manibusque palpabi- mus; Et hic finis est ultimus vivificationis no- stræ spiritualis, de qua proxime Apostolus, inque ea consistit salus nostra, de qua v. sq. Nec vero si ostensio illa intelligatur, quæ fit in regno gratiæ, hæc restringi commode potest ad secula succedentia resur- rectionem Christi, vel tempora Novi Testamenti, quandoquidem opes gratiæ in Christo etiam ostensæ fuerint priscis fidelibus, qui non alia gratia salutem adepti sunt Actor. XV. 11. In Paulo quidem πρώτῳ ἐνδείξηται ἰησοῦς χριστὸς τὴν πᾶσαν μακροθυμίαν πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν τῶν μελλόντων πιστεύειν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον 1. Tim. I. 16. quem locum pulchre huic nostro respondere ait Crocius: Sed ibi agitur de singulari Pauli exemplo, quod merito aliis sistitur ad excitandam fidem in longanimitatem DEI; hìc vero commune celebratur beneficium, quod omnibus obtigit, quia omnes in Christo vivificati sumus. Non ergo hic ἐνδείκνυσθαι est speciem præbere, & exemplum proponere: Sed iisdem, quibus acquisita est vita, ostendere in altero seculo divitias gratiæ, quemadmodum illustris ἔνδειξις vel ostensio justitiæ est, quæ exhibetur in nostri justificatione, per propitiationem Christi, & ἀπολύτρωσιν sanguine ejus factam, Rom. III. 26. Quapropter non debet restringi hæc gratia ad Judæos & gentes istius temporis, quasi illis exhibita, ut in ipsis specimen ostendatur seculis sequentibus. Beneficia enim hæc omnibus communia sunt, quemadmodum communis erat, fatente Crocio, miseria. Omnes ergo concernit, quod ad divinam intentionem attinet, siquidem DEUS cum Christo omnes vivificavit, ut in omnibus ostenderet divitias gratiæ. Etsi, quod ad actualem fruitionem, fidelibus hæc solum obtingant. Quid? quod hic immediate de gentibus sermo non sit, tantum abest, ut illi in exemplum sistantur. Adhibet enim Apostolus Pronomen ἡμᾶς nos, de se, & aliis fidelibus è Judæis loquens, quum ita se distinguat ab Ephesiis, & gentilibus, quos Pronomine ὑμᾶς vos expressit, v. 1. etsi conjunctim utrosque illa beneficia concernant, ideoque etiam ad Ephesios fideles applicentur: Quod etiam in sequentibus fit.

## 2:8
Verse 8. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God) To be saved here is to be cleansed from vices: to be rendered just, as in Acts 2:40 and 1 Cor. 1:21. Namely, just as life in sins is called death, so to be freed from them is called being saved. The Apostle shows at length in the epistle to the Romans that this is done through faith. That faith or trust in God proceeds not from arguments discovered by human means, such as the philosophers used, but from those things which God, unasked, exhibited to us in the miracles and death and resurrection of Christ. Therefore he deservedly ascribes this to the goodness of GOD, and calls it His gift. This, that is, that very thing, that we have believed Phil. 1:29.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσωσμένοι διὰ τῆς πίστεως, καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν, Θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον) Σώζεσθαι hic est purgari à vitiis: Justum reddi, ut Act. II. 40. & 1. Cor. I. 21. Nem- pe sicut vita in peccatis mors dicitur, sic ab iis liberari appellatur servari. Hoc autem per fidem fieri late osten- dit Apostolus in epistola ad Romanos. Ea fides sive in Deum fiducia procedit non ab argumentis humanitus re- pertis, qualibus utebantur Philosophi, sed ab iis, quæ Deus non rogatus in Christi miraculis & morte & resurrectio- ne nobis exhibuit. Merito igitur hoc DEI bonitati adscri- bit, ejusque donum vocat. Τῦτο, id est, illud ipsum, quod credidimus Phil. I. 29.

## 2:9
Not of works) supply from the preceding, you have been saved. You did not acquire that righteousness by long exercise, in the way philosophers say virtues are acquired. Suddenly, and without labor, it came to you by the compendious way of faith. See Rom. 4:2 and what is said there.

That no one may boast) Lest anyone attribute that to his own praise, as if by his own ingenuity or labor he had arrived at that righteousness, which holiness and holy works follow. Whatever is in the river is owed to the fountain.

The Apostle proves that those dead in sins have been made alive in Christ, because they have obtained salvation then through faith. All things are referred to Christ. As he had taught in chapter 1 that we are blessed in Christ, chosen in Christ, redeemed through Christ, etc.: So he taught that we have been made alive in Christ when we were dead, raised up in Christ, and placed in the heavenly places in Christ; applying these things primarily to the Ephesians. Which he demonstrates from the salvation which they have obtained only through faith in Christ. Thus the harmony of the decree and the execution is also consistent with itself, and the application of the same life by faith is deservedly joined to salvation. To be saved (Σώζεσθαι) here therefore is to be saved, which the force of the word properly implies: from which one should not rashly depart. Moreover, salvation is understood concerning salvation both in the kingdom of grace and in the kingdom of glory. Since the former consists in peace, righteousness, and joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. 14:17, that salvation is obtained when we are justified; it happens through the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. Therefore, salvation or blessedness and justification are used interchangeably by the Apostle, Rom. 4:2, seqq. This will be situated in the eternal vision of God, whom we see here as in a mirror in the Word, and there we shall see face to face, 1 Cor. 13. The word 'having been saved' (σεσωσμένοι) can be understood in both ways: concerning the blessedness of justification, which the Ephesians had obtained through faith; and of salvation, which they likewise possessed through faith: but only as regards hope and a foretaste, not as regards the thing itself and its completion. However, because of the certainty of hope, they are said to be saved in the past tense for the present, and that through faith: just as we are justified solely through faith, so also we are saved solely through faith. If, therefore, Grotius understands the purgation from vices as the remission of sins, and as that justification which the Apostle taught is brought about through faith, Rom. 3, 4, 5, we do not deny it: but we have taught in its proper place how he perverted that doctrine there: namely, he describes justifying faith not through the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ, but through a trust in God conceived from the miracles, death, and resurrection of Christ. He by no means holds the death of Christ as the object of saving faith, insofar as it is a satisfaction for our sins.

The Apostle, however, notably adds, 'and this is not of yourselves': it is the gift of God; which do not refer to faith, although this also is a gift of God, Phil. 1:29, but to salvation. Because we contribute nothing of our own to salvation: salvation is in no way from us, but solely from the gift of God and pure grace. For it was enough to have said that we are saved freely, he adds, 'and this is not of yourselves': and lest even the beginning be attributed to grace, while good works are thought to contribute something to the completion, he teaches that this whole thing is a purely gratuitous gift of God, just as he shows in Rom. 6:last that eternal life is a gift (χάρισμα) in Christ Jesus: Nor does he rest there, but adds in addition the antithesis 'not of works' (οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων). Thus, therefore, he teaches that nothing should be ascribed to our own powers, but everything in the matter of salvation to the grace of God alone, and nothing to our merits, but everything to the merits of Christ, apprehended by faith. He asserts with a resounding voice that salvation is a purely gratuitous gift of God, and that it can in no way be ascribed to our works, removing any works whatsoever from the circle of salvation just as from that of justification, Rom. 3:25, so that it may be established that salvation is obtained through faith, and in no way from works, and that the glory of salvation is left solely to the grace of God and the merit of Christ: 'that no one may boast' (Ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται), so that we may have no cause for boasting for any reason, however small, but that he who boasts, may boast only in the Lord, 1 Cor. 1:31. It is not a question here of the acquisition of habitual and inherent righteousness, but of the manner of obtaining blessedness and salvation, from which our works are entirely removed. If habitual and inherent righteousness had a place here in that hinge of our salvation, then we would indeed have something in ourselves of which we could boast, and not only the grace of God and the merit of Christ, but also our own righteousness would contribute to obtaining salvation. For even if Grotius ascribes the same to divine grace, he does not, however, exclude the human will. But it is not of him who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy, Rom. 9:16. The words are clear

and most weighty: By the grace of God you have been saved, and not of yourselves: the gift of God, i.e., not of works, lest anyone should boast. Crocius is correct: The word grace excludes all human works and merits, and the word 'have been saved' contains the whole rationale of salvation. Therefore, as Beza notes, he did not say 'you have been justified,' which is indeed most true, but is eluded by the adversaries; nor did he say 'you are beginning to be saved,' or 'you will be saved,' but 'you have been saved,' to show that they already have the right to eternal life in Christ by grace. Some refer the particle 'and this' (καὶ τοῦτο), 'and that not of yourselves,' to faith, such as Jerome, Chrysostom, Piscator, and Crocius. But it is more correctly referred to the word 'having been saved' (σεσωσμένοι). For it is a question here of the causes of salvation, not of faith. Consequently, however, it is also referred to faith. For if in the whole matter of salvation nothing is obtained except by grace, if our salvation is the gift of God, our works have no place here, nor is anything that contributes to salvation from us, then faith, by which we are saved, must by no means be from us. For nothing by which we are saved is from us. If anything by which we are saved were from us, we would indeed have something of which we could boast. Therefore, the opposition of faith and works in the matter of salvation must be carefully noted against the Papists and the Calixtines. The opposition of faith and works in this cause is perpetual, not because they fight against each other by their own nature: for works are the fruits of faith: but because they do not tolerate each other in the work of being saved. For the latter is attributed to faith in such a way that it is taken away from works. The reason for the exclusion of works must also be carefully observed: lest anyone should boast. For he who is saved through faith despairs of his own powers and merit, but seriously acknowledges his own demerits, and relies solely on the grace of God and the merit of Christ. But he who is persuaded that his own works are also necessary for salvation, he boasts before the Lord of his own works, as if they were required for salvation alongside the merit of Christ: therefore, he does not believe that he will obtain salvation by the grace of God alone, and by the merit of Christ alone.

Latin:

Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων) supple ex prioribus, servati estis. Non acquisivistis istam justitiam longa exercitatione, quomo- do Philosophi dicunt acquiri virtutes. Subito, & sine la- bore ea vobis obvenit per compendiosam viam fidei. Vid. Rom. IV. 2. & ibi dicta.

Ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται) Ne quis id laudi sibi tribuat, quasi suopte ingenio aut labore pervenisset ad istam ju- stitiam, quam sanctitas & sancta opera sequuntur. Quic- quid est in flumine, fonti debetur.

Probat Apostolus, mortuos in peccatis vivificatos in Christo esse, quia salutem consequuti sunt tum per fidem. Omnia ad Christum referuntur. Ut benedici nos in Christo, electos esse in Christo, re- demptos per Christum &c. cap. I. docuerat: Ita nos in Christo vivificatos esse, cum mortui essemus, in Christo resuscitatos, in Christo in cælestibus col- locatos docuit; imprimis ea ad Ephesios applicans. Quod demonstrat è salvatione, quam non nisi per fidem in Christum consecuti sint. Ita sibi et- iam constat harmonia decreti & executionis, & merito vitæ applicatio ejusdem per fidem ad falu- tem jungitur. Σώζεσθαι ergo hic falvari est, quod proprie vis vocis infert: A qua non temere re- cedendum. Salus autem intelligitur de salute tum in regno gratiæ, tum in regno gloriæ. Illud quum in pace, justitia & gaudio in Spiritu Sancto con- sistat, Roman. XIV. 17. falus ea obtinetur, cum justificamur. per remissionem peccatorum & im- putationem justitiæ Christi contingit. Ideo salus vel beatitudo & justificatio permutantur ab Apo- stolo, Roman. IV. 2. seqq. Hoc æterna DEI visio- ne situm erit, quem hic velut in speculo videmus in Verbo, illic à facie ad faciem visuri, 1. Cor. XIII. Utroque modo intelligi potest verbum σεσωσμέ- νοι, de justificationis beatitudine, quam per fidem consequuti erant Ephesii; & salvationis, quam itidem per fidem possidebant: Sed solum quoad spem, & prægustum, non quoad rem & comple- mentum. Ob spei autem certitudinem præterito adhibito pro præsenti falvati dicuntur, idque per fidem: quod ut unice per fidem justificamur, ita etiam unice per fidem salvemur. Si ergo purga- tionem à vitiis de remissione peccatorum intelligat Grotius, & de ea justificatione, quam per fidem fieri Apostolus docuit, Rom. III. IV. V. capp. non abnuimus: Sed quomodo illam doctrinam ibi per- verterit, suo docuimus loco: Nimirum non per apprehenfionem justitiæ Christi, sed per fiduciam in Deum conceptam è miraculis, morte, & resurre- ctione Christi fidem justificantem describit. Mor- tem vero Christi nequaquam pro objecto fidei sal- vificæ habet, quatenus satisfactio pro peccatis no- stris est.

Notanter autem Apostolus addit, καὶ τῦτο ἐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν: Δῶρον Θεῡ est; quæ non de fide agunt, li- cet hæc etiam donum DEI sit, Phil. I. 29. sed de salute. Quod nihil de nostro conferamus ad sa- lutem: Nullatenus ex nobis salus sit, sed unice ex dono DEI & mera gratia. Nam satis erat di- xisse, gratis nos salvari, addit, & hoc non ex vo- bis: Et ne initium quidem τῇ χάριτι tribuatur, ad complementum vero aliquid bona opera con- ferre censeantur, totum hoc DEI donum mere gratuitum esse docet, quemadmodum Rom. VI. ult. vitam æternam χάρισμα esse ostendit in Chri- sto Jesu: Nec adhuc eo acquiescit, sed subjungit insuper ἀντίθεσιν ἐκ ἐξ ἔργων, non ex operibus. Ita ergo nihil viribus nostris, sed solius DEI gratiæ omnia in negotio salutis, nihil meritis nostris, sed omnia meritis Christi, fide apprehensis, ad- scribi debere docet. Donum DEI mere gratui- tum esse salutem, nec ullatenus operibus nostris adscribi posse, sonora voce asserit, à salutis æque ut justificationis circulo, Rom. III. 25. opera quæ- vis removens, ut salutem per fidem, nullatenus ex operibus obtineri constet, & gloria salvatio- nis unice gratiæ DEI & merito Christi relinqua- tur: Ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται, ne ulla vel minima ratione gloriandi causam nos habeamus, sed qui gloriatur, unice in Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. I. 31. Non de acquisitione justitiæ habitualis, & inhæren- tis hic agitur, sed de ratione beatitudinem & sa- lutem consequendi, à qua opera nostra penitus re- moventur.
