Si justitia habitualis & inhærens hic locum haberet in illo salutis nostræ cardine; ita haberemus utique in nobis, de quo gloriari pos- semus, nec gratia DEI, & Christi meritum solum, sed etiam justitia nostra ad salutem consequen- dam faceret. Nam etsi eandem divinæ gratiæ ad scribat Grotius, non tamen voluntatem humanam excludit. Non est autem volentis aut currentis, sed miserentis DEI, Rom. IX. 16. Verba sunt luculenta

& ponderosa maxime: Gratia Dei servati estis, & non ex vobis: Donum Dei h. e. non ex operibus ne quis glorietur. Recte Crocius: Vox gratia omnia hu- mana opera & merita excludit, & Verbum SERVATI totam salutis rationem continet. Ideo ut annotat Be- za, non dixit justificati estis, quod quidem verissimum, sed eluditur ab Adversariis; nec dixit servari in- cipitis, aut servabimini, sed servati estis, ut osten- dat, jam habere jus vitæ æternæ in Christo ex gra- tia. Referunt nonnulli particulam καὶ τοῦτο, idque non ex vobis, ad fidem, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Piscator, & Crocius. Sed rectius refertur ad vo- cem σεσωσμένοι. Nam de causis salutis, non fidei hic agitur. Consequenter tamen ad fidem etiam refertur. Nam si in toto salutis negotio nihil nisi gratia obtinet, si salus nostra donum DEI est, opera nostra nullum hic locum habent, nec quic- quam, quod ad salutem facit ex nobis est, utique fides, qua salvamur, nullatenus ex nobis sit, opor- tet. Nihil enim, quo salvamur, ex nobis est. Si aliquid, quo salvamur, ex nobis esset, haberemus utique, unde gloriari possemus. Notanda itaque sedulo contra Pontificios & Calixtinos oppositio fidei & operum in negotio salutis. Perpetua est fidei & operum in hac causa oppositio, non quod ratione sui inter se pugnent: Opera enim sunt fructus fidei: Sed quod mutuo se non ferant in opere servandi. Illud enim sic fidei tribuitur, ut operibus derogetur. Observanda etiam pro- be ratio exclusionis operum: ne quis glorietur. Qui enim per fidem servatur, is de suis viribus & merito desperat, demerita vero sua serio agno- scit, & sola DEI gratia ac Christi merito niti- tur. Qui vero opera sua etiam ad salutem esse ne- cessaria persuasus est, is gloriatur coram Domi- no operibus suis, ac si juxta cum merito Christi ad salutem requirantur: Non ergo sola DEI gra- tia, non solo Christi merito se salutem consequu- turum credit.

## 2:10
Verse 10. 'For we are His workmanship' (Αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν ποίημα). From Deut. 32:6 and Isa. 43:21 and 44:21. God had made the Israelite people for Himself by delivering those Israelites from the servitude of Egypt. God made the Christian people for Himself by delivering us from the servitude of vices. This is a new creation, 2 Cor. 5:17, Gal. 6:15. Whence it follows here:

Created in Christ Jesus for good works) that we might produce good works. Just as God founded the earth from a crude mass, that it might produce fruits: So God made men, who were disorderly, into ordered men, that they might then produce good works. Teaching is similar to nature, says Theodoret. Add what we have said about this word in the Prolegomena to the Gospels. Here ἐπὶ signifies that for the sake of which something is, in the way the Greeks say, for gain, for a reward.

Which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them) He prepared them both by prescribing the form of works, and by giving the Spirit, who leads us to all best things: As if someone in the sea were both to mark out a way, and at the same time provide favorable winds.

That he may further set forth the grace of GOD, as the sole and solitary cause of our salvation, he says that we, that is, the reborn and faithful, are the work of GOD, created in Christ Jesus, that is, through and on account of Christ, just as this expression in Christ has already been frequently used by the Apostle in this epistle, or that we may be a new creature in Christ, 2 Cor. 5. Gal. 6. Regarding good works he says: Here it becomes clearer that we contribute nothing to faith, and that it also is a gift of GOD. For as man contributes nothing to his own creation, but this work is of GOD alone: So we can contribute nothing to our regeneration or new creation, but whatever we are, we are the workmanship of divine grace and power. He had said that good works contribute nothing to our salvation. But lest one should think that they are not required at all from Christians or the faithful, he teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, and are prepared by God for that purpose, that we may walk in them, lest we fall from salvation. Good works are indeed excluded from justification and salvation: but they altogether become those who have been justified and have attained salvation, since they are created in Christ unto good works. Whence the rule of the Theologians: Good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one justified. It is to be observed here, however, that the Apostle again changes persons, so that he may teach that there is no διαςολὴν here, that all are justified and saved by grace, and that this is not of any of us, but is the gift of GOD, and in no wise from the works of anyone: nor can anything be attributed here to any of the faithful from among the Jews more than to any from among the Gentiles, all being saved by the grace of GOD alone, so that he may oppose the Pseudo-Apostles, who mix the law and the Gospel, and require works together with faith for salvation. He had said before that we were dead before conversion; now he intimates that we are nothing. For when God creates something, He produces it out of nothing. Some refer this to the first creation, along with Nazianzen and Basil in Theophylact: Created in Christ Jesus unto good works. Thus the Apostle would call us the work of GOD by ἀνάκτισιν, just as we were once created in the Son of GOD unto good works, or in good works, created in true righteousness and holiness. But it is simpler to refer everything to the second creation, because in respect of it we are called a new creature in Christ Jesus. And the discourse here is of the faith of those who are called both ποίημα, the work of GOD, and κτισθέντες ἐν Χριςῷ ἰησοῦ. Therefore Chrysostom says that regeneration is indicated here. Crocius notes that, although both creations were made unto good works, and both in Christ: yet there is a great distinction between the first and the second creation. In the first creation the gift of persevering in good works was not given, but it is in the second. The former was not made through Christ as Mediator, but the latter was so made. The latter distinction is correct, the former is not. The gift of persevering in good works was not lacking to Adam: which is granted to the faithful through Christ. But that was not unloseable. Nor is an unloseable gift given to these. For many lose it totally, many even finally. Crocius therefore rashly assumes an absolute unloseability of grace along with his absolute decrees of predestination. That, however, is correctly noted by Crocius, when the Apostle calls them good works, they are to be understood not only as external, but also internal, nay even thoughts, desires, and words. When he says good, he understands those done from faith, agreeable to the divine will; not those which we fashion for ourselves, I add, or which are done without faith. For these are truly good works.

Furthermore, God prepares good works not through predestination, as Augustine and Thomas wish. For although we have been chosen for this, that we might be holy and blameless, yet there is no talk here of election, much less are we said to be prepared and disposed to good works through predestination. But GOD προητοίμασε, prepared, that we might walk in them. Nor did GOD properly prepare us through the law, as Grotius wishes with the Pelagians, because through the law we are only informed about good works and directed in them, but good works are not prepared, nor are we prepared for them, since the law does not bestow the Spirit, Gal. III. 2. But God prepares good works, that we might walk in them, as most wish it to be said in the Attic style οἷς προητοίμασε, or rather, retaining the Ablative, by which (namely, the things said thus far, that He saved and created us for good works, that is, through justification and renewal) He prepared, or disposed (us) that we might walk in good works, while He, as Musculus has it in this place, makes us a good tree and fruitful in works:

He who rendered: He prepared in us: Not, however, as if He does not further help, strengthen, and support those already working. He who prevents, the same accompanies those doing right. Thus οἷς can be said to be placed for ἐν οἷς, and this pronoun is to be referred not to good works, but to κτισθέντες. He prepares us, however, while He illuminates through His Spirit, bends the will, rules the affections, supplies strength, excites, inclines, and by His own power He Himself works and effects good works in us, ἵνα ἐν αὐτοῖς περιπατῶμεν, that we might live or walk in them, so that we might spend our life occupied in them promptly with a ready mind and constantly, not desisting but proceeding: always in the course of piety, while we are on the way, until we arrive at the goal. He did not say, that we might be saved through good works: But since we have been saved through faith, He indicated that we must not rest, but must perpetually walk in good works. Theophylact: Lest by chance, he says in this place, if you understand that we have not at all attained righteousness from works, you be rendered more sluggish to perform anything rightly, after faith (he says) has been received, there is need of deeds. For you are created in Christ Jesus, and you are a new work, having been affected by death now that the old man has been removed from you through baptism, and you have been changed into a new creation. And just as God created you from nothing to being: So now He has advanced you to well-being. Furthermore, you have been founded, and created, not that you might be idle and sluggish, but that you might do something, and walk in good works, that is, that you might spend every path of this life in such good works. Bernard called good works the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. But they are not even called the way of the kingdom, unless this is explained rightly. For Christ alone is the way, John XIV. 6. In the kingdom of Christ one must walk in the way of good works: But good works are not the way of the kingdom of Christ. One does not go to the kingdom of Christ through good works, but we walk in the kingdom of Christ, to which we have arrived through regeneration, John III. 5.

PART II. The status of the Ephesians outside of Christ, and a comparison in Christ.

Latin:

Vers 10. Αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν ποίημα) Ex Deut. XXXII. 6. & Esa. XLIII. 21. & XLIV. 21. Populum Israeliticum Deus sibi fecerat, liberando eos Israelitas a servitute Ægypti. Populum Christianum sibi Deus fecit, liberando nos a servitute vitiorum. Hæc est nova creatio, 2. Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. Unde hic sequitur:

Κτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς) ut bona opera ederemus. Sicut ex rudi mole terram Deus con- didit, ut fruges ederet: Ita ea hominibus ἀτάκτοις Deus fe- cit compositos homines, ut deinde bona opera ederent. Παραπλησίως τῇ φύσει ἡ διδασκαλία, ait Theodoretius. Adde quæ de hac voce diximus in Prolegomenis ad Ev- angelia. Ἐπὶ hic significat id, cujus causa aliquid sit, quo- modo Græci dicunt, ἐπὶ κέρδει, ἐπὶ μισθῷ.

Οἷς προητοίμασεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἵνα ἐν αὐτοῖς περιπατῶμεν) Præ- paravit tum præscribendo formam operum, tum dando Spiritum, qui ad optima quæque nos agat: Quasi in mari aliquis & viam præsignaret, & simul ventos daret ferentes.

Ut gratiam DEI amplius adferat, ceu unicam ac solitariam salutis nostræ causam, nos, hoc est, renatos & fideles, opus DEI esse, creatum in Chri- sto Jesu, id est, per & propter Christum, quemad- modum frequenter loquutio hæc ἐν Χριστῷ ab Apostolo jam in hac epistola adhibita, vel ut simus nova creatura in Christo, 2. Cor. V. 7. Gal. VI. Ad opera bona ait: Hic clarius evadit, nos ad fidem nihil conferre, eamque etiam ex dono DEI esse. Nam ut nihil homo ad sui creationem confert, sed opus hoc solius DEI est: Ita nos ad nostri re- generationem vel novam creationem nihil con- ferre possumus, sed quanti quanti sumus, divinæ gratiæ & virtutis ποίημα sumus. Opera bona ni- hil facere ad salutem nostram dixerat. Ne autem ea a Christianis vel fidelibus nullatenus requiri existimet, nos creari in Christo Jesu ad bona ope- ra, & a Deo ad id præparari, ut in iis ambulemus, ne salute excidamus, docet. A justificatione qui- dem & salute excluduntur bona opera: Sed justi- ficatos & salutem consequutos omnino decent, quum conditi in Christo sint ad bona opera. Unde regula Theologorum: Bona opera non præcedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justificatum. Obser- vandum autem hic, quod iterum mutet personas Apostolus, ut nullam hic esse διαςολὴν, omnes ju- stificari & servari ex gratia, & hoc non esse ex ullo nostrum, sed donum DEI, nec ullatenus ex cujusquam operibus doceat: Nec ulli fidelium ex Judæis hic magis tribui posse quicquam, quam cuiquam ex gentilibus, omnes sola DEI gratia servari, ut occurratur Pseudo-Apostolis, legem & Evangelium miscentibus, ac cum fide opera ad salutem simul requirentibus, Mortuos nos esse ante conversionem antea dixerat; Jam nihil nos esse in- nuit. Nam cum Deus aliquid creat, ex nihilo id producit. Nonnulli hoc ad primam creationem cum Nazianzeno & Basilio apud Theophylactum referunt: Conditi in Christo Jesu ad bona opera. Sic opus DEI nos diceret esse Apostolus per ἀνάκτισιν, quemadmodum conditi quondam su- mus in Filio DEI ad bona opera, vel in bonis operibus, creati in justitia & sanctitate vera. Sed simplicius est, omnia referre ad secundam crea- tionem, quia ejus respectu dicimur nova creatura in Christo Jesu. Et de fide illorum hic sermo est, qui & ποίημα opus DEI dicuntur, & κτισθέντες ἐν Χριςῷ ἰησοῦ. Ideo Chrysostomus regenerationem inquit, hic indicat. Crocius notat, etsi utraque creatio ad bona opera, utraque in Christo facta sit: Inter primam tamen, & secundam creationem ma- gnum discrimen dari. In prima creatione donum perseverandi in bonis operibus non datum, sed in secunda. Illam non factam per Christum ut Me- diatorem, hanc autem ita factam. Posterius dis- crimen recte se habet, prius non item. Non deerat Adamo donum perseverandi in bonis ope- ribus: quod fidelibus conceditur per Christum. Sed non erat illud inamissibile. Nec his datur inamissibile donum. Multi enim amittunt totali- ter, multi etiam finaliter. Supponit ergo temere absolutam gratiæ inamissibilitatem cum absolutis suis decretis prædestinationis Crocius. Id autem recte notatur à Crocio, cum Apostolus vocat bo- na opera, intelligi non tantum externa, sed et- iam interna, imo etiam cogitationes, desideria & verba. Bona cum dicit, intelligit ex fide facta, voluntati divinæ consentanea; non quæ ipsi no- bis fingimus, addo, vel quæ sine fide facta. Hæc enim sunt vere bona opera.

Porro bona opera præparat Deus non per præ- destinationem, sicut Augustinus & Thomas vult. Quamvis enim ad id electi simus, ut sancti & im- maculati simus, non tamen hic de electione ser- mo est, nedum præparati dicimur & dispositi ad bona opera per prædestinationem. Sed DEUS προητοίμασε, præparavit, ut in iisdem ambulemus. Neque proprie DEUS præparavit nos per legem, ut cum Pelagianis Grotius vult, quia per legem solum informamur de bonis operibus & dirigi- mur in iisdem, non vero vel præparantur bona opera, vel nos ad eadem, quum lex non largia- tur Spiritum, Gal. III. 2. sed præparat Deus bo- na opera, ut in iisdem ambulemus, ut Attice ple- rique dictum volunt οἷς προητοίμασε, vel potius retento Ablativo, quibus, (scilicet hactenus di- ctis, quod servarit & crearit nos ad bona opera, hoc est, per justificationem & renovationem) præparavit, vel disposuit (nos) ut in operibus bonis ambulemus, dum nos, ut h. l. habet Muscu- lus, facit arborem bonam & fructuum feracem:

Qui reddidit: Præparavit in nobis: Non tamen, quasi jam operantes non juvet porro, firmet, ful- ciat. Qui prævenit, idem comitatur recte facien- tes. Ita οἷς positum dici poterit pro ἐν οἷς, & Pro- nomen hoc non ad bona opera, sed ad κτισθέντες referri. Præparat autem nos, dum per suum Spi- ritum illuminat, flectit voluntatem, regit affe- ctus, vires sufficit, excitat, inclinat, & virtute sua operatur & efficit ipse in nobis bona opera, ἵνα ἐν αὐτοῖς περιπατῶμεν, ut in iis versaremur vel ambularemus, ut prompte alacri animo ac con- stanter iis occupati vitam transigamus, non desi- stentes sed pergentes: semper in cursu pietatis, dum sumus in via, donec ad metam perveniamus. Non dixit, ut per bona opera salvemur: Sed quum salvati simus per fidem, indicavit non quiescen- dum nobis esse, sed perpetuo ambulandum in operibus bonis. Theophylactus: Ne forte, inquit hoc loco, si ex operibus haudquaquam nos fuisse justitiam assecutos intelligas, segnior ad recte per- agendum aliquid reddaris, post fidem (inquit) sus- ceptam factis est opus. Es namque in Christo Jesu creatus, & in novum es opus, sublato à te per ba- ptismum veteri homine jam morte affectus, in no- vamque es immutatus facturam. Et quemadmo- dum ex nihilo ad esse aliquid creavit te Deus: Sic nunc ad bene esse provexit. Conditus præterea es, & creatus, non ut otio vaces & torpeas, sed ut ali- quid agas, & in bonis operibus ambules, hoc est, ut omnem vitæ hujus semitam in bonis hujusmodi transigas. Bernhardus bona opera viam regni di- xit, non causam regnandi. Sed nec via regni di- cuntur, nisi dextre hoc explicetur. Solus enim Christus est via, Joh. XIV. 6. In regno Christi am- bulandum est in via bonorum operum: Non au- tem bona opera via sunt regni Christi. Per bona opera non itur ad regnum Christi, sed ambula- mus in Christi regno, ad quod per regeneratio- nem pervenimus, Joh. III. 5.

PARS II. Status Ephesiorum extra Christum, & in Christo comparatio.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. Διὸ μνημονεύετε) He concludes from the aforementioned that all who have been converted to Christ owe thanks to God perpetually, but especially those from the Gentiles.

That you once in the flesh, that is, by carnal origin (For thus flesh is taken in Rom. 1:3, 9:3, 1 Cor. 10:18) were Gentiles גוים. For by that name were called those who were not of the people of Israel, Matt. 6:32 and often elsewhere. In the Manuscript: That once you &c.

Those called uncircumcision by the so-called circumcision in the flesh made by hands) You were spoken of contemptuously even by pious Jews as uncircumcision, that is, having uncircumcision, which we read in Acts 11:3, the uncircumcised Jud. 14:3, 15:18, 1 Sam. 14:6, 17:26, 30, 31:4, 2 Sam. 1:20, 1 Chron. 10:4, Isa. 52:1, Ezek. 28:10, 31:18 and often elsewhere. Which Hebrew word is for the most part translated by the Greeks as uncircumcised, and in Joshua 5:7 as uncircumcised. We have had the word uncircumcision for the uncircumcised, and Rom. 2:25, 26, 27. Thus circumcision by a like metonymy for the circumcised, Rom. 3:30, 4:9. But not in vain is added in the flesh and made by hands, because there is also another mystical circumcision of the heart or soul, which is not made by hands, Col. 2:11. This has been made common to Jews and Gentiles through the Gospel.

Thus far concerning the misery and grace common to the Ephesian Gentiles with the Jews. Now he describes the state of the Ephesians as Gentiles specifically, both outside of Christ and in Christ, and so first recalls to their memory what they were under Gentilism, verse 11, 12, afterwards, what they have become under Christianity, he presents them with the same, so that they may be led more and more to acknowledge the grace of God. Theophylact comments thus: When he had said that God had made them alive, when they were dead, now indeed he is about to say, to whom he had made [them] the same and equal co-heirs, and in what manner he equaled them to the Israelites, whose dignity was greatest at that time. Μνημονεύετε, recall to memory, never forget, that you were once Gentiles in the flesh: by which expression he does not so much express the origin as the carnal state, that they were devoid of the Spirit of God. For by the word τὰ ἔθνη, an origin distinct from the Israelite lineage had already been expressed: as Grotius acknowledges, that those were called by that name who were not, as to origin, of the people of Israel. Concerning the passages Rom. I. 3. IX. 5., it has been treated in its proper place, that by the restriction κατὰ σάρκα, his human nature in Christ is noted there. He says the Gentiles were once in the flesh. Therefore they were no longer in the flesh. There is noted, therefore, both the hereditary carnal corruption, which is common to all, and the carnal conversation, because they were only in the flesh under Gentilism, and therefore were an abomination to God, Rom. IIX. 8. The Gentiles are called ἀκροβυσία or uncircumcised, as from περιτομῇ, i.e. to the circumcised Jews (the abstract being put for the concrete) they are distinguished, and thus not out of contempt, but primarily for the sake of distinction and separation. Circumcision was held in contempt rather among the Gentiles, which among the people of God was held in value as a means of salvation and a seal of the righteousness of faith, and also as a token of discretion from the Gentiles. Therefore, pious Jews called the Gentiles ἀκροβυσία, contemners of the divinely ordained Sacrament, not to insult them, but to separate themselves from them, whose plight they rather lamented than reproachfully cast in their teeth. Nor were only those Gentiles held profane who had not received circumcision; but also those who had received it, but out of κακοζηλίᾳ, not as a means of grace and a sacrament, such as were the Egyptians, Ethiopians, Syrians, and Colchians according to Herodotus. Therefore, all who were outside the boundaries of the Church, not initiated by the sacrament of circumcision, were noted by the word of the foreskin: Jerem. IX. 25. Roman. II. 26. 27. chap. III. 29. Galat. II. 7. and by the name of the uncircumcised, Genes. XXXIV. 14. Jud. XIV. 3. chap. XV. 18. 1. Sam. XIV. 6. chap. XVII. 26. 36. 2. Sam. I. 20. Uncircumcised and unclean Esa. LII. v. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Διὸ μνημονεύετε) Concludit ex antedictis, o- mnes ad Christum conversos perpetuo gratias Deo debere, sed maxime illos ex gentibus.

Ὅτι ὑμεῖς ποτε τὰ ἔθνη ἐν σαρκὶ) carné, id est, origine carnali (Nam ita caro sumitur Rom. I. 3. IX. 3. 1. Cor. X. 18.) eratis גוים. Eo enim nomine vocabantur, qui non erant de Israelis populo, Matth. VI. 32. & alibi sæpe. In Manuscripto: Ὅτι πότε ὑμεῖς &c.

Οἱ λεγόμενοι ἀκροβυστία ὑπὸ τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ χειροποιήτου) Contemptim à Judæis etiam piis dice- bamini ἀκροβυστία, id est, ἀκροβυστίαν ἔχοντες, quod legimus Act. XI. 3. הערלים Jud. XIV. 3. XV. 18. 1. Sam. XIV. 6. XVII. 26. 30. XXXI. 4. 2. Sam. I. 20. 1. Paral. X. 4. Esa. LII. 1. Ezech. XXVIII. 10. XXXI. 18. & alibi sæpe. Quæ vox Ebræa à Græcis plerumque vertitur ἀπερίτμητοι, ac Jo- suæ V. 7. ἀκρόβυστοι. Ἀκροβυστίας vocem pro ἀκροβύστοις ha- buimus, & Rom. II. 25. 26. 27. Sic περιτομὴ pari μετωνυμίᾳ pro circumcisis, Rom. III. 30. IV. 9. Non frustra autem additur ἐν σαρκὶ & χειροποιήτου, quia est & alia circumcisio mystica cordis sive animi, quæ est ἀχειροποίητος, Col. II. 11. Hæc per Evangelium communis facta est Judæis & gentibus.

Hactenus de miseria & gratia Ephesiis gentili- bus cum Judæis communi. Nunc statum Ephesio- rum ceu gentilium proprium, tum extra Chri- stum, tum in Christo describit, adeoque in me- moriam primum revocat ipsis, quales fuerint sub gentilismo vers. 11. 12. postea, quales sub Christianismo evaserint, iisdem sistit, ut ad agnoscendam DEI gratiam magis magisque ad- ducantur. Theophylactus ita commentatur: Cum Deum dixisset, hos salvos fecisse, cum mortui essent, nunc quidem dicturus est, quibus eosdem & pares feciffet & cohæredes, & quemadmodum Ifraelitis æquaverit, quorum maxima esset tunc dignitas. Μνημονεύετε memoria recolite, nunquam obliviscamini, quod quondam gentes fueritis in carne: Qua voce non tam originem, quam statum carnalem, quod expertes Spiritus Dei fuerint, exprimit. Nam voce τὰ ἔθνη origo distincta ab Israelitica prosapia expressa jam erat: ut agnoscit Grotius, eo nomine vocatos, qui non erant, quod ad originem de Israelis populo. De locis Rom. I. 3. IX. 5. in propria sede actum, per restrictionem κατὰ σάρκα in Christo humanam ejus naturam illic notari. Dicit gentes quondam fuisse in carne. Non ergo amplius in carne erant. Notatur ergo cum corruptio carnalis hæreditaria, quæ communis omnibus est, tùm conversatio carnalis, quia nonnisi in carne erant sub gentilismo, ideoque Deo erant abominatîoni, Rom. IIX. 8. Vocantur gentes ἀκροβυσία vel præputiati, ut à περιτομῇ, h. e. Judæis circumcisis (abstracto pro concreto posito) distinguantur, adeoque non per contemptum, sed imprimis distinctionis & separationis causa. Contemptui habebatur potius penes gentiles circumcisio, quæ in populo Dei ceu medium salutis, & sigillum justitiæ fidei in pretio erat, nec non tessera discretionis à gentilibus. Ideo pii Judæi ἀκροβυσίαν gentiles, contemptores Sacramenti divinitus ordinati, dicebant, non ut insultarent ipsis, sed ut sese ab iisdem separarent, quorum vicem potius dolebant, quam contemptim ipsis exprobrabant. Nec tantum illæ gentes profanæ habebantur, quæ circumcisionem non susceperant; sed etiam, quæ susceperant, sed ex κακοζηλίᾳ, non ceu medium gratiæ & sacramentum, quales erant Ægyptii, Æthiopes, Syri & Colchi apud Herodotum. Notabantur ergo omnes, qui extra pomœria Ecclesiæ erant, non initiati per sacramentum circumcisionis, voce præputii: Jerem. IX. 25. Roman. II. 26. 27. cap. III. 29. Galat. II. 7. & incircumcisorum nomine, Genes. XXXIV. 14. Jud. XIV. 3. cap. XV. 18. 1. Sam. XIV. 6. cap. XVII. 26. 36. 2. Sam. I. 20. Incircumcisi & impuri Esa. LII. v. 1.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. Ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς χρισῦ) because the promises concerning the Messiah had been announced by the Prophets to the Jews alone. See Rom. IX. 4. Now you possess him no less than those to whom he had been promised.

Ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τῦ ἰσραὴλ) In that Republic instituted by God, not only could you not take honors: but you could not even be held as citizens: So far did the institutions differ. See Esth. III. 8. and Tacitus concerning the Jews. But now God has made another Republic for himself, namely the Church, in which you can be promoted through all degrees of honors, no less than the Jews. Thus was the prediction of Esa. LV. vers. 5. eminently fulfilled.

Καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Those covenants made with Abraham, then with Isaac and Jacob, and then the legal covenant given through Moses, pertained nothing to you, that is, they spoke nothing of you, Psalm. CXLVII. v. 20. Now that covenant which Christ brought equals you to the Jews. But all those old covenants are rightly called covenants τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, because they have annexed promises on God's part, which can be seen in their own places.

Ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντες) Of the resurrection, namely, and of eternal life, as this is explained below IV. 18. All time after the return from Babylon was the vestibule of the Gospel. The resurrection and eternal life were to be fully and certainly revealed through the Messiah. But from the mystical explanation of the Prophets made by Ezra, the Jews had received some taste of those things, as appears from the Maccabean books, the description of the Pharisaic opinions which is in Josephus, and Act. XXIII. 8. The Gentiles, however, had no divine revelation concerning that matter. Epicurus and Aristotle believed nothing of it. The Stoics thought souls remained, but not beyond the time of the ἐκπυρώσεως. The Platonists thought souls in perpetual cycles became now blessed, now miserable. Whatever they said were uncertain, vague, and fragile conjectures,

Καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ) that is, through all the shores of the earth, you either were ignorant of the true GOD, the maker of the world, or certainly did not worship him, but instead of him, gods fashioned by men. But the sense is taken from Hosea IV. v. 1. ואין־דעת אלהים בארץ, οὐκ εἰδότες Θεὸν, Gal. IV. vers. 8.

How miserable the state of the Ephesians was under Gentilism, the Apostle now explains by parts, 1. as to faith and religion, that they were without Christ, destitute of true religion. Χωρὶς Χριστõ is not without promises concerning the Messiah. For those pertained to all the nations of the earth, Genes. XII. 3. even if for the most part and ordinarily the Prophets were sent to the Jews alone; yet that some of them were sent to the Gentiles also is certain, and that their sermons not rarely looked to the Gentiles as well is by no means obscure. The Gentiles were certainly not excluded from the promises concerning the Messiah, who was destined for the whole world, and before the distinction of Jews and Gentiles arose, was announced to Adam in the former world, to Noah in the other, and to other Prophets through many centuries. But those who remained in Gentilism were without Christ, that is, destitute of faith in Christ, and devoid of the saving knowledge of the same.

2. As for the ecclesiastical polity, the Gentiles were formerly separated from the polity of Israel: which, although it may be true also of the civil, here the ecclesiastical is nevertheless regarded, by which God had associated that people to Himself peculiarly by a covenant, and had furnished them with laws and statutes, as well as with various privileges and benefits above the rest of the peoples, in which He ordinarily manifested Himself then, who also was His peculiar treasure and royal priesthood, Ex. XIX. 5. Psal. CXVIII. 20.

3. As for the divine covenants: Because they were strangers from the covenants of promise, where the word τῆς ἐπαγγελίας teaches that the legal covenant is not regarded, because the promise of Evangelical grace is hinted at: such as was made in the covenants with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which were truly Evangelical and distinct from the legal ones, as the Apostle interprets, Gal. III. The promise on the part of GOD was indeed universal, but the Gentiles were not received into the covenant of grace through their own fault. For they could have become proselytes.

4. As regards the hope of eternal life. Not that there was no hope of resurrection and eternal life for the ancients before the coming of Christ, but that it was lacking to the Gentiles. Grotius would prefer to deprive even the faithful Jews of it, and leaves them only a certain taste of it, and that only in the final times of the Prophets: as if the Patriarchs and almost all the Prophets before Ezra either themselves had no hope of the resuscitation of the dead and eternal life, or if they are believed to have had it, they gave no hope to the people of their own time. And yet, in Paradise itself through the Proto-Evangelium, and among the Patriarchs through the proclamation of the same, and the repetition made divinely, that hope was published, and being illustrated from time to time by Prophetic sermons, it uniquely comforted and sustained the faithful in miseries both corporal and spiritual, which can be taught by the examples of Lot, Gen. XIX, of David, Psalm XVI, Psal. XVII, and CXIX. & of the Prophets throughout the Old Testament, and the holy Apostle demonstrated it at length, Heb. XI. Nor was it handed down only mystically by the Prophets, but was included in their sermons, taken in the literal sense. Concerning the mystical explanation of Ezra, who supposedly handed it down peculiarly, Grotius brought forward nothing. The comforts by which the faithful sustained themselves in the most grievous sufferings and martyrdoms, of which there is mention in the Maccabees, arose from the common faith and hope, not one peculiar to those times. By what reason, however, could other faithful ones of earlier times have otherwise raised themselves in calamities and persecutions and death itself, if they had no hope of the resurrection of the dead, no blessed life after this; they would certainly have been the most miserable of all mortals, 1 Cor. XV. 19. The nations also conceived hope regarding their false deities, but a vain one, not true, not living. As the deities were, such also was their worship, and such was their hope. Destitute of Christ, who is our hope, 1 Tim. I. 1, how could they have a living hope? They lacked regeneration, through which we are made heirs according to hope, 1 Pet. I. 3; they were devoid of the consolation of the scriptures, through which they had hope, Rom. XV. 4, whence then could they have had hope? Therefore, 1 Thess. IV. 17, they are said to be, μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα. 5. As to the knowledge of God. Because the nations were without GOD in the world, inasmuch as they were ignorant of the true God, Gal. IV. 8, it does not say the nations did not worship God, but it says you were ἄθεοι while living. How could the nations worship the true God, when they were ignorant of him, as such. For there is no true God, except the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one in essence, three in persons. Those who are ignorant of Him are ἄθεοι, inasmuch as they are ignorant of that one true God. Concerning which in the Appendix to the Syncretism of Calixtus and Vol. III of the System of Theology. Diverse classes of atheists can be established: The first of them is those who have no God, such as the Epicureans are said to be: The second of them is those who worship none but fictitious deities, such as the Ephesians were. The third of them is those who indeed acknowledge God as the Creator of heaven and earth, but are ignorant of who He is, while they do not know the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be that true God, such as the Jews, Turks, and Arians. The fourth of them is those who indeed acknowledge that true God, but deny Him by their deeds, Tit. I. 16, such as Pseudo-Christians. There is added ἐν κόσμῳ, because such as he had described lived in the world without Christ, outside the Church, outside the covenant of grace, without a living hope, and devoid of God. For this particle pertains to all the preceding.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς χρισῦ) quia promissiones de Messia ad solos Judæos a Prophetis annunciatæ fuerant. Vid. Rom. IX. 4. Nunc eum non minus possidetis vos, quam ii, quibus promissus fuerat.

Ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τῦ ἰσραὴλ) In illa Republica à Deo instituta non modo honores non poteratis capere: sed nec pro civibus haberi: Adeo distabant instituta. Vid. Esth. III. 8. & Tacitum de Judæis. Nunc vero aliam sibi Rempublicam Deus fecit, Ecclesiam scilicet, in qua per omnes honorum gradus provehi potestis, non minus, quam Judæi. Sic impleta eminenter prædictio Esa. LV. vers. 5.

Καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Pacta illa cum Abrahamo facta, deinde cum Isaaco & Jacobo, ac deinde pactum legale per Mosen datum, nihil ad vos pertinebant, id est, nihil de vobis loquebantur, Psalm. CXLVII. v. 20. Nunc pactum illud, quod Christus attulit, vos Judæis æquat. Omnia autem ista pacta vetera recte vocantur pacta τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, quia annexas habent promissiones ex Dei parte, quæ videri possunt suis locis.

Ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντες) Resurrectionis scilicet & vitæ æternæ, ut hoc explicatur infra IV. 18. Omne tempus post reditum ex Babylone erat vestibulum Evangelii. Resurrectio & vita æterna plene & certo revelanda erant per Mesfiam. Sed ex mystica Prophetarum explicatione per Esdram facta, aliquem rerum illarum gustum Judæi acceperant, ut ex Maccabaicis libris, Pharisaicarum sententiarum descriptione, quæ est apud Josephum, & Act. XXIII. 8. apparet. Gentes vero nullam ea de re habebant divinam revelationem. Epicurus & Aristoteles nihil ejus credebant. Stoici animas putabant manere, sed non ultra, quam ad tempus ἐκπυρώσεως. Platonici animas perpetuis vicibus nunc beatas nunc vero miseras fieri. Quicquid dicebant, conjecturæ erant incertæ, vagæ, fragiles,

Καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ) id est, per omnes terrarum oras, verum DEUM, mundi scilicet opificem, aut ignorabatis, aut certe non colebatis, sed pro eo Deos ab hominibus fictos. Est autem sensus desumptus ex Oseæ IV. v. 1. ואין־דעת אלהים בארץ, οὐκ εἰδότες Θεὸν, Gal. IV. vers. 8.

Quam miserabilis Ephesiorum sub gentilismo fuerit status, jam per partes explicat Apostolus, 1. quod ad fidem & religionem, quod sine Christo fuerint, vera religione destituti. Χωρὶς Χριστõ non est sine promissionibus de Messia. Illæ enim ad omnes nationes terræ pertinebant, Genes. XII. 3. etsi plerumque & ordinarie Prophetæ ad Judæos solos mitterentur; Quorum tamen nonnullos ad gentes etiam missos, constat, & conciones eorum gentes quoque non raro spectasse, minime obscurum est. Non erant utique gentes exclusæ à promissionibus de Messia, qui toti mundo destinatus erat, & ante enatum discrimen Judæorum & gentium Adamo in priori, Noæ in altero mundo, aliisque Prophetis per complura secula annunciatus fuit. Qui autem in gentilismo manebant, sine Christo erant, hoc est, fide in Christum destituti, & salutaris ejusdem notitiæ expertes.

2. Quod ad politiam Ecclesiasticam, olim separati erant gentiles à politia Israelis: quod etsi de civili etiam verum sit, hic tamen respicitur Ecclesiastica, qua Deus populum illum sibi peculiariter fœdere consociaverat legibus & statutis, nec non variis privilegiis & beneficiis præ reliquis populis instruxerat, in quo ordinarie tum se manifestabat, qui etiam ejus peculium & Regale sacerdotium erat, Ex. XIX. 5. Psal. CXVIII. 20.

3. Quod ad pacta divina: Quia peregrini erant à pactis promissionis, ubi non legale pactum respici vox τῆς ἐπαγγελίας docet, quia promissio gratiæ Evangelica innuitur: qualis in pactis cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Jacobo facta est vere Evangelicis, & à legalibus distinctis, interprete Apostolo, Gal. III. Promissio ex parte DEI universalis quidem erat, sed in pactum gratiæ non receptæ erant gentes culpâ propriâ. Poterant enim fieri proselyti.

4. Quoad spem vitæ æternæ. Non quod veteribus ante adventum Christi nulla spes resurrectionis & vitæ æternæ fuerit, sed quod ea gentibus defuerit. Grotius eâ etiam fideles Judæos privare mallet, nec nisi gustum quendam illis, & quidem temporibus demum Prophetarum ultimis, relinquit: quasi Patriarchæ & Prophetæ plerique omnes ante Esdram, vel ipsi nullam resuscitationis mortuorum & vitæ æternæ spem habuerint, vel si habuisse credantur, populo sui temporis nullam spem fecerint. Atqui in ipso Paradiso per Prot-Evangelium & penes Patriarchas per ejusdem præconium, & repetitionem divinitus factam spes illa publicata, & concionibus Propheticis subinde illustrata unice solabatur & sustentabat in miseriis tum corporalibus tum spiritualibus fideles, quod exemplis Lothi Genes. XIX. Davidis, Psalm. XVI. Psal. XVII. & CXIX. & Prophetarum passim in Veteri Testamento doceri potest, & sanctus Apostolus prolixe, Ebr. XI. demonstravit. Nec tantum mystice per Prophetas illas tradita, sed in ipsorum concionibus, sensu literali acceptis, comprehensa. De Esdræ explicatione mystica, qui peculiariter eam tradiderit, nihil adduxit Grotius. Solatia, quibus sese in gravissimis passionibus & martyriis sustentabant fideles, de quibus in Maccabaicis, è fide ac spe communi non istorum temporum propriâ, enata sunt. Qua ratione autem alias sese erigere potuissent in calamitatibus & persecutionibus ac morte ipsa, alii fideles superiorum temporum, si nullam mortuorum resurrectionem, nullam beatã vitam post hanc sperassent; miserrimi certe fuissent omnium mortalium, 1. Cor. XV. 19. Concipiebant & gentes spem de falsis suis Numinibus, sed inanem, non veram, non vivam. Qualia erant numina, qualis eorum cultus, talis quoque spes ipsorum erat. Christo, qui spes nostra est, 1. Tim. I. 1. destituti, quo- modo spem vivam habere poterant? Regeneratio- ne, per quam heredes efficimur secundum spem, 1. Petr. I. 3. carebant; consolationis scripturarum, per quam spem habebant, Rom. XV. 4. expertes e- rant, unde ergo spem habuissent? Ideo 1. Thess. IV. 17. dicuntur, μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα. 5. Quod ad Dei a- gnitionem. Quia gentes fuerunt sine DEO in mun- do, utpote verum Deum ignorantes, Gal. IV. 8. non dicit gentes non coluisse Deum, sed ἄθεοι inquit degentibus eratis. Quomodo colere gentes ve- rum Deum poterant, quum ignorarint eum, qua tales. Verus enim Deus non est, nisi Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus, unus essentia, Trinus in per- sonis. Quem qui ignorant, ἄθεοι sunt, utpote unum illum verum Deum ignorantes. Quo de in Syncret. Calixt. Append. & Tom. III. System. Theol. Atheorum diversæ classes constitui pos- sunt: Prima eorum est, qui nullum Deum habent, quales Epicurei dicuntur: Secunda eorum, qui non nisi fictitia Numina colunt, quales Ephesii fuerunt. Tertia eorum, qui Deum quidem Crea- torem cæli & terræ agnoscunt, sed quis ille sit, ignorant, dum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum san- ctum verum illum Deum esse nesciunt, ut sunt Judæi, Turcæ, Ariani. Quarta eorum, qui agno- scunt quidem illum verum Deum, factis autem abnegant, Tit. I. 16. quales sunt Pseudo-Christiani. Additur ἐν κόσμῳ, quod tales, quales descripserat, in mundo vixerint sine Christo, extra Ecclesiam, ex- tra fœdus gratiæ, citra spem vivam, & expertes Dei. Hæc n. particula ad præcedentia omnia pertinet.

## 2:13
Verse 13. But now in Christ Jesus) Through Christ Jesus. You who once were far off) who were far from the knowledge of the true God, and from the hope of heavenly life. You have been made near) You clearly perceive those things, as those are accustomed to do who have approached near to some thing. In the blood of Christ) The death of Christ and the resurrection that followed it have made you certain of these things. Verse 14. For He Himself is our peace) Christ is the cause of concord between those converted from the Jews and the nations. See above I. 10. A similar expression in Micah V. 4. He who made both one) both, namely, the races. One, namely, one body קרב אותם אחד אל- אחד Ezech. XXXVII. 17, the mystical fulfillment of which place is taught here. See John X. v. 16. And having broken down the middle wall of partition). קיר פרץ: A partition (so Pliny speaks) separating. For the genitive here is in the Hebrew manner in place of an adjective. Thus in Terence a wall is ordered to be torn down, so that one house may be made.

Now follows the blessed state of the Ephesians: 1. That they are no longer without Christ, but in Christ Jesus. 2. That they are no longer ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι, separated from the Republic of Israel and the true Church; but whereas they were once μακρὰν, far from it, Acts II. v. 39, they have now been made near through the blood of Christ, not that they were rendered certain of the hope of heavenly life through the passion and death of Christ and the resurrection that followed (of which there is no word here), but that through the death of Christ that nearness was acquired for all, and through the sprinkling of the blood of Christ and faith in his blood they belong to the Royal priesthood of God, 1. Petr. I. v. 2, cap. II. vers. 9, Apocal. I. vers. 5, 6, cap. V. v. 9. For since Christ is our peace, who earned peace for us all by his blood, Roman. V. v. 9, therefore by the virtue of his merit he made those two kinds, which were once divided, of Israelites and Gentiles one, τὸ μεσότοιχον

having broken down the partition, he founded the two in peace and concord into a new body, and reconciled both in one body to GOD through and because of the merit of his cross, having put to death enmity on the cross or through his cross. There could not be true and solid peace among men, much less among peoples so separated, unless Christ were our peace. We had to coalesce in GOD; therefore we both had to be reconciled to God first through Christ the Mediator. With peace with God broken, no peace could exist or be restored on earth, unless peace with God were sanctioned again, which was done by the blood of Christ. Therefore Christ is our peace, by reconciling peace for us with GOD. Who, since he is appeased toward us all, all who are in Christ are united to God in Christ. Faith in Christ is that bond by which they are bound together, to which the nations being called, they themselves become one with the Jewish people in Christ: So that there is no longer Jew, nor Greek, nor slave, nor free, but all are one in Christ, Galat. III. v. 28, Col. III. vers. 11. Christ therefore made both one, by bringing the nations to the Jews, so that they constitute one flock, John X. v. 16, one body, 1 Cor. XII. 13. In the word middle wall of partition there is a metaphor from two houses, or two rooms, which are torn down by a partition wall, by the removal of which one house, one room is made. Such a wall was the ceremonial law. This separated the Jews and the Gentiles in the Old Testament. And therefore it had to be removed, so that they might coalesce into one ecclesiastical polity. A partition is not a solid wall of solid material, but a hedge or fence, through which we can still reach something with our eyes in neighboring buildings. The Apostle therefore wished to say that the polity of the Jews was so distinguished from the Republic of the Gentiles by a fence, that they could nevertheless look at the ceremonies and laws of the Jews as if from a distance, just as they also mutually took not a few things into their own sacred rites and statutes, as the blessed Balduinus holds here. But this fence was thoroughly torn down, so that from both peoples one might be made, because both peoples were redeemed by the blood of Christ, both were reconciled to God, therefore both became partakers of the fruit of the blood and passion through the preaching of the Word.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Νυνὶ δὲ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Per Christum Jesum. Ὑμεῖς οἱ ποτὲ ὄντες μακρὰν) qui longe eratis à cognitio- ne Dei veri, & à spe vitæ cœlestis. Ἐγγὺς ἐγενήθητε) Clare illa conspicitis, ut solent, qui prope ad rem aliquam accessere. Ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ χριστοῦ) Mors Christi & eam secuta re- surrectio vos rerum istarum certos fecere. Vers. 14. Αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ εἰρήνη ἡμῶν) Christus causa est concordiæ inter conversos ex Judæis & gentibus. Vide supra I. 10. Similis locutio Michæ V. 4. Ὁ ποιήσας τὰ ἀμφότερα ἓν) τὰ ἀμφότερα nempe γένη. ἕν nempe σῶμα, unum corpus קרב אותם אחד אל- אחד Ezech. XXXVII. 17. cujus loci mystica impletio hic docetur. Vide Joh. X. v. 16. Καὶ τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ λύσας). קיר פרץ: Inter- gerinum (ita Plinius loquitur) separans. Nam Genitivus hic more Ebræo est vice ἐπιθέτου. Sic apud Terentium ju- betur maceria dirui, ut fiat una domus.

Sequitur jam status Ephesiorum beatus 1. Quod non amplius sine Christo sint, sed in Christo Jesu. 2. Quod non amplius sint ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι separati à Republ. Israelis & verâ Ecclesiâ; sed quum quon- dam μακρὰν longe ab illa fuerint, Actor. II. v. 39. jam propinqui facti sint per Christi sanguinem, non quod per passionem & mortem Christi, & resurrectionem sequutam (de qua hic nullum ver- bum extat) certi redditi spei cœlestis vitæ, sed quod per mortem Christi omnibus illa propinqui- tas acquisita sit, & per aspersionem sanguinis Chri- sti & fidem in sanguinem ejus ad sacerdotium Dei Regale pertineant, 1. Petr. I. v. 2. cap. II. vers. 9. Apocal. I. vers. 5. 6. cap. V. v. 9. Quum enim Chri- stus pax nostra sit, qui nobis omnibus pacem san- guine suo promeruit, Roman. V. v. 9. Ideo virtute meriti sui duo illa genera, quæ erant olim divisa, Israelitarum & gentium unum fecerit, τὸ μεσότοιχον

τῶ φραγμῶ λύσας, duos pace & concordia facta in novum corpus condidit, & utrosque in uno cor- pore DEO reconciliavit per & propter crucis suæ meritum, mortificatà inimicitià in cruce vel per crucem suam. Non posset inter homines pax vera & solida esse, nedum inter populos ita separatos, nisi Christus pax nostra esset. Coalescere in DEO debuimus; utrique ergo prius Deo eramus con- ciliandi per Christum Mediatorem. Pace cum Deo ruptà nulla in terris esse poterat aut redintegrari pax, nisi cum Deo pax iterum sanciretur, quod fa- ctum Christi sanguine. Pax ergo nostra Christus est, pacem nobis cum DEO conciliando. Qui quum nobis omnibus placatus sit, omnes qui in Christo sunt, Deo in Christo uniuntur. Fides in Christum est vinculum illud, quo colligantur, ad quam vocatis gentibus unum ipsæ fiunt cum po- pulo Judaico in Christo: Ut non sit amplius Ju- dæus, nec Græcus, non servus, nec liber, sed omnes unus sint in Christo, Galat. III. v. 28. Col III. vers. 11. Fecit ergo Christus utrosque unum, gentes ad Judæos adducendo, ut unum gregem, Joh. X. v. 16. unum corpus, 1. Cor. XII. 13. constituant. In voce μεσότοιχον τῶ φραγμῶ Metaphora est à duabus do- mibus, aut duobus conclavibus, quæ pariete in- tergerino diruuntur, quo sublato una fit domus, unum conclave. Paries ejusmodi erat lex ceremo- nialis. Hæc separabat Judæos & gentiles in Veteri Testamento. Ideoque tollenda erat, ut in unam politiam Ecclesiasticam coalescerent. φραγμὸς non est paries solidus ex solida materia, sed sepes seu se- ptum, per quod adhuc oculis aliquid in vicinis ædi- bus assequi possumus. Voluit ergo dicere Aposto- lus, politiam Judæorum à gentilium Republica ita fuisse distinctam septo, ut tamen ceremonias & leges Judæorum quasi eminus adspicere potuerint, quem- admodum etiam non pauca suis in sacris & statutis mutuo sumpserunt, ut hic habet B. Balduinus. Di- rutum autem penitus fuit hoc septum, ut ex utro- que populo unus fieret, quia uterque populus Christi sanguine redemptus, uterque Deo recon- ciliatus fuit, ideo uterque fructus sanguinis & pas- sionis particeps factus est per Verbi præconium.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. The enmity) It is a preposition and at the same time a metonymy. He says, that cause of enmity, on account of which the Gentiles were despised by the Israelites, and in turn the Israelites were in hatred among the Gentiles, as being unmixable, of a different race, and unassociable. A comma should be placed here.

In his flesh) Refer this to that 'having made one' and 'having broken down'. He did that not by the flesh of victims, through which they were accustomed to sanction covenants, as we said at Matt. 26:27-28. It is the same as what he says shortly after: By the cross.

The cause of the enmity was the ceremonial law, although by accident, for from different forms of worship and ceremonies the occasion for enmity between the Jews and the Gentiles was seized. This cannot be understood of the moral law. For that was common to Jews and Gentiles. But it was not the partition wall. We acknowledge, however, a comma here, and we allow the words 'in his flesh' to be referred to that 'having made one' and 'having broken down'. For in the flesh, and through the flesh of Christ, the union of Jews and Gentiles was made, and the removal of the partition wall as the cause of dissension. Christ removed this cause of enmity by the sacrifice of his death, by which he brought an end to the ceremonial law.

The law of commandments in ordinances) katargein corresponds to the Hebrew batel, in which way it is also translated here by the Syriac. Those things are said to be katargeisthai which lose their force. The force, however, which is understood here, is the force of binding. The 'law of commandments' is called that part of the law which consists in things neither honest nor base in themselves, and the word entole corresponds to the Hebrew chukkim, as can be seen in Deut. 16:12, 1 Kings 2:23, 3:14, Ezek. 18:21. By this name are understood precepts concerning days, concerning victims, concerning forbidden foods, and the like. The force of these Christ removed by dogmas, Col. II. verse 14. which is here called ἐν δόγμασι, namely by his own dogmas, as the Syriac, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact have rightly understood here. For he taught through his Apostles that these things have nothing excellent in themselves, and that God grants liberty either to follow or not to follow these things, so that men might be more intent upon the most important matters. Δόγμα is a Greek word, which is frequent for signifying the doctrines of philosophers: Paul uses it here, writing to men versed in the writings of philosophers. Thus the Greek Fathers often call Christian doctrine by the name of philosophy.

Now the Apostle explains how Christ is our peace, about to exhibit the third of the moments of the blessed state of the Ephesians after their conversion, namely that they are no longer outside the covenant of grace, or ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, but through Christ enjoy grace and peace. For whose sake he here claims for Christ 1. the destruction of the law, 2. the reconciliation of men with God, 3. the proclamation of peace, 4. the access and approach to God the Father procured for us, from which he concludes that we are no longer ξένος καὶ παροίκυς, ἀλλὰ συμπολίτας τῶν ἁγίων, καὶ οἰκείους τοῦ Θεοῦ. Concerning the first he has this here: Τὸν νόμον τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐν δόγμασι καταργήσας. It is asked, what law is understood here, what dogmas, what that καταργήσας is. Most understand the ceremonial law. But its λύσις had also been indicated before, since that is the middle wall of partition taken out of the way through the flesh of Christ. And thus νόμων τῶν ἐντολῶν is restricted to that part of the law which consists of things in themselves neither honest nor base. We do not deny that that word ἐντολῶν sometimes corresponds to the Hebrew חקים, when there is talk of the ceremonial law. Nor does the reason sufficiently appear why the mandates of both kinds should not be understood. For the word of the law is general, as is ἐντολῶν. Therefore they are not to be restricted here to the ceremonial only. Crocius notes that it is said in the plural of laws, of commandments, because there are many laws concerning ceremonies and rites. Aretius rashly wishes both the moral law and the ceremonial to be understood. By dogmas Crocius, with Beza, and with the approval of the blessed Balduinus, likewise [understands] rites and ceremonies. But in this way Beza inserts the word ὄντα, (which) (is placed) in rites, which does not please others, who prefer to interpret the word ἐν δόγμασι with the Syriac, WITH DECREES: And they connect the same with the following participle καταργήσας. If it is rendered in this way, it can be explained as the law of commandments with decrees, or that he has evacuated both the ceremonial law and the rites themselves, as Beza understands the Syriac, or that he has evacuated not only the law of temporal commandments, but also the decrees concerning rites (although for a different reason). Camerarius: But it is altogether consistent that we should include ἐν δόγμασι with that which he had said, ἐντολῶν. So that the law is signified, containing precepts and decrees. Grotius wishes to understand dogmas as the Apostolic precepts by which Christ through the Apostles evacuated the ceremonial law. But the Apostle is not dealing here with the doctrine or precepts or commands of Christ, where it is clear that the discourse is rather about the effects of the cross or death of Christ; nor in the parallel passage which Grotius cites, Col. II. verse 14. by the word δόγμασι are understood not Apostolic precepts, but the decrees of the law, which lost their force through the cross of Christ, with that which was against us in them, the handwriting, being deleted, and taken out of the way, and affixed to the cross. Grotius appeals rashly to Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact. Chrysostom says: The Apostle calls either faith a decree, or the precept of Christ, Matt. V. But I say to you. Oecumenius and Theophylact explain it no differently. Theodoret thinks that the evangelical doctrine is called decrees or placita, to which some more recent [authors] also subscribe. But the Apostle is speaking about the evacuation which was done through the cross, not through the evangelical doctrine. Wherefore it is more correctly understood by dogmas as decrees pertaining to the moral law, for instance, those by which all and each are obligated to observance if we wish to obtain salvation, and the law threatens a curse to all who do not observe all things written in the book of the law. Thus CHRIST removed the law of commandments. But in these decrees, or regarding these decrees, [he removed] the necessity of obligation and the curse. For it is manifest from Col. II. verse 14 that these decrees are to be understood.

What the word καταργήσας means is not at all obscure. Aretius says the ceremonial law was abrogated by reason of obligation, because it is no longer necessary to be observed: But the moral law by reason of condemnation, so that it cannot condemn the elect. There is no doubt that the evacuation of the ceremonial law is discussed here: To which the cross, or the death of the cross of CHRIST, brought an end, which the ceremonies prefigured, and in which they attained their completion. But if it seems inconvenient to anyone that the moral law has been evacuated, let him weigh the passage 2 Cor. III. verse 11, where the same word occurs: Εἰ γὰρ τὸ καταργούμενον διὰ δόξης, and let him compare the parallel Coloss. II. verse 14, in which the Apostle teaches that the handwriting in these dogmas, decrees, which were contrary to us, obligating us to the most exact observance or to punishment, was deleted through Christ, and affixed to the cross, through which he took it out of the way.

That he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace) Just as the whole people is one civil person, so too is the Church. Κτίσῃ, that is, might form, as above at 10. Τοὺς δύο, which below is τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους, namely Jews and Gentiles, for which he had said before ἀμφότερα, namely γένη, as we have already said. Ἐν ἑαυτῷ is a metonymy of the efficient cause for the effect, in himself, that is, through his doctrine. Καινὸν ἄνθρωπον, that is, a new body, using not those ancient laws, but new ones. Ποιῶν εἰρήνην, concord having been established. See above at 14. In the manuscript it is ἐν ἀυτῷ for ἐν ἑαυτῷ, with the same sense.

A twofold end of the abrogated law is now expressed, designated by these and the following words: Namely, that Jews and Gentiles might be reconciled among themselves into one new man, and that both might be reconciled with God. By which at the same time the other point pertaining to the admission of the Gentiles into the covenant of grace is dispatched. The former pertains to the ceremonial aspects of the law, the latter to the abrogation of the moral law. Regarding the former end, the means and the term must be considered first. The means here is not doctrine, but the flesh of Christ, which was sacrificed on the cross, or delivered unto death. Nor indeed is there need here for a metonymy, IN HIMSELF, that is, through his doctrine. For Christ himself is the Mediator, in whom and through whom the two are created into one man, nor is the doctrine of CHRIST new laws, just as he himself is not a new lawgiver. Grace and truth came through him, but the law did not come through him, but was given through Moses, John 1:17. He preferred, however, to say ONE MAN in designating the term, rather than one people. For thus the union and unity is more expressed, into which those peoples, so greatly separated, come together, who become one man, that is, one body and one soul, and are one in Christ Jesus, Galatians 3:28. And indeed a NEW man, not because of new laws, because new laws do not make or constitute a new man, but because of the renewal of the Spirit. For it was not acquired by the merit and blood or cross of CHRIST that new laws should be created, but that a new Spirit should be given to us, and we might become a new creature in Christ, so that we might be the chosen people of God, and a Royal priesthood. It is also indicated what kind of unity it is, namely not numerical, not political, not economic, but spiritual or mystical: by which we are rendered one mystical body and one soul, Acts IV. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Τὴν ἔχθραν) Est πρόθεσις simul & Metony- mia. Causam, inquit, illam inimicitiæ, ob quam gentes ab Israelitis spernebantur, contra Israelitæ in gentium erant odio, tanquam ἄμικτοι, ἀσύμφυλοι, ἀκοινώνητοι. Ponenda hic ὑποστιγμή.

Ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἀυτῦ) Hoc refer ad illud ποιήσας ἓν & λύσας. Fecit illud non victimarum carne, per quas fœdera sancire solebant, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 27. 28. Idem est, quod mox dicit: Per crucem.

Causa inimicitiæ erat lex ceremonialis quamvis per accidens, Nam ex diversis cultibus & ceremo- niis arripiebatur occasio inimicitiæ inter Judæos & gentes. De lege morali hoc intelligi nequit. Nam illa Judæis & gentibus communis fuit. Non autem paries intergerinus. Agnoscimus autem hic ὑποστιγμὴν, & verba ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἀυτῦ ad illud ποιήσας ἓν & λύσας referri permittimus. Nam in carne, & per carnem Christi facta est Judæorum & gentium unio, & parietis intergerini ceu cau- sæ dissensionis remotio. Sustulit autem hanc ini- micitiæ causam Christus mortis suæ sacrificio, quo finem attulit legi ceremoniali.

Τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασι καταργήσας) καταργῆν respondet Ebræo בִּטֵּל, quomodo & à Syro hic vertitur. Dicuntur autem καταργεῖσθαι ea, quæ vim amittunt. Vis au- tem, quæ hic intelligitur, est vis obligandi. Νόμος τῶν ἐντο- λῶν dicitur ea pars legis, quæ consistit in rebus per se nec honestis, nec turpibus, & respondet vox ἐντολὴ Ebraicæ חֻקִּים, ut videre est Deut. XVI. 12. 1. Reg. II. 23. III. 14. Ezech. XVIII. 21. Hoc nomine intelliguntur præcepta de diebus, de victimis, de cibis vetitis & similia. Horum vim sustulit Christus δόγμασι, Col. II. vers. 14. quod hic dici- tur ἐν δόγμασι, per dogmata nempe sua, ut hic recte intel- lexerunt Syrus, Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophyla- ctus. Docuit enim per Apostolos suos hæc in se nihil ha- bere egregii, & Deum istorum aut sequendorum aut non sequendorum indulgere libertatem, quo intentiores sint homines ad potissima. Δόγμα vox est Græca, quæ frequens ad significandas Philosophorum doctrinas: Ea hic utitur Paulus, scribens hominibus tritis in Philosophorum scri- ptis. Sic Græci Patres sæpe Christianam doctrinam φι- λοσοφίας nomine appellant.

Jam explicat Apostolus, quomodo Christus pax nostra sit, tertium momentorum beati Ephe- siorum post conversionem status exhibiturus, quod nempe non amplius extra fœdus gratiæ, vel ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας sint, sed per Christum gratia & pace fruantur. Cujus causâ Chri- sto hîc vendicat 1. legis destructionem, 2. hominum cum Deo reconciliationem, 3. pacis annunciationem, 4. ad Deum Patrem aditum & accessionem nobis partam, è quibus concludit, nos non esse amplius ξένος καὶ παροίκυς,ἀλλὰ συμπολίτας τῶν ἁγίων, ᾐ οἰκείυς τῦ Θεῦ. De primo hic ita habet: Τὸν νόμον τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐν δόγμασι καταργήσας. Quæritur, quænam lex hic intelligatur, quæ dogmata, quid- nam illud καταργήσας. Legem ceremonialem in- telligunt plerique. Sed ejus λύσις etiam antea indi- gitata erat, cum illa sit paries intergerinus è medio sublatus per Christi carnem. Et ita νόμων τῶν ἐντο- λῶν restringitur ad eam legis partem, quæ consistit in rebus per se nec honestis, nec turpibus. Non ab- nuimus vocem illam ἐντολῶν Ebræo חקים quan- dóque respondere, cum de lege ceremoniali ser- mo est. Nec satis apparet ratio, cur non utriusque generis mandata intelligenda sint. Vox enim legis pariter, & ἐντολῶν generalis est. Non ergo hic ad ceremonialem tantum restringendæ sunt. Crocius notat, ideo in plurali dici legum, mandatorum, quod plurimæ sint leges de ceremoniis & ritibus. Aretius temerè & legem moralem, & ceremonia- lem intelligi vult. Per dogmata Crocius cum Beza, annuente B. Balduino, itidem ritus & ceremonias. Sed ita ingerit Beza Verbum ὄντα, (quæ) in ritibus (posita est) quod aliis non placet, qui malunt vo- cem ἐν δόγμασι cum Syro interpretari, CUM DE- CRETIS: Et connectunt eandem cum partici- pio sequenti καταργήσας. Quo pacto si reddatur, exponi potest, legem mandatorum cum decretis, vel quod & legem cæremonialem, & ritus ipsos eva- cuarit, ut Beza Syrum intelligit, vel quod non tan- tum legem mandatorum temporalium, sed etiam decreta de ritibus, (quanquam dispari ratione) evacuarit. Camerarius: Omnino autem consenta- neum est, ut complectamur ἐν δόγμασι, cum eo, quod dixerat ἐντολῶν. Ut significatur lex, præceptiones & decreta continens. Grotius dogmata intelligere ma- vult de præceptionibus Apostolicis, quibus Christus per Apostolos legem ceremonialem evacuarit. Sed non agit hic Apostolus de doctrina vel præ- ceptis seu jussionibus Christi, ubi potius de crucis vel mortis Christi effectis sermonem esse, luculen- tum est; neque in loco parallelo, quem affert Grotius, Col. :I. vers. 14. voce δόγμασι intelligun- tur Apostolica præcepta, sed legis decreta, quæ per crucem Christi vim suam amisere, deleto eo, quod contra nos in illis erat, chirographo, & sub- lato è medio, crucique affixo. Ad Chrysostomum, Oecumenium & Theophylactum temere provocat Grotius. Chrysostomus dicit: Apostolum aut fidem vocare decretum, aut præceptum Christi, Matth. V. Ego vero dico vobis. Non aliter Oecumenius & Theophylactus explicant. Theodoretius decreta seu placita appellari putat doctrinam Evangeli- cam, cui etiam nonnulli recentiores suffragantur. Sed de evacuatione, quæ per crucem facta, non per doctrinam Evangelicam loquitur Apostolus. Quapropter rectius per dogmata decreta intelliguntur ad legem moralem spectantia, puta, quibus ad omnium & singulorum observationem obligantur, si salutem adipisci velimus, & maledictionem minatur lex omnibus, qui non observant omnia, scripta in libro legis. Ita legem mandatorum sustulit CHRISTUS. Sed in hisce decretis, vel quoad hæc decreta, necessitatem obligationis, & maledictionem inferentia. Nam hæc decreta intelligi è Coloss. II. vers. 14. manifestum est.

Quid sibi velit vox καταργήσας, minime obscurum est. Aretius legem ceremonialem abrogatam dicit ratione obligationis, quia non amplius necessaria sit observatu: Legem autem moralem ratione damnationis, ut electos condemnare non possit. De evacuatione legis ceremonialis hic disseri, nullum est dubium: Cui finem attulit crux, vel mors crucis CHRISTI, quam ceremoniæ præfigurarunt, & in qua complementum suum consecuta sunt. Moralem autem legem evacuatam esse, si cui inconveniens videatur, locum expendat 2. Corinth. III. vers. 11. ubi eadem vox occurrit: Εἰ γὰρ τὸ καταργούμενον διὰ δόξης, & parallelum Coloss. II. vers. 14. conferat, in quo chirographum in his dogmatibus, decretis, nos ad exactissimam observationem, vel ad pœnam obligantibus nobis contrarium per Christum deletum, & cruci, per quam illud sustulit è medio, affixum docet Apostolus.

Ἵνα τοὺς δύο κτίσῃ ἐν ἑαυτῷ εἰς ἕνα καινὸν ἄνθρωπον, ποιῶν εἰρήνην) Sicut populus totus est una persona civilis, sic & Ecclesia. Κτίσῃ, id est, formaret, ut supra 10. Τοὺς δύο, quod infra τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους, Judæos nempe & gentes, pro quo ante dixerat ἀμφότερα, nempe γένη, ut jam diximus. Ἐν ἑαυτῷ est Μετωνυμία efficientis pro effecto, in se, id est, per suam doctrinam. Καινὸν ἄνθρωπον, id est, novum corpus, non priscis illis, sed novis utens legibus. Ποιῶν εἰρήνην, concordia constituta. Vide supra 14. In Manuscripto est ἐν ἀυτῷ pro ἐν ἑαυτῷ, sensu eodem.

Finis geminus jam exprimitur evacuatæ legis, his & sequentibus verbis designatus: Nimirum ut inter se concilientur Judæi & gentiles in unum novum hominem, & ut utrique reconcilientur cum Deo. Quo simul alterum punctum pertinens ad gentium in fœdus gratiæ admissionem expeditur. Prior ad legis ceremonialia, posterior ad moralis evacuationem pertinet. Circa priorem finem imprimis medium respiciendum, & terminus. Medium non est hic doctrina, sed caro Christi, quæ in cruce immolata, vel in mortem tradita. Neque vero hîc Metonymiâ opus est, IN SE, id est, per suam doctrinam. Mediator enim Christus ipse est, in quo & per quem duo in unum hominem conduntur, nec doctrina CHRISTI novæ sunt leges, quemadmodum nec ipse novus νομοθέτης est. Gratia & veritas per ipsum facta, non vero lex per ipsum, sed per Mosen lata, Johan. I. vers. 17. Maluit autem dicere UNUM HOMINEM in designando termino, quam unum populum. Nam ita unio & unitas magis exprimitur, in quam illi tantopere dissiti populi coëunt, qui unus homo, hoc est, unum corpus & una anima evadunt, & unus in Christo Jesu sunt, Galat. III. vers. 28. Et quidem καινὸς NOVUS homo non ob novas leges, quia novæ leges non faciunt, aut constituunt novum hominem, sed ob renovationem Spiritus. CHRISTI enim merito & sanguine vel cruce ejus acquisitum id non est, ut novæ conderentur leges, sed ut novus nobis daretur Spiritus, & nova fieremus creatura in Christo, ut populus Dei electus, & Regale sacerdotium essemus. In- dicatur etiam qualis sit unitas, scilicet non nume- rica, non politica, non œconomica, sed spiritualis, vel mystica: qua unum corpus mysticum & una anima reddimur, Act. IV. 32.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. And might reconcile both in one body to God) Here he said body, which he just called man, just as among the Latins associations are called bodies. Thus Livy spoke of the body of the state, and the King of his own body. These are bodies from things divided, as the Greeks say, compacted from distant things, as Pomponius the Jurisconsult says. Might reconcile, namely among themselves. To God is briefly said for that they might serve God.

Through the cross) When he says cross, he simultaneously understands the doctrine, sanctioned by the cross. But he preferred to say cross, so that we might understand how much that matter cost Christ, so that we might value this benefit all the more.

Having killed the enmity in it) in it, namely the cross, as the Syrian rightly understood here. The same word having killed has the same value here as he just used for having loosed, but with the mention of the cross the translation of the word having killed was more apt, because the cross brings death. A similar allusion in Gal. V. 24.

It must be explained here 1. who are reconciled; 2. in what; 3. by what, and 4. how. As to the first: It is not now a matter of the union and reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles among themselves, but as the Apostle expressly has it, with God. For what is clearer than that might reconcile to God? This construction introduces the object of reconciliation, and thus reconciliation with God, especially since the other party of the dissidents is also expressed. Reconciliation is between two who are at odds. One party of the dissidents is men, Jews and Gentiles: The other is God. Both he reconciled to GOD. We have therefore those who were to be reconciled: We have also God, to whom they were to be reconciled. That gloss, that they might serve God, is not held in the text, but is inserted: just as the Apostle does not have that AMONG THEMSELVES: And therefore it is added rashly. Of doctrine sanctioned by the cross there is also no trace here. Nor did Christ die so that he might sanction doctrine. His cross was not a testimony or proof and confirmation of doctrine, but a ransom or price of redemption. Finally, the enmity which was killed in the cross and through the cross is not here the enmity between Jews and Gentiles, but between those whom the Apostle said were reconciled to each other, that is, between both of those on one side, and God on the other. For there was need of that extinction of enmity above all, so that true peace might be sanctioned among men, as it is that whose foundation is union with God: Those who are united to Him can also cultivate solid peace among themselves. For there is no solid peace, except in God. As to the second, our reconciliation with God was made in one body, which Grotius, along with certain others, understands of the body of the Church, insofar as both Jews and Gentiles were reconciled to God in one mystical body of the Church: nor is there any doubt that both are reconciled by the merit of the cross through faith, as being reconciled by the blood of Christ, who killed the enmity on the cross, and coming preached peace to us, so that we might actually enjoy the reconciliation made through Christ. But here it is a matter of the acquisition of reconciliation, not of the application: therefore Johannes Crocius, although he notes that not only Ambrose, Haymo, Thomas, and Cornelius à Lapide take it of the body of the Church, but that Bucer, Musculus, Piscator, and indeed even his own Calvin incline to it, and that this sense is orthodox, he nevertheless preferred with Bullinger, Zanchius, and Beza to interpret it of the proper body of Christ. A manifest parallel passage is Col. I. 22. 23. But now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death. This is in one body, which is there in the body of his flesh: What is here

διὰ σταυρᾶ there is διὰ τῶ θανάτε. He said, however, ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι, either because he made mention of two peoples, who were reconciled through one body of his flesh, or because of the comparison of types. Reconciliation in the types was accomplished through many bodies, many victims: This reconciliation, however, in the antitype was accomplished in a single body, a single sacrifice, Heb. X. 8, 9, 10. Thus with Chrysostom, Theophylact: In one body, however, that is, in his own. And Theodoret: He reconciled both, namely those who were from the Gentiles, and those who were from the Jews, in one body, which was offered for all, so that they themselves might be one body. With whom E. Hunnius also agrees. In his one most holy body through the cross, while he did not hesitate at all to expose it to be crucified for the salvation of the world and that desired peace.

As to the third, through what was the reconciliation accomplished? Διὰ τῶ σταυρᾶ, says the Apostle, through the cross, with no mention made of the doctrine, which Grotius said was sanctioned through the cross in a heterodox sense; as if the cross of Christ were viewed in these things not so much as a λύτρον, but as a μαρτύριον. Theophylact is more correct, that he paid the penalties owed by us for wicked deeds through the cross. He did not, however, say through the cross to exclude the penalties endured before the passion, but because the completion of them was on the cross, whence he is said to have been made obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross, Phil. II. v. 7.

4. How was the reconciliation accomplished? The Apostle adds, ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν ἀυτῷ, which is rightly understood concerning the σταυρῷ with the Syriac, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact, even if some seem to have read ἐν ἑαυτῷ in himself, as B. Luther rendered it with the Vulgate, and Beza testifies that he found it in certain codices. The matter comes to the same thing: because in himself, namely, immolated on the cross, through which he had already said the reconciliation was accomplished, he took away the enmities, in which he affixed the handwriting, Col. II. v. 14, so that the enmity of God and men might be taken away. It had arisen from sin, because of which GOD justly turned away from man, and man, indeed, being evilly conscious of himself, fled from God. Therefore, sin having been taken away through the sacrifice of the cross, that enmity was destroyed. Διὰ τῶ σταυρᾶ, says Photius, for having loosened sin by his death, he also loosened the enmity.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ ἀποκαταλλάξῃ τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι τῷ Θεῷ) Hic corpus dixit, quod modo ἄνθρωπον, sicut Latinis collegia vocantur corpora. Sic corpus civitatis di- xit Livius, & sui corporis Regem. Hæc sunt corpora ἐκ διηρημένων, ut loquuntur Græci, ex distantibus compacta, ut Pomponius Jurisconsultus. Ἀποκαταλλάξῃ, nempe in- ter se. Τῷ Θεῷ breviter dictum pro ut Deo serviant.

Διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ) Cum crucem dicit, simul intelligit do- ctrinam, cruce sancitam. Sed crucem dicere maluit, ut intelligamus, quanti res ista Christo steterit, ut eo majoris faciamus hoc beneficium.

Ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν αὐτῷ) ἐν αὐτῷ nempe σταυρῷ, ut recte hic accepit Syrus. Idem hic valet ἀποκτείνας, quod modo λύσας, sed crucis facta mentione aptior fuit trans- latio verbi ἀποκτείνας, quia crux mortem affert. Similis allusio Gal. V. 24.

Explicandum hic 1. qui reconciliati sint; 2. in quo; 3. per quod, & 4. quomodo. Quod ad pri- mum: Non jam de unione & reconciliatione Ju- dæorum & gentilium inter sese, sed ut expresse Apo- stolus habet, cum Deo agitur. Quid enim clarius, quàm illud ἀποκαταλλάξῃ τῷ Θεῷ? Hæc constru- ctio reconciliationis objectum, adeoque recon- ciliationem cum Deo infert, imprimis cum altera dissidentium pars etiam expressa sit. Reconcilia- tio est inter duos, qui dissident. Una dissidentium pars homines sunt, Judæi & gentes: Altera Deus. Τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους utrosque reconciliavit DEO. Ha- bemus ergo eos, qui reconciliandi erant: Habe- mus & Deum, cui reconciliandi. Glossa illa, ut Deo serviant, in textu non habetur, sed ingeri- tur: quemadmodum nec illud INTER SE Apo- stolus habet: Ideoque temere additur. De do- ctrina cruce sancita nullum etiam hic vestigium. Nec mortuus est Christus, ut doctrinam sanciret. Crux ejus non μαρτύριον erat vel doctrinæ testi- monium & confirmatio, sed λύτρον vel redemptionis pretium. Inimicitia denique, quæ in cruce & per crucem interfecta est, hic non est inimicitia in- ter Judæos & gentes, sed inter eos, quos mutuo sibi reconciliatos dixit Apostolus, hoc est, inter utrosque illos ex una, & Deum ex altera parte. Nam illa imprimis inimicitiæ extinctione opus erat, ut vera pax sanciretur inter homines, utpo- te cujus fundamentum est unio cum Deo: Cui qui uniti sunt, illi inter se pacem solidam etiam colere possunt. Nulla enim pax solida, nisi in Deo. Quod ad alterum, reconciliatio nostri cum Deo facta ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι, quod de corpore Ecclesiæ intelligit Grotius, cum quibusdam aliis, quatenus scilicet tum Judæi tum gentes in uno Ecclesiæ corpore mystico Deo reconciliati: neque dubi- um est, utrosque merito crucis reconciliari per fidem, utpote reconciliatos sanguine Christi, qui inimicitiam interfecit in cruce, & veniens evan- gelizavit nobis pacem, ut actu frueremur recon- ciliatione per Christum facta. Sed hic de acqui- sitione reconciliationis agitur, non de applicatione: ideo Johannes Crocius etsi non tantum Ambro- sium, Haymonem, Thomam & Cornelium à Lapide de corpore Ecclesiæ accipere notet, sed etiam eo inclinare Bucerum, Musculum, Piscatorem, imò etiam Calvinum suum, eumque sensum orthodo- xumque esse, maluit tamen cum Bullingero, Zanchio & Beza de proprio Christi corpore inter- pretari. Locus parallelus manifestus est Col. I. 22. 23. Νυνὶ δὲ ἀποκατήλλαξεν ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρ- κὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου. Hic est ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι, quod illic ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ: Quod hic est

διὰ σταυρᾶ ibi est διὰ τῶ θανάτε. Dixit autem ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι, sive quod duorum mentionem fecerit populorum, qui per unum corpus carnis ipsius reconciliati, sive ob typorum collationem. Reconciliatio in typis per multa fiebat corpora, victimas multas: Hæc vero reconciliatio in antitypo facta est in unico corpore, unico sacrificio, Ebr. X. 8. 9. 10. Ita cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: In uno autem corpore, hoc est, in suo. Et Theodorets: Reconciliavit autem utrosque, nempe eos, qui erant ex gentibus, & qui erant ex Judæis, in uno corpore, quod pro omnibus oblatum est, ut ipsi essent unum corpus. Quibus E. Hunnius etiam suffragatur. In uno suo sanctissimo corpore per crucem, dum illud crucifigendum pro mundi salute & optata illa pace exponere minime dubitavit.

Quod ad tertium, per quod facta sit reconciliatio? Διὰ τῶ σταυρᾶ, inquit Apostolus per crucem, nulla facta mentione doctrinæ, quam per crucem sancitam heterodoxo sensu dixit Grotius; quasi crux Christi non tam ut λύτρον, quam ut μαρτύριον in his spectetur. Rectius Theophylactus, quod pœnas nobis ob prava facinora debitas ille per crucem luerit. Non autem per crucem dixit, ut pœnas ante passionem exantlatas excluderet, sed quod complementum earum in cruce fuerit, unde obediens dicitur factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. II. v. 7.
