Eph. IV. 4. and following, it sets forth primarily this, that they have one hope of their calling. (3.) Partakers of the promise of God, which is not partakers of the Holy Spirit. For nowhere is the Holy Spirit called the promise of God, but the Spirit of promise. But those who are partakers of the Evangelical promise, they have the hope of eternal life, which the Gospel promises to those who believe. That this promise is indeed understood, it is manifest: because it is added, in Christ, by whom it was acquired for us, and in whom we have it uniquely, through the Gospel, that is, received by faith. For what is offered through the Gospel, that is received through faith. The Gospel is the medium of the giving, and on the part of God, faith is the medium of the receiving, and on the part of men.

Latin:

V. 6. Εἶναι τὰ ἔθνη συγκληρονόμα κὴ σύσσωμα κὴ συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ἀυτὸ ἐν τῷ χριστῷ) Gentes intellige natos ex gentibus, manentes in sua libertate: non factos prose- lytos. Συγκληρονόμα pari jure vocatos ad vitam cœlestem, quæ hæreditas dicitur, vide Rom. VIII. 17. Ebr. XI. v. 9. 1. Petr. III. 7. σύσσωμα concorporeas, partes ejusdem cor- poris, id est, Ecclesiæ, vide supra II. 16.

Συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ἀυτῦ) participes Spiritus san- cti, qui dicitur ἐπαγγελία Θεῦ, ut vidimus supra I. vers. 13. Ἀυτῦ enim hic refertur ad illud Θεῦ, quod satis longe præ- cessit. Ἐν χριστῷ per Christum, qui ista bona nobis obtinuit.

Διὰ τῦ Εὐαγγελία) tanquam per instrumentum, quo Christus ad res illas efficiendas utitur. Per Evangelium colligitur Ecclesia, credentibus datur jus ad vitam cœle- stem, & interim dona Spiritus.

Explicat jam Apostolus spem gentium quoad hæreditatem cœlestem, cujus gratia potissimum il- lam de revelatione hujus mysterii præmiserat, & deinceps porro de ministerio suo disserere con- stituit. Nimirum τὰ ἔθνη esse 1. συγκληρονό- μα, quod respectu Christi, cujus cohæredes dici- mur, Rom. IIX. 17. intelligit Hieronymus, alii con- venientius textui ratione Judæorum, qui spem vitæ æternæ habuerant, quum gentes sine spe essent in mundo. Nunc autem cohæredes eosdem esse quoad spem, & jus ad vitam æternam affirmat Apostolus. Non accesserunt Judæi ad gentes, sed gentes ad Judæos, ideo cohæredes horum dicun- tur. 2. Σύσσωμα, concorporeos sunt gentes, quia ad unum corpus mysticum pertinent, cujus unitas

Eph. IV. 4. feqq. exposita imprimis id infert, quod unam spem vocationis habeant. (3.) Συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod non est participes Spiritus sancti. Nam nuspiam Spiritus sanctus ἐπαγ- γελία Θεοῦ dicitur, sed πνεῦμα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας. Qui autem participes sunt promissionis Evangeli- cæ, illi spem habent vitæ æternæ, quam credenti- bus promittit Evangelium. Eam vero promissio- nem intelligi, manifestum est: quod addatur, ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ, a quo nobis ea acquisita, & in quo eam unice habemus, διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου per Evangelium, fide scilicet receptum. Nam quod per Evange- lium offertur, id per fidem accipitur. Evangelium est medium τῆς δόσεως, & ex parte Dei, fides est me- dium τῆς λήψεως, & ex parte hominum.

## 3:7
V. 7. Of which I became a minister) The word minister being taken more generally, as 1 Cor. III. 5, 2 Cor. III. 6, VI. 4, XI. 23, Coloss. I. 23, 25.

According to the gift of the grace of God, which was given to me according to the working of his power) The gift here denotes tongues, an excellent effect of admirable divine power for converting the nations, 1 Cor. XIV. 18. according to the working or by working, we have above I. 19. and below IV. 16. and Phil. III. 21. and Coloss. I. 23. I am bound, but God is even now effective through me.

It is rashly said that only the gift of tongues is understood by the gift of the grace of God: Which, although it did [something] to convert the nations, yet it was not sufficient alone, nor was it granted divinely only to the Apostle. Therefore, all the gifts which were given to Paul for the sake of the Apostolic ministry are to be understood. Theophylact requires three things for a minister: first, a spirit that will fearlessly approach any dangers; then, wisdom and understanding; finally, integrity of life, and that all these things are obtained by divine grace. To which, indeed, extraordinary gifts must be added in Paul. Compare Acts XV. verse 12, Rom. XV. verses 18, 19, 1 Corinth. XV. verse 10, Gal. II, 8.

Latin:

V. 7. Οὗ ἐγενόμην διάκονος) Voce nempe διακόνου sum- pta generalius, ut 1. Cor. III. 5. 2. Cor. III. 6. VI. 4. XI. 23. Coloss. I. 23. 25.

Κατὰ τὴν δωρεὰν τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ, τὴν δοθεῖσάν μοι κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ) Donum hic notat lin- guarum, eximium effectum admirabilis potentiæ divinæ ad convertendas gentes, 1. Cor. XIV. 18. κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν aut καθ' ἐνέργειαν, habemus supra I. 19. & infra IV. 16. & Phil. III. 21. & Coloss. I. 23. vinctus sum ego, sed Deus e- tiam nunc per me est efficax.

Per δωρεὰν τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ solum lingua- rum donum intelligi temere dicitur: Quod etsi ad convertendas gentes fecerit, non tamen vel sufficiebat solum, vel solum Apostolo concessum est divinitus. Omnia ergo dona, quæ διακονίας Apostolicæ causa data erant Paulo, intelligenda sunt. Ad ministrum tria requirit Theophylactus, animum primo, quæcunque discrimina intrepide aditurum; deinde sapientiam & intellectum; de- nique vitæ integritatem, & hæc omnia obtingere divina gratia. Quibus vero in Paulo addenda dona extraordinaria. Conf. Act. XV. vers. 12. Rom. XV. vers. 18. 19. 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 10. Gal. II, 8.

## 3:8
V. 8. To me, the least of all) In manuscripts and in other books, 'of the saints' is added. He returns to the discourse which he had interrupted by a parenthesis, but with a changed construction, as we just said. 'Least' is a comparative made from a superlative. Thus, a superlative from a superlative, 'least' (pauxillum), in the Glossary. Such are found among the poets: 'most extreme', 'worse', 'more graceful', 'most noble', 'better', 'more former', 'easier'; but Paul's highest modesty is to be noted, where he speaks of himself, not of his office; compare 1 Cor. XV. 9, where the word is 'least'. הַדַּל

This grace was given to preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ) In the manuscript, 'in' is absent. Understand 'riches' of grace, as above I. 7 and II. 7, most abundant grace; we have 'unsearchable' also in Rom. XI. v. 3, it corresponds to the Hebrew אֵין חֵקֶר, as can be seen in Job V. verse 9, chapter IX. 10, chapter XXXIV. verse 24.

There is no need for either a parenthesis or a changed construction. For this dative corresponds to the preceding: 'given to me', 'to me the least of all the saints', this grace was given to me, I say, the least of all the saints. Theophylact observes here the humility of blessed Paul: when he is about to explain the magnitude of divine grace, see how modestly he speaks of himself. For after such great things well done, he calls himself the least, not only of the Apostles, but even of all the saints, that is, the faithful. Which, without doubt, by reason of humility, is far greater than that which he says: 'I am not worthy to be called an Apostle.' Here that grace is explained, which the Apostle had said in v. 2 was given to him for the nations, that it was given for evangelizing among the nations, which, however, is not to be taken exclusively, because he evangelized among the Jews, Acts XIII. verse 16, chapter XIV, chapter XVII. 1, 10, 16, but preeminently or primarily. For he had been appointed especially as Teacher of the nations, Acts IX. 15, Rom. XI. 13, 1 Tim. II. 9, 2 Tim. I. 11.

The object of the Gospel designates τὸν ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλῦτον τῦ χρισῦ, the unsearchable riches of Christ, by which name, even when placed simply, the riches of mercy and kindness are understood, especially the riches of the grace of Christ, which are unfolded in the Gospel most of all, although the riches of glory and wisdom are also explained in the same, 2 Cor. 8:9, 2 Cor. 2:8, Col. 2:3. Those riches are called the grace of Christ so that they may be distinguished from the wealth of the world, and they are the remission of sins, justice, holiness, hope, certainty of glory, eternal salvation. They are unsearchable, both because they cannot be investigated by the benefit of human reason without divine revelation, and because in this age, even if they have been revealed through the Word, they cannot be comprehended by the mind. From which Theophylact refutes Eunomius, who said that he comprehended the nature and essence of Christ. Whereby it happens, he says, that if the riches of GOD are unsearchable, far more can his substance not be tracked. By what pact, therefore, did that heretic Eunomius boast that he comprehended such a substance of God? But how do those things become known to the Angels through the Church? Augustine explains it concerning the triumphant Church in book 5 of Genesis to the letter, chapter 19. But this is foreign. For it is a matter of the grace exhibited to the Church in these lands. Thomas [speaks] of the experience of vision, that they see that which they previously knew only through revelation, 1 Tim. 3:16. Others explain it thus concerning experimental notification, that, having been taught by the testimonies of things, they understand that gratuitous salvation in Christ is offered not only to the Jews, but also to the Gentiles, even by him who a little before was an incensed enemy, and is received through faith, [they understand] the will of GOD concerning saving the Gentiles equally as the Jews, through faith, without the ceremonial law; which reason they had previously known not at all, much less that the Gentiles, swelling with doctrine, would yield to such an easy kind of teaching, as is learnedly explained by Crocius. Which notification, however, is not to be accepted solitarily, whether as an object or as a mode. For not only was the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles made more manifest to the Angels, but also other mysteries of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:12. And not only from real experience, but also from further revelation: διὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, not indeed as if the Angels learned by receiving the Word from the mouth of a minister in the Church, like men who have faith from hearing, Rom. 10:17, but because they know what is done in the Church, 1 Cor. 11:10, Luke 15:10. Indeed, they announce to the Church itself things received from God, as was done in the conception, birth, resurrection, and ascension of Christ into heaven, and also in the calling of the Gentiles, when Peter had to enter them first, Acts 10. For neither is διὰ explained here necessarily as cause or medium, since it is also the same as IN or AMONG, as 1 Tim. 2:15, Gal. 3:19, among the ecclesiastical assemblies, such things were notified either through the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the Apostles and other θεοπνεύςες men, so that he might reveal hidden mysteries; or through immediate revelation made from heaven, or manifested by the Son of God, or through the disclosure which was made to the Angels themselves for the sake of the Church. It can also be explained διὰ Ἐκκλησίας as 'because of the Church.' For the notification to the Angels was made for its sake, as the particle διὰ also occurs with the Genitive, Rom. 6:4, 1 Tim. 4:14, 2 Pet. 1:3.

Latin:

V. 8. Ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων) In Manuscriptis & in aliis libris additur τῶν ἁγίων. Redit ad sermonem, quem per παρενθήκην interruperat, sed mutata constructione, ut modo diximus. Ἐλαχιστότερος comparativum ex superla- tivo factum. Sic superlativum ex superlativo ἐλαχιστότατον pauxillum, in Glossario. Talia sunt apud Poetas ἐσχατώ- τατος, χερειότερος, χαριστότερος, κυδίστατος, λωΐτερος, προτεραίτερος, ῥαοίτερος, notanda autem Pauli, ubi de se, non de munere suo agit, summa modestia, confer. 1. Cor. XV. 9. ubi est vox ἐλάχιστος. הַדַּל

Ἐδόθη ἡ χάρις αὕτη ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν εὐαγγελίσασθαι τὸ ἀνεξι- χνίαστον πλοῦτον τοῦ χριστοῦ) In Manuscripto abest ἐν. Πλοῦ- τον intellige χάριτος, ut supra I. 7. & II. 7. gratiam uber- rimam, ἀνεξιχνίαστον habemus & Rom. XI. v. 3. respondet Ebræo אֵין חֵקֶר, ut videre est Jobi, V. vers. 9. cap. IX. 10. cap. XXXIV. vers. 24.

Non opus est sive παρενθήκῃ sive mutata con- structione. Respondet enim Dativus hic præce- denti: δοθεῖσάν μοι, ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ, datam mihi, mihi inquam minimo omnium sanctorum data est hæc gratia. Observat hic B. Pauli humi- litatem Theophylactus: Cum sit divinæ gratiæ ma- gnitudinem explicaturus, vide quam modeste de se loquatur. Post tantas namque res optime gestas mi- nimum se appellat, non modo Apostolorum, sed omnium etiam sanctorum, hoc est fidelium. Quod procul dubio ratione humilitatis majus est longe, quam illud quod inquit: Non sum dignus vocari Apostolus. Explicatur hic χάρις illa, quam sibi datam ad gentes v. 2. dixerat Apostolus, quod ea sit data ad evangelizandum inter gentes, quod ta- men exclusive non est accipiendum, quia evange- lizavit inter Judæos, Act. XIII. vers. 16. cap. XIV. cap. XVII. 1. 10. 16. sed ἐξοχικῶς seu primario. Nam præcipue gentium Doctor constitutus erat, Act. IX. 15. Rom. XI. 13. 1. Tim. II. 9. 2. Tim. I. 11.

Objectum Evangelii designat τὸν ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλῦ- τον τῦ χρισῦ, non pervestigabiles divitias Christi, quo nomine etiam simpliciter posito divitiæ mi- sericordiæ & benignitatis intelliguntur, imprimis divitiæ gratiæ Christi, quæ in Evangelio pandun- tur cum maxime, quamvis & divitiæ gloriæ & sa- pientiæ in eodem explicentur, 2. Cor. IIX. vers. 9. 2. Cor. II. 8. Col. II. 3. Divitiæ illæ gratiæ Christi dicuntur, ut ab opibus mundi discernantur, sunt- que remissio peccatorum, justitia, sanctitas, spes, certitudo gloriæ, salus æterna. Impervestigabiles sunt, tum quod citra divinam patefactionem hu- manæ rationis beneficio investigari nequeant, tum quod in hoc seculo, etiamsi per Verbum revelatæ sint, comprehendi mente non possint. Ex quo Theophylactus redarguit Eunomium, qui naturam & essentiam Christi se comprehendere dicebat. Quo sit, inquit, ut si ininvestigabiles sunt DEI opes, longe magis nec ejus vestigari substantia possit. Quo ergo pacto Eunomius hæreticus ille comprehen- dere se bujusmodi Dei substantiam jactabat? Quo- modo autem nota illa fiunt Angelis per Ecclesiam? Augustinus de Ecclesia triumphante exponit libr. V. de Genesi ad lit. cap. 19. Sed hoc alienum est. Nam de gratia exhibita Ecclesiæ in his terris agi- tur. Thomas de experimento visionis, quod id vi- deant, quod antea solum per revelationem nove- rint, 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. Alii de notificatione experimentali sic exponunt, quod rerum testimo- niis edocti non solum Judæis, sed & gentibus offerri gratuitam salutem in Christo etiam ab eo, qui paulo ante infensus erat hostis, & recipi per fidem intelligant voluntatem DEI de servandis gentibus æque ac Judæis, per fidem, absque lege ceremoniali; quam rationem antea minime co- gnoverint, multo minus, quod tam facili generi doctrinæ gentes cessuræ essent, doctrina tumentes, ut erudite exponitur a Crocio. Quæ vero notifica- tio non accipienda solitarie, sive qua objectum, sive qua modum. Nam non tantum mysterium vocatio- nis gentium Angelis magis patefactum fuit, sed etiam alia Christi mysteria, 1. Petr. I. 12. Nec solum ab experimento reali, sed etiam a revelatione ulterio- ri: διὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας non quidem, quasi Angeli didi- cerint ex ore ministri in Ecclesia accipiendo Ver- bum, ut homines, qui fidem ex auditu habent, Rom. X. 17. sed quod cognoscant, quæ in Ecclesia geruntur, 1. Cor. XI. 10. Luc. XV. 10. Imo Ecclesiæ ipsi annuncient accepta a Deo, ut in conceptione, nativitate, resurrectione, ascensione Christi in cœ- lum factum est, nec non in vocatione gentium, cum Petrus ad easdem primum ingredi debuit, Act. X. Neque enim διὰ hic necessario de causa vel medio explicatur, quum etiam sit idem, quod IN vel INTER, ut 1. Tim. II. 15. Gal. III. 19. inter Eccle- siasticos conventus, talia sunt notificata sive per Spiritum sanctum, qui loquutus est per Aposto- los, aliosque viros θεοπνεύςες, ut mysteria abs- condita revelaret; sive per immediatam revela- tionem de cœlo factam, aut a Filio Dei manifesta- tam, sive per patefactionem, quæ Ecclesiæ causa ipsis Angelis facta est. Explicari etiam potest διὰ Ἐκκλησίας propter Ecclesiam. Nam ejus causa facta est Angelis notificatio, ut particula διὰ etiam cum Genitivo occurrit, Rom. VI. vers. 4. 1. Tim. IV. 14. 2. Petr. I. 3.

## 3:9
V. 9. Καὶ φωτίσαι πάντας) To fulfill eminently the prophecy, Isa. 42:16. See above 1:18. Φωτίζειν, האיר, to teach, as Ps. 119:130, and it is rightly constructed with the Accusative of the person, as John 1:9. Ignatius, writing to the Roman Church, calls it πεφωτισμένη ἐν θελήματι Θεῦ.

Although τὸ Φωτίσαι happens through doctrine, it nevertheless inserts not only the external information of the Word, but the internal illumination of the mind, Acts XXVI. 18. 2. Cor. IV. 5. 6. and the light of heavenly refreshment, grace, joy, life, and every good thing, as Kircher observed from the Hebrew אור in his Concordance regarding the prophecy of Is. XLII. 16. It was shown around that prophetic passage that it deals not only with the mystical sense, which Grotius was accustomed to call eminent, but with the literal sense concerning the illumination of the Gentiles. The Apostle therefore means this: to bring into the light what had been as if hidden in darkness, and to expose it to the eyes of the Gentiles as well as the Jews, and to open the eyes of those who were previously blind and did not see the riches of Christ, by the preaching of the word, and to cause them now to see what they had previously not seen at all; not that he himself has the power of illuminating by himself, but that God uses him as His instrument by which He infuses light into both Gentiles and Jews, as Grotius rightly notes here along with Musculus and Zanchius.

Τίς ἡ οἰκονομία τῦ μυσηρίυ ) the dispensation or execution of that mystery.

Τῦ ἀποκεκρυμμένε ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ) Ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων here means from a very long time. See 1. Cor. II. 7. Ἐν τῷ Θεῷ within God, as above I. 9.

Τῦ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι διὰ Ἰησῦ χρισῦ ) See above II. 10. 15. for what κτίζειν means, and in our Prolegomena to the Gospels; Christ made all things new, 2. Cor. V. 17. and this creation is more divine than that former one.

Οἰκονομία τῦ μυσηρίε (thus Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, the Syriac read it, and Beza found it so in ancient codices) not only the execution of the mystery in God, but primarily that eternal dispensation of grace by which God tempered His justice and wrath against sinners with His grace and mercy, so that He might give His only-begotten Son for us, which is that highest mystery of divine wisdom, which was hidden not from a very long time, but from eternity in God, because we were chosen in Christ from eternity, Ephes. I. verse 4. Therefore here ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων is the same as πρὸ τῦ αἰώνων, 1. Cor. II. v. 2. which there signifies from eternity. Compare Col. I. 26. Nor is τὸ κτίζειν to be understood here as a new creation, even if it is added 'through Jesus Christ,' because through the same Logos, the eternal Son of God, all things were made that were made, John I. 2. All things were created in Him, through Him, and for Him, Col. I. 16. For it is signified that this mystery concerning Christ was hidden from eternity in God, who created all things through the Son, before anything at all was created, Eph. I. 4. And it is indicated at the same time that the work of redemption and reparation through Christ is of no less power than the creation made from nothing. And not only does the property of the word κτίζειν demand this sense, but also the designation of the object of creation, which is τὰ πάντα, all things. For were all things that exist repaired? But reparation only concerns the human race. But in the beginning of creation all things were created through the Son, John I. 3. through whom God also created the ages, Heb. I. 3. Therefore Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Jerome, and others understand this as the first creation, and God is accustomed to be described by it, even when there is talk of the promise of the Messiah, Is. XL. 22. 25. 26. ch. XLII. 5. 6. 7. XLV. 12. 13. Acts XIV. 15.

Latin:

V. 9. Καὶ φωτίσαι πάντας) Ad implendum eminenter vaticinium, Es. XLII. 16. Vide supra I. 18. Φωτίζειν האיר docere, ut Psal. CXIX. 130. & recte construitur cum Accu- sativo personæ, ut Joh. I. 9. Ignatius Romanæ Ecclesiæ scribens vocat eam πεφωτισμένη ἐν θελήματι Θεῦ.

Etsi τὸ Φωτίσαι per doctrinam fiat, insert tamen non externam tantum informationem Verbi , sed internam illuminationem mentis , Act. XXVI. 18. 2. Cor. IV. 5. 6. & lucem cœlestis refocillationis , gratiæ , lætitiæ , vitæ , omnisque boni , ut de Ebræo אור observavit in Concord. Kircherus in vaticinio Es. XLII. 16. non tantum sensu mystico , quem emi- nentem dicere consvevit Grotius, sed literali de illu- minatione gentium agi, circa locum illum Prophe- ticum ostensum fuit. Id ergo vult Apostolus , quod in tenebris quasi occultum fuerat , in lucem proferre , atq; id tam gentium quam Judæorum oculis exponere , & eorum , qui antea cæci erant , nec opes Christi vide- bant , verbi prædicatione oculos aperire , atque effice- re , ut nunc videant , quæ antea minime viderant , non quod ipse per se habeat vim illuminandi , sed quod Deus ipso utatur , tanquam suo instrumento , quo lu- cem infundat tam gentibus , quam Judæis , ut non male hic Grotius cum Musculo & Zanchio.

Τίς ἡ οἰκονομία τῦ μυσηρίυ ) dispensatio sive executio istius arcani.

Τῦ ἀποκεκρυμμένε ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ) Ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων hic valet a longissimo tempore. Vide 1. Cor. II. 7. Ἐν τῷ Θεῷ intra Deum , ut supra I. 9.

Τῦ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι διὰ Ἰησῦ χρισῦ ) Quid sit κτίζειν vide supra II. 10. 15. & in Prolegomenis nostris ad Evange- lia , omnia Christus fecit nova , 2. Cor. V. 17. & divinior hæc creatio , quam prior illa.

Οἰκονομία τῦ μυσηρίε ( sic legit Chrysost. Theo- doretus , Theophylactus , Oecumenius , Syrus , idque in veteribus codicibus invenit Beza ) non tantum executionem arcani in Deo , sed imprimis æter- nam illam gratiæ dispensationem , qua Deus justi- tiam & iram adversus peccatores gratia & miseri- cordia sua temperavit , ut Filium Unigenitum pro nobis daret , quod est summum illud sapientiæ divi- næ mysterium , quod non a longissimo tempore , sed ab æterno in Deo absconditum fuit , quia ab æterno in Christo electi sumus , Ephes. I. vers. 4. ideo hic ἀπὸ τῦ αἰώνων idem est , quod πρὸ τῦ αἰώνων, 1. Cor. II. v. 2. quod ibi significat ab æterno. Conf. Col. I. 26. Nequè τὸ κτίζειν hic de nova creatione accipiendũ , etsi addatur per Christum Jesum , quia per eundem Λόγον, æternum Dei Filium omnia facta sunt, quæ fa- cta , Joh. I. 2. Omnia condita sunt in ipso, per ipsum, & ad ipsum, Col. I. 16. Significatur enim ab æterno in Deo qui omnia per Filium condidit, hoc myste- rium de Christo absconditum fuisse, antequam ad- huc quicquam conderetur, Eph. I. 4. & indicatur simul, non minoris virtutis opus esse redemptionis & reparationis per Christum, quam creationis ex nihilo factæ. Nec solum verbi κτίζειν proprietas hunc sen- sum poscit, sed etiam objecti creationis designatio, quod sunt τὰ πάντα, omnia. Num enim omnia, quæ sunt, reparata sunt? Sed reparatio tantum ge- nus humanum concernit. At in principio creatio- nis omnia condita sunt per Filium, Joh. I. 3. per quē Deus & secula condidit, Ebr. I. 3. Ideo de creatione prima hæc intelligunt Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Hieronymus, alii, soletque Deus ab ea describi, etiam cum de promissione Messiæ ser- mo est, Es. XL. 22. 25. 26. c. XLII. 5. 6. 7. XLV. 12. 13. Actor. XIV. 15.

## 3:10
V. 10. Ἱνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς κὲ ταῖς ἐξυσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις ) That it might be made known even to the highest orders of Angels, that which before both they and the Prophets were ignorant of, God retaining that counsel with Himself; concerning the matter see 1. Pet. I. 2. But concerning the names of the principalities and powers, see above I. 21. and what was said there.

Διὰ τῦ Ἐκκλησίας ) see what great honor belongs to men, that God willed these secret counsels to be made known to the Angels through them, especially through the Apostles. Therefore, after this time, the Angels do not wish to be worshipped by the Apostles as if they were placed in a greater ministry, Rev. XIX. 1. and deservedly so. For many great commands had been given to the Angels, but none equal to this.

The manifold wisdom of God, truly a wondrous and varied dispensation of God. He gave easy laws to Adam: He allows him to fall to curb human pride: He allows vices to grow before the flood, and again after the flood: When vices and especially idolatry had increased again, He raised up one man, through whom the worship of the true God might be restored; He willed his descendants to experience by their own misfortune how great a difference there was between the institutions of Abraham and those of other nations, even those which were considered the most wise; then, as idolatry grew among other nations, and many Israelites were also drawn to imitate it, He led the descendants of Abraham out of that contagion, and in solitary places for forty years, even by inflicting diseases and deaths upon the stubborn, He purged them; then He gave them an excellent land, and rulers endowed with the Spirit of God, so that they might see what a great thing it was to be ruled by God; to those who wished, He permitted them to have Kings, and for the most part, evil ones. Under the Kings, however, the borders were well protected and they extended them, but they made bad use of those good things, and following the examples of the Kings, they lapsed into idolatry, and into all other vices, which usually follow idolatry as the leader of impiety. God warned them by degrees: first by the splitting of the kingdom, then by both parts being much vexed by foreign Princes; after the part of the ten tribes was first taken away, then what remained, so that they themselves might be corrected, and others might be terrified by that example; when the tribes that remained had not made good use of even this so severe a warning, He caused them also to be led away, and by a long and hard exile of seventy years He willed them to experience what kind of character idolaters had, so that they might the more abhor idolatry in the future; which medicine was so effective that the Jews afterwards relapsed into all other things rather than into idolatry; in that exile they led many from the nations to the knowledge of the true God by their instruction and example; having taken this experiment from them, God restored them to their homeland through Cyrus the King, who was not an idolater, yet not with full liberty, so that they might gradually become accustomed to the contempt of earthly things, and the hope of heavenly things, which the Messiah was fully about to reveal: And this whole time up to the Messiah was truly, as I just said, the vestibule of the Gospel. For many from the nations also acknowledged the true God during those times through the example of the Jews; but when that same people had fallen again, not indeed into idolatry, but into many other vices, which themselves are rightly called idolatry in a figurative sense, He repressed their ferocity first through the Macedonians, then through the Romans: and since most were not corrected at all, He sent Elijah, that is, John the Baptist, then the Messiah Himself, who for three years, by the holiness of His life and by miracles, surpassing all the Prophets and Moses himself, did everything that could be done to correct the Jews; He gathered some fruit, but in such a multitude, a small amount; the same thing happened to His Apostles after Him, being so badly treated by the Jews: What did God do? He abolished that ritual law, which had in itself nothing of either good or evil, but was devised for this purpose: first, so that the people, burdened with these rites and loving rites, might have that much less cause to follow idolatrous rites; second, so that under those figures they might understand greater things; since neither the former before the Babylonian exile, nor the latter after the Babylonian exile, had succeeded very well. He began a matter that was clearly new, unheard of, and incredible, and showed that He considered those from the nations who wished to follow the piety commanded by Christ, even if they did not become proselytes, as of no less value than either the Jews or the proselytes; and for that reason, He brought many Jews to piety by the example of the nations they had despised, and He brought an innumerable multitude of men, especially through the ministry of Paul, to that degree of piety and contempt for all earthly things and for this life itself, to which not even the best of the Jews had attained. Whoever has weighed these things well (and yet I have told only a small part of that dispensation, for it is not mine to conceive or to utter everything) he will certainly have a cause why he should admire and venerate the manifold wisdom of God, see Isaiah 55:9.

Latin:

V. 10. Ἱνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς κὲ ταῖς ἐξυσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπυρανίοις ) Ut patefiat etiam maximis Angelorum ordini- bus, id quod ante & ipsi & Prophetæ ignorarunt, Deo istud consilium apud se retinente, de re vide 1. Petr. I. 2. De no- minibus vero ἀρχῶν & ἐξυσιῶν supra I. 21. & ibi dicta.

Διὰ τῦ Ἐκκλησίας ) vide , quantus honos hominum , quod hæc arcana consilia per ipsos , maxime per Aposto- los , Deus innotescere Angelis voluit. Ideo Angeli post hoc tempus nolunt ab Apostolis coli tanquam in ministerio majore collocatis , Apoc. XIX. 1. & merito. Multa enim magna mandata data fuerant Angelis , sed nullum huic par.

Ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τῦ Θεῦ ) vere miranda tam varia Dei dispensatio. Adamo leges dedit faciles : Labi sinit ad coercendam humanam superbiam : sinit vitia crescere ante diluvium, rursus post diluvium: Auctis iterum vitiis & vi- tiorum maxime idololatria, unum hominem excitavit, per quem veri Dei cultus instauraretur, ejus posteros voluit ex- periri suo malo, quantũ esset discriminis inter instituta Ab- rahami & aliarum gentium, etiam earum, quæ sapientis- simæ habebantur, deinde gliscente apud alias gentes idolo- latria, multis quoque Isräelitis ad ejus imitationem tractis, eduxit ex ea contage Abrahami posteros, eosque in locis so- litariis per quadraginta annos, etiam morbis mortibusque immifsis in contumaces, purgavit, deinde dedit eis terram egregiam, & rectores Dei Spiritu donatos, ut viderent, quan- ta res esset, a Deo regi, volentibus permisit habere Reges, & pleròsque malos. Sub Regibus tamen fines bene tutati sunt & protulere, sed illis bonis male usi, & Regum secuti exem- pla, prolapsi sunt in idololatriam, & ad omnia alia vitia, quæ plerumque idololatriam, ut impietatis ducem sequi solent. Deus per gradus eos admonuit: Scisso primum regno, dein- de parte utraque multum vexata per Principes externos; post decem tribuum parte primum exigua, deinde, quod reliquum erat, abductis, ut & ipsi corrigerentur, & exemplo isto terrerentur alii, cum ne hac quidem tam severa admo- nitione recte usæ essent tribus, quæ restabant, eas quoque abduci fecit, & longo ac duro septuaginta annorum exilio experiri eos voluit, quali essent ingenio idololatræ, quo magis imposterum ab idololatria abhorrerent, quæ medici- na ita fuit valida, ut ad omnia alia potius, quam ad idolola- triam relapsi sint postea Judæi, in illo exilio multos ex gen- tibus sua institutione & exemplo ad cognitionem veri Dei perduxerunt; hoc de ipsis sumpto experimento Deus per Cyrum Regem non idololatram eos in patriam restituit, non tamen cum plena libertate, ut paulatim ad contemptũ rerum terrenarum, & spem rerum cœlestium, quas plene e- rat revelaturus Messias, assuescerent: Et hoc tempus omne ad Messiam usque vere, ut modo dixi, vestibulum fuit Ev- angelii. Nam & multi ex gentibus per ea tempora Deum verum agnovere Judæorum exemplo; at cum rursus idem ille populus non quidem ad idololatriam, sed ad alia vitia plurima, quæ & ipsa ωςικῶς recte dicuntur idololatria, de- cidiffet, per Macedonas primum, deinde per Romanos re- pressit eorum ferociam: ac plerisque nihil correctis misit Eliam, id est, Johannem Baptistam, deinde Messiam ipsum, qui per triennium & vitæ sanctitate & miraculis omnes Pro- phetas ipsumque Mosen superans, omnia fecit quæ fieri po- terant ad corrigendos Judæos, frugem collegit aliquam, sed in tanta multitudine exiguam, idem post ipsum tam ma- le tractatum a Judæis evenit Apostolis ejus: Quid fecit Deus? Legem illam ritualem nihil in se habentem aut boni aut mali, sed in hoc repertam, primum ut istis ritibus onerata plebs rituum amans, eo minus causæ haberet sequendi ritus idolatricos, deinde ut sub illis figuris res intelligerent majores, cum nec prius illud ante Babylonicum exilium, nec posterius illud post Babylonicum exilium ἐπιτοπολὺ be- ne successiffet, antiquavit: Rem orsus est plane novam, inauditam atque incredibilem, ostenditque, se illos ex gen- tibus, qui pietatem a Christo præceptam vellent sequi, etiamsi non fierent proselyti, nihilo minoris ducere, quam aut Judæos aut proselytos, eaque ratione tum Judæos mul- tos, exemplo gentium, quas contempserant, ad pietatem adduxit, tum innumeram hominum multitudinem, Pauli maxime ministerio, ad eum perduxit pietatis gradum & re- rum omnium terrenarum, atque ipsius vitæ hujus contem- ptum, ad quem ne optimi quidem ex Judæis pervenerant. Hæc qui bene expenderit (& tamen exiguam tantum par- tem dixi illius dispensationis, neque enim omnia aut con- cipere, aut eloqui meum est) is certe causam habebit, cur admiretur ac veneretur τὴν πολυποίκιλον σοφίαν τῦ θεῦ, vide Es. LV. v. 9.

## 3:11
V. 11. According to the most ancient purpose, the evidence of which is the promise made to Abraham concerning the great goods which the nations were to obtain through one of Abraham's descendants. Thus we interpret from Titus 1:2. Concerning the word purpose, see Romans 8:28, chapter 9:11, and concerning the verb to purpose, Romans 3:25, above 1:9. Which He wrought in Christ Jesus, our Lord; wrought, that is, He executed through Christ.

Grotius places the object of the notification made to the Angels, the manifold wisdom of God, in merely legal matters, even though he also uses the name of the Gospel, which, however, Grotius understands in his own way, that is, perversely, concerning the more perfect Mosaic legal commandments, along with the Pelagianizing Socinians. Hence, in such a prolix explanation of the dispensation of divine grace, he does not mention by a word the reconciliation made through the blood of Jesus Christ, or redemption, and the merit of Christ, and similar things, but he says only that he did everything which could be done for the correcting of the Jews. Although indeed the dispensation of the calling of the Gentiles, which was truly done for the fruition of that redemption and reconciliation of Christ, is intended by the Apostle here: yet that is not the only nor the chief thing in the mystery τῆς οἰκονομίας, or οἰκονομία τõ μυστηρίε and the evangelization of the unsearchable riches of Christ, and the notification made to the principalities and powers, in which, beyond controversy, in the great mystery of godliness, the first place is deservedly obtained by Φανέρωσις θεõ ἐν σαρκὶ, 1 Tim. III. 16. into which, along with other mysteries of Christ concerning his sufferings and the glory that followed the same, and similar things ἐπιθυμõσιν Ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι, the angels long to look, 1 Pet. I. v. 12. Theophylact noted that this was the sense of Nyssen: Gregory, he says, of Nyssa affirms that before the incarnation the celestial powers had a certain simple knowledge of God, namely that he created all things by his will alone, and they understood that it was permitted to him to moderate all things and wisely to care for all things. But when the Word of God was incarnate, contrary effects were produced by the contrary. For through death life succeeded, through weakness power, through ignominy glory, and finally through the baser things were attained those which were worthy of God. Thus therefore now the multiform wisdom and power of God is known to the celestial beings, which, when they became known to us, those powers, having perceived through us the Church, how great were the goods with which it was endowed (held worthy), were led to a more certain knowledge of divine wisdom. Nor indeed is either σοφία τõ θεõ, or that notification κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶν αἰώνων, ἣν ἐποίησεν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησõ, or the purpose itself ἐν χριστῷ restricted to the calling of the Gentiles, but it embraces the whole mystery concerning Christ, which the Apostle had expounded in the two previous chapters: just as Grotius himself extends it to the immense goods which the Gentiles were to obtain through Christ, not only the Gentiles, who are so called in particular, but, as we add, all the nations of the earth: but that πρόθεσις denotes not some ancient, but an eternal purpose, which was made πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων in Christ: for these words sound of an eternal decree, not of a temporal execution of a decree. Whence it is a distortion when Grotius explains the word ἐποίησεν as 'he executed,' when it properly signifies the purpose WHICH God MADE in Christ. Wherefore πρόθεσις αἰώνων is not a predefinition concerning future ages, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Cornelius a Lapide explain it concerning men of any ages. But as Theodoret explained: According to the predefinition of the ages, that is, he had proposed these things before the ages. For πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων is a Hebraism, that is, αἰώνιος, as Jerome, Haymo, B. Luther, and most others have also rendered it. πρόθεσις περὶ τῶν αἰώνων and πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων are different. Jerome, Photius, and Theophylact refer the pronoun ἣν (ἐποίησεν) to σοφίαν. But there is no reason why it should not be referred to the closer noun, τὴν πρόθεσιν, which was done by Haymo, Hugo, Lombard, Thomas, Lyranus, Hunnius, Calvin, Beza, and others.

Latin:

V. 11. Κατὰ πρόθεσιν ὤ αἰώνων) secundum propositum antiquissimum, cujus indicium est promissio facta Abraha- mo de ingentibus bonis, quæ per aliquem ex posteris Abra- hami gentes essent adepturæ. Sic interpretamur ex Tito I. v. 2. De voce πρόθεσεως vid. Rom. VIII. 28. cap. IX. 11. & de verbo προτίθεσθαι Rom. III. 25. supra I. 9. ἧν ἐποίησεν ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησῦ, τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν ) ἐποίησεν, id est, executus est per Christum.

Objectum notificationis Angelis factæ τὴν πολυ- ποίκιλον τῦ Θεῦ constituit Grotius in mere legalibus, etsi nomine Evangelii etiam utatur, quod vero suo modo, id est, perverse de mandatis perfectioribus legalibus Mosaicis cum Socinianis Pelagianizanti- bus intelligit Grotius. Hinc in tam prolixa dispen- sationis gratiæ divinæ explicatione ne verbo me- minit reconciliationis per sanguinem Jesu Christi factæ, aut redemptionis, & meriti Christi ac similium, sed tantum fecisse eum omnia dicit, quæ fieri po- terant ad corrigendos Judæos. Quanquam vero vocationis gentium dispensatio, quæ vere facta est ad illius redemptionis & reconciliationis Chri- sti fruitionem, ab Apostolo hic intendatur: ea tamen non sola nec præcipua est in mysterio τῆς οἰκονομίας, vel οἰκονομία τõ μυστηρίε & evangeli- zatione impervestigabilium divitiarum Christi, ac notificatione principatibus & potestatibus facta, in quo citra controversiam magno pietatis mysterio, primum locum merito obtinet Φανέρωσις θεõ ἐν σαρκὶ, 1. Tim. III. 16. in quod cum aliis Christi mysteriis de passionibus ejus, & de gloria eandem consecuta ac similibus ἐπιθυμõσιν Ἄγγελοι παρα- κύψαι, gestiunt Angeli introspicere, 1. Petr. I. v. 12. Hunc sensum fuisse Nysseni notavit Theophyla- ctus: Gregorius, inquit, Nysses ante incarnationem affirmat simplicem quandam potestates cælestes ha- buisse Dei cognitionem, videlicet quod sola voluntate cuncta creaverit, & eidem licere omnia provide- bant, moderarique universa & sapienter curare omnia intelligebant. Incarnato autem Dei Verbo ex contrario contraria sunt effecta. Nam per mortem vita successit, per infirmitatem potentia, per igno- miniam gloria, per viliora denique sunt consecuta, quæ Deum decerent. Sic igitur nunc multiformis cognita cælestibus Dei est sapientia atque potentia, quæ ubi nobis innotuere, potestates illæ per nos per- specta Ecclesia, quantis esset dignata (digna habita) bonis; ad certiorem sunt divinæ sapientiæ cognitio- nem deductæ. Neque vero vel σοφία τõ θεõ, vel no- tificatio illa κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶν αἰώνων, ἣν ἐποίησεν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησõ, aut ipsa πρόθεσις ἐν χριστῷ est restri- cta ad vocationem gentium, sed complectitur uni- versum mysterium de Christo, quod prioribus duobus capitibus exposuerat Apostolus: quemad- modum Grotius ipse id extendit ad ingentia bona, quæ per Christum gentes adepturæ essent, non gentes tantum, quæ in specie ita vocantur, sed quod addimus, universæ nationes terræ: πρόθεσις vero illa non antiquum aliquod, sed æternum pro- positum notat, quod πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων factum est in Christo: De decreto enim æterno, non de tempo- rali executione decreti hæc sonant. Unde στρεβλό- της est, cum Grotius verbum ἐποίησεν exponit, exe- cutus est, quum proprie significet propositum, QVOD FECIT Deus in Christo. Quapropter πρό- θεσις αἰώνων non est præfinitio de seculis futuris, ut Chrysostomus, Theophylactus & Cornelius a Lapide id explicant de hominibus quorumvis seculorum. Sed ut Theodoretius exposuit: Secundum præfinitio- nem seculorum, hoc est, hæc ante secula proposuerat. Est enim Ebraïsmus πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων, id est, αἰώνιος, ut reddidere etiam Hieronymus, Haymo, B. Lutherus, & plerique alii. Diversa sunt πρόθε- σις περὶ τῶν αἰώνων & πρόθεσις τῶν αἰώνων. Prono- men ἣν (ἐποίησεν) ad σοφίαν referunt Hieronymus, Photius, Theophylactus. Sed non est, cur non ad propius nomen, τὴν πρόθεσιν, referatur, quod fa- ctum ab Haymone, Hugone, Lombardo, Thoma, Lyrano, Hunno, Calvino, Beza, aliis.

## 3:12
V. 12. Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν παῤῥησίαν) παῤῥησία by its origin of speaking signifies liberty, but by a meaning drawn further, confidence, as can be seen in Levit. XXVI. 16, where in the Hebrew is רבמיות, and that Spirit produces great confidence, testifying that God is Father to us, Rom. VIII. 15, Gal. IV. 6. Philo on the heir of divine things: 'When do you have παῤῥησία, a servant toward a master? Is it not when he is not conscious of having done wrong, but both says and does everything on behalf of his possessor? When then is it worthy for the servant of God also to speak freely toward his own and the ruler and master of all, if not when he is pure from sins, and judges the love of the master from his conscience, using greater joy in being a servant of God than if he ruled over the whole race of men?'

Καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν) free access, above II. v. 18. קרבת אלהים, Isa. LVIII. 2. In the Manuscript, τὴν is missing.

Ἐν πεποιθήσει) With great hope of future things. The Hebrew בטח is for the most part translated as ἐλπὶς: but πεποίθησις is found in 2 Kings XVIII. 20. See 2 Cor. I. 15, III. 4, VIII. 22, X. 2, Phil. III. 4.

Διὰ πίστεως ἀυτῦ) that is, through that faith which Christ has produced in us. This genitive does not signify the cause from which, as above in 1, but the object, as in Mark XI. 22, where see the things said.

These things again serve to confirm the hope and certainty of the eternal inheritance. Some explain παῤῥησίαν as confidence, others as liberty. Blessed Luther, whom Crocius here prefers to the rest, rendered it Freudigkeit, by which means both the confidence of the heart and the παῤῥησία of prayer are denoted, by which they do not lay down their prayers timidly, as servants before masters, but with confidence, as children before parents. In whom, as Mediator, 1 Tim. II. 5, we have [it] through faith: For the application is held in the Word ἔχομεν, and that is expressed subsequently διὰ τ' πίστεως; it hints at a cheerful and joyful παῤῥησίαν or confidence, Phil. I. 20, Heb. III. v. 6, c. IV. 16, c. X. 19, 35, Philem. v. 8, 1 John II. v. 21, c. III. v. 21, c. IV. 17, c. V. 14. προσαγωγή concerns free access, such as that of subjects to a Magistrate or a Prince devoted to them, or of children to their Parents, which Christ has prepared for us through reconciliation, and which we who are justified through Christ possess, Rom. V. 2, Eph. I. 18, ἐν πεποιθήσει in confidence, boasting, hope. The word is used in relation to men, 2 Cor. VIII. 22, and to God, as here, and 2 Cor. III. 4, where we do not deny that the same hope is implied, just as it occurs here concerning the hope of being heard and of the inheritance of heavenly goods, by which, approaching God, we seek these things. The Apostle adds διὰ πίστεως ἀυτᾶ, through faith in him, that is, in him. We admit that the object is noted, just as faith in Christ is expressed, Rom. III. 22, Gal. III. v. 16, 20, 22, Phil. III. 9, Rev. XIV. 12, by which he signifies the same thing as Eph. I. 15, Gal. III. 26, Col. I. 4, faith in Christ Jesus, and Rom. III. 23, 1 Tim. III. 13, 2 Tim. III. 15. faith in his blood, and what denotes faith in Christ, Acts XX. 21, c. XXIV. 25, c. XXVI. 18, Col. IV. 15, Philem. v. 5. But the fact that the Papists object from this passage that faith is not confidence, because it is distinguished from confidence, is easily resolved. Naturally, the Apostle here accumulated different names to express the nature of faith: παῤῥησίαν, πεποίθησιν, and πίσιν, which distinctly designate parts of faith. For faith specially denotes knowledge, though not excluding other acts; confidence denotes assent and certain persuasion; boldness brings in trust: But neither does confidence exclude knowledge or trust, nor does boldness exclude knowledge or assent. Add that faith is as it were the whole, boldness as it were a part; since the former embraces all three degrees, and trust is as it were its soul.

Latin:

V. 12. Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν παῤῥησίαν) παῤῥησία ex origine quidem loquendi significat libertatem, sed longius per du- cta significatione fiduciam, ut videre est Levit. XXVI. 16. ubi in Ebræo רבמיות, magnam autem fiduciam parit Spi- ritus ille attestans Deum nobis esse Patrem, Rom. VIII. 15. Gal. IV. 6. Philo de hærede rerum divinarum: Πότε ἐν ἄγεις παῤῥησίαν οἰκέτης πρὸς δεσπότην ἆρ' ὀυχ ὅταν ἠδικηκότι μὲν ἑαυ- τῷ οὐκ συνειδῇ, πάντα δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶ κεκτημένε κὶ λέγοντι κὶ πράττοντι. Πότε ἓν ἄξιον κὶ τὸν τῶ θεῶ δõλον ἐλευθεροστομεῖν πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτõ κὶ τõ παντὸς ἡγεμόνα κὶ δεσπότην, ἤ ὅταν ἁμαρτημάτων καθαρεύῃ, κὶ τὸ Φιλοδέσποτον ἐκ τῶ συνειδότος κρίνῃ, πλείονι χαρᾷ χρώμενος ἐπὶ τῷ θεράπων γενέσθαι Θεõ, ἤ εἰ τõ παντός ἀνθρώπων γένες ἐβασίλευσε.

Καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν) aditum liberum supra II. v. 18. קרבת אלהים, Es. LVIII. 2. In Manuscripto deest τὴν.

Ἐν πεποιθήσει) Cum spe magna rerum futurarum. בטח Ebræum plerumque; ἐλπὶς vertitur : πεποίθησις autem 2. Reg. XVIII. 20. Vide 2. Cor. I. 15. III. 4. VIII. 22. X. 2. Phil. III. 4.

Διὰ πίστεως ἀυτῦ) id est per eam fidem, quam Christus in nobis effecit. Iste Genitivus non causam ex qua, ut su- pra 1. sed objectum significat, ut Marci XI. 22. ubi dicta vide.

Hæc iterum ad confirmandam spem & certitu- dinem hæreditatis æternæ faciunt. Παῤῥησίαν alii de fiducia exponunt, alii de libertate. B. Lutherus, quem hic cæteris præfert Crocius, reddidit Freu- digkeit, quo pacto & fiducia cordis, & παῤῥησία orationis, qua non timidiufcule, ut servi coram Dominis, sed cum confidentia, ut liberi coram pa- rentibus suas deponunt preces, denotatur. In quo, ut Mediatore, 1. Tim. II. 5. habemus per fidem: Nam applicatio in Verbo ἔχομεν habetur, idque expri- mitur deinceps διὰ τ' πίστεως; παῤῥησίαν vel fidu- ciam innuit hilarem, & lætam, Phil. I. 20. Ebr. III. vers. 6. c. IV. 16. cap. X. 19. 35. Philem. v. 8. 1. Joh. II. vers. 21. c. III. v. 21. c. IV. 17. c. V. 14. προσαγω- γὴ de libero aditu, qualis est subditorum ad Ma- gistratum, vel Principem sibi addictum, liberorum ad Parentes, quem Christus nobis per reconcilia- tionem paravit, quemque justificati per Christum habemus, Rom. V. 2. Eph. I. 18. ἐν πεποιθήσει in confidentia, gloriatione, spe. Adhibetur vox in re- latione ad homines, 2. Cor. VIII. 22. & ad Deum, ut hic, & 2. Cor. III. 4. ubi non abnuimus, spem ean- dem inferri, quemadmodum hic de spe exaudi- tionis & hæreditatis bonorum cœlestium, qua ac- cedentes ad Deum ea expetimus, occurrit. Addit Apostolus διὰ πίστεως ἀυτᾶ, per fidem ipsius, hoc est, in ipsum. Objectum notari admittimus, uti fides Christi exprimitur, Rom. III. 22. Gal. III. vers. 16. 20. 22. Phil. III. 9. Apoc. XIV. 12. quo idem signifi- cat, quod Eph. I. 15. Gal. III. 26. Col. I. 4. πίςις ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησᾶ, & Rom. III. 23. 1. Tim. III. 13. 2. Tim. III. 15. πίςις ἐν τῷ ἅιματι ἀυτᾶ, quodque notat πίσις ἐις τὸν χριστὸν, Act. XX. 21. c. XXIV. 25. c. XXVI. 18. Col. IV. 15. Philem. v. 5. Quod vero Pontificii ex hoc loco fidem non esse fiduciam objici- unt, quia a fiducia distinguitur, facile expeditur. Nimirum cumulavit hic Apostolus diversa nomi- na ad fidei naturam exprimendam τὴν παῤῥησίαν, τὴν πεποίθησιν καὶ τὴν πίςιν, quæ partes fidei distin- cte designant. Nam πίςις specialiter notitiam, non exclusis tamen cæteris actibus, πεποίθησις as- sensum & persuasionem certam, παῤῥησία fiduciam infert: Sed nec πεποίθησις notitiam aut fiduciam, nec παῤῥησία notitiam aut assensum excludit. Ad- de quod πίςις veluti totum sit, παῤῥησία veluti pars; Siquidem illa omnes tres gradus comple- ctatur, ejusque veluti anima sit fiducia.

## 3:13
V. 13. Wherefore I ask) Since our confidence in God is so just, I pray you.

Not to lose heart) To lose heart is indeed elsewhere to grow sluggish, but here rather to be terrified. For the Greeks also often call those who are timid cowardly; the fear of danger and of labor are neighbors. In the Glossary, I fail.

In my tribulations) on account of these chains and other evils which I bear.

For you) He repeats what he had said above 1. These things happen to me for your sake; it is right that you should not be ashamed of the thing of which I am not ashamed.

The Syrian, Theodoret, and Jerome understand prayers directed to God, that Paul might not grow sluggish or lose heart on account of his afflictions; but that the Apostle is praying the Ephesians, when he could warn and command, that they themselves should not grow sluggish on account of the afflictions which he sustains for their sake, as Blessed Luther renders it with Theophylact, that you do not grow weary, which sense of the word, because it is more accepted, Luke XVIII. v. 1, 2 Cor. IV. v. 1, Gal. VI. 9, 2 Thess. III. 13, there is no reason why we should desert the same. Chrysostom notes here a great argument for divine love, because not only did the Son of GOD have to die in their stead, but also His servants had to be afflicted for His good. Moreover, they endured chains for their good, both because they were confirmed by the same in the truth of the doctrine, for which he did not hesitate to undergo great afflictions own example he taught both patience in afflictions, 2 Cor. I. 6. and the way into the kingdom of God through many tribulations, 2 Cor. VI. 8. Acts XIV. 22. 2 Tim. II. 9.

Which is your glory) He could have said, which are your glory, which evils bring you much honor, but both among the Hebrews, and among the Greeks and among the Latins, the relative pronoun is accustomed to be conformed as much to the latter as to the former part. Such is that of Cicero: The fires which you call stars. It was truly the honor of all Christians, especially those who had been called from the Gentiles, that Paul refused to suffer no evils for the discipline which he was handing down.

Some others refer the glory not to the martyrdom of Paul, but to the constancy of the Ephesians in a not inconvenient sense, that this would be their own glory, if they do not grow sluggish, so as to fail because of Paul's afflictions, but remain constant. But the explanation of Grotius is more common, and declares that 'for you', and provides an argument for the Apostolic admonition, that you ought not to be deterred from the Gospel by that which is glorious to you. But my chains are glorious to you. Thus Jerome, Theophylact, and most others.

PART II. Euktike with doxology.

Latin:

V. 13. Διὸ ἀιτᾶμαι) Cum tam justa sit nostra in Deum fiducia, precor vos.

Μὴ ἐκκακεῖν) Ἐκκακεῖν alibi quidem est segnescere, sed hic potius expavescere. Nam & Græci κακὸς sæpe vocant eos, qui sunt timidi, vicina sunt timor periculi & laboris. In Glossario ἐκκακῶ deficio.

Ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσί με) ob hæc vincula & mala alia, quæ fero.

Ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν) Repetit, quod dixerat supra 1. Vestri causa hæc mihi eveniunt, æquum est, ne vos pœniteat rei, cujus me non pœnitet.

Preces ad Deum directas, ne Paulus segnescat vel deficiat ob afflictiones, Syrus, Theodoretius, & Hieronymus intelligunt; at Apostolum precari Ephesios, quum monere ac jubere posset, ne ipsi segnescant propter afflictiones, quas ipsorum cau- sa sustineat, ut B. Lutherus reddit cum Theophyla- cto, daß ihr nicht mude werdet, qui sensus verbi, quia receptior est, Luc. XIIX. vers. 1. 2. Cor. IV. vers. 1. Gal. VI. 9. 2. Thess. III. 13. non est, quod eundem deseramus. Magnum hic notat divini a- moris argumentum Chrysostomus, quod non tantum Filius DEI illorum vice mori debuit, sed & servi ejus illius bono affligi. Bono autem eorum sustine- bant vincula, tum quod confirmati iisdem sint in veritate doctrinæ, pro qua non dubitavit magnas afflictiones subire, tum quod exemplo suo do- cuerit & patientiam in afflictionibus, 2. Cor. I. 6. & viam in regnum Dei per multas tribulationes, 2. Cor. VI. 8. Act. XIV. 22. 2. Tim. II. 9.

Ἥτις ἐςὶ δόξα ὑμῶν) Potuerat dicere, αἵτινές εἰσι δόξα ὑμῶν, quæ mala multum vobis honoris adferunt, sed & apud Ebræos, & apud Græcos & apud Latinos relativum Pronomen tam posteriori quam priori parti conformari so- let. Tale illud Ciceronis: Ignibus quæ sidera vocatis. Vere honos erat omnium Christianorum, maxime eorum, qui ex gentibus vocati erant, quod Paulus nulla mala pati recusabat pro ea, quam tradebat, disciplina.

Alii nonnulli gloriam referunt non ad marty- rium Pauli, sed ad constantiam Ephesiorum sensu non incommodo, quod hæc ipsorum gloria futura sit, si non segnescant, ut defecerint ob Pauli affli- ctiones, sed constantes permæserint. Sed explicatio Grotii communior est, & declarat illud ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, atque argumentum præbet monitioni Apostoli- cæ, quod vobis gloriosum est, eo absterreri non debe- tis ab Evangelio. At gloriosa vobis sunt vincula mea. Ita Hieronymus, Theophylactus, & alii plerique.

PARS II. Ἐυκτικὴ cum δοξολογίᾳ.

## 3:14
V. 14. For this cause) Namely for this, that you may not waver, terrified by my evils.

I bow my knees) which is the custom of those praying in anxious matters. See what is said at Matt. VI. 5. Mark XV. 19. Luke XXII. 41. Acts VII. 60. IX. 40. XX. 36. XXI. 5.

To the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ) see above I. 2. In the Manuscript those words 'of our Lord Jesus Christ' are missing, and without them the following parts cohere better, and Jerome teaches us that these were absent from the Greeks at their own time as well. The sense remains the same.

Therefore the words which are found in most Codices are not to be rashly questioned, nor do they hinder the sense at all; indeed, they contribute to fostering confidence, because when we invoke God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we also profess with confidence that the same is our Father in our Lord Jesus Christ, John XX. 17. Of those whose Lord Christ is by right of actual redemption, He is their Father by right of adoption; thus the Apostle simultaneously separates himself by this invocation from the Gentiles, who worship their fictitious gods, and from the Jews, who do not invoke the Father of Jesus Christ, and declares that he does not wish to join his prayers with them. Moreover, the prayer follows conveniently after the exposition of the state of grace of the Ephesians, so that they may be preserved in it, to which he had indeed exhorted them with his prayers, namely, that they should not grow sluggish or fail. But since that is not situated in human powers, therefore he bends his knees to the Father of Jesus Christ, that He may deign to strengthen them: such prayers are frequent for the Apostle for the faithful to whom he wrote, Phil. I. 9. Col. I. 9. 2 Thess. I. 9. Philem. v. 6. But the Apostle pours himself out into this prayer in the middle of the course of the epistle because of the fervor of the Spirit and his love toward the Ephesians, even though he had already mentioned his prayers in the first chapter, and had conceived them for the same. Furthermore, this prayer of the Apostle concerns both the salvation of the Ephesians and the honor of God: he prays that the former be promoted, and the latter be celebrated through the Church. There the prayer is euktike, here it is doxological. The strengthening of the Spirit, the indwelling of Christ, and the being rooted in the love of God look toward the salvation of the Ephesians. That we may be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner man, it is necessary that Christ dwell in us through faith; that that dwelling place or temple of Christ may be prepared, it is necessary that we be rooted in the love of God toward us; which is as it were the foundation and root of faith, through which we are built up and rise into the dwelling place of Christ. But when we are properly rooted in the love of God, we know the immensity of the love of God and Christ, and we are filled with all the fullness of God. With which prayers the Apostle lays down as a base both the divine power, by which He is able to do superabundantly more than we ask or can conceive in our mind, and the grace, which one may gather from the power working in us, and from the doxology, and the celebration of God in Christ, by which it is subjoined with a certain confidence of grace, as if the prayer had already been heard: But he also constitutes a part of the prayer, as that by which the Apostle contends that the glory of God be celebrated in the Church through Christ Jesus, through all generations for ever and ever: which prayer he seals with the word of faith: Amen.

Jerome refers genuflection to the knees of the mind, which the Apostle undoubtedly bent first; but in order to bend them more devoutly, with due humiliation, he also bent the knee of his body to the ground, and the literal sense implies this, from which one should not rashly depart, especially because by this sign he wished to express the thing itself, namely his devotion, and thus to testify his love to the Ephesians. Theophylact: When he says (he says) I bend my knees, he shows that he is praying with great ardor of spirit. Chrysostom says that by this he declares that he is praying in the way that those who pray in afflicted circumstances are accustomed to do.

Latin:

V. 14. Τύτε χάριν) Nempe in hoc, ne malis meis territi labascatis.

Κάμπτω τὰ γόνατά μυ) qui mos precantium in rebus anxiis. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. VI. 5. Marci XV. 19. Luc. XXII. 41. Act. VII. 60. IX. 40. XX. 36. XXI. 5.

Πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα τῦ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χριςῦ) vide supra I. 2. In Manuscripto desunt illa τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χριςῦ & sine illis melius cohærent sequentia, & suo quoque tem- pore a Græcis hæc abfuisse, docet nos Hieronymus. Sensus idem manet.

Non ergo temeræ verba solicitanda, quæ in Codicibus plerisque reperiuntur, nec sensui quic- quam officiunt, imo ad fiduciam fovendam faciũt, quia cum Deum Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Chri- sti invocamus, eundem etiam Patrem nostrum in Domino nostro Jesu Christo esse cum fiducia pro- fitemur, Job. XX. 17. quorum Christus Dominus est jure actualis redemptionis, eorum Pater est jure adoptionis; ita simul separat Apostolus se hac in- vocatione ab Ethnicis, qui Deos suos fictitios adorant, & a Judæis, qui non invocant Patrem Je- su Christi, ac declarat, se nolle cum illis preces suas conjungere. Sequitur autem commode precatio expositionem status gratiæ Ephesiorum, ut in illo conserventur, ad quod ipsos quidem precibus suis hortatus erat, ne scilicet segnescant aut deficiant. Sed quum id in viribus humanis situm non sit, ideo genua sua flectit ad Patrem Jesu Christi, ut eos- dem corroborare dignetur: quales precationes Apostolo pro fidelibus, ad quos scripsit, frequen- tes sunt, Phil. I. 9. Col. I. 9. 2. Thess. I. 9. Philem. v. 6. Sed in hanc precationem in medio cursu epistolæ effunditur Apostolus præ Spiritus, & amoris sui fervore erga Ephesios, tametsi preces suas in pri- mo capite jam commemorarit, & conceperit pro iisdem. Cæterum hæc precatio Apostoli con- cernit tum Ephesiorum salutem, tum Dei honorem: Illam promoveri, hunc per Ecclesiam celebrari precatur. Ibi oratio est ἐυκτικὴ, hic δοξολογική. Ad salutem Ephesiorum spectat corroboratio Spiritus, inhabitatio Christi, & fundatio in amore Dei. Ut Spiritu corroboremur in interiori homine, opor- tet, ut per fidem in nobis habitet Christus; ut habi- taculum vel templum illud Christi præparetur, oportet, ut in dilectione Dei erga nos radicemur; quæ est veluti fundamentum & radix fidei, per quam ædificamur & assurgimus in habitaculum Christi. Cum vero probe radicamur in Dei dile- ctione, cognoscimus immensitatem amoris Dei & Christi, & implemur omni plenitudine Dei. Quibus precibus substernit Apostolus pro basi divinam tum potentiam, qua valet superabundanter plura facere, quam petimus, aut mente concipere possu- mus, tum gratiam, quam e vi operante in nobis colligere licet, & e δοξολογίᾳ, & celebratione Dei in Christo, qua subjungitur e certa gratiæ fiducia, quasi jam exaudita esset precatio: Sed etiam par- tem constituit precationis, utpote qua Apostolus contendit, ut gloria Dei celebretur in Ecclesia per Christum Jesum, per omnes generationes in se- cula seculorum: quam precationem obsignat ver- bo fidei: Amen.

Genuflexionem Hieronymus ad genua mentis re- fert, quæ sine dubio flexit imprimis Apostolus, sed ut devotius flecteret, cum debita humiliatione, cor- poris etiam poplite in terram flexit, idque τὸ ῥητὸν importat, a quo temere non est discedendum, ma- xime, quia hoc signo exprimere rem ipsam voluit, nempe devotionem, adeoque amorem suum te- stari Ephesiis. Theophylactus: Cum autem (inquit) flecto genua dicit, ostendit, se ingenti animi ardore precari. Chrysostomus ait, per id ita se precari decla- rare, quomodo solent, qui rebus afflictis precantur.

## 3:15
V. 15. Ἐξ ὗ πᾶσα πατριὰ ἐν ὐρανοῖς κὴ ἐπὶ γῆς ὀνομάζεται is family, as can be seen in Exod. VI. 25. XII. verse 1. and in a great number of other places. It is customary for the Hebrews, as we also touched upon above, when they speak of angels and pious men, to call them the superior and inferior family of God; both are called sons of God, both are called the family of God, and this is what is said here. Not far removed is that of Simplicius in his commentaries on Epictetus: Αἱ πολλαὶ ἀρχαὶ πάντων ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς ἔχουσι τὸ τ’ ἀρχῆς ἀξίωμα, and this of Proclus on the Timaeus: Πάντα τὰ δημιεργικὰ αἴτια ὡς ὑφ’ ἓν κέντρον συνέπει τὴν μίαν τῶν πάντων πατρικὴν αἰτίαν. The Hebrews think it magnificent that they can trace their lineage to Judah, Reuben, and the other sons of Jacob; but we are reckoned by God the Father: Τοῖυ παρ τρὸς ἐυχόμεθ’ εἶναι.

Although there are not lacking even among Christians those who wish for angels to be included here, such as Lombard, Thomas, and others among the Papists, with Theodoret designating God the Creator as the Father of all here, and Jerome even judging that archangels and other superior beings are brought in when he speaks of the Fathers of the angels, but he brings this forward without foundation. More conveniently, however, the name of Father, by which he addressed God here, is regarded, for whose sake it is to be believed that every family is named, as indeed every family, but descending from this one Father in Christ Jesus, or as He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and thus of all who are in Christ Jesus. Which is a fatherhood not according to the inner nature, but according to the outer, not with respect to the divine nature of Christ, by which He is the Son of God begotten from the substance of the Father from eternity, but by reason of the human nature which He assumed for our sake, according to which He is consubstantial with us and our brother, Heb. II. 11. Yet by a different reasoning He is called the Father of Christ, and the Father of the faithful of Christ, because He adopted us as His sons when we were by nature children of wrath, but He raised the flesh of Christ, devoid of all sin, into the hypostasis of His only-begotten Son, of which elsewhere. Here every family is spoken of with regard to those who descend from God the Father through Christ. Whence some refer the pronoun (ἐξ) to Christ himself, such as Calvin, Zanchius, Musculus, and Aretius, which, however, is more correctly referred here to the Father, following the ancients Chrysostom, Theodoret, Jerome, and Theophylact; but by Bullinger and Gualther, πατριὰ is not inappropriately explained as family, which is noted not only among the LXX Interpreters, when אבות is joined with בית, but also when it is joined with ראשו, or with שרו, as can be seen from the Concordances, and it corresponds to the Hebrew משפחה, Exod. VI. v. 15. 17. 19. Deut. XXIX. 18. 1. Sam. IX. 21. etc. That name also occurs in this way in Acts c. II. 4. c. III. v. 24. nor is it read anywhere else, nor does it denote paternity But the family in heaven is to be understood not of the Angels, but of the elect triumphing in heaven, just as the family on earth is to be understood of the faithful militant in the Church, who are all sons by adoption, all have arrived in Christ at υἱοθεσίαν, since the Angels are sons of God not by adoption, but by creation, nor do they have Christ as Mediator or Redeemer. This πατριὰ, however, is founded in Christ the Mediator. The Apostle had also taught that the Gentiles belong to this family, who have become fellow-citizens of the saints & σύσσωμοι & οἰκεῖοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, for whose sake he prays here, that they may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit, etc. Thus the blessed Hunnius: He understands, he says, the kinship by which Christ is bound to us, and we to Christ, by the communion of one Father already, so that the sense is: That Father is the common Father, not only of our Lord Jesus Christ by nature, but also of all believers, whether they are triumphing in heaven or still militant on earth, He is their Father through the grace of adoption. Thus he not only opposes the one true God to the many gods of the Gentiles, but also rebukes the pride of the Jews, so that they may no longer exclude the Gentiles from the family of God, or wonder that they are brought to salvation from a common Father through Christ, says Crocius here.

Latin:

V. 15. Ἐξ ὗ πᾶσα πατριὰ ἐν ὐρανοῖς κὴ ἐπὶ γῆς ὀνομάζεται est familia, ut videre est Exod. VI. 25. XII. vers. 1. & locis aliis magno numero. Solenne autem est Ebræis, ut & supra attigimus, cum de Angelis & hominibus piis loquuntur, nominare eos familiam Dei superiorem & inferiorem, utrique Dei filii dicuntur, utraque vocatur Dei familia, & hoc est, quod hic dicitur. Non longe abit illud Simplicii in Epicteteis: Αἱ πολλαὶ ἀρχαὶ πάντων ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς ἔχουσι τὸ τ’ ἀρχῆς ἀξίωμα, & hoc Procli ad Timæum: Πάντα τὰ δημιεργικὰ αἴτια ὡς ὑφ’ ἕν κέντρον συνέπει τὴν μίαν τῶν πάντων πατρικὴν αἰτίαν. Magnificum putant Ebræi, quod genus suum referre possunt ad Judam, Rubenum, & alios Jacobi filios; at nos Deo Patre censemur: Τοῖυ παρ τρὸς ἐυχόμεθ’ εἶναι.

Quanquam non desint etiam inter Christianos, qui Angelos quoque hic comprehendi velint, Lom- bardus, Thomas, aliiique e Pontificiis, Theodoreto hic Deum Creatorem universorum Parentem desi- gnante, Hieronymus etiam Archangelos & alios su- periores inferri censeat, cum Angelorum Patres di- cit, sed sine fundamento, adferat. Convenientius tamen hic Patris nomen, quo Deum nuncupavit, respicitur, cujus gratia πᾶσαν πατριὰν dici creden- dum, ut familia quidem omnis, sed ab hoc uno Pa- tre in Christo Jesu descendens, vel qua est Pater Dn. nostri Jesu Christi, adeoque omnium, qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Quæ est paternitas non κατ’ ἔσω, sed κατ’ ἔξω, non respectu divinæ Christi naturæ, qua est Dei Filius ex substantia Patris ab æterno genitus, sed ratione naturæ humanæ, quam nostri causa assum- psit, secundum quam nobis est ὁμοούσιος & frater noster, Ebr. II. 11. dispari tamen ratione ita Pater Christi, & Pater fidelium Christi dicitur, quia nos ad- optavit in filios suos, quum essemus natura iræ filii, carnem autem Christi expertem omnis peccati e- vexit in hypostasin Filii sui unigeniti, de quo alias. Hic πατριὰ πᾶσα dicitur quoad eos, qui a Deo Pa- tre per Christum descendunt. Unde Pronomen (ἐξ) ⅌ nonnulli referunt ad ipsum Christum, ut Calvinus, Zanchius, Musculus, Aretius, quod tamen hic rectius ad Patrem refertur, præeuntibus veteribus Chry- sostomo, Theodoreto, Hieronymo, Theophylacto; A Bullingero autem & Gualthero πατριὰ de fa- milia non incommode exponitur, quæ non tantum apud LXX. Interpretes notatur, quando אבות cum בית, sed etiam quando cum ראשו, vel cum שרו jungitur, ut e Concordantiis videre est, & respondet Ebræo משפחה, Exod. VI. v. 15. 17. 19. Deut. XXIX. 18. 1. Sam. IX. 21. &c. Occurrit etiam ita nomen illud in Actis c. II. 4. c. III. v. 24. nec uspiam alias legitur, aut paternitatem notat, sive apud LXX. Interpretes, sive in Novo Testamento. Familia autem in cælis non de Angelis, sed de electis in cælis triumphantibus intelligenda, ut familia in terris de fidelibus in Ecclesia militantibus, qui omnes filii sunt per adoptionem, omnes in Christo ad υἱοθεσίαν pervenerunt, quũ Angeli non per adoptionem, sed creationem filii Dei sint, nec Christum Mediatorem aut Redemptorem habeant. Hæc a. πατριὰ fundata est in Christo Mediatore. Ad hanc familiam etiam pertinere gentes docuerat Apostolus, qui concives facti sunt sanctorum & σύσσωμοι & οἰκεῖοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, quorum causa hic orat, ut corrobbrentur per Spiritum S. &c. Ita B. Hunnius: Cognationem, inquit, intelligit eam, qua Christus nobis, nos Christo unius jam Patris communione sumus devincti, ut sit sensus: Pater ille est communis Pater, non solum Domini nostri Jesu Christi per naturam, sed etiam cunctorum credentium, sive in cælis triumphantium, sive in terris adhuc militantium Pater est, per gratiam adoptionis. Sic non solum multis gentiliũ Diis unum verum Deum opponit, sed etiam Judæorum superbiam retundit, ne deinceps gentes a Dei familia excludant, aut mirentur, a communi Patre ad salutem adduci per Christum, inquit hic Crocius.

## 3:16
V. 16. That He may grant you according to the riches of His glory) glory signifies Majesty: But here metonymically it signifies the very power of God, which Majesty follows, just as among the Hebrews עז is accustomed to be placed now with this, now with that meaning. πλοῦτος is the abundance of that power. See above I. 7. 18. II. 7.

Δυνάμει κραταιωθῆναι) to be increased in strength.

Διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον) that is ἐν τῷ ἔσω ἀνθρώπῳ, in the mind itself. See Rom. VII. 22. and what is said there. They are mistaken who confuse the inner man with the new man.

The word Majesty is fuller than power, and the riches of Majesty bring in not only glorious power, Col. I. 11. but also glorious grace that is very rich, Eph. I. 7. c. II. 7. Because the power and grace of God is not common, but magnificent and full of Majesty. He prays, therefore, that they be strengthened not with common but with singular strength, so that they may be able to stand against any temptations whatsoever, therefore he adds, in power. Yet he does not understand an extraordinary, but an ordinary strengthening. By the inner man, however, he does not denote the mind of man, but the Spirit, which is opposed to the exterior man or flesh, Rom. VII. 15. sqq. Gal. V. 17. that is, the whole man, insofar as he has been renewed, to whom not only the mind, but also the will, and the affections, and any faculties of man, insofar as renewal falls upon them, pertain. He prays, therefore, for strength and perfection in knowledge, faith, holiness, chastity, and other gifts and goods of the Holy Spirit, which are not obtained except through the Spirit of God. Thus Crocius, although he asserts with his Calvin that the inner man can be taken as the mind, he nevertheless admits that it can also be taken as the whole man, who is regenerate, so that he is confirmed in every part of himself, so that neither the mind nor any sense fails. The blessed Hunnius: From this (he means to say) I ask ardently, that you may be so confirmed in the doctrine of truth, that you may not waver on account of any afflictions, whether mine or yours, much less fail: but according to the inner man in knowledge, faith, hope, and tolerance you may be made more robust by new acts and increments from time to time: And that through the Holy Spirit, who may support your faith with His divine power. This strengthening of the inner man is constituted by some as a general benefit, of which the special parts are the indwelling of Christ, the confirmation of love, the increase of knowledge, the perfection of gifts. Our analysis was provided above.

Latin:

V. 16. Ἵνα δῴη ὑμῖν κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ) δόξα Majestatem significat: Sed hic μετωνυμικῶς ipsam Dei potentiam, quam sequitur Majestas, quomodo Ebræis עז poni solet modo hoc, modo illo significatu. πλοῦτος est ejus potentiæ abundantia. Vide supra I. 7. 18. II. 7.

Δυνάμει κραταιωθῆναι) augeri viribus.

Διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον) id est ἐν τῷ ἔσω ἀνθρώπῳ, in mente ipsa. Vid. Rom. VII. 22. & ibi dicta. Falluntur, qui ἔσω ἄνθρωπον confundunt, cum καινῷ ἀνθρώπῳ.

Vox Majestatis plenior est, quam potentiæ, & divitiæ Majestatis non tantum potentiam gloriosam, Col. I. 11. sed etiam gloriosam gratiam valde divitem inferunt, Eph. I. 7. c. II. 7. Quia potentia & gratia Dei non est vulgaris, sed magnifica & Majestatis plena. Corroborari ergo non vulgari sed singulari robore eosdem vovet, ut ad quasvis tentationes consistere possint, ideo addit, in potentia. Nec tamen extraordinariam, sed ordinariam corroborationem intelligit. Per τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον autem non mentem hominis, sed Spiritum notat, qui exteriori homini vel carni opponitur, Rom. VII. 15. sqq. Gal. V. 17. hoc est totum hominem, quantum renovatus est, ad quem non mens tantum, sed & voluntas, & affectus, ac quævis facultates hominis, quatenus in eas cadit renovatio, pertinent. Robur ergo & perfectionem in cognitione, fide, sanctitate, castitate, aliisque donis, & bonis Spiritus S. precatur, quæ non nisi per Spiritum Dei obtinentur. Ita Crocius, etsi cum Calvino suo posse accipi interiorem hominem de mente asserat, posse tamen etiam accipi fatetur de toto homine, qui est regenitus, ut omni sui parte sic confirmetur, ut nec mens, nec sensus ullus deficiat. B. Hunnius: Ab hoc (vult dicere) peto ego ardenter, ut ita confirmemini doctrina veritatis, ne ob ullas afflictiones vel meas vel vestras vacilletis, multo minus deficiatis: sed secundũ internũ hominem in agnitione, fide, spe & tolerantia novis subinde actibus & incrementis robustiores efficiamini: Idque per Spiritum sanctum, qui fidem vestram divina virtute sua fulciat. Hæc corroboratio interioris hominis spiritualis constituitur a nonnullis generale beneficium, cujus speciales partes sunt inhabitatio Christi, confirmatio dilectionis, in- crementum cognitionis, perfectio donorum. Ἀνάλυσις nostra supra tradita est.

## 3:17
V. 17. That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts;) This also is constructed with 'may grant', and is asyndeton. Concerning the sense, see John XIV. 23.

Some connect this with the preceding, with Theodoret, so that through the grace of the Spirit our souls may be the dwelling place of Christ, and with Theophylact, that Christ dwells in the inner man, but it is more correctly separated from the former and connected with the following. But the distinction of Beza between 'to dwell as a stranger' and 'to dwell as an inhabitant' is more subtle than true, because the former implies an indwelling for a time, the latter forever, by which he wished to serve his hypothesis concerning inamissible grace. He dwells, however, through faith, and thus spiritually, but it is not to be inferred from this with Crocius that Christ does not dwell in us at all according to His human nature as to substance: For the former pertains to the mode of indwelling, the latter to the indwelling subject. Nor indeed does only a part of Christ, but the whole Christ dwell in our hearts, although not so that the flesh of Christ is mixed with the bodies of the faithful, as Crocius cavils; for the presence is divine. But when God is present with us, He is not mixed with our bodies, nor does He have need to leave heaven in order to dwell in us. The whole Christ comes to us, not indeed His bare Deity, as the Father, and makes His abode with us, John XIV. 23. Therefore that arrival is not to be feigned with a substantial absence, so that a bare presence of power is believed. Is the Father or the Holy Spirit present with us only by His power, is the Word, the Son of God, present only by His power? But where He is present substantially after the incarnation, since the human nature of Christ subsists in His hypostasis, this cannot be absent. Nor are the faithful to be deprived of the comfort which they have from the presence and indwelling and communion of the whole Christ, since He does not diffuse His grace and power except through His flesh, and that not absently, but presently, for our great protection, Matt. XXIX. 20.

Faith is the medium of indwelling: because through faith Christ is received, who comes to us through the Word and through the sacraments, John XIV. 23. 1 John V. 6. Through faith He remains in us, lives in us, works in us, Gal. II. 20. Phil. IV. 13. Rom. XV. 18. Through faith we participate in His flesh and blood in the Word spiritually, John VI. Through faith we also receive salvifically in the holy supper under the Eucharistic bread His body, and under the blessed wine His blood, not however merely the naked efficacy or virtue of His body and blood, 1 Cor. X. 16. Blessed Chemnitz here against the Calvinists observes the true reasons why Paul says that Christ dwells in us by faith: in his book on the two natures in Christ, ch. 30, p. 505. Thus to the Ephesians, after Paul had discoursed much concerning the mystery of Christ, through whom God restored all things in His blood, who dissolved enmities in His flesh, whom the Father, having raised from the dead, set at His right hand above every name, through whom we have access to God, which circumstances manifestly show that Paul is speaking of the whole person of Christ, and specifically denotes the assumed nature in Christ; afterwards he adds in chapter III that Christ dwells by faith in our hearts. But here some seize upon the appeal to faith, and oppose it to presence, and wish the sense of this saying to be that the person of Christ dwells in our hearts, not by His essence, as He consists of two natures and subsists in them, but that He dwells in us by faith, as if indeed faith in this place were a fantasy, or an imagination concerning Christ, who is not truly present to us, but is feigned by imagination to dwell in us, whereas faith, Heb. XI, is ἔλεγχος, because those things which in the word are delivered, although they neither appear to the senses, nor are perceived, yet they truly and certainly are so, and are so constituted, just as faith from the Word and according to the Word believes and determines.
