But the true causes, which Paul states, that Christ dwells in us by faith, are these: to show that faith is the medium, organ, or instrument by which we apprehend, receive, and retain Christ in the Word, so that he does not pass by as if a stranger, or stay with us only as a guest for the night, but that through the grace of indwelling he may remain, and perpetually dwell in us, so that we may always be and remain members of God's household. (2.) Because faith in this place is opposed to open vision & the senses, as 2 Cor. V: we walk by faith, not by sight or vision: And John XX: Blessed are those who do not see or touch, but believe. (3.) Christ is said to dwell in us by faith, because he does not dwell in our hearts by any reason or condition of this age that is sensible, visible, or local, which could be perceived by the senses or comprehended by the intellect or reason, but in a heavenly, divine, and incomprehensible manner, which is believed by faith alone from the promise, so that even if we neither feel nor understand what and how Christ is in us, we may nevertheless by faith according to the promise certainly determine that he truly dwells in our hearts. And I think this is what Nazianzen means when he writes in his first epistle to Cledonius, that Christ dwells in our hearts οὐ κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ νοούμενον. Since, therefore, the promises concerning the presence of Christ in the Church, concerning his whole and entire person, which consists of two natures and subsists in two natures, speak, why should we exclude from there the presence of the other nature, through which Christ is our brother, and does not hate us as his own flesh, and allow it to be snatched from us? For where Scripture does not restrict, neither ought we to restrict the promises concerning Christ to his divine nature alone. But lest this deduction from the circumstances of the text, which is manifest and firm, be called into doubt, the Son of God himself, after his ascension, residing in glory in the heavens, clearly and expressly delivered to Paul a solemn testimony and public sealing, that by his body and blood, that is, that by his whole person even according to the assumed nature, he wishes to be present with the Church on earth in that and with that, 1 Corinthians XI. And Paul himself teaches that we have not only the κοινωνίαν of the Spirit, 2 Cor. XIII, but also the κοινωνίαν of the body and blood of Christ, 1 Corinthians X. If, therefore, we wish Scripture to be the voice of the Judge in this dispute, and not the subject matter of the litigation, the matter is plain and defined concerning the presence of the whole or entire Christ in the Church according to both natures. Bucer examines that which is in John VI, where Christ teaches how we remain in Christ, and Christ in us; there is explicit mention of the flesh and blood of Christ, to which when we are joined, Christ, God and man, remains in us, and we in him. And indeed, the head of the Church is not torn away or separated from his members, but is most closely joined to them. Moreover, Christ is our head not only according to his divine nature, but also according to that nature by which he is related and consubstantial to us, his members. For the Scholastics also rightly say that this pertains to the nature of the head. And briefly, it is certain that it pertains to the office of Christ, as Mediator, High Priest, King, and our head, that he be present with his Church, and being present, hear, help, govern, etc. It is, however, acknowledged that Christ does and effects those things which pertain to his office in and with both, through and according to both his divine and human natures. Since, therefore, concerning that presence, which from the words of Scripture we can rightly name the indwelling, habitation, and presence of Christ with us or in us, we have a certain word and express promise that the whole Christ, his whole and entire person, God and man according to both natures, wishes to be present with his Church, not only triumphing in the heavens, but also still militant on earth, the matter is plain and full of consolation, that he wishes to be present with us also in that nature by which he is consubstantial, related, and our brother, and we are of his flesh and of his bones, in which he paid the price of redemption and acquired us for himself, and was tempted, so that he might be able to sympathize with our miseries, through which we have access to the divinity.

Latin:

V. 17. Κατοικῆσαι τὸν χριστὸν διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν ;) Hoc quoque construitur cum δῴη, & est ἀσύνδετον. De sensu vide Joh. XIV. 23.

Nonnulli connectunt hoc cum præcedentibus cum Theodoreto, ut per gratiam Spiritus nostræ animæ sint habitaculum Christi, & Theophylacto, habitare Christum in interiore homine, sed rectius sejungitur a prioribus, & connectitur cum sequen- tibus. Subtilior autem est, quam verior distinctio Bezæ τοῦ παροικεῖν & τοῦ κατοικεῖν, quod illud inha- bitationem ad tempus, hoc in perpetuum impor- tet, qua suæ ὑποθέσει de gratia inamissibili δουλεύειν voluit. Inhabitat autem per fidem, adeoque spiri- tualiter, sed inde non est inferendum cum Crocio, Christum secundum Humanam naturam in nobis quantum ad substantiam minime habitare: Nam illud ad modum inhabitationis, hoc ad inhabitans suppositum pertinet. Nec vero Christi pars tantum, sed totus Christus inhabitat in cordibus nostris, etsi non ut misceatur caro Christi cum fidelium cor- poribus, ut cavillatur Crocius; nam præsentia est divina. Deus autem cum adest nobis, non misce- tur cum corporibus nostris, nec cælum deserere necesse habet, ut in nobis habitet. Totus Christus ad nos venit, non vero nuda ejus Deitas, ut Pater, & mansionem apud nos facit, Joh. XIV. 23. Non ergo adventus ille cum substantiali ἀπουσίᾳ fin- gendus est, ut nuda virtutis præsentia credatur. Num sola virtute sua adest nobis Pater aut Spiritus sanctus, num sola virtute ὁ λόγος, Filius Dei? At ubi hic substantialiter post ἐνσάρκωσιν præsto est, quum in hypostasi ejus subsistat humana natura Christi, abesse hæc non potest. Nec privandi sunt fideles solatio, quod a præsentia & inhabitatione ac communione totius Christi habent, quum non nisi per carnem suam jam diffundat gratiam & virtu- tem suam, idque non absenter, sed præsenter ma- gno nostro præsidio, Matth. XXIX. 20.

Fides medium est inhabitationis: quia per fi- dem suscipitur Christus, qui per Verbum ad nos venit & per sacramenta, Joh. XIV. 23. 1. Joh. V. 6. Per fidem manet in nobis, vivit in nobis, operatur in nobis, Gal. II. 20. Phil. IV. 13. Rom. XV. 18. Per fidem participamus carnem ejus & sanguinem in Verbo spiritualiter, Joh. VI. Per fidem etiam salu- tariter percipimus in sacra cœna sub pane Eucha- ristico corpus, & sub vino benedicto sanguinem ejus, non v. tantum nudam efficaciam vel virtutem corporis & sanguinis ejus, 1. Cor. X. 16. B. Chemni- tius hic contra Calvinianos observat veras causas, cur dicat Paulus, Christum fide inhabitare in nobis: libr. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 30. p. 505. Ita ad Ephesios, postquam Paulus multa disseruisset de my- sterio Christi, per quem Deus universa restituit in sanguine ejus, qui inimicitias solvit in carne sua, quem Pater a mortuis resuscitatum constituit ad dextram suam super omne nomen, per quem aditum habemus ad Deum, qua circumstantiæ manifeste ostendunt, Paulum de tota persona Christi loqui, & nominatim denotare assumptam naturam in Christo; postea subjicit cap. III. Christum habi- tare per fidem in cordibus nostris. Sed hic quidam arripiunt appellationem fidei, & eam opponunt præsentiæ, ac sensum hujus dicti esse volunt, per- sonam Christi inhabitare in cordibus nostris, non essentia sua, sicut duabus naturis constat, & in illis subsistit, sed fide inhabitare in nobis, quasi ve- ro fides hoc loco sit phantasia, seu imaginatio de Christo, qui revera nobis non adsit, sed per ima- ginationem fingatur in nobis inhabitare, cum fides Ebr. XI. sit ἔλεγχος, quod ea, quæ in verbo traduntur, licet sensibus nec appareant, nec perci- piantur, vere tamen ac certe ita sint, atque ita se ha- beant, sicut fides ex Verbo ac juxta Verbum credit ac statuat. Veræ autem causæ, quod Paulus dicit, Chri- stum fide inhabitare in nobis, hæ sunt, ut ostendat, fidem esse medium, organon seu instrumentum, quo Christum in Verbo apprehendimus, accipimus, ac re- tinemus, ut non quasi peregrinus transeat, vel ut ho- spes pernoctet tantum apud nos, sed ut per inhabita- tionis gratiam maneat, ac perpetuo in nobis inhabi- tet, ut semper nos simus ac maneamus Domestici Dei. (2.) Quia fides hoc loco opponitur apertæ vi- sioni & sensibus, ut 2. Cor. V. per fidem ambula- mus, non per speciem seu visionem: Et Joh. XX. Beati qui non vident aut palpant, sed credunt. (3.) Christus dicitur fide inhabitare, quia non ratione aut conditione aliqua hujus seculi sensibili, visibili, aut locali, quæ vel sensibus percipi, vel intellectu seu ratione comprehendi possit, sed cælesti, divino, ac incomprehensibili modo, qui sola fide ex promissio- ne creditur, Christus inhabitat in cordibus nostris, ut etiamsi nec sentiamus, nec intelligamus, quod & quomodo Christus sit in nobis, fide tamen juxta pro- missionem certo statuamus, ipsum vere habitare in cordibus nostris. Et hoc existimo, Nazianzenum velle, quando scribit epistola I. ad Cledonium, Chri- stum habitare in cordibus nostris ἠ κατὰ τὸ Φαινό- μενον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ νούμενον. Cum itaque promissio- nes de præsentia Christi in Ecclesia, de tota & integra ejus persona, quæ constat duabus naturis, & subsi- stit in duabus naturis, loquantur, cur alterius na- turæ præsentiam, per quam Christus frater noster est, ac nos ut carnem suam odio non habet, inde excluderemus, & nobis inde eripi pateremur? Ubi enim scriptura non restringit, nec nos promissiones de Christo, ad solam divinam ejus naturam restringere debemus. Ne vero hæc collectio ex circumstantiis textus, quæ manifesta & firma est, in dubium voce- tur, ipse Filius Dei post ascensionem in cælis residens in gloria, diserte & expresse tradidit Paulo solennem testificationem & publicam obsignationem, quod corpore & sanguine suo, hoc est, quod tota persona etiam secundum assumptam naturam in illa & cum illa velit Ecclesiæ in terris adesse, 1. Corinth. XI. Et Paulus ipse docet, nos non tantum habere κοινωνίαν Spiritus, 2. Cor. XIII. verum etiam κοινωνίαν corpo- ris & sanguinis Christi, 1. Corinth. X. Si itaque scripturam volumus esse in hac disputatione vocem Judicis, & non materiam litis, res plana & definita est de præsentia totius seu integri Christi in Ecclesia secundum utramque naturam. Bucerus expendit illud, quod Joh. VI. ubi Christus docet, quomodo nos maneamus in Christo, & Christus in nobis, diserte fit mentio carnis & sanguinis Christi, cui quando conjungimur, Christus Deus & homo ma- net in nobis, & nos in ipso. Ac profecto caput Eccle- siæ non est a membris suis avulsum vel separatum, sed ipsis conjunctissimum. Est autem Christus caput nostrum non tantum secundum divinam natu- ram, sed & secundum eam naturam, qua nobis membris suis cognatus & consubstantialis est. Illud enim ad rationem capitis pertinere, etiam Scholastici recte dicunt. Ac breviter, certum est ad officium Christi, Mediatoris, Pontificis, Regis, & capitis nostri pertinere, ut Ecclesiæ suæ adsit, ac præsens exaudiat, juvet, gubernet &c. In confesso autem est, Christum ea, quæ ad officium suum pertinent, agere & efficere, in & cum utraque, per & secun- dum utramque suam naturam divinam & huma- nam. Cum igitur de illa præsentia, quam ex scri- pturæ verbis recte nominare possumus mansionem, habitationem & præsentiam Christi apud nos seu in nobis, certum verbum & expressam promissionem habemus, quod totus Christus, tota sua & integra persona Deus & homo secundum utramque natu- ram Ecclesiæ suæ, non tantum in cælis triumphanti, verum etiam in terris adhuc militanti adesse velit, res plana est, & plena consolationis, quod ea etiam natura nobis adesse velit, qua nobis consubstantia- lis, cognatus & frater noster est, ac nos de carne ejus ac de ossibus ejus, in qua pretium redemptionis persolvit, ac nos sibi acquisivit, tentatus est, ut pos- sit miseriis nostris compati, per quam aditum habe- mus ad divinitatem.

## 3:18
V. 18. Ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐῤῥιζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι, ἵνα ἐξισχύσητε καταλαβέσθαι σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις) There is a transposition of the word ἵνα, such as in John XIII, verse 29, Rom. XI. 31, 1 Cor. IX, v. 15, 2 Cor. II, verse 4, Gal. II, verse 10. Constancy is rightly expressed by two similitudes: of a tree striking roots deep, Matt. XIII, verse 6, 21, Mark IV, verse 6, 17, Luke VIII, verse 13, and of a building well founded, Matt. VII, verse 24, Luke VI, 28, where the word is θεμελίῳ. See also above II, verse 20, and Rev. XXI, verse 14, and compare Coloss. II, v. 7. Philo on the confusion of tongues: Πηπηγότα βεβαίως τῇ τοῦ τετραγώνου σχήματος οἰκειόμιτα φύσει. Ἀκράδαντοι γὰρ τοῦτό γε' ἵνα πλῦθύ τινα τρόπον ἐρερεισμένα βεβαίως καὶ τὰ ἐποικοδομούμενα δέχηται.

Τί τὸ πλάτος, καὶ μῆκος, καὶ βάθος, καὶ ὕψος) There is an allusion to the passage in John XI. 7. God's goodness both pours itself out most widely to all men, and extends in length, that is, into all ages, and frees man from the lowest depression, and lifts him to the highest places. The motions of the offered things looked to the same, the former into the height and depth, which was called תרומה, then the other into the breadth and length, which was called תנופה.

Photius finally acknowledged that trajection in the Greek scholia, even though he had previously posited either a σφάλμα γραφικὸν or an enallage of case. Most Papists, as well as Calvin and Bullinger, understand it as concerning our love toward God and neighbor: others, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, as concerning God's love toward us. Some, such as Bucer, Zanchius, and Musculus, wish for both loves to be noted. But this is less consistent with the unity of the sense. Indeed, our love is not of such value that it can found a spiritual edifice which might stand against infernal winds and tempests, or the gates of hell. For it is very imperfect, very impure, very languid, and weak. An immovable foundation of such a kind is to be sought only in God, who alone is our rock, Psalm 18:2, Psalm 73:26. Crocius acknowledges this; who, although he argues on behalf of Bucer and Zanchius against Beza—who contended that the name of root and foundation is less correctly attributed to fruits, namely the love of God and neighbor—that it can be explained as concerning divine and our love, not that our charity is the root or foundation of our election or salvation; but that it is necessary for the faithful to be properly established in the charity both of God toward us and of us toward God, yet he calls this explanation most apt, because he seeks to be founded and rooted in the charity of God toward us, so that they may feel more and more that they are truly loved by God in Christ and may place firm confidence and the hope of salvation in this love. But what he adds, that from the sense of divine love toward us we are in turn established in love toward God, so that our love may not be volatile, but firm and constant, so that nothing may move them from it, that is indeed a consequence in terms of the matter, but it is not inferred by the words of the Apostle, nor does it exhibit their sense; and Crocius admits that that love does not depend on our virtue, just as the Ephesians were not rooted in themselves, but rather in Christ, as is held concerning the Colossians, Colossians 2:7. If, however, we are rooted only in Christ, or in the grace of God in Christ, then we are not correctly said to be rooted or founded in our love toward God. Add that it is explained later what that love is, the knowledge and sense of which he prays for the Ephesians, namely, whose breadth and length and depth and height is here designated (which do not befit our charity) and whose sense is desired from that rooting together with the sense of the charity of Christ. But there is no need for us to have the sense of our love toward God and neighbor from that rooting, since the spirit of man knows altogether those things which are in man, 1 Cor. 2:10. Finally, who would explain more correctly than the Apostle himself, Rom. 5:5 sqq. and ch. 8:38, 39, what charity renders us unmoved against the whirlwinds of temptations, who testifies this concerning the love of God toward us infused into our hearts, by which he embraces us in Christ Jesus, not concerning our love. What if the Apostle also explained the very phrase used here, Col. 2:7, ἐῤῥιζωμένοι, κὴ ἐποικοδο- μύμενοι ἐν ἀυτῷ κὴ βεβαιόμενοι ἐν τῇ πίσει. Wherefore Grotius rightly explains it concerning the goodness of God. Nor could Crocius deny that those four dimensions pertain to the love of God: but no mention of it is made in the aforementioned, unless it be understood through charity, v. 18.

Although indeed most wish the immense magnitude of the mystery of Christ to be delineated by these dimensions, yet it especially explains itself in grace and love in this mystery, and all its parts, as that which everywhere dominates and prevails in the entire economy of grace, exhibited in Christ. And finally, almost all interpretations return to this. Ambrose wishes the immensity of God to be signified in the dimensions, so that just as in a sphere there is as much length as breadth, and as much height as depth, so also in GOD all things are equal by the immensity of infinity. Therefore, the same must be said equally of the love and grace of GOD, which is in GOD. For the mercy of God is as great as He Himself is. Sir. 2:23. Bernard indeed explains it concerning the different attributes of God, yet he did not pass over the grace of God here, book 5 de considerat. What is God? Length, breadth, height, and depth. One thing, manifold effect, and diverse operations. And that one thing is length because of eternity, breadth because of charity, height because of Majesty, depth because of wisdom. Photius says that the mystery has its length, because the salvation of the Gentiles was decreed from eternity; breadth, because it extends to all; depth, because Christ by his presence and power penetrated to the underworld and despoiled the Principalities; height, because he ascended into the heavens; in all of which the love of Christ exerted itself most of all: which indeed was most abundantly demonstrated in the mystery of the cross, to which Gregory of Nyssa, Jerome in this place, Augustine epist. 120, ch. 26, book 2 de doctr. Christ. ch. 41, serm. 7 de Verbo Apostoli refer these dimensions. Concerning which explanation Theophylact says thus: Gregory of Nyssa, he says, says that by breadth, depth, and length of this kind the cross is signified: and he asserts that the Apostle prayed for the Ephesians that they might be able to contemplate the mystery of the cross. Since indeed by this cross the whole dispensation was contained, which is certainly more convenient. For by the cross the charity of God toward us is made most clear, just as the Lord also says, and Paul now subjoins. But without doubt Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Theophylact refer these dimensions more correctly to the magnitude of the mystery concerning Christ, where Chrysostom expressly teaches that the immensity of love and affection is simultaneously hinted at: Τυτέσι, τὸ μυσήριον τὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν οἰκονομηθὲν μετὰ ἀκριβείας εἰδέναι, κὴ τὸ πλάτος,

and the length, and the depth, and the height. That is, the magnitude of the love of God, how it is extended everywhere, and he described it with bodily figures. What he had begun and prayed for earlier, says Theophylact, that the Spirit might be granted to them with both wisdom and revelation, so that they might understand what the hope of their calling was, and other things of this kind, he pursues the same thing at present, saying that you may be able to embrace with mind and thought together with the other faithful, what kind of mystery that is, which was dispensed for your sake, and has advanced to such a magnitude that it has been most amply propagated everywhere on earth. Whence he also described this, which encompasses everything, under a bodily figure. For I myself have explained this sacrament as I could, yet nothing can be comprehended from my words unless it be revealed through the Spirit. Nor will it be permitted for you to conceive of such a thing in your mind, unless you are strengthened by the Spirit. This sense as the simplest is approved by Crocius, and has been approved by the Blessed Osiander, as if to say, I ask God that you may be able, together with other sincere Christians, to embrace in some way with your mind the immense love of God toward you, which, to use a metaphor, extends itself into all dimensions. Hyperius indeed refers the designation of these dimensions to the certainty and fullness of the knowledge of the love of Christ, just as mathematical dimensions are most certain and perfect, when length, breadth, height, and depth are observed in solid bodies. But this geometry of divine love itself is ἀγεώμετρος καὶ ἄμετρος, and not that of our knowledge, which is occupied with the love of God; and just as that is truly immense, so our knowledge is indeed certain, yet not perfect and absolute in all numbers and dimensions. Others, however, unfold the individual dimensions: Nor can that be displeasing. For they are not enumerated distinctly without cause. Hemmingius in his Commentary on this passage understands the mystery of the grace of God and the love of Christ toward us, for the Apostle explains himself thus, that you may know the immense love of Christ toward you. For just as the mercy of the Father exceeds all his works, according to the opinion of David: So the love of the Son of God surpasses every measure. For if you look at its breadth, it is enclosed by no limits: If you consider its length, it extends itself to all the ends of the world: If you attend to its depth, it embraces the most humble and abject things in the world: If you regard its height, it surpasses the heavens. This sense of this passage is simple and true; let us leave aside trifles about the wooden cross of the Lord and a spherical figure. Blessed Aegidius Hunnius explains these dimensions thus, paraphrasing the whole text in this way: That you may be able to attain what is the breadth &c. I pray also that with the rest of the Christians you may be able in some way to weigh through faith what is the breadth, length, depth, and sublimity of the mystery of the grace and mercy of God exhibited through Christ: Namely, that its breadth suffers itself to be enclosed by no boundaries anywhere: That its length stretches itself from the rising of the sun even to its setting, and extends itself into the world of all nations: That its depth lowers itself to lift up all the most despised things from the mire of misery: that finally its height transcends the intelligence of all men and Angels, and thus lies open in all dimensions without measure and limit. This explanation pleases me above others. How Daniel Heinsius applies this to buildings and the commemoration of dimensions, since mention has been made of the dwelling or temple of Christ, see his exercises on this passage. We easily acquiesce to the Hunnian interpretation, yet by breadth [we understand] the universality of divine love extending itself most amply to the whole human race, supposing that by length eternity is designated from before and after, by height the immense sublimity, established above mind, above reason, above every comprehension of created nature, by depth the abyss of the mystery of love, and the unsearchable depths of mercy, Rom. XI. verse 33. a sacred mathematics, and as it were measures the love of Christ according to four dimensions, attributing to it breadth, length, depth, and height. But by this measurement, instituted in an anthropopathic manner, he indicates its immensurability and immensity in the truth of the matter, as if he were to say, it is higher than the heavens, deeper than the sea, broader than the height of the earth, longer than all time, as it endures for all eternity.

Latin:

V. 18. Ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐῤῥιζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι, ἵνα ἐξισχύ- σητε καταλαβέσθαι σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις) Est trajectio vocis ἵνα, qualis Joh. XIII. vers. 29. Rom. XI. 31. 1. Cor. IX. v. 15. 2. Cor. II. vers. 4. Gal. II. vers. 10. Constantiæ duabus similitudinibus recte exprimitur: arboris in altum radices agentis, Matth. XIII. vers. 6. 21. Marci IV. vers. 6. 17. Luc. VIII. vers. 13. & ædificii bene fundati, Matth. VII. vers. 24. Luc. VI. 28. ubi vox θεμελίῳ. Vide & supra II. vers. 20. & Apoc. XXI. vers. 14. & conf. Coloss. II. v. 7. Philo de linguarum confusione: Πηπηγότα βεβαίως τῇ τοῦ τετραγώνου σχήματος οἰκειόμιτα φύσει. Ἀκράδαντοι γὰρ τοῦτό γε' ἵνα πλῦθύ τινα τρόπον ἐρερεισμένα βεβαίως καὶ τὰ ἐποικοδο- μούμενα δέχηται.

Τί τὸ πλάτος, καὶ μῆκος, καὶ βάθος, καὶ ὕψος) Est allusio ad locum Joh. XI. 7. Dei bonitas & latissime se effundit in omnes homines, & in longum, id est, in omnia secula se extendit, & ex infima depressione hominem liberat, & in loca suprema evehit. Eodem spectabant motiones rerum oblatarum, prior in altum & profundum, quæ dicebatur תרומה, deinde altera in latum & longum, quæ diceba- tur תנופה.

Trajectionem illam tandem in scholiis Græcis agnovit Photius, etsi prius vel σφάλμα γραφικὸν, vel Enallagen casus statuerit. De amore nostro erga Deum & proximum Pontificii plerique, ut & Calvinus & Bullingerus intelligunt: De amore Dei erga nos alii cum Chrysostomo & Theophyla- cto. Nonnulli utrumque amorem notari volunt, utpote Bucerus, Zanchius, Musculus. Sed hoc minus convenit unitati sensus. Amor vero noster tanti non est, ut possit fundare ædificium spiritua- le, quod adversus ventos & tempestates inferna- les, vel portas inferorum consistat. Valde enim imperfectus, valde impurus, valde languidus est & infirmus. Fundamentum immotum ejusmodi non nisi in Deo quærendum, qui unice est petra nostra Psal. XIIX. vers. 2. Psal. LXXIII. vers. 26. Agnoscit hoc Crocius; qui etsi contra Bezam, ar- guentem, quod radicis & fundamenti nomen minus recte tribuatur fructibus, dilectioni Dei & proximi, pro Bucero & Zanchio disputet, de di- lectione divina & nostra explicari posse, non quod nostra charitas sit electionis aut salutis nostræ radix aut fundamentum; sed quod necessarium sit, fideles probe stabiliri in charitate tum Dei erga nos, tum nostra erga Deum, hanc tamen ex- plicationem aptissimam dicit, quod petat fundari & radicari in charitate Dei erga nos, ut magis ac magis sentiant, se in Christo a Deo vere diligi & in hac dilectione fiduciam firmam, & spem salutis immotam collocent. Quod autem addit, ex sen- su divini erga nos amoris vicissim nos stabiliri in amore erga Deum, ne sit volatilis amor, sed firmus & constans, ut nihil eos inde dimoveat, id conse- quens quidem est ex parte rei, sed non infertur per verba Apostoli, aut sensum eorum exhibet; & fatetur Crocius, non pendere amorem illum a nostra virtute, ut Ephesii non ideo in seipsis, sed potius in Christo radicati fuerint, ut de Colossensibus habetur, Colos. II. vers. 7. Si autem solum in Christo, vel gratia DEI in Christo radicamur, non ergo in amore nostro erga Deum nos radicari vel fun- dari, recte dicimur. Adde quod explicetur postea quænam illa sit dilectio, cujus cognitionem & sen- sum precetur Ephesiis, nimirum cujus latitudo & longitudo & profunditas & sublimitas hic designa- tur (quæ non conveniunt nostræ charitati) & cu- jus sensus ex radicatione illa cum sensu charitatis Christi exoptatur. Amoris autem nostri erga De- um & proximum sensum non opus est ex illa radi- catione habeamus, quum Spiritus hominis omnino novit ea, quæ in homine sunt, 1. Cor. II. 10. Denique quæ charitas nos immotos reddat adversus tenta- tionum turbines, nemo rectius exposuerit, quam Apostolus ipse, Rom. V. 5. sqq. & cap. IIX. 38. 39. qui de dilectione Dei erga nos infusa in cordibus nostris, qua nos complectitur in Christo Jesu, testatur hoc, non de dilectione nostra. Quid quod etiam phrasin ipsam exposuerit Apostolus hic adhibitam, Col. II. 7. ἐῤῥιζωμένοι, κὴ ἐποικοδο- μύμενοι ἐν ἀυτῷ κὴ βεβαιόμενοι ἐν τῇ πίσει. Qua- propter recte Grotius de Dei bonitate explicat. Neque diffiteri potuit Crocius, ad dilectionem Dei pertinere quatuor illas dimensiones: Ejus vero nul- la in ante dictis facta mentio, nisi per charitatem, v. 18. ea intelligatur.

Quanquam vero hisce dimensionibus magni- tudinem immensam mysterii Christi delineari velint plerique, ea tamen præcipue sese in gratia & di- lectione explicat in hoc mysterio, & omnibus ejus partibus, utpote quæ ubique dominatur & præva- let in universa οἰκονομίᾳ gratiæ, in Christo exhibi- tæ. Et eo denique redeunt omnes pene interpre- tationes. Ambrosius in dimensionibus immensi- tatem Dei significari vult, ut sicut in sphæra tanta longitudo est, quanta latitudo, & tanta altitudo, quantum & profundum, ita & in DEO omnia æqualia sint immensitate infinitatis. Id itaque de dilectione & gratia DEI, quæ in DEO est, pa- riter dicendum. Tanta enim est Dei misericordia, quantus ipse est. Sir. II. 23. Bernhardus explicat quidem de diversis Dei attributis, non tamen præ- teriit hic gratiam Dei, libr. V. de considerat. Quid est Deus? Longitudo, latitudo, sublimitas, & pro- fundum. Res una, effectus multiplex, operationes- que diversæ. Et illa una res est longitudo propter æternitatem, latitudo propter charitatem, sublimi- tas propter Majestatem, profunditas propter sa- pientiam. Photius ait, mysterium suam habere lon- gitudinem, quia ab æterno decreta fuerit salus gen- tium; latitudinem, quia ad omnes extendatur; profunditatem, quia Christus sua præsentia & po- tentia ad inferos penetraverit, & expoliaverit Prin- cipatus; altitudinem, quia in cælos adscende- rit; in quibus omnibus vel maxime sese exeruit Christi dilectio: Quæ vero abundantissime de- monstrata est in mysterio crucis, ad quam has di- mensiones referunt Gregorius Nyss. Hieronymus in h. l. Augustinus epist. CXX. cap. 26. libr. II. de doctr. Christ. cap. 41. serm. VII. de Verbo Apo- stoli. De qua explicatione ita Theophylactus: Gregorius Nysses, inquit, per latitudinem hujus- modi, profunditatem & longitudinem crucem dicit significari: comprecatumque Ephesiis fuisse Aposto- lum afferit, ut quirent crucis mysterium contemplari. Siquidem hac cruce omnis contineretur dispensatio, quod sane est convenientius. Per crucem enim maxime Dei erga nos charitatem perspicuam fieri, sicuti & Dominus dicit, & Paulus modo subjungit. Sed rectius sine dubio has dimensiones ad magnitu- dinem mysterii de Christo referunt Chrysostomus, Theodoretus & Theophylactus, ubi Chrysostomus expresse simul immensitatem dilectionis & amoris innui docet: Τυτέσι, τὸ μυσήριον τὸ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν οἰκονομηθὲν μετὰ ἀκριβείας εἰδέναι, κὴ τὸ πλάτος,

| καὶ τὸ μῆκος, καὶ τὸ βάθος, καὶ τὸ ὕψος. Τουτέστι τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Θεοῦ, πῶς πανταχοῦ ἐκτέ- ταται, καὶ σωματικοῖς αὐτὴν ὑπέγραψε σχήμασι. Quod prius, inquit Theophylactus, fuerat exorsus & comprecatus, ut Spiritus his cum sapientia tum revela- tionis concederetur, ut intelligerent, qualis eorum voca- tionis spes esset, & hujusmodi reliqua, idipsum im- praesentiarum prosequitur, ut possitis (inquiens) mente & cogitatione complecti cum fidelibus caeteris, quale illud mysterium sit, quod vestri gratia est dis- pensatum, & eo est magnitudinis provectum, ut sit terrarum ubique amplissime propagatum. Unde & hoc undique circumplexus sub corporali figura de- scripsit. Explicavi enim ipse, ut potui, hoc sacra- mentum, nihil tamen potest meis ex verbis, nisi per Spiritum patefiat, comprehendi. Neque aliter vobis licebit ejusmodi mente concipere, nisi a Spiritu corro- boratis. Hic sensus ceu simplicissimus probatur Crocio, probatus & Beat. Osiandro est, q. d. rogo Deum, ut possitis una cum aliis sinceris Christianis aliquo modo mente vestra complecti immensam Dei erga vos charitatem, quae, ut Metaphora utar, in omnes dimensiones sese extendit. Hyperius quidem refert harum dimensionum designationem ad cer- titudinem & plenitudinem cognitionis dilectionis Christi, sicut certissimae sunt Mathematicae di- mensiones, & perfectae, cum in corporibus soli- dis longitudo, latitudo, altitudo & profunditas observatur. Sed dilectionis ipsius divinae haec est geometria ἀγεώμετρος καὶ ἄμετρος, non vero cognitionis nostrae, occupatae circa dilectionem Dei; atque ut illa vere immensa est: ita nostra cognitio certa quidem est, non tamen perfecta, & omnibus numeris ac dimensionibus absoluta. Alii tamen evolvunt singulas dimensiones: Nec id dis- plicere potest. Non enim praeter causam distin- cte enumeratae sunt. Hemmingius in Comment. in h. l. intelligit mysterium gratiae DEI & dilectionis Christi erga nos, ita enim se exponit Apostolus, ut cognoscatis charitatem Christi immensam erga vos. Quemadmodum enim Patris misericordia excedit omnia opera ejus, juxta Davidis sententiam: Ita omnem mensuram superat amor Filii Dei. Nam si latitudinem ejus spectas, nullis limitibus clauditur: Si longitudinem consideras, ad omnes fines orbis ter- rarum sese extendit: Si profunditatem attendis, hu- millima & abjectissima in mundo complectitur: Si altitudinem respicis, superat caelos. Hic sensus hu- jus loci simplex & verus est, nugas de lignea cruce Domini & sphaerica figura relinquamus. Beat. Aegid. Hunnius ita hasce dimensiones explicat, totum textum sic παραφράζων. Ut valeatis assequi, quae sit latitudo &c. Precor etiam, ut cum reliquis Chri- stianis valeatis aliquo modo per fidem pensitare, quae latitudo, longitudo, profunditas, & sublimitas my- sterii gratiae & misericordiae Dei per Christum ex- hibita: Quod videlicet ejus latitudo nullis uspiam terminis se claudi patiatur: Quod longitudo ejus se porrigat a solis ortu usque ad occasum, & in omnium gentium orbem se extendat: Quod profunditas illius ad contemptissima quaeque e caeno miseriae attollenda se demittat: quod denique altitudo ejus omnium ho- minum & Angelorum intelligentiam transcendat, atque sic in omnes dimensiones citra mensuram & modum pateat. Quae explicatio prae aliis placet. Quomodo id ad aedificia & dimensionum comme- morationem, cum mentio facta sit habitaculi vel templi Christi, applicet Dan. Heinsius, de eo vid. exercitationes ejus in h. l. Nos facile acquiescimus Hunnianae interpretationi, per latitudinem ta- men universalitatem dilectionis divinae sese am- plissime porrigentis ad totum genus humanum, per longitudinem æternitatem a parte ante & post, per altitudinem sublimitatem immensam, ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιςῆς φύσεως constitutam, per profunditatem mysterii dilectionis abyssum, & τὰ βάθη misericordiæ investigabilia, Rom. XI. vers. 33. designari autumantes. Hic sacram, inquit Beat. Glassius in Dom. XVI. post Trin. pag. 553. mathematicam instituit Apostolus, & secundum quatuor dimensiones dilectionem Christi quasi metitur, latitudinem, longitudinem, profunditatem & sublimitatem illi tribuens. Verum mensuratione ista ἀνθρωποπαθῶς instituta, ejusdem immensurabilitatem & immensitatem in rei veritate indicat, quasi dicat, altior est cælis, profundior mari, latior altitudine terrarum, longior omni tempore, utpote in omnem æternitatem durans.

## 3:19
Verse 19. And to know the surpassing love of Christ which surpasses knowledge.

In the Manuscript: The surpassing love of the knowledge of Christ: that supreme love, namely of GOD and neighbor, which arises from the knowledge of Christ. It seems that in Jerome's time some books also had it this way: for he himself explains this passage thus, See Phil. III. 8. And to know here is to experience in oneself.

His interpretation is held here, what the Apostle understands by 'to comprehend what is the breadth' etc., namely to acknowledge the charity of Christ as superior to all knowledge. The Apostle had spoken of being rooted in the love of GOD; he had spoken of the comprehension of the mystery of divine love according to all dimensions: now for the sake of explanation he adds the knowledge of the love of Christ, and indeed by which it is known that it is truly incomprehensible by us, and transcends all our knowledge, so that we may understand that he is not dealing with any other mystery of love than that which is in Christ, and that he exhibits its dimensions as comprehended in such a way that we acknowledge that they can by no means be comprehended by us, and that it surpasses all knowledge, not only ours, but even that of Angels, because knowledge is posited generally without restriction to human knowledge. Concerning which Ambrose in this place. After the infinite and incomprehensible knowledge and ineffable clemency of God the Father, he also wants us to acknowledge the charity of Christ, because it is of supereminent knowledge, and it is understood as human, so that the love of Christ may be held as above the knowledge of men. For who can gather the reason for this mystery of charity, that GOD should be born man for the sake of man, then die for men, the Lord for servants, the Creator for the creature, the pious for the impious? For what reason did he love us so? Or why should he have anything of ours, who is in need of nothing, is this not charity above the knowledge of men? Or what man could show this charity to anyone, although he is unequal to it, and by this it surpasses human inventions? Therefore he wants us to know this, because our sense cannot attain, nor perceive the depth of the benefits of Christ toward us, so that we may always be simple and devoted to him, and as we cannot satisfy our debts in any way, we may persevere in his faith even unto death. For he, for the magnificence of his Majesty, did those things for us which are unworthy of him, so that we also, as much as we can, may serve him. The Grotian gloss concerning the love of God and neighbor is clearly alien. For it in no way agrees with the words of the text. Therefore a new text is substituted, and all other codices are corrected from one MS., which new text, however, does not introduce our love, but the love of Christ transcending knowledge. And if the Grotian translation concerning supreme love, which arises from the knowledge of Christ, is admitted; even so it does not fit our charity, which the imperfection of our love forbids us to call supreme and surpassing in relation to God and neighbor, unless one likes to invent works of supererogation with the Papists. Nor is there any support for this gloss from Phil. III. 8; where the subject is the faith and righteousness of Christ, which is to be apprehended through faith, compared with which our inherent righteousness is to be estimated as mere loss, nay, as refuse on account of the imperfection and impurity adhering to it.

That you may be filled unto all the fullness of God) I take fullness here actively, John I. 16, Col. II. 9. The sense is, that you may be filled with all those gifts with which God is accustomed to fill men.

Crocius rightly explains the sense here: Let that fullness of gifts be understood, of which God makes us participants through Christ dwelling in us. Thus Theophylact. Therefore the Apostle prays that the Ephesians may not be adorned with ordinary gifts, or attain only some degree, but that they may be accumulated here in every way with every kind of the most excellent gifts, for example, knowledge, faith, charity, every fruit of righteousness, Rom. XV. 14, Phil. I. 9, 11, so that they may become more and more similar to God, until at length they are most perfectly filled with God in the other world, when he shall be all in all, 1 Cor. 15, 28. Beza said he preferred to translate it as fullness, because it was said a little before that Christ dwells in our hearts, so that God in a certain way may fill us in him, and we may be as it were filled with God in him.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Γνῶναί τε τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς γνώσεως ἀγάπην τοῦ χριστοῦ.

In Manuscripto: Τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν ἀγάπην τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ χριστοῦ: summam illam dilectionem, DEI scilicet & proximi, quæ ex cognitione Christi oritur. Videntur etiam Hieronymi tempore libri quidam sic habuisse: nam ipse sic hunc locum exponit, Vide Philipp. III. 8. Et γνῶναι hic est in semet experiri.

Interpretatio ejus hic habetur, quidnam intelligat Apostolus per τὸ καταλαβέσθαι τί τὸ πλάτος &c. nimirum agnoscere charitatem Christi omni cognitione superiorem. Dixerat Apostolus de radicatione in dilectione DEI; dixerat de comprehensione mysterii dilectionis divinæ secundum omnes dimensiones: nunc ἐξηγήσεως causa addit dilectionis Christi cognitionem, & quidem qua cognoscitur illa vere incomprehensibilis a nobis, omnemque nostram cognitionem transcendens, ut intelligamus, non de alio mysterio dilectionis, quam quæ in Christo est, se agere, ejusque dimensiones ita exhibere comprehensas, ut agnoscamus, easdem comprehendi a nobis minime posse, omnemque non nostræ tantum, sed Angelicæ etiam cognitionis, quia generatim cognitio ponitur sine restrictione ad humanam cognitionem, superare. Quo de Ambrosius in h. l. Post Dei Patris infinitam & incomprehensibilem cognitionem & inenarrabilem clementiam, Christi quoque agnoscere nos vult charitatem, quia supereminentis est scientiæ, & subintelligitur humanæ, ut super scientiam hominum habeatur dilectio Christi. Quis enim potest colligere mysterii hujus charitatis rationem, ut & DEUS hominis causa homo nasceretur, deinde moreretur pro hominibus, pro servis Dominus, pro creatura Creator, pro impiis pius? Propter quid ita dilexit nos? Aut ut quid nostrum haberet, qui nullius indiget, numquid non charitas hæc super scientiam hominum est? Aut quis hominum hanc poterit charitatem alicui exhibere, quanquam impar sit, ac per hoc supereminet humana commenta? Hoc ergo vult nos scire, quia sensus noster assequi non potest, nec perspicere profunditatem beneficiorum Christi erga nos, ut perinde semper ei simplices & devoti, & qui debitis nulla ratione satisfacere possumus, vel in fide ejus usque ad mortem perseveremus. Ille enim pro magnificentia Majestatis suæ ea gessit pro nobis, quæ sibi indigna sunt, ut & nos, in quantum possimus, ei famulemur. Grotiana glossa de dilectioneDei & proximi plane ἀλλότριος est. Ea enim verbis textus nullatenus convenit. Ideo novus textus substituitur, & ex uno MS. alii codices omnes emendantur, qui tamen novus textus non infert dilectionem nostram, sed dilectionem cognitionis Christi transcendentem. Ac si admittatur translatio Grotiana de dilectione summa, quæ ex cognitione Christi oriatur; ne sic tamen charitati nostræ convenit, quam summam & ὑπερβάλλουσαν dicere in ordine ad Deum & pro- ximum imperfectio nostræ dilectionis vetat, nisi fingere cum Papistis, opera supererogationis li- beat. Neque a Phil. III. 8. quicquam huic glossæ præsidii est; ubi de fide & justitia Christi, quæ per fidem apprehendenda est, cum qua collata inhæ- rens nostra justitia pro mero damno, imo pro σκυβάλοις ob imperfectionem & impuritatem adhærentem æstimanda est, agitur.

Ἵνα πληρωθῆτε εἰς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ) πλήρωμα hic sumo Active, Joh. I. 16. Col. II. 9. Sensus est, ut im- pleamini omnibus illis donis, quibus Deus implere homi- nes solet.

Recte sensum hic exponit Crocius: Intelligatur igitur illa donorum plenitudo, cujus nos Deus per Christum in nobis habitantem reddit participes. Sic Theophylactus. Proinde orat Apostolus, ut Ephesii non vulgaribus donis ornentur, aut aliquem tantum gradum consequantur, sed omnibus modis bic cu- mulentur omni præstantissimorum donorum genere, puta, cognitione, fide, charitate, omni fructu justi- tiæ, Rom. XV. 14. Phil. I. 9. 11. ut magis ac magis Deo fiant similes, donec tandem perfectissime in altero seculo impleantur Deo, cum futurus est omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15, 28. Beza plenitudinem se maluisse vertere dixit, propterea quod paulo ante dictum est; Christum in cordibus nostris habitare, ut Deus quo- dammodo in ipso nos impleat, & nos Deo veluti im- pleamur in ipso.

## 3:20
Verse 20. Now to him who is able to do above all things above abundantly, than we ask or think) The epistle to the Romans ends with a similar doxology. First he says he is able to do above all things, namely those which have been seen thus far. Then he adds also much above those things which we might dare to ask or think, 'above abundantly' are several cumulative intensifying particles, which kind of speaking Paul loves, as can be seen also in 2 Cor. III. v. 9, VII. 13, Philipp. I. 9, 1 Thess. IV. 1, 10, Rom. V. 10, 2 Cor. VII. 4, 1 Tim. I. 14, above I. 21, below IV. 10.

According to the power that works in us) In the Manuscript 'in you', that is, in such a way as it began to work. For 'according to' often signifies likeness.

By this doxology, as we have said, the Apostle testifies that he does not in the least doubt about being heard. Moreover, he describes the power of God not only with a notable eulogy and great weight of words, that He can do ALL things which we ask, but he says that He can do above all those things which we ask, nay, ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ superabundantly, which can be rendered with infinite redundancy. Nor does it consist in that, but he adds also above all things which we conceive in our mind, that He can do more than we can think. Let those, therefore, says Crocius in the cited places, be far removed from Christians, who say, we do not understand how it can be done: Therefore God cannot do it. We must not, therefore, invent contradictions so that we may conclude an impossibility. But if two things seem to us contradictory, we must nevertheless believe, provided that Scripture affirms both. Which admonition can not undeservedly be opposed to the associates and Patriarchs of Crocius, nay, to Crocius himself, since they deny those things which are expressly brought forward in Scripture, because they seem to us contradictory and impossible. The things which are added concerning the power that works in us serve not only to illustrate the divine power, but also to prove the will of God from clear examples of grace. Whence Hyperius rightly observes, according to the reasoning from the will of God already discovered from certain signs, God not only can do good, but also wills to. That He does will to, however, can be known from this, that we already now acknowledge His power, effectively acting in us; God adorns His Church with admirable gifts, from which believers can understand that God wishes them very well.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑπὲρ πάντα ποιῆσαι ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ, ὧν αἰτούμεθα ἢ νοοῦμεν) Simili ferme δοξολογίᾳ fi- nitur ad Romanos epistola. Primum dicit posse super omnia nempe quæ visa sunt hactenus. Deinde addit etiam pluri- mum supra ea, quæ petere aut cogitare audeamus, ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ, sunt particulæ plures αὐξητικαὶ cumulatæ, quod loquendi genus amat Paulus, ut videre & 2. Cor. III. v. 9. VII. 13. Philipp. I. 9. 1. Thess. IV. 1. 10. Rom. V. 10. 2. Cor. VII. 4. 1. Tim. I. 14. supra I. 21. infra IV. 10.

Κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν ἐνεργουμένην ἐν ἡμῖν) In Manuscri- pto ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, ita, ut incepit operari. Nam κατὰ sæpe similitudinem significat.

Hac δοξολογίᾳ, ut diximus, Apostolus testatur, se minime de exauditione dubitare. Non autem tantum insigni elogio & magno verborum pon- dere potentiam Dei describit, quod possit facere OMNIA, quæ petimus, sed super omnia illa facere posse ait, quæ petimus, imo ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ super- abundanter, quod reddi potest cum infinita redun- dantia. Nec in eo consistit, sed addit etiam super omnia, quæ mente concipimus, quod plura possit facere, quam nos cogitare. Facesseant ergo, inquit in LL. CC. Crocius, a Christianis procul, qui dicunt, non intelligimus, quomodo fieri possit: Ergo Deus fa- cere non potest. Non igitur contradictiones fingere debemus, ut concludamus impossibilitatem. Sed si duo videantur nobis contradictoria, nihilominus credere debemus, modo scriptura utrumque affirmet. Quæ commonitio non immerito sociis & Patriar- chis Crocii, imo Crocio ipsi opponi potest, cum ideo negant, quæ ῥητῶς in scriptura afferuntur, quod ea nobis contradictoria & impossibilia vi- deantur. Quæ adduntur de δυνάμει τῇ ἐνεργουμένῃ ἐν ἡμῖν non tantum ad illustrandam potentiam di- vinam, sed etiam ad voluntatem Dei ab exemplis luculentis gratiæ comprobandam faciunt. Unde recte observat Hyperius, secundum rationem a voluntate Dei jam ex certis signis comperta Deus non solum potest benefacere, sed vult quoque. Quod autem velit, cognosci hinc potest, quod jam nunc agnoscamus ejus vim, efficaciter in no- bis agentem Deus suam Ecclesiam admirandis donis ornat, ex quibus intelligere possunt creden- tes, quod Deus optime ipsis velit.

## 3:21
V. 21.

V. 21. To Him be glory in the Church in Christ Jesus) In the Church, just as it is the custom to give thanks to God through Christ for sins, so also [it is the custom] through Christ, Rom. I. 8. VII. 25.

To all the generations of the age of ages. Amen.) Here also, for the sake of amplification, the Apostle mixed two Hebrew expressions, of which the former is לְדֹר וָדֹר, Psal. X. 6. the latter עַלְמֵי עַד, Es. XLV. 17. and elsewhere. Churches were accustomed to acclaim such doxologies with Amen: which Paul leads them to do.

Let there be glory, that is, let God be glorified on account of the grace exhibited in Christ, both to the whole human race and especially to the Gentiles; in the Church: because outside the Church there is no true glorification pleasing to God; since that ought to be done through Jesus Christ, or in his name, Col. III. ver. 17. and thus through faith, Heb. XI. ver. 6. That εἰς πάσας τὰς γενεὰς, which the Vulgate rendered κατὰ πόδα, into all generations, Beza translated into all ages. It is an age of a century, says Crocius, which is not an age of ages. For a century is often taken for a defined time. But here a perpetual duration is noted. And not without reason. The grace of GOD is eternal, why therefore should He not be glorified eternally? He wishes, therefore, that the Ephesians learn to glorify God, and teach this to their own, so that glory may be attributed by posterity as well, until the eternal glorification in heaven succeeds the glorification which is made here through faith. This perpetual duration, as Hemmingius warns, admonishes us of the glory of God regarding two things. First, that we, who are members of Christ, should perpetually proclaim the glory of God in Christ, by the example of David, singing in this manner: Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you over the judgments of your righteousness. Then, that we may know that the Church of GOD will remain perpetually. For if glory is to be attributed to GOD perpetually, and that cannot be done except in the Church, it follows that the Church will not be abolished. Therefore, it will be preserved here in the world until the judgment, and then after the resurrection it will remain, celebrating God in all eternity. Regarding the little word Amen, Crocius rightly says: It is a seal, with which he seals the discourse, and both testifies to his own trust toward God, and inflames and strengthens in the minds of the Ephesians his zeal for glorifying Him.

Latin:

V. 21.

V. 21. Αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) In Ecclesia sicut mos est per Christum peccata, ita etiam per Christum gratias Deo agere, Rom. I. 8. VII. 25.

'Εις πάσας τὰς γενεὰς τοῦ αἰῶν© τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.) Hic quoque augendi causa duas loquutiones Ebraicas miscuit Apostolus, quarum prior est לְדֹר וָדֹר, Psal. X. 6. altera עַלְמֵי עַד, Es. XLV. 17. & alibi. Solebant talibus δοξολο- γίαις Ecclesiæ acclamare, Amen: quod ut faciant, præit eis Paulus.

Sit gloria, id est, glorificetur Deus ob gratiam, tum universo generi humano, tum imprimis gen- tibus exhibitam in Christo; in Ecclesia: quia extra Ecclesiam nulla est vera, Deoque grata glorifica- tio; siquidem illa per Jesum Christum, vel in no- mine ejus fieri debeat, Col. III. vers. 17. adeoque per fidem, Ebr. XI. vers. 6. Illa εἰς πάσας τὰς γε- νεὰς, quæ Vulgatus reddidit κατὰ πόδα, in omnes generationes, Beza transtulit in omnes ætates. Est ætas seculi, ait Crocius, quæ non est seculi seculo- rum. Seculum enim pro definito tempore sæpe capi- tur. Hic vero duratio perpetua notatur. Nec im- merito. DEI gratia est æterna, cur igitur non æternum glorificaretur? Vult igitur, ut Ephesii discant glorificare Deum, & doceant id suos, ut a posteris quoque gloria tribuatur, donec glorificatio- ni, quæ hic fit per fidem, succedat in cælo glorifica- tio æterna. Hæc perpetua duratio, monente Hem- mingio, gloriæ Dei de duabus rebus nos admonet. Primum ut nos, qui Christi membra sumus, perpetuo gloriam Dei in Christo prædicemus, exemplo Davi- dis, in hunc modum canentis: Septies in die lau- dem tibi dixi super judicia justitiæ tuæ. Deinde ut sciamus, perpetuo mansuram Ecclesiam DEI. Nam si perpetuo DEO tribuenda est gloria, & id fieri non potest, nisi in Ecclesia, sequitur, Ecclesiam non abolitum iri. Proinde & hic in mundo usque ad judicium conservabitur, & deinde post resur- rectionem manebit, in omni æternitate Deum cele- brans. De vocula Amen Crocius recte: Est sigil- lum, quo obsignat sermonem, atque tum suam testatur erga Deum fiduciam, tum ejus glorificandi studium in Ephesiorum animis inflammat, robo- ratque.

## 4:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE EPISTLE, PARÆNETIC, ON the Christian Life, worthy of the calling to the faith of Christ. SECTION I. GENERAL MORAL PRECEPTS. CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle now exhorts that they walk worthily of their calling, and especially that they strive to keep the unity of the Spirit, with the most weighty reasons added from the mystical rationale of unity, and the dispensation of the various gifts, which Christ distributed after his ascension into heaven, ordaining Doctors, for the edification of the whole body, so that we all may be able to rise to the just measure of his stature. Then he recalls them from their former conversation of gentilism to the true newness of life, from various vices to Christian virtues.

There are therefore two parts: The former is an exhortation to concord and peace, up to v. 16. The latter, to the holiness of life, up to v. 32.

PART I.

Exhortation to concord and peace.

Vers. 1. I beseech you) The part of doctrine being completed, he comes, as is his custom, to exhortations.

I the prisoner in the Lord) It is the same as what he says above III, 1. prisoner of Christ. For ב among the Hebrews signifies 'on account of' just as other things.

Worthily of the calling, with which you were called) In such a way as it is fitting for those to live, whom God has affected with so great and so unexpected a benefit. A similar manner of speaking [is found in] Rom. XVI. 2. Philipp. I. 27. Colos. I. 10. 1. Thess. II. 12.

He sets forth the summary of the entire parenetic treatment: that they may walk worthily of their calling, concerning which he had brought forward such august things. That treatment he subsequently executes both with moral precepts and common ones up to chapter V. 21, and particular ones, concerning a certain state, such as spouses, in the remainder of the fifth chapter; children and parents, servants and masters, chapter VI, in the first 9 verses: and then with warnings about the spiritual armor against the temptations of the Prince of darkness, v. 10 seqq. In the generic exhortation he makes mention of his bonds, which Jerome understands as the bonds of Paul's charity and love, but others more correctly understand as the bonds of his captivity, of which he also made mention in c. III. 1 and c. IV. 20. He calls himself a prisoner in the Lord, although others might prefer that he is exhorting in the Lord, just as in the other part he adjures in the Lord, verse 17. Therefore, he intermixes with the exhortation arguments that might move them, whether from his bonds for the Lord, or from the authority of the Lord, and especially from their own state, which demands a life worthy of the calling received. Theophylact says: It befits a Master not only to command his disciples what is more upright, but also to serve them for their salvation. Therefore, Paul also prays in the manner of a servant, and proposes both the things to be prayed for and his bonds. For he says, I, a prisoner in the Lord, as if he were to say: Not by any wicked crime of mine, but on account of the grace of the Lord have I been cast into bonds. Venerate, therefore, also those who have endured shackles for Christ the Lord. But what do I pray for? For myself, indeed, nothing, but for you, that just as your calling demands, so you may walk. For you have been called to certain great things, namely, that you may sit together with Christ, being future participants of the same heavenly kingdom. Wherefore, this dignity of yours will not be to be disparaged by works unworthy of Christ. He makes the calling the norm of Christian conversation, just as the calling is the norm of duty. Conf. 1 Cor. VII. verse 1, chapter IIX. verse 17, Tit. II. v. 11, 1 Petr. I. 3, chapter II. 9.

Latin:

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ PARÆNETICA, DE Vita Christiana, vocatione ad fidem Christi digna. SECTIO I. GENERALIA PRÆCEPTA MORALIA. CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Hortatur jam Apostolus, ut digne ambulent vocatione sua, & imprimis, ut studeant ser- vare unitatem Spiritus, additis causis gra- vissimis e mystica unitatis ratione, ac diver- sorum donorum dispensatione, quæ Chri- stus post ascensionem in cælos distribuit, or- dinans Doctores, ad ædificationem totius corporis, ut nos omnes possimus ad justum staturæ ejus modum assurgere. Deinde re- vocat eos a pristina gentilismi conversatione ad veram novitatem vitæ, a vitiis variis ad Christianas virtutes.

Partes proinde duæ sunt: Prior est exhortatio ad concordiam & pacem, ad v. 16. Posterior, ad vitæ sanctitatem, usque ad v. 32.

PARS I.

Adhortatio ad concordiam & pacem.

Vers. 1. Παρακαλῶ ὑ̂ς ὑμᾶς) Parte doctrinæ absoluta venit, ut solet, ad adhortationes.

Ἐγὼ ὁ δέσμιος ἐν Κυρίῳ) Idem est, quod supra III, 1. dicit δέσμιος τῦ χριστῦ. Nam ב Hebræis ut alia ita & propter significat.

Ἀξίως τ̃ κλήσεως, ᾗ ἐκλήθητε) Ita ut par est eos vivere, quos tanto & tam inexpectato beneficio Deus affecit. Simile loquendi genus Rom. XVI. 2. Philipp. I. 27. Colos. I. 10. 1. Thess. II. 12.

Summam præmittit universæ Paræneticæ tractationis: ut digne vocatione sua, de qua tam augusta adduxerat, ambulent. Illam vero tractationem deinceps exequitur tum præceptis morum & communibus usque ad cap. V. 21. & particularibus, certum statum concernentibus, utpote conjugum, capite quinto reliquo; liberorum & parentum, servorum & Dominorum, cap. VI. versibus 9. prioribus: tum monitis de armatura spirituali adversus tentationes Principis tenebrarum, v. 10. seqq. In adhortatione generica vinculorum suorum meminit, quæ Hieronymus de vinculis charitatis & amoris Pauli, sed alii rectius de vinculis captivitatis ejusdem intelligunt, quorum etiam c. III. 1. c. IV. 20. mentionem fecit. Vinctum autem se dicit in Domino, etsi alii malint, ipsum adhortari in Domino, quemadmodum in parte altera obtestatur in Domino, vers. 17. Adhortationi itaque immiscet argumenta, quæ moveant ipsos, sive a vinculis pro Domino, sive ab autoritate Domini, & imprimis a statu ipsorum, qui dignam vocatione accepta vitam postulat. Theophylactus inquit: Non imperare modo discipulis, quæ rectiora sunt, decet Magistrum, sed iis etiam pro eorum salute inservire. Propterea & Paulus in servi morem precatur, proponitque precanda & vincula. Vinctus enim ego inquit in Domino, perinde ac si dicat: Non pravo aliquo meo facinore, sed ob Domini gratiam sum conjectus in vincula. Veneremini ergo & eos, qui pro Christo Dn. compedes tolerarunt. Verum quid precor? Pro me equidem nihil, sed pro vobis, ut quemadmodum vestra deposcit vocatio, sic incedatis. Estis namque ad magna quædam vocati, ut cum Christo videlicet consideatis, regni cælestis eidem futuri participes. Quocirca non erit vestra hac dignitas indignis Christo operibus vituperanda. Normam Christianæ conversationis facit vocationem, quemadmodum norma officii est vocatio. Conf. 1. Cor. VII. vers. 1. cap. IIX. vers. 17. Tit. II. v. 11. 1. Petr. I. 3. cap. II. 9.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. Μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης. Acts XX. 19. Phil. II. 3. Coloss. II. 18. 23. III. v. 12. This is a great virtue, unknown to almost all philosophers, to which the memory of what they were before such a benign calling, from which other goods flow, ought especially to have led men. Therefore, the Apostles mention it so often.

Καὶ πραότητος κ̃ μακροθυμίας) It is of gentleness, not to be moved by light matters: of long-suffering, to restrain anger even in more serious matters; concerning this see Matth. XVIII. 6. 29. 1 Cor. XIII. 4. 1 Thess. V. 14. 2 Cor. VI. 6. Gal. V. 22. You have both joined together also in Coloss. III. 12.

Ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ) Thus also Colos. III. verse 13. Ἀνέχεσθαι is סבל, to bear gently with the ignorances of others, although they are troublesome to us. A similitude derived from a burden. He made the construction, however, as if he had said not περιπατῆσαι but περιπατῆτε. It is frequent for Paul to look to the sense.

He encourages concord, partly by enjoining charity in general, partly by enjoining unity in the Spirit in particular. But because pride is the greatest obstacle to both, he admonishes them toward humanity; since a readiness for agitation and anger is very harmful to both, he exhorts them to gentleness, to long-suffering, and also to mutual tolerance. Theophylact considers that humanity is brought forward not only for the sake of concord, but also for the sake of holiness, as the foundation of all virtues. He shows in this place how it is permitted for each one to lead a life in accordance with the dignity of his calling. For if, he says, you show yourself to be humble, and have an understanding of yourself, and understand with what goods you have been gifted by GOD, you will surely be humbled and will draw back, and you will strive to show obedience to Him who has been beneficent toward you. Moreover, humility is the mother and foundation of all virtues. And for that reason, and from this, the Lord, naming the kinds of virtues, declares those blessed who were more humble in Spirit, and who would display humility before others. With all humility, he says, as that which is to be preferred not only in words, but in deeds, and in habit and gesture itself. Nor will this humility be for one or another, but it is to be observed toward all, whether you speak of the lowly and abject, or the opulent and famous. Most people, however, refer the pursuit of unity here to charity, because concord is preserved if we live humbly with one another, and the bond of spiritual peace and all concord is easily dissolved by the proud and arrogant. Therefore, he commends humility before God and men. Pride, haughtiness, and arrogance think magnificently of themselves, value all their own things highly, hold others and the gifts and all the deeds of others in low esteem, are fierce, suffer nothing, stir up quarrels, disturb everything, and are the contrary genius of humility. Meekness is a kind of offspring of humility, which moderates anger, suppresses the unjust, curbs the just, and contains the agitated so that it does not overstep the limits prescribed by GOD. To this, long-suffering (μακροθυμία) provides support, so that one may be slow to anger, easily forgive injuries, and lay aside the desire for vengeance: and tolerance, by which we bear the infirmities of others with an even mind, nor do we withdraw from the friendship of a neighbor because of those things in him that displease us, but we constantly love the person, even if we hold their vices in hatred. This tolerance must be mutual if concord is to be preserved, which the Apostle hints is the end of this exhortation. The Apostle admonishes in this place, says Theophylact, what gain is to come from meekness, and what follows from patience. Then, lest anyone should say, how could he be able to bear his neighbor, who is more prone to anger, and is clearly convicted? He therefore introduces the manner of tolerance in charity, saying: For if we attain this, we will tolerate one another.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης. Actor. XX. 19. Phil. II. 3. Coloss. II. 18. 23. III. v. 12. Magna hæc virtus est, Philosophis ferme omnibus incognita, ad quam præcipue ducere homines debuit memoria ejus, quod fuerunt ante tam benignam vocationem, unde cætera bona fluunt. Ideo toties ejus meminere Apostoli.

Καὶ πραότητος κ̃ μακροθυμίας) Lenitatis est, non moveri ob res leves: Μακροθυμίας etiam in gravioribus cohibere iram, de hoc vide Matth. XVIII. 6. 29. 1. Cor. XIII. 4. 1. Thess. V. 14. 2. Cor. VI. 6. Gal. V. 22. utrumque conjunctum habes & Coloss. III. 12.

Ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ) Sic & Colos. III. vers. 13. Ἀνέχεσθαι סבל est aliorum ignorantias, quanquam nobis molestas, leniter ferre. Similitudo ab onere deducta. Ita autem fecit constructionem, quasi dixisset non περιπατῆσαι sed περιπατῆτε. Frequens Paulo respicere τὸ ἰσύμφωνον.

Ad concordiam excitat, partim in genere chari- tatem, partim in specie unitatem in Spiritu præci- piens. Quia vero utrique maxime obstat super- bia, ad humanitatem commonefacit; quum officiat utrique multum facilitas commotionis & iræ, ad lenitatem, ad longanimitatem, nec non ad mutuam tolerantiam hortatur. Theophylactus non tantum humanitatem concordiæ, sed etiam sanctitatis cau- sa adduci censet, ceu virtutum omnium funda- mentum. Ostendit hoc loco, quemadmodum cuique liceat pro vocationis dignitate & vitam ducere. Si enim, inquit, humilem te ipse præstiteris, & tui ipsius habueris notionem, & quibus fueris à DEO bonis dignatus intelliges, delebis profecto & contraheris, & ei gerere morem studebis, qui in te fuerit benefi- cus. Est præterea cunctarum virtutum mater hu- militas & fundamentum. Eoque & ex hac Domi- nus, virtutum genera nominans, beatos affirmat, qui Spiritu essent humiliores, præ seque ferrent humilita- tem. Cum omni inquit humilitate, ut quæ non ver- bis modo, sed factis, habituque ipso & gestu sit præfe- renda. Nec in unum alterumve hæc erit humili- tas, sed in omnes servanda, sive tenuem dixeris & ab- jectum, sive opulentum & clarum. Ad charitatem vero plerique referunt hic unitatis studium, quod concordia servetur, si humiliter invicem vivamus, & vinculum pacis spiritualis omnisquæ concordiæ facile solvatur à superbis & arrogantibus. Ideo humilitatem coram Deo & hominibus commen- dat. Superbia, fastus, & arrogantia magnifice de se habet, omnia sua magni æstimat, alios, & alio- rum dona, ac facta omnia parvi pendet, est ferox, nihil suffert, movet lites, turbat omnia, contra- rius humilitatis genius. Humilitatis quædam veluti proles mansuetudo est, quæ iram modera- tur, injustam supprimit, justam frænat, commo- tam continet, ne limites egrediatur à DEO præ- scriptos. Cui μακροθυμία longanimitas admini- culatur, ut tardus ad iram quis sit, facile injurias condonet, & vindictæ studium deponat: Et tolerantia, quâ aliorum infirmitates æquo animo ferimus, nec ob ea, quæ nobis in proximo displi- cent, ab ejus amicitia recedimus, sed personam con- stanter amamus, etsi vitia odio habeamus. Quam tolerantiam mutuam esse oportet, ut concordia servari debeat, quem finem cohortationis hujus esse innuit Apostolus. Commonefacit hoc loco Apostolus, inquit Theophylactus, quidnam obventu- rum sit ex mansuetudine lucrum, & quid ex patien- tia subsequatur. Deinde ne quis diceret, quo pa- cto quiverit proximum ferre, qui ad iram sit prom- ptior, & plane convictetur? Inducit itaque toleran- tiæ modum in charitate, inquiens: Hanc enim si con- sequemur, nos invicem tolerabimus.

## 4:3
Vers. 3.

Σπουδάζοντες τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ Πνεύματος ἐν τῷ συνδέσμῳ τῆς εἰρήνης.) He calls the unity of the Church, which is a spiritual body, ἑνότητα τοῦ Πνεύματος; it cannot be preserved where haughtiness, emulation, envy, and other things contrary to love reign. See both [epistles] to the Corinthians.

Here he descends from the general precept of charity to the preservation of spiritual unity. Strive to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, which does not pertain to all, as charity is to be shown to all men, but to the faithful or members of the Church. Whence this exhortation is wrongly snatched by the Syncretists to preserve unity with those who differ in faith. The subject of this unity are the faithful, who preserve the bond of peace among themselves mutually. The form is that it is the unity of the Spirit, that is, not simply the consensus and concord of minds, as Calvin explains, but the unity of the Spirit, which prevails in the reborn, inasmuch as they are governed by the Holy Spirit. Crocius, along with Musculus, Beza, and Zanchius, prefers this sense, namely that internal and spiritual charity is denoted, which is distinguished from external and secular [charity] by this very fact, that it is called the unity of the Spirit. Through the Spirit, others understand the Holy Spirit, to whom as the Author the unity of the Church is certainly to be referred: Concerning which Theophylact says: Just as in the body the spirit contains and unites all things, and the members are diverse, so the Holy Spirit governs in us the faithful, who makes all unanimous, and binds them, although they differ in nation and customs or arts, and through this same Spirit we are all made one. The matter comes to almost the same thing. It is from the Holy Spirit that the Spirit dominates in us, not the flesh. Nothing, however, prevents understanding the unity of the Spirit in the former way, that all ought to be one body and one soul in such a way that there is, as it were, one Spirit of all. Which is the form and spiritual soul of this unity. By the bond of peace, the manner of preserving the unity of the Church is shown: peace with God and men. As remaining in the unity of the Church, peace with GOD is to be retained, which is retained, according to Crocius, by faith and the pursuit of obedience. But here the Apostle speaks of mutual peace among the pious, which is friendly and quiet conversation. That is the bond by which the unity of the Church is contained, just as a body has its ligaments by which the members are bound together, which the Greek word εἰρήνη, derived from the verb εἴρειν, from ἴρω, which is to bind, signifies. Nor does Hyperius note inconveniently that it is not called peace simply, but the bond of peace, so that it may be signified that a solid peace is required, which is not dissolved for any reasons, but remains most amicably joined. For if we do not attain this bond of charity, as Theophylact warns, and are not more peaceable toward one another, we are undoubtedly going to lose the unity which the Spirit has conferred upon us. Nor will it be dealt with us otherwise than if the hands or feet were to make a schism with the rest of the body, and were cut off from the bond and connection of the other parts of the body. For they are no longer contained under one spirit as members. There is therefore need for the greatest diligence on our part, so that where one has yielded, the other may follow. For there are those of this kind who are not bound by one bond, so that they may have no power of their own; thus, without a doubt, we will be under one Spirit. Charity is σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος, the bond of perfection, Gal. 3, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Σπουδάζοντες τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ Πνεύματος ἐν τῷ συνδέσμῳ τῆς εἰρήνης.) Ἑνότητα τοῦ Πνεύματος vocat uni- tatem Ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus spirituale, ea servari non potest, ubi regnant fastus, æmulatio, invidentia, & alia di- lectioni contraria. Vide utramque ad Corinthios.

Hic à præcepto charitatis generali ad unitatis spi- ritualis custodiam descendit. Studete servare uni- tatem Spiritus in vinculo pacis, quæ non ad omnes spectant, ut charitas omnibus hominibus exhi- benda, sed ad fideles vel membra Ecclesiæ. Unde hæc parænesis male à Syncretistis ad servandam cum illis, qui in fide discrepant, unitatem abripi- tur. Subjectum hujus unitatis sunt fideles, qui in- ter se mutuo vinculum pacis servant. Forma est, quod sit unitas Spiritus, hoc est, non animorum consensio & concordia simpliciter, ut Calvinus explicat, sed Spiritus, qui in renatis prævalet, utpo- te qui à Spiritu Sancto reguntur, unitas. Quem sensum cum Musculo, Beza, Zanchio præfert Crocius, internam scilicet ac spiritualem notari charitatem, quæ ab externa & seculari hoc ipso distinguitur, quod dicitur unitas Spiritus. Per Spiritum alii Spiritum Sanctum intelligunt, ad quem ceu Autorem utique unitas Ecclesiæ referenda: Quo de Theophylactus: Quemadmodum in corpore Spiritus omnia continet, unitque & diversa sunt membra, sic Spiritus Sanctus in nobis fidelibus regit, qui cunctos facit unanimes, nectitque, quamvis natione & moribus vel artibus differant, & per eundem hunc Spiritum omnes unum sumus effecti. Res eodem fere recidit. A Spiritu Sancto est, quod Spiritus in nobis dominetur, non caro. Nihil tamen prohibet unitatem Spiritus priori modo intelligere, quod ita unum corpus una anima omnes esse debeant, ut unus omnium veluti Spiritus sit. Quæ est forma & anima spiritualis hujus unitatis. Per vinculum pacis modus servandæ unitatis Ecclesiæ monstratur pax cum Deo & hominibus. Ut manens in unitate Ecclesiæ retinenda est pax cum DEO, quæ retinetur secundum Crocium, fide & obedientiæ studio. Sed hic loquitur Apostolus de pace mutua inter pios, quæ est amica & quieta conversatio. Ea est vinculum, quo continetur unitas Ecclesiæ, sicut corpus sua habet ligamenta, quibus membra colligantur, quod vox Græca εἰρήνη à εἴρειν verbo ἴρω, quod est necto, deducta significat. Nec incommode notat Hyperius, non nude pacem, sed vinculum pacis nominari, ut significetur, requiri solidam, quæ nullis ex causis dissolvatur, sed amicissime juncta maneat. Nam si charitatis hunc nexum, ut Theophylactus monet, nequaquam adipiscemur, nec pacatiores ad invicem fuerimus, perdituri haud dubie sumus, quam Spiritus nobis contulerit, unitatem. Nec secus nobiscum agetur, quam si cum reliquo corpore manus vel pedes dissidium fecerint, & ab aliarum corporis partium nexu & copula proscindantur. Non enim ultra sub uno spiritu membra continentur. Est itaque nobis summa diligentia opus, ut quo unus concesserit, eodem & alius subsequatur. Sunt enim hujusmodi, qui non uno sunt vinculo alligati, ut vel nullam habeant suimet potestatem, sic procul dubio sub uno Spiritu erimus. Charitas est σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος, vinculum perfectionis, Gal. 3, 14.

## 4:4
Vers. 4.

Ἓν σῶμα) We are one body by reason of the consciousness of religion, and the unity of discipline, and the covenant of hope, says Tertullian in his Apologeticus: Moreover, it is briefly said one body, for the Church is one body. The figure of this is the one tabernacle of the Hebrews, and its way afterwards the one temple.

Καὶ ἓν Πνεῦμα) One Spirit, supply, is, who governs the Church: Not Satanic, not human, but Divine, 1 Cor. 12, 4.

Καθὼς καὶ ἐκλήθητε ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι τῆς κλήσεως ὑμῶν) that is, εἰς μίαν ἐλπίδα, and he calls the thing itself hope, to the hoping of which we have been called, that is, eternal life. See above 1, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἓν σῶμα) Corpus sumus de conscientia religionis, & disciplinæ unitate & spei fœdere, ait Tertullianus in Apologetico: Est autem breviter dictum unum corpus, pro Ecclesia est unum corpus. Hujus figura unum tabernaculum Ebræorum, & ejus viæ postea templum unum.

Καὶ ἓν Πνεῦμα) Unus Spiritus, supple, est, qui Ecclesiam gubernat: Non Satanicus, non humanus, sed Divinus, 1. Cor. 12, 4.

Καθὼς καὶ ἐκλήθητε ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι τῆς κλήσεως ὑμῶν) id est, εἰς μίαν ἐλπίδα, & spem vocat ipsam rem, ad quam sperandam vocati sumus, id est, vitam æternam. Vide supra 1, 18.

## 4:5
Vers. 5.

Εἷς Κύριος) Christ is the Lord of the Church by the decree of God the Father, 1 Cor. 8, 6.

Μία πίστις) One rule of faith, of which we spoke at Matthew 28, 19.

Ἓν βάπτισμα) One mode of professing that faith, namely through baptism. See at the same passage of Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Εἷς Κύριος) Christus Ecclesiæ Dominus ex Dei Patris decreto, 1. Cor. 8, 6.

Μία πίστις) Una regula fidei, de qua diximus ad Matthæi 28, 19.

Ἓν βάπτισμα) Unus modus profitendi eam fidem, nempe per baptismum. Vide ad eundem Matthæi locum.

## 4:6
Εἷς Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ πάντων) You have this also in the said passage 1 Cor. 8, 6.

V. 6. Ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων) That is ἐπάνω πάντων, who has authority over us all.

Καὶ διὰ πάντων) He diffuses his providential government through all.

Καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν) ὑμῖν is absent in the Manuscript. He acts within you through the Spirit, proceeding from himself.

Reasons why the unity of the Spirit must be preserved are now brought forward, derived from the nature of that spiritual unity and from its causes, both principal and instrumental. The Principal Efficient Cause is the most holy Trinity. Therefore, it first brings forward the unity of the Holy Spirit, as the one to whom, in a peculiar way, the work of sanctification and the preservation of the Church is attributed, who consequently animates, vivifies, and vegetates the body of the Church, and glues us together into one body: by whom we are called and gathered to the Church into one hope of our calling. Next, it brings forward the unity of the Lord, who redeemed us and rules us as King and head, to whom we are bound in the unity of the faith by one and the same Sacrament of baptism. Third, it commemorates one God and Father of all by reason of eminence, who is above all, by reason of care and providence, who is through all, and by reason of motion and presence, who is in all. But those things which singularly concern all the faithful here, as well as the universal Church, are that the Father is [Father] by reason of regeneration, above all by reason of governance, through all by reason of special care, and in all by reason of the indwelling of grace. Therefore, three times three reasons for guarding unity can be established: The first can be referred to the third article concerning the Holy Spirit: in which class the first reason is, because there is one body, which, if it is to be preserved, requires the concord of its members. For if they are dissenting, how will the unity of the body remain? Which argument the Apostle executes in verse 16 and especially in 1 Cor. 12:14 ff. The second: because there is one Spirit, just as one body is ruled by one soul: so this mystical body has one Spirit, through whom we are baptized into one body, 1 Cor. 12:13; therefore also there is deservedly one mind for all, one heart, Acts 4:31. Since the faithful, says Theophylact, are joined by the body, it is necessary that they also have one Spirit: Since there is one Spirit received by us through faith, you all ought to think one thing and agree. Theophylact indeed adds another explanation, or he calls the Spirit an equal readiness of mind and good conspiracy, as if he were saying, one body and the same mind: But these pertain to the conclusion. Here, however, the argument for preserving unity is handed down. The former explanation concerning the Holy Spirit is therefore more correct. The third: There is one hope of all: just as you were also called into one hope of your calling. The medium of the calling is the Word of the Gospel, which is unique; the same word of salvation and life is announced to all. The end is one, eternal life, to which we are called. The effect of the Holy Spirit, calling us to eternal life, is one for all believers, namely, the excitement of hope: For this same Spirit kindles this in all, when we are regenerated by the Spirit to a living hope, John 3:5, 1 Pet. 1:3.
