God, says Theophylact in interpretation, has called us all equally, and has bestowed (spiritual) life upon all, and is equally the head of all, has raised all together, and from there received a seat, and finally has received all with equal honor, and we all hope for the same and one thing. It is necessary, therefore, for this bond of charity, that you be one out of many. For we are all going to be equal in heaven, even though we were once dissimilar on earth. The three following reasons can be reduced to the second article concerning Christ: The fourth reason is, there is one Lord, Christ Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him, 1 Cor. 8:6. Phil. 2:11, who is called Lord by right not only of creation, but also of redemption, and indeed of governance, because he is the Redeemer and head of the Church, Eph. 5:23, 25. To him, therefore, we all ought to serve with one mind and one shoulder, Zeph. 3:9, Zech. 14:9, 16, Luke 1:75. For it is not fitting that the servants of one Lord should be discordant. The fifth is: There is one faith. For there is one object of faith, Jesus Christ, who is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13. Outside of his name there is no other name given to men, Acts 4:12. True faith is operative through charity, Gal. 5:6. Where, therefore, there is true faith, there charity ought not to be absent. But where there is no true faith, there neither is there true charity: because that is the mother and root of charity. There is one faith, both that which is believed and that by which it is believed: The former, because there is one doctrine of salvation; the latter, because although the subjects are diverse, the object is nevertheless one. There is one grace in Christ. All the saints believe in one Christ, not in one before the law, another under the law, another after the law: Not in one for the Jews, another for the Gentiles, Acts 15:11. Here the one faith, by which it is believed, is properly understood. For other things pertain to the object of faith, namely, one Spirit, one Lord, and one God. The sixth reason is, one baptism. It is the same medium of regeneration and salvation, not only the audible Word, the doctrine of the Gospel, which is the same for all, but also the visible Word, the sacrament of baptism, because through one Spirit we are all baptized into one body, just as in the Eucharist we are all made to drink into one Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:13. He did not add the sacrament of confirmation here, but comprehended it under the one sacrament of baptism by reason of parity: which, because it is common to all, both infants and adults, and through it we are regenerated, and we all become children of God through faith, Gal. 3:27, he wished to express particularly. However, he does not exclude the unity of the Eucharist, 1 Cor. 10:17, we being many are one bread, one body. For we all participate from one bread. Briefly, Theophylact has encompassed this triad of reasons thus: One Lord, one faith, and one baptism. For you have not obtained a greater Lord, and he a lesser: Nor have you been redeemed by faith, and he by works. Nor, finally, have you attained salvation through baptism, and he not at all. The third triad of reasons pertains to one God and Father of all, so that in the place of the seventh reason is that one God the Father of all is above all. For those who are under the empire of one God, it behooves them to nourish mutual charity: But the faithful are under one God in a peculiar way, because they all acknowledge him as their Father. It is necessary for children to cultivate peace and spiritual unity. How can they love God, whom they do not see, if they do not love their brother, whom they do see? 1 John 4:20, cf. ch. 5:1. The eighth reason is, because there is one God and Father of all who is through all. He not only commands all, but also provides for all: He is, as it were, through all by His paternal care and prudence, and as it were diffused through all. Since therefore God is devoted to all the faithful with a special love, why should we not love those whom our God and our Father so loves? Musculus, Zanchius, and Aretius explain this concerning the universe, that God rules all things, concerning which the Poet says, 'For God goes through all lands and tracts of the sea'; but Crocius, with Calvin, Beza, and Hemmingius, rightly departs from them and acknowledges that this is more fittingly referred to the Church, through whose members the providence of God is led as diffused. Not that it does not extend further, but that Paul here has a special regard for the Church, concerning whose unity he is discoursing. Finally, the ninth reason is, because God and Father of all is in all of us. Here he now expressly indicates the faithful. For although Jerome does not read the pronoun here, yet all the Greek and other codices have it with Ambrose. It signifies therefore a gracious indwelling in the faithful, as Chrysostom explains. If one God dwells in all the faithful, therefore those who rend the unity of the faithful do just as if they wished to rend the one God and Father into parts: All the faithful are the temple of God: He who separates himself from the faithful through schism and discord. Theophylact embraces this triad of reasons thus: One GOD and Father of all, who both presides over us, and pervades all things with prudence and moderation, and dwells within us all. And these things concerning the motives of spiritual concord; which Crocius urges in his Anti-Becanus in his dedication to the Queen of Sweden and the Landgrave of Hesse, that he might induce Calvinists and Lutherans to a spiritual brotherhood in the Lord. But we gave a response to those in the dedication of the Critici sacri to the Queen of Sweden, and the most illustrious tutors of the same, which also appeared separately, under the title, Consultatio Cassellana. To which things of ours he himself was more mute than a fish. Now let him answer for himself. Is it therefore only, he asks on page 441, in this place, that peace is to be cultivated with those with whom we are one in Spirit? Spiritual peace is to be cultivated with them ONLY, external peace also with others, who are outside the unity of the Church, Rom. 12, 18. How are they one in Spirit, who do not have one faith?

Latin:

Εἷς Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ πάντων) Habes & hoc dicto loco 1. Cor. 8, 6.

V. 6. Ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων) Id est ἐπάνω πάντων, qui imperium in nos omnes habet.

Καὶ διὰ πάντων) Per omnes diffundit providam suam gubernationem.

Καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν) ὑμῖν abest in Manuscripto. Intra vos agit per Spiritum, à se procedentem.

Rationes, cur servanda sit unitas Spiritus, jam ad- ducuntur a natura spiritualis illius unitatis, & causis ejusdem tum principali, tum mediis desumptæ. Causa Efficiens Principalis est sacrosancta Trinitas. Spiritus sancti ergo unitatem primo adducit, utpote cui peculiari ratione opus sanctificationis, & conser- vationis Ecclesiæ tribuitur, qui proinde corpus Ec- clesiæ animat, vivificat & vegetat, & nos in unū cor- pus conglutinat: a quo vocamur & colligimur ad Ecclesiam in unam spem vocationis. Deinde addu- cit unitatem Domini, qui nos redemit, & tanquam Rex & caput nos regit, cui in unitate fidei devincti sumus uno eodemque Sacramento baptifmatis. Tertio unum Deum commemorat, &. Patrem omnium ratione eminentiæ, qui est super omnia, ratione curæ & providentiæ, qui est per omnia, & ra- tione motionis ac præsentiæ, qui est in omnibus. Quæ vero singulariter hic concernunt fideles quoscun- que, ut & universam Ecclesiam, quia Pater est ra- tione regenerationis, super omnes ratione guberna- tionis, per omnes ratione curæ specialis, & in omnibus ratione gratiæ inhabitationis. Constitui ergo pos- sunt ter tres rationes unitatis custodiendæ: Prima, ad tertium articulum de Spiritu S. referri potest: in qua classe prima ratio est, quia unum est corpus, quod si conservandum sit, concordia membrorum requiritur. Illis enim dissidentibus, quomodo u- nitas corporis manebit? Quod argumentum exe- quitur Apostolus v. 16. & imprimis 1. Cor. 12, 14. sqq. Altera: quia unus est Spiritus, ut corpus unum ab una anima regitur: Ita corpus hoc mysticum unum habet Spiritum, per quem in unum corpus baptizamur, 1. Cor. 12, 13. ideo etiam unus omnium merito est animus, unum cor, Act. 4, 31. Cum fide- les, inquit Theophylactus, juncti sint corpore, unum etiam Spiritum habeant, necesse est: Cum unus sit Spiritus a nobis per fidem acceptus, & unum sentire debetis omnes & convenire. Addit quidem Theo- phylactus & aliam explicationem, vel Spiritum æ- quam animi promptitudinem dicit, & bonam conspi- rationem, tanquam id dicat, corpus unum & animus idem: Sed hæc ad conclusionem pertinent. Hic vero traditur argumentum servandæ unitatis. Re- ctior ergo prior explicatio de Spiritu Sancto. Ter- tia: Una est spes omnium: quemadmodum & voca- ti estis in unam spem vocationis. Medium voca- tionis Verbum Evangelii est, quod unicum est, o- mnibus idem salutis & vitæ verbum annuntiatur. Finis est unus, vita æterna, ad quam vocamur. Ef- fectus Spiritus Sancti, nos vocantis ad vitam æter- nam, unus est omnium credentium, spei scilicet ex- citatio: Hanc enim idem ille Spiritus in omnibus accendit, cum ex Spiritu regeneramur ad spem vi- vam, Joh. 3, 5. 1. Pet. 1, 3. Deus, inquit, interprete Theophylacto, pariter nos omnes vocavit, & vitam (spiritualem) omnibus largitus est, & æque est omni- um caput, cunctos simul suscitavit, & inde consessum recepit, ac demum omnes pari honore suscepit, eadem- que & una universi speramus. Necesse est ergo pro charitatis hac copula, ut unum ex pluribus sitis. Nam in cælo sumus pares omnes futuri, tametsi in terris olim eramus dissimiles. Tres sequentes ratio- nes ad secundum articulum de Christo possunt re- duci: Quarta ratio est, unus est Dominus, Christus Jesus, per quem omnia, & nos per illum, 1. Cor. 8, 6. Phil. 2, 11. qui Dominus jure non creationis tan- tum, sed & redemptionis dicitur, imo & regiminis, quia Redemptor & caput est Ecclesiæ, Ephes. 5, 23. 25. Huic ergo omnes una mente & uno humero servire debemus, Zeph. 3, 9. Zach. 14, 9. 16. Luc. 1, 75. Non enim convenit, ut servi unius Domini dif- cordes sint. Quinta est: Una est fides. Nam unum objectum est fidei Jesus Christus, qui idem heri, ho- die & in secula, Ebr. 13. Extra ejus nomen non est aliud nomen hominibus datum, Act. 4, 12. Vera fides per charitatem operosa est, Gal. 5, 6. Ubi er- go vera est fides, ibi charitas abesse non debet. Ubi autem non est fides vera, ibi nec charitas vera: quia illa est mater & radix charitatis. Una est fides, tum quæ, tum qua creditur: Illa, quia una salutis doctrina est; hæc, quia licet subjecta diversa sint, objectum tamen unum est. Una est gratia in Chri- sto. In unum Christum omnes sancti credunt, non in alium ante legem, alium sub lege, alium post le- gem: Non in alium Judæi, alium gentes, Act. 15, 11. Hic una fides, qua creditur, proprie intelligitur. Nam ad objectum fidei alia pertinent, unus Spiritus nempe, unus Dominus, & unus Deus. Sexta ratio est, unum baptisma. Idem medium regenerationis & salutis est, non tantum Verbum ἀκυστὸν doctrina Evangelii, quæ omnibus eadem, sed & Verbum ὁρατὸν, baptismatos sacramentum, quia per unum Spiritum omnes ad unũ corpus baptizamur, quem- admodum & in Eucharistia omnes ad unum Spiri- tum potamur, 1. Cor. 12, 13. Hoc sacramentum con- firmationis hic non addidit, sed sub uno baptisma- tis Sacramento ex paritatis ratione comprehendit: quod, quia commune est omnibus tam infantibus, quam adultis, & per id regeneramur, & filii Dei evadimus omnes per fidem, Gal. 3, 27. peculiariter exprimere voluit. Non excludit autem unitatem Eucharistiæ, 1. Cor. 10, 17. unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Omnes enim ex uno pane participamus. Breviter hanc rationum trigam ita complexus est Theophylactus: Unus Dominus, una fides, & unum baptisma. Neque enim majorem tu nactus es Domi- num, ille minorem: Neque ipse ex fide, ille ex operi- bus est redemptus. Nec demum tu per baptismum salutem es consecutus, ille minime. Tertia triga ra- tionum ad unum Deum & Patrem omnium perti- net, ut septimæ rationis loco sit, quod unus Deus Pater omnium super omnes sit. Qui enim sub unius Deo imperio sunt, eos oportet mutuam alere cha- ritatem: At peculiari ratione sub uno Deo sunt fi- deles, quia illum Patrem suum agnoscunt omnes. Filios vero necessum est colere pacem & unitatem spiritualem. Quomodo possunt Deum amare, quẽ non vident, si fratrem non amant, quem vident? 1. Joh. 4, 20. conf. cap. 5, 1. Octava ratio est, quia unus Deus & Pater omnium est per omnes. Non tan- tum imperat omnibus, sed etiam prospicit omnibus: Omnes cura & prudentia sua paterna veluti per- means, & per omnes quasi diffusus. Quum ergo o- mnibus fidelibus Deus speciali amore addictus sit, qui non amemus eos, quos sic amat Deus noster, & Pater noster? Musculus, Zanchius, & Aretius de universo hoc explicant, quod Deus regat omnia, de quo Poeta, Deum namque ire per omnes terrasq; tractusq; maris; sed recte ab iis discedit, & ad Ec- clesiam commodius hoc referri agnoscit Crocius cum Calvino, Beza, & Hemmingio, per cujus mem- bra diffusa Dei ducatur providentia. Non quod non longius se extendat, sed quod Paulus hic spe- cialem Ecclesiæ rationem habeat, de cujus unitate disserit. Nona deniq; ratio est, quia Deus & Pater omnium est in omnibus nobis. Hic jam fideles expres- se indicat. Etsi enim Pronomen hic non legat Hie- ronymus, habent tamen omnes Codices Græci & alii cum Ambrosio. Significat ergo gratiosam in fi- delibus habitationem, ut Chrysostomus explicat. Si unus Deus in omnibus fidelibus habitat, ergo qui fidelium unitatem scindunt, perinde faciunt, ac si unum Deum & Patrem in partes scindere velint: Fideles omnes sunt templum Dei: Qui à fidelibus sese separat per schisma & discordiam. Hanc trigam rationum ita complectitur Theophylactus : Unus DEUS & Pater omnium, qui & nobis præsidet, & omnia prudentia & moderatione pervadit, & in nobis universis inhabitat. Atque hæc de motivis concordiæ spiritualis; quæ Crocius urget in Anti-Becan. sua dedicatione ad Reginam Sueciæ & Landgravium Hassiæ, ut Calvinianos & Lutheranos inducat ad spiritualem in Domino fraternitatem. Sed illi responsum dedimus in Critici sacri dedicatione ad Reginam Sueciæ, & Tutores ejusdem Illustrissimos, quæ seorsim etiam prodiit, sub titulo, Consultatio Cassellana. Ad quæ nostra ipse magis mutus fuit, quam piscis. Jam sibi ipsi respondeat. Ergone tantum, quærit pag. 441. hoc loco, cum illis pax colenda,cum quibus sumus unum Spiritu? Pax spiritualis cum illis TANTUM colenda, externa etiam cum aliis, quæ sunt extra unitatem Ecclesiæ, Rom. 12, 18. Quomodo unum Spiritu sunt, quibus non est una fides?

## 4:7
Ver. 7.

But to each one of us was given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ) Because it could be objected, we have not all received the same, he answers: They are gifts, the measure of which depends on the will of the giver, and these very things serve not one, but all, Romans XII. v. 3. 6. Thus not to all tribes was given the same amount of land, but more to the more populous ones. - This is not added, however, by way of objection. He provides a new argument. From the diversity of gifts ordered to the unity of the Church. For it is so far from the case that the body of the Church should be split on account of diverse gifts, which is done by Schismatics, that rather for this reason the unity of the Spirit should be cultivated, because not all things were granted to one, but some gifts to others, so that no one may serve another, and all with one mind may confer their gifts for the use of the Church. For He distributes them to each one as He willed, for the profit, 1. Cor. 7, 7. 11. which argument is afterwards applied especially to the unity of Teachers in the Church, to whom for that reason diverse gifts are granted.

Grace does not signify justifying grace, as Bellarmine wishes, but any gifts granted by GOD. Nor does it seem to be restricted to ministering gifts, even if the Apostle afterwards passes particularly to Teachers. For here the Apostle speaks generally of any gifts whatsoever to each one of us, grace is given, i.e., a gratuitous gift, a certain charism, Cf. Rom. 12, 3. Theophylact on this place: Someone will say, if all things are, as you say, common, why therefore does this one have less grace, and that one more? Since such an unequal partition would be a seedbed of envy, just as happened to the Corinthians, and to very many others. Therefore, resolving this, the Apostle says that a gift was bestowed upon each one according to the judgment of the bestowing God. Since therefore it is free and given as a gift, it will be enough for you that you have received something, and are not entirely devoid of grace. For nothing has been paid out to you as a debt: And because GOD has predetermined the measure for each, you shall investigate nothing, nor should it be a care if you have not received all things alone. For if GOD has once measured out grace, He surely did it for our utility. But those things are undoubtedly common, without which Christianity cannot consist; if anyone has obtained a little more grace beyond these, do not grieve at all. For perhaps he also expends more labor, as he is about to say in the progress of the discourse. For he did not say according to the measure of faith, which each one has, lest he should lead into desperation those who had less, but he left the mode to the judgment of the giver, lest an occasion for dissension be offered to them from that. According to the measure of the gift of Christ. Therefore, he establishes that one Lord, of whom v. 5, as the Author of the gifts, who distributes them by his own authority in the whole Church, which is an argument for the Deity of CHRIST; and thus the gifts given to CHRIST according to his Human nature are distinguished, not according to measure, that is, immense, and the gifts which are given to us by CHRIST according to the measure of the gift of Christ, which pleases Him.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ἑνὶ δὲ ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ἐδόθη ἡ χάρις κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ) Quia objici poterat, non eadem omnes accepimus, respondet : Dona sunt, quorum mensura pendet à voluntate donantis, & hæc ipsa non uni, sed omnibus serviunt, Roman. XII. v. 3. 6. Sic non omnibus tribubus tantundem datum terræ, sed plus copiosioribus. - Non hoc tamen κατ᾽ ἀνθυποφορὰν additur. Novum præbet argumentum. A diversitate donorum ordinata ad unitatem Ecclesiæ. Tantum enim abest, ut ob diversa dona scindendum sit corpus Ecclesiæ, quod à Schismaticis fit, ut potius ideò colenda sit Spiritus unitas, quia non uni omnia, sed aliis alia concessa sunt dona, ut nullus alteri inserviat, omnesque una mente dona sua ad usum Ecclesiæ conferant. Distribuit enim illa unicuique prout voluit, πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον, 1. Cor. 7, 7. 11. quod argumentum postea imprimis ad unitatem Doctorum in Ecclesia,quibus idcirco diversa conceduntur dona, applicatur.

Χάρις non significat gratiam justificantem, ut Bellarminus vult, sed quævis à DEO concessa dona. Nec restringenda videtur ad dona ministrantia, etsi peculiariter ad Doctores postea transeat Apostolus. Nam generaliter hic de quibusvis Apostolum loqui ἑνὶ δὲ ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν, unicuique vero nostrum data est gratia, h. e. donum gratuitum, χάρισμα quoddam, Conf. Rom. 12, 3. Theophylactus in hunc locum : Dicet aliquis, si omnia sunt, ut inquis, communia, cur ergo hic gratiæ minus, ille plurimum habet? Siquidem ejusmodi non æqua partitio invidiæ seminarium esset, quemadmodum & Corinthiis evenit, & aliis plurimis. Id itaque solvens Apostolus,unicuique dicit donum fuisse pro Dei largientis arbitrio mensura quadam collatum. Cum itaque gratis sit illud & dono datum, sat tibi fuerit, quod acceperis quippiam, nec prorsus immunis sis gratia. Non enim pro debito tibi est aliquid persolutum : Et quia DEUS mensuram cuique præfinivit, nihil scrutabere, nec curæ sit, si non omnia solus acceperis. Nam si semel gratiam mensus est DEUS, in nostram profecto utilitatem id fecit. Atqui ea communia haud dubie sunt, sine quibus constare Christianismus haud potest, hæc præter si quis est gratiæ plusculum nactus, nihil doleas. Nam & laboris forsitan plus ille impendit, ut in orationis progressu dicturus est. Neque enim secundum fidei dixit mensuram, quæ cuique est, ne in desperationem induceret, qui minus haberent, sed donantis arbitrio modum permisit, ne inde his dissidendi offerretur occasio. Κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς χρισ̃. Dom 1:m ergo illum unum, de quo v. 5. constituit Autorem donorum, qui ἀυτεξουσίως illa distribuit in universa Ecclesia, quod argumentum est Deitatis CHRI- STI; & distinguuntur ita dona CHRISTO se- cundum Humanam naturam data, ὀυκ ατὰ μέτρόν, sine mensura, hoc est, immensa, & dona, quæ no- bis dantur à CHRISTO κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δω- ρεᾶς τ̃ χρισ̃, secundum mensuram donationis Christi, quæ ipsi libet.

## 4:8
Ver. 8.

Ἀναβὰς ἐις ὕψος ἠχμαλώτευσεν αιχμαλωσίαν, καὶ ἔδωκε δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) In the Greek the first words are the same: except that there the discourse is to GOD, here it is about GOD: Then ἔλαβες δόματα ἐν ἀνθρώποις. But Paul, in order to draw these things better to a mystical sense, took לקח as 'he took' in the sense of 'giving': nor is that surprising, since we receive what we wish to give, so that we may give, as can be seen in Exodus 25:2 and 1 Kings 17:10. Wherefore also it is translated by ἐκβάτων in Job 22:22, Jeremiah 23:30, and thus with the word כ taken, it will mean 'on account of', concerning which meaning we spoke above 1. This passage, however, fits Christ most excellently, who was seen ascending into heaven, then conquered through the doctrine of the Apostles, and led idolatry and other vices as if captive: and he took gifts from the Father, which he might distribute to men. Αιχμαλωσία שבי in the Psalms, and Numbers 31:12, is a multitude of captives.

Because he establishes CHRIST as the Author of the gifts, which is to be understood of CHRIST also according to his Human nature, according to which he was established Lord by his ascension into the heavens, Acts 2:36, he proves from Psalm 68 that CHRIST was so exalted that he might receive gifts for men, and the power of giving them. Nor is this a mystical, but the proper and literal sense of the Psalm, just as we showed in the Illustrious Bibles of the Old Testament regarding the cited Psalm, so far is it from the case that anything here is drawn by Paul to a mystical sense. We note only the consensus of Junius and Crocius on account of Calvin. For he says thus on this passage: Since they are not said of David, (those rebels dwelling you make captives Jah God) it remains that they are said of GOD, but of GOD manifested in the flesh. This indeed does not please the Jews, whence some refer it to the time of the giving of the law, but the Psalm itself overturns the gloss. For previously it was treated of that time in which GOD appeared about to bring the law to his people; but because that glory, which GOD, when the law was given, the people led forth and sent into the possession of the land, the kingdom established, the enemies defeated, was interrupted by very many afflictions, by which that glory seemed to languish and wither, therefore the Prophet passes over to the preaching of another advent, namely that in which the Word was made flesh, and the Angels of GOD ascended and descended upon the son of man, until the ascent into the sublime made captivity captive. Thus Franciscus Junius learnedly explains in his Parallels. Moreover, it is added, he led captivity captive, because gifts could not have been distributed to men, unless Satan, who held us captive, had been defeated by CHRIST, which was shown when in the triumph of his ascension he led captivity captive. But he was not conquered only through the doctrine of the Apostles, when he led idolatry and other vices as if captive: but through death, by which he destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil, Hebrews 2:14, and stripped principalities and powers, and made a show of them ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ, triumphing over them in himself, which the Apostle says was done on the cross, Colossians 2:14, 15. Nor indeed would the doctrine of the Apostles have availed anything here against Satan and Satanic vices, unless the power of Satan had been overcome through his death, and we had been liberated from the power of darkness through ἀπολύτρωσιν [redemption] through the blood of CHRIST, Coloss. 2, 13. 14. Some have explained the captivity as referring to captive men. Lyranus, as referring to the fathers detained in limbo. Thomas, as referring to both them and the living captured by sin. Ruffinus, as referring to the whole human race. But, setting aside limbo, which is a mere fable, that this does not treat of captive men here, but of the Devil, the enemy of the human race, the Davidic phrase teaches, because the Hebrews did not signify by it that captives are led into freedom, but that enemies are led into captivity, Deut. 31, 10. 2 Chron. 28, 11. See also the parallel passage Coloss. 2, 14. Wherefore Chrysostom: What captivity does he speak of? The captivity of the Devil, to be sure. He apprehended the tyrant Devil, and death, and the curse, and sin. You see the spoils and the booty! Theophylact has similar things, and most other interpreters, even from the Reformed, Calvin, Beza, Aretius, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἀναβὰς ἐις ὕψος ἠχμαλώτευσεν αιχμαλωσίαν, καὶ ἔδωκε δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) In Græco prima verba eadem: nisi quod ibi ad DEUM sermo, hic de DEO: Deinde ἔλαβες δόματα ἐν ἀνθρώποις. At Paulus ut melius ad mysticum sensum hæc traheret לקח sumpsit in sensu dan- di: nec id mirum, cum, quæ dare volumus, accipia- mus, ut demus, ut videre est Exod. XXV. v. 2. & 1. Reg. XVII. v. 10. quare & per ἐκβάτων vertitur Job. XXII. 22. Jerem. XXIII. 30. & sic sumpto verbo כ valebit propter, de quo significatu diximus supra 1. Optime autem Chri- sto convenit hic locus, qui in cœlum afcendere conspe- ctus est, deinde per Apostolorum doctrinam vicit, & velut captivam egit idololatriam & vitia alia: sumpsit- que à Patre dona, qui hominibus dispartiretur. Αιχμα- λωσία שבי in Psalmis, & Num. XXXI. 12. est captivorum multitudo.

Quia CHRISTUM Autorem donorum con- stituit, quod de CHRISTO etiam secundum Hu- manam naturam, secundum quam per ascensio- nem in cœlos Dominus constitutus est, Actor. 2, 36. intelligendum è Psalm. 68. probat CHRI- STUM ita exaltatum esse, ut acciperet dona pro hominibus, & potestatem ea dandi. Neque hic mysticus, sed proprius est, & literalis Psalmi sensus, quemadmodum in Bibliis Illustr. Vet. Testam. ad Psalmum allegatum ostendimus, tantum abest, ut hic quicquam trahatur à Paulo ad sensum my- sticum. Notamus solum propter Calvinum Ju- nii & Crocii consensum. Hic enim ita in hunc locum: Cum de Davide non dicantur, (illa rebel- les habitando captivos facis Jah Deus) restat, ut dicantur de DEO, sed de DEO patefacto in carne. Hoc quidem Judæis non placet, unde aliqui refe- runt ad tempus editæ legis, sed ipse Psalmus glos- sam evertit. Prius enim actum est de illo tempo- re, quo DEUS apparuit laturus legem populo suo; quia vero gloriam illam, quam DEUS, data lege, deducto populo & in terræ possessionem misso, regno constituto, hostibus debellatis, interrumpebant affli- ctiones quamplurimæ, quibus illa gloria flaccescere & marcescere videbatur, propterea transilit Pro- pheta ad prædicationem adventus alterius, nempe quo Verbum caro factum est, & Angeli DEI ad- scenderunt & descenderunt super filium hominis, donec ascensus in sublime captivam fecit captivi- tatem. Sic erudite explicat Franciscus Junius in Parallelis. Additur autem, captivam duxit ca- ptivitatem, quia non potuissent hominibus do- na distribui, nisi, qui nos captivos tenebat, Sa- tanas devictus fuisset à CHRISTO, quod osten- sum, cum in triumpho ascensionis captivam duxit captivitatem. Non autem victus est tantum per doctrinam Apostolorum, cum idololatriam & alia vitia captiva velut egit: sed per mortem, qua destruxit eum, qui habebat mortis imperium, hoc est, Diabolum, Ebr. 2, 14. & Principatus ac pote- states exuit, & traduxit ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ, triumphum agens super ipsis in semetipso, quod in cruce fa- ctum ait Apostolus Coloss. 2, 14. 15. Neque ve- ro doctrina Apostolorum hic quicquam valuisset contra Satanam & vitia Satanica, nisi Satanæ po- testas per mortem ejus devicta fuisset, nosque e tenebrarum potestate liberati per ἀπολύτρωσιν per sanguinem CHRISTI, Coloss. 2, 13. 14. Non- nulli exposuere captivitatem de hominibus capti- vis. Lyranus de patribus in limbo detentis. Tho- mas & de illis & de viventibus peccato captis. Ruffinus de toto genere humano. Sed misso limbo, qui mera est fabula, non agi hic de homi- nibus captivis, sed de Diabolo, hoste generis hu- mani, phrasis Davidica docet, quia Ebræi ea non significabant, captivos duci in libertatem, sed hostes in captivitatem, Deut. 31, 10. 2. Chron. 28, 11. Vid. & locus parallelus Coloss. 2, 14. Quare Chryso- stomus: Quam captivitatem dicit? Captivitatem scilicet Diaboli. Captivum apprehendit Diabolum tyrannum, & mortem, & maledictum & peccatum. Vides spolia & prædam! Similia habet Theophy- lactus, & plerique alii interpretes, etiam e Refor- matis Calvinus, Beza, Aretius, &c.

## 4:9
Verse 9.

Now this, he ascended, what is it, but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth?) Even GOD, of whom the Psalm treats in the sense first obvious, had first descended, but onto Mount Sinai: CHRIST, however, much lower, into that part in which men are accustomed to live. See John 3, 13. ch. 6, 33. 37. 41. 42. 50. 51. 58. Thus κάτω [below] is taken in John 8, 23. Acts 2, 19. Someone might believe that this treats of the maternal womb because of the place in Ps. 139, 15, but it is more credible that it treats of the Divine power of Christ exercised on earth before many witnesses, of which it also treats in 1 Tim. 3, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Τὸ δὲ ἀνέβη, τί ἐστιν, εἰ μὴ ὅτι καὶ κατέβη πρῶτον εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς) Etiam DEUS, de quo sensu pri- mum obvio agit Psalmus, primum descenderat, sed in montem Sinai: CHRISTUS vero multo inferius in eam partem, in qua homines solent vivere. Vid. Johan. 3, 13. cap. 6, 33. 37. 41. 42. 50. 51. 58. Sic κάτω sumitur Joh. 8, 23. Actor. 2, 19. Posset aliquis credere, agi hic de utero ma- terno ob locum Ps. 139, 15. sed credibilius est, agi de Divi- na Christi potentia in terris exercita coram multis testi- bus, de quo agitur & 1. Tim. 3, 16.

## 4:10
Verse 10. He who descended) See the passages of John just mentioned. He is also he who ascended above all the heavens) That is, above the air and the ethers, which region is called the third heaven, and the heaven of heavens, and in the plural ὀρανοὶ [heavens], and by way of excellence ὁ ὀρανὸς [the heaven], see Acts 2, 24. and ch. 1, 10. 1 Cor. 15, 48. and here below in ch. 6, 19.

That he might fill all things) The neuter for the common: that he might fill or satisfy all, namely the faithful, with his gifts. See above ch. 3, 19.

The Apostle pursues the power of that one Lord, which he has for enriching and endowing the Church, and for freely distributing gifts for the building up of the Church, for which Satan was to be overcome, and captivity was to be led captive, so that ascending into heaven he might gather the Church to himself through the Doctors of the Word, and by his gifts might instruct these by his grace, and might adopt, join together, and coagulate the saints into one body, under whom, as head, the Church might be built up through mutual love. He executes this victory of CHRIST with his omnipresent rule in such a way that, combining the ascent above all heavens with the descent to the lowest parts of the earth, he confirms the πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων [filling of all things] of our Lord exalted for us by the Spirit and in a truly Apostolic manner, thus, namely, that he ascended with triumph over captivity into the heights and above all heavens, so that he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth; both of which pertain to the state of Christ's exaltation, because in the descent to hell, which is opposed to the highest heaven, or rather to the supercelestial, so that these things may be handed down humanly and for our capacity, he led away the Diabolical Principalities and powers, demonstrating himself as victor over them, so that in his glorious ascent he publicly celebrated a triumph over them before Angels and men, so that he might show the head of the infernal serpent crushed. In his descent he conquered captivity, which was taking us captive, the Devil, and the gates of hell; in his ascent he led captivity with him, as is accustomed to be done in a public triumph. Nor, however, did he wish to ascend unless he had first descended, and shown himself to the Spirits, both Satanic and those of the formerly incredulous, as the victor of Satan, and as the Savior from these things, having been indignantly despised and rejected by them through their incredulity, with their own eternal damnation and disgrace. The lower parts of the earth do not denote either the part in which men are accustomed to live, that comes under the name of the earth, not of the lowest parts of the earth, just as they do not designate the maternal womb in this place, where there was no place for treating of conception in the womb; nor is there a convenient opposition between the descent in conception and the ascension above all heavens, as that descent is not to be considered as an emptying in the phrase of scripture, to which the ascension is opposed as an exaltation, and the lower parts of the earth import a greater emphasis when they are opposed to that which is above all the heavens, than when those things are expressed absolutely, outside of such an antithesis, in Psalm 139, v. 15. For here this precise passage, if I may so speak, is opposed absolutely to the highest by the force of the antithesis, which does not happen in the Psalm, where there is no such antithesis, nor can the lowest parts of the earth be understood simply, when the maternal womb is noted, for who would call the womb the lower parts of the earth in such an excellent manner? That hell can come under that name by antonomasia is not in doubt, at the very least in our mode of speaking. Concerning which Theophylact: Into hell: namely, which he calls the deepest parts of the earth according to the common opinion of men, just as Job also says, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow into hell. And David: I am counted with those descending into the pit. To the lower parts, therefore, Christ descended, beyond which there is nothing further, and he ascended above all heavens, than which there is nothing higher. Finally, that filling of all things does not agree so well with a descent into the womb. But truly, when it is said that he both descended into hell and ascended above the heavens, without local progress, it is rightly inferred that he fills all things by his omnipresence, as one who could present himself as victor to the inhabitants of hell and be raised above all heavens at will, and had no need to descend to the infernal regions locally and by progressive motion, and to be raised through all the heavens and above all the heavens, just as GOD is said to ascend at one time and descend at another, not by a change of presence, but by a manifestation of his omnipresent power. For the flesh of CHRIST is not present to those above and those below, and fills all things, by any other presence than the Divine, by which, namely, in the Word, in whose hypostasis it subsists, it is present and fills all things, from which it is inseparable both among those in hell and among those in heaven, constituting one thing with the Word subsisting. Compare on this passage our Theological College's Beständige Widerlegung, in Consil. Theol. Witteb. Vol. I, page 881. B. Gesnerus, disp. XIV. for the Book of Concord, p. 499. B. Hutterus in the explanation of the Book of Concord, art. IX. p. 967. B. Mylius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 74. Lord Dr. Johan. Meisnerus, disp. on the descent of Christ to the underworld, p. 72. We deny that the Psalm treats of God ἀσάρκῳ (without flesh), since, as the Apostle testifies, it treats of Christ, who is God manifest in the flesh, to whom is ascribed in 1 Tim. 3:16 that ascension or reception into glory. But the same one, according to the Apostle, who descended is he who also ascended, namely Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God-man), just as not so much in the descent into the womb, which is of the λόγε ἀσάρκε (Word without flesh), as in the descent into hell, the same Christ is God and man, who also ascended into heaven: which the Apostle not without reason repeats and inculcates, so that we may deservedly acknowledge that this victory over Satan, and the distribution of gifts in the Church, and the entire government of the Church are to be ascribed to the merit of Christ, of which his descent to the underworld and his ascent to the heavens provided a manifestation and clear testimony, he who on account of our sins was delivered, and was raised again for our justification, by whose blood and cross we have redemption and reconciliation, Ephes. 1, 7. chap. 2, 16. in whom we also have been quickened with CHRIST, and raised up, and made to sit in the heavenly places, chap. 2, 5. 6. That this ἀνάβασιν or ἀνάληψιν, 1. Timoth. 3, 16. or βάσιν is to be explained by the power of Christ exercised below before many witnesses, is unheard of before Grotius. But that Πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων is the satisfying of the faithful through the gifts of Christ from the passage Coloss. 3, 19. in no way appears, and the reasoning there is quite different. For there we are said to be filled with all his fullness; here Christ is said to fill all things, and to have descended into the lower parts of the earth, and to have ascended above all heavens, that it might be established that he himself fills all things; If it be explained by way of declaration; since things are said to happen in men when they are declared, or demonstrated; or that he might fill all things, by the power of his exaltation above all heavens, and his lifting up to supreme power, which he then obtained over those below and those above, through that exaltation, which he always had, by reason of κτήσεως; but now he exerts it κατὰ χρῆσιν, and exercises it in his ceaseless dominion in heaven and on earth, filling all things with his omnipresent and Divine dominion, Matth. 28, 19. 20. Ephes. 1, 20. seqq.

The Calvinists also interpret that πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων sometimes with Hugo and Thomas as the granting of gifts in the Church, but they are not even consistent with themselves, since they sometimes take it with Bernard, Anselm, and Lombard as the fulfillment of scripture, which, however, the Holy Spirit is accustomed to designate not by πλήρωσιν πάντων, but with the addition of the name of scripture or some Prophet, a thing of which kind does not occur here at all: Nor if it be admitted that the granting of gifts in the Church is noted, it does not exhaust πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων, inasmuch as it extends itself even to those things which are outside the Church, and it pertains not only to the kingdom of grace and glory, but also to the kingdom of power, because when there is talk of gifts, mention of gifts is also added to the verb of filling, as is done in Coloss. 1, 9. Phil. 1, 4. But what it designates by the filling of all things, the parallel passage teaches, Jerem. 23. v. 13. & Jacob. 1. v. 7. namely not the granting of gifts, but Divine omnipresence: In which sense Oecumenius on this passage says: He says, he formerly filled all things by his naked Divinity, but having become incarnate he descended and ascended, that he might fill all things μετὰ σαρκὸς. And what kind of gloss will this be from the mind of the Calvinists: He ascended according to his humanity, that he might fill the Church with gifts according to his Divinity? But then, could he not have filled the Church with gifts, even if he had not ascended ABOVE all heavens. Finally, others of the Reformed explain this filling of all things as the operation of all things in all. Crocius on this passage, page 431, has it thus: The filling of gifts presupposes the filling of power and dominion. For in this CHRIST exerts power and dominion, that he fills the whole Church with his gifts. Nor could he fill all things with gifts, unless he perfected, or ruled and moderated all things by his power. B. Hunnius thus presses the Calvinists: since this operation of all things in all is without doubt an action of uncreated power alone, which (uncreated power), if it is not really communicated to Christ as he is man, how will he be able as man to act omnipotently, that is, to work all things in all? And if they concede that the Λόγος now works all things according to his flesh also: why do they not by this very fact also establish his presence among all creatures? For how absurd it is that the λόγος present should administer present creatures through a Humanity that is in every way really absent and remote, was shown above on page 82 in the explanation of the first chapter. And the word itself of filling primarily designates the presence of the one filling or working; but secondarily or subordinately declares the operation of the one present. For that reason mention is made of places, both of those below and those above, in the description of this filling: so that presence in all places might be designated, not that successive and local one, of which above: But a personal presence according to the manner of the right hand of God described. Just as from the testimony of Jeremiah chap. 23 it is evident what it means to fill all things, the Lord saying there: Do I not fill heaven and earth? And he renders that same thing more clearly by these immediately preceding words, when he says: Am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off? Where to the Lord, to fill all things and to be present to all at hand is the same thing. In the same way it is taken in Wisd. 1. The Spirit of the Lord fills the round world. Where similarly the word of filling denotes not a naked operation without the presence of the operator, but presence first, and then the operation of the one present. These are the words of B. Hunnius, concluding that this is the simplest sense of Paul's words, that Christ according to his flesh was elevated not by a manner customary to other saints into heaven, but by a singular privilege above all heavens to the very right hand of omnipresence, so that he might be present to all, and work all things in all. This explanation agrees with the scope of Paul, with the comparison of other sayings which treat of the ascension of Christ into heaven, and subsequently join the article of sitting at the right hand, and thus declare that for the Apostle, to sit at the right hand of GOD and to fill all things is the same, it agrees with the declaration of the word of filling, Jerem. 23. v. 33. Moreover it agrees with the Interpreters Oecumenius and Theophylact, of whom the former has already been produced, but the latter has it thus: That he might fill all things by dominion and operation, and that IN THE FLESH, since he already filled all things by his Divinity. B. Hunnius also adds the words of Stapulensis, who wrote thus before the sacramental struggle was stirred up: The body of Christ fills heaven and earth. For it is wherever the Word is. For the Word was made flesh. Wherefore the Word is nowhere without the flesh, nor that flesh without the Word. Finally, B. Hunnius notes the proper confession of the Calvinists, when they prove the omnipresence of Christ from this filling of all things in Ephes. 4, 10, in demonstrating his Deity, Sohnii in disp. Heidelb. §. 31. Grabii and others.

Now, that we may still offer some advice regarding the other phrase of the Apostle, by no means are the lower parts of the earth here to be understood as places properly called subterranean, toward which St. Augustine indeed seemed to incline in book XII of De Genesi ad Litteram, chapter XXXIII. But he explains his own mind in the cited place, chapter XXXIV: Therefore, the underworld is called or believed to be beneath the earth, because it is fittingly demonstrated in the Spirit through those likenesses of corporeal things, so that since the souls of the departed sinned by being worthy of the underworld through love of the flesh, this is exhibited to them through those likenesses of corporeal things, which is customary for the dead flesh itself, that it be hidden beneath the earth. Finally, the underworld is called inferi in Latin because it is below. Just as, however, according to the body, if they keep the order of their weight, all lower things are heavier: so according to the Spirit, all lower things are sadder. Whence also in the Greek language the origin of the name by which the underworld is called seems to resonate from the fact that they have nothing pleasant. Whence it appears that it is said κατ᾽ αναλογίαν and improperly, according to Augustine of the lower regions, not by reason of a place properly called subterranean: And since heaven and earth are to perish, where will such an infernal place, which Bellarmine in book IV de Christo chapter XV places within the bowels of the earth, and Calvin in book II of the Institutes chapter 16, with his followers, sells as a subterranean place, remain? And this can also be seen from the opposite, concerning which Athanasius against the followers of Sabellius says: Let them learn, he says, that that expression 'up' and 'on high' is not to be heard corporally alone, but is to be understood in a new way, namely, explaining it concerning the majesty of the visible Deity, which he says is called sublimity. Conf. B. Hunnius on this passage, who observes among other things the emphasis in the word ὑπεράνω FAR ABOVE all heavens, and infers that Christ by His humanity is thus IN heaven, that is, in the blessed life, (where this is revealed to the elect, it is not for us to define, since, as Isaiah and Paul testify, eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man) so that nevertheless in another more Divine respect of His MAJESTY He transcends by His height ALL heavens, exalted ABOVE everything that is named not only in this, but also in the future age. Unless perhaps the Calvinists have conceded that their heaven, in which they falsely claim CHRIST IS HELD, can be named neither in this nor in the future age, that is, that it is nothing and nowhere. Marloratus acknowledged the truth here, when, on Matthew 27, he says: The heaven into which the Lord ascended is the invisible glory of the Father, and the inaccessible light of the Divinity.

Regarding the Apostolic consequence, 'but that he ascended, what is it, except that he first descended?', a doubt might be raised, because according to our interpretation a previous descent is gathered from the ascent? And it certainly pleased Calvin, Musculus, Aretius, Hemmingius, and Crocius to conclude here that the Apostle concludes the descent from the ascent; who also understand the descent of the incarnation from this, because the Son of God had to descend to earth before He ascended into heaven, since an ascent cannot be said of God unless a descent is presupposed, as Crocius holds here. But others among the Reformed do not acknowledge the consequence here. For to Zanchius, as the same Crocius notes, it seems simpler that we should say that the Apostle only wished to interpret the words of the Prophet, which also pleases Fr. Junius: But, even admitting the Apostolic inference, it still does not follow that the descent of the incarnation is designated. For it can be said that the Apostle does not argue simply from the ascension, but from that ascension which he described with the words of the Prophet, namely, by which He led captivity captive. For from that he gathers that not the Son of God ἀσαρκὸν (without flesh) descended to earth first, but Christ, when on the cross, as is held in the parallel passage Colossians 2 (for Crocius acknowledges this as a parallel), He took away from the midst the handwriting which was against us, about to triumph over captivity, and about to lead the same captive in the ascension, having first had to descend into the lowest parts of the earth, so that He might capture captivity, and lead them openly before Principalities and powers. Which consequence and interpretation would have been of no human ingenuity, but is produced by the Holy Spirit, by whom the holy Apostle was impelled, most worthy of Apostolic illumination. Nor indeed can the Calvinists find where to fix their foot, ignorant of where they ought to place the locations and the lowest parts of the earth in the descent of the incarnation: They designate nothing solid or certain. Calvin, Aretius, and Hemmingius take it simply concerning the earth, so that the sense is that Christ descended from such an exalted seat into our deep abyss: But thus the force and strength of the argument perishes: 'What he ascended, what is it, except that he first descended?' For the ascent is believed by them to be local, but the descent metaphorical: The ascent is of Christ according to His human nature, the descent of the λόγος ἀσάρκος (the Word without flesh). How therefore is it the same, which the Apostle intends, 'he who descended, who also ascended'? What are the κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς (lowest parts of the earth), in a sense clearly improper, that deep abyss of misery for an ascent into the third local heaven, which the Calvinists imagine, to a place properly so called? Therefore Beza and Piscator, when they see that those κατώτερα (lowest parts) were not designated in vain, do not acquiesce in Calvin's interpretation, but contend that the words of the Apostle should perhaps be taken concerning the conception, so that the lowest parts of the earth signify the Virgin's womb. But what stands in the way of this exposition has already been said. Nor do others stop there. For Bullinger understands the whole mystery of the incarnation and passion, namely, that He emptied Himself, that He lowered Himself to the lowest things that are on earth, namely, to the very most shameful death of the cross. But thus an emptying in a different sense, in the same place, must be admitted, namely, improperly for the inclination of the Divinity in the ἐνσαρκώσει (incarnation) in the Patristic sense, and properly for the true emptying in the Apostolic sense, concerning which in Phil. 2, which is not of the λόγος (Word) or of the simple Divinity, but of the person of Christ Jesus συνθέτε (composite): Nor yet will the antithesis of the lowest parts of the earth, which are thus explained clearly metaphorically, and the supercelestial place or in the third heaven, which they assign to the same, properly so called, hold together for the Reformed, not to repeat what I said about the force of the consequence thus about to perish! Whence Musculus, finding nothing certain, finally says it matters little which you accept, whether that Christ descended to us into this world, or into the sepulcher, and to the lower regions. But this is not sufficiently pious, that it matters little what the true sense of the Apostle is in such a notable passage. Musculus, however, sees well that the force of the phrase concerning the descent into the lowest parts of the earth does not exhaust the coming of the Son of God into this world, unless the sepulcher and the descent into hell are added. But Crocius denies a real descent into hell, yet he fights for a real and local ascent as if for hearth and home, even though he sees that Musculus's opinion concerning the descent into hell also pleases Zanchius here, nor does the Apostolic Creed remain whole without it, the article concerning the descent being omitted, which is expressly contained in it, nor can it be confused with the passion, death, or burial of Christ as an article of faith distinct from them. What then? Finally Crocius: To me, he says, it is pleasing that by the descent into the lowest parts of the earth the whole incarnation and humiliation are signified, to which it is certain that the burial pertains. That, however, ought to have pleased least of all. For thus things that are most disparate are joined together. For the incarnation neither entails a real, proper, or local descent, such as an ascent into heaven, properly so called and local (according to Crocius's opinion), demands by force of real opposition: nor does it properly pertain to humiliation; nor is it of Christ the θεανθρώπε, but of the Word, which was from eternity with the Father, John 1, 1. 14. The ascent, according to Crocius, signifies local motion. For he ascended by reason of the flesh, to which local motion is appropriate. The descent does not signify local motion, insofar as it is referred to the incarnation. For he did not exchange a higher place with a lower one while he assumed flesh, he who was everywhere according to the immensity of his Deity. How, therefore, can that opposition, which the Apostle shows and urges so clearly, be consistent for them, especially because the descent as regards the soul is neither a descent simply into the earth, but is designated as εἰς κατώτερα τῆς γῆς, and indeed, in opposition not to an ἀνάβασιν simply, but to an ἀνάβασιν ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὐρανῶν: with which ἀντιθέσει observed, that descent is not [appropriate] to the incarnation can be applied, nor to the humiliation of Christ universally, inasmuch as it consists in the κένωσις (emptying) of Divine Majesty, and the assumption of the form of a servant, and obedience even unto the death of the cross, not in the descent to the lowest parts of the earth, nor finally to the burial. For if that descent be drawn hither, because he then remained ὑπὸ γῆς ἐν τῷ μνημείῳ (under the earth in the tomb), as Ignatius to the Trallians designates the burial, and was in the heart of the earth, that was indeed a real descent, just as the disciple stooped down to look into the tomb, John 20:15. from which Crocius infers a real descent: But neither for that reason can Christ be said to have descended into the lower parts of the earth when he was buried, nor will the humiliation be noted by the descent in such a way, inasmuch as it is said to be a descent not properly, but improperly, just as the descent into hell is sometimes taken improperly concerning extreme humiliation, and the suffering and sense of infernal pains, which indeed the metaphorical descent into hell has nothing in common with the lowering of the body of Christ into the tomb. Finally, what does the burial, what does the humiliation of Christ have to do with the words brought from the Psalm, in which Paul is occupied? Thus in no part does this Crocian commentary, or any gloss of the Calvinists, hold together for itself: But it must be admitted that the descent to the שׁאול (Sheol) of the damned is designated, not indeed that Christ might suffer there: For we do not admit that Christ felt any pains after death, but that he might show himself as victor, which Crocius says is not impious, yet not probable. But why? Because the soul of Christ was in Paradise on the same day, namely immediately after death; But neither did Christ descend immediately after death in our opinion, but ζωοποιηθεὶς (having been made alive), after he was vivified, nor do the διαστήματα (intervals) of places have anything to do with this, since the Son of Man was even then in the heavens when he spoke with Nicodemus on earth, John 3:13. And shall we think that Christ descended from heaven when he appeared to Paul in the Jerusalem barracks, Acts 23:11.

Now as regards the ascension above all heavens, the blessed Hunnius had noted against the Calvinists that the eminence of Majesty, not of place, is designated. What of Crocius? He acknowledges that the sublimity of Majesty is noted in chapter 1, 20, 21, 22. But he says he hears no serious reason why the eminence of place should be excluded here. Why then did he not seek the sublimity of place there in the word ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις (in the heavenly places)? And is it not a sufficiently serious reason that Christ is said to have ascended ABOVE ALL HEAVENS? How then can he be contained in the place of any heaven? He says he ascended far above all visible heavens, namely into the third heaven, which is called the heaven of heavens. But the Apostle does not say, far above all visible heavens, but simply far above ALL heavens. Are the regions of the air and the starry heaven ALL the heavens? Is not the third heaven, is not the heaven of heavens also a heaven? But he ascended ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν (far above all the heavens), as Paul says. Crocius on the contrary says that Paul says this once, but that Scripture affirms more often that Christ was taken up into heaven, Mark 16:19, Acts 1:11, Heb. 9:24, and will descend from heaven, 1 Thess. 4:16. These, however, so that they do not conflict with each other, must be reconciled according to Scripture in this way: that he ascended above all visible heavens into the third heaven. But are things that are said once in Scripture as certain as those that are said more often? And what contradiction is there here, even an apparent one at least? Where has Scripture reconciled it as Crocius has? Grant me some place of Scripture! He says he ascended into heaven, but not so that he is contained by heaven, or that heaven itself contains him, as Crocius with Beza perverts the place in Acts 3:21, much less that he is contained by heaven, which was indeed Beza's earlier depravation, against which in the examination concerning the perfection of Christ, p. 533 ff., we have acted, for the opinion of Nazianzen's second oration concerning the Son was freed from that distortion; but so that he might occupy the heavenly kingdom, and thus reign in the heavens sitting at the right hand of God, not by a local session, but by a Majestatic rule, just as Oecumenius observed that Peter did not say ὅτι ὁ ὀυρανὸς ἐδέξατο τὸν Χριστὸν (that heaven received Christ), but vice versa, ὅτι ὁ Χριστὸς ἐδέξατο τὸν ὀυρανὸν (that Christ received heaven). Then indeed, if Christ with respect to his flesh, having been received into heaven once, dwells in it as in his Royal palace, and holds his place there, how is he said to have ascended far above ALL HEAVENS? Is there some local palace or some material place above all heavens? Crocius wants this: not indeed that a place subject to corruption is there, but a place suitable for spiritual bodies; not a place which Aristotle defines, but a place, if you define it with Scaliger by the space of a created thing. But where has Scripture assigned a material place to spiritual bodies, by reason of which we shall be ἰσάγγελοι (equal to angels)? Where a local palace for Christ? Where are the spaces of Scaliger found in the Scriptures, assigned to the elect, to angels, or to Christ according to the flesh? And where will those material spaces and palaces remain when heaven and earth shall burn with fire and are about to cease? Concerning which Augustine in Ps. 22: If we have understood that corporeal heaven, which we see with our eyes, to be the habitation of God, the habitation of God is about to pass away, because heaven and earth will pass away. Furthermore, if the human nature of Christ is left only in a place, and is not raised beyond a place, how is it believed to be truly raised to the right hand of God, where there are no places. If it is enclosed in a certain place of heaven, how is it said to have penetrated the heavens, Heb. 4:14. And is Christ about to carry away that material heaven, which the Calvinists posit above all heavens, when he will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God, so that he may again have need to ascend ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν (far above all the heavens), so that he may return to his palace and regain his former place? These are Calvinian phantasms, not Apostolic teachings. He will come from heaven, but not from a place: He will descend and be revealed from heaven, not by a certain local descent from the upper parts of the world: but He will come forth from His heavenly Majesty, as if from unapproachable light, and will appear in the clouds of heaven, Matt. 26, just as it is said of God Himself, that He descends from heaven, not as if He sits in some transmundane place and comes to earth from on high through the spheres of the planets by local motion: for He is not far from each one of us, Acts 17:27, but because He comes forth from His unapproachable light and manifests His Majesty by some illustrious work, as B. Balduinus rightly says here.

Crocius also solicited our explanation concerning the filling of all things, which he says Hunnius and other Ubiquitarians interpret concerning the filling of all places and the omnipresence of the reigning Christ. But, setting aside the calumny familiar to the Ubiquitarians, if not perpetual, even though he knew that the Majesty of omnipresence is asserted by us for the flesh of Christ, and that ubiquity, which is of infinite immensity, is not attributed to the same. We do not say that the filling of all things is the filling of all places, much less an expansive, extensive, or local one, which the Calvinists are accustomed to attribute to us. B. Hunnius had warned about this, not only in his own words, but also in those of Stapulensis. His own: That there is to be imagined here no local diffusion or extension, nor an affixing of the humanity to creatures, or some physical contact of them or inclusion in things, but that according to the nature of this heavenly mystery an illocal and Divine presence, rejecting all these paradoxes, is declared, has been shown sufficiently and more than enough partly above and partly elsewhere. Stapulensis: See that a corporal imagination does not deceive you, you multiply places and extend spaces.

Neither is a multiplication of places or an extension of spaces understood here, but a fullness without place above every place, below every place without space, above and below space. Nor does the blessed Hunnius assert so nakedly that CHRIST ascended, so that according to the flesh He would exist substantially in all places, but he explained the filling of all things with Jeremiah, that He is present to all things nearby, not from afar, and from Wisdom ch. 1, that the word of filling denotes not a naked operation without the presence of the operator, but presence first, then the operation of the present one. That Crocius croaks that our explanation fights with the ascension and with the return from heaven is frivolous. Omnipresence or the omnipresent rule and government of Christ according to his flesh ought not to be opposed to his ascension and return, just as Scripture cannot be contrary to Scripture. If he was made everywhere through the ascension, he says, therefore by ascending he did not depart from the earth. But he did depart from the earth, Acts 1:9. Whence Paul, if he were on earth, would not be a Priest, Heb. 8:4. But who says that Christ, through that ascension by which a cloud took him away from the eyes of the Apostles, Acts 1:9, was made everywhere? When he ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things, we say that Christ was exalted according to the flesh, so that present he might rule and sustain all things, which in no way fights with that visible elevation from the earth to the clouds. But if Christ was not a Priest on earth, which the Socinians might prefer, how did he offer his sacrifice on earth? The words of the Apostle, therefore, are to be understood in a certain respect: If he were still on earth in the former manner, he would certainly neither have offered himself as a sacrifice, nor, having entered into the holy of holies through his blood for us, would he have interceded there, and thus he would not be a Priest. What has this to do with the present matter, that the filling of all things, through Divine omnipresence, does not suit Christ according to the flesh, or cannot be understood, when it is said that he ascended above all heavens that he might fill all things? But perhaps this will fight with the return from the earth. Thus Crocius argues: if he is everywhere according to the flesh, he cannot return from heaven into the air. We admit this, if local ubiquity and local return are understood. But that calumny and this phantom we have already discussed. Does he not have power in the air, who has obtained all power in heaven and on earth: which if he exercises according to the flesh, according to which it was given to him in time, does he exercise the same there absent or truly present? If present, what need has he of local and progressive motion from a place above all heavens, perhaps to be completed only after many lustra or centuries of years, in order to be present in the air. Scripture describes the advent of Christ through the manifestation and appearance of his presence, 2 Thess. 1:8, and through the manifestation of his glory, Tit. 2:13. Thus he unsuccessfully battered our interpretation. Now Crocius also strives to overturn his Hunnian foundations, but with no happier success. He denies 1. that it agrees with the scope of Paul. The scope of Paul, he says, is to excite the Ephesians to preserve the unity of the Spirit by the contemplation of the unity of the origin of all gifts, which he refers to Christ. What does the ubiquity of the flesh have to do with this? Not ubiquity, but the omnipresence of the flesh has everything to do with this. For the Apostle refers this to Christ, exalted above all heavens, and filling all things according to the flesh. For will the Calvinists say that according to the Divine nature he was exalted or ascended above all heavens into the place of his palace? But how would Christ distribute all gifts throughout the entire Church, and to all the faithful, according to the flesh, if he is absent from his faithful by as great an interval as the highest heaven is distant from the earth according to the flesh? He denies 2. that our explanation agrees with other sayings, the comparison of which declares that for the Apostle to sit at the right hand of God and to fill all things is the same. But what the blessed Hunnius affirmed only in a certain respect, namely for the underlying subject matter, that Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, fills all things. If to fill all things and to sit at the right hand of God are the same, therefore, he says, the filling of all things is not the ubiquity of the flesh, because sitting at the right hand of God is not the ubiquity of the flesh, but to reign, 1 Cor. 15. But this is no opposition. For Christ reigns according to his Human nature, not absent, but present even in the midst of his enemies. But how would he reign present according to the flesh on earth, and in the midst of his enemies, if he remained confined in a certain place in his palace in the heavens? Concerning which the blessed Hunnius p. 84: If anyone grants that Christ by his human nature sits everywhere at the right hand of God, he will not be able to deny that he is also everywhere and reigns. Since that sitting primarily and first designates presence, but secondly involves the dominion of the kingdom. Now, however, it is certain that Christ according to the flesh sits everywhere at the right hand of God. Therefore it should also be certain that Christ, as he is man, is and reigns everywhere. The evidence of the minor premise appears from this. For if he does not sit everywhere at the right hand, but sits at it in only that one place in which he is according to the property of nature visibly and naturally, as the Adversaries argue: then his sitting at the right hand of God will be subject to the condition of place, terminated in that one place, and according to places movable and changeable. But since it is profane to wish to measure the heavenly mystery of the most Divine sitting at the right hand of the power and Majesty of God by place, and to subject it to the condition of places and the accident of mobility: we piously and with full assurance conclude that the Messiah in his assumed nature sits at the right hand of God, not in one place only, but everywhere, and therefore is also personally present everywhere. Nor does Crocius admit that our explanation agrees with the passage of Jeremiah. In Jeremiah, he says, filling is understood through the immensity of essence. Does that suit the flesh of Christ? The Book of Wisdom attributes the filling of the world to the immense Spirit of God. Does the Apostle thus attribute it to Christ according to the flesh? Resp. The passage of Jer. 23. & Wis. 1. is compared not regarding the suitability of the mode, but regarding the equivalence of the phrase, so that it may teach, namely, what the fulfillment of all things signifies, (which implies for them a substantial nearness and an ἐνεργητικὴν power, or one joined with operation, because the word for fulfilling always implies the presence of the one fulfilling, but never, when it is applied to the kingdom of God, operation only without the presence of the operator,) but not the mode or even the reason & cause of the same. For GOD is present to us through the immensity of His essence, which is not to be said of the flesh of CHRIST. Although in GOD also omnipresence & immensity must be distinguished, as we taught in Tom. II. System. Theol. Furthermore, even if the flesh is not omnipresent through the immensity of essence, yet its omnipresence is not therefore to be entirely denied. The consequence from the negation of the mode to the negation of the thing is not valid. This is not a local or diffusive, but an illocal & Divine presence, not according to the mode of immense extension, but according to the mode of the right hand of GOD, as Blessed Luther explained in the Conf. Maj. concerning the Lord's Supper, by which arrangement neither is anything detracted from the finitude of the human nature of Christ, nor can diffusion from one place to another be feared, since at the right hand of Majesty neither one nor another place either exists, or can be piously and rightly conceived: But with respect to this presence & session at the right hand of Majesty All places, otherwise most separated in the world, are as one place by their exalted Humanity, or rather they scarcely obtain the ratio of a single point. Therefore, just as in local ubiquity there would be no proportion between the quantity of the Human nature and those immense intervals of places: so with respect to the illocal presence of the man Christ at the right hand of power, all created things and all places are reduced and contracted to such straits that the smallness of the assumed Humanity, remaining undiffused with respect to its own quantity, holds in a divine manner this most vast machine of heaven and earth in its hands, just as all those things are also read to have been delivered into his hands, John 3 and 13. And thus in that way, in which he is at the right hand of God, he is not contained, not subjected, not measured, not comprehended by creatures; but rather he contains, comprehends, has subjected to himself, and the universe delivered into his hands, and already before transcending and containing the universe, he presentially rules and moderates all things in heaven and on earth, as the blessed Hunnius piously explained this with the blessed Luther, page 84.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὁ καταβὰς) Vide modo dicta Johannis loca. Αὐτός ἐστι καὶ ὁ ἀναβὰς ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀρανῶν) Id est, supra aërem & æthera, quæ regio cœlum tertium di- citur, & cœlum cœlorum, & pluraliter ὀρανοὶ, & κατ᾿ ἐξο- χὴν ὁ ὀρανὸς, vide Act. 2, 24. & cap. 1, 10. 1. Cor. 15, 48. & hic infra cap. 6, 19.

Ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα) Neutrum pro communi: ut impleret sive satiaret omnes, nempe fideles, donis suis. Vide supra c. 3, 19.

Persequitur Apostolus Domini illius unius potestatem, quam habet ad ditandam & dotan- dam Ecclesiam, libereque distribuenda dona ad ædificandam Ecclesiam, ob quam superandus erat Satanas, & captiva agenda captivitas, ut ascen- dens in cœlum & Ecclesiam sibi colligeret per Doctores Verbi, & donis suis ejus gratia hosce instrueret, & sanctos adoptaret, compaginaret & coagularet ad unum corpus, sub quo, ceu ca- pite, Ecclesia per dilectionem mutuam ædifice- tur. Quam CHRISTI victoriam cum omni- presente ejus regimine ita exequitur, ut ascensum super omnes cælos cum descensu ad infimas terræ partes componens, Spiritu & more vere Aposto- lico πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων Domini nostri pro no- bis exaltati confirmet, sic scil. ascendisse cum tri- umpho super captivitate in sublime & super omnes cælos, ut prius descenderit in partes terræ inferio- res; quæ utraque pertinent ad statum exaltationis Christi, quia in descensu ad infernum, qui oppo- nitur cælo supremo, vel potius supercœlestibus, ut ἀνθρωπίνως, & pro nostro captu hæc tradantur, traduxit Principatus & potestates Diabolicas, de- monstrans se illis victorem, ut in ascensu glorioso publice coram Angelis, & hominibus triumphum de iisdem egit, ut caput serpentis infernalis con- tritum ostenderet. In descensu expugnavit ca- ptivitatem, nos captivantem, Diabolum, & in- ferorum portas, in ascensu captivam secum duxit, ceu in triumpho publico fieri solet, captivitatem. Neque tamen ascendere voluit, nisi prius descen- deret, & Spiritibus tum Satanicis, tum incredu- lorum quondam sese ostentaret ceu victorem Sa- tanæ, & Salvatorem ab hisce per incredulitatem cum æterno ipsorum damno & opprobrio indi- gne contemptum & reprobatum. Κατώτερα τῆς γῆς non notant vel partem eam, in qua homines solent vivere, ea terræ nomine venit, non infima- rum partium terræ, quemadmodum nec uterum maternum designant hoc loco, ubi de conceptio- ne in utero non erat agendi locus; nec oppo- sitio commoda inter descensum in conceptione, & ascensionem super omnes cælos, uti descensus il- le non est pro exinanitione phrasi scripturæ ha- benda, cui opponatur ascensus exaltatio, & ma- jorem emphasin importat τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς, cum illis opponitur τὸ ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν, quam cum absolute illa, extra talem ἀν- τίθεσιν, in Psalm. 139. v. 15. exprimuntur. Hic enim præcise imus locus, ut ita loquar, abso- lute summo vi ἀντιθέσεως opponitur, quod in Psalmo non fit, ubi nulla ἀντίθεσις ejusmodi est, neque intelligi possunt simpliciter infimæ par- tes terræ, cum uterus notatur maternus, quis enim tam excellenti modo τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς μέρη uterum diceret? Uti infernum eo nomine venire posse κατ᾿ ἀντονομασίαν dubium non est, ad mini- mum nostro loquendi modo. Quo de Theophy- lactus: In infernum: nimirum quem profundissimas terræ partes pro communi hominum opinione appel- lat, quemadmodum & Job, deducetis (inquit) canos meos cum dolore in infernum. Et David: Affimi- labor descendentibus in lacum. Ad inferiora itaque Christus descendit, ultra quæ nihil est amplius, & su- per omnes cælos ascendit, quibus nihil est altius. Denique πλήρωσις illa τῶν πάντων cum descensu in uterum non adeo convenit. At vero cum & in infernum descendisse, & super cælos ascendisse, ci- tra localem progressum, dicitur, omnia ipsum im- plere sua omnipræsentia recte infertur, ut qui præ- sens & inferis sese victorem sistere, & super omnes cælos evehi pro libitu potuit, neque localiter & motu progressivo & ad inferna descendere, & per omnes cælos ac supra omnes cælos evehi opus habuit, quemadmodum DEUS ascendere modo, modo descendere dicitur, non mutatione præsen- tiæ, sed manifestatione omnipræsentis potentiæ. Non enim alia præsentia adest caro CHRISTI superis & inferis, & implet omnia, quam Divina, qua scilicet λόγῳ, in cujus hypostasi subsistit, adest, & implet omnia, a qua & penes inferos & penes superos ipsa est inseparabilis, unum cum Λόγῳ constituens ὑφισάμενον. Conf. de hoc lo- co Collegii nostri Theologici Beständige Widerle- gung, in Consil. Theol. Witteb. Tom. I. pag. 881. B. Gesnerus disp. XIV. pro libro Concordiæ pag. 499. B. Hutterus in explicat. libr. Concord. art. IX. pag. 967. B. Mylius in August. Confess. pag. 74. Dn. D. Johan. Meisnerus disp. de descensu Christi ad infer. pag. 72. De DEO ἀσάρκῳ age- re Psalmum inficiamur, quum teste Apostolo de Christo agat, qui est Deus manifestatus in carne, cui adscribitur 1. Tim. 3, 16. illa ascensio vel susce- ptio in gloriam. Idem autem est, juxta Aposto- lum, qui descendit, qui & ascendit, Christus nem- pe θεάνθρωπος, sicut non tam in descensu in uterum, qui est λόγε ἀσάρκε, quam in descensu in infernum idem est Christus Deus, & homo, qui & ascendit in cælum: quod non abs re repetit & inculcat Apostolus, ut merito Christi nos hanc victoriam Satanæ, & distributionem donorum in Ecclesia, totamque gubernationem Ecclesiæ ad- scribendam esse agnoscamus, cujus φανέρωσιν & luculentum testimonium præbuere descensus ad inferos, & ascensus ad cælos ejus, qui propter peccata nostra traditus, & propter justitiam no- stram resuscitatus est, per cujus sanguinem & crucem redemptionem & reconciliationem habe- mus, Ephes. 1, 7. cap. 2, 16. in quo & nos vivificati sumus cum CHRISTO, & resuscitati, & in supra- cœlestibus collocati, cap. 2, 5. 6. De potentia Christi inferius exercita coram multis testibus hanc sive ἀνάβασιν vel ἀνάληψιν, 1. Timoth. 3, 16. sive βάσιν explicari, inauditum est ante Grotium. Πλή- ρωσιν vero τῶν πάντων esse satiationem fidelium per dona Christi e loco Coloss. 3, 19. nullo pacto appa- ret, ac ibi disparrima est ratio. Nam illic im- pleri nos dicimur omni ejus plenitudine; hic Chri- stus dicitur implere omnia, & descendisse ad infi- mas terræ partes, atque ascendisse supra omnes cœlos, ut constaret ipsum implere omnia; Si ra- tione declarationis id explicetur; quum res in hominibus dicantur fieri cum declarantur, vel demonstrantur; vel ut impleret omnia, vi exal- tationis supra omnes cœlos, & evectionis ad sum- mam potestatem, quam supra inferos & superos, per illam exaltationem tum obtinuit, quam sem- per habuit, ratione κτήσεως; nunc autem exerit κατὰ χρῆσιν, & exercet in cessante dominio in cœ- lo & in terra implens omnipræsente & Divino suo dominio omnia, Matth. 28, 19. 20. Ephes. 1, 20. seqq.

Interpretantur & Calviniani illam πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων quandoque cum Hugone & Thoma de concessione donorum in Ecclesia, sed nec ipsi sibi constant, quum de impletione scripturæ non- nunquam cum Bernhardo, Anselmo, Lombardo accipiant, quam vero non per πλήρωσιν πάντων, sed cum addito scripturæ aut Prophetæ alicujus nomine solet Spiritus Sanctus designare, quale quid hic minime occurrit: Nec si admittatur, donorum concessionem in Ecclesia notari ea ta- men non exhaurit πλήρωσιν τῶν πάντων, utpote quæ se etiam ad ea extendit, quæ extra Eccle- siam sunt, nec regnum solum gratiæ & gloriæ, sed etiam ad regnum potentiæ accedit, quod cum de donis sermo est, verbo implendi etiam dono- rum adjiciatur mentio, ut fit Coloss. 1, 9. Phil. 1, 4. Quid autem impletione omnium designet, locus parallelus docet, Jerem. 23. v. 13. & Jacob. 1. v. 7. nimirum non donorum concessionem, sed omni- præsentiam Divinam: Quo sensu Oecumenius in hunc locum: Nuda, inquit, Divinitate olim omnia implebat, incarnatus autem descendit & ascendit, ut μετὰ σαρκὸς omnia impleret. Et quæ- nam isthæc glossa erit ex mente Calvinianorum: Ascendit juxta humanitatem, ut impleret donis Ecclesiam juxta Divinitatem? Tum vero annon potuisset donis implere Ecclesiam, etiamsi non SUPRA omnes cœlos ascendisset. Denique explicant alii è Reformatis hanc omnium imple- tionem de operatione omnium in omnibus. Cro- cius in h. l. pag. 431. ita habet: Donorum imple- tio præsupponit impletionem potentiæ ac dominii.
