In eo enim exerit CHRISTUS potentiam ac do- minatum, quod universam Ecclesiam suis donis complet. Nec complere posset omnia donis, nisi omnia perficeret, seu regeret sua virtute ac mode- raretur. B. Hunnius ita urget Calvinianos: quum hæc operatio omnium in omnibus citra dubita- tionem actio sit solius increatæ potentiæ, quæ, (poten- tia increata) si Christo, qua est homo, communica- ta realiter non est, quomodo qua homo omnipotenter agere, hoc est omnia in omnibus operari poterit? Et si concedunt, Λόγον jam juxta carnem quoque suam operari universa: quidni hoc ipso præsentiam quoq; illius apud cunctas creaturas stabilient? Quam enim sit absurdum, ut λόγος præsens præsentes crea- turas administret per Humanitatem omni modo rea- li absentem ac remotam, supra pag. 82. in explicatio- ne primi capitis ostensum est. Et vox ipsa implendi πρώτως quidem præsentiam implentis seu operantis designat; δευτέρως autem seu secundario præsentis operationem declarat. Ideo enim & locorum fit mentio, cum inferorum tum superorum in descriptio- ne impletionis hujus: ut præsentia in omnibus locis designetur, non illa successiva & localis, de qua su- pra: Sed personalis & juxta modum dextræ Dei de- scriptæ præsentia. Sicut ex testimonio Jeremiæ cap. 23. est evidens, quid implere omnia significet, di- cente ibi Domino: Nunquid non cœlum & terram ego impleo? Idq́; ipsum his immediate præcedenti- bus verbis dilucidius reddit, cum ait: Nonne Deus in propinquo ego sum, & non Deus à longe? Ubi Domino idem est, implere omnia, & adesse omni- bus in propinquo. Eodem modo accipitur Sap. 1. Spiritus Domini replet orbem terrarum. Ubi si- militer replendi vox non nudam operationem sine operantis præsentia notat, sed præsentiam primo, dehinc præsentis operationem. Hæc B. Hunnius, concludens, hunc esse simplicissimum verborum Pauli sensum, quod Christus juxta carnem non ra- tione aliis sanctis consueta in cœlum, sed privilegio singulari supra omnes cœlos ad ipsam dextram omni- præsentiæ elevatus sit, ut præsens adesset omnibus, & in omnibus operaretur omnia. Hæc explicatio congruit cum scopo Pauli, cum collatione aliorum dictorum, quæ de ascensu Christi in cœlum agunt, & subinde sessionis ad dextram articulum conjun- gunt, adeoque declarant, idem esse Apostolo, sedere ad dextram DEI, & omnia implere, con- gruit cum declaratione verbi implendi, Jerem. 23. v. 33. Insuper congruit cum Interpretibus Oe- cumenio & Theophylacto, è quibus ille antea jam productus, hic vero ita habet: Ut omnia impleat dominatione operationeq́;, idque IN CARNE, quan- doquidem Divinitate jam omnia compleret. Addit & verba Stapulensis B. Hunnius, qui ante motum certamen sacramentarium ita scripsit: Corpus Chri- sti cœlum implet & terram. Est enim, ubicunque Verbum est. Nam Verbum caro factum est. Qua- re verbum nusquam est sine carne, neque caro illa sine Verbo. Denique notat B. Hunnius confessionem Calvinianorum propriam, quando ex hac imple- tione omnium Ephes. 4, 10. omnipræsentiam Chri- sti probant, in demonstranda ejus Deitate, Sohnii in disp. Heidelb. §. 31. Grabii & aliorum.

Jam ut ad phrasin alteram Apostoli aliquid ad- huc moneamus, nequaquam hic inferiores partes terræ sunt de locis proprie dictis subterraneis intel- ligendæ, quo S. Augustinus quidem inclinare visus fuit libr. XII. de Gen. ad Lit. cap. XXXIII. Sed mentem suam sic explicat loco citato cap. XXXIV. Ideo sub terris inferi dicuntur vel creduntur, quia congruenter in Spiritu per illas corporalium rerum similitudines sic demonstrantur, ut quoniam defun- ctorum animæ inferis dignæ carnis amore peccave- runt, hoc eis per illas corporalium rerum similitudi- nes exhibeatur, quod ipsi carni mortuæ solet, ut sub terram recondatur. Deniq́; inferi eo, quod infra sint, Latine appellantur. Sicut autem secundum corpus, si ponderis sui ordinem teneant inferiora omnia sunt graviora: Ita secundum Spiritum inferiora sunt omnia tristiora. Unde & in Græca lingua origo no- minis, quo appellantur inferi, ex quo, quod nihil sua- ve habeant, resonare videtur. Unde apparet κατ᾽ αναλογίαν & improprie dici secundum Augustinum inferos, non ratione loci subterranei proprie di- cti: Et quum coelum & terra peritura sint, ubi talis locus infernalis, quem Bellarm. intra viscera terrae collocat libr. IV. de Christo cap. XV. Calvinus libr. II. Instit. cap. 16. cum suis, pro subterraneo lo- co venditat, manebit? Idque etiam ex opposito videre est, de quo Athanas. contra Sabell. gregal. Discant, inquit, sursum illud & in alto esse non cor- poraliter duntaxat audiendum, sed nova ratione in- telligendum esse, scil. explicans id de majestate vi- sibilis Deitatis, quam sublimitatem vocari ait. Conf. B. Hunnius in hunc locum, qui observat in- ter alia emphasin in voce ὑπεράνω LONGE SU- PRA omnes coelos, infertǵ, Christum sua Humanita- te sic esse IN coelo, hoc est in vita beata, (qua ubi reve- letur electis, nostrum non est definire, cum, Esaia & Paulo testantibus, oculus non viderit, auris non audi- verit, nec in cor hominis ascenderit) ut nihilominus alio Diviniore respectu MAJESTATIS sua celsi- tudine transcendat OMNES coelos, exaltatus SU- PRA omne, quod nominatur non tantum in hoc, sed etiam in futuro seculo. Nisi forte Calviniani suum coelum, in quo CAPI CHRISTUM per crimen falsi dictitant, neque in hoc, neque in futuro seculo nominari posse, hoc est, nihil & nullibi esse concesse- rint. Marloratus hic agnovit veritatem, cum, in Matth. 27. Coelum, inquit, in quod Dominus ascen- dit, invisibilis Patris gloria est, & inaccessa lux Divi- nitatis.

De consequentia Apostolica, caeterum illud ascendit, quid est, nisi quod prius descendit, dubium moveri possit, quod juxta nostram interpretatio- nem ex ascensu colligatur descensus praevius? Et placuit sane Calvino, Musculo, Aretio, Hemmingio & Crocio, hic concludere, Apostolum ex ascensu de- scensum; qui etiam descensum incarnationis hinc intelligunt, quod prius Filius DEI descendere in terram debuerit, quam ascenderet in coelũ, quum de Deo ascensus dici nequeat, nisi descensus prae- supponatur, ut hic habet Crocius. At consequen- tiam hic non agnoscunt alii è Reformatis. Zan- chio enim, notante eodem. Crocio, simplicius vide- tur, ut dicamus, tantùm Apostolum verba Prophetae interpretari voluisse, quod & placet Fr. Junio: Sed, admissa etiam illatione Apostolica, nondum tamen sequitur, descensum incarnationis designatum. Di- ci enim potest, non simpliciter Apostolum ex a- scensione argumentari, sed ex ea, quam verbisPro- phetae descripsit, ascensione, nimirum qua captivam duxit captivitatem. Ex ea enim colligit, prius de- scendisse non Filium Dei ἀσαρκὸν in terras, sed Christum, quando in cruce, ut in loco parallelo Coloss. 2. habetur, (hunc enim pro parallelo agno- scit Crocius) è medio sustulit chirographum, quod ad- versus nos erat, triumphum acturus de captivitate, eandemq́; captivam ducturus in ascensione, prius de- buisse in infimas terrae partes descendere, ut captiva- ret captivitatem, & coram Principatus & potestates traduceret. Quae consequentia & interpretatio nullius humani ingenii fuisset, sed à Spiritu Sancto, à quo impulsus fuit sanctus Apostolus, proditur, illuminatione Apostolica dignissima. Neque sa- ne possunt Calviniani invenire, ubi pedem figant, nescii, ubi loca, & infimas terrae partes locare debeat in descensu incarnationis: Solidi utique & certi ni- hil designant. Calvinus, Aretius, Hemmingius sim- pliciter de terra accipiunt, ut sensus sit, Christum ex sede tam excelsa in profundum nostrum bara- thrum descendisse: Sed ita vis & robur argumento perit: Quod ascendit, quid est, nisi quod prius descen- dit. Nam ascensus creditur ab ipsis localis, descen- sus vero Metaphoricus : Ascensus est Christi se- cundum Humanam naturam, descensus λόγυ ἀ- σάρκε. Quomodo ergo idem est, quod vult Apo- stolus, qui descendit, qui & ascendit? Quid κατώ- τερα μέρη τῆς γῆς, sensu plane improprio, profun- dum illud barathrum miseriæ ad ascensum in cœlũ tertium localem, quem fingunt Calvinistæ, ad locũ proprie ita dictum? Ideo Beza, & Piscator cum vi- deant, non frustra κατώτερα illa designata, haud ac- quiescunt Calvini interpretationi, sed de conceptio- ne forte accipienda esse verba Apostoli dimicant, ut infimæ partes terræ Virginis uterum significent. Sed quæ obstent huic expositioni, jam dictum est. Nec in ea subsistunt alii. Bullingerus enim totum incarnationis & passionis mysterium, nempe quod exinaniverit seipsum, quod ad infima, quæ in terris sunt, se demiserit, ad ipsam scilicet mortem crucis turpissimam, intelligit. Sed ita exinanitio diverso sensu, loco eodem, admittenda, nempe improprie pro inclinatione Divinitatis in ἐνσαρκώσει sensu Patristico, & proprie pro vera exinanitione sensu A- postolico, de qua Phil. 2. quæ non λόγε aut Divinita- tis simplicis est, sed Christi Jesu personæ συνθέτε: Nec tamen sibi constabit antithesis infimarum par- tium terræ, quæ plane Metaphoricè sic explicantur, & loci supercœlestis vel in tertio cœlo, quem eodem assignant, proprie ita dictum, Reformati, ut non re- petam, quæ de vi consequentiæ ita peritura dixi! Unde Musculus, nihil certi inveniens, tandem pa- rum referre ait, quodcunœ accipias, sive quod Chri- stus ad nos in hunc mundum descenderit, sive quod in sepulchrum, & ad inferos. At hoc non satis pium, parum interesse, quisnam verus sit Apostoli sensus in tam insigni loco. Videt autem probe Musculus, non exhaurire vim phraseos de descensu ad infi- mas partes terræ adventum Filii Dei in hunc mun- dum, nisi sepulchrum addatur & descensus ad infe- ros. Sed Crocius realem ad inferos descensum ne- gat, pro ascensu tamen reali & locali, tanquam pro aris & focis dimicat, etsi Zanchio etiam Musculi sententiam de descensu ad inferos hic placere vi- deat, nec sine eo Apostolicum symbolum inte- grum manear, omisso scilicet articulo de descensu, qui expresse in eo continetur, nec cum passione, morte aut sepultura Christi potest confundi ceu distinctus ab iisde fidei articulus. Quid ergo? De- nique Crocius: Mihi, inquit, placet, descensu in infi- mas terræ partes incarnationem totąmœ, humiliatio- nem significari, ad quam sepulturam pertinere certũ. Id vero minime omnium placere debebat. Nam ita maxime disparata conjunguntur. Incarnatio e- nim nec realem proprium aut localem descensum infert, qualem vi oppositionis realis proprie ita di- ctus & localis (juxta Crocii sententiam) ascensus in cœlum, vi oppositionis postulat: nec proprie ad humiliatione pertinet; nec est Christi θεανθρώπε, sed verbi, quod ab æterno apud Patrem fuit, Joh. 1, 1. 14. Ascensus, secundum Crocium, localem motum significat. Adscendit enim ratione carnis, in quam localis motus competit. Descensus motum localem non significat, quatenus ad incarnationem refertur. Non enim locum superiorem cum inferiore commuta- vit, dum carnem assumpsit, qui ubique erat secundum Deitatis immensitatem. Quomodo ergo sibi illa oppositio, quam tam exerte monstrat & urget A- postolus, constare potest, imprimis quia descensus quoad animam neque descensus simpliciter in ter- ram, sed εἰς κατώτερα τῆς γῆς, & quidem, in opposi- tione non ad ἀνάβασιν simpliciter, sed ad ἀνάβασιν ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὐρανῶν, designatur: qua ἀντι- θέσει observatâ nec incarnationi descensus ille ap- plicari potest, nec ad Christi humiliationem uni- versaliter, utpote quæ in κενώσει Majestatis Divinæ, & assumptione formæ servilis, ac obedientia usque ad mortem crucis consistit, non in descensu ad infi- mas terræ partes, nec denique ad sepulturam. Nam si huc trahatur ille descensus, quod tum ὑπὸ γῆς ἐν τῷ μνημείῳ manserit, ut Ignatius ad Trallian. se- pulturam designat, & in corde terræ fuerit, realis quidem descensus ille erat, quemadmodum disci- pulus sepulchrum inspecturus sese incurvavit, Joh. 20,15. è quibus realem descensum Crocius colligit: Sed nec ideo in inferiores terræ partes Christus de- scendisse dici potest, cum sepultus est, nec ita per descensum humiliatio notabitur, utpote quæ non proprie, sed improprie descensus dicitur, quomo- do descensus ad infernum improprie quandoque sumitur de extrema humiliatione, & perpessione ac sensu dolorum infernalium, qui vero descensus ad inferos Metaphoricus nihil commune habet cum demissione corporis Christi in sepulchrum. Denique quid sepultura, quid humiliatio Christi ad verba è Psalmo adducta, in quibus occupatur Paulus, facit? Ita nulla parte sibi constat hic Crocianus commen- tarius, aut ulla Calvinianorum glossa: Sed fateri oportet, descensum ad שׁאול damnatorum designa- ri, non quidem, ut illic pateretur Christus: Nam post mortem Christum dolores ullos sensisse, nec nos admittimus, sed ut se victorem ostenderet, quod impium non esse, ait Crocius, probabile tamen non esse. Cur vero? Quia anima Christi eodem die fuit in Paradiso, nempe statim à morte; Ast nec statim à morte Christus descendit nostrâ senten- tiâ, sed ζωοποιηθεὶς, postquam vivificatus est, nec locorum διαστήματα huc quicquam faciunt, quum Filius hominis etiam tum in cælis fuerit, quando cum Nicodemo in terris loquutus est, Joh. 3, 13. Et num descendisse cælo Christum putabimus, cum Paulo apparuit in castris Hierosolymitanis, Act. 23, 11.

Jam quod ad ascensum supra omnes cælos attinet, notarat contra Calvinianos B. Hunnius, Majestatis, non loci eminentiam designari. Quid Crocius? Ma- jestatis sublimitatem notatam cap. 1, 20.21.22. agno- scit. Sed hic loci eminentia cur excludatur, causam nullam gravem se audire, ait. Cur ergo illic in voce ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις loci sublimitatem non quæsivit? Et annon satis gravis causa est, quod Christus SU- PRA OMNES COELOS adscendisse dicatur? Quomodo ergo cæli alicujus loco concludi po- test? Dicit, adscendisse longe supra omnes cælos aspe- ctabiles, scil. in cælum tertium, quod cælum cælo- rum appellatur. At Apostolus non dicit, longe su- per omnes cælos aspectabiles, sed simpliciter longe super OMNES cælos. An aëris regiones & cæ- lum sidereum OMNES sunt cæli? Annon cælum tertium, annon cælum cælorum etiam est cælum? At ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν ascendit, dicente Paulo. Crocius contra, id Paulum semel dicere, sed Christum in cælum evectum, scripturam sæpius affirmare, Marci 16, 19. Act. 1, 11. Ebr. 9, 24. & è cælo descensurum, 1. Thess. 4, 16. Hæc autem, ne pugnent inter se, concilianda ita esse juxta scriptu- ram, adscendisse supra omnes cælos adspectabiles in cælum tertium. Sed tàm certa sunt, quæ semel di- cuntur in scriptura, quàm quæ sæpius? Et quænam hic contradictio, etiam apparens saltem? Ubi ita scriptura conciliavit, ut Crocius? Cedo aliquem scripturæ locum! In cælum dicit adscendisse, sed non ut contineatur cælo, aut ut cælum ipsum capiat, ut locum Act. 3, 21. cum Beza Crocius pervertit, nedum ut capiatur cælo, quæ quidem pri9 fuit Bezæ depravatio, contra quam in exam. de perf. Christi p. 533. sqq. egimus, liberata enim Nazianzeni orat. II. de Filio eo detorta sententia; sed ut regnum cœ- leste occuparet, adeoque in cœlis regnaret sedens ad dextram Dei non locali sessione, sed Majestatico regimine, quemadmodum Oecumenius observavit, Petrum non dixisse, ὅτι ὁ ὀυρανὸς ἐδέξατο τὸν Χριστὸν, sed vice versa, ὅτι ὁ Χριστὸς ἐδέξατο τὸν ὀυρανὸν. Tum vero si Christus carnis suæ respectu in cœlum semel receptus in eo commoratur, ut in suo pala- tio Regio, ibique locum suum teneat, quomodo dicitur longe supra OMNES COELOS adscen- disse? An supra omnes cœlos est aliquod palatium locale, aut locus aliquis materialis? Id vult Crocius: non locum quidem corruptioni obnoxium ibidem esse, sed locum spiritualibus corporibus convenientem; non locum, quem Aristoteles definit, sed locum, si cum Scaligero per spatium rei creatæ definias. Sed ubi scriptura corporibus spiritualib9, quorum ra- tione ἰσάγγελοι erimus, materialem locum assigna- vit? Ubi Christo locale palatium? Ubi spatia Sca- ligeri in scripturis inveniuntur, electis, Angelis aut Christo secundum carnem assignata? Et ubi ma- nebunt spatia & palatia illa materialia, cum cœ- lum, & terra igne conflagrabunt, atque desitura sunt? Quo de Augustinus in Ps. 22. Si cœlum illud corporeum, quod oculis videmus, intellexerimus esse habitationem Dei, transitura est habitatio Dei, quia cœlum & terra transibunt. Porro si humana Christi natura tantum in loco relinquitur, neque ultra locum evehitur, quomodo evecta vere cre- ditur in Dei dextram, ubi loca nulla sunt. Si in loco quodam cœli conclusa est, quomodo penetrasse cœ- los dicitur, Ebr. 4, 14. Et num cœlum illud materia- le, quod supra omnes cœlos statuunt Calviniani, Christus deferturus est, cum de cœlo descendet cum tuba Dei, ut rursum op9 habeat ὑπεράνω πάν- των τῶν ὀυρανῶν adscendere, ut in palatium suu red- eat, locumq; suum pristinu repetat? Φαντάσματα hæc Calviniana sunt, non ἀκόσματα Apostolica. Veniet de cœlo, non autem de loco: Descendet & pate- fiet de cœlo, non locali quodam descensu e superioribus mundi partibus: sed e cœlesti sua Majestate prodibit, tanquam ex luce inaccessa, & in nubibus cœli appa- rebit, Matth. 26. quemadmodum de Deo ipso dici- tur, ipsum de cœlo descendere, non quasi in loco trans- mundano quodam sedeat, & e supernis per sphæras planetarum ad nos motu locali veniat in terram: non enim procul est ab unoquoq; nostrum, Act. 17, 27. sed quia ex luce sua inaccessa prodit, & Majestatem suam illustri aliquo opere manifestat, ut hic recte B. Bal- duinus.

Solicitavit etiam nostram explicationem de im- pletione omnium Crocius, quam de locorum omnium impletione & regnantis omnipræsentia Hunnium, & alios Ubiquitarios interpretari ait. Sed missa calumnia Ubiquitarioru ipsi familiari, si non per- petua, etsi non nescierit, Majestatem omnipræsentia carni Christi a nobis adseri, ubiquitatem, quæ im- mensitatis infinitę est, eidem haud tribui. Imple- tionem omnium non dicimus esse impletionem omnium locorum, nedum expansivam, extensivam, localem, quam affingere nobis solent Calviniani. Monuerat de eo B. Hunnius, non suis tantum, sed etiam Stapulensis, verbis. Suis: Esse autem hic nul- lam fingendam localem diffusionem aut extensionem, nec affixionem humanitatis ad creaturas, vel earun- dem contactum quendam physicum aut inclusione in rebus, sed pro natura cœlestis hujus mysterii præsentia illocalem & Divinam, cuncta hac paradoxa respuen- tem declarari partim supra partim alibi satis superq ostensum est. Stapulensis: Videte ne corporalis ima- ginatio vos ludat, loca multiplicas & spatia distendes.

Neque hic locorum multiplicatio, neque spatiorum distensio intelligitur, sed plenitudo sine loco supra lo- cum omnem, infra locum omnem sine spatio, supra & infra spatium. Neque ita nude asserit B. Hun- nius, CHRISTUM ascendisse, ut secundum car- nem existeret substantialiter in locis omnibus, sed impletionem omnium exposuit cum Jeremia, quod in propinquo adsit omnibus, non à longe, & è Sapient. cap. 1. quod vox implendi non nudam operationem sine operantis præsentia notet, sed præsentiam primo, dehinc præsentis operationem. Quod pugnare nostram explicationem cum ascen- su & cum reditu è cælo crocitat Crocius, frivolum est. Omnipræsentia vel omnipræsens regimen & gubernatio Christi secundum carnem ejus ascensui & reditui tam opponi non debet, quam scriptura scripturæ adversa esse non potest. Si factus est per ascensum ubique, inquit, Ergo ascen- dendo non recessit è terra. At recessit è terra, Act. 1, 9. Unde Paulus, si esset in terra, non esset Sacerdos, Ebr. 8, 4. Sed quis dicit, Christum per ascensum illum, quo sublatum nubes subduxit oculis Apo- stolorum, Actor. 1, 9. factum esse ubique. Cum ascendit super omnes cælos, ut omnia impleret, di- cimus, exaltatum esse Christum secundum car- nem, ut præsens omnia regeret ac sustentaret, quod minime pugnat cum illa visibili è terra ad nubes elevatione. Si autem Christus in terra Sacerdos non fuit, quod Sociniani malint, quomodo in terra sacrificium suum obtulit? Verba ergo Apostoli κατά τι intelligenda: Si adhuc pristino more in ter- ris esset, utique nec obtulisset sese in sacrificium, nec per sanguinem suum in sanctum sanctorum in- gressus pro nobis ibi interpellaret, adeoque non esset Sacerdos. Quid hoc ad rem præsentem, im- pletionem omnium, per omnipræsentiam Divinam, Christo secundum carnem non convenire, aut non intelligi posse, cum ascendisse super omnes cœlos dicitur, ut impleret omnia? Sed forte cum reditu è terra hoc pugnabit. Ita arguit Crocius: si est secundum carnem ubique, è cælo redire non potest in aërem. Admittimus, si localis ubiquitas & loca- lis reditus intelligatur. At illam calumniam & Φάντασμα hoc jam discussimus. Annon in aërem potestatem habet, qui omnem potestatem nactus est in cælo & in terra: quam si exercet secundum carnem, secundû quam ei in tempore illa data est, num absens an vero præsens eandem ibi exercet? Si præsens, quid opus habet motu locali & progref- sivo de loco supra omnes cœlos multis forte anno- rum lustris aut centuriis demum expediundo, ut in aëre adsit. Scriptura per manifestationem & ap- paritionem præsentiæ describit adventum Christi, 2. Thess. 1, 8. & per manifestationem gloriæ ejus, Tit. 2, 13. Ita infeliciter arietavit nostram interpreta- tionem. Jam fundamenta etiam ejus Hunniana evertere satagit Crocius, sed successu haud feliciori. Negat 1. quod cum scopo Pauli ea conveniat. Pau- li, inquit, scopus est, ad unitatem Spiritus servandam excitare Ephesios contemplatione uniό originis omniũ donorum, quam ad Christum refert. Huc quid facit ubiquitas carnis? Non ubiquitas, sed omnipræsen- tia carnis omnino huc facit. Nam ad Christum hoc Apostolus refert, exaltatum supra omnes cœlos, & implentem omnia secundum carnem. Secundum enim Divinam naturam num exaltatum aut ascen- disse supra omnes cœlos in locum palatii sui dicent Calvinistæ? Quomodo verò dona omnia per u- niversam Ecclesiam, omnibusque fidelibus distri- bueret Christus secundum carnem, si tanto inter- vallo à fidelibus suis abest, quanto intervallo supre- mum cœlum distat à terra secundum carnem? Negat 2. quod explicatio nostra cum aliis dictis, quo- rum collatio declarat, idem esse Apostolo sedere ad dextram Dei, & omnia implere, congruat. Quod vero B. Hunnius secundum quid tantum affirma- vit, nimirum pro substrata materia, quod Christus sedens ad dextram Dei, impleat omnia. Si implere omnia, & sedere ad dextram Dei, idem sunt, ergo, in- quit, impletio omnium non est ubiquitas carnis, quia sedere ad dextram Dei non est carnis ubiquitas, sed regnare, 1. Cor. 15. Ast nulla hæc oppositio. Nam regnat Christus secundum Humanam naturam, non absens, sed præsens etiam in medio inimico- rum suorum. Quomodo autem præsens regnaret secundum carnem in terris, & in medio suorum inimicorum, si in cœlis in palatio suo in certo loco conclusus maneret? Quo de B. Hunnius p. 84. Si quis largiatur, Christum natura humana sua ubique sedere ad dextram Dei, is negare haud poterit, quia etiam ubique sit & regnet. Quandoquidem illud se- dere principaliter ac primo præsentiam designat, se- cundo autem regni Dominatum involvit. Jam vero certum est, Christum juxta carnem ubique sedere ad dextram Dei. Ergo certum etiam sit, Christum, qua homo est, esse & regnare ubique. Minoris evidentia hinc apparet. Nam si non ubique sedet ad dextram, sed in uno tantum eo loco ad illam sedet, in quo est juxta naturæ proprietatem visibiliter & naturaliter, sicut Adversarii disputant: tum ipsius ad dextram Dei sessio erit subjecta conditioni loci, terminata uno illo loco, & secundum loca mobilis atque mutabilis. Cum autem profanum sit, cœleste mysterium Divinis- simæ sessionis ad dextram virtutis & Majestatis Dei, metiri velle loco, & locorum conditioni & accidenti mobilitatis subjicere: nos pie & cum πληροφορίᾳ concludimus, Messiam in assumpta natura ad dextram Dei sedere, non uno tantum in loco, sed omnino ubiq̄, & proinde etiam ubique personaliter adesse. Neque admittit Crocius, congruere explicationem no- stram loco Jeremiæ. Apud Jeremiam, inquit, intel- ligitur impletio per essentiæ immensitatem. Num ea convenit carni Christi? Liber Sapientiæ immenso Dei Spiritui tribuit orbis terrarum impletionem. Num sic Apostolus tribuit Christo secundum carnem? Resp. Locus Jerem. 23. & Sap. 1. confertur non quoad modi convenientiam, sed quoad phraseos æ- quipollentiam, ut nempe doceat, quid significet im- pletio omnium, (quod inferat ea propinquitatem substantialem vimque ἐνεργητικὴν, vel cum opera- tione conjunctam, quod implendi vox semper præ- sentiam implentis inferat, nunquam autem, cum de regno Dei adhibetur, operationem tantum sine præsentia operantis,) non autem modum vel etiam rationem & causam ejusdem. Nam DEUS per es- sentiæ immensitatem nobis adest, quod de carne CHRISTI dicendum non est. Quanquam in DEO etiam omnipræsentia & immensitas distingui de- beant, ut Tom. II. System. Theol. docuimus. Porro etsi caro non per essentiæ immensitatem omnipræsens est, non tamen ideo prorsus neganda ejusdem omnipræsentia. A negatione modi ad ne- gationem rei non valet consequentia. Est hæc non localis aut diffusiva, sed illocalis & Divina præsen- tia, non juxta modum immensæ extensionis, sed juxta modum dextræ DEI, ut B. Lutherus. Conf. Maj. de cœna Domini exposuit, quo pacto nec fi- nitati humanæ naturæ Christi quicquam deroga- tur, nec diffusio de loco uno in alterum metui po- test, cum in dextra Majestatis nec unus nec alter lo- cus vel sit, vel cogitari pie recteque possit: Sed respectu hujus præsentiæ & sessionis ad Majestatis dextram omnia loca, alias in mundo disjunctissima eorum ex- altata Humanitate veluti locus unus sunt, imo vix unius puncti rationem obtinent. Proinde sicut in ubiquitate locali nulla esset proportio inter quantita- tem Humanae naturae, & immensa illa locorum inter- valla: Sic respectu illocalis praesentiae Christi hominis in dextra virtutis, res creatae omnes & loca omnia ad eas angustias reducta contractaque sunt, ut assumptae Humanitatis parvitas respectu quantitatis suae indif- fusa permanens divino modo hanc vastissimam caeli terraeque machinam in suis manibus habeat, sicut et- iam illa omnia in manus tradita leguntur, Joh. 3. & 13. Atque sic eo modo, quo in dextra Dei est, non continetur non subjicitur, non mensuratur, non com- prehenditur a creaturis; sed potius continet, compre- hendit, subjecta sibi habet, & in manus tradita uni- versa, & jam antequam transcendens atque conti- nens universorum praesens regit ac moderatur omnia in caelis & in terra, ut haec pie cum B. Luthero ex- posuit B. Hunnius pag. 84.

## 4:11
Verse 11.

• Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔδωκε τῆς μὲν Ἀποστόλες) Just as God had appointed through Moses the princes of the tribes, the commanders of thousands, the centurions, and so on in order, so also Christ has done now. The Apostles correspond to the princes of the tribes.

Τὸς δὲ Προφήτας) Who are always placed next to the Apostles, as above chapter 3, 5. 1 Cor. 12, 28.

Τὸς δὲ Εὐαγγελισάς) Helpers of the Apostles, Acts 21, 8. 2 Tim. 4, 5. Such for a time were Titus, Timothy, Apollos, Silas, Mark, Luke. See 2 Cor. 8, 18.

Τὸς δὲ ποιμένας) פרנסין pastors. A pastor among the Jews was called the governor of the Synagogue; that name is appropriate to the one presiding, to the one laboring in the word, 1 Tim. 5, 17, who is called by way of eminence Bishop, the inspector of the flock. For to teach is to feed.

Καὶ διδασκάλος) These were Bishops themselves also, but placed in a more eminent rank: such as were later called metropolitans, as we said Rom. 12, 7 and 1 Cor. 12, 28.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

• Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔδωκε τῆς μὲν Ἀποστόλες) Sicut Deus per Mosen constituerat tribuum Principes, chiliarchos, centu- riones, atque ita deinceps, ita & nunc fecit Christus. Apo- stoli tribuum Principibus respondent.

Τὸς δὲ Προφήτας) Qui semper proximi Apostolis po- nuntur, ut supra cap. 3, 5. 1. Cor. 12, 28.

Τὸς δὲ Εὐαγγελισάς) Adjutores Apostolorum, Act. 21, 8. 2. Tim. 4, 5. tales aliquandiu fuere Titus, Timotheus, A- pollo, Silas, Marcus, Lucas. Vide 2. Cor. 8, 18.

Τὸς δὲ ποιμένας) פרנסין pastores. Pastor apud Ju- daos vocabatur gubernator Synagoga, id nomen com- petit τῷ προεςῶτι, τῷ κοπιῶντι ἐν λόγῳ, 1. Tim. 5, 17. qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν dictus Ἐπίσκοπος, inspector gregis. Nam do- cere est pascere.

Καὶ διδασκάλος) Hi erant Episcopi & ipsi, sed in emi- nentiore gradu positi: quales dicti postea μητροπολῖται, ut diximus Rom. 12, 7. & 1. Cor. 12, 28.

## 4:12
Verse 12.

Πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων εἰς ἔργον διακονίας) There is a transposition here also. For the genuine construction would have been, εἰς ἔργον διακονίας πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων, the work is enjoined upon them, and indeed, that they may minister to the saints, by perfecting them more and more both in faith and in the knowledge of those things which in some way pertain to the Gospel. See concerning this word 1 Cor. 1, 10. 2 Cor. 13, 11. Gal. 6, 1.

Εἰς οἰκοδομὴν τῷ σώματος τῷ Χριστ) So that in that way they also, the saints, may be made fit for the building up of the Church, that is, by teaching others.

Just as the Apostle attributes the concession of gifts regarding all the faithful in general to Christ exalted and the omnipotent Lord present everywhere, so he now ascribes to the same person, specifically, the constitution of the Doctors of the Church, which is likewise a fruit of the victorious ascension of Christ. He designates first their rank, then their office and work, and finally their end and scope. As regards rank, some are extraordinary, who are moved by an immediate Divine impulse, such as Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists; others are ordinary, such as Pastors and Doctors, to whom no peculiar assembly of the Church is entrusted, through whom Grotius rashly understands a more eminent rank and metropolitans. Theophylact, on the contrary, by the name of Pastors understands Presbyters and Bishops, and by Doctors, Deacons and whatever ministers of the Church. But they are more correctly called Pastors who rule the Church, and Doctors who rule the School. But we have already spoken of these at 1 Cor. 12:21. The office and work is the work of the ministry for the edifying of the saints. The Vulgate rendered καταρτισμὸν as consummation; Erasmus more correctly as restoration. But others most conveniently as joining together, as καταρτίζειν is to fit together neatly, to join together, Heb. 10:5, 1 Cor. 1:10, where it is opposed to dissensions; and therefore this work of the ministry is directed both to the saints, as they are viewed individually, so that they may be aptly perfected, and to the same in communion. For they think the metaphor is taken from a building, when stones and wood are not only adorned and

prepared: But are also aptly joined among themselves, so that they admit no fissure, which kind of conjunction he hints is especially necessary in the Church, since this exhortation is directed toward concord. Others more correctly note the metaphor of a body, which is in a right state when the members are not dissipated, not dislocated, but duly joined by their joints. The end, therefore, is οἰκοδομὴ, the edification of the mystical body of Christ, not so much that the saints may also be apt for teaching others—for the order of Doctors and hearers must be preserved in the Church—as that that work of the sacred ministry may be directed to the edification of the whole building of the Church, which is called the body of Christ, so that by this twofold reason unity may again be urged, namely, of both the building and the mystical body: which the following verses declare more abundantly.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων εἰς ἔργον διακονίας) Est & hic trajectio. Nam genuina constructio fuerat, εἰς ἔρ- γον διακονίας πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων, opus illis in- junctum est, & quidem, ut sanctis ministrent, eos perficien- do magis & magis & fide & cognitione rerum earum, quae ad Evangelium aliquo modo pertinent. Vide de hoc verbo 1. Cor. 1, 10. 2. Cor. 13, 11. Gal 6, 1.

Εἰς οἰκοδομὴν τῷ σώματος τῷ Χριστ) Ut ad eum mo- dum illi quoque sancti apti fiant aedificandae Ecclesiae, id est, docendis aliis.

Ut donorum concessionem quoad omnes fideles in genere Christo exaltato, & omnipotente Domino ubiq; praesenti tribuit Apostolus; ita eidem adscribit jam in specie Doctorum Ecclesiae constitutionem, quae fru- ctus itidem est ascensionis Christi victoriosae. Eo- rum autem primum gradus designat, deinde officium & opus, denique finem & scopum. Gradus quod attinet, alii sunt extraordinarii, qui immediato im- pulsu Divino acti, quales Apostoli, Prophetae, Evan- gelistae, alii ordinarii, ceu sunt Pastores & Doctores, quibus non est peculiaris coetus Ecclesiae creditus, per quos temere eminentiorem gradum & metropo- litas intelligit Grotius. Theophylactus contra nomi- ne Pastorum Presbyteros & Episcopos, Doctorum & Diaconos & quoscunque Ministros Ecclesiae in- telligit. Sed rectius Pastores dicuntur, qui Eccle- siam, Doctores, qui Scholam regunt. Sed de his jam diximus ad 1. Cor. 12, 21. Officium & opus est ἔργοντ διακονίας πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων. Καταρ- τισμὸν Vulgata reddidit consummationem: Erasmus rectius instaurationem. Sed commodissime alii co- agmentationem, uti καταρτίζειν est concinne coapta- re, coagmentare, Ebr. 10, 5. 1. Cor. 1, 10. ubi dissidiis id opponitur; ideoque tum ad sanctos, qua singuli spectantur, id opus ministerii directum est, ut illi apte perficiantur, tum ad eosdem in communione. Metaphoram enim sumptam ab aedificio censent, quum lapides & ligna non tantum adornantur &

præparantur: Sed etiam apte inter sese conjungun- tur, ut nullam fissuram admittant, quali conjuncti- one imprimis non opus esse in Ecclesia innuit, cum ad concordiam directa sit hæc parænesis. Alii re- ctius Metaphoram corporis notant, quod tum recte habet, cum membra non sint dissipata, non luxata, sed suis juncturis rite conjuncta. Finis itaque est οἰκοδομὴ ædificatio corporis mystici Christi, non tam, ut sancti etiam apti sint aliis docendis; ordo enim Doctorum & auditorum in Ecclesia conservandus; quàm ut illud ministerii sacri opus dirigatur ad to- tius ædificii Ecclesiæ ædificationem, quæ corpus Christi dicitur, ut gemina hac ratione unitas ite- rum suadeatur, puta tum ædificii tum corporis mystici: Quam sequentia uberius declarant.

## 4:13
V. 13. Until we all come into the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man) It is again a communion. For Paul, perfect above others, counts himself among the imperfect: And εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα is put for ἐν τῇ ἑνότητι; each person has need of other Teachers for so long as until he himself also has been consummated in faith and in the knowledge that is added to faith (concerning which see above ch. 1:17, Col. 1:10, 11, 12). A perfect man is called by Lucian and other Greeks one who has completed the growth of his powers, which Macrobius says in the sixth book of his Saturnalia happens in the fifth hebdomad of years. For the same, 'man' without addition is read in 1 Cor. 13:12; the name of that condition is here transferred from the body to the soul.

Unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ) To that measure of stature which is full of Christ, that is, of the knowledge concerning Christ. We saw that ἡλικίαν is stature in Matt. 6:27.

From the common end concerning the whole Church, the edification of the body of Christ, the Apostle proceeds to the special end, concerning each of the saints, that all may arrive and come into the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God unto a perfect man. The verb καταντάω does not denote only to meet, but also to arrive, Acts 16:1, etc., as also to escape, according to Arethas in his commentary on the Apocalypse. Grotius seems to understand this of the perfection of this life, but others refer it to the other life. However, our blessed Hunnius favors that explanation, along with blessed Luther in Sermon II on Matt. VIII, Vol. VI, Altenburg, fol. 467, and Osiander in his paraphrase, and indeed also Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and not least among the Latins, Jerome, Ambrosiaster, and Haymo. Add also Augustine, book XXII, De Civitate Dei, ch. 18. Estius praises Thomas and Sasbold here, and pursues that opinion at greater length in IV Sententiarum, dist. XLIV. Theophylact: It is to be desired, he says, by all who are not immune to grace, and labors are to be expended to build up one faith, until this unity of faith is reached, that is, until at length we are all convinced, and hold the same faith, and differ in nothing concerning the dogma of Christ, nor dissent from one another while we live. Thus, indeed, the conjunction of faith itself will be optimal; thus, I say, we are to know the Son of God, when we think rightly concerning dogmas and keep the bond of charity. Estius on this passage: The very words of the Apostle, he says, absolutely demand such an understanding. For to meet and to arrive into the unity of the faith is not of the future age, in which, faith ceasing, we shall see face to face, 1 Cor. 13, but of the present, in which we walk by faith and not by sight, 2 Cor. 5. But what others explain as 'into the unity of the faith,' that is, 'through unity,' is forced and contrary to the usage of the Greek preposition. But what follows in v. 14 squares very well with this understanding. Most Latins, however, take it concerning the future age, such as Calvin and Aretius, who explain it concerning the full consensus of the whole Church after the final judgment. Crocius embraces both senses: Here, he says, the unity of faith and knowledge begins, by which we are separated from the world and joined into one body, but it is finally consummated in heaven, because the flesh, while we are here, is always entangled with the remnants of ignorance and incredulity.

Although indeed all-encompassing perfection follows finally in the state of those whom they call the comprehenders, yet here it is a matter of the joining together of the saints in this life, and of the increases of knowledge, so that we may not be children, but may grow up into CHRIST in all things to manly perfection, according to the measure of the stature of the adult CHRIST: which things pertain to the state of wayfarers. For that distinction does not appear here between the childish, adolescent, and manly age, as if the first two states were of this life, but the last were of the other life. But they are all referred to the present age, in which concord and unity are urged to be kept; and therefore the perfection of which the Apostle speaks in 1 Corinthians 13:9, which will succeed when that which is in part shall cease, is altogether different from the perfection of which he speaks in the present. For there we are always left as children in this world, so that we may finally emerge as men according to the likeness employed in that same place, but here we are forbidden to be children, we are commanded to grow up, and to emerge into a perfect man. There, perfection of not only parts, but also of degrees is understood: Here, not of degrees, but of parts. For who, whether in this life or in the other, attains that perfection of degrees which was Christ's ἐν τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τῦ πληρώματος? Therefore the blessed Osiander explains it as: that we may approach as closely as possible to perfection: Just as CHRIST was in the perfect manly age, when He undertook to conquer death for us. (He, however, who exhorts to perfection does not thereby teach that a man can arrive at solid perfection in this life, so that nothing is lacking to him, nor can he progress any further. Let us, however, strive toward perfection, as much as can possibly be done in this life.) But how Paul wishes this figurative discourse about the age of CHRIST to be understood, he now explains more clearly, saying: That we may no longer be little children, etc.

Vain, therefore, are the disputes here and altogether foreign, both those of certain people in Augustine, Book XXII of The City of God, chapter 27, concerning the resurrection of bodies; whether all are to rise again in the male sex, which error is imputed to Origen by Jerome in Epistle LXI to Pammachius, and which has a patron even to this day, that all women, except the Blessed Virgin Mary, will rise again in the male sex: and also those of the Scholastics, who with Anselm and Thomas conclude in this passage that all will also rise again in the youthful age and manly stature. For there is nothing here about the resurrection of bodies: And that locution is metaphorical, that the knowledge of men is perfect, that of children is imperfect; the discourse is not about bodily, but spiritual perfection.

Furthermore, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ is not to be understood with Beza in this way, that CHRIST is said here to grow up not in Himself, but in us, for our increase in CHRIST, and His in us, nor yet is it to be explained by that full stature of the body of CHRIST. For although He Himself in His natural body had received various increases according to the degree of age, yet that is not noted here, nor is the exemplar of our perfection placed in the quantity of the body of manly age: But in the measure of knowledge, which Christ had, as to the habitual knowledge in age, as the Vulgate, or stature, as Beza translates, of the fullness, that is, complete: because as He grew in age and stature, so also He grew in habitual wisdom, Luke 2:52. That which Grotius has is forced, to that mode of stature which is full of CHRIST, that is, of knowledge about Christ. For neither is CHRIST the same as knowledge about Christ, nor is spiritual stature understood, but the knowledge or wisdom of Christ in the full stature and manly age, into the measure (understand, of the knowledge which was) of the stature of the fullness (that is, into the full stature) of Christ. What Grotius has concerning the knowledge approaching to faith, we do not admit, unless it is understood rightly. For faith itself consists in the knowledge and full knowledge of the Son of God, to which, however, there is no doubt that a richer full knowledge can be added. For faith is common to all the faithful. But in some of these, for example in the Doctors, a richer knowledge is added. Here, therefore, faith and full knowledge of the Son of God are spoken of exegetically.

Latin:

V. 13. Μέχρι καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα ΍ πίστεως καὶ ΍ ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ ὑιῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ, εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον) Est rursum κοινωνία. Nam Paulus supra alios perfectus se im- perfectis accenset: Et εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα positum est pro ἐν τῇ ἑνότητι, tamdiu aliis Magistris quisque opus habet, donec ipse quoque in fide & accedente ad fidem cognitione (de qua supra c. 1, 17. Col. 1, 10. 11. 12.) consummatus fuerit. Ἀνὴρ τέλειος dicitur Luciano & Græcis aliis is, qui virium complevit augmentum, quod quinta fieri annorum hebdo- mada ait Macrobius Saturnalium l. 6. Pro eodem ἀνὴρ sine adjectione legitur 1. Cor. 13, 12. ejus habitudinis no- men hic à corpore ad animum transfertur.

Εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ) Ad eum staturæ modum, qui est plenus Christi, id est, cognitionis de Christo. Ἡλικίαν esse staturam vidimus Matth. 6, 27.

A communi fine totam Ecclesiam concernente ædificatione corporis Christi ad specialem pergit Apostol9, sanctorum quemq; attinentem, ut omnes perveniant & concedant in unitatem fidei & cogni- tionis Filii Dei in virum perfectum. Verbum καταντάω non notat tantum occurrere, sed etiam pervenire, Act. 16, 1. &c. ut etiam evadere apud A- retham in Asc. Grotius videtur de hujus vitæ per- fectione intelligere, sed alii ad alteram vitam refe- runt. Illi tamen explicationi favet B. Hunnius noster cum B. Luthero Serm. II. in Matth. VIII. Tom. VI. Altenburg. fol. 467. & Osiandro in pa- raphr. imò & Chrysostomo, Oecumenio, nec non in- ter Latinos Hieronymo, Ambrosiastro, Haymone. Adde & Augustinum lib. XXII. de C. D. cap. 18. Estius laudat hic Thomam, Sasboldum, eamque sententiam prolixius exequitur in IV. sentent. dist. XLIV. Theophylactus: Tamdiu, inquit, optan- dum est omnibus, qui gratiæ sunt non immunes, & in- sumendi ad ædificandum fidem unam labores, quo- usque ad fidei unitatem hanc pertingatur, hoc est, quoad tandem arguamur omnes, & eandem tenere fi- dem, & nihil de Christi dogmate discrepare, nec ad in- vicem dissidere, dum vivimus. Sic sanc optima futura est fidei ipsius conjunctio, sic inquam sumus, & Dei Fi- lium cognituri, cum de dogmatibus recte sentimus, nexumque charitatis servamus. Estius in h. l. Ipsa Apostoli verba, ait, prorfus exigunt hujusmodi intel- lectum. Nam occurrere & pervenire in unitatem fi- dei, non est futuri seculi, in quo fide cessante videbi- mus facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. 13. sed præsentis, in quo per fidem ambulamus, & non per speciem, 2. Cor. 5. Quod autem alii exponunt in unitatem fidei, id est, per unitatem, coactum est, & præter usum Græcæ Præpositionis. Optime vero quadrat huic intellectui, quod sequitur v. 14. Plerique tamen Latini de fu- turo seculo accipiunt, ut Calvinus & Aretius, qui explicant de pleno consensu totius Ecclesiæ post judicium novissimum. Crocius utrumque sen- sum complectitur: Hic, inquit, incipit unitas fidei & agnitionis, qua à mundo separamur, & in unum corpus conjungimur, at in cælo demum consum- matur, quia caro, dum hic sumus, ignoran- tia & incredulitatis reliquiis, semper est implicita.

Quanquam vero omnimoda perfectio sequatur demum in statu comprehensorum, quos vocant, hic tamen de coagmentatione sanctorum in hac vita, & de incrementis cognitionis, ut ne simus pueri, sed adolescamus in CHRISTUM per omnia ad virilem perfectionem, secundum mensuram staturæ adulti CHRISTI agitur: quæ ad statum viatorum pertinent. Nec enim ista distinctio hic apparet inter puerilem, adolescentem & virilem ætatem, quasi priores duo status hujus, ultimus vero alterius vitæ sit. Sed referuntur omnes ad præsens seculum, in quo concordia & unitas servanda suadetur; ideoque alia omnino est perfectio, de qua 1. Corinth. 13, 9. Apostolus, quæ succedet, cum id, quod ex parte est, cessabit, alia perfectio, de qua in præsenti. Nam illic semper pueri relinquimur in hoc mundo, ut viri demum evadamus secundum similitudinem ibidem adhibitam, hic vero prohibemur esse pueri, jubemur adolescere, & evadere in virum perfectum. Illic perfectio non tantum partium, sed & graduum intelligitur: Hic non graduum, sed partium. Ecquis enim sive in hac, sive in altera vita eam graduum perfectionem assequitur, quæ Christi fuit ἐν τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τῦ πληρώματος? Ideo B. Osiander exponit, ut quam proxime accedamus ad perfectionem: Sicut CHRISTUS fuit in perfecta virili ætate, cum pro nobis mortem vincendam susciperet. (Qui autem ad perfectionem hortatur, non propterea docet, hominem ad solidam perfectionem in hac vita pervenire posse, ita ut nihil illi desit, nec amplius proficere queat. Contendamus autem ad perfectionem, quantum omnino in hac vita fieri potest.) Hunc autem figuratum sermonem de ætate CHRISTI, quomodo Paulus intelligi velit, jam dilucidius explicat, dicens: Ut jam non simus parvuli, &c.

Vanæ ergo hic sunt & prorsus alienæ disputationes, tum quorundam apud Augustinum libr. XXII. de Civitate Dei cap. 27. de corporum resurrectione; anne omnes in virili sexu resurrecturi sint, qui error Origeni imputatur ab Hieronymo Epist. LXI. ad Pammach. Scotumque hactenus Patronum habet, quod omnes fœminæ, excepta B. Maria virgine, sexu virili resurrecturæ sint: tum Scholasticorum, qui cum Anshelmo & Thoma hoc loco colligunt, omnes etiam juvenili ætate & virili statura resurrecturos. Nihil enim hic de corporum resurrectione: Et Metaphorica illa locutio est, quod virorum cognitio perfecta sit, puerorum imperfecta, non de corporali, sed spirituali perfectione sermo est.

Porro mensura staturæ τῦ πληρώματος τῦ Χρισῦ non intelligenda cum Beza hoc modo, quod CHRISTUS dicatur hic non in sese, sed in nobis adolescere, pro nostri in CHRISTO, & ipsius in nobis incremento, nec tamen illa cum statura plena corporis CHRISTI explicanda. Nam quamvis ipse in corpore suo naturali diversa ceperat incrementa pro ætatis gradu, non tamen id notatur hic, aut exemplar nostræ perfectionis in quantitate corporis ætate virili locatur: Sed in mensura cognitionis, quam Christus habuit, quantum ad notitiam ἑκτικὴν in ætate, ut Vulgata, vel statura, ut Beza vertit, τῦ πληρώματος, hoc est, completa: quia ut ætate & statura, ita & sapientia crevit habituali, Luc. 2, 52. Coactum est, quod habet Grotius, ad eum staturæ modum, qui plenus est CHRISTI, id est, cognitionis de Christo. Nam nec CHRISTUS idem est, quod cognitio de Christo, nec spiritualis statura intelligitur, sed cognitio vel sapientia Christi in statura plena & virilis ætatis, in mensuram (subintellige, cognitionis quæ fuit) staturæ ple- nitudinis (id est, in statura plena) Christi. Quod de accedente ad fidem cognitione Grotius habet, non admittimus, nisi dextre intellectum. Nam fides ipsa in γνώσει & ἐπιγνώσει Filii DEI consi- stit, cui tamen accedere uberiorem ἐπίγνωσιν pos- se, nullum est dubium. Nam fides communis est omnium fidelium. At in nonnullis horum, v. g. Doctoribus uberior cognitio accedit. Hic ergo πίστις καὶ ἐπίγνωσις τῆ ὑι̃ τ̃ Θε̃ dicta ἐξηγη- τικῶς.

## 4:14
Verse 14.

That we may no longer be little children.) He shows more fully what that manly habit is, by comparison with others who have not yet arrived that far. Little children are those who still ought to be instructed or strengthened, Rom. 2:20, 1 Cor. 3:1, chapter 13:11, Heb. 5:13.

Tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine)

He shows not only what could happen, but also what had happened to many at Ephesus. For they had been shaken by the doctrines partly of the philosophers, partly of the Jews, and had been tossed hither and thither, as if by storms. For this is the surge in Proverbs 23:34, Jonah 1:4, 11, 12, Luke 8:24, James 1:6, whence to be tossed by waves. It seems, however, to allude to the passage of Isaiah 57:13, where in the Greek: For a wind shall take all these, and a storm shall carry them away. Seneca at the end of his book On the Happy Life: A certain whirlwind rotates and entangles your minds, fleeing and seeking the same things, and now it snatches them lifted on high, now dashed into the lowest depths.

In the sleight of men

He alleviates their fault by gravely accusing the seducers themselves. Κυβεία is a Greek word, but it is also frequent among the Talmudists and Rabbis as קוביא. And because in the game of dice simpler people are accustomed to being cheated, therefore this word is accustomed to being transferred to any kind of circumvention. For:

The better a gambler is at his art, the more wicked he is.

& thus it appears that he accepted the Syrian here.

In craftiness)

He explains more clearly what he had said, and in both places ἐν signifies by.

Unto the wiles of error

In the manuscript: τὰς μεθοδείας τῆς πλάνης τοῦ Διαβόλου, namely so that we may understand that those men act craftily, and that from the art of seducing, which they have from the Devil. The Pythagoreans seem to be indicated most of all, most of whom were magicians. But we see that magical arts were much practiced at Ephesus, Acts 19:19. μεθοδεία is the same as μέθοδος, a way and method of acting; compare what is below at 6:11, where Ambrose translates it not badly as 'reasons'. Μεθοδεύειν is רגל, to act with craft, 2 Sam. 19:27.

The metaphor is threefold: the first is from children, who are unrefined, changeable, fickle, and easily believe, and therefore are easily deceived; the second is from sailors, who are destitute of a helmsman and are tossed here and there, wherever the wind drives them, so that they cannot keep a straight course but wander on an uncertain path and, driven onto sandbanks, suffer shipwreck; the third is from the erratic and slippery game of dice, in which various frauds are also committed. Therefore, some here wish to refer to the slipperiness of the game, the uncertain outcome, and the dangerous state, with Beza and Drusius; others to the craft, the deceitful artifice, and the artificial fallacy, which Crocius notes pleases both the ancients and the moderns. Whence πανυργία, that is, crafty versatility, by which someone with all their effort leans into the task of circumventing others in any way possible.

For the sake of explanation, the 'method of deceit' seems to have been added; it is itself as it were a method and art of leading others away from the right path and circumventing them, by which especially the arts of the Pseudo-Apostles and other heretics are noted, from whom greater danger was to be feared than from the Pythagoreans. Jerome in this place has it thus: We shall attain the term of a perfect man, yet so that the whole crowd of those present may arrive at the completed age of the fullness of Christ, and by no means wavering in dogmas, like little children, be carried uncertainly in the whirlpool of infidelity, while winds blowing from here and there—namely, of heretics or of the wise of the world—diverse and conflicting reasons, either bring or threaten shipwreck to the hearers, while some, without the will of deceit, nevertheless preach things that are false: Others, however, composing the snares of error with all cunning, hasten to deceive and conquer us.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἵνα μηκέτι ὦμεν νήπιοι.) Plenius ostendit, qualis sit illa virilis habitudo, comparatione aliorum, qui nondum eo usque pervenere. Νήπιοι נערים sunt, qui adhuc institui aut roborari debent, Rom. 2, 20. 1. Cor. 3, 1. cap. 13, 11. Ebr. 5, 13.

Κλυδωνιζόμενοι καὶ περιφερόμενοι παντὶ ἀνέμῳ τῆς διδα- σκαλίας)

Ostendit non tantum, quod evenire poterat, sed & quod multis Ephesi evenerat. Doctrinis enim partim Philoso- phorum, partim Judæorum concussi, & huc illuc jactati fuerant, tanquam procellis. Hoc enim κλύδων Proverb. XXIII. 34. Jon. I. 4. 11. 12. Luc. VIII. 24. Jacob. I. 6. un- de κλυδωνίζεσθαι. Videtur autem alludi ad locum Esaiæ LVII. 13. ubi in Græco : Τούτους γὰρ πάντας ἄνεμος λή- ψεται, καὶ ἀποίσει καταιγίς. Seneca fine libri de vita bea- ta: Turbo quidam animos vestros rotat & involvit, fugien- tes petentesque eadem, & nunc in sublime allevatos, nunc in infima allisos rapit.

Ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων)

Illorum culpam sublevat, graviter accusando ipsos seductores. Κυβεία Græca vox est, sed Thalmudicis quoque & Rabbinis frequens קוביא. Et quia in aleæ ludo solent simpliciores circumveniri, ideo ad quamvis circumventionem hæc vox transferri so- let. Nam:

Aleator quanto in arte est melior, tanto est ne- quior.

& ita apparet hic Syrum accepisse.

Ἐν πανυργίᾳ)

Planius explicat, quod dixerat, & utroque loco ἐν valet per.

Πρὸς τὴν μεθοδείαν τ̃ πλάνης)

In Manuscripto: τὰς μεθοδείας τῆς πλάνης τοῦ Διαβόλου, nempe ut intelligamus versute agere illos homines, id- que ex arte seducendi, quam habent à Diabolo. Vi- dentur Pythagorei maxime indicari, quorum plerique magi. Magicas autem artes multum exercitatas fuisse Ephesi, videmus Actor. XIX. 19. μεθοδεία idem, quod μέθοδος via ac ratio agendi, confer, quod infra VI. 11. ubi rationes vertit Ambrosius non male. Μεθοδεύειν רגל astu agere, 2. Sam. XIX. 27.

Triplex est Metaphora, prima à pueris, qui rudes, mutabiles, leves & facile credunt, adeo- que facile decipiuntur; altera à navigantibus, qui rectore destituuntur, hinc inde jactantur, quocunque ventus impulerit, ut rectum cursum tenere nequeant, sed incerta via oberrent, & in Syrtes depulsi faeiant naufragium. Tertia à ludo taxillorum erratico atque lubrico, in quo etiam fraudes variæ committuntur, ideo alii hic ludi lubricitatem incertum eventum & pe- riculosum statum cum Beza & Drusio respici vo- lunt, alii astum, fallax artificium, & artificiosam fallaciam, quod veteribus & recentibus placere notat Crocius. Unde πανυργία, id est, vete- ratoria versutia, qua quis toto nisu in id incum- bit, ut quovis modo alios circumveniat.

Ἐξηγήσεως causa videtur addita μεθοδεία τῆς πλά- νης, est ipsa velut methodus & ars alios extra re- ctam viam abducendi & circumveniendi, qua im- primis Pseudo-Apostolorum & hæreticorum alio- rum artes notantur, à quibus majus periculum metuendum erat, quam à Pythagoreis. Hiero- nymus in h. l. ita habet: Vocabulum perfecti viri sortiemur, ita tamen, ut ad consummatam ætatem plenitudinis Christi omnis præsentium turba perve- niat, & nequaquam in dogmatibus fluctuans, ad in- star parvulorum gurgite infidelitatis feratur incer- to, dum venti hinc inde perflantes, hæreticorum vi- delicet, sive sapientium sæculi, diversa compugnan- tesque rationes naufragium audientibus aut inferunt aut minantur, dum alii absque voluntate fallaciæ, ea tamen, quæ falsa sunt, prædicant: Alii vero omni calliditate erroris laqueos componentes nos decipere & vincere festinant.

## 4:15
Ver. 15.

But speaking the truth in love) Just as 'truth' signifies sincerity, Matt. 22:16, Tob. 8:9. So 'to speak the truth in love' is to love others sincerely.

Let us grow up into him in all things) Again 'into him' for 'in him', in himself, that is, let us progress in the knowledge of him through all things, 'the all things' as 'all things', 1 Cor. 9:31, through all things in all things worthy of being known. Thus in that to the Colossians ch. 1:10 it is said 'increasing in the knowledge of God', which is the same as that which follows in ch. 11:19, 'increases with the increase of God'.

Who is the head, Christ) The native construction would have been, 'into him Christ, who is the head'.

According to others, the pursuit of both truth and love is more rightly inculcated; so that, namely, they may be zealous for truth and charity, according to that of Zech. 8:16, 'Only love truth and peace.' For 'to speak the truth' in Gal. 4:16 is to speak the truth. Whence Bullinger, Calvin, Beza, Gualther, Hemming, teach that the pursuit of both truth or Evangelical doctrine, and of charity, is to be enjoined: Or as pleases others, that the word 'in love' should cohere with the word 'let us grow', so that following the truth in charity we may grow up. The former sense, however, is more suitable because of the comma interposed. It is an antithesis, says B. Hunnius, by which he opposes the pursuit of truth to the seduction of the Pseudo-Doctors. And he wishes this to be commended to the Ephesians, that having omitted those impostors they should follow the simple truth of the doctrine preached by the Apostles, and devote effort that in the acknowledgment of the truth, and also in charity, which is the other part of Christianity, they may grow up into Christ through all things, or in all things which are required in a Christian man. B. Balduinus: The scope, he says, of our instruction ought to be truth, especially the truth of doctrine: This he commands us to do or follow in charity, or with the pursuit of charity toward God and neighbor: Thus we shall happily grow as members under one head, Christ, who is the truth itself, and who leads those following him by his Holy Spirit into all truth; From this pursuit, full perfection will finally follow, the perfect conjunction of the members of the Church. 'Into him' seems to be retained in the more received sense, INTO HIMSELF, so that it is the same as v. 13, 'into a perfect man, into the measure', etc. so that progressing by such increases we may finally look to our head, whose members we are, that is, Christ, as Estius has it. 'The all things' he rightly explains as 'through all things', which Estius draws to the members, as if this word were to be understood. But the Greeks more rightly explain it as 'through all our things', namely, doctrine and life.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ) Sicut ἀλήθεια sincerita- tem significat, Matth. 22, 16. Tob. 8, 9. Ita ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ est sincere alios diligere.

Αὐξήσωμεν εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα) Rursum εἰς αὐτὸν pro ἐν αὐτῷ, in ipso, id est, ipsius cognitione proficiamus per omnia, τὰ πάντα ut πάντα, 1. Corinth. 9, 31. per omnia in omnibus scitu dignis. Sic in illa ad Colossenses c. 1, 10. dicitur αὐξανόμενοι εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod idem est cum illo, quod sequitur cap. 11, 19. αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ Θεοῦ.

Ὅς ἐστιν ἡ κεφαλὴ ὁ Χριστός) Nativa constructio fuerat, εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν Χριστὸν, ὅς ἐστιν ἡ κεφαλή.

Secundum alios rectius & veritatis & dilectionis studium inculcatur; ut nempe veritati studeant & charitati, juxta illud Zach. 8, 16. Tantum veritatem & pacem diligite. Nam ἀληθεύειν Gal. 4,16. est ve- rum dicere. Unde Bullingerus, Calvinus, Beza, Gualtherus, Hemmingius, & veritatis seu doctrinæ Evangelicæ, & charitatis studium præcipi docent: Vel quod aliis placet, ut vox ἐν ἀγάπῃ cohæreat cum voce αὐξήσωμεν, ut veritatem sectantes in charitate adolescamus. Prior tamen sensus magis convenit ob comma interpositum. Antithesis est, inquit B. Hunnius, qua studium veritatis Pseudo- Doctorum seductioni opponit. Idque commendatum vult Ephesiis, ut omissis impostoribus illis simplicem sectentur veritatem doctrinæ per Apostolos prædica- tæ, & operam dent, ut in agnitione veritatis, nec non in charitate, quæ est altera Christianismi pars, ado- lescant in Christum per omnia, sive in omnibus, quæ in homine Christiano requiruntur. B. Balduinus: Scopus, inquit, nostræ institutionis debet esse veritas, præsertim veritas doctrinæ: Hanc nos facere seu se- ctari jubet in charitate, seu cum studio charitatis er- ga Deum & proximum: Ita feliciter crescemus, ut membra sub uno capite Christo, qui ipsa veritas est, quique sequentes ipsum Spiritu suo Sancto ducit in omnem veritatem; Ex hoc studio plena tandem se- quetur perfectio, perfecta conjunctio membrorum Ecclesiæ. Εἰς αὐτὸν sensu receptiori retinendum vi- detur, IN IPSUM, ut idem sit, quod v. 13. εἰς ἄν- δρα τέλειον εἰς μέτρον &c. ut hujusmodi incremen- tis proficientes tandem respiciamus capiti nostro, cujus membra sumus, id est, Christo, ut habet E- stius. Τὰ πάντα recte exponit διὰ πάντα, quod ad membra trahit Estius, quasi hæc vox subaudienda sit. Sed rectius Græci exponunt, per omnia no- stra, doctrinam scilicet & vitam.

## 4:16
Ver. 16.

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of every single part, makes the increase of the body) Better in the Manuscript: 'Of every single member', the body is the Church: Its members are individuals, Rom. 12:4, 5, 1 Cor. 12:12, 14, 18, 19, 20.

22, 25, 26, and another Hebraism, that in the second place he said 'the body' for 'itself', that is, he repeats the noun where another would have placed a reciprocal pronoun. Christ in the Church has the role not only of the head, but also of the heart, whence both blood and Spirit are carried through many interconnected channels to the outermost parts, and provides increase to individuals, while they have need of increase. 'I fitly join' in the glosses. It is said also of a building, as above ch. 2:12, and of a body, as here. It is the same as 'to fit together'. Xenophon: 'I have fitted the body to you.' 'I compact' in the Glossary seems to signify a certain tighter coagulation than the preceding word. See the twin passage to this in Col. 2:2 and 19. 'Joint' in the plural 'joints' in that place to the Colossians, where the word 'bands' is also added, are the joints of the body, because through contact they cohere mutually to themselves and with other members, like veins and arteries. But those 'joints of supply' are called so, the genitive signifying the use of the thing, because they supply Spirit and sap to the body: Just as in that place to the Colossians the body is said through those joints 'to be supplied', that is, to receive what is necessary for itself. And this 'supply', that is, sub-administration or nourishment, is done through the operation into each single member, and that 'in measure', that is, according to the mode in which each member needs nourishment, both for sustenance and for its own increase. As of a building, so of the body, all those ranks of those set over, of which above ch. 1:21 and this chapter 11, correspond to the joints in the Church.

Εἰς οἰκοδομὴν ἑαυτῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ) He mixes a comparative rendering; these things, he says, pertain to this, that that body, that is, the Church, may be built up through mutual love, that is, through the duties of love, that is, may be more and more instructed. Moreover, it is a work of great love to teach others.

Because not only Grotius's Manuscript, but other approved Codices and Greek Interpreters also, along with the Vulgate and the Codices of Beza and Stephanus, have μέλος in Curcellaeus: B. Luther and Piscator do not interpret it badly thus, although the matter comes to the same thing if, with Augustine (book XXII de Civit. Dei, ch. 18), Erasmus, and most Greek Codices, you render it 'part,' because a part in a body is a member of the body. However, the designation 'member' is more customary when the discourse is about the human body, or a metaphor is drawn from it. See below, ch. 5, 25, 30. But the application of the simile is more suitable when Christ is compared not to the heart, but to the head, as the Apostle expressly called him. For just as the Spirit, descending through the nerves from the brain itself, imparts sense to all members in proportion to each, so Christ supplies his gifts to our souls, which are his members. And not fortuitously and rashly, but according to the measure of each member, that is, as each is able to receive, and in this manner he makes the whole body to be built up for itself and to coalesce. For otherwise the soul would be unable to receive what is supplied by the Spirit descending from above, from whom we have received both life and growth, unless we were compacted and joined together by charity like a body. For as a hand torn from the rest of the body is by no means any longer receiving the life-giving Spirit, as one that is severed from the connection of the members, so indeed we too, unless we preserve unity and the conjunction of souls, are by no means ever going to admit the grace of the Spirit which has flowed forth from Christ (who is our head). Therefore he also said the body is compacted and connected, that is, with the members not rashly disposed, but coupled, or each one clinging in its own place, not scattered or lying without form, as Theophylact interprets with Chrysostom. To these corresponds the word ἐπιχορηγίας, whether you take it passively with Theophylact, Beza, and Camerarius, that the Spirit directed and supplied from the head reaches all things, or actively with Luther and most of the Reformed, so that they are called ἀφαὶ ἐπιχορηγίας, because through them one member [supplies] the vital Spirit which is diffused from the head into the members, and communicates all gifts received. For the living members of the Church, just as they receive nourishment and growth from Christ the head, so also they supply it to other members. For in this sense the word ἐπιχορηγίας is taken in Phil. 1, 19. For God supplies the Spirit, Gal. 3, 5. as Crocius here.

PART II. Exhortation to holiness.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἐξ ὗ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα συναρμολογούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον διὰ πάσης ἁφῆς τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας, κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους, τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ σώματος ποιεῖται) Melius Manuscriptus: Ἑκάστου μέλους, corpus Ecclesia: Ejus membra singuli, Rom. 12, 4. 5. 1. Cor. 12, 12. 14. 18. 19. 20.

22. 25. 26. & alius Ebraïsmus, quod secundo loco τὸ σῶ- ματὸς dixit pro ἑαυτῦ, id est, nomen repetit, ubi alius posuisset nomen reciprocans. Christus in Ecclesia non capitis tantum, sed & cordis habet rationem, unde & sanguis & Spiritus per multos inter se cohærentes meatus ad extimas partes fertur, incrementumque præstat sin- gulis, dum incremento habent opus. Συναρμολογῶ com- pagino in glossis. Dicitur & de ædificio, ut supra cap. 2, 12. & de corpore, ut hic. Idem est, quod συναρμόζειν. Xenophon : Τὸ σῶμα συνήρμοσάγ σοι. Συμβιβάζω cogo in Glossario videtur arctius quoddam coagulum signifi- care, quam vox præcedens. Vide geminum huic locum Coloss. 2. v. 2. & 19. Ἁφὴ in plurali ἁφαὶ in illo ad Co- lossenses loco, ubi & συνδέσμων vox additur, sunt jun- cturæ corporis, quia per contactum mutuo sibi & cum aliis membris cohærent, ut venæ & arteriæ. Vocantur autem illæ ἀφαὶ τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας, Genitivo significante usum rei, quia Spiritum & succum corpori suppeditant : Sicut in illo loco ad Colossenses dicitur corpus per illas juncturas ἐπιχορηγῆσθαι, id est, accipere, quæ sibi sunt necessaria. Fit autem ista ἐπιχορηγία, id est, submini- stratio sive alitura, per operationem in membrum u- numquodque, idque ἐν μέτρῳ, id est, pro modo, quo quodque membrum alimenti indiget, tum ad sustenta- tionem, tum ad incrementum sui. Sicut ædificii, ita corporis juncturis respondent in Ecclesia omnes illi præ- positorum gradus, de quibus supra cap. 1, 21. & hoc ca- pite 11.

Εἰς οἰκοδομὴν ἑαυτῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ) Miscet comparati- ve ἀπόδοσιν; hæc, inquit, eo pertinent, ut corpus il- lud, id est, Ecclesia, per dilectionem mutuam, id est, per dilectionis officia ædificetur, id est, magis magisque in- struatur. Magnæ autem dilectionis opus est docere alios.

Quia non tantum Grotii Manuscriptum, sed alii etiam probati Codd. & Græci Interpp. cum Vulga- ta & Codicibus Bezæ, & Stephani, Curcellæi μέλος habent: B. Lutherus & Piscator non male ita inter- pretantur, quamvis eodem res redeat, si cum Au- gustino lib. XXII. de Civit. Dei cap. 18. Erasmo, & plerisque Codd. Græcis partem reddas, quia pars in corpore est membrum corporis. Usitatior au- tem est membri appellatio, cum de corpore huma- no sermo est, aut metaphora inde petitur. Vid. infra 25. cap. 5, 30. Convenientior autem est si- militudinis applicatio, cum Christus non cordi, sed capiti, ut eundem diserte Apostolus appella- vit, confertur. Quemadmodum enim Spiritus per nervos à cerebro ipso descendens sensum omnibus membris ad proportionem cuique impertitur, sic Christus nostris animis, qui illius sunt membra, sua dona suppeditat. Nec fortuito & temere, sed pro mensura membri cujusque, hoc est, ut quodque capere potest, & hunc in modum coædificari sibi u- niversum corpus & coalescere facit. Alias enim nequiret anima à superne Spiritu descendente, à quo & vitam accepimus & incrementum, sub- ministrata excipere, nisi charitate corporis instar unius compacti essemus & juncti. Nam ut ma- nus à reliquo corpore avulsa, haud quaquam ul- tra est vegetantem Spiritum receptum, ut quæ à membrorum sit nexu discissa, sic sane & nos, nisi unitatem servemus, & animorum conjunctionem, haud quaquam aliquando sumus Spiritus gratiam admissuri, qui à Christo, (qui caput est nostrum) profluxit. Idcirco & corpus compactum & con- nexum dixit, hoc est, nihil temere dispositis mem- bris, sed copulatis, vel singulis suo loco hærentibus, non disjectis vel sine forma jacentibus, ut cum Chrysostomo interpretatur Theophylactus. His convenit vox ἐπιχορηγίας, sive cum Theophyla- cto, Beza, & Camerario passive accipias, quod Spiritus à capite directus & suppeditatus omnia contingat, sive cum Luthero & Reformatis ple- risque active, ut ἀφαὶ ἐπιχορηγίας dicuntur, quia per eas unum membrum alteri vitalem Spiritum, qui à capite in membra diffunditur, & omnia dona accepta communicat. Membra enim Ecclesiæ vi- va, sicut à capite Christo accipiunt alimentum & incrementum, ita & aliis membris suppeditant. Hoc sensu enim vox ἐπιχορηγίας accipitur Phil. 1, 19. Deus enim Spiritum suppeditat, Gal. 3, 5. ut hic Crocius.

PARS II. Adhortatio ad sanctitatem.

## 4:17
V. 17. This therefore I say) He returns to that which he had begun to say at the beginning of this chapter.

And I testify in the Lord) that is, I adjure you through Christ, I declare it openly as if witnesses were brought forward העירתי see Acts 20, 26. Gal. 5, 3.

That you no longer walk, as also the rest of the Gentiles walk) That you do not lead that life which they lead from among the Gentiles, who have not been converted to Christ.

In the vanity of their mind) He touches especially upon the philosophers, as also in Rom. 1, 2. where the word ἐματαιώθησαν. See what is said there. The Hebrews call such men אבירי לב, Is. 46, v. 12.

Latin:

V. 17. Τῦτο ὖν λέγω) Redit ad id, quod cœperat dice- re capitis hujus initio.

Καὶ μαρτύρομαι ἐν Κυρίῳ) id est, per Christum vos ob- testor, palam quasi testibus adhibitis denuntio העירתי vide Act. 20, 26. Gal. 5, 3.

Μηκέτι ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν, καθὼς κὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη περιπατεῖ) Ne eam vitam ducatis, quam illi ducunt ex gentibus, qui ad Christum conversi non sunt.

Ἐν ματαιότητι τῦ νοὸς αὐτῶν) Philosophos maxime tan- git, ut & Rom. 1, 2. ubi verbum ἐματαιώθησαν. Vide ibi dicta. Ebræi tales homines vocant אבירי לב, Es. 46, v. 12.

## 4:18
V. 18. Darkened in their understanding) Corrupt appetites also cloud the mind, Rom. 1, 21.

Being alienated from the life of God) Far removed from that life which is according to God. See Gal. 2, 19. We had the word ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι also above in c. 2, 12.

Because of the ignorance that is in them) He explains that which he had just said about darkness.

Because of the hardening of their heart) We said at Mark 6, 52 that all ingrained vices are designated by the word πωρώσεως. Thus also in Latin they are said to have developed a callus, who do not perceive good warnings.

He does not so much return to that which he had said at the beginning of the chapter, as he pursues that very thing. He had exhorted them to a life worthy of Christians. To which the pursuit of both concord and holiness pertains. However, the state of this kind was not only that of the philosophers or the Gentiles of that time. It is the state of all who are not converted. Who, as regards the mind, are filled with vanity and the darkness of errors, being as they are alienated from the life which is from God, in God, and according to God, because of their native ignorance (to which an affected ignorance had been added in the Gentiles, Rom. 1, 20. seqq.), and as regards the will, they labor under hardening and vices, whether habitual by nature or by custom, and for that reason also they are alienated from the life of God. For where there is nothing in the intellect but ignorance, where there is hardening in the heart and will, how can the life of God be in them? They are said to walk in the vanity of their mind, because conversation, pursuits, and acts are instituted according to the idea of the mind or intellect, when the mind is occupied with vain opinions or persuasions, how will the pursuits and practices of life be of a better sort? But it is not only the vanity of the mind in simple apprehension, or composition and division, or, as they speak, in the first and second operation of the mind; but also the darkness of the understanding, darkness in the reasoning or the third operation of the mind is designated, because the whole intellect is corrupt and filled with vanity and darkness outside the grace of conversion. The corruption of the mind is followed by the depravity of the will, in which hardening is designated on account of habitual corruption, which the Vulgate indeed rendered as blindness. But it is more correctly translated here by Ambrose and others as hardness, or obduration, although examples of both meanings are not lacking. Since the heart or will is joined here with mind and reason; for to the latter properly belong darkness, obscuration, and blindness, but to the former hardness and obduration. But as we have by nature a hard and stony heart before conversion: so πώρωσις (callousness) is increased by the habit of sinning, when we walk and order our life according to the vanity of the mind and the darkness τῆς διανοίας (of the understanding), just as the Gentiles harden themselves more and more in their mind. For Crocius acknowledges that πώρωσιν (callousness) is to be taken here not passively, but actively. Wherefore, that the Apostle may recall or deter the Ephesians from the old habit of life to the newness of life, he teaches that the effect of the former is not only alienation from the life of God, but also stupor and wantonness for the perpetrating of all impurity, of which it now follows.

Latin:

V. 18. Ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ) Appetitus corrupti et- iam mentem obnubilant, Rom. 1, 21.

Ὄντες ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῇς ζωῆς τῦ Θεῦ) Longe remoti à vita illa, quæ secundum Deum est. Vide Gal. 2, 19. Vo- cem ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι habuimus & supra c. 2, 12.

Διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν ὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς) Explicat id, quod de tenebris modo dixerat.

Διὰ τὴν πώρωσιν τῇ καρδίας αὐτῶν) Diximus ad Marcum 6, 52. omnia vitia inolita designari voce πωρώσεως. Sic & Latinis callum obduxisse dicuntur, qui bona monita non persentiunt.

Non tam redit ad id, quod initio capitis dixerat, quam persequitur id ipsum. Hortatus erat ad vi- tam Christianis dignam. Ad quam & concordiæ & sanctitatis studium pertinet. Non autem Philoso- phorum tantum vel gentium istius temporis status hujusmodi fuit. Est omnium non conversorum. Qui quod ad mentem vanitati & tenebris errorum, utpote alieni à vita, quæ ex Deo, in Deo, & secun- dum Deum est, ob inscitiam eorum nativam, (cui affectata in gentilibus accesserat, Rom. 1, 20. seqq.) repleti sunt, quod ad voluntatem, πωρώσει & vi- tiis, sive per naturam, sive per consuetudinem habi- tualibus laborant, atque ea etiam ratione alieni sunt à vita Dei. Nam ubi in intellectu nihil nisi ἄγνοια, ubi in corde & voluntate πώρωσις, quo- modo illis vita Dei inesse potest? Περιπατεῖν di- cuntur in vanitate mentis suæ, quia conversatio, studia, & actus instituuntur juxta mentis vel intel- lectus ideam, quum vanis opinionibus vel persua- sionibus mens occupata est, quomodo vitæ stu- dia & praxes melioris commatis erunt? Non au- tem vanitas tantum τῦ νοὸς in apprehensione sim- plici, vel compositione & divisione, aut, ut lo- quuntur in prima, & secunda mentis operatione; sed etiam σκότος τῆς διανοίας, tenebræ in ratiocina- tione vel operatione mentis tertiæ designantur, quia totus intellectus corruptus est vanitate & te- nebris repletus extra conversionis gratiam. Mentis corruptionem sequitur voluntatis depravatio, in qua πώρωσις ob habitualem corruptionē designa- tur, quam Vulgatus quidem cæcitatem reddidit. Sed rectius hic ab Ambrosio & aliis durities, vel obdura- tio vertitur, quamvis utriusque significatus exem- pla non desint. Quandoquidem cum mente & ra- tione cor seu voluntas hic conjungatur; ad illam enim tenebræ, obscuratio & cæcitas proprie spe- ctant, ad hanc vero durities & obduratio. Ut au- tem natura cor habemus durum & lapideum ante conversionem: Ita πώρωσις augetur per consue- tudinem peccandi, cum juxta vanitatem mentis & tenebras τῆς διανοίας ambulamus & vitam institui- mus, quemadmodum gentiles se magis magisque in mente sua obdurant. Πώρωσιν enim non pas- sive, sed active hic accipiendam esse, agnoscit Cro- cius. Quapropter ut revocet aut absterreat A- postolus Ephesios à veteri vitæ consuetudine ad vitæ novitatem, illius effectum docet esse non ab- alienationem tantum à vita Dei, sed & stuporem & proterviam ad omnem impuritatem perpetrandam, de quibus jam sequitur.

## 4:19
Vers. 19.

Οἵτινες ἀπηλγηκότες (Who being past feeling) He explains further what he understands by πώρωσιν (callousness). Just as certain parts of the body deprived of vital spirit feel no pain, so for them the mind, even when they do most shameful things, is moved by no pain on that account. Ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ (They gave themselves over to lasciviousness) ἀσελγεῖαι (lasciviousnesses) are the beginnings of impudicity, the first lines, as they say, we have spoken of this at 2 Cor. 12:21. Εἰς ἐργασίαν ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης (To work all uncleanness) Basil to Diodorus: Τῷ τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας ὀνόματι τάς τε κὴ τῶν ἀῤῥένων ἀῤῥητοποιΐας κὴ τὰς θηλειῶν περιλαμβάνων (Under the name of uncleanness, including both the unspeakable acts of males and those of females). Jones, whose Princes were the Ephesians, soft as Martial, had learned Persian customs: and so those vices reigned among them which Paul notes under the name of ἀκαθαρσίας (uncleanness) at Rom. 1:24, ch. 6:10, as also among the Corinthians, 2 Cor. 12:21, and Gal. 5:19. Ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ (In covetousness) He adds this because many males prostituted themselves for a price.
