Therefore Sallust says: Avarice makes body and mind effeminate. בצע (betza) signifies gain to the Hebrews. But πλεονεξία is often translated.

These are rather effects of the old habit of life, as we have said. The Old [Version] rendered the word ἀπηλγηκότες as 'despairing'. Whence Beza thinks he read ἀπηλπικότες. But Crocius rightly warns: the Old [translator] could have read as we do, and yet translated otherwise, because ἀπαλγέω in Polybius is the same as ἀπογινώσκω, I despair. Jerome: 'Ἀπηλγηκότες, he says, are those who, after they have sinned, do not feel pain: who, by no means sensing their ruin, are carried headlong, and like beasts, seeing the iron, rush into death.' Let us express, if we can, word for word, and say 'indolentes' (indolent) or 'indolorios' (pain-less). For some of the Philosophers also preached ἀπαλγησίαν (indolence), i.e., painlessness. Ἀσελγεῖαι (Lasciviousnesses) are explained either specifically concerning impudicity or wantonness, or generally concerning wantonness in words and deeds, as this word is explained by Bullinger, Calvin, Beza, Aretius, Zanchius, and Crocius, as any perpetual lust, or explained as petulance, by which the flesh, not restrained by the Spirit of God, exults intemperately and licentiously. Other passages in the New Testament support the former sense: Mark 7:22, Rom. 13:13, 2 Cor. 12:21, Gal. 5:19, 1 Pet. 2:3, 2 Pet. 2:7, 18. In which sense that word is also read in Wisdom 14:6, in Philo lib. I de vita Mof., and elsewhere passim, namely, concerning wanton lasciviousness. But where the first lines and beginnings of impudicity are noted by this word, I do not find: nor does that suit this place, because the Gentiles are said to have delivered themselves to lasciviousness, παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ, and indeed after they ceased to feel pain, they contracted that πώρωσιν (callousness), or drew over themselves a callus of such a kind that they had no longer any sense of sin, which stupor is not followed by the beginnings of impudicity, but rather of wanton lasciviousness: and therefore it is not inappropriately rendered by 'wantonness', which kind of sense occurs in verse 4 of the Epistle of Jude, especially because it is added specifically that the discourse is about that wantonness which is detected in impurity. For the Apostolic variation of cases is not to be neglected, that they were delivered τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ (to lasciviousness), to what end? Εἰς ἐργασίαν τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης (to work all uncleanness), how? Ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ (in covetousness); they are not said to be delivered both to lasciviousness, and to uncleanness, and to covetousness. One kind of vice therefore is primarily designated, which was most customary, namely, that after they had no longer any pain or sense of sin on account of the πώρωσιν τῆς- had hearts, they had given themselves most especially to impurity of every kind, which he expresses more emphatically as τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ εἰς ἐργασίαν ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης, for the operation of all impurity, where it is manifest that it is not about any wantonness and petulance of sinning licentiously, although the heart is prone to any sins, and the native πώρωσις of the heart extends itself to any sins, but specifically to the wantonness in impurity and any unchastity being committed, as B. Luther, Piscator, Musculus, and others with the old Vulgate have specifically explained, and thus wanton lust, which exerts itself in impurity of every kind, is to be understood. When a concrete thing, says Chrysostom on this passage, is gathered into one place, it is a dead member and lacking in sense, and whether you burn it, or cut it, or do anything to it, it does not feel. So also those who have once given themselves to unchastity, even if you apply prayer to them like fire, even if like iron, nothing touches them, nothing reaches them. For their member is clearly dead. And unless you take away from them the emptiness of sense, so that you may touch healthy members, you do everything in vain. Ἐν πάσῃ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ that, according to Chrysostom, is, every adultery, fornication, pederasty, envy, every lust, and intemperance. Some interpret πλεονεξίαν as an insatiable desire for sinning, just as in the greedy there is an insatiable desire for wealth, as Jerome, Theodoret, Bullinger, Aretius, Calvin, and others explain it as avarice, Chrysostom, Ambrose, B. Luther, and most other interpreters. The usage of scripture favors these, Mark VII. v. 22. Luke XII. 16. Col. III. 5. 1 Thess. III. 5. But to those, because here not so much a special kind of sin is expressed, as the manner of the working of all impurity, which is done in greed. Which Grotius understands as the price or gain of the prostitution of bodies, from which it is established that harlots have their name. Which, although it can be admitted to that extent, that they indulge in unchastity so far that they even hire out harlots for a price, or prostitute their bodies. Yet the explanation of Jerome does not displease. And since they have omitted nothing at all that is unclean, to do all this in greed, since they are never satisfied by luxuriating, nor does their pleasure have an end. Thus Thomas on greed, that is, ardently and insatiably, according to that of Peter 2. ep. II. 14. and Estius, here the discourse is about the greed of shameful pleasures. Therefore Beza rendered it: To perform all impurity WITH COMPETITION.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Οἵτινες ἀπηλγηκότες) Amplius explicat, quid per πώ- ρωσιν intelligat. Sicut partes quædam corporis à spiritu vitali destitutæ dolorem nullum sentiunt, ita illis animus, etiam cum turpissima faciant, nullo ob id dolore commo- vetur. Ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ) ἀσελγεῖαι sunt impu- ditiæ initia, primæ, ut loquuntur, lineæ, diximus ad 2. Cor. 12, 21. Εἰς ἐργασίαν ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης) Basilius ad Diodo- rum: Τῷ τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας ὀνόματι τάς τε κὴ τῶν ἀῤῥένων ἀῤῥη- τοποιΐας κὴ τὰς θηλειῶν περιλαμβάνων. Jones, quorum Prin- cipes Ephesii, molles Martiali, didicerant mores Persicos: itaque regnabant apud eos ea vitia, quæ ἀκαθαρσίας no- mine Paulus notat ad Rom. 1, 24. c. 6, 10. ut & apud Co- rinthios, 2. Cor. 12, 21. & Gal. 5, 19. Ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ) Hoc ideo addit, quia multi mares ob pre- tium se prostituebant. Ideo Salustius dicit: Avaritia corpus animumque effœminat. בצע Ebræis lucrum signi- ficat. Sæpe autem vertitur πλεονεξία.

Hi effectus potius sunt veteris vitæ consuetudinis, ut diximus. Vocem ἀπηλγηκότες desperantes red- didit Vetus. Unde Beza legisse eum putat ἀπηλπι- κότες. Sed recte monet Crocius: Veterem potuisse legere, ut nos, & tamen aliter vertere, quia ἀπαλγέω apud Polybium idem est, quo ἀπογινώσκω despero. Hieronymus: Ἀπηλγηκότες autem, inquit, hi sunt, qui postquam peccaverint, non dolent: qui, nequa- quam sentientes ruinam suam, feruntur in pronum, & tanquam bestiæ, ferrum videntes, in mortem ruunt. Exprimamus, si possimus, verbum de verbo, & di- eamus ἀπηλγηκότες indolentes sive indolorios. Nam & quidam Philosophorum ἀπαλγησίαν, i. e. indoloriam prædicavit. Ἀσελγεῖαι vel speciatim de impudicitia aut lascivia explicantur, vel gene- ratim de protervia in dictis & factis, ut vox hæc ex- plicatur à Bullingero, Calvino, Beza, Aretio, Zanchio, Crocio, de libidine quavis perpetua, seu pro petu- lantia explicatur, qua intemperanter quidem & li- centiose exultat caro, Spiritu Dei non coërcita. Pro priori sensu faciunt alia loca in N. Testamen- to, Marc. 7, 22. Rom. 13, 13. 2. Cor. 12, 21. Gal. 5, 19. 1. Pet. 2, 3. 2. Pet. 2, 7. 18. Quo sensu etiam vox illa legitur Sap. 14, 6. apud Philonem lib. I. de vita Mof. & alibi passim, de proterva nempe lascivia. Ubi vero impudicitiæ primæ lineæ & initia hac voce notentur, non reperio: neque id huic loco con- gruit, quia gentes seipsos tradidisse dicuntur lasci- viæ, παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ, & quidem postquam dedoluerunt, eam πώρωσιν contraxerunt, vel callum ejusmodi obduxerunt, ut nullum amplius sensum pec- cati haberent, quem stuporem non sequuntur ini- tia impudicitiæ, sed protervæ potius lasciviæ: Id- eoque non incommode per proterviam redditur, cujusmodi sensus vers. 4. in epistola Judæ occurrit, imprimis, quia peculiariter additur, quod de pro- tervia illa, quæ deprehenditur in impuritate, ser- mo sit. Nam non negligenda casuum variatio A- postolica, quod traditi sint τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ, ad quid? Εἰς ἐργασίαν τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης, quomodo? Ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ non traditi dicuntur & ἀσελγείᾳ, & ἀκαθαρσίᾳ, & πλεονεξίᾳ. Unum ergo genus vi- tiorum imprimis designatur, quod maxime so- lenne erat, quod nempe postquam nullum am- plius dolorem vel sensum peccati ob πώρωσιν τῆς- καρδίας haberent, sese maxime dederant omnis gèneris impuritati, quod ἐμφατικωτέρως effert τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ εἰς ἐργασίαν ἀκαθαρσίας πάσης, proterviæ ad operationem omnis impuritatis, ubi manifestum est, quod non de quavis licentiosè peccandi protervia & petulantia, licet cor ad quævis peccata proclive sit, & πώρωσις nativa cordis sese ad quævis peccata extendat, sed spe- ciatim ad proterviam in impuritate & impudici- tia quavis patrandi notari, ut B. Lutherus, Pisa- ctor, Musculus, alii cum veteri Vulgata speciatim exposuere, adeoque proterva libido, quæ se exe- rit in omnis generis impudicitia, intelligatur. Quando concreta, inquit Chrysostomus in hunc lo- cum, defluxio in unum locum cogitur, membrum sit mortuum & sensu defectum, & sive usseris, sive secueris, sive quidvis feceris, non sentit. Ita etiam illi, qui se semel dederunt impudicitiæ, etiamsi in- star ignis, etiamsi instar ferri orationem eis appli- caris, nihil eos tangit, nihil ad eos pervenit. Est enim plane membrum eorum mortuum. Et nisi eis ademeris sensus vacuitatem, ut membra sana tangas, frustra facis omnia. Ἐν πάσῃ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ id secundum Chrysostomum est, πᾶσα μοιχεία, πορνεία, παιδερασία, φθόνω, πᾶσα ἀκολασία, καὶ ἀσέλγεια, in omni immunditia, in omni adul- terio, scortatione, pædicatu, invidia, omni libi- dine, & intemperantia. Πλεονεξίαν interpretan- tur nonnulli insatiabilem peccandi cupiditatem, sicut in avaris inexplebilis est opum cupiditas, ut- pote Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Bullingerus, Are- tius, Calvinus, alii avaritiam exponunt, Chryso- stomus, Ambrosius, B. Lutherus, & plerique cæte- ri Interpp. His favet usus scripturæ, Marci VII. v. 22. Luc. XII. 16. Col. III. 5. 1. Thess. III. 5. Illis verò, quod hic non tàm speciale genus peccati, quàm modus ἐργασίας τῆς πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας exprimatur, quod fiat ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ. Quam de pretio vel lucro prostitutionis corporum Grotius intelligit, à quo meretrices nomen habere con- stat. Quod etsi admitti eatenus possit, quod eo usque indulgeant impudicitiæ, ut pro pretio etiam conducant meretrices, vel prostituant corpora. Non displicet tamen Hieronymi ex- plicatio. Et cùm nihil omnino prætermiserint, quod immundum sit, hoc totum facere in avaritia, cum nunquam luxuriando satiantur, nec eorum terminum habet voluptas. Ita Thomas in avari- tia, id est, ardenter & insatiabiliter, juxta illud Pe- tri 2. epist. II. 14. & Estius, hic sermo est de avaritia turpium voluptatum. Ideo Beza reddidit: Ad CERTATIM patrandam impuritatem omnem.

## 4:20
Verse 20. But you did not so learn Christ) Christ, that is, the doctrine of Christ, by a frequent metonymy: You did not learn it in such a way that you ought to imitate those shameful deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὑμεῖς δὲ ὐχ ὕτως ἐμάθετε τὸν Χριστὸν) Christum, id est, doctrinam Christi, per μετωνυμίαν frequentem: Non ita didicistis, ut scilicet illa flagitia imitari debeatis.

## 4:21
Verse 21. If indeed you have heard him) That is, if only you have well understood the Gospel. Thus we had ἀκούειν also above c. III. v. 2.

And in him you were taught as the truth is in Jesus) And if you have been so taught the Gospel, how it truly is, just as it was preached by Jesus himself, he says this because after his departure some under the name of the Gospel had taught a certain profane liberty, as also at Corinth.

It is not about the Gospel or the glad tidings of grace in Christ, but about the doctrine of Christ in general, from which they could perceive that not only faith or knowledge of the truth, but also piety and a zeal for holiness were required.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Εἴγε αὐτὸν ἠκύσατε) Id est, si modo Evange- lium bene comprehendistis. Sic ἀκύειν habuimus & supra c. III. v. 2.

Καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐδιδάχθητε καθώς ἐστιν ἀλήθεια ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ) Et si ita edocti estis Evangelium, quomodo illud revera se habet, prout à Jesu ipso prædicatum est, hoc ideo di- cit, quia post suum abitum quidam sub nomine Evan- gelii profanam quandam docuerant libertatem, ut & Co- rinthi.

Non de Evangelio seu læto nuncio gratiæ in Christo, sed de doctrina Christi in genere sermo est, ex qua percipere poterant non tantum fidem vel cognitionem veritatis, sed etiam pietatem, & studium sanctitatis requiri.

## 4:22
Verse 22. That you put off according to the former conversation, the old man) He explains what kind of people they were, and what the doctrine of the Lord Jesus requires Matt. XII. 24. and elsewhere, predicted by Isaiah LV. 7. and it is a transposition: that you put off the old man, that is, him who was in your former way of living.

We had the old man also in Rom. VI. v. 6. which is here to put off, that is, to strip off, Coloss. III. 9. the opposite of which is to put on, which will now follow, both alluding to the rite of baptism, in which clothes were laid aside and put back on. Conversation is a certain kind of life among men, as Gal. I. v. 13. James III. 13. 1 Pet. I. 15. 18. II. 12. III. 16. 2 Pet. II. 7. III. 11. Tob. IV. 19. thus Seneca also said to converse for to associate.

The one being corrupted) Who tends toward destruction Galat. chap. VI. v. 8.

And the desires of deceit) That is, through seducing desires. A sweet root, but most bitter fruits: the Homeric lotus.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἀποθέσθαι ὑμᾶς κατὰ τὴν προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν, τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον) Explicat, quales fuerint, & quid exi- gat Domini Jesu doctrina Matth. XII. 24. & alibi, prædicta ab Esaia LV. 7. & est trajectio: ut exuatis veterem homi- nem, id est, eum, qui erat in priore vestro vivendi genere.

Veterem hominem habuimus & Rom. VI. v. 6. quod hic ἀποθέσθαι, id est, ἀπεκδύσασθαι, Coloss. III. 9. cujus contrarium est ἐvdύσασθαι, quod jam sequetur, utrumque alludens ad ritum baptismi, in quo vestes deponebantur & refumebantur. Ἀναστροφὴ est vitæ quoddam genus inter homines, ut Gal. I. v. 13. Jacob. III. 13. 1. Petr. I. 15. 18. II. 12. III. 16. 2. Petr. II. 7. III. 11. Tob. IV. 19. sic conversari pro συνομιλεῖν dixit & Seneca.

Τὸν φθειρόμενον) Qui tendit ad exitium Galat. cap. VI. v. 8.

Καὶ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τ’ ἀπάτης) Id est, per cupiditates seducentes. Dulcis radix, sed fructus amarissimi : lotos Homerica.

## 4:23
And to be renewed in the spirit of your mind) Here the spirit of the mind is the mind itself. Thus the Hebrews say clay of mud, earth of dust, where the Genitive is explanatory.

Latin:

Ἀνανεᾶσθαι δὲ τῷ Πνεύματι τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν) Hic spiritus mentis est ipsa mens. Sic Ebræi dicunt lutum cæni, terram pulveris, ubi Genitivus est ἐξηγητικὸς.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. And to put on the new man) which he called τὸν νέον ἄνθρωπον in the same sense in Colossians III. 9.

Created according to God) who is formed according to the will of God. Concerning the verb κτίζεσθαι see above II. 10. III. 9. 2. Cor. V. 17.

In righteousness and holiness of truth) The former is δικαιοσύνη צדק, that is, innocence, which is חסד, ὁσιότης, as the Hebrews distinguish them thus. Moreover, Paul adds τ’ ἀληθείας for ἀληθίνῃ, that is, such innocence, and then holiness, which are in being, not in appearing.

The old man corrupted according to the lust of error is original sin, which is called man, because it has pervaded the whole man and all the powers of soul and body, so that the natural man appears as nothing but sin. Old from the origin, both of the first seduction of the Protoplasts, and of the derived conception and birth of the carnal man, through which sin is propagated. Corrupted, because sin is nothing but damnable and abominable lust, through the lust of any sins whatsoever, to which nature is led, James chap. I. 14. Of error, because the whole sea of sins arises from the depraved judgment of corrupted reason. The old man therefore does not denote a former way of life in Heathenism, which the Apostle had already designated by τὴν προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν, but rather the corruption of the old Adam, which he contracted by sin, and transmitted to his descendants. Whence the blessed Balduinus: This, he says, is that old man, namely the mind and will of man corrupted, and he is so called, 1. because he is prior to the new, for such he is born from the mother's womb, whereas the new is only reborn, 2. because he grows old and is corrupted, while he is daily resisted through the Holy Spirit, 3. because he proceeds from that old and first Adam, and is begotten in his image, 4. because he is occupied with, acts in, and lives this old and carnal life. Which corruption, although it begins to be put off in baptism, as the washing of the renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III. 5. yet the remnants of oldness always adhere to the reborn: and therefore it must be our perpetual task that that old man be put off, Heb. chap. XII. vers. 1. For it is a matter here of the reborn, who had been converted, and in baptism, having put off the old man, were putting on the new. Which that rite of baptism, in which garments were put off and new ones were put on, signified.

They are therefore commanded to put on the new man, so that being renewed more and more by the Spirit of the mind, they may strive for true newness, and become more fully new men. The new man is spoken of in antithesis, says the blessed Nicol. Hunnius in Exam. error. Photin. de statu Integr. p. 20. to the old, who is from Adam by hereditary received wickedness and impiety, Rom. chap. VI. v. 6. Eph. IV. 22. Coloss. III. 9. 1. Corinth. V. 1. 8. and is corrupted according to the desires of error, vers. 22. as therefore nothing is more rightly opposed to impiety, wickedness, and erroneous desires than holiness and justice, so nothing more rightly constitutes the new man than these.

Furthermore, renewal, by the force of the word ἀνανεῦσθαι, implies the former state, which we had in our first Parents. For he who must be RENEWED, it was necessary that he should have first been NAKED in the Spirit of his mind. But we were not new, except in Adam, when we were first created in him according to God, or to the image of God in true righteousness and holiness. Therefore he says, who was created and image of GOD. Similarly, the word ἀνακαί- νωσις, renewal, looks back to the first creation, Rom. XII. 2. Tit. III. 5. Which two words the blessed Nic. Hunnius, in the place cited a little before, most elegantly joins, Paul Col. III. 11. Put on τὸν νέον τὸν ἀνακαινόμενον, the new, the renewed, or the new-ancient, so that he may evidently show that the new man is the renewal of the first one created in holiness, nor can these words so joined be explained otherwise, whence this hypothesis arises for us: To put on the new man, who is created according to God &c. is to be renewed to the ancient holiness and righteousness once possessed by man, who was founded according to God, or to his image.

To which primal condition the Apostle also recalls us with the word κτισθέντα. For this must properly be taken concerning the first creation, since there is no necessity to abandon the proper meaning of the word. And the passage Col. III. 10 is to be compared here entirely, where the Apostle speaks of the image of him who created us, and thus the first creation is expressly looked back upon, in which we were created to the image of God. For this is a most customary and frequent periphrasis of God in the scriptures, that he is our Creator, or that he created us. The blessed Nicol. Hunnius adds in the same place that the manner of speaking here clearly agrees with the first creation. Here, he says, the discourse is about the new man renewed, but he was originally created entirely to the image of him. Adam is said to be created to the image of God, and the new renewed man is created to the image of God: the manner of speaking agrees, and no reason for a different interpretation is given, wherefore no one justly doubts that the discourse is about the same thing. If you say that τὸν καινὸν ἄνθρωπον is described here, and thus a new creation is designated, it can be answered that what we ought to put on is expressed in two ways: first by the new man, then by him who is founded according to God, or to the image of God; the first indicates renewal, the latter indeed the first creation, and that is because both bring in true righteousness and holiness, which is to be put on, and pertains to the new man, and also pertained to the man κτισθέντα κατὰ τὸν Θεόν. Since we were all founded in Adam according to God, or to the image of God, Gen. ch. I. 26. 27. and we ought to put on in turn, through renewal, that man who was founded according to God to the image of God. Which we have brought up elsewhere against the Socinians who deny that the image of God in Adam consisted in righteousness and holiness. Thus the blessed Ægydius Hunnius in this place, who, having explained the truth or the true reason for living in Christ Jesus, and the putting off of the old man, who is corrupted according to the former conversation of sin and uncleanness, has it thus: The dissolute manners of a shameful life that have gone before do not befit this light of the knowledge of Christ, nor do inveterate pursuits, nor the thoughts and lusts of former errors, nor the ancient perversity and distorted disposition of the old Adam. But concerning the renewal and the putting on of the new man, he gives this paraphrase: But rather the new Evangelical profession of the doctrine of CHRIST demands other manners, that you may be renewed by the internal innovation of your Spirit and mind, which, having been sprinkled by the blood of CHRIST through faith, and purged from sins, has now been made otherwise, and thus having put on the new man, in disposition, thoughts, manners, and pursuits, [he is] in all things repugnant and opposed to the old Adam. Who was once founded according to GOD or to the image of GOD in true righteousness and holiness. To the idea of which primal image it befits you to strive, and to labor toward this, that it may be restored more and more.

Although indeed some understand the word κτισθέντα not of the first creation, but of renewal, which can also be seen in the blessed Balduinus, they do not doubt, however, that the first creation is alluded to here, and from this Apostolic phrase they likewise gather that the image of GOD was situated in righteousness and holiness. Thus he alludes, says Crocius, to the first creation, in which man was made to the likeness of GOD. For this was corrupted through the fall; therefore there is need of restoration. Most explain righteousness concerning the duties of the second table, and holiness concerning piety toward GOD according to the first table. Which interpretation is also approved by Calvin, Musculus, and Crocius. But Crocius is here more unfair than the matter warrants to the most excellent Theologian Flacius Illyricus, whom he dishonors with the term of the unhappy offspring of the Manichaeans, as if he had said that sin is a substance, and regeneration is the creation of a substance. Concerning whose opinion we have treated in Article II of the Augustan Confession. The blessed Balduinus also praises the words of Flacius on this place, that the very mind of man is the image of Satan or of GOD, according as it is whole or corrupted. What? That Crocius himself praises the words of Chrysostom: The very essence of the new man is in righteousness, and in the holiness of truth.

Aretius explains Τὸν Φθειρόμενον concerning the daily abolition, by which the old man is mortified daily by the reborn. But Crocius rightly corrects that. Judging that it alludes rather to the oldness, which is almost next to corruption, because unless it is put off daily, it is increased, and corrupts the man himself more, and that both by rendering him worse, or more prone to sin, and more unhappy or more worthy of punishment. The Greek Scholia do not say ἐφθαρμένον, but in the present Participle φθειρόμενον, so that a continuous act may be signified. For the old man never ceases from vice, he is incessantly occupied in wicked desires, by which he is led from error into error, and through individual days, hours, and moments he is corrupted, intercepted, violated, as Jerome speaks, and is never not deceived. Which explanation is to be preferred to the Grotian one. The old man, I say, is corrupted, not by perishing (for although the Apostle might wish this most of all, it does not happen through depraved concupiscences, by which he is rather preserved), but by increasing his native corruption through deceitful desires, so that he who is corrupted becomes continually more corrupt. This the opposition teaches. For just as in the renewal the fruit or consequence of the same is not expressed, but what it is like and in what it consists: so in the description of the old Adam, he does not designate the destruction which it brings, but the state and kind of the same, that it corrupts itself more and more through depraved desires.

Moreover, by the mention of the old and new man, the Apostle implies that not only the inferior faculties of man are corrupted and in need of renewal, but the whole man; therefore he indicates the renewal of the mind, which is that principal thing in man by which he is distinguished from the brutes, the seat of reason, and the leader of the will. Which is also called transformation through the renewal of the mind, Rom. chap. XII. ver. 1. not by a transformation of substance, but by a conformation of a new mind, just as the putting on of the new man occurs not regarding substance, but quality. For it is opposed to the old, which is not the first Adam, but the corruption drawn from Adam. Indeed, by this likeness it is declared that the new and the old man differ from the one putting on and putting off from him who puts it off and on. As the old man is original sin: So the new man is the χάρισμα of sanctification effected by the Holy Spirit in the regenerate man, by which sin is crucified, wicked concupiscence is resisted, and the pursuit of a life pleasing to God takes increments from day to day, as the blessed Glassius has it on the 19th Sunday after Trinity, p. 819.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Καὶ ἐνδύσασθαι τὸν καινὸν ἄνθρωπον) quem τὸν νέον ἄνθρωπον eodem sensu dixit Coloss. III. 9.

Τὸν κατὰ Θεὸν κτισθέντα) qui formatus est secundum Dei voluntatem. De verbo κτίζεσθαι vide supra II. 10. III. 9. 2. Cor. V. 17.

Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ὁσιότητι τ’ ἀληθείας) Prior est δικαιοσύνη צדק, id est, innocentia, quam חסד, ὁσιότης, ut ita distinguunt Ebræi. Addit autem Paulus τ’ ἀληθείας pro ἀληθίνῃ, id est, tali innocentia, & deinde sanctitate, quæ sint in esse, non in videri.

Vetus homo corruptus secundum concupiscentiam erroris peccatum originale est, quod homo dicitur, quia totum hominem & omnes animæ ac corporis vires pervasit, ut homo ψυχικὸς nihil nisi peccatum videatur. Vetus ab origine, tùm prima Protoplastorum seductionis, tùm derivata conceptionis & nativitatis hominis carnalis, per quam peccatum propagatur. Corruptus, quia peccatum non nisi concupiscentia damnabiles & abominabilis est, per concupiscentiam quorumvis peccatorum, ad quæ natura ducitur, Jac. cap. I. 14. Erroris, quia totum peccatorum pelagus oritur è pravo corruptæ rationis judicio. Vetus ergo homo non prius vivendi genus in Ethnicismo notat, quod per τὴν προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν jam designarat Apostolus, sed potius corruptionem veteris Adami, quam peccato contraxit, & ad posteros transmisit. Unde B. Balduinus: Hic est, inquit, vetus ille homo, mens nimirum hominis & voluntas corrupta, & sic dicitur, 1. quia prior est nova, talis enim nascitur ex utero matris, cum novus demum renascatur, 2. quia inveterascit & corrumpitur, dum ei quotidie per Spiritum Sanctum resistitur, 3. quia ex veteri illo, primoque Adamo provenit, & ad ejus imaginem gignitur, 4. quia circa hanc veterem carnalemque vitam versatur, agit & vivit. Quæ corruptio, etsi in baptismo exui incipiat, ceu lavacro renovationis Sp. Sancti, Tit. III. 5. semper tamen renatis adhærent vetustatis reliquiæ: ideoque perpetuo id nobis agendum, ut vetus ille homo deponatur, Ebr. cap. XII. vers. 1. Agitur enim hic cum renatis, qui conversi erant, & in baptismo, deposito veteri homine, novum induebant. Quod ritus ille baptismi, in quo vestes deponebantur, & novæ induebantur, significabat.

Novum ergo hominem induere jubentur, ut subinde magis magisque Spiritu mentis renovati veræ novitati studeant, ac plenius novi homines evadant. Novus homo dicitur in ἀντιθέσει, ait B. Nicol. Hunnius Exam. error. Photin. de statu Integr. p. 20. ad veterem, qui est ab Adamo hæreditario accepta nequitia & impietas, Rom. cap. VI. v. 6. Eph. IV. 22. Coloss. III. 9. 1. Corinth. V. 1. 8. & corrumpitur secundum desideria erroris, vers. 22. ut ergo impietati, nequitiæ, & erroneis desideriis nihil opponitur rectius, quam sanctitas & justitia, sic nihil rectius, quam ea, novum hominem constituunt.

Porro renovatio, vi vocis ἀνανεῦσθαι, pristinum statum, statum, quem in primis Parentibus habuimus, in- nuit. Qui enim RENOVARI debet, ille prius NUDUS fuerit Spiritu mentis suæ, oportuit. Non autem fuimus novi, nisi in Adamo, cum in ipso primum creati sum9 secundum Deum, vel ad ima- ginem Dei in justitia & sanctitate vera. Ideo di- cit, qui creatus est non à Deo, sed secundum Deum, hoc est, ad exemplar & imaginem DEI. Similiter respicit primā creationem, vox ἀνακαί- νωσις renovatio, Rom. XII. 2. Tit. III. 5. Quam utramque vocem elegantissime conjungit, dicente lo- co allegato paullo ante B. Nic. Hunnio, Paulus Col. III. 11. Induite τὸν νέον τὸν ἀνακαινόμενον, novum, re- novatum, seu nov-antiquum, ut evidenter monstret, novum hominem esse renovationem primi in sanctita- te creati, nec possunt hæ voces ita junctæ exponi ali- ter, unde hac nobis surgit hypothesis : Induere no- vum hominem, qui secundum Deum est creatus &c. est renovari ad antiquam sanctitatem & justi- tiam olim aliquando possessam ab homine, qui se- cundum Deum, sive ad ejus imaginem est conditus.

Ad quam primævam conditionem etiam nos re- vocat Apostolus voce κτισθέντα. Hæc enim pro- prie accipienda de prima creatione, quum nulla sit necessitas propriam significationem vocis de- serendi. Et conferendus hic omnino locus Col. III. 10. ubi imaginem dicit Apostolus ejus, qui condidit nos, adeoque exerte respicitur prima creatio, in qua conditi sumus ad imaginem Dei. Est enim hæc periphrasis Dei usitatissima & fre- quentissima in scripturis, quod Creator noster sit, vel nos condiderit. Addit B. Nicol. Hun- nius l. c. modum loquendi hic plane congruere primæ creationi. Hic, inquit, sermo est de ho- mine novo renovato, is autem primitus omninò creatus fuit ad imaginem ejus. Adam creatus di- citur ad imaginem Dei, & novus renovatus homo ad imaginem Dei creatus: congruit loquendi mo- dus, & ratio diversæ interpretationis non datur, quare de re eadem sermonem esse, nemo juste ambi- git. Si dicas, τὸν καινὸν ἄνθρωπον hic describi, adeo- que designari novam creationem, responderi po- test, duobus modis exprimi id, quod induere de- bemus: primo per novum hominem, deinde per eum, qui conditus est secundum Deum, vel ad ima- ginem Dei; primum innuit renovationem, alte- rum vero primam creationem, idque ideo, quia utrumque infert justitiam & sanctitatem veram, quæ induenda est, & ad novum hominem perti- net, pertinuit etiam ad hominem κτισθέντα κατὰ τὸν Θεόν. Siquidem in Adamo conditi omnes si- mus secundum Deum, vel ad imaginem Dei, Gen. c. I. 26. 27. atque illum hominem, qui secundum Deum conditus fuit, debeamus per renovatio- nem ad imaginem Dei vicissim induere. Quod contra Socinianos negantes imaginem Dei in Ada- mo constitiisse justitia & sanctitate, alias adduxi- mus. Sic B. Ægydius Hunnius in h. l. qui expo- sita veritate seu vera ratione vivendi in Christo Je- su, & veteris hominis depositione, qui juxta priorem conversationem peccati & immunditiei corrum- pitur, ita habet: Hanc lucem agnitionis Christi non decent antegressæ flagitiosæ vitæ mores dissoluti, non inveterata studia, non cogitationes & concu- piscentiæ errorum pristinæ, non veteris Adami vetusta perversitas ac distortum ingenium. De renovatione autem & induitione novi hominis hanc reddit paraphrasin: Quin potius nova pro- fessio Evangelica de CHRISTO doctrinæ alios mores postulat, ut renovemini interna Spiritus atque mentis vestræ innovatione, quæ sanguine CHRISTI per fidem aspersa, & à peccatis per- purgata, jam aliter effecta sit, atque sic indutis novum hominem, ingenio, cogitationibus, moribus, atque studiis veteri Adamo per omnia repugnantem & oppositum. Qui juxta DEUM sive ad DEI imaginem olim conditus est in vera justitia & sanctitate. Ad cujus primævæ imaginis ideam decet vos contendere, atque huc laborare, ut illa magis magisque restauretur.

Quanquam vero nonnulli vocem κτισθέντα non de prima creatione, sed renovatione intelligant, quod etiam in B. Balduino videre est, non dubitant tamen illi, ad primam creationem hic alludi, & ex hac phrasi Apostolica pariter colligunt, imaginem DEI sitam fuisse in justitia & sanctitate. Sic alludit, inquit Crocius, ad primam creationem, in qua homo factus est ad DEI similitudinem. Hæc enim per lapsum corrupta; ideo opus est instauratione. Justitiam de officiis tabulæ secundæ, sanctitatem de pietate erga DEUM secundum primam tabulam plerique explicant. Quæ interpretatio Calvino, Musculo, Crocio etiam probata. Iniquior autem hic præter rem est Crocius Theologo Præstantissimo Flacio Illyrico, quem infelicis Manichæorum germinis vocabulo dehonestat, quasi peccatum substantiam, & regenerationem creationem substantiæ esse dixerit. De cujus sententia egimus Artic. II. August. Confess. Laudat & B. Balduinus verba Flacii in hunc locum, ipsam mentem hominis esse imaginem Satanæ aut DEI, prout integra vel corrupta est. Quid? quod Crocius ipse laudet Chrysostomi verba: Ipsa novi hominis essentia in justitia est, & sanctitate veritatis.

Τὸν Φθειρόμενον de abolitione quotidiana exponit Aretius, qua indies à renatis mortificatur vetus homo. Sed id merito corrigit Crocius. Alludi potius censens ad vetustatem, quæ fere corruptioni proxima est, quia nisi exuatur indies, augetur, magisque hominem ipsum corrumpit, idque tùm reddendo deteriorem, seu ad peccatum proniorem, tùm infeliciorem seu digniorem supplicio. Non inquiunt Scholia Græca ἐφθαρμένον, sed in præsenti Participio φθειρόμενον, ut continuus actus significetur. Nunquam enim vetus homo cessat à vitio, indefinenter versatur in pravis desideriis, quibus ex errore in errorem ducitur, & per singulos dies, horas atque momenta corrumpitur, intercipitur, violatur, ut loquitur Hieronymus, & nunquam non decipitur. Quæ explicatio præferenda est Grotianæ. Corrumpitur, inquam, vetus homo, non intereundo, (hoc enim cum maxime vellet Apostolus, sed id per pravas concupiscentias non fit, quibus potius ipse conservatur,) sed corruptionem nativam per deceptrices cupiditates augendo, ut qui corruptus est, subinde fiat corruptior. Quod oppositio docet. Nam ut in renovatione non exprimitur fructus aut consequens ejusdem, sed qualis ea sit, & in quo consistat: Ita in veteris Adami descriptione non exitium designat quod affert, sed statum genusque ejusdem, quod magis magisque se corrumpat per pravas cupiditates.

Veteris autem & novi hominis mentione Apostolus innuit non tantum inferiores facultates hominis corruptas esse & renovatione indigere, sed totum hominem; ideo mentis, quæ præcipuum illud in homine est, quo à brutis distinguitur, sedes rationis, ac dux voluntatis renovationem indicat. Quæ & transformatio dicitur per renovationem mentis, Rom. cap. XII. vers. 1. non substantiae μεταμορφώσει, sed animi novi conforma- tione, sicut & indutio novi hominis sit non quoad substantiam, sed qualitatem. Veteri enim oppo- nitur, qui non est primus Adamus, sed corruptio ex Adamo tracta. Imo hac similitudine declara- tur, novum & veterem hominem ab induente & exuente differre, sicut vestis res diversa est, ab eo, qui exuit & induit. Ut vetus homo est peccatum originale: Ita novus homo est χάρισμα sanctifica- tionis à Spiritu Sancto effectum in homine regenito, quo peccatum crucifigitur, concupiscentia prava re- sistitur, & vitae Deo placentis studium de die in diem incrementa sumit, ut habet B. Glassius ad Dom. XIX. Trin. p. 819.

## 4:25
Ver. 25. Wherefore putting away lying) He says this against those who, in order to gain the thanks of either Jews or Gentiles, said other things than they felt.

Speak truth each one with his neighbor) From Zech. chap. VIII. v. 10. where the same words are in Greek, except that for with his neighbor it is toward his neighbor. Speak openly what you feel, not only among Christians, but also among others, who just as before the law were called neighbors, as Exod. chap. XI. v. 2. so also in the new law. Thus Augustine interprets this place in his book against lying. Contrary to this is to speak a lie, Ps. XII. v. 2.

For we are members of one another) That is, besides that society of which we have treated, there is also another certain society of either the state or the human race: And this also must be observed, which cannot happen if the tongue says one thing while the mind conceives another.

The Apostle now delivers special precepts making for renewal, 1. that detesting lying we speak the truth, which pertains primarily to governing the tongue of the new man. He prohibits lying, however, not of such hypocrites who in the cause of religion speak otherwise than they feel, but also in common life, and thus in general any kind. Which unless we put off the old man, we do not strive to put off. Which must be held likewise concerning other vices, just as on the contrary, that we may put on the new man, it is necessary to imply the contrary virtues. I said primarily. For we easily agree here with Crocius, who by lying understands not only lying speech, but also all hypocrisy, pretense, duplicity, as Haymo speaks, imposture, calumny, deceit, snares, fraud, flattery, and indeed even the disease of lying, with which corrupt nature is intensely afflicted. And further: I interpret truth as integrity and candor, by which he who is a good man seeks to deceive no one, but to deal sincerely and faithfully with those with whom he has business, in word and deed. Nor does it matter what the Apostle says, speak; for if candor is required in words, much more so in work. For where things do not correspond to words, there is no truth, but mere pretense and lying. But that reason of the Apostle is not, for we are members of one another by the common bond of men or of the faithful (although we are also bound by the same to speak the truth) but by a closer one, by which Christians are more mutually bound to the pursuit of sincerity and truth, namely, taken from the condition of the faithful. We are all indeed joined by the bond of nature, which is violated by lies. Whence the pursuit of truth is generally commended, Matt. chap. V. v. 37. Jas. c. V. v. 22. but specifically here the mutual duty of candor is prescribed to be cultivated among the Ephesian Christians themselves; because it adheres to the allegories proposed from the condition of the members: For we are not only members with respect to the head CHRIST, but also mutually among ourselves. Therefore, as members in a body serve one another without fraud and pretense: So also sincerity ought deservedly to be commended to the faithful in mutual intercourse. The blessed Glassius explains this beautifully on the 19th Sunday after Trinity. Just as one member of a human body that is in a right state does not exercise deceits and fallacies toward another, but rather seeks and promotes its advantages sincerely; and if anything happens to one member, whether of pain or joy, it is known to all the rest by a real sympathy and is common: So Christians ought to behave toward one another candidly and openly without lying and simulation out of sincere charity. Thus Christians ought to communicate to one another not the poison of hatred, vengeance, envy, and malice, but the vital Spirit of love, sympathy, and rejoicing together. Just as the tongue in the human body does not speak those things which result in harm to the other members: So also let Christians not speak to one another things that are harmful, and which either stir up scandal or injure reputation, but things that are salutary, true, good, and useful, etc. This therefore is the fruit of faith and love, which if it be absent, and thus there be lying in a man, that is, if heart and tongue disagree for the sake of doing harm deceitfully, if one deals deceitfully and craftily with a neighbor, etc., charity is also absent, and its very mother and fountainhead, true faith: And in such a man the renewal of the Holy Spirit is not, but on the contrary, the oldness of the flesh, the captivity of Satan, the wrath of GOD, whence also follows the punishment which David threatens to liars and the unjust, Psalm LV. 22.

But what Grotius observes from Exod. chap. XI. ver. 2, that those who were called neighbors before the law, in it something deceitful is hidden, as if that appellation varied in and under the law, and that precept, you shall love your neighbor as yourself, did not have a place in it, which is against Christ's interpretation in Luke X. as noted elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Διὸ ἀποθέμενοι τὸ ψεῦδος) Hoc adversus eos dicit, qui ut gratias captarent aut Judaeorum aut gentium, alia dicebant, quam sentirent.

Λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν ἕκαστος μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ) Ex Zach. cap. VIII. v. 10. ubi eadem verba in Graeco, nisi quod pro μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον est πρὸς τὸν πλησίον. Aperte loquimini, quod sentitis, non tantum apud Christianos, sed etiam apud alios, qui sicut ante legem dicebantur οἱ πλησίον, ut Exod. cap. XI. v. 2. ita etiam in nova lege. Sic Augustinus hunc locum interpretatur libro contra mendacium. Contrarium huic mendacium loqui, Ps. XII. v. 2.

Ὅτι ἐσμὲν ἀλλήλων μέλη) Id est, praeter illam societa- tem, de qua egimus, est & alia quaedam societas aut ci- vitatis aut humani generis: Et haec quoque observanda est, quod fieri nequit, si aliud lingua dicat, quam mens concipit.

Specialia jam praecepta ad renovationem fa- cientia tradit Apostolus, 1. ut mendacium de- testantes veritatem loquamur, quod ad regen- dam novi hominis linguam imprimis pertinet. Mendacium autem non hypocritarum talium, qui in causa religionis aliter loquuntur quam sen- tiunt, sed etiam in vita communi, adeoque in ge- nere quodvis prohibet. Quod nisi deponamus veterem hominem, deponere non annitimur. Quod pariter de aliis vitiis habendum, quem- admodum contra ut novum hominem indua- mus, virtutes contrarias innuere oportet. Dixi imprimis. Nam facile annuimus hic Crocio, qui per mendacium non tantum intelligit sermonem mendacem, sed & omnem hypocrisin, fucum, duplicitatem, ut loquitur Haymo, imposturam, calumniam, dolum, insidias, fraudem, adulatio- nem, imo & mentiendi morbum, quo natura corrupta impense laborat. Et porro: Veritatem interpretor integritatem & candorem, quo nemi- nem fallere, qui vir bonus est, sed sincere & fide- liter cum illis, cum quibus negotium est, agere studet sermone & facto. Nec refert, quod Aposto- lus ait, loquimini; Si enim candor in verbis re- quiritur, multo magis in opere. Ubi enim res verbis non respondent, non est veritas, sed merus fucus & mendacium. Non autem ratio illa A- postoli, nam sumus alii aliorum membra à com- muni hominum, aut fidelium vinculo, (quanquam eodem etiam adstringamur ad veritatem dicen- dam) sed ab arctiori, quo Christiani magis ad sin- ceritatis & veritatis studium mutuo devincti sunt, nempe à conditione fidelium petita. Omnes uti- que sumus naturae vinculo conjuncti, quod men- daciis violatur. Unde veritatis studium genera- tim commendatur Matth. cap. V. v. 37. Jac. c. V. v. 22. speciatim autem hic Ephesiis Christianis inter se colendum mutuum candoris officium praescribitur; quia propositae à membrorum conditione allegoriae inhaeret: Non enim so- lum membra sumus respectu capitis CHRISTI, sed etiam inter nos mutuo. Ideo ut membra in corpore sibi invicem inserviunt sine fraude & fuco: Sic etiam fidelibus sinceritas in mutua consuetudine merito commendata esse debet. Pulchre hoc explicat B. Glassius Domin. XIX. Trinit. Quemadmodum unum membrum cor- poris humani recte se habentis erga alterum non exercet dolos ac fallacias, sed potius ejus commoda εἰλικρινῶς quærit ac promovet; & si quid uni membro contingit sive doloris sive gaudii, id omni- bus cæteris reali συμπαθείᾳ constat & commune est: Sic absque mendacio & simulatione candide aperteque versari invicem ex sincera charitate Christiani debent. Sic Christiani sibi invicem non odii, vindictæ, invidiæ & ἐπιχαιρεκακίας vene- num, sed vitalem amoris συμπαθείας συγχαρείας Spiritum communicare debent. Sicut lingua in corpore humano non proloquitur ea, quæ cæteris membris in noxam cedunt: Sic & Christiani non loquantur invicem, quæ noxia sunt, & vel scandalum movent, vel existimationem lædunt, sed salutaria, vera, bona, & utilia &c. Hic igitur fructus fidei & dilectionis est, qui si ab- sit, sicque in homine mendacium sit, hoc est, si cor & lingua mendaciter nocendi causa discre- pent, si dolose & subdole cum proximo &c. aga- tur, abest etiam charitas, & ipsa ejus mater ac scaturigo vera fides: Et in tali homine renova- tio Spiritus Sancti non est, sed contra, vetustas carnis, captivitas Satanæ, ira DEI, unde & pœ- na insequitur, quam mendacibus & injustis com- minatur David, Psal. LV. 22.

Quod autem Grotius è cap. Exod. XI. vers. 2. observat, qui ante legem οἱ πλησίον dicti, in ea ὕπουλόν τι occultatur, quasi in, & sub lege ea ap- pellatio variarit, nec in illo istud præceptum, di- liges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum, locum ha- buerit, quod est contra Christi interpretationem Luc. X. ut alias notatum.

## 4:26
Ver. 26. Be angry and do not sin) I wonder that there are those who doubt whether this is from Psalm IV. ver. 5. For the LXX version has the same words there: Be angry and do not sin, where we said it could be rightly translated: Are you angry? But do not sin, by that kind of speaking which we have in Jas. V. v. 14.

Ὁ ἥλιος μὴ ἐπιδυέτω ἐπὶ τῷ παροργισμῷ ὑμῶν) This is a Hebrew idiom concerning that which must not be prolonged, Deut. XXIV. 15. and at the same time an application of that law which is in Deut. XXI. 23. By an argument from the lesser to the greater. If punishments prescribed by law are not to be extended until evening, much less ought anger privately conceived be extended beyond it. Plutarch: Πυθαγορικοὶ γένει μηδὲν προσήκοντες ἀλλὰ κοινῇ λόγῳ μετέχοντες, εἴποτε προαχθεῖεν εἰς λοιδορίας ὑπ᾽ ὀργῆς, πρὶν ἢ τὸν ἥλιον δῦναι τὰς δεξιὰς ἐμβάλλοντες ἀλλήλοις καὶ ἀσπασάμενοι διελύοντο.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε) Miror, esse, qui dubitent, an hoc sit ex Psalmo IV. vers. 5. Nam versio LXX. eadem ibi habet verba: Ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμάρ- τάνετε, ubi diximus, recte verti posse: Irascimini? At ne peccate, eo loquendi genere, quod habemus Jac. V. v. 14.

Ὁ ἥλιος μὴ ἐπιδυέτω ἐπὶ τῷ παροργισμῷ ὑμῶν) Est lo- cutio Ebræa de eo, quod protrahendum non est, Deut. XXIV. 15. & simul applicatio ejus legis, quæ est Deut. XXI. 23. Argumento à minori ad majus. Si pœnæ lege præscriptæ non extendantur usque ad vesperam, multo mi- nus extendi ultra eam debet ira privatim suscepta. Plu- tarchus: Πυθαγορικοὶ γένει μηδὲν προσήκοντες ἀλλὰ κοινῇ λό- γῳ μετέχοντες, εἴποτε προαχθεῖεν εἰς λοιδορίας ὑπ᾽ ὀργῆς, πρὶν ἢ τὸν ἥλιον δῦναι τὰς δεξιὰς ἐμβάλλοντες ἀλλήλοις καὶ ἀσπα- σάμενοι διελύοντο.

## 4:27
Vers. 27. Μήτε δίδοτε τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ) An excellent admonition. For if the movements of the mind are fostered by neglect, they pass into a habit, the Devil obtaining a certain right over such persons, concerning which matter we have spoken at Luke XXII. 3. John XIII. 27. Acts V. v. 3. Thus:

Neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris.

A second special warning directs the heart: namely, that we should lay aside the emotion of illicit anger, which is both sinful in itself and tends toward leaving a place for the Devil, the author of all enmity. We assent here to the interpretation of Grotius, which Crocius also brought forward from Bullinger, Musculus, Hemmingius, Piscator, and indeed even Beza, namely that this is indicated: since there is no one who is not sometimes moved to anger, with a certain propensity toward it inherent in nature itself, Christians must take care, if it happens that they become angry—as we are all men subject to passions and infirmities—not to become angry for any reason or for a trivial one, nor to loosen the reins of anger to such an extent that they consent to it or act upon it, what sudden impulse suggests, or dictates, to devote effort, that they should rather repress the first impulse, lest it break out into a more serious sin. What is said about the setting of the sun, Haymo, with Jerome, understands as the Sun of righteousness. But this measure of anger is prescribed, which would not be sufficiently consistent in that sense, nor should one rashly depart from the dispute. Whence neither the allegory of Lombard concerning the sun of reason, which ought not to be darkened by the clouds of anger, can be approved. More correctly, Ambrose says one is warned that anger should end with the day as it arose with the day, lest, namely, the bed receive those who are agitated, or sleep overwhelm them, which can easily turn into the sleep of eternal night. Therefore, the memory of an injury is to be washed from the mind in this way, before the setting of the sun, which arose from goodness itself, lest returning anger disturb rest, impede nocturnal prayer, and, confirmed by longer delay, depart with more difficulty. How the Father and the Son, says Jerome on this passage, stand before the door and knock, that they may enter and dine with him who has received them: So also the adversary is always prepared to break into us, and, when we have given him a place, he enters. But he is accustomed, before he comes, to send certain darts ahead, and to make a thought the precursor of his arrival: If we have nurtured this in our heart once received, and have made it grow, when he has made his offspring in us increased, he himself will dare to enter.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Μήτε δίδοτε τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ) Optima mo- nitio. Nam si motus animi negligendo foveantur, trans- eunt in ἕξιν, Diabolo jus quoddam in tales nanciscente, qua de re diximus ad Luc. XXII. 3. Joh. XIII. 27. Act. V. v. 3. Sic:

Neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris.

Monitum speciale alterum cor dirigit: ut nempe affectum iræ illicitæ deponamus, quæ tum in se peccaminosa est, tum eo tendit, ut Diabolo autori omnis inimicitiæ locus relinqua- tur. Annuimus hic interpretationi Grotii, qua- lem etiam è Bullingero, Musculo, Hemmingio, Piscatore, imo & Beza protulit Crocius, id nempe indicari: cum nemo sit, qui non aliquando ad iram commoveatur, in naturæ ipsa hærente qua- dam ad eam propensione, cavendum esse Christia- nis, si irasci contingat, ut omnes homines sumus affectibus & infirmitatibus obnoxii, ne vel ulla, vel levi de causa irascantur, vel iræ frena la- xent, eo usque, ut in id consentiant, aut faciant, quod subitus impetus suggerit, dictarve, ad dan- dam operam, ut primum impetum potius repri- mant, ne in peccatum gravius exeat. Quod de solis occasu dicitur, Haymo cum Hieronymo de sole justitiæ intelligit. Sed hic modus iræ præ- scribitur, qui eo sensu non satis constaret, nec à litem temere recedendum. Unde nec Lom- bardi allegoria de sole rationis, qui non debeat obtenebrari nebulis iræ, probari potest. Re- ctius, Ambrosius moneri ait, ut iræ cum die orta cum die desinat, ne scilicet lectus commotos re- cipiat, aut somnus opprimat, qui facile æternæ noctis somnus evadere potest. Ideò ita injuriæ memoria ex animo diluenda, priusquam immi- neat solis occasus, ab ipsa bonitate exorti, ne ira recurrens quietem turbet, orationem no- cturnam impediat, & mora longiore confirmata difficilius recedat. Quomodo Pater & Filius, inquit Hieronymus in hunc locum, stant ante ostium & pulsant, ut introeant & cœnent cum eo, qui se receperit: Ita & adversarius semper in nos est paratus irrumpere, &, cum locum dederimus, ingreditur. Solet autem, antequam veniat, quædam jacula præmittere, & præcurso- rem adventus sui facere cogitationem: Hanc si nos in corde nostro susceptam nutrierimus intrin- secus, & crescere fecerimus, cum in nobis pro- lem suam auctam fecerit, & ipse audebit in- trare.

## 4:28
Vers. 28. Ὁ κλέπτων μηκέτι κλεπτέτω) That is, ὁ κλέψας. For among the Hebrews, just as a past tense verb is used for the present, so a present participle is used for the past, because the Hebrews do not have more forms.

Μᾶλλον δὲ κοπιάτω ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθὸν ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν) A similar manner of speaking 1 Cor. ch. IV. vers. 12. 1 Thess. ch. IV. vers. 11. Add Acts ch. XX. vers. 34. But he well adds τὸ ἀγαθὸν, lest anyone think that any gain is approved, such as that of harlots and pimps.

Ἴνα ἔχῃ μεταδιδόναι τῷ χρείαν ἔχοντι) It is a brief expression. For the sense is, that he may not only have himself, from which to live, but also in addition something by which he may help the needy, like that poor widow in Luke XXI. 2.

This is the third commandment directing the hands, that we should not extend them to the handling of another's property, or theft or robbery, but apply them to the works enjoined upon us, and suitable, so that we may not only acquire for ourselves by divine blessing those things which make for food and clothing, but also be able to impart something to a needy neighbor to relieve his necessity. Nor indeed does he say, as Jerome warns, but rather let him labor by working with his own hands, which is good, so that he may not be in need, and may have food, and cause trouble to no one: but let him labor, he says, with his hands, which is good, so that he may have something from which to share with the needy. Whoever, therefore, labors to this extent only, that he himself may not be in need, and draws back his hand from others, although he may applaud himself, yet he has not fulfilled the Apostle's commandment. The sense, which Jerome adds, or rather prefers, concerning the spiritual theft of the False Prophets, who steal words, each one from his neighbor, Jer. XXIII. who come as thieves and robbers, John X. this is foreign, where labor of the hands is opposed to theft, and the end of this is established as the communication of temporal goods. But he does not so strictly bind everyone to manual labors. For Bullinger rightly says: If what you do is convenient and useful to the republic, if you defraud no one, the labor to which you have devoted yourself is holy, whether you labor with your hands, or feet, or body, or finally with your mind. Therefore, from the prior and more common organ, labor is described as theft through unjust manual extension, 1 Thess. III. So here the Apostle describes due labor through the good operation of hands. There are lawful, honest, useful, necessary works; there are illicit, base, useless, unnecessary ones. He commends the former, he excludes the latter, although they have their own labor. Cf. 1 Thess. IV. 11. Luke VI. 35. Eccles. XII. 4. But he prohibits theft generally. Johannes Molanus denies that theft is committed in a very small thing. But theft is simply prohibited, Exod. XX. 15. whether it be of a great thing or a small one. Bellarmine grants that theft of a small thing is a sin, but denies that it is mortal. But every sin by its nature deserves death because of the offense to divine justice. The wages of sin is death, Rom. VI. v. last. Emanuel à Sa thinks it is permissible to take something secretly from a rich man who is bound to help a poor man. But no exception is applied here. Cf. August. lib. VI. de mendac. cap. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ὁ κλέπτων μηκέτι κλεπτέτω) Id est, ὁ κλέ- ψας. Nam apud Ebræos sicut verbum Præteritum usur- patur pro Præsente, ita Participium Præsens pro Præteri- to, quia plures formas Ebræi non habent.

Μᾶλλον δὲ κοπιάτω ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθὸν ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν) Simile loquendi genus 1. Cor. cap. IV. vers. 12. 1. Thessal. cap. IV. vers. 11. Adde Actor. cap. XX. vers. 34. Bene autem addit τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ne quis putet, quemvis quæ- stum probari, qualis est scortorum & lenonum.

Ἴνα ἔχῃ μεταδιδόναι τῷ χρείαν ἔχοντι) Est brevis lo- quutio. Sensus enim est, ut non tantum ipse habeat, unde vivat, sed & insuper aliquid, quo egenos adjuvet, ut illa paupercula Luc. XXI. 2.

Tertium hoc est præceptum manus dirigens, ne easdem extendamus ad rei alienæ contrecta- tionem, vel furtum aut rapinam, sed adhibea- mus ad opera nobis injuncta, & competentia, ut non tantum nobis acquiramus divina be- nedictione ea, quæ πρὸς τὰ ἄλφιτα faciunt ad victum & amictum necessaria, sed etiam egenti proximo impertiri aliquid possimus ad suble- vandam ejus necessitatem, Neque vero ait, mo- nente Hieronymo, magis autem laboret operando manibus suis, quod bonum est, ut non indigeat, & habeat victum, & nulli molestiam exhibeat: sed la- boret, inquit, manibus suis, quod bonum est, ut ha- beat, unde communicet indigentibus. Qui igitur ad hoc tantù laborat, ut ipse non egeat, & à cæteris con- trahit manum, quamvis applaudat sibi, tamen Apo- stoli præceptum non fecit. Sensus, quem addit, imo præfert Hieronymus de furto spirituali Pseudo- Prophetarum, qui furantur sermones, unusquis- que à proximo suo, Jer. XXIII. qui veniunt, ut fu- res & latrones, Joh. X. alienus hic est, ubi furto labor manuum opponitur, & finis hujus commu- nicatio bonorum temporalium constituitur. Non vero ita ad manuarias operas quemvis adstringit ἀποτόμως. Nam recte Bullingerus: Si commo- dum & utile reipublicæ est, quod agis, si neminem fraudas, sanctus est labor, cui te dedideris, sive ma- nibus, sive pedibus, sive corpore, sive animo tandem labores. A priori itaque & communiori organo labor describitur ut furtum per extensionem ma- nuam injustam, 1. Thess. III. Ita hic laborem debi- tum per operationem manuum bonam describit Apostolus. Sunt operæ licitæ, honestæ, utiles, ne- cessariæ; sunt illicitæ, turpes, inutiles, non ne- cessariæ. Illas commendat, has excludit, quam- vis suum habeant laborem. Conf. 1. Thess. IV. 11. Luc. VI. 35. Eccles. XII. 4. Prohibet autem gene- ratim omne furtum. Johannes Molanus negat, fur- tum in re minima committi. At simpliciter pro- hibitum est furtum, Exod. XX. 15. sive sit rei magnæ, sive minimæ. Bellarminus rei minimæ furtum pec- catum esse largitur, negat autem esse mortife- rum. Sed omne peccatum natura sua mortem meretur ob offensam justitiæ divinæ. Stipen- dium peccati mors est, Rom. VI. v. ult. Emanuel à Saa putat, licere à Divite, qui pauperi subvenire tenetur, rem clam accipere. Sed nulla hic adhi- bita exceptio. Conf. August. lib. VI. de mendac. cap. 7.

## 4:29
Vers. 29. Πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω) It is said to go out from the mouth, what we speak, Matt. IV. 4. XV. 18. λόγος σαπρὸς דָבָר בָּאשׁ, or רַקָבוֹן Joel II. 20. Job XLI. 19. a rotten word, that is, obscene, of which we would have many, I believe, if the Ephesiaca of Xenophon existed. In the Glossary σαπρὸς is foul.

Ἀλλ’ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας) But let that word go out, which is apt for that instruction which is necessary for each one. The genitive for an adjective, in the Hebrew manner; χρεία is a frequent word in Sirach.

Ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσι) Through which you may deserve well of the hearers. Thus we had ἐπιτελεῖν χάριν 2 Cor. VIII. v. 6. he deserves well of someone, who leads them away from vices. May the Latin rightly profit here.

This fourth commandment governs speech. The former required the harmony of heart and mouth, excluding lying. Now it wishes to exclude not only foul and filthy speech, but also, as the word σαπρὸς properly implies, rotten speech, see Matt. VII. 17, ch. XII. 20, ch. XIII. 48, Luke VI. v. 43. That the old man may be put off, those things which corrupt the use, the hands, the tongue, and other members of man must be laid aside. In a servant of God, says Ambrose, all things ought to appear good, nor should his purity be stained in any part. For what does it profit to have a clean life and a filthy mouth, when the Lord says that everyone shall be justified or condemned by his own words. Nor can it seem credible that he lives well who speaks ill. For speaking ill is drawn into many vices. Impure speech is an index of an impure heart, and a precursor and inventor of evil deeds. The Vulgate rendered it the edification of faith. But in the Greek Codices τῆς χρείας is held, not τῆς πίστεως. Whence Jerome explained it as for the edification of opportunity. But χρεία denotes necessity, or rather utility. Beza explains it by hypallage: for the use of edification. But without hypallage the sense is entirely convenient. If anyone is convenient for the edification of present necessity, that is, where that opportunity of Jerome is also to be heeded: As often as someone profits from our speech, and according to the opportunity of time, place, and person edifies those who hear, good speech has proceeded from our mouth. But as often as we speak either not in time, or in an opportune place, or not as is fitting for the hearers: so often does evil speech proceed from our mouth to the destruction of those who hear. Let us therefore consider what we speak, because we are to render an account for every idle word on the day of judgment. And even if we do not harm, yet if we do not edify: the penalty of an evil word must be paid by us. Beza, along with Hemmingius, interprets χάριν as any kind of convenience and utility, but that is already included in οἰκοδομῇ. Therefore, we prefer to interpret it not indeed of grace which speech may produce for the speaker with the hearer, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, but of holy delight with Blessed Luther, whom Crocius also prefers here, translating: 'That it is pleasant to hear': 'The children of this world,' he says, 'prepare their speeches for the delight of the flesh, ea is something else, just as the joy of the world differs greatly from the joy of the Spirit. A fragrant rose and odoriferous flowers are not only useful for restoring and maintaining the health of the body, but they also delight with their sweetness; thus, he who hears holy speech perceives the fragrance of a sweet odor. Thus, therefore, the Apostle wishes the speech of Christians to be prepared so that it may be pleasant and lovable to the spirit. To this pertains what he says, 'think on things that are lovely,' Philippians ch. IV, v. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω) Exire ex ore dicitur, quod loquimur, Matth. IV. 4. XV. 18. λόγος σαπρὸς דָבָר בָּאשׁ, vel רַקָבוֹן Joël. II. 20. Job. XLI. 19. sermo putridus, id est, obscœnus, qualia multa, ut credo, haberemus, si existe- rent Ephesiaca Xenophontis. In Glossario σαπρὸς fœdus.

Ἀλλ’ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας) Sed is ser- mo exeat, qui aptus est ad institutionem eam, quæ cuique est necessaria. Genitivus pro Adjectivo, more Ebræo; χρεία vox frequens apud Sirachidem.

Ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσι) Per quem bene merearis de auditoribus. Sic ἐπιτελεῖν χάριν habuimus 2. Cor. VIII. v. 6. bene de aliquo meretur, qui à vitiis abducit. Prosit hîc Latinus recte.

Quartum hoc præceptum sermonem modera- tur. Prius cordis & oris consonantia requirebat excludens mendacium. Jam omnem sermonem non fœdum tantum & spurcum, sed, quod pro- prie vox σαπρὸς infert, putrem exclusum vult, vid. Matth. VII. 17. cap. XII. 20. cap. XIII. 48. Luc. VI. v. 43. Ut homo vetus exuatur, quæ usui, quæ manus, quæ linguam & alia membra hominis vi- tiant, deponenda sunt. In Dei servo, inquit Ambro- sius, omnia debent bona videri, nec ex aliqua parte puritas ejus debet maculari. Quid enim prodest mundam vitam habere & os sordidum, cum dicat Dominus, quod unusquisque verbis suis aut justifica- bitur aut condemnabitur. Nec credibile potest vi- deri, bene vivere eum, qui male loquatur. Male enim loqui ad multa trahitur vitia. Sermo impurus est impuri cordis index, & facti mali præcursor in- ventorque. Vulgatus ædificationem fidei reddidit. Sed in Græcis Codicibus τῆς χρείας habetur, non τῆς πίστεως. Unde Hieronymus exposuit ad ædifica- tionem opportunitatis. Sed χρεία necessitatem, vel utilitatem potius notat. Beza per hypallagen expli- cat: ad usum ædificationis. Sed sine hypallage sen- sus omnino commodus est. Si quis commodus est ad ædificationem necessitatis præsentis scilicet, ubi illa opportunitas Hieronymi etiam attendenda: Quotiescunque ex sermone nostro aliquis proficit, & juxta opportunitatem temporis, loci, & personæ ædi- ficat audientes, bonus de ore nostro sermo processit. Quoties vero loquimur aut non in tempore, aut op- portuno loco, aut non ut convenit audientibus: toties sermo malus procedit de ore nostro ad destructionem eorum, qui audiunt. Consideremus itaq;, quid loqua- mur, quia pro omni otioso verbo reddituri sumus ra- tionem in die judicii. Et etiamsi non lædamus, non tamen ædificemus: mali verbi nobis luenda sit pœna. Χάριν interpretatur etiam Beza cum Hemmingio de quovis commodi & utilitatis genere, sed id jam in οἰκοδομῇ comprehensum. Ideo non quidem de- gratia, quam sermo dicenti apud auditorem pariat cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, sed de sancta ob- lectatione malumus interpretari cum B. Luthero, quem hic præfert etiam Crocius, vertentem: Daß es holdselig sey zu hoͤren: Filii, inquit, hujus mundi ad carnis delectationem suos sermones comparant, eam quærentes in obscœnitate & scurrilitate. Alia est oblectatio sancta, sicut gaudium mundi a gaudio Spiritus plurimum differt. Rosa fragrans & flores odoriferi non solum utiles sunt reparandæ, tuendæ- que sanitati corporis, sed etiam suaveolentia sua ob- lectant, sic odoramentum odoris grati percipit, qui sanctum sermonem audit. Sic ergo vult Apostolus, sermonem Christianorum esse comparatum, ut spiri- tui jucundus sit & amabilis. Quo pertinent, quod dicit, cogitate, quæ sunt amabilia, Philipp. cap. IV. v. 8.

## 4:30
Verse 30. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is greater than the angels, yet the Israelites were often warned not to offend an angel, Exodus ch. XXIII, v. 21, where in Hebrew it is אַל־תַּמֵּר, in Greek μὴ ἀπείθει αὐτῷ, Isaiah LIII. 10, 'they provoked the Holy Spirit.' Hermas II. 10: 'For sadness is the most wicked of all spirits and the worst for the servants of God, and it drives out the spirit of all and torments the Holy Spirit.' Afterwards: 'This sadness enters into a man and makes the Holy Spirit sad and vexes him.' Soon after: 'Do not offend the Holy Spirit, who dwells in you.' Nor is that saying of Seneca, Epistle XLI, entirely foreign to this: 'I say this, Lucilius, a holy spirit sits within us, an observer and guardian of our good and evil deeds; as he is treated by us, so he treats us.' Tertullian on spectacles: GOD has commanded the Holy Spirit, as being tender and delicate for the good of His nature, to be treated with tranquility, and gentleness, and peace, and quiet.

In whom you were sealed unto the day of redemption: By whom you were sealed, so that you may be certain of the coming day of redemption: namely, of the bodies, which is the resurrection, Rom. VIII, v. 23. Thus 'unto redemption' above I. 14, where the word 'you were sealed' also preceded. See what is said there.

That comparison with the angels seems out of place here, nor does it fit the passage in Exodus ch. XXIII, verse 21, where the speech is not about any created angel, but an uncreated one. The Ephesians are said to be sealed not 'of' the day, but 'unto' the day of redemption; therefore, it is not only certainty about that coming day, but the confirmation of our hope of redemption and eternal salvation is sealed in us by the Holy Spirit until the very day of redemption, until hope is converted into reality. That redemption can be understood both as the redemption of the soul, which occurs at the end of life when the soul is thoroughly freed from all sin and misery, and as that of the body, which is expected in the blessed resurrection: nor is there any reason why it should be restricted to this in the present passage. It is different in Rom. ch. VIII, v. 23. For there the speech was about the universal liberation of the creature. Blessed Baldwin, with Jerome, refers it to the day of baptism, where GOD made us His servants marked with a brand. But in the Greek it is 'unto the day of redemption,' not as the Vulgate has it, 'in the day of redemption.' Some refer this precept to the preceding, others to the following. But it can be established as a peculiar warning, or argument, pertaining to all the hortatory warnings, that we should not in any way, whether by those things which he has said, or by those which he was still about to say, grieve the Holy Spirit by our vices, which is therefore placed as if in the middle. The Spirit is said to be grieved 'anthropopathically,' which is also customary regarding GOD the Father; therefore, the Socinians rashly challenge the Deity of the Holy Spirit based on that way of speaking. Regarding which Jerome says: 'The grief of the Holy Spirit is to be understood in the same way as the wrath of GOD, and sleep, and the rest of the passions of human likenesses.' Cf. Isaiah ch. LXIII, v. 16. He is not grieved here, says Ambrose, so as to suffer, since He is impassible, but when he says He is grieved, he signifies this for our sake, because He deserts us, because we have injured Him by despising His warnings. Therefore, His grief is our indignity, which forbids us from being called children of God. For He Himself is the Holy Spirit, who signifies that we are children of God, remaining in us.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Καὶ μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον) Major est Spiritus Sanctus Angelis, at moniti sæpe Israelitæ, ne An- gelum offenderent, Exod. cap. XXIII. v. 21. ubi in Ebræo אַל־תַּמֵּר, in Græco μὴ ἀπείθει αὐτῷ, Es. LIII. 10. παρώξυναν τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον αὐτῶ. Hermas II. 10. tristitia enim omni- um spirituum nequissima est & pessima servis Dei, & omnium spiritus exterminat, & cruciat Spiritum Sanctum. Postea: Tristitia hæc intrat in hominem & tristem facit Spiritum Sanctum & vexat eum. Mox: noli offendere Spiritum Sanctum, qui in te habitat. Nec plane alienum hinc est illud Senecæ epist. XLI. ita dico, Lucili, sacer intra nos Spiritus sedet, bonorum malorumque nostrorum observator & custos, hic prout a nobis tractatus est, ita nos ipse tra- ctat. Tertullianus de spectaculis: DEUS præcepit Spi- ritum Sanctum, utpote pro naturæ suæ bono tenerum & de- licatum, tranquillitate, & lenitate & pace & quiete tra- ctari.

Ἐν ᾧ ἐσφραγίσθητε εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως) Per quem signati estis, ut certi sitis de ventura die redemptionis: nempe corporum, quæ est resurrectio, Rom. VIII. v. 23. Sic εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν supra I. 14. ubi & verbum ἐσφραγίσθητε præcessit. Vide ibi dicta.

Illa cum Angelis comparatio & aliena hic vi- detur, nec loco Exod. cap. XXIII. vers. 21. con- venit, ubi non de Angelo quopiam creato, sed increato sermo est. Obsignati autem dicuntur Ephesii non de die, sed ad diem redemptionis, non certitudo itaque tantum de ventura illa die, sed confirmatio spei nostræ redemptionis & sa- lutis æternæ in nobis obsignatur per Spiritum Sanctum usque ad ipsum redemptionis diem, donec spes in rem convertatur. Potest autem ἀπολύτρωσις illa intelligi cum de animæ redem- ptione, quæ in fine vitæ, cum anima ab omni peccato & miseria penitus liberatur, tum de corporis, quæ expectatur in beata resurrectione: nec est, cur ad hanc in præsenti loco restringa- tur. Alia est Rom. c. VIII. v. 23. Nam ibi de universali creaturæ liberatione sermo fuit. Ad diem baptismi refert cum Hieronymo B. Baldui- nus, ubi DEUS nos servos suos fecit stigmati- cos. Sed in Græco est, in diem redemptionis, non ut Vulgata habet, in die redemptionis. Re- ferunt hoc præceptum alii ad præcedens, alii ad subsequens. Sed peculiare id statui potest mo- nitum, aut argumentum, ad omnia monita de- hortatoria pertinens, ne ullo modo sive iis, quæ dixit, sive, quæ adhuc dicturus erat, vitiis contristemus Spiritum Sanctum, quod idcirco in medio veluti collocatur. Contristari autem Spi- ritus dicitur καθ’ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν, quæ de DEO Patre etiam usitata est, idcirco temere ex ea lo- quendi ratione Sociniani solicitant Spiritus San- cti Deitatem. Quo de Hieronymus: Mæror Sancti Spiritus sic intelligendus, quomodo ira DEI, & somnus, & cætera humanarum similitudinum passiones. Conf. Es. cap. LXIII. v. 16. Non hic, inquit Ambrosius, contristatur, ut patiatur, quippe cum impassibilis sit, sed cum eum contri- statum dicit, nostri causa hoc significat, quia de- serit nos, quod læserimus eum, contemnendo mo- nita ejus. Contristatio itaque ejus nostra indi- gnitas est, quæ filios Dei nos prohibet appellari. Ipse enim est Spiritus Sanctus, qui significat filios Dei, manens in nobis.

## 4:31
Verse 31. All bitterness) Evil-speaking, see Rom. III, v. 14.

And wrath) The first inflammation of the mind, Rom. ch. II, v. and 2 Cor. XII. 20. Gal. V. 20. Col. III. 8.

And anger) A movement passing into a passion.

And clamor) Clamor is the horse of anger, says Chrysostom here, when you have thrown it, you have unhorsed the rider.

Καὶ βλασφημία) Indeed, all evil speaking is called βλασφημία, but so that it may be distinguished ἀπὸ τῆς πικρίας, the words to be understood here seem to be those which in any way harm the honor of God. For Menander also used this word in this way: and it is accustomed to be used in this way in our own writings. See Matt. IX. 3. 2 Kings ch. XIX. 6. 22. Isa. LII. 5.

Ἀρθῆτω ἀφ' ὑμῶν) Let it be far away הוסר. Σὺν πάσῃ κακίᾳ) See Rom. I. 29. 1 Cor. V. 8. XIV. 20. Coloss. III. 8. Tit. III. 8.

This is a new commandment, that the Apostle dissuades from bitterness, which does not boil up in the heart so as to break forth through the tongue. Therefore, bitterness is not evil speaking here, but the root of heat and anger. Excessive severity, which argues a will to strike, to move, to irritate, rather than to amend and correct. Indeed, he dissuaded from anger above, but here he roots it out, says Theophylactus. For bitterness is the root of irascibility and fury. But where a sharper storm of anger bristles, it overcomes the lid of the mouth more vehemently with its waves, and is diffused through the whole body, and makes the man himself savage; let it be taken away (he says) and clamor, so that not even any trace of it may remain. Clamor indeed presents the figure of a horse, anger presents the rider; bind the horse with fetters, and you will overthrow the one sitting upon it; remove besides the curses and quarrels, which are born from anger. Vociferation indeed inflames anger all the more. And because there are many who are silently angry, and suppress their anger by keeping silent, and are bitten by clandestine stings, and keep an obscure and hidden indignation, he added to it, with all wickedness, that is, whether it be small or great. Theophylactus says this excellently: Chrysostom preceded him: He refers these things to the preceding, in this way: How the race of bees will never descend into an unclean vessel or garment: For this reason, those who are skilled in these matters sprinkle the place with fumigations and good perfumes and ointments, and smear with sweet-smelling wines and all other things the baskets in which are the swarms going out from the hives, lest a heavy and unpleasant odor drive them away again: So also in the Holy Spirit. Our soul is a certain vessel and a certain basket filled to receive the swarms of spiritual graces. But if there is bile inside, and bitterness, and anger, the swarms fly away. See, therefore, how he purges and cleanses our heart. He expelled lying, he expelled anger. He shows again how evil can be rooted out. If we are bitter in mind, they say: as is accustomed to happen in bile, which is bitter, if there should be some small movement with the receptacle broken. For when it has become sharper than is proper for the vehemence of its quality, and the vessel that was receiving it, and previously containing it, has been eaten away as if by a vehement fire, it can no longer control it and contain it within defined limits, but, torn apart by the immoderate acrimony, it lets it go forth to destroy the whole body. But when the dominion of anger has prevailed, with the barriers that were interposed broken, and it is able to leap out, it fills the city with every tumult and disturbance.

and drives them all away. So also in bile, as long as it is contained within its own boundaries, it does us no great harm. But after the membrane that contained it is ruptured, nothing prevents it from henceforth diffusing into the whole nature; then, even if it is a thing very small in quantity, because of its exceeding power in quality, it infects all other elements with its vice. For also, having found blood, which is near both in place and quality, it makes the heat that is in it sharper, and whatever is near, leaping over the boundaries of the symmetry and moderation that is in the humor, and rendering it bile, relying on these aids, it subsequently wages war even against other members, and then, when it has instilled its bitterness into all, it makes the man mute, and causes him to expire, expelling the soul. And afterwards: Let all bitterness be taken away from you. Let not even the remnants remain. For if this is moved, it knows how to stir up a whole pyre within, as if from another spark. What bitterness is, therefore, let us consider accurately. As if a man were fraudulent and insidious, deceitful, and prepared for doing evil, suspicious. From him always is born anger and indignation. For it cannot be that a mind of this kind is tranquil. But the root of anger and indignation is acerbity and bitterness. For he who is of this kind is prone to grave anger, and never relaxes his mind, as one who is always pensive, always sad. For they themselves, as I said, are the first to feel their own evils. And clamor, he says, why do you take away even clamor? For it behooves him who is meek to be such. For clamor is a horse carrying a rider, namely anger and indignation. Stop the horse, and you have overturned the rider. Finally, towards the end of this XV homily: And blasphemy, he says, let it be taken away from you. See how evil proceeds. Bitterness brought forth anger, anger indignation, indignation clamor, clamor blasphemy, that is, curses, but blasphemy brings forth blows, blows wounds, wounds death. But Paul did not wish to say any of these, but said, with all malice. In this he defines. There are, however, some like dogs biting secretly, who do not bark at one approaching, nor do they bear him ill will, but fawning and showing a semblance of gentleness and meekness, when they have caught those not on their guard, they inflict teeth upon them. They are more grave than those who undertake open enmities. Since, therefore, men are also dogs, neither shouting, nor becoming angry, nor bearing ill will, they threaten: But secretly weaving deceits, and constructing innumerable evils, and avenging themselves by deeds and facts themselves, these also he tacitly signified. Let it be taken away, he says, from you with all malice. Do not spare even in words, but avenge yourself in deeds. I therefore chastised the tongue, and cut off its clamor, lest it should kindle a more vehement pyre. But if you do the same things even without clamor, and nourish a pyre and coals within, what does silence profit you?
