Do you not know that those fires are most grave which, while they are nourished within, do not appear to those who stand around? And wounds, which do not exist and do not appear on the surface? And fevers, which burn internally? So also anger is more grave, which consumes the soul. But it too, he says, let it be taken away with all malice, both small and great. Let us therefore obey him, and let us take away all bitterness and malice, lest we afflict the Holy Spirit with sadness. Let us take away bitterness by the root, let us cut it off. Nothing good will be able to arise from a bitter soul, nor anything healthy. All things are calamities, all things are tears: all things are lamentations, mourning, and wailing. These things Chrysostom: Similarly almost our Blessed Baldwin: These are more vehement affections, and primarily the kin and effects of irascibility. Πικρία is the first motion of irascibility, when the mind is plucked by a less pleasing object: this is followed by θυμός ἡ ὀργὴ, ferocity and anger, or a vehement impulse of an excited mind, thence arises κραυγὴ, insane clamor, such as is that of those who, out of the fury of irascibility, exclaim against those with whom they are angry, there is added moreover blasphemy or contumely, by which the reputation of others is torn apart, and finally malice, which seeks an occasion of harming those with whom we are angry. All of which the Apostle wishes to be alien to Christians. Jerome distinguishes these thus: Bitterness is contrary to sweetness, whence they are commonly called bitter and sweet. But fury is foolish anger, and indignation boiling in the mind. But anger is that, of which bitterness and fury are species, which, with fury extinguished, desires vengeance, and wishes to harm him whom it thinks to have done harm. After bitterness, fury, anger, clamor and blasphemy are also rightly prohibited in us. Because he who has once been overcome by fury, it is necessary that he should leap into clamor, and turbulently roaring, be tossed here and there like a leaf and say, O the iniquity of things! O the unjust judgments of God! and the rest which those are accustomed to say who, through the fury of indignation, have lost the judgment of the mind. Ambrose has it thus: He mentions that all these things, which can provide destruction to souls, are to be removed. For through anger comes indignation, through indignation clamor, as it were the voice of one insane, which is alien to the servant of God. Through clamor creeps in blasphemy, which cannot but be evil, this renders life bitter, drawing it to death. Σὺν πάσῃ κακίᾳ, this they refer either to bitterness, as Theophylact not inconveniently. or as they have the sum of forbidden things. To which also Jerome's explanation goes. But malice is to be understood either as contrary to virtue, which by another name we call vice; or malignity and wickedness, which is felt in tergiversation and craftiness. Yet this κακία seems to be taken more restrictively and in order to bitterness. With Chrysostom, Ambrose has: But because some can retain malice in the mind, with anger and clamor suppressed, for retribution when an occasion is found, therefore he added these are to be taken away with all malice: because it is not only malice to blaspheme, but also to feign peace in the face, and to meditate discord in the mind.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Πᾶσα πικρία) Maledicentia, vide Rom. III. v. 14.

Καὶ θυμὸς) Prima inflammatio animi, Rom. c. II. v. & 2. Cor. XII. 20. Gal. V. 20. Col. III. 8.

Καὶ ὀργὴ) Motus transiens in πάθος.

Καὶ κραυγὴ) Clamor equus est iræ, ait hic Chrysostomus, cum prostraveris, equitem dejeceris.

Καὶ βλασφημία) Omnis quidem maledicentia dicitur βλασφημία, sed ut distinguatur ἀπὸ τῆς πικρίας, videntur hic intelligenda verba, quæ Dei honorem quoquomodo læ- dunt. Nam sic & Menander usurpavit hanc vocem: & in nostris literis sic usurpari solet. Vide Matth. IX. 3. 2. Reg. c. XIX. 6. 22. Es. LII. 5.

Ἀρθῆτω ἀφ' ὑμῶν) Longe absit הוסר. Σὺν πάσῃ κακίᾳ) Vide Rom. I. 29. 1. Cor. V. 8. XIV. 20. Coloss. III. 8. Tit. III. 8.

Novum hoc præceptum est, quod ab amaru- lentia dehortatur Apostolus, quæ non in corde ebullit, ut per linguam prorumpat. Non ergo hic est maledicentia, sed excandescentiæ & iræ radix amarulentia. Nimia severitas arguens potius vo- luntatem pangendi, movendi, irritandi, quam emendandi & corrigendi. Supra quidem ab iræ dehortabatur, sed hic stirpitus eam evellit, inquit Theophylactus. Amaritudo namque iracundiæ & furoris est radix. At ubi acrior ira tempestas inhor- ruit, vehementius oris operculum superat fluctibus, & per omne corpus diffunditur, & hominem ipsum efferat, tollatur (inquit) & clamor, ita ut nec vesti- gium ejus aliquod sit reliquum. Clamor quidem equi præfert figuram, sessorem ira prætendit, con- stringe compedibus equum, & insidentem prosternes, deme præterea maledicta & jurgia, quæ ab ira na- scuntur. Iram quidem magis incendit vociferatio. Et quia plerique sunt, qui tacite irascuntur, & iram comprimunt conticendo, & stimulis mordentur clandestinis, obscuramque & reconditam indigna- tionem asservant, eo adjecit, cum omni nequitia, hoc est, sive exigua, sive magna illa sit. Hæc eximie Theophylactus: Cui præivit Chrysostomus: Refert hæc ad superiora, hoc modo: Quomodo in vas & vestimentum immundum se nunquam demiserit genus apum: Propterea enim & suffitibus & bonis odoramentis unguentisque locum aspergunt, qui ha- rum rerum sunt periti, vinisque suaveolentibus & a- liis omnibus illinunt calathiscos, in quibus sunt insef- suræ exeuntes ex alveis, ne gravis odor & insuavis eas rursus abigat: Ita etiam in Sancto Spiritu. Vas quoddam & quidam calathiscus est nostra anima re- ferta ad excipienda examina gratiarum spiritua- lium. Sed si sit intus bilis, & amaritudo, & ira, evo- lant examina. Vide ergo, quomodo expurgat & emundat cor nostrum. Expulit mendacium, expulit iram. Ostendit rursus, quomodo malum radicitus evelli possit. Si mente quidem simus amari,inquiunt: quomodo solet accidere in bile, quæ est amara, si fuerit aliquis parvus motus rupto receptaculo. Nam quan- do facta fuerit acrior, quam pro vehementia ejus qualitatis, & vas quod eam suscipiebat, & prius con- tinebat eam ferens, tanquam vehementi igne facto fuerit exesum, non potest eam amplius regere & con- tinere in definitis terminis,sed ab immodica divulsum acrimonia dimittit eam egressam totum corpus per- dere. Quando vero iræ dominatus invaluerit, per- fractis, quæ interjecta erant, repagulis, & poterit exi- lire omni tumultu & conturbatione replet civitatem,

& omnes abigit. Ita etiam in bili, quamdiu qui- dem continetur suis finibus, nobis nullum magnum facit malum. Postquam autem rupta, quæ eam continebat, membrana, nihil vetat, quo minus de cætero in universam diffundatur naturam, tunc, etiamsi sit res admodum parva in quantitate, pro- pter exuperantem in qualitate virtutem, omnia alia elementa suo inficit vitio. Nam & invento sanguine, qui est propinquus & loco & qualita- te, efficiens acriorem, qui est in illo, calorem, & quicquid est propinquum, ab ea, quæ est in humo- re symmetria, & moderatione terminos transiliens, & bilem reddens, his freta auxiliis deinceps etiam in alia membra bella gerit, & deinde, quum omni- bus suam indiderit amaritudinem, mutum efficit hominem, & facit exspirare, animam expellens. Et postmodum: Omnis amaritudo tollatur à vobis. Ne maneant quidem reliquiæ. Nam si hoc motum fuerit, scit tanquam ab alia scintilla integrum intus excitare rogum. Quid sit ergo amaritudo, accurate consideremus. Utpote sit homo fraudulentus & insidiosus, dolosus, & ad male faciendum paratus, suspiciosus. Ab eo sem- per nascitur ira & indignatio. Fieri enim non po- test, ut tranquillus sit ejusmodi animus. Sed iræ & indignationis radix est acerbitas & amarulentia. Nam qui est hujusmodi, est ad gravem iram pro- pensus, & nunquam remittit animum, ut qui sem- per cogitabundus, semper tristis. Nam ipsi, ut dixi, primi sua mala sentiunt. Et clamor inquit, Curnam tollis etiam clamorem? Nam eum, qui est mitis, oportet esse talem. Clamor enim est equus ferens ascensorem, nempe iram & indignationem. Equum impedi, & evertisti ascensorem. Denique sub finem homiliæ istius XV. Et blasphemia, in- quit, tollatur à vobis. Vide quomodo procedat ma- lum. Amarulentia peperit iram, ira indignatio- nem, indignatio clamorem, clamor blasphemiam, hoc est maledicta, blasphemia vero plagas, plaga vulnera, vulnera mortem. Sed nihil horum voluit dicere Paulus, sed dixit, cum omni malitia. In hoc definit. Sunt autem quidam sicut canes mordentes latenter, qui accedenti quidem non allatrant, neque eum ægre ferunt, blandientes autem & lenitatis & mansuetudinis ostendentes speciem, quum non sibi caventes apprehenderint, eis dentes infligunt. Ii sunt graviores, quam qui apertas suscipiunt inimici- tias. Quoniam ergo homines sunt quoque canes, neq; clamantes, neque irascentes, neque ægreferentes mi- nantur: Sed clam dolos consuentes, & mala struen- tes innumerabilia, & rebus ipsis & factis ulciscentes, hos quoque tacite significavit. Tollatur, inquit, à vo- bis cum omni malitia. Ne verbis quidem parcas, fa- ctis autem ulcifcaris. Ego ideo linguam castigavi, & clamorem ejus amputavi, ne vehementiorem rogum accenderet. Si autem etiam absque clamore eadem facis, & intus alis rogum & carbones, quid tibi prod- est silentium? An nescis, incendia illa esse gravissima, quæ cum intus alantur, non apparent singulis, qui cir- cumsistunt? & vulnera, quæ non exststunt & non ap- parent superficie? & febres, quæ interna adurunt? Ita etiam ira est gravior, quæ depascit animam. Sed ipsa quoq;, inquit, tollatur cum omni malitia & par- va & magna. Ei ergo pareamus, & omnem tollamus amaritudinem & malitiam, ne tristitia afficiamus Spiritum Sanctum. Auferamus radicitus amaritu- dinem, eam abscindamus. Nihil boni oriri poterit ex amara anima, neque sani. Sunt omnia calamitates, omnia lacrymæ: omnia lamentationes, luctus & eju- latus. Hæc Chrysostomus: Similiter fere B. Baldui- nus noster: Sunt hi vehementiores affectus, & im- primis iracundiæ cognata ac effectus. Πικρία est primus iracundiæ motus, cum carpitur animus obje-żto minus grato: hanc sequitur θυμός ἡ ὀργὴ, fero- cia & ira, seu vehemens animi concitati impetus, inde oritur κραυγὴ, clamor insanus, qualis eorum est, qui præ furore iracundiæ exclamant adversus eos, quibus irascantur, accedit insuper blasphemia seu contumelia, qua aliorum proscinditur fama, & de- nique malitia, quæ quærit occasionem nocendi, quibus irascimur. Quæ omnia à Christianis aliena vult esse Apostolus. Hieronymus hæc ita distinguit: Ama- ritudo contraria dulcedini est, unde amari vulgo ap- pellantur & dulces. Furor vero insipiens ira est, & fervescens in animo indignatio. Ira autem est, cujus amaritudo & furor species sunt, quæ furore restincto desiderat ultionem, & eum, quem nocuisse putat, vult lædere. Post amaritudinem, furorem, iram, recte clamor quoque & blasphemia prohibentur in nobis. Quia qui semel furore fuerit superatus, necesse est, ut profiliat in clamorem, & turbide fremens huc atque illuc in modum folii ventiletur & dicat, O rerum iniquitas! O injusta Dei judicia! & cætera quæ solent loqui, qui per indignationis furorem mentis judi- cium perdiderunt. Ambrosius ita habet: Omnia hæc, quæ perniciem possunt præstare animis, amo- venda memorat. Per iram enim fit indignatio, per in- dignationem clamor, quasi vox insanientis, quæ ali- ena est à Dei servo. Per clamorem surrepit blasphe- mia, quæ non potest non mala esse, hæc amaram præ- stat vitam trahens ad mortem. Σὺν πάσῃ κακίᾳ, hoc vel ad amarulentiam referunt, ut non incommode Theophyl. vel ceu sumnam habent vetitorum. Quo etiam abit Hieronymi explicatio. Malitia autem vel contraria virtuti intelligenda est, quam alio no- mine vitium nominamus; vel malignitas & nequi- tia, quæ in tergiversatione & calliditate sentitur. Restricte tamen & in ordine ad amarulentiam potius accipienda videtur hæc κακία. Cum Chry- sostomo Ambrosius habet: Sed quia possunt aliqui pressa in animo ira & clamore retinere malitiam ad retributionem nacta occasione, idcirco subjecit hæc auferricum omni malitia: quia non solum blasphe- mare malitia est, verum etiam fingere pacem in fa- ciem, & in animo meditari discordiam.

## 4:32
Vers. 32. γίνεσθε δὲ εἰς ἀλλήλυς χρηστοὶ) Kind, such as Abraham was towards Lot, Gen. XIII. 8.

Εὔσπλαγχνοι) Merciful. Thus 1 Pet. III. 8. the same sense, where Paul commends σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν Coloss. III. v. 12.

Χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς) Forgiving, namely offenses, according to the command of Christ, Matt. XVIII. 22. Concerning this use of this word see 2 Cor. II. 7. 10. Ἑαυτοῖς here is one another, as also Coloss. III. 13. and here below V. 19.

These virtues are opposed to the vices just proscribed. We are therefore commanded, that we should not only put off the old man, but also put on the new, and those vices having been laid aside, to be above all χρηστοὶ κὲ εὔσπλαγχνοι, the former of which Theophylact wishes to be opposed to anger, the latter to bitterness. But Jerome more correctly vice versa opposes χρηστότητα to bitterness, just as τὸ εὔσπλαγχνον is not undeservedly said to be opposed to hot-temperedness. But forgiveness or τὸ χαρίζεσθαι is opposed to anger, and to the sprouts of the same, clamor with railing. These are related virtues, says Blessed Balduinus, χρηστότης is sweetness or kindness opposed to bitterness and harshness of manners; mercy feels for those inflicting injury rather than allowing the mind to think of revenge, forgiveness entirely removes all anger, while it forgives the delinquent. Therefore is added χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, which the Vulgate rendered, forgiving one another. Jerome, forgiving that to yourselves, referring that to a gift; because what is done well to another is stored up more for him who performed it than it is given to the other, he who will pity the poor, he himself will be satisfied, & he who gives to him, lends to God. But τὸ χαρίζεσθαι is explained in Col. 3, 13. concerning forgiveness, so that it is fitting to wonder that the donation should have come into Jerome's mind here. More correctly, therefore, Chrysostom and the Greek scholia: χαριζόμενοι ὅ ἐστι, συγγνωμονικοὶ γίνεσθε.

As also Christ forgave you.) This sense is not bad. But most and the best Codices have: God in Christ forgave you. Thus also the Syrian, and Chrysostom, and Theophylact, and the Latin read. In Christ, that is, on account of Christ, with Christ interceding, Is. 53, 12. Luke 23, 34.

This is entirely the common reading, which the Latins also have, Jerome, Ambrose, and the Vulgate interpreter, etc. But it is not only in Christ because of the intercession of Christ, but primarily on account of the merit of Christ, upon which his intercession rests. In what way in Christ? asks Theophylact, that is, with the risk and death of his own Son. You, however, would by no means have contributed anything at your own risk. But he [did so] far otherwise. For he [forgave] his brother and neighbor, but he [God] forgave and bestowed upon you as an enemy, and one hostile because of sins. He notes, therefore, a twofold weight of the Apostolic reasoning: both that God expended his Son for us, that he might show grace by forgiving our sins, and that he bestowed that mercy upon us, who were enemies. Chrysostom proposed yet another point to us, that mutual forgiveness is given among men, but we can do nothing to gratify God. He says, therefore, forgive one another. And yet they are by no means sparing. For if you now indeed give and gratify, he in turn will give and gratify you. But you have given nothing to God, nor have you gratified him; and you indeed [forgive] a fellow servant; but God [forgives] a servant and an enemy, and one who hates him. Just as also God, he says, in Christ gave to us. This also has a great enigma. Not absolutely, he says, did he give to us without risk, but with the risk of his son. In order to forgive you, he sacrificed his Son. You, however, often see καὶ ἀκίνδυνον κὰὶ ἀδάπανον τὴν συγχώρησιν, forgiveness both without risk and without cost, [and] you do not do it. Chrysostom connects this admonition with the following, and refers it not to this, but to the subsequent chapter. Bullinger, Calvin, and Crocius judge that those who divided the chapters ineptly separated them from the preceding.

Latin:

Vers. 32. γίνεσθε δὲ εἰς ἀλλήλυς χρηστοὶ) Benigni, qualis Abrahamus erga Lothum, Gen. XIII. 8.

Εὔσπλαγχνοι) Misericordes. Sic 1. Pet. III. 8. idem sen- sus, ubi σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμῶν commendat Paulus Coloss. III. v. 12.

Χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς) Condonantes, nempe offensas, ex præcepto Christi, Matth. XVIII. 22. De usu hoc hujus ver- bi vide 2. Cor. II. 7.10. Ἑαυτοῖς hîc est alter alteri, ut & Coloss. III. 13. & hîc infra V. 19.

Virtutes hæ opponuntur vitiis modo proscriptis. Jubemur ergo, ut non veterem tantum hominem exuamus, sed novum etiam induamus, vitiis que il- lis depositis, imprimis esse χρηστοὶ κὲ εὔσπλαγχνοι, quorum prius iræ, alterum amarulentiæ opponi vult Theophylactus. Sed rectius vice versa Hierony- mus τὴν χρηστότητα opponit amarulentiæ, uti τὸ εὔ- σπλαγχνον excandescentiæ non immerito opponi di- citur. Ignoscentia vero vel τὸ χαρίζεσθαι iræ, & ger- minibus ejusdem clamori cum contumelia. Cognatæ sunt virtutes, inquit B. Balduinus, χρηστότης suavitas seu benignitas opposita amaritudini & asperitati morum; misericordia condolet potius injuriam infi- rentibus, quam ut animum de vindicta cogitare pa- tiatur, condonatio prorsus omnem iram tollit, dum delinquenti ignoscit. Ideo additur χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, quod Vulgata reddidit, donantes invicem. Hieronymus, donantes id vobismetipsis, referens id ad donationem; quia quod bene in alium fit, magis ei reponitur, qui præstitit, quam alii datum est, qui miserebitur pauperis, ipse saturabitur, & qui dat ei, Deo foenerat. Sed τὸ χαρίζεσθαι explicatur Col. 3, 13. de condonatione, ut mirari OPorteat donationem Hieronymo in mentem hic venisse. Rectius itaque Chrysostomus, & Graeca scholia, χαριζόμενοι ὅ ἐστι, συγγνωμονικοὶ γίνεσθε.

Καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν.) Est sensus hic non ma- lus. Sed plerique & optimi Codices habent: ὁ θεὸς ἐν χρι- στῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν. Sic legit & Syrus, & Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus, & Latinus. Ἐν χριστῷ, id est, ob Christum, Christo deprecante, Es. 53, 12. Luc. 23, 34.

Est omnino haec lectio communis, quam & La- tini habent, Hieronymus, Ambrosius, & Vulgatus interpres &c. Non autem in Christo tantum est propter intercessionem Christi, sed imprimis ob meritum Christi, quo nititur ejus intercessio. Quo pacto in Christo? quaerit Theophylactus, hoc est, cum Filii sui discrimine & morte. Ipse vero haud quaquam tuo cum periculo quicquam contuleris. At ille longe aliter. Nam ipse in fratrem & proximum, ille vero tibi ut hosti, & ob peccata infenso errata di- misit & largitus est. Geminum ergo notat mo- mentum rationis Apostolicae, tum quod Filium Deus nobis impenderit, ut gratiam exhiberet, peccata nobis condonando, tum quod nobis eam misericordiam praestiterit, qui hostes eramus. Chrysostom. aliud adhuc nobis proposuit momen- tum, quod inter homines detur mutua condona- tio, Deo vero nos nihil gratificari possumus. Di- cit itaque, donate vobis invicem. Atqui minime sunt parca. Nam si tu nunc quidem dones & gra- tificeris, ille rursus tibi donabit & gratificabitur. Deo autem nihil donasti, nec gratificatus es; & tu quidem conservo; Deus autem servo & inimico, & ei, qui ipsum odit. Sicut & Deus, inquit, in Christo donavit nobis. Hoc quoque magnum ha- bet aenigma. Non absolute, inquit, sine periculo no- bis donavit, sed cum periculo filii. Ut tibi ignosceret, sacrificavit Filium. Tu autem saepe videas καὶ ἀκιν- δυνον κὰὶ ἀδάπανον τὴν συγχώρησιν, condonationem & sine periculo & sine sumptu, non facis. Connectit Chrysostomus hoc monitum cum sequentibus, & refert non ad hoc, sed ad subsequens caput. Inepte ea à superioribus diremisse, qui capita distinxit, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Crocius judicant.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Furthermore, the Apostle exhorts to charity by the example of God and Christ, to the avoiding of impurity and avarice, as also drunkenness, so that they may be filled with the Spirit of God; and specifically he admonishes wives concerning obedience toward their husbands, and these concerning the love of their wives, by the example of the obedience of the Church toward Christ, and the love of Christ toward the Church, and by a comparison of the matrimonial law (Gen. II. 24.), and he illustrates his admonitions with a great mystery concerning Christ and his Church.

There are two parts: The first is still general concerning charity and the avoidance of vices that are by no means becoming to saints, up to verse 20. The second is special, concerning the duties of spouses up to the end of the chapter.

PART I. GENERAL.

Vers. 1. Be therefore imitators of God) Which is done especially by doing good to all, Matt. 5, 48. For thus man is a God to man.

as beloved children) Of God, that is. It is the duty of children to reflect their Father in their character.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Exhortatur porro Apostolus ad charitatem exemplo Dei, & Christi, ad vitandam im- puritatem, & avaritiam, ut & ebrietatem, ut Spiritu Dei impleantur; & speciatim uxores de obedientia erga maritos, & hos de dilectione uxorum commonet, exemplo obsequii Ecclesiae erga Christum, & dilectio- nis Christi erga Ecclesiam, & collatione le- gis matrimonialis, (Gen. II. 24.) ac magni de Christo ejusque Ecclesia mysterii monita sua illustrat.

Partes duae sunt: Prima generalis adhuc est de charitate, & vitiorum sanctos minime decentium vitatione, ad v. 20. Altera specialis, de officiis con- jugum ad finem usque capitis.

PARS I. GENERALIS.

Vers. 1. Γίνεσθε ὗν μιμηταὶ θεῦ) Quod praecipue fit, bene omnibus faciendo, Matth. 5, 48. Nam sic homo ho- mini Deus.

ὡς τέκνα ἀγαπητά) Dei nempe. Liberorum est, Patrem moribus referre.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. and walk in love) περιπατεῖν, הלך, does not signify one act or another, but a perpetual tenor of life.

and gave himself up for us) To death, of course, just as Gal. 2:20. He brings the greatest testimony of love, John 15:13, Rom. 5:8, and following.

An offering and a sacrifice to God) You have these two together also in Ps. 40:7, where for προσφορὰν in Hebrew is מנחה, an oblation, namely of wheat, concerning which see the things said at Levit. 2 and Mark 9:49; wherefore θυσία is to be understood as זבח, which otherwise is general concerning victims. The similarity lies in the fact that from both, the consecrated part placed upon the altar was consumed in honor of God.

For a sweet-smelling savor) This is used also concerning victims in Levit. 1:9 and concerning the Manna, Levit. 3:16, and it first occurs in the history of Noah, Gen. 8:21, ריח הניחח, where there is an allusion to the very name of Noah. Christ is the other Noah, who saves from the flood of vices, the Prince of the new age; no sacrifice can be more pleasing to God than where the same one is both Priest and victim. It is added that in no sacrifice is there more perfect obedience, and its fruit is the salvation of the human race.

He proposes as an exemplar not himself, as in 1 Cor. 4:16, 2 Thess. 3:9, but God; not of wisdom, justice, mercy, and truth, and holiness, which pleased Haymo, but of charity, as most other interpreters rightly teach. Now, for the imitation of someone, Zanchius not badly requires these three things: that you do what he does, that you do it with the zeal of imitating the exemplar, and that you conform your work to his likeness, as far as it can be done. Applying these specifically to forgiveness, one must forgive one's neighbor, just as God forgives us promptly, sincerely, fully, freely, and constantly. Moreover, we ought to imitate God, not as disciples their Master, but as children their Parent; and indeed as beloved children, whom He adopted in Christ, and in that beloved Christ He loves. Where Chrysostom beautifully says: Whence did you become a son? From the fact that it was forgiven you. Therefore, for that cause, from which you have been affected by such great honor, for that very cause, I say, forgive also your neighbor. Now the impulsive cause of forgiveness, προηγουμένη, is uniquely charity. God forgives us our sins out of mere charity. Let us also forgive in this way by the example of GOD, Matt. 18.

And thus the Apostle leads us to Christ the Son of God, in whom he had said that God χαρίζεσθαι to us, that is, forgives sins, and he sets forth the charity of the Son of GOD, proclaimed as a most illustrious document of far-eminent love, as an example by which grace and paternal forgiveness have been reconciled to us; where, however, the particle καθώς is only of similarity, not of equality. For no one can show that love to a brother which Christ showed to us; it designates indeed the sincerity, ardor, and perpetuity of love, in which we ought to imitate Christ. Nor does it look only to the affection, but also to the effect. For we also ought to lay down our life for the brethren, just as He laid down His life for us, 1 John 3:18. For although a brother cannot merit salvation for a brother with his blood ἱλαστικῶς, or appease God Himself, Ps. 49:8. It can, however, happen that by his temporal death he may in some way be able to avert the danger of eternal death from his neighbor, to which he is entirely bound by divine law and the example of Christ, in a case of supreme necessity, if it cannot be avoided otherwise.

Moreover, all the words testify to the love of Christ: He loved us, he says, not that we loved Him first, but He loved us, which is said of the Father in 1 John 4:10, with whom the Son is one, John 10:30, when we were still ungodly and sinners, Rom. 5:6, 8, He gave Himself out of love. He was not given up unwillingly, but although He is said to be given up by the Father, Rom. 5:24, yet He gave Himself up αὐτεξουσίως, John 10:18, and He did the will of the Father willingly, Ps. 40:7, Heb. 10:7, 9. He gave up not something outside of himself, as he had all things in his own hand, John 13:2. He is said to have delivered his own flesh, John 6:51. His own body, Luke 22:19. His own soul, Matt. 20:21. John 10:8. But himself entirely, just as there also the whole is understood by naming a part, which is also expressed in Gal. 1:4. ch. 2:20. 1 Tim. 2:6. Tit. 2:14. for ours, not only for our good, but in our place, which the particle ὑπὲρ implies, 2 Cor. 5:19. And from there also the preposition ἀντὶ, which signifies in the stead and place of, is used, Matt. 20:28. Mark 10:45. 1 Tim. 2:6. He delivered [himself], however, into death, Eph. 5:26. Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his soul for his friends, John 15:13. As if he were saying, how can I more clearly demonstrate my love toward you than by pouring out my life for you, so that I may make you friends of God the Father and of me? Never has it shone more clearly that the Lord loved us than in his own passion and wounds. He delivered himself into a bloody death, which the word θυσία, derived from slaughtering, indicates. For expiatory victims had to be slaughtered, and their blood offered to the Lord; therefore Christ, who was prefigured by the victims, had to pour out his blood, Matt. 26:28. Heb. 9:14. While the Apostle says that Christ offered himself as a victim, he comprehends all things at once that Christ suffered, both elsewhere in his great passion and on the altar of the cross, 1 Pet. 2:24. How many testimonies here to the most ardent love of Christ? The Apostle used two words, προσφορὰν and θυσίαν, but with them he encompassed all sacrifices, because all sacrifices foreshadowed his sacrifice, Psalm 40:7, 8. Heb. 10:5. Or if you prefer it so, those two species are designated here, as figures of the sacrifice of Christ, מנחה and זבח; in them the charity of Christ is also sufficiently foreshadowed, in that he willed also to be slaughtered and to pour out his blood, as we have already said, for us, and underwent the fire of divine wrath, and by it was roasted and burned for us. For we ought to have been scorched by the flames of eternal fire because of our sins, which he took upon himself, offering himself for us. Who can attain to such love even in thought, or express it in words?

Socinus denies that that oblation was made on the altar of the cross; he contends that the death of Christ was only a preparation for the sacrifice of Christ, but that the sacrifice itself is performed in heaven. But here the Apostle openly testifies that Christ delivered himself into death, into a sacrifice. And Crellius had to admit, in his response to Grotius on the satisfaction of Christ, page 533, that a θυσία is properly completed by slaughtering, just as θύειν is to slaughter. But Christ was not slaughtered in heaven, but on the altar of the cross; see Socinismus profligatus, page 353 et seqq. Schlichting in his commentary on this passage: He delivered himself for us, namely into death, see ch. 5:25, than which love there is none greater. He delivered himself, however, so that he might be a victim for our sins. But as to what he adds, the Apostle is not speaking here of the oblation by which Christ offers himself to God in heaven, of which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews treats, as if a twofold oblation of Christ must be established, one made in death, another which is made in heaven; in this he begs the question, since a twofold oblation of Christ has never been proven, and he openly contradicts Paul, who recognizes no other than a single oblation of Christ, and teaches that it was made on earth, in the very epistle which he wrote to the Hebrews, ch. 7:27, ch. 9:14, ch. 10:10, 14. Furthermore, Schlichtingius provides this gloss on the present passage: An oblation and a victim to God for a sweet-smelling savor. By apposition he declares how Christ, doing this, was pleasing and acceptable to God; it is a metaphor from the peace offerings and victims of old, from whose incense it was said that an odor of a sweet savor was carried to God, and therefore he was acceptable to God. You have a similar apposition in Phil. 4:18. Moreover, this act of Christ and this love of Christ toward us was so pleasing and acceptable to God that, because of it, he wills to bestow the same inheritance as Christ upon all who apply themselves to Christ through faith and, imitating him, walk in charity, whom he also for this very reason delivered into death for us, so that by his blood he might inscribe that he would surely do this. Regarding which these things are to be noted: 1. That it is not so much an apposition, 'he delivered himself for us, namely into death, an oblation and a victim,' wherefore the preposition IN is to be understood, so that the manner in which he delivered himself into death for us might be explained, namely, that by that pact he became a victim and an oblation to God, indeed, through this delivery and his death; 2. Therefore it is not declared by apposition how Christ, doing this, was pleasing and acceptable to God, but how Christ by this oblation reconciled God to us, for whom he delivered himself as a victim, and rendered us pleasing to Him. For the priest did not render himself pleasing to God by offering a victim for the people, but he reconciled God to the people, since the offered victims were for the expiation and remission of sins. 3. Not only in peace offerings and victims, but also in expiatory sacrifices, it was said that an odor of a sweet savor was carried to God from the incense, Lev. 1:4, 5, 9, 13, 17. 4. The passage Phil. 4:18 is not similar, but dissimilar. For there it is not a matter of delivery into death, but of alms collected; not of an expiatory sacrifice, but of peace offerings. 5. It is not taught here how the love of Christ was pleasing to God, or his delivery into death, but what it profited us, because he delivered himself for us. Nor is that act of Christ regarded here as an act, when Christ is said to have been made a victim for our sins: But the death of Christ, inasmuch as the nature of the sacrifice consists in it, which is owed to the love of Christ, John 15:13. The propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, viewed formally, is not properly a deed or any action, but the passion and death of Christ, which is satisfactory for our sins. 6. The Apostle does not teach that our love was pleasing to God, but that the victim of Christ, by which he delivered himself up to death for us, was an odor of a sweet smell to God, just as the offering of victims was ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας; this, however, was not because of the love of the Priest offering, even though the obedience of the office in the Priest was pleasing to God, but because of the victim itself offered, by which Christ, as a victim to be offered for us, was prefigured; nor does the Apostle hint at how the Priest was made pleasing to God, but how those who presented them to the priest to be offered, so that their sins might be expiated, were brought back into favor with God through the offering of the victims. And therefore, the expiation made for our sins, and the appeasement and reconciliation of God obtained through the expiatory sacrifice of Christ, is properly designated, so that the analogy and correspondence between the type and the antitype may be consistent. 7. It is not taught here that God delivered Christ to death for us so that by his blood he might inscribe that he wishes to bestow upon the faithful the same inheritance as Christ: thus the death of Christ would only be a μαρτύριον, not a λύτρον, a certification of grace, not an expiation of sin or a propitiation of God. 8. God does not bestow the heavenly inheritance upon us because someone applies himself to Christ through faith and imitates him by walking in love. For nothing is attributed here to our love, but it is uniquely ascribed to the love of Christ and his delivery as an expiatory victim that the remission of sins comes to us, just as it once did to those who offered sacrifices, by virtue of the antitype, since from the offering of the sacrifice of Christ an ὀσμὴ ἐυωδίας, an odor of a sweet smell, uniquely redounded, and thus grace

of God and the remission of sins is to be credited to the offering of Christ, who poured out his blood and gave himself up to death for our sins, and for the remission of our sins. 9. Nor is Christ said anywhere to have obtained the heavenly inheritance through love for us, for he did not need to merit anything for himself: nor do we obtain or secure the heavenly inheritance through the imitation of Christ in charity, but solely through faith in Christ, or through the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith, since by his obedience he did not indeed merit justification and salvation for himself, yet he did for us, and justifies us by the faith of his obedience, Is. 53, 11. 10. Therefore we do not become heirs by applying ourselves to Christ through faith, but by apprehending Christ with his obedience and merit through faith, and by applying them to ourselves, we obtain the ἐξουσίαν, to become τέκνα θεῦ, as many as believe in his name, Joh. 1, 12.

Joh. Coccejus attempts here to carve out his particular satisfaction for the elect in his Commentary on this passage: If he gave himself up out of love, and for those for whom he gave himself up, he obtained what he asked (inasmuch as he was made a sweet-smelling savor), it follows that Christ, as Priest, did not ask for the salvation of all without exception, although as man and servant he might have felt compassion for the perishing according to the law: But that he gave himself up for those who were given to him by the Testament: who are those very ones who believe in such a way that they love. But Coccejus confuses general love, which extends to all, and special love, which is proper to the faithful. For the former is the cause of his being given up to death, the latter arises from faith, which applies that giving up to itself. And although nothing is expressly held here concerning Christ's intercession, but only his sacrifice is treated, in which he is said to have been made a sweet-smelling savor, there is no doubt, however, that just as he gave himself up for all, he also interceded for all, Is. 53, 12. Luc. 23, 34. which prayer of his was entirely heard, because he obtained reconciliation for the world, and the grace of forgiving sins, which he offers to all, by the power of that καταλλαγῆς through the ministry of the καταλλαγῆς, but confers it upon believers. Vain also is the distinction of Christ as Priest, and as man and servant. For both as Priest he offered sacrifice and intercedes for all, and as a servant of God he was made just and obedient to the Father for all, Is. 53. Phil. 2. Nor, however, is it the same thing to be a servant and a man. For the latter is a name of nature, the former of status. He remains a man, he has ceased to be a servant; just as he is not Priest as God alone, because this is a name of office; to which also the obedience of Christ, being subject under the law, is referred. But the names of office belong to Christ according to both natures; and the form of a servant looks to the state of humiliation, in which his obedience, both active and passive, was performed. But what that compassion of Christ the man according to the law might be, I confess that I do not grasp, since according to the law he would rather condemn the unbelievers. But that he gave himself up only for those who were given to him by the testament is foreign to Scripture, nay, it is contrary to Scripture, since he gave himself up for all, 1. Tim. 2, 6. so that he might acquire the inheritance for all, to which we aspire by faith alone, and not indeed by faith and charity. For the inheritance is not acquired by virtue, but by the right of τῆς ὑοθεσίας, which we do not obtain except by faith, Joh. 1, 12. Rom. 8, 16. Gal. 3, 26. Crocius himself certainly acknowledged in this place that Christ was not given up in death for the faithful only, but for all men. Moreover, he says, he does not say, for us, so as to restrict it to a certain absolute fewness of men for whom he gave himself, with others excluded for whom he in no way gave himself. For elsewhere he says he gave himself for all, 1. Tim. 2, 8. but then, both to include himself and to profess his own faith, and so that individual Ephesians might subsume it particularly, saying: And he gave himself for me. I ought therefore to walk with charity. For wherever the Apostles say for us, there every believer ought to include himself and say: He loved me, and gave himself for me, which the Apostle does in Gal. 2, 20.

Latin:

Vers. 2. καὶ περιπατεῖτε ἐν ἀγάπῃ) περιπατεῖν הלך non actum unum aut alterum significat, sed perpetuum vitæ tenorem.

καὶ παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) In mortem scilicet, sic & Gal. 2, 20. affert maximum dilectionis testimonium, Joh. 15, 13. Rom. 5, 8. & sequentibus.

Προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ Θεῷ) Hæc duo simul habes & Ps. 40, 7. ubi pro προσφορὰν in Ebræo est מנחה oblatio, nimirum triticea, de qua vide dicta ad Levit. 2. & Marci 9, 49. quare θυσία זבח, quod alioqui generale est de victimis intelligendum. Similitudo in eo, quod de utroque pars sacrata in honorem Dei imposita altari absumebatur.

Εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) Usurpatur id & de victimis Levit. 1, 9. & de Maná, Levit. 3, 16. ac primum occurrit in Noæ historia, Gen. 8, 21. ריח הניחח, ubi ad ipsum Noæ nomen sit allusio. Christus alter Noë, qui ex diluvio vitiorum servat, Princeps novi seculi, nullum sacrificium Dei potest esse gratius, quam ubi idem est & Sacerdos & victima. Accedit, quod in nullo sacrificio perfectior obedientia, & fructus ejus salus humani generis.

Exemplar proponit non se, ut 1. Corinth. 4, 16. 2. Thess. 3, 9. sed Deum, non sapientiæ, justitiæ, misericordiæ, & veritatis, ac sanctimoniæ, quod Haymoni placuit, sed charitatis, ut alii plerique Interpp. recte docent. Ad imitationem autem alicujus Zanchius tria hæc non male requirit, ut facias, quod ille facit, ut facias studio exemplar imitandi, & ut opus tuum ad illius instar, quoad ejus fieri potest, conformes. Hæc ad condonationem specialiter applicando, condonandum erit proximo, sicut Deus nobis condonat prompte, sincere, plene, gratis, constanter. Imitari autem Deum debemus, non ut discipuli Magistrum, sed ut filii Parentem; & quidem ut dilecti filii, quos in Christo adoptavit, in Christo dilecto illo diligit. Ubi Chrysostomus pulchre: Unde factus es filius? Ex eo quod remissum est tibi. Ex ea itaque causa, unde tanto affectus es honore, ex ea, inquam, ipsa causa ignosce & proximo tuo. Condonationis autem causa impulsiva προηγουμένη unice est charitas. Deus ex mera charitate nobis condonat peccata. Condonemus & nos ita exemplo DEI, Matth. 18.

Atque ita deducit nos Apostolus ad Christum Dei Filium, in quo nobis Deum χαρίζεσθαι dixerat, condonare peccata, & charitatem Filii DEI opere ipso ceu amoris longe eminentissimi documento illustrissimo, declamatam in exemplum sistit, quo conciliata est nobis gratia, & condonatio paterna; ubi tamen particula καθώς similitudinis tantum est, non æqualitatis. Nemo enim eam dilectionem fratri præstari potest, quam Christus nobis præstitit, designat utique amoris sinceritatem, ardorem, perennitatem, in quibus imitari Christum debemus. Nec affectum tantum, sed etiam effectum respicit. Nam & nos animam pro fratribus ponere debemus, sicut ille animam pro nobis posuit, 1. Joh. 3, 18. Quamvis enim salutem non possit fratri frater mereri sanguine suo ἱλαστικῶς, aut ipsum Deum placare, Ps. 49, 8. Fieri tamen potest, ut temporali sua morte periculum æternæ mortis à proximo avertere aliquo modo queat, ad quod divina lege, & exemplo Christi omnino tenetur, in necessitatis supremæ casu, si aliter id declinari nequeat.

Omnia autem verba amorem Christi testantur: Dilexit nos, inquit, non priores ipsum dileximus, sed ille nos, quod de Patre dicitur 1. Joh. 4, 10. quo cum Filius unum est, Joh. 10, 30. cum adhuc impii essemus & peccatores, Rom. 5, 6. 8. tradidit se ex dilectione. Non traditus est invitus, sed etsi à Patre traditus dicatur, Rom. 5, 24. semetipsum tamen αὐτεξουσίως tradidit, Joh. 10, 18. & voluntatem Patris fecit libenter, Ps. 40, 7. Ebr. 10, 7. 9. Tradidit non aliquid extra se, uti omnia habuit manu sua, Joh. 13, 2. Tradidisse carnem suam dicitur, Joh. 6, 51. corpus suum, Luc. 22, 19. animam suam, Matth. 20, 21. Joh. 10, 8. Sed se totum, sicut & illic parte nominata totum intelligitur, quod etiam expres- sum est Gal. 1, 4. cap. 2, 20. 1. Tim. 2, 6. Tit. 2, 14. Tradidit non sui causa, sed nostri, non bono tan- tum nostro, sed nostri loco, quod particula ὑπὲρ in- fert 2. Cor. 5, 19. atque inde etiam præpositio ἀντὶ, quæ significat vice & loco, adhibetur, Matth. 20, 28. Marc. 10, 45. 1. Tim. 2, 6. Tradidit autem in mortem, Eph. 5, 26. Majorem hic dilectionem nemo habet, quam ut animam suam ponat quis pro amicis suis, Joh. 15, 13. quasi dicat, quomodo clarius pos- sim demonstrare meum erga vos amorem, quam quod vitam meam pro vobis profundo, ut faciam vos amicos Dei Patris & meos? Nunquam illuxit clarius, quod nos dilexit Dominus, quam in ipsius passione & vulneribus. Tradidit sese in mortem cruentam, quam vox θυσία à mactando dicta indi- cat. Victimæ enim expiatoriæ mactandæ erant, & sanguis earum offerendus Domino, ideo effun- dere Christus, qui per victimas figuratus est, de- buit sanguinem suum, Matth. 26, 28. Ebr. 9, 14. Victimam dum Christum sese obtulisse dicit Apo- stolus, omnia simul comprehendit, quæ Christus passus est, tum alias in passione sua magna, tum in ara crucis, 1. Pet. 2, 24. Quot hic testimonia arden- tissimi Christi amoris? Voces duas adhibuit Apo- stolus, προσφορὰν, & θυσίαν, sed illis omnia sacrificia complexus est, quia omnia sacrificium ipsius adum- brarunt, Psalm. 40, 7. 8. Ebr. 10, 5. Vel si ita mavis, duæ illæ species hic sunt designatæ, ceu figuræ sa- crificii Christi מנחה & זבח; satis in illis etiam adumbrata charitas Christi, quod & mactari, ac sanguinem profundere, ut jam diximus, pro nobis voluerit, ignemque iræ divinæ subierit, & eo pro nobis assatus & crematus sit. Nos enim æterni ignis flammis ustulari debebamus propter peccata, quæ in se suscepit, offerens semetipsum pro nobis. Quis tantum amorem vel cogitatione assequi, vel verbis efferre potest?

Socinus negat, oblationem illam factam esse in ara crucis; mortem Christi contendit tantum præparationem fuisse sacrificii Christi, sacrificium vero ipsum in cælis peragi. Sed hic aperte testa- tur Apostolus, Christum se tradidisse in mortem, in sacrificium. Et fateri debuit Crellius resp. ad Grot. de satisf. Christi pag. 533. θυσίαν proprie ma- ctatione perfici, ut θύειν mactare est. At Christus in cælis mactatus non est, sed in ara crucis; Vid. Socinismus profligatus pag. 353. seqq. Schlichting. in Commentario ad h. l. Tradidit se ipsum pro no- bis, nempe in mortem, vid. cap. 5, 25. quanta dile- ctione nulla est major. Tradidit autem, ut esset victima pro peccatis nostris. Quod autem addit, non loquitur hic Apostolus de obligatione, qua sese Christus in cælis Deo offert, de qua autor epistolæ ad Ebræos agit, quasi gemina statuenda sit Christi oblatio, alia in morte facta, alia quæ in cælis fiat, in eo principium petit, quum nunquam gemina Christi oblatio probata sit, & Paulo aperte con- tradicit, qui non nisi unicam Christi oblationem agnoscit, eamque in terris factam docet, in ipsa, quam ad Ebræos perscripsit, epistola, cap. 7, 27. cap. 9, 14. cap. 10, 10. 14. Glossam porro hanc tra- dit præsentis loci Schlichtingius: Oblationem & victimam Deo in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ. Apposi- tione declarat, quam Christus hoc faciens Deo fuerit gratus & acceptus, metaphora est ab oblationibus & victimis olim pacificis, ex quarum incenso diceba- tur odor ad Deum ferri bonæ fragrantiæ, proinde acceptus Deo. Similem appositionem habes Phil. 4, 18. Adeo autem hoc Christi factum, & hæc Christi dilectio erga nos fuit grata & accepta Deo, ut ob eam omnibus, qui se se Christo per fidem applicant, & eum imitantes in charitate ambulant, eandem cum Christo hæreditatem largiri velit, quem etiam ob id ipsum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, ut sanguine ejus hoc sese omnino facturum inscriberet. Ad quam hæc notanda: 1. non tam oppositionem esse, tradidit seipsum pro nobis, nempe in mortem, oblationem & victimam, quare subintelligi præpositione IN, ut, qua ratione se in mortem pro nobis tradiderit, explicetur, ut scilicet fieret eo pacto victima & oblatio Deo, nimirum, per hanc traditionem & mortem suam; 2. Non ergo appositione declaratur, quam Christus, hoc faciens, Deo fuerit gratus & acceptus, sed quomodo Christus hac oblatione Deum nobis, pro quibus se tradidit in victimam, placaverit, gratosque illi nos reddiderit. Nam non Sacerdos se Deo reddebat gratum, offerens pro populo victimam, sed Deum conciliabat populo, quum oblatæ victimæ fuerint in expiationem & remissionem peccatorum. 3. Non tantum in oblationibus & victimis pacificis, sed etiam in sacrificiis expiatoriis dicebatur ex incenso odor ad Deum ferri bonæ fragrantiæ, Lev. 1, 4. 5. 9. 13. 17. 4. Locus Phil. 4, 18. non similis est, sed dissimilis. Ibi enim non de traditione in mortem, sed de eleemosyna collecta, non de sacrificio expiatorio, sed de victima pacificis gemina agitur. 5. Non quomodo grata fuerit Deo Christi dilectio, aut ejusdem in mortem traditio, sed quid nobis profuerit, hic docetur, quia tradidit se pro nobis. Nec illud factum Christi hic respicitur, ut factum, cum victima pro peccatis nostris Christus factus dicitur: Sed mors Christi, utpote in qua consistit sacrificii ratio, quæ dilectioni Christi debetur, Joh. 15, 13. Propitiatorium Christi sacrificium formaliter spectatum proprie non est factum, vel actio aliqua, sed passio & mors Christi pro peccatis nostris satisfactoria. 6. Non docet Apostolus, dilectionem nostri gratam Deo fuisse, sed victimam Christi, qua seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, odorem bonæ fragrantiæ fuisse Deo, quemadmodum oblatio victimarum erat ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας, hoc vero erat non ob dilectionem Sacerdotis offerentis, etsi obedientia officii in Sacerdote Deo placeret, sed ob ipsam victimam oblatam, qua Christus, ut victima, pro nobis offerenda, figurabatur, nec quomodo gratus Deo factus sit Sacerdos, innuit Apostolus, sed quomodo in gratiam cum Deo reducti sint per hostiarum oblationem, qui eas, ut offerrentur, sacerdoti sistebant, ut peccata ipsorum expiarentur. Ideoque proprie expiatio pro peccatis nostris facta, Deiq; placatio & reconciliatio per sacrificium Christi expiatorium impetrata designatur, ut typi & antitypi sibi constet analogia & convenientia. 7. Non hic docetur, Deum Christum pro nobis in mortem tradidisse, ut sanguine ejus inscriberet, se fidelib. eandem cum Christo hæreditatem largiri velle: Ita tantum μαρτύριον foret Christi mors, non λύτρον, certificatio gratia, non expiatio peccati, aut propitiatio Dei. 8. Non largitur nobis Deus hæreditatem cœlestem, ideo quod quis Christo per fidem se applicet, & eum in charitate ambulando imitetur. Non enim nostræ charitati hic quicquam tribuitur, sed charitati Christi, & traditioni ejus, ceu victimæ expiatoriæ id unice adscribitur, quod remissio peccatorum nobis obtingat, ut olim iis, qui offerebant sacrificia, virtute antitypi, quum è sacrificii Christi oblatione ὀσμὴ ἐυωδίας odor bonæ fragrantiæ unice redundarit, adeoque gratia

Dei & remissio peccatorum oblationi Christi ac- cepta ferenda sit, qui sanguinem suum effudit, se- que in mortem tradidit pro peccatis nostris, & in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. 9. Nec Christus per dilectionem nostri hæreditatem cæle- stem consequutus uspiam dicitur, non enim sibi quicquam mereri debuit: neque nos per imitatio- nem Christi in charitate adipiscimur aut impetra- mus cælestem hæreditatem, sed unice per fidem in Christum, vel per meritum Christi vera fide appre- hensum, quum obedientia sua non quidem sibi, nobis tamen justificationem & salutem prome- ruerit, nosque fide obedientiæ suæ justificet, Es. 53, 11. 10. Non ergo nos per fidem Christo nos ap- plicando hæredes evadimus, sed Christum cum obedientia & merito ejus per fidem apprehen- dendo, nobisque applicando ἐξουσίαν consequi- mur, τέκνα θεῦ γενέσθαι, quotquot in nomen ejus credimus, Joh. 1, 12.

Joh. Coccejus hic particularem suam pro electis satisfactionem exsculpere conatur in Comment. ad hunc locum: Si ex amore se tradidit, & pro qui- bus sese tradidit, iis impetravit, quod petivit, (quippe odor fragrantiæ factus) sequitur Christum, ut Sacer- dotem, non petivisse omnium sine exceptione salutem, licet ut homo ac servus pereuntibus condolesceret se- cundum legem: Sed se tradidisse pro iis, qui ipsi dati sunt Testamento: qui sunt ii ipsi, qui sic credunt, ut diligant. At confundit Coccejus amorem genera- lem, qui ad omnes se porrigit, & specialem, qui fi- delium proprius est. Ille enim est causa traditionis in mortem, hic oritur è fide, applicante sibi illam traditionē. Et quanquam hic nihil exerte de Chri- sti intercessione habeatur, sed tantum de sacrificio ejus agatur, in quo odor factus dicitur bonæ fra- grantiæ, non dubium tamen est, quin ut se tradidit pro omnibus, & pro omnibus interpellarit, Es. 53, 12. Luc. 23, 34. quæ oratio ejus omnino exaudita est, quod impetrarit orbi reconciliationem, & gra- tiam condonandi peccata, quam omnibus offert, vi istius καταλλαγῆς per ministerium ῦ καταλλα- γῆς, confert autem credentibus, Vana etiam est distinctio Christi ut Sacerdotis, & ut hominis ac ser- vi. Nam & ut Sacerdos obtulit sacrificium atque intercedit pro omnibus, & ut servus Dei justus obe- diens factus est Patri pro omnibus, Es. 53. Phil. 2. Ne- que tamen idem est, esse servum & hominem. Nam hoc naturæ, illud status nomen est. Homo manet, servus esse desiit; uti nec Sacerdos est qua Deus so- lum, quia nomen hoc officii; ad quod etiam obe- dientia Christi, sub legem subditi, refertur. Nomi- na autem officii conveniunt Christo secundum u- tramq; naturam; & forma servi ad statum exinani- tionis spectat, in quo obedientia ejus tum activa, tum passiva, peracta est. Quænam autem illa condo- lentia Christi hominis sit secundum legem, fateor, me non capere, quum secundum legem potius in- credulos damnet. Pro iis vero tantum se tradidisse, qui ipsi dati sunt testamento, à scriptura alienum est, imo scripturæ contrarium est, quum pro omnibus se tradiderit, 1. Tim. 2, 6. ut omnibus hæreditatem acquireret, ad quam fide sola, non vero fide & cha- ritate adspiramus. Hæreditas enim non acquiritur virtute, sed jure τῆς ὑοθεσίας, quam non, nisi fide, consequimur, obtinetur, Joh. 1, 12. Rom. 8, 16. Gal. 3, 26. Agnovit certe Crocius ipse hoc loco, Christū non pro fidelibus tantum traditum esse in morte, sed pro omnibus hominibus. Cæterum, inquit, non ait, pro nobis, ut ad absolutam quandam hominum, pro quibus se dederit, paucitatem restringat, aliis ex- clusis, pro quibus seipsum nullo modo dederit. Alibi enim dicit, dedisse pro omnibus, 1. Tim. 2, 8. sed tum, ut seipsum includat, suamque fidem profiteatur, tum ut singuli Ephesii particulariter subsumant, dicen- tes: Et pro me dedit semetipsum. Debeo igitur am- bulare cum charitate. Ubicunque enim Apostoli di- cunt pro nobis, ibi unusquisque fidelis debet se inclu- dere & dicere: Dilexit me, & pro me dedit semet- ipsum, quod facit Apostolus Gal. 2, 20.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. πορνεία δὲ) He has now named the vices which were especially reigning in Ephesus. Under the name of πορνείας you may rightly include here both adulteries, just as the Latins do under the name of stuprum.

καὶ πᾶσα ἀκαθαρσία) Sodomy, tribadism, lewdness, lesbianism, see above 3, 19.

ἢ πλεονεξία) because Ephesus is a merchant city, L. 2. concerning that which it is necessary to give in a certain place. But in such cities the desire to increase one's wealth by fair means or foul reigns most of all: For it is not asked whence you have it, but it is necessary to have it.

μηδὲ ὀνομαζέσθω ἐν ὑμῖν) A similar manner of speaking 1. Cor. 5, 1. let no Christian even be suspected of those names.

καθὼς πρέπει ἁγίοις) Because no one arrives at holiness unless he is first freed from such vices.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πορνεία δὲ) Jam nominavit vitia, quæ Ephesi ma- xime regnabant. Sub πορνείας nomine recte hic & adulte- ria comprehendas, ut & Latini sub stupri nomine.

καὶ πᾶσα ἀκαθαρσία) Ἀρσενοκοιτία, τριβαδικὴ ἀσέλγεια, λεσβιασμός, vide supra 3, 19.

ἢ πλεονεξία) quia urbs mercatrix Ephesus L. 2. de eo, quod loco certo dare oportet. In talibus autem urbibus maxime regnat per fas & nefas rem augendi cupido: Nam non quæritur, unde habeas, sed oportet habere.

μηδὲ ὀνομαζέσθω ἐν ὑμῖν) Simile loquendi genus 1. Cor. 5, 1. nemo Christianus illis nominibus vel suspectus sit.

καθὼς πρέπει ἁγίοις) Quia ad sanctitatem nemo perve- nit, nisi liberetur prius à talibus vitiis.

## 5:4
Vers. 4. καὶ αἰσχρότης) Which he calls αἰσχρολογίαν in Col. 3, 8. shamelessness in words, which the Stoics approved. See Cicero's letter to Papirius Paetus IX. 12. In the Glossary αἰσχρολογία is foul language.

ἢ μωρολογία ἢ εὐτραπελία) That is, μωρολογία, which men, using a diminutive, call εὐτραπελία. Such are the sayings of mimes, and likewise of parasites, in Greek and Latin comedies, which abound with such sayings, called γελοῖοποιοὶ by the Greeks, and ridicularii by the Latins. But such things do not befit a more serious person, such as a Christian man is. Chrysostom explains this passage excellently and describes those γελοῖοποιοὺς in Homily VI on Matthew.

τὰ ἐκ ἀνήκοντα) In the manuscript, ἃ ἐκ ἀνῆκεν, אשר לא יעשה.

Ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐυχαρισία) Let the principal subject of your speech be thanksgiving for benefits received from God. Compare what is below at 19.

He continues the precepts of holiness, and according to Chrysostom, passes from the irascible faculty to the concupiscible. And when he had said that Christ gave himself up for us as a fragrant odor, he teaches that we ought to be a fragrant odor among men, and therefore he commands us to beware, regarding deeds, of filthiness in the abuse of the body, and avarice; and regarding words, of obscenity, foolish talk, and scurrility. He includes that filthiness under two names: πορνείας, which designates every mixing of the sexes outside of marriage; and ἀκαθαρσίας or uncleanness, which is referred by Thomas to other lusts and pollutions which are against nature and cannot be ordered toward generation. Jerome understands πλεονεξίαν as the insatiable desire to satisfy lust; but from Colossians 3:5 and the predicate of idolatry, it is clear that an insatiable desire for wealth is noted; and the effort to multiply wealth to the injury of another was already dealt with above in chapter 4, verse 24. Since it is called idolatry here, it is manifest that avarice or immoderate desire and trust in wealth is designated. For this is a violation of the first commandment, Matthew 6:24, Colossians 3:5. By αἰσχρότητα, although we might understand with Lombard obscenity in kisses and embraces, and with Musculus whatever deviates from honesty in words, deeds, or gestures, the others are nevertheless inferred by consequence rather than by immediate sense. Here, however, it imports base words; and the things that are added also pertain to the directing of speech, in which: 1. Filthiness of words is to be avoided, 'schandbare Wort' (shameful words), as Piscator rendered it with Blessed Luther, which Crocius approves. 2. Μωρολογία, foolish and inept and profane speeches, whether they be serious or jocular, whether the foolishness is feigned or not feigned. Jerome. Stultiloquium (foolish talk), he says, I consider to be not only that of those who tell base things to move laughter, and by feigned foolishness mock those whom they desire to please: but also that of those who are thought to be the wise men of the age, and disputing about physical things, say that they have clearly comprehended the sands of the shores, the drops of the ocean, the expanse of the heavens, and the point of the earth. There is also foolish talk in the Church:

If anyone thinks the heaven is curved like a vault: deceived by the language of Isaiah which he does not understand: also that a throne is placed in the heavens, and God sits upon it, and in the manner of an Emperor and Judge, angels stand in a circle, who obey the words of the one commanding, and are sent on various duties. But because foolish talk follows scurrility, foolish talk is rather to be transferred to vain and inept fables. 3. Ἐυτραπελίαν, which has its name from being versatile, the Vulgate rendered as scurrility. The word denotes urbanity, namely a moderate, timely, and honest manner of joking: and scurrility, by which, without regard for the person, place, time, or the thing itself, nothing is sought except laughter. Which Jerome called jocularity. Not the former, but the latter is prohibited. Concerning which see B. Luther, Tom. I. Jen. Lat. fol. 160. Eutrapelia or scurrility, which is facetiousness, or urbanity, which Aristotle thinks is a virtue, namely when not base, nor foolish, but pleasant and learned things are said at the same time, so that utility may enter under the sweetness of courtesy. Therefore courtesy, or affability, or urbanity, or facetiousness, which causes the sad and those tempted in the Spirit to be refreshed, is praiseworthy. But that which is done without cause, only for the consolation of vanity and the flesh, especially when the cause of this is always nothing but levity, and only the desire for telling stories and laughing moves it, does not befit Christians. By ἐυχαρισίαν Jerome understands not that by which we give thanks to God, but that by which we are reputed as grateful, gracious, and witty among men. Whence Calvin and Musculus translate it as grace, because our speech ought to be imbued with true sweetness and grace. But ἐυχαρισία is nowhere used in that way. The Apostle calls us back from ἐυτραπελία, by which we strive to please men, to ἐυχαρισία, which pleases God above all. Therefore afterwards, those vices having been overthrown, the Apostle particularly inculcates ἐυχαρισία.

Latin:

Vers. 4. καὶ αἰσχρότης) Quam αἰσχρολογίαν vocat Col. 3, 8. inverecundiam in verbis, quam Stoici probabant. Vi- de Ciceronis epistolam ad Papirium Pætum IX. 12. In Glos- sario αἰσχρολογία turpiloquium.

ἢ μωρολογία ἢ εὐτραπελία) Id est, μωρολογία, quam ho- mines ὑποκοριζόμενοι vocant ἐντραπελίαν. Talia sunt dicta Mimorum, item Parasitorum, in comœdiis Græcis & Lati- nis, qui talibus dictis scatent, γελοῖοποιοὶ Græcis, ridicularii Latinis. Talia vero personam graviorem, qualis est homi- nis Christiani, non decent. Egregie hunc locum explicat & γελοῖοποιοὺς illos describit Chrysostom. Hom. VI. in Matth.

τὰ ἐκ ἀνήκοντα) In Manuscripto, ἃ ἐκ ἀνῆκεν, אשר לא יעשה.

Ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐυχαρισία) Sermonis vestri præcipua ma- teria sit gratiarum actio pro beneficiis à Deo acceptis. Con- fer, quod infra 19.

Continuat præcepta sanctitatis, & à θυμικῷ se- cundum Chrysostomum transit ad τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν. Et quum Christum se pro nobis tradidisse in odo- rem fragrantiæ dixisset, nos odorem fragrantiæ apud homines esse debere docet, atque ideo cave- re quoad facta jubet fœditatem in abusu corporis, & avaritiam, quoad verba turpitudinem, stultiloquium & scurrilitatem. Fœditatem illam comprehendit duobus nominibus πορνείας, quæ omnem sexuum commixtionem extra conjugium designat:& ἀκα- θαρσίας vel immunditiæ, quæ ad cæteras libidines & pollutiones à Thoma refertur, quæ contra natu- ram sunt, & ad generationem ordinari non pos- sunt. Πλεονεξίαν de insatiabili libidinis explendæ cupiditate Hieronymus intelligit; sed è Col. 3, 5. & idolatriæ prædicato liquet, opum cupiditatem inexplebilem notari; & supra jam de studio mul- tiplicandi opes cum alterius injuria c. 4, 24. actum. Hic quia idololatria nominatur, avaritiam vel im- moderatam cupiditatem & fiduciam in opibus designari, manifestum est. Hæc enim primi præ- cepti violatio est, Matth. 6, 24. Col. 35. Per αἰσχό- τητα, etsi cum Lombardo obscænitatem in osculis & amplexibus, cum Musculo, quicquid vel in verbis, vel in factis, vel in gestibus ab honestate abludit, in- telligere possimus, cætera tamen per consequens potius, quàm immediato sensu inferuntur. Hic au- tem verba turpia importat; &, quæ adduntur, ad sermonem dirigendum etiam pertinent, in quo. 1. fœditas verborum cavenda, schandbare Wort, ut cum B. Luthero reddidit Piscator, quod approbat Crocius. 2. Μωρολογία, sermones stulti & inepti, ac profani, sive serii, sive jocosi, sive fatuitas simule- tur, sive non simuletur. Hieron. Stultiloquium, in- quit, esse existimo, non solum eorum, qui aliqua nar- rant turpia, ut risum moveant, & fatuitate simulata magis illudant eis, quibus placere desiderant: Sed et- iam eorum, qui sapientes seculi putantur, & de rebus physicis disputantes dicunt se arenas littorum, guttas oceani, & cælorum spatium, terræque punctum li- quido comprehendisse. Est & in Ecclesia stultiloquiū:

Si quis cœlum putet fornicis more curvatum: Esaia quem non intelligit sermone deceptus: Solium quoque in cœlis positum, & super eo sedere Deum, & in ri- tum Imperatoris & Judicis Angelos stare in circui- tu, qui verbis jubentis obtemparent, & in diversa mittantur officia. Sed quia sequitur stultiloquium scurrilitas, magis stultiloquium ad vanas & ineptas fabulas transferendum. 3. Ἐυτραπελίαν, quæ à versatili nomen habet, Vulgatus reddidit scurrilı- tatem. Notat vox & urbanitatem, moderatam nempe, tempestivam ac honestam jocandi ratio- nem: & scurrilitatem, qua non habita ratione per- sonæ, loci, temporis, rei ipsius, nihil præter ri- sum quæritur. Quam jocularitatem dixit Hiero- nymus. Non illa, sed hæc prohibetur. Quo de B. Lutherus Tom. I. Jen. Lat. fol. 160. Eutrapelia seu scurrilitas, quæ est facetia, seu urbanitas, quam Aristoteles virtutem esse putat, quando scilicet non turpia, neque stulta, sed jucunda & erudita simul dicuntur, ut utilitas intret sub dulcedine comitatis. Itaque comitas, seu affabilitas, seu urbanitas, seu fa- cetiatatis, quæ fit, ut tristes atque tentati in Spiritu recreentur, laudabilis est. Verum quæ fit sine causa, tantum ad consolatiunculam vanitatis & carnis, præsertim cum bujus semper non sit, nisi levitas, cau- sa, & sola libido fabulandi atque ridendi moveat il- lam, non convenit Christianis. Per ἐυχαρισίαν Hie- ronymus non eam, qua gratias Deo agimus, sed qua grati, gratiosi & salsi apud homines reputa- mur, intelligit. Unde Calvinus & Musculus ver- tunt gratiam, quod sermonis nostri debeant vera suavitate & gratia esse perfusi. Sed ita nuspiam ἐυχαρισία adhibetur. Revocat Apostolus ab ἐυ- τραπελία, qua hominibus placere studemus, ad ἐυχαρισίαν, quæ Deo imprimis placet. Ideo post- ea, vitiis illis profligatis, ἐυχαρισίαν peculiariter inculcat Apostolus.

## 5:5
Vers. 5. τῦτο γάρ ἐστε γινώσκοντες) I think it is an imperative rather than an indicative. For Paul begins a warning of equal sense in this way in 1 Cor. 6:9, μὴ πλανᾶσθε, and ἔστε γινώσκοντες is a Greek circumlocution for γινώσκετε. But in the manuscript it is ἴστε γινώσκοντες, that is, know well, in the Hebrew idiom.

ὅτι πᾶς πόρνος) That is, a fornicator. For thus our writers use this word, as we have shown. A universal word followed by a negation among the Hebrews stands for a universal negative, as we have already often seen.

ἢ ἀκάθαρτος) These are the μαλακοὶ and ἀρσενοκοῖται in the aforementioned place to the Corinthians.

ἢ πλεονέκτης) You have this also in the aforementioned place to the Corinthians. Cyprian interprets it as a defrauder in epistle LII.

ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης) Rightly, as also in Col. 3:5. For they have Mammon, that is, riches, as God, Matt. 6:24; they place all their hope in them, they devote themselves entirely to them, they do everything for their sake. There is a similar way of speaking, whose God is their belly, Phil. 3:19. A passage of Philo in his first book περὶ μοναρχίας serves beautifully to explain this saying: Διελόγχυσαν εἰ κελίζως τὺς φιλοχρημάτυς, οἳ πανταχόθεν καὶ ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον ἐκπορίζουσι, τὸ δὲ πορισθὲν, ὡς ἄγαλμα θεῖον, ἐν ἀδυνάτοις θησαυροφυλακῦσιν, ἀγαθῶν αἴτιον καὶ τῆς συμπάσης εὐδαιμονίας τῦτ’ εἶναι νομίζοντες, the same author in his book on rewards and punishments calls the passions of pleasure τὰ ἔδωλα.

ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ χριστῦ καὶ θεῦ) The kingdom of Christ is in judgment, the kingdom of God is after judgment, 1 Cor. 15:24. The Hebrews would say אין לו חלק בעולם הבא.

The Syriac takes the word ἐσὲ as indicative, and the sense is indicative: You are aware. Furthermore, that distinction of the kingdom of Christ and God seems to sail for the Socinians. The kingdom of Christ and God are not different kingdoms, either by the boundaries of the empire or by the time of reigning. Nor in judgment, whether you understand the government of the Church or of the whole world, or the final judgment, does Christ alone reign or will he reign without the Father: nor after judgment does the Father alone reign without the Son. But it is called the kingdom of Christ and God, because it was given to Christ as Mediator by God, (or rather because Christ as man was raised to the same government and kingdom, which is God's, that is, of the Father, Son, and

Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he has been exalted to the throne of divine Majesty. Where God is, both the Father and the Son can be understood, says Jerome on this passage. Furthermore, what we say about the Father and the Son, let us think the same about the Holy Spirit. We pass over the fact that the copulative here can be understood as placed for a relative: Christ, who is God. See the Grammar of S. Glassius, page 188. To which it contributes that the article is not repeated.

Latin:

Vers. 5. τῦτο γάρ ἐστε γινώσκοντες) Imperativum potius esse reor, quam Indicativum. Nam & sic paris sensus mo- nitum Paulus inchoat 1. Cor. 6, 9. μὴ πλανᾶσθε, & ἔστε γινώ- σκοντες pro γινώσκετε circumlocutio Græca. At in manuscri- pto est, ἴστε γινώσκοντες, id est, bene scitote locutione Ebræa.

ὅτι πᾶς πόρνος) Id est, Scortator. Sic enim nostri scri- ptores hanc vocem usurpant, ut ostendimus. Universalis vox sequente negatione apud Ebræos est pro negativa uni- versali, ut jam sæpe vidimus.

ἢ ἀκάθαρτος) Hi sunt μαλακοὶ & ἀρσενοκοῖται in dicto ad Corinthios loco.

ἢ πλεονέκτης) Habes & hoc dicto ad Corinthios loco. Fraudatorem interpretatur Cyprianus epistola LII.

ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης) Recte, ut & Col. 3, 5. Nam pro Deo habent Mammonam, id est, divitias, Matth. 6, 24. in iis spes totas collocant, iis totos se devovent, earum causa ni- hil non faciunt. Par loquendi genus est, quorum Deus est venter, Phil. 3, 19. Facit pulchre huic dicto explicando locus Philonis περὶ μοναρχίας primo: Διελόγχυσαν εἰ κελίζως τὺς φι- λοχρημάτυς, οἳ πανταχόθεν καὶ ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον ἐκπορίζουσι, τὸ δὲ πορισθὲν, ὡς ἄγαλμα θεῖον, ἐν ἀδυνάτοις θησαυροφυλα-κῦσιν, ἀγαθῶν αἴτιον καὶ τῆς συμπάσης εὐδαιμονίας τῦτ’ εἶναι νομίζοντες, idem libro de præmiis & pœnis, τὰ πάθη τῆς ἡδονῆς vocat τὰ ἔδωλα.

ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῦ χριστῦ καὶ θεῦ) Re- gnum Christi est in judicio, regnum Dei post judicium, 1. Cor. 15, 24. Ebræi dicerent אין לו חלק בעולם הבא.

Syrus verbum ἐσὲ indicative accipit, estque sen- sus Indicativus: Gnari estis. Cæterum Socinianis velificari videtur illa regni Christi & Dei distin- ctio. Non diversa regna sive finibus imperii, sive regnandi tempore sunt regnum Christi & Dei. Nec in judicio sive gubernationem Ecclesiæ in- telligas, aut mundi universi, sive novissimum ju- dicium, solus regnat aut regnabit Christus sine Pa- tre: nec post judicium solus Pater sine Filio. Chri- sti autem & Dei regnum dicitur, quia Chri- sto ut Mediatori datum à Deo, (vel potius quia Christus ut homo ad idem evectus est regimen & regnum, quod Dei est, hoc est, Patris, Filii, &

Spiritus Sancti, utpote qui in thronum Majestatis divinæ exaltatus est. Ubi Deus est, tam Pater, quam Filius intelligi potest, inquit Hieronymus in hunc locum. Porro quod de Patre & Filio di- cimus, hoc idem & de Spiritu Sancto sentiamus. Tacemus, quod copulativa hic pro Relativo posi- ta intelligi possit: Christi, qui est Deus. Vide Gramm. S. Glassii pag. 188. Quo facit, quod arti- culus repetitus non sit.

## 5:6
Vers. 6. Let no one deceive you with empty words) A similar warning 1 Cor. 3, 18. He notes, however, the philosophers who taught that there is nothing evil in incest and ἀρσενοκοιτία, and who praised κοινογαμίαν, and who thought it lawful for buyers and sellers to circumvent one another, for the reason that no injury is done to a willing person, and civil laws permit it; but also the Jews, who said that all who Judaize, however they may have lived, would have a part in the other world.

For because of these things comes the wrath of God) Divine vengeance, Rom. 1, 8. Coloss. 3, 6.

upon the sons of disobedience) Against those who spurn the Gospel, above 2, 2. Coloss. in the place already mentioned בנים לא־אמן בם Deut. 33, 20.

Latin:

Vers. 6. μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς ἀπατάτω κενοῖς λόγοις) Similis mo- nitio 1. Corinth. 3, 18. Notat autem Philosophos, qui doce- bant, nihil mali esse in incestibus & ἀρσενοκοιτία, & qui lau- dabant κοινογαμίαν, & qui putabant, vendentibus & ementibus licitum, circumvenire se invicem, ideo quod volenti non fiat injuria, & leges civiles id permittant; sed & Judæos, qui omnibus Judaizantibus, quo- modocunque vixissent, partem fore dicebant in seculo altero.

διὰ ταῦτα γὰρ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τῦ Θεῦ) Divina ultio, Rom. 1, 8. Coloss. 3, 6.

ἐπὶ τὺς ὑἱὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας) In eos, qui Evangelium sper- nunt, supra 2, 2. Coloss. dicto jam loco בנים לא־אמן בם Deut. 33, 20.

## 5:7
do not therefore become partakers with them) Such as those who are described Ps. 50, 18. and Job 34, 8.

We do not deny that the philosophers and others, whom Grotius says are named, are noted. But we do not admit that they alone are noted. Bellarmine, book 1 de amiss. grat. cap. 6, says that obscenity and foolish talk and scurrility ought indeed to be foreign to the mouth of the sanctified, but he thinks that they are not of such a kind by their nature as to exclude one from the inheritance of Christ and God. Who is refuted, however, both by the general reason that because of all these things which the Apostle commemorates, the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience, and by the Apostolic dehortation: Do not therefore be their consorts. For those who are consorts in guilt will also be consorts in punishment, Apoc. 13, 4. and the Apostle pronounced that the wages of any sin is death, Rom. 6, last verse. Just as Moses pronounces a curse on everyone who has not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. 27, 26. Add that he said the Holy Spirit is grieved by filthy and rotten speech, chap. 4, 29. 30. and that an account must be rendered for every idle word, Matt. 12, 36. Finally, εὐτραπελία also sins both by foolish talk and because they provide scandals and because they pave the way for other more serious vices. λόγοι τῶν πραγμάτων ὁδοὶ, words are approaches or paths to the things themselves, as Chrysostom says here.

Latin:

μὴ ὖ γίνεσθε συμμέτοχοι ἀυτῶν) Quales illi, qui descri- buntur Pf. 50, 18. & Job. 34, 8.

Philosophos & alios, quos nominari ait Gro- tius, notari non abnuimus. Sed eos solos notari haud admittimus. Bellarm. libr. I. de amiss. grat. cap. 6. obscœnitatem ac stultiloquium & scurrilitas- tem debere quidem aliena esse ab ore sanctificato- rum ait, sed non ex genere suo talia esse, quæ ex- cludant ab hæreditate Christi & Dei, putat. Qui v. tum generali ratione, quod propter hæc omnia, quæ commemorat Apostolus, ira Dei veniat in fi- lios τῆς ἀπειθείας, refellitur: tum dehortatione A- postolica: Ne igitur estote consortes eorum. Qui enim consortes in culpa sunt, consortes etiam e- runt in pœna, Apoc. 13, 4. & cujusvis peccati stipen- dium esse mortem, pronunciavit Apostolus, Rom. 6. v. ult. Uti Moses maledictum pronunciat o- mnem, qui non in omnibus permanserit, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, Deut. 27, 26. Adde, quod sermone spurco, & putri contristari Spiritum Sanctum dixe- rit, cap. 4, 29. 30. quodque de verbo quovis otioso reddenda sit ratio, Matth. 12, 36. Denique peccat etiam εὐτραπελία cum μωρολογίᾳ, tum quod scan- dala præbeant, tum quod aliis vitiis gravioribus viam sternant. λόγοι τῶν πραγμάτων ὁδοὶ, sermo- nes aditus sunt, vel viæ ad res ipsas, ut hic Chryso- stomus.

## 5:8
Vers. 8. For you were once darkness) By metonymy those are called darkness here who are elsewhere in darkness, Rom. 2, 19. 1 Thess. 5, 4. who are involved in great ignorance of good things. See Rom. 3, 12.

But now light in the Lord) Enlightened through Christ, above 1, 18. The mystery of the lamp kindled in the temple is fulfilled in you: and you are like the Angel, of whom Dan. 10, 6.

as children of light walk) A Hebrew expression בני אור; which signifies men bathed in light. Thus also 1 Thess. 5, 5. for the same thing, walk in the light, John 1, 17 said.

By darkness is understood not only ignorance of God and divine things, but also a flagitious life, which is its companion. Nor were they immersed only in the darkness of ignorance and errors, but also of various vices before conversion, illumination of the mind, and liberation from the darkness of the heart. By light, however, is noted not only the knowledge of God and divine things, but also purity of life, both of which arise from God, that true light in whom there is no darkness, and the Father of lights, 1 John 1, 5. James 1, 17. For one cannot aspire to it by the proper light of nature, but by the illumination of Him who, as the true light, desires all men to be enlightened, John 1, 9. Therefore it is said, you are light in the Lord; who in the passage of Dan. 10, 16 is also to be understood, not indeed any created Angel. They are called from thence also children of light, because from Christ, who is the true light, their illumination and light is, or that they are from GOD through the grace of regeneration. Although they are also rightly called children of light through a Hebraism, that is, very luminous. From this an argument is drawn, that they ought to walk in the light, as children of light, John 12, 35. and thus avoid darkness, and have no fellowship with the works of darkness, Conf. Matt. 5, 16. Rom. 12, 12. 13. Phil. 2, 15. 1 Thess. 5, 5. 1 John 1, 7. The children of darkness have their way, the children of light have theirs, in which the light of the Word shines before them, Ps. 119, 105.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἦτε γάρ ποτε σκότος) Per μετωνυμίαν hic σκότος esse dicuntur, qui alibi ἐν σκότει, Rom. 2, 19. 1. Thess. 5, 4. qui in magna rerum bonarum ignorantia versantur, Vide Rom. 3, 12.

Νῦν δὲ φῶς ἐν κυρίῳ) Illuminati per Christum, supra 1, 18. Impletur in vobis mysterium lychni incensi in templo: & similes estis Angelo, de quo Dan. 10, 6.

ὡς τέκνα φωτὸς περιπατεῖτε) Locutio Ebræ בני אור; quæ significat homines luce perfusos. Sic & 1. Thess. 5, 5. pro eodem, ambulate in luce, dixit Joh. 1, 17.

Per tenebras non tantum ignorantia Dei re- rumque divinarum, sed etiam, quæ illius co- mes est, vita flagitiosa intelligitur. Nec igno- rantiæ solum & errorum, sed etiam vitiorum variorum tenebris immersi erant ante conver- sionem, illuminationem mentis, & liberatio- nem à tenebris cordis. Per lucem verò non tantum cognitio Dei ac rerum divinarum, sed etiam vitæ puritas notatur, quæ utraque à Deo, vera illa luce, in qua non sunt tenebræ, & Patre luminum oritur, 1. Joh. 1, 5. Jac. 1, 17. Nam ad eam non potest quis adspirare proprio naturæ lumine, sed illuminatione ejus, qui ceu lux vera omnes ho- mines illuminatos cupit, Joh. 1, 19. Ideo dicitur, lux estis in Domino; Qui in loco Dan. 10, 16. etiam in- telligendus est, non vero Angelus quispiam crea- tus. Dicuntur inde & filii lucis, quod à Christo, qui vera lux est, illorum illuminatio sit, & lux; aut quod ex DEO sint per regenerationis gratiam. Quanquam & filii lucis recte dicantur per Ebrai- smum, id est, valde lucidi. Ex eo argumentum defumitur, quod ambulare debeant in luce, ut filii lucis, Joh. 12, 35. adeoque tenebras vitare, & cum operibus tenebrarum nihil habere commercii, Conf. Matth. 5, 16. Rom. 12, 12. 13. Phil. 2, 15. 1. Thess. 5, 5. 1. Joh. 1, 7. Habent filii tenebrarum suam viam, habent suam filii lucis, in qua praelucet ipsis lux Verbi, Ps. 119, 105.

## 5:9
Ver. 9. For the fruit of the Spirit) In the manuscript, for the fruit of the light, which coheres better with the preceding. These are soon opposed to the works of darkness. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call works by the name of fruits, Matt. 3, 8. John 15, 16. Gal. 5, 22. from which passage this reading was poorly changed by the scribes. This whole clause, however, is to be read as a parenthesis.

These reasons are not pregnant enough to abandon the received reading, even if not only the MS of Grotius, but also the Claromontanus, Bezae, and even the Vulgate and the Syriac have 'of the light,' and Jerome retains it. For all other Codices have 'of the Spirit.' And why should we reject that? Is it new to pass from one metaphor to another in scripture? It is received that the fruits of the Spirit are named. But the fruits of light are nowhere read.

in all goodness) Rom. 15, 14. Gal. 5, 21.

and righteousness) Which is opposed to covetousness, which he condemned above.

and truth) Which is opposed to the lie, which he likewise condemned above 2, 25.

Thus Chrysostom says that goodness is led against bitterness, righteousness against covetousness (where he signifies by 'just' in contradistinction to 'good' that by which one's own is rendered to each), truth against false pleasure, so that it may be opposed to feigned pleasure and the lie, just as it can be said to be opposed to hypocrisy and every simulation and dissimulation.
